TitreApplicationTitle: The efficacy of a computer-based prompting system to develop self-care skills in children with autism
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITIES OF DAILY LIVING; ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE; AUTISM; PROMPTING; SELF-CARE; TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Much attention has focused on developing effective strategies to enable children with autism to achieve functional independence in self-care, such as the use of prompts.  However, the literature has shown that prompting is most successful when the task and prompts are presented systematically and invariantly, using a variety of delivery modalities, which is often difficult for a caregiver to perform.  As such, the goal of this research project is to develop and determine the efficacy of a computerized system that can automatically monitor progress, and deliver prompts to children with autism while they complete a self-care activity. This project will be completed in three phases:  1) an observational study; 2) development of a working prototype; and 3) an efficacy study.  The observational study will involve videotaping parent-children dyads, observing the types of prompting strategies that are currently used to assist children with autism through the task of handwashing.  A linguistic analysis of these data will be completed in order to develop preliminary guidelines with respect to the type of verbal and non-verbal prompts that may be effective with this target population.  Next, these guidelines will be used to inform the development of a computerized prompting system, which will be based on a previous system developed by the research team.  Finally, this system will be tested within the homes of five children with autism, again during handwashing. It is expected that these findings could have a significant impact on the care of children with autism, especially within the home and school.   Information on the types of effective prompting strategies could be extremely useful to parents and caregivers, while the development of a new technology could provide much needed assistance and support to not only the child, but to families and caregivers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the Nature and Improving the Treatment of Kidney Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ABLATION THERAPY; GENOMICS; INTERVENTIONAL RADIOLOGY; KIDNEY CANCER; SMALL RENAL MASSES; THERMOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common kidney cancer and the most lethal urological cancer with>33% mortality in Canada.  The incidence of kidney cancer is similar to leukemia and increasing at>1% per year, apparently due to earlier detection.  New cases are now frequently diagnosed incidentally, without symptoms, as small renal masses (SRMs) or spots on the kidney that usually grow very slowly frequently in older persons.  Despite earlier treatment, the expected decrease in death rate from RCC has not been realized.  We have initiated initial watchful waiting after biopsy in selected cases, in order to delay surgery until tumour growth is detected.  However, we do not know which tumours will grow or why.  Our two research initiatives will directly improve management of SRMs: molecular studies and minimally invasive therapy.  We know much about the genetics and molecular pathways that lead to RCC, mainly because some RCCs occur as a consequence of hereditary Von Hippel Lindau (VHL) Disease.  We will define the VHL gene mutations initiating SRMs and the progressive molecular changes that cause progression to advanced large RCC.  By understanding the molecular changes we will identify targets for therapeutic intervention.  We will develop new and improved tools for minimally invasive image guided therapy of those localized kidney cancers that need treatment, starting with radiofrequency ablation (RFA).  By inserting a new type of electrode through the skin and meaduring the heating effect in the tumour by MRI images (called thermometry), we will be able to treat larger tumours and potentially reduce the use of invasive surgical procedures for kidney cancer.  Wyeth and CIHR support for the Chair and these studies will advance knowledge and treatment of kidney cancer, heighten awareness of kidney cancer research, facilitate multidisciplinary approaches to research and patient care, and enhance local, provincial, national and international collaborations.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: The promyelocytic leukemia protein and nuclear domain function in DNA damage signaling and repair.
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE AND REPAIR; LIGHT AND ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MECHANISMS OF ONCOGENESIS; NUCLEAR STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION; PROMYELOCYTIC LEUKEMIA NUCLEAR BODIES
Abstract-Résumé: The repository of genetic information in each of our cells is the nucleus. In eukaryotic cells, the nucleus is a highly organised and dynamic structure, complete with specialised compartments responsible for processes such as transcription, RNA splicing, DNA repair and replication. The various sub-nuclear compartments appear to serve as excellent markers for cellular health, often being disrupted in disease states such as cancer or viral infection. This concept is most elegantly demonstrated by the promyelocytic leukemia nuclear body (PML NB), which is disrupted in the white blood cells of patients with acute promyelocytic leukemia. PML NBs have also been implicated in DNA repair and tumour suppression. We have recently discovered that PML NBs respond to DNA damage by increasing in number through fission from pre-exisiting bodies. This response is regulated by cell cycle progression and several key molecular pathways that help to prevent cancer following DNA damage. PML NB numbers appears to provide a novel biomarker for the cellular response to DNA damage and control of cellular proliferation. Further characterization of the role of PML NBs in DNA repair will provide needed insight into how our cells respond to genotoxic stress and how this response is subverted during cancer development.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Cerebral Representation of Pain in Self and in Others
Keywords-MotsClés: FMRI; IMAGERY; MOTOR SKILLS; PAIN; PHANTOM LIMBS; SENSORI-MOTOR FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: When we observe the behaviors of other people, the level of activity in numerous regions of our brain is very similar to what is observed when we perform the same behaviors. Similarly, when we imagine behaviors without external stimulation (like an athlete before a performance), parts of our brain respond as if we were executing them (or practicing). This characteristic of brain functioning, which has been referred to as "shared representations", holds for actions, sensations as well as emotions and pain. Such a mechanism may explain in part how we learn through imitation and observation of others. A series of studies is proposed with healthy subjects and people with orthopedic or neurological disorders to investigate the variables that promote the shared representation of behaviors. The studies will also help identify the brain systems involved in these processes, and test whether they can be useful in rehabilitation in some cases to improve motor performance and in others to modulate pain such as phantom pain. It is expected that a better understanding of the shared representations in the context of neurological rehabilitation will open the door to new interventions for improving motor function and pain management.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of Integrin Function in Muscle Formation and Maintenance.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL-ECM ADHESION; DEVELOPMENT; DROSOPHILA; GENETICS; INTEGRIN; MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Cells in multicellular organisms are arranged in highly complex three-dimensional structures. Achieving such a complex organization necessitates that cells form both transient and stable adhesive contacts with their extracellular environment. In animals, cells attach to their environment through the action of specialized cell adhesion proteins. Integrins are an important type of cell adhesion molecules that attach cells to the extra cellular matrix that surrounds most cells. Defective integrin-mediated adhesion has been implicated in a wide variety of pathological disorders such as skin blistering diseases, muscle degeneration, thrombosis, blood clotting disorders, and cancer. Our work explores the mechanisms that regulate the activity of integrins as well as the role of integrins in preventing muscle degeneration. For our studies we use the fruit fly, a common genetic model system, Because the mechanisms of integrin function are conserved between flies and humans, we can take advantage of the powerful molecular genetic technologies available in fruit flies to rapidly derive novel insight into how these mechanisms operate in humans. This will greatly improve our understanding of the aetiology of diseases where integrin function is disrupted.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immune mechanisms of food allergy induced by concurrent exposure to microbial products and food antigens
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGY; DENDRITIC CELL; IMMUNOLOGY; INFECTION; INTESTINE; T CELL
Abstract-Résumé: As many as 2-8% populations suffer from food allergy or food allergen related immune inflammation. The mechanism is not clear. Since no effective therapy is available at present, elucidation of the underlying mechanisms of food allergy may contribute to the development of novel therapeutic strategies.     The proposed study will use animal cell model to study a novel mechanism of food allergy. We postulate the simultaneous exposure to microbial products and food antigens initiates food allergy. Therefore, we will expose mice to microbial products and food antigens together; to examine intestinal immune cell response. This study may create a new animal model to be used in further study of food allergy and other allergic disorders. Also, several therapeutic targets may be identified in this study to be used to attenuate or inhibit allergic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development of complex vision in primates
Keywords-MotsClés: FACE; IMMEDIATE-EARLY GENE; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INFEROTEMPORAL CORTEX; MONKEY; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: The temporal lobe of the primate brain is known to be specialized for processing complex visual information, including faces. The existence of such high-level visual processing at the cellular level has led many psychologists and neuroscientists to wonder whether this property develops only after postnatal exposure to visual stimuli or whether it is fundamentally innate such that primates are born with at least some level of complex visual analysis. There is some evidence to suggest that the latter may be the case, which in turn leads to the tantalizing possibility that the complex circuitry needed to encode facial stimuli is somehow genetically specified.  It has not been possible to address this question to date because neonates are extremely difficult to work with because they are sensitive to the manipulation and stress that accompanies scientific studies on living animals. As a result, the standard method of physiologically exploring the brain to study its function can not be applied to newborn animals. To get around this problem, we have developed an imaging technique that provides maps of brain activity at the cellular level. The major advantage of our technique is that it can be applied to awake animals at all ages and with minimal handling stress.  The objective of our study will be to expose newborn monkeys to face and other complex stimuli followed by an application of our imaging technique to map out the temporal lobe. If the hypothesis that primates are born with the ability to process complex visual information is true, then our activation maps will not only confirm this hypothesis but will provide significant insight into the layout of neural circuits in the temporal lobe that mediate these functions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Methods and tools for integrative meta-analysis of neuroscience microarray data
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; DATABASES; GENE EXPRESSION; META-ANALYSIS; MICROARRAY; NEUROSCIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Dozens of neuroscience laboratories around the world are using "gene expression microarrays" to simultaneously monitor the activities of thousands of genes in a sample of brain tissue or cells. The goal of these studies vary but might be aimed at understanding what happens to the brain when it is diseased (as in Alzheimer's disease or schizophrenia) or damaged by injury such as stroke. These studies generate huge amounts of data but surprisingly comparing the results across laboratories is very difficult. This means that many interesting discoveries are waiting to be made from these data, but cannot be accessed because the data are too complex or too difficult to analyze. The aim of this project is to develop methods, databases and software that will help address this problem. Our earlier work showed how it is possible to compare microarray results across laboratories to increase their usefulness. This project is specifically targeted at simultaneously expanding the capabilities of our tools while increasing their specific usefulness to neuroscience research. The tools we develop will allow brain researchers to submit their own data, compare it to published data or that of their collaborators, and combine microarray data with other types of information. We are working with experts on schizophrenia, depression and other neuropsychiatric disorders to develop our software and apply our ideas to studies of importance to human health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of white adipose tissue metabolism by AMPK
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTE; AMPK; FAT METABOLISM; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; LIPOGENESIS; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Adipocytes are specialized and differentiated cells with a great capacity to store triglycerides (TG). However, the fat cell also possesses the biochemical oxidative machinery to dissipate energy within itself. In fact, white adipocytes can be transformed into very effective "fat burning machines". These remarkable functional and structural transformations of white adipocytes confer high metabolic versatility to fat tissue with important therapeutic implications for the treatment of obesity and its related metabolic disorders. The experiments proposed here are aimed at investigating the molecular and physiological mechanisms involved in energy dissipation within the adipocyte. We are particularly interested in the role played by a protein called AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). Activation of this protein switches on alternate pathways that deplete fat and generate ATP. Since obesity is characterized by excessive accumulation of adipose tissue, physiological and/or pharmacological activation of AMPK to promote fat oxidation in adipocytes has become of great therapeutic interest. However, very little is known about the effects of AMPK activation on lipid metabolism in fat cells. Here, we intend to unravel the physiological effects and the molecular mechanisms involved in AMPK activation in adipose tissue. The significance of the proposed research is: It will develop a greater understanding of the basic fundamental physiological and molecular mechanisms involved in TG storage and energy dissipation in white adipocytes, and in the regulation of whole-body glucose and lipid metabolism. This is important because adipocyte function and its metabolic adaptations to diet, exercise, and hormonal secretions are involved in the pathogenesis of a large number of major debilitating diseases. These include insulin resistance (muscle, liver, and fat), dyslipidemia and hypertension (cardiovascular system), and beta-cell failure and death (pancreas).

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Phase II Metabolism and MRP Transport in Carcinogen Detoxification
Keywords-MotsClés: ARSENIC; GLUTATHIONE S-TRANSFERASES; MEMBRANE TRANSPORT; MULTIDRUG RESISTANCE PROTEIN; SANDWICH-CULTURED HEPATOCYTES; TOBACCO CARCINOGENS
Abstract-Résumé: To protect our bodies from daily exposure to cancer causing chemicals, cells have protective pathways in place. These include surface (or membrane) protein pumps that can prevent harmful chemicals getting into cells. If chemicals by-pass the pumps and enter the cell, metabolic enzymes (or proteins that speed up change within the cell) can modify them to a less harmful more water soluble form, that must be pumped out across the cell membrane. We are investigating how protein-pumps work together with metabolic enzymes to protect cells from cancer causing environmental toxins such as arsenic and tobacco smoke components. We will identify the specific protein pumps and metabolic enzymes that work to remove harmful chemicals from cells. Not everyone who is exposed to environmental chemicals and tobacco components will develop cancer.  We will investigate how slight variations in the genetic code of protein pumps and metabolic enzymes can influence their ability to protect cells from cancer causing chemicals.  Identification and characterization of metabolic pathways and protein pumps involved in preventing the accumulation of cancer causing chemicals lays the foundation for identifying inter-individual gene differences that could predispose people to chemically-induced cancers. In addition, although these protein pumps and metabolic pathways are protective in healthy tissue they can also protect cancer cells and make tumours unresponsive to cancer drug treatment.  Thus, understanding how these proteins function is important for effective cancer prevention and treatment strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The TIPS (Tips for Infant and Parent Sleep) Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIGRAPHY; DEPRESSION; FATIGUE; INFANT; MATERNAL; SLEEP
Abstract-Résumé: A mother's sleep is linked to her baby's sleep.  Every new mother expects her baby to wake up during the night, but these awakenings have an effect on the mother's amount of sleep and her feelings of fatigue.  Many mothers also have difficulty managing their baby's sleep and babies' development benefits from having fewer awakenings and less awake time between sleep episodes.  This study will determine if teaching women about strategies for improving mothers' and babies' sleep and giving them support for dealing with sleep concerns can improve the amount of sleep new mothers get at night and can lengthen the periods of sleep that a baby gets between awakenings.  The TIPS Trial will also look at effects on other sleep issues, fatigue and depression in new mothers, and breastfeeding at 6- and 12-weeks after the baby is born.  Healthy, first time mothers who have given birth to a healthy, full term baby will be enrolled in the study at one of two hospitals in downtown Toronto.  Mothers' and babies' sleep will be measured using a wrist-watch sized device called an actigraph at 6- and 12-weeks after the baby is born.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of Assessment Tools for Fatigue Related to Systemic Sclerosis:  Research, Diagnostic, and Screening Applications
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSESSMENT; DIAGNOSIS; FATIGUE; ITEM RESPONSE THEORY; SCLERODERMA; SYSTEMIC SCLEROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Fatigue refers to the common experience of feeling weak, tired, and lacking energy. Although fatigue may come and go in normal circumstances, chronic fatigue in patients with medical illness involves ongoing exhaustion that is not alleviated by rest. Patients with chronic disease rate fatigue as one of the most important factors leading to disability and diminished quality of life. Among patients with scleroderma, several studies have found that fatigue is rated among the most bothersome of all symptoms, including pain. Fatigue is often overlooked, however, by clinicians and researchers. Among rheumatologists, almost 90% say that they never assess patients for fatigue. One reason that fatigue is typically overlooked is that protocols for identifying patients with high levels of fatigue do not exist for most chronic diseases. As a result, it is not clear how many patients have high levels of fatigue, and there has been little research on interventions for fatigue. A working set of diagnostic criteria for fatigue related to chronic disease is important for both research and treatment planning. In cancer, for instance, when a protocol for diagnosing a syndrome called Cancer-Related Fatigue was developed, researchers were able, for the first time, to consistently identify patients with high levels of ongoing fatigue. The objective of this proposal is to adapt research tools from other chronic disease patient groups for scleroderma so that fatigue levels can be measured precisely in research seeking, for instance, to identify factors leading to greater fatigue; to adapt the Cancer-Related Fatigue program for patients with scleroderma so that patients with clinically significant levels of fatigue related to scleroderma can be identified; and to develop a set of 1-3 questions that rheumatologists can ask patients to accurately identify patients who are likely to have clinically significant fatigue based on a more thorough evaluation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bioinformatics Detection and Experimental Validation of Functional Transcripts in Mammalian Genome
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; COMPARATIVE GENOMICS; HUMAN GENOME; NONCODING RNA; RNAI; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: Widespread transcription activities in the human genome were recently observed from a number of high-resolution tiling array experiments, which revealed many novel transcripts that are outside of boundaries of known protein or RNA genes. Termed as "TARs" (Transcriptionally Active Regions), these regions represent the "dark matter" in the human genome, and their origin and functionality remain as mystery. Increasing evidence suggest that they encode for previously unknown proteins or RNAs. . I am interested in using a combination of computational and experimental approaches to characterize these regions, aiming to identify novel protein-coding or non-coding genes, especially those that are primate-specific or involved in human disorders.   Our proposed research has three specific aims: (i) we will use bioinformatics techniques to characterize these TARs, and investigate their possible functional roles; (ii) we will select those TARs that are likely to be human- or primate-specific, and to sequence their orthologous regions in other primates to infer their evolutionary history; (iii) we plan to use RNAi to knock-down selected ncRNAs in vivo to infer their cellular functions.   This proposed research will enhance our understanding of the complexity of the transcription activities in the human genome. The resultant list of the primate-specific transcripts will not only have direct impact in the field of human genetics, but also extend our understanding on primate evolution. Many RNAs have been implicated in human disorders and cancer, thus a comprehensive catalogue of RNAs provides invaluable resources for biomedical research, especially in cases where there are no obvious protein suspects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oxidative stress, fetal growth and programming of the metabolic syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; DEVELOPMENTAL PROGRAMMING; GESTATIONAL HYPERTENSION AND DIABETES; IUGR; MACROSSOMIA); PERINATAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; PREGNANCY OUTCOMES (PRETERM BIRTH; THE METABOLIC SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: The fetal "origins" or "programming" of the metabolic syndrome (obesity, hypertension, dislipidemia, impaired glucose tolerance) associated with adverse fetal growth has received increasing cognition. The underlying mechanisms of fetal "origins" remain unresolved. Because many commonly known or suspected causes of or conditions associated with adverse fetal growth have been associated with oxidative stress, we hypothesize that oxidative stress may be a key common link underlying fetal origins of the metabolic syndrome and associated disorders. We propose to test several links in this novel hypothetical framework. 270 pregnant women at 24-27 weeks of gestation will be recruited, and their infants will be followed up at delivery, 3 months and 1-year of age. Fasting blood insulin, 32-33 split proinsulin, leptin, and grehlin levels among infants at 1-year of age will be assayed and correlated with levels of oxidative stress markers in the mother (24-27 weeks, 32-35 weeks of gestation) and baby (cord blood). Gender-based analysis will be used to explore whether the associations may differ among boys and girls. The proposed study will be the first to assess the potential role of oxidative stress in adverse developmental programming in humans. Findings from the proposed study will contribute new knowledge to understanding the mechanisms of fetal "origins" of the metabolic syndrome and associated disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Signal Transduction Mechanisms Underlying Circadian Timekeeping in Mammals
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL ASSAYS; CELL AND TISSUE CULTURE; CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; FLUORESCENCE IMAGING; GENE TARGETING; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Living organisms have internal biological clocks that drive daily (ie., circadian) rhythms in behaviour and physiology, and that allow such rhythmic processes to be adapted beneficially in response to environmental change. It is important to understand how the circadian clock is regulated, because a dysfunctional clock¿as a result of genetic inheritance (eg., familial advanced sleep phase disorder), disease (eg., cancer, bipolar disorder), or environmental conditions (eg., jet lag, night-shift work)¿has profound, adverse consequences to the individual and his society. The goal of this proposal is to elucidate the intracellular signaling mechanisms that couple the circadian clock to environmental time cues (eg., light), and those that are needed by the clock to maintain self-sustaining circadian rhythms. Recent work has implicated two key signal transduction systems, the MAPK and G-protein signaling pathways; however, the precise molecular mechanisms by which they exert their effects on the clock remain to be determined.  Here we propose to use a combination of molecular, cellular, genetic and behavioural approaches to explore the roles of Dexras1 and RKIP, key regulatory factors in MAPK and G-protein signaling, in resetting and synchronization of the circadian clock.  To this end, we have generated a suite of transgenic and gene 'knock-out' mouse models that allow us to selectively manipulate the expression and/or activities of Dexras1 and RKIP, as well as clock reporter mouse models that allow us to monitor molecular oscillations in real time in live tissues.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES DU FOIE; METABOLISME ET NUTRITION
TitreApplicationTitle: Noninvasive prediction of hepatic fibrosis using serum markers in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
Keywords-MotsClés: FIBROSIS; LIVER BIOPSY; NONINVASIVE; SERUM MARKERS; STEATOHEPATITIS; STEATOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a common condition, affecting 15-30% of the population. It is frequently associated with obesity, diabetes and hyperlipidemia, and may lead to inflammation and scarring within the liver. Some patients develop progressive liver scarring which may lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, and liver cancer. At present, the only method of determining the amount of liver damage in people with NAFLD is liver biopsy. This procedure is invasive, prone to complications such as bleeding and death, and is not perfectly accurate. Moreover, assessing changes in the degree of liver damage with repeat liver biopsies is not feasible. Therefore, the goal of my study is to develop blood tests that can accurately determine the amount of liver damage in patients with NAFLD, so as to reduce the need for liver biopsy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and Network Analysis of Olfactory Bulb
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM IMAGING; DENDRITES; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; SYNAPSE
Abstract-Résumé: Neurons are the most anatomically complex cells in the body and this structural complexity is integrally woven into their signaling functions. Neuronal dendrites, which resemble the branches of a tree in winter, are the site where synaptic inputs from tens to thousands of presynaptic neurons arrive and are integrated. Most dendrites simply receive synaptic inputs but some like those in mitral and granule cells of the olfactory bulb also release transmitter. Dendrites are usually not passive electrical elements but instead express a diversity of voltage sensitive ion channels that interact with the neurotransmitter gated channels to produce a complex, activity and time dependent, transformation of synaptic currents into dendritic voltage changes. The electrical properties of dendrites therefore determine the way in which a neuron responds to input from other neurons and thus the flow of information through a neural circuit. In our work we study how various ion channels in dendrites of olfactory granule cells interact with glutamate-gated channels to amplify particular kinds of synaptic inputs. We also study how potassium currents in dendrites of granule cells control the initiation and spread of dendritically generated APs. Our studies on mitral cells in olfactory bulb focus on the role of transient low threshold calcium channels that we have identified by immunocytochemistry in the apical dendrite. For our work we use a combination of electrophysiology and fluorescence imaging techniques that measure changes in calcium ion concentration. Much of the calcium influx into dendrites occurs through voltage gated channels so measurements of calcium can serve as an indicator of local electrical activity in these small structures. We also focus on measuring calcium because transmitter release is driven by elevations in calcium ion concentration and many forms of synaptic plasticity (changes in synaptic strength with time) depend on calcium activated cellular processe

TitreApplicationTitle: A Study to Prospectively Validate a Clinical Decision Rule for the Investigation of Alert Patients Suspected of Having Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL DECISION RULE; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; HEADACHE; SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE; VALIDATION STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: This study builds on our previous work which developed clinical decision rules (or guidelines) to help emergency physicians determine which patients with headache require investigation for possible subarachnoid hemorrhage. This study will validate, or test, these previously developed decision rules. A subarachnoid hemorrhage is type of stroke caused by a bleeding brain aneurysm present in 1 out of every 100 emergency department patients with headache. Approximately half of all patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage die, and of those who survive, half have permanent neurological deficits. Subarachnoid hemorrhage is diagnosed with a CT scan (type of X-Ray) and/or lumbar puncture (needle in patient's back to obtain spinal fluid). CTs miss up to 10% of subarachnoid hemorrhages and while lumbar punctures miss few cases, they are painful and invasive procedures. Over 95% of the CTs and lumbar punctures are negative for subarachnoid hemorrhage suggesting overuse of these tests. Yet, some patients are misdiagnosed due to under investigation. There are no guidelines to help physicians decide which headache patients require investigation. Our previous study developed three potential decision rules to determine high and low risk groups of headache patients. These rules will improve the efficiency of current investigations while identifying high risk individuals who would otherwise not be tested. This study will validate the proposed rules to ensure their reliability to correctly categorize patients as high or low risk for subarachnoid hemorrhage. Validation is a necessary step the development of any clinical decision rule. During this study, patients will be investigated at the discretion of their physician and physicians will be told not use the proposed rules until after validation has proven them to be safe and reliable. The best rule will become the "Canadian Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Rule".

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF; CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: The control of ribosome synthesis and cell growth by the target-of-rapamycin (TOR) pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL GROWTH; DROSOPHILA; GENE EXPRESSSION; RIBOSOME SYNTHESIS; TOR
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how cells grow and multiply is a fundamental question in biology.  The processes that control cell growth are remarkably similar across different species.  For example, in humans and fruit flies, similar genes regulate cell growth.  Mutations in such genes can often lead to cancer. We therefore use the fruit fly as a simple, yet powerful genetic system to study these genes.  Our work focuses on the control of ribosome production.  Ribosomes synthesize all the proteins and enzymes in a cell, including those essential for growth.  Abnormal overproduction of ribosomes is very often seen in cancer cells, and may contribute to the runaway cell growth characteristic of the disease. Using fruit fly genetics, we will identify the genes responsible for controlling ribosome production, and examine how these genes function.  This work should help determine how the regulation of ribosome production controls cancer cell growth, and may lead to new ways to target cancer cells for therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure-function studies of purine riboswitches
Keywords-MotsClés: FLUORESCENCE SPECTROSCOPY; FRET; GENE EXPRESSION AND REGULATION; RIBOSWITCHES; RNA FOLDING AND DYNAMICS; RNA STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Riboswitches are structured RNA elements typically found in the 5' untranslated regions (5'-UTR) of mRNAs, where they regulate gene expression by binding to small metabolites. A major goal of our research is to unravel the molecular mechanisms by which the purine riboswitches harness the binding of ligands to selectively control gene expression. An understanding of the interactions between riboswitches and their metabolite ligands should provide insights into the ability of RNA to act as a genetic switch. This knowledge might empower future efforts to design novel general antimicrobial drug development approaches for generating analogs of riboswitch ligands, disrupt regulation of key metabolic pathways, and thus be selectively toxic to bacteria that carry these RNAs.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; ARYTHMIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels: crystallographic and electrophysiological investigation of interactions with SNARE proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: CALORIMETRY; ION CHANNELS; NEUROTRANSMITTER RELEASE; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; VOLTAGE-GATED CALCIUM CHANNELS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Our thoughts and memories are formed by complex signaling networks in our brains. These networks are formed by a vast amount of neuronal cells. The signaling occurs in two stages: within a neuron, fast electrical signals are used, whereas slower chemical signals bridge the gap between two different neuronal cells. A particular switch is needed to convert the electrical signal into a chemical signal. That switch is formed by "voltage-gated calcium channels", specialized proteins that are embedded in the membrane of the neurons. When an electrical signal arrives, they open and let calcium flow into the cell. The calcium then triggers the release of the chemical signals.  The calcium channels are important for many physiological events: they play a primary role in the generation of heartbeats, contraction of muscle, and release of hormones and neurotransmitter. They are the primary targets for drugs used to treat cardiovascular diseases, epilepsy, and chronic pain. It is very hard to know how these channels work without knowing their architecture. In this project, we will study how the calcium channels from the brain are regulated by other proteins necessary for the release of the chemical signals. We will use X-ray crystallography, a technique that allows us to describe their threedimensional structure in high detail. Once we know crucial parts of the structure, we will employ various methods to investigate how they are regulated. Knowing how calcium channels look like and how they are regulated will lay the basis for novel strategies to interfere with their function in several types of genetic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Embodied selfhood and person-centred dementia care: Exploring an arts-informed educational intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; DEMENTIA; FOCUS GROUPS; INTERVIEWS; MULTIPLE CASE STUDY DESIGN; OBSERVATION
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive brain disorder that currently affects 280,000 Canadians, and is characterized by impaired memory, thought, and speech. Once institutionalized, behavioural problems have been found to occur in up to 90% of residents with dementia. Non-pharmacological interventions are recommended as the first line approach to behavioural management. Nevertheless, the use of tranquillizers and physical restraints in nursing homes remains common because of the belief that the behaviour of persons with Alzheimer's disease is symptomatic of dementia itself, rather than being due to a response to physical discomfort or social isolation. This study introduces a new approach to person-centred dementia care. It is based on the concept of embodied selfhood, which refers to the ways in which persons with dementia use nonverbal communication to express themselves. Pilot work suggests that when health practitioners recognize and respond positively to expressions of embodied selfhood by residents with dementia, residents' agitation and the need for tranquillizers and physical restraints is reduced, and caregiving interactions are more cooperative and less stressful. An educational intervention for dementia care practitioners will be implemented in two Alzheimer support units. The intervention is a 12-week course that uses drama and critical reflection to enhance understanding of embodied selfhood, and will be tailored to the units for relevance and practicality. The study will collect information from residents, health practitioners, and administrators through the use of questionnaires, in-depth interviews, focus groups, and observations of day-to-day activities in the units in order to explore why the intervention and adoption strategies worked or failed, the impact on staff and residents, the needs for refinement, and the factors important for replication.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cannabis and traffic collisions: A case crossover study of patients presenting to tertiary care centres in Toronto and Halifax
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYTIC TOXICOLOGY; CASE CROSSOVER DESIGN; DRIVING UNDER THE INFLUENCE OF CANNABIS/ALCOHOL; INJURY PREVENTION; SURVEILLANCE; TRAFFIC COLLISION
Abstract-Résumé: Impaired driving is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Canada, and is an important issue to researchers, policymakers, and the public. Epidemiological evidence points to the profound effect of alcohol on road safety, and a number of important initiatives to combat this problem have been introduced. Concern about the effects of other drugs on road safety, in particular cannabis, has been growing in recent years; however, much less is known about this issue. The purpose of this research project is to understand the effects of cannabis consumption, either alone or in conjunction with alcohol, on the risk of traffic collision among patients presenting to emergency departments in Halifax and Toronto. This study is the first of its kind to explore the effects of cannabis on collision risk in multiple sites and provinces, and one of only a handful that will have examined the issue in Canada. The results of this research have clear implications on road safety and population health. Collectively, this project is an important multidisciplinary effort between clinicians, epidemiologists, social scientists, and policy makers, and fulfills CIHR's objective to fund interdisciplinary, collaborative, and policy relevant research with the goal of improving the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Increased eNOS activity and NO bioavailability through regulated eNOS-Caveolin-1 antagonism: new therapeutic avenues for vascular tone control
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD PRESSURE; CAVEOLIN; CELL CULTURE; CELL PERMEABLE PEPTIDES; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; ENOS; NITRIC OXIDE
Abstract-Résumé: A plethora of clinical data demonstrates deficient vascular tone regulation in patients, the most common condition being hypertension.  Considered a 'silent killer' since it does not cause symptoms unless severely high, considerable epidemiological evidence suggests hypertension is linked with aging and is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis, strokes, myocardial infarction, hypertensive cardiomyopathy and chronic renal failure.  Nitric oxide (NO) is a potent vasodilator that under normal conditions significantly contributes to resting vasodilator tone and participates in maintaining the non-thrombogenic surface of the vascular endothelium. However, hypertension and aging help cause a pathogenic state called endothelial dysfunction that results in impaired NO release by the blood vessels.  We have previously described how the endothelial NO synthase (eNOS), the enzyme that synthesizes NO in blood vessels, is inhibited under basal conditions.  With this knowledge in mind, we have elaborated a novel approach that prevents eNOS inhibition under basal condition, and leads to increased NO release and profound vasorelaxation.  Interestingly, this vasorelaxation is observable only in aged (old) and not in young vessels, which suggests that we might have uncovered a mechanism responsible for the attenuated NO response observed in settings in aging.  Future work will focus on characterizing this mechanism and how we can translate our research data to human pathologies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ethics in Translational Research: Navigating the Interface between the Bench and Clinic
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL TRIALS; INFORMED CONSENT; PHASE 1 RESEARCH; RESEARCH ETHICS; RISK; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: This research proposes to extend my previous work on gene therapy by examining the ethics of testing drugs in human beings for the first time-- a process called "translational clinical research."  I propose to study the ethics of three aspects of this research: when to make the "leap" from animal studies to human trials, changes in how cancer drugs are tested in clinical trials, and the ways that researchers communicate exciting (or disturbing) discoveries to the public. This proposal is aimed at addressing a major gap in ethical scholarship at a time when governments are increasing their investment in translational research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stress-induced dopamine release in subjects at clinical high risk for psychosis: a [11C]-(+)-PHNO PET study
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL HIGH RISK FOR PSYCHOSIS; DOPAMINE AGONIST RADIOTRACERS; SCHIZOPHRENIA; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia affects 1% of the population. Schizophrenics suffer from abnormal perceptual experiences (hallucinations) and thoughts (delusions). This results in enormous personal, social and economic costs. One characteristic of this disease is that schizophrenics, and people who are at a high risk of developing schizophrenia (prodromals) get very much sicker when they experience stress or take certain drugs of abuse such as amphetamine. Dopamine is a natural chemical of the brain that carries signals between nerve cells. We and others think that schizophrenics have too much dopamine especially when they are under stress or take amphetamine. However we don't know if stress results in too much dopamine in the brains of prodromals and those that became schizophrenics, as compared to healthy controls; and this is what we propose to find out in this study.  We also want to see if this excess of dopamine in the brain due to stress results in more hallucinations and delusions like experiences. We have recently developed a method to measure dopamine amounts in the human brain as it has never been possible to do so before, using a radioactive dye that can exquisitely "sense" dopamine levels in the brain when looked at with a special camera. Thus, we propose to compare stress-induced dopamine release in healthy volunteers and prodromal subjects using this technique. If our hypothesis is true, we could potentially help prodromals, by finding new treatments to regulate stress-induced DA release and may be potentially avoid a full blown psychotic episode.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of Synaptic Plasticity and Memory by Beta-Adrenergic Receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: HIPPOCAMPUS; MEMORY; PROTEIN KINASES; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Learning is the acquisition of new information, and memory is its retention over time.  Much of what we do in the present and future is determined by our past experiences, which are accessible only through memory storage and retrieval. In essence, we are what we are because of what we learn and what we remember. Memory disorders, such as amnesia (memory loss), can be devastating, as anyone familiar with the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease can attest to.  An understanding of how memories are formed in our brains, and of which genes and molecules are important for normal learning and memory formation, can lead to better strategies to treat and alleviate memory disorders in the young and in the elderly.  Research in Peter Nguyen's laboratory, at the University of Alberta, is addressing the general question: What factors can modulate and alter the ability to learn and remember new information ?  Nerve cells (neurons) in the brain are connected to each other by way of structures called synapses, and neurons communicate with each other by way of synaptic transmission (much like the way you can talk to a neighbour on the telephone). Synaptic transmission between connected nerve cells is vital for memory formation. Neurons can change the physiological strength of transmission at their synapses, in response to alterations in their electrical activity. This "synaptic plasticity" may be a cellular mechanism for memory formation in the central nervous system, and is itself modifiable (that is, the ease of inducing  of long-lasting changes in synaptic transmission can be altered by chemical transmitters and drugs,  by previous electrical activity of neurons,  and by ageing). A key goal of my reearch is to identify the mechanisms by which transmitters modulate synaptic strength and memory function. One such transmitter is noradrenaline, which is an important regulator of multiple brain functions, including arousal, mood, memory, and attention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel pathways in the metabolic regulation of insulin release from pancreatic beta-cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; INSULIN SECRETION; ISLET FUNCTION; METABOLISM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PANCREATIC BETA-CELL
Abstract-Résumé: A primary defect in type 2 diabetes mellitus is the inability of the insulin-secreting beta-cells to sense and respond to changes in blood sugar levels. How insulin-secreting beta-cells sense glucose is incompletely understood. This lack of understanding hinders development of new cell-based and drug therapies for both major forms of diabetes. Our group has developed a modern set of tools that provide a unique opportunity to gain major new insights in this area. The goals of the laboratory are to apply these newly developed tools to study stimulus/secretion coupling mechanisms in insulin-secreting beta-cells. These studies will provide new insights into relevant pathways involved in sensing sugar levels in the blood by insulin-secreting beta-cells and will have important applications for therapy of both major forms of diabetes. More specifically, since the demand for human islets for transplantation far exceeds the supply, our findings may influence genetic engineering approaches for creation of cells or cell lines that can be used for transplantation therapy to treat diabetes mellitus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term consequences of prenatal exposure to maternal cigarette smoking on brain structure, function and mental health in adolescence: role of genes and environment in brain development
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ADOLESCENCE; GENETICS; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; SMOKING DURING PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: This application seeks funding for the continuation of the Saguenay Youth Study (SYS), a research program that has been initiated five years ago through the CIHR New Emerging Team (NET) program "Neurodevelopment and Early Life Events". The SYS is a retrospective study of long-term consequences of prenatal exposure to maternal cigarette smoking (PEMCS) on brain & behaviour and cardiovascular & metabolic health of the adolescent offspring. Multiple quantitative phenotypes are acquired over four sessions (home, hospital, laboratory and school). To facilitate the search for genes that modify an individual's response to an in utero environment (i.e. PEMCS), the study is family-based (adolescent sibships) and is carried out in a relatively geographically isolated population of the Saguenay Lac-Saint-Jean (SLSJ) region in Quebec, Canada. DNA is acquired in both biological parents and in adolescent siblings. A genome-wide scan will be carried out with sib-pair linkage analyses, and fine mapping of identified loci will be done with familybased association analyses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the Anaphase Promoting Complex in Cancer and Viral Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-CANCER AGENTS; APOPTOSIS; CANCER BIOLOGY; CELL CYCLE REGULATION; P53; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Viruses often produce proteins that are highly toxic to human cells.  In some cases, such proteins are able to kill cancerous cells more effectively than normal ones, meaning that these agents have the properties of ideal cancer therapies.  The research strategy of our lab has been to study how viral proteins specifically destroy cancer cells in the hope of identifying new ways of treating cancer.  Using this approach, we have identified a critical molecular complex in cells called the Anaphase Promoting Complex/Cylosome, or APC/C.  Two different viral proteins that specifically kill cancer cells were found to bind and inhibit the APC/C.  Cancer is essentially a disease in which cells lose their normal restraints on cell division.  Research over the past several years has identified the APC/C as one of the most critical points controlling when cells divide, yet little is understood about its role in cancer or viral infection.  This proposal aims to study the mechanisms that viral proteins use to inhibit the APC/C.  Ultimately we seek to determine whether the APC/C can be utilized as an intervention point for designing novel drugs for the treatment of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting The Risk of Infection In Children Receiving Chemotherapy For Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE MYELOID LEUKEMIA; BACTERIAL AND FUNGAL INFECTION; CHILDREN; MULTI-CENTER STUDY; PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISMS
Abstract-Résumé: One in 10 children with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is expected to die from infection. Infections also increase hospitalization, decrease the amount of chemotherapy we can give, compromise quality of life and increase costs. If we could predict those at highest risk for infection, we could target strategies to prevent or improve the outcome of infection. We believe that we can use genetic information to determine who is at highest risk. We propose to obtain DNA from children soon after AML diagnosis and look for variations in genes related to the immune system. We will then determine if some genetic changes can predict infections while on treatment. We plan to include children from all 17 centres in Canada and 2 large US centres that treat children with cancer. This study will require four years to complete. We have already determined that the study is feasible and we have successfully recruited 68 patients in a pilot study. This will be the first large study to carefully measure infections in children with AML and will be the first study that will predict the risk of infection for future children with AML. With the information that we will obtain from this study, we will be able to appropriately target treatment and we should be able to improve the outcome for children with AML.

TitreApplicationTitle: Développement et évaluation des stratégies d'amélioration de la qualité des soins et d'implantation des guides de pratiques cliniques en santé de la reproduction
Keywords-MotsClés: AMELIORATION DE LA QUALITE DES SOINS; AUDIT AVEC RETRO-INFORMATION; DIMINUTION DES CESARIENNES; ESSAI CONTROLE RANDOMISE EN GRAPPE; INTERVENTIONS COMPLEXES; TRANSFERT DES CONNAISSANCES
Abstract-Résumé: L'amelioration de la qualite des soins et des pratiques cliniques en obstetrique represente un souci constant au Canada. La Societe des Obstetriciens et des Gynecologues du Canada (SOGC) a developpe des Guides de Pratique Clinique destines a ameliorer la qualite des soins. Cependant, leurs effets sur les pratiques cliniques restent limites. Le defit consiste maintenant a developper et mettre en ¿uvre des strategies adaptees d'implantation de ces Guides de Pratique afin de promouvoir les pratiques optimales. Le taux de cesariennes ne cesse d'augmenter dans les pays industrialises. Au Quebec, il est passe de 18,5% en 2000 a plus de 22,9% en 2005 en depit des recommandations de l'Organisation Mondiale de la Sante (OMS) qui preconise qu'au plus 15% des accouchements soient faits par cesarienne. Depuis le milieu des annees 1990 plusieurs etudes ont mis en evidence un risque plus eleve de complications maternelles et foetales associe a un accouchement par cesarienne. L'augmentation des taux de cesariennes constitue plus que jamais une importante question de sante publique et necessite de mettre en ¿uvre cet essai afin de repondre de maniere appropriee a la problematique de l'augmentation des taux de cesariennes au Quebec. Le programme QUARISMA, base sur le concept d'une pratique fondee sur des donnees probantes, integre une formation des professionnels de sante aux pratiques optimales ainsi qu'une evaluation des pratiques cliniques par les pairs et met l'accent sur l'implication des professionnels de sante dans le processus d'evaluation, selon la definition de l'OMS sur les methodes d'evaluation de la qualite des soins en obstetrique. Les resultats permettront de mobiliser les professionnels de sante pour ameliorer la qualite des services obstetricaux et repondre aux besoins des patientes en matiere d'information concernant les differents modes d'accouchement, et ainsi reduire durablement les taux de cesariennes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of T Cell Development, Function and Transformation by IL-7.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE AND MEMORY RESPONSES TO PATHOGENS; ANIMAL MODELS OF HUMAN DISEASE; CYTOKINE RECEPTORS; LYMPHOMA PROGRESSION; PROTEOMIC ANALYSES; T CELL ONTOGENY
Abstract-Résumé: Immune disorders such as immunodeficiencies, leukemia and lymphoma, autoimmunity, and allergy are global problems. For example, cancers of the immune system such as leukemia and lymphoma, are the most common cancers among children, accounting for 42% of such cases, and about 5600 deaths annually in all age groups. Estimates of direct and indirect costs and loss of labour from cancer of nearly $12 billion make it the second highest cause of economic loss from illness to Canada's economy. Cancer will replace heart disease as the leading cause of deaths in Canada by 2010. Current treatments (e.g., chemotherapy and radiation treatment) have significant shortcomings. Manipulating the immune system has great potential as shown by successful immunization that eradicated diseases such as smallpox. Immunological memory is the basis of vaccination and is vital since the follow up response to germs is more targeted and effective. New disease-specific therapies or vaccines with less side effects are needed.  Cytokines regulate immune cells by interacting with specific proteins on their surfaces. These "receptor" proteins trigger biochemical pathways that control normal development and function of these cells. Loss of control of these cytokines or the signals they activate can lead to diseases, such as cancer and inadequate response to infection. Treating diseases with few side effects requires knowing the signals involved in disease development. Mouse models have many advantages in the study of cytokine regulation in lymphoid development. We use gene-targeted mouse models and global protein analysis to identify the steps that are necessary for normal immune cell development, cancer of the immune system and responses to microbes that are controlled by the cytokine IL-7. A better knowledge of cytokine signaling will further our understanding of immune regulation to identify potential therapeutic strategies to cancer and to enhance vaccines for long-term immunity.

TitreApplicationTitle: The OSCILLation for ARDS Treated Early (OSCILLATE) Pilot Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME; CRITICAL CARE; HIGH FREQUENCY OSCILLATION; MECHANICAL VENTILATION; VENTILATOR-INDUCED LUNG INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a common and catastrophic complication of critical illness related to burns, motor vehicle accidents, or overwhelming infection. ARDS kills 40-70% of affected patients. Patients with ARDS require life support in the form of a ventilator to breathe for them while their lungs heal. Ironically, ventilators can cause further damage to the lungs. We propose a study comparing 2 methods to protect the lungs from further damage. One method uses standard mechanical ventilators and the other uses a new type of ventilator, called a high frequency oscillator. We propose to test whether this high frequency oscillation will reduce the relative risk of dying from ARDS. 60 patients from 10 intensive care units in Canada will participate in this preliminary study to test the feasibility of our study methods. If feasible, we plan to move on and conduct a large multinational study to definitively answer this question.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nkr-p1 receptor-ligand interactions in missing-self recognition of tumour cells and infected targets
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CYTOMEGALOVIRUS; GENE REGULATION; INFECTION; INNATE IMMUNITY; NATURAL KILLER CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The innate immune system protects us from bacteria, viruses, and cancer. Natural killer (NK) cells are innate immune cells that can detect and destroy infected and tumour cells. How NK cells do this requires understanding of the molecules they use to sense what is harmless or dangerous, and how these molecules assist in the decision to ignore or kill the target cell. We have identified a receptor-ligand pair (NKR-P1B:Clr-b) on NK cells and their targets, respectively, that mediates immune recognition at the molecular level. Because the NKR-P1B receptor is inhibitory, normal cells express the Clr-b ligand to prevent NK cell attack, while infected and cancerous cells lose Clr-b expression and are killed by NK cells. This suggests a role for the NKR-P1:Clr interactions in fighting cancer and infectious disease. I propose to advance our understanding of NK-target interactions by studying how the NKR-P1B:Clr-b interaction affects our immune defenses in fighting cancer and infection. I intend to study the structure, function, and control of ligand expression, and how pathogens can evade this NK/immune recognition. This knowledge could lead to therapies in cancer treatment and control of infectious disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies of the molecular reaction mechanisms of drugs for chemotherapy, radiotherapy and photodynamic therapy of cancers using novel ultrafast biophotonics technology
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICANCER DRUGS; CANCER THERAPY; DNA DAMAGE & CELL DEATH; MEDICAL BIOPHYSICS; TIME-RESOLVED ULTRAFAST LASER SPECTROSCOPY; ULTAFAST BIOPHOTONICS
Abstract-Résumé: The conquest of cancer continues to pose great challenges to medical science.  Overall, anticancer drug discovery remains a somewhat empirical process.  There is pressing need for molecular mechanistic understanding of action of existing anticancer drugs, which can, in turn, lead to mechanism-based design of new drugs. This proposal describes an innovative program to study molecular reaction mechanisms of anticancer drugs using novel ultrafast biophotonics technology combined with biochemical methods. By investigating how anti-cancer drugs work at a molecular level, the applicant hopes to improve our knowledge of how to treat more challenging types of cancers. Using ultrafast biophotonics - a technology that works like a high speed camera capturing real-time observations of cancer drugs at work - the applicant expects to be able to gauge the effectiveness of existing treatments and to develop new cancer therapies. These studies will lead to the developments of more effective therapies with few toxic side effects and no/little resistance to various types of cancer.  The work may also lead to the findings of molecular switches for regulating DNA damage and cell death in human systems associated with various diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Integration of Emotional and Cognitive Processing in the Brain
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL MEMORY; FRONTAL LOBES; LESION METHOD; NEUROIMAGING; TEMPORAL LOBES; THEORY OF MIND
Abstract-Résumé: There is little understanding of the brain regions and networks that support the combining of feeling with thinking to influence behaviour. While brain damage may cause obvious deficits in cognitive abilities such as attention and memory, it may also lead to subtler, yet equally devastating mental deficits, such as the inability to use feelings to make inferences about other people's mental states, what is known as 'theory of mind.' Our capacity for cooperation, deception, empathy, and humour rests on this ability to recognize in others a set of beliefs that might not correspond to our own beliefs. The loss of this ability can thus have enormous social consequences for patients and their families. The proposed research uses an innovative approach of combining the examination of theory of mind impairment following brain lesions, with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that allows visualization of on-line brain activity as participants perform various tasks. A first set of studies examines how damage to discrete regions of the frontal and temporal lobes can impair the integration of emotional and cognitive function on a wide range of tests known to be sensitive to theory of mind impairment. The relationship between theory of mind and self-referential processing during autobiographical memory, which draws on similar brain regions and processes, will then be investigated using a novel real-world 'family photos' test. Patients will be scanned with fMRI to explore differences in brain regions recruited as they recollect their own mental states while viewing personal photos of past events, and as they infer the thoughts and feelings of other people when viewing strangers' photos. These studies will also help to reveal how damage to a region can affect the remaining network of regions. These findings could lead to new diagnostic tools and rehabilitation techniques to help individuals with brain injury lead emotionally and socially fulfilling lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Spatial Chromatin Organization in Genome Regulation
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMOSOME STRUCTURE AND ORGANIZATION; EPIGENETIC REGULATION; GENE REGULATION AND EXPRESSION; GENOME ANALYSIS; GENOMICS; SYSTEMS/NETWORK BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: All human cells contain genomic DNA composed of thousands of genes coding for all the elements required for life. The genomic DNA is divided into very long molecules called chromosomes that measure approximately one meter in combined length. In order to fit inside the small volume of each cell, chromosomes must be tightly packaged and organized. Incorrect packaging of chromosomes can result in improper gene expression and may lead to disease. Therefore, the physical organization of chromosomes might be an important diagnostic marker of human diseases. I have devised a new and unique methodology termed "Chromosome Conformation Capture Carbon Copy" (5C) to map the architecture of genomes. The 5C technology measures physical DNA contacts inside living cells, and can be used to characterize the organization of the genomic DNA at very high resolution and at the genome scale. The goal of this project is to define the relationship between chromosome organization and correct gene expression. The 5C approach will be used to analyze the conformation of large genomic domains containing genes required for proper development and involved in various types of cancers. Studies will be conducted in human and mouse cells under various differentiation conditions and the gene expression will be analyzed using state-of-the-art molecular biology techniques.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancing Effectiveness and Efficiency: The Federal-Provincial Medical Surveillance Program to Detect Tuberculosis in New Immigrants and Refugees
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADIAN IMMIGRATION MEDICAL EXAMINATION; IMMIGRANTS AND REFUGEES; MASS SCREENING; PREDICTION MODELS; STATISTICS AND EPIDEMIOLOGY; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The medical surveillance program for tuberculosis is a large federal-provincial program that represents the primary line of defence against the importation of tuberculosis into Canada. However, this program, which is highly interconnected across governmental jurisdictions, detects less than 15% of foreign-born tuberculosis cases in the province of Ontario. The primary objective of this proposal is to rigorously evaluate the effectiveness of the medical surveillance program for tuberculosis in Ontario and develop specific evidence based tools to enhance its effectiveness and efficiency. By linking federal immigration data with Ontario's tuberculosis surveillance data, we will identify key areas of program inefficiency while concurrently developing and validating a prediction tool to determine how finite medical surveillance resources should best be utilized. Enhancing efficiency within the medical surveillance program for tuberculosis in Ontario could greatly improve tuberculosis control efforts and concurrently save substantial health and human resources. The lessons learned and program developed for Ontario could also serve as a model for other Canadian provinces and potentially other industrialized nations around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cervical cancer screening in the era of HPV vaccination: using mathematical and economic models to guide screening policy
Keywords-MotsClés: CERVICAL CANCER; CLINICAL POLICY; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HPV VACCINATION; NETWORK MODELS; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: In 2006, an estimated 1,350 Canadian women were diagnosed with cervical cancer, of whom 390 died.  Cervical cancer has declined by 60% since the Pap test was first introduced in 1960, and each year approximately 40% of Canadian women aged 18-69 undergo cervical cancer screening.  Recently introduced technologies will change the landscape of cervical cancer screening and treatment.  For instance, sensitive new screening tests have improved the detection of precancerous lesions.  Likewise, a new vaccine against the most common types of human papillomaviruses that cause cervical cancer is being introduced in universal vaccination programs.   It is crucial to maintain screening programmes in this new era.  However, it is is not known whether, or how, to modify current screening recommendations in response to the advent of vaccination, because (1) this would require knowledge of the future prevalence of cervical cancer, and (2) there are tradeoffs between between clinical, economic, and practical/logistic considerations that make formulation of policy difficult.   Computer models that integrate disease transmission processes, economic and logistic factors, and clinical/treatment factors can estimate future disease prevalence, and are increasingly recognized as a way of integrating disparate types of evidence to inform policy.   Our multi-disciplinary team consisting of experts in all aspects of HPV infection, interventions, and cervical cancer will develop a computer model to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of current and possible modified screening strategies using new technologies, in light of vaccination.  The model will also study potential behavioural changes brought on by vaccination (for instance, the effects of a decrease in the frequency of screening sought by vaccinated women).  This will help provinces to develop new screening recommendations in the vaccine era, with a goal of further reducing cervical cancer incidence in Canada.

However, it is is not known whether, or how, to modify current screening recommendations in response to the advent of vaccination, because (1) this would require knowledge of the future prevalence of cervical cancer, and (2) there are tradeoffs between between clinical, economic, and practical/logistic considerations that make formulation of policy difficult.   Computer models that integrate disease transmission processes, economic and logistic factors, and clinical/treatment factors can estimate future disease prevalence, and are increasingly recognized as a way of integrating disparate types of evidence to inform policy.   Our multi-disciplinary team consisting of experts in all aspects of HPV infection, interventions, and cervical cancer will develop a computer model to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of current and possible modified screening strategies using new technologies, in light of vaccination.  The model will also study potential behavioural changes brought on by vaccination (for instance, the effects of a decrease in the frequency of screening sought by vaccinated women).  This will help provinces to develop new screening recommendations in the vaccine era, with a goal of further reducing cervical cancer incidence in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic variation in the one carbon transfer pathway and ovarian cancer risk: a replication-association study
Keywords-MotsClés: FOLATE AND DIET; GENETIC ASSOCIATION STUDY; GENETIC REPLICATION; ONE CARBON METABOLISM PATHWAY; OVARIAN CANCER RISK; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISMS
Abstract-Résumé: Ovarian cancer will affect 2,400 Canadian women in 2007 and 1,700 are expected to die. Only 30% of women survive 5 years. Unfortunately, few known risk factors exist and they cannot account for the occurrence of the majority of ovarian cancers, indicating a large gap in our understanding of the causes of this disease. It is likely that genes play an important role and interact among themselves or with environmental factors (such as diet) in complex ways. We previously studied 2,000 women with and without ovarian cancer and found that 10 gene variants (or sites of DNA variation between individuals) were each linked to developing ovarian cancer. These sites of DNA variation were found in genes that are necessary for DNA synthesis, cell division, growth and proper DNA function in healthy cells. Importantly, these processes also depend on the essential vitamin folate, which is critical for DNA synthesis. The findings are an important, initial report of potential causal variants, novel for their previously-unexamined association with cancer risk. However, these initial findings must be evaluated further in order to generalize the initial findings to a larger number of women with ovarian cancer. We hypothesize that our findings for the 10 gene variants will also be linked to ovarian cancer in an independent sample of 2,000 women with and without ovarian cancer who participated in a research study in British Columbia. We also hypothesize that newly-examined genetic variants within this pathway will also be important to ovarian cancer risk. Upon completion, we will have confirmed the importance of up to 10 gene variants to ovarian cancer risk in a total of 4,000 women and identified additional gene variants that may also be important. Our ultimate goal is to identify women at genetic risk of ovarian cancer and to design appropriate intervention strategies (lifestyle or medical) to prevent this fatal disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional analyses of the mechanisms of protein penetration through membranes.
Keywords-MotsClés: AAA ATPASE P97; ANTHRAX TOXIN; ELECTRON CRYOMICROSCOPY; ERAD; MOLECULAR MACHINES; PROTEIN TRANSLOCATION ACROSS MEMBRANE
Abstract-Résumé: Lipid membranes are barriers separating the cell from its outside environment and organizing the inside of the cell into biochemically distinct compartments in which specific cellular functions are performed. My research focuses on understanding the mechanisms used by proteins to cross cellular membranes in two important biological systems, anthrax toxins and ERAD. I will use a multidisciplinary approach combining biochemical and structural biology (cryo-EM) techniques.  With the threat of emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases, combined with potential risk of terrorist attacks, there is an urgent need to examine the initial steps of infection (entry into the host cell). I will use anthrax toxins as a model system to study how bacteria inject toxins into the host cell. In particular, I will investigate how the two anthrax toxic factors, LF and EF, interact with the pore forming moiety PA, how PA inserts into the cell membrane and enables the entry of LF and EF into the cell.  Abnormal (or short-lived) proteins in the ER are selectively transported back across the ER membrane to the cytosol for degradation by the proteasome (ERAD). Malfunction of this process, which can be caused by aging, genetic mutations, or environmental factors, result in various diseases such as diabetes, inflammation, and neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Paget's disease (the second most common bone disease) and bipolar disorder. The AAA ATPase p97 plays a central role in ERAD but its exact mechanism of action is not known. I will investigate its function by studying its interactions with other important players of the ERAD pathway such as the ER membrane proteins Derlin-1 and VIMP, the p97-co-factor Ufd1-Npl4 and substrates. I will also study the complexes assembled by p97 during ERAD on cellular membranes (equivalent to taking snapshot images of the complexes during the biological pathway) and correlate these images with biochemical data.

TitreApplicationTitle: Indigenous Knowledge Network for Infant, Child, and Family Health
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY BASED HEALTH PROGRAMMING; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MATERNAL CHILD HEALTH; ORAL HISTORY; PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: First Nations and Metis children and their families do not enjoy the same good personal and community health that is enjoyed by other Canadians.  One reason for this is that health planners, managers and workers in First Nations and Metis communities often don't have the the health information they need to do their jobs. Information about health in their local area and information that fits with their local culture is required. This research project will test a new way of trying to get First Nations and Metis health planners, managers, and workers the health information they need, so that they can make use it in their local parenting and child health programs.  Building on the informal networks that already exist in First Nations and Metis communities, this project will link Indigenous health planners,managers, and workers together through their participation in a more structured Indigenous knowledge network.  In partnership with academic researchers the members of this network will work on gathering, organizing, exchanging and using health information.  They will work with both cultural information from their home communities and scientific information from the project scientists and apply this new information to a local parenting or infant/child health promotion program. Ultimately, this project can contribute to the improvement of the personal and community health of First Nations and Metis people in Canada by testing out a new way of getting health planners, managers, and workers the information they need to improve health policies, programs, and services for young Aboriginal families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bridging the translational gap between basic science and clinical medicine in pulmonary fibrosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CLINICAL MANAGEMENT; DISEASE MECHANISMS; PULMONARY FIBROSIS; TRANSLATIONAL MEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive lung disease that is characterized by excessive scarring in the lungs. The cause for this process is as yet unknown. There are approximately 20,000 people in Canada affected by IPF and approximately 20% of them die each year. The disease is unresponsive to current treatment, which underscores the need for development and evaluation of new drugs.  I am a clinical expert in interstitial lung diseases and also have received extensive training in basic research in this field, which allows me to facilitate the translation between basic science and clinical arenas. My research investigates the mechanisms of progressive scarring in lungs by using animal disease models and analyzing human blood and tissue. The purpose is not only to better understand the nature of the disease but also to identify potential drug targets and biomarkers, which are naturally occurring events in living organisms, cells or molecules that can be used as indicators of disease progression. I evaluate new drugs and biomarkers in disease models in animals and aim to translate these findings into clinical practice to improve the management and care of affected patients.
