TitreApplicationTitle: The role of H-NS and related molecules in regulating bacterial virulence gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIOLOGY; GENE REGULATION; GENOMICS; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MICROBIAL EVOLUTION; PATHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Free-living bacteria are constantly swapping genetic material (DNA) with other bacterial species.  By doing so they are able to rapidly evolve in response to their ever-changing environment.  Genes responsible for antibiotic resistance are often obtained by gene swapping; a fact that accounts for the rapid spread of drug resistant bacteria.  The virulence genes of most bacterial pathogens were also obtained by gene swapping.  Genetic exchange can come with an associated cost for the bacterial cell, however, if the new genes they acquire are incompatible with the genes they already have.  We have found that a bacterial protein found in E. coli and Salmonella, called H-NS, can distinguish "self" genes from those genes acquired from other bacteria and subsequently turn the foreign genes off.  By shutting these genes off the bacteria can acquire foreign genes without compromising their own fitness by doing so.  Over a longer period of time the bacteria can develop ways of turning the foreign genes on under the right conditions.  Evidence indicates that H-NS regulates the vast majority of virulence genes in the enteric bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli, Vibrio and Yersinia).  We wish to explore exactly how H-NS shuts foreign virulence genes down and, subsequently, how such genes are turned on under the right conditions.  By understanding these processes we hope to develop new therapeutic strategies for the control of bacterial infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Non-invasive imaging of pathological neoangiogenesis using targeted multivalent nanoparticles
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CANCER; INTRAVITAL IMAGING; METASTASIS; NANOTECHNOLOGY; VASCULAR TARGETING AGENTS
Abstract-Résumé: New imaging techniques that light up tumour "signatures" hold great promise for the early detection and treatment of cancer. The ability to detect tumours without biopsy or surgery should lead to more effective cancer screening strategies, lower healthcare costs and ultimately a higher quality of life. The growth of new blood vessels is particularly important at the early stage of tumour formation. Because current imaging techniques are unable to detect these blood vessels specifically, there is a need to develop new methods to address this. We propose to evaluate a novel "target" called EGFL7 for these imaging strategies. This target is present only at sites of new blood vessel growth in growing tumours. Using an innovative approach that capitalizes on recent advances in nanotechnology and non-invasive imaging, this study will increase our understanding of new blood vessels growth in cancer and result in new imaging techniques to detect early stage cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Complementary therapy decision-making processes of advanced cancer patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVANCED CANCER; COMPLEMENTARY AND ALTERNATIVE MEDICINE; GROUNDED THEORY METHODOLOGY; PALLIATIVE CARE AND END OF LIFE CARE; TREATMENT DECISION-MAKING
Abstract-Résumé: A growing number of patients with incurable cancer are choosing to use complementary therapies. With the increasing variety of complementary therapies, patients are faced with difficult choices and require support and education to make treatment decisions. The specific aims of this project are to describe the unique and dynamic characteristics of complementary therapy decision-making processes, the differences in these decisions between women and men and across cancer types, the social context within with these decision-making processes take place; and lastly, to describe the information resources used by advanced cancer patients as well as their unmet information needs. Thirty women and thirty men with a variety of cancer diagnoses will be invited to take part in two interviews that will be conducted approximately 4 months apart to capture any changes in treatment decisions. Interviews will also take place with an individual who was influential in the decision-making process. As the first known study to explore complementary therapy decisions within the context of advanced cancer care, the study findings may inform decision making research in other palliative populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Skeletal muscle dysfunction in COPD
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC OBSTRUTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; EXERCICE TOLERANCE; MUSCLE BIOPSY; MUSCLE WASTING; SKELETAL MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is highly prevalent and the burden of this disease is only expected to increase in the coming 15-20 years.  Once viewed as a disease limited to the lung, COPD is now recognized as a disease involving various organs.  The impairment in lower limb muscle function is one of the most devastating systemic manifestations of COPD.  Over the course of my CIHR-fundfed research program my group have established the impact of muscle wasting and poor lower limb muscle endurance on survival and functional status impatients with COPD.  We wish pursue this research in order to understand why a significant portion of patients with COPD become susceptible to muscle fatigue or loose muscle mass.  On the long term, we hope to contribute to therapeutic development in this area, and ultimately, to impact on functional status, quality of life and survival in patients with COPD.

Abstract-Résumé: There are important knowledge gaps concerning the long-term impact of various adverse prenatal risk factors (social, behavioral, environmental and genetic) on the health of future generations. This is in part due to the lack of prospective clinical research on large cohorts, transcending pregnancy and extending to the neonatal period and the pediatric years. To untangle the complex casual pathways and to identify potential effective preventive measures for many adverse birth outcomes, these gaps must be bridged. Our proposed network-based clinical research program is poised to rise to these unmet challenges, addressing the intrauterine determinants of important perinatal health outcomes. Reproductive health issues are critically important public health concerns to Canadians: they create long-term societal and family burdens and have major costs implications. Our program, which crosses CIHR¿s four pillars, will promote knowledge transfer from the basic sciences to clinical research, culminating in evidence based practice guidelines and public policy. IRNPQ will provide much needed new knowledge to legislators, policy makers, clinicians and consumers, so that policy decisions will result in improved health and well being for all Canadians.

Abstract-Résumé: For nearly two decades, the Canadian HIV Trials Network (CTN) has been central to Canada¿s research response to HIV/AIDS.  The CTN is proud to have created an organization that encourages and facilitates high quality investigator-driven research, while linking or connecting resources and expertise from across Canada.  And the need for reliable and well-structured trials has not diminished in the current context.  While research alone has tremendous value, its worth compounds when it translates into new knowledge, better treatments and improved services and public policies.   The CTN has developed a plan for its next funding cycle 2008-2013 that includes five strategic priorities and the actions needed to realize them. Critiques from past external reviews, recommendations from the CTN¿s operational review conducted in 2006, and ideas garnered from CIHR¿s RFA planning session in May in Ottawa, have all been taken into consideration in setting the Network¿s 5-year agenda,  These five strategic priorities create a framework for action and continuous improvement:  1. Deliver on the value of a Canadian clinical trials network for HIV/AIDS research. 2. Ensure the CTN is a high-performance, service-oriented and accountable organization that supports researchers and scientific excellence. 3. Enable scientific excellence by facilitating HIV/AIDS clinical trials in Canada and beyond. 4. Translate and transfer scientific knowledge into action. 5. Position the CTN to be an integral player in the Federal Initiative to Address HIV/AIDS in Canada (FI).

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Cell Survival Genes in Promoting Neural Regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH AND SURVIVAL GENES; CORTICAL DEVELOPMENT; NEURAL STEM CELL BIOLOGY; NEUROGENESIS; REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: The discovery of stem cells in the adult brain has generated hope for a future where brain regeneration can occur. The long term objective of this research, therefore, is to "help the brain heal itself".  Currently the low numbers of stem cells in the adult brain limits their ability to restore brain function following an injury. The goal of this project is to develop a strategy to expand the number of stem cells within the brain and manipulate them to generate new nerve cells to replace those lost due to neurodegenerative diseases (ie. Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases) or following acute injuries such as stroke.   Stem cell numbers in the adult brain are tightly regulated by a balance between expansion (cell division) and elimination (cell death). To increase the numbers of stem cells and promote brain regeneration, we need to understand what factors regulate their survival. This project examines the role of Mcl1 which has been shown to promote the survival of both blood stem cells and mature neurons. To determine what role Mcl1 plays in the nervous system, we will manipulate its expression using two approaches: (i) loss of expression and (ii) increasing Mcl1 expression in brain stem cells.  These strategies will allow us to assess whether Mcl1 is a survival factor for stem cells in the brain and whether we can expand their numbers by manipulating Mcl1 expression. Finally, we will examine whether increasing Mcl1 expression in brain stem cells will facilitate the production of new neurons. These experiments will identify a novel approach to promoting neural regeneration and restoration of function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Violence and Victimization: Reducing Risk and Promoting Health and Well Being for Girls and Young Women
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD AND ADOLESCENT DEVELOPMENT; MENTAL AND PHYSICAL HEALTH; QUALITATIVE; QUANTITATIVE; VICTIMIZATION; VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Until recently, research on aggression and violence has focused primarily on boys. This is understandable given the fact that compared to girls, boys engage in more serious acts of violence and inflict greater physical injury on others at every stage of development. Nonetheless, rates of violent crime have increased among young women and these trends are similar in what girls report about their own behaviour. We know that many girls involved in aggression and violence have experienced severe and chronic victimization and they struggle with a myriad of social and mental health issues. Such findings signal the need to fast track research on aggression, victimization and violence in the lives of girls, with the goal of informing social policy, and developing programs to promote health and well-being. More specifically, we need a better understanding of the factors that place girls at risk, the developmental course of these problems among girls, potential factors that buffer girls from risk and promote their healthy transition into young adulthood, and the effectiveness of interventions to reduce risk.    This program of research in four central areas that relate to the health and well-being of adolescent girls and young women:  1. The etiology, developmental course and health consequences of exposure to victimization and involvement in violence;  2. The unique factors and needs related to cultural and social marginalization that place young women at risk for poor health outcomes.  3. The development of effective intervention and the promotion of community capacity to reduce risk and promote health and well-being;  4. The development of an international collaborative team to study risk, resilience, prevention and intervention related to gender, sex, victimization and violence.  Mentorship, capacity building (both research capacity and community capacity), and knowledge translation is discussed thematically is a key focus throughout this program of work.

Abstract-Résumé: The United Nations' First Millennium Development Goal is to eradicate extreme poverty and hunger by 2015.  The elimination of hunger would yield a food security dividend beyond any other global achievement, and it would improve the lives of women and their children more than any other human development action.  This program of research seeks to listen to women in many parts of the world who struggle to meet their food needs and the food needs of their families and in turn produce a shared voice, solidarity of purpose, and novel strategies that might be overlooked without a gendered analysis of women's food provisioning experiences.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of the sex differences in radiation-induced bystander effect in vivo
Keywords-MotsClés: BYSTANDER EFFECT; EPIGENETICS; IONIZING RADIATION; MICRORNA; SEX DIFFERENCES; SEX HORMONES
Abstract-Résumé: One third of the live people today are likely to contract some form of carcinoma, and more than half of which are likely to receive some form of radiotherapy. While modern cancer radiation therapy has led to increased patient survival rates, the risk of treatment-related secondary complications and adverse effects is becoming a growing clinical problem.  The bystander effect   is included in these secondary complications, and may occur upon any type of radiotherapy. Of critical importance, the bystander effect has been linked to treatment-induced secondary radiation carcinogenesis. Despite the obvious associations, however, firm and conclusive evidence that IR-induced bystander effect in vivo is indeed operational is limited. Furthermore, pending conclusive evidence of its existence, the exact molecular mechanisms of bystander effect in vivo have yet to be identified.  Tumors, including radiation-induced secondary malignancies, have been reported to occur to a different extent in males and females. Congruently, some studies hinted that somatic bystander effects are also sex specific. Is there a link between the two phenomena? Before any far-reaching conclusions can be made, animal models are very useful tools in elucidating sex differences in bystander responses and their molecular mechanisms. Uncovering the molecular underpinnings and biological repercussions of sex differences in somatic in vivo bystander phenomenon will allow the development of strategies for the prevention or mitigation of bystander effects in humans, thus increasing patient survival rates.

TitreApplicationTitle: New Perspectives on Sex/Gender, Diversity and Health Reform in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: DIVERSITY; GENDER/SEX-BASED ANALYSIS; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH REFORM; HEALTH SERVICES; HOME CARE; INTERSECTIONALITY; PRIMARY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Health care reform is a global phenomenon aimed at improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the health sector in the face of limited government resources, demographic changes and technological innovations.  Most recently in Canada, the government of British Columbia concluded a consultative process entitled The Conversation on Health, intended to lead to historical transformations to the health care system in the province.  Even though reforms to the health care system differentially affect vulnerable and marginalized populations including those in need of care, those who work in the formal care system and those who provide informal or unpaid care, most health care reform interventions are designed and implemented with little attention to gender and diversity.  The goal of this research program is two-fold: to apply a gender and diversity analysis - using a mixed methods approach that prioritizes action and knowledge translation - to the most recent health reform initiative in Canada (i.e., the BC Conversation on Health) and to evaluate current approaches and tools of GBA for assessing the effects of health reform for women in all their diversity.  Moreover, because the research will be informed by a gender and diversity analysis, the project also provides an opportunity to apply, evaluate and further refine current approaches to GBA in Canada to methodically capture not only gender but factors that intersect with gender including age, class, geography, language, race/ethnicity, ability and sexuality.  The results of this program of research, focused on various aspects of health reform and aimed at improving existing GBA, will contribute to gender equity and equitable health outcomes in research, policies, programs and legislation.

Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO PRENATAL CARE; DIVERSITY ANALYSIS; HEALTH BEHAVIORS IN PREGNANCY; MIXED METHODS; VULNERABLE/MARGINALIZED WOMEN; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: As a Mid-Career Research Chair in Gender, Sex and Health, my program of research will focus on women's health as it relates to pregnancy and childbirth.  Pregnant women are not a homogeneous group and significant differences may exist among women.  This program of research will use a gender and sex-based analysis to conceptualize and measure health care use and quality of health care from the perspectives of pregnant women in diverse social, economic, and geographic locations.  My research program has the following specific aims: (1) to examine inequities and disparities in women's prenatal health and access to prenatal care, (2) to explore how these disparities are related to other health determinants such as income, ethnicity, migration, and geography, and (3) to study the association of disparities in women's prenatal health and use of prenatal care with adverse pregnancy outcomes.  In particular, the experiences of poor women, Aboriginal women, and immigrant women will be studied.  One project will examine factors associated with inadequate use of prenatal care among inner-city women.  The results of this project will be used to develop and test new service delivery models of prenatal care for inner-city women.  Another project will explore perspectives of both women and health care providers regarding quality of prenatal care.  Data gathered from the qualitative interviews will be used to develop an instrument to measure quality of prenatal care.  This instrument will then be used in studies to compare and contrast quality of care across socioeconomic and geographic areas, and to determine the association of quality of prenatal care with pregnancy outcomes.  Knowledge translation will be an important component of this program of research, with research users integrated in all phases, ensuring that results will be used to influence program and policy development.  Training of the future generation of researchers in women's health will be given high priority.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ocanku Duta Amani: Paths to Living Well for Aboriginal Youth
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL YOUTH; COMMUNITY BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; CULTURALLY COMPETENT CARE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; ON-RESERVE HEALTH AND WELL-BEING; PHOTOVOICE
Abstract-Résumé: Numerous publications and reports have shown that the health status of young Aboriginal Canadians is lower than that of non-Aboriginal Canadians the same age. Although this disparity highlights a challenge, current research suggests building on the strengths of Aboriginal youth and their communities is more effective than reflecting on problems and deficits. This research will seek the perspectives of Aboriginal on-reserve youth about their "paths to being and becoming well". A select group of on-reserve youth in Saskatchewan will explore the meaning and strategies to being well in a holistic context using sharing circles and photovoice. The youth will also develop an interactive activity through which they will share their knowledge and experiences with other Aboriginal on-reserve youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autophagy mediator Beclin 1 as a suppressor of three-dimensional growth of ras oncogene-driven tumors
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; BECLIN 1; CANCER; CELL DEATH; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; RAS
Abstract-Résumé: The cells lining many human organs (epithelial cells) form a single layer. Cells that detach from this layer die. Most tumors are composed of epithelial cells that became cancerous. These cells now have to survive outside of the epithelial layer in order to be able to form a three-dimensional tumor mass and spread throughout the body. We are investigating the mechanisms allowing detached cancer cells to survive.  Cellular protein called Ras is normally activated by signals coming from outside of the cell. Ras can, in turn, trigger events that change cellular levels of many proteins. Genetic alterations in cancer cells can make Ras active at all times and this contributes to the progression of many cancers. One of the properties of Ras that is thought to make it a major factor in cancer is its ability to block death of tumor cells growing outside of the epithelial layer. We have begun to identify the mechanisms of this effect of Ras but our knowledge about these mechanisms is far from complete.   We found recently that Ras triggers the reduction in the levels of a cell death-inducing protein called Beclin 1 in cancer cells. The role of Beclin 1 in the Ras-driven survival of cancer cells growing outside of their original location has never been explored. We will examine this role in the present study. We expect that re-introduction of Beclin 1 into cancer cells will block Ras-dependent survival and growth of these cells outside of the epithelial layer and prevent growth of Ras-driven tumors in mice (which are often used as models for studying tumor growth).   We expect that our studies will reveal the mechanisms allowing tumors to grow outside of the epithelial layer. Suppression of these mechanisms can be anticipated to stop or slow down tumor progression. If successful, our work could give rise to a new type of cancer therapy based on blocking the formation of the three-dimensional tumor mass and the spread of cancer cells throughout the body.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preventing bone loss in osteoporosis and other osteolytic diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE RESORPTION; EARLY BIOMARKERS; INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIS; ION TRANSLOCATION; OSTEOARTHRITIS; OSTEOCLASTOGENESIS; OSTEOCLASTS; OSTEOPOROSIS; PERIODONTAL DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Preventing bone loss is an essential issue in women's health.  One in four women over the age of 50 has osteoporosis. Rheumatoid arthritis, which results in bone loss around the affected joint, has been reported to be 2-4 times higher in females than males. Bone is the most frequent site of metastasizing breast cancer and is the source of the most deleterious effects of breast cancer, resulting in severe pain from nerve compression in the spinal cord, decreased mobility, and ultimately bone fractures. The goal of my research is to prevent pathological bone loss. Towards this objective, my lab has three projects underway which focus on osteoclasts, the cells responsible for resorbing bone.  The first project is based on the observation that osteoclasts residing in joints affected by inflammatory arthritis are larger and more active.  Our objective is to try to elucidate differences in the signaling and activation mechanisms between these large osteoclasts involved in pathological bone loss and the smaller osteoclasts involved in maintaining healthy bone.  The goal is to provide the groundwork for designing methods for selective inhibition of osteoclasts involved in excessive bone loss. Secondly, my lab is studying the molecular mechanisms by which osteoclasts pump acid over the bone surface, an essential step in dissolving bone.  We are currently screening for compounds that prevent this process, to be used as therapeutics for alleviating pathological bone loss.  Finally, my lab is part of a CIHR New Emerging Team that is exploring the hypothesis that variations in osteoclastogenic capacity in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis could underlie variation in predisposition for disease and disease severity.  The goal of this work is to establish osteoclastic parameters strongly related to presence and severity of bone and joint destruction and to determine if these biomarkers are predictors of patient progression and responsiveness to different treatment regimens.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a valid and reliable self-report index of frailty
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DISABILITY; FRAILTY; MEASUREMENT; MORTALITY; PHYSICAL PERFORMANCE; PREDICTIVE VALIDITY; PREVALENCE; SELF-REPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Traditionally, the health of older persons has been assessed based on the presence of chronic disease, mental status, and/or disabilities in carrying out basic activities such as bathing. Using this approach, clinicians may overlook older persons who are functionally independent, but who have identifiable markers of frailty that make them vulnerable to adverse health outcomes, such as acute illness, falls, or disability. In primary care practice, the potential to identify frailty in independent older persons can lead to interventions that prevent or delay the onset of disability. In specialized care where older persons are receiving complex interventions such as chemotherapy and cardiac surgery, screening for frailty may allow for interventions tailored to the heterogeneous levels of vulnerability in the older population. Currently, several large Canadian research projects have been initiated with the purpose of broadening our understanding of frailty. Investigators of these studies are faced with the challenge of selecting appropriate measures to assess frailty. Several types of measures have been proposed for the identification of frailty: physical performance tests are based on the measurement of a specific physical function, such as the strength of a person's grip; clinical assessments are based on a clinician's gestalt about how frail the person is; physiological measures use laboratory-based tests of features such as inflammation or coagulation; and self-reported measures rely on the older person's responses to questions that are indicative of their level of frailty. Self-report is widely used in the assessment of disability in older persons, and is potentially the most cost-effective type of measure. There is insufficient research about the most appropriate self-report measures for the assessment of frailty status. The objective of this study is to develop a self-reported index that can be used to assess frailty in both clinical and research settings.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Image Guidance for Prostate Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES; IMAGING; MINIMALLY INVASIVE; MULTIMODALITY; PROSTATE CANCER; QUALITY OF HUMAN LIFE; TRANSLATIONAL; TUMOR CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer remains a significant health care problem: in Canada in 2007, over 22,000 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer and over 4000 will die from the disease. The last decade has seen a 20% increase in the number of men diagnosed with prostate cancer and this trend is projected to continue in the coming decade. Management options for men with localized prostate cancer include active surveillance, radical prostatectomy, external beam radiotherapy, or brachytherapy. Currently, decisions about treatment are based on a limited set of clinical data: blood PSA levels, extent of the cancer on rectal examination, and cancer grade on biopsy. This information is used to estimate the probability of prostate cancer spread, help select the appropriate treatment and predict the treatment success. While helpful, such estimates are based on groups of men and are limited in their ability to predict outcome or tailor therapies for individuals. There is a pressing need for new techniques that can identify and characterize cancers in individual men to better select treatments and enable minimally invasive therapies to improve outcomes and reduce side effects. We propose to combine different prostate cancer images using computed tomography, magnetic resonance, ultrasound and nuclear medicine techniques to create "hybrid imaging maps" that can be used to predict the location of cancer within the human prostate with millimetre accuracy. We will evaluate the potential impact of hybrid imaging maps on patient outcomes and quality of life through clinical studies where our hybrid maps are used to guide diagnosis and treatment. Finally, we will use animal models to develop new methods of imaging prostate cancer biologic processes that could be translated into new techniques for human use. Through the knowledge gained we hope to develop innovative techniques that will benefit cancer patients broadly through improved abilities to detect, map and treat cancer.

Abstract-Résumé: Reports of numerous commissions in Canada and abroad suggest that the rate of adaptation of health care delivery systems has been too incremental or insufficient. Our research program focuses on three interdependent dimensions of the process of governing change within health care networks: management of change and innovations, performance management and the management of knowledge. Comparative analysis will be done with networks in Ontario, Alberta and UK. The organization of forums with decision-makers and the production of systematic reviews to support the development of guidelines for network governance will be performed. Our research program will support health care managers and clinical leaders in their attempt to reorganize the delivery of health care services to improve patient care.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Mucosal Innate Immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC LUNG INFLAMMATION; DENDRITIC CELLS; EPITHELIAL CELLS; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; LUNG AND BOWEL INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; NK CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The majority of human pathogens initiate infection through mucosal surfaces and there are differential immune responses to invading pathogens, depending on the tissue of entry (lung, gut or genitor-urinary tract), and due to exposure to commensal microflora, physiologic requirements of the tissue and the nature of the infecting organism or environmental exposure. However, little is understood about the communication between the innate systems at different mucosal sites, a very much understudied area of mucosal immunology. We wish to uncover novel ways to manipulate this mucosal innate response to the benefit of acute and chronic respiratory disorders, GI diseases, as well as sexually transmitted diseases. We will use new approaches (gnotobiotic facility) and integrate our findings from the diverse mucosal sites to understand the rules governing the interaction between the host (i.e. the mucosa) and environmental and biological entities (i.e. bacteria, viruses, food and aeroallergens and hormones) which determine whether the specific and local outcome will be protection, homeostasis or immunopathology, with comparison and cross-talk between the mucosal sites being paramount. We will explore the influence of commensal and/or pathogenic microflora on the host mucosal innate response at the various tissues. We will determine the extent of the Common Mucosal Innate Response by comparing the effects of exposure to relevant pathogens at one mucosal site to changes seen in the components of the innate response at a second mucosal tissue site. We will also determine the extent and interaction of the various mucosal innate responses when perturbed by non-microbial environmental factors. These findings will directly inform us about pathways and mechanisms involved in the innate and adaptive response at the mucosa, how the cross-talk informs the innate response in other mucosal tissues and how we might intervene for beneficial and therapeutic outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Maternal Infant Care
Keywords-MotsClés: INFANTS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MOTHERS; OUTCOMES; QUALITY OF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: A major weakness in health research is the inability to effectively, efficiently and rapidly translate knowledge into improved quality of care, better patient outcomes and reduced health care costs. Preterm birth is a prime area for developing knowledge translation models to improve quality of care. The costs of preterm birth are estimated to exceed $1 billion annually in Canada and include NICU care, which is expensive and often prolonged. Unfortunately, little is known about how to reduce preterm births and the outcomes for preterm infants have not improved in recent years. This research program is designed to improve outcomes and reduce costs through a better understanding of how different practices and risks affect the long-term health of preterm infants, how improved methods of knowledge translation can enhance quality of care, and how the use evidence can be extended to patients for counseling and decision making.      Our objective is to conduct an integrated program of research, training and knowledge translation aimed at creating innovative methods and models for improving quality of care for pregnant women, infants and their families. We will involve researchers, clinicians, administrators, professional bodies and community groups from across Canada. We will establish a unique national database that spans the entire period from pregnancy to childbirth, infancy and developmental follow-up, and use it to develop and test innovative methods and models for quality improvement. We will conduct 5 projects that will assess the therapy and non-therapy related risk factors for preterm infants, use evidence to identify best practices and indicators, develop and evaluate decision support tools to facilitate practice change, implement and evaluate an evidence-based practiceidentification and change (EPIC) system for improving care for newborn infants and their families, and develop updated prognostic tools for family counseling and decision making.

TitreApplicationTitle: The CIHR Team in Driving in Older Persons (CanDRIVE II) Research Program
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; COLLISION RATES; DRIVING; DRIVING PATTERNS & HABITS; EVIDENCE BASED RESEARCH; GERIATRICS; OLDER DRIVERS; PHYSICAL IMPAIRMENT; PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY; QUALITY-OF-LIFE; RESTRICTED DRIVING; SENIORS
Abstract-Résumé: Besides falls, motor vehicle crashes (MVCs) are the most common cause of injury in seniors. Of all age groups, those over 65 years have one of the highest crash rates per kilometers driven where the crash rate is 4-6X higher for older persons compared to middle-aged drivers.  Increased crash rates in older drivers is due to the increased prevalence of health conditions that can affect fitness to drive.  While morbidity and mortality rates related to MVCs have declined substantially recently, death and injury rates for those over 65 continue to climb. Older drivers also pose an increased risk to their passengers, pedestrians and occupants of other vehicles.  Therefore, the impact of the increased crash rates of older persons extends beyond older drivers, and imposes a significant cost to society.   However, at the individual level, the loss of one's driver's license also has serious consequences. The mobility provided by the ability to drive allows the maintenance of community independence, and holding a driver's license has symbolic importance for older drivers.  Loss of driver licensure can lead to depression, social isolation and stress on families. Older drivers often feel angry with those who deem them unfit to drive, often straining personal and professional relationships.  The CIHR Team in Driving in Older Persons (CanDRIVE II) research program builds on the momentum of its CIHR-funded predecessor (CanDRIVE I) in taking a national collaborative, inter-disciplinary approach to identifying, analyzing and addressing issues pertaining to the mobility, injury prevention, and quality-of-life of older drivers.  The objective of the CanDRIVE II Team is to conduct innovative, methodologically sound, practical clinical research that can be translated into policy renewal and improved clinical practice, and that will help maximize the health and independence of older adults.

Abstract-Résumé: Although large strides have recently been taken in the characterization of innate response to microbes, deficit in host resistance to infection remains a primordial problem.  Host genetic factors play an important role in the onset, progression, and ultimate outcome of infection with pathogens. To effectively address the challenge of emerging and established infectious diseases in human health, we propose the creation of a large multidisciplinary team of Canadian scientists and international collaborators to systematically identify and characterize mouse genes conferring host resistance against infectious pathogens of global relevance: malaria, influenza and enterobacteria. Ultimately, the mutated genes identified in mice will be tested as candidates for infectious disease susceptibility among well-defined affected human populations and will serve as a substrate for biochemical and medical chemistry studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the Nature and Improving the Treatment of Kidney Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ABLATION THERAPY; GENOMICS; INTERVENTIONAL RADIOLOGY; KIDNEY CANCER; SMALL RENAL MASSES; THERMOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common kidney cancer and the most lethal urological cancer with > 33% mortality in Canada. The incidence of kidney cancer is similar to leukemia and increasing at >1% per year, apparently due to earlier detection. New cases are now frequently diagnosed incidentally, without symptoms, as small renal masses (SRMs) or spots on the kidney that usually grow very slowly frequently in older persons. Despite earlier treatment, the expected decrease in death rate from RCC has not been realized. We have initiated initial watchful waiting after biopsy in selected cases, in order to delay surgery until tumour growth is detected. However, we do not know which tumours will grow or why. Our two research initiatives will directly improve management of SRMs: molecular studies and minimally invasive therapy. We know much about the genetics and molecular pathways that lead to RCC, mainly because some RCCs occur as a consequence of hereditary Von Hippel Lindau (VHL) Disease. We will define the VHL gene mutations initiating SRMs and the progressive molecular changes that cause progression to advanced large RCC. By understanding the molecular changes we will identify targets for therapeutic intervention. We will develop new and improved tools for minimally invasive image guided therapy of those localized kidney cancers that need treatment, starting with radiofrequency ablation (RFA). By inserting a new type of electrode through the skin and measuring the heating effect in the tumour by MRI images (called thermometry), we will be able to treat larger tumours and potentially reduce the use of invasive surgical procedures for kidney cancer. Wyeth and CIHR support for the Chair and these studies will advance knowledge and treatment of kidney cancer, heighten awareness of kidney cancer research, facilitate multidisciplinary approaches to research and patient care, and enhance local, provincial, national and international collaborations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Tissue Injury and Novel Approaches to Tolerance Induction to Promote Long Term Transplant Survival
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; EPITHELIAL CELL; KIDNEY; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal describes three major areas of research we are engaged in.  The first looks at mechanisms by which kidneys and likely other organs are injured following transplantation.  The very nature of transplantation is associated with organ injury, as all organs are at least temporarily removed from a blood supply with the procurement procedure.  While not preventable, the extent of injury may be modifiable by studies of the molecular pathways by which cells undergo injury.  Our hope is that these can be modified to minimize injury not only with organ procurement but also after transplantation, with rejection.  The second area is the development of genetically modified plants that express human proteins for applications in medicine.  Plant systems overcome many of the hurdles currently facing the production of biotherapeutics, including high cost, ability to produce abundant amounts, easy scale-up, and freedom from human pathogens and viruses.  Finally, we are developing protocols for human transplantation by testing those strategies most extensively tested in mouse models, to non-human primates.  It is our hope that we will define strategies that allow immune acceptance of transplant with limited or no ongoing immunosuppressive drugs.  Overall these projects are linked by a desire to utilize basic discoveries to strategies that will lead to human therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ex-vivo Repair of Injured Donor Lungs for Transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICALLY REJECTED HUMAN DONOR LUNGS; CYTOKINES; EX-VIVO NORMOTHERMIC LUNG PERFUSION AND LUNG REPAIR; EX-VIVO THERAPEUTIC GENE THERAPY; INHIBITION OF PRO-INFLAMMATORY FACTORS; LARGE ANIMAL MODELS; LUNG TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last two decades, lung transplantation has become the mainstay of therapy for selected patients suffering from many types of end-stage lung diseases (e.g. emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension and cystic fibrosis) refractory to medical management. Lung transplantation has enjoyed increasing success with better early and late survival rates. However, the number of patients requiring lung transplantation has been increasing and largely exceeds the number of donors available. As a result, the death rate on the waiting list is 20% to 30% in most lung transplant centers.   The best alternative will be to expand the number of donors. Indeed, we currently are able to use only 15% to 25% of the lungs that are offered to us from brain dead donors; 75% to 85% of donors are rejected due to various forms of lung injury. Hence, any strategy that would increase our utilization rate of lung donors from 15% to even 40 -50% could potentially double and even triple the number of lung transplants performed every year.   Our project, using a large animal model and human injured donor lungs will study a very novel concept: ex-vivo (outside the body) repair of damaged lungs for transplantation. After organ retrieval and ischemic storage we will treat the donor lungs ex-vivo for 6 to 12 hours in a special pump perfusion system while repairing the organ with gene therapy. We will be able to evaluate the lung function in the perfusion system to document improved lung function and confirm that after transplantation. The consequent improvement in the quality of donor lungs with ex-vivo repair will have a significant impact on the number of transplants performed each year and on the outcome after lung transplantation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of neuronal aging and neurodegeneration: an examination of the roles of oxidative stress and mitochondrial trafficking.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; MITOCHONDRIA; NEURONS; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: In aging neurons, mitochondria are a source of, and target for oxidative stress. It has been proposed that disruption of mitochondrial trafficking may play a role in the generation or exacerbation of neuronal injury.  Impairment of mitochondrial trafficking may compromise a neuron's ability to deliver energy to regions of metabolic demand.  Preliminary studies have shown that the generation of reactive oxygen species can disrupt mitochondrial trafficking; however a linkage between impairment of mitochondrial trafficking and the aging process has not been established. Therefore, using a novel model of neuronal aging, we will examine the hypothesis that progressive oxidative stress mediated disruption of mitochondrial trafficking is a factor in aging. Through this study, we hope to gain a greater understanding of the neurobiology of aging, by examining the roles of, and relationship between oxidative stress and mitochondrial dynamics in the context of aging.

Keywords-MotsClés: FRACTURE HEALING; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL; TIBIA; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: While results of a number of small randomized trials have suggested that therapeutic ultrasound may improve fracture healing, their findings are not definitive, and the therapy remains controversial.  We therefore propose a study of 500 patients to determine the effect of low-intensity, pulsed ultrasound on functional outcomes following operatively treated tibial shaft fractures in skeletally mature adults at least 18 years of age. This study has the potential to resolve the role of therapeutic ultrasound in healing of the most common long bone fracture, the tibia, an issue that has remained unresolved for over five decades.  If therapeutic ultrasound does significantly reduce time spent disabled following tibia fracture the socioeconomic benefits would prove substantial.

TitreApplicationTitle: Eating disturbances, depression and medical complications in girls and women with type 1 Diabetes: 8 and 10 year follow-up
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; BULIMIA NERVOSA; DIABETES-RELATED MEDICAL COMPLICATIONS; EATING DISORDERS; FEMALE DEVELOPMENT; LONGITUDINAL STUDY.
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (DM) is a common chronic condition of childhood and adolescence.  Our research has shown that eating disorders are more common in pre-teen and teenage girls with DM than in their non-diabetic peers, and some early risk factors, including higher BMI, lower self-esteem and disturbed maternal eating attitudes, are beginning to emerge from this in-progress longitudinal study.  Eating disorders add to the health consequences of DM by worsening blood sugar control and increasing the risk of serious DM-related medical complications.  This can impose a tremendous burden, both in terms of human suffering and of increased health care utilization.  There is an urgent need to identify risk factors that predict the development of eating disorders in this high-risk group, and to better understand their long-term course and progression.  This 10-year longitudinal study is following girls with DM from the pre-teen years to young adulthood, to determine risk factors and progression of eating disorders, the relationship of eating disorders to depression, and the associated long-term medical complications in this high-risk group.  This study will help in developing prevention and intervention strategies aimed at treating eating disorders, improving quality of life, and diminishing the risk of serious long-term DM-related medical complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting hyperapoB100 versus hypercholesterolemia to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes in obese subjects; mechanism of action
Keywords-MotsClés: FATTY ACID TRAPPING (OXIDATION/STORAGE OF 13C-FATTY MEAL); INFLAMMATION (IN SERUM AND ADIPOSE TISSUE); INSULIN SENSITIVTY (CLAMP); LIPIDS & APOB-LIPOPROTEINS (LDL SIZE; NUMBER & OXIDATION); RANDOMIZED INTERVENTIONS/ GROUP: DIET OR STATIN (24WKS)+ F/U; RCT GROUPS: HIGH SERUM APOB VS NORMAL APOB OBESE; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Type 2 diabetes results in the yearly death of ~ 40,000 Canadians. Some obese subjects have higher risk for diabetes than others do & my research will examine why. The risk for type 2 diabetes in obese subjects increases in the presence of resistance of the body to insulin action (or reduced insulin sensitivity) which leads to increased blood sugar & diabetes. I believe that insulin resistance is promoted by the elevated numbers of the atherogenic particles that carries cholesterol in the blood (like LDL) rather than by elevated cholesterol alone. Accordingly obese subjects with elevated particle numbers have higher risk for developing type 2 diabetes than those with elevated cholesterol & normal particle numbers.   Methods: I will recruit obese subjects without diabetes or chronic disease (>45 years). Subjects with high particle numbers will be compared to subjects with normal particle numbers & high blood cholesterol (64 subjects/ group) at 1) at baseline, 2) before & after 6-months of intervention with either low calorie diet to reduce weight by 10%, or statin therapy to reduce the particle numbers & cholesterol, and 3) before & after withdrawal of interventions. Mechanisms examined to explain the differences in insulin sensitivity between the 2 groups are; fat oxidation & storage, inflammation, blood atherogenic particles & genes affecting metabolism. I expect that compared to subjects with normal particle number, obese subjects with high particle numbers have 1) lower insulin sensitivity at baseline, 2) greater decrease in particle numbers & increase in insulin sensitise after diet or statin interventions and 3) greater increase in particle numbers & decrease in insulin sensitivity after withdrawal of statin    Significance: My study will identify obese subjects with high atherogenic particle number as a high-risk group to develop type 2 diabetes & will demonstrate that targeted treatment of these subjects may aid in the prevention of diabetes

TitreApplicationTitle: Colorectal cancer: Distress, couple dynamics, and psychological adjustment
Keywords-MotsClés: COLORECTAL CANCER; COUPLES; GENDER DIFFERENCES; POSTTRAUMATIC GROWTH; PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer is the third most common type of new cancer cases and second most common cause of cancer-related deaths for both men and women. In 2007 alone, 20,800 Canadians are expected to develop colorectal cancer. Colorectal cancer affects individuals in myriad ways; patients report that it brings changes to their physical, psychological, and social functioning. Cancer survivors report that coping with these changes is not just an individual matter, but also an interpersonal concern. It is widely accepted that social support plays an important role in reducing psychological distress (PD) for both cancer patients and their caregiving partners. Despite the potential for cancer to create suffering and stress, cancer can also generate positive, transformative experiences. Posttraumatic growth (PTG), defined as positive life changes that result from having cancer, appears to occur in the context of meaningful relationships, such as the couple. Relationship dynamics may play an important role in whether couples expereince PD or PTG.   However, the impact of negative and positive relationship dynamics on the subsequent development of PD and PTG has been largely ignored in colorectal cancer patients and their caregiving partners. Furthermore, research is severely lacking on potential gender differences in couple's relationship dynamics for cancers diagnosed in both men and women, such as colorectal cancer. The proposed research will examine these issues in a sample of 100 newly diagnosed colorectal cancer patients and their partners. The primary aim of this study is to examine the contribution of relationship dynamics to the development of PD and PTG in colorectal cancer patients and their partners. Additionally, an important aim of this research is to examine the degree to which gender (being male or female) has an effect on the association of couple's relationship dynamics, PD and PTG in couples, where one partner has been diagnosed with colorectal cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assembly and Trafficking of Homo- or Heterodimers of Chemokine HIV Co-Receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: BRET; G PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTOR; IMAGING; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; SIGNALING SPECIFICITY; TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: The past decade has witnessed extraordinary advancements in the therapy of HIV infections. Despite the undeniable efficacy of anti-HIV therapies, important limitations arise including emergence and transmission of multi-resistant strains and difficulties with side effects. HIV infection occurs via the attachment of the virus on cell surface receptors, particularly CD4, CXCR4 or CCR5. But as for most cell surface receptors, very little is known regarding the method used by the receptor to travel inside the cell after their synthesis. The first question we want to answer is where are the different components of HIV receptors assembled inside the cell? Defining the exact composition of the proteins forming HIV receptors is certainly key to develop an appropriate therapy. Other questions arise from this: Is there any influence of other proteins on the trafficking route used by receptors to be functional? Is there any specific partners that are found in certain signaling complexes and not others? And if there are some, can we target them for new and more specific therapies? These are the questions this Research Proposal want to answer, to understand the basic mechanisms leading to the formation of HIV receptors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the effectiveness of antiretroviral therapy in preventing heterosexual transmission of HIV among HIV sero-discordant couples in Eastern Uganda
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; COUNSELLING; HIV TRANSMISSION; RISK REDUCTION; SERO-DISCORDANT COUPLES; SEXUAL BEHAVIOUR
Abstract-Résumé: While HIV prevalence in Uganda has fallen dramatically since the early 1990's, it remains unacceptably high with 7.3% of adult women and 6.3% of adult men infected in 2005. There is concern that HIV incidence has remained largely unchanged in Uganda over the last decade and indeed may be on the increase. In this setting, antiretroviral therapy (ART)has become increasingly available in Uganda, beginning in 2003.  Uganda is still only treating about 8% of the total HIV infected population in the country.  Recently, the largely unrecognized value of ART in preventing new HIV infections in industrialized countries has been highlighted with population-based studies. However, the estimates of the added preventive value of ART in sub-Saharan are limited by the lack of data on the effectiveness of ART in reducing HIV transmission through heterosexual contact.  In theory HAART, should be highly effective in reducing heterosexual transmission as the risk HIV transmission is very dependant on the level of HIV in and infected individuals blood.  However, only two studies, have derived estimates for the effectiveness on reducing ART. We propose to conduct an observational study of two groups of HIV sero-discordant, co-habiting heterosexual couples; one group where the HIV positive partner is on ART because of meeting clinical or laboratory eligibility requirements and the second group will be composed of individuals where the infected partner is not ART eligible.  We propose to conduct this study among clients of The AIDS Support Organization in Mbale and Soroti districts in Eastern Uganda.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing capacity for knowledge translation: Identifying and evaluating factors that improve the effectiveness of practice guideline implementation
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; RANDOMIZED TRIAL; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Practice guidelines summarize available research and describe how health care services should be delivered. They can improve health care outcomes but are not consistently implemented or used. There may be multiple reasons why this occurs. Responsibility for implementation may not be clearly designated or prompted with incentives, and it is time-consuming and costly. Implementation is a five-step process: creating actionable messages, assessing user environment, tailoring of implementation strategy, use of a credible messenger, and evaluation of the impact. Guideline developers may lack knowledge of, or guidance on how to undertake this process. It is not known whether various messengers are used, or how they could best contribute to more thorough guideline implementation. This study will examine whether, and how these factors influence guideline implementation by interviewing representatives from three Ontario programs producing or endorsing guidelines for: 1) depression, diabetes, 18-month well baby visit, palliative care; 2) cancer treatment; and 3) prevention of surgical site infections. We will also review the research literature to understand how much direction is currently available in guidelines and instructional manuals, and how other groups have used messengers to assist with guideline implementation. For modifiable implementation processes (directions within guidelines, engaging different individuals) we will evaluate their effectiveness and cost by measuring the short- and long-term impact of implementing a particular guideline. No previous study has investigated the many factors that may be influencing the process of guideline implementation, particularly in the Canadian setting, for a range of different guidelines, and according to how various individuals are engaged in the process. This will generate recommendations to improve the way that guidelines are applied and used.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examination of prognostication, end-of-life decision-making and organ donation after cardiocirculatory death in severely brain-injured pediatric patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICS; NEUROCRITICAL CARE; PEDIATRIC ORGAN DONATION; PROGNOSIS; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Independently of patient characteristics, physician characteristics such as specialty and subspecialty, age, experience, religion and practice setting have been shown to influence end-of-life care in the intensive care unit (ICU). This variability creates challenges for the rigorous and systematic approach needed with the recent acceptance in Canada of organ donation after cardiocirculatory death (DCD).  Within end-of-life decision-making and DCD, establishing a sound prognosis is medically crucial but often extremely challenging. This vexing problem is less well documented and defined in the literature for the severely brain-injured population and for the pediatric population. However, prognostication is fundamental in the care of severely brain-injured pediatric patients given that patient preferences are often indirectly articulated by a proxy decision-maker, that severe brain injury can lead to life-long impairments and that emerging practices of DCD directly touch brain-injured patients and their families. Aims: Examining prognostication in end-of-life decision-making in the pediatric DCD context  With Canadian DCD practices emerging, there is a need for a clear assessment of physician prognostication and variability in the severely brain-injured pediatric population. This study will: 1.Identify prognostication practices and assess quantitative variability based on physician characteristics regarding end-of-life decision-making for severely  brain-injured pediatric patients in the context of DCD; 2. Identify and define qualitative variability in language used by physicians for prognostication and end-of-life decision-making for severely  brain-injured pediatric patients in the context of DCD; 3. Make recommendations on ethical prognostication and DCD for severely brain-injured pediatric patients based on the results of this research, literature reviews and an interdisciplinary workshop.

TitreApplicationTitle: Can Fish Oil a Day Keep Depression Away?  The Effectiveness of Fish Oil in Preventing Postpartum Depression in Mothers at High Risk.
Keywords-MotsClés: HISTORY OF DEPRESSION IN MOTHERS; OMEGA 3 FATTY ACIDS; PREGNANCY AND POSTPARTUM; PREVENTION OF POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION; RCT; REPRODUCTIVE RELATED MOOD DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a common and recurring illness.  Its symptoms are serious with both immediate and future consequences not only for the mother but also for her infant and her family.  Unfortunately most women who experience PPD do not seek professional help; for those that do, the available treatment options are not supported by extensive research evidence.  Whether PPD can be prevented is an important public health question but to date, no specific biological or non-biological preventative interventions can be strongly recommended for clinical practice.  Omega-3 fatty acids (fish oil) are nutritional compounds with established health benefits.  Several lines of research have linked omega-3 fatty acids (omega-3) and PPD.  Although it has already been recommended that perinatal women consume an adequate intake of omega-3 to potentially prevent PPD, there is a lack of research evidence - a significant gap in the mental health field.  The proposed research is a multi site double blind randomized controlled trial to determine the effectiveness of omega-3 in preventing depression during the first 24 weeks postpartum in women with a history of depression.  Participants will be equally randomized to either omega-3 or placebo at 18 weeks of pregnancy and will take the study capsules daily.  Research personnel will telephone all the women over the course of their pregnancy and post delivery to determine depressive symptoms and other variables of interest.  Participants will be take the study capsules until they become clinically depressed or up to the first 24 weeks post-delivery.  Investigating whether omega 3 fatty acids can prevent PPD is particularly attractive because unlike other biological interventions available for PPD, omega-3 supplementation has beneficial effects on many levels for both the mother and her child.  The results from this trial can alter clinical practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the folate status of Canadian women of childbearing age: An analysis of the Canadian Health Measures Survey (CHMS) to assess and guide folate recommendations.
Keywords-MotsClés: FOLATE STATUS                  REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH; FOLIC ACID                      WOMEN OF CHILDBEARING AGE; NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS       CANADIAN HEALTH MEASURES SURVEY; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Adequate nutrition during pregnancy is important for the health of both mother and child. Folate deficiency is a common women¿s health problem that may lead to neural tube defects (NTDs) such as spina bifida. Folic acid supplements of 0.4 mg/d are recommended for women of childbearing age in Canada, in addition to folate-rich foods, such as fortified grain products. A higher dose folic acid supplement of 5 mg/d is recommended for women at risk for NTD birth, for example, women with a family history of NTD. Some medical practitioners argue, however, that all women of childbearing age need higher dose folic acid supplements, regardless of risk factors. The necessity and practicality of these higher doses are not yet fully understood. Research is needed to better examine the folate status of Canadian women and their intake of folate-rich foods and supplements.   For the first time, a national survey is being conducted that includes direct measures of folate status in Canadian women. Statistics Canada¿s Canadian Health Measures Survey (CHMS) is collecting health data from 5000 Canadians, aged 6 to 79 years, from spring 2007 to spring 2009.  The CHMS will provide a rich source of data on women¿s health, including direct measures of folate status. This research will investigate the CHMS data to better understand the factors surrounding folate recommendations, and whether the folate needs of Canadian women are being met. Canadian women¿s intake of folate-rich foods, supplement intake, pre-existing health conditions and measures of red blood cell folate will be examined.  Comparisons will be made to international data to explore these factors in relation to other countries. The results of this research will inform nutrition policies and contribute to improving the health of women and children.

TitreApplicationTitle: How stress alters memory formation, reconsolidation and forgetting
Keywords-MotsClés: EXTINCTION; FORGETTING; MEMORY FORMATION; RECONSOLIDATION; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: We all know what happens when we are stressed out. We forget things or we keep remembering things we really do not care to remember. How does this happen. This proposal will study at the level of individual neurons how stressful events alter memory formation. We will show that sometimes stress makes a memory better. This may or may not be a good thing. We will also study why a stressful event can cause forgetting of a previous event. Finally, we will attempt to uncover at the cellular level the biological basis of post traumatic stress syndrome. All of these experiments will be performed on an invertebrate model system developed in my laboratory over the past 15 years. This system is applicable to human research because nature is conservative and what works in less complicated brains appears to work in a similar manner in our brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: A global view of host cell manipulation by Salmonella
Keywords-MotsClés: HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; PHOSPHOPROTEOMICS; SALMONELLA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; UBIQUITIN-PROTEASOME SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Salmonella bacteria reside in the intestinal tracts of livestock or wild animals and can be transmitted to humans via contaminated food or water to cause typhoid fever and diarrhea, which pose major health problems throughout the world. White blood cells can normally destroy invading microorganisms by engulfing them and then delivering destructive enzymes that kill the bacteria. This part of our innate immune system is one of the primary lines of defense against invading pathogens but Salmonella species have evolved mechanisms to avoid this destruction; the bacteria is able to get into other cell types on its own, such as the cells lining our intestines, where it can halt the delivery of the destructive enzymes, allowing the bacteria to live and multiply within the cell. Ultimately the bacteria can either cause food poisoning-like symptoms from inside these cells or it can escape the confines of the cell and spread throughout the body to cause typhoid fever. The work proposed here focuses on trying to understand, from a broad view, how Salmonella is able to so efficiently control its host cells.Previous work from many other laboratories has made significant progress in understanding some aspects of this process but we aim to apply some cutting edge technology that we have had a role in developing in order to take a step backwards and ask: What is going on in the cell as a whole? As our group has led some of the technology development and also has significant background in the biological aspects of this problem, we have a unique ability to contribute to the overall picture of how this important pathogen affects us.The anticipated benefit of this work will be a much better understanding of how pathogens such as Salmonella are able to bypass our immune system. Such knowledge will allow us to make a more rational approach to drug design and therapies since we will be able to target specific processes unique to Salmonella.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bacterial complex II homologs as models for mitochondrial electron transfer
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL MEMBRANE; ELECTRON PARAMAGNETIC; FUMARATE REDUCTASE; HEREDITARY PARAGANGLIOMA; RAPID REACTION KINETICS; REACTIVE OXYGEN
Abstract-Résumé: Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), also called Complex II, is a key enzyme in all cells that can utilize oxygen for growth. The enzyme has two essential functions: It participates both in carbon metabolism and the respiratory chain in which the energy of the food we eat is converted to adenosine triphosphate  (ATP) the energy currency of the cell. Importantly, the amino acid sequence and the structure of the enzyme are highly conserved from simple bacteria to humans. In bacteria, the enzyme is localized to the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane. In higher organisms, it is found in the mitochondrial inner membrane. The enzyme is composed of four different protein subunits which form the scaffold for an electron transfer relay of cofactors within the protein. In recent years, it has been found that specific amino acid mutations in the relay scaffold can result in tumors referred to as pheocytomas and paragangliomas. We have developed methods to express and purify large quantities of SDH from the bacterium Escherichia coli suitable for biochemical and biophysical study of the electron transfer relay as it is not possible to isolate the eukaryotic enzyme in sufficient quantity for study. We use site-directed mutagenesis to create mutations in the electron transfer relay which mimic human variations in order to learn how altered enzymes can result in tumors.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Psychobiology of Caregiving for a Spouse with Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREGIVING; CHRONIC STRESS; CORTISOL; DEPRESSION; INFLAMMATION; PSYCHONEUROIMMUNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Caring for a family member with a chronic illness is a demanding experience. Research indicates that caregiving not only diminishes the quality of peoples' lives, but it also increases their vulnerability to various mental and physical illnesses. Despite these powerful consequences, little is known about the mechanisms through which caregiving 'gets inside the body' to influence disease, or the coping strategies and personal resources that enable some to thrive under these demanding conditions, while others succumb to distress and illness. The goals of this research project are (1) to document the psychological and biological consequences of caring for a family member who is being treated for a serious and disabling medical illness like cancer, and (2) to identify personal resources and coping strategies that enable caregivers to manage this demanding experience successfully.  We will study 120 adults who are caring for a family member with brain cancer, and 60 control subjects whose family members are in good health. The subjects will be assessed four times over a one-year period to evaluate their psychological functioning, the status of their immune systems, and how at risk they are for serious medical problems like diabetes and heart disease. The data culled from this project will be used in the long-term to develop preventive interventions that can facilitate caregivers~ adjustment to these demanding circumstances.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention d'équipe - Réseaux de recherche clinique
TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Familial Risks of Breast Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER SUSCEPTIBILITY; CANCER RISK PREDICTION MODELS; ETHICAL AND LEGAL ISSUES; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; KNOWLEDGETRANSFER AND IMPLEMENTATION; PSYCHOSOCIAL; RISK COMMUNICATION
Abstract-Résumé: The overarching goal of this integrated team grant program is to  thoroughly evaluate the prediction of breast cancer risk and its  communication to individuals with a family history of breast  cancer. The 4 components of the proposed program are  designed: 1) To determine the contribution of uncommon or rare  intermediate-risk variants in selected candidate genes to the  genetic population attributable fraction and the familial relative  risk of breast cancer, and to assess the robustness of their risk  in women ascertained through clinic-based and population- based studies. 2) To improve estimation of breast and ovarian  cancer risks associated with mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2  genes by identifying the genetic and environmental modifiers  that may influence these risks. 3) To integrate the knowledge on  newly identified genetic and environmental factors, as well as  biologic markers, in breast cancer risk prediction models  providing individual risk estimates. 4) To assess communication  of risk prediction information by health professionals and the  impact of such information on women at moderate to high risk  of the disease. We expect this program to identify specific  genetic factors contributing to breast cancer susceptibility, in  particular yet poorly explored uncommon or rare intermediate- risk variants that potentially explain a significant proportion of  the missing familial risk of breast cancer. Some of these could  enter clinical cancer genetics practice in the foreseeable future.

Abstract-Résumé: . . Many of the drugs that are commonly used to treat inflammatory disorders, such as arthritis, can cause ulcers and bleeding in the stomach and small intestine.  These can be painful for the patient and can lead to significant bleeding requiring hospitalization.  In the past decade, new anti-inflammatory drugs have been brought onto the market claiming to be much safer than older drugs.  However, these claims have largely turned out to be unsubstantiated, and 3 of these new drugs (COX-2 inhibitors) have now been withdrawn from the Canadian (and other) marketplace.  The research proposed in this application is aimed at determining why existing anti-inflammatory drugs cause ulcers to develop in the stomach and intestine.  We will then use that knowledge to develop much more safe and effective anti-inflammatory drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ageing of the vascular endothelium
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE-RELATED ENDOTHELIAL DYSFUNCTION; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; MOUSE MODEL OF HUMAN DYSLIPIDEMIA; PATIENT'S ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; STRESS-INDUCED PREMATURE SENESCENCE; TELOMERE-DEPENDENT REPLICATIVE SENESCENCE
Abstract-Résumé: The inner layer of cells that are in contact with the blood are called the endothelial cell and constitute the endothelium. The function of the endothelium is important because it dilate the arteries to allows more blood to feed the organs, prevents blood clotting, is the first barrier against foreign organisms such as bacterias and viruses and regulates the diffusion of nutrients from the blood to the organs. With ageing, this function declines and favours plaque formation that close arteries inducing a heart attack if this artery feed the heart. Increase in cholesterol, high blood pressure, smoking or high sugar, all these increase the risk of heart attack and I beleive this is through an acceleration of the ageing of the endothelium. The aim of this project is validate this hypothesis and the mechanisms by which this occurs. We could then develop strategies to protect the endothelium and slows this abnormal ageing process that lead to premature heart attack.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Poxvirus Control of Ubiquitination
Keywords-MotsClés: BTB/KELCH; F BOX PROTEIN; POXVIRUS; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: The degradation of proteins is necessary for the proper regulation of many cellular processes. Significantly, alterations in protein degradation have been linked to a number of human diseases including cancer. Proteins can be marked for degradation by the addition of a small protein called ubiquitin, this process is essential for the normal function of healthy cells. Given the importance of regulated protein degradation, many viruses regulate protein degradation to their own advantage. We have recently found that poxvirus infection ultimately influences the fate of cellular proteins by exploiting the ubiquitin system. Understanding how viral proteins modulate protein degradation will provide clues regarding regulation of protein degradation and the future development of therapeutic interventions.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation and function of circadian clocks in the limbic forebrain
Keywords-MotsClés: CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; CLOCK GENES; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; LIMBIC FOREBRAIN; MICROSCOPY; RNAI
Abstract-Résumé: Circadian clocks are present in all living organisms.  They control the temporal organization of biological processes necessary for adaptation to the environment.  In humans, circadian rhythmicity is required for physical health and psychological well being.  Disorders of circadian rhythms have been linked to physiological and psychological disturbances associated with shift-work, air travel across time zones, aging, depression, and Alzheimer's disease (for example, disorders of sleep and mood, cognitive disturbances, decreased vigilance, anorexia). Despite growing interest in the role of circadian rhythms in health and disease, and accumulating knowledge about the molecular and cellular bases of circadian rhythmicity, fundamental questions concerning the neurobiological mechanisms that regulate circadian rhythms remain. Mammalian circadian rhythms are believed to be regulated by a system of internal clocks in which a master brain pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, synchronizes, or entrains, networks of subordinate clocks in the rest of the brain and periphery that control specific behavioral and physiological rhythmic outputs.  We recently discovered novel clocks in several nuclei of the rat limbic forebrain that play important roles in the regulation of motivational and emotional state.  This finding provided a way to study how the master clock controls rhythmicity within regions of the brain that influence motivated behavior and emotional state as well as suggested a mechanism by which motivational events and emotional states can affect circadian rhythms directly, downstream from the master clock.  The aim of this proposal is to study further how the novel clocks that we discovered in the limbic forebrain are affected by conditions that disrupt behavioral state, such as restricted feeding and exposure to drugs of abuse, and how disruptions of clocks within select limbic forebrain nuclei affect physiology and behavior.
