TitreApplicationTitle: Selection and validation of target genes implicated in the clinical and biological features of ovarian cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER ETIOLOGY; CLINCAL CORRELATES; GENE EXPRESSION; MODEL SYSTEM; MOLECULAR ONCOLOGY; OVARIAN CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: In women, ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related deaths in North America and the second most common gynecological cancer. Early detection of ovarian cancer is rare and screening programs in the general population have for the most part been unsuccessful. Largely asymptomatic, over 70% of patients with ovarian cancer are diagnosed at an advanced stage of the disease. Despite various modifications in the treatment regimen, minimal improvements in survival have been achieved over the last three decades. The high rate of recurrence and mortality of this disease underscores the need for a greater understanding of the molecular basis of the disease and the subsequent development of new clinical tools for both detection and management of the ovarian cancer patient. We have assembled a multi-disciplinary team, and using new high-throughput genomic approaches, we have created a research program whose ultimate goals are twofold:  the identification of new diagnostic and prognostic markers for ovarian cancer and the identification of new therapeutic targets for the management of this disease. In this proposal we will continue to identify possible interesting target genes, we will validate their expression in normal and diseased ovarian tissues, and we will correlate their expression to clinical parameters. Finally, we will address whether any of these candidates play a role in the initiation or development of ovarian cancer. This research builds on the strong models we have generated, on an extensive infrastructure between the laboratory and the clinic, and the molecular analysis of the disease we have already undertaken and leaves us poised to impact significantly on the study of ovarian cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of phosphatidylinositol-3 kinase (PI3K) coupled signaling pathways in mammary tumorigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SURVIVAL; LIPID PHOSPHORYLATION; MAMMARY TUMORS; METASTASIS; MUTATION; TRANSGENIC
Abstract-Résumé: The progression of a primary mammary epithelial cell to the malignant phenotype is thought to involve multiple genetic events including the activation of dominant acting oncogenes and the loss of specific tumor suppressor genes. The principle objective of this proposal is to elucidate the role of oncogene known as PI-3K in breast cancer progression. The first experimental aim will investigate whether of an activated form PI-3K is directly involved in induction of mammary tumors. To accomplish this, we will establish whether expression of this activated PI-3K in the mammary gland of mice is capable of inducing mammary tumors. Conversely, we will assess whether loss of PI-3K function interferes with mammary tumour induction. The results of these studies will provide important insight into the role of PI-3K in mammary tumor induction and progression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Carbohydrate-recognition in bacterial pathogenesis: structural and functional analysis of virulence-associated Clostridium perfringens enzymes.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARBOHYDRATE BINDING; GLYCOSIDE HYDROLASE; MICROBIAL PATHOGENESIS; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; SMALL-ANGLE X-RAY SCATTERING; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Clostridium perfringens is the most widely distributed pathogen in Nature. It can cause deadly diseases, such as gas gangrene, meningitis, and necrotising enteritis, but more commonly causes gastroenteritis. It is one of the World's leading causes of gastrointestinal disease (in the top 3) and a leading cause of death from food borne illness. Though exactly how this bacterium causes disease is not entirely understood, it is clear that its battery of toxins play an important role in making us sick. Among these toxins are proteins that interact with and modify the carbohdyrates present in our tissues. How the relatively large number of C. perfringens carbohydrate-active enzymes work has not been well studied and is the focus of this proposal. In general, this work will lead to a better understanding of how C. perfringens causes disease and perhaps inform new approaches to developing therapeutic agents to treat illnesses caused by this germ.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lymphocyte Proteinases
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CYTOTOXIC T LYMPHOCYTES; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; PROTEINASES
Abstract-Résumé: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes protect us against a wide variety of virus and tumours. When their activities are unchecked they can lead to the destruction of healthy tissues in autoimmune diseases and upon transplant rejection. Our research program aims to determine, at the molecular level, how these important cells work. We will employ a variety of biochemical, genetic and immunologic techniques to achieve this goal. The knowledge gained will allow the design of drugs that might enhance or inhibit the activities of CTL. Such drugs will be useful in suppression of autoimmunity and transplant rejection, and immunotherapy for infectious diseases and cancer.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE; MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS
TitreApplicationTitle: Nuclear signaling in human neutrophils
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CHEMOKINES; GOUT; INFLAMMATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Arthritis is one of the most prevalent chronic inflammatory disorders in North America, and is affecting over 4 million people in Canada alone. It is characterized by a chronic inflammation of the joints and a progressive destruction of cartilage and bone. One of the distinctive features of arthritic joints is their massive infiltration by white blood cells, and in particular neutrophils. The latter have been proposed as a source of several inflammatory mediators (including cytokines and chemokines) that are present at high levels inside inflamed joints. A recent study, which found that neutrophils are indeed essential to the initiation of arthritis in a murine model, strongly supports this view.   In this proposal, we will focus our efforts on a cellular signaling pathway that controls the production of chemokines by neutrophils in response to inflammatory biochemicals in the micro-environment. This pathway (the IKK/NF-kB cascade) has many unique features in neutrophils, and we aim to identify key regulators of this pathway that can be exploited for future therapeutic intervention. There is indeed increasing evidence for a link between dysregulated signaling cascades and a number of inflammatory disorders, and some new drugs targeting specific signaling intermediates are already under development. Accordingly, we believe that strategies such as the ones we propose herein have the potential to reap important benefits for the health of Canadians, and in particular ageing citizens.

TitreApplicationTitle: Timing of Surgery for Crossed Eyes in Infancy: A Clinical Evaluation of Sensory and Motor Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: INFANTILE ESOTROPIA; MOTION PERCEPTION; MOTION VEP; OPTOKINETIC NYSTAGMUS; STEREOPSIS; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Infantile esotropia (crossed eyes in infancy) is a common health problem among children. While there is uniform agreement among pediatric ophthalmologists that infantile esotropia requires surgical correction, the proper timing of surgery is controversial. In North America, the typical age at surgery ranges from 11-18 months. Despite surgery, a number of visual abnormalities, including subnormal three-dimensional depth perception and abnormal eye movements, often persist. Although a few studies have reported favourable outcomes after early surgery, no study has been performed to evaluate the effects of early (at or before 11 months) versus standard surgery (11-18 months) on a number of visual and eye movement functions that are important for daily activities. The goal of this study is to determine the age at which surgery can prevent the maldevelopment of visual deficits typically associated with infantile esotropia. We will measure visual motion processing by the brain, three-dimensional depth perception, visual following eye movements, and motion perception in children who have early versus standard surgery. The proposed study will help establish clinical guidelines for the ultimate timing of surgery for infantile esotropia, which is a critical issue that is hotly contested in the pediatric ophthalmic community.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: Memory TH2 cell responses during helminth infection
Keywords-MotsClés: CD4 T CELLS; GASTROINTESTINAL; GUT HOMING; HELMINTH INFECTION; IMMUNOLOGICAL MEMORY; RETINOIC ACID
Abstract-Résumé: An estimated two billion people worldwide are infected with soil-transmitted helminth parasites. Field and experimental studies have shown that immunity in infected individuals is associated with expression of T helper type 2 (TH2) cytokines, the same family of proteins that are over-expressed in asthma, allergies and some forms of inflammatory bowel disease. Although there is strong evidence that there is resistance to re-infection, it is unclear how this 'immunological memory' develops nor how it works. The goals of this proposal are to understand how the immune system remembers helminth parasites and to employ this knowledge to design successful anti-helminth vaccines. At the same time, this information will be extremely useful in the development of new therapies that treat diseases caused by dysregulated TH2 cells. Thus, the results of these studies will provide insights into the nature and function of memory TH2 cells and will be broadly applicable towards optimizing anti-parasite immunity as well as limiting inflammatory diseases caused by TH2 cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in APOBEC3G-mediated innate immunity to HIV infection
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; ANTIVIRALS; APOBEC3G; CYTIDINE DEAMINATION; HIV; INNATE IMMUNITY
Abstract-Résumé: Infection by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) can lead to a progressive deterioration of the body's immune system. AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) represents the stage when a HIV-infected individual becomes susceptible to life-threatening parasitic infections that are normally destroyed by the immune system of healthy individuals. Although HIV is capable of evading detection by the body's immune system, several factors exist nevertheless that can protect us against HIV infection. One of these endogenous antiviral factors is a protein called APOBEC3G that is part of the innate component of the human immune system. This protein can bind and heavily mutate HIV DNA, ultimately leading to the inactivation and destruction of the virus. APOBEC3G has also other very powerful, but less characterized, methods of blocking HIV infection that are tightly regulated by yet unidentified cellular factors. In most circumstances, these factors maintain APOBEC3G in an inactive state thus preventing APOBEC3G to fully deploy its potent antiviral effect on HIV. This research project will enable us to identify these factors and further our understanding on how they interact with APOBEC3G. This work will hopefully establish new therapeutic targets and contribute to the development of a new generation of molecules capable of recruiting one's own innate immune system to fight and prevent HIV infection. Regulating and recruiting the full antiviral potential of APOBEC3G could undoubtedly not only inactivate infectious HIV particles in HIV/AIDS patients but also help prevent HIV infections in high-risk individuals.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; TUMEURS
TitreApplicationTitle: Anaerobic Nucleolar Proteome Dynamics
Keywords-MotsClés: ANAEROBIC METABOLISM; ARGININE METHYLATION; EXTRACELLULAR ACIDOSIS; HYPOXIA; NUCLEOLUS; SUBCELLUAR TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Tumors of various tissue origins, such as breast, ovary or kidney occur because of mutations in very different genes.  However, cancers do shares some near-universal features including the fact that the center of tumors often lacks oxygen (termed hypoxia).  Our cells are program to produce energy exclusively from the catabolism of sugar, called glucose, in the absence of oxygen in a process that is called fermentation or anaerobic metabolism.  Yeasts produce alcohol when they ferment glucose in the absence of oxygen.  In the case of higher organisms, like humans, we produce lactic acid.  Therefore, the middle of tumors is often very acidic compared to normal tissues.   It is generally agreed upon that tumors that are hypoxic and acidic are likely to be more aggressive.  That's because cells in the middle of the tumors have been able to survive this particularly harsh environment whereas cells that did not are already dead.  My laboratory is interested in the study of this process of cellular adaptation to anaerobic metabolism.  Our group has published papers that demonstrate that cells that engage in anaerobic metabolism are able to store or hide several proteins in a cellular closet (called the nucleolus) because they do not need them, or want them, in the absence of oxygen.  We also showed that when we prevent this hiding of proteins, cells cannot survive anaerobic metabolism an die.  This proposal is to continue studying this process in the idea of preventing the aggressive cancer cells to survive in the core of tumors as a way to treat cancer.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the HIF2a Oncogenic Pathway in Human Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: EGFR; HYPOXIA; HYPOXIA INDUCIBLE FACTOR; TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT; TUMORIGENESIS; VHL
Abstract-Résumé: Project summary: The major goal is to understand why people get kidney cancer when a kidney cell losses on of its gene; the VHL tumor suppressor gene.  Our laboratory focuses more on the study of the role of different proteins that can be targeted by known drugs already in clinical trials.  Research update: We have made two recent important observations.  The first one, published in Cancer Research, is that a protein called TACE, is involved in kidney cancer.  Removing this protein from kidney cancer cells prevent these cells from making tumors.  Of interest is the fact that TACE inhibitors are readily available in clinic.  These inhibitors are used to treat patients with inflammatory diseases, such as arthritis.    We are suggesting that patients with kidney cancer undergo treatment with TACE inhibitors.  The second observation was very recently published by my group in the Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA.   It has been known for a long time that the EGFR protein, a protein involved in growth of several cancer cells (breast, ovarian, kidney etc) is very often overproduced in human cancers.  Scientists have been sequencing the EGFR gene for several years to find mutations in this gene to explain why it is often overexpressed.  Surprisingly, this gene is not often mutated in human cancer.  We showed that the tumor microenvironment, not genetic mutations, upregulates the EGFR protein in human tumors providing a non-mutational explanation for this phenomenon.    Project description: We will continue investigating the mechanisms involved in kidney cancer formation following mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene to find possible targets, such as EGFR and TACE, for therapy.  We plan to apply this knowledge to other human cancers because of our observations that what causes kidney cancer may also cause other type of cancers.  This would suggest that different tumors might share more things in common than originally thought by scientists and clinicians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Post-transcriptional gene regulation during Drosophila development
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; GENE REGULATION; GENETICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Genes can be regulated at many different levels. Best understood are the machineries that generate a messenger RNA (mRNA) copy from the DNA and then translate the information encoded in the mRNA into protein. It is well known that cells are instructed to take on distinct fates (e.g., skin, nerve cells, etc.) during development in large part through different genes being turned 'on' and 'off' in their ability to make an mRNA (and, therefore, the encoded protein). Recently it has become clear that a great deal of control is, in fact, exerted after an mRNA is made rather than just in its synthesis. For example, an mRNA may be made in two cell types but only allowed to be translated into protein in one of the two cells. Likewise the stability of an mRNA can be controlled so that it is made in both cell types but is degraded in one of the two, preventing protein production. Furthermore, the sub-cellular location of the mRNA within a cell is highly regulated and may influence whether the mRNA is stable and/or translated into protein. Defects in these post-transcriptional events lead to developmental defects as well as to disease. The machinery of post-transcriptional control is highly conserved from lower animals (e.g. the fruit fly, Drosophila) to mammals, including humans. We use the fruit fly - which is amenable to sophisticated molecular and cellular methods - to understand the role of post-transcriptional regulation in development and disease.

OrgNm: Ottawa Hospital Research Institute/Institut de recherche de l'Hôpital d'Ottawa
TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of a novel gene for brachydactyly-A1
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE DEVELOPMENT; DISEASE GENE DISCOVERY; GENETICS; LINKAGE; POSITIONAL CLONING
Abstract-Résumé: The brachydactylies are a group of rare, congenital developmental disorders that affect normal bone development and patterning resulting in shortened digits. First classified by Bell into types A, B, C, D and E, the brachydactylies were reclassified based on the bones and digits involved. The first group, Brachydactyly Type A1 (BDA1), was the first human trait described in terms of a dominant Mendelian inheritance. In 1903, as part of his PhD thesis, William C. Farabee described a large family from Pennsylvania with a hand disorder and correctly surmised that the trait was transmitted as an autosomal dominant condition. Individuals affected by the disorder were characterized by short, broad hands and overall short stature. X-rays of the hand revealed that the middle phalanges of affected individuals were either absent or severely hypoplastic. Recently, the Indian Hedgehog gene (Chromsome 2) was found to contain mutations in a subset of patients with BDA1. We have identified two new genes and a second locus at 5p13 responsible for BDA1 and our application is directed at cloning and characterizing this novel gene.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of ABCA1 and apolipoprotein E in brain lipid metabolism and amyloidogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ABC TRANSPORTERS; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; APOLIPOPROTEIN E; CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT; MOUSE MODELS; PRIMARY CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer~s Disease (AD) is a devastating illness that affects half of the population over 85 years of age. The brains of AD patients accumulate amyloid plaques, which are composed mainly of a toxic peptide called Abeta.  Recent research has shown that cholesterol, a type of fat, plays a major role in AD, particularly in the formation or removal of amyloid plaques.  My laboratory studies genes that control cholesterol in the brain and how they affect AD.  One such gene is called ABCA1, and is known to be involved in cholesterol transport.  Because cholesterol is a fat, it separates from water and does not move well in the watery bloodstream.  ABCA1 is a protein that moves cholesterol onto carrier proteins called apolipoproteins, which can then transport cholesterol through the bloodstream.  We have shown that mice that lack ABCA1 have a number of defects in brain cholesterol transport that involve apolipoprotein E (apoE), which is the major cholesterol carrier in the brain and a very well known risk factor for AD.  Mice that lack ABCA1 are unable to produce normal amounts of apoE, and the little apoE that remains does not transport cholesterol well.  Together, these defects lead to more amyloid in the brains of ABCA1-deficient mice.  We have also shown that mice with excess ABCA1 have absolutely no amyloid in their brains.  These studies demonstrate that ABCA1 is a key factor in AD. In this proposal, we propose to learn more how about ABCA1 affects apoE function to affect amyloid levels, and we will begin to determine whether drugs that increase ABCA1 can protect from AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Energy substrate metabolism in the ischemic and non-ischemic heart
Keywords-MotsClés: AMP-ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASE; FATTY ACID OXIDATION; ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE; ISOLATED WORKING HEART; MALONYL COA; MALONYL COA DECARBOXYLASE
Abstract-Résumé: The high energy demands of the heart are met by the metabolism of both sugars and fatty acids.  Normally, there is a balance between the use of these sugars and fatty acids.  However, if blood flow to the heart muscle is interrupted, termed myocardial ischemia,  oxygen supply to the heart is interrupted  and energy supply to the muscle is compromised.  If blood flow is then re-introduced to the muscle, called reperfusion, alterations in the control of energy metabolism occur, such that fatty acids dominate as a source of fuel, unfortunately at the expense of sugar use.  This excessive use of fatty acids can compromise the ability of the heart heart to recover from the myocardial ischemia insult.   We have shown that a major contributor to this excessive use of fatty acids is due to changes in the levels of a molecule called malonyl CoA that is present in heart muscle cells.  The studies proposed in this grant application will determine the cellular mechanisms responsible for how malonyl CoA levels are regulated,  and how malonyl CoA regulates fatty acid use by the mitochondria, which are the furnaces of the heart cell that burn fats and sugars to produce energy.  We will use a number of molecular, biochemical and physiological approaches to examine the importance of key proteins that regulate the levels of malonyl CoA in the heart.  We will also determine if preventing the switch from  sugar to fatty acid metabolism, by increasing malonyl CoA levels, can be used as a therapeutic strategy to protect the heart following a heart attack  or in the failing heart.  Understanding how energy metabolism is regulated in heart should lead to the development of  therapies that optimize  energy use by the  heart and protect the failing heart.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ovarian cell differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: FOLLICULOGENESIS; GENE REGULATION; GRANULOSA CELLS; LUTEINIZATION; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; OVULATION
Abstract-Résumé: The superfamily of nuclear receptors function primarily in modulating transcription of their target genes.  Many display ubiquitous distribution and they can effect multiple functions, even in a single cell type.  The steroid receptor family, in particular, the estrogen and progesterone receptors play important roles in differentiation of ovarian somatic cells, with consequences on germ cell maturation and, as a result, on fertility.  We propose to continue investigation of the process of ovarian somatic cell differentiation with a focus on the role of nuclear receptors, in particular the nuclear receptor NR5A2, also known as liver receptor homolog.  Multiple animal and cell models will be employed including the mouse model in which we have achieved granulosa cell-specific deletion of the Nr5a2 gene and phenotype of complete abrogation of the ovulation.  Using molecular and cellular tools, we will examine the consequences of Nr5a2 deletion on follicle formation, on ovulation and on the terminal differentiation of the follicular cells into the corpus luteum.  Global strategies will be employed to determine Nr5a2 target genes and these will be further investigated in the primary cultures of ovarian cells an cell lines to establish the mechanisms of nuclear receptor regulation of the ovary.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
TitreApplicationTitle: Relationship between neural activity and blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signals in the primate frontal eye fields
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL IMAGING; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; PRIMATE; SACCADE; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has been performed on human subjects for more than a decade and numerous articles have appeared in Nature, Science, Neuron and other leading journals. Surprisingly, the relationships between behavior, neural coding and functional brain imaging with fMRI are still poorly understood, leaving uncertainty over these interpretations. Furthermore, it is unlikely that neural events, which occur in complex serial and parallel pathways on the scale of milliseconds, can be completely interpreted on the basis of the static maps produced with conventional fMRI. These issues become clouded even further when fMRI studies are performed in patient populations where the underlying metabolism, biochemistry, and neuroarchitecture are disrupted by disease or trauma. It is therefore necessary to use animal models to fully understand the relationship between neural activity and fMRI as well as their relationship to behaviour. The only suitable model that allows such linkages is that of the non-human primate. Single-neuron recordings in non-human primates have provided crucial information for our current knowledge of the information processing in the primate brain. The last decade has witnessed a renaissance in the study of brain and behavior in non-human primates due to new techniques in multi-unit recording and data processing. Here we will investigate how the fMRI in the frontal cortex -  a brain region involved in many psychiatric disorders - relates to neural activity. This research has fundamentally important and far-reaching consequences. The links between subthreshold and spiking neural activity, metabolism, and behaviour can be put on firm footing " and establishing these relationships will result not only in further methodological advances in the field of functional brain imaging but also help us to interpret brain imaging data in psychiatric patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Determinants of Apoptosis in Heart
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL CULTURE; GENES; HEART FAILURE; MITOCHONDRIA; VENTRIUCLAR MYOCYTES
Abstract-Résumé: One of the most compelling issues to impact on contemporary cardiology to date is arguably  the concept of 'apoptosis'. Since ventricular myocytes have exited from the cell-cycle, loss of potentially viable cells through an apoptotic process may influence cardiac structure/function given the limited and meager capacity of the heart for repair after  injury. We plan to study the role of a gene called Bnip3 that we had cloned several years ago. We believe that Bnip3 is a key factor responsible for promoting the death of heart cells during  heart attack. Our goal is to understand the regulation and function of this gene so that we can ultimately prevent its expression and heart cell death which will disease the morbidity and mortality of patients after heart attack.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structures and Processes of Care in Colorectal Cancer Surgery (SPoCCS) Study
Keywords-MotsClés: COLORECTAL CANCER; PROCESSES OF CARE; QUALITY OF CARE; STRUCTURAL EQUATIONS MODELING; STRUCTURES OF CARE; SURGICAL ONCOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer is the second most common cause of death from cancer in Canada.  Most patients who develop colorectal cancer require surgery at some point in their illness, and the quality of surgical care they receive varies substantially. This research project is an in-depth evaluation of the quality of surgical care provided to residents of Ontario with colorectal cancer. We will use an innovative approach for the collection of information, including use of electronic health databases and cancer registries, review of medical records, hospital site visits, and field observation of surgeons in the operating room. Our proposed analysis will deconstruct the complex relationship between patient, surgeon and hospital factors that affect the outcome of surgery for colorectal cancer.  The results of our research will be immediately useful to Canadian cancer agencies and health care providers, by identifying a set of "best practices" for surgical care, and by focusing attention on those areas that should be targeted for quality improvement programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Shutting down the innate immune response: Mechanisms and  strategies utilized by human herpesvirus 6 to persist within the  infected host.
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE ACTIVATION; HERPESVIRUS 6; IMMUNE EVASION; INFECTION; INTERFERON; ISRE
Abstract-Résumé: Herpesviruses are among the most successful infectious organisms colonizing the human host. To efficiently do so, these large double stranded DNA (dsDNA) viruses manipulate the host immune system many different ways, allowing them to partly evade immune surveillance and ensure their existence within infected individuals. One of the first antiviral defense mechanisms triggered following viral infections involves the synthesis and release of alpha and/or beta interferons (IFN) by infected cells. IFNs are key antiviral molecules and not surprisingly, many viruses including herpesviruses, have countermeasures that negatively influence IFN production. This application is directed toward the identification and characterization of IFN regulation by the IE1 protein of HHV-6. In the present proposal we plan to dissect the mechanisms through which the IE1 protein causes a defect in the IFN pathway which could lead to favor HHV-6 persistence within the infected host.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aryl 2-chloroethylureas as thioredoxin and cellular redox homeostasis inhibitors: Structure-activity relationships and mechanisms of anticancer activity
Keywords-MotsClés: AMINO ACID ALKYLATION; APOPTOSIS; CANCER; CELL CYCLE; CYTOTOXICITY; DRUG DESIGN; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; MECHANISM OF ACTION; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY; PHARMACOMODULATION; RADIOLABELING; REDOX SYSTEM; SAR; THIOREDOXIN; THIOREDOXIN INHIBITION; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Modern chemotherapy is now embracing a "strategy of personalization" of cancer treatments based on genetic and biochemical differences between cancers born by different patients. However, such a strategy does not only require a better understanding of genetic and biochemical differences between normal and tumor cells. It also presupposes the development of new molecules capable of specifically and efficiently rectifying faulty biochemical mechanisms that are identified.  It is in that context that we have conducted for the last eighteen years our research program on the discovery of new small molecules capable of controlling tumor cell proliferation through new mechanisms of action. Our present proposal aims principally to achieve two main objectives. The first one is to understand how a newly discovered family of drugs modulates the biological activity of an extremely important protein named thioredoxin-1.  Thioredoxin-1 is a key element of the so-called cellular redox system. Thioredoxin is involved in numerous cellular pathways that control cell life and death.  The second objective of the proposal is to prepare a series of new drugs based on the molecular structure of our prototypical thioredoxin activity "modulator" to determine the relationships between the molecular structure of the drugs and their effects on thioredoxin-1. Our experiments are performed in view of producing a potent drug suitable for testing on animal models of cancers and eventually for clinical trials. We believe that our research program is of utmost importance to insure the availability of molecules that could synergize the curative effect of other known drugs for the treatment of cancer tumors that are still nowadays resilient to modern chemotherapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Oxygen as a Regulator of Tumour Cell Plasticity and Metastatic Potential
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; HYPOXIA; MELANOMA; METASTASIS; NODAL; STEM CELL PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Rapidly growing tumours contain many areas of low oxygen (hypoxia), and the presence of these hypoxic regions is associated with cancer metastasis and a poor clinical outcome.  In a manner similar to stem cells, sub-populations of aggressive cancer cells express embryo-associated proteins, such as Nodal, that enable them to grow forever (self-renew).  Recent studies have revealed that low oxygen levels allow stem cells to grow forever (self renew).   We propose that low oxygen levels similarly allow cancer cells to grow forever and metastasize. As such, the effects of hypoxia on the expression of stem cell-associated genes (with an emphasis on Nodal) as well as the contribution of these factors to tumour progression and metastasis will be investigated.  It is our hope that this research will uncover novel targets for the treatment and prevention of cancer progression and metastasis.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of natural killer cell contributions to the known, elevated risks for maternal and fetal pathologies in diabetic pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: DISTURBED HOMING OR ACTIVATION OF NATURAL KILLER LYMPHOCYTES; ENDOMETRIAL ANGIOGENESIS; HYPERTENSION; PREGNANCY AND PREGNANCY-INDUCED SPIRAL ARTERY MODIFICATION; QUANTITATIVE REALTIME PCR; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Pregnancy in type 1 and type 2 diabetic women carries major risks for poor fetal and maternal outcomes despite good pre-pregnancy counselling and gestational control of blood sugar and blood pressure. Although type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease that deviates lymphocyte functions, its impact on key functions of lymphocytes found in the pregnant uterus are virtually unknown. Very early in normal pregnancies, specialized lymphocytes known as uterine Natural Killer (uNK) cells, amass within implantation sites where they contribute to uterine (maternal) blood vessel growth and tissue remodelling necessary to support healthy pregnancy. We propose that diabetes limits the functional interactions between uNK cells and endothelial cells, the cells that initiate branching blood vessel growth. Further, we postulate that therapeutic promotion of uterine blood vessel growth will improve both maternal and fetal outcomes for diabetic patients. We have developed pre-clinical models that we will use to evaluate several treatment strategies. Early in pregnancy, the major implantation site arteries of women and mice change dramatically in structure and dilate. This does not occur in the acute, pregnancy-associated disease pre-eclampsia, the major disease risk for pregnant diabetic women. In 3 mouse models, we dissociated implantation site vessel structure from high blood pressure and defined 5 distinct phases of blood pressure regulation over pregnancy. We will characterize the regulatory mechanisms in each phase to aid in design of novel therapeutic agents of value in human pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure-Function Relationships of Bacterial Polysaccharide Co-Polymerases
Keywords-MotsClés: MODAL LENGTH CONTROL; MUTAGENESIS; O-ANTIGEN BIO SYNTHESIS; PROTEIN EXPRESSION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Bacterial cells have complex sugar molecules decorating their external surfaces. These molecules have important functions during infection as they can protect bacteria form being engulfed by phagocytic cells and being destroyed by host molecules and antibiotics. Bacteria make these sugar molecules by a complex process that starts in the bacterial cytoplasm and eventually results in the movement of sugar intermediates across the bacterial cell membrane, followed by additional reactions that result in the formation of a variety of complex sugar chains. These processes require special proteins that are located in the bacterial cell membrane. Blocking the formation of these sugars could represent a novel way to treat infections, but unfortunately very little is known about the mechanism of action of the proteins involved in this process. We have recently elucidated the detailed structure of one class of these proteins, which is involved in determining the length of the sugar chain. We will use this information to design experiments that will explain how these types of proteins work, with the long range goals to design inhibitors that would block the synthesis of bacterial surface sugars.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Steroidal hormone programming in heart.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS; DNA METHYLATION; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC MEASUREMENT OF HEART FUNCTION; EXPRESSION ANALYSES; GONADECTOMY AND HORMONE REPLACEMENT; HISTONE MODIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is the number one killer of women and men in the industrialized world. Women are somewhat protected from heart disease, but only until menopause. Observational studies suggested that female hormones protect the heart from damage but clinical trials indicated the opposite. Thus it is entirely unclear how female hormones affect cardiac function. Our data lead us to think that hearts are 'feminized' or 'masculinized' very early in life, that steroid hormones are required for this and that this is an active process that needs continual hormone presence to be maintained. We have identified proteins necessary for normal contraction that are targets for this feminizing and masculinzing phenomena. In our project we will manipulate the timing and amount of female and male steroid hormones and measure cardiac function and the amount of these proteins made. Our goal is to find out when and how hearts are feminized and masculinized and how this affects how the heart functions. We suspect that the steroids alter the genes without altering the gene sequence. We will use molecular biology techniques to find out how the steroid hormones are able to alter the gene or histones that attach to the gene so that hearts become or remain sex-determined. This work will provide fundamental and basic information about the role of female and male hormones in heart. These results will help us understand how and why women and men do not always develop, modulate or respond to heart disease the same.

TitreApplicationTitle: Energy Coupling in ATP Synthase
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOENERGETICS; ENERGY COUPLING; PROTEIN STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Living organisms derive usable energy by a process called oxidative phosphorylation, in which they combine the food molecules they consume with oxygen.  The energy released in this process is captured in the form of ATP, an intracellular molecule that drives muscle contraction, biosynthetic reactions, and a host of other processes that are essential to maintaining a living state.  The enzyme that makes the ATP is called ATP Synthase.  This is an ancient enzyme, present in all forms of life due to the extreme importance of energy to all types of living organisms.  Every day a human produces, and uses, his/her own body weight in ATP. The goal of this proposal is to determine how ATP synthase works to capture as much of the available energy as possible.  The multi-component enzyme has been called the "worlds smallest motor" because of its surprising mechanism, in which some components literally rotate relative to others to drive ATP formation.  Sometimes however, mutations or damage to some of the parts cause the motor to work inefficiently; that is, rotation may occur but ATP is not made.  The types of changes that cause inefficient operation are surprising, and why they have these effects is not understood.  In this project we will study the detailed aspects of how the enzyme operates to produce a healthy state, and why it is that certain changes cause loss of its efficiency.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Querying cognition and pharmacologic treatment of urinary incontinence in the elderly
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; ELDERLY; MEDICATION; URINARY INCONTINENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Urinary incontinence is a common and devastating geriatric condition with important physical, psychological and economic consequences.  Among individuals older than 50 years living in the community, incontinence affects almost 20 percent of men and 50 percent of women. Drug therapy, consisting of a growing number of acetylcholine-blocking agents, is currently prescribed to approximately one third of incontinent individuals to help relax their bladder. However, the same acetylcholine-blocking mechanism that controls unwanted contractions in the bladder forms the basis of many of the theories underlying memory loss in Alzheimer's disease patients. A number of patients on incontinence medication have experienced sudden memory problems. Surprisingly, few large studies have investigated whether bladder relaxant medications indeed affect memory and function in older individuals. The goal of this project is to systematically evaluate whether medications used to treat incontinence affect memory and function in older adults, by asking them to undergo detailed neuropsychological testing before and after they begin their therapy. We also intend to discover the most sensitive screening test for physicians to use to detect if any of their patients are at risk for having memory side effects from their incontinence treatment. In this way proper screening and prevention can be done in the future to allow patients to continue reaping the benefits of treatment for their incontinence without suffering undue harm.

ClasseRechercheFR: ASTHME; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Intracellular Mechanisms in Eosinophil Exocytosis:  Contribution to the Development of Airway Inflammation.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALPAIN; CHIMERIC MICE; CYCLIN-DEPENDENT KINASE; P35; P39; RAB27A; SEC1-MUNC PROTEINS; TRANSGENIC MICE; VAMP-2; VESICLE ASSOCIATED MEMBRANE PROTEIN-7 (VAMP-7)
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a serious disease affecting millions of sufferers in North American and Canada.  The disease is characterized by inflammation which damages the lining of the airways.  This damage is thought to be the result of release of toxic proteins generated by specialized white blood cells called eosinophils. These cells are found in large numbers in the airways of asthmatics.  Eosinophils manufacture, store and release many different proteins thought to be involved in the inflammation changes associated with this disease.  Our research programme is aimed at understanding the events inside the cell which, at a molecular level, cause the release of these mediators to the outside of the cells.  Our study will focus particularly on understanding how this secretion is regulated, especially by investigating 4 different and very important intracellular proteins that have a specialized role in delivering these nasty mediators out of the cell. Our project is aimed at characterizing these molecules and develop methods to block their effect within the cell and prevent mediator secretion.  By doing so, we can prevent the inflammation associated with asthma.  We will apply novel methods to inhibit the various molecules involved in regulating mediator secretion in genetically-modified mouse models of asthma.  The purpose is to translate our test tube data to actual disease conditions.  We are confident that such a new tratment strategy will help reduce or remove the effects of inflammation in the airways with the ultimate aim of improving the clinical condition of asthmatic sufferers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hepatic Organic Anion Transporting Polypeptide (OATP) drug uptake transporters as determinants of drug disposition
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY; DRUG DISPOSITION; DRUG TRANSPORTERS; LIVER TRANSPORTERS; PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCES; PHARMACOGENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Liver is widely known as an organ capable of breaking down (metabolism) foreign chemicals and drugs that we ingest, and then secrete such breakdown products into bile for subsequent elimination out of the body. In the past decade, remarkable progress has been made in a field called drug transporters. Specifically, we now know that the cells that make up organs such as the liver possess proteins called transporters on their cell membrane that allow drugs, foreign chemicals, hormones, and nutrients to enter or leave the cell. For many drugs that circulate in our body, a subset of drug transporters known as Organic Anion Transporting Polypeptide (OATP) found in liver cells facilitate the movement of drugs from blood into liver. The activity of these OATP transporters appears to be critical to the efficient removal of many drugs including the 'statin' class of lipid lowering drugs that millions of Canadians currently take to lower their cholesterol. Currently however, little is known regarding how these liver OATP transporters recognize drugs for uptake into liver, or the processes that govern their expression. For example, we know that people vary significantly in their ability to take up and eliminate 'statin' drugs and that in human liver samples, expressed levels of these OATP transporters markedly differ. Therefore we plan to study and create model systems in relation to liver OATP transporters to determine how these transporters recognize drugs, how we could better predict drug effects in humans by using Oatp transporter deficient mice, and then to study the factors that regulate the expression of these OATP transporters in cell based systems and also in human subjects. It is expected that our findings will provide important new insights to how drugs are taken up by the liver, mechanisms of drug-drug interactions, and better prediction of drug response based on genetic makeup of an individual and thereby further enable the emerging field of personalized medicine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of the Interplay Between Histone MTases, DNA Methylation and Proviral Silencing
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; COVALENT HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; DNA METHYLATION; ENDOGENOUS RETROVIRUSES; SODIUM BISULPHITE SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Normally, cells in the body grow, divide, and die in an orderly manner. Although there are many kinds of cancer, all develop when cells begin to divide abnormally. DNA is the material in every cell that directs all of its functions, the genetic blueprint of life. Tumor-suppressor genes are a subset of genes that encode the proteins that regulate cell growth. Mutation of the genes encoding these proteins leads to the development of cancer. In many cancer cells, these proteins are no longer produced, not because the genes that encode them have become mutated, but rather because the genes that encode them have been shut-off. This process frequently involves a specific chemical change in the DNA of these genes called methylation. Paradoxically, coincident with the methylation of tumor-suppressor genes, most of the genome in tumor cells, including vestigial "endogenous" viruses, becomes demethylated. The underlying cause of these alterations in DNA methylation patterns remains a mystery. The aim of this proposal is to characterize the underlying mechanism(s)/biochemical pathway(s) leading to DNA methylation of the genome in normal cells, using the mouse as a model system. Knowledge gained from this work may lead to the development of pharmaceuticals that counteract or inhibit aberrant DNA methylation observed not only in cancer, but in other diseases as well, such as Fragile X, ICF and ATRX syndromes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adversity and Resilience among early teens: What predicts positive outcomes in later adolescence?
Keywords-MotsClés: (CROSS) CULTURAL RESEARCH; MEASUREMENT DESIGN AND VALIDATION; MULTIPLE SERVICE USE PATTERNS; POSITIVE YOUTH DEVELOPMENT; RESILIENCE; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: This research extends the work of a three-year National Crime Prevention Centre study. It will tell us more about how to effectively measure resilience among high-risk youth across French, English and Aboriginal communities. We are particularly interested in understanding how adolescents achieve outcomes like a sense of citizenship, healthy family relationships and commitment to education. This research will help both policy makers and front-line human services workers understand the pathways to well-being among diverse populations of young people. Because the study focuses on different cultures and contexts, it will position Canada as a world leader in the study of resilience as a culturally-embedded concept.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering a novel ubiquitin-dependent signaling pathway during the DNA damage response
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE; DNA DAMAGE CHECKPOINTS; DNA REPAIR; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; RIDDLE SYNDROME; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Our genetic information is encoded into our chromosomes, which are made of DNA. To become cancerous, a cell must acquire changes in its DNA. Thus, DNA must be damaged and mis-repaired for this to happen. Normally, cells have a policing system that helps them detect damaged DNA. My laboratory has recently discovered a novel means by which cell communicates its damaged DNA. I propose in this grant to build on this discovery to understand in detail how this novel means of cellular communication helps cells indicate where DNA is damaged, when DNA is repaired and ultimately how this new process helps stave off cancer.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Thalamic regulation of the nucleus accumbens
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; DEPRESSION; DOPAMINE; DYNORPHIN; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; OREXIN
Abstract-Résumé: Dopamine is an important neurochemical in the brain where it plays a critical role in controlling movement and motivation.  Consequently, changes in dopamine levels have been implicated in a number of important neurological and psychiatric disorders.  The nucleus accumbens, which forms a large part of the ventral striatum, plays a key role in regulating normal behavior and is the area of the striatum most closely associated with psychiatric conditions (e.g. schizophrenia, drug addiction, depression, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder).  We plan to determine if an area of the thalamus called the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) regulates the activity of dopamine neurons in the midbrain and the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens.  We hypothesize that in response to different arousal states, the PVT regulates dopamine release by modulating feedback regulation of dopamine neurons.  A change in the sensitivity or activity of this arousal system may play a key role in the production of maladaptive behaviors associated with some psychiatric disorders including drug addiction and depression. We hope that results from the proposed research may provide preclinical data that may be useful for designing new therapeutic approaches for the treatment of psychiatric disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aging of male germ cells
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; MALE GERM CELLS / SPERMATOZOA; NICHE; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; STEM CELLS; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Male germ cells are made on an ongoing basis in the testes of adult non-seasonal mammals. Little is known about how the quality of sperm is affected by advancing age. Do spermatogonia that divide to produce subsequent generations of germ cells accumulate damage as years go by? In man, there is an increasing rate of abnormalities in chromosomes with aging.  There is a strong correlation between the age of the male partner and decreased sperm motility and normal morphology, decreased pregnancy rates, increased time to pregnancy, and higher incidences of schizophrenia and autism. Yet, the lack of robust prospective studies makes it difficult to draw firm conclusions from human data. The BN rat is an excellent model to study the effects of aging on the male reproductive system. We have found that during aging there are clear effects on progeny outcome, on sperm morphology and motility, and on the ability of sperm to withstand oxidative stress. However, the underlying factors that result in these clear age related effects are not clear. We hypothesize that, during the process of aging, both the nuclear proteins and DNA (chromatin) of germ cells are modified, thus resulting in spermatozoa of functionally poorer quality. Our three specific aims are: First to determine what specific molecular changes occur in organelles of sperm (nuclear matrix/cytoplasmic droplet) during aging. Next, to assess how altered expression of glutathione peroxidase 4 affects the ability of sperm to withstand modifications of oxidative stress that occur during aging. Third, to use stem cell transplantation to determine how aging of spermatogonial stem cells affects their potential for proliferation and differentiation. Together these studies will provide a clear indication of how aging affects both germ cell chromatin and function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Early identification of rheumatoid arthritis in First Nations
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; AUTOANTIBODIES; ORAL HEALTH; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease that, once established, causes progressive lifelong joint damage. Previous studies have shown that healthy people who are genetically susceptible and who have RA antibodies in their blood are highly likely to develop RA in the future. Since RA is common and severe in First Nations (FN) people, we have been testing the healthy family members of FN RA patients for RA antibodies and predisposing genes, and then following them to detect early signs of disease.     We would now like to get a better understanding of the complex factors involved in the development of RA in these high risk individuals. We have found a number of important clues, including an association between the RA antibodies and a bacteria that causes gum disease. Our studies will follow this high risk group, along with a control group, with questionnaires, joint exams, and blood samples. If signs of joint inflammation start, we will examine an affected joint in detail by MRI and pathology. Our study will also screen a population sample from a single FN community, St Theresa Point, for the presence of arthritis symptoms, RA antibodies, and gum disease. We hope this will help us to get a better understanding of the link between these conditions, and to get a better estimate of how common these problems are.   We anticipate our study will shed important light on the factors involved in starting RA, and give us the opportunity to treat it very early. We hope to develop a community based approach to detecting RA in FN communities, and to address unmet health needs in these communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of G protein-coupled receptor trafficking
Keywords-MotsClés: GPCR TRAFFICKING; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; INTRACELLULAR TRAFFICKING; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells communicate with each other by sending chemical messages that are perceived at their surface by proteins named "receptors". The messages bind to the receptors and transmit a signal towards the interior of the cell. This will result in modifying the activity of the cell. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) constitute the largest family of cell surface receptors. They also form the biggest target for prescribed drugs on the market. Problems in routing these receptors to the cell surface after their synthesis inside the cell may result in diseases. Understanding how these receptors are targeted to the cell surface is thus crucial and may lead to future therapeutic targets. We have identified two novel pathways controlling the targeting of GPCRs at the cell surface. Our research project aim at characterizing in detail these new mechanisms.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - B: Clinical Behavioural Sciences
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: The Genetic Epidemiology of Autism; Family and Molecular Studies
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; GENETICS; WHOLE GENOME ASSOCIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Autism is a neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by impairments in social-communication and by a preference for repetitive activities. It is one of a group of disorders called the autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and is perhaps the most handicapping disorder of childhood in terms of prevalence, morbidity, outcome and cost to society. It has been clear for some that that autism has a genetic basis but it has been difficult to identify the genes that cause the disorder. Recently, our group came together with the other major autism genetics research groups in the world and formed the Autism Genome Project (AGP). Together, we uncovered important new findings which form the basis of this renewal. We now propose to complete a new study to identify genetic markers associated with autism and with variations in severity of the disorder. The plan is to collect 500 children affected with ASD and their families. We will exclude children with the most severe form of intellectual disability and with sub-microscopic chromosome abnormalities so that we can focus on the most familial cases. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, blood is taken from these children and their relatives and a battery of behavioural measures is obtained on affected and unaffected family members.  We intend to assess the degree of impairment in social reciprocity, IQ, inflexible behaviour and language in affected children and similar measures of social impairments and language in parents and sibs. Collecting data on unaffected relatives is important since we argue that families in which the unaffected relatives also have impairments in social reciprocity and language will be the ones in which it easiest to find the genes associated with the disorder. We will then conduct a whole genome association study with roughly five (5) controls per case and 1 million genetic markers to see which genetic markers are associated with the risk for autism and with variation in the behavioural measures of affected children.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Links between antibiotic production and resistance in producer organisms
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICS; BACTERIA; BIOSYNTHESIS; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; REGULATION; RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Since their introduction, the antibiotics have significantly reduced infant mortality, post-operative infection, injury-acquired sepsis, pneumonia and countless other causes of premature death. Sadly, resistant pathogens have emerged for all the antibiotics we have. We can still treat many hospital-acquired and most community-acquired infections but the options are eroding steadily. We need new antibiotics and better versions of the old ones. Most antibiotics are produced by the Streptomyces bacteria and we know that this genus makes molecules we have not discovered yet. Finding new producers and manipulating the biosynthetic mechanisms that produce antibiotics are two approaches to solving the resistance crisis. But there are significant challenges. First, many species do not produce significant antimicrobial activity in the laboratory. Second, manipulating in vivo biosynthesis is hampered by a lack of understanding of biosynthesis. This proposal addresses these challenges. The producer bacteria encode membrane proteins that protect them from the agents they produce. We have discovered a fascinating mechanism that links these proteins to biosynthesis: we think cells respond to intermediates in the antibiotic biosynthetic pathways by activating resistance genes " we refer to this as the 'feed-forward' hypothesis. It also appears that the resistance proteins coordinate the assembly of multi-enzymes complexes that complete biosynthesis. This new and very exciting biology has important implications for drug discovery. First, to modify the biosynthesis of known drugs, we must understand how these multi-enzyme complexes are assembled. Second, we have found that constitutive expression of the resistance genes massively increases in antibiotic production. This might provide a new way activating the genes for production of un-characterized antibiotics, leading to new drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comprehensive analysis of mouse and human transcription factor DNA-binding specificities
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA-BINDING; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE REGULATION; GENOMICS; MICROARRAYS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Most physiological processes - growth, metabolism, development, reproduction, the immune response, and even most diseases - are controlled by transcription factors. Transcription factors are proteins that determine which genes are turned on and off, and to what level, by binding to specific DNA sequences within or nearby the genes they control. A key objective of genomics research is to understand how all of the genes are regulated, and a critical missing piece in this puzzle is that the DNA-binding specificity of most transcription factors is either unknown or poorly defined. Our major objective is to systematically determine the DNA binding specificities of all ~1,500 known and predicted transcription factors in the mouse and human genomes - most of which are nearly identical, such that knowledge gained can be followed up by genetic experimentation with mouse mutants. Full knowledge of transcription factor binding specificities will enable us to understand how gene regulation is controlled in disease states, and which transcription factor (or factors) is involved, providing a rational path towards improved therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of HIF in Endocytosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; ENDOCYTOSIS; HYPOXIA; HYPOXIA-INDUCIBLE FACTOR (HIF); OXYGEN-SENSING PATHWAY
Abstract-Résumé: Oxygen homeostasis or balance is an important organizing principle for human development and physiology. A universal response to compromised oxygen availability involves a protein called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), which accumulates during low oxygen levels or hypoxia to trigger the expression of numerous genes including those that promote new blood vessel formation (angiogenesis), anaerobic metabolism, and the production of oxygen-carrying red blood cells. These cellular responses facilitate adaptation and survival in low oxygen environment, and help to restore normal oxygen balance. The significance of HIF in cancer is underscored by the finding that HIF is inordinately overexpressed in virtually all human tumours. Tumour cells express high level of HIF because regions within a growing tumour mass inevitably and progressively become more hypoxic as the diffusional capacity of oxygen from the nearest blood vessel is surpassed. In addition, cancer-causing mutations on critical tumour suppressor genes have been shown to increase the expression of HIF. Clinically relevant is the fact that the expression of HIF correlates with cancer progression, resistance to radiation and chemotherapy, and poor prognosis. Emerging evidence suggests that tumour hypoxia by largely unknown mechanisms leads to deregulated accumulation of and signalling via receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) that are critical for driving cancer development and progression. Our preliminary data have revealed an unprecedented role of HIF in modulating RTK function via endocytosis, a major cellular process of deactivating and recycling receptors. The objective of this research proposal is to elucidate the molecular mechanisms governing HIF-mediated endocytosis with the supposition that lessons learned would provide significant and original insight into the multifaceted adaptive response to hypoxia and advance our understanding of cancer biology.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of brain adenosine levels by ecto-enzymes and membrane transporters.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOSINE TRANSPORT; ATP; BEHAVIOR; ECTO-5'-NUCLEOTIDASE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Adenosine is a natural compound found in all cells.  Adenosine is a signalling compound that activates a family of receptors, termed adenosine receptors.  In brain, adenosine receptor function has been implicated in a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions, including stroke injury, epilepsy, insomnia, ethanol intoxication, neuroinflammation, Parkinson's Disease and depression.  As adenosine is a break-down product of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the energy molecule of cells, adenosine levels increase dramatically when ATP synthesis fails, for example during stroke.  However, many of adenosine's receptor mediated effects are observed without significant loss of ATP.  The research described in this proposal will examine adenosine formation and adenosine receptor mediated effects in wild type and two genetically modified lines of mice to determine how adenosine levels are regulated.  This research will identify ways of manipulating adenosine levels to therapeutic advantage for treatment of diseases ranging from epilepsy to depression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biotransformation and Molecular Toxicity of Pulmonary Carcinogens
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOTRANSFORMATION; CHEMICAL CARCINOGENESIS; DNA REPAIR; LUNG CANCER; ONCOGENES; PULMONARY TOXICOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The respiratory system is unique because of its very large surface area, which is constantly exposed to the environment through inhalation of air. The purpose of the proposed research is to ascertain what processes are involved in making the lung a target for cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens). We will study how lungs handle two carcinogens; the fungal metabolite, aflatoxin B1, and the tobacco-specific nitrosamine, NNK. We will examine how lung cells chemically alter these carcinogens, and what effects the carcinogens have on DNA repair. Such information will be valuable for developing strategies to prevent lung damage due to carcinogens.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuropeptides and peptidomimetics as parmacological tools and potential drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS OF PEPTIDES AND PEPTIDOMIMETICS; OPIOID ANALGESICS; OPIOID PEPTIDES AND RECEPTORS; OPIOID TOLERANCE AND DEPENDENCE; PEPTIDE HORMONES AND NEUROTRANSMITTERS; PEPTIDE-BASED DRUG DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Opiates have a unique place in medicine. Their usefulness in the treatment of severe pain is undeniable. For example, pain remains a serious and disabling symptom of cancer and 30% of all cancer patients require opiate analgesics. Among patients with bone, oral and GU cancer, opiate use is even higher, around 80%. The World Health Organization estimates that pain represents a major symptom in 70% of patients with advanced cancer. Opiates remain the mainstay of treatment but not without side effects, such as respiratory depression, nausea, vomiting, dysphoria, constipation, sedation, tolerance and dependence, which often limit their use. Obviously, the development of opioid compounds that are devoid of these serious side effects represents a high priority goal. In addition, the illicit use of opiates remains a major problem, particularly with the recent association of AIDS with intravenous dug abuse. Developing analgesic drugs with very low abuse potential would facilitate treating pain patients by diminishing concerns of physicians and would minimize the diversion of illicit drugs. In the present application we propose to develop novel bifunctional compounds containing a mu opioid agonist peptide and various neuropeptide antagonists, including delta opioid-, cannabinoid (CB1)-, substance P (NK1)- and opioid receptor like (ORL1)-antagonists. These compounds are expected to be potent analgesics for the treatment of severe pain with a low propensity to produce the typical side effects of mu opiod agonists like morphine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of cardiac fatty acid and glucose metabolism by lipins
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FATTY ACID METABOLISM; FUEL PARTITIONING; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; HORMONAL ACTION; LIPOTOXICITY; TRIACYLGLYCEROL SYNTHESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Control of cardiac fatty acid and glucose metabolism by lipins   Press release  There is an epidemic in the increase of heart disease associated with increases in obesity and diabetes in the Canadian population.  In obesity and diabetes, there is an increased use of fats versus glucose as fuels in the heart.  This impairs the function of the heart and its ability to recover from heart attacks.  The proposed work on the heart will study a newly discovered family of proteins called lipins.  These proteins control the synthesis of fats called triglycerides.  They also have the unique property of being able to regulate the balance of the use of fats versus glucose as fuels in the liver. Almost nothing is known about the regulation of lipin expression in the heart. We will study how the expression of the lipins is regulated by hormonal changes that are relevant to diabetes and obesity. We will also investigate how fat and glucose metabolism is changed in the hearts of mice that lack lipin activity and we will relate the results to the mechanical performance of the hearts.  This project is unique in that the lipins and their role in controlling fuel selection was only discovered in 2006 and we have no direct knowledge of their functions in the heart.  Our work will provide an exciting opportunity for studying a new dimension of how heart function is changed in obesity and diabetes. Understanding how to prevent adverse changes in fat and glucose metabolism will enable us to devise strategies for improving heart function and the ability of the heart to recover following heart attacks.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biosynthesis and role of eicosanoids in inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: 5-LIPOXYGENASE PATHWAY; EICOSANOIDS; EOSINOPHILS AND NEUTROPHILS; HPLC AND MASS SPECTROMETRY; OXIDATIVE STRESS AND INFLAMMATION; POLYUNSATURATED FATTY ACIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Arachidonic acid, a fatty acid abundant in all cells, is converted to a large number of biologically active products. Several years ago we discovered a new pathway that results in the formation of a substance (5-oxo-ETE) that causes the accumulation of certain types of white blood cells (eosinophils and neutrophils) in tissues. These cells normally play an important role in defending the body from parasitic and bacterial infections, but they are also associated with asthma and other allergic diseases and can cause lung damage. In addition, other research groups found that 5-oxo-ETE can promote the growth of tumor cells. We propose to determine how the formation of 5-oxo-ETE is regulated in inflammatory cells and tumor cells and to investigate its biological effects. We will examine its role in inflammatory diseases such as asthma, both in humans and in animal models. Because of the proinflammatory effects of 5-oxo-ETE and its proliferative effects on tumor cells we will attempt to devise ways to block its formation and biological activity. To this end, we are working jointly with a group of chemists in the United States to develop chemically-synthesized substances that can either block the actions of 5-oxo-ETE (a 5-oxo-ETE receptor antagonist) or its synthesis by cells in the body (an inhibitor that will selectively block the enzyme that is required for its formation). We will evaluate the effectiveness of these substances in various cell types as well as in animal models of disease. Such substances could be useful in the treatment of inflammatory diseases and cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: A role for SPARC in the Regulation of CNS Repair
Keywords-MotsClés: GLIAL MIGRATION AND MITOSIS; GLIAL-MEDIATED REPAIR; MICROGLIA; MYELINATION; NEURO- AND GLIAL-GENESIS; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: This grant focuses on the activity of a matricellular protein, Secreted Protein Acidic and Rich in Cysteine (SPARC), that is made by glia can be either intracellular or secreted. Secreted SPARC can interact with multiple growth factors and extracellular matrix components to shift the state of Schwann cells into one more capable of promoting the outgrowth of specific fibre tracts in the spinal cord. Preliminary evidence in our laboratory suggests that SPARC can regulate glial cell motility and migration, two crucial processes involved in control of development of the CNS, and mechanisms that need to be manipulated to promote CNS repair. SPARC has already been implicated in the regulation of bone and blood vessel formation. In this proposal, we propose to attack how SPARC may be a key mediator of multiple events in CNS repair.  A greater understanding of how SPARC works in mediating multiple cellular events that are beneficial to the damaged NS will allow us to develop new and innovative methods to strengthen our translational approach to the problem of promoting repair after stroke and spinal cord injury. In order to achieve these goals, we have established specific aims to better understand how SPARC functions in the context of regulating neurogenesis and gliogenesis from CNS progenitors, regulates microglial activation and motility, and regulates reperfusion and blood-brain barrier formation in the damaged CNS. A dual role for SPARC in regulating these processes is hypothesized to depend on whether SPARC is secreted or whether it remains inside the cell or nucleus. Based on our preliminary data, we propose that abundant levels of intracellular SPARC is a characteristic of a more quiescent cell.  Informaiton gained from this research will provide us with a stronger understanding of SPARC function that we will use to design ways to manipulate SPARC activation to promote CNS repair

TitreApplicationTitle: Adaptive mechanisms of spinal locomotion
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; INTRATHECAL INJECTIONS; KINEMATICS; LOCOMOTION; NEUROIMAGING; NEUROPHARMACOLOGY; PARAPLEGIA; REFLEXES; REHABILITATION; SPINAL LESIONS; SPINAL PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Several sensory and motor deficits result from spinal lesions. However, in most species, including humans, motor functions such as locomotion can recover to some degree depending on the severity of the spinal lesion. Various mechanisms may account for this recovery. Undamaged fiber tracts from the brain may undergo anatomical and physiological reorganization. Even some damaged fibers may regrow to reinnervate targets below the spinal lesion. However, based on our previous experiments on complete spinal cord lesion, it is clear that changes within the intrinsic spinal circuitry  (named Central Pattern Generator or CPG) below the lesion may account for some recovery of function. The general hypothesis underlying this grant proposal is that this CPG is as important for the recovery of locomotion in cats with partial spinal lesions as those with complete lesions. This hypothesis is strongly supported by our preliminary experiments showing that cats trained to walk after a partial lesion can walk within 24 hours after a second and complete spinal section. Furthermore, the quality of locomotor recovery is highly correlated with the amount of treadmill locomotor training received after the first lesion.  This work therefore suggests that the locomotor recovery after the first initial partial spinal lesion depends largely on intrinsic changes in the spinal cord since, after the second and complete lesion at T13, the isolated spinal cord shows an immediate ability to express locomotion. In this proposal, I intend to investigate the mechanisms involved in the recovery of locomotion after partial spinal lesions using electromyographic recordings, video recordings and also intracellular techniques to evaluate changes occurring within these spinal circuits. This research has important clinical implications for human rehabilitation since it will identify how locomotor training induces profound and persistent changes within the spinal cord itself.

ClasseRechercheFR: TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Brain Lipid Binding Protein in Growth-Promoting Glia
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDYNOGLIA; CNS REGENERATION; GLIAL DEVELOPMENT; GLIAL MIGRATION AND MITOSIS; OLFACTORY ENSHEATHING CELLS; RADIAL GLIA
Abstract-Résumé: For many years, successful and consistent functional neurogenesis and restoration of neuronal connectivity has been reported within the rodent olfactory system, and recently, much attention has been focused on the role of Olfactory ensheathing cells (OECs) in this process. We have found that a gene, BLBP (aka FABP7) that was previously thought restricted to embryonic glial cells, is highly expressed by OECs and a subpopulation of growth-promoting glia in the CNS. Because OECs possess a unique ability to promote neurogenesis and axonal targeting across the PNS:CNS boundary in the olfactory system, they have become a prime candidate for transplant-mediated repair following a variety of CNS lesions, including spinal cord injury. The considerable variability in functional or anatomical outcome reported in OEC transplant studies, however, has prompted us to closely examine how the intrinsic properties of OECs change in vitro and in vivo, and led us to test specific OEC-driven repair mechanisms that may contribute to neuronal outgrowth, regeneration, sprouting and protection.  BLBP expression declines with passage and time in vitro, (and with age of animal in vivo) coincident with a reduction in the ability of OECs to promote regeneration. Here, we will directly test pathways that regulate BLBP in OECs. We will directly test if OECs expressing high and low levels of BLBP possess differential abilities to promote CNS regeneration or remyelination.  This proposal thus focuses on identifying specific signals we could use to manipulate the endogenous state of growth-promoting glia, in order to shift the lesioned CNS into a state more capable of promoting repair and regeneration.
