TitreApplicationTitle: Functions of alpha-4 integrins in monocyte emigration.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION MOLECULES; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; BETA-2); BIOASSAYS; CELL BIOLOGY; CHEMOKINES; EMIGRATION; FLOW CHAMBER STUDIES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; INTEGRIN AFFINITY; INTEGRIN AVIDITY; INTEGRINS (ALPHA-4; LYMPHOCYTES; MONOCYTES; SIGNALING PATHWAYS; TIRF MICROSCOPY; TRANSFECTIONS; VCAM-1
Abstract-Résumé: The emigration of white blood cells (leukocytes) from the blood into tissues is a key process in atherosclerosis, autoimmune conditions and rejection of transplanted organs. Monocytes are leukocytes that play a critical role in atherosclerosis, a disease that results in heart attacks and strokes. Inhibition of monocyte emigration can constitute an important therapeutic approach, and understanding mechanisms of monocyte emigration is critical to achieving this goal. Significant advances have been made. Numerous adhesion molecules, such as VCAM-1, have been identified on endothelial cells (cells that line the inner surface of blood vessels), and integrins (molecules that bind to endothelial cell adhesion molecules) were found on leukocytes. Chemokines are soluble molecules that are adsorbed onto the endothelial cell surface and stimulate blood leukocytes that come into contact with endothelial cells. Chemokine stimulation up-regulates the adhesive function of integrins, and is critical for monocyte adhesion to endothelial cells and their subsequent emigration out of the blood vessels and into tissues. Our goal is to determine which biochemical signaling pathways that are activated by chemokines in monocytes are required for up-regulating the adhesive function of an integrin called alpha-4. We will also assess the roles of signaling molecules that are activated after alpha-4 integrins bind to VCAM-1. We will use biochemical assays, state-of-the-art microscopy and functional assays, as well as cells where signaling molecules are inhibited or their expression is reduced by genetic engineering.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering pathways of transcriptional regulation in Schizosaccharomyces pombe
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELLULAR NETWORKS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; MICROARRAY; SYNTHETIC GENETIC ARRAY; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Proper transcriptional regulation of gene expression in all cell types is essential for normal growth and development and governed by a particular class of proteins called transcription factors. Changes in gene expression caused by alterations in transcription factor activity have been linked to several diseases states. To decipher the transcriptional control program of a cell, it is essential to determine how the activities of each transcription factor and their interactions with gene targets are appropriately coordinated in a regulatory network. Mapping such networks in humans has been difficult due to the challenges associated with studying transcription factors and the complexity of our genome. The yeast model system has proven to be extremely powerful in research because it possesses well-developed genetic, molecular and functional genomic tools that are not available to studies in humans. This allows for faster progress in the functional characterization of transcription factors and the identification of their gene targets. We plan to systematically characterize all 99 transcription factors in fission yeast to rapidly map the entire transcriptional-regulatory network in an organism. Basic studies in the fission yeast transcriptional-regulatory network are expected to develop methods and approaches for dealing with such complex networks in metazoans. Furthermore, since many genes are conserved from fission yeast to humans, results from these studies will likely facilitate knowledge in the transcriptional control of various genes linked to human diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of osteoclast formation and function by cell-cell interactions in the bone microenvironment
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; BONE REMODELING; CALCIUM SIGNALING; ERYTHROBLASTS; HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA; OSTEOCLAST
Abstract-Résumé: Musculoskeletal disorders affect people of all ages, severely compromising their health and well-being.  The destruction of bone is characteristic of several classes of diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis, and periodontitis. Osteoclasts are the cells responsible for resorbing bone normally in health (during bone remodeling) and abnormally in these disorders. The molecular factor RANKL has been identified as a critical stimulator for osteoclast formation and function, and was shown to play an important role in mediating bone destruction in inflammatory arthritis, periodontitis, and cancer metastasis to bone. However, we have recently found that although RANKL is necessary during initial stage of osteoclast formation, in the later stages, proliferating bone marrow cells produce factors that can substitute for RANKL and induce successful osteoclast formation.  The studies proposed in this grant application are aimed at 1) characterizing the effects of proliferating bone marrow cells on osteoclasts; 2) examining the changes induced by bone marrow cells in osteoclast intracellular milieu and 3) identifying the mediators of the osteoclastogenic effect of proliferating bone marrow cells. Taken together, these data will provide new insights into the regulation of bone remodeling in the complex bone microenvironment, and may lead to the development of new avenues for targeted therapeutic interventions in these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Micro-RNA's in Human Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
Keywords-MotsClés: EBV; MICRO-RNAS; NASOPHARYNGEAL CANCER; PREDICTIVE GENES; RADIATION THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Current treatment for patients with nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) comprise of radiation therapy (RT) alone, or RT combined with chemotherapy (CT), which achieves only modest results. We propose that through the development and use of predictive gene signatures, based on mini-genes, or micro-RNAs, we could customize therapies for each individual patient, thereby improving outcome by increasing cure, and reducing side effects.  The predictive gene sets will be developed using an initial group of 173 NPC patient samples, then validated using an independent group of 189 NPC patient samples.  The biological effects of these new micro-RNAs will also be examined using laboratory models of NPC.  Their potential role as non-invasive markers of cancer burden will also be explored. If such predictive gene signatures could be developed, this will have significant benefit in the clinical management, and ultimate outcome for future patients with NPC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of correction of deltaF508CFTR
Keywords-MotsClés: CORRECTOR; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; DISEASE MECHANISM; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; RESPIRATORY DISEASES; THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Cystic fibrosis is the most common lethal genetic disease. Affected individuals have persistent lung infections and fibrotic lesions, pancreatic and digestive deficiencies and males are sterile. The disease results from mutations in the CFTR gene discovered in Canada in 1989. The most common mutation, deltaF508, results in a mutant CFTR protein that is functional but is retained in the wrong location in the cell. However, if the mutant deltaF508 CFTR protein can be induced to traffic to its correct location on the cell surface it functions as a chloride ion transporter. Despite the almost 20 years of our knowledge of the basic defect underlying the disease there is no therapy that is directly based on correcting this defect. We have found compounds that act as potent correctors of this disease in mutant human airway cells and in a mouse cystic fibrosis model. This application is directed at determining how some of these compounds correct the deltaF508 CFTR trafficking defect.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CANCER; MOLECULAR IMAGING; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: New cancer therapies based on reduction of tumour feeding blood vessels (angiogenesis) are now having a significant impact on patient outcomes when used in combination with other front line therapies.  This project seeks to develop ultrasonic approaches to test the value of new combinations of therapies for control of cancer growth in experimental mouse models of breast cancer and melanoma.  The new approaches to be developed will enable the important molecules associated with angiogenesis to be followed in time course studies with out having to sacrifice mice at every time point.  This, inturn, will greatly speed up the process of screening new combination therapies that might be taken forward to the clinic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oncogenes and the interaction of retroviruses with the host
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER STEM CELLS; MAMMARY STEM CELLS; MAMMARY TUMORS; NOTCH1
Abstract-Résumé: Notch1 (N1) is a gene which is highly conserved among species and which is known to control the fate of many distinct cell populations of the body.  In particular, its expression is known to keep specific tissue stem cells in an undifferentiated state.  N1 has been found to be overexpressed in a significant percentage of human breast tumors and such overexpression is associated with aggressive tumors.  We previously found that N1 is involved in some mouse mammary tumors and that a truncated version of this gene can induce mammary tumors in transgenic (Tg) mice.  In addition to tumors, N1 Tg mice exhibit a severe developmental defect of the mammary glands related to their stem or progenitor cells. In the present proposal, we intend to characterize the stem/progenitor pre-malignant cells of these young Tg mice and to compare them to the tumor stem cells giving rise to tumors.  Considering that Notch1 is involved in human breast tumors, it is likely that this newly-developed mouse model of these tumors will be instrumental in understanding the biology of these specific mammary tumors and in finding specific and unique pathways which may be targeted for therapy.

Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN SLICE PREPARATIONS; CORTICAL EXCITABILITY; ELECTRO-PHYSIOLOGY; EPILEPTOGENESIS; EXCITATORY AMINO ACIDS; EXPERIMENTAL EPILEPSY
Abstract-Résumé: Our studies will elucidate several unanswered questions that are important pathogenic issues in epileptology, specifically with regard to temporal lobe epilepsy. This is a common form of partial epilepsy that afflicts approximately 0.2% of adult Canadians. Seizures in these patients are poorly controlled by antiepileptic drugs, and thus these individuals know only a life of unexpected disruptions that deeply affect their personal and professional activities. In the absence of alternative treatments many of them must undergo trials of elaborate, costly surgery, in which portions of their brains are removed. Therefore, understanding the pathophysiogenesis of temporal lobe epilepsy is an important challenge in epilepsy research. We are confident that our findings will help in the identification of novel therapeutic strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroanatomic features specific to pedophilia
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; MAGNETIZATION TRANSFER; MRI; PEDOPHILIA; SEXUAL OFFENSES
Abstract-Résumé: This project will use state-of-the-art brain imaging technologies to learn more about what in the brain causes pedophilia.  Brain scans will include conventional MRI's, as did our previous research on pedophilia, plus two recently developed types of brain scans, called "Diffusion Tensor Imaging" and "Magnetization Transfer."  We will identify the parts of the brain that relate to pedophilia by comparing pedophiles with three different control groups: men who committed nonsexual crimes, men who have atypical sexual interests other than pedophilia (such as exhibitionism), and healthy non-offenders.  These scans will permit us to test a theory of what in the brain causes pedophilia: Our previous MRI research of pedophiles suggested that the disorder is caused by a disconnection among different parts of the brain that normally serve to identify stimuli in the environment as sexually relevant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms of DN regulatory T cell-mediated donor specific transplantation tolerance.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN SPECIFIC SUPPRESSION; AUTOIMMUNE DISEASE; CANCER; CARDIAC TRANSPLANTATION; DONOR LYMPOCYTE INFUSION; DOUBLE NEGATIVE REGULATORY T CELLS; GRAFT REJECTION; GRAFT VERSUS HOST DISEASE; IMMUNE REGULATION; TRANSPLANTATION TOLERANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Current treatment for preventing rejection of transplanted organ grafts relies on the use of non-specific immunosuppressive drugs, which are toxic and have significant side effects for recipients.  More importantly, these drugs are not effective in inducing long-term organ graft survival.  On the other hand, accumulating evidence indicate that regulatory T lymphocytes (Treg) may be used to prevent the immune response associated with autoimmune diseases and graft rejection.  Further understanding of the mechanisms leading to activation, expansion and function of Treg cells is required before we are able to use these cells as a novel therapy for treating graft rejection.  Our laboratory has recently identified and cloned a novel antigen-specific Treg cell, called DN Tregs, and demonstrated that injection of these DN Tregs into recipients before transplantation leads to permanent acceptance of donor-specific grafts in mice without treatment with immunosuppressive drugs.  The objective of this proposal is to use our well-established mouse transplantation model to identify the cellular and molecular mechanisms whereby DN Treg cells induce and maintain donor-specific transplantation tolerance.  The results from these studies will enhance our understanding of the mechanisms of antigen-specific suppression mediated by DN Tregs, and bring us closer to using DN Tregs in the clinic to prevent organ graft rejection and autoimmune diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel roles for Cdx proteins in development
Keywords-MotsClés: AXIAL ELONGATION; CDX; POSTERIOR SPECIFICATION; SOMITE; TRANSCRIPTION; WNT
Abstract-Résumé: The development of the main body axis, including the neural tube and the spinal column, begins during early development and involves complex interactions between a number of different cell populations. Lesions in any one of the numerous events essential to the completion of this process can lead to severe congenital malformations common in the human population, such as neural tube defects (NTD).  A number of signaling molecules have been implicated in normal axial development, including retinoic acid (RA), fibroblast growth factor and Wnts.  These molecules ultimately function by regulating the expression of target genes which then impact on cell differentiation.  Work from our group, together with our laboratories, has led us to form a hypothesis that Wnt, FGF and RA signaling impact, in part, on patterning of the main axis through regulation of a family of genes, the Cdx genes (Cdx1, Cdx2 and Cdx4).  The Cdx genes encode transcription factors, and are essential regulators of downstream target genes essential for normal axial development.  However, the precise roles of the Cdx proteins, is poorly understood.  Novel genetic models developed by our group have revealed new and surprising roles for the Cdx transcription factors in development of the posterior embryo.  In the present application, we propose further analysis of these novel mutants, with particular emphasis on defining the target genes and pathways that are dependent on Cdx function.  The information forthcoming from these studies should have important bearing on our understanding not only of basic processes related to embryonic development, but may also shed light on the basis for certain congenital defects prevalent in the human population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Polymicrobial Infections and Pathogenesis of the Streptococcus Milleri Group
Keywords-MotsClés: CYSTIC FIBROSIS; INVASIVE INFECTIONS; PATHOGENESIS; POLYMICROBIAL INFECTIONS; STREPTOCOCCUS MILLERI
Abstract-Résumé: The Streptococcus milleri group (SMG) represents a distinct group of Streptococcus composed of three closely related species (S. constellatus, S. intermedius and S. anginosus). This group of bacteria is difficult to isolate and identify and has therefore been under-reported and under-studied. They are a leading  cause of liver, brain and lung abscesses. Using new methods developed in my lab for isolation and identification of SMG, we have shown that it contributes to respiratory tract infections in cystic fibrosis and bronchiectisis and we predict that it will also be a major contributor to bacterial pneumonias. We have also obtained almost complete genome sequences for isolates of each of the three species in this group. As a pathogen, the SMG are almost always associated with other bacteria in polymicrobial infections.We propose investigate the mechanisms of pathogenesis of SMG and how they interact with other bacteria in infections. This work will lead to improved diagnostics and improved treatment strategies for SMG related infections.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural analysis of the molecular machinery involved in protein secretion and membrane protein assembly.
Keywords-MotsClés: MACROMOLECULAR X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; MEMBRANE PROTEIN ASSEMBLY; PROTEIN TARGETING; PROTEIN TRANSLOCATION; SIGNAL PEPTIDASE; SIGNAL PEPTIDE PEPTIDASE
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately one third of the proteins coded for in the genome of any organism need to cross or partition into hydrophobic membranes of the cell. Cells have evolved a conserved general system to facilitate this mass transport process called the general secretory system that consists of three steps: 1) protein targeting to the membrane, 2) protein translocation across or into the membrane and 3) release and hydrolysis of the signal peptide of secreted proteins. Each of these steps utilizes protein based molecular machines that work together to perform this fundamental task of moving proteins to their final functional location within the cell or outside the cell.  Our lab uses X-ray crystallography, protein chemistry and molecular biology to investigate the proteins and protein complexes involved in the general secretory system. The basic components of the general secretory system are essential to the life of all cells, yet we know from prior research that bacterial and human cells differ in some of the components of the machinery. We will, along with our collaborators, use the three-dimensional structures and functional observations that result from our research to design molecules that will inhibit the function of essential bacterial components of the general secretory system thus killing the bacteria. These compounds could lead to the development of a novel class of antibiotics. One example of this is our collaborative efforts with both industry (Basalia Pharmaceutica Ltd.) and academia (The Scripps Research Institute) to develop a novel antibiotic (a derivative of Arylomycin A2) based on the inhibition of bacterial type 1 signal peptidase.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Development of new pharmacological therapeutic strategies for long-term tinnitus.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; BEHAVIORAL MODELS OF PATHOLOGIES; NEUROPHARMACOLOGY; NEW THERAPEUTIC STRATEGIES; PATHOLOGIES OF AUDITORY PERCEPTION; TINNITUS
Abstract-Résumé: With 10% of the adult population experiencing ringing in the ear, tinnitus is a major problem of public health, worsened by the deleterious combination of aging of the population and drastic increase of noise pollution in Western countries. Unfortunately, the neuronal mechanisms underlying tinnitus are not yet fully understood, nor are effective treatments available. Taking step on important preliminary data, we aim here to develop new and efficient therapeutic strategies to cure long-term noise-induced tinnitus (the more clinically relevant form of tinnitus) by generating integrated pre-clinical data, using a combination of behavioral and pharmacological approaches. Specifically, using validated animal models of tinnitus, we will investigate the modifications of cognitive behaviors induced by long-term tinnitus, and test the effect of local application pharmacological agents on the blockade of tinnitus, ranging from simple situation (short-term and long-term tinnitus), to more clinically-relevant ones (long-term tinnitus modulated by anxiety). The expected output of this project constitutes a necessary prerequisite for the development of efficient therapeutic strategies to cure tinnitus.

ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: Low dietary folate and colorectal carcinogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DNA DAMAGE; FOLATE; METHYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this research program is to determine the mechanisms by which deficiency of the B vitamin folic acid increases the risk for colon cancer and possibly other types of cancer. We have recently identified intestinal tumors in mice fed low folate diets. These mice represent a new animal model for intestinal neoplasia that may be more similar to the human disease than previous rodent models.      We shall use these mice to determine if folate deficiency increases cancer risk by damaging DNA or by disrupting DNA methylation. We shall attempt to identify specific genes with altered methylation patterns that may be involved in tumor formation. We shall also determine whether diets low in choline, a nutrient that intersects folate metabolism, can also cause intestinal tumors. We shall assess whether low dietary folate contributes to a wide range of solid tumors and whether low dietary folate during pregnancy affects cancer risk in newborn mice.        We have observed that the low folate diets do not cause intestinal neoplasia in a different strain of mice (C57Bl/6) in contrast to the studies described above for the BALB/c strain. This finding suggests that the C57Bl/6 strain possesses mechanisms to block tumor formation; we shall try to identify these mechanisms of tumor resistance by comparing the 2 strains for DNA damage, methylation changes, and relevant measurements of folate pathway activity. Finally, since folic acid supplementation has been implemented in North America, we will determine whether folic acid in high quantities increases tumor formation in mice.       This work will increase our understanding of the nutritional impact on cancer development and may identify novel genes that can be exploited as therapeutic targets.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the effects of monoaminergic regulation of frontostriatal systems in different aspects of impulsive decision-making.
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE; FRONTAL CORTEX; GAMBLING; IMPULSIVITY; SEROTONIN; SUBCORTICAL
Abstract-Résumé: Impulsivity is a characteristic of human behavior that can be both beneficial and detrimental in our everyday lives.  An impulsive decision can allow us to seize a valuable opportunity or make a disastrous choice which we live to regret.  High levels of impulsivity are not only considered socially unacceptable, but they are a key symptom in a range of psychiatric illnesses including bipolar disorder, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), pathological gambling, personality disorders and substance abuse.  Understanding the neurobiological basis of impulsivity could therefore provide valuable insight into these afflictions and potentially lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies.  In this grant, we propose to explore the role of different regions of the brain on aspects of impulsive decision-making and gambling using tests which measure these cognitive processes in rats.  We also want to determine whether changing levels of brain chemicals such as dopamine and serotonin within these different brain regions can affect impulsive choice.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impacts of disulfide bond CD40/CD40 dimers in the biological responses.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGY; AUTOIMMUNE DISEASE; CELL SIGNALING; IG SWITCHING; IMMUNOPRECIPATION; INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE DIRECT SITE MUTAGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: As a part of our assignment, we have certain leads and we are trying to understand the role of some surface molecules such as CD40 on B cells and its ligand (s) on T cells which are central in the regulation of the immune response and in the pathogenesis of autoimmune disease in general and rheumatoid arthritis in particular. We have shown that CD40 can exist at level in B cells in a dimeric form (CD40/CD40). We were surprized when we noticed that the presence of CD40/CD40 did not attract the attention of the researcher till we showed its constituitive presence in so many cells. We further showed that its oligomerisation can trasnslocate it to designated or more favoured domains (lipid rafts) to be able to relay signals toward down stream substrates for the final effector response. Now we are interested to go after these downstream messages one by one to be able to best focus our efforts to target the disease more precisely.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; APOPLEXIE, INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of TRPM Channels in Ischemic Brain Damage
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ANTIOXIDANTS; BRAIN ISCHEMIA; CATION CHANNELS; CELL CULTURES; FREE RADICALS
Abstract-Résumé: TRP channels are proteins that have only recently been investigated as possible key players in tissue ischemia, including stroke. Of these, TRPM7 and TRPM2 have been shown to be activated by free radicals, and to mediate anoxic damage in cultured neurons. However, their investigation has been hampered by the lack of pharmacological modulators and transgenic animals. Here we propose to use genetic disruption approaches to regionally suppress TRPM channels in the  mature mammalian CNS, and to use high throughput screens to derive small molecule inhibitors of these channels. Using these tools, we will investigate the roles of TRPM2 and TRPM7 in cultured neurons, brain slices, and whole animals both under normal (physiological) conditions, and during stroke. The information gained will provide tools for the study of these important membrane channels, and potential therapies for ischemic brain damage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pannexin-1 Hemichannel Activation in Neurons.
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GLUTAMATE EXCITOTOXICITY; ISCHEMIA; NMDA RECEPTOR; PANNEXIN HEMICHANNEL; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke occurs when a blood vessel to the brain is blocked or ruptures.  This results in rapid death of neurons due to energy deprivation (i.e. loss of oxygen and glucose).  These dead cells form the beginning of an infarct (dead tissue), which release neurotransmitters that become harmful to neighboring cells.  This process, called excitotoxicity, culminates in a final brain lesion that will determine the severity of impairment experienced by the patient - including loss of motor control, epilepsy and death.  In both the cases of pathological oxygen / glucose deprivation and glutamate excitotoxicity, death of the neurons involves a loss of membrane potential (depolarization), dysregulation of ionic balance, and mitochondrial inhibition.  I recently reported that a novel and unique type of ion channel, pannexin-1 is activated by oxygen / glucose deprivation and by glutamate receptor stimulation.  The goal of this proposal is to test the hypothesis that neuronal necrosis induced by excitotoxic insults requires the activation of pannexin-1 hemichannels.  The ultimate goals are to understand the mechanisms regulating pannexin-1 hemichannels, and to determine if these channels contribute to neuronal death.  The work will greatly increase understanding of fundamental neuronal pathologies and potentially lead to the development of novel treatments for neurodegeneration.

OrgNm: Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM)
TitreApplicationTitle: Redox regulation of the RSV-induced proinflammatory response in airway epithelial cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; GENE REGULATION; PROINFLAMMATORY RESPONSE; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; RESPIRATORY SYNCYTIAL VIRUS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Infection by the Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in young children and ederly is associated with acute severe respiratory tract illness, such as broncholitis or pneumonia, which are associated with morbidity and mortality. Despite intensive research, the development of efficient vaccine or treatment failed. The search for novel RSV treatment remains a priority and requires a better understanding of the RSV immunobiology. In particular, more information is needed on the molecular basis that control the first line of immune response, known as innate immune response. This response is of particular importance as it is essential to limit virus spreading, but also as it orchestrates the subsequent specific immune responses. The innate immune response involves the production of cytokines and chemokines, which are factors that have the ability to limit virus replication, and attract and activate immune cells to the site of infection. The inflammatory process is a normal response to foreign invaders. However, in the context of RSV infection the production of cytokines/chemokines is exaggerated and the levels of specific chemokines in the lung of children infected with RSV are correlated with the severity of the virus-associated disease, thus suggesting that the production of chemokines is a potential target for the development of new therapies. Most of the known signaling molecules that link virus recognition to the innate immune response genes have been identified in the past 5 years and much remain to be done to understand how they are regulated. Our research endeavor is aimed at characterizing the molecular mechanisms involved in the regulation of these signaling pathways in order to define how the production of cytokines could be limited. Our work specifically focuses on the role of oxygen derivatives, which we recently identified as being key regulators of this response. We believe that our research will help design new therapeutic agents that are urgently needed.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: SCIENCES DENTAIRES/BIOLOGIE ORALE; MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional studies and experimental manipulation of ameloblastin expression
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CALCIFIED TISSUES; CELL BIOLOGY; DENTAL/PERIODONTAL DISEASES; ENAMEL PROTEINS; GENE TRANSFER
Abstract-Résumé: Bone, mineral and tooth disorders affect large segments of the population. The combination of rare forms of these diseases with very common ones has a major impact on quality of life, and represents an important financial burden for society. The decoding of the human genome and identification of specific genes associated with diseases has raised high hopes. Since biological processes occur through the action of one or more proteins, elucidating the nature and function of proteins encoded by the genome is the next challenge scientists face in understanding how the body functions and how disease alters this pattern. This information is essential in order to develop novel, biologic therapies, based on the body's own elements, and to select relevant drug targets.  In calcified tissues, noncollagenous matrix proteins (NCPs) play important roles in both cell and matrix events. We will be working on elucidating the function of ameloblastin, a unique tooth NCP that is necessary for formation of enamel, whose absence in knockout mice favors the development of odontogenic tumors, and for which one of its sister proteins is showing an interesting potential for the treatment of periodontal disease and bone repair. This protein also appears essential for maintaining the integrity of the gingival seal around teeth, the first line of defence for preventing periodontal diseases.  To achieve our objectives we will use well-established animal models and gene transfer. The proposed integrated set of experiments is expected to generate new information about the role of ameloblastin in calcified tissues and in the gingival seal, and assess its potential for therapeutic applications. They are also expected to help with the application of gene therapy protocols for the treatment of calcified tissue diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic dissection of the host response to intestinal infections
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS OF HUMAN DISEASE; GASTROENTEROLOGY; GENETICS; HOST:PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; INNATE IMMUNITY; POSITIONAL CLONING
Abstract-Résumé: Infectious diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide, and host genetics play an important role in determining the ultimate outcome of many infections. Performing genetic analyses in mouse models of infection has many advantages over genetic analyses in humans, and a number of important breakthroughs in our understanding of the human response to infection have come through mouse genetic studies. Here, we propose to apply a genetic approach to a mouse model of enterohemorrhagic and enteropathogenic Escherichia coli infection. These pathogenic bacteria colonize the lumen of the intestinal tract, and cause diarrhea with potentially fatal complications. Our preliminary studies indicate the presence of a gene that controls the susceptibility of mice to these types of infections. We aim to identify and characterize this gene in order to understand how it controls susceptibility to infection. These studies promise to identify new mechanisms of host defense, and to help us understand the variability of host response to infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Rap1 in regulating cell function
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL ADHESION; CELL MOTILITY; CYTOSKELETAL FUNCTION; DEVELOPMENT; ONCOGENES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Rap1 is a signaling protein that is involved in the regulation of a number of cell functions, including motility, cell shape, adhesion and phagocytosis, and its mis-regulation can lead to cancer. The challenge is to understand how this single protein can regulate such a myriad of cell functions.  We will determine the various ways in whch the protein is activated and the various ways in which the signal is then transduced.

ClasseRechercheFR: AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE; TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Control of movement: Brain stem control of locomotion
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN STEM; CENTRAL PATTERN GENERATOR; LOCOMOTION; RETICULAR FORMATION; SPINAL CORD; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: It has been known for about one century that the spinal cord contains the nerve cells and networks necessary to produce the basic rhythm and pattern of walking. These networks are often called "central pattern generators" or CPGs. Over the last few decades, several laboratories have investigated the pathways that the brain uses to control these spinal CPGs. However, there is a paucity of details regarding these pathways. This project will use new mouse transgenic technology combined with advanced imaging techniques to study the neurons and pathways involved in activating spinal CPGs. The neurons will be identified, and their properties will be studied. The understanding of these pathways is essential to the development of strategies aimed at regenerating motor control pathways following spinal cord injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Dissection of Host Response Against Respiratory Virus Infections in Recombinant Congenic Strains of Mice
Keywords-MotsClés: DISEASE MODELS; GENE EXPRESSION/GENE CLONING; GENETIC CONTROL; QUANTITATIVE TRAIT LOCI; RECOMBINANT CONGENIC MICE; VIRAL INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: This application proposes a novel approach towards the understanding of susceptibility and resistance to infections with clinically-important respiratory viruses in a unique mouse model. Research progress of our group and others over the last 3 decades clearly indicated that host genes play an essential role in the onset, progression and ultimate outcome of infection with many pathogens. These genetic factors are often impossible to find in human patients and infected populations, without the prior knowledge of their existence, location, regulation and function, which can only be discovered in experimental animals, primarily the mouse.  We have preliminary data which suggest that various inbred mouse strains are, genetically, either resistant or susceptible to infection with influenza virus (FLU-HK), a mouse-adapted agent of pandemic influenza, with coronavirus (MHV1) which produces SARS-like disease and with ectromelia (ECTV) virus, causing a smallpox-like disease. Our group has developed a special gene-discovery platform, namely the recombinant congenic strains (RCS) of mice, each carrying a unique recombinant genotype derived from virus-susceptible and virus-resistant parents. This proprietary platform will be used to dissect the individual genetic and functional components of the host responses to these viral infections and will provide invaluable information as to the genes, and mechanisms regulated by these genes, in our search for new anti-viral drugs and vaccines in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: A longitudinal study to identify factors that trigger ventricular tachyarrythmias among persons with implanted cardioverter defibrillators
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENT; IMPLANTED CARDIOVERTER DEFIBRILLATORS; SUDDEN CARDIAC ARREST; TRIGGERING FACTORS; VENTRICULAR TACHYARRHYTHMIAS
Abstract-Résumé: Sudden death from heart rhythm disorders (arrhythmias) is one of the leading causes of death in Canada. It is widely accepted that cigarette smoking, obesity, lack of exercise, high blood pressure, high levels of cholesterol increase the likelihood of developing and dying from cardiovascular disease. However, the chain of events leading up to sudden cardiac death from abnormal heart rhythms is not well understood. We know that persons with cardiovascular disease are at very high risk but there is little high quality information regarding what factors "trigger" these fatal heart rhythms. Many people at high risk have defibrillators implanted under the skin to detect these abnormal rhythms and correct them through electrical pacing and shocks. Because these devices record cardiac rhythms (ECG) in their electronic memories, we propose to follow a group of patients (a 'cohort') through time to determine whether certain factors, such as increasing air pollution, higher temperatures, anger, and drugs cause these abnormal heart rhythms. In this study we will follow a group of persons, age 50-75 years, living in Montreal who have received a new defibrillator. At the beginning of the study, we will characterize their illnesses and ask them questions about lifestyle (e.g., smoking) and other relevant questions.  They will be given a questionnaire about daily activities and ask them to fill this out from time to time.  They will also complete the same questionnaire when they receive a shock from the defibrillator, and so we will be able to compare their activities when they did and did not have a shock. In addition, by making use of hourly measurements of air pollution in the city, we will be able to determine whether these shocks occurred more frequently when air pollution was higher or lower.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proteomic Analysis of the Ubiquitin Proteasome System and the Protein Quality Control Machinery
Keywords-MotsClés: MASS SPECTROMETRY; PARKINSON DISEASE; PROTEASOME; PROTEIN AGGREGATE; QUALITY CONTROL; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: The cell has an elaborate system for eliminating proteins that can be compared to a garbage collecting and recycling system. First, a quality control machinery specifically recognizes proteins that are damaged or not properly folded. These unwanted proteins are then tagged by the attachment of a small protein called ubiquitin. Finally, the ubiquitin-tagged proteins are recognized by the proteasome, a complex protein structure that selectively destroys them. Perturbation of this system has dramatic consequences for the cell. Unwanted proteins accumulate until they form large aggregating structures in the cell. Parkinson~s disease, affecting more than 1.5 million people in North America, has long been associated with the impairment of this degradation machinery. However, very little is known about the exact mechanism of this process and which proteins are affected.  My laboratory has developed techniques for specifically identifying proteins that are targeted to the proteasome. The focus of my study will be to identify which proteins are actually targeted by the quality control machinery for recognition by the proteasome. In addition, I will identify which other genes are associated with the quality control machinery. My work has the potential of providing fundamental knowledge for the understanding of the quality control mechanism and how this system may be involved in pathologies like Parkinson~s disease. It might also uncover new biomarkers for diagnosis and targets for new therapeutic treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Experimental therapies for vascular remodeling diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; DHEA; K+ CHANNEL; NUCLEAR FACTOR OF ACTIVATED T CELLS; PI3KINASE; VASCUAR REMODELING DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: The thickened wall of blood vessels characterizes many and common diseases. This results from excessive growth of cells within the blood vessel wall but the mechanism causing this abnormality are unknown. Although we have learned much about prevention of blood vessel disease, we know very little about how to reverse established disease. This is particularly challenging because the therapies ideally have to remove the excessive cells in the diseased blood vessels (for example a thickened coronary artery following an angioplasty procedure) without affecting the normal vessels in other areas of the body (for example the kidney blood vessels). We have evidence that a very simple drug (similar to hormones that normally circulate in the blood stream) called DHEA might indeed be able to achieve this. We believe that this drug acts on mechanisms that are activated only in rapidly growing cells in the wall of a disease vessel but not in the quiet resting cells in the wall of a normal blood vessel. Therefore it might be able to completely spare the normal blood vessels in the body from adverse effects. We propose to use several animal models as well as tissues from human beings (taken at the time of surgery) and many cutting edge techniques to show that a thickened artery in the neck of rats and mice (the carotid artery, which is very frequently diseased in humans causing strokes) can become thin again, improving the blood flow to the brain. If we succeed we will be able to convince physicians to try this medication in human clinical trials. The possibility that this drug might reverse the thickening of blood vessels without affecting normal vessels and the fact that this drug is easy to take (as a pill) and cheap (its available as an over the counter medication) is very exciting.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
TitreApplicationTitle: Diabetes, neuron degeneration and insulin signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETIC PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY; DIABETIC POLYNEUROPATHY; INSULIN; NERVE REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes mellitus is rising in prevalence worldwide.  Up to one-half of diabetic patients may suffer neurological complications, particularly polyneuropathy (damage to peripheral nerves).  Peripheral nerve damage results in loss of sensation, intractable pain, and later muscle weakness.  Currently there is no therapy to arrest or reverse the disorder.  There has been disagreement whether polyneuropathy arises because of high glucose levels or because of lack of insulin.  This grant addresses the accumulating evidence that lack of insulin or inappropriate insulin signaling on nerve cells contributes to damage.  The Zochodne laboratory has demonstrated that nerve cells have receptors for insulin and that they can dramatically alter their behaviour (increase regeneration, survive damage) when insulin is directly applied to them irrespective of glucose levels in blood.  The proposed grant would explore this relationship further in both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes. We want to discover whether insulin, correctly applied directly to neurons is capable of reversing the earliest molecular changes of nerve damage, whether nerve cells become resistant to the effect of insulin in Type 2 diabetes, what the impact of diabetes and insulin are on nerve regeneration and finally how new forms of delivery directly to nerve cells or related therapies that impact insulin pathways in cells might potentially reverse neuropathy and open the way for better treatments.
