TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics of Reading Disabilities
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSOCIATION; LINKAGE; READING DISABILITIES; SIB-PAIR ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Reading disabilities (RD) are a major social, educational, and mental health problem with prevalence conservatively estimated between 3 to 6% of school children.  Twin and family studies have produced evidence for a strong genetic component, prompting investigations by several groups into the molecular genetic basis of this disorder. Linkage studies have pointed to ten different chromosomal regions and fine mapping in these regions have provided association to specific genes. In our previous studies, we have collected DNA on 376 families with a child with reading problems and their siblings (502 children).  These children have been assessed for all aspects of reading, language and spelling ability.  We have identified several genes with evidence for association to RD in our families (KIAA0319, KIAA0319L, EKN1, Protogenin). In the continuation of this project, we will recruit an additional 400 families.  We will collect a blood sample and isolate DNA from the families.  We will continue to study the genes that we have previously identified as associated to confirm their association and determine how they function differently in children at risk for reading problems.  We will also begin fine mapping for gene identification in 5 additional linkage regions.  The finding of genetic susceptibility factors for RD will be an invaluable step forward in understanding the molecular mechanisms of this disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: EF-hand proteins and calcium-mediated modulation
Keywords-MotsClés: BINDING; CALCIUM; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; EF-HAND PROTEINS; REGULATION; STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Calcium (Ca2+) is involved in the regulation of a vast array of cellular processes.  Ca2+-binding proteins and/or domains, such as EF-hand motifs, bind Ca2+ and result in the regulation of specific molecular functions.  For example, calmodulin (CaM) is such a protein that plays a central role in the signalling of Ca2+.  EF-hand Ca2+-binding proteins, including CaM, interact with their targets using a variety of novel, structural mechanisms.  We are constantly discovering new interactions between CaM with novel proteins, even including CaM with other EF-hand proteins.  Moreover, we are learning that the EF-hand domains may also have a function that is independent of its regulatory function.  Calcineurin is a Ca2+/CaM dependent phosphatase (i.e. removes phosphate groups) which has been linked to neurological disorders such as schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease, as well as to the immune response system in cases such as organ rejection.  Our goals of this project will be to study the interaction of calcineurin with CaM, its regulation by CaM, in addition to the novel function of the EF-hand motif.  Calpain is a Ca2+-dependent protease which has been linked to a wide range of disorders including, but not restricted to, Parkinson's disease, muscular dystrophy, diabetes, and gastric cancer.  We have recently discovered a new association between the calpain EF-hand small subunit, CaM and beta-PIX.  The second goal of this project will be to investigate the specific interactions involved in these associations and the functional implications thereof.  Through our research, we hope to gain a better understanding of the specific interactions involving these Ca2+-dependent proteins and their regulation, in order to furhter our knowledge on the processes they affect.  Morever, this should aid in developing specific therapeutic strategies against the various disease that they have been associated with.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the Phosphoinositides and Moesin on the Actin/Microtubule crosstalk during cell division.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN; CELL DIVISION; DROSOPHILA; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; MICROSCOPY; MICROTUBULE
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of this project is to understand the molecular basis underlying how cell division is deregulated in cancer cells. This study will be performed using drosophila fly as a model using modern genetic and cell biology tools to identify and characterize novel genes involved in the control of cell division. In the last past years, Drosophila melanogaster has proven to be an excellent model organism to study such aspects of cell biology. Since most of the molecular functions are conserved throughout evolution, this work will provide new avenues to study the process of cell division across species. Deregulation of cell division being one of the major causes leading to cancer and metastasis, this work will enable a better understanding on the molecular pathways that prevent this disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; ARTHRITE/ARTHROSE
TitreApplicationTitle: Constitutive and regulated pathways of hyaluronan degradation
Keywords-MotsClés: EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; HYALURONAN TURNOVER; JOINT DISEASE; LYSOSOMAL ENZYMES; LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISORDER; MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Hyaluronan (HA) is a large polysaccharide secreted from cells to assemble their surrounding matrix.  It is abundant in many tissues, but has its highest concentration in connective tissues such as cartilage and synovial fluid of the joint.  The functions of HA differ depending on its concentration, size, and association with other matrix molecules. Large sized HA maintains tissue structure and integrity, while small sized HA promotes inflammation and other processes related to tissue injury.  However, no one knows whether small-sized HA is produced in living organisms.  We are studying hyaluronidases, the enzymes that break HA down, and are presumed to control the levels and sizes of HA.  There are three broadly distributed hyaluronidases (Hyal1, Hyal2, and Hyal3) and a deficiency in one of these (Hyal1) results in a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by joint and skin problems.  We have already generated mice with deficiencies in each of these three hyaluronidases, which we propose to characterize further to determine how each of these enzymes function. We will cross the hyaluronidase deficient mice with mice deficient in other enzymes involved in HA breakdown or synthesis in order to determine which enzymes are essential to break down HA.  In our Hyal1-deficient mice we have observed indicators of cartilage loss as early as 3 months. We will examine these abnormalities in more detail in order to better understand why they result from hyaluronidase deficiency.  Once we understand how the hyaluronidases function it may be possible to regulate their activity as a means of controlling HA function.  These studies are especially important given that HA is used in a broad range of medical devices.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ampakine Therapy to Alleviate Respiratory Depression
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAINSTEM; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MOTONEURONS; PREBOTZINGER COMPLEX; RESPIRATION; RESPIRATORY NEURAL CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Suppression of central respiratory drive by anesthetics and narcotics is a clinical problem. A pharmacological approach to alleviate respiratory depression without loss of analgesia and sedation is desirable. Further, advancements in drug treatment to counter endogenous respiratory disorders such as those that occur in some newborns. My laboratory has recently demonstrated that a novel class of drug, called ampakines, is very effective in countering respiratory depression in a variety of rodent models. We now have access to ampakines that have been proven safe for human use. Thus, we are proposing a comprehensive series of studies toward gaining necessary pre-clinical data. This will be essential for achieving the ultimate goal of having ampakines being used routinely in clinical settings.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular activity of prion protein oligomers in health and diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; CELLULAR TRAFFICKING; LYSOSOME EXOCYTOSIS; NEURONAL DEGENERATION; PRION DISEASES; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Prion diseases, also known as transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs), are a group of fatal neurological diseases of humans and animals. These diseases have achieved enhanced visibility in the media due to the appearance of bovine prion disease or "mad cow disease" and its transmission to humans. They are characterized by deterioration of the central nervous system which causes vacuoles (sponge-like holes) in the brain. Appearance of spongiform degeneration of the brain is a consequence of extensive neuronal cell loss. The toxic neuronal molecule is the prion protein, identified by Nobel Prize winner Stanley Prusiner. This protein accumulates as fibrils in the central nervous system of affected humans and animals. The mechanism whereby prion protein mediates neuronal cell death remains unclear. We are studying how this abundant neuronal protein switches from a harmless state to a neurotoxic state. Eventually, our research will directly improve human health, and also indirectly by improving health of animals entering the human food chain. The acquired knowledge will also have implications in other neurodegenerative diseases characterized by the transformation of innocuous endogenous neuronal proteins into toxic molecules. As society ages, these incurable, disabling, and often fatal neurodegenerative diseases will become increasingly common and our research will benefit the health of populations.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Hippocampal Plasticity: Cellular & Molecular Physiology of the K-Dependent Na/Ca-Exchanger, NCKX2
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS; MEMBRANE TRANSPORT; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NEURONAL FUNCTION; SODIUM-CALCIUM EXCHANGE; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Ionized calcium (Ca2+) is a critical signaling molecule in brain neurons. The concentration of Ca2+ is controlled by membrane transporters, including surface Na/+Ca2+-exchangers. Our previous work has helped establish that newly identified K+-dependent Na+/Ca2+-exchangers play a predominant role in controlling Ca2+ flux at numerous neuronal sites. Recent studies to characterize the NCKX2 protein have identified important new modes of regulation for this transporter. Further work established that when the gene for NCKX2 was knocked out, the mice display dramatically reduced long term potentiation in the hippocampus (a change in neuronal connectivity thought to be associated with behavioural changes), and very specific deficits in motor learning and memory. The experiments proposed here will lead to an in depth understanding how the NCKX2 protein functions and is regulated, as well as to further knowledge of how Ca2+ transport by NCKX2 contributes to the changes in nerve transmission that underlie memory and learning. These advances will further our understanding of the molecular events that are responsible for critical behaviours " such as learning and memory " and thus lead to insights into how these processes go awry in disease states, possibly leading toward in clinical and therapeutic interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Distinct insulin exocytotic actions of Syntaxins-1 and -2
Keywords-MotsClés: CAPACITANCE MEASUREMENTS; DIABETES; EVANESCENT MICROSCOPY; EXOCYTOSIS; INSULIN SECRETION; SNARE PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: In diabetes, both first and second phases of insulin release are severely reduced.  First phase insulin release from pancreatic islet b-cells is from insulin granules already docked onto the plasma membrane, which undergo fusion with the plasma membrane, called primary exocytosis. We hypothesize that primary exocytosis is mediated by Syntaxin-1A. The ensuing second phase insulin release arises from recruitment of insulin granules to fuse with those granules undergoing exocytosis, called compound exocytosis.  This mechanism is under-utilized even in normal islet b-cells and even less so in diabetes. We postulate that insulin granule-granule fusion is mediated by Syntaxin-2A. Here, we will dissect the role of Syntaxin 1A and 2A in primary exocytosis and granule-granule fusion, and also examine their possible influences on ion channels that regulate the secretory process. We will use an islet b-cell specific knockout of Syntaxin 1A and global Syntaxin 2A knockout mice. We will examine the various components of insulin secretion using a battery of state-of-the-art assays to very finely measure insulin granule exocytosis (islet perifusion, electron microscopy, imaging single granule exocytosis, and capacitance measurements) and membrane ion channel activities (electrophysiology). This work will reveal therapeutic targets that can selectively rescue first and second phase insulin secretory deficiencies in diabetes.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - C: Behavioural Studies, Neuroscience and Cognition
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
TitreApplicationTitle: The Cortical Sites of Amblyopia and Suppression in Humans
Keywords-MotsClés: AMBLYOPIA; BINOCULAR VISION; BRAIN IMAGING; HUMANS; STRABISMUS; SUPPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Amblyopia or lazy eye (incidence 3%) is the greatest single cause of unilateral blindness in the North American adult population.  It results from a disruption to normal visual development in childhood.  The view we have of the type of brain deficit underlying amblyopia is now out of date as it relies on findings in the 70s and 80s suggesting that the site is restricted to the cortex and involves loss of binocular connections. My recent work suggests that binocular connections within the brain are not lost but are intact and can be strengthened.  Also I have shown that the cerebral cortex is not the only site of amblyopia, a subcortical structure named the Lateral Geniculate Nucleus is also affected.   The present grant directs itself to these two new findings that lie at the heart of the amblyopic problem and therefore hold the key to developing new therapeutic approaches to reverse this visual loss in adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: Insulin sensitivity of protein in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION ASSESSMENT; CELLULAR PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; HYPERINSULINEMIC CLAMPS; INDIRECT CALORIMETRY; INSULIN RESISTANCE; STABLE ISOTOPE KINETIC TECHNIQUES
Abstract-Résumé: We have established that body protein balance deteriorates in obese adults with poorly controlled diabetes, when blood sugar levels are elevated. Further, by either intensive insulin treatment or by the combination of calorie-reduced diets and oral medications, these abnormalities can be corrected. We examined the role of resistance to the action of insulin upon protein balance. By using a sophisticated test named the 'hyperinsulinemic, euglycemic, isoaminoacidemic clamp' we kept the levels of amino acids or building blocks of protein constant in blood and found that insulin could induce considerable protein synthesis in nondiabetic young volunteers. However, in obese persons without diabetes, protein synthesis was less. The research now goes forward in persons with type 2 diabetes, known to have insulin resistance of glucose and explore the effects of high blood sugar and high levels of amino acids as well as those of diabetes treatment and low protein diets, on the insulin resistance of protein and glucose. The outcomes will have implications for the appropriate prescription of dietary protein for obese persons with diabetes, to improve their health while avoiding the risk of loss of essential body protein. This is critical, as the worsening epidemic of obesity is causing alarming rises in incidence of diabetes in the Canadian population, including children and teens.

ResearchClassEN: METABOLISM AND NUTRITION; LIPOPROTEINS, LIPID TRANSPORT
ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; LIPOPROTEINES, TRANSPORT LIPIDIQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Phosphatidylcholine metabolism and obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: CTP:PHOSPHOCHOLINE CYTIDYLYLTRANSFERASE; HIGH DENSITY LIPOPROTEINS (HDL); LOW DENSITY LIPOPROTEINS (LDL); OBESITY; PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE; PHOSPHATIDYLETHANOLAMINE N-METHYLTRANSFERASE
Abstract-Résumé: Cholesterol and fat are carried in the circulatory system by particles called lipoproteins.  In addition, these particles contain specific proteins and phospholipids.  Phospholipids are molecules that are insoluble in water and form the membranes of cells and also the surface of lipoproteins.  The major phospholipid in lipoproteins is phosphatidylcholine (PC). Two major classes of lipoproteins, VLDL and HDL, are secreted from the liver into the bloodstream where VLDL is converted to LDL, the lipoprotein that delivers cholesterol to other body tissues such as muscle. We have discovered that the liver has to make PC in order to secrete VLDL and HDL. In the last few years we have found that an enzyme in PC biosynthesis called PEMT is important in the secretion of VLDL. Moreover, mice that lack PEMT are greatly protected from atherosclerosis. Strikingly, we have found that mice that lack PEMT are protected from diet-induced obesity. We shall investigate the mechanism for this protection against becoming fat. Such information should be very useful for the discovery of drugs that selectively inhibit PEMT and thereby lower atherosclerosis and obesity. Another recent finding is that PC on LDL can be delivered to the liver and that half of this PC is converted into TG. We shall study how important PC on lipoproteins is for formation of TG in liver, adipose and muscle.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biology of Trophoblast Giant Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: HORMONE; KNOCKOUT MICE; MOLECULAR GENETICS; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: The placenta is essential for growth and survival of the fetus and abnormalities in its development are associated with common problems affecting the course of human pregnancy. Placental cells normally invade into the uterus to help promote the flow of blood to the implantation site. The placenta also produces a large variety of hormones whose primary functions include altering the physiology of the mother in order to promote fetal survival and growth. During pregnancy, maternal adaptations to pregnancy are known to include increasing the production of blood cells, neurons in the brain associated with the sense of smell, and the number of insulin producing cells in the pancreas. Defects in placental development are associated with a common disease of pregnancy called preeclampsia and in some cases restricted growth of the baby. The underlying molecular basis for human placental pathology is poorly understood and therefore there is no effective treatment or prevention. Also, the specific hormones that induce the range of normal maternal physiological changes are poorly understood. In the last five years we have used the power of genetic approaches available in the mouse model to identify genes that control the formation of the invasive and hormone-producing cell type in the placenta, called trophoblast giant cells. We have recently discovered an unexpected diversity in these cells. In the proposed work, we will use molecular and genetic approaches to determine the origins of these different subtypes and define their physiological roles during pregnancy.

ResearchClassEN: MULTIPLE DISEASE RELEVANCE; CANCER THERAPY GENERAL
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The RNA binding protein HuR is a key player in muscle cell differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: ELAV; HUR; MRNA EXPORT; MRNA STABILITY; MUSCLE SPECIFIC MOUSE KNOCKOUT; SKELETAL MUSCLE DIFFERENTIATION
Abstract-Résumé: The integrity of skeletal muscle tissue is vital for an organism to ensure normal locomotor activity, postural behavior, and breathing. Since these are basic functions, muscle fibers are under constant pressure and undergo minor and local injuries, which need to be immediately repaired. However, under intense physical activities, laceration or as a consequence of chronic diseases such as cancer, inflammation or innate genetic defects, muscles activate a sophisticated mechanism to replace the lost fibers. This regeneration process requires the sequential activation of specific genes that encode for key proteins. Over the last few decades, a lot of progress was made in delineating these molecular mechanisms, which had a direct impact in improving the strategies used to ameliorate lean muscle in domestic animals or to combat human muscle related diseases. Recently, we discovered a new layer of control needed to ensure normal muscle development. This type of control involves the regulation, through a protein named HuR, of the messages that are sent by the genes to translation machinery located in the cytoplasm to acquire the synthesis of specific proteins. The aim of this grant is to define the exact mechanisms by which HuR affects muscle adaptation to environmental changes. This grant application is built upon our previous observation showing that HuR protein is a key player in muscle development and decay resulting from strong inflammatory response. Thus, in this proposal, by using in vitro and in vivo models, we aim to define the HuR-dependent regulatory network that affect the fate of muscle tissues. By establishing this new level of regulation for muscle regeneration and decay, we hope to define HuR as a potential target for to either improve regeneration or combat some muscle-related illnesses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation and function of Dlx homeobox genes in the developing forebrain of vertebrates.
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT; GENE REGULATION; HOMEOBOX; TELENCEPHALON; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory is interested in the role played by a family of genes, the Dlx genes, in specifying the development of different types of neurons during brain development. We have identified DNA sequences whose role is to regulate expression of these genes to various cell types. These DNA sequences also position the Dlx genes in cascades of regulation that are important for brain development. We are using transgenic animals to test the function of these regulatory sequences. By defining their role, we will better understand brain development and the disease that result from abnormal brain development.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - A: Reproduction, Maternal, Child and Youth Health
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Models of Intraocular Pressure and Endothelin-1 Induced Optic Nerve Damage
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ENDOTHELIN-1; GLAUCOMA; GLIA; INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE; RETINAL GANGLION CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Optic neuropathies are among the leading causes of blindness in Canada.  Of these diseases, open-angle glaucoma is by far the most common affecting 1-2% of persons over the age of 40 years.  It leads to visual disability and blindness by damaging retinal ganglion cells which are specialized neurons in retina which transmit signals to the brain via their axons which make up the optic nerve.  The precise mechanism of how these messages are interrupted and how retinal ganglion cells actually die is unknown.  To address this question, this research programme will use experimental models of optic neuropathy in rats.  Our work to date has suggested that a class of supporting cells called astrocytes are intimately involved in retinal ganglion cell health by their interaction with their axons.  Specifically we have shown that a specific receptor called endothelin B (ETB) is expressed more readily by astrocytes in damaged eyes.  Using a variety of techniques we will determine the mechanism of ETB expression and its relation to retinal ganglion cell loss.  We will also use a strain of knockout rats in whom ETB is not functional to determine the modulating role of ETB.  The knowledge from this programme will lead to new therapeutic approaches targeted to ETB which will have a positive impact in the treatment of the optic neuropathies.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - A: Reproduction, Maternal, Child and Youth Health
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Bcl-2 family members in regulating placental cell fate
Keywords-MotsClés: BCL-2 MEMBERS; CELL DEATH; CELL PROLIFERATION; PLACENTA; PREECLAMPSIA/IUGR
Abstract-Résumé: Over 400,000 children are born annually in Canada and an estimated 10% of these births will be complicated by preeclampsia and/or intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Such babies are at significantly increased risk of death and serious illness and in adulthood have higher chances of developing cardiovascular disorders and diabetes. The major hurdle in developing therapies to prevent these complications of pregnancies is that their underlying cause remains an enigma. However, it is accepted that a common element in preeclamptic and IUGR pregnancies is the failure of normal placental development. In particular, the accelerated death and failure of trophoblast cells to adequately invade the maternal uterine tissue in order to establish connection between the mother and the baby as well as the optimal environment for the developing fetus. This proposal builds upon a series of novel experiments in which we have defined that two unique members of the Bcl-2 family (a family comprising pro-survival and pro-death molecules) play a major role in regulating trophoblast cell fate in normal and pathological pregnancies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of extracellular matrix by myofibroblasts in cardiac hypertrophy and failure
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FIBROSIS; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; HEART FAILURE; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; MYOFIBROBLASTS; SMADS
Abstract-Résumé: Despite recent advances in treatments for cardiac patients, most who survive the acute complications of a large heart attack (myocardial infarction or MI) go onto develop congestive heart failure from one to five years thereafter, and their prognosis is grave.  During the development of congestive heart failure, altered expression of several hormones occurs that confer significant changes to structure of the surviving heart and excessive healing of the cardiac scar.  This healing is so pronounced, it may eventually "spill over" from the scar to the rest of the heart.  Thus changes include abnormal growth  marked by fibrosis and inappropriate stiffening of all different regions of the damaged heart.  All events that lead to heart fibrosis are mediated by specialized non-muscle cells called cardiac myofibroblasts. TGF-b1 is a hormone known to activate other proteins called Smads, and Smads are linked to heart fibrosis.   Long-term exposure to TGF-b1 generates an imbalance, favouring a class of Smads called R-Smads.  We have found that R-Smads tend ramp up fibrosis and recently that they also cause myofibroblasts to contract just like a true muscle cell.  All of these changes are good for normal wound healing, but we also know that too much healing leads to heart failure.  Finally, we know that Smads can induce a special calcium transport protein called NCX1. Calcium is needed for activation of a broad range of cell functions.  We believe that Smads are important for stimulating myofibroblast function and one of the mechanisms for managing this is by changing NCX1 expression and/or function.  We have shown that NCX1 is found in heart myofibroblasts, but its influence on myofibroblast function has not been well studied. This proposal will provide answers about Smads and how they influence NCX1, and how this sequence of events may change calcium delivery in and thereby activate myofibroblast function.  These changes, in turn, contribute to heart fibrosis and failure.

CommitteeNameEN: Social & Developmental Aspects of Children's & Youth's Health
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Insulin resistance and beta cell dysfunction in early childhood: the role of maternal and infant metabolic risk factors
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOKINES; BETA CELL DYSFUNCTION; DIABETES; INSULIN RESISTANCE; METABOLIC SYNDROME; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Infants born to women with diabetes diagnosed during pregnancy are at an increased long-term risk of developing obesity and diabetes which results, in part, from the effects of exposure to high blood sugars before birth.  High blood sugars during pregnancy may result in reprogramming of important enzyme pathways involved in glucose (sugar) and insulin regulation in the developing baby.  Very little is known about how these processes evolve from birth to early childhood.  The overall goal of this study is to evaluate changes in growth, body fat and measures of glucose and insulin in infants over time from birth to 5 years of age born to mothers who had diabetes during pregnancy. We have previously studied these children from birth to one year of age, and for this study will extend the observation period from 2 to 5 years of age.  Annual measurements of growth and body fat will be taken, and at age 3 and 5 years a single blood sample will be taken to look at various factors associated with increased risk of obesity and diabetes.  These infants will be compared to a similar group of children of the same age, whose mothers did not have diabetes during pregnancy.  This study will allow us to assess early risk for obesity and diabetes, and determine how diabetes in pregnancy influences outcomes in children.  This could lead to early intervention studies to prevent obesity and diabetes in at-risk children.

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Functions and regulation of the papillomavirus E1 and E2 proteins in the viral life cycle
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; DNA REPLICATION; HELICASE; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are the cause of benign and malignant lesions of the epithelium. Notably, infection by oncogenic HPV types can lead to cervical cancer, the second most common cancer in women worldwide. HPV infections can also play a role in the development of anal cancer as well as non-melanoma skin cancers. Infection by non-oncogenic HPV types causes benign genital warts (condylomas), a less serious condition but one of the most frequent sexually transmitted disease. More rarely, they can also cause recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, a debilitating infection of the larynx and trachea acquired by infants during birth from an infected mother. Two proteins of the virus, E1 and E2, are absolutely necessary for replication of the viral genome and for disease development. Our studies are aimed at understanding the functions of these critical viral proteins, in particular how they subvert the host cell to promote replication of the viral genome. We propose to investigate which proteins of the infected cells E1 and E2 must interact with to achieve their function and what are the consequences of these interactions. A better understanding of how E1 and E2 interface with infected cells will suggest new ways to interfere with viral replication and thus open new avenues for the treatment of HPV infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Image-guided surgery for epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; DIGITAL HISTOLOGY; EPILEPSY; IMAGE-GUIDED SURGERY; IMAGING; RELAXATION MAPPING
Abstract-Résumé: The objective of this proposal is to integrate cutting-edge MRI tools, such as relaxation mapping and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to provide both enhanced localization of epileptic foci as well as optimal planning of resection. This approach is intended to ultimately eliminate the need for invasive and traumatic procedures  such as the Wada test (anesthetising a hemisphere) and the application of cortical and deep brain EEG electrodes commonly employed to lateralize epileptogenic activity and identify seizure foci. It will also combine the results of multiple MR testing protocols within a single environment. Key to this work will be the incorporation of these approaches with tools recently developed in our laboratory. The endpoint of this research will be an integrated analysis environment, which can serve as botha multi-spectral image analysis and diagnosis platform, as well as a surgical planning and guidance system. A unique feature of this system will be the ability to validate the MRI acquired tissue signatures based on relaxation mapping and diffusion, with high resolution digital histology volumes.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
ResearchClassEN: DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS; SCHIZOPHRENIA
ClasseRechercheFR: DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES; SCHIZOPHRENIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Dopaminergic circuits and risky decision making
Keywords-MotsClés: DECISION MAKING; DOPAMINE; MICRODIALYSIS; NUCLEUS ACCUMBENS; PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Impairments in decision making entailing cost/benefit evaluations about risks and rewards have been observed in a number of disorders such as schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease and stimulant addiction. In each of these conditions are thought to be due in part to dysfunction in brain dopamine transmission.  Similarly, drugs that increase dopamine activity can promote risk-seeking behaviours, such as pathological gambling.  These drugs stimulate proteins or "receptors" that dopamine interacts with to facilitate movement and cognition. However, is unclear are what parts of the brain, and what specific receptors dopamine may act on to alter risk-based decision making.  We intend to clarify these issues using an animal model of "gambling" behaviour. We have observed that drugs that increase dopamine release in the brain increase "risky decision-making" in a rodent version of a gambling task.  This research project will investigate where in the brain, and on which receptors dopamine acts on to promote risky choices.  We will also monitor changes in brain dopamine levels that are associated with risk-based decision making. These studies will provide important new information about how different brain circuits interact to solve these types of risk/reward decision making problems. Furthermore, the information provided by these studies may yield important insight into the brain dysfunction that underlies impairments in this form of cognition associated with a number of psychiatric disorders.

ClasseRechercheFR: RETARD MENTAL; TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic analysis of Williams-Beuren syndrome: linking genes with cognition and behaviour
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; COGNITION; GENETIC PATHWAYS; LEARNING DISABILITY; MOUSE MODELS; WILLIAMS-BEUREN SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Williams-Beuren syndrome (WBS) is a genetic disorder that presents with a complex set of medical and cognitive symptoms.  People with WBS have a range of disabilities such as  intellectual impairment, severe anxiety and poor spatial skills, yet have relatively well preserved language abilities and a natural friendliness and empathy. WBS is caused by the deletion of a small region on one copy of chromosome 7 that removes key genes involved in the development and function of the human brain. Understanding how these key genes contribute to the features of WBS will further our understanding of the genetic basis of cognitive function and give insight into common problems like mental retardation and anxiety disorder. We will use both human patients and mouse models to interrogate the role of specific genes that have been implicated in WBS, and so take advantage of this unique opportunity to link genes with human behavior and brain function.

OrgNm: Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM)
ResearchClassEN: MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; BRAIN TUMORS (INCL. RETINAL TUMORS)
ClasseRechercheFR: SCLEROSE EN PLAQUES; TUMEURS CEREBRALES (ET RETINIENNES)
TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Adhesion Molecules of the Blood-Brain Barrier Regulating CNS Inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION MOLECULES; BLOOD BRAIN BARRIER; ENDOTHELIUM; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NEURO-INFLAMMATION; TH17 LYMPHOCYTES
Abstract-Résumé: Immune cells travel from the blood to local sites of inflammation where they initiate and maintain tissue-specific immune responses. Normally, the brain is not easily accessible to cells of the immune system due to the presence of the endothelial blood-brain barrier (BBB). However, in the central nervous system (CNS) disorder Multiple Sclerosis (MS), a large number of immune cells known as TH1 and TH17 lymphocytes readily cross the BBB to infiltrate the brain and eventually lead to the formation of lesions. The movement of such aggressive immune cells from the blood to the CNS is orchestrated by many factors, including cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) that enable immune cells to adhere and cross over the BBB. We have identified MCAM (for Melanoma cell adhesion molecule) as a novel CAM expressed by endothelial cells of the BBB, and found it to play a central role in the migration of aggressive immune cells into the CNS. This research focuses on this newly discovered molecule used by immune cells to enter the CNS and to promote the development of MS lesions. This project expands our research program which aims at identifying attractive target for the development of novel therapies for the treatment of MS and other inflammatory diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: MRI of learning and memory
Keywords-MotsClés: LEARNING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI); MEMORY; NEUROANATOMY
Abstract-Résumé: Brain imaging has made tremendous advances in identifying which areas of the brain are active during a given task. The longer term implications of learning and memory on the brain have, however, remained elusive. There are cellular changes that are known to occur in the learning process whose aggregate could procue a local volume displacement that can be captured with imaging. A recent study by our group set out to test for this phenomenon using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) in mice; we indeed were able to detect subtle brain volume changes when the mice learned to navigate a maze. This proposal will expand on that research in order to establish a solid methodology for localizing the effects of learning in the brain. In particular, we intend to investigate the timecourse of these brain changes in response to learning and identify the cellular components that are their cause. We will also assess whether the alterations in the brain's response to learning can provide an early indicator of Alzheimer's Disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Bacterial Conjugation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-SENSE RNA; ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; BACTERIAL CONJUGATION; PROTEIN:RNA INTERACTIONS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Antibiotic resistant bacterial infections are becoming an increasingly serious health issue. Many of the pathogenic bacteria that infect humans have acquired this resistance through a process called bacterial conjugation, whereby bacteria exchange specialized portions of their DNA, called plasmids. In this way, many of the bacteria that infect humans have been able to rapidly acquire resistance from other bacterial species in which the resistance initially evolved. We have focused our work on the F family of plasmids, which are found in intestinal bacteria that cause diseases such as hemorrhagic colitis (hamburger disease). Our aim is to understand how a set of proteins made from the F plasmid coordinate the transfer of the plasmid from one cell to another. The insights gained from these studies could provide a rational basis for the design of new ways to control the spread of antibiotic resistance.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Epithelial cell signalling responses to attaching-effacing intestinal pathogens
Keywords-MotsClés: EPITHELIAL CELLS; ESCHERICHIA COLI; INFLAMMATION; PROTEIN KINASE C; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; STAT 1
Abstract-Résumé: Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC) O157:H7 is a non-invasive pathogen, which results in both sporadic cases and outbreaks of bloody diarrhea (hemorrhagic colitis) and kidney failure (hemolytic-uremic syndrome) in humans. Current therapy is limited to supportive care, because antibiotics likely increase the risk of harmful consequences, due to the release of bacterial-derived toxins. Improving future management options is likely to be based on a better understanding of how this bacterial pathogen causes disease.  We have demonstrated subversion of signal transduction responses in host cells infected with EHEC. The current application will focus on three complementary study aims to further characterize three inter-related signal transduction responses to EHEC, and the related murine enteric pathogen Citrobacter rodentium, following challenge of epithelial cells of human and mouse origin, respectively. We will: 1) determine whether nucleotide-binding domain-like receptors (Nod1 and Nod2) mediate EHEC- and C. rodentium-induced inhibition of the transcription factor, nuclear factor (NF) kappa B, 2) define bacterial and host factor(s) mediating bacterial inhibition of the interferon-gamma - Jak1,2 - Stat1 signal transduction cascade, and 3) delineate the role of atypical isoforms of protein kinase C (PKC) present in cholesterol-enriched microdomains of the plasma membrane in EHEC-  and C. rodentium-infected epithelia.  The model systems we employ have proven effective for testing the benefits of novel intervention strategies that are currently under development, and will define new target molecules and therapeutic approaches for use in managing this infectious disease. This research program will advance knowledge in the area of intestinal inflammation induced by a bacterial infection that causes both serious short-term disease and death and has the potential to induce chronic illnesses, including irritable bowel syndrome, in affected Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Signal crosstalk in lung injury and repair
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY AND REPAIR; CELL BIOLOGY; PATHOPHYSIOLOGY; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) means severe acute lung injury. It has very high mortality. SARS is one particular type of ARDS. It is a good example to let us know how severe this syndrome could be. Death of lung epithelial cells is an important component for this syndrome. Damaged lung tissue also cannot repair properly, which require cells to grow and migrate. Cell survival, proliferation, migration are fundamental functions controlled by intracellular signaling pathways. One of them is so-called PI3K/Akt pathway. Recently, we discovered a novel protein, and named it as XB130. We found it controls the PI3K/Akt pathway in lung epithelial cells, thus, controls cell survival, proliferation and migration. Transgenic mice with xb130 gene knocked out, antibodies, and molecular constructs have been generated. In this proposal, we will use these powerful molecular tools to determine the roles and mechanisms by which XB130 protect lung from injury (reducing cell death), and promote lung repair (enhance cell growth and migration). These studies may reveal new therapeutic target to reduce severity of lung injury and help patients to recover from this syndrome.

ClasseRechercheFR: ENDOCRINOLOGIE; CANCER DE LA PROSTATE ET DE LA VESSIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanism of action of the membrane-bound transcription factor AIbZIP
Keywords-MotsClés: AIBZIP; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; CONDITIONAL EXPRESSION; GENE EXPRESSION; PROSTATE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: AIbZIP (Androgen-Induced bZIP) is a transcription factor that is expressed in several organs of the endocrine and reproductive systems, and it is most abundant in the prostate gland. In addition, higher levels of AIbZIP are found in prostate and liver tumors, which suggests that AIbZIP may be linked to cancer. We previously found that the AIbZIP protein localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), a cellular organelle that is responsible for several critical biological functions, including protein synthesis. We recently discovered that AIbZIP becomes transcriptionally active and travels to the cell nucleus when prostate cells are exposed to drugs that interfere with protein maturation in the ER, thereby causing ER stress. In order to understand the consequences of AIbZIP activation we performed microarray experiments to identify genes that are regulated by AIbZIP. These studies revealed that AIbZIP induces the expression of CREB3, a transcription factor that is structurally related to AIbZIP. Subsequent studies revealed that ER stress activates AIbZIP before it activates CREB3, suggesting that AIbZIP plays an important role in the early phase of the ER stress response. Although these exciting discoveries shed new light on the physiological role of AIbZIP, several important questions remain unanswered. In the present research project we propose to determine precisely which genes are activated by AIbZIP during ER stress as well as the order in which they are activated. We will define the DNA sequences that are recognized by AIbZIP as well as transcription factors that cooperate with or otherwise modulate the transcriptional activity of AIbZIP. Given the importance of the ER stress response in health and disease, a better understanding of the mechanism of action of AIbZIP during ER stress could ultimately lead to the development of new therapeutic approaches for diseases in which ER stress plays a significant role.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mapping the human auditory cortex: low-level features and higher-order interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY CORTEX; COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: We will study the human auditory cortex using brain imaging techniques. Our work will help to map the basic characteristics of how the human auditory brain responds to different types of sounds, how it changes in response to training, and how it interacts with other parts of the brain. The research has implications for understanding differences in how individuals are able to learn to perceive sounds, such as speech sounds of a foreign language, or musical sounds. The research also helps to establish the basic mechanisms of cortical hearing, which is relevant for disorders such as developmental language impairment, or tinnitus, and is also relevant for improving the way that deaf people learn to interpret sounds coming from cochlear implants.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Molecular Cytology of Membrane Dynamics
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BASED ASSAY; CELL FREE ASSAY; CRYO-ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; CRYO-ELECTRON TOMOGRAPHY; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; NOVEL PROTEINS; QUALITY CONTROL; RNAI
Abstract-Résumé: Diseases of the secretory pathway include cancer, cystic fibrosis, diabetes and metabolic syndrome. Furthermore, all proteins found in body fluids which may be biomarkers for human diseases originate from the secretory pathway. These are either soluble secretory proteins such as alpha fetoprotein or shed proteins from the cell surface such as carcino embryonic antigen. Understanding the molecular mechanisms by which proteins and other macromolecules traverse the secretory pathway to exit the cell or from the plasma membrane is the key to developing diagnostics and therapeutics to human disease. The resource of the fundamental knowledge base we shall provide is even relevant to biofuel production since biofuels are a product of cellulose which must be elaborated and transported through the secretory pathway of plants. The detailed molecular machineries which regulate secretion as well as the productive folding of proteins in the secretory pathway is the object of this grant proposal. It will build on past work which has uncovered 345 new candidate proteins of the secretory pathway, as well as on past work which has led to the innovation of cell based and cell free assays. These assays will elucidate the mechanistic functions of proteins newly uncovered, as well as those proteins known to be found in the secretory pathway, in order to provide the knowledge base and resource to address human disease and biomarker discovery.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; BIOLOGIE MOLÉCULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Control mechanisms of fin regeneration in zebrafish
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE REGENERATION; BRANCHING MORPHOGENESIS; FIN REGENERATION; HEDGEHOG SIGNALLING; MICROARRAY ANALYSIS; ZEBRAFISH TRANSGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Fish fins and limbs of mammals evolved from similar structures.  Fish have the ability to regenerate their fins after injury.  Regeneration depends on the formation of a blastema, a group of proliferative and undifferentiated cells which will progressively differentiate as the regenerate is growing. This process involves the reactivation of genetic programs that took place during development of the embryo and larvae. One important question to address mechanisms of regeneration is to determine how this blastema is formed and maintained during the regeneration process.   My laboratory is studying the molecular pathways for cell-cell communication that we think is crucial for the formation and maintenance of the blastema and for the synthesis of new bone during regeneration.  We are using techniques that allow us to inactivate gene function or, conversely, to activate the gene function in places where this gene does not normally function.  We are using other techniques to eliminate specific cells of the regenerate to examine the impact of the loss of these cells on the regeneration process.  This work will allow us to better understand how cells communicate with one another to assure the growth of the fin regenerate and to precisely position the newly-forming bone.  The relative simplicity of the fin regenerate make it an excellent model to study regeneration mechanisms, more specifically the relative ability of various cell types to trigger and/or maintain regeneration, a fundamental knowledge that will be important in establishing strategies to develop methods, drugs or tools to induce a regeneration response to injury, trauma or degenerative event in species that do not regenerate, including humans.

ResearchClassEN: CNS ORGANIC; ATTENTION DEFICIT HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER (ADHD)
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; TROUBLE D'HYPERACTIVITÉ AVEC DÉFICIT DE L'ATTENTION (THADA)
TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying development and plasticity of prefrontal attention circuitry
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTICOTHALAMIC NEURONS; DENDRITIC MORPHOLOGY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS; NICOTINIC ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTORS; PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are thought to play a key trophic role in brain development, and aberrant regulation of nicotinic receptors is seen in several serious neurodevelopmental conditions, such as autism, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. It is not well understood how perinatal brain development is changed by the drug nicotine, a partial agonist of nicotinic receptors; however, it is clear that children with prenatal exposure to nicotine are at elevated risk for developing attention deficit disorder. The drug nicotine binds to nicotinic receptors, which are also stimulated by the endogenous neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Nicotine can activate these receptors, but it can also inactivate or desensitize them. The goal of this proposal is to test specific hypotheses about how aberrant nicotinic receptors or developmental nicotine exposure disrupts the development of attention circuitry. We will focus on the corticothalamic neurons, a group of neurons that direct attentional focus by modulating information flow through the thalamus to the cortex. We have previously shown that there is strong developmental regulation of nicotinic acetylcholine currents in these neurons. Here, we will examine the molecular composition of these receptors, test mechanisms through which nicotinic stimulation can alter the properties and plasticity of corticothalamic neurons, probe how these neurons are affected by chronic exposure to nicotine during development, and ultimately test the in vivo effects of corticothalamic nicotinic receptors on attention.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of the Melanin-Concentrating Hormone System in the Regulation of Energy Balance
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; BROWN ADIPOSE TISSUE; ENERGY BALANCE; ENERGY EXPENDITURE; HYPOTHALAMUS
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the progresses made, the complex etiology of obesity remains poorly understood. Etymologically derived from the Latin word >obedere~ -- to eat in excess -- obesity has to be first and foremost seen as an energy-balance-regulation-associated disorder. Energy balance regulation depends on controls exerted on food intake and energy expenditure, and the brain as well as the peripheral organs or tissues sensitive to variations in energy stores and nutritional status are determinant in such a regulation. Within the brain, the controls exerted on food intake and energy expenditure are insured by interconnected neurons producing different peptides and classical neurotransmitters that have been regrouped into >anabolic~ (promoting energy deposition) and >catabolic~ entities. The main goal of the proposed research program is to further delineate the mechanisms whereby certain neural control food intake and energy expenditure. Using various techniques and approaches, we proposed a research plan aimed at describing the mechanism whereby a key neurosystem in energy balance regulation, namely the melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH) system, exerts its effect on food intake and energy expenditure. The three objectives of the program are (i) to explore the mechanisms whereby the MCH system acts to increase food intake and to decrease locomotion; (ii) to determine the circuitries implicated in the effects of melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH) on the activity of the sympathetic nervous system in brown and white adipose tissues; (iii) to characterize the metabolic phenotype of a transgenic (knock-in) mouse expressing the human MCH receptor 2.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES A VIRUS
TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization and improvement of the intrinsic adjuvant properties of papaya mosaic virus-like particles: An innovative vaccine platform.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUVANT; ADJUVANTED INFLUENZA VACCINES; CROSS PRESENTATION; INNATE IMMUNE RESPONSE; PAPAYA MOSAIC VIRUS; PATHOGEN ASSOCIATED MOLECULAR PATTERN
Abstract-Résumé: Vaccination has been the most efficient method for the control of infectious diseases, leading to eradication of small pox. Paradoxally, most vaccines on the market provide partial protection. Therefore, the development of vaccine platforms and adjuvants have been identified as the second and third top ten priorities by an eminent group of researchers and health specialists for improvement of health worldwide. The threats of pandemics and the vulnerability of elderly to emerging infectious diseases and cancers generates a medical need for novel and efficient immunomodulatory molecules that could improve vaccines and be used in treatments of cancer.  We have recently shown that virus like particles (VLPs) derived from the nucleocapsid of papaya mosaic virus (PapMV) are excellent adjuvant that can trigger both arms of the immune system, the humoral (antibodies) and the cellular (CTL) responses. Therefore, this adjuvant respond to an unmet need because it can contribute to increase the immune response to current vaccine and serve as a platform for the vaccine design of more sophisticated subunit candidate vaccine. In this proposal, we propose to elucidate the mechanisms of action of this adjuvant to better comprehend how it interacts with the immune cells. Furthermore, we propose to take advantage of the plasticity of the PapMV platform to generate improved versions of this adjuvant using rational design and protein engineering. We believe that the outcome of this research proposal will have a major impact in the field of vaccinology and vaccine design.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms and Modulation of Spatio-temporal Organization of Human Ventricular Fibrillation
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN PHYSIOLOGY; SUDDEN DEATH; VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Sudden cardiac arrest has been called the number one health problem in Canada and the United States.  It is responsible for approximately 40,000 and 450,000 deaths a year, in Canada and United States respectively.  It is an equally serious health problem in most developed countries of the world. A large fraction of cases of sudden cardiac arrest are caused by the arrhythmia ventricular fibrillation.  As opposed to normal cardiac rhythm in which a steady, regular, organized electrical activation sequence of the ventricles leads to an organized contraction of the ventricular muscle that causes the efficient pumping of blood throughout the body, during ventricular fibrillation the cardiac electrical activation sequence is extremely rapid and much less organized, leading to tremulous, almost imperceptible, ventricular muscular contraction and the absence of blood flow. In the absence of blood flow, death quickly ensues.  While heart failure is primarily considered a disease that leads to power failure and poor cardiac output, approximately half of all deaths associated with heart failure are due to sudden cardiac arrest, suggesting that the heart failure process influences ventricular fibrillation. However the mechanisms of organization of electrical waves that maintain human ventricular fibrillation have not been studied. Currently electrical shock is the only available therapy to halt ventricular fibrillation. The objective of the project is to perform hanging human heart mapping studies to understand the mechanisms of waveform behavior of VF that is thought to be important in the mechanism of VF. Armed with this knowledge we also plan to modulate VF by strategies of pharmacological intervention and pacing therapies that would be give us potential interventions that would treat this life threatening arrhythmia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interplay of Transporters, Enzymes, and Nuclear Receptors in First-Pass Drug Absorption
Keywords-MotsClés: ABSORPTION; ENZYMES AND TRANSPORTERS; FARNESOID X RECEPTOR; FIRST-PASS METABOLISM; IN VITRO; IN VIVO; INTESTINE AND LIVER; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; REGULATION; VITAMIN D RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The intestine and liver are important tissues that regulate the extents of oral drug absorption.  The intestine offers a barrier to absorption, and is endowed with enzymes that modify chemicals to either active or inactive forms, and possesses different proteins or transporters that can facilitate absorption or even remove the absorbed drug from the intestine. If a substantial portion of the absorbed dose is removed by the intestine, then less will reach the liver, the proximal organ, which also contains an abundance of transporters and enzymes. It is widely accepted that vitamin D prevents cancer and prolongs life. Its active metabolite, 1alpha,25-Dihydroxyvitamin D3, is capable of binding to the vitamin D receptor (VDR) to alter the production of transporters and enzymes in both the intestine and liver. Rats treated with 1alpha,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 showed increased intestinal absorption of bile acids. The higher levels of absorbed bile acids reaching the liver will in turn stimulate another receptor, the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), to result in activation or inhibition of liver enzymes and transporters.  We propose to administer varying doses of 1alpha,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 to the rat and the genetically altered mouse in which FXR was rendered inert.  Liver tissue treatments will further include the bile acids.  Levels of the transporters/enzymes will be measured and correlated with their functions unveiled by test probes.  From the observations, we would be able to decipher the impact of 1alpha,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 usage on VDR and FXR, and the roles these receptors play on controlling intestinal and liver transporters and enzymes in oral drug absorption.

TitreApplicationTitle: Estrogenic 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases contributing to breast cancer stimulation: 3D-structure, function and inhibition
Keywords-MotsClés: 17BETA-HYDROXYSTEROID DEHYDROGENASES; ANIMAL MODEL FOR BREAST CANCER; BREAST CANCER DEVELOPMENT; ENZYME KINETICS AND VARIATION; PROTEIN CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; RATIONAL INHIBITOR DESIGN
Abstract-Résumé: Most breast tumors are estrogen sensitive meaning that the natural hormone, estrogens, support their growth.  Different approaches can be used to limit the role of estrogen in tumor growth. Among these are the uses of drugs like Tamoxifen to block the estrogen receptor, or the use of inhibitors that block the activity of the aromatase enzyme which has a role in estrogen synthesis. Both approaches limit the availability of estrogen for tumor stimulation. The major estrogen synthesis though is via the sulphatase pathway that involves a class of proteins called the 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases (17beta-HSDs) which are responsible for the last step synthesis of estrogens. As limiting the availability of estrogen to the tumor is key to halting its growth, the blockade of all estrogen synthesizing pathways is thus desirable. We propose building on our extensive experience obtained from many years of study of the 17beta-HSD enzyme family, by refining the structural knowledge of these proteins in order to design efficient inhibitors to block estrogen production specifically. By identifying the role of individual enzymes in estrogen synthesis we can focus on estrogenic 17beta-HSD family members that play an active role in breast cancer cell proliferation. Further intensive study of the protein structures of such enzymes will yield information leading to the rational design of potential inhibitors. These compounds can be synthesized, tested for efficacy in a cellular system and refined as required for optimization before advancing to further testing in more complex models. This has already led to the design and synthesis of an hybrid inhibitor of the 17beta-HSD type 1 enzyme thus supporting the validity of our multidisciplinary approach. The further improvement of the efficacy of the latter inhibitor will be pursued, and finally tested in an animal model.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advanced anatomical and dynamic micro-computed tomography for arthritis research
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE BIOMECHANICS; COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; DUAL-ENERGY IMAGING; OSTEOARTHRITIS; SMALL-ANIMAL IMAGING; TOTAL JOINT REPLACEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Musculoskeletal disorders, such as arthritis, are the most common cause of severe long-term pain and physical disability affecting hundreds of millions of people around the world.  As the world~s population ages, the extent of the problem will increase, placing huge burdens on societies and health care systems.  Despite the worldwide impact of diseases like arthritis, they do not receive the attention they deserve and are often inadequately funded.  This proposal describes the development of new imaging techniques " using high-resolution computed tomography (CT) " to be used in research applications related to arthritis.  Arthritis is a significant cause of pain and disability, and there are few effective treatments available.  Basic research to understand arthritis and develop improved treatments is often carried out in small laboratory animals (such as the rat) and on human bone specimens (obtained from cadavers).  Our group has experience with animal models of arthritis, in surgical treatment of arthritis, and in the development of CT imaging systems for clinical applications and basic research.  Over the next five years, we intend to develop innovative CT-based tools that will address fundamental challenges associated with basic OA research using micro-CT.  We have four major objectives: 1) to implement a novel 'tilted-detector' approach, increasing the volumetric spatial resolution of benchtop micro-CT systems by up to two orders of magnitude; 2) to develop and test a new intra-vascular contrast agent that is optimized for dual-energy imaging of blood vessels near bone; 3) to develop a new procedure for characterizing joint replacement components using micro-CT prior to implantation; and 4) to develop techniques to see inside human bones while they are being tested for mechanical strength.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics of Antipsychotic-Induced Metabolic Syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIPSYCHOTICS; GENETIC ASSOCIATION; OBESITY; PHARMACOGENETICS; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SIDE EFFECTS
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a debilitating illness affecting 1% of the general population, or more than 300,000 people in Canada. The disease is treated with antipsychotic drugs, however, no particular drug is effective in completely minimizing the symptoms. There are two types of drugs that are used for the treatment of the disease but each of these is associated with side effects. Besides this, ~ 30% of patients have poor response to either the older or newer drugs. A second class of drugs was introduced in early 1980s, (clozapine is a well-known example) which were well tolerated and associated with very few muscle movement side effects (Tardive Dyskinesia). Although clozapine and drugs of this class are effective in treatment of a wide range of symptoms of schizophrenia, unfortunately they are also associated with serious side effects of weight gain along with blood sugar (diabetes), chlolesterol and fat molecule abnormalities. Groups of these side effects can fit the criteria for metabolic syndrome, a well known and serious problem in heart disease. These side effects do not develop in all patients treated with clozapine-like drugs, but do arise in a significant subset of the patients. This suggests a genetic basis, and specific genes might be involved in these side effects. In this research proposal we have carefully selected a set of genes that we think are important in appetite and metabolic syndrome, including members of the dopamine and insulin signaling pathways. We aim to identify the variants of these genes that might be causing the development of these side effects. The elucidation of the genetic causes of these side effects can result in the prediction of who will be at risk for weight gain and diabetes, and this information can be used to help clinicians decide the right medication for a particular patient. Furthermore, the gene discoveries may lead to important clues for the design of new drugs that are free of these unwanted side effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study of pre-T cell receptor signals regulating thymocyte differentiation.
Keywords-MotsClés: LYMPHOCYTE DEVELOPMENT; NOTCH SIGNALING; PRE-TCR SIGNALING; STROMAL CELLS; T CELL DEVELOPMENT; THYMUS
Abstract-Résumé: The thymus is the essential organ that supports and allows for the development of T  lymphocytes from bone marrow-derived stem cells. Thymic contributions result in the generation of mature T cells that are capable of recognizing foreign antigens/pathogens, while at the same time producing T cells that are tolerant to their own uninfected cells, preventing the initiaion of autoimmune disease. This proposal provides a comprehensive study of key signaling pathways occuring at a critical checkpoint in T cell development. A deeper understanding of signaling cascades employed during normal T cell maturation is essential, as mutations in components of these signaling pathways may result in oncogenic events, leading to the onset of leukemia, such as aggressive thymomas or lymphomas. Cellular signals and molecular mechanisms underlying the differentiation of immature T cells remain unclear, hence our proposal aims to create in vitro and in vivo experimental systems in which to study the events governing a key stage during T cell differentiation.

CommitteeNameEN: Social & Developmental Aspects of Children's & Youth's Health
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
DomainesScientifiquesFR: MÉTABOLISME/DIABÈTE; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Sleep and Obesity in Children and Adolescents: Identifying Pathogenic Pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: One in four Canadian children is overweight or obese.  Over the past 25 years, the level of overweight and obesity has doubled.  This is worrying because it has long term health consequences.  Childhood obesity increases risk for many diseases such as high blood pressure, heart disease, and diabetes.  While obesity levels have been rising, the amount of time children spend sleeping has been decreasing.  Recently, researchers found that children who sleep less have a larger body size.  Even small decreases in children~s sleeping time are related to greater body size.  It is not clear why sleep and obesity are linked.  Researchers have started to look at many factors that may explain the link between sleep and obesity.  Some factors include hormones dealing with appetite, stress, breathing problems during sleep, eating habits, and changes in metabolism and sensitivity to insulin.  Most researchers look at these factors singularly.  Also, most studies use only self (or parent) reports of sleep times.  This may not be the best way of capturing what happens during sleep.  The goal of the current project is to consider three factors that may link sleep to obesity at the same time to see how they are related.  Sleep will also be measured objectively using a device to measure brain activity when children sleep at home.  The project will result in new information about why sleep may be linked to obesity.  This information might then be able to help prevent and treat obesity.

CommitteeNameEN: Social & Developmental Aspects of Children's & Youth's Health
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Everyday Pains in Young Children
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; FAMILY; PAIN; PARENTS; PSYCHOLOGY; SOCIAL LEARNING
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain is a serious health problem for many children and adolescents. The understanding and management of children's pain still lags considerably behind what is known about adult pain. Much of what is known about the psychological and social factors that influence children's pain comes from studying children with chronic pains like headaches or stomachaches or from observing children undergoing painful medical procedures such as blood draws. The research outlined in this application will use innovative observational methods and a longitudinal design in a cohort of children aged 18 to 30 months to determine the importance of "everyday pains" (the minor bumps and scrapes experienced often by young children during the course of their everyday activities) and parental response to these pains in influencing how children later cope with a painful procedure (immunization). This research will provide important information about how children learn to respond to and cope with pain as well as parents' roles in this process and will be able to provide parents with recommendations on how to best respond when their children experience minor bumps and scrapes.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: BIOLOGIE MOLÉCULAIRE; GÉNOMIQUE, PROTÉOMIQUE ET BIOINFORMATIQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the mechanisms of alternative reading of genetic code
Keywords-MotsClés: PROGRAMMED FRAMESHIFT; PROGRAMMED READTHROUGH; RIBOSOME STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION; RNA STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The biology of different retroviruses, including HIV, requires the presence in the cell of particular viral proteins in exact proportions to each other. This is achieved through a tiny regulation of the synthesis of these proteins, which is based on such rare events as the shift of the reading frame and the readthrough of stop codons. Although the existence of such regulation has been known for almost twenty years, its mechanism remains unclear. The elucidation of the details of this mechanism would pave the way to development of new anti-viral treatments. Also, the understanding of why such events as the frameshift and readthrough, normally considered as errors, can sometimes proceed with high efficiency is important for understanding of the fundamental of protein synthesis. This knowledge, in its turn, will affect different areas of molecular and cellular biology. The events that we discuss in this proposal take place on the ribosome, the cellular machine that synthesizes proteins. The recent progress in the crystallography of the ribosome has given a new push to the research concerning the mechanisms of frameshift and of readthrough of stop codons. In this project, we will study these phenomena using a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches. Based on the analysis of the available ribosome conformations we will be able to build the molecular model that explains the mechanisms of both phenomena. Then, using different biochemical techniques, we will verify the model.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and cellular characterization of early human hematopoietic lineage determination
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE TRANSFER; GLOBAL GENE EXPRESSION; LINEAGE DETERMINATION; STEM CELL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: We know very little of the early stages of blood development because it has not been possible to purify and assay human stem cells and the immediate progeny of HSC that become increasingly restricted in differentiation potential. Our studies over the past 15 years have developed the first human stem cell assays by transplanting them into special immune-deficient NOD/SCID mice. We have been able to partially purify them and determine what genes they express. In this way we can gain increased understanding of which genes control their development. These stem cells can also be transduced with viral vectors to directly determine how a specific gene functions to control the stem cell. With all these methods in place we propose to provide the first detailed examination of HSC and all the downstream progeny that become increasingly restricted to one of the twelve specific mature blood lineages. We will purify each stage of development and then determine the gene expression profile that is distinctive for each stage. We will also determine the how signaling pathways function together to maintain stem cell function or lineage restricted cell function. In this way we will be able to determine which are the key regulators that control what a cell will be. Finally we will use gene transfer to express each of the newly identified regulators in each stem cell or lineage restricted cell type. In this way we can determine the actually mechanism of how the regulatory protein works. Ultimately the new information we will learn from this research program will enable better understanding of blood diseases and aid in the development of new therapeutics that affect each blood cell type. This information will be important in the future development of new stem cell-based therapies including stem cell transplantation, gene therapy, and stem cell expansion.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: REPRODUCTION/GROSSESSE; EFFETS ENVIRONNEMENTAUX SUR LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Sex-specific susceptibility for fetal origins of adult disease and transgenerational effects
Keywords-MotsClés: FETUS; FOLATE; GERM CELLS; SEX-SPECIFIC; TRANSGENERATIONAL
Abstract-Résumé: The prenatal period is a key time of fetal programming. In particular, one of the tissues of the fetus, the germ line, undergoes a genome-wide programming event that is critical for fertility of the resulting offspring and the health of future generations. Recent animal and human studies have indicated that environmental exposures of male germ cells either during the period of fetal programming of male germ cells or prepubertally can lead to adult-onset diseases that are passed through a number of generations. Animal studies have linked these sex-specific, male-line transgenerational effects to epigenetic changes to the DNA of the developing germ cells. The epigenetic change identified was in the level of methylation of the DNA.  DNA methylation is a chemical modification of genes that is essential for normal developmental programs; it regulates gene expression and provides a way for genes to be turned on or off at specific times. The fetal period is the key period when DNA methylation is reprogrammed in germ cells. However, while DNA methylation is erased in both male and female fetal germ cells, it is only re-established  before birth in male germ cells whereas the DNA of female germ cells doesn~t become methylated until after puberty. Due the presence of fetal germ line DNA methylation reprogramming in the male but not the female, we hypothesize that male fetal germ cells are uniquely vulnerable to epigenetic abnormalities resulting from environmental insults occurring during pregnancy.  Since epigenetic abnormalities are heritable, once induced, they have the potential to be passed on to future generations. Folate and methyl-donor deficiencies are dietary exposures known to alter DNA methylation. In our research we are studying how perturbations of a key enzyme in the folate pathway, methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) and/or folate deficiency affect male germ cell DNA methylation patterns in the mouse and human.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the human embryonic stem cell niche
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN STEM CELL NICHE
Abstract-Résumé: We now know that adult stem cells can be found in many tissues of the human body that require regeneration from damage or disease. Therefore, it~s important to better understand the nature of these stem cells so that this information can be used to induce stem cell regeneration when needed, eg. pancreas damage in diabetes, spinal cord injury, etc. Recently, a large amount of data from around the world has indicated that stem cells determine how and when they regenerate based on their immediate surroundings. This has been called the >stem cell niche~, or home in which the stem cells reside. Our laboratory has recently revealed that a series of growth factors is responsible for niche-to-stem cell interplay that uses one specific factor called, >insulin-like growth factor~. Our proposal aims to better understand this factor and others recently discovered by our team to understand how these can be applied to stem cell regeneration in the clinic.
