TitreApplicationTitle: Dissociating cognitive and motor components of healthy and dysfunctional expressive language development in children
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE; LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHY; MOTOR CONTROL; SPEECH-LANGUAGE IMPAIRMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Language production is a complex skill that involves brain areas that plan and select the words to be spoken, and then coordinates the mouth muscles and tongue to articulate, or produce, the selected words.  Although healthy children become proficient in language production very quickly, neuroscientists are still puzzling over the brain mechanisms, network, and developmental trajectory involved in producing language.  The first aim of this project is to use a neuroimaging technique called MEG to understand healthy language development.  There are serious consequences when children fail to learn to produce language.  It is not clear why some children fail at this task, but two possibilities include:  failure of the brain to appropriately select words for production, or, failure of the motor system to properly produce the words.  Children with speech-language impairment often have the former problem while subgroups of children with autism spectrum disorder have the latter problem.  The second aim of this project is to use MEG to examine the brain activity related to these two aspects of language in these two groups of children to identify and dissociate the dysfunctional brain mechanisms involved in their disorders.  We propose to test children, aged 4-16 years with specific language impairment and autism spectrum disorder, who will have experienced various degrees of speech-language intervention.  The third aim of our study is to use MEG to examine the interaction between age, type of disorder, and therapy duration; this will allow us to correlate the relative efficacies of intervention with the different underlying neural deficits.  The outcome of this study is increased knowledge about healthy language development, improved understanding of dysfunctional language development in children with speech-language impairments and autism spectrum disorder, and recommendations for identifying the most efficacious intervention for specific clinical condition

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and biochemical impact of TDP-43 mutants in ALS
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; CELL DEATH; MOTOR NEURON; MUTATION; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATION; TDP-43
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is an adult-onset rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disease. The genetic cause of only 1-2% of all ALS cases is accounted for by mutations in the SOD1 gene. Consequently the identification of novel ALS-causative genes remains imperative. TDP-43 has been demonstrated to be a major component of the protein aggregates seen in ALS patients but no mutation had been identified till recently. Our group just identified and genetically validated mutations of TDP-43 in sporadic and familial ALS cases. This suggests that mutant TDP-43 is the sole cause of ALS in a subset of patients. This project will help to determine and understand the negative impact of TDP-43 mutations in ALS and motor neuron degeneration. Given TDP-43 is mutated in a significant number of individuals affected by ALS it will be an important advance to demonstrates that the mutated protein has a role in ALS and that it~s not just a pathological hallmark. The characterization of mutant TDP-43 will help to determine what roles the protein normally has in motor neuron biology. This should open avenues for the development of therapies that could delay or prevent disease onset and progression in all ALS patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sex hormone-based differences in cardiac electrical activity
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIA; CARDIAC REPOLARIZATION; CELLULAR ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY (PATCH CLAMP); EXPRESSION STUDIES (WESTERN AND QPCR); SEX STEROID HORMONES; SEX-BASED DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Sex-related differences in electrocardiographic (ECG) variables and susceptibility to arrhythmia exist. For instance, men have a higher prevalence of atrial fibrillation, which is the most common arrhythmia in the population. Conversely, women are at higher risk of developing life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia following the administration of a variety of clinically useful drugs. The basis of these sex-related distinctions is far from being understood. However hormonal status clearly emerged as an important factor in the development of some types of cardiac arrhythmia. Accordingly, the primary objectives of this research proposal will be to explore the exact contribution of male and female sex steroid hormones on the regulation of cardiac electrical activity and to determine whether there are sex differences in the basic mechanisms responsible for the electrical activity of the human heart. These studies will be realized using a combination of electrophysiological and biochemical techniques. This work will provide important information related to the understanding of the basic mechanisms of action of sex steroid hormones in electrical activity of the heart. Ultimately, understanding the mechanism responsible for gender differences in cardiac arrhythmias may help to develop improved strategies for the prevention and the management of cardiac arrhythmias in both men and women.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; APPAREIL DIGESTIF ET FOIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Distension-Activated Contractility in Lymphatic Vessels: Importance for edema resolution
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ENDOTHELIUM-DEPENDENT; INFLAMMATION; INFLAMMATORY MEDIATORS; LYMPHATIC PUMPING; LYMPHATIC VESSELS
Abstract-Résumé: Edema occurs in many inflammatory diseases such as heart/renal failure, arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, with debilitating consequences and a huge health impact. Edema is generally seen as a consequence of increased vascular permeability and most studies are focus on this particular aspect. Few resources however are allocated to the understanding of why the edema is not properly handled by the lymphatic system, which is designed to maintain our body fluid homeostasis. Although we know that rhythmical contractions of lymphatic vessels help drain fluid, proteins and lipids away from interstitium and propel them back into the blood stream, our understanding of the processes allowing lymph transport and its modulations in physiological and pathological conditions remains extremely limited.  The lymphatic system is composed of an extended network of vessels, which actively and phasically constrict to propel lymph. This lymphatic pumping is initiated by electrical events (spontaneous transient depolarization and action potentials) leading to mechanical contraction of the vessels and forward propulsion of the lymph. Increasing interstitial fluid pressure, as it occurs in edema, is one of the most efficient ways to augment lymphatic pumping. Fluid loading of the vessels distends them, causing a potent contraction. This distension-induced contraction implies activation of a mechanosensitive mechanism, which has not been investigated. Using electrophysiological, pharmacological and biochemical tools, we will investigate in this research proposal the mechanisms of distension-induced contractions in lymphatic vessels and examine the effects of experimental edema and inflammation on these mechanisms. Outcomes of these studies will improve our understanding of lymphatic contractility and its regulations under physiological and pathological conditions, such as edema. They could open novel therapeutic avenues to prevent edema formation by modulating lymphatic activity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Charting the Territory: Determining and Documenting Trajectories for Families Where a Child Has a Life-Threatening Condition
Keywords-MotsClés: LONGITUDINAL STUDY; METABOLIC DISORDERS; NEUROLOGICAL DISEASE; PEDIATRIC PALLIATIVE CARE; PSYCHOSOCIAL; SYMPTOM MANAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Children living with severe life-threatening conditions and their families require specialized care to enhance their quality of life. Prevention and relief of physical symptoms, as well as emotional, social, and spiritual difficulties, needs to begin at diagnosis because little can be done to stop or slow these diseases, which typically result in death before adulthood. We know that while the number of children affected by such conditions is relatively small, the impact is extensive as a child's life and death affect parents, siblings, extended family, peers, community, and the health professionals who care for the child.  The purpose of the proposed five year study is to identify and follow approximately 300 children with these conditions, and their families, from across Canada to determine and document the how the child's condition affects them physically and the associated emotional, social, physical, and spiritual experiences of the family over time.  New knowledge obtained from this study will be very helpful to families because it will offer information about the child's disease which they can use in decision-making about their child's care and in advocating for required resources. Currently, they have no such information and are 'navigating uncharted territory.' This proposed study will develop the map they need to help them through the illness experience. The study also will assist health professionals to provide families with information on what to expect as their child's illness progresses and how to make the most of their child's shortened lifetime. Further, interventions that may be helpful to families can be identified and then form the basis for future studies to determine which treatments are most effective to strengthen the positive and reduce the negative impact of living with and caring for a child with a life threatening condition, from diagnosis through bereavement.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional regulation of follicle stimulating hormone synthesis
Keywords-MotsClés: HORMONE; PITUITARY; PROMOTER REPORTER ASSAYS; PROTEOMICS; TRANSCRIPTION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: The pituitary gland synthesizes two hormones important for reproductive function: follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). As its name indicates, FSH stimulates the development and maturation of ovarian follicles in women. Follicles are structures in the ovary in which the eggs (or oocytes) mature and from which the oocytes are ovulated each month. LH stimulates ovulation. The precise control of FSH synthesis and secretion is critical for reproduction, partilcuarly in women. Indeed, suppressed or elevated FSH levels are observed in women seeking treatment for infertility.  In many of these cases, the underlying cause of altered FSH is unknown or idiopathic. The primary objective of the research proposed here is to understand how FSH is normally synthesized by specialized cells of the pituitary gland.  This information will aid in the identification of causes of, and therefore treatments for, some forms of unexplained infertility.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional and Structural Genomics of Bacteriophage
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIAL ACTIVITY; BACTERIOPHAGE GENETICS; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY; STRUCTURAL PROTEOMICS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Viruses that infect bacteria are widespread in nature and play an important role in controlling bacterial populations. In addition, they play an important role in human infectious disease as they can spread antibiotic resistance between bacterial species. Many toxins that are harmful or fatal in humans such diptheria, cholera and botulism, are  produced by bacteriophages. Recently, there has been an interest in harnessing the ability of bacteriophages to specifically kill bacteria, and they have been shown to be effective in a number of systems. In the U.S., phages are in use as pesticide sprays on crops, as well as in antibacterial spray used on ready-to-eat lunchmeat and chicken products. Our research aims to determine the specific interactions that allow phage to efficiently infect and kill bacteria. Knowledge gained will have direct relevance to the development of novel antibacterial agents.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Structure-function studies of glycosyltransferases
Keywords-MotsClés: GLYCOSYLTRANSFERASES; HUMAN ABO(H) BLOOD GROUP; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: All disease states and all disease therapies stem from a molecular basis.  We use a tool called x-ray crystallography to determine the structures of the biological molecules involved in disease and disease therapies with the objective of taking that knowledge of structure and using it to advance our understanding of how these biological molecules work and, in the longer term, exploiting that knowledge in the development of new diagnostic and therapeutic agents.  Research in my laboratory is focused on understanding the interactions of proteins with carbohydrates.  In this project we are examining how a family of enzymes called 'glycosyltransferases' (GTs) make the complex carbohydrates that all organisms require.  GTs are important new targets in the generation of antibiotics as many bacterial GTs use carbohydrate molecules not found in the human body.  It may be possible to target these bacterial GTs with designer molecules that can inhibit their action and so kill the bacteria.  Several GTs are being studied.  Some belong to important pathogens, some belong to harmless organisms but are related to bacterial GTs, and some belong to humans.  The GTs from pathogens offer great insight into how these enzymes can be therapeutically inhibited, but the other GTs (even the ones from humans) have properties in common with their relatives in the pathogenic bacteria.  Careful study has to be made to understand how the bacterial GTs can be inactivated without harming the human enzymes.  Relatively few of the tens of thousands of GTs in nature have been studied in sufficient detail for us to be confident that we know how they work, and it is important to determine new structures and to develop model GT systems to understand at the molecular level how they may be inhibited by new medicines.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Androgen sensitive pathways to the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFECTIVE DISORDERS; BEHAVIOR; FUNCTIONAL NEUROANATOMY; SEX STEROIDS AND SEX DIFFERENCES; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a neuroendocrine system that regulates the release of glucocorticoids from the adrenal gland (cortisol in humans), a catabolic steroid that is essential for withstanding the metabolic demands of homeostatic threat (i.e. stress).  Glucocorticoid hypersecretion, however, has been implicated in the pathogenesis of several forms of systemic, neurodegenerative and affective disorders, including depression and anxiety.  A wealth of studies have shown that testosterone exerts robust effects on the activity of the HPA axis, contributing to individual and sex-related differences in HPA dysfunction associated with affective disorders.  Despite this knowledge, we truly know very little about how sex steroids act in the brain to regulate the HPA response to stress.  To address this question, we use several types of functional anatomical techniques in the rat, superimposed over a battery of sex steroid manipulations.  Our most recent findings underscore the importance by which sex steroids can operate on the development of the HPA axis.  Furthermore, we have new evidence implicating arginine vasopressin as a neuropeptide mediator of testosterone's central actions on behavior, as well as HPA function.       Mounting clinical evidence suggests an involvement of vasopressin in mood related disorders in humans.  Further, depressed male patients who show a decrease in testosterone secretion can be rescued by androgen replacement therapy.  Thus, we hypothesize that normal adaptation to stress occurs as a consequence of testosterone's actions on vasopressin activity in the brain.  In the current application we will examine how testosterone acts and interacts with vasopressin on HPA function and behavior in response to different types of challenges.  The studies proposed should provide novel insights on the basic underpinnings by which testosterone regulation of the HPA axis could influence susceptibility to stress-related disorders

TitreApplicationTitle: Major transitions in eukaryotic cell evolution.
Keywords-MotsClés: EVOLUTION OF EUKARYOTE CELLS; EXPRESSED SEQUENCE TAGS; GENOMIC SURVEY; IMMUNOLOCALIZATION; LATERAL GENE TRANSFER; ORGANELLE FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how complex single-celled organisms have evolved into the major super-kingdoms of Life remains a fundamental problem in biology.  Indeed, we are largely ignorant of the inner-workings of the vast majority of single-celled organisms that inhabit every corner of the biosphere.  We propose to use advanced genomic sequencing, microscopical, computational and cell-biological methods to probe the diversity of complex cells and to understand the genetic mechanisms that led to the evolution of this diversity over the last two billion years on Earth.  Several major evolutionary transitions will be examined.  We will address how a wide diversity of unicellular organisms have independently adapted to life without oxygen. These include organisms that are free-living in the environment, those that live in symbiosis with animals and those that parasitize them. We will investigate how these organisms have modified their cells and genomes to acquire new biochemical pathways in adaptation to low-oxygen environments. We will also investigate the ways in which their genomes have evolved to allow them parasitize their hosts. Although our primary goal is to clarify how complex Life arose in evolutionary history, there are a number of potential practical benefits of the proposed research. The organisms we are studying are close relatives of serious human pathogens and understanding the unique aspects of their genomes and cells could lead to the identification of potential drug targets. Furthermore, we aim to understand the mechanisms by which free-living organisms evolve into disease-causing parasites which should help us better evaluate the risks associated with emergence of new pathogens.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sensory Inflow Through the Spinothalamic Tract During Normal vs. Restricted Sleep
Keywords-MotsClés: (NON)REM SLEEP; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; SLEEP DEPRIVATION; SPINAL CORD; SPINOTHALAMIC TRACT; WAKEFULNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Interactions between sleep and pain are commonly assumed to exist but to this day remain poorly understood. For example, during normal sleep, pain sensitivity is dampened. On the other hand, pain thresholds decrease when sleep deprivation, a phenomenon common in today's society, occurs while sleep quality and quantity worsen when pain is present. Virtually nothing is known on how classical pain transmission neurons in the spinal cord behave under natural conditions, i.e., during the state of wakefulness or during the transition into and during the state of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and REM sleep. Exactly how and why pain thresholds decrease upon protracted periods of sleep restriction is also not known.        The overall objective of this research proposal is to employ chronic extracellular recording techniques in a unique chronically instrumented animal preparation to provide a detailed description, and hence, the first privileged view, of how STT neurons actually "behave' and are modulated by higher brain centers during wakefulness vs. sleep. This will be accomplished in a longitudinal research design fashion where the same animal preparations that employ unique chronic recording and microdialysis techniques will be used to obtain control baseline data when sleep quantity is normal, vs. when sleep is abnormal following sleep deprivation, and again, during recovery of normal sleep.        Such efforts will undoubtedly bridge two traditionally insular fields of sleep and pain science by providing fundamental knowledge on how sleep, or lack thereof, modulates pain processing. These efforts are necessary for providing novel therapeutic strategies for millions of Canadians suffering from inadequate sleep, chronic pain, or a combination of both.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms for (subcellular) regulation of cAMP in normal and diseased heart
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRENERGIC RECEPTORS; CALCIUM; CAMP; CONTRACTION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HEART DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Previous studies have established that changes in the electrical and contractile properties of the heart during excercise depende crtically on the levels of an intracellular messanger called cAMP. Our recent studies have establsihed that cAMP is tightly regulated in subcellular domains of the muscle cells (i.e. cardiomyocytes) of the heart. This subcellular regulation is accomplished in cardiomyocytes by the co-assembly of functional and signaling protein molecular into large marcomolecular complexes. Our recent results suggest that changes in these macromolecular complexes occur in heart disease. We will study the structure and function of these macromolecular complexes. The infomration from these studies will be used to develop new strategies for the treatment of heart disease.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Defining therapeutic inflammation for articular cartilage regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; BIOMATERIALS; BONE MARROW; CARTILAGE REPAIR; COAGULATION; INNATE IMMUNE CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Walking on damaged cartilage can cause pain and stiffness, loss of quality of life, and eventually lead a patient to seek clinical help.  To post-pone total joint replacement, many surgeons treat eroded cartilage with a pick or drill to make holes in the bone at base of the lesion to induce bleeding and stimulate cartilage repair.  These resurfacing procedures when successful can re-stabilize the joint and slow the progression of OA.  To improve the current standard of care, we have developed therapeutic implants for cartilage repair which are made of patient whole blood mixed with chitosan, a natural polymer that stimulates the immune system. The implant is placed over the holes made in the bone resulting in the formation of a  bioactive implant that stimulates the bone and recruits blood vessels and cartilage stem cells to re-grow new cartilage. Since every patient has a unique genetic makeup and knee condition, we are researching how to stimulate universal responses by immune cells, to ensure both safety and efficacy of the procedure.  Results from this research project will teach us how to use the immune system to boost repair of damaged cartilage. This research is, therefore, important to people with osteoarthritis since it has the potential to lead to novel and improved therapeutic approaches that stimulate the regeneration of cartilage that will alleviate the discomfort and pain of arthritis patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of pro-inflammatory cytokines on cardiac repolarization and arrhythmogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIA; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL TECHNIQUES (PATCH-CLAMP; HIV-RELATED HEART DISEASE; PRO-INFLAMMATORY CYTOKINES; TELEMETRY); TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS; VENTRICULAR REPOLARIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that 28-73% of all AIDS patients will experience heart problems, such as cardiac arrhythmias. Cardiac arrhythmias are disturbances in the electrical activity of the heart and can result in death. However, at this time it is not understood how HIV/AIDS changes the electrical activity in the heart. Electrical activity in the heart is regulated by ionic currents such as potassium, calcium and sodium currents. Preliminary studies show that potassium current is reduced in HIV mice. This changes cardiac electrical patterns and alters how the heart beats. In HIV/AIDS patients the body~s immune system produces high levels of small toxic proteins called cytokines to try to fight the disease. Moreover, studies have shown that cytokines can affect cardiac ionic currents and how the heart beats. Therefore, it is possible that the cytokines produced in response to the HIV virus change the electrical and contractile function of the heart. Furthermore, cytokines are also elevated in other cardiac disease states. In heart failure, the cytokines levels are elevated. Interestingly, there also is an increased incidence of arrhythmia in failing heart which could be attributable, in part, to the high cytokine levels. Accordingly, in the present research proposal we plan to establish the influence of cytokines on electrical and contractile functions of the heart by means of electrophysiological and biochemical techniques on cultured cardiac myocytes, cytokine-treated mice and genetically manipulated mouse models. Identifying how cytokines lead to the development of arrhythmias will help developing better treatment for this condition. These treatments could be used to improve the health of HIV/AIDS patients experiencing cardiac rhythm disturbances. This knowledge also could be used to prevent the development of arrhythmias in patients suffering from HIV/AIDS or from an inflammatory condition where cytokines levels are elevated.

TitreApplicationTitle: Leukocyte Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs) in Arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CHEMOKINES; COLLAGEN; CONNECTIVE TISSUE; MACROPHAGE; MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASES (MMP)
Abstract-Résumé: In arthritis, the cartilage and other tissue components are destroyed by enzymes called Matrix Metalloproteinases or MMPs. Some white blood cells, such as "PMNs" and "macrophages", have specific MMPs that are only found in these white blood cells. In chronic inflammation we predicted they would have specific roles in the disease process, perhaps causing the normal tissue to be destroyed. In arthritis this can result in sore and swollen joints. We studied the specific MMP collagenase (MMP-8) that is made only by white blood cells called "polymorphonuclear neutrophils" or PMNs. The gene for MMP-8 was knocked out genetically and we crossed this mouse onto the Mrl background, which is prone to autoimmune disease. We found this mouse showed worse arthritis with massive PMN accumulations revealing the anti-inflammatory effects of this enzyme. This is a new paradigm for MMPs which always are presumed to be destructive. We found that MMP-8 activates the chemoattractant molecular beacons called chemokines for PMNs. In mice lacking this enzyme the initial ingress of PMNs is reduced through reduced chemokine cleavage. Later these PMNs show reduced apoptosis or cell death hence explaining PMN accumulation late in disease. We also found that the macrophage-specific MMP-12 cleaves and inactivates these chemokines so stopping PMN ingress. Following these successes we propose to cross the MMP-12 knockout onto the arthritis model. Does it also increase inflammation and arthritis? We can then easily cross this mouse with the MMP-8 mouse to study the double knockout in arthritis. Our goal is to understand how MMP-12 and macrophages work in normal tissues and how they may go wrong in inflammation and chronic inflammatory diseases such as arthritis. Thus, this research will point to more effective treatment that spares the beneficial activities of MMP-8 and takes into account the effects of MMP-12 and macrophages in arthritis that our research will uncover.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac growth control by E2F4
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMYOCYTES; CELL DEATH; CELL GROWTH; HEART FAILURE; HYPERTROPHY; PROLIFERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is the leading cause for morbidity and mortality in all Western countries including Canada. Although current medical managements have been shown to improve the outcome for patients with heart failure, the prognosis is still poor. In fact, the mean survival rate of patients with advanced heart failure compares well to that of patients with highly malignant tumours. The reason for this gloomy perspective is the apparent lack of restoration of healthy cardiac function under current medications. The attenuation of the disease progression rather than cardiac regeneration is all what our current heart failure managements can achieve. In order to manufacture new drugs with a more profound effect on quality of life and prognosis for patients with heart failure, we need to better understand underlying molecular pathways controlling cardiac growth and regeneration.  E2F4 is a member of the E2F-family of transcription factors and as such a potent negative regulator of gene expression. Although it is known for some time that this factor is highly expressed in the mammalian heart, little is known about its cardiac function. We have conducted in vitro experiments suggesting that E2F4 may exert key functions relevant to the control of proliferative and hypertrophic growth as well as cell death in the heart. Based on these preliminary experiments we hypothesize that E2F4 represents an important cardiac survival factor. To test this hypothesis, we want to perform a series of gain and loss of function studies using in vitro cell culture models as well as genetically modified mouse strains with a disrupted E2F4 gene or targeted expression of E2F4, respectivelly. The verification of our hypothesis could ultimately lead to the development of novel compounds which directly target the heart leading to the restoration of normal cardiac function and by that means greatly improve the quality of life and prognosis for patients suffering from heart failure.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: In Vivo Brain Mapping in the Dementias: A Longitudinal Brain-Behaviour Study With a Focus on interactions of Alzheimer's and Cerebrovascular Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; DEMENTIA (ALZHEIMER'S; FRONTOTEMPORAL; GAIT DISORDER; LEWY BODY); LONGITUDINAL COHORT; MRI (STRUCTURAL/FUNCTIONAL); NEUROPSYCHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The prospect for disease-modifying therapies for Alzheimer~s Disease (AD) has intensified efforts to find brain imaging changes that will help in screening, differential diagnosis, monitoring disease course and response to new interventions.  In this rapidly moving field, longitudinal studies are an important way to understand differences in disease patterns and rates of decline in the common dementias.  An important emerging concept is the destructive interplay between AD and Cerebrovascular Disease (CVD) in our aging population, especially since these disorders share common risk factors and respond to similar interventions for prevention and treatment.  Together, they account for 80% of all dementias, including the 25% of stroke patients who show significant cognitive decline post-stroke.  Computerized brain mapping techniques capitalize on the fact that different neurodegenerative diseases target particular brain areas.  Brain shrinkage and stroke disease can be quantified on Magnetic Resonance Imaging using computerized analysis.  Our proposed study will apply advanced MR imaging analysis techniques and genetic testing to measure and monitor longitudinal change in patients with AD, Vascular Cognitive Impairment and other dementias to understand interactions of vascular and neurodegenerative diseases, and potentially to measure modifying effects of the emerging therapies.  Over the last years, we have assembled an important database of almost 800 patients with Alzheimer~s, Vascular, Frontotemporal and Lewy Body Dementia, and 92 normal elderly being followed over time with serial MRI, functional imaging and cognitive assessments.  By continued accrual and follow-up, we will be able to compare and contrast the cognitive and brain profiles of these different disorders, and improve our ability to distinguish between them and to monitor the change over time.  Such data is crucial to monitor disease-modifying therapies currently in development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hypertension at nexus of the thrifty, thirsty and accelerated ageing genotypes: evolution of a complex disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AGEING; GENETICS; HYPERTENSION; METABOLIC SYNDROME; SALT
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity, diabetes, atherosclerosis and other common human diseases are frequently appearing in patients with high blood pressure. We adhere to a hypothesis that these conditions reflect the interplay between the recent shifts in the environment, especially dramatic increase in energy intake and reduction in physical activity, and the genetic heritage that allowed our ancestors to survive adverse conditions. So, selection fixed in our genomes those variants allowing survival during periods of largely irregular nutrient availability («thirsty» genes), variants facilitating salt and fluid retention when exposed to heat or infections like cholera («thirsty» genes), even though at the expense of accelerated ageing of the cells of our bodies. These pressures acted upon humankind for thousands of years, allowing the carriers of thrifty and thirsty genes reach reproductive age. However, as the last century witnessed dramatic increase of human life expectancy, the very same genes became detrimental in the long-term and in combination with overabundancy of both food and salt.  We hypothesize that insulin resistance with its «thirsty» genotype, sodium retention and its proposed «thirsty» genotype are both associated with accelerated ageing, all playing substantial role in the development of common forms of hypertension.  In order to validate the hypothesis, we plan to use a bona fide model of human hypertension, spontaneously hypertensive rat. In this strain, we and others have uncovered indications of simultaneous occurrence of both thrifty and thirsty genotypes together with anomalies in salt handling and accelerated ageing. In series of targeted experiments, we will pursue the common hereditary denominators of these processes - their nexus - and its link to development of high blood pressure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innate immune signaling in hematopoiesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION; CLONOGENIC PROGENITOR ASSAYS; INNATE IMMUNE SIGNALS; MICRO RNA; MYLEODYSPLASTIC SYNDROME; TRAF6
Abstract-Résumé: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of diseases in which the bone marrow produces too few blood cells, and which may progress to acute leukemia. Within this group of disorders is a specific subset of disease in which the patients are missing part of chromosome 5. Patients with this type of MDS, which is called 5q- syndrome, have a lower risk of developing acute leukemia and tend to live longer than other MDS patients. Further, the level of one type of blood cell called platelets is not decreased in these patients, but the cells that makes platelets called megakaryocytes look abnormal under the microscope. Because a large part of chromosome 5 is missing in patients with this disease, it is not clear which of the genes on this chromosome are important in this disease. We have identified a new type of RNA called microRNAs that we believe play a role in keeping the platelets increased in these patients. This grant is designed to understand the function of these microRNAs on chromosome 5, and determine their role in causing MDS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Polycystin-2: cellular function, regulation and mechanism of renal cyst progression
Keywords-MotsClés: AND ER PROTEIN HERP; APOPTOSIS; CELL PROLIFERATION; CULTURED CELLS; CYST PROGRESSION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; KINASE PERK; KNOCKOUT MICE; ORGAN CULTURE; OVER-EXPRESSION; POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE; POLYCYSTIN-2; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; SIRNA; TRANSLATION FACTOR EIF2
Abstract-Résumé: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is characterized by formation of multiple fluid-filled cysts in kidneys, ultimately destroying kidney function. The most predominant form of PKD, autosomal dominant PKD (ADPKD), due to mutations in membrane proteins polycystin-1 and polycystin-2, affects 0.2% of population and accounts for about 10% of end stage renal failure. At the cellular level, dysfunctions of polycystins are associated with abnormal cell growth, apoptosis and maturation, among others. However, how alterations in polycystins result in these cellular defects remains elusive. To ultimately elucidate the underlying mechanisms we should first learn how normal and mutant polycystins are handled and regulated by cell, and then how they impact cellular machineries that are critical to cell life. Polycystin-2 is an ion channel mainly present in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. We recently reported interaction between polycystin-2 and an ER membrane protein called Herp, and discovered an important link between polycystin-2 and a cellular protein-synthesis machinery component called eIF2-alpha that is essential for cell growth and apoptosis. The objectives of this study are to study 1) how the polycystin-2 amount and channel function are regulated by Herp, 2) how polycystin-2 regulates the activity of eIF2-alpha, and 3) how eIF2-alpha or Herp regulates polycystin-2 dysfunction-elicited cyst progression. For this, we will employ interdisciplinary experimental approaches, such as protein-protein interaction, molecular biology, gene expression and interference, and electrophysiology, in combination with different models, including cultured cells, knockout mice and embryonic kidneys. Elucidating how eIF2-alpha and Herp modulate polycystin-2-associated cyst progression is very important to understand ADPKD pathogenesis and will allow discovering novel molecular targets for therapeutic treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Spatial and temporal plasticity of neurotransmitter release at a developing central synapse
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY FUNCTIONS AND DEFICITS; DEVELOPMENTAL PLASTICITY OF SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; DUAL-ELECTRODE PATCH-CLAMP; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; PRESYNAPTIC COUPLING BETWEEN CALCIUM AND VESICULAR RELEASE; VOLTAGE-GATED CALCIUM CHANNELS
Abstract-Résumé: The brain exhibits robust synaptic plasticity during its critical period of development in the early postnatal stage. Using the mouse auditory brainstem as a model system, our research focuses on understanding the cross-talk between nerve cells at highly specialized connections (i.e. synapses) in the developing brain.  Our goal is to gain insights into the precise cellular and molecular mechanisms that govern developmental changes in the efficacy of neuronal communication and establish novel theories on experience-independent and -dependent plasticity in young brain. Our work will improve our understanding of how sensory experience shapes up brain functions, particularly auditory perception and related disorders such as deafness, hearing loss and audiogenic seizures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of postsynaptic expression and function of GABA-A receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN SLICES; CELL BIOLOGY; CULTURED NEURONS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EPILEPSY; GABA-A RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Communication between neurons occurs at specialized junctions known as synapses via a process known as synaptic transmission: neurotransmitter molecules are released from presynaptic neurons, bind to membrane receptors on the surface of postsynaptic neurons, and initiate various processes within this neuron. The strength of the synaptic transmission may then, theoretically, be regulated by either altering the presynaptic neurotransmitter release or the responsiveness of postsynaptic receptors. Research in our laboratory has focused on the mechanisms by which postsynaptic receptors are regulated. We have provided the first evidence suggesting that the number of receptors expressed on postsynaptic domains can be rapidly regulated, and that these rapid changes in postsynaptic receptor number may be a novel and efficient means by which the strength of synaptic transmission can be altered. In this application we propose experiments to investigate how such rapid changes in the number of postsynaptic receptors, and hence, synaptic transmission strength, are initiated and regulated. Interneuronal communication is fundamental to all aspects of brain function, and alteration of this process underlies many brain disorders, including epilepsy, stroke, and anxiety disorders. As such, our proposed studies can be expected to lead to better treatments for these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathophysiology of sleep disordered breathing
Keywords-MotsClés: APNEES DU SOMMEIL; MUSCLES RESPIRATOIRES; STIMULATION MAGNETIQUE; VOIES AERIENNES SUPERIEURES
Abstract-Résumé: Normal respiration requires the maintenance of a constant patency of the anatomical structures above the trachea (upper airway). When these tissues are not supported by rigid structures, upper airway patency depends on the activity of dedicated muscles (so called stabilizing upper airway muscles). The activity of these muscles is closely linked with that of respiratory muscles (i.e. Diaphragm) and there is a fine tuning between the timing and amplitude of their respective neuromuscular activation. The loss of this equilibrium (i.e. reduction in the amount of upper airway muscles activity or delay in this activation process) may occur during sleep and will result in upper airway closure and obstructive apnea. Transcranial magnetic stimulation can be used to characterize the skeletal muscles response to a brief cortical stimulus. The aims of this research program are to investigate the factors that govern the corticomotor activity of upper airway muscles during wakefulness and sleep, their impact in the occurrence of sleep-induced breathing disorders, and evaluate the potential of this technique to stimulate upper airway muscles as a potential treatment of this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Histone modifications and the epigenetic state of transcribed chromatin
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; HISTONE DEACETYLASES; HISTONE KIANSE; HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; MASS SPECTROMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: The genetic information is composed of long molecules called DNA. To package these long DNA strands into the cell~s nucleus, the DNA is covered with proteins called histones, forming a structure called chromatin. There are about 30,000 human genes coding for the production of specific proteins. In a particular cell type not all of these genes are expressed. Hence genes expressed in a liver cell will be different from those expressed in a muscle cell, and determining which genes are turned on or off will make a cell a liver cell and not a muscle cell. Chromatin has a pivotal role in deciding which genes are turned off or turned on. In a particular cell type certain parts of chromatin will have an accessible, open structure such that the genetic information held in the DNA can be expressed. In contrast, the sections of chromatin containing genes that are turned off will have an inaccessible, condensed structure. Thus for each cell type in the body there are decisions as to which genes are turned on or off, and it is the job of chromatin to expose genes to be turned on and to hide genes to be turned off. The job of chromatin is accomplished, in part, by a group of tightly regulated enzymes that modify the histone proteins. These histone modifications act as signals to recruit other proteins which in turn drive the chromatin into open or closed structures. Our research explores the way by which these histone modifying enzymes are directed to specific genes and how these specific histone modifications signal to attract other proteins to allow for chromatin to have an open structure that enables a gene to be turned on. These processes must be tightly regulated or else genes that should be off are turned on. This is the case in many human diseases and particularly a problem in cancer. Understanding how histone modifications and chromatin structure manage the turning on and off will provide new insights into the treatment of human diseases such as cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Fetal Growth
Keywords-MotsClés: FETAL GROWTH; FETAL GROWTH RESTRICTION; GENE TARGETING; INSULIN-LIKE GROWTH FACTORS; PLACENTAL GROWTH; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Pregnancies in which fetuses are smaller than expected (low birth weight) called fetal growth restriction have higher perinatal mortality and morbidity. Low birth weight infants have greater incidence of physical growth impairment and neurological problems in infancy and childhood. Recent epidemiological studies have also shown that the incidence of cardiovascular disease (such as hypertension, coronary heart disease and stroke) and endocrine and metabolic diseases (such as diabetes and hyperlipidemia) is increased when these infants become middle aged adults. This predisposition of adult diseases as a result of growth restriction in utero is called "developmental programming". This proposal will address the role of a family of small protein molecules called insulin-like growth factors, their receptors and binding proteins in the regulation of normal and abnormal fetal and placental growth using molecular biology and genetic manipulation studies in mice. In addition, this proposal will utilize genomic approaches to determine the genetic basis of fetal programming. These studies will lead to improved diagnosis and management of pregnant women with intrauterine growth restriction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lipidomics of neurodegenerative disease: A systems and cell biology approach to reverse neuronal vulnerability
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; BETA-AMYLOID; GLYCEROPHOSPHOLIPIDS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; NEURODEGENERATION; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer Disease is the most common neurodegenerative disorder with 24.3 million patients worldwide.  One new patient is diagnosed every seven minutes.  The emotional toll is incalculable. Prognosis is bleak.  Insidious cognitive decline eliminates a patients identity and renders victims dependent upon custodial care within 5-8 yrs.  Death occurs within 8-12 yr of diagnosis.  The financial cost is staggering.  $5.5 billion/yr is spent on afflicted Canadians.  There is no means of preventing or slowing down the disease.  Current medications afford a modest boost in brain cell function, temporarily masking decline in brain function, but do not alter outcome.  There is a pressing need for strategies that target the brain cell changes observed early in Alzheimer Disease.  If we can maintain brain cell function, we can help patients retain their identity and their dignity.  In this proposal, we argue that changes in the lipid composition of brain cells precedes memory loss and renders brain cells vulnerable to Alzheimer Disease.  Lipids are fat soluble molecules.  There are thousands of different lipids in each brain cell.  It is known that families of lipids are altered over the course of Alzheimer Disease but they have, for the most part, been ignored given the technical challenges associated with identifying lipid subtypes.  As such, we have been unable to separate 'good' from 'bad' lipids in diseased brain.  In this proposal, we have developed a new methodology to compare the individual types of lipids present in diseased and healthy brain.  Using this methodology, we have identified a series of potentially damaging lipid species.  We propose studies to establish whether accumulation of these lipid subtypes affects brain cell viability and function.  Using this information, we will determine whether preventing the accumulation of specific lipids in Alzheimer Disease can be used to reduce brain damage and prevent memory loss.

TitreApplicationTitle: Delineating the Molecular Mechanisms Underlying BMP Action
Keywords-MotsClés: CARTILAGE FORMATION; REGULATORY NETWORKS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR BETA SUPERFAMILY; TRANSGENIC AND KNOCKOUT MICE
Abstract-Résumé: The bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) are a family of proteins that stimulate cartilage and bone formation.  At present, some of the BMPs have been approved clinically to enhance spinal fusion for the treatment of degenerative disc disease and also for some types of non-union fracture repair.  These factors are also in clinical trials for a number of other indications related to augmenting cartilage and/or bone formation, some of which include sinus lifts to increase maxilla bone thickness, fracture repair, and osseous-integration.  Mutations in the BMPs or their receptors are associated with a number of skeletal defects, with the most severe being fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, a progressive and deadly disease where much of the soft tissue is slowly replaced by bone.  Together, these observations highlight the critical roles of BMP in maintenance and development of the skeleton, however, very little is known about how these molecules accomplish these activities.  Over the last several years my laboratory has studied the mechanisms underlying BMP action in cartilage formation and recently we have made substantial progress on determining how BMPs stimulate this process.  The present grant application seeks to extend these studies and define at the molecular level how BMPs regulate the chondrogenesis.  Results from these studies are expected to impact the clinical usage of BMPs, but also to provide new therapeutic avenues for the treatment of diseases and trauma to the skeleton.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
TitreApplicationTitle: Adaptive Cortical Plasticity Following Deafness
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTICAL; CORTICAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO BEHAVIOR; CROSS-MODAL CORTICAL PLASTICITY; DEAFNESS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL RECORDING; REVERSIBLE DEACTIVATION
Abstract-Résumé: Hearing loss is the third most common chronic disability, affecting one in ten Canadians. Moreover, hearing loss is the most common birth defect in Canada, yet little is known about what occurs to the brain as a consequence of deafness. In this proposal we will be studying what happens inside the brain following the onset of deafness during the time around birth. Specifically, we will be studying the regions of the brain that normally process sounds in hearing individuals. To do this we will examine deafness in an animal model. This approach will permit us to examine the activity of individual neurons, to examine changes in brain circuitry, and to examine how changes in the brain affect perception and behavior. If the part of the brain that normally processes hearing is not receiving sound, then what is it doing? Is it processing visual information? Is it processing information concerning touch? If it is processing sight, then it may very well help explain the increased visual abilities of deaf humans. Changes in the brain such as this are known as "plastic" changes, or simply "plasticity". These changes are also called "adaptive" because they help the patient enhance their ability to use their remaining senses. Therefore, the goal of this study is to examine the natural adaptive plasticity of the brain. Knowing how the brain responds to changes in its inputs in this way will help us develop appropriate therapeutic strategies to help increase brain plasticity and help patients to overcome conditions such as deafness and blindness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Visual perception deficits in children after mild traumatic brain injury: psychophysics, electrophysiology and impact on postural stability
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MILD TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY; PERCEPTUAL DEFICITS; PSYCHOPHYSICS; SENSORY INTEGRATION; STANDING POSTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last 10 years, the importance of detecting deficits after a mild traumatic head injury (mTBI) has grown significantly. Although cognitive, behavioural and physical symptoms are reported by the families and children with mTBI, the results of quantitative tests to objectively document these impairments are often negative and perhaps not sensitive enough.  Studies by our team have shown that deficits in children with mTBI are revealed in situations requiring difficult motor or visuomotor tasks. Our hypothesis is that the deficits arise because of poor integration of information at high functioning levels. Using psychophysical and electrophysiological methods to test visual perception, we will evaluate high levels of sensory integration and processing in the brain. Simple and complex visual stimuli and optic flow patterns will be used to evaluate perception thresholds and visual evoked potentials. Visual perception deficits will also be studied in relation with standing postural stability and variables pertaining to the trauma (severity scores, duration of loss of consciousness, duration of post-traumatic amnesia, characteristics of the head injury sustained). If children with mTBI show persistant deficits, sensitivity to complex visual information may be used to understand motor and cognitive deficits important in daily life. Furthermore, these experimental procedures could be adapted for clinical use as a tool to disclose perceptual deficits, evaluate their evolution in time and the effects of rehabilitation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcription Networks Controlling Human Embryonic Stem Cell Fate
Keywords-MotsClés: EMBRYONIC STEM CELL; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE TRAP MUTAGENESIS; INTEGRATIVE BIOLOGY; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TRANSCRIPTIONAL NETWORKS
Abstract-Résumé: Embryonic and adult stem cells have tremendous therapeutic potential. However, there is much more to learn before these cells could be safely used to treat a variety of diseases. When stem cells divide, the daughter cells can either remain stem cells (a process known as self-renewal) or differentiate into cells whose daughters will form specific functions within the body. Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into all of the cells of the body. Hence, embryonic stem cells are known as pluripotent. Recently, several groups have generated mouse and now human embryonic stem-like cells (called induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells) from adult skin cells by expressing specific genes known to be required for pluripotentiality. Unfortunately, these iPS cells eventually form cancer. In addition to the future therapeutic potential of embryonic stem cells and iPS cells, these cell types can be used to better understand the properties of adult stem cells, which are difficult to study directly. We have recently identified novel genes that regulate the self-renewal (pluripotency) and differentiation of mouse embryonic stem cells and found that some of these genes functioned in similar roles in mouse adult stem cells. Our goal in this grant is to test the ability of these genes to control human embryonic stem cell self-renewal and differentiation and to determine how these genes work together in networks to control embryonic stem cell function. We will test these networks by manipulating the expression of the regulatory genes known as transcription factors and determine if the stem cells self-renew or differentiate in culture normally. We will then determine if these genes can be used to isolate safe iPS cells for future clinical use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Cytosolic Calcium in the Regulation of Osteoclasts and Bone Resorption
Keywords-MotsClés: ACIDOSIS; BONE; CALCIUM; ION CHANNELS; LYSOPHOSPHATIDIC ACID; OSTEOCLAST
Abstract-Résumé: Role of Cytosolic Calcium in the Regulation of Osteoclasts and Bone Resorption  i) Objectives: Drs. Sims and Dixon will measure the concentration of calcium and the membrane ionic currents in osteoclasts, and investigate their regulation and function.  ii) Background: Bone remodelling involves osteoblasts, which lay down bone, and osteoclasts, which resorb bone. Little is known about the ways in which osteoclasts are activated to resorb bone.  iii) Theory: Calcium in the osteoclasts serves a critical role integrating and transducing diverse stimuli.  iv) Methods: Drs. Sims and Dixon will study osteoclasts isolated from the long bones of neonatal rats and mice.  They will use innovative imaging and biophysical techniques to monitor the concentration of calcium in cells, and the ion channels that regulate levels of calcium. They will study the effects of calcium on osteoclast function and on expression of genes.  v) Significance: Understanding the basis of diseases involving bone loss, such as rheumatoid arthritis and osteoporosis, depends on knowledge of the cellular events involved in bone remodelling. Calcium-mobilizing receptors and channels on osteoclasts may represent targets for the development of therapies directed at arresting resorption in inflammatory and metabolic diseases of bones and joints.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of pRb phosphorylation on development and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CDKS; HOMOLOGOUS RECOMBINATION; KNOCK-IN; MOUSE GENETICS; PHOSPHORYLATION; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: The tumor suppressor pRb is thought to play a crucial role in cell cycle control, survival and differentiation and its loss represents one of the hallmarks of cancer. Rb can be inactivated by mutations in the gene or by hyper-phosphorylation of the protein via cyclin dependent kinases CDK4 and CDK6. To address the importance of pRb phosphorylation, the Zacksenhaus lab created mice in which a cluster of 7 CDK sites in pRb were substituted to Ala, a related but unphosphorylatable amino-acid. The phospho-mutant Rb mice developed apparently normally, were alive and fertile. However, starting at 8-10 months of age, the mutant mice exhibited signs of accelerated aging, and developed insulin sensitive diabetes, associated with reduced pancreatic islets. Thus, both activation and inactivation of pRb are harmful. Dr. Zacksenhaus proposes a series of experiments to determine how pRb phosphorylation affects diabetes, cell cycle progression and breast cancer progression as well as to develop a mouse in which additional phosphorylation sites in pRb are blocked. This research will unravel fundamental mechanisms by which pRb phosphorylation affects cell proliferation, survival and differentiation during normal development and disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons in synaptic plasticity and cognition.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; AGING; CHOLINERGIC MECHANISMS; COGNITION; TRANSGENIC MICE; VESICULAR ACETYLCHOLINE TRANSPORTER
Abstract-Résumé: Canada faces significant aging of its population as the proportion of adults 65 years of age or older increases more rapidly than all other age groups. Since the incidence and prevalence of dementing disorders such as Alzheimer~s disease increase with advancing age, the number of persons with dementia is expected to increase as the Canadian population grows older. It has been estimated that by the year 2031 there will be approximately 4 million Canadians with dementia. During aging and in many types of age-related dementia neurochemical changes are believed to play significant roles in altered cognitive function. One of the key chemical messengers that are altered in old individuals and in various forms of dementia is the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Hence, it is important to understand how this neurotransmitter can affect learning, memory and pathological changes in Alzheimer´s disease. To reach this objective we have generated a collection of mutant mice presenting altered release of acetylcholine in the brain. In this proposal, one of the questions we will address is:  How cholinergic neurons (acetylcholine releasing neurons) influence acquisition, storage and retrieval of information? With these studies we expect to uncover basic mechanisms that can participate in cognitive alterations during dysfunction of the cholinergic system. We also want to investigate whether the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (a protein that regulates the amount of ACh stored in vesicles at the nerve terminal) or the high affinity choline transporter (a protein that regulates the uptake of choline at the nerve terminal), can be a target to regulate the amount of acetylcholine stored and released by cholinergic nerve terminals. These experiments will test the possibility that these cholinergic transporters can function as drug targets to augment cholinergic tone in disorders where decreased release of acetylcholine affects cognitive processing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Restoration of upper extremity function with a novel implanted neuroprosthesis.
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL ELECTRICAL STIMULATION; HAND FUNCTION; IMPLANTED STIMULATOR; NEURAL PROSTHESIS; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Background: In North America over 3 million people have weak or paralyzed hands and arms as a result of stroke or spinal cord injury (SCI). Functional electrical stimulation (FES) combined with daily exercise over several weeks can improve hand function, but in most cases subjects still benefit from continued use of FES. FES is usually delivered via surface electrodes. The disadvantage of surface stimulators is that they must remain accurately positioned to stimulate only the targeted muscles. Small shifts of the splint or garment containing the electrodes can produce unwanted movements and sensations. Implanted stimulators with electrodes that lead directly to nerves, provide more focused stimulation and therefore better selectivity, but they are costly and require invasive surgery. Three years ago we proposed a novel implant called the Stimulus Router System (SRS), the core component of which is a flexible lead.  One end of the lead is implanted under the skin and picks up current delivered through the skin by an external stimulator.   The other end terminates in a cuff attached to a target nerve.  The current in the lead activates this nerve, producing muscle contractions.  The SRS has the advantages of an implanted stimulator: selectivity, reproducibility and convenience, but at a fraction of the cost. The main aim of the project is to do the first implants of the SRS for motor function in 20 human subjects whose hands are paralyzed as a result of spinal cord injury.  Hypothesis: Implanted SRS systems will provide clinically significant improvements in tasks of daily life.  Significance: If the SRS works as well as the preliminary animal and human data suggest, it will provide an important management option, not only for SCI and stroke, but also for a variety of other neural disorders.  This project will provide the first crucial scientific test of this new type of neuroprosthesis, invented and developed in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chromatin Assembly during DNA Replication
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CHROMATIN; CHROMATIN ASSEMBLY; CHROMOSOME; HISTONE; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Each cell in the human body contains about 2 metres of DNA packaged within a cell nucleus that is roughly 6 micrometers in diameter. Thus, the nucleus of each cell is far smaller than what is visible with the naked eye and yet, this tiny nucleus contains two meters of DNA! This impressively tight packaging of DNA within cells is accomplished with the help of extraordinary molecular machines. The sequence of DNA and the genes are analogous to the letters and words of a book, albeit an extremely long one. A book can only make sense to the reader when the letters and words in it are in the correct order and this is also the case for DNA. DNA can thus be regarded as the book of life. Errors in DNA packaging within the cell can result in DNA damage, a sort of scrambling of the DNA message that ultimately can lead to cancer and several other genetic diseases. Our laboratory studies the molecular machines that package DNA in human cells with the aim of uncovering novel sources of DNA message scrambling implicated in human disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of fat-induced hepatic insulin resistance in vivo
Keywords-MotsClés: FAT; INFLAMMATION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LIVER; OBESITY; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: More than 25% of Canadians are obese. Obesity is the major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, which affects 6% of Canadians.  Elevated levels of circulating and tissue fat may predispose obese individuals to develop type 2 diabetes.  For example, it is known that fat can lead to decreased insulin action (i.e., induce insulin resistance). Insulin resistance is a key characteristic of type 2 diabetes and is a risk factor for atherosclerosis and cancer. Our objective is to investigate the mechanisms of fat-induced insulin resistance in the liver, which is a key insulin target tissue and a very important organ for the maintenance of normal blood glucose levels. We will measure liver insulin action after fat infusion in rats treated with inhibitors of key signaling pathways potentially activated by fat and in mice that lack key molecules of these signaling pathways. Liver tissue, which cannot be taken in humans, will allow us to assess these pathways. By understanding the mechanisms of fat-induced insulin resistance we will identify targets for nutritional and pharmacologic intervention aimed at prevention and treatment of obesity- associated diseases, such as type 2 diabetes, atherosclerosis and cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nuclear receptors and dopamine neurotransmission: A yin-yang relationship
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE; DRUG ABUSE; IN SITU HYBRIDIZATION; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS
Abstract-Résumé: Nuclear receptors are a large family of transcription factors acting as molecular switches directly controlling gene expression.  The molecular switches are triggered by a variety of signals including steroids, hormones, fatty acids and vitamins. Nuclear receptors regulate growth, development and metabolic homeostasis in multicellular organisms. Dopaminergic systems in the brain are involved in multiple neuroadaptation processes in response to a variety of stimuli from the internal or external world. Dopamine-mediated neuroadaptation is associated with Parkinson's disease, addiction, schizophrenia and their treatments. In recent years, data supporting an important role for a subgroup of nuclear receptors (Nurs) in dopamine-mediated neurotransmission, through their actions as transcription factors, have emerged. Nur family members, namely Nurr1, Nur77 and Nor-1, are closely associated to dopamine systems and to retinoids which, in turn, are also involved in dopamine-mediated signalling. Current knowledge suggests a kind of yin-yang relationship between Nur77 and dopamine; Nur77 levels of expression are modulated by manipulation of dopamine neurotransmission and in turn, Nur77 expression modulate dopamine neurotransmission. Our global objective is to investigate in depth the reciprocal relationship between Nurs (Nurr1, Nur77 and Nor-1) and dopamine neurotransmission. We propose studies aimed at investigating the role of these orphan nuclear receptors in: 1) the behavioural sensitization induced by repeated amphetamine administration, and 2) dopamine cell death and neuroprotection. This opens a totally new heuristic area for our basic understanding of molecular and cellular effects associated with dopamine neurotransmission, in addition to offer new possibilities for drug development

TitreApplicationTitle: Étude prospective sur l'impact psychologique et social de la victimisation criminelle avec violence
Keywords-MotsClés: SOUTIEN SOCIAL; VICTIMISATION CRIMINELLE; ETAT DE STRESS POST-TRAUMATIQUE; ETUDE PROSPECTIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Le risque de developper des sequelles psychologiques et sociales suite a un acte criminel avec violence varie en fonction des individus et des evenements auxquels ces derniers sont exposes. Tres peu d'etudes ont tente d'identifier de facon longitudinale les facteurs qui protegent ou qui mettent a risque les individus exposes a la victimisation criminelle avec violence. De plus, les connaissances sont tres restreintes concernant le recours a des services d~aide dans les heures et les jours suivant un tel evenement et la possibilite de prevenir l'apparition de troubles de sante mentale tel que l~etat de stress post-traumatique. L'objectif general de la presente etude est de preciser les determinants psychosociaux de l'impact psychologique et social de la victimisation criminelle avec violence et de verifier si une prise en charge rapide et precoce impliquant un proche permet d'attenuer le risque de developper des troubles de sante mentale chez les individus exposes. Trois cent quarante victimes d'un acte criminel avec violence seront recrutees. Des evaluations multimodales (entrevues et questionnaires) visant a evaluer les differents types de facteurs previsionnels, la symptomatologie et l'efficacite d'interventions precoces seront effectuees a differents intervalles apres l'evenement. Les resultats de cette etude aideront a mieux comprendre les facteurs associes a l'adaptation suite a un acte criminel avec violence. Ils apporteront egalement des precisions sur les aspects associes au recours aux services ainsi qu'a l'efficacite d'une intervention precoce offerte aux victimes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of sensory systems development
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; CELLULAR SIGNALING; MOUSE GENETICS; NEURONAL DIFFERENTIATION; SENSORY SYSTEMS
Abstract-Résumé: The development of the nervous system relies on the tight control of several processes that regulate the generation of neurons and the formation of precise connections between neurons to ensure appropriate information processing. Some families of molecules have the ability to regulate several of these processes throughout development of the nervous system. It will be critical to understand how these molecules affect neuronal development for our ability to design future regenerative therapies to repair the nervous system after injury or neurodegeneration. Our research proposal is aimed at understanding the molecular mechanism that underlie the role of the transmembrane protein Neogenin in the development of the murine nervous system using a combination of in vitro and in vivo approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bases moléculaires de la fonction du récepteur AT1 de l'angiotensine II
Keywords-MotsClés: MODELISATION MOLECULAIRE; MECANISMES POSTRECEPTEURS; RECEPTEUR GPCR; SIGNALISATION INTRACELLULAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: En Amerique du Nord, les maladies cardiovasculaires demeurent la cause la plus importante de deces. Parmi ces maladies, l'hypertension arterielle a regresse de facon significative grace au developpement entre autres de medicaments pouvant contrer l'effet de l'angiotensine, une hormone impliquee dans le maintien de la pression sanguine. Cependant, cette hormone pourrait aussi jouer un role important dans l'hypertrophie ventriculaire et autres maladies cardiovasculaires. L'angiotensine produit ses effets en activant le recepteur AT1 situe a la surface des cellules des organes-cibles tels que les vaisseaux sanguins, le coeur, le rein, les glandes surrenales, l'hypophyse et le cerveau. Notre groupe etudie les mecanismes par lesquels l'angiotensine et son recepteur interagissent pour engendrer l'effet biologique. En utilisant diverses approches experimentales, nous voulons obtenir beaucoup d'information sur les sites de contact entre l'angiotensine et les divers domaines du recepteur AT1. Nous voulons aussi obtenir de l'informnation sur les sites de contact entre le recepteur AT1 et les proteines de signalisation activees par celui-ci. Enfin nous voulons obtenir de l'information sur les changements structuraux qui se produisent lorsque le recepteur AT1 passe de l'etat inactif a l'etat actif. Avec notre approche pluridisciplinaire (chimie, pharmacologie, biologie moleculaire, pharmacologie structurale), l'acquisition de nouvelles connaissances sur les mecanismes de reconnaissance de l'angiotensine par son recepteur pourrait paver la voie vers le developpement de nouveaux agents therapeutiques.

TitreApplicationTitle: Plasticity of neuroendocrine and autonomic synapses
Keywords-MotsClés: CANNABINOIDS; NEUROENDOCRINE; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; OXYTOCIN; VASOPRESSIN
Abstract-Résumé: Until approximately 15 years ago, most neuroscientists thought that information was past sequentially through the nervous system wherein the nerve cell received information at one of it's terminations, called the dendrite, processed the information in the cell body and then sent the information down a long cable called the axon to activate the next cell in the progression. However, over the past 15 years has come the appreciation that information can also be passed in the other direction. This type of communication utilizes transmitter molecules called retrograde transmitters, which gate incoming information by allowing the dendrite to signal back to the incoming axon terminal. The neuronal cells that I work on in the supraoptic nucleus are very well known for their involvement in body water and salt balance and for their involvement in birth process and lactation. They offer a particularly approachable group of neurons for studying this process of retrograde transmission. My work focuses on the roles of peptide neurotransmitters (arginine vasopressin and oxytocin), brain marijuana-type transmitters called endocannabinoids, and another peptide known for it's role in the cardiovascular system, endothelin in regulating the activity of this important neuroendocrine nucleus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms underlying the normal operation and the physiological role of the renal Na-K-Cl cotransporter splice variants.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL KNOCKOUT; BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL AND REGULATION; CARDIOVASCULAR SYSTEM; CATION-CL COTRANSPORTERS; CLONING; EXTRACELLULAR VOLUME
Abstract-Résumé: The Na-K-Cl cotransporters (CTs) are proteins that form holes in the lipid envelop of most cells. They operate in conjunction with other transporters to regulate the simultaneous transfer of Na and/or K and Cl into/or out of the fluid compartment of cells. By controlling the salt and water content of this compartment, the Na-(K)-Cl CTs allow individual cells to maintain a normal function. Their presence in renal cells, in addition, enables the body of mammals to reabsorb or excrete salt and water normally and, secondarily, to maintain blood pressure at a optimal levels. To date, several Na-(K)-Cl CTs have been identified: the Na-K-Cl CTs type 1 and 2, the Na-Cl CT, the K-Cl CTs type 1, 2, 3 and 4, and the orphan Na-(K)-Cl CT-like proteins type 1, 2 and 3. For this proposal, we are interested mainly in the Na-K-Cl CTs "2" and in 4 of its variants (called A, B, F and AF) that are all localized in the kidney specifically, albeit in different types of renal cells. To understand better how these variants operate and what is their role in mammals, we have produced mutant A, B, F and AF variants as well as mutant mice in which the A or B variant has been removed and will study their behavior through various types of analyses. Such mutants will allow us to determine which regions in the proteins are responsible for the movement of ions or binding to certain drugs and how these proteins affect blood pressure control in general. A refined knowledge of how the Na-(K)-Cl CTs work in the kidney could lead to the identification of new therapeutic targets, the interruption or activation of which could halt a variety of clinical disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms underlying the production and homeostasis of the incretin hormone GLP-1
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CATENIN; DIABETES; GLP-1; INSULIN; TCF-4; WNT
Abstract-Résumé: Pancreatic and gut endocrine cells produce a number of hormones that are important in control blood glucose level and food intake. Among them, a gut hormone namely GLP-1, and its long term effective derivatives has been utilized in clinic for treating both diabetes and obesity. We are examining mechanisms that control the production of GLP-1 and the genesis of hormone producing cells. In this application, we propose to study the role of a signaling cascade, namely the 'Wnt' signals, in stimulating GLP-1 production in gut. Our studies will eventually lead to the methods for engineering hormone producing cells, and the identification of novel drug targets in treating diabetes and other disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of CD40 ligand in athero-thrombosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION & AGGREGATION; ALPHA5BETA1& ALPHAIIBETA1 INTEGRINS; ANIMAL MODELS/THROMBOSIS & ATHERO-THROMBOSIS; BLOOD FLOW MONITORING; CD40; CD40 LIGAND; CD40 LIGAND MUTANTS; CELL ACTIVATION; CONFOCAL; EXPRESSION; FLOW CYTOMETRY; KNOCKIN MICE; LIPID RAFTS/CAVEOLAE; PLATELETS; RECEPTOR BINDING; SIGNALING; WESTEN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Atherothrombosis is the underlying cause of events such as myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and vascular death. It is characterized by a sudden disruption of an atherosclerotic plaque, which leads to clot formation (thrombosis). CD40 Ligand (CD40L) is an inflammatory molecule that has been recently associated with athero-thrombosis. Indeed CD40L was shown to interact with the major players in blood homeostasis and thrombotic events, platelets. Moreover, platelets have been shown to express CD40L as well as its three receptors, CD40, alpha5 beta1 integrin, and alphaII beta3 integrin. However, the exact role of CD40L in platelets remains to be elucidated since controversial data exist in this matter. Moreover, the discovery of the new CD40L receptor, the alpha5 beta1 integrin, which is expressed on vascular cells, including platelets calls for a thorough investigation into the relative importance of each CD40L receptors (CD40, alphaIIb beta3, alpha5 beta1) and their signaling pathways in platelets and in platelets-related diseases such as athero-thrombosis. In addition, we have generated soluble CD40L mutant proteins capable of specifically interfering with the binding of CD40L to CD40, alphaIIb beta3, or alpha5 beta1.  Therefore, the goal of our current proposal is to investigate the role of CD40L and its receptors in platelets, and to determine, using animal models, the implications of CD40L/receptors interactions in diseases such as atherothrombosis, and the therapeutic efficiency of CD40L mutants in preventing such diseases.  We expect to provide considerable insights into the role of CD40L, CD40, alphaIIb beta3, and the new receptor alpha5 beta1 in athero-thrombosis, and to highlight new approaches for the treatment of human vascular diseases.
