TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms for cardiovascular dysfunction in offspring born intrauterine growth restricted
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FUNCTION; FETAL ORIGINS OF ADULT DISEASE; MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASES; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PREGNANCY COMPLICATIONS; VASCULAR ENDOTHELIUM FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease continues to be the leading cause of death and a major source of disability in the aging population. Poor fetal growth in the uterus (intrauterine growth restricted) increases your risk for developing cardiovascular disease in adult life. However the specific effects on the cardiovascular system in adults born growth restricted are not well understood. Many cardiovascular diseases are mediated by oxidative stress. In this proposal, we hypothesize that offspring born from a poor intrauterine environment have increased risk for cardiovascular problems due to enhanced oxidative stress that activates enzymes (such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). We will expose pregnant rats to low oxygen in their last week of pregnancy to induce intrauterine growth restricted offspring. Vascular and cardiac function (in the absence or presence of antioxidants or inhibitors of MMPs) will be assessed in male and female offspring at 3, 9, and 15 months of age who had been born growth restricted compared to controls. These studies will ultimately lead to new therapeutic approaches to intervene either at the time of the complicated pregnancy or, importantly, to provide novel therapeutic options for those adults who have greater cardiovascular risks due to their prenatal history.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of inflammation in pathogenesis and immunotherapy of ALS
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROINFLAMMATION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is an adult-onset disease characterized by the selective degeneration of motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord resulting in progressive paralysis and death. Here, we will study what are the contribution of inflammation processes to ALS disease onset and progression. This will be done with transgenic ALS mouse models through ablation of selective cell types known to proliferate at time of disease symptoms. In addition we will examine with the use of a new method of real time imaging the effects of immunotherapy on the inflammatory responses and on pathological changes in ALS mice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular regulation of layer formation in the developing CNS
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL NUMBER CONTROL; LAYER FORMATION; P53 TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENE; PI3K SIGNALING; RETINA; ZAC1 TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: For the central nervous system (CNS) to function properly, it is necessary that during development; 1) correct numbers of neurons are generated, 2) individual neuronal populations acquire their specific molecular and morphological properties that help them to carry out their unique functions, and 3) individual neuronal populations migrate to settle in their correct final locations. In some regions of the brain, such as the retina, neocortex and cerebellum, neurons migrate in highly stereotyped patterns, resulting in the formation of distinct layers that are each distinguished by unique neuronal compositions. Genetic mutations that disrupt layer formation are associated with severe cognitive (neocortex), visual (retina) or movement (cerebellum) disorders. We are examining how genetic pathways regulate the formation of neuronal layers in the developing CNS. Specifically, this grant will focus on understanding how a specific gene (Zac1) and its downstream effector molecules [i.e., genetic pathway(s)] regulate the formation of a precisely organized, three-layered retina. We have evidence that in the absence of Zac1, the retina generates extra neurons and that these extra neurons migrate inappropriately to form a four-layered (rather than three-layered) retina. Similarly, we have evidence that Zac1 is required to ensure that appropriate numbers of the correct types of neurons migrate to their specific layers in the developing neocortex and cerebellum. To now elucidate the mechanism(s) by which Zac1 regulates layer formation, we will perform genetic, molecular and cellular studies, focusing on the developing retina. However, the insights we gain in the retina will likely be applicable to understanding how layered structures form in other regions of the CNS, including the neocortex and cerebellum.

TitreApplicationTitle: Basal Telencephalic Limbic System Development
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYGDALA; BRAIN DEVELOPMENT; LIMBIC SYSTEM; NEURONAL PRECURSOR; TELENCEPHALON
Abstract-Résumé: The mammalian brain contains a region termed the basic limbic system. This region is composed of several complex structures that are involved in the processing and regulation of emotions and particular aspects of memory. Despite the very important role of specific components of the basal limbic system in the mediation of behavior, little is know about how the limbic system forms during development. In this proposal, we aim at investigating developmental mechanisms important for the generation of specific types of nerve cells that populate particular structures of the limbic system. We plan to utilize a combination of in vitro and in vivo approaches to determine the mechanisms that direct selected precursor cells to differentiate into neurons that will become part of the basal limbic system. The information obtained from these studies will help understand the mechanisms that build a functional brain during development. This knowledge will help to understand the functional roles of particular structures of the basal limbic system and their involvement in normal and abnormal behaviors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathogenic Mechanisms in Persistent Pulmonary Fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL AND MOLECULAR REGULATION OF FIBROGENESIS; GENE TRANSFER IN ANIMAL MODELS OF FIBROSIS; PULMONARY FIBROSIS; TGFBETA AND EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic lung disease that involves progressive scarring of the lung over a number of years leading to a decrease in lung function and in many cases to severe compromise and death. The origin of the disease is unknown and there are currently no therapeutic interventions that can stop the persistence of the disease and/or reverse the scarring and return the lung to proper function. Our investigations will determine how the growth factor TGF-beta is directly involved in this disease, how genes that are regulated by TGF-beta contribute to the persistence of fibrosis and how cells that are in circulation in the blood are involved in maintaining the structure of the lung after damage, with a goal of identifying new viable targets for drug development and therapies for this chronic and dangerous lung disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Life Course Analysis of Family Structure, Stress, and Mothers' Mental Health: Setting the Stage for a Prospective Study of Families
Keywords-MotsClés: FAMILY STRUCTURE; LIFE COURSE PERSPECTIVE; MENTAL HEALTH; STRESS AND ADVERSITY
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past decade, the structure of Canadian families has undergone considerable change.  Although the majority of children are born to married couples, recent estimates suggest that more than 30 percent of all Canadian children are born to other kinds of families, mainly to cohabiting couples or to single mothers.  Relatively little research has examined the effects of these different family structures on maternal mental health.      We propose a survey of 2,100 mothers between 18 and 29 years of age at the time of their child~s birth  so that we can construct three subsamples of approximately equal size of married, cohabiting, and single mothers.  These women will be interviewed within three months of their delivery.     The aims of this study are: 1.  To estimate rates of psychological and substance use problems and disorders among mothers and to determine whether these rates vary by family structure.    2.  To examine the significance of exposure to social stress for mothers~ mental health and substance use problems.  Components of stress include major traumas and adversities, intimate partner violence, recent life stress, and neighbourhood poverty. 3. To determine whether social support or mastery/personal control) affect the relationships between stress and mothers~ psychiatric and/or substance use problems. 4. To assess the importance mothers~ outcomes of pregnancy context (i.e. reproductive history, attitudes regarding non-marital births, contraception practices, planned/wanted pregnancy) and the context of paid work (e.g.  full- versus part-time employment; the availability of maternity/paternity leaves).   5.  To assess the importance of socio-economic circumstances for the health and well-being of 18-29 year-old new mothers.  These include factors such as education, income, and the quality of housing.  6.  To estimate rates of birth complications among the children of these mothers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Executive Functions and stress reactivity in 5-7 year olds following prenatal serotonin reuptake inhibitor exposure
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD DEVELOPMENT; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH; PRENATAL ANTIDEPRESSANT MEDICATION EXPOSURE; PRENATAL DEPRESSION AND STRESS; STRESS REACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Prenatal exposure to maternal depression and antidepressants are common, yet little is known about the long term impact of these developmental risk factors on cognitive development at entry to school. This study will investigate whether prenatal exposure to serotonin reuptake inhibitors antidepressants (SRI) leads to sustained changes in key regulatory central brain functions (as reflected in executive functions and stress reactivity)in 5-7 year olds. We will also study whether these effects can be distinguished from the effects of exposure to prenatal and concurrent maternal depressed mood and whether these outcomes are modified by genetic factors. Since 2002 we have studied a cohort of mothers and their children from mid second trimester, during infancy and early childhood. We expect that some children, whether because of a constitutional advantage or sensitive care taking environment may have high levels of stress reactivity and cognitive and behavioral self-regulation that buffers them from environmental risk. Our goal is to identify the genetic or other constitutional factors that interact with early life experience that alters developmental trajectories in this setting. We anticipate that this work will assist us in understanding the antecedents to key areas of child behavior and development, and lead to improved clinical management of exposed children and their mothers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endothelial to mesenchymal transformation
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC CUSHION DEFECTS; CELL SIGNALING; CONDITIONAL GENE-TARGETED MOUSE MODELS; ENDOTHELIAL MESENCHYMAL TRANSFORMATION; HEART DEVELOPMENT; NOTCH; RETROVIRAL GENE TRANSFER; RNA INTERFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Heart malformations are the most frequent type of congenital birth defects, present in ~1-2% of newborns. Defects of the heart valves and the membranous walls that separate the chambers of the heart are the most common congenital heart problems seen. A key process in the formation of the valves and membranous septum of the heart is the formation and differentiation of embryonic tissue (called endocardial cushion), which partitions the initial single heart tube into an atrium and ventricle, and the single outflow tube into an aorta and pulmonary artery. Endocardial cushion development takes place by the transformation of cardiac endothelial cells (that line the inside of the heart tube) into cells that have the characteristics of cells within the membranous walls. This process is referred to as endothelial-to-mesenchymal transformation (EMT). We have discovered that a specific cell surface receptor called Notch has the capacity to cause EMT in the heart. In this grant we propose to understand how this receptor signals the endothelial cells to transform. Specifically, we are proposing that Notch switches on in a subset of endothelial cells of the endocardial cushion, which then become mesenchymal cells. At the same time, we propose that Notch also affects adjacent endothelial cells (in which Notch is turned off), such that these adjacent cells secrete a gas called nitric oxide to make the Notch "switched-on" cells migrate into the membranous walls. We hope that a better understanding of the processes that make the heart valves form will provide direction for genetic diagnosis and potentially tissue engineering efforts to create artificial valves.

TitreApplicationTitle: Salmonella Spi 2 Type III effectors that alter host cellular functions
Keywords-MotsClés: FIBROSIS; GASTROENTERITIS; SALMONELLA; TYPE III SECRETION; TYPHOID; VIRULENCE FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Salmonella species continue to cause much morbidity and mortality worldwide, causing human diseases ranging from gastroenteritis to typhoid fever.  In addition, there is an ever increasing incidence of antibiotic resistant Salmonella worldwide.  This application proposes to examine the molecular mechanisms of S. Typhimurium intracellular parasitism and virulence, using tissue culture and murine typhoid models. We will examine how several known secreted bacterial virulence factors (Spi-2 effectors) that are injected into host cells interact with cognate host cellular components, and determine how these interactions affect the function of human cells.  In addition, we will determine the impact of these factors on pathogenesis in relevant murine models of typhoid, gastroenteritis and fibrosis. Collectively this information will yield new information about Salmonella as an enteric pathogen, infectious disease mechanisms, and explore the interactions that occur between bacterial virulence factors and host defense mechanisms.  It is hoped that by understanding the basic mechanisms of disease, potential lines of therapeutics can be developed.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Structure/Function of Reovirus Core: Host Proteomic Perturbations
Keywords-MotsClés: PROTEOMICS; VIRUS & CORE TRANSFECTION; VIRUS PATHOLOGY; VIRUS TEMPERATURE-SENSITIVE MUTANTS; VIRUS UNCOATING
Abstract-Résumé: Viruses are responsible for more disease in humans, animals, and plants than any other type of pathogenic organism. The most significant viruses are those with RNA genomes and a more detailed understanding of virus assembly processes would benefit efforts to combat such viruses. We will continue to examine molecular mechanisms responsible for assembly of reovirus, a virus with numerous characteristics that makes it uniquely well suited for these studies. Assembly-defective mutants will be further analyzed by Reverse Genetics. Additionally, reovirus may be useful for killing cancer. Since all viruses depend intimately and exclusively upon host cells to replicate and virus infection causes profound changes in infected cells, it will be beneficial to better understand reovirus-mediated cell- and cancer-killing properties. We will use novel high-resolution mass spectrometry-based analysis of some of the above virus mutants (defective at each of various stages) to examine and measure changes that take place in host cell proteins at each of various stages within the reovirus replicative cycle. Functional roles of proteins will be determined by selectively silencing each host protein to determine how each cell protein contributes to how viruses induce disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The phagosome proteome and systems biology: insights into novel phagosome functions
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; EVOLUTION; PHAGOCYTOSIS; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Phagocytosis leads to the formation of phagosomes where pathogens are killed and degraded. To understand the molecular mechanisms governing phagosome functions, we have undertaken a large-scale proteomics program that led to the identification of ~ 800 proteins, unraveling novel biological findings of this organelle.  In the next 5 years, we will apply new methods in proteomics and bioinformatics and functional assays to characterize the dynamic modulation of the phagosome proteome in various conditions linked to innate and adaptive immunity. Our first aim will be to use quantitative proteomics to define the dynamic changes in composition and phosphorylation stoichiometry during phagosome maturation.  Preliminary experiments led to the identification of more than 2000 proteins and 3000 unique phosphorylation sites providing by far the most detailed analysis of any organelle.  Our second aim will be to investigate the plasticity of the phagosome proteome and phosphoproteome in response to various cytokines enhancing the immune functions of this organelle. Preliminary results indicate that microbicidal properties induced by interferon-g are due to a major remodeling of the phagosome proteome and phosphoproteome. Findings obtained through our proteomics discovery studies will be validated using morphological and functional assays to reveal the fine molecular mechanisms underpinning the functions of the phagosome in immunity and during disease development.  Thirdly, we will initiate a systems biology study to understand the evolutionary changes of the phagosomes leading to functions associated with innate and adaptive immunity. Detailed proteomics and bioinformatics analyses of phagosomes from amoeba (nutritional functions), insect (innate immunity), and mammals (adaptive immunity) will be performed to highlight evolutionary pressures that led to structural changes in protein orthologues and the inheritance of novel phosphorylation sites of functional significance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of epithelial polarity
Keywords-MotsClés: CRUMBS; DEVELOPMENT; DROSOPHILA; EPITHELIAL POLARITY; ORGANOGENESIS; PHOTORECEPTOR CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The human retina contains cells called photoreceptors that are specialized to receive light and thus allow us to see. Photoreceptor cells have a complex architecture that emerges during development and that is essential for the normal function and survival of these cells. Mutations in several genes are known that presumably compromise photoreceptor cell structure and lead to the degeneration of the retina and blindness. The crumbs gene that we study is one of those genes. Humans that carry a mutant crumbs gene become blind during early childhood. Photoreceptors belong to a large group of cells known as epithelial cells, which include cell in our skin, gut, liver, and lungs to mention a few examples. All epithelial cells share a polarized cell structure that is critical for their shape and function as in the case of photoreceptors. Crumbs is needed to shape many different epithelial cells in addition to photoreceptors. On a fundamental level, we try to understand the mechanisms that shape epithelial cells by studying crumbs and several other genes that interact with crumbs. Our work is also relevant for the understanding of cancer. Cancer cells derived from most organs originate from epithelial cells in these organs. In fact, more that 80% of all cancers derive from epithelial cell. Thus, understanding epithelial tissue organization and developing strategies for maintaining epithelial tissue integrity is critical for addressing the cancer problem.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of kidney cell determination and morphogenesis by BMPs and Beta-catenin
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CATENIN; BONE MORPHOGENETIC PROTEINS; RENAL DEVELOPMENT; RENAL DYSPLASIA; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Abnormal kidney formation, which is complete by the end of human pregnancy, is the root cause of kidney malformation. Failure to generate a sufficient number of filter units (nephrons) is now thought to be an important determinant of adult-onset high blood pressure. Despite the importance of kidney development to human health and disease, the molecular mechanisms that control kidney formation are largely undefined. The goal of my research program is to define these mechanisms. Using the mouse, a model of human kidney development, we are determining how molecular signals named bone morphogenetic proteins (BMP) and their effectors and beta-catenin control nephron number. Here, we propose to further define the actions of BMP effectors during kidney development in mice in which deficiency of these molecules is targeted to specific types of embryonic kidney cells. We will determine how very early events during kidney formation, determined by a BMP effector, ALK3, determine the overall form of the mature kidney. We will then establish how ALK3 also controls the number of filter units formed. Next, we will determine how BMP effectors, newly implicated in kidney development in my lab, control nephron formation using genetic mouse models. Based on our results showing that the dose of beta-catenin is critical to normal renal development, we will determine the genetic contribution to kidney malformation in mice with elevated beta-catenin. Finally, we will investigate the contribution of beta-catenin dependent gene expression to human renal malformation. Together, our results will provide new insights into the mechanisms that guide kidney formation. Further, they will provide a basis for development of therapies aimed at preventing and treating these disorders.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF; LIPOPROTEINES, TRANSPORT LIPIDIQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Gaining insight into cholesterol homeostasis in the small intestine: a special role for PCSK9
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT AND HOMEOSTASIS; CONVERTASE; INTESTINAL LIPID ABSORPTION; INTESTINAL ONTOGENY AND REGULATION; LIPOPROTEIN ASSEMBLY
Abstract-Résumé: Dietary cholesterol contributes to high concentrations in the blood circulation system and to coronary heart disease. However, more and more studies stress that the response of blood cholesterol concentration to changes in dietary cholesterol varies widely in humans and animals and largely depends on cholesterol absorption. Even if there is considerable interest in lowering cholesterol and thereby reducing morbidity and mortality, efforts are unfortunately hampered due to our incomplete understanding of the transport processes.   The intestine (i) represents the entry point of dietary cholesterol; (ii) constitutes one of the major sites of cholesterol synthesis; (iii) is a very active organ for low-density lipoprotein uptake; and (iv) plays a key role in overall cholesterol balance. In the last years, our laboratory has considerably contributed to the elucidation of mechanisms responsible for identifying cholesterol transporters and regulating cholesterol uptake, which make up processes relevant for the prevention of cardiovascular diseases. However, future studies are needed to determine whether intestinal cholesterol transporters and other key proteins (involved in cholesterol balance) act independently or in a coordinated fashion. Fresh and preliminary data from our laboratory indicate that a novel protein, PCSK9, could orchestrate various processes related to intestinal cholesterol metabolism. Therefore, in the present research proposal, time and efforts will be dedicated to define the role of PCSK9 in intestinal cholesterol processing, since increased knowledge may rapidly be translated into the design of novel and effective therapeutic agents.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms by which Afferents Regulate Striatal Neuronal Loss and Motor Activity in Movement Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFERENTS; BASAL GANGLIA; GROWTH FACTOR; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; MOVEMENT DISORDERS; STRIATUM
Abstract-Résumé: A part of the brain known as the striatum is a key structure that  helps control movement and thought in humans and other  mammals. Progressive loss of nerve cells in the striatum occurs  in Huntington's disease, and results in abnormal movements and  disorders of thought and mood. We hypothesize that the nerve  supply to the striatum, also known as its 'afferent input', is an  important factor in producing the abnormalities seen in  Huntington's diseases. Specifically, we propose that afferents  that provide information to striatum nerve cells by using the  chemical messenger glutamate, work with a survival factor  BDNF, to sustain subgroups of neurons in normal striatum, and  this function is impaired in Huntington's disease. Loss of trophic  support produces a specific form of cell death known as  apoptosis, which can be studied in developing cells. Finding out how glutamate and BDNF control survival of striatum neurons, may provide important clues to how cells may be rescued in Huntington's disease and other degenerative disease of the brain. We will use 3 main  approaches: 1) Examine how glutamate and growth factors  cooperate to survival vulnerable striatum neurons in rodents.  2) Determine how afferent inputs producing glutamate and  growth factors provide a sustaining influence for subtypes of  striatum neurons. 3) Determine how production and survival of  neurons may be controlled by afferents in rodent models of  Huntington's disease and in pathology specimens of patients  who died of Huntington's disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Cdc42 Regulates Asymmetric Cytokinesis in Polar Body Extrusion
Keywords-MotsClés: ASYMMETRIC; AURORA KINASES; CDC42; CENTRALSPINDLIN; OOCYTE MATURATION; POLAR BODY; RHOA; SPINDLE; XENOPUS
Abstract-Résumé: In cell division, the duplicated chromosomes are assembled into a structure called spindle, which separates the chromosomes into equal halves for each daughter cells. To complete cell division, the cell itself needs to be divided as well. The structure responsible for cell splitting is called contractile ring. Chromosome separation (aka, 'anaphase') and cell splitting (aka, 'cytokinesis') must be coordinated in both time (anaphase before cytokinesis) and space. Defects in anaphase or cytokinesis result in chromosome aneuploidy which is a major cause of human cancers. Anaphase-cytokinesis coordination is well understood in symmetric cell division in which a mother cell splits into two identical daughter cells. However, in asymmetric cell division, in which the two daughters receive identical chromosomes but different non-chromosomal materials, the coordination between anaphase and cytokinesis is more complex and less well understood.  We propose to study the this problem in an extreme form of asymmetric cell division: egg maturation in which half of the chromosomes are discarded with minimum cell contents in a diminutive cell called polar body (the Danny DeVito half!) and the other half are retained by the robust egg (the Arnold Schwarzenegger half!). We have found that a protein called Cdc42 plays the role of ensuring that the spindle achieves a highly lopsided position before allowing cytokinesis to proceed. The frog egg, with the giant size of a million average human cancer cells put together, offers unparallelled experimental advantages for this work. Current theory of cancer origin focuses on cancer stem cells, thought to be the 'seeds' of all cancers. Like all stem cells, cancer stem cells undergo asymmetric cell division to self-renew and, simultaneously, to produce progenies of different properties. Cdc42 may play a similar role in regulating cancer stem cell division. Cdc42 may prove to be an effective therapeutic target in treating human cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phenotypic and molecular heterogeneity of bipolar disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; GENE EXPRESSION; GENETICS; LINKAGE ANALYSIS; LITHIUM; NEUROBIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Bipolar disorder is recognized as having a strong familial basis. Identification of genes influencing the risk of illness in families will help better understand the disease processes as well as open new treatment opportunities. Search for these susceptibility genes has been progressing only slowly, most likely due to the fact that the condition we label as bipolar disorder may comprise several different disorders, each associated with specific genes as well as with specific clinical characteristics. Building on our previous work, which pointed to several specific chromosomal regions, we will test whether our findings apply to forms of bipolar disorder characterized by specific clinical features such as symptoms, family history, long term clinical course, and also the response to particular long terms treatments. Our studies thus could also help in linking patients' genetic makeup with a choice of effective long term treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional analysis of a developmentally regulated Jumonji-family histone demethylation pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; DEVELOPMENTAL GENETICS; EPIGENETICS; HISTONE DEMETHYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: My work utilizes a powerful model organism, the single-celled yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, to elucidate important aspects of gene function. As is the case with yeast, nearly every cell of all organisms resides in either of two developmental states: replicative or quiescent, which can fundamentally be thought of as dividing and non-dividing. Entry into, maintenance of, and exit from these states underlie critical events during normal development and dysfunction of these events can cause disease. Under certain environmental conditions, S. cerevisiae can undergo a developmental process called sporulation, resulting in the production of differentiated quiescent spores. We have determined that an evolutionarily conserved yeast gene called JHD2 functions to accomplish proper gene expression during sporulation in S. cerevisiae. Intriguingly, Jhd2 is the yeast relative of a human gene called Rbp2 and Rbp2 functions to regulate quiescent states in human cells. Indeed, defects in an Rbp2-associated gene called Rb are associated with most human cancers. My ambition is to elucidate fundamental genetic mechanisms governing development using S. cerevisiae in order to advance our understanding of related mechanisms functioning in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Unraveling the Molecular Mechanisms of Non-homologous DNA End-joining
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DNA DOUBLE STRAND BREAK REPAIR; NON-HOMOLOGOUS DNA END JOINING; SEVERE COMBINED IMMUNE DIFFICIENCY; V(D)J RECOMBINATION; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Maintaining the integrity of genetic information is central to all aspects of life.  DNA, the molecule in which this information is stored, is continually under attack from exposure to many types of harmful agents.  Estimates put the frequency of DNA damage at up to 1,000,000 events each day in every cell.  Although DNA is damaged in many ways, the most severe form of occurs when the long thread-like DNA molecule is broken in two or more pieces. If not repaired, a cell harboring this kind of damage will die. If repaired improperly, genetic information will be lost rendering such a cell susceptible to misregulation that can ultimately manifest itself in the onset of cancer. Fortunately, cells harbor a number of proteins which collectively act as guardians of the genome. Several such guardian proteins have now been identified in humans, however the way in which they come together to form a functional DNA repair machine is not yet understood. Using a technique (X-ray crystallography) that permits the detailed 3-dimensional visualization of proteins, it is possible to approach the understanding of DNA repair machinery from the perspective of a molecular mechanic. Specific parts or proteins can be studied both individually and in context of other parts of the machine. By first achieving a better understanding of how the DNA repair machinery functions normally, it may then be possible to evaluate why an individual~s DNA repair machinery malfunctions and ultimately take measures to fix the repair machinery before harmful mutations are acquired.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of TNFalpha in synaptic plasticity and during neurodegeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GLIA; INFLAMMATION; NEURODEGENERATION; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of almost every neurological disorder, from acute head injury and stroke to most neurodegenerative diseases, and is thought to be a major contributor to the disruption of neuronal function and cell death. This grant will study the effects of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the regulation of synaptic transmission.  This research will yield new insight into a variety of dysfunctions of the nervous system, where neuronal inflammation, seen during neural trauma and neurodegenerative disease, may lead to cell death.  Many of these dysfunctions are without effective therapies, and a fundamental understanding of these disorders will be necessary to develop more effective regimens. This research could lead to potential therapies for a variety of neuronal disorders and neurodegenerative diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: High Tibial Osteotomy: Lessening the Load
Keywords-MotsClés: GAIT ANALYSIS; KNEE OSTEOARTHRITIS; ORTHOPAEDIC SURGERY; PHYSICAL THERAPY; PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) ranks amongst the most common, disabling and costly health conditions in adults and its prevalence is projected to increase sharply over the next two decades. Lower limb alignment and the distribution of loads on the knee during walking are strong risk factors for progression of knee OA. The main purpose of this project is to evaluate the effect of surgery to improve limb alignment and redistribute joint loads. We will measure the effect of surgery on walking, x-ray and patient-reported outcomes over a five year period. We will also directly evaluate whether males and females respond differently to the procedure and whether strengthening the knee muscles prior to surgery improves outcomes. The study will build upon an existing study and will ultimately include 200 patients followed for five years. We will also use the information to explore new ways to more accurately measure knee joint motion during walking. We believe that knee realignment surgery is a highly effective, yet underused, treatment for knee OA and could substantially improve the health of many thousands of Canadians.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGRICULTURAL; ENVIRONMENT; HEALTH; HEALTH SERVICES; RURAL
Abstract-Résumé: The primary research focus of our team is to investigate the effects of living and working in the rural environment on the health of people. In Saskatchewan 36% of the population lives outside of cities in what can be termed "rural and remote" areas, compared to 20% in the overall Canadian population. There is evidence that physical, social and health service delivery circumstances may affect the health of farmers and other rural people. There may be adverse effects on respiratory health in the form of chronic bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), as a rseult of personal, normal and physical factors. The goal of our team is to look at rural environments as determinants of respiratory health by evaluating sentinel environmental exposures and health services issues. Our program seeks to both carry out the research indicated, and to devise better ways to get the information back to farmers and other rural dwellers and to those who plan for and deliver health services to rural people.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing CT Functional and Molecular Imaging Techniques for the Diagnosis of Disease and Monitoring of Treatment Effects in Stroke, Cancer, and Heart Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CT FUNCTIONAL IMAGING; DIAGNOSIS OF DISEASE; HEART DISEASE; MOLECULAR IMAGING; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases including heart attack and stroke and cancer rank first and third in health care spending and cost the Canadian economy $18.5 and $14.2 billions respectively each year. To stem the drain in our resources, there is an urgent need to develop diagnostic methods to understand the biological mechanisms of disease and make informed decision on the best treatment for individual patients.       The applicant's research effort has focused on developing physiology and molecular biology based imaging methods for the diagnosis of disease and monitoring of treatment effects in stroke, heart attack and cancer.  He has pioneered the CT Perfusion method for the measurement of tissue blood flow using CT scanning.  The method is licensed to General Electric Healthcare (GE) and widely adopted around the world in the study of stroke patients and more recently cancer patients.  Based on this prior work and existing collaboration with GE, the proposed research program will focus on improving/extending the application of CT Perfusion in four key areas: (1) measurement of blood flow in heart muscle to better predict heart attack in patients with coronary artery disease; (2) measurement of injury to the brain in stroke patients to better predict whether there is a risk of bleeding if a clot dissolving drug to restore blood flow is given to rescue the brain; (3) measurement of blood flow to the liver as an early predictor of the conversion to liver cancer from cirrhosis (inflammation and 'hardening' of the liver); (4) measurement of clearance of lipids from dietary fat by the liver as another early predictor of liver cancer.

Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Nutrition and food hygiene
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic disorders such as obesity, adult-onset diabetes, heart disease and certain types of cancers and inflammatory bowel diseases are on the rise, and there is evidence that diet interacts with genetic make-up and gender to influence risk of these disorders. The major goal of my Nutrigenomics research program is to gain insight into how nutrients and hormones regulate expression of genes and coordinate metabolic processes. Using cutting edge molecular techniques, I aim to learn what genes are involved in the absorption and processing of dietary fats, cholesterol, and bile acids; and how these processes are affected by diet and gender, and how they regulate metabolic pathways in different individuals. Ultimately I aim to promote health and wellness by improving our understanding of the cause of specific disease states, and to provide the medical community with insight into developing individualized diet-related strategies to prevent and to treat chronic diseases.

Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The glucagon-like peptides are hormones produced by the intestines. These hormones play important roles in the prevention of type 2 diabetes, by promoting insulin secretion and increasing the growth of the beta cells that produce insulin, as well as in maintaining normal intestinal function and promoting intestinal growth. The proposed studies will take a 3-pronged approach to: 1) determine the regulation of release of the glucagon-like peptides from the intestine; 2) establish the pathways by which they increase tissue growth; and 3) examine the potential roles of these hormones in the development and prevention of diabetes and intestinal disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell, and defects in mitochondrial function have been implicated in aging, cancer and a range of degenerative diseases, especially of muscle, brain, kidney and the endocrine system. Advances in genomics and proteomics during the past few years now make it possible to study mitochondrial function in previously-unimagined detail. We are using model experimental systems to understand how mitochondria are assembled and how their functions are regulated. This work has also led to our discovery of a ribozyme (an enzyme composed of RNA instead of protein) in mitochondria that can catalyze biological reactions at rates much faster than previously thought possible for RNA enzymes. This ribozyme provides us with a unique experimental system to investigate how ribozymes, which lack the catalytic chemical groups found in proteins, can nonetheless catalyze reactions at comparable rates.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chaire de recherche du Canada en Biologie de la Chromatine et Epigénétique Moléculaire/Canada Research Chair in Chromatin Biology and Molecular Epigenetics
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: All cells in a multicellular organism contain the same genetic material. Despite this fact, different cell types must carry out different functions. How each cell expresses the required proteins at the correct times and represses unnecessary ones is a primary goal of gene regulation. Deregulation of this process can result in malfunctioning cells, cell death or uncontrolled growth (cancer). It is now clear that activities modifying chromosome structure are an intricate part of the process controlling gene expression. Our goal is to characterize the structure and functional roles of these activities. Through this research program we will elucidate how these activities not only regulate genome expression and but also its maintenance and integrity, which in turn controls cell proliferation. Studying the fundamental processes which govern cell growth and differentiation allows us to better understand the mechanisms of a properly functioning cell. This in turn will point to new scientific approaches in applied research and ultimately lay grounds for developing new diagnostic tools and therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Women's Cardiovascular Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The Davidge laboratory studies cardiovascular physiology with specific interests in womens health. Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of death in women. Our laboratory is unique for studying cardiovascular effects of aging/estrogen deficiency in females. We also investigate vascular complications in the pregnancy disorder, preeclampsia. Both aging and preeclampsia are associated with oxidative stress which is a common link for investigation. Pregnancy complications may also alter cardiovascular health in the offspring which is another aspect of our studies. Our research provides a unique opportunity to develop new therapeutic strategies for women that will potentially benefit the health of future generations.

Abstract-Résumé: The brain is composed of synergistically interacting networks. Fast excitatory transmission mediated by the neurotransmitter glutamate is at the heart of this network. Glutamatergic neurotransmission is implicated in all brain functions (sensory-motor, cognitive, mood etc). Moreover, the involvement of glutamate is strongly suspected in most neuropathologies. Despite its pivotal role in the CNS, little is known on the involvement of glutamate in psychiatric or neurological diseases. The main goal of the present project is i) to increase our knowledge on glutamate in the normal and pathological brain and ii) to develop new diagnostic or therapeutical tools targeting glutamatergic neurons.
