TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of susceptibility variants for rheumatoid arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC ASSOCIATION ANALYSIS; INFLAMMATION; LYMPHOCYTE ACTIVATION; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal is aimed at identification of the genes/proteins which confer susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a chronic inflammatory disease in which the tissues lining the joints become severely inflamed and ultimately damaged. As a result most patients experience systemic illness and chronic pain and disability, requiring frequent hospitalizations and surgical interventions. At present treatment of RA is far from satisfactory, such therapy often being unsuccessful and/or associated with considerable toxicity. Development of better treatment or preventive strategies in RA has been impeded by lack of understanding of the basic cause(s) of this disease. However, a major role for genetic factors in development of RA is widely recognized. The goal of this proposal is to identify these genetic factors using DNA markers to compare RA patient gene status with that of healthy controls. We have already identified several regions of the genome which appear to harbor RA risk genes. We will now characterize these regions in detail so as to pinpoint the gene lesions causing RA. Once identified, the susceptibility genes and the proteins they encode will be studied for their effect on disease risk as well as severity and outcome. We will also focus on characterizing the molecular pathways linking one known RA risk variant to disease. These data will pave the way for earlier diagnosis, improved therapy and, ultimately, prevention of RA.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Structure-function studies of methionine recyclying enzymes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-MICROBIAL DRUG DESIGN; METHIONINE RECYCLING; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; STRUCTURE-BASED DRUG DESIGN; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRPAHY
Abstract-Résumé: Enzymes are a particular class of proteins, which speed up chemical reactions that otherwise would not take place or take place very slowly.  They are found in all organisms in both the plant and animal kingdoms and are essential for the maintenance of life.  Knowing the structure of an enzyme and how the enzyme works has allowed novel drugs to be designed to combat AIDS.  We intend to use the same strategy, structure-based drug design, to design novel therapeutics to target two enzymes in the methionine recycling pathway: the dual substrate specific enzyme 5'-methylthioadenosine/ S-adenosylhomocysteine (MTA/SAH) nucleosidase and 5-methylthioribose (MTR) kinase. A difference exists in the way in which MTA, SAH and MTR are broken down in various organisms. MTA/SAH nucleosidase and MTR kinase are found in various bacteria and plants but are not present in humans.  Inhibitors of these enzymes therefore have the potential to be excellent antibiotics, selectively killing the infectious organism while leaving the human host unharmed.  The primary goals of the research outlined in this proposal are to determine detailed enzymatic mechanisms for MTA/SAH nucleosidase and MTR kinase using biochemical and biophysical techniques such as NMR and X-ray crystallography, and to use this understanding to develop novel specific inhibitors for both enzymes.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Short and longterm effects of sports concussions in athletes
Keywords-MotsClés: IMAGING; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; MILD TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY; MOTRICITY; SPORTS
Abstract-Résumé: Sports concussion is a major problem affecting thousands of people in North America every year. In the United States alone, close to 300,000 sports-related concussions are reported annually, though the actual number of sustained concussions is likely much higher when unreported and undiagnosed incidences are factored in (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1997). There has been an increasing amount of research dedicated to investigating the effects of concussions "or mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI)- including work conducted in our laboratories. In particular, we have shown electrophysiological anomalies in asymptomatic concussed athletes up to several years post-injury, suggesting reduced attention and information processing capacities.  In parallel, we have also shown long-term changes in motor cortex excitability consecutive to sports concussion and at a functional level, studies have demonstrated an association between sports concussions and balance problems that persisted at least 30 days post-injury. Moreover, we have recently found that, compared to non-concussed former athletes of the same age (60 years old), older athletes with a history of concussion displayed a lower performance on neuropsychological tests of episodic memory as well as electrophysiological and motor anomalies accompanied by bradykinesia, a profile that may suggest the emergence of dementia. These various findings stress the importance of better assessing the short and long-term effects of concussions on the brain. The general objective of the present research program will be to investigate these effects in three different sets of studies: 1) changes cognitive function and its uderlying electrophysiology; 2) changes in motor function and 3) biochemical changes.  This research program should allow us to assess whether sports concussions may be considered a risk factor in the early deterioration of brain functions.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES
TitreApplicationTitle: Structure/function studies of adenovirus in the infected cell
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRUS; CHROMATIN; DNA; GENE EXPRESSION; HISTONE
Abstract-Résumé: Adenovirus is a common virus that causes mild illness in most patients, primarily respiratory disease, but can be lethal in immunocompromised individuals, or pediatric and geriatric populations.  Currently, there are no effective treatments to combat infection with this virus.  Adenovirus has evolved to very effectively take-over the host cell and redirect all cellular processes to the production of new viruses.  To accomplish this, soon after entering the host cell, the virus must begin to efficiently express genes from the incoming viral DNA that are necessary for co-opting cellular functions.  Little is known about the structure of the viral DNA within the infected cell:  whether it is wrapped in cellular proteins, called histones, that are crucial for expression and regulation of normal cellular genes was unknown.  Our recent studies have shown that in the infected cell the viral DNA is wrapped in histones, and that this event is necessary for efficient expression of viral genes.  We will now expand these studies to determine the cellular proteins that are involved in depositing histones on the Ad DNA, and the impact this event has on virus replication and growth.  Our studies may identify new targets for therapeutic intervention, which will lessen the impact of Ad-induced disease and virus spread.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Oxidative Stress and Neonatal Pulmonary Vascular Resistance Control
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; FETAL; LUNG; NEWBORN; SMOOTH MUSCLE; VASCULAR
Abstract-Résumé: The lung is exposed to high oxygen content and requires a protective mechanism to prevent oxygen-induced damage to cells.  Birth is associated with a significant increase in oxygen exposure when compared with fetal life.  Although neonates and newborn animals appear to withstand a lack (hypoxia) or excess of oxygen (hyperoxia) more so than adults, once the lung cells are injured the newborn can develop a serious condition called "pulmonary hypertension".  The purpose of my project is to understand the mechanism accounting for the newborn increased resistance to hypoxia and/or hyperoxia and the factors leading to the development of pulmonary hypertension.  The study will be conducted in normal and genetically modified mice and a novel potentially beneficial drug for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension will be tested.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Rac1 Signaling in Myocardial TNF-alpha Expression in Sepsis
Keywords-MotsClés: LIPOPOLYSACCHARIDE; NITRIC OXIDE; SEPSIS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TUMOR NECROSIS FACTOR-ALPHA
Abstract-Résumé: Sepsis is one of the main consequences of infectious diseases and occurs in 2-11% of all hospital or intensive care unit admissions. Mortality is 20-30% in sepsis and 40-80% in septic shock. Cardiac dysfunction is a common complication of septic shock. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), the endotoxin of Gram-negative bacteria induces tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), a pro-inflammatory cytokine. TNF-alpha is one of the main mediators responsible for cardiac dysfunction in sepsis. However, mechanisms leading to TNF-alpha production in the heart in sepsis are not fully understood. The goal of this proposal is to study the role of Rac1, a signaling molecule in the regulation of myocardial TNF-alpha expression and cardiac function during sepsis. The proposal will increase our understanding on mechanisms regulating TNF-alpha expression in sepsis, and may have therapeutic implications in the treatment of sepsis.

TitreApplicationTitle: The function and regulation of short-stature genes during limb development
Keywords-MotsClés: EMBRYONIC PATTERNING; ENHANCERS; LIMB DEVELOPMENT; SHOX; SHOX2; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Transcription factor proteins introduce pattern into the embryo by controlling gene expression.  One such patterning process is the formation of the limbs (arms and legs).  Different transcription factors are necessary for the development of specific segments of the limbs, and birth defects can result when the function of a transcription factor is missing.  Because developmental patterning is similar in all mammals, we use limb development in the mouse as a model.  For example, we have found that the mouse transcription factor gene Shox2 is necessary to form the proximal segment of the limbs (the humerus in the arms and the femur in the legs).  Shox2 is closely related to a human gene called SHOX whose disruption causes the malformed limbs in people with Turner, Leri-Weill and Langer syndromes, which together affect approximately 1 in 3,000 people.  We hypothesize that mouse Shox2 and human SHOX have similar cellular functions that are exerted in different parts of the embryo depending on where the genes are expressed.  As a first step to test this hypothesis we need to identify the genes that mouse SHOX2 regulates. We will test potential SHOX2-target genes by changing their expression in transgenic mice.  If we can reproduce the Shox2-mutant phenotype by specifically changing the expression of putative targets this will confirm the importance of regulating these genes during limb patterning. Second, we will investigate how the expression of Shox genes is controlled by DNA sequences called enhancers.  This analysis is important because deletions on the human chromosome near the SHOX gene can cause limb malformations without disturbing the SHOX gene itself, presumably by removing enhancer sequences. Because human DNA elements are generally functional in mouse embryos, we propose to test the activity of putative human DNA enhancers in transgenic mice to determine how their absence might be involved in the human pathology.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU POUMON; CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: TGFbeta receptor trafficking and signaling in lung cancer cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL MOTILITY; MIGRATION AND INVASION; NON-SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER (NSCLC); RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SUBCELLULAR FRACTIONATION
Abstract-Résumé: Transforming growth factor-beta (TGFB) is a cytokine that normally acts as a tumor suppressor.  However, in lung tumors it switches roles and aides tumor cells to become metastatic.  We will investigate the regulation of this switch and how TGFB signals are regulated in lung cell tumors. TGFB associates with cell surface receptors, which internalize rapidly into the cell body.  The interaction of these activated receptors with different molecules in their cellular travels will affect signaling outcome.  In this study we propose to analyze a novel aspect of TGFB regulation; the relationship between TGFB receptor traffic and signal transduction. We propose to analyze how proteins that associate with the receptors alter TGFB receptor trafficking and signaling.  These proteins will then be tested for their TGFB-dependent metastatic potential of lung cancer cells.  This will be tested by analyzing lung cancer cell growth, migration and invasion in cell culture models.  This research will identify molecules that will be eventually used as therapeutic targets in lung cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of microbial RNA trans-splicing and editing - an integrated genomics and bioinformatics approach
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGY AND EVOLUTION OF MICROBIAL PATHOGENS; EVOLUTION OF TRANS-SPLICEOSOME AND EDITOSOME; GENOME AND TRANSCRIPTOME SEQUENCING; IN SILICO PREDICTION OF TRANS-SPLICING AND EDITING SIGNALS; MOLECULAR MECHANISM OF TRANS-SPLICING AND RNA EDITING; PROTEIN COMPLEXES CATALYSING TRANS-SPLICING AND RNA EDITING
Abstract-Résumé: According to the central dogma of biology, genes encoded by DNA are transcribed into RNAs, which are then translated into proteins. Today, we know that RNA transcripts undergo numerous maturations steps to yield translatable RNAs. Typically, post-transcriptional RNA processing includes removal of introns and addition of a tail consisting of the base A. In addition, the sequence of some transcripts is changed ('RNA editing') or pasted together from distinct RNAs ('trans-splicing'). Several such instances have been observed in human, and they have been linked to the generation of enzyme isoforms in specialized tissue cells. Yet, the underlying molecular mechanisms of RNA editing and trans-splicing are not fully understood. We propose here to investigate RNA editing and trans-splicing in eukaryotic microbes - diplonemids - where these otherwise rare events are the rule. This work has potential long-term impacts on health research. First, dissection of the cellular machineries catalyzing these processes may expand the molecular tools for treating hereditary disorders at the RNA level. Second, these studies may also shed light on the evolution of the pathogenic microbes Leishmania and Trypanosoma, the causative agents of leishmaniasis and Chagas disease, since diplonemids are their free-living sistergroup.

TitreApplicationTitle: Approaches to understand the regulation of microtubules and microtubule motor proteins in mitotic spindle assembly and the positioning of intracellular structures.
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOSKELETON; MICROSCOPY; MICROTUBULES; MOLECULAR GENETICS; MOTOR PROTEINS; SPINDLE ASSEMBLY
Abstract-Résumé: A single cell division can herald the beginning of life or portend the development of a devastating disease such as cancer. With each division, all animal cells must partition genetic material correctly into the future daughter cells. To do this, the cell first replicates its genetic material and then builds a complex 3D structure to physically separate the duplicated genetic material. This structure is called the mitotic spindle and it is largely composed of long rigid tube-like polymers termed microtubules. In addition to forming the mitotic spindle, microtubules give cells their shape, they help cells move, and they provide a scaffold for the transport of proteins to and from the outer reaches of the cell. How does a simple polymer provide all of these functions within a cell? The simple answer is that the cell contains many proteins that serve as cellular architects, regulating when and where microtubules form. In ways that we do not understand, the microtubule regulators work together to coordinate the assembly and disassembly of microtubules at specific intracellular locations in a timely manner.  In order to better understand the regulation of microtubules in the cell, we are using molecular genetics to identify proteins required for microtubule-based processes such as mitotic spindle assembly. With specialized microscopy assays, we can further characterize the role of the regulatory proteins by determining if they instruct microtubules to grow, shrink, or move. For example, one molecular pathway we are studying is implicated in controlling the stability of microtubules in the mitotic spindle, and another project focuses on understanding how the mitotic spindle is positioned by nano-scale motors that pull on microtubules. Knowledge gained from these studies will help us understand how cells control microtubules during cell division. It could also provide new approaches to interfere with microtubule function as a way to halt renegade cell division in cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Auditory perception in infancy:  Event-related potential measures of development and effects of experience
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY; DEVELOPMENT; EVENT-RELATED POTENTIALS; HEARING; INFANCY; MISMATCH NEGATIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: The perception and acquisition of language and music depend critically on developing efficient brain networks for complex sound processing.  The research in this proposal examines the brain's response to sound in infants and children.  The auditory system has evolved to respond to change, whether the onset of a new sound that could signal, for example, a dangerous predator, or a change in a sound, for example signaling emotion in a voice. During the previous grant period we discovered that the cortical response to a change in a sound feature (e.g., pitch, timing or location) undergoes a radical development during early infancy.  Here we apply this knowledge to study the development of (1) pitch processing, including pitch patterns as found in speech intonation and melodies, (2) "auditory scene analysis", whereby infants learn to process the sounds from more than one object at the same time, (3) the effects of learning and specific experience with sounds on brain development, and (4) the development of oscillatory brain activity that reflects attention and memory processes.  The proposed studies examine aspects of complex auditory processing that are critical for the acquisition of language and music.  Only by understanding these mechanisms will we be able to understand why language and music do not develop optimally in certain special populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: The CAP study:  Cardiovascular Disease After Preeclampsia
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CAROTID INTIMA-MEDIA THICKNESS; CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE; PREECLAMPSIA; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: A group of researchers from McMaster University is studying women who had preeclampsia (high blood pressure during the last half of pregnancy along with leakage of protein in their urine) because they seem to be at double the risk for early heart disease and stroke.However, the studies which have been published did not determine if preeclampsia itself is a cardiovascular risk factor because they did not account for all of the other known risk factors.  In particular, they did not study leakage of protein in the urine (microalbuminuria) which is a risk factor. We seek to address these issues in the current study.  Women will be studied 10-20 years after the pregnancy in which they had preeclampsia and compared to women with uncomplicated pregnancies.  We will send an invitation to participate to both groups.  A research nurse will schedule an appointment with those who agree.  At the appointment, the research nurse will ask questions about their health, exercise, smoking, stress, diet and other risk factors for heart disease.  She will measure their blood pressure, height, weight, waist circumference and hip circumference.  Participants will have urine and blood tested for risk factors for heart disease.  They will have an ultrasound of the blood vessels in their neck to measure the thickness of the blood vessel wall.  The amount of early atherosclerosis (thickening of the blood vessel wall) will be compared in women with a history of preeclampsia to women with uncomplicated pregnancies.  This study would add to existing knowledge by i) determining for the first time the prevalence of early (called subclinical) atherosclerosis in relatively young women in their 40's and 50's who have had preeclampsia, ii) explaining the cause of any increase in subclinical atherosclerosis with a complete assessment of current cardiovascular risk factors which will allow us to determine if preeclampsia itself is a risk  for heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of the Interplay Between Histone MTases, DNA Methylation and Proviral Silencing
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; GENE REGULATION; HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; RETROVIRUSES
Abstract-Résumé: Normally, cells in the body grow, divide, and die in an orderly manner. Although there are many kinds of cancer, all develop when cells begin to divide abnormally. DNA is the material in every cell that directs all of its functions, the genetic blueprint of life. Tumor-suppressor genes are a subset of genes that encode the proteins that regulate cell growth. Mutation of the genes encoding these proteins leads to the development of cancer. In many cancer cells, these proteins are no longer produced, not because the genes that encode them have become mutated, but rather because the genes that encode them have been shut-off. This process frequently involves a specific chemical change in the DNA of these genes called methylation. Paradoxically, coincident with the methylation of tumor-suppressor genes, most of the genome in tumor cells, including vestigial "endogenous" viruses, becomes demethylated. The underlying cause of these alterations in DNA methylation patterns remains a mystery. The aim of this proposal is to characterize the underlying mechanism(s)/biochemical pathway(s) leading to DNA methylation of the genome in normal cells, using the mouse as a model system. Knowledge gained from this work may lead to the development of pharmaceuticals that counteract or inhibit aberrant DNA methylation observed not only in cancer, but in other diseases as well, such as Fragile X, ICF and ATRX syndromes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Generation of hematopoietic stem cells from embryonic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFERENTIATION; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; SCREENING; SIGNALING PATHWAYS
Abstract-Résumé: The focus of this research proposal is to understand how to direct embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and reprogrammed pluripotential stem cells (iPSCs) to generate blood forming stem cells in a tissue culture dish. The experiments in this proposal are based on recent findings from our laboratory that have identified a cell type that can make most of the different types of blood cells, suggesting that it could represent the earliest blood forming stem cell.  The studies proposed in the first part of this application will further characterize these cells to determine if they are blood forming stem cells.  The studies outlined in the second part of the application are aimed at identifying strategies that will enable us to generate large numbers of blood-forming stem cells from these different pluripotent stem cell populations. While the application is focused on mouse ESCs, we anticipate that the findings will be easily translated to human cells. The outcome of these studies have a number of important implications for improving public health.  First, understanding how blood-forming stem cells are generated from ESCs and iPSCs will provide a novel and unlimited source of these cells for transplantation.  Transplantation of blood-forming stem cells is a routine proven treatment for certain types of leukemia and blood cell disorders.  Being able to generate unlimited numbers of these cells will significantly expand the patient pool that can be treated by transplantation.  Second, the ability to recreate blood formation in a petri dish from ESC and iPSCs provides an unprecedented opportunity to study and identify the causes of blood cell disease such as leukemia and certain types of anemias.  Understanding the events that initiate these diseases will provide new approaches for developing therapies that specifically target the cells that cause the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Quantitative Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Neurodevelopment
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; COGNITIVE ABILITY; DEVELOPMENT; FETAL ALCOHOL SPECTRUM DISORDER; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MRI
Abstract-Résumé: The primary goal is to develop and use state-of-the-art Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to study the development of the brain in both healthy and disabled children. As a child matures into adolescence and young adulthood, major structural changes occur in various parts of the brain. Much remains unknown on how the brain evolves with age in healthy development and how it relates to cognitive ability such as math and reading in individuals. In other words, why are some people better at certain tasks than others? Sophisticated MRI acquisition techniques and image analysis can safely and non-invasively evaluate when, where, and how much specific brain regions change in a person. A comparison of the integrity of the brain white matter (i.e. the "wiring"), the thickness of the cortical gray matter (i.e. the "computers"), and the volume of deep gray matter (i.e. the "relay stations") to cognitive assessments will be performed in a large number of healthy individuals. Understanding how the healthy brain develops is important to understand the consequences when something goes wrong.  While many children develop normally, there are others who suffer from cognitive, neurological, and behavioural problems. Some children have permanent structural brain damage because of the consumption of alcohol by the mother during pregnancy, leading to a broad condition known as fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD). Children with FASD often have motor delays, and deficits in attention, learning and memory, executive functioning, mathematics, and language. Quantitative MRI may identify regions of brain abnormality that are not detected with conventional clinical MRI. Differences in the severity and location of brain changes may explain the range of cognitive deficits seen amongst FASD children. Knowledge of the responsible brain regions could lead to improved therapies and individual-based treatment strategies since all patients may not show the same structural abnormalities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering signalling complexity at the single cell level using high-throughput microfluidic imaging.
Keywords-MotsClés: GENOMICS; HIGH-THROUGHPUT; LIVE CELL IMAGING; MICROFLUIDICS; PROTEIN SIGNALLING NETWORKS; SINGLE CELL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells respond to external stimuli through the complex interaction of molecules which is referred to as signalling.  The proper regulation of these responses is crucial for proper development while misregulation is associated with onset of diseases including cancer.  A major obstacle in understanding and ultimately manipulating cellular responses is the inherent variability of individual cells that is difficult to capture using conventional techniques.  This proposal will exploit newly developed methodologies based on micro-scale channels and valves to enable, for the first time, the detailed analysis of signaling at the single cell level.  These studies will shed light on fundamental processes relevant to all aspects of human health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Extracellular nucleotides in inflammatory cell reactions to pathogenic determinants
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; APYRASE; ARTHRITIS; BIOCHEMISTRY; CD39; CELL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Leukocytes and endothelial cells play key roles in inflammation and arthritis by releasing chemokines such as IL-8. IL-8 promotes the migration of neutrophils that rapidly accumulate in the inflamed and eliminate the danger. We have made the novel observation that in human monocytes, IL-8 secretion is regulated by extracellular nucleotides; blocking either the action of extracellular nucleotides or the nucleotide receptor P2Y6 prevented IL-8 expression and secretion as well as leukocyte migration to the inflammatory site. Extracellular nucleotides (ATP, ADP, UTP, UDP) are signalling molecules secreted in large amounts by injured and activated cells, especially at sites of inflammation. The signalling and functions induced by extracellular nucleotides in leukocytes and endothelial cells is a new but fast developing research area. Indeed nucleotides are suspected to regulate a variety of proinflammatory responses of these cells via a number of specific P2 receptors such as P2Y6. The concentration of extracellular nucleotides and thus the activation of P2 receptors are tightly regulated by cell surface enzymes called ectonucleotidases. We have discovered the first member of a new family of such enzymes that break down these molecules at the surface of macrophages and neutrophils. We engineered mice deficient in this enzyme, named NTPDase1 that represent a powerful tool to explore the function of nucleotides in inflammation. Our preliminary data suggests the involvement of two P2 receptors in cell migration, and we have obtained mice that do not express these receptors from a collaborator. In this project, using the mutant mice mentioned above together with various cellular and in vivo models, we will elucidate the function of nucleotide signalling in inflammation. We anticipate that our studies will lead to the identification of novel therapeutic targets that will help understand and treat inflammatory diseases such as arthritis as well as infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Specificity profiling and prediction of protein networks for peptide recognition domains
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL PATHWAYS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; PEPTIDE LIBRARIES; PHAGE DISPLAY; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Protein-protein interactions are involved in almost all cellular processes, and in particular, eukaryotic signaling pathways are controlled by complex protein networks.  These networks are essential for normal development and cell function, and furthermore, many diseases are caused by imbalances in particular signaling networks.  Thus, a major goal of modern biology  is to define the interacting partners in cellular networks and to elucidate the molecular basis for key protein-protein interactions.  Many of these interactions are mediated by modular peptide recognition domains, which are usually imbedded in large scaffolding proteins and function by recognizing distinct linear motifs within binding partners.  Our laboratory has pioneered the use of combinatorial peptide libraries for identifying high affinity ligands for peptide recognition domains.  We propose a large-scale project that will define the binding specificities of all human SH3 and WW domains, polyproline recognition modules that are involved in many important signaling pathways.  This analysis will contribute to the understanding of cell signaling in normal and diseased cells, and the peptide ligands will be useful as inhibitors that can be used to study protein function inside cells.  Immediate benefits of the research include new advances in Canadian biomedical science, more efficient use of Canadian research resources, and an increased pool of highly qualified personnel in the nationally underrepresented field of combinatorial biology.  Longer term benefits for Canada from obtaining a better understanding of cell signaling networks include potential therapies for many diseases, including cancer and infectious diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Corticolimbic Endocannabinoid Signaling Regulates Adaptation and Neurobehavioral Plasticity to Stress
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; EMOTIONAL BEHAVIOR; ENDOCANNABINOID; NEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; NEUROPHARMACOLOGY; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Cannabis contains chemicals named cannabinoids which exert their effects on behavior by acting upon cannabinoid receptors in the brain. It is known that the brain also produces its own cannabinoids, known as endocannabinoids. One important function of endocannabinoids is to regulate emotional behavior and stress responsivity through interactions with cannabinoid receptors in the brain. Our laboratory has recently shown that endocannabinoids may be involved in the development of major depression as endocannabinoid levels are reduced in individuals with major depression and increased following antidepressant treatment. One mechanism by which endocannabinoids may influence the development of depressive illness is by modulating the physiological and behavioral responses to stress. The aim of this research is to examine the role endocannabinoids play in the ability of the brain to adapt to stress and if endocannabinoids are involved in the changes in emotional behavior that are induced by exposure to stressful stimuli. Ultimately, this research will help us to understand the role of endocannabinoids in resilience to stress and how deficits in this system may increase human vulnerability to stress-related mental illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brain degeneration and regeneration in preclinical models of Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AXONAL REGENERATION; CHOLINERGIC NEURONS; NERVE GROWTH FACTOR; REMOVAL OF AMYLOID BETA
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease is associated with the damage of a particular type of brain cell, the neuron. A specialized part of the neuron, termed the axon, is primarily and most severely affected by the toxicity of amyloid beta, present in the Alzheimer brain.   It is well established that the degeneration of cholinergic neurons is significant in Alzheimer's disease and that it is related to learning and memory deficits. Enhancing cholinergic neurotransmission has been a main therapeutic focus with the use of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, to prolong the action of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. However, through the course of the disease, cholinergic axonal degeneration progresses and cholinergic cell bodies, deprived of nutrients such as nerve growth factor (NGF), ultimately die. Once such severe cholinergic degeneration occurs, treatments with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors have limited hope of success. The levels of acetylcholine, which could be protected by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, are insufficient.  Our goal is to develop a multi-component therapeutic strategy that will restore cognitive function by halting the toxicity of amyloid-beta using novel and effective methods including immunotherapy combined with non-invasive MRI-guided focused ultrasound delivery, scyllo-inositol, and rescuing cholinergic neurons by delivering NGF to specific areas of the brain. We hypothesize that limiting the toxicity of amyloid-beta will enhance the regenerative potential of cholinergic neurons in presence of NGF. In mouse models of Alzheimer's disease, this combined treatment is expected to restore axonal networks leading to the recovery of behavioral functions.  The proposed research provides an improved basis for current and novel therapeutic interventions by reducing amyloid deposition and promoting neuronal regeneration to ameliorate cognitive function, and eventually to improve the quality of life for Alzheimer's patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the leukemia-inducing NUP98-HOXA9 oncogene using Drosophila and mouse models
Keywords-MotsClés: DROSOPHILA GENETICS; GENETIC SCREENS; LEUKEMIA; MOUSE HEMATOPOIESIS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Oncogenes have the capacity to transform cells and promote cancer. They often result from specific mutations that hyper-activate or change normal gene function and thereby force a cell to engage in a path that it normally does not follow. While a large number of oncogenes have been identified to date, we still know little about the molecular disorders they create. This is in part due to the complexity of the effects as well as the slow pace associated with mammalian-based experimental models. Several other organisms have proven invaluable to elucidate basic cellular processes. For instance, the fruit fly Drosophila has already provided seminal information regarding a large range of  human afflictions, such as neurodegeneration, obesity and aging to name a few. Here, we propose to use Drosophila as a tool to speed-up the characterization of human oncogenes and to verify our findings in mouse models. Because Drosophila genetics is extremely well developed, countless tools are available to rapidly identify novel genes.   We recently generated a fly model that recapitulates the ability of a human oncogene (NUP98-HOXA9) to induce proliferation and tumor-like formation. Expression of NUP98-HOXA9 during Drosophila eye development produces defects that depend on fly genes related to known mammalian collaborators of NUP98-HOXA9. Moreover, co-expression of NUP98-HOXA9 and one of these collaborators, induces strong cell proliferation behavior that produces large tumor-like formation. We now propose to use this model to identify new partners of NUP98-HOXA9 activity by genetic screening and then test the new partners in mouse leukemia models to ascertain their implication.   HOX gene dysregulation is often linked to acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This project should unveil a repertoire of genes modulating the action of NUP98-HOXA9. Once validated in mouse models, each of these new genes may represent as many potential targets against HOX-dependent leukemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of endothelial gene expression by epigenetic signalling pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; CYTOKINE SIGNALING; DNA METHYLATION; HISTONE; HISTONE DEACETYLASE; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Diseases of the cardiovascular system, such as coronary heart disease   and stroke due to atherosclerosis, are known to start in the vascular   endothelium. This research laboratory has a long-term interest in   understanding how endothelial genes are regulated in health and   disease. We argue that we need to understand how genes are expressed   in the endothelial cells of the body and how these pathways become   abnormal in disease. What makes an endothelial gene turn off in   diseased human blood vessels? Classically the nucleus has been viewed   as the key regulator of gene expression. Yet all cells have the same   DNA. Why do endothelial cells express only certain genes in healthy   tissue? In disease many of these genes turn off. Why does the nucleus   get affected? These processes are chromosome-based or chromatin-based,   and are also called epigenetic processes. What we inherit from our   parents, or what one cell passes on two cells when it divides,   represents the "nature" side of the equation. These processes are   influenced by the environment. This represents the "nurture" side of   the equation. Whatever our cells sense in their external world   interacts with genetic material in the nucleus to influence gene   expression. Epigenetics is broadly defined as the mechanisms that   control gene expression that do not involve the DNA sequence per se.   We are among the first to study these concepts in the cardiovascular   sciences. We believe that the principles we uncover in endothelial   cells will teach us about blood vessels gene regulation in general.   Our understanding of these newer concepts offers the hope of   innovative approaches to preventing and treating the underlying   problem in diseased blood vessels of patients. We anticipate findings   that will provide important new insight into how genes are turned on   and off in disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of insulin resistance of protein metabolism in human obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: INSULIN RESISTANCE; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MUSCLE BIOPSIES; OBESITY; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS AND CATABOLISM; STABLE AND RADIOACTIVE ISOTOPE STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: Muscle is the principle tissue with high protein content in the body, so it plays a central role in the whole body's protein balance. Insulin is the main anabolic (tissue-building) hormone, and it affects protein metabolism during meal absorption and between meals.  How it increases muscle synthesis and decreases muscle breakdown are not fully understood. Furthermore, a prominent feature of obesity is that tissue responses to insulin's effects are blunted. When this reaches the point that hypersecretion of insulin to overcome this insulin resistance can no longer occur, high blood sugar, i.e., type 2 diabetes develops. We have shown insulin resistance of protein metabolism in obesity.  We wish to better understand this defect in obese persons, as the main objective of the proposed study. Specific amino acids from protein, especially leucine, also directly stimulate protein synthesis, and obesity may also have an as yet unrecognized defect at this level. To define these defects, we will use our method, the "hyperinsulinemic, hyperglycemic, hyperaminoacidemic clamp" test with studies of leg muscle.  In this, we raise insulin, glucose and amino acids (protein) to levels found after meals by giving them intravenously for several hours. This simulates the situation after a meal, during which most anabolism takes place. This will be combined with measurements in needle biopsies of the muscle. The biopsies will give direct access to tissue so that we can assess its rates of protein accretion in response to insulin and amino acids. The most novel aspect of the work is that we will be able to learn more about what happens inside the muscle cell that controls its rates of protein metabolism, including using "gene-chip" technology.  We expect that obese persons' muscle will be less responsive to the effects of insulin and amino acids. These studies can help not only basic understanding of obesity but also; to give insights into dietary requirements for treatment of obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inherited Disorders of Vitamin B12 Metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: CAENORHABDITIS ELEGANS; COMPLEMENTATION GROUPS; MITOCHONDRIA; MUTATION; PROTEIN COMPLEX; VITAMIN B12
Abstract-Résumé: Vitamin B12 is an essential nutrient by helping maintain the metabolic activity of all cells. At least eight genetic diseases have been discovered which are blocked in the metabolism of vitamin B12 to its active forms, resulting in severe, potentially fatal illnesses in children. Our goal has been to identify the affected genes and determine how vitamin B12 is metabolized in cells. To date, seven of the genes have been identified and, with our colleagues, we have identified five of them. In the last grant period, we investigated the biochemical steps governed by the newly identified genes, investigated the mutations causing B12 diseases in patients and have continued to search for additional genes in human cells and other organisms that use B12 as a nutrient. We now propose to investigate the mechanism by which B12 is metabolized in human cells. We predict the existence of protein complexes, or small self-contained factories, in cells that process B12 to active form from beginning to end. We will isolate the complexes, determine their composition and how they metabolize B12 and how the predicted complexes are disrupted in patients. Our studies will increase our knowledge of vitamin B12 metabolism in humans and lead to the therapeutic strategies for the treatment of affected patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of podocalyxin in hematopoietic and vascular function
Keywords-MotsClés: ASYMETRIC CELL DIVISION; BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION; CANCER; CELL ADHESION; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; HEMOPOIESIS; HOMING AND MIGRATION; LEUKOCYTE TRAFFICKING; METASTASIS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; TRANSGENIC MICE; VASCULAR ENDOTHELIA; VIDEO MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: All blood cells, including those that help fight infection, transport oxygen or stop bleeding by forming clots at the site of a wound are derived from a very rare stem cell in the bone marrow.  These cells are an extremely valuable clinical commodity since they can be used to regenerate all blood cells of the body in patients with genetic diseases or undergoing treatment for cancer.  My laboratory is studying a family of cell surface proteins expressed by these rare cells in order to understand how they help regulate stem cell behavior. We have preliminary data to suggest that one of these proteins, podocalyxin, regulates the trafficking of the stem cells to the appropriate site in the bone marrow during transplantation and that it also regulates the expansion of these cells once they reach this site.  The goal of this project is to clarify the molecular mechanisms governing this behavior with the long-term goal of manipulating podocalyxin's role in stem cell migration and expansion for clinical therapy.  Since we also have evidence that this mechanism is subverted by a variety of tumors, this could also lead to approaches to suppressing tumor metastasis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Retinopathy of Prematurity: Role of PAR-2 in restoration of retinal microvascular bed
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH; ENDOTHELIUM; NITRIC OXIDE; NITROSATIVE STRESS; OXIDATIVE STRESS; RETINA
Abstract-Résumé: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is the major serious eye disorder of the child. This condition is associated with long term complications, including strabismus, myopia, abnormal color discrimination, and blindness. ROP evolves from a relatively high extrauterine oxygen exposure of the premature child, which results in arrest in vascular development and degeneration of present vasculature. This anomaly leads to an excessive attempt of the tissue to repair itself, leading to abundant neovascularization that penetrates the vitreous, and predisposes to hazardous retinal detachment. Our laboratory has identified numerous mediators that cause vascular degeneration and new ones that are proliferative. However, to date the mechanisms that unable vessels to reform in vascular depleted areas are unknown. If one would identify these factors, desirable therapies can be envisaged.  We therefore set out to begin to tackle this challenge and have identified a notable candidate, namely protease-activated receptor type 2. Activation of this receptor restores vascularity of the vascular depleted areas of the retina in ROP models. This important pilot information sets the basis of our current grant application, and opens the door for readily amenable therapeutics, superior to currently utilized ones.

TitreApplicationTitle: c-Myb-dependent proliferation & differentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; C-MYB; CELL CYCLE; DEVELOPMENT; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELL; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Heart attack and stroke occur because of hardening of the arteries, which remains the leading cause of death in our society. The unregulated growth of vessel smooth muscle cells (VSMC) is a key feature of this condition. Despite enormous efforts aimed at understanding why VSMC undergo disease-causing growth, it is unfortunate how little of our knowledge has translated into successful treatments. We believe that these difficulties are due to redundancies inherent in biological systems and the failure of therapies aimed at single targets. Accordingly, we have focused our efforts on improving our understanding of the final common pathway of events controlling cell division. It is also noteworthy that the ability of adult VSMC to grow by dividing is unique among muscle cells, as heart and skeletal muscle cells lose their ability to divide following their differentiation from their muscle precursor cells. By contrast, the property of VSMC to continue to divide following differentiation is the very basis of their disease-causing potential. Studying the unique differentiation and development of VSMC may thus help explain how they cause disease.

OrgNm: CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Jewish General/CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Hôpital juif
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of the anti-cancer actions of arsenic.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARSENIC; BIOMARKERS; EXPLORATORY TRANSLATIONAL CANCER RESEARCH; NOVEL PHARMACEUTICAL AGENT; SIGNALING; TARGETED THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Although considerable progress has been made in understanding the biology of cancer, effective novel therapeutics are still urgently needed in human malignancies.  We have studied the mechanism of action of arsenic and found that it turns on specific cellular signaling pathways and can induce cancer cells to undergo a form of programmed cell death.  Through understanding of these signaling pathways, we can develop combinations with other drugs currently used or under development.  This application proposes to further study the mechanisms by which arsenic kills tumor cells and use arsenic to enhance the tumor killing with other drugs.  Our goal is to increase anti-tumor activity without significantly increasing toxicity to the normal cells.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: The behavioral readout of long term plasticity is an active molecular process.
Keywords-MotsClés: CONSOLIDATION; MEMORY EXPRESSION; PLASTICITY; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: The mechanisms involved in memory storage have been intensively studied during the last decades. These investigations gave rise to the now dominant view that protein-synthesis dependent processes are required to store memories over time.  Early studies demonstrating that protein-synthesis inhibitors (PSIs) disrupt memory storage when administered shortly after learning also suggested that the expression of long-term memory during a retention test is not impaired when protein-synthesis is inhibited by systemic PSI injections.  Since then, memory expression has been modeled as a relatively passive readout of memory representations that does not engage the molecular, protein-synthesis dependent mechanisms engaged during learning.  Mainly for this reason, little is known about the molecular events associated with memory expression.  We will attempt to shed some light on this area using behavioral paradigms.  Employing drugs targeting specific molecular pathways that were thought to only be involved in learning, we will challenge memory expression, and monitor changes in expression of receptors associated with memory formation.  So far, we have striking results suggesting that memory expression might be mediated by rather dynamic molecular mechanisms.  If the experiments proposed here confirm these findings, our current understanding of how memory is expressed would be in need for fundamental revision.  The implications would not only be of theoretical nature, but would touch directly on the clinical treatment of memory related disorders. For example, the clinician may be able to control retrieval of specific memories in patients suffering from aversive, traumatic experiences, and, on the other hand, may help those who suffer from apparent amnesia, in cases where this memory loss represents a failure in the retrieval of memory that still exists but is repressed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Magnetic Resonance Imaging for Ischemic Heart Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; TISSUE CHARACTERIZATION; VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA
Abstract-Résumé: A major cause of sudden death is the development of a sustained very rapid heart rate associated with damage to cardiac muscle due to reduced blood supply. Several treatments have been developed to avoid this situation including the use of drugs to manage heart rate, implantable devices to reset the heart rate if an irregular rhythm is detected, and interventions where segments of cardiac muscle are destroyed to avoid conditions which can cause the rapid heart rate. Unfortunately, it is difficult to predict who will benefit from these therapies. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is proving very effective in characterizing damage to the cardiac muscle. Several studies  suggest that such information can be used to better manage patients at risk of sudden death due to sustained rapid heart rates. Our goal is to better understand how such information is related to the underlying causes of this condition and to exploit this information to improve patient management. To do so, we plan to characterize the movement of electrical signals in the heart via correlation of  electrical properties to spatial maps of tissue damage determined from MR images, studying these measurements initially in animal models and explanted hearts,and finally in patients at risk of developing rapid heart rates. Through these studies, we hope to be able to better plan and assess interventions aimed at adjusting the electrical circuitry of the heart, yielding better outcomes for this patient population.

ResearchClassEN: CONGENITAL ANOMALIES; NONE OF THE ABOVE
ClasseRechercheFR: ANOMALIES CONGENITALES; AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES
TitreApplicationTitle: Cx43 mutations linked to human disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNEXINS; DISEASE; GAP JUNCTIONS; MUTATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: In normal human physiology, most cells directly talk to each other through specialized conduits or channels that are built between contacting cells within tissues and organs. The protein molecules used to assemble these specialized cell-cell channels, known as gap junctions, are called connexins. Inherited mutations in the genes that encode these connexins cause severe diseases ranging from deafness to developmental disorders. Most organs in the human body express one particular member of the connexin family called connexin43. Inherited mutations in this connexin lead to a wide range of developmental abnormalities in the hands, feet, facial bone and teeth, and frequently cause chronic disease of the bladder, eyes and nerves. Our group has specialized and published extensively on this disease known as oculodentodigital dysplasia. In the present application, we will use cell and mouse models of oculodentodigital dysplasia to examine how connexin43 mutations lead to moderate or severe disease in some tissues but cause little or no disease in other organs where connexin43 is present. Importantly, we will obtain cells and tissues from patients suffering from this disease to facilitate our studies. Through our multidisciplinary approach of using genetically manipulated cells, mouse models of the disease and human samples from patients, we will provide much needed insight into the basis of how connexin43 mutations cause disease. Finally, our studies should provide important leads into potential therapeutic interventions that may alleviate the severity of the disease in patients suffering from chronic and degenerative problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: MHC II antigen presentation: Modulation by E3-ubiquitin ligases of the MARCH family
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTATION; CYTOKINES; DENDRITIC CELLS; E3 UBIQUITIN LIGASE; MHC CLASS II; MONOCYTES
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system protects humans against pathogens and inflammation (redness, heat, swelling...) is part of the healing process. However, the body must put an end to these reactions in order to prevent complications and even auto-immune diseases. We have identified a molecule (MARCH1) that acts as a brake in the presence of anti-inflammatory messages such as the cytokine IL-10. MARCH1 acts by modifying the structure of other proteins through the addition of a ubiquitin tag. Our goal is to understand the regulation of MARCH1  in immune cells, identify its molecular targets and to characterize its structure and function. These results will help understanding inflammation, autoimmunity and possibly control organ transplantation.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE; GÉNOMIQUE, PROTÉOMIQUE ET BIOINFORMATIQUE
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; TUMEURS
TitreApplicationTitle: Control of the function and activity of the anaphase promoting complex by phosphorylation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANAPHASE-PROMOTING COMPLEX; CELL CYCLE REGULATION; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEOMICS; UBIQUITINATION; YEAST CELL BIOLOGY AND PHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The most critical moment in the life of a cell is when it separates its replicated chromosomes into two daughter cells.  Errors in the timing of this event can be catastrophic and lead to the damage and loss of chromosomes, both of which can lead to the generation of a cancerous cell.  A similar error in a maturing egg can lead to devastating chromosomal disorders, like Down syndrome.       How do cells integrate different signals, such as the size and environment of the cell, or if the cell's chromosomes are fully replicated and properly attached to the division machinery, to determine when to separate its chromosomes?  My hypothesis is that a complex of proteins, called the anaphase promoting complex or APC, keeps track of this information by the addition or removal of special marks, called phosphorylation, on members of this complex.  I want to determine how many different marks there are, how they change during the life of the cell and what happens when they are never added.  Understanding how the APC keeps track of this information will lead to a greater understanding of why errors occur during chromosome separation and how we can prevent these errors from ever happening.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent

TitreApplicationTitle: The Iowa Flood Project: Effects of prenatal maternal stress on pregnancy outcomes and infant development.
Keywords-MotsClés: FETAL DEVELOPMENT; INFANT DEVELOPMENT; NATURAL DISASTER; PREGNANCY OUTCOMES; PRENATAL STRESS; QUESTIONNAIRES
Abstract-Résumé: Stressing pregnant female animals result in damage to the foetus, subsequently affecting later development. Studying prenatal maternal stress (PNMS) in humans is hampered by ethical constraints: researchers cannot randomly assign pregnant women to stress and no-stress conditions. Disasters create natural experiments in which the degree of stress may be randomly assigned to large numbers of pregnant women. In January 1998, Southern Quebec experienced the worst disaster in Canadian history, an ice storm which knocked out electrical power to more than 3 million people for as long as 45 days. McGill researchers recruited over 150 pregnant women in June 1998 and have been following the women and the development of their children ever since. Results show that more severe in utero exposure to PNMS is associated with worse cognitive, behavioural, motor, and physical development during infancy and earlier childhood. Yet Project Ice Storm has weaknesses: there were no pre-disaster measures on the women, the sample size has diminished to about 140 families 10 years later, and no biological samples (i.e., fetal and maternal blood, placenta, umbilical cord), needed to test hypotheses about the way PNMS effects the foetus, were obtained. In June 2008, Iowa experienced the worst flooding in 50 years. Before the flooding, University of Iowa researchers had already recruited 135 pregnant women and assessed their psychological functioning, coping, and social support to study the effects of everyday stress on pregnancies. The goal of the current grant is to increase our understanding of the effects of PNMS on pregnancy and fetal outcomes, and on early childhood development. An additional 300 women will be recruited to participate. The current grant will allow us to test biological markers to determine the manner in which PNMS influences development. It will also allow for a thorough prospective follow-up of mothers and children annually between the ages of 1 and 5 years.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Impact of an Aging Population on the Delivery of Critical Care Services in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CRITICAL CARE; HEALTH SERVICES AND POLICY RESEARCH; INTENSIVE CARE UNITS; MECHANICAL VENTILATION
Abstract-Résumé: We hypothesize that the aging of Canada's population is creating a looming crisis for our healthcare system.  Elderly patients already comprise the majority of acutely ill and critically ill patients in Canadian hospitals, and we anticipate that this issue will intensify.  We predict that Canada's aging population (the 'Baby Boomers') is expected to increase the demand for ICU care by nearly 60% over the next 20 years.  If successful, our research will examine the implications of these trends on the Canadian healthcare system.  By examining the effects of age on ICU utilization and outcome and on post-ICU healthcare utilization and outcome, we will provide vital information to help citizens, researchers, and policy makers anticipate future costs and resource requirements. We believe the findings of our research will be essential for planning healthcare delivery to the increasing number of elderly Canadian patients who will require ICU care in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery and characterization of clinically important changes in axillary node-negative breast cancer.
Keywords-MotsClés: AXILLARY NODE-NEGATIVE BREAST CANCER; BIOSTATISTICAL METHODS CLUSTERING; GENE EXPRESSION MICRO ARRAYS; MICRO-DISSECTION; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; PRE-MALIGNANT BREAST LESIONS; PROGNOSTIC MARKERS; TUMOUR ARRAYS
Abstract-Résumé: Axillary lymph node status in breast cancer is the most important factor in predicting a patient's risk of recurrence of disease. Patients whose disease has not spread to the lymph nodes (axillary node-negative, ANN) generally have a good prognosis; however, 20-30% of ANN patients will experience disease recurrence. This limit in prognostic ability of lymph node status has led our team to a search for markers with prognostic power to aid in determining which ANN patients may benefit from therapy.   We recruited women with ANN breast cancer from eight Toronto hospitals to participate in the study. We obtained biospecimens and clinical follow-up information from the group. We have found that certain genetic changes in the tumor, such as increased number of copies of the HER2 gene, can predict those patients most likely to have a recurrence.  We also found that the presence of lymphatic invasion is predictive of recurrence. We have identified novel patterns of genes that distinguish tumors with and without lymphatic invasion and related to recurrence. We will continue to investigate the alterations in breast tumors. We will evaluate how the patterns can be used to predict recurrence. We will study the genes to discover how changes in the genes can be involved in breast cancer.  Our studies may lead to the identification of novel genes involved in breast cancer. By studying tumors from a large number of women with ANN breast cancer we will be able to determine the clinical importance of the genetic changes. The protein products of some of these genes may be targets for the development of new cancer treatments, as Herceptin has been for tumors that overexpress HER2. Our goals are to explore the clinical importance of these genes to diagnose women early enough to prevent or diminish the effects of breast cancer, to tailor treatment to increase the likelihood of a cure, and to identify novel targets for new cancer therapeutics.

ClasseRechercheFR: SUBSTANCES CANCERIGENES (ET ENVIRONNEMENTALES); LES EFFETS ENVIRONNEMENTAUX SUR LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of the sex differences in radiation responses
Keywords-MotsClés: BYSTANDER EFFECT; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; IONIZING RADIATION; SEX DIFFERENCES; SEX HORMONES
Abstract-Résumé: While modern cancer radiation therapy has increased patient survival rates, the risk of secondary treatment-related complications and adverse effects is becoming a growing clinical problem. Radiation-induced tumors and other toxic radiation effects have been reported to occur to a different extent in males and females. Mechanisms of these differences remain elusive. The DNA content of each cell in a given higher organism is identical: our liver and brain cells contain the same DNA, but they are very different in their shapes and functions. This is due to the existence of different patterns in reading and translation of genes for the type of cells in question, referred to as 'gene expression'. This is the domain of the emerging science of epigenetics  (literally, 'beyond genetics'). Remarkable features of epigenetic changes include simple chemical modifications of the 'C' base in DNA by attachment or removal of methyl (-CH3) groups. Highly methylated regions of DNA are turned off or silenced - a kind of cellular dimmer switch.  Most amazing and contrary to popular opinion that DNA sequences determine everything, epigenetic changes can extend beyond cell division to reproduction. Although epigenetic changes are inheritable, they are reversible. A lot still has to be learned about the role of epigenetic changes in living cells and organisms and their interactions with the environment. In my laboratory, we have found that males and females respond to radiation differently due to distinct epigenetic changes in DNA methylation. These changes may lead to different levels of radiation toxicity. Currently, we would like to understand (i) which epigenetic changes occur in males and females; (ii) why epigenetic changes in males and females are different; (iii) which cellular processes they affect. We will use a set of novel state-of-the art techniques to answer these questions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of placental VEGF-A and FLT1/sFLT1 in placental vascularity, fetal growth, and maternal function in mice
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; MOUSE MODELS; PLACENTA; PREECLAMPSIA; PREGNANCY; VEGF-A
Abstract-Résumé: The placenta is a critically important organ for successful pregnancy.  In the placenta, maternal blood rich in oxygen and nutrients bathes the fetal villi.  They absorb these substances and they are transported to the fetus in the umbilical cord to support fetal growth.  The villi are packed full of fetal blood vessels in a healthy placenta, but blood vessels may be sparce in fetuses whose growth is abnormally slow during pregnancy.  Similarly, the flow of blood from the maternal side is often low in women with preeclampsia, a life-threatening disorder in the mother.  In women with small fetuses or who have preeclampsia the normal increase in sflt1, a factor that inhibits blood vessel growth, is accelerated.  Evidence suggests high sflt1 inhibits blood vessel growth and can cause these diseases.  Treatments to block the rise in sflt1 are contemplated, yet the normal function of the late-pregnancy rise is unknown.  The current proposal investigates the normal role for sflt1 in placental blood vessel density and maternal function in mutant mice.  Since evidence suggests sflt1 is produced by the fetal trophoblast cells that form the placenta, we will use mutant mice to specifically delete sflt1 in these cells.  We anticipate that this will blunt the normal increase in sflt1 in late gestation in the mother.  We will then examine the effect of this intervention on the placenta and the mother.  sflt1 is believed to act by reducing levels of the blood vessel growth factor, VEGF.  So, we will see if inhibiting VEGF production by trophoblast cells using other types of mutant mice reduces placental vessel density and/or causes preeclamptic changes in the mother.  These studies will help us understand the role of sflt1 and VEGF in normal pregnancy leading to a better understanding of how abnormal levels of these substances cause disease in pregnancy.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent

ClasseRechercheFR: AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES; METABOLISME ET NUTRITION
TitreApplicationTitle: Pre-clinical trial of docosahexaenoic acid supplementation in AMD
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION (AMD); ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MECHANISMS OF RETINA DEGENERATION AND DHA THERAPEUTIC ACTION; MOUSE MODEL; NUTRITION; VISUAL FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of registered blindness in the elderly of the western world. Each year, 78,000 Canadians are diagnosed with AMD, a number expected to triple within the next 25 year as our population ages. The dry form of AMD comprises over 90% of all cases and a cure as yet to be found for it. A major hurdle for developing a treatment has been the lack of optimal animal models of AMD. The newly developed ELOVL4 transgenic mouse shares similar pathological processes to dry AMD. During the past 2 years of funding by CIHR we have undertaken a detailed analysis of this novel model, which further supports anatomical and functional similarities in the degenerating retinas of ELOVL4 mice and humans with dry AMD. We also have obtained conclusive preliminary results supporting that retina function can be partially preserved by dietary supplementation with DHA (a type of omega-3 fatty acid) in ELOVL4 mice. More exhaustive experiments are required to better understand the mechanisms underlying retina degeneration and the therapeutic effect of DHA in ELOVL4 mice. These experiments must be undertaken before we can consider and optimally plan a large-scale clinical trial of DHA supplementation in dry AMD patients. Since dry AMD is the greatest risk factor for developing wet AMD, then preventing dry AMD is likely to thwart most cases of wet AMD.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Regular Exercise on Cerebrovascular Reserve in Older Adults: Role in the Prevention of Age-Related Cognitive Decline
Keywords-MotsClés: AEROBIC EXERCISE TRAINING; AGING; CARDIORESPIRATORY FITNESS; CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW; COGNITIVE FUNCTION; STROKE PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Cerebral blood flow (CBF) is highly regulated by carbon dioxide and oxygen in the arterial blood. This process becomes impaired with cerebrovascular disease processes and by aging.  Aging is associated with a progressive decline in CBF, which is a major risk factor for stroke. In premenopausal women, this decline is not as pronounced as in men but it appears to be accelerated after menopause and persists into old age. This biphasic phenomenon might be explained by ovarian hormone modulation of CBF before menopause, followed by a predominant influence of other factors thereafter. Physical inactivity, a modifiable risk factor for stroke and cognitive decline, may be one of those factors. However, the mechanism by which physical activity exerts its protective effect on the cerebral circulation is unclear.   If physical activity is a significant modulator of CBF, one would predict that men and women who are more active would have fewer incidences of cerebrovascular disease than those who are sedentary. A suitable experimental design would require a set of studies in sedentary men and women, followed by the same studies in active men and women, and then placing the sedentary and physically-active groups on similar training programs. This approach would enable the possibility of using this knowledge to impact predictors for stroke, or at least how active living may prevent cardiovascular problems in the brain from occurring.   We propose studies in sedentary men and women to address the question: What are the effects of physical activity on CBF and cognitive function in older men and women? This approach will allow us to study the interactions between the cerebral circulation and cognitive function, and may provide powerful diagnostic tools to help identify those individuals at risk of stroke. This work may have a positive impact in helping delay or prevent the onset of disabilities due to diseases like stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Design and Application of Combinatorial Libraries of Synthetic Antibodies and Alternative Scaffolds
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODIES; CANCER; CELL SIGNALING; PHAGE DISPLAY; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Protein-protein interactions are involved in essentially all biological processes.  Furthermore, most diseases are caused by or are associated with aberrant protein-protein interactions.  Thus, understanding and manipulating protein-protein interactions holds great potential for enhancing our understanding of how cells work, and also, for developing therapies for devastating diseases such as cancer and infectious disease.  This project will develop synthetic antibody libraries as a source of ligands to selectively target proteins inside cells.  These antibodies will be invaluable tools for probing cell function and could even be used as therapies for unmet medical needs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of HLA-driven immune escape on HIV replicative capacity
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOTOXIC T-LYMPHOCYTES (CTL); HIV EVOLUTION AND DIVERSITY; HIV/AIDS; HUMAN LEUKOCYTE ANTIGEN (HLA); IMMUNE ESCAPE; VIRAL FITNESS
Abstract-Résumé: With over 30 million people living with HIV/AIDS globally, the need for an HIV vaccine has never been so urgent.  Yet the recent failure of a major phase 2b vaccine trial highlights the sobering reality that 25 years after the discovery of HIV, we are nowhere close to a vaccine.  In response to major knowledge gaps in our understanding of HIV immunobiology, experts are now calling for a major paradigm shift "back to the basics of vaccine research".  One of the major challenges is the virus' extreme mutational capacity, which allows the virus to escape recognition by the immune system.  Understanding how HIV adapts to immune responses will help us design better vaccines.    Specialized immune cells called "killer" T-cells eliminate HIV-infected cells by recognizing small viral fragments presented by Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) molecules on the infected cell surface. Possession of certain HLA molecules is associated with slower rates of HIV disease progression, although the reasons behind this are not well understood.  It has been hypothesized that certain "protective" HLA molecules mediate a particularly strong and effective immune response that selects for escape mutations that compromise the virus' ability to replicate. The resulting "disabled" virus yields a more benign disease course.   If substantiated, this hypothesis could have important implications for vaccine design.   This proposal represents the first large-scale study investigating the impact of immune escape mutations on viral replicative capacity in HIV sequences obtained from infected patients.  The identification of specific escape mutations that influence HIV replication capacity (and the HLA molecules that drive these changes) will help illuminate which parts of the virus would be most important to include in future vaccine strategies.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - B: Heart and Circulation
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; GÉNOMIQUE, PROTÉOMIQUE ET BIOINFORMATIQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Chromosome Y-dependent modulation of the effects of androgen receptors on mouse cardiac cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN RECEPTORS; CARDIAC FUNCTION; CHROMOSOME Y; EARLY LIFE PROGRAMMING; GENETICS AND GENOMICS; SEX DIFFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Sex differentiation, in addition to being responsible for the obvious differences between males and females, also has consequences on general health.  In particular, cardiovascular diseases affect women and men differently.  In addition to sex steroids (mostly estrogens in females and testosterone in males), there is now evidence that genes present on sex chromosomes (including the male-specific chromosome Y) also play critical roles. However, little is known about the functions of chromosome Y genes besides their effects on male reproductive organs, and there is almost no information explaining how they might affect cardiovascular health.  We have obtained evidence that genetic variants of chromosome Y are responsible for differences in the size and contractile properties of cardiac cells from different mouse strains.  Preliminary experiments have revealed that these effects are complex, as chromosome Y variants transform the manner in which several cardiac genes respond to testosterone, in part by programming around the time of birth how cardiac cells will respond to testosterone later during adult life.  We have therefore designed experiments aimed at elucidating how chromosome Y could affect the characteristics of cardiac cells and their responsiveness to testosterone, and identify the mechanisms responsible for these effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of nitric oxide and its effects:  A pivotal point of control of mast cell phenotype and function.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDOLASE A; ALLERGY; ASTHMA; B BISPHOSPHATE; BIOENERGETICS; EPIGENETICS; FRUCTOSE 1; INFLAMMATION; INFLUENZA; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTERFERON GAMMA; MAST CELLS; NITRATION; NITRIC OXIDE; NITRIC OXIDE SYNTHASES; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Mast cells are involved in allergy and other inflammatory diseases. These cells store and rapidly secrete several powerful chemicals that cause the symptoms of allergic reactions.  In recent years it has also been discovered that mast cells help defend us against bacterial and viral infections.  Our goal is to understand how mast cell functions are controlled so that we will be able to prevent or inhibit the unwanted symptoms of allergy, but at the same time enhance the benefits that mast cells bring in our defence against infections.    We were one of the first research groups to discover that mast cells make nitric oxide, the gas that was the subject of the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1998.  Nitric oxide produced by mast cells inhibits their allergic reactions and appears to enhance their role in host defence.  We are studying precisely how this works and the factors that control how and when mast cells make nitric oxide to regulate their functions.  Our research is aimed at identification of new drugs or therapeutic targets for allergic and infectious diseases.

NomDuComitéFR: Bourses destinées à un professionnel de la santé - Nouveaux chercheurs
TitreApplicationTitle: Cerebral small vessel disease and beta-amyloid deposition in subjects with mildly impaired cognition
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; COGNITION; LEUKOARAIOSIS; MRI; PET
Abstract-Résumé: More than one-quarter of people over age 65 will develop memory problems that impair their basic activities of life. The overall goal of our project is to understand the relationship between memory and brain blood flow, brain damage from lack of blood flow, and Alzheimer's disease. The knowledge gained from this study will allow us to tell who is most at risk for memory difficulty related to blood flow problems or related to Alzheimer's disease. Our results will help us to identify the right groups for future studies of treatments to prevent memory loss.
