NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Function of the Gab1 and Gab2 scaffolding adapter proteins in angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CANCER; ENDOTHELIAL CELL; GAB1/2; KNOCKOUT MICE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Much progress has been made over the last decade in our understanding of the cellular mechanisms leading to cancer. In spite of this, cancer still remains a major cause of human death. A novel anticancer therapy, based on the destruction of blood vessels within tumors, however offers new hope for the successful treatment of cancer. It is derived from the principle that tumor cells, like healthy cells, require oxygen and nutrients to survive. Thus, tumor cells release factors to act on nearby blood vessels to stimulate their growth into the developing tumor. This formation of new blood vessels, a process called angiogenesis, is essential for the aggressive growth of tumor cells, and allows their dispersal in the organism and the formation of metastases. To develop effective means of blocking the growth of tumor-associated blood vessels, we need to understand the molecular events that underlie their formation. In this context, we are proposing to deepen our understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating angiogenesis with special emphasis on proteins called Gab1 and Gab2, which represent important signal amplifiers in cells. We have shown over the last funding period that these proteins play essential roles in the formation of blood vessels in vitro. Therefore, our goal for the next five years is to investigate their in vivo role during angiogenesis and tumor progression, and determine their potential as new therapeutic targets. To do this, we will generate mice in which the Gab1 and Gab2 genes are deleted from blood vessel cells, and we will investigate the consequences on angiogenesis, tumor-associated angiogenesis, and the ability of tumor cells to grow and metastasize. In a complementary fashion, we will also develop and test small peptide inhibitors that neutralize Gab1 and Gab2. The potential impact of these studies on the burden of cancer is that the knowledge generated may lead to the development of novel strategies to block angiogenesis and tumor growth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Safety and Effectiveness of Sitagliptin in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; HEALTH OUTCOMES; MORBIDITY & MORTALITY; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; RESTROSPECTIVE COHORT; SAFETY
Abstract-Résumé: Treatment of type 2 diabetes often requires the use of several oral drugs. Overall, these drugs help to lower blood sugars levels and reduce the risk of kidney, eye, and nerve damage. Differences appear to exist, however, with respect to the effect of each drug's on the risk of cardiovascular disease (i.e., heart and stroke disease). For example, previous research has suggested that metformin may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, while newer agents such as the thiazolidinediones may in fact increase the risk. Given the wide spread use of newer drugs in the treatment of diabetes, better evaluation of the cardiovascular effects of these agents is required.   The range of drugs available to treat diabetes in Canada has recently expanded with the approval of a new oral antidiabetic drug - sitagliptin.  These drugs are rapidly being used to control blood sugars in patients with diabetes, yet there effects on heart disease and stroke are not known.   This study will measure the risk of heart disease and stroke in people using sitagliptin relative to other drugs, like metformin or glyburide. Information from this study will help clinicians better determine which combination of drugs is safe and effective for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Behavioural dysfunction and map alterations in epilepsy.
Keywords-MotsClés: MODELING BRAIN REORGANIZATION IN EPILEPSY
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is the most common and expensive neurological disorder worldwide.  Between seizures people with epilepsy may have any number of behavioural comorbidities that include anxiety/depression, memory disruption, sexual dysfunction, sensory and motor disturbances.  My laboratory has documented motor disturbances in rats that had seizures elicited from the area in the neocortex that regulates forelimb movement.  Furthermore, neocortical movement representations or "motor maps" become larger in rats with seizures much like the anomalous motor maps reported in people with frontal lobe epilepsy.  Thus, we have developed a homologous rat model for the altered motor behaviour and motor map reorganization observed in a population of people with frontal lobe epilepsy. The framework for this grant application is that alterations in neural network functioning underlies inter-ictal behavioural comorbidities with epilepsy.  Neural network functioning can be assessed by deriving high resolution motor maps.  The motor maps are in turn based on the interplay between excitatory and inhibitory cells and seizures alter the synaptic communication and/or cellular firing properties of the cells in the neocortical circuits.  Through the studies proposed here we will test the general hypothesis that expansion and reorganization of neural networks, manifested as changes in motor maps, will be related to alterations in motor behaviours in rats.  This grant utilizes a multi-level integrated approach that encompasses the behavioural, network, cellular and synaptic levels.  The novelty and innovative aspects of these studies are based upon the fact that my laboratory is the only one that uses detailed kinematic behavioural analysis and high resolution intracortical microstimulation to derive motor maps following induced seizures.  Thus my laboratory is in a unique position to discover the relationship between functional network level organization and skilled motor behaviour after seizures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of miRNA action in translation and mRNA decay.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; IN VITRO MICRORNA ASAYS; IN VITRO TRANSCRIPTION; MICRORNA; RNA METABOLISM; TRANSLATIONAL CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: A newly discovered class of small RNA molecule, called microRNAs, has recently been shown to be involved in muscle differentiation, stem cell development, and cancer formation.  MicroRNAs bind to certain tails of the genetic material (messenger RNA) that serves as a the template for the synthesis of all proteins in the cell.  We are studying how microRNAs, once bound to messenger RNAs, shut down protein synthesis and lead to messenger RNA degradation.  Understanding the basic mechanisms of how miRNAs function will allow us to design new treatments for a variety of microRNA-related diseases

TitreApplicationTitle: Vasoactive peptide and growth factor-induced signaling in vascular smooth muscle cells in health and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOTENSIN -II; CALCIUM; CALMODULIN; ENDOTHELIN; GROWTH FACTORS; HYPERTENSION
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension is associated with abnormal vascular resistance due to vessel wall thickness.  The increase in wall thickness of the vessels is due to a greater vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) mass, because of the abnormal growth and proliferation of these cells.  The exact mechanism for this abnormality in hypertension is not clearly understood at the present.  The studies proposed in this grant application are aimed at delineating the molecular mechanism of the abnormal VSMC growth in animal models of hypertension. More specifically,we propose to investigate if vasoactive peptide and growth factor -induced proliferative and hypertrophic signaling pathways are defecive in animal models of hypertension , and if correction of this aberration by pharmacological or genetic interventions can  improve the hypertension.     The results obtained from these studies will eventually provide a basis for new approaches to the management of cardiovascular disease, more particularly, hypertension.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of the immune receptor dectin-1 signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; DECTIN-1; FUNGAL INFECTION; IMAGING; MACROPHAGES; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Infectious diseases continue to be a major cause of mortality worldwide, emphasizing the need for constant expansion of our knowledge on the mechanisms involved in the immune control of pathogens. Understanding how our bodies respond to such life threatening microbes is a priority. By developing new experimental approaches, designed to further detail the relationship between the host and its pathogens, I wish to contribute to the development of new strategies for fighting infectious diseases. Recent discoveries in the domain of innate immunity have highlighted the important role of a new family of proteins. Through these proteins, specialized cells of the innate immune system recognize unique molecule present on the surface of pathogens. These proteins have been named pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) due to their capacity to bind specific pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Dectin-1, a member of this family of immune receptors, is the major receptor for fungal and bacterial beta-glucans. An important feature of this particular PRR relies in its capacity to activate several important processes in immune cells required to counteract microbial infections. The long-term objectives of this project are to elucidate, at the molecular level, the determinants of dectin-1 mediated activation of the immune system. Classical biochemical and biophysical approaches, combined with the use of single molecule analysis, will address questions about the molecular organization of the receptor, specifically, how ligand binding triggers phagocytosis and cellular activation. Such techniques, with the ability to resolve individual molecule behavior, will certainly shed light on yet undetermined mechanisms and thus strengthen our understanding of the regulation of immune system responses to microbial challenges.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endobiotics glucuronidation: a novel therapeutic avenue for metabolic and endocrine diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES; ENDOBIOTICS METABOLISM; GENE REGULATION; HORMONAL DISEASES; LIVER DISEASES; MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Glucuronidation is an enzymatic reaction very well studied for the role its plays in drug elimination. However, this reaction also affects a wide variety of endogenous substance. The aim of our research program is to determine whether controlling the elimination of specific endogenous compounds through the use of novel drugs can be of therapeutic value in the treatment of various pathologies such as liver diseases, cardiovascular diseases or prostate cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of female sex hormone action on susceptibility and immune responses to HSV-2 infection
Keywords-MotsClés: HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS; IMMUNE RESPONSES; KNOCKOUT MICE; PRIMARY CELL CULTURES; SEX HORMONES; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES; SUSCEPBILITY; WOMEN'S REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Genital herpes is a major health problem. An estimated one in four sexually active adults has actve or inactive genital herpes infection. For some time now, it is known that menstrual cycle of women can influence susceptibility to STDs and disease severity. Clinical studies also show that use of oral contraceptives and other hormonal contraceptives such as Depo-Provera by women correlate with increased chance of getting STI infections, including HIV, HSV-2, Chlamydia. Our previous research has shown that sex hormones control both susceptibility and immune responses to sexually transmitted infections including chlamydia and HSV-2. We recently reported that female mice treated with estradiol were protected from herpes infection while progesterone treated mice had severe genital herpes and inflammation. In the current study, we propose to understand how the hormonal environment in the reproductive tract affects immunity to hereps infection in this mouse model. We will study how certain hormones can affect body's defence mechanism in a certain way resulting in better or worse protection. We will also examine how local environment in the genital tract affects body's protective mechanisms. These studies will help us understand how hormones affect ability of females to defend against sexually transmitte infections. This information will be useful particulaly for women who are on hormonal contraceptives on hormone replacement therapies. It will also help us to understand how we can make use of natural hormones to make better vaccine against herpes, targeted specifically for women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of a novel, caspase-8 dependent survival pathway in inflammatory neutrophils
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL SIGNALING; CRITICAL ILLNESS; INNATE IMMUNITY; NEUTROPHILS; SEPSIS
Abstract-Résumé: White blood cells known as neutrophils form the body's first line of defense against infection.  They release a potent array of substances that kill invading bacteria, and so are essential to surviving a life-threatening infection.  But these same substances can cause unwanted damage to healthy host tissues.  Tissue injury by neutrophils, for example, contributes to a condition known as sepsis in critically ill patients in an ICU, and to joint injury in patients with arthritis. In health, the potential for injury is minimized because of the neutrophil lives for only a very brief period, before dying a death by cellular suicide through a process known as apoptosis.  During inflammation, the neutrophil's ability to undergo apoptosis is inhibited, with the result that its capacity for both host defense and tissue injury is enhanced.  We have found that neutrophil survival is dependent on changes to the structure of an enzyme called caspase-8 that initiates the process of apoptosis.  The addition of a phosphate molecule to an amino acid in capase-8 (a process called phosphorylation) blocks its activity.  In the studies proposed here, we will first determine whether phosphorylated caspase-8 is needed to activate a protein known as PI3 kinase, which regulates the survival program in the neutrophil.   We will define the role in neutrophil survival of a new survival gene that we have recently identified and called ILIP-1 (Interleukin-1-Induced Protein-1).  These processes - caspase-8 phosphorylation, PI3 kinase activation, and expression of ILIP-1 - comprise an integrated complex that we have termed the 'casapase-8 survivalsome'.  Finally, we will determine whether modulation of the survivalsome in neutrophils from critically ill patients with sepsis can restore the normal expression of apoptosis.  Together the studies will provide the insights necessary to develop new treatments for life-threatening inflammation that are based on preventing the persistence of inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anomalies dans le contrôle de la réponse des cellules endométriales à l'IL-1 : rôle dans la physiopathologie de l'endométriose.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESE; CELLULES ENDOMETRIALES; CELLULES ENDOMETRIOSIQUES; CULTURE CELLULE; CYTOKINES; ELISA; ENDOMETRE; ENDOMETRIOSE; GEL SHIFT; IL-1; IMMUNOCYTOFLUORESCENCE; INFLAMMATION; MODELE IN VIVO; PROLIFERATION; PROMOTEUR; REAL TIME-PCR; RECEPTEURS; SIGNALISATION; SIRNA; SURVIE CELLULAIRE; TRANSFECTION; WESTERN BLOT; ZYMOGRAPHIE
Abstract-Résumé: L'endometriose, croissance de tissu endometial souvent dans l'abdomen, est une maladie frequente (8 a 10% de femmes en periode reproductive) causant infertilite et douleurs abdominales. La maladie depend des hormones du cycle, mais elle est souvent associee a de l'inflammation dans l'abdomen et dans l'endometre a l'interieur de l'uterus. Nos recherches on montre l'existence d'une deficience dans un systeme specifique de controle de cette inflammation dans l'endometre (le recepteur de l'interleukine-1 type 2), laquelle se conjugue a une surexpression du recepteur d'activation type 1 dans les implants. Cette deficience peut jouer un role cle dans l'initiation de l'inflammation dans la cavite abdominale, la ou on trouve les lesions d'endometriose, dans l'aptitude de ces cellules a se developper a l'exterieur de la cavite uterine et former des lesions d'endometiose et notre but est d'en connaitre les mecanismes, et les implications quant au developpement de la maladie. Nous croyons que la recherche proposee pourrait avoir un impact considerable dans l'endometriose pour mieux comprendre la physiopathologie de cette maladie et la mise en place de nouvelles approches diagnostiques et therapeutiques.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toward Reducing the Risk for Violence-Related Adverse Events among People with Major Mental Disorders: A Prospective, Repeated-Measures Study
Keywords-MotsClés: LONGITUDINAL COHORT DESIGN; MENTAL HEALTH; RISK REDUCTION; SUICIDE-RELATED BEHAVIOUR; VICTIMIZATION; VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Unfortunately, people who suffer from major mental disorders such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression are at heightened risk to experience violence-related events in their lives. This includes suicide and suicide attempts, being victims of violence, and also engaging in violent behaviour. These adverse events are also related to one another. That is, people who experience one of these events are more likely to experience the others, compared to people who do not experience any of them. Separate lines of research have identified numerous risk factors for each adverse event. However, an integrated study of all three adverse events has yet to be undertaken, despite the great promise this holds for reducing the risk of these multiple adverse events. Such a line of research can enhance the health and safety of persons with major mental disorders by increasing the understanding of what factors lead to increased and decreased risk, and informing treatments that can reduce the risk for multiple adverse outcomes. This research project will follow a group of 300 persons with major mental disorders, and a matched comparison group of 150 persons without mental disorders, in order to determine (a) what the common and unique risk and protective factors are for suicide-related behaviour, victimization, and violence, (b) which of these risk and protective factors change over time, and hence would be particularly promising areas for risk-reduction intervention programs. In order to accomplish these goals, the study will include comprehensive baseline assessments of risk and protective factors, and three follow-ups within 12 months.

TitreApplicationTitle: Finding the endocrine and genetic determinants of obesity: The Newfoundland study
Keywords-MotsClés: CCK; FOOD INTAKE AND MACRONUTRIENTS; GENETICALLY HOMOGENEOUS NEWFOUNDLAND POPULATION; GHRELIN; GUT HORMONES; PPY AND PYY3-36; SNPS; WILLETT FOOD FREQUENCY QUESTIONNAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: Eating more than one needs is a major cause of human obesity. The gut produces chemicals called hormones that tell the brain how much we need to eat. If the level of these hormones is abnormal, one may eat too much leading to obesity. We think that one of the reasons why more people in Newfoundland are overweight/obese may be due to abnormal levels of these hormones. This abnormality may be genetic. We will study the role of genes in causing this abnormality in the Newfoundland population. We will measure food intake, total body fat, the level of gut hormones and relate these with any abnormality found in the genes we study. This information will help for development of medication to control abnormal gut hormone levels, food intake and obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Search for genes of hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENTAL EXPOSURES; EPIGENOMICS; HYPERTENSION; OBESITY; PERSONAL RISK PREDICTION; WHOLE-GENOME ASSOCIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension (HT) is a well recognised global disease burden, which has yet to be resolved. Genomic determinants contribute significantly to HT and cardiovascular outcomes, which tend to cluster in families; however, their impact is blurred with age and progressive exposure to environmental factors. That is probably one of the reasons for only moderate success in determination of common genomic variants causative for HT in spite of significant endeavours in genomic analysis of hypertension. The so far identified variants contribute only modestly to overall risk. While genomic determinants are not modifiable, the degree of DNA methylation (epigenomics), resulting in modification of transcription of specific genes, and the telomeric length, are modifiable, reflecting past and current impacts of environmental factors. We hypothesize that integrating the information from genomic signatures of HT with progressively modifiable parameters will enhance our capacity to predict and prevent cardiovascular outcomes. To achieve this we will: a) analyze outcomes, temporal characteristics and familial clustering using hospital and genealogical records; b) partition hypertension into clinically and genetically defined subsets along phenotypic and genomic characteristics; c) search for genomic signatures of early nonfatal and fatal cardiovascular outcomes utilizing enhanced level of combined genomic and epigenomic analyses in defined subsets of hypertensive families d) use results of the above to develop "Personal Risk Prediction" tools in collaboration with our bioinformatics co-investigators and in partnership with IBM Research. The goal of our research is to develop predictive medicine tools to help doctors diagnose risks before they manifest, with a potential of primary prevention to reduce diseases burden.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular basis of synaptic communication between inhibitory interneurons in the hippocampus
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; INHIBITORY INTERNEURON; NETWORK COMPUTATION; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; TWO-PHOTON MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: How circuits of neurons process information depends on the dynamic dialogue between two network elements: principal cells and local circuit inhibitory interneurons. As network gatekeepers, GABAergic inhibitory interneurons control all stages of information processing by principal neurons, from signal integration to generating spikes and synchronized network oscillations. To perform these precise operations, inhibitory interneurons must be tightly organized in functional ensembles. In the hippocampus, the brain structure involved in learning and memory, a specific population of inhibitory interneurons selectively innervates other GABAergic cells, and may provide the cellular basis for such higher-level control of network computations. However, the physiological properties and the role of these cells in the local circuit dialogue remain unknown. We propose that the specific physiological organization of these interneuron-specific interneurons (ISIs) allows them to efficiently integrate multiple cortical and subcortical inputs and to act as a fine-tuning device sculpting the inhibition received by principal cells. We will use a combination of whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, two-photon microscopy, and pharmacology in acute slices of mouse hippocampus to investigate: (1) how ISIs integrate signals and produce spikes; (2) how their signal integration is affected by the activation of subcortical inputs; (3) how connections between inhibitory interneurons are modified by changes in activity; and (4) how the inhibitory control of local circuit inhibition directs the network activity. This investigation should provide essential information about the functional organization of inhibitory interneurons specialized to control network inhibition. It will also yield new important insights into how the interactions between specific neural elements form working neural circuits, and how these may break down in brain disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: The implications of adolescent health and health risk behaviors for  health in early adulthood: Sources of continuities and discontinuities in developmental trajectories over 10 years
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT HEALTH; HEALTH PROMOTION; LIFESPAN HEALTH; LONGITUDINAL RESEARCH; MENTAL HEALTH; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Can we predict adult health based on youth characteristics and experiences? This question is addressed in an interdisciplinary program of research that will use six waves of data to follow a cohort of youth (initially ages 12 to 18) across a total of 10 years. Our research aims to inform strategies for community development, policy and education that can to advance healthy foundations for young adults. Assuming a lifespan, perspective, we hypothesize that health and health risk behaviors affect each other and are affected by risks and protective factors that characterize both individuals and the contexts in which the live. We highlight an important set of indicators that, together, paint a profile of health and health risks in the early adult years (physical health, mental health, stable relationships, low health risk behaviors and accruing labour market capital).We hypothesize that changes in  these five interdependent indicators of health in young adulthood are, to some degree, founded on stable individual differences that are already evident in adolescence. We also examine the prospective effects of multivariate risk factors (including disruptions and conflict in family of origin, deviant peer associations, serious injuries, weight gain, early school leaving, and early parenting, relationship aggression) and protective factors (family support [financial and emotional], peer support, on time graduation from high school, postsecondary school engagement, stable romantic relationships). These predictors can be and have been targeted by policy and prevention programs aiming to improve health across the lifespan and they have been extensively shown to effect late adolescent outcomes, however, their significance for health in young adulthood is largely unknown.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the disease-modifying potential of calcium channel blockers in Parkinson's disease: Using population-based administrative data to inform clinical trials.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKERS; HEALTH CARE ADMINISTRATIVE DATABASES; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PROGNOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: There is evidence from laboratory models that a class of medication commonly used to treat high blood pressure (dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, DHP CCBs) may be protective against the progression of Parkinson's disease.  This project will explore the impact of greater exposure to DHP CCBs on the rate of progression of Parkinson's disease using the health care administrative databases of Ontario.  Rate of progression will be assessed by time to requiring drug treatment, admission to long term care and death.  If slower rate of progression is identified in those taking DHP CCBs, this will provide important justification for studies of DHP CCBs in Parkinson's disease patients.  There is a critical need for treatments that slow the progression of Parkinson's disease.  This project will lay the foundation for other projects investigating the effects of commonly used medications on outcomes in Parkinson's disease.  Together these projects will form an integral part of the research program that will be supported by this New Investigator Award.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Translational Approach to Neuro-Inflammation and Behavioral Outcomes After Spinal Cord Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; HUMAN CLINICAL TRIALS; MULTIPLEX BEAD ARRAY TECHNOLOGY; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injuries result in devastating paralysis, often in young, otherwise healthy individuals. A great deal of scientific research into spinal cord repair/regeneration has been conducted over the past 30 years, offering much hope to individuals with this catastrophic injury. Despite this, all therapies which have shown great promise in animal models of spinal cord injury have failed to demonstrate benefit in human clinical trials. Hence, there are no treatments currently available to reverse the paralysis of spinal cord injury. When the spinal cord is injured, an inflammatory reaction is triggered. This inflammatory response is thought to contribute to further damage. In this research project, we will investigate the inflammatory response to spinal cord injury in human patients by sampling their spinal fluid and measuring proteins that regulate inflammation. We will correlate these inflammatory proteins with the severity of paralysis and the behavioral/functional recovery of these patients. This will establish a method of classifying patients according to biological, rather than functional criteria. We will then test whether these proteins are influenced by a drug called minocycline, which is currently being tested in patients with acute spinal cord injuries. This will help us identify biological methods of measuring treatment response.  Establishing biomarkers of injury severity and treatment response will be extremely valuable in facilitating clinical trials of new SCI treatments, and will potentially speed up the process of validating new therapies for this devastating injury. Also, by revealing new information on the human inflammatory response to injury, we will identify important aspects of the acute pathophysiology of spinal cord injuries that may be important targets for new treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: CXC chemokines in basal cell carcinomas
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL CELL CARCINOMA; CELL SINGALING; CXC CHEMOKINES; RODENT MODELS; SKIN CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: A form of skin cancer called basal cell carcinoma (BCC) develops due to sun light induced gene mutations in skin and hair follicle cells. Over 70,000 cases of BCC occur in Canada each year which are normally treated by expensive surgical removal. Recent studies by the grant applicants have identified a number of genes that are highly expressed in BCCs as compared to healthy skin. In particular we have found CXC chemokines are produced at high levels by BCCs. CXC chemokines are proteins that are released by the cells as a way to communicate with each other. We will use cell cultures and cancer models to identify the importance of CXC chemokine communication in BCC growth. First we will show how these products can stimulate BCC growth. Then we will try to prevent BCC development by blocking the actions of these CXC chemokines. This study will help us to understand the mechanisms involved in BCC development and we may identify new ways to block their growth. New drug treatments for BCC may reduce or even avoid the need for surgical removal of the cancer. Drug application should be a cheaper and less physically and psychologically damaging treatment approach for patients than surgical removal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hypercapnia as Therapy for Neonatal Pulmonary Hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: CARBON DIOXIDE; HYPERCAPNIA; HYPOXIA; INFLAMMATION; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary hypertension (high blood pressure in the lung) is a complication that requires medical treatment in about 1 in 500 newborn infants and commonly leads to death in the most severe cases.  This disease is common in the newborn period because of two factors: 1) a failure of the normal dilation of blood vessels in the lung at birth that allows oxygen to enter the blood, and 2) rapid development of thickening of the walls of blood vessels (known as remodeling), which blocks the normal passage of blood through the lung and prevents vessels from properly relaxing.  The treatments we currently have available to treat babies with pulmonary hypertension often do not work, do not improve remodeling of blood vessels and have not been shown to decrease death or to improve outcome in the long term.  The overall goal of my research is to develop more effective treatments for the prevention and treatment of pulmonary hypertension in newborns.  To facilitate this goal, my laboratory has developed two newborn rat models of chronic pulmonary hypertension, which have many similarities to human newborns that do not respond to conventional treatments.  Published and preliminary work from my laboratory indicates that the induction of high carbon dioxide levels in the blood (hypercapnia) can prevent lung injury and improve pulmonary hypertension in newborn rats.  The aims of our proposed work are to further define the "dose" of hypercapnia that is required to effectively treat pulmonary hypertension, to better understand how hypercapnia works, to ascertain its effects on lung development and to see whether its beneficial effects will last into adult life.  This work will provide new insights with a high potential for clinical translation.  Hypercapnia has great potential as an effective and enticingly simple therapeutic approach to an otherwise intractable problem.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural mechanisms of familiarity assessment
Keywords-MotsClés: DEJA VU; EPILEPSY; FMRI; MEDIAL TEMPORAL LOBE; MEMORY IMPAIRMENTS; RECOGNITION MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to distinguish between new and previously encountered parts of the environment and people is of critical benefit to daily behaviour. We constantly take advantage of this ability, such as when we greet a colleague from work at the shopping mall, but don't greet strangers. Recognition of prior occurrence is thought to rely on two distinct mental processes, i.e. familiarity and recollection. We can find ourselves in situations in which we experience a sense of familiarity with another individual or with a specific place, but cannot recollect anything about the circumstances of a prior encounter. In other situations, we may experience feelings of familiarity in combination with a detailed recollection of a past episode involving this person or place. The general goal of the proposed research is to understand how the human brain generates feelings of familiarity. Although familiarity has long been known as an essential memory component in psychological theory, the underlying brain mechanisms remain unclear. From a health perspective, it is critical to elucidate these mechanisms because impairments in feelings of familiarity represent a clinical feature of various neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, stroke, and epilepsy. It is easy to see that they would be debilitating in daily life given that such impairments can even affect the ability to recognize close relatives. Under some circumstances, they can also result in clinically abnormal feelings of deja vu, i.e., in persistent experiences 'that things look more familiar than they should'. Here, we plan to shed light on the brain mechanisms that cause impairments in feelings of familiarity in epilepsy. We also plan to examine the brain mechanisms of intact feelings of familiarity by using modern brain imaging methods in healthy individuals. Together, the proposed research promises to lead to a better understanding of fundamental memory mechanisms with important clinical applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Viral host interactions of the dicistroviridae family
Keywords-MotsClés: IRES; POLYSOME; RIBOSOME; RNA; TRANSLATIONAL CONTROL; VIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Viruses have evolved strategies to infect host cells and disrupt normal cellular functions while hijacking critical host machineries to express viral genes. However, the host can counteract by using innate antiviral responses to detect and defend against viruses. Revealing the molecular mechanisms between the battle of the virus and host is vital in our fight against clinically relevant viruses. One mechanism that some viruses use is through an IRES. In our cells, molecular machines, called ribosomes, translate our genes into proteins, but some viruses, such as hepatitis C virus and poliovirus, possess an IRES to hijack the ribosome to preferentially express their viral proteins. We need a better understanding of these mechanisms in order to fight viral infections.       This proposal will gain insight into these viral IRESs by elucidating the mechanisms by which a unique IRES, found within an insect virus called the cricket paralysis virus (CrPV), can hijack the ribosome. Because the CrPV IRES directly recruits ribosomes without any factors, it provides a simple and powerful model to study IRES functions and will lay the foundation for studying more complex IRESs. Our previous work was seminal in delineating important CrPV IRES functions. Building on this work, we aim: 1) to use innovative techniques to map the specific IRES elements that interact with the ribosome, 2) to determine how the CrPV disrupt cellular functions that leads to IRES activity in Drosophila (fruit fly) cells, and 3) to elucidate the host antiviral responses in Drosophila cells, which have not been fully investigated. Because molecular signals are often conserved, the study of Drosophila antiviral responses is relevant in revealing fundamental virus host interactions in humans. Armed with these interdisciplinary approaches, we will gain valuable into details of viral IRES mechanics, the host disruptions by the CrPV that leads to IRES activity, and the identity of key antiviral responses.

ClasseRechercheFR: TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION; AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE
TitreApplicationTitle: Signaling mechanisms of the p75 neurotrophin receptor
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; JUN KINASE; NEUROTROPHIN; NF-KB; TRAF PROTEINS; TRK
Abstract-Résumé: Loss of neuronal cells is a hallmark of many diseases of the nervous system. and in many cases, this is mediated by loss of survival signals and activation of a process of cell suicide, termed apoptosis. My lab is concerned with identifying the precise cellular signals that regulate cellular life and decisions in the nervous system.       This proposal is designed to examine the cellular pathways activated a cell surface receptor termed p75NTR. Previous studies have shown that this single receptor can, in some circumstances, cause cells to survive but in others, to facilitate their death. The mechanisms controlling these processes are complicated but are beginning to be clarified.       In this proposal, we will address i) how p75NTR causes cells to commit suicide, ii) how p75NTR present in non-neuronal cells activates death pathways in neurons and iii) how p75NTR can, in some cases, facilitate cellular survival pathways.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of auditory and cognitive deficits on speech understanding in the elderly
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; AUDIO-VISUAL INTEGRATION; AUDITORY AGING; COGNITIVE PROCESSES; HEARING; HEARING DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Older adults often find it difficult to understand speech in everyday listening situations.  These difficulties could reflect age-related deterioration in hearing abilities, in cognitive abilities (e.g., memory), or both. For example, when listening to a conversation, hearing declines might cause older adults to mishear individual words more often than younger adults.  This, in turn, will often cause older adults to misinterpret the intended message.  Alternatively, cognitive declines may make it more difficult for older adults to integrate information coming from different conversationalists, leading to misinterpretation of what was said. Our research program is designed to determine the relative contribution of these two kinds of declines to spoken language comprehension so that appropriate steps can be taken to improve language comprehension in older adults (e.g., assistive listening devices for hearing declines; medication and/or therapies for cognitive declines). To date, we have been able to show that declines in hearing abilities rather than declines in cognitive abilities are responsible for most of the comprehension difficulties experienced by healthy older adults when they are listening to sentences, lectures, or simple two-person conversations. We now plan to investigate the relative contribution of these two factors when the speech material becomes cognitively more complex (e.g., multi-talker conversations), and when listening becomes more difficult (e.g., the background contains intelligible but irrelevant speech). In addition, because real-life conversations are usually face to face, we will be studying spoken language comprehension when the listener can both hear and see the talkers so that the results of this research will generalize more readily to real-life situations.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal correlates for spatial self-motion estimation and motor planning
Keywords-MotsClés: MOVEMENT CONTROL; NEURAL COMPUTATION; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; SENSORY INTEGRATION; SPATIAL ORIENTATION; VESTIBULAR
Abstract-Résumé: Whether running to catch a ball or turning to reach for a coffee cup, our ability to interact behaviorally with the environment depends critically on knowing our motion and orientation in space. As we move, the brain integrates multiple sensory signals to compute estimates of our self-motion. However, this poses a challenge because the way that sensory signals must be combined and interpreted depends on the conditions (context) in which they are sensed. One important contextual influence is gravity. Gravity provides a world-fixed reference (i.e., which way is up/down) for interpreting our motion. To navigate during locomotion or maintain upright posture we rely on information about our motion with respect to this fixed spatial reference. However, because each of our sensors is attached to different body parts, no one sensor provides this information. For example, our vestibular sensors (semicircular canals and otoliths) signal head movement along axes fixed in the head. Thus, when running to catch a ball, the same movement in space (e.g., forward motion) is sensed by one combination of sensors when the head is upright and a different set when the head is tilted backward to look up at the ball. To maintain balance as we run, we must also know our tilt relative to gravity. This too requires combining sensory signals in a head-orientation-dependent way. Gravity thus serves as a fundamental contextual cue for interpreting the motion our sensors encode. The goal of this work is to investigate the contextual role of gravity on the integration of multisensory (vestibular, visual) signals in the brainstem and cerebellum. By better understanding how the brain computes spatial motion estimates that are essential for tasks such as navigation and postural control, it is hoped that this research will lead to improved rehabilitative strategies to counteract spatial disorientation, balance and dizziness disorders, debilitating problems that are particularly common in the elderly.

TitreApplicationTitle: Matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) in myocardial cell death  from oxidative stress injury
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL DEATH; MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASES; NECROSIS; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PROTEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Enhanced oxidative stress is common to several cardiac diseases and can damage heart muscle cells, sometimes leading to cell death.  This of course can result in heart failure.  There are enzymes in heart cells which may be activated as a result of enhanced oxidative stress and contribute to cell injury and death by cutting other proteins into smaller pieces.  These enzymes, known as proteases, are very important in cell injury pathways and inhibiting their activity may prevent injury from oxidative stress.  This proposal will focus particularly on one such protease, matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2), which has newly discovered biological roles inside of heart muscle cells which may contribute to cell injury and death.  We particularly would like to understand the role of MMP-2 in cell injury and death, and compare its role to other known proteases, as we believe it has distinct undiscovered roles and targets.  We will use a combination of approaches including molecular, to cultured heart muscle cells, to intact hearts isolated from rats which have been given treatments to enhance oxidative stress.  We will determine if inhibiting MMP-2 will protect the cells and the hearts from cell injury and death resulting from oxidative stress.  The relevance of this research is that an entirely new class of inhibitor drugs which target MMP-2 may prove useful for the treatment of a broad range of cardiovascular diseases, as enhanced oxidative stress is common to many.

TitreApplicationTitle: Melanoma and neurofibromatosis: Genetic diseases linked by dark skinned mouse mutants
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; G PROTEINS; GENETICS; MELANOMA; MOUSE; NEUROFIBROMATOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Melanoma is a type of cancer that originates in the pigment cells of the skin. The number of melanoma cases in North America has more than doubled in the past 20 years and continues to rise. When not treated at an early stage of disease progression, melanoma patients often have a poor survival outcome, since metastatic melanoma is very aggressive. It is generally believed that cancer is caused when individual cells develop a series of changes in their DNA or genetic material. These changes allow them to escape normal growth restrictions.   Our main goal is to understand how melanoma forms in people. We began this project by using mice to model the genetics of skin pigmentation. We focused on three genes that we found darkened the mouse skin when mutated: GNAQ, GNA11 and NF1. We have since identified a mutation in GNAQ in 46% of uveal melanomas, a cancer of the pigment cells in the uveal tract of the eye. GNAQ is the first oncogene identified in this type of cancer and suggests novel therapeutic strategies for its treatment. In this application, we propose to further study the role of GNAQ, GNA11 and NF1 in skin pigmentation and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Processing of proIAPP: Role in islet amyloid formation
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYLIN; AMYLOID; BETA CELL; CELL BIOLOGY; HISTOLOGY; IAPP
Abstract-Résumé: Many people with type 2 diabetes must take insulin by injection because of the loss of insulin-producing cells, called islet beta cells, in their pancreas. It is thought that this loss of islet beta cells is due islet amyloid, a toxic accumulation of protein.  In order to better understand why protein builds up in people with type 2 diabetes, we propose to study the forms of a protein hormone called pro-islet amyloid polypeptide (proIAPP).  ProIAPP is made within the insulin-producing islet beta cells. When it is cut by enzymes, it becomes a smaller protein hormone called islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP). Islet amyloid forms when, for unknown reasons, IAPP forms aggregates that kill the islet beta cells.  We believe that in type 2 diabetes, the process through which proIAPP is cut to form IAPP is defective, leading to an accumulation of incompletely cut forms of proIAPP, that then aggregate to form amyloid.   We will study the forms of proIAPP in the blood of persons with type 2 diabetes and in mice that make excessive amounts of the protein hormone. Through this research, we hope to understand why islet amyloid occurs in people with type 2 diabetes. Our goal is to contribute to developing new therapies that may prevent this protein buildup and the resulting destruction of the pancreas' insulin producing cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Action observation in people with Down syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: DEMONSTRATIONS; DOWN SYNDROME; IMITATION; MOTOR LEARNING; OBSERVATIONAL LEARNING; SKILL ACQUISITION
Abstract-Résumé: In British Columbia 2 in every 1000 births are of children with Down syndrome. This is a genetic disorder which results in an array of symptoms including mental and sensory-motor difficulties. People with Down syndrome are at high risk for obesity and cardiovascular disease as they age and inactivity is a significant risk factor. The acquisition of basic motor skills enables and motivates engagement in activities for life. This program of research is designed to fill a knowledge gap about the action-observation process in people with Down syndrome. The specific aim is to study how these people observe and attend to actions in others in order to facilitate the learning of physical skills. Surprisingly very little is know about how to effectively teach people with Down syndrome motor skills and the processes engaged during observation and motor learning. These individuals appear to learn well from demonstrations, in comparison to mental age matched controls, yet there is evidence from brain imaging studies that this process is different to typically developing individuals, not involving activation of motor-areas of the brain. Further, no one has systematically studied what information drives this observational learning process. During actual movement, there is evidence that people with Down syndrome have difficulties predicting the future effects of their action, in terms of how an action looks and feels. We do not know whether this difficulty extends to the observation process and hence this research will help answer this question through studies requiring the prediction of movement effects when watching others. We will use behavioural methods to study these questions, involving the measurement of responses to demonstrated actions, both in the short term and long-term learning of novel actions. This research will direct evidence-based interventions for the teaching of motor skills and help to promote engagement in physical activity among people with Down syndrome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Plasticity of inhibition in spinal sensory pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL PHARMACOLOGY; CELLULAR IMAGING; CHRONIC PAIN; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GABA / GLYCINE; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY
Abstract-Résumé: The nerve cells of the sensory portion of the spinal cord in humans and animals are responsible for the relay of pain related information from the body to the brain, leading to a perceived sensation. Injury to the nervous system can induce persistent changes in spinal cord function that cause pain and tenderness to develop and be maintained for very long periods (days to years) after healing. The present project aims at determining how inhibitory control of nerve cell function is regulated and how it is altered in the spinal cord under pathological conditions such as peripheral neuropathy. Understanding the long term alterations which take place in the spinal cord after injury is of critical importance to design treatments for the prevention and alleviation of chronic neuropathic pain syndromes such as postherpetic neuralgia, causalgia following damage to a major nerve, diabetic neuropathy, allodynia, hyperalgesia, and spontaneous or phantom limb pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards Understanding the Consequences of Mild Bilateral and Unilateral Hearing Loss in Early Childhood
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; DEVELOPMENTAL OUTCOMES; MILD HEARING LOSS; NEWBORN SCREENING; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; UNILATERAL HEARING LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: Permanent hearing loss is one of the most common childhood disorders and interferes with the typical acquisition of speech and language and influences academic, social, and quality of life outcomes.  Several Canadian provinces and much of the world have implemented universal newborn hearing screening programs to identify hearing loss early so that children have a better start in life. About 30 to 40% of the children who may be identified through screening present with mild bilateral or unilateral hearing loss (one ear).   Prior to screening, the majority of these children were not identified until 4 to 6 years of age.  While studies have shown that late-identified hearing loss affects these children's behavior and abilities in school, the impact of hearing loss when it is identified very early in life is less clear. Therefore, there is considerable uncertainty amongst practitioners about the best ways to help children and their families.  This study will follow a group of early identified children over several years to identify the difficulties they are experiencing compared to a group of children with normal hearing. The study will measure children's progress in several areas and interview parents to elicit their perspective of their child's development.  In addition, we will examine the factors that may predict which children will have difficulty.   We will also try to determine what supports families need to care for their child with hearing loss in the early years.  This study will provide useful information for decision-making regarding the severity of hearing loss that should be targeted in newborn hearing screening programs and the interventions that might be appropriate for children with mild and unilateral hearing loss.

TitreApplicationTitle: Computational and structural studies of gene silencing mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTATIONAL MODELING; GENE EXPRESSION MECHANISMS AND PATHWAYS; NMR; PHYSICOCHEMICAL PROPERTIES; STRUCTURAL AND GENOMIC DATA; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Nature has developed mechanisms to protect living organisms against external intruders such as viruses, or internal dysfunction such as cancer. One such security mechanism is shutting down genes, also known as gene silencing. Gene silencing is at the heart of development and specialization. It has thus recently been widely used to study human and model organisms' genetics and development, and to create transgenic plants developing resistance to viruses. Increasing evidences suggest that diseases such as cancer are the result of multiple gene deregulations. A normal cellular reaction in front of such deregulations is shutting down these genes.  However, in the case of cancer for unknown reasons, the cell is unable to do so and tumors develop and progress. We need to understanding better gene silencing mechanisms if we wish to discover why the cell cannot defends itself against cancer, or if we want to intervene efficiently in gene silencing to fight cancer. Gene silencing is based on a class of ribonucleic acids called microRNAs. One of the aims of this research proposal is to study the molecular basis of these microRNAs, and in particular the binding mechanism by which they bind the messenger RNAs of targeted genes. Predicting accurately the targeted genes of microRNAs is among the most important unresolved questions of gene silencing at this moment. Dr. Major proposes the application of an RNA computer-modeling framework he developed over the last 20 years to obtain high-resolution 3-D structures of microRNAs as well as of their targeted messenger RNAs. These 3-D structures will help him get insights into how and where microRNAs bind their targets, and prepare biological assays to confirm these insights.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and processing of slipped-DNAs in patient tissues: Mutagenic Intermediates of Disease-Associated CAG/CTG Trinucleotide Repeat Instability
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA MUTATION; DNA REPAIR; DNA REPLICATION; DNA STRUCTURE; GENETIC INSTABILITY; GENOME STABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: About 40 human diseases, including myotonic dystrophy, are inherited in a manner that the symptoms become worse down generations as well as worsening as the individual ages.  These diseases are caused by DNA mutations involving repeated DNA sequences.  If one considers a gene as though it were a sentence such as THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT RAT, typical mutations would pose as spelling errors.  For instance THE GAT ATE THE FAT FAT RAT.  This mutation would be the same in all individuals in the family, all with the same symptoms.  However, in repeat-associated diseases the mutation would be THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT RAT, and their children would inherit a further mutation; THE CAT ATE THE FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT RAT and have more severe disease than their parents.  These mutations also continue through the life of the patient; progressively making symptoms worse.  My research focuses on understanding this form of mutation with the long-term goal of being able to prevent or treat affected families.  Being able to arrest or reverse this repeat mutation (reducing or preventing the expansion of the number of "FAT" repeat units) presents a therapeutic pathway to reduce disease severity; a pathway whose elucidation will be facilitated by understanding of the mutation process.   To understand this mutation we will focus on: 1) unusual DNA structures that form at the repeating units that are thought to be involved in the mutation; 2) mistakes during the process of DNA replication, which duplicates the DNA when making a new cell: and 3) DNA repair which repairs broken DNA and unusual DNA structures.  Mistakes during replication and repair are thought to cause the mutation of repeats in these diseases.  Our studies will decipher the mechanisms of this disease-causing mutation and will reveal candidate targets for research avenues aimed at therapeutic treatment by arresting or reversing the expansion mutations (FAT FAT FAT FAT FAT RAT.......down to......FAT FAT R

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of the high-affinity ligand binding and selective ion permeation  in voltage-gated K-channels
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC POTASSIUM CHANNELS; MEMBRANE PHARMACOLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOPHYSICS; MOLECULAR MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: This project is aimed towards better description of the molecular mechanism, which governs an inhibition of ion currents in  cardiac K-channels by the novel anti-arrhythmic and anti-convulsant drugs. Selective transport of potassium ions across  cellular membranes is a key component for the normal heart function. Theoretical simulations create a in silica model  systems that allows in silica mutagenesis. Insights from models will then be validated or refuted by in vitro expression of  native and mutated potassium channels followed by voltage clamp experiments. The information allows feedback refinement  of the 3d molecular structure of the channels. The projects will lead to understanding of mechanisms of how membrane  proteins select ions for their functional activity, of the mechanism of drug binding and block in different K+ channels, and  structural determinants of cardiovascular diseases. Since inadvertent drug block is a major causes of Long QT Syndrome  and potentially lethal arrhythmias in humans this work is clinically relevant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure, dynamics and contingency in signaling regulatory networks
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL REGULATORY NETWORKS; GENE REGULATORY NETWORKS; PROTEIN KINASES; PROTEIN PHOSPHATASES; PROTEIN-FRAGMENT COMPLEMENTATION ASSAYS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: If you wanted to understand an electronic device like an iPod, you would likely look at the individual components, see how they are wired together and then figure out how individual and groups of components dynamically respond to inputs and what signal come out.  You'd start with individual components and then look at hierarchically more complex two, three or more component relationships.  Along the way, you'd make lists of motifs, groups of different components that behave the same way, to try to figure out the modular organization of the whole.  Can the same logic be applied to life?  In fact it can and extraordinary efforts are aimed at breaking down cellular processes in this way.  But it is an arduous task and some aspects, such as dynamics are not easy to study.  We have developed novel experimental strategies that allow us to both study the dynamics of regulatory circuits in cells involving genes and proteins and to dissect these circuits by disrupting, very specifically, the relationships between individual components.  Further, we can perform these analyses en-masse, allowing us to obtain enough information to see if life has come up with a definable set of motifs with unique properties. The central aim of our proposal is to build on evidence for simple three component motifs that have been characterized in a model of the eukaryotic cell, that of the bakers yeast, by identifying and characterizing the behavior of these motifs.  The advantage of working on yeast is that they share many genes with humans and most notably those that are most primordial and become dysfunctional with age and in diseases such as cancers.  As we discuss in the proposal, we have shown how certain types of cell regulation, are particularly vulnerable to disruption of certain genes. The results of our efforts may help us to more generally define how certain cell regulation is more vulnerable to dysfunction than others and what kinds of strategies could re-stabilize them.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and validation of a lung cancer risk prediction model
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE-CONTROL STUDIES; EPIDEMIOLOGIC RESEARCH; LUNG CANCER; PROBABILITY FUNCTIONS; RISK PREDICTION; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to assess an individual's risk of lung cancer can have important implications for public health, clinical medicine and for individual decision-making regarding lifestyle changes. We will develop and validate a series of inter-related statistical models that will enable accurate assessment of lung cancer risk on an individual and population level.  We will use the data from two case-control studies that have been carried out in Montreal by Dr Jack Siemiatycki. These studies were characterized by development of a unique methodology for assessment of various exposures based on detailed interviews with over 4000 lung cancer cases and age- and sex-matched population-based controls. Base on these data, advanced statistical methodology for studying the roles of smoking history and occupational and chemical factors has been developed by our team.  Based on the above-mentioned case-control data, we will develop multivariable statistical models. The set of candidate risk indicators (selected from the study database, comprising hundreds of variables) will include those representing tobacco smoking history (both first-hand and environmental), age, sex, occupational exposures (in particular, selected dusts and fumes), history of hay fever and respiratory illnesses (emphysema, chronic bronchitis), and some others.   The models derived from this study can be applied to the scientific practice of lung cancer risk assessment, diagnosis, and prevention. At a community level they can be used to predict the numbers of cases of cancer that will arise, and thus be used for health services planning. For clinical purposes they can be used to triage people into screening programs.  For the subjects themselves, these models can also be used to motivate lifestyle changes or at least to inform them of the potential consequences of lifestyle changes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Patient and neuroimaging studies of mental state representations
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL MEMORY; FRONTAL LOBES; LESION METHOD; NEUROIMAGING; TEMPORAL LOBES; THEORY OF MIND
Abstract-Résumé: There is little understanding of the brain regions and networks that support awareness of past and current mental states belonging to oneself and to other people. While brain damage may cause obvious deficits in cognitive abilities such as attention and language, it may also lead to subtler, yet equally devastating deficits, such as the inability to decipher other people's thoughts and feelings, what is known as 'theory of mind.' Our ability to cooperate, deceive, and empathize rests on theory of mind, which allows us to recognize in others a set of beliefs that might not correspond to our own beliefs. The loss of this ability can thus have enormous social consequences for patients and their families. The proposed research uses an innovative approach of combining the examination of theory of mind impairment following brain lesions, with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a technique that allows visualization of on-line brain activity as participants perform various tasks. A first set of studies examines how damage to discrete regions of the frontal and temporal lobes can impair the ability to represent mental states on a wide range of tests known to be sensitive to theory of mind impairment. The relationship between theory of mind and remembering one's own past mental states during autobiographical memory, which draws on similar brain regions and processes, will then be investigated using a novel real-world 'family photos' test. Patients will be scanned with fMRI to explore differences in brain regions recruited as they recollect their own mental states while viewing personal photos of past experiences, and as they infer other people's current experiences when viewing strangers' photos. These studies will also help to reveal how damage to a region can affect the remaining network of regions. These findings could lead to new diagnostic tools and rehabilitation techniques to help individuals with brain injury lead emotionally and socially fulfilling lives.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTH CARE DATABASES; ADVERSE DRUG EVENTS; CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY; GERIATRICS; NESTED CASE-CONTROL STUDY; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: A wide variety of medications possess anticholinergic properties, meaning they block a chemical called acetylcholine in the body. The anticholinergic effects of these drugs can be especially concerning in older adults for several reasons. First, they can lead to acute urinary retention (the sudden, painful inability to void). Second, anticholinergic drugs can also interfere with memory and thinking, which is especially dangerous for older people with dementia. In fact, another group of drugs called the cholinesterase inhibitors, which are used to treat dementia, essentially have the opposite effect of anticholinergic drugs. Despite their opposing actions, anticholinergics and cholinesterase inhibitors are sometimes prescribed together. This practice may provoke serious adverse effects such as acute urinary retention and worsening confusion. We will find out how commonly these drugs with opposing actions are prescribed together, and whether this prescribing practice leads to safety problems in frail older adults with dementia. If we find evidence of harm, a policy to help alert physicians to the hazards of co-prescribing these drugs may help to limit this problem.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effects of C-type natriuretic peptide and its receptors on sinoatrial node function, heart rate regulation and arrhythmogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIAS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HEART RATE; NATRIURETIC PEPTIDE; SINOATRIAL NODE; TRANSGENICS
Abstract-Résumé: Natriuretic peptides are a family of related hormones produced in the heart that are very important in the context of normal heart function and heart disease. Heart rate (the number of times the heart beats per minute) regulates the delivery of blood to all regions of the body and is determined by specialized 'pacemaker' cells in a region of the heart called the sinoatrial node. My lab is interested in how natriuretic peptides regulate the specialized sinoatrial node region of the heart. Since we began studying this topic we have found that one kind of natriuretic peptide, called CNP, can potently reduce heart rate by binding to a specific receptor called the natriuretic peptide C receptor (or NPR-C). Originally, scientists thought this NPR-C receptor had no function, but our work is helping to change this idea. Many more experiments are necessary to understand how CNP and the NPR-C receptor affect heart rate and the sinoatrial node. CNP also binds to a second kind of receptor called NPR-B. Very little is known about the role of the NPR-B receptor in the sinoatrial node; therefore, we are also studying this receptor so that we may ultimately understand how both NPR-C and NPR-B contribute to heart rate regulation by CNP. This work is important because heart failure is characterized by the occurrence of life threatening arrhythmias, some of which are associated with dysfunction of the sinoatrial node. The body increases its production of natriuretic peptides in heart disease because these peptides help prevent heart failure from worsening over time. We hypothesize that natriuretic peptides will be effective in treating or preventing arrhythmias during heart failure in people and believe our work will help lead to significant improvements in the use and development of synthetic natriuretic peptides for the treatment of people suffering from heart failure, arrhythmias and other forms of heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolic regulation by a network centered on a conserved Mediator subunit
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE EXPRESSION/ TRANSCRIPTION; GENETICS OF REGULATORY NETWORKS; LIPID METABOLISM; STRESS RESPONSE / DETOXIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Like all organisms, humans must adapt to changing conditions. Failure to do so can cause health problems; for example, inappropriate responses to food intake can cause diabetes and obesity, which are global health concerns today. These metabolic diseases are caused by a myriad of genetic and environmental factors. Accordingly, the pathways that assure normal metabolism are very complex. Fortunately, such mechanisms are conserved in lower animals to a significant extent. Thus, I want to exploit the genetically tractable roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans to discover and characterize new regulators that control lipid biology and the response to nutrition-related stresses. I will focus on a protein, called MDT-15, which plays a key role in the regulation of these processes. Importantly, this protein has a relative in humans, so I can potentially learn about human metabolic regulation by studying a model organism. In summary, I shall identify and characterize new genes and pathways that contribute to human (metabolic) disease. This work will add significantly to our knowledgebase of pathways regulating metabolism, and - in the long term - may aid the development of new preventative and/or therapeutic strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural Processes Underlying Action Valuation
Keywords-MotsClés: DECISION-MAKING; ELECTRICAL MICROSTIMULATION; FRONTAL CORTEX; NON-HUMAN PRIMATE; PROBABILITY; REWARD
Abstract-Résumé: We make thousands of decisions every day. Scientists have been quite successful in studying the brain processes underlying simple decisions such as navigating a traffic light, in which sensory cues indicate the correct choice. However, in many situations we must decide in the face of uncertain outcomes. For example, we must weigh the risks and rewards with the probability of each outcome when deciding on a proper medical treatment (e.g., chemotherapy treatment or surgical removal of a tumour). My research attempts to uncover how these different factors are represented in the brain and the rules by which they are combined to guide behaviour. One goal is to understand at the biological level the reasons normal individuals make appropriate and inappropriate decisions. Moreover, certain clinical populations such as pathological gamblers, obsessive-compulsives and substance abusers routinely make poor decisions that have more severe effects on their own well-being and on society at large. A second goal is to identify the differences in brain processing that underlie normal and pathological decision-making which is a critical step towards proper diagnosis and therapeutic intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bidirectional cell signaling networks that control cell movement and segregation.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIDIRECTIONAL CELL SIGNALING; CELL SORTING; EPH RECEPTORS AND EPHRINS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEOMICS/MASS SPECTROMETRY; TYROSINE KINASES
Abstract-Résumé: Communication between cells in the human body is essential for the formation, maintenance and functions of tissues. Conversely, diseases such as cancer result from aberrant signaling, that results in inappropriate cell growth and migration. In normal tissues, cellular communication is a two-way process, such that different cell types signal back and forth. A striking example involves two types of transmembrane proteins found on the surfaces of distinct cells, termed Eph receptors and ephrins. These proteins contact one another, and by transmitting molecular information into both cell types drive a sorting process, such that Eph receptor- and ephrin-expressing cells segregate into two spatially distinct populations. This type of bidirectional cell signaling is also important in disease tissues, such as cancers, in which the tumour and surrounding stromal cells exchange signals in a reciprocal fashion to support the growth of the tumour. We have developed a novel biochemical technique that allows us, for the first time, to directly analyze bidirectional signaling when different cells types are cultured together, for example cells expressing Eph receptors or ephrins. We will couple this proteomic approach with a functional analysis of proteins required for cell sorting, and use computational and experimental tools to define the network of signaling proteins that allows bidirectional signaling between Eph receptor- and ephrin-expressing cells to mediate cell segregation. We will then apply this approach to other sets of cells undergoing reciprocal signaling, including tumour and stromal cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protein interaction domains and adaptor proteins in cell signaling.
Keywords-MotsClés: DOCKING AND ADAPTOR PROTEINS; MOUSE GENETICS; NEURAL DEVELOPMENT; PHOSPHOTYROSINE SIGNALING; PROTEIN SIGNALING DOMAINS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The functions of cells in the human body are largely organized by proteins, and the great majority of therapeutic drugs are targeted to proteins. Most human proteins are themselves constructed in a cassette-like fashion, from building blocks termed domains. One key function of such domains is to allow proteins to interact with one another, to form functional networks that allow the cell to respond to signals from its environment. Defects in these domain-based protein-protein interactions can underlie diseases, such as cancer and diabetes. To understand how human proteins work, and the defects characteristic of disease, we need to understand the properties of their constituent domains, both with respect to their biochemistry and their functions in the intact organism. In this project, we will investigate the properties of specific domains, and the proteins in which they reside, to understand more about how the body normally works, and what goes awry in disease states. Our work will focus on a so-called adaptor protein termed Grb2, and enzymes that add phosphate groups onto the amino acid tyrosine, one of the key regulatory devices used in normal and cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Antiretroviral Drug Transport in the Brain
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; ASTROCYTES; BIOCHEMICAL STUDIES; BRAIN; BREAST CANCER RESISTANCE PROTEIN; CELL CULTURE; DRUG; ENDOTHELIAL MICROVESSEL CELLS; HIV( HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS INFECTION); MICROGLIA; MORPHOLOGY AND IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; MULTIDRUG RESISTANCE PROTEINS; ORPHAN NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; P-GLYCOPROTEIN; RT-PCR ANALYSIS; TRANSPORT; TRANSPORT STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: In the brain, Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infects primarily the immune cells called microglia, and to a lesser extent, the supporting cells called astrocytes.  It is well established that antiretroviral drugs are not as  effective in the treatment of HIV-1 infection of the brain and equally well established that the brain concentrations of antiretroviral drugs are much less than those seen in other organ tissues.  The brain is unique in that it is separated from the rest of the body by a number of barriers that prevent  drugs from entering this organ. We believe that the lower brain concentrations of anti-HIV drugs  are not only due to the effect of the physical brain barriers, but also due to membrane proteins  (i.e., P-glycoprotein, Multidrug Resistance Proteins and Breast Cancer Resistance Protein) that can efficiently extrude these compounds out of the brain into the peripheral circulation as well as metabolic enzymes. We also propose that common regulatory mechanisms, such as the presence of specific cell receptors called , Pregnance X receptor (PXR) in rats and steroid  and xenobiotic receptor, SXR in humans,  control the production of these transporters and metabolic enzymes in the brain. Using various cell culture systems of the brain barrier and brain tissue isolated from both human and rat brain as well as in animal models, we propose to investigate the role that these receptors, membrane transporters and metabolic enzymes  play  in the accumulation and distribution of anti-HIV drugs. If these transporters and metabolic enzymes are  significantly active, then blocking their activity will result in higher drug concentrations and improved efficacy in the brain. This information is novel and clinically important since identifying mechanisms by which antiretroviral drugs accumulate or fail to accumulate in the brain can provide therapeutic strategies that will optimize delivery of these drugs in the treatment of the neurological consequences of HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of SPARC in Cancer Therapy Sensitization
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER BIOLOGY; CANCER GENOMICS; CHEMOTHERAPY RESISTANCE; COLORECTAL CANCER; GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: The goal to improving mortality from cancer is to achieve complete response to therapy.  However, chemotherapy resistance has been a difficult problem to overcome. In order to better understand this phenomenon, our laboratory used a whole genome approach to obtain a snapshot of the changes that occur when cancer cells develop resistance to chemotherapy.  This allowed us to identify SPARC as a gene that may play a role in changing the sensitivity of cancer cells to chemotherapy.  We have been able to demonstrate that low SPARC levels in chemotherapy resistant human MIP101 colon cancer cells was associated with cancer cells that were resistant to therapy.  However, if SPARC was restored by either re-expressing this gene at higher levels, or by introducing the SPARC protein in tissue culture, colon cancer cells became more sensitive to chemotherapy.  In animal models, treatment with SPARC also allowed colon cancer cells to respond better to chemotherapy, and this was demonstrated by greater tumor regression in animals receiving SPARC with chemotherapy than in animals receiving chemotherapy alone. These exciting preliminary results serve as the basis of this research grant, as it proposes to study the mechanisms by which SPARC changes the sensitivity of colon cancer cells to chemotherapy.  The ultimate goal in understanding these mechanisms is the possibility of developing additional agents that would be useful in the treatment of colon cancer, especially in cases of previously failed cancer therapy.
