Abstract-Résumé: The Ontario HIV Treatment Network (OHTN) / St. Michael¿s Hospital-led Centre for Interdisciplinary Training and Research in HIV and AIDS (CITRHA) is an innovative model for learning, mentorship, training and research. CITRHA will build an national interdisciplinary learning network -- connecting faculty in six major academic training hubs (Dalhousie, Queen¿s, St. Michael¿s Hospital, University of Windsor, University of Calgary, and Simon Fraser University) as well as faculty in 20 other universities across the nation -- 14 front-line organizations and 7 policy-makers. The Centre will provide a dynamic academic and service learning environment that will attract outstanding students across a wide range of disciplines and develop 60 to 70 new social science researchers skilled in interdisciplinary research, community-based research, ethics, and knowledge translation who are able to work collaboratively with other researchers, community and policy makers to have a national and global impact on the HIV/AIDS epidemic.  Major Aims and Objectives of CITRHA: 1) Establish a National Training Network; 2) Build an Interdisciplinary Training Model and Approach; 3) Broaden Content Learning Opportunities; 4) Offer Practical Training Opportunities; and 5) Monitor and Evaluate the Success of CITRHA.

Abstract-Résumé: Understanding protein folding and protein interactions is one of the central concerns in biology. While the structure of the protein native state is dictated by the amino acid sequence of the protein, the mechanisms of spontaneous and chaperone-assisted folding remain elusive. Furthermore, the mechanisms by which protein aggregation causes neurotoxicity is also poorly understood. Building on our previous six years of funding, the CIHR Training Program in "Protein Folding and Interaction Dynamics: Principles and Diseases" will facilitate research into these fundamental questions by providing an excellent training environment and by encouraging the use of multidisciplinary and transdisciplinary approaches. Our program brings together scientists from various disciplines to encourage cross-disciplinary research encompassing computational, in vitro, in vivo, and disease-related aspects of protein folding.

Mucosal inflammatory diseases affect the lining of the mouth, GI tract, respiratory tract, and genito-urinary tract and are caused by infections, allergens, environmental and food toxins, and auto-immune reactions.  The goal is to implement an interdisciplinary training network to educate a new generation of investigators who will apply team-oriented research training to the generation of new diagnosis/treatment strategies for the prevention and management of mucosal inflammatory diseases.

Abstract-Résumé: Cancer remains a leading cause of disability and death in Canada.  Aging of the population and advances in cancer screening and treatment means that more individuals are now living with the aftermath of cancer such as important psychological, physical, financial and social ramifications. PORT (Psychosocial Oncology Research Training) is a transdisciplinary research training program whose goal is to prepare a new generation of scientists from coast-to-coast in the development, implementation, evaluation, and transfer of theoretically-based approaches to cancer supportive care and survivorship. This much-needed initiative began its operation in 2003 at four participating universities (UBC, Manitoba, McGill, and Dalhousie).  PORT offers a core evidence-based seminar, internships, continuing research training and fellowships to promising young researchers. This renewal application seeks to broaden the scope of the program through the inclusion of 3 new research sites (U. Toronto, U. Calgary and U. Laval). The renewed critical mass of internationally-renowned researchers in the field and their promising graduate students will ensure that cutting-edge cancer survivorship knowledge continues to be developed to make a significant difference in the lives of individuals and their families living with cancer.

The goals are to encourage these students to consider the implications of their research in the global field of transplantation and to provide opportunities for them to develop careers in all aspects of Transplantation. It is expected that the students will consider the impact of their research on the advancement of patient care.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL; CHILD HEALTH; CLINICAL RESEARCH; CLINICIAN-SCIENTIST; CURRICULUM; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICES; INTERDISCIPLINARY; TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: Clinician scientists, expert in clinical and research disciplines, are uniquely qualified to link science to human health. Yet, a shortage of clinician scientists exists across all child health professions in Canada. The Canadian Child Health Clinician Scientist Program (CCHCSP) was founded in 2002 with the goal of training a new generation of child health clinician scientists trained to lead interdisciplinary research. CCHCSP created a financial model to enable child health clinicians to train in research, recruited 46 clinicians in 7 clinical disciplines at 11 Canadian universities to its training pathways, and created an innovative on-line curriculum that fosters the knowledge and skills needed for success as a clinician scientist. In addition to CCHCSP trainees, 393 other clinicians and research trainees and 94 faculty from 7 child health clinical disciplines have participated in the on-line curriculum, a strong demonstration of its 'added-value' beyond existing curricula. Our graduates have been recruited to clinician scientist faculty positions at Canadian universities. During the next 6 years, CCHCSP will continue to recruit clinicians across the breadth of child health disciplines for training as clinician scientists since the human resource gap is far greater than the 46 individuals recruited to date. Second, CCHCSP will introduce a new curriculum aimed at educating CCHCSP trainees in the theory and practice of team research (as compared to individual led research), since evidence shows that successful solutions to health problems are likely achieved by multidisciplinary research teams. Third, CCHCSP will introduce a new curriculum in which trainees will be mentored individually with their supervisors on the integration of knowledge translation into their research proposals to enable them to impact health care delivery via their research. With these approaches, CCHCSP will continue at the vanguard of clinician scientist training at the international level.

Abstract-Résumé: Pain in Child Health (PICH) is an innovative cross disciplinary research training consortium that originally linked research centres in 5 cities across Canada and created a community of scholars in pediatric pain. The consortium has expanded, with funding from Mayday Foundation in New York,to include mentors and trainees from around the world.  The trainees in PICH are becoming the next generation of pediatric pain researchers.  They have published over 370 peer-reviewed papers during the first phase of PICH. We continue to create a virtual community of pediatric pain research training centres using information technology, trainee exchanges and a summer/fall institute.       Pain in infants and children is of critical importance both because of its immediate biological, psychological and social effects and because of the potential long term effects on pain sensitivity and on learning and social functoning.  PICH faculty have been at the forefront of research in this area and this initiative has lead to significant strengthening of the skills of trainees and an increase in the number of highly qualified personel in this area.  These are the prerequisites for further advances in the science of pediatric pain. The consortium has garnered strong support from its academic and industry partners and the international community.    The training consortium familiarizes trainees with knowledge that is outside their own focus and fosters cross fertilization and greater collaboration across disciplines and across centres.  This initiative will create new understanding of how to protect our most vulnerable citizens from the scourge of unnecessary pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Strategic Training Program in the Social Aetiology of Mental Illness
Keywords-MotsClés: AETIOLOGY; COMMUNITY BASED RESEARCH; DIVERSE POPULATIONS; MENTAL DISORDERS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS; TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: Mental health and addiction disorders account for five of the top ten leading causes of disability worldwide. The reasons why people develop these illnesses are complex with biological, psychological and social factors interacting at multiple levels.  Biological investigation, such as molecular, genetic, and brain-imaging research increased understanding of the mechanisms involved but this work needs to be combined with an understanding of social processes in order to convert discoveries into public health advances.    The quality and quantity of mental health researchers with expertise in social causation has not kept pace with those interested in biology.   The recent World Health Organization report, "Closing the Gap in a Generation" underlines the importance of social determinants in improving health and notes improved training of health researchers is vital.    Sophisticated inter-disciplinary expertise is required to integrate work on social, psychological, and biological causes.  In Canada, an advanced research training program is needed to encourage the development of evidence-based prevention methods and effective ways to deal with the social determinants of recovery.  The Social Aetiology of Mental Illness training program will create a new generation of advanced experts through an interdisciplinary collaboration focusing on the social determinants of mental disorders and models of causation. It will train researchers from diverse fields including medicine, health sciences, social work, and social sciences and produce a new cadre of researchers equipped to investigate causation and ultimately translate into health prevention and promotion initiatives.  It will produce national and international networks of interested professionals that will further build capacity while leading the field. The faculty, from a number of institutions in Canada, the USA, the UK, and the Netherlands are world experts.

Abstract-Résumé: This proposal is for the renewal of our Training Program at the interface between Neurosciences, Photonics, the Nanotechnologies and Computational sciences.  The objective of this training program is to create a generation of Health Scientists with a truly transdisciplinary attitude and ability to apply and develop novel approaches derived from the fields of Physics, Chemistry and Computational Sciences for the study of neural mechanisms and disorders, including epilepsy, Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, depression and anxiety disorders, multiple sclerosis, neuropathies and chronic pain.  Fields of research covered include: neuroanatomy, neurophysiology, neuropharmacology, ion channel biophysics, molecular biology, biochemistry, advanced microscopy, transgenic technology and studies ranging from cell cultures to whole animals, computational neurosciences, non-linear optics, laser science, fibre-optics, tissue spectroscopy, scanning-probe microscopy, micromachining, physical organic chemistry, bioanalytical chemistry, lipid-protein interactions, novel biosensors and image analysis approaches.

Abstract-Résumé: For those who are lucky enough to spend a portion of their research career in a developing country, a common sentiment is that the experience changed their lives and refocused their field of investigation.  Imagine the impact on a young researcher of being involved in a training program that not only focuses on international health issues using a multidisciplinary approach, but does so from four major international training sites.  From these sites the trainees, both Canadian and international, conduct their research, work as teammates on joint study projects and come together annually for intensive coursework at one of the major training sites. The theme of the International Infectious Disease and Global Health Training Program is "Four Continents, One Shared Experience".  The goal of this Training Program is not only to inform the trainees about the issues, challenges and opportunities of multidisciplinary international health research but to have them experience it for themselves.

Abstract-Résumé: The McGill Integrated Cancer Research Training Program (MICRTP) seeks to support the development of future scientific leaders with the mission of developing and maintaining a diverse educational program that stimulates and supports basic and clinical research training thus encouraging the translation of discoveries for the benefit of patients.  Our vision is to bridge basic, translational and clinical Cancer research.   This program will also promote the development of well-rounded scientists through the interdisciplinary activities offered to our trainees and the expansion of their management skills facilitating their participation in large-scale projects and biopharmaceutical initiatives.  We propose to strengthen our programs by combining our existing programs, the Montreal Centre for Experimental Therapeutics in Cancer (MCETC) based at the Segal Cancer Centre (SCC), and the McGill Cancer Centre, now called the Goodman Cancer Centre (GCC), into one and supplementing critical skills needed by the next wave of cancer trainees.  The program is intended to catalyze a change in graduate education for students, for faculty and for the institution by establishing innovative models of education.  In bridging our efforts within and across multiple departments in our institutes and hospitals, we now have the opportunity to develop combined scientific workshops and symposia, thus providing a framework for integrating innovative research (basic, clinical and translational) with essential skills (ethics, knowledge translation, bioinformatics and professional skills).  We believe that this dynamic program will provide trainees with the edge needed to become talented biomedical scientists and clinicians as well as leaders in Cancer research.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Integrated Training Program in Basic and Clinical Aspects of Neuroinflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: CNS - IMMUNE INTERACTIONS; CNS INFLAMMATION; MULTIDISCIPLINARY; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammation occurs as a response of the body to infections, injury or as an abnormal attack of the immune system against certain tissues or organs (autoimmune disease).  Neuroinflammation, which refers to inflammation occurring in the nervous system, is recognized as having negative or positive consequences in a variety of neurological disorders. Understanding the mechanisms underlying these inflammatory responses can lead to the development of novel therapies for various neurological conditions. Our Neuroinflammation Training Program is focused on (i) multiple sclerosis (MS), an autoimmune inflammatory disease of the nervous system that is particularly prevalent in Canada; (ii) spinal cord injury, and spinal mechanisms underlying pain; and (iii) the effects of maternal infections on brain development leading to schizophrenia. Our aim is to educate the next generation of neuroscientists and clinician scientists interested in neuroinflammation in these conditions to acquire a broad multidisciplinary knowledge and expertise in immunology, neuroscience, animal models, neuroimaging, pre-clinical translational work, clinical trials, epidemiology and health outcomes.  To this end we have assembled a diverse team of expert mentors from three Montreal area Universities - McGill University, Universite de Montreal, and Universite du Quebec. This application is a renewal of a successful, on-going program, which currently has 106 trainees, 40% of whom were funded directly by this program in the form of studentship and fellowships. Our Program also provides travel awards. It also includes formal courses, and a variety of regular group meetings including monthly laboratory presentations, seminars, annual symposia and workshops. These activities have contributed to an excellent record of success in mentoring productive trainees with multidisciplinary knowledge and expertise in the area of neuroinflammation.

Keywords-MotsClés: FORMATION EN RECHERCHE; POLITIQUES PUBLIQUES; PROMOTION DE LA SANTE; PREVENTION; SANTE PUBLIQUE ET DES POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: La complexite des problemes auxquels les autorites de sante publique (SP) et les autorites responsables des politiques et de l'organisation des services sociaux et de sante (POSSS) au Canada seront confrontes requiere une amelioration de la capacite de recherche transdisciplinaire et du partage de connaissance.  Il manque une masse critique de chercheurs ayant les habiletes necessaires en recherche en intervention pour generer les nouvelles connaissances requises et soutenir la prise de decision.  Nous proposons la poursuite du programme de formation entrepris en 2003 pour augmenter la capacite de realiser des recherches directement utiles et applicables aux decideurs de SP et POSSS.  Nos objectifs sont d'inciter les etudiants a entreprendre une carriere de recherche en SP ou POSSS appliquee et de creer une communaute d'interet dans ce domaine; d'offrir aux etudiants des laboratoires de formation dans les milieux de pratique et de decision, et de favoriser l'adoption d'une vision large, ethique et transdisciplinaire a la formulation d'hypotheses, a la conception d'etudes, a l'analyse de donnees et a l'interpretation des resultats.  Pour ce faire, nous recruterons des etudiants au Ph. D. et au post-doctorat qui feront leurs travaux sur un sujet applique de recherche en intervention et sous la supervision directe d'un mentor et localises dans les organisations formelles de SP ou POSSS.  Ils seront aussi exposes a un curriculum de formation complementaire en recherche transdisciplinaire.  Nous avons reuni un groupe de mentors exceptionnels provenant de six universites quebecoises et de 10 organisations de SP et POSSS qui offriront des opportunites de formation en recherche appliquee a des problemes concrets et actuels de SP contribuant ainsi a augmenter la qualite et l'applicabilite des recherches et pour permettre la prise de decisions basee sur des evidences probantes.

Abstract-Résumé: Most chronic disease (cancer, heart disease, and diabetes) is preventable. But these diseases afflict millions of Canadians and strain the health care system. Leading Canadian researchers will train students to do studies that provide evidence needed by those responsible for developing policies designed to reduce the number of people with chronic disease in Canada, using approaches that will reduce disease rates as much as possible, as fast as possible. In supporting this training program, CIHR is contributing to the health of Canadians by advancing federal and provincial strategies for preventing cancer, heart disease and diabetes (and increasing physical activity, and healthy eating, while decreasing tobacco use and obesity) through policies and programs that change living conditions.     Although we have developed scientific methods to study treatments (e.g., effectiveness of drugs) for individual people, we need to develop new methods to study ways to prevent disease in the entire population.  This training program will train the research leaders of tomorrow in doing research that will increase our ability to prevent disease in the population at large. Trainees from across Canada will work and learn together, so that they understand how to collaborate across fields to do studies that make a difference. They will learn by actually doing research, through a distance education course, web-conferencing and through an annual meeting.

Keywords-MotsClés: EQUITY; GLOBAL HEALTH RESEARCH; GRADUATE STUDENTS; NEW INVESTIGATORS; RESEARCH CAPACITY STRENGTHENING; TRAINING PROGRAMME
Abstract-Résumé: The GHR-CAPS Program builds on a partnership between the four Teasdale-Corti teams of Quebec and the Global Health Research Network (GHRN) of the Reseau de recherche en sante des populations du Quebec. The research agenda of the teams is representative of the wide spectrum of themes that constitute global health: land use, environment and eco-system health (UQAM), mental health of populations exposed to organized violence and complex emergencies (McGill), foodborne, waterborne and zoonotic diseases (Laval), and vulnerability and equity in public policies and health systems (Montreal). The teams are led by established researchers and partners in Canada, Africa, Asia and Latin America and the Caribbean. The Canadian investigators collaborate closely with their partner investigators and knowledge users in low and middle income countries to ensure the effective translation of knowledge into sustainable and equitable health policies and practices. The GHR-CAPS program unites the four Teasdale-Corti teams on an integrated training platform. The overarching goal of the GHR-CAPS Program is to contribute to the production of an integrated ontological and methodological platform for global health research (GHR) through the establishment of an international network for GHR and capacity building in Quebec, Canada and selected low and middle income countries. The main objective of the GHR-CAPS Program is to strengthen research capacity in global health through an integrated and systemic approach. Examples of activities include: field fellowships, bursaries for students, partnership development grants, a GHR summer school, mentoring support, thematic seminars, and the development of a best practices guide for the training of future GHR leaders. We expect that the GHR-CAPS Program, implemented in complementarity with ongoing GHR-Teasdale-Corti, GHRN and FRSQ initiatives, will produce a significant and sustainable impact on the field of GHR in Canada and abroad.

Keywords-MotsClés: APPLIQUEE; APPRENTISSAGE ACTIF; ARTHROSE; CLINICIENS-CHERCHEURS; COMPETENCES; CYCLES SUPERIEURS; DEFICITS NEUROMOTEURS; DEFORMATIONS; FONDAMENTALE; FORMATION; MENTORAT; MULTIDISCIPLINAIRE; POSTDOCTORAT; RECHERCHE; RECHERCHE CLINIQUE; RIGUEUR; STAGIAIRES; TRANSFERT ET APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES; TRAUMATISMES; TRAVAIL D'EQUIPE; ETHIQUE; EVALUATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Ce projet concerne specifiquement le renouvellement du programme MENTOR, programme de formation a la recherche sur l'evaluation et les traitements des troubles de la mobilite et de la posture.  Ce programme a ete mis sur pied en 2002 a la suite d'une subvention des IRSC dans le cadre de l'Initiative strategique pour la formation dans le domaine de la sante. Grace a cet octroi, le groupe de mentors a l'origine du programme a cree un environnement de formation enrichie qui favorise l'exposition a la recherche multi/interdisciplinaire, le travail d'equipe, l'utilisation des nouvelles technologies, le transfert et l'application des connaissances, le developpement du sens critique et de la rigueur scientifique ainsi que la sensibilisation aux considerations ethiques. Depuis sa creation, le programme a accueilli pres de 75 stagiaires de tous les cycles d'etudes, du Canada ou d'ailleurs, provenant des sciences fondamentales, cliniques ou appliquees. Le programme a favorise l'integration de ces jeunes chercheurs et cliniciens-chercheurs dans des equipes de recherche multidisciplinaires et milieux industriels de pointe. Devant ce succes, les mentors souhaitent poursuivre leur mission qui est de former des chercheurs et cliniciens-chercheurs en mesure d'apporter des solutions pour ameliorer la sante des canadiens. En effet, les troubles de la mobilite et de la posture affectent une proportion importante de la population. Or, il existe toujours une penurie de personnel qualifie dans ce domaine. Une attention particuliere sera donc accordee a la formation de stagiaires exceptionnels, en fin d'etudes doctorales et postdoctorales, et en voie de debuter une carriere scientifique, afin qu'ils s'integrent rapidement et aisement dans differents milieux de recherche.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Training Grant in Interdisciplinary Primary Health Care Research
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; RESEARCH METHODS; TRAINING; TRANSDISCIPLINARY
Abstract-Résumé: This is a one-year, national interdisciplinary research training program funded by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) with mentor representation from the disciplines of: Family Medicine, Nursing, Psychology, Social Work, Epidemiology, Pharmacy, Sociology and Interprofessional Education. This program will be of interest to graduate students or post-doctoral fellows from Canadian Universities (as well as mid-career clinicians) who are engaged in primary health care research regardless of their home discipline.  The program has an innovative curriculum (primary health care research skills and interdisciplinary theory and process) which includes: 1)An on-site 3 day symposium in May; 2) 2 on-line workshops on research methods or primary health care related topics; 3) 2 on-line interdisciplinary discussion groups including: a) Interdisciplinary Collaborative Team Development during which trainees present their research project to peers and receive transdisciplinary feedback and b) Interdisciplinary Grant Writing during which trainees work together in an interdisciplinary team to create a primary health care research proposal.  Students can remain at their home university/institution while participating in the on-line training.  This program will prepare health researchers in areas (e.g., health services, health human resources, chronic disease management, electronic medical records) relevant to primary health care.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Training Program in Reproduction, Early Development, and the Impact on Health (REDIH)
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT; ETHICS; MATERNAL FETAL HEALTH; ORIGINS OF DISEASE; REPRODUCTION; TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: We propose a training program in Reproduction, Early Development, and the Impact on Health (REDIH). REDIH will be a collaborative training program across institutions in Quebec and Ontario, with mentors who are basic biomedical, clinical, population health, education, and ethics researchers. A main focus will be on very early development and how perturbations during gametogenesis, embryogenesis, and fetal development affect both health during development and the long-term health of offspring. A key emphasis will be on infertility and assisted reproduction technologies (ART), widely used in treating human infertility, and the effectiveness and safety of emerging technologies. The objective of REDIH will be to provide increased opportunities for excellent training in reproduction and early development for graduate students and fellows, to build research, clinical, regulatory, decision-making, and industry capacity in Canada. REDIH builds on three successful, collaborative, and interdisciplinary research networks that have been funded by CIHR Strategic Initiative program grants. Considerable added value will be provided by cross-program training modules in ethical/legal/social issues, training in knowledge translation including using a 360-degree model incorporating end users as well as teaching by recognized KT experts, semi-annual group meetings with a broad range of training modules, off-site workshops, and training opportunities provided in research groups outside that of the trainee's mentor and in clinical settings. An expertly-designed evaluation strategy will be embedded in REDIH. Canada has considerable, internationally-recognized expertise in this area of research, but needs additional capacity. Therefore, a cross-disciplinary training program such as REDIH, encompassing a wide range of methodologies including basic biomedical, clinical, population health, and ethical, legal and social science research, is needed.

This proposal will extend the number of core WRTC sites from three to six, adding diversity and strength to the WRTC training mission to enhance health services and policy research capacity in western Canada.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODIES; BREAST CANCER; CANCER; DEVELOPMENTAL NEUROBIOLOGY; DRUG DELIVERY; DRUG METABOLISM; EPILEPSY; G-PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTORS; IMMUNE SYSTEM; IMMUNITY; INFECTION; LIPOSOMES; NERVOUS SYSTEM; OCULAR; ONCONGENES; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PEPTIDES; PHARMACEUTICALS; RADIOPHARMACEUTICALS; REGENERATION; RETINOBLASTOMA; RNAI; SIRNA; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The use of nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA, peptides, proteins, and viruses is rapidly becoming a dominant facet of drug therapy.  The development, production, and use of peptides, proteins (including antibodies), small interfering RNAs, and viral-based vectors including RNAi for reducing or increasing the amounts of proteins in the body represents a new wave of pharmaceutical therapy that is applicable to both animal models of disease and human therapeutics.  The objective of this strategic training program is to bring together leaders in the fields of biological drug development in the Toronto research core to address a rapidly growing yet unmet need, namely to train young scientists in the design, development, and delivery of biologically-based medicines.  The emphasis will be on drug development and therapeutics, not diagnostics or biomarkers.  The program will encompass three major therapeutic areas of application: neuroscience/CNS, cancer, and infection and immunity.  The researchers (Mentors) in this proposed training program have laboratories based at the University of Toronto, the University Health Network including the Ontario Cancer Institute, MaRS, and the Toronto Western Research Institute.  Postdoctoral Fellows and graduate students will receive training in cutting edge techniques and tools such as bioinformatics, the use of RNAi, new methods and formulations for the delivery of nucleic acids and proteins, and the analysis of the metabolism and fate of these macromolecules (pharmacokinetics) in animal models of disease.        An attractive aspect of the proposed training program is the partnerships with pharmaceutical companies whereby selected graduate students and PDFs will spend 2 - 6 months working at a pharmaceutical company.  We already have agreements to participate from at least 8 pharmaceutical companies in Toronto and elsewhere and more companies are expected to sign on.

Abstract-Résumé: Building on the strengths of the current IMPART, which focuses on training in transdisciplinary research on women, gender and addictions, the new IMPART will also directly address the intersections of addictions and substance use with mental health, violence and trauma.  The program will provide a transdisciplinary context, including all 4 pillars of health research, plus policy, for a range of trainees.  Training will consist of mentorship, learning plans, research projects, an online course in the core concepts, monthly seminars, an annual research day, and student-driven, transdisciplinary collaborative projects.  The goal of the program will be to enhance the capacity of researchers in BC in applying a gendered approach to the study of addictions and its intersections with mental health, trauma, and violence.  IMPART will result in increased knowledge and appreciation of the complexities and breadth of these issues in women and men, girls and boys that can be applied nationally and internationally.

TitreApplicationTitle: Incorporating laboratory-based measures of compensatory postural control into the clinical setting
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSESSMENT; BALANCE; FALL PREVENTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OLDER ADULTS; PHYSIOTHERAPY; POSTURAL CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Falls are a significant concern for older adults, which occur when the neuromuscular system is not able to successfully recover when thrown off balance. There is currently a lack of appropriate clinical tools for assessing the ability to perform balance recovery, largely due to traditional reliance on laboratory-based techniques to measure these extremely rapid reactions. Healthcare clinicians need to be able to objectively assess postural recovery in order to fully understand balance abilities and to prescribe appropriate treatment if needed. The objective of this work is to address the gap between the basic and clinical measurement of compensatory postural using embedded Knowledge Translation (KT) strategies. The purpose of doing so is to encourage the uptake of objective balance assessment in clinical practice. This objective will be realized in three phases. (i) Firstly, focus groups with clinicians will probe the perceived barriers associated with implementing laboratory-based measures. (ii) These findings will be incorporated into the development of a clinical assessment of compensatory balance tool, which will then be evaluated for feasibility with clinicians. (iii) Finally, following revision of the assessment based on clinical perspectives, it will undergo reliability and validity testing in comparison to traditional laboratory measures. Incorporating current practice with physiological evidence and addressing perceived barriers when developing the clinical balance assessment should facilitate uptake of the tool, thus advancing treatment planning and ultimately, more effectively reduce risk of falling.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comprehensive intervention strategies with young HIV-positive women in Canada: individual, social, and cultural factors that make sexual health promotion programs successful.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; EVALUATION; FAMILY; FOOD SECURITY; GENDER; HIV/AIDS; INTERVENTION MAPPING; PREVENTION; QUALITATIVE METHODS; SEXUAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Despite extensive global efforts to combat HIV/AIDS through prevention, treatment, and care services, HIV infection rates continue to rise and approximately 25% of new infections are among young people. Young women are especially vulnerable to infection due to developmental, biological, social, and cultural factors contributing to the feminization of the pandemic. Research that extends beyond behavioural models of sexual health promotion is urgently needed to help curb the spread of HIV and provide support and care for those already living with HIV/AIDS. This proposed research is Pan-Canadian and aims to both develop and evaluate innovative sexual health interventions with HIV-positive young women. Given evidence of the multiplicity of factors impacting on health and wellness outcomes for women living with HIV, the objectives of the study include examining social and community influences. As a qualitative program of research, this work will enhance the understanding of developing successful interventions with groups of marginalized young women through using qualitative and community-based methodologies. This will involve combining various qualitative methods including naturalistic observation and in-depth interviews with young women and other key stakeholders such as family members and service providers. It will use intervention mapping, a step-wise systematic method of determining relevant stakeholders, community needs, program directions, and evaluation. The proposed research explores and addresses support and service needs of young women living with HIV in various geographic and cultural communities as it relates to their sexual health. In addition to the development of theoretically and empirically-based interventions, the project will serve to illicit cultural knowledge including understandings about the daily experiences of these young women in relation to their medical institutions, community-based services, and family systems.

Keywords-MotsClés: ABDOMINAL OBESITY; ADIPOSE TISSUE METABOLISM; AGING; BEHAVIOUR; DIABETES; ENERGY EXPENDITURE; ENERGY METABOLISM; ENVIRONMENTAL ASPECTS; FOOD INTAKE; GENETICS; HEART; HYPERTENSION; INFLAMMATION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LIPID METABOLISM; LIVER METABOLISM; LUNG; METABOLIC SYNDROME; MORBID OBESITY; OBESITY; RESEARCH; TRAINING PROGRAM
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the increasing prevalence of obesity and the detrimental impact of this condition on health and health costs, there is as yet no consensus on either a mechanism or a cure for adult and childhood obesity. It appears therefore urgent to intensify the research effort to better understand the complications, etiology and treatment/prevention of obesity in an integrative approach.     To achieve this objective, there is an urgent need for scientists specifically devoted to obesity research. There is an evident lack of such researchers in Canada and it has become imperative that we develop programs to train highly qualified personnel in the field of obesity. In addition, the exponential increase in knowledge pertaining to the basic, clinical and social aspects of obesity calls for the development of tools devoted to helping health professionals have rapid access to cutting-edge information.     The GLOBAL OBJECTIVE of this proposal is to consolidate, develop and implement distinctive and efficient training initiatives in order to expand the capacity of the Canadian health research community to confront the problem of obesity in Canada and throughout the world. We intend to provide the next generation of scientific leaders with the knowledge, skills, ethics and motivation required to tackle the major public health threat that constitutes excess body weight.

Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; RESPIRATORY BIOLOGY; RESPIRATORY EPIDEMIOLOGY AND HEALTH; STUDENT EXCHANGE PROGRAMS; TRANSDISCIPLINARY TRAINING AND RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Respiratory diseases are the third most important source of  health burden, after cardiovascular disease and cancers.  They  reflect a complex interplay between genetic factors, biological  exposures, inflammatory responses, psychosocial determinants,  and health services.  Future research must combine focused  questions and abilities with broader understanding of respiratory  disease, in both biological and societal context.   Future  researchers will require key crosscutting competencies to take  projects from great ideas to successful completion.  They will  need to develop research questions with diverse colleagues and  "consumers."  They will need to disseminate the resulting new  knowledge effectively, so as to improve relevant health  outcomes.   As a first step, in 2003 the CIHR funded a Quebec- wide multidisciplinary research training program in respiratory  disease.  We now aim to broaden the scope of our program, to  secure its long-term viability, and to further increase the impact  of Canadian respiratory research.

Abstract-Résumé: Cancer research requires a combined effort by many different individuals and organizations.  Funds are gathered; therapies are proposed, based on new knowledge, to prevent and treat cancer; clinical trials are designed and conducted; and patients, their families, and the public are educated with respect to new cancer knowledge.  Synergies among key partners are essential to generate and translate knowledge to the clinic and the community, but are not well-developed in Canada.  Basic and clinical researchers must develop interactive links with each other, with the private sector, and with the public to achieve true transdisciplinary synergy.  The London Strategic Training Initiative in Cancer Research and Technology Transfer trains researchers to forge these linkages and use them productively to translate new knowledge from the laboratory to the clinic and the community.

Abstract-Résumé: The proposed Training in Health Research Using Synchrotron Techniques (THRUST) program is a cross-disciplinary training and mentoring program in the development and use of synchrotron techniques to address key questions in Canadian health research. The program is centred at the University of Saskatchewan and will provide health researchers with comprehensive training in the use and development of the novel techniques at the Canadian Light Source, Canada's first synchrotron. A world-class cadre of synchrotron health experts will collaborate with other health researchers locally, nationally and internationally to mentor the brightest and best young researchers. Together, mentors and trainees will develop techniques and address priorities in Canadian health such as cancer metastasis, neurodegenerative disease and rational drug design. The unique combination of facilities and mentors gives THRUST the potential to become an international standard in synchrotron health research training.

Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR; CELL AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; CLINICAL RESEARCH; CLINICIAN-SCIENTIST; ENVIRONMENT; GENE; GENOTYPING; IMAGING; MENTORING; PHENOTYPING; PHYSIOLOGY; PULMONARY; TEACHING; TRAINING; TRANSDISCIPLINARY THEMATIC RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: IMPACT focuses on training PhD and MD post-doctoral research fellows with research targeted at the role of inflammation and repair processes in pulmonary and cardiovascular disease.  IMPACT aims to improve our ability to translate basic research findings into improved patient care and, accordingly, is transdisciplinary.  IMPACT focuses on post-doctoral trainees because it is at this level that we can most effectively introduce PhD trainees to key clinical research issues and MD trainees to key basic research techniques and thought processes - and initiate this collaborative approach early in their careers.  We accomplish this by bringing both categories of post-doctoral fellows together and ensuring that each post-doctoral fellow has both a basic and clinical IMPACT mentor.  We have developed a rich curriculum to support these post-doctoral trainees and help them to excel as career scientists, a curriculum that has also attracted grad students and many others in our institutions thus providing significant broad value added to research and clinical training environments.  The role of IMPACT mentors exceeds the usual post-doctoral supervisory role by contributing to the shared curriculum and by mentoring our trainees through to their initial faculty appointments.  Our focus on this career step recognizes and addresses the concerning rise in age of independent investigators first obtaining peer-reviewed grant support in North American institutions and particularly targets the need for effective translation of basic research into improved clinical outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Training Program in Bridging Scientific Domains for Drug Safety and Effectiveness
Keywords-MotsClés: & HEALTH POLICY RESEARCH; BIOSCIENCES; CLINICAL; CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY; COLLABORATIVE & PROFESSIONAL SKILL DEVELOPMENT; DRUG SAFETY AND EFFECTIVENESS; INTERDISCIPLINARY TRAINING PROGRAM; KT AND EVALUATIVE RESEARCH METHODS; MEDICATION USE IN OLDER ADULTS; POPULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Medications, when used optimally, are a key management strategy in health promotion, disease prevention, and acute and chronic disease management, especially for older adults. However, little is known about the real world effectiveness of many therapies currently in widespread use. Part of this gap stems from the lack of research that engages the various disciplines involved in the drug development, prescribing, and use systems. Researchers skilled in health research design, molecular and clinical pharmacology, biostatistics, health services research, behavioural sciences and health technology assessment, are essential to the drug discovery, use and policy system in Canada and around the world.  The goal of this training program is to provide an innovative, multidisciplinary training environment for future scientists in Canada with a focus on integrating the generation and use of drug effectiveness, safety, and adverse event data into everyday clinical practice and policy. The program will focus on training individuals who will be leaders and practitioners in the research methods that are required to impact the use of medications for older adults in the real world. The main objectives of this training program are to: 1) create an innovative training program that links complementary disciplines at both trainee and mentor levels; 2) provide a rich learning environment that is content and research method focused; 3) increase the use of multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches towards drug safety and effectiveness research; 4) provide tangible opportunities to develop collaborative research skills; 5) foster the development of professional skills through direct opportunities to learn and practice these skills; and 6) incorporate knowledge translation learning and activities at all stages of the training program.

Abstract-Résumé: Our understanding of human development - from embryo to adult -is being unravelled at a rapid pace. Specifically, the sequencing of the human genome and advances in modern genetics and experimental biology in model organism systems, are allowing for an understanding of how specific genes determine the formation of tissues in the body. At the same time, we are developing a greater understanding of how the interplay between genetics and the early environment control childhood development. However, for our healthcare system to take advantage, there is an urgent need to bridge the communication and knowledge gaps between biomedical scientists, clinical researchers and healthcare professionals no one of which can individually keep up with advancements outside of their own fields. The aims of the Training Program in Genetics Child Development and Health are to: i) further enhance the training activities and special events of our transdisciplinary educational environment; ii) improve the opportunities for team research across themes and with distant collaborators; and iii) emphasize the importance of knowledge translation and the ethical and social implications of genetics and child health research.

Abstract-Résumé: Dans le contexte des Initiatives strategiques pour la formation en recherche dans le domaine de la sante, le Reseau de medecine genetique appliquee (RMGA) du Fonds de la recherche en sante du Quebec (FRSQ) souhaite elargir le panel des activites offertes dans le cadre de son programme de formation. Le RMGA est un organisme sans but lucratif, fonde il y a plus de 20 ans. La transmission des connaissances est la base de la creation du Reseau. Le RMGA propose un programme de formation en recherche de grande qualite, axe sur un enseignement dans des domaines d'etudes varies et transversaux en genetique translationnelle, en genetique en general et en genomique. L'objectif du RMGA est de developper les quatre evenements phares de son programme : les ateliers de formation, les Journees genetiques, les bourses de formation et le programme de formation multi-et transdisciplinaire en co-supervision. Le RMGA souhaite etendre la portee et l'acces de son enseignement dans des domaines specifiques reconnus comme essentiels par la communaute scientifique et la population en general. Le programme de formation est dirige par les responsables d'infrastructures du Reseau qui ont en charge de developper un programme d'etude transversal a celui etabli dans les 7 infrastructures de recherche du Reseau(les Plateformes de recherche appliquee, la Genetique du developpement, les Interventions genetiques en Sante, l'Epidemiologie genetique neuropsychiatrique, l'Oncogenetique, la Genetique des populations et l'infrastructure socio-ethique et juridique). Les mentors de notre programme sont d'excellents chercheurs et professeurs, d'une renommee internationale parmi la communaute scientifique.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGRICULTURAL HEALTH; ECOSYSTEM HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH; RURAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Few industries are so fundamental to society as is agriculture,such that our expanding global population increasingly pushes us to sustain ourselves.  This also drives the growing  mechanization and use of chemical fertilizers, herbicides, and pesticides in agriculture.  While these have increased our productivity, they also take their toll on the health of farm  operators and families globally.  In addition, rural-based industries such as mining, petroleum, forestry and others contribute significantly to the toll on the health and wellness of inhabitants of the global rural ecosystem.  These issues are complex, but must be addressed.  Evidence from all countries  around the world clearly indicates that the health of those who live and work in the rural agricultural ecosystem suffers disproportionately relative to that of their urban counterparts, and not just modestly so.  Under the proposed program, we will bring together Canadian professionals from many disciplines to provide critical training to young scientists from across Canada as well as from abroad, in order to increase our research  capacity and infrastructure, and thereby promote the health of rural-agricultural sector workers and families.

Abstract-Résumé: The SARS crisis, the tainted blood scandal, the massive public health burden due to tobacco products, controversy over the HPV vaccine, and many other recent events highlight both the importance of public health and the central role of public policy in maximizing the health of populations. Despite the importance of public health policy, no formal academic training in this field currently exists in Canada. The Strategic Training Program in Public Health Policy will address this gap, bringing together faculty from a broad range of disciplines and areas of expertise, to offer an outstanding training program in public health policy that is sustainable in the long term. Fellows will be trained in public health policy research, policy evaluation, policy analysis and policy change, and will be exposed to a variety of content areas including tobacco control policy, food security and nutrition policy, immunization policy and environmental health policy. They will also gain real-world experiences through work with public health policy professionals and participation in public health policy action teams, and will develop important professional skills, including a strong grounding in research ethics and public health ethics, through public health policy rounds, a summer institute, and a variety of opportunities for sharing their findings. Mentors are accomplished public health leaders:  they represent a range of academic units including the Dalla Lana School of Public Health, the Department of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation, the Department of Nutritional Sciences, the School of Public Policy and Governance, the Faculty of Law, the Joint Centre for Bioethics, and organizations such as the Public Health Agency of Canada and the Ontario Agency for Health Protection and Promotion. By addressing society's pressing and emerging public health priorities, the proposed training program will have a direct impact on improving the health of populations in Candada and abroad.

TitreApplicationTitle: Knowledge Translation Canada:  A CIHR Strategic Training Initiative in  Health Research
Keywords-MotsClés: EDUCATION AND TRAINING; EVIDENCE-BASED HEALTH CARE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; QUALITY OF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Much of the $100B/year worldwide investment in biomedical and health research is wasted because of challenges to knowledge translation (KT) that remain understudied.  KT is the science and practice of putting knowledge into action.  Health systems fail to optimally use evidence with resulting inefficiencies and reduced quantity and quality of life.  We have developed a multidisciplinary collaborative network involving colleagues from 8 universities to improve the health of Canadians and the effectiveness of health services by identifying and studying solutions to ensure that Canadians have tools and skills necessary for KT.  The objective of this STIHR is to create an internationally-recognised national training initiative to enhance capacity in KT and KT research by providing excellent training centres and laboratories for trainees from various disciplines to develop skills in KT and KT research; linking trainees and mentors who will work collaboratively to advance the science and practice of KT; and partnering with other national and international networks to promote KT research and training across a range of settings and health system issues.  Support for this program will place Canada in a leadership position by providing a unique training model through the nurturing of transdisciplinary collaborations and will result in the creation of the next generation of KT researchers and practitioners, and in improved health of Canadians.

Abstract-Résumé: The exponential expansion of knowledge in the basic and clinical sciences in perinatology requires that health professionals and researchers develop new expertise to integrate the biological, social, cultural and ethical issues of new reproductive technologies in their research. Moreover, researchers must develop leadership in knowledge transfer, ethics and gender-related issues in reproductive and perinatal health in order to play a more active role in developing and implementing policies that will impact favourably on the health of women and their families. The Quebec Training Network in Perinatal Research (QTNPR) will bring together five existing multidisciplinary research teams/networks, each with complementary expertise in specific areas to create a broadly accessible curriculum on the impact of environmental exposures to maternal and children health. Our objectives are to provide trainees the knowledge, skills and values that will allow them to address the complex interdisciplinary challenges of the current reproductive and perinatal health environment. QTNPR will train a new generation of researchers and improve Canadian population health care.

Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer¿s Disease (AD) followed by Parkinson¿s Disease  (PD)are Canada¿s most common and devastating  neurodegenerative disorders. Insidious cognitive and physical  decline renders victims dependent upon custodial care at an  annual cost of $9 billion.  The lack of therapeutic options has  been dubbed the ¿biggest unmet medical need in neurology¿  Arguably, the next major advance in rational therapeutic design  will come in tying a cell¿s metabolome into genomic and  proteomic maps of disease. TitreApplicationTitle: The Bridge Program: CIHR Strategic Training Program bridging public  health, engineering and policy research.
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH; HEALTH POLICY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH; TRANSDISCIPLINARY TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: Some of the largest gains in life expectancy in the last century  were made by prevention measures using engineering solutions,  reinforced by public policies. Examples include safe drinking  water, sanitary sewage disposal, changes in heating fuels from  coal to oil to natural gas, seatbelts in cars, and workplace safety  systems. In spite of the importance of linking engineering, policy  and public health, in typical university structures, engineering  and medical faculties tend to operate very separately, and often  do not interact with policy makers.  To bridge this divide, we propose to renew and build upon our  successful Strategic Training Program, the Bridge Program, an  innovative training model centred at the University of British  Columbia with links to government, the private sector, and other  research institutions. It aims to create a paradigm shift in the  search for solutions to public health issues by bridging the  realms of engineering, public policy, and the environmental,  occupational, and public health sciences. The goal is to train the  next generation of researchers, professionals, and policy makers  so they will be able to work as partners to develop prevention  strategies for the public health problems facing Canadians today  and in the years to come.

TitreApplicationTitle: The CIHR ACHIEVE Research Partnership: Action for Health Equity Interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH DISPARITIES; INNER CITY HEALTH; INTERVENTIONS RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION AND EXCHANGE; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The ACHIEVE Research Partnership will be Canada's first praxis-oriented, engaged research immersion program aimed to advance use of research evidence for effective and sustainable inner city health interventions. ACHIEVE will mentor highly-trained  health researchers to collaborate across scientific disciplines and with influential program and policy decision makers, in order to address inner city health problems and reduce health inequities. Across all health conditions, lower income families and individuals face highest rates of illness and experience greatest unmet need for health care. This is especially true in low-income urban neighbourhoods, where residents may face deep poverty, homelessness or unstable housing, social exclusion, family disruption, substance abuse and mental health disorders, barriers to service utilization, and social and economic isolation. During the last two decades, Canada has fallen behind many other nations in taking action to address health inequity. Relevant interventions research and strong cross-sectoral partnerships are needed to generate better evidence of "what works and why" in the Canadian context, and to move evidence into action. ACHIEVE will provide a training platform for new scientists to develop skills in complex interventions research and to work effectively in partnership with inner city health service providers, policy makers, and stakeholders. Over the course of this intensive, two-year program, Fellows will develop competencies that are unavailable through traditional graduate training yet necessary for closing the gap between monitoring urban health disparities and reducing them. ACHIEVE will be based at the Centre for Research on Inner City Health at St. Michael's Hospital. This dynamic setting offers unparalleled opportunities to generate evidence and alliances for urban health equity and to launch the careers of ACHIEVE Fellows.

Abstract-Résumé: Autism is a serious and not so rare disorder that affects young children in the first 3 years of life (and 52,000 young Canadians under age 20). It is a lifelong handicap, with no cure yet available. Genetic susceptibility, abnormal patterns of brain growth, and specific neuropsychological deficits are well characterized.  Recent progresses in genetics, early detection and diagnosis, and early intensive behavioural interventions, are accumulating; however, families and professionals remain frustrated by lack of service availability. Well trained researchers in both basic and clinical disciplines are urgently needed in Canada. Since 2003, we have successfully developed an Autism Research Training (ART) program that trained over 40 PhD and post-doctoral students conducting research in various disciplines (from molecular genetics to outcome intervention studies) at 9 Canadian universities. This renewal application will expand this innovative program, adding new faculty, new disciplines and research environments at 14 Canadian universities. The training program involves a one-year stipend; 3 years of active mentoring (34 faculty, including 11 endowed Research Chairs) and 3 years of attendance at a summer school; travel stipends to facilitate recruitment and attendance at international conferences; regular trainee and program evaluation; a Winter Institute to increase faculty-fellow mentoring and organize with partners and stakeholders a joint national conference; a new initiative that will advance training outside Canada by funding international students to attend the ART Summer School. ART is administered from McGill which will separately fund its administrative support. Partners have committed at least  $675,000 of matching funds. The Program is designed to address the pressing needs of Canadians affected by autism as well as their families and service providers by optimizing the development of a new cohort of exceptionally well-trained researchers.

Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C infection remains a serious health problem both worldwide and in Canada. It is estimated that over 250 000 Canadians are chronically infected and over 6000 new cases occur each year.  The annual death rate in Canada from Hepatitis C is 4700. Moreover, at least 15% of HIV-infected individuals are co-infected with hepatitis C. The majority but by no means all new cases of Hepatitis C are observed in current and former injection drug users, Aboriginals and new immigrants. Over the last 5 years, the National Canadian Research Training Program has gathered 30 stellar Canadian mentors in clinical, social and basic sciences such as virology, addiction, HCV-HIV co-infection, nursing, molecular biology, immunology, etc. The program has recruited 23 students all of whom participate in a transdisciplinary curriculum. This proposal is targeted at renewing and further developing the program to increase student recruitment, strengthen its transdisciplinary component and enable collaborative research initiatives among the mentors and with colleagues internationally, the common goal being to eradicate hepatitis C and avoid complications in currently infected individuals.

Abstract-Résumé: With breakthroughs in scientific discovery comes the need for advances in the legal and ethical frameworks necessary to ensure advances are implemented in the health care system without harm.  With a 2001 CIHR grant we built a Health Law and Policy Training network at Dalhousie University, the University of Alberta and the University of Toronto.  By combining expertise both across universities and across disciplines we provide sophisticated multi-disciplinary training in order to address challenges such as use of patient data for research purposes, the development of regulatory frameworks for new drugs, or the ethical use of stem cells.  Our 71 trainees are all employed as academics or decision makers (in government, in non-governmental organizations and international agencies) or are pursuing further study.  In addition to our success preparing urgently needed graduates, we have also provided an unprecedented forum for experts in Canadian health law and policy.  Well over 500 academics, decision-makers, and scholars in fields as diverse as sociology and physics have attended our annual conferences and seminars.  Our website, on which our faculty put their course curricula, has become a valuable tool for Canadian teachers of health law (particularly those who are not lawyers teaching law to, for example, to medical students) and to scholars internationally.  We seek CIHR funding to continue this Program and to expand it in the following ways: to support training in French and exchange with Quebec researchers; to expand internationally through a new exchange program; to add new disciplines to speak to emerging health challenges in, for example, aboriginal health, mental health, and nanotechnology; to weave and strengthen ethics training throughout the Program; and to provide a  mentorship matrix for our Master¿s students that enhances their multi-disciplinary research skills and their ability to translate their knowledge to achieve impact in the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Seat-human interface: Optimizing car seat properties to the individual for injury prevention.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; CAR SEAT KINEMATICS; ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; HUMAN SUBJECTS; INJURY PREVENTION; NECK MUSCLE RESPONSE; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; STARTLE RESPONSE; WHIPLASH INJURIES
Abstract-Résumé: Whiplash injury is the most common form of injury associated with low-speed rear-end collisions. In 2000, the direct and indirect costs associated with whiplash were estimated at over $500 million dollars in British Columbia. Currently, the exact physiological reason for these injuries is not known but most researchers agree that injury occurs in the joints and muscles of the neck. One possible factor associated with whiplash injuries is the mechanical properties of car seats, such as head restraint position and seat rigidity. Most car seats have been designed to reduce neck injuries using a crash test dummy representing an average male occupant.  However, most occupants are not the average male occupant and car seats are not optimized to prevent neck injury for each individual. The International Insurance Whiplash Prevention Group (IIWPG) uses four performance criteria to evaluate and rate the ability of head restraints and seats to prevent whiplash injury in rear end collisions. The objective of this project is to investigate how mechanical properties of car seats influence males and females of different mass and height according to the four IIWPG criteria during whiplash-like perturbations. We hypothesize that as seat rigidity increases, males and females of greater mass and height will exhibit greater head acceleration and neck muscle activity than with subjects of lower mass and height. Greater neck muscle activity and head accelerations will increase the likelihood of whiplash injuries. For the proposed project, 90 human volunteers will be subjected to a series of whiplash-like perturbations on four car seats with various seat rigidity levels.  Subjects will be separated into 6 groups (3 male/3 female groups) with specific mass and height ranges.  We intend to identify car seat factors that will best protect individuals with different height and mass during whiplash collisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular physiology of T-type calcium channels
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICS; CALCIUM CHANNELS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EPILEPSY; HYPERTENSION; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Calcium plays a number of highly important roles in human physiology.  In the brain, calcium entering into nerve cells controls nerve to nerve communication and triggers a variety of intracellular signaling processes.  At the same time, too much calcium is toxic, and hence, the amount of calcium entering brain cells must be precisely controlled.  One key player in the regulation of calcium entry is a family of proteins termed "calcium channels".  Several differenct types of calcium channels have been identified in mammalian brain, each with a unique role in the function of the nervous system.  T-type calcium channels, the focus of this proposal, contribute to the regulation of cell growth, and how effectively nerve impulses are conducted.  Genetic abnormalities in these channels have been linked to absence epilepsy in children, and they are considered important pharmacological targets in the treatment of seizures.  In this application, we propose to investigate in detail how the function of these channels is controlled at the molecular level, and how mutations linked to childhood epilepsy affect nerve cell function.  In addition, we will examine how channel function can affect other types of ion channels.  This will be accomplished through a combination of state of the art molecular and neurophysiological techniques.  We anticipate that our findings will help guide new therapeutic strategies towards treatment of disorders linked to these channels.

TitreApplicationTitle: The functional architecture and neural substrates of perception and action
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; OBJECT VISION; OPTIC ATAXIA; VISUAL FORM AGNOSIA; VISUOMOTOR CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Why do we need vision? As it turns out, there are two answers to this question. On the one hand, we need vision to give us detailed knowledge of the world beyond ourselves - knowledge that allows us to recognize things from minute to minute and day to day. On the other hand, we also need vision to guide our actions in that world at the very moment they occur. These are two quite different job descriptions, and research by Dr. Goodale at the University of Western Ontario is revealing that nature has given us two different visual systems to carry them out. One system, vision-for-perception, allows us to recognize objects and build up a 'database' about the world. The other system, vision-for-action, provides the visual control we need to move about and interact with objects. The idea of two visual systems in a single brain might seem initially counter-intuitive. Our visual experience of the world is so compelling that it is hard to believe that some other quite independent visual signal - one that we are unaware of - is guiding our movements. Nevertheless, using brain imaging and case studies of neurological patients, Dr. Goodale's research is providing evidence that the two systems are quite separate, even though they work together in the production of everyday behaviour. His research is revealing that vision-for-perception sends information to the temporal lobe of the brain where it makes contact with cognitive areas involved in memory and semantics -- whereas vision-for-action sends information to the parietal lobe where it interacts with areas involved in motor control. Dr. Goodale's work is providing useful insights into visual and visuomotor deficits in patients with brain damage, leading to more efficient diagnosis and rehabilitation.  In addition, the models of visual function that are emerging from his research are being applied to the development of more efficient human-machine interfaces and robotic control systems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innate Immunity and Hepatitis C Virus Infection.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC LIVER DISEASES; GENE REGULATION; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTERFERON AND CYTOKINE; SIGNALING TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: With more than 170 million people infected worldwide, the hepatitis C virus (HCV) is an important cause of human chronic liver diseases and a major public health problem. Clinically, of those individuals exposed to HCV, 80% become continuously infected, a disease state that is often associated with significant liver disease, including chronic active hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Recent investigations have demonstrated that the interferon pathway is very important in controlling HCV disease, and in fact interferon is one of the few medical treatments available for HCV infected patients.  A new pathway called RIG-I appears to be very important for the host cellular antiviral response to HCV infection. However the virus has 'learned' through millions of years of evolution to counteract or evade the immune response in general, and one particular viral protein NS3/4A is able to specifically inactivate the RIG-I mediated antiviral response. The goal of this research project is understand how host response to HCV infection and how HCV evades the IFN response and to begin to understand the functions of the viral and cellular proteins involved. Our research objective is to investigate host innate antiviral response during HCV infection and to characterize the role of HCV encoded E2 glycoprotein in the regulation of expression of host antiviral defense genes. Understanding these virus-host interactions will provide important insights concerning HCV infection and disease; we believe these studies will contribute to the development of novel strategies for antiviral and immune modulatory therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure, function and regulation of the yeast SAGA complex.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; GENE EXPRESSION; MOLECULAR GENETICS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Most disease states result from or are manifest by alterations in expression of one or more genes. By manipulating gene expression, we have the potential to prevent or reverse these conditions. Many multicomponent enzyme complexes regulate gene expression in eukaryotic cells. These influence the basal transcriptional machinery, alter chromatin composition and structure, and interface with molecules involved in RNA processing and export from the nucleus. Our project centres on the SAGA-complex, a prototypical regulatory complex found in budding yeast and with closely related counterparts in human cells. Several of the human SAGA components are implicated in disease, most notably cancer, and thus represent excellent candidate therapeutic targets. We have focused our studies on the yeast molecules because this organism facilitates the combination of molecular, biochemical and genetic studies. Our objective is to characterize the structure, function and regulation of the SAGA complex with the goal of manipulating its activity and thus altering disease states.

Abstract-Résumé: This proposal describes an innovative national research network, the CIHR HIV Prevention Social Research Centre, to be housed at the Dalla Lana School of Public Health, University of Toronto. We are responding to the need for leadership in developing integrated programs of prevention research, capacity building and knowledge translation, aimed at improving services, increasing resilience, decreasing vulnerability to HIV, and ultimately achieving a reduction in HIV transmission. In the earlier phases of the HIV epidemic, focus was on rapid development of essential services and achievement of urgent near-term goals in prevention and care. As the epidemic continues and new issues and vulnerable populations emerge, we need more than ever to pursue longer-term goals with multilevel interventions grounded in increased understanding of social and cultural driving forces.  Through strong multi-sectoral and multi-disciplinary collaborations, and through capacity building and KTE activities with policy and community partners, the Centre will develop multi-site, theoretically and methodologically novel approaches to HIV prevention and intervention research, will support promising trainees/students and attract new researchers to the field. Our working model is a public health approach which integrates multi-level analyses of vulnerability and risk, ensuring KTE across research, program and policy domains.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of CTGF in tissue repair and fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; FIBROSIS; KNOCKOUT AND TRANSGENIC MICE; SCLERODERMA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TISSUE REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Fibrotic (scarring) diseases cause about 40% of the health care costs in Canada. There is no treatment for scarring diseases, which are believed to arise due to a failure of normal wound repair to terminate.  One protein called CTGF is not normally present in skin, but is present in tissue repair.  Abundant levels of CTGF exist in conditions of scarring. Blocking the action of CTGF may be a good treatment to control the extent of tissue repair and scarring. The key cell type resposible for scarring and fibrosis is the fibroblasts. I wish to use mice lacking CTGF in fibroblasts to see if these animals show defects in tissue repair and a resistance to skin fibrosis.  I wish to use mice in which large amounts of CTGF exist in fibroblasts to see if these mice get fibrosis. I also want to determine how CTGF works, with a long-term goal of developing ways of blocking CTGF action and hence fibrosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of stem cell proliferation in the C. elegans germ line
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC EPISTASIS; GERMLINE DEVELOPMENT; NOTCH SIGNALING; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; STEM CELLS; TUMOUR FORMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Stem cells provide the source material for the generation of tissues in the developing animal, as well as for the turnover of tissues in the adult.  They are able to serve these functions due to their unique ability to yield two general types of cells when they divide.  One type of cell enters a path to differentiation, thereby forming the needed tissue.  The other type of cell is essentially identical to the parental stem cell, with the continued ability to produce two types of cells.  A dividing stem cell is able to produce both types of daughter cells.  A balance must be maintained between cells that take on the character of the parental cell (self-renew) and those cells that differentiate into the desired tissue.  If too many of the cells differentiate, the pool of self-renewing cells is depleted, which prevents tissues from being made in the future.  Conversely, if too many cells self-renew, a tumour of proliferating cells is formed at the expense of the differentiated tissue.  In my lab, we study the genetic and molecular mechanisms that control the balance between self-renewal and differentiation.  We are using the germ line of a small nematode worm, C. elegans, as a model to study how stem cell self-renewal is regulated.  To build upon our current understanding of how stem cell proliferation is controlled, we are studying the activities of genes that cause a tumour, when mutant.  One of these genes, puf-8, encodes a protein that is similar to proteins in humans that are expressed in germline stem cells.  Another protein, KIN-10, is similar to a human protein that has been implicated in forming tumours.  By studying how the balance between stem cell self-renewal and differentiation is controlled in the C. elegans germ line, we will be able to uncover themes that may be found in other stem cell niches.  The full therapeutic potential of stem cells depends upon our understanding how stem cell behavior is regulated.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural analysis of the ATP synthase and V-ATPase
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOSTATIN; ATP SYNTHASE; CANCER; ELECTRON CRYOMICROSCOPY; MEMBRANE PROTEIN STRUCTURE; VACUOLAR ATPASE
Abstract-Résumé: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) synthase and Vacuolar-type ATPase (V-ATPase) are important biological machines involved in converting energy from one form to another. ATP synthase converts the energy in an electrical and pH gradient into chemical energy, whereas V-ATPase converts chemical energy back into an electrical and pH gradient. These machines play important roles in the healthy functioning of cells and also in the dysfunction of cells in cancer and other diseases. Knowledge of the structure of biological machines is a prerequisite to understanding how they work and provides a major advance towards generating drugs that target them. We will use an advanced form of molecular microscopy to study the structures of ATP synthase and V-ATPase, elucidate their mechanisms, and discover how they interact with other molecules within the cell. The understanding of the ATP synthase and V-ATPase mechanisms that will result from this research will affect the lives of many Canadians living with diseases such as cancer, osteoporosis, and renal tubule acidosis.
