TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the Na+/H+ exchanger in the mammalian myocardium
Keywords-MotsClés: ERK1/2; INTRACELLULAR PH; ISCHEMIA; KINASES; NA+H+ EXCHANGER; PHOSPHORYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: The object of our study is to examine the control of the activity of the Na+/H+ exchanger protein, that removes acid from inside the heart. Handling acid is a problem in all organisms. These cells of the heart use food such as glucose and fat, to produce energy for the heart so that it can contract and pump blood. When this occurs, they produce waste products, and one of these is acid. Too much acid is bad for the heart. It inhibits the ability of the heart to contract - that is the heart cannot pump blood well if there is excess acid inside the cells of the heart. In certain conditions such as ischemic heart disease, acid builds up, and this causes an inhibition of the heart's ability to contract and pump blood. We are studying the mechanism that deals with acid removal from inside heart cells and how it is regulated. There is a protein called the sodium proton exchanger (Na+/H+ exchanger) and its function is to remove the excess acid from inside the cells of the heart and take it out of the cells. In so doing, this protein brings in excess sodium into the heart. During heart disease, this results in an accumulation of intracellular sodium and this results in excess intracellular calcium through the actions of a sodium calcium exchanger protein. This exacerbates the problems that occur in ischemic heart disease and results in cell death and damage. We are studying how the protein is regulated in the heart which will give us insights into why its excess activity damages the heart.

TitreApplicationTitle: The neurobiology of motivation

Abstract-Résumé: We are generally interested in the parts of the nervous system that underlie motivation, and we use opiates and nicotine as tools to study motivational processes because they are such potent motivational stimuli. Opiates (morphine, heroin) and nicotine produce rewarding or noxious effects depending on the circumstances under which they are administered. We and others have previously characterized a number of places in the brain where opiates and nicotine produce rewarding effects. The present proposal investigates the question of whether a single brain circuit underlies all opiate and nicotine reward or whether multiple parallel pathways in the brain are substrates for opiate and nicotine motivation.

Abstract-Résumé: The proposed CIHR Centre for REACH in HIV/AIDS is a collaborative, national partnership among leading health researchers in Canada in a wide array disciplines from over 20 academic institutions, people living with HIV, front-line service providers, knowledge translation and exchange (KTE) specialists, and federal, provincial and regional policy makers.  OUR VISION is to bring together critical practice, research, and policy skills as well as the lived experience of people with HIV to enhance the health of individuals and communities disproportionately affected by HIV. OUR MISSION is to provide the core infrastructure support required to: engage community, policy-makers and researchers in interdisciplinary teams; break down geographical, theoretical, and conceptual barriers; and solve problems in the use, uptake and implementation of research evidence. OUR WORK will strengthen policy, programs and practices, and make a measurable difference in the health and well being of people with HIV and communities most vulnerable to HIV.  Using an interdisciplinary approach and working collaboratively at the intersections of social science, population health and health services research, the Centre will use an interdisciplinary approach to focus on three thematic areas: (1) UNDERSTANDING THE PROBLEMS AND FACTORS DRIVING THE EPIDEMIC ¿ reaching beyond individual behaviour to explore the impact of broader structural and cultural factors as well as the social determinants of health (i.e.,  poverty, stigma, discrimination, racism and gender inequality) on risk, resilience, behaviour and access to health services within communities; (2) FIND INNOVATIVE AND PRACTICAL SOLUTIONS ¿ taking an integrated approach to prevention and treatment, developing evidence-based interventions and strategies; and (3) MOVE RESEARCH EVIDENCE INTO ACTION ¿ developing effective KTE strategies, relationships and networks and having a measurable impact on policy and practice.

Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ISCHEMIA; DRUG CARRIER FOR BIOLOGICAL MATERIAL; MELANOMA; POLYMERIC ARTIFICIAL CELLS; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE: LIVER
Abstract-Résumé: (1)Coronary arterial obstruction can lead to heart attack. Oxygen carrier in solution can perfuse through the obstruction to supply oxygen. However, this can result in the release of damaging oxygen radicals. We have prepared an oxygen carrier-enzyme complex that can supply oxygen and at the same time remove oxygen radicals. We have shown earlier that this can prevent oxygen radical damage in a rat stroke model. With the importance of coronary heart diseases, we propose now to study its effect in an ischemic heart model. This will also avoid the side effects of heart attack when using oxygen carriers as blood substitute in transfusion. (2)Melanoma is a deadly skin cancer that cannot be adequately treated at present. We have prepared a new enzyme carrier to rapidly lower systemic tyrosine level. Daily injections slow the growth of melanoma in mice. We shall be doing using a new method of nano artificial cells that have a  longer duration of action to study if it can suppress rather than just retard the growth of melanoma in a mice model.  Results obtained may lead to a treatment for melanoma  (3) The liver of patients with severe acute liver failure can have a chance to recover if the patients are maintained alive with short term support for their liver functions. Donor source for human liver cells is rare, but donor human bone marrow is routinely available.  Bone marrow stem cells can differentiate into liver cells and can secrete growth factors to help the liver to recover.  We are studying artificial cells containing rat bone marrow cells in a rat model of acute liver failure.  Our early results show an increase in survival of animal treated this way. We are proposing to carry out more detailed studies using this approach.

TitreApplicationTitle: Low Glycemic index diet to improve glycemic control and cardiovascular disease in type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD GLUCOSE AND LIPID CONTROL; DIETARY INTERVENTION; INTIMA MEDIA THICKNESS (IMT); INTRA PLAQUE HEMORRHAGE (IPH); LOW GLYCEMIC INDEX (GI); MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI); TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Current oral anti-diabetic medications have been very successful in controlling glycemia and reducing the microvascular complications of diabetes but have largely failed to deliver the anticipated benefit of reduced macrovascular disease. One notable exception has been the alpha-glucosidase inhibitor, acarbose, which effectively converts the diet into a low-glycemic index diet through slowing the rate of carbohydrate absorption.  This manipulation has resulted in reduced progression of high risk people to diabetes, hypertension and coronary heart disease.  To determine whether dietary advice to lower the glycemic index of the diet can also reduce the burden of macrovascular disease, 160 subjects with type 2 diabetes taking oral hypoglycemic medications will be randomized to receive advice to consume either a low glycemic index (GI) diet or a conventional high fibre diet in a 3y parallel design. The main outcome of vascular disease will be measured by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as arterial damage assessed by the extent of plaque and its vulnerability at 1y and 3y. Other outcomes will include HbA1c, blood glucose, body weight, cholesterol profile, and markers of inflammation.  These data will indicate whether a dietary strategy to lower the glycemic-index of the diet is more effective in reducing or slowing the progression of macrocvascular disease than conventional high fibre advice in people with type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Randomized Trial of Thymoglobulin to Prevent Chronic Graft versus Host Disease in Patients Undergoing Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation from Unrelated Donors
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTITHYMOCYTE GLOBULIN; CHRONIC GRAFT VERSUS HOST DISEASE; HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANTATION; PREVENTION; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Chronic Graft versus Host Disease (cGVHD) is a common long term complication of bone marrow transplantation.  cGVHD causes chronic illness in people whose bone marrow disease has been cured, resulting in a severe decrease in quality of life and increased risk of death.  The Canadian Blood and Marrow Transplant Group (CBMTG) outlines a key study of a preventive treatment that promises to ameliorate or prevent suffering. Complications of cGVHD occur despite the use of current treatments which are therefore ineffective and which have serious side-effects.  Prevention is a better strategy.  The most promising strategy is the administration of antithymocyte globulin (ATG, Thymoglobulin®) just prior to transplantation.  The proposal: Patients will be randomized to receive, or not to receive, Thymoglobulin®, and the incidence and severity of graft versus host disease will be compared between the two study groups.  Information Regarding Graft Versus Host Disease: a)Bone marrow transplantation cures otherwise fatal bone marrow disorders b)The bone marrow contains the cells for the development of the immune system and those for the development of other blood cells. c)The recipient adopts the immune system of the donor. d)The donor¿s immune system may attack the recipient¿s tissues.  When the attack is against the diseased marrow this is termed Graft versus Leukemia reaction (GVL) and is responsible in a major way for the success of the transplant.  On the other hand, when the donor immune system attacks the recipient¿s normal tissues (Graft Versus Host Disease, GVH) the result is organ damage with death or chronic long term illness. e)Graft Versus Host Disease may be Acute (aGVHD), occurring within the first 100 days, or it may be Chronic (cGVHD), occurring beyond 100 days.  cGVHD may be fatal but more often it is debilitating, the degree of illness being compounded by the side effects of the drugs used to treat it.

Keywords-MotsClés: DOUBLE BLIND; FETAL GROWTH RESTRICTION; FOLIC ACID; HYPERTENSION; KIDNEY DISEASE; PLACEBO CONTROL; PREECLAMPSIA; PREGNANCY; PRETERM BIRTH; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SOLUBLE ENDOGLIN; SUPPLEMENTATION
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed project aims to conduct a study in the next five years on a new prevention strategy for preeclampsia in women with a high risk of developing preeclampsia: supplementation of folic acid starting in early pregnancy (12-16 weeks of gestation) until delivery, using randomized controlled trial, the scientific sounding method. Preeclampsia is hypertension that develops in pregnancy with proteinuria, affecting at least 5% of pregnancies worldwide.  Preeclampsia has serious health consequences to affected women and their offspring, with enormous economic impact on society.  No cure or prevention for this serious pregnancy complication is available.

Abstract-Résumé: Many infants require surgery in early life. It has been assumed  that there are no adverse effecs of general anesthesia in this age  group. However there is increasing evidence from animal studies  of  detrimental effects on brain development at a cellular level  and on memory and learning. Human studies following infants  exposed to anesthesia at an early age also show poorer  performance in a range of neuropsychological tests and in  school performance. All these studies have defects: translation  of animal data to humans; study groups having congenital  anomalies, being sicker than control groups. It is therefore  essential to prospectively study human infants having one type  of surgery which can be performed with either general or  regional anesthesia to determine if anesthesia itself has an  adverse effect on neurodevelopment in this age group.

TitreApplicationTitle: Birth insult and the development of medial prefrontal cortical function
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE; GLUTAMATE; MEDIAL PREFRONTAL CORTEX; MICRODIALYSIS; PERINATAL ANOXIA; VOLTAMMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: Obstetric complications at or close to the time of birth have long been thought to increase the risk for several mental disorders.  Such complications are suspected to produce subtle changes in brain maturation, the impact of which may become apparent only much later in life.  One consequence common to many obstetric problems is an episode of oxygen deprivation or anoxia to the newborn.  In this research project, I will examine in rats how birth anoxia alters the development of the prefrontal cortex, a brain area that plays a critical role in decision-making, memory and the control of impulsivity. This brain region and in particular the brain messenger molecule dopamine is known to function abnormally in kids with ADHD and in schizophrenia patients.  My question is, could birth complications involving anoxia contribute to this abnormal development of cortical dopamine function?

TitreApplicationTitle: Multi-center randomized placebo-controlled trial of nocturnal oxygen therapy in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease - The Canadian Nocturnal Oxygen (CANOX) trial
Keywords-MotsClés: COPD; OXYGEN THERAPY; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SURVIVAL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) is the only component of the management of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) that improves survival in patients with severe daytime hypoxemia.  In Canada, LTOT is usually provided by a stationary oxygen concentrator and is recommended to be used for at least 15-18 hours a day.  Sleep-related oxygen desaturation often occurs in patients with COPD who do not qualify for LTOT. The suggestion has been made that the natural progression of COPD to its end stages is dependent upon the severity of nocturnal desaturation.  A number of patients are currently treated with nocturnal oxygen although the beneficial effects of this therapy have not been confirmed.  Our primary objective is to determine, in patients with COPD not qualifying for LTOT but who present significant nocturnal oxygen desaturation, whether nocturnal oxygen therapy provided for a period of 3 years decreases mortality or delays the prescription of LTOT.  We propose a multi-center, experimental study comparing the effect of nocturnal oxygen therapy added to usual care vs. usual care alone in patients presenting sleep-related oxygen desaturation who do not qualify for LTOT.  We hope to reduce mortality from all cause and requirement for LTOT over the study period.

TitreApplicationTitle: The BK: KIDNI Trial (BK: Kinase Inhibition to Decrease Nephropathy  Intervention Trial)
Keywords-MotsClés: BK VIRUS; CHRONIC ALLOGRAFT NEPHROPATHY; INFLAMMATION AND FIBROSIS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED CLINICAL TRIAL; SIROLIMUS AND LEFLUNOMIDE; TRANSPLANT FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: This is a randomized controlled trial to determine whether specific  therapy aimed at reducing viral damage to the transplant kidney  will have a better outcome than standard therapy, which currently  consists of reducing immunosuppression. Infection with the BK  virus in kidney transplants can lead to transplant failure. We have  chosen this therapy with two immunosuppressive medications  based upon the biology of the BK virus. This virus hijacks the  cellular machinery to reproduce itself, and in passing activates  inflammation and scarring. Our therapy will interrupt this process,  and result in less scarring and will maintain renal transplant  function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Organization of Auditory Cortex Following Cochlear Implant
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY CORTEX; COCHLEAR PROSTHETICS; CONGENITAL DEAFNESS; DEVELOPMENT; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL RECORDING; REVERSIBLE DEACTIVATION
Abstract-Résumé: Hearing loss is the third most common chronic disability, affecting one in ten Canadians.  Moreover, deafness is the most common birth defect in Canada. Cochlear implants are extremely useful tools in providing auditory sensations to profoundly deaf individuals and have restored hearing to tens of thousands of people around the world. The use of cochlear implants in the profoundly deaf makes human speech comprehension possible. In hearing subjects, auditory cortex of the brain receives acoustic input and develops in the typical way. However, in deaf individuals the auditory cortex is deprived of acoustic input. Other senses, such as vision and touch, exploit the unused "deaf" region of cortex for their own purposes. This commonly results in enhanced visual or tactile abilities reported in the deaf. However, if the dormant auditory system is then activated by a cochlear implant; how does "deaf" auditory cortex respond? Does all of "deaf" auditory cortex begin to process sound again? Does the visual or tactile processing that invaded "deaf" auditory cortex retreat? Do the different auditory cortical areas begin to perform the same functions identified in a hearing subject? By better understanding the plastic properties of the cerebral cortex following implantation of a cochlear prosthetic, it will be possible to develop cochlear prosthetics and implantation strategies to better serve the needs of the brain. The greatest benefit of cochlear prosthetics has been found to occur in young children. Therefore, in these proposed studies, cochlear prosthetics will be implanted in young subjects. We will examine auditory cortical function in the congenitally-deaf cat following cochlear implant. The congenitally-deaf (or deaf, white) cat is the only known natural model for human congenital deafness. The results from these studies will be directly applicable to clinical studies presently investigating the functional outcomes of cochlear implants in young children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cascades of Non-selective cation channels that mediate cell signaling or cell death in the Hippocampus
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMERS; CONVERT STROKE; NON-SELECTIVE CATION CHANNELS; PATCH CLAMPING; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; TRANSIENT RECEPTOR POTENTIAL CHANNELS
Abstract-Résumé: Providing new types of pharmacological therapy for the elderly facing Alzheimer's and related disease is likely the most important health and social concern for Canada and the developed world. With aging, covert strokes, and in age-related degenerative diseases brain cells are lost and the ability of these cells to communicate information is impaired.  This results in deficits of learning and memory, and in thinking abilities in general.  Alzheimer's disease is a major example of where  there are changes in excitatory communication between brain cells.  This proposal examines how a unique ion channel, TRPM2, is correlated with aging and with the degenerative mechanisms underlying Alzheimer's like conditions.  It examines how TRPM2 channels interact with one of the excitatory synaptic channels (NR2B) that is know to cause cell damage and death.  The function and expression of TRPM2 will be examined with aging, metabolic stress and in mouse models of Alzheimer's. The toxic interactions of TRPM2 and NR2B and their co-regulation will be studied.  An agent that prevents this toxic action will be tested for potential benefits in preventing the degenerative changes underlying age-related degenerative diseases and Alzheimer's disease. We have identified a potential candidate drug for preventing such injury

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and Physiological Function of Protein Tyrosine Phosphatase Alpha (PTPa): Investigation of PTPa-Deficient Mice and Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL MIGRATION; CYTOSKELETON; IGF-1; INTEGRIN; INVASION; MAST CELLS; METASTASIS; PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION AND DEPHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN TYROSINE PHOSPHATASES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TUMOUR CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Cell motility or migration is an important process that determines many physiological events, including development, tissue repair, and immune responses. Migration is controlled by the interactions between the cell and the surrounding matrix that are co-ordinated with the continual re-organization of the structural elements within a cell (the cytoskeleton) that determine its shape. Proteins at the cell surface called integrins are the nodes of this co-ordination, as they form contacts with the matrix and relay these signals to the cytoskeleton. Integrin-mediated signal relay is highly complex and involves a multi-protein communication network within the cell.  Furthering our understanding of this network and how its components function will allow us to pinpoint molecular alterations in diseases involving aberrant cell migration, notably cancer.  Cancer mortality usually arises as a result of tumor cell migration to new sites in the body, with the consequent formation of new tumors.  We have discovered that a molecule called PTPa plays key roles in the integrin signaling network, as it performs two different functions in this process.  Our previous work has shown that PTPa acts in conjunction with integrins to stimulate early signaling molecules.  We have recently identified another requirement for PTPa further along in the signaling relay that is critical for migration.  In our proposed research we will elucidate this novel second role of PTPa that we believe is fundamental to the migration of numerous cell types.  Knowledge of precise molecular functions in integrin signaling will promote the development of targeted molecular therapies, perhaps to PTPa, to combat migration-based diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of MARK2:TORC2:CREB signaling in beta cell regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK KINASE FAMILY; BETA CELL REGENERATION; BETA CELLS; CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT; CREB; TORC2/CRTC2
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing our understanding of beta cell survival mechanisms is critical to the improvement of treatment of type I and  type II diabetes. While islet transplantation offers a promising treatment, this approach is limited by graft immune  rejection and impaired function and survival of transplanted islets. The switch protein CREB is critical for the long-term  survival of insulin-producing islet cells. Loss of CREB function in islet cells leads to islet cell death and to diabetes. We  have identified a complex of signaling proteins - those that detect signals from outside the cell and transmit this  information within the cell - that control CREB function in islet cells. This complex includes the enzyme MARK2 and a protein called TORC2 which is required to turn CREB on.  We hope to establish what  contribution MARK2 and TORC2 makes to the control of CREB activity in islet cells, and to determine whether or not drugs that  modify TORC2 activity could be used to promote islet cell function and survival. The knowledge gained will be applied to  preserve islet cell survival during islet transplantation for children with Type I diabetes, and to improve islet cell  function in Type II diabetes patients who display impaired glucose control.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and genetic basis of polygenic hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDOSTERONE PATHWAY; ANIMAL MODELS OF HUMAN DISEASES; CONGENIC STRAIN; EPISTASIS; VERTEBRATE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension is one of the most common diseases. So far, very little is known about the genes whose defects can cause inherited hypertension in the majority of human populations. Because naturally existing human populations are genetically heterogeneous and because environmental factors impacting on how hypertension occurs are impossible to be controlled in any given population, it has been difficult to identify hypertension genes by directly studying humans. As an alternative, inbred animal models can be experimentally manipulated and, therefore, can be more aptly utilized to identify genes. It is expected that some of theses genes may be extrapolated to humans. One animal model for hypertension is the inbred spontaneously hypertension Dahl salt-sensitive rats. Our overall objective is to identify hypertension genes using this particular strain of rat. The current research is to pursue molecular identifications of multiple genes on Chromosome 10 which have human homologues.

TitreApplicationTitle: Glycosome Biogenesis:  The Role of LdPEX14 in Protein Targeting and Import
Keywords-MotsClés: GLYCOSOME; LEISHMANIA; PEROXIN; PROTEIN CHEMISTRY; PROTEIN REGULATION; STRUCTURE FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The protozoan parasite Leishmania is the causative agent of leishmaniasis, a disease that is characterized by clinical symptoms ranging from disfiguring lesion to death in the absence of drug treatment.  Presently no effective vaccine is available for immunization against this disease and the drugs that are used to treat these infections have moderate-highly toxic side effects, require hospitalization, and are expensive.  Of greater concern however, is the up surge in leishmaniasis in Afghanistan and Iraq, coupled with the emergence of drug resistant Leishmania.  The aim of our research is to identify unique biological features in Leishmania that can be exploited for the development of new drugs that selectively target this parasite.  Perhaps one of the most unique structural features found in Leishmania is small round microbody called the glycosome, which contains a large number of enzymes needed for energy production or synthesis of new molecules.  Correct targeting of these proteins to the glycosome is crucial for parasite survival.  Efforts in my laboratory focus on understanding the molecular machinery involved in the assembly of the glycosome.  This knowledge will ultimately be used to design new classes of drugs that block the import of proteins into the glycosome, an event that is lethal to the parasite.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of PKC in the nervous system
Keywords-MotsClés: APLYSIA; G PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTORS; GFP IMAGING; LEARNING AND MEMORY; PROTEIN KINASE; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: An experience leaves a molecular trace inside neurons and identifying this trace is the goal of my research. We believe that memories are defined by these molecular traces and thus, understanding these traces is critical for our understanding of memory. For example, if the traces encoding short-term memories and long-term memories are made in parallel, one can paradoxically make a long-term memory without a short-term memory.  To study memory, we use a simple model system, the marine mollusk Aplysia, because in this system the neurons that hold the memory trace have been identified. Moreover, these neurons can be cultured and the changes that occur during memory can be studied under controlled conditions. This is a valuable model for studying memory formation, as seen by the Nobel Prize awarded to Dr. Eric Kandel in 2000 for his pioneering work in this system.  In this application, we study a family of molecules that are important for both generating and in some cases encoding memory traces. This family is called protein kinase C (PKC). PKCs encode memories by adding phosphate residues to molecules that determine how well neurons are connected, regulating the strength of these connections, and thus forming memories. When PKCs are persistently activated, they can encode the memory trace, since changes in synaptic strength are maintained by the active kinase. In this application we will determine the rules by which different experiences activate and/or persistently activate distinct members of the PKC family and thus learn how different types of experience lead to different types of memory traces. Understanding how memories are formed has important health implications both for pathological conditions such as mental retardation, and physiological conditions such as aging. A better understanding of how memories are formed is important for developing strategies for improving memory in both healthy and diseased individuals.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of NADPH oxidases in Inflammatory Bowel Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; GENETIC VARIATION; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASES; NADPH OXIDASES; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES
Abstract-Résumé: Our immune system has many weapons to defend us from infection by microbes.  One of these weapons is the generation of reactive oxygen species (or oxidants).  These are typically thought of as 'bad' molecules of oxygen since they can lead to damage of cellular components.  Under normal circumstances our cells use a variety of anti-oxidant molecules and enzymes to protect our cellular components from damage caused by reactive oxygen species.  However, during infection our cells utilize specific enzyme systems to generate large amounts of reactive oxygen species to kill the invading microbe.  The enzymes, members of the NOX/DUOX family, are found in all cell types and can act within different compartments of our cells. By delivering the NOX/DUOX enzymes to where the microbes are, the cell can effectively deliver a lethal burst of reactive oxygen species that fatally damage the microbe. Genetic deletion of the genes  encoding the NOX/DUOX enzymes is known to make mice susceptible to bacterial infection. So these enzymes, and the reactive oxygen species that they generate, play an important role in our immune defences.  Recent studies suggest that the function of NOX/DUOX enzymes may be altered in some individuals with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD).  Here we will test this idea by determining if any naturally occuring genetic variations in the NOX/DUOX enzymes are linked to IBD.  These studies will involve genetic testing of individuals with IBD, and comparing their genes with individuals that do not have the disease. Based on our preliminary data we expect that at least four members of the NOX/DUOX family will display altered function in IBD patients.  We will then examine how the function of these enzymes is altered, and how this affects the immune responses of cells from individuals with IBD. These studies will provide important insight into the genetic causes of IBD, allowing the development of better treatments of the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Viral Determinants of Infectious Hepatitis C Virus Production
Keywords-MotsClés: FORCED EVOLUTION; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; IMMUNFLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; INFECTIVITY ASSAYS; VIRUS ASSEMBLY; VIRUS CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 300,000 Canadians are currently infected with the hepatitis C virus, and as many as 80,000 of these people may not yet know it. Up to 70% of these individuals will progress to develop liver cirrhosis, and some will go on to develop hepatocellular carcinoma. Currently available therapies show limited efficacy with uncomfortable side-effects and poor tolerance. Treatment for this large number of people will translate to an enormous impact on public health in our country. The main focus of my research will be to identify novel targets for anti-HCV therapy, and it is my hope that these efforts will contribute to the development of novel antiviral drugs to help fight this disease. Until recently there was no robust cell culture system available for the study of HCV, but in 2005 a fully infectious HCV cell culture system was established that allows secretion of infectious virus particles upon transfection of human hepatocyte cell lines. Using this system, it is now possible to study all aspects of the viral life cycle, including virus entry and assembly, as well as the role of critical cellular factors in these processes. Presumably, HCV particle formation is driven by the core structural protein. At some point, either during or after core has assembled a genome-containing capsid, viral glycoproteins E1 and E2 are incorporated into the virion. Using the infectious HCV system, I plan to characterize the role of the viral core protein in the virion assembly process. My previous work suggests that the viral p7 and NS2 proteins also contribute in some way to the virus assembly process. I plan to elucidate the mechanisms by which these proteins play a role in virus assembly and production of infectious virions. The information obtained from these studies will not only contribute to the basic understanding of the HCV life cycle, but will also help to identify putative new targets for specific antiviral therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetic regulation of neuroprogenitor behavior: Role of the Snf2l chromatin remodeling protein.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN REMODELING; EPIGENETICS; ISWI; NEURODEVELOPMENT; SNF2H; SNF2L
Abstract-Résumé: Mental handicap is a common clinical problem affecting 2-3% of the population, where ~0.3% of individuals are so severely handicapped they cannot live independently and often require continuous nursing care. If we estimate the Canadian population at 35 million, it suggests there are 700,000 affected individuals with mental handicap, of whom ~100,000 are severely debilitated and represent a significant expense to healthcare resources. Understanding the molecular basis of mental handicap is essential for the development of treatments that can improve the quality of life for these individuals. We have recently established that proteins that regulate gene expression by modifying chromatin structure are mutated in several disorders of mental handicap. In the present proposal we examine the specific role of a chromatin remodeling protein in neuronal differentiation during brain development. A complete understanding of how chromatin remodelling proteins regulate cellular differentiation and how this process proceeds will provide valuable information for scientists and clinicians alike interested in stem cell therapy of such developmental disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interrogation of neuron-mediated morphogen signaling in the nervous system
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL BIOLOGY; LIVE IMAGING MICROSCOPY; MOUSE MODELS; PRIMARY NEURON CULTURE; TRANSFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: The Sonic hedgehog protein plays a critical role in the development of the brain and altered Sonic hedgehog signaling is associated with brain malformations and cancer in humans.  Neurons represent an important source of this protein in the developing and adult brain, and the goal of this study is to understand how unique characteristics of neurons, including long distance transport of proteins in axons and electrical activity, regulate the secretion of this protein.  Findings from these studies have the potential to enhance our understanding of normal development, disease and regeneration in the brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms for eye-hand coordination in the human
Keywords-MotsClés: ARM MOVEMENTS; BRAIN IMAGING; COGNITION; EYE MOVEMENTS; PERCEPTION; TMS
Abstract-Résumé: Eye-hand coordination is central to the basic life-skills, work, and recreational activities of all people. Eye-hand coordination is more complicated than we generally assume, because it depends on proper vision, eye movements, perception, cognition, and arm control. Consequently, it breaks down in many diseases, developmental disorders, and injuries of the central nervous system. The purpose of this project is to understand how the brain uses vision to guide arm movements, and how this degrades during brain damage and across the normal lifespan. We will test how the cerebral cortex represents movement goals in sensory space and transforms this into actions. We will test how humans incorporate different types of complex perceptual information into their movement plans. Finally, we will explore how these processes fail to develop or decline with age, and test a paradigm that we developed from our last grant for rehabilitation of patients with cortical damage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prévention des récidives des tentatives de suicide : étude des parcours de soins selon le genre
Keywords-MotsClés: PARCOURS DE SOINS; PREVENTION DU SUICIDE; TENTATIVES DE SUICIDE; ETUDE DE COHORTE
Abstract-Résumé: Le but de la presente recherche est d'identifier les pratiques et interventions qui peuvent contribuer a la diminution de la recidive de suicide,tout en tenant compte des besoins des differentes clienteles qui se presentent a l'urgence d'un centre hospitalier suite a une tentative de suicide. Plus specifiquement,les objectifs sont de decrire les pratiques actuelles de soins aupres des patients suicidaires et d'evaluer les caracteristiques liees aux interventions qui favorisent une diminution des taux de recidives de tentatives de suicide.Cette recherche comprend trois grands volets. Le Volet 1 documentera le parcours de soins d'une cohorte de 700 patients ayant fait une tentative de suicide, en milieu intra et extra hospitalier. Des indicateurs du parcours de soins seront etablis en fonction d'un ensemble de criteres inspires de guides de pratiques cliniques internationaux deja existants, valides aupres d'informateurs cle des milieux hospitaliers participants. Ce volet s'interesse egalement aux consequences des pratiques aupres des patients. Des mesures longitudinales sur 18 mois permettront d'identifier quels criteres ou quels ensembles de criteres sont plus efficaces en termes de diminution des recidives de tentatives de suicides en fonction du genre. Plusieurs sources d'informations seront utilisees: dossiers medicaux, entrevues avec le patient, questionnaires auto completes. Le deuxieme volet consiste en une etude qualitative de l'experience du parcours de soins aupres d'un echantillon intentionnel de 60 personnes. Finalement, le troisieme volet sera consacre a l'elaboration d'outils d'application des connaissances. L'aspect novateur de cette demande est d'outrepasser la verification empirique d'une intervention pour, au contraire, identifier des modeles d'intervention qui tiennent compte des variables personnelles, sociales et demographiques du patient tout en analysant la repercussion des soins recus selon le genre.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural coding in Deep Cerebellar Nuclei
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICS; BURST DISCHARGE; CALCIUM CHANNELS; CALCIUM SPIKE; DENDRITIC PHYSIOLOGY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The cerebellum is a highly organized structure that rests near the back of the brain to coordinate all aspects of movement.  It receives sensory input from joints and muscles during movement that inform the circuit of where in space a limb is positioned, and the current status of a requested movement (ie arm or leg).  Sensory input is received by the cerebellar cortical circuit that is centered around a layer of Purkinje cells.  All output from Purkinje cells is then transmitted to a set of three Deep Cerebellar Nuclei (DCN) as a series of electrical impulses down its nerve fiber, with the DCN in turn taking charge of sending all final output from cerebellum to various motor centers. What makes the cerebellum unique is that all Purkinje cell output to the DCN is inhibitory, meaning that DCN cells must translate an inhibitory signal to an excitatory output that reflects the pattern or frequency of arriving nerve impulses.  We use recordings of single cells in animal model preparations to understand the "neural code" used by DCN cells to translate Purkinje cell inhibition into an excitatory "rebound excitation" that accurately reflects incoming information.  In this way we can understand where the circuit fails to function correctly in cases of ataxia or tremor.

TitreApplicationTitle: Individual Differences Underlying Substance Abuse and Addiction: At the Intersection of Brain, Cognition, Genetics and Personality
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; DOPAMINE; EVENT-RELATED BRAIN POTENTIALS; GENETICS; INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES; REINFORCEMENT LEARNING
Abstract-Résumé: Substance abuse is a major public health concern: In Canada, tobacco alone is consumed by an estimated 15-20% of the population, and 20% of all drinkers engage in hazardous alcohol use. The total cost to society--in terms of the burden placed on the Canadian health care system, law enforcement, and workplace productivity--is estimated to be about $40 billion per year. But why is it that only some people who use drugs actually become addicted? Can sufficient exposure to substances of abuse cause anyone to become dependent or do addicts simply lack the will-power to resist? In fact, addiction depends on a far more complicated process involving a confluence of biological, behavioral, cognitive, social, and personality-related factors. Notably, all addictive drugs act on a neural system for reinforcement learning called the midbrain dopamine system, which projects to and regulates the brain's system for cognitive control, called frontal cortex. Further, the development and expression of the dopamine system is determined in part by genetic factors that vary across individuals such that dopamine-related genes are partly responsible for addiction-proneness. We have recently found that young adults who are dependent on substances of abuse produce an abnormal brainwave response to reinforcing events, and further, that they behave abnormally on a decision making task that is diagnostic of dopamine dysfunction. In this project, we propose to conduct a series of experiments that will investigate whether this atypical brain response  is 1) associated with abnormal reinforcement learning, 2) elicited by drug rewards, 3) present in adolescence even before acute drug use, and 4) associated with genes that code for the expression of the dopamine system. In so doing we hope to tease apart biological, cognitive and personality-related factors underlying substance abuse that will be amenable to treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Drug metabolism in the Brain: Expression and Regulation of Cytochrome P450
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL; CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM; CYTOCHROME P450 ENZYMES; DRUG METABOLISM; EXTRAHEPATIC; NICOTINE
Abstract-Résumé: Metabolism of drugs by liver enzymes is the principal mechanism the body has for removal of drugs, including nicotine and ethanol. For drugs that enter the brain and have their actions in the brain, such as nicotine and alcohol, many effects on brain function have been demonstrated after both one-time and long term use. Recently we have shown that the liver enzymes that inactivate nicotine and ethanol are also made in the brain in very specific regions and cells. We have also shown that they are increased after even very low doses of nicotine or ethanol (or in the brains of human smokers or alcoholics). The increased activity of these enzymes can have a number of consequences. 1) Increased levels of these enzymes can increase the speed of inactivation (or activation) of drugs in the brain as a safeguard or this may provide an incentive for increased use, for example for drinking more alcohol or lighting up the next cigarette to replenish the drug that is removed by metabolism. 2) Increased levels may alter the activation/inactivation of other drugs which also use this enzyme, for example smokers may require more sedative than nonsmokers. 3) The higher levels of activity could increase the metabolism of other chemicals in the brain, both chemicals that are required for normal brain function, and other pharmaceutical drugs. We will investigate the consequences of the presence and induction of these enzymes in the brain in animal drug-induced behavioural models. This information will improve our understanding of the brain and its response to drugs and will also provide opportunities for altering this process to decrease the harm done by these drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lipid signaling in the eye: Pharmacology of cannabinoid receptors and their ligands.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; ENDOCANNABINOID SYSTEM; INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE; OCULAR PHARMACOLOGY; RECEPTORS; VASCULATURE
Abstract-Résumé: Increased pressure in the eye is a key risk factor in glaucoma, an age-related blinding eye disease that results in death of neurons in the retina, the tissue at the back of the eye responsible for transmitting light signals to the brain.  In addition, abnormal blood flow in the eye may also contribute to glaucoma. Drugs that decrease eye pressure are important in the treatment of glaucoma and are able to slow down the loss of vision in this disease.  Our research is examining drugs called cannabinoids which include naturally occurring chemical constituents of the cannabis plant and their synthetic derivatives. Cannabinoids are able to reduce eye pressure and may have beneficial effects on blood flow in the eye. These chemicals mimic the actions of natural compounds found in the eye called endocannabinoids. We want to determine how cannabinoids and endocannabinoids work in the eye and whether the ocular endocannabinoid system constitutes a therapeutic target in the treatment of glaucoma and ischemic eye disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of mTOR and p53 signaling pathways on the MHCI immunopeptidome of cancer cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER CELLS; CHROMATOGRAPHY; IMMUNOPEPTIDOME; MASS-SPEC; MHCI; MTOR; P53; T-CELL THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer cells can be killed effectively by T lymphocytes. In accordance with this concept, studies in mice and humans have clearly shown that T lymphocytes can cure cancer. In order to do so however, T lymphocytes must recognize abnormalities on the surface of cancer cells that are not usually present on normal cells. In essence, T lymphocytes recognize a specific group of small molecules (peptides) that are bound to cell surface proteins called MHCI. Collectively, these peptides are referred to as the MHCI immunopeptidome. We know so far that translation of T-cell therapeutic potential in the clinical setting is still extremely limited, mainly because our knowledge of cancer cells MHCI immunopeptidome is rudimentary. Therefore, in order to develop effective therapies, we must understand the mechanism controlling the MHCI immunopeptidome. Without such understanding, a customized and time consuming identification and/or preparation of cancer specific peptides would be required de novo for each patient. Since the immunopeptidome is dependent on both protein translation and degradation, we intend to analyze how major signaling pathways known to play pivotal roles in cancer cells would affect the immunopeptidome. Such understanding will lead us to select particularly attractive peptide targets to prime T-cells ex-vivo for cancer immunotherapy. We will test the efficacy of these peptides to i) prevent the occurrence of spontaneous tumors, and to ii) treat established tumors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Quality control in the secretory pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: CA HOMEOSTASIS; CALNEXIN; CALRETICULIN; ER QUALITY CONTROL; PROTEIN FOLDING; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS
Abstract-Résumé: In my laboratory we study the structure and functions of proteins of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. This intracellular organelle is involved in the control of virtually every aspect of normal and diseased cellular function including ion transport and storage, muscle contraction and relaxation, protein and lipid synthesis, protein modification and folding. The focus of our work is on endoplasmic reticulum chaperones, proteins involved in folding of other proteins. Impaired protein folding has been implicated in many devastating diseases such as Alzheimer, neurodegenerative diseases, atherosclerosis, cystic fibrosis to name just a few. Work from our laboratory indicates that endoplasmic reticulum proteins are essential for neuronal development and play a critical role in myelin formation. Therefore, our work is directly relevant to fundamental clinical problems such as multiple sclerosis and other myelin diseases. Endoplasmic reticulum associated proteins may become the future targets for clinical management of many neuropathies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Function of the FMR1 gene product in protein synthesis
Keywords-MotsClés: FRAGILE X SYNDROME; GENE REGULATION; MENTAL RETARDATION; MRIBONUCLEOPARTICLE; NEURONS-CULTURES; RNA-BINDING PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: The Fragile X syndrome, one of the most frequent genetic disease, is the most common form of inherited mental retardation. It affects 1 person out of 5000 in the population all over the world. The syndrome results from the absence of the Fragile X mental Retardation Protein (FMRP). This protein is normally involved in the transport and metabolism of messenger RNA that are required for the synthesis of specific proteins necessary for normal neuron circuitry and development. We are currently using normal as well as defective cells in culture to understand the missing functions that leads to mental retardation. We are also studying how FMRP interacts with its RNA targets in order to understand its functions. These studies will provide critical data to better understand the pathology of mental retardation and possibly to device strategies for therapeutic interventions in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of astrocytes in blood-brain barrier regulation and CNS immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTES; BLOOD BRAIN BARRIER; ENDOTHELIUM; HEDGEHOG; NEURO-INFLAMMATION; TIGHT JUNCTION PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: The Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB) restrict the passage of noxious molecules and cells from the blood to the brain. In diseases like Multiple Sclerosis (MS), the BBB fails to prevent entry of aggressive white blood cells (leukocytes) into the brain. These leukocytes are thought to be the effectors of damage to brain cells. Our work focus on both the intact and damaged BBB and its role on the development of inflammatory diseases directed to the brain. We intend to understand the molecular mechanisms involved in the formation of a tight and impermeable BBB and to study the dysregulation of these mechanisms in MS. As MS is the most prevalent neurological disorder of young adults in Canada and the first cause of permanent handicap, our research can have a significant impact on the health status of thousands of young canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of a novel urate transporter in the kidney and colon.
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HETEROLOGOUS EXPRESSION; METABOLIC DISEASE; PCR; SITE DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; URATE TRANSPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Humans have very high circulating levels of urate in their blood compared to other mammals. The physiological reason for this is not known, however even small additional increases in this concentration is associated with several metabolic diseases including gout and diabetes. The normal regulation of urate in the blood is controlled primarily by the kidney through several proteins which can either reabsorb urate from the urine or secrete it back into the urine. We have recently discovered a new protein which can transport urate in the kidney and we proposed that this protein may be a key player in secreting urate into the urine, i.e. lowering plasma urate concentrations. Further, a genetic screen indicates that a series of polymorphisms (slight genetic variations) within the gene coding for this protein may be related both to the incidence of gout and/ or hypertension in some populations. This project contains experiments designed to test just how this protein moves urate out of (or into) different cell types and in particular tests our hypothesis that it plays a key role in the kidney. If our hypothesis proves to be correct this may identify a new drug target for the treatment of gout and hypertension

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechnisms dictating control of neuroendocrine function by estrogen.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CONTRACEPTION; ESTROGEN; FERTILITY; GENE ARRAY; GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory is studying the biology of gonadotropin-releasing hormone(GnRH)-secreting neurons located in a specific region of the brain, the hypothalamus. GnRH is the primary regulator of reproduction, and is controlled by estrogen levels in the body. Infertility, and conversely, safe contraceptive methods are both major reproductive health concerns, and knowledge of the signals involved in the control of GnRH synthesis is therefore important for our comprhension of reproductive function and failure. Neuropeptide Y (NPY) and Kisspeptin (KISS), hormones produced by other specific hypothalamic neurons, have a profound impact on reproduction. Yet despite the significance of NPY and KISS on the overall control of reproductive capability, little is known about how NPY/KISS neurons directly affect the GnRH-producing neurons.  We are studying both the direct action of these neurons on the GnRH neuron, and more generally how the NPY and KISS neurons are regulated by estrogen. Our research will provide insights into the control of the expression of GnRH, NPY, and KISS genes by estrogen. Further, unravelling the complexities involved in the control of GnRH neuronal activity by NPY and KISS at the molecular level will contribute critical knowledge for applications with both physiological and therapeutical relevance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genomics of mycobacterial pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE DELETION; GENOMICS; MICROARRAYS; MYCOBACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; TRANSCRIPTOME; VIRULENCE
Abstract-Résumé: The availability of genome sequence data has permitted a renewed approach to understanding how certain bacteria cause disease. This has been particularly valuable in understanding the bacteria that causes tuberculosis, called Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and the closely related bacteria used as a vaccine against tuberculosis, called BCG. In this project, we plan to continuing studying mycobacterial pathogens, using a variety of genomic methods. Previously, these organisms were characterized by their loss of DNA, but studies by our group and others have shown that these organisms are also able to gain new genetic elements. The goal of our research is to understand how the acquisition of new genes by these organisms mediates virulence, which is their capacity to cause disease. The ultimate goal is to have a better understanding of the basis of disease, towards the development of improved diagnostic tests and vaccines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lytic transglycosylases as new antibacterial targets
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOLYSINS; BACTERIOL PHYSIOLOGY; ENZYMOLOGY; LYTIC TRANSGLYCOSYLASES; NEW ANTIBIOTIC TRAGETS; PEPTIDOGLYCAN METABOLISM
Abstract-Résumé: The insoluble peptidoglycan (PG) sacculus encloses the cytoplasmic membrane of bacterial cells to maintain their structural integrity.  This fact, together with its uniqueness to the bacterial cell, have made the enzymatic machinery responsible for the biosynthesis of PG a popular and prime target for antibacterial therapy.  Indeed, the beta-lactams and vancomycin have proven to be very useful classes of antibiotics, but their efficacy now appears to be limited in view of the various forms of resistance that have emerged over the past 50 years.  New targets have to be identified which, ideally, should be common to both Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens thereby permitting the development of broad spectrum antibiotics.   We propose that the lytic transglycosylases (LTs) present an attractive target for the development of new antibacterials.  These enzymes would be ideal targets because: i) their PG substrate is unique to, but common amongst, almost all bacteria; ii) the component sugar residues remain consistent in all PGs; iii) the lack of variation in the glycan chain implies less chance for resistance to evolve; iv) they are required for a host of essential functions, including secretion/transport, insertion of appendages, cell growth, and cell division; and v) an inhibitor specific for the active site region for any one of the LTs will likely prove to be reactive against all in the same way that penicillin binds all PG transpeptidases. The major aims of this research proposal are to: i) Continue to characterize the structure and function relationship of LTs; ii)Develop a high throughput screen for the search of inhibitors of LTs; and iii)Continue to investigate the biological role and organization of LTs in PG metabolism.  These studies will involve a combination of microbiological, molecular biological, and analytical biochemistry techniques, including insertion and site-directed mutagenesis, enzyme kinetics, and electron microscopy.

TitreApplicationTitle: System specific chaperones and the Tat protein translocation system
Keywords-MotsClés: CHAPERONES; ESCHERICHIA COLI; PROTEIN SECRETION; PROTEIN TRANSLOCATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; REDOX ENZYMES
Abstract-Résumé: Redox enzymes are responsible for the energy production and maintenance of cells.  Many different bacterial bioenergetic enzymes use alternatives to oxygen in their respiratory chains.  These enzymes are complex with multiple components that interact with the cell membrane.  In many cases the production of these enzymes and their final cellular location are on opposite sides of the cell membrane.  Moving proteins across biological membrane is a fundamental process in cell biology. I discovered 10 years ago, a system that moves or translocates these bioenergetic enzymes across the membrane.  In order to target such proteins to this translocase, these proteins have unique leader sequences that act as an address for the protein.  We are interested in proteins that interact with this leader address, and chaperone the protein to the membrane and help the protein mature into a functional respiratory system.  Our group has identified a number of these chaperone like proteins.  The goal of this research is to understand how these proteins recognize different leader address signals and how they play a role in these proteins' maturation events leading to a healthy bacterial cell.  This research is important, as it has been observed that bacteria deficient in the translocase have lost their pathogenic properties and grow as a community of cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Systematic analysis of RNA-protein interaction specificities
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE REGULATION; GENOMICS; MICROARRAYS; RNA STRUCTURE; RNA-BINDING; SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: In order to understand how human beings work under the hood we need to understand how all of our parts work.  While the genome sequence has been described as a blueprint, it is really more like a self-extracting computer program:  all of the information needed to decode the message is contained in the message.  What we need now is to understand how the parts encoded by the genome interpret the genome.  Human genes make RNA and most go on to make proteins.  Hundreds of human proteins bind RNA and regulate when it is made and what it does.  The purpose of this project is to catalogue the RNA-binding preferences (e.g. preferred sequences) for all human RNA-binding proteins.

TitreApplicationTitle: Knee Joint Contractures: Reversibility and Molecular Pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: EXPERIMENTAL SURGERY; GENETICS; HISTOMORPHOMETRY; JOINT CAPSULE; MECHANOBIOLOGY; MICROARRAY
Abstract-Résumé: A contracture is a pathologic condition limiting range and function of joints. Contractures of large and small joints alike will affect one's ability to independently perform daily activities such as eating, dressing or walking. Current treatments for contractures include physical stretching, the use of assistive devices or, rarely, surgery. Despite prolonged treatments, patients with contractures rarely regain complete mobility. Progress in preventing and treating contractures will be possible only through an understanding of the biological and molecular processes involved. In the past 12 years our group has established and validated an animal model to study the histological events and the molecular mechanisms involved in joint contractures. We have provided evidence for capsule stiffness, characterized cartilage degeneration, and identified four genes whose expression is altered in the cartilage of a knee joint with contracture. The work we propose in the current application aims at studying the reversibility of joint alterations after immobility and at finding genes and pathways in the joint capsule associated with knee joint contractures. The results will identify new avenues for treating the large number of patients suffering from contractures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional analyses of novel heterodimeric kinesin motors
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-FUNGAL DRUGS; HETERODIMER; KINESIN; MICROTUBULE DYNAMICS; MITOSIS; NUCLEAR MIGRATION; PATHOGENIC FUNGI; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Kinesins are nanosized protein machines that help move a wide variety of subcellular components around the cell on protein tracks called microtubules. One of the key functions kinesin-based movement serves is to facilitate timely and equal segregation of genetic material between dividing cells. Recent research has come to show that inhibition of this type of kinesin-based movement in disease causing cells, such as pathogens and tumors, could offer a powerful and side effect-lowering therapeutic intervention when cell-type or mechanism-specific kinesins are targeted. A new form of kinesin, which functions in movement of genetic material in budding yeast, appears to exist exclusively in budding yeast relatives that cause deadly fungal infections in a significant proportion of the human population. This form of kinesin has also recently been shown to move its genetic cargo by an unprecedented mechanism. Together, these factors could form the basis for development a new generation of anti-fungal drugs once sufficient information is obtained about their mode of movement and breadth of roles in the more pathogenic species. Our research proposal describes our approach toward attaining this information.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chemical genomic investigations in Escherichia coli
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBACTERIAL; CHEMICAL BIOLOGY; CHEMICAL GENETICS; CHEMICAL GENOMICS; ESCHERICHIA COLI; SMALL MOLECULE SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: In the past forty years only two new classes of antibiotics have reached the clinic for treatment of bacterial infections.  During the same time we have seen an alarming increase in reports of "superbugs" with resistance to existing drugs. Indeed, multidrug resistance in bacteria is due largely to the limited repertoire of drugs that eradicate bacteria and with a narrow range of mechanisms. Recognizing the need for new therapies with novel mechanisms, we seek to better understand the most basic elements of poorly understood but core physiology in bacteria to reveal chinks in the armor of important pathogens.  In the work proposed here we hope to break fresh ground in the discovery of new probes of the model microbe Escherichia coli with the hope that this work will lead to novel leads for new antibiotics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular studies of von Willebrand factor pathobiology.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; INHERITED BLEEDING DISORDER; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MOLECULAR GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: von Willebrand factor (VWF) is a large adhesive pro-coagulant protein that is required for two key functions in normal blood clotting: the initial attachment of blood platelets to sites of blood vessel damage, and the carriage of clotting factor VIII in blood. Inherited quantitative or qualitative abnormalities of VWF result in the inherited bleeding disorder, von Willebrand disease (VWD). The aim of these studies is to investigate how changes to the amount and function of VWF affect blood clotting. The first group of studies will characterize genetic sequences involved in regulating how much VWF is made within the body. These studies will initially be based upon results obtained in the investigation of a large population of patients with low blood levels of VWF. Abnormalities to the genetic control sequences documented in these patients will be investigated for their functional significance. In the later stages of the project, we will also begin to evaluate the influence of more distant sequences on VWF gene expression. In the second and third aims of this project, we will investigate the effects of qualitative changes to the VWF protein that result in abnormal blood clotting. Variant forms of the protein that show altered cleavage by the processing enzyme ADAMTS13 and abnormal binding to platelets will be assessed though a variety of in vitro and in vivo approaches. Initial studies will confirm the functional deficits of these variant proteins through standard in vitro analysis. Subsequently, recombinant forms of the variant proteins will be infused into mice with severe VWF deficiency to assess their recovery and circulation times. Finally, in vivo analysis of these variant forms of VWF will be evaluated following delivery of mutant transgenes through a hydrodynamic injection approach. These in vivo studies will involve a comprehensive series of investigations to determine the influence of these VWF protein changes on normal blood clotting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Influenza A virus infection activates PI3K/Akt pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: FRET-FLIM; INFLUENZA A VIRUS; LIVE CELL IMAGING; PATHOGENESIS OF INFLUENZA A VIRUS; PI3K/AKT SIGNALING PATHWAYS; REVERSE GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza viruses continue to pose a severe threat worldwide. The major difficulty in defending against influenza virus infection is the high genetic variability of the virus. This results in the rapid generation of reassortant viruses that can escape the acquired immunity against previous virus strains or gain resistance to antiviral agents. During virus infection, virus-host interactions determine the virus life cycle and pathogenesis. One important strategy from the virus perspective is to activate cellular signaling pathways and hijack the cellular machinery to augment viral replication and propagation. Thus, cellular events that are essential for efficient virus replication and propagation might be the target for anti-influenza interventions. The proposed research is designed to focus on the cellular function, specifically, to dissect how influenza virus infection leads to the activation of cellular Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases (PI3K)/Akt signaling pathway, which is essential for efficient virus replication and propagation. The rationale is that a missing cellular function is more difficult for the virus to adapt to, and should affect virus infection independent of the virus strain and antigenic properties. The knowledge gained from this research will increase understanding of the pathogenesis of influenza virus and provide new insights for the development of antiviral therapeutics for this emerging disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the Cytoskeleton in Collagen Phagocytosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL ADHESION; CYTOSKELETON; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; PERIODONTIUM; REMODELING; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Many high prevalence and serious diseases of liver, kidney, heart and gum tissues cause serious alterations to the structure and function of the tissue. These alterations cause the formation of excessive fibrous tissue, which prevents normal function from occuring. The purpose of this application is to determine how a type of cell called a fibroblast, contributes to excessive production of fibrous tissue. Specifically, this project will examine how fibroblasts normally break down fibrous tissue by a process called phagocytosis. The specific aim of this project is to determine how fibroblasts regulate the breakdown of collagen by phagocytosis. It is hoped that a better understanding of these processes could lead to the development of therapies that might help fibroblasts to reduce fibrosis in chronic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal mechanisms of muscle spasms after spinal cord injury.
Keywords-MotsClés: INTRACELLULAR RECORDING; MONOAMINE RECEPTORS; MOTONEURON; MUSCLE SPASMS; PERSISTENT CALCIUM CURRENTS; REFLEXES AND EPSP
Abstract-Résumé: A prerequisite for normal movement is that motoneurons in the spinal cord are sufficiently excitable to be able to produce sustained muscle contractions in response to command signals from the brain. Motoneuron excitability is facilitated by monoamines like norepinephrine and serotonin that come from the brainstem.  Spinal cord injury causes loss of brainstem monoamine innervation, which leads to dramatically decreased motoneuron excitability and muscle weakness. Yet in the weeks after injury, motoneurons undergo a remarkable recovery, becoming very excitable. While this aids in the recovery of residual motor function, it also leads to the development of debilitating muscle spasms because the motoneurons are not under normal descending inhibitory control. We recently found that this recovery of motoneuron excitability and development of spasms involves monoamine receptors that somehow become activated despite the loss of most monoamines. We hypothesize that this occurs because the monoamine receptors become constitutively active - spontaneously entering their active state without the binding of monoamines. We will test this hypothesis with a new class of drugs that selectively block constitutively active receptors, which may prove useful as novel antispastic medications. These studies are possible because of our unique in vitro rat spinal cord preparation, which for the first time allows study of chronic injury and spasticity with comprehensive pharmacological methods (spasticity in a dish). In summary, the proposed experiments evaluate a novel mechanism of spinal cord plasticity, involving constitutive receptor activity, that will have broad ranging implications to normal and pathological control of movement. Considering that we have recently shown that muscle spasms are caused by a similar cellular pathology in rats and humans, the proposed experiments will directly translate to understanding and treating spasticity in humans with spinal cord injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inborn errors of cobalamin and folate metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: COBALAMIN; FOLATE; HOMOCYSTEINE; INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM; METHYLMALONIC ACID
Abstract-Résumé: The overall theme of my research is the use of carefully collected clinical samples for the genetic and biochemical characterization of human inherited diseases involving two critical vitamins, folic acid and vitamin B12. With collaborators from around the world, we have identified all the known genes responsible for the inherited disorders of vitamin B12 metabolism and have discovered new steps in the pathway. We are in the process of characterizing the function of the products of these genes, constructing mouse models, and studying possible therapeutic approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: DNA Copy Number Variation in Li-Fraumeni Syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENETICS; COPY NUMBER VARIATION; LI-FRAUMENI SYNDROME; P53
Abstract-Résumé: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is a familial disorder characterized by the development of multiple cancers in children and young adults. These individuals carry a mutation in a gene, called p53. p53 normally behaves to protect cells from becoming cancerous. It does so by being able to recognize when DNA (the genome) of a cell is unstable, and then directing the cell to stop dividing or to kill itself. But people with LFS carry an abnormal copy of the p53 gene in every cell in their body, and if they lose or mutate the second normal copy in a cell, then that cell's DNA becomes unstable and the transformation of that cell to a cancer cell is initiated. We do not know what other genetic changes are required that determine what age or what type of cancer will develop in any particular LFS individual. However, using novel experimental techniques we have shown that there may be other abnormalities in a person's DNA that modify the effect of the mutant p53 gene. It appears that, in addition to the abnormal p53 gene, these people also inherit or acquire dramatic sub-microscopic structural alterations in their DNA in every cell in their body, and in cell's that become cancerous, these changes become even more pronounced. The studies outlined in this application seek to determine whether these genomic changes are a result of the p53 defect or are more universal. We will examine the DNA from blood of LFS patients, and compare these with children with a variety of cancers, their parents (to determine if the changes are inherited) and a healthy control population to answer these questions. This information would be enormously helpful in predicting who develops cancer, when and what cancers occur, as well lead to a better understanding of the underlying genetic basis of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms of Invasive Aspergillosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; ASPERGILLUS; BIOFILMS; CELLULAR BIOLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The mold Aspergillus fumigatus causes a severe, and often fatal pneumonia in patients whose immune systems do not function normally.  This project will identify the factors made by the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus that allow it to attach to and invade human lungs.  Through the identification of these molecules, we hope to develop new tests to diagnose this infection, as well as new treatments to help cure this disease

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of DOG-1/FANCJ in Fanconi Anemia Repair and Genome Stability
Keywords-MotsClés: C. ELEGANS GENETICS; CANCER SUSCEPTIBILITY; DNA REPAIR; FANCJ HELICASE; FANCONI ANEMIA; GENOME STABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Fanconi Anemia is a severe inherited disease leading to a wide range of clinical problems including predisposition to cancer.  Defects in any of thirteen genes can result in problems of DNA repair, specifically sensitivity to DNA interstrand cross-links.  Unrepaired DNA results in gross chromosomal rearrangements generating genomic instabilities that lead to tumour formation and cancer syndromes.  Initially the inherited defects express as blood anemias.  Even if the anemia can be treated by transfusion or marrow transplant, ultimately FA patients develop cancer.  Thus, treatment of the anemia is not sufficient to protect sufferers of this disease.  A better understanding of the repair defects leading to the gross genomic instabilities is needed to help prevent the progression to cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Aha1p in the Hsp90 Chaperone Cycle
Keywords-MotsClés: HSP90; MOLECULAR CHAPERONES; PROTEIN FOLDING
Abstract-Résumé: The heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) is a molecular chaperone that plays a central role in the development and progression of cancer.  Many of the regulatory changes that occur in cancer cells are mediated by Hsp90 and inhibition of Hsp90 by drugs has been demonstrated to halt the growth of cancer cells in a variety of systems.  The development of Hsp90 as a target in the treatment of cancer is hampered by the lack of understanding of its mechanism of action.  Hsp90 itself is regulated by a large number of proteins called co-chaperones but how these proteins influence Hsp90 activity is only beginning to be revealed.  This proposal is aimed at understanding how Hsp90 works on the molecular level and how its action changes the growth properties of cells that ultimately give rise to cancer cells. This research will allow for the potential of Hsp90 as a target in the treatment of human disease to be realized.

TitreApplicationTitle: Morphogenesis of fungal pathogens
Keywords-MotsClés: CAPSULE; FUNGAL DISEASE; GENE DELETION; SECRETION; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Infections of humans by opportunistic fungal pathogens are increasingly common due to the AIDS epidemic and the use of immunosuppressive therapies for procedures such as organ transplants. Diseases caused by fungi are difficult to treat because anti-fungal drugs have limited effectiveness and often have side effects. We are applying a combination of genomic and molecular genetic techniques to discover the mechanisms by which fungal pathogens cause disease. Specifically, we seek to understand how the fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans adapts to the host environment during the infection process. C. neoformans causes meningitis and is one of the most common fungal pathogens that infects AIDS patients. In addition, strains of C. neoformans are currently causing an outbreak of infections in otherwise healthy people in British Columbia with over 200 human cases reported. We plan to examine the mechanisms by which the fungus delivers disease-promoting molecules to its surface during infection.  By understanding the way that C. neoformans causes disease, we hope to discover new targets for the development of anti-fungal drugs. These drugs and the information that we obtain will help in treatment of fungal infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Glutamate in Bone Metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHOTONICS; BONE METASTASIS; BONE PAIN; GLUTAMATE; OSTEOLYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with advanced breast and prostate cancer frequently suffer from debilitating bone pain and fractures resulting from the spread of cancer to the bone (metastasis). In the bone, cancer cells commandeer normal bone cells and begin to degrade the fine architecture of bone, making it weaker and prone to fracture. Understanding the communication systems between bone cells and tumour cells is vital for the design of drugs that specifically target the devastating effects of cancer. The goal of this proposal is to study the role of one of the possible mediators of pain, namely glutamate. This molecule is an important transmitter of pain and hence, it may provide a link or an association between cancer cells and bone pain. Dr. Singh's team thinks that not only is glutamate responsible for much of this pain, it may even be important in the process of formation of the bone metastases. If this holds out true, then we will have a very useful target to control bone metastases and the pain it causes. There is presently a large array of well-studied pharmaceuticals that target this biological process, mostly used in the treatment of neurological diseases. We therefore have a rich source of potential compounds to screen and study for the purpose of bone metastasis treatment, foregoing the costly and time-consuming process of drug development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanosensitive ATP release in the lungs
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOSINE TRIPHOSPHATE RELEASE; AIRWAY EPITHELIA; ASTHMA; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; EXOCYTOSIS; TIRF MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Adenosine 5'-triphosphate (ATP) functions as extracellular signaling molecule in most tissues. In the lungs, ATP is a potent stimulator of surfactant secretion and modulator of muciliary clearance but sources and mechanisms of its release remain unknown. We have previously discovered, that non-lytic mechanical stimuli, such as cell stretch, cell deformation, shear stress and hypotonic swelling, result in calcium-dependent ATP secretion from lung epithelial cells. Our goal is to identify and characterize the mechanisms of such ATP release. Understanding these mechanisms may help to design new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of several diseases, including chronic bronchitis, cystic fibrosis and asthma.
