TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms underlying sympathetic sprouting in sensory ganglia after nerve injury
Keywords-MotsClés: GROWTH FACTORS; NOCICEPTIVE; PAIN; RECEPTORS; SYMPATHETIC; TRANSGENIC
Abstract-Résumé: In response to various types of pathologies including hypertension and diabetes, sympathetic neurons extend numerous aberrant fibers, which coincide with elevated levels of nerve growth factor (NGF).  Following peripheral nerve injury, sympathetic fibers also extend aberrant sprouts into damaged sensory ganglia.  In contrast to random sprouting seen in other diseased tissues, sympathetic axons invading the damaged sensory ganglia of adult mammals target individual sensory neurons, forming a basket-like plexus of fibers around cell bodies.  This phenomenon, referred to as sympatho-sensory sprouting, has been linked to the development of neuropathic pain conditions (including hyperalgesia and allodynia), which occur following nerve injury.  Importantly, destroying aberrant sympathetic axons that invade the affected sensory ganglia in both laboratory animals and humans can alleviate neuropathic pain.  In this investigation, we propose a new model for the cellular mechanisms that initiate and sustain the abnormal association between sympathetic axons and sensory neurons that is seen in adult mammals having nerve injury and neuropathic pain behaviors.  It is hoped that by gaining a greater understanding of this pathological condition, strategies may be designed to perturb the coupling between sympathetic fibers and sensory neurons induced by nerve injury, and thus counteract the subsequent onset of neuropathic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structures and Mechanisms of Proteins Involved in Parkinson's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: E3 LIGASE; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; PROTEIN FOLDING; THREE DIMENSIONAL STRUCTURE; UBIQUITYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Mutations in genes frequently result in disease. In particular, one form of Parkinson's Disease, autosomal recessive parkinsonism, is caused by missense mutations in the gene coding for parkin, resulting in single amino acid substitutions in the protein. Parkin is an enzyme responsible for the removal of other unwanted proteins from the cell. This is a complicated process requiring the involvement of other enzymes and substrates (ie. unwanted proteins) that must associate with the parkin protein.  The substitutions in parkin cause its function to be compromised. Our lab is examining the three-dimensional structure and function of parkin and its disease-causing substitutions to understand how mutations cause dysfunction of the protein.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reorganization of adult prefrontal cortex plasticity and function by neonatal hippocampus lesion - role of cortical alpha-1 adrenergic receptor signaling.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRENERGIC SIGNALING; ANIMAL MODEL; FEAR CONDITIONING; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing evidence suggests that many human neuropsychiatric conditions have their origins in the faulty development of brain before or around birth.  It has been shown that rat pups with defined damage to a brain region called hippocampus grow up to show many behavioral features analogous to those seen in human schizophrenia and other mental disorders, including cognitive deficits, sensorimotor abnormality and abnormal sensitivity to psychostimulants.  In search of neural mechanisms that may mediate behavioral changes in neonatal ventral hippocampus lesioned rats, we have observed several changes in the cortical alpha-1 adrenergic receptors and associated signalling pathways.  The goal of the present proposal is understand the specific role of alpha-1 adrenergic system in cognitive deficits of fear learning seen in the lesioned animals.  We will try to see if specific manipulations of signaling or plasticity can normalize cognitive changes in the lesioned animals.  We hope that our studies will lead to a better understanding of the  cognitive problems in schizophrenia and other developmental mental disorders.  Hopefully, they may aid in the developmental of novel therapeutic strategies in treating these disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of antibiotic resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC; ENZYME; GENE; INHIBITOR; PROTEIN STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Bacterial resistance to antibiotics is a significant problem facing the health care sector.  In the past, antibiotic resistance has been largely confined to bacterial infections associated with hospitals and other centers where intense antibiotic use provides the evolutionary pressure to select for resistant organisms.  However, resistance is now becoming a major issue for infections originating in the community.  Antibiotic resistance is therefore an acute problem that requires our attention.  The research we plan to undertake addresses the problem of resistance on 2 fronts.  First, by understanding the molecular basis of resistance, we will provide the necessary information to understand where resistance comes from and how we might overcome it.  Second, we will search for molecules that block resistance.  Such compounds could be leads towards new therapies that would extend the life of antibiotics currently in the clinic and imperiled by resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics of high density lipoproteins(HDL)
Keywords-MotsClés: CHOLESTEROL; GENETICS; HIGH DENSITY LIPOPROTEINS; LIPOPROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Heart attacks often have a genetic or familial basis. We have focused our work of the genetics of a common cardiovascular risk factor, high density lipoproteins (the "good" cholesterol. Taking advantage of large families in the province of Quebec, we have identified a new gene on chromosome 16 that is associated with HDL levels in man. This gene, called WWOX is well known in the cancer field, because it acts as a tumor-suppressing gene. A new role for this gene in the metabolism of cholesterol has recently been found. We will now explore the role of WWOX in HDL and in cardiovascular disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neonatal and Maternal Creatine Synthesis
Keywords-MotsClés: AMINO ACIDS; ORGAN METABOLISM
Abstract-Résumé: Creatine, in the form of creatine monohydrate, is well known to the public since it is used by athletes to increase muscle strength. However, we also synthesize creatine and obtain it from our food. We now know that the synthesis of creatine plays a crucial role in neonatal development, since infants who cannot synthesize this compound because of genetic defects, suffer from serious neurological symptoms. We propose to employ piglets, as a model system for human infants, to discover how neonatal animals synthesize creatine as well as how this process is controlled.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and physiological mechanisms of longevity in Mclk1+/- mutants
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING AND LIFESPAN; IMMUNE SYSTEM; INFECTION; MITOCHONDRIA; MOUSE MUTANTS; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: We are studying a strain of mouse mutants (Mclk1+/-) that live longer than normal mice. We have found that when we compare aged mutants to normal mice of the same age, the mutants appear physiologically younger, that is, they are healthier and more youthful. We have also found that these mutants have a stronger than normal immune reactivity against infectious agents, which seems to allow them to recover more completely from infection. Finally, we have found that these mutants might live longer than normal mice only under conditions that are not completely aseptic, as if their enhanced longevity was mostly due to their more efficient immune system. Our hypothesis is that sustaining infections throughout life, repeatedly or chronically, participates in creating the damage to tissues and organs that is central to aging. In the project that we are proposing we seek to test this hypothesis and to understand in detail the biological mechanisms that allow Mclk1+/- mice to have a particularly robust immune system. Understanding these mechanisms might allow us to learn how to strengthen the immune system of people as well.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms of Peroxisome Biogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; INHERITED DISORDERS; MODEL ORGANISMS; ORGANELLE BIOGENESIS; PEROXISOME; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Peroxisomes are ubiquitous intracellular organelles that perform a myriad of important biochemical functions, most notably in lipid metabolism and the detoxification of reactive oxygen species. The requirement of peroxisomes for normal human development and physiology is underscored by the lethality of the peroxisome biogenesis disorders, genetic diseases in which peroxisomes fail to assemble. As the peroxisome biogenic pathway has been highly conserved during evolution, we exploit yeast as a model system to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the peroxisome biogenesis disorders. Our research aims for a better understanding of the molecular bases of the peroxisome biogenesis disorders to provide for future rational genetic and/or therapeutic intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Peer abuse and adolescent health: A biopsychosocial perspective
Keywords-MotsClés: ABUSE BY PEERS; BEHAVIORAL GENETICS; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MENTAL HEALTH; PHYSICAL HEALTH; TWIN STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Peer abuse among children and adolescents is a severe problem in many countries around the world. Canadian data show that 30% of boys and 24% of girls are being beaten up, threatened, taunted, or humiliated by their peers. Although physical peer abuse tends to decline over the course of primary school, nonphysical forms of abuse such as rumor spreading or social exclusion actually increase with age, with a sizable peak between ages 11 and 15 when children experience puberty and enter high school. Previous research shows that peer abuse in the early primary school years is an important environmental stressor that significantly impairs the mental and physical health of the victims. However, the neurophysiological pathway underlying the association between peer abuse and physical and mental health problems is still not well understood. Moreover, little is known about the effect of long-term exposure to peer abuse on youngsters' physical and mental health as they reach adolescence. Finally, from a disease prevention perspective, it is crucial to identify protective factors that can mitigate the negative health consequences of peer abuse. To address these issues, the proposed research aims to: 1) assess the effect of peer abuse on mental and physical health problems after the transition from primary school to high school 2) investigate the neurophysiological pathway through which peer abuse impacts on adolescent physical and mental health, specifically the mediating role of HPA axis activity (cortisol) in the stress-disease linkage, 3) examine the potential exacerbating effect of genetic vulnerability and of prior peer abuse experiences during elementary school on the link between peer abuse, HPA axis activity, and health problems, 4) test the potential mitigating effect of social support resources on the link between peer abuse, HPA axis activity, and health problems, and 5) explore potential gender differences in regard to the previously described linkages.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of transposable elements on mammalian genomes
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; GENE REGULATION; MOUSE GENETICS; RETROVIRUSES; TRANSPOSABLE ELEMENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Sequencing of the human genome revealed that nearly half of our DNA is composed of over two million mobile genetic elements that inserted into our chromosomes throughout evolutionary history.  This surprising finding means that mobile elements, also termed "jumping DNA", have made major contributions to our genome.  Studies have shown that such elements can cause disease by inserting into (thereby inactivating) genes and by inducing gene deletions.  Mobile elements can also affect the regulation of nearby genes in a variety of ways.  The goal of this research is to understand how mobile elements in human and mouse affect various genetic processes, most notably gene regulation. Gaining a better appreciation of mobile elements in the human genome and how they affect our genes will help us to understand the basis of some human genetic diseases which are due to abnormal gene regulation, such as cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms underlying alphaB-crystallin function in multiple sclerosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHAB-CRYSTALLIN; AUTOIMMUNITY; EXPERIMENTAL ALLERGIC ENCEPHALOMYELITIS (EAE); MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NEUROIMMUNOLOGY; NEUROPROTECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease leading to central nervous system (CNS) degeneration in approximately 2.5 million people worldwide including 55,000-75,000 Canadians. Current therapies for MS are useful in some patients but they do not prevent progression of the disease and are ineffective in many patients signifying a vital need for new therapies. My research interest is to identify endogenous protective molecules and/or mechanisms in MS that suppress autoimmunity and CNS damage in order to prevent the progression of MS. This research has tremendous potential for discovering novel strategies to treat MS.   AlphaB-crystallin (alphaBC) is the most abundant gene found to be upregulated in early, acute MS plaques with localization to CNS glia. Free alphaBC is also detected in sera and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of all relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) patients but only a proportion of individuals with other neurological disorders (eg. epilepsy, cancer). We found that in mice with experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE), an animal model of MS, this crystallin acted as a "brake" on inflammation by attenuating the pro-inflammatory activity and CNS infiltration of leukocytes. Most significantly, recombinant human alphaBC (rhualphaBC) was therapeutic in ameliorating clinical EAE. However, the underlying mechanisms of rhualphaBC treatment, and the translation of the EAE results to MS, remain undefined.   This study aims to identify the immunological mechanism(s) underlying rhualphaBC therapy in EAE, as well as test the ability of this crystallin to suppress the activity of immune cells from MS patients. I will also investigate the role of alphaBC in the physiology of oligodendrocytes, the cells primarily targeted for death in MS. This research will advance our knowledge on the role of alphaBC in MS, as well as place us one step closer to determining whether this crystallin may have therapeutic potential in MS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular basis of tenascin elasticity and mechanotransduction
Keywords-MotsClés: ATOMIC FORCE MICROSCOPY; EHLERS-DANLOS SYNDROME; EXTRACELLULCAR MATRIX; MECHANOTRANSDUCTION; TENASCIN; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: Mechanical force is an important physiological signal. In living tissues, mechanical force is transmitted to cells through extracellular matrix, which serves as a structural scaffold for cells to adhere, migrate and differentiate. Tenascins are an important family of extracellular matrix proteins and play important roles in modulating cell-matrix interactions. Tenascins are expressed in adult tissues that are subject to heavy tensile loading or undergo remodeling. Deficiency and mutations in tenascin-X were found to link directly to one recessive form of Ehler-Danlos Syndrome, which is characterized by abnormal mechanical properties of skin tissues and joints. However, little is known about the molecular basis of tenascin mechanics and mechanotransduction. The long term goal of this proposal is to determine the molecular basis of the fine-tuned nanomechanics of tenascins and understand how tenascins function in mechanotransduction in connective tissues. Towards this goal, we will combine the state-of-the-art single molecule atomic force microscopy, protein engineering and cell biology techniques to investigate the mechanical architecture and design of tenascins. We will focus our studies on tenascin-C and tenascin-X. We will examine the mechanical phenotype of disease-causing point mutants of FnIII domains, and explore the possible mechanism linking point mutations to connective tissue disorder. We will examine the mechanical effect of the binding of various receptors and/or ligands to tenascins to test various hypotheses on the roles of tenascins in tissue modeling and connective tissue disorder. We will also develop novel tools to quantitatively probe the force experienced by tenascins in living cells. These proposed experiments will provide insights into molecular basis of tenascin mechanics and the role of tenascin-X in biomechanics of connective tissues. These insights will also offer useful information for tissue engineering strategies in skeletal repair.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the role of sterol transport by the oxysterol binding protein (OSBP) gene family in cellular cholesterol homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHOLESTEROL TRAFFICKING; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; GOLGI APPARATUS; OXYSTEROL BINDING PROTEINS; OXYSTEROLS; PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL 4-PHOSPHATE
Abstract-Résumé: Excess cholesterol is an important risk factor in heart disease and stroke, and is implicated in neurological and metabolic diseases.  These diseases all result from a defect in cholesterol removal from cells, which causes abnormal accumulation within specific cellular compartments.   Cholesterol accumulation, together with other factors, ultimately leads to the disease condition, for instance, in the cells lining the arteries of the heart.  How cholesterol is moved around the cell to prevent accumulation is not well understood but seems to involve cholesterol-binding proteins.  We are investigating one such group of proteins, termed oxysterol-binding proteins (OSBP), that bind cholesterol and transport it around the cell.  We propose to investigate how cholesterol is transported by two of these OSBPs, and what affect this has on cholesterol removal from cells and cell survival.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms orchestrating epithelial cell polarity
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; COLON CANCER; EPITHELIUM; INTESTINE; MORPHOLOGY; POLARITY
Abstract-Résumé: Epithelia, composed of epithelial cells, delimit the frontier between the external environment and the inside of complex organisms. Therefore, epithelial cells cover the surface of the body (e.g. skin) and line internal cavities of organs (found in the intestine, lung, liver, etc). An important function of epithelia is to selectively transport selected molecules to adjust the chemical composition of the different compartments of the body. This function relies on the asymmetric distribution of many cellular constituents, a structural organization referred to as epithelial polarity. The polarized architecture of epithelial cells is also required to maintain the homeostasis of epithelia as loss of epithelial polarity is associated with the progression of many cancers. Mechanisms linking the loss of cell polarity with cell division and invasion in the context of cancer are still poorly understood.  We have previously identified genes important for the establishment and maintenance of epithelial cell polarity. Mutations in these genes result in loss of tissue integrity similar to what is observed during cancer progression. The aim of our research program is to identify new genes regulating epithelial polarity and to understand how these genes control the normal physiology of epithelia and how alteration of their function contribute to cancer progression. By identifying genes involved in the control of epithelial polarity, our study will identify potential therapeutic targets to fight cancer of epithelial origin, which account for 80% of all human cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular genetic functional analysis of nuclear transactions focusing on developmental genome reorganization involving an RNAi pathway with an animal model system; a unicellular eukaryotic ciliated protozoan
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN REMODELING; EXPRESSION MICROARRAY; GENOME REORGANIZATION; GENOME SURVEILLANCE/SILENCING; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MODEL ORGANISM
Abstract-Résumé: The unicellular eukaryotic microorganisms, the ciliated protozoa, are recognized as exceptionally useful and important animal models for addressing basic biological questions with relevance for practical applications including human health. One well studied member of this group, Tetrahymena thermophila has typical eukaryotic biology. Its ultrastructure, cell physiology, development, biochemistry, genetics, and molecular biology have been extensively investigated. This organism displays a degree of cellular, structural, and functional complexity comparable to that of human and other metazoan cells. At the molecular level, Tetrahymena's rich and complex genome conserves a rich set of ancestral eukaryotic functions. In addition, Tetrahymena's special elaborations of certain basic eukaryotic mechanisms have facilitated discoveries opening the door to major new fields of fundamental research such as telomeres and telomerase, catalytic RNA and ribozymes, histone modification and epigenetic developmental mechanisms, and much more. The richness of Tetrahymena's biology makes it a genetic unicellular animal model organism "for all seasons." An impressive array of novel molecular genetic technologies places Tetrahymena at the forefront of experimental, in vivo functional genomics research, and complements a wealth of favorable biological features. The recent complete sequencing of the 104 MB somatic genome with the identification of many orthologs of human disease genes provides additional experimental opportunity for addressing basic biological questions of significance and with implications for human health. Our research will focus on molecular and biochemical studies of developmentally programmed gene reorganization and genome surveillance and silencing via an RNAi-dependent heterochromatin mechanism, as well as on gene expression and   proteomics to identify and analyze interesting and important proteins including orthologs of human disease genes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the BACE1 gene expression in the Alzheimer's Disease pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: AD PATHOGENESIS; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID PRECURSOR PROTEIN; BACE1; GEL SHIFTING ASSAY; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Deposition of amyloid beta protein (Abeta) in the brain is a central pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Proteolytic processing of beta-amyloid precursor protein (APP) at the beta site by the Beta site APP Cleaving Enzyme 1 (BACE1), the beta-secretase in vivo, is essential to generate Abeta. BACE1 gene expression is tightly regulated and it shows tissue specificity with its enzymatic activity mainly in central nervous system. Increased beta-secretase activity was reported in the cortex of AD patients and abnormal BACE1 gene regulation links vascular factors to AD. We propose to continue studying the molecular mechanisms of BACE1 gene regulation and its role in AD. Our working hypothesis is that transcriptional dysregulation of the human BACE1 gene plays an important role in the development of AD. This proposal seeks to further examine transcriptional regulation of the BACE1 gene and the mechanism underlying the 5'UTR regulating BACE1 translation initiation, as well as their role in the development of AD. Results from this proposal will thoroughly characterize the transcriptional regulation of the human BACE1 gene, and the role of abnormal gene transcription in the development of AD. It will provide much needed information regarding the cell signal transduction in APP processing and has an important pharmaceutical implication in AD therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) and multifactorial diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH DEFECTS; CANCER; FOLATE; GENES AND NUTRITION; HOMOCYSTEINE; METHYLENETETRAHYDROFOLATE REDUCTASE
Abstract-Résumé: Folic acid is an important B vitamin which is involved in several different common disorders, including neural tube defects (such as spina bifida), vascular disease and cancer. Other less well-characterized associations with folate deficiency include pregnancy complications and neuropsychiatric disorders. We had isolated an important gene in folate metabolism (MTHFR) and identified a mutation that increases risk for having a child with spina bifida and for developing vascular disease. In contrast, we found that this mutation decreased risk for colon cancer under certain conditions. Approximately 10 - 15% of North Americans and Europeans may be implicated, particularly if their folate intake is low. We have generated mice which serve as an animal model for MTHFR deficiency in human populations. In this application, we shall determine whether pregnant mice that carry this mutation, in combination with nutritional deficiencies, exhibit pregnancy complications and birth defects in their offspring. We shall examine the impact of this mutation on brain development and behaviour and determine whether there is a different response to infection in mice with MTHFR deficiency. Since food is fortified with folate in Canada and the US, we shall repeat some of the afore-mentioned studies in mice fed very high levels of folic acid. Our work will have an impact on prevention and modulation of common diseases that are influenced by genetic and nutritional disturbances in folate metabolism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Biology of Calcium Sensing Systems
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM SIGNALING; LYMPHOCYTE ACTIVATION; NMR; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Non-scientific Abstract As the most abundant mineral in the body, calcium has long been recognized as vital to the formation and maintenance of living systems.  Bones, where calcium is stored, continuously release the mineral into the system where it plays a central role as an intracellular messenger.  To make use of this unbreakable and toxic messenger, cells have developed sophisticated and clever mechanisms with many components that can sense, magnify, and transmit the calcium signal.  Physiological outcomes of these calcium signaling processes include fertilization, proliferation, development, learning and memory, contraction and secretion.  In order to understand how the biological systems function in response to the calcium signal, we first need to understand how biological components sense the calcium signal to make use of the information.  We employ molecular and structural experimental tools that enable us to visualize three-dimensional atomic structures of calcium sensing components in living cells, which are typically proteins belonging to a well-known protein family that share the same calcium binding motif so-called EF-hand.  In this proposal, we focus on newly-identified calcium ion sensor proteins called STIM1 and STIM2. These proteins play a crucial role in immune response and disruption of their function could lead to an immune disease as seen in severe combined immune disease (SCID) patients. The proposed studies will contribute to our understanding of how lymphocytes respond to foreign objects in human body. Deeper understanding of these calcium sensing systems may also provide insights into therapeutic approaches for those patients with autoimmunity or inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Circumventricular Organs - New CNS sites for the Regulation of Energy Homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; CIRCUMVENTRICULAR ORGANS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; FOOD INTAKE; METABOLISM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: We have identified new brain regions which may play critical roles in the regulating food intake, metabolism and thus body weight. These structures known as the circumventricular organs are unique in that they are the only regions of the brain with the ability to sense multiple satiety signals including glucose, leptin, amylin and many other signaling molecules as they lack the blood brain barrier. Our proposal outlines studies which will describe the roles of two of these circumventricular organs in the integrated regulation of energy metabolism. These studies will potentially provide important new targets for the treatment of obesity and other metabolic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cell signaling and tissue growth by Nemo and Hipk protein kinases
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL PATTERNING; DROSOPHILA SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; HOMEODOMAIN-INTERACTING PROTEIN KINASE; KINASE CASCADES; NEMO-LIKE KINASE; WNT SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: The information needed for a cell to properly function is encoded in its genes. Therefore, normal development of a multicellular organism requires regulation of gene activity. This occurs through proteins, known as transcriptional regulators, that turn genes on or off. The focus of the proposed project is two specific protein kinases and their role in controlling the activity of a proteins involved in regulating genes.  Protein kinases can modify their target proteins (substrates) and change their function or inhibit their activity.  In the Verheyen lab we study the Nemo kinase and the Homeodomain-interacting protein kinase (Hipk) in the fruit fly Drosophila.  Both Nemo and Hipk are conserved across many species including humans, and disruptions of their activity can result in profound alterations in cell growth and tissue and organ development. Because of their conserved functions, findings from studies in fruit flies will provide invaluable insight into the role these proteins play in higher organisms such as humans.  The harmful effects on growth and tissue patterning that occur when Hipk and Nemo are disrupted are likely due to unregulated substrate activity, which would normally be modulated by Nemo and Hipk.  Our lab has already identified a number of substrates, and in the next granting period we will expand on these findings as well as begin to examine the regulation of Nemo and Hipk kinase activity.  Some of the known target proteins are themselves implicated in cancers in humans, and thus the understanding of their regulation can provide insight into management and prevention of malignancies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rôle des interactions cellulaires avec la matrice dans la physiopathologie de l'épithélium intestinal humain
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE ET MOLECULAIRE; CANCERS COLO-RECTAUX; DIFFERENCIATION; EXPRESSION DES GENES; FONCTIONS EPITHELIALES; INTEGRINES; PROLIFERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Les cellules epitheliales qui tapissent la paroi interne de la cavite intestinale sont maintenues en place par le biais de molecules d'adhesion et de recepteurs membranaires qui les rattachent a la matrice extracellulaire. Les integrines sont les principaux recepteurs impliques dans ces interactions avec la matrice extracellulaire. Les integrines peuvent regulariser une multitude de fonctions cellulaires incluant la migration, la proliferation et la differenciation.   Le present programme de recherche vise a identifier les mecanismes cellulaires et moleculaires de la regulation de l'expression des genes par la matrice extracellulaire chez les cellules epitheliales de l'intestin humain en conditions normales et en conditions pathologiques.  Dans ce projet, nous analyserons plus particulierement les interactions entre differentes formes moleculaires de l'integrine a6b4 que nous avons identifiees au cours des dernieres annees chez les cellules epitheliales intestinales et les laminines. Des alterations importantes des formes de l'integrine alpha6beta4 sont observees particulierement au cours de la progression des cancers colo-rectaux.  La realisation de ce programme de recherche permettra d'elucider les mecanismes regulateurs de la proliferation et de la differenciation en reponses aux interactions cellulaires mediees par alpha6beta4 en conditions normales et pathologiques. L'identification des molecules impliquees et de leurs voies effectrices represente une etape essentielle pour la caracterisation d'outils diagnostiques et l'identification de cibles d'interet therapeutique.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of beta-amyloid peptides in regulating the function/survival of central cholinergic neurons and its implications in Alzheimer's disease pathology
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BETA AMYLOID PEPTIDES; CHOLINERGIC NEURONS; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROPROTECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by a gradual loss of memory followed by deterioration of higher cognitive functions such as language, calculation and judgment. The neuropathological features associated with AD include abnormal extracellular deposits of amyloid beta (Ab) peptide in neuritic plaques, intracellular accumulation of filamentous structures termed neurofibrillary tangles and loss of neurons (nerve cells) in selected regions of the brain. Accumulated evidence indicates that deposition of Ab peptides may trigger the loss of neurons and subsequent development of AD pathology. Among vulnerable neurons, the basal forebrain neurons which use acetylcholine (ACh) as a neurotransmitter (chemical messenger) and play an important role in learning and memory processing are known to be most severely affected in the AD brain. However, very little is known about why these neurons are preferentially vulnerable in AD pathology. We have earlier reported that short-term exposure of rat brain slices to Ab peptides can markedly inhibit ACh release from the hippocampus and cortex - the regions which receive inputs from the forebrain cholinergic neurons, whereas long-term exposure to the peptides can lead to the loss of cultured forebrain cholinergic neurons. However, the cellular mechanisms by which Ab peptide can cause the inhibition of ACh release or the loss of forebrain cholinergic neurons remain unclear. To address this issue our laboratory is currently investigating how various Ab-related peptides can mediate their effects on the basal forebrain cholinergic neurons in normal rat brain as well as in mice that have been genetically modified to produce excess Ab peptides. This study will determine the underlying basis of functional interrelationships between Ab peptides and brain cholinergic system and will define whether inhibition of Ab production can prevent the onset and/or retard the progression of AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the balance between repair and regeneration in skeletal muscle
Keywords-MotsClés: FIBRO/ADIPOGENIC PRECURSORS; MUSCLE DEGENERATIVE DISEASE; MYOGENIC PRECURSORS; PROSPECTIVE PURIFICATION; REGENERATION VS REPAIR; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Tissue damage can lead to complete regeneration and the return of the tissue to full functionality, or can be followed by the generation of of a scar that ensures the continuity of a  tissue but does not restore, and often impedes, its function. Several factor affect the balance between these two processes. For example, aged tissues are more likely to be repaired via scar formation than young tissues. Chronic disease and inflammation are well known to eventually lead to scar formation and failure to regenerate. The precise mechanisms determining whether regeneration or scar formation predominates are unknown, but they are likely to act at the level of the progenitor cells involved. However, while the progenitors involved in regeneration have been identified and studied in depth, little is know about those involved in scar formation. Our laboratory has recently identified such progenitors from skeletal muscle. Here, we propose to take advantage of this advance to investigate the mechanisms with which their activity is regulated in aging, disease and inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: In Vivo Studies to define the Role of Progranulin Mutations in Frontotemporal Dementia
Keywords-MotsClés: DEMENTIA; MOUSE MODELS; NEURODEGENERATION; PROGRANULIN
Abstract-Résumé: Much has already been learned from established mouse models of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) that are known to be caused by mutation of the MAPT gene, the first genetic form of FTD identified. In 2006, mutations were identified in the Progranulin gene (PGRN) that cause a common type of familial FTD associated with a specific pattern of protein aggregation in the brain (FTLD-U). These PGRN mutations result in significantly decreased levels of progranulin protein which appears to be an important growth factor for brain cells (neurons). My laboratory has an established track record of excellence in both experimental therapeutics, neurogenetics, and the generation of genetically-modified mouse models of human neurologic disease. We will examine the effects of modulating progranulin levels in cell culture systems and in the whole mouse brain. We have developed a mouse model of human FTLD-U by producing mice that can be selectively induced to lack the PGRN gene that makes progranulin in specific cells or at specific times in development. These mice represent the first established conditionally-targeted PGRN animal, are a critical tool to study the function of progranulin in the brain, and may be a model of this common type of hereditary dementia. The development of such a model will be crucial for future studies examining how the loss of progranulin causes the dysfunction and death of neurons in FTD, and for the eventual development of treatments for this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms and regulation of IgE-dependent mast cell activation
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGY; ASTHMA; IGE; INFLAMMATION; MAST CELL; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Allergic diseases such as asthma, rhinitis or atopic dermatitis have reached epidemic proportions worldwide. Mast cells play a central role in allergic inflammation. This is because allergen binding on mast cells initiates a cascade of signaling events leading to excessive secretion of biologically potent mast cell mediators. Accordingly, understanding of mechanisms involved in controlling mast cell mediator secretion is essential for the development of effective therapy for the treatment of allergy and asthma. We recently identified a novel molecule, Rcan1 which was not previously associated with mast cells, as a potent endogenous inhibitor of mast cell activation. However, how Rcan1 inhibits allergen-induced mast cell mediator secretion is still unclear. In this application, we will use biochemical and genetic approaches (1) to investigate the molecular targets of Rcan1 in mast cells, (2) to investigate how Rcan1 is regulated in mast cells and (3) to determine the significance of Rcan1 in the development of asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunobiology of bacterial superantigens
Keywords-MotsClés: MHC CLASS II MOLECULES; STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS; STREPTOCOCCUS PYOGENES; SUPERANTIGENS; T CELL RECEPTORS; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal is designed to study a group of bacterial toxins produced from the notorious human bacterial pathogen Streptococcus pyogenes. This project will evaluate the role that superantigen toxins play in the development of severe disease such as bacteremia and Kawasaki diesease, and colonization of the bacteria in animal models of tonsil infection. The proposal is also focused on understanding the mechanism by how these superantigen toxins bind to important proteins (called T cell receptors) on the surface of white blood cells - this binding causes the white blood cells to over-react which can result in a patient developing shock. In this proposal, we are also developing drug inhibitors which will bind and neutralize the activity of these toxins.

TitreApplicationTitle: Drosophila models of human obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOR; CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM; DROSOPHILA; GENETICS; LIPIDS; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: In the past decade, obesity has been recognized as an increasing threat to the global health of children and adults.  This has prompted considerable efforts to understand the pathogenesis of obesity in order to develop potential treatments.  While lifestyle (i.e. diet and exercise) are known to play an important role in maintaining normal body weight it is increasingly clear that genes also play a role in determining who is at risk of becoming obese and developing obesity-related disorders.  However, to date, only a handful of genes have been identified and many more remain to be discovered.  In this proposal, we will describe how we will use powerful genetic approaches available in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, to search for genes that regulate normal body weight.  We will also determine whether these genes control body weight by affecting appetite, feeding behavior or how fat is processed within the body.  In the long-term, we will detemin whether the genes we identify in the fruit fly also play a similar role in maintaining body weight in mice and humans and, finally, how we will use our fly models to screen for new treatments for obesity and its numerous life-threatening complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Psychosocial Demands and Cardiovascular Risk
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR RISK; PSYCHOSOCIAL; SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Individuals lower in socioeconomic status (SES) are more likely to get sick, to have more severe illnesses, and to die from diseases, compared to higher SES individuals. This project seeks to understand how daily life experiences contribute to these relationships.  We will describe the types of daily life experiences low SES individuals face- for example, whether lower SES individuals experience more competing demands whereby responsibilities in one domain spillover and conflict with responsibilities in other domains.  In turn, we will examine whether these daily life experiences are associated with biological markers of risk for cardiovascular disease.  Second, we will investigate whether some individuals have characteristics that protect them from adverse social environments.  For example, certain low SES individuals may believe that there are ways in which even difficult environments can be beneficial, and we will test whether these beliefs buffer individuals from poor biological outcomes.  The knowledge gained from this study will increase our understanding of how social factors such as SES shape biology, with the potential for informing future interventions aimed at maximizing health across individuals in our society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular control of iron homeostasis in the central nervous system
Keywords-MotsClés: FERROXIDASES; FREE RADICALS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; IRON; KNOCKOUT AND MUTANT MICE; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Iron is essential for life.  It plays an important role in the functioning of enzymes required for a whole host of cellular functions.  However, iron can also generate toxic free radicals that can damage cells if it is not properly handled. Therefore, although iron accumulation results in free-radical-mediated cell death, lack of cellular iron can also lead to loss of cell viability. In the central nervous system (CNS) which consists of the brain and spinal cord, iron is required for the survival of neurons. It is also required for myelination which is essential for proper conduction of nerve impulses. How iron from the circulation is delivered to different cell types in the nervous system is still not fully understood.  A number of molecules that transport and detoxify iron are involved in the safe delivery of iron from one cell type to another.  The aim of this proposal is to study the role of an iron transporter called ferroportin, two ferroxidases called hephaestin and ceruloplasmin, and an iron binding protein called lipocalin 2, in iron trafficking in the nervous system.  This work has important implications for various neurodegenerative diseases in which iron accumulation occurs as well as for neuropathies that affect peripheral nerves.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of epigenetic regulation and hematopoietic lineage specification
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETIC REGULATION; GENE EXPRESSION; HEMATOPOIESIS; HUMAN BONE MARROW; LEUKEMIA; MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: The abnormal expression of genes can induce diseases including cancers. Abnormal gene expression frequently results from gene mutations or chromosomal translocations but it can also result from the environment of the gene. Indeed, the chromatin, which is composed of DNA and proteins required for the DNA compaction in cell nucleus, can be influenced by the sub-nuclear environment and adopts variable organizations (chromatin organizations). The chromatin organization can be favourable or refractory to gene expression and thus, alteration of the chromatin organization can induce diseases. If we understand how and what determine the chromatin organization, we will be able to find ways to change this organization and prevent abnormal gene expression. For this study, we are characterizing the BETA-globin genes, which are expressed in red (erythroid) cells. The material that we are using includes transgenic mice containing the human BETA-globin genes (mouse model) and human bone marrow cells. We will try to define the 'normal' chromatin organization of human BETA-globin genes. The chromatin organization of a gene can be variable in different types of cells. Indeed, genes like the BETA-globin genes are expressed only in specific tissues but not in others. Then, their expression in unwanted cell types (tissues) can induce cell death and or diseases. Little is known about mechanisms involved in gene repression in cells not expressing the BETA-globin genes. This will be investigated. Thus, this study will provide information concerning the influence of the chromatin organization on globin gene expression and repression in non-erythroid cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of GATA transcription factors in the heart
Keywords-MotsClés: MOLECULAR AND CELL BIOLOGY; PROTEIN CHARACTERIZATION; TRANSCRIPTION / SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS / HEART DEVELOPMENT; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; TRANSGENIC MICE / CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE / HEART FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: In human, cardiac abnormalities represent 25% of congenital malformations, and heart failure is the leading cause of death in industrialized countries.  Unfortunately, the cellular and molecular mechanisms controlling cardiac growth and differentiation remain poorly understood.  In human and other mammals, the heart is the first functional organ but its development into the mature four-chamber heart is a complex multistep process involving different cell types.  The establishment and maintenance of the cardiac phenotype require the activation of cardiac-specific genes in a tightly regulated temporal and spatial manner.  This process is governed by the combinatorial action of a limited number of regulatory proteins known as cell-restricted as well transcription factors.  Transcription factor GATA-4 has emerged as a key regulator of heart development.  Heterozygote mutations in the human GATA4 gene cause congenital heart disease.  Our studies are aimed at understanding the essential role of GATA-4 at various stages of heart development and in different cardiac cells.  In addition to its crucial role in the embryonic heart, GATA-4 appears to be essential for post-natal myocyte survival and adaptive response to various stressors.  Since heart failure is caused by loss of myocytes and impaired responsiveness of the remaining cardiac cells, the GATA-4 pathway may represent a novel target for cardioprotection.  We propose to define, at the molecular level, the mechanisms responsible for GATA-4 action in the developing and postnatal heart. Our studies also suggest that another member of the family, GATA-5 is essential for heart valve formation and may be a congenital heart disease causing genes. We propose to further analyze the role of GATA-5 in the heart and its interactions with other heart regulators.

TitreApplicationTitle: Influences of homing endonucleases on gene structure and function
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE REGULATION; GENOME STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION; HOMING ENDONUCLEASES; INTERRUPTED OPEN READING FRAME; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; PROTEIN-DNA INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: A significant fraction of the genome of any organism is composed of mobile genetic elements, discrete units of nucleic acid that promote their own spread within and between genomes. Commonly referred to as junk or selfish DNA, mobile elements have profound influences on evolution by promoting genomic rearrangements that can be both beneficial and deleterious to organisms. Mobile elements can impact on human health in a number of was, by inserting into genes and disrupting function, by influencing expression of genes, and by promoting dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes among pathogenic bacteria. The goal of our research is to determine how mobile elments regulate their activity so that they do not effect genomic instability. Results from our research will lead to a greater understanding of the dynamic interplay between mobile elements and genomes, and identify cellular mechanisms that regulate the spread of mobile elements to minimize deleterious effects on gene structure and function. In particular, research proposed in this applications deals with insertion of mobile elements into the genes for ribonucleotide reductase and topoisomerase, key targets of chemotherapeutic agents. We are in a position to provide critical insight into the molecular mechanisms by which these proteins function, with potential benefits in improving the mode of action of chemotherapeutic drugs targeted against the proteins.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Post-stroke neuroplasticity and neuroprotection: impact of prolonged hypothermia treatment.
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOR; HISTOPATHOLOGY; HYPOTHERMIA; NEUROPLASTICITY; NEUROPROTECTION; STROKE (ISCHEMIA AND HEMORRHAGE)
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke devastates 50,000 Canadians each year. The aim of my research proposal is to evaluate the protective effects of mild therapeutic hypothermia (reduction in body temperature) on the brain damange caused by stroke. Hypothermia is a promising neuroprotective (cell saving) treatment that is used in cardiac arrest survivors and has much potential for stroke victims. Specifically, I will determine how effective hypothermia is following several types of stroke (e.g., ischemia, hemorrhage) and I will study how cooling the brain affects the brain's natural response to injury. Various neuroplasticity mechanisms are set in motion by brain injury. For instance, synaptogensis is an increase in the number of connections between existing cells. Such responses are stimulated after stroke and act to repair the brain to improve behavioral recovery. I wish to determine whether cooling the brain affects its natural neuroplasticity response (e.g., to impede it). Thus, I will use rat models of stroke and induce brief to prolonged cooling periods, as would be used clinically, to investigate how hypothermia affects brain injury and neuroplasticity. These findings should improve treatment choices in clinical trials of hypothermia for stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Facilitating access to health data for research and planning in light of laws and ethical norms
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOBANKS; CONFIDENTIALITY; CONSENT; DATA QUALITY; DATABASES; ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORDS; PERSON-LEVEL DATA; PRIVACY; PROCEDURAL & STATISTICAL; REGISTRIES; RESEARCH GOVERNANCE; SAFEGUARDS
Abstract-Résumé: Our objective is to identify the conditions under which scientifically valid health research using data and biological samples may proceed using: the evolving Canadian interoperable electronic health record system; registries, biobanks, and longitudinal cohort studies; and archived pathology samples and records. Through a series of evidence-informed deliberative dialogues, we will identify areas of consensus and divergence on the topics relevant to key conditions of use: (a) the role of consent and privacy, (b) models of governance, and (c) necessary safeguards. Deliberations will be grounded in real-world research scenarios and informed by relevant ethical, legal, philosophical, technical, and empirical literature. Following the dialogues, findings and policy recommendations will be fed back to the affected stakeholders for their comments. A series of workshops will be prepared for the annual meetings of the associations of research ethics board chairs, ethicists, privacy commissioners, public health researchers, health services and policy researchers, and informatics researchers. The evidence syntheses will be published as a book and the results of the dialogues in peer-reviewed journals.  Through our literature syntheses, legal analysis, and dialogues, we will be well positioned to make statements about what an ideal framework for research use of electronic health information ought to be and the values and principles that should be taken into consideration when making policy decisions around use of personal information and biosamples for health research. By working closely with policy makers at all stages, we expect to have an impact on future legislative and policy development, including future revisions to the TCPS.  This work will be ground-breaking internationally, and could make Canada a leader in the use of research data to improve the health care system and the population's health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Schizophrenia as a genomic disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: 22Q11 DELETION SYNDROME; GENETIC SYNDROME; GENETICS; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a serious psychiatric illness that affects 1 in 100 people.  In schizophrenia, 1 in 100 people have a genetic syndrome called 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome (22qDS) that is associated with a 22q11.2 deletion (piece missing from a region on one chromosome 22) that can be confirmed with a blood test. We are international leaders in the study of adults with 22qDS. Individuals with 22qDS have a high (about 1 in 4) chance of developing schizophrenia. This makes 22qDS an especially valuable group to better understand genetic factors that lead to schizophrenia. We will perform detailed clinical assessments and laboratory investigations comparing two groups: 100 adults with schizophrenia and 100 adults with no psychotic illness, all of whom have 22q11.2 deletions.  We will use advanced genetic techniques to find changes in the genetic sequence and architecture that interact with the 22q11.2 deletion to cause schizophrenia.  Results from this study should help us to understand more about the genetic mechanisms that predispose to schizophrenia in the general population.  Improved knowledge about these genetic changes will help us understand the brain changes that lead to schizophrenia.  Eventually this new knowledge will help us to develop improved treatments for those who suffer with this serious illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the ERK/MAPK cascade function during mouse development
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR DIFFERENTIATION; EMBRYONIC DEVELOPMENT; ERK/MAPK CASCADE; MOLECULAR GENETICS; PLACENTA PATHOLOGIES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The development of a normal placenta is essential for fetal growth and survival, and defects in its development are associated with common problems affecting the course of human pregnancy. The abnormal differentiation of the trophoblast cells that are involved in the implantation of the embryo and in the establishment of the maternal blood flow is linked to preeclampsia and, if severe, may affect fetal growth resulting in intrauterine growth restriction. By producing and analyzing Map2k1 and Map2k1 Map2k2 compound mouse mutants, we have established the essential and unique role played by MAP2K1 and MAP2K2 during placenta formation. Both MAP2K proteins are required for the normal response of the cell to specific signals during the formation of the placenta. However, they do not seem to be involved in the same processes. MAP2K1 is essential for the normal growth of the labyrinthine region of the placenta whereas MAP2K2 seems to be required for the differentiation of the syncytiotrophoblasts in absence of one Map2k1 allele. Both type of mutations are characterized by the underdevelopment and hypovascularization of the labyrinthine region leading to a non-functional placenta and the death of their progenies. The molecular mechanisms responsible for the specific functions of MAP2K1 and MAP2K2 are poorly understood. This application is aimed at elucidating the unique role(s) of Map2k1 and Map2k2 genes in signal transduction during embryonic and extra-embryonic development, as well as identifying the mechanisms involved in the specificity of signal transduction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chromatin Regulation of Estrogen-Mediated Transcription in Hormone-Dependent Cancer. / Rôle de la chromatine dans la régulation des gènes dépendants des récepteurs de l'oestrogène.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; CHROMATIN REMODELLING; GENE EXPRESSION; HORMONE-DEPENDENT CANCERS; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; PROMOTER
Abstract-Résumé: Estrogens are physiologically important steroid hormones that regulate growth and differentiation in a broad range of target tissues including the mammary gland, uterus and ovary. The biological effects of estrogens are mediated through two forms of nuclear estrogen receptors (ER) named ERalpha and beta which control gene expression in conjunction with coregulatory proteins as ligand-regulated transcription factors. Inside cells, genes that are regulated by ER are assembled into a nucleoprotein structure known as chromatin that restricts the ability of these genes to be activated by ER and their coregulatory proteins. One of the roles of ER and their coregulatory proteins is to overcome the repressive effects of chromatin, allowing the genes to be appropriately activated. Although we understand the basic scheme of how estrogens control gene expression, we do not yet comprehend fully how ER and its coregulatory proteins work at chromatin level. The overall objective of this proposal is to achieve a better understanding of the role of chromatin architecture and its biochemical composition in transcriptional activation of ER-regulated genes. We will use molecular and cellular biology techniques in conjunction with biochemical tools that will help to unveil the functions of chromatin structure in gene expression. Together, these results should provide significant insight relevant to the understanding of the exploitation of ER and their coregulatory proteins as targets for drug therapy in human diseases, such as breast and ovarian cancers.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE DE PARKINSON; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Pathophysiology of Parkinson's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; MOTOR CORTEX; MOVEMENT DISORDERS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the commonest neurodegenerative diseases and is due to dysfunction of parts the brain known as the basal ganglia.  Advances in the understanding of the connections of the basal ganglia have led to new treatment of PD such as deep brain stimulation (DBS).  However, the functions of the basal ganglia, how PD affects the brain and how DBS leads to improvement in PD remain poorly understood.  In the first experiment, we will determine how the part of the brain that directly mediates movement, known as the motor cortex, is affected in PD.  In the second experiment, we will examine how movement affects the activities of the basal ganglia by direct recording of electrical activities from DBS electrodes implanted in the basal ganglia in PD patients.  We will determine if the basal ganglia works by oscillating at different speeds and if DBS works by changing this oscillation.  In the third experiment, we will determine how stimulation of the basal ganglia changes the surface of the brain known as the cortex by detailed analysis of electrical brain rhythms.  How DBS affect the ability of the brain to adapt to changes will be examined in the fourth experiment. These experiments will result in much greater understanding of the functions of the basal ganglia, how the basal ganglia are abnormal in PD and how DBS works.  This will advance our knowledge of PD, and may lead to improved treatment for PD patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulating Excitability in Spinal Sympathetic Preganglionic Neurons: focus on nitric oxide and electrotonic coupling
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ELECTRONIC COUPLING; HYPERTENSION; IN VITRO SLICE PREPARATION; NITRIC OXIDE; PREGANGLIONIC NEURONS; RODENT; SPINAL SYMPATHETIC OUTFLOW
Abstract-Résumé: Persistently high blood pressure is a prevalent problem among the population, also common in obesity, ultimately posing major risk factors for stroke, myocardial infarction and kidney failure. Identifying causes is difficult, so efforts to reduce blood pressure over the long term have become a clinical objective. In humans, as in experimental models of chronic hypertension, over activity in the sympathetic nerves to many organs (e.g. kidney) and to blood vessels suggests that the brain cells forming these pathways are "hyperactive", possibly indicating reduction in the "brake" that controls the sympathetic nervous system. Designing therapeutic approaches to target selectively these components of the nervous system would seem a reasonable goal. Achieving this objective needs more a focused approach based on an understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms that underlie the principles governing sympathetic nerve activity. To this end, we use a rodent model to acquire information specifically from the spinal neurons that give rise to the sympathetic outflow pathways to the cardiovascular system, kidneys and adrenal glands. We are particularly interested in nitric oxide (NO), a gas-like molecule that is best known for its actions to reduce angina when taken under the tongue. NO is made in sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord, and our preliminary data indicate that it may serve as the "brake" to control sympathetic nerve activity. Assessing how this molecule works selectively on these spinal neurons may aid in the design of a drug that could target these neurons selectively, much as nitroglycerin does for the heart, and have a therapeutic value in the long term control of hypertension.

TitreApplicationTitle: Overcoming Antibiotic Resistance:  Targeting the AmpC beta-lactamase induction pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC DRUG RESISTANCE; DRUG DISCOVERY; ENZYMOLOGY; GLYCOBIOLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Our most safe and effective antibiotics are the Beta-lactams; however, the protection they offer against infection is being eroded by the increasing prevalence of bacterial pathogens expressing AmpC beta-lactamase.  AmpC is found in many bacteria including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a significant opportunistic pathogen of humans that is associated with considerable morbidity and mortality in intensive care units (ICU) and cystic fibrosis patients. Capable of hyper-producing AmpC in response to beta-lactam exposure, P. aeruginosa rapidly develops clinical resistance to most available beta-lactams; thus, there is a need to better understand how P. aeruginosa regulates ampC gene expression in response to beta-lactams, and to develop alternative approaches to surmount ampC mediated antibiotic resistance.  Production of AmpC depends on the activity of three proteins:  AmpR, NagZ and AmpG.  Exposure to beta-lactams prompts these proteins to turn on AmpC production to destroy the antibiotic and promote bacterial survival. Because AmpC itself is highly resistant to clinically available inhibitors, we are examining the structural and functional biology of NagZ, AmpR and AmpG and using this information to guide the development small molecules that block their function. We hypothesize that blocking the function of these proteins with small molecules will increase the efficacy of beta-lactams against bacteria that harbor ampC.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: Control of enteropathogenic Escherichia coli virulence by the Cpx envelope stress response
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL DIARRHEA; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; MICROARRAY ANALYSIS OF GENE EXPRESSION; MICROBIAL GENETICS & MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MICROBIAL PATHOGENESIS; VIRULENCE DETERMINANT EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Microbial antibiotic resistance is rapidly becoming wide spread, making infections that were once easily treated difficult, or impossible, to eradicate.  Our need for new therapies is more pressing than ever.  In order to develop new therapies that short-circuit the infectious process, a detailed understanding of how bacteria cause infection is required.  To cause infection, microbes must produce specialized factors called virulence determinants after entering our bodies.  For example, diarrhea-causing Escherichia coli must assemble hair-like structures called pili on the bacterial cell surface that allow adherence to intestinal cells.  Next, a more intimate attachment is formed between human and bacterial cells and a bacterial secretion system injects virulence determinants directly into intestinal cells.  This ultimately causes diarrhea and the symptoms of E. coli infection.  Bacteria use special regulatory proteins or pathways to control expression of virulence determinants so that they are only produced when needed (i.e. inside our bodies).  My lab has evidence that one such regulatory pathway, the Cpx envelope stress response, is capable of shutting off the pili and secretion system required for E. coli to cause diarrhea.  This effect is also observed in other microbes that cause diarrhea.  Accordingly, it is our hypothesis that multiple disease-causing bacteria use the Cpx response to shut down expression of virulence determinants when they are not needed or are detrimental to the microbe.  Our goal is to characterize the mechanism by which the Cpx response accomplishes this task in E. coli, with the hope that this knowledge will be exploited in the future to develop new treatments for infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: The neural substrates of human decision making: A component analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; DECISION MAKING; FRONTAL-EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; HUMAN; LESION METHODS; REWARD
Abstract-Résumé: We make many decisions, large and small, every day, yet know very little about the brain processes that underlie these decisions. What brain mechanisms allow us to calculate the value of possible options, and to weigh that value against the costs (such as time and effort) of a particular course of action? This research will help to answer these questions, by examining how specific regions within the brain's frontal lobes are involved in the basic building blocks of decision making. This work is done with the help of patients who have suffered injury to specific parts of the frontal lobes, and so also provides a better understanding of why such patients have problems with motivation, judgment, and decision making in their everyday lives. In addition, this research has implications for understanding the brain basis of common psychiatric conditions that are characterized by poor decisions, such as drug addiction.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of sumoylation in mitochondrial signaling and function.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; CELL SIGNALING; MITOCHONDRIA; MITOCHONDRIAL DYNAMICS; PROTEOME; SUMO
Abstract-Résumé: The mitochondria are found in all cells of the body, and are often considered the "furnace" of the cell where sugar and fat are broken down.  This process requires the oxygen that we breath and results in the production of energy that is used in all of cellular functions, from the production of hormones, to cell division, brain function and muscle contraction.  Our lab asks questions about how the mitochondria know how much energy to produce in each cell, how they deal with the damaging biproducts of combustion, and how they know where to position themselves in complex cells like neurons or muscle.  This grant proposal expands upon some of our previous studies that have identified novel ways that the mitochondria communicates with the other parts of the cell, most particularly with the nucleus.  Given the central role of the mitochondria in metabolism, cell toxicity and death, this research program will help us develop new ways to treat metabolic disorders, cancer and neurodegenerative disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Group V and Group X secretory phospholipases A2 in myocardial infarction.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOACTIVE LIPID MEDIATORS; BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION; CARDIAC REMODELLNG; GROUP V AND GROUP X SECRETORY PHOSPHOLIPASES A2; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is the most common cause of death in Canada. Two of the most well known forms of heart disease are congestive heart failure, in which the pumping function of the heart is severely impaired, and heart attacks (or myocardial infarction) in which blood supply to the heart is slowed or stopped because of a blockage and part of the heart dies. The key to saving lives and preventing premature death and disability caused by heart attacks lies in science research investigations.Its role in understanding the basic mechanisms of how heart disease and strokes develop is a critical step to early prevention and treatment. It is well established that alterations in prostaglandin and leukotrienes biosynthesis occur in the myocardium of patients who sustain a myocardial infarction, some of whom go on to develop congestive heart failure, and that these prostaglandins have diverse effects on cardiac function. The secretory phospolipases A2 enzymes are involved in the pathway that generates bioactive lipid mediators by resident cardiac cells and also by recruited myeloid cells in the heart - we have identified that two of these enzymes, Group V and Group X secretory phospholipases A2, were present in several myeloid cells including PMN and also in heart tissue after infarction. Currently, there is almost no information regarding the role that Group V and Group X secretory phospholipases A2 enzymes play in the regulation of heart function or the heart response to injuries, such as a heart attack. An in depth analysis of the role that Group V and Group X secretory phospholipases A2 play in the heart may lead to a better understanding of the effect of these enzymes on cardiac remodeling and function after myocardial infarction.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - A: Reproduction, Maternal, Child and Youth Health
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of endothelial cell dysfunction in preeclampsia
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIUM; MYOGRAPH; NITRIC OXIDE; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PREECLAMPSIA; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Preeclampsia is a common disorder of pregnancy and is a leading cause of sickness to the mother and her child. It is diagnosed primarily by the onset of high blood pressure and protein in the urine during the last half of pregnancy. The cause for preeclampsia is not known. The only cure is to deliver the baby, which results in the risk of delivering a premature infant. In addition, women who have experienced preeclampsia are at a greater risk for cardiovascular disease later in life.    There is evidence that the elevated blood pressure that occurs in preeclampsia is due to dysfunction of endothelial cells that are the cells that line the lumen of all blood vessels. Endothelial cells produce many substances that can relax and constrict blood vessels. Since delivery of the baby and placenta removes the symptoms of preeclampsia, it is proposed that the placenta releases factors into the blood stream that affects vascular function by promoting endothelial cells to produce more constrictors and less dilators.     We will study blood vessel function in an animal model that has similar features as women with preeclampsia. In this model, blood flow to the uterus is reduced and this leads to the placenta releasing factors in the blood that results in high blood pressure. Our studies are designed to determine the vascular pathways that lead to the high blood pressure. In addition, we will determine if circulating factors are responsible for the impaired blood vessel function. Our last aim is to study the vascular effects of previous exposure to preeclampsia on later life cardiovascular function.    These studies will increase our understanding of the vascular problems in preeclampsia in order to develop new therapies to improve the outcome of the mother and her child.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
ResearchClassEN: MUSCULO SKELETAL; DENTAL DISEASE (INCL. ORAL BIOLOGY)
ClasseRechercheFR: MUSCLES ET OS; AFFECTIONS DENTAIRES (ET BIOLOGIE BUCCO-DENTAIRE)
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of biomineralization by osteopontin
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMINERALIZATION; BONE; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; OSTEOMALACIA; PATHOLOGIC CALCIFICATION; TEETH
Abstract-Résumé: In bones and teeth, small calcium- and phosphate-containing crystals (and calcium- and carbonate-containing crystals in inner ear otoconia) are deposited within a scaffolding of proteins called the extracellular matrix. Exciting new evidence describes the importance of protein-crystal interactions, which in bones and teeth, define properties of the mineral making the tissues strong, and which in the inner ear, provide for small mineralized structures which help maintain balance. Our work is particularly relevant to understanding the defective/decreased mineralization occurring in osteomalacias - diseases where bone is incompletely calcified, soft and prone to fracture. It is also relevant to pathologic calcification diseases of "soft" tissues. Compelling evidence indicates that a bone and tooth protein - osteopontin (OPN) - controls mineralization. Equally important is that processing of OPN by enzymes leads to mineralization-inhibiting protein fragments (peptides) with different potencies. Processing of OPN protein and its peptides might define a control mechanism affecting biomineralization in different tissues. Here we propose to investigate this possible regulation, guided by the general hypothesis that OPN in bones, teeth and other tissues, and peptides derived from enzymatic processing of OPN, control mineralization by modulating (pyro)phosphate-regulating genes, and by binding to crystal surfaces in a very specific way to control their growth. We will examine these mechanisms in cell-free systems, cell culture models, and mouse models using biochemical measurements, high-resolution imaging approaches, biophysical approaches to characterize mineral, and computational modeling to simulate atomic-scale binding. Such work should provide insights into keeping bones and teeth strong and healthy, and maintaining balance, and may suggest ways to treat patients where these tissues are defective.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lineage development in the mouse blastocyst
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL LINEAGE SPECIFICATION; EMBRYO DEVELOPMENT; GENE REGULATION; LINEAGE TRACING; PLURIPOTENCY; STEM CELL IDENTITY
Abstract-Résumé: In the early development of either a mouse or human embryo, the first stage at which different cell types can be identified is the blastocyst. At this stage, the embryo has about 100 cells, is the size of a speck of dust and has not yet attached itself to the mother's womb. One of the cell types in the blastocyst is the epiblast-the pluripotent cells that give rise to all the later cells of the body. It is from the epiblast that embryonic stem cells arise-the stem cells that have the potential to make so many different therapeutically important cells for treating degenerative diseases. However, the other two cell types in the blastocyst, the trophectoderm and the primitive endoderm, are also important. They provide signals that tell the epiblast cells how to make the body plan and they directly make the tissues like the placenta that the embryo needs to survive in the womb. We have identified some of the key genes whose expression tells cells to become epiblast, primitive endoderm or trophectoderm. Now we need to understand the way in which those genes are turned on and off in time and space to make the organized structures of the blastocyst. Using live cell imaging in cultured mouse embryos, combined with experiments to alter cell behaviour, cell signaling and gene expression, we will be able to provide new insights into the form and function of the mouse and, by extension, the human blastocyst. These studies will inform reproductive technologies and improve stem cell maintenance and differentiation.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; ANOMALIES CONGENITALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Tracking the yeast telomerase RNA
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER; GENOME STABILITY; MOLECULAR GENETICS; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Telomerase is an essential enzyme that ensures genome stability by replenishing the special DNA sequence repeats at the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes, the telomeres. Two components are required for telomerase activity in vitro: a protein that is believed to work like other enzymes that synthesize DNA using an RNA template, and such an RNA template molecule that harbours a specific sequence element that is used for sequence copying. Inadequate expression, maturation, modification of subunits and/or regulation of telomerase components is associated with a number of human disease states, foremost cancer, but also dyskeratosis congenita (DKC). In fact, it has been shown that DKC can be caused by mutations in the RNA component of telomerase. Using budding yeast as a model system, here we propose to investigate the biology of the yeast telomerase RNA. In particular, we wish to determine all the components of the yeast telomerase, learn more about how the RNA is regulated and localized and how the enzyme operates at its most important location, namely the catalytic center. Given the fact that telomerase function and regulation generally is very highly conserved across many species, including humans, we speculate that these studies provide critical clues and input into questions how this enzyme affects human health.
