ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Integrin-Linked Kinase in Mitotic Spindle dynamics and Centrosome clustering in cancer cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CENTROSOMES; INTEGRIN LINKED KINASE; INTEGRINS; MITOSIS; MITOTIC SPINDLE
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer cell division is abnormal. Cancer cells often acquire extra centrosomes which normally control proper segregation of genetic material into daughter cells during cell division. The extra centrosomes make cancer cells vulnerable to cell death, but many types of cancer cells acquire ways to cluster the centrosomes to form bipolar spindles and undergo cell division. Recently we have identified a protein called ILK as a component of centrosomes. Our preliminary work shows that this protein is critical for proper cell division and that in cancer cells this protein facilitates the clustering of multiple centrosomes . Here we propose to dissect exactly how ILK works to perform its functions in the centrosomes, and whether inhibiting its function, or the function of other associated proteins in cancer cells will induce centrosome declustering and specific cell death. We also propose to develop assays for the discovery of novel compounds capable of inhibiting cancer cell division by targeting centrosome clustering. This work will provide fundamental new knowledge to the field of cell division mechanisms, but importantly may identify specific ways of blocking cell division and inducing cell death in cancer cells and identify novel cancer therapeutic agents.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; OBESITE
TitreApplicationTitle: Feeding Behaviour & Satiety: Cellular & Molecular Physiology of the K-Dependent Na/Ca-Exchanger, NCKX4
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS; MEMBRANE TRANSPORT; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NEURONAL FUNCTION; OBESITY; SODIUM-CALCIUM EXCHANGE
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity and eating disorders represent an enormous problem in western society, with obvious cost to both individual health and the health care system. Despite intensive investigation and steady advances in our knowledge about the ways in which appetite and eating work, we still do not have a complete picture of how the brain controls these behaviours. Further new insights are necessary to combat this escalating health problem.  We have recently discovered that mice lacking the gene for the specialized calcium transport protein known as the K+-dependent Na+/Ca2+-exchanger type 4 or NCKX4 for short, are healthy but weigh 30% less than normal mice because they eat about 30% less food. Although various hormones and brain circuits have previously been suggested to control feeding behavour, this is the first time that a membrane calcium transport protein has been shown to have an effect on eating behaviour. Our discovery creates a whole new opportunity both to understand the way eating is normally controlled, and to study an unexpected target for the development of new treatments for eating disorders and obesity.  The experiments proposed here will lead to an in depth understanding of where and how the NCKX4 protein works in brain nerve pathways that control feeding behaviour and satiety. This information will be critical in understanding normal feeding behaviour and the events that underlie its dys-regulation, possibly leading toward the development of novel therapeutic agents for eating disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Antibiotic Resistance Through the Systematic Characterization of TetR-like Transcription Factors and Their Target Genes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; PROTEIN/DNA INTERACTIONS; PROTEIN/LIGAND INTERACTIONS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Modern medicine depends on our ability to control bacterial infections. At present the only way to do this is to administer antibiotics. This is important for treating routine infections such as bacterial pneumonia, meningitis, ear and upper respiratory infections (especially in children) and for managing infections that arise post-surgically and due to immune suppression resulting from disease and chemotherapy. More than 80 million antibiotic prescriptions are given each year in North America alone.   The rapid rise in antibiotic-resistant infections is therefore an extremely serious problem. Resistance has emerged and proliferated within a few years of the introduction of every single antibiotic. Where does this resistance come from? How does it arise and spread so quickly? Growing evidence strongly suggests that resistance for most or all of the antibiotics exists already in Nature. This is because the antibiotics themselves come from Nature - most of them are purified from soil bacteria. There is no ready alternative source of antibiotics so we are stuck with this sorce of theraputic agents. But if we could understand these antibiotic resistance mechanisms before they arise it would allow us to use antibiotics more intelligently, reduce clinical resistance and increase efficacy. Furthermore, we could develop resistance protein inhibitors that would restore the usefulness of those drugs subject to widespread resistance.  Our research suggests that the large family of bacterial transcription factors known as TetR-like proteins (TLPs) and the genes ("effectors") that they regulate are a large component of this uncharacterized environmental resistance. Our plan is to identify the antibiotics that they act on and understand their biological importance. We will argue that this work will provide new ways of combating antibiotic resistance and facilitate antibiotic discovery.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular control of cardiac repolarization and the substrate for lethal ventricular arrhythmias
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTION POTENTIAL RECORDING; ANTIARRHYTHMIC DRUGS; CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIAS; ION CHANNELS; PATCH CLAMP; REMODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Every year, about 30,000 Canadians die suddenly. Very rapid heart rhythms are a major cause of sudden cardiac death. Tiny membrane channels control cardiac electrical function and heart rhythm. When these channels don't function right, they cause very rapid abnormal rhythms. Rapid abnormal rhythms impair heart function and cause sudden death. Both heart disease and rhythm problems can in turn impair channel working. This study focuses on how channels are made up and how heart disease and rhythm problems affect channel make-up. We have created new models of heart function using single heart cells. These models respond like the intact heart to disease conditions. We will use these models to understand how disease conditions affect channel make-up. We will then learn how these changes in make-up can lead to serious heart rhythm problems. This knowledge will allow us to design new treatments to prevent sudden death in man.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of Physical Activity on Muscle Function in growing children: Implications for adult health?
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; EMG; GROWTH AND MATURATION; MUSCLE STRENGTH; NEURO-MOTOR FUNCTION; NEUROMUSCULAR DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Physical activity during youth is known to be very beneficial for adults' cardiovascular and bone health. In fact, physical activity of various types can unmistakably result in better bone development during youth, which is believed to promote bone health and strength in adulthood and thus, reducing the risk of osteoporosis. By comparison, it is unclear whether physical activity during youth can also affect neuromuscular function (the way nerves make muscles work) and health and if so, which types of physical activity will be most beneficial for this purpose in children. In fact, the effects of physical activity on neuromuscular function in youth are practically unknown. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to examine the effects of growth and maturation, as well as physical activity participation during youth on neuromuscular function. Neuromuscular function (strength and electrical activity within the muscle) will be examined in children over a period of three years, in a mixed-longitudinal fashion, spanning an age range of 8-16 year olds. Changes in neuromuscular function with maturation and physical activity will help answer the question of whether physical activity can improve neuromuscular function and whether childhood provides a "window of opportunity" for neuromuscular health, similar to that provided for bone health. Additionally, muscle strength development is different in males and females. This study will examine whether these sex-differences are related to differences in the way their muscles are activated (the electrical activity within the muscle). Finally, changes in neuromuscular function with maturation will be instrumental in the revision of current practices and the development of child-oriented physical therapy programs. That is, the results of this study will provide the basis of neuromuscular function during childhood, which can then be applied in various childhood chronic diseases that affect the neuromuscular system.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition

TitreApplicationTitle: Using eye movements to probe brain function and dysfunction in humans
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHD; BRAIN; FMRI; FUNCTION AND DYSFUNCTION; FUNCTIONAL NEUROIMAGING; PARKINSON DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: An important aspect of intelligence - and part of what makes us 'human' - is the ability to exert flexible control over our behaviour. Think of our response to a crosswalk light: when green, we can cross the intersection; when red, we should wait. But what if something jumps into the intersection, even though we have the right of way? We must continually adapt our behaviour based on our intentions and the changing environment. Here we present a multi-tiered project that is designed to investigate how the brain provides this flexible control over behaviour by using the saccadic eye movement system as the model platform. The eye movement system is used because we have extensive knowledge of both the sensory component (vision) and the motor component (eye movement) of the system. Specific experiments have been designed to combine high speed eye movement recording with modern brain imaging techniques to identify brain regions that provide flexible control over behaviour. We will investigate the maturation of this flexible control across the lifespan and we will conduct these same experiments in various patient groups (e.g., attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and Parkinson's disease) in which flexible control over behaviour is compromised.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of vascular inflammation in septic shock: Role of bacterial DNA
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; BACTERIAL CONSTITUENTS (DNA; CELL AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY TECHNIQUES; ENDOTHELIAL DYSFUNCTION/DAMAGE; LEUKOCYTES; LPS); SEPSIS; SEPTIC SHOCK
Abstract-Résumé: Sepsis is a major growing health problem and remains the leading cause of death in critically ill patients. Only 55 to 65 percent of patients with sepsis survive. Sepsis, currently defined as a systemic inflammation in the presence of infection, is increasingly being considered an exaggerated, poorly regulated response of the immune system to microbial products. Severe sepsis develops when an organ system begins to fail. Cells of the immune system recognize bacteria and bacterial products (for example, lipopolysaccharide or LPS, and bacterial DNA) through proteins called Toll-like receptors and produce inflammatory mediators. When properly regulated, these host responses destroy invading bacteria; in excess, they devolve into sepsis. Recent results, including ours, suggest that bacterial DNA, which differs from our own DNA, is a potent activator of immune cells.   In this application, we propose to investigate if bacterial DNA could affect the functions of endothelial cells (the cell lining the blood vessels inside) and white blood cells called neutrophil granulocytes, events that are critical to the development of unregulated inflammation. We will also investigate whether promoting removal of neutrophil granulocytes from the injured organs reduces inflammation and accelerates healing. We will use neutrophil granulocytes and endothelial cells from healthy donors and also those from genetically altered mice which lack the gene for the protein that recognizes bacterial DNA. We will combine pharmacological, immunological, cell and molecular biology techniques and mouse models of sepsis. The research in this proposal will address fundamental questions in the pathobiology of sepsis. We anticipate that our results may provide a rational basis for development of novel therapeutic approaches, i.e. targeting bacterial DNA, to prevent multiple organ failure and ultimately to reduce the high death rate associated with severe sepsis.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: BIOCHIMIE; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Properties of Prothrombinase
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD COAGULATION; FACTOR V; FACTOR XA; KINETICS; PROTEIN CHEMISTRY; PROTHROMBIN ACTIVATION
Abstract-Résumé: The circulatory system can elicit  a complex mechanism known as the blood coagulation cascade to make the blood clot. The mechanism is for the most part latent, but it is locally activated when needed to prevent excessive blood loss in the event of injury. Once activated, the cascade can be very powerful; if it is not properly regulated it can have rapid and lethal consequences, such as heart attack and stroke. The prothrombinase complex operates within the cascade and catalyses the formation of the blood clotting enzyme thrombin from its latent precursor, prothrombin. The proposed work is directed at obtaining a better understanding of the functional properties of this complex. The work will be accomplished by measuring the function of the complex reconstructed from purified components. Its down regulation by two physiologic regulators, known as antithrombin and activated protein C, will be quantitatively characterized in real time during the process of prothrombin activation. The mechanism of prothrombin activation will be investigated in molecular detail. The binding of prothrombin and thrombin to blood platelets and the consequences of that binding will be measured. In addition, a determination of  whether prothombinase exhibits thresholding, all-or-none qualities will be made. If so, a fundamentally new view of the regulation of prothrombinase will arise. These studies should provide a clearer picture of how prothrombinase works and is regulated. This clearer understanding will provide both new insights into the molecular details which underlie dysfunctional operation of the cascade and new rationale for reducing or preventing heart attacks and strokes with drugs.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Developing RNA-cleaving DNAzymes as Molecular Tools for Cancer Study and as Cancer Therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: BCL-XL; CANCER; DNAZYME; IN VITRO SELECTION; RNA CLEAVAGE; THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: DNA is widely known as the material used by all living organisms on Earth to store and transmit genetic information. Recently however, DNA has been shown to have other talents as well, one of which is to act as a catalyst to make or break molecules of biological significance. DNA-made catalysts, known as 'DNAzymes', are usually made by scientists either to address fundamental scientific questions or to provide unique solutions to problems of medical importance. Because DNA is an exceptionally stable polymer and can be easily produced commercially, DNAzymes with tailor-made functions are regarded as very desirable molecular tools and are being tested in many research labs around the world as diagnostic kits and therapeutic agents. In this project, we will study a class of DNAzymes denoted here simply as 'RNase DNAzymes' because they can function as special molecular scissors to cut an extremely important class of biological molecules known as 'RNA'. RNase DNAzymes are medically valuable because they can catalytically destroy a specific RNA of interest (such as a cancer-causing RNA molecule). The proposed work is to design DNAzyme based molecular tools for facilitating biomedical research on cancer and develop some potent DNAzymes into therapeutic agents for this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Angiogenesis During Lung Development, Injury and Repair
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRUS MEDIATED GENE TRANSFER; ALVEOLI; ANGIOGENESIS; BRONCHOPULMONARY DYSPLASIA; ENDOTHELIAL PROGENITOR CELLS; LUNG INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a chronic lung disease that follows ventilator and oxygen treatment for acute failure to breath in babies born very prematurely (24-28 weeks of gestation instead of 40). BPD is a major complication of prematurity with a short and long term burden for infants and their families. Damage to the still developing lung stops the normal formation of the alveoli (the air sacs in the lung that allows the uptake of oxygen and release of waste carbon dioxide). Currently there is no treatment for this disease. Our laboratory is seeking new medications to either protect or heal the damaged lung. We try to understand if the tiny blood vessels that run along the air sacs contribute to normal lung growth and if stimulating the growth of these vessels can prevent lung damage or repair an already damaged lung. We are exploring if a "master" transcription factor called HIF (hypoxia inducible factor) that turns on several blood vessel-making growth factors, is important for normal lung development and can prevent lung injury. Very recent evidence suggests that the lung also contains the very first cells that make blood vessels, so called endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs). We will be exploring how important these cells are for normal lung development and if they can be used to prevent lung injury. Our proposal will test if HIF or EPCs can repair lungs in experimental BPD induced by high oxygen concentrations. This research could lead to new treatments to improve the outcome of premature babies, but also of adults with incurable lung diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Angiogenesis During Lung Development, Injury and Repair

TitreApplicationTitle: Breast cancer risk assessment using optical transillumination spectroscopy
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL OPTICS AND SPECTROSCOPY; BREAST CANCER; EPIDEMIOLOGY; RISK GROUPS
Abstract-Résumé: Conquering cancer needs next to early diagnosis and effective therapy also a preventive strategy.  Any preventive strategy requires means to detect the persons at highest risk and to monitor changes in that risk when preventive interventions are applied.  Means to detect individuals at risk are commonly based on risk factors and biomarkers, which in turn can be genetic, demographic, environmental or physical in nature. For breast cancer the BrCa ½ genes, family history, lifestyle and also mammographic density have been demonstrated to be risk factors, so their ability to identify women at risk vary wildly. Only mammographic density can monitor the efficacy of preventive intervention.  Here we plan to develop an optical technique to identify women at risk and monitor their change in risk over a 4 year period. The study comprises 3 cohorts of women with anticipated different rates of risk change over this period.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: Longitudinal Study of Cognition in Older Adults with Bipolar Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIPOLAR DISORDER; COGNITION; LINEAR MIXED MODEL; LONGITUDINAL FOLLOW-UP; PREDICTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Bipolar disorder (formerly called manic-depressive illness) affects about 3 percent of older Canadians. Many older persons who suffer from bipolar disorder experience significant problems with their memory, attention, and other cognitive functions.  These changes put them at risk to develop dementia or to lose their ability to take care of themselves and live independently in the community. This project will study the factors that influence these changes in memory, attention, and other cognitive functions. Identifying and understanding these factors will provide new targets for interventions in these vulnerable elders.  In turn, new or improved interventions will help to preserve their independence and quality of life as they age.

TitreApplicationTitle: A study of novel anti-cancer immunomodulatory fusion proteins and transgenic cell therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENE THERAPY; CYTOKINES; IMMUNOLOGY; INTERLEUKINS; MARROW STOMAL CELLS; RETROVIRAL VECTORS
Abstract-Résumé: We are focusing on investigating the use of therapeutic synthetic proteins which elicit an anti-tumor immune response.  These synthetic proteins encode for coupled cytokine genes not otherwise found in nature, hereafter referred to as "fusokines".  As part of on-going CIHR funding -here considered for renewal - we have had tremendous success in developing and characterizing fusokines borne of the marriage of GMCSF and IL2 (aka GIFT2), GMCSF and IL15 (aka GIFT15).  Interleukin-21 is a recently discovered cytokine which promotes the potent Th17-driven immune response.  As a new objective, we here propose to study the use of GMCSF and IL21 (aka GIFT21).  We have also discovered that GMCSF coupled to truncated forms of chemokines also induce apoptosis and cell death of malignancies expressing specific chemokine receptors.  Indeed we've published the use of a GMCSF and Monocyte Chemotactic Protein (MCP)-1 fusokine (aka GMME1) which kills tumor cells expressing chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2) at their surface.  We also propose to study the use of GMCSF & MCP3 fusokine (aka GMME3) as a means of targeting and destroying tumor cells expressing chemokine receptor 5 (CCR5) for which it has a specific affinity.  Lastly, we have demonstrated that tumor cells escape immune rejection in large part due to their production of TGFbeta.  To address this issue, we created a fusokine which couples a decoy TGFbeta receptor and IL2 (aka FIST) and propose to examine its use in cancer immunotherapy.  We will also determine if normal bone marrow stromal cells engineered to secrete these novel fusokines can be used in the treatment of cancer.  In sum, we have developed novel anti-tumor biopharmaceuticals that have been shown to be effective in animal models of cancer.  These same tools and concepts are being specifically developed in a novel approach harnessing the immune system for the treatment of cancer that may benefit patients with otherwise "incurable" or recurrent malignancy.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic control of artery and vein specification
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ARTERY; COUPTFII; DEVELOPMENT; ISLET2; VEIN
Abstract-Résumé: The vascular system (blood and vessels) arises from the same initial cell population which differentiates into different cell types. Blood and vessels are the first to differentiate. Next arteries and veins form, and finally all the smaller vessels of animals form from the initial first vessels. We are studying the genetic mechanisms that lead to these different 'choices'. In particular, the choice between artery and vein has great clinical impact- up to 1% of the population has cerebral cavernous mutations where arterial and venous blood mix due to improper vessel development. Arteries have different origins, properties and structures as compared to veins. We are interested in how these differences arise at the genetic level. We use the transparent zebrafish model to identify new genes and manipulate their expression. In this proposal we will study the Islet2 and the CoupTFII transcription factors in their role in vein development and sprouting of new blood vessels. We will determine how they work at the molecular level, and whether they interact. We will also study the Numb protein, which affects blood development to determine how it guides cells to their fates.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel mechanism in controlling the expression of ChREBP and liver lipogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRAMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION (CHIP); CHREBP; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LIVER LIPOGENESIS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REPRESSION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Increased lipogenesis (fatty acid production) is tightly associated with many metabolic diseases, including atherosclerosis, fatty liver disease, diabetes, obesity and metabolic syndrome. we are working  towards exploration of mechanisms underlying the expression of a protein namely ChREBP, a newly identified "master" switch in the control of lipogenesis. This gene is important as in obese and diabetic mouse models, expression of ChREBP is increased (too much expression of this gene is no good), while mice without this gene show protection from the development of obesity.  Our study may lead to the identification of novel therapeutic targets fro controlling abnormal lipogenesis in the diseases including diabetes.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors and CNS development
Keywords-MotsClés: CNS DEVELOPMENT; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; FRAGILE-X MENTAL RETARDATION; GLUTAMATE RECEPTOR PLASTICITY; NEUROTROPHIC SIGNALS; RETT'S SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Rett syndrome and Fragile-X mental retardation are debilitating neurodevelopmental disorders that strike young infants after apparently many months of normal growth and development. Although there is currently no effective medication, the time delay suggests a "window of opportunity" for therapeutic intervention may exist. Each disorder presents with a spectrum of symptoms, however, afflicted children commonly possess autistic features. This finding has suggested to some that Rett syndrome and Fragile-X mental retardation may have a common molecular basis. In this grant application, we provide evidence for a novel signaling pathway triggered in early brain development by the neurotransmitter, L-glutamate. Importantly, this pathway is absent in a mouse model of Fragile-X mental retardation. We hypothesize it is also deficient in Rett syndrome. Experiments are planned to study the properties of this signaling pathway with the aim of rescuing its expression. Our work demonstrates for the first time a missing molecular event in the brains of Fragile-X sufferers that may also be lacking in Rett syndrome. The benefit of this work is that it may provide a basis for the development of clinically relevant compounds to treat these disorders early on in childhood.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of colonic short chain fatty acids in obesity and insulin resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: COLONIC FERMENTATION; GUT HORMONES; HUMANS; INSULIN SENSITIVITY; OBESITY; WHOLE BODY METABOLISM
Abstract-Résumé: The high rate of obesity in Canada is a major public health concern because obesity increases risk for diseases such as diabetes and heart disease.  Research shows that people who eat a high amount of dietary fiber gain less weight and are at lower risk of getting diabetes than those with low fiber diets.  This may be because fibers are broken down (fermented) by bacteria in the large intestine (colon) to form gases (the cause of flatulence) and substances known as short chain fatty acids (SCFA).  The most abundant SCFA is acetic acid, which is commonly consumed in vinegar.  SCFA may be beneficial; our research shows that they influence the secretion of hormones such as glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), peptide YY (PYY), ghrelin and adiponectin which help control appetite and blood glucose levels.  On the other hand, research suggests that obese people have different bacteria in their colons which break down fiber to produce more SCFA than lean people and that this causes weight gain because of the extra energy obtained from the SCFA.  However, it is unknown if obese people produce more SCFA or not.  The purpose of this research is to see if the types of colonic bacteria, and the absorption, metabolism and metabolic effects of SCFA differ in lean and obese subjects.  Using a series of tests in human subjects involving intravenous and rectal infusion of acetate and measuring blood SCFA responses after feeding a fermentable fiber we will determine the rates of production, absorption and metabolism of acetate in lean and obese subjects and in people with different kinds of bacteria in their colons and whether these treatments have different effects on hormones and metabolites which control appetite and blood glucose.  This research will help us to understand if and how colonic SCFA are involved in the development of obesity in humans so that treatments can be developed to help correct the problem(s) identified and ultimiately help to prevent or treat obe

NomDuComitéFR: Santé publique, santé communautaire et santé de la population - A
TitreApplicationTitle: Scaling up treatment to reduce population HIV incidence
Keywords-MotsClés: CLUSTER SAMPLING; HIV/AIDS; HOUSE TO HOUSE TESTING; INCIDENCE MEASUREMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is a threat to global health and economic stability. In spite of ongoing prevention efforts, such strategies have had limited success in decreasing the number of new infections. Combination Antiretroviral Therapy (cART) is a successful multi-drug therapy for reducing illness and death among those receiving it. CART reduces the amount of virus in the body and has been successfully used to prevent mother-to-child transmission of the infection. We aim to determine if expanded cART use in populations with a high level of HIV infected people can reduce the number of new infections in the community. The scientific logic behind this is that successful treatment of an individual will make them less infectious to their sexual partners. We will sample many households in the Bushenyi and Gulu districts of Uganda. With our implementing Ugandan partners, The Joint Clinical Research Centre, we will conduct ongoing HIV testing and collect sexually transmitted infection (STI) data on consenting adults (15-59). We will conduct a yearly survey with participants addressing risk factors. We will dramatically scale-up cART access in these districts using a novel design called a 'step'wedge' design that allows us the increase access to specific populations at specific time points. We will measure incidence of STIs and HIV on a yearly basis and determine if there is a lower number of new infections with expanded cART use. We will determine if new infections are caused by individuals receiving treatment or by high-risk individuals.We will survey the population about HIV risk factors. This study will provide strong inferences about the use of cART to prevent new HIV infections. It will identify infected individuals early and provide clinical care to them. Finally, it will provide strong inferences on risk factors for HIV/AIDS in these communities.

CommitteeNameEN: Public, Community and Population Health - B
NomDuComitéFR: Santé publique, santé communautaire et santé de la population - B
TitreApplicationTitle: HPV Infection and Transmission Among Couples Through Heterosexual Activity (The HITCH Cohort Study)
Keywords-MotsClés: CERVICAL CANCER; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS; RISK FACTORS; SEXUAL BEHAVIOUR
Abstract-Résumé: Genital infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection today.  Most of the time, such infections are not noticed or cause only external warts. Although benign, warts are difficult to treat and lead to social stigmatization. However, there is a more ominous health consequence of HPV infection: cancer of the uterine cervix, a disease that can be fatal in about 40% of the women who are affected by it. Most HPV infections will not lead to cervical cancer, only those that involve certain types of this virus and that persist for a long time. Testing for HPV is a novel screening strategy that has the potential to detect more cases of precancerous cervical lesions than the traditional Pap test. As more and more physicians order these tests, there is increased awareness of how common such infections are among Canadian women (depending on age, 15%-40% have them). Women, their partners, and their physicians are left with many unanswered questions on how the infection is transmitted, how much risk there is after a sexual encounter, and what measures of protection can be achieved. This project will be the first in Canada to try to find answers to these questions.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - C: Behavioural Studies, Neuroscience and Cognition
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of sleep and aging in the consolidation of motor memories
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CONDITIONING; FUNCTIONAL AND ANATOMICAL MRI TECHNIQUES; MOTOR MEMORY CONSOLIDATION; POLYSOMNOGRAPHY; SLEEP STAGES
Abstract-Résumé: Throughout our life, we learn an impressive number of new sequences of movements that can only be performed in a fast and automatic fashion after extensive practice. Current research crucially indicates that the memory trace created after an initial, short amount of practice needs to be consolidated so that it can be retained on the long term. A role for sleep in this consolidation process has been reported but still has to be fully characterized. Our research program aims at establishing a more qualitative link between the consolidation of a motor sequence memory trace and sleep. More specifically, the endeavour is to establish a causal relationship between the occurrence of sleep spindles during stage 2 and motor sequence consolidation in young volunteers as well as to assess the impact of normal aging, in which this specific sleep component is affected, on memory consolidation. A variety of state of the art neuroimaging techniques that allow mapping in vivo brain activity will be employed, along with more classical behavioural and electrophysiological approaches, to test our hypotheses (notably regarding the role of the striatum and hippocampus) in both young and elderly healthy individuals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Allograft Vasculopathy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ANIMAL MODELS OF TRANSPLANT REJECTION; CARDIAC TRANSPLANT; CELLULAR PERMEABILITY; TRANSPLANT REJECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Hardening of the arteries occurs in blood vessels of one's own heart and those that have been transplanted, in people throughout Canada and worldwide. The nature of this hardening is distinct and more accelerated than that which occurs in our own hearts. The reasons why this devastating condition occurs in transplanted hearts, often leading to silent heart attacks and death of the organ recipient, are unknown. We do know that the immune system of the recipient responds against the transplanted heart, but we do not know how the vessels in the heart are injured nor how they become narrowed.  Endothelial cells (EC) line the inner surface of the blood vessels, separating the vessel wall from the bloodstream, and when injured early post-transplantation, lead to many adverse consequences, including artery narrowing. Substances responsible for injury and subsequent poor function of EC are only partially known. Among factors of interest in this regard, Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) on one hand causes EC renewal or healing, as well as the recruitment of stem cells which may help heal the endothelium, and on the other hand, appear to diminish EC integrity. VEGF is increased in availability in artery walls of transplanted hearts, and when present in excess, as it is in this disease, may be adverse to arterial health.  We will define in detail how the integrity of the endothelium is modified by VEGF and how this factor works to do so. As well, we will identify the role of the recipient's bone marrow, and how it may repair and replace damaged EC. This work will be accomplished using state-of-the-art technology and cell culture models using human EC. As well, we will examine the degree and contribution of bone marrow-derived stem cells in our mouse model of heart transplantation. The results from this study will provide unique insight into the beneficial and detrimental roles of VEGF, and allow for the use of specific therapies at specific times to address these.

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
TitreApplicationTitle: Recruitment of the DDB1-CUL4-DCAF1 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex by the HIV/SIV Vpr/Vpx accessory proteins: implications for viral infection, persistence and pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE ARREST; HIV/AIDS; HOST CELL RESTRICTION FACTORS; HOST CELL UBIQUITIN-PROTEASOME SYSTEM; MACROPHAGE INFECTION; VIRAL PROTEINS R AND X (VPR AND VPX)
Abstract-Résumé: AIDS is a slow degenerative disease of the immune and nervous systems resulting from HIV-1 infection. Despite considerable progress made in our understanding of HIV infection, we still do not completely understand how the virus causes disease and how it maintains itself in infected individuals in presence of a vigorous immune response and highly suppressive antiretroviral regimens. HIV-1 viral protein R (Vpr) is a virion-associated protein that is required for efficient infection of macrophages and dendritic cell, two cellular compartments that play a major role in HIV persistence and pathogenesis. In addition, Vpr has the ability to arrest infected T lymphocytes at a specific step of the cell cycle (G2) presumably to optimize viral replication. Interestingly, recent evidence from our laboratory suggests that Vpr biological activities are dependent on the association of the protein with a host protein destruction complex. The overall goal of this research project will be to test the hypothesis that HIV-1 Vpr binds a protein destruction complex to cause destruction of cellular proteins that may be part of antiviral defense systems. First, we will characterize the association of Vpr with the host protein destruction complex. Second, we will identify cellular proteins that are destroyed by Vpr to induce cell cycle arrest and to promote efficient infection of macrophages. Finally, we will investigate whether Vpr via its cell cycle arrest activity affects the function of cellular components of innate immunity. Ultimately, the elucidation of the interaction between HIV-1 Vpr and host target cells will lead to a heightened comprehension of viral replication and pathogenesis. Additionally, a greater understanding of host cell resistance factors restricting HIV replication may lead to the development of pharmacological agents that can boost their potency and thereby lead to treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biology of iron overload: oxidative stress, gene expression, and cellular energetics
Keywords-MotsClés: ATP; CHELATION; IRON REGULATORY PROTEINS; IRON TOXICITY; ROS
Abstract-Résumé: Iron is essential for life, but in some individuals genetic diseases cause an accumulation of too much iron.  Also, some kinds of anemias require repeated blood transfusions that lead to progressive iron overload in sensitive tissues.  In these circumstances, drugs called chelators are used to control the effects of excess iron.  With the identification of new proteins and regulatory pathways, we know much more about iron physiology and toxicity than we did a decade ago.  Iron reacts with oxygen in the body to create chemical forms of oxygen that are damaging to cells.  We now know that iron can also have additional effects on how cells express their genes, that are unrelated to direct effects of these forms of oxygen.  Our current research is directed to distinguishing these different effects, using endpoints of toxicity linked to clinical disease.  One aspect of this work is to understand how iron interacts with the energy-producing unit of the cell called the mitochondrion.  We have also found that a protein intimately involved in iron metabolism, called IRP-1, binds and reacts with the cell's energy-carrying molecule, ATP.  This provides a link between cellular iron levels and energy production, and we are studying the underlying chemistry of this sensing mechanism.  Our ultimate objectives are to gain a deeper understanding of how iron causes organ damage, particularly to the heart and liver, and thus to provide additional insight into the design and implementation of therapies with iron chelators.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the Polo kinase by the Aurora and Greatwall kinases in Drosophila
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CYCLE; DROSOPHILA; GENETICS; POLO KINASE; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Every living organism must control precisely when and how its cells divide. Complex molecular mechanisms inside the cell have evolved to enforce this regulation. In humans, mutations in some of the genes involved in these processes can result in uncontrolled and unrestricted proliferation known as cancer. Understanding the molecular mechanisms that regulate cell division in normal cells, and how they are altered in cancer cells, allows the design of drugs that modify the activity of targeted molecules to stop the division of cancer cells. Moreover, because evolution has conserved these very important genes and proteins across organisms, we can exploit the relative simplicity and laboratory convenience of model organisms in our research. My model of choice is the fruitfly Drosophila melanogaster. The Polo-like kinases are a family of proteins that are crucial in regulating cell division. These proteins promote cell division by modifying the structure and activity of other proteins. The first protein of this family to be discovered was the Polo kinase of Drosophila. In humans, the equivalent protein (Plk1) is often overactive in cancer cells. For this reason, drugs that can inhibit Plk1 are being developed to treat cancer. Unfortunately, we do not yet fully understand the mechanisms by which the Polo-like kinases are controlled in the cell. I have recently found two additional kinase proteins that appear to regulate Polo in the fly. I will use genetic, biochemical, molecular and cell biological approaches to elucidate how these kinases control Polo, and to assess the biological consequences of failures in these mechanisms. This knowledge will improve our molecular understanding of cancer and suggest new ways to interfere with Polo-like kinases as a way to treat cancer.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
ResearchClassEN: DIABETES MELLITUS; NONE OF THE ABOVE
ClasseRechercheFR: DIABETE SUCRE; AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES
TitreApplicationTitle: Abnormalities of signaling pathways in diabetic cardiomyopathy: Implications for new treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS; DIABETIC CARDIOMYOPATHY; HEART FUNCTION; MITOCHONDRIA; PROTEIN KINASE C; RHO KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: It is well established that people with diabetes are more likely to suffer from heart failure and are three times more likely to die from it than the rest of the population. One of the reasons for this is that people with diabetes develop a specific form of heart disease called diabetic cardiomyopathy. In this condition, the heart does not beat as well because the ability of the heart cells to contract is impaired. Our recent studies suggest that increased activity of a specific signaling pathway, known as the RhoA-rho kinase pathway, plays a very important role in this condition, because when rats with type 1 diabetes are treated with drugs that block signaling through this pathway, the ability of their hearts to contract improves. We have found that this occurs after administration of a single dose of the drugs, both in isolated hearts and in intact animals. Preliminary evidence suggests that this pathway is also hyperactive in hearts from rats with type 2 diabetes as well, meaning that it is a common consequence of diabetes. In the proposed research, we will investigate why inhibition of this pathway leads to improvement of the ability of the diabetic heart to contract. We have identified some targets of the RhoA-rho kinase pathway in diabetic hearts and we will determine if they are responsible for the poor contraction of the heart. This research has the potential to lead to new information about the causes of diabetic cardiomyopathy, and to provide new strategies for its treatment.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE SUR LES MÉDICAMENTS; SYSTÈME NERVEUX
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Design and Synthesis of Disease Modifying Agents for Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BETA-AMYLOID; DEMENTIA; DRUG DESIGN; NEURODEGENERATIVE; PROTEIN MISFOLDING
Abstract-Résumé: There are currently no disease-modifying therapeutics available to treat Alzheimer's disease (AD).  As such, onset of the disease is inevitably followed by increasing deficits in memory and worsening behavioral disturbances, eventually resulting in death.  By targeting the neuropathological hallmarks of AD, i.e. aggregates of beta-amyloid peptide and intraneuronal aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau, we aim to interrupt and reverse the processes involved in neurodegeneration.  A small molecule that succeeds in these goals is likely to prevent the relentless cognitive and behavioural decline in people with AD.  Computer aided drug design will be used to design such an agent.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional dissection of the microRNA pathway.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL ASSAYS; C. ELEGANS GENETICS; GENE REGULATION; MICRORNA PATHWAY; RNA FUNCTION; SMALL NON-CODING RNA
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer development is constituted of series of event where normal cells suffer alterations leading to a growth advantage on normal cells and loss of function.  These novel capabilities acquired during tumor formations originate from the same initial event: genetic changes affecting various cellular pathways. Our research project focus on the understanding of how the microRNA pathway, a new process discovered less than fifteen years ago, contributes to cancer formation and progression in human.  We are using the worm as model system to study in details the microRNA pathway and thus how misregulation of components of this new cellular pathway can lead to cellular anomalies and cancer. We will study how the newly identified genes implicated in this cellular pathway are important for maintaining healthy cells. A better understanding of how these RNA molecules function will lead to significantly improve detection and treatment of cancers.  It is clear that cancer is a very complex disease, in part because many uncharacterized regulatory molecules, such as microRNA, are playing an essential role in modulating the progression of the disease. Understanding how the new cellular pathway inferring microRNAs maintains cells healthy is important because altering microRNA expression can cause cancer, and thus correcting the inappropriate expression of these tiny RNAs can contribute to treat cancer patients. A better comprehension of the microRNA pathway and identification of novel genes implicated in this pathway is important for developing new ways to detect cancerous cells as well as developing new treatments to correct anomalies found in cancer cells.

AreasOfScienceEN: ENVIRONMENTAL INFLUENCES ON HEALTH; POPULATION HEALTH

TitreApplicationTitle: Étude des effets de l'exposition à certains contaminants émergeants sur la croissance du foetus et de l'enfant d'âge scolaire
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPOSES PERFLUORES; CONTAMINANT ENVIRONNEMETAUX; CROISSANCE DE L'ENFANT; CROISSANCE FOETALE; DIPHENYL ETHER POLYBROMES; GROSSESSE; PERINATALITE; EPIDEMIOLOGIE; ETUDE LONGITUDINALE
Abstract-Résumé: Au cours des 20 dernieres annees, un nombre grandissant d'etudes ont demontre un lien entre l'exposition a certains contaminants environnementaux au cours de la grossesse et des effets sur le developpement foetal et postnatal de l'enfant. Ces toxiques ont la capacite de traverser la barriere placentaire et de se rendre jusqu'au foetus, ou ils ont la capacite de perturber la maturation des organes en developpement provoquant ainsi des modifications permanentes dont les repercussions se feront sentir bien au-dela de la naissance. Parallelement, la quantification de nouvelles substances chimiques aupres d'individus provenant de differentes populations ont demontre l'emergence d'une nouvelle generation de contaminants au niveau mondial. L'incorporation massive de ces substances dans une multitude de produits commerciaux d'usage courant a mene a ce constat inquietant. A ce jour, les etudes evaluant les effets possiblement nefastes des ces produits chimiques sur le developpement du foetus et de l'enfant en developpement sont quasi inexistantes, et ce malgre le fait que ces substances aient ete detectees dans le sang de cordon ombilical de nouveau-nes et dans le lait maternel. Une equipe de chercheurs de l'Universite Laval et de l'Universite de Montreal ont donc initie une etude a travers le Canada aupres de 2000 femmes et de leurs enfants afin de determiner leur exposition a ces nouveaux contaminants et d'en evaluer les effets sur la croissance foetale et neonatale. Ils investigueront egalement les effets de ces contaminants sur la croissance d'enfants inuits d'age scolaire, puisque cette population est connue pour etre exposee a des niveaux eleves de contaminants de part leur consommation de mammiferes marins. Ces nouvelles connaissances permettront de mettre en place des mesures et des politiques afin de diminuer l'exposition a ces contaminants a l'echelle nationale et ainsi de prevenir des troubles developpementaux potentielles chez cette population vulnerable.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of antifungal drug resistance in Candida albicans
Keywords-MotsClés: AZOLE DRUGS; CANDIDA ALBICANS; DNA MICROARRAYS; MULTIDRUG RESISTANCE; PHOSPHOLIPIDS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The fungus Candida albicans is one of the most commonly encountered human pathogens.  It causes a wide variety of infections, ranging from mucosal infections in healthy individuals (oral thrush, vaginitis) to life-threatening systemic infections in individuals with an impaired immune system (candidemia).  The drugs most widely used for the treatment of these infections are azoles.  However, treatment failure due to the emergence of azole-resistant strains of C. albicans in patients receiving long-term therapy, such as AIDS patients, is an important medical problem.  During the past funding period of this project by CIHR, we have found that many azole-resistant C. albicans clinical isolates overexpress the PDR16 gene.  This gene produces a protein whose predicted function is to transfer specific lipids (phospholipids) between different sub-compartments of the cell.  We have also shown that deleting this gene from azole-resistant C. albicans cells significantly decreases their resistance to azole drugs, by an unknown mechanism.  Finally, we have shown that PDR16 overexpression in azole-resistant clinical isolates is due to mutations in a protein called TAC1.  This protein is a transcription factor whose role is to control the expression of genes into proteins (for example, the PDR16 gene).  Our proposed research project uses genetic, genomic, molecular biology and biochemical approaches and is aimed at better understanding the function of these proteins in the response of C. albicans cells to azole drugs.  The results from our studies will help to better understand the molecular mechanisms of azole resistance, with the aim of circumventing or preventing it.  Our studies will also contribute to a better knowledge of the biology of this as well as other medically important fungi.

TitreApplicationTitle: Beyond the estrogen receptor: Involvement of kinases in estrogen dependence and independence in human breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; BREAST CANCER; ESTROGEN RECEPTOR; KINASE; MOLECULAR ENDOCRINOLOGY; MOLECULAR PATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Targeting ER, using drugs like tamoxifen, is successful in treating and preventing breast cancer. Nevertheless, such therapies are limited by development of resistance. Newer therapies, targeting ER, are also likely to be limited by development of resistance. Understanding the mechanisms of ER action holds promise for increasing further the arsenal of approaches to treat ER+ breast cancer, the most frequent type of breast cancer. The more targets, the more likely we will be able to control this disease. The development of more precise biomarkers of therapy response is valuable, so that the most appropriate therapies can be used quickly with minimal side-effects. We have potentially identified more precise markers of response to endocrine therapies. As well identification of the enzymes that are responsible for phosphorylating ER and pathways that control their activity, may offer specific targets and alternative approaches to develop new endocrine therapies for treating and preventing breast cancer.

NomDuComitéFR: Génomique: Biologie computationnelle et biologie des systèmes
AreasOfScienceEN: GENOMICS, PROTEOMICS, AND BIOINFORMATICS; INTERNATIONAL HEALTH
DomainesScientifiquesFR: GÉNOMIQUE, PROTÉOMIQUE ET BIOINFORMATIQUE; SANTÉ INTERNATIONALE
TitreApplicationTitle: The global genomics of human malaria parasites: deep resequencing to identify genetic control points of transmission, drug resistance and immune evasion in Plasmodium falciparum
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG RESISTANCE; GENETIC RECOMBINATION; GENOMICS; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MALARIA; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: Human malaria is one of the most serious global public health problems, causing over 500 million infections and 1.12 millions deaths per year.  Almost all of the deaths are caused by the parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Controlling malaria has proven to be unusually challenging as the parasites quickly adapt to human interventions by becoming resistant to drugs and remaining refractory to vaccines. Here we propose a study which uses newly developed sequencing technologies to address many of the outstanding questions of malaria science.   We will be able to generate whole-genome sequence data from a global collection of P. falciparum isolates and use statistical and bioinformatic methods to address issues of emerging virulence, vaccine design, and drug resistance in human malaria.  We plan to locate regions of the P. falciparum genome associated with immune evasion and drug resistance, to elucidate the mechanisms that allow these changes to arise, and to develop a comprehensive understanding of genome change that can help to direct future studies in vaccine and drug design.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of glypicans in the regulation of hedgehog signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: GLYPICANS; HEDGEHOG; OVARIAN CANCER; RHABDOMYOSARCOMA
Abstract-Résumé: Glypicans are proteins that regulate the activity of various families of growth factors including Hedgehogs. The activity of these growth factors is frequently altered in cancer and other genetic diseases. The goal of this project is to investigate the molecular mechanisms by which the various glypicans regulate the activity of Hedeghogs. We expect that a better understanding of the role of glypicans in the regulation of the activity of Hedgehogs will facilitate the development of therapies that target such growth factors in cancer and other genetic diseases.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: How does the rate of drug delivery influence the potential for addiction?
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; DRUG SELF-ADMINISTRATION; GLUTAMATE; NUCLEUS ACCUMBENS; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; RATE OF DRUG DELIVERY
Abstract-Résumé: The faster drugs reach the brain, the more addictive they are. As such, drug addiction is more likely and more severe in individuals who use routes that rapidly deliver drugs to the brain (e.g., smoking or intravenous injection). However, it is not known why this is. We have found recently that when drugs like cocaine and nicotine are delivered rapidly, they more readily activate neurons within the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and within a region that receives glutamate-containing inputs from the mPFC, the nucleus accumbens (NACC). This is significant because drug-induced activation of the mPFC-NACC circuit plays a critical role in the development and maintenance of drug addiction. Our goal is to determine whether rapidly delivered drugs promote addiction because they more readily engage the mPFC-NACC pathway.  To this end, we will allow rats to voluntarily self-administer rapid or slower intravenous cocaine or nicotine injections and we will determine (1) whether disrupting function within the mPFC with a chemical lesion suppresses the voluntary intake of rapid drug injections, (2) whether the intake of rapidly delivered drugs is regulated by glutamate receptors in the NACC, (3) whether the intake of rapidly delivered drugs increases glutamate levels in the NACC, and (4) whether the intake of rapidly delivered drugs alters the expression of glutamate receptors within the NACC.  This research could provide unique information on the brain mechanisms by which the rate of drug delivery influences the potential for addiction. Such findings could help to reduce the burden of drug addiction in two major ways. First, the mechanisms identified can aid in the development of new anti-addiction treatments designed specifically for addicts who use "rapid" routes of drug administration. Second, the mechanisms identified can contribute to the design of new formulations for potentially addictive medications (e.g., Ritalin) in order to reduce non-medical use.

ResearchClassEN: CANCER THERAPY GENERAL; MULTIPLE DISEASE RELEVANCE
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: MRP Mediated Multidrug Resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; DRUG RESISTANCE; MEMBRANE PROTEIN BIOCHEMISTRY; PROTEIN/LIGAND INTERACTION; PROTEIN/PROTEIN INTERACTION; TRANSMEMBRANE TRANSPORT
Abstract-Résumé: The Multidrug Resistance Proteins (MRPs), which are the focus of our research, act as energy dependent molecular pumps that can prevent drugs from reaching their targets within cells. These proteins recognize a vast array of drugs that are used to treat cancer and other diseases. When they are present in various types of tumours, they have the potential to make the tumour resistant to many commonly used chemotherapeutic agents. These proteins are also present in normal tissues and they play an important role in protection against environmental toxins, as well as potentially harmful components in the diet. However, their presence at certain locations, such as in the barriers between the blood and the central nervous system, can serve as an obstacle that limits the effectiveness of drugs that need to cross these barriers to reach their targets, such as certain drugs that are used to treat various neurological disorders. Because of their important roles in normal physiology, as well as their potential as therapeutic targets in pathological conditions, it is essential that we understand the possible consequences of manipulating the way in which these proteins function. Our research aims at understanding how the MRPs recognize their "cargo" and how they transport it across biological membranes. This research will assist in the design of drugs that will allow controlled alteration of the activity of these transport proteins and provide a greater understanding of the potential consequences of inactivating them when treating diseases such as cancer.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Morphogenetic regulation of interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM)
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBELLUM; DIFFERENTIATION; GRANULE CELL; MICROSCOPY; MIGRATION; PAR6; POLARITY; PROGENITOR; PROTEOSOME; SIAH
Abstract-Résumé: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant  pediatric brain tumor and the more aggressive,  forms of the disease result from misregulated  granule neuron differentiation. Granule neuron  progenitor (GNP) migration may be an  unappreciated component of MB tumorigenesis as  GNPs locked into progenitor migration pathway  would be unable to leave the cerebellar germinal  zone and continue dividing. The Par6 complex has  been shown to mediate migration of differentiated  granule neurons and is absent from GNPs. This  proposal aims de to  cipher the molecular  mechanisms regulating GNP migration and  differentiation by examining the regulation of  Par6 complex function by the Siah ubiquitin  ligase. The development of techniques able to  distinguish between progenitor and differentiated  migration modes may lead to the development of  therapies specifically targeting motile MB cells  while sparing normally functioning neurons.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic manipulation of the mouse SirT1 locus to investigate cancer susceptibility, response to calorie restriction, and fertility.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALORIE RESTRICTION; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; FERTILITY; HOMOLOGOUS RECOMBINATION; MOUSE GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: The lifespan of a species is a characteristic determined by the genetic composition of the organism.  Genes of the sir2 family are known to modulate the lifespan of simple organisms.  We are studying a member of this gene family in mammals and plan to modify this gene in mice to test the idea that the gene determines the response of animals to the onset of diseases such as cancer that terminate life.  This application describes a variety of gene modifications that will allow us to modulate its activity and hence determine whether ablation or activation has effects on the animals' health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Baycrest Research About Volunteering in Older adults (BRAVO)
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITIVE FUNCTIONING; PHYSICAL FUNCTIONING; PSYCHOSOCIAL FUNCTIONING; VOLUNTEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Physical activity, cognitive activity, and social activity have all been identified as protective factors against dementia in seniors. Volunteering should protect seniors' physical, cognitive, and psychosocial functioning because it gets people out into the community engaging with others in work. Existing research has identified physical and psychosocial benefits of volunteering, but the vast majority of this work has relied on subjective reports of functioning, and very little attention has been paid to the cognitive benefits of volunteering. Moreover, no prior research has specifically linked volunteering benefits to the demands of the volunteer placement. To address these issues, we plan to study the physical, cognitive, and psychosocial benefits of one year of volunteering among 200 older adults (aged 55+), using not only subjective measures, but objective measures and qualitative interviews as well. We will also rate each volunteer placement in terms of its physical, cognitive, and psychosocial demands. We hypothesize that the benefits of volunteering will depend not only on socio-demographic and health factors, but also on the number of hours volunteered, as well as on the the specific demands of the volunteer placements. This work will advance our understanding of how real-world, useful activity can improve seniors' functioning.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sensory processing and plasticity at peripheral arterial chemoreceptors in co-culture
Keywords-MotsClés: CAROTID BODY; CELL CULTURE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HYPOXIA; NEUROMODULATORS; PERIPHERAL CHEMORECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The body contains cells know as peripheral chemoreceptors that help maintain important blood chemicals at particular levels via control of our breathing. In particular, these cells sense blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, acidity, and glucose, and send corrective signals to the brain via reflexes, and these in turn control the rate and depth of breathing. Abnormalities in this pathway have important consequences on the health care system and are associated with such common conditions as sleep apnea (where breathing in intermittent) and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Our investigations are aimed at understanding how these cells work, how they communicate with the nervous system, and how their properties are altered by disease conditions or environmental factors (e.g. nicotine in cigarette smoke). To simplify the analysis, our approach is to isolate these receptor cells and grow them in tissue culture, either alone or in combination with the nerve cells that normally contact them. Then we can apply a variety of techniques (e.g electrophysiology, imaging, molecular biology) to help us understand how they communicate with each other, and how they respond to the blood chemicals listed above.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical and functional significance of a pathognomonic FOXL2 mutation in granulosa cell tumours of the ovary
Keywords-MotsClés: GRANULOSA CELL TUMOURS; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; OVARIAN CANCER; PATHOLOGY; SOMATIC MUTATIONS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: In North America, ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death due to gynaecological malignancies.  Ovarian cancers can be divided into subtypes based on their tumour cell types.  These specific subtypes are essentially different diseases and are associated with different molecular characteristics and different prognosis.  Granulosa cell tumours are one of the ovarian cancer subtypes and represent approximately 5% of all malignant ovarian tumours.  For women with this disease, the success of traditional chemotherapy has been limited, suggesting the need for more effective and subtype specific treatments.  We have recently shown that 95% of granulosa cell tumours have an identical mutation in a gene called FOXL2.  FOXL2 is a transcription factor - a protein that regulates other genes by, turning them 'on' or 'off'.  We suspect that the FOXL2 mutation found in granulosa cell tumours disrupts this regulation, which ultimately results in uncontrolled growth of granulosa cells and cancer.    Our research will attempt to elucidate the specific role of FOXL2 and how a mutation in this protein contributes to granulosa cell ovarian cancer.  We will firmly establish how common this mutation is in both granulosa cell tumours and also other similar tumours (sex cord-stromal tumours).  In addition, through carefully designed experiments, we will determine how FOXL2 influences cell growth and whether this is altered with mutated FOXL2.  We will attempt to specifically identify which genes are regulated by both the normal and mutated versions of FOXL2.  Finally, we will investigate how FOXL2 participates in cellular functions involving well known signalling pathways.  This research will contribute to the understanding of FOXL2 and its role in granulosa cell tumours.  These findings could lead to the development of new therapeutics and diagnostics for granulosa cell tumours which would result in improved management and outcomes for this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lipopolysaccharide signaling in the vasculature
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIUM; GENE TARGETED MICE; LIPOPOLYSACCHARIDE; SASH1; SEPSIS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: When bacteria or viruses enter the bloodstream, the body has to recognize these foreign infectious agents and then respond to contain these agents. Infectious agents are recognized by a family of proteins on the cell surface called Toll-like receptors (TLR). When TLRs recognize the presence of an infection they send a signal to the inside of the cell called an innate immune signal. Innate immune signals immediately begin a process called inflammation. Inflammation is the response of the body to contain infectious agents by bringing white blood cells (infection-fighting cells) to the site of the infection. However, depending on the type of infection and/or the response of the person getting the infection sometimes the process of inflammation functions incorrectly which causes various organs in the body to fail. This response of the body that occurs when various organs function poorly during severe infections is called septic shock. Septic shock occurs because the body responds inappropriately to chemicals that make up bacteria and viruses, which then impair the normal process of inflammation. Despite the continuing development of new antibiotics, when specific bacteria enter the blood and cause septic shock, the death rate is very high. It is thought that alteration of blood vessel stability plays a crucial role in this process. This proposal is designed to understand how the cells lining the inside of blood vessels, called endothelial cells, respond to bacterial and viral components through TLR. We are interested in the molecular signals within the endothelial cell that regulate the responses to infections. We have discovered a new gene that we believe plays a role in regulating the signal transmitted by specific TLRs. The studies in this grant are designed to understand how this molecule functions to send signals within the endothelial cell, and to determine whether blocking this signal can alter the outcome during septic shock.

TitreApplicationTitle: Non-specific stimulation of the immune function in early age through Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination and occurrence of childhood asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATABASES; ASTHMA; BCG VACCINATION; EPIDEMIOLOGY; POPULATION HEALTH; VACCINATION REGISTRY
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is the most common chronic disease among children, a challenge for health care, and a burden for individuals and the society. The Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine, given to protect against tuberculosis, stimulates the general immune response but inhibits some immune mechanisms related to allergic diseases such as asthma and hay fever. As a result, the BCG vaccine could indirectly help in asthma prevention. Studies relating to the effect of BCG vaccination on asthma occurrence have not provided a clear answer, some suggesting no effect, while others observed increased and decreased risks. A program of BCG vaccination was held in Quebec between 1949 and 1974, and all vaccinations were compiled in a registry. Our study aims to determine whether BCG vaccination, through its influence on immunity during early life, is associated with the occurrence of asthma in the Quebec population. We will use existing administrative databases to follow a group of 70,000 individuals born in 1974 for occurrence of asthma until 1994. The databases that we will use include the Birth, Death, and BCG Vaccination registries, and Medical Services and Hospitalizations databases from the public health system. We will compare the proportion of asthmatics, those who had medical visits or hospitalizations with a diagnosis of asthma, between subjects BCG vaccinated and those not vaccinated. We will also conduct interviews on a subset of 1,600 participants to document individual characteristics, especially those that may have influenced whether they received the BCG vaccine and their risk of asthma. This will allow us to take into account in our analyses factors such as occupation and smoking status of the parents. Statistical techniques are available to combine the results from the whole population and from the subset interviewed. Our study will contribute to the knowledge on mechanisms and factors linked to asthma occurrence, which ultimately will help establish preventive strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Femoroacetabular Impingement: Correlating Hip Morphology to Changes in Cartilage and Subchondral Bone
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS PREVENTION; CARTILAGE IMAGING; HIP IMPINGEMENT; HIP MOBILITY/DEFORMITY; SURGICAL PLANNING; THREE DIMENSIONAL IMAGING AND KINEMATICS
Abstract-Résumé: Femoro-acetabular impingement (FAI) is a known cause of hip pain and possibly a major cause of adult hip osteoarthritis. The relationship between cam-type FAI deformity characteristics and joint degradation to better identify 'at-risk' patients requiring corrective surgery will be scrutinized to gain a better understanding of the condition's natural history.  The influence of certain morphologies (e.g. size and location of the deformity) will be analyzed to determine if this leads to aberrant loading of regions of the cartilage and subchondral bone, resulting in cartilage damage and joint degradation. Additionally, this research will determine if changes in the subchondral bone precede cartilage degeneration.   The methodology for establishing the morphology/cartilage degeneration relationship includes Magnetic Resonance Image analysis, three-dimensional motion analysis and computer simulation/finite element analysis.   The outcomes of this research may lead to a reduction in total hip replacement cases by as much as 70%, saving many Canadians from a painful and debilitating condition and reducing costs to the Canadian health care system by as much as $290 million annually.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the E74-like transcription factor 3 (ELF3) in airway immune responses to antigen
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY IMMUNE RESPONSES; INFLAMMATION; LUNG; T CELL DIFFERENTIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma has increased dramatically in prevalence and severity over the past three decades. Reduced early life exposure to infectious microbes has been attributed to this increase, which becomes the basis for the "Hygiene Hypothesis". Asthma is caused by dysregulated immune responses in the respiratory mucosa and both genetic as well as environmental factors are involved. This dysregulation is due to exaggerated T-helper 2 (TH2)-driven responses that lead to the production of cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-4, -5, and -13. These cytokines promote eosinophil infiltration, immunoglobulin E (IgE) production, mucus hypersecretion and airway hyperreactivity. Therefore, knowledge of T cell differentiation in relation to pulmonary immune responses is critical to the understanding of the pathogenesis of asthma. Our work previously funded by the CIHR has revealed that the E74-like transcription factor, (Elf3), regulates cytokine induction in the lung. Our recent work in a knockout mouse model suggests that Elf3 is involved in T cell differentiation. Our present application is to investigate the role of Elf3 in T cell differentiation both in vitro with cultured primary T cells and in vivo with mouse models. Our proposed research will gain insights into the mechanisms of T cell differentiation in pulmonary immune responses.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and functional characterization of cardiac progenitor cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC PROGENITOR CELLS; CARDIAC REGENERATION; CELL PROLIFERATION AND DIFFERENTIATION; CELL TRANSPLANTATION; DEVELOPMENTAL PHARMACOLOGY; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Heart function is compromised in several forms of heart disease due to the loss of muscle cells. It is believed that increasing the number of muscle cells will have a positive impact on the contractile ability of the diseased heart. Cell transplantation is emerging as a favorable strategy to repair the damaged heart tissue. A variety of donor cells (e.g. fetal and stem cell derived heart muscle cells, skeletal myoblasts, and adult stem cells) were shown to improve heart function after transplantation into diseased hearts. There is no general consensus on the type of cell that is better suited for myocardial repair. We have recently discovered the existence of muscle precursor cells in the embryonic mouse heart after chambers are fully formed. We confirmed that these precursor cells can generate mature heart muscle cells. We believe that embryonic heart precursor cells have ideal features of a donor cell such as a) potential to form new heart muscle cells that can communicate with the host heart cells, b) higher growth potential compared to mature heart muscle cells and c) no tendency to form non-cardiac cell types as might be the case with stem cells. In this application, we propose to undertake further molecular and functional characterization of embryonic heart precursor cells. By better understanding mechanisms controlling heart muscle cell formation from precursor cells, we hope to reveal novel strategies for heart muscle regeneration which may ultimately facilitate the development of new cell based therapies. Further, these studies will reveal potential interactions between drugs and developing heart cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of midbody ring biogenesis during cytokinesis.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DIVISION; CYTOKINESIS; DROSOPHILA MELANOGASTER; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; RNA INTERFERENCE; SPINNING DISC CONFOCAL MICROCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Errors in cell division can lead to cancer and targeting the cell division machinery is an attractive strategy for anti-cancer therapies. Using powerful genetic tools available with the fruitfly model organism, together with high-resolution microscopy techniques, we will analyze and dissect an essential but poorly understood step in the cell division process. Our preliminary studies have identified several genes that are important at this stage of cell division and we will focus on these. Because the mechanisms of cell division have been well conserved through evolution, our findings will be relevant to our understanding of the division of human cells. Thus our findings may guide future strategies for anti-cancer therapies.
