TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the Effects of Alcohol Misuse on the Neuropsychological and Neuropathological Outcome from Traumatic Brain Injury: A Longitudinal Study.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL INTOXICATION; CHRONIC ALCOHOL ABUSE; CONCURRENT DISORDERS; MR BRAIN IMAGING; NEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL ASSESSMENT; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is one of the leading causes of death and disability in persons under the age of 50 years. Alcohol misuse is a significant risk factor for TBI. The prevalence of alcohol intoxication in hospital patients presenting to the Emergency Department with head trauma ranges from 37% to 53%. Patients who are intoxicated at the time of TBI have been found to be more difficult to manage and treat, have worse recovery, and consequently place an increased economic burden on the health care system. However, it is unclear whether poor recovery following an intoxicated-TBI is due to the negative effects of acute alcohol intoxication at the time of injury, or simply due to the consequences of pre-injury alcohol abuse that is common in this population. To date, our current understanding of the effects of alcohol misuse on outcome from TBI is limited. The purpose of this study is to examine the relative contributions of day-of-injury alcohol intoxication and pre-injury alcohol misuse on the neuropsychological and neuropathological outcome from TBI. This study will recruit patients treated at the Emergency Department of Vancouver General Hospital and Lions Gate Hospital who have sustained a TBI. Participants will undergo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and neuropsychological testing at 6 weeks and 12 months post injury. Neuropsychological outcome will focus on various neurocognitive abilities (e.g., attention and memory) and neurobehavioural outcomes (e.g., emotional and quality of life factors). Neuropathological outcome will be evaluated using a sophisticated MRI technology, diffusion tensor imaging, that will assess microstructural damage in the brain. This study will lead to a greater understanding of the role of alcohol on outcome from TBI which will facilitate the development of more effective treatment and rehabilitation options for this population.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathogenesis of age-related macular degeneration (AMD)
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVANCED GLYCATION ENDPRODUCTS; AGE RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID BETA; CHRONIC INFLAMMATION; DRUSEN
Abstract-Résumé: Age related macular degeneration (AMD) is the most common cause of irreversible vision loss in the elderly. Each year 80,000 Canadians are diagnosed with a form of AMD. At present, there are an estimated 1 million people in Canada with AMD, and this number is expected to double by 2031. There are treatments to slow the progression of AMD and vision loss, but we do not know how to prevent AMD from occurring. In order to prevent AMD, we need to know more about how and why AMD develops.  Earlier studies identified that AMD is a disease in which the photoreceptor cell in the retina degenerates and eventually dies. These cells do not regenerate. Once these cells die, they are never replaced. The loss of the photoreceptor cell causes blindness. Neighboring cells in the eye, the retinal pigment epithelial cells (RPE), support and maintain the health of the photoreceptor cell. However, in AMD, RPE do not function normally, and therefore they no longer support the photoreceptor cell.  We will determine what causes the RPE cells to become abnormal in the early stages of AMD. Drusen accumulate near the RPE. Drusen are a hallmark of the early stage or 'dry' form of AMD. We will focus on two components of drusen, advanced glycation end products (AGEs) and amyloid beta. Our experiments will focus on the effects of these two abnormal products on RPE function. We showed that these products caused RPE to abnormally secrete cytokines. These cytokines promote swelling and inflammation in the retina. Our hypothesis is that AGEs and amyloid beta cause RPE to change their gene expression patterns, with these newly induced gene products causing retinal inflammation. Inflammation is known to promote AMD. If proven correct, we will be the first to show that drusen components, specifically AGEs and amyloid beta, cause pro-inflammatory events in the eye. These results will allow us to develop novel first-in-class strategies using AGEs and amyloid beta as targets to prevent and treat AMD.

TitreApplicationTitle: PPARalpha as a Mediator of Sex Differences in Autoimmunity
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES; EXPERIMENTAL AUTOIMMUNE ENCEPHALOMYELITIS; PEROXISOME PROLIFERATOR-ACTIVATED RECEPTOR ALPHA; SEX DIFFERENCES AUTOIMMUNITY; SEX HORMONES; T HELPER CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease where the individual's own immune system goes awry and mounts repeated attacks on brain and spinal cord myelin. Myelin is the protective coating on nerves that enables them to conduct signals from the brain to other parts of the body. When myelin is destroyed, nerve conduction is disrupted, resulting in such symptoms as muscle weakness, blindness, loss of sensation, and cognitive dysfunction.  For reasons that are still unclear, MS affects women three times more often than men. The goal of this research program is to determine the underlying reasons for the sex-based differences in the prevalence of MS. To this end, we conduct studies using the animal model of MS, experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). Previous work by our group and others has revealed that sex differences in the development of EAE may relate in part to the ability of male sex hormones (androgens) to dampen the activity of myelin-reactive T cells. Additionally, we have made progress towards identifying the genes that mediate the effects of androgens on the immune response. Our studies have shown that male sex hormones induce the expression of Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARalpha) in T cells and that this gene has suppressive effects on the activity of these cells.  The major objective of our research is to study in more depth the mechanism of how male sex hormones limit the activity of myelin-reactive T cells during EAE and to test the hypothesis that these hormones suppress the activity of T cells by increasing the expression of PPARalpha. This research will provide insights into why females preferentially develop multiple sclerosis. Moreover, elucidation of the molecular mechanism of how male sex hormones dampen the immune response may lead to the discovery of new targets for drug development in the treatment of MS.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Serine carboxypeptidases that inactivate short vasoactive peptides: roles in vasoconstriction and proliferation of vascular SMCs
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOTENSIN; CARBOXYPEPTIDASES; CATHEPSIN A; ENDOTHELIN; REMODELLING; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; TRANSGENIC MICE; VASCULAR PEPTIDES
Abstract-Résumé: Blood flow in organs is controlled by small peptide hormones (vasoactive peptides) that influence both arterial blood pressure and the ability of arterial wall to rebuild itself after injury (so called remodelling).  The blood and tissue levels of these peptides are controlled by 2 mechanisms: through their synthesis and through their inactivation by the enzymes that are capable of cleaving them.  Our previous studies identified one of such enzymes, cathepsin A that in addition to its primary location inside the cellular vesicles responsible for degradation of big molecules, can be also transported to the cell surface and even secreted from cells.  We have developed a genetically modified strain of mice that do not produce active cathepsin A and demonstrated that these mice rapidly develop high blood pressure, enlargement of the heart and the deterioration of its function.  Aorta, lungs, and skin of cathepsin A-deficient mice also produce fewer elastic fibers that are normally responsible for high resiliency of those tissues.  Now we will use this experimental animal model to explore detailed mechanism by which cathepsin A affects structure and function of vascular system.  We will also study mice deficient in serine carboxypeptidase 1, another enzyme that can also inactivate vasoactive peptides. By testing an additional mice strain, deficient in both cathepsin A and serine carboxypeptidase 1, we will get insight into the functional engagement of these two enzymes in pathophysiology of hypertension and explore whether their induction would have any therapeutic value.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diagnosis, pathophysiology and treatment of adult somnambulism
Keywords-MotsClés: EEG; PARASOMNIAS; POLYSOMNOGRAPHY; SLEEP DEPRIVATION; SPECT
Abstract-Résumé: Despite almost 5 decades of clinical and laboratory investigations of sleep disorders, relatively little is known about the mechanisms which give rise to sleepwalking (somnambulism). Sleepwalking occurs in 4% to 17% of children and is far more common in adults (approximately 4%) than commonly acknowledged. Patients suffering from this sleep disorder often consult due to a history of aggressive and/or injurious behaviour during sleep. In a significant number of cases, patients report having suffered serious injuries (e.g., contusions, fractures to limbs, rib cage, multiple lacerations) and/or having attacked a bed partner during an episode. Diagnosing sleepwalking with objective instruments such as sleep laboratory assessments is often difficult as episodes rarely occur in the laboratory. Establishing a correct diagnosis is vital for the patient's proper treatment as well as in light of the growing number of medico-legal cases of sleep-related violence. One aim of the proposed research program is to develop an investigative protocol that will allow researchers and clinicians to establish a laboratory-based diagnosis for sleepwalking. The infrequency with which episodes occur in the laboratory has also hampered the study of physiological variables associated with sleepwalking. In a series of studies, we showed that sleep deprivation significantly increases the frequency and complexity of somnambulistic events recorded in the laboratory.  A second aim of the proposed research is to elucidate our understanding of sleepwalking by recording sleepwalkers' brain activity during sleep and wakefulness both before and after a period sleep deprivation.  We also plan to study underlying brain processes during the episodes themselves. Taken together, these studies should a) lead us to a better understanding of why some people suffer from sleepwalking, b) help develop an objective protocol for its diagnosis, and c) guide future clinical treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of global post-translational modifications, histone variants and linker histones in chromatin folding and function.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYTICAL ULTRACENTRIFUGE; CHROMATIN; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; FLUORESCENCE RECOVERY AFTER PHOTOBLEACHING; HISTONES; MASS SPECTROMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: DNA is the repository molecule for genetic information. In multicellular organisms, like humans, the DNA strands are associated with specific proteins called histones. Portions of the DNA are wrapped around histones forming tight coils. The association between DNA and histones, called chromatin, helps to store the large amount of DNA within the limited space of the cell nucleus. This also helps to regulate the expression of genes. Expression of genes results in the downstream synthesis of a functional gene product. This gene product may be a protein or an RNA that is required to carry out activities within the cell. The way in which the different histones are precisely arranged onto the DNA is very important for chromatin function. Also, metabolic (chemical) modifications of histones such as acetylation and/or phosphorylation, play a critical role in fine-tuning the histone-DNA interactions which allow for the proper storage and expression of genes. Understanding the transitions undergone by chromatin as a result of these structural and metabolic changes is of utmost importance in order to ascertain the mechanisms involved in altered chromatin conformations which occur in many genetic diseases such as cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pharmacological and Social Smoke Exposure as Differential Predictors of Smoking Initiation in Adolescents: The AdoQuest Cohort
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ADOLESCENTS; NICOTINE DEPENDENCE; PSYCHOSOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SMOKING; TOBACCO
Abstract-Résumé: Recent surveys show that many children and teenagers in Canada live with smokers at home and inhale secondhand smoke.  Quebec is the province where the percentage of smokers is highest, which means that children and teenagers in Quebec are more likely to live with a smoker than anywhere else in Canada.  Importantly, inhaling secondhand smoke is linked to serious diseases, even among non-smokers.  Studies now show that inhaling secondhand smoke is not only linked to diseases, but possibly also to starting to smoke.  Scientists have found that non-smoking children who inhale secondhand smoke are more likely to start smoking when they are teenagers, compared to children who do not inhale secondhand smoke.  Other scientists have found that non-smoking adults who inhale secondhand smoke at work are more likely to feel negative physical sensations similar to withdrawal effects.  Another group of scientists found that non-smoking children who inhale secondhand smoke are more likely to report having symptoms of feeling dependent on nicotine (the addictive substance in cigarettes).  Scientists can measure exposure to secondhand smoke in people's saliva or hair.  Recently, scientists found that the speed with which people metabolize nicotine in their body is determined by certain DNA genes.  Our project seeks to recruit students in 7th grade in French-speaking high schools, a time that is typically before students start smoking.  Students will answer questions about their beliefs about smoking and its consequences.  We will collect a saliva and hair sample to measure exposure to secondhand smoke.  We will also rub a swab on the inside of their mouth to help us identify the gene for nicotine metabolism.  The students will be contacted twice each year during high school so we can identify those who start smoking.  The aim of the study is to see whether there is a physiological pathway, due to secondhand smoke exposure, that leads to increased smoking risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Régénération différentielle de la peau humaine: Voies de spécialisation des cellules souches cutanées
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULES SOUCHES; CULTURE CUTANEE; DIFFERENCIATION ET PROLIFERATION DES CELLULES CUTANEES; GENIE TISSULAIRE; PEAU; PLAIES ET BRULES
Abstract-Résumé: Ce projet s'inscrit dans le cadre de la chaire de recherche du Canada en Cellules Souches et Genie Tissulaire qui vise a reconstruire differents organes humains in vitro a partir de cellules postnatales, dont la peau, la cornee (oeil), les vaisseaux sanguins et les valves cardiaques. Il porte sur la regeneration de la peau humaine et les voies de specialisation des cellules souches (cellules responsables de la regeneration et du maintien des tissus) cutanees postnatales. La peau est un organe fascinant pour l'analyse des cellules souches et de leurs voies de differenciation puisque l'epiderme se renouvelle a tous les 28 jours. Nous avons identifie 2 populations des cellules souches dans la peau au niveau des follicules pileux (FASEB Journal 22:1404, 2008). Le but du projet est d'ameliorer nos connaissances des cellules souches de l'epithelium et de mieux definir certains signaux provenant du derme ou de l'epithelium, qui permettent le maintien des cellules souches ou leur differenciation terminale. Les informations nouvellement acquises serviront a ameliorer la qualite des peaux reconstruites in vitro par genie tissulaire. Les retombees de ce projet s'inscrivent dans la generation de modeles in vitro de culture d'epiderme et de peaux reconstruites qui sont utiles pour des etudes fondamentales ou appliquees en physiologie, pathologie et dermatoabsorption. Ainsi, ils ont servi a demontrer l'effet drastique sur les cellules humaines de composants actifs utilises dans les produits cosmetiques antirides (British Journal of Dermatology 156(3):433, 2007). Les retombees cliniques se situent dans le domaine de la guerison des plaies chroniques tels les ulceres cutanes ou les blessures graves comme celles dont souffrent les patients brules profondement sur une surface etendue. Il s'agit d'ameliorer la technique de culture d'epiderme autologue qui est effectuee par le LOEX pour le traitement des grands brules depuis plus de 20 ans.

ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; MALADIES A VIRUS
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of retinoid action in respiratory virus infections: potential for both benefit and harm
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; INNATE IMMUNITY; MICRONUTRIENTS; PARAMYXOVIRUSES; RETINOIDS & VITAMIN D; VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & SUPPLEMENTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Vitamins are among the most common health products used, often in mega-doses. However, relatively little is known about the mechanisms of vitamin action in either health or disease. Vitamin A has powerful effects on the eyes, on tissue repair and in maintaining immunity. Large doses of vitamin A are routinely used in developing world infants to prevent blindness and to improve resistance to childhood infections, particularly viral diseases like measles. Measles is a member of a group of viruses that cause serious disease in humans throughout the world including mumps, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and the paramyxoviruses. The last agents are responsible for a large proportion of the childhood hospitalizations in Canada and may be involved in the development of asthma. Despite these benefits, recent work has demonstrated that vitamin A and other retinoids do not always have positive effects. Several studies have shown that vitamin A supplements can actually make some virus infections worse. We have shown that retinoids can inhibit the growth of several members of this virus family in the laboratory and we have developed animal models for studying vitamin A-virus interactions. Most recently, we have shown that vitamin A supplements can relieve ferrets of many of the symptoms of severe canine distemper virus infection (CDV or 'dog measles'). We have identified key pathways that retinoids use to protect individual cells (and possibly animals) from these infections. We propose to expand these studies to better understand which of the childhood viruses are susceptible to inhibition by retinoids and which might be made worse by exposure to retinoids. We will study this interaction at multiple levels; from the genes activated by viruses and retinoids all the way to animal models of disease. This knowledge will be critical to pursue improved treatments for these infections and may also give insight into the targeted use of vitamin A supplements.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES A VIRUS
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism-based sialidase inhibitors as potential therapeutics for influenza and trypanosomal diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRALS; CHAGAS; INFLUENZA; INHIBITORS; SIALIDASE; TRYPANOSOMES
Abstract-Résumé: The development of therapies for treatment of viral diseases has proved to be much more challenging than for bacterial infections. Despite stunning successes such as the AIDS drugs, the development of resistant virus strains has generally required use of combination therapies of two or more drugs. A new therapeutic strategy has recently been developed for influenza, involving a drug that slows a viral enzyme, a sialidase, which cuts a sugar (sialic acid) off the surface of the cell that has been invaded, thereby stopping spread of the virus. The drugs currently available, Tamiflu and Relenza, are now being stockpiled in large quantities by many countries in the face of the very real danger of an influenza pandemic, especially one evolving from avian influenza. Unfortunately, at the same time, strains of influenza virus that are resistant to Tamiflu are now in common circulation. Consequently new influenza therapeutics are urgently needed, preferably incorporating a design that minimizes the probability of development of resistance. Our laboratory has recently uncovered the detailed mechanism by which these enzymes, sialidases, work, and thereby developed and synthesized effective inhibitors of these enzymes that are highly specific for viral enzymes, and do not affect their human counterparts. Since they closely mimic the structure of the natural sialic acid substrate they should be much less likely to induce resistance development. These compounds work as highly effective anti-viral agents against most, but not all, viral strains in cell-based assays. We now propose a series of studies to probe why they show such strain-dependent variability, to see if the compounds work as anti-viral agents in animals (mice), and to design and synthesise even more effective inhibitors based upon what we have learned. We shall also apply a parallel approach to the development of anti-trypanosomal agents for treatment of Chagas disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Perceptual and cognitive mechanisms of audio-visual speech perception in older and younger adults
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; AUDITION; AUDITORY-VISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION; COGNITION; LANGUAGE; SENSORY FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: With notable exceptions (e.g., communicating by telephone), a person can both hear the speech signal and see the speech cues produced by his/her communication partner.  Using auditory and visual speech information (i.e., lipreading) to understand speech is referred to as audio-visual (AV) speech perception.  Both normal-hearing and hearing impaired persons perform markedly better on AV speech perception tasks than on auditory (A) or visual (V) tasks alone.  This is ecologically advantageous because speech perception typically takes place in less than ideal acoustical environments (e.g., noise, etc.).  Recent studies of AV speech perception in older adults have left many issues unresolved. We will investigate the AV speech perception abilities of healthy young and older adults.  Our short-term objectives are to describe and understand aspects of bimodal (auditory and visual) speech processing and integration by investigating the sensory, perceptual, and cognitive processes involved in AV speech perception.  Our long-term objectives are to understand the individual differences that contribute to AV speech perception and the brain mechanisms that which underlie the integration of speech signals.  Given the importance of communication in society, our research promises to address quality of life issues for elderly individuals, many of whom have hearing loss (estimated at more than 60 % among individuals aged 75+ years).  Our results may inform guidelines for communication strategies that could be used by and intervention programs that could be developed for older persons with communication difficulty due to hearing/visual disabilities or cognitive impairments/declines.  Finally, our results should provide information for models of bimodal speech-perception across the lifespan.

TitreApplicationTitle: The RECOVER Program: Phase I Towards RECOVER - Outcomes and Needs Assessment in Survivors of Prolonged Mechanical Ventilation and Their Caregivers
Keywords-MotsClés: FAMILY CAREGIVING; ICU SURVIVORS; MULTI-CENTRE PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY; PHYSICAL FUNCTIONING; QUALITATIVE NEEDS ASSESSMENT; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Towards RECOVER will be the very first study to provide an in-depth characterization of the long-term functional, mental health, quality of life outcomes and rehabilitative needs of a broad sample of Intensive Care Unit (ICU) survivors of prolonged mechanical ventilation and their caregivers. It will provide essential quantitative and qualitative outcomes data needed to design the RECOVER trial- a future multidisciplinary rehabilitation intervention including early physical rehabilitation and a family psychoeducational intervention - to optimize patient and caregiver outcomes after an episode of critical illness.     In Towards RECOVER, we will collect in-person multi-centre follow-up data on 300 ICU survivors (mechanically ventilated for at least one week) and their family caregivers for the first two years after their ICU stay. Survivors and caregivers will complete standardized outcome assessments of physical and mental functioning and quality of life 1-week, 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post ICU stay. A sub-set of participants (2 survivors and 2 caregivers per research site) will also participate in qualitative interviews 6, 12, and 24-months post ICU stay to examine their experiences and support needs during their recovery, rehabilitation and return to community living. We will perform a detailed evaluation of the patient and caregiver long-term outcomes and qualitative data and the results of these quantitative and qualitative analyses will inform the design of the RECOVER trial.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring and predicting cognitive impairment in the geriatric clinic
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITIVE REHABILITATION; COGNITIVE SCREENING; DEMENTIA; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Disability due to cognitive or mental impairment is an increasing concern for older Canadians. People notice changes in their mental abilities as they age and some worry they may develop dementia. Health care professionals would like to improve their ability to measure mental abilities and identify those patients who are most in need of interventions to slow the rate of cognitive decline. Sophisticated techniques such as brain imaging, genetic testing or neuropsychological assessment can help predict whether mental functioning will remain stable or decline.  Unfortunately, these are too costly for regular use in most clinics.     Fortunately, brief and inexpensive screening tests are already available to most clinics. These are simple pencil-and-paper tests of memory and other mental abilities that say whether or not a person has mental impairment. With this project we will test whether these screening tests can tell us much more than just if there is cognitive impairment or not. We believe that the way people respond to specific test questions can tell us a lot about an individual's strengths and weaknesses in mental abilities. This information will guide decisions about which methods can help a particular patient compensate for impairment. We will also test whether the response to specific questions can predict who can sustain mental functioning over the next few years, so that additional expensive tests are not necessary. Finally, we will develop a new test for measuring mental ability that takes less time to complete, even for people with significant cognitive impairment. This work is important because the results will have immediate practical applications for people working in geriatric health care, even where resources are limited.

TitreApplicationTitle: An ethno-epidemiological investigation of social and environmental contexts of HIV vulnerability among IDU
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNO-EPIDEMIOLOGY; ETHNOGRAPHY; HARM REDUCTION; HIV/AIDS; ILLICIT DRUG USE AND HARMS; INJECTION DRUG USE; PUBLIC HEALTH; RISK BEHAVIOURS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Outside of Africa, it is estimated that two-thirds of new HIV infections are occurring among people who inject illicit drugs. Experts have pointed to the need to develop innovative methods of examining high-risk environments which are implicated in the transmission of HIV, and have pointed to the potential of combining ethnographic and epidemiological research methods. Innovative approaches to examining how participation in particular social contexts and environments fosters vulnerability to HIV are crucial to the development of effective interventions designed to reduce HIV transmission among this highly vulnerable population. The proposed research project will employ ethnographic methods to develop empirical information regarding how transitions into particular social contexts influence HIV risks and individual ability to engage in risk reduction among injection drug users. This information will be integrated with findings from ongoing epidemiological studies in the same locales to test socially-oriented hypotheses regarding the relationship between HIV vulnerabilities and particular social contexts. This research will help to advance the study of HIV risks among injection drug users and inform the development of social and community interventions to reduce HIV transmission.

TitreApplicationTitle: FXR: a promising target for prostate cancer treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL CYCLE; FXR; PROSTATE CANCER; URSO; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in Canadian males and the third leading cause of cancerrelated death in men in most Western industrialized countries. Estimations assume that approximately 660,000 men worldwide will be diagnosed with this form of cancer and 250,000 men will die from it in 2010.  We discovered that a series of natural or synthetic compounds, which modulate gene expression through activation of a protein named FXR, are efficient blockers of the growth of common prostate cancer cell lines.  In this application, we propose to determine the therapeutic interest of these molecules in vitro and in animals models.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of mutated GABAA receptors in the pathogenesis of idiopathic generalized epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EPILEPSY; GENETICS; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a common neurological disease affecting approximately 300 000 Canadians.  Almost half of the new cases are children. With the anti-epileptic drugs that are currently available, up to 30% of individuals with epilepsy still have uncontrolled seizures. For many others, the medication will achieve control of the seizures, but with significant side-effects, impairing their quality of life. The objective of the proposed work is to identify genes that predispose to epilepsy, and to determine how mutations in these genes lead to the disease.  The identification of these genes will allow a better understanding of epilepsy, and will eventually facilitate the design of more specifically targeted drugs to treat this chronic and disabling disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Induction of a murine model of anti-phospholipid syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ANTI-PHOSPHOLIPID ANTIBODIES; ANTI-PHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME; APOPTOTIC CELLS; ELISAS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; IMMUNIZATION; SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS
Abstract-Résumé: Anti-phospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune disease that occurs in approximately 50-70% of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) who possess anti-phospholipid antibodies (aPL), but it can also occur in individuals without SLE.  APS is defined as the presence of aPL plus a clinical event associated with aPL (such as "thrombosis" [blood clot], heart attack, or stroke).  Currently, while it is clear that aPL are associated with adverse clinical events in SLE and APS, little is known about the mechanisms that lead to their occurrence.  It is also not clear why some patients with aPL develop symptoms, while others do not.  We hypothesize that a minimum of two factors are needed to produce APS: (1) persistent and high levels of aPL in the blood; and (2) exposure of the individual to a factor (e.g., infection, inflammation, or injury) that initiates a process called "innate immune activation".  "Innate immune activation" can cause localized changes in the blood vessels that make them more prone to blood clots.  Together, aPL and "innate immune activation" can predispose patients to blood clots, especially if other risk factors (e.g., smoking) are present.  We propose to directly test this hypothesis in a mouse model by creating an environment in which both factors (aPL and "innate immune activation") are present.  The findings from this proposal have the potential to improve the quality of life for individuals living with APS.  Thrombosis is a devastating clinical manifestation of APS that can be life-threatening or result in long-term disability and life-long anticoagulation.  If we find that activation of the innate system plays a role in APS, this will provide a new approach to monitoring and treating patients with APS.  Thus, findings from our studies have the potential not only to improve the quality of life of these individuals, but also to significantly reduce the cost of medical care for patients with APS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sulfatase and aromatase pathways for estradiol synthesis in human breast cancer cells, tissues and animal models: identifying a combinatory therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: A COMBINATORY THERAPY FOR BREAST CANCER; ANIMAL XENOGRAFT MODELS; COMBINED USE OF ENZYME INHIBITORS; ENZYME KINETICS IN BREAST CANCER CELLS; ENZYMES ACTIVATING ESTROGENS; SULFATASE AND AROMATASE PATHWAYS
Abstract-Résumé: It is now well-known that most breast tumours are sensitive to estrogens, that is, these steroid hormones contribute to their growth. Inhibiting the synthesis of these molecules within the body of cancer patients has thus been explored as a means of fighting cancer. Among the present used drugs there are selective estrogen receptor modulators, such as tamoxifen. However, the existing products only give partial results, not to mention sometimes severe side effects, even for example promoting endometrial cancer. The aromatase inhibitors blocking partially estrogen synthesis gives better results, but not yet a complete therapy. We now intend to find new ways of blocking more generally the synthesis of estrogens, by deepening our understanding of how the body produces them through the action of enzymes that activate estrogens, such as estrone sulfatase and 17betahydroxysteroid dehydrogenases. We will notably experiment, in cancer cell lines and mice, a number of inhibitors able to block the action of these enzymes, in other words, able to deprive cancerous cells of active estrogens that stimulate their growth. We will identify the necessary combined use of the enzyme inhibitors. The efficacy of using a new selective estrogen receptor modulator Raloxifen alone, inhibitors of the most important enzymes proved above, or both of them, will be tested in animal models for breast cancer. In the end of this study, we will identify a combinatory therapy for different sub-types of breast cancer with varying enzyme expression profiles, for further pre-clinical studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multi-potency and Noise-induced cell fate commitment
Keywords-MotsClés: FLUORESCENT PROTEINS; GENE NETWORK; MICROFLUIDICS; MOUSE STEM CELL LINES; MULTIPOTENCY; SINGLE-CELL PCR
Abstract-Résumé: To harness the capacity of stem cells to produce many different cell types for therapy, we need to know how stem cells make the decision into which cell type to differentiate. It now appears that to a great extent stem cells play dice: randomness of fluctuations in gene activities contributes to the cell fate choice. However, the decision is also controlled by intricate genetic circuits. It is the interplay between chance and control that somehow orchestrates the production of various cells types in correct proportions. This project studies in detail the contribution of both in the example of blood stem cells that have to decide between becoming red or white blood cells. A variety of state-of-the art single-cell analysis technologies will be used to gain insight into the dynamics of cell fate decision. A practical outcome will be a better understanding of how we can more efficiently reprogram cells into a desired cell type for therapeutic purposes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Smoothelin like-1 interacts with apo-calmodulin and tropomyosin to regulate Ca2+-dependent contractile signaling in vascular smooth muscle cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM DESENSITIZATION; CALMODULIN; CONTRACTION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEIN STRUCTURE/FUNCTION; RELAXATION; SMOOTHELIN; TROPOMYOSIN; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension, referred to as high blood pressure, is a medical condition in which the blood pressure is chronically elevated. Persistent hypertension is one of the risk factors for strokes, heart attacks and heart failure, and it is a leading cause of chronic renal failure. However, only in a small minority of patients with high blood pressure can a specific cause be identified. Certain proteins that control the contraction of smooth muscle cells in the cardio-vascular system are thought to contribute to hypertension. We are investigating the role of a newly discovered protein (smoothelin-like 1, SMTNL1) in generating contractile tension in vascular smooth muscle cells. Recently, deletion of the SMTNL1 protein in animal models was found to produce a cardiovascular condition similar to that achieved with endurance-exercise training. So the SMTNL1 protein may make smooth muscle cells more contractile, leading to cardio-vascular dysfunction and contributing to morbidity and mortality. The work is expected to generate additional information about new therapeutic targets that could be of clinical significance in controlling hypertension. This will help in designing strategies to maintain proper blood pressure during healthy and diseased conditions.

ClasseRechercheFR: AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE; MALADIE DE PARKINSON
TitreApplicationTitle: Neural control of locomotor movements: Brainstem mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: LOCOMOTION; LOCOMOTOR CENTERS; MOTOR CONTROL; NEUROANATOMY; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; RHYTHMIC MOVEMENTS
Abstract-Résumé: . Locomotion is a basic motor function generated and controlled by genetically defined neuronal networks. The pattern of muscle synergies responsible for locomotor movements is generated in the spinal cord, whereas neural centers located above the spinal cord in the brainstem and brain are essential for initiating and controlling locomotor movements. One such locomotor control center in the brainstem is the Mesencephalic Locomotor Region (MLR), first discovered in cats and later found in all vertebrate species tested to date. Recent studies using functional MRI suggest that this locomotor region is also present in humans and plays a role in locomotion. Such high conservation among vertebrates is a good indication of the key importance of this structure in the functioning of the brain. In animal models, stimulation of the MLR induces locomotion and fine-tunes the power of the locomotor output - somewhat like a rheostat. The cellular mechanisms for this regulation are not yet understood and we propose to analyze this problem. For that purpose, the relative simplicity of the lamprey model is far more favourable than higher vertebrates. We propose to apply an array of neurobiological techniques in the lamprey model to examine how the MLR activates downstream brainstem cells to control locomotion and gate sensory inflow. The information we will gain is fundamental for comprehending how the nervous system initiates and controls locomotor movements. Transposed to mammals, including humans, we believe that this knowledge will be important to elaborate strategies for restoring normal function in patients with motor disorders. An example of knowledge transfer to clinical practice involves Parkinson's patients who show a loss of neurons in the MLR. Electrical stimulation of the MLR has been recently shown to improve locomotion in these patients, an exciting new approach for treatment. It is thus very important to understand better how the MLR regulates locomotion.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: B cell development
Keywords-MotsClés: B CELL DEVELOPMENT; DIFFERENTIATION; HEMOKININ 1; INTERLEUKIN 21; INTERLEUKIN 7; PREB CELL RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The white blood cells that make antibodies are called B cells.  These cells help maintain health in a world of infectious agents by providing key components to the immune systems.  Mature, functional B cells develop from less well development precursors by passing through a number of stages.  At each stage there are checkpoints which determine if everthing is in order for that stage of development.  Failure to follow the "rules" of B cell development can result serious diseases such as  immunodeficiencies, autoreactivity, or malignant transformation.  Attempts to elucidate these rules have created a rich body of knowledge that not only reveals key features of the B cell developmental pathway but more general facts widely applicable to biological systems.  Despite progress, there remain key gaps in our understanding of the developmental pathways. This grant is designed to close those gaps.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE DE PARKINSON; MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: An ecologically minded multiple hit hypothesis of Parkinsonism: Inflammatory processes.
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; CYTOKINE; MICROGLIA; NEUROINFLAMMATORY; NEUROPROTECTION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Substantial evidence suggests that the cumulative effects of multiple environmental toxins (e.g. pesticides) contribute to the development of Parkinson's disease (PD). It has also recently become apparent that viral and bacterial agents may enhance the vulnerability of neurons to environmental toxins by over-stimulating the brain's own specialized inflammatory cells, called microglia. In fact, PD brains display signs of excessive microglial activation, as well as accumulation of messenger proteins of the inflammatory system, called cytokines. In this proposal, we plan to assess the specific role of cytokines and microglial cells in the death of dopamine neurons (the same cells that are lost in PD patients) that occurs in response to exposure to an inflammatory agent in combination with the commonly used herbicide paraquat. We hypothesize that certain pro-inflammatory cytokines will contribute to the loss of dopamine neurons, whereas anti-inflammatory cytokines and associated growth factors will protect these neurons from the impact of an inflammatory challenge and paraquat administration.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux

TitreApplicationTitle: A window on promoting memory
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; CAMP; CONDITIONED PREFERENCE LEARNING; CREB; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; REAL TIME PCR
Abstract-Résumé: We will pursue the understanding of formation and prolonging of memory at the behavioural and cellular level.  We will use a relatively simple learning model in neonate mammals (rats, mice) to investigate how two inputs come together (associate) to produce learning; similar in concept to the famous Pavlov's dogs.  In our model we use odor associated with a reward signal such as stroking the neonate animal (giving pleasure such as would occur with the mother licking the pup).  The stroking actually causes stimulation of norepinephrine in the brain.  Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter with widespread influences in the brain and has been shown to be involved in memory and other brain functions.  Within cells, certain pathways seem to be important in memory formation and for even prolonging memory.  Our research is focused upon unlocking mysteries of these pathways in memory formation.  Additionally, we have found that the memory we study is sensitive to enabling longer memories than normal if certain targets in the cell are manipulated.  Our studies may lead to developments in treating developmental learning disorders or lead to understanding memory which could provide memory enhancement approaches in young and aged adults.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: The reovirus FAST proteins: Structure-function relationships and role in virus replication and pathogenesis.
Keywords-MotsClés: MEMBRANE FUSION; MEMBRANE FUSION PROTEINS; PROTEIN STRUCTURE-FUNCTION; REOVIRUSES; VIRAL PATHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Membrane fusion is an essential process involved in a diverse range of normal biological phenomena including the formation of muscle, bones and the placenta. Membrane fusion also influences how viruses infect and spread between cells. All of these processes require the activity of specific membrane fusion proteins. My research group discovered a new family of membrane fusion proteins that promote fusion of virus-infected cells to neighbouring uninfected cells. These proteins contribute to rapid cell-cell spread of the infection and virus-induced disease. We are striving to understand how these proteins function. We are also using the information obtained from these studies to identify the cellular membrane fusion proteins involved in the processes listed above.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: Emerging structural insights into prokaryotic phosphorylation systems
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; KINASE; PHOSPHATASE; REGULATION; STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins in living cells "talk" to each other for many cellular functions. One of the most common communications in all organisms is by adding (or removing) phosphate groups to proteins. As such, protein phosphorylation is a critically important regulatory mechanism. For example, addition of a phosphate group to a protein can serve to turn on (or off) the protein and triggers its biological activity. As an analogy, it would be like attaching a switch to a light bulb. Protein phosphorylation has been extensively studied in mammalian systems. By contrast, protein phosphorylation research in lower organisms such as bacteria has lagged far behind.   Our laboratory was successful in determining the first structure of a bacterial tyrosine kinase - E. coli tyrosine kinase (Etk) which is involved in cell surface protection - using a technique called crystallography. This powerful technique can provide direct visualization of the three-dimensional structure of a protein. A picture is worth a thousand words! Based on the "picture", we were able to uncover important functional insights into Etk. We are also studying a unique bifunctional bacterial enzyme, serine/threonine kinase/phosphatase AceK. (Phosphatases remove phosphate groups, in contrast to kinases.) AceK enables bacterial growth in a low-glucose, high-acetate environment. It is very rare to have both phosphate addition and removal activities within a single protein; in fact, there are only two known examples. As such, Acek is an excellent target to learn how two opposing functions are accommodated in one protein, in addition to revealing biological insights.   Through our research, we hope to gain a better understanding of bacterial phosphorylation. Since some of these proteins are uniquely found in bacteria, our knowledge of these key enzymes may have potential for the development of selective antibiotics in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism and Structure of G Protein-Coupled Receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY; CO-OPERATIVITY; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTOR; G PROTEIN-MEDIATED SIGNALLING; HEART DISEASE; LIGAND-RECEPTOR INTERACTION; M2 MUSCARINIC RECEPTOR; MATHEMATICAL MODELS; MECHANISM; OLIGOMERS; PURIFIED AND RECONSTITUTED RECEPTOR; RECEPTOR BIOPHYSICS; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Cells receive external signals--everything from light to hormones--at hundreds of different proteins or 'receptors' located on the cellular surface.  Most receptors act via transducing agents known as G proteins, and such G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are ubiquitous throughout biological systems.  They are implicated in many diseases, and they are the targets of many drugs.  Since GPCRs are so numerous, they also represent the largest pool of potential targets for new drugs and future therapeutic intervention.  The critical events of G protein-mediated signalling derive from the interaction between the receptor and the G protein, and that interaction is known to be impaired in conditions such as heart disease, Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia.  The importance of this process is self-evident, yet the nature of the interaction itself and its impairment in disease remain unknown.  Our investigation is aimed at an understanding of the mechanism whereby GPCRs signal to and through their attendant G proteins.  Our approach is based on biophysical, biochemical and pharmacological studies of natural receptors and of mutants engineered for specific experiments.  The techniques yield information on the state of the system at the molecular level.  The data are interpreted in the context of mathematically formulated, mechanistic models wherein we strive to achieve a realistic description of the signalling process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Placental Insufficiency and Aortic isthmus Flow (PIAF)
Keywords-MotsClés: AORTIC ISTHMUS FLOW; DOPPLER VELOCIMETRY; NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES; UTERO-PLACENTAL INSUFFICIENCY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, the rate of babies with foetal growth restriction is ~3.7%. In 60% of pregnancy with foetal growth restriction, the primary cause is placental insufficiency. Placental insufficiency is characterized by an increase in placental vascular resistance with a secondary decrease in placental blood flow. These physiological modifications occur between 20 and 22 weeks of gestation. Available tools to detect babies at risk of brain damage related to circulatory problems are not sensitive enough to permit delivery before these injuries occurred.  The need for tools is obvious in babies with growth restriction due to insufficient exchange at the level of the placenta. Using ultrasound techniques (Doppler velocimetry), blood flow can be measured in specific area of baby circulation including that of the placenta, the brain and many other organs. By detecting changes in flow in a specific portion of the aorta called "the aortic isthmus (AoI)", the present study aims at identifying a precise marker of the stage when the baby is about to suffer irreversible brain injury due to lack of oxygen. We have completed 2 preliminary steps, one establishing the normal pattern of flow through the AoI and the second testing on a small group of foetuses the reliability of an isthmus flow index (IFI) as a marker of lack of oxygen at the level of the brain.  A cut-off value for the IFI of 0.7 has been found, below which preventive preterm delivery would be indicated. The objective of this study is to confirm in a greater number of growth restricted babies gathered from many centers across Canada, the cut-off value of 0.7 for the IFI, as a marker for baby delivery before occurrence of cerebral damage due to lack of oxygen.  In a following study, the IFI will be incorporated in the protocol leading to the decision to deliver growth-restricted babies. A decrease in developmental problems and learning disabilities is expected with this management protocol.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fusion and cell entry by oncogenic sheep retroviruses
Keywords-MotsClés: ENTRY; ENVELOPE; FUSION; LOW PH; RECEPTOR; RETROVIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Virus entry to host cells is an essential yet poorly understood process. It can occur at the cell membrane triggered by binding to cognate receptors or in an intracellular compartment induced by a low pH. While entry of retroviruses, typified by HIV-1, is pH-independent, we have recently found that oncogenic sheep retroviruses use a pH-dependent mechanism for fusion and cell entry. The objective of the proposed research is to understand the mechanisms of fusion and cell entry by these oncogenic sheep retroviruses and their possible implications for pathogenesis. Results from these studied will also provide crucial insights into a better understanding of fusion and entry of other enveloped viruses, and may offer valuable information to the development of novel antiviral therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toward Key Principles for Assessing Integrated Knowledge Translation
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE CREATION FUNNEL; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MIXED METHODS RESEARCH; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; PARTNERSHIP; PROGRAM EVALUATION; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH METHODOLOGY; SYSTEMATIC REALIST REVIEW METHODOLOGY; TOOL FOR APPRAISING INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Health researchers are increasingly collaborating with representatives from populations under study to make research more relevant and effective. This collaboration means that research participants work alongside researchers to design, implement and analyse research that affects them. An assumption exists that participatory research enhances the health of populations because it increases the probability that health knowledge produced from the research will be adopted by the population and that the research will be more relevant to the needs of the people. The present study investigates that assumption by interviewing 30 lead investigators of participatory research projects to uncover critical issues in measuring the effectiveness of participatory research. The outcome will be a research instrument that will help academics, decision-makers, and community leaders better understand and assess the benefits of participatory research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies of the role of an Ets family protein in prostate cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CARCINOGENESIS; PROSTATE CANCER; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: This project is aimed at defining the molecular and cellular pathways which lead to prostate cancer (PCa). PCa is the most common cancer in North American males, but the mechanisms underpinning PCa emergence and progression are poorly understood. We have recently found that mice lacking a protein designated Ese3 develop prostate intraepithelial neoplasia as well as invasive PCa. Ese3 is normally expressed at high levels in the epithelial cells of the prostate gland, but our data suggest that Ese3 levels are decreased in human PCa samples. These data suggest that Ese3 may inhibit malignant transformation of prostate epithelial cells and conversely, that the loss of Ese3 may lead to PCa. To address this hypothesis, we propose to define Ese3 roles in development of PCa.   For these studies, we will capitalize on the availability of Ese3-deficient mice to first define Ese3 roles in prostate epithelial cell function and transformation. Prostate tissue/cells from the Ese3-deficient mice will be characterized in terms of prostate epithelial cell development and features and biologic properties of the malignant cells. We will then define the mechanisms whereby Ese3 influences malignant transformation, by determining how Ese3 controls one specific cell growth pathway and searching for other proteins/pathways that may be regulated by Ese3. Tissue samples from PCa patients will be examined for changes in Ese3 level and the genetic basis for such changes and their relationship to clinical/pathologic features assessed so as to define the extent to which, mechanisms whereby and clinical consequences when Ese3 expression is lowered in human PCa. These data will allow us to establish the relevance of Ese3 to human PCa and the mechanisms whereby Ese3 deficiency leads to PCa. As Ese3 is also expressed in lung, breast and skin, defining the pathways that link reduced Ese3 expression to PCa provides a unique opportunity to unravel the pathogenesis of several major epithelial cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1)  plays an innate protective role in Clostridium difficile-induced colitis
Keywords-MotsClés: CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE; COLITIS; EPITHELIAL BARRIER DYSFUNCTION; HYPOXIA INDUCIBLE FACTOR-1 ALPHA; MUCOSAL INFLAMMATION; POST-TRANSLATION MODIFICATIONS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Clostridium difficile (Cdf) is a serious concern in hospitals throughout Canada and around the world. The majority of Cdf cases occur in hospitalized elederly patients on antibiotic medications. Antibiotic treatment disrupts the colonic flora, allows Cdf to over-populate the colon, and results in Cdf-associated colitis. This condition is characterized by severe diarrhea and abdominal pain, affects ~25% of hospitalized patients who undergo antibiotic treatment, and if left untreated, can develop into acute toxic megacolon. Colonic tissue from Cdf colitis displays marked pathological similarities with tissue from patients with ischaemic colitis. One hallmark of ischaemic colitis is hypoxia (i.e. a lack of oxygen), and a key regulator of the cellular response to hypoxia and other stresses is the hypoxia inducible factor (HIF). HIF has been found to play a protective role in intestinal tissue from patients with Inflammatory Bowel Diseases. We have recently found increased HIF protein in colonic tissue removed from patients with Cdf colitis. Furthermore, we have identified that purified Cdf toxins are novel activators of HIF. These preliminary studies suggest that HIF is an important regulator of the intestinal inflammation and damage that occurs in response to Cdf. This proposal will employ biochemical and physiological methods to define the link between Cdf and HIF in the development of Cdf-colitis and toxic megacolon. Model systems (i.e. genetically modified mice) will be used to examine the contributions of HIF to the development of inflammation following exposure to Cdf. In summary, this proposal will assess whether HIF plays a protective role in Cdf disease progression to acute toxic megacolon. We need to understand the specific molecular mechanism(s) by which Cdf induces colonic inflammation and tissue damage so that more effective therapeutic interventions for the Cdf-infected patient population can be developed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bcl-xL regulation and function during G2 and mitotic spindle assembly checkpoints
Keywords-MotsClés: BCL-XL; CELL CYCLE CHECKPOINT; CHECKPOINT KINASE; CHEMOTHERAPY; PHOSPHATASE; PHOSPHORYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: The Bcl-2 family of proteins stands among the most crucial regulators of cell death (apoptosis) and performs vital function in deciding whether a cancer cell will live or die after cancer chemotherapy and radiotherapy. In addition, recent studies reveal that members of the family also interface with cell cycle progression and DNA repair pathways, effects that are generally distinct from their functions in apoptosis. This study will focus on one member of the Bcl-2 family, and further analyse the mechanisms by which Bcl-xL plays roles during the cell cycle checkpoints. Many efforts are already being pursued to develop new drugs targeting anti-apoptotic bcl-2 and cell cycle regulatory family members, with the ultimate goal of improving or developing alternative therapeutic protocols for cancer therapy. Thus, it is important to explore how these key regulatory molecules interface together to improve our understanding for potential clinical use of these novel cancer chemotherapy molecules.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathogenesis and treatment of immune thrombocytopenia: Are there fundamental differences between anti-GPIba and anti-GPIIbIIIa mediated thrombocytopenia?
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNE THROMBOCYTOPENIA (ITP): AUTOIMMUNE BLEEDING DISORDER; INTRAVENOUS IMMUNOGLOBULIN G (IVIG); MONOCLONAL ANTIBODY EPITOPE MAPPING; PLATELET ANTIGENS: GPIIBIIIA VERSUS GPIB; PLATELET CLEARANCE AND PHAGOCYTOSIS; PLATELET FUNCTION AND PLATELET GENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Platelets are small blood cells responsible for forming clots at the site of bleeding. They aggregate to form a cellular plug, strengthen the coagulation system when blood vessels are injured, and are critical in preventing blood loss. Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is a disease where the immune system mistakenly produces antibodies which destroy the patient's own platelets. Thus, the patient cannot stop bleeding properly, which can lead to severe health problems or death. The antibodies in this disease attack two proteins (antigens), called GPIIbIIIa and GPIb, which are on the surface of platelets. These proteins are responsible for physically connecting platelets together and sticking to the vessel wall to stop bleeding. Approximately 70-80% ITP patients have antibodies to GPIIbIIIa, 20-40% patients have antibodies to GPIb, and some patients have antibodies to both proteins. Currently, it is not clear whether the antibodies to GPIIbIIIa and GPIb work the same (mechanism of disease), and if ITP caused by antibodies to these two proteins can be treated successfully by the same therapies. We also do not know whether some patients have more severe bleeding than others because of the specific type of antibodies in their blood (i.e. whether severity is related to the protein or the sub-section of the protein that the antibody attacks). We propose to address these questions and investigate whether antibodies against GPIb and GPIIbIIIa may act differently by causing: i) a change in platelet signalling activity, or ii) changing the physical structure of GPIIbIIIa and GPIb proteins, or iii) affecting platelet generation. We think that different antibodies may affect platelet function in a different manner, determine where platelets are destroyed, and how patients respond to current clinical therapies (e.g. removing patient's spleen or treatment with IVIG).

TitreApplicationTitle: Single gene deletions in the nematode C. elegans -working towards a mutation in every gene.
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPARATIVE GENOME HYBRIDIZATION; DEEP SEQUENCING; IDENTIFYING MUTATIONS; PCR ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Our goal in this project will be to continue providing researchers with deletion mutations in genes in the small soil nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. We will focus on a target list of genes with human homologs. This group of genes is of practical importance in human health and disease and the nemtode offers a suitable model to efficiently determine novel gene functions at the cellular and intercellular level.    Many biochemical pathways are conserved between the nematode and humans and genes within the nematode can be functionally replaced by their human homologs. In many cases these genes when dysfunctional within humans lead to inherited diseases, susceptibility to cancers or other health related problems. Understanding the basic biological function of these genes in the nematode could have direct consequences for medical diagnosis and treatment in humans. On a broader level, the availability of thousands of gene knockouts in C. elegans will provide a powerful resource to study a range of basic problems in developmental biology. The impact of this project will be to accelerate the pace of gene discovery and functional analysis of individual genes and complex gene systems.   The C. elegans Gene Knockout Facility at the University of British Columbia is part of an International Consortium. As such it is internationally recognized as a major research center for C. elegans genetics and genomic studies. The mutant strains we provide to the research community are a priceless resource. Because nematodes can be frozen these mutant strains are a permanent resource. This will be a significant and enduring legacy of Canadian science.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation and Dynamics of Mitotic spindle Assembly
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DIVISION; CHEMICAL BIOLOGY; FLUORESCENCE LIGHT MICROSCOPY; KINESIN MOTOR PROTEINS; LIVE CELL IMAGING; MITOTIC SPINDLE ASSEMBLY
Abstract-Résumé: When a cell divides, a complex machine is built to accurately separate genetic material (DNA) into two daughter cells. This machine is called the mitotic spindle, due to its shape: a broad barrel, pointed on both ends.  The spindle composed of mainly cable-like polymers called microtubules, which can connect to and move the DNA. We will study key protein molecules that interact with these polymers and understand how they are coordinated to build this DNA-segregation machine. Improper segregation of DNA can cause cells to have an abnormal amount of genetic material, an outcome often associated with cancer. Our cells have surveillance systems to monitor whether this DNA-segregating machine is properly assembled, they will not divide until the spindle is properly formed and connected to DNA. Since cancer is a disease of uncontrolled cell divisions, inhibiting spindle formation thus provides a way to block cells from dividing. Understanding how this DNA-segregation machine is built could help us to identify new targets for developing improved anti-cancer drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hedgehog signalling during mammary gland development and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; HEDGEHOG PATHWAY; MALIGNANT TRANSFORMATION; MAMMARY GLAND DEVELOPMENT; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Our lab is concerned with the mechanisms that are used by mammals to control the development of the mammary gland (mice) or breast (humans).  We are interested in these processes in embryonic animals, where mammary gland development begins, as well as in postnatal animals.  In particular we study a class of protein molecules called the Hedgehog proteins. These proteins are very important in helping to organize the three-dimensional structure of embryos and of individual tissues.  The Hedgehog proteins work by binding onto other molecules, called receptors, which then dictate how cells will participate in the formation of a tissue.  We recently discovered that a defect in the Hedgehog receptor stopped the development of the mammary gland in mice. This mouse seems also to be blocked for forming tumours in the mammary gland of some mice carrying a particular cancer gene, but not in mice carrying a different class of cancer gene.  Thus, our studies will show how the Hedgehog proteins help direct breast development as well as to understand how, when altered, they are involved in the formation of cancer in the mammary gland.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissection of growth control by the atypical cadherin Fat in Drosophila melanogaster
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DROSOPHILA; HIPPO PATHWAY; KINASES; PROLIFERATION
Abstract-Résumé: The Hippo pathway is a newly discovered genetic pathway that regulates growth that was discovered through research on the fruit fly. Mutations of this pathway have been found to lead to cancer in man and tissue overgrowth in flies. Scientists understand how defects in Hippo pathway components lead to rapid cell division and a block of normal cell death control, but do not know how the pathway is normally controlled. We will investigate the regulation of the Hippo pathway using the fruit fly as a model system.  Genetic studies have implicated 3 molecules in the regulation of the Hippo pathway (1) a cell-cell adhesion molecule called Fat, (2) a structural protein called Ex, and (3) a protein that can modify others (a kinase) called Dco. We have  found that the Dco binds to Fat and modifies it. We also found that Ex localizes to cell-cell contacts and also binds to Fat, and that growth control by Ex correlates with Ex localization to cell-cell contacts. We will determine if Dco binding to Fat is needed for growth regulation, and how Dco controls Fat activity. We will use flies to understand if the location of Ex at cell contacts is needed for stopping cell division, and use genetic screens to identify new components of the Hippo pathway to understand how it is regulated.  Mutation of the Hippo pathway is a common defect in many forms of cancer including colon, breast, lung and ovarian cancer. All known elements of the Hippo pathway are highly conserved from flies to man. By finding the genes that regulate this pathway, and understanding how it is regulated in fruit fly, we can rapidly understand the regulatory mechanisms that normally inhibit cell division, and promote death of unwanted cells. This information can be used to understand the regulation of the human Hippo pathway, and set the groundwork for studies to diagnose and treat people who develop cancer due to defects in the Hippo pathway.

TitreApplicationTitle: Androgen Receptor Corepressors, PSF and p54nrb, in Prostate Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN RECEPTOR; PROSTATE CANCER; STEROID HORMONE; STEROID RECEPTOR COREPESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Introduction - Androgens are steroid hormones produced and secreted by the testes that have been strongly implicated in prostate cancer. These hormones act by activating a protein inside the cell called the androgen receptor (AR). AR regulates specific target genes and promotes tumor growth through protein interactions with AR cofactors. Abnormal expression and function of AR cofactors was suggested promote prostate cancer progression from the androgen-sensitive into the advanced androgen-insensitive stage, for which no curative option is available. We recently found two such cofactors, called PSF and p54nrb, inhibit AR functions regardless the presence of androgens. The hypothesis of this proposal is that PSF and p54nrb play important roles on AR functions and contribute to prostate cancer progression to the advanced androgen-insensitive state.  Project description - To test these hypotheses, we will 1) define whether changes in protein levels of PSF and p54nrb affect prostate cancer growth and measure the protein levels of PSF and p54nrb in tissue samples from prostate cancer patients; 2) investigate whether changes in the activities of PSF and p54nrb impact on AR function; and 3) determine whether PSF and p54nrb regulate the expression of the AR regulated gene, clusterin. Clusterin was shown to enable prostate cancer become resistant to anti-cancer therapies.  Significance - Current therapy is only effective for androgen sensitive prostate cancer, and no cure is available when prostate cancer develops into the advance state that is androgen insensitive. Treatments that block AR function would benefit both androgen-sensitive and insensitive prostate cancer. Studies from this proposal would establish whether PSF and p54nrb can be served as novel exciting targets to control AR function in prostate cancer, providing an urgently needed alternative to current anti-androgen therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Central nervous system (CNS)controls of cancer anorexia - cachexia syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: ANOREXIA - CACHEXIA; APPETITE; HYPOTHALAMUS; PALLIATIVE CARE; SKELETAL MUSCLE; WASTING SYNDROMES
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer patients often enter into a syndrome of malnutrition and wasting, and an important part of this problem is loss of appetite (anorexia). Cancer patients generally fail to take in enough essential nutrients and this malnutrition worsens as the disease progresses. Loss of appetite is also distressing, because food and eating are an important part of family and social life and because we understand that food is essential to sustain life.  When children with cancer lose appetite, this is particularly distressing to thier parents and family.  Cancer anorexia remains a problem that is difficult to treat in advanced cancer patients.  Only a few treatments are available and these have the unwanted side effect of causing muscle wasting. Recent clinical research has alsobeen disappointing, perhaps in part due to a relatively poor understanding of the fundamental nature of cancer anorexia.    Our research team brings together experts on appetite, nutrition and weight loss, to begin a program of basic research in laboratory animals. We will identify the key pathways of cancer anorexia which occur in the brain centres where appetite is regulated, and also identify factors related to muscle wasting.  This work will be done with a view to developing treatments for the palliation of cancer -associated malnutrition and wasting in cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The sexual health of young rural Canadians: Examining positive outcomes and the gendered dynamics of power
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; GENDER; INTERVIEWS; POSITIVE SEXUAL HEALTH; POWER; QUALITATIVE; QUANTITATIVE; RURAL; SURVEY
Abstract-Résumé: Research has shown that gendered power dynamics within heterosexual relationships influence sexual health outcomes in both positive and negative ways. Gendered power dynamics are generally characterized by inequity. This inequity or imbalance in power often means that women have less power within relationships as compared to males. This imbalance in power often stems from gender - the social expectations of what it means to be a man or a woman.    This project proposes to investigate the positive aspects of sexual health and the gendered dynamics of power among young heterosexual Canadians living in rural and Northern settings in British Columbia. Adolescents living in rural and Northern communities face unique challenges as compared to their urban counterparts which may impede their ability to achieve positive sexual health. First, this project will use interviews to talk to young people about how they experience and use power within their sexual relationships. The results of these interviews will be used to develop a survey to explore the links between the gendered dynamics of power, social determinants of health (e.g. income, ethnicity), and positive (e.g. communication, pleasure) and negative (e.g. sexually transmitted infections) sexual health outcomes.   This research will improve our understanding of the sexual health of young rural and Northern Canadians, a unique and often overlooked population. The addition of a positive perspective will provide a more complete picture of young people's sexual health, which extends beyond risk and negative outcomes. Moreover, this project will help us understand how the gendered power dynamics influence both positive and negative outcomes and provide insight into issues of gender equity. This enhanced perspective will allow for the creation of programs and interventions that reach young people more effectively to improve their sexual health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation into the role of MIER1 alpha, a novel estrogen receptor co-regulator
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CHROMATIN REMODELING; CO-REGULATOR FUNCTION; NUCLEAR RECEPTOR CO-REGULATORS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: While there are many different kinds of cancer, they are all linked by a common thread: cancer cells do not know when to stop growing. In normal tissues, cells receive signals, like estrogen, from their surroundings that tell them what to do: to grow, to migrate, to die and so on. Cells pick up these signals which are then translated inside the cell into the appropriate action. In cancer cells, the signaling circuitry that controls cell growth has gone awry and the signal to grow does not get switched off. We need to know more about how this signaling circuitry works. What happens when a cell is stimulated to grow? What happens as a cell "decides" to become a cancer cell? Can we change the signaling and make the cell become normal again? These are some of the questions that we are trying to answer by studying a new cancer related gene called mier1 alpha. Our most recent work has led to the discovery of a role for MIER1 alpha specifically in breast cancer. We have found that MIER1 alpha can control the cell's response to estrogen, an important hormone for the growth of most breast cancers. When we force the tumour cells to overproduce MIER1 alpha, breast cancer growth is blocked. Our research in this proposal is aimed at uncovering how MIER1 alpha works. This will provide us with a better understanding about how the estrogen response and breast cancer growth is controlled by MIER1 alpha and ultimately, help us identify potential targets for the design of new drugs and alternative breast cancer treatments.
