TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular links between coagulation and innate immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: COAGULATION; COMPLEMENT; HEMOLYTIC UREMIC SYNDROME; INFLAMMATION; PROTEIN C; VASCULAR ENDOTHELIUM
Abstract-Résumé: In the last few decades, it has been recognized that the lining cells of the blood vessels, the endothelial cells, play a major  protective role in health and disease. When not functioning properly, disease occurs, and this is most commonly manifest by atherosclerosis, heart attacks, angina, strokes, and blood clots in the legs and lungs, all of which continue to be major causes of disability and death. The mechanisms that protect the blood vessel endothelial cells from damage are complex and not fully understood. One well-characterized system prevents blood from abnormally clotting.  Another prevents the immune system, the so-called complement system, from over-reacting and destroying any injured endothelial cells.  It is not clear how these two mechanisms are co-ordinated.  We have recently identified links between the two, but much more work is necessary to better understand the relationship. This new knowledge will lead to a clearer view as to why disease occurs, and will allow for the development of new therapies that enhance the protective activities of both, thereby preventing blood vessel disease.   The overall goal of our studies is to understand how the blood clotting system interacts with the complement system, and how these two systems are co-ordinated to protect the blood vessel endothelial cells from damage that would lead to heart disease and stroke.  We hope to determine how genetic abnormalities in some of the components of these systems increase the risk of disease, which will allow for the development of new and more effective therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Basis of Profibrinolytic Platelets and White Blood Cells in Quebec Platelet Disorder.
Keywords-MotsClés: BLEEDING DISORDERS; FIBRINOLYSIS; GENETIC TESTING; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Normally, platelets help clot formation by sticking at sites of blood vessel injury and releasing substances that protect clots from being dissolved too rapidly.  We are studying an inherited illness, called the Quebec Platelet Disorder (QPD), that causes excessive bleeding.  Individuals with this condition have increased levels of a "clot busting" enzyme activator called urokinase (uPA) in their platelets; this enzyme is found in trace amounts in normal platelets.  uPA is a potent activator of the clot dissolving pathway in blood.  In the QPD, changes in uPA convert platelets from "clot formers" into "clot busters".  The result is a high risk of bleeding.  We have been looking at normal and QPD cells to understand how normal clot-protective platelets are produced and how platelets and some other types of blood cells are changed into "clot busters" in the Quebec Platelet Disorder.  We now know that the QPD increases uPA as stem cells mature to make platelets and white blood cells (cells that fight infection and normally make uPA to help break down clots). We have identified that patients with QPD have a duplicated copy of the uPA gene, and we have developed tests to detect this extra copy to help diagnose individuals with bleeding problems. We now want to determine how and why this extra copy of the uPA gene changes platelets, and some white blood cells, into "clot busters". This will help us work on designing better treatments for this serious bleeding disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of synaptic vesicle recycling
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOCYTOSIS; GENE TRANSFER; HIPPOCAMPAL CULTURES; SIRNA; SYNAPTIC VESICLES
Abstract-Résumé: Synaptic vesicles contain chemicals that allow cells in the brain to communicate.  Synaptic vesicles are re-used, and recent evidence suggests that the rate of vesicle recycling may be limiting in some circumstances.  Controlling this rate may allow some brain connections to work more efficiently, thereby strengthening some circuits.  This is thought to contribute to learning and memory.  Interestingly, the protein Sept3 appears to interact with a critical component of the recycling process, dynamin-1, and may be a crucial regulator of synaptic vesicle recycling.  The studies outlined in this proposal will shed new light on how synaptic vesicles recycle and may provide new insights into diseases such as Schizophrenia were the release and recycling of synaptic vesicles may be abnormal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional studies of Na/Ca -K exchangers (NCKX)
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS; MEMBRANE TRANSPORTERS; MOLECULAR MODELLING; RETINAL PIGMENT EPITHELIUM; SKIN PIGMENTATION; SODIUM-CALCIUM EXCHANGE
Abstract-Résumé: Calcium homeostasis in cells is of critical importance for the proper functioning of cells in all tissues in our body. Our laboratory has a long standing interest in the SLC24 gene family of NCKX proteins that are important for proper calcium homeostasis in retinal rod and cone photoreceptors, in many neurons in the brain and in pigment producing cells in the skin and in the eye. We conduct structure-function studies of NCKX proteins to elucidate how NCKX proteins work. One part of our research concerns the role of NCKX5 in pigment synthesis in the skin and in the eye. The human population displays a striking variation in skin, hair and eye pigmentation and the underlying molecular mechanism remains one of the outstanding problems in human biology. Work during the past several years has yielded great progress in the identification of sequence variants in the few genes within the human genome that are associated with variations in human skin pigmentation. One of the more striking examples is the recent identification of a sequence variant in the SLC24a5 gene (encoding the fifth member of the family of NCKX proteins) that, when present on both chromosomes, is responsible for light skin in people from European descent. It is possible that the same sequence variant constitutes a risk factor for people from European descent for developing age-related macular degeneration, the most prevalent blinding disease in the elderly. Other members of the NCKX family are involved in calcium transport, although NCKX5 function in pigment producing cells remains elusive. NCKX5 is also found in the eye where it plays a major role in melanin pigment synthesis in the retinal pigment epithelium. In this application we propose experiments to elucidate the role of the NCKX5 protein in pigment synthesis in the skin and in the eye.

TitreApplicationTitle: Activity-driven structural synaptic remodeling
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; LEARNING AND MEMORY; NEUROLIGIN; NMDA RECEPTORS; PHOTOCONDUCTIVE STIMULATION; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Changes in synaptic connections are thought to underlie learning and memory, and are a fundamental part of human cognitive function. Using hippocampal neurons grown on silicon wafers, we have established a unique and robust experimental paradigm to investigate the 3 parts of this process - the Dendrite, the Axon and the Synapse between them. Combined with our discovery of a new way to guide axons to their target, we can use our neuronal-silicon interface to understand the mechanisms underlying this important part of brain function. By determining the roles of key molecules involved, insight into the mechanism of cognitive dysfunction in conditions such as autism could be gained and may ultimately provide a target for therapeutic intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Built environments as determinants of health in young Canadians, and the role of social environments as intermediary factors
Keywords-MotsClés: BUILT NEIGHBOURHOOD ENVIRONMENTS; BUILT SCHOOL ENVIRONMENTS; CHILD HEALTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; INJURY; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Two important aspects of physical health in children are obesity and injury.  We will explore whether features of the built environment contribute to obesity and injuries in Canadian children.   As part of an organized effort to collect health data on children in 45 countries, we conduct a survey every 4 years in grade 6-10 Canadian youth.  In 2004, CIHR funded us to perform in-depth analyses of this Canadian survey, and to develop a follow-up survey of Ontario students. This research focused on risk-taking and injury.  Additional analyses allowed us to understand other aspects of child health.    The focus of our renewal grant is the "built environment" and its effects on the physical health of children.  The built environment refers to physical features of the environment such as the presence and condition of parks, walking paths, school facilities, and safe homes. We contend that, if we make changes to the built environment, we can reduce injuries and obesity in young Canadians.      In 2009-10, we will survey 90,000 Canadian children.  It is possible to link these survey data with public information describing school, neighbourhood and home environments.  Using these sources, we will study the effects of the built environment on obesity and injury. We will also study whether social, behavioural and geographic factors influence the ability of the built environment to impact obesity and injury.  Social factors will include wealth, behavioural norms, and cohesion within schools and neighbourhoods.  Behavioural factors will include diet, physical inactivity, and risk-taking. Geographic factors will include the province, community size, and climate of the communities in which youth live.    Our long-term goal is to inform health policies and prevention strategies for obesity and injury. CIHR suggests that both are leading research priorities, as are studies of the built environment.  Study of these relationships will lead to novel research for Canadian youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Betaine-dependent methylation pathways in preimplantation embryos and their contribution to fetal, placental and offspring health
Keywords-MotsClés: EMBRYO; GENE EXPRESSION; GENOMIC IMPRINTING; INFERTILITY; METHYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: There is strong evidence that the mother's nutrition, health, and environment during the earliest stages of pregnancy immediately after conception can significantly affect the health of the embryo and the fetus and placenta into which it develops. Also, the treatment of human infertility by assisted reproduction technologies (ART), in which multiple eggs are obtained from women, fertilized, and cultured for an extended period before being transferred into the uterus, has been very effective and produced millions of babies, but there is increasing evidence that how eggs and very early embryos are handled during ART can cause health problems in the fetus, placenta, and offspring. In this work, we will be investigating mechanisms that may be important in causing such problems, concentrating on one biochemical pathway that we have identified in embryos that may be involved in setting up patterns of gene expression in the fetal/placental unit that can then last throughout life. This pathway involves the metabolism of a compound called betaine. A part of the betaine molecule called a methyl group is transferred to many other compounds in cells, and such "methylation" is instrumental in setting gene expression patterns among other important processes. We hope to show that creating the conditions in which this pathway can function normally in very early embryos will prevent some of the problems that arise in fetuses and placentas during pregnancy, and in babies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Serotonin and reward-related behaviours: opposing roles of 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; DOPAMINE; DRUG ABUSE; IMPULSIVITY; NICOTINE; SEROTONIN RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Neurons using the neurotransmitter serotonin (5-HT) project widely through the brain, and 5-HT alters neuronal function via multiple receptors.  Given the ubiquitous and complex nature of 5-HT signalling it is not surprising that manipulations of 5-HT function alter a wide range of different behaviours, and that 5-HT has been implicated in many psychiatric disorders including anxiety, depression, schizophrenia, impulse control disorders, eating disorders and addiction.  My research has found that activating 5-HT2C receptors reduces addiction-like behaviour and impulsiveness.  Blocking the 5-HT2A receptor also reduces some of these behaviours.  The present proposal explores the potential clinical utility of 5-HT2C receptor agonists and 5-HT2A receptor antagonists for treating "motivational" disorders such as addiction, impulsivity and abnormal feeding.  We are especially interested in 1) how these drugs alter nicotine self-administration,  relapse to nicotine seeking and impulsiveness, 2) the sites in the brain that mediate the effects of these drugs, and the circuits that mediate these different behaviours, and 3) how 5-HT2A receptor blockade and 5-HT2C receptor activation alter dopamine function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sex Differences in Cardiac Excitation-Contraction Coupling: Impact of Calcium Load and Ischemia/Reperfusion
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIAS; CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS; ISCHEMIA; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; REPERFUSION; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: There are important differences in heart function between men and women.  Men and women also tend to get different heart diseases.  Sex differences in heart function and heart diseases might be caused by differences in individual heart cells.  One possibility is that the control of calcium levels inside heart cells differs between men and women.  The heart needs calcium to contract, but too much calcium can lead to heart disease.  Still, we know very little about sex differences in the control of calcium in heart cells, because most experiments use cells from male animals or don't specify the sex.  Our study will look at how sex differences in the control of calcium affect the ability of the heart to contract normally and when the heart is exposed to high calcium loads.  We will also look at how male and female heart cells deal with calcium in conditions such as a heart attack, where the blood supply to the heart is blocked.  The goal of our study is to discover whether sex differences in the control of calcium change the way heart cells function, especially when cells are stressed with high calcium loads or a heart attack.  This will allow us to find out if changes in the heart cells themselves are responsible for differences in heart function between males and females.  Our results are important because they will help us understand why men and women respond differently to diseases like heart attacks.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunoregulatory functions of the IL-27 p28 subunit-CLF complex
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNITY; CYTOKINE RECEPTORS; CYTOKINES; HEMATOPOIESIS; INFLAMMATION; MYELOMA
Abstract-Résumé: Cytokines of the IL-6 family are mediators released in large amounts at sites of infection or injury. They induce and control the protective body responses such as fever, recruitment and activation of immune cells. These cytokines play also important roles in pathologies involving undesirable local inflammation such as multiple sclerosis or uncontrolled immune cell proliferation such as multiple myeloma. We study a new composite cytokine of the IL-6 family, p28/CLF. We identified p28/CLF receptor and characterized p28/CLF biological activities. Our observations suggest that p28/CLF could have beneficial anti-inflammatory functions. We will investigate the effects of p28/CLF in models of multiple sclerosis and multiple myeloma. New therapies that could improve treatments would be helpful for both pathologies: multiple sclerosis remains difficult to control and can result in patient disability. Multiple myeloma is the second most common hematological cancer and current median survival times of patients are only 3-5 years.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery and Validation of Pharmacological Probes for Understanding Protein-Protein Interactions of Focal Adhesion Signalling in Invasive Cancer Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL MIGRATION AND INVASION; CHEMISTRY; FOCAL ADHESION KINASE; FOCAL ADHESION SIGNALING; PRECLINICAL AND PHARMACOLOGICAL STUDIES; SMALL MOLECULES
Abstract-Résumé: The capacity of primary cancer to invade neighboring tissues and distant organs (metastases) is controlled by a mechanism broadly referred to as focal adhesion signaling. This mechanism allows cancer cells to become motile and to migrate to distant sites. Focal adhesion signaling is mediated by important proteins, among which the focal adhesion kinase (FAK) plays a central function. FAK is an intracellular protein that localizes to specific structures of  cell membrane called focal adhesions. Focal adhesions are important for the regulation of cancer cell's capacity to become motile and invasive. Inhibition of FAK function using genetic manipulations can prevent cancer cells from spreading and invading distant organs. Therefore, discovery of chemicals that can inhibit focal adhesion signaling proteins such as FAK will help understanding the process of cancer cell invasion, and to discover novel therapeutics to prevent cancer from metastasizing. The focus of this application is to investigate the chemistry, pharmacology, biology, and therapeutic implications of novel chemicals we identified as inhibitors of FAK function in invasive cancer cells. The outcome of this research will be to deepen our understanding of mechanisms that control cancer invasion. In addition, this research will accelerate our strides towards discovery of efficient therapy to manage invasive cancers, where the currently available therapies have only a limited efficacy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural Encoding in the Visual Cortex: Engineering Principles for Advanced Neural Prosthetics
Keywords-MotsClés: DATA COMMUNICATION; DELTA-SIGMA MODULATION; ELECTRICAL-ENGINEERING: DATA ENCODING; NEURONAL MODELLING; NEUROSCIENCE: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; VISUAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: This research examines how the electrical activity of neurons in the visual areas of the brain (visual cortex) represents information. This question is commonly referred to as revealing the 'neural code'. We will study the neural code by using an interdisciplinary approach, which combines electrical-engineering theory and electrophysiological recordings of neural activity.    Neural prosthetic devices show tremendous promise for restoring damaged sensory and motor functions, in addition to treating neurological conditions ranging from Parkinson's disease to depression. Using a synergistic combination of electrical engineering and experimental neurophysiological testing, we will develop novel models of the neural code that better account for the biological activity of the brain.    Accordingly, this research will enhance our ability to design advanced neural prosthetics and will expand our basic knowledge of brain functions, which is critical for understanding the basis of diseases that affect mental health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Permeation and Gating of Inwardly-Rectifying Potassium Channels
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; INWARD-RECTIFIER POTASSIUM CHANNEL; KATP CHANNEL; PATCH CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: In the cardiovascular system, inwardly-rectifying potassium (Kir) channels are a critical component in the cardiac action potential, regulating both the shape and duration of the electrical events that underlie each heartbeat. A unique feature of this family of proteins is the range of cellular factors that regulate their activity, including inorganic cations, products of cellular metabolism, changes in cellular acidity, and even properties of the cell membrane. Adding further diversity, the activity of Kir channels is regulated dynamically, from moment to moment, by voltage-dependent block by intracellular cations, and more tonically regulated by ligands that influence channel gating. Recent studies have begun to link genetic mutations that disrupt blockade or gating of specific Kir channels to various cardiac arrhythmias, vascular defects, and more severe disorders including Andersen's syndrome, Bartter's syndrome, and DEND (Diabetes with Epilepsy and Neuromuscular Defects), demonstrating a broad spectrum of physiological roles of this class of channels. The long-term goal of the proposed research is to understand the general and specific mechanisms underlying regulation of Kir channels by (1) their permeating ions, (2) soluble cellular factors that alter channel activity, and (3) interactions with other proteins. To tackle these questions, detailed experiments measuring the electrical activity of Kir channels will be combined with computer modelling, and powerful new biochemical techniques to introduce useful artificial/unnatural amino acids at specific locations in proteins. A detailed understanding of the fundamental mechanisms of Kir channel regulation will provide a basis for ultimately developing interventions to regulate disorders of electrical excitability in the heart, vasculature, and beyond.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the chymase-dependent production of Endothelin-1 in the cardiovascular system
Keywords-MotsClés: CHYMASE; ENDOTHELIN-1; REAL-TIME PCR; WESTERN IMMUNOBLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Endothelin-1 (ET-1) is a small protein secreted by the endothelium, a cell layer lining all blood vessels and which is in direct contact with circulating blood. In healthy subjects, several mechanisms maintain ET-1 blood levels to a strict minimum. In cardiovascular diseases, on the other hand, the production of ET-1 is enhanced in particular due to the loss of protective 'clearance' mechanisms of the peptide. Albeit ET-1 blockers (antagonists) are prescribed to over 50,000 pulmonary hypertensive patients worldwide, the use of these drugs for the treatment of other diseases such as heart failure, hypertension and atherosclerosis is yet to be conclusive.  We wish to investigate, in this proposal, the role of one particular enzyme, chymase, in the production of ET-1 in the cardiovascular system. Chymase, derived from inflammatory mast cells, has previously been reported to produce another constrictor peptide, angiotensin II, within vascular and cardiac muscular walls. Our project hypothesises that chymase may well be involved in the production of ET-1 in the cardiovascular system in whole animals albeit this has yet to be demonstrated. We will therefore assess, in a healthy mouse model, the role of chymase in the synthesis of ET-1. In a second part, we will attempt to circumvent the contribution of the same enzyme in the pathological roles of ET-1 in an atherosclerotic mouse model. We suggest that a better understanding of the enzymes involved in the production of endothelin-1 in physiological and pathological settings may provide important information towards the development of more efficacious antagonists for the treatment of atherosclerosis and other cardiovascular dysfunctions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Determinants of Alternative Splicing and Gene Isoform Expression
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION; GENETIC DISEASE; GENOMICS; RNA PROCESSING; SPLICING REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Small differences in our DNA may have drastic effects on the expression levels of our gene. Moreover, even small differences can vastly influence the final composition of the encoded protein. This is due to the process called alternative splicing, whereas different "chunks" of each gene can be excluded or included in the final protein product. This proposal aims to characterize the effect of DNA differences on gene expression levels and types of the final gene products. Using genomics, we will identify large number of differences influencing gene expression. Using computational approaches, we will determine sets of rules that govern the effects of detected polymorphisms - with the final goal of building predictive models. Finaly, using cell culture systems, we will study the phenotypic effects of variation in expression of the affected genes. Our approach will help us understand the role of common genetic variation in determining human phenotypic traits, such as susceptibility to genetic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dopamine and synaptic plasticity in human substantia nigra pars reticulata
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY-DEPENDENT SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; FIELD EVOKED POTENTIALS; INTRAOPERATIVE MICROELECTRODE RECORDING; MOVEMENT DISORDERS SURGERY; PARKINSON'S DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: The substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) is a deep subcortical nucleus that serves as the output of the basal ganglia. It receives two major inputs from the striatum, a direct and an indirect pathway, and sends its output to premotor centers in the brainstem and thalamus. Parkinson's disease (PD) results from the loss of dopamine supply to the striatum, and this leads to abnormal rhythmic activity of neurons in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) which project to the SNr via the indirect pathway. How these abnormal rhythms affect the output neurons and lead to the motor symptoms is still not understood. The implantation of chronic indwelling deep brain stimulation electrodes in the STN can be very effective for treatment of severe cases of PD. During this operation we can monitor and test the responsiveness of the output neurons to short bursts of electrical currents which enhances their responsiveness, a process termed activity-dependent synaptic plasticity. We recently found that  dopamine causes a dramatic enhancement of the synaptic plasticity in the SNr, and we know from previous work that dopamine abolishes the abnormal rhythmic activity in STN. Therefore we wish to determine whether there is a link between the abnormal STN rhythms and the lack of synaptic plasticity. We propose to electrically stimulate the SNr with a rhythm that mimics the abnormal activity to see what changes occur in the synaptic plasticity. This work will give us a much clearer picture of the mechanisms at work so that specific drugs can be developed to change or prevent these alterations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chromosomal and epigenetic abnormalities after ICSI treatment for male infertility
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEUPLOID SPERM; CHROMOSOMAL ABNORMALITY AND ITS ORIGIN; ICSI PREGNANCIES; INTRACYTOPLASMIC SPERM INJECTION (ICSI); MALE INFERTILITY; MEIOTIC DEFECTS
Abstract-Résumé: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is an assisted reproductive procedure in treatment of male infertility. It involves the injection of a sperm into an oocyte to facilitate fertilization. Because natural barriers to fertilization are bypassed, ICSI may facilitate the transmission of genetic (DNA related) and epigenetic (DNA independent mechanisms that influence gene expression) abnormalities to the next generation. These abnormalities include a deviation from the normal complement of chromosomes (46 units of compacted DNA) in a cell. There is also concern that the injection procedure of ICSI disrupts the organization of the oocyte and this may effect the development of the resulting embryo. These alterations in pregnancies can potentially lead to pregnancy loss, birth defects, and low birth weight. We hypothesize that ICSI presents both procedure-dependent and independent risks to the fetus. We will investigate of the incidence of chromosomal abnormalities and epigenetic changes in the pregnancies of three assisted reproductive techniques - intrauterine insemination, in vitro fertilization (IVF), and ICSI - and evaluate how the differences among the techniques, namely the use of cell culture, the genetic background of different types of infertility involved, and the method of fertilization, effects the development of these abnormalities.  Furthermore, we will examine key steps of cell division in the development of sperm when a chromosomal abnormality in a child is determined to be passed on from the father. Our long-term aims are to identify chromosomal and epigenetic risk factors to conceptions of ICSI, and to develop strategies to prevent abnormal offspring from being born after ICSI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural and behavioural correlates of autobiographical memory performance  in patients with post-traumatic stress disorder and/ or major depression following motor vehicle crash
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL MEMORY; CO-MORBIDITY; MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER; NEUROIMAGING; PTSD; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: The mental and behavioral consequences of trauma affect scores of North Americans, yet little research has been conducted examining changes in memory and in brain functioning thought to follow exposure to traumatic events.  The proposed studies will explore the effects of trauma exposure on brain functioning and on autobiographical memory for trauma and related events in survivors of motor vehicle crashes. These studies will be an important first step in developing more targeted pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions that can improve brain functioning and memory performance, and assist in reducing the psychological aftermath that accompanies trauma exposure.

TitreApplicationTitle: SNARE regulation of potassium channels in neuroendocrine cells
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; EVANESCENT MICROSCOPY; EXOCYTOSIS; PANCREATIC ISLET; PATCH CLAMP; POTASSIUM CHANNELS
Abstract-Résumé: In insulin-secreting pancreatic islet beta-cells, membrane excitability which controls calcium influx required to cause exocytosis of insulin secretory granules, is regulated by two K+ channels,  ATP-sensitive K+ (KATP) channels (sulfonylurea receptor 1-SUR1/Kir6.2 subunits) and voltage-gated K+ (Kv2.1) channels. Current treatment for diabetes with sulfonylureas is unsatisfactory since these drugs act on islet beta-cell SUR1 receptors to stimulate insulin secretion in a manner independent of glucose levels, which can cause hypoglycemia. More appropriate strategies would be to close the KATP channel in a glucose (or ATP)-dependent manner or to delay the closure of Kv2.1 channels, the latter prolonging glucose-evoked membrane depolarization, resulting in more sustained insulin secretion.  We found that a class of proteins called SNAREs, originally shown to mediate exocytosis, directly bind and inhibit both KATP (at SUR1) and Kv2.1 channels. We will now examine the finest aspects of the structure-functional interactions between SNARE proteins and these K+ channels in absolute detail using a battery of state-of-the-art biophysical and imaging methodologies. We also propose that some of these interactions could actually influence exocytosis per se independently of ion channel regulation. This research into the novel SNARE-K+ channel interaction sites could reveal novel therapeutic targets to treat diseases of secretory deficiency (diabetes) or excels (hypersecreting endocrine tumors).

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Bone Fracture and their Clinical Applications
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BONE MECHANICS; HIP FRACTURE; OSTEOPOROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: This project studies fundamental mechanisms of hip fracture with the goal of better predicting hip fracture, especially a second hip fracture.  At the newly established Center for Hip Health and Mobility, the research team with expertise in engineering, bone biology, medical imaging, and orthopaedic surgery will work together to answer one question: How does osteoporosis related structural changes make a hip susceptible to fracture?  By combining both macroscopic and microscopic fracture analyses with high resolution CT imaging of the fracture femoral components from patients, we will be able to understand the material and structural nature of hip fragility. More importantly, we will provide more accurate risk prediction of a secondary hip fracture, thus bringing immediate impact to the patient group with primary hip fracture.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Determinants of Pancreatic Beta Cell Homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CRE LOX P; DIABETES; EPO SIGNALING; ERYTHROPOIETIN; KNOCKOUT MICE; PANCREATIC BETA CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Erythropoietin (Epo) is largely known for its role in erythropoiesis.  However, recent studies have reported the presence of the Epo receptor (EpoR) on non-erythroid tissues, including the neuronal cells, the kidney, the heart, and the pancreatic beta cells.  These findings have led to further investigations of the possible non-hematopoietic effects of Epo.  Indeed, emerging evidence shows cytoprotective roles of Epo in neuronal and other tissue injury models.  The non-hematopoietic roles of Epo in pancreatic beta cells and in diabetes is not well understood. The objective of our study is to investigate the direct effects of Epo on the pancreatic beta cells during physiological and diabetic states.  We hypothesize that Epo can directly promote beta cell survival and growth, and protect against diabetes development through activation of its receptor and downstream signaling pathways.   In order to assess the direct effects of Epo on the beta cells, we will investigate the essential roles of EpoR and its immediate downstream signaling molecule JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) specifically in the pancreatic beta cells by using beta cell-specific knockout mice. These mice will be examined during their normal growth to assess the role of endogenous Epo during normal physiological growth of the pancreatic beta cells.  We will also study the role of endogenous and exogenous Epo during models of diabetes.    Our proposed experiments will determine the physiological roles of Epo in promoting beta cell growth and survival, and identify Epo or Epo-related agents as potential novel therapeutic targets for diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and molecular mechanisms implicated in the metabolism and actions of endocannabinoids and other arachidonic acid-derived lipid mediators in leukocytes.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARACHIDONIC ACID; EICOSANOIDS; ENDOCANNABINOIDS; LEUKOCYTES; LEUKOTRIENES; NEUTROPHIL
Abstract-Résumé: Although cannabis has been used in medicine for centuries, nobody clearly understands how it exerts its effects in humans. Cannabis does much more than increasing appetite: it also decreases pain and inflammation. However, our understanding of how cannabis prevents inflammation is very limited. Over the last decade, two molecules that mimic the effects of cannabis were found in the human body (N-arachidonoyl-ethanolamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoyl-glycerol(2-AG)). Because of that, they have been termed endocannabinoids.  Endocannabinoids contain a lipid named arachidonic acid, which can be transformed into several other lipids that worsen diseases such as arthritis and asthma. Among these lipids are the prostaglandins and the leukotrienes. Endocannabinoids are normally seen as anti-inflammatory while leukotrienes and prostaglandins augment inflammation.   Our preliminary data indicate that endocannabinoids can be transformed into leukotrienes. We believe that if we can prevent this transformation, we will decrease inflammation.   We will initially characterize how endocannabinoids are transformed into leukotreienes by incubating inflammatory cells with endocannabinoids. We will next evaluate the consequence of such a transformation on the activation state of inflammatory cells by measuring their recruitment, the release of pro-inflammatory molecules, and the ingestion of microbes.   Our long term objective is to develop a therapy promoting the anti-inflammatory effects of endocannabinoids. We believe this can be achieved with a compound that would prevent their transformation into arachidonic acid. Such a therapy would increase the quality of life of many Canadians suffering from inflammatory diseases such as asthma and Rheumathoid Arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biological significance of SALL4, a novel homeobox gene that is aberrantly expressed in ALK-expressing anaplastic large cell lymphoma
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS ASSAY; CLONOGENIC ASSAY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; NPM-ALK; ONCOGENIC TYROSINE KINASE; SALL4; SIRNA; STAT3
Abstract-Résumé: Tyrosine kinase is a type of enzyme that provides many important biological functions in our body. When abnormally activated, tyrosine kinases are known to cause cancer. It is important to fully understand the mechanisms by which these over-active enzymes cause cancer, since one can design new anti-cancer therapy based on these information. In this proposal, the fellow will explore one novel pathway by which an over-active tyrosine kinase, NPM-ALK, can cause a specific childhood cancer. We believe that NPM-ALK allows SALL4 to be expressed in cells in which SALL4 expression should have been shut-off. SALL4 in turns mediates the tumor-forming effects for NPM-ALK. If our hypothetical model turns out to be correct, we may be able to treat this type of cancer by interrupting the interaction between NPM-ALK and SALL4.

TitreApplicationTitle: Agonistic activities of angiopoietins on neutrophils
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOPOIETINS; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL SIGNALING; CHEMOTACTIC ACTIVITIES; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; FACS; GROWTH FACTORS; INFLAMMATION; INTEGRINS; NEUTROPHILS; TIE2 RECEPTOR; TYROSINE KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: An overexcessive and uncontrolled formation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis) occurs in the setting of numerous diseases such tumor growth and metastasis, ocular diseases, arthritis, psoriasis and atherosclerosis.   Consequently, our general hypothesis is that the blockade of pathological angiogenesis is a potential therapeutic target to treat and/or to prevent the development and the progression of chronic diseases.   The induction of pathological angiogenesis requires the contribution of various proteins (growth factors).  One of those growth factors is VEGF, this latter induces an acute inflammatory response, which is promoting the formation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis).  During the last years, our research group discovered how VEGF is inducing the inflammatory response.  In our most recent studies, we observed that another family of growth factors (namely the Angiopoietins) which are involved in the angiogenic process are also capable to mediate the synthesis of an inflammatory mediator (platelet-activating factor) by circulating blood cells (neutrophils) and to promote biological activities related to the induction of inflammatory responses.  Based on these observations, we are trying to understand how the angiopoietins are activating the neutrophils, and how they mediate their inflammatory activities.  These studies might provide pivotal information on the mechanisms required not only to promote but also to abrogate angiogenesis in function of the needs.  Our data could set the bases for future therapeutic strategies designed to prevent and/or to treat vascular diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Visually-guided arm movements: cerebral cortical neuronal mechanisms of motor and non-motor decisions
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL CORTEX; DECISION MAKING; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; NON-HUMAN PRIMATES; REACHING MOVEMENTS; SINGLE-NEURON RECORDINGS
Abstract-Résumé: The world continually bombards us with sensory inputs that offer many opportunities for action. However, our behaviour is not slavishly driven by any and all sensory inputs. Instead, normal behaviour while interacting with our complex environment usually involves the selective and often very arbitrary response to only certain stimuli, usually during the focussed pursuit of a short or long-term goal, such as the sequences of arm and leg movements elicited by green, yellow and red lights while driving a car from home to the office. That simple example also illustrates how much of our voluntary behaviour is flexible, context-dependent, and acquired by personal experience. Failure to impose this rational introspective control on voluntary behaviour leads to many behavioural problems at both the level of the individual and society, including impulsive behaviour (e.g., distraction, inability to pursue a goal to its accomplishment), compulsive behaviour (e.g., gambling), perseverance (e.g., persistent use of inappropriate or counterproductive behaviour), and socially inappropriate behaviour (e.g., physical aggression, theft). The overall objective of this proposal is to gain further insight into the cerebral cortical single-neuron decision-making mechanisms underlying the selection of the appropriate action from among multiple competing alternatives, using as our experimental model visually-guided arm movements in non-human primates that have been trained to perform conditional motor tasks.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Minimal Effective Dose of Antipsychotic Medication in Older Patients with Schizophrenia: A PET Study
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANTIPSYCHOTIC MEDICATION; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a life-long illness requiring daily treatment with antipsychotic medication. Even though older patients are well-known to be very sensitive to medications, we still do not know the lowest effective dose of antipsychotic medication that is necessary in older patients with this condition. This information has traditionally been acquired through large drug studies. Binding of antipsychotics to brain dopamine receptors has previously been used to predict the least effective dose in younger patients using relatively few patients compared to large clinical studies. We therefore seek to study the lowest antipsychotic dose needed to maintain wellness in older patients with early-onset schizophrenia. To do this we plan to conduct a PET study in 40 patients 60 years and older who have had schizophrenia since their young adulthood and have been maintained for > 12 months on risperidone, a very commonly used antipsychotic medication. Participants will undergo a gradual dose reduction up to 40% of their baseline dose to a target dose not lower than the lowest recommended dose 1.25 mg/day. A PET scan will be completed after gradual dose reduction. They will then be followed for 6 months to determine whether they remain well at this low dose.  If they experience any new symptoms, they will have their dose increased to treat these symptoms and then undergo a second PET scan. This study will provide new information about the mechanisms involved in antipsychotic drug sensitivity in older patients. This information can be translated to the determination of the lowest effective antipsychotic dose necessary for maintenance of therapeutic effect in older patients with schizophrenia, a clinical question of major public health significance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of cytokines in perinatal brain lesions and subsequent cerebral palsy: towards effective and safe neuroprotective therapies targeting IL-1beta and TNF-alpha.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CEREBRAL PALSY; CYTOKINES; NEUROINFLAMMATION; NEUROPROTECTION; PERINATALITY
Abstract-Résumé: La paralysie cerebrale provoque des handicaps moteurs et cognitifs durables constituant un probleme majeur de sante publique. Les molecules inflammatoires produites en reponse a des infections bacteriennes perinatales survenant dans l'environnement foetal, particulierement la synthese de cytokines proinflammatoires, jouent un role central dans la genese des lesions cerebrales responsables de la paralysie cerebrale. Notre objectif est, grace a des approches utilisant plusieurs modeles animaux, de preciser la combinaison de cytokines impliquees dans les dommages cerebraux neonatals et de tester l'effet neuroprotecteur de substances bloquant leur action. Les resultats de cette recherche devraient deboucher sur des essais therapeutiques humains neuroprotecteurs dans le but de reduire la frequence et la severite de la paralysie cerebrale.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pharmacogenetic study of warfarin
Keywords-MotsClés: BLEEDING; GENETIC TESTS; INR FLUCTUATIONS; PHARMACOGENOMICS; WARFARIN
Abstract-Résumé: Warfarin is the most widely prescribed blood thinner medication for the treatment and prevention of blood clots. Its use, however, is greatly complicated by the drug's narrow therapeutic dose range and by the extensive variation in safe doses among different individuals to avoid exposing patients to clots formation or to bleeding events. Recent studies showed that two genes, together with environmental factors, can explain some of the variability between patients. New blood thinner medications are being developed that could eventually provide an alternative to warfarin treatment. In order to identify patients who are most likely to be exposed to serious bleeding or clot formation we propose to evaluate the genetic and clinical determinants of adverse responses to warfarin treatment. These include: (i) severe and potentially fatal bleeding, the most serious adverse response; (ii) major complications related to clot formation; and (iii) fluctuations in the International Normalised Ratio (INR), a parameter used to monitor warfarin treatment in order to establish the safe therapeutic dosage for each patient. This study will recruit 2,500 patients initiating warfarin therapy over a 2-year period. Patients will be selected from the warfarin clinics of 4 greater-Montreal area. They will be followed-up for 1 year as part of this research project. The prediction of adverse events in warfarin therapy is expected to allow a better management of treatment with blood thinner medications. This effort offers great potential for the improvement of personal and public health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the molecular and cellular links between cilia, cGMP signaling, physiology and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BARDET-BIEDL SYNDROME; CGMP SIGNALING; CILIA; DISEASE; SATIETY/OBESITY; SENSORY PERCEPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Primary cilia are small hair-like cellular appendages that are found on most human cells and perform key roles in sensory perception, including smell, vision and hearing. Our recent studies have shed new insights into the physiological functions of cilia, and their association with human disease. Specifically, we showed that Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS), a genetic disorder that affects nearly all organs, is caused by functional defects in cilia. BBS patients have, in addition to sight, smell, and hearing problems, several other serious ailments, including severe obesity, kidney cysts, diabetes, and skeletal anomalies. The central hypothesis of our research is that cilia coordinate a cellular signaling response by using a molecule termed cGMP. Although this cGMP signaling pathway is known to be important for vision and smell, the precise molecular mechanisms involved, and link to other physiological functions, such as weight control, have not been explored. We propose to make use of two innovative and complementary experimental systems to dissect the link between cilia function and cGMP signaling. The first is the nematode C. elegans, a simple yet powerful model organism widely used to study cilia function and their roles in cellular and organismal physiology. Our proposed genetic and cell biology studies are directly relevant to human biology and disorders, including obesity. The second involves cultured human cells, which allow for detailed studies at the cellular level. In addition to shedding new, fundamental insights into the role of cilia in normal human physiology, an important goal of our proposed research is to provide essential information on the roles that cilia and different sensory molecules play in controlling satiety, the sensation of having eaten sufficiently. As such, our studies may ultimately help tackle the current obesity epidemic by providing new targets that can be used for preventing and treating abnormal weight gain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of a kinase-HDAC-MEF2 signaling axis in normal and oncogenic cellular programs
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DIFFERENTIATION; CELL SIGNALING; CHROMATIN; EPIGENETICS; HISTONE DEACETYLASE; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: In the past decade, my colleagues and I have discovered and studied a group of important proteins called histone deacetylases. These proteins are important regulators able to control the way by which the genetic material is organized in human cells. Like genetic mutations, abnormal organization of the genetic material has recently been recognized as oneimportant reason for various human diseases, including cancer. Clinical trials with chemical compounds that are able to inhibit the activities of these regulators have yielded very promising results. For example, one such compound (now known as Zolinza, Merck) was approved as the first histone dacetylase-based drug, for treating cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. One problem with these compounds is serious toxicity or side effects. To develop agents able to target different histone deacetylases more selectively and precisely, it is necessary to understand the function and regulation of these regulators themselves. In this grant application, we propose to continue our studies of these important proteins, by carrying out molecular and genetic analyses of a subgroup of such regulators.  Our recent results identified modulators of the histone deacetylases. Excitingly, this modulator is directly linked to lung cancer and the Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (a genetic disease characterized by the development of benign polyps and other tumor-like growth in the gastrointestinal tract), so the proposed studies shall yield new insight into the molecular basis of cancer and other human diseases. This is one of the very first steps towards developing new methods of diagnosis and therapy.  Compounds able to inhibit histone deacetylase activity have been isolated from garlic, broccoli and fruits, and there are animal studies indicating that physical exercise regulates the activity of histone deacetylases. Therefore, the proposed studies shall also shed light on how to adjust diet and life style for disease prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: The molecular basis of trafficking defect of cystic fibrosis mutations in respiratory epithelia
Keywords-MotsClés: APICAL TARGETING; CFTR MUTATIONS; CONFORMATIONAL DEFECT; PROTEIN QUALITY CONTROL; PROTEIN SORTING; RESPIRATORY EPITHELIA
Abstract-Résumé: The cystic fibrosis gene dictates the synthesis of a protein (called CFTR) which is normally resides in the limiting membrane of cells and responsible for the normal water content or hydration of the lung. Genetic mutations in the cystic fibrosis gene can impair the protein's ability to accumulate at cell surface and/or remain there long enough to execute its function. The mechanism of delivery of the normal CFTR to and the premature removal of mutants from plasma membrane is not known and constitutes the major focuse of the present proposal. We propose to identify the molecular basis of CFTR normal delivery to its appropriate cellular location, as well as the cellular mechanisms that discriminate between the normal and mutant CFTR structure. We will investigate the cellular and biochemical mechanisms of mutant CFTR recognition and premature elimination, one of the most common causes of cystic fibrosis at the cellular level. The results may identify novel drug targets in cystic fibrosis that could help to alleviate the clinical symptoms in this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Visual and cognitive development in premature and full term children
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY EVOKED POTENTIALS; COGNITION; FULL TERM INFANTS; MAGNO AND PARVOCELLULAR SYSTEMS; PREMATURE INFANTS; VISUAL EVOKED POTENTIALS
Abstract-Résumé: The great progress that has been achieved in infant care has gradually raised survival rates, especially in those born early (premature) and with low birth weights. For many infants, this means severe problems in sensory functions (ex. visual deficits), and so-called minor ones in brain functions, such as learning disabilities and attention deficit disorders with or without hyperactivity. The general objective of this research program consists in better identifying one of the major consequences of prematurity, impairment of the visual system, and establishing the brain activity patterns of the so-called minor impairments (ex. attention, language functions). Despite technological improvements in brain imaging, there is still no method for adequately determining problems at all levels of visual function. This is even truer in cases where little or no brain lesion has been detected. Moreover, the effects of prematurity on brain function (i.e. cognitive) development are not adequately defined. Evoked potentials (EPs) represent a non-invasive and objective method for measuring electrical responses from the brain following the presentation of specific stimuli. Our team has carried out developmental studies of EPs in response to various visual and auditory stimuli. These paradigms were developed in adults and healthy children, and will now be used to compare the development in full term and premature infants (0-3 years). This research should provide a better understanding of which factors can best predict a premature child's neurological future and her/his cognitive future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Harsh parenting conditions and fear circuitry function in anxious and healthy youths.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE CARE-GIVING; ANXIETY DISORDERS; FEAR CIRCUITRY; FEAR CONDITIONING; FMRI; YOUTHS
Abstract-Résumé: Links have been established between adverse care-giving and anxiety disorders. These links could reflect long-term changes within the brain's neural fear circuit. Very few studies in youths have ever investigated these links. Understanding the links among harsh parenting, fear circuitry and anxiety in youths will provide key insights on the biology of harsh parenting and anxiety during development. Identifying biological perturbations related to anxiety while individuals are still young is crucial as it could lead to early interventions that would effectively interrupt the development of these perturbations early in their course, before they become chronic and exceedingly debilitating. The main objective of this CIHR research project is thus to understand the functioning of the fear circuit in anxious and non-anxious adversely-reared and non-adversely reared youths. Here, adverse care-giving is defined as harsh parenting: hostile and coercive (i.e., aggressive, cold, critical, punitive) parenting behaviours. To reach this goal, we will recruit 4 groups of 30 youths aged between 11-12 years old. Groups will be: youths with (1) current high-harsh parenting and current anxiety symptoms, (2) current high-harsh parenting, but no current anxiety symptom, (3) current low-harsh parenting, but current anxiety symptoms, (4) current low-harsh parenting and no current anxiety symptom. Subjects will be recruited through the Research Unit on Children's Psychosocial Maladjustment (University of Montreal and Laval University). To study the functioning of the fear circuit, we will use tasks measuring the acquisition and extinction of a fear response to emotionally arousing cues. These tasks have been adapted for the functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanner and have been recognized as safe by previous pilot-studies performed in healthy anxious youths.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pleiotropic effects of oxytocin
Keywords-MotsClés: (OT); CARDIOPROTECTION; CELL DIFFERENTIATION; DIABETES; GLUCOSE UPTAKE; HEART; OT ELONGATED FORM- (OT-GKR); OXYTOCIN
Abstract-Résumé: We have recently uncovered a functional oxytocin (OT) system in the human and rat heart, linked natriuretic peptides (NPs) and nitric oxide (NO) as well as shown an important role in cardiac development and cardiomyogenesis. We now propose to investigate the hypothesis that specific interaction (and balance) between the OT, nitric oxide (NO) and atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) systems exists to maintain cardiac homeostasis by controlling cardiac cell differentiation and cellular and metabolic effects in the heart. To substantiate this hypothesis, we are proposing to: i) characterize the molecules OT and elongated form of OT (OT-GKR) which is the main form present in the fetal and newborn heart and elucidate their signaling pathways in the heart cells. ii) study OT and OTX action on glucose uptake in newborn and adult rat CM in normal, ischemic and pathological conditions such as diabetes. The present studies will provide a comprehensive analysis of cardiac OT biology. Particular attention will be given to the OT control of cardiac cell functionality and the evidence that modulation of OT signalling could serve as a versatile strategy for improving cardiovascular functions and preventing abnormalities associated with cardiovascular pathologies. These observations may lead to new therapeutic approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Living Kidney Donor Safety Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; COHORT STUDY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HYPERTENSION; KIDNEY DONATION; KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: When donating a kidney to someone you love, there are a few things to think about. There are surgical and long-term medical risks from having one kidney removed. On the other hand, the person receiving the kidney has the benefit of a longer and better life. We understand the surgical risks of donating a kidney quite well. But we know less about the long-term medical and psychosocial risks of donating a kidney. This study will help us understand these risks better. We will follow 620 people from 12 transplant centres in Canada for 7 years. First, we want to find out if kidney donation increases a person's risk of getting high blood pressure. Next, we will use surveys to help us understand the psychosocial health of donors. Finally, we will collect blood and urine each year to test how well the kidney works. This will be the largest and most accurate study of its kind in the world. The knowledge we gain will improve how we select donors and the information we tell people who want to donate. It will help doctors maintain the health of former and future living donors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcription and Translesion Synthesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CUX1; GENOMIC ANALYSIS; KU; POINT MUTATIONS; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS; REV1; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; TRANSLESION SYNTHESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is believed to be caused by the accumulation of mutations that cause the activation of oncogenes and the inactivation of tumor suppressors. While much progress has been made in the elucidation of various mechanisms of DNA repair, very little is known about the processes by which point mutations are introduced in our genome. The aim of this proposal is to verify whether the rate of mutagenesis can vary in response to certain treatments and to investigate a mechanism by which error-prone DNA polymerases are targeted to specific genomic regions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Azapeptides: A new class of CD36 ligands for the treatment of ischemic heart disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AZAPEPTIDES; CARDIAC METABOLISM; ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Despite optimal drug regimen, coronary disease remains the highest cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, giving birth to heart attack and stroke. The aims of the present proposal are to characterize the cardioprotective effects of a new class of drugs, acting through a receptor called CD36. We have obtained preliminary evidence, in a mouse model of heart attack, that these drugs may reduce the size of the damage to the heart after infarction. In the present study, we will identify the effects of these drugs on cardiac function and characterize the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying their beneficial action. Considering the aging population and the steady increase in heart disease and its complications, effective and novel therapeutic strategies are thus warranted.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cystic Fibrosis and ER Quality Control.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHAPERONE/PROTEIN FOLDING; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; DISEASE MECHANISMS; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; QUALITY CONTROL GENETICS; RNAI
Abstract-Résumé: The respiratory disease Cystic Fibrosis results from mutations in a cell membrane protein, the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR). The mutant CFTR protein is recognized by the endoplasmic reticulum quality control system (ERQC) and retained within the cell and proteolytically degraded.  Thus Cystic Fibrosis is termed, a "protein trafficking disease". If the mutant CFTR can traffic correctly to the cell surface it is functional as a transporter of chloride ions. That is, if the ERQC can be subverted the mutant CFTR can traffic correctly to the cell surface where it can function and alleviate the symptoms of the disease. This application addresses the fundamental mechanism of the retention of mutant CFTR in the ER by the ERQC, and thus how the mechanism can be subverted. Cystic fibrosis is the most common fatal genetic disease in Canada. Although the gene and the most frequent allele were identified nearly 20 years ago by groups in Canada and the US, there is no therapy based on the alleviation of the basic defect. This project is designed to explore the mechanism of ERQC that we have identified targets that controls the recognition of mutant CFTR. There are a large number of "protein trafficking" diseases - including immune disorders, cystic fibrosis, emphysema and others, that arise from the retention of otherwise functional proteins in the ER by the ER quality control system. The goal of this project is to discover its mechanism and approaches to therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cortical plasticity in children who are deaf
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY DEVELOPMENT; BILATERAL COCHLEAR IMPLANT; CENTRAL AUDITORY SYSTEM; CORTEX; DEAFNESS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Children who are deaf cannot communicate through listening and talking unless we find a way for them to hear. Cochlear implants (CIs) can restore some hearing but it is not normal.  This means that children using CIs work hard to learn to hear and speak. These challenges might occur because the brain is starved of sound for the first months or years of life and/or because we are not providing enough hearing through the CIs. We have already found that brain responses in these children are different from those in children with normal hearing.  Although CI technology continues to improve, we might be able to help children who are deaf immediately by providing a CI in both ears (bilateral) rather than continuing to offer only one (unilateral) CI.  We follow one of the largest groups of such children in the world and have developed special tools to look at their brain activity.  In this study, we ask: 1) How do young brains develop without hearing?, 2) How does the brain change after unilateral or bilateral CIs are used, and 3) Can children who already use a unilateral CI benefit from a second CI?  We record brain responses and hearing in children who are deaf in both ears as well as in children who used a unilateral CI for months or years.  All children then use bilateral CIs and we measure changes in brain function and hearing over the first 12 months.  More detailed recordings will also be done in some of these children as well as in children who used bilateral CIs for longer than 3 years to identify which areas of the brain are working. Our results will tell us whether using a unilateral CI changes the way the brain normally uses sound coming from both ears. It will also identify what parts of the brain are working to hear sounds coming through unilateral or bilateral CIs.  Any differences from normal brain function will help us to understand why hearing is poorer than normal in children using CIs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of Critical Lung Cancer Targets Using Genetically Engineered KRas and BRaf Mice
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICALLY ENGINEERED MOUSE MODELS OF DISEASE; LUNG CANCER; RAS RAF SIGNALING; SENESCENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in globally and in Canada, killing more people than breast, prostate and colorectal cancers combined. Unfortunately, for the majority of Canadians diagnosed with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLCs) today, the prognosis remains the same as it did twenty years ago, less than a 5% five year survival rate.  While standard chemotherapies have failed, there is hope. A coalescence of human genetic and biochemical data have identified a number of "cancer genes" that may be good targets for future chemotherapeutic drugs.  Indeed, several recent high-profile examples of new therapeutics have enjoyed success in the clinic - where it matters to the average Canadian.  Despite these successes, these new therapies fail to provide clinical benefit for the vast majority of NSCLC patients.  RAS and BRAF genes are the most prevalent mutated oncogenes in many human cancers, particularly in NSCLCs (>25%), yet available data suggest these mutant oncogenes do not act on their own: they require additional cooperating genes for cancer genesis and progression. This proposal aims to uncover what these cooperating genes are, how they work at molecular level, and when they are important in the evolution of a fully malignant metastatic cell - all of which are paramount to discovering new and effective cancer treatments.   Genetically modified mouse models (GEMMs) are presently the gold standard for whole organism cancer modeling.  We will make use of our novel GEMMs of human lung cancer where we can control the site, the number, the timing and the genetics of tumour initiation.  This enables us to query fundamental questions regarding the genetics of tumour initiation, progression, maintenance and ultimately, metastasis.  Furthermore, these GEMMs of human lung cancer provide platforms for both the engineering and validation of targeted therapies with the goal of developing new therapies to alleviate suffering inflicted by this dreaded disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Cell Death Mechanisms in Transformed/Cancer Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; MEMBRANE TRAFFIC; ORGANELLE DYNAMICS; PROGRAMMED CELL DEATH; RHO GTPASES; SRC KINASES
Abstract-Résumé: Physiological cell death widely occurs through induction of a cell suicide program called apoptosis. Apoptosis provides a self-cellular defense against detrimental assaults and also against aberrant cellular growth that leads to cancer, by eliminating cells bearing anomalies. Acquired resistance to apoptosis is a hallmark of human tumors and contributes to the resistance of these cells to many anti-cancer agents. Other modes of cell death also exist, but the molecular mechanisms are poorly understood. Furthermore, a number of viral and cellular proteins have been identified, which possess the remarkable ability to destroy cancer cells, while sparing normal cells. Hence, these products seem to activate novel modes of cell death that operate selectively in cancer cells, by sensing and exploiting critical lesions common to cancer cells. This research program aims to comprehend how one of these cancer cell-selective killers, the viral protein named E4orf4, functions at the molecular level. We found that E4orf4 interferes with cellular functions that are deregulated during cell transformation and that depend on key enzymes (Src tyrosine kinases) participating to cancer progression. The study of the mode of action of E4orf4, in cancer cells and in mouse models, could help developing new anti-cancer agents that would be more efficient and less toxic to normal cells.
