TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of TrkA receptor trafficking and signaling by Calnuc
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SURFACE RECEPTORS; CONFOCAL IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; ENDOCYTOSIS; HETEROTRIMERIC G PROTEIN; INTRACELLULAR TRAFFICKING; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Extracellular signaling molecules bind to specific receptors at the cell surface that will initiate a cascade of signal inside the cell and control a wide variety of biological responses such as proliferation, differentiation, migration and modulation of cell survival. Signal termination from these receptors is triggered by a number of mechanisms including an uncoupling of the cell surface receptor from its intracellular effector or the internalization and degradation of the receptor. It has been established that elevated expression of cell surface receptor, enhanced receptor signaling and impaired receptor deactivation are frequently implicated in hyperproliferative diseases such as cancer. Therefore, gaining a better understanding of key proteins  involved in the regulation of the signaling pathway and receptor downregulation is crucial. Our research team is studying Calnuc which might be one of these critical protein. Our main goal is to understand the importance of calnuc in the regulation  of normal and altered cellular responses in the context of cancer. By carefully studying the receptor signaling cascades and trafficking regulated by Calnuc, we will gain insights on the role of this protein. Results generated from these studies may lead to the identification of new therapeutic targets, and the developments of new drugs for the treatment of a broad variety of pathological conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Heterogeneous vesicle pools and their function in the presynaptic terminal
Keywords-MotsClés: HIPPOACAMPUS; NEUROTRANSMITTER RELEASE; PRESYNAPTIC MECHANISMS; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; ZINC
Abstract-Résumé: Neurones in the nervous system communicate via synapses. Neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic cell and this signals is sensed by the receptors of the potsynaptic cell. Neurotransmitter is packaged into small vesicles, which release their content up activation. It is generally accepted that presynaptic vesicles form a homogenous population in terms of their content and the variety of proteins embedded into the vesicle membrane. In contrast, our data show that vesicles are heterogeneous, their membrane contains different proteins and their release is triggered by different stimuli. The current grant will explore the functional consequences of this heterogeneity within the presynaptic terminal. We will investigate how different vesicles are generated, why their presence is necessary for the normal function of the brain. We will study how synaptic transmission and memory formation is influenced by the presence of different vesicle pools in the terminal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of improved glucose metabolism after bariatric surgery in type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: BARIATRIC SURGERY; DIABETES MELLITUS; FATTY ACID METABOLISM; INSULIN RESISTANCE/SECRETION; OBESITY; POSTPRANDIAL METABOLISM
Abstract-Résumé: Glucose tolerance reverts toward normal within 3 to 6 days after bilio-pancreatic diversion (BPD) in obese subjects with type 2 diabetes (T2D) even before any significant weight loss. The mechanisms for this dramatic improvement, however, are not understood. We have previously shown that impaired fat tolerance (i.e. increased circulating fat upon intravenous infusion of fat) occurs before development of T2D in subjects at high-risk of this disease, is present in subjects with T2D, and is reverted with weight loss after BPD. We propose that improvement of glucose metabolism following BPD may involve rapid reversal of impaired fat tolerance in T2D. Subjects without or with T2D who undergo either gastric restrictive (gastric banding) or intestinal bypass surgery for treatment of obesity will be studied before and 5-7 days, and 3 and 18 months after surgery. Two out of three metabolic protocols will be performed on each occasion, the first one to measure intravenous glucose tolerance and insulin secretion, the second to measure circulating fat metabolism and intravenous tolerance, insulin resistance, and adipose tissue function, and the third one to measure glucose and lipid tolerance and metabolism, and hormone secretion after a mixed meal. The present study will determine some mechanisms underlying the profound improvement of glucose homeostasis after bariatric surgery, a very successful treatment approach for some patients with T2D that is now becoming more widely available. The proposed studies will provide novel and unique information on the potential role of gut endocrine regulation of adipose tissue function after bariatric surgery. As this work will be performed in human subjects, results will directly identify relevant pathophysiological mechanisms that will become prime targets for the development of preventive and therapeutic interventions for T2D.

TitreApplicationTitle: Involvement of the DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PK) in p53-mediated apoptosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; DNA DAMAGE; DNA-PK; P53
Abstract-Résumé: Throughout everyday life, our cells are exposed to many environmental factors (UV light, chemical carcinogens in the air, food or cigarettes) that could potentially cause them considerable harm, particularly to the cell's genetic material, DNA. If this DNA damage remains unchecked, it can be passed onto daughter cells (i.e., new cells produced after the division of the parent cell), eventually leading to the development of a cancer. To avoid this, the cell has a protein called p53 that acts as a cellular policeman. This protein tells the cell to immediately stop growing, allowing the cell time to repair this damage; or, should the damage be too severe, commit suicide by triggering a cellular process called apoptosis. In either event, the damaged DNA would not be passed onto daughter cells. The important questions remain: how is the damage sensed by p53 and how does it choose between cell growth arrest and apoptosis? It turns out that p53 does not sense the damage itself. Rather, damaged DNA is sensed by other proteins which then relay the message to p53 either directly, or via messengers. The identity of the sensor(s) and/or messenger(s) is crucial to our understanding of cancer development and predisposition, and the design of anti-cancer strategies. Previously, we identified one such messenger as a large protein called DNA-PK. We have since carried out a range of studies to support this claim. We demonstrated that when the cell has sustained severe DNA damage (damage beyond repair), DNA-PK and p53 quickly become closely associated, and communicate with each other. Specifically, DNA-PK informs p53 to carry out the suicidal process. The proposed research focuses on the precise mechanisms whereby DNA-PK executes this command, thereby preventing cancer development.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; ANOMALIES CONGENITALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of the role of the Gumby gene in angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CRANIOFACIAL SYNDROMES; DEVELOPMENT; MOLECULAR GENETICS; MOUSE GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels from pre-existing vasculature, important in normal development and in human patholgies, such as diabetic retinopathy, macular degeneration, and importantly cancer. Vascular cells are less likely than cancer cells to gain resistance to therapeutics, thus targeting tumor vasculature is an attractive strategy for treating cancer patients.  Angiogenesis in tumors, termed neoangiogenesis, appears to be regulated by the same pathways that govern it during normal development. Using mouse genetics we have identified the novel Gumby gene, which is required for normal angiogenesis. Most angiogenic genes belong to gene families and are expressed not just in blood vessels, but in other adult tissues. Thus, it is challenging to design anti-angiogenesis drugs that affect only a single family member, and anti-angiogenic drugs often have deleterious side effects on other tissues.  By contrast, Gumby is the only member of its family in mice and humans and is expressed predominantly in blood vessels and, thus, may provide a unique target for future anti-angiogenesis tumor treatments. Here we will explore the molecular and biological roles of Gumby during angiogenesis.

ClasseRechercheFR: ANOMALIES DE LA COAGULATION/THROMBOSE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of von Willebrand factor gene expression in endothelial cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; PROMOTER ANALYSIS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; TRANSGENIC MICE; VASCULAR DYSFUNCTION; VON WILLEBRAND FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Leading causes of mortality include cardiovascular disease, stroke and cancer. What all these diseases have in common is that vascular endothelial cells that cover the lining of blood vessels directly participate in the generation and /or progression of these diseases. Damage or dysfunction of cardiovascular and brain vascular endothelial cells is the major cause of heart disease and stroke respectively. While growth of endothelial cells to generate new blood vessels that vascularize tumors is the route of cancer metastasis. A major obstacle in developing effective therapies for these diseases is the lack of knowledge of how endothelial cells are different from other cell types, how in various organs endothelial cells differ from each other, and how endothelial cells respond to injuries.  This knowledge is essential for determining why endothelial cells of specific organs, but not all vascular endothelial cells become susceptible to dysfunction in these diseases. We propose to determine the molecular mechanisms that are invoked in response to injuries such as irradiation and hypoxia. We have developed a system to target expression of desired genes in endothelial cells of specific organs and we will use this system to explore the response of endothelial cells of target organs to injury in transgenic mice in addition to cell culture. These studies will provide necessary information to develop therapeutic approaches to inhibit processes that are activated in endothelial cells in response to injury and finally target the endothelial cells of each organ specifically for future effective therapies for vascular diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of urotensin II function
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; PEPTIDE HORMONES; PROTEOLYTIC PROCESSING; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; STRUCTURE-FUNCTION STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: The cardiovascular system is affected by a variety of stimuli, many of which are peptidic in nature. In order to become active most peptidergic hormone precursors are submitted to cleavage by proteases. This permits the production of the bioactive peptide, which is later secreted from the cell. This peptide then interacts with cell-surface receptors enabling the hormone to transmit its signal to the cell, which in turn emits a response. Deregulation of these peptidergic and receptor systems often leads to diseases such as hypertension, heart failure and other cardiovascular-related pathologies. Recently, two new hormonal peptides, urotensin II (UII) and urotensin-related peptide (URP) and the receptor with which they interact have been identified in man. Not only is UII amongst the most vasoactive peptide known but recent evidence shows that it also acts as an important chemotactic factor, a substance that attracts cells of the immune system in situations of tissue injury or infection. A vital area of activity in biomedical research is the identification of structural determinants within proteins that dictate or regulate their interaction with other proteins. We propose an integrated, multidisciplinary and multi-laboratory project intended to examine various facets of these interactions using the UII system as a model. Specifically, we will identify those 'molecular signatures' that are responsible for proUII and proURP's recognition and cleavage by specific proteases. We will determine what are the important amino acids involved for the recognition and activation of the UT receptor by UII and URP. Finally we will explore a novel concept called collateral efficacy, a way in which a single receptor can behave differently depending on the type of ligand it interacts with. Our studies will have an important impact in understanding how peptide hormones are produced and how they can influence cardiovascular function by their interaction with their receptor.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adaptation to hypoxia in cancer through the unfolded protein response
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; HYPOXIA; MRNA TRANSLATION; RADIOBIOLOGY; TUMOR BIOLOGY; UNFOLDED PROTEIN RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: Poorly oxygenated (hypoxic) tumor cells represent a major limitation to the success of current cancer treatment due to their resistance to conventional cancer therapy and their ability to promote malignancy. We aim to identify processes that hypoxic cells rely on for their survival, with the ultimate goal of targeting these cells in the clinic. We focus on the role of a recently discovered hypoxia adaptive pathway known as the unfolded protein response. We have discovered that this pathway induces a pro-survival process during hypoxia known as autophagy, a process in which the cells consume and recycle their own contents to maintain survival. By genetically and pharmacologically disrupting the function of pathways that are responsible for these processes, we will evaluate their importance for survival during hypoxia. Likewise, we will evaluate their impact on important tumor characteristics in mouse tumor models, and their potential for being targeted therapeutically. Lastly, we will use tumor samples from patients with cervix cancer to investigate whether UPR and autophagy are associated with hypoxia in tumors, and how this impacts on patient prognosis. Our studies are expected to lead to new approaches to identify and target hypoxic cells and by doing so improve our ability to successfully treat patients with these aggressive types of tumors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Basis of Calcium Sensitization in the Arterial Myogenic Response
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM SENSITIZATION; CONTRACTILE APPARATUS; MYOGENIC RESPONSE; MYOSIN LIGHT CHAIN PHOSPHATASE TARGETING SUBUNIT 1; RHO-ASSOCIATED KINASE; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Failure to properly regulate the diameter of small calibre arteries results in hypertension, vasospasm and/or end-organ damage. The molecular basis of the processes that regulate the diameter of small blood vessels is not known with certainty. Small vessels are difficult to study owing to the limited amount of tissue that can be obtained for biochemical analysis of the molecular mechanisms involved. We have developed new methods of greater sensitivity to permit identification of the molecular events controlling arterial diameter. Small arteries react to changes in pressure within the vessel lumen by constricting to pressure elevation and dilating to pressure reduction. This is a fundamentally important mechanism for control of blood pressure, regulating blood flow to the different organs of the body and preventing pressure-induced damage to downstream structures. Changes in arterial diameter are produced by varying the level of contraction of smooth muscle cells within the vessel wall. Previous experiments have focused on the mechanisms that turn the contraction on and off, but our knowledge of the processes that control the magnitude of contraction and, therefore, the extent of change in diameter, is limited. Our recent findings provide evidence for the contribution of a process that enhances the ability of the contractile apparatus of smooth muscle cells to react to pressure. Specifically, they produce more contraction for the same level of stimulation when pressure is increased. The proposed experiments will define the molecular basis of the mechanism by which this process is activated by pressure. Understanding the molecular basis of these mechanisms will define how arterial diameter is regulated in health and provide the foundation for future experiments to identify the dysfunctional mechanisms that contribute to abnormal control of arterial diameter in disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dysregulated STAT-3 activation underlies lung fibroblast heterogeneity: Implications for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: FIBROBLASTS; FIBROSIS; HUMAN; LUNG; REMODELING; RESPIRATORY; SIGNALING; STAT-3
Abstract-Résumé: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a devastating disease since there is no cure or effective therapy. In North America and Canada there are over 200,000 patients with this disease. Of these more than 40,000 die annually. Currently we think that the pathology of IPF follows a pathway similar to normal wound healing, although there is progression of the disease because the normal "braking" mechanisms do not function properly. As a consequence, too much connective tissue is produced in the lungs and the ability to transfer oxygen to the bloodstream is severely impaired. My research focuses on the cells that produce the connective tissue, called myofibroblasts. We have identified a protein that we think regulates how myofibroblasts appear in the lung and produce connective tissue but do not die. By reducing the activation of this protein, the hope is that we can make myofibroblasts function normally.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - A: Reproduction, Maternal, Child and Youth Health
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: A Murine Model to Investigate the Mechanisms Underlying DOHaD
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL HEALTH; DEVELOPMENTAL ORIGINS OF HEALTH AND DISEASE; FETAL GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT; METABOLIC SYNDROME; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: Recent studies have clearly established a relationship between sub-optimal intrauterine and post-natal development, and later life predisposition to adult disease, including type II diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, stroke and other neurologic disorders - a relationship termed "developmental origins of health and disease" (DOHaD). While adverse pre- and postnatal development increases the risk of DOHaD, it does not determine that an individual will acquire these disorders suggesting that interactions between an individual's genotype and the environment may contribute to the eventual outcome. Increasing evidence suggests that premature activation of the fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a central component linking adverse pre and/or post-natal environmental exposures to later poor health outcomes. We have developed a novel mouse model in which dietary restriction of the mothers during pregnancy leads to symptoms of DOHaD disorders in the offspring.  We will use this model to define gene-environment interactions that result in DOHaD disorders. We anticipate that this study will enhance progress towards future intervention strategies aimed at reducing the burden of these disorders.

ClasseRechercheFR: RETARD MENTAL; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Target-Dependent Neuronal Differentiation in Drosophila
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DIFFERENTIATION; CIS-REGULATORY MODULE; DEVELOPMENTAL NEUROSCIENCE; DROSOPHILA MOLECULAR GENETICS; SIGNALLING PATHWAY; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Normal nervous system function requires the generation of an enormous diversity of neurons during development. Differences in neuronal identity and function depend upon the repertoire of genes expressed in different neurons. We are examining how differences in neuronal gene expression are specified by the intersection of 1) transcription factors intrinsic to the neuron, with 2) extrinsic signals that neurons receive from the target cells that they innervate. Using the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, as our model, we have found that the signals that neurons receive from their target cells activate different gene expression profiles in different neurons. Because this is a conserved mechanism for neuronal differentiation, we can take advantage of the powerful molecular genetic technologies of Drosophila to rapidly derive novel insight into how these mechanisms operate in humans. Disruptions in transcription factor function has been linked to congenital disorders and disruption of target-derived signal trafficking has been strongly implicated in neurodegenerative disorders. Our studies will provide a mechanistic understanding of how these factors control neuronal function. This will greatly improve our understanding of the aetiology of diseases where these factors have been disrupted

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of circadian clocks in reproduction
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL CLOCK; CIRCADIAN  RHYTHMS; CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT MOUSE; CRE/LOXP SYSTEM; DISRUPTION OF CLOCK FUNCTION; ENDOCRINE RHYTHMS; GENE EXPRESSION; HISTOLOGY; INFERTILITY; NEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; OVARY; PITUITARY; RADIOIMMUNOASSAY; REPRODUCTIVE DISORDERS; REPRODUCTIVE PHYSIOLOGY; SCN
Abstract-Résumé: Humans and rodents alike possess a circadian timing system that drives 24-hour rhythms in physiology and behavior. We now know that circadian clocks reside in many organs and tissues throughout the body but their individual contributions to physiological functions is largely unknown. Intriguingly, also the pituitary gland and the ovary, both key structures of the reproductive system, harbor their own circadian pacemakers. Numerous aspects of reproductive physiology are under distinct temporal control such as the onset of puberty, the menstrual cycle, as well as ovulation and gestation. Together with the observation that several mouse models with body-wide impairments of circadian function show reproductive deficits, it seems likely that in particular the circadian clocks in the ovary and the pituitary act as integral players within the reproductive system. The proposed research aims to address the hypothesized role of circadian oscillators along the reproductive axis by employing mouse models that are specifically engineered to allow manipulation of circadian clock function in a tissue-restricted fashion. We will generate animals that lack clock function exclusively in the ovary, pituitary or the entire central nervous system and then test for reproductive consequences. These experiments may critically contribute to a better understanding of the physiological program that ensures reproductive success and will therefore likely help to elucidate new avenues for the treatment of infertility.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rational design of an effective TB vaccine: Immunology-driven reshaping of conventional BCG
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTATION; CATHEPSIN S; DENDRITIC CELLS; M. BOVIS BCG; MACROPHAGE; MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) is primarily an illness of the respiratory system, and is spread by coughing and sneezing.  TB is currently a global health problem of monumental proportions: each year about 8 million new cases of TB develop and about 3 million people die of the disease. The TB pandemic continues in spite of increased attention to the disease globally, the expansion of therapeutic regimes, and the widespread use of an existing vaccine.  TB is now a leading cause of death in the developing world. More than 90% of TB cases and deaths occur in low/middle income countries comprising 76% of the world's population. The recent increase of TB in developing countries has been exacerbated by many causes including pandemic HIV, war and political instability, drug resistance, and increasing poverty.  Moreover, if multi-drug resistant TB increases, TB could become even more difficult to control throughout the world.  BCG (Bacille Calmette-Guerin), developed in the early 1900s, is the vaccine used against TB today.  However, the high incidence of TB in developing countries where BCG immunization is widely practiced indicates that BCG is not highly efficacious over the many years that people are at risk for contracting the disease.  Clearly a better vaccine against TB is urgently needed.  In this respect, the objective of our research is to manipulate molecular interactions between the vaccine BCG and the immune system cells with a special focus on how to induce these cells to develop efficient TB immunity.  The results expected will significantly advance our understanding of host interactions with the BCG vaccine and will open avenue for testing a novel protective anti-TB vaccine.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Endothelial ion channels, nitric oxide and the cellular mechanisms regulating vasorelaxation
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ENDOTHELIUM; HYPERTENSION AND DIABETES; NITRIC OXIDE; VASCULAR MYOGRAPHY AND FLUORESCENCE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Vascular endothelium is a cell layer that lines the lumen of blood vessels and regulates blood pressure by producing and releasing chemical substances that regulate the level of contraction in the smooth muscle layers in the wall of the blood vessel. In diabetes mellitus, dysfunction of the endothelium is considered clinically to be an early causative event that leads to more serious cardiovascular complications, such as atherosclerosis, kidney damage and heart failure. Preventing or reversing endothelial dysfunction should thus halt the progression of cardiovascular disease. In the accompanying research proposal, we will examine the cellular mechanisms underlying the synthesis and actions of nitric oxide (NO), an important vasoactive substance produced by the endothelium that lowers blood pressure by relaxing smooth muscle and further acts to prevent the formation of atherosclerotic plaques. In particular, we will define the critical roles for membrane ion channels and cell signaling pathways in the synthesis of NO by human endothelial cells and in active resistance arterioles from mouse models of human diabetes. Our experiments will incorporate biochemistry, molecular biology and state-of the-art recording techniques to measure directly NO production and ion channel activities in single endothelial cells. These proposed studies will reveal important, new insights regarding NO synthesis and action in blood vessels, as well as potential new therapeutic strategies to reverse disease-related changes in these events.

TitreApplicationTitle: In vivo neuroimaging analysis of salt taste sensory pathway in C.elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: C.ELEGANS; CALCIUM; CLONING; GENETICS; IN VIVO NEUROIMAGING; SALT TASTE SENSATION
Abstract-Résumé: Salt sensation, unlike other tastes including sweet, sour, bitter, and umami (savory), is poorly understood. Knowing how we taste salt is important, as regulation of salt in the diet is essential for managing high blood pressure. We are studying salt sensation using the microscopic round worm C. elegans. Using powerful genetic, imaging, and behavioral tests, we are trying to find the genes responsible for salt sensation and understand how they help the worm (and people) to taste salt. These studies will lead to the development of salt substitutes that can be used to prevent high blood pressure.

ClasseRechercheFR: LEUCEMIES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Biomarkers for Chronic Graft-Versus-Host disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; BLOOD AND MARROW TRANSPLANTATION; GRAFT-VERSUS-HOST DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: In 2005, approximately 17,000 people world-wide received an allogeneic Blood and Marrow Transplantation (BMT) as a life saving procedure. Of those transplant recipients, >1900 died of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). The chronic form of GVHD (cGVHD) now occurs in about 50% of all allogeneic BMT and its treatment is limited by a poor ability to diagnose, determine whether it is high or low risk, and evaluate how it has responded to treatment. These limitations are primarily due to a poor understanding of the underlying biological factors causing the disease. This current proposal strikes at these primary limitations by utilizing a comprehensive approach to validate biomarkers that will lead to improved ability to assign treatment and develop new therapeutic approaches to cGVHD.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
AreasOfScienceEN: DENTAL SCIENCE - Oral Biology; CELL BIOLOGY
ResearchClassEN: DENTAL DISEASE (INCL. ORAL BIOLOGY); SKIN AND SUBCUTANEOUS TISSUS
ClasseRechercheFR: AFFECTIONS DENTAIRES (ET BIOLOGIE BUCCO-DENTAIRE); PEAU ET TISSUS SOUS-CUTANES
TitreApplicationTitle: Critical role for alpha-v-beta-6 integrin in enamel biomineralization
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA-V-BETA-6 INTEGRIN; CELL CULTURE; EPIDERMIS; EXPERIMENTAL PERIODONTITIS; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: Enamel is the hardest mineralized tissue in the human body. It covers the crowns of teeth and protects the teeth from decay and functional wear during chewing and grinding the teeth together. It is the only calcified tissue in the body that is produced by epithelial-derived cells called ameloblasts. During enamel formation, ameloblasts produce and process extracellular matrix that then becomes calcified to form fully mineralized enamel. A number of proteins that are crucially important for enamel formation have been discovered. Human mutations in some of these proteins cause inherited conditions in which enamel is poorly developed or calcified (called Amelogenesis Imperfecta; AI). This can lead to extensive wear and decay in both the primary and permanent dentition. Often, patients with AI lose their teeth at a young age or need to go through extensive restorative work to protect teeth from decay and attrition. We have recently discovered that mice lacking ameloblast surface protein alpha-v-beta-6 integrin show weakly calcified rough enamel that poorly resists wear during chewing. This integrin regulates cell adhesion to proteins that have an arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (RGD) amino acid motif but its function in ameloblasts is not known. In this grant proposal, we will characterize in detail the enamel defect caused by alpha-v-beta-6 integrin deficiency and investigate the molecular mechanism by which alpha-v-beta-6 integrin regulates calcification of enamel. Understanding the molecular mechanism of enamel calcification would help us not only to better diagnose genetic and acquired conditions that affect enamel formation and prevent destruction of crowns of teeth but also facilitate future endeavours aimed at tooth regeneration.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Autophagic Regulation of Memory T Cell Survival
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CELL DEATH; HYPOXIA; IMMUNE RESPONSE; LCMV; MEMORY T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: When a host becomes infected with a virus or bacteria the immune system responds by generating a large number of immune "T cells" to seek and destroy the microorganism.  This expansion in cells can be in excess of ten fold so that adequate T cells can neutralize the infection.  When the infection is eliminated most T cells die so that normal numbers of circulating T cells are restored.  However, a small proportion of T cells do not die but instead survive and transform into "memory T cells".  Memory T cells go on to survive for the lifetime of the host so that a second infection with the same microorganism leads to stronger immunity.  In this way, the host develops "memory" to the infectious agent.  This is one of the most basic aspects of the immune system and is the principle on which the development of every successful human vaccine is based.  Despite this achievement, we do not fully understand how memory T cells survive for the entire lifespan of the host which in the case of humans can be greater than 60 years.  Based on our initial experiments, we have found that memory T cells turn on a survival program called "autophagy".  We believe that this distinct form of survival is necessary for the generation and maintenance of memory T cells.  We also have evidence to suggest that autophagy is switched on when memory cells are exposed to low levels of key metabolites.  In this proposal, we will:  1) determine whether autophagy is required for memory T cell development, and 2) determine what factors activate memory T cell autophagy and how this is accomplished at the molecular level.  This information can be used to understand how other cell types including rare long-lived cancer stem cells that may be responsible for the development of primary as well as recurrent tumors, are endowed with this survival property.  The answers to these questions may enable us to exploit this property to develop more effective treatments for diseases such as HIV/AIDS and cancer.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
ResearchClassEN: MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL DISEASES; PSYCHO-SOCIAL AND BEHAVIOURAL RESEARCH
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; RECHERCHES PSYCHOSOCIALES ET COMPORTEMENTALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Maturational and psychosocial factors' relation to substance use in  adolescence for children with early physical aggression and hyperactivity
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; AGGRESSION; DEVELOPMENT; HYPERACTIVITY; LONGITUDINAL; NEUROCOGNITION
Abstract-Résumé: Substance use seems to wax in adolescence and wane in early adulthood. Yet adolescents know as well as adults about the hazards of substance use but do not seem to make good use of this information. The frontal lobes, which are important in decision making, develop steadily throughout adolescence. However, puberty begins slowly in late childhood, accelerates in mid adolescence and slows down by late adolescence. Researchers have noticed that the rate at which pubertal maturation proceeds initially exceeds that of the frontal lobes. They think that this may create a maturational gap that would drive adolescent substance use; it is only by late adolescence and young adulthood, when pubertal maturation slows down and when the brain has matured sufficiently to handle the motivational changes brought up by puberty, that the gap begins to close. However, not all children experience puberty in the same manner. And it may be those for whom the gap between pubertal and brain maturation is greatest who are most at risk for smoking, drinking, and taking drugs, particularly if they spend time with deviant peers, lack positive relations with adults, and already have a history of behaviour problems since childhood.  This research project will follow several hundreds of adolescents yearly from the ages of 13-17 years to examine behaviour, pubertal changes, and decision-making. These children have been followed yearly since birth and our previous documentation of their developmental history including behaviour, early puberty, social environment, and decision making will prove extremely valuable. Identifying mechanisms at play in childhood and adolescence will further help current prevention initiatives, which rely mainly on universal approaches, to become more targeted.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Investigations on 4-hydroxy-2-alkylquinoline (HAQ) derivatives produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Burkholderia species.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE / ALTERNATIVE ANTI-INFECTIVE DRUGS; BIOWARFARE AGENT / MELIOIDOSIS; CELL-TO-CELL COMMUNICATION (QUORUM SENSING) /GENE REGULATION; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMIC / GENETIC / WHOLE-GENOME TRANSCRIPTOME; IMMUNOMODULATORY ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a prevalent opportunistic human pathogen. Individuals who are immunocompromised or have breaches in normal barriers are especially susceptible to P. aeruginosa infections, such as cancer patients, those with indwelling medical devices, and AIDS patients. Moreover, P. aeruginosa is the primary cause of mortality among individuals suffering from the fatal genetic disorder cystic fibrosis (CF). The genus Burkholderia comprises more than forty species that inhabit remarkably diverse ecological niches. The pathogen B. pseudomallei is the causative agent of melioidosis, a common cause of human pneumonia that can turn into an often fatal septicemic infection. This bacterium is now considered a potential biothreat agent. Also, a number of Burkholderia species are increasingly prevalent opportunistic human pathogens. Burkholderia species are notoriously highly resistant to antibiotic treatments. «Quorum sensing» (QS) is an intercellular communication system used by many bacterial species to regulate virulence factors and gene products required for bacteria-host interactions. P. aeruginosa and Burkholderia control the expression of a wide spectrum of virulence/survival factors through QS. Because of their adaptability, persistence and multi-resistance to antibiotics, the opportunistic pathogens P. aeruginosa and B. cepacia complex species such as B. ambifaria, are virtually impossible to eradicate. Furthermore, the potential severity and difficulty of treatment of melioidosis pose a bioterrorism threat. It is therefore imperative to search for new therapeutic approaches. We have been uncovering a remarkable mechanism required for the full virulence of P. aeruginosa. This new intercellular communication system is based on the production of 4-hydroxy-2-alkylquinolines (HAQs). Furthermore, we have identified HAQ-like molecules in Burkholderia species. We believe HAQ signalling is a target for antiinfection therapeutics targeting these bacteria.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms in Scar Formation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ORAL MUCOSA; SCAR; SKIN; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: Scar formation following injury to skin is a common, unwanted outcome of the wound healing process.  Clinically, scars can range from fine lines to expansive, disfiguring hypertrophic or keloid scars.  Regardless of the type of scars, they lead to considerable psychosocial impacts or physical complications or both for the individuals.  At least 45 million patients in the United States alone undergo procedures that could benefit from therapies that reduce scar formation, resulting in a $4 billion anti-scarring therapy market annually.  During the last decades, using various animal models, steady progress has been made to identify factors that may reduce scar formation.  In spite of these advances, no effective therapy to prevent scar formation exists today.  This is likely because information from the animal models cannot always be applied to humans.  Thus, better models to compare scar-free and scar-forming wound healing are needed.  Intriguingly, there is a common impression among clinicians that human oral mucosal wounds heal with minimal scar formation.  However, there has been no rigorous experimental evidence that support this notion.  Systematical studies of experimental wound healing in humans are, however, difficult to perform for ethical reasons.  We have, therefore, developed a red Duroc pig model.  Skin wound healing in these pigs has been extensively characterized and closely resembles human skin wound healing and results in abnormal scar formation.  We have shown that wounds in the oral mucosa of these animals heal with significantly reduced scar formation compared to skin wounds.  We have also confirmed that oral mucosal wound healing in these pigs is similar to that in human oral mucosa.  By using this model, we will identify novel mechanisms that promote scarless healing and reduce scar formation.  We believe that the present study will provide novel information that can be used to design therapies to reduce scar formation in human skin.

TitreApplicationTitle: STeroid-induced Osteoporosis in the Pediatric Population: Canadian Incidence Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE FRAGILITY; CHILDREN; CHRONIC ILLNESS; GLUCOCORTICOIDS; OSTEOPOROSIS; VERTEBRAL COMPRESSION FRACTURES
Abstract-Résumé: Children with serious chronic illnesses such as leukemia, nephrotic syndrome (a kidney disorder) and rheumatic conditions (such as arthritis, dermatomyositis and lupus) are frequently treated with a medication known as glucocorticoids. While effective in treating the underlying conditions, glucocorticoids have the potential to cause osteoporosis in children, a thinning of the bones. We have learned through a prior grant funded by CIHR, that children receiving glucocorticoids for serious illnesses have a higher than expected rate of osteoporosis, which causes painful vertebral (spine) fractures. In this next phase of our research project, known as the STeroid-induced Osteoporosis in the Pediatric Population (STOPP) study, we plan to determine the ongoing rate of spine fractures in children with chronic disease and the clinical profile of children at greatest risk for developing such fractures in the long-term. In addition, the young skeleton differs greatly from that of adults since children with osteoporosis have the potential to recover from spine fractures through bone growth.  As pediatric researchers, it is important that we determine to what extent children are able to reconstruct fractured vertebrae, and the clinical profile of the child with the greatest potential to do so. The information that we gain from this study will allow us to develop national guidelines for the early identification, treatment and prevention of osteoporosis in children with serious underlying disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diffuse brain damage effects on distributed systems: multimodal brain imaging and rehabilitation
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSE BRAIN DAMAGE; EEG; FUNCTIONAL MRI; REHABILITATION; STRUCTURAL MRI
Abstract-Résumé: Diffuse brain damage affects communication in distributed systems that support complex information processing, yet few neuropsychological or brain imaging studies directly address the effects of diffuse injury or apply interventions targeting neuropsychological disabilities. The objectives of this research are to 1) improve assessment of diffuse injury effects through behavioral assessment and multimodal brain imaging and 2) apply a rehabilitation specifically  for complex information processing deficits in three populations: mild-to-moderate traumatic brain injury (TBI), multiple sclerosis (MS), and small vessel white matter stroke. Patients will be assessed pre-intervention, post-intervention, and at long-term follow-up using a battery of behavioral and functional neuroimaging tasks.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Synaptic Growth and Function at the Drosophila Larval Neuromuscular Junction
Keywords-MotsClés: BMP SIGNALING; DROSOPHILA NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION; GENETICS; IMAGING; RHO GTPASES; SYNAPTIC GROWTH AND FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: It is well accepted that in the developing nervous system neuronal connections undergo tremendous remodeling, and evidence is accumulating that in fact this is true for the adult brain as well. We use a combination of genetic and molecular tools in combination with imaging and electrophysiological techniques in fruit fly nervous system to identify genes and characterize mechanisms that underlie the ability of neurons to maintain their ability to change and remodel. In parallel experiments, we study the role of human disease genes in this process, by focusing on the fly counterparts of human genes or by transgenically expressing the human genes in the nervous system of the fly. Our findings will provide important insight into how the brain is wired up and how it functions as well as paving the way for novel therapeutic approaches aimed at curing brain diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU POUMON; THERAPIE DU CANCER DU POUMON
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of antigen processing machinery in carcinomas
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTATION; IMMUNOGENICITY; LUNG/BREAST CANCER; MHC I; TAP; TRANSCRIPTIONAL ACTIVATOR
Abstract-Résumé: An effective immune system is essential for limiting the emergence of cancers and for aiding in the recovery from cancer. It has recently been recognized that the failure of the immune surveillance system is primarily the result of defects in the antigen presentation machinery of certain malignant cells. The immune response detects abnormal peptides, or antigens, in the context of a multi-part molecule known as MHC I on the surface of cells, and this functions as an effective tumour detection system. However, many lung carcinomas exhibit a loss of MHC I on their surface and transporter of antigen processing (TAP) downregulation, as do other cancers such as breast, ovarian, prostate, and cervical cancer. Failure of this antigen presentation system allows malignant cells to grow and in some cases, to develop into metastatic cancers. Overall, 90% of carcinomas lack functional MHC I molecules. Thus, these tumour cells are hidden from the cellular arm of the immune system and grow into tumours that may eventually result in death. We show strong evidence of strategies to increase the recognition of cancers by the immune system will halt tumour growth and metastases. Key Research Aim: We have found that metastatic carcinomas lack positive regulators of the TAP-1 gene. We have thus cloned candidate regulators and plan to express these regulatory genes to confirm they can enhance immune recognition of cancer in tumour bearing animals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Traitement des blessures tendineuses : analyse de l'impact de différents protocoles d'exercice sur la matrice extracellulair
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYSE D'IMAGES; CONTRACTION CELLULAIRE; FIBROSE; IONS CALCIQUES; MARQUEURS FLUORESCENTS; MATRICE EXTRACELLULAIRE; MICROSCOPIE; MYOFIBROBLASTES; MECANOTRANSDUCTION; REPARATION TISSULAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: Myofibroblasts (MFs) are cells implicated in wound healing through their strong contraction and remodeling of injured tissues. These cells can also play a significant role in pathological fibrosis. However, the mechanisms of MF contraction are still unclear. Spontaneous intracellular oscillations of a chemical mediator, the calcium ion (Ca2+), have been shown to coordinate between contacting MFs. Inhibition of mechanical coupling structures of cells abolishes coordination of oscillations. We thus propose that contraction is dependent on interplay between mechanical coupling of cells and Ca2+ movements. In addition, this process would be influenced by intra- and extracellular mechanical environment.  Consequently, we will perform live videomicroscopy on MFs incorporated in collagen gels. Using fluorescent indicators, we will analyze Ca2+ oscillations in relation to cell contraction. The effect of Ca2+ signaling inhibitors will be tested under these conditions. Next, we will evaluate Ca2+ movements under varying cellular tension, which will be modulated by growing MFs on substrates and in gels of defined rigidity or on extendable membrane. Finally, we will excise rat dorsal wounds and mount tissue sections for microscopic observation. We will assess how Ca2+ oscillations change during the course of wound healing. The role of mechanical coupling structures will also be analyzed by adding specific inhibitors.  Tissue healing is a necessary process to maintain body integrity and function. Pathological changes leading to fibrosis occur in various anatomical structures like skin, lungs, liver and others. Considering the personal and socio-economical burdens associated with fibrosis, it is crucial to deepen our understanding of key players, like MFs, implicated in this process. This project will thus provide useful insights on mechanisms of MF contraction and remodeling of tissues, making another important step towards the definition of possible therapeutic targets.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE PULMONAIRE CHRONIQUE OBSTRUCTIVE; LES EFFETS ENVIRONNEMENTAUX SUR LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) induced cardiovascular disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTION; BIOMARKERS; COPD; EXACERBATION OF COPD; SYSTEMIC INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or better known as Chronic Bronchitis & Emphysema, is a progressive inflammatory condition of the lungs predominantly causes by cigarette smoke and air pollution. COPD is a worldwide public health problem has been projected to be the 3rd leading cause of death and 5th leading cause of disability by 2020 worldwide. COPD is a major health burden in Canada, effecting ~750,000 Canadians and accounts for over 100,000 hospitalizations and 10,000 deaths each year at an annual economic cost of $1.67 billion dollars in direct health care expenditures and $4.1 billion in total costs to Canadians.  The Lung Health Study has shown that the majority of disability and death in COPD subjects are caused by heart and blood vessel disease (heart attacks and strokes). The reason for this association is unclear. We postulate that the lung inflammation in COPD spills over into the bloodstream causing systemic inflammation which activates blood vessels resulting heart attacks and strokes in susceptible individuals. We have developed a novel animal model to test this hypothesis and have selected to explore the role of a pro-inflammatory mediators, IL-6, that is known to be associated with heart disease and elevated in the blood of COPD subjects. This model would also allow the development of targeted interruption of inflammatory mediators as a new therapeutic approach to impact heart disease causes by inflammatory lung conditions such as COPD.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; TROUBLES DE SOMMEIL
TitreApplicationTitle: High-throughput, in vivo, Nuclear Receptor-targeted drug discovery
Keywords-MotsClés: HIGH THROUGHPUT; LIGAND; METABOLISM; NUCLEAR RECEPTOR; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Hormones are chemicals that circulate within the body and trigger specific responses in target tissues. Steroids, such as the estrogens used to treat or postpone menopause and the muscle building steroids taken by some athletes, are  some well known examples. These particular hormones penetrate cells and elicit responses by binding to a family of proteins called nuclear receptors (NRs). NRs control many of the metabolic pathways in our body as well as related processes such as memory, behaviour and aging. Consequently, a large number of human diseases, for example diabetes, obesity, heart disease and Alzheimers, are caused, or enhanced, by NR malfunctions. Fortunately, the ability of these proteins to respond to small molecules that move efficiently within the body make them ideal drug targets. In fact, a disproportionate percentage of the most successful and important pharmaceuticals target specific NRs. This is despite the fact that hormone partners have yet to be identified for more than half of NRs. We have devised new methods to identify new human hormones using live fish. These methods allow us to screen chemical libraries for hormones that act in specific cells or tissues, that do not cross-react with other NRs, and that do not cause detrimental side effects. These are common problems in drug discovery that usually only come to light later during lengthy and costly clinical trials. These advantages will provide us with enormous advantages in terms of time, costs and successful compound identification.
