TitreApplicationTitle: An epidemiologic assessment of the risk of acute lumbar disc herniation from chiropractic care.
Keywords-MotsClés: BAYESIAN METHODS; BELIEF ELICITATION; CHIROPRACTIC; COMPLICATIONS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LUMBAR DISC HERNIATION; POPULATION-BASED; PRIMARY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Chiropractic care is popular for low back pain, but may increase the risk for lumbar disc herniation.  Although research suggests that chiropractic treatment can benefit low back pain, little is known about possible complications of chiropractic care for low back pain.  This lack of information is an important problem because an effective treatment is one that improves health while leading to few complications.  The main purpose of this research is to investigate associations between chiropractic visits and acute low back disc herniations that require surgery in the Ontario population and to contrast this with primary care physician visits and low back disc herniations.  A secondary goal is to examine beliefs about the risk of lumbar disc herniation from chiropractic care and the impact of epidemiological evidence on these beliefs.  Data will be collected for the population-based study from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long Term Care.  Advanced epidemiologic methods will be used to analyze the associations between the two health care services and acute low back disc herniation surgery.  The belief elicitation study will apply a Bayesian approach to health services research in order to formally incorporate prior beliefs about the risk from chiropractic treatment into epidemiological analyses of the association between chiropractic care and sudden low back disc herniation.  This research will provide important information that will help to inform clinical practice and health services policy development.  It represents epidemiologic policy-relevant research that has the potential to protect the health of Canadians and ensure the safety of the Canadian health care delivery system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of meiotic defects as an underlying cause of male factor infertility
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNOCYTOGENETICS; IMPRINTING GENES; INTRACYTOPLASMIC SPERM INJECTION (ICSI); MALE INFERTILITY; MEIOTIC DEFECTS; SPERM CHROMOSOMAL ABNORMALITIES
Abstract-Résumé: Infertility is regarded as a major health problem, affecting approximately one in six couples in Canada.  It is estimated that 30-40% of couples seeking fertility treatments are diagnosed with male-factor infertility due to abnormal sperm production.  In the majority of these cases, the cause of infertility remains unknown.  It is suspected that genetic and epigenetic factors may both play an important role in the onset of male infertility. Recent studies have shown that errors in this meiotic division are more prevalent in infertile men and may play an important role in idiopathic male infertility.  We recently provided evidence that meiotic errors in infertile men may also be associated with the production of aneuploid sperm, that is, sperm containing either extra or missing chromosomes.  There is increasing evidence in the literature to suggest that infertile men may be at risk of having abnormal DNA methylation (a chemical modification of genetic sequences) in their sperm, which may affect sperm production. Recently, we also found that a subgroup of infertile men had increased imprinting defects (defects in the methylation of specific DNA sequences) in their sperm. We will use recently developed techniques to further characterize the meiotic defects that lead to the production of aneuploid sperm and male infertility in two unique infertile male groups (men with very low sperm counts with and without chromosome rearrangements).  We will also investigate the prevalence of imprinting defects among infertile men, and its possible association with meiotic errors within the same study population.  Detailed meiotic and imprinting studies of infertile men will begin to reveal the underlying genetic causes of male infertility.  The results of this study could lead to improved treatment and reproductive outcomes for couples undergoing infertility treatments, such as intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI).

TitreApplicationTitle: An investigation into risk-taking behaviour, bone microstructure and fracture between the sexes: What underpins fracture in boys compared to girls during growth?
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION; BONE STRUCTURE; BOYS HEALTH; FRACTURE; LIFESTYLE FACTORS; RISK-TAKING BEHAVIOR
Abstract-Résumé: It has been suggested that "falls and fracture at any age are no accident" More boys (42-51%) than girls (27-40%) sustain a fracture during the growing years. Despite this sex difference in fracture rates, factors that contribute to fracture in this age group are not well understood. Reasons for higher fracture rate might include children partaking in higher risk activities or having less fear of injury, having higher body fat relative to body weight, falling more often (poor balance) or having more fragile bones. Thus we aim to determine if there are, 1) differences in whether all or some of these factors predict fractures in boys compared with girls and, 2) whether these factors track forward similarly in boys compared with girls as children advance through the growth spurt at puberty. Our project is novel because it integrates factors related to fracture in boys compared with girls - previous research has examined some of these factors in isolation. To address our aims, we will recruit 200 boys (12-14y) and 200 girls (10-12 y)[these ages match the children for maturity]. We will recruit 100 girls and 100 boys who have sustained a fracture within the last 6 weeks. These children will be compared with 100 same age and sex friends who have not sustained a fracture. We will measure children across 4 years of childhood and adolescent growth. We will assess risk behaviours, lifestyle in boys and girls using questionnaires as well as age-appropriate measures of balance (stability). We will use advanced medical imaging to measure fat and muscle mass as well as to characterize bone strength. We have one of only a few instruments world-wide that is able to safely and precisely measure the fine microstructure of bone. Our research team has a strong history of collaborating with key stakeholders (parents, teachers, clinicians) to develop key messages and tools and to move knowledge into programs, practice and policy that benefit children's health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of AboriginalYouth Health Leadership Through Theatre
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL YOUTH HEALTH; ABORIGINAL YOUTH LEADERSHIP; ARTS-BASED RESEARCH; DECISION-MAKING AND HEALTH; THEATRE AND HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Our research project is based on our previous research with Aboriginal youth in which we used theatre workshops to help participants to examine healthy decision-making. The participants reported that the workshops helped them overcome shyness and develop confidence, attributes that are necessary for making independent decisions in a context of constant peer pressure that has often resulted in participation in unhealthy activities. The Aboriginal youth participants who experienced the transformative power of theatre actitives during these workshops have taken the initative to lead younger children in theatre activities in an effort to help them overcome shyness and develop self-confidence. In this research project, we will continue to work with Aboriginal youth to examine how to best have an impact on the process of healthy desision-making. We will use theatre and other art forms to determine how Aboriginal youth make decisions regarding healthy and unhealthy behaviours. Based on our previous research, we know that these theatre activities provide the space for the the participants' Indigenous knowledge to emerge, thus empowering them to be aware of their decision-making and to take leadership in assisting other Aboriginal youth do the same.   This research will document the process of Aboriginal youth becoming health leaders and will include Elders and other supportive adults in the process. We will also examine how theatre and other arts-based methods engage Indigenous youth in healthy decision-making. The researchers will collaborate with youth to determine the specifics of the research project within the parameters set by the overall design. In collaboration with the youth participants, we will share our findings with other Aboriginal youth, community members, and policy makers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Centre for Research Development in Gender, Mental Health and Violence Across the Lifespan
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER; GENDER AND SEX-BASED ANALYSIS; KNOWLEDGE; MENTAL HEALTH; MIXED METHODS; PREVENTION; SECONDARY DATA ANALYSIS; TRANSLATION; VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: The mental health of children and adults across many areas, including substance use, mood and personality disorders can be profoundly affected by violence in the home. These effects often persist, and can contribute to ongoing cycles of violence and poor health. Child maltreatment (CM) and intimate partner violence (IPV) are global public health problems for which there are few proven interventions; also, while thought to affect primarily females, there is evidence that exposure to child physical abuse is at least as, if not more, common in males, and both women and men are victims of IPV and its mental health consequences. Despite the known link between mental health and family violence, they have received relatively little research focus, especially in the areas of intervention. With family violence affecting at least 30% of Canadians, there is a pressing need for a coherent and integrated approach to the problem of family violence and its mental health outcomes, and to look at this for both males and females. Our proposed Centre for Research Development in Gender, Mental Health and Violence Across the Lifespan has three main goals:  (1) to increase our understanding of the links between mental health problems and CM and IPV; (2) to develop strategies to prevent or reduce CM, IPV and subsequent mental health problems; and (3) to share and exchange knowledge within the team of Centre investigators and with stakeholders such as policy-makers, health and social service providers, advocates and members of the public. We will do this by: (1) creating an international network of researchers, clinicians and policy-makers to set priorities for research to reduce family violence, and to better understand the links between CM, IPV and mental health by analysing data from existing studies, (2) understanding and fostering resilience in mental health outcomes after exposure to violence and (3) developing innovations in knowledge exchange tailored to the area of violence.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Centre for intercultural research on prevention of gender violence (CIHR-CIPREV)
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; ADDICTIONS; ENCULTURATION; GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE; IMMIGRANTS; KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS AND TRANSLATION; MENTAL HEALTH; PRIMARY PREVENTION; RESEARCH DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Ethnic minority and migrant status are recognized risk factors for gender-based violence and related mental health problems. This Centre develops research, theory, methods, and proposals for the prevention of gender-based violence (GBV) and associated mental health problems, including addictions, among four cultural minorities in Canada, with a focus on parenting and 'resilience of origin' -- resilience rooted in the culture of origin -- as potential protective factors across the lifespan.  The research development focuses on gendered enculturation and its influence through parenting as a turnkey if not invariably positive intervention to reduce GBV. Key theoretical touchstones are enculturation and decolonization.   The driving force is research use in partner communities of origin and related urban communities: Alexis Nakota Sioux and urban Nakota Sioux (Edmonton); Akwesasne and urban Mohawk (Ottawa and Toronto), Inuit living in Ottawa, and a subgroup of the Ottawa Latin American immigrant community. The Centre will generate proposals for in-depth research with and for each of these partner groups, training researchers from each group to play lead roles in the future research.   The Centre will also build skills in partner groups and organizations to use the products of GBV prevention research in mental health programs with partners engaged from the outset. A community of practice that includes policy-makers and other stakeholders will accompany the development of the major proposals generated by the Centre, contributing to an enabling environment for their future implementation.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Centre for Research on Gender and Social Disparities in Mental Health and Addictions
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER AND SEX BASED ANALYSIS; INTERSECTIONAL ANALYSIS; MENTAL HEALTH; MULTI-METHODS (QUALITATIVE AND QUANTITATIVE); SOCIAL INEQUITIES; SUBSTANCE ABUSE
Abstract-Résumé: Through the support of innovative research, knowledge exchange, and training activities, the Centre for Research on Gender and Social Disparities in Mental Health and Addictions aims to create a better understanding of why disparities in mental health and addictions outcomes persist so that appropriate programs, policies, and interventions can be developed and implemented, ultimately leading to improved mental health for men and women, boys and girls in Canada and internationally.  The Centre, located at Simon Fraser University, will foster relationships among groups of academic and community researchers, community service providers, policy makers, practitioners, advocates, and those who have experience with mental illness from across Canada, the US, UK, and Australia, who will explore the use of gender and sex-based analysis tools and other relevant methods in the following five key theme areas:  mental health reform; recovery and housing; reproductive mental health; violence, mental health, and substance use, and; the criminal justice system, mental health, and substance use.  In addition, through its partnership with the Mental Health Commission of Canada (MHCC), the Centre will develop mechanisms for sharing research findings emerging from the Centre with regional, provincial, national, and international governments, service providers, researchers, and the general public to facilitate access to information about gender and social disparities in mental health and addictions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Perceptions, Experiences and Management of Knee Symptoms in Adults Age 35-65 Years
Keywords-MotsClés: GENERALIZED ESTIMATING EQUATIONS; HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; MODELS OF CARE; ORTHOPAEDICS; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PATIENT OUTCOMES; SPECIALIZED PHYSIOTHERAPISTS
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) or 'wear and tear' arthritis is a chronic condition that produces joint pain and stiffness with resultant physical disability. OA affects 10% of the population.  As the population ages, the number of people with OA is expected to increase. There are shortages of health care providers, such as orthopaedic surgeons (OS), to provide care to this growing population. Typically, patients are referred to OSs for consultation about surgery. Yet, about 30% of people with OA who see a surgeon don't need surgery. In response to health system challenges, some hospitals use specially trained physiotherapists (PTs) to assess patients referred for orthopaedic consultation to determine if they need to see an OS for consideration of surgery. For people who don't need surgery, the PT provides care, such as exercise and education. There has been little research on the benefits of this way of delivering care and no information on how it changes patient outcomes or health services used by patients. The main objective of this study is to compare the outcomes of people who don't require surgery at 6 and 12 months following their visit to an OS (group 1) or to a specially trained PT (group 2). The main outcome is physical function but pain, participation in social roles, knowledge and self-efficacy (confidence in managing OA) will also be compared between groups. A second objective is to compare use of health services related to OA (e.g. physician or therapy visits) between groups after 1 year. Information will be collected using questionnaires and health care datasets that routinely collect data on medical care. This study will provide important information to help us understand if this new way of delivering health services improves pain and function in people with non-surgical OA. The results will be shared with study participants, health care providers and health agencies who make decisions about services for people with OA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring the impact of musculoskeletal disorders on work: The development of a comprehensive approach to capture health-related worker productivity loss.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; ITEM RESPONSE THEORY; LATENT VARIABLE MODELING; MUSCULOSKELETAL DISORDERS; OUTCOME MEASUREMENT; PSYCHOMETRICS; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING; UPPER-LIMB DISORDERS; WORK PRODUCTIVITY LOSS; WORKPLACE DISABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Work is a central part of peoples' lives. A person's ability to work can be profoundly affected by a musculoskeletal (MSK) disorder. Examples of a MSK disorder can include an acute injury to a specific body part, like the shoulder, or more chronic conditions like arthritis. As such, MSK disorders can affect workers of all ages and of all professions. MSK disorders can affect worker productivity in different ways and to varying degrees, depending on variables like the severity of injury or job factors. Some will only be mildly affected at work, but others may need a leave of absence. Still others may be able to remain productive with some modifications to their work duties. Currently, there is no simple way to quantify the impact of MSK disorders on work. To that end, there is a need to develop an approach to measure health-related worker productivity loss that can be used as an outcome for clinical studies.    The purpose of this research is to apply advanced statistical methods to map out the relationships between different expressions of workplace disability (e.g. being off work, job accomodations), and to understand the factors or variables that affect these relationships. From these insights, we will then develop a novel approach to the measurement of worker productivity loss that considers all the possible ways in which this can be expressed for an individual worker. We will use patient-based data collected from workers with MSK disorders (e.g. upper-limb disorders, arthritis) to perform this work.  Developing a sensible way to measure worker productivity loss is an essential first step towards understanding how MSK disorders affect workers over time, and for estimating the associated economic costs to workers, employers, and insurers. This work will also set the stage for future research to evaluate the effectiveness of new therapies or workplace interventions aimed at reducing the burden of MSK disorders for the Canadian society at-large.

TitreApplicationTitle: School Functioning in Children after Traumatic Brain Injury: Developing A New Outcome Measure
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; FOCUS GROUPS; FUNCTION IN SCHOOL; MEASUREMENT TOOL DEVELOPMENT; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; PEDIATRIC; QUESTIONNAIRE; SCHOOL EDUCATION; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Unfortunately, trauma continues to be the leading cause of death and disability for children under the age of 18 years.  Children are also more susceptible to suffering head injuries as part of their trauma than are adults.  Successful rehabilitation and reintegration of these children into their surroundings is key to the prosperity of society as a whole.  After rehabilitation, these children are likely returned to their regular school environment.  There is currently no reliable or valid means to objectively assess the overall function in school of this specific patient population.  All currently used instruments assess single areas of function, but none has integrated them into a global measure.  We propose a new tool to assess how children function in school after head injury.  Through literature review, focus groups, and expert opinion, a new questionnaire will be designed that will then be admninistered to educational personnel.  It will be validated against various functional scales.  The end result will be a new measure that will prove invaluable in the rehabilitation and reintegration of these children into society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mutation of KCC3: Understanding a sensory motor neuropathy
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MOLECULAR PATHOGENESIS; SENSORY MOTOR NEUROPATHY
Abstract-Résumé: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with agenesis of the corpus callosum (HMSN/ACC) is a severe and progressive hereditary disease that affects the brain and spinal cord. The main features of the disease include malformation of the bridge connecting the two halves of the brain, progressive nerve and muscle wasting, and mental retardation. Symptoms of HMSN/ACC appear within the first year of life; by the time patients are adolescents all muscle movements are severely impaired and most patients are confined to wheel chairs or bedridden. The average life expectancy is 30 years; patients commonly die of complications related to respiratory problems. There is no specific treatment for HMSN/ACC. The disease is particularly common in the Northeastern part of the province of Quebec, where 1/2000 infants are born with the disease. Because HMSN/ACC is a genetic disease (it runs in families), it must be caused by a problem within a gene. We have identified the gene responsible for this disease and we will now determine how the malfunctioning of this gene leads to the disorder. With this added knowledge we should be able to develop much needed treatments and management strategies, which will improve the quality of life and life expectancy of HMSN/ACC patients. It may also shed some light on how the brain develops and functions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bone Marrow-Derived Cells as Gene Delivery Vehicles in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; BONE MARROW-DERIVED CELLS; MICROGLIA; MONOCYTE; MOTONEURON; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: We will explore the utility of bone marrow-derived cells as a delivery mechanism in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Our previous work has shown that bone marrow cells enter the brain and spinal cord in an animal model of ALS. We also have found that we can engineer the cells that enter the central nervous system to produce beneficial substances within the nervous system that could prevent neuron death and slow the progression of the disease. We anticipate that these bone marrow cells can be used as delivery vehicles that could aid in the survival of sick or dying cells in the nervous system of patients with ALS. We will identify which bone marrow-derived cells enter the nervous system so that we can restrict production of the substances to this specific population of bone marrow cells. Knowing the relevant population will allow us to restrict production of these substances which will minimize side effects, such as the uncontrolled proliferation of bone marrow stem cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Peripherin Abnormalities in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; BIOMARKERS; NEUROPATHOLOGY; TRANSGENIC MICE; UBIQUITINATED INCLUSIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating adult-onset neurodegenerative disease characterized by the loss of motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord, progressing from a mild muscle weakness to complete paralysis and eventual death, usually from respiratory failure, within 2-5 years from diagnosis. The incidence is about 2 per 100,000 with 2000-3000 Canadians suffering from the disease at any one time. There is no cure, nor effective treatment. Peripherin is a protein that is found associated with many of the pathological abnormalities found in the diseased motor neurons of patients with ALS. Overexpression of peripherin in transgenic mice leads to the formation of pathological abnormalities similar to those seen in ALS, that precedes a massive age related motor neuron degeneration, closely modeling the disease. This evidence suggests that peripherin may be an important factor contributing to motor neuron degeneration in ALS. This is supported by the finding of mutations in the peripherin gene in a few ALS cases. We have shown that many different peripherin species, or isoforms, can be generated by a process called alternative splicing, and that changes in peripherin isoform expression causes peripherin aggregate formation, and in some cases, neuronal death. We have shown that there is deregulation of alternative splicing of peripherin in ALS generating disease specific isoforms that may have utility as diagnostic markers. This proposal is aimed at further characterizing peripherin abnormalities in ALS as a means to understanding the underlying pathogenic process, which will aid in the development of effective therapeutics and eventual cure.

Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; GENE TRANSFER; MUSCLE; MUTANT G93A SOD1 TRANSGENIC MICE; NEUROMUSCULAR; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is an insidious and rapidly progressing disease affecting the brain, spinal cord and muscle function. ALS is a disease of motor neurons, which are specialized cells needed for muscle control. Diagnostic features of the disease are muscle weakness and paralysis, with an invariably fatal outcome. The swiftness of the disease progression makes ALS devastating for the affected individuals as well as their loved ones. Much progress has been made in understanding the disease mechanisms underlying the inherited form of ALS with the aid of an excellent mouse model. Mounting evidence from numerous studies suggests that ALS is actually a multi-systemic disorder, and disease progression is influenced by cells other than motor neurons. A recent study suggests that muscle is also a primary target organ affected in the familial form of ALS. In our preliminary study, specific genes expressed in muscle alone significantly modulated disease onset and progression in an ALS mouse model expressing a human ALS gene (the mutant G93A human SOD1 gene). The proposed studies aim to determine the skeletal muscle properties important for modulating ALS disease progression. These studies may lead to the development of effective muscle-based therapies for ALS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Formation of the tRNALys packaging complex in HIV-1
Keywords-MotsClés: GAG; GAGPOL; GENOMIC RNA; HIV-1 ASSEMBLY; LYSYL-TRNA; PRIMER TRNALYS3 FOR REVERSE TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: During HIV-1 assembly, a cellular molecule, tRNALys3, is selectively incorporated into the new virus, and anneals with a region in the viral RNA genome called the primer binding site (PBS). When this virus infects new cells, tRNALys3 is used to prime the initiation of reverse transcription, which produces new viral DNA. Infectivity of the viral population is directly proportional to the amount of tRNALys3 incorporated into the viruses, and this is an essential reaction in the HIV-1 life cycle.  We are examining the molecular mechanisms involved in tRNALys3 incorporation in order to find new targets for anti-viral therapy. Specifically, this involves discovering the viral and cellular proteins involved in facilitating tRNALys3 packaging into HIV-1. Our past studies have shown that this involves formation of a tRNALys3 packaging complex composed of tRNALys, viral genomic RNA, the viral proteins Gag and GagPol, and the cellular protein lysyl-tRNA synthetase (LysRS), a major tRNALys3 binding protein. One part of this project is devoted to developing an in vitro system for assembling this complex, so these interactions can be examined more closely, and it can be determined how the reactants can assemble at the particular region of the viral RNA where primer tRNALys3 is annealed.  The other part of this project further investigates why HIV-1 produced in mouse cells is unable to incorporate tRNALys3, even though all components of the tRNALys3 packaging complex described above are present in the formed virus. tRNALys3 incorporation in mouse cells is rescued by some factor (s) on human chromosome 16, and we will determine what this factor is.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study of the cellular and molecular mechanisms of HIV associated nephropathy (HIVAN)
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; ANIMAL MODEL; FOCAL SEGMENTAL GLOMERULOSCLEROSIS; HIV-1; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Kidney disease is a relatively frequent manifestation of HIV-1 infection in individuals of African origin and is designated HIV-1 associated nephropathy (HIVAN). It progresses rapidly and leads to end stage renal failure. It is thought to be induced by HIV-1 itself. The kidney lesions in HIVAN are very special and are only seen in other relatively rare genetic forms of kidney disease. Over the last few years, we have generated a mouse model of AIDS by expressing HIV-1 genes in mice. These mice develop all the immune manifestations of AIDS, such as loss of T cells. They also develop HIVAN very similar to human HIVAN. We plan to use this mouse model to understand how HIVAN develops; which kidney cells express host genes affecting HIV-1; what are the consequences of expression of these genes in different kidney cells; what are the main genes controlling the development of HIVAN; and is there genetic ways to block the development of this disease, etc. We believe this unique model reflects the human disease very well and its likely to be instrumental in providing answers to the above questions and to give us very good insights on how this disease occurs in this context.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of IL-12 family of Th1 cytokines IL-12, IL-23 and IL-27 by HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE REGULATION; HIV; IL-12 FAMILY OF CYTOKINES; MONOCYTIC AND DENDRITIC CELLS; TLRS
Abstract-Résumé: Immune response to infection is governed by cytokines secreted by various cells of the immune system. Cytokines have been classified into T helper (Th) type 1 and type 2 cytokines. Th1 cytokines promote cell mediated immune responses (CMIR) whereas Th2 cytokines mediate antibody responses. In HIV infection, the protective CMI responses diminish as disease progresses from the asymptomatic stage to the onset of AIDS. By down-regulating protective CMIR, HIV avoids an effective immune response resulting in progressive immunodeficiency and eventually the onset of AIDS related symptoms. We hypothesize that HIV infection disrupts the Th responses causing down regulation of Th1 cytokines such as IL-12, IL-23 and IL-27 (members of the IL-12 family of cytokines) thereby resulting in the loss of immune competence. An important key to elucidating the immune unresponsiveness associated with a profound down regulation of Th1 cytokines, therefore, lies in deciphering the molecular mechanism involved in this process. The mechanism by which IL-12, IL-23 and IL-27 production is regulated following infection of monocytic and dendritic cells is not clear at present. Our preliminary results suggest that the HIV regulatory gene products vpr and nef modulate Th1 cytokines production in LPS-stimulated human monocytic cells. In this research proposal, we will investigate the mechanisms by which the HIV regulatory proteins nef, tat and vpr down regulate the production of Th1 cytokines namely IL-12, IL-23 and IL-27 in monocytic and dendritic cells. The results of these studies will provide further insights into the molecular mechanisms by which HIV induces immunodeficiency.  Understanding the signaling pathways in HIV-induced dysregulation of Th1 cytokines may allow the development of effective therapeutic strategies aimed at enhancing immune responsiveness and potentially eliminating virus from the tissue reservoirs in HIV infected individuals who receive potent anti-retroviral therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of maternal immune responses and viral determinants of hepatitis C virus during pregnancy.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; CELL-MEDIATED IMMUNITY; HCV; HEPATITIS C; HIV; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: The clinical course of hepatitis C improves during pregnancy but worsens thereafter. In addition, women who carry hepatitis C virus (HCV) can transmit the infection to their infant during pregnancy and at the time of childbirth. In women who are infected with both HCV and human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), the causative agent of AIDS, transmission of HCV to the infant is 4 times more common. It is thought that maternal immune responses play a role in preventing disease progression and in protecting the child against infection. However, the means by which this protection is effected are unknown. To better understand the relationship between HIV-1, HCV, and maternal immunity, we will study immune responses and viral proteins in a group of pregnant women infected with HCV or coinfected with HCV and HIV-1. Results from these experiments will enable us to perfect the methods and protocols currently used to prevent transmission of viral infections from mother to child.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the role of structural inequities, gender-based violence, and power in shaping STI/HIV transmission dynamics in public place-based sex work
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER INEQUITIES; SEX WORK; SOCIAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; STI/ HIV; STRUCTURAL INEQUITIES; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Street-involved women who exchange sex for money, drugs, shelter, food or other commodities across Canadian cities remain highly vulnerable to violence, exploitation, homelessness, substance use, mental health issues, suicide, and premature mortality. Of particular concern, increasing evidence suggests this population is at elevated risk for acquiring HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with preliminary findings in Vancouver suggesting an HIV prevalence of 25% among female sex workers (FSWs). Importantly, emerging theoretical paradigms and global environmental-structural HIV/STI prevention research highlight the need to re-conceptualize women's HIV/STI risk as negotiated interactions, embedded in gendered power dynamics and access to resources, and the broader social, physical, and policy environment. While previous research has identified the individual risk factors for STI/HIV acquisition among FSWs, data has been largely drawn from studies among injection drug users and street involved youth, and there remains a dearth of longitudinal research evaluating the impact of the broader risk environment on HIV/STI transmission among street involved women who exchange sex. The proposed study aims to prospectively investigate how structural inequities (eg. housing insecurity, enforcement), gender-based violence, and power may shape the negotiation of risk reduction with clients and STI/HIV incidence among FSWS in public place-based sex work settings (e.g. bars, streets). As the first prospective study of FSWs and HIV/STI incidence in Canada, this research has a strong potential to contribute to innovative public health and HIV prevention strategies for some of the most vulnerable women in Canadian society. This research is also particularly timely and has the potential to inform ongoing legal proceedings and public policy discussions, as well as serve to help monitor the health and social impacts of major international events (e.g., 2010 Olympics).

TitreApplicationTitle: Studying the antiviral activity of bone marrow stromal cell antigen 2 and the countering mechanism from HIV-1 Vpu
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; BST-2; HIV; VIRAL PATHEGENESIS; VIRUS ASSEMBLY; VPU
Abstract-Résumé: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) has claimed the lives of 25 million people since the beginning of the AIDS epidemic in the early 1980s and endangers the life of 33 million infected individuals. Finding an effective treatment or a cure for this deadly virus is the goal of AIDS research. The currently available antiretroviral drugs are potent enough to lower the viral load in patient below the detection level and thus can extend the patient's life for more than 25 years on average. Yet, the inevitable appearance and circulation of multi-drug resistance HIV-1 strains quickly exhausts the effectiveness of these HIV-1 inhibitors. Without an HIV-1 vaccine in hand, developing new antiretrovirals is essential to control this epidemic. Research proposed in this grant application is aimed to study one recently host factor named bone marrow stromal cell antigen 2 (BST2) that potently block HIV-1 production when viral Vpu is not expressed. Understanding how BST2 restricts HIV-1 production and how Vpu counteracts BST2 is expected to reveal new strategies for developing novel HIV-1 therapeutic approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of the CD4 pathogenicity island on HIV susceptibility and disease progression
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV INFECTION; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; RECEPTOR POLYMORPHISM; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: As humans we all share the same set of gene, however, we all possess slightly different versions of those gene and that is what makes us all unique as individuals.  These genetic differences, called polymorphisms, also have been shown to be associated with differing susceptibility to disease, such as HIV.  Our lab has previously demonstrated a link between increased susceptibility to HIV infection and a particular version of the gene that encodes the main host protein that HIV uses to enter into a cell, called CD4.  Recent studies from our lab have shown that the genes that surround CD4 could also be linked to altered HIV susceptibility.  We have termed this group of genes the CD4 pathogenicity island and this proposal seeks to explore the genetic linkages between these genes and also determine at a molecular level how they affect susceptibility to HIV infection.  These studies could lead to be better understanding of the molecular events necessary to HIV to infect a cell which would provide a foundation for further anti-HIV drug development.

TitreApplicationTitle: University of Montreal Cardiac Surgery Clinical Investigation Group
Keywords-MotsClés: Unspecified/Non Spécifié
Abstract-Résumé: Despite improvements in cardiac surgery and anaesthesia in the face of sicker and elderly patients, numerous issues remain to be clarified concerning the best treatment options for ischemic mitral valve regurgitation and novel therapy for pulmonary hypertension. These important questions are difficult to answer with single center trials even in centers with a high volume of complex valvular surgery. The NIH has decided to form a network of clinical centers to address this challenge. The U of Montreal Cardiac Surgery Clinical Investigation Group (UMCSCIG) is proposing to join the NIH Network to help attain its goals of bringing innovative experimental strategies for the treatment of cardiac surgical pathology from the laboratory to the bedside. The U of M investigation Group is made up of 3 tertiary university hospital centers on 5 sites in the city of Montreal, treating over 3000 patients by 17 surgeons which represents close to 50% of the cardiac surgical volume of the Province of Quebec (population 8 million). The Group has a number of special attributes, and brings with it expertise that would be helpful for the NIH network as a whole. Its members belong to a single payer socialized medicine system, which facilitates patient follow-up and data generation. The close collaboration of cardiac surgical investigators with extensive experience in clinical trials with cardiologists, clinician-scientists and basic researchers within the research centers of the 3 hospital centers by their affiliation to the University of Montreal plus the hook-up with the Canadian East-West Network and the Quebec Heart Failure Society dedicated to Heart Failure Research are definite advantages. The MHI has a long and successful tradition of working with the NIH, it has an experienced clinical research co-ordinating center. The group has access to state of the art investigative technology, expertise in blood sampling, transportation and performs a large spectrum of open and minimally invasive coronary, valvular and aortic surgery as well as heart transplantation and implantable artificial heart program and emerging strength in cell therapy and seven new hybrid technology operating rooms are currently under construction at MHI. The U of Montreal Research Group proposes a project to evaluate the effect of a new treatment option for severe ischemic mitral regurgitation and a second project test as a new pharmacological management of pulmonary hypertension in patients experiencing difficulty separation from cardiopulmonary bypass.

TitreApplicationTitle: Équipe des IRSC en Comorbidité des troubles cérébraux et autres problèmes de santé : Recherche sur le développement d'approches novatrices de prévention du VIH et du VHC chez les usagers de cocaïne souffrant de problèmes de santé mentale
Keywords-MotsClés: COCAINE; ENTRETIEN MOTIVATIONNEL; INTERVENTION BREVE; PREVENTION; SANTE MENTALE; TOXICOMANIE; VIH / VHC
Abstract-Résumé: La concomitance sante mentale et consommation problematique de cocaine est rarement consideree dans les etudes sur les risques d'infection et dans l'offre de service en prevention du VIH et de l'hepatite C. Or, plusieurs etudes montrent que la consommation problematique de cocaine est associee aux conduites de consommation a risque de ces infections. De plus, les problemes de sante mentale frequents chez les usagers peuvent nuire a leur capacite d'avoir des comportements securitaires. Malheureusement, l'acces a des interventions individuelles efficaces et adaptees aux besoins de ces usagers, surtout ceux atteints de problemes de sante mentale, est tres limite. Le but du programme de recherche est de contribuer a la prevention de la transmission du VIH et de l'hepatite C liee a la concomitance de la consommation problematique de cocaine et des problemes de sante mentale. Nous menerons des travaux de recherche permettant de comprendre les liens entre les problemes de sante mentale et les conduites de consommation a risque chez les usagers fumant ou s'injectant de la cocaine. Nous explorerons egalement l'acceptabilite et les effets d'une nouvelle intervention de prevention leur etant destinee. Finalement, nous realiserons des activites ciblees en vue d'articuler et soutenir l'integration continue du programme et associer les milieux de pratiques et les decideurs dans la demarche de generation et d'application des connaissances. Reunissant des chercheurs de trois universites appartenant egalement a des milieux cliniques diversifies, et des partenaires des milieux communautaires et institutionnels, notre equipe sera en mesure d'assurer un environnement de recherche et de formation de haut niveau et de participer au developpement de la releve dans ce domaine de recherche. Les resultats du programme auront egalement le potentiel d'influencer directement l'offre de services destines aux usagers problematiques de cocaine souffrant de problemes de sante mentale.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Vascular Cognitive Impairment: Animal Models of Co-morbidity
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; DIABETES; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROINFLAMMATION; STROKE; VASCULAR COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Investigations in humans clearly demonstrate a relationship between Alzheimer Disease and other diseases affecting blood vessels, particularly those of the brain. These diseases include stroke, diabetes, high blood pressure, and clogged arteries. For example, even the risk of developing Alzheimer Disease is increased in individuals who have these diseases that affect blood vessels. In rats, we have created a brain condition that is similar to that of an older brain or the earliest stages of Alzheimer Disease. The combination of this Alzheimer-like brain condition with a small stroke results in much greater brain damage and is accompanied by a much greater loss of memory or the ability to learn. Similarly, we have shown that when we create this Alzheimer-like brain in a rat model of diabetes, we have much greater amount of degenerative changes in the brain than either alone. Thus, examining animal models of stroke, diabetes and hypertension in the presence of brain chemistry that is associated with old age or early Alzheimer Disease will provide insight into the changes that take place which lead to early reduction in brain function with aging. We have assembled a team of investigators with considerable wide ranging experience, including expertise in animal models of Alzheimer Disease, stroke, diabetes and hypertension, pathology, brain imaging techniques, generation of new brain cells and biochemistry. This allows us to examine multiple changes in the deterioration of the brain and the changes in brain function of animal models of stroke, diabetes and hypertension in the presence of elevated levels of a chemical in the brain associated with brain aging and Alzheimer Disease. These models will be critical in allowing us to understand the mechanisms which lead to brain deterioration with combined disease, be able to diagnose these conditions and determine which new drugs being developed will be most effective to treat the brain before full dementia occurs.

Abstract-Résumé: Mechanisms of inflammation may be involved with a host of  comorbid disorders affecting behaviour. In the aging brain,  inflammatory mechanisms may interact with diseased blood vessels  and diminished brain reserve capacity to result in problems of  learning and memory, and in depression. In younger adults,  inflammatory mechanisms may be an integral part of the way  exposure to viral infections can influence thinking, memory and  mental illnesses such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Better  understanding of the risk factors for viral infection may also be  important in limiting the prevalence of comorbid mental illness,  addiction and infectious disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; CO-MORBIDITIES: PSYCHIATRIC & SUBSTANCE USE DISORDERS; DEVELOPMENTAL TRAJECTORIES & LONGITUDINAL STUDIES; EFFECTIVE TREATMENTS; INNOVATIVE MODELS OF SERVICE DELIVERY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION & EXCHANGE; YOUTH & FAMILIES
Abstract-Résumé: This research will develop and evaluate innovative, developmentally-informed, integrative service delivery models to address co-occurring disorders (CDs) using a community-collaborative framework. We will 1) prepare the groundwork for improved child, youth and family treatment 2) increase collaboration amongst disciplines and service sectors 3) develop strategies to reduce barriers to effective treatment 4) help establish an integrated health services and research network and 5) identify distinct profiles of youth with concurrent disorders that informs prognosis and  practice. There are four inter-related subprojects: 1. A three-year longitudinal Cohort study using school-based and clinic-referred samples to investigate diverse trajectories of emerging CDs and to track service utilization and treatment barriers. We focus on the transition from childhood to adolescence, a critical  period for steep increases in substance use, psychological distress, and behaviour problems. 2. Screening and Diagnosis: screening tools for youth CDs will be validated on school-based and clinic-referred samples. The tools will be validated with other mental health and substance use measures through the Cohort Study. 3. Service Delivery and Treatment.  We will evaluate three treatment components: 1) individual motivational enhancement for adolescents, 2) skills training groups for youth based on dialectal behaviour therapy, and 3) skills training groups for families. 4. Knowledge Translation and Exchange. Stakeholder involvement, from design to implementation to evaluation, is essential for successful approaches with community end users. We will build collaborative cross-sectoral networks with community service providers involved with youth. Community agencies will participate in one or more of subprojects and the experience with and information from these subprojects will inform capacity building and enhance service utilization.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in The Epidemiology and Impact of Comorbidity on MS in Canada (ECoMS)
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; EPIDEMIOLOGY; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; QUALITY OF LIFE; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: This Team Grant in Comorbidity and Multiple Sclerosis (MS) represents a joint initiative of four academic centres in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and Nova Scotia and will create a multi-disciplinary team with complementary expertise. The research program has three objectives. First, we will develop methods for using health claims data to identify and monitor co-existing health conditions (comorbidities) among persons with MS and in the general population. Second, we will identify the type and frequency of comorbidities among persons with MS as compared to the general population, determining how this varies according to age, gender, region and socioeconomic status. Finally, we will assess the impact of comorbidity on MS in two ways. By focusing on health-related quality of life we will gain a broad perspective on how comorbidity influences health. By focusing on use of disease-specific treatments for MS we will gain an understanding of how comorbidity influences treatment decisions and access, as well as treatment tolerability and adherence. We will partner with decision makers and the Multiple Sclerosis Society of Canada to ensure that our findings are disseminated. Anticipated benefits from our population-based research program include individualized disease management, novel insights into the pathophysiology of MS, and ultimately improved health care in MS.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in using a mobile community research laboratory to improve understanding, treatment and prevention of addiction and mental illness co-morbidities at the individual and community level : The Ontario Communities Project
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY AND INDIVIDUAL LEVEL INFLUENCES; COMMUNITY INDICATORS; DATA LINKAGE; MENTAL HEALTH AND ADDICTION CO-MORBIDITIES; MOBILE COMMUNITY RESEARCH LABORATORY; MULTI-LEVEL MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: The CIHR Community Studies in Co-morbidities Team will bring together community partners and investigators from many disciplines to better understand mental health and addiction (MHA) co-morbidities. An innovative community-based approach will be used, involving use of a mobile research laboratory to collect data in a diverse set of communities. The overall objectives of the Team are to: assess the contributing roles of individual and community level factors on MHA co-morbidities in rural, high risk and other communities; integrate biological, social and behavioural science research to gain a better understanding of MHA co-morbidities; develop a database for a minimum of 20 communities collected at both the individual and community level that will form the basis of an ongoing community indicator system;  evaluate the extent of unmet need related to co-morbidities in communities; and assess and improve the capacity of community services to respond to unmet need. To address these objectives, the team will support and coordinate pilot research using a mobile research laboratory in communities and coordinate full-scale projects developed from these pilot studies. Each study will include a common set of variables related to key measures of MHA, including: mood and anxiety disorders; violence; alcohol, marijuana and tobacco use and problems; burden of disabilities related to co-morbidities on individuals and their families; and biomarkers of stress. Community partners will take an active role in all phases of the research, and be especially important in applying research knowledge to improving health services and support systems. This community based approach will lead to a better understanding of causes and mechanisms of co-morbidity, increased sharing of findings among relevant disciplines, and strategies for improving prevention and treatment programs for those with co-morbid conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR team in Mobility in Aging: Quantifying, characterizing and modeling the whole-body mobility of individuals in their natural environment; from normal aging to Parkinson's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CLINICAL APPLICATIONS; COMMUNITY MOBILITY; HOME MONITORING; MOBILITY; PARKINSON
Abstract-Résumé: Research on mobility has been mostly confined to the laboratory, providing fairly good insight about intrinsic obstacle brought about aging or disease. However, the challenges facing the aging population at home and in the community, i.e., extrinsic obstacles brought about the environment in which they navigate have been largely unexplored. Furthermore, the relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic obstacles has been rarely examined, probably due to a lack of proper technology to examine these issues.  To understand the changes in mobility that occurs with normal aging, or with disease of the central nervous system such as Parkinson's disease, we must quantify, characterize and model movements in the natural environment, e.g., in and around the home. Here, we will record whole-body 3D movement during extended periods of time (hours) with a newly-developed highly portable, light-weight camera-free system that can provide 3D body rendering in the home. Community mobility will be explored using a GPS-based system that allows us to examine the sphere of mobility, and how it is influence by age or disease. We will develop the mathematical means to assess the quantity of movement, characterize and model that movement, identify key features of mobility to improve quantitative assessment of movement, and finally correlate our results with those obtained by clinical scales of mobility. Based on this new understanding of the effect of age and disease on home and community mobility, we will propose improvements to current clinical scales so that they better reflect the mobility at home and in the community. We will also and clinically-friendly technological tools to assess that mobility. One ultimate goal is to better identify barriers to mobility within a person's home and find characteristics to predict "adverse events" (e.g., falls) that may jeopardize the health of elderly individuals or persons suffering from neurological ailments.

Abstract-Résumé: Falls are the number one cause of injury in older adults, including 90% of hip fractures and wrist fractures, and a substantial portion of head injuries and vertebral fractures. Seniors living in long-term care (LTC) facilities have twice the rate of falls of those living independently. Yet few studies have examined the factors that influence risk for falls in LTC. Furthermore, no previous study has captured (through video or other means) objective measures of the initiation, descent, and impact stages of falls as they occur in real life, in order to identify the cause and circumstances of these events. This represents a fundamental barrier to the development of effective prevention strategies. The primary goal of this team grant is to create a novel program of collaborative research between universities, government agencies, and end users, for the development of new technologies to prevent falls in older adults. Our efforts address the following objectives: (1) to utilize networks of video cameras to record and interpret the mechanisms of real-life falls in older adults; (2) to develop wearable sensor systems to accurately detect and record movement characteristics associated with falls and near-falls; (3) to determine how fall mechanisms are influenced by physical abilities, cognitive function, cardiovascular status, medication use, assistive devices, and environmental features; and (4) to engage stakeholders in the design and implementation of the research, in order to facilitate the utilization of our technologies and study results. Our outcomes will include new knowledge on ¿how and why¿ falls occur, and novel strategies to prevent falls in the high-risk LTC environment. Our efforts will also promote a greater awareness of these outcomes in the academic and stakeholder community, and ultimately, a significant reduction in the burden of fall injuries in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: CanWheel CIHR Team in Wheeled Mobility for Older Adults
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT; MEASUREMENT; REHABILITATION INTERVENTIONS; SKILL TRAINING; WHEELED MOBILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Power wheelchairs are an expensive yet essential form of assistive technology that can compensate for impaired mobility and improve quality of life for older adults. Despite this benefit, the safe use of these devices can be compromised by decreased cognition and/or functional ability as well as insufficient training; is not uncommon for these devices to be abandoned because they do not meet the needs of the wheelchair user. The overall purpose of this Emerging Team Grant is to improve the mobility opportunities of older adults who use power wheelchairs by addressing three basic questions: 1) How are power wheelchairs used now? 2) How can power wheelchairs be used better?, and 3) How can power wheelchairs be better?   Our research plan will specifically enable us to: 1) describe the trajectory of mobility status in older power wheelchair users; 2) develop and assess strategies to maintain and restore wheeled mobility; 3) assess a toolkit of subjective and objective measures to improve research and clinical practice through better assessment of power wheelchairs; and 4) develop clinical approaches and technology to provide environmental support enhancing mobility for existing power wheelchair users as well as an estimated 61-91% of current manual wheelchair users who could benefit from these advances.  Our team of 14 clinical researchers and basic scientists have developed a program of research that will use a mixed-methods approach, including lab-based, qualitative and quantitative methodologies, spanning 5 key research projects. These projects will ultimately converge at the end of the 6-year grant when we will leverage our results into a new proposal and funds to conduct a randomized controlled trial in year 7 of the team's existence. Our plan is to assess the effectiveness of our new, collaboratively-controlled wheelchair, in combination with the Wheelchair Skills Program, using the outcome toolkit we will have validated during the tenure of this team grant.

Keywords-MotsClés: HUNTINGTON DISEASE; LIPID MODIFICATION; PALMITOYLATION ASSAYS AND SCREENS; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; SYNAPTIC FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Protein palmitoylation is a dynamically regulated posttranslational modification critical for proper cellular trafficking. Our recent studies show that defects in palmitoylation of selected neuronal proteins are associated with Huntington Disease. We will effectively explore this process by using our novel proteomic technology to identify most of the neuronal proteins showing altered palmitoylation in HD, and define the relationship between defects in palmitoylation of these proteins and HD. The discovery of enzymes that remove palmitate will be important for the identification of small molecule inhibitors that target these enzymes and the development of therapeutic tools. This CIHR Team brings together investigators who have made landmark discoveries in the field, including the development of technologies to detect palmitoylation, description of the palmitoyl proteome, identification and characterization of the first palmitoyl transferases, and the first demonstration of altered palmitoylation in Huntington Disease. Thus, our overall goals are to determine the mechanism by which altered palmitoylation contributes to the pathogenesis in HD, and to develop therapeutic tools designed to increase palmitoylation, thereby improving the outcomes for patients with this devastating disease for which there is currently no effective therapy.

Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL ASSAYS OF LUNG DISEASE; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; DIFFERENTIATED RESPIRATORY EPITHELIUM; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT CELLS; MOLECULAR RECOGNITION; SMALL MOLECULES
Abstract-Résumé: New treatments are currently being found through screening of compound libraries that, rather than addressing the consequences of the genetic defect, target the underlying abnormality in CF itself. However, the mechanism of action of most of these compounds remains unknown and the validation of these "leads" in relevant model systems and in patients is a major hurdle to drug development. These new therapeutic approaches therefore require a framework that clarifies the underlying mechanism of promising compounds and uses this information to improve their efficacy. In parallel, tests need to be developed that can be used to assess the efficacy of compounds in cell based assays, in tissue samples from CF patients and ultimately in studies in CF subjects. This will be achieved by parallel research projects on the cellular mechanisms of promising chemical compounds, the development of a stem cell based assay that can be used for compound testing as well as patients based tests that can show efficacy in tissue derived from patients and in clinical studies on patients. The ultimate goal of this research is to bring new therapies that will substantially improve life expectancy into clinical care of patients with cystic fibrosis.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; AUTOPHAGY; CANCER; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; SMALL MOLECULE INHIBITORS; THERAPEUTIC TARGET
Abstract-Résumé: A biological process called autophagy has recently generated tremendous attention due to the recognition that autophagy is involved in various human diseases including cardiomyopathies, bacterial and viral infections, neurodegenerative disorders, bone disease, neuromuscular disorders and cancer. Autophagy acts as a guardian of cells, protecting them from adverse environmental conditions. In a similar manner, autophagy protects cancer cells from the damaging effects of anticancer treatments intended to eradicate them. Thus, a promising strategy to improve cancer treatment efficacy is to inhibit autophagy in combination with anticancer therapies. We have assembled a team of scientists and clinicians with the expertise required to develop specific and potent inhibitors of autophagy components and then translate our findings into treatments beneficial for cancer patients. Our focus will be directed toward late stage and recurrent/treatment resistant cancer patients that are in desperate need of improved treatment options.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in the Leigh Syndrome French Canadian Type (LSFC): Translating LSFC gene discovery into treatments for patients
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CYTOCHROME OXIDASE DEFICIENCY; ENERGY METABOLISM; LACTIC ACIDOSIS; LRPPRC; MITOCHONDRIAL DYSFUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Leigh syndrome French Canadian Type (LSFC) is an inherited metabolic disorder that usually kills children before 4 years of age. First described in 1993 by Dr Morin & colleagues, LSFC is characterized by an energy deficit and deadly lactic acidosis episodes commonly referred to as "crisis". The current incidence of this disease is 1/2000 and it is highly prevalent in the north-eastern region of Quebec where the number of carriers is estimated at 1/23. In 2003, Dr Rioux & colleagues identified the mutations responsible for the LSFC in the LRPPRC gene thereby enabling prenatal screening. The challenge is now to translate this information into treatment. Currently, therapeutic options for LSFC children undergoing crisis are practically nonexistent due to our lack of understanding of the (1) function of the normal LRPPRC protein, and (2) circulating factors that trigger the crisis and precipitate death. Hence, we have formed a multidisciplinary team of basic and clinical researchers, which includes Drs Morin and Rioux, and headed by Dr Des Rosiers, to tackle these issues using state-of-the art technologies. The ultimate goal of this team's research project is to identify circulating biomarkers for early detection and molecules for effective treatment in order to improve survival of LSFC patients undergoing a lactic acidosis crisis without any detrimental consequences such as brain injury. Our team includes pediatricians who treat children with inborn errors of metabolism such as the LSFC and works in close partnership with the Lactic Acidosis Association to insure rapid translation of research results to the target population. Anticipated findings of the proposed research go beyond LSFC patients as they may apply to other conditions involving mitochondrial energetic defects including common chronic diseases such as diabetes and heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy  (ARVC): From Genes to Proteins, Cells, Tissues and Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMOGENIC RIGHT VENTRICULAR CARDIOMYOPATHY; CARDIOMYOCYTE CULTURE; CONDUCTION VELOCITY; GENE TRANSFECTION; MULTIPARTICLE IMMUNOGOLD; SIRNA
Abstract-Résumé: Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is present in up to 1/1000 individuals and is the 2nd most frequent cause of sudden death in young individuals. We follow the largest cohort of (219) young individuals identified with ARVC, collaborate with adult cardiac EP colleagues, and are a North American clinical testing centre for ARVC genes.  Mutations in five ARVC genes result in abnormal desmosomal proteins, and mutations in the new ARVC gene, TMEM43, result in abnormal expression of desmosomal proteins. These six genes account for 50% of ARVC families, and result in early reduced connexin43 (Cx43) gap junction expression as a final common pathway, slowing myocardial conduction, & leading to arrhythmias. We seek to identify all genes underlying ARVC, understand how mutations affect desmosomal gap junction expression and function,  and evaluate therapies based on these common pathways of ARVC expression. To achieve these goals, we study gene suppression and transfection of human mutations into  (HL1) cardiomyocyte cultures, assessing downstream effects by immuno-fluorescence, multiparticle gold electron microscopy, dye transfer & micro-electrode array assessment of conduction velocity (providing functional assays of ARVC mutations). We assess animal models of ARVC (JUP heterozygous mouse, Boxer dog) as well as our large bank of human cardiac biopsy tissue from individuals with ARVC. We perform high-throughput assessment of protein interactions, and evaluate binding partners as potential new candidate genes for analysis in our patient cohorts. We are also evaluating the gene underlying Boxer dog ARVC, using a 20,000 SNP array, and will assess the human homolog as a candidate gene in our ARVC patients.In our tissue culture models, we assess potential rescue therapies in a high-throughput system, and evaluate candidate therapies for effects on connexin expression and function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuromodulation of executive function in the rodent hippocampus
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; COGNITIVE FUNCTION; INTRACRANIAL INFUSIONS; NEUROANATOMY; PSYCHOPHARMACOLOGY; STEREOTAXIC SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: The role of the hippocampus in executive function is an emerging topic of interest. Its damage leads to several cognitive deficits such as poor working memory, impulsivity and perseveration, that lead to general disorganization of behaviour, thereby hindering ones ability to plan, organise and generate novel problem-solving strategies. These behavioural deficits are features of prefrontal dysfunction, raising the question whether the hippocampus (HC), whose main outputs innervate the prefrontal cortex (PFC), is instrumental in shaping executive behaviour. The present research plan is a comprehensive study of the role of the HC in executive function. Combining techniques of neuropsychology and psychopharmacology in rodents, the goal of the proposed research is to gain a better understanding of the functional roles of the dorsal and ventral subdivisions of the HC in executive function, and their respective modulation by the neurotransmitters dopamine (DA) and serotonin (5-HT), both of which are known to be important in modulating prefrontal-executive function. Executive deficits are characteristic of neurodegenerative disorders (e.g., Alzheimer's disease) and chronic mental illnesses (e.g., schizophrenia); for these patients, the disruption of attention, memory, planning, and behavioural flexibility that can persist long after their acute symptoms subside, act to severely compromise their quality of life. Unfortunately, current pharmacotherapies fail to improve these enduring executive deficits and they are important targets for treatment. An understanding of the basic neural mechanisms that underlie cognitive function will help us develop new, more comprehensive and effective treatments for disorders of executive function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Motor Learning and Sensory Systems
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN MOTOR LEARNING; INTERNAL MODELS; MOTOR LEARNING BY OBSERVING; MULTIJOINT ARM MOVEMENT; PROPRIOCEPTION; ROBOTIC MANIPULANDUM
Abstract-Résumé: This research will explore the bidirectional relationship between motor learning and sensory systems in humans. Project 1 will focus on how vision modulates the motor system. We will investigate motor learning by observing, that is, our ability to learn about how to execute novel motor skills, by observing the actions of others. Several behavioural experiments will test the idea that the same neural circuitry that underlies our ability to learn new motor skills actively, by moving, are also activated when we observe the actions of others. Project 2 will focus on how the motor system modulates the proprioceptive system - that is, our sense of body position. We will build on exciting pilot data showing that after we practice a motor task, proprioceptive acuity is modulated in a spatially local fashion - essentially resulting in a flexible proprioceptive fovea. In order to understand the basis of motor dysfunction in disease it is necessary first to understand the basis of motor control and motor learning in the intact nervous system. The results of the studies proposed here could influence our view of motor learning in two important ways: first, by accounting for observational learning, and second, by incorporating sensory change as part and parcel of the learning process. This work could have significant implications for how we design and implement empirically based treatment programs for neuromotor rehabilitation, by focusing not only on motor systems but sensory systems as well.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Emerging Team in Integrative Biology of Inflammatory Diseases: IL23R as a confirmed immune disease pathway: a model for translating genetic discoveries into better diagnosis and treatment of common diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR IMMUNOLOGY; GENETICS; GENOMICS; INFLAMMATORY DISEASES; PROTEOMICS; THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Given the recent successes in identifying genetic risk factors for common diseases, there now is a major scientific challenge to translating the discovery of disease genes into better clinicalpractice.  It is therefore imperative to develop scientific strategies to address this challenge.  Our Emerging Team will endeavor to meet this challenge with its initial focus on a biological pathway that has been implicated in multiple diseases of the immune system. Specifically, we and others have shown that genetic variation in four genes of an important cell signaling for the immune system hormone IL-23 pathway (including the R381Q variant in IL-23 cell surface receptor) is associated with Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis and psoriasis. Our Team, which includes basic and clinical researchers, has the diverse set of expertise necessary to understand the mechanisms by which the associated genetic variants influence disease susceptibility as well as to design and test potential therapies.  Our Team also has the structures and partners in place for the scientific planning, teaching, dissemination of information, and commercialization of findings. We feel that our proposal is of great clinical relevance as (1) this pathway is a current target in clinical trials; (2) we have developed IL23 receptor-specific bioactive peptide antagonists and (3) we are creating novel models for pre-clinical testing. The Team's program could have significant impact on the well-being, health and productivity (currently a loss of $1.064 billion annually) of inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) patients (approximately 201, 000 cases) and the enormous burden on our healthcare system caused by these diseases ($753 million in 2008).

TitreApplicationTitle: Costimulation of  Human T cell Responses
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV; HUMAN; INFLUENZA; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISMS; T CELLS; TUMOR NECROSIS FACTOR RECEPTOR ASSOCIATED FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: When an individual is infected with a virus, white blood cells of our  immune system are mobilized to fight the infection. One kind of white blood cell, called a cytotoxic or killer T cell, is important in killing virus-infected cells.  During an acute  viral infection the virus replicates for a few days and makes us ill, but within a week or so, the immune system succeeds in fully clearing the infection. However, sometimes the immune system cannot handle the infection, such as with HIV infection, and the infection becomes chronic. Under these conditions, the cytotoxic T cells can become inactivated. Our laboratory has shown that we can reactivate these T cells outside the body to kill HIV-infected cells.  Therefore we wondered why the T cells are not working within the infected individuals. We found that a molecule called Tumor necrosis factor receptor associated factor 1 (or TRAF1) is important in the T cells in fighting HIV infection, but it disappears from the T cells over time of chronic infection. We would like to know why this happens more in some individuals than others and the mechanisms involved. TRAF proteins show small sequence differences among different individuals in the population, referred to as polymorphisms. We will investigate how these polymorphisms in TRAF proteins affect the ability of individuals to respond to acute infections such as influenza, as well as chronic infections, such a HIV. Understanding the role of TRAF1 and TRAF protein polymorphisms in immunity to acute viral infections, such as influenza, as well as chronic viral infections, such as HIV, will help us to design better vaccines and therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determinants of the progression and outcome of mitral regurgitation
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMETABOLIC RISK; DOPPLER-ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; EXERCISE TESTING; HEART VALVE DISEASE; LEFT VENTRICULAR FUNCTION; MITRAL REGURGITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Mitral regurgitation (MR) is a frequent and serious cardiac disease that is characterized by a leak at the level of the mitral valve. When MR becomes severe, the only efficient treatment is to repair or replace the diseased valve. However, the optimal timing of this open-heart surgery remains uncertain and controversial. The current guidelines for clinical practice recommend waiting for the development of symptoms or cardiac chamber dysfunction to perform surgery, whereas some investigators believe that all patients with severe MR should be operated even if they have no symptoms or signs of cardiac dysfunction. In the current clinical practice, the patients are generally evaluated at rest, which does not necessarily represent the physiological conditions of the patient during his or her daily activities. In this large prospective follow-up study of >400 patients with at least moderate MR, we will perform a comprehensive evaluation of valve and cardiac function not only at rest but also during exercise. We believe that the indices of MR and cardiac function measured during exercise will provide important new information that will help the clinician to better predict the progression rate of the disease and thereby to better select the optimal timing for surgery. We will also determine whether or not patients with abdominal obesity have a more rapid progression of MR and associated cardiac dysfunction. This study is the first of its kind, as it will measure prospectively in a large cohort of patients: 1) MR severity at rest and exercise and its progression over time, 2) the patient's maximum exercise capacity; 3) several hormones produced by the heart muscle; 4) the metabolic abnormalities associated with abdominal obesity; and 5) the occurrence of adverse events (symptoms, deaths, heart failure etc.). The new knowledge generated by this study will contribute to improve the risk evaluation and the therapeutic management of the patients with this disease.
