TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Prion Protein Expression, Trafficking and Function.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; BAX PROTEIN; CELL DEATH; PRION PROTEIN; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Prion protein is well known for it's involvement in the transmission of neurodegenerative conditions but much less is known on the normal function of prion protein in normal tissues. Yet, prion protein is expressed everywhere. Recent evidence suggests that too much prion protein can promote cancer and offer resistance against cancer drugs. In this proposal, we investigate in cancer cells and in neurons, the regulation of prion protein expression, where the protein is localized within the cell and what the prion protein does relative to survival and cell death. THis work will help us understand the role of the normal prion protein and how this function may be lost in disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Induction of Allograft Vasculopathy by CD8+ T cells under conditions of immunosuppression.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOGRAFT VASCULOPATHY; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Although most transplanted hearts survive well for the first year (95% survival), there is a chronic ongoing rejection process which results in heart transplant malfunction in about 50% of patients by 10 years post transplant. This process continues such that 20 year survival is less than 10%. Given that the average age of a heart transplant recipient in Canada is 50 years old this is a significant clinical problem that has yet to be resolved. Unfortunately, the anti-rejection drugs that work so well to prevent early transplant rejection do not prevent this late response. This is primarily because the biological basis of the two responses is quite different. Late transplant rejection is due to a growing lesion in the inside of the coronary arteries that eventually results in blockage. This lesion is caused by the immune response and is called allograft vasculopathy. Because it looks somewhat like naturally occurring arteriosclerosis it is sometimes called allograft arteriosclerosis. A significant limitation to successful development of novel therapies for allograft vasculopathy is the uncertainty regarding the nature, origin and mechanism of development of the lesion. In our experiments in mice we have shown that immunosuppressive drugs (similar to the kind used in human transplant patients) block the activities of some parts of the immune system but not others. The primary part to escape these immunosuppressive drugs are the CD8+ T cells. In our last grant supported by the CIHR we showed that these CD8+ T cells are responsible for causing allograft vasculopathy under conditions of clinically relevant immunosuppression. In this renewal project we are now trying to understand how these CD8+ T cells cause this lesion and the resulting loss of transplanted hearts. In the end our aim is to achieve a sufficient understanding of this process to be able to intervene with therapeutic agents to shut down this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental influences on multidrug efflux gene expression and antibiotic resistance in P. aeruginosa
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; EFFLUX; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA; REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a bacterium that causes severe and often lethal infections in humans debilitated as a result of disease, burns, surgery or severe injury. The organism is innately resistant to many antibiotics and often develops what might be termed high-level antibiotic resistance during antibiotic therapy, both of which complicate effective treatment of P. aeruginosa infections.  Primary contributors to this innate and acquired antibiotic resistance are pumps within the bacterial cells that extrude antibiotics before they reach levels sufficient to kill the bacterium.  Despite their contributions to antibiotic resistance, however, these pumps have other than antibiotic export as their intended function (antibiotic extrusion being a fortuitous and poorly understood 'benefit' of their operation in these bacteria) and are naturally produced in response to a variety of environmental conditions, some of which occur within the human body. Thus, invading P. aeruginosa causing infections may be expressing these efflux systems and, so, be less susceptible to antibiotic therapy.   The focus of this proposal, then, is the detailed characterization of these pumps, including the identification of the specific conditions in the human body that activate antibiotic pump production in P. aeruginosa.  Insights gained from this study should assist efforts to overcome resistance in treating P. aeruginosa infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: PCSK9: Functions and mechanisms of action in liver and adipocytes
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CHOLESTEROL AND FATTY ACIDS; MECHANISMS AND PHYSIOLOGY; MOUSE KNOCKOUT AND TRANSGENIC MODELS; PROTEASES; STUCTURE-FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Our group has been at the forefront of discovering and characterizing a family of enzymes known as the proprotein convertases and in unraveling their role in normal biology and in human disease. In this application we propose to continue this line of research with a particular focus on the role of the convertase PCSK9. Recently, we functionally and genetically linked PCSK9 to the development of cardiovascular diseases in humans, including dyslipidemias and fat metabolism, and showed that PCSK9 triggers the degradation of receptors that regulate cholesterol levels. The absence of functional PCSK9 lowers the levels of circulating low density lipoprotein (LDL)-cholesterol by 80%. The proposed research will define the mechanisms behind the molecular functions of PCSK9 in the test tube, cell lines, mouse knockout and transgenic models. The identification of Annexin A2 as a physiological PCSK9 inhibitor, will allow us to design inhibitory peptide mimics. We will identify the proteins targeted by PCSK9 in live cells and mice and use state-of-the-art technology to study the mechanisms underlying their functions, with the aim of developing new treatment strategies for PCSK9-dependent diseases. These include hypercholesterolemia, fatty liver (steatosis), fat distribution, atherosclerosis and hepatitis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating and addressing injection drug use and other harms among street-involved youth: The ARYS Project
Keywords-MotsClés: HCV; HIV/AIDS; ILLICIT DRUG USE; INJECTION DRUG USE; RISK ENVIRONMENT; STREET-INVOLVED YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: This research will address the urgent challenge of illicit drug use among street-involved youth. By studying a large group of street-involved youth in Vancouver, we will acquire the evidence-based information necessary to inform appropriate responses to this health crisis locally, nationally and internationally. Specifically, the project will examine patterns of illicit drug use and the risk environment in which they are used, and evaluate their effects on initiation of injection drug use, sexual risk behaviour, and incidence of hepatitis C and HIV among a cohort of 500 street-involved youth from 14 to 24 years of age. The study will investigate not only individual circumstances but also social, structural and environmental influences on risk behaviour. For instance, the study will assess specific factors such as homelessness and sex-trade involvement on sexual and drug risk-taking and infectious disease incidence, with the aim of informing pragmatic intervention strategies. The study will be carried out by inviting youth to conduct a standardized survey every six months for five years. The knowledge gained through this research should prove useful in guiding HIV and hepatitis C prevention measures, as well as initiatives to prevent the initiation of injection drug use among youth. Street youth represent one of the most vulnerable populations in Canada, and research to determine how to reduce harm among this population will be of benefit to all Canadians.

Keywords-MotsClés: BROMINATED FLAME RETARDANTS; CRYPTORCHIDISM; ETHICAL; FETAL AND POSTNATAL EXPOSURE; LEGAL AND SOCIAL ISSUES; MALE AND FEMALE FERTILITY; REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEMS
Abstract-Résumé: During the past thirty years, brominated flame retardants (BFRs) have been used worldwide as fire retardant chemicals in a wide variety of consumer products (textiles, foam furniture, electrical equipment and electronics). Unfortunately, the BFRs leach out of these products: at present, greater than 80% of human exposure to the BFRs is due to contaminated dust in our immediate living spaces (home, car, workplace) with the remainder from food. As a result of increasing exposure, BFR levels in North Americans (serum, tissues) are some of the highest in the world. Of particular concern is the fact that newborns and young infants have the highest serum levels, since it is generally believed that infants are more vulnerable to toxicological insults. Animal studies of BFR exposure have demonstrated interference with male as well as female reproductive organ development and function. Limited clinical studies suggest an association with abnormal male reproductive development (cryptorchidism in newborns, lower sperm levels in young adults). These data suggest that the BFRs are impacting early stages of human development and that at least one outcome is abnormal male reproduction.  This is a serious issue: not only is an individual's health potentially at risk but that of future generations. There is a clear need for additional data, to address the concerns of Canadians about the use of BFRs and to provide the information that is essential for policy makers and regulators. Our multidisciplinary team of expert clinical and basic scientists from five Canadian universities in partnership with Health Canada will address these concerns. Our goals are: 1) to use animal models to mimic human BFR exposures and to investigate the mechanisms underlying effects on development and reproduction; 2) to elucidate the impact of BFR exposure on human reproduction (cryptorchidism, fertility); and 3) to explore the ethical, legal and social issues raised by these results.

TitreApplicationTitle: Human cytomegalovirus tropism for dendritic cells and fibroblasts
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOMEGALOVIRUS; DENDRITIC CELLS; ENDOCYTOSIS; FIBROBLASTS; TROPISM; VIMENTIN
Abstract-Résumé: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections are a serious source of morbidity and mortality for immunocompromised individuals such as AIDS patients, transplant recipients, and newborns. Because of this, the development of novel strategies to block viral infection and virus-mediated inhibition of host immune defenses is a priority. CMV's exceptionally broad tissue tropism contributes greatly to the severe multi-organ disease caused by this virus in immunocompromised people. The molecular mechanisms mediating viral entry into such a variety of different cell types, however, are still ill defined. In this proposal, we seek to establish the mode of entry of CMV into two cell types of fundamental importance during infection, fibroblasts and dendritic cells, and to determine the role played by the cellular protein vimentin in facilitating entry of viral particles. These studies will identify candidate cellular factors and pathways of importance for the development of improved antiviral compounds targeting viral entry, and for the enhancement of immune responses to CMV vaccines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Leukotriene B4 in Leukocyte Functions
Keywords-MotsClés: RECEPTOR EXPRESSION AND FUNCTION; RECEPTOR-MEDIATED SIGNALING; STRUCTURE-FUNCTION RELATIONSHIP
Abstract-Résumé: Les leucotrienes sont des lipides derives des membranes cellulaires qui possedent des proprietes biologiques tres puissantes: ils sont dimportants facteurs dans plusieurs maladies inflammatoires, telles l'arthrite, l'asthme et les maladies inflammatoires de l'intestin.  Le leucotriene B4 (LTB4) est particulierement actif comme agent d'attraction et d'activation des neutrophiles aux sites inflammatoires.  Il est aussi capable de moduler diverses phases de la reponse immune telle la cytotoxicite des lymphocytes T et "natural killer".  Son action passe par deux recepteurs cellulaires (BLT1 et BLT2) qui sont clones. Notre projet vise a etudier la structure et la fonction de ces recepteurs et a determiner les facteurs qui influencent leur expression dans les cellules inflammatoires.  Une meilleure comprehension de ces elements permettra d'elaborer des strategies de traitement plus precises et idealement plus efficaces dans les maladies inflammatoires.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure, function and trafficking of bicarbonate transport membrane proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: ERYTHROCYTE; GLYCOPROTEIN BIOSYNTHESIS; ION TRANSPORT; KIDNEY; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; PROTEIN STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Each cell in our body is surrounded by a thin membrane made up of specialized lipids and proteins.  Some of these membrane proteins allow certain ions like sodium, chloride or bicarbonate to enter or exit the cell.  We are studying a bicarbonate/chloride transport protein that is present in our red blood cells and also in acid-secreting cells in the kidney.  We would like to find out how this protein works at the molecular level.  Studies have indicated that it operates somewhat like a revolving door, where bicarbonate enters as chloride exits.  Bicarbonate ions are important for maintaining a proper pH balance within cells and the body.  When cells become too acidic through metabolism, bicarbonate enters to neutralize the acid.  In the red blood cell, carbon dioxide that builds up in tissues such as muscle enters the cell and is converted to bicarbonate, which then exits the cell via a specific transport protein called AE1, for anion exchanger 1.  In the kidney a similar process happens where bicarbonate is moved back into the blood to maintain the pH balance of the body by a kidney form of AE1.  Unfortunately, there are inherited mutations in the AE1 gene that result in human diseases that affect bicarbonate transport in the red blood cell and the kidney.  We are very interested in determining how these mutations affect the working of the AE1 transport protein.  To see how AE1 works, we are trying to determine the structure of this molecular machine using powerful biochemical techniques like X-ray crystallography.  One approach we are using is to study similar proteins from bacteria, which are much simpler and easier to study.  One goal of our work is to develop drugs that correct the defects in AE1 that may be useful in treating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidation of the role of the RhoGEF Lfc in human epithelial tumors
Keywords-MotsClés: AKAPS; GUANINE NUCLEOTIDE EXCHANGE FACTOR; MOUSE MODELS; OVARIAN CANCER; PHOSPHATASES; PKA; RHOGTPASE
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal investigates an enzyme that controls the way a cell is shaped and the way it moves. We have discovered that this enzyme called Lfc, is important in cancer initiation and/or progression. A normal break down product of the membranes of our cells is called lysophosphatidic acid or LPA. LPA can function like a growth factor for cells. It can stimulate cells to survive under low nutrient conditions and induce cells to grow, change shape and become motile. LPA is an important growth factor created by our own bodies that can potently stimulate cancer growth. LPA levels are extremely high in certain types of tumors specifically ovarian, breast and colon. LPA binds to protein receptors on the cell surface which then activates biochemical cascades within the cell to instruct the cell to change. We have discovered that Lfc is one of the enzymes that is activated by LPA. We have shown that Lfc must be present in a cell in order for it to respond to LPA. We have examined over 200 ovarian cancers and discovered that Lfc is abnormally expressed at high levels. This means that not only is LPA elevated in patients with ovarian cancer but so is the machinery inside the cell necessary to activate the pathway that make the cell grow and move. We propose to analyze how Lfc is normally controlled in the cell. What turns it on, what turns it off? We have discovered that another molecule that binds to Lfc called Tctex1 which brings Lfc to the LPA receptor. Once LPA binds to its receptor Lfc is somehow discharged from its inhibitory complex and becomes activated. We will endeavor to discover the mechanism underlying this process. We will analyze the role of Lfc in human tumors by protein expression analysis of primary ovarian tumors. We will remove Lfc from these tumor cells and determine if they can still behave as tumors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Osteopontin and Aldosterone on Lung Structural Remodeling and Right Ventricular Function in Congestive Heart Failure
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDOSTERONE; CELL CULTURE; CONGESTIVE HEART FAILURE; LUNG REMODELING; OSTEOPONTIN
Abstract-Résumé: Congestive heart failure is an important health problem affecting more than 350,000 Canadians. Subjects with heart failure are principally limited because of shortness of breath that, according to disease severity, can interfere with daily activities or even occur at rest. This symptom has been attributed to passive congestion of the lung with blood because of failure of the heart to pump efficiently, akin to a dam on a lake. Although blood congestion into the lungs no doubt contributes to the process, reactive structural modifications of the lung itself with thickening of the wall between the air spaces and the lung vessels play a more important deleterious role. This thickening (remodeling) of the lung will reduce the capacity for oxygen to enter into the blood and elevatre the pressure in the lung, further increasing the work demand of the right side of the heart. There have been deceivingly little research efforts to study the evolution and the determinants of lung remodeling in congestive heart failure. Osteopontin is a substance that is known to be involved in various lung disorders, but its role in lung disease associated with heart failure is unknown.  The drug spironolactone is recommended for the treatment of advanced heart failure: its mechanisms of action are however still unclear and it is unfortunately  under-used. This grant application proposes to evaluate the hypothesis that increased lung production of  osteopontin contributes to lung remodeling and that the drug spironolatone can block osteopontin activation and improve lung function in heart failure. The results of this grant will provide a better understanding of the processes responsible for the major symptom of heart failure, shortness of breath,  and explore a novel pharmacological pathway for subjects suffering from heart failure.

Abstract-Résumé: Most of the disabling consequences of chronic inflammatory joint diseases are the result of damage to the joints and surrounding cartilage and bone. Pathological local bone resorption associated with immune arthritis like rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, crystal-induced arthritis, and chronic infection of joints and bones, remains a major medical problem implicating enormous socio-economic costs. Etiology and initiating events of these inflammatory arthritis are unknown and our knowledge dealing with the tissue degrading process during inflammation remains too fragmentary. In recent years, factors of intercellular communication have been the subject of intense research which is promoting an increasing number of mediators involved in the inflammatory process. Among the numerous factors, osteoprotegerin, osteoprotegerin ligand and its receptor RANK are substances of particular interest since they appear to be involved in bone resorption and inflammation and they are targets for pharmacological modulation. A goal of the present study will be to evaluate the role of neutrophils through their expression of these compounds in bone resorption related to chronic arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Infants' Motor Abilities: A validation of the Alberta Infant Motor Scale Normative Data
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNO-CULTURAL ETHNICITY; INFANT MOTOR DEVELOPMENT; NORMATIVE VALIDITY; STATISTICAL SCALING METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: The Alberta Infant Motor Scale (AIMS) is a measure of infant gross motor abilities that is used worldwide. The AIMS motor growth curves, similar to height and weight growth curves, were developed by assessing 2200 infants in Alberta in 1990-1992. We are concerned that this data may not be an appropriate 'yardstick' for the motor abilities of present Canadian infants for two reasons.  The first reason to evaluate the motor growth curves is that many infants now spend less time on their tummies because of 'back to sleep' campaigns to prevent Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS). Some research suggests that babies today achieve some motor milestones later than babies did before the 'back to sleep' campaigns.  For example, babies may roll from tummy to back at older ages now.  If so, then the present motor growth curves would identify a baby as being delayed in motor skills when actually the age of achieving the skill has changed for all babies.  This has important implications for accurately identifying infants who are truly delayed in their motor skills.  The second reason is that the data does not represent the changing cultural face of Canada today. If cultural child rearing practices influence the development of motor skills, then it is important that all cultures in Canada are represented in the growth curves.  We plan to assess 675 babies across Canada, making sure to include families from different cultural groups, and then compare their scores with the scores of babies of the same age who were assessed to make the motor curves.  If differences emerge, then the present motor curves will be adjusted to reflect changes in the ages that babies now achieve motor skills.  This study will ensure that the AIMS, a made in Canada measure, continues to be an important assessment of infant gross motor abilities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of movement: regulation of spinal-muscular circuits
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; LOCOMOTION; MOTONEURONS; MUSCLE SPINDLES; NEUROMODULATION; SPINAL CORD
Abstract-Résumé: Quality and longevity of life may be significantly impacted by diseases or injuries affecting the spinal cord. One disability resulting from such diseases and injuries is the reduction in or loss of the ability to move. This application addresses neural circuits between the spinal cord and muscles that ensure that limbs move appropriately during behaviour.  The nerve cells that cause muscles to contract are called "alpha motor neurons." These nerve cells receive commands from many other types of nerve cells in the spinal cord, process these commands, and send messages to muscles causing them to contract. The muscles in turn can relay information about their position and their speed of contraction back to the spinal cord. Much of this sensory information is carried by sensory nerve fibres receiving information from organs embedded within the muscle called "muscle spindles." These spindles are controlled other nerve cells in the spinal cord called "gamma motor neurons." Little is known about the control of these gamma nerve cells.   In this application, I propose to study alpha and gamma motor neurons, and the ways by which the activity of these nerve cells is controlled to ensure that limbs move appropriately during behaviour (walking). These studies involve a number of cutting edge techniques in which we will use transgenic mice and advanced microscopy techniques which together allow visualisation and manipulation of the activity of identified nerve cells. In addition, we propose to genetically modify these neurons to study the mechanisms underlying the control of these neurons in behaviour.  By the conclusion of the 5-year granting period, we will have a greater understanding of the communication between the spinal cord and muscles. Knowledge of this circuit will assist in the development of strategies to improve the function of people living with spinal cord injuries and diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Apoptosis Prevention Therapy for the Treatment of Retinal Degeneration:  Basic Science to Clinical Application
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; GENE THERAPY; RETINAL DEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: The socio-economic burden of visual impairment and blindness is tremendous and will increase dramatically as our population ages.  This underscores the urgent need for Canada to develop a comprehensive national vision plan aimed at the treatment and prevention of blinding disorders.  Diseases affecting the retina such as retinitis pigmentosa, glaucoma, retinal ischemia and age-related macular degeneration cause visual loss in millions of people in North America alone, and yet little is known about the mechanisms or causes of many of these diseases.  What is known, however, is that cell death through apoptosis is the final common pathway for many forms of retinal disease.  Our research program has provided compelling evidence showing that a therapy that targets the X-linked inhibitor of apoptosis (XIAP) to the retina can prevent cell death and significantly preserve vision in animal models of retinal ischemia, retinal detachment and in genetic forms of retinitis pigmentosa (RP). With the current Emerging Team Grant, we propose a strategy for the development of XIAP therapy for the treatment of retinal disease.  We will establish a multidisciplinary team of basic and clinical scientists with expertise in the basic science of visual structure and function, in anti-apoptotic mechanisms and therapies, in vector delivery to the eye, in animal models of retinal disease, and in the establishment and follow-up of clinical trials.  By the end of the five-year granting period, we will have conducted all the studies necessary to bring XIAP therapy to the clinic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Roadblocks to Nerve Regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: NERVE INJURY; NERVE REGENERATION; PERIPHERAL NERVE; PERIPHERAL NERVE REGENERATION; PTEN; RHOA
Abstract-Résumé: Peripheral nerves are the essential connections that exist between the brain and spinal cord, and the body. Without peripheral nerves, there is no movement, no sensation. Damage and disease of peripheral nerves (neuropathy is a disease of the peripheral nerve) are very common, usually irreversible and disabling. Out lab is interested in a new approach toward improving regeneration of peripheral nerves. This approach involves inhibiting molecular "brakes" or roadblocks that exist within nerve cells and that restrain growth. While restraint may be necessary in normal stable adults, these roadblocks limit regenerative growth of neurons. Two molecules, named PTEN and RHOA are key roadblocks and our laboratory has evidence that by inhibiting either, improved regeneration activity ensues. We propose to evaluate mechanisms of their action, the long term impact on regrowth of nerves when they are inhibited and whether these molecules operate together or are independent "brakes". If independent, inhibiting both may have substantial benefits during regeneration after nerve injury or neuropathy. Our work focuses on neurons in culture, nerve regeneration in rats and mice and occurs within a milieu of several neuroscientists interested in improving the outcome of regeneration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and functional analysis of host resistance to cryptococcus
Keywords-MotsClés: CRYPTOCOCCUS NEOFORMANS; FUNGAL INFECTION; GENETIC ANALYSIS; HOST RESISTANCE; INBRED MOUSE STRAINS; INNATE IMMUNITY
Abstract-Résumé: Infectious diseases are a major threat to human health and account for 25% of all deaths throughout the world. Fungal infections are particularly dangerous for individuals with weakened immune defenses due to conditions such as advanced or severe chronic illness, HIV infection, cancer treatment, or organ transplantation. During the past three decades, Cryptococcus neoformans has emerged as a serious global human fungal pathogen that may cause fatal infection involving the lungs and brain. The basic mechanisms by which humans defend themselves against this fungus are not well understood. Using a mouse model that closely resembles the human disease we have identified three important chromosomal regions, or loci, that control the development of severe cryptococcal infection. The first aim of this proposal is to complete the identification of the loci that control antifungal immunity in our model. Second, we will use genetic tools to dissect apart the effects of each locus on host immunity. Third, we will analyze the effects of each individual locus on the immune response of lung cells and tissue against Cryptococcus neoformans. Finally, we will focus on the precise identity of the host resistance genes contained within each locus by combining the information we have gathered with a series of modern molecular technologies. The knowledge arising from this research will advance our understanding of how serious fungal diseases develop and will have excellent potential to improve prevention and treatment measures for individuals as well as for the population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cross-modal integration and plasticity: organization and limits
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING AND CONNECTIVITY; EARLY BLIND SUBJECTS; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MMN MISMATCH NEGATIVITY; TACTITLE  AND VOICE DISCRIMINATION; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: The human brain shows remarkable capacities to modify its organization and function in response to external demands. In neurologically normal subjects, these changes occur during regular maturation and learning. In individuals with sensory loss due to damage to peripheral organs, such as in the blind, these normal changes are also accompanied by modifications that allow the individuals to adapt and possibly compensate for their loss. We have examined this problem using behavioural, electrophysiological and imaging studies and plan to continue and extend them in the present proposal. Thus, at the behavioural level, we plan to examine if blind subjects outperform sighted ones in voice discrimination and whether performance is related to stronger activation of brain structures that control for voice perception. We have shown in the past that they excel in auditory and tactile functions. We shall thus examine, using functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging if this is due to recruitment by auditory or tactile stimulation of the visual cortex that no longer receives visual inputs. We shall specifically examine the nature of this recruitment at three levels: a) by investigating whether it follows the specific function of the area or adapts to the functions of the sensory systems which they now treat, b) we shall try and define the mechanisms and pathways through which this occurs and d) we shall analyze whether these recruitments of visual areas are truly responsible for the superior abilities of the blind by temporarily inactivating the recruited visual structures, using Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, and determining if performance is affected.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sharing the Harvest: A Community and Regionally-Based Intervention Strategy Addressing Food Security and Sustainability Issues in First Nations of the Mushkegowuk Territory
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENTAL/CULTURAL SUSTAINABILTY; FOOD INSECURITY; HARVEST SHARING; LEAD AND NON-TOXIC AMMUNITION; NUTRIRION AND OBESITY; STABLE LEAD ISOTOPE RATIOS
Abstract-Résumé: Food security "is the assurance that all people at all times have both the physical and economic access to the food they need for an active, healthy life¿the food itself is safe, nutritionally adequate, [and] culturally appropriate" (Food Security Assembly, 2004). Food insecurity exists when people do not have adequate physical, social or economic access to food as defined above. Food security has been recognized as a determinant of health and individuals experiencing food insecurity are at a greater risk for many negative health consequences. Historically, the Omushkego Cree of northern Ontario, Canada, have had to deal with recurring periods of food insecurity. At present, one of the barriers to the consumption of healthy traditional foods is the expense associated with harvesting. Thus, people that formerly consumed a more nutritious wild meat diet became more dependent on cheap, non-nutritious, store-bought food. Our intervention would support First Nations people who could not afford to harvest traditional game by transporting them up to Cape Henrietta Maria, Ontario, to hunt spring snow geese (Chen caerulescens); the harvesters would use only steel shotshell, so as not to lead contaminate the meat. It should also be noted that the over-population of snow geese is destroying the environment; this is well documented. So the First Nation harvesters through the proposed intervention would be receiving many benefits: an uncontaminated, nutritious source of traditional food (snow goose); participating in the harvesting aspect of their culture, which also has important social benefits associated with well-being; protecting the environment for future generations by participating in the North-American wide, snow goose harvest initiative; and addressing the food security issue not only at the harvester level, but at the community level by "sharing the harvest". We would evaluate the effectiveness of the program both qualitatively and quantitatively.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery of cellular targets of ER-routed protein toxins
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PAHTOGENS; DRUG DISCOVERY; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PEPTIDE SYNTHESIS; PROTEOMICS; RIBOSOME INACTIVATING PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Many plants and bacteria produce some of the deadliest natural molecules known as ribosomal-inactivating proteins or RIPs. They do so to protect themselves (Castor bean plants avoid being eaten by herbivores and omnivores by producing ricin for instance) or to propagate by exiting from infected hosts (for example, the Walkerton bacteria O157:H7 that cause diarrhea). Consequently, common bacterial outbreaks arising from food and water supplies contaminated with Shigella desenteria and E. coli O157:H7 strains, do lead to hemorrhagic forms of diarrhea in humans that can cause death. To intoxicate cells, these RIPs must enter and travel inside cells to reach a cellular compartment known as the Endoplasmic Reticulum or ER. Upon reaching this site, they are then able to relocate themselves outside the ER near the cell's protein synthesis machines known as ribosomes and inactivate them. Each RIP has evolved to recognize which cells they want to intoxicate (they bind to different cells). However, they all share the same mechanism to travel inside cells and damage ribosomes. We want to understand how these toxins commonly exploit the cellular machinery to travel inside cells and dock themselves on ribosomes to block their action. This information may provide generic strategies (cellular targets) to counter the action of all RIPs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure-fonction de la protéine StAR
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOCORTICOTROPINE; CHOLESTEROL; HYPERPLASIE LIPOIDE CONGENITALE DES SURRENALES; MUTATIONS CLINIQUES; RESONANCE MAGNETIQUE NUCLEAIRE; STEROIDOGENIC ACUTE REGULATORY PROTEIN (STAR)
Abstract-Résumé: Dans les tissus steroidogeniques le cholesterol est transforme en pregnenolone par une enzyme localisee a la membrane interne mitochondriale. Le transfert du cholesterol de l'exterieur vers l'interieur de la mitochondrie est l'etape limitante de la production des steroides et l'importance d'une proteine nommee StAR (Steroidogenic Acute Regulatory) pour ce transfert a ete demontree sans equivoque par des donnees biochimiques et genetiques. Plusieurs mutations cliniques repertoriees rendent la StAR inactive, incapable de proceder au transfert du cholesterol vers la membrane interne mitochondriale, resultant au developpement de l'hyperplasie lipoide des surrenales, une maladie fatale. En effet, sans apport de cholesterol a la membrane interne mitochondriale, il n'y a pas de formation de corticoides, ce qui entraine la mort de la personne si non traitee adequatement et a temps! Notre objectif de recherche touche la comprehension du mecanisme d'action de la StAR au niveau moleculaire, a sa structure et a sa fonction. A date nos etudes biochimiques et structurales ont ete a la base de l'elaboration d'un modele du mecanisme d'action de la StAR pour lier et relacher le cholesterol et pour evaluer l'impact des mutations cliniques dans la maladie de l'hyperplasie lipoide congenitale des surrenales. La determination definitive de la structure tridimensionnelle de la StAR est une etape cruciale pour valider notre modele. En conclusion, notre recherche contribuera significativement a l'elucidation de la structure de la StAR qui pourrait mener ulterieurement au developpement de molecules ou peptides pharmacologiques capables de retablir son activite steroidogenique dans l'hyperplasie lipoide congenitale des surrenales.

TitreApplicationTitle: Smooth Muscle Mechanics in Airway Hyperresponsiveness and Asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN; IN VITRO MOTILITY ASSAY; MYOSIN HEAVY CHAIN; MYOSIN LIGHT CHAIN PHOSPHORYLATION; QUICK RELEASE ASSAY; SM22
Abstract-Résumé: Airway muscle from asthmatics and from animal models of asthma exhibits increased rate and extent of shortening as well as increased force generation. Many hypotheses on the mechanisms responsible for this enhanced contractility have been formulated but have never been tested thoroughly. Our data from human bronchial biopsies indicate that the gene expression of certain contractile proteins is altered in asthmatics compared to normal subjects. These proteins are responsible for the movement and force generating capacity of muscle as well as its activation. It is therefore conceivable that the altered expression of these proteins directly enhances airway muscle contractility in asthma. Thus, we propose to use state of the art technology and combine mechanics measurements directly at the molecular, muscle strip, and whole animal levels to elucidate the causes of airway muscle abnormality in asthma. Understanding the fundamental abnormality of airway muscle in experimental models of asthma will help formulate strategies to alleviate asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determinants of Active Involvement in Leisure for Youth: DAILY Living with Disability
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT; CONGENITAL HEART DEFECTS; DETERMINANTS; LEISURE; PREMATURE INFANT
Abstract-Résumé: Children who were either born extremely premature or had a congenital heart defect that required open heart surgery in the first weeks or months of life are two groups of children at high risk for motor, behavioral, cognitive and other developmental disabilities. As such, these children are likely to exhibit limitations in their participation in activities at home, in school and in the community. This study aims to clarify the extent of involvement in leisure activities, known to be critical in promoting health and minimizing risk for cardiovascular and psychosocial sequelae. In particular, this study will identify the facilitators and obstacles to a physically and socially active and satisfying life for these two target groups of survivors of early intensive care. The child, family and environmental attributes that are associated with participation in active physical and other leisure activities will be determined. Involvement and enjoyment of leisure activities is critical for developing life skills, promoting healthy and fit lifestyles, fostering friendships, increasing self-worth and personal autonomy. Of note, a sedentary lifestyle is detrimental to the cardiovascular health of all children, and health risk is likely to be compounded by any chronic illness or disability. Recognition of the factors that influence leisure participation is essential to guide the development of targeted adaptive and remediation strategies and health promotion initiatives that foster health and well-being.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Tn10 and Tn5 Transposition
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; BACTERIAL GENE EXPRESSION; DNA TRANSPOSITION; GENETICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NUCLEOID BINDING PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Bacteria cause a variety of human and animal diseases. Antibiotics provide protection against many such diseases by preventing bacterial growth. However, bacteria are adept at acquiring DNA from foreign sources, a process known as lateral gene transfer, including genes that confer resistance to antibiotics. The acquisition of multiple antibiotic resistance genes can lead to the development of bacterial strains that are resistance to a broad range of antibiotics and subsequently infections caused by these bacteria can become life threatening. Transposons are mobile genetic elements found in almost all bacteria and contribute greatly to lateral gene transfer, including the mobilization of antibiotic resistance genes. We are studying mechanisms by which the movement of two reasonably well-characterized transposons, Tn10 and Tn5, are regulated. In particular, we are interested in defining how proteins encoded by the host bacteria (as opposed to the transposon itself) regulate transposon mobility and if/how this regulation is linked to existing pathways that help the bacteria adapt to changing environmental conditions and/or cellular stress. Our studies focus on two proteins considered to be global regulators of gene expression in bacteria, H-NS and Hfq, and which we have shown are important regulators of Tn10 and Tn5 transposition. Ultimately, our studies should provide insight into how lateral gene transfer is controlled, and into factors in the environment that promote this process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study of the pathogenesis and reversibility of airway damage and repair (remodeling) during chronic mucosal immune response to environmental allergens in a large animal model of asthma.
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE REMODELING; EQUINE HEAVES; EXPRESSION ARRAYS (SSH; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; LASER  MICRODISSECTION; LUNG FUNCTION; MICROARRAYS)
Abstract-Résumé: In human asthma, repeated exposure to environmental allergens leads to persistent inflammation and damage (remodeling) of the lungs, and a progressive loss of airway function. Our proposed studies aim to determine 1) if the lesions present in the lung tissue of asthmatic individuals are reversible by decreasing the level of allergen exposure or by the administration of corticosteroids and antileukotrienes, two common therapeutics for this condition, and 2) if so, identify the cells and the mediators responsible for these changes. These results will provide insight to the relationship between inflammation, remodeling and airway function and may lead to the discovery of novel anti-remodeling therapy. These studies are conducted in equine heaves, a natural disease of horses that shares many similarities with human asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cortical synaptic remodeling in Alzheimer's disease and animal models
Keywords-MotsClés: ABETA AMYLOID; AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; INFLAMMATION; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT (MCI); TRANSGENIC MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Our lab has contributed significantly towards the understanding of cellular and molecular aspects of the earliest stages of the Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology through the generation of novel cell and transgenic animal models as well as studies in the human brain. An example of the latter is our paper "A paradoxical upregulation of glutamatergic presynaptic boutons during Mild Cognitive Impairment," (highlighted in Nature Clinical Practice Neurology). The present grant application is the natural continuation of these studies, aimed at responding to key questions related to the cellular and molecular pathology of this devastating disease. Questions such as: Is the paradoxical increase in cortical synaptic numbers at the early stages of AD a compensatory response or pathological event? Does the early pathological accumulation of toxic Abeta peptides unleash an inflammatory process? What is the molecular organization of these Abeta peptides which are lodged inside neurons in brain regions vulnerable to the AD pathology? Are these Abeta peptides responsible for the pre-amyloid-plaque inflammatory process? Will this pre-amyloid-plaque contribute to the dysregulation of the ERK/CREB pathway (a pathway affecting synaptic plasticity essential to memory formation)? Is this newly identified "pro-inflammatory" process also found in key brain areas of Mild Cognitive Impairment sufferers (MCI is a clinical stage preceding AD)? Is this pro-inflammatory process apparent and related to cognition before MCI and correlated with cognitive decline? These essential questions are formulated in a research plan under three guiding Hypotheses and will significantly contribute to our current understanding of the molecular and cellular events leading to brain dysfunction in the "twilight" region between the healthy brain and the start of AD. These investigations will render valuable clues for possible early therapies or prevention of AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translation regulation of the inhibitor of apoptosis, cIAP1, during cellular stress.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER; INTERNAL RIBOSOME ENTRY SITE; RNA BINDING PROTEINS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSLATIONAL CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: My research program involves the study of the regulation of gene expression at the level of protein synthesis (translation), in particular how it is regulated during conditions of cellular stress. We have discovered that there exists an alternative mode of translation that utilizes an RNA regulatory element termed IRES. Importantly, this mode of translation persists during conditions of stress when normal cellular protein synthesis is shut down. I propose here to continue our analysis of the IRES mechanism of translation during conditions of cellular stress.

TitreApplicationTitle: MRE11-RAD50-NBS1: at the crossroads of DNA double-strand break repair and Fanconi anemia
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL AND CELLULAR ASSAYS; CANCER RESEARCH; DNA REPAIR; DOUBLE-STRAND BREAKS; FANCONI ANEMIA; MRE11-RAD50-NBS1
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a constant treath for humans. All organisms have evolved mechanisms that allow the maintenance of genomic integrity. The consequences of damaged DNA, and especially double-strand breaks, may be disastrous and lead to cancer if left unrepaired. All organisms can suffer DNA damage, during normal cellular processes or as a consequence of DNA damaging agents such as ultraviolet light and ionizing radiation.   The present project involves the characterization of key enzymes (MRE11-RAD50-NBS1) involved in the repair of double-strand breaks but also Fanconi anemia. Understanding how these proteins function in cell is critical to improve radiotherapy on cancer cells. Moreover, it will greatly improve our knowledge on several genetic disorders (such as Ataxia telangiectasia like-disorder and Fanconi Anemia) that are characterized by defective DNA damage responses.

TitreApplicationTitle: ProNGF and neurodegeneration in aging and Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BASAL FOREBRAIN CHOLINERGIC NEURONS; NERVE GROWTH FACTOR; NEUROTROPHIN RECEPTORS; PRONEUROTROPHINS; RETROGRADE TRANSPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Neurotrophins are small but essential proteins found in the brain and nervous system that govern critical aspects of cell-cell communication, neuronal function and survival, and repair after injury. We were one of the first labs to demonstrate that protein precursors called proneurotrophins are the predominant form of these molecules in the brain and that they have biological activity, although the nature of that activity is now hotly debated. In Alzheimer's disease, one of these proneurotrophins, proNGF, accumulates in areas of the brain necessary for cognition, learning and memory, and this accumulation correlates with cognitive decline. The mechanisms causing abnormal proNGF accumulation and how that affects neuronal function are not well understood. In this application we hypothesize that the survival- or death-promoting activities of proNGF depend upon the balance of receptors present, that proNGF is transported within neurons from axon terminal to cell body and that it supports cell body survival. Moreover, we propose that when one of the receptors is lost in aging and in Alzheimer's disease, proNGF is no longer transported, accumulates and becomes harmful to neurons.  Our proposed research will use cell culture approaches to examine the biological effects of proNGF accumulation and elucidate the roles of receptor loss and defective proNGF transport and signalling in neuronal degeneration. Understanding the conditions under which proNGF causes survival or death, and how it signals and is transported within the cell, is important to our basic knowledge of the normal nervous system and to the molecular mechanisms of cognitive decline.  The overarching goal of our research is to prevent cognitive decline.  This project will provide new understanding and new targets for therapeutic intervention for aging and neurodegenerative disease and will thereby promote advances in health care for older Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Insight into sensorimotor cortex function and plasticity by monitoring and interrogating the brain-muscle interface using light.
Keywords-MotsClés: 2-PHOTON IMAGING; CHANNELRHODOPSIN; IMAGING; MOTOR CORTEX; PLASTICITY; SENSORIMOTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The action of the motor system, that controls our bodies muscles, is critical for everything that we do. The remarkable abilities of the brain's motor control system allow us to learn how to walk and later as adults learn new tasks. My lab will apply new techniques to further address classic work on the structure and function of the motor system. The ability of the motor system to change is also essential for recovery after debilitating injuries such as stroke or damage to the spinal cord. We hope that by understanding the motor system's circuits on a basic level that new insight into treatment of those affected by diseases that impact the sensory and motor system will achieved. To do this, we believe we need to unravel the motor system's complex circuits. The brain is organized much like a circuit diagram within a computer with discrete wires or connections. However, none of the brain circuits or cells have color-coding or labels which enable technicians to service them. Here, using new genetic technologies we will employ strategies, which label select mouse neurons with fluorescent proteins, which enable them to glow under particular wavelengths of light. Not only can the glowing neurons be found by light, but they can also be controlled by light using new light-sensitive protein ion channels, which transmit light energy into excitation or inhibition. Using these fluorescing neurons, which can be controlled by light, we plan to unravel how the motor system can control specific muscles, but yet be flexible to change. We also will understand how this system can be modulated or altered by ongoing experiences. Lastly, we plan to understand how different behavioral states (for example awake versus asleep), and brain rhythms impact the function of the motor system. Overall, our goal is that through insight into motor system function novel treatments will ensue, permitting better lives for those affected by diseases that alter motor function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Circadian clock gene expression on night shifts
Keywords-MotsClés: BRIGHT LIGHT; CYTOKINES; PERIPHERAL BLOOD MONONUCLEAR; PLASMA CORTISOL; PLASMA MELATONIN; SHIFT WORK
Abstract-Résumé: In humans and animals, most body and mental rhythms are governed by internal biological clocks. The master biological clock is located centrally, deep in the brain. Its function relies on sophisticated feed-back loops of genes transcription within its cells. In lower animals, it was discovered that even cells located in peripheral tissues could express cycles of genes transcription akin those observed in the central clock. This exciting finding suggests that molecular mechanisms can be studied in peripheral tissues as an indicator of what is happening in the brain. We recently discovered that this was true for human beings and that genes related to the biological clock were expressed in a rhythmic manner in white blood cells. We also demonstrated that their rhythm is affected by irregularities in the schedule of sleep. In the present project we will study the impact of working nights on clock gene expression and the immune function in humans.  This line of investigation has enormous potential for substantial breakthroughs in our comprehension of health problems associated with disorders of the sleep/wake cycle such as shift work, jet lag, and chronic insomnia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism and Function of the Specialized Nuclear Export of mRNA Encoding Secreted and Mitochondrial Proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: MRNA NUCLEAR EXPORT; NUCLEAR PORE COMPLEX; ORGANELLES; PROTEIN BIOSYNTHESIS; RNA LOCALIZATION; SECRETION
Abstract-Résumé: Gene expression plays a critical role in regulating and modifying various cellular functions, which impact on processes such as development and homeostasis. In eukaryotic cells, gene activation begins in the nucleus, where DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA). After the mRNA is processed it is exported into the cytoplasm where it is translated into protein.   Previously, I discovered that a subset mRNAs encoding secreted and mitochondrial proteins are exported by a specialized mRNA nuclear export pathway. These mRNAs contain an element, the SSCR/MSCR, that  is found within the open reading frame and is translated in the cytoplasm into a cleavable leader peptide that targets the newly made protein for secretion or to an organelle. I discovered that SSCRs and MSCRs derived from mammalian genes not only encode targeting peptides, but also act as RNA elements that promote mRNA nuclear export. In humans, approximately 10 to 15% of all genes have this export element. We believe that this export pathway evolved only recently as the sequence characteristics that promote export is only seen in vertebrate SSCRs and MSCRs. In unpublished work, I found that at least one model SSCR binds to a set of nuclear proteins that have been implicated in nuclear export and may regulate mRNA localization in the cytoplasm.   In this proposal I will describe my plans for investigating the molecular mechanisms responsible for the specialized export of mRNA encoding secreted and mitochondrial proteins. In the process I will gain a deeper understanding of the role of this mRNA export pathway in the production and function of newly synthesized proteins.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analyses of the multiple functions of the Drosophila foraging gene: a cGMP dependent protein kinase
Keywords-MotsClés: DROSOPHILA; FAT; FORAGING BEHAVIOUR; LEARNING AND MEMORY; NEUROGENETICS; PLEIOTROPY
Abstract-Résumé: Many serious diseases such as obesity and diabetes and are related to an excess of stored fat. This is especially common in affluent countries where overeating and a lack of exercise are common. Stored fat also affects the physiology of the entire organism including its behaviour. We use the fruit fly to investigate natural variation in the foraging gene which encodes a signalling molecule called PKG. Variation in the foraging gene results in two behavioural types, rovers and sitters, which differ in a suite of traits including their food intake, food related movement, learning and memory and lipid metabolism. We use the fruit fly to investigate how this single naturally varying gene which is also found in humans exerts its multiple effects on metabolism and behaviour. Our studies will help us understand how excess fat  affect behaviours important to our well-being and survivorship.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Architecture of the CFTR Chloride Channel
Keywords-MotsClés: CYSTIC FIBROSIS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNELS; PATCH CLAMP; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; STRUCTURE-FUNCTION RELATIONSHIPS
Abstract-Résumé: Cystic fibrosis is a common, fatal hereditary disease that occurs in children who inherit a mutant gene from each of their parents. Only one gene is involved, and this gene controls the production of a protein called CFTR that is found in the membrane surrounding cells in the lungs, pancreas, sweat glands, reproductive system, and other organs. The role of CFTR is to allow chloride ions to move across the cell membrane, which is important in controlling fluid movement within each of these organs. Research in my lab uses precise electrical recording techniques to study the movement of chloride ions through CFTR in cell membranes, in order to understand how CFTR carries out this transport role and how its normal function is disrupted by cystic fibrosis-causing genetic mutations. To understand the CFTR protein at the molecular level, we change its structure by introducing changes into the gene sequence. Forms of CFTR bearing these structure-changing mutations are then introduced into cells growing in culture, allowing any changes in their activity to be investigated in fine detail by electrical recordings. We are particularly interested in understanding the structure of the pathway in the CFTR protein through which chloride ions move as they cross the cell membrane, and how this movement is controlled. We believe that understanding how CFTR carries out its normal role in controlling chloride movement is key to understanding the cellular defects in cystic fibrosis, and perhaps in developing new ways to correct these defects.

ClasseRechercheFR: RETARD MENTAL; TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of palmitoylation in the trafficking of the lysosomal sorting receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; LYSOSOMAL TRAFFICKING; NEURONAL CEROID LIPOFUSCINOSIS; PALMITOYLATION; SORTILIN
Abstract-Résumé: The efficient sorting and trafficking of proteins in the cell has important consequences in human health. Our work focuses on the sorting and trafficking from the Golgi apparatus to the lysosomal compartment. To date, three lysosomal sorting receptors have been identified that bind cargo in the Golgi apparatus to deliver it to the lysosomal compartment. In order to maintain efficient sorting and trafficking, the cell recycles the receptors back to the Golgi apparatus. Several cytosolic components have been identified that are required for the Golgi to lysosome trafficking and the recycling pathway. Interestingly, we and others have shown that palmitoylation, a lipid modification found on proteins, is important in the efficient recycling of the lysosomal sorting receptors. However, the exact function of this modification and the mechanism the cell uses to add and remove the palmitoyl group has not been investigated. We have identified an enzyme that modifies the sorting receptors with a palmitoyl residue that is required for the proper recycling of the sorting receptors. If the enzyme is absent or the receptor can not be modified due to a mutation in the sorting receptor itself, then the receptor is not brought back to the Golgi but is instead degraded. This leads to the improper sorting of lysosomal cargo and eventually cell death. Proper and efficient lysosomal sorting is significant to human health as over 40 lysosomal storage disorders have been identified with the majority being genetically inherited. No cures or treatments exist for the majority of these conditions which usually result in premature death in childhood. Our work will lead to a greater understanding of the molecular details the cell employs to sort and traffic the lysosomal sorting receptors which could lead to an increase in our knowledge of the mechanism of lysosomal storage disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aging and degeneration in the mammalian nervous system: role of the p53 family
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; CELL SURVIVAL; NEURODEGENERATION; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The mechanisms that maintain the integrity and function of the mammalian brain for an entire lifetime are still poorly understood.  We have recently identified a gene, p73, that when mutated, causes nervous system degeneration and age-dependent cognitive decline.  In this project, we are asking how this gene and a number of related genes maintain the brain in the face of aging, and what goes wrong to cause degeneration when they are mutated. Such information is important as we attempt to generate new approaches to promote healthy aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the O-GlcNAc post-translational protein modification in epigenetic regulation of gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETICS; GENE SILENCING; GLYCOSYL TRANSFERASE; O-GLYCOSYLATION; POLYCOMB GROUP; TRITHORAX GROUP
Abstract-Résumé: Proper functioning of an enzyme called OGT, which puts a simple sugar residue on various proteins, has been implicated in insulin signaling, neurodegenerative diseases, and cellular stress response.  We recently found that OGT regulates the turning on and off of certain genes, with potential consequences for important processes such as developmental regulation, stem cell maintenance, genomic imprinting, and cancer.  Our proposed work will provide more information on how OGT plays a key role in such diverse cellular events.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hypoxia:  Effects on Tumour Response and Progression in Cervix Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER STEM CELLS; CERVIX CANCER; HYPOXIA; METASTASIS
Abstract-Résumé: Most human tumors contain regions that are abnormally low in oxygen (hypoxia). Hypoxic cancer cells in these regions respond poorly to conventional cancer treatment and are associated with metastatic spread to other organs. The research conducted in this project is aimed at understanding how exposure to hypoxia affects the ability of the tumour cells to resist treatment and to metastasize. Recent research from our group has identified specific genes that may be turned on under hypoxic conditions and that can affect the ability of the cells to spread and form metastases. We have already shown that blocking the activity of one of these genes can reduce the effect of hypoxia on metastasis. Studies conducted in this project will work with tumour tissue directly from patients or recently established tumours growing from such tumour tissue in animals (xenografts). It will compare the hypoxic environment in early xenografts with that in the primary (patient) tumour from which they were derived and investigate the effects of hypoxia on the genes already identified to determine their role in the metastatic process in cervix cancers. We will test whether drugs which can inhibit the activity of these genes can reduce metastases. The studies will also involve investigation of so-called "cancer stem" cells in cervix cancers. These cells are of particular interest because they may represent the subpopulation of the cancer cells which are most able to form metastases. First we will develop methods to identify such cells and then establish whether hypoxia promotes their ability to form metastases and to resist treatment.  We believe that understanding how hypoxia limits the success of current cancer therapy both at the local site and as a result of distant metastatic spread and testing the ability of new drugs to target specifically the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms involved will lead to improvement in the efficiency of current cancer therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Depression and disability in diabetes: a prospective community study
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY SAMPLE; DEPRESSION; DIABETES; DISABILITY; LONGITUDINAL RELATIONSHIP
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is also a highly prevalent but treatable disorder and is a leading cause of disability, work place absenteeism, and increased use of health care resources. Depression has been shown to be a common co-morbidity in diabetes, affecting 10 to 30 % of the diabetic population. Growing evidence from clinical studies indicates that diabetic patients with depression demonstrate poor adherence to antidiabetic regimens and are at increased risk for diabetes specific complications The purpose of this project is to follow the cohort of the Montreal Diabetes Health and Well-Being Study (DHS) for additional three years and to study the incidence of and risk factors for depression, disability, and mortality. The DHS is a nationally representative sample of the general adult population in Quebec that was recruited through random digit dialing in 2008 (n=2,003; 1 year follow-up: January-March 2009; PI: Schmitz, Wang, Malla, Lesage, Boyer, Strychar, funded by CIHR).  Our specific objectives are:  a)To estimate the number of new cases of depression, disability and mortality in diabetes; b)To identify the role of depression in the development of disability in diabetes; c)To identify the role of disability in the development of depression in diabetes;  e)To identify the impact of depression on health service utilization in diabetes. The follow-up assessment of this unique cohort will give us an opportunity not only to estimate incidence of depression and disability in the community but also to study the complex interaction of risk factors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of Loci and Genes for Autosomal Recessive Mental Retardation and Autism in Consanguineous Pakistani Families
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE; DISEASE GENE IDENTIFICATION; MENTAL RETARDATION; MUTATION SCREENING; PHENOTYPE
Abstract-Résumé: Mental retardation  is believed to occur with a prevalence of approximately 2% within the population. Autosomal recessive forms of non-syndromic mental retardation (where no additional symptoms are presnet and the disease causimg mutation is inherited from both unaffected parents) are believed to account for a large proportion of these individuals. Mapping genes for autosomal recessive disorders can be performed with great efficiency in families with a high proportion of consanguineous marriages using microarray data for high-density DNA markers. We have recruited in total 57 consanguineous families with MR (autistic individuals are also present in some families) from Pakistan - a country where consanguineous marriages are commonplace.  We propose to simultaneously map the disease loci and genes in these families, while refining the clinical descriptions for each family. To date we have mapped and identified the disease genes for 4 families, including 2 new, and two previously known genes. We also plan to recruit additional Pakistani MR families to the study.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the E4orf6/E1B55K E3 Ubiquitin Ligase in the Adenovirus Life Cycle
Keywords-MotsClés: CULLIN-BASED UBIQUITIN LIGASES; HUMAN ADENOVIRUSES; MRNA TRANSPORT; PROTEIN COMPLEXES; PROTEIN DEGRADATION
Abstract-Résumé: Viruses have many obstacles to overcome in order to infect cells and multiply effectively. All cells possess multiple processes for protection against viral replication, but most viruses have evolved multiple ways to counteract these processes, or merely promote a more efficient infectious process. Human adenoviruses (Ad) cause upper respiratory, eye and gastrointestinal infections. They also induce tumours in rodents and although no evidence yet exists to suggest they cause any human cancer, they have been tremendously valuable as models to better understand the molecular basis of cancer.  They are also important vectors used in gene therapy, and replicating forms are in clinical trials for use in treating cancer. We believe that they are excellent models to understand an emerging strategy used by many viruses, that of creating a complex that destroys cellular proteins that block their ability to replicate. An Ad protein, termed E4orf6, has evolved to form a complex, termed a Cullin-based E3 ubiquitin ligase, that degrades cellular proteins. Another Ad protein, termed E1B55K, binds to a range of cellular proteins and then introduces them to the E4orf6 ligase complex so that these bound proteins can be degraded. We already know that several cellular proteins are destroyed by this process, including one that kills cells before the virus can complete replication (p53), two that cause problems for newly-made viral DNA to be assembled into new viruses (Mre11 and DNA ligase IV), and our new discovery, a protein that may limit spread or yield of the newly made viruses (integrin a3).  We propose to conduct detailed studies on the Ad E4orf6/E1B55K complex, including the identification of additional cellular protein targets, to gain insight into the nature of substrates that may be targeted by Ad and perhaps other more clinically relevant viruses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nutrient sensing in the Gut
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES/OBESITY; FOOD INTAKE; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; GUT NUTRIENT SENSING; GUT/BRAIN/LIVER AXIS; PANCREATIC CLAMP / INTESTINAL ADMINISTRATION IN VIVO
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes and obesity are characterized by increased blood glucose levels and body weight, which are caused partly by increased glucose production by the liver and appetite. We and others have demonstrated that nutrients such as lipids activate sensing mechanisms in the duodenum to lower glucose production and food intake through a neuronal network. We here test the working hypothesis that nutrients activate distinct signaling pathways in different parts of the small intestine to lower glucose production and appetite through a neuronal network. These findings will reveal new therapeutic strategies and molecular candidates targeting the intestine to lower glucose levels and body weight in diabetes and obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: The importance hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1)in vessel physiology and pathology.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL BIOLOGY; GENE REGULATION; HIF-1; HYPOXIA; VASCULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The human body is constantly subjected to low oxygen conditions (hypoxia) in everyday living. Exercise, cold temperatures and changes in altitude all effect the oxygen concentration in our body's tissues and organs. For survival, we must adapt to these changes in oxygen. Fortunately, our body is highly able to respond quickly and efficiently to hypoxia. A large number of genes important for survival are finely controlled by oxygen through a protein complex called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1). These genes play a critical role in blood vessel development, growth and maintenance and have been shown to be involved in different vascular pathologies. Given the possible importance of HIF-1 in cardiovascular disease, understanding of how HIF-1 is controlled can lead to beneficial effects. Since its conception, our laboratory has been studying how HIF-1 activity is controlled in cells and tissues. We have found that in addition to hypoxia, different hormones can increase HIF-1 and hypoxic genes in cells isolated from blood vessels. We are convinced that this type of gene induction of is important in how blood vessels react in the normal healthy body and in various disease situations. We believe that changes in the normal regulation of this factor could cause major blood vessel problems and lead to hypertension, vascular remodeling atherosclerosis and other vascular diseases. The goal of our work is to understand the mechanisms involved in this type of HIF-1 regulation, to evaluate the genes that are activated and to demonstrate the importance of this regulation of HIF-1 in vascular biology. When the pathways are well mapped out, we hope that this knowledge will identify targets to help fight cardiovascular disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Demands and Resources in Work and Family Life and their  Implications for Stress and Health among Canadians
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFLICT; FAMILY; HEALTH; SPILLOVER; STRESS; WORK
Abstract-Résumé: The experiences of stress in work and family life have implications for health and well-being of Canadians. The proposed research seeks to investigate the specific conditions that influence the exposure to stressors and the potential resources that might mitigate their effects on health. We focus particular attention on the ways that job-related demands generate stress in the ways that people navigate the borders between work and family life. Moreover, we explore the impact of personal, social, household, and organizational resources as protective factors in these processes. The discovery of knowledge about these processes can inform the public about ways that they can avoid or minimize stressors in these core role domains of daily life. At a broader level, the proposed research could inform policy makers about personal and organizational conditions that present risk and/or protective factors for stress in the intersection of work and family life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Isolation of therapeutic fractions from intravenous immunoglobulins using the triple transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: 3XTG-AD; ABETA; ALZHEIMER; INTRAVENOUS IMMUNOGLOBULIN; TAU
Abstract-Résumé: Immunoglobulins (or antibodies) are proteins found in blood or other body fluids that are produced by the immune system to identify and neutralize foreign particles, such as bacteria and viruses. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) therapy consists in injecting to a patient a mixture of immunoglobulins that have been extracted from plasma pools of thousands of blood donors. This approach is successfully used to treat immunodeficient patients that do not produce enough immunoglobulins by their own blood cells. These patients completely rely on IVIg therapy to live. An increasing number of autoimmune or inflammatory diseases are also treated with IVIg. Recent evidence suggests that Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients may benefit from IVIg. However, the total pool of immunoglobulin available for this use is very limited. Thus, we need to better understand how IVIg therapy works if we want to be able to offer it to AD patients on a large scale. In the present grant application, we propose to identify the small fraction(s) of IVIg preparations displaying full efficiency and to study its mechanism of action. In summary, our research project aims to demonstrate the efficacy of IVIg therapy in an animal model and to shed light on the underlying mechanisms necessary for its clinical application in AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of mast cell activation and inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNITY; INFLAMMATION; MAST CELLS; PROTEIN KINASES AND PHOSPHORYLATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Mast cells are part of our immune system that can protect us from some infections.  However, mast cells can also contribute to allergic diseases and promote tumour growth. In this proposal we investigate several important proteins that can regulate the accumulation of mast cells and the amounts of inflammatory mediators they release.  Our goal is to identify new therapeutic targets to treat mast cell-related diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of immunosuppressive medication use on patient outcomes following kidney transplant failure
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE MEDICATION; KIDNEY TRANSPLANTATION; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with end-stage kidney disease can be treated with long-term dialysis or receive a kidney transplant.  Research has shown that patients who receive a kidney transplant have an improvement in survival and quality of life. Unfortunately, not all kidney transplants last forever and many patients have to go back on dialysis treatments. Patients who have transplant failure and resume dialysis have a significantly increased risk of complications and death compared to those who maintain kidney transplant function. They also have worse outcomes compared to other dialysis patients who never received a transplant. The cause of this poor outcome is not known. We speculate that it is due to patients remaining on immunosuppressive medications for too long after the transplant has failed. In this study, we will evaluate patients who suffer kidney transplant failure at all of the adult kidney transplant programs in Canada. We will carefully measure the amount of medication taken, the occurrence of complications such as serious infections as well as their survival. Information from this study will be used to guide practice in this area. This study will show health care professionals the best methods to manage medication in order to improve outcomes for this patient population. Such improvements for the growing number of patients with end-stage kidney disease would represent an important advance in the management of this very disabling and lethal long-term condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms involved in the neuroendocrine-immune interaction
Keywords-MotsClés: GLUCOCORTICOIDS (HPA AXIS); INFLAMMATION/INFECTION/CYTOKINES; MOLECULAR NEUROBIOLOGY; NEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; NEURONAL CIRCUITS; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: It is now well accepted that the occurrence of the immune activation must be conveyed to the brain to allow coordination of the appropriate metabolic, behavioral, and endocrine changes necessary for the restoration of the homeostasis.  In this concept, the hypothalamus, an area of the brain containing many of the peptides that modulate the neuroendocrine functions, is considered central to the bilateral functional communication pathways between the immune and neuroendocrine axes.  The demonstration that cytokines, especially interleukin-1 (IL-1), tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and IL-6, can stimulate neuroendocrine corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) neurons and the finding that subsequent activation of adrenal steroid release can convey feedback signals to immune cells, is a clear example of the bilateral communication linking the immune and the neuroendocrine systems.  Stimulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary adrenal (HPA) axis has been the subject of a great deal of interest because of its major impact on the regulation of the immune response.  Glucocorticoids have long been recognized as being among of the most powerful anti-inflammatory agents known, and their use in restraining excessive immune responses has been common in clinical practice since more than 50 years.  Inappropriate plasma levels of glucocorticoids may therefore play a crucial role as contributing to deviant regulation of the immune response, indicating the importance to identify and characterize the mechanisms through which local inflammatory process interact with the neuroendocrine system.
