TitreApplicationTitle: In utero insults and adult insulin resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETIC REGULATION OF MUSCLE DEVELOPMENT; IN VIVO FETAL HYPOXIA AND MUSCLE DEVELOPMENT; MITOCHONDRIAL BIOGENESIS AND OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION; MTOR AND MUSCLE OXIDATIVE FUNCTION; ORIGINS OF ADULT DISEASES; PPARS AND MUSCLE ENERGY BALANCE
Abstract-Résumé: When the placenta does not develop normally during pregnancy, babies receive a reduced nutrient supply, are born small, thin and lack muscle mass. This outcome is called Intrauterine Growth Restriction (IUGR) and affects approximately 8% of newborns. Despite being born small, these babies grow very quickly after birth once they receive normal or excessive nutrient supply and undergo what is termed 'catch up growth'. It appears that as these babies grow, they develop a reduced ability to use dietary sugars and fats correctly and store these important nutrients in fat tissue rather than use them to build organs, bone and muscle. Later in life, this change in utilization of nutrients, and exposure to high-fat foods and reduced physical activity, dramatically increases the chance of developing diseases such as obesity, high blood pressure, heart disease and type-2 diabetes, a group of diseases now called the 'metabolic syndrome' or syndrome X. An understanding of how we may regulate the body's use of fats and sugars in our diet, to prevent the development of the metabolic syndrome, is critical, as rates of metabolic syndrome continue to climb in Canada.  The key to this change in utilization of nutrients is thought to be in the muscle, where changes in the sensitivity to insulin, one of the body's main regulators of nutrient use, are seen long before other symptoms of metabolic syndrome become apparent. The unifying theme of this research proposal is to define the processes that lead to these alterations in the muscle's response to insulin and use of nutrients, which are set in early life and lead to the newborn being at risk for metabolic syndrome in adult life. This research will help doctors manage IUGR babies, as young adults, and will provide preliminary information on the potential role of new drugs, currently used in adults to treat obesity and resistance to insulin, in modifying this early change in use of nutrients and the prevention of metabolic syndrome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Systems Immunology of S. aureus Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNOLOGY; SEPSIS; STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS; SUPERANTIGENS - TOXIC SHOCK; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Research on the mechanisms of disease is the foundation to improve health care and ultimately quality of life.  Recent advances in DNA and protein technology and in handling of biological information have allowed us to explore fundamental aspects of Biology in the complex milieu of progression and treatment of diseases.  Such a study of biological phenomena in "holistic terms" is known as Systems Biology, and it involves the acquisition and analysis of large amounts of gene and protein data and their computer modeling to learn how a biological system works.    The current grant explores the Systems Immunology of infection by Staphylococcus aureus (Staph), a microbe that is the second most common cause of infections outside hospitals and the most common cause of hospital infections.  We have recently discovered that the wall of Staph is able to turn off the response of some immune cells to the toxins this microbe makes.  This discovery has two different implications.  On one hand, it helps explain why up to 50% of healthy individuals carry Staph in their bodies but do not develop disease. On the other hand, it reveals a mechanism by which Staph may evade our immune system and cause severe infections.  In this grant application, we propose to identify the mechanisms that determine the balance between colonization and disease by Staph using a Systems Biology approach.   The information gathered by this research will be a first step towards the design of novel strategies, different from conventional antibiotics, to prevent and treat infections by this microbe.  It is also important because infections by Staph are one of the most important causes of death in patients with flu, making this study very timely in the context of the ongoing threat of a flu pandemic and the need to be prepared for it.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibition of retroviral replication by the restriction factor TRIM5alpha, and its applications
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE THERAPY; GENETIC SCREENS; HIV-1; INNATE IMMUNITY; MOLECULAR VIROLOGY; RETROVIRUSES
Abstract-Résumé: TRIM5alpha is a natural inhibitor of retroviruses, a family of viruses that includes HIV-1, the AIDS virus. Unfortunately, HIV-1 is not affected by the human version of TRIM5alpha, but it is efficiently inhibited by this protein in other primates. My laboratory is working at deciphering the mechanism of action of TRIM5alpha, in particular by identifying its cellular partners. We are also developing potential therapeutic gene transfer applications. This approach would involve modifying blood cells in AIDS patients so that they express a version of TRIM5alpha targeting HIV-1. Toward this end, we are using genetics to introduce mutations in human TRIM5alpha in order to boost its antiviral potential.

TitreApplicationTitle: The axo-myelinic synapse
Keywords-MotsClés: 2 PHOTON MICROSCOPY; AXON; CALCIUM IMAGING; GLUTAMATE; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; MYELIN
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis, stroke and spinal cord injury are common and devastating human disorders.  The central nervous system is composed of two different types of tissue: gray matter, which comprises the nerve cell bodies, and white matter, which represents the nerve fibers connecting nerve cells to each other.  Nerve fibers in the brains of mammals are highly specialized, being very thin (to pack millions of fibers into a small volume) and wrapped by an insulating fatty material called myelin to prevent short circuits.  How this all-important myelin is damaged in human neurological disorders, and how the nerve fiber tells the myelin to start wrapping and insulating it, remain mysteries.  This project will focus on chemical communication between axons (nerve fibers) and their myelin sheaths.  We proposed that, just like nerve cells communicate with each other using chemical neurotransmitters, so do axons talk to their myelin sheaths to promote the development and continued health of this vital insulating material.  A breakdown of this communication may underlie divers diseases such as MS, cerebral palsy and even psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia.

TitreApplicationTitle: The early course of bipolar disorder: From genetic risk to illness onset
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; CHILD AND ADOLESCENT; CLINICAL COURSE; HIGH RISK; PRODROME; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a severe, heterogeneous psychiatric illness for which there is a lack of information about the origins and early natural history. As BD has strong genetic underpinnings, longitudinal studies of the offspring of carefully diagnosed parents is an important strategy to describe the early clinical course and to study factors influencing illness onset in those predisposed.    With previous funding, we have identified a large unique cohort of offspring of bipolar parents classified by the parent response to lithium treatment, which is a strategy to identify more homogeneous subgroups. We were able to describe for the first time the early clinical stages of BD.  Clinical staging has tremendous potential to advance early diagnosis and treatment, as well as to inform neurobiological research. In related work, we identified factors associated with the risk of BD including: temperament, current life stress and abnormalities in cortisol, a stress-sensitive hormone.     We now propose to extend our longitudinal high-risk study in order to characterize the early clinical stages of BD and investigate the influence of risk factors in illness development. This high-risk study is the largest and longest in duration of its kind worldwide. Results from this study will form the basis of a working model of BD and will provide a clinical staging framework that will inform the way we diagnose, treat and study BD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Natural variation in perturbed phenotypes in C. elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: DISEASE GENETICS; GENETIC INTERACTIONS; NATURAL VARIATION; POPULATION GENETICS; QUANTITATIVE PHENOTYPING; RNAI PHENOTYPES
Abstract-Résumé: Why do patients respond differently to the same drug? Why do two people that inherit the same mutation develop such different diseases? These are critical problems in modern health care -- solving them opens new areas for personalised medicine. At present we are far from understanding this variability between people, and cannot predict it at all.  At the heart of this problem is the way that genes interact. If two people inherit the same mutated copy of a particular gene, one reason they develop such different diseases is that the rest of their genes are not identical. People have millions of genetic differences and these combine to change the effect of a drug or a mutated gene. We propose to take a systematic view of how natural variation between individuals affects the outcome of a single treatment and thus to learn the rules for how the changes in each of our genomes combine.  We cannot do direct experiments in humans, so we turn to the nematode worm, C. elegans. This simple animal shares half its 20,000 genes with humans including many pathways mutated in genetic diseases. Critically, in the worm we can turn off any gene using a technique called RNAi and examine the effect. We have already looked at the effect of removing each gene in the worm and found ~1500 genes that strongly affect the animal.  However, when we now repeat exactly the same experiments in a different naturally occurring worm strain, we often obtain strikingly different effects. This is like examining the differences between people in response to the same drug, and the question is the same -- why do these individuals respond differently? We will answer this in worms by first examining the effect of removing each gene on a whole series of naturally occurring worms, then using genetics to map down the exact changes that cause these differences. We will thus get insight into how genetic variation affects our responses to drug treatments or genetic mutations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular pharmacology of the neuroprotective peptide hormone PACAP (pituitaty adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide) and its receptors.
Keywords-MotsClés: A NEUROPEPTIDE HORMONE; BINDING AND PHOTOLABELING STUDIES; ELDERS' HEALTH; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES; PACAP; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PEPTIDE SYNTHESIS AND MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) is a neurohormone with a wide distribution in the central nervous system and peripheral tissues, suggesting that this peptide is involved in a large array of physiological processes. In fact, PACAP biological activities were described in most systems, including the nervous system, and interestingly, PACAP was shown to exhibit beneficial properties in several pathophysiological states such as Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, cerebral ischemia and traumatic brain injury. Parkinson's disease is characterized by a neurodegeneration of the dopaminergic cells in the midbrain with concomitant loss of dopamine innervations resulting in a dysfunction of motor activation. It is ranked second in terms of prevalence among neurodegenerative diseases affecting 1-2% of the population over 65. Considering the report from the Department of Economics and Social Affairs of the United Nations stating that population ageing is unprecedented, pervasive and enduring, it is likely that the number of patients with the Parkinson's disease will increase in the next decades. The neuroprotective effects of PACAP appear to be mediated by a cellular receptor protein named PAC1. Therefore, this receptor has been proposed as a potential target for the treatment of several neurodegenerative diseases, including the Parkinson's disease. Hence, we propose to evaluate the molecular and functional aspects of PACAP and its receptors using synthetic analogues discriminating its various actions. This approach is a key step in the development of a new therapeutic strategy focusing particularly on the treatment of nervous alterations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechamisms of glomerular barrier dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOMERULAR PODOCYTES; PROTEINURIA; RHO-GTPASES; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: The glomerulus is the filtration unit of the kidney. It filters water and small molecules including body wastes while retaining large molecules essential for body function. When this barrier function is impaired, proteinuria occurs, which is often followed by kidney failure. Visceral glomerular epithelial cells (commonly known as 'podocytes') are critical for structural integrity as well as barrier function of the glomerulus.  Recent researches highlighted the importance of the structural proteins (actin cytoskeleton) in podocytes for their function. The proposed research will define how podocytes maintain the structural and functional integrity and how podocyte injury leads to proteinuria. We hypothesize that various small Rho-GTPases act together to modulate the actin cytoskeleton and maintain podocyte morphology and function and that when the balance of various signaling pathways is disturbed, it leads to proteinuria. Cultured cells as well as experimental models will be used to address this hypothesis. The result of the research is likely to give insights into the pathogenesis of various proteinuric glomerular diseases such as membranous nephropathy, minimal change disease, and diabetic nephropathy, and contribute to the development of the better therapeutic approach to glomerular disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dopaminergic control of locomotion in the neonatal mouse
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT; LOCOMOTION; MONOAMINE; RECOVERY; SPINAL CORD
Abstract-Résumé: One of the success stories in treatment of spinal cord injury has been the adoption of active locomotor-based rehabilitation. While the underlying mechanisms may never be fully known, a consensus has emerged that part of the recovery is due to activity-driven reorganization of spinal circuits. These spinal circuits are essential for producing many motor behaviors including walking. Despite the success of these programs, patients do plateau in their recovery over time, and indeed activity-dependent rehabilitation does not work for some patients. It would be beneficial to have drug-based therapies promoting activation of spinal circuits that would accelerate activity-dependent recovery of function. Our work and that of others has established that spinal circuits can be awakened by application of exogenous drugs or by electrical stimulation of nerves. Promising candidates are chemical transmitters (monoamines) that are released by the brain within the spinal cord and normally activate and modulate spinal circuits. Perhaps the biggest impediment to future success is our lack of basic knowledge about the spinal circuits that generate walking and consequently where and how these drugs may be acting. Our work explores this issue using an innovative mouse model. We use mice that 'light up' cells involved in walking. We can then target these cells and circuits to test drug combinations that turn on the dormant walking engine downstream of the injury. Our expectation is that these approaches will lead to new drug-based therapies that will dramatically increase the effectiveness of current rehabilitation strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of lyososomal cholesterol in the regulation of ABCA1 expression and HDL formation
Keywords-MotsClés: ABCA1; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CHOLESTEROL; CORONARY HEART DISEASE; HDL; INTRACELLULAR CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT
Abstract-Résumé: High density lipoproteins or HDL in human blood are the good cholesterol particles, in that a higher level of HDL is associated with protection against heart attacks, while a low level of HDL increases the risks of heart attacks.  Increasing the formation of new HDL particles in the body is a major goal, along with healthy diet and regular exercise, in preventing heart attacks and strokes. We have found that the flow of cholesterol out of a particular area of the cell known as lysosomes is a major determinant of how well the cell can turn on HDL formation.  We are continuing our studies on this pathway to confirm how important this mechanism is, including how important the cholesterol that comes out of lysosomes is for the cell to make new HDL.  The planned studies will further our understanding of the way cells make new HDL, and determine whether the flow of cholesterol out of lysosomes is something that could be increased as a new treatment to increase HDL formation for the prevention of heart attacks and strokes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Calcium-activated proteases in health and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM; CALPAINS/PROTEASES; INHIBITORS; MOLECULAR MODELING; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Calpains are enzymes in every cell of our body that are regulated by calcium ions to cut other proteins in a selective and highly controlled way. This is a normal and essential process required for cell functions like motility, cell division, and developmental changes. However, in certain diseases such as stroke, heart attack, blunt trauma, cataract and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Huntington's, calcium levels rise inside the cell. This triggers the calpains to become over-active and unregulated. They then cause extensive tissue damage to the affected areas.  We have several objectives in this application. The first is to develop better inhibitors of calpain that are more effective than present ones and that do not affect other enzymes in the cell. For inhibitor development we have two approaches. One is to use modeling and simulations to design better inhibitors based on the structures we have recently solved by X-ray crystallography, including that of calpain bound to its natural inhibitor, calpastatin. The other is to use a high-throughput screening assay to look through tens of thousands of compounds for better inhibitors At the same time we are studying the metabolism and turn-over of the main calpains to see how they are normally controlled and what other opportunities there are to stop them from becoming too active. We are also extending this investigation to include tissue-specific forms of calpain to see how these minor calpains of uncertain function might be affected by inhibitors we design.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tissue factor in tumour progression and angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CANCER STEM CELLS; COAGULATION; GLIOBLASTOMA; ONCOGENES; TISSUE FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Blood clotting helps tumours with new blood vessel growth and with spread around the body. The protein that is responsible for these effects is called tissue factor (TF), and is produced in large amounts by some cancer cells. Indeed, cancer cells are not equal. Some of them, the so called cancer stem cells (CSCs) or tumour initiating cells (TICs), are believed to be essential for starting tumour growth (tumour initiation). They are also involved in diesase spreading and failure of treatment. In contrast, the majority of other tumour cells are thought to be less deadly at causing the disease, and they may eventually stop dividing by themselves. For this reason much research now focuses on eliminating CSCs. Our laboratory discovered that some CSCs express high levels of TF, provoke blood clotting and use such clots as protective and nurishing nests, the so called CSC 'niches'. CSCs may also exploit normal cells as a source of TF and clotting niches. We would like to explore these new findings further, and in the context of presently incurable brain tumours (gliomas), where the clotting system is activated and may contribute to the disease. We will study how CSCs 'talk' to the clotting system and whether we can change their properties by depriving them of TF (e.g. by using certain antibodies). We will also test whether the surrounding host cells are induced to provide their own TF activity to 'help' CSCs in forming a tumour. We have unique mice which make low levels of TF and could mimick this situation. We will also study what do CSCs 'sense' when they come into contact with the activated clotting proteins and wheter they can be made more vulnerable to therapy when such contacts are interrupted (e.g. by antibodies or blood thinners), Ultimately we aim at finding ways to deny CSCs in the brain the support of the clotting system, to devise new treatments for this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: ATP-sensitive potassium channels: common variants, pharmacogenomics and type 2 diabetes risk.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATP-SENSITIVE POTASSIUM CHANNELS; BETA-CELL; COMMON GENETIC VARIANTS; METABOLISM; PATCH-CLAMP; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: ATP-sensitive potassium channels are important membrane proteins that regulate a number of cellular processes that control blood sugar levels including insulin secretion. Indeed, drugs that target this channel are used to stimulate insulin secretion in type 2 diabetics. Common genetic variants in this channel are associated with an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes (20% or type 2 diabetics have two copies of these genetic variants). However, the mechanisms by which these variants 1) trigger diabetes and 2) alter sensitivity to commonly used drugs has not been determined. It is therefore the aim of this research to further understand how common genetic variants increase the risk for type 2 diabetes and determine if current drug management of this disease can be optimized for these patients with these variants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization and Roles of Hepatic Ectonucleotidases
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; APYRASE; CHOLESTASIS; CIRRHOSIS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; NUCLEOTIDASES
Abstract-Résumé: Nucleotides (e.g. ATP) and nucleosides (e.g. adenosine) act as hormones by activating a variety of functions in all systems and cells.  In the liver, these small molecules regulate a number of metabolic functions as well as inflammation and therefore a number of liver diseases.  The level of these molecules is regulated by enzyme at the cell surface that break them down and therefore these enzymes regulate in the mean time the functions played by nucleotides and nucleosides.  Interestingly, these enzymes transform the former molecule, ATP, into adenosine which has often opposite effect to the former molecule showing the importance of these regulatory enzymes.  We have discovered a novel form of these enzymes that is almost exclusively present in this tissue and that it is the most important enzyme to regulate the level of these molecules.  We will evaluate whether this and other similar enzymes in the liver regulate the functions of these molecules and therefore if they can regulate liver functions and diseases such as cirrhosis.  To address this goal we will generate a mouse that is invalidated for this enzyme.  This mouse will help us to understand the function and importance of this enzyme in liver diseases and functions.  We anticipate that these studies will help define new molecular mechanisms that could be targeted as novel pathways to control liver diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic dissection of leprosy susceptibility
Keywords-MotsClés: CANDIDATE GENE ANALYSIS; LEPROSY; LINKAGE DISEQUILIBRIUM; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Leprosy is an ancient scourge of mankind.  Despite advances in the treatment of this disease still several million people suffer from short term or long term consequences of leprosy.  Our group has been a major contributor to establish that leprosy susceptibility is strongly influenced by host genetic factors.  In this application we propose to identify the genes and their variants that make a person susceptible to leprosy using the latest advances of genetic analysis and genome research.  A major focus will be to understand the mechanisms of action of identified susceptibility genes which will open new avenues of controlling and restricting the health damage to individuals already suffering from leprosy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the microenvironment in liver metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ANTI-INFLAMMATORY DRUGS; CANCER METASTASIS; GENE TRANSFER; IGF AXIS; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: The liver is the major site of metastasis for some of the most common human malignancies, particularly cancers of the GI tract such as colorectal carcinoma. While improvements in surgical techniques have significantly improved disease outcome, most patients with liver metastases still die of their disease. To improve these statistics and prevent liver metastasis, a better understanding of the underlying biology is essential. Our previous work identified the liver microenvironment, in particular the host inflammatory response as a promoter of the early stages of metastasis and implicated the receptor for the growth factor IGF-I in the regulation of this response. Here we propose to continue our studies on the crosstalk between these two systems as well as to test the effect of anti-inflammatory drugs on metastasis of human tumor cells. The results should provide further insight into the interaction between tumor cells and their microenvironment and determine the therapeutic benefit of several novel treatment strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of cell death induced by poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation
Keywords-MotsClés: AKT; AMPK; APOPTOSIS; CANCER; CELL DEATH; CHEMOTHERAPY; DNA DAMAGE; ERK; FACS ANALYSIS; LKB1; MICROSCOPY; MTORC; NUDIX; PARG; PARP
Abstract-Résumé: Human cells suffer DNA damage during normal cellular processes or as a consequence of exposure to DNA damaging agents such as ionizing radiation and UV. Cells have evolved mechanisms to detect DNA damage and repair lesions which could otherwise lead to cancer if left unrepaired. However, in the presence of large amounts of DNA damage, the cell may instead undergo a form of suicide, termed apoptosis, if it detects too much damage and cannot repair all of it properly. Treatment of cancer by chemotherapy and radiotherapy is actually taking advantage of the cell's ability to commit suicide. Chemotherapeutic agents and ionizing radiation both aim at damaging the DNA of cancer cells sufficiently to trigger their death. However, many cancer cells have altered their biology to circumvent cell death and therefore, the biochemistry of these cells is unique.  This project aims at understanding how cancer cells sense that there is too much damage to repair and how they trigger death signals. Specifically, we want to understand how PARP-1, a protein that rapidly detects DNA damage, and PAR, a molecule synthesized by PARP-1 at sites of DNA damage, send death signals within the cell, and which protein partners are involved in transmitting these signals. Identifying the molecules involved in death signals and understanding their functions is critical to design better cancer therapy treatments and to improve clinical outcome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Macrophage CD36 in Atherosclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CD36; ENDOCYTOSIS; MACROPHAGE; RECEPTOR; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL) is thought to be the main causative agent of vascular disease.  This modified form of LDL is ingested by cells of the immune system, specifically macrophages, with consequent accumulation of cholesterol.  As a result of cholesterol loading, the behavior of the macrophages becomes aberrant: the cells become immobile, lose the ability to fight infections and instead cause local inflammation, which ultimately damages the vessel wall.   The goal of our proposal is to minimize the deleterious effects of cholesterol intake, while preserving the ability of the macrophages to clear from the circulation the excess modified LDL.  Towards this end, we are trying to differentiate the molecular mechanisms that mediate the beneficial and detrimental effects of the receptors that mediate the clearance of oxLDL.  We hypothesize that different subpopulations of oxLDL receptors exist. Our studies will focus on a particular scavenger receptor, CD36, which was recently found to be the major factor responsible for the formation and rupture of atherosclerotic plaque, the underlying causes of stroke and infarction.  To selectively observe CD36, we will use novel microscopic techniques capable of detecting single molecules. If subpopulations of receptors are found, therapeutic approaches can be developed that would selectively antagonize the damaging, i.e. inflammatory, effects of the immune receptors, while preserving their benign (antimicrobial and lipid-clearance) properties.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brain mechanisms and sympathetic hyperactivity in genetic models of salt-sensitive hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDOSTERONE; BRAIN; GENETIC MODELS OF SALT-SENSITIVE HYPERTENSION; NA+-TRANSPORT; OUABAIN; SYMPATHETIC ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension (or high blood pressure) is very common in our society. By 60-70 yrs of age >50% of people develop high blood pressure.  It is among the leading causes of stroke, heart attacks, heart failure.  Most hypertension is a combination of genetic and environmental (ie diet and lifestyle) factors.  Besides obesity, excess salt intake is a major contributor to high blood pressure in those people with a genetic predisposition but which genes are involved is still unknown.  About 50% have so-called salt-sensitive hypertension.  Regarding the mechanisms involved, it was commonly assumed that in this group of people, genetically determined changes in the kidney predispose to salt and water retention and this then would lead to high blood pressure.  Studies in animal-models of salt-sensitive hypertension by our and other groups established that effects of high salt intake on brain-mechanisms regulating blood pressure also play an important role.  It appears that the same mechanisms controlling salt retention in the kidneys also function in the brain, leading to increased concentrations of salt in the brain, which then increase the activity of the sympathetic nervous system and thereby cause hypertension.  In the present grant proposal we focus on abnormalities in genes which may be involved in these salt-transporting mechanisms in the brain and the pathways in the brain being activated.  These studies will lead to a better understanding of the genetic determinants of salt-sensitive high blood pressure in animals, which then can be tested in ongoing studies by our group in humans.  Together, these studies may then lead to more precise diagnosis of salt-sensitive hypertension and more specific prevention and treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Synapse Development and Neuronal Activity by a Novel Cation Channel
Keywords-MotsClés: C. ELEGANS LOCOMOTION; CATION CHANNEL; GENETIC SUPPRESSOR SCREEN; NEURONAL EXCITABILITY; SYNAPSE DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Human brain consists of numerous neurons that communicate with each other, and to other target cells through electrical and chemical activities. Abnormal communications, such as the inability of neurons to fire signals, or to control the intensity of their signals, to their target cells are associated with various neurological and cognitive disorders. We discovered a family of evolutionarily conserved cation channels that modulate how active the neuron is in communication, and also influence the structural development of the nervous system. How this channel controls the activity and development of neurons are unknown. Here we propose to use C. elegans and murine neurons as our model systems to study what proteins constitute and modulate the activity of this channel, and how this channel affects the communications between neurons. Interestingly, in humans, some components of this channel reside in a genomic region that is known to associate with several neurological disorders, such as epilepsy, bio-polar and Schizophrenia. Our studies therefore will not only elucidate the fundamental mechanisms on how the brain works, but also provide potential new drug targets and therapeutic interventions for neurological disorders.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE SUR LES MÉDICAMENTS; SANTÉ MENTALE
TitreApplicationTitle: Towards a systems approach to antidepressant drug design
Keywords-MotsClés: ANHEDONIA; ANIMAL MODEL; ANTIDEPRESSANT DRUG ACTION; DEPRESSION; LIGAND-SPECIFIC CONFORMATIONS; NUCLEUS ACCUMBENS
Abstract-Résumé: Antidepressant drug research has traditionally been guided by the notion that the therapeutic efficacy of these agents derives from their capacity to correct neurochemical imbalances in serotonergic and/or noradrenergic neurotransmission.  Despite the fact that we still do not understand how modifying monoamine levels may translate into antidepressant action, drug design of currently available antidepressants is nonetheless based on this mechanism of action.  As a result, all antidepressants have similar shortcomings: 1) reduced side-effects but sub-optimal therapeutic efficacy, 2) dangerously long delays in therapeutic response (2-4 weeks), and 3) inability to alter the course of the illness; most patients relapse subsequent to drug withdrawal.  We have recently observed that direct stimulation of the serotonergic 4 receptor (5-HT4R) can produce behavioral, electrophysiological, cellular and biochemical changes predictive of antidepressant action. More importantly, these changes are observed after only three days of treatment as opposed to the 2-4 weeks necessary with currently-available antidepressants.  One of the behaviors that is reversed by 5HT4R stimulation is anhedonia, which is defined as a reduction in the capacity to experience reward (pleasure).  Understanding how stimulation of this receptor sub-population leads to fast antidepressant action has the potential to be a significant breakthrough in the treatment of a serious mental disorder.  We propose to combine biochemical, immunohistochemical, cellular, pharmacological and behavioral approaches to understand where and how stimulation of 5HT4Rs leads to this unusually fast antidepressant effect.  In addition to elucidating the mechanisms of action of 5HT4R agonists, results of the proposed research may lead to the rational design of fast-acting, more effective antidepressants.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of innate phagocytic function in control of inflammation from infection or injury
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; DENDRITIC CELL; INNATE IMMUNITY; MACROPHAGE; NEUTROPHIL; PHAGOCYTOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: White blood cells play a critical role in control of inflammation. The mechanisms in humans can be best understood by the study of their cells as they try to control inflammation after infection or injury. I propose to continue my CIHR-funded research by extending studies done during the past five years. I have been studying the interaction of cells which ingest bacteria (phagocytes) and bacteria to better understand the reasons why the system can go awry and inflammation can be damaging to the human host. I propose to study the interaction of phagocytes with two different types of bacteria (one which causes infection in cystic fibrosis and one which causes tuberculosis). I will also study people in whom there is loss of control of inflammation. By studying such "experiments of nature," a clearer understanding of the control mechanisms of inflammation should be uncovered.

TitreApplicationTitle: Unintentional Injuries: Influences on school-age children's risk taking and strategies for prevention
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD ATTRIBUTES; DETERMINANTS OF RISK TAKING; PEER INFLUENCES; RISK OF UNINTENTIONAL INJURY; SCHOOL-AGE CHILDREN; STRATEGIES TO REDUCE RISK TAKING
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, accidential injuries rank as the number one cause of death and a leading cause of disability for children beyond 1 year of age. This research will increase knowledge for understanding and preventing unintentional injuries in school-age children (7-12 years of age). Because many injuries in this age range occur when with peers and unsupervised by adults, the research explores how different types of peer communications influence children's risk taking decisions (i.e., engaging in behaviors that elevate risk of injury when there are alternative behaviors that do not do so), and if these influences vary with child attributes (i.e., age, sex, personality traits, immediate mood state). The findings will allow us to determine if personality attributes make certain children more susceptible to peer influence than others, particularly when in an aroused positive mood state.

TitreApplicationTitle: Signaling complexes between G protein coupled receptors and N-type calcium channels
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IMMUNOSTAINING; N-TYPE CALCIUM CHANNEL; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; SITE DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: Calcium plays a number of highly important roles in human physiology.  In the brain, calcium entering into nerve cells controls nerve to nerve communication and triggers a variety of intracellular signaling processes.  At the same time, too much calcium is toxic, and hence, the amount of calcium entering brain cells must be precisely controlled.  One key player in the regulation of calcium entry is a family of proteins termed "calcium channels".  Several different types of calcium channels have been identified in mammalian brain, each with a unique role in the function of the nervous system.  N-type calcium channels, the focus of this proposal, contribute to the release of neurotransmitters from nerve terminals, and they are critical for the transmission of pain signals at the spinal level.  As a result, inhibitors of these channels mediate analgesia.  In this application, we propose to investigate in detail how the function of these channels is controlled at the cellular and molecular level.  This will be accomplished through a combination of state of the art molecular and neurophysiological techniques.  We anticipate that our findings will help guide new therapeutic strategies towards treatment of pain and central nervous system disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of immune status is necessary for full recovery in Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID; CEREBROVASCULAR FUNCTION; IMMUNOLOGY; MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Amyloid disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia, are characterized by loss of CNS homeostasis and neurodegeneration leading to cognitive decline.  The common and central feature of these diseases is amyloid deposition, of which the major component is the amyloid beta peptide (Abeta).  To improve treatment of patients and thereby decrease the associated mortality and morbidity, we propose that only early and prolonged treatment with multiple therapeutic strategies will be effective.   One component of a multi-drug approach is to re-balance the immunological status of the CNS to promote homeostasis and decrease secondary injury.  Using an in vivo model, we will examine the physiological outcome of antagonizing inflammation within the brain to determine the extent of cognitive improvements. Our preliminary results suggest that both parenchymal and perivascular amyloid contribute to disease pathogenesis and only by addressing both will we improve the life of afflicted individuals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ethnic and sex differences in presentation of acute coronary syndromes and in accessing cardiac care
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO CARE; ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROMES; ETHNIC; MIXED METHODS; SEX; SYMPTOMS
Abstract-Résumé: People often recognize that pain or pressure in the middle of the chest may be heart symptoms. It is very important that people suffering from these symptoms recognize that they should seek medical attention quickly. People may have different or unusual (atypical) symptoms of these problems based on their ethnicity and/or sex. This can lead to them taking much longer to get the care they need, and may result in more damage being done to their hearts or them dying unnecessarily. We will interview 1827 men and women of different ethnic backgrounds (European--Caucasian; Chinese, and South Asian) who have been admitted to hospital in Toronto, Vancouver or Calgary with chest pain or heart attack. We will ask them questions about their symptoms (i.e., Where was your pain/discomfort?, What other symptoms did you have?, Was the chief or main symptom?). We will also ask them about the process of getting to the hospital (i.e., How long did you have symptoms before you went to the hospital?, Did you see a health care provider for these symptoms within 72 hours before going to hospital?, If so, who did you see?, Who brought you to the hospital?). We will also ask more 'open-ended' questions to determine how, why or the context in which their behaviours/decisions occurred. Interviews will be conducted in English, Cantonese, Mandarin, Punjabi, Tamil, Urdu, Hindi or Gujarati. Finally, once the person is discharged from hospital, we will look at their health record to collect information about their illness and treatments received while in hospital. We aim to compare this information between the ethnic groups (and between men and women within each ethnic group) to see if there are differences based on ethnicity and sex. If there are differences, we will describe them. This information will be helpful to men and women from each ethnic group when trying to make a decision about seeking health care and to health care providers when these people arrive at their offices or hospital.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal type-specific regulation of NMDA receptor signaling and toxicity
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL TRANSFECTION; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; PATCH CLAMP RECORDING; PRIMARY NEURONAL CULTURE; SELECTIVE NEURODEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: The objective of this proposal is to investigate mechanisms for regulating brain cell pathways that contribute to learning and memory ("plasticity"), and also brain damage during stroke or neurodegenerative disease. We will study rat brain tissue from cortex, hippocampus and striatum, which are regions involved in controlling movement and memory, and are also vulnerable to damage in stroke and age-related neurodegeneration.  Brain cells from hippocampus and cortex show differences from those of striatum, however, in their responses to stimulation that induces plasticity or death. We will directly study brain tissue, and also study isolated brain cells that are maintained in a dish for ~3 weeks. Neurons from the different brain regions will be compared in terms of composition and function of the NMDA-type glutamate receptor. This receptor normally mediates cell-cell communication and is critical for learning and memory; however, it becomes over-activated in some neurological diseases and triggers a series of events leading to cell death. We will study natural cellular mechanisms by which these NMDA receptors are regulated, by recording electrical activity and cell death mediated by these receptors, and how it is affected by manipulating activity of other cellular proteins closely linked to the receptors. Using this approach, we will contribute to a detailed understanding of how pathways involved in learning and memory, or cell death in neurological disease, can be regulated in different brain regions. Our results may lead to development of new drugs to diminish NMDA receptor activity in specific brain regions and neurologic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigations on the role of p21-activated kinase (PAK) in Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER; ANIMAL MODEL; DOCOSAHEXAENOIC ACID; INTEGRATIVE; PAK; TAU
Abstract-Résumé: ------------------------------------------------------------------------- 17% of Canadians have someone with Alzheimer disease (AD) in their immediate family. It is thus imperative to identify new drug targets to help the patients and their caregivers.   PAK (p21-activated kinase) is an enzyme in the brain. Defects in PAK have been associated with mental retardation. Our hypothesis is that PAK progressively becomes defective in AD as well. This hypothesis is first based on observations made in the brain of patients who died with AD. For example, we found that the more severe were the clinical symptoms of AD, the greater was the decrease of PAK. We then discovered that a decrease of PAK was also present in an animal model of AD. We are thus proposing here to investigate the role of PAK in this animal model using various strategies. Will inactivating PAK make the animals sicker? Conversely, will stimulating PAK be beneficial for the mice? For example, we will use omega-3 fatty acids as one of the strategy to boost PAK activity in the brain. If we succeed in confirming that PAK plays a key role in our AD model, we could then develop drugs that target PAK. In summary, we hope to decipher a molecular mechanism in the brain that could lead to the development of new treatments for AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Judgments and health innovation: How do upstream knowledge transfer and exchange among stakeholders contribute to the design of innovations
Keywords-MotsClés: DESIGN OF INNOVATIONS; HEALTH INNOVATION; KTE; QUALITATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this five-year research program is to examine, from a health care perspective, the ways in which knowledge, preferences and norms of designers, R and D funders, users, regulators and media shape the design of new health technologies. More specifically, we are interested in understanding the extent to which the strategic decisions made during the R and Dprocess address health care system challenges, such as access, equity and sustainability. The program builds on one Core Research Project, around which Satellite Studies will be developed throughout the five-year timeframe. The Core Project consists in examining the development of three award-winning innovations: a catheter-based cryotherapeutic treatment for cardiac diseases, a decision-support software for delivery monitoring and a home-based clinical monitoring system for patients with chronic diseases. We will do interviews with designers, interviews and focus groups with stakeholders (R and D funders, health care providers, patient representatives, journalists, etc.) and document analysis. By bridging two perspectives that rarely cross-fertilize each other --the industry and the health care system-- this research program will inform health innovation design and policy, research on knowledge transfer and qualitative research methods.

TitreApplicationTitle: A study of genetic and epigenetic factors influencing obesity-related metabolic complications.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSOCIATION STUDIES; CHANGES; GENETIC; METABOLIC COMPLICATIONS; OBESITY; TRANSCRIPTIONAL
Abstract-Résumé: According to a recent report form the World Health Organization (WHO), the prevalence of obesity is reaching epidemic proportions in both developed, and less developed countries around the world. Obesity places a substantial burden on the health of Canadians. The increased morbidity related to obesity may be largely accounted for by the presence of several risk factors that define the metabolic syndrome. However, a significant proportion of obese individuals remains healthy, while the risk profile of other obese subjects may vary from mild to severe. Our knowledge of the factors determining the severity of the metabolic syndrome or the conversion from a healthy state to cardiovascular diseases or diabetes remains largely incomplete, but there is strong evidence of the involvement of hereditary/molecular factors. Given its dramatic impact in our society, there is an urgent need to identify these molecular factors. Our goal is to gain further understanding of the genetic and epigenetic events that contribute to the metabolic syndrome in obese individuals. The knowledge of molecular factors involved has considerable public health implications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Acid tolerance mechanisms of Streptococcus mutans
Keywords-MotsClés: ACID TOLERANCE; BIOFILMS; CARIES; QUANTITATIVE REAL-TIME PCR; REPORTER GENES; STREPTOCOCCUS MUTANS
Abstract-Résumé: Streptococcus mutans is a bacterium that lives in dental plaque and is known to cause cavities. It is able to dissolve the tooth enamel by converting dietary sugars into acids.  By producing acids it also lowers the pH of the plaque environment causing a shift in the populations of the many normal bacteria that live in 'healthy' plaque. S. mutans has evolved specialized mechanisms that allow it to withstand an acidic environment, giving it an 'ecological edge' over these other bacteria.  One of the main features of S. mutans is its acid tolerance that gives it the ability to survive in acid that it and other bacteria produce from sugars. The aim of this project is to gain understanding of the genes and enzymes that the bacterium uses so that we may eventually block this process, hopefully stopping the ecological changes in dental plaque that lead to cavities. We have already identified a number of proteins involved in the process and now wish to examine the genes involved.  We have used DNA microarrays to help us determine which genes are activated when S. mutans senses a pH drop.  We are now examining the proteins that S. mutans uses to sense its environment hopefully to find the switches that turn on the genes. We are also examining a way of blocking protective metabolic activities that S. mutans uses to survive low pH. Ultimately our goal is to design a treatment that will prevent healthy plaque from becoming 'caries-causing' plaque.

TitreApplicationTitle: Compulsive reassurance seeking in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD): A new focus on an old symptom
Keywords-MotsClés: AMBIGUITY; OBSESSIVE COMPULSIVE DISORDER; PERCEIVED THREAT; REASSURANCE SEEKING; SCALE DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Repeated reassurance seeking (asking for information over and over again) is a hallmark feature of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) that has a significant impact upon those struggling with the problem as well as upon their friends, family members and loved ones. Although reassurance seeking has been studied in the context of low self-esteem and depression (e.g., "Do you really love me?"), it has not been investigated in the context of OCD (e.g., "Do you really think that my hands are clean?"). We propose to conduct a series of interconnected studies that will establish a measure of reassurance seeking in OCD and that will experimentally manipulate a variety of factors which are proposed to contribute to repeated reassurance seeking (e.g., perceived threat and ambiguity of feedback) in clinical and nonclinical participants. Results from these investigations will be communicated to scientific, community and clinical populations and we expect that our findings will help to refine and improve psychological treatments for this complicated type of OCD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interaction of Bcl-2 family apoptosis regulatory proteins with cellular membranes
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER; CHEMOTHERAPY RESISTANCE; FLUORESCENCE SPECTROSCOPY; PROTEIN OLIGOMERIZATION AND PORE FORMATION; PROTEIN-MEMBRANE INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Programmed cell death or apoptosis normally prevents cells that have lost growth control from going on to form tumours. During apoptosis, holes are formed in the membranes inside of cells, causing cells to die. Chemotherapy kills cancer cells by causing apoptosis, and certain gene products including the protein Bcl-2 inhibit this process; expression of Bcl-2 in cancer causes resistance to treatment. We have discovered that Bcl-2 prevents the formation of holes in membranes by changing its shape after it becomes attached to the membrane. In this new shape, Bcl-2 binds and inhibits other proteins that make the holes in the membrane. We will use new techniques in biophysics to study exactly how holes are formed and how Bcl-2 and other proteins control the formation of these holes inside cancer cells. Understanding how formation of holes in membranes is regulated will advance treatment options currently being explored with Bcl-2 inhibitors and is expected to open up new possibilities for cancer treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Lysine Methylome
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; METHYLATION; PEPTIDE FINGERPRINTING; PROTEOME-SCALE ANALYSIS; PROTEOMICS; SET DOMAIN PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Thousands of biochemical reactions take place simultaneously in each cell.  Among those, chemical alterations of proteins, the building block of any living organism, are of pivotal importance in eliciting a given biological response.  Correlatively, if these chemical reactions cannot take place properly, diseases such as cancer and Alzheimer arise.  Our laboratories seek to identify, locate and precise the role of a specific modification named lysine methylation, which is recognized as a key modification during many pathology's.  Our discoveries will 1) provide the biochemical bases underlying the role of lysine methylation in a biological process 2) further our understanding on the linkages between this chemical modification and various forms of cancer and 3) provide new and innovative therapeutic strategies to treat these diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: ASTHME; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Mediation of allergic airway inflammation and pathology by Oncostatin M
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRUS EXPRESSION VECTORS; CELL SIGNALING; ELIZA; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; GENE REGULATION; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INFLAMMATORY CYTOKINES; SIRNA; TAQMAN
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic inflammation such as that seen in asthma results in local events in lungs that compromise lung function. These include the accumulation of inflammatory cells such as eosinophils, and increases in tissue deposition (also termed matrix remodelling). Common allergens such as house mite and ragweed pollen, known to drive symptoms in allergy-induced asthma, can induce asthma-like inflammation in mouse models when introduced through the airway. The control of the inflammatory response involves numerous molecules, however we hypothesize that the hormone-like molecules called gp130 cytokines play a crucial role in the development of the lung pathology. We believe that one of these cytokines in particular, called Oncostatin M, is up-regulated in asthma and interacts with cells in synergistic fashion with other molecules important in immunity. We believe that this causes increased symptoms and pathology of the lungs. We will use approaches that examine responses in gene knockout mice and that examine in vitro responses of cells of the airway including human smooth muscle cells and lung fibroblasts. We predict that these studies will demonstrate the importance of gp130 cytokines in models of asthma, and thus point to new approaches in the study and treatment of human allergic asthmatic disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: SCLEROSE EN PLAQUES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging of multiple sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MAGNETIZATION TRANSFER; MR RELAXOMETRY; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a devastating condition and is the most common chronic neurological disease affecting young adults in Canada.  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has revolutionized the detection of MS in the brain and spinal cord and is now an essential tool in the diagnosis and monitoring of the disease.  However, as it is routinely used, MRI is very sensitive to MS disease detection in the white matter of the brain but is not good at differentiating between different characteristics of MS lesions such as inflammation versus destruction of myelin, an important component of brain tissue.  Conventional MRI is also not very sensitive to MS disease in the grey matter of the brain.  In this application we propose to develop a new MRI technique that will enable whole brain quantitative assessment of tissue destruction.  After verifying the performance of this technique using postmortem MS brains we will use it to study the pattern of white matter and grey matter damage in MS patients.  Specifically, we wish to determine if damage to the grey matter is the result of prior damage to the white matter or is independent.  We will also study the relationship between the location of brain tissue damage and specific aspects of the patients' disability.  This project will provide new tools for comprehensive and quantitative assessment of tissue damage in MS patients and will reveal new information on the natural evolution of the disease.  This research will also enable the evaluation of badly needed new therapies that attempt to slow or stop the progression of this disease.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - C: Behavioural Studies, Neuroscience and Cognition
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional and structural correlations in prosopagnosia
Keywords-MotsClés: FACE RECOGNITION; FUNCTIONAL MRI; PROSOPAGNOSIA
Abstract-Résumé: Prosopagnosia is a family of disorders in which patients lose the ability to recognize faces after some form of brain damage, such as a stroke, infection or tumour. Face recognition is a complex process involving a number of perceptual and memory functions. Likewise, the lesions that cause prosopagnosia can vary a lot, in whether the temporal lobe or occipital lobe is affected, and if the damage is in the right and/or the left side. Although it is a rare disorder, understanding the mechanisms of prosopagnosia can provide us with great insight into how the brain creates meaningful visual experiences. This is an international collaboration that brings in subjects from around the world for state-of-the-art functional and structural imaging to carefully characterize their lesions, and a thorough battery of neuropsychological and experimental tests aimed at answering key theoretical questions about what aspects of face and object processing are impaired or spared, and thus how this is related to the anatomic damage.

ResearchClassEN: MULTIPLE DISEASE RELEVANCE; MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL DISEASES
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Gonadal hormone effects on adult hippocampal neurogenesis in the male and female rodent
Keywords-MotsClés: DENTATE GYRUS; ESTRADIOL; HIPPOCAMPAL NEUROGENESIS; HORMONES; LEARNING AND MEMORY; TESTOSTERONE
Abstract-Résumé: The hippocampus is a brain region that has continual neuronal birth throughout life, in all mammalian species studied to date, including the human. Women are more likely to suffer from Alzheimer's disease and depression than males, which may be linked to the levels of hormones in men and women.  Estrogen, a mainly female hormone, enhances the production but potentially suppresses the survival of these new brain cells in the hippocampus of adult female, but not male, rodents.  Testosterone, a mainly male hormone, enhances the survival of new brain cells in the hippocampus of male rodents, but it is not known how it affects female rodents. The proposed experiments are designed to investigate the effects of estrogen and testosterone on neuronal birth and survival in the hippocampus of adult male and female rodents.  The objectives are: to determine the effects of repeated exposure to estradiol and testosterone on neuronal birth and survival; to determine the mechanisms of how estradiol and testosterone augment neuronal birth (how these hormones actually work to exert their effects on new cell growth in the brain); and finally to determine whether changes in new neuron survival by estrogen or testosterone affect learning and memory.  We expect that estradiol will suppress new neuron survival by influencing their specific receptors.  These findings will help determine how new neurons are produced in the adult brain and provide clues as to how estrogens and androgens exert their protective effects in patients with depression or Alzheimer's disease.  The results of these experiments will elucidate the gender-specific mechanisms controlling the hormone-induced changes in neuronal birth which may ultimately lead to ways of inducing new brain cell growth to repair or replace lost cells in the gender-related diseases that have neuron loss.

TitreApplicationTitle: Use of indicator acid oxidation to determine amino acid requirement
Keywords-MotsClés: AMINO ACID REQUIREMENTS; CHILDREN; ELDERLY; PREGNANCY; STABLE ISOTOPES
Abstract-Résumé: The diet supplies both protein and calories.  The living parts of our bodies (such as the brain, muscles, heart, kidneys) are all made of protein.  Proteins are big molecules which are made up of 20 buiding blocks, which are called amino acids.  Nine of these cannot be made in the body, so must be provided in the diet; hence these 9 are known as essential amino acids.  We have very poor information on requirements for these essential amino acids throughout life, except in young adults, due to a lack of suitable methods.  Over the past 5 years our group has developed a novel method to determine essential amino acid requirements in childern and have shown it to work and to be practical.  Over the next five years we plan to use this method to determine amino acid and protein requirements in women who are pregnant and in elderly women and men

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of neuronal polarity formation
Keywords-MotsClés: AXONAL OUTGROWTH; AXONAL SPECIFICATION; CELL CULTURE; CELL POLARITY; MOUSE GENETICS; NEURONAL DIFFERENTIATION
Abstract-Résumé: The ability of cells to polarize is critical for complex biological activities, such as the organization of a fully functional nervous system. The functional units of the nervous system, the neurons, are an exquisite example of highly differentiated and polarized cell types; typically extending a long thin process called axon, which is engineered to propagate signals, and several shorter and thicker processes called dendrites, which are designed to receive signal inputs. The asymmetric localization of proteins within the axons and dendrites is crucial for a neuron to develop its fully functional architecture, but how the axonal and dendritic compartments are specified remains unclear. The major question that we are going to address in this project is how is the characteristic morphology of neurons acquired? Specifically, we will focus on the function of a recently identified gene, called Inscuteable (Insc), on the process of axonal specification. Recent studies, mostly conducted in invertebrates, have shown that Insc is part of an important polarity complex that regulate cellular function in various cell types, but its role in neuronal cells remain unknown. Here, we propose to use a combination of mouse genetic and cell biology approaches both in vitro and in vivo to determine the function of Insc in mouse neurons. We will test the hypothesis that Insc is involved in the specification of axons and dendrites in neurons, and that disruption of Insc activity leads to the formation of abnormal neurons. Based on mouse and human genome sequence data, no other gene was duplicated from the invertebrate Insc ancestor, suggesting that loss of Insc will lead to potent defects when inactivated in mouse, or when mutated in humans. Our work should help identify key developmental defects caused by Insc loss of funtion, which could lead to identification of similar conditions in humans with Insc mutations.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ; RECHERCHE SUR LES MÉDICAMENTS
TitreApplicationTitle: Efficacy and safety of methylxanthines in very low birthweight infants
Keywords-MotsClés: APNEA OF PREMATURITY; DRUG SAFETY; METHYLXANTHINES (CAFFEINE); RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; SCHOOL-AGE FUNCTION; VERY LOW BIRTH WEIGHT INFANTS
Abstract-Résumé: At least 5 of every 1000 live-born babies are very preterm and weigh only 500 to 1250 grams at birth. Approximately 50% of the surviving children have serious school difficulties and require special educational assistance. The aim of this research is to reduce this heavy burden of illness. A multi-centre controlled trial is underway in which over 2000 very low birth weight infants have been enrolled. Our goal for this application is to determine if caffeine therapy for apnea of prematurity affects educational and motor skills and increases behavior problems at middle school age. Caffeine is one of the most commonly used drugs in preterm infants. Caffeine is prescribed to treat periodic breathing and breath-holding spells, but evidence for long-term drug efficacy and safety has been lacking. Laboratory research suggests that caffeine may have toxic effects on the immature brain. This large and long-term trial has been designed to clarify whether caffeine therapy is safe in very preterm infants.

TitreApplicationTitle: C-Reactive Protein: a Link between Inflammation and Acute Coronary Artery Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROMES; C-REACTIVE PROTEIN; CELL AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY TECHNIQUES; ENDOTHELIAL CELL BIOLOGY; LEUKOCYTE ACTIVATION AND APOPTOSIS; VASCULAR INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Evidence accumulated over the past decade supports a fundamental role for ongoing inflammation in mediating all stages of atherosclerosis ("hardening" of the blood vessels) from initiation through progression to the culmination in acute coronary heart disease (angina and heart attack). The search for clinical biomarkers that reflect low levels of inflammation and are useful in predicting risk for acute coronary artery disease (CAD) and cardiac death led to identification of C-reactive protein (CRP). Clinical and laboratory evidence indicates that CRP is not only a marker, but rather an active part-taker of inflammation that contributes to CAD. Recent research, including ours, revealed the existence of distinct forms of CRP, called native CRP, which is present in the blood, and modified CRP (mCRP), which is present in tissues. This latter protein possesses potent pro-inflammatory actions.  We propose to examine how mCRP is formed by activated platelets and white blood cells and to investigate how mCRP affects interactions between platelets, white blood cells and endothelial cells (the cells lining the blood vessels inside), events that trigger heart attack. We will explore the contribution of mCRP to destabilization of atherosclerotic plaques and examine whether anti-inflammatory lipids that are formed inside the body following administration of aspirin can reverse the deleterious actions of mCRP. We will study these events using isolated human cells, mouse models, pharmacological, immunological and molecular biological techniques. We believe that identifying the process that lead to formation of mCRP as well as better understanding how this molecule influences inflammation will likely identify novel therapeutic targets, including mCRP itself or the process of its formation, for reducing inflammation localized to the coronary arteries and for the prevention and/or treatment of acute CAD.

ResearchClassEN: CANCER THERAPY GENERAL; DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES
TitreApplicationTitle: P-glycoprotein Drug Pump: How Does it Work and How Can it be Turned Off?
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG RESCUE; DRUG TRANSPORT; MEMBRANE PROTEIN; MULTIDRUG RESISTANCE; P-GLYCOPROTEIN; PROTEIN FOLDING
Abstract-Résumé: The P-glycoprotein drug pump is a critical defense mechanism because it is found at high levels in the lining of the intestine,in the kidney and liver, and at the blood-brain barrier where it functions to block entry or extrude toxins found in food or the environment from entering our body or brain. If you eat a food that contains a toxin (many plants produce toxins to protect themselves from being eaten), then P-glycoprotein in the intestine will prevent these toxins from being absorbed. If toxins do enter your bloodstream then P-glycoprotein expressed in the liver or kidney will extract these chemicals from the bloodstream so that they will be eliminated in the urine (kidney) or bile (liver).P-glycoprotein can cause problems in treatments for diseases such as cancer or brain diseases however, because it prevents therapeutic drugs from entering cancer cells or getting into the brain.  The long-term goals of Dr. David Clarke's laboratory are to determine how P-glycoprotein is able to pump so many different kinds of drugs and to find out ways to turn it off during treatment of diseases. The ability to turn off this drug pump would improve the effectiveness of cancer chemotherapy, treatments for brain disorders as well as treatments for other diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: How is the epigenetic landscape re-established after DNA synthesis?
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETIC LANDSCAPE; HISTONE POST TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATION; NUCLEAR SORTING; POLYCOMB GROUP; REPLICATION FORK; TRITHORAX GROUP
Abstract-Résumé: DNA is packaged by many different kinds of proteins. The proteins establish a local environment that allows genes to be active, or keeps genes off.  The problem is that DNA synthesis removes most or all of the proteins that establish the correct environment, so these proteins have to be re-assembled on newly synthesized DNA. We don't have any idea which steps occur early and which steps occur later during this re-establishment. We will use fruit flies as a model system to address this question.  Errors in this process lead to developmental defects,cancer, and are important for the normal function of stem cells.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Physiological factors that determine quantity of in vivo synthesis of palmitate, palmitoleate, stearate and oleate in humans
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE RISK; DE NOVO LIPOGENESIS; FAT METABOLISM; HUMAN RESEARCH; STABLE ISOTOPES; SUBSTRATE UTILIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Health Canada's current recommendations for healthy eating suggest that Canadians reduce total fat and saturated fat in their diets. Reducing fat in the diet results in increased carbohydrate intake, and this can lead to undesirable changes in fat metabolism in some people. Reducing fat and increasing carbohydrate consumption can result in the body making more fat. More importantly, it is mostly saturated fat, potentially increasing the amount of saturated fat to which the body is exposed. High amounts of saturated fatty acids may increase the risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes and heart disease, particularly when these fats are present in the bloodstream or in the liver where there is the greatest influence. In this research, we will test to see which physiological factors result in the least amount of saturated fat production and transport. This is done by utilizing a recent technology that follows fat processing in the body with isotope tracers. This tracer can be ingested just like water, and a few hours later we are able calculate how much fat was made from the carbohydrate in food. For example, does a Western-style diet that is already high in fat prevent fat synthesis? Does reducing fat consumption result in increases in the saturated fats produced by the body, thereby adding saturated fat indirectly? Is a high fat Mediterranean-style diet best for reducing both saturated fat intake and production by the body? Hence, if low fat diets increase saturated fat, then perhaps this is not the best diet strategy for some people. This research will identify individuals who may be able to decrease dietary fat intake with no rebound increase in saturated fat in their bodies, and which people should adopt other dietary changes such as replacing saturated fat in their diet with monounsaturated fat, as in the Mediterranean-style of eating.

TitreApplicationTitle: Homeostatic regulation of CD4 T cells during lymphopenia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTING CELLS; CD4+; HOMEOSTATIC EXPANSION; IL-7; LYMPHOPENIA
Abstract-Résumé: White blood cells known as T lymphocytes, or T cells, are essential components of the immune system. They can be divided into two major groups: CD4+ T cells, which act as helper cells, directing the activity of other immune cells, and CD8+ T cells, which kill infected cells and tumor cells. The function of the thymus, the organ where T cells differentiate in order to perform specific functions, declines with age. When T cells become depleted in adults, they can undergo spontaneous, or homeostatic, proliferation in an attempt to restore their numbers. Although homeostatic proliferation efficiently regenerates CD8+ T cells, it is much less efficient in regenerating CD4+ T cells. For example, after high dose chemotherapy or stem cell transplantation, patients recover essentially each type of white blood cells within six to eight months except for CD4+ T cells that remain below normal levels for several years. As a result, lymphopenic patients are vulnerable to common and opportunistic infections, tumor recurrence and second malignant neoplasms. Dendritic cells are a specialized type of white blood cells that are important for naive CD4+ T cell maintenance. We recently identified a regulatory circuit interfering with the capacity of dendritic cells to support naive CD4+ proliferation. This grant will provide critical information about how lymphopenia (low T lymphocyte counts) affects dendritic cells and prevents CD4 regeneration. Furthermore, we will investigate how disruption of this regulatory circuit translates into safe and rapid CD4 regeneration. Finally, we will also investigate the recovery of other cell subsets (CD4+CD25+ T cells) important for the regulation of the immune system during lymphopenia.

NomDuComitéFR: Déterminants psychosociaux, socioculturels et comportementaux de la santé

TitreApplicationTitle: Insomnia Following Myocardial Infarction: A Prospective Study to Determine Prevalence, Contributors and Consequences
Keywords-MotsClés: INSOMNIA; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; PREVALENCE; PROSPECTIVE; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Insomnia is characterized by difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, waking up to early and/or waking up unrefreshed. Certain medical conditions (i.e. arthritis, cancer) appear to increase the risk of sleep disruptions, which in turn may worsen the condition, causing further complications (i.e. depression) and adding to the disability associated with the chronic condition. Yet insomnia remains underrecognized, underdiagnosed and undertreated among the chronically ill, including patients with coronary heart disease (CHD). The few studies available suggest that between 42-44% of patients with CHD experience insomnia symptoms, with problems persisting up to one-year following a cardiac event. Untreated insomnia can negatively impact prognosis and further deteriorate functioning, well-being and quality of life in this patient population.  Insomnia has received limited research attention in terms of identifying its prevalence, chronicity and impact on health-related quality of life in patients who have had a heart attack. This study will survey 376 patients 4 weeks following a heart attack and track the occurrence and maintenance of insomnia over the course one year. We will measure a number of variables (i.e. sociodemographic, medical, lifestyle and psychosocial) in order to identify factors associated with insomnia following in patients who have had a heart attack. This study will provide a better understanding of the factors which contribute to disrupted sleep in patients who have suffered a heart attack and will help health care professionals to better identify and manage insomnia in this patient population and ultimately improve quality of life.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Systems biology approach to elucidating the role of TAL1/SCL in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION DEEP SEQUENCING (CHIP-SEQ); GENE EXPRESSION; ICAT QUANTITATIVE PROTEOMICS; KNOCKDOWN BY RNA INTERFERENCE; SCL; T-CELL ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA; TAL1; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive cancer occurring in children and adults wherein cells belonging to the immune system acquire a defect in their normal regulatory circuitry and grow in an uncontrolled manner. In many instances, T-ALL is caused when the TAL1 protein (which is normally present in red blood cells) is aberrantly produced in white blood cells.  This disrupts the growth control mechanism of specific cells of the immune system.  To understand how this mis-expression of TAL1 in white blood cells leads to leukemia, we have recently identified the genes that are deregulated in diseased cells. In this new application, we will further these studies to examine how TAL1 interacts with specific proteins present in white blood cells, leading to deregulation of these genes. Our novel approach could lead to new therapy for treating children and adults affected with this deadly disease.
