NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
ResearchClassEN: STROKE, HEART FAILURE; PSYCHO-SOCIAL AND BEHAVIOURAL RESEARCH
ClasseRechercheFR: APOPLEXIE, INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE; RECHERCHES PSYCHOSOCIALES ET COMPORTEMENTALES
TitreApplicationTitle: New Directions in Stroke Prevention and Rehabilitation
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL NEUROSCIENCE; MOTOR SYSTEM; RECOVERY OF FUNCTION; SKILLED MOVEMENT; STRESS AND GLUCOCORTICOIDS; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the primary cause of long-term disability in Western societies. A common consequence of stroke is loss of motor control to some degree. Although some treatment options are available, most treatments do not fully restore motor function. Therefore, it is important to not only develop better therapies for stroke, but to also learn about prediction of stroke risk to prevent an infarct. Early experience might represent a key to stroke prevention. For example, recent research suggested that maternal stress during pregnancy leads to disease later in life, including high blood pressure, diabetes and glucose intolerance. These factors are known to elevate the risk of cardiovascular disease and stroke.    The aim of the proposed research is twofold: to explore new avenues to recognize individuals at risk of having a stroke, and to improve current treatment strategies once a stroke has occurred. The proposed research will investigate if stress during pregnancy predisposes the offspring to enhanced stroke risk. Furthermore, the research will explore if aging and stress affect stroke risk and recovery. The proposed research will also use a new rat model of "silent stroke" to determine the consequences of repeated stroke on recovery and if life style changes can promote recovery. It will also be tested if life style changes, such as an enriched environment, can help prevent recurrent stroke in young and old animals. This research will lead to new insights into the influence of experience and life style on stroke risk, and how experience and life style can be used as a therapy to enhance recovery after stroke. This will result in new recommendations for a healthier life style. The results might also offer new information how to predict and prevent stroke. The unique focus on recurrent and silent stroke, on stress and aging will address a vital issue for Canada's aging population.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - A: Reproduction, Maternal, Child and Youth Health
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Gene-environment interactions underlying the developmental origins of health and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL ORIGINS OF HEALTH AND DISEASE; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; HYPOTHALAMIC-PITUITARY-ADRENAL AXIS; METABOLIC SYNDROME; PREGNANCY COMPLICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Recent studies have clearly established a relationship between sub-optimal intrauterine and post-natal development, and later life predisposition to adult disease, including type II diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, stroke and other neurologic disorders - a relationship termed "developmental origins of health and disease" (DOHaD). While adverse pre- and post-natal development increased the risk of DOHaD, it does not determine that an individual will acquire these disorders suggesting that interactions between an individual's genotype and the environment may contribute to the eventual outcome. Increasing evidence suggests that premature activation of the fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adreal (HPA) axis is a central component linking adverse pre and/or post-natal environmental exposures to later poor health outcomes. We propose to integrate population genetics approach to investigate gene-environment interactions underlying DOHaD. Identification at birth of genetic signatures that enhance risk of diabetes, coronary heart disease or stroke will provide opportunities to develop lifestyle or medical intervention strategies aimed at preventing these adverse outcomes. The potential to impact on the global disease burden is immense.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - C: Behavioural Studies, Neuroscience and Cognition
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
TitreApplicationTitle: Investigations of the cause and treatment of deprivation-induced vision impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; NEUROANATOMY; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; VISION DEPRIVATION; VISION IMPAIRMENT; VISION RECOVERY
Abstract-Résumé: Interference with normal vision early in life, as with congenital cataracts or strabismus (turned eye), can promote aberrant development of neural circuitry that leads to permanent vision impairments - notably amblyopia. For decades, selected visual deprivation has been used to study the role of early sensory experience on brain organization, function, and development. Depriving normal visual input during a formative period early in life provokes conspicuous changes in the structure and function of neurons and their connections, all of which are believed to underlie a consequent and pronounced impairment to visual perception. Experiments in this proposal are designed to investigate the neural changes that lead to amblyopia and that accompany recovery.  We have three specific aims: (1) to understand the intracellular processes that enable neurons to change structure in the context of amblyogenic rearing; (2) to develop a novel treatment for amblyopia designed to promote recovery beyond what is typically achieved by conventional approaches; (3) to directly measure and characterize the functional and structural neural recovery brought about by novel and conventional treatment procedures. The more general objective of these investigations is to clarify the origin and etiology of deprivation-related vision impairments. This insight is expected to enable a more focused approach to treatment and recovery that will have direct health implications for conditions that disrupt sensory input and preclude normal brain development.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional roles of glycogen synthase kinase-3 in cellular regulation and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CATENIN; COLON CANCER; DEVELOPMENT; LYMPHOMA; PROTEIN KINASE; STEM CELL
Abstract-Résumé: We have been studying a pair of proteins that have an unusual function as gate-keepers in tissues by providing a throttle to signals that normally promote growth and adoption of particular cell fates. The growth inhibitory effects of these proteins is cleverly bipassed in a large number of human cancers. We have created strains of mice and engineered cells in which we can turn off these proteins  in specific  tissues and cell types (such as liver, brain and immune cells). When switched off in the liver and immune cells, all of the animals succumb to liver overgrowth and lymphoma, respectively. This proposal aims to understand the roles of these proteins in cancer, how inhibition of these proteins promotes tumorigenesis and whether turning them back on again can block tumour growth, once it has occurred.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting Carbonic Anhydrase IX and Hypoxia for the diagnosis and treatment of aggresive breast cancers
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODIES; BREAST CANCER; CAIX; HYPOXIA; METASTASIS; PET IMAGING; SMALL MOLECULE INHIBITORS
Abstract-Résumé: Mortality from breast cancer is primarily due to the formation of distant metastases. However, the molecular properties of primary breast tumors that dictate metastattic potential are poorly understood. Such knowledge would identify patients with high risk for systemic disease and would allow for the development of specific therapeutic strategies with significant potential for decreasing mortality. We have recently demonstrated that primary breast tumors with high metastatic potential express genes induced by hypoxia. One of these genes codes for a protein called carbonic Anhydrase IX ( CAIX), which we have now shown to be vital for the survival of metastatic breast tumor cells. Genetic ablation of this protein in a mouse model of breast cancer results in dramatic regression of breast tumors and complete inhibition of distant metastasis. Most significantly, ananlysis of 4,000 human breast cancer samples demonstrates that patients with tumors that express high levels of CAIX protein, have a poor survival outcome and high potential of distant metastases. In this aplication we wish to extend this exciting findings and propose to: 1) validate the vital role of CAIX in breast cancer metastasis by examining additional breast cancer models and perform detailed structure-function analysis of CAIX protein to understand its role in protecting hypoxic tumor cells; 2) develop novel imaging reagents as diagnostic an prognostic tools for identifying and following therapeutic response of agressive breast cancers; and 3) develop novel antibody and small molecule compounds that inhibit CAIX function for use as cancer therapeutics therapeutics.  Our studies should result in the ability to identify breast cancer patients with high risk of metastasis, and in the development of novel prognostic and therapeutic reagents for aggresive breast cancers

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
ClasseRechercheFR: TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The effects of cellular senescence on tissue regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BONE MARROW; MICROENVIRONMENT; PLASTICITY; SENESCENCE; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Tissue regeneration and repair is delayed as we get older. One possibility is that as we age, our tissues accumulate tired (or senescent) cells that either no longer divide or prevent healthy ones from dividing. Adult stem and progenitor cells are responsible for the repair of tissues, mainly due to their capacity to divide and differentiate in several cell type (i.e. skin, bone, muscle). We have observed that the environment in which stem cell reside has a large influence on the number of time a given stem/progenitor cell will divide and perhaps more importantly in which cell type it will differentiate. Purification and injection of cells supporting stem cells (i.e. supporting fibroblasts) helps even further wounded tissues to repair (i.e. wounded skin). Our hypothesis is that accumulation of senescent cells in the microenvironment of stem cells prevents adequate regeneration of tissues. This hypothesis is supported by results we obtained showing that senescent cells are deficient in the activation of certain responses required for tissue repair following an injury. Also, in comparison to normal cells, senescent cells secrete molecules that may influence stem cell response. In conclusion, our objective is to identify how the accumulation of senescent cells possibly impairs tissue regeneration. The goal will be to either eliminate senescent cells or to complement their deficiencies in order to improve age-associated diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic determinants of eating behaviors, dietary intake and obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSOCIATION STUDIES; EATING BEHAVIOR; GENETICS; LINKAGE STUDIES; NUTRITION; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Overweight and obesity result from an imbalance between energy intake and energy expenditure. Although it is established that obesity is influenced by genetic factors, little is known about the role of genes in determining eating behaviors and dietary intake and the role of these genes in determining the genetic susceptibility to obesity. The objective of this research is to investigate how genetic factors influence the relationships between eating behaviors, dietary intake and obesity related traits and identify new genes that could influence these traits. This research will be conducted on 951 adult men and women from 223 French Canadian families in which habitual food intake and several obesity-related traits have been measured. Finding genes influencing traits related to eating behaviors will contribute to increase our understanding of the biological relationships between eating behaviors, dietary intake and obesity, which will eventually improve our capacity to better prevent and treat obesity.

NomDuComitéFR: Soins palliatifs et soins de fin de vie
ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; MUSCLES ET OS
TitreApplicationTitle: Function of USP19 deubiquitinating enzyme in muscle wasting
Keywords-MotsClés: CACHEXIA; CANCER; DEUBIQUITINATING ENZYMES; MUSCLE ATROPHY; MYOSIN HEAVY CHAIN; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Cachexia is a major complication of cancer that causes significant morbidity and loss of quality of life. A major feature of cachexia is muscle wasting which causes weakness. We are exploring the biochemical pathways in muscle that lead to loss of muscle proteins and wasting.  We have identified a gene, USP19, in the ubiquitin pathway which is the major pathway of protein breakdown in cells.  USP19 is activated in rats in skeletal muscle wasting from cancer.  We have recently observed that mice lacking USP19 lose less muscle mass in conditions of muscle wasting.  Furthermore, lowering USP19 levels in muscle cells results in accumulation of the major contractile proteins in muscle.  Thus, we propose in this application to further define how USP19 exerts these effects on skeletal muscle, identify mechanisms for inhibiting it and explore its role in patients with cancers that predispose them to cachexia.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Cytoprotective role of nuclear factor kappa beta in heart
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRUS MEDIATED GENE TRANSFER; ADULT VENTRIUCLAR MYOCYTES; APOPTOSIS; CELL CULTURE; GROWTH FACTORS; HEART FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the substantial progress that has been made during the past two decades in heart research, cardiac disease still represents a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in North America. When oxygen delivery to the heart muscle is decreased such as seen during heart attack or myocardial infarction, the cells of the heart begin to die by a genetically regulated process known as Apoptosis. This is a major clinical problem since once injured cardiac cells die they are not replaced by new ones. Consequently, the loss of heart cells through an apoptotic process decreases the heart's ability to pump blood which ultimately manifest as heart failure. Heart failure represents a major financial and socio-economic burden to Canada, since individuals with heart failure require costly long-term care. Understanding the signaling pathways and cellular factors that regulate cell death/survival processes in the heart would be of substantial importance toward developing new therapeutic agents that could prevent excess cardiac cell death and heart failure. The proposed studies will specifically address this issue by testing the postulated role of the cellular factor Nuclear factor -kB (NF-kB) as a survival factor in the heart. This innovative research will provide new important information regarding the molecular mechanisms that regulate cardiac cell survival during disease conditions. The long-term therapeutic objective of this research is directed toward improving the quality of life of patients with heart disease by developing novel agents that would reduce apoptosis during heart attack. The spin-off benefit to this research would be realized by a substantial reduction in costly medications and need for long-term patient care. It can be seen that this research will have a major and positive impact on society and Canada's health care system in particular.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
AreasOfScienceEN: MUSCLE, BONE, OR JOINT; CELL BIOLOGY
DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Ion transport and signaling in skeletal cells: P2 nucleotide receptor function in bone
Keywords-MotsClés: LIVE-CELL IMAGING; OSTEOBLAST; OSTEOCLAST; P2 NUCLEOTIDE RECEPTORS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Our research focuses on ion transport and signaling in skeletal cells. Osteoblasts are the cells that form bone and osteoclasts are the cells that remove bone. In this application, we propose to examine the mechanisms involved in the actions of a cell surface receptor that binds extracellular nucleotides. Nucleotides are small molecules that serve a number of biochemical functions within the cell, but mediate cell-cell signaling when released into the extracellular environment. We will examine the ways in which extracellular nucleotides act through P2X7 nucleotide receptors to regulate the activity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts. Relatively frequent genetic differences among individuals lead to differences in the function of this receptor. There is growing evidence that these differences affect bone density, predisposing these individuals to diseases such as osteoporosis. We will use genetically modified mice to examine whether this receptor also plays a role in fracture healing and the response of bone to mechanical stimuli such as whole-body vibration. Receptors and ion channels are among the most common targets for pharmacological agents. Therefore, these studies may identify new targets for the development of drugs to prevent the loss of bone and to promote the formation of new bone in metabolic diseases such as osteoporosis, and in inflammatory diseases such as periodontitis (gum disease) and rheumatoid arthritis.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE; APPAREIL DIGESTIF ET FOIE
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES DU FOIE; METABOLISME ET NUTRITION
TitreApplicationTitle: Keratins 8/18 in the liver: cell death, metabolism and disease association
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL CULTURE; CIRRHOSIS; FAS; GENE TRANSFER; GLUCOSE; HEPATOCANCEROGENESIS; INSULIN; KERATINS; LIVE CELL IMAGING; NECROSIS; PANCREATITIS; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; SIRNA; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Keratins constitute a family of cytoskeletal proteins present in epithelial cells of both keratinizing (e.g. skin) and non-keratinizing (e.g. liver) tissues. Monoclonal antibody technology has established them as reliable markers of epithelial cells when they emerge from stem cells. However, their role(s), particularly in internal organs like liver, remains unclear. The data accumulated largely by us in recent years suggest that keratins play a pivotal role in the liver cell responses to death-receptor and insulin-receptor stimulation and to oxidative stress. This research proposal uses mice lacking keratins in their liver as a model system to investigate how keratins regulate these cellular activities.  The experimental strategies are based on use of complementary molecular biology, biochemistry and high-resolution microscopy tools. The proposed research will shed new light on the involvement of keratins in liver disease development, for instance when mutations in human keratin genes result to liver cirrhosis.

ResearchClassEN: BREAST CANCER THERAPY; BONE CANCER THERAPY
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN; THERAPIE DES CANCERS OSSEUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Co-targeting parathyroid-hormone related protein (PTHrP) signaling and osteoclast activation to counter breast cancer metastasis to bone
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE METASTASES; BREAST CANCER; CO-TARGETED THERAPY; NEUTRALISING ANTIBODY; PTHRP
Abstract-Résumé: Bone metastases are catastrophic consequences of breast cancer progression and are present in up to 70% of patients who die from breast cancer. Skeletal metastases cause considerable suffering due to high serum calcium, pathological fractures and intractable pain, and once metastases invade bone, they are usually fatal. Breast cancer easily spreads to the skeleton; tumor cells first escape the primary site in the breast, then migrate through the bloodstream and reach the bone marrow. There, they stimulate bone-destroying cells (osteoclasts) to create niches in the bone where the cancer cells can multiply and start the skeletal invasion. Breast cancer cells are known to overproduce a biochemical factor called parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) which stimulates the bone-resorption activity of osteoclasts, allowing the creation of a favorable environment for cancer invasion. PTHrP also promotes growth of the invading tumor cells, and is suspected of controlling the spread from the primary site to the metastasis area. Bone metastases are currently treated with bisphosphonates, a family of drugs that impair osteoclasts' bone-destroying capacity. Bisphosphonates are not a cure, however, and reduce bone complications in only 20% of patients. Importantly, bisphosphonates specifically target osteoclast activity, and do not address other aspects of bone metastasis such as tumor cell growth and spread from the primary site. Our recent results suggest that PTHrP may play a crucial role in these other aspects of skeletal metastasis. In order to improve the efficacy of the current therapy, this application proposes to examine the possibility of countering breast cancer metastatic spread through PTHrP inhibition in combination with bisphosphonate treatment. We will use a neutralizing anti-PTHrP antibody developed in our laboratory with the goal to create an enhanced therapy addressing additional aspects of metastatic spread to the skeleton.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
ClasseRechercheFR: VIEILLISSEMENT; MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: FMRI studies of age related differences in brain networks and brain variability
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DEFAULT MODE NETWORK; FUNCTIONAL MRI; MEMORY; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Our brains change as we age and recent research has identified a number of ways in which older brains differ from younger ones.  Some brain networks are less active in older adults while others are more active.  We also have found that brain activity in older adults is surprisingly less variable than that seen in younger adults.  Both activity in these brain networks and how variable they are may be fundamental aspects of aging that we need to understand.  The projects in this proposal will address these important issues.

ResearchClassEN: DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS; CANCER THERAPY GENERAL
ClasseRechercheFR: DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Image-Guided Design of an Actively Targeted Liposomal Drug Formulation for Treatment of Lung Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVE TARGETING; CISPLATIN; CT IMAGING; DRUG DELIVERY; LIPOSOMES; LUNG CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer-related death worldwide and results in 1.3 million deaths each year. Currently, platinum-based chemotherapy, in particular cisplatin, plays a major role in the management and treatment of lung cancers.  However, conventional cisplatin therapy is associated with inadequate delivery of drug to tumours, major dose limiting toxicities and development of multi-drug resistance.  These obstacles may be addressed by the development of actively targeted therapies that are effectively transported to tumors while minimizing accumulation in healthy tissues. The overall goal of this research is to use nanotechnology to provide targeted delivery of the chemotherapeutic agent, cisplatin, to lung cancer tumor cells. Advanced image-based methods will be used to inform on the pathway and fate of the targeted nanoparticles in animal models in order to design the optimal targeted nanoparticle formulation of cisplatin. This research should lead to the development of a superior formulation of cisplatin that results in major improvements in tumor control and long-term survival for lung cancer patients.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - C: Digestive, Endocrine and Excretory Systems
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - C : Systèmes digestif, endocrinien et excrétoire

TitreApplicationTitle: Preventing chronic kidney disease by avoiding acute, transient elevations in serum creatinine
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; CABG SURGERY; CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS PUMP; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; SERUM CREATININE
Abstract-Résumé: When individuals suddenly lose their kidney function, it is known as acute kidney injury (AKI). This frequently occurs in patients who are ill and having major surgery. AKI is identified when there is a temporary rise in serum creatinine levels. Since serum creatinine levels often return to normal values, it has been believed that AKI has no long-lasting effects. Recently, there have been an increasing number of reports suggesting that people who have had AKI demonstrated permanent kidney dysfunction years later. This proposal will determine whether preventing these temporary slowings of kidney function while someone has surgery will prevent long term kidney dysfunction. We are in a unique position to do this by testing the benefits of cardiac surgery established by an existing study known as CORONARY.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanical Properties Of Human Airway Smooth Muscle In Vitro And In Vivo: Normal Structure And Function And Abnormalities In Asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTATION; AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE; ASTHMA; BRONCHIAL HYPERRESPONSIVENESS; LENGTH TENSION RELATIONSHIP; SMOOTH MUSCLE PLASTITICY
Abstract-Résumé: The frequency and severity of asthma have increased in industrialized nations for the last couple of decades, despite the opposite trend for many other chronic diseases. It is estimated that more than 10% of the population are asthmatic, with a greater proportion in children.  According to the Asthma Society of Canada, 500 Canadians die every year from asthma and 3 million Canadians are suffering from the disease.  The economic burden on our health care system is enormous.  There is no cure for asthma and the cause has not been identified.    One of the few consensuses among asthma researchers is that excessive contraction of airway smooth muscle, the muscle layer that surrounds the airways and can constrict the airways when stimulated, is an important mechanism. Many drugs for asthma therapy attempt to relax the muscle.  Although the treatment alleviates the symptoms, hypersensitivity of the airways to inhaled irritants remains. To find a cure for asthma, we need to understand why the airway muscle contracts excessively to cause difficulty in breathing.  In the proposed research we will systematically compare the mechanical and biochemical properties, as well as the subcellular organization of the protein structures of airway smooth muscle in human asthmatic and non-asthmatic control subjects. This has not been done before because of the difficulty in obtaining suitable lung tissues. We have established a unique source of human tissues, the International Institute for the Advancement of Medicine (http://www.iiam.org/) through which human tissue obtained at autopsy is donated for research purposes. Findings from this project will help identify defects in asthmatic airway muscle and aid the design of a new generation of drugs that can better alleviate or eliminate asthma symptoms.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
TitreApplicationTitle: A beta-adrenoceptor-mediated memory circuitry in rats
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-ADRENOCEPTOR; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IMAGING; MEMORY; OLFACTORY LEARNING; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to create associations among objects or events enriches the brain's capacity for new memories and permits a wide array of cues to trigger the recall of past memories. My proposal explores the cellular mechanisms governing memory formation in a simple mammalian associative learning model. Classical conditioning of odor preference learning in the neonatal rat provides us with an excellent model for the study of associative memory. Young rats learn to prefer odors associated with a stimulus such as stroking the pup that mimics the maternal care of licking pups. The unconditioned stimulus, stroking, is mediated by norepinephrine release in the olfactory bulb (the first odor processing center) acting at beta-adrenoceptors. The conditioned stimulus, an odor, is represented by activity in olfactory bulb mitral cells. How does norepinephrine via beta-adrenoceptor activation in the olfactory bulb promote learning? I propose to create an in vitro working model using olfactory bulb slices. The learning association will be mimicked by pairing electrical stimulation of the olfactory nerve (mimicking odor input) with application of a beta-adrenoceptor agonist. I will measure the physiological changes in different types of neurons in order to understand the circuitry underpinning the odor associative learning. I hypothesize that beta-adrenoceptor activation in the olfactory bulb facilitates the communication between olfactory receptor neurons (which form the olfactory nerve) and olfactory bulb mitral cells so that mitral cells enhance their responses to the same odor input.   My proposed research in understanding one form of memory will shed light on what underneath memory loss during pathological conditions. A deeper understanding of memory mechanism in animal models has implications for the treatment of memory dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease and other age-related disorders, which significantly affect quality of life of millions of people.

NomDuComitéFR: Santé publique, santé communautaire et santé des populations
DomainesScientifiquesFR: SANTÉ DES POPULATIONS; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Methods for the analysis of complex life history data
Keywords-MotsClés: DESIGN OF CLINICAL TRIALS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; INTERVAL CENSORING; LIFE HISTORY DATA; ONCOLOGY; RECURRENT EVENTS
Abstract-Résumé: New and emerging challenges in the health sciences have arisen in recent years due to greater appreciation for the complex multifactorial nature of chronic disease processes, increasing ability to capture massive amounts of data, and a growing interest in making use of existing health data bases to answer medically important questions. This research program is directed at the development of innovative, rigorous and efficient biostatistical methodology to achieve a better understanding of the underlying etiologies of disease in population studies, a clearer appreciation of biological mechanisms of activity and progression in longitudinal studies of patients with chronic disease, and powerful methods for assessing the value of experimental therapeutic interventions in clinical trials involving complex outcomes. Because statistical methods are at the foundation of any rigorous scientific inquiry, methodologic advances in biostatistics have bearing in the full spectrum of health research.   One of the problems to be considered is how to make most efficient use of datasets from randomized and observational studies with only partial information on risk factors and outcomes due to incomplete observation. Predictive models will also be developed to guide therapeutic decision making and facilitate personalized therapy in cancer research. Models which lead to better understanding of risks for side-effects to treatments will give insight into the risks of potentially fatal adverse drug reactions and help guide use of treatments and improve patient care in orthopedic surgery. Additional topics involve the development of innovative methods for the design and analysis of clinical trials.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: The Roles of MicroRNA miR-17-3p in Wound Healing and Angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CELL BIOLOGY; GENE EXPRESSION; MICRORNA; SELF-RENEWAL; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: Different kinds of heart diseases are the leading cause of death in developed countries.  Among them, vascular disease is the most important manifestation resulting from extensive inflammation and fibrosis due to blood vessel injury. Cell self-renewal is an integration of growth control. It is important to maintain organ integrity and functions. We are interested in studying regulation of tissue regeneration and blood vessel formation by microRNAs. MicroRNAs are a group of newly discovered tiniest genetic materials. MicroRNA is known to play important roles in physiological and pathological conditions, including heart disease-associated formation of new blood vessels. We will study the role of a microRNA named miR-17-3p in regulation of the expression of a number of proteins associated with tissue regeneration and blood formation. We will develop an anti-sense construct (to combat against miR-17-3p) and to promote new blood vessel formation for the recovery of heart diseases. With such an approach, it is possible to inhibit the function of a particular microRNA by producing an anti-sense construct against that microRNA. Since chemically synthesized RNAs are unstable and it always produces off-target results (side-effect), body-expressed microRNAs are under strict control of the body system and can exert normal physiological functions. Fulfillments of the proposed experiments will provide new information in understanding the regulatory roles of miR-17-3p in factors associated with blood vessel formation and wound repair. This could lead to the development of a new method to treat vascular diseases, which could increase the chance of survival and recovery in patients with myocardial ischemia, cerebral ischemia myocardial infarction and stroke.

ClasseRechercheFR: SURDITE; AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE
TitreApplicationTitle: Using Drosophila to investigate mechanisms underlying planar cell polarity
Keywords-MotsClés: ATROPHIN; DEVELOPMENT; DROSOPHILA MELANOGASTER; FAT; GENETICS; PLANAR CELL POLARITY
Abstract-Résumé: The basic mechanisms of the control of tissue organization are the same in man, mice and flies. Work from the fruitfly has identified many genes that control tissue organization, and subsequent studies have shown that these genes also function to control tissue organization in mammals. Loss of a specific form of tissue organization called Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) leads to numerous developmental defects, such as neural tube closure defects, as well as defects in adults such as deafness and cystic kidney disease in mammals. Studies in the fruitfly are more rapid and cost-effective than vertebrate models, and the sophisticated genetic tools available in the fruitfly allow a rapid understanding of basic mechanisms of tissue organization. This grant will use the fruitfly to determine the basic mechanisms of PCP, focusing on the role of a large cell adhesion molecule called Ft. Our previous studies have identified two proteins that bind the cytoplasmic domain of Ft that also regulate PCP (a transcriptional co-repressor called Atrophin, and a kinase called Discs Overgrown). Biochemical, molecular and genetic approaches will be used to understand how Ft regulates PCP, to identify the transcription factors that function downstream of Ft and Atrophin in regulation of PCP, and the targets of the kinase Discs Overgrown in PCP regulation.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: The herpes simplex virus virion host shutoff protein: mechanisms of translational regulation.
Keywords-MotsClés: HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS; HOST SHUTOFF; IMMUNE EVASION; RNA TURNOVER; STRESS GRANULES; TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: All viruses must use the host cell's protein synthesis machinery to decode the viral genetic instructions (messenger RNAs) in order to make the building blocks of new virus particles. Many viruses therefore manipulate the protein synthetic machinery to their own advantage. We are studying a herpes virus protein called vhs, which destroys cellular messenger RNAs. We discovered that it also modifies the messenger RNA decoding process (translation), and showed that this modification is needed for efficient virus growth. We will now determine exactly how vhs reprograms translation. The results will improve our understanding of how viruses take over the host cell machinery, and may lead to improved ways of preventing and treating virus infections.

AreasOfScienceEN: MENTAL HEALTH; SOCIETAL & CULTURAL DIMENSIONS OF HEALTH
DomainesScientifiquesFR: SANTÉ MENTALE; DIMENSIONS SOCIALES ET CULTURELLES DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: New Mothers in a New Country: Understanding Postpartum Depression among Recent Immigrant and Canadian-Born Chinese Women
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCULTURATION; IMMIGRANT WOMEN; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION; SOCIAL SUPPORT; TRADITIONAL POSTPARTUM RITUALS
Abstract-Résumé: Many mothers from diverse cultures experience postpartum depression (PPD), a serious form of maternal morbidity with well-documented health consequences for the mother, child, and family. While the cause of PPD remains unclear, recent research suggests recent immigrant status is an important predictor. The purpose of this longitudinal study is three-fold: (1) to determine the prevalence of PPD, when it started, and whether the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is a good way to assess for PPD among recent immigrant Chinese mothers; (2) to examine the relationships between recent immigrant status, PPD, acculturation, acculturative stress, social  support, income, and the practice of traditional postpartum rituals; and (3) to determine patterns of PPD help-seeking behaviours and barriers to health services among recent immigrant Chinese mothers. Following a comprehensive recruitment program, eligible and consenting mothers will receive follow-up calls by trained research assistants matched on maternal language ability. Diverse study outcomes will be assessed at baseline, 12, 24, and 52 weeks postpartum. The study results will make substantive contributions in seven areas: (1) provide information about PPD prevalence rates among recently immigrated and Canadian-born Chinese women; (2) establish the validity of using the EPDS in detecting PPD among these Chinese mothers; (3) advance our understanding of the relationship between recent immigrant status, the acculturation process, and PPD; (4) determine which traditional postpartum rituals are maintained post-migration and the effect of these practices on the development of PPD; (5) investigate health service utilization barriers and help-seeking behaviours related to PPD; (6) promote cultural sensitivity among health professionals; and (7) guide the development of a future randomized controlled trial.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Disruption of axonal transport by soluble A-beta oligomers
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AXONAL TRANSPORT; CULTURED HIPPOCAMPAL NEURONS; LIVE CELL IMAGING; NEURODEGENERATION; VESICLE TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Healthy nerve cells are vital to the function of the nervous system.  Nerve cell deterioration leads to neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's. A critical factor in neurodegeneration is the disruption of transport pathways inside neurons. Literally cellular highways, these pathways transport molecular signals that are needed for neuronal development, communication, and survival. Our project aims to characterize how a particular molecule implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) leads to defective transport in nerve cells. A likely culprit in AD is a small protein called the amyloid-beta (Abeta) peptide. Although fibrous forms of Abeta are involved in AD pathogenesis, a recently discovered non-fibrous form of Abeta (ABO) may be more neurotoxic than the Abeta form. ABOs are short, modified versions of Abeta that lead to abnormal synaptic function, inhibit normal cellular functions in experimental models of learning, and contribute to plaque formation in the brains of AD mice. Notably, ABOs cause chemical alteration of a cytoskeletal component of nerve cell transport structures. We have new data showing that ABOs reduce axonal transport of molecules that are essential for nerve cell function and survival. When neurons are treated with an Alzheimer's drug, however, the ABO-induced reduction in transport is prevented. Our results also point to the protein glycogen synthase kinase as a pivotal regulator of intracellular transport, and when this function is derailed, transport is disrupted. Our proposed experiments will use primary cultures of mammalian nerve cells and employ imaging technology that enables us to observe transport events as they occur in the living cells. This powerful experimental system will allow us to assess the role ABOs play in disrupting transport functions in neurons.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
TitreApplicationTitle: High Frequency EEG Oscillations in Epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: DETECTION; EEG (ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY); EPILEPSY; LOCALIZATION; PREDICTION; SEIZURE
Abstract-Résumé: The electroencephalogram (EEG) has been considered until recently to contain signals with frequencies up to 100Hz. Recent work has demonstrated the presence of signals of very low amplitude and high frequency (100 to 500Hz), which may be of importance in epilepsy. The purpose of this application is to establish an efficient methodology to record and quantify this activity, and to assess its importance in the localization of the brain regions generating epileptic discharges, to improve the chances that the surgical treatment of epilepsy is successful. It is also expected that these high frequency activities will help in understanding how abnormal tissue can generate seizures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathogenesis of tendinopathy: Clinical and laboratory studies
Keywords-MotsClés: REPETITIVE USE INJURIES; TENDINOPATHY; TENDON
Abstract-Résumé: Repetitive-use tendon injury (typically called "tendinitis") is a major clinical burden in many Canadian industries. Unfortunately, how and why this condition develops is poorly understood.  Improved treatment will require increased knowledge of the causes of this common, costly condition.  In everyday clinical medicine, it was presumed that painful 'tendinitis' was due to inflammatory cells damaging tendon tissue. In detailed studies of tendon tissue from patients undergoing surgery for repetitive-use tendon injury, we found that inflammatory cells were very scarce or absent, despite the presence of tendon pain.  Instead, we could see  a large number of new blood vessels (microvessels) within painful tendons.  These microvessels were actively proliferating, and producing a small protein (peptide) that stimulated vessel development (VEGF; vascular endothelial growth factor). Microvessels are associated with pathology in other tissues such as in the eye, where they impair vision, in cancer progression, and in osteoarthritis.   These data are of potential importance in understanding the cause of repetitive-use tendon injuries, because clinical imaging techniques have revealed that overgrowth of vessels in tendon is strongly associated with chronic pain.    This research is tests the theory that tendon vessels become more prominent during periods of repetitive use as a result of local VEGF production, and that this compromises tendon structure and function.  If this is proven, it will provide novel avenues for drug therapies to treat tendon problems.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms of Electrogenesis in the Neonate Heart: Etiology of Junctional Ectopic Tachycardia
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIAS; CARDIAC MYOCYTES; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; JUNCTIONAL ECTOPIC TACHYCARDIA
Abstract-Résumé: Congenital heart disease (CHD), normally caused by genetic mutations that are inherited from the child's parents, is one of the most common congenital diseases exceeding 1% of all live births.  Many types of CHD require open heart surgery to correct the structural defect while the child is still very young, sometimes within days of birth.  Open heart surgery normally requires the patient to be put on a heart-lung machine to do the work of the heart while the heart is being operated on.  Open heart surgery is challenging under the best of circumstances but it is much more complicated and risky in a newborn.  Most infants come off the heart-lung machine with a weakened heart and are at high risk for developing a serious arrhythmia known as Junctional Ectopic Tachycardia or JET.  The mechanisms underlying JET are not well understood and therefore the treatment is frequently not very effective.  The purpose of this grant proposal is to understand the mechanisms behind JET and to propose novel therapies based on this knowledge.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
ResearchClassEN: DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS; MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL DISEASES
ClasseRechercheFR: DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES; TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Alterations in amygdala-prefrontal cortex circuitry by repeated psychostimulants: Electrophysiological and behavioural analyses
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYGDALA; DOPAMINE; DRUG ADDICTION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; REWARD LEARNING
Abstract-Résumé: Emotional processes and higher-order executive functions are governed in part by interconnected neural networks linking the amygdala (a brain nucleus in the temporal lobes) and dopamine input arising from the from the midbrain, to the frontal lobes. Drug addicts, particularly those abusing psychostimulants such as amphetamine or cocaine, display impairments in cognitive functions mediated by these neural circuits. In addition, recent experimental evidence suggests that the brain regions comprising this circuit may be particularly susceptible to long-term neurochemical, anatomical and neurophysiological alterations following repeated exposure to these drugs of abuse. The main objective of the present proposal is to elucidate the neuroadaptations that occur in these circuits following repeated exposure to psychostimulants. We will use amphetamine-induced behavioural sensitization as an animal model of the neural changes that occur following repeated drug exposure, in combination with multidisciplinary analyses combining electrophysiological and behavioural measures that are a hallmark of our research program. Specifically, we will characterize how repeated amphetamine exposure i) disrupts reward-related learning for natural reinforcers such as food, ii) may affect behaviour guided by conditioned aversive stimuli and iii) perturbs in the neurophysiological properties of amygdala neurons and how the actions of dopamine on these cells are altered. Using animal models to investigate the changes that chronic drugs of abuse can induces in these circuits will provide important insight into the aberrant brain function that underlies drug addiction, and may in turn facilitate the development of treatments for the cognitive dysfunction that occurs in this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional genomics to identify stem cell fate determinants
Keywords-MotsClés: BAC COMPLEMENTATION; CHIMERIC MOUSE; CHROMOSOME ENGINEERING; COMPARATIVE GENOMIC HYBRIDIZATION ARRAY; ES CELLS; IN VITRO DIFFERENTIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Stem cells have received considerable public attention in part because of their potential application in regenerative therapies. Stem cells can be operationally defined as cells that have the unique property to self-renew as well as to generate more differentiated progeny (differentiation). However, much remains to be learned about the genes regulating stem cell differentiation and renewal, their relationship to each other, and the signalling pathways that control their expression and/or activity. In this application, we propose to use a new resource developed in our laboratory in the last 6 years -called DelES, for chromosomal Deletion in ES cells, see www.bioinfo.iric.ca/deles- to efficiently identify novel genes and other elements which are essential for stem cell activity.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of Nod proteins on the inflammatory response to differentially compartmentalized intracellular pathogens
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; IMMUNITY; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Detection of microbes by the host is critical to initiate a program to develop inflammation, leading to the successful clearance of the infection. Specific receptors inside the host cell are critical for the initiation of this program. Our laboratory studies Nod1 and Nod2, which are key mediators of this intracellular surveillance system. In this proposal, we wish to explore the cellular mechanisms of how Nod proteins detect different invasive bacteria and how this impacts on the inflammatory program, and ultimately, recovery from infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional studies of protein/protein and protein/DNA interactions regulating hematopoietic development
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVATORS; BLOOD CELL DEVELOPMENT; CANCER; LEUKEMIA; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that between 3,000-4,000 Canadians will be diagnosed with leukemia this year alone and over 2,000 persons will die from the disease. In children, one fourth of all new cancers and one third of cancer deaths are the result of some form of leukemia.  Therefore, leukemia is the most common form of childhood cancer.    Most leukemia's result from a disruption or alteration in the normal formation of the different blood cells (red cells, white cells, immune cells). All blood cells are derived from a common  cell called the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) that can be converted into the other types of blood cells. The process by which the HSC is converted to the other blood cells is referred to as hematopoiesis. The conversion of the HCS to the over 15 other blood cell types requires a series of highly regulated signals.  Although tremendous advances have been made in our understanding of how the various signals lead to specific types of blood cells, there is still much about the process that is poorly understood.  However, it is clear that the body must maintain a certain balance between the  different types of blood cells. In this project, I will be investigating how the signals convert the HSC to red blood cells and how the body maintains a balance between the different types of blood cells. This information is crucial to the development of new therapeutic strategies for treatment of leukemia's and other blood related diseases including anemia's.  Our goal is that these studies will help in the development of these new therapeutic strategies.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
ResearchClassEN: CNS ORGANIC; MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL DISEASES
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Brain noise and variability in sensory and cognitive function.
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN; LEARNING; NEURAL NETWORKS; NEUROIMAGING; PERCEPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Intuitive notions of the brain would suggest that if there is too much noise, behavioral and cognitive function would be compromised.  However, given the brain is a nonlinear dynamical, or chaotic, system, it is possible that a certain level of noise is actually central to normal function.  Like an inverted-U, noise needs to be at a moderate level for optimal function, and above or below this level, function drops off.  We will examine the benefits of brain noise in the detection of weak stimuli, and how brain noise changes with learning and across adulthood.  Our hypothesis is that brain noise is a vital enabler of normal behavior.   In a certain way it could be stated that a noisy brain is a healthy brain.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Recovery of function following stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BEHAVIOUR; CO-MORBIDITY; NEUROPLASTICITY; RECOVERY OF FUNCTION; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: We are presently facing a growing epidemic of obesity and related health concerns (e.g. diabetes) as a result of diets high in fat and sugar (HFS) combined with physical inactivity. It is likely that these lifestyle factors, along with an aging population, will increase the incidence of stroke but they also may worsen stroke outcome. Our research uses animal models that closely reproduce the pattern of brain damage and functional impairments commonly seen in stroke patients. Recently we have developed treatments (e.g. stimulating enriched environments) that when initiated at the optimal time after stroke, greatly improve behavioural recovery. Our research findings have created considerable interest among clinical rehabilitation specialists, however all of our findings have been obtained in young, healthy animals. In our proposed experiments we will determine whether treatments effective in these young, healthy animals are also effective in older animals and in animals that have a history of dietary metabolic challenges similar to humans. Interestingly, older people use additional parts of the brain such as the prefrontal cortex in order to compensate for reduced brain function resulting from aging and metabolic stress. This compensation may be even more important after brain injury such as stroke. Thus we will also try to enhance the function of the prefrontal cortex during rehabilitation with the aim of producing more complete functional recovery after stroke. These experiments are of fundamental importance if we are to develop more effective stroke rehabilitation therapies.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - B: Heart and Circulation
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Harnessing the immune system to achieve cardiac restoration by allogeneic cell transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOGENEIC REJECTION; ALLOGENEIC TRANSPLANATION; CELL TRANSPLANTATION; HEART FAILURE; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients who survive a heart attack remain at risk of developing heart failure. This is because a heart attack damages the heart's blood vessel network, kills heart cells, and alters the structure of the heart itself. Heart failure results when the heart can no longer keep up with its increased workload. Cell therapy involves implanting the body's own "stem cells" directly into the heart. The stem cells can help to repair damaged tissue and blood vessels, and decrease the workload of the remaining heart cells. These strategies were very helpful in animals, but produced weaker effects in patients. One main difficulty is that stem cells from patients who are aged and sick are less effective than those from younger, healthy individuals. We need to find a better source of stem cells for aged patients. Ideally, we would like to use healthy bone marrow stem cells prepared from younger donors. Cells that come from a donor rather than the recipient themselves are called "allogeneic" cells. However, just as the body's immune system can "reject" a donated organ, a patient's heart can reject or eliminate donor cells from another individual. We confirmed that allogeneic bone marrow stem cells were not rejected soon after they were implanted into the heart. However, the cells were rejected by the recipient's immune system later, after they developed into muscle cells. Our first objective is to discover exactly why this happens. We will determine which proteins are produced by bone marrow stem cells both before and after they mature inside the heart. This will tell us which proteins the immune system uses to identify allogeneic cells. Next, we will develop new treatments that protect implanted cells from rejection. Clinical trials testing allogeneic cell therapy are already underway. Therefore, we need to learn as much as we can about allogeneic cells in the heart. Our findings will be used to interpret the results of the trials, and to suggest improvements for future trials.

OrgNm: Ottawa Hospital Research Institute/Institut de recherche de l'Hôpital d'Ottawa
NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cell motility by the Ste20-like kinase SLK
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL MIGRATION; KINASES; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: As normal cells become cancer cells, they develop new phenotypes. One such characteristic is the ability to invade surrounding tissue and enter the blood stream. In order for a cancer cell to invade, it also has to become more motile. Our previous research has identified SLK as a protein regulating cell motility. This project will use cultured cells and animal models to investigate the mechanisms of SLK-stimualted motility. We will attempt to disrupt SLK regulators and their interaction to anlayse the effect on cell movement. Finally, we will examine the effect of SLK gene deletion on the induction of tumors in animal models of cancer.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Epidemiology of cognitive dynamics in older adults
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; COHORT STUDIES; DEMENTIA; SECONDARY ANALYSES
Abstract-Résumé: As people age, on average, their brains work less efficiently, especially their memory. With dementia, it is even worse. People with Alzheimer's disease, the most common cause of dementia, usually experience relentless decline. Their decline is both faster and more widespread than what normally happens with age. Even so, relentless decline is not what happens to everybody.  Instead, even with dementia, some people decline much more slowly than do others, some stabilize and a few even improve.  Stability and improvement are not studied very often, but that is what we aim to do.   The reason to study more than decline is that we believe improvement is fundamental - and not just a fluke - and will tell us a lot about brain aging and dementia. We can do this using a type of mathematics known as dynamic systems modeling, which is well suited when things can get better or worse (e.g. weather forecasting). We have devised a dynamic systems model which has shown exceptional promise so far - so much so that leading dementia experts from the US and the UK are willing to share their very expensive data with us.  One example of why we need this type of modeling is to understand how dementia prevention might work. It turns out that some interventions which might lower the risk of dementia also lower the risk of dying. This is a good thing, but it might also have a down side. Because the risk of developing dementia increases rapidly with age, if mortality is improved, some interventions could actually make dementia more common, by having more people live longer, to the ages at which dementia is very likely. (For example, past age 85, about one person in three has dementia.) So it is possible that unless a drug very markedly reduces the risk of dementia, the burden of dementia will increase. This is a tricky issue, which is why we need a sophisticated means of understanding all the ways in which prevention might change the burden of these progressive, damaging illnesses.

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Analysis of Osteopetrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE HOMEOSTASIS; HEMATOPOIESIS; MOUSE GENETICS; OSTEOCLAST; OSTEOPETROSIS/OSTEOPOROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Our ultimate goal is to understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms that regulate bone homeostasis. Throughout life, equilibrium between two opposite phenomena, bone formation and bone resorption, has to be maintained. Specific cells, osteoblast and osteoclast are responsible respectively for bone tissue synthesis and degradation. The osteoclast is from hematopoietic origin and when its activity is lost, severe diseases as osteoporosis and osteopetrosis can occur. Particularly, osteopetrosis is observed when osteoclast cells are deficient or absent, thereby causing an excess of bone mass and a poorly developed bone marrow cavity, leading to death. To gain insights into osteopetrosis, we are studying a mouse model of this disease called grey-lethal (gl) that reproduces the human infantile and most severe form of this disorder. We recently isolated and characterized the gene responsible for this disease using a positional cloning approach. We have now entered a new phase of our studies that consists in the characterization of the grey-lethal gene function and its normal biological role in bone homeostasis and hematopoiesis at large. In addition, we will investigate into the intracellular function of gl in the osteoclast activation pathway. The characterization of this osteopetrotic gene is fundamental for the future development of potential therapeutic strategies.

ResearchClassEN: LIPOPROTEINS, LIPID TRANSPORT; METABOLISM AND NUTRITION
ClasseRechercheFR: LIPOPROTEINES, TRANSPORT LIPIDIQUE; METABOLISME ET NUTRITION
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of intestinal lipoprotein overproduction in insulin resistant states
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; APOLIPOPROTEIN B; CELL BIOLOGY; DIABETES; INSULIN RESISTANCE; INTESTINE
Abstract-Résumé: Insulin resistance is a very common disorder observed in subjects with conditions such as obesity and type 2 diabetes and is now considered to be an important risk factor in the development of heart disease (and higher risk of heart attacks). The incidence of insulin resistant states has been increasing at an alarming rate in not only adults but also adolescent and pediatric populations. Patients with the so called "insulin resistance" syndrome develop hyperlipidemia (high blood fat and cholesterol) which puts them at a greater risk of developing atherosclerosis (narrowing of blood vessels) and coronary heart disease.  Our laboratory is studying the mechanisms underlying a very important link between insulin resistance/diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Our aim is to determine how development of an insulin resistant state leads to the development of hypertriglyceridemia (high blood fat levels) and other lipid disorders. The main objectives of the present proposal to CIHR include: a) to determine the role of the intestine in lipid and lipoprotein metabolism in insulin resistance; b) to investigate hormonal networks in the intestine that control lipid metabolism and their dysregulation in insulin resistance; and c) to understand the pathways mediating inflammation of the intestine that lead to insulin resistance and intestinal dysfunction. Significance: The long term objective of this research is to increase our understanding of this common disorder in humans, and identify potential drug targets, allowing the development of nutriceutical and pharmaceutical measures which can help us control insulin resistance in patients and thus reduce the risk of development of heart disease and other diabetic complications.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurotensin modulation of limbic neurotransmission
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; AMPHETAMINE; DOPAMINE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GLUTAMATE; NEUROTENSIN
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia, major depression, anxiety disorders and drug addiction are among major mental health diseases that are associated to abnormal functions of deep brain regions that belong to a neuronal network that we call the "limbic system".  Pharmacological treatments used to date to reduce and control emotional and motivational symptoms that characterize these disorders target neurochemical communications within the limbic network.  For instance, abnormal limbic dopamine neurotransmission is associated with psychosis and drug addiction and the current medications target this neurotransmitter. But the limbic network is highly complex and dopamine is obviously not the sole relevant neurochemical messenger involved. Results from previous reseach show that neurotensin, a peptide (small protein-like) that modulates neurotransmission with several limbic regions plays a key role in psychosis and vulnerability to drug addiction.  We propose to use complementary multi-technical approaches to further understand the modulation of limbic neurotransmission by neurotensin. Studies are designed to investigate the mechanisms by which this peptide initiates sensitization to the stimulant and the rewarding effect of amphetamine; we will attempt to determine its site of action, its interaction with other neurochemical messengers such as dopamine, glutamate and GABA and the intracellular events that are triggered within neurons of the limbic system by the action of neurotensin.  The use of complementary technical approachs is a promising avenue to reveal mechanisms that subserve funtional changes in the brain that lead to abnormal mental states like psychosis and addiction.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
ResearchClassEN: MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL DISEASES; MULTIPLE DISEASE RELEVANCE
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular mechanisms of multiple intrinsic theta pacemakers in hippocampus
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN DISORDERS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GABAERGIC INTERNEURONS; HIPPOCAMPUS; PHARMACOLOGY; THETA RHYTHM
Abstract-Résumé: Memory requires that large number of neurons interact together. How neurons can do this remains a mystery. This is important to know since this interaction is defective in Alzheimer's disease and may explain why memory is deficient in this disease. In this proposal, we will provide experiments to explain these complex population interactions. Such answers will provide new insights into the treatment of memory disorders.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Atherogenic adipocyte dysfunction induced by TSH
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTE BIOLOGY; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; INFLAMMATION; TSH SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Fat cells produce a lot of factors that are important for healthy metabolism and circulation. When fat cells malfunction, they make too many of these factors, and that can raise the risk of heart disease and diabetes (type 2 or adult-onset form). We are interested in what causes fat cell to malfunction. We have discovered that TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone), known for its role in controlling the thyroid, also acts on fat cells and can cause fat cell to malfunction. We want to study how TSH activates the fat cells, because other research shows that people that have high TSH levels (~5-10% of the population; a condition called subclinical hypothyroidism) have a higher risk for heart disease. We will obtain fat cells from volunteers, place them in dishes in the lab, and study how TSH causes the over-production of these factors that promote artery blockages. We will also study the levels of these factors from blood samples of patients who receive short-term TSH treatment (as a test for thyroid cancer care).

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: FGF2 Isoforms in Cardiac Hypertrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; FIBROBLAST-MYOCYTE INTERACTION; FIBROSIS; GROWTH FACTOR ISOFORM; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSGENIC MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Many cardiovascular diseases are characterized by abnormal heart growth, which predicts poor cardiac outcome. Our previous studies have indicated that a protein, believed to be involved in promoting abnormal growth, FGF2, is more complex than generally known: FGF2 is made as both a 'long' version (Hi-FGF2) and a 'short' version (Lo-FGF2, and our data suggest that only the Hi-FGF2 version promotes hypertrophy (the 'bad' FGF) while the Lo-FGF2 version is actually beneficial. This poposal uses experimental mouse models of abnormal heart growth, as well as in vitro systems, to confirm and expand our data, and potentially provide a strategy that would convert the 'bad' FGF2 to its beneficial version (Lo FGF2). They may provide a means to prevent and even regress pathological hypertrophy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the physiological functions of apoptosis effectors in Nod-like receptors signaling, mucosal immunity and colitis
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; COLITIS; COLORECTAL CANCER; INFLAMMATION; PATHOGEN CLEARANCE; PATTERN-RECOGNITION RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Two of the main challenges that multicellular organisms faced during evolution were to cope with invading microorganisms and eliminate and replace dying cells. The innate immune system evolved to handle both tasks. Key aspects of innate immunity are 1) the detection of invaders or tissue injury and 2) the induction of an inflammatory response. Both of these functions are governed by specific receptors of the innate immune system termed « pattern recognition receptors » (PRRs). In the gut, PRRs interact with commensal bacteria and induce a physiological level of inflammation, which is necessary for tissue integrity (homeostasis) and repair. While PRR activation in the intestine is essential for host resistance, it is detrimental when induced chronically or in excess and is linked to various diseases, notably inflammatory bowel diseases and cancer. Recent evidence from our laboratory has identified a tight crosstalk between innate immunity and proteins involved in apoptosis, or programmed cell death. The contribution of apoptosis to innate immunity is not restricted to the elimination of infected and damaged cells, as various effectors of the apoptosis machinery are emerging as critical for PRR signaling. We are investigating three classes of apoptosis effectors: 1) The Inflammatory caspases, 2) The inhibitors of apoptosis proteins (IAPs) and 3) The Bcl-2 family proteins. Our research program is aimed at understanding how these effectors contribute to the regulation of mucosal immunity in the intestine. Our ultimate goal is to find ways to manipulate their activity or modulate their downstream effects for therapeutic interventions. We will use experimental and genetic models of colitis, colorectal cancer and diarrheal disease, novel chemical compounds and genome-wide RNA interference to achieve our goals.

OrgNm: CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Jewish General/CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Hôpital juif
TitreApplicationTitle: T-regulatory cells and vascular injury in hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGENIC AND CONSOMIC RATS; GENETIC AND EXPERIMENTAL HYPERTENSION; IMMUNITY; INFLAMMATORY MEDIATORS; T-LYMPHOCYTES; VASCULAR REMODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Low-grade inflammation participates in the mechanisms leading to elevated blood pressure. This occurs in part via injury of blood vessels and the kidney. These mechanisms contribute to strokes and heart attacks. The inflammation found in these conditions may be triggered by the body's defenses, which are mediated in part by circulating white blood cells called T lymphocytes. Among these T lymphocytes are regulatory cells called Treg. Lack of activity of Treg that suppress inflammation may be involved in enhancement of inflammatory responses in hypertensive animal models, and this may be favored by heredity (genetic predisposition). We will test whether genes influence the role of these T regulatory lymphocytes on inflammation in rats with genetic hypertension facilitated by salt loading, which leads to blood vessel and kidney injury that contribute to elevated blood pressure. These findings will create totally new opportunities for treatment of high blood pressure.

ClasseRechercheFR: TRAUMATISMES, EMPOISONNEMENTS, VIOLENCE; SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of gender on functional outcome following mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI):  Do women experience worse sequelae and longer recovery than men?
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY; GENDER DIFFERENCES; RECOVERY FROM INJURY; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Although women comprise 50% of the athletic population and they are 3 times more likely than men to suffer a sport-related mild Traumatic Brain Injury (mTBI) (also known as concussion), the current diagnostic tools and return to play safety guidelines are entirely based on scientific evidence from a male athlete population. This not only places women in danger of experiencing more and graver traumatic injuries but also of suffering from long-term consequences of these injuries. The only two studies that investigated gender-based differences indicate that women have greater cognitive deficits than men; however, these investigations did not extend beyond 3 days post-injury. A recent study from our group with female university athletes found persisting cognitive deficits 6 to 8 months after the injury. Cumulating research indicates that if an athlete returns to the game before recovery is completed, they become 5 times more at risk of suffering from subsequent head injuries. Further, a new mTBI on top of a lingering injury will lead to worse deficits, will take longer to recover, and may even lead to death. Finally, the accumulation of mTBIs may increase the presence of cognitive deficits during aging and even lead to Alzheimer's disease. The objectives of the current proposal are to 1) establish gender specific norms for the assessment tools currently used in sport mTBI (symptoms checklist, cognitive tests, balance assessment, and electroencephalography (EEG)), 2) compare symptoms, cognitive deficits, impairments in balance, and anomalies in EEG's caused by a mTBI in male and female athletes, 3) chart the recovery period for the different assessment tools and different brain functions in female versus male athletes as a function of injury history (i.e., number of previous mTBI), and 4) ultimately develop a diagnostic and return to play protocol adapted for women.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - B: Heart and Circulation
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Endothelin, vascular inflammation and injury, and hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR INJURY; HYPERTENSION; MOLECULAR AND CELLULAR TECHNIQUES; PHARMACOLOGIC TECHNIQUES; PRESSURIZED VESSELS; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Endothelin is a substance produced by the endothelium, the inner lining of blood vessels. It is a powerful contrictor of blood vessels and has been shown to participate in many cardiovascular diseases such as high blood pressure, atherosclerosis which obstructs arteries and leads to heart attacks and strokes, and failure of the heart and the kidneys by contributing to injury of blood vessels, the kidney and the heart. We have generated a mouse that produces human endothelin in the endothelium and develops vascular injury. We have shown However, in this mouse endothelin is produced from very early development which may confound our findings. We are therefore proposing to generate a mouse that will produce human endothelin only when we trigger the production, which will allow better understanding of what happens in humans. We will also cross these mice with mice that have elevated cholesterol or increased or decreased inflammation, so that we will be able learn which are the mechanisms whereby endothelin leads to injury in cardiovascular disease. This will help develop strategies to treat cardiovascular diseases in humans.

AreasOfScienceEN: GENOMICS, PROTEOMICS, AND BIOINFORMATICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
DomainesScientifiquesFR: GÉNOMIQUE, PROTÉOMIQUE ET BIOINFORMATIQUE; BIOLOGIE MOLÉCULAIRE

TitreApplicationTitle: Charting Bacterial Pathways and Functional Interaction Networks Using E. coli Synthetic Genetic Arrays
Keywords-MotsClés: E.COLI; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; FUNCTIONAL MODULES AND NETWORKS; GENETIC (GENE-GENE) INTERACTIONS; SYNTHETIC GENETIC ARRAYS; SYNTHETIC LETHALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how all the genes encoded by the genome of a microbe work together to form a living cell requires a complete description of the 'wiring circuits' that underlie the various fundamental cellular processes. A key feature is the tendency of genes to form molecular pathways that serve as communication links between specific combinations of genes. Genes with similar or overlapping biological roles generally belong to the same pathway. Here, we propose to explore the global pathway architecture of the classical model bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) using powerful new technology developed by our group.  Our experimental approach will enable us to generate circuit diagrams for all the pathways and genes involved in important biological processes essential for bacterial cell growth and infection. Since many bacterial genes are conserved across microbial evolution, the identification of the pathway architecture of E. coli should also reveal the organization of pathways in other bacterial species, including pathogens. The data generated in this project will therefore serve as a valuable resource for the entire biomedical research community, and should spur on the development of new antibiotics.

ClasseRechercheFR: AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE; MALADIE DE PARKINSON
TitreApplicationTitle: Signaling mechanisms induced by the axon guidance cue netrin-1
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; CYTOSKELETAL DYNAMICS; DCC/UNC5 RECEPTORS; NETRINS; RHO GTPASES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: During brain development, neurons navigate over long or short distances to reach their targets and make the appropriate neural connections. To achieve this important task, they will be guided by molecular cues present in their cellular environment. Netrins are guiding neurons during brain development. In this research proposal, our goals are to understand how netrin-1 regulate the navigation of neurons and what are the molecular targets of netrin-1. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying netrin-1 function will help to identify novel therapeutic strategies for tumor therapy, neurodegenerative diseases, and spinal cord injuries.
