NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The importance of dopamine, dopamine receptors, and dopaminergic pathways for analgesia and pain modulation in humans.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIETARY DOPAMINE DEPLETION; DOPAMINERGIC NEUROTRANSMISSION; FIBROMYALGIA; HUMAN PAIN PROCESSING; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; PSYCHOPHYSICS
Abstract-Résumé: The brain chemical dopamine is best known for its role in motivation and motor control. More recently, however, animal studies have implicated dopamine also in pain relief. Studies that point at impaired dopamine systems in the brains of some patients with chronic pain suggest that a thorough understanding of the role of this chemical, its receptors and pathways is clinically relevant.  No experimental study has yet investigated the effects of reduced dopamine availability in the brain on human pain perception. We therefore propose to decrease brain dopamine in healthy volunteers using acute dietary dopamine depletion to study the role of dopamine in pain sensitivity and the individual's capacity to modulate pain sensations. By combining thorough psychophysical studies with Positron Emission Tomography of the brain, we will also examine the localization of any pain increase due to reduced dopamine levels. Thereby, we will gain insight as to which dopaminergic pathways are involved in pain relief. We will assess certain character traits in all participants because we have preliminary data suggesting that certain traits make people less vulnerable to a pain-augmenting effect of reduced dopamine levels. All experiments will be performed in men and women. This is of crucial importance because the pain conditions for which impairment of dopamine systems has been shown are more often diagnosed in women. The proposed research is likely to yield important insights into the importance of dopamine for human pain processing and why some chronic pain syndromes occur more frequently in women than in men. This knowledge could potentially be used to devise new diagnostic and therapeutic option for affected patients.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Normal aging and the cholinergic hypothesis of cognitive impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; AGING; ATTENTION AND LEARNING; BASAL FOREBRAIN; CHOLINERGIC CORTICAL DEAFFERENTATION; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Canada is going to face a growing crisis of seniors living with a decline in cognitive faculties, such as attention, learning, and memory, as a common consequence of normal aging. Understanding the biological and cognitive changes during aging is critical to improving our elders' quality of life. This proposal will focus on the role of the cholinergic basal forebrain (BF) in the cognitive impairments associated with normal aging. The BF region of the brain is poised to play an important role in how the brain takes in information because it is the major source of the chemical acetylcholine (ACh) for brain areas critical to cognition. Extensive loss in this chemical's function and pathology at its source are prominent in Alzheimer's disease (AD); thus, they are hypothesized to contribute to the cognitive decline associated with normal aging. The proposed studies will examine how this region and chemical affect how the aging brain 'binds' information. Although the human cognitive literature has yielded substantial insights into the attention-dependent nature and broad brain systems involved in feature binding, the chemistry and specific downstream correlates of feature binding remain unknown. The proposed studies will (1) selectively remove ACh cells in brain regions important to feature binding in rats to establish an animal model of cholinergic BF dysfunction, (2) test aged rats, and (3) collect behavioural and functional neuroimaging data in normally-aging humans to test the validity of this rat model to normal aging across the lifespan in humans. Thus allowing us to compare the behaviour and brain regions of rats and humans while performing the same feature binding task. Success of these studies may provide an understanding of the mechanisms by which the cholinergic BF system contributes to normal cognition and cognitive deficits associated with cholinergic deficiency that have significant societal consequence, such as normal aging and pathological aging, like AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors in airway  chemoreceptors: Molecular characterization and physiological  functions
Keywords-MotsClés: BPD; CARBON DIOXIDE SENSING; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; CONTROL OF BREATHING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; K/O MICE MODELS; MOLECULAR; NEONATAL RESPIRATORY ADAPTATION; NICOTINE INDUCED NEB CHANGES; OXYGEN SENSING; PATCH-CLAMP METHOD; SIDS; TISSUE CULTURE; TRANSGENICS
Abstract-Résumé: We study specialized groups of lung cells called neuroepithelial bodies or NEB, located within airways of human and animal lungs. NEB are postulated to function as oxygen and potentially carbon dioxide sensors in lung with greatest importance during neonatal adaptation to air breathing . We found that NEB can signal airway oxygen levels (low oxygen) via a presumptive cell membrane localized oxygen sensor protein complex operating cooperatively with specialized ion channels. This activity leads to secretion of effector molecules that include amines and neuropeptide hormones. We propose to establish that this oxygen sensor complex is situated on the cell surface membranes of NEB in proximity to the airway microenvironment and associates specifically with proteins that regulate ion transport. We will characterize the carbon dioxide sensor complex component which also appears to be functional in NEB cells. The NEB functions to sense both oxygen and carbon dioxide and relay messages back to the central control of breathing via the vagus nerve. For our studies we use tissue and cell culture methods, animal models carrying alterations or defects in one of the sensing complex components, so called transgenics and knockouts. We study these models with morphological, biochemical, molecular and electrophysiological methods, all further refined for studies of NEB.We will also study changes in NEB in a variety of pediatric lung disorders such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia and SIDS. Understanding the molecular mechanism of how NEB sense ambient gas conditions will provide insights into the pathobiology of perinatal diseases and breathing disorders and provide a greater understanding of the physiological functions of lung.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: A Murine Model for Understanding the Implications of Adynamic Bone Disease on Bone Quality
Keywords-MotsClés: ADYNAMIC BONE DISEASE; ANIMAL MODELS; BIOMECHANICS; BONE; FRACTURE; FRAGILITY; OSTEOPOROSIS; QUALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Adynamic bone disease is a serious condition in which the bone cells that build and maintain our bones become inactive or impaired. This condition is observed in patients with renal failure receiving dialysis, geriatric patients, and sometimes in patients receiving long-term treatment with bisphosphonates (drugs used to treat osteoporosis). The disease often results in bone fragility but we do not clearly understand how the fragility or weakness develops because there are multiple ways the bone can become weakened. The Grynpas Laboratory at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto (in collaboration with the Alman Laboratory at the Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto) proposes to develop a mouse model of adynamic bone. Basically, we are able to turn off the cells that build and repair bone. We will confirm the adynamic bone disease condition using standard techniques that pathologists use when they are diagnosing if a human patient has the disease. We will also use specialized laboratory techniques to determine the condition of the bone. We call this "assessment of bone quality" and our laboratory is one of only a few laboratories in the world that does this kind of work. We will also test the role of ageing in adynamic bone disease. Additionally, we will study how the adynamic bone condition effects bone fracture healing. Ultimately, we hope that this work will lead to improved health and quality of life for patients who have adynamic bone disease by developing improved understanding of how their bone fragility develops, how painful fractures may be avoided and if fracture occurs increased understanding of issues in fracture healing.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Beta cell-stimulus secretion coupling: The role of zinc transport and its link to type 2 diabetes.
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA CELL; GLUCAGON SECRETION; INSULIN SECRETION; TYPE 2 DIABETES; ZINC TRANSPORTER MUTATIONS AND DIABETES RISK; ZNT8 TRANSPORTER FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The maturity onset form of diabetes, Type 2 diabetes (T2D), afflicts more than 2 million Canadians and costs the healthcare system billions of dollars annually. As the disease progresses T2D can cause many severe health problems including; blindness, kidney failure and heart attacks. T2D is in part caused by genetics and by environmental influences like obesity. We have recently shown that a large population of humans are at risk to develop T2D because they possess a genetic variant of a protein called ZnT8. At present, the function of this protein is not well understood, but it is expressed in insulin producing B cells and can regulate the transport of zinc ions into cells from the blood. It has been known for many years that zinc is an extremely important element to B cells because it is required for both the production of insulin. Additionally, zinc is co-released with insulin from B cells to inhibit the secretion of glucagon, a hormone known to counter insulin's actions and raise blood sugar. Thus, zinc can greatly influence blood sugar by stimulating insulin production and by suppressing glucagon secretion. In the present application, we propose 3 distinct experiments. First will determine how ZnT8 functions in B cells to control insulin secretion by studying mice that are designed not to possess this protein. In a second set of studies we will determine how one specific human genetic variant of the ZnT8 protein called ZnT8325R that is found in the majority of people, increases your risk of developing T2D. To do this, we will study mice that are genetically modified to express human ZnT8325R in their insulin-producing B cells. In a third set of experiments we will determine if new drugs that increase ZnT8 protein activity, can enhance insulin secretion and thereby be used to treat T2D. Overall these studies will allow us to better understand how ZnT8 increases T2D risk and may lead to new methods to treat this disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; EPIDEMIOLOGIE
TitreApplicationTitle: An investigation of risk factors common to cancer at different sites
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; MAMMOGRAPHIC DENSITY; MELANOMA; THYROID CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Cancers that develop at different sites on the body may share common risk factors.  Knowledge about these shared factors can help us understand the causes of these cancers and eventually lead to ways to prevent them. The goal of this research is to find out if mammographic density, a strong risk factor for breast cancer, is also associated with the risk of developing melanoma (a type of skin cancer) and thyroid cancer.  Mammographic density refers to the amount of fibro-glandular tissue in the breast as seen on a mammogram and is one the strongest known risk factors for breast cancer. In a cohort of women with extensive mammographic density we have observed a higher than expected number of melanoma and thyroid cancers. In the research proposed in this application we will determine whether mammographic density is associated with the risk of melanoma and thyroid cancer by studying women who have mammograms as part of the Ontario Breast Screening Program and have developed melanoma or thyroid cancer.  We will compare the amount of mammographic density in the mammograms of those who developed these cancers and those who did not. The finding that mammographic density is associated with melanoma and/or thyroid cancer would lead to future studies to understand the genetic and biological factors responsible for these associations so that preventive strategies can be developed.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS CEREBRALES (ET RETINIENNES); THERAPIE DES TUMEURS CEREBRALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular targeting of the Rho-GTPase pathway in human astrocytomas
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTOMA; INVASION; MIGRATION; NANOPARTICLES; RHO-GTPASE
Abstract-Résumé: Human astrocytomas are the most common primary brain tumour and are incurable with present treatment strategies. The principle reason for therapeutic failure is the invasion of astrocytoma cells invade into regions of the normal brain which prevent complete surgical removal or effective radiation therapy.  In addition, chemotherapy frequently fails in astrocytomas because of the ''blood brain barrier'' which blocks the delivery of drugs to the brain. Our study examines a key pathway involving a family of proteins called the Rho-GTPases that regulate how cancer cells migrate out of the tumour mass and invade into normal brain tissue. Our recent studies have identified individual proteins in this pathway that are abnormally found in astrocytomas and may be potential targets for novel therapeutics.  To this end we have designed experiments to use drugs currently available to block the Rho-GTPase pathway, to generate novel nanoparticle delivery vehicles targeting specific Rho-GTPases, and to use the technique of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-directed focused ultrasound to focally disrupt the blood brain barrier to enhance the delivery of our reagents to astrocytomas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Donor Human Milk Versus Preterm Formula as a Substitute for Mothers' Own Milk for Feeding Very Low Birth Weight Infants
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT; DONOR MILK; HUMAN MILK; ILLNESS; INFANT NUTRITION; VERY LOW BIRTH WEIGHT INFANTS
Abstract-Résumé: Health authorities recommend mothers' own milk as the sole source of nutrition for infants for the first 6 months of life.  For very low birth weight (VLBW, less than 1500g) infants who are at elevated risk of developmental delay, provision of mothers' own milk improves their cognitive, physical and visual development, feeding tolerance and reduces their of  risk of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC).  NEC, a life-threatening gastrointestinal emergency, is 6-10 times lower among infants fed mothers' own milk versus formula.  Unfortunately for many VLBW infants, their mothers are unable to supply an adequate volume of milk for a variety of reasons, such as maternal illness and stress. In these instances, preterm formula is provided.  In response to evidence supporting the benefits of mothers' own milk in the VLBW population, donor human milk banks are being established internationally at an unprecedented rate; there is significant interest in doing the same in Canada. It is unclear, however, whether donated milk that requires pasteurization is better than preterm formula as a supplement to mothers' own milk.  To answer this question, health care professionals from a consortium of neonatal nurseries in the greater Toronto area have assembled to carry out a research study to examine the potential benefits, risks and costs of using donor milk versus preterm formula as a supplement to mothers' own milk.  This study will be pivotal in setting public policy for milk banks in Canada. In this clinical trial, when mothers' own milk is unavailable, VLBW infants will be fed either donor milk or preterm formula by random assignment until hospital discharge.  Both groups of infants will be followed for 2 years to determine if there are improvements in development, a reduction in illness and they grow normally using donor milk.  Costs, including direct hospital dollars spent and productivity losses experienced by the families, will be compared between the two supplement options.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the role of group IIA secreted phospholipase A2 in inflammatory arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; AUTOIMMUNITY; INFLAMMATION; LIPIDS; MOUSE MODELS; PHOSPHOLIPASE A2
Abstract-Résumé: With a prevalence of ~0.6%, rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is the most common form of human inflammatory arthritis.  In Canada alone, it is estimated that more than 100 000 people are diagnosed each year with this disorder, with a societal monetary cost measured in the billions.  Since the pathogenic mechanisms of RA remain poorly understood, and current therapies are not preventive and remain only partially effective, further understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms and regulatory pathways active in synovial inflammation promises to yield more effective treatment for patients afflicted with this devastating illness. Among the different proteins detected in joints of patients with RA, the secreted phospholipase A2 (sPLA2) enzymes attracted considerable attention but the actual roles of these proteins in RA were never delineated. The sPLA2 family of enzymes, numbering 9 members in humans, is most studied for their role in generating substrate fatty acid for biosynthesis of lipid mediators. Given the recent insights into sPLA2 diversity, we reexamined sPLA2 expressions and contributions in inflammatory arthritis. Although several sPLA2 isoforms could be detected, our studies confirm the dominant expression of sPLA2-IIA in RA synovial fluids (SF). Importantly, we demonstrate a prominent proinflammatory activity for the sPLA2-IIA isoform in a murine model of arthritis. To our surprise, we also unveil an anti-inflammatory function for another sPLA2 isoform, sPLA2-V. This present research study will aim to unfold the mechanisms by which sPLA2-IIA contributes to arthritis and will examine the predicted necessity for highly selective therapeutic compounds targeting sPLA2-IIA -and not sPLA2-V- as a novel therapeutic for treatment of RA.

NomDuComitéFR: Génomique: Biologie computationnelle et biologie des systèmes
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural variation in medical genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOGENOMICS; DISEASE PREDISPOSITION; DNA AND CHROMOSOME VARIATION; GENOMIC MICROARRARY; QUANTITATIVE AND COPY NUMBER ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic variation forms the basis of evolution and human diversity. In some instances deleterious changes in DNA can occur resulting in disease. The Human Genome Project told us we were 99.9% DNA identical with the majority of changes in our genomes being single letter (nucleotide) differences called SNPs. Over the past five years our group with others have used state-of-the-art technologies to discover that the human genome also contains an abundance of larger previously undetected structural alterations. We now know that the complexity of genetic information related to such 'structural variation' in DNA is greater by an order of magnitude than that for SNPs. These differences among humans reflect the dynamic nature of genomes, and account for both normal variations among us, and those that predispose to conditions of medical consequence. With an international consortium we have generated massive datasets cataloguing the structural copy number variation content in world populations. Our public Database of Genomic Variants has become the primary resource for structural variation data and it is used by thousands of clinicians and scientists. Here, we will expand our database to meet the ever-increasing needs of geneticists and to capture the enormous data coming from personal genome-sequencing projects. We will also investigate novel forms of structural variation, and develop predictive models of how rare genetic variants can influence susceptibility to common complex disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Membrane transport and ion homeostasis in cardiac muscle.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM TRANSPORT; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; MEMBRANE RECONSTITUTION; SODIUM-PROTON EXCHANGE; STRUCTURE-FUNCTION; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Inside of our cells, ion levels are used to control a variety of physiological processes, such as muscle contraction and relaxation. Muscle contraction and relaxation occur as a direct response to oscillations in the cytosolic calcium concentration. To do this, the cell relies on the cyclic release and reuptake of calcium between external and internal stores and the cytosol. In addition, the metabolic processes that allow muscle contraction-relaxation to occur increase the cytosolic proton concentration (acidosis). However, the contractile apparatus in heart muscle is compromised by acidosis. Therefore, the regulated control of both of these ions (calcium and protons) is essential for heart muscle contractility. Calcium metabolism is primarily controlled by the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) - a calcium storage compartment containing a pump (SERCA) that plays a central role in muscle relaxation. Additional proteins 'phospholamban' (PLB) and 'sarcolipin' (SLN) regulate SERCA in response to stress, exercise, and disease. Proton metabolism in the heart is primarily controlled by the plasma membrane, which contains a sodium-proton exchanger (NHE1) that removes intracellular protons. Most intriguing is the pathological role of NHE1 in heart disease. The reduced blood flow that occurs in heart disease activates NHE1; however, under disease conditions NHE1 indirectly triggers cell death. Our research encompasses structure-function studies of these calcium and proton transport systems. First, we use membrane reconstitution systems to provide insights into the mechanism of ion transport. Second, we use techniques called 'x-ray crystallography' and 'electron microscopy' that allow us to determine the arrangement of atoms in the proteins from the interaction with a beam of x-rays or electrons (special forms of light). This will provide us with a molecular picture of the ion transporters, and take us one step closer to the rational improvement of heart performance in patients

TitreApplicationTitle: Athero-protective shear stress signalling in the vasculature
Keywords-MotsClés: AND FISTULA; ANGIOTENSIN; ANIMAL MODELS OF ATHERSCLEROSIS; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; HYPERTENSION; IN VIVO AND CELL IMAGING; MOLECULAR AND CELL BIOLOGY; SHEAR STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases are by far the most prevalent cause of death in developed countries. These diseases, including heart attacks and strokes, often result from atherosclerosis, a fatty deposit of cholesterol, blood cells and fibres in the wall of arteries. Atherosclerotic plaques are not found uniformly in the vasculature; their distribution depends on local blood flow. Vessel segments exposed to high flow, and consequently high "shear stress", are typically devoid of atherosclerotic lesions. On the contrary, vessel segments exposed to low or oscillatory blood flow are prone to atherosclerotic plaque formation. "Shear stress" is the frictional force created by blood on endothelial cells, the inner lining of blood vessels. Our hypothesis is that shear stress is athero-protective because it reduces local angiotensin II (AngII) generation in vessels and decreases the expression of its receptor (AT1R) in endothelial cells. We will define the molecular mechanisms that regulate AT1R expression in endothelial cells exposed to shear stress. We will also determine whether shear stress regulates the generation of AngII in the vascular wall. We will then establish how localised AngII and AT1R expression may increase the risk for atherosclerotic plaque formation in vessels, at the molecular level. Finally, we will determine to what extent endothelial AT1R receptor expression regulates plaque formation in atherosclerotic mice. This study should help us to identify the molecular mechanisms that underlie the athero-protective effects of shear stress. This will point the way to novel therapeutic approaches that could impact on the prevention and treatment of atherosclerosis.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
TitreApplicationTitle: Adult neurogenesis and the central control of energy homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT NEUROGENESIS; BODY WEIGHT SET POINT; CENTRAL CONTROL OF ENERGY HOMEOSTASIS; DIET-INDUCED OBESITY; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; HIGH CALORIC DIET; HYPOTHALAMUS; ICV SURGERY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MOUSE MODEL; NEURAL PLASTICITY; NEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; OBESITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is on the rise at an alarming rate particularly in the developed world and so are obesity-related diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. Yet efforts to reverse this trend through promotion of lifestyle changes or via medical intervention had only limited success so far. Towards developing effective ways to intervene with the obesity pandemic, we want to investigate how the generation of new cells in the adult brain influences body weight. We have previously shown that treatment with a particular anti-obesity drug, ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF), initiates large-scale birthing of new cells in the hypothalamus, a brain area that plays a key role in feeding control. Our research further indicates that these newly born cells are crucial for the weight-lowering effect of the drug. However we do not yet understand how these cells are able to influence body weight. Towards this end, we plan to comprehensively characterize adult-born hypothalamic cells with regard to their function and the ways they mesh into the brain's neuronal network. Moreover we want to know if the cells that are produced by the hypothalamus on its own, i.e., in the absence of CNTF, are required for weight maintenance as well. Because the proposed research approaches body weight regulation from a novel angle, the investigations may open up avenues to more effective obesity treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biology of the fetal-maternal interface
Keywords-MotsClés: DECORIN; PLACENTA; PREECLAMPSIA; REPRODUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT; TROPHOBLAST; VEGF-RECEPTOR-2
Abstract-Résumé: The human placenta is an invasive "tumor- like" structure that invades the pregnant uterus and its arteries to tap on the maternal blood supply and derive nourishment for the fetus. However unlike tumors, placental growth and invasion of the uterus is exquisitely controlled by certain locally derived molecules. Poor placental invasion can result in poor blood flow to the placenta leading to retarded fetal growth and a serious maternal disease called "preeclampsia", whereas excessive invasion is a property of placental cancers. We discovered that two molecules, transforming growth factor beta (TGFbeta)and a TGF-beta-binding proteoglycan called decorin , both produced by cells of the pregnant uterus, independently control placental growth and invasion We also found that  placental cancers defy this control. We have identified molecular mechanisms underlying TGF-beta mediated control of placental growth and invasion, whereas those responsible for decorin action on placental cells remain unknown. Present proposal is to define mechanisms underlying  decorin action and its possible derangements in preeclampsia. This knowledge is critical for prevention, early diagnosis and treating this serious pregnancy associated disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The complex dynamics of Hepatitis C virus and HIV infections among injection drug users: A comprehensive approach.
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTEXTUAL FACTORS; DRUG INJECTION BEHAVIOUR; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEPATITIS C; HIV; LONGITUDINAL COHORT
Abstract-Résumé: Injection drug use accounts for the majority of new cases of Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections and for 30% of all new cases of AIDS in Canada. Despite considerable prevention efforts, HIV incidence in Montreal injection drug users (IDUs) remains among the highest for North American cities, and studies have shown modest or no effect of HIV prevention programs on HCV transmission. In Montreal, up to one in three IDU will contract HCV in the next year, and these figures do not include re-infections. There is a crucial need to estimate the true burden of HCV infection among IDUs and to better assess the determinants of HCV/HIV infections to improve prevention efforts. We recently demonstrated that high-risk injection behaviour among IDUs living in Montreal was associated with neighbourhood educational attainment and low income, and that IDUs living in socioeconomic disadvantaged areas or with a high level of crimes were at higher risk of acquiring HCV. Cumulative duration of injection appeared to influence such relationships. Following acute infection, approximately 26% of recently infected individuals spontaneously clear HCV. Hence, a key question for future HCV vaccine development is whether protective immunity against HCV occurs after HCV clearance. This renewal application seeks to further investigate how individual and contextual factors constitute key potential influences that may exacerbate or attenuate the rate of viral transmission, thereby presenting opportunities for intervention. We will also expand the scope of our research by studying the course of HCV infection, including primary infection, re-infection and clearance among injection drug users.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural mechanisms governing eukaryotic protein kinase signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: CATALYTIC SWITCHING MECHANISMS; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY X-RAY; PHOSPHOREGULATION; PROTEIN KINASE; SIGNALLING DOMAINS; SUBSTRATE RECOGNITION
Abstract-Résumé: The Raf family of protein kinases regulate many aspects of cell function including instructing cells to live or die, to replicate and to form specific types of tissues. Raf kinases are mutated in a large proportion of human cancers suggesting that they play a critical role in cancer formation. This identifies the Raf kinases as good targets to develop drugs to treat disease. Using X-ray microscope techniques, our primary aim we will obtain an atomic level view of how Raf proteins function normally and how genetic mutations cause Raf function to go awry and to cause cancer. A detailed understanding of how Raf proteins function normally and in human cancers may reveal novel strategies to develop drugs to treat cancers caused by rogue versions of Raf proteins.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissection of the complex genetics of host defense against salmonella infection
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEX TRAIT ANALYSIS; FONCTIONAL GENOMICS; QTL MAPPING; SALMONELLA; SEPTIC SHOCK; TRANSCRIPTIONAL PROFILING
Abstract-Résumé: Gram-negative bacilli of the genus Salmonella are ubiquitous in nature.  They are able of producing a spectrum of clinical disease in both animals and man ranging from asymptomatic carriage to life-threatening sepsis.  Human infection occurs in two major patterns, a systemic disease known as typhoid fever or a gastrointestinal illness termed salmonellosis. On a global scale, there are over 16 million cases of typhoid fever reported annually and 600 000 cases of mortality associated with untreated infection. The incidence of reported nontyphoidal salmonellosis has increased dramatically since 1980.  At present, up to 3.7 million cases of salmonellosis are estimated to occur annually in the United States.  The overall aim of this project is to use mouse models of Salmonella infection and a genetic approach to study the pathogenesis of Salmonella infection. Due to the great degree of conservation between the mouse and the human genome, elucidation of the pathways responsible for host resistance in mice can help determine the pathways for the immune response to bacterial infections seen in humans.  A better understanding of the host response to Salmonella infection may have a direct implication on more effective public health interventions and the design of efficient treatments against Salmonella or other intracellular pathogen.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: EGFR Interactions and Phosphorylation
Keywords-MotsClés: EGFR; EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; KINASE; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: A major form of regulation in cells occurs through the addition and removal of phosphate groups to proteins, which is a mechanism to turn them on and off. This process is aberrant in cancers often because enzymes, such as the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), which attach phosphate groups to proteins, are activated as a consequence of genetic mutations. The EGFR and other enzymes (kinases) related to it are drug targets for cancer therapy, but knowing which target(s) is responsible in any given cancer remains a challenge. We have developed methods to characterize the phosphate groups in the proteins of tumors, and believe this "phospho profile" information will be useful in determining what kinases are activated in tumors, and which drug or drug combinations may be effect to treat them. We plan to use this technology to better understand how the activated EGFR causes tumor growth, and how to monitor its activity in tumors. Another process by the EGFR is normally turned off, is by a process called endocytosis. When stimulated, the EGFR is "endocytosed", which causes it to be destroyed. In many cancers including breast and lung, this process is disrupted, and mutant activated EGFR proteins escape being destroyed by endocytosis. Our research has uncovered new information on how this process is regulated, and we will further investigate this important process towards the design of new therapies to trigger the destruction of cancer-causing EGFR proteins.

TitreApplicationTitle: Differential Actions of the Novel Adipokine Chemerin Signaling Through Multiple Receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTE; ADIPOKINE; DIABETES; GENE REGULATION; OBESITY; PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, a growing number of our population have excess fat and are termed obese.  This condition is a major cause of disability and early death. Obese individuals are also at increased risk for diabetes, heart disease and some cancers. However, our understanding of how obesity increases the risk for developing these other disorders remains incomplete. We have identified a chemical called chemerin that is released in increasing amounts from fat with obesity. We propose to study how the changes in chemerin secretion relate to obesity related disorders and to identify new methods to modify the release of chemerin from fat or modify the actions of chemerin in the body.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of neuronal injury induced by dopamine and exogenous toxicants in mice with selective dopamine transporter overexpression.
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENTAL TOXICANTS; NEUROBIOLOGY; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic, progressive neurological disorder characterized by resting tremor, bradykinesia, postural instability and rigidity, resulting from the loss of dopamine (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc). The most vulnerable neurons affected in Parkinson's disease (PD) have the highest density of the phenotypic marker of DA neurons, the plasma membrane dopamine transporter (DAT). DAT is the major controller of DA neuron homeostasis being critically important not only for clearance of released DA from extracellular space but also for maintenance of intracellular DA stores. Thus by altering expression levels of the DAT it is possible to significantly change both extracellular and intracellular DA levels. We recently developed a novel strain of mice over-expressing 6 copies of the DAT gene (DAT-Tg). We propose here to use this strain of mutant mice to evaluate the effect of environmental toxicants known to induce DA cell loss and Parkinosnian phenotypes. There is ample evidence of gene/environment interaction resulting in increased susceptibility of individuals to the deleterious effects of toxicants. Here we propose to directly evaluate whether increases in DAT levels and intracellular DA may increase the toxicity induced by three model toxicants, namely MPTP, rotenone and paraquat. In parallel, we will also directly address whether augmenting DAT levels will lead to increased vulnerability of DA neurons to physiological concentrations of DA and of MPTP. For this, we will use cultured postnatal SN neurons from transgenic mice with varied expression levels of DAT (wild-type (normal expression), DAT-tg (increased expression) and DAT-KO (lack of expression) animals. Using this approach it will be possible to test how DA induced toxicity correlates with DAT levels. This will hopefully allow us to address the specific importance of DAT in DA induced toxicity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cholinergic activation of dopamine neurons in dependence
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; DOPAMINE; ETHANOL; MOUSE; MUSCARINIC; OPIATES
Abstract-Résumé: Opiates are abused drugs that activate midbrain dopamine neurons indirectly via opioid receptors. Opioid receptors are associated with non-dopamine neurons, however, so how opiates cause abuse has not been clear. Ethanol abuse is treated by the opiate receptor blocker naltrexone in humans, suggesting shared mechanisms for opiate and ethanol drug choices.    Morphine's activation of dopamine output in the nucleus accumbens was blocked by lesions of midbrain cholinergic neurons, by muscarinic receptor blockers, or by knockout of the M5 muscarinic receptor gene expressed by dopamine neurons. Furthermore, mice lacking the M5 muscarinic receptor showed less morphine-induced locomotion, drank less ethanol in two-bottle choice tests than wild type mice, and were less sensitive to the opioid receptor antagonist naltrexone in both tasks. M5 knockout males also showed fewer courtship calls during mating, but these were not affected by naltrexone.     We propose to reverse these opiate sensitivity deficits in M5 knockout mice in three different ways: 1) By adding the M5 muscarinic receptor gene into dopamine neurons using the herpes simplex virus. 2) By infusing the growth factor BDNF into the same midbrain area to induce an opiate-dependent-like state. 3) By long-term opiate or ethanol exposure followed by withdrawal. The effects of these procedures on morphine-induced locomotion, ethanol preference, courtship calls in sex, and dopamine output will be measured in knockout and wild-type mice, to better understand dopamine-related changes in opiate and ethanol dependence. These studies will help us understand how the midbrain changes in opiate addiction, and how naltrexone works to treat alcoholism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Somatic cell reprogramming and therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: INCOMPLETE REPROGRAMMING; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; NON-VIRAL REPROGRAMMING; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; TETRACYCLINE INDUCIBLE SYSTEM; TRANSPOSON SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: It has recently become possible to derive stem cells directly from completely differentiated adult cells, like the skin, through a mechanism referred to as reprogramming.  Reprogramming is achieved by forced expression of 2-4 transgenes, which push the cells to a more primitive, pluripotent state. Such so called induced Pluripotent Stem (iPS) cells from individual patients can be grown in large numbers and then turned into a large variety of cell types. These cells could then be used to treat patients suffering from regenerative diseases, while eliminating the risks associated with immune rejection. The current methods of generating iPS cells are associated with numerous viral insertions in the chromosomes of cells, which raises serious safety concerns. My laboratory pioneered the first non-viral production of iPS cells from both mouse and human cells. Interestingly, the other risk factor is the pluripotency of the iPS cells itself, which could cause tumors if pluripotent cells are transplanted into an adult individual. Here we propose a strategy in which we only partially reprogram somatic cells to a stage where they can still "remember" their origin and go back to the original cell type if the transgene expression is stopped. This partial reprogramming will be used to develop models for cell-based therapies of diabetes. Ultimately, the experiments outlined in this proposal will greatly contribute to improve the efficiency and safety of future clinical applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic determinants of plasma lipoproteins
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CORONARY HEART DISEASE; GENETICS; LIPOPROTEINS; METABOLISM; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Disturbances in the blood levels of lipids are strongly associated with increased risk of heart attacks and strokes.  The main lipids are cholesterol and triglyceride.  Blood lipids are a risk factor for atherosclerosis, also called hardening of the arteries. While we have made much progress in understanding and treating disturbances of blood lipids, many patients cannot be treated with current medications, either because such medications are ineffective or because they cause side effects.    The objective of this project is to learn more about the pathways, enzymes and molecules that regulate blood lipid levels by studying the genomes of patients with extremely high or low levels of blood lipids.     The applicant has spent two decades collecting data and samples from patients and families referred to the Lipid Genetics Clinic, London Health Sciences Centre (www.lipidgeneticsclinic.ca) for medical advice and care.  This patient resource converges physically with access to the London Regional Genomics Centre (www.lrgc/ca), and this physical proximity has accelerated and will continue to accelerate discovery of the altered metabolic pathways in patients, beginning the process with close examination of their genetic code.  The newly available genomic technologies will help uncover new aspects of the disease process that have not been previously appreciated or understood.

TitreApplicationTitle: Differential affects of personal and community resources on breast cancer care and long-term survival in Canada and the United States, 1995 to 2015
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER CARE; COMMUNITY SERVICE ENDOWMENTS; INTERNATIONAL COMPARISON; LONG-TERM SURVIVAL; PHYSICIAN SUPPLY; SOCIOECONOMIC FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Publics in both Canada and the US rate health care as a top concern. American advocates, primarily concerned with access problems among the uninsured, call for a more Canada-like single payer system, while Canadian advocates, concerned with health care shortages, call for a more American-like system that would open up more payer (private) options. Our CIHR-funded study aimed to add the voice of science to these debates. It focused on a health problem of great significance: breast cancer. Its funds were invested in the enhancement of public cancer databases so that the most valid conclusions could be drawn from the best available data. We found strong evidence of better cancer care access and survival among low-income Canadians (versus low-income Americans), but we also identified regions of Canada with significant physician shortages. We have routinely reported to researchers, legislators and the public. Some of our findings have been provocative in their contrast with political rhetoric. For example, we observed that low-income American patients wait as long as or even longer than low-income Canadians for chemotherapy. We aim to be a part of making the best possible use of the natural policy laboratory comprised of the adjacent, but distinctly different Canadian and American health care systems. This CIHR renewal grant would enable us to do that. Our first project focused on the lowest economic third of Canadians and Americans. These include not only poor to very poor people, but also the near poor and the lower middle-class. Using large samples of women with breast cancer from diverse urban and rural places in Ontario and California, this next project would focus on their most vulnerable areas: areas of extreme impoverishment and areas of extreme physician shortages. It would provide timely scientific insights into the past, present and future cancer care experiences (1995-2015) of the most vulnerable Canadians and Americans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Problems, Predictors, and Progression of Sexual Functioning among Adolescents
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; GENDER; QUALITATIVE METHODS; RISK AND RESILIENCY; SEXUAL HEALTH; SURVEYS
Abstract-Résumé: The general goal of this proposed multidisciplinary program of research is to assess the prevalence, onset and progression of problems in sexual functioning, risk and protective factors, and associated longer-term outcomes. Adolescents' sexual functioning will be explored using an integrated mixed methods approach that incorporates both qualitative interviews and online longitudinal survey data. This program of research will extend knowledge in several ways. First, it will clarify the extent to which adolescents' lives are affected by problems in their sexual lives, including sexual pain, and the extent to which health professionals are addressing these problems.  Second, it will establish the prevalence of sexual problems among adolescents and help to determine the point of onset. Third, it will identify risk and protective factors related to sexual problems. Fourth, it will establish the longer term impact of decreased sexual health. Finally, the findings will be carefully integrated to inform the development of a gender-sensitive model of adolescent sexual health care and care delivery, and to identify priority areas in adolescents' sexual health to be targeted for future educational initiatives as well as trainings for health care providers serving adolescents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of PTP1B in Her2+ breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; HER2; PTP1B
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the second most common cause of cancer related death in women. One subtype of breast cancer is characterized by the overexpression of a receptor molecule, called HER2. When HER2 is overexpressed, breast cells are stimulated to divide inappropriately. The importance of HER2 overexpression in breast cancer pathogenesis has been dramatically illustrated by the ability of antibodies against HER2 to improve survival of HER2+ breast cancer patients. However, these antibodies are not a panacea, and many women with HER2+ disease will still die of their disease. We have found that a molecule that normally regulates HER2, called protein-tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B), is required for HER2-overexpressing cells to cause breast cancer, at least in mice. Specifically, mice rendered genetically deficient for PTP1B are resistant to the ability of HER2 over-expression to induce tumors. However, PTP1B also affects several other pathways in mice - for example, it regulates insulin responses and body weight - so the exact reason why PTP1B deficiency causes breast cancer resistance remains unclear. We will determine how PTP1B deficiency causes breast cancer resistance at the cellular and molecular level, and also determine whether PTP1B deficiency and/or inhibition of PTP1B activity, prevents or reverses carcinogenesis in human HER2+ breast cancer cell lines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lipid-based nanopharmaceuticals alone and in combination to treat aggressive forms of cancer: Design and development of formulations capable of causing tumor specific blood vessel damage
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; COMBINATIONS; NANOTECHNOLOGY; PRECLINICAL; TREATMENTS; TUMOR VASCULATURE
Abstract-Résumé: The environment where tumor cells thrive is highly dependent on the tumor's ability to co-opt existing blood vessels and promote development of new blood vessels. Thus a key to limiting the growth of existing tumors and stopping the spread of cancer involves targeting blood vessels within tumors. Previously this research identified a drug formulation that exerts some of its therapeutic effects through a mechanism that involves tumor specific vascular damage. This was a fortuitous and unexpected discovery and more research is needed to better understand this therapeutic effect. The formulation is composed of synthetic and naturally occurring biodegradable lipids (fat molecules) that self associate to form small (100 times smaller than a red blood cell) spheres which can enclose 10,000 or more drug molecules inside. This new formulation (called Irinophore C) will be tested in cancer patients for the first time next year (2010). Importantly, it is expected that other drug formulations can be designed to cause more selective damage to the blood vessels within tumors. Before this can be done, however, several important questions need to be answered: How does vascular damage occur? What are the biological consequences? What formulation parameters can be modified to achieve more selective damage? Answers to these questions will be used to help design drug candidates that achieve unmatched treatment outcomes when used to treat experimental models of aggressive cancers. This research is focused on developing drug candidates that have the potential to be effective in patients with relapsed and metastatic disease as well as patients with cancers that are not effectively treated with currently available drugs. The treatments developed will build on existing treatment standards which use multiple drugs to achieve significant increases in the time patients live free of detectable disease when treated at doses that have little or no impact on the patient's quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functions of the activating E2fs beyond cell cycle control
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; CHROMATIN; CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUTS; DNA REPAIR; E2F; NEUROGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: The E2f family play crucial roles in human cancer.  In some cases they can drive cancer by promoting cell division.  In other cases low E2f activity facilitates tumor growth, but it is now clear how this occurs.  There are drugs in the clinic that inhibit E2f activity.  It is important to understand the contexts in which these inhibit (good) or promote (bad!) cancer  We have discovered that many normal cell types do not need E2fs to divide.  Instead, their critical role appears to be to promote survival and to prevent DNA damage.  In their absence, cells divide, but are stressed.  This stress is seen as increased cell death and a molecular signature common to cells with damaged DNA.  We believe that in this context, the cells are trying to prevent mutations occuring in genes that could promote cancer.  In otherwords, it appears that E2fs may prevent cancer by ensuring safe DNA replication.  Here, we will examine the effect of E2f loss in multiple tissues.  We are especially interested in those cell types that show increased DNA damage, and we believe these may be the ones that generate tumors when E2f activity is low.  Elucidating the contexts and mechanism through which low E2f activity leads to tumor formation, will guide the appropriate use of E2f inhibitors for the safe treatment of human cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: "Spot Sign" Selection of Intracerebral Hemorrhage to Guide Hemostatic Therapy (SPOTLIGHT): A Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE STROKE; CLINICAL; HEMOSTATIC THERAPY; INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE; NEUROIMAGING; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: This study tackles the problem of intracerebral hemorrhage, a serious type of stroke caused by bleeding into the brain from a ruptured blood vessel. It accounts for 10-30% of all strokes worldwide, often affecting young people, and is the deadliest, most disabling, and least treatable stroke type. Sadly, there are no proven emergency medical treatments available. We urgently need to develop an effective therapy and identify which patients will benefit most from treatment. The ideal treatment is one that can act quickly to stop bleeding and prevent hemorrhages from enlarging to a critical, life-threatening size. Now, an exciting treatment called "Factor 7", which has been used for years for other bleeding disorders, holds great promise for treating brain hemorrhages. Recently, "Factor 7" was shown to reduce the amount of bleeding in the brain by 58%! However, this did not translate into improved survival or reduced disability when given to a group of unselected patients. We believe this treatment will work best when given to a specific subgroup of brain hemorrhage patients that we call the "spot sign" patients. This study will test whether treatment in the emergency room with "Factor 7" is beneficial for brain hemorrhage patients who have a "spot sign" on brain scanning.  A "spot sign" is detected by a contrast CT scan of the blood vessels in the head. Our group described this sign in 2007 as a bright dot within a hemorrhage, corresponding to leakage of contrast dye (extravasation) from a bleeding blood vessel. If a "spot sign" is present, it predicts a very high risk of worsening due to continued bleeding in the brain. About one-third of patients have a "spot sign" (indicating active bleeding) and two-thirds do not have a "spot sign" (indicating the bleeding has already stopped). Therefore, this sign should predict which patients will respond best to "Factor 7" therapy. If proven correct, this approach could revolutionize the management of hemorrhagic stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chemokines and chemoattractants: a hierarchy of signals to allow neutrophil chemotaxis to sites of infection
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CHEMOTAXIS; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; NEUTROPHIL; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Our first line of defense against bacteria and other invading organisms are white cells called neutrophils.  To find these bacteria, the neutrophils must follow cues or road signs provided by our own immune system called chemokines.  However, when in close enough proximity to bacteria, the neutrophils begin to sense the bacteria directly and must ignore our own chemokines.  Understanding how this transpires is the main theme of this grant.  We have set up a simple system of 3 wells where we put neutrophils in a center well and we place a chemokine in a left well and bacterial products in a right well.  We will begin to study the molecules within the cells that signal the cells to decide to go right instead of left.  We believe there are two separate signaling pathways involved inside the neutrophils that include p38 MAPK, PIXa and PLA2 for bacterial products and PI3K, PTEN and SHIP1 in response to chemokines.  Finally, we developed a way to watch neutrophils make these decisions in vivo, using a technique termed intravital microscopy.  We believe that in a live animal, the crawling of neutrophils will be a very complex situation.  The final series of experiments will involve the use of bacteria to ascertain that results from our simplified systems do in fact apply to a relevant infection model.  The mechanisms will be elucidated in mice that lack the aforementioned molecules.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of yeast H2A.Z effector pathways involved in gene expression (Caractérisation de voies effectrices de H2A.Z impliquées dans l'expression génique chez la levure)
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER; CHROMATIN; GENE TRANSCRIPTION; GENETICS; H2A.Z
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory uses budding yeast as an experimental system to study how proteins that compact our genomes can actually regulate how genes are expressed.  Moreover, we also study other types of proteins and enzymes that can change this levels of chromosomal compaction.  Importantly, these proteins are well conserved in humans, and mis-regulations of its actions may lead to cancer progression in certain cases.  To achieve our goals, we use a variety of state-of-the-art technologies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of gene expression by aryl hydrocarbon receptor and estrogen receptor alpha
Keywords-MotsClés: ARYL HYDROCARBON RECEPTOR; BREAST CANCER; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; ESTROGEN RECEPTOR; GENOMICS; TOXICOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common non-skin cancer and second leading cause of cancer death in Canadian women. Although breast cancer is significantly influenced by genetics, the risk of breast cancer is influenced by lifestyle and environment. Exposure to certain chemicals is suspected to contribute to increases in the risk of developing breast cancer. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) and estrogen receptor alpha (ERalpha) are two proteins that play key physiological roles in cells, but are also implicated in diseases such as breast cancer. AHR mediates most, if not all, of the toxic effects of environmental contaminants called dioxins, whereas ERalpha is the key regulator of estrogen action and an important pharmaceutical target for breast cancer therapy. Previous studies have shown that these two proteins and their associated networks interact with each other and that this interplay is regulated by activation of AHR by dioxins. However, the molecular mechanisms remain elusive. The overall objective of this study is to elucidate the mechanisms of reciprocal interplay between AHR and ERalpha. To attain this objective, we will use molecular and cellular biology techniques in conjunction with biochemical approaches and animal models to better understand of the AHR/ERalpha interplay. These results will enable better estimates of the health risks associated with the combined environmental and dietary exposure to modulators of AHR and ERalpha activity and clarify the role of AHR in diseases such as breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cloning and functional analysis of nuclear gene defects for respiratory chain disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL GENETICS; FUNCTIONAL COMPLEMENTATION; MAMMALIAN CELL CULTURE; MITOCHONDRIAL DISEASE; MOLECULAR GENETICS; OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: All cells in the body require a steady source of chemical energy to carry out their normal physiological functions. The majority of this chemical energy, which is packaged as a compound called ATP, is produced by the oxidation of carbohydrate and fat in a biochemical process called oxidative phosphorylation. This process takes place in a compartment of the cell called the mitochondrion, and is carried out by several large protein complexes that constitute the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Respiratory chain dysfunction interferes with the normal supply of energy, and this produces a wide variety of different diseases, the nature and severity of which depend on the exact genetic defect. The genetics of respiratory chain diseases is complicated by the fact that some components of the system are encoded in nuclear genes, others in a small genome that is contained within the mitochondria themselves. Diseases caused by nuclear gene defects generally produce the most severe phenotypes (neurodegeneration, heart or liver failure) with onset at birth or during early infancy, and are usually fatal.   The aim of this proposal is to identify nuclear gene defects in these patients. We will do this by complementing the defect in patient cells by the transfer of normal human chromosomes. This permits us to map the position of the defective gene on a chromosome, and ultimately to identify it. Successful identification of the defective gene leads directly to the development of diagnostic tests that are made freely available to patients and their physicians. Characterization of the function of the genetic mutation provides biological insight into the normal assembly and function of the respiratory chain, which may ultimately permit us to devise treatments for these devastating disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biochemistry and genetics of wall teichoic biogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC; BACTERIAL GENETICS; ENZYMOLOGY; GRAM-POSITIVE BACTERIA; INFECTION; WALL TEICHOIC ACID
Abstract-Résumé: Resistance has developed to virtually all antibiotics used in the clinic today.  Particularly worrisome are Gram-positive infections caused by organisms such as Staphylococci that cause often-fatal hospital infections and are increasingly a cause for concern in the community setting.  The problem is that in the last 40 years or so only two truly novel chemical compounds have been discovered for the treatment of bacterial infections.  Indeed most of the antibiotics currently in use were discovered prior to 1960.  Since then, the lion's share of antibacterial drug development has involved minor changes to these chemicals.  Bacterial resistance to these modified drugs has never been far behind these minor structural changes.    Modern approaches to antibacterial drug discovery have emphasized strategies to discover truly novel chemicals with unique mechanisms.  The thinking is that a focus on new targets in the bacteria will give rise to new chemical matter that kill bacteria with novel mechanisms for which there are no pre-existing resistance mechanisms.  The problem with this approach is that bacterial physiology and the interactions of bacterial pathogens with patients are remarkably complex.  Success in drug discovery is critically dependent on a deep understanding of the biology behind new targets.   In the work proposed here we are laying the groundwork for a meticulous understanding of the physiology of wall teichoic acid synthesis in Gram-positive bacteria.  Our work aims to test the hypothesis that wall teichoic acid is a critically important component of the cell walls of pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus and that there are druggable targets in the teichoic acid biosynthetic pathway.  Ultimately, it is hoped that these studies will contribute to the development of new antibacterial drugs.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; CARDIOLOGIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Electromechanical- and intersubunit coupling in voltage-gated ion channels
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EPISODIC ATAXIA; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; SINGLE MOLECULE FLUORESCENCE; VOLTAGE-CLAMP FLUOROMETRY; VOLTAGE-GATED ION CHANNELS
Abstract-Résumé: Voltage-gated ion channels are responsible for the electrical signals in our central nervous system and for the heart beat. Defects in genes encoding for voltage-gated ion channels lead to severe inherited diseases, which include episodic ataxia I (sporadic discoordination) and LQT syndrome (irregular heart beat). Ion channels are therefore a major drug target, and it is important to achieve a thorough understanding of their structure-function relations. The channels respond to the electrical voltage over the cell wall of e.g. nerve cells and open, in response to higher potentials, a central pore that allows ions to pass through the cell wall between the inside and outside of the cell. The channels are formed of two modules, the voltage-sensor and the pore. It is known that the voltage sensor moves in response to voltage. This movement in turn has to be transferred to pore opening, a process called electromechanical coupling. In this project, we are investigating how this electromechanical coupling is working.  The channels consist of four identical units, which are thought to influence each other (cooperativity). We will also investigate the coupling of the four subunits as it is closely related to electromechanical coupling. To achieve our goal, we will investigate modified (mutant) channels using simultaneous electrophysiology and fluorescence spectroscopy (voltage-clamp fluorometry). This technique allows us to visualize the movement in the order of a few A (10e-10m) of a specific point in the protein and - at the same time - measure the opening of the channel. We can even see the movement (fluorescence) of a single channel so that we can identify how the four identical parts of the channel are coupled to each other. We found several mutations that influence the coupling also to cause the disease episodic ataxia. If we understand the coupling mechanism in detail, we will also be able to define strategies to design drugs to correct abnormal coupling

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of susceptibility genes for calcific aortic valve stenosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIFIC AORTIC VALVE STENOSIS; CASE-CONTROL POPULATION; GENOME-WIDE ASSOCIATION STUDY; GENOMICS; GENOTYPING; SUSCEPTIBILITY GENES
Abstract-Résumé: The aortic valve is a key component of the heart that ensures proper circulation of blood. Calcification of the aortic valve, or more specifically aortic stenosis, is the third leading cause of heart disease in adults. The incidence increases with age and with the current shift toward an older population, it is likely to become a major societal and economic burden. There is currently no medical treatment available other than open heart surgery to replace the diseased native valve by a prosthetic heart valve. It is thus urgent to understand the cause of the disease at the most fundamental levels in order to elucidate new therapeutic options. Many factors are predicted to cause the disease and an important genetic predisposition is anticipated. However, only a small number of studies have tried to identify the susceptibility genes. In this research program, we plan to expand this work using a new genomic approach called genome-wide association (GWA) study. This approach is the gold standard to identify susceptibility genes in human diseases. To achieve the first GWA study on aortic stenosis, we propose to recruit a cohort of control individuals to match an existing cohort of patients with the disease that we have collected during the last few years. This strategy will allow us to build a case-control series of patients with aortic stenosis (750 cases and 750 controls) and to perform the most effective genetic analyses. In addition, the creation of this large case-control cohort will serve as a major research resource to study the genetics of aortic stenosis for many years to come. The ultimate goal is to develop a comprehensive research program on the genetics of aortic stenosis in order to elucidate its genetic determinants. Overall, identifying causal and susceptibility genes will increase our understanding of the disease process, which can subsequently lead to innovative therapeutic strategies to treat this life-threatening and frequent disease.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal mechanisms underlying the emergence of selective attentional control
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTIONAL CONTROL; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NEURONAL SYNCHRONIZATION; NONHUMAN PRIMATES; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; VISUAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Our brains contain billions of cells. These cells need to interact to ensure that we successfully achieve our aims in a dynamically changing environment. When aiming to read a newspaper article we narrow our attention to the words and sentences ahead, but we are influenced by the value of alternative actions, like grasping the cup of coffee that promises to be tasty. Thus, controlling what to attend to at any moment in time is effortful, and it is influenced by the reward promised by alternatives.  This control is achieved by brain cells. Some cells are known to be crucial to control where to attend to, whereas other cells are crucial to evaluate the reward value of the current and alternative goals. Our research program aims to understand how these two gross types of brain cells interact to control successfully attention to achieve our goals. Our research program is particularly innovative in focusing on the dynamic interplay between brain cells in different regions of the brain. This interplay is known to involve rhythmic coordination among many cells from many different regions. And disturbance of rhythmic coordination during attentional control has been implicated in many severe neurological diseases.  Despite clear indications of its importance, it is unknown whether rhythmic coordination of brain activity has causal consequences for failures of attentional control. We aim to uncover this missing knowledge by recording brain activation patterns at the highest spatial resolution in monkeys while they perform a selective attention tasks in a dynamic environment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Polynucleotide kinase: its role in DNA single-strand break repair and a potential therapeutic target to enhance radio- and chemotherapy.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICAL APPROACHES; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR; IONIZING RADIATION; SMALL MOLECULE INHIBITOR
Abstract-Résumé: A problem frequently encountered in cancer therapy is that of tumour cell resistance to therapeutic agents, so that although the majority of cells in a tumour will be destroyed, a small fraction will survive, and have the potential to metastasize. At present our ability to predict tumour response to treatment or diminish the resistance to radiation or drugs is very limited. Such methods are only likely to be developed when we have a clearer understanding, at the molecular level, of how cells respond to these agents. For many of these agents, DNA is considered to be the main target leading to cell death. It is known that cells have the capacity to repair much of this damage. Uncovering all the enzymes responsible for repair and learning how they operate is still a major task. This proposal focuses on a particular type of damage, DNA strand breaks, and on the role of a particular enzyme, polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP), in mediating the repair of these lesions. We intend to learn how it interacts with other proteins required to mend strand breaks and if it plays an important role in making cells resistant to a variety of anti-cancer drugs. We also intend to develop inhibitors of this enzyme that may be used clinically to counter its activity in cancer cells and thereby improve the ability of the therapeutic agents to kill tumour cells.

ResearchClassEN: BRAIN TUMORS (INCL. RETINAL TUMORS); BRAIN TUMORS THERAPY
ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS CEREBRALES (ET RETINIENNES); THERAPIE DES TUMEURS CEREBRALES
TitreApplicationTitle: GATA4 and GATA6 Transcription Factors in Gliomagenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: GATA TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; NEUROONCOLOGY; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENE
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last 4yrs we demonstrated how a well-characterized mouse transgenic glioma model we created can be used to discover novel genetic alterations which are relevant in human gliomas, by a technique called gene-trap. We isolated and proved that loss of GATA6,a gene that encodes a transcription factor which is expressed in normal embryonic and adult brain,is involved in human glioma progression. A close but distinct family member of GATA6 is GATA4, which our published and submitted data also demonstrates loss in both low and high grade human gliomas. In this application we will: 1-Characterize where in the overall transformation process from normal astrocytes to low-grade and subsequent high-grade astrocytomas does loss of GATA4 and GATA6 play a role. We will undertake this by transgenic mouse glioma models; 2- We will determine whether alterations in GATA4 and GATA6 play a role in human glioma stem or initiating cells; 3-Determine and validate genes regulated by GATA4 and GATA6 and their role in astrocytoma formation; 4- Determine interactions of GATA4 and GATA6 loss with other genetic alterations towards human astrocytoma prognosis and how loss of these transcription factors may facilitate resistance to chemotherapies currently used in human gliomas. Collectively our past and proposed work illustrates how replenishable well-characterized mouse models of human cancers, in our case gliomas, can be utilized towards increasing our understanding of their human counterparts towards potential of identifying and testing novel biological therapeutic targets.

AreasOfScienceEN: NERVOUS SYSTEM; MUSCLE, BONE, OR JOINT
DomainesScientifiquesFR: SYSTÈME NERVEUX; MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS
ResearchClassEN: STROKE, HEART FAILURE; MULTIPLE DISEASE RELEVANCE
ClasseRechercheFR: APOPLEXIE, INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Visuomotor control of locomotion
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGING; KINEMATICS; LOCOMOTION; REHABILITATION; STROKE; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Vision is a powerful source of information to control locomotion. We have previously shown that persons with stroke have an altered processing of visual motion information (optic flow) to control their speed and direction of walking. It remains unclear if such altered walking behaviours are caused by difficulties in discriminating visual motion or in integrating multiple sources of sensory and motor information during gait. Whether the expression and severity of the altered walking behaviours is explained by the brain lesion location is also unclear. We aim to understand, using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), normal brain structures that are involved in the discrimination of heading and active control of steering when exposed to optic flow. We will also investigate whether optic flow speed modifies brain activation while discriminating heading direction. The ability of stroke and healthy individuals to discriminate heading and control steering during simulated self-motion in sitting will be examined. Steering performances in sitting vs. walking will further be investigated to assess the contribution of sensorimotor deficits related to postural and gait dysunctions post stroke. Finally, we will determine whether individuals post stroke can adapt and hence learn to enhance their steering performance in response to repeated optic flow exposure. The visual control of walking is essential to safely navigate in the environment. The proposed studies will provide insights on brain functions, in particular visual perception in the control of walking after stroke. Results will also lead to the development of a virtual reality-based locomotor training protocol that incorporates manipulation of visual motion information.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - B: Clinical Behavioural Sciences
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of CNS inflammation in schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE; INFLAMMATION; MICROGLIA; OXIDATIVE STRESS; POST-MORTEM; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a serious mental illness that will affect approximately 1% of Canadians at some point in their lifetime. It is a chronic condition and symptoms evolve over time. Although the prevailing theory is that this disorder results from abnormal brain development, new evidence suggests that brain pathology gets progressively worse over the course of the illness. The cause of these ongoing changes has not yet been identified. We propose that inflammation is present in the brains of individuals with SCZ and is involved in the evolving brain pathology observed in this disorder. Inflammation can lead to behavioural changes, such as alterations in mood and cognition. In addition, brain inflammation is known to result in pathology similar to that observed in chronic SCZ patients. Although markers of inflammation have been found in the blood of patients with SCZ, it is not yet clear whether inflammation is also present in the brains of these individuals. While our preliminary evidence suggests that this is the case, further studies are required. We therefore propose to carry out a comprehensive study of markers of brain inflammation, including measurement of microglial cells, cytokines, complement protein and transcription factors, in post-mortem brain tissue obtained from individuals with SCZ and from non-psychiatric controls. These studies will advance our understanding of the pathology of this disorder and could provide new targets for medications.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: ASPECTS PSYCHOSOCIAUX/COMPORTEMENTS; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
ResearchClassEN: ATTENTION DEFICIT HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER (ADHD); PSYCHOSOCIAL AND HEALTH BEHAVIOURS
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLE D'HYPERACTIVITÉ AVEC DÉFICIT DE L'ATTENTION (THADA); SANTE ET FACTEURS PSYCHOSOCIAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Adult ADHD: exploring gender, symptoms and social outcomes using a population-based survey
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHD
Abstract-Résumé: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a commonly diagnosed childhood psychiatric disorder. Clinical studies have found that ADHD can continue into adulthood and be associated with increased negative social outcomes, including substance abuse, risky driving, poorer health status, although there is controversy about how often these negative outcomes occur and whether they are due to other disorders. Controversy also relates to gender. Among children, boys are 3 to 9 times more likely to be assessed with ADHD compared to girls, while the few adult studies suggest that ADHD rates in men are similar to women. These gender and age differences could be due to differences in symptoms displayed (e.g. inattentive vs. hyperactive/impulsive), diagnosis and acting-out behaviours associated more with ADHD boys. Recent research has highlighted the importance of examining these different symptom domains as they may be associated with different negative social outcomes and the need for different treatments.  No Canadian studies examining ADHD in the general adult population are available. The proposed study will examine ADHD by adding ADHD questions to the Ontario Monitor, an on-going provincial survey of health and well-being.  Specifically, we will analyze ADHD screening questions, previous diagnosis and medication use by gender and age. Additionally, we will examine whether negative social outcomes are due to ADHD, or other psychiatric problems. Better understanding of adult ADHD by gender and age through a population-based survey can provide evidence of potentially gender-differentiated symptom patterns, outcomes, under-diagnosis and can guide diagnosis and treatment. For example, knowledge on whether the underlying problems are related to ADHD or anxiety would lead to different treatment approaches. Assessment of adult ADHD in a sample of Canadians would also provide important data to regulatory bodies for treatment planning and resource allocation.
