NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
ResearchClassEN: MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL DISEASES; MENTAL DISABILITY
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; RETARD MENTAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Genomics of idiopathic intellectual disabilities
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRAY-CGH; BIOINFORMATICS; FUNCTIONAL GENE ANALYSIS; GENOMICS; HEALTH CARE; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Intellectual disability (ID) is a diagnosis given to persons who have life-long cognitive and adaptive impairments that commence in early life. ID affects about 1-3% of the population, thus nearly 1 million Canadians have an ID. The cause of ID is unknown in at least 40% of all cases. Recent reports have shown that very tiny chromosome changes are the cause of many cases of ID. These tiny chromosome anomalies are usually not seen using routine microscopic analysis. We are using the technology of genomic arrays to look for tiny chromosomal abnormalities in children with ID and have identified them in 10% of children studied so far.  In the next stage we wish to understand how these tiny chromosomal changes cause ID by studying the function of genes they contain (their sequence, expression, replication). In order to facilitate the selection of candidate ID genes to study, we will create a unique database which will integrate clinical and genetic information from the current and future children we plan to study with genomic arrays. Such a database will also enhance our ability to recognize common clinical features of children who share a genetic alteration, lead to description of novel syndromes and development of Health Care Watches to assist in their health management.

TitreApplicationTitle: Calcium perturbation, ER stress and the pathogenesis of dilated cardiomyopathy
Keywords-MotsClés: CA2+ REGULATION; CARDIOMYOPATHY; ER STRESS; HEART FAILURE; IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: A heart beat is a cycle of contraction and relaxation of the heart muscle. Contraction occurs when extracellular calcium and calcium located in intracellular membrane stores flows into the muscle cell through calcium channels. Relaxation begins when calcium is pumped out of muscle cells or into internal stores by calcium pumps. If the calcium pumps are maximally active, calcium will be removed from the heart cells at a higher rate and the heart muscle can relax more rapidly and completely. If the internal store is maximally filled by more active calcium pumps, the amount of calcium released into the heart muscle is greater and the force of the subsequent contraction is greater. Calcium pumps in the heart do not always work maximally. They are associated with an inhibitor protein called phospholamban so that calcium pumping activity is reduced sharply. The association between the calcium pump and phospholamban is disrupted, however, when special demands on the body are met by release of adrenalin into the blood. Adrenalin changes the structure of phospholamban so that it can no longer inhibit the calcium pump. Now calcium stores can be loaded with calcium more rapidly and fully so that the heart undergoes a more rapid and complete relaxation and subsequent contractions have greater force. Specific mutations of phospholamban can cause cardiomyopathy. Our laboratory has investigated a mouse line carrying a phospholamban mutation, R9C, which causes dilated cardiomyopathy and premature death in both humans and mice. We have found that the R9C mutation causes changes in the heart that "stress" the ER membrane system which synthesizes secreted proteins and regulates calcium concentrations. In our application, we propose experiments aimed at understanding how the R9C mutation, which alters cellular calcium dynamics, can cause ER stress and how ER stress can alter calcium dynamics. Since ER stress pathway offer many potential drug targets for reversing cardiomyopathy.

CommitteeNameEN: Psychosocial, Sociocultural & Behavioural Determinants of Health
NomDuComitéFR: Déterminants psychosociaux, socioculturels et comportementaux de la santé
ResearchClassEN: PSYCHO-SOCIAL AND BEHAVIOURAL RESEARCH; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES PSYCHOSOCIALES ET COMPORTEMENTALES; RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: PATHWAYS: Evaluating the Transition of Psychiatric Services from Hospital to Community
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL AND BEHAVIOURAL OUTCOMES; CONSUMER SATISFACTION AND QUALITY OF LIFE; DEINSTITUTIONALIZATION; HEALTH SERVICES; MENTAL HEALTH; RISK ASSESSMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Individuals living with mental health problems have traditionally been segregated from the general population and placed in large psychiatric hospitals. The separation of psychiatric patients from family and the stigma that results from forcing mentally ill individuals to essentially live outside of the greater community has been seriously criticized. Partly as a result of these issues, throughout Canada and the world, psychiatric beds are being closed and large hospitals are shutting their doors. Increasingly, the delivery of psychiatric services is being transferred to community settings. Consistent with this approach, the British Columbia Ministry of Health has put into place a plan to close Riverview Hospital. Despite the staggering fiscal and humanitarian implications of implementing such dramatic changes in health policy, we have very little research to inform our understanding of the effects of moving psychiatric patients out of large hospitals and relocating them in the community. Given the dramatic gap between knowledge and practice, our team will intensively track the movement of a cohort of psychiatric patients for a 2-year period initially, and ultimately for 5 and 10 years, to determine pre-post transfer changes in patients': (1) mental health, physical health, and health related behaviours (e.g., substance misuse); (2) contacts with social agencies (e.g., homeless shelters, criminal justice system), and (3) quality of life and satisfaction with the setting and services. Our study will provide previously unavailable information to guide mental health policy in Canada and abroad. The results will also have important clinical relevance to the Canadian and international health communities.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
ClasseRechercheFR: EPILEPSIE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular targets of kainate-induced neuron death in the hippocampus
Keywords-MotsClés: CHIMERAS; HIPPOCAMPUS; KAINIC ACID; MOUSE MODEL; NEURON DEATH
Abstract-Résumé: Proper brain function relies on the communication between cells (neurons) in the brain and this largely depends on excitatory and inhibitory actions between neurons. The disruption of this balance can result in epilepsy and seizures and the death of neurons that are over-stimulated. In the laboratory, we have developed a mouse model to study the cellular signatures of neuron death using an agent, kainic acid, which overstimulates neurons. An experimental, whole animal model is used that has mixtures of neurons that are sensitive or resistant to the detrimental effects of kainic acid and we will study the factors that are within the neurons or that are part of the environment that determine whether neurons will die. This will lead us to therapeutic approaches to limit neuron death that often follow epileptic episodes or stroke.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - A: Reproduction, Maternal, Child and Youth Health
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Studies concerning the roles of the ADAMTS at the maternal-fetal interface during early pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOMETRIUM; IMPLANTATION; MATERNAL-FETAL INTERFACE; PLACENTA; PREGNANCY; TROPHOBLAST
Abstract-Résumé: Infertility affects approximately 10% of couples trying to establish a family. These statistics are rapidly increasing in developed countries as women continue to choose to delay child-bearing. A major underlying cause of infertility is believed to be the inability of the embryo to interact with the lining of the uterus (endometrium), a condition known as pregnancy loss.  Furthermore, preeclampsia is a disorder of pregnancy that has severe consequences for the mother and her unborn child. A better understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms of pregnancy would reduce the emotional and physical toll that these reproductive health problems have on women and alleviate the huge financial burden that they create for the health care system.  In the studies outlined in this application, we will use cells isolated from human placenta or endometrium and grown in culture to answer the following questions 1) how do placenta cells and endometrial cells interact with one another to create an interface between the mother and fetus that permits the exchange of essential nutrients and waste products? and 2) what hormones regulate this process? We believe that disruption(s) in the activity of these developmental pathways is the underlying cause(s) of pregnancy loss and, in less severe cases, preeclampsia. The long term goals of these studies are to develop, novel cell-based diagnostic tools and therapies for the management and/or treatment of these and other related, reproductive health problems.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: Secreted Effectors From Shigella flexneri That Target the Ubiquitin Proteasome System.
Keywords-MotsClés: INNATE IMMUNITY; PATHOGENESIS; SHIGELLA; TYPE III EFFECTORS; TYPE III SECRETION; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Shigella spp. is a food and water-borne pathogen and is the causative agent of dysentery, a severe diarrheal disease, which kills a million people yearly. Most of these victims are children under the age of 5 in the developing world. Our understanding of how Shigella spp. causes disease is limited and as a result, there is currently no effective vaccine against Shigella infection. The Shigella bacterium injects more than 20 proteins into the infected mammalian cells. These proteins, known as effectors, interfere with the immune response and are required for Shigella to cause disease. Recently, we have discovered the function of the largest class of these effector proteins, the IpaH proteins. IpaH proteins are a new class of enzymes that mark human proteins for destruction using the host cell's own machinery. By determining what human proteins the IpaH enzymes target we will learn what proteins are impaired by Shigella in order for it to cause disease.  A basic understanding of how the IpaHs work will also aid in our understanding of Shigella pathogenesis and provide insight to novel therapies to treat dysentery.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical Outcomes and Tissue Changes in Knee Osteoarthritis:  A Novel Approach Using Cumulative Knee Loading
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOMECHANICS; GAIT; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Knee osteoarthritis causes chronic pain, limits mobility and reduces quality of life for thousands of Canadians.  The magnitude and repetition of mechanical loads placed on the knee during daily activities are very important to understanding why knee osteoarthritis worsens over time.  Unfortunately, studying the loads in a laboratory setting does not provide a complete understanding of the pain and mobility limitations people with this condition experience. We need fresh approaches to understanding and correcting these joint loads to improve health for people with knee osteoarthritis.   Our innovative approach to measuring the magnitude and repetition of knee joint loads that occur during every day activity is called "cumulative knee load."  To identify magnitude, we will measure the loads a person places on their knees during walking in a laboratory. To identify repetition, we will use a device like a pedometer to count a person's activities over one week. Cumulative load will be calculated by multiplying the loads by the week-long activity count. The relationships between cumulative load and knee alignment, obesity and muscle strength will be investigated.  We will also investigate the link between cumulative knee load and damage of knee cartilage and bone using magnetic resonance imaging.  Ultimately, our goal is to predict knee osteoarthritis progression and cartilage damage over 3 years by evaluating the magnitude and repetition of loads experienced throughout daily activity.   Clinicians can use cumulative load to facilitate early detection of knee OA by identifying overuse due to physical activity in people at risk. Clinicians can also use cumulative load to track the progression of this disease and to tailor exercise programs for each person. As a result, cumulative load is a novel approach with great potential to advance care for people with knee osteoarthritis.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: A novel Src/ezrin signalling network as a potential marker for breast cancer metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CELL INVASION; MET/INTEGRINS; METASTASIS; SRC/EZRIN; TUMOUR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The team has previously shown that certain scafolding proteins in tissues surrounding cells can "turn on" the growth factor receptor Met expressed on the surface of breast cancer cells, and they are now trying to learn more about this interaction. They have discovered that an oncogene (a cancer-causing gene) called Src helps control Met's activity. They have also learned that by interacting with a protein called ezrin (that tethers the outer cell membrane to internal cytoskeleton structures), Src can stimulate breast cancer cells to spread to other parts of the body (termed metastasis). Furthermore, ezrin is required for local invasion and distant metastasis of breast cancer cells. This proposal will investigate how Src and ezrin may regulate local tumour spreading and metastasis, using defined culture and animal models of human breast cancer. A better understanding of the Src and ezrin signalling pathways that regulate these processes may lead to new approaches to early detection and effective predictors for treatment response of breast cancer metastasis in the future.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - C: Behavioural Studies, Neuroscience and Cognition
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Integration of decision making and motor planning in primate premotor cortex
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL CORTEX; DECISION-MAKING; MOTOR PLANNING; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; NON-HUMAN PRIMATES; VOLUNTARY MOVEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: This project investigates how the brain makes decisions about voluntary actions. Recent studies motivate the hypothesis that the brain regions involved in the guidance of actions such as reaching are also involved in the process of deciding about which action to take. This hypothesis suggests that populations of neurons in the cerebral cortex, each representing a different reach direction, can simultaneously encode several potential reaching actions. These representations compete by mutually trying to suppress each other until a single winner emerges. The competition is biased by a variety of influences, including estimates of possible payoffs of the different actions, such that the most desirable action wins the competition and is released into execution. This project investigates how that competition takes place. It involves recording neural activity from the cerebral cortex of monkeys trained to perform a variety of reach decision tasks. One experiment studies how biasing influences such as the relative expected payoffs associated with different actions interact and influence neural representations of those actions. A second experiment studies how neural activity evolves while the monkey makes guesses about which action to perform. Ultimately, the project is expected to shed light both on questions of decision-making and on questions of movement planning and execution. This will lead to important insights into the neural organization of voluntary behavior and to a better understanding of both the cognitive and motor aspects of Parkinson's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Homéostasie intestinale de la vitamine D chez la fibrose kystique: Rôle du CFTR.
Keywords-MotsClés: CFTR; CULTURE CELLULAIRE; FIBROSE KYSTIQUE; MALABSORPTION; PHYSIOLOGIE INTESTINALE; VITAMINE D
Abstract-Résumé: La fibrose kystique (FK) represente la maladie hereditaire la plus repandue et la plus mortelle chez les jeunes Canadiens.Outre les infections respiratoires qui sont responsables de la mortalite de ces patients avant l'age de 40 ans,les personnes atteintes de FK souffrent tres precocement de complications gastro-intestinales qui entrainent des repercussions sur l'etat nutritionnel de ces patients.L'une de ces repercussions touche la vitamine D dont la prevalence de deficience peut atteindre 90% chez des enfants et adultes FK et ce, malgre la prise quotidienne de doses massives de cette vitamine.La vitamine D revet une importance de plus en plus grandissante au sein de multiples processus biologiques.Elle joue un role au sein de la mineralisation osseuse, de la force musculaire, de la defense immunitaire, de la protection contre le cancer du colon et le diabete. Ainsi, un statut nutritionnel insuffisant en vitamine D chez l'enfant et l'adulte FK aura des repercussions majeures sur la fonction de plusieurs systemes, ce qui contribuera a la progression des complications, deja fort nombreuses, de cette maladie. On reconnait, a l'heure actuelle, l'inefficacite des protocoles de supplementation en vitamine D a normaliser le statut nutritionnel en cette vitamine chez le patient FK.Nous postulons que la deficience en vitamine D chez les patients FK est le resultat de perturbations severes de son absorption et metabolisme intestinal.Ces travaux viseront a etudier le processus d'absorption et le metabolisme de la vitamine D dans le contexte de la FK a l'aide de modeles cellulaires et animaux FK. Les connaissances acquises sur la vitamine D pourront s'etendre, non seulement a la population FK, mais a l'ensemble de la population generale compte tenu du haut taux d'insuffisance en vitamine D recense au Canada. Ces travaux serviront a justifier une hausse des apports nutritionnels de reference en vitamine D qui sont,a l'heure actuelle,en pleine revision.

ResearchClassEN: CANCER THERAPY GENERAL; DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular-Mechanism-Based Target Identification and Drug Discovery for Radiotherapy of Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICANCER DRUGS; BIOPHYSICS; CANCER RADIOTHERAPY; MEDICAL PHYSICS; RADIATION BIOLOGY; ULTRAFAST TIME-RESOLVED LASER SPECTROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: The conquest of cancer continues to pose great challenges to medical science. Despite the introduction of numerous chemotherapeutic agents, cancer survival rates for clinically advanced tumors (e.g. lung, breast, prostate) remain disappointingly low. Using a somewhat empirical process, screening of more than 10000 compounds typically yields only about one new anticancer drug. The compelling need is for a more fundamental, mechanistic understanding of human cancers and anticancer drugs to design more appropriate new drugs. This proposal focuses on a new perspective on the molecular-mechanism of drug action to develop novel drugs that synergize with radiotherapy for high performance cancer treatment. It also aims to integrate the novel femtobiology/femtomedicine technology in Waterloo with the state-of-the-art STTARR facility housed within the Radiation Medicine Program of the Princess Margaret Hospital/MaRS in Toronto. This combination provides an ideal vehicle to bring innovations arising from studies in femtobiology to clinical formulation and evaluation. We anticipate that this project will provide greater understanding of the mechanisms of chemo-radiation and quickly lead to the development of powerful, translatable agents for highly effective radiotherapy of prostate cancer, lung cancer and breast cancer.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTÉ; SANTÉ INTERNATIONALE
ClasseRechercheFR: POLITIQUE SANITAIRE; RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating Knowledge-Translation Platforms in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE STUDY; EVALUATION; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SYSTEMS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; SURVEY
Abstract-Résumé: The health status of many countries' citizens suffers when poorly considered policies weaken or fail to strengthen health systems and when health systems fail to ensure the safe, efficient, and equitable delivery of effective services and technologies. A number of units are beginning to experiment with efforts to address the challenges of linking research evidence to policy about health systems. We call these units "knowledge-translation (KT) platforms" because they seek to convert the knowledge arising from research into the types of action on the ground that can mean the difference between life and death or the difference between good health and bad health. We have been asked to lead the evaluation of KT platforms that are being launched in municipalities (e.g., Beijing), countries (e.g., Mexico), and regions (e.g., east Africa) around the world. We plan to describe regularly what these KT platforms are doing, which of their efforts can be improved, and which combinations of their activities and outputs can be matched to particular contexts and (infra)structure in order to optimize desired outcomes and impact. Our research findings have the potential to inform future research and decision-making about KT platforms, both in Canada (where such units have been proposed by CIHR, but not yet funded) and in low- and middle-income countries.

TitreApplicationTitle: D-serine and plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: DEMENTIA; GLUTAMATE; HIPPOCAMPUS; NMDA RECEPTOR; WHOLE-CELL PATCH-CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Short-term (or "working") memory, is the memory function that we rely on in order to accomplish day-to-day tasks, like remembering a telephone number, or where we left our car keys.  These memories are formed and stored via circuits of brain cells that co-ordinate many different spatial and temporal inputs.  When we try and remember where our keys are, spatial cues (e.g."on the table") and temporal cues (e.g."last night") are blended into a unique neural network and stored in a brain region called the hippocampus.  Interestingly, the hippocampus is also involved in the formation of navigational memories, so the route to the local Tim Hortons for example, is also contained in the hippocampus, but in a totally separate network of neurons.  These networks are naturally transient and can be easily remodeled or broken when the memory needs to be changed or when it is no longer of use. For reasons that remain elusive, these hippocampal circuits are particularly vulnerable to malfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients. Indeed, one of the stereotypical clinical pathologies of AD is degeneration in short-term memory and learning, due to the death of these hippocampal neurons over a prolonged period of time. The major challenge we face, as medical experts, is the fact that when we diagnose AD, it is likely too late to initiate effective treatment. Our lab is interested in addressing this challenge. Using a well-defined experimental protocol based on the firing pattern of neurons recorded from a mouse who is forming a short term memory, we aim to record the electrical activity from multiple neurons in a network to determine how the memory is set up, used, and ultimately discarded.  We will then attempt to disrupt memory formation in a way similar to that believed to occur in AD to see how the network is affected.  We will even go as far as to you're going to kill a neuron in the network to see if memories can be re-routed or changed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health Outcomes and Physical activity in Preschoolers: The "HOPP" Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCELEROMETRY; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HEALTH-RELATED FITNESS; MOTOR PROFICIENCY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PRESCHOOL CHILDREN
Abstract-Résumé: The preschool years are a period of growth for which we know the least about the impact of physical activity. Since society has traditionally thought of little kids as "active enough", important questions regarding physical activity and health in preschoolers have gone unanswered. Because Canada is facing a childhood obesity epidemic, there has never been a greater need to understand how physical activity during the early years is related to health. If we do not fill this gap in our knowledge, it will be impossible to develop evidence-based policies to promote physical activity for preschoolers. The goal of our study is to measure physical activity in preschoolers and determine how activity levels relate to key health outcomes, including body composition (obesity), how well blood vessels work (heart health), fitness levels, and information related to quality of life. To know if active preschoolers are really healthier preschoolers as they grow up, we will make these assessments in 408 children ages 3 to 5 years (equal number of boys and girls) who will be tested once per year for 3 years, until the 3-year-olds are 5 and the 5-year-olds are 7. Since preschool children are still developing movement skills, we will also test their ability to perform basic movement skills at each yearly assessment along with their parents' beliefs about physical activity for their preschooler - two pieces of information that could be used to help influence preschooler physical activity. In preparation for this study, we have adapted existing tests and even developed new ones for use with preschoolers, and our research team is involved in several initiatives related to physical activity for preschoolers including the possibility of developing physical activity guidelines. Canada could be a leader in this area. Our study will provide the evidence to create public policies that work and optimize the spending of precious public funds for physical activity promotion during the early years.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proteomic Analysis of Platelet-Monocyte Aggregate Formation and Function
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD RESEARCH; CELL CULTURE; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PLATELET-MONOCYTE AGGREGATES; PROTEOMICS; QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The formation of platelet-monocyte aggregates is a known early marker of cardiovascular disease, which if untreated can lead to stroke or heart attack, and ultimately to death.  Recent evidence suggests that platelet-monocyte aggregates also play a direct functional role in these processes.  Our knowledge on these aggregates is limited, however.  Having a detailed understanding of how they are formed, and how they interact with the surface of blood vessels to elicit their deleterious physiological effects, is critical for our ability to design appropriate measures for prevention or treatment.  Proteomics is a new, high-throughput approach that aims at providing a comprehensive analysis of all of the proteins in a biological system.  Owing to recent technical advances, it can now routinely identify hundreds, or even thousands of proteins that are present in cells and tissues, and detect and quantify any changes they may undergo.  We propose to use proteomics to identify the proteins that are involved in platelet-monocyte aggregate formation and function, determine the changes platelets, monocytes, and cells lining the blood vessels undergo, and establish the exact sequence of these evenets.  Such information is particularly helpful as it can be used to develop and test intervention strategies to block or counter these events.  We are uniquely qualified to carry out the proposed research, as we have the necessary equipment, experience, and track record of success for each aspect of the proposal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Angipoietins and vascular protection: therapeutic implications
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY; ANGIOGENIC FACTORS; ANGIOPOETINS; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; PERMEABILITY; VASCULAR INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Using stem cells to prevent people dying of influenza? Sounds like science fiction, but this actually represents a novel type of treatment that could potentially save the lives of many patients suffering from severe influenza, and other causes of 'white out' lungs; a condition that occurs when the lungs become flooded due to a breakdown in the normal barrier function of the blood vessels in the lung. The proposed research will study a family of blood vessel growth factors known as, angiopoietins, which play critical roles in stabilizing and maintaining the normal properties of healthy blood vessels, such as preventing vessel leakage and inhibiting inflammation. The manipulation of these growth factors, coupled with the delivery of stem cells bearing powerful anti-inflammatory properties, has already shown remarkable benefits in preclinical animal models. The therapeutic potential of this strategy will be evaluated in more clinically relevant models, in particular H1N1 influenza, in order to establish its suitability for full-scale clinical testing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cornée reconstruite in vitro par génie tissulaire pour des applications expérimentales et cliniques
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE ET MOLECULAIRE; CELLULES SOUCHES; CORNEE; GREFFE; GUERISON DES PLAIES; GENIE TISSULAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: Ce projet s'inscrit dans le cadre de la chaire de recherche du Canada en Cellules Souches et Genie Tissulaire. Il porte sur la reconstruction d'une cornee humaine in vitro par genie tissulaire pour des applications experimentales et cliniques.  La cornee est un tissu de l'oeil d'une grande importance car il protege des atteintes externes et maintient la transparence pour une vision claire. La deficience en cellules souches epitheliales ainsi que les blessures peuvent diminuer la vision voir meme mener a la cecite. Le LOEX a developpe une expertise en genie tissulaire qui permet de reconstruire en laboratoire des tissus et organes qui peuvent servir a des experiences in vitro ou a des greffes in vivo. Notre equipe a ete la premiere, en 1999, a recreer une cornee entierement composee d'elements humains.  Notre approche totalement originale, la methode d'auto-assemblage, est basee sur la reconstruction de la cornee in vitro a partir des cellules prelevees d'une biopsie de l'oeil. De plus, notre matrice nanostructuree permet d'orienter les cellules et le collagene du stroma reconstruit, ce qui est essentiel pour la transparence.  Le present projet permettra de developper des reconstructions de cornee qui seront plus sophistiquees et plus apparentees au tissu natif. D'abord, un modele simple comprenant des cellules epitheliales cultivees sur un gel de fibrine vise le traitement des deficiences en cellules souches limbiques. Puis, une cornee reconstruite a partir des trois populations de cellules (epitheliales, fibroblastes et endotheliales) de la cornee normale vise a traiter des pathologies necessitant une greffe de cornee complete. Ce projet comprend de l'experimentation fondamentale et pre-clinique et exploitera des techniques de pointes tel que l'identification des signatures d'expression genique. De plus, notre modele servira a mieux comprendre la guerison des plaies corneennes et l'effet des medicaments afin d'ameliorer les traitements offerts aux patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms underlying the role of UL24 in Herpes simplex virus 1 replication and pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; MOUSE MODEL OF INFECTION; NUCLEOLUS; UL24 OF HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS 1; VIRAL GENETICS; VIRAL LATENCY AND REACTIVATION
Abstract-Résumé: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections are highly prevalent worldwide.  HSV initially infects mucosal surfaces such as the lip, eye or vaginal lining causing blistering sores, and then goes on to infect sensory neurons where it goes dormant.  Through poorly understood mechanisms, stress induces reactivation of the virus from this quiescent state leading to the production of new infectious particles.  HSV sometimes causes encephalitis, and recurrent infection of the eye can lead to blindness.  HSV is especially dangerous for neonates and immunocompromised individuals, such as those undergoing certain cancer therapies or people living with AIDS.  Epidemiological evidence has identified genital HSV infection as a significant risk factor for the transmission of the human immunodeficiency virus.  Thus, the prevalence of genital herpes is an important problem in the fight to control the incidence of AIDS.  Despite extensive efforts, there is no vaccine against HSV.  Furthermore, the development of strains resistant to anti-herpesviral drugs presently available is an especially serious problem for those with weakened immune systems.   Our research is aimed at understanding how this virus causes life-long infections and recurrent disease.  Our objective is to identify intermolecular interactions that are critical for pathogenesis, and which may constitute targets for the development of new therapeutics to treat this common, but potentially life-threatening infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: A role in cell polarity for INF1, a novel microtubule-associated formin
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN CYTOSKELETON; CELL POLARITY; CYTOSKELETAL REMODELING PROTEINS; FORMIN HOMOLOGY PROTEINS; MICROTUBULES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: During the course of our growth and development many of the cells within our bodies have to migrate to find their place within a growing tissue or organ. Once they arrive at their home destination they must maintain their sense of direction to ensure that they stay in the correct position and point in the right direction for the tissue to function. Often this sense of direction is lost during the formation of a tumor and this allows tumor cells to wander off and invade the surrounding tissue. We study a novel protein called INF1 that we think is important for setting the cell's internal guidance system. This guidance system consists of two separate networks of structural proteins, one called the microfilament cytoskeleton and one called the microtubule network. It has been proposed that microfilaments provide the force that makes the cell move while microtubules point that movement in the right direction. Our initial experiments suggest that INF1 gives the cell its sense of direction by connecting the microfilaments to the microtubules so that they may work together to point the cell in the right direction. We will test this idea by asking how the loss of INF1 function affects the cellular sense of direction and by examining how INF1 is able to connect microfilaments and microtubules to allow the cell to orient itself.

TitreApplicationTitle: Post-transcriptional control of Sox9 during endocrine pancreas  development: role of microRNAs
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT; DIABETES; HUMAN EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; MICRORNA; SOX9; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: To date, the only successful approach for curing insulin-dependent diabetes is to replace the insulin-producing B-cells that have been destroyed by disease. Pancreas and islet cell transplantation are promising therapeutic strategies; however, scarcity of transplantable tissue has limited their widespread adoption. One way to produce enough B-cells to cure diabetes is to determine how the B-cells develop normally within the embryo and apply this knowledge to the generation of B-cells in the culture dish.  This proposal focuses on a novel group of genes, known as microRNAs (miRNAs) that play important roles in the development of many tissues. MiRNAs function by binding to their targets and preventing them from being made into proteins.  I have demonstrated that miRNAs control the formation of B-cells but it's unclear how they do so.  Here I hypothesize that a protein necessary during the formation of B-cells called Sox9 is regulated by miRNAs.  I have shown that Sox9 levels are lower when potential miRNAs regulators of Sox9 are present, at a critical time during development.  Preliminary results also suggest Sox9 levels are elevated if miRNAs are not present during development.  Here I propose the expansion of our understanding of the role of miRNAs in Sox9 regulation by answering three key questions: 1) Is Sox9 repression required for generating B-cells?  2) Can miRNAs target Sox9 during B-cell development? 3) Is regulation of Sox9 by miRNAs necessary for B-cell development in both mice and humans? These studies will identify miRNAs that directly regulate Sox9 expression during B-cell development. That knowledge will provide a better understanding of B-cell formation and will assist in the development of methods for producing sufficient numbers of B-cells to cure diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: A multidimensional approach to vulnerability to schizophrenia and bipolar-depression: transgenerational genetic modeling of trajectories of cognitive deficits in kindreds affected by schizophrenia and bipolar-depression.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DEPRESSION; DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOPATHOLOGY; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; NEUROCOGNITION; RISK TRAJECTORIES; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic/environmental factors are undoubtedly in cause in schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar depression (BP). These disorders complexity complicate the identification of involved genes. First, current definitions of SZ and BP include different disease entities, each having its own causes; second, some of these disease entities result from the joint action of many different causes, both genetic and environmental, and third, the clinical manifestations of these disorders are varied and complex to measure.  We believe that in order to detect the gene/environment interactions involved in these disorders, analyses should be improved by greater phenotype accuracy. Thus, we investigated cognitive intermediate phenotypes (CIP), considering that CIPs would be closer to genotype than clinical diagnosis. Our study involved a 20-year long accumulated sample of 2500 members from 48 well-characterized multigenerational families of Eastern Quebec that are densely affected by SZ or by BP. This transgenerational sample permitted us to extend our analyses to the young high risk offspring (HRs) for SZ and BP of the third or fourth generations and allowed us to innovatively combine a developmental psychopathology with a genetic approach.  The interdisciplinary combination of expertise of our research team allowed us to demonstrate that HRs and non-affected adult relatives (NAARs) displayed important cognitive impairments similar to those observed in adult patients. Moreover, particular cognitive deficits were proved to present distinct generational patterns from childhood to adulthood. In particular, impairments of the visual episodic memory were common to patients and HRs and, as such, act as a predictor of illness.  This proposal objective is to characterize further the phenotype in this unique sample by investigating CIPs. This will allow us to look at trajectories of cognitive deficits from childhood to adulthood and at the genetic mechanisms involving cognition in SZ an BP.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Ghrelin Signaling on Peripheral Nuclear Receptors and the Regulation of Lipid and Energy Metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTES; FATTY ACID METABOLISM; GHRELIN; OBESITY; PPAR NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; THIAZOLIDINEDIONES
Abstract-Résumé: The epidemic of excess body weight in our society and its increasing prevalence in children indicate that health problems related to obesity will continue to impact our national health care system. The adipocyte is the major site of fatty acid storage in the body and plays a critical role in maintaining normal blood glucose and lipids. Excessive accumulation of lipids in fat tissues and nonadipose depots, such as in liver, pancreas, and muscle cells, is associated to many metabolic dysregulations globally referred to as the metabolic syndrome, which include central obesity, type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance. We have obtained preliminary evidence of a novel cellular pathway by which the hormone ghrelin regulates PPARgamma, a key protein involved in lipid and glucose metabolism. The present study will characterize such beneficial regulation of PPARgamma and other related nuclear receptors in order to elucidate the mechanisms contributing to obesity and diabetes, and to warrant effective and novel treatment strategies for metabolic disorders.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Early Developmental Trajectories in Autism: From Infancy to Age 8
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; CHILD DEVELOPMENT; EARLY DETECTION; LONGITUDINAL STUDIES; TEMPERAMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Autism is a form of disability that affects a person's ability to communicate and interact with other people, and is associated with disabling obsessions and repetitive behaviours. About 1 in 150 individuals have autism, most of who require lifelong supports, achieving only limited independence and participation in their communities as adults, despite talents and areas of strength. The profound impacts on affected individuals and their families and costs to society through health, education and social services argue for strong efforts aimed at improving outcomes.  This project aims to better understand the developmental course of autism from infancy through early childhood. With previous support from CIHR, we have assessed and followed 400 infants at increased risk of autism (younger siblings of children with autism) from age 6 months to 3 years. In doing so, we have identified some of the earliest signs of autism ever reported, and have gained important new insights into some of the least understood aspects of this disorder, such as differences between affected boys and girls and patterns of onset, including 'regression' or skill loss. By following this unique cohort (the largest of its kind in the world) to age 5 and 8 years, we hope to further understand how early behavioural features can be used to predict risk of autism and variation in developmental course (including changes in diagnostic classification over time) and how such relationships may vary between boys and girls. We will also investigate how specific characteristics such as early temperament may influence risk of later mental health and behavioural problems in both children with and without autism. Findings from this study will provide a stronger empirical basis for clinical service and policy development aimed at supporting the unique needs of children with autism identified early in life, and helping each of them to achieve their full potential.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stemming the epidemic of liver related morbidity and mortality in HIV-HCV co-infection: Is ART enough?
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; CO-INFECTION; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; HIV; IMMUNOPATHOGENESIS; PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: An increasing number of people are infected with both Hepatitis C (HCV) and HIV. HIV appears to make HCV related liver disease progress more rapidly. Liver disease is now one of the leading causes of illness and death in HIV-HCV-infected persons. By restoring the immune system, it was expected that effective HIV treatments would lead to improved liver health. However, it remains unclear why liver disease continues to be such a large problem in co-infection. We have created a cohort study of 950 HIV-HCV infected persons from 16 centres across Canada to study how HIV and HCV therapy impacts HCV related liver disease. We will look at social and biologic factors that may contribute to liver disease and evaluate non-invasive methods to measure liver health. We will also examine the immune function of participants receiving HIV therapies compared to those not treated. This work will allow a greater understanding of how these two viruses interact to cause disease and will provide insights into to how best to design and target therapies so that in the future, HIV-HCV infected individuals may be able to derive full benefits from the treatment advances being realised for HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechano-chemical signal transduction in myofibroblasts during skin wound healing and fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: MECHANOTRANSDUCTION; MYOFIBROBLAST PATHOLOGY; SKIN FIBROSIS - SCLERODERMA; TISSUE REPAIR AND REGENERATION; TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR BETA; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: After skin injury our body rapidly repairs the damage, often leaving behind a stiff scar. Scarring is a clinical burden because skin is losing vital functions. After burns or trauma, scarring makes the skin so inflexible that it can impede the function of muscles, limbs and digits. Worse, uncontrolled wound healing accumulates fibrous tissue. This condition, called fibrosis, is fatal in skin systemic sclerosis and in lung, heart, liver, and kidney fibrosis. To date, no therapy is effective to treat fibrosis.  Fibroblasts promote wound healing and fibrosis by secreting fibrous collagen and the growth factor TGFb1. As fibroblasts crawl they pull on the initially soft fibre matrix and make it stiffer. At one point, the matrix is too stiff to be reorganized but still too weak to stabilize the skin. Like cellular Popeyes fibroblasts then turn into powerful contractile 'myofibroblasts'. To make this switch the cells need to get at their 'spinach' - the TGFb1 sitting in the matrix. Using innovative soft culture substrates, we have discovered that cells unlock TGFb1 via a purely mechanical process. In a sufficiently rigid matrix, cell pulling allows the TGFb1 to pop out, like candy from a wrapper. With TGFb1 available, fibroblasts express the muscle proteins needed to contract. The stronger pulling liberates yet more TGFb1 that stimulates other cells to become contractile - a vicious loop is closed.  We will use our understanding of mechanical fibroblast activation to fight fibrosis. We can intercept mechanical TGF-beta activation by interfering with integrins, the proteins that cells use to grab on the inactive TGFb1. To identify these yet unknown integrins, we will turn selected integrins on and off, using molecular biology and pharmacological drugs. Effective drugs will be tested in animal models of wound healing and fibrosis. It is our ultimate aim to block TGFb1 activating integrins as a novel clinical strategy to treat fibrosis and to achieve scarless healing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lab-on-a-chip platform for single rare cell genomic and proteomic analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYTICAL CHEMISTRY; LAB-ON-A-CHIP; MICRO ANALYSIS; SINGLE CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Performing laboratory operations on small scale has many benefits for chemical research. For biological and medical research it can become paramount to work with very small volumes particular when comprehensive analysis of single cells is the long term goal. In this proposal we want to implement the so called lab-on-a-chip technology for single cell analysis. In  particular to study rare cells, such as those which have the ability to self-renew and transform into particular lineages of differentiated cells as required in repair of certain organs. The envisioned tool should enable ultimately to further understand the chemical and signaling pathways triggering the transformation of these cells into the differentiated cells. The importance of developing a microchip lies in the ability to work with very small volume containing only a few of the rare cells of interest. The microchip is designed to incorporate laser technology to trap and manipulate and transport cells within microfluidic channels. The selected cells can then be lysed in a controlled manner to analyze contents within the cell such as proteins, RNA and DNA. These molecules are selected using a variety of chemical modifications to the microchannel to trap and adsorb these molecules which enable analysis of the contents comprising protein, RNA or DNA by techniques such as capillary electrophoresis and laser induded fluopresence, or permit harvesting of particular analytes for other secundary analysis.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Diabetic Brain resulting from Insulin Deficiency and loss of PI3K/Akt signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL ATROPHY; COGNITIVE DECLINE; DIABETES; INSULIN; WHITE MATTER ABNORMALITIES
Abstract-Résumé: As first described nearly one century ago, the brain is targeted by diabetes, which leads to brain shrinkage, loss of brain white matter and slowed thinking and memory. Thus, diabetes can initiate or accelerate dementia, a major problem in our aging population. Diabetes-related brain changes are related to long duration and severity of diabetes, but there is additional evidence that the brain is starving for insulin in diabetes. We have developed the only experimental model of the diabetic brain which demonstrates changes analogous to the human condition. This diabetic brain also has disrupted insulin levels. Our work demonstrated that insulin replacement prevents changes in the DM brain, but giving insulin systemically is complicated by low blood sugars. In response, we have developed an alternative method of delivery, intranasal insulin which gives insulin through the nose, targeting the brain - this slowed the onset of brain changes found with magnetic resonance imaging and imrpoved memory performance, when compared to similar dosing of systemic insulin.  Now, I would like to target the molecules modified by insulin called CREB and GSK3B with small molecules that can also be delivered through the nose without effects upon blood sugars. I also plan to use specialized mice genetically modified to have more or less of CREB and GSK3B. Then, I will use a new form of magnetic resonance imaging called diffusion tensor imaging to specifically examine brain white matter tracts injured by diabetes. If beneficial, these concepts could easily be translated to studies in human populations, and may also extend their value to brains affected by Alzheimer's Disease as well.

AreasOfScienceEN: GENOMICS, PROTEOMICS, AND BIOINFORMATICS; CELL BIOLOGY
DomainesScientifiquesFR: GÉNOMIQUE, PROTÉOMIQUE ET BIOINFORMATIQUE; BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the human T-cell receptor repertoire by massively parallel sequencing
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNOPROFILING; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; T CELL RECEPTOR; T CELL REPERTOIRE
Abstract-Résumé: T-cells circulating in blood are the key players in your adaptive immune system and are particularly important in recognizing and killing other cells that are infected with viruses, or that carry cancer causing mutations.  Because there are a vast number of different infectious agents or cancer causing mutations possible, a vast number of T-cell variants are required to recognize them. The component of the T-cell responsible for this recognition is the T-cell receptor, and the variation required for recognition is generated mainly by shuffling the large number of short DNA segments that comprise T-cell receptor genes.  Although the central importance and T-cell receptor in adaptive immunity is well established, the actual number and diversity of T-cells that exist in an individual (ie. the T-cell repertoire), how this changes in response to immune challenge, and how it varies from one individual to the next, remains unknown.  We have used the latest DNA sequencing technologies to develop an approach for examining the T-cell repertoire in a given blood sample by directly sequencing T-cell receptor genes.  In the study proposed here we will work on improving the performance of this method and we will use it to determine the number of different T-cell receptors in a typical blood sample, how this varies from person to person, how it changes with age, and how it is affected by persistent viral infections. The results of this study will improve our understanding of adaptive immunity and will facilitate the future development of immunoassays for diagnostic testing and immune intervention in cancer, infectious disease and auto-immunity and transplantation medicine.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: FONCTION RÉNALE, NÉPHROLOGIE, UROLOGIE; APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Distributed autoregulation of renal blood flow
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOREGULATION; BLOOD FLOW; DYNAMICS; KIDNEY; LASER SPECKLE PERFUSION IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: High blood pressure is the single most important cause of kidney disease.  So we need to understand how the kidney normally  is protected from episodes of high blood pressure.  In relation to their size the two kidneys have the highest blood flows in the body. A human kidney contains a million functional units called nephrons. Each nephron consists of a glomerulus, the tiny filter where fluid is removed from blood, and the tubule that leads fluid away. The glomerulus is a delicate structure and must be protected from episodes of high blood pressure that occur routinely in all of us.   Humans and other animals have a process that adjusts the caliber of the small blood vessels that feed the glomeruli. The process is called autoregulation because it occurs entirely within the kidney. It stabilizes kidney blood flow and pressure at the glomerulus when blood pressure varies. Typically it is thought that autoregulation at each glomerulus acts independently. However, neighboring nephrons (about 20 in a cluster) exchange information and tend to work together. We suspect that these interactions are important to the effectiveness of autoregulation but we really know very little about them.  We acquire images of perfusion at the surface of the kidney and analyze them to examine the signatures left when autoregulation is active. This will tell us how important it is for the nephrons in a cluster to work together. We will define how big the cluster is and how its size varies under normal conditions. Then we will use several experimental tricks to change the number of nephrons in the cluster. We expect that autoregulation provides better protection  when nephrons act together. We are well placed to perform these studies because we have expertise in the subject and a long-standing interest in autoregulation. We were the first to define the problem and how to address it. We have a team made up of a physiologist, a kidney doctor, and an engineer who specializes in data analysis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ventricular Tachycardia Ablation vs Enhanced Drug Therapy In Structural Heart Disease:  The VANISH Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIARRHYTHMIC DRUGS; CATHETER ABLATION; IMPLANTABLE CARDIOVERTER DEFIBRILLATOR; VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA
Abstract-Résumé: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT) is a dangerous heart rhythm that frequently causes sudden death in people who have survived heart attacks, even years later.  It is caused by 'short circuits' of the heart's electrical system which are inside heart attack scar.  Doctors will usually put in a device called an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) if a person is at risk for VT.  This device can shock the heart back to a normal rhythm if VT recurs.  Shocks can save lives, but a person may get lots of shocks and they may be painful and have other adverse effects.  Approximately 50,000 people in Canada have ICDs, and about 3400 per year experience at least one shock.  To prevent shocks, we can use heart rhythm drug therapy or a procedure called a catheter ablation (ablation).    The drugs which are available to control VT are better than nothing, but they have been quite disappointing.  They have quite a few side-effects (some of which are dangerous) and work only moderately well.  Ablation is a procedure which is an alternative to drug therapy.  Heart rhythm specialists do this procedure by putting wires up through the blood vessels of the legs into the heart, and by testing the electrical properties of the heart attack scar.  One of the wires has a special tip that can be used to cauterize the short circuits that are in the heart attack scar.  This procedure may be complex, is not always perfectly successful, and has a small risk of complications which could be serious.  We don't know whether it is better to use drugs or ablation for people who get shocks from their ICD.  The VANISH Trial is a study which will be carried out across multiple specialized hospitals to compare ablation to drug therapy for patients with VT.  260 patients who need VT treatment will (randomly) receive either drugs or ablation and the outcomes will be studied.  This will determine whether there is any advantage of one over the other for better survival or for reduction/delay in shocks.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development and function of cholinergic-nicotinic synapses in sympathetic ganglia
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT OF FUNCTIONAL SYNAPTIC CONNECTIONS; NICOTINIC ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTORS; SYMPATHETIC GANGLIA; SYNAPTIC ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: The autonomic nervous system consists of sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons collected in several ganglia throughout the body and most organs and tissues rely on the autonomic nervous system to regulate their function. The synapses in autonomic ganglia represent the final output of various CNS structures that regulate autonomic activity; if these synapses do not develop or function properly, this vital link between the CNS and the periphery is disrupted, and a wide range of abnormalities and unique syndromes ensue. These syndromes include abnormal heart rate that predisposes a person to life-threatening arrhythmias, gastrointestinal problems, poor bladder control, and erectile dysfunction. Collectively these symptoms and abnormalities are referred to as autonomic neuropathies or dysautonomias and adversely affect a person's quality of life and life expectancy. This proposal has two major goals. One is to understand how neural circuits in autonomic ganglia are established during development. Our overall hypothesis is that synapses that make the postsynaptic neuron fire are useful and become stabilized whereas those that cannot are inappropriate and are eliminated. To test this we will investigate different mouse models that have targeted mutations in genes that result in a disruption of either pre- or postsynaptic function. Our second goal is to understand how diseases disrupt the function of synapses in autonomic ganglia and produce dysautonomia. We showed recently that mild elevations in cytosolic reactive oxygen species (ROS) inactivate nAChRs on sympathetic neurons and produce a long-lasting depression in synaptic transmission in sympathetic ganglia. Elevated ROS have been implicated in a number of diseases, including diabetes, and recently, we showed that synaptic transmission in sympathetic ganglia is depressed in diabetic mice. We plan to determine how ROS disrupt the function of receptors at synapses in autonomic ganglia and produce dysautonomias.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: SCIENCES DENTAIRES/BIOLOGIE ORALE; MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cell behaviour on implants by surface topography
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BEHAVIOUR; CELL SIGNALING; DENTAL IMPLANTS; EPITHELIUM & FIBROBLASTS; GENE ARRAYS; OSTEOBLASTS & MACROPHAGE
Abstract-Résumé: Artificial implants are now used in a host of applications including hip joints, catheters, heart valves, and dental implants. The shape of the surface at the micometer and nanometer scale, that is its topography, has been found to influence cell and tissue responses to implants but our current knowledge of how cells may be specifically controlled by topography is limited, and compromises our ability to develop improved surfaces. This proposal will study the effects of surface topography on four types of cell that often contact implants: fibroblasts, epithelium, bone cells and macrophages. Using sophisticated methods of microfabrication and nanofabrication, novel and precisely characterized surfaces will be produced and examined for their effects on cell structure, migration, and cell-cell interactions, as well as gene and cell signaling activities.  Particular attention will be focused on the macrophage as this cell orchestrates the body's response to foreign bodies such as implants, and the intent is to develop surfaces that induce macrophages to promote healing rather than destructive inflammation. Our past work has been used to modify some types of dental implants. We anticipate the proposed work will lead to the rational, cell behaviourly-based design of specific engineered surfaces that improve implant tissue integration for multiple clinical applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of ventilator-induced pulmonary fibrosis and its therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY; ARDS; MECHANICAL VENTILATION; RESPIRATORY DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Patients who develop a disease known as Acute Lung Injury or Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) have a very high mortality. Mortality is particularly high in the subset of patients with ARDS who develop fibrosis (scarring) in their lungs while they are on a breathing machine (called a ventilator) in the intensive care unit. Our hypothesis is that the ventilator which helps saves the patient's life by taking over the breathing function while they are ill, may actually contribute to the development of the scarring (fibrosis). Our studies will use animal models to see whether our hypothesis is correct, and will also try various therapies to prevent and/or treat the fibrosis. If our hypothesis is true that the ventilator can cause lung fibrosis, the increased understanding generated our studies may lead to new therapies that can be tested in patients with acute lung injury to decrease the high mortiality of this deadly syndrome.

ClasseRechercheFR: APOPLEXIE, INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE; AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the Functional Distribution of Aquaporin 4 in Brain
Keywords-MotsClés: AQUAPORIN 4-MEDIATED WATER TRANSPORT; ASTROCYTES; BRAIN EDEMA; CONFOCAL AND ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; DYSTROGLYCAN INTERACTION WITH THE EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; FLUORESCENCE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is one of the leading causes of death in Canada. Mortality due to stroke is in large part due to abnormal water accumulation that leads to brain swelling and compression within the skull. Current treatment options to reduce the swelling of the brain, also called edema, due to stroke are limited, more than 70 years old and generally require surgical intervention. The limited development of new therapies attests of an incomplete understanding of the regulation of water accumulation in the brain. Thus, the major challenge in the development of new therapies is to better define the mechanism of water transport in brain. A key regulator of water transport in the brain is the water permeable channel, aquaporin 4, which is expressed in non-neuronal cells called glial cells. It is the goal of the present proposal to identify molecules that modulate aquaporin 4 function in glial cells and test whether they may prove to be useful in reducing water accumulation in models of brain edema.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Control of skeletal development by the chromatin remodeling protein ATRX
Keywords-MotsClés: ATR-X SYNDROME; CHROMATIN REMODELING; GENETIC DISEASE; MOUSE MODELS; OSTEOBLASTS; SKELETAL DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: ATR-X syndrome is one of several inherited diseases characterized by both mental retardation and skeletal defects. It is currently not known whether mental and skeletal defects in these patients are caused by similar molecular mechanisms. Moreover, the function of the normal form of this gene (the ATRX gene) in the healthy skeleton is not known. Our proposal aims to address these questions. We are currently generating mouse models of the skeletal aspects of the human disease, by selectively inactivating the ATRX gene in specific components of the skeleton (e.g. bone) and in the brain which controls skeletal development through secreted growth factors and hormones. Analyses of these mice will reveal the normal roles of ATRX in the growth and development of the skeleton as well as the processes that are disrupted in ATR-X syndrome. In parallel, we will perform biochemical and cell biological assays to determine the molecular mechanisms used by ATRX to control the development of skeletal cells. Together, these studies will give novel insights into the mechanisms responsible for skeletal defects in ATR-X syndrome and related disorders and will ultimately contribute to better treatment of these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac Calreticulin: Cell & Developmental Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION & CYTOSKELETON; CALCIUM BINDING PROTEINS; CARDIOMYOCYTE; CARDIOMYOGENESIS; ES CELLS; HEART
Abstract-Résumé: Several years ago we discovered that a calcium-binding protein, calreticulin, initially found in a skeletal muscle, is also present in cardiac and smooth muscle and in non-muscle cells.  In addition, evidence has been accumulating as to suggest that calreticulin is more than a calcium-storage protein, since it modulates gene transcription in response to steroid hormones and it is involved in regulation of cell adhesiveness.  Genetic knockout of calreticulin prevents embryonic heart from developing. Using transgenic mice expressing green fluorescent protein under control of the calreticulin promoter we have shown that the calreticulin gene is transiently activated in the developing heart. In the adult, calreticulin abundance increases in cardiac hypertrophy. On the other hand, targeted overexpression of calreticulin in the heart leads to bradyarrhythmia and complete heart block, followed by sudden death. Hence, the protein plays an important role both in cardiac development and pathology.  Nonetheless, almost nothing is known about function of calreticulin in cardiomyocytes.  Not even its precise distribution in the heart is known.  Therefore, the general objective of my research is to unravel cell role of calreticulin in heart development and function, while the most immediate objective of this proposal is to the cell biological basis for the role of calreticulin in cardiomyocyte differentiation and function.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of SPARC in chemotherapy sensitization
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER BIOLOGY; CHEMOTHERAPY RESISTANCE; COLORECTAL CANCER; GENE EXPRESSION/GENOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: The goal to improving mortality from cancer is to achieve complete response to therapy.  However, chemotherapy resistance has been a difficult problem to overcome.  In order to better understand this phenomenon, our laboratory used a whole genome approach to obtain a snapshot of the changes that occur when cancer cells develop resistance to chemotherapy.  This allowed us to identify SPARC as a gene that plays a role in changing the sensitivity of cancer cells to chemotherapy.  We have been able to demonstrate that low SPARC levels in chemotherapy resistant human MIP101 colon cancer cells is associated with cancer cells that were resistant to therapy.  However, if SPARC is restored by either re-expressing this gene at higher levels, or by introducing the SPARC protein in tissue culture, colon cancer cells become more sensitive to chemotherapy.  In animal models, treatment with SPARC also allowed colon cancer cells to respond better to chemotherapy, and this is demonstrated by greater tumor regression in animals receiving SPARC with chemotherapy than in animals receiving chemotherapy alone.    In this grant application, we propose to conduct experiments that will allow us to gain a better understanding of the mechanisms by which SPARC improves the sensitivity of colorectal cancers to chemotherapy.  The results will allow us to determine if SPARC has any potential as a therapeutic, and as well, allow us to develop better drugs and tests that will be useful in the treatment and management of patients with colorectal cancer, especially in cases where therapy has failed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA BINDING; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE EXPRESSION; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; TRANSCRIPTION; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how gene regulation is controlled, and how cells interpret their own genome, is one of the great challenges of our era.  Gene expression - the process of turning genes and their products on and off - is controlled by the joint activity of hundreds of proteins that recognize specific DNA and RNA sequences present in or encoded by the genome.  These proteins work together in ways that are largely uncharted, executing programs such as development, differentiation, homeostasis, and cell reprogramming, but also aging and disease.  The details of how these processes work remain extremely difficult to decipher because of the complexity of cells, and this limits our ability to understand, harness, diagnose, and fix biological systems.  As with any type of problem, if one does not know how the system works, it is impossible to make rational decisions, and the results of any intervention will be unpredictable.  In order to change medicine and biotechnology into disciplines driven by principles and basic knowledge, rather than by trial-and-error, we need to understand how all of the parts controlling cells work, and how they work together.  We make use of a powerful model system -- the budding yeast -- to explore regulators of gene expression. We have also developed and applied new technologies that have enabled us to understand aspects of gene regulation that have so far been elusive. We expect our studies of gene expression in model systems to provide conceptual, and ultimately practical, approaches to disease treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of saposin proteins in glycosphingolipid catabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: ATOMIC FORCE MICROSCOPY; FLUORESCENCE SPECTROSCOPY; LIPID STORAGE DISEASES; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; PROTEIN-LIPID INTERACTIONS; XRAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: The lipids that constitute cellular membranes are in constant flux.  New lipids are constantly being made while old lipids are being degraded.  Normally, this process is finely balanced, and the levels of lipids remain constant.  Lipid storage disorders, such as Gaucher disease,  Fabry disease and Niemann-Pick disease, result from a disrupted balance where lipids accumulate to abnormal levels.  The lipids accumulate because of a problem with their degradation, and this research studies a class of proteins called the saposins that are essential for the normal breakdown of lipids.  Our studies will help clarify the role of saposins in this process, and will help us understand how these proteins can recognize particular lipids and target them for degradation.

TitreApplicationTitle: PTHrP and osteoblast biology: Relevance to osteoporosis
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE; METABOLIC BONE DISEASE; OSTEOBLAST; OSTEOPOROSIS; PARATHYROID HORMONE RELATED PEPTIDE; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis is an increasingly common medical problem afflicting the elderly population. Although its consequences are already a major drain of the allocated health care budget, there is clear indication that osteoporosis will be an increasingly important medical issue over the next several decades. After age 65, approximately one in three women and one in five men will suffer a bone fracture as a consequence of osteoporosis. However, little is known about the mechanisms that may be involved in the pathogenesis of this bone loss with age. Recent clinical trials have shown a significant benefit of daily administered parathyroid hormone (PTH) in increasing bone mass and preventing fractures in osteoporotic patients. Work in our laboratory has shown that transgenic mice with decreased or absent levels of the PTH-related protein from the osteoblasts, the bone-forming cells of the skeleton, develop premature osteoporosis. Here we will use novel mouse transgenic technologies to investigate the mechanism by which PTHrP in turn influences osteoblast proliferation, differentiation, and regulated programmed death. Such knowledge will have direct implications in our understanding of the pathogenesis of osteoporosis and will serve as a guide for the development of novel treatment modalities for this disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mapping the reference genetic network of a eukaryotic cell with automated yeast genetic analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEX GENETICS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENETIC CONSERVATION; GENETIC NETWORKS; SYNTHETIC GENETIC ARRAY; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Genome sequencing projects have revealed the massive catalogue of genes in a variety of organisms, from yeast to man. Biologists are faced with a major challenge as they confront this embarrassment of riches; how to assign functions to thousands of uncharacterized genes, and how to use this information to identify the proteins that function together to regulate fundamental cellular processes. Functional genomics technologies enable researchers to study all genes simultaneously and systematically in a specific assay and their development and application is providing unprecedented, global, views of gene function. We are developing novel genomics technologies and applying them in large-scale studies using a yeast model system. Yeast are single celled microorganisms that are related to humans evolutionarily, with thousands of genes homologous to those in humans. Our systematic approaches will accelerate the pace of yeast research and provide proof-of-principle analyses for analogous approaches in more complex cells and organisms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting 7 transmembrane receptor's pathways through designed separation of function.
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-ARRESTIN; CELL SIGNALLING; EVOLUTIONARY TRACE ANALYSIS; FUNCTIONAL SELECTIVITY; G PROTEINS; SEVEN TRANSMEMBRANE RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Seven transmembrane receptors (7TMR) represent the largest class of therapeutic targets for the development of new drugs in a vast diversity of clinical indications. Although these receptors have been the object of intense research for the last 30 years or so, our understanding of how drugs can target these receptors to have specific therapeutic activities remains very incomplete. Results obtained in the last few years by our group and others have open new avenues toward a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying the selectivity of drug actions through 7TMR. Recent advances in bioinformatic and phylogenomic analysis offers new means to explore these avenues with the hope of developing new drugs with better therapeutic profiles. The present grant application proposes to combine the use of such new bioinformatic analytical tools with molecular and cellular biology methods in order to unravel the molecular determinants of drug action selectivity.
