TitreApplicationTitle: The role of interstitial cells of Cajal in control of  gastrointestinal motility
Keywords-MotsClés: ENTERIC NERVOUS SYSTEM; GASTROINTESTINAL MOTILITY; GASTROINTESTINAL MOTILITY DISORDERS; INFLAMMATION; IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME; PATCH CLAMP TECHNIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, at least 2 million people suffer from some form of disorder of gastrointestinal motility. This is causing these patients to assess their quality of life as severely impaired. It also costs the health care system between $370 million and $1 billion per year. The indirect costs such as staying home from work are even higher. Although the need for treatment is high, there are few options and some good drugs such as cisapride and tegaserod have been taken off the market. This has also led to the pharmaceutical industry withdrawing research support. Hence it is critical that research is conducted into the causes of gastrointestinal motor abnormalities and it is critical that we find new targets for pharmaceutical intervention. The health care costs are driven by frustration of patients related to the limited availability of treatment. And this is based on our limited understanding of the underlying pathophysiology, which we will address in this application. We will investigate new hypotheses related to the mechanisms behind peristalsis and segmentation, the major motor activities of the stomach and small intestine. We are proposing that the study of the role of interstitial cells of Cajal (the pacemaker cells of the gut) is a very promising avenue for understanding of motor control and motor abnormalities. We will study the electrophysiological basis of pacemaker activity using the most advanced electrophysiological techniques in combination with calcium imaging. We will investigate comprehensive and unique hypotheses related to the mechanism behind segmentation. We will study how these control systems are affected by inflammation and we will investigate our hypotheses in humans in collaboration with clinical investigators at McMaster University.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
TitreApplicationTitle: Acute Hormonal Regulation of Steroidogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT; HORMONES; LEYDIG CELLS; STEROID BIOSYNTHESIS; TESTIS
Abstract-Résumé: Eukaryotic steroid hormones are responsible for the maintenance of the organism's homeostasis, adaptability to the environment, and developmental and reproductive functions. Many tissues of the body have the ability to metabolize steroids. However, few tissues are able to synthesize steroid hormones from the substrate cholesterol. These tissues are the adrenals, gonads, placenta and brain. Steroidogenesis in adrenal and gonadal cells and its regulation by peptide trophic hormones has been well studied. The primary point of control of the acute stimulation of steroidogenesis by hormones and by the second messenger cAMP, involves the first step in this biosynthetic pathway where cholesterol is converted to pregnenolone by a cytochrome P450 enzyme, localized at the inner mitochondrial membrane. Pregnenolone then leaves the mitochondrion to undergo enzymatic transformation in the endoplasmic reticulum that will give rise to the final steroid products. The rate-determining step in this pathway is the transport of the precursor, cholesterol, from intracellular stores into mitochondria. To date, there are many questions on the mechanisms allowing minimal hormone and cAMP levels to induce maximal stimulation of cholesterol transport and steroid formation by the cells within minutes. This application deals with the mechanisms underlying the hormone-induced transport of substrate cholesterol from intracellular stores into the mitochondria. This intracellular trafficking of cholesterol is a fundamental aspect of cell biology and critical in reproductive and adrenal biology, since this is the rate-determining step in the formation of steroids. Understanding the mechanisms underlying this process would also pave the way for the development of novel pharmacological strategies for manipulation of the reproductive and adrenal function and might help unveiling the physiopathology of endocrine diseases associated with abnormal cholesterol metabolism and steroid synthesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brain Fuel Uptake and Cognitive Decline in the Elderly
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BRAIN; COGNITION; GLUCOSE; KETONES; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: In certain brain regions, glucose uptake decreases significantly in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Decreased brain glucose uptake can occur decades before the clinical onset of AD, making it the earliest reported pathophysiological change associated with AD. Using positron emission tomography (PET), we have preliminary evidence showing that in the healthy elderly, brain glucose uptake declines 11-13% in the same regions as in AD but that brain ketone uptake is unaffected. We have also shown that rats in mild, experimental ketonemia (MEK; 1-2 mM total plasma ketones for 2 wk) have a 2-3 fold increase in brain uptake of both ketones and glucose. If confirmed in humans, this novel finding might explain why, in short term studies, MEK improves cognition in AD. The amnestic form of mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) is the condition most likely to lead to AD. We hypothesize that - (i) aMCI predisposes to AD in part because it exacerbates the age-related trend towards lower brain uptake of glucose in brain regions affected in AD, and (ii) MEK has a beneficial effect on cognition because it bypasses or corrects lower brain glucose uptake. The objective is to better understand the link between deteriorating glucose uptake and risk of declining cognition in the adult/aging brain. Specifically, before and after inducing MEK, we will assess cognitive function and use our PET method to assess the brain uptake of ketones and glucose in human studies involving the healthy elderly and aMCI. In aged rats, we will examine mechanistic aspects of different models of MEK including brain fuel uptake, and brain glucose and ketone transporter expression. Whether gradually deteriorating brain glucose uptake with aging can be corrected is unknown. MEK is currently the only known way to raise brain glucose uptake so it has important implications for nutritional strategies to reduce the risk of developing aMCI or, potentially, its conversion to AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms for the gating of voltage-activated potassium channels
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIA; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GATING; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; POTASSIUM CHANNELS; STRUCTURE FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The direct aims of this project are to understand how these small proteins that regulate the electrical activity of the heart work.  When they control the beating of the heart they must open and then close at the appropriate time during the heartbeat.  To allow them to do this they have specialized parts that move and change shape.  We want to understand how the parts work together to make a smoothly functioning channel.  in this way we can fully appreciate the complexity of these channels, and begin to understand how the disease process modifies this normal pattern of function.  Finally we can begin to devise ways to correct malfucntions in these small proteins both from birth, and also as a result of modificaitons that occur as a result of diseases, and perhaps correct the manifestations of disorders of heart rhythm that can be so serious.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and functional studies of the vascular Ca2+-activated K+ channel of intermediate conductance KCa3.1.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOPLASTY; ENDOTHELIAL AND SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; K CHANNEL; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MOLECULAR STRUCTURE; PATCH CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: The voltage insensitive KCa3.1 channel is a membrane protein that forms a pore in the cell membrane through which K+ ions diffuse down their electrochemical gradient. The channel is activated by internal Ca2+ so that its activity varies in response to a variety of chemical (hormones, neurotransmitters) and physical (shear stress) external stimuli. Channel activity is also controlled through intracellular chemical modifications involving several protein kinases including AMPK which is sensitive to the cell energy status. Recent studies have demonstrated that the activation of KCa3.1 constitutes an obligatory step in the control of vascular tone by the endothelial cells which are expressed at the internal surface of blood vessels. This channel is also  documented to be involved in the proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells in pathological conditions. As a result, KCa3.1 is now emerging as a therapeutic target for cardiovascular disorders such as atherosclerosis, restenosis after angioplasty and traumatic-induced edema. In the proposed research program we intend, using electrophysiological measurements, computer-based modeling and tools from molecular biology,  1) to identify the amino acids which are responsible for controlling the K+ ion flow through the channel pore, and 2) to determine how the structural changes induced by the binding of Ca2+ to the channel are conveyed to the amino acid responsible for channel opening. The preliminary results we obtained to date indicate in this regard that a region of the channel referred to as the selectivity filter plays a crucial role in the Ca2+ dependent control of K+ ions flow and represents an important binding site for KCa3.1 potentiators and inhibitors. This information is essential to understand the mechanisms by which pharmacological agents known to affect KCa3.1 activity exert their action, while constituting an essential step to design molecules capable of either stimulate or block KCa3.1 activity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and inhibitory analysis of antibiotic resistance mechanisms and novel antibiotic targets in pathogenic bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; CELL-WALL BIOGENESIS; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; STRUCTURE-BASED DRUG DESIGN; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: The growing resistance of bacterial infections to standard antibiotic therapies has quickly become a major and frightening health concern around the globe. The causative agents of serious illnesses such as hospital staph infections, tuberculosis and meningitis are showing increasing numbers of antibiotic resistant strains both within the hospital and community settings. Some particular bacterial infections, often termed "superbugs", have become entirely resistant to all clinically utilized antibiotics. Our research aim is to understand both the way in which bacteria resist current families of antibiotics and to design new antibiotic drugs based on inhibiting specific features of the bacterial life-cycle. We will undertake this research by characterizing the three-dimensional atomic structures of molecules critical to the viability of the bacteria. By knowing these structures in such fine detail, a molecular blue-print if you will,  we can design drugs (antibiotics) that specifically inhibit or "turn off" these critical molecules of the bacteria, destroying the infection in the process. In this way we hope to continue the era of control over bacterial pathogens that we have had the privilege of living in this past half century.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cerebrovascular effects of endothelial NMDA receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: 2-PHOTON IMAGING; ASTROCYTE; D-SERINE; DEMENTIA; ENDOTHELIUM; NMDA RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Brain cells are normally protected by a mechanism that delivers enhanced blood flow to areas that have increased demand. Defects in this protective mechanism are assocaited with development of dementias including Alzheimer's Disease. Our lab has identified a protein inside the lining of brain blood vessels that reponds to neurotransmitters released during brain activity by increasing the vessel diameter and, consequently, the amount of blood that can flow through the vessel. This is the first description of this mechanism. Thus our proposal is to thoroughly characterize the structural and functional characteristics of this receptor target, and then to examine how brain cells communicate with this blood vessel protein in intact brain models, including a) thin slices of brain that contain both brain cells and blood vessels in native form in a complex known as the "neurovascular unit," and b) whole animal brain using intricate surgical and imaging procedures. These experiments will produce results with important implications for all research streams involving this protein, including stroke, brain inflammation and Alzheimer's Disease

TitreApplicationTitle: The Transition from Acute Postsurgical Pain to Chronic Pain: The Role of Pain Anxiety and Parental Influences in Paediatric Pain
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PAIN; PAIN ANXIETY; PARENT-CHILD RELATIONSHIP; PEDIATRIC POST-OPERATIVE PAIN; QUANTITATIVE; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Although the exact prevalence of pediatric chronic postsurgical pain is not known, recent estimates indicate that between 10% and 50% of children experience pain six months after common surgical procedures. Very little is known about the mechanisms responsible for the transition from acute to chronic postsurgical pain in children. Well-validated models, based in part on work our group has conducted with adults and children, have lead us to propose testable psychological and behavioural mechanisms that are involved in the transition from acute to chronic pain among children undergoing surgery. We will use a prospective, longitudinal design to evaluate the role of specific biomedical, psychological and behavioural processes associated with the development of chronic postsurgical pain and pain-related disability up to one year after surgery. The identification of such mechanisms has important implications for developing psychological interventions to prevent children from developing chronic postsurgical pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Plasma exchange and glucocorticoid dosing in the treatment of anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibody associated vasculitis: an international randomized controlled trial
Keywords-MotsClés: GLUCOCORTICOID; PLASMA EXCHANGE; PLASMAPHERESIS; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL; VASCULITIS; WEGENER'S GRANULOMATOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Severe, anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibody associated vasculitis (AAV) is an uncommon but serious disease of the immune system that is diagnosed in approximately 1 in 100,000 Canadians each year. AAV is important because up to 50% of patients will die or develop kidney failure within 5 years of diagnosis. There are two major problems in the treatment of AAV: 1) current treatment strategies fail to bring the disease under control quickly, before it causes major organ damage, and 2) current treatments have a serious toxicity profile. We propose a study to examine these problems in patients with severe AAV that affects their kidneys or lungs. Patients will be randomly assigned to receive plasma exchange, a method of rapidly removing harmful antibodies to rapidly gain control of AAV, in addition to standard therapy or standard therapy alone . Patients will also be randomly assigned to receive either a standard dose of steroids or a reduced-dose scheme which is predicted to reduce treatment related toxicity. By addressing both these critical problems we hope to significantly improve patient survival and reduce the frequency of kidney failure in patients with severe AAV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engineering Gold Nanoparticle Radiosensitizers for Cancer Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DOSIMETRY; NANOPARTICLES; RADIATION THERAPY; SENSITIZERS; TRANSPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer remains the second leading cause of death in Canada. Radiation therapy is used in the management of over 50% of all individuals suffering from cancer. A major focus of cancer research is to develop strategies that are minimally invasive and provide cure or control with negligible side effects. Recently there has been significant interest in exploring nanotechnology for imaging, diagnostic and therapeutic applications in cancer. Animal studies have shown that nanoparticles formed from gold can be used as a potent radiation sensitizer that enhances the effect of the radiation dose delivered. At present, the major challenge associated with the use of gold nanoparticles for cancer therapy is the inability to preferentially target tumor tissues and avoid sensitization of normal critical structures. As well there is a limited understanding of the relationship between the distribution of gold nanoparticles at the cellular level and the resulting radiobiological effects. The goal of the current proposal is to design gold nanoparticle contructs that target tumor tissue and achieve the optimal subcellular distribution in cancer cells to enable full exploitation of their radiosensitizing effect for improved cancer outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Connexin regulation and glioma growth control
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; GAP JUNCTIONS; GLIOMA
Abstract-Résumé: Connexin43 is a member of a large family of proteins that form pores between two adjacent cells so that the exchange of materials can occur. This direct communication between cells is important in many normal and diseased organs.   Brain cancer often arises from cells that originally contain high levels of connexin 43 that disappear when the cells become cancerous. However, our preliminary results show that connexin43 is also present at the tumor boundary where there is active invasion of the normal tissue by the cancer cells.  Recent evidence has revealed the pivotal role of tumor cells changing the fate of the surrounding normal cells and vice versa, eventually leading to an advanced stage of tumor progression. The brain presents one of the most complex environments with numerous factors being released by brain cells that might directly or indirectly affect tumor growth.   Connexin43 has already been shown to be important for the interaction between tumor  cells and blood vessels, facilitating the spread of tumors cells to the rest of the body. We now propose connexin43 is also critical for the communication between tumor and normal cells. We will determine whether Cx43 affects the spread of brain cancer by altering the characteristics of the cancer cells, or by allowing direct communication between tumor and surrounding cells. Lastly, we will investigate the possible mechanisms by which Cx43 can mediate these effects.   The study of Cx43 will provide a better understanding on the lethality of brain cancer, often untreatable due to the aggressive invasion of the cancer cells to the surrounding healthy tissue. Our study might ultimately lead to a treatment to prevent cancer cells from taking over the whole brain

TitreApplicationTitle: Mitochondrial vulnerability to stress: An early maladaptive response in adverse ventricular remodelling.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH; HEART PERFUSION / ISCHEMIA-REPERFUSION; ISOLATED CARDIOMYOCYTES / STRESS RESPONSE; ISOLATED MITOCHONDRIA / PERMEABILITY TRANSITION PORE; MITOCHONDRIA; MYOCARDIAL HYPERTROPHY AND FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the known association between cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure the mechanisms involved in the transition from compensated hypertrophy to failure remain poorly understood. Several evidences indicate that in the failing stage mitochondria (the cellular powerhouses) display overt defects, which can contribute to energy starvation. In addition, mitochondria contribute to cell death observed in the failing heart by their capacity to trigger cell death. This phenomenon is important as loss of cardiac cells is viewed as a critical contributor to the failure process. However, the factors that set the stage for these events in the failing heart remain poorly understood. Identification of contributing factors early during the disease is critical in order to develop treatments to prevent or attenuate the relentless progression of this pathology. We have recently shown that mitochondrial vulnerability to stress develops early in compensated hypertrophy at a time when overt mitochondrial defects are not yet apparent. This observation is highly relevant as hypertrophied hearts are often exposed to prolong periods of stress well before the occurrence of cardiac failure. The general objective of this proposal is to further define whether mitochondrial vulnerability to stress represents an early factor contributing to cardiac decompensation. This will be done by determining 1) when and how mitochondrial vulnerability develops in the hypertrophied heart following myocardial infarction, 2) how it impacts of heart function and cell death mechanisms in response to acute stresses and 3) if genetic and pharmacological inhibition of mitochondrial vulnerability affects the tolerance of the heart to acute stress and disease progression. This program will increase our understanding of the role of mitochondria in myocardial patho-physiology and contribute to the identification of therapeutic means to prevent of reduce the progression towards heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure function analyses of bacterial staphyloferrin systems
Keywords-MotsClés: CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; ENZYMOLOGY; IRON UPTAKE; SIDEROPHORE
Abstract-Résumé: Iron is growth essential for almost all human pathogens and thus bacterial iron acquisition systems are recognized generally as virulence factors. This proposal focuses on investigation of the mechanisms employed by a key iron transport system in a clinically important human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus that cause debilitating and life threatening infections. The rapid spread of methicillin resistant S. aureus (MSRA, a.k.a. the superbug) in both community and hospital settings, has accelerated the need for understanding this pathogen's virulence repertoire for the development of new therapeutic approaches. Staphyloferrin A and staphyloferrin B siderophores are low molecular weight iron chelators that are used by S. aureus to scavenge iron. These iron transport systems have components shown to be required for optimal growth under iron limitation and for colonization or pathogenesis in model animal systems. We will make use of the complementary strengths from our two labs to drive a concerted approach to understand the mechanisms of key steps in staphyloferrin A and B synthesis and uptake. Specifically, we will crystallography to determine high resolution structures of the enzymes and receptors to gain insight into their function. Assays will be used to test hypotheses concerning specificity of these proteins.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of the Safety of C-Spine Clearance by Paramedics
Keywords-MotsClés: CERVICAL SPINE INJURIES; CLINICAL DECISION RULE; COHORT STUDY; EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES; IMPLEMENTATION STUDY; PARAMEDICS
Abstract-Résumé: Each year, Canadian Emergency Medical Services (EMS) bring 1.3 million patients who may have injured their neck (c-spine) in falls or motor vehicle collisions to local emergency departments (ED). Less than 1% of all these patients have a c-spine injury (bone or ligament), and even less (0.5%) have a spinal cord injury (nerve damage). Most spinal cord injuries occur before EMS arrival and not during transport to hospital, yet most trauma victims (with or without c-spine injury) are transported in ambulances using backboard, collar, and head immobilizers. They stay fully immobilized until an ED bed is made available (sometimes up to 3 hrs, also holding up the EMS crew), or until physician assessment and/or X-rays are complete. This prolonged immobilization is often unnecessary, adds considerably to patient discomfort, and also adds to the burden of our EMS system and overcrowded Canadian EDs. A clinical decision rule helps health care workers make clinical decisions using information from the history, examination, or simple tests. We have developed the Canadian C-Spine rule (CCR) to be used by physicians, nurses, and paramedics for alert and stable trauma patients. After evaluating more than 30,000 patients, the CCR has never missed a significant injury. Physicians and nurses already use the CCR in clinical practice to remove immobilization devices without the need for X-rays. Paramedics recently evaluated 1,949 patients using the CCR and identified all injuries. The goal of this project is to evaluate the safety and potential impact of an active strategy to empower paramedics to evaluate and not immobilize the c-spine of very low-risk trauma patients before transport.  Our ethics board believe that teaching paramedics to evaluate the c-spine of very low-risk trauma patients is safe and has the potential to significantly improve patient care in our busy EMS system and Canadian EDs. We expect the results of this study to be used by paramedics throughout Canada.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; AUTRES MALADIES VENERIENNES
TitreApplicationTitle: Gonococcal Opa protein binding to the CEACAM receptors: Impact on infection and immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; CELL BIOLOGY; GONORRHEA; IMMUNOLOGY; MUCOSAL INFECTION; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The sexually transmitted infection gonorrhea is one of the most prevalent infections in the world, and remains one of the leading causes of female infertility and blindness in new infants who are born to infected mothers. These outcomes of infection result from an overly aggressive 'innate' immune response that causes damage to tissues that are infected by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Despite this fact, the immune system does not 'remember' the infection, allowing an individual to get repeatedly infected with these bacteria. This research proposal describes work that aims to explain these observations based upon our finding that the bacteria express a family of proteins, known as the Opa proteins, which bind to human CEACAM receptor proteins that can either activate or suppress a variety of human cell functions depending upon the cellular and immunological context.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying progression in open-angle glaucoma
Keywords-MotsClés: FOLLOW-UP STUDY; GLAUCOMA; NEW TECHNIQUES; OPTIC NERVE HEAD IMAGING; PERIMETRY; PROGRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Glaucoma is an age-related visual disorder that affects the lives of 2% of the population aged over 40 years and up to 5% of those aged over 70 years.  Glaucoma places a large burden both on the health care system with increasing treatment costs, and on care-givers from physicians to family members of the affected.  More importantly, studies have repeatedly shown that glaucoma is a disabling disease that significantly diminishes the patient's quality of life, even with mild to moderate disease severity. Successful treatment outcomes depend primarily on early detection of disease and its progression.  The current grant proposal deals with strategies to detect early disease progression and their translation into clinical practice to ensure not only success in stalling the biological progression of the disease but maintaining good quality of life.  In order to do this we will investigate a variety of tests to measure the field of vision which is affected in this disease and image the optic nerve which is damaged.  We are tracking the progress of patients with glaucoma who are tested with a variety of tests and developing analysis techniques to translate the findings to clinical practice. If we can show that we can detect progression of the disease earlier, we may be able to identify individuals that need different intervention in their management and therefore provide a better prognosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Study to Prospectively Assess the Safety and Effectiveness of The Ottawa SAH Strategy for the Investigation of Alert Patients Suspected of Having Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (Renewal - Phase III)
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL DECISION RULE; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; HEADACHE; SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE
Abstract-Résumé: This study will validate, or confirm the accuracy, of two new ways to determine which headache patients seen in emergency require investigation for possible subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). One is the Ottawa SAH Rule which will determine which patients with severe headaches need any investigations. The second is the 6-Hour CT Rule, which says that patients who have a CT scan (a type of X-Ray) within 6 hours of headache onset do not need a lumbar puncture (LP) (where a needle is put into the lower back to get spinal fluid). SAH is a type of hemorrhagic stroke caused by a rupture of a brain aneurysm. One percent of emergency department visits for a headache have a SAH. Half of all patients who have a SAH die and of those who survive, almost half have permanent neurological symptoms. Currently SAHs are diagnosed using CT and LP. Once the accuracy of these rules has been confirmed, we will also conduct a targeted implementation study to determine if physicians will use these rules. During implementation, we will also further assess the safety of the rules, use of testing and the length of time patients spend in the emergency department. Given the need for a correct diagnosis and the cost and invasiveness of over-investigating patients, clinical decision rules, which physicians will use, are needed to determine which headache patients require evaluation and how best to investigate patients requiring evaluation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Primary EBV Infection in the Immunosuppressed Setting of Organ Transplantation: Determinants of the Outcomes of Virus-Host Interaction
Keywords-MotsClés: EPSTEIN-BARR VIRUS; GENE EXPRESSION; LYMPHOPROLIFERATION POSTTRANSPLANT; MICROARRAY; RT-PCR; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISMS
Abstract-Résumé: This will be a multi-centre Canadian study to be done over 4.5 years. We will be  studying children and young adults with primary Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection after weakening of their immune systems. In this regard, we will use the example of organ transplantation. The EBV can cause a wide range of problems in individuals who get infected. The virus often infects white blood cells, causing the cells to multiply out of control in some individuals with weakened immune systems. Doctors are in need of more information to help them to better understand the reasons why some individuals do well with EBV infection, while others do not. This will help them to design the best treatments, particularly for those with weakened immune systems. This is a growing concern given the large numbers of patients who are currently receiving various forms of treatments that weaken the immune system.  We will be trying to find out if there are special protein-like substances, referred to as genes, that could explain why some people get mild infection while other get more severe infection.  We will study patients with new-onset EBV  after organ transplantation and compare these patients with different groups, including those who are otherwise healthy with EBV infection.  We will assess the transplant patients with EBV infection during the early and later stages of infection. In addition to clinical assessment, we will measure the amount of virus in the blood. We will also measure special proteins that are produced in response to infection. In addition, we will be identifying particular genes that are responsible for controlling infection and determine how the transplant patients with EBV differ from those without transplantation or EBV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional characterization and fine mapping of a type 2 diabetes risk locus near IRS1.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN STRUCTURE; DIABETES GENETICS; DIABETES PATHOGENESIS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE EXPRESSION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Adult-onset diabetes frequently occurs in family members as a result of inherited changes in the sequence of their genes. We have discovered a number of changes in DNA can make people more prone to developing diabetes. In the current project, we will study the physiologic effects of one of these these DNA changes to determine how it increases a person's risk of developing diabetes. In particular, we will determine how a genetic change on human chromosome 2 affects insulin's ability to alter cellular metabolism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Benznidazole Evaluation For Interrupting Trypanosomiasis Trial (BENEFIT)
Keywords-MotsClés: BENZNIDAZOLE VS PLACEBO; CHAGAS CARDIOMYOPATHY; CHAGAS DISEASE; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Chagas' disease is caused by the bite of a mosquito that transmits the parasite known as Trypanosoma Cruzi. This is a disease that affects more than 10 million people in Latin America and with the increase in immigration there is the potential to see some cases in Canada. Once the individual is infected susceptible individuals will develop severe cardiac complications that occur in 20% to 30% of infected individuals. The most frequent manifestation is chronic heart failure characterized by severe shortness of breath and marked exercise limitation. The disease has a rapid course and a high mortality due to heart failure and sudden cardiac death being the most frequent causes of death. To date no specific therapy is available to delay or halt the progression of heart damage. Recently the parasite has been closely linked to the progression of the disease and the use of an antitrypanosomal drug such as Benznidazole has been suggested but never tested in the setting of a large clinical trial. This study will assess whether the administration of Benznidazole in patients with established Chagas' heart disease reduces the progression of the cardiac involvement. The BENEFIT Pilot trial is currently being conducted in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Colombia and over 1700 patients have been recruited, demonstrating the safety and feasibility of this study. This renewal request will focus on the long-term follow-up, and completion of recruitment (2700)and establish whether treatment will erradicate or reduce the amount of parasites in chronically infected people and thereby halt or reduce the progression of this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bordetella pertussis Lipid A
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL VIRULENCE FACTORS AND PATHOGENESIS; BORDETELLA PERTUSSIS; INNATE IMMUNITY; LIPOPOLYSACCHARIDE AND LIPID A; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Our immune system can detect an integral component of bacterial surfaces called lipid A. This is mediated by a receptor complex called TLR4-MD-2, that when activated, results in the production of proteins called cytokines that are important in controlling infection.  Although not completely understood, much of what is known about this process has arisen from studying lipid A from laboratory strains of E. coli and a handful of pathogens. These studies have shown that lipid A molecules vary not only between bacterial pathogens but also within a given strain. This can result in immune responses that differ both in the magnitude, and in the pattern of cytokines produced. This can ultimately shape the outcome of infection.   Bordetella pertussis, the causative agent of whooping cough, which has a lipid A molecule that is very different from that of E. coli, can alter its lipid A to either increase or dampen the immune response to it.  How this happens is not known. We will decipher the mechanisms by which very small changes in B. pertussis lipid A influence immune responses. We will also look at the mechanisms by which the lipid A molecule is modified in B. pertussis. This work will contribute to the basic knowledge on how a fundamental building block of an important bacterial surface structure is made, and how the host responds to it.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gait Variability as Predictor of Cognitive Decline and Risk of Falls in MCI. A Cohort Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGES; DEMENTIA; FALLS; GAIT; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; VASCULAR RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: A decrease in walking speed (gait slowing) is a common problem in older persons and is frequently overlooked though it is a strong predictor of future disability and adverse events. Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a transitional state between normal cognition and mild dementia, however, not all older people having MCI will develop dementia. Recently, a Canadian consensus on dementia called for better characterization of MCI emphasizing the need to identify potential clinical, imaging, and biological changes that may serve as predictors of further dementia. To date, such a predictors have not been identified. However, since an association between gait slowing and dementia has been established, gait itself might be able to serve as  such a predictor. This study plans to assess the ability of quantitative gait analyses, specifically gait variability under a dual-task condition (e.g. walking while counting backwards), to predict time to progression to dementia in older persons with MCI. A secondary objective is to determine if there are particular physical changes in the brain that are associated with gait variability and slowed gait velocity. Our hypotheses: 1) High gait variability in people with MCI will predict future progression to dementia. 2) Further gait variability during dual-task conditions is an independent predictor of dementia. 3) Gait variability and a faster progression to dementia will be associated with specific physical changes in the brain.  If the hypotheses are confirmed, conducting practical assessments of gait in people with MCI may help determine who may eventually progress to dementia. Since dementia is a prevalent and important public health problem, improved detection of those at higher risk is a priority. Better detection will help the Canadian health system to optimize available resources and strategies to implement early interventions to preserve function and to improve the quality of life of seniors.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; SANG
TitreApplicationTitle: A Systems Approach to Sepsis: Pathological versus Adaptive Microvascular Responses
Keywords-MotsClés: INTRAVITAL VIDEO MICROSCOPY; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; MICROVASCULAR OXYGEN TRANSPORT; SEPSIS; SPECTROPHOTOMETRY; TISSUE OXYGENATION
Abstract-Résumé: Sepsis occurs when an infection initiates an inflammatory response that involves not just the local site of initial injury but the whole body resulting in failure of otherwise healthy organs.  Due to the nature of the disease and limited treatment options, patients may spend a prolonged period in an intensive care unit receiving expensive state-of-the-art medical treatment yet ultimately die or, if they survive, have dramatically reduced quality of life. Sepsis is the primary cause of death in the ICU.  There has been an ongoing debate whether sepsis damages the molecular machinery (mitochondria) responsible for producing energy in the cell through the consumption of oxygen or damages the vasculature responsible for delivering oxygen and other nutrients needed by the cell.  Our research using an animal model of sepsis, which has been confirmed in other laboratories and in patients, shows that sepsis can results in 50% of capillaries in an organ to longer carry oxygen to the tissue.  Although we have interpreted this to support vascular injury as the cause of organ failure, others have interpreted the loss of capillaries as a normal adaptive response to the reduced demand for energy that occurs with mitochondrial damage.  It is extremely important to determine which interpretation is correct since the treatment strategies will be very different, i.e. protecting the mitochondria will fail if the vasculature is unable to adequately deliver the necessary oxygen.  The goal of this research is to determine whether the vasculature in an animal model of sepsis is able to respond normally to changing demands for oxygen. If the vasculature responds appropriately, the loss of capillaries is likely an adaptive response.  But if the vasculature fails to respond, it will be strong evidence that failure of the vasculature leads to organ failure, and hence that treatment strategies need to focus on either protection or restoration of vascular function to preserve organ function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathobiology and ribosomal insufficiency in Shwachman-Diamond syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW FAILURE; EXOCRINE PANCREATIC DYSFUNCTION; MOUSE DISEASE MODELS; RIBOSOME BIOGENESIS; SHWACHMAN-DIAMOND SYNDROME; TRANSLATIONAL INSUFFICIENCY
Abstract-Résumé: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) is a genetic disorder with food digestion problems leading to poor growth, and blood cell deficiencies leading to severe infections and susceptibility to leukemia.  The proposed investigations build on our previous family studies that led to the identification of a major gene that leads to SDS, known as SBDS, and our disease models that implicate problems in protein production.  SDS is one of a series of bone marrow failure disorders including Diamond-Blackfan anemia, Dyskeratosis congenita and the acquired 5q deletion syndrome that share clinical features of poor growth and leukemia susceptibility.  We propose to understand the function of SBDS and the consequences of its loss, and to learn how impaired protein production affects growth and leads to clinical problems.  Our long term goals are to improve strategies for patient management and to develop rationalized therapies for SDS and related bone marrow failure syndromes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Quantitative MRI for Multiple Sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IRON; FAST SPIN ECHO IMAGING; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; PHASE IMAGING; SUSCEPTIBILITY-WEIGHTED IMAGING; T2 QUANTIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a debilitating diseae typically beginning in young adulthood.  The cause is unknown and there is no cure. magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides a way to visualize the MS brain and has been used for clinical diagnosis and research inMS for many years. However findings on MRI do not correlate with the actual physical symptoms of the patient.  New MRI methods are needed, which is the focus of this application.  Studies of extracted brain after death have shown that MS brains often have iron buildup and that many lesions are not seen on MRI.  We introduce new MRI approaches to gain a greater understanding of MS in patients.  The new methods focus on two main areas of MS that need further investigation: lesion detection, and brain iron content. The methods introduce a living iron "stain" to determine relative iron content,and a new "microscope" that enables visualization of previously invisible lesions. The new methods all require significant advances in MRI technical development by applying physics insight. An additional step forward is that all new methods are "quantitative" which means they supply an absolute measure that can be used to follow disease over time. Most of the methods are performed with a rare MRI system at strength 4.7 T, which is roughly 90,000 times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.  After all of the methods have been created and tested in normal volunteers, we apply the methods to a time course study of MS evolution in patients to gain new insight into the disease.  This work is a collaborative effort between an MRI physicist, four MS neurologists, a neuroradiologist, two computer scientists and a statistician.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the epigenome in spermatogenesis, sperm function and embryo health
Keywords-MotsClés: EMBRYO HEALTH; EPIGENETICS; HISTONES; MALE INFERTILITY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; SPERMATOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Globally there have been reported increases in male infertility and reproductive disorders such as testis cancer. Both these conditions are associated with changes to what is known as the epigenetic program. Epigenetics is used to describe heritable biochemical information that sits on the DNA and is attached to the DNA packaging proteins the histones. Importantly the epigenetic layer regulates whether a gene is turned on or not, and can be influenced by the food we eat, the drugs we take and the toxins we are exposed to.  In the formation of sperm, the layer of epigenetic information in part controls how male germ cells develop and also packages the DNA for the safe delivery to the embryo.  If this setting of the epigenome is disturbed during male germ cell development there will be negative consequences for fertility and the health of offspring. This research program will investigate how the epigenetic information carried on sperm DNA contributes to male fertility and embryo health.  The information generated from these studies will contribute new information on male infertility and as to how fathers can cause disease in their offspring through heritable information outside of the DNA.

ResearchClassEN: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL DISEASES

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of synaptic plasticity by the amyloid precursor protein (APP)
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; CALCIUM IMAGING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GENETIC MUTATIONS; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; TWO-PHOTON IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD), a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, is the most common form of dementia in the elderly. The prime candidate for the cause of Alzheimer's disease is the peptide beta-amyloid (A-beta), which is formed by biochemical processing of the amyloid precursor protein (APP), and is part of the plaques found in the brain of AD patients. However, memory deficits in AD patients do not correlate well with A-beta plaque burden, but, rather, with the loss of synaptic markers. Synaptic plasticity is the best cellular approach available for how learning and memory occurs in the brain, and it was, therefore, of great interest that the rules for synaptic plasticity are changed in animal models of Alzheimer's disease. How these changes take place, however, is largely unknown. Therefore, we propose a set of experiments to examine how the different parts of APP, such as A-beta, affect synaptic plasticity and, thereby, affect learning and memory. We hope to further elucidate the mechanisms underlying Alzheimer's disease as well as provide potential targets for future AD treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular controls of jaw identity and limb patterning
Keywords-MotsClés: EMBRYO DEVELOPMENT; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; GROWTH FACTOR SIGNALLING; JAW IDENTITY; LIMB PATTERNING; PEPTIDASE INHIBITORS
Abstract-Résumé: In previous work we found that the levels of retinoic acid, a vitamin A derivative, and Bone Morphogenetic Protein are essential factors in jaw development. The tweaking of these two molecules in early chicken embryos changed the side of the face (cheek bones) to the centre of the face. The present application is testing the model that RA and BMPs and other molecules downstream are necessary for specifying jaw identity. We are focusing on a secreted protein that not only can replicate the effects of BMP and RA on the face but also has effects on limb patterning. Here we will increase and decrease the levels of this protein in the early chicken embryo to determine its roles in shaping the skeleton of the limbs and face. Our work will not only shed light on inherited birth defects that affect the upper face such as cleft lip and midine clefts but also will help us to understand disturbances in the number of digits in the hands or feet.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of apoptosis by insulin signaling in C. elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; CHEMOTHERAPY; GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Adult organisms must maintain a relatively constant number of cells by sustaining a critical balance between cell division and cell death. If this intricate balancing act is tipped to favour too much cell survival an organism can develop tumors. Genes that regulate cell survival and cell death are well conserved from simple organisms to humans. We use the microscopic nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans as a model to understand how these genes make life and death decisions. We recently discovered that insulin signaling has a profound effect on survival by engaging the cell's internal suicide machinery.  Yes, all of our cells can kill themselves if they are a threat to the organism.  Insulin signaling can be thought of as a way to transmit information from one cell to another.  These signals from neighbours can dictate whether the cell divides more or kills itself for the greater good of the organism.  Cancer cells are not aware of what is good for the organism and only care about living forever.  This is a major problem for the organism if one group of cells grows out of control and forms a tumor. We found that insulin signaling from neighbouring cells assists severely damaged cells to kill themselves (sort of like assisted suicide).  We use C. elegans to study the regulation of this process because of its remarkable similarity to insulin signaling in humans and the efficiency by which genes can be turned on or off in this organism.  Because we can manipulate genes so easily in this organism it is possible to discover new ways to manipulate insulin signaling to kill cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal Correlates of Spontaneous Fluctuations in Blood-Oxygenation Imaging Signals and Functional Connectivity at Rest
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY; FUNCTIONAL MRI; LARGE SCALE NETWORKS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGICAL RECORDINGS; OPTICAL IMAGING; RESTING STATE
Abstract-Résumé: Visual, auditory, and other sensory stimuli presented to human subjects evoke increases in brain activity. Modern Magnetic Resonance Imaging scanners are capable of detecting such increases in neuronal activity in an indirect manner: they detect increased blood flow triggered locally by the increased neuronal activity. This method is termed 'functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging' (fMRI). Recent fMRI studies have demonstrated changes in brain activity not only when stimuli are presented to subjects, but also at rest. Importantly, these spontaneous (i.e. with no external stimuli) fluctuations in fMRI signals demonstrate 'functional connectivity': they increase or decrease in a synchronous manner over large parts of the human brain. It has been suggested that spontaneous brain activity is an important principle of brain function. This proposal is aimed at investigating the neuronal electrical activity that is represented by spontaneous changes in fMRI signals. We will pursue experiments that will determine the extent to which spontaneous fluctuations in fMRI signals reflect similar fluctuations in the underlying local neuronal activity. Furthermore, we will test whether the synchronization in spontaneous fMRI signals observed over remote regions of the brain (i.e., the functional connectivity) reflect synchronization in the overall level of neuronal activity measured within these areas. Last, we will pursue experiments towards understanding the mechanisms employed by neurons to mediate functional connectivity. To this end, optical imaging of blood oxygenation signals will be combined with neurophysiological recordings. The results may validate fMRI as a method for investigating spontaneous activity and functional connectivity in the resting state in healthy human subjects. Moreover, they may validate resting-state fMRI for diagnostic measurements in neurological and psychiatric diseases, based on changes in functional connectivity observed in these diseases.

ResearchClassEN: BRAIN TUMORS (INCL. RETINAL TUMORS); BRAIN TUMORS THERAPY

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery and characterization of C19MC a novel oncogenic miRNA locus in malignant brain tumors
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL MARKER; BRAIN TUMORS; MICRORNA; NEURAL STEM CELLS; ONCOGENES
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumors are the most common cause of childhood cancer-related deaths, however unlike for childhood leukemia, treatment of childhood brain tumors remains relatively crude and ineffective. Inorder to advance brain tumor treatment it is critical to identify and study how specific genes and pathways are altered and may be targeted for therapy. In contrast to most cancers, genetic knowledge regarding most pediatric malignant brain tumors is very limited. Recently my laboratory undertook a large international collaboration to study SPNET - a particularly aggressive and often fatal maligant brain tumor in young children for which no significant genetic investigations have been undertaken to date.  Our investigations, which represented the first comprehensive genetic studies of these "orphan" tumors resulted in the discovery of a novel cancer causing gene, C19MC, which has to date not been discovered in other human cancers. Our studies show that C19MC, which codes for a cluster of microRNAs - a newly discovered class of cancer molecules, can alter growth of human neural stem cells and make them more resistant to normal growth stopping signals. Indeed, we find that tumors with high levels of specific C19MC microRNAs have very aggressive behaviours. Interestingly, recent studies in breast and other cancers suggest that other C19MC  microRNAs genes may also predict bad tumor outcomes. In this grant application, we propose to carry out in depth studies of the function of these C19MC microRNA genes in order to understand how these genes can lead to cancer development. We also propose to manipulate the C19MC microRNas to generate the first mouse model of SPNET brain tumors. We believe our studies will provide important new information about the role of microRNAs genes in a spectrum of other human cancers, and how they maybe exploited for novel cancer therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect insulin on Ventral Tegmental Area dopamine neurons
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; INSULIN; MOTIVATION; OBESITY; VENTRAL TEGMENTAL AREA
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity now poses a epidemic health crisis in the developed world. The abundant availability of palatable and highly caloric foods in the western diet is a major contributor to this disease. Traditionally, most research focuses on energy balance regulation in the hypothalamus. However, much less is known about how peptides that signal the cessation of eating, such as insulin, modulate motivation and reward. Dopamine neurons of the Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA) are a critical component of the neural circuit that mediates reward seeking behaviours, either for drugs of abuse or natural rewards. Indeed, dopamine has been shown to reinforce ingestive behaviours like food intake. Furthermore, evaluation of reward or motivation can be substantially modified by the metabolic status of the animal or by the administration of insulin into the brain. Dopamine neurons may serve as a direct target for insulin in these paradigms.  Receptors for peptides that increase food intake and modulate dopamine neural activity, such as ghrelin and orexin, in addition to others that decrease food intake such as insulin and leptin are abundantly expressed in dopaminergic neurons. Recently we have identified that orexin increases the neural activity of dopamine neurons to motivate animals to forage for food. Therefore, we are interested in how these reward signals are turned off. Insulin is released after meals and recent evidence suggests that the post-ingestive consequences of food can alter reward pathways. The proposed experiments will examine how insulin can modulate neuronal activity and output of VTA dopamine neurons. Further, we will determine if this insulin modulation the reward system is dysregulated in either genetically-prone or diet-induced models of obesity. These experiments will expand our knowledge of the mechanisms of insulin action on the dopamine reward circuit and ingestive behaviour and may lead to the development of therapeutic agents for the treatment of obesity.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Monte Carlo-based mixed electron/photon beam inverse treatment planning, delivery and verification
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTRON BEAM; ENERGY MODULATION; INVERSE PLANNING; MONTE CARLO SIMULATIONS; RADIATION PHYSICS; RADIATION THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Radiation therapy, the cancer therapy that makes use of ionizing radiation, can be performed with different types of radiation. The majority of therapy is done with photons, which have the property that they deposit dose in healthy tissues beyond the tumour, i.e., tissues that we would like to avoid giving radiation. Electron radiation is used currently at a much smaller scale although it could be very useful since the electron penetration depth can be accurately controlled and hence used to avoid dose delivery to healthy tissues. In this project we develop techniques to upgrade electron therapy technology. In the previous research we have invented, designed and built a new type of "(few-leaf) collimator" (or "FLEC"), i.e., a device that focuses the electron radiation for radiation therapy and that can be used on current commercial radiation equipment for cancer treatment. The collimator blades move during the treatment and the energy of the electrons is made to change during the treatment. These actions are termed "modulation" hence the term "modulated electron therapy". By doing so we can conform the high electron radiation dose tightly around the tumor and much better avoid normal healthy tissues. We have established that modulated electron radiation can help in a great way to reduce dose to healthy organs but that its performance and range of application can be greatly enhanced if it is used in conjunction with traditional photon radiation (hence, mixed-beam therapy). We use Monte Carlo simulation techniques with which we can follow the individual radiation particles and their path as they emerge from the radiation equipment through the collimator into the patient and we calculate how they deposit energy in the patient. Mixed beam therapy is very complex to plan and deliver so we develop novel techniques to verify mixed-beam therapy using sophisticated dose measurement techniques.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and molecular characterization of lupus susceptibility genes using congenic mouse strains
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGENIC; IMMUNOGENETICS; MURINE MODELS; SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system plays an important role in discriminating between proteins that are foreign to the body, such as those in the bacteria and viruses that cause infections, and proteins that are normal parts of the body, such as those found in organs like the kidney and the brain.  Foreign proteins are attacked preventing overwhelming infection while self-proteins are normally left unharmed.  We believe that Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) results from defects in the immune system that lead to abnormal activation of cells that react to self-proteins, however the precise defects remain to be identified.  In addition to humans, many strains of mice develop a lupus-like illness and study of these mice has provided important insights into the human disease.  My laboratory has been studying one of these mouse strains, the New Zealand Black (NZB) mouse.  In both humans and mice, SLE results from the interaction of multiple genes.  To facilitate identification of these genes, we have produced genetically manipulated mice, called congenic mice.  In these mice most of the DNA is from a normal mouse strain, but a small region of DNA has been introduced from the NZB mouse that is known to contain at least one of the genes that causes disease.  This allows us to study the effects of individual genes in isolation, with the ultimate goal of identifying the specific genes that cause disease.  Identification of these genes and the abnormalities they produce could ultimately lead to characterization of similar defects in humans and more effective therapies for this condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sleep and mild cognitive impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGING; EVENT RELATED POTENTIALS; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES; QUANTIFIED EEG; SLEEP DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: The prevalence of dementia is increasing at a rapid pace and Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the number one cause. The promise of future treatment, and even prevention, of AD with neuroprotective agents calls for the identification of reliable markers. The presence of a long and progressive preclinical period, termed mild cognitive impairment (MCI), offers the opportunity to detect incipient AD before the dementia phase. The aim of the present study is test the power of computerized EEG analysis and of brain imaging performed during sleep to identify MCI subjects at risk of developing AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cell surface regulation of G protein-coupled receptors in neuroendocrine systems
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL AND ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; DESENSITIZATION AND INTERNALIZATION; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; HYPOTHALAMUS; NEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; RECEPTOR TARGETING AND TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) represent the largest class of cell surface receptor molecules and are the targets of most drugs used in the therapy of metabolic and neurological disorders. They transmit extracellular signals, e.g. provided by endogenous signalling molecules or by medical drugs, inside the cells and induce a cascade of reactions on the part of the target cells. In order to fulfil this function, receptor molecules have to be delivered to the cell surface. Sst1, sst2, and sst5 are members of a family of GPCRs mediating the effects of somatostatin (SST), a member of the neuropeptide family of signalling molecules. There are marked differences between these receptor subtypes in their delivery from intracellular stores to the cell surface but only a few studies have addressed how cells control the availability of individual GPCR types at their surface membrane. Therefore, I propose to investigate how SST-responsive cells control the availability of SST receptor subtypes at the cell surface. Thereby, they effectively regulate their sensitivity to SST and, by extension, to drugs acting at the same receptors. SST plays a critical role in the control of hormone release from the pituitary gland by the brain and in fine tuning other neurotransmitter and hormonal systems. Dysfunctions of the SST system are frequently caused by neuroendocrine tumours of the pituitary or the gastro-intestinal system and have been implicated in a number of disorders such as acromegaly, gigantism, Alzheimer's disease and major depression. The proposed studies will provide a deeper insight into the mechanisms regulating the sensitivity of the SST receptor family and, by analogy, other GPCR signalling systems. They will also demonstrate the roles of gender and endogenous rhythms (e.g. hormonal rhythms) in the regulation of cell surface receptors and potentially break ground for the design of more effective drugs and new therapeutic approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of intrinsic B cell defects and their role in the immunopathogenesis of murine lupus
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGENIC; IMMUNOGENETICS; MURINE MODELS; SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS; TOLERANCE; TRANSGENIC
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system plays an important role in discriminating between proteins that are foreign to the body, such as those in the bacteria and viruses that cause infections, and proteins that are normal parts of the body, such as those found in organs.  Foreign proteins are attacked preventing overwhelming infection while self-proteins are normally left unharmed.  We believe that Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) results from defects in the immune system that lead to abnormal activation of cells that react to self-proteins.  Many strains of mice develop a lupus-like illness and study of these mice has provided important insights into the human disease.  In the immune system two classes of cells, T and B cells, act in concert to mount an immune response.  In both humans and mice with SLE, B cell functional abnormalities play a central role in the pathogenesis of disease.  However the precise genetic changes that lead to this altered function and mechanisms through which they act to promote disease remain to be identified.  My laboratory has been studying the New Zealand Black (NZB) mouse strain.  In previous work we have identified a number of B cell abnormalities in these mice.  To facilitate identification of the genes that produce these abnormalities, we have produced genetically manipulated mice.  In these mice most of the DNA is from a normal mouse strain, but a small region of DNA has been introduced from the NZB mouse that is known to contain at least one of the genes that leads to altered B cell function.   We have shown that mice with genes derived from NZB chromosomes 1 or 13, develop lupus, and that this is the result of altered B cell function.  In this grant we propose to further investigate how this altered function produces disease, with the ultimate goal of identifying the specific genes that alter B cell function.  Identification of these genes and the abnormalities they produce could ultimately lead to characterization of similar defects in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of aortic valve calcification by matrix biomechanics
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; CALCIFICATION; HEART VALVE DISEASE; MATRIX MECHANICS; MECHANOTRANSDUCTION; MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Diseases of the heart valves are among the most frequent causes of heart disease in Canada and cause significant morbidity. The most common valve disease is calcific aortic valve sclerosis. In aortic valve sclerosis, the valve leaflets thicken, stiffen, and calcify. Ultimately, these changes prevent the valve from opening and closing properly, which leads to serious heart problems. Currently, there is no effective treatment for aortic valve sclerosis except to replace the valve when the disease is advanced. The goal of this research is to better understand the biomechanical and biochemical factors that contribute to the progression of valve disease.  In preliminary work, we discovered that the aortic valve contains a large population of mesenchymal stem cells, a primitive type of cell that can become various mature cell types. We showed that the stiffness of the valve tissue modulates whether these cells convert to osteoblasts that make bone or myofibroblasts that cause fibrosis when grown under disease conditions. The objective of this project is to determine the molecular mechanisms by which tissue stiffness modulates valve cell pathological differentiation. Using novel bioengineering approaches and biomaterial systems, we will determine how matrix stiffness affects signalling pathways within the cell that regulate differentiation, with particular focus on pathways that are known to play an important role in skeletal bone formation. We will then confirm these findings in normal pigs and in pigs with valve disease by measuring valve tissue stiffness and correlating it with biological markers of valve cell function.  The knowledge gained by these studies will help to identify and develop novel therapeutic strategies that prevent or arrest aortic valve sclerosis, thereby reducing the impact of the disease and leading to improved health and quality of life for millions of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: McMaster Evidence Review and Synthesis Centre (MERSC)
Keywords-MotsClés: DISEASE PREVENTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; METHODOLOGY; PRACTICE GUIDELINES; PUBLIC HEALTH; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: The McMaster Evidence-based Practice Center (MU-EPC) and the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) are proposing to jointly create an Evidence Review and Synthesis Centre at McMaster University (MERSC).  The MERSC will support the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care (CTFPHC) by conducting between 8 and 10 'knowledge syntheses' per year.  Together, the MU-EPC and EPHPP have a solid, core group of researchers and staff who have conducted over 40 knowledge syntheses, all successfully completed on time and on budget, over the last 12 years.  The core group will be geographically based in Hamilton.  However, the group's researchers will use their vast number of contacts to recruit other researchers from within and outside Canada to form working groups of content experts for each knowledge synthesis.  The MU-EPC and EPHPP understand all of the steps and methods that are involved in designing and undertaking a knowledge synthesis.  Following the assignment of the topic and the refinement of the research question(s) in conjunction with the CTFPHC, a comprehensive literature search will be conducted to find all relevant articles.  We will use inclusion/exclusion criteria, developed before the literature search, to decide which articles should be included for review as part of the synthesis.  We will also use established standards to assess the methodological quality of included articles, as well as explicit methods to extract and synthesize data from included articles.

TitreApplicationTitle: The involvement of the epigenome in the mechanism of action and efficacy of pharmacotherapeutic interventions for bipolar disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIPSYCHOTIC; BIPOLAR DISORDER; BRAIN; EPIGENETICS; GENETIC ANIMAL MODEL; MICROARRAY-BASED DNA METHYLATION PROFILING; MOOD STABILIZER; SODIUM BISULFITE SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Bipolar disorder is a prevalent and devastating mental illness that is characterized by recurrent manic and depressive episodes. Medication is the cornerstone for treating bipolar disorder and includes mood stabilizers and antipsychotics. The development of new and improved treatments is greatly limited by our lack of understanding on how current treatments work. I will investigate the possibility that epigenetic factors may have an important role in the mechanisms of action of treatments for bipolar disorder. Epigenetics processes control gene activity without changing the DNA sequence. It acts as a "second code" of programming on top of the DNA code that, unlike DNA, can change over a lifetime. DNA methylation is an epigenetic mechanism that has been shown to be abnormal in bipolar patients, and treatments for this illness may ameliorate symptoms by causing changes in DNA methylation. To explore this possibility, mood stabilizers and antipsychotics will be administered to animal subjects, and changes in DNA methylation will be measured across the entire genome using a microarray technique. The microarray-based approach is unbiased and is a productive means of finding new genes affected by bipolar treatments via an epigenetic mechanism. The microarray findings will be confirmed with highly sensitive fine-mapping techniques. Epigenetic changes in response to drug treatments will be measured in both the normal mouse brain and in the brains of mutant mice that exhibit biochemical and behavioral disturbances resembling the symptoms of bipolar disorder. Nerve cells that originated from unmedicated human bipolar patients will also be exposed to bipolar medications and changes in DNA methylation will be measured. Overall, this study will provide insight on how treatments for bipolar disorder work and will reveal new gene targets involved in drug response. Identification of novel genes influenced by bipolar medications will fuel the development of improved treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: eHealth Mentoring: Building pathways to health careers for Aboriginal youth
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT; EDUCATION; INFORMATION TECHNOLOGIES
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal learners are under-represented in the post-secondary education system.  This is particularly evident in health science programs. The largest barrier is that only 9% of Aboriginal students are eligible for post-secondary entry. The low rates may be due to a number of reasons, including inadequate academic preparation, a lack of student development services, and feelings of isolation and exclusion. Mentoring relationships have been shown to positively influence various youth outcomes, including academic achievement and self-confidence. Online communications technology can support mentoring relationships and connect youth with inspirational role models they may otherwise be unable to meet. This concept, called "eMentoring", can provide Aboriginal youth with the support, knowledge and confidence they need to successfully enroll in university/college health science programs. The proposed plan is to implement an eMentoring pilot program for Aboriginal youth in grades 6-10, in collaboration with Aboriginal communities. Mentor-student relationships will last a minimum of one year, and consist of online activities that address some of the barriers Aboriginal students face in their transition to post-secondary education. Specifically, the evaluation will seek to understand: 1) how best to implement an eMentoring model in First Nations communities; 2) how mentors and youth interact with each other; and 3) how eMentoring can promote awareness, interest and enrolment in post-secondary health science programs. Connecting Aboriginal students to mentors using technology can overcome geographical and social boundaries. eMentoring has the potential to improve Aboriginal health by addressing some of the key factors that influence health outcomes, including education, social support networks, employment and culture.

TitreApplicationTitle: BACTERIAL OUTER MEMBRANE VESICLES and THEIR ROLE in PATHOGENESIS
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; OUTER MEMBRANE VESICLES; PORPHYROMONAS GINGIVALIS; PROTEIN SECRETION; SALMONELLA; VIRULENCE FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Many bacteria produce membrane vesicles that may be used as "long distance rockets" loaded with toxins. It is believed that these vesicles play a role in the establishment of the infection.  We work with two important bacterial pathogens, Porphyromonas gingivalis, a major cause of chronic gingivitis and recently implicated in pregnancy complications, and Salmonella typhimurium, one the most common agents that cause gastroenteritis world-wide. We have discovered that these bacteria can selectively pack toxins in these vesicles. The main goal of this project is to understand how the toxins are packed in the vesicles and to study the roles of the vesicles in pathogenesis. Achieving the goals may have an impact in human health by opening new opportunities for intervention against pathogenic bacteria. Understanding how proteins are selectively packed into vesicles may be useful to improve the current vesicles-based vaccines, which have been already used in humans in different parts of the world.

ClasseRechercheFR: DIABETE SUCRE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Immunogenetics of a rare T cell subset in autoimmune diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNE DISEASES; GENETICS; IMMUNOLOGY; MICROSATELLITE MARKERS; MURINE MODEL; T LYMPHOCYTES
Abstract-Résumé: Autoimmune diabetes is one of the most common of chronic childhood illnesses. North America shows one of the highest prevalence, with an incidence of 3 affected individuals for 1000 population. Daily insulin injections are able to control the disease; however, they do not prevent the clinical complications such as blindness, kidney failure, and heart attacks.  Autoimmune diabetes results from the destruction of insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. A specific subset of white blood cells, known as T cells, is sufficient to mediate this destruction and lead to the progression to autoimmune diabetes.  In this proposal, we aim to characterize a rare T cell population, which instead of destroying the pancreatic beta cells, may protect them. Indeed, we have recently shown, in our diabetes-resistant mouse model, that this rare T cell population can specifically eliminate destructive B cells. Interestingly, these rare protective T cells associate with resistance to diabetes, as they were found in higher proportion in our diabetes-resistant mice compared to our diabetes-susceptible mice. Importantly, the rare T cell subset is present in humans and their numbers can be easily increased. Thus, these rare T cells carry a high potential for cellular therapy.  Herein, we aim to compare the protective T cells obtained from diabetes-resistant and diabetes-susceptible mice to: (1) Help identify new effective drug targets, promoting the development of vaccine approaches, (2) Lead to the identification of susceptibility genes for diabetes, a step which is necessary for the development of early diagnostic tools, (3) Create a potential for developing cellular therapy treatments for patients at risk of developing diabetes and newly diagnosed patients. In summary, this proposal promotes the study of a rare T cell population, which carries a high potential for cellular therapy to prevent autoimmune diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of ALDH+/CD44+ stem-like cells in breast cancer progression and treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDH1; BREAST CANCER; CANCER STEM CELLS; CD44; METASTASIS; RESPONSE TO THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is a leading cause of cancer death in women. This is primarily due to difficulty in treating metastasis, which occurs when tumor cells spread from the original breast tumor to other parts of the body (lymph nodes, bone, lung, liver, or brain). Recent studies have demonstrated the existence of novel cells called "breast cancer stem cells". These aggressive cells are believed to be the cells that started the cancer growing in the first place; however their role in metastasis remains poorly understood. The goal of this study is to test the hypothesis that these cells are also responsible for metastasis and for determining how patients respond (or don't respond) to treatment. We will test this hypothesis using a combination of molecular biology/cell culture approaches, animal models, and patient-based studies.   The objectives of this proposal are (1) To use animal models of breast cancer and novel MRI imaging technology to determine the role that "stem-like" cancer cells play in metastasis, including whether these cells grow preferentially in certain common metastatic sites such as lymph node, lung, liver, brain, or bone; (2) To investigate the functional role of two specific proteins called aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) and CD44 in determining aggressive "stem-like" behavior and metastasis; and (3) To use a combination of cell culture and animal models as well as assessment of breast cancer patient samples in order to determine whether "stem-like" versus "non stem-like" cancer cells respond differently to cancer therapies and to determine the mechanisms by which they do so. These innovative and clinically relevant research studies will allow us to gain a greater understanding of metastasis and potentially identify new approaches for effective treatment of breast cancer.
