TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms underlying the sarcomere length dependence of force and muscle activation
Keywords-MotsClés: MYOFIBRIL; MYOFILAMENT; MYOSIN-ACTIN INTERACTION; NANOTECHNOLOGGY; SARCOMERE; TITIN MOLECULES
Abstract-Résumé: Muscle contraction is responsible for vital functions in humans. Skeletal muscles are responsible for movement of legs and arms, eyes, and hands. Lung muscles are responsible for breathing and blood oxygenation. Heart muscles are responsible for heart beating and pumping blood with oxygen and nutrients to all regions of our body throughout the entire life. Therefore, understanding how muscles work is of fundamental importance. However, the detailed mechanisms of muscle contraction are not well understood yet. The events that happen inside the muscles, at the molecular and cellular levels are under investigation in many laboratories without conclusive results. The current proposal intends to use an array of cutting-edge, experimental preparations ranging from single muscle molecules to cells to understand the basic mechanisms of contraction and force production. The results will add important information to our knowledge on how muscle work, and therefore will be essential for understanding the mechanisms of diseases that affect the muscular system, such as muscle dystrophy, cardiac arrests and asthma. Furthermore, understanding how muscles work may help us to delineate strategies to compensate muscle wasting commonly observed with aging, and consequently improving the quality of life of many Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sympathetic neuropathy during IBD: causes and consequences
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASES; NEUROSCIENCE; NEUROTRANSMITTER RELEASE; VASCULAR REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Summary: Neurotransmitters do more than cause muscles to contract and glands to secrete, they play an important role in modifying the activity of the immune system.  Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are caused by overactive immune responses, so dampening the immune system is an important means of treating IBD.  A branch of the nervous system, the sympathetic nervous system (SNS), participates in the regulation of the gastrointestinal tract and can modulate intestinal inflammation.  Therefore, the SNS potentially has the ability to suppress inflammation during IBD.  A recent study in an animal model of IBD reported that a drug which targets a receptor for a sympathetic neurotransmitter can decrease disease severity.  However, we have found that IBD inhibits the release of this neurotransmitter, which limits the ability of these receptors to suppress inflammation.  Therefore, this grant proposes to use a mouse model of IBD to examine how inflammation inhibits sympathetic neurotransmitter access to its receptors and how the immune system is modulated by the SNS. Where possible, findings in the mouse model will be confirmed by studying human tissue from biopsies of IBD patients and normal patients undergoing routine surveillance screening for colon cancer. By examining the reciprocal interactions between the immune system and the SNS, we hope to develop strategies to enhance the immunosuppressive actions of the SNS in IBD patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Community Social Capital and Population Health in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY EFFECTS; HEALTH DISPARITIES; HEALTH SOCIOLOGY; MULTILEVEL MODELING; SOCIAL CAPITAL; SOCIAL NETWORKS
Abstract-Résumé: The concept of community social capital--the resources that exist within community social ties and networks--has received intense interest by health researchers and policymakers.  This interest has emerged in trying to understand how the social conditions of neighborhoods and other local areas contribute to the health and well-being of residents.  However, existing data on social capital in British Columbia (BC) (as well as in Canada overall) provide insufficient information for policy and practice aimed at improving health and well-being in general and, more specifically, early childhood development (ECD)--a critical period of the lifespan for preventing or ameliorating many potentially harmful adult health outcomes.    The objective of this project is to examine how neighborhood social networks and the resources they provide matter for the health and well-being of two subpopulations in British Columbia (BC): young children and adults.  The project will analyze a comprehensive dataset of neighborhood conditions and child and adult well-being.  Survey data on community social ties and adult health will be collected from over 3000 respondents located in 100 rural and urban BC neighborhoods.  This unprecedented BC data will be merged with area census data and an existing BC population database of kindergarteners' ECD score records.  This project has 2 major benefits.  First, it will provide an improved--and Canadian-specific--examination of the different ways that urban and rural neighborhood social conditions matter for the health and well-being of the young children and adults who live within these locations.  Second, it will provide a crucial--and rare--resource for informing policies and interventions aimed at developing neighborhoods into environments that promote health and well-being from the early years onward.  The information generated by this project will be useful for residents, parents, researchers, policymakers, and practitioners.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sugar-coated designer immunogens to elicit HIV-1 neutralizing antibodies
Keywords-MotsClés: EPITOPE TARGETING; IMMUNOGEN  DESIGN; NEUTRALIZING ANTIBODIES; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; RECOMBINANT ANTIBODY DISPLAY; VACCINE ADJUVANTS
Abstract-Résumé: An effective vaccine is required to reverse the global spread of HIV-1. A consensus viewpoint is that a prophylactic HIV vaccine will need to incorporate a component that elicits so-called broadly neutralizing antibodies, which are those with the capacity to recognize a large variety of circulating viral isolates -primary viruses--and prevent infection upon exposure to HIV. This application seeks to determine whether a set of engineered proteins can stimulate the production of neutralizing antibodies targeted to a relatively conserved segment of a protein on the surface of the virus. Specifically, it is proposed to (i) investigate the significance of formulating the engineered proteins with different immunological stimulants to elicit neutralizing antibodies, (ii) to determine the power of incorporating immunostimulatory protein sequences into the engineered proteins on the induction of neutralizing antibodies, and (iii) to determine the potential importance of the mode of presentation of the engineered proteins on stimulating the production of neutralizing antibodies. Our long-term goal is to understand features required for eliciting antibodies with broad neutralizing activity against HIV-1, in particular to specifically targeted segments, and identify promising candidates that may be moved forward for preclinical vaccine development.

TitreApplicationTitle: From doing good to feeling good: The health benefits of prosocial behaviour.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTRUISM; HAPPINESS; HEALTHY AND SUCCESSFUL AGING; PROSOCIAL BEHAVIOURS; SPENDING CHOICES; VOLUNTEER WORK
Abstract-Résumé: Can helping other people improve one's own health? Consistent with this possibility, recent research has demonstrated that individuals who provide help to others exhibit reduced risk of mortality, as well as better overall health. Almost nothing is known, however, about the pathways through which prosocial behavior might influence health. In addition, there is virtually no experimental research in this area due to the challenges associated with assigning people to engage in generous behavior.   Providing the opportunity to overcome these limitations, our team has recently developed paradigms that enable us to study prosocial behavior using experimental methodology. Applying these paradigms, we will investigate whether and how prosocial behavior influences biological variables related to health. Because money and time represent the two primary resources that people can give to others, we will examine the health consequences of using money (Study 1) and time (Study 2) to benefit others. Although engaging in prosocial behavior may be beneficial across the life span, there is some evidence that such behavior may be particularly valuable early and late in life. Thus, the proposed research will examine aging adults and university students. In Study 1, an aging sample of participants will be asked to use money in prosocial ways over a period of weeks and their sleep quality, cortisol, and blood pressure will be measured before, during, and after this. In Study 2, a sample of university students will be given the opportunity to use time in prosocial ways over the course of a school year and the impact of this experience on sleep and cortisol will be examined. We will further test whether the biological effects of prosocial behavior are mediated by social and emotional well-being. Thus, the core objective of this research is to illuminate the basic pathways through which helping behavior may "get inside the body" to bolster health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preserving local knowledge to protect health among Anishinabe communities in the Great Lakes Region
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE; FIRST NATIONS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LOCAL KNOWLEDGE; QUALITATIVE METHODS; YOUTH AND ELDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Research with Canada's First Nations has identified important links between the health of local physical environments and the health of local communities. The health of First Nation communities is strongly influenced by the ability to use, and benefit from, local environmental resources. In the Great Lakes region, Anishinabe (Ojibway) communities have endured several decades of environmentally exploitative resource development, that which has often had long-term consequences (e.g., compromised drinking water). As a result, the relationship between the Anishinabe and their land has changed over time and local elders have articulated an urgent need to preserve the traditional knowledges, cultural identities and social values intrinsic to Anishinabe concepts of health. In response, the proposed project will draw from an integrated knowledge translation framework to train and hire Anishinabe youth from various communities in the Great Lakes region to undertake qualitative research with their respective community elders. The research will address elders' perceptions of the causes and consequences of changes to health and environment over time, document special places, medicines, plants and animals within their traditional territories, and culminate in an Elder gathering. The main goals of this project are to preserve local elder knowledge about health and environment, to provide a knowledge transfer mechanism between youth, elders and researchers, and to expand the skill set, knowledge base and research potential of participating youth and community collaborators. This research will pioneer a critically important area of First Nation's health research by preserving local elder knowledge, and documenting how this process can be used in a way that will enhance local capacity, protect the environment and improve health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genome structure variations (SVs) and the origin of novel genes
Keywords-MotsClés: C. ELEGANS; GENOME; GENOME REARRANGEMENT; INSERTION/DELETION; NOVEL GENE; STRUCTURAL VARIATION
Abstract-Résumé: How novel genes form is a fundamental question in evolution and critical for understanding devastating disease conditions. In the past, the origin of novel genes has been attributed primarily to duplication of genome DNA sequences. However, other mechanisms, including exon-shuffling, retroposition, horizontal gene transfer, as well as de novo gene formation from non-coding sequences, have also been demonstrated to contribute to the generation of novel genes.   In this project, we are interested in examining the contribution of breakpoints associated with structural variations to the formation of novel genes. Genome structural variations, which are generated by rearrangement events, can be divided into two categories: (1) copy number variations that contain insertions and deletions; (2) balanced rearrangement events that contain inversions, transpositions, and translocations. The formation of each genome structural variation event is inevitably accompanied with the creation of one or more breakpoints. While most breakpoints in both somatic and germline genomes are deleterious and may cause various types of cancers and mental retardation in humans, reports from other research groups and recent data from our group demonstrate that some breakpoints can be the source of novel genes. In this project, we will examine the formation of novel genes at the "cutting edges" (i.e., structural variation breakpoints). In short, we will use the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans as a model system to demonstrate the importance of structural variation breakpoints in the origin of novel genes.   Specifically, we will first use computational methods to identify and experimental means to validate genome structural variations in two C. elegans strains, one of which is a laboratory strain and the other one is a wild isolate (isolated from an island in Hawaii). Then, we will identify these structural variations that impact protein coding genes and reconstruct the novel genes models.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hyperpolarized Helium-3 Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Healthy Aging Lung
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTHY AGING; HYPERPOLARIZED HELIUM-3; LUNG BIOMECHANICS; LUNG IMAGING; MRI; RESPIRATORY STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: To maximize transport of oxygen to the blood, the lungs are uniquely designed to contain approximately 2,400 km of airways and approximately 500 million alveoli, with a total gas exchange surface area that is roughly the area of a tennis court.  As we age, lung structure changes and function diminishes to the extent that the predicted lifespan of the normal healthy lung does not surpass about  120 years.  As the aging population increases in the developed world, it is increasingly important to understand the physiology, structure and function of the aging lung in order to establish appropriate strategies for its functional improvement.  The effects of the aging pulmonary system, that along with environmental factors is thought to be implicated as directly responsible for 10,000 deaths and 100,000 hospitalizations each year in Canada, is not well understood.  Despite the staggering societal burden and decades of active research,little is known about how to differentiate "usual aging" representing the effects of aging mixed with lifestyle and environmental factors, from "successful aging" reflecting not only a lack of apparent disease but physiological performance that is not significantly different from that of healthy young adults.  We recently were the first to report the unexpected 3He magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) finding that healthy elderly subjects exhibited lung functional changes similar to subjects with smoking-related lung disease suggesting that significant and unexpected age-related airway changes were occurring in healthy elderly never-smokers.  Our surprising imaging findings provide important mechanistic information about the aging lung and identify the potential for lung imaging measurements to help better quantify healthy aging lung changes. We will exploit our previous novel findings in a large longitudinal imaging study of healthy elderly lung.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transformation of normal to abnormal myocardium by diabetes: role of Rac1-mediated calpain activation
Keywords-MotsClés: CALPAIN; CARDIOMYOPATHY; DIABETES; RAC1
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is a disease. Patients' body with this disease can not properly utilize sugar (glucose). Thus, there is an increased concentration of sugar in blood of diabetic patients. There are two main types of this disease: type-1 and type-2 diabetes. The prevalence of diabetes is growing rapidly. Globally, the number of adults affected with diabetes is estimated to increase from 135 million in 1995 to 300 million by 2025. Patients with diabetes are at increased risk for heart and blood vessel diseases. Heart and vessel diseases are the leading cause of diabetes-related death. Diabetes can directly damage heart and cause the heart not working properly, a condition called diabetic cardiomyopathy. Diabetic cardiomyopathy occurs independently of other heart disorders such as heart vessel disease and high blood pressure. However, how diabetes causes diabetic cardiomyopathy remains not fully understood. Excessive oxidant products have been linked to the onset of diabetic cardiomyopathy. Recent studies have found that damage caused by oxidant products plays a critical role in diabetic cardiomyopathy. Oxidant products are generated by different sources, among which an enzyme called NADPH oxidase has been suggested as a main source in heart muscle cells. A protein called Rac1 is an important subunit of this enzyme and is required for this enzyme's activation. However, the role of Rac1 in diabetic cardiomyopathy has not been fully elucidated. Thus, the present study is aimed to understand if Rac1 plays a role in development of diabetic cardiomyopathy and how Rac1 causes this heart disorder. The results from this study will help to design the treatment methods for diabetic cardiomyopathy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immuno-endocrine interaction in gut: role in inflammation and host defense
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES; ENTEROCHROMAFFIN CELLS; GUT; HOST DEFENSE; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: The enormous mucosal surface of gastrointestinal (GI) tract is continuously exposed to a large numbers of food and waterborne microbes and toxic stimuli and is clearly more susceptible to inflammation than any other organ in the body. However, despite this challenge, the gut is rarely overwhelmed by microbial pathogens, suggesting that the GI tract has effective defense system. GI tract contains the largest endocrine organ in the body, and interactions among immune, endocrine and nervous systems are considered to comprise an integrated network of host defense in gut. Hundreds of thousands of endocrine cells are present throughout the GI tract and react to changes in gut contents by releasing hormones. The best characterized subset of enteric endocrine cells is enterochromaffin (EC) cells, which synthesize and release serotonin (5- hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT). 5-HT contributes to gut physiology and is considered to be important in maintaining the integrity of gut. 5-HT has been implicated in a number of diseases including functional disorders like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and in a number of GI infections. The association between alteration in 5-HT production and various GI diseases highly emphasizes the significance of 5-HT in intestinal pathophysiology. However, the mechanisms regulating the changes in EC cells/5-HT content during infection and inflammation, or the precise role of 5-HT in gut pathology and host defense is still not clear. This research proposal examines the mechanisms by which immune system regulate turnover of EC cells and 5-HT production and the role of 5-HT in gut pathology and host defense in enteric infection. Understanding the role of 5-HT in gut pathology and host defense will provide new insights into the mechanisms of gut function which may ultimately lead to improved therapeutic strategies in GI functional and inflammatory disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the Polo kinase by the Aurora and Greatwall kinases in Drosophila
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CYCLE; DROSOPHILA; GENETICS; POLO KINASE; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Every living organism must control precisely when and how its cells divide. Complex molecular mechanisms inside the cell have evolved to enforce this regulation. In humans, mutations in some of the genes involved in these processes can result in uncontrolled and unrestricted proliferation known as cancer. Understanding the molecular mechanisms that regulate cell division in normal cells, and how they are altered in cancer cells, allows the design of drugs that modify the activity of targeted molecules to stop the division of cancer cells. Moreover, because evolution has conserved these very important genes and proteins across organisms, we can exploit the relative simplicity and laboratory convenience of model organisms in our research. My model of choice is the fruitfly Drosophila melanogaster. The Polo-like kinases are a family of proteins that are crucial in regulating cell division. These proteins promote cell division by modifying the structure and activity of other proteins. The first protein of this family to be discovered was the Polo kinase of Drosophila. In humans, the equivalent protein (Plk1) is often overactive in cancer cells. For this reason, drugs that can inhibit Plk1 are being developed to treat cancer. Unfortunately, we do not yet fully understand the mechanisms by which the Polo-like kinases are controlled in the cell. I have recently found two additional kinase proteins that appear to regulate Polo in the fly. I will use genetic, biochemical, molecular and cell biological approaches to elucidate how these kinases control Polo, and to assess the biological consequences of failures in these mechanisms. This knowledge will improve our molecular understanding of cancer and suggest new ways to interfere with Polo-like kinases as a way to treat cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Combined telomerase inhibition and drug screen as novel therapies for tumor initiating cells in pediatric nervous system tumors.
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMORS; NEUROBLASTOMA; TELOMERASE; TREATMENT; TUMOR INITIATING CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Tumor recurrence is still the most devastating event in childhood cancer. Although we can achieve minimal disease with our current aggressive therapies, some tumors tend to recur, eventually causing these children to succumb to their disease.  Over the last several years our group discovered the existence of tumor initiating cells (TIC) within pediatric tumors. These cells have endless replicative potential and are resistant to conventional chemoradiotherapies. TIC are a major component of tumor relapses. Furthermore, over the last several years we have shown that specific structures in the cells called telomeres, which determine the ability of cells to grow indefinitely, are maintained by an enzyme called telomerase in tumors which recur, and specifically, in the TIC component of these tumors. We recently found that telomerase inhibition using a novel drug could inhibit these TIC. We also used novel techniques to screen for multiple compounds which TIC may be sensitive to.  In this project, we will combine telomerase inhibition with known and novel compounds to determine which combinations are optimal for TIC clinical testing.  This collaborative effort with industrial drug company (GERON) and the strong basic and clinical expertise of our group in telomere biology and stem cell research will enable us to complete our aims and will be the last validation step before incorporating telomerase inhibition into childhood clinical trials. Furthermore, these experiments would shed new light on cancer stem cell and the ability of tumors to recur which will be expanded for the general cancer community.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of ABC transporters-mediated sterol transport
Keywords-MotsClés: ATP BINDING CASSETTE TRANSPORTERS; CELL CULTURE; CHOLESTEROL EFFLUX; HIGH DENSITY LIPOPROTEIN; PROTEIN PROTEIN INTERACTION; PROTEIN PURIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Atherosclerosis leads to cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death and morbidity in Canada. More than 50,000 strokes and 75,000 heart attacks occur in Canada every year, causing at least one in three deaths annually. Current therapeutic strategies to prevent atherosclerosis are primarily based on the use of lipid-lowering drugs, statins, which decrease concentrations of low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol (sometimes referred as the 'bad' cholesterol) in the blood. The treatment of patients with statins reduces cardiovascular events by about 20 to 40%. Moreover, mounting evidence shows that lowering LDL cholesterol might not be enough for people at high risk of heart disease. Thus, there is an important and urgent need for new therapies. Numerous studies have provided unquestionable evidence that plasma levels of HDL cholesterol, sometimes referred as the 'good' cholesterol, are positively associated with protection against atherosclerosis. One of the most important roles of HDL in protection against atherosclerosis is the removal of cholesterol from macrophages. The initial and rate-limited step in this biological process is the removal of cholesterol from cells.Two proteins that play an important role in this step are the so-called ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters, ABCA1 and ABCG1. We are investigating how these proteins help macrophages get rid of excessive cholesterol. We will conduct the research using a broad range of cutting edge techniques in biochemistry, cell biology and molecular biology. Outcomes of our studies will provide fundamental information for the future design of new therapies to reduce the rates and severity of atherosclerosis, thereby benefiting millions of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of Insulin on Ventral Tegmental Area Dopamine Neurons
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE; INGESTIVE BEHAVIOUR; INSULIN; OBESITY; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; VENTRAL TEGMENTAL AREA
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity now poses a epidemic health crisis in the developed world. The abundant availability of palatable and highly caloric foods in the western diet is a major contributor to this disease. Traditionally, most research focuses on energy balance regulation in the hypothalamus. However, much less is known about how peptides that signal the cessation of eating, such as insulin, modulate motivation and reward. Dopamine neurons of the Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA) are a critical component of the neural circuit that mediates reward seeking behaviours, either for drugs of abuse or natural rewards. Indeed, dopamine has been shown to reinforce ingestive behaviours like food intake. Furthermore, evaluation of reward or motivation can be substantially modified by the metabolic status of the animal or by the administration of insulin into the brain. Dopamine neurons may serve as a direct target for insulin in these paradigms.  Receptors for peptides that increase food intake and modulate dopamine neural activity, such as ghrelin and orexin, in addition to others that decrease food intake such as insulin and leptin are abundantly expressed in dopaminergic neurons. Recently we have identified that orexin increases the neural activity of dopamine neurons to motivate animals to forage for food. Therefore, we are interested in how these reward signals are turned off. Insulin is released after meals and recent evidence suggests that the post-ingestive consequences of food can alter reward pathways. The proposed experiments will examine how insulin can modulate neuronal activity and output of VTA dopamine neurons. Further, we will determine if this insulin modulation the reward system is dysregulated in either genetically-prone or diet-induced models of obesity. These experiments will expand our knowledge of the mechanisms of insulin action on the dopamine reward circuit and ingestive behaviour and may lead to the development of therapeutic agents for the treatment of obesity.

Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE; INGESTIVE BEHAVIOUR; INSULIN; OBESITY; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; VENTRAL TEGMENTAL AREA

TitreApplicationTitle: Viral Determinants of Infectious Hepatitis C Virus Production
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE SYSTEMS; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; VIRUS ASSEMBLY; VIRUS ENTRY; VIRUS INFECTIVITY; VIRUS REPLICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 300,000 Canadians are currently infected with the hepatitis C virus, and as many as 80,000 of these people may not yet know it. Up to 70% of these individuals will progress to develop liver cirrhosis, and some will go on to develop hepatocellular carcinoma. Currently available therapies show limited efficacy with uncomfortable side-effects and poor tolerance. Treatment for this large number of people will translate to an enormous impact on public health in our country. The main focus of my research will be to identify novel targets for anti-HCV therapy, and it is my hope that these efforts will contribute to the development of novel antiviral drugs to help fight this disease. Until recently there was no robust cell culture system available for the study of HCV, but in 2005 a fully infectious HCV cell culture system was established that allows secretion of infectious virus particles upon transfection of human hepatocyte cell lines. Using this system, it is now possible to study all aspects of the viral life cycle, including virus entry and assembly, as well as the role of critical cellular factors in these processes. Presumably, HCV particle formation is driven by the core structural protein. At some point, either during or after core has assembled a genome-containing capsid, viral glycoproteins E1 and E2 are incorporated into the virion. Using the infectious HCV system, I plan to characterize the role of the viral core protein in the virion assembly process. My previous work suggests that the viral p7 and NS2 proteins also contribute in some way to the virus assembly process. I plan to elucidate the mechanisms by which these proteins play a role in virus assembly and production of infectious virions. The information obtained from these studies will not only contribute to the basic understanding of the HCV life cycle, but will also help to identify putative new targets for specific antiviral therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biophysics of Functional MRI
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICAL MODELLING; BRAIN MICIRCULATION; BRAIN PHYSIOLOGY; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEUROVASCULAR COUPLING; TWO-PHOTON MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Functional magnetic resonance imaging has greatly enhanced our understanding of how the healthy human brain processes information. To date, however, this technology's promise of revolutionizing clinical practice has not been realized, to a large extent due to the lack of a detailed knowledge of the biophysical mechanism that links brain activity to signal changes detected by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Although it is well established that brain activity is associated with local changes in brain's blood flow that MRI can detect, an understanding of these blood flow changes and their relationship with brain activity has not been fully developed. Moreover, the alterations in this relationship that occur with disease are largely unknown. To address these issues, we will perform detailed microscopic and functional MRI investigations in animals, allowing the development of a biophysical model of functional MRI to aid in the interpretation of functional MRI data in patients and providing a platform for future studies of the growing list of diseases that are thought to alter the relationship between blood circulation and activity in the brain, such as stroke and Alzheimer's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The risk of lung cancer related to occupational and recreational physical activity and to dietary intake of flavonoids
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE-CONTROL STUDY; DIET; FLAVONOIDS; LUNG CANCER; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the most deadly cancer among Canadian men and women. Although smoking causes most lung cancers, some people who have never smoked in their life also sometimes get lung cancer. Also, only about 15% of smokers eventually get lung cancer. It is therefore clear that other factors are involved in lung cancer risk. Our research focuses on identifying other lifestyle behaviours that men and women can change in order to prevent lung cancer.   Being physically active and eating lots of fruits and vegetables have been shown to reduce the risk of some cancers. However, the role of physical activity and diet in the development of lung cancer is not well established. There are different types of physical activity that a person may be involved in, including activity at work and recreational activities. Fruits and vegetables have many nutrients and bio-active compounds that may prevent cancer, including compounds called flavonoids, which are also found in tea and wine. New studies are needed to fully understand the impact of these factors on lung cancer risk.   In this research, we will examine how lung cancer risk is associated with physical activity levels and dietary intakes of flavonoids. Our research will be based on a study conducted between 1996 and 2005 that included men and women newly diagnosed with lung cancer in Montreal, and a group of people without lung cancer that were representative of Montreal area residents at risk of lung cancer. The interview asked detailed questions on smoking, occupation, diet, and recreational activities. This study thus offers a valuable opportunity to examine whether these lifestyle factors play an important role in lung cancer risk.   There are many ways to prevent lung cancer and the more we know about the factors that may cause lung cancer, such as poor diet and low physical activity, the more weapons we will have in the battle to prevent this deadly disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: A beta-adrenoceptor-mediated memory circuitry in rats
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-ADRENOCEPTOR; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IMAGING; MEMORY; OLFACTORY LEARNING; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to create associations among objects or events enriches the brain's capacity for new memories and permits a wide array of cues to trigger the recall of past memories. My proposal explores the cellular mechanisms governing memory formation in a simple mammalian associative learning model. Classical conditioning of odor preference learning in the neonatal rat provides us with an excellent model for the study of associative memory. Young rats learn to prefer odors associated with a stimulus such as stroking the pup that mimics the maternal care of licking pups. The unconditioned stimulus, stroking, is mediated by norepinephrine release in the olfactory bulb (the first odor processing center) acting at beta-adrenoeceptors. The conditioned stimulus, an odor, is represented by activity in olfactory bulb mitral cells. How does norepinephrine via beta-adrenoceptor activation in the olfactory bulb promote learning? I propose to create an in vitro working model using olfactory bulb slices. The learning association will be mimicked by pairing electrical stimulation of the olfactory nerve (mimicking odor input) with application of a beta-adrenoceptor agonist. I will measure the physiological changes in different types of neurons in order to understand the circuitry underpinning the odor associative learning. I hypothesize that beta-adrenoceptor activation in the olfactory bulb facilitates the communication between olfactory receptor neurons (which form the olfactory nerve) and olfactory bulb mitral cells so that mitral cells enhance their responses to the same odor input.   My proposed research in understanding one form of memory will shed light on what underneath memory loss during pathological conditions. A deeper understanding of memory mechanism in animal models has implications for the treatment of memory dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease and other age-related disorders, which significantly affect quality of life of millions of people.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of TNFalpha in synaptic plasticity and during neurodegeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GLIA; INFLAMMATION; NEURODEGENERATION; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of almost every neurological disorder, from acute head injury and stroke to most neurodegenerative diseases, and is thought to be a major contributor to the disruption of neuronal function and cell death. However, it remains unclear how the inflammation, driven by the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, is contributing to the damage. Cytokines, by increasing synaptic content of calcium-permable glutamate receptor, could be causing cell death through excitotoxicity. We are studying the role of cytokines in the regulation of synaptic function, both during the normal functioning of the nervous system and during inflammation. This research could lead to potential therapies for a variety of neuronal disorders and neurodegenerative diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Prescription Adaptation and Renewal by Pharmacists
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; OBSERVATIONAL RESEARCH; PHARMACARE; PHARMACEUTICAL POLICY; PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
Abstract-Résumé: In January 2009, a policy change in British Columbia (BC) gave pharmacists the authority to independently modify and renew prescriptions. The policy is intended to improve patient access to drugs and reduce the already heavy burden on primary care physicians. However, physicians and others have raised concerns about potential negative effects on patient safety due to inappropriate medication modifications and reduced continuity of care. While several other provinces have either implemented or proposed similar policies, there have been conspicuously few rigorous evaluations of these changes. We will use the world-class health research datasets in BC to study the effects of this policy change on drug utilization and costs, patient adherence to medication, the number of visits to physicians and hospitalization. Our study will benefit Canadians by informing the future design and refinement of these important and controversial policies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physical Activity for Overweight Youth at Risk for Type 2 Diabetes (POWER) Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD OBESITY; EXERCISE; LIPOTOXICITY; MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY; PATHOGENESIS; YOUTH-ONSET TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: In youth it remains unclear how effective physical activity is at lowering the risk for type 2 diabetes and if it does, how much activity is needed. This information is critical for developing guidelines and policies for diabetes prevention in youth. We hope to address this issue by conducting a physical activity intervention study on risk factors for type 2 diabetes in youth. We are going to test the theory that higher intensity physical activity will be better for reducing the risk for type 2 diabetes in overweight youth than lower intensity physical activity. To accomplish this aim we plan to recruit 120 overweight youth 13-18 yrs of age that have signs suggesting that they are at risk for type 2 diabetes. Eligible youth will be randomly assigned to either (1) low intensity activity; (2) high intensity activity or (3) 6-month delayed activity (control) group for a period of six months. Youth will be exercise trained at YMCA locations in Winnipeg supervised by trained staff at least 3 days each week for a period of 6 months, after which all measurements of diabetes risk will be repeated. The data will not only provide us with important information for how much physical activity an adolescent needs to reduce their risk for type 2 diabetes, but we will also gain insight into the reasons why some adolescents progress to diabetes while others remain protected. This information will help clinicians and policy makers tailor messages and practical efforts for the prevention of type 2 diabetes in the growing number of at-risk Canadian youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Plasticity in the undamaged hemisphere following motor cortical infarct in a primate model
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNECTIONS; CONTRALESIONAL HEMISPHERE; ISCHEMIC LESION; MONKEY; PLASTICITY; SINGLE-NEURONS ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: A stroke is a vascular lesion within the brain. Following a stroke located within the motor cortex, patients have several deficits including loss of upper extremity function. However, patients undergo substantial motor recovery in the weeks and months following the lesion. One hypothesis, for which there is now remarkable support, is that the recovery is dependent upon adaptive reorganization of intact, remaining brain structures. The changes in the hemisphere that had sustained the lesion (ipsilesional) are generally believed to be beneficial to the recovery. Conversely, the role of the reorganization that occurs in the hemisphere opposite to the lesion (contralesional) is controversial. Some studies conclude that plasticity in that hemisphere supports recovery, while others conclude that it actually interferes with it. The goal of the present project is to study the nature of the reorganization in the contralesional hemisphere in order to understand how it can either participate or interfere in recovery. This will be achieved using single-neuron recording techniques in a primate model of stroke. This project is designed to address particularly pressing clinically relevant questions and the information it will generate will help to refine current experimental protocols in humans. The knowledge of physiological principles underlying normal and abnormal function is instrumental in the refinement of effective clinical practice aiming at the maximization of recovery following stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of nutrition information on menus: evidence to inform policy.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIET; HEALTH POLICY; NUTRITION; NUTRITION LABELS; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: More than half of adult Canadians are overweight or obese, with alarming increases in paediatric obesity. An increasing number of Canadians eat restaurant and fast-food as part of their daily diet. Nutrition labels have become a prominent policy tool for promoting healthy eating habits for pre-packaged foods; however, existing regulations do not apply to restaurants or fast-food outlets. We propose to conduct 2 studies to examine the impact of nutritional information on menus. In Study 1, a community sample of 660 adults will be recruited for a study in which they will consume a meal from a leading fast-food chain after being randomly assigned to order from 1 of 4 menus: 1) a typical menu with no calorie information, 2) menus with calorie content listed next to the price, 3) menus with calorie content and Daily Recommended Intake amounts, and 4) menus with calorie content presented with Traffic Light symbols. The main analysis will examine differences between experimental conditions in the calorie content of the meal consumed by participants. In Study 2, 4 food outlets located at the University of Waterloo (2 "sit-down restaurants" and 2 fast-food outlets) have agreed to participate in a naturalistic study of menu labelling. Following a 1-month "baseline" period, one restaurant and one fast-food outlet will be randomly selected to display calorie information next to each food and beverage item on their menus for a 1-month period, with the remaining 2 outlets serving as controls. Surveys will be conducted during the baseline and intervention periods at each of the 4 outlets to examine differences in menu selection and calorie consumption among patrons. Sales data will be provided by each outlet and analysed. This research has the potential to make important contributions to the evidence base on nutritional labelling. The findings also have implications for menu labelling legislation before the Ontario legislature and in other jurisdictions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mobilizing Evidence into Action to Improve Health Outcomes of Vulnerable Seniors
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE HEALTH; FALLS PREVENTION; HIP FRACTURE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MOBILITY; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, there are over 25,000 fall-related fractures at the hip annually with significant personal and societal consequences. Approximately 20% of people die within 12 months of fracturing and half do not regain their previous level of mobility. The decreased mobility leads to muscle weakness and an increased risk of falling; this combined with poor bone health can contribute to the risk of additional injuries. Consequently, understanding both falls risk factors and bone health are vital if we aim to improve outcomes and reduce falls risk after hip fracture.  We and others have shown significant breakdowns in the recommended care pathway (post-discharge) after fall-related hip fractures. More recently, several publications have tested different strategies to improve follow-up care for seniors after hip fracture, and some succeeded in improving investigation rates for osteoporosis. However, the prevention of future fractures requires assessment of both bone health and falls risk factors. Therefore, we aim to add a novel dimension to post-discharge hip fracture management by incorporating falls risk and bone health follow-up with an evidence-based exercise program within a dedicated clinical service for older adults after hip fracture. Our objective is to test the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of comprehensive post-discharge hip fracture management for two key health domains, bone health and falls risk ( balance, cognition and continence), that can contribute to future falls and injuries in seniors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring and modeling the spread of infections, beliefs and behaviours
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURS; CIRCUMCISION; HIV; MATHEMATICAL MODELS; NORMS; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: This salary award will allow the investigator more time to pursue and supervise already-funded research into the spread of infectious diseases, with a particular focus on the interaction between disease spread, and the spread of related beliefs and behaviours.  One disease of interest is HIV, and initiatives to combat HIV spread through male circumcision.  The proposed research aims to bring an explicit gendered perspective lacking from much existing research in this topic.  Another disease of interest is canine rabies, an underappreciated and significant killer of people in the less-developed world.  The research program will also focus on improving statistical methodologies for quickly characterizing new epidemics, like the new H1N1 influenza, or SARS.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ; IMAGERIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Harsh parenting conditions and fear circuitry function in anxious and healthy youths.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE CARE-GIVING; ANXIETY DISORDERS; FEAR CIRCUITRY; FEAR CONDITIONING; FMRI; YOUTHS
Abstract-Résumé: Links have been established between harsh parenting, i.e., hostile and coercive (aggressive, punitive) parenting behaviours, and anxiety disorders. These links could reflect long-term changes within the brain's neural fear circuit, encompassing a region in the middle (the amygdala) and in the front (prefrontal cortex) of the brain. Very few studies in youths have ever investigated these links. Identifying biological perturbations (i.e., alterations in amygdala and prefrontal cortex function) related to harsh parenting and anxiety in youths is crucial as it could lead to early interventions that would effectively interrupt the development of these perturbations early in their course, before they become chronic and exceedingly debilitating. The main objective of my CIHR research project is thus to understand the functioning of the fear circuit in anxious and non-anxious harshly-reared and non-harshly reared youths. To reach this goal, I will recruit 4 groups of 30 youths aged between 12-16 years old. Groups will be: youths with (1) current high-harsh parenting and current anxiety symptoms, (2) current high-harsh parenting, but no current anxiety symptom, (3) current low-harsh parenting, but current anxiety symptoms, (4) current low-harsh parenting and no current anxiety symptom. Subjects will be recruited through the Research Unit on Children's Psychosocial Maladjustment (University of Montreal and Laval University). To study the functioning of the fear circuit, I will use tasks measuring the acquisition and extinction of a fear response to emotionally arousing cues. These fear acquisition and extinction tasks have been adapted for the functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanner and have been recognized as safe by previous pilot-studies performed in healthy or anxious youths.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; TUMEURS
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Targeted Phosphatase Activity in the Regulation of Cell Proliferation
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CHROMATIN; FLUORESCENCE IMAGING; PP1; QUANTITATIVE PROTEOMICS; REPOMAN
Abstract-Résumé: The human body is composed of billions of cells, and these cells in turn are composed of thousands of proteins that work together in complexes and networks to carry out all cellular functions.  One important function is "programmed cell death", or the triggering of cells to die at a particular point in their life cycle.  In cancer cells, it is this programmed cell death that is disrupted, allowing them to continue growing and dividing.     A major mechanism that regulates protein function in cells is the reversible addition of phosphate groups (protein kinases add them while protein phosphatases remove them).  Abnormal phosphorylation has been linked to the progression of certain types of cancer, and my laboratory studies the targeting of protein phosphatase activity within living cells to better understand the phosphorylation-mediated processes that give rise to cancers in humans.  These processes can then be targeted for disruption in therapeutic approaches.   We have developed a unique fusion of techniques that combines imaging of fluorescent phosphatases in live cells with recovery of these phosphatases and identification of all of the proteins with which they associate.  Using this approach we identified RepoMan, which specifically directs protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) activity to proteins associated with DNA.  RepoMan is highly expressed in certain aggressive tumor types, suggesting that it is suppressing systems that regulate programmed cell death.  Indeed, reducing levels of RepoMan in cells led to rapid and massive cell death.     In order to exploit the therapeutic potential of RepoMan in the treatment of certain cancers, we must gain a better understanding of its mode of action.  These studies will aid the design of drugs that target specific phosphatase complexes involved in cell survival, to provide more efficient treatment of certain types of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of vascular tone by sphingosine 1-phosphate in pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: INTRAUTERINE GROWTH RESTRICTION; PRESSURE MYOGRAPH; SPHINGOSINE 1-PHOSPHATE; VASCULAR PERMEABILITY; VASCULAR TONE
Abstract-Résumé: The movement of blood containing oxygen and nutrients from the mother to the fetus is important for proper fetal growth. Blood from the mother flows to the uterus and placenta to reach the fetus. If this blood flow is decreased, the growth of the fetus is reduced. Growth restricted newborns suffer many adverse consequences and are also at increased risk for cardiovascular disease when they become adults. Blood flow is controlled by changes to the diameter of arteries (vascular tone) through constriction or relaxation. Arteries contain endothelial cells which are surrounded by the smooth muscle cells. One factor that can act on both cell types is a lipid called sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P). This lipid causes relaxation or constriction depending on whether it binds to receptors on the endothelial or smooth muscle cells, respectively. This study looks at a novel role for S1P in vascular tone regulation of arteries that are important for blood flow to the fetus: uterine and placental arteries. Understanding these responses in normal pregnancy will help to develop methods to prevent or treat fetal growth restriction. Our hypothesis is that when S1P binds to receptors on the endothelial cells, there will be increased relaxation of uterine arteries in pregnancy which will be lost in pregnancies with growth restricted babies. This relaxation is important because it provides a balance for constriction by S1P and other factors. This balance is what maintains the blood flow from mother to fetus. We will use two approaches to examine this question: 1) We will compare the response to S1P in uterine arteries from pregnant and non-pregnant mice; 2) We will also use arteries from human placentas of normal babies and compare their response to S1P to that from growth restricted babies. We predict that the increased relaxation response to S1P in normal pregnancy will be lost in growth restricted pregnancies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroendocrine Regulation of Energy Homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY WEIGHT; DIABETES MELLITUS; FOOD INTAKE; METABOLISM; NEUROENDOCRINE FACTORS; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity and diabetes are debilitating diseases reaching pandemic proportions in developed countries. According to Statistics Canada reports, 23.1% of adult Canadians and 26% Canadian children and adolescents are obese.  Approximately 1 billion of the global population is obese. About 5% of Canadians have diabetes. Several hormones, produced in the body are involved in the regulation of blood glucose levels and body weight. Defects in the production, secretion and/or action of these hormones could contribute to certain types of obesity and/or diabetes. There is a great deal of interest in using natural appetite and glucose regulating hormones to treat obesity. Nesfatin is a recently discovered appetite inhibitory hormone. My preliminary research, as well as studies by other researchers have shown that nesfatin-1 administration causes a decrease in food intake and body weight. We also found nesfatin in the insulin producing cells of the pancreas, and observed that nesfatin infusion causes an increase in insulin secretion. The presence of nesfatin-1 in the pancreas, and its food intake inhibitory and insulin stimulatory effects suggest an important role for this novel peptide in regulating metabolism. However, the biological functions and mechanisms of actions of nesfatin remain largely unknown. I hypothesize that nesfatin is involved in the regulation of blood glucose levels and metabolism. Using experimental models, I propose to study the role of nesfatin in regulating blood glucose levels, insulin secretion, and the mechanisms that mediate these actions in animal models of diabetes and obesity. I anticipate nesfatin to decrease blood glucose levels and reduce body weight. If found effective in reducing food intake and promoting weight loss and blood glucose levels, nesfatin could become beneficial for developing potential therapies for diabetes and obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Blood telomere length and breast cancer risk
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; QUANTITATIVE POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION; SINGLE-TELOMERE LENGTH ANALYSIS (STELA); TELOMERE; TERMINAL RESTRICTION FRAGMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The overall goal of our research is to understand the causes of breast cancer. The research proposed in this application will determine whether blood telomere length is associated with the risk of developing breast cancer in a prospective study.  Telomeres are pieces of DNA on the ends of chromosomes that protect them from damage.  Telomeres shorten with age, and the length of telomeres in cells in the blood may be an indicator of biological aging and susceptibility to cancer.  If the length of telomeres in blood cells from women who develop breast cancer is different from that in women who do not have breast cancer, then blood telomere length may be a useful marker to identify women at increased risk for breast cancer. Further research to understand the reason for this difference may lead to ways to prevent breast cancer in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of circadian clocks in reproduction
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL CLOCK; CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; CONDITIONAL KO; CRE RECOMBINASE; GENE EXPRESSION; HISTOLOGY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; IN SITU HYBRIDIZATION; LOCOMOTOR BEHAVIOR; NEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; OVARY; PITUITARY; RADIOIMMUNOASSAY; REPRODUCTIVE PHYSIOLOGY; SCN; SEX HORMONS; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Humans and rodents alike possess a circadian timing system that drives 24-hour rhythms in physiology and behavior. We now know that circadian clocks reside in many organs and tissues throughout the body, but their individual contributions to physiological functions is largely unknown. Intriguingly, also the pituitary gland and the ovary, both key structures of the reproductive system, harbor their own circadian pacemakers. Numerous aspects of reproductive physiology are under distinct temporal control such as the onset of puberty, the menstrual cycle, as well as ovulation and gestation. Together with the observation that several mouse models with body-wide impairments of circadian function show reproductive deficits, it seems likely that in particular the circadian clocks in the ovary and the pituitary act as integral players within the reproductive system. The proposed research aims to address the hypothesized role of circadian oscillators along the reproductive axis by employing mouse models that are specifically engineered to allow manipulation of circadian clock function in a tissue-restricted fashion. We will generate animals that lack clock function exclusively in the ovary, pituitary or the entire central nervous system and then test for reproductive consequences. These experiments may critically contribute to a better understanding of the physiological program that ensures reproductive success and will therefore likely help to elucidate new avenues for the treatment of reproductive disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: PATHWAYS: Evaluating the Transition of Psychiatric Services from Hospital to Community
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL AND BEHAVIOURAL OUTCOMES; CONSUMER SATISFACTION AND QUALITY OF LIFE; DEINSTITUTIONALIZATION; HEALTH SERVICES; MENTAL HEALTH; RISK ASSESSMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Individuals living with mental health problems have traditionally been segregated from the general population and placed in large psychiatric hospitals. The separation of psychiatric patients from family and the stigma that results from forcing mentally ill individuals to essentially live outside of the greater community has been seriously criticized. Partly as a result of these issues, throughout Canada and the world, psychiatric beds are being closed and large hospitals are shutting their doors. Increasingly, the delivery of psychiatric services is being transferred to community settings. Consistent with this approach, the British Columbia Ministry of Health has put into place a plan to close Riverview Hospital. Despite the staggering fiscal and humanitarian implications of implementing such dramatic changes in health policy, we have very little research to inform our understanding of the effects of moving psychiatric patients out of large hospitals and relocating them in the community. Given the dramatic gap between knowledge and practice, our team will intensively track the movement of a cohort of psychiatric patients for a 2-year period initially, and ultimately for 5 and 10 years, to determine pre-post transfer changes in patients': (1) mental health, physical health, and health related behaviours (e.g., substance misuse); (2) contacts with social agencies (e.g., homeless shelters, criminal justice system), and (3) quality of life and satisfaction with the setting and services. Our study will provide previously unavailable information to guide mental health policy in Canada and abroad. The results will also have important clinical relevance to the Canadian and international health communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics of antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIPSYCHOTICS; DNA SEQUENCING; EPIGENETICS; METABOLIC SYNDROME; MOLECULAR GENETICS; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a relatively common disorder with a lifetime prevalence of approximately 1% and typically arising in late adolescence or early adulthood. The discovery of the first antipsychotics in the 1950s has revolutionized treatment. However, antipsychotic drugs are still not effective in treating a broad range of symptoms and treatment with also remains problematic because of their frequent side effects. One major side effects occurring with some classic and modern antipsychotics (particularly with clozapine and olanzapine) is substantial weight gain, which further adds stigmatization to our patient population. Obesity then often leads to diabetes and high blood pressure; a condition known as the metabolic syndrome. The metabolic syndrome is likely a major factor for the significantly reduced life expectancy of patients. However, it has to be kept in mind that while some patients encounter substantial weight gain, others may not develop this side effect. The underlying molecular, cellular or hormonal mechanisms are not well understood thus far, but the observed inter-individual variability is known to be significantly determined by genetic factors. In our efforts to unravel genetic factors associated with antipsychotic induced weight gain, we will 1) collect a large sample of at least 400 schizophrenia patients treated with antipsychotics bearing high risk for weight gain 2) conduct detailed analyses of genes hypothesized to be involved in the crosstalk between the mechanism of action of antipsychotics and body energy regulation using novel sophisticated genetic analyses and 3) establish collaborations with more groups to conduct joint analyses in larger samples allowing to detect also subtle genetic effects. In conclusion, our studies will lead to determine patients at higher risk for weight gain and thus optimize the choice of prescribing drugs. Furthermore, the identified genes will help to find new targets for the development of novel medications.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de formation : épidémiologie génétique - demande détaillée

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR STAGE (Strategic Training for Advanced Genetic Epidemiology): An integrated program in statistical & epidemiological training for genetics with a population health impact
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL SCIENCES; CHRONIC AND COMPLEX DISEASES; ETHICS & KT & PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY & STATISTICAL GENETICS; INTERNATIONAL & NATIONAL INTERNSHIP; POPULATION GENETICS & POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The STAGE (Strategic Training for Advanced Genetic Epidemiology) program of the University of Toronto Dalla Lana School of Public Health with affiliated institutions, in collaboration with National and International partners, offers innovative and integrative graduate and post-doctoral training at the interface between statistical, biomedical and human population health sciences, with a focus on genetics and genomics. The fundamental premise of STAGE is that in order for genetics to have an impact on population health, trainees require substantial experience in leading-edge research at the interface of statistics, epidemiology, and biomedical sciences, which builds on fundamental training in their core disciplines, and is enriched by cross-disciplinary and integrative curriculum activities. The program includes coursework in the trainees¿ core academic program, and cross-disciplinary as well as integrative courses. These courses are also available to post-doctoral trainees. The curriculum incorporates rich opportunities for cross-disciplinary "hands-on" practica in industry and government agencies, as well as national and international research internship opportunities. Upon completion of training, a new generation of investigators will be well equipped to take up positions in academia, government, and industry. Based on the current demand for such expertise, graduates of the program will find a wide range of opportunities to contribute to the current economy by exercising leadership in scientific investigations aimed at understanding and addressing the etiology of common chronic and infectious diseases, and improving associated population health outcomes.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse nouveau chercheur - Annonce de priorités : recherche biomédical/clinique sur le HIV/SIDA
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of exosomes in acute HIV-1 infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE INFECTION; CD4 IMMUNODEPLETION; DENDRITIC CELLS; EXOSOME PURIFICATION; HIV-1; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Immature dendritic cells (iDCs) which reside in these mucosal tissues capture internalize and serve as hidden reservoirs for the virions. This helps the virus escape immune surveillance during the DCs migration to the secondary lymphoid organs where the virions are transmitted to CD4 cells. The virus can replicate in these T cells which are severely depleted in less than 10 days after primary infection. In fact, HIV infection is controlled by CD4 T cell responses and depletion of these cells during primary infection affects the initiation of the specific immune response, which could explain the long-term inability of the host immune response to control the infection. Based on preliminary data, we propose a mechanism by which exosomes released by HIV-1-iDCs can induce functional defects in CD4 T cells. We have observed that iDCs stimulated with HIV-1 release particles akin to HIV-1 and called exosomes, and these exosomes contain at their surface several molecules which are able to eliminate the CD4 T cells. It should be pointed out that the link between the surface molecules associated with exosomes and the effects of the latter on the activity of the various CD4 T cell sub-populations has not been studied in the context of HIV-1 infection. Filling this gap is a major aim of the present application. Two distinct but interlinked research objectives are proposed to test this hypothesis. AIM I: To further characterize exosomes and determine the mechanisms involved in their release from iDCs after HIV-1 capture. AIM II: To investigate the effects of HIV-1-iDC-derived exosomes on the functional responses of CD4 T cells. Altogether the proposed research project should contribute to our comprehension of the various mechanisms underlying the complex interplay occurring between iDCs-exosomes HIV-1 and CD4 T cells. This study is of utmost importance to elucidate the mechanisms of immune depletion in HIV-1 patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multiplex screening assays for HIV and co-infections: will they benefit patients, providers and health care systems?
Keywords-MotsClés: CO-INFECTIONS; HIV; IMPACT; MULTIPLEX ASSAYS; SCREENING STRATEGY; VULNERABLE
Abstract-Résumé: Targeted screening of at risk individuals is a proven cost effective strategy. Vulnerable at risk populations are difficult to follow up, so that regular screening for all co-infections and HIV is often not conducted in them. Due to the asymptomatic nature of early infections and the lack of consistent screening, a vast majority of affected individuals are living with un-diagnosed infection. Early diagnosis and early treatment are proven to reduce morbidity and mortality, health care costs and transmission. Recently developed multiplex strategy makes it possible to inexpensively test individuals multiple infections with just a single drop of blood, with immediate results precluding the need for follow-up visits. Multiplo(TM) (MedMira Inc, Halifax, Canada), is one such multiplex point-of-care device that detects four infections (i.e., HIV, HBV, HCV and Syphilis) with a small 5 micro-litre finger stick blood sample in 5 minutes. In this proposal, we will investigate whether introducing Multiplo(TM) as a first line screening assay helps impact: a) detection of new infections and expedite initiation of treatment in patients; b) facilitate clinical decision making by health care providers; c) improves estimates of co-prevalence; and, d) lastly, offer cost and time savings to the health care systems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anal cancer screening in HIV: Progression and transmission
Keywords-MotsClés: ANAL CANCER; CANCER SCREENING; HIV ILLNESS; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS; TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer of the anus occurs at much higher rates in HIV-infected men who have sex with men (MSM).  Both anal and cervical cancers are caused by a sexually transmitted virus called human papillomavirus (HPV), so these conditions may be passed on to sexual partners. Anal Pap smears can be used to screen for precancerous anal growths.  If the pap is positive, then a high powered examination can be done to identify the precancerous growth which can then be removed using laser treatment. Our team has used HPV tests, anal Pap smears and high-power examinations of the anal canal to look for pre-cancerous changes in a large group of HIV-infected MSM. We found that the Pap smear was moderately accurate and that ¼ of our group had advanced pre-cancerous growths.  These findings are important but more knowledge is needed before formal screening programs can be instituted. In the current project, we intend to evaluate how precancerous anal growths have changed over a 4 year period in the original group of HIV-infected men that we studied.  The sexual partners will also be examined to see if they have the same kinds of HPV as the original subjects. These studies will help us determine: a) how often HIV-infected men to be re-checked in order to find advanced pre-cancer, b) how effective their previous treatments have been and c) whether their partners are at risk for similar conditions. These results will help design screening programs for anal cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Statins and Renovascular Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; PROGNOSIS; RENAL ARTERY STENOSIS; STATINS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with obstructed kidney arteries are said to have 'renovascular disease' (RVD).  Affected individuals are at risk for a number of important kidney-related complications such as acute kidney failure and uncontrolled high blood pressure.  Promising animal studies suggest that a common class of cholesterol-lowering drugs known as statins might favourably affect the natural history of this disorder.  At present, less than half of patients with established RVD are receiving these agents.  The objective of this research is to test whether statins are associated with a reduced risk of kidney complications in RVD and provide planning data for a definitive clinical trial.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relationship between amputation-induced plasticity and motor control of the phantom limb
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN PLASTICITY; EEG; MOTOR CONTROL; PAIN; PHANTOM LIMB; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Pain has an inhibitory effect on the motor areas of the brain, and interferes with motor control. In patients who have both pain and a motor deficit the pain might hamper proper activation of motor areas during attempts to move, thereby limiting motor improvement during rehabilitation. Therefore it is important to have a comprehensive understanding of the pathophysiology of disorders that include both motor deficits and pain. An innovative approach to studying interactions between the motor system and pain is to study the phantom limb phenomenon, which is the vivid sensation that a missing body part is still there after an amputation. The majority of amputees report pain in the missing limb, called phantom limb pain, as well as the perceived ability to perform voluntary movements with their phantom limb.  Amputation induces a reorganisation of the motor areas of the brain (motor plasticity), and this plasticity appears to be related to phantom limb pain as well as to the perceived ability to perform movements with the phantom limb. The main objective of this research program is to gain a better understanding of the relationship between pain, motor control, and motor plasticity using neuroimaging and neurostimulation approaches. First, in healthy individuals, experimentally-controlled pain and experimentally-induced nerve block (that produces reversible amputation-like effects in the brain) will be used to look at how brain motor areas reorganise as a function of whether pain or nerve block occur alone or in combination. Second, in amputees suffering from phantom pain, a non invasive brain stimulation technique will be used to induce transitory changes in the excitability of motor areas in order to study the relationship between physiological changes induced and clinical changes in pain levels and voluntary movements of the phantom limb. Finally, in upper limb amputees, the effect of prosthesis use on motor area plasticity and phantom sensations will be assessed.

Abstract-Résumé: This project develops a process for bridging the gaps between scientific research and community expertise and priorities in order to inform best practices in policy action to address urban environmental health inequities. Our team plans to design, implement, and evaluate a three-part process that includes: (1) building a community of researchers, policy-decision-makers, and community leaders who will set knowledge translation priorities together; (2) designing a comprehensive systematic review methodology that synthesizes multiple forms of knowledge from research, policy, and the community that can be used to improve understanding of, and ultimately reduce environmental health inequities; and (3) promoting a national multi-stakeholder discussion using accessible web-based tools in order to translate our findings into concrete policy actions to be carried forward by our team. We will evaluate our process to ensure that it is a meaningful and relevant experience for all participants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Passive smoke during pregnancy and within-city disparities in intrauterine growth restriction? Linking molecular markers with population data in support of evidence-based policy.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE PREGNANCY OUTCOMES; BIOMARKERS OF EXPOSURE; EFFECTS OF PASSIVE SMOKING ON FOETAL GROWTH; ENVIRONMENTAL CONTAMINANTS; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; SOCIOECONOMIC GRADIENTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: As in many Canadian cities, babies born to mothers who live in socially and materially poorer parts of Vancouver are more likely to be born too small than babies born in other parts of the city. We know that there are more smokers in poorer areas, and so it is possible that active and passive smoking are some reasons for the differences in birth outcomes in different parts of the city. We will test passive smoking by measuring cotinine, a byproduct of nicotine, in serum (blood) samples from nonsmoking pregnant women. We will then investigate whether non-smoking women with higher levels of serum cotinine (and thus with higher passive smoke exposures) are more likely to have a baby that is too small. We will also test whether some babies are genetically more susceptible to adverse effects of passive smoke during pregnancy. Finally, we will test whether non-smoking pregnant women who live in poorer areas of Vancouver have higher levels of serum cotinine compared to others, which would suggest that they were exposed to more passive smoke. Taken together, our study will provide good evidence for whether reducing exposures to passive smoke would reduce the disparities in how likely a baby is to be born too small in poorer and richer areas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Revealing the Role of Adolescent Growth, Bone Accrual and Physical Activity to Adult Bone Strength at the Wrist and Hip
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE HEALTH DETERMINANTS; BONE STRENGTH; FRACTURE PREVENTION; MRI; MUSCULOSKELETAL IMAGING; OSTEOPOROSIS PREVENTION; PQCT
Abstract-Résumé: Bone mass gain, lifestyle behaviors (such as physical activity) and other factors (such as muscle mass development) during adolescence affect bone strength development, and consequently are thought to be important in reducing risk of osteoporotic fractures later in life. However, only studies that follow the same individuals from childhood to adulthood can tell us how important childhood and adolescent growth, bone development and lifestyle are for adult bone strength. Currently no study like that exists. Thus, our main purpose is to examine the relationship of bone development and physical activity during the adolescent growth period to bone strength at wrist and hip in young adulthood (30 years of age). This study is an extension of the Saskatchewan Pediatric Bone Mineral Accrual Study which measured children (age 8-15 years) growth, bone mass accrual and lifestyle factors over 7 years (1991-1998). These participants are now entering their 4th decade of life. The proposed study provides a unique opportunity to address an important question: Do growth and lifestyle factors during childhood and adolescence affect long-term bone strength?

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of genome mutators governing adaptive and innate immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DNA MUTATIONS; GENOME INTEGRITY; HIV; IMMUNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: A unique way that the body enhances immunity to pathogens is through introducing subtle changes at the genetic level.  There are two main categories of genetic changes.  The first type occurs in the genome of our B cells.  B cells are the white blood cells of the immune system which produce antibodies necessary to fight pathogens.  The genetic changes in B cells are carried out by Activation induced cytidine deaminase (AID), an enzyme that makes changes to the antibody genes, leading to stronger antibodies.  The second type of genetic changes are those that take place in the genes of viruses.  A set of AID-related enzymes known as APOBECs introduce changes in the genes of viruses as a means of deactivating the virus.  They specifically act on retroviruses, most notably HIV.  Overall, genetic alterations are an effective means to boost immunity; however, these processes are not perfect and can be misdirected to the wrong genes.  Such unwanted genetic changes have been shown to result in cancers of immune cells, namely lymphoma/leukemia.  Thus, these processes are a double-edged sword. The focus of my research is to understand the mechanisms of the processes which introduce genetic changes in the immune system, the facets through which they modulate immunity, and how they are targeted to certain genes. These studies are essential in order to understand how a system that is there to help immunity can actually result in the generation of cancer. Our results and future studies will have implications on strategies for treatment of leukemia/lymphomas and  HIV.
