Abstract-Résumé: En Amerique du Nord, entre 7 et 45 % des jeunes ages de 13 a 20 ans (filles et garcons) ont deja ete victimes d'au moins un episode de violence en contexte amoureux. De meme, il semble que certains jeunes sont davantage vulnerables a vivre de la violence dans les relations amoureuses. A long terme, ces phenomenes engendrent des couts importants de par les blessures physiques et la detresse psychologique engendrees. L'exploration des mecanismes impliques dans la violence au sein des relations amoureuses chez les jeunes est donc prioritaire, de meme que l'etude des relations harmonieuses et egalitaires. Ainsi, la programmation de  recherche proposee par l'equipe verra a etudier de plus pres ces phenomenes, particulierement chez les jeunes (filles et garcons)ages entre 14 et 18 ans. Une attention particuliere sera accordee tant aux adolescents en provenance de la population generale qu'en provenance de populations plus vulnerables, tels les jeunes ayant ete victimes d'agression sexuelle ou les jeunes des minorites sexuelles. Les resultats issus du present programme de recherche contribueront entre autres a cibler, en collaboration avec les milieux partenaires, des pistes pertinentes quant a l'elaboration de programmes de prevention et d'intervention specifiques aux clienteles et aux problematiques etudiees. A plus long terme, la mise sur pied et l'evaluation de ces programmes bases sur des donnees probantes contribueront a reduire la violence dans les relations amoureuses des jeunes, ainsi que les couts y etant associes.

Abstract-Résumé: High velocity/low amplitude (HVLA) spinal manipulation, a non-invasive manual procedure applied to specific body tissues with therapeutic intent, is the most common complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) practice in North America. Manipulation is most commonly provided by chiropractors although it is also provided by physiotherapists, physicians and osteopaths. At present, there is no formal reporting mechanism to document adverse events associated with HVLA manipulation. The study team aims to create a culture of safety around manipulation by developing instruments that practitioners can use to record and report adverse events. Volunteer community-based manipulation providers will pilot these tools through active surveillance with the goal of implementing the refined tools into the routine practice of manipulation providers. The ultimate goal of this team grant is to develop, pilot, evaluate and support a culture of safety for regulated professionals (chiropractors, physicians, physical therapists and osteopaths) who provide SMT in Alberta and Ontario. Our partners will not only help disseminate findings, they will apply the research findings to inform policies, programs and practice through their provincial regulatory responsibilities, and their strong ties with national associations and educational colleges.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Child and Youth Injury Prevention
Keywords-MotsClés: BURDEN OF INJURY; CHILD AND YOUTH INJURY; HIGH-RISK POPULATIONS FOR INJURY; PEDIATRIC TRAUMA; PUBLIC HEALTH APPROACH; SPATIAL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The CIHR Team in Child and Youth Injury Prevention addresses calls for improved Canadian child and youth injury prevention initiatives by focusing on research and its application for prevention, training and capacity building, and enhanced communications within the injury prevention community. Activities include assessing: the burden of child and youth injury by looking at the long-term costs to the individual, family and society; paediatric trauma systems - getting the right patient to the right place at the right time; Aboriginal child and youth injury; and high risk injury groups based on stages of childhood (supervision of young children, child pedestrian injury, snowboarding injury, junior high curriculum-based sports-injury prevention, and identifying adolescent risk takers). The Team will use novel methods (e.g. spatial analysis) to identify risk factors based on injury hotspots; virtual reality environments to study child behaviour; and web-based interventions to deliver information to youth. Innovative products will include a Web Portal, a Child and Youth Injury Indicators Dashboard, and an Atlas of Child and Youth Injury. The Dashboard will provide current information on injury indicators to inform the development of injury prevention policies, prevention and research. The Atlas will include maps and spatial analyses from the Burden, Trauma and Aboriginal Injury studies. The Web Portal will serve as a communications platform for on-line discussions, seminars, meetings, and communiques; house the Dashboard and Atlas, providing current surveillance information; serve as a repository for injury prevention knowledge, evidence and tools; display team abstracts, presentations, publications and reviews; and link and present information from other sources. This research systematically builds on past advancements and will be undertaken in co-operation with many child and youth injury prevention partners, including Safe Kids Canada and the Assembly of First Nations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Detection and compensation for mass motion induced signal artifacts in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (FMRI); HUMAN BRAIN FUNCTION; IMAGE PROCESSING; IMAGING; INDEPENDENT COMPONENTS ANALYSIS (ICA); MOVEMENT ARTIFACT; NEUROSCIENCE; PREPROCESSING
Abstract-Résumé: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a powerful tool to non-invasively measure brain activity by changes in signal intensity over time. Any motion during a scan presents a difficulty for fMRI as it leads to signal intensity variations that can either mask or mimic the signal changes due to neuronal activation. Even if the head remains perfectly still, movement of masses outside the head will distort the static magnetic field and contaminate the brain scans. This is an inherent limitation of all fMRI experiments, and one of the remaining hurdles keeping fMRI from regular clinical use.  My Ph.D research will develop strategies to distinguish mass movement artifacts from genuine brain activation. Since real subjects might move while in the scanner and will always have other physiological sources of noise (e.g. breathing, swallowing, attentional fluctuations), we will perform this study using a phantom (an inert, fluid filled volume guaranteed to remain stationary), and a simulated arm that we can control to mimic the reaching actions studied by this research group.  This will allow us to determine the spatial and temporal characteristics of the signal, which could then be subtracted from real data.   Any person who undergoes fMRI testing is bound to move on their first time.  Instead of increasing the number of trials, this research would allow researchers to improve the quality of the data they acquire.  This research could also expand the types of tasks that can be studied by fMRI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparative Effectiveness of Disorder-Focused vs. Transdiagnostic Cognitive Behavioural Group Therapy for Panic Disorder: A Pilot Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY DISORDERS; CLINICAL RESEARCH; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; EMPIRICALLY SUPPORTED TREATMENTS; PANIC DISORDER; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Anxiety disorders are among the most common psychiatric disorders, affecting over 1.2 million Canadians per year; however, many of those affected, particularly those in rural or underserved communities, do not receive evidence-based treatments. Although effective psychological treatments are available, many mental health care providers are unable to learn independent therapy protocols for each anxiety diagnosis throughout the course of their training; therefore, the availability of therapists who can provide such treatments is limited. In addition, over half of anxiety patients report symptoms of at least one additional mood or anxiety disorder, suggesting that current treatments are only targeting some of the difficulties that people are experiencing. To address these concerns, new transdiagnostic treatments are being developed which target the common underlying features of anxiety disorders, rather than disorder-specific symptoms. These treatments provide people with strategies that they can use for a wide range of anxiety and mood problems, potentially reducing treatment duration and the need to seek subsequent therapy for other anxiety disorders. They also allow individuals with different anxiety disorders to receive treatment in the same groups, which is more cost-effective, efficient, and may reduce wait times. While initial evidence is promising, research has yet to examine whether transdiagnostic protocols are as effective as disorder-specific treatments. Therefore, this study will be one of the first randomized controlled trials to compare transdiagnostic treatment for Panic Disorder to cognitive behavioural therapy. Before we can recommend these new protocols above the current treatment of choice, studies, such as the one proposed, are necessary to provide empirical support for their effectiveness. Given the practical benefits, transdiagnostic interventions have the potential to greatly improve the provision of mental health care services in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the Parietal Lobe in Reading and Writing
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGULAR GYRUS; COGNITION; FMRI; LANGUAGE; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; NEUROSURGERY; PARIETAL LOBE; READING; WRITING
Abstract-Résumé: The precise role that the angular gyrus plays in cognition has been difficult to establish. Dejerine's 19th century examinations of the brains of patients who after a stroke could no longer read or write revealed extensive lesions within the left posterior parieto-occipital area, leading Dejerine to the conclusion that the angular gyrus is essentially involved in reading and writing. However, modern neuroimaging techniques, such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), rarely find any angular activity that correlates with reading and writing in healthy subjects (for review, see Price et al., 2000). Why have so few imaging studies confirmed the neurological model? We plan to use fMRI to investigate angular gyrus function in healthy subjects as a test of the hypothesis made by the neurological model that the angular gyrus is in fact critical for reading and writing. We hope to better understand how and when the angular gyrus is engaged in reading and writing. Once we have fMRI tasks that yield reliable angular activations in healthy subjects, we will adapt them for clinical use in patients with low-grade tumors in and around the angular gyrus to test whether the angular tissue is functioning so that the surgeon can use this information to plan the surgery, such as to avoid functional tissue. We will also test the patients in the operating room to monitor any changes to the patients' performance on the tasks intraoperatively. This stage in the research will be part of a large research project, already being carried out in Dr. Petrides' laboratory in collaboration with Dr. R. Del Maestro (neurosurgeon), to apply fMRI for the preoperative evaluation of patients with brain tumors in the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of gut mucosal immunity in HIV immunopathogenesis and transmission
Keywords-MotsClés: GASTROINTESTINAL TRACT; HIV/AIDS; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; TRANSMISSION RISK
Abstract-Résumé: The success of antiretroviral therapy (ART) has dramatically increased the life expectancy of HIV infected individuals. However, previously underestimated illnesses, particularly cardiovascular disease, are responsible for persistently elevated morbidity and mortality despite ART. One major limitation of current therapy is its relative inability to reverse HIV induced gut immune defects and HIV-associated immune activation; both phenomena are interrelated and associated with morbidity.  The gut houses most of the body's activated CD4+ T cells, which are critical targets for HIV.  In contrast to blood, CD4+ T cells in the gut are dramatically depleted within weeks of infection, and normalize slowly and incompletely upon initiation of ART. Loss of these immune cells may impair important barrier functions of the gut, enabling for normal gut bacteria to "leak" into the bloodstream.  This may cause immune activation in both the gut and the rest of the body, contributing to CD4+ T-cell death and co-morbid conditions.  Moreover, gut mucosal immune activation may explain why levels of HIV are higher in the rectum than in the blood or the semen. Since this gut immune activation persists despite ART, this may have important implications for HIV sexual transmission during ART.  Therefore, for my PhD thesis research I propose to: 1) study the impact of HIV infection and it's treatment on key aspects of gut mucosal immunology; and 2) examine the levels of rectal HIV and their correlation with gut immunology and immune activation. We believe that a better knowledge of these mucosal events will lead to novel strategies to therapy improvements HIV infection and to prevent HIV transmission.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional characterization of NleA, a type III secreted virulence factor of enteropathogenic and enterohemorrhagic E. coli
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CULTURE; CELL FRACTIONATION; CHROMATOGRAPHY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; PROTEIN SECRETION; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Enteropathogenic and enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EPEC & EHEC) are bacterial pathogens able to cause severe diarrheal illnesses in otherwise healthy individuals.  EPEC is a diarrheal pathogen that kills several hundred thousand children each year in developing countries. EHEC is known as the causative agent of 'hamburger disease', is more prevalent in developed countries, and causes diarrheal outbreaks with fatal complications. Currently no specific therapeutic regimens for EHEC infections have been developed; antibiotic use is not recommended as it exacerbates disease.  This project aims to elucidate the mechanisms behind how EPEC and EHEC cause disease. To accomplish this we look at the bacterial protein NleA (non- LEE-encoded-protein) that is delivered into the host cell by both EPEC & EHEC.  NleA has been shown to dramatically contribute to the virulence of these pathogens, bind to a mammalian secretory protein Sec24, and decrease host cell secretion of a reporter protein by 50%.  Recently we have found that NleA plays a role in the disruption of the tight junctions that form between epithelial cells lining the lumen of the gut.   This disruption is hallmark to EPEC pathogenesis and allows the pathogen to systemically disseminate through the host.  With these results combined with future studies we hope to develop therapeutics that inhibit NleA and attenuate EPEC and EHEC pathogenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fanconi Anemia signaling and Mus81-Eme1: role in replicative stress and development
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; EMBRYONIC DEVELOPMENT; FANCONI ANENIA; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; KNOCK-OUT MICE; MUS81-EME1; TUNEL
Abstract-Résumé: We are exposed to various substances on a daily basis that have the ability to damage our DNA. The body has developed a number of processes to sense and remove damage to DNA. One process involves a protein known as Mus81-Eme1 which behaves like a pair of molecular scissors that helps to snip out pieces of damaged DNA.  Mice missing Mus81-Eme1 have problems snipping out pieces of damaged DNA-the DNA of these mice is then easily corrupted by chemicals known as DNA crosslinking agents.  A similar problem exists in patients afflicted with a hereditary syndrome known as Fanconi anemia.  Patients afflicted with this disease also exhibit congenital defects that point to a role for this repair process during prenatal development.  The relationship between DNA repair and congenital defects in Fanconi anemia is not known.  We have recently discovered that both Mus81-Eme1 and the repair process affected in Fanconi anemia are required to make a mouse, as mice missing both processes often die before birth.   We want to figure out how and why both these processes are necessary for embryonic development of mice, and how this is related to DNA repair.  This research can help us understand how and why patients with Fanconi anemia are afflicted with congenital defects that occur during gestation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Résurrection scientifique ? L'utilisation secondaire rétrospective de l'information et du matériel génétique de personnes décédées en recherche
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOBANQUE; BIOMEDICALE; BIOETHIQUE; COMPARE; DROIT; GENETIQUE; INTERNATIONAL; RECHERCHE
Abstract-Résumé: Depuis le sequencage du genome humain, le developpement de banques de donnees genetiques permet un essor important de la recherche biomedicale, notamment epidemiologique.  Le nombre important d'echantillons contenus dans les banques de donnees genetiques permet la validation des resultats de recherche dans des delais nettement inferieurs a la periode generalement requise lors de recherches effectuees aupres d'un petit nombre de sujets.  Forte de cette reussite, la communaute de recherche biomedicale ne cesse de developper de nouvelles banques.  Afin d'optimiser l'utilisation de ces ressources, plusieurs chercheurs combinent desormais les informations contenues dans differentes banques de maniere a creer «virtuellement» de mega-cohortes de sujets.  Cette volonte se manifeste particulierement par la creation de consortiums nationaux et internationaux de banques de donnees genetiques. Puisque l'utilisation secondaire est encadree de maniere differente d'une juridiction a l'autre, les echanges interprovinciaux et internationaux d'echantillons et de donnees genetiques soulevent plusieurs questions juridiques et ethiques.  Ces questions sont exacerbees lorsque les echantillons et informations proviennent de personnes aujourd'hui decedees.  Ce projet a pour objectifs d'etudier les enjeux juridiques et ethiques souleves par l'utilisation secondaire retrospective des donnees et du materiel genetique de personnes decedees dans le cadre de partenariats nationaux et internationaux de recherche et de proposer un modele facilitant cette utilisation secondaire.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification des déterminants moléculaires du récepteur CXCR4 impliqués dans la liaison à des composés anti-VIH ainsi qu'au niveau de son activation.
Keywords-MotsClés: CXCR4; GPCR (RECEPTEURS COUPLES AUX PROTEINES G); SCAM (SUBSTITUTED CYSTEINE ACCESSIBILITY METHOD); SIGNALISATION; STRUCTURE; VIH
Abstract-Résumé: Chaque annee, plus de 2,5 millions de personnes sont infectees par le VIH (virus de l'immunodeficience humaine). Plusieurs groupes de recherche s'interessent a la conception de medicaments qui pourraient empecher ce virus d'infecter les cellules du systeme immunitaire de l'organisme humain. Il existe d'ailleurs plusieurs composes qui ont ete synthetises a cet effet, mais la plupart d'entre eux n'ont pas reussi a etre commercialises. Dans notre laboratoire, nous etudions, au niveau moleculaire, l'interaction d'une drogue avec sa cible. Le recepteur CXCR4 est une cible pour beaucoup de drogues anti-VIH, car il permet a certaines souches de ce virus d'infecter les cellules immunitaires. Dans mes etudes, je propose de caracteriser l'interaction entre certaines drogues anti-VIH et ce recepteur. Le but de cette etude vise a comprendre comment ces differentes drogues specifiques a CXCR4, bloquent l'infection au VIH. Ceci permettra l'elaboration rationnelle de nouveaux medicaments qui pourraient avoir davantage d'effets benefiques tout en limitant les effets secondaires.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying the Pathways by Which Interleukin-7 Enhances CD8 T-Cell Activation.
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; CD127; CYTOKINES; CYTOTOXIC CD8 T CELLS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HIV; INTERLEUKINS; PROLIFERATION; REAL TIME RT-PCR; TAT PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: HIV infection is marked by low or lack of immunity which allows infections to enter and persist in the body.  The link between HIV infection and lack of immunity is clear. However, it is not fully understood at the molecular level.  HIV disrupts many processes and mechanisms in the white blood cells. One of the mechanisms that is impaired by HIV and is crucial for body immunity is mediated by Interleukin (IL)-7. IL-7 is a 'messenger' molecule which is produced when an infection enters the body and travels through the blood stream to alert immune cells to the presence of the invader. Some immune cells, including CD8 T-cells, have a special receptor on their surface that allows them to detect IL-7 and respond to the alarm. We recently showed that one of the HIV products, the Tat protein, is able to bind to the IL-7 receptor and remove it from the surface of CD8 T-cells.  As a result, the CD8 T-cells cannot "hear" the alarm and fail to activate in the presence of infection leaving the body vulnerable. In this study, we will first identify the details of how IL-7 helps CD8 T-cells to grow and become functional.  Then we will examine the effects of IL-7 in presence of the HIV Tat protein. The main goal of this project is to identify the exact effects of Tat on CD8 T-cell functions.  If we understand how IL-7 activates CD8 T-cells and how HIV disables them, we may be able to design drugs that could reverse the effect and restore immune function in HIV+ patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Origin of antibodies with long CDR-H3 loops in HIV-1 infection and autoimmune disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY NEUTRALIZATION; ANTIBODY STRUCTURE; AUTOIMMUNITY; B CELL BIOLOGY; HIV/AIDS; HUMORAL IMMUNOLOGY; IMMUNOGENETICS; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; VACCINE DESIGN
Abstract-Résumé: It is likely that any prophylactic vaccine against HIV-1 will require the induction of both cell-mediated immunity and broadly-neutralizing (bNt) antibodies (Abs) to be successful. bNt Abs against HIV-1 are rarely-produced Abs with unusual structures that are able to bind and neutralize a large number of viral variants, and confer protection from infection when transferred into non-human primates. One of these unusual structures is a long "CDR-H3" loop, a feature that is sometimes found associated with autoimmune Abs. Normally, cells that produce Abs which bind to the body's own proteins are destroyed during development; failure of these so-called "tolerance" mechanisms can lead to life-threatening autoimmune disease. Recently, it has been proposed that bNt Abs are autoimmune Abs that arise when immunological tolerance is broken and only coincidentally bind to HIV-1.  Our lab's unpublished analyses have revealed that long CDR-H3s are a more general feature of anti-protein Abs, and in particular those that arise during chronic viral infection. Thus, elucidation of the cellular origins of bNt Abs is necessary to guide HIV-1 vaccine design. We are currently investigating the genetic features of Abs isolated from patients with HIV, autoimmune diseases, or healthy controls, and trying to relate these features to functional properties including self-reactivity. We expect to determine if long-CDR-H3 Abs are present in HIV-1 infection vs. a truly autoimmune state, and whether distinct autoreactivities or generalized polyreactivity is present in bNt serum. Our goal is to define cellular and molecular features associated with clinical outcome, particularly broad neutralization. In addition to its pertinence to HIV-1 vaccine design, our work will increase basic knowledge of the genetic and functional properties of B cell subsets, as well as the shaping of antibody responses to natural infection, both of which are generally applicable to vaccinology.

TitreApplicationTitle: Linkage of KIR/HLA genotype combinations with NK cell cytolytic potential: Role in protection from HIV infection.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR MEDIATED IMMUNITY; HIV/AIDS; HOST RESPONSE; INNATE IMMUNITY; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Human immunodeficiency virus type-1 (HIV-1) is the primary cause of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and is one of the 3 greatest infectious disease killers globally. Some people appear to be resistant to HIV infection, remaining uninfected despite exposure. Among those who become infected a small subset of about 5% progress slowly without treatment. There is epidemiological evidence that Natural Killer (NK) cells, through interactions between certain NK receptors (KIR3DL1) and their ligands (HLA-Bw4), play a role in HIV resistance as well as slow disease progression in infected subjects. In this project I will work with cells from HIV exposed uninfected individuals typed for KIR3DL1 and HLA-Bw4 and study the linkage between the anti-viral function of NK cells from individuals having KIR/HLA receptor ligand pairs that are associated or not with favorable outcomes following exposure to HIV. In particular I will investigate the ability of NK cells to kill cells after they detect changes that occur on the surface of HIV infected cells. This proposal will contribute to improving our understanding of the role of NK cells in protection from HIV observed in HIV resistant and/or slow disease progressors. Such information would be relevant to vaccine design by providing a rationale for modulating NK activity at the time of vaccination to favor the development of protective immunity.

TitreApplicationTitle: A photographic exploration of housing and health among persons living with HIV in Vancouver
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; BODY MAPPING; CARE GIVING; HIGH RISK SEXUAL BEHAVIOUR; HIV/AIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Against a backdrop of rising adult morbidity and mortality fuelled by the world's largest HIV epidemic, there exists a growing demographic of adolescents in South Africa who are thrust into the precarious situation of having to provide care to their infected and affected family members. It is well documented in the literature how the stress of care giving undermines household capacity and stability, increasing the vulnerability of informal caregivers, but few studies have sought to assess the prevalence and characteristics of home care provided by adolescents and the associated risk for HIV exposure and acquisition. Young carers are additionally vulnerable due to a myriad of factors that are known predictors of high-risk sexual behaviour: loss of parental guidance at a crucial development stage; loss of income due to illness or death of a parent, which may be a driver of survival sex; and loss of opportunity to pursue education and income generating activities. While South Africa struggles to cope with the enormity of the HIV epidemics impact on their communities, adolescents remain both the hope and the angst of HIV prevention in this setting, where 2 million of the estimated 6 million HIV infections are amongst people between the ages of 15 and 24 years. While there is widespread speculation and little evidence regarding adolescent sexual health needs, the aims of this project are to contribute new knowledge regarding an important and neglected population by exploring caretaking responsibility, an understudied explanatory variable in South Africa's epidemic. The findings will advance new understandings of youth vulnerability and resiliency, which may help to address the sexual health needs of this globally important group in diverse socio-cultural and geographic contexts, including with at-risk and vulnerable youth in Canada. The findings of this study will empower the next generation of caregivers, policy-makers and educators to turn the tide on this pandemic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Individual, social and health services factors in vulnerability to co-infection with hepatitis C virus and human immunodeficiency virus and the role of a peer-based intervention and integrated health services model in addressing hepatitis C virus treatment readiness and access among injection drug users living with hepatitis C and concurrent substance use and mental illness.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESSIBILITY OF HEALTH SERVICES; CO-INFECTION HIV/STI; CONCURRENT SUBSTANCE USE AND MENTAL ILLNESS; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; GROUP-COMPARISON/LONGITUDINAL COHORT STUDY; HEPATITIS C VIRUS TREATMENT READINESS; INJECTION DRUG USERS; PEER-BASED INTERVENTION; QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DATA/ANALYSIS; THEORETICAL BEHAVIOURAL FRAMEWORK
Abstract-Résumé: The overall aim of the present research is to examine the impact of a peer-based intervention for injection drug users (IDUs) diagnosed with hepatitis C virus (HCV) on treatment readiness, access and barriers to health services, and issues of co-infection with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and concurrent mental illness. Infectious diseases of HCV and HIV are serious public health concerns in Canada, and the integration of care for vulnerable populations affected by these infections is a major policy goal. The target population experiences stigma, isolation, limited support, homelessness, poverty, social marginalization, and barriers to treatment access. Not many IDUs have successfully accessed treatment for HCV and they continue to be an underserved vulnerable population. Non-traditional health care approaches to treating people with HCV who use drugs and who have co-infection with HIV and/or concurrent mental illness can be successful with regards to treatment delivery, and managing side effects. The study will utilize quantitative and qualitative data collected from IDUs in the peer-based intervention and IDUs not a part of the intervention but receiving primary care at partnering health centers. A theoretical behavioural framework will guide the analysis of the behavioural, structural and epidemiological aspects of infectious disease risk behaviours and prevention including co-infection HCV/HIV, treatment readiness, barriers to treatment, integration of care, substance use, mental illness, risk reduction strategies, stigma, social support, homelessness, poverty, and social marginalization. The proposed study has important implications for the development of targeted, culturally-appropriate, applied public health interventions and community-based research on vulnerable populations focused on improving the quality and accessibility of services.

TitreApplicationTitle: The contribution of cellular PRMT6 to HIV-1 pathogenesis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGININE METHYLATION; HIV/AIDS; HOST RESTRICTION FACTOR; PRMT6; PROTEASOMAL DEGRADATION; RAPID DISEASE PROGRESSION; SITE DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; SNP VARIANTS; UBIQUITINATION ASSAY; VIRUS PROPAGATION AND TITERING
Abstract-Résumé: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) readily replicates in human immune cells, evades the host immune response by mutating frequently, and causes disease by ultimately depleting the cells humans use to protect themselves. However, HIV-1 infection may be controlled for a number of years prior to the onset of disease and this progression towards AIDS is a result of complex host and viral determinants. The natural development of HIV-1 infection varies widely from person to person and can result in rapid disease progressors to asymptomatic long term non progressors. The reasons for this are still obscure; however, the recent discovery of host restriction factors, which function to inhibit retroviral activities, may shine light on this process. Host restriction factors PRMT6, a protein arginine methyltranferase, compromises HIV-1 protein function by methylating HIV-1 Tat, Nef and nucleocapsid (NC). However over the natural course of infection HIV-1 eventually manages to circumvent the restrictive effects of PRMT6. Our preliminary data suggest that PRMT6 is targeted by Vif for degradation and we aim to elucidate the mechanism behind this degradation. The importance of PRMT6 in HIV-1 pathogenesis was further demonstrated by a recent publication by Le Clerc et al. that establishes in a genome wide study, the association between a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the PRMT6 gene and rapid progression of the disease. We also wish to study the  PRMT6 variant and its effect on HIV-1 protein methylation and its susceptibility to Vif-mediated degradation.  In light of the latest intriguing findings on PRMT6 and with the expertise of Dr. Wainberg and his team, we believe that studying HIV-1 PRMT6 interaction will most certainly reveal exciting insight into the regulation of HIV-1 transcription, the innate immunity against the virus, viral latency and AIDS disease progression. Such insight will ultimately provide new drug targets and enable better disease management

TitreApplicationTitle: International Nurse Migration on the Global Distribution of Resources for Persons Living with HIV/AIDS in Developing Nations: A Critical Discourse Analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADIAN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH POLICY; CRITICAL PERSPECTIVES; GLOBAL NURSING SHORTAGE; HEALTH PROMOTION; HIV/AIDS IN DEVELOPING NATIONS; INTERNATIONAL NURSE MIGRATION; MIGRATION AND FOREIGN AID POLICIES
Abstract-Résumé: The global nursing shortage extends beyond a lack of personnel to fill vacancies. There is an extreme imbalance in the proportion of healthcare workers worldwide. As the largest body of healthcare professionals globally and as experts of human caring science, nurses are integral players in the well being of society. And yet, many developing countries lack the resources to educate, employ and sustain a nursing workforce within their national public sector, often resulting in inadequate access to healthcare services for already vulnerable populations such as those affected by HIV/AIDS.  Canada holds a unique position on the international health stage. As an affluent industrialized competitively positioned to attract nurses, Canada is also a significant contributor of foreign aid. As Canada responds to its national nursing shortage, it is important consider the implications for the global context. This research will give particular attention to the policy change process focusing on the collective as the instrument for health service delivery. Specifically, this study will examine how Canadian migration and foreign-aid policies contribute to the production and distribution of social and economic resources that shape health for persons living with HIV/AIDS in developing nations.  By providing theoretical and methodological insights into international health policies in the form of health service delivery and the social determinants of health, this work will benefit healthcare practitioners, policy makers and researchers. Further contributing to the body of global health research, the findings from this study will illuminate how Canadian health policies and practices shape the international distribution of resources, and opportunities for Canada to optimize its global contribution.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Palmitoylation in Huntington Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CONDITIONAL KNOCK OUT MOUSE MODEL; CRE/LOXP SYSTEM; HIP14; HUNTINGTON DISEASE; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES; PALMITOYL ACYL TRANSFERASE; PALMITOYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington disease (HD) is a degenerative disease starting in mid-life that affects the neurons of an area of the brain called the striatum, which regulates movement. HD affects the part of the striatum responsible for inhibiting unwanted movement such that the primary symptom of HD is chorea or involuntary movement. There are presently no effective treatments or cures and death occurs, on average, 15 years after disease onset. HD is caused by an inherited mutation in the huntingtin gene, where a short sequence at the beginning of the gene is multiplied more than 36 times. The mutation has many effects on the function of the huntingtin protein (htt), including interfering with how it interacts with other proteins. One of these other proteins is Huntingtin Interacting Protein 14 (HIP14). HIP14 is a "PAT" which is a type of enzyme that adds a fatty acid to other proteins, including htt, in a process called palmitoylation. This process controls where in the cell a protein is located, like the address on an envelope, and what function it performs at that location. In a mouse model of HD, htt and other proteins are less palmitoylated. We have created a genetically modified mouse model that lacks the HIP14 gene to determine if HIP14 is involved in HD. This mouse model is born with a very severe form of HD; however, because people and HD model mice are not born with the disease, we are unable to definitively show that HIP14 is involved in HD. We are therefore engineering a new kind of mouse model called a "conditional knockout" mouse that works a little like a light switch. We will be able to "turn off" HIP14 when and where we want like turning a light off in one room but not another. We will then look for the symptoms of HD in this mouse model.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Parental Involvement in a Group-based Multidisciplinary Childhood Obesity Treatment Program
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION; CHILDHOOD OBESITY; FITNESS; NUTRITION; OBESITY; PARENTS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SOCIAL SUPPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Treatment programs for childhood obesity require varying degrees of parental involvement. The goal of this research program is to investigate the optimal level of parent involvement in such programs. Three studies will be conducted to achieve this goal. Study 1 will track body composition (% fat, muscle mass), physical activity (PA), and diet in 60 obese children and their parents and compare to healthy weight children and their parents over 3 months. This will be the first study to comprehensively monitor these factors and will help clarify the relationship between lifestyle behaviours and obesity. These findings will be used to guide the development of a 3-month structured diet and exercise intervention to be used in the next study. In Study 2, obese children and their parents will be randomized into 1 of 3 conditions: (1) no parental involvement, (2) parallel parental involvement, or (3) interactive parental involvement. All children will participate in diet and exercise sessions; however parental involvement will be manipulated across conditions. Specifically, Group 1 will not involve the parents, Group 2 will involve the parents in separate identical diet and exercise sessions, and Group 3 will involve the parents interacting with their children during diet and exercise sessions. During the sessions, participants will be taught how to regulate their diet and exercise behaviour. This will be the first study to experimentally manipulate parental involvement in a childhood obesity intervention. Finally, Study 3 will examine the long-term effects of this intervention through following up with the same assessments after an additional 3 months. Children whose parents are involved the most are expected to exercise the most, and experience the greatest short- and long-term improvements in all lifestyle factors. The identification of the optimal amount of parental involvement in this intervention will help in the design of future childhood obesity treatment programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Telerehabilitation:  an innovative approach to cognitive strategy training with brain injury survivors
Keywords-MotsClés: ACQUIRED BRAIN INJURY; ACTIVITIES OF DAILY LIVING; COGNITIVE REHABILITATION; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; STRATEGY TRAINING; TELEREHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Recent research has shown that a real-world strategy training program is effective in improving functional performance on daily life activities (e.g. accomplishing tasks at work, preparing a meal, passing a test) for brain injury survivors.  To date, this real-world strategy training has been administered face-to-face with the therapist visiting the participants' homes or other community environment.  However, many brain injury survivors do not have access to this type rehabilitation due to the lack of available service in their area.  This is particularly true in northern and rural areas. This study evaluates the use of video teleconferencing or telerehabilitation in administering this training protocol to make this program available to any brain injury survivor regardless of their location.  This research has the potential to improve the quality of life and day to day functioning of brain injury survivors living in any community and to greatly improve access to rehabilitation services, especially those in northern and rural areas.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Effects of a Pivotal Response Treatment-Based Community Intervention on Social Interactions of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; OBSERVATIONS; PEERS; SOCIAL INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Severe and persistent impairment in social functioning is a core feature of ASD that has a significant impact on real world adaptive success (Rutter, 2005). Left untreated, social dysfunction results in substantial burden on families, educators and health care providers.  As a result, the treatment of social skills deficits is the focus of many interventions for children with ASD.  However, little is known about the translation of social skills into naturalistic settings among peers. When assessed, social skills are examined qualitatively or informally, in clinic settings, often facilitated by an adult (Lord et al., 2005).  While successful peer interaction is the most valued outcome for parents whose children have ASD, this critical outcome has been surprisingly overlooked (Mesibov, Shea & Adams, 2001). In attempt to address this gap, the proposed observational study seeks to examine peer interactions of children with ASD in a real world setting after participating in a community based EIBI program (NS EIBI).  This innovative program provides evidence-based intervention that is feasible, cost-effective and sustainable in community settings (Bryson et al., 2007).  The sample will consist of children previously enrolled in the NS EIBI program and children who received alternative intervention.  Children will be observed in one-on-one and group free play settings.  The study will utilize a one-zero time-sampling procedure (Martin & Bateson, 1995) at 30-second intervals.  Social skills will be examined using a multi-faceted approach, obtaining parent and teacher report measures in addition to direct observation (MacIntosh & Dissanayake, 2006; Sparrow, Cicchetti & Balla, 2005).  The proposed research will evaluate whether skills acquired in the NS EIBI program are maintained and generalized to a real world setting. Moreover, these findings will have broad implications for more effective interventions that target valued outcomes for children with ASD.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of primary care reform in Ontario for individuals with mental illness
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; MENTAL HEALTH CARE; PATIENT ENROLLMENT MODELS; PRIMARY CARE DELIVERY
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Among physicians, primary care doctors play the largest role in care of Canadians with mental health problems. Ontario has introduced patient enrolment models (PEMs) which include patient rostering--patients sign up with a specific provider or team. Some patients, however, receive services from their physician without being enrolled. There are three PEM model types: enhanced fee-for-service (FFS); blended capitation; and team based capitation models. Despite similarities, model types differ in physician compensation. In enhanced FFS, claims are paid in full. In contrast, reimbursement in capitation models is largely based on the age and sex distribution of rostered patients and only to a minor degree (10% of claims) on FFS. Critics assert that physicians in capitation may preferentially select the least complex patients, known as 'cream skimming'.   The aim of the proposed study is to investigate how enrolment in different models influences access and quality of primary care for individuals with mental illness. Specifically, this study will investigate if when compared to FFS models, capitation models provide better quality care, but are less likely to serve people with mental illness including severe and persistent mental illness.   Method: Patients will be assigned to one of three groups: psychotic disorders; non- psychotic disorders; and no mental illness. Utilization, access to care, and quality of care will be compared for patients in different model types, as well as between enrolled and non enrolled individuals. This study will be conducted at ICES using non nominal data from linked administrative databases.    Results: Results will indicate how the introduction of PEMs in Ontario has affected access and quality for primary care for mental illness.   Discussion: Findings from the present study have implications for policy-makers at the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long Term Care and in professional associations, clinicians and patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Primary health care: Assessing levers for change within the Canadian system
Keywords-MotsClés: FOCUS GROUPS; HISTORICAL POLICY ANALYSIS; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; SEMI-STRUCTURED INTERVIEWS
Abstract-Résumé: Primary health care (PHC) is the foundation of Canada's health care system.  It is the provision of essential health care services for individuals and families in the community by a family physician who acts as a first point of consultation with the health care system and a coordinator of secondary care services.  Canada lags well behind most industrialized nations in terms of quality of, and access to, PHC and myriad experts as well as the public, have advocated for fundamental change to the system.  Although significant innovation has occurred on a very small scale, system-level reform remains elusive.   This project attempts to take the first steps necessary to address why we seem unable to make sweeping change to PHC by examining constitutional, legislative, and historical structures that may be acting as barriers to change. This study will also examine one or more international examples of successful system-level reform with the goal of understanding the factors that facilitated the change process.   In the final phase of the study, options for reform will be presented to individuals who are responsible for making management and/or policy decisions in Canadian health care. Options will fit within Canada's existing constitutional frameworks, but may involve changes at the legislative, policy, and/or delivery levels, informed by the results of the international studies. A focus of these interviews will be strategies for successful integration of any of the options for change, and the likelihood of success.   An in-depth study of the barriers to and facilitators of system-level change will be instrumental for moving beyond the small-scale, towards systems-level innovation. This work will be the first set of projects in an interdisciplinary research portfolio, the goal of which is to elevate Canada's profile as a world leader in the provision of outstanding primary health care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Primary Care Resident Physicians' Knowledge About Health Equity: A Multi-Institutional Survey in Canada and Brazil
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENDER; HEALTH DISPARITIES; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH SERVICES; INTERNATIONAL HEALTH; MEDICAL EDUCATION; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Primary health care has an important role to provide a more effective and equitable health care for population. The relation between health in equity and health care is a priority theme in the world. Brazil and Canada consider primary health care as essential to improve and to maintain the health of population.Education for family physicians is important for achieving high quality in primary health care. Aim:This study aims to evaluate the actual and perceived knowledge about health inequities among residents in family medicine in Canada and Brazil. Objectives:1-Critically review the content of existing medical and health curriculum in health equity and skills training programs in shared decision making and cultural competency and evidence of their effectiveness in reducing health care equity gaps, 2-Conduct a needs assessment survey, assessing knowledge about health inequities among residents in family medicine in Brazil and Canada and compare the results. 3- Develop a workshop or course in health equity and decision-making skills will address identified needs using data from critically review of the health curriculum for family physicians and the needs assessment survey,4)Conduct and evaluate a workshop about health equity for family physicians in Brazil and Canada. Hypothesis: Family physicians have low actual and perceived knowledge about health equity.Methodology: We will use quantitative and qualitative approaches.A cross-sectional survey will assess actual and perceived resident knowledge on health equity.The total of participants will be distributed to residents and directors of medical schools in Canada and Brazil.The questionnaires will include all the recommendations from experts in health equity that specifically addressed family physician education in health equity.Expected Results:We expect that this study will contribute to improving the quality of life of Canadians and Brazilians by helping making primary care more equitable.

Keywords-MotsClés: BEST PRACTICE GUIDELINES; COLLABORATION; EVIDENCE-BASED CARE; HEALTHY WORK ENVIRONMENTS; LONG TERM CARE; NURSING HOMES; ORGANIZATIONAL PERFORMANCE; RECRUITMENT AND RETENTION; TEAMWORK; WORKLIFE
Abstract-Résumé: The population of elderly people in Canada is growing at an unprecedented rate. Many elderly people will require long term care services that are provided by nursing homes. It is vitally important that nursing homes have sufficient numbers of qualified staff to provide the required care and services. The key to keeping staff in nursing homes and attracting new staff may lie in understanding the work environment and how to make it one that is supportative of staff. A tool has been developed by RNAO that would allow a health care organization to use research to improve the work environment. My research will evaluate the use of this tool to learn how it needs to be implemented and what it's impact will be on the work environment.The results will serve to educate nursing homes and improve worklife for staff and care for the elderly, which is ultimately the goal.

TitreApplicationTitle: A longitudinal study of neurocognitive and neuroimaging markers of remission in first-episode psychosis
Keywords-MotsClés: FIRST-EPISODE PSYCHOSIS; MARKERS OF REMISSION; NEUROCOGNITIVE; NEUROIMAGING; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: People with a first episode of psychosis (FEP) exhibit substantial heterogeneity with respect to severity and course over time. In the summer of 2004 and following the award of a CIHR operating grant we initiated a large longitudinal study on neurocognitive and neuroimaging markers of clinical outcome following a first episode of psychosis. The first objective of this study was to characterize from clinical, neurocognitive, and neuroimaging perspectives this cohort of patients at the time of initial presentation. A second objective consisted in the exploration of the predictive value of neurocognitive and neuroimaging measures in determining short-term (6 months post baseline) response to treatment. A third and ongoing objective is to document neurocognitive and neuroimaging changes over a two year period and evaluate how these changes may relate to good or poor clinical outcome. With respect to baseline assessment, we have characterized this large cohort in terms of deficits in social cognition (Bertrand et al., 2007), level of insight (Lepage et al., 2008) and memory impairments (Achim et al., 2007). We have also examined the functional and structural neural correlates of memory impairments (Achim et al., 2007), social cognition (Bertrand et al., 2008; Montreuil et al., in submission) and the effects of untreated psychosis on gray matter density (Malla et al., submitted).  We have also explored the predictive value of neurocognitive and neuroimaging measures on short-term response to treatment. Response to treatment is only the first step in the journey towards remission and eventual recovery or lack thereof. Therefore, as part of this project, I intend to pursue this unique longitudinal study involving an already well characterized large FEP patient cohort and a smaller cohort of healthy comparison subjects for understanding predictors of variations in remission and functional recovery. The aim is to focus all efforts on markers of remission at 1  year.

Abstract-Résumé: Genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein, and this information flow is regulated at several points. How the information encoded by RNA is regulated depends on proteins that bind to the RNA, which affect how the RNA is used to make new proteins. Importantly, the flow of information from RNA to protein is changed in diseases such as cancer due to changes in the activities of RNA-binding proteins. One such RNA-binding protein is the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A1 (hnRNP A1), which has a well-characterized role in regulating how newly-made RNA is processed into mature RNA capable of making new proteins. The regulation of RNA maturation by hnRNP A1 occurs in the nucleus of the cell; however, hnRNP A1 also plays important roles outside of the nucleus in the cytoplasm, where it regulates how long a RNA exists (RNA stability) and how RNA is used by the machinery that makes new proteins (RNA translation). Little is known about how hnRNP A1 performs its cytoplasmic activities, and therefore we do not know what may happen to change hnRNP A1 cytoplasmic activity in cancer cells. Furthermore, we do not know which RNAs are affected by deregulated hnRNP A1 activity in cancer cells. I propose to investigate how hnRNP A1 affects RNAs in the cytoplasm through the identification and characterization of the protein partners that bind to hnRNP A1 to regulate its activity. I will also identify and characterize the RNAs that are dependent on hnRNP A1 for their translation into protein to gain a better understanding of the cellular activities that are affected by cytoplasmic hnRNP A1. These studies will help us understand how RNA is made into protein, which will provide insight into what goes wrong in cancer cells. Moreover, by identifying the RNAs that are affected by hnRNP A1 cytoplasmic activities we will also understand more about the cellular functions that are changed in cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding reward motivation and expectancy in early phase psychosis smokers: a neuroimaging and genetic approach
Keywords-MotsClés: EXPECTANCY; MOTIVATION; NEUROIMAGING; PSYCHOSIS; SMOKING; TOBACCO ADDICTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Psychotic disorders, such as schizophrenia, are severe mental illnesses affecting approximately 3% of the population.  These disorders typically begin in late adolescence or early adulthood and are often associated with lifelong, psychological and social impairments. Smoking rates are highly elevated in these disorders; 75-85% of patients smoke, compared to approximately 20% of the general population. Individuals with psychotic disorders also have extremely low smoking-cessation rates even though they can be motivated and persistent in their attempts. The purpose of this study will be to further understand motivations for smoking and the brain mechanisms underlying tobacco craving and expectancy in patients with psychotic disorders.  By manipulating visual smoking-related cues, the effects on specific brain pathways (e.g., the reward pathway) will be examined. Given the diversity in characteristics of people with these disorders, we will also attempt to gain a better appreciation for the effects of different genes on patients' sensitivity to smoking-related cues.    Methods: Smokers (patients and controls) will be exposed to smoking and neutral videos while the researchers perform a brain scan. Activation in relevant brain regions of will be examined while varying the subjects' perceived drug availability.  Patients' experience of smoking cravings will also be assessed. Additionally, clinical assessment of patients' smoking patterns and reasons for smoking will be collected. A saliva DNA collection method will allow for analyses of the genes of interest to determine whether patients with certain genetic profiles show particular brain responses suggesting sensitivity to reward, when they are exposed to smoking videos.        The proposed study has the potential to uncover brain, genetic, and psychological explanations for the high rates of tobacco use and dependence in people with psychotic disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protection of CNS neurons by Heat Shock Proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL AND CELLULAR ANALYSES; CELL CULTURE OF CNS NEURONS; CYTOSKELETON AND AXONAL TRANSPORT; IMAGING AND CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; NEURONAL TOXICITY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease is thought to be caused by cumulative effects of beta-amyloid that can result in structures in the brain known as plaques and tangles.  The plaques often consist of beta amyloid, as well as other proteins that can include those that are increased with stress.  The tangles, also known as neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) can be made of proteins that provide integrity to the neuronal processes or axons; these include proteins such as neurofilaments and the microtubule-binding protein knonw as tau.  A group of proteins known as the Heat Shock Proteins (Hsps) are often increased in cells in response to various different stresses. One of these proteins, the small heat shock protein, Hsp27, has been shown to protect various cell types against different agents that could cause cellular damage. With respect to Alzheimer's Disease, Hsp27 has been reported to be increased in AD brains, with accumulation in plaques and tangles. Whether this is a protective response to the stress or is part of the disease process is not known. While most brain neurons do not express Hsp27, there are some selective populations that do.  Are these neurons less vulnerable to the cumulative effect of a life time of stressors?  In our experiments we can increase the expression of Hsp27 in neurons and have been able to show that this prevents neuronal death triggered by exposure to beta-amyloid.  However, we do not know how this occurs and our objectives are to understand how Hsp27 functions and how its expression might be regulated in brain neurons.

TitreApplicationTitle: Men's health promotion and workforce engagement in the context of workplace bullying
Keywords-MotsClés: GROUNDED THEORY; HEALTH PROMOTION; MEN'S HEALTH; WORK ENGAGEMENT; WORKPLACE BULLYING
Abstract-Résumé: Canada has one of the highest rates of workplace bullying in the world. Workplace bullying has negative social, health, and economic outcomes. Little is known about how workplace bullying affects men's capacity to look after their health or continue in the workforce. Employed men are essential to Canada's economy. Knowing how men promote their own well-being in situations of workplace bullying and what affects the way they work is important for sustaining a healthy workforce. In this grounded theory study, we will seek men to be interviewed individually about their workplace bullying experiences. We will examine how being bullied at work affects men's patterns of health promotion and their work. From this, we will provide a theoretical understanding of these experiences. Importantly, the findings of this research will help employers and service providers design more relevant policies and programs to address workplace bullying and support men's engagement in the workforce.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exit Strategies:  The Timing and Impacts of Physician Retirements
Keywords-MotsClés: PHYSICIAN RESOURCE POLICY; PHYSICIAN RETIREMENT PATTERNS
Abstract-Résumé: Exit Strategies - The Timing and Impacts of Physician Retirements  Much has been made over the past fifteen years about the actual or impending shortage of physicians in Canada.  The aging of the patient population increases the need, while the aging of the physician population reduces the supply.  Recent dramatic increases in the number of medical students being trained in Canada should go some distance in addressing supply concerns.  Less well-understood is the potential effect of changes in physicians' decisions about when, and how quickly, to retire.  Despite the fact that retirement decisions can have a large influence on the total available supply of physicians, surprisingly little is known about those decisions.  The purpose of this project is to fill in some of those gaps in our understanding.    This project involves a collaboration between UBC's Centre for Health Services and Policy Research, the B.C. Ministry of Health Services, four of the province's health authorities, and the Western and Northern Health Human Resources Planning Forum.  It will focus on whether retirement patterns of B.C. physicians have changed over recent decades and, if so, the implications for future physician supply; whether the financial market turmoil in 2008-09 has affected those retirement decisions or patterns; and what happens to patients of primary care physicians who retire or reduce their hours of clinical work.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a New Clinically Relevant Method for Meta-Analysis of Continuous Outcomes (Ratio of Means), and the Evaluation of the Effectiveness of Treatments in Critical Illness Using Meta-Analytic Techniques
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE KIDNEY FAILURE; ACUTE RESPIRATORY FAILURE; CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; CRITICAL ILLNESS; META-ANALYTIC TECHNIQUES; RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Meta-analysis is used to combine results from multiple randomized controlled trials to provide an overall measure of a therapy's effectiveness.  I recently developed a new method, the ratio of means (RoM), to combine continuous outcome results that may be more easily interpretable by clinicians compared to traditionally-used mean difference methods.  Using comprehensive simulation and comparison to actual data, I have shown that this new method gives comparable results to traditionally-used methods.  Other biostatisticians have suggested an alternative ratio method, involving geometric means, a measure unfamiliar to most clinicians.  Using comprehensive simulation and comparison to actual data, I plan to determine how the statistical properties of RoM compares to the ratio of geometric means.  If RoM provides comparable results, then the use of this measure may make it easier for clinicians to interpret how the meta-analytic results of continuous outcomes apply to their particular patients. This research will also use meta-analytic techniques to evaluate the effectiveness of therapies for critically-ill patients requiring life support therapies to treat either kidney failure or severe breathing failure, both of which have very high mortality.  Different methods for providing continuous forms of dialysis in kidney failure and different specialized therapies to improve oxygenation in breathing failure are used without clear guidance whether these methods improve survival.  I plan to conduct separate systematic reviews and meta-analyses in both these areas to determine the effectiveness of each of the following therapies:  high vs standard dose dialysis and type of clearance (hemodialysis vs hemofiltration) in acute kidney failure; and high frequency oscillation and inhaled nitric oxide in patients with the most severe low-oxygen breathing failure.  This will provide effectiveness data to clinicians and identify areas where further research is required.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism and modulation of spatio-temporal organization of human VF
Keywords-MotsClés: HEART FAILURE; MAPPING; VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Sudden cardiac arrest has been called the number one health problem in Canada and the United States. It is responsible for approximately 40,000 and 450,000 deaths a year, in Canada and United States respectively. It is an equally serious health problem in most developed countries of the world. A large fraction of cases of sudden cardiac arrest are caused by the arrhythmia ventricular fibrillation. As opposed to normal cardiac rhythm in which a steady, regular, organized electrical activation sequence of the ventricles leads to an organized contraction of the ventricular muscle that causes the efficient pumping of blood throughout the body, during ventricular fibrillation the cardiac electrical activation sequence is extremely rapid and much less organized, leading to tremulous, almost imperceptible, ventricular muscular contraction and the absence of blood flow. In the absence of blood flow, death quickly ensues. While heart failure is primarily considered a disease that leads to power failure and poor cardiac output, approximately half of all deaths associated with heart failure are due to sudden cardiac arrest, suggesting that the heart failure process influences ventricular fibrillation. However the mechanisms of organization of electrical waves that maintain human ventricular fibrillation have not been studied. Currently, electrical shock is the only available therapy to halt ventricular fibrillation.   The objective of the project is to perform hanging human heart mapping studies to understand the mechanisms of waveform behavior of VF that is thought to be important in the mechanism of VF. Armed with this knowledge we also plan to modulate VF by strategies of pharmacological intervention and pacing therapies that would be give us potential interventions that would treat this life threatening arrhythmia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Emergent Care and Outcomes of Acute Heart Failure in the Population
Keywords-MotsClés: EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEART FAILURE; HOSPITALIZATION; MORTALITY; OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure occurs when the pump function of the heart is weakened or when the heart becomes stiff and relaxation of the heart becomes impaired. The initial indication that heart failure is present is the occurrence of shortness of breath and "fluid in the lungs" on chest x-ray. One in every 5 adults aged 40 years or more will develop heart failure, and thus, in Canada, over 1.6 million Canadians will develop heart failure in the future. Patients with heart failure symptoms seek care in the Emergency Department (ED) from which about one-third are discharged home. However, heart failure patients who were thought to be "safe" to discharge home from the Emergency Department have a substantial risk of death. In Ontario, 6.1% of patients died within 30 days of discharge home from the Emergency Department. In addition, nearly one-fourth of heart failure patients discharged from the Emergency Department return for emergent care or are hospitalized for heart failure within 3 months after the initial ED discharge. In this grant proposal, we will develop ways to identify heart failure patients in the Emergency Department who are at high risk of death, repeated ED visits, or hospitalization. Currently, there is no way to determine if a heart failure patient should be admitted to hospital or discharged home. This study will provide much needed tools to aid decision-making about heart failure patients, and may prevent thousands of deaths and repeated hospital visits for heart failure every year. The results of this grant may improve the survival and quality of life of heart failure patients by providing ED physicians with new information on the risks of death or repeated hospital visits. Knowing who the high risk patients are will allow doctors and nurses to target their efforts to at-risk populations, who may benefit from rapid heart failure care delivery, and will lead to greater efficiency of heart failure care in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of cell adhesion factors implicated in leukemic cell survival
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER STEM CELLS; HEMATOPOIETIC MICROENVIRONMENT; RNA INTERFERENCE; STEM CELL NICHE
Abstract-Résumé: Most blood cells are made inside the marrow of long bones, arising from blood-forming stem cells. These stem cells reside in a supportive environment called the stem cell niche. There is mounting evidence that cancers of the blood cells, such as leukemias and lymphomas, tend to grow inside the bone marrow because they benefit from factors found inside the stem cell niche. It is thought that cancers begin by suberting this natural support system for their own growth, and to become more resistant to conventional anti-cancer treatments. The goal of this project is to identify which adhesion factors are particularly important for the homing and survival of cancerous cells inside the stem cell niche. Using RNA interference techniques, we plan to downregulate the expression of selected cell adhesion factors in leukemic cells, and test their impact on leukemic cell proliferation after implantation in mice. This work will potentially identify new pathways affecting cancer cell growth and survival that could eventually lead to the development of new anti-cancer treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Experience-dependent structural and functional plasticity of auditory-motor systems in the human brain
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHD; ADOLESCENCE; COGNITION; DAYTIME FUNCTIONING; DEVELOPMENT; EMOTION; GENETICS; LEARNING; MEMORY; POLYSOMNOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Both attention deficit and hyperactivity disordered (ADHD) patients and sleep-deprived healthy children display similar maladaptive behaviours and have poor performance on certain complex learning tasks. If present over long periods, these symptoms are associated with poor academic performance, poor social interactions, lower intelligence scores, more accidents, and even higher obesity rates in later life. Between 5 and 10% of otherwise healthy children and adolescents are diagnosed with ADHD, and approximately 30% suffer from insufficient sleep.  Progress in preventing, diagnosing, and effectively treating these problems is limited by insufficient knowledge of the underlying brain systems and how they change as a child matures, since most studies have been done with adults. In particular, almost nothing is known about the role of sleep in memory and learning in adolescence - a period of life characterized by growth and change in both the mind and body, and by a lifestyle that reduces sleep duration.   My research involves a large-scale study which examines the interplay between sleep and memory in healthy and ADHD-affected adolescents, and in healthy children and young adults for comparison. The effects of moderate amounts of sleep reduction over the course of three consecutive nights on memory performance will be studied, as well as the relative efficiency of post-learning sleep vs. waking periods to facilitate memory. Physiological, genetic, and performance data will be collected to answer specific questions about differences between normal and reduced sleep periods, and differences between groups within the study.  Our results will help to clarify the complex relationships between sleep and cognitive function in healthy and ADHD subjects, and will help to inform sleep-related decisions, practices, and treatments for the large number of affected young people affected by these problems. We will use these data to establish new research paths.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rare Obesity Disorders Informing Common Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION; EXTREME PHENOTYPES; GENOMIC COPY NUMBER VARIANTS; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; LIPODYSTROPHY; MORBID; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, 16% of adults and 10% of children are obese. Obesity  in children is now five times as common as it was in 1981, and  is set to replace smoking as the major cause of preventable  death. Obesity makes people more likely to get diabetes and  heart disease, and costs Canada $12.5 billion per year. A  targeted investment of health research money will pay for itself  many times over, if it makes even a small dent in obesity. Many  see it as a lifestyle disease, caused by eating too much and not  exercising enough. Though it is true that you won¿t get fat  unless you eat more calories than you burn, your genes strongly  influence appetite and calorie burning. Genes also strongly  influence who gets diabetes and heart disease. I am a doctor  who specializes in genetic diseases that affect body fat. My  group¿s work is guided by the idea that ¿extreme phenotypes¿  (e.g. severe childhood obesity and unusual disorders of fat loss)  teach us much about obesity and its diseases. Our strategy is to  seek uncommon genes and mutations that force people to gain  or lose fat. In this project we will study children with either  severe fat gain or inexplicable fat loss, to look for extra or  missing copies of whole genes. This will uncover new genes and  pathways relevant to human body weight. These pathways will  be good candidates for anti-obesity treatments, and will also  teach us about key molecular players in  obesity, diabetes and  heart disease in the general population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Histone Lysine Methylation in Medulloblastoma and Cerebellar Development
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENETICS; EPIGENETICS; HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; MEDULLOBLASTOMA; MOUSE MODELS; PEDIATRICS
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood brain cancer is the most common type of solid cancer seen in children, and the most common cause of cancer deaths in children.  Current therapies that include surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy do terrible damage to the developing brain, so that even survivors are often left with significant disabilities.  We have recently discovered that there are frequent mutations in a family of genes that control how DNA is wound up inside of cells.  These mutations are found in childhood brain cancer, but not in normal cells.  This application describes experiments to study the mutations in DNA winding genes, and to determine how we can exploit this difference betweent the cancer cells and the normal cells, in order to develop more effective, less toxic treatments for children with brain cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: BRUISE CONTROL: BRidge or continUe coumadIn for device SurgEry randomized CONTROLled Trial.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICOAGULATION; ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; DEFIBRILLATOR; HEPARIN; PACEMAKER; WARFARIN
Abstract-Résumé: Many patients requiring cardiac arrhythmia device surgery are on chronic blood thinners, usually Coumadin, to prevent stroke. The management of their blood thinners around the time of surgery presents a dilemma to physicians. Physicians usually treat these patients with a strategy known as "bridging anti-coagulation". In this strategy tablet blood thinners are discontinued for a few days before the surgery (it takes a few days for the effects of tablet blood thinners to be cleared) and the patient is bridged with injection blood thinners (Heparin). After surgery the patient is restarted on injection blood thinner for a few days while tablet blood thinner effect is building up to therapeutic levels. However there are a number of downsides to bridging anti-coagulation around device surgery. In particular there is a substantial risk of significant device pocket hematoma (large collection of blood around the device battery). Pocket hematoma in this situation is not always benign. Despite these risks the accepted standard of care in most centers is to bridge patients who are at moderate to high risk of stroke. Recently in response to these issues a number of centers have explored the option of performing device surgery without stopping tablet blood thinners. The early observational data from single centers would suggest a greatly reduced hematoma rate with this strategy. Despite these encouraging results most surgeons are reluctant to move to operating without stopping tablet blood thinners. Hence a direct head to head comparison of the two strategies at multiple centers with multiple surgeons is required. BRUISE CONTROL is a prospective, single blind, randomized, controlled trial. Patients will be randomly assigned to one of two treatment arms. In the conventional arm patents will be bridged. In the experimental arm patients will continue on tablet blood thinners. The primary outcome will be clinically significant hematoma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Patient and public involvement in defining quality of care: Engaging  citizens in clinical practice improvement
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PATIENT PARTICIPATION; PUBLIC PARTICIPATION; QUALITY INDICATORS; QUALITY OF CARE; SOCIOLOGY OF SCIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Quality of care is at the heart of health care renewal in Canada. The rise of chronic disease, with its emphasis on the active involvement of patients and communities, means that patients and the public are becoming key players in quality improvement. However, the growing call for their involvement in quality initiatives is hampered by a poor evidence base.   Knowledge tools, such as quality indicators and clinical practice guidelines, help define how practice should be organized and delivered to provide quality health care. This doctoral thesis will document how patients and the public can be most effectively involved in the development of knowledge tools used in quality improvement. We will: 1) conduct a realist review of evidence, based on existing literature and consultation with an international working group of experts; 2) conduct a cluster randomized controlled trial to assess the impact of a patient and public involvement program on the process of knowledge tool development, its validity, responsiveness to public expectations, and implementation by decision-makers.   This doctoral program is conducted under the direction of leading experts in quality of care and public involvement: Richard Grol and Jako Burgers (Scientific Institute for Quality of Healthcare, the Netherlands), and Pascale Lehoux (Universite de Montreal, my nominating institution in Canada). Empirical work will be carried in rural Quebec in close collaboration with local decision-makers, thus strengthening capacity for primary care research while laying the foundation for a clinician-researcher career of international standard. This thesis will advance the evidence that supports patient and public involvement in defining quality of care, thus fostering upstream engagement of Canadians¿ in clinical practice improvement.
