TitreApplicationTitle: Host-pathogen interactions in malaria and tuberculosis: experimental models and translation to novel adjunctive therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: INNATE IMMUNITY; MALARIA; MYCOBACTERIA; NITRIC OXIDE; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis and malaria are leading causes of disease and death around the world.  Understanding how the body fights these diseases, how they may interact, and looking for new treatments may have important implications for human health.    The first two questions we explored were:  (1) does malaria make mycobacterial (tuberculosis-like) disease worse; and (2) does a cell surface molecule called CD36 contribute to the body¿s defences against mycobacteria?  We used cells and mouse infections to model aspects of human disease.  We showed that malaria exacerbates mycobacterial infection, which may be important for people living in areas where both diseases are common who may become co-infected (manuscript submitted, J Infect Dis).  We next showed that mycobacterial infection is attenuated in CD36 deficient mice which  may explain why many people living in areas where tuberculosis is common have genetic mutations in CD36 (manuscript submitted, Am J Pathol).  We are proposing new experiments to further examine the mechanism of this finding.  Next, we are designing a clinical trial of another treatment strategy for severe malaria, inhaled nitric oxide (iNO).  We are proposing this human trial because animal studies and a human trial using the NO donor L-arginine have suggested that NO is effective against malaria, and clinical experience and numerous trials of iNO for other conditions have shown that its use is safe in humans.  We have validated a way to objectively measure malaria severity in a recently published mansucript (Lovegrove et al.,PLoS ONE, 2009), which will serve as a primary endpoint of this trial.  This program of research is multi-disciplinary and spans a wide range of techniques, all the way from bench research and animal models to direct translation to human disease with a clinical trial of an innovative adjuvant treatment for severe malaria.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigations of the Phenomenology and Neurobiology of the Negative Symptoms of Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANHEDONIA; APATHY; FMRI; FUNCTIONAL OUTCOME; MOTIVATION; NEGATIVE SYMPTOMS; PHENOMENOLOGY; PLEASURE; SCHIZOPHRENIA; VIRTUAL REALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is an illness that affects approximately 1% of the population, and is accompanied by profound functional impairment and enormous emotional and financial costs. The symptoms of this illness are commonly thought of in separate categories, including Positive (hallucinations and delusions), Cognitive (memory, attention, and planning problems), and Negative symptoms (including decreased facial expressions, reduced speech, difficulty in experiencing pleasure, and a lack of motivation). Despite advances in treatment, particularly for positive symptoms, recovery of functioning in those with schizophrenia remains elusive. There has been a lack of effective methods for the treatment of negative symptoms despite research suggesting that these symptoms have a substantial impact on functioning in schizophrenia. The research program being undertaken aims to advance understanding of the core components of negative symptoms in schizophrenia, and to guide the development of effective treatments. We have already begun a long-term study of negative symptoms, which for the first time looks specifically at both motivation and pleasure and their impact on functioning in schizophrenia over the course of one year. Initial results from this work indicate that lack of motivation is the critical link to functioning, while this is not the case with other symptoms, including the experience of pleasure. Based on this work, we have also begun the development a novel test of motivation with direct relevance to the everyday lives of individuals with schizophrenia, using virtual reality technology. This unique and innovative method will be combined with functional brain imaging to explore the neurobiology of motivational problems in schizophrenia, which will ultimately guide the development of new strategies for treatment of schizophrenia and the promotion of functional recovery.

OrgNm: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (Toronto)/Centre de toxicomanie et de santé mentale
TitreApplicationTitle: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) to Evaluate the Role of Clozapine Potentiation of GABA in the Treatment of Schizophrenia.
Keywords-MotsClés: GABA; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PHARMACOLOGY; RECEPTOR; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a serious and prevalent mental illness that affects approximately 1% of Canadians and is characterized by a number of symptoms, such as disorganization, unusual beliefs and poor cognitive functioning. The brain mechanisms that lead to schizophrenia are poorly understood; however, recent studies suggest that impaired brain inhibition may be involved in the development of psychotic symptoms in schizophrenia.  Inhibition refers to a brain process that filters out excessive information in the environment, so that information can be processed effectively.  Clozapine - one of the most effective medications used to treat schizophrenia - has also been related to brain inhibition. Our recent studies using transcranial magnetic stimulation have shown that clozapine results in a significant increase in brain inhibition when compared to other antipsychotic medications. This increase in brain inhibition is also accompanied by neurophysiological changes which suggest that GABAB - a specific brain receptor - is increased. Our preliminary molecular experiments also suggest that clozapine enhances brain inhibition by acting directly on the GABAB receptor.  In this proposal, we intend to further our understanding of this promising data through experiments that will investigate the effects of clozapine on brain inhibition, as compared to other antipsychotic medication, in brain regions that are most affected in this disorder. We will also investigate the genetic basis of this response. These studies may ultimately help us to better understand the brain mechanisms involved in schizophrenia, as well as potentially provide new pathways through which future medications may be developed to treat this devastating disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic determinants of left ventricular outflow tract obstruction
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYSIS OF STRUCTURAL GENOMIC VARIATION; ANIMAL MODELS OF CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; CANDIDATE GENE MUTATION SCREENING; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; GENOTYPE-PHENOTYPE CORRELATIONS; RESEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Congenital heart disease is the most common birth malformation and occurs in 1 of every 100 newborns. A very large share of the burden of congenital heart disease is caused by blockages of the outflow from the left heart. This part of the heart is crucial to the perfusion of the body. It has now become clear that genetic factors largely influence the development of this group of diseases.  We have now carried out studies which pinpoint several regions of the human genome as culprits in these diseases. Several approaches led to these findings: first, we have established a large database with families in whom several members are affected; second, we have access to the French-Canadian founder population; third, we have screened the genome at very high resolution for several types of genetic variation that is linked to those diseases.  We propose to extend the current cohort in order to confirm our current findings, and to study in detail the most promising regions and types of variation of the human genome that are linked to disease. These studies will reveal why children are born with heart malformations, and hold the promise to allow more targeted therapies and the prevention of complications from these diseases in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: A mixed methods inquiry into multi-level factors that influence immigrant women's postpartum health and access to primary health care services
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMIGRANT HEALTH; MIXED METHODS; PERINATAL HEALTH; POPULATION HEALTH; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Immigrant women in Canada face unique health challenges that differ from women born in Canada.  Some of these challenges, such as language and cultural differences, are apparent.  However, less obvious are obstacles that many immigrant women experience such as lower income and education, lack of social support, and difficulty accessing health services.  Immigrant women are particularly vulnerable during the times surrounding pregnancy, both during the pregnancy and the postpartum period after giving birth.   My PhD research seeks to understand the factors influencing Canadian immigrant women's postpartum health and access to primary health care services.  I will compare the health of immigrant and Canadian-born women at three time points during the first year after birth.  I will also look specifically at postpartum depression (PPD) and attempt to identify factors to understand who is more likely to get PPD and if there is a relationship between PPD and the neighbourhood in which the women live.  Finally, I will investigate women's perceptions about their own health as well as their thoughts on their ability to access the primary health care services needed. This study will address knowledge gaps related to how various factors interact to influence immigrant women's postpartum health. Poorer postpartum health and increased risk for PPD in immigrant women has implications for a woman's health, but also that of her partner, children, and community. To develop healthy public policy and address issues such as equity and access to services, it is important to better understand the factors that contribute to differences in health, as well as those that influence immigrant women's ability to access necessary services. My research will inform decision-makers and service providers in the planning of effective health and social services to meet the needs of diverse communities, and ultimately help enhance the health of a growing population of immigrant women in Canada.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CELL CULTURE; CELL PROLIFERATION; DYSGLYCEMIA; EPITHELIAL OVARIAN CANCER; GLUCOSE TRANSPORT; METABOLISM; RODENT MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Metabolic disorders associated with obesity are a growing problem in Canada. In particular, states of high blood sugar such as type 2 diabetes affect a large proportion of the population. Recent research has shown that cancer cells require greater amounts of blood glucose to fuel their activities than normal cells, which suggests that if there is increased glucose available, tumours may be able to grow more rapidly. High blood sugar is also known to stimulate the growth of new blood vessels, which are essential in a growing tumour to provide nutrients and remove waste.  Ovarian cancer is the most lethal cancer of the female reproductive tract and is known as a "disease that whispers" because of its vague symptoms. Due to the fact that there are no reliable screening tools, the disease is usually not detected until an advanced stage where treatment is often ineffective. We plan to investigate whether ovarian cancers grow more aggressively in animals that have high blood sugar compared to normal animals. There are a number of glucose-lowering drugs that are used to treat diabetes, and we plan to use these to see whether ovarian tumour growth can be slowed down or reversed if glucose levels are returned to normal. We believe that starving tumours of an energy supply as well as a blood supply will significantly reduce ovarian cancer growth and increase the length and quality of life of those suffering from this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sous-types neuropsychologiques du trouble déficitaire de l'attention / hyperactivité: Existe-t-il une association entre les déficits cognitifs et les symptômes comportementaux du TDAH?
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION; COGNITION; DEVELOPPEMENT DE L'ENFANT; FONCTIONS EXECUTIVES; MOTIVATION; MEMOIRE DE TRAVAIL; NEUROPSYCHOLOGIE; SANTE MENTALE; SYMPTOMES COMPORTEMENTAUX; TROUBLE DEFICITAIRE DE L'ATTENTION/HYPERACTIVITE (TDAH)
Abstract-Résumé: Le projet de these doctorale propose vise a demontrer l'existence de profils neuropsychologiques distincts chez les enfants presentant un trouble deficitaire de l'attention/hyperactivite (TDAH) et a verifier si ces profils sont associes a des symptomes comportementaux specifiques. Dans les dernieres annees, certains auteurs se sont interesses aux deficits cognitifs presents dans le TDAH et en viennent a la conclusion que ces deficits sont tres variables d'un enfant a l'autre, appuyant ainsi la pertinence d'etablir des clusters neuropsychologiques. Toutefois, lorsque les sous-types de TDAH retrouves dans le DSM-IV-TR et etablis a partir de manifestations comportementales (predominance inattentive, predominance hyperactive/impulsive et type combine) sont correles avec les deficits cognitifs, aucune relation n'en ressort. Comme second objectif, ce projet vise donc a verifier si les profils cognitifs seront associes avec des symptomes specifiques plutot que des syndromes generaux du TDAH (agitation motrice, couper la parole, etc.). A cette fin, 60 enfants avec TDAH seront evalues sur la presence de troubles cognitifs, de symptomes comportementaux et de traits pathologiques co-morbides et compares avec un groupe d'enfants sans TDAH. Des analyses statistiques permettront de statuer sur la presence de deficits cognitifs, sur l'association entre ces deficits et les symptomes comportementaux, et sur la contribution de chacune des variables cognitives aux symptomes comportementaux. Ce projet vise donc l'amelioration du diagnostic de TDAH en permettant de baser ce dernier sur des elements cognitifs et comportementaux. De plus, il permettra une meilleure comprehension des relations entre les deficits cognitifs et l'apparition des symptomes comportementaux, permettant ainsi une meilleure prise en charge de cette pathologie.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the development of endotoxin tolerance in sepsis.
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNOSUPRESSION; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; INFLAMMATION; SEPSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The innate immune response is the first line of defense against microorganisms. However, if this response is highly stimulated, it can result in excessive inflammation that can lead to organ injury and high mortality. Sepsis, often caused by bacterial infection in the bloodstream, is an example of the consequences of uncontrolled inflammation. In the United States, sepsis is the leading cause of death in critically ill patients with more than 200,000 fatalities annually. Sepsis can be initiated by bacteria or bacterial products such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Initially, septic patients exhibit a pronounced and vigorous innate immune response, but eventually, this shifts towards an immunosuppressive state. This state is related with a phenomenon called endotoxin tolerance, which is basically the reduced or null capacity of the immune cells to respond to bacterial products, after they have been in previous contact with these products. The purpose of endotoxin tolerance may be to reduce the immune response and lessen the consequences of excessive inflammation, although this may also increase the risk of subsequent infections and death. Therefore, the main aim of this project is to explore the development of endotoxin tolerance during sepsis, and to analyze how this may increase fatality. Studying cells from patients with human sepsis during the different stages of the syndrome, will allow me to see changes in the immune response, and to find possible markers of endotoxin tolerance that can be correlated with mortality. In the long term, the potential blockage of these markers in septic patients undergoing an endotoxin tolerance stage, could lead to improvements in their clinical outcome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of monocyte-macrophage differentiation and activation in radiation-induced fibrosis of breast cancer patients
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CYTOKINE ARRAYS; ELISAS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; MACROPHAGE POLARIZATION; MONOCYTE DIFFERENTIATION; QUANTITATIVE REAL-TIME PCR; RADIATION TOXICITY; SKIN FIBROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Globally, 1.3 million women are diagnosed with breast cancer each year.  Radiation therapy is standard treatment for many of these women as it significantly improves survival and decreases chances of relapse.  One of the most common side effects of radiation therapy, however, is skin fibrosis, a condition characterized by hardening of normal tissue affected by radiation.  Approximately half of all breast cancer patients receiving radiation treatment will develop skin fibrosis.  This condition causes discomfort, pain, and changes in breast shape and/or volume.  At the site of radiation, irradiated normal tissue adjacent to the tumour will send wound signals to recruit a number of other cells in the body to help repair any injury incurred.  In patients with skin fibrosis, the wound signals are irregular and the repair process is heightened, causing accumulating tissue masses which harden.  Monocytes are immune cells which exist in the blood and are recruited to the radiation area.  Monocytes change into macrophages at the irradiated site and macrophages are the cells that work to continue the abnormal repair process.  My project aims to understand how the monocytes and macrophages are functioning in breast cancer patients with radiation-induced skin fibrosis.  We will also resolve the differences in the monocytes/macrophages between patients who develop skin fibrosis with radiation and ones that do not.  Our goal is to be able to predict which breast cancer patients needing radiation therapy will develop skin fibrosis before or early in the course of treatment so that clinicians can better manage this major side effect.  Ultimately, our research project will improve the quality of life of the large number of breast cancer patients receiving radiation therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancing HIV/AIDS service organizations' capacity to engage in community-based research to address social and health inequities
Keywords-MotsClés: CAPACITY BUILDING; COMMUNITY ORGANIZATIONS; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HIV/AIDS; PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH; SOCIAL INEQUALITIES
Abstract-Résumé: Canada's strategy to fight HIV/AIDS, "Leading Together", identifies priority actions to improve social factors that affect health: poverty, gender, disability, and discrimination. Community-based research (CBR) methods involve collaboration between university researchers, community partners, and the people affected by the research, and are well suited to study the effects of social factors on health. More and more, funding bodies and governments are requiring a CBR approach. Community organizations are demanding to play a more active role in research. The results obtained through CBR identify ways to improve services, help strengthen funding applications, and help make programs more sustainable. However, community organizations face challenges to participate in CBR: tight time constraints, high staff turnover, and limited resources and funding. The applicant will study what helps HIV/AIDS service organizations to conduct CBR, and what prevents them from doing so. She will determine how best to enhance their capacity for research, and study the potential impact this would have on addressing the social factors that affect health. She will explore the potential role that a national organization, the Canadian AIDS Society, could play in enhancing HIV/AIDS organizations' capacity for CBR. Research Questions: 1. What helps HIV/AIDS service organizations to engage in CBR, and what hinders them? Is there a role for a national organization to play in making it easier for HIV/AIDS service organizations to conduct CBR? 2. What are the potential impacts of enhancing CBR for addressing the social factors that make communities more vulnerable to HIV/AIDS? What forms of CBR are best suited to achieve this? Enhancing HIV/AIDS service organizations' capacity to engage in forms of CBR that are best suited to address the social factors that affect health would lead to better community services, and ultimately to reduced social and health factors that drive the HIV/AIDS epidemic.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Cedar Project: Exploring resiliency and its influence on HIV  vulnerability among young Aboriginal people who use drugs in  two Canadian cities.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; COHORT STUDY; GENDER; HIV/AIDS; INJECTION DRUG USE; PUBLIC HEALTH; RESILIENCE; TRAUMA; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS; YOUTH HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The increasing rates of HIV among young Aboriginal people in BC are deeply concerning. Few studies have  investigated the role that historical trauma plays in HIV vulnerability of young Aboriginal people who use drugs. A  holistic resiliency approach is a critical component of re-building healthy families and communities that have been  heavily impacted by the effects of colonization, including multigenerational trauma. It is unknown how Aboriginal  young people who use drugs define resilience for themselves. The Cedar project is a cohort study of Aboriginal young  people who use drugs in 2 Canadian cities. The proposed study will utilize mixed methods to investigate the impact  of resiliency on HIV vulnerability among Aboriginal young people who use drugs. Through quantitative and qualitative  inquiry the influence of structural factors, age, gender and trauma on young peoples perceptions of resilience will be  explored. It is hypothesized that structural factors, trauma, resiliency, age and gender are significant determinants of  HIV vulnerability for Aboriginal young people. Through ethnographic interviews of Cedar Project participants the  relationship between protective-resiliency and risk factors for HIV will be investigated. The proposed study aims to  provide recommendations for fostering resiliency and preventing HIV vulnerability among Aboriginal young people  who use drugs.

Abstract-Résumé: There is evidence that certain types of physical activity cause hip osteoarthritis (OA). OA occurs when the cartilage (the gristle that lines the ends of the bone) is damaged. OA is the most common form of hip arthritis and responsible for more than 90% of hip replacements (more than 21,000 hip replacements are done per year in Canada). Recently, subtle deformities of the hip have been linked to hip OA. It is believed that certain types of physical activity such as hockey, soccer and bicycling combine with the deformity to cause hip damage.   The goal of this CIHR team is to show how physical activity while interacting with one or more subtle deformities can cause cartilage damage and eventually OA. We will determine the frequency of the deformities in the population, compare the frequency in groups thought to have a lower frequency (Chinese) or higher frequency (Aboriginal Peoples) of OA compared to Caucasians and see if physical activity over one's lifetime is important in causing hip pain and eventually hip OA.    In addition, we will: 1) See how the physical motion and the deformity combine to damage cartilage using Canada's only magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machine that allows testing with the person standing up and with movement; 2) Use new techniques that show changes in the cartilage even though it is normal on a regular MRI; and, 3) Get the results out to Canadians better than has ever been done before.  These questions will be addressed by a collaborative team of researchers from four medical specialties (orthopaedics, rheumatology, physiotherapy, radiology), six research disciplines (basic and clinical sciences, population health, epidemiology, biostatistics, health services research and knowledge translation), as well as stakeholders from the arthritis community. This research program will generate the new knowledge needed for major breakthroughs in the prevention, detection and treatment of hip OA.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Physical Activity, Mobility and Neural Health
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTONOMIC NERVOUS SYSTEM; CARDIOVASCULAR CONTROL; CORTEX; CORTICAL NETWORKS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HEAT SHOCK PROTEINS; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MICRONEUROGRAPHY; MOTOR CONTROL; MOTOR NEURON; NERVE BLOOD FLOW; NEURAL PROPERTIES; NEUROPROTECTION; ULTRASOUND IMAGING; VASCULAR DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to move freely (mobility) depends on the coordinated activity of muscles and bones. In turn, muscles and bones require a healthy system of blood vessels (the cardiovascular system) to deliver blood and remove metabolic waste.  However, no muscle can move without nerves from the brain to cause them to contract with coordinated purpose. Also, nerve pathways originating in muscle and joints are required to communicate information to the brain about how the muscles and limbs are moving.  In turn, as with muscle, nerves do not function without adequate blood supply. Furthermore, the blood vessels within nerves are regulated by the very nerves to which they supply blood flow.  So, what happens to nerves and their ability to affect mobility when the blood vessels supplying these nerves become diseased?  This project will examine the role of vascular disease on blood supply to, as well as the structure and function of, nerves in the brain, spinal cord and the periphery related to the control of muscular movement and cardiovascular control. Finally, just how exercise that reduces vascular disease also improves neural vascularization and function will be examined. Both human and rodent models of disease, incorporating exercise interventions, will be performed by specialists in the fields of Physiology, Neuroscience, Cardiology, Family Medicine and, Rehabilitation. Mechanistic details about how vascular disease affects the properties and plasticity of nerves will be examined. This information will be delivered to, and studied in, patients with coronary artery disease in a program that links researchers, exercise specialists and medical practitioners in community-based health programs.

Abstract-Résumé: The objective of our research team is to study physical activity and health-related fitness to improve breast cancer survivorship from the time of diagnosis and for the balance of life. We propose to achieve this objective by establishing a large cohort of breast cancer survivors with a comprehensive assessment of subjective and objective measures of physical activity and health-related fitness (e.g., physical fitness, physical functioning, body composition). This cohort will allow us to address important questions related to physical activity and health-related fitness including: (a) examining associations with important outcomes such as disease outcomes, symptoms, late effects, psychosocial outcomes, and quality of life, (b) examining determinants such as medical, social cognitive, and environmental, and (c) examining mechanisms and moderators of observed associations. These data will help inform strategies to promote physical activity and health-related fitness to improve breast cancer survivorship.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Linking Exercise, Physical Activity and Pathophysiology in Childhood Arthritis: A Canadian Collaborative Team.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; EXERCISE/PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; JUVENILE IDIOPATHIC ARTHRITIS; OUTCOMES; PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) afflicts approximately 10,000 children and youth, causing pain, disability and long-term joint and bone damage. JIA often results in poor physical function and reduced quality of life into adulthood, and imposes a large burden on affected children, their families and the health care system. Emerging evidence suggests that increased levels of physical activity might favourably influence the outcomes of children with JIA although it is also evident that these children are less physically active than their healthy peers, or indeed others with chronic disease. Our research program aims to uncover the factors, specific to children with JIA, that affect their ability to participate in physical activities and the barriers to such participation.  We will also determine how varying levels of physical activity affect the inflammation of arthritis, and also its effects on the developing bones and muscles, of children with JIA.  Finally, we will study the effects of two different 'novel' physical activity programs on these same outcomes in children with JIA.  Our research team is uniquely positioned to conduct this important research, using a cross-Canadian approach, and involving expert researchers in bone health in childhood.  We will also use state-of-the-art techniques to examine developing bone and muscle structure and new methods to accurately measure physical activity.  The major aim of our research program is to develop new evidence that will support the need for, and promotion of, increased levels of physical activity in children with JIA with the ultimate objective of improving their overall health and well-being.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing disease burden and health inequalities arising from chronic dental disease among Indigenous children: an early childhood caries intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; DENTAL SYSTEMS NAVIGATION; EARLY CHILDHOOD CARIES; ORAL HEALTH LITERACY; ORAL HEALTH PROMOTION; PREGNANT WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Profound disparities in early childhood caries (ECC) exist between Indigenous and non-Indigenous children in Australia, New Zealand and Canada. If the burden of ECC and associated oral health inequalities experienced by Indigenous children in these nations are to be reduced, more needs to be done to ensure that information about achieving and maintaining optimal oral health reaches those who are caring for such children in the early life stages. This will be an interventional study, with all participants receiving the intervention benefits. Pregnant Indigenous women residing in the three countries, and their families, will be included. The intervention will be implemented from birth and continue for the first three years of a participating child's life. It will be tailored at the individual- or family-level, with each carer or family progressing to the next level only when they are ready. The intervention will be based on a range of contexts including oral health promotion, oral health protection, dental disease prevention, oral health care and maintenance, dental systems navigation and oral health literacy. Developing a functional, context-specific ECC intervention that aims to improve child oral health, in full partnership with the Indigenous communities involved, may  provide useful evidence in the policy-making arena to lead to more appropriate oral health and oral health promotion program initiatives for Indigenous child groups.

TitreApplicationTitle: Educating for equity: Exploring how health professional education  can reduce disparities in chronic disease care and improve  outcomes for Indigenous populations.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; HEALTH OUTCOMES MEASUREMENT; INDIGENOUS HEALTH; MEDICAL EDUCATION INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Indigenous people in Canada, Australia and New Zealand  experience a greater burden of chronic diseases such as  diabetes, heart disease and mental illness than non-Indigenous  people. This is partly due to differences in access to health care  and in the standard of care received. Indigenous patients tend to  receive poorer quality health care than non-Indigenous people,  which is partly due to health professionals¿ clinical decision  making, communication and engagement with patients and  families. One way to address these factors is through education  of current and future health professionals, yet there is currently  little known about how educational approaches influence these  ¿health professional factors¿ or what approaches work best.  This project is about comparing, building and sharing  experiences and approaches to Indigenous health teaching and  learning in the area of chronic disease. It begins by describing  existing educational approaches and the contexts in which the  study is being undertaken. Indigenous health curriculum  developers will be interviewed to identify the specific  approaches used and the reasons underlying their use. We will  conduct focus groups with learners, educators, patients and  other stakeholders (e.g. non-Indigenous colleagues) to study  the impact of different educational approaches. This will result  in development of an Indigenous chronic disease education  ¿toolkit¿ and methods to evaluate the effectiveness of  educational approaches. A major focus of the project will be on  ensuring that the lessons from the project are translated into  practice. The research will make a substantial and enduring  contribution to improving the quality of health care for  Indigenous people with chronic disease and thus health  outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of HIV infection and antiretroviral therapy on mucosal and systemic memory CD4 T cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CD4 MEMORY CELLS; HIV/AIDS; MICROBIAL TRANSLOCATION; MUCOSAL IMMUNITY; PRIMARY HIV INFECTION; T CELL ACTIVATION
Abstract-Résumé: Despite major improvements in the treatments of HIV infected individuals, the mechanisms that contribute to AIDS development is not fully understood. It is important to understand how HIV attacks the immune system both in the circulating blood and at the primary site of viral replication, the mucosal rectum. Recently, it has been shown that the cells that fight HIV (immune memory CD4 T cells) express mucosa marker called alpha4beta7 that can be preferentially infected and killed by HIV. These memory alpha4beta7 CD4 T cells have a very important role in mucosa protection. It has been hypothesized that the loss of these cells may facilitate the microbes present in the stools that inflame and activate a large number of the body's immune cells, leading to a rapid progression to AIDS. The following proposal will measure how memory alpha4beta7 CD4 T immune cells change over time in both blood and mucosa tissue. We will do this by obtaining a small piece of the rectum using a non-invasive method. We will assess the effect of HIV on these cells and their potential reconstitutions while patient undergo treatment for their infection. We will also compare the changes of these memory alpha4beta7 CD4 T immune cells in relation with factors associated with fast progression to AIDS such as inflammation, viral load, CD4 cells decay, and neurological testing changes. To address these important questions, we plan to expand the well established Montreal primary HIV cohort throughout many hospitals and private medical clinics across Canada. We will collect clinical, socio-demographic, neurocognitive and behavioural data, which will be analyzed in association with study immunological findings. Collectively, new data generated will allow the expansion of how HIV attacks the immune system and will contribute to the development of new therapeutic HIV vaccines.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; CANCER GENOMICS; CHILDHOOD LEUKEMIA; DISEASE ETIOLOGY; ETHICAL AND SOCIAL ISSUES; EXOME AND TRANSCRIPTOME SEQUENCING; FUNCTIONAL VALIDATION; GENE-EXPRESSION ANALYSIS; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; GWAS; HIGH-THROUGHPUT RNAI; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; TREATMENT RESPONSES
Abstract-Résumé: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common cancer in children but the underlying causes of this disease remain poorly understood. The development of new genomics tools and the availability of a unique and well-characterized cohort of French-Canadian ALL patients now allow us to simultaneously detect common and rare genetic changes as well as tumor-specific mutations and novel inherited variants. We propose to examine whole-genome (all the genes) sequence variation from a sample of childhood leukemia patients with the following aims : 1) to identify novel sequence and structural variants in childhood ALL genomes; 2) to explore changes in gene expression associated with ALL by examining the transcriptome and allelic expression; 3) to assess the impact of selected genes on disease susceptibility and disease outcomes and  investigate the functional significance of these genes in vitro; and 4) to translate our genetic discoveries into appropriate health care policy and services. These findings will ultimately lead to the development of powerful research and clinical tools that could improve detection, diagnosis and treatment of childhood leukemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Terry Fox New Frontiers Program Project in ultrasound for Cancer Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL DEATH; QUANTITATIVE ULTRASOUND; ULTRASOUND THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: We are proposing to develop and enhance the use of ultrasound techniques to improve cancer treatment. We will continue developing quantitative ultrasound methods to detect and track the progression of the effects of cancer therapies on cell death. In addition, we will develop novel ultrasound-based therapies in order to improve current conventional cancer treatments. The ultimate goal is to apply both aims integrated clinically at the end of the proposed research period, with clinical evaluations of enhanced imaging and cancer treatment derived from these research objectives.  There are four integrated complementary projects proposed that arecritical to bringing these technologies to the clinic. The first will see the continued development of quantitative ultrasound methods for the detection of tumour responses to cancer therapies at high and low frequency, for preclinical and clinical applications, respectively. The second will focus on correlative analyses with quantitative ultrasound approaches and will focus on correlating dynamic contrast enhanced MRI tumour data, and whole mount three-dimensional histopathological data, with the ultrasound data. The third project will be centered about evaluating quantitative ultrasound data from patients receiving cancer therapy using established methods in quantitative ultrasound and be guided by ongoing developments from the first two projects. The last project will further develop recent innovations in using ultrasound as an enhancing agent for cancer therapy based on our discovery of bubble enhanced ultrasound potentiation of tumor response.  The overarching goal is to use our ultrasound methods to detect tumour responses to therapy. If a therapy is detected early on to be ineffective such methods could be used to guide changes from ineffective therapies to more efficacious ones. Such therapies can include chemotherapy, radiation therapy or new therapies including those to be developed as part of this application.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Terry Fox New Frontiers Program Project in genomics of forme fruste tumours: new vistas on cancer biology and management
Keywords-MotsClés: NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; PATHOGNOMONIC MUTATIONS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; UNUSUAL CANCERS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a complex and challenging disease to study, partly because many common cancers are not defined by a single driving event.  Rather, a constellation of many different genetic changes can occur in these cancers, only some of which will be present in any particular patient. It follows that common cancers are extremely heterogeneous, both molecularly and clinically. The situation is very different in many rarer tumours which often share a single, identical defect that translates into uniform clinical presentation and prognosis. We call such cancers forme fruste tumours. Identification of the defects responsible for rare tumours is beneficial for affected patients, but also, the study of rare tumours has historically led to insights into basic biology which has advanced cancer research overall. In this project, we will take study a series of 12 forme fruste tumours that lack effective diagnostics and treatments with the aim of understanding both these diseases and cancer in general. In our first project, we will use new DNA sequencing technology to analyse the entire suite of expressed genes in these tumours with the hope of identifying the genetic changes that are the root cause of their cancerous behaviour. Our second project will exploit new advances in microfluidics to enable genomic analysis of very small amounts of sample and single cells; the technology developed as part of this sub-project will be applied to all other projects. Our final three projects will use new DNA sequencing technology to explore the role of the novel biologic concepts of RNA editing and asymmetrical cell division in cancers. Our last project will study the functional consequences of the discovered mutations in order to better understand their potential as either direct or indirect therapeutic targets. This work will lead to direct improvements in diagnosis and ultimately the treatment for Canadians who have rare cancers and provide insights into the biology of common cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modelling Translation Inhibition as Cancer Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPY; EIF4A; EIF4E; MOUSE MODELS; MTOR SIGNALLING; RAPAMYCIN; RNAI INHIBITION; TRANSLATION INITIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Recent large scale analyses of mutations in human cancers have revealed that cancer cells exhibit on average approximately 60 to 90 mutations per tumor, with most of these occurring in genes implicated in a limited set of key regulatory celullar pathways. These results indicate that strategies targeting genetic mutations in human cancers are not probably not the way to develop broad acting chemotherapeutic compounds. However, because most of the mutations in human tumors occur in genes that reside in a small number of cellular processes, a better strategy is to develop drugs that inhibit cellular processes that occur downstream of the cancer causing lesions. We know that one such pathway is the regulation of protein synthesis (called translation), a process that is deregulated in many human cancers and which supports the higher growth rate of tumor cells.  This therefore provides a therapeutic opportunity in which we can attempt to  specifically turn down the rate of protein synthesis in transformed cells and hence interfere with tumor growth.  In the current proposal, we  propose to experimentally test this hypothesis by generating mouse cancer models in which we can specifically and reversibly interfere with the process of protein synthesis. These new cancer mouse models will allow us not only to assess the consequences of interfering with translation at the cellular level, but also in the tumor as the cancer cells divide in  the mouse. Specifically, we will use a lymphoma cancer model were we can easily monitor if we cause tumor regression or growth inhibition. This proposal takes advantage of novel technology developed to shut down any gene desired in the mouse in an inducible and reversible manner. We expect that our experiments will identify a key vulnerability in cancer cells that will inform us as to the direction to proceed in developing novel molecular-targetted chemotherapeutics

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of spasticity after spinal cord injury and cerebral palsy
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL PALSY; MOTONEURONS; PERSISTENT INWARD CURRENTS; SENSORY INPUTS; SPASTICITY; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: The main goal of this research is to understand the neuronal mechanisms that mediate the development of spasticity and motor dysfunction after spinal cord injury and cerebral palsy. We examine how neurons and neuronal circuits in an injured nervous system adapt to produce the uncontrolled and unwanted muscle contractions that affect the majority of patients with spinal cord injury and cerebral palsy. One of the neurons that we study is the motoneuron that excites the muscles of the limbs to produce movement. Previously, we have shown that after spinal cord injury, the excessive and uncontrolled activity of motoneurons during muscle spasms is mediated, in large part, by the activation of voltage-dependent persistent inward currents (PICs) in the human motoneuron. In human patients we have used dual motor unit recording techniques to estimate the contribution of PIC activation in the motoneuron.  In this proposal, we study why motoneurons recover PICs and self-sustained activity after chronic spinal cord injury. Because PICs require the presence of the monoamines serotonin (5HT) and norepinephrine (NE) to activate, and these monoamines are greatly reduced after injury, we examine if PICs recover because the 5HT receptors become spontaneously active without the need for 5HT to bind to the receptor. We also examine how manipulation of the NE system in patients with spinal cord injury affects PIC activation and muscle spasms. Finally, we examine in patients with cerebral palsy if spasticity is produced by augmented activation of the motoneuron by PICs, involuntary descending inputs and/or sensory inputs. These research results will pave the way to develop new pharmacological and rehabilitative therapies to both control spasticity after spinal cord injury and cerebral palsy and augment residual motor movements in these patient groups.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural composition and regulation of neuronal gap junctions in the CNS
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALLING; CONNEXINS; ELECTRICAL SYNAPSES; GAP JUNCTIONS; NEURONS; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: James Nagy, physiology, is working to understand how electrical synapses in the brain contribute to normal central nervous system (CNS) function and to the development of CNS disease. Neuroscientists have identified numerous chemical messengers that nerve cells in the brain employ to communicate with each other. But recent research by Nagy and others indicates that electrical synapses are present in the central nervous system and Nagy¹s group is pioneering the idea that these types of synapses may be as important a means of communication as chemical transmission. Nagy¹s team is focusing on this mode of intercellular information transfer that occurs by direct contact between the cells at what are called gap junctions. Gap junctions form electrical synapses and mediate electrical transmissions between neurons. Nagy is working to understand the types and locations of neurons that form gap junctions, to identify the members of the gap junction forming connexin proteins that are produced in neurons, to identity proteins that as associated with electrical synapses, and to determine how these proteins regulate and contribute to the functions of electrical synapses. To achieve this, Nagy's group will use state-of-the-art imaging equipment allowing rapid and efficient visualization and mapping of gap junctions throughout the brain. In addition, he will use biochemical approaches, cell culture model systems and various drugs to manipulate gap junction associated proteins, and thereby discern how these proteins govern the operations of electrical synapses. This work is expected to open up entirely new possibilities for considering ways in which inappropriate or abnormal cell-cell communication in brain may contribute to various CNS diseases such as Parkinson¹s disease, schizophrenia, depression and epilepsy.

TitreApplicationTitle: NMR Structures and Dynamics of Cardiac Muscle Proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOTONIC DRUGS; CARDIOVASCULAR; MECHANISM; MUSCLE BIOLOGY; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; PROTEIN DYNAMICS; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is the leading cause of death of men and women in Canada, and results in the highest economic burden to our health care system. While death rates from heart disease in Canada have fallen over the last 10 years, the good news is offset by the fact that heart disease is affecting more women, and becoming more prevalent as a complication of diabetes and obesity. The role of the cardiac muscle proteins in heart disease is being recognized as clinical evidence indicates a strong correlation between many cardiac dysfunctions and altered myofilament protein structures. For example, mutations of myofilament proteins have been associated with familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; one of the most frequently occurring inherited disease that often cause sudden cardiac death in young healthy athletes. This proposal is focused on the elucidation of the detailed mechanism of the regulation of cardiac muscle contraction. Only then can we truly understand how cardiac muscle works. We use high resolution NMR spectroscopy to determine the three dimensional structures of the calcium regulatory proteins, to delineate their interactions with other proteins as well as cardiotonic drugs, and to evaluate the effects of mutations on their structure. The outcome of this research is a detailed understanding at a molecular level, which can then be exploited to rationally design and develop possible therapeutic intervention strategies and advanced diagnostics for the treatment of heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Neuronal Encoding of Self-Motion
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTATIONAL MODELS; MOTOR CONTROL; MOTOR LEARNING; SINGLE UNIT RECORDING; VESTIBULAR; VOLUNTARY BEHAVIOUR
Abstract-Résumé: The vestibular system functions to detect the motion of the head-in-space. Head velocity is detected by vestibular hair cells that are located within the semicircular canals of the inner ear labyrinth. The vestibular nerve projects from the labyrinth directly to the vestibular nuclei of the brainstem. Bilateral loss of labyrinthine functional causes 1) the visual world to move on the retina with head movements, 2) an inability to keep the head/body erect during common activities, and 3) an inability to perform tasks that require spatial orientation such as determining the direction of body motion or navigating through space in the absence of visual cues. My research addresses how the vestibular information is processed by the brain during our normal daily activities. The results of the proposed research will further increase our understanding of how the brain modulates vestibular reflex pathways during common voluntary behaviours. This information, in turn, will lead to a better understanding of disorders that affect patients who suffer from disorientation,vertigo, dizziness, and motion (and space) sickness. Patients with such symptoms are extremely common, however to date the fundamental causes of these disorders are not well understood.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Structure and Function of Molybdoenzymes.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOENERGETICS; ELECTRON PARAMGNETIC RESONANCE; ELECTRON TRANSPORT PROTEINS; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; MOLYBDOENZYMES
Abstract-Résumé: Bacteria, plants and animals require molybdenum as an essential nutrient. It is found in trace amounts in food, is taken up by our cells, and is incorporated into enzymes critical for human health. For it to be incorporated into enzymes, it must be combined with a complicated chemical compound to form what is called molybdenum cofactor. There are two critical molybdenum enzymes that impact human health: these are sulfite oxidase and xanthine oxidase. Sulfite oxidase is required for normal brain development and children born with a genetic defect in this enzyme are gravely ill and die soon after birth. In some patients, the defect has been traced to an inability to make molybdenum cofactor, and it has recently been demonstrated that treatment is possible by injecting them with molybdenum cofactor isolated from bacteria. Xanthine oxidase is another molybdenum enzyme that degrades certain chemicals called purines in our body. If this enzyme does not function correctly we develop gout, a painful disease caused by crystal formation of purines in our joints. We and others discovered that many species of bacteria, including many that cause bacterial infections, use molybdenum enzymes to convert the nutrients they subsist on into more usable forms of energy, allowing them to grow and multiply. Thus understanding molybdenum enzymes has important implications for fighting bacterial infections. Why have some enzymes evolved to require molybdenum? How is the molybdenum-containing cofactor made in cells? How is it incorporated into enzymes? What does the cofactor do in enzymes, that is, how does it work? As there is great similarity between molybdenum-containing enzymes from bacteria to humans, we use bacterial enzymes for our research as they are easier to isolate and modify by genetic manipulation. In our research we address these questions by conducting sophisticated experiments using cutting edge techniques.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of murine calcium and bone metabolism during pregnancy, lactation and post-weaning
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCITONIN; CALCITONIN RECEPTOR; CALCIUM AND BONE METABOLISM; KNOCKOUT/TRANSGENIC MICE; MICROARRAY AND PROTEOMICS; PARATHYROID HORMONE; PARATHYROIDS; PREGNANCY AND LACTATION; PTHRP
Abstract-Résumé: During pregnancy and lactation (breast-feeding), a woman will lose calcium from her body in order to provide it to the developing fetus and suckling neonate, respectively.  During pregnancy, a woman meets this calcium demand by doubling intestinal absorption of calcium and by losing some calcium from her skeleton.  During six months of lactation, a woman meets the neonate's demand for calcium by losing 5 to 10% of the calcium content of her skeleton.  The rate of loss of skeletal calcium during lactation is extremely fast when it is considered that a loss of more than 1% per year is termed "rapid" in a woman at menopause.  After weaning the baby, calcium that was lost from the skeleton during pregnancy and lactation is completely restored at rates that far exceed what current treatments for osteoporosis can accomplish.  The recovery is especially remarkable when it is considered that, apart from pregnancy and lactation, losses of calcium from the adult skeleton are at best only slowly and incompletely restored (eg from estrogen deficiency, illness, weightlessness, etc).  In this work we are trying to understand how the skeleton recovers lost calcium so quickly and readily after lactation because this knowledge might lead to new ways to restore calcium to the skeleton in people with osteoporosis or other conditions of low bone mass.  This work involves mice, which lose up to 55% of skeletal calcium during 3 weeks of lactation, and fully restore the skeleton within 10-14 days after weaning.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOBANKING; BIOMARKERS; INFORMATION MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS; QUALITY ASSURANCE; TRANSLATIONAL CANCER RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Tumor Repository Network (CTRNet) was established in order to create a virtual web-based tumor bank network.  The main focus of CTRNet has been to improve accessibility for researchers to tumor materials contained in existing biobanks, to detail and harmonize standards across Canada (and beyond), and to ensure quality processes are in place and well utilized by participating biobanks.  It is generally recognized that networks enhance and harmonize biospecimen and data standards as well as heightening awareness and access by research initiatives.  To date, 47 tissue banking standard operating procedures and seven policies have been completed, widely disseminated, and uniformly utilized by CTRNet banks and accessed worldwide.  A standardized tissue accession and annotation tool (ATiM) has been developed and deployed and is being enhanced and improved.  The www.ctrnet.ca web portal has been developed and provides the required interface for biobanking activities to Canadian and international researchers.    CTRNet proposes to continue to address the needs to increase the quality and standardization of processes involved in biospecimen collection, to increase capacity for accrual and broad tumor representation by facilitating inclusion of existing biobanks and establishment of new biobanks supported by CTRNet, and by expanding and establishing new activities in training and education, biobank certification, and promotion of network resources.  CTRNet will continue to take a leadership role in national and international networks dedicated to strengthening biobanks.    CTRNet will maintain and enhance a crucial national resource for translational cancer research, which will be utilized to delineate biomarkers for early detection and monitoring of cancer and for the design and development of new therapies to reduce the burden of cancer worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immune regulation by SAP, the X-linked lymphoproliferative (XLP) gene product
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTORS; AUTO-IMMUNITY; IMMUNODEFICIENCY; KINASES; RECEPTORS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: SAP is a small protein that resides inside the cell and is termed "adaptor". It is present only in cells of the immune system. SAP is mutated in a human immunodeficiency named X-linked lymphoproliferative (XLP) disease, which is characterized by an abnormal ability to fight certain viruses and immune cell cancers. Over the past years, we uncovered how SAP regulates the normal immune system. We also provided insights into the mechanisms by which SAP mutations can lead to immunodeficiencies and cancers. Lastly, we found that SAP may be involved in the unfortunate capacity of some humans to develop auto-immune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. In the current proposal, we will continue to study the role and regulation of SAP. The results of these studies will not only augment our comprehension of the normal immune system, but will also help elucidate and, perhaps, treat certain human diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of reflex gain in an osmoregulatory circuit
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MECHANOSENSITIVITY; OSMORECEPTOR; SUPRACHIASMATIC NUCLEUS; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; VASOPRESSIN
Abstract-Résumé: Vasopressin (VP, the antidiuretic hormone) is produced by a small group of neurons in the hypothalamus. The electrical activity of VP neurons (and thus its secretion into the blood) normally increases when body water is low (a condition termed hyperosmolality) to promote water conservation by the kidney. Hyperosmolality is detected by other neurons, termed osmoreceptors, that excite VP neurons via synaptic connections. The endocrine response mediated by this simple neuronal circuit is vital for body fluid balance and changes in its performance are linked to significant pathological conditions. For example, an exaggerated response of osmoreceptors contributes to hyponatremia and pulmonary congestion following a heart attack, and may be involved in the development of hypertension linked to excessive salt intake. Conversely, inadequate (i.e. weak) osmoreceptor control of VP neurons causes night time polyuria and enuresis (overfilling of the bladder and bed-wetting). More importantly, weak osmoreceptor control of VP neurons also contributes to the increased risk of mortality of elderly individuals during summertime heat waves, and in patients hospitalized with septic shock. Although defects in osmoreceptor signaling clearly contribute to disease, virtually nothing is known about the molecular and cellular mechanisms that mediate these functions in either normal or pathological conditions. In this project Dr. Bourque and his collaborators will use in-vitro models of rodent brain to investigate how neurons in the biological clock (the suprachiasmatic nucleus) interact with osmoreceptor neurons and VP neurons to increase in the electrical activity of VP neurons during late sleep. Bourque's team will also investigate how a peptide neurotransmitter called angiotensin II may increase in osmoreceptor signaling during dehydration. The findings of these studies could help define important new approaches for the treatment of conditions related to impaired osmoreceptor signaling.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of muscle glucose transporters by Rac and Rabs during insulin action and lipotoxicity
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN REMODELLING; GLUCOSE TRANSPORTERS; INSULIN ACTION AND SIGNALLING; INTRACELLULAR COMPARTMENTS; MUSCLE CELLS; VESICLE TRAFFIC
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes is alarmingly on the rise, urging us to investigate its molecular underpinnings. Sugars from our meals go to the blood and then are stored in our muscles, entering through glucose transporters called GLUT4. This process is triggered by insulin, and when it fails (in insulin resistance) this leads to Type 2 diabetes. We have studied for over 25 years how insulin signals within muscle cells regulate glucose uptake. GLUT4 is stored in vesicles inside muscle cells that move to the cell surface in response to insulin. With this grant we discovered new insulin signals mediated by 'G-proteins' called Rac and Rabs. We now propose to map what activates Rac and Rabs and how they, in turn, connect to GLUT4 vesicles. For this purpose, we have generated muscle cells in culture and a transgenic mouse in which GLUT4 is 'tagged' so we can follow it by fluorescence microscopy. We propose to test the hypothesis that Rac regulates structural elements of the cell ('hardware') and Rabs are on/off switches ('software') that carry GLUT4 vesicles to the cell surface. We also propose to map the circuit that GLUT4 transits inside live muscle cells. With our new transgenic mouse model with 'tagged' GLUT4, we will be able for the first time to track GLUT4 in the mature muscle. Finally, we have shown that saturated fats given directly to muscle cells markedly lower the response of GLUT4 to insulin. We will now study how these fats affect insulin signals, with emphasis on Rac and Rabs. In this way, we hope to generate useful knowledge that can shape therapeutic approaches to prevent Type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pain-Attention Interactions and the Descending Pain Modulation System
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION; CATASTROPHIZING; COGNITION; FMRI; PAIN; STRUCTURAL MRI
Abstract-Résumé: The pain experience is shaped by brain activity along pathways, including descending pathways collectively known as the descending pain modulation system.  This system can produce pain-relieving effects. Attention can also influence the pain experience.  Sometimes, engagement in a cognitive task can reduce pain, but in other situations, pain interferes with attention and cognition (e.g., reasoning, thinking). The outcome of pain-attention interactions impacts how chronic pain interfers with cognitive function, and also the potential for pain control through cognitive coping strategies.  We previously showed: 1) In some people pain diminishes cognitive abilities but in others cognitive performance improves during pain; 2) Performance of a demanding task concurrent with painful stimulation reduced activity in the brain's pain areas in people who perform better during pain; 3) People who catastrophize (e.g., ruminate) about pain, show high brain activity in pain areas and low activity in pain modulation areas.  This project will study inherent factors that may predispose an individual to either develop chronic pain or contribute to poor pain coping and reduced ability to maintain cognitive performance during pain.  I hypothesize that the ability to balance pain with cognitive performance depends on the integrity of the descending pain modulation system. This system is reduced in people who catastrophize about pain.  Therefore, MRI will be used to assess the anatomical and functional integrity of this system and the relationship with behaviour responses and pain catastrophizing.  This project will provide a new view on the brain's descending pain modulation system by assessing factors than impact its effectiveness in light of biological (brain structure and function) and psychology. The findings will impact our fundamental understanding of pain-attention interaction and will provide a framework for future individualized therapeutic approaches for pain coping.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Intestinal Stem Cell Proliferation in Response to Microbial Challenges.
Keywords-MotsClés: INNATE IMMUNE SIGNALING; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTESTINAL IMMUNITY; INTESTINAL STEM CELL; JNK; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Guts are major entry sites for numerous pathogens and gut cells perform essential barrier functions against invading microbes. Thus, it is essential to ensure that gut cell proliferation keeps pace with the rate at which a microbial assault damages gut cells. A failure to do so may result in catastrophic intestinal breaches and chronic disease states. A groundbreaking series of studies uncovered a striking evolutionary conservation of the formation and cellular architecture of mammalian and fly guts. Furthermore, the regulatory circuits that control immune responses in flies tend to be highly conserved throughout evolution. Thus, the genetically accessible fruitfly serves as an ideal tool to study gut cell proliferation during intestinal infections. We recently developed a novel experimental method that allowed us to rapidly survey the entire fruitfly genome for genes that control the activation of immune responses. In this study, we showed that detection of foreign microbes results in the production of a secreted molecule, Pvf2, which drives the cellular proliferation of numerous cell types. More recently, we showed that Pvf2 is specifically expressed in the gut during infection. Overlapping studies revealed that Pvf2 controls the proliferation of damaged gut cells. These observations led us to propose that bacterial damage of gut cells triggers the intestinal production of Pvf2, which drives a compensatory cellular proliferation in the gut. Such proliferative responses are essential to ensure the maintenance of an intestinal barrier to invading pathogens. Remarkably, the mouse equivalent of Pvf2 appears to perform related functions in the control of cellular proliferation in the gut. Thus, it appears that Pvf2 may perform evolutionarily conserved roles in the formation and maintenance of animal guts. In this research project, we will perform a comprehensive characterization of the role of gut cell proliferation in fly immune responses to pathogenic microbes

TitreApplicationTitle: Cell Response to Electrical Stimulation Mediated by Conductive Scaffold
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CONDUCTIVE POLYMERS; CYTOKINES; ELECTRICAL STIMULATION; GENE EXPRESSION; SKIN HEALING; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Injury of tissues like skin or bone can be repaired by the cells originally presented in the tissues. Cellular activities and tissue repair are coordinated by many kinds of proteins called cytokines and chemokines produced by the repairing cells. Such proteins are produced by different types of cells during injury or infection to fight invasion and to repair damaged tissues or organs. One of the fundamentally important tasks in tissue regeneration is to understand and, even more importantly, to modulate the activities in the repairing cells in order to favour the regeneration of the damaged tissues. We have previously reported that the production of two types of important biomolecules in wound healing, interleukin-6 and interleukin-8, was dramatically increased through electrical stimulation using our unique electrically conductive material. We also showed that one type of skin cells (fibroblasts) have the possibility to be transformed into a different type of cells called myofibroblasts. Myofibroblasts are important in wound healing by helping the closure of wound. This highlights the possibility of using electrical signals to promote tissue regeneration. The current grant application is to investigate the mechanisms behind the electrically stimulated cell response, and to expand our knowledge on how cells react to conductive polymer-mediated electrical stimulations. The scientific knowledge anticipated from this research is directly applicable to regenerative medicine and therefore beneficiary to the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cell biology and function of glutamate co-transmission in mesencephalic dopamine neurons.
Keywords-MotsClés: COTRANSMISSION; DOPAMINE; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; GLUTAMATE; TRANSGENIC MICE; VESICULAR GLUTAMATE TRANSPORTER
Abstract-Résumé: Neurons in the brain are usually characterized by the type of chemical transmitter molecules that they produce and release in the context of neuronal cummunication. However, recent work suggests that some neurons can produce and release more than one type of small chemical messengers. In the current project, we will study the capacity of dopamine-containing neurons to produce and package the amino acid transmitter glutamate. In particular, we will evaluate whether single neurons have the capacity to release dopamine and glutamate from the same or different axon terminals. In addition, we will use a genetic approach to prevent dopamine neurons from releasing glutamate and determine the impact of this on the activity and morphology of dopamine neurons. This work could help understand how dopamine neurons modify their properties in context of diseases such as Parkinson's, drug abuse and schizophrenia.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Hyperpolarized Helium-3 Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Healthy Aging Lung
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTHY AGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NON-INVASIVE IMAGING; PHENOTYPES; SENILE EMPHYSEMA; THORACIC IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: To maximize transport of oxygen to the blood, the lungs are uniquely designed to contain approximately 2,400 km of airways and approximately 500 million alveoli, with a total gas exchange surface area that is roughly the area of a tennis court. As we age, lung structure changes and function diminishes to the extent that the predicted lifespan of the normal healthy lung does not surpass about 100 years. As the aging population increases in the developed world, it is increasingly important to understand the physiology, structure and function of the aging lung in order to establish appropriate strategies for its functional improvement. The effects of the aging pulmonary system, that along with environmental factors is thought to be responsible for 10,000 deaths and 100,000 hospitalizations each year in Canada, is not well understood. Despite the staggering societal burden and decades of active research, little is known about how to differentiate "usual aging" representing the effects of aging mixed with lifestyle and environmental factors, from "successful aging" reflecting not only a lack of apparent disease but physiological performance that is not significantly different from that of healthy young adults. We recently were the first to report the unexpected 3He magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) finding that healthy elderly subjects exhibited lung functional changes similar to subjects with smoking-related lung disease suggesting that significant and unexpected age-related airway changes were occurring in healthy elderly never-smokers. Our surprising imaging findings provide important mechanistic information about the aging lung and identify the potential for lung imaging measurements to help better quantify healthy aging lung changes. We will exploit our previous novel findings in a large longitudinal imaging study of healthy elderly lung.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: Host-parasite interactions alter joint inflammation in mouse model systems
Keywords-MotsClés: HELMINTH PARASITES; INFLAMMATION; NEUROGENIC; PAIN; REGULATORY IMMUNE CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The incidence of arthritic disease is increasing globally. Joint inflammation is severely debilitating and impacts millions of Canadians, disrupting the quality of life of the patients and their families, and has a major socio-economic implication (eg healthcare costs & lost productivity).   A variety of drugs are used to treat the symptoms of arthritic disease, such as pain and swelling, but these often have undesirable side-effects and while they can be effective in providing symptom relief there is currently no cure for arthritis. A more comprehensive knowledge of the mechanisms that cause inflammation, and those of the resolution phase, is required to develop better therapies and advance towards a cure for arthritis.  This research proposal presents a novel way to address this issue. Recent studies show that infection with worm parasites in laboratory models of human disease can alleviate the disease. While the exact mechanism of this effect is unclear, and varies between model systems, it appears that the hosts' natural response to infection with a worm parasite can block concomitant disorders. Using a mouse model of joint inflammation, preliminary data show that mice infected with the tapeworm, Hymenolepis diminuta, have significantly less joint swelling and recover quicker from the inflammatory insult. Thus, we have designed a series of investigations to explore how infection with H. diminuta exerts this anti-inflammatory effect. These studies will assess immune and neural derived factors in the development and recovery from the inflammatory insult and will use measurements of inflammation (ie. immune cell infiltrate) and disease symptomatology (ie. joint swelling & pain perception) to assess the effectiveness of parasitic infection to block arthritic disease. We anticipate that we will identify new immune and nervous mechanisms that regulate the extent of arthritis and that these findings can lead to progress in the treatment of these disabling conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of an automated blood counter for quantitative molecular imaging applications
Keywords-MotsClés: POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: "Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) are well established molecular imaging modalities used in many fields of the biomedical sciences, most notably in neurology, cardiology and oncology.  They allow in vivo investigations of biological processes at the molecular level, and provide valuable information on the onset and  progression of diseases. PET and SPECT are routinely used for diagnostic purposes and increasingly used to monitor the response to therapy, and in both cases they are key aspects of patient management.  These functional imaging modalities also play an important role in the development of new drugs at clinical and preclinical stages.  PET and SPECT images are fundamentally based on a measurable number of nuclear disintegrations and as such are inherently quantitative. The quantitative nature of PET and SPECT can be assessed down to nanomolar concentrations and constitutes a powerful investigation tool for research and clinical purposes.  The quantitative nature of PET and SPECT however is typically dismissed in most studies, largely because quantitative protocols are cumbersome and time-consuming.  Accurate quantification in PET and SPECT indeed requires frequent assessments of blood activity through direct sampling and measurement in a well-counter, an error-prone task that increases exposure for personnel and potentially interferes with data acquisition. The objective of this project is to develop a device for the automated determination of blood activity for quantitative molecular imaging applications. The device will rely on Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT), a room-temperature semi-conductor compatible with clinical requirements such as stability, sturdiness and compactness.  This device will dramatically decrease the overhead associated with quantitative PET and SPECT imaging protocols and consequently favor their clinical adoption and development. These studies potentially can provide additional diagnostic clues and valuable information regarding the response to therapy compared to traditional PET and SPECT studies based mostly on visual interpretation and semi-quantitative analysis. This in turn has a direct clinical and economical impact through better patient management. A systematic access to accurate quantitative data in molecular imaging promises to positively change how PET and SPECT studies are used in the clinic and in research protocols. "

TitreApplicationTitle: New Polymer Composites Based on Natural Compounds for Dental Applications
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN
Abstract-Résumé: "The research outlined in this proposal is expected to yield substantial knowledge related to understanding, assessing and treatment of Blast-Induced Traumatic Brain Injury (BI-TBI) cases. This knowledge will be translated into a Decision Support System (DSS) to be used by healthcare providers for immediate intervention as well as short-term resource management  and for long-term treatment BI-TBI patients.  The development of the DSS is based on the results of numerical models validated through different levels of experiments under simulated blast load conditions.  The numerical tasks will focus on correlating the frequency contents of different sub-lethal explosion scenarios to natural (resonance) frequencies of different parts of the brain using high resolution finite element models. The tasks will also identify critical brain regions that are most susceptible to damage by different blast shock wave levels and frequency content. Isolating such critical brain areas will facilitate the quantification of the mechanical strain and strain rate levels developed within different brain areas under different explosion scenarios.  The experimental tasks will include testing of physical skull/brain models under a wide range of blast shock wave parameters. This will facilitate visualising of blast wave propagation and reflection processes in the brain. These experiments will also be used to validate the results of the numerical models. The experiments will also include testing animal models under different levels of sub-lethal combination of blast pressure and impulse. In addition, this project will evaluate the cellular response of neuron cells in culture to different strain and strain rate levels (obtained from the numerical and physical head models) to generate injury threshold relationships.  Integration of the data generated through the different research tasks in the form of a DSS software tool and identification of the different injury levels in terms of expected acute and chronic neurological outcomes are the ultimate goals of this project.   Meeting these objectives will ensure quality of life to Canadians who may be victims of possible BI-TBI. The proposed research program, with the support from NSERC and CIHR, will make significant strides in the BI-TBI research areas, resulting in optimized clinical resource management, immediate and effective medical intervention and improved long-term management of Canadians who may become victims of BI-TBI."
