TitreApplicationTitle: Ice-binding proteins: structure function and evolution
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIFREEZE PROTEINS; FLUORESCENCE TAGGING; ICE NUCLEATION; ICE-BINDING PROTEINS; MOLECULAR MODELING; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; PROTEIN EVOLUTION; PROTEIN EXPRESSION; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: We are studying several types of ice-binding proteins. These include antifreeze proteins (AFP) which bind to the surface of ice crystals and stop them from growing. These proteins help organisms like fishes and some insects to avoid freezing through this lowering of the freezing point. One medical application of these AFPs is to help cool organs and tissues below zero prior to transplantation into patients without damage to the organs by ice crystals. The colder the organ, the longer it will last. We have discovered that some AFPs are ten times better at lowering the freezing point than others and we want to learn why this is and how their activity can be further improved by the addition of enhancer proteins, about which little is known. When ice freezes, the presence of some AFPs can make it form sharp needle-like crystals which are useful in cryosurgery for killing tumour cells. Again we need to know more about how these proteins interact with ice to change its shape. Other AFPs seem to help organisms tolerate freezing. Here their role seems to be stopping the growth of large ice crystals at the expense of small ones. In other words, they are ice recrystallization inhibitors, which are finding many uses in frozen products to stop freeze-thaw damage. Again, there are medical applications for the cryopreservation of cells and tissues. We are also exploring the link between AFPs and ice nucleating proteins. The latter have applications in rain/snow making and controlled freezing. We are investigating the hypothesis that ice nucleating proteins are like AFPs in structure but are 10- to 20- larger. If so, we should be able to protein engineer the interchange by making one smaller and the other larger. Learning how these different ice-binding proteins are related and how they function mechanistically will pave the way for biotechnological applications in the medical and biological fields.

TitreApplicationTitle: The central role of the vagus nerve in high fat diet-induced obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ENERGY EXPENDITURE; GENE REGULATION; HIGH-FAT DIET; NUTRITION; VAGUS NERVE
Abstract-Résumé: The incidence of obesity in Canada is increasing at a staggering rate. The number of Canadians afflicted by Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus continues to grow, and we know that increased body mass is associated with the development of this disease. The rate of heart disease and stroke, the largest cause of death and disability in Western Society, is significantly elevated in those with obesity and Type 2 Diabetes. Consequently much effort has been spent on understanding how our bodies respond to excess dietary fuel and the mechanisms involved in diet-induced obesity.  The body controls fuel usage, in part, through the communication of metabolic information between organs. It is becoming apparent that this communication consists of factors secreted into the blood and neuronal connections between tissues. The main objective of this project is to explore the role of neuronal connection between the brain and liver in controlling whole-body energy usage. The vagus nerve, one of the most important nerves in the body, is a two-way highway of communication between the brain and many organs. The liver-branch of this nerve controls many aspects of food intake and energy metabolism, though exactly how remains largely unknown To investigate the role the vagus nerve plays in the development of obesity, we will surgically disrupt the action of this nerve in mice. Following surgery, mice will be fed a high-fat diet for 10 weeks which normally causes weight gain and impairs insulin action. Our subsequent experiments will allow us to elucidate the role of the brain-liver axis in the development of obesity. We believe that by understanding the mechanism by which these neuronal signals alter weight gain, hormone action and fuel partitioning we will discover new targets for the prevention/treatment of obesity, diabetes and heart disease.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of AMPK in the Regulation of Cardiac Hypertrophy and Hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; ANIMAL MODELS OF DISEASE; CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CELL SIGNALLING; HYPERTENSION; RESVERATROL
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a major cause of death worldwide and occurs as a consequence of a number of diseases related to the heart or to the blood vessels.  A common condition that can lead to heart failure is abnormal heart muscle growth.  We have identified a new pathway that contributes to abnormal heart growth as well as found a drug that can rescue this pathway and prevent this condition.  In addition to the direct effects on the heart, this pathway also contributes to elevated blood pressure.  As a result, we will perform pre-clinical studies using rats and mice to determine how this drug alters the aforementioned pathways to prevent a rise in blood pressure and abnormal heart growth. Since abnormal heart growth and high blood pressure are major risk factors for the development of a number of other heart related illnesses, understanding how our newly identified pathway is involved in these diseases will contribute significantly to understanding abnormal heart growth and high blood pressure.  In addition, studying how our drug regulates this pathway to prevent these diseases could one day lead to this drug being used clinically.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aging and the Neural Architecture Supporting Perceptual Organization of Speech
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ATTENTION; AUDITORY CORTEX; EVENT-RELATED POTENTIALS; HEARING; PERCEPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Older adults often experience difficulties in understanding speech, especially when several people are talking at the same time as during a cocktail party or at the restaurant. There are several possible reasons why older adults, even those with good hearing, experience difficulty in understanding speech in adverse listening situation (e.g., cocktail party), including age-related changes in peripheral and central auditory processing as well as changes in attention and memory. In this research program, we measure brain activity while participants of varying ages listen to various sounds. The aims are to relate participant's perception with specific patterns of brain activity and to assess how these patterns of brain activity changes with age. From these measurements, we will learn about the areas involved in auditory perception and we will be able to better understand the cause of speech perception problems commonly observed in older adults. It is expected that the outcomes of this research will lead to a better understanding of how aging affects the ability of older adults to communicate in complex auditory environments that they encounter in everyday life and will inform the development and implementation of new rehabilitative strategies to enhance speech perception in noisy environments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining HIV related vulnerabilities among conflict-affected populations in Gulu and Amuru Districts Northern Uganda
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFLICT/POST-CONFLICT; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIV/AIDS; UGANDA; YOUNG PEOPLE
Abstract-Résumé: The protracted conflict in Northern Uganda has lasted over twenty years, it has affected the whole population and its impact has been cross-generational. In August 2006, the signing of the landmark Cessation of Hostilities Agreement took place. Although the search for durable solutions is ongoing, several hundred thousand Internally Displaced Peoples (IDPs) have started to return to their home villages. Accordingly, the Government of Uganda is reinstating plans for resettlement as relative peace prevails. While NGOs have consistently reported grave concern that HIV/AIDS may be devastating the region, epidemiological data describing the legacy of the conflict are scarce. Without this data it is difficult for donor agencies and NGOs to prioritize effective responses. Given the identified gap in evidence and the potential for rapid progression of HIV infection post conflict, due to the combination of high vulnerability and increased exposure opportunities, it is vital that an aggressive and deliberate approach to evidence-based research and programme design be developed as the previously encamped resettle. This initiative aims to address the paucity of HIV related epidemiological data for the Northern region of Uganda by assessing HIV prevalence and incidence rates and trends of disease among a cohort of individuals aged 13-39, in order to better inform post-conflict intervention planning. The implications of this new research initiative have great significance for developing policies and programs to confront HIV in the context of post-conflict.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Nuclear envelope-DNA attachments in cellular lifespan control
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CHROMATIN; CHROMOSOME BIOLOGY; LAMINOPATHIES; NUCLEAR MEMBRANE PROTEINS; REPETITIVE DNA; RESVERATROL; RIBOSOMAL RNA GENES (RDNA); SIRTUINS; TELOMERES
Abstract-Résumé: In pursuit of longevity and health, scientists have uncovered dietary, metabolic, and genetic factors involved in the aging process.  Our bodies are built from millions of living units called cells.  Each cell has a copy of our DNA, which is arranged in thousands of units called genes.  Not all genes are used in a cell and this is how an eye cell is different from a liver cell.  Genes are arranged on linear structures called chromosomes.  At both ends of each chromosome lies a special structure termed telomere, which protects our DNA and controls which genes are expressed in a cell.  Telomeres have generated much excitement in recent years and the 2009 Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded to their discoverers.  The excitement stems from the fact that telomeres become defective as we age but cancer cells have unusually strong telomeres.  This led scientists to suspect that telomeres may act like a clock controlling how long our cells and we live.  Scientists have also learned a lot by studying patients that age too fast.  In the most extreme of these cases, young children start to look and be old as they suffer from heart attacks and strokes.  In fact, scientists now know that these patients have defects in a group of proteins located at the edge of the balloon-like envelope in which genes are located in a cell.  My lab has new data indicating that these proteins actually attach telomeres to the edge of this envelope.  This attachment allows telomeres to function properly.  These proteins also attach other parts of our DNA.  Together, these attachments act like hooks holding up a tent, or the DNA, in place.  We propose that removing these DNA-hooking proteins causes normal cells to behave like old ones.  Also, once these proteins are lost such as in premature aging, we test if artificial DNA hooks introduced at the envelope or pharmaceuticals can make cells young again.  This study may allow us to slow down normal or premature aging and prevent age-related diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Striking A Balance: Health and Employment Outcomes Related to Role Overload and Role Balance Among People with Arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CHRONIC EPISODIC CONDITIONS; EMPLOYMENT; MEASUREMENT DEVELOPMENT; PROSPECTIVE STUDY DESIGN; PSYCHOSOCIAL FACTORS; QUESTIONNAIRES; ROLE BALANCE; ROLE OVERLOAD
Abstract-Résumé: Workforce health is a critical driver of the economy. However, many Canadians live with chronic or episodic physical disabilities, such as arthritis, multiple sclerosis, colitis, diabetes, and HIV. Statistics Canada reports that 51% of people with disabilities were employed in 2006 compared to 75% of people without disabilities. Psychological processes and workplace circumstances have been identified as critical to helping people remain employed. In particular, perceived role overload in managing health and work is a key stressor related to absenteeism, reducing work hours, and work disruptions. We will examine different types of role balance/overload (e.g., time-based overload, demand-based role interplay, role strain, role facilitation) as early warning indicators of health and workplace difficulties. The research will focus on people with arthritis. Although arthritis is often thought of as a disease of aging, 3 of 5 people with arthritis are under age 65 and most of them are in their prime earning years. In fact, arthritis is the second most frequent cause of disability in the working population with about 50% of adults with arthritis disability reporting being out of work. Telephone and mailed, self-administered questionnaires will assess study objectives related to better describing role interplay, the factors associated with it, and its impact. The study will capitalize on an existing cohort of 400 individuals with inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis and recruit an additional 100 participants for longitudinal analyses. Participants will be assessed at 3 time-points, each 12 months apart. The proposal brings together a team from clinical, health services, and population and public health, as well as organizations focused on arthritis, work, and health. Findings will result in a more comprehensive assessment of role balance and a better understanding of its impact.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of mammalian homologous recombination
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA REPAIR; DNA REPLICATION; HOMOLOGOUS RECOMBINATION; MAMMALIAN; MOLECULAR GENETICS; RAD52 EPISTASIS GROUP PROTEINS; RECOMBINANT DNA
Abstract-Résumé: Homologous recombination is the process by which genetic information is exchanged between DNA molecules. It is of fundamental importance in living organisms. During the generation of eggs and sperm, homologous recombination between chromosomes generates genetic diversity. In the dividing cells of the body, homologous recombination is important in repairing breaks that occur in chromosomes. When homologous recombination doesn't work correctly, broken chromosomes can trigger cell death or chromosome rearrangements and mutations that are linked to cancer. Much of our knowledge of how homologous recombination works, comes from studies conducted in model organisms, such as yeast and bacteria. Unfortunately, we know less about this process as it occurs in mammalian cells. The research work of my laboratory is focused on understanding how homologous recombination aids in the repair of DNA breaks in mammalian cells and of the mechanisms involved. Our research contributes to an understanding of how cells maintain the stability of the DNA in their chromosomes. Eventually, there is the hope that this research will help in the design of therapeutic drugs and processes that can aid in cancer prevention.

CommitteeNameEN: Social & Developmental Aspects of Children's & Youth's Health
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Fetal programming of infant stress reactivity
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTISOL; FETAL/INFANT DEVELOPMENT; HEART RATE VARIABILITY; MATERNAL PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; MOTHER-INFANT INTERACTION; STRESS REACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Recent studies suggest that pregnant women who report high levels of stress, anxiety, or depression have babies who are at increased risk for poor developmental outcomes. For example, infants of distressed mothers have a higher incidence of 'difficult' temperament, behavioural and emotional problems, and physical disease. Unfortunately, these effects can last a lifetime.     Research also suggests that when women are stressed, anxious, or depressed during pregnancy, the way in which these psychological problems affect their babies is through 'stress hormones'. Exposure to maternal stress hormones during formation of the baby's stress response system can alter its function and make it over-reactive to stress throughout the child's life. These changes may explain why children whose mothers were distressed during pregnancy are at increased risk for developmental and health problems.    The current proposal examines the biological processes that may cause changes in the development of babies born to stressed, anxious, or depressed mothers. The primary questions we address are: (1) does exposure to maternal stress hormones during gestation alter infants' stress responses? and (2), does the way a mother interacts with her infant after birth have the potential to change the effects of prenatal exposure to the mother's stress hormones? To address these questions, we repeatedly measure maternal cortisol during pregnancy and infant stress reactivity at 3 and 6 months of age.    Given that the prevalence of harmful levels of stress, anxiety, and depression in expectant mothers is high (13%), understanding the association between maternal stress hormones and infant stress responses has the potential to influence policies aimed at reducing psychological distress in mothers in the prenatal and postpartum periods. Children and society stand to gain from reducing the health and developmental problems associated with exposure to maternal distress during pregnancy.

ClasseRechercheFR: DIABETE SUCRE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: T-cell tolerance versus the genetic resistance to spontaneous autoimmune diabetes in mice
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE T-CELL TRANSFER; AUTOIMMUNITY; CYTOKINE ASSAYS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; IMMUNOGENETICS; IMMUNOPATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Insulin-dependent or type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D) results from immune dysregulation (autoimmunity) leading to destruction of the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas (beta cells) by beta cell-killer white blood cells. Susceptibility to T1D is genetically determined, but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood.  Our studies to date have explored mechanisms underlying the genetic risk to T1D afforded by 3 different genes, and have discovered that all 3 affect the development and function of a type of white blood cells whose job is to protect us against autoimmune disease ('suppressor white blood cells'). Particularly significant with regards to human T1D are our studies of the mouse 'Interleukin 2' gene. Like its mouse counterpart, the human Interleukin 2 gene is associated with human T1D. We have shown that the variants of this gene that afford T1D risk in mice do so because they work slightly less than normal (i.e. make less interleukin 2 protein). Since the 'suppressor white blood cells' require interleukin 2 to function, mice that make less interleukin 2 than normal have 'suppressor' cells that don't work very well; this is the reason why this gene is associated with T1D.  This prompted us to investigate a related gene that is also associated with human T1D: 'Interleukin 2 receptor alpha'. This gene codes for a protein on the surface of the 'suppressor' cells that allows them to capture 'Interleukin 2' from the blood. We hypothesize that the variants of this gene that are associated with T1D are those that make less 'Interleukin 2 receptor alpha' protein. The objective of this grant is to investigate if relatively small variations in the function of the genes coding for 'Interleukin 2' and 'Interleukin 2 receptor alpha' (alone and in combination) result in significant variations in the function of 'suppressor' cells leading to T1D. This work will help identify new therapeutic targets for T1D and other autoimmune diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Educational, health and well-being outcomes of children born to immigrant and refugee families in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN AND YOUTH; DEVELOPMENTAL OUTCOMES; IMMIGRANT FAMILIES; POPULATION STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Canada as a whole, and BC in particular (e.g., BC Settlement & Adaptation Program), has been working hard to create settlement services for immigrant and refugee families in communities and in the schools with the aim of assisting these families in the process of integration into Canadian society. The programs established to assist immigrant and refugee families also work in partnership with communities and schools to create environments that are inclusive of the cultural beliefs and practices of Canadian newcomers and to which newcomers can contribute their skills. Little research, however, has been done that specifically studies the development, health and well-being of immigrant children over their school years in Canada. This proposed research will study the developmental trajectories including physical and mental health and academic achievement from Kindergarten through High School completion for children of four of the largest immigrant groups in BC; Chinese, South Asian, Filipino, and South East Asian; and for all other immigrant and refugee groups in BC. The knowledge gained from this study will expand our understanding of the cultural, familial, and neighborhood factors associated with the different immigrant populations that support successful long-term outcomes for the children of these newcomer groups, and has the potential for informing future intervention efforts aimed at maximizing successful developmental outcomes for the children of Canada's growing immigrant population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic analysis of the C. elegans cytoskeleton
Keywords-MotsClés: C. ELEGANS; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; GENETICS; MEIOSIS; MORPHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells contain several types of internal protein "skeletons", termed the cytoskeletons. One type provides structural support, while another generates force, the cellular "muscle" and "bone", respectively. We study how cells rearrange the cytoskeleton as embryos develop. We find mutations in genes controlling these processes; and by examining what goes wrong when the genes malfunction, we can infer the roles of the normal genes. Our work uses the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Its small size, the ease of growing large numbers of animals and rapid generation time make this worm ideal for genetic analysis - three recent Nobel Prizes were awarded for work on this animal. Because basic biological processes are very similar in all animals, we can use the worm to study genes in ways that are impossible with humans or other mammals. We have found a series of C. elegans genes, similar to those controlling human blood pressure and tumour metastasis, that regulate how the cytoskeleton changes cellular shapes. We also found cytoskeletal genes that are required for the accurate distribution of chromosomes to daughter cells in the specialized type of division that produces eggs. Disruption of this process in humans results in birth defects such as Down's syndrome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multidrug resistance in pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER RESISTANCE PROTEIN; CYTOKINES; EPIGENETICS; FETAL PROTECTION; INFECTION / INFLAMMATION; MATERNAL / FETAL THERAPY; MULTIDRUG RESISTANCE P-GLYCOPROTEIN; OBESITY; PLACENTA; PRREGNANCY DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Drug transporting P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) were first discovered in tumour cells that exhibited resistance to anticancer drugs. P-gp is encoded by the ABCB1 gene and BCRP by the ABCG2 gene. Both drug transporting proteins are located at the cell surface where they actively extrude (pump out) a large range of substances from cells. P-gp and BCRP can extrude a large number of medically relevant compounds. These include anticancer drugs, several forms of common herbicides and pesticides, cardiac drugs and synthetic steroids. Recently, P-gp and BCRP have been reported in normal tissues including the brain and placenta, and we have recently shown that placental P-gp levels fall rapidly in late gestation in humans and mice. The presence of these multidrug resistance proteins in the placenta, indicates a role in protection of the fetus from drugs, environmental toxins and hormones present in the maternal blood. Results from our current CIHR-funded research indicating that this is indeed the case. Our objective is to understand the role and regulation of placental multidrug resistance in normal and abnormal human pregnancy, as this will allow the development of innovative new treatment strategies in pregnancy. Studies will be undertaken using human placentae. We will also utilize the mouse (normal & genetically modified) to carry out in vivo studies, not possible in the human.

TitreApplicationTitle: Disserting the mechanisms of palmitoylation of the HCV core protein and its influence on formation of lipid droplets; a crucial function in the virus life cycle.
Keywords-MotsClés: 5 CELLS; CORE PROTEIN; DHHC ENZYMES; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; HUH7; JFH1; LIPID DROPLETS; PALMITOYLATION; PARTICLE FORMATION; UBIQUITINYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a plus-strand RNA virus that causes acute and chronic liver disease. More than 3% of the worldwide population is infected, making HCV infection one of the most devastating infectious diseases of our time. The main function of the HCV core protein is the encapsidation of the viral RNA. HCV core plays also an important role in the pathogenesis of the virus since this protein is intimately associated with lipids and can potentially be one of the cause of the disorders observed in the HCV infected patients. This proposal is dedicated to the study of HCV core and its interaction with the lipids. We recently found that palmitoylation (addition of a lipid moety by the cell) of core influences its interaction with cellular membranes, viral assembly and infectivity of the virus. Those events are complex and are related to specific interactions with several host proteins of the lipid metabolism that are not currently well understood.  Our major objective is to bring some light of those interactions to hopefully, discover new targets for the development of specific therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional genomics of the response to DNA double-strand breaks
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR; DNA REPLICATION; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENOME INTEGRITY; RNA INTERFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: A hallmark of cancer cells is their rearranged chromosomes. To arrive at this point, chromosomes must experience breakage. The questions I will try to answer in this proposal is: what are the genes that prevent chromosome breakage, what are those that tell the cell that there is a breakage and those involved in repairing them? I propose to employ the powerful technology of RNA interference to systematically examine the ~22,000 human genes in order to identify those genes involved in the formation of or response to chromosome breakage. I hypothesize that those genes will likely be enriched in genes that normally safeguards us from cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pregnancy, beta-interferon exposure, and long-term disability in Multiple Sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: DATA LINKAGE; DRUG ADVERSE EFFECTS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH OUTCOMES; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a relatively common disease of the brain and spinal cord, leading to disability and coordination problems; its cause is unknown. Women and men are often diagnosed with MS just as they are considering starting a family, making pregnancy-related issues of great importance. Historically, women with MS were advised against pregnancy because of assumed adverse effects on the course of their MS disease. We now know that short-term benefits can be gained during pregnancy, but it is unclear whether long-term benefits also occur in MS. We will examine the effect of pregnancy on long-term disability outcomes in MS. The need for pre-pregnancy planning is also important in MS, particularly since the introduction of new drugs for MS, such as the beta-interferons (IFNB). We will investigate the effect of MS on delivery and the newborn and how the newborn might be influenced by IFNB treatment. Fathers are often neglected in pregnancy studies; we will explore how IFNB treatment in fathers with MS might impact the newborn. Given the estimated 75,000 Canadians with MS, the relatively young age at MS onset and the increasing popularity of the MS drugs; issues surrounding pregnancy and MS and a possible negative effect of MS drugs on pregnancy are of real importance. This research will link, for the first time, extensive province-wide databases related to MS and pregnancy, enabling data collected by specialist physicians for over two decades to be examined. To date, there have been few studies as comprehensive as ours investigating all these aspects of pregnancy in MS. In addition, this important information will help develop a framework to evaluate the risk of future new MS drugs on pregnancy and may also have implications for other patient groups using similar drugs (the interferons), such as hepatitis C. Our study is a cost-effective way of spending research dollars, costing the equivalent of placing just 5 people with MS on IFNB treatment for 5 years.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the molecular components of Ca++ signal-induced alternative pre-mRNA splicing
Keywords-MotsClés: CAMK IV; CELL CLUTURE; PRE-MRNA SPLICING; PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION; RNA INTERFERENCE; SPLICING ASSAYS
Abstract-Résumé: From genes to the production of proteins, there are still a lot for us to learn to uncover the many mysteries in life and diseases. A gene's initial product from its DNA is a long thread of RNA containing various regions in a way like "several to dozens of beads interspersed on a long chain". The beads (called "exons") have to be accurately "spliced" together in a process called "RNA splicing" to produce proteins. During splicing, the combination of the exons can vary according to cell's needs so as to produce up to thousands of proteins with different properties from a single gene, which is called "alternative splicing".       Alternative splicing is an important mechanism by which cells can generate a vast pool of proteins to carry out complex functions such as learning and memory. However, if it goes wrong due to genetic mutations, improper exon combinations can be produced and cause human diseases such as spinal muscular atrophy, Frasier's syndrome and dementia. Yet, despite its importance for cell function and its role in diseases, still little is known of how cells splice together the exons accurately in response to changes in its environment (a "signal" as in the project title) and how we can use this process to correct the mutations in human diseases.       This research is to uncover the molecular components and mechanisms using our published model system started more than 10 years ago with calcium signals that are critical in almost every cells/tissues to understand how cells choose a proper combination of exons through alternative splicing in general. The knowledge to be obtained will also help us understand how those genetic mutations cause human diseases to provide better diagnosis and even treatment approaches in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure/function analysis of the ubiquitin/proteosome system
Keywords-MotsClés: CATALYTIC SWITCHING MECHANISM; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY XRAY; E3 UBIQUITIN LIGASE; PHOSPHOREGULATION; PROTEIN KINASE; SCF COMPLEX
Abstract-Résumé: In all cells of the body, proteins are selectively targeted for removal by attachment to a small protein tag called ubiquitin. Ubiquitin is attached to its target proteins through a series of enzyme steps denoted E1 -> E2 -> E3. The ubiquitin tag typically marks a protein for rapid destruction by a large protease called the 26S proteasome. The elimination of critical proteins by this mechanism affects many aspects of cellular function, and often goes awry in diseases such as cancer, immune dysfunction, neurological disorders, and viral and bacterial infection. The most critical regulatory step in the E1 -> E2 -> E3 process is the recognition of the target protein by the E3 enzyme. In this proposal, we characterize the structure and function of two different types of E3 enzymes, called the SCF ligases and a new class of E3 enzymes encoded by bacterial pathogens termed IpaH ligases. We will build on our structural analyses to develop chemicals that influence the recognition of substrates and/or the activity of E2 and E3 enzymes. We have already identified a number of interesting lead compounds and determined their structures when bound to E2 and E3 enzymes. These compounds will allow us to probe the biochemical mechanisms of the ubiquitin transfer reaction and serve as potential leads for the development of novel drugs to treat cancer, inflammation, infection and other human diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Risk and Resilience among Bisexual People in Ontario:  A Community-Based Study of Bisexual Mental Health
Keywords-MotsClés: BISEXUAL; COMMUNITY BASED RESEARCH; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; MENTAL HEALTH; SERVICE UTILIZATION; SEXUAL ORIENTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Bisexual people have poorer mental health outcomes compared to lesbian, gay and heterosexual people. However, little is known about why bisexual identity is associated with poor outcomes.  Recent qualitative research suggests that experiences of marginalization may contribute to these outcomes; however quantitative research is needed to confirm these findings. Similarly, bisexual people report high rates of mental health service use, but few studies have examined bisexual peoples' satisfaction with services, or mental health outcomes associated with service use. In this study, quantitative and qualitative methodology will be used to address these research gaps. A community based research approach, where bisexual people are involved in all parts of the research process will ensure relevance of the project.  Specifically, the study aims: a) to measure the rates of mental health problems in bisexual people  b) to examine which factors are associated with the marginalization of bisexual people c) to examine whether the marginalization experienced by bisexual people is related to mental health status d) to determine whether access to or satisfaction with mental health services is associated with mental health status e) to explore experiences with mental health services and help seeking strategies and f) to combine research results with social action to improve bisexual mental health.  Respondent-driven sampling will be used to identify 800 participants from Ontario, who will complete a survey that includes assessments of mental health status, marginalization variables and mental health service use. Forty participants will be interviewed about the factors enabling them to maintain good mental health. This project will be the most comprehensive study of bisexual mental health conducted to date. It will address critical gaps in knowledge and create information that will assist health providers in the provision of optimal mental health care to bisexual people.

TitreApplicationTitle: Randomized Controlled Trial of the Efficacy of Carrageenan as a Topical Microbicide Against HPV Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: CARRAGEENAN; CLINICAL TRIAL; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS; SEXUAL TRANSMISSION; TOPICAL MICROBICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide, cervical cancer is the second leading cause of cancer in women. Cervical cancer is most common in Latin and in sub-Saharan Africa, and the Caribbean. Because it is much more common in developing countries, it has been described as a disease of poorer nations. We now know that human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is the cause of cervical cancer. HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection, and most sexually-active women acquire HPV infection over their lifetime.  Usually these infections are not noticed or only cause external warts, which although benign, are difficult to treat and often lead to social stigmatization. Most HPV infections will not lead to cervical cancer, only those that involve certain types of this virus and that persist for a long time. There is currently a vaccine available that prevents two of the types of HPV infection that cause cervical cancer, but unfortunately it is effective only before and not after the infection is established. Furthermore, HPV vaccination is too expensive for use in developing countries. A HPV inhibitory compound in the form of a topical microbicide that kills viruses might be useful for blocking the spread of HPV. Researchers have identified carrageenan (an inexpensive gelling agent) as a potent HPV infection inhibitor in laboratory and animal studies. If an inexpensive topical microbicide is identified that eliminates HPV, this would serve as a very useful method to help reduce the burden of HPV infection and cervical cancer in developing and developed countries, in a cost-effective way. It could also reduce the risk of women's precancerous lesions of the uterine cervix and eventually help reduce the need for costly Pap test screening and treatment procedures. This study is the first to investigate whether a topical microbicide that contains carrageenan is effective in preventing transmission of HPV.

TitreApplicationTitle: A biomedical engineering approach to investigating bone quality across the lifespan
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; BONE AND JOINT HEALTH; BONE QUALITY; MEDICAL IMAGING; MICRO-COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; OSTEOPOROSIS; QUANTITATIVE X-RAY TECHNIQUES
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis is a disease of decreased bone density and deterioration of tissue resulting in an increased risk of fracture, most often in the hip, spine and wrist. In our aging Canadian population, the prevalence of osteoporosis is rapidly increasing. One in four women (and one in eight men) over the age of 50 has osteoporosis, and currently about two million Canadians suffer from the disease. This represents a significant health concern, and a burden on our health care system with costs estimated to be $1.3 billion each year in Canada. The proposed research develops a new approach to diagnosing and monitoring the disease through the use of a newly developed medical imaging technology called high resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) that provides high resolution images of bone in patients. To date, the normal way that osteoporosis patients are diagnosed or monitored is to simply measure their areal bone mineral density. New HR-pQCT technology is a significant advancement for monitoring patients because it measures volumetric bone density and three-dimensional structure. This technology, in combination with the finite element method (a computer modeling technique), provides a novel method to estimate the breaking strength of bones directly from patients, rather than trying to estimate a patients bone strength from the density alone. Our research seeks to establish the use of HR-pQCT on a representative Canadian population to identify the normal variation of bone structure as a function of age and sex. These data will provide a critically needed reference data against which the bone measurements of potential osteoporosis patients can be measured. We will explore research questions such as how increased porosity affects bone strength, and whether physical activity is a predictor of bone quality. This research will provide important new insight into bone quality in Canadians, and establish a new tool for monitoring bone health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ghrelin and the CNS control of appetite.
Keywords-MotsClés: FMRI; GHRELIN; OBESITY; REWARD; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is a major health problem in the developed world. It is now clear that the main cause of obesity is over-eating. It has been suggested then that obesity should be viewed as a brain disease.We plan to study how the brain controls appetite by focussing on a hormone called ghrelin. Ghrelin is made by the stomach and its main effect is to enter the brain and activate hunger centres. We will administer and measure ghrelin in healthy volunteers, and in obese individuals undergoing weight loss regimens while simultaneously measuring brain activity using functional magnetic resonance imaging. We hope to gain insights into the causes of obesity, and develop methods to assess treatments, whether pharmacological or behavioral.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and Function Studies of Nonribosomal Peptide Synthetases
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICS; BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER DRUGS; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ENZYMES; MICROBIOLOGY; MOLECULAR MACHINES; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; REACTION MECHANISMS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Many of the drugs and medicines that we rely on today are so-called natural products, made by the earth's flora and fauna. One important class of these compounds is made by fungi and bacteria using massive enzymes called nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPS). NRPSs synthesize all sorts of antibiotics, which can kill dangerous fungi and bacteria, as well as compounds that can help us fight off viral infections and cancers. For example, these compounds include viomycin, an antibiotic used for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, cyclosporin, which has been widely used as an immunosuppressant in organ transplants and can inhibit hepatitis virus C replication, and penicillin, the famous antibiotic.   The goal of this research is to expand our knowledge of NRPSs and the mechanisms they employ to synthesize important drugs. I will use biochemistry and biophysics, including techniques known as X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy, to capture three-dimensional pictures of an NRPS at different points in the process of making these antibiotics. I will study several NRPSs, including the penicillin synthesizing enzyme and the cyclosporin synthesizing enzyme, but the results of the work will be applicable to all NRPSs. The subjects addressed will range from elucidating the precise details of how building blocks are chemically assembled into the antibiotics, to understanding the large-scale rearrangements these enzymes need to perform to these drugs.  NRPSs hold a vast potential to produce new drugs. Because NRPSs are divided into segments, with each segment adding one building block to the drug, we can switch around the order and specific type of segment to produce variants of the drug.  My studies can help us learn how best to re-arrange NRPS segments to make millions of new compounds. Among these compounds could be important drugs to fight antibiotic resistant bacteria, viruses and cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: ASP Deficient and ASP Excess Mice Models: Immune-Metabolic Interactions in Adipose Tissue and Energy Expenditure Regulation
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE TISSUE; CELL BIOLOGY; DIABETES; MICE MODELS; OBESITY; PEPTIDE HORMONES
Abstract-Résumé: There is now considerable evidence that obesity, and in particular abdominal obesity, is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease, diabetes and hypertension.  The exact reason for this association is not clear. However, there is currently a wide interest in understanding the factors that control how and where the dietary fat is deposited in fat tissue. Fat is released into the bloodstream to provide an energy source to other tissues.  There are many different fat depots in the body and the efficiency of fat deposition and release of fat into the bloodstream varies widely. However, if too much fat is released, then the amount exceeds what is required by the muscle and other tissues for energy, and the excess may cause problems in both the liver and in the arteries. Our studies have focused on determining the role of a hormone (ASP) produced by fat tissue in increasing the efficiency of fat storage. In mouse models that do not have ASP, the mice are leaner, with reduced fat tissue in spite of eating more food. This increase in food intake is counterbalanced by an increase in energy expenditure. Our present goals are to understand the mechanisms in the body which change in order to increase energy expenditure and reduce energy storage in these mice. One of the primary questions is: Is the ASP acting at the level of the brain (centrally) or peripherally (on adipose and muscle)?  We will also determine the effect of providing too much ASP on the mice: we hypothesize that this will result in increased fat storage and can lead to problems in insulin sensitivity (important for sugar regulation) as well as inflammatory response (abnormal immune activation). We are using a combination of animal studies and genetic analysis to identify the sequence of steps involved. These studies will help us to understand the regulation of fat storage in humans, and future studies may allow us to design pharmacological compounds to control obesity and reduce its profound health consequences.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigations of low energy electron damage to cellular constituents: application to Chemoradiation therapy.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMOLECULAR DAMAGE; BIOMOLECULES; CANCER TREATMENT; CELLULAR MOLECULES; CHEMORADIATION THERAPY; CONCOMITANCE; DNA DAMAGE; ELECTRON SPECTROSCOPY; ELECTRON STIMULATED DESORPTION; GOLD NANOPARTICLES.; LOW ENERGY ELECTRONS; RADIATION DAMAGE; RADIOSENSITIZERS; RADIOTHERAPY; SECONDARY ELECTRONS
Abstract-Résumé: In the battle against cancer, clinicians are constantly seeking innovative strategies to expand treatment modalities.  Among the different strategies to improve therapy, the combination of drugs with radiation has had a strong impact in achieving better tumor treatment. This combination increases the amount of harmful products that can kill cancerous cells.  Our group has recently shown that the majority of these products are generated by secondary low electrons, which are produced by the primary radiation as it enters the cancer cells. In other words, we now understand more precisely how radiation destroys those cells. Within our research program, we will apply this new knowledge and comprehension to radiotherapy combined with chemotherapy. We will investigate the damage caused by low energy electrons to vital cellular constituents, when in these latter we incorporate new radiotherapeutic agents or drugs which are presently (or will be) used with radiotherapy.  Our results will be applied to the development of improved therapeutic modalities for the treatment of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study of the mechanism of secretion of calprotectin
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CELL CULTURE; CYTOKINE; ELISA; INFLAMMATION; SECRETION
Abstract-Résumé: A new hereditary syndrome called hypercalprotectinaemia has been recently described. It is characterised by the extremely high concentration of a protein called calprotectin in the serum. Patients with this syndrome suffer from anemia, diffuse joint pain and frequent infections. Works from our laboratories indicate that calprotectin participates in the development of autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn disease.   Preliminary results indicate that hypercalprotectinaemia is not due to the overproduction of calprotectin, but rather to its hypersecretion. Sadly, we know very little of the mechanism of secretion of calprotectin. This research project is aimed at investigating the mechanism of secretion of calprotectin. We will compare the mechanism of secretion of calprotectin to that of IL-1 alpha and IL-1 beta, two cytokines presumed to be secreted via similar alternative secretion pathways.  Results from these studies will provide clues as to the cause of hypercalprotectinaemia. They will also indicate new ways to target calprotectin which could benefit people living with autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of ErbB2-14-3-3 sigma signaling axis in cancer and development
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL POLARITY; ERBB2; METASTASIS; TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: The development of breast cancer involves the coordinate loss of genes that negatively regulate the capacity epithelial cells to divide termed tumour suppressors and the elevated expression of other gene termed oncogenes that promote epithelial cell division. The major objective of this proposal is to investigate the role of 14-3-3 sigma tumour suppressor in breast cancer development. Using a well defined mouse model of human breast cancer, we hope to elucidate the molecular basis for the ability of this tumour suppressor to stop breast cancer cells from dividing.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of FUS in neurodegeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: INCLUSION BODIES; KINASES; LIVE CELL IMAGING; NEURODEGENERATION; SITE DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; STOCHASTIC COMPUTER MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: In the brain misfolded and damaged proteins accumulate with age or as the consequence of mutations in inherited disorders such as Huntington's disease.  A hallmark of many forms of human neurodegenerative disease is the formation of inclusion bodies within neurons; these structures are thought to represent concentrations of misfolded proteins that have been sequestered away from other cellular constituents.  We have recently shown that a protein called FUS becomes concentrated into such inclusions, and this may have deleterious effects on cell survival.  We propose to study this process using live cell imaging and computer modelling.  We will identify the signalling pathways that impinge on FUS and determine if these pathways can be therapeutically manipulated.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the Dynamics of Large Ribonucleoprotein Complex Maturation
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY CHROMATOGRAPHY; BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL BIOLOGY; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; FLUORESCENT MICROSCOPY; PROTEOMICS; RIBONUCLEOPROTEIN MATURATION PATHWAYS; RIBOSOMES; RNA; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: One of the central tenets of biology is that DNA makes RNA, which then makes protein. The DNA sequence in genes is copied into a messenger RNA, whose encoded information is then read by ribosomes, the cellular protein translation machinery, and used to produce proteins. Ribosomes consist themselves of RNA and proteins, and the communication of correct DNA-encoded information, does not only depend on proper conversion of a genes sequence into messenger RNA, but also on the presence of functional ribosomes within cells. Ribosome biogenesis is the process of making ribosomes and involves the coordinated function of over 200 proteins in the synthesis and processing of four ribosomal RNAs, as well as assembly of those ribosomal RNAs with the ribosomal proteins. Incorrect processing and assembly of ribosomal RNAs, which comprise the catalytic part of the protein translation machinery, can result in serious diseases such as various cancers, hematopoietic diseases, and even Altzheimer's Disease. Understanding the molecular mechanisms that define the order of maturation events during ribosome biogenesis is therefore of great interest and importance. The main aim of the proposed research is to study the dynamic changes that take place during the maturation of ribosomal RNA-protein complexes in the unicellular eukaryotic model systems Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which will allow us to gain insight into how the ordered assembly of molecular interactions controls the regulation of ribosome maturation. Since ribosomes and their biogenesis have been highly conserved during evolution, the results from this study will be used in the future to understand how ribosome biogenesis events can affect the development of certain diseases as well as the fate of cells and organisms as a whole.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using the Internet for Self-management and Monitoring Patients with Heart Failure at a Distance
Keywords-MotsClés: HEART FAILURE; INTERNET; TELEHEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is the result of the heart not being able to pump blood. Heart failure is becoming an increasing burden to Canadians and health care. In recent years, the number of hospital admissions due to heart failure and its costs has increased. Many hospital admissions due to heart failure can be prevented through patient self-management (patient awareness of how they feel). Clinics that help patients with self-management result in less hospital admissions and improved patient quality of life. Patients with heart failure who live in smaller urban and rural areas do not have access to these special heart failure clinics. Therefore, patients with heart failure in smaller urban and rural areas do not receive the same health care.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; BIOLOGIE MOLÉCULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Artificial zinc finger transcription factors targeting the utrophin promoter as a potential therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENO-ASSOCIATED VIRUS; DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; DYSTROPHIN; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; UTROPHIN; ZINC FINGER
Abstract-Résumé: In Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), repeated cycles of muscle fiber destruction lead to progressive paralysis and death. The basic cause of this is the lack of an essential protein located at the surface membrane of muscle fibers, due to a mutation of the dystrophin gene on the X chromosome. A promising approach to the therapy of DMD is the transfer into muscle fibers of a normal dystrophin gene. Another approach to DMD therapy is a substantial increase of an analogue of dystrophin, the protein utrophin, so that it becomes present throughout the surface membrane of muscle fibers, instead of its normal, very restricted localization. Several pieces of evidence in mouse and dog models of DMD indicate that a substantial increase of the amount of utrophin will decrease or eliminate muscle fiber damage caused by lack of dystrophin. We have previously published a means of directly increasing the amount of mouse utrophin using proteins called artificial transcription factors. In this proposal, we will use the same approach to design artificial transcription factors which target the human utrophin gene in order to increase the amounts of human utrophin. It is hoped that these may eventually be used as part of therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Serotoninergic mechanisms in depression and its SSRI treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: 5-HT1A RECEPTORS; CELLULAR AND SUBCELLULAR LOCALIZATION; DEPRESSION AND SSRI ANTIDEPRESSANTS; INTERNALIZATION; SEROTONIN (5-HT); SEROTONIN TRANSPORTER (SERT)
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a heavy burden for individuals and society. The brain neurotransmitter serotonin (5-HT) is incriminated in this disease, and drugs that block its re-entry into 5-HT nerve cells, so-called  SSRIs, are commonly used as antidepressants. Yet, little is known of the neurobiological bases of the depressed state, and especially of the molecular mechanisms underlying the efficacy of SSRI antidepressants. We will therefore investigate, in rat models of depression, the subcellular localization of two proteins which determine the activity of 5-HT neurons: the 5-HT1A receptor regulating their firing and release, and SERT, the 5-HT transporter on their plama membrane and primary target of SSRIs. Both proteins will be visualized by immuno-electron microscopy, before and during a chronic treatment with the prototypic SSRI, fluoxetine (Prozac®, and after its cessation. In each condition, the functional state of 5-HT1A receptors will be assessed by examining their capacity to translocate from the surface (membrane) to the inside (cytoplasm) of 5-HT neurons (internalize) when activated with a selective agonist (8-OH-DPAT), and that of SERT by measuring its relative amount on the membrane versus the cytoplasm of 5-HT neurons. Behavioral tests performed in the same animals will allow to correlate observed changes in the functional localization of 5-HT1A receptors and SERT with the behavioral responsiveness to the treatment. Signalling molecules presumably involved in the internalization of 5-HT1A receptors will also be investigated. Such novel information on key parameters of 5-HT function in depression as well as under and after SSRI treatment should help to develop better antidepressant treatments, and also prompt further brain imaging studies eventually applicable to the early diagnosis and therapeutic management of the depressed state in human.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARgamma) in cartilage development and osteoarthritis in vivo
Keywords-MotsClés: CARTILAGE; CHONDROCYTES; INFLAMMATION; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PPARGAMMA; PTEN/AKT PATHWAY
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is commonly described by joint pain and reduced joint movement associated with narrowing of joint space, cartilage destruction and changes in bone formation. It is a leading cause of disability in Canada with economic expenses close to $22 billion in Canada. With increasing life expectancy, OA is a major clinical concern. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms by which OA can be stopped remains to be determined. Our animal and cell based studies suggest that PPARgamma (a biological factor) is an attractive target for the treatment of OA. Activation of this biological factor by certain drugs such as rosiglitazone (FDA approved anti-diabetic drug) has been shown to reduce inflammation and symptoms related to OA in animal models. However, one of the key problems of these drugs is that they activate not only PPARgamma but also other variety of factors resulting in serious side effects in patients such as heart attack and stroke. Since these drugs activate other factors, the exact role of PPARgamma in cartilage development and in OA is unknown. Therefore, this study for the first time will investigate the specific role of PPARgamma in cartilage development and OA using mice in which PPARgamma is genetically absent only in the cartilage and then we will compare mice data to cartilage samples collected from normal human and OA patients and specifically answer the following questions: (1) Does PPARgamma control growth and development of the cartilage? (2) Does PPARgamma control cartilage damage observed during OA? (3) Does PPARgamma inhibit inflammation and production of harmful mediators which destroy the bone and cartilage during OA? I anticipate that this study will show that PPARgamma is the key target likely to control inflammation and damage to bone and cartilage observed in OA. Therefore, this project has the potential to generate new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of OA and other forms of arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Natural Antisense Transcripts in Silencing Transforming Growth Factor Beta Regulated Genes in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LEUKEMIA; CYCLIN-DEPENDENT KINASE INHIBITORS; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; HISTONE H3K9 METHYLATION; HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; NATURAL ANTISENSE TRANSCRIPTS; TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR BETA
Abstract-Résumé: Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-B) is a hormone that is required for regulating blood cell production by controlling cell growth, death, and maturation. Inactivation of TGF-B regulated genes plays a key role in the development and abnormal growth of leukemia.   Epigenetic silencing, due to modifications of DNA and histone proteins around which the DNA winds, is one mechanism cancers lose the ability to activate genes. p15 and p21 are TGF-B regulated genes that instruct cells to stop growing and are activated by TGF-B in normal cells but not in cancer cells. Recently, large RNA molecules, referred to as natural antisense transcripts (NATs), have been implicated in epigenetic silencing of p15 and p21. We showed that TGF-B fails to activate p15 and p21 but that the response to TGF-B can be regained in leukemia cells by treatment with so called epigenetic drugs that inhibit DNA methylation and modify histones. We now have preliminary data showing that by reducing the levels of p15 and p21 NATs in leukemia cells we can restore the responsiveness of p15 and p21 to TGF-B.   The objective of this proposal is to characterize the role of NATs in keeping these critical growth suppressing genes in an unresponsive state. We will use genetic engineering techniques to deplete leukemia cells of p15 and p21 NATs and then characterize these effects on DNA methylation, histone modifications, gene activation, interaction with epigenetic drugs, responses to TGF-B, and leukemia cell growth.  Understanding the role of NATs in epigenetic silencing of TGF-B regulated genes is essential for developing therapies to restore TGF-B responsiveness and thereby treat leukemias. This knowledge is vital for designing new treatment strategies to re-express individual genes silenced by epigenetic mechanisms in leukemias. As these disease mechanisms are likely to be fundamental to cancer cell biology, the insights gained from our study are likely to have broad applicability to other cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding DNA end fate
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; DNA DOUBLE-STRAND BREAKS; SACCHAROMYCES CEREVISIAE; TELOMERES
Abstract-Résumé: The overall objective of this project is to understand how cells protect their chromosomes.Acquiring this knowledge is critical to understand how normal cells usually prevent the mutations that promote the formation of cancer. Dr. Durocher proposes to use the baker's yeast as a more rapid and simpler system to discover basic mechanisms that operate within the cell to protect the integrity of chromosomes. The project builds on Dr. Durocher's discovery of six genes that enable cells to make mistake in the repair of broken chromosomes. Dr. Durocher proposes to understand how these six genes work and how one could counteract their action.

TitreApplicationTitle: The S100A8/A9-RAGE Axis in Airway Inflammation, Hyperresponsiveness, and Remodeling
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY REMODELING; AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE; ASTHMA; MOUSE MODELS OF ASTHMA; NEUTROPHILS; RAGE
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease that affects ~12% of children and ~6% of adults in Canada where disease occurrence has nearly doubled in the past two decades. In most patients symptoms can be controlled by common therapies such as steroids. However, 15% of patients are "difficult-to-treat", being resistant to steroid control, and exhibit a severe asthma phenotype. Notably this patient subpopulation accounts for well over 50% of asthma health care costs. Our project examines a unique protein complex called S100A8/A9 released by neutrophils, which are inflammatory cells that excape the bloodstream and populate the bronchial airways of severe asthmatics. We will study the effects of the S100A8/A9 protein on human airway cells that contribute to disease worsening over time. We will use human lung cell cultures and mouse models of "asthma" to assess the role of S100A8/A9 in airway inflammation, lung function, and cell responses. We will also determine how these effects occur by examining whether a specific receptor for S100A9/A9, called RAGE, is involved. Ours will be the first study examining these proteins in allergic airway inflammation, thus they have potential to uncover new means for future treatment of asthma, particularly in those patients that suffer from difficult-to-treat severe disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular mechanisms of distal renal tubular acidosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; EPITHELIAL CELLS; KIDNEY DISEASE; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; MUTAGENESIS; PROTEIN BIOSYNTHESIS
Abstract-Résumé: The kidney is our body's filter that ensures we get rid of all waste products, while retaining vital components. One vital molecule is bicarbonate, which we must retain to compensate for the acid produced while processing food. Inside the kidney, a specialized pump ensures bicarbonate reabsorption. Some people are unable to properly retain this precious bicarbonate because the bicarbonate pump in their kidney is not working properly, thus bicarbonate is expelled instead of reabsorbed. As a result, these children and adults produce kidney stones, experiencing difficulties to thrive, and developing bone disease. Our goal is to understand why these specialized pumps do not function properly, with the aim to further develop strategies to better the lives of these patients. We can study these defective bicarbonate pumps in cells, which behave just like those in our kidney to determine if the disease appears because these dysfunctioning pumps are targeted to the wrong place or because they are unable to function properly in these cells. Our studies will tell us how these pumps work in our body to keep us healthy and how defective pumps cause kidney diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Sarcolipin in Thermogenesis, Diet-induced Obesity and Glucose Intolerance
Keywords-MotsClés: CA2+ PUMP; INDIRECT CALORIMETRY; INSULIN SECRETION; METABOLIC RATE; MUSCLE GLUCOSE UPTAKE; SARCOLIPIN; SKELETAL MUSCLE; TRANSGENIC MOUSE
Abstract-Résumé: We are currently facing an 'obesity epidemic' worldwide. Promoting inefficient metabolism in muscle represents a potential treatment for obesity and its complications. Muscle contraction and relaxation are energy-dependent processes that are regulated by Ca2+. A major aim of this research is to determine if altering Ca2+ cycling efficiency in muscle has significant effects on metabolic rate and susceptibility to obesity and type II diabetes. Ultimately, understanding the link between Ca2+ pump energetics in muscle and obesity could lead to the development of new drugs that will reduce susceptibility of those most likely to develop obesity and other related metabolic disorders such as diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Therapeutic properties of the innate immune response by microglia
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUVANTS; BRAIN REPAIR; CELL PROLIFERATION; MICROGLIA; MOUSE MODELS; NEUROPROTECTION; NEW DRUGS; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Microglia are the main resident immune components of the complex cellular structure of the brain. These cells react quickly to pathogens and injuries, they accumulate in degenerating regions and produce a wide variety of inflammatory molecules. Together these phenomena have generated actively debated concepts regarding their exact roles and whether they have beneficial or detrimental effects. These obviously depend on the models, context and origin of microglia.  Others and we have contributed to unravel numerous neuroprotective roles of microglia, although they may create an environment that is highly toxic to brain elements when they do not receive appropriate inhibitory cues.  One very interesting potential therapeutic avenue is to activate these cells to better clear pathogens, cell debris and toxic substances that are produced in acute injuries and chronic diseases.  Such a natural immunotherapy by microglia would have the advantage to respond quickly, efficiently and more specifically than conventional approaches. The essential objective of this grant renewal is to use new drugs to regulate the innate immune response in the brain toward neuroprotective properties. This work should help us developing more innovative therapeutic strategies to help repairing the injured brain and ultimately find cures for brain diseases, which are desperately needed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Purinergic signaling and the role of enteric glia in the enteric nervous system in intestinal inflammation.
Keywords-MotsClés: COLITIS; ENTERIC NERVOUS SYSTEM; INTESTINAL INFLAMMATION; PURINERGIC SIGNALING; SYMPATHETIC NERVOUS SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: After eating, food is digested in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.  The process of digestion requires the food to be moved along from the stomach and through the intestines, because absorption of nutrients takes place at various points along the length of the gut. What is left after digestion has to be removed or the system becomes blocked.  The movement of digestive contents is very carefully controlled; too fast, and digestion is not complete and nutrients are wasted, too slow, and there is the risk of blockage and excessive growth of bacteria that live in the gut.  The control of gut movements is exercised by a rich system of nerves called the enteric nervous system or 2nd brain, because it is so large and complex. Nerves do not work alone.  They require support from special cells called glia, which form a network around the nerves.  Through my research, we know that nerves communicate with the glial cells by releasing substances called chemical messengers.  This nerve-glial communication is important for the system to work effectively.  This chemical communication appears to go wrong when the gut is diseased.  In fact, some of the symptoms of gut diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), may occur because of inadequate communication between nerves and glial cells in the gut.  We propose to study one of the most important chemical messengers called ATP that is used in the dialogue between nerves and glial cells.  We will study it in normal tissues in order to understand how the healthy gut behaves. Then we will study this chemical messenger (ATP) in animals that have been treated to give them a condition like IBD.  We do this in order to understand how the chemical signaling is altered when the gut is diseased.  These studies will give us new insights into the chain of events that leads to the development of GI disease. The new knowledge that we gain will also be used to develop better treatments for GI disorders, including IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effects of obesity on the immune response to infection: mechanisms and sites of action
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOKINES; FEVER; IMMUNE RESPONSE; IMMUNOASSAYS; INFECTION/INFLAMMATION; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is now considered to be a major global health issue mainly because of the number of diseases with which it is associated. These include cardiovascular diseases such as high blood pressure and, metabolic ailments, which include diabetes. In addition to the suffering caused to individuals from these illnesses their treatment and management presents a considerable socioeconomic burden.  Investigating the causes of the diseases associated with obesity would be of great benefit in designing new treatments. One factor common to the diseases documented in obese individuals is the presence of background inflammation. This appears to be linked to an abnormally high  production of inflammatory immune mediators such as those belonging to the cytokine family. Although associated mainly with circulating blood cells, it is now well established that white fat, which increases dramatically in obesity, is a very important source of these mediators. Importantly, this tissue is now known to present an important target for invading pathogens such as bacteria which act on fat cells to cause the production of cytokines and their subsequent release into the circulation. This results in further inflammation and contributes to the many diseases associated with obesity. In the present proposal we will investigate the mechanisms regulating the inflammatory response in obese rodents subjected to infection with bacterial pathogens by trying to identify the mediators involved and their target organs or systems. By doing this we will establish the link between obesity, the immune system and its role in the development of the documented health risks associated with the chronic increase in body weight and fat mass.

TitreApplicationTitle: Développement de nouvelles stratégies thérapeutiques pour enrayer la dissémination métastatique et les douleurs chroniques consécutives au cancer du sein
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALGESIQUES OPIOIDERGIQUES ET NON OPIOIDERGIQUES; DOULEURS CHRONIQUES; IMAGERIE MEDICALE; METASTASES OSSEUSES; QUALITE DE VIE; RECEPTEURS COUPLES AUX PROTEINES G
Abstract-Résumé: Malgre les progres constants accomplis dans la detection precoce et le traitement chirurgical des tumeurs primaires, la mortalite des patientes atteintes du cancer du sein depend de plus en plus de la formation de metastases osseuses. Apparaissant chez 75% des patientes, cette dissemination vers l'os est source de douleurs osseuses importantes et est a l'origine d'une alteration considerable de la qualite de vie. Le but de notre equipe, aux expertises multidisciplinaires, est de rechercher de nouvelles therapies pour traiter efficacement les douleurs osseuses et enrayer la propagation des metastases au sein de l'os et enfin de developper de nouveaux biomarqueurs pour leur detection precoce. Avoir le cancer ne devrait pas necessairement signifier vivre dans la douleur. Pourtant, plus de 50% des patientes souffrant d'un cancer des os recoivent des medications inadequates et ne sont pas soulagees par les traitements antalgiques actuels. Plus grave encore, certains analgesiques, tels que la morphine, conduisent a l'apparition d'effets secondaires et favorisent meme la dissemination des metastases a l'os. Nous testerons sur un modele animal de cancer osseux l'efficacite de nouvelles classes de molecules pour les traitements prophylactique et palliatif des douleurs osseuses. Dans la mesure du possible, il est preferable de soulager la douleur en traitant le cancer. Nous etudierons donc, en utilisant des techniques d'imagerie de pointe, l'impact de ces nouveaux composes sur la progression tumorale et sur le metabolisme de l'os. Detecter de maniere precoce la presence possible de metastases constitue egalement une etape cle du traitement du cancer du sein metastatique. Nous examinerons si la nouvelle generation d'agents de contraste que nous avons developpee pour l'IRM peut etre utilisee comme test diagnostic pour la detection precoce et l'etablissement d'un pronostic favorable dans le traitement des metastases osseuses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies on novel anti-tuberculosis agents
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBACTERIAL DRUGS; ANTIMICROBIAL AGENTS; CHEMOTHERAPEUTIC AGENTS; DRUG THERAPY; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY
Abstract-Résumé: Incidence of tuberculosis (TB) has been increasing in recent years posing a major global health challenge. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), TB kills more adults per year than any other single pathogen worldwide. Close to 5000 people die from TB every day. TB is the most common infection among people living with HIV/AIDS, leading to killing of one of every three of them. A disturbing fact is that TB is the only opportunistic infection of HIV (and other immunocompromised patients), which is a public health threat to people they contact as it spreads by aerosol through coughing, laughing and sneezing. Each individual with infectious TB is estimated to infect 10-14 more individuals per year. WHO has spotlighted that TB could become a major epidemic worldwide including North America and Europe if not controlled. Most alarmingly, multi-drug resistant TB (MDR-TB) with a mortality rate of ~89%, continues to rise worldwide. Further, deadly new extensively-drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) with 100% mortality among HIV/AIDS and non-HIV people, has put this disease at a top priority. XDR-TB has been reported in 45 countries including United States, Japan, Canada and Europe. XDR-TB is virtually incurable. There is a real unmet need to discover novel anti-TB drugs. We have made innovative discovery of new classes of compounds, which exhibit potent activity against various pathogenic mycobacteria and drug-resistant strains, and would work by a novel mechanism distinct from the current drugs. In the proposed work, we will investigate anti-mycobacterial properties of these promising molecules in cultures and in animal models. The proposed studies will contribute significantly to the knowledge and understanding of new approaches for the treatment of TB infections. Promising agents may emerge from these studies, which could then be developed as a new generation of drugs for TB and MDR/XDR-TB to improve the life expectancy and quality of life of infected people worldwide.
