NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: MMP-7: Key mediator in hypertension and heart disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: GROWTH FACTOR; HYPERTENSION; HYPERTROPHY; MMPS; SIGNALLING; VASCULAR TONE
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory studies hypertension, a disease that affects millions of Canadians (close to 30% of all adults). Characterized by sustained high blood pressure, hypertension is accompanied by heart disease leading to heart failure. Since hypertension can be lethal, but has no obvious symptoms, it is often called the silent killer. Previous discovery of factors such as the hormones angiotensin II and adrenaline which, in high levels, cause hypertension has paved the way to important anti-hypertensive drugs. These drugs include the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (the well-known ACE inhibitors) and adrenaline receptor blockers (best known as alpha or beta blockers). Although these drugs are highly specific, they can fail when the disease is caused by different or by multiple pro-hypertensive hormones. Drug combinations have side-effects. In the 21st century, over 60% of all treated individuals still do not meet current treatment goals and are at risk of heart disease. These facts underscore the need for better knowledge of the mechanisms of pro-hypertensive hormones and how they cause hypertension and heart disease. Interestingly, research from my laboratory suggests that many pro-hypertensive hormones work through rather similar mechanisms. Molecular scissors (also known as proteases with names such as MMP-2, MMP-7 and ADAM-12), which are specialized in cleaving cell proteins, work downstream of pro-hypertensive hormones. Therefore, we propose to address some very important questions such as: 1) Do different pro-hypertensive hormones cause hypertension using the same proteases? 2) Do these proteases take turns to work? Do they work together? How do they regulate each other? For example does MMP-7 somehow assist MMP-2 and ADAM-12 to cause hypertension and affect the heart? 3) Which protease(s) is a good target to treat hypertension and the accompanying heart disease, when the causes of these diseases are complex or unknown?

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional networks in trophoblast stem cell development
Keywords-MotsClés: ENHANCER ACTIVITY; GENE REGULATION; STEM CELL; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; TRANSCRIPTIONAL NETWORKS; TROPHOBLAST
Abstract-Résumé: Embryonic stem (ES) cells are a very powerful tool for the development of cell-based therapy and for understanding early human development. They are cells that can make every cell type of the body. However, they are derived from a stage of development, the blastocyst, when other cell types are set aside to make the placenta and other supporting tissues for the fetus. In the mouse, trophoblast stem (TS) cells arise from the blastocyst and give rise to most of the placenta. It is important to understand the genetic regulation of TS cells, if we are to understand better the problems of pregnancy caused by trophoblast deficiencies. And it is important to understand the genes that make sure that ES cells do not diverge into TS differentiation, in order to better control pluripotency and the production of induced pluripotent stem cells. Building on our studies of genes necessary for TS formation and maintenance in the mouse, we will undertake genome-wide approaches to identify the core TS regulatory networks and their interrelationship to the pluripotent networks. We will mine this dataset for putative novel regulators of TS cell development and differentiation and test their function. Study of mouse TS cells is uniquely positioned to provide new insights relevant to human stem cell development and reprogramming, since only in the mouse is it currently possible to compare and contrast lineage decisions in different blastocyst cell lines.  These studies will provide the initial data on which to build the interaction networks that drive lineage development in both mouse and human development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protein transport into and across cellular membranes
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; FLUORESCENCE PROTEINS; GTP BINDING PROTEINS; HIGH CONTENT SCREENING BY FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; HUMAN CELL LINES; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; PROTEIN TARGETING; RNAI; YEAST GENE DELETION LIBRARY
Abstract-Résumé: The outer cell membrane holds cells together and creates a barrier to the outside world. The membranes inside cells enclose chemical reactions that would harm the cells. However, cells must be able to move things across these membranes and therefore complex machinery exists that inserts proteins into membranes so cells can pass signals, small molecules and other proteins across the membranes.      For many proteins, we now have a good understanding of the machinery that inserts them into membranes. However, there is a class of proteins, called tail-anchor proteins, about which we know very little. We and others have found that tail-anchor proteins are involved in a wide variety of crucial cellular processes. They have also been linked to a number of diseases states including diabetes, myotonic dystrophy, (ALS) Lou Gehrig's disease and, most relevant to this proposal, are cancer and auto-immune diseases.       To better understand these proteins, we have used bioinformatics, biochemical and cell biology approaches to identify all of the tail-anchor proteins in humans and plants. We propose to continue this work to refine our identification and assign these proteins to specific sub-classes to help understand how these proteins function. We propose testing many different variations of the sequence within tail-anchor proteins that targets them to membranes to derive a signature sequence that specifies transport to the correct membrane. We propose extending the image-based genetic screening approach we have used to study membrane assembly to identify the machinery that inserts tail-anchor proteins in membranes. Finally, we propose to study in detail the role of the tail-anchor sequence for a class of proteins involved in cancer and auto-immune diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Behavioural and neurochemical responses to acute, subchronic, and chronic intermittent stressors in relation to depression: Contribution of 5-HT, CRH and BDNF to the depressive phenotype
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; BDNF; CRH AND CRH RECEPTORS; DEPRESSION; GENETIC; SEROTONIN
Abstract-Résumé: Stressful events have been associated with several illnesses, such as anxiety and major depressive disorder. These adverse outcomes may represent a failure of adaptive biological processes when stressor experiences are prolonged and occur on an intermittent basis. Essentially, when a stressor is unpredictable, occurs on a haphazard basis and goes on for a lengthy period, our adaptive systems become overloaded and psychological disturbances may result. Moreover, just as all humans do not respond similarly to stressful experiences, it seems that some strains of mice are especially vulnerable to the adverse effects of stressors, whereas other strains are relatively resilient. The proposed investigation, which involves different strains of mice, is aimed at assessing the role of several brain chemical changes elicited by stressful events in promoting a depressive-like state as well as anxiety. It is expected that the appearance of certain chemical changes in brain will accompany stressful experiences and that these will be more pronounced in mice at risk for stress-related disturbances, but will be largely absent in a stress-resilient strain.  Through various techniques we will determine whether altering the biological effects of stressors will reduce anxiety and depression that otherwise occurs. The data obtained may provide information regarding the stressor processes leading to depression and anxiety, and may suggest biological processes that should be targetted in treating depression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of reactive oxygen/nitrogen species in normal and aberrant postnatal lung growth
Keywords-MotsClés: ALVEOLOGENESIS; LUNG DEVELOPMENT; LUNG INJURY; MORPHOMETRY; OXIDATIVE/NITRATIVE STRESS; OXYGEN TOXICITY
Abstract-Résumé: The major focus of this research is the lung of the newborn infant and the role of oxygen in regulating normal lung growth and, in excess, causing lung injury. A neonatal rat model is used to define biochemical pathways involved in normal and abnormal (injured lung) growth. This allows interventions to be developed and tested which may limit/prevent lung injury. Neonatal lung injury can be lethal or have life-long consequences, and is second only to asthma for health care costs of paediatric diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role and signaling mechanism of EAT-2, an adaptor involved in anti-tumor immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTORS; IMMUNE CELLS; NK CELLS; RECEPTORS; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: EAT-2 is a small molecule named "adaptor" that is expressed in cells of the immune system. A closely related protein, SAP, is mutated in boys suffering from X-linked lymphoproliferative (XLP) disease. Our recent work shows that the EAT-2 protein plays a critical role in the normal immune response, in particular against cancer cells or cells infected by viruses. In keeping with this, we found that mice that were engineered to lack the EAT-2 molecule have an altered capacity to eliminate cancer cells.   This grant proposal is aimed at understanding better the molecular mechanism of action and role of EAT-2 in immune cells, especially in anti-cancer responses. We hope that this work will not only improve our comprehension of the processes controlling the normal immune response, but will also help identify new ways of treating human illnesses such as cancer and viral infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of a novel function for PABPN1: the product of the oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy disease gene.
Keywords-MotsClés: CULTURE HUMAN CELLS; FISSION YEAST; FLUORESCENT IN SITU HYBRIDIZATION; GENOMICS; NONCODING RNAS; OCULOPHARYNGEAL MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; POLY(A)-BINDING PROTEIN NUCLEAR 1; POSTTRANSCRIPTIONAL GENE REGULATION; SIRNA-MEDIATED GENE SILENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Muscular dystrophies are genetic disorders that afflict more than 50,000 Canadians and for which there are currently no cures. Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (OPMD) is an adult-onset form of muscular dystrophy that is found worldwide, but that is more frequent in the French Canadian and Jewish populations. OPMD is a disorder of skeletal muscle cells that is primarily associated with eyelids drooping, swallowing difficulties, and proximal limb weakness. The underlying genetic defects of OPMD are small GCG insertions in the PABPN1 gene that expands the amino terminal polyalanine tract of PABPN1 from 10 to 12-17 residues. To date, the underlying mechanism by which short GCG insertions in the PABPN1 gene causes OPMD remains completely unknown. Furthermore, limited knowledge exists about the cellular functions of PABPN1. The objective of this application is therefore to provide better understanding about the mechanistic function of PABPN1. The central hypothesis of our research project, which is based on our preliminary findings, is that PABPN1 functions in a specialized nuclear pathway of RNA degradation. We propose to make use of two innovative and complementary experimental systems to characterize this novel PABPN1 function. The first is the yeast S. pombe, where we have identified the homolog to human PABPN1. This simple yet powerful model organism is widely used to study mechanisms of gene regulation. The second involves cultured human cells, which allow for detailed cellular studies of human PABPN1. In addition to shedding new, fundamental knowledge into the role of PABPN1 in gene regulation, our studies are expected to further the understanding into the molecular basis of OPMD. As such, our studies may ultimately address why OPMD is restricted to specific skeletal muscles, and therefore, lay the groundwork for developing much needed therapies.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN; CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of ARF proteins in breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ADP-RIBOSYLATION FACTOR; CANCER; GROWTH FACTOR; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALING; MIGRATION; PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Progression of cancer involves two important processes. First cancer cells grow at an accelerated rate and second, a proportion of them move in the body to go to different organs in order to form metastasis. In our laboratory, we refer to these events as proliferation and migration, respectively. The proposed research project aim at defining the intracellular events that are turned on in cancer cells to increase their proliferation and give the cells the ability to detach from the primary tumor and move to secondary sites. Our preliminary experiments indicate that a protein inside breast cancer cells, named ARF1, act as a switch to initiate cell proliferation and migration when cells are in the presence of growth factors. If we lower the amount of this protein in cancer cells, we totally prevent proliferation and migration. The proposed experiments will help us understand exactly how this protein works, and delineate which cellular events its activation initiate. A better understanding of the mechanisms that are altered when cell transform during the progression of cancer will allow us to design more effective anti-cancer therapies that have less secondary effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: The functional role of titin in muscle contraction
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL PALSY; MECHANISMS OF MUSCLE CONTRACTION; MUSCLE; SKELETAL AND CARDIAC MUSCLE; TITIN
Abstract-Résumé: For the past fifty years, muscle contraction has been assumed to be exclusively governed by the contractile proteins actin and myosin. However, recent experiments from our group demonstrate that titin, a structural protein so far believed to play a purely passive role in muscles, is likely to regulate active forces too. Furthermore, it is well accepted that titin functionally adapts in muscle diseases and muscle degeneration as observed for example in heart disease, such as cardiac myopathies, and in muscle degeneration associated with aging, injury, disuse and Botox treatments. In this proposal we try to achieve two goals: first, we would like to demonstrate directly how titin regulates force in contracting muscles. This will be done by quantifying titin elongations under passive (no calcium) and active (high calcium) stretch conditions, which will provide insight into titin's possible interactions with the contractile protein actin and its force and stiffness regulation in the presence of calcium. Second, we would like to identify how titin produces the dramatic passive forces measured in spastic muscles from cerebral palsy children. The experiments will be performed on single myofibril preparations that are stretched under active and passive conditions, and on isolated titin segments using atomic force microscopy. These experiments will provide novel insight into force regulation in normal and diseased (cerebral palsy) muscles and will shed light into titin's role in muscle force regulation and cardiac and skeletal muscle diseases.

ResearchClassEN: CONGENITAL ANOMALIES; DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS
ClasseRechercheFR: ANOMALIES CONGENITALES; DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES
TitreApplicationTitle: Embryonic stress response as a determinant of developmental toxicity
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE EFFECTS OF DRUGS; BIRTH DEFECTS; DEVELOPMENTAL TOXICOLOGY; STRESS RESPONSE; TERATOGEN
Abstract-Résumé: Many drugs and environmental toxicants induce a stress response.  The embryo is uniquely sensitive to insult during the time when organs are developing. We hypothesize that the ability of the embryo to respond to stress is an important determinant of developmental outcome.  Furthermore, we suggest that there are specific signaling pathways which are uniquely sensitive to stress and mediate this response.  Elucidation of the role that these signalling pathways play in protecting the embryo against insult will permit us to develop new strategies to prevent birth defects.

CommitteeNameEN: Social & Developmental Aspects of Children's & Youth's Health
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
ResearchClassEN: ATTENTION DEFICIT HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER (ADHD); MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL DISEASES
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLE D'HYPERACTIVITÉ AVEC DÉFICIT DE L'ATTENTION (THADA); TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Parenting in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION-DEFICIT/HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER; PARENTING
Abstract-Résumé: About 1 in 20 people have Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). People with ADHD have problems such as not being able to concentrate or pay attention, being impulsive, and being overactive or feeling restless. We used to believe that only children had ADHD. Now we know that ADHD occurs at all ages. Given their problems with inattention and impulsiveness, the behaviour of people with ADHD can lead to problems in getting along with their families. Although we know quite a lot about how children with ADHD get along with their families, very few studies have looked at parents with ADHD and how they interact with their children. This study is one of the first to focus on parents with ADHD. We will compare families where both a parent and a child have ADHD to families where just the child has ADHD or families where no one has ADHD. We will ask parents about their parenting strategies and relationship with their children, and we`ll observe how the parents and children get along in a variety of situations. There are two important aspects of this study. First, we will include both mothers and fathers. Second, we will measure, not only the problems that parents with ADHD have, but also the positive aspects of their parenting. For example, do parents with ADHD have more energy or empathy for their children? This study will provide critical answers to questions about the functioning of families of parents and/or child with ADHD. Once we understand how adults with ADHD meet the challenges of parenting, we will be able to design treatments that build on their strengths and support them in raising their children.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
AreasOfScienceEN: MUSCLE, BONE, OR JOINT; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; BIOLOGIE MOLÉCULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Articular chondrocyte differentiation and Osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CATENIN; DEVELOPMENT; HUMAN SAMPLES; MOUSE MODELS; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PLURIPOTENTAIL CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis, affecting over 200 million people worldwide, and about one million Canadians. This condition causes substantial pain associated with the degeneration of joint cartilage. There is no known cure for this condition, and in advanced cases it is treated with surgical replacement with an artificial joint. During normal fetal development cells change behavior to form the various tissue types making up the bones and joints. We found that a protein, called hedgehog, changes the way the cells develop so that they do not form as many joint cartilage cells. Using mice that develop osteoarthritis we found that blocking the action of hedgehog in cartilage cells also substantially reduces osteoarthritis severity.   We began investigating another protein that regulates the way the cells develop to form joint cartilage cells, called beta-catenin, and found that this protein also modulates osteoarthritis severity.   This suggests that agents that enhance the way the cells develop to form joint cartilage also will attenuate the severity of osteoarthritis.  In this proposal, we will build on this work to find other proteins that control how cells form joint cartilage during fetal development.  Proteins that enhance the ability to form these cells may also be able to be used to reduce the severity of osteoarthritis. We will test these proteins using mice that develop osteoarthritis, and using human osteoarthritis samples. This information will not only help us understand how joint cartilage develops, but will also identify novel drug therapies that can be used to reduce the degeneration associated with osteoarthritis, and help patients heal damaged cartilage.

AreasOfScienceEN: SOCIETAL & CULTURAL DIMENSIONS OF HEALTH; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH
DomainesScientifiquesFR: DIMENSIONS SOCIALES ET CULTURELLES DE LA SANTÉ; RECHERCHE SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Mobilizing New Meanings of Disability and Difference: Using Arts-Based Approaches to Advance Health Care Inclusion for Women with Disabilities
Keywords-MotsClés: EVALUATION OF ARTS BASED METHODS IN HEALTH CARE; HEALTH CARE INTERACTIONS; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE AND INTRAPROFESSIONAL EDUCATION; NARRATIVE AND ARTS-INFORMED METHODS; PARTICIPATORY ARTS-BASED RESEARCH; WOMEN WITH DISABILITIES AND PHYSICAL DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Women living with disabilities and physical differences are often represented negatively in our society and encounter a number of stereotypes about their abilities, needs, and interests. There is evidence that negative stereotypes inform the experiences that over two million Canadian women with disabilities and physical differences have with their health care providers and constitute a significant barrier to these women receiving satisfactory access to preventive and primary healthcare services in Canada. Existing studies indicate that encountering such barriers to health care resources is linked with an increased risk of mental health problems and chronic disease for women with disabilities and physical differences compared to disabled men and to their non-disabled female counterparts. In this qualitative, participatory arts-informed research project we analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of two arts-based approaches to alter and transform pervasive stereotypes, including negative cultural and medical views of body differences held by health care professionals, that contribute to health inequities experienced by women living with disabilities and physical differences. The arts-based methods we use are: i) Digital stories or autobiographical videos made by health practitioners and women with disabilities and differences; and ii) Research-based drama with health providers in community and institutional settings. These methods will be evaluated using focus groups and interviews to determine the ways that they might impact on patient-clinician interactions and enhance clinical competences thereby improving access to and quality of health care for women living with disabilities and physical differences.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanotransduction and sensory information coding
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MECHANORECEPTION; SENSORY INFORMATION; SYSTEMS ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Detection of mechanical stimuli is important in many human functions. Mechanical sensitivity underlies the senses of touch, hearing, balance and awareness of limb and joint positions. It also gives important internal feedback to organs such as the heart, lungs and stomach to control things like blood pressure, respiration rate and pulse rate. We are trying to understand the fundamental processes that allow us to detect mechanical stimuli, and also how information from such stimuli is coded and transmitted to the central and autonomic nervous systems. A special feature of our research is the use of a range of quantitative methods that engineers have developed for understanding how machines can be controlled and kept stable during rapid movements and other changes. These methods are particularly useful for understanding the time-varying properties of sensory receptors, such as the different mechanisms required for a touch receptor compared to a vibration receptor. In humans and other vertebrate animals, mechanically sensitive cells, such as those in the tips of the fingers, are too small for us to record the electrical signals produced by external stimuli near the places where these signals are first detected. Instead, we use preparations from model animals such as spiders that have large vibration detecting neurons that are well suited to these experiments. Although insects and spiders are very different animals to humans, their basic mechanisms of sensation and nervous signaling seem to be very similar. Increased understanding of how mechanical stimuli are detected should eventually create drugs and therapies that allow us to modulate crucial regulatory processes. For example, drugs that could raise the sensitivity of pressure detectors in the heart, arteries and veins would be useful for reducing blood pressure. Similar possibilities exist for respiratory function, gastrointestinal motility and muscle contraction.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and cell biological analysis of calpain: a potential therapeutic target in breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CALPAIN; CANCER; HER2 / NEU; TRANSGENIC / KNOCKOUT MICE; TRASTUZUMAB
Abstract-Résumé: In order for cancer to evolve, grow and spread, the transformed cancer cells must evade the normal safeguards that usually cause programmed cell death of transformed cells.  Then they must acquire the ability to enter the vascular system, travel to distant tissues and escape the blood vessel to establish metastatic tumors.  Calpain is an enzyme that cleaves other proteins, thereby modifying their functions.  In this way, calpain is involved in the regulation of a number of important cell functions including proliferation, survival, programmed cell death and migration.  Paradoxically, calpain can either promote or inhibit cell death in response to different toxic challenges, including many therapeutic approaches currently used to treat cancers.  The reasons for this are complex, but appear to relate to the many different roles of calpain in the cell.  Thus, calpain inhibition is predicted to have cumulatively different effects depending on the cellular context in which it occurs.  In our previous work, we have explored these apparently opposing roles for calpain in an attempt to identify specific therapeutic challenges where calpain inhibition enhances the death of tumor cells, but either protects normal cells or at least does not further sensitize them to the toxic effects of the therapy.  We have found that blocking calpain reduces the ability of human breast cancer cells to grow into tumors when transplanted into mice.  This appears to involve a requirement of tumor cells to engage a specific survival mechanism that requires calpain.  Interestingly, breast tumor cells that become resistant to a drug called trastuzumab can be made sensitive to this drug again when calpain is inhibited.  This supports our hypothesis that calpain inhibition will promote tumor cell death in response to specific therapeutic challenges.  We will pursue this observation and identify other cancer treatments that can be made more effective by combining them with calpain inhibition.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; METABOLISME ET NUTRITION
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the PGC-1 transcriptional coactivators in the regulation of breast cancer metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOENERGETICS; BREAST CANCER; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; PGC-1; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer occurs when cells divide uncontrollably. In order to proliferate, cells need a lot of energy to build all the components necessary for making new cells. It is therefore not surprising that cancer cells display metabolic reorganizations tailored for their high and rapid energy demands. However, this metabolic reorganization of cancer cells is poorly understood. The focus of my laboratory is to reveal the metabolic abnormalities, as well as the molecules driving them, during the development of the tumor state. We are particularly interested in PGC-1, key regulators of metabolism. It is known that the expression of PGC-1 is reduced in various forms of cancer. The central aim of the proposed research program is to understand the role of PGC-1 in the overall metabolic reorganization of breast cancer cells and to determine if elevating PGC-1alpha levels in these cells could limit tumour growth. Finally, we want to assess if PGC-1alpha is a potential target for the treatment of breast cancer.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: A molecular and genetic analysis of the fer proto-oncogene: A potential novel therapeutic target in cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CANCER; CELL MIGRATION; HER2 / NEU; METASTASIS; PROTEIN-TYROSINE KINASE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; VESICULAR TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a complex continuum of diseases caused by gene mutations that disrupt the mechanisms controlling normal cell proliferation and survival.  Unfortunately, many genes can be involved, which explains why cancers are so diverse in clinical behaviour and response to treatment.  This knowledge has led to the expectation that more effective treatments will come from characterizing the defective regulatory pathways in individual cancers and inhibiting key components of each of these pathways.  In practical terms this means that more effective cancer treatments will involve many therapeutic targets and a further refined understanding of how these targets regulate both normal and cancer cell behaviour.    In our previous work we have studied the function of an enzyme called FER in the hope that it might represent a potential novel therapeutic target in cancer.  We genetically engineered mice which no longer produce functional FER and found that they are overtly healthy, suggesting that humans might also tolerate inhibition of FER without serious toxicity; an important consideration for any therapeutic target.  When these FER-deficient mice were bred to a separate strain of transgenic mice which develop breast cancer, we observed a significant reduction in tumor development.  This result suggests that FER might represent a novel therapeutic target in breast cancer, and potentially other cancers as well.   In this research proposal we aim to validate the effect of blocking FER on breast tumor development and determine if it is specific to one type of breast cancer or might also apply to other subtypes.  We also learned a great deal in the previous grant term about how FER contributes to regulating cellular behaviour.  We propose to extend this analysis to further refine that understanding in order to more fully appreciate how FER inhibition might block tumor development or metastasis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Magnetic resonance imaging of epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN MORPHOMETRY; CORTICAL DYSPLASIA; EPILEPSY; EPILEPSY SURGERY; EXTRA-TEMPORAL EPILEPSY; IMAGE ANALYSIS; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI); TEMPORAL LOBE EPILEPSY
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy affects about 1% of the general population. One-third of epilepsy patients suffer seizures that do not respond to drug treatments. Uncontrolled epilepsy has devastating socio-economic consequences, is harmful to the brain and is associated with higher mortality. In these patients, there is a lesion that irritates the brain and causes seizures. Surgery is the only effective treatment for them, provided that the lesion is found. Indeed, more than 90% become free of seizures and enjoy greatly improved quality of life when the lesion is removed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has made it possible to detect lesions. However, many times, the brain abnormality is tiny and very difficult to find. In these circumstances, patients have electrodes surgically inserted inside their brain. Such procedures are time consuming and expensive as they involve prolonged hospitalizations. Moreover, in many cases, these invasive procedures are not able to find the abnormal area. This project aims at developing new MRI automated techniques for improving the detection of brain lesions. We will also devise methods to inform patients about their chance to become seizure free after surgery. Thus, our research could make surgery available to many more patients, and reduce the complexity and cost of the pre-surgical evaluation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Strategies to Improve the Efficacy of BCG
Keywords-MotsClés: BCG; EFFICACY; METABOLISM; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TUBERCULOSIS; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major worldwide health problem, which causes ~2 million deaths and 10 million new infections annually. During recent years, the situation has worsened with the advent of M. tb/HIV coinfection and the emergence of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant TB. As such, effective approaches alternative to antibiotics are urgently needed for the control of TB. BCG, an attenuated live bacterium, is currently the only available vaccine against TB. However, BCG has a limited effect against pulmonary TB in adults and disconcerting safety record in immunocompromised individuals. During the past three-year granting period, my laboratory has made significant progress in understanding why current BCG vaccines do not provide optimal protections and we have identified several molecular factors that influence the vaccine properties of BCG, including safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy. Equipped with this knowledge, my current proposal aims to improve on BCG by several novel approaches. One approach is to genetically manipulate two regulatory proteins (PhoP, Lsr2) involved in the production of multiple antigens, allowing the modified BCG to have an improved immunogenicity hence protective efficacy. Another approach is to generate a recombinant BCG overproducing a key metabolic enzyme (GlnA1), allowing the BCG to grow better within host, thus providing a longer duration of protection. I describe in this proposal a number of experiments to test these different strategies. The outcome of our study will provide novel strategies for designing more effective and safe TB vaccines to replace BCG.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - C
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE; DIABETE SUCRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional markers of neuro-retinal complications in adolescents with early type 1 diabetes.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; RETINOPATHY; STRUCTURAL IMAGING; TYPE 1 DIABETES; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 Diabetes (Juvenile Diabetes) affects children and often disrupts their vision. Twenty five to thirty years after the diagnosis of Type 1 Diabetes, loss of vision and even blindness are common. The number of children with Type 1 Diabetes is increasing. It is vital to detect eye problems early so that the best medical treatment can be given, reducing problems occurring years after diagnosis.  In Type 1 Diabetes, damage to the eye occurs in the retina. The retina is a sensory lining at the back of the eye and can be compared to the film in a camera; a damaged film results in a damaged "picture". This damage may be microscopic at first and may not be detected in a standard eye exam. If children and adolescents have Diabetes, the retina is often damaged before vision loss is apparent or the damage detected.  Over a five-year period, we will recruit and follow 145 adolescents with Type 1 Diabetes, who have had the disease for more than 5 years. Over the same 5-year period, we will also collect data from 145 adolescents who have no illness or eye problem (control subjects). We will compare the results between the data from those with Type 1 Diabetes and normal controls.  Our project will find very earliest signs of damage in diabetes. We will collect high resolution images of the structure of the retina, and test how well the different retinal cells are working. Knowledge about the best early signs of Diabetes to look for, and follow over time, will allow better treatment of Diabetes before the damage has a larger impact on vision. At the Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto, Canada, we are uniquely positioned to perform this study as we see very many young children with Diabetes. We have a world-renowned visual function testing facility and a new, state of the art, retinal imaging lab, both dedicated to the pediatric patient population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular analysis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis Signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PHOSPHOPROTEINS; PROTEIN KINASES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (mtb) is the causative agent of Tuberculosis (TB) and is considered to be the leading cause of death from a single organism in the world. Understanding how the disease works in the body is crucial for developing effective therapies to treat this deadly disease.  Mtb primarily infect human white blood cells called macrophages, which represent the first line of cellular defense against microbial invasion. Our research is focusing on understanding how Mtb senses its surroundings enabling it to adapt to the hostile environment of the macrophage. We have previously shown that a family of proteins is essential for the physiology and virulence of the bacterium.  One of the proteins, PtpA, is required for "successful" infection of macrophages. We had shown that PtpA acts by alteration of the white blood cells "normal" signaling mechanisms. Other members of this family are proposed to control key metabolic pathway in the bacterium enabling it to adapt to its host environment and to control the shift between growth and latency.  The objective of this research is to further investigate the role, and mechanism of action of this "eukaryotic-like" family of protein kinases and phosphatases. We will reveal the networking and signal transduction pathways within this bacterium and between it and the human macrophage host. By examining these internal and external signaling pathways new therapies can be sought that will eventually improve the health of millions of people worldwide that suffer from TB.

ResearchClassEN: METABOLISM AND NUTRITION; LIPOPROTEINS, LIPID TRANSPORT
ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; LIPOPROTEINES, TRANSPORT LIPIDIQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of medium-chain triglycerides on chylomicron secretion and expression of genes that regulate intestinal lipid metabolism in men with dyslipidemia associated with the metabolic syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE EXPRESSION; INTESTINAL LIPOPROTEIN METABOLISM; METABOLIC SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Insulin-resistant states such as diabetes mellitus and the metabolic syndrome are metabolic disorders affecting more than 15% of the world's population and their prevalences are on the increase due mainly to more sedentary lifestyles associated with rising obesity rates and aging of the population. Because insulin-resistant states are so closely associated with major health problems such as high blood pressure, high blood cholesterol and cardiovascular disease, they have a huge impact on the health care costs of our society. Major efforts should therefore be undertaken to tackle from a societal perspective this critical problem. Although elevated blood cholesterol levels observed in insulin-resistant states have largely been attributed to overproduction by the liver, recent studies from our group have indicated that the small intestine also contributes significantly to elevated blood cholesterol levels. In this regard, diets supplemented with medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) have been shown to exert beneficial effects on the intestinal cholesterol production in animal models. However, the effects of MCTs on the intestinal production of cholesterol and expression of genes regulating intestinal cholesterol metabolism represent key issues that have yet to be investigated in humans.  This study will allow us to investigate whether MCT intake could reduce intestinal cholesterol production in patients with the metabolic syndrome. We will also examine the impact of MCTs on expression of the major genes involved in the regulation of intestinal cholesterol metabolism. Identification of therapeutic strategies using non-pharmacologic agents such as MCTs is likely to lead to significant advances in our attempts to reduce cardiovascular disease risk in this vulnerable population.

AreasOfScienceEN: MUSCLE, BONE, OR JOINT; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH
DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; RECHERCHE SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Fixation using Alternative Implants for the Treatment of Hip Fractures (FAITH): A Multi-Centre Randomized Trial Comparing Sliding Hip Screws and Cancellous Screws on Revision Surgery  Rates and Quality of Life in the Treatment of Femoral Neck Fractures
Keywords-MotsClés: HIP FRACTURE; INTERNAL FIXATION; MULTICENTRE; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED TRIAL; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: Hip fractures occur in 280,000 Americans (over 5000 per week) and 36,000 Canadians annually. The number of hip fractures is likely to exceed 500,000 annually in the United States and 88,000 in Canada as the population ages. Hip fractures can be fixed with multiple cancellous screws or a single large screw with a plate (sliding hip screw). Experimental data suggest that multiple cancellous screws offer greater preservation of blood and supply while sliding hip screws provide greater biomechanical stability to bending stresses.  Although clinical studies suggest that a sliding screw may reduce re-operation rates, the evidence remains far from definitive. We, therefore, propose multi-centre, concealed randomized study.  Surgeons will use one of two surgical strategies in 1,500 patients who have sustained a femoral neck fracture. The first strategy involves fixation of the fracture with multiple small diameter cancellous screws (cancellous screw group). The second treatment strategy involves fixation of the fracture with a single larger diameter screw with a side plate (sliding hip screw group). Study personnel will monitor critical aspects of peri-operative care and rehabilitation. Our primary outcome is the need for revision surgery and our secondary outcomes include patient function and quality of life. We will independently adjudicate revision surgeries that occur within 2 years of the initial fixation.

NomDuComitéFR: Santé publique, santé communautaire et santé des populations 2
ClasseRechercheFR: SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL; CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: Association between allergy history, immunologic genetic variants and pancreatic cancer risk
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGIC DISEASE; CASE-CONTROL STUDY; ETIOLOGY; GENETIC VARIANTS; PANCREATIC CANCER; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Pancreatic cancer is a leading cause of cancer death and only 5% of patients survive five years. Causes of pancreatic cancer are poorly understood. There is a growing body of evidence suggesting history of allergies may be associated with reduced pancreas cancer risk. This finding is intriguing and  must be further explored to help provide insight into the causes of  pancreas cancer.  The proposed study will improve upon the previous studies and will obtain detailed information on specific allergies and medication taken for allergies. Also, it is possible that the reduced cancer risk may be due to common underlying genetic factors whereby inherited genetic variants may be associated with both increased susceptibility to allergies and reduced risk for pancreas cancer; thus, we will investigate this. We propose a case-control study design, using pancreas cancer patients (cases) (800) identified using the Ontario Cancer Registry (OCR) and persons without cancer (controls) (1600).  Recently the OCR implemented an electronic reporting system so as to obtain pathology reports (indicating cancer diagnosis) very rapidly - this is crucial for the study of fatal pancreas cancer and this will enhance our study design. Questionnaires (allergies, medications, diet, etc) will be mailed to participants along with a saliva collection kit.  DNA from saliva samples will be analysed in a laboratory to detect common variations in many immune system genes. Statistical analyses will be performed to compare the risk of pancreas cancer among persons with and without these genetic variants, and to compare, the risk of pancreas cancer among those who have allergies compared to those that have no allergy history.  Understanding the role that allergic diseases and genes involved in the immune system may play in the development of pancreatic cancer is important given pancreas cancer is extremely fatal, causes are poorly understood, and there is no screening test.

AreasOfScienceEN: NERVOUS SYSTEM; MUSCLE, BONE, OR JOINT

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the development of neural circuits involved in locomotion.
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; CENTRAL PATTERN GENERATORS; CEREBELLAR DEVELOPMENT; CONDITIONAL MUTANT MICE; MOTOR NEURON INNERVATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Our laboratory is interested in understanding how we walk. Walking requires coordinated movements from the left and right side of the body in an alternating manner. This process is regulated by the spinal cord, with input from the brain. Interestingly, a number of disorders identified as 'mirror movement disorders', in which people move both the right and left arms simultaneously, and spastic movement disorders including a 'bunny-hop gait' in some children, have given us some insights into how the nervous system controls movement. Despite this we still understand little about how the spinal cord controls movement. My laboratory uses genetic approaches, combined with molecular and physiological approaches to understand the cells and molecules in the spinal cord that control walking. The goal of our research is to understand how we walk and provide insights into how we can repair the spinal cord following injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel  functions  for p21 and cyclinD1 in TGFB-mediated breast cancer metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CYCLIN D1; P21; PROTEASOMAL DEGRADATION; SIRNA KNOCKDOWN; TGFB/SMAD SIGNALING; TUMOR METASTASIS
Abstract-Résumé: According to the Canadian Cancer Statistics, an estimated 166,400 new cases of cancer and 73,800 deaths from cancer will occur in Canada in 2008. Everywhere in the world and Canada, breast cancer is the most common cancer among women. In fact, 22,400 Canadian women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in 2008 and this is associated with a high rate of morbidity and mortality. Breast cancer has a high rate of developing osteolytic skeletal metastases, which once established, will result in bone pain, pathological fractures and death. This grant proposal is to elucidate the mechanisms of action of tumor-permissive growth factors, such as TGFB, that promote tumor metastasis. Our group recently found that TGFB increases the level of a protein, called cyclin D1. We will now investigate how this cyclin D1 protein affects cell migration, cell invasion and tumor metastasis at large in aggressive human breast cancer. Based on these finding, we will develop small antagonist compounds that will block breast cancer metastatic and osteolytic lesion development. This will open new avenues for the development of anti-breast cancer therapies and we expect the outcome to help contribute to a better survival rate and tumor remission for breast cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Histone methyltransferase-dependent regulation of T helper cell differentiation and function
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; CD4 T CELLS; CHROMATIN; COLITIS; EPIGENETICS; G9A AND SET7; HELMINTH INFECTION; HISTONE LYSINE METHYLTRANSFERASE; T CELL MEMORY; T CELL PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: The human body fights off infections by using a wide variety of white blood cells to kill invading germs ('microbes'). One type of white blood cell is a CD4 T helper (Th) cell that patrols the blood and tissues. Once CD4 Th cells encounter a foreign microbe, they can develop into one of several types of activated cells including Th1, Th2 or Th17 cells. This 'choice' is absolutely critical as each type of cell has a different function in the body- Th1 cells kill bacteria and viruses, Th2 attack worm parasites and Th17 cells control fungal infections. In addition, uncontrolled or inappropriate Th cell responses result in disease. For example, Th1 cells can cause inflammatory diseases like arthritis, Th2 cells are the main cause of asthma and allergies and Th17 cells are associated with Multiple Sclerosis. Thus, the control of this choice is critical for both killing infections and not developing diseases. The focus of this proposal is to understand how this choice is made. I have identified two molecules called G9a and Set7 that play an important role in this decision process. G9a and Set7 act by modifying other proteins and affecting their functions.  In the absence of G9a, Th cells can not become Th2 cells. This is a good thing if you have asthma or allergies but a bad thing if you are infected with a worm parasite. In direct contrast, Set7 is critically required for Th1 responses. How G9a and Set7 control this choice is completely unknown and is the major focus of this proposal. The results from these studies will shed light on this important yet poorly understood question and may identify new drug targets that could possibly aid in the treatment of asthma and other allergies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Right parietal cortex updates internal representations of space, time and intention: neurological, computational and neuroimaging investigations.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION; COMPUTATIONAL MODELING; FUNCTIONAL MRI; NEUROLOGICAL PATIENTS; PARIETAL CORTEX; UPDATING REPRESENTATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: In order to guide behaviour efficiently, the brain must create internal representations of the external environment and the organism's goals for future action. One brain region in particular - known as the right inferior parietal cortex - is exceptionally well placed to maintain and update internal representations of the external world. One crucial need in the context of an everchanging physical and mental landscape, is the need to 'update' our representations. In other words, a static representation of either the external world or an organism's goals would not be useful in guiding behaviour. The current proposal will examine the behaviour of people who have suffered injury to the right parietal cortex to determine the role played by this brain region in updating internal representations. In addition, healthy younger participants will undergo functional MRI scans that provide an in vivo look at how the brain completes various updating tasks. Finally, mathematical models of brain function will be developed that will be tested against the human data obtained in the first two projects. Together, these projects will lead to a more precise understanding of how the right inferior parietal cortex creates and updates internal representations of the world and an organism's goals for future behaviour. Developing a comprehensive model of how this brain region functions is a critical step in then creating interventions for patients who suffer damage to this region.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fate-determining mechanisms in the epithelium during fibrogenesis: the role of cell contacts
Keywords-MotsClés: EPITHELIAL-MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION; IDIOPATHIC PULMONARY FIBROSIS; INTERCELLULAR CONTACTS; KIDNEY; LASER MICRODISSECTION; LIVE VIDEOIMAGING; LIVER); MICROPATTERNED SURFACES; ORGAN FIBROSIS (LUNG; TGFBETA SIGNALING; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Organ fibrosis is an aberrant healing process or a failed attempt to repair tissue injury, which occurs as a consequence of many common disease conditions, such as long-lasting inflammation, diabetes, hypertension and drug abuse. Organ fibrosis is a devastating and ultimately lethal condition that characterizes a large variety of pathologies, including many chronic lung and kidney diseases and liver cirrhosis. It is estimated that 45% of all deaths in the western world can be attributed to some form of chronic fibrotic disease. A major common factor in these disease states is the formation and activation of a motile and aggressive muscle-like cell type, the myofibroblast (MF), which produces a tissue-destroying matrix. Recent studies from several laboratories including our own have demonstrated that MFs can derive from injured epithelial cells, through a process called epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). It is known that the disruption of intercellular contact is key trigger for EMT and thereby fibrosis, but the underlying mechanisms are not well defined. Our previous research has identified new cell fate-determining changes in the localization and expression of key proteins during EMT. We would like to know how the injury of cell-cell contacts impacts on these newly recognized mechanisms, i.e. how disruption of the coupling between cells facilitates the conversion of tight epithelial layers to loosely organized, contractile, scar-forming and destructive MFs.  We would also like to test whether these new molecular mechanisms contribute to the development of disease in animal models of lung fibrosis or in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.  We will use a variety of cell and molecular biology techniques, live video microscopy and histology to address these important questions. We hope to gain key insights into the basic mechanisms underlying organ fibrosis, and identify therapeutic targets to halt or lessen this fatal disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of the prorenin processing enzyme
Keywords-MotsClés: HYPERTENSION; PRORENIN; PROTEASE; RENIN; RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: High blood pressure affects roughly 3 out of 10 Canadians and almost every one 9of us will become hypertensive at some point in our lives. There are several effective medications to treat high blood pressure, but they don't all work as well in every patient and many of them have side effects. As a result, only 2 of 3 hypertensive patients are properly controlled by current therapy. One of the major contributors to high blood pressure in humans is a protein called renin. Renin is first made as an inactive protein called prorenin. Prorenin has to be cut by an enzyme present in the kidney to be activated. The identity of the enzyme that activates prorenin is not known and the goal of this research is to identify that enzyme. Ultimately, development of a drug that could block this enzyme might lead to a new treatment for high blood pressure.

Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD; EXERCISE; INSULIN SENSITIVITY; MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY; OBESITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: The Physical activity for OverWEight youth at Risk for type 2 diabetes (POWER) Trial  is a randomized controlled clinical trial designed to study the effects of different exercise training programs on the risk for type 2 diabetes in overweight youth.  We will recruit 120 overweight adolescents and randomly assign them to one of two six-month intervention: (1) a low intensity continuous activity arm (2) a vigorous intensity intermittent activity arm or a wait-list control group. The relevance of the project for the prevention of type 2 diabetes in youth is two-fold: (1) it will provide strong evidence for the optimal intensity of physical activity required to reduce the risk for diabetes, and (2) it will provide evidence for ta novel mechanism to explain why some youth progress to diabetes and others do not.

TitreApplicationTitle: Microvascular endothelial cell loss in pulmonary arterial hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; BMPR2; CONDITIONAL TRANSGENIC MICE; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; INFLAMMATION; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION; VASCULAR CELL PROLIFERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary hypertension is a lethal disease that often affects young women and results in high blood pressure in the arteries of the lung. Despite all available treatments, it is usually progressive, ultimately resulting in heart failure and death between 3 and 5 after diagnosis. The present research proposal seeks to define the underlying cause of pulmonary hypertension, specifically damage and degeneration of the cells lining the inner surface of blood vessels, called endothelial cells. It is hypothesized that these cells within the fragile lung blood vessels are particularly vulnerable to injury, particularly in patients that have genetic defects known to be associated with this disease. Experiments will be carried out in genetically engineered mouse models of pulmonary hypertension. It is hoped that this work will lead to more effective strategies to prevent and treat this devastating disease, particularly for families carrying the pulmonary hypertension gene.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural control of gaze using coordinated eye and head movements
Keywords-MotsClés: EYE-HEAD COORDINATION; FRONTAL LOBE AND MOTOR CONTROL; GAZE MOVEMENT; MOTOR CONTROL; NEURAL RECORDING IN ALERT MONKEY; SACCADES; SUPERIOR COLLICULUS
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple brain regions are implicated in organizing the complex activity, which regulates posture and initiates coordinated and precise voluntary movements. Our knowledge of these systems is still very limited. In the clinical environment this implies that the fundamental causes of movement disorders are not well understood. Coordinated eye and head movements, which are used to orient the visual axis towards a target of interest, represent an elegant example of how the nervous system controls simultaneously two mobile body segments. To assure accuracy in orienting to, and fixating a target, three major brain motor systems must interact: the saccadic eye movement system, the vestibular system, and the head movement system.  The neural networks in the first two systems are among the brain's best understood neural systems. This knowledge is a major advantage when studying how eye and head movements are coordinated.  The general objective of my research program is to understand how the brain creates the nervous signals that guide together the eyes and the head. The technique used will be to record the electrical activity of individual neurons and with these results to develop theoretical models of the neural networks that control head and eye movement trajectories. These models in turn can lead to a formal understanding of disorders of the vestibular and motor systems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of gut bacterial derived peptidoglycan in the induction of immune inflammation in the intestine
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; INTESTINE
Abstract-Résumé: Intestinal inflammation compromises human health and social economy. Chronic intestinal inflammation, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and chronic diarrhea, causes significant morbidity in general populations. The incidence rate of IBD is estimated at 0.5% in Canada, which has a substantial negative impact on human health and social economy and has emerged as one of the major health problems. Current therapeutic remedies for IBD are not satisfactory. Therefore, there is an urgent need for novel and more effective therapeutic approaches for IBD. On the other hand, elucidation of the underlying mechanisms of IBD also contributes to the development of novel therapeutic strategies.       Bacterium-derived factors are involved in the pathogenesis of intestinal inflammation. The most commonly accepted etiology of IBD is a loss of tolerance to luminal microflora. The distal ileum and colon are the areas with the highest bacterial concentrations in the body and represent the sites of inflammation in IBD Sartor . Rats raised in germ-free conditions do not develop colitis Sellon . Colonization of these animals with bacteria rapidly induces gut inflammation. These observations support the notion that IBD is mediated by aberrant immune responses directed at enteric microflora Packey; gut microbial components such as peptidoglycan (PGN) have a close relation with the pathogenesis of intestinal inflammation.        The proposed study will use a set of updated research technique to take further insight into the mechanism by which gut microbial components in the induction of intestinal immune inflammation that include: (1) Examination of intestinal epithelial innate defense mechanism in IBD patients; (2) investigate into the mechanism by which microbial products impair the innate defense mechanism in the gut and (3) restoration of the impaired innate defense mechanism in the intestine with immune inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging of Small Vessel Disease in Dementia
Keywords-MotsClés: DEMENTIA; DIFFUSION; MAGNETIC RESONANCE; PERFUSION; PERMEABILITY; SMALL VESSEL DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Today, up to 255,000 Canadian seniors suffer from a brain disorder known as vascular dementia. By 2031, the number is expected to rise to upwards of 675,000, primarily due to aging of our population. Vascular dementia is a complex disease that is difficult to define and diagnose. Changes to the small blood vessels in the brain (with diameters of less than 0.6 mm) represent a common element and over time these changes will result in a reduction of brain function, known as dementia. Reduction in brain function is dependent on the location and nature of the blood vessel disease. We propose to develop and evaluate new magnetic resonance imaging-based techniques that can assess the health of these small blood vessels and therefore provide important information about the potential for brain function deterioration. Our methodologies are unique as they are geared to providing quantitative measurements in the brain for variables that are implicated in causing brain changes due to early disease in small vessels. Magnetic resonance imaging is very safe and is an ideal way of repeated scanning the human brain. It uses magnetic field and radio waves, instead of x-rays, to form images. The long-term goal is to develop accurate methods for detecting small vessel disease at an early stage, thus allowing for steps to be taken to avert or delay brain deterioration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genome-wide Association Study of Childhood Obsessive-Compulsive Traits in a General Population Sample
Keywords-MotsClés: COPY NUMBER VARIANTS; EXTREME TRAIT ANALYSIS; GENOME-WIDE ASSOCIATION STUDY; OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER; QUANTITATIVE TRAITS; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISMS
Abstract-Résumé: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a common and debilitating psychiatric disorder usually beginning in childhood. Scientists are convinced that genetic factors are an important cause of OCD because OCD runs in families and is highly heritable. So far it has been difficult to find genes involved in the disorder. Genetic studies have focused on people who come to clinics for help and who get a diagnosis even though obsessive-compulsive (OC) traits are present to varying degrees throughout the population. We propose to take a novel approach to this disorder by first collecting a large sample of children and adolescents identified not in a clinic, but in the general population. From this sample we will select individuals with high (top 12%) and low (bottom 12%) scores on measures of OC traits; in other words those with the most and those with the least OC characteristics. This strategy has worked in other diseases but has never been tried in OCD. Once we find the extreme groups, we will conduct a genome-wide survey comparing high and low OC individuals. Next, we will obtain data from a second independent study of individuals with clinical OCD in order to find out if genes for OC traits also predispose to the disorder. Our approach is cost-effective and involves cutting edge genetic technology.  The proposed research has the potential to discover OCD-related genetic risk factors, which will ultimately shed light on the biological basis of a common disorder, provide insight into mechanisms of illness, enabling identification of individuals at high-risk for adverse health outcomes, and development of tailored treatments. Ultimately, it is hoped that identification of risk genes will lead to more effective treatment of OCD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Is IGF-IR Mediated Mammary Tumorigenesis Influenced by the Mammary Developmental Stage
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; BREAST CANCER SUSCEPTIBILITY; IGF-IR; MAMMARY DEVELOPMENT; SOY
Abstract-Résumé: Since breast cancer develops primarily in women over the age of 40 it is often thought that the genetic changes leading to breast cancer also occur later in life. However a number of studies have shown that alterations in hormone or growth factor levels and exposure to chemicals or radiation early in life influences the risk of developing breast cancer as an adult. One area of research that has not been explored is whether breast cancer oncogenes are more potent at particular developmental stages. Using a mouse model where the expression of a breast cancer oncogene known as the type I insulin-like growth factor receptor can be controlled by an inducing agent, we will increase the expression of this gene during embryonic development, puberty and in adults and determine the effects on mammary tumorigenesis. We will also examine whether pregnancy protects the mammary gland from oncogene-induced tumor development as observed in humans. In addition, mice will be fed soy-based diets to promote mammary gland differentiation and the ability of a breast cancer oncogene to induce mammary tumors in soy-fed and control mice will be examined. These studies will determine whether a more differentiated mammary gland is less susceptible to tumor formation and whether changes in diet can promote mammary differentiation and protect against breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functions of Related Ets Transcription Factors in B Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNE DISEASE; B CELL DEVELOPMENT; B CELL MATURATION; GENE REGULATION; TOLERANCE; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Antibodies are proteins manufactured by our immune system that recognize and inactivate invading bacteria and viruses. Antibodies are made by B cells, a type of white blood cell that resides in lymphatic tissues. B cells are made initially in the bone marrow, but then migrate to the spleen where they differentiate into different subsets. B cell differentiation is controlled by several factors including proteins called transcription factors. Transcription factors regulate gene expression. The goal of this project is to identify transcription factors that control B cell differentiation. We have preliminary evidence that three related transcription factor proteins called PU.1, Spi-B, and Spi-C are important for B cell differentiation. This work is important because the consequences of impaired B cell differentiation include diseases such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, or leukemia. Successful accomplishment of this research could lead to novel therapies for treatment of autoimmune diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Longitudinal study of brain mechanisms underlying visual working memory in children with autism
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; FMRI AND MEG; FRONTAL LOBE DEVELOPMENT; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Working memory allows the temporary storage, rehearsal and manipulation of information - keeping things 'in mind' - and relies on the frontal lobes of the brain.  The development of the frontal lobes continues into adulthood, making it the brain area most at risk for developmental disturbances.  Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have a range of strengths and weaknesses with respect to memory, but deficits in working memory are usually found, particularly with difficult working memory tasks.  Moreover, in ASD, abnormal maturation of the frontal lobes has been documented.  The link between memory impairments and frontal lobe structure and function has not been established in ASD.  We have demonstrated that we can reliably complete brain imaging in young children, including ASD children; the current project will allow us to track the development of the brain-behaviour relations using working memory tasks with several levels of difficulty. We will acquire measures of brain function (fMRI and magnetoencephalography (MEG)) and brain structure (MRI and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)) in children with high functioning ASD and age and IQ matched control children without ASD (7-13yrs), using two complementary memory tasks.  One will test working memory maintenance (the length of time one can hold items in mind), and the second will measure working memory capacity (the number of items one can hold 'in mind' at one time).  Children will be tested twice, 2 years apart to allow us to examine development over time.  This research will introduce new knowledge on brain development underlying memory functions in typically developing children and will characterise deficits in ASD children.  The results will contribute to our understanding of how the brain structure affects brain function and behaviour over childhood.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and Biological Studies of Human Ubiquitin Specific Protease 7
Keywords-MotsClés: MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN CRYSTALLIZATION; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Ubiquitin specific proteases are enzymes that remove a tag (ubiquitin) from specific proteins. These proteases are found in all eukaryotic organisms and are involved in many cellular processes including DNA repair and cell cycle progression, and their malfunction can lead to cancer. There is very little information regarding how these proteases recognize and interact with their target proteins. This research program focuses on understanding the roles of USP7, a tumor suppressor protein, in cancer, using a combination of biochemistry and structural biology. USP7 has been linked to lymphomas and carcinomas (lung and renal), however its ability to cause cancer has not been fully investigated. How USP7 interacts with specific cellular proteins and how lack of interaction with these proteins leads to cancer is being studied. The ability to better understand the structure and function of USP7 may lead to the design of anti-cancer therapeutics or cancer prevention strategies to the benefit of all Canadians.  Our research focuses on expanding this knowledge primarily by determining three-dimensional structures of proteases with their target proteins. These structures will reveal the molecular mechanism of interaction and allow for the design of drug therapies to prevent or enhance these interactions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Les troubles de comportement au féminin: évolution, facteurs de persistance et de rémission, et contribution des services
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFERENCES SELON LE SEXE; ENFANTS D'AGE SCOLAIRE PRIMAIRE; FACTEURS DE PERSISTANCE/DE REMISSION; FILLES; TROUBLE DES CONDUITES PRECOCE
Abstract-Résumé: Les troubles de comportement qui surviennent des l'enfance chez les filles sont associes a d'importants problemes de sante et d'adaptation sociale a l'adolescence et a l'age adulte, dont les troubles mentaux, la delinquance, la toxicomanie, la violence conjugale et a l'egard des enfants. Malgre leur gravite et leurs consequences potentielles, ces troubles precoces chez les filles n'ont fait l'objet que d'encore peu d'etudes pour comprendre les facteurs qui affectent leur persistance ou leur remission, en raison de leur faible prevalence dans la population feminine. Il n'en demeure pas moins que les connaissances les entourant se limitent encore souvent aux resultats d'etudes obtenus aupres de garcons, tout comme les theories qui guident le travail d'intervention aupres des enfants. Ce projet de recherche est base sur l'hypothese que l'evolution des troubles precoces des filles different de celle des garcons et peut etre plus negative en raison des niveaux de risque indiquant de plus grandes vulnerabilites individuelles et sociales chez les filles. Il propose le suivi longitudinal d'un groupe de filles et de garcons (6-9 ans) suivis a l'ecole pour des troubles de comportement afin d'etablir les trajectoires des difficultes selon le sexe et dans les facteurs associes a la presence des troubles et a leur evolution. Determiner si ces facteurs varient selon le sexe est primordial lorsque, en raison du nombre nettement plus eleve de garcons identifies avec ces troubles, ce sont surtout les caracteristiques de ces derniers qui sont determinantes dans la definition des services de sante et des services sociaux offerts aux enfants. Disposer de ces informations est donc essentiel pour differencier ces services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical Assessment of Thrombosis in Children after Heart surgery: The CATCH study
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC SUGERY; COMPLICATIONS; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; DIAGNOSIS; PEDIATRICS; THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Nearly 2000 infants are born in Canada each year with a severe heart problem. Most of these infants will need surgery at least once in their lifetime. These surgeries often require the use of an external life support system that puts these children at high risk for developing blood clots. Having a clot makes infants and children more likely to have severe immediate and longterm health problems. Unfortunately, many children with clots do not have obvious symptoms. The only way to confirm a child has a clot is by using imaging equipment that can see if the blood flow is blocked. For a number of reasons, this equipment is not used on a regular basis. In children, there is a high risk of clots not being identified and treated which can lead to even more severe long-term problems or even death.       This study will help create a regular routine for screening patients for clots. It will also identify areas for future research on clots prevention. Children will be enrolled in the study before surgery. A number of laboratory measurements will be taken during and after surgery of factors that indicate or increase the chances of clot formation. After the surgery all the children will have an ultrasound (a scan) of their full body and heart to see if they have developed a clot. They will be seen again 1-2 years after surgery at a blood clotting clinic.      Most of the existing research on blood clots is on treatment of clots and their complications once they develop. This study will begin moving research in this area toward prevention and early detection of clots. Through this study we will determine the effectiveness of routinely screening for clots, and identify factors associated with clot development. The formation of blood clots in children after heart surgery is a very serious but under-researched topic. This original study will reduce and ultimately prevent the negative effects of clots in children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the mechanisms through which Rac Isoforms regulate neutrophil chemotaxis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMOTAXIS; INNATE IMMUNITY; NEUTROPHILS; RAC; RHO SMALL GTPASES
Abstract-Résumé: Background: The microbicidal functions of neutrophils (PMN) are highly dependent on their ability to migrate from the vasculature into infected sites. This directed migration, or chemotaxis, involves two key steps: 1) compass-like sensing of the chemoattractant gradient; and 2) actin assembly in the leading lamella mediated through the actin binding protein cofilin, which drives cell migration towards the chemoattractant. Rho family small GTPases including Rac, Rho and Cdc42, are important regulators of cell migration that impact health and disease. For example, patients with a Rac2 mutation exhibit a severe PMN chemotactic defect and experience life threatening bacterial infections. Severe PMN chemotactic defects typify Rac1 and Rac2 null mice, experimental models which we developed to study Rac isoform function in PMNs.  Goal: Define how these highly homologous Rac proteins carry out their unique signaling roles during PMN chemotaxis and recruitment to sites of infection.  Significance: The transgenic mouse models and the combination of novel techniques used in this grant will permit biochemical and functional examination of the local signaling roles played by Rac1 and Rac2 and their downstream ROS activated signaling elements in actin-mediated PMN chemotaxis. Over the long-term, this knowledge will allow us to identify key downstream mediators of PMN recruitment to sites of infection and inflammation. By better understanding the signaling elements involved in the key aspects of PMN chemotaxis we will be able to translate this information into more specific and promising anti-inflammatory drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Converging circadian and arousal signaling in thalamic paraventricular nucleus
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN SLICE PREPARATIONS; CELLULAR ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; CHANNEL SUBUNIT MRNA EXPRESSION; DAY/NIGHT DIFFERENCES/RT-PCR; INTRINSIC MEMBRANE CONDUCTANCES; MIDLINE THALAMUS; PATCH CLAMP TECHNIQUES; SIGNALING; STRESS RESPONSES/ CIRCADIAN RHYTHMICITY DISRUPTION; SUPRACHIASMATIC NUCLEUS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells in living organisms contain "clock" genes that regulate cellular processes over an approximately 24 hr cycle. In mammals, these clock genes are particularly important in neurons located in a brain structure called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN). SCN receives information from the eye and, via connections with other brain centers, regulates rhythms in  behavior (e.g. sleep-wake cycles) and physiology (e.g. hormones, blood glucose) in synchrony with the solar day. This tuning of inner biology allows us to cope with the outside world. Disruption in these rhythms e.g. by shift work, travel, or sleep deprivation, is now recognized as a health hazard and a contributing factor to the development of obesity, diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular and mental disorders. Collectively, these represent an enormous burden on society. Although we now have an understanding as to how clock genes operate, we are still uncertain how SCN neurons communicate this synchrony to other brain cells. Knowledge here would help us understanding how "clock disruptors" relate to disease, and may suggest therapeutic measures. Our approach uses live brain slice preparations from the rat and single cell electrophysiological techniques to assess the mechanisms through which chemical messengers in SCN neurons communicate with neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of thalamus (PVT). Because PVT neurons are known to be sensitive to various stressors and to connect not only with SCN but also to brain areas governing arousal, mood and reward, we anticipate that this research will allow insight into the cellular mechanisms whereby the SCN clock "signaling" in brain could be perturbed by environment (e.g. stressors) and by internal (e.g. psychological) factors.
