TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the mechanisms required to regulate metabolism and tumour growth downstream of LKB1/AMPK signalling.
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; AUTOPHAGY; C. ELEGANS; CELL POLARITY; DAUER; LIPID HYDROLYSIS/METABOLISM; LKB1; PEUTZ JEGHERS SYNDROME; RNAI; TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS) is a genetic disease that makes patients succeptible to tumour growth and cancer. These patients have a 500-fold increased risk of developing cancer in the small intestine, and also in other tissues/organs. The mutation that causes this predisposition occurs in a protein kinase-a gene product that makes an enzyme which activates and inactivates numerous other proteins. This protein, called LKB1, is particularly curious because it plays multiple, seemingly unrelated roles in the cell. We do not understand how LKB1 carries out these essential tasks, nor which ones are absolutely required to block the formation of tumours but we intend to use a simple model and modern genetic and molecular approaches to resolve this problem with the hope of finding ways to better harness this activity and block tumour growth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting and understanding patterns of service utilization within children's mental health agencies
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN AND YOUTH; MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES; SERVICE UTILIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Children's mental health has been labelled the "orphan's orphan" of Canada's health care system. About 20 percent of children and adolescents have psychosocial problems (i.e., problems in with learning, behaviour, emotions, or peer interactions). We know a minority of these children receive specialized mental health treatment. Much less is known about patterns of service use. In Ontario, children's mental health centres are the main source of public, not-for-profit specialized mental health care providing care for over 150,000 children and their families annually. Using regularly collected by these agencies our study will examine how factors such as children's sex and age, parental psychopathology and child psychopathology predict patterns of service use. We will also see how these same factors predict children who have two or more episodes of care and we will explore differences in the status of children (e.g., dropout) at the end of care. We will look at patterns of use over a 4-year period among children age 4 to 11 years at the time of their first recorded visit to the centre. This study will help in the development of new models to guide treatment within the children's mental health system.

TitreApplicationTitle: GABA-A receptor plasticity in response to experimental and human epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EPILEPSY; GABA-A RECEPTORS; IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is one of the most expensive health care costs the Canadian medical health care system must bear. Nearly one third of those with epilepsy have seizures that are uncontrolled by current pharmacotherapy. For these people epilepsy becomes a life long affliction, resulting in underemployment and low living standards. The goal the this research proposal is to indentify brain abnormalities that may account for seizures and their intractability. We will use a combination of techniques that will tell us how the brain inhibitory system may be perturbed due to seizures. This will be done in both an animal model of epilepsy and in tissue that has been obtained from humans who have undergone brain surgery to treat their drug resistant epilepsy. The goal of these studies is understand how drugs fail to treat seizures and develop better strategies for the management of this important neurological disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Carotid chemoreception and sympathetic nervous activity in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD FLOW; CHEMORECEPTION; CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; EXERCISE; REHABILITATION; SYMPATHETIC NERVOUS ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is defined as a respiratory disorder largely caused by smoking and  characterized by airway obstruction. While originally considered a disease specific to the lung, typified by breathlessness with exercise, it is now appreciated that there are important secondary issues that develop as a result of COPD such as cardiovascular disease. COPD patients are almost three times more likely to die of heart failure than smokers not diagnosed with COPD, indicating that it is something specific to the disease of COPD, and not simply smoking history that is causing cardiovascular disease. COPD patients have increased resting sympathetic activity. While initially beneficial, chronically elevated sympathetic activity results in cardiovascular disease and increased mortality. Importantly, the exact cause for the increased sympathetic activity in COPD is unknown. We believe that the carotid chemoreceptors (CC) are important in regulating the sympathetic nervous system and cardiovascular function in COPD. Like heart failure, we believe that there is an increased sympathetic nervous response to exercise in COPD due to increased CC activity, which reduces muscle blood flow and decreases exercise capacity. We will perform experiments to modify CC activity at rest and during exercise to determine how this affects sympathetic activity and blood flow in COPD. Exercise training is now recognized as an important therapy for COPD. Exercise training has been shown to improve exercise capacity, quality of life and may even improve mortality in COPD; however, the physiological adaptations from rehab are not well understood. Based on previous work, we believe that exercise training will improve: CC activity, sympathetic activity and cardiovascular function in COPD. These studies will help to understand why COPD are at increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease, and help us understand how to improve functioning in COPD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving detection of disease genes involved in gene-gene and gene-environment interactions through joint modeling of the disease and a subphenotype
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOPHENOTYPE; FAMILY-BASED ASSOCIATION ANALYSIS; GENE-GENE INTERACTION; GENETIC LINKAGE ANALYSIS; GENETIC STUDY DESIGN; PSYCHIATRIC DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Most diseases with serious health impacts such as cancer, cardiovascular disease and psychiatric disorders are called complex due to the large number of genes and environmental factors that combine to cause them. For many complex diseases, comparing the frequencies of differences in the DNA sequence (called genetic variants) between patients and healthy subjects has identified genes contributing to cause them. However, the individual effects of the genes on disease risk are usually small, and researchers will need to jointly analyze other genes and environmental factors with which they interact to accurately predict individual disease risk. It is also recognized that faulty genetic variants may cause impairments associated to a disease. One way to facilitate the detection of disease genes and better understand their action is to measure various traits relevant to a disease in non-affected relatives of patients. A memory impairment in a relative of a schizophrenic patient, or an allergy in a relative of an asthmatic patient is a hint that the relative shares some but not all of the disease-causing variants with the patient. This proposal aims at developing statistical methods to use these hints of disease in two types of gene finding approaches: linkage analysis, which finds regions of the genome transmitted from the parents to their children together with an observable trait, and association analysis, which finds genetic variants overrepresented in people with a trait. The proposed methods model genetic variants in two genes or one gene and one environmental factor simultaneously, and aim the identification of variants making the difference between having the disease or merely an associated impairment. We will also compare different ways of choosing the family members to determine which ones maximize chances of finding such variants. Finding those variants will provide a better understanding of complex diseases to improve preventive and therapeutic interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The E. coli Cell Envelope Interactome: Identifying Protein Complexes Critical for Bacterial Cell Growth and Pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY PURIFICATION; BACTERIA; GENOMICS; INFORMATICS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MEMBRANE PROTEIN COMPLEX
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how all the proteins encoded by the genome of a microbe work together to form a living cell requires a complete description of the 'wiring circuits' that underlie the various fundamental cellular processes. A key feature is the tendency of proteins to interact physically to form molecular complexes that serve as molecular machines. Proteins with similar or overlapping biological roles generally belong to the same complex. Here, we propose to explore the physical interaction architecture of complexes of membrane proteins found at the outer bacterial cell envelope in the classical model bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) using powerful technology developed by our group. Our experimental approach will enable us to generate circuit diagrams for all the membrane bound proteins involved in important biological processes essential for bacterial cell growth and infection, which represent important targets for antibiotics. Since many bacterial genes are conserved across microbial evolution, the identification of the pathway architecture of E. coli should also reveal the organization of membrane proteins in other bacterial species, including pathogens. The data generated in this project will therefore serve as a valuable resource for the entire biomedical research community, and should spur on the development of new antibiotics.`

TitreApplicationTitle: A transport metabolon in the apical membrane of the proximal tubule alters sodium and water (re)absorption
Keywords-MotsClés: HYPERTENSION; MICROSCOPY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; SODIUM HOMEOSTASIS
Abstract-Résumé: Blood pressure is controlled by regulating the amount of sodium and water in the blood space. This regulation occurs in the kidney where daily 180L of blood is filtered and then 178-179L is reabsorbed back into the blood via a process that generates urine. The bulk of renal (kidney) regulation occurs in the first part of the kidney's functional unit the nephron, called the proximal tubule. Inappropriate absorption of salt and water from the proximal tubule causes increased blood pressure/hypertension. It is known that sodium and water (re)absorption occurs in this segment through a complex series of events mediated by several different membrane proteins capable of coupling water, sodium and bicarbonate movement. In order to most efficiently mediate the flux of this prodigious quantity of salt and water we propose that a physical interaction exists between these proteins. Specifically, we propose that the physical attachment, or "stickiness", of one protein to another enables the product of one transport event to be readily available as the substrate for the next, thereby enhancing the ability for this large amount of sodium and water to be absorbed. To test our hypothesis we will perform two types of studies. The first will look at sodium and water transport across kidney cell membranes (in petri dishes).  Experiments will  be performed with individual proteins and then in the presence of the other proteins we predict will increase the transport process. This will show a functional interaction between the proteins we are studying. To demonstrate a physical interaction we will use classic biochemical approaches where purified proteins are employed to demonstrate that one sticks to the other. Ultimately we will show that such a physical and functional interaction occurs in the intact functioning kidney (through the use of genetically modified mice). Identifying these interactions are fundamental to understanding and developing treatments for increased blood pressure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Echocardiographic assessment of global and regional left ventricular function using an original modality of coupled wall-fluid dynamics mapping.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL EXPERIMENTS; CATHETERIZATION; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; LEFT VENTRICULAR FUNCTION; PIV EXPERIMENTS; STRAIN RATE AND PRESSURE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in Canada and the most common cause of hospitalization. Among cardiovascular diseases, heart failure - a cardiac disorder that impairs the ability of the heart to pump sufficiently - is the most rapidly raising disorder that will impact on the lives of Canadians. Around 2% of the adult population has heart failure, although it mainly affects elderly people: 6 to 10% of people over the age of 65 years have this disorder. Heart failure affects approximately 400,000 Canadians and the number of cases is continually rising due to the aging of the population. It contributes significantly to cardiac mortality and represents an extremely costly public health problem.  A detailed examination by ultrasound imaging often reveals whether a patient has heart failure. Cardiac ultrasound is recognized as the most important investigation tool for the patient with this disease. It may provide extensive information on the abilities of the heart pump. This technique is nonetheless subject to important limitations and further technical development is still necessary.  The objective of this project is to develop a new ultrasound imaging technique that can provide a deeper look at the cardiac mechanics. This technique will take account of the blood flow within the principal cardiac chamber as well as the properties of the cardiac wall. New information derived from this novel imaging modality will allow the physician to assess the heart pump ability rapidly and objectively.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brain anatomy in auditory and motor learning: predispositions and plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY PROCESSING; DEVELOPMENT; LEARNING; MOTOR PROCESSING; STRUCTURAL NEUROIMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: The brain is the source of all behavior, but in turn is modified anatomically and physiologically by the behaviors it produces. In the planned research, we propose to understand the relationships between anatomical brain structure and behavior in the context of learning. Musical production and perception provide a particularly good model system to understand these interactions because they involve complex yet highly determined movements that produce organized sequences of sound. We will study the relation between brain structure and the ability to learn these auditory-motor processes by considering three major influences on that relationship: the effects of explicit training, the developmental stage at which the training takes place, and the influence of individual differences in pre-existing anatomical features on the behaviors of interest. The significance of this work lies in its contribution to understanding the interplay between neural structure and function in the context of learning. Our focus here is on the basic science behind these relationships; but understanding the anatomical substrates that may enhance or limit learning has potential implications for everything from pedagogy to rehabilitation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Villous Trophoblast Turnover
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC REGULATION; GLIAL CELL MISSING; IUGR; PLACENTAL DEVELOPMENT; PLACENTAL EXPLANTS; PLACENTAL INSUFFICIENCY; PREECLAMPSIA; VILLOUS CYTOTROPHOBLAST
Abstract-Résumé: A healthy placenta is critical for growth and survival of the fetus, and failure of proper placental development can lead to severe perinatal diseases, including preeclampsia (PE) and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR).  The epithelial layer of the placenta, in direct contact with maternal blood is called trophoblast and some of its functions include nutrient, gas and waste exchange as well as metabolic and endocrine activity.  The dynamic trophoblast layer undergoes tightly regulated proliferation, differentiation, fusion and apoptosis events throughout the entire gestation.  This recurrent process permits expansion of the epithelial surface are of the placenta and maintains its continuity and thus function.  Transcriptional factor GCM1 controls the balance between villous trophoblast proliferation and differentiation.  Furthermore, placental pathologies PE and IUGR are characterized by alterations in trophoblast turnover and divergent expression of GCM1.  The aim of this project is to gain further understanding of how converse expression of GCM1 in PE and IUGR contributes to their placental phenotype via genetic and epigenetic regulation of GCM1 expression.

TitreApplicationTitle: The dilated heart: insights from an animal model of left ventricular volume overload.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTORS; CELL SIGNALLING; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; HEART HYPERTROPHY; HEART VALVE DISEASES; LIFESTYLE AND DIET
Abstract-Résumé: In developping countries, heart valve diseases such as aortic or mitral insufficiency (AR and MI; regurgitation) are frequent and mostly due to endemic rheumatic fever. Immigrants to Canada from such countries should be considered at high risk of having significant rheumatic aortic or mitral valve disease. Rheumatic fever has declined dramatically in Canada but still accounts for a major percentage of cardiac morbidity in developing countries. Aboriginal Canadians are also at higher risk due to their lower socio-economic status and sometimes improper access to health care. Other causes of aortic or mitral insufficiency are either congenital anomaly, disease of the ascending aorta, degenerative or secondary to an infarct (MI). These valve diseases cause heart dilatation which can sometimes go unnoticed for years before apparition of symptoms such as shortness of breath, fatigability and eventually heart failure if the valve is not surgically replaced by a prosthesis soon enough. Our goal is to better understand in a rat model how the heart adapts to these valve diseases, what are the mechanisms of heart dilatation and why the heart muscle capacity of forming enough energy to fulfill its pump function decrease over time. Our animal model is also unique in giving us the capacity to study a pre-heart failure situation and the slow decline towards this state. It offers us a window to observe over months the mechanisms leading to heart failure in a controlled fashion. In this proposal, we intend to study more in details how the dilated heart manages the formation of its energy to fulfill its function and how lifehabits changes (exercise or diet) can alter positively or not this parameter.

TitreApplicationTitle: NK cell receptor-ligand interactions in recognition of tumour cells and infected targets.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CYTOMEGALOVIRUS; GENE REGULATION; INFECTION; INNATE IMMUNITY; NATURAL KILLER CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The innate immune system protects us from bacteria, viruses, and cancer. Natural killer (NK) cells are innate immune cells that can detect and destroy infected and tumour cells. How NK cells do this requires understanding of the molecules they use to sense what is harmless or dangerous, and how these molecules assist in the decision to ignore or kill the diseased cell. We have identified a receptor on NK cells, called NKR-P1B, that binds to a protein, named Clrb, on all other cells. Because the NKR-P1B receptor turns off NK cells, normal cells display the "self" Clrb protein to prevent NK cell attack, while infected and cancerous cells lose Clrb protein ("non-self") and are eliminated by NK cells. On the other hand, NKG2D is a different receptor that turns on NK cells. NKG2D binds to "danger" proteins displayed on infected and tumour cells, but not normal cells, and these "danger" flags alert the immune system and NK cells that something is wrong. The combination of receptors that either turn off or turn on NK cells provides a sensitive balance to allow NK cells to discriminate between "good" and "bad" cells. It also suggests a role for multiple NK cell receptors allowing NK cells to fight cancer and infectious disease. I propose to advance our understanding of the role of NK cells in disease, cancer, and infection by studying how NK cells "see" diseased cells. This proposal will study how NK cells use their receptors to interpret levels of different good or bad proteins, what makes these proteins go up or down on diseased cells, and how infectious pathogens or malignant tumour cells can escape this immune recognition. This knowledge could lead to therapies in cancer treatment and vaccines to control infectious disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of caspase mediated DNA damage and repair in cell differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFERENTIATION; DNA DAMAGE; GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: DNA damage is typically characterized as a negative outcome for the health and survival of all cell types.  Moreover, DNA damage is often considered a trigger event in the formation of many forms of cancer.  Despite the wealth of information demonstrating the negative consequences of DNA damage, our investigations have shown that DNA damage occurs during the normal maturation of cells and is in fact required for this process.  For example, if the occurance of DNA damage is blocked, muscle cells fail to develop.  These observations have significant repercussions for our understanding of both basic biology as well as many disease processes that have been consdiered to arise from DNA damaging events.  In the current application, we propose to continue our investigations of this novel and exciting area of research

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural basis of memory for context and association in young and older adults
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE; FUNCTIONAL MRI; HIPPOCAMPUS; MEMORY; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; STRUCTURAL MRI; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Human memory can some times be precise, accurate, and vivid but it can also be vague, hazy or absent altogether.  As  people age, their memory for experiences seems more often to fall in the latter category than the former one.  Research has  shown that while the ability for older persons to recognize when an isolated "item" - a face or a word, for instance - has been  previously encountered is relatively preserved, the concomitant ability to recover details about the context in which that item  had been embedded becomes far more difficult as people age.  In the present project we employ functional neuroimaging  techniques to investigate the neural mechanisms that support rich, detailed, and accurate memories in young and old adults.  Our goal is to define how variation in the behavior of brain systems known to be important for memory can predict how well  older adults perform on difficult memory tests.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies of alpha granule formation in human megakaryocytes and platelets
Keywords-MotsClés: BLEEDING AND CLOTTING; BLOOD; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; GFP-FUSION PROTEIN; HA-FUSION PROTEIN; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; MYC-FUSION PROTEIN; PLATELET ALPHA GRANULES; SBP-FUSION PROTEIN; VESICLE TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Platelets are the key blood cells that are involved in preventing blood loss after injury. Platelets are also responsible for chronic changes in blood vessels (atherosclerosis) and the acute presentation of heart attack and stroke. Heart attack and stroke account for approximately half of all deaths in the Western world. Platelets develop from precursor megakaryocyte cells found in the bone marrow, which are released into the bloodstream. Platelet development is poorly understood. Alpha granules are the major storage granules found in platelets that contribute to the development of atherosclerosis and blood clotting during an acute vessel occlusion. The focus of my research is to understand the development of platelet alpha granules from precursor megakaryocytes. We have previously discovered that a protein called VPS33B is essential for platelet alpha granule formation. The goals of this grant are to understand how proteins like VPS33B, interact with other proteins identified in my laboratory, to promote platelet alpha granule formation. These investigations will provide insights into the mechanisms of alpha granule formation and platelet development. This knowledge will help in the design of strategies for controlling platelet involvement in processes leading to heart attack and stroke. It may also point the way to novel approaches for exploiting the ability of platelets to carry and secrete proteins and other molecules in the treatment and prevention of disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bcl-2 Family Proteins, Cell Death and the Endoplasmic Reticulum
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; AUTOPHAGY; BAP-31; BCL-2 FAMILY PROTEINS; CALCIUM; CHAPERONS; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; MITOCHONDRIA; NAF-1; PROGRAMMED CELL DEATH
Abstract-Résumé: Elimination of cells is an important process, essential for development, maintaining normal tissue status and eliminating damaged or virus-infected cells and as a front line defense for eliminating cancer cells. The elimination of cells is programmed into the cell's DNA and pathways for self-destruction of the cell are activated in response to stress signals. Mutations that interfere with the ability of a cell to kill itself or lead to killing of otherwise normal cells has serious consequences and can result in diseases such as cancer or degenerative diseases. The Bcl-2 family of proteins are amoung the key regulators of the programmed cell death pathway. Our research aims to elucidate the function of this protein family at multiple levels. Such studies have been translated into therapy with the discovery and development of obatoclax, a drug that antagonizes Bcl-2 survival proteins. This drug is currently in clinical trials to assess its promise as a new targeted anti-cancer agent.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional studies to elucidate the role of the DOCK180 pathway in cell polarity, myoblast fusion and podocyte integrity
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTO-INHIBITION; CELL MIGRATION; CELL POLARIZATION; DOCK180; ELMO; MYOBLAST FUSION; PODOCYTE; RAC GTPASES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: DOCK180, an evolutionarily conserved protein, acts in concert with ELMO in regulating the activity of the small GTPases of the Rac family. Work in model organisms uncovered a role for these proteins in crucial developmental processes such as cell migration, myoblast fusion and phagocytosis of apoptotic cells. Yet, the mechanisms governing their activities and their biological functions in mammalian systems are poorly understood.  As such, the long-term objectives of this proposal are to (i) uncover the biological functions of DOCK180/ELMO complex in mice and (ii) decipher the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of the signaling activity of the DOCK180/ELMO complex.       We recently uncovered a central role for DOCK180 in mammalian myoblast fusion. The podocyte, a specialized cell type of the kidney, shares remarkable similarities to myoblasts. In our first aim, we will study the biological functions of two signaling pathways involving DOCK180 in the orchestration of the formation/maintenance of the kidney filtration barrier. In addition, we will pursue our studies on myoblast fusion by characterizing a putative mammalian fusion receptor. In the second aim, we propose to test the hypothesis that intramolecular constraints in ELMO maintain the protein in a "dormant" state and that activation by small GTPases is needed to permit DOCK180-mediated Rac signaling. Finally, in aim 3, we will investigate the molecular mechanisms of cell polarity and leading edge formation by DOCK180/ELMO. In summary, this work will help define the contribution of the DOCK180/ELMO/Rac signaling axis on biological events such as myoblast fusion, kidney filtration and cell polarity that require precise spatiotemporal remodeling of the cytoskeleton.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of organelle inheritance
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC DISEASES; MODEL ORGANISMS OF HUMAN DISEASE; ORGANELLE INHERITANCE; PEROXISOMAL MYOSIN RECEPTOR; PEROXISOME; PEROXISOME BIOGENESIS DISORDERS; PROTEASE; PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION; VIDEO MICROSCOPY; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Organelles are membrane-surrounded compartments present within the cells of higher organisms, including humans. Cells contain many functionally distinct organelles that house different, specific and complex biochemical functions that are necessary to the existence of higher life forms. Accordingly, cells have developed mechanisms that ensure the inheritance of their organelles so as to maintain the benefits of having organelles. One essential biological question is how does the cell maintain the population of an organelle during cell division. With every round of cell division, organelles must be duplicated and distributed to daughter cells, while some fraction of the organelles must still be retained in the mother cell. Peroxisomes are organelles involved in fat metabolism and the elimination of toxic chemical substances from the cell. There are inherited diseases called peroxisome biogenesis disorders in which peroxisomes are absent from cells. Patients with a peroxisome biogenesis disorder rarely live beyond the first year. We are investigating how peroxisomes are inherited at cell division and the molecular factors required for this process. Insight into how peroxisomes are inherited will provide increased understanding of the role of organelle inheritance in normal physiology and disease and will further our knowledge of the molecular basis of the peroxisome biogenesis disorders with a view to their future rational treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular analysis of nuclear pore complex function and assembly
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CYCLE; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; NUCLEAR STRUCTURE; NUCLEAR TANSPORT; PROTEIN SORTING
Abstract-Résumé: Genome sequencing has begun to reveal the blueprints of life.  The daunting challenge now facing the scientific community is to understand how genes are specifically and coordinately expressed to control cell growth and differentiation.  The DNA in every eukaryotic cell is housed within a spherical, membrane-enclosed compartment, termed the nucleus. Cells have made use of this physical separation to control cellular function by regulating the passage of molecules into and out of the nucleus.  The passage of molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm is regulated by elaborate macromolecular gateways, termed nuclear pore complexes (NPCs).  The NPCs control the access of proteins to the DNA, which, in turn, defines the amount and types of messenger RNAs that will be made in the cell, and thus the functions the cell will perform. In this proposal, we outline experiments to investigate how NPCs control transport into the nucleus at specific times during the growth and division of cells. In particular, we focus on understanding how the movement of molecules into the nucleus is controlled prior to and during mitosis, when copies of the DNA must be equally separated and distributed to the daughters. When this process is disrupted catastrophic consequences arise, including birth defects and cancer.  In addition to controlling access of proteins to the genome, NPCs also directly interact with chromatin (structures containing the DNA). Recent evidence suggests that, like puppeteers, the NPCs can manipulate chromatin structure. Using state-of-the-art proteomic and genomic techniques, we are investigating how NPCs interact with factors that alter chromatin structure and how NPC assembly determines the structure of chromatin and the epigenetic regulation of gene expression.  Defects in these processes are linked to the pathogenesis of a variety of disorders including Alzheimer's disease, type 1 diabetes, heart disease, and the metastatic potential of cancer cells.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - C : Systèmes digestif, endocrinien et excrétoire
TitreApplicationTitle: Studies of plasma DNA in sepsis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH; COAGULATION; CRITICAL CARE; INFLAMMATION; PLASMA DNA; PROGNOSTIC MARKER; SEPSIS PATHOPHYSIOLOGY; SEVERE SEPSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Severe sepsis (ie. life-threatening infections) is triggered by harmful microorganisms or their toxins in the blood or tissues.  These harmful agents damage the lining of blood vessels which can lead to inflammation, blood clot formation, and vessel obstruction.  In Canada, there are approximately 90,000 patients with severe sepsis each year.  Of these, 30% to 50% will die.  The identification of highly reliable outcome predictors in severe sepsis patients is important for several reasons including: to help describe the severity of sepsis, to classify patients for enrolment in clinical studies, and to monitor a patient's response to treatment and procedures.  In our lab, we examined the incremental usefulness of adding multiple biomarkers to clinical scoring systems for predicting ICU mortality in patients with severe sepsis.    In a preliminary study of 80 patients with sepsis, we found that high levels of plasma DNA predicted ICU death better than any other clinical or biological factor.  In this grant, we propose to confirm these findings in an external group of 400 patients in a blinded fashion.  We also plan to study how plasma DNA levels change over time and whether high plasma DNA levels can be used to distinguish sepsis from other critically ill conditions.  Finally, we will examine how high levels of plasma DNA cause death using a mouse model of sepsis.   Our research thus has the potential to significantly improve the management and treatment of septic patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The blood-epididymis barrier, A key determinant of male fertility
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR BIOLOGY; CLAUDINS; ENDOCRINOLOGY; EPIDIDYMIS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; TIGHT JUNCTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 12-15% of couples experience fertility problems and male infertility accounts for half of these cases. In patients with normal spermogram and diagnosed as idiopathic infertile, it is thought that post-testicular factors are responsible for the infertility, as the problem appears associated with the process of sperm maturation. While spermatozoa are formed in the testis via spermatogenesis, these spermatozoa do not have the ability to fertilize or swim. These functions are acquired in the epididymis.  If we are to understand the normal and pathological conditions attributable to human epididymal function, we must establish the physiological, cellular and molecular regulation of the human epididymis, develop tools to characterize these functions and develop clinical strategies to improve treatment. This study will address two critical function of human epididymal physiology: the molecular regulation of the tight junctions which make up the blood-epididymis barrier, and the regulation of epididymal sperm maturation. Our hypothesis is that cellular and molecular regulation of proteins, including those which comprise epididymal tight junctions and essential secreted proteins, represent clinical targets that can be exploited to improve epididymal function and fertility in obstructive and non-obstructive azoospermic infertile patients following epididymostomy. To address this hypothesis we intend to understand how claudins, the protein which make up tight junctions, are regulated in the human epididymis and using recently developed cell lines, understand epididymal sperm maturation.

ClasseRechercheFR: AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE; MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: P2 purinoceptors in the spinal dorsal horn
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; CALCIUM; CALCIUM MEASUREMENT; DORSAL HORN; GLIA; MICROGLIA; PURINOCEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past several years my research group has developed a new framework for understanding the basis of neuropathic pain. This type of pain typically arises from injury to pain-processing neurons in the peripheral or central nervous system, and is nearly always resistant to known treatments, such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or even narcotics. We have discovered that stimulating P2X4 receptors, a subtype of purinergic receptor, on microglial cells in the sensory region of the spinal cord causes them to release the protein brain-derived neurotrophic factor which then acts to amplify the activity of pain-processing neurons in the spinal cord. Our main goal is to understand how the function P2X4 receptors is regulated in microglia.  From this we anticipate developing entirely new types of drugs to block neuropathic pain and hence relieve the suffering of tens of millions of people around the globe.

ResearchClassEN: DISEASES AFFECTING SPEECH/VISION/HEARING; STROKE, HEART FAILURE

TitreApplicationTitle: Face expression and identity processing in the occipitotemporal cortex
Keywords-MotsClés: FACE EXPRESSION; FACE RECOGNITION; FMRI; PSYCHOPHYSICS; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: How the brain extracts meaning from the visual world remains a mysterious process, particularly in the case of complex objects like the human face. The face is one of the best examples of the challenging high-level object recognition tasks we perform: not only is its shape intricate, but it can convey a wide variety of information, including age, gender, expression and identity, among others. A dominant theory is that this information is not all processed by a single region, but dispersed to specialized modules. This may be particularly true for expression and identity. Our goal is to test hypotheses generated by this concept, using patients with brain lesions and functional imaging, to determine if the evidence supports this modular view of face processing by the brain. This may shed light on the different processing problems experienced by patients with different types of strokes and may help pinpoint the systems that are dysfunctional in other diseases that may affect face processing, like autism and Asperger syndrome.

OrgNm: London Health Sciences Centre Res. Inc. (Ont.)
TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a photoacoustic imaging system for lesion characterization during breast cancer diagnostics
Keywords-MotsClés: PHOTOACOUSTIC IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of the research program will be to develop a method for breast cancer detection using laser light and ultrasound, called photoacoustic breast imaging.  The technology we will develop has great potential for characterizing breast lesions that are unidentifiable by mammography and ultrasound.  This advanced technology could benefit a large fraction of women who have a diagnostic breast imaging procedure and receive an uncertain result.  These women are often sent home without a clear indication about the status of their condition.  Some will return for follow-up only to discover that they had no disease or that they in fact had malignancies that have progressed.  Photoacoustic breast imaging could potentially offer the clinician additional information to help identify breast lesions, thereby enhancing patient care.

ClasseRechercheFR: RESPIRATION; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Preclinical assessment of therapeutic hypercapnia
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME; CARBON DIOXIDE; CRITICAL CARE MEDICINE; ISCHEMIA REPERFUSION; LUNG INJURY; MECHANICAL VENTILATION
Abstract-Résumé: Patients in ICU usually have severely injured lungs. We showed that carbon dioxide, a waste gas, protects against lung injury in the laboratory. There are now two key questions. How should we administer carbon dioxide? And, how does it work?  AIM 1 addresses whether we should add carbon dioxide to the gas that the animal breathes or if we should arrange the breathing machine so that the animal recycles their own carbon dioxide. Our preliminary results suggest that adding carbon dioxide protects best. We will test this on 2 different types of lung injury: where lung injury (mouse) is caused by lung stretching by a life support machine, and where the lung injury (rat) results from shock to the intestine. Both models represent important elements of critical illness in man. AIM 2 looks at the timing of therapy. Previous work showed that when given before injury, carbon dioxide is effective. However, we usually only know about lung injury when it is severe. Thus we will ensure that injury is established, and then administer carbon dioxide. Our preliminary results show that even when given late, it is protective. We will confirm this in several models. If these two aims are successfully investigated, we will know better how to administer carbon dioxide for testing (in the next aim, and in potential preliminary clinical trials).  AIM 3 focuses on how carbon dioxide works. First, we examine in which lung cells the inflammation occurs, and in which the carbon dioxide may be effective. We selected cells representing all the important parts of the lung (air sacs, blood vessels). In concert with this, we examine a major series of molecules called the Nuclear Factor kappa B family that is centrally involved in inflammation. Although known for years, the only drugs that block this pathway are lethal, except carbon dioxide. If we understand the cells and molecules carbon dioxide acts on, we have the best chance of selecting the context to maximize benefit and avoid harm.

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of G-protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (Gprk2) in Hedgehog signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; DROSOPHILA; G-PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; HEDGEHOG SIGNALING; MOLECULAR GENETICS; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Hedgehog (Hh) proteins are an evolutionarily-conserved family of growth factors that are secreted from cells and convey information to neighbouring cells within tissues. These proteins play a critical role in controlling the growth and organization of embryonic and fetal tissues in species ranging from flies to man. They are also important for stem cell function, and consequently for maintenance of adult tissues. Due to their central role in these processes, misregulation of Hh activity can result in congenital birth defects and cancer. Much of our understanding of how Hh proteins work comes from studies in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster. The main initiator of intracellular signaling in response to Hh is a protein called Smoothened (Smo). Upon exposure of cells to Hh, Smo moves to the cell surface and becomes active, sending a signal that is relayed to the nucleus to change patterns of gene expression. We have shown that a protein called G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (Gprk2) is involved in Hh signaling in flies, as loss of this protein affects Smo regulation and blocks changes in gene expression in response to Hh. Our studies are aimed at identifying how Gprk2 regulates Smo, and how this contributes to the relay of the Hh signal to the nucleus. Gprk2-related proteins in mammals have also been implicated in Hh signaling. Thus, we expect that our studies in flies will provide important basic insights into how Hh proteins normally signal in humans, and how this can be misregulated in disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering epigenetics plasticity during hematopoietic stem cell differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD DEVELOPMENT; CHIP-SEQUENCING; CHROMATIN; EPIGENETICS; GENOMICS; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELL; HISTONE; LEUKEMIA; RNA-SEQUENCING; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: All the different types of cells present in the blood originate from a common progenitor cell called hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). HSCs can differentiate into various cell types specialized in performing different functions. For instance, red blood cells are used to transport oxygen molecules from the lungs to the various organs, whereas a series of white blood cells play various roles in innate and adaptive immunity. Understanding the differentiation process that allows HSCs to produce various blood cell types is critical since cancers such as leukemia and lymphomas can arise if this process is perturbed. In cells, the genetic material (DNA) is associated with various proteins. While all cells from an individual carry essentially the same DNA, these cells have very different characteristics and functions. What makes the different cells in our body mostly lies within the way DNA is packaged with proteins. This "packaging" is heritable just like the sequence of DNA itself. Interestingly, while mutations in cancer cells cannot be repaired by therapeutic interventions, some drugs can modify DNA packaging. Therefore, researchers are developing drugs to treat cancer by modifying DNA packaging in cancer cells. In that context, it becomes of high importance to study DNA packaging in key cells like HSCs and their derivatives. The objective of this proposal is to characterize the way that DNA is packaged in HSCs and, more importantly, to determine how this packaging changes as HSCs differentiate into the various blood cell types.  This will inform us about how HSCs can give rise to all kinds of blood cells, will constitute a framework to understand how leukemia and lymphoma arise, and will provide important clues about how to cure these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cardiolipin metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: ACYLTRANSFERASE; BARTH SYNDROME; BIOCHEMISTRY; CARDIOLIPIN; CELL CULTURE; GENETIC DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiolipin is an important phospholipid (phosphorus containing lipid or fat) found in mammalian cells. It is the major phospholipid found in mitochondria (a cellular organelle responsible for the synthesis of energy for the cell to function). Some enzymes (proteins which synthesize or breakdown compounds) in mitochondria that produce energy have an absolute requirement for cardiolipin. Cardiolipin contains four fatty acid side chains that are important for activation of these mitochondrial enzymes. My research program focuses on examining how cardiolipin is remodelled, that is, how are these fatty acids placed on the cardiolipin molecule. We know that the remodelling of cardiolipin is defective in children with Barth Syndrome, a rare genetic disease. There are many different mutations that cause Barth Syndrome. One of the enzymes involved in cardiolipin remodelling is called MLCL AT-1. In this application we are proposing to characterize this enzyme and examine whether increasing the amount of this enzyme in cells from Barth Syndrome patients with different mutations restores cardiolipin levels and mitochondrial function. We also propose to examine how MLCL AT-1 functions in regulating the level and activity of other cardiolipin remodelling enzyme.

TitreApplicationTitle: Insight and schizophrenia: Psychological and neuronal determinants
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; INSIGHT; LACK OF AWARENESS; NEUROIMAGING; PSYCHOSIS; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychiatric illness characterized by delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder, emotional dysfunctions, social withdrawal and cognitive dysfunctions. Persons with schizophrenia often are unaware of major aspects of their illness. Such a lack of awareness of illness also referred as poor insight has very profound prognostic and therapeutic consequences for these patients. To date, not a single intervention has been shown to have a major positive impact on insight in schizophrenia. In the last 20 years, studies have examined the neurocognitive, metacognitive, psychopathological, psychological, and neuroanatomical correlates of poor insight but no studies have examined within the same cohort these determinants of insight. Recent studies suggest that insight may have multiple dimensions including awareness of mental illness, capacity to recognize symptoms as abnormal, perceived need for treatment, and perceived social consequences of the illness among others. We propose to conduct a large cross-sectional study of multiple dimensions of insight in a cohort of persons who suffer from schizophrenia. We will focus our investigation on chronic patients since recent data indicates that insight is fluctuating during the first years following the onset of psychosis. We will recruit 150 persons with schizophrenia and 75 healthy control subjects matched on sociodemographical variables. Insight will be assessed with multiple clinician rated and self-report measures. A semi-structured interview will be used to assess positive symptoms, negative symptoms, depression and anxiety. An exhaustive neuropsychological evaluation will be administered to all participants along with measures of metacognitive abilities. A structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging scan will be performed to assess the volumetry of multiple key brain regions using manual and automated approaches. We hope to identify malleable factors that could become the target of future interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms by which long-term exposure to free fatty acids inhibit glucose-induced insulin secretion
Keywords-MotsClés: CA2+ CHANNELS; DIABETES; EXOCYTOSIS; FREE FATTY ACIDS; INSULIN; ISLETS OF LANGERHANS
Abstract-Résumé: A reduced capacity for insulin secretion by pancreatic islet beta-cells underlies the development of type 2 diabetes. This is underscored by recent observations that insulin release is impaired in obese pre-diabetic individuals, and that most identified genetic risk factors for type 2 diabetes impact pancreatic islet function. We recently demonstrated that increased free fatty acid levels impair insulin secretion from rodent islets in vitro by selectively uncoupling the insulin secretory granules from sites of calcium entry (i.e. the voltage-dependent Ca2+-channels). This results in an impaired efficiency of exocytosis, the process that underlies insulin release into the blood. We now propose to further our findings through the examination of 'exocytotic uncoupling' in rodent models of diabetes, human islets treated in vitro with free fatty acids, and islets from human donors. This work can be expected to elucidate the mechanistic dysfunction that occurs in pancreatic islets leading to type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Daytime functioning and sleep disorders in older adults: Predicting sleep apnea in a prospective primary care study.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CASE IDENTIFICATION; HEALTH RISKS; POLYSOMNOGRAPHY; PRIMARY CARE; SLEEP APNEA; SYMPTOMS
Abstract-Résumé: A very high percentage of individuals who have obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) are not recognized or diagnosed by health professionals and, therefore, not referred for appropriate evaluation and treatment. Untreated OSA appears to have serious correlates and consequences with respect to health (e.g., metabolic syndrome components such as diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity), daytime functioning (e.g., sleepiness, fatigue), and quality of life. Recent literature suggests that OSA may be an independent risk factor for the metabolic syndrome, and vice versa. Little is yet understood about the time course of these conditions and the factors that mediate them in the real world of primary care. Therefore, the key objectives of this investigation are to (1) improve identification of OSA in older primary care patients, (2) evaluate the relationship between OSA and metabolic syndrome components such as diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity, and (3) chart the OSA related course of those with differing numbers of metabolic syndrome components. We will do this in the context of a naturalistic, clinically-based, prospective study, which addresses the identification, causes, correlates and consequences of OSA, an important, but under recognized disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Organization and reflex control of spinal locomotor networks.
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTATIONAL MODELS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; INTRACELLULAR IN VIVO RECORDING; LOCOMOTION; REFLEX REVERSAL; SPINAL CORD ORGANIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: The detailed patterns and sequences of leg muscle activity during walking, standing and stabilizing the body are generated by centres in the spinal cord that are activated by  commands from the brain. Movements such as walking are often impaired after spinal cord injury because the brain is no longer able to activate the spinal centres that in many cases remain undamaged. One huge obstacle to repairing spinal cord injuries is our poor understanding of how spinal cord centres controlling muscles function. It is very difficult to repair a system without an instruction manual or an understanding of how it works! My research is designed to learn how the healthy spinal cord produces complex movements. I am investigating how neurons in the spinal cord are inter-connected and how they work together. In essence, we are creating a wiring diagram of spinal neuronal networks and the systems that control them. This knowledge is essential to understanding how information from the brain and sensory information from the legs are brought together to produce safe and stable walking. These investigations are important for guiding future transplantation and stem cell therapies to restore function in damaged spinal cord pathways. By understanding the most critical features of spinal cord organization, we can identify the best targets for biological interventions to restore function.

ResearchClassEN: LEUKAEMIAS; DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS
ClasseRechercheFR: LEUCEMIES; DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic determinants of the resistance to corticosteroids, vincristine and asparaginase in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA; CORTICOSTEROID; DRUG; DRUG ACTION; DRUG METABOLISM; VINCRISTINE / ASPARAGINASE
Abstract-Résumé: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common cancer of childhood. Patients vary widely in their response to drug therapy. This difference can result in too little treatment, leading to treatment failure and disease relapse. Variations in genes that code for enzymes that are important for drugs effects and thus named candidate genes, may underlie these differences, offering a powerful tool in predicting treatment outcome. For example, gene variations (polymorphisms) may change the rate at which a drug is eliminated by the body, the rate at which a drug is moved into and out of the cell, or the activity of an enzyme inhibited by a drug. We propose to analyze such genetic variations in patients with ALL. Since ALL is treated by protocols that include many different drugs, the effect of each drug is dependent of the activity of several enzymes. Therefore, we will simultaneously consider several candidate genes and their polymorphisms. Genetic variants will be compared with ALL outcome. The functional effect of these polymorphisms will also be addressed. Identification of genetic variants with high predictive value might allow optimal use of drugs on an individual basis leading to higher cure rates.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of action of DNA methyltransferase (DNMT1)  inhibitors and their therapeutic potential
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICANCER DRUGS; ANTISENSE; CELL GROWTH PARAMETERS; MECHANISMS OF ACTION OF DRUGS; SIRNA; WESTERN BLOT ANALYSES
Abstract-Résumé: Human DNA is coated with chemical marks called methyl groups. The methyl groups (DNA methylation) program how genes function. This program is critical for normal life. In cancer, the distribution of the methyl groups on the DNA is altered. Drugs that modify the markings of DNA, called epigenetic drugs, are considered a novel approach to cancer therapy as well as to other diseases. However to be able to take advantage of these drugs we need to understand their mechanism of action. A drug blocking DNA methylation (Vidaza) is now approved for treating certain blood cancers. However, we discovered in the previous term of the grant that Vidaza does not only cause loss of methylation from tumor blocking genes, but it also removes the methyl marks from genes that cause metastasis, raising the concern that this anticancer drug would induce metastasis, the most morbid aspect of cancer. Our challenge is to discover ways to utilize this class of drugs to block cancer while avoiding metastasis. The first step is to understand the mechanisms of action of these drugs. Since multiple proteins called DNMTs 1 to 3 are involved in DNA methylation and Vidaza blocks them all, we first propose to test the impact of depleting just one of these proteins on the distribution of methyl groups in cancer and normal cells. We believe that by blocking a specific form of DNMT1 we will reduce the risk of metastasis.  Second, we will determine whether inhibitors of DNMT will work in only in cells that are dividing and will thus be limited to fast growing tumors or also in nondividing cells and will therefore be useful in treating slow growing cancers, brain diseases and other diseases in organs where cell division does not occur. Third, we discovered that DNMT1 inhibitors could block cell growth without affecting the methyl coating, thus avoiding the risk of metastasis. We will define how DNMT1 is involved to determine whether this activity should be targeted in our drug design.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES DU FOIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Signatures of a Successful Immune Response against HCV
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES; HEPATITIS C; LIVER DISEASE; MICROARRAYS; T CELL MEMORY; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection usually causes a life-long persistent infection in humans that can lead to irreversible liver damage and even cancer. It is estimated that the number of persons currently infected with HCV in the world is approximately 130 million individuals. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C and the only available treatment is expensive, has many side effects and is effective only in half of the infected population. Despite the progress we made in understanding the immune response against hepatitis C, we still lack a great deal of knowledge about what distinguishes a good immune response against HCV that can protect against new infections. Our previous results demonstrated that a successful immune response is characterized by an increase in the expression of molecules associated with the long-term survival of white blood cells specific for hepatitis C. In this proposal, we plan to study the early events following infection with hepatitis C. We will use novel techniques that will measure the activity of genes that are activated in individuals who can successfully clear Hepatitis C infection without the need for therapy. This will help us develop methods to predict early whether someone will clear the virus or not. Defining this successful immune response profile will set the ultimate characteristic that should be achieved by new vaccines and should be used as a measure of their efficacy and success.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; RETARD MENTAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The organization of recent and remote memory
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTEX; GENETICALLY-ENGINEERED MICE; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; MEMORY CONSOLIDATION; MEMORY DISORDERS; PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The brain is a complex structure, and is made up of many interconnected sub-regions. When we remember something, that information is thought to be stored in a distributed manner- that is, a large network of sub-regions might be involved in storing a particular memory. When memory fails- for example in old age or in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease- this might reflect a deterioration of that network (e.g., in the way the network is organized, or communication within the network). The goal of our studies is to explore how these memory networks are organized, and how this organization might be altered in disease states. These studies are conducted in mice, allowing us, for example, to over-express disease genes (and therefore model conditions such as Alzheimer's disease). We believe that understanding the network properties of memory lays an essential foundation for the development of targeted treatments for memory loss associated with disease or aging.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - B: Heart and Circulation
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Distribution of systemic blood flow: importance of reservoir flow
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOENGINEERING; BLOOD FLOW DISTRIBUTION; DOPPLER BLOOD VELOCITY; HEMODYNAMICS; VASCULAR PHYSIOLOGY; WINDKESSEL
Abstract-Résumé: When the left ventricle (LV) contracts, it forcefully propels blood into the arterial system.  Therefore, it may seem surprising that some of the vital organs (e.g., the brain, and the heart itself) derive most of their blood flow not when the LV is contracting but later, when the LV is relaxing.  This is possible because when the LV contracts, it "stores" much of its ejected blood in an arterial reservoir and this stored blood is distributed later, during diastole.  Previous approaches could not provide an adequate conceptual framework but we have developed a promising new "reservoir-wave approach".  The objective of this proposal is to understand better how blood flow is distributed to the vital organs of the body, to each according to its changing needs.  We will measure blood flow in the human brain and pressure by non-invasive techniques.  Preliminary data suggest that we can explain how brain flow responds to changes in O2 and CO2.  By also measuring blood flow and pressure in the leg, we can study the effect of exercise and determine if exercise compromises brain flow.  Previously, in dogs, we studied the coronary circulation, at rest and under the influence of drugs that increased or decreased blood flow.  We will re-analyze those data based on our new understanding of the arterial reservoir.  The innovative feature of this project is our conceptual framework and we believe this new approach will help us understand better how blood is distributed to vital organs.  An adequate volume in the arterial reservoir is necessary to maintain blood flow to the brain and heart.  This volume decreases when we get older, because the vessels get stiffer.  Exercise and drugs that interfere with the action of a natural hormone (i.e., angiotensin) can increase the volume (i.e., decrease the stiffness) of this reservoir.  Demonstrating how this reservoir works might persuade people to exercise more and lead to the development of new drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Quebec Administrative health databases linkage-based study on First Nations and Inuit birth and infant outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL MATERNAL AND INFANT HEALTH; ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTH DATABASE LINKAGE; GESTATIONAL DIABETES; GESTATIONAL HYPERTENSION; INFANT MORTALITY; MACROSOMIA; PERINATAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; PERINATAL MORTALITY; PRETERM BIRTH
Abstract-Résumé: Available limited research data indicate that First Nations and Inuit birth outcomes are much worse than their non-Aboriginal counterparts in Canada. The causes and consequences are poorly understood. There are significant data gaps in Aboriginal (First Nations, Inuit, Metis) birth outcomes in Canada. In particular, there is a lack of linked mother-infant administrative health data for Aboriginal births in Quebec and Canada. In collaboration with Quebec Aboriginal community stakeholders, we propose to create a linked database from multiple existing birth-related administrative health databases in Quebec for more in-depth studies on First Nations and Inuit birth and infant outcomes. Study findings will inform policy makers and Aboriginal community health stakeholders and planners about the needs and gaps for developing perinatal and infant health promotion programs to improve Aboriginal birth and infant health outcomes in Quebec. The creation of this linked database will lay the foundation for Quebec researchers and Aboriginal community stakeholders in further future studies to address other perinatal and infant health questions of concern to Quebec Aboriginal communities to inform perinatal and infant care program developments to improve Aboriginal birth and infant outcomes in Quebec and Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epithelial-mesenchymal (endothelial)interactions regulate postnatal lung development
Keywords-MotsClés: ALVEOLARIZATION; BRONCHOPULMONARY DYSPLASIA; CAPILLARY FORMATION; HYPOXIA INDUCIBLE FACTOR; SEMAPHORINS; SONIC HEDGEHOG
Abstract-Résumé: Lung diseases resulting from premature birth are major health issues for children. Lung anomalies occur less frequently, but are usually fatal. Currently the care of these babies is supportive with no specific therapy available to prevent or treat the lung defect. To understand the pathogenesis of these childhood diseases, we first need to understand normal lung development. Normal lung function requires the development of an air-blood barrier of maximal surface area and minimal thinness. This is achieved by the formation of alveoli, a largely postnatal process that requires appropriate vessel development. In this grant we propose to investigate the importance of a variety of molecules for the formation of vessels and alveoli using genetically modified mice. In these mice we can delete the molecule of interest specifically in the lung distal airway cells or blood vessels and study the impact of such deletion on postnatal vessel and alveolar formation. This information can then be used to develop new therapeutic strategies or to improve existing therapies for infants with developmental lung disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of monocyte recruitment and intimal cell proliferation in atherosclerosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; GM-CSF; INFLAMMASOMES; MONOCYTE RECRUITMENT; PROLIFERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Atherosclerosis is a disease caused by risk factors such as elevated levels of LDL-cholesterol and involves the formation of lesions or plaques on the inner portion of the artery wall.  As lesions enlarge, they cause narrowing or blockage and loss of blood supply to tissues, resulting in a heart attack or stroke.  In some regions, the inner layer of arteries contains white blood cells (leukocytes).  At the early stages of lesion formation, leukocytes take up lipid and become foam cells, undergo cell division (proliferation) and there is excessive leukocyte entry into the artery wall (recruitment).  With time, lesions become larger and other cell types accumulate in addition to leukocytes, and cells die, which leads to deposition of calcium or sudden rupture (thrombosis).  The goal of our research is to gain a better understanding of the cellular and molecular basis of lesion formation during the development of atherosclerosis. Our recent success in tracking cell proliferation of leukocytes as well as leukocyte recruitment from blood into the aorta revealed that both processes take place in early stages of lesion formation. We will utilize this approach to determine the roles played by leukocyte recruitment and proliferation and the relationship between these events during distinct stages of lesion formation.  We will also monitor the extent of cell death at each stage, since cell survival versus death influences the outcome of lesions.  The contribution of specific molecules that are critical for leukocyte recruitment and proliferation will be explored. We will also investigate the roles of a newly emerging family of proteins, called Nod-like receptors (NLR) that mediate the response of cells to signals that are sensed as danger.

TitreApplicationTitle: High resolution genetic analysis of genetic loci implicated in colorectal cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLELE-SPECIFIC EXPRESSION; COLORECTAL CANCER; GENE REGULATION; GENETIC ASSOCIATION; GENETIC VARIATION; LINKAGE DISEQUILIBRIUM; MOLECULAR GENETICS; SUSCEPTIBILITY GENES
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer is a major public health challenge. While killing thousands of Canadians each year, mortality and severe morbidity due to the disease is potentially highly preventable through detection and treatment of precursor lesions and early stage disease.  A large portion of individual risk for colorectal cancer is genetically inherited. While this was determined from family studies, only recently have individual genetic variants been identified through direct study of the genomes of those affected.   Our team contains talented and experienced cancer researchers.  The senior applicants, Drs. Hudson and Gallinger have worked together with other Canadian, US, and UK scientists in identifying several chromosomal regions that harbour genes that predispose to colorectal cancer. Drs. Lemire and Peltekova were recruited to the Ontario Institute for Cancer Research to bring statistical and molecular genetics expertise needed to refine the information derived from the genomic screens and pinpoint the specific genes and mutations involved in colon cancer.  With the support of the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the applicants will will identify and characterize new genetic determinants of risk. This may be used in the development of screening programs for high risk individuals and inform scientists on the biology of colon cancer (particularly early lesions) that may be used in future treatment strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Where is Autism Located in the Brain?
Keywords-MotsClés: ANATOMICAL PHENOTYPE; AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; BRAIN; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING (DTI); MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI); MOUSE MODELS OF DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Autism is a complex neurological disorder that hinders a person's ability to relate to and communicate with others. It is part of a group of disorders known as autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Approximately 6 in 1,000 people have an ASD. Individuals with Autism can have multiple variations in the sequence and structure of their DNA that can lead to similar symptoms. Since there are a variety of genes that have been shown to be related to Autism, one working hypothesis, which attempts to explain this variance in the disease, is that many factors can disrupt the brain from developing the connections necessary for sociability. Here we propose to take advantage of this diversity in Autism genetics by examining mouse models of 13 mutations associated with ASD. Using high resolution Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) we will reveal the consistently detectable effects of autism in the brain. This study thus has great potential to identify novel pathways and mechanisms of ASD and will thereby speed the search for a cure for this set of disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: CSF1 pathway inhibitors in tenosynovial giant cell tumors and leiomyosarcoma
Keywords-MotsClés: CSF1; EXPERIMENTAL THERAPEUTICS; MACROPHAGE; SARCOMA; SOFT TISSUE TUMORS; TRANSGENIC MOUSE; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Macrophages are normal cells in our immune system that are sometimes recruited by cancers, because of their ability to help tumor cells invade, spread and to obtain a blood supply. The main signaling protein used by cancers to recruit macrophages is called CSF1. As a creative new approach to treat cancer, researchers and drug companies around the world are busy developing drugs that block CSF1, some of which are now entering clinical trials.  Our previous work helped to identify some specific tumor types that are especially dependent on CSF1 production. One, called tenosynovial giant cell tumor, is to date the only tumor type known to have activating mutations in the CSF1 gene itself. Another, called leiomyosarcoma, directly produces CSF1 in some cases, and these patients have particularly aggressive disease and a high death rate.  However, testing new CSF1 inhibitors has been hampered by a lack of experimental systems where macrophage recruitment can be measured. We recently developed a new technique (implanting tumor under the kidney capsule of mice) that allows us to do this, and found that CSF1 inhibitor drugs indeed do block macrophage recruitment. In this grant application, we propose to use this model to understand how CSF1 promotes cancer progression, and to test a new generation of especially good candidate drugs for their effect on these diseases, to guide future clinical trials. We also plan to develop a new transgenic mouse model of tenosynovial giant cell tumor that would greatly accelerate future research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Complex RNA regulatory networks in the human pathogen Leishmania and their role in developmental gene expression and pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: 3'UTR ELEMENTS; DEVELOPMENTAL GENE REGULATION; LEISHMANIA; MICROARRAYS; MRNA DECAY; PATHOGENESIS; PROTEOMICS; RNA REGULATORY NETWORKS; RNA SEQUENCING; RNA STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Leishmania is an important human pathogen that causes leishmaniasis, a vector-borne parasitic disease with a large spectrum of clinical manifestations, and infects more than 12 million people worldwide. In order to survive within its mammalian host, Leishmania has to differentiate from the extracellular promastigote form found in the insect vector into the amastigote stage inside the phagolysosomes of macrophages. The ability of Leishmania to survive within the acidic phagolysosome milieu depends upon the developmental regulation of a variety of genes which is controlled by complex RNA regulatory pathways. Genes preferentially expressed in response to various environmental stimuli in the macrophages should play a central role in the parasite's intracellular survival and pathogenesis. Very little is known, however on the mechanisms underlying their stage-specific expression and their putative function. In the past 10 years, we have made important contributions to our understanding of how differentially expressed genes throughout the developmental stages of Leishmania are regulated using global genomics and proteomics approaches. Our main research interest is to delineate the molecular mechanisms that control stage-specific regulation of gene expression in Leishmania and contribute to parasite pathogenesis. These studies would possibly depict novel mechanisms of gene regulation and pinpoint promising targets for the development of novel therapeutic strategies against these important but neglected human parasitic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Peau reconstruite par génie tissulaire: Étude de l'influence de l'innervation cutanée sur la guérison des plaies
Keywords-MotsClés: CICATRISATION; GRANDS BRULES; GENIE TISSULAIRE; HISTOPATHOLOGIE; IMMUNOHISTOCHIMIE; INNERVATION
Abstract-Résumé: L'objectif de ce projet est d'etudier l'influence de l'innervation sensitive sur la cicatrisation d'une plaie cutanee grace a un nouveau modele de peau reconstruite in vitro par genie tissulaire. Ce modele permet de combiner a la fois le derme, l'epiderme, le systeme vasculaire et le systeme nerveux sensitif presents dans une peau normale. Il suffit ensuite de creer une plaie dans l'epiderme avec un poincon de 10mm de diametre pour pouvoir ensuite etudier l'influence de divers composants sur sa vitesse de fermeture. On etudiera en particulier l'influence du systeme nerveux sensitif via la secretion de Substance P et de CGRP sur la reepithelialisation et sur l'angiogenese cutanee. Une meilleure comprehension de l'effet du systeme nerveux sensitif sur la cicatrisation pourrait deboucher sur de nouvelles alternatives de traitement des plaies chroniques, en favorisant par exemple la regeneration nerveuse.

TitreApplicationTitle: DNA methylation and its association with neural tube defects
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH DEFECT; EPIGENETICS; FOLATE; NEURAL TUBE DEFECT
Abstract-Résumé: Neural tube defects (NTDs) as a group represent one of the most common serious birth defects and result from growth abnormalities of cells during very early embryo development. They are thought to result from a complex interaction between genetic and environmental influences. NTDs have been shown to be reduced, but not eliminated, through population-wide folate supplementation programs. We suggest that poor folate uptake by the placenta is a major contributor to NTDs. Low folate may lead to abnormal DNA methylation, a chemical modification to the DNA that helps regulate how genes are turned on and off  in the cell. We plan to study methylation differences in the DNA of placentas and fetuses affected with NTDs.  By identifying the specific changes associated with abnormal fetal development we will be better able to understand the causes and identify those chemicals in our environment that might have detrimental effects on development. Furthermore, such changes may be useful to subgroup NTDs into folate pathway dependent and independent causes and thus improve our ability to evaluate the impact of folate supplemenation on NTDs.
