ResearchClassEN: CANCER THERAPY GENERAL; HEALTH CARE DELIVERY
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; DISTRIBUTION DES SOINS DE LA SANTE
TitreApplicationTitle: Transition to Survivorship: Translating knowledge into action for testicular and endometrial cancer populations.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER SURVIVORSHIP; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Over 60% of Canadians diagnosed with cancer are now expected to survive. As primary treatment ends, and the patient transitions to the follow-up period (survivorship phase) they face a number of challenges to restoring and maintaining their health and overall well-being. There is a need to provide a summary of what has happened to the patient and what their plan is moving forward. This is called a Survivorship Care Plan (SCP). The SCP has the potential to help patients understand and navigate the survivorship phase and cope with the challenges that they face. It may also be useful for health care professionals involved in the patient's on-going care. While SCPs are recommended as a critical element of survivorship care, few organizations currently use SCPs and there remain a number of barriers to its use. The purpose of this study is to conduct a pilot demonstration of implementing SCPs as part of routine cancer care. An established knowledge translation approach will be used, integrating those who will use SCPs (i.e. patients' and health care providers) throughout the process. Two distinct cancer sites (testicular and endometrial) which are distinct allowing for comparisons and who already exhibit readiness to embrace change will be involved. The project deliverables will include: 1)development of appropriate SCPs; 2)pilot feasibility testing of the model of implementation; 3)use of a multifaceted strategy to implement the use of SCPs;and 4) evaluation of the process of implementation and short-term outcomes. This project is largely focused on improving the experience of the survivorship phase and ensuring that patients are empowered with the information and support needed to thrive. Using a systematic approach to the development and implementation of SCPs combined with the use of an integrated KT model will help to ensure the sustained and effective use of SCPs in practice and will promote survivorship care planning as a valued component of clinical practice.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and cellular basis of cardiac hypertrophy caused by Noonan syndrome-associated RAF1 mutations
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC DISEASE; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Heart diseases are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the Western World. In many types of heart disease, the heart thickens as a consequence of enlargement of the heart muscle; this process is called "cardiac hypertrophy". Chronic cardiac hypertrophy can cause heart failure, abnormal heart rhythm or sudden death. Despite its substantial medical importance, the detailed way in which cardiac hypertrophy develops in heart disease is largely unknown.  Noonan Syndrome (NS) is a fairly common inherited genetic disorder that affects about 1:1000- 2500 live births. Approximately 20% of NS cases show cardiac hypertrophy with cardiac dysfunction, called hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). Recent studies have established that NS is caused by enhanced activation of a specific biochemical pathway, called the RAS/ERK cascade, which controls many important biological processes. In addition to the effects of aberrant RAS/ERK activation in the heart, abnormal regulation of this pathway also contributes to many cancers.  Interestingly, different NS mutations appear to have somewhat different effects. For example, inherited mutations in the RAF1 gene account for only 3-5% of NS cases, but these patients frequently exhibit HCM. However, the detailed mechanism by which RAF1 mutants cause abnormal activation of RAS/ERK pathway and how they induced HCM is largely unknown. The goal of our research is to use unique mouse models of NS that we have generated in our laboratory to understand the cellular and molecular mechanism of cardiac hypertrophy. We will also attempt to use genetic and pharmacological agents to prevent or treat HCM in our mouse models. Our study will help us to understand cardiac hypertrophy, and may also aid in the development of new therapeutic strategies for cardiac hypertrophy as well as acquired heart diseases. Because of the central role of the RAS/ERK pathway in many cell types, our results may also provide insight into other diseases, such as cancer.

ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of nutrition and metabolism in breast cancer patients
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION; BREAST CANCER; EXERCISE; LIPID; METABOLISM; MUSCLE; NUTRITION; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Although successful new treatments have developed with cancer research, breast cancer patients often gain fat and lose lean mass while receiving chemotherapy. These unhealthy changes in body composition relate to poor quality of life and fatigue during cancer treatment. In non-cancer populations, these negative body composition changes are linked to unhealthy metabolic changes including poor lipid and glucose metabolism, which may increase the risk of cancer recurrence, cardiovascular disease and diabetes in cancer survivors. Although these changes in body composition have been identified, the nutrition and metabolic changes associated with these body composition changes that may develop during the treatment time-course have not been comprehensively examined. The first objective is to characterize the changes in nutrition, metabolism, physical function, and body composition that occur during treatment in breast cancer. Nutrition and exercise programs are known to promote healthy body composition and metabolism in non-cancer populations. While exercise during chemotherapy reduces fatigue and enhances quality of life, the metabolic benefits of combined nutrition and exercise in breast cancer patients are unclear. The second objective will examine the metabolic benefits of nutrition and exercise intervention in breast cancer patients receiving chemotherapy. We expect that a combined exercise and nutrition program will prevent poor body composition changes and potentially improve lipid and glucose metabolism in recently diagnosed breast cancer patients who are receiving chemotherapy. Understanding the effects of nutrition and exercise in breast cancer patients will provide a strong foundation for future research studies and for the development of effective nutrition and exercise programs that reduce the risk of cancer recurrence and other chronic diseases in survivorship.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Modeling cardiovascular development using human stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC DEVELOPMENT; CARDIAC PROGENITORS; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL SURFACE; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEOMICS; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death and disability in Ontario and Canada, results in an enormous loss of productivity to society and represents a growing burden on the health care system. With dramatic improvements in the treatment of the acute stages of heart disease, the health system now faces the challenge of escalating chronic cardiovascular disease, including systolic and diastolic heart failure, hypertensive and diabetic heart disease, stroke, and vascular atherosclerosis. Unfortunately, these conditions are often diagnosed at the presentation of symptoms, which occurs in the later stages of disease. Advances in treating and managing these debilitating conditions requires a shift from the traditional focus on end-stage complications towards the development of novel diagnostic, prognostic, and targeted therapeutic and preventive tools and strategies. This research proposal brings together an outstanding research team to build on the success of these previous studies involving mouse models of cardiac disease and to extend the approach to include human pluripotent stem cells as a cellular model of disease that can provide novel populations for the identification of new markers and can also be used to validate marker sets and to test the therapeutic potential of new markers. To accomplish this goal, we will combine our expertise in stem cell biology and differentiation, cardiac biology and disease and proteomics and bioinformatics to identify and mechanistically investigate novel cell-surface markers by advance mass spectrometry. We feel that this type of study will provide important data as we design the next generation of treatments for cardiac disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects and Mechanisms of B7-H4 Pathway on Inhibition of the Development of Type 1 Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: B7-H4 KNOCKOUT MICE; B7-H4 PROTEIN; B7-H4 TRANSGENIC MICE; INHIBITION OF THE DEVELOPMENT OF T1D; NEGATIVE CO-SIGNALING PATHWAY; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the cells of the pancreas that secrete insulin, called beta cells, are destroyed by the patient's own immune system. Despite decades of research, we are still not able to prevent or reverse this disease process in humans.  We believe the best chance for a cure is to restore functional beta cells by either activating regeneration of these cells in the pancreas, or by replacing them through transplantation. Our goal with this proposal is to assess a novel compound that we believe could be used to treat type 1 diabetes. In previous research, we determined that a naturally occurring protein called B7-H4 can selectively suppress the immune cells that are responsible for killing insulin-secreting beta cells and thereby reduce the incidence of diabetes in mice. Our studies also suggest that increasing the amount of B7-H4 protein within pancreatic cells (through genetic engineering) prior to transplantation may inhibit the recurrence of diabetes in mice receiving the transplanted cells.   We therefore aim to determine: (1) Can B7-H4 protein influence the development of diabetes in mouse models of the disease, if we: (a) inject B7-H4 protein directly into the mice; (b) increase the amount of B7-H4 protein in islet beta cells by genetic engineering; or (c) induce B7-H4 deficiency through genetic engineering? (2) If B7-H4 does prevent diabetes, then through what mechanism(s)? We will determine: (a) the effect of B7-H4 protein on the response, function, amount and balance of the various immune cells that either protect or destroy beta cells, and (b) the level of B7-H4 protein in beta cells required to protect beta cells from death. The use of B7-H4 protein may help to prevent and reverse the development of T1D and provide a more natural compound to treat the underlying autoimmune disease process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Space-Time Exposure to Foodscapes, Diet and BMI: Combining Travel Surveys, Objective Measures of the Food Environment, and individual-level measures of Dietary Intake and BMI
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY SPACES; FOODSCAPE EXPOSURE; MOBILITY PATTERNS; OBESITY; SPACE-TIME GEOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Researchers have been interested in understanding if the environment we live in contributes to the observed rising rates of overweight and obesity in the Canadian population. Whereas most studies until now have looked at the characteristics of the food environment around people's place of residence, none has yet taken into account how and where people move to fulfill their daily activities to better assess the opportunities for food that arise as we are mobile. Research in geography has been trying to improve our consideration of both geographic space and time to understand people's options for mobility and related actual travel behaviour. By mapping the different locations people visit during a day to fulfill their activities, we hope to obtain a more precise measure of the types of food environments they get exposed to. These measures and related models will be used to assess whether the types of food stores we are exposed to in our daily living play a role in what we eat and on how much we weigh.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms controlling the signaling efficacy and selectivity of dynamic G protein-coupled receptor signaling complexes
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; DURG TARGETS; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; RESONANCE ENERGY TRANSFER; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The discovery and development of new drugs with better therapeutic efficacy and lesser undesirable effects remains an unmet need for many clinical indications. In recent years, the rate of discovery and commercialization of truly innovative drugs has sensibly decreased. Many factors contribute to this biopharmaceutical crisis but one of the causes is certainly that the low hanging fruits have already been harvested. In other words, a significant number of drugs acting in conventional ways by directly binding to and inhibiting or activating enzymes, channel or receptors have already been developed and, improving on that theme is increasingly challenging. Obviously, improving on drugs directly inhibiting or activating conventional therapeutic targets is still needed. However, taking advantage of recent knowledge on how potential drug targets can be controlled in novel ways will be essential to create the next generation of drugs. New findings on one of the most prominent family of drug targets, the G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), indicate that many cellular factors can regulate their activity. Targeting these processes offers new opportunities for the development of innovative therapeutic agents. Therefore, the present proposal aims at further understanding the mechanisms regulating the activity of GPCRs with the intention of identifying novel regulatory process that could be pharmacologically targeted for therapeutic purposes. The studies proposed also include the search for new chemical entities that will serve as tool to better probe the role of the various mechanisms unravelled and could represent interesting lead candidates for the development of new classes of drugs for various diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The interactome of the human G-protein coupled receptors.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; G-PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTORS; MEMBRANE YEAST TWO HYBRID; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: The G-protein coupled receptors form the largest family of cell surface proteins with over 1,000 members. They are involved in the recognition and response to stimuli as diverse as hormones, neurotransmitters, calcium, odorants, gustatory signals or light. Their key roles in cells have made them the target of more than 60% of all currently prescribed drugs, including drugs to treat heart failure, chronic pain, obesity, neuropsychiatric disorders and carcinomas. Although the symptoms of these diseases are well understood, the molecular mechanisms that underlie them are not. The overall objective of our project is to identify and characterize the role of proteins associated with one hundred selected human G-protein coupled receptors as well as to understand how these proteins, when impaired, contribute to the development and progression of various human diseases. To that end, we are using a state-of-the-art technology developed in my laboratory that is able to detect interactions involving proteins on the cell surface. In addition, we will investigate the cellular mechanisms in which these proteins are involved using computational approaches as well as traditional techniques, including biochemical, cell biological and molecular biological assays. We hope to provide a more complete understanding of the role of these proteins in the normal operation of human cells, and to gain insight into the cellular mechanisms involved in human diseases that result from the malfunction of these proteins. This understanding should provide potential avenues for additional therapeutic interventions against heart failure, chronic pain, obesity, neuropsychiatric disorders and carcinomas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multiple medication use in the Quebec elderly and the risk of motor vehicle crash
Keywords-MotsClés: DATABASE; ELDERLY; MEDICATIONS; MOTOR VEHICLE CRASH
Abstract-Résumé: Over 60% of Canadian elderly consume multiple medications.  Many of these drugs have been implicated with impairment of the psychomotor skills required for driving and could increase the risk of injurious car crashes.  Because we live in an aging society with an increasing number of elderly drivers, it is of interest to assess the impact of the interactions between commonly used drugs on driving safety in the elderly.  This study will use the cohort of over 700,000 patients, all elderly drivers from the Province of Quebec between 1999-2008, identified from the computerized databases of the Societe de l'Assurance Automobile du Quebec (SAAQ).  These data will be anonymously linked with those of the Regie de l'Assurance Maladie du Quebec (RAMQ) to identify medication use.  Together they will allow estimating the relative risk of accident associated with combinations of drugs commonly prescribed to the elderly.  Although, elderly people are heavy consumers of several commonly used drugs with known psychomotor impairment, no studies have assessed the impact of the use of multiple drugs by elderly drivers on the risk of motor vehicle crash.  As the proportion of the elderly driving is increasing, the rate of car crashes causes by medication use will increase and will represent a growing concern for public health because of the associated morbidity and mortality.  The results of the research will be useful for the development of appropriate policies regarding preventive driving measures, as well as clinical guidelines for the management of elderly patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tumor immunotherapy: enhancing the efficacy of cytotoxic T lymphocytes by IL-21 and IL-15
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE CELL THERAPY; CPG DEMETHYLATION; CYTOTOXIC T CELLS; GADD45; GENE EXPRESSION; INTERFERON GAMMA; INTERLEUKIN-15; INTERLEUKIN-21; TUMOR IMMUNOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system actively guards against cancer using the 'cytotoxic T lymphocytes', commonly referred to as CTLs. CTLs become activated upon recognition of certain proteins called 'tumor antigens' that are expressed on tumor cells. These tumor-specific CTLs infiltrate the tumor and kill the cancer cells. When the tumor is aggressive and grows into a larger mass, it secretes a variety of substances that neutralize the killing ability of CTLs. These tumor-infiltrating CTLs can be obtained from the tumor, grown in the laboratory outside the suppressive influence of the tumor and injected back into the same patient so that they can now efficiently kill the tumor. This method is called 'adoptive cell therapy' or ACT. ACT is being used in clinical trials to treat melanoma patients. However, the success of this treatment is unpredictable because the biomarkers that define the clinical efficacy of CTLs used for ACT have not yet been adequately defined. In this project, we will use a new strategy developed in our laboratory to optimize the conditions for generating antitumor CTLs with superior antitumor efficacy. Using a mouse model of melanoma, we will determine the parameters that correlate with the clinical efficiacy of antitumor CTLs. We will also investigate the feasibility of generating tumor-specific CTLs from outside the immunosuppressive environment of the tumor, an approach that could pave the way for generating antitumor CTLs from the blood of human cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Use of Extended Peri-operative Low Molecular Weight Heparin to Improve Cancer Specific Survival Following Surgical Resection of Colon Cancer: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: GASTRO-INTESTINAL CANCER; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SURVIVAL; THROMBOPROPHYLAXIS
Abstract-Résumé: The human body has a natural stress response to surgery, including the fomation of blood clots. This response to surgery has been shown to increase metastases (the spread of cancer cells to other organs in the body). These metastases cannot be seen at the time of surgery but when they grow into new tumors, the cancer has recurred (come back). A blood thinner called "low molecular weight heparin" (LMWH) can suppress the development of metastases after surgery in animal experiments. We want to see if giving patients with colon cancer the blood thinner, LMWH, around the time of surgery can decrease the chance of their cancer spreading to other organs (metastases) and coming back (recurrence).  We need 1075 patients to answer our scientific question. Patients who give informed consent will be randomly put into one of two groups, the experimental group and the control group. The patients in the control group will be treated with LMWH starting a few hours after surgery and every day until they leave the hospital. This is how most patients are treated after colon cancer surgery (standard care). The patients in the experimental group will be treated with LMWH for a longer period of time, starting on the day they agree to have surgery and continuing for two months after surgery. All the patients will be followed for at least three years after surgery to find out if their cancer has recurred (come back). If LMWH treatment around the time of surgery reduces the chance of recurrence in patients with colon cancer, it would improve the health and quality of life for these patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Dissection of Airway Hyperresponsiveness and Susceptibility to Allergic Asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGIC ASTHMA; ASTHMA PHENOTYPES; CANDIDATE GENES; GENE MAPPING; GENETICS OF ASTHMA; RECOMBINANT STRAINS
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a complex respiratory and immune disease. The environment and its interaction with the genetic make-up of the host determine the onset, progression and severity of the lung inflammatory response associated with asthma. The limited success in identifying genes regulating  asthma is not only due to the inherent genetic complexity of the disease, but also to the very limited number of genetic models suitable for studying the disease. By taking advantage of a new mouse model of asthma together with a unique genetic platform, we have shown that genes confering susceptibility to asthma are tractable.  We have identified several candidate mouse chromosomal regions that coincide with asthma susceptibility loci identified in humans, indicating that our approach will yield genes with a high probability of being relevant to the development of asthma. In this proposal our initial efforts will be directed towards identifying asthma susceptibility genes within a chromosomal region that has gone undetected in previous studies. This region shows a strong effect and therefore will be more easily amenable to gene identification. In addition, the region harbors several candidate genes that may provide new insights into the mechanisms of asthma susceptibility. Another important aspect of the proposal involves understanding the various pathological characteristics of asthma. It will address the question of whether the same genes and pathways underly asthma and allergy, and aid the identification of allergy susceptibility genes.   We anticipate that the proposed studies will provide us with a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying asthma which may enable the identification of new treatments and targets for new drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Title: Molecular Mechanisms of Lung Protection from Ventilator Induced Lung Injury (VILI)
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY; CELL STRETCH; KNOCK OUT MICE; MECHANOTRANSDUCTION; MICROARRAY; TRANSCRIPTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; VENTILATOR INDUCED LUNG INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a common and devastating problem affecting many patients in the intensive care unit. This syndrome is characterized by severe lung inflammation which prevents patients from breathing independently - so most patients need to be placed on life support. Although mechanical ventilation in these patients can be life saving, studies have shown that repeated lung stretch that occurs during artificial ventilation can also increase lung injury and promote further inflammation. This is called ventilator induced lung injury (VILI). VILI contributes significantly to the mortality and long term morbidity of ARDS patients.  There are no known specific treatments for ARDS. The only strategy shown to decrease mortality in these patients is the use of lower tidal volumes - which minimizes lung stretch. My lab is dedicated to understanding how the ventilator causes this type of injury and using this knowledge to develop new therapeutic approaches to reduce lung injury. Using novel genomic technology we have identified a new transcription factor (a molecule that regulates the function of other molecules) that we believe may be important in protecting the lungs from mechanical injury. The mechanism of this protection is unknown. Therefore, in this grant we propose to identify the mechanisms by which ATF3 may protect lungs from VILI. We will use both in-vivo (animal) and in-vitro (cell) models to determine which cells (circulating vs. tissue) play a major role; and which mechanisms (inflammation, cell death [apoptosis] or/and oxidative stress) enable ATF3 to protect lungs from lung injury. This is very important because identifying and understanding novel mechanisms of lung protection is fundamental to developing novel treatment approaches for these and possibly all other patients on life support.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of early adversity on the developing serotonin system in humans:  A monozygotic twin study of epigenetic mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH WEIGHT; EMOTION REGULATION; EPIGENETICS; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEURODEVELOPMENT; SEROTONIN
Abstract-Résumé: A number of studies have shown that individuals born to mothers who were exposed to severe stressors during pregnancy are at increased risk of developing psychological problems later in life. The brain chemical serotonin may be important in this process. Animal studies have shown that adversity during pregnancy can alter the activity of serotonin and the function and structure of brain regions playing a role in the regulation of emotions in the newborn. These alterations can persist until adulthood. In the proposed project, we will investigate whether these long-lasting alterations also occur in humans. To study this, adolescents will undergo a brain scan (called fMRI) while viewing faces with emotional expressions. This is a standard procedure to measure, in the laboratory, how the brain reacts to situations that elicit emotions. Adversity will be indexed by birth weight since lower birth weight is indicative of greater adversity during pregnancy. We expect that birth weight will predict the function of those parts of the brain that are important in emotion regulation. We will also investigate one of the mechanisms by which adversity during pregnancy may affect the brain: via changes in gene expression. One of the genes that we will look at is the serotonin transporter, a gene that determines how much serotonin is used in the brain. These questions will be examined in twin pairs that have been followed almost yearly since they were born.  We hope that this project will increase our understanding of the specific role of early environmental influences on brain development, gene expression and mental health. Results should eventually lead to a better understanding of possible early ways to foster optimal brain development and prevent mental health problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intrinsically Disordered Domains and Cellular Pathways in Virus-Mediated Cell-Cell Fusion.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENS JUNCTIONS; INTRINSICALLY DISORDERED DOMAINS; MEMBRANE FUSION; PROTEIN STRUCTURE-FUNCTION; REGULATED INTRAMEMBRANE PROTEOLYSIS; REOVIRUSES; VIRAL MEMBRANE FUSION PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Numerous viruses, such as HIV and influenza virus, induce virus-infected cells to fuse their membranes with those of neighboring uninfected cells, thereby promoting spread of the infection. Cell-cell membrane fusion is not only induced by viruses, but it is an essential feature of numerous biological processes such as muscle and bone development, fertilization, and formation of the placenta and the lens of the eye. There is therefore considerable interest in trying to understand how cellular membranes fuse together. While the cellular proteins responsible for membrane fusion remain elusive, numerous viral membrane fusion proteins have been identified. These viral proteins have become the models for how proteins induce membrane fusion. Our research is focused on a new family of viral membrane fusion proteins encoded by the fusogenic reoviruses. These fusion-associated small transmembrane (FAST) proteins are unlike all previously characterized membrane fusion proteins. Our research efforts are focused on trying to understand how the FAST proteins function, and to use this information to characterize the cellular factors and pathways that contribute to this process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of importance of sCD200 levels for prognosis in CLL patients
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA; MONITORING TUMOR THERAPY; SERUM MARKERS OF DISEASE; TUMOR CLASSIFICATION; TUMOR DIAGNOSIS; TUMOR PROGNOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Gorczynski is studying chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), the most common adult leukemia in western countries. It is recognized that there is a need to identify "high-risk" disease and design more effective treatment strategies for them, without exposing patients with less aggressive disease to the same therapies. The Gorczynski laboratory proposes that a new marker, namely the presence of increased levels of a soluble molecule CD200 in the serum of patients, may help identify such "high risk" patients, and that treatments directed at antagonizing the function of CD200 will improve outcome in CLL.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toward personalized immunotherapy: identifying tumour-specific factors that dictate the response of spontaneous mammary cancers to T cells
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CD8+ T CELLS; CELL MIGRATION; CELL-CELL INTERACTION; CYTOKINES; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; IMMUNOTHERAPY; TUMOR STROMA; TUMOR-INFILTRATING LYMPHOCYTES; WHOLE TRANSCRIPTOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research will investigate how the immune system responds to breast cancer, and how best to manipulate the immune response to treat established tumors. Our group developed a transgenic mouse model of breast cancer, in which mice develop spontaneous mammary tumors at 6-9 months of age. Tumors are engineered to express a model antigen (ovalbumin) that can be recognized by the immune system. We then try to cure tumors by infusing immune cells (specifically "helper and killer T cells") that recognize the tumor. Using this system, we have shown that ~35% of mammary tumors can be completely eradicated by T cell infusion without the need for any other form of treatment. This is among the most striking examples of successful T cell therapy ever reported. However, ~65% of tumors somehow survive the T cell attack. In our first cycle of funding, we showed that many tumors resist T cell attack by physically blocking the entry of T cells into the centre of the tumor; such tumors are said to have an "infiltration barrier". In Aim 1, we will use modern genomic approaches to dissect tumors at a molecular level to better understand what makes tumors sensitive or resistant to T cell therapy. In Aim 2, we will alter the expression of key genes in tumors and test whether this increases or decreases their sensitivity to T cell therapy. Finally, in Aim 3 we will apply similar approaches to human breast tumors that have elicited either strong or weak T cell responses in patients. This study will advance our understanding of the immune response to breast cancer and generate new strategies to enhance immune-based treatments. In future, it may be possible to better predict which patients will respond to immunotherapy, and how best to enhance the immune response as a new form of treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cooperation between the Notch and the kRas signaling pathways in pancreatic cancer progression.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPY; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL SIGNALING; KRAS/RAF/MEK/ERK SIGNALING PATHWAY; NOTCH SIGNALING PATHWAY; PANCREATIC CANCER; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: With an overall 5-year survival rate under 5% and a median survival of 6 months, pancreatic cancer is the most devastating human malignancies. Moreover, the almost identical annual incidence and mortality rates make it the fourth leading cause of cancer-related death in Canada and worldwide.  Despite enormous progress in medicine, the survival of patients with pancreatic cancer has not significantly improved over the last 40 years. The main reasons for the dismal prognosis of this type of cancer remains the late diagnosis of the disease, hence rendering surgical resection rates exceedingly low in addition to yielding poor clinical response to chemotherapy. This raises the urgent need for the identification of biomarkers to aid in the early detection of pancreatic cancer as well as in the development of new and effective treatment strategies.  To attempt this goal, a better understanding of the detailed mechanisms of disease pathogenesis is critical.  Previous studies have identified two signaling pathways aberrantly re-activated in cancerous pancreatic tissues compared to normal pancreatic tissues: the kRas and Notch pathways.  Our results suggest that these two signaling pathways cooperate to promote pancreatic carcinogenesis.  The general aim of our research is thus to understand how these two signaling pathways interact in order to promote progression of pancreatic cancer and evaluate whether inhibition of one of this pathway (the Notch pathway) blocks pancreatic cancer progression and thus can be envisaged as a new therapeutic avenue. To answer these questions, we will use both pancreatic cell lines and mouse models of pancreatic cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Steroids In caRdiac Surgery trial (SIRS)
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC SURGERY; CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS PUMP; CORONARY ARTERY BYPASS GRAFT; STEROIDS
Abstract-Résumé: SIRS trial is a large simple study in which high-risk patients undergoing cardiac surgery requiring the use of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) are randomly allocated to receive a pulse dose of steroids or a matching placebo.  Cardiopulmonary bypass initiates a systemic inflammatory response that contributes to post-operative complications.  A review of the available literature demonstrates that there is evidence that steroids decrease this unfavorable response and may have clinical benefit while having an excellent safety profile.  In fact, from the available evidence, the 2004 AHA guidelines for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) support liberal prophylactic use in patients undergoing extracorporeal circulation.  However, cardiac surgeons are resistant to adopt this practice for fears of adverse effects of peri-operative steroids and because the available studies are too small to make conclusive statements. This study of 7500 patients will address whether pulse dose steroids result in improved early survival and less heart injury in cardiac surgery requiring CPB.  This inexpensive and accessible treatment has the potential to save many lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel functions of histone acetylation.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; GENETICS; HISTONE ACETYLATION; HISTONE METHYLATION; SACCHAROMYCES CEREVISIAE
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately two metres of DNA is packaged into the nucleus of a single human cell. This event is facilitated by a class of proteins known as histones that, akin to thread on spools, compact the DNA into a compartment that is only 0.00002-0.00004 metres in diameter. Current data suggests that only 5% of the human genome codes for proteins, the basic building blocks of our cells. Storing the remaining 95% of DNA in an inaccessible form is important for both genome stability and for protection of our cells from the dangerous effects of the parasitic retroviral DNA elements that reside within our genomes. Our cells are therefore challenged with the task of keeping 5% of the genome in an active and accessible state, while maintaining the remaining 95% as inactive and inaccessible. This is analogous to playing "Three Card Monte" with twenty cards.  The research in my lab strives to understand how our cells "cheat" at Monte by marking the coding regions of our genomes as "active" and protecting these regions from factors that inactivate the remaining parts of the genome. We are specifically interested in understanding the role of a chemical modification of histones, known as acetylation, that our cells use as a molecular flag to label regions of gene expression. Histone acetylation controls gene expression and changes in histone acetylation occur during aging and cancer development.  Drugs are currently being developed that can regulate histone acetylation, and in addition to their use as cancer treatments, they are being studied for efficacy in treatment of a wide range of diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Huntington's disease, Lupus, and rheumatoid arthritis.  However despite the applicability these drugs in the treatment of multiple diseases, there remain large gaps in our knowledge regarding the establishment and function of histone acetylation.   We study the importance of histone acetylation on gene expression using baker's yeast as a model organism.

TitreApplicationTitle: A calreticulin-cytomechanical switch in osteoblast-adipocyte fate choice in an ES cell model
Keywords-MotsClés: CA BINDING PROTEINS; CHONDRO/OSTEOGENESIS; DEVELOPMENT; ES CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Work from several laboratories has demonstrated that cell shape, cytoskeletal tension and substratum elasticity direct differentiation in many cell types including embryonic stem cells. Calreticulin, a Ca-binding protein either by its role in intracellular Ca homeostasis or as a helper protein, modulates signalling pathways that control cell lineage specification and tissue formation. The growth substratum also influences the formation of tissues by affecting the cell adhesion and shape, which are modulated by calreticulin. Thus, both cell shape and signalling pathways are affected by calreticulin expression level. Consequently, we postulate that the cell fate choice is controlled by the combinatorial action of calreticulin level of expression and biomechanics of the substratum.  While the role of calreticulin in adipogenesis and cardiomyogenesis from ES cells has been established, its role in skeletogenesis is not yet clear.  In the present proposal, we thus wish to first elucidate the role of calreticulin in differentiation of embryonic stem cells towards skeletal tissue. Next, we will elucidate the role of substratum biomechanics in directing differentiation of embryonic stem cells in the presence or absence of calreticulin.   These experiments will allow us to delineate the role of calreticulin in cell differentiation from embryonic stem cells and will address the emerging question of the impact of the biomechanics of the environment on cell fate. The results may have important implications for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of LDL Receptor Degradation by PCSK9
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM BINDING; ENDOCYTIC RECEPTOR RECYCLING; EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR-LIKE DOMAINS; LOW-DENSITY LIPOPROTEIN RECEPTOR; PROPROTEIN CONVERTASE SUBTILISIN/KEXIN TYPE-9; PROTEIN CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION
Abstract-Résumé: Low-density lipoprotein (LDL), the so-called "bad" cholesterol, is a major cause of heart disease and stroke.  More than 25 million people worldwide take a class of drugs known as statins to help lower their LDL cholesterol level to within recommended healthy limits. The LDL receptor is a protein on the cell surface that juts out and latches onto "bad" cholesterol in the bloodstream, drawing it into cells.  A protein in blood called PCSK9 can also latch onto the LDL receptor, however, this binding triggers LDL receptor destruction.  With fewer receptors available, more "bad" cholesterol remains in the bloodstream.  The research undertaken will aid in the design of drugs that neutralize PCSK9 by determining how binding of PCSK9 to LDL receptor is regulated and also how the LDL receptor is destroyed in cells.  While statins drugs work by increasing the number of LDL receptors that are made in the body, a drug to inhibit PCSK9 would keep the existing receptors from being degraded.  A combination of these two drugs promises to be a very effective treatment for lowering "bad" cholesterol levels in the blood.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cell migration by a Rap1 GTPase-dependent sensor of extracellular matrix density that controls cytoskeletal and focal adhesion dynamics.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL ADHESION; CELL MIGRATION; CYTOSKELETON; INTRAVITAL IMAGING; LIVE CELL IMAGING; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION
Abstract-Résumé: The ability of cells to move within the body, which requires them to attach to and pull themselves along a web of matrix proteins, is a highly regulated component of tissue and organ development. When cancers metastasize, this process is co-opted such that tumor cells move abnormally from the tissue of origin (ie. breast or prostate) to distant sites (ie. bone or brain) during the terminal endstages of the disease. We have recently determined that a cell's ability to sense the number of attachment proteins present in the matrix web is a key regulator of cell migration and metastasis. Therefore, this project has been designed to identify the key molecular components of this 'sensor' such that new therapeutic strategies can be developed to prevent metastatic spread by overriding it.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Vibrio cholerae Type VI Protein Secretion System and its Role in Microbial Competition
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PROTEIN SECRETION; BACTERIAL TOXINS; BIOLOGICAL MEMBRANES; DICTYOSTELIUM DISCOIDEUM; GENE REGULATION; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; MICROBIAL PATHOGENESIS; PERSISTENCE; VIBRIO CHOLERAE; VIRULENCE FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The emergence of new and drug-resistant variants of microbial agents of disease (also known as pathogens) represents a challenge to human health. The objective of the proposed research is to understand how these disease-causing entities interact with other microbes and host cells in an attempt to identify novel drug targets for alternative therapies. We are studying Vibrio cholerae, the bacterium that causes cholera - an infection of the small intestine that causes severe watery diarrhea, dehydration, and too often death.   While cholera is endemic in many regions of the world causing over 120,000 deaths every year, it is also one of the first diseases that emerge when a country is faced with an economic crisis or a natural disaster, mostly because the health care system and sanitation infrastructure breaks down. The most recent examples are Zimbabwe which experienced a major cholera outbreak in 2009 with 100,000 cases and 4,300 deaths, and Haiti which suffers from the consequences of a major earthquake in early 2010. Cholera then becomes a health threat to those Canadians who travel to these affected regions as relief workers or health professionals.  The delivery of poisonous substances (toxins) is a common mechanism bacteria use to cause disease. We have discovered a novel mechanism by which V. cholerae delivers toxins to kill other bacteria as well as eukaryotic cells. We hypothesize that V. cholerae uses this system to cope with competitors in the environment and in the human host where they cause disease.   This project is designed to expand our knowledge on how this delivery mechanism contributes to microbial infections.  We plan to do this by studying when the toxins are produced, where the toxins go, and what the toxins do in the infected host cell. We anticipate that our findings will help us identify weaknesses that can be exploited therapeutically for the large number of pathogens whose genomes contain the information for this virulence mechanism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolic network analysis in apicomplexan parasites: Mechanistic insights into coccidian pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: APICOMPLEXA; BIOINFORMATICS; FLUX BALANCE ANALYSIS; GENE KNOCKDOWNS; GENOMICS; METABOLIC PATHWAYS; PARASITES; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TOXOPLASMA
Abstract-Résumé: Parasites inflict devastation and misery on the lives of their victims, leaving millions of people debilitated and incapacitated. For example, malaria affects over 300 million people worldwide, while almost one fifth of the population of North America is chronically infected with a related parasite - Toxoplasma (the causative agent of toxoplasmosis). Indeed, in terms of prevalence and disease burden toxoplasmosis is considered the most important parasitic infection in the North American Arctic. The high prevalence of Toxoplasma has severe implications for pregnant women and those whose immune systems have been compromised (e.g. individuals affected by HIV/AIDS). Occasionally infections in otherwise healthy adults can result in the loss of vision, motor and cognitive function. Despite the terrifying impact of these parasites, relatively few effective treatments and vaccines are currently available.  Our team seeks to exploit available genome information to identify parasite protein targets for therapeutic intervention. Due to their fundamental role and mode of operation, metabolic enzymes represent ideal candidates for the development of new drugs. Examining these enzymes in the context of the pathways in which they are involved, allows the identification of those which perform essential roles. We will combine sophisticated mathematical models with state-of-the-art functional genomics to identify metabolic enzymes and pathways critical to the survival of the parasite within the host. Those which show promise as amenable drug targets will be subsequently characterised through a series of experimental assays.  With new insights into the molecular basis of parasitism, this program of research promises to deliver a host of new candidate drug targets that may be exploited through existing drug development pipelines.

TitreApplicationTitle: The physiological basis of hearing and balance by hair cells of the inner ear
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HAIR CELLS; HEARING AND BALANCE; INNER EAR; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Hearing disorders affect two in 1000 newborns and yet the molecular underpinnings of hearing are poorly understood.  Hearing loss increases with age, eventually affecting 40% of adults over 75.  Hearing loss and vestibular disorders are usually caused by the loss of the sensory receptor cells, called hair cells, located in the inner ear.  Hair cells can be damaged due to disease, noise exposure (including cell phones) or drug toxicity.  Hair cell death is irreversible and leads to permanent hearing loss.  We will tackle these important health issues by discovering genes that contribute to auditory function and finding ways to preserve and regenerate hair cells.  This includes a combination of physiological and molecular approaches using mice and zebrafish to find the genes that are essential for converting sound and head movements into electrical potentials as well as screening gene targets for their ability to promote hair cell regeneration.  Our findings will enhance our understanding of the genetic basis of auditory and vestibular disorders, a critical step toward developing successful therapies.  Results from this research will contribute to the health of Canadians through the discovery of ways to regenerate inner ear sensory cells.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Genomic changes in human miscarriages and their functional consequences
Keywords-MotsClés: ABNORMAL HUMAN PRENATAL DEVELOPMENT; EMBRYO AND PLACENTA DEVELOPMENT; GENE FUNCTION; GENOMIC ARRAYS; RECURRENT PREGNANCY LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: Pregnancy loss is a significant health concern as 15 percent of clinically recognized pregnancies end in miscarriage, with the highest rate in the first trimester. Although finding the cause of pregnancy loss is essential for prognosis, recurrence risk counseling, and the management of all future pregnancies, the cause remains unknown in 30-50 percent of all cases. Our recent studies of sporadic and recurrent miscarriages showed that previously not described and very tiny chromosome changes, detectable only by genomic array technology, occur in 30 percent of miscarriages. In addition, our studies revealed that these tiny (submicroscopic) chromosomal abnormalities may also occur in couples with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss and may represent predisposing genetic factors for recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL). We propose to expand our screening for submicroscopic chromosomal abnormalities to additional miscarriages and couples with RPL in order to identify new genetic causes for RPL. Furthermore, we propose to determine if the function of the genes affected by these submicroscopic rearrangements (candidate miscarriage genes) is altered. We will focus on genes which have a suspected function in reproduction and early embryo/placenta development. The benefit of our study is that costly multiple testing and searching for causes of miscarriage can be eliminated for couples found to carry or transmit the candidate miscarriage genes to their pregnancies. In addition, new genes important for maintaining a successful pregnancy will be identified. The better understanding of genetic factors that contribute to pregnancy loss will pave the path for their future prevention and treatment and facilitate optimal care for reproductive health of families wishing to have a successful future pregnancy.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Studies of the molecular mechanisms by which mutations in the SUR2A NBDs cause cardiovascular diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: ATP-SENSITIVE POTASSIUM CHANNELS; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; NUCLEOTIDE BINDING DOMAINS; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN DYNAMICS; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Potassium ion channels in cells are essential for healthy function of the heart. These channels are formed from two different types of proteins. One protein, called Kir6.2, forms the channel pore while the other protein, known as SUR2A, regulates opening and closing of the pore. Proper control of the channel is essential as mutations in the gene for SUR2A cause cardiovascular disorders.  We will study the molecular details by which SUR2A mutations result in potassium channel dysfunction in the heart. SUR2A mutations cause many disease-causing defects, including altered ability of SUR2A to sense the cellular concentration of ATP (the energy currency of cells) and the inefficient transport of the channel from the site of protein synthesis to the cell membrane where it functions. These defects likely result from changes in (1) the 3-D arrangement of atoms in SUR2A, (2) movement of specific regions in SUR2A, and (3) the way that SUR2A interacts with other parts of the channel.  Thus, obtaining a 3D picture of SUR2A is critical to understanding cardiovascular diseases. We will focus on the regions of SUR2A that are the sites of disease-causing mutations. These regions, called nucleotide binding domains (NBDs), utilize the energy of ATP to control opening and closing of the pore. Knowledge of the changes in the molecular details of the NBDs caused by the mutations will help develop new treatments for disease.  We will use a technique very similar to medical MRI to get a detailed 3D picture of the SUR2A NBDs alone and bound to other parts of the channel. These experiments will also give information regarding how the 3D shape of the NBDs changes in time, which is important for function. We will compare mutants of SUR2A NBDs that cause disease to the SUR2A NBDs in their normal state. These studies promise to enhance our understanding of how SUR2A mutations cause cardiovascular diseases and this molecular level knowledge will help design new molecules to treat disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: E2A proteins in acute lymphoblastic leukemia: Structural and functional analysis and inhibition of oncogenic protein-protein interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: B-CELL DEVELOPMENT; BIOPHYSICAL APPROACHES; CANCER; NMR; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common cancer in children. ALL often arises due to defects in the normal development of blood cells, which then grow in an uncontrolled manner. A high percentage of cases of pediatric ALL is caused when the E2A protein, which is normally present in developing B-cells, is fused to another protein PBX1. This linkage disrupts the normal control mechanism in B-cell development. To better understand how E2A contributes to ALL we have recently identified a specific protein that E2A interact with, and that this interaction is key to the onset of ALL. In this new application, we will determine how specific regions of E2A interact with their target protein, what changes in E2A structure affect these interactions, and identify/design small molecule inhibitors that can be used as molecular probes to better characterize the role of E2A-PBX1 in leukemia. Our novel approach could lead to new therapies for treating children afflicted with ALL.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Iron and Heme Metabolism in Erythroid Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CLONING; DMT1; ERYTHROID CELLS; FERRITIN; HEME SYNTHESIS; HYPOCHROMIC MICROCYTIC ANEMIAS; IRON REGULATOR PROTEINS 1 AND 2; MITOCHONDRIAL FERRITIN; TRANSFECTIONS; TRANSFERRIN RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Iron is an essential nutrient for all cells and tissues.  However, because of iron in hemoglobin of red blood cells, these cells contain up to 70% of the total iron in a normal adult.  Therefore, by far red blood cells have the highest requirement for iron, but our knowledge on iron translocation in developing red blood cells is rather limited.  We shall investigate the mechanisms involved in the acquisition and intracellular transport of iron in immature red blood cells.  Defects either in iron acquisition by red blood cells or in its translocation within the cells lead to anemias.  We shall use various experimental and animal models to identify and characterize such defects in iron acquisition and translocation.  This research will be very important for understanding some of the anemias occurring in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mitochondrial Uncoupling in Skeletal Muscle: Molecular Mechanisms to Whole Body Implications
Keywords-MotsClés: MITOCHONDRIA; MUSCLE; OBESITY; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS; UNCOUPLING PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Over 60 percent of Canadian adults are currently overweight or obese. Within the last generation, the percentage of overweight or obese children has also risen dramatically.  The health risks associated with obesity are well known, and include type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and cardiovascular disease, both of which are increasingly an issue in young adults. An early risk factor for T2DM is 'insulin resistance' - a situation in which insulin is no longer effective in stimulating glucose entry into many cell types including muscle. Interventions that decrease insulin resistance can prevent the full development of T2DM. Causes underlying individual susceptibility to obesity and T2DM are complex and include many environmental and biological factors. The overall goal of this research is to address some biological mechanisms in muscle that protect against obesity and T2DM. Detailed mechanistic analyses will be conducted on the metabolic function of proteins that reside in the 'powerhouses' of cells, the mitochondria.  Specific objectives will examine the molecular mechanisms of uncoupling protein-3 (UCP3) function. UCP3 is a mitochondrial protein that facilitates fat oxidation, and protects cells from oxidative stress - but the molecular mechanisms are as yet unknown. Recent findings from our laboratory identify novel roles for UCP3 in glucose metabolism on the surface of mitochondria, and in mitochondrial proton leak.  The metabolic implications of these processes for the efficiency of energy transduction processes in muscle will be studied in mice lacking UCP3; mice that have higher than normal levels of UCP3 in muscle, and in normal control mice.  An epigenetic model of obesity and T2DM susceptibility in mice will also be examined. Additional determinations will be conducted in biopsied muscle from obese adults. The research is expected to improve our limited understanding of the role of impaired mitochondrial metabolism in obesity and obesity-related disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Bedside Paediatric Early Warning System: a cluster randomized trial of mortality and processes of care
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ARREST; HEALTH SYSTEMS; PAEDIATRICS; PREVENTION; RESUSCITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiac arrest in children cared for in hospital wards is often fatal, and survivors may have brain damage. Nearly 5000 children have near or actual cardiac arrest each year in Canadian and American paediatric hospital wards. It is estimated that 80% of these events could have been prevented. Despite all the expertise available to treat children in hospitals, it is apparent that current systems of cardiac arrest prevention are not working. With a multi-disciplinary team we developed a new documentation-based system of care to prevent cardiac arrest in children. We called it the Bedside PEWS. Our research to date shows that the Bedside PEWS has potential. However the actual benefits of Bedside PEWS are not known. We want to know if the Bedside PEWS can help identify children-at-risk earlier, prevent cardiac arrest, and save lives. It is a big deal to introduce systems like the Bedside PEWS into hospitals. It is important to be sure that it is worth the effort. This research is to study the effect of the Bedside PEWS when used to help care for children in hospital wards. We think the Bedside PEWS may improve the quality of patient records, and that it will improve hospital efficiency. We hope that the Bedside PEWS prevents cardiac arrest and saves lives. This study will answer the question: "Can the Bedside PEWS prevent cardiac arrest and improve the outcomes of hospitalized children?". Knowing this is important. Knowing will allow doctors, nurses and other hospital leaders to confidently make the major decisions about how best to care for hospitalized children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ensuring effective newborn screening: The case of cystic fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTH DATA; CHILD HEALTH POLICY; MIXED METHODS RESEARCH; POPULATION SCREENING; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SURVEY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada and most developed countries, all infants are tested shortly after birth for signs of certain rare disorders that must be identified and treated before clinical symptoms become apparent. The initial test "screens" infants to find those who might be at risk; those identified to be at risk must have further testing to find out whether they do have the disorder (called "true" positive), do not have the disorder (called "false" positive), or cannot be immediately diagnosed (called "uncertain" positive). Newborn screening (NBS) is performed to find and provide care for "true" positives, but it always affects other families who get "false" or "uncertain" results. In the past, very few conditions were tested for, so the implications of NBS for families and health care providers were limited. In recent years, however, NBS programs have begun to test for a much larger number of conditions. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is one such condition that has recently been added to NBS programs in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario, Canada, and in other places around the world. Very good evidence exists to show that infants with CF will be better off if they are identified as newborns and given the best possible care, but evidence regarding the experience of all families who receive positive screening results, the implications for health care providers and health services, and ways to ensure the best care, is limited. This study will examine NBS for CF in Ontario as a case study to ensure a fulsome assessment of the health service and familial implications of expanded NBS in the Canadian context, and generate evidence to support planning and policy development. We have 3 main objectives: To explore the impact of CF newborn screening on (1) mothers of CF screen positive infants, (2) health care providers (primary care and specialists), and (3) use of health services by CF screen positive infants and their mothers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of dasatinib cytotoxicity and sensitization to standard therapy in chronic lymphocytic leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CHLORAMBUCIL; CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA; DASATINIB; FLUDARABINE; P53
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is the most common leukemia in adults. Even though individuals with chronic lymphocytic leukemia do better after they have been treated they eventually became tolerant to the treatments available. Thus there is no actually cure for the disease. In a previous project funded by the CIHR, our group find that a drug called dasatinib prevents the malignant lymphocytes from surviving when used alone or in combination with standard therapeutic agents. In the present proposal we intend to further understand the mechanisms by which dasatinib kills CLL lymphocytes. Also we want to confirm our preliminary results that suggests that the drug may be really effective in killing the lymphocytes of patients which are resistant to other treatments. These lymphocyte patients display a genetic abnormality associated with poor response to standard therapy and poor survival. Our understanding of the mechanisms of action of dasatinib so far, predicts that dasatinib may exacerbate the killing effect of other anticancer agents used to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia. We will perform all the experiments using cancer cells isolated from the blood of CLL patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: IL-7 and IL-15 as Potential Immunotherapies for Cancer and Chronic Viral Infections
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC VIRAL INFECTIONS; IL-7; IMMUNOTHERAPY; IN VIVO MOUSE MODELS; MOLECULAR SIGNALLING; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: The immune responses mounted by our bodies to persistent viruses often do not clear these threats, resulting in chronic virus infections. Our group is studying the possibility of using an intercellular messenger molecule (a cytokine) called IL-7 to bolster the body's attack on these assaults. The proposed experiments will be performed using a combination of genetically modified mice and variant viruses that will allow us to monitor a specific anti-viral immune response and the effects of IL-7 therapy on that response.       IL-7 stimulates cells of the immune system, prolonging their survival and increasing their capacity to kill virus-infected cells. Unlike other cytokines tried as therapies, IL-7 in large quantity is not toxic. Thus, IL-7 is a promising agent for human immunotherapy. However, the mechanism by which this cytokine acts is unknown, and whether this approach can be safely and effectively translated to human patients in the clinic is not clear. We intend to investigate how IL-7 works and to determine in mice how broadly applicable its effects might be. The specific experiments we will undertake involve infecting mice with a particular virus strain known to establish a chronic infection. The animals will be treated with IL-7 or a control reagent and the course of disease will be monitored. We will analyze cells from the affected mice and determine at the molecular level what intracellular signalling molecules have been altered and why.      IL-7 treatment designed to bolster anti-tumour responses in mice with cancer has led to highly encouraging results, and we hope that IL-7 will be similarly effective against chronic virus infections. Our findings may translate well to humans and thus have wide applicability, including to the treatment of intractable virus infections such as HIV and hepatitis C.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular analysis of chromosome assembly
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMOSOME; CONDENSIN; HIGH RESOLUTION IMAGING; MITOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Uncontrolled cell division is a fundamental hallmark of cancer. Chromosome assembly (termed "condensation") occurs prior to each cell division in order to compartmentalize the genome into manageable packages. Without condensation, each chromosome would be approximately 1000x longer that the cell length, making this process central to accurately segregating the genome to the daughter cells. This proposal uses high-resolution imaging and analysis techniques coupled to targeted protein depletion in the soil nematode C. elegans to uncover fundamental properties of chromosome condensation. Mechanisms discovered in this work will likely be prime targets for chemotherapeutics in the treatment of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of diabetes on tau pathogenesis in vivo
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; DIABETES MELLITUS; TAU PATHOLOGY; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia. It is an incurable, degenerative and terminal disease that afflicts an estimated 27 million people worldwide. In the brain, it is characterized by the presence of two protein aggregates: amyloid plaques, and neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs). NFTs are composed of bundles of aggregated tau protein. There is clinical evidence that diabetes is associated with an increased risk of AD, but there is very little understanding of the mechanism by which diabetes could affect AD. The overall goal of this project is therefore to clarify the impacts that diabetes has on tau protein pathogenesis, one of the pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease. My hypothesis is that diabetes will induce tau pathology by deregulating signaling cascades in the brain. In turn, this will result in tau dysfunction and memory impairment. To address my hypothesis, I will develop the three following specific aims: Aim 1: To characterize the effect diabetes on tau pathogenesis in vivo Aim 2: To elucidate the mechanisms of tau pathogenesis in diabetes in vivo Aim 3: To investigate the functional and behavioral effects of tau pathology during diabetes The aims focus on one aspect of Alzheimer's disease: tau pathogenesis. Completion of those aims will help clarify the impact of diabetes on Alzheimer's disease pathology. In turn, this understanding will help the development of treatments or life-style strategies destined to check the advance of the disease. In light of the increased incidence of diabetes in the young population that predict higher incidence of senile dementias in the coming years, our study may provide invaluable information for the treatment and prevention of sporadic AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of receptor tyrosine kinases in the initiation and progression of colorectal cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ANIMAL MODELS; CARCINOGENESIS; COLORECTAL CANCER PROGRESSION; CONDITIONAL MICE KNOCKOUT; METASTASIS; RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASE; RNAI INTERFERENCE; THERAPEUTIC TARGETS; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer represents the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in North America. Despite adequate surgical removal of the primary tumor, relapse of the disease occurs within 5 years in nearly half of the patients, who will eventually die principally due to metastatic spread of the disease. Colorectal cancer represents a progressive disorder arising through the accumulation of multiple heterogeneous genetic and molecular changes that may never be fully identifiable for each colorectal tumor. Hence, one of the challenges in the development of new therapies relies on the identification of targets that regulate biological processes required for the initiation and/or malignant progression of colorectal cancer, i.e.: cell division, survival, invasion, and motility, as well as the formation of new blood vessels, a process termed angiogenesis. These are biological processes under the control of a family of growth factor cell surface receptors with tyrosine kinase activity, which are frequently deregulated in colorectal malignancies, such as the hepatocyte growth factor receptor, also known as the Met receptor. In this project, we will use molecular and cellular approaches, both in vitro and in vivo, to define in the context of the Met RTK, the functional significance of RTK signaling proteins in the initiation and malignant progression of colorectal cancer. These studies will determine which signaling proteins engaged by RTKs represent valid targets for the eventual development of new therapeutic strategies to reduce the growth of primary colorectal tumors and/or the incidence of metastases. Thus, it may have significant impact on future treatments for patients afflicted by this dreadful disease that is colorectal cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innovative Approaches to Functional Characterization of the Androgen Receptor in Prostate Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN RECEPTOR; DNA METHYLATION; EXON ARRAYS; GENE EXPRESSION; PROSTATE CANCER; PROTEOMICS; RNA SPLICING; SOMATIC MUTATIONS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Hormones play a vital role in normal physiology, but they do not work alone. In order to understand hormones, we must understand how their receptors work. For every hormone made and circulated in the body, there is a specific receptor on or within cells that binds to that hormone. We focus on how male hormones (androgens) work by investigating the androgen receptor. Many times studying a mutant receptor can be very informative when we are trying to understand how a normal receptor works. We study androgen receptor mutations that cause several different diseases, and specifically prostate cancer, in which men develop resistance to anti-androgen treatment. We will use a proteomics approach (large-scale analysis of proteins) to identify proteins that interact with normal and mutant androgen receptors. We will also examine how different androgen receptors and hormones affect which genes are "turned on" or "off" in cells. When we study mutant receptors we can relate certain parts or structures of the androgen receptor to its functions. In this way we can get a better idea of how the androgen receptor works and how mutations cause disease. In the end, knowing more about normal and mutant androgen receptors should lead to better screening and treatments for prostate cancer.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal derived Semaphorin 3A contributes to vascular degeneration and  misdirected pathological vessel growth in proliferative ischemic retinopathies
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ENDOTHELIAL CELL; GUIDANCE CUES; PROLIFERATIVE RETINOPATHIES; RETINAL GANGLION CELLS; SEMAPHORIN
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) and retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) (collectively termed proliferative retinopathies (PRs)) are the leading causes of blindness in the world. Like a cancerous tumor, they are characterized by excessive blood vessel growth inside the eye, on the surface of a neuron-rich structure called the retina. In a healthy individual, the retina captures and transforms light into electrical pulses that are transmitted to the brain as images. Adequate retinal function ensures vision. The clinically demonstrable features of PRs have lead to the inference that these diseases are entirely of a vascular nature. Yet a body of evidence now points to changes in neurons in the retina as early events in these diseases. We recently published that neurons which intimately interact with blood vessels are important effectors of the excessive vessel growth associated with PRs. Recently, we found that these same retinal neurons in a stressed context (as in PRs) produce a molecule named Semaphorin 3A (Sema3A) that binds to a receptor named Neuropilin-1 (Nrp-1) thus provoking the repulsion of blood vessels away from desired regions of the retina into zones where they will interfere with vision. It is thus compelling to hypothesize that these neuron-derived Sema3A is an important contributor to the abnormalities observed in these diseases. The proposed grant is designed to investigate the relevance of Sema3A and its receptor Nrp-1  as a cause of blindness by addressing in the following aims: i) Determine quantitatively during the development of PR the retinal localization of the Sema3A and Nrp-1.  ii) Assess the therapeutic relevance of the Sema3A and Nrp-1 axis in PRs.  iii) Establish the influence of Sema3A on vessel guidance and vessel death.  The therapeutic options to counter PRs are limited to invasive interventions. Applications of findings are broad and can be harnessed for cancer and cerebral-vascular infarcts where vascular growth is perturbed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics of natural killer cell response to virus infection
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEX TRAIT ANALYSIS; CYTOMEGALOVIRUS INFECTION; DNA SEQUENCE ANALYSIS; GENE IDENTIFICATION; GENOMICS; INNATE IMMUNITY; MODELS OF INFECTION; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; NATURAL KILLER RECEPTORS; POXVIRUS INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Natural Killer (NK) cells are a critical arm of the host antiviral response in humans and mice alike. Our laboratory and others have previously shown that key mechanisms of NK cell function can be discovered using mouse genetic models of virus infection, even without the prior knowledge of their existence, location, and function. For example, this approach has provided a fresh view on how NK cells recognize and eliminate virally-infected cells. Here we propose to build on this productive strategy by exploiting mouse models of experimental infections relevant to human disease, new genetic resources unique to our laboratory, and the latest advances in genome research to identify genes that control the NK response against virus infections. A major focus will be to understand the mode of action and mechanisms regulated by the identified genes, as a means to open new avenues in our search for strategies to harness the NK cell antiviral activity in the clinic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determinants of Genome Stability
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEUPLOIDY; CANCER THERAPY; CELL CYCLE REGULATION; CHROMOSOME TRANSMISSION FIDELITY; KINETOCHORE; MITOSIS; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of our work is to identify and characterize genes required for mitotic chromosome transmission in yeast and to relate our studies to human biology, and in particular to human cancer.  Mutations that cause a chromosome instability (CIN) phenotype in cancer cells are now widely recognized to be a major predisposing condition in cancer initiation and/or progression.  Yeast has proven to be an excellent experimental model organism for the study of cell division and the chromosome transmission cycle. We will develop yeast/human cross-species comparisons to identify and characterize molecular determinants of chromosome transmission that are highly conserved in evolution, and to determine which CIN genes are mutated in cancer cells.  Using yeast genetic techniques, in particular, global synthetic lethality analysis, we will also identify genes in yeast, and the corresponding human gene counterparts, that could define potential therapeutic targets for selective killing of cancer cells relative to adjacent normal tissue.  The results of our proposed research will provide a basic understanding of the mechanisms of chromosome transmission, and will therefore be directly relevant to an understanding of cancer mechanisms.  The results will also be useful in identifying new drug targets that could be used to screen for new cancer therapeutics for the selective killing of cancer cells in patients.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; MUSCLES ET OS
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of microfibril biogenesis and function in health and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOGENESIS AND FUNCTION OF SUPRAMOLECULAR MICROFIBRILS; CELL-MATRIX INTERACTIONS; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX BIOLOGY; GROWTH FACTOR REGULATION; MARFAN SYNDROME; PATHOGENETIC PATHWAYS OF MICROFIBRILLOPATHIES; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells are connected to each other by an array of proteins known as connective tissue that play an important role in optimal cell function. When connective tissue fails, a multitude of disease states can ensue. From genetic disorders and aging to orthopaedic impairments, health care costs and quality of life are severely impacted by dysfunction of connective tissue.  More research, both basic and applied, is urgently needed to better understand the specific steps that result in connective tissue failure and how these conditions can be better treated. This project aims to examine some of the molecular mechanisms involved in connective tissue related disease. Connective tissue contains very fine fiber-like strands, called microfibrils, that play an important role in both structural support of the tissue and the way cells function.  If the fundamental composition of these microfibrils become altered, or mutated, it gives rise to severe and sometimes life threatening complications that can affect blood vessels, bones and eyes. Correct formation and function of these fibers is essential, since these aspects are frequently disturbed in these disorders. The goal of this project is to investigate the molecular mechanisms involved in the formation and function of these microfibrils in normal and in disease situations using cell biological, biochemical and animal approaches. We intend to determine the significance of specific active regions in the major protein of microfibrils (fibrillin). We will determine the role of an important protein (fibronectin) which guides the formation of microfibrils. The effects of mutations in the fibrillin protein on its ability to function and on cell behavior will be studied. It is expected that the information obtained from this project will not only contribute to the fundamental understanding how these fibers work, but will also help in the development of new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for the entire group of these disorders.
