TitreApplicationTitle: Ameliorating Affective Disorder Induced by Circadian Rhythm Disruption
Keywords-MotsClés: ALERTNESS; CIRCADIAN RHYTHM; MELATONIN; MOOD; OPTICAL FILTERS; PHASE SHIFTS; SHORT WAVELENGTHS; SLEEPINESS
Abstract-Résumé: Social and professional obligations often compel individuals to stay up late and be exposed to light at night. This behavioral pattern adversely affects the body's internal clock which regulates the timing of key physiological processes including the sleep-wake cycle and timing of peak alertness and cognitive performance. The biological clock synchronizes its own time to environmental cues, of which light exposure is the strongest cue allowing us to maintain a 24 h rhythm known as circadian rhythm. Nocturnal light exposure causes the clock to set late bed times and later waking times that are often past the usual daily work start times. Therefore, individuals often find themselves to be excessively sleepy and lack alertness especially during the early part of the day. Furthermore, many individuals find it difficult to maintain a daily regular routine in sleep-wake habits. This irregular sleep-wake habit and late night light exposure can induce conflicts between important physiological rhythms including cognitive processes and mood and can promote pathological states like chronic fatigue, depression and anxiety disorder. The biological clock is most sensitive to short wavelengths light and we have recently demonstrated in a rat model that filtration of a narrow bandwidth (470-480 nm) within the wavelength dependent sensitivity spectrum of circadian photoreceptors can prevent the disruption of melatonin and corticosterone levels by nocturnal lighting. Our preliminary results in humans also demonstrate that filtering short wavelengths below 480 nm is effective in preventing alterations in hormone levels and improves mood, alertness and vigilance during simulated night shift work. These important findings indicate that biological clock disruption may be attenuated by filtering a very narrow bandwidth of light. This novel approach may provide a simple, economical countermeasure to ameliorate mood and cognitive impairment associated with circadian rhythm disruption.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of neuropeptides in the control of breathing during physiological stress
Keywords-MotsClés: CAROTID BODY; CONTROL OF BREATHING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IN SITU PREPARATIONS; NEONATAL APNEA; STRESS RESPONSES
Abstract-Résumé: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (cote death) is a primary cause of death of infants between 1 month and 1 year. We know that environmental stress (including pathogens, temperature and soft bedding) combine with genetic abnormalities to put infants at risk.   We found a gene associated with Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) that produces three types of brain signaling molecules (neuropeptides). Two of these are known, the third is novel. Here we test the role of all three peptides in the control of neonatal breathing during physiological stress. We test whether these peptides are (1) necessary to breath when neonates are exposed to SIDS related risk factors, (2) released during respiratory stress and (3) stimulate breathing. We also test whether a genetic variant found in the novel neuropeptide of some SIDS victims affects neuropeptide production and/or efficacy to stimulate breathing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Psychological problems associated with transition to insulin therapy in people with type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; COMMUNITY STUDY; COPING; DEPRESSION; DIABETES; EPIDEMIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes is a chronic disease that is recognized as a major public health problem. Studies have shown that treatment with insulin is associated poorer health status.The initiation of insulin therapy is considered as a critical life event: it may be associated with biological complications and psychological problems. Using a community sample of people with type 2 diabetes, we plan to identify psychological and psychosocial factors associated with change of health status due to the transition from oral hypoglycemic agents to treatment with insulin injections. The two main objectives are a) to identify if psychological problems, social support, diabetes related distress and negative attitudes toward insulin are predictors for change in health status and b)to identify how people manage the initiation of insulin therapy and stay in good health condition. We propose to conduct a community based cohort study in Quebec with 2,500 insulin naive type 2 diabetes patients at baseline. Participants will be recruited through the Regie de l'Assurance Maladie du Quebec (RAMQ), the provincial public health insurer. This cohort will be re-assessed after one, two and three years. We expect that 20% of the participants will switch to insulin treatment within 2 years after baseline assessment.  We will use different strategies to evaluate change in health status: we will use models where we will study the change of health status over time and we will use models where we will study incidence of poor health status for those with good health status at baseline.  The proposed study will provide knowledge about psychological problems associated with decline of health status after transition to insulin. This information will allow us to develop tailored interventions to reduce the psychosocial impact of the transition. Knowledge of effective individual coping strategies may help us to guide individuals likely to experience greater difficulty.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vascular Metabolism and Angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ARTERIOGENESIS; ENDOTHELIUM; HINDLIMB ISCHEMIA; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA
Abstract-Résumé: Many people have diseases where increasing or decreasing growth of new blood vessels might help. For example, in coronary artery disease and peripheral artery disease, arteries are blocked, and growing new blood vessels might prevent symptoms or damage. In cancer, reducing blood vessel formation might prevent tumor growth. Recently, in cancers, there has been recognition of new ways that mitochondria, the parts of cells that supply most of the energy, interact with a system called HIF that detects oxygen. Changes in the metabolism of cells alter the function of mitochondria, which can in turn change the HIF system. Since the HIF system is like a switch that turns on new blood vessel growth, changing the metabolism and mitochondrial function with drugs might be a new way to increase or decrease new blood vessel formation. This has not been studied in blood vessels yet. Since there are reports that thiazolidinediones, diabetes medicines that affect mitochondria and metabolism, might decrease new blood vessel formation in people in ways that are harmful, studying this mechanism is very important. In addition to understanding how these medicines might cause bad side effects, this work might lead to new ways of increasing new blood vessel growth in vascular disease and decreasing new blood vessel growth in cancer.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Broad spectrum beta lactamase inhibitors to counter antibiotic resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; BETA LACTAM ANTIBIOTICS; BETA LACTAMASE INHIBITORS; CARBAPENEMS; MICROBIOLOGY; PROTEIN CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Human pathogenic bacteria are becoming increasingly resistant to currently available antibiotics. This problem is particularly acute for patients in hospitals where the frequent use of antibiotics can encourage the development and spread of resistance. In recent years, bacteria that are commonly encountered in the environment or are part of the bacterial flora that normally exist in the body and are completely benign towards those with healthy immune systems have been found to be potentially lethal towards those hospitalized patients whose immune systems are compromised in some way, such as in the case of AIDS patients, those undergoing cancer chemotherapy, burn victims, organ transplant patients and cystic fibrosis patients.  In recognition of this problem, special restrictions have been put in place in regard to the use of antibiotics called the carbapenems that are reserved exclusively for use in hospitals for the treatment of life-threatening bacterial infections that are resistant to all other antibacterial drugs. Despite these precautions, high level resistance to carbapenems has become a serious emerging problem as a consequence of the ability of bacteria to produce enzymes that destroy the carbapenem antibiotics.  Resistant hospital acquired infections result in extended stay in healthcare facilities and high treatment costs and so pose a substantial economic burden in addition to concerns about potential fatalities caused by such infections. The goal of the present proposal is to create new classes of drugs that can inactivate the bacterial enzymes and that can be given in combination with the carbapenems to restore their potent antibacterial activity.

TitreApplicationTitle: HOLD IT: Health Outcomes of Low vitamin D In Toddlers: A TARGet Kids!longitudinal cohort study
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; BONE HEALTH; CHILDREN; LONGITUDINAL COHORT STUDY; OBESITY; VITAMIN D DEFICIENCY
Abstract-Résumé: Because of Canada's northern latitude, understanding vitamin D deficiency and associated preventable health problems is of major importance to Canadian children and their parents.    There is reason for concern that low vitamin D levels may be contributing to the development of some of the commonest health issues affecting Canadian children including fractures, asthma, respiratory infections, obesity and high blood pressure.  With previous support from CIHR, we have developed an innovative and powerful pediatric primary care practice based research network called TARGet Kids! to conduct studies on the nutritional health of Canada's young children.  Using TARGet Kids!, we have recruited 2000 children between 1 and 5 years of age with detailed clinical and laboratory measurements including vitamin D level.  Early results are suggesting that up to eighty percent of these young children have insufficient vitamin D levels.  In this proposed longitudinal cohort study, we will follow children for 4 years during their regularly schedule primary healthcare visits to determine whether their vitamin  D level increases their risk of developing asthma, respiratory infections, obesity or high blood pressure.  Collectively, fractures, asthma and respiratory infections make up one third of all emergency department visits for children in Ontario and obesity alone costs Canada's health care system 1.8 billion dollars annually.  If low vitamin D level is contributing to the development of any of these health conditions, measures to increase vitamin D levels may offer a significant benefit in reducing population wide illness and associated short-term and long-term healthcare costs.  This study will launch Canada as a leader in childhood vitamin D research.   Information from this study will assist parents, clinicians and policy makers in determining practice recommendations and health policy related to vitamin D supplementation and health policy for Canadian children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging the Mechanisms of Diastolic Dysfunction and its Role in Cardiovascular Performance
Keywords-MotsClés: DIASTOLIC FUNCTION; EXERCISE; HEART FAILURE; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; VENTRICULAR RELAXATION; VENTRICULAR STIFFNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a modern day epidemic, affecting 1.5-2% of Canadians with $3 billion in hospital costs annually, and the burden will double in the next 1-2 decades.  One-third of patients will die within one year of diagnosis, and all patients have a low quality of life.  Surprisingly, up to half of these patients have seemingly preserved systolic (pumping) heart function, and are diagnosed with "diastolic" heart failure (which refers to how their heart relaxes and fills with blood).  There are unfortunately no proven therapies for diastolic heart failure, and there is no direct evidence that abnormal relaxation and filling are the actual cause of the heart failure in these patients.  The underlying health issue is thus the limited understanding of the mechanisms of heart failure in patients who have seemingly normal pumping function.  In this program, we are motivated by the need for new diagnostic tools and targeted studies to identify and understand these mechanisms.  We will develop and evaluate new medical imaging (MRI) techniques for the measurement of the mechanisms of diastolic dysfunction.  Ultimately, accurate diagnosis and effective treatment plans and therapies for diastolic heart failure cannot be developed without knowledge of the underlying disease mechanisms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Viral transgenic mice as a model for understanding tolerance, autoimmunity and tumor immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVATION; AUTOIMMUNITY; CELLULAR IMMUNOLOGY; CYTOKINES; DENDRITIC CELLS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; INFLAMMATION; TOLERANCE; TRANSGENIC MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how the immune system works is essential to design new ways to treat and cure disease. Many different types of cells are involved in the immune response.  T cells are a population of white blood cells that protect our bodies against infection.  These cells also have the potential to protect our bodies against tumor growth.   However, T cells also have the ability to cause diseases such as diabetes or arthritis, where T cells in our bodies attack our own tissues.  Another population of cells in the immune system is called dendritic cells.  These cells are essentially the 'directors' of the immune response and can motivate T cells to do their job.  Therefore, it is critical to understand how the dendritic cells function to control the immune response.  If the dendritic cells are in a resting state, then an immune response is not initiated. If the dendritic cell receives activation signals, then this initiates an immune response.  Very little is known about the nature of the signals that initiate dendritic cell maturation against our own self tissues in the case of autoimmune disease.  Similarly, little is known about how the dendritic cell is activated in the setting of a tumor.  The goal of this research is to understand how dendritic cells can be activated and the molecules that are involved in this process.  The identification of key molecules and pathways that control the immune response will provide novel targets and approaches to direct new therapies for cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Eph receptor function in neuronal circuit development
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; CHICKEN; DEVELOPMENT; ELECTRICAL ACTIVITY; EMBRYONIC DEVELOPMENT; EPH TYROSINE KINASE; IN VIVO ELECTROPORATION; MOTOR NEURON; MOUSE GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: The basic units of nervous systems are circuits formed by precisely interconnected neurons. Neurons connect by extending processes called "axons" that are guided to their targets over long distances. Loss of accuracy of this guidance can have disastrous effects on the wiring of our nervous system, including mental retardation and even death. Some studies have suggested that diseases such as autism and schizophrenia might be caused by inappropriate connections formed between specific regions of the brain. Knowing how our nervous system is wired is therefore extremely important if we want to understand how such diseases develop and what could be done to cure them. In this proposal I outline experiments that address the role of the axon guidance protein family called "Eph receptors".  Specific Objectives: (1) Determine how Eph receptor function is modulated by proteins that bind to it. (2) Determine how Eph receptors relay their signals inside the neurons. (3) Determine how Eph receptors work together with other kinds of axon guidance receptors.   Hypothesis. To achieve a greater variety of responses, the Eph receptor function is modified by interacting with other proteins.   Methods: I will test this hypothesis by using the mouse and chick model systems. Both share similar spinal cord anatomy, and use very similar proteins in their development. The mouse has the advantage of the possibility of using animals with "knocked out" genes, but chick embryos are more accessible and can be manipulated while inside the egg.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Gut Involvement in Dietary Protection from Autoimmune Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNITY; DIET; GASTROINTESTINAL TRACT; NUTRITION; PANCREAS; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Objective:  To understand the role of the gastrointestinal tract and food proteins in the development of autoimmune type 1 diabetes (T1D) by studying the link between a damaged gut immune system and destruction of insulin-producing cells in the pancreas.   Background:   We have shown in diabetes-prone rats that some diets protect against diabetes, while others containing wheat promote the disease.  These rats have a leaky gut barrier, which allows large amounts of food proteins to contact the immune cells in the gut, possibly triggering an immune  attack on the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas.  Treatment with a drug to block gut leakiness prevents T1D, suggesting that the defects in the gut barrier and immune system are important in understanding how diabetes occurs.  Hypothesis: We propose that defects in controls for the gut immune responses to food proteins and a leaky gut barrier, enable an immune attack on the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. Project Design:  We will study the cells that control the immune response in the gut of a well described rat model of T1D to examine these questions.  We will inject diabetes-prone animals with antibodies to block the function of key regulatory cells called CD163 macrophages to see whether this will increase the incidence of T1D.  Various immune regulatory cells will also be examined in gut biopsy samples from human patients and controls.  We will also treat animals fed protective and diabetes-promoting diets with drugs that prevent gut leakiness to study the effect of these treatments on diabetes development and the number and function of the immune cells that populate the gut.  Significance:  These studies will reveal the role of the gut in T1D, and whether changes in the regulation of gut immune cell populations affect gut leakiness and contribute to disease development.  This will increase our understanding of the basic causes of T1D and could provide new avenues for treatment or prevention of diabetes.

ClasseRechercheFR: TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION; AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE
TitreApplicationTitle: Axon guidance and cell migration mechanisms in C. elegans.
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; CELL MIGRATION; NOVEL TGF-BETA SIGNALING; PATHWAY FUNNELING; SENSITIZATION TO GUIDANCE CUES; UNC-6/NETRIN PATHWAY
Abstract-Résumé: We have discovered a novel TGF-beta, UNC-129, which is largely dedicated to functioning in guiding growing neurons and migrating cells during development. TGF-betas have many known functions in development and cancer, however, UNC-129 was one of the first (and still one of the few) TGF-beta molecules that functions to regulate guidance of migrating cells and (growing) axons. We showed that this TGF-beta acts through a novel signaling mechanism not utilized by other TGF-betas for non-migration functions in development. Our major goal is to understand how the UNC-129 signaling mechanism works at a molecular level to guide migrations. We have shown that UNC-129 acts by modulating UNC-6/Netrin guidance functions. UNC-6/Netrin and its receptors represent a major cell migration guidance system first discovered by our laboratory using C. elegans and later discovered to have analogous functions in the developing vertebrate spinal cord and brain. Our recent evidence suggests that UNC-129 regulates the sensitivity of alternate receptor pathways for the UNC-6 guidance cue by interacting with UNC-5, one of the two UNC-6/Netrin receptors we discovered and characterized. Thus UNC-129 provides our first insights into the way sensitivity to gradients of morphogens and guidance cues are regulated at a molecular level. This information should prove vital to understanding how cells migrate normally, how axons migrate and grow to construct and repair the nervous system and how cancer cells become metastatic. The elucidation of these mechanisms could provide important insights into mechanisms to promote spinal cord regeneration and to prevent cancer morbidity.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role and molecular mechanism of Sonic hedgehog in neural circuit formation
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; GENETICS; HEDGEHOG; MOUSE; NERVOUS SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SPINAL CORD
Abstract-Résumé: The brain is composed of billions of interconnected neurons. To correctly form neuronal circuits, the developing axons (a long extension of a neuron) require attractive and repulsive molecules to lead them to their appropriate targets. One such molecule is called Sonic Hedgehog (Shh). Dr. Charron discovered that Shh acts as an axonal attractant for brain and spinal cord neurons. However, how Shh elicits this effect remains unknown. Thus, the objective of this proposal is to understand, at the molecular level, how Shh regulates the guidance of axons. This will be done using a novel technique invented by the lab of Dr. Charron which allows researchers to control and observe the behavior of axons in response to guidance molecules.  Connecting axons with their correct set of targets is a very complex task. Inappropriate wiring or damage to these neuronal connections leads to severe abnormalities of the nervous system. This work is expected to speed up the discovery of drugs that control axon pathfinding and will thus pave the way to new therapies to treat spinal cord injuries, neurodevelopmental disorders, and neurodegenerative diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Characterization of the Food Environment in Saskatoon for Families with Children
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY MASS INDEX; CHILD HEALTH; DIETARY ASSESSMENT; INTERVIEWS; LOCAL FOOD AND NUTRITION ENVIRONMENTS; OBESITY; SURVEYS
Abstract-Résumé: The neighbourhoods in which we live and how easily we can access nutritious food (sometimes called the food environment), particularly for our children, can make a difference in children's health. This study will help us understand  the food environment for families with children aged 10-13 years in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and its impact on obesity and overweight in children. First, using research tools such as Geographic Information Systems and the Nutrition Environment Measures Survey, this study will show where grocery and convenience stores and fast-food restaurants in Saskatoon are located and how nutritious the foods are that are carried within them.  Then, we will ask 2000 children between the ages of 10-13 years in 20 neighbourhoods to participate in a dietary assessment survey. We will also collect information on height and weight in the children. Using these research data we will understand the relationships between diet quality, body weight and the food environment in Saskatoon neighbourhoods. By gathering information on the nutritional health of children living within neighbourhoods in Saskatoon and by linking that to information on the accessibility of healthy food in Saskatoon neighbourhoods, ultimately we hope  to support the development of improvements to health policy and practice in Saskatoon, and also provide information that would benefit nutrition and health of children and their families elsewhere.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oral Micronized Progesterone for Perimenopausal Vasomotor Symptoms
Keywords-MotsClés: MENOPAUSAL TRANSITION; ORAL MICRONIZED PROGESTERONE; PERIMENOPAUSE; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; VASOMOTOR SYMPTOMS (HOT FLUSHES AND NIGHT SWEATS)
Abstract-Résumé: Perimenopausal hot flushes affect an estimated 2 million Canadian women and 200 000 experience severe symptoms that strongly disturb sleep and quality of life. Although hot flushes and night sweats begin in perimenopause (the transition to menopause) almost all therapies have only been tested with menopausal women. Therapies that work in menopause, when estrogen and progesterone levels are low, may not work in perimenopause, when estrogen levels are variable and elevated (25% above earlier reproductive years) with lower progesterone levels. Neither estrogen (the strongest medicine in menopause) nor birth control pills have been proven helpful for perimenopausal hot flushes. We believe that progesterone will improve perimenopausal hot flushes. We have found that a synthetic cousin of progesterone (medroxyprogesterone) is as good as estrogen in menopause. We also believe that progesterone is safe because when given without estrogen it does not increase the risk of blood clots or breast cancer. In clinical experience, when we have given progesterone to perimenopausal women, they had fewer and less intense hot flushes. Our recent study showed that natural progesterone as a pill (Prometrium) is effective for menopausal flushes; we want to test it in perimenopause. The purpose of this 4-year study is to compare the frequency and intensity of hot flushes over three months for women taking Prometrium daily at bedtime with women taking identical inactive capsules. We will randomize 175 women to active or placebo therapy. During the study, neither investigators nor the participants will know who is taking what. Each participant will record hot flushes daily for 1 month before the 3 months' treatment. This study is important because currently a large number of perimenopausal women with intense night sweats are having trouble doing their jobs and enjoying life. If natural progesterone is effective for hot flushes, perimenopausal women's health will improve.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel regulation and targets of matrix metalloproteinase-2 in the ischemic heart
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC MYOCYTES; DRUG-PROTEIN INTERACTION; ENZYME ASSAYS; ISCHEMIA-REPERFUSION; ISOLATED HEART; MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASE; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; REACTIVE OXYGEN/NITROGEN SPECIES
Abstract-Résumé: Ischemic heart disease is a major health problem in Canada which affects millions of people worldwide.  It is caused by either the constriction or blockade of arteries which supply heart muscle.  When blocked, heart muscle is starved of oxygen and nutrients required for contraction, and harmful metabolic by-products accumulate.  Further injury occurs when blood flow is restored by either drug or mechanical means (as cardiologists are able to do), a term called 'reperfusion' as reactive oxygen metabolites are synthesized in heart cells which damages them.  Ischemia and reperfusion (I/R) together causes heart muscle to contract more poorly, and this is due in part to reactive oxygen metabolites activating an enzyme we found to be located inside heart muscle cells, matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2).  We found that MMP-2 is found near certain proteins which are part of the contraction and structural machinery of these cells.  MMP-2 damages by acting as a molecular scissors, cutting certain target proteins into smaller pieces.  Here we wish to study the molecular structure of intracellular MMP-2 as its shape and function should be distinct from that of extracellular MMP-2. Knowing its precise shape will help us to understand which of the current drugs which are known to block MMP activity in general may be specific for the intracellular MMP-2.  We will also make artificial proteins which should be cut by MMP-2 and could be used in tests of MMP-2 activity, to help us find new drugs to inhibit it. We will also determine which of the contractile and structural proteins is most susceptible to MMP-2 in I/R injury and whether a hormone known to be elevated in persons with cardiovascular disease increases MMP-2's damage to these proteins.  We will test MMP-2 inhibitor drugs to see if we can protect mouse or rat hearts, or heart muscle cells, from I/R injury.    Our research may identify new drugs useful to treat ischemic heart disease, and which have fewer side effects.

ClasseRechercheFR: CHOREE DE HUNTINGTON; MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Altered balance of synaptic/extrasynaptic NMDA receptor signaling in Huntington disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HUNTINGTON DISEASE; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; NEURONAL CELL SIGNALING; NEURONAL CULTURE; NMDA RECEPTOR; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Brain cells require precise communication in space and time in order to orchestrate movements and thinking.  Communication between these cells occurs at highly specialized points of contact called synapses, at which an electrical signal in one brain cell is converted to a chemical signal which is sensed by receptors on the next cell in the circuit.  One key receptor in the brain is called the "NMDA" receptor, which mediates mechanisms underlying learning and memory ("synaptic plasiticity"); however, when over-activated, NMDA receptors can signal cell death.  Recent studies show that NMDA receptors located in synapses are beneficial, signaling cell survival and contributing to learning, whereas NMDA receptors residing outside synapses predominantly signal cell stress or death. Previous work suggests these receptors are upregulated on the surface of brain cells and show increased numbers outside synapses in the hereditary disorder Huntington disease (HD). HD is caused by a mutation in the gene coding for the protein huntingtin, and is associated with selective loss of brain cells with onset in mid-life, resulting in abnormalities of movement, mood and memory.  The proposed study will investigate the mechanisms underlying altered location of NMDA receptors, and the consequences to brain cell signaling such as synaptic plasticity and cell death pathways, in a mouse model of Huntington disease.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Interhemispheric contributions to neuroplasticity and motor learning after stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY; LEARNING; MOTOR LEARNING; NEUROPLASTICITY; REHABILITATION; STROKE; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: After a stroke the excitability of the brain decreases on the stroke side and increases on the opposite, non-stroke side. These changes make use of the stroke-affected arm difficult and slow recovery. Rehabilitation exercises that increase arm use after stroke help increase brain excitability, but the net effect of this approach is low. New therapies are needed that restore more equal levels of brain excitability between the two sides. Brain stimulation is a noninvasive way to affect activity the excitability of brain cells.  Pairing brain stimulation with exercises that require patients to learn new movements may help the brain to learn.  Using stimulation that reduces activity in the side opposite to the stroke can increase activity on the stroke-affected side, through connections between the two brain hemispheres. The purpose of this study is to test if brain stimulation on the side opposite to the stroke, paired with arm movement exercises, can help patients learn new arm movements and improve arm function.      In this study people with stroke will receive brain stimulation over two different areas on the side of the brain opposite to the stroke: 1) those areas responsible for movement and 2) those responsible for sensation. These experiments will test both the short and long term effects of brain stimulation on patients' learning and arm function and will allow us to identify which area of the brain best improves learning and arm function. These experiments have the potential to improve the effectiveness of rehabilitation after stroke. The proposed study is among the first to test stimulation over the side of the brain opposite to the stroke damage and at multiple sites. This unique approach may help stimulate the development of new methods for stroke rehabilitation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Consumption of chocolate in pregnant women with non severe hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD PRESSURE; ENDOTHELIAL FUNCTION; GRAVIDIC HYPERTENSION; POLYPHENOLS; PREECLAMPSIA; THEOBROMINE
Abstract-Résumé: Preeclampsia (PE), syndrome defined by gestational hypertension and proteinuria originates in the placenta and is characterized by maternal dysfunction of the endothelium, leading to the clinical symptoms of the mother. PE is one of the most common medical disorders affecting pregnancy, with potentially severe consequences for mother and child, especially in developing countries. Despite intensive research, PE remains a disease for which no effective prophylactic measures are available to patients. Recent literature confirmed that flavanol-rich chocolate has a beneficial influence on endothelial function and reduces systolic and diastolic blood pressure (BP). One study suggested that chocolate consumption during pregnancy may lower risk of PE, but effects of black chocolate among pregnant women have never been studied in a clinical design. Our hypothesis is that flavanol-rich chocolate consumption reduces the risk of PE via improvement of endothelial function in pregnant women. The primary objective of this trial is to investigate the acute and chronic effect of consumption of flavanol-rich chocolate on endothelial function in pregnant women at high risk for PE.  The proposed trial is a 4-group randomized clinical trial.  Non-smoking PE-high-risk women between the ages of 18 and 35 years will be eligible for participation in the study.  Women wishing to participate should present themselves at the research Centre for a total of 4 visits. Acute effects of chocolate will be assessed only during the randomization visit. The sustained effect will be evaluated after 6 and 12 weeks of chocolate consumption. The study participants must consume 3 chocolate squares per day (30 g/day) for 12 weeks. If results from our clinical trial confirmed that flavanol-rich chocolate improves endothelium function in pregnant women at high-risk of PE, a larger randomized clinical trial would be implemented with clinical mother and foetal outcomes.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of 14-3-3 proteins in axon guidance and extension
Keywords-MotsClés: 14-3-3; AXON GUIDANCE; GROWTH CONE DYNAMICS; REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Growth cones are specialized tips at the end of growing nerve cells that are critical for appropriate wiring of the nervous system. Appropriate connectivity in the nervous system is a fundamental process for appropriate neuronal development and is a key component of nervous system regeneration following trauma. In a screen to identify proteins within the growth cone that are critical for their dynamic functions, we have identified a family of adapter proteins, coined 14-3-3 proteins, that play critical roles in regulating the cytoskeleton. The cytoskeleton is the underlying support system within growth cones. In this proposal we will explore the roles of 14-3-3 proteins in nervous system development and regeneration. This research will lead to a better understanding of nervous system development and may identify new therapeutic targets for repair following CNS injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Elucidation and Characterization of Bacterial Virulence Factors from Pathogenic Bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL INFECTIONS AND DISEASES; BACTERIAL VIRULENCE FACTORS; BIOINFORMATICS; ENZYME INHIBITORS; ENZYME MECHANISMS; FLUORESCENCE SPECTROSCOPY; PROTEIN CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: We are using a technique called "Protein Crystallography" to elucidate the three-dimensional structures of bacterial toxins in complex with their host cell target proteins.  We believe that this new knowledge of protein structure of these toxins will improve our understanding of their mechanisms of action.  This enhanced knowledge will aid in the design and characterization of inhibitors against these bacterial factors that should translate into therapeutics for the treatment of bacterial diseases in man.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Vascular (patho)biology of TRPM7 chanzymes in hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; INFLAMMATION; ION TRANSPORT; MAGNESIUM; RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASES; RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN-ALDOSTERONE SYSTEM; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; VASCULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: High blood pressure (BP), also called hypertension, affects 30% of adult Canadians and is the leading cause of death worldwide, since it is a major risk factor for heart disease, kidney failure and stroke.  Despite extensive research and availability of many antihypertensive drugs, we still do not know exactly what causes high BP and why some individuals are more predisposed than others. Moreover, even though there are many different drugs to treat high BP, only a small percentage of patients are adequately managed. More research investigating the causes of hypertension will facilitate a better understanding of the disease so that improved therapies can be developed, which would reduce BP and hence improve the health of Canadians. We know that hypertension is associated with damage to blood vessels, especially the small arteries, which contribute to the processes of blood pressure elevation. However we still do not know exactly what causes the damage. My laboratory focuses on special proteins that may influence the function of vessels, which when altered could result in inflammation, injury and thickening of arteries. Such damage to small arteries leads to blood pressure elevation. Specifically, we examine a protein called TRPM7, which regulates the magnesium levels as well as other cellular processes that ultimately influence the function (contraction) and structure (artery wall thickness) of vessels. TRPM7 may also influence heart and kidney function. We believe that abnormal TRPM7 activity contributes to processes that cause injury to blood vessels and hence to the development of hypertension. If this is correct, then we could develop special drugs to "normalize" TRPM7, which would prevent or improve the vascular damage and hence reduce BP. Such strategies could improve the well-being of the Canadian population at large.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of cytochrome P450 enzymes in pathogenesis of cardiac hypertrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: ARACHIDONIC ACID; CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CARDIOVASCULAR PHARMACOLOGY; CYTOCHROME P450; DRUG METABOLISM; GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Enlargement of the heart is one of the most common causes of heart failure in Canada. Once cardiac failure develops, the condition is irreversible and is associated with a very high death rate. Fifty percent of patients whose heart failure has progressed to include shortness of breath without physical activity do not survive beyond one year. As the heart becomes enlarged, it also disrupts the production of small lipid molecules that control the heart function, causing further damage and increasing the risk of sudden cardiac death. The heart enlargement reduces the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules called epoxyeicosatrienoic acids and increase the production of cardiotoxic molecules called hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid. While most patients can be treated with drug therapy, these treatments have side effects and are not effective in all patients. The objectives of our work are to control and prevent enlargement of the heart to improve treatment options for patients and reduce mortality. By increasing the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules (epoxyeicosatrienoic acids) and inhibiting the production of cardiotoxic molecules (hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid) in the heart, we can prevent the progressive deterioration of heart function and the development of heart failure. Our research will identify the molecules that are responsible for the enlargement of the heart and heart failure. In addition, we will test new chemicals that are known to increase the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules (epoxyeicosatrienoic acids) and inhibiting the production of cardiotoxic molecules (hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid) in the heart. This will prevent the progressive deterioration of heart function and the development of heart failure. This research will help to diminish health care costs, as well as to design strategies that improve treatment of heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: The roles of RGMa and Neogenin in the control of axonal growth
Keywords-MotsClés: AXONAL GROWTH; CELL SURVIVAL; CNS DEVELOPMENT; ELONGATING AXON; MEMBRANE PROTEIN; VISUAL SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: During development, various parts of the brain establish connections with each other. In this process, nerve cells extend processes towards specific target areas in the brain. These connections are organized in a very precise manner and each nerve cell targets one brain cell. Proteins present in the brain environment guide projections to the correct target. One of these proteins is the RGMa protein. We showed that several parts of RGMa guide nerve cells within the brain. Furthermore, we demonstrated that RGMa uses the membrane protein Neogenin to this aim. In this application we want to understand the exact contribution of each one of these different RGMa parts in guiding nerve cells.  Findings from this study will allow us to characterize a key protein for the establishment of a well functioning nervous system. In this study, we make use of the developing chick brain to uncover the mechanisms by which RGMa and Neogenin control connections. The mechanisms we uncover here may well play a role in many nerve diseases. Indeed RGMa restricts recovery when nerve cells are damaged. Understanding the mechanisms of action of RGMa may offer a means to promote nerve cell recovery and restore nerve cell functions. Here, we propose to modulate the Neogenin/RGMa pathway to help nerve cell recovery following injury.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Characterization of P4-ATPases and Their Role in Membrane Lipid Asymmetry, Photoreceptor Cell Structure and Function, and Retinal Degenerative Diseases.
Keywords-MotsClés: ENZYMATIC ACTIVITIES; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; MEMBRANE RECONSTITUTION; P4-ATPASES; PHOSPHOLIPID ASYMMETRY; PHOTORECEPTOR CELLS; PROTEIN CHARACTERIZATION; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; PROTEOMICS; RETINAL DEGENERATIVE DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Phospholipids are known to be asymmetrical distributed across biological membranes. This asymmetry plays a crucial role for a wide variety of cellular processes including membrane fusion and vesicle trafficking, aging, cell survival, phagocytosis and general membrane associated protein activities.  P4-ATPases are a class of membrane proteins which have been implicated in the generation and maintenance of phospholipid asymmetry, but to date little is known about their structure, function or regulation in cells.  In this proposal the P4-ATPase, Atp8a2, will be purified and characterized in order to define its role in photoreceptor cell function and retinal degenerative diseases.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: The neurogenetic basis of social interactions in Drosophila
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: The presence and existence of others around us permeates our lives. It is interesting to consider that social interactions with the people we meet shape our character and are also shaped by the character of our schools, our commerce, our government, our media, our military, our children. Humans are not unique in this regard. Scientists have shown that group life is evident in many life forms from bacteria to humans. In all cases the primitive ability to cooperate strengthens the quality of life in the face of external challenges. For instance, it has long been appreciated that overcrowding may be harmful (for insects as well as mammals) but a too few in the group also expose an individual to danger and yet an optimal number of individuals does better than either extreme.  Survival of the fittest requires adequate numbers (at the very least it takes two to reproduce). The observation that group life is important for many different forms of life suggests that at least some features of social interactions are inherited. Here we are proposing to extend our earlier studies funded by CIHR. These studies published in leading journals like Nature and Current Biology identify molecular, cellular, and behavioural mechanisms of social life in the fruitfly. We have shown that flies are like us: they synchronize their activities, form groups and find the scent of others attractive or repulsive. The studies proposed here will enable us to understand the inherited mechanisms controlling group life. Our studies are relevant to autism and schizophrenia.

TitreApplicationTitle: The MiTY Trial (Metformin in Women with Type 2 Diabetes in Pregnancy)
Keywords-MotsClés: PREGNANCY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: The incidence of type 2 diabetes is rising at a remarkable rate, and with it we see the rise of type 2 diabetes in pregnancy.  Insulin is the standard of care for the management of type 2 diabetes in pregnancy; however, despite treatment with insulin, these women continue to face increased rates of poor maternal and fetal outcomes. Metformin is presently being used in other populations with insulin resistance, with some benefit.  We plan to study the use of metformin, in addition to insulin, in pregnant women with type 2 diabetes, by conducting a multicentre, randomized trial, randomizing 500 pregnant women with type 2 diabetes, to receive either metformin or placebo, in addition to their usual insulin regimen.  We hypothesize that metformin use, when added to the treatment with insulin, will improve these outcomes by reducing maternal high blood sugars, high maternal insulin doses, excessive maternal weight gain and pregnancy-induced high blood pressure, all of which should reduce poor outcomes in the baby.  Our primary outcome will be the reduction of a composite outcome, which will include pregnancy loss, preterm birth, birth injury, respiratory distress, low blood sugar, and neonatal intensive care admissions over 48 hours.  With the rising rate of type 2 diabetes in pregnancy, and the poor neonatal outcomes, it is important to attempt to improve such outcomes for this growing population.  This trial will address the efficacy and safety of using metformin to prevent adverse neonatal outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional regulators of Leydig cell differentiation and function
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; CELL DIFFERENTIATION; GENE EXPRESSION - TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; HORMONE-DEPENDENT CANCERS; HORMONES; MALE REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH; REPRODUCTION; TESTOSTERONE
Abstract-Résumé: Testicular Leydig cells produce two hormones that are indispensable for proper development of the male reproductive system: INSL3 and testosterone. INSL3 regulates testicular descent and testosterone is essential for the development of the male external genitalia, sex accessory glands, as well as production of mature sperm. Abnormal Leydig cell development and function results in insufficient hormone production leading to impaired male reproductive health. Despite the physiological importance of Leydig cells, the transcription factors controlling the development and function of these cells remain poorly understood. Transcription factors are proteins that bind to genes in order to regulate their expression. The goal of the present research project is to identify transcription factors regulating Leydig cell development and function. To do so, different but complementary in vitro and in vivo approaches will be used. Understanding these processes may eventually lead to better diagnosis and treatment of several human pathologies associated with defective Leydig cells and/or sex steroid hormone production.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: Knowledge to Action Processes in SHRTN Collaborative Communities of Practice
Keywords-MotsClés: AGED; CASE STUDY; COMMUNITIES OF PRACTICE; EVIDENCE INFORMED PRACTICE; HEALTH AND AGING; KNOWLEDGE NETWORKS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OUTCOME ASSESSMENT; SOCIAL LEARNING
Abstract-Résumé: This research will help us to understand how a Community of Practice (defined as a group of people who work together to identify innovations, translate evidence and help implement changes to improve care) creates and shares knowledge in ways that improve quality of healthcare and quality of life for seniors. The investigators will work with the leaders and members of Ontario's Seniors Health Research Transfer Network Collaborative, which is a network of networks that includes the Seniors Health Research Transfer Network Knowledge Exchange, the Alzheimer Knowledge Exchange and the Ontario Research Coalition.   The collaborative facilitates the sharing of knowledge through a library service, knowledge brokers, local implementation teams, collaborative technology, and, most importantly, Communities of Practice (CoPs).  The research will help us to understand the types of activities and organizations that are most successful at bringing new innovations to the frontlines of Canadian healthcare.  Over a three year period, the investigators will focus on at least nine detailed case studies that demonstrate how important new research findings and best practices are identified, confirmed, and then shared with frontline caregivers.  By studying these cases, the research team will learn how to support the development of these communities of practice, and what factors are needed to support the adoption of better caregiving practices.  They will also gain a better understanding of the importance of having everybody who participates in the creation of new innovations (researchers, policy makers, caregivers and others) involved throughout the knowledge generation process.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Control of Myometrial Contractile Activity During Pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES; INFLAMMATION; LABOUR; LEUKOCYTES; MYOMETRIUM; PREGNANCY; PRETERM BIRTH
Abstract-Résumé: Pre-term birth (birth at <37 completed weeks of gestation) is the most significant clinical problem facing contemporary clinical obstetrics in the developed world and is the single most important cause of perinatal mortality and morbidity in industrialized countries. Approaches to the prevention of preterm labor that have focused on inhibition of myometrial contractile activity have proven largely ineffective, probably because they target events late in the labour process.  Our recent studies suggest a new model for labour initiation.  In this model the term uterus is stimulated to produce chemicals that attract peripheral white blood cells to leave blood vessels and enter the uterine muscle where they induce an inflammatory reaction.  This inflammatory reaction in turn generates further chemicals that contribute to the initiation of labour and delivery of the baby.  As such these white blood cells and the pathways that lead to their activation may represent novel targets for preterm birth prevention.  Using animals, our study will test the validity of the model through a series of experiments that will 1) define the pattern of the uterine inflammatory response during pregnancy and labor, 2) determine the molecular mechanisms that induce the myometrium to activate and recruit circulating immune cells to the myometrium, and 3) define the contributions of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) to the regulation of uterine inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Small molecule SHIP agonists for inhibiting the phosphoinositide 3-kinase pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS OF DISEASE; HEMOPOIETIC CANCER; PHOSPHOINOSITIDE 3-KINASE PATHWAY; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TARGETTED THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: The growth and survival of cells requires the action of an intricate network of pathways and mechanisms inside the cell. The PI3K pathway is one key component and anti-cancer drugs are being developed which block this pathway in order to kill cancer cells. However, a novel and powerful approach for inhibiting the PI3K pathway involves activating the natural brakes of this system. This brake is the protein SHIP which serves normally to limit cell growth and action.We developed a way to turn SHIP using a small molecule we isolated by screening a library of marine natural products for  activators of SHIP. This molecule, pelorol and subsequent structurally related derivatives AQX-016A and AQX-MN100 are not only able to activate SHIP in an enzyme assay in vitro, but as predicted is also able to inhibit multiple myeloma tumour cell growth. However, the known role of SHIP in regulating blood cell function suggest that SHIP activators could have additional beneficial actions on the multiple myeloma disease process. Studies are now proposed to examine these possibilities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering and reconstituting genetic events in oral cancer progression
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRAY CGH; CANCER PROGRESSION; CELL MODELS; HEAD AND NECK; ORAL CANCER; SHRNA
Abstract-Résumé: Oral cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed types of cancer worldwide.  Unfortunately, those diagnosed with this disease rarely survive longer than 5 years.  Given that survival statistics for oral cancer have not changed for 20 years, there is a clear need for new approaches for diagnosing and treating this disease.  Like many cancer types, oral tumors develop by progression from precancerous tissues through increasingly aggressive stages.  Accumulated DNA mutations that alter gene behavior are the driving force behind the transformation of normal cells into invading cancerous cells.  By identifying the DNA changes that exist in cells at each stage of oral cancer development, we will define the critical order of gene mutations that lead to an invasive tumor.  Specific DNA changes will then be used to more accurately determine the stage of a given precancerous lesion, the likelihood that that lesion will progress to later disease stages, and the treatment that will work best against that lesion (since the underlying DNA changes can govern how a cell responds to drugs).  The genes identified by this analysis will also be assessed in model systems of oral cancer in order to 1) better understand the mechanisms driving tumor cell behavior and 2) define targets for the next generation of chemotherapeutic agents.  This work will create a new and valuable model for oral cancer research and has the potential to greatly impact survival rates associated with this dangerous disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The roles of p53 and p73 in DNA repair and oncogenesis.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER; CHROMOSOMAL INSTABILITY; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; INFLAMMATION; SENESCENCE; TUMORIGENESIS; TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Tumour suppressors are proteins that prevent cells from becoming cancerous by triggering programmed cell death pathways. The most important tumour suppressors belong to the p53 family, which includes p53, p63 and p73. These proteins have activating forms (termed "TA") and interfering forms (termed "DeltaN"). Our laboratory has genetically engineered two strains of mutant "knockout" (KO) mice, one that does not express the TA form of p73 (TAp73), and another that does not express the DeltaN form of p73 (DeltaNp73). TAp73 KO mice show increased inflammation and high rates of tumorigenesis, whereas DeltaNp73 KO mice show neurodegeneration and high sensitivity to DNA damage. We are characterizing the tumours appearing in these mice and determining whether the inflammation that occurs in the absence of TAp73 enhances the onset and progression of cancer. In addition, we are screening other genes for their capacity to enhance or hinder the ability of p53 to trigger the death of damaged cells.

NomDuComitéFR: Recherche en interventions et en évaluation dans les services de santé 2
TitreApplicationTitle: RADAR: A new screening tool to improve the recognition of delirium among older persons.
Keywords-MotsClés: DELIRIUM; DETECTION; GERIATRIE; SOINS INFIRMIERS; VIEILLISSEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Delirium is a sudden, usually temporary condition that affects the normal functioning of the brain. It is characterized by a disturbance in consciousness, attention, orientation, memory, thought, perception and behaviour. It is a common and serious problem among older people admitted to hospital or a nursing home. Consequences for elderly patients who develop delirium include decline in functional autonomy, cognitive deficits, prolonged hospital stay and even death. Despite its importance, delirium is often missed by nurses. This is a serious concern because early recognition of delirious patients is essential for both prompt management of the underlying causes of the delirium and rapid implementation of intervention aimed at reducing its severity and duration. Our team has been working on the development of a new screening instrument to address the issue of barriers to the recognition of delirium. We call this instrument RADAR. It is quick to administer, suitable for use by both nurses and nurse assistants, can be integrated into routine care, is suitable for use among patients with or without dementia and is suitable for use in hospitals and nursing homes. These characteristics enable a continuous and frequent assessment of signs of delirium which is essential given the fluctuating nature of delirium throughout the course of a day. This is also achieved without significant increase in nursing staff workload. Our team undertook a pilot test of RADAR among 57 older persons and in so doing, demonstrated that the proposed study design is feasible in both hospitals and nursing homes. The use of the RADAR in these settings was positively received by the participating nursing staff and preliminary information on the properties of RADAR has yielded positive results. The objective of the proposed project is to further develop and validate RADAR by applying the methodology used for the pilot study in a large-scale study.

NomDuComitéFR: Déterminants psychosociaux, socioculturels et comportementaux de la santé 2
TitreApplicationTitle: A web-based person-centred navigation tool for newly diagnosed colorectal cancer patients: A clinical trial to assess empowerment and cost-effectiveness
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER SURVIVORSHIP; COLORECTAL CANCER; EMPOWERMENT; MULTIMEDIA INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY; PATIENT EDUCATION AND NAVIGATION; PERSON-CENTRED CARE; PSYCHOSOCIAL ONCOLOGY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: For individuals diagnosed with colorectal cancer, exposure to up-to-date cancer information and support as well as guidance to access the most appropriate health care services is crucial for cancer self-management and support. Timely access to high quality cancer information is suggested to contribute to patient empowerment - defined as the perception of being better able to manage illness demands.  With the advent of the information age, individuals increasingly are turning to online health information resources. The use of rigorous web-based tools is found to be an engaging and convenient way to access health information, while being tailored to people's needs and preferences. The present study seeks to examine the effects of a recently developed high quality and person-centred web-based tool, the Oncology Interactive Navigator (OIN) on patients' empowerment as well as document its cost-effectiveness. Participants newly diagnosed with colorectal cancer will be randomly assigned to experimental or control groups with the former having unrestricted access to the OIN for 8 months. Participants in the control group will receive care as usual. Information on background, medical characteristics, and empowerment will be collected as well as cost-effectiveness indicators. If producing the desired effects, the OIN could be proposed for national implementation across Canadian cancer centers. Work is currently underway to add over 23 types of cancer diagnoses to the OIN.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Hippocampal dentate gyrus damage and cognitive deficits: An evaluation of restoration of function after regrowth of neural circuitry
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRENAL; AMNESIA; CORTICOSTERONE; GRANULE CELL; HIPPOCAMPUS; NEUROGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: A simple rat model of slowly developing brain injury producing memory problems has been developed. Current work has focused on describing in detail the injury and the type of memory problem.  The model involves a slow loss of cells in the hippocampus, a region responsible for memory problems in Alzheimer's dementia and other related diseases. The loss of cells is caused by removing the adrenal glands. This removal eliminates a corticosterone, a hormone, that is necessary for keeping alive certain brain cells in the hippocampus. Another important fact about this part of the hippocampus is that it has the ability to produce a small number of new brain cells, even in adults. We have shown that we can regrow lost cells in the hippocampus using treatments that dramatically increase adult birth of new brain cells. We plan to measure reversal of brain and memory dysfunctions.  We do this in 3 ways by studying memory in rats who have lost and regrown cells in the hippocampus, by measuring activation of certain genes in these new cells that respond to learning, and by recording from individual newborn cells from freely moving rats. From these experiments we can determine if the cells we have created truly replace the functions of lost ones. The long-term goals are to rationally develop treatments for cognitive disorders, especially due to anti-cancer therapies, age-related dementias, and related forms of brain injury.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; RECHERCHE SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTÉ

ClasseRechercheFR: CARDIOLOGIE; DIMENSIONS SOCIALES ET CULTURELLES DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Acute Coronary Syndrome Management in South Asian, Chinese and White patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME; ADHERENCE; COHORT STUDY; ETHNICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) (heart attack or unstable angina)is one of the leading causes of death in North America.  Prognosis from ACS appears to vary by ethnicity with higher early mortality in Chinese patients and higher risk of recurrent heart attack in South Asian and White patients compared to Chinese patients. As we know that proper ACS management and health behavior change like taking cardiac medications and quitting smoking significantly improves prognosis, one possible explanation for ethnic differences in prognosis is variations in ACS management and adoption of heart healthy behaviors. The goals of this study are to (1) systematically compare ACS management and health behavior change in South Asian, Chinese and White patients with ACS and (2) to examine potential patient level - cultural factors that may influence cardiac care and health behavior change such as language barriers, poor knowledge of cardiac risk factors, and use of traditional therapies. To achieve this goal, we will follow 1827 patients with recent ACS (609 from each ethnic group) in Vancouver, Calgary and Toronto who have already been enrolled in one of our other studies called ACS cross sectional study. Patients who agree to join this study will receive telephone interviews at 3,6 and 12 months after ACS to collect the data. We will carefully translate all of the study documents so that South Asian and Chinese patients who do not speak english can also take place in this study.  This study will help us learn where the care gaps in ACS management occur in these ethnic groups and also help us learn how culture affects chronic disease management and cardiac care. These findings will be instrumental in developing targeted interventions aimed at improving ACS management in a culturally sensitive manner.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Immune signatures predicting development and progression of Alzheimer Disease: impact of immunosenescence and Cytomegalovirus infection.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; CELLULES T; CMV INFECTION CHRONIQUE; CULTURE DE CELLULES; FACSCAN; FONCTIONS ET PHENOTYPES DES CELLULES T; MACROPHAGES; SIGNALISATION INTRACELLULAIRE; VIEILLISSEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most frequent cause of dementia in the ever increasing elderly population. AD causes a great deal of suffering to the patients, their families and caregivers. AD was considered for a long time a disease of the brain only, but it is now well recognised that, fundamentally, it also affects the rest of the body. It is widely suspected that a protein fragment (amyloid beta peptide, Ab) which accumulates in the brain in AD could be partly responsible. The accumulation of Ab also causes inflammation. Inflammation is a beneficial process when it is aimed at eradicating aggressors like the Ab, but if it becomes chronic, it can then harm individual organs as well as the whole body. The inflammatory process is mediated by our defence, or innate immune system. Following this first reaction , cells of the adaptive immune system - T lymphocytes - become sensitized to Ab and try to eliminate it by various strategies including helping specific autoantibody production by B cells. Interestingly, despite their apparent link to AD, Ab-reactive cells are also found in healthy people. Aging by itself alters our immune system for several reasons including infection with a common persistent virus (Cytomegalovirus), resulting in a less vigorous immune system, state termed: immunosenescence. We propose that with advancing age, the immune system becomes less effective in clearing Ab. Through its continuing but failing attempts to get rid of Ab, the immune system tires which then has deleterious side effects. Moreover, tiring of the immune system is accelerated by CMV infection, so we propose that CMV and AD could be linked. The objective of this project is to investigate immune status in patients with AD compared to patients with mild cognitive impairment and healthy elderly controls, in relation to CMV infection. This could lead to novel treatment strategies targeting inflammation and CMV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Gab Family Signal Amplifiers in Tumorigenesis and Invasion
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN REMODELLING; BREAST CANCER; CELL MIGRATION AND INVASION; ORGANOID CULTURE; POLARISED CELL SIGNALLING; RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASE; SCAFFOLD PROTEINS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TUMOR METASTASES; VESICLE TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: The Met receptor is dysregulated in many human cancers and Gab proteins are elevated in many human cancers. Hence, it is critical to understand at the mechanistic level how Met and the Gab proteins contribute to and mediate loss of epithelial organization and invasive responses, which contribute to tumor progression and metastases when dysregulated in human cancers. These experiments will identify key and possibly unknown genes and proteins that regulate tumor progression and invasion. Since signalling networks and receptors, such as Met, are potentially suitable sites for drug intervention, the identification of proteins involved in loss of epithelial polarity and invasion will facilitate the rational design of compounds to interfere with these signaling networks in cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Drugs and Human Milk: mammary xenobiotics transporter
Keywords-MotsClés: ABC TRANSPORTERS; CANCER; HUMAN; MILK; RIBOFLAVIN
Abstract-Résumé: Mother's milk provides tremendous medical benefits to the infant, which range from infection prevention to improved brain function. However, medications the mother needs and food toxins the mother ingests are excreted into milk, exposing the infant to these potentially toxic substances. This study is to find out the way to block drug excretion into mother's milk by giving vitamin B2. Also, we will develop a laboratory tool to predict levels of drug entry into mother's milk. The approachs we wil use are laboratory experiments using human and mouse cells of mammary gland, and mouse studies. The results will be used as a foundation of human trials and to develop a tool to assess drug safety during lactation.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: MÉTABOLISME/DIABÈTE; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Basis of Fuel Surfeit Detoxification in Pancreatic beta-Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: FUEL DETOXIFICATION; GLUCOLIPOTOXICITY; GLYCEROLIPID/FREE FATTY ACID CYCLING; LIPID METABOLISM; LIPOLYSIS; PANCREATIC BETA CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Nutrient fuels, including carbohydrates, proteins and fats, are essential for body and function of the cells. However, continuous supply of any of these nutrients in excess can be toxic due to interference with normal functions of the cells in the body, resulting in obesity and diabetes. Thus, beta cells of pancreas, which produce insulin in response to glucose in blood, fail to do so if they are continuously exposed to high fat and glucose. Under such conditions of excess fuel supply, other body tissues also do not respond normally to insulin and cannot use blood glucose effectively. These toxic effects of excessive fuels result from the accumulation of fat in tissues, decreased useable energy production, abnormal protein synthesis and increased production of harmful oxygen free radicals. The mechanisms by which, cells handle and dispose-off toxic chemicals coming from environment, are relatively well understood. Surprisingly, we know much less about the way the cells escape from the toxicity of excess fuels. This is particularly important in conditions like obesity and diabetes, which are often associated with fuel oversupply. In the present proposal, we are planning to investigate how the beta cells of pancreas get rid-of excess fuels. Many cells harbor a central cyclic process, which handles fatty acids coming from fat and glycerol coming from glucose. This procedure is important in storing excess fatty acids as fat droplets in the cells, and in transporting some of the breakdown products produced during this process out of the cell. We will study different steps of this process and their relative contribution to dispose of excessive fuels. This information will help in understanding how cells and tissues cope-up with the toxicity due to too much fuel supply, how they fail in this process, and what therapeutic measures can be implemented to prevent this failure.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
ResearchClassEN: SKIN AND SUBCUTANEOUS TISSUS; INJURY, REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the role of dermal stem cells in wound healing and the influence of niche-derived factors that govern their behavior
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DERMIS; HAIR FOLLICLE; STEM CELL BIOLOGY; STEM CELL DIFFERENTIATION; STEM CELL MAINTENANCE; TISSUE REGENERATION; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: In 2005, 11 million skin wounds (burns, trauma) were treated in emergency departments in the United States. At least 3 million adults in the North America are reported to have pressure ulcers yearly. The result is chronic pain, immobility, disfigurement and in many cases infection leading to further medical complication or death. The cost of chronic wound care alone in North America is estimated at $10 billion annually. The physical and emotional recovery can often require years of treatment and have devastating impact on quality of life. Therefore understanding the mechanisms involved in skin regeneration and wound healing and the potential for stem cell-based therapies to improve repair are of tremendous importance. Unlike other adult tissues, the mammalian hair follicle repeatedly regenerates itself, without formation of scar tissue. This remarkable regenerative capacity is due to the presence of stem cells that are maintained within the hair follicle throughout life. We have recently identified a multipotent dermal stem cell from adult hair follicles that functions to regulate hair follicle regeneration and growth. We have also obtained evidence to suggest that these cells may play a role in skin wound healing. Therefore, the objectives of the proposed studies will be to understand: 1) how dermal stem cells contribute to wound healing, 2) whether supplementing wounds with dermal stem cells improves healing, and 3) how the hair follicle micro-environment maintains these stem cells throughout adulthood. These studies will provide important insights into adult stem cell biology and tissue regeneration. Dermal stem cells may provide a novel source of cells for hair follicle restoration and improved skin repair for burns and chronic ulcerations. Understanding how these cells are regulated may also provide clues as to the cause of diseases such as alopecia areata, keloid and neurofibromatosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the mTOR/S6K1 and RSK pathways in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE TISSUE; ANIMAL MODELS; CELL CULTURE; DIABETES; GLUCOSE TRANSPORT; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LIVER; MUSCLE; NUTRIENT SENSING
Abstract-Résumé: This CIHR-funded project has focused on the potential role of the mTORC1/S6K1 signaling pathway in the induction of insulin resistance for glucose metabolism in insulin target cells and tissues. We found that IRS-1 Ser phosphorylation by mTORC1 and S6K1 is involved in the development of insulin resistance induced by nutrient satiation and obesity. In the current proposal, we will study the detailed mechanisms by which overnutrition activates the mTORC1/S6K1 pathway in animal models of obesity. We will also determine the potential role of another kinase, RSK, in mediating IRS-1 Ser phosphorylation and inhibition of insulin action on glucose metabolism. These studies will further establish the roles and mechanisms of the mTORC1/S6K1 and RSK pathways in mediated insulin resistance in obesity and upon nutrient satiation, and thus help define novel therapeutic strategies to combat this metabolic syndrome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Better Contraceptive Choices for Marginalized Women:  Immediate vs. Interval Insertion of Intrauterine Contraception after Second Trimester Abortion
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORTION; CLINICAL RESEARCH; CONTRACEPTION; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH SERVICE DELIVERY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Women seeking abortion beyond 12 weeks (2nd trimester) are at high risk of recurrent unwanted pregnancy.  Often, women seeking a 2nd trimester abortion are disadvantaged by lower education and socio- economic status.  The best reversible contraception to prevent repeat abortion is long acting, such as intrauterine contraception (IUC).  Current medical practice and package labelling require waiting 4 weeks after a 2nd trimester abortion to insert the IUC. However, most women who receive an abortion do not return for follow-up, and so do not have the IUC inserted.  With prompt IUC insertion, more women will benefit from effective birth control for up to 5 years.  While there may be a slightly higher risk of the IUC falling out compared to insertion 4 weeks later, on balance the potential benefit to the patient is very high. This Randomized Controlled Trial will be the first to compare the effectiveness of immediate IUC versus 4 week IUC after a 2nd trimester abortion by looking at pregnancy rates one year later. To find one year pregnancy rate we will use a provincial health information database.  In this way the research outcome does not rely on follow up participation by enrolled women. The investigators will also conduct an in-depth health economic analysis of the costs and cost savings.  The findings of this trial will provide new evidence to inform policy-makers and health care professionals and offer better contraceptive choices to women. Our proposed research aims to improve the health and well-being of women at risk of repeated unwanted pregnancies, and their families, throughout Canada and internationally.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mutations in the SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex genes: an alternative mechanism for ovarian carcinogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN REMODELLING; CLEAR CELL CARCINOMAS OF THE OVARY; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; OVARIAN CANCER; PATHOLOGY; TUMOUR SUPRESSORS
Abstract-Résumé: In North America, ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death due to gynaecological malignancies.  Ovarian cancers can be divided into subtypes based on their tumour cell types.  Clear cell carcinomas of the ovary are one of the ovarian cancer subtypes and represent approximately 12% of all malignant ovarian tumours.  For women with this disease, the success of traditional chemotherapy has been limited, suggesting the need for more effective and subtype specific treatments.  We have recently shown that over one-third of ovarian clear cell tumours contain mutations in a gene called ARID1A.  This gene encodes the BAF250a protein which is a member of a large complex of proteins termed the SWI/SNF complex. This complex is involved in remodelling DNA, ultimately influencing which genes are turned 'on' or 'off'.  It may be that mutations in ARID1A and related genes disrupt this regulation, which could result in uncontrolled growth and cancer.    Our research team will harness the power of new genomic technologies to investigate the involvement of the SWI/SNF complex of proteins in clear cell cancers of the ovary.  We will firmly establish how common mutations in ARID1A and other SWI/SNF genes are in both clear cell tumours of the ovary, other ovarian carcinomas and their precursor lesions.  In addition, through carefully designed experiments, we will determine how SWI/SNF proteins influence cell growth and whether this is altered when specific components of the complex are mutated.  Finally, it may be that disruption of ARID1A confers a specific sensitivity to cancer cells that could be used to selectively kill these cells as a potential therapy for clear cell cancers of the ovary; this will be investigated through a screening experiment.
