ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: The Motor Side of Amblyopia (Lazy Eye)
Keywords-MotsClés: AMBLYOPIA; EYE MOVEMENTS; EYE-HAND COORDINATION; LIMB MOVEMENTS; POINTING; SENSORIMOTOR TRANSFORMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Lazy eye (amblyopia) is a decrease in vision in one eye caused by inadequate use during early childhood and cannot be corrected by prescription glasses. It affects 3-5% of people in the western world, and is the number one cause of blindness in one eye. Despite the millions of dollars spent in treatment, many people with lazy eye continue to have significant visual problems throughout their adult lives. A main function of the brain is to use vision to guide actions. Although we know a lot about the visual problems in lazy eye, little is known about how these visual problems impact on day-to-day actions, such as moving our eyes to track a bouncing ball and using our hand to catch the ball. In this research, we will investigate how visual problems affect the motor activities in people with lazy eye. We will look at how the control of three-dimensional eye movements is altered in lazy eye, how these changes affect eye-hand coordination in a pointing task, and how people with lazy eye adapt to these changes. This information will tell us that lazy eye is not just a visual problem, but it also affects many motor activities. It will also have significant clinical implications for the treatment and rehabilitation of lazy eye.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chemical genomics: Linking biologically active compounds to cellular pathways and targets
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMICAL GENOMICS; NATURAL PRODUCTS; YEAST FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: We are applying yeast functional genomics methodology towards the analysis of an extensive collection of natural products, which are sophisticated chemical compounds produced by living organisms, with the goal of linking these compounds to their cellular targets. Natural products are often selected for specific biological activity and, therefore, may be of therapeutic value.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of  novel mechanisms  underlying  pathophysiologic  remodeling of atrial myocytes during the genesis of atrial fibrillation.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; ATRIAL MYOCYTE; GIRK CHANNEL REGULATION; KATP CHANNEL REGULATION; PARASYMPATHETIC SIGNALING; REGULATOR OF G-PROTEIN SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a condition of the upper heart chambers in which the normal transmission of electrical signals in the heart is lost.  AF is the most common electrical abnormality of the human heart, and is especially common in the aging population (for example 10 % of people in their 80's show signs of AF).  The random electrical signals produced during AF result in improper communication (timing of coordinated pumping) between upper and lower heart chambers and impaired upper chamber function (pumping).  Thus, long-lasting bouts of AF significantly increase the risk for stroke and other cardiovascular complications.  Lastly, a single bout of prolonged AF is believed to reprogram the cells of the upper chambers so that they are more susceptible to future AF events.  In other words once you have an AF episode, it becomes much more likely you will have another.  Our preliminary work in dog hearts and genetically altered mice and has identified Rgs4 as a key protein that normally protects hearts from AF.  Once Rgs4 function is compromised the susceptibility to AF dramatically increases, especially in aging mice.  Using the same mouse and dog models described above we have also shown that that AF can expression another protein, Kir6.2 that contributes significantly to the adverse electrophysiology remodeling of upper chambers.  This work aims to understand the molecular connections between RGS4 and Kir6.2 function during the development of persistent AF.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of signaling and dendritic cell functions by CD45
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; DENDRITIC CELLS; DISEASES ASSOCIATED WITH IMMUNE CELL DYSFUNCTION; KNOCKOUT MICE; PROTEIN TYROSINE KINASES; PROTEIN TYROSINE PHOSPHATASES
Abstract-Résumé: Dendritic cells are key regulatory cells of the immune system that determine whether an immune response should be initiated and if so, what type of response it should be. Receptors on the surface of dendritic cells sense disease causing agents and send signals to the dendritic cell to tell it how to respond. These signals result in the secretion of specific messenger molecules called cytokines that direct effector T cells to respond appropriately. CD45 is a regulatory molecule expressed on the surface of dendritic cells. It has an enzyme activity that modulates the signals transmitted in dendritic cells. We hypothesize that CD45 modulates the signals and messengers produced by dendritic cells to dampen inflammatory immune responses and to help prevent the immune system from attacking itself. The aim of this grant is to perform basic research to determine how CD45 modulates these signals and messengers, and how this affects the outcome of an immune response. We will use a loss of function approach to determine the role CD45 plays in regulating these responses and determine how dendritic cells lacking CD45 fight bacterial and parasitic infections. Understanding the factors that regulate dendritic cells and promote or inhibit specific types of immune responses will be of help in the design of new treatments to modulate immune responses. This is relevant to the improved health of Canadians, especially to those who suffer from inflammatory and autoimmune diseases where the magnitude and type of immune response has gone awry.

ClasseRechercheFR: ÉQUITÉ EN SANTÉ; SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the impact of barriers to health insurance coverage in maintaining health inequalities: The Health Insurance Access Database
Keywords-MotsClés: CROSS-NATIONAL COMPARISONS; ECONOMETRICS; HEALTH INEQUALITIES; HEALTH INSURANCE; HEALTH SYSTEMS; LIFECOURSE; PUBLIC POLICY; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Health spending in most developed countries has recently grown faster than gross domestic product, leading governments to search for alternative financing structures, such as increases in private expenditures. However, as these increases are generally not randomly distributed in the population, these transformations have raised concerns about their impact on population health and social inequalities in health. Finally, as the extent of private spending varies between developed countries, it appears that certain countries are better able to limit the erosion of health insurance coverage, notably through greater public regulation of the health insurance market. In order to examine this hypothesis, we propose here to build a database of indicators pertaining to the interplay of public and private health insurance coverage and regulation, with an emphasis on the identification of groups at higher risk of out-of-pocket payments. We will proceed in two phases, the first descriptive, and the second analytic.  In the first phase, we will create the Health Insurance Access Database (HIAD) by extracting policy information on 18 (of 30) Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries, for a range of 14 services, and over the period ranging 1990-2010. With the HIAD, we will 1. Summarize information on policies over time and by service; 2. Highlight similarities in policy instruments and functions between health systems; 3. More parsimoniously describe access to public health insurance and public regulation of private insurance.  In the second phase of the project, the HIAD will be linked to cross-nationally harmonized, longitudinal, micro-level data for these same 18 countries. With this linkage, we will estimate the impact of these health systems arrangements on individual health and health inequalities.  This research will therefore lead to the development of evidence-based health policies better able to protect population health and equity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lipolysis: Biochemical Genetics, Physiology and Molecular Circuitry
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL GENETICS; LIPASES; LIPIDOLOGY; MOUSE MODELS; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity results from excess fat cells in the abdomen and under the skin. Fat cells are filled by a droplet made of triglycerides. The process by which they are broken down is called lipolysis. Lipolysis may be important in determining whether people are obese or thin, and may regulate the development of diabetes. We discovered that fat cells have more than one way to degrade fat and slim down. There is reason to think that one or more previously-unrecognized pathways degrade fat to provide energy and to serve other functions essential for health. We hope to understand the different ways that fat cells slim down. We will compare normal mice with genetically-altered mice that we have created, which lack essential components of fat breakdown. The goal is to discover new genes and other components important for getting and maintaining a healthy body weight. Eventually we wish to be able to adjust these pathways for medical purposes. This would be a new approach to health restoring to people with obesity or diabetes and to children with certain hereditary metabolic diseases. In obesity and in some hereditary diseases of children, tissues like the liver and muscle accumulate fat. People with too much fat in the liver or muscle can develop complications in these organs. Fat breakdown is not well understood in liver and muscle and we will use genetically-modified mice with deficiency of important steps of the breakdown pathway to study how complications might arise and how they might be treated.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sustained ovulation-associated inflammatory signaling in fallopian tube epithelium as a predisposing factor of serous carcinoma
Keywords-MotsClés: FALLOPIAN TUBE; GLUCOCORTICOID; INFLAMMATION; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; OVARIAN CANCER; OVULATION; SEROUS CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Epithelial ovarian cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in Canadian women and is the most lethal cancer of the female reproductive tract. Unfortunately, there are no reliable tests for early detection of the disease, and symptoms that might alert a woman to seek medical treatment at an early disease stage are easily dismissed as being due to minor ailments. A major barrier in developing tests for early detection is our lack of knowledge of how this cancer develops. Women with a family history of breast or ovarian cancer are at very high risk of developing ovarian cancer, with much of this risk being due to a mutation within the breast cancer susceptibility gene 1, referred to as BRCA1. Promising recent studies indicate that the most common and lethal form of ovarian cancer may actually arise from cells lining the fallopian tube. The fallopian tube is a structure that carries the egg cell to the uterus following its release from the ovary. Each woman has two fallopian tubes, one for each of the two ovaries. In a preliminary study comparing fallopian tubes from women with BRCA1 mutations to fallopian tubes from control patients, we have identified molecular differences in the tubes from BRCA1 mutation carriers that could contribute to cancer development. Of particular interest, these differences may appear only during the period of the menstrual cycle following the release of the egg cell from the ovary (ovulation), suggesting that factors associated with ovulation may contribute to predisposition to ovarian/fallopian tube cancer development. During a typical menstrual cycle, an egg cell is released from only one of the ovaries, and thus these changes may occur in the fallopian tube near the ovulating ovary and not the fallopian tube on the other side.  The purpose of this study is to determine if this is indeed the case, and to identify potential molecules that likely participate in turning cells within the fallopian tube to cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging-based assessments of knee mechanics
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; CARTILAGE; IMAGING; KNEE; OSTEOARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: The overall benefit of this project will be to help explain why people get osteoarthritis, which must be understood to develop ways to prevent and treat the disease.  The aims of this project are a) to develop new methods for measuring how knees move and transmit load b) to develop new methods for measuring early degeneration in cartilage and c) to assess how the changes in joint movement and load transmission produced by an operation performed for early osteoarthritis are linked to degeneration of cartilage.  To date, these links have not been well-studied because we have not previously been able to make appropriate measurements of joint movement and load transmission and cartilage degeneration in living people.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Function and Activitiy of ABCA1
Keywords-MotsClés: ABCA1; ADIPOSE TISSUE; CHOLESTEROL METABOLISM; DIABETES; MICRORNA; PALMITOYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Regulation of intracellular cholesterol levels is crucial for cell function. ABCA1 is a critical protein for maintaining proper cholesterol levels in a variety of cell types by transporting excess cholesterol out of cells. Failure of ABCA1 to function properly leads to problems in many cell types. For example, if ABCA1 does not work properly in the liver and intestine, there is an inability to produce HDL or 'good' cholesterol which can result in an increased incidence of cardiovascular disease. If ABCA1 does not work normally in the pancreas, insulin is not properly secreted and can result in an increased risk for type-2-diabetes, the fastest growing disease in Canada. Failure of ABCA1 to work in the brain leads to inflammation and problems in communication between neurons which can lead to neurodegenerative disorders such as dementia, which Alzheimer's Disease International estimates afflicts more than 35 million people worldwide. Due to the importance of ABCA1 in the proper functioning of various tissues, it is vital that we understand how to regulate ABCA1 activity. Previous studies identified a way to effectively regulate ABCA1 at the level of the gene. Unfortunately, the benefits of increasing ABCA1 through these means are compromised by a variety of deleterious off-target effects. Our work aims to understand alternate pathways to regulate ABCA1 function in different tissues safely and effectively with minimal off-target effects. We will focus on two pathways, one involving the role of a lipid known as palmitate in controlling the location of ABCA1 in a cell, and another involving the role of microRNAs in controlling ABCA1 protein levels in a cell, both of which are correlated to ABCA1 activity levels. This work will provide insights into novel mechanisms of regulating ABCA1 and in doing so; identify means of controlling ABCA1 activity in different tissues, focusing on the liver, the pancreas, the brain and adipose tissue.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pain at Home in Children following Major Surgery: Physical, Psychological, and Economic Consequences
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTION; PAIN; PSYCHOLOGICAL; RECOVERY; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Pain has long-term negative consequences for children. Early experiences with medical pain are related to a host of negative outcomes including heightened pain sensitivity, medical fears, and even avoidance of future health care. Pain in childhood may also lead to declines in learning ability and can affect physical and mental health and quality of life. For thousands of children across Canada each year, surgery is an excessively painful experience. Literature on minor surgery suggests that postoperative pain in children is not well managed, especially at home, where children often receive less than prescribed doses of analgesia and non-pharmacological strategies are underused. Children undergoing major surgery are at a particularly high risk of suffering significant pain because these procedures are typically highly invasive, cause significant tissue damage, and require long recovery periods at home. Literature from adult studies suggests that postoperative pain and associated physiological processes may interfere with physical recovery, return to function, quality of life, and may be associated with the development of chronic pain. Despite evidence from adult studies, there has been little research on postoperative pain in children following major surgery. In particular, there has not been systematic prospective research examining the severity, trajectory, and treatment of children's pain at home following major surgery. There has also been little research examining the physical, emotional, and economic consequences of children's postoperative pain. Thus, the purpose of this research is to examine the prevalence, treatment, and impact of postoperative pain following children's major surgery This project brings together a team of scientists and practitioners from psychology, surgery, anesthesia, nursing, and biostatistics who have the interests and skills to carry out the research and translate the knowledge gained.

AreasOfScienceEN: RENAL FUNCTION, NEPHROLOGY, UROLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
DomainesScientifiquesFR: FONCTION RÉNALE, NÉPHROLOGIE, UROLOGIE; BIOLOGIE MOLÉCULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Factors that Protect the Vasculature in Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOPOIETIN; CRE-LOXP; DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY; MTOR; RETINOPATHY; TIE2; TRANSGENIC MICE; VEGF
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is increasing at an alarming rate worldwide and is associated with complications that include kidney failure, blindness and heart disease.  The primary defect in diabetes is elevated blood sugar due to a lack of insulin production or resistance to the insulin that is produced; in turn, the metabolic disturbances injure the tiny blood vessels resulting in the complications listed above.  Up until now, most research has focused on understanding how elevated blood sugar injures the blood vessels.  In our lab, we have discovered that growth factors, naturally produced by the body, can protect the kidney, eyes and heart from diabetic injury.  In this grant, we will use a number of 'designer mice' developed in our laboratory, to further understand how these growth factors can protect the blood vessels of diabetics.  With this knowledge in hand, we will be able to design new treatments to slow and/or prevent the devastating complications of diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathophysiology and treatment of restless legs syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES; CYCLIC ALTERNATING PATTERN; DOPAMINERGIC AGONISTS; PERIODIC LEG MOVEMENTS; RESTLESS LEGS SYNDROME; SLEEP DISTURBANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Sleep is a universal biological experience and is an integral part of our health and life. Most people have learned from their own experience that sleep is essential to health, and the body restoration provided by sleep promotes wakefulness and a sense of well-being. However, sleep disturbance may disrupt this sense of well-being and produce a wide range of physical and psychological symptoms. Sleep disruption is one of the most frequent complaints of RLS sufferers, which also bring them to consultation. Symptoms of RLS occur or worsen in the evening or night and cause difficulty in initiating or maintaining sleep leading to sleep loss and fragmentation. RLS represents one of the more frequent causes of insomnia and it has major impact health and daytime functioning. For example, data from the Sleep Heart Health Study showed that daily symptoms of restless legs were associated with a twofold increase in the risk for cardiovascular diseases. In addition, patients with RLS have stereotyped and repetitive leg movements during sleep (PLMS). Hundreds of PLMS are often seen in these patients every night and each of these movements is associated with a 15 to 40 mmHg increase in systolic blood pressure which lasts 10 to 20 sec. The aim of the present study is to look at determinants of cardiovascular changes in patients with RLS and to assess effects of various treatment modalities on RLS symptoms, nocturnal sleep and risk of developing hypertension and coronary heart disease in RLS patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: A randomized trial of a shorter radiation fraction schedule for the treatment of localised prostate cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL CLINICAL FAILURE; DOSE ESCALATION; HYPOFRACTIONATION; PROSTATE CANCER; RADIOTHERAPY; RANDOMIZED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer affecting Canadian men, and radiotherapy given from the outside (external beam) is frequently chosen by patients as an alternative to surgery to eradicate the tumour and cure the disease.  Recent improvements in radiation treatment allow more radiation dose to be safely given than before, but this has extended the duration of a treatment course from a traditional 6-7 weeks to up to 8-9 weeks.  Extending radiation treatment courses has improved cancer control, but is more inconvenient to patients and has placed a substantial economic burden on the health care system. Canadians often live remotely from radiation treatment centres, and prostate cancer patients have also been burdened with additional financial, emotional and social costs from the added weeks of  treatment.  This randomized trial is being conducted in centres across Canada and in Australia to determine whether an 8 week course of radiotherapy can be safely compressed into 4 weeks with the same effectiveness as a longer course, by using very high-precision radiotherapy techniques to direct the radiation to the tumour and away from the healthy tissues. So far 700 patients of a total 1204 have been entered.  If a shorter course is proved to be equivalent to a longer course, then using it will increase overall treatment capacity and possibly access to care, and reduce the emotional, financial and social impact of treatment on men with prostate cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Early Developmental Model of Overeating, Obesity and Executive Dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION DEFICIT; DOPAMINE; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; FETAL ADVERSITY; FOOD REWARD; GENES; IMPULSIVITY; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood obesity rates have nearly tripled in the last 25 years, with 26% of Canadian children ages 2-17 years currently overweight or obese. Despite significant efforts, our understanding, prevention and treatment of childhood obesity has fallen well short of established goals.This is highly problematic as obesity is associated with a myriad of medical and emotional complications, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, depression and a decreased lifespan.  Historically, most obesity research has fallen into one of two separate traditions. The  majority of obesity work has examined metabolic factors and weight regulation, with a strong focus on diabetes and insulin. A separate tradition has focused on behavioural factors such as food reward processes and binge eating as a cause of obesity over time.   It can be argued that a major limitation of obesity research has been a failure to integrate these two areas of work, and to characterize distinct forms of obesity that might involve both types of problems in the same individual. The goal of this proposal is to study obesity from both a metabolic and behavioural perspective, focusing on overeating driven by brain mechanisms related to Attention Deficit (Hyperactivity) Disorder (ADHD). There is significant evidence that both children and adults with ADHD have increased rates of overeating and obesity than does the population at large. This may be due to alterations related to the brain chemical dopamine, which is known to play a role in food reward processes,impulsivity and ADHD.  It is likely that several new findings related to childhood and adult obesity will emerge from this work, and lead to entirely new preventative and treatment strategies for children and adults alike.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimisation à visée clinique des aspects physiologiques et biomécaniques d'un vaisseau sanguin humain de petit diamètre produit par génie tissulaire.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE; CELLULES ENDOTHELIALES; GREFFE VASCULAIRE; GENIE TISSULAIRE; SUBSTITUTS VASCULAIRES AUTOLOGUES; VASA VASORUM
Abstract-Résumé: Le Laboratoire d'Organogenese Experimentale (LOEX) poursuit un programme hautement specialise en culture cellulaire pour reproduire in vitro des vaisseaux sanguins humains de petit diametre (moins de 6 mm). Cette initiative s'inscrit dans un domaine relativement nouveau de la biotechnologie que l'on nomme le genie tissulaire et la medecine regeneratrice, ou le LOEX est tres actif. Le present projet s'appuie sur une methode originale du genie tissulaire developpee par notre equipe n'utilisant que des cellules humaines normales et leurs proprietes intrinseques: l'AUTOASSEMBLAGE. Les vaisseaux ainsi obtenus sont les structures les plus proches de vaisseaux naturels jamais produits en laboratoire. Il s'agissait, en 1998, d'une premiere mondiale qui nous a permis de poursuivre nos travaux et publier plusieurs resultats sur les proprietes biomecaniques et physiologiques des tissus vasculaires. Nous poursuivons activement nos travaux sur ce modele. Le present projet propose d'ameliorer ce modele sophistique de vaisseau sanguin pour pouvoir eventuellement l'utiliser comme source fiable de greffons de haute qualite produits avec les propres cellules du patient. Nous allons etudier les effets de differentes modifications de conditions de culture et de production des vaisseaux pour optimiser leurs proprietes mecaniques et fonctionnelles. Ce vaisseau reconstruit en laboratoire possede des caracteristiques uniques qui permettent d'etudier des questions touchant la sante cardiovasculaire. L'objectif a long terme est donc de pouvoir fournir un petit vaisseau produit par genie tissulaire avec les propres cellules du patient pour des applications telles que les pontages coronariens ou les greffes vasculaires au niveau des jambes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Immune Biomarkers that Predict Influenza in the Nursing Home Elderly
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOMARKERS; IMMUNOSENSCENCE; INFLUENZA; NURSING HOME ELDERLY
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza is a major threat to the health of residents of nursing homes. Almost half of all deaths from influenza occur in residents of nursing homes despite high rates of influenza vaccination. It is hypothesized that the increased risk of infection stems from an aging immune system. It is known that immune system parameters change with age and these altered parameters (also referred to as immune biomarkers) can predict death. It is unknown whether immune biomarkers can predict risk of influenza infection and its complications. The goals of this study are to: 1) identify immune biomarkers predictive of influenza infection in nursing home residents; and 2) test whether an immune biomarker that rises during influenza infection will predict worsening mobility. To accomplish these goals, we will enroll 1600 nursing home residents over two influenza seasons. Residents will be eligible to participate if they are over 65 years, if they receive the seasonal influenza vaccine and if they are not taking medications that affect the immune system. Blood for immune cell analysis will be obtained prior to the influenza season. Residents will be closely monitored throughout the influenza season. In the event of respiratory symptoms, a nose swab will be obtained, and tested in the laboratory for influenza. The immune biomarkers of residents who acquire influenza will be compared to residents who do not acquire influenza. Changes in mobility during influenza infection will be recorded. The ability of the influenza specific biomarker to predict a decrease in mobility will be tested. This study aims to establish an effective way to identify nursing home residents at highest risk for influenza infection and its complications. These residents may benefit from heightened surveillance for influenza and alternative prevention strategies such as preventative anti-influenza medications. Residents who are at risk of a decline in mobility following influenza may benefit from rehabilitation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interplay between women's stress and reproductive axes: The dynamic transition from post-postpartum infertility to ovarian cyclicity
Keywords-MotsClés: INTER-BIRTH INTERVAL; INTERACTIONS BETWEEN STRESS AND REPRODUCTION; MIXED MODELS; REPRODUCTIVE AXIS - HYPOTHALAMIC-PITUITARY-GONADAL AXIS; STRESS AXIS - HYPOTHALAMIC-PITUITARY-ADRENAL AXIS; TRANSITION FROM POST-PARTUM AMENORRHEA  TO  EUMENORRHEA; WOMEN'S REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The effects of stress on health are well recognized, yet most research in this area does not adequately account for the biological differences in those effects between men and women. In both sexes there is a relationship between stress and reproductive biology. However, in women this interaction is more dynamic due to their continuous transition between different reproductive phases, from menstrual cycles to pregnancy to post-partum infertility and back to menstrual cycles. Little is known about the effects that daily life challenges have on women's reproductive biology and how those effects change as women transition between said reproductive phases. Most research in this area has been narrowly focused on subgroups of women. This study will provide new knowledge about the interactions between stress and reproductive biology in a population of healthy women from rural Guatemala. Our preliminary research on these women suggests that daily challenges may reduce the chance of conception and increase the risk of miscarriage. In this study, we will use data previously collected from these women to study another critically important and understudied transition: the period between birth and the resumption of menstrual cycles. We will evaluate hormonal levels in urine specimens collected from these women as they recovered their fertility after giving birth and use that information to develop a model of the interactions between stress and reproductive biology during this transition. This study will shed new light on how stress responses change as women transition across different reproductive phases. The result will also help explain how those changes in stress response affect women's health and reproductive outcomes. This will provide the foundation for future research into the prevention and treatment of a broad range of women's reproductive health issues such as unplanned pregnancies and problems conceiving a new pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autophagy and Apoptosis Cross-talk
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; AUTOPHAGY; CANCER; CELL LINES; CELL SURVIVAL; DROSOPHILA; FAT BODY; OOGENESIS; PROGRAMMED CELL DEATH; RNAI
Abstract-Résumé: A biological process called autophagy has recently generated tremendous attention due to the recognition that autophagy is involved in various human diseases including neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. Autophagy acts primarily as a guardian of cells, protecting them from stressful environmental conditions such as low nutrients, low oxygen and toxic insults. Another process that occurs in response to such stresses is called apoptosis, a well-studied form of cell death.  Recent studies suggest that there is a complex relationship between the processes of autophagy and apoptosis. Under some conditions and in some cell types, they act in opposition, representing a struggle between life and death. In other conditions, however, they can act coordinately to kill cells. The main objective of our research proposal is to determine how autophagy and apoptosis components interact with each other, and how this can lead to cell survival versus cell death.  Our findings will provide new insights into normal animal development and also have important implications for human disease. Since components of apoptosis and autophagy pathways are being investigated as therapeutic targets, it is important to know how modification of one process may affect the other, and what that will mean for the final fate of the cell: life or death.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel therapeutic agents for Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; LIPOPROTEIN; THERAPEUTIC
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in the elderly, and causes an enormous financial and emotional burden on patients and their families. Our research has demonstrated that the amount of cholesterol carried on apolipoprotein E (apoE), the best-established risk factor for AD, determines how much A-beta, a neuropathological hallmark of AD, is deposited in AD brains. The proposed research will determine the potential of using certain compounds to remove A-beta from the brain, thereby forming the potential basis of a new therapeutic strategy to treat this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Systemic host protein changes and requirements for Influenza virus infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-VIRALS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; PROTEOMICS; VIRUS INFECTION; VIRUS PATHOLOGY; VIRUS UNCOATING
Abstract-Résumé: A hallmark of influenza virus is its genetic variability. Antigenic drift and shift lead to rapid (approx. yearly) generation of distinct virus clones that the human immune system normally does not recognize. All viruses depend upon host cells to replicate. Virus infection causes profound changes in infected cells and some of these have been determined by "gene arrays". However, the way(s) viruses alter host proteins (the effecter molecules in cells) remains poorly understood in most virus systems. We will use an integrated 2-pronged approach to determine how influenza virus infection alters host proteins and which "non-critical" host genes are absolutely required by the virus for its replication and pathogenesis. Preliminary studies have been completed in tissue-culture cells. Here, we will extend these analyses to more relevant primary cells. Cells will be infected with various H1N1 viruses, including non-pathogenic, mildly pathogenic seasonal flu strains, and pathogenic strains, including the current pandemic swine-origin H1N1 virus and the 1918 virus. Changes in 1000s of host protein levels will be measured by "SILAC" (Stable Isotope Labeling with Amino acids in Cell culture), and processed by multi-dimensional liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry. Critical, but "non-essential" host genes will be identified by genome-wide RNA interference screens and resultant cells that survive virus infection characterized and tested for their capacity to resist infection by other influenza viruses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the innate immune response to virus particle entry
Keywords-MotsClés: HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS TYPE 1; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTERFERON; MOLECULAR VIROLOGY; VIRUS-HOST INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells respond to virus infections by rapidly producing a set of proteins that function collectively to block virus replication and spread. We previously found that cells recognize virus entry and that they respond to the entry event by rapidly producing a small number of proteins that work within that cell to prevent virus replication. In this grant, we propose to characterize how different cell types respond to virus entry, including cells that are normally the first to encounter virus, along with blood cells that are important components of the immune response. We also propose to study how viruses fight back by blocking the production or function of these response proteins. By understanding how viruses and cells counteract each other, we can learn more about the immune response and how to better design antiviral drugs to successfully fight off virus infections, especially new emerging viruses that have not been fully identified and characterized.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Integrated Real-Time 3D Ultrasound Guidance System for Multi-catheters Breast Brachytherapy
Keywords-MotsClés: 3D IMAGING; AUGMENTED REALITY; BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; BRACHYTHERAPY; BREAST CANCER; MEDICAL PHYSICS; OPTIMIZATION ALGORITHMS; ROBOTIC DEVICES; TREATMENT PLANNING SYSTEM; ULTRASOUNDS IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer affects more than 20 000 women each year in Canada. The treatment recommended for the majority of patients with stage I and II breast cancer is conserving surgery followed by radiation therapy. The radiation therapy treatment is usually performed in 4 to 5 weeks with 5 days of treatment per week. Various studies and current ongoing randomized trials have investigated methods to accelerate treatment, in which the irradiation portion of the treatment would be no more than a single week. This has become possible with the use of advanced imaging devices in the design and delivery of the radiation therapy treatments. Of all the methods used to deliver an accelerated breast treatment, brachytherapy offers the greatest potential to deliver a high dose to the tumor while sparing normal tissues because it brings a source close or inside the area to be treated. In prostate brachytherapy, this potential has reached an enhanced state with the recent combination of real-time 3D imaging of the tissues and the catheter/needle positioning, and modern planning tools. However to reach that level, breast brachytherapy (BBT) requires the use of an efficient imaging system. This proposal combines the unique strengths of two laboratories in Canada to demonstrate that a 3DUS guidance system can be used with efficacy in BBT for real-time tumor visualization, 3D contouring and choosing the right number and position of catheter used during insertion. Therefore, 3DUS will be the central technology for a complete treatment system, bypassing the need for CT imaging (extra radiation), increasing the precision and decrease the procedure time for BBT delivery. We anticipate that the 3DUS system will show superiority in term of procedure time, reduced CT dose, dose distribution and reduced # of catheters used (related to cosmetic and side effects). If proven, the system will have a tremendous impact on BBT procedures worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Silent Victims: Stigma Surrounding the Mentally Ill and Stress Effects on Spouse and Their Children
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CAREGIVERS; MENTAL HEALTH; STIGMA; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Stress associated with caring for a mentally ill spouse can adversely affect the health status of caregivers and their children. Adding to the stress of caregiving is the stigma often placed against spouses and children of people with mental illness. The goal of this study is to measure physiological markers of stress (stress hormones measured in saliva samples) as well as psychological markers of stress in spouses and children of patients suffering from mental health disorders and to compare these results to non-caregivers families and families with a member with cancer.  Comparison of physiological and psychological markers of stress in these different groups will allow to disentangle the impact of stigma against mental health disorders on chronic stress markers in caregivers and their children.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Sex & Gender Based Analysis of the Effects of Chronic Stress on Physiological and Psychological Determinants of Health in Workers
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOCRINOLOGY; GENDER; MEN AND WOMEN; SEX; STRESS; WORKERS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic stress in the workplace is becoming a very important problem in Canada, both in terms of health and economics. Although previous studies have used psychological questionnaires to assess stress in workers, we now know that these psychological questionnaires are of little help in trying to understand how stress 'gets under the skin' in workers, contributing to physical and mental health problems. In recent years, biomarkers of stress in saliva and blood have been developed and various studies have shown their efficacy at predicting physical and mental health problems in humans. However, to this day, no study has assessed factors that could differentially contribute to chronic stress in men and women in the workforce. Clearly, today's men and women in the workforce are faced with different challenges related to gender role and gender identity. These factors, along with biological differences in sex steroids in men and women could render them differentially vulnerable to the effects of chronic stress. The main goal of this study is to thus perform the first Sex and Gender-Based study of chronic stress in men and women in the workforce. In order to disentangle the effects of sex (biological factors; sex steroids in men and women) and gender (gender role and identity) on chronic stress in workers, we will measure biomarkers of basal, reactive and chronic stress in samples of saliva and blood in a population of 360 workers from a large hospital in the Montreal, Quebec region, and we will measure sex factors (sex hormones) and gender role and identity with various validated questionnaires.  By combining these sex and gender-based measures with factors associated with workplace (job content, resources, etc.) and family (parental role, financial strain, etc.) stress, we will provide the first set of scientific data determining the role of biological and psychosocial factors in contributing to chronic stress in men and women from the Canadian workforce.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Determinants of Li-Fraumeni Syndrome Associated Cancers
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRENOCORTICAL CARCINOMA; CANCER GENETICS; CHOROID PLEXUS CARCINOMA; COPY NUMBER VARIATION; LI-FRAUMENI SYNDROME; P53
Abstract-Résumé: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is the most common form of hereditary cancer known to predispose both children and adults to a wide spectrum of malignancies. Inherited mutations of the p53 tumor suppressor gene are the most common primary genetic event in LFS. Our research team is studying two groups of cancer patients to determine what genes are important in cancer development: very young children with a kind of brain tumor commonly seen in LFS, called choroid plexus carcinoma, and children and adolescents with another tumor commonly seen in LFS, called adrenocortical carcinoma that arises in the adrenal gland. We will investigate the role played by the p53 gene in the development of both tumors. We will also identify and examine regions of variation in DNA copy number in the blood and tumors of these patients, comparing them with patients who have the same kinds of tumors, but do not carry inherited p53 mutations, to identify genes that are important in the development of these tumors. Finally, we will use this genetic information together with clinical information of the patients to develop a clinical surveillance algorithm that doctors can use to detect cancers early and institute early therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: MCL-1: Functions in the nucleus regulating cell cycle and DNA damage response
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; BCL-2 FAMILY; CANCER; CELL DIVISION; DEVELOPMENT; DIFFERENTIATION; DNA DAMAGE; KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: There are a group of proteins present in all cells that are related to the founding member of the family, Bcl-2. Depending on which of the proteins are present in any given cell, their quantity, and their level of activity, they can control whether a cell continues to live, or whether it makes a decision to undergo suicide. Mcl-1 is a member of this family, but in addition to its role in promoting cell survival, it is well known to cause changes in the rate at which cells divide. By breaking Mcl-1 down into smaller fragments, and changing some parts of the protein, we can introduce the altered forms into cells to investigate the key features that controls this alternate activity. We have strong evidence that Mcl-1 acts as an important adaptor protein in the nucleus, close to the DNA molecules, and it can participate in the machinery that allows a cell to make the decision to divide into two daughter cells. We also have evidence that it functions when DNA is damaged by chemicals and it plays a role in telling the cells not to divide. Taken together, Mcl-1 may have several functions that could determine whether a cell may grow inappropriately and thus develop into cancer. We think that abnormal functioning of Mcl-1 may allow cells to divide when they should not, and could thus lead to build-up of abnormal cancerous cells. In future, a better understanding of Mcl-1's involvement in these processes may be useful in better understanding some aspects of cancer development. The knowledge gained from our studies will help us to understand many aspects of cell division, and it may be possible to utilize the new information to interrupt the abnormal processes, by designing drugs to disrupt Mcl-1 functions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Should I Stay or Should I Go? Understanding Overweight Children and Their Families Referred For and Discontinuing Weight Management Care
Keywords-MotsClés: FAMILY; HEALTH SERVICES; MULTI-SITE; OBESITY; PEDIATRIC; QUALITATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Over 2 million Canadian children meet criteria for weight management. While many researchers have tested family-based interventions to improve health, very few have studied family factors that underlie families' decisions to initiate or continue weight management care. Using a qualitative, multi-centre design, we will explore the following questions: (1) After being referred for pediatric weight management, what factors are involved in families' decisions regarding whether or not to initiate weight management care? (2) After commencing pediatric weight management, what factors are involved in families' decisions regarding whether or not to continue weight management care?  We will recruit 120 obese children/youth and 120 parents (to conduct 240 individual interviews) from Vancouver, Edmonton, Hamilton, and Montreal. Participants will be recruited into one of the following groups: (1) Initiators (n=10 families/site): referred for weight management within the past 6 months and did follow-up the referral with at least one clinic appointment; (2) Non-Initiators (n=5 families/site): referred for weight management within the past 6 months and did not follow-up the referral with a clinical appointment; (3) Continuers (n=10 families/site): completed a formal weight management intervention within the past 12 months and did continue with follow-up care for at least 6 months; and (4) Non-Continuers (n=5 families/site): completed a formal weight management intervention within the past 12 months and did not continue with follow-up care.   Demographic and anthropometric data will also be retrieved from families. This study will help us to better understand families' experiences so we can optimize the care they receive. As well, data from this study will be used in future research to develop a survey that health care professionals offering weight management care can use to understand and improve their own health services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of HCN channel opening by cyclic nucleotides
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC PHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNEL BIOPHYSICS; ION CHANNEL PHARMACOLOGY; ION CHANNEL STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: This grant focuses on "pacemaker" channels, a special class of protein tubes found in large amounts on the surface of pacemaker cells of the sino-atrial (SA) node of the heart. The SA node is the primary pacemaker and sets the natural beating rate. When pacemaker channels open, they produce electrical activity that helps cells  to contract and beat. Pacemaker channels also contribute to changes in heartbeat that occur in response to hormones such as adrenaline, which is released during the "fight or flight" response to a stressor. Adrenaline triggers the production of a small molecule, cyclic (c)AMP, inside the pacemaker cell which then attaches itself to the channel, allowing it to open more easily. Greater electrical activity and a faster beating rate result, permitting an adaptive, heightened physical reaction to the stressor. The way cAMP facilitates pacemaker channel opening has been actively studied, but findings are mainly inferred from the impact of this molecule on channel function. Specific determinants for binding of cAMP to the pacemaker channel, the strength and nature of this interaction, and the process by which function is altered remain unknown. In this application, direct binding approaches are implemented to understand the process by which cAMP facilitates channel opening. Importantly, we will measure the strength with which cAMP attaches itself to the channel using an approach called calorimetry in which the very small amounts of heat that are released when the two molecules interact are directly measured. This is the first time calorimetry has been utilized successfully with pacemaker channels; together with concurrent analyses of channel function, direct assessments of binding by calorimetry will greatly aid in the design of new drugs and therapeutic strategies to control heart rate, disorders of which include abnormally slowed or increased heart rate, pauses, and arrest with the associated risk for compromised quality of life and even death.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: Composition, Structure and Function of Human Acquired Enamel Pellicle
Keywords-MotsClés: ACIDIC PRP; ACQUIRED ENAMEL PELLICLE; AFM; ENAMEL HOMEOSTASIS; HISTATIN; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEOMICS; SALIVA; SALIVARY PROTEINS; STATHERIN
Abstract-Résumé: The acquired enamel pellicle (AEP) is a protein film with unique composition and properties which is formed in a selective manner on tooth enamel surfaces. The composition and the structure of this protein film are still mainly unknown but play functionally a vital role with important physiological/clinical implications. Its presence has important consequences both with respect to the protection of tooth enamel mineral and with respect to the nature of oral bacteria which colonize this tooth integument leading ultimately to bacterial colonization and the formation of dental plaque. The overall goal of this project is to gain insight into the biologic formation and function of the human acquired enamel pellicle. A major driving force of this application is therefore to use state-of-the-art proteomics to better characterize the components of the in vivo formed pellicle. It is also planned to explore the structural and functional properties of those in vivo AEP components by in situ and in vitro experiments.  The results of the work proposed herein will contribute significantly to the characterization of human AEP in vivo, and to our understanding of the biological functions of its components. In addition, this study may provide insights into the pathological processes underlying the initiation of dental caries and periodontal diseases.  Moreover, the functional characterization of novel proteins and peptides may lead to the development of therapeutics aimed at controlling biofilm growth, remineralizing early carious lesions and providing new salivary substitutes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of the genomic determinants of childhood leukemia using next-generation sequencing
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; BIOSTATISTICS; CANCER GENOMICS; CHILDHOOD LEUKEMIA; EPIGENETICS; FUNCTIONAL ANALYSIS; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; SNP ARRAYS
Abstract-Résumé: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most frequent cancer in children, accounting for approximately 25% of all pediatric tumors. We have previously shown that the origins of childhood leukemia could be explained by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Our main goal now is to obtain a detailed catalogue of the genetic mutations (errors in DNA sequences) involved in ALL to better understand the underlying causes of this cancer type as well as the mechanisms of disease progression. We propose to shift the paradigm of leukemia genomics research by using a new technology, next-generation sequencing, to investigate all the human genes (the genome) and identify mutations implicated in childhood leukemia. To our knowledge, this is the first study to use this powerful tool to search for novel candidate genes involved in leukemia. Successful identification of ALL causal genes will have significant implications for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of this disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; SANTE ET FACTEURS PSYCHOSOCIAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Emotion regulation and self-harm in borderline personality disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER; EMOTIONS; IMPLICIT ASSOCIATIONS; RELIEF; SELF-HARM
Abstract-Résumé: Self-harm is a serious health risk behaviour with many negative consequences. Yet, despite the seriousness of self-harm, research on why people keep harming themselves has been limited. Several articles have suggested that people harm themselves to feel better - for emotional relief. Most of this research, however, has focused on individuals' conscious beliefs about why they harm themselves. Yet, people might not be consciously aware of some of the factors that influence self-harm. As such, research is needed to tap into peoples' implicit (outside conscious awareness) beliefs about self-harm. Our first goal is to examine the implicit link between self-harm and emotional relief among self-harming individuals with and without borderline personality disorder (BPD), and controls without any history of self-harm (n = 96 per group; N = 288). We will use a validated measure (the Implicit Association Task) to examine implicit associations of self-harm with relief. Our second goal is to examine factors that strengthen the link between relief and self-harm. For instance, we will examine whether the link between relief and self-harm increases when people are upset, and whether persons with BPD show stronger associations of relief with self-harm. In doing so, we will identify the situations and individuals for which the positive emotional effects of self-harm are strongest, thereby placing people at risk for self-harm. Our third goal is to examine whether implicit associations of relief with self-harm predict future self-harm over one year. We wish to examine whether implicit associations might actually maintain self-harm over time. The proposed research has the potential to improve our understanding of why people keep self-harming despite negative emotional and interpersonal consequences. As a result, our findings will help to improve treatments for self-harm and suggest interesting directions for new treatments (e.g., modifying implicit associations).

TitreApplicationTitle: In-vivo analysis of mechanisms of cell death in inherited retinal degeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH; ERAD; RETINITIS PIGMENTOSA; RHODOPSIN; TRAFFICKING; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS
Abstract-Résumé: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is an inherited disorder in which the light detecting cells of the retina progressively die. Eventually, people with RP may become completely blind.    A key challenge to tackling RP is the diversity of genetic changes that are linked to the disease. Unlike other inherited disorders which are often caused by a single genetic change, RP can result from any one of hundreds of different mutations in several different genes. Does this mean RP is really a hundred different diseases, just one, or several? More specifically, do we need a hundred different treatments for these patients, just one, or several? To answer these questions, we will characterize several strategically chosen genetic mutations that cause different types of retinitis pigmentosa, in order to clarify the mechanisms of disease. These studies will provide valuable information about the progress of retinal degeneration, and help us to better understand how we might design treatments for this disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of scleraxis in cardiac collagen gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FIBROSIS; COLLAGEN; FIBROBLASTS; GENE EXPRESSION; KNOCKOUT MICE; MYOFIBROBLASTS; THORACIC AORTIC BANDING; TRANSCRIPTION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: The walls of the heart are strengthened by a supporting framework called the extracellular matrix, made primarily of a protein called collagen. In response to stresses such as high blood pressure or heart attack, cells in the heart called myofibroblasts make additional collagen, which strengthens the damaged heart wall and helps the heart to maintain its function. However, over time too much collagen can be made, causing the heart walls to stiffen and impairing heart contraction and relaxation. This excessive collagen accumulation (« fibrosis ») is a significant clinical challenge, affecting millions of patients worldwide. Drug treatments for fibrosis are limited and show modest effects. This is likely due to the fact that these drugs do not target fibrosis itself, but rather the underlying conditions. To design better drugs to specifically target fibrosis, we must better understand how and why excess collagen is made.  Our previous research indicates that a protein called scleraxis is an important new player in the process of collagen synthesis. Our work shows that scleraxis directly regulates the gene encoding a key cardiac collagen that is largely responsible for fibrosis. The current proposal will expand on these discoveries by determining whether the loss of scleraxis will blunt collagen projection.  To undertake this work, we will study mice in which the gene encoding scleraxis has been deleted. We will test whether these mice become resistant to fibrosis. We will also determine where and when scleraxis is active in the heart during the development of fibrosis. Finally, we will determine whether scleraxis interacts with other cellular pathways known to impact collagen formation, and if so, how this occurs. Our work will thus identify scleraxis as a critical player in the progression of fibrosis, and as a potential target for therapeutic anti-fibrosis drug design. This is a first and critical step towards the development of better treatments for fibrosis.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; AUTISME
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuron-Glia Interactions in Retinotectal Map Development
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY-DEPENDENT; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ELECTROPORATION; IN VIVO IMAGING; MORPHOMETRY; NEURON-GLIA INTERACTION; NITRIC OXIDE; RETINOTECTAL; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; VISUAL SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The current model for brain development posits that initial guidance of axons and formation of connections is largely predetermined and controlled by molecular cues, whereas the plasticity leading to precise refinement of these connections is activity-dependent and can be influenced by sensory experience.  We have studied this developmental interplay between molecular signalling and sensory experience using the retinotectal system of Xenopus laevis tadpoles.  This model system has the advantages of being amenable to repeated imaging of living cells, electrophysiological recording, and single-cell genetic manipulations all in the intact, living animal.  In addition to the neurons from the eye that project to synapse onto neurons in the brain, there is a third, often unappreciated player in this process:  radial glial cells.  The radial glia have long been known to be a source of the molecular guidance cues that help target retinal axons in the tectum.  However, we made the surprising discovery that radial glial cells are also extraordinarily structurally dynamic cells, even more motile than the neurons with which they interact.  During retinotectal map formation, they continually extend and retract long filopodial processes in all directions, greatly increasing their probability of interacting with ingrowing axons.  Even more interestingly, we found the rate of their motility was modulated by sensory input.  This means that rather than serving as passive molecular guideposts for ingrowing axons, the behaviour and presumably function of radial glia is also activity-dependent.  The experiments in this proposal will elucidate the signalling pathways by which sensory experience regulates the motility of radial glia and the consequences of glial cell dynamics on neural circuit refinement and function.  This work will provide new insights into how all the cells in the brain respond to early sensory experience to help build a highly efficient neural circuit.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of TGFbeta Signalling by Polarity Complexes
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CELL POLARITY; METASTASIS; ORTHOTOPIC CANCER MODELS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR BETA
Abstract-Résumé: Metastasis is a critical step during the progression of cancer, that involves tumour cells leaving the site of the tumour and migrating to distant parts of the body, such as the lung or bone. It is most often this event that leads to mortality in cancer patients. Therefore it is critical to understand exactly how tumour cells are altered such that they gain this capacity. One key step in this progression is changes in the shape and movement of tumour cells. Work in my lab has focussed on a factor (Transforming Growth Factor beta, or TGFbeta) that plays a key role in promoting this process in breast cancer. In previous work supported by this grant we reported on the discovery of a novel pathway that connects TGFbeta to the changes in cell shape and behaviour and showed that in breast cancer this pathway is critical for metastasis. We also discovered that the TGFbeta pathway is also linked to another cancer causing pathway that controls tissue growth. In this proposal we aim to investigate how these pathways intersect to promote tumour progression and the metastatic behaviour of cancer cells. This work will lead to new insights into how cancers grow and transition to metastasis and may illuminate new targets for the development of anti-cancer therapeutics.TGFbeta pathway is also linked to another cancer causing pathway that controls tissue growth. In this proposal we aim to investigate how these pathways intersect to promote tumour progression and the metastatic behaviour of cancer cells. This work will lead to new insights into how cancers grow and transition to metastasis and may illuminate new targets for the development of anti-cancer therapeutics.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Investigations of cardiac metabolism using mass isotopomer analysis: A paradigm for biomarker and therapy discovery.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ENERGY METABOLISM; CARDIOMYOPATHY; CGMP SIGNALING; DIABETES; HEART PERFUSION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MITOCHONDRIA; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Despite improvements in terms of management and treatment over the past 30 years, cardiovascular diseases still represent the leading cause of death in Western societies. Moreover, a raising number of patients suffer from diabetes, of which 80 percent will die of a heart attack. Accordingly, in light of (i) socioeconomic considerations; (ii) the need for new treatments for these patients; as well as (iii) the need for discovery of biomarkers (molecules that could be measured in blood or urine) to predict the risk of developing heart diseases or diabetes, there has been a major resurgence of interest in the role of nutrients and their assimilation by the body in general, and its implication for the heart in particular. In fact, it is now recognized that the diseased heart is "energy-starved in the midst of plenty", because he is unable to efficiently use blood nutrients or metabolites (sugars and lipids) for the production of energy essential for contraction. For this reason, "metabolic therapies" aiming at enhancing the efficiency of nutrient utilization are currently being considered as alternatives to the currently used treatments. However, the ultimate success of this approach relies in part on a better understanding of the cellular mechanisms governing the utilization of these nutrients by the diseased heart as well as their fate, which include energy production, but also the formation of side-products that can potentially be toxic for the heart.   The objective of this research project is to dissect the cellular mechanisms responsible for altered nutrient utilization by the diseased heart using various animal models, including models of diabetes, and pharmacological interventions that specifically target them. Furthermore, we will develop state-of-the-art technologies for screening of new molecules in biological fluids, which could improve our capability to predict disease development in a given individual.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using Novel Canadian Resources to Improve Medication Reconciliation at Discharge
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVANCED INFORMATION TECHNOLOGIES; ADVERSE DRUG EVENTS; HEALTH SERVICES OUTCOMES; MEDICATION RECONCILIATION
Abstract-Résumé: People who are hospitalized often already take many medications. Many of these medications will be stopped or changed during a hospital stay.  When patients are discharged from hospital and return home, they can sometimes get ill from the medications they were given because of problems in communication between the hospital treatment and their community-based health care providers. This study will test the advantages of using available information from provincial drug plans and community pharmacies to provide better information about community medications patients are taking at the time of hospital discharge, and improve the communication of changes made during a patient's hospital stay back to the community pharmacists and doctors. Computerized lists of community medications will be used to help patients and health professionals check which medications are being prescribed and taken. Doctors, pharmacists and nurses in the hospital will then be able to make sure new hospital and previous community drug lists are correctly matched and that the information is shared with the community doctors and pharmacists. This study will take place in three hospitals which are part of the McGill University Health Centre. There are a total of 28 medical, surgical and psychiatric units that provides treatment to 1.3 million Quebecers living in the western part of the province, spanning the area from Montreal to James Bay. We will randomize half of the hospital units to a discharge medication reconciliation and communication module, and compare these units to usual care to find out if the use of these computerized tools will decrease the number of people getting ill from medication problems that make them come back to hospital after they have been discharged home.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predictive value of inflammatory biomarkers for untreated HIV disease progression, and their response to initiation of antiretroviral therapy: a sub-study of CTN-240 (VALIDATE) and CTN-238 (MAINTAIN) Trials.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; COHORT STUDY; HIV; HSV-2; INFLAMMATORY BIOMARKERS; MICROBIAL TRANSLOCATION; MICRONUTRIENTS; NATURAL HISTORY
Abstract-Résumé: Recent research has shown that HIV may stimulate the immune system to generate a high degree of inflammation.  This inflammation can be detected using specialized blood tests that measure molecules known as 'inflammatory markers'.  Inflammation is important in HIV because it may shorten the time until treatment with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) is needed.  Inflammation also contributes to heart , kidney and liver disease.  Little is known about these inflammatory markers in the early stages of HIV infection and among people not yet treated with HAART.  In related research, Canadian researchers are leading two large clinical trials studying whether the anti-herpes drug valacyclovir (in the VALIDATE trial), or, a micronutrient/ antioxidant supplement (in the MAINTAIN trial), may be able to prolong the time before HAART is needed. One way these treatments might work is by decreasing inflammation.  Objectives: 1.What are the levels of inflammatory markers in people with HIV who are not yet on HAART, and how do these levels change over time? 2.Can blood levels of specific inflammatory markers help predict when HAART will be needed? 3.Can the anti-herpes drug valacyclovir or micronutrient/antioxidant supplementation decrease blood levels of these inflammatory markers? 4.Does herpes type 2 infection increase inflammatory markers? 5.What is the effect of starting HAART on inflammatory markers? This research will provide important insights into the levels of inflammation in people with untreated HIV.  The results will help determine whether these blood tests should be done routinely in all people living with HIV in Canada, to improve individual health by predicting how quickly HIV will lead to symptoms and other serious infections. This information will also contribute to the ongoing debate about the best time to start HAART.  The analysis will be invaluable in interpreting the final results of the VALIDATE and MAINTAIN trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of leukocyte recruitment in liver microcirculation compared to other vascular beds
Keywords-MotsClés: HEPATITIS; INFLAMMATION; INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY; LEUKOCYTE RECRUITMENT; MICROCIRCULATION
Abstract-Résumé: White cells get into different tissues to either kill bacteria or, when inappropriately activated, to cause damage as occurs in hepatitis and inflammatory bowel disease.  If we could block their recruitment into tissues we might be able to prevent some of the diseases.  Our understanding of how white cells are recruited is incomplete, but we now have a brand new imaging system that lets us look in blood vessels of living mice at all the different white cells.  We will look at how different white cells enter the liver vasculature during various inflammatory and infectious conditions.  There are at least 2 types of white cells that live in the blood vessels of the liver that can help to detect infections and injuries and release factors that initiate inflammation.  We can watch the behavior of these cells.  Using microscopy approaches that allow us to watch white cells in blood vessels we will assess how important different molecules are for white cells to stop in the liver blood vessels despite lots of flow pushing them out of the liver.  In addition, most investigators have examined the role of recruitment pathways in simple systems but not in complex conditions like liver disease.  We will investigate how white cells move into this tissue and whether any of the recruitment pathways are important in inflammation.  Finally, white cells include neutrophils, monocytes, Kupffer cells as well as iNKT cells which are a subset of lymphocytes.  We now have different strains of mice in which each of the cell types glow.  This will help tell us which white cells are adhering via which recruitment pathways in which inflammatory conditions and may reveal strategies to reduce the over-exuberant inflammatory response.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal mechanisms of compensation for dynamic force field perturbations in cerebral cortex: on-line correction, predictive adaptation, and skill generalization
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL CORTEX; COMPUTATIONAL MODELS; MOTOR SKILL LEARNING; NON-HUMAN PRIMATES; SINGLE-NEURON RECORDING
Abstract-Résumé: When our arm or hand is perturbed by an external force or obstacle while making a movement, the brain possesses mechanisms that rapidly detect the error and make a corrective adjustment to complete the movement as originally intended. This is called feedback control. If the same perturbation is encountered many times, the brain gradually learns to anticipate the effect of the perturbation and adjusts the motor command to reduce its effect. This is called predictive or feedforward control, and the learning process is called adaptation. Similarly, when we try to learn a new motor skill, we make many mistakes at first but gradually reduce the errors as our skill improves. In both adaptation and motor learning, the errors sensed during the initial feedback error-correction phase are used to modify the neural circuits responsible for the planning and execution of movements. As the circuits are modified and errors are reduced, the motor system gradually functions more and more in predictive feedforward mode. This project investigates the neural mechanisms in the motor cortex and parietal cortex that are believed to play a critical role in the detection and correction of errors during feedback control while learning a skill, and how their activity changes to permit feedforward control during skilled performance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oncolytic Virus Therapy for HTLV-1 induced Adult T cell Leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT T CELL LEUKEMIA; HTLV-1; INTERFERON SIGNALING; ONCOLYTIC VIRUS; TAX; VIROTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: HTLV-I virus is the causative agent of adult T cell leukemia (ATL), an aggressive and fatal leukemia of CD4+ T lymphocytes, and is also associated with a neurological demyelinating disease, tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP). In some areas of the world, these diseases are major causes of mortality. Using a genomics approach, we identified many genes that were upregulated during HTLV-1 infection, including suppressor of cytokine signaling (SOCS-1). SOCS-1 was stimulated during HTLV-1 infection and acted to inhibit the host antiviral response. Preliminary data argued that SOCS-1 functions by a unique mechanism, and targets interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) for degradation, thus shutting down the immune response. We are proposing to investigate the interactions between SOCS-1 and IRF-3 and how these mechanisms influence HTLV-1 infection.   Decreased antiviral responses in tumor cells help these cells to avoid the immune response but also poise them as a unique niche for the growth of oncolytic viruses (OVs) - a group of viruses that specifically infect and kill cancer cells. Because established chemotherapeutic regimens have failed in the treatment of ATL and because these cancer cells also suppress the antiviral response,  we propose to investigate the efficiency of OV as a treatment for ATL patients.  ATL cell lines and small animal models of ATL disease will be examined, either alone or in combination with another class of drug (HDI), to determine the sensitivity of adult T cell leukemia to OV treatment. This combination approach represents a potential treatment for a fatal and aggressive leukemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Folding and aggregation of ALS-associated mutant superoxide dismutases
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; BIOPHYSICAL TECHNIQUES; PROTEIN AGGREGATION; PROTEIN DYNAMICS; PROTEIN FOLDING
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a progressive, fatal neurodegenerative disorder.  In Canada and USA, ALS is the most common cause of neurological death on an annual basis. The mean age of onset for ALS is ~55 years, and the average disease duration is 3-5 years.  This devastating disease causes rapid degeneration of nerve cells and pathways in the brain and spinal cord, leading to progressive muscle paralysis, with little impairment of the intellect or senses. There is no cure and very little in the way of treatment for ALS. The major known cause of ALS is mutations in a protein called superoxide dismutase (SOD).  In vivo data from ALS patients and studies on mice indicate that mutant SOD have gained an as yet unidentified dominant toxic property. In recent years many different diseases, including transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, Alzheimer's disease and Huntington's disease, have been shown to be protein misfolding diseases.  In these diseases, variant forms of a naturally occurring protein are altered or mutated, and consequently rather than folding to the functional conformation adopted by the wild-type protein, the variants misfold and form toxic aggregates.  Our hypothesis is that mutations in SOD decrease the stability and increase structural fluctuations or dynamics of this protein, leading to increased formation of toxic aggregates which give rise to the ALS disease. We propose to measure the stability, dynamics and aggregation of recombinant mutant SOD in vitro, to identify correlations between biochemical characteristics of mutant SOD with disease properties in ALS patients.  These studies will provide important information regarding ALS disease mechanisms, and contribute to the developing urgently needed therapeutic approaches for treating ALS and other prominent and devastating protein misfolding diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genome-wide analysis of the regulation of alternative splicing
Keywords-MotsClés: COMBINATORIAL AND CONTEXT-DEPENDENT REGULATION; DNA AND RNA REGULATORY ELEMENTS; GENE REGULATION; MACHINE LEARNING; MAMMALIAN GENE VARIANTS; SPLICING AND ALTERNATIVE SPLICING
Abstract-Résumé: Twenty  years after the proposal of the double helix, it was discovered that DNA does not directly encode messenger RNA, but that a process called splicing assembles each mRNA based on carefully selected DNA subsequences. Because of this, a gene can encode many different mRNAs and which mRNAs are generated can depend on cell type, age and disease. There are 22,000 human genes, but there are over 1,000,000 different mRNAs produced by splicing. For example, one fruit fly gene encodes 38,000 mRNAs that control wiring in the brain.  Roberts and Sharp received the Nobel Prize for their work in 1993, but the genetic information that controls splicing in general has remained a mystery. Unraveling this mystery is important for fundamental science, but also for medicine, since many diseases are associated with errors in splicing. Recently, my group proposed a new approach whereby hundreds of new and known RNA features are assembled into a "splicing code" that accounts for tissue-dependent changes in alternative splicing (Nature, accepted subject to minor revisions). In this project, my group will use this approach to develop the first every, comprehensive human splicing code. This code will elucidate new classes of tissue-regulated alternative splicing patterns, identify distinct regulatory programs in different tissues, correctly predict splicing patterns in healthy tissues and find associations between disease-associated mutations and the codes needed for normal splicing. I anticipate that these results will provide a foundation for understanding and predicting the complicated, genome-wide regulation of splicing, and how diseases can cause this process to go wrong.
