TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team Grant in "Saving Vision in Glaucoma: Novel Mechanisms and Therapeutic Targets."
Keywords-MotsClés: GLAUCOMA; GLUTAMATE RECEPTORS; MUELLER GLIA; NUCLEAR FACTOR KAPPA B; RETINAL GANGLION CELL; TUMOR NECROSIS FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Glaucoma is a leading cause of blindness worldwide. At present, there is no cure for glaucoma and current therapies are often inadequate. Loss of vision in glaucoma results from the irreversible death of retinal ganglion cells, the neurons that send visual information from the retina to the brain. The current proposal will focus on novel observations made by our team to provide an in-depth characterization of key pathways leading to retinal ganglion cell death and will use this knowledge to develop novel therapeutics for glaucoma. We have brought together a multidisciplinary team of experts in a wide range of fields, from molecular biology to execution of clinical trials. It is anticipated that this research program will lead to groundbreaking discoveries, will provide an outstanding training environment, and will serve as a knowledge-translation springboard to engage our clinical, institutional and industrial partners towards rapid clinical development.

TitreApplicationTitle: British Columbia Hospitals: examination and assessment of Payment Reform - BCHeaPR
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY BASED FUNDING; HEALTH SYSTEM EXPENDITURES; HOSPITAL CARE; HOSPITAL FUNDING POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: A fundamental change to the method of funding acute hospital activity is being implemented in British Columbia (BC) in April 2010.  Activity Based Funding (ABF) is a mechanism for directing operating funds to hospitals that increase their volume of services relative to other participating hospitals.  This change is significant in an industry accustomed to historically-based global budgets and unaccustomed to detailed scrutiny of what services are provided, to whom, and with what results.  The primary objective of this study is to examine the impact of ABF on acute care hospital and related services in BC.  We are motivated to conduct this study since changes in hospital funding policy have the potential to affect health system expenditures, residents' access to care and impact care quality.  BC is the first province to adopt this acute hospital payment method on a large scale.   Although there have been no formal studies of the effects of this policy in Canada's publicly financed health care system, several provinces are also considering making a similar policy change.  This project will provide an evidence base on the impacts of ABF - including changes to the types and volume of services provided, as well as performance on quality metrics - for policy-makers in BC and elsewhere in Canada to base adaptations and modifications.  We expect these findings will be relevant across the country and in other countries where similar programs are being adopted.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissection of the NuA4 acetyltransferase complex in nuclear functions
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATIONS; CHROMATIN REMODELING; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE REGULATION; GENOME MAINTENANCE AND STABILITY; HISTONE ACETYLTRANSFERASE; HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; HISTONE VARIANTS; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: All cells in a multicellular organism contain the same genetic material.  Despite this fact, different cell types must carry out different functions.  How each cell expresses the required proteins at the correct times and represses unnecessary ones is a primary goal of gene regulation.  Deregulation of this process can result in malfunctioning cells, cell death or uncontrolled growth (cancer). It is becoming increasingly clear that the remodeling of chromosome structure is an intricate part of the process controlling gene expression.  Activities involved in this remodeling include multiprotein complexes which disrupt the basic structure of the chromosomes, the nucleosome, where DNA is wrapped around a structural protein core. These complexes are highly conserved in eukaryotes throughout evolution from unicellular organisms (ex. yeast) to mammals.  They are intimately linked to gene transcription control and implicated in the development of many human cancers.  Subunits of these activities interact with viral oncogene and tumor suppressor gene products.  Our goal is to characterize the structure and functional roles of NuA4, a specific multisubunit histone acetyltransferase complex essential for cell viability.  A combination of molecular biology, genetics, biochemistry and functional genomic techniques will be used to elucidate how this activity controls cell proliferation and gene expression, and also to characterize its role in the maintenance of the genome.  Studying the fundamental processes which govern cell growth and differentiation allows us to better understand the mechanisms of a properly functioning cell.  This in turn will point us to new scientific approaches in applied research and ultimately lay the grounds for developing new industrial production systems, diagnostic tools and therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Combinatorial Creation of Targeted Therapeutics for Breast Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; BCLXL AND GRP78 INHIBITORS; BREAST CANCER; COMBINATORIAL BIOSYNTHESIS; DEPSIPEPTIDE; DRUG DESIGN; DRUG DISCOVERY; NATURAL PRODUCTS; SMALL MOLECULES; TARGETED THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Natural products have long been a source of innovative anticancer therapeutic agents. With respect to breast cancer, natural products and chemical derivatives of them constitute a large majority of clinically used chemotherapeutic agents. One class of natural products known as depsipeptides have been the focus of much attention in recent times for their capacity to kill breast cancer cells and act on targets that would lead to less toxicity. Two of the targets of depsipeptide natural products, BclXl and GRP78, are known to be upregulated in breast cancer cells leading to cancer cells ability to resist programmed cell death (apoptosis). The focus of this grant is to harness, and strategically re-engineer, the natural biosynthetic enzymes for making anticancer depsipeptides to create improved chemical analogs for breast cancer therapeutic development. We have designed a strategy to combine structural features of distinct anticancer depsipeptides to make possible new chemotherapeutic agents that have a much greater capacity to kill breast cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels by mu-Conotoxins - mechanisms, targeting, and applications
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALGESIC; CONE SNAILS; CONOPEPTIDES; CONOTOXINS; PAIN TRANSMISSION; RESONANCE ENERGY TRANSFER; SINGLE-CHANNEL RECORDING; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; VOLTAGE CLAMPING; VOLTAGE-GATED SODIUM CHANNELS
Abstract-Résumé: Elaborately patterned cone shells house predatory snails, which are specialized to live on unlikely seeming prey ranging from fish to other mollusks or marine worms, depending on the species of snail.  Cone snails have adapted to these life styles by using a combination of stealth and venoms, which contain a deadly array of neuromuscular toxins and are injected via microscopic harpoons.  Individual conotoxins target various ion channel and receptor proteins which underlie signaling in the nervous system, and trigger muscle contraction.  Some toxins inhibit signaling activity while others enhance it.  These conotoxins, in some cases deadly to humans, are peptides (small proteins), whose well-defined structures are keyed to bind tightly to the targeted proteins and modify their essential signaling functions.  For example, members of the µ-conotoxin family (µCTXs) inhibit sodium channels that generate the impulses which convey rapid signals along nerve and muscle fibres.  Recent work shows that some µCTXs (e.g. µCTX GIIIA) preferentially block the sodium channels in muscle, while others selectively inhibit the closely related, but distinct, forms of sodium channel in pain-sensing nerves (e.g. µCTX KIIIA).  The proposed work will define the molecular lock-and-key structures on toxin and channel responsible for these remarkably selective actions, with the a long-term vision of developing safer, better targeted strategies to combat pain, and perhaps other hyper-excitability disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Integration of genetic determinants of lipoprotein(a), concentration and isoform size in relation to risk of coronary heart disease in a multi-ethnic population
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; GENETICS; LIPOPROTEIN(A); LIPOPROTEINS; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is a leading cause of death in Canada. In addition to risk factors such as smoking and diabetes, increased fats and cholesterol in the blood can lead to narrowing and blockage of the blood vessels to the heart. These fats and cholesterol are carried in the blood in packages called lipoproteins. Increased amounts of one of these packages in the blood, called lipoprotein(a)[ Lp(a) ], is associated with increased risk of heart and blood vessel disease.  However, the real importance of Lp(a) is not yet clear because people of differing genetic ancestry have varying amount and sizes of Lp(a).  The size of Lp(a) is determined by our genes. The different sizes of Lp(a) make it difficult to measure in the blood. Another challenge is that smaller size Lp(a) packages lead to larger number of the Lp(a) packages in the blood.  People can have their Lp(a) measured using different types of tests. The tests can either measure how much of the lipoprotein is in the blood, determine the Lp(a) gene type or  look at the size of Lp(a).  At the moment, we are not sure if there is one best test to use in all ethnic groups or if it is better to use a combination of tests.  We plan to use 4 different laboratory techniques. One will measure the amount of Lp(a). The second will identify the genetic factors. The other two will determine the different sizes of Lp(a) in each blood sample. We will use blood samples from a very large international study (the INTERHEART study) which was designed to allow us to understand the factors that can be used to predict the risk of someone having a heart attack. The INTERHEART study involved more than 20,000 women and men, young and old, from 52 countries and many ethnic groups.  The study we propose is the first to combine these 4 laboratory techniques in a large number of people from many ethnic groups to try to fully understand Lp(a) and its value in helping to predict the risk of developing heart and blood vessel disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Cytoprotective Responses Triggered Following Initial Exposure to Targeted Therapy: Defining Improved Treatment Strategies for Patients with HER-2 Positive Breast Cancer.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; BREAST CANCER; CYTOPROTECTIVE RESPONSES; DRUG COMBINATIONS; TRASTUZUMAB RESISTANCE; TUMOUR MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: This research program is focused on the development of drug combinations for use in patients with relapsed breast cancer. More specifically, a significant number of women suffer from advanced breast cancers that express HER-2, a protein that is associated with more aggressive metastatic breast cancer. Trastuzumab is a drug specifically designed to treat individuals with HER-2 positive disease. Unfortunately, many patients who initially respond, when first treated with trastuzumab, will relapse with a disease that will be resistant to this drug. Therefore, we need to develop new effective drugs for this group of patients. The goal of this research program is to gain new insights into the mechanisms contributing to the behavior of HER-2 positive cancers when initially exposed to different drugs and learn how to fight these mechanisms to make treatments more effective and avoid problems with drug resistance. Here, we propose two research approaches. The first one is focused on addressing a transient (reversible) adaptive response called autophagy, a cellular mechanism protecting the cancer cells from cell death while treated with anti-cancer drugs. The studies proposed here will determine whether improved treatment responses can be achieved when we combine drugs that inhibit this protective response. The second goal is designed to identify other protective responses in HER-2 positive breast cancer cells that occur when they are first exposed to selected drugs. Once these protective responses are understood, then, genes or products of these genes, will be identified as new targets for treatment. Drugs against these targets would be extremely valuable when used in a combination with the agents that first elicited the protective response of cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: The "forgotten client": What factors influence levels of psychological distress among spousal caregivers Alzheimer's patients?
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANXIETY IN CAREGIVERS; BEHAVIOURAL OBSERVATIONS; CAREGIVER BURDEN; CAREGIVER STRESS; DEPRESSION IN CAREGIVERS; INTERPERSONAL MODELS; LONGITUDINAL MODELS; SOCIAL SUPPORT; SUPPORT TRANSACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: An ever-increasing number of Canadians are providing care for spouses with Alzheimer's disease. Although in-home care is associated with better outcomes for persons with Alzheimer's disease, caregivers are at increased risk for becoming depressed as a result of the caregiving role. Specifically, compared to caregiving for patients without dementia, depression rates are nearly twice as high among caregivers of people with dementia. The first goal of our project is to better understand what factors increase the likelihood that a spousal caregiver will experience symptoms of depression. To answer this question, we will examine individual characteristics of the caregiver, characteristics of the care receiver and the context in which the care is occurring. We would also like to investigate the processes by which providing care to a patient with Alzheimer's disease leads to depression in caregivers. Answering these questions will help us identify individuals who are at greatest risk for experiencing negative outcomes as a result of their caregiving role and to refine existing interventions, in an effort to provide caregivers with skills and resources to better manage their stress. In our study, we will also follow caregivers over time. Doing so will help us understand how caregiver functioning changes over time and what factors predict better long-term health and well-being of caregivers. We are focusing on caregivers who are spouses because this group represent the majority of caregivers and because, compared to other family members, spouses in the caregiving role are particularly likely to experience negative mental health outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dynamic regulation of NMDA receptor function in the adult hippocampus
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTICOSTERONE; HOMEOSTASIS; PATCH-CLAMP RECORDING; PHOSPHORYLATION; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing findings suggest that even reaching the adult stage, our brains remain plastic and display adaptive changes in response to environmental influences.  However, unrestrained plasticity could derail normal brain functions and ultimately lead to diseases.  Thus, our brain must possess mechanisms to maintain a tight balance between plasticity and stability.  The primary objective of this proposal is to understand how the stability of a molecule named N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) is maintained in the adult brain.  NMDAR is an important molecule for learning and memory, so that deficient NMDAR activation has been implicated in the cognitive impairments of brain diseases.  Nonetheless, excessive NMDAR activation could be neurotoxic.  Because of the crucial functional roles of NMDAR and its potential contribution to neurotoxicity, it is not surprising to observe that stable NMDAR function is tightly controlled in the adult brain.  Interestingly, NMDAR in the adult brain remains changeable by environmental influences such as psychological stress.  Given the importance of maintaining NMDAR stability, we hypothesize that there are homeostatic mechanisms to stabilize the levels of NMDAR function after it is altered by stress.  This hypothesis is supported by our preliminary findings that after enhancing NMDAR function using a stress hormone corticosterone, we observed a delayed-onset alteration of the molecular composition of NMDAR.  This delayed alteration after corticosterone exposure could be a stabilizing mechanism to achieve homeostatic levels of NMDAR function in the adult brain.  In this proposal, we will examine the functional roles and molecular mechanisms underlying this potential homeostatic mechanism.  Since compromised NMDA receptor functions have been implicated in various brain diseases, our findings could provide important insights for developing therapies to restore normal NMDA receptor function in these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of vascular stability by FGF9
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; GROWTH FACTORS; VASCULAR REMODELING; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Diseased tissues that become starved of oxygen sometimes respond by growing new blood vessels.  In addition, there have been several attempts to stimulate the growth of new blood vessels in patients with artery disease.  In both cases however, the vessels that form are often fragile and fail to effectively deliver blood.  We have identified a factor, known as fibroblast growth factor 9, that has the potential to activate a population of cells that can stabilize newly formed blood vessels.  We will use novel human cell cultures that we developed and genetically altered mice to study the role played by this poorly understood growth factor.  We will focus on understanding how thin walled vessels can be converted into multilayered structures, using specialized microscopy techniques and molecular analyses.

Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH HUMAN RESOURCES; PHYSICIAN SERVICES; PRACTICE VARIATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Doctors make a majority of the decisions about how health care services are used, but we know very little about the demand each doctor makes on overall resources. This project is a first attempt to measure patterns of practice both for physicians and regions in BC. The four main research questions this project will address are: 1)For patients with similar needs, what are the variations in doctors' and regions' patterns or practice and health care system cost? 2)Are there certain types of services for which variations in practice are greater than others? 3)What factors contribute most to variations in footprint size? 4)Is there a relationship between variations and difference in patient outcomes?  The results of this project will be used by policy-makers and managers as they continue to try and improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the health care system. They will also be beneficial to other researchers interested in variations in and outcomes of physician practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Longitudinal Examination of Interpersonal and Individual Factors in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; CLOSE RELATIONSHIPS; COGNITION; LONGITUDINAL; POSTTRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER; SOCIAL SUPPORT; STANDARDIZED SELF-REPORT AND INTERVIEW ASSESSMENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a severe mental health condition that occurs in approximately 10% of Canadians following exposure to a traumatic event (Van Ameringen et al., 2008). Though a number of individual factors have been associated with the occurrence of PTSD (e.g., severe distress at the time of the traumatic event), social support after a traumatic event is one of the strongest factors associated with successful recovery. Furthermore, traumatized individuals indicate that intimate relationship problems are among their greatest concerns and PTSD is strongly associated with poorer intimate relationship functioning. This study aims to extend prior research in this area by testing a model that identifies individual and interpersonal risk and resilience factors that predict the course and severity of PTSD and relationship problems over time. A sample of 250 dyads (romantic and other close relationships) in which one member has PTSD symptoms will be recruited from the Greater Toronto Area and assessed four times. This research investigating individual and interpersonal factors associated with posttraumatic adjustment will lead to more effective prevention and treatment interventions for those with PTSD, as well as their loved ones.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION TREATMENT; HARM REDUCTION; HEALTH CARE UTILISATION; ILLEGAL DRUGS; ILLICIT USE OF DRUGS; INJECTION DRUG USERS; OVERDOSE; PRESCRIPTION DRUGS; SPACE-TIME TRENDS; WASTEWATER ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The use of illegal drugs imposes a devastating cost on Canadians, both in terms of lives lost and dollars spent. More recently, the abuse of prescription opioids (POs) has captured media headlines and the attention of the medical community. Since the early 2000s, the rate of prescribing opioids has increased close to one hundred-fold and more Canadians are now dying of accidental overdoses from POs than from street drugs such as heroin and cocaine.   Prevention efforts are needed urgently, but detecting individuals likely to experience a PO overdose is currently difficult, as there is little research to suggest how these people are unique. Our goal is to identify personal characteristics and patterns of healthcare use associated with unintentional death from PO overdose.   Identification of characteristics associated with PO overdose is a critical first step towards developing methods for detecting individuals in need of timely intervention and directing these high-risk individuals to appropriate clinical and social services.  We propose to use health data from multiple sources, including the Coroner's Office, hospital records and drug prescribing databases, to identify characteristics of PO abusers who are likely to die from an accidental overdose. This information should allow public health policy-makers to optimize treatment services and harm reduction efforts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diabetes and the mechanism(s) of renal tubular apoptosis in db/db mouse kidneys
Keywords-MotsClés: ALBUMIN; ANGIOTENSINOGEN; CASPASE-12 GENE EXPRESSION; DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY; MOLECULAR AND CELL BIOLOGY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; RENAL PROXIMAL TUBULAR CELLS; RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN SYSTEM; TRANSGENIC MICE; TUBULAR APOPTOSIS AND ATROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in both type 1 and type 2 diabetics. It is estimated that approximately 30-50% of diabetic patients in Canada and in the USA will eventually develop chronic renal failure (or end-stage renal disease). Clinical and animal experimental studies have demonstrated that intensive insulin treatment and chronic administration of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers are effective in delaying the progression of nephropathy but are not cures. These findings suggest that hyperglycemia and renin-angiotensin system activation are major risk factors for DN. Tubulointerstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy are closely associated with the progression of DN although the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This proposal, which concerns the molecular mechanism(s) of intrarenal RAS and albumin action on the development of cell death in kidney proximal tubular cells in diabetes, will increase our knowledge and understanding of their role(s) in the pathogenesis of DN, thereby contributing directly to improved clinical treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fundamental processes impacting Campylobacter jejuni pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL CELL SHAPE DETERMINANTS; BIOCHEMISTRY; BIOFILMS; CAMPYLOBACTER JEJUNI; CELL INFECTIONS; COLONIZATION; DIARRHEA; FOOD POISONING; FUNDAMENTAL PROCESSES; GASTROENTERITIS; GENOMICS; GUILLAIN-BARRE; INNATE IMMUNE ACTIVATION; MOLECULAR GENETICS; OSMOTIC STRESS RESPONSE; STRESS SURVIVAL; TRANSMISSION; TRANSPOSON MUTAGENESIS SCREENS AND SELECTIONS; VIRULENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Campylobacter jejuni is a major human pathogen, causing more foodborne diarrheal illness than any other bacterium in the developed world. However, much less is understood about its pathogenesis and survival strategies than those of less prevalent organisms such as Salmonella and E. coli. Our lab is a leader in the C. jejuni field for identifying and understanding bacterial factors important for the pathogenesis cycle, including colonization of animal hosts, causing disease in humans, and survival in the harsh transmission environment. Interestingly, we have consistently found that C. jejuni utilizes "fundamental" processes not only to survive significant stresses but also to engage in pathogenic activities such as colonization and virulence. The importance of these fundamental processes is underscored by a lack of dedicated "virulence" factors, thus also distinguishing C. jejuni from other diarrheal pathogens. This proposal seeks to better understand several newly identified novel factors and to uncover additional means by which C. jejuni persists in the environment, colonizes animals, and causes human disease. We will use genetics, biochemistry, molecular biology, and other technologies to study these processes, including several novel approaches pioneered by our group. Many of our findings will have implications for future therapy, prevention, and control strategies. Our current and future findings will also contribute greatly to emerging models of pathogenesis in other important organisms.

Abstract-Résumé: The cell is a complex machine made of many interacting parts. Parts include proteins, encoded by genes in the genome, and other molecules, like fats and sugars. The goal of this research is to develop a map of how parts of the cell work together. This map can then be used to learn how genes function in cellular processes and what happens when specific genes fail in disease, such as cancer, heart disease and autism. With this information, researchers can better understand the underlying causes of disease in their quest to develop more timely diagnosis and better medical treatments. Immediate benefits of this research include new advances in Canadian biomedical science, more efficient use of Canadian research resources, due to the public availability of software to predict protein interactions, and an increased pool of highly qualified personnel (HQP) in the nationally underrepresented fields of Computational Biology and Bioinformatics. Longer term benefits to Canada from better understanding of cell regulatory networks include the potential for improved medical treatments that will extend the comfortable life of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Further studies of the pathophysiology of vitamin B1 deficiency: effects on neural progenitor cell function
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTE; EXCITOTOXICITY; NEURAL STEM CELLS; NEUROGENESIS; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; RNA INTERFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Wernicke's encephalopathy (WE) is one of two components of the Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a neuropsychiatric disorder resulting from vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency (TD), that often develops in alcoholic patients and other individuals with a grossly impaired nutritional status. WE is associated with irreversible brain damage, particularly in forebrain and midbrain structures. These patients often have a history of recurrent bouts of TD. While thiamine administration represents a well-established treatment for acute WE nowadays, such lesions and the resulting neurological impairment are not responsive to thiamine treatment. Thus, we plan to 1) examine the effects of TD on neural precursor cells capable of forming new neurons and thereby replacing the damaged structures, and 2) the ability of these cells to respond to the injury when administered to the intact TD animal.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR Team in Novel molecular approaches in the treatment of retinal disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CELL DEATH; GENE THERAPY; NEUROPROTECTION; RETINAL DISEASE; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: In recent years a wealth of new information has become available on the causes of retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy and retinitis pigmentosa. This has highlighted two, connected problems: firstly, it is now clear that very many different genetic mutations and pathological mechanisms can underlie any given disease. Secondly, and because of this, some therapeutic approaches might be impractical since they will target only small numbers of patients or might have limited impact on resultant blindness because only one of a number of pathological mechanisms in that disease has been corrected. By instead targeting pathological mechanisms, therapeutic interventions can be made more generally applicable to a wider a variety of disease. For example, work on inhibiting inflammation is relevant to blindness due to age-related macular degeneration and also diabetic retinopathy. In addition, such a molecular approach is ideal for studying potential synergies - more effective outcomes might be achieved by targeting multiple points of a pathogenic pathway e.g. greater impact might be achieved through concurrently targeting protein misfolding, inflammation and cell death in retinitis pigmentosa.  Our team of four scientists, all located at one site, have a committed track record in studies of retinal disease. We propose a series of molecular studies in model systems. From this we will select candidate molecules, targeted at correcting retinal cell apoptosis, protein misfolding or inflammation, to take forward into pre-clinical trials in model systems (zebrafish, xenopus, or rodent). Finally, the most promising molecules will be combined to study synergies to improve outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Development and Ageing of Binaural Hearing
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE RELATED HEARING LOSS; BINAURAL HEARING; COCHLEAR IMPLANTATION; DEVELOPMENTAL PLASTICITY; PRESBYACUSIS; SOUND LOCALIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Our ability to hear is important for communication and social interactions. Hearing loss can loss can result in many difficulties and a reduced quality of life. Normally we hear with both ears (we call this binaural hearing), but deafness often results in loss of function in one ear which can also cause significant problems. Our research team has come together to explore how we use hearing from two ears, how this aspect of hearing develops from birth and how it becomes degraded in old age.  Having two ears to hear provides an important advantage over one ear and this is especially true when listening in noisy situations.  Individuals who suffer from hearing loss find it extremely challenging to hold a conversation in a large crowd or other noisy situation and thus could benefit considerably if we could restore binaural functions. We have assembled a team of investigators, already well known for their research on hearing and deafness in children and adults, and in animal models. They will determine how binaural hearing develops during childhood and how it suffers as we age.  The research will help us understand what is important about using two ears rather than one, how binaural hearing develops and how we might restore the benefits of binaural hearing in deaf children and adults. We will examine how hearing loss begins in the inner ear and how it affects the auditory nerves which run from the ears, along the brainstem, and up to the brain.  We are interested in how these nerves link the two ears and what happens to these links when there is hearing loss in both ears or only on one side.  We expect that any changes to these nerves will make it difficult to benefit from binaural hearing but that some degree of binaural function can be restored using bilateral auditory prostheses (e.g. cochlear implants).  The results of this study will enable us to establish better hearing in children with hearing loss and to improving hearing after any decline with ageing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expression of the Hepatic Glucokinase Gene in the Progression and Treatment of Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; GENE EXPRESSION; GLUCOKINASE; LIVER
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is characterized by the loss of control of blood sugar levels.  Diabetes is a complex disease with many causes, both genetic and environmental.  The liver has a primary role in maintaining proper blood sugar levels as it is a major site of production of glucose, when blood levels are low, and storing excess levels when blood levels are high.  Both high and low levels of blood glucose have serious health consequences.  The enzyme glucokinase is the key gatekeeper of glucose metabolism in liver cells as it regulates the production of glycogen and metabolism of glucose.  Glucokinase gene expression and enzymatic activity are carefully regulated so that it is only active when there is excess glucose, but in Diabetes the regulation of glucokinase is impaired, thus the uptake of glucose by liver cells is reduced.  Activators of glucokinase enzymatic function have been identified and have promise in the treatment of Diabetes.  Unfortunately, glucokinase also functions at other sites in the body, and activation of glucokinase function at these sites may have negative health impacts, thus efforts are underway to identify mechanisms that could lead to the liver-specific enhancement of glucokinase function.  We propose to investigate mechanisms that regulate the expression, as well as the consequences of impaired regulation, of the glucokinase gene in the liver.  An understanding of the mechanisms that regulate glucokinase gene expression, as well as genes and enzymes miss-regulated by glucokinase deficiency, should allow the development of alternate strategies to treat Diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Occupational and selected nonoccupational risk factors for lung cancer: analysis of a case-control study in Montreal
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CASE-CONTROL; ENVIRONMENT; EPIDEMIOLOGY; ETIOLOGY; OCCUPATION; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the most common cancer in Canada, accounting for 25% of all cancer deaths. Prevention of lung cancer depends on the discovery and elimination of its causes. Each cancer case results from the conjuncture of a complex of circumstances (e.g., genetic predisposition, environmental exposures, lifestyle habits) which combine over a lifetime to initiate cancers. Cigarette smoking is the single most important cause of lung cancer. Since it has proven so hard to eliminate smoking, it is very important to identify other modifiable causes. Apart from smoking, there are several recognized or suspected lung carcinogens in the occupational milieu and there are several suspected non-occupational risk factors as well, such as alcohol intake, domestic radon, and urban air pollution. In 1996 we undertook a large study of lung cancer whose aim was to elucidate environmental causes of lung cancer. All lung cancer cases occurring in Montreal from 1996 to 1998 were approached, as well as a representative sample of people in the general population.  Interviews were carried out with 1211 cases and 1539 controls. The questionnaire focused on lifetime occupational history, but also included detailed info on many other factors.  The occupational history was subsequently evaluated to infer a list of occupational exposures. The statistical challenge is to compare the cases with the controls to determine which factors, if any, occurred more often among cases than among controls, and that might be causally related to lung cancer. This is a lengthy and painstaking process. We have started working our way through the long list of about 600 different variables at our disposal, and this has resulted in a number of results and publications. The purpose of the present application is to extend the comprehensive program of statistical analysis and reporting of this study. We will continue to make significant contributions to the identification of modifiable risk factors for lung cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Walking after stroke: Is learning enhanced through attention or distraction?
Keywords-MotsClés: KINEMATICS; MOTOR LEARNING; SPLIT-BELT TREADMILL; STROKE; WALKING
Abstract-Résumé: Regaining the ability to walk is an important goal for many individuals with stroke, and the demand for walking training in Canada is growing.  Our research will help the health care system cope with this increasing demand by discovering more effective training methods for walking.  We will study whether conscious effort during training improves or worsens the learning of walking.  Adults and children, some healthy and some with stroke, will learn to walk on a split-belt treadmill.  This treadmill has two belts, one for each leg, that run at different speeds.  Some subjects will focus on their feet while learning to walk on the split-belt treadmill (attention group).  Others will watch a TV show when split-belt walking (distraction group).  We will compare how well the attention and distraction groups learn to walk on the split-belt treadmill.  By testing children and adults we can study how attention level affects learning across the lifespan.  By testing subjects with and without stroke we can see how an injury affects the learning of walking.  Our work will help individuals with stroke become successful walkers.  This will increase their quality of life and reduce their risk of health complications as they become more physically active.  Our research findings can be applied quickly by health professionals, and thus our research has the potential to have an immediate, positive impact on the delivery of rehabilitation in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prenatal hypoxic programming of vascular dysfunction: role of MMP-2 and endothelin.
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIN; FETAL PROGRAMMING; HYPOXIA; MATRIX-METALLOPROTEINASES; NITRIC OXIDE; VASCULAR FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in Western countries, and is predicted to become the leading cause of death worldwide. Studies in the last 20 years have shown that adverse events during pregnancy can permanently affect the long-term health of a fetus. That is, someone exposed to stress during fetal life is at a greater risk of developing high blood pressure, stroke and heart attacks as adults. One of the most common complications in pregnancy is low oxygen supply to the fetus. We have shown that low oxygen supply to the fetus is linked to blood vessel damage in adults, although the exact causes are not known. This aim of this project is to identify the mechanisms by which low oxygen supply causes blood vessel dysfunction. The project focuses on endothelin (ET), which is an important player in various cardiovascular disorders. The project aims to determine if and how ET activity goes awry. To carry out these experiments, rats will be put in a chamber with low oxygen (12%) during the last trimester of pregnancy; these will be compared to rats that were kept at normal oxygen (21%) throughout pregnancy. Once the rats give birth, the offspring will be raised normally. When the rats become young adults (4 months), or aged adults (12 months),blood vessels will be removed from anesthetised animals, and will be mounted in a myograph system, in which we can assess vascular function. We will conduct experiments with various drugs to determine if ET, and other systems with which it interacts, are altered. Using treatments immediately after birth, we will also attempt to prevent the blood vessel damage from occurring.  This work ultimately seeks to uncover events in very early life that increases one's risk CVD, thereby giving us information about early treatment options to prevent its eventual onset.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the airway epithelium inflammasome in asthma pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; EPITHELIAL MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION; EPITHELIUM; GROWTH FACTORS; INFLAMMASOME; MOUSE; REPAIR; TRANSGENICS
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a world-wide respiratory disease that affects more than 300 million individuals and causes considerable burden on health care systems due to direct (medicare and drugs) and indirect (mortality, quality of life, lost productivity in workplace)costs. The airway epithelium is the first line of defense against inhaled allergens, viruses, bacteria, and environmental pollutants. Recently the airway epithelium in asthmatics has been shown to different from non-asthmatics in it's ability to repair itself. Understanding the mechanisms underlying why asthmatic epithelium and it's repair processes differ from non-asthmatics will provide insight into disease development and shed light on new therapeutic options.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effets à long terme de l'intervention précoce sur les troubles des conduites et comportements à risque: Comment fonctionnent-ils et pour qui?
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPORTEMENTS A RISQUE; DEVIS LONGITUDINAL; DIFFERENCES SEXUELLES; ENFANTS NES PREMATUREMENT; ESSAI RANDOMISE; INTERVENTION PREVENTIVE; MECANISMES D'INTERVENTION; TROUBLE DES CONDUITES
Abstract-Résumé: L'objectif de ce projet de recherche est d'etudier comment l'intervention precoce aupres des enfants mene a la reduction a long terme des troubles des conduites et de leurs consequences. Les jeunes qui presentent des troubles des conduites (comportements agressifs et non-respect recurrent des regles et des lois), sont plus a risque que les autres de fumer, de consommer, d'avoir des relations sexuelles non-protegees et de decrocher au secondaire. Ce projet de recherche s'appuiera sur les donnees d'une grande etude americaine a laquelle ont participe 985 familles ayant donne naissance a des enfants prematures et de petit poids. Le tiers de ces familles, selectionnees au hasard, ont recu des services pendant les trois premieres annees de vie de l'enfant (visites a domicile, services educatifs prescolaires de qualite, rencontres de parents). Pendant leur enfance, les enfants du groupe d'intervention et leurs familles ont montre plusieurs gains comparativement a ceux du groupe controle, mais ce n'est qu'a l'age de 18 ans qu'on a aussi note moins de problemes de comportement, un phenomene surprenant, mais qu'on a observe dans d'autres etudes similaires. Ce projet vise donc d'abord a mieux comprendre les mecanismes par lesquels l'intervention precoce parvient a prevenir les problemes de comportement : est-ce en stimulant le developpement cognitif des enfants, en favorisant l'emploi de la mere, ou en ameliorant l'environnement familial et les comportements parentaux ? On examinera ensuite s'il existe des differences dans les mecanismes les plus importants pour les garcons et les filles, ou pour les enfants qui presentent differentes caracteristiques. Mieux comprendre comment et pour qui l'intervention precoce permet de prevenir les troubles des conduites permettra de mieux diriger les efforts et les ressources publiques qui y sont consacres, et ainsi eviter que ces problemes compromettent la sante de ces jeunes et leurs chances de reussir aux plans social et economique.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroprotection in cerebral ischemia by inhibition of the interleukin-1 system: involvement of age-dependent central and peripheral inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BEHAVIOURAL ANALYSIS; CEREBRAL ISCHEMIA; CYTOKINES; IN VIVO IMAGING; INFLAMMATION; NEUROPROTECTION; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a major health problem, being the third leading cause of death in Canada. About 15% of stroke patients will die and 75% will suffer from long-lasting disabilities, requiring constant medical support and putting a huge strain on their families with important associate cost on the economy. Stroke occurs during any period of development, from neonate to the adult, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms leading to brain damage differ depending on age. New treatments for stroke are therefore urgently required but, in order to successfully treat all ages, it is necessary to understand the differences between neonatal and adult brain response after a stroke. Both central and peripheral inflammation, and especially the pro-inflammatory and neurotoxic mediator interleukin-1, plays a crucial role in brain damage induced by a stroke. We hypothesize that interleukin-1 is a central player in brain damage after a stroke in both neonates and adults, and we will study the neuroprotective potential of systemically administered new interleukin-1 blockers. This study will enable a better understanding of the central and peripheral mechanisms underlying brain damage after a stroke, especially the differences between neonates and adult responses, and will highlight new age-dependent processes that could be targeted to develop new therapeutic strategies.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSAFETY LEVEL 3 CONTAINMENT LABORATORY; ENVELOPE GLYCOPROTEINS; GENETIC ANALYSIS; HIV/AIDS; MOLECULAR VIROLOGY; MUPFURE SCHISTOSOMIASIS AND HIV COHORT; PATHOGENESIS; PROTEIN MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is an enveloped virus and a member of the retrovirus family that causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). An estimated 33 million people are living with HIV infection worldwide. One striking feature of this global epidemic is the geographical distribution of different HIV-1 subtypes. Most of the current research regarding HIV-1 pathogenesis has been focused on the study of HIV-1 subtype B (B-HIV), which is predominantly found in western countries. However, more than 50% of all people infected with HIV-1 and 20% of the entire adult population in much of sub-Saharan Africa are infected with subtype C (C-HIV). HIV-1 infects vital cells of our immune system by entering through a receptor called CD4, and a coreceptor, which can be either CCR5 (R5) or CXCR4 (X4). B-HIV has been shown to use both coreceptors although at late stages of infection, it preferentially uses X4. In contrast, C-HIV isolates exclusively use the R5 coreceptor for viral entry. Studies have shown that during B-HIV infections, the viruses that use R5 acquire natural mutations that increase pathogenesis thereby making the patient's illness worse. We believe that C-HIV viruses also acquire mutations during the course of an infection that allows the virus to be more efficient at entering and killing immune cells. To verify our hypothesis, we propose to use a consented cohort of 196 individuals from Zimbabwe with C-HIV. Samples were taken at different times spanning the asymptomatic stages of infection through to AIDS. Using these samples, we will identify naturally occurring changes in the C-HIV envelope and verify how these mutations affect HIV-1 entry and death of immune cells. Our findings will not only be important for better understanding how C-HIV evolves over the course of time but also for the development of novel vaccines and/or entry inhibitors designed to treat the millions of people suffering from C-HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism and biological consequences of alternative 3' end processing in the nervous system
Keywords-MotsClés: 3'-UTR; ALTERNATIVE POLYADENYLATION AND CLEAVAGE; CANCER BIOLOGY; DEEP SEQUENCING; ONCOGENES; ONCOGENIC TRANSFORMATION; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; RNA-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENES
Abstract-Résumé: The process by which normal cells become cancer cells is a highly complex process. The transition from a normal cell to a cancer cell can often be attributed to genetic mutations in proto-oncogenes; however, activation of the protein products of cancer-causing oncogenes sometimes occurs without mutations in DNA.   One newly discovered characteristic of cancer cells is that they tend to produce some mRNAs (molecules used as templates to synthesize proteins) with tail-ends called 3' Untranslated Regions (3'UTRs) that are shorter than in normal cells. This change is important because the 3'UTR of mRNAs contain repressive elements that cause decreased protein expression. The shorter mRNAs produced in cancer cells have usually lost 90% of the 3'UTR and express on average 10-times more protein than their longer counterparts.   The process of generating mRNAs with these shorter 3'UTRs is called alternative polyadenylation and cleavage (APA). It has been found that mice injected with a short 3'UTR mRNA that codes for an oncogene called IMP-1 develop tumors. On the other hand, mice injected with a corresponding long 3'UTR mRNA coding for IMP-1 remain healthy. Thus, APA-mediated activation of IMP-1 leads to oncogenic transformation without mutations in DNA.   I want to understand the molecular events that cause cancer cells to produce these mRNAs with shorter 3'UTRs. Specifically, I plan to identify protein factors found in cancer cells that influence the production of shorter 3'UTR mRNAs. Since the production of shorter 3'UTR mRNAs by cancer cells is not caused by genetic mutations, the process could be reversible. Therefore, understanding the factors involved in APA may lead to new cancer treatments.

Abstract-Résumé: Premature birth, defined as birth before 37 completed weeks gestation, has been identified as one of the most important health problems for babies in developed nations. Immature newborn babies often have quite complex medical conditions that require the sophisticated care provided within level III Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs). In 2009, the March of Dimes Foundation released a report that shows that premature birth is actually on the rise. Doctors and nurses who look after these babies within NICUs need to quickly and accurately analyse and interpret data shown on a number of medical devices to provide optimal care for these babies while they grow and develop. Despite the availability of newer information technologies in the NICU, most tasks performed by neonatologists, nurses, and other healthcare providers are manual as there is no system which integrates the data from all the different medical devices used on a baby on an ongoing basis. Recent medical research has discovered that nosocomial infection and other conditions of the premature and/or critically ill newborn may have common early indicators in aspects that are seemingly unrelated such as heart rate and breathing rate. In our research we have created a system that is capable of receiving and analysing a range of data from the babies and looking for nosocomial infection and other conditions of interest in real-time. We have an established academic collaboration between the Canadian Neonatal Network and the People's Republic of China (PRC) to train Chinese neonatologists. We have commenced a clinical research study in Canada focussed on supporting earlier detection of nosocomial infection, which if detected late can result in devastating outcomes for these babies. In this research proposal we merge and extend those initiatives to pursue collaborative clinical research between the PRC and Canada in the area of onset behaviours in physiological streams for patients that develop nosocomial infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Quality of care following injury in British Columbia and the Yukon: a study to validate the use of linked administrative data sources to evaluate care
Keywords-MotsClés: LINKED ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTH DATABASES; MULTIVARIATE ANALYSIS; RE-HOSPITALIZATION FOLLOWING SEVERE INJURY; REHABILITATION AND PSYCHOLOGICAL SUPPORT SERVICES
Abstract-Résumé: Nearly 10,000 persons are permanently or temporarily disabled each year in British Columbia due to injury. However, we do not know how frequently these patients are re-hospitalized after discharge and whether these re-hospitalizations could be prevented through improved access and utilization of outpatient support services. This limitation poses a serious deficiency to injury surveillance programs.  I propose to study preventable re-hospitalizations following severe injury in British Columbia and the Yukon. My hypothesis is that reduced access and utilization of outpatient rehabilitative and psychological support services leads to increased rates of re-hospitalization. Furthermore, these risks will be higher among certain segments of the population, including women, patients who reside in rural and remote communities, and among populations with greater socio-economic disadvantage.   I will test my hypothesis by estimating the adjusted odds ratios for re-hospitalization among injury survivors between 2001 and 2009, using linked administrative health, socio-economic, and geographic databases to build my analysis at the population-scale. I will administer an online survey of key stakeholders to identify which clinical indicators currently used to measure long-term functional outcomes can be reconstructed using linked administrative health databases. These stakeholders will include trauma surgeons, rehabilitation and return-to-work specialists, and medical health officers.   The primary importance of this study is that it will recapture, for the first time, an entire trauma patient population since their initial discharge and assess whether current systems of care prevent re-hospitalization. This analysis will also identify where and among which populations increased re-hospitalization rates are occurring, thus providing a highly detailed population-wide perspective of barriers that delay reintegration back into work and society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dietary and genetic predictors of antioxidant status and risk of cardiovascular disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIOXIDANTS; BIOMARKERS; BIOSTATISTICS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; DIET-GENE INTERACTIONS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENETICS; GENOME-WIDE ASSOCIATION; NUTRITION; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability in North America and is known to be caused by both genetic and dietary factors. Because low levels of antioxidants in the blood have been shown to increase the risk of CVD, many studies of CVD and dietary antioxidants, such as vitamins A, C and E, have been conducted, but the results have been mixed. Our previous research suggests that this inconsistency may be due to genetic differences in the subjects studied that lead some people to have higher levels of antioxidants in their blood after consuming antioxidants than others. We will expand this research to find out whether these genetic differences in response to dietary antioxidants can predict the risk of CVD events such as heart attacks. Recent technologies have made it possible to examine the whole genome of subjects, and so it is timely to conduct a thorough analysis of genetic predictors of CVD and examine how their combined influence can enhance the prediction of CVD risk by dietary and conventional risk factors. The Nurses' Health Study (NHS) of women and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study (HPFS) of men are among the largest and longest running (>20 years) health investigations, and have produced landmark data on CVD, showing that diet, physical activity and other lifestyle factors can powerfully promote better health. Now that genome-wide data is available for 1000 NHS and HPFS subjects who have had a heart attack and 2000 controls who have not, we plan to combine the genetic, dietary, lifestyle and other risk factors to create a CVD risk predictor score that will be more useful in predicting heart attacks than any single risk factor alone. This research will also help to determine the optimal dietary recommendations of antioxidants for preventing CVD in individuals and populations, enable future studies of antioxidants to be more consistent, and provide a template for creating predictor scores for other complex diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing Structural, Functional and Cognitive Changes in Multiple Sclerosis (MS) using High-Resolution Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI)
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL IMAGING; COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING (DTI); FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (FMRI); MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NEURODEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a relatively common, early-onset disorder in which the immune system attacks the myelin coverings of axons throughout the central nervous system.   There is no known cause or cure and symptoms are variable across individuals, but can include sensory, motor, and cognitive dysfunctions.  However, because the neural systems responsible for higher-level cognitive functions appear to be more adaptable than those for sensory and motor functions, cognitive abilities are spared in a subset of patients, despite MS-damage.  Therefore, identifying the structural and functional brain changes associated with this type of neural plasticity, and the reason(s) for this neural reorganization, could improve predictions of cognitive decline on an individual basis, and could identify treatments that enhance natural adaptation to restore or prolong cognitive function.  The primary goal of this project is to test whether normal genetic variations linked to cognition and neural plasticity are related to structural or functional brain changes that enable individuals to compensate for MS damage and maintain cognitive function.  This will require a thorough assessment of individuals with MS, as well as healthy controls, to characterize: (1) the degree of white matter integrity in specific brain tracts using high-resolution diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), (2) the neural activity in brain regions recruited during cognitively-demanding tasks using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and (3) known genetic variations through genetic screening.  Determining whether specific genetic variants are associated with the structure and function of healthy cognitive neural systems, and whether these genetic variants are related to the degree of MS-related cognitive preservation is critically important.  These findings will pave the way for clearer prognosis, better disease management, and future interventions for preventing or reversing MS-related cognitive decline.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Gut Microbiota:  Its Regulation by and Impact on the Host Immune Response
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICS; COLITIS; GASTROINTESTINAL; GUT MICROBIOTA; IMMUNOLOGY; MICROBIOLOGY; SALMONELLA TYPHIMURIUM
Abstract-Résumé: In the last several years a great deal of attention has been given to understanding the role of commensal microbiota in the development and progression of diseases.  In particular, alteration in the gut microbiota have been suggested to be important in various conditions such as irritable bowel disease (IBD) and Crohn's disease.  However, it is not clear what host factors play a role in determining the composition of the microbiota.  We hypothesize that various components of the immune system are important in regulating the normal microbiota.  We hope to assess this hypothesis by comparing the composition of the gut microbiota of mice with various innate and adaptive immune system alterations to determine what aspects of the immune response are responsible for shaping the microbiota.  We are also interested in understanding what role the microbiota plays in the induction of an immune response against Salmonella Typhimurium infection.  WE hope to examine this relationship by utilizing various antibiotic treatments to cause different shifts in the gut microflora community and examining the immune response generated in response to Salmonella Typhimurium infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the role of Nrf2 and HNF4alpha in in utero high fat diet-induced nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: FETAL ORIGINS OF NONALCOHOLIC LIVER DISEASE; MATERNAL HIGH FAT DIET RELATED FETAL EPIGENETIC CHANGES; ROLE OF TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS IN FETAL PROGRAMMING
Abstract-Résumé: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a serious liver condition because severe cases can lead to end-stage liver disease, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality. NAFLD is the most common cause of liver disease in adults and children and its prevalence has increased dramatically over the past few decades. There is evidence that high fat diet (HFD)-induced hyperlipidemia during pregnancy contributes to the development of NAFLD in human, nonhuman primate, and mouse offspring. The mechanisms of this effect are unclear; however, likely involve aberrant fetal hepatic lipid metabolism, oxidative stress, and epigenetic changes. The transcription factor Nrf2 and nuclear receptor HNF4a are implicated in the etiology of adult NAFLD. Nrf2 regulates genes involved in lipid metabolism and oxidative stress. In addition, Nrf2 null mice fed a HFD have an increased incidence of NAFLD than wildtype mice. HNF4a regulates hepatic development and lipid homeostasis. Hepatic specific knockout of HNF4a in mice results in the accumulation of lipids in the liver. Therefore, we hypothesize that Nrf2 and HNF4a are major regulators of fetal liver lipid homeostasis and oxidative stress gene expression and further play a role in maternal HFD-induced aberrant gene expression leading to permanent alterations in lipid homeostasis that predispose the offspring to developing NAFLD. By using Nrf2 null, Nrf2 enhanced, and hepatic-specific HNF4a null pregnant mice fed a control or HFD, we will fully investigate this hypothesis by correlating markers of NAFLD in the fetal and postnatal offspring with 1) expression changes of lipid metabolism and oxidative stress response genes, and 2) epigenetic changes in Nrf2 and HNF4a genes and target genes. These experiments will provide valuable insight into mechanisms of the developmental origins of NAFLD and provide knowledge on lipid metabolizing and oxidative stress response gene regulation in the fetal and postnatal liver during development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating and training the brain in chronic pain
Keywords-MotsClés: 'TRAINING THE BRAIN' TREATMENT; BRAIN IMAGING; CHRONIC BACK PAIN; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; HEALTH LITERACY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; NEUROSCIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic back pain (CBP) is commonly disabling and very costly. Current treatments that focus on treating physical structures in the back itself are usually ineffective. This may be because changes in the nervous system and brain that often occur in people with CBP are responsible for the pain instead. Treatment guidelines for CBP recommend general exercise and physical activity but these treatments do not address brain changes. A further issue is that patients and clinicians are often unable to make effective decisions about treatment because they do not have the necessary understanding of these complex processes. This project integrates two exciting new areas of research. First, we now know that the brain changes that occur in chronic pain can be corrected and when they are, pain and disability are reduced. Second, we now know that giving people the required understanding to make effective health-related decisions improves their health. Building on the latest advances in these 2 areas, we will investigate if the combination of a new treatment ('training the brain') plus giving patients the resources to improve their health literacy, will decrease pain and disability in CBP. We will test this using the gold standard approach - a randomized controlled trial. Importantly, we are also using input from patients, clinicians, and stakeholders (eg, employers) to determine the best way to transfer and translate this knowledge into optimized clinical practice. This research could revolutionize how we treat CBP. If our theory is correct, it could lead to a reduction of the huge burden, on individuals and on society, of CBP. We expect to see improved rates of return to work and a large proportion of people resuming meaningful and productive lives. This project will have direct implications for the 1 in 5 Canadians who have a CBP problem that limits their life activities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of factors involved in the development of CD8+ memory T cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE TRANSFER; CD8 T CELL MEMORY; FLOW CYTOMETRY; MOLECULAR IMMUNOLOGY; MOUSE MODELS; RNA MICROARRAY
Abstract-Résumé: Undoubtedly one of the revolutions of modern medicine has been the development of vaccines. These have allowed for the control of several infectious agents afflicting humans, such as those causing smallpox and polio. The illustrious success of certain vaccines suggests that this technology could provide the solution to current epidemics, including HIV and tuberculosis, or cure certain cancers. However, the engineering of a successful vaccine is poorly understood. One of the characteristics of efficacious vaccines is the induction of long-term memory T cells. These are capable of a rapid and strong response upon exposure to the targeted pathogen. Using a mouse model, we plan to elucidate some of the molecular mechanisms that favour the establishment of memory T cells. Through the use of two different immunization protocols, we are able to induce a strong or a weak memory T cell response. Therefore, by comparing the molecular signature of T cells induced through either protocol, we will identify factors associated with efficient production of a memory pool. Subsequently, the molecular factors suspected to play a role in T cell memory development will be abrogated in genetically modified mice. Qualifying the immune response in these mice should confirm the importance of these factors in efficient T cell memory production. Clarifying the molecular events involved in this process will allow for the development of optimal vaccination strategies that are needed to curtail current epidemics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of IGFBP7-mediated apoptosis in oncogenic BRAF melanomas
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; BCL-2 PROTEINS; IGF2R; IGFBP7; MAP KINASE PATHWAY; MELANOMA; ONCOGENE ADDICTION; STAT1
Abstract-Résumé: Melanoma is a type of cancer that occurs in melanocytes, the pigmented cells of the skin, and is the deadliest form of skin cancer. The incidence of this disease is rising faster than any other cancer (American Cancer Society, 2006) and therapeutic interventions remain only marginally effective. With this in mind, a huge investment is being made to understand melanoma signaling networks in an attempt to identify new targets or combinations of targets for therapeutic intervention. At the genetic level, greater than 90% of all melanomas show continuous hyperactivity in a particular signaling pathway known as the MAPK pathway, which is responsible for the rapid growth and division of these melanoma cells. In 60% of all melanomas this phenomenon is the result of a particular mutation in the protein BRAF, which is part of the MAPK pathway. Unfortunately drugs that target this pathway do not kill melanoma cells but only slow their growth, which will slow tumour growth but not shrink tumours. Hence these drugs have performed poorly in clinical trials. The lab of Michael Green at the University of Massachusetts Medical School has discovered that the protein IGFBP7 effective kills melanoma cells that contain this BRAF mutation, shrinking melanoma tumours. The aim of the research proposed here is to fully understand how IGFBP7 kills these cells. This knowledge may further the potential for IGFBP7 to be used clinically to treat melanomas that contain this BRAF mutation. More importantly, since only 60% of melanomas have this mutation, IGFBP7 will not be effective in treating all melanomas. However, by using this protein as a guide we can hopefully identify key drug targets for killing all melanoma cells, and use this knowledge as a platform for therapeutic intervention.

Abstract-Résumé: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are rare cells capable of initiation and maintenance of malignancy. Most therapeutic strategies tend to target the bulk of the tumor composed of cells that can not initiate malignancy. Hence, the focus of cancer research has shifted to identification and characterization of CSCs in the hope of developing therapies that would specifically target these cells. Leukemic stem cells (LSCs) are among the most well characterized CSCs and initiatives to specifically target these cells, while leaving normal hematopoeitic stem cells (HSCs) unharmed, have already begun. However, it is very difficult to distinguish an HCS from an LSC and thus to develop therapies which specifically target the LSC without harming the normal HSC pool. Therefore, there is great need for identification and the characterization of the differences between HSCs and LSCs. I will utilize two well defined mouse acute myeloid leukemia (AML) models in conjunction with normal HSCs to generate a common gene expression signature for AML LSCs at the single cell level. This expression signature can be further utilized to explore molecular differences between these two cell types. The findings of this project can potentially be applied to human AML samples for prognosis assessment and possibly aid in the development of LSC-specific therapeutic strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparative genetic and proteomic analysis of late-outgrowth endothelial progenitor cells from pulmonary arterial hypertension patients bearing mutations in bone morphogenetic protein receptor type II
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MORPHOGENETIC PROTEIN 9; BONE MORPHOGENETIC PROTEIN RECEPTOR TYPE II; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; ENDOTHELIAL PROGENITOR CELLS; PULMONARY ARTERIAL HYPERTENSION
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a disease that causes a narrowing and loss of the blood vessels in the lung, leading to increased stress on the heart and eventual death by heart failure. There are currently no effective treatments for this devastating disease, which often affects individuals in their 30s and 40s and women over men at a ratio of two to one. Current therapies offer patients a partial relief from symptoms, but only marginally extend survival and are extremely expensive (between $20,000 to $200,000 per patient per year, depending on the treatment). Recently, the onset of PAH was linked to a mutation in a gene encoding the protein BMPR-II. While it is still unknown how defects in BMPR-II can lead to disease, the investigation of this relationship remains the best hope for understanding how this disease progresses and for finding an effective treatment. We believe that mutations in BMPR-II cause disease by altering the functional capacity of endothelial cells, the cells that line the blood vessels.  Previous work has been limited by the difficulty associated with isolating endothelial cells from the lungs of both healthy individuals and patients with PAH.  However, recent discoveries have led to the development of techniques to isolate circulating stem cells from the blood and drive them towards a cell type that is similar to lung endothelial cells.  These techniques offer an alternative cell source from PAH patients that we will use to test the impact of BMPR-II mutations on blood vessel structure, integrity and repair. We will also use advanced genetic techniques to scan the many thousands of genes in the human genetic code and determine how cells isolated from patients with mutations in BMPR-II differ, on a molecular level, from those isolated from healthy individuals. We believe that this work will increase our understanding of PAH and help to identify and test new targets for advanced therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal and biochemical underpinnings of aversion-related processing: A translational approach in humans and rats
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; GABA; GLUTAMATE; HUMAN; MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY; MICRODIALYSIS; NEUROSCIENCE; PSYCHIATRY; RATS
Abstract-Résumé: A punishment is any aversive event that an animal or human will expend energy to minimize or avoid. Aversive/stressful events are well known triggers for the onset and relapse of many psychiatric disorders (e.g. depression, addiction); there is evidence that brain circuitry involved in the processing of aversive stimuli may be impaired in these individuals. For instance, people with major depressive disorder (MDD) - which has the fastest growing disability costs to Canadian employers and is experienced by nearly 8% of Canadians (www.mooddisorderscanada.ca) - may show alterations in key brain areas associated with the processing of aversion, such as the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex. The neurotransmitters glutamate and GABA are essential to the healthy functioning of these areas. Despite recent advances, it is not yet known how these brain areas and their related neurotransmitters contribute to healthy and abnormal aversive/emotional processing. This project will combine state-of-the art brain imaging and animal-based techniques to investigate and directly compare the levels of glutamate and GABA in the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex during the presentation of aversive stimuli in humans and animals. Simultaneous investigation in humans and animals (a translational approach) will facilitate the mapping of this basic circuitry and will help to elucidate the basic processing in healthy subjects which can subsequently be extended directly to the study of subjects with neuropsychiatric disorders. This project will lead to the creation of new knowledge related to emotion-related brain functioning and may lead to the development of new drugs and therapies for psychiatric disorders such as MDD. In addition, data which results in a clearer understanding of the biologically rooted nature of psychiatric disorders may ultimately help reduce the stigma associated with mental illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Validation of separate pain biomarkers using combined fMRI and TMS
Keywords-MotsClés: EMOTIONS; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (FMRI); PAIN; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION (TMS)
Abstract-Résumé: Pain is a fundamentally subjective experience. As a result, subjective pain ratings have proven to be the most reliable indexes of pain. Nevertheless, pain ratings are still subjected to the same biases as other self-reported measures. The proposed experiment is part of a larger project aiming at defining brain-based biomarkers for pain that can augment self-reported pain as outcome measures. Two networks of brain regions seem to be particularly relevant for the generation of pain ratings: 1) a pain-processing network (PPN) involved in the primary perception of painful stimuli and 2) an emotional appraisal network, involved in the evaluation of emotional stimuli, including pain. The objective of the proposed project is to test the respective contribution of the PPN and EAN to the generation of pain ratings by selectively disrupting these two networks with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and measuring the resulting effects on brain activation with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). If TMS is proven effective in reducing pain, the results of this study could also support the use of TMS for pain treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive networks in behavioural flexibility
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; BRAIN LESION; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; FRONTAL LOBE; FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY ANALYSIS; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (FMRI); PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION (TMS); WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: For people with disorders of the basal ganglia, which are brain regions that modify neural signals related to movement, activities such as walking and writing can be difficult to control. Parkinson's disease (PD) is the most common example of a basal ganglia (BG) disorder, and researchers now have sophisticated models to understand why movements, or 'motor functions', are impaired. However, the prefrontal cortex of frontal lobe, which is responsible for 'cognitive' functions such as decision making and planning, is also wired-in with the BG. Thus, many problems we associate with motor dysfunction in BG disorders may actually be problems with cognitive functions, affecting the decisions and planning mechanisms that must be in place prior to movement initiation. It is extremely important that we gain a better understanding of this prefrontal cortex-BG system, because medications utilized to treat motor dysfunction can adversely affect cognitive function in the prefrontal cortex.   My current laboratory at Queen's University is a world leader in studying motor function. In this laboratory, I have developed novel methods to examine how cognitive processes, such as planning and decision making, affect the motor system. We have studied the ability of healthy young adults and people with PD to switch suddenly from one planned behaviour to another, while activity in their BG and prefrontal cortex was scanned with an MRI machine. We did this to understand how the cognitive function of planning can impact motor behaviour. In the next laboratory, at UC Berkeley, I will learn the most advanced methods of using MRI to examine activity in prefrontal-BG networks, and will be combining these methods Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation of the prefrontal cortex, which is a non-invasive way to modify neural activity in humans. The goal is to change neural activity in these networks, to observe how cognitive control signals are transmitted from the prefrontal cortex through the BG.

TitreApplicationTitle: Thyroid Hormone and Ovarian Follicle Growth  and Steroidogenesis.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CULTURES; FOLLICLE CULTURES; GONADOTRIPIN ACTION; HYPOTHYROIDISM; INFERTILITY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; OOCYTE-DERIVED FACTORS; OVARIAN FOLLICULAR GROWTH; THYROID HORMONE
Abstract-Résumé: Thyroid hormone [TH (T3 and T4)] is important for normal reproduction function and dysregulation of TH support is associated with reproductive disorders, including impaired follicular development. The hypo- and hyper-thyroidism are associated with dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis and suppressed ovarian follicular growth and function. The destiny of the ovarian follicle (growth/ovulation and atresia) is dependent on a delicate balance in the expression and actions of factors promoting follicular cell proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis. While follicle development is markedly hampered in hypothyroidism, this ovarian condition can be markedly improved by TH, especially in the presence of FSH. FSH and T3 interact in promoting preantral follicular growth and this regulation is mediated through GDF-9-dependent FSH receptor mRNA expression. However, the nature of this TH--FSH--GDF-9 interaction is poorly understood. Also, although TH nuclear receptors are expressed in the follicle and mediates the growth promoting action of TH, mechanism of action of TH in regulating follicle development is not known.
