Keywords-MotsClés: CTLA-4; GLOBAL HEALTH; HUMAN IMMUNOLOGY; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; MYCOBACTERIA; PD-1; T CELL EXHAUSTION; TIM-3; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis is one of the most deadly infectious diseases in the world, with an estimated 9.27 million new cases in 2007. Also,many strains are now resistant to current drug regimens. Therefore, designing new immune based strategies to fight this infection are needed. We know that only about 10% of people infected with tuberculosis actually go on to develop a potentally fatal disease. This proposal plans to team up the expertise from two researchers, Xiaoxing Cheng at the TB institute in Beijing, China, and Mario Ostrowski at the University of Toronto. They both bring diverse areas of expertise in human immunology and infectious diseases. We will study immune cells from people that get TB disease and compare them to those that are infected but donot have disease (latent TB).It is hoped that this combined project will give us new insights as to why TB gets reactivated and causes disease, by studying defects in an immune cell called the T cell. Our findings should help us new vaccines and therapies to this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the role of NF-kB in Neuroblastoma Cancer Stem Cells survival and self-renewal
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER STEM CELLS; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL SIGNALLING; IMMUNOBLOTTING; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; NEUROBLASTOMA; NUCLEAR FACTOR KAPPA B; RNA INTERFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Neuroblastoma (NB) is one of the most common childhood cancers.  Despite intensive treatment, survival rates of children with an aggressive form of the disease are below 30%.  Therefore, further understanding of the events that contribute to disease progression is required, in order to design new and more effective therapies.  Our lab has previously isolated unique cells from NB tumors and bone marrow metastases, which we believe are responsible for the disease progression.  These cells are called "cancer stem cells" since injection of only 1-10 cells recreates a human tumor in an immuno-deficient mouse.  We are specifically interested to explore which key signals contribute to survival and growth of these cells.  In this proposal I will access the importance of one such potential factor, called NF-kB, on the growth and survival of NB cancer stem cells.  NF-kB refers to a group of proteins that play a crucial role in various cellular events, such as inflammation, survival and growth.  NF-kB activity is often found to be deregulated in different cancers, which usually contributes to abnormal cellular growth and escape from death.  According to my preliminary results, NB cancer stem cells are sensitive to treatment with several drugs that block NF-kB activity, which gives me a reason to believe that it is indeed an important survival factor.  Therefore, in the current proposal I will first examine whether NB cancer stem cells exhibit enhanced NF-kB activity.  I will then block specific NF-kB molecules in a culture dish and see whether this inhibition interferes with vital cellular functions.  Finally, I will also evaluate whether tumor growth in a mouse can be suppressed following treatment with drugs, which inhibit NF-kB activity.  I believe that findings from this project will provide valuable information not just for better understanding of neuroblastoma, but also for implementing potential novel treatments into the clinic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gestational Diabetes: Reprogramming the Genome, a Potential Risk Factor for Adult Disease?
Keywords-MotsClés: BI-SULFITE PYROSEQUENCING; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; GESTATIONAL DIABETES; NEONATAL OUTCOME; OBESITY; PROGRAMMING; TYPE II DIABETES; WHOLE GENOME ARRAYS
Abstract-Résumé: Gestational diabetes frequently occurs during pregnancy.  Numerous epidemiological human studies and animal studies have shown that an altered intrauterine environment, as is the case with gestational diabetes, impacts development leading to the onset of disease later in life.  Specifically, there is an increased risk of developing obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.  Given the prevalence of gestational diabetes and the emerging pandemic of obesity and type 2 diabetes, it is imperative that we determine the underlying mechanism(s) involved.  Strong evidence in literature now suggests that epigenetic modification of genes underlies disease.  More recently, early life exposure has been shown to modify the epigenome of offspring, impacting adult health.  I wish to undertake new studies aimed at elucidating the mechanisms involved in adverse neonatal outcome and late onset adult disease that result from an altered intrauterine environment.  Further, I plan to identify at risk human populations.  I now hypothesize that an altered metabolic intrauterine environment permanently changes fetal gene expression leading to adverse neonate outcome and disease in adulthood. Utilizing a combination of state-of-the-art molecular techniques and bioinformatics on mouse tissues (placenta, heart, pancreas and liver) and T-cells, in addition to biological data (i.e. glucose tolerance test) I plan to test my hypothesis. The results from this study will provide a better understanding of how an adverse intrauterine environment can lead to early life pathologies and late onset metabolic disease. Further, establishing correlations between specific epigenetic changes observed and outcome, will permit us to identify vulnerable human populations and subject them to preventative interventions.  This intervention will hopefully reduce the rate of metabolic disease development and may also potentially minimize the risk of transmission of metabolic disease to future generations.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; AUTISM; GERONTOLOGY; HEALTH MEASUREMENT; LONGITUDINAL STUDIES; SCREENING TOOL DEVELOPMENT; VALIDATION STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Autism is a lifelong disability characterized by an onset before age 3, involving deficits in social relationships, communication, and a repetitive pattern of activities.  Current prevalence rates in Canada suggest that about one in 200 people have an Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), or approximately 150,000 Canadians.  However, the prevalence of ASDs in adulthood is unknown.  As children were only diagnosed with autism in the 1940's, this group, which is in their 60's today, is the first group ever to age with an autism diagnosis.  Therefore, this is a new group of older adults that we know very little about.  Older adults with autism have unique characteristics and needs compared to those without autism.  It is therefore important to understand these issues in order to provide appropriate care, services and supports.  As the diagnosis and management of autism has been based on childhood assessments and therapies, there is a need for a measure that can be used to identify older adults with autism. The goal of this study is therefore to address this gap by developing and evaluating an appropriate screening measure to identify older adults with an Autism Spectrum Disorder.

Abstract-Résumé: Virus-caused heart muscle disease is an important cause of death in China and North America. A pathogen called Coxsackie B3 virus (CVB3) is the commonnest virus associated with the occurrence of heart muscle disease. So far, it is unknown how CVB3 causes heart muscle disease and there is no treatment for this disease.The only definite treatment currently available for heart muscle disease is heart transplantation. Heart muscle disease has been a huge burden in North American since it accounts for about 50% of all patients requiring heart transplantation. The present project is to study whether and how a protein called calpain plays a role in CVB3-caused heart muscle disease. The results from this study will help to better understand the disease and to find new treatment for this life-threaten disease.

Abstract-Résumé: Glucose, in the heart in diabetes, may cause tissue damage by a specific mechanism named oxidative stress. In our body there are naturally occurring molecules named metallothionein, which may prevent such tissue damage. Metal molecules such as zinc and other molecules normally present in the body such as fibroblast growth factor may stimulate such actions of metallothionein. However, use of these molecules may have other harmful effects. In the laboratory, Chinese researcher Dr Li has been able to engineer these molecules so that they don't have any such bad effects. In the proposed research, in models of type1 and type2 diabetes, routinely used in the laboratory of Dr. Chakrabarti in Canada, we will examine whether such molecules can be effectively used to prevent diabetic heart disease. We will also simultaneously examine the mechanisms leading to diabetic heart disease. This project, we believe, will be helpful in the identification of potential novel therapeutic avenues for future treatment of diabetic heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antidepressant-Like Effect of Deep Brain Stimulation: Neurobiological and Neurogenic Mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL BEHAVIOUR; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; DEPRESSION; HIPPOCAMPUS; LIMBIC CEREBELLUM; NEUROGENESIS; NEUROTROPHIC FACTORS; PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a debilitating psychiatric illness affecting about 10% of the population in any given one-year period. Symptoms include low mood, lack of motivation and suicidal thoughts. It is projected to be a leading cause of disability by 2010. A staggering health care cost is allotted to manage depression. Although, several types of antidepressant drugs are available, these possess many limitations in efficacy. For example, these drugs curb symptoms only after several weeks of continuously taking them. A third of patients do not respond at all to these drugs and many more treated patients experience relapse. Furthermore, our understanding about depression is not complete. It is a complex disorder likely affecting many aspects of the brain, including chemical deficiency and cell death. There is a pressing need to explore alternative treatments. A potential novel treatment approach is called deep brain stimulation (DBS). This technology involves implanting an electrode that delivers electrical current into brain regions adversely affected in depression. The prefrontal cortex and the medial cerebellum, brain structures involved in cognitive, psychomotor and emotion-related functions, have been stimulated using DBS in depressed patients, as well as, in animals showing depression-like behaviours. These attempts to assess DBS for depression have proven to be promising, with patients completely improving symptoms. However, the mechanisms and principles by which DBS conveys its effectiveness remain poorly understood. We shall therefore examine DBS, using animal subjects, on its ability to modify protein interactions commonly affected by antidepressants, and to enhance cell birth in the hippocampus, a structure known to be modified by antidepressant drugs. It is necessary to exhaustively understand these mechanisms in order to gain more insights into the cause of depression, better characterize the effects of this disease in the brain, and optimize treatment efficacy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Age Related Effects of Nicotine on the Transcriptome, Epigenome, and Behaviour
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; BEHAVIOUR; EPIGENOME; GENE EXPRESSION; NICOTINE
Abstract-Résumé: Cigarette smoking is an addiction that is the most preventable cause of premature death in the world.  Approximately 90% of adult smokers initiate tobacco use before age 18, and this early behaviour could be critical to addiction.   There is evidence that early exposure to nicotine, the addictive component of tobacco, can affect immediate behaviours but more interestingly can have persistent effects on behaviour long after nicotine exposure.  Nicotine has also been shown to induce gene expression changes in an age-related manner.  One possible explanation for nicotine induced changes in behaviour and gene expression could be a result of epigenetic modifications.  Epigenetic modifications are changes that lead to structural remodeling of the genetic material without altering the DNA sequence and can result in gene expression alterations.   In fact, recent evidence indicates that nicotine exposure can induce epigenetic modifications which could explain immediate and persistent changes involved in the addiction process.  To study some aspects addiction, mouse models provide excellent research tools as they are available on defined genetic backgrounds and because environmental factors can be well-controlled.  In this system, the effect of nicotine exposure can be systematically assessed in an age dependent manner for gene expression changes, the role of epigenetic modifications, and behavioural modifications by controlling the environmental factor (nicotine) in genetically identical mice at varying adolescent ages and at adulthood. We propose nicotine exposure will have dramatic age-related behavioural, epigenetic and transcriptomic changes in regions of the brain involved in reward.  Identifying these changes will provide unique insight into the effects of age-related nicotine exposure on gene expression, the underlying mechanisms mediated by epigenetics, and behavioural alterations, thereby suggesting possibilities about how we may intervene in the addiction process.

Abstract-Résumé: Respiratory infections present a serious health risk worldwide. Influenza virus infections are particularly problematic due to the capacity of the virus to rapidly mutate its coat proteins and evade antibody responses. This characteristic means that current vaccines, which primarily elicit antibody responses must be reformulated on a yearly basis. Viral infections typically yield a population of cells called memory T cells that are able to rapidly respond to a subsequent infection with a related virus. As opposed to antibodies, these cells are able to recognize  relatively conserved internal viral proteins. Therefore, developing vaccine strategies that elicit potent memory T cell response may provide broader immunity against several different strains and will not require yearly refomulation. The presence of memory T cells directly in the lung airways plays a critical role in the ability of the host to defend against subsequent respiratory infections. However, it is not understood how these cells are recruited to the lung airways. The goal of the  project is to identify some of the steps that are required for memory T cells to gain access to, and be maintained, within the lung airways. As such, the information obtained as the result of the experiments proposed here may allow for the development of more effective vaccines that provide long-term protection against viruses like influenza.

TitreApplicationTitle: A mechanistic study of major depressive disorder: Role of oligodendrocytes
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; GENETICS; MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER; MRI; MYELIN; OLIGODENDROCYTES; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Major depressive disorder affects 10% of the world's population and is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide. Research suggests that the brain, genetics, and environmental factors contribute to depression. Although the cause of major depression is unknown, it is accepted that there is a network problem in the brain as opposed to a problem in a single neurotransmitter or brain region. Research suggests that white matter damage in the brain may be a critical factor. White matter is composed of cells in the brain that have a protective coating around them called myelin. Myelin insulates the brain cells much like the coating on a wire and allows cells to send electrical messages to each other rapidly and efficiently, forming the basis of movement, thought, and behaviour. Abnormalities in myelin results in communication disruptions and deficits follow. Our research team has designed a project that will span human clinical studies, animal models of depression, and cell biology to examine the role myelin in depression and the effect of antidepressant treatment on myelin. The human studies will examine if there are specific genes associated with depression. MRI's will be used to detect if myelin is damaged in patients with depression, if myelin abnormalities are related to gene alterations, and if antidepressants have an effect on myelin. The animal model of depression studies will tell us how myelin causes depression symptoms and how antidepressants can prevent myelin damage using cell biology methods. This project will greatly enhance our understanding of what causes major depression. It will tell us how myelin causes depression, and what can be done to interrupt or reduce these abnormalities and improve the symptoms of depression. This could lead to changes in the way antidepressants are used and guide the development of new drugs that target myelin more directly, all of which would lead to improvements in the lives of people suffering from depression.

Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; FORWARD GENETIC SCREEN; GUIDEPOST NEURON; SYNAPTOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Our nervous system is comprised of numerous neurons that communicate with each other in a complex network of neural circuits. The establishment of these neural circuits is a tightly regulated, multi-step developmental process. For example, following their birth, neurons develop membrane extensions with distinct functions, so that they can both receive (via dendrites), and transmit (via axons) signals in the network. A challenge for a neuron to integrate into the network is to find its correct partners, which often requires the neuron to migrate and extend its axons over a long distance, in order to receive and transmit information. Incorrect migration of the axon, or mis-selection of its targets will result in a faulty nervous system, with detrimental consequences in human physical and mental development.  In this proposal, we investigate how axons are guided towards, and establish connections with their target cells. Specifically, we will use the simple nervous system of a nematode, called C. elegans to identify essential genes that are required during this process. C. elegans is a well-established model to examine this process as it shares not only many genes, but also the fundamental structural units of the nervous system with higher organisms including humans. The functional conservation of the identified genes in this study will further allow us to explore the potential involvement of their human counterparts in development and mental disorders. In addition, they provide candidate therapeutic targets to treat these disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms underlying processing of social rejection and vulnerability to depression: investigating neural correlates of psychological, immunological and hormonal responses to social rejection paradigm in a population vulnerable to depression.
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTISOL; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (FMRI); GLUTAMATE RECEPTORS; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY (PET); PSYCHOLOGICAL STRESS; UNIPOLAR DEPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a severe, debilitating and in many cases, chronic illness, which is often preceded by extreme or prolonged psychological stress. Individuals afflicted by depression show impairment in regulating their emotions and thoughts. Not surprisingly, this impairment is reflected in maladaptive brain activity patterns within key brain areas responsible for the regulation of emotions and thoughts. Yet, neurobiological mechanisms underlying these brain activity patterns still remain largely unknown. Recent studies suggest a contribution of glutamate and one of its specific receptor types, mGluR5, in these processes. Glutamate is the most common messenger in the brain, generally carrying excitatory messages. The mGluR5 have been suggested to play a role in mediating one's response to stress. Furthermore, substances that interfere with function of the mGluR5 have antidepressant-like effects, at least in animal models. However, no study to date has investigated the contribution of the mGluR5 to the changes in brain activity assessed via functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) during rest and in response to psychological stress. Therefore, the goal of the present study is to apply two different neuroimaging technologies (Positron Emission Tomography and fMRI) in order to investigate whether there are differences in levels of the mGluR5 between the groups of healthy, at-risk and depressed subjects, as well as to examine how the levels of mGluR5 may be linked to the brain activity both at rest and in response to a psychological stress task, within and across each study group. Investigating the contribution of glutamate receptors to maladaptive changes in brain activity can help further our understanding of the neurobiology underlying this complex illness and therefore advance the development of more specific prevention and treatment approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of Ser/Thr kinase regulation of peptidoglycan biosynthesis in M. tuberculosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CLONING; ENZYMOLOGY; FLIPPASE COMPLEX; PEPTIDOGLYCAN BIOSYNTHESIS REGULATION; PROTEIN COMPLEX; PROTEIN COMPLEX ASSOCIATION IN VITRO AND IN VIVO; PROTEIN COMPLEX CRYSTALLIZATION; PROTEIN KINASE; TUBERCULOSIS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Protein phosphorylation is a ubiquitous regulatory mechanism that plays essential roles in wide range of cellular processes. Intracellular protein phosphorylation by Ser/Thr protein kinases (STPKs) regulates cellular pathways in all aspects of metabolism, cell growth and cell division.  The human pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis, is a major health problem worldwide responsible for the deaths of over two million people every year. The rapid recent emergence of multi-drug resistant strains of Mtb and the lack of new anti-tubercular drugs, led the WHO (World Health Organization) to declare Mtb a global emergency. Mtb encodes phospho-signaling components, including receptor STPKs, an antagonistic phosphatase and kinase regulatory proteins, that mediate bacterial growth and host-pathogen interactions. Although these signaling components can be recognized by sequence analysis, the functional implications and mechanisms by which they integrate into signaling networks are largely unknown.  We propose to determine for the first time how a master kinase of Mtb, called PknB, regulates biosynthesis of the bacterial cell wall.  The cell wall plays critical roles during the infection of bacterial pathogens, but little is known about the regulation of this process. We will use biochemical, structural and cell biological approaches to identify the partners of the PknB kinase, as well as a "flippase" protein that delivers the building blocks of the cell wall to the outside of the cell where they are used.  We will identify, build and characterize molecular complexes of the flippase regulatory domain that reveal how PknB phosphorylation controls its function. The information obtained from this analysis of the STPK signaling network that regulates cell-wall biosynthesis provides novel targets of antibiotic intervention for treating serious bacterial infections such as tuberculosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of Resting-State and Sleep Brain Activities in Consolidation of Sequential Behaviors in Health and Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; CONSOLIDATION; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; LEARNING; MEMORY; MOTOR; NEUROIMAGING; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SLEEP
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a devastating syndrome affecting approximately 1% of the population worldwide. This illness is known by many to be defined by dramatic positive (psychosis, hallucinations and delusions) and negative (lack of drive and motivation) symptoms. Although overlooked for a long time, cognitive deficits are also a cardinal feature of schizophrenia and they contribute substantially to disability too. In fact, cognitive deficits that are already seen prior to the onset of illness and in unaffected family members are better predictors of social function and functional outcome than the symptoms that define this illness. Among other cognitive impairments, people suffering from schizophrenia fail to consolidate and retain novel sequential motor behaviors. This ability is essential for a vast array of human activities, including speech, writing, music playing, sport practice or tool-use. The present research project thus seeks to identify abnormal brain activity in schizophrenia that may account for deficits in motor memory consolidation, the offline process by which an initially fragile memory trace becomes more robust. In particular, this research will aim at dissociating how deficient brain mechanisms occurring respectively during wakefulness and sleep are at play in schizophrenia, as compared to health. To this end, we will use state-of-the-art brain imaging techniques (functional magnetic resonance imaging, fMRI and electroencephalography, EEG) to map neural activity during practice on a novel sequence of finger movements both at training and retrieval as well as during posttraining rest, in the framework of a sleep deprivation paradigm. It is hoped that findings emerging from this research program will help identifying essential mechanisms in normal memory consolidation and suggest new avenues for translational studies of novel and practical interventions that could ameliorate disabling cognitive deficits in schizophrenia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the Molecular Basis for improved Metabolism following low-protein feeding
Keywords-MotsClés: BILE ACIDS; GLUCOSE TOLERANCE; INSULIN SECRETION; ISLET; METABOLISM; PANCREAS; TGR5
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes is a disease characterized by elevated blood glucose and is commonly associated with obesity, reduced physical activity and aging. As the prevalence of type 2 diabetes is increasing in epidemic proportions, so has the need for more effective treatments and a better understanding of the metabolic and genetic factors behind this disease. The gall bladder is a storage site for bile acids, which are secreted into the intestine when we eat, and play an important part in breaking down ingested fat. Interestingly, it was found that bile acids can also travel throughout the body and tell muscle and fat cells to burn more energy. When rodents on a high-fat diet are supplemented with bile acids, they lose weight, improve their diabetes and have increased function of the cells in the pancreas that make insulin (the beta-cells). This last point is important, as the beta-cells of the body are pivotal in maintaining normal blood sugar and their function is impaired in people with diabetes. However, an important matter that remains to be understood is whether bile acids have beneficial actions directly on the pancreatic beta-cells. In this application, we are proposing to study the effects of bile acids on the function and welfare of beta-cells using 2 approaches: 1) by directly treating beta-cells in grown in culture dishes with bile acids and 2) testing if the anti-diabetic effect of bile acids is altered in mice whose beta-cells lack a critical bile acid receptor.

TitreApplicationTitle: Quantitative assessment of how Salmonella bacteria control the processes in our cells
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PEPTIDE SYNTHESIS; QUANTITATIVE PROTEOMICS; SALMONELLA INFECTION; STABLE ISOTOPE LABELING
Abstract-Résumé: A large proportion of human disease results from bacterial pathogens that invade and infect host cells. Diseases like malaria and tuberculosis result from such intracellular infection and cause widespread illness and premature death worldwide. A versatile intracellular pathogen, Salmonella enterica, is capable of infecting diverse hosts and causing different diseases. In humans, S. enterica strains can cause typhoid or gastroenteritis, both responsible for much morbidity and mortality throughout the world. A central aspect for pathogenesis of S. enterica and other bacterial pathogens is their ability to hijack host cell processes for their own benefit. Upon encountering a human cell, Salmonella delivers a choreographed series of virulence factors (also known as 'effector' proteins) into the cells using needle-like structures. These effector proteins are key players that hijack natural host cell processes and ensure survival, invasion and replication of these types of bacteria. To date we only know bits and pieces of the impact of these effector proteins and their role in Salmonella invasion on host cells. I am proposing here to test the effects of Salmonella on a variety of host processes. The central analytical method that I will use to investigate this is mass spectrometry. This powerful technique allows us to monitor all or most of the early processes downstream of invasion. Thereby I hope to tease apart the effects of these closely-related effectors, and to look at the impact of all the effectors on human proteins that we know are targeted by Salmonella. So the studies proposed here will allow us to make a quantum leap forward in our understanding of how Salmonella controls its host. In particular, a detailed map of key players and their actions during Salmonella invasion will be constructed. Ultimately, therapeutic strategies for treating salmonellosis can be based on key players that will be identified and characterized in these studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) Agonists As A Potential Therapy for Childhood Acute Lymphatic Leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LYMPHATIC LEUKEMIA; BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION; CANCER IMMUNOLOGY; CELL DEATH (LEUKEMIC BLASTS); CHEMOIMMUNOTHERAPY; CHILDHOOD; IMMUNOGENICITY; NOVEL THERAPEUTIC AGENTS; SIGNALLING; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTOR AGONISTS
Abstract-Résumé: The most common form of childhood blood cancer is acute lymphatic leukemia (ALL). ALL is characterized by an uncontrollable growth of immature white blood cells. Approximately 80% of ALL cases can be successfully treated with chemotherapy.  However, if the disease returns, which occurs in 15-20% of cases, these children often cannot be saved, even if a blood and marrow transplantation (BMT) is performed. For these children, new treatment options are urgently needed in order to enable them to survive this disease. In fact, recurring ALL is the sixth most common cancer diagnosis in childhood highlighting the importance of finding a cure for this disease.   In healthy children the immune system is capable of detecting and killing defective cells. When this ability is lost, for yet not fully known reasons, leukemia can develop. One reason why ALL returns in these children is that ALL cells become resistant to chemotherapy. Therefore, alternative treatment options, possibly in combination with chemotherapy, are needed. When a child receives a BMT from a healthy individual, the immune system's ability to recognize defective cells, such as ALL cells, can be restored and the child healed. In a similar way, new drugs that affect the immune system may be a promising way of finding and ultimately destroying ALL cells.   A new drug that is directed towards the toll-like receptor - a marker that is found on the surface of many blood cells of the immune system - is such an exciting innovative approach to developing a new immune therapy. Recent research indicates that the immune system can be triggered to recognize ALL cells by stimulating the toll-like receptors on various immune cells.  However, further research is urgently needed to make this promising lab-based knowledge applicable for clinical treatment. Ultimately, this work will lead to new treatment options for curing recurring ALL.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of neighbourhood environment on risk for HIV/STIs and barriers to accessing prevention, treatment and care among women involved in sex industry work
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; COMMERCIAL SEX WORK; COMPLEX ADAPTIVE SYSTEMS; GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEMS; HEALTH SERVICES ACCESS; HIV/AIDS; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOCIAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; SUBSTANCE USE
Abstract-Résumé: Women in sex industry work in urban Canadian settings continue to experience high rates of HIV and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), violence and poor access to health services. Despite increasing evidence of the limitations of individual-level focused interventions, there remain major research gaps in our understanding of the social and structural determinants of HIV/STI risk to inform evidence-based policies and programs. Therefore, in the proposed fellowship project I aim to investigate the intersecting relationships between neighbourhood and sex work environment at the macro level and the distribution of individual sexual HIV/STI risk patterns and access to health services among a sample of sex industry workers in an urban Canadian setting (Metropolitan Vancouver). This project is part of a larger study, a five-year longitudinal cohort of women in sex industry work in Metropolitan Vancouver that began enrolment in Jan-10, in partnership with local sex work and service agencies. Women will be followed up every six months over five years through interviews. I will use empirical data gathered in the larger project, and combine advanced social epidemiology methods and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) mapping technology, developing a GIS database. I will also explore the use of novel complex adaptive systems approaches and develop a unique model that incorporates factors at multiple levels of influence, including social, structural and environmental, in understanding how neighbourhood environment impacts sexual risk patterns and health services access. The results from the research conducted during this fellowship will be exceedingly important in informing the ongoing development of health policy and structural interventions that improve the health of women involved in sex industry work in Canadian settings and will support ongoing knowledge translation of evidence into policy and practice through our extensive community partnerships.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of Rare Pathogenic Copy Number Variants in Neurocognitive Disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: GENOMICS; NEUROCOGNITIVE DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Autism, developmental delay and schizophrenia (together referred to as neurocognitive disorders) are thought to be the result of individually rare, but collectively common, alterations of specific genes, yet traditional technologies have identified a likely genetic cause for only15-17% of cases.  In less than 5% of cases, however, has the association been proven. Initial studies using modern genome screening technologies have begun to identify rare submicroscopic (not identifiable by conventional cytogenetic screening) genomic lesions, but this is complicated by the discovery of significant genetic variations between normal, healthy individuals. Thus, a large number of cases and controls (thousands) will be essential to distinguish disease-causing events from rare, benign variants.  To this end I aim to identify genes and copy number variations that cause neurocognitive disorders.  This will be accomplished through the application of modern, high resolution whole-genome screening tools to the largest panel of children with developmental disorders studied to date (11,000 controls and 25,000 cases). By utilizing such large, detailed sample sets, we will be able to avoid the challenges that plague conventional studies of rare variants by detecting genomic lesions that are specific to disease in as few as 0.05% of cases. These lesions will be validated in an independent set of 4,525 cases and 2,500 controls by targeted profiling with a clinically transferable method (Illumina BeadXpress). Additionally, we will apply targeted DNA sequencing of the genes we identify in 1,500 cases to identify novel mutations in additional cases.  Based on preliminary studies, we anticipate that this project will result in the identification of genetic causes for an additional 5-10% of neurocognitive cases.  This will greatly increase our knowledge of intellectual disabilities and the genes affected as well as provide tools for clinical screening and diagnosis..

TitreApplicationTitle: Gut Hormones and the Resolution of Diabetes after Bariatric Surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: BARIATRIC SURGERY; BODY WEIGHT; DIABETES; GHRELIN; GLP-1; GOAT; INSULIN CLAMP; OBESITY; ROUX-EN-Y GASTRIC BYPASS; VERTICAL SLEEVE GASTRECTOMY
Abstract-Résumé: The 2004 Canadian Consumer Health Survey estimated that 5.5 million Canadians aged 18 or older are obese and another 8.6 million overweight. The health consequences of obesity are well known, especially with respect to the risk of type II diabetes. Currently over 3 million Canadians have diabetes and that number is expected to reach 3.7 million by the year 2020, with an estimated cost to the Canadian health care system of nearly 17 billion annually. Bariatric surgery is currently the only effective treatment for morbid obesity, and it prolongs life as well as ameliorating obesity and diabetes. Operated patients can expect to lose 75% or more of their excess fat within 6 months after surgery, and the weight loss is likely to be maintained for the rest of the patient's life. The effect of bariatric surgery on diabetes is rapid, with some patients leaving the hospital without the need for further diabetes medication. The rapidity of this effect has led to the hypothesis that bariatric surgery reduces diabetes independent of weight loss, but the underlying mechanism has not been identified. The frequency of bariatric surgeries has increased in Canada every year over the past decade, and the current average wait time is 5 years. Understanding the mechanism(s) that produce the benefits of bariatric surgery is critical for three reasons. First, it is our responsibility to understand how we are affecting these patients. Second, mechanistic studies are critical for developing less invasive and more cost-effective procedures. Finally, mechanistic studies are critical for identifying those patients most likely to benefit from this treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Influence du sommeil diurne (sieste) sur les corrélats cérébraux de la consolidation des mémoires de séquences motrices chez les sujets jeunes et âgés, explorée à l'aide de l'imagerie par résonance magnétique fonctionnelle (IRMf)
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; CONSOLIDATION; IMAGERIE PAR RESONANCE MAGNETIQUE FONCTIONNELLE (IRMF); MEMOIRE; NEUROSCIENCES; POLYSOMNOGRAPHIE; SOMMEIL; SUJETS JEUNES ET AGES; SEQUENCES MOTRICES; VIEILLISSEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Il est maintenant clairement admis que les sommeils nocturne et diurne jouent un role important dans les mecanismes de consolidation des memoires de sequences motrices chez l'homme. Chez les sujets jeunes, les phenomenes de consolidation observes apres une nuit de sommeil s'accompagnent d'une restructuration des reseaux cerebraux (dans le striatum et l'hippocampe par exemple) utilises pour realiser la tache afin de permettre l'optimisation du comportement moteur. Chez les sujets ages, de tels gains de performance ne sont pas observes. Ceci pourrait etre du a l'alteration de l'architecture du sommeil survenant avec l'age et a l'alteration de ces circuits neuronaux. Dans ce projet de recherche de 3 ans, nous tentons de determiner l'influence du sommeil diurne (sieste), encore inexplore, sur les correlats cerebraux de la consolidation des memoires de sequences motrices chez les sujets jeunes et ages, par la technique d'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle (IRMf). Nous planifions par la suite d'explorer plus finement les determinants comportementaux et cerebraux, associes a l'apprentissage sequentiel moteur, dont la consolidation sera specifiquement dependante du sommeil chez les sujets jeunes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Syntactic changes in Primary Progressive Aphasia
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION MODEL; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; COGNITIVE NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; INHIBITION; LANGUAGE IMPAIRMENT; SYNTACTIC IMPAIRMENT; WERNICKE'S APHASIA; WORD FINDING IMPAIRMENT
Abstract-Résumé: To perform tasks successfully in daily life, we all need to be able to ignore information that is not important to the task we are trying to accomplish. For example, when talking with a friend, we must be able to ignore what is said by the people next to us. It has been proposed that we use this ability to ignore distracting information in three important ways: 1) ignoring new information that is not important, 2) deleting information in our minds that is no longer important, and 3) not responding when it is inappropriate. It is believed that our ability to ignore information in these ways is responsible for individual differences on such things as memory tasks, and also for the reduced abilities of healthy older adults compared to younger adults, on these tasks. Recent studies have suggested that an impaired ability to ignore distracting information could also be responsible for the language difficulties in people with Wernicke's aphasia. This is a devastating language disorder that can occur after a stroke, leaving a person with difficulty understanding what people are saying and difficulty speaking, even at the word level. To date, there are only a few studies providing evidence for effective treatments for people with Wernicke's aphasia. In recent investigations, scientists have found that people with this disorder have trouble ignoring new information that is not important. They have also found that this difficulty ignoring new information is linked to the person's language difficulties. The goal of the current study is to investigate in more depth the difficulties that people with Wernicke's aphasia have ignoring distracting information, and how this may relate to their language difficulties. By gathering information about the causes of the language difficulties in Wernicke's aphasia, it is more likely that future treatments will be more successful. This will allow people with Wernicke's aphasia to lead a more successful and independent life.

Abstract-Résumé: Atherosclerosis (AS) and its vascular complications, atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases (ASCVD) account for a staggering burden of disease globally affecting both developed and developing societies. Abnormal blood cholesterol has long been recognized as an important risk factor for ASCVD. Despite the proven benefit of lowering of LDL cholesterol, or the so-called bad cholesterol by a class of pharmacological agents called statins, there remains a significant treatment gap. Recent studies on a class of plant-derived compound called Anthocyanin showed great promise in producing further benefit. A proof of principle clinical trial by Dr Ling's group in China suggested that Anthocyanin targets not only LDL cholesterol, it also significantly raises HDL-C in healthy subjects. In this China-Canada joint venture, Dr Ling and Dr Ng will intergrate their respective expertise to address the important questions through combined basic science studies and human clinical trials. The major research aims are to address (1) whether Anthocyanin treatment are also effective in raising blood level of HDL-C and in improving other biomarkers of ASCVD in at risk subjects selected on the basis of low HDL-C, (2) detailed mechanisms as to how Anthocyanin impacts on blood level as well as function of HDL. These findings will provide crucial information as to the potential of this class of naturally occurring plant compounds in the treatment of heart diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fast multispectral diffuse optical imager applied to pharmacokinetics of cancer.

Abstract-Résumé: Diffuse optical imaging is a new functional imaging modality with great promise in oncology. Optical mammography has emerged as a new imaging technique that is safe and can be used towards breast cancer screening. Recent clinical studies indicate that monitoring image contrast produced by optical blood pooling contrast agents may lead to enhanced diagnostic information. To be able to use this diagnostic information, new instruments need to be developed that can inform on the dynamical changes in optical images. However the optical technology to perform fast and spatially resolved pharmacokinetic measurements is lacking.  The goal of this project is to develop a unique micromirror-based multispectral optical imager for in vivo real time 3D optical imaging of optical contrast agents. The instrument will be validated on a small animal model of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Neuroimaging of White Matter Integrity in Cognitive Dysfunction: Linking Neuroscience Research with Clinical Evaluation
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; DEMENTIA; DIAGNOSIS; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; FUNCTIONAL BRAIN IMAGING; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NEUROLOGY; STROKE; WHITE MATTER
Abstract-Résumé: Normal function of the human brain relies on distributed neural network systems, where neural fibers (white matter) link specialized processing regions (gray matter). Using the basic analogy of lines connecting dots within a network, almost fifty percent of brain tissue is comprised of white matter "lines". This proposal focuses on role of these white matter connections in brain conditions with cognitive dysfunction. Disruptions in white matter have long been known to cause problems in mental functioning, yet current functional imaging approaches focus almost exclusively on gray matter. We have developed advanced imaging to examine function in white matter. The next step is to apply this discovery to improved diagnosis in neurological patients. The current Canada-China collaboration takes advantage of an existing two year relationship between our team at Dalhousie University and the corresponding team at Tianjin Medical University in China. Joint research is already underway and highly skilled personnel are being exchanged for advanced training opportunities. This application proposes to significantly expand on this progress by developing white matter functional imaging as a clinical diagnostic method. The Chinese team will focus on large scale clinical testing of neurological patients and integration of white matter function with existing structural imaging approaches. Importantly, this work will not focus on a given disease per se, but rather in cognitive processing affected by range of neurological conditions. These conditions will include not only common white matter diseases like multiple sclerosis, but will also expand the scope to diseases not commonly considered as white matter diseases (e.g., stroke and dementia). Findings of this research will allow better understanding fundamental mechanisms underlying functional neural connection/disconnection in cognitive dysfunction with an emphasis on significantly improving diagnostic imaging in neurology.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identify and characterize the genetic changes in cholesterol-regulator genes in late-onset Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ABETA PRODUCTION; APP PROCESSING; CHOLESTEROL METABOLISM; GENES; LATE-ONSET ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; RISK FACTORS; SECRETASE ACTIVITIES; SNP
Abstract-Résumé: AD is characterized by accumulation and deposition of pathogenic Abeta peptides in the brain.  Family AD results from inherited mutations in genes involving Abeta peptide production.  The majority of Alzheimer's patients are sporadic late-onset cases (LOAD).  The pathogenic mechanisms of LOAD are still elusive.  A number of epidemic and genetic studies including genome-wide association studies (GWAS) suggested that altered cholesterol metabolism is linked to LOAD pathogenesis.  Experimental studies have shown that increased levels of cellular cholesterol promotes the production and deposition of Abeta peptides in the brain. ApoE proteins (ApoE2, 3, and 4) are the main cholesterol transport proteins in the brain.  ApoE4 which is not efficient in cholesterol transport is a recognized risk factor of LOAD. Changes in genes (such as single nucleotide polymorphisms -SNP) involving cholesterol/lipid metabolism may predispose the carriers to the development of LOAD.  Our previous study has demonstrated that cholesterol retention occurs in LOAD brain with increased beta-and gamma secretase activities and increased ABeta production.  We have also identified nine nuclear receptors (transcription factors) involving cholesterol/lipid metabolism from LOAD brain.  The levels and activities of these nuclear receptors are altered in LOAD brain as compared to age-matched non-demented controls (ND). This collaborative study is aimed to identify the SNPs in these nuclear receptor genes in LOAD vs. ND humans and to characterize the effects of the identified genetic changes on the expression of the nuclear receptors, cholesterol/lipid metabolism, secretase activities and Abeta processing/production using in vitro cell model systems. This will validate whether genetic changes in these nuclear receptor genes that regulate cholesterol metabolism are responsible for altered cholesterol metabolism in the brain and are involved in LOAD pathogenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of AKF-PD-mediated protection of diabetic nephropathy in db/db mice
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL BIOLOGY/SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; DB/DB MICE; DIABETES; DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY; SIRNA
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 8.8% of Canadians and 5% of Chinese have diabetes, with one-third of them developing diabetic nephropathy. A large number of these patients will have their disease progress towards end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Currently, we cannot control the progression of diabetic nephropathy towards ESRD, nor can we effectively treat ESRD. Therefore, diabetic nephropathy is a major and serious complication of diabetes and there is an urgent need to develop drugs to treat or effectively control the disease. Professor Tao's research group in China has recently invented a very promising drug, called AKF-PD (also known as Fluorofenidone). In their research involving mice with diabetic nephropathy, AKF-PD has been shown to effectively control the progression of diabetic nephropathy. In the current research proposal, Dr. Tao's research group in China and Dr. Tang's laboratory in Canada will work together to investigate 1) whether AKF-PD can prevent diabetic nephropathy when the drug is given to diabetic mice before developing diabetic nephropathy, 2) whether AFK-PD can effectively control further progression of diabetic nephropathy towards ESRD at time when the disease is already at an advance stage, 3) how AKF-PD prevents or cures diabetic nephropathy. This information will be essential in our effort to prevent diabetic nephropathy and to control the disease even at advance stages. As more than 3 million Canadians suffers from diabetes and its complications, this research offers a promising hope to find a novel therapy to control diabetic nephropathy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and drug screen for modulators of aggressive behavior in genetic model systems
Keywords-MotsClés: AGGRESSION; BEHAVIORAL RESEARCH; DROSOPHILA; DRUG SCREEN; GENETIC MODEL; GENETIC SCREEN; NERVOUS SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Aggression is an important behavior evolutionarily conserved in animals, and is essential to the survival and evolution of animals. In humans, excess aggression is observed in patients with certain neurological diseases. In this application, the two groups (i.e. Dr. Yong Rao at McGill University Health Centre and Dr. Yi Rao at Beijing University) will perform a genome-wide genetic screen to identify new genes that are involved in the control of aggressive behavior. The two groups will also perform a large-scale drug screen to isolate new compounds that modulate aggressive behavior. Such research will not only provide novel and important insights into the molecular mechanism of aggression, and also provide invaluable information for the development of new therapeutic approaches to treat neurological and psychiatric diseases associated with excess aggression.

TitreApplicationTitle: A New Tool for the Comprehensive Analysis of Peptides and Proteins in Biological and Biomedical Research
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTRON CAPTURE DISSOCIATION (ECD); MASS SPECTROMETRY; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS; PROTEIN AND PEPTIDE STRUCTURAL CHARACTERIZATION; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins perform a multitude of functions within the body, many of which have a profound impact on the health of individuals. For this reason, the characterization of proteins is a central activity in biological and biomedical research. The comprehensive analysis of proteins requires sophisticated instrumentation, and mass spectrometers are currently the preferred tools for these analyses. Up until the last couple of years, the mass spectrometers utilized in protein analyses had only limited ability to determine certain important characteristics of the proteins, known as post-translational modifications (PTMs), but new technology has arisen which is now capable of providing the desired information. Unfortunately, instruments equipped with the new technology are expensive and thus not readily available to many researchers. The proposed research project has as its primary goal the development of a new cost-effective tool for determining PTMs of proteins, so that biological and biomedical researchers can obtain the information they require at a fraction of the cost of existing solutions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Integrative Genomic Strategies to Discern Cancer Progression Risk in Early Oral Dysplasia
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRAYCGH; BIOMARKER; HEAD AND NECK; LEUKOPLAKIA; PREMALIGNANT; PROGRESSION; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Oral cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed types of cancer worldwide. Unfortunately, only half of those diagnosed with this disease will be alive 5 years after the diagnosis. Given that survival statistics for oral cancer have remained static for 20 years, it is clear that new diagnostic and treatment tools are needed. Like many cancer types, oral tumors develop by progression of precancerous tissues through increasingly aggressive stages. It is the accumulation of genomic aberrations during this process that drives progression to invasive disease. By characterizing alterations at both the DNA and protein levels in various stages of oral cancer, we will identify new markers that are able to predict whether an early oral lesion will become an invasive cancer. We will then use cell models to study the importance of each of the candidate genes in cancer development. The main product of this work will be new molecular tools that can be used to facilitate early diagnosis and management of those lesions at risk of becoming cancer. In addition, the genes we implicate in cancer progression will represent the best candidates for novel targeted therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The therapeutic effect and safety of collagen binding vascular endothelial growth factor on myocardial infarction
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ANIMAL EXPERIMENT; GROWTH FACTOR IMMOBILIZATION; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; VASCULAR ENDOTHELIAL GROWTH FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Ischaemic Heart Disease is the most common cause of death in several countries around the world. Recent advances in the understanding of the mechanisms of neovascularization and the identification of potent angiogenic growth factors have led to the development of therapeutic angiogenesis for treatment of severe ischemic heart disease. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is an important active protein for the induction of angiogenesis. Clinical trials of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy have proven that high dose of VEGF has beneficial effects on ischemic heart disease; however, potential problems associated with the prolonged and excessive production of VEGF remain a major concern. Our tremendous amount of work has been focused on improving cytokine therapy efficiency and decreasing associated side effects by increasing the local cytokine concentration in the injury sites. Here we propose to increase the local VEGF concentration in the infarction zone for achieving better therapeutic effect and lower VEGF diffusion risk in the circulation. As the main components of cardiac extracellular matrix (ECM) are type I and type III collagen, and about 85% of total collagen is type I, we propose to modify VEGF with a collagen-binding domain with gene engineering methods to enhance VEGF binding ability to cardiac collagen. The fused protein is expected to share the abilities of both angiogenesis and collagen binding. As pig coronary vascular system is more similar to that of human, the therapeutic effect for ischemic heart disease could be detected in the myocardial infarction model of pigs. By detecting the heart function, regional blood flow, scar size, capillary vessel number, VEGF diffusion in circulation, the therapeutic efficiency and safety would be analyzed. This work would be beneficial for developing a novel efficient and safe VEGF protein drug for ischemic heart disease therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proteomics in Human Health and Disease: An Organelle Approach for Human and Rodent Liver Samples
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; ORGANELLES; PROTEOMICS; TANDEM MASS SPECTROMETRY; TEST SAMPLES
Abstract-Résumé: The human liver is key to our understanding of human physiology.  The liver is the major site of energy storage in the body via sugar stored as glycogen.  It is the organ positioned anatomically to receive directly the blood supply from the insulin and glucogen producing cells from islets of Langerhans of the pancreas which regulate the storage and breakdown of glycogen in the liver.  Liver is also the major site of drug detoxification in the human body and this same machinery regulates cholesterol formation and its elimination from the body.  One major cell type accounts for 90% of liver, the hepatocyte which secretes most proteins into the bloodstream. The other cell types are important in nutrient uptake and the delivery of the plasma proteins from the liver to the circulation.  In addition, important immune cells are found between the blood and the hepatocytes. Clearly, the make up of the protein complement of liver is important for understanding liver function in health and what goes wrong in liver diseases including cirrhosis, hepatitis and liver cancer.  The objective of this grant is to transform the data amassed by several hundred Chinese investigators in 11 labs and assign the data quantitatively to a new gene-based protein coding data base using tools developed in Montreal, as well as to assign proteins to intracellular structures (organelles) in liver cells in order to decipher the abundance location and function of all proteins made in human liver and reveal the diagnostic proteins of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Osteoinductive Biomaterials
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: This renewal seeks to build on successes of the past five years in the field of osteoinductive biomaterials.  This first phase has enabled the establishment of a functional laboratory with appropriate protocols in place.  The aim of the proposed chair is to develop synthetic bone graft substitutes that have the same biological properties as the current 'gold standard' that is bone autograft, namely pieces of the patient's own hip or rib etc.  A further goal is to achieve this without recourse to use highly expensive recombinant proteins since this will make the technology more widely and hopefully more safely available.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Virology and Pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Virus infection is responsible for a significant proportion of human and animal disease. Yet the majority of viral diseases still remain untreatable. Over the course of millions of years viruses have evolved with their hosts resulting in the development of effective strategies to exploit key cellular signaling pathways that affect virus replication. We will use a combination of molecular biology and proteomics to unravel the strategies that viruses use to ensure their survival. The study of how viruses exploit cellular signaling pathways will provide novel insights into virus immune countermeasures with the ultimate goal of developing therapeutic anti-viral strategies.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Structural Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Our ability to treat infectious diseases has been severely compromised, principally due to a dramatic rise in antibiotic resistance.  We aim to address this problem by studying how microbial pathogens evade the effects of antibiotics, and by exploring novel strategies to treat infectious diseases.  To accomplish this, we will examine in atomic detail microbial proteins that are involved in resistance or that can be exploited as drug targets, using structural biological techniques. Guided by our findings we will initiate and pursue the development of next-generation antimicrobial drugs, employing structure-based drug design methods.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Knowledge Transfer for Musculoskeletal Care
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: I will broaden my research focus from evidence-based medicine to the creation of evidence-based healthcare policy. I will develop innovative Knowledge Translation and Exchange programs, and I will facilitate multi-sectorial collaborations between a range of stakeholders to develop measures of quality assessment and studies of quality improvement for musculoskeletal care. The success of these initiatives will hinge on my training of qualified personnel who will develop specialized research expertise in these emerging areas. These initiatives will provide the evidence and impetus for health-system changes, and will ultimately lead to health system innovation, positioning Canada as a leader in this field.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Clinical Cyberpsychology / Chaire de Recherche du Canada en Cyberpsychologie Clinique
Keywords-MotsClés: Other research relating to social structures and relationships, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: This Chair advances our understanding and confidence in the mental health applicationsof cyberpsychology, especially virtual reality and telepsychotherapy. Six objectivesare set out, three relevant to virtual reality and three to telepsychotherapy: (a)developing VR interventions for complex anxiety disorders and document theirefficacy, (b) clarifying the therapeutic mechanisms behind VR therapy, (c)further contribute to the reduction of costs of therapeutic VR environments, (d)documenting the efficacy of telepsychotherapy with new disorders, (e)circumscribe the therapeutic mechanisms associated with favourable outcome, and (f)delineating the characteristics of patients who benefit from telepsychotherapy anddevelop selection guidelines.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Rehabilitation Engineering
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed program will be the first in the world to study facial temperature profiles and blood flow in the brain as alternative access pathways for children and youth who have severe disabilities, but are cognitively capable. The program will use state-of-the-art instrumentation and engineering analyses to tease out patterns of blood flow and temperature changes that occur when a child makes a mental selection or intends to communicate. This research will open up new doors for communication, interaction, recreation and education for over 90,000 Canadian children without speech and useful movements.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Neural Circuit Formation
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Chen is interested in the principles underlying how brains wire up complex circuits with extreme precision.  To uncover the different molecules and strategies cells use to form such highly organized neural circuits, Dr. Chen combines high-resolution imaging techniques with advanced molecular genetics in different model systems to look inside living animals while their neurons form synapses.  Dr. Chen uses invertebrate organisms to identify underlying genetic mechanisms, and vertebrates to investigate common molecular rules.  His research will provide insight into how the brains wiring diagram is encoded within a genome, and how these may go awry in common brain disorders.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Membrane Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: The goals of Dr. David Clarke's laboratory are to develop novel drug therapies forthe treatment of cystic fibrosis and to improve cancer chemotherapy by prevention of multidrug resistance. Patients develop cystic fibrosis because they produce a CFTRchloride channel that does not fold properly due to a genetic defect. Dr. Clarke's laboratory is developing an innovative drug-rescue approach to repair the folding defects in the mutant CFTRs so that they work properly. His team is also developing novel methods to turn off a drug pump called P-glycoprotein during chemotherapy because expression of this protein in cancer cells makes them resistant to anticancer drugs.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Endothelial Cell Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: In the last few decades, it has been recognized that the lining cells of blood vessels  the endothelial cells  play a major protective role in health and disease.  They not only participate in preventing blood from abnormal clotting, but they prevent our immune system from over-reacting to invading organisms, such as infections.  There are many diseases that are caused by abnormal functioning of endothelial proteins that are defective due to gene mutations. Our goal is to determine which endothelial proteins are important in protecting against blood clotting and immune diseases, and to identify the patients who have mutant forms of these proteins. We will then use several techniques to determine how these mutations cause disease. Hopefully, this will lead to more effective treatments.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Common Spinal Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Whether measured in terms of related medical visits, industrial injury claims, disability pensions or prevalence of symptoms among the general population, lower back ailments are among the most common and costly musculoskeletal problems facing Canada and other developed countries. Finding ways to prevent or reduce the severity of these prevalent and disabling disorders would significantly improve quality of life for those who would be affected and decrease society's associated financial burden. But in order to develop more effective prevention and treatment strategies and improved health care policies, we must advance knowledge of the conditions underlying common spinal disorders and their risk factors. This is the goal of my research program.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Brief Interventions for Problem Drinkers
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: An unfortunate reality for people who suffer from drinking problems is that most will never seek treatment. If people with drinking problems wont come to treatment, can we take treatment to them? Dr. Cunningham studies how people solve their drinking problems. Using this information, he takes treatments that have been shown to work in clinical settings and modifies them so that people with alcohol problems can use them without having to come to a clinic for treatment. Dr. Cunninghams research is diversifying the ways we help problem drinkers by providing effective new options for people to access care.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Genetic Modeling
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: With the completion of the human genome sequence, one great challenge for scientists is to determine the biological functions of the genes encoded by these sequences and to investigate the roles of these genes in the development of human diseases. Dr. Ding's program uses powerful and elegant genetic tools to modify the mouse genome in order to examine where genes are normally expressed, and how alterations in genes can affect their functions. Specific changes in mouse genes are introduced in order to understand how each affects normal development or to generate a disorder that mimics that of a human condition.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Prokaryotic Membrane Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Membrane transporters function to mediate the transfer of material or information from the inside or the outside of a cell.  The Sec complex, or translocon, is a prototypical example.  Studying this machine is essential to understand how bacteria secrete toxins and other weapons.  It is difficult to study the transporter in vitro however, since the machine stops working as soon as removed from the membrane.  We are now developing a new technology called Nanodisc, which is a water-soluble particle that mimics a small patch of the membrane.  The resulting nano-membrane resembles a sushi roll or hockey puck with the transporter embedded in the middle.  This is considered the best and most original way to investigate how membrane protein transporters truly work.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Physical Activity & Health Studies
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Our knowledge of the altered physical activity on the locomotor system is incomplete. The proposed research will examine the effects of chronically increased (exercise wheels) and decreased (restricted hindlimb weight-bearing) activity, in the rat, on physiological and gene expression properties of motor and sensory neurons involved in locomotion. The properties of motor neurons will be determined during locomotor activity (brainstem stimulation), while properties of sensory (dorsal root ganglion) neurons will be measured in isolated cells in vitro.  This knowledge is necessary for the use of exercise as rehabilitation for the compromised nervous system.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Traumatic Brain Injury -  Cognitive Neurorehabilitation Science
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Green's research focuses upon traumatic brain injury (TBI), a ubiquitous and debilitating disorder that can cause decades of disability due to its prevalence among young adults. TBI causes cognitive impairments (e.g., to memory, problem solving, self-awareness) and emotional dysfunction. Such impairments markedly impede functioning, whether at home, school or work, and people with moderate or severe TBI rarely recover fully. Dr. Green asks new questions, employing novel methods to better understand the basic brain and behavioural mechanisms of cognitive and emotional impairments as well as the processes that underlie their recovery (or lack thereof) in order to develop treatments that target the root causes of dysfunction.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Neonatal Mucosal Immunology
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Vaccination is one of the most effective tools for managing infectious diseases, but for many enteric viral and bacterial infections, no effective vaccines exist.  The development of protective vaccines and effective vaccine delivery  remain large challenges for these diseases.  This Canada Research Chair program focuses on diseases which enter the body through mucosal surfaces such as are found in the intestines; and on the possibility of developing  vaccines which protect  these same surfaces. If successful, this novel approach could open the way to prevent neonatal enteric infections which cause lifelong disease.  In conjunction with the mucosal vaccine "delivery" challenge there is also a need to create  immunotherapeutic agents which target persistent pathogens.  The Chair's program will encompass both these opportunities and will go forward in close conjunction with allied R&D at the University of Saskatchewan and industrial research laboratories. Benefits will accrue both in human health and the veterinary sector.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive Neuroscience
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Drug abuse and addiction
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Holroyd is interested in the neurobiological mechanisms that underlie cognitive control - how people regulate their attention, thoughts, and behaviors in accord with high-level goals and intentions. In pursuing this interest he has asked two specific questions: How do people detect and correct their errors and how do they learn from the consequences of their actions? To investigate these issues he adopts a variety of empirical and theoretical approaches including the event-related brain potential technique (i.e., brainwaves) and computational modeling. His research is advancing the study and treatment of addiction, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, schizophrenia, and many other neurocognitive disorders.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive Neuroimaging and Neurodevelopmental disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: Other research, Education, training, recurrent education and retraining
Abstract-Résumé: Social cognition refers to the set of mental skills necessary to understand how people interact and behave in groups. Dr. Itiers research uses behavioural and neuroimaging techniques to examine the neural basis of fundamental aspects of social cognition including the processing of face identity, emotions and gaze direction across the life span. Important insights into these functions are made by studying patients with brain lesions, and developmental disorders in which social interactions go awry (e.g. autism, Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders). This fundamental work will contribute to a better understanding of the social deficiencies seen in these pathologies and will ultimately lead to rehabilitation programs.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive Neuroscience
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research program examines the importance of knowledge and experience in speech comprehension in noisy environments. The proposed research is important both for a basic understanding of the cognitive neuroscience of speech comprehension, and for tackling the problem of impaired real-world speech comprehension in the coming decades. As people age and the fidelity of the input deteriorates, top-down cues to speech comprehension become increasingly important. A more complete understanding of the factors that can facilitate speech comprehension is instrumental to optimizing them and promoting their use, helping Canadians lead full and rich lives as they age.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Spinal Function
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Low back pain is an epidemic within our society. Unfortunately, alleviating this epidemic has proven to be difficult largely because the causes of back pain remain elusive; less than 1% of all cases have an identifiable cause. Without a specific target on which to focus treatment, spinal disorders remain highly prevalent and exceedingly expensive. These facts suggest that current strategies are not optimal; novel approaches will be necessary to create the transformative knowledge needed to reduce the substantial cost and morbidity burdens associated with common spinal disorders. The primary objective of this CRC is to delineate the mechanisms that initiate and sustain spinal disorders. To achieve this objective, it is critical that the relation between spinal function and pathology/dysfunction be understood. The CRC will probe the basic mechanisms of this relation by understanding spinal function at the genetic, tissue and human level. With this knowledge, it will be possible to identify spinal dysfunction as well as the factors which regulate its onset.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and Molecular Neurophysiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
