TitreApplicationTitle: Reconstruction of Regulatory Networks Mediating Persistent Inflammation in HIV Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; HIV; IMMUNE ACTIVATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; PATHOGENESIS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Substantial progress has been made in the treatment and prevention of HIV/AIDS, especially in resource-rich regions where antiretroviral drugs are readily available. The continuous development of new antiretroviral drugs, together with the current use of combination antiretroviral therapy (cART), has resulted in substantial declines in AIDS-associated morbidity and mortality, reducing the frequency of opportunistic infections and prolonging survival. Despite the success of cART, there is great variability among individual therapeutic responses. Poor therapeutic responses are frequently associated with increased mortality as well as non-AIDS associated morbidities, including cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and cancer. Understanding the cellular mechanisms that regulate immune reconstitution is important for optimizing current treatment strategies. HIV causes early severe damage to the gut, which leads to activation of the immune system and chronic inflammation, even in patients on treatment. These findings have focused attention on the pathological processes of immune activation in HIV-infected individuals and its potential role in treatment failure. The goal of this proposal is to understand the dysfunctional immune responses that drive chronic inflammation and limit therapeutic responses in HIV-infected individuals on current treatments. The study will identify molecular signatures and develop computational models that predict therapeutic responses to antiretroviral therapy. To accomplish these goals, we will use advanced technologies to analyze complex immune regulatory networks. These innovative studies involve the assembly and analysis of large datasets using state-of-the-art statistical and computational methods. This information may provide insights that will enable the development of immune-based or other new therapeutic strategies that can be used in conjunction with current treatment regimens to improve therapeutic outcomes.

Abstract-Résumé: Finding a HIV vaccine has been identified as a major scientific milestone for the control of the worldwide AIDS pandemic. However, past attempts using conventional vaccine methods developed for other viruses have failed in significantly protecting individuals against new HIV infections. Surely, modified or novel strategies will need to be elaborated for the design of an effective HIV vaccine. In the current proposal, we put forward new strategies to identify and define vulnerable sites on the surface of HIV that could be exploited in the design of an effective vaccine. By using state-of-the-art methods and automated equipment for structure determination, we attempt unprecedented efforts to give a refined understanding of the only protein present on the surface of HIV. In collaboration with world-class scientists of the International AIDS Vaccine Consortium, our atomic structural characterization of the HIV surface will allow to design candidate vaccine molecules exposing the few vulnerable sites of HIV.  The past 25 years of HIV vaccine research suggest to us that a refined understanding of the HIV surface is a necessary pre-requisite in designing a vaccine that can elicit antibodies capable of preventing new HIV infections.

Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; ANIMAL MODELS; DICER; PHOSPHORYLATION; TAUOPATHIES
Abstract-Résumé: Thirty five millon people worldwide are estimated to be living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementia. This number is expected to double every 20 years. Alzheimer's disease represents 70% of demented disorders. Others include Lewy body dementia, vascular dementia and tauopathies such as frontotemporal dementia and progressive aphasia. Tauopathies are a group of dementing disorders characterized by Tau pathology. In Alzheimer's disease, microtubule-associated protein Tau is the major component of paired helical filaments inside degenerating neurons referred to as neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs). However, aggregation of Tau inside neurons or glial cells is observed in more than twenty neurological disorders, which together form the so-called Tauopathies. For instance, the Tau / MAPT gene locus is associated with the development of frontotemporal dementia. In some of the patients, Tau pathology may be related to early changes in tau alternative splicing. When aggregated, one of the major questions that to be answered is whether there is a loss or gain of toxic functions of Tau. Recent development of transgenic animal models may be useful to address this question. NFTs seem to be of a lesser importance since they represent end-stages of aggregation. In contrast, it has been proposed that the real toxic entity is misfolded non-aggregated tau. Indeed, turning off the expression of the human tau transgene in a mouse model with repressible expression of tau, reverses memory defects even if NFTs continue to accumulate. Likewise, in mouse tauopathy models various pathologies become apparent, including activated microglia and behavioural deficits, before the appearance of NFTs. Therefore, NFTs are neither necessary nor sufficient to cause a cognitive decline. These results altogether do not completely rule out a possible role of tangles in neurodegeneration; however, the memory decline induced in relationship with tau pathology, particularly during the earliest, pre-symptomatic stages of dementia, most probably relies on unknown mechanisms. Among new mechanisms involved in neurodegeneration in AD and related disorders, micro RNAs are of particular interest. miRNAs are a class of conserved noncoding RNAs, which depend on the RNAi machinery. Recent data have shown that they have a role in learning-related synaptic plasticity and brain functioning. The present project aims to understand the relationships between mRNAs and Tau pathology. Its scope is widened to all tauopathies and not only AD. It also explains why we are focussing on the Tau side of the pathology. The strength of the project is the synergy and complementary of two research laboratories (one Canadian, specialized in miRNAs in neurodegenerative disorders and one expert in neurofibrillary degeneration in Alzheimer and Tauopathies in France) with promising preliminary data. The double approach is original and hopeful for diagnosis and new innovative therapeutic strategies.

Abstract-Résumé: The amyloid cascade hypothesis in AD has fulfilled its aim in fostering research but appears to be now insufficient to explain the mechanisms of the disease. The role of molecules interacting with Abeta peptide appears essential. Associated proteins have been thoroughly investigated. However, technical difficulties makes the study of lipids much more difficult. Cholesterol is an abundant component of the senile plaque, modulates A¿ secretion, and is transported by ApoE whose E4 allele is the most significant risk factor of AD. This large scale project will bring together researchers from France, Canada and Quebec who have been successfully working in this field for many years and have complementary areas of expertise (genetics, neuropathology, mass spectrometry, molecular and cellular biology, animal models, gene therapy). The project also involves experts who have developed new technological tools such as MALDI and SIMS imaging of human tissue. These new tools will increase the chance of making discoveries in poorly explored territories of AD research. We will improve our knowledge on the role of cholesterol in the formation of amyloid deposits through an exhaustive investigation on human tissues, in vivo transgenic models and in vitro transfected cells, exploring transport and efflux of A¿  and cholesterol, modulation of APP processing by cholesterol (and cholesterol derivatives) and finally gene therapy. The project will have practical implication on finding  1) new genetic risk factor for AD 2) new biomarkers (enlarged endosome) and 3) new therapeutic approaches that could be translated into clinics. Moreover, the project will also bring results in the development of new microscpy capacities (mass spectrometry imaging) that could deeply modify the way human and animal material are investigated.

Abstract-Résumé: This research project is to generate critical knowledge on the molecular mechanisms underlying Alzheimer's disease and prion diseases with potential developments of new avenues in therapeutical approaches. The improvement of amplification methods for AB and the expected new specific antibodies are settled for direct application in blood diagnosis. This ambitious large-scale project brings together 4 experienced groups with complementary competences to explore the molecular connections between AD and prion diseases. - Partner 1 (Deslys, CEA) has developed the BSE diagnostic test most used in the world and has a strong experience of in vivo experiments and is coordinator of the European network of excellence NeuroPrion - Partner 2 (Rezaei, INRA) is expert in biophysical approaches of PrP conformation, in vitro transconformation and polymerization kinetic analysis. Moreover, he proposes a complete platform of biophysic analysis including spectroscopy in a high-secured environment. - Partner 3 (Roucou, University of Sherbrooke) has contributed in the understanding of the molecular activity of specific isoforms of the prion protein and the initiation of protein aggregation in cultured cells. - Partner 4 (Cashman, University of British Columbia)has developed the first diagnostic test for prions in blood (epitope protection), and has discovered unique protein misfolding epitopes for the prion protein and superoxide dismutase-1, with applications to diagnosis and therapy. He is Scientific Director to PrioNet Canada.  The general and specific objectives of this project are relevant of three of the major research themes of this call for proposals, including:  1- The development of original animal models transgenic for both APP and PrP proteins; 2- Development of diagnostic tools through the creation of specific antibodies 3- Development of original therapies  Moreover, This new area of research between France and Canada will be improved if powerful collaborative tools are put in place to enable a day-to-day communication between distant teams. Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is one of the most common causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide. The high mortality rate from breast cancer is largely due to the metastatic spread of the disease. Metastasis is the ability of a cancer to spread from where it starts to other parts of the body. Therefore suppression of dissemination is an important issue in the treatment of the disease.     We have identified proteins namely 'arrestins' that are highly expressed breast tumor cells and stimulate their ability to migrate and invade, two processes required for metastasis. We will now assess the ability of arrestins to regulate metastasis, using animal models of metastasis. We will deplete arrestin proteins from breast cancer cells, and evaluate the effect on tumor formation and growth. The tumors in animals will be tracked using fluorescent (glowing) tags, which will allow us to monitor their growth and number.  We will determine if less tumours develop and if cancer spread is reduced if arrestins are depleted from the breast cancer cells. This will establish for the first time a direct role for arrestin proteins in regulating metastasis.       Additionally, we will use cell model systems to understand how arrestin proteins signal in breast tumor cells to regulate cell invasion. This will enable us to identify specific small molecule inhibitors that interfere with arrestin signaling in tumor cells.  These studies will provide a better understanding at the molecular events regulating breast cancer metastasis, and may reveal novel drug targets for the treatment and prevention of this disease.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de fonctionnement - Annonce de priorités : cancer du sein
ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: The cellular implications of breast tumor kinase induction in mammary tumorigenesis.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; BREAST TUMOR KINASE; MAMMARY TUMORIGENESIS; METASTASIS; MIGRATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; XENOGRAFT MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women worldwide and a serious public health issue in Canada with 1 in 9 women at risk. Statistics Canada reports more than 22,000 new diagnoses in Canada every year and over 5,000 deaths. Elevated expression of BReast tumor Kinase (BRK) occurs in about 60% of breast tumors, but the oncogenic, prognostic, diagnostic and physiological roles of BRK overexpression have not been clarified. The human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), overexpressed in about 25-30% of breast cancers, is targeted for breast cancer treatment with the drug Herceptin. We have previously established that BRK contributes to the oncogenic effects of HER2 in breast cancers. To assess if BRK is associated with specific breast tumor subtypes and/or tumor grades, we will measure the expression of BRK in a panel of clinically classified breast cancer cell lines and human breast tumors and tissue microarrays. We will next knockdown BRK in breast cancer cells and introduce BRK into normal cells and determine the effect on tumor formation and breast cancer cell morphogenesis and metastasis in vitro and in vivo.  Together, these studies will define the physiological role of BRK in mammary tumorigenesis and position BRK as a targeting alternative to breast cancer therapy.

ProgramNameEN: Operating Grant - Priority Announcement: Breast Cancer
NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de fonctionnement - Annonce de priorités : cancer du sein
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN; CARDIOLOGIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Multidisciplinary Approach to Novel Therapies in Cardiology-Oncology REsearch
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CHEMOTHERAPY CARDIOTOXICITY; HEART FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: A growing number of women are diagnosed with breast cancer each year and it is one of the most common causes of death.  A new chemotherapy drug called trastuzumab has been shown to decrease the risk of cancer recurrence and improve patient survival.  Unfortunately, this breast cancer treatment may also result in significant damage to the heart muscle that can ultimately lead to heart failure.  We have recently shown that women receiving trastuzumab develop heart enlargement, an early sign of heart failure.  Effective medications for heart failure are available but have not been well studied in the prevention of this chemotherapy related heart damage.  The main objective of this project is (1) to determine if two commonly prescribed heart failure medications called ACE-inhibitors and beta blockers can prevent MRI evidence of early heart damage in breast cancer patients receiving trastuzumab.  Other objectives of this project are: (2) to determine if a blood test can also detect early signs of heart damage, (3) to better understand the cause of the heart damage by studying relatively new blood tests and an in-depth MRI of the heart, (4) use MRI to determine if the damage to these patients' hearts continues in the year following chemotherapy.  We will perform a study called a randomized controlled trial.  Patients will receive either a heart failure pill or a placebo for the 1 year duration of their chemotherapy.  They will each undergo blood tests and a heart MRI before chemotherapy, at 3 months, at 12 months and at 24 months.  On the MRI, we will measure if the heart failure pill prevents the heart from enlarging.  On the 24 month scan, we will be interested to see if the heart enlargement remains over time, worsens or gets better.  We will also determine if any of the blood tests seem to predict heart enlargement.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de fonctionnement - Annonce de priorités : cancer du sein

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: The Eph family of receptor tyrosine kinases in breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION; BREAST CANCER; EPH RECEPTORS; INVASION; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Metastatic activity of cancer cells is defined by their adhesive and migration properties.  Eph receptors execute their functions through the control of both cell adhesion and cell migration, and, therefore, may represent very effective targets for cancer therapy Previously published observations strongly suggest that the suppression of EphB6 receptor expression correlates with the increased metastatic activity in breast cancer cells. However, the exact functions of EphB6 and the mechanism of its action have not been addressed. Our observations show that the EphB6 receptor acts in breast cancer cells to mediate their adhesion to EphB receptor ligand, ephrin-B2, and to the extracellular matrix protein, fibronectin. EphB6 also initiates a very specific combination of signaling events. Moreover, in our experiments re-expression of EphB6 in metastatic breast cancer cells reduced their invasive activity in cell culture and forced them to behave in a manner similar to non-metastatic cells.    Our team plans to further investigate the ability of the EphB6 receptor to regulate breast cancer cell adhesion to extra-cellular matrix proteins and to modulate cell-cell attachment. We will examine the specific molecular mechanisms allowing EphB6 to control cell attachment and block breast cancer invasiveness. We will also analyse, how EphB6 regulates metastasis and aggressiveness of breast cancer tumors in the animal model of breast cancer, and determine if EphB6 re-expression or activation blocks breast cancer metastasis. To further understand the role of EphB6 in human breast cancer we plan to use a collection of breast cancer samples to examine the co-operation between this protein and other adhesion molecules in the regulation of metastatic activity. Our work will lead to a better understanding of breast cancer invasiveness and may support the development of new treatment approaches allowing to block the initiation and progression of breast cancer metastatic disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathogenic mechanisms associated with neurofilament disorganization
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; AXONAL TRANSPORT; CYTOSKELETON; MICROTUBULES; NEUROFILAMENTS; NEUROPATHIES; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Abnormal accumulations of neurofilaments are a pathological hallmark of many human neurodegenerative disorders including peripheral neuropathies and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, the exact molecular mechanisms underlying the toxicity of neurofilament disorganization are unknown. We will address this question by the characterization of new transgenic mouse models with neurofilament abnormalities generated in our laboratory. First, propose to elucidate the pathogenic mechanisms of Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2E (CMT2E) neuropathy and to rescue it by gene therapy using a mouse model with conditional expression of NF-LP22S mutant that recapitulates key features of CMT2E disease. Second, we will investigate the role of peripherin in transgenic mice models of ALS overexpressing human genomic fragments encoding TDP43 or ALS-linked TDP43 mutants. Our general hypothesis is that IF abnormalities can contribute to CMT2E neuropathy and to ALS disease by causing axonal transport defects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Motor, multisystemic and social participation assessment in myotonic dystrophy type 1: a 9-year longitudinal study.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING PROCESSES; CLINICAL RESEARCH; DIRECT OBESERVATIONS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; MYOTONIC DYSTROPHY; NERVOUSS SYSTEM; NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS; PSYCHOSOCIAL RESEARCH; QUESTIONNAIRES
Abstract-Résumé: Myotonic dystrophy (DM1), an autosomal dominant disorder, is the most common adult form of muscular dystrophy.  The natural history and variable patterns of motor and multisystemic progression in DM1 have not been well delineated.  This multidisciplinary team want to reassess 152 DM1 patients, 9 years after baseline evaluation, using measures of muscular strength, daytime sleepiness, fatigue, respiratory and metabolic impairments, cognition and behavioral impairments, functional status, social participation and quality of life.  The project will improve the understanding of the natural history of DM1, highlight major determinants of social participation, well-being and quality of life for affected patients and their families and promote the emergence of comprehensive disease management strategies.  The project will also generate estimations of annual change of several impairments in DM1 that will be valuable for the design of therapeutic trials in DM1.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting protection of functionally intact motor units in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; CDNA MICROARRAY; CLINICAL NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; ELECTRODIAGNOSTIC MEDICINE; PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY
Abstract-Résumé: Lou Gehrig's disease, also known as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or ALS, is a disease that causes the death of nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. The disease specifically targets the motor neurons that are essential for producing movement. Individuals with the disease become progressively weaker until fully paralyzed and die within 3-5 years of diagnosis. While motor neurons are particularly susceptible to ALS, we recently found that motor neurons connected to fast twitch muscle are especially vulnerable whereas motor neurons connected to slow twitch muscle show some resistance to the disease. We have used three types of interventions to convert fast into slow twitch muscle and have preliminary evidence that all three enhance the survival of motor neurons. We think it is likely that the molecular mechanisms that result in protecting the motor neurons are common for the three interventions. We will test this hypothesis by measuring changes in gene expression that are common across the three interventions. These results will identify which genes and proteins are ultimately responsible for the protective effect that results when the fast twitch muscles are converted to slow. These results will be translated into specific exercise training recommendations for people with ALS and will aid in the development of evidence based treatments for this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing specific motoneuron subtypes from embryonic stem cells, and induced pluripotent stem cells, to treat neuromuscular disorders and paralysis due to injury.
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; MOTONEURON; MUSCLE; NEUROGENESIS; NEUROMUSCULAR ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; REGENERATION; TISSUE CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Motor neuron diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are devastating neurodegenerative disorders caused by the selective loss of motoneurons. As spinal motoneurons die, muscles become progressively weaker, to the point of complete paralysis, due to muscle denervation.  Patients succumb to the disease when they lose the ability to control voluntary and rhythmic movements such as breathing. There is currently no cure for ALS.  Motoneurons also die in patientssuffering from a spinal cord injury (SCI).  Fracture and/or dislocation of the vertebrae produce massive damage to the delicate underlying tissue of the spinal cord resulting in the death of motoneurons innervating skeletal muscles.  Motoneurons do not regenerate.  Consequently the only means to restore function to muscles denervated by the loss of motoneurons resulting from ALS or SCI is to replace them with healthy motoneurons.   The aim of this proposal is to first develop different subtypes of motoneurons from mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells and then show that they are capable of restoring muscle function when transplanted near paralyzed muscles.  We aim to show that different subtypes of motoneurons can be generated from mouse ES cells that normally innervate leg or postural muscles.  We will then show that muscle recovery is better when the paralyzed muscle is reinnervated by their appropriate subtype of motoneuron (e.g. paralyzed leg muscles will recover better when reinnervated by leg motoneurons).  Finally, we will determine whether induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS) cells have the same capacity to make different subtypes of motoneurons and restore muscle function when transplanted near paralyzed muscles.   Together, these experiments will be the first ever to examine whether different motoneuron subtypes can be generated from ES cells and iPS cells and whether their creation and use will lead to better function of paralyzed muscles in patients with ALS or in those suffering from a SCI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of HAART expansion on community levels of HIV viral load and HIV risk behaviours among MSM in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: HAART; HIV VIRAL LOAD; MSM; RISK BEHAVIOURS
Abstract-Résumé: Recently the BC Ministry of Health endorsed expanding access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) as a strategy that could reduce the number of new HIV infections by reducing community infectivity levels. Guidelines have also been revised so that many more HIV-infected people may now access ART. The success of ART expansion in reducing new HIV infections might be affected if "ART optimism" causes higher levels of risk behaviour for HIV transmission. Men who have sex with men (MSM) remain the risk group most affected by HIV in Canada and BC. We wish to examine the impact of expansion of access to ART on risk behaviour among the MSM population in Greater Vancouver and on community HIV viral load as a marker of community infectivity. We will conduct two cross-sectional surveys of MSM, spaced over a 5-year period. The surveys will be designed to be representative of the ethnic and sub-cultural diversity of MSM in Greater Vancouver. We will sample 1000 MSM aged 15 years and over at each survey, using members of different sub-populations of MSM (seeds) to recruit a diverse group of MSM. All study participants will be asked to sign a consent form, complete a questionnaire, a rapid HIV blood test, syphilis test, hepatitis C serology, and to provide consent to allow researchers access to health services databases. HIV+ participants in the surveys will be invited to enroll in a longitudinal sub-study with follow-up at 6-month intervals that will examine the effectiveness of a peer-based treatment literacy intervention for increasing ART uptake among HIV+ men currently not on treatment, and on risk behaviour for HIV transmission. The study results will assist service providers and program planners to respond to potential increases in HIV risk behaviours. The results will also directly inform policy makers in Canada and other countries with regards to the added preventive value of ART and influence decisions regarding the further expansion of ART in industrialized countries.

TitreApplicationTitle: Can intensified anti-retroviral therapy during acute/early HIV-1 infection reduce and/or eliminate viral reservoirs in HIV-1 infected individuals?
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE HIV INFECTION; AIDS; HAART; HIV INFECTION; MARAVIROC; PROGRESSION; RALTEGRAVIR; RANDOMIZED TRIAL; TREATMENT; VIRAL RESERVOIRS
Abstract-Résumé: Although the current standard of therapy for Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection is able to control the progression of the disease and prevent AIDS in most persons, these persons must take the drugs for life. Thus, there is no cure for AIDS because the current standard therapies can not get rid of the virus completely in infected persons. One reason for this, is that the virus can hide in places called reservoirs. HIV establishes residence in these reservoirs very early in infection. It is currently unclear whether treatment of infected persons very early in the infection is beneficial. The proposed study is a pilot, randomized controlled clinical trial comparing a standard therapy regimen to a more intensified therapy regimen that uses new anti-viral agents named Raltegravir and Maraviroc, in acute/early HIV infection to see whether the more intense regimen is able to reduce or even get rid of virus reservoirs. The results of this study, if favourable, will inform on developing larger trials for the treatment of very early HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms underlying the development of resistance to apoptosis in response to HIV-Vpr protein and HIV infection in monocytic cells
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; HIV; IN VITRO INFECTION; MONOCYTE DERIVED MACROPHAGES; MONOCYTIC CELLS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; VPR
Abstract-Résumé: HIV infection resulting in Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) is dramatically affecting the health of nations worldwide. People infected with HIV progressively lose the function of their immune system and the ability to recover from disease. The virus incapacitates the patients' immune system in a variety of ways, one of which is its ability to enter immune cells mainly T cells, monocytes and macrophages. The virus can remain inside these cells, effectively hiding from current anti-HIV treatment therapies, as well as the patients' immune system. Therefore one of the many challenges facing scientists is how to eliminate virus from these cells. HIV infection normally kills immune T cells; however, monocytes/macrophages are somehow able to survive HIV infection.   One of the HIV proteins, termed Vpr, has been shown to cause cell death in T cells and neuronal cells. Our preliminary results show that this protein can also kill monocytes but not differentiated macrophages. It is well known that HIV patients get infected with opportunistic infections primarily because of their deficient immune system. These patients contain various microbial products including bacterial DNA in their blood. We have found that when patient's monocytes come in contact with microbial products such as their DNA (CpG) cannot be killed by Vpr protein. Overall, this proposal is directed towards understanding mechanisms by which monocytes/macrophages are essentially protected from death caused by the killing effect of either HIV or its viral proteins. The results of this study will help in understanding how macrophages evade the killing effect of HIV or its toxic proteins such as Vpr with a view to designing novel strategies that may prove useful towards HIV eradication from infected people.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study of immunopathogenic consequences of HIV-1/Leishmania interactions in human primary cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; DENDRITIC CELL; DNA MICROARRAY; HIV-1; LEISHMANIA; MACROPHAGE
Abstract-Résumé: We are proposing to investigate the consequence(s) of biological and pathological interactions that may occur between HIV-1 and the protozoan parasite Leishmania within natural targets of both pathogens (i.e. macrophages and dendritic cells). It is crucial to improve our understanding of the complex interactions which may occur between both infectious agents because Leishmania is considered as an emerging disease in at least 30 countries worldwide where HIV-1 is frequently prevalent. It is anticipated that the data from the planned studies described herein will contribute also to our overall understanding of the immunopathogenesis and mechanisms of HIV-1 transmission. A better comprehension regarding the impact of a co-infecting agent such as Leishmania on HV-1 biology is crucial because in countries where antiretroviral drug are not widely available there is also a high incidence of opportunistic and endemic infectious diseases such as leishmaniasis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Potential of pathogen-specific egg yolk antibodies (IgY) for treating Clostridium difficile infections.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESINS; ANTI-INFECTIVE; CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE; DIARRHEA; EGG YOLK ANTIBODIES; EXOTOXINS; NOSOCOMIAL INFECTIONS; PASSIVE IMMUNITY; THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: C. difficile causes a condition now called C. difficile infection(CDI) in hospitalized patients. This occurs when hospital patients are treated with antibiotics in order to prevent opportunistic infections. In some cases, however, eradicating the normal gut microflora (NF) with antibiotics leaves the GI tract of these subjects vulnerable to colonization by C. difficile. Once these organisms, which display an inherent resistance to many common antibiotics, gain a foothold, they produce two high molecular weight exotoxins (TcdA and TcdB) which are primarily responsible for the clinical symptoms associated with these infections. In many cases, the condition can be successfully treated by replacing the offending antibiotic with one, typically metronidazole, to which C. difficile is sensitive. In approximately 20% of cases, however, the condition will return once the antibiotics are withdrawn and it is only a matter of time before multi-drug resistant C. difficile strains begin to appear in hospitals. The hypothesis to be tested is that toxins and adherence to host intestinal cells both contribute to CDI pathogenesis and, as a consequence, anti-infective agents designed to neutralize C. difficile toxins as well as inhibit C. difficile colonization of the GI tract will provide greater therapeutic benefit in subjects suffering from this infectious condition. The proposal is to assess, in vitro and in vivo, the potential therapeutic benefit of using C. difficile-specific egg yolk antibodies (IgY) to inhibit colonization of the GI tract by these organisms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Telomere attrition rate as predictor of cardiovascular complications of type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; DIABETES MELLITUS; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; TELOMERE LENGTH
Abstract-Résumé: Telomeres are the chromosome caps that are necessary to keep chromosomes from unraveling. As with each cell division a piece of the telomere end is lost, the length of telomeres is a marker of biological aging of the cells and the organism as a whole. Recently, the telomere length has been linked to several frequent human diseases involving heart and circulatory system.  In this project, we will assess the predictive value of the shortening of telomeres over time for frequent complications affecting the heart, blood vessels and the kidneys  of patients suffering from type 2 diabetes. We will build upon our access to data and DNA samples from a large clinical study on the  treatment of diabetes and high blood pressure, called ADVANCE. We will measure the telomere lengths in several thousands of study participants repeatedly during a five year period and assess how this information together with other characteristics (genetic, clinical) can help to predict cardiovascular complications in diabetic patients. The accrued knowledge will serve as a stepping stone for establishing telomere attrition rate as a novel tool for prediction of cardiovascular complications of diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of changes in Quebec's prescription drug insurance policy on low-income pregnant women
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER EPIDEMIOLOGY; MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Over half a million women continue to die each year from pregnancy and childbirth-related causes. The slow progress in reducing maternal deaths could be attributed to the myriad and complex causes of maternal mortality. Socioeconomic and cultural issues that confer secondary status on women may also hinder them from obtaining essential obstetrical care. When women consistently lag behind men in areas such as education, employment and political participation, a gender gap is created, which can affect the health of women.  Objective: We hypothesize that the lower the status of women in a country, or the greater the gender gap, the higher the maternal mortality rate for that country. Consequently, the objectives of our study were to evaluate whether the existence of a gender gap is associated with maternal mortality in 130 countries. Methods: We propose to conduct an ecological cross-sectional study using measures of gender inequity obtained from the World Economic Forum gender gap report. The gender gap index created will incorporate female economic and political participation, education and health, as compared to men. Poisson regression analyses will be used to assess the relationship between the gender gap index and maternal mortality. Longitudinal analyses will also be performed to examine whether maternal mortality decreases with reductions in gender inequity.  Relevance: This study will be relevant to public health organisations and policy-makers in order to target the specific spheres where women lag behind men. Reducing maternal mortality and improving the general health of women will have greater implications on the health of their children and the productivity of society in general.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring Family-Centred Issues in Adult Rehabilitation Settings: Health care professionals', patients', and families' experiences
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DESEASE MANAGEMENT; FAMILY/CLIENT-CENTRED CARE; HEALTH SERVICES EVALUATION; MEASUREMENT DEVELOPMENT; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: People live longer today, but do they live better? Of the more than 50,000 Canadians who will suffer a stroke this year, and the 3 Canadians who will be diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis (MS) each day, most will require on-going rehabilitation services from a variety of health care professionals. Given that hospital stays are getting shorter, improving the planning and delivery of rehabilitation services is essential. Research has shown that strong partnerships between patients and clinicians can improve outcomes, enhance patient and professional satisfaction with care, and decrease family anxiety. However, the elements involved in creating this partnership are not always clear. The goals of this study are to 1) develop a measurement tool that will capture the extent to which this partnership is experienced by patients, their families, and health professionals; 2) understand the needs of patients and families in terms of ways in which this partnership could be improved; and 3) explore the potential partnership barriers experienced by health professionals, patients and families. A two-phase study will be carried out in two organizations specializing in providing care to people with chronic diseases: Regional/District Stroke Programs, and the MS Clinic of Southwestern Ontario.  Patients, families and clinicians at these facilities will be asked to complete a survey and to participate in personal interviews. The results of this study will help to improve our understanding of specific rehabilitation needs of patients who live with chronic illness and disability and their families. It will also provide knowledge and advice as to how to create strong partnership for educators and medical professionals. In turn, this will facilitate communication between families and health professionals and provide future directions to inform planning and evaluation of rehabilitation services, enhancing the health-related quality of life for adults with long-term rehabilitation needs.

Abstract-Résumé: The gastrointestinal tract is a particular environment that is constantly exposed to commensal bacteria and dietary "foreign" antigens, but generally does not succumb to inflammation directed at these non-self constituents. Indeed, the intestinal immune system can mount a protective response against pathogens maintain tolerance towards commensal bacteria and dietary antigens. Perturbations in tolerance mechanisms lead to chronic inflammatory disorders of the intestine, such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which are collectively referred to as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Patients tend to be diagnosed in early adulthood and inflammation becomes a lifelong state. IBD afflicts over 200,000 and 9,200 new cases are diagnosed every year. This puts Canada among the countries with the highest reported prevalence rates of IBD in the world. This generates and economical burden estimated to $1.8 billion per year.In recent years, various IBD mouse models have shed light on our understanding of the pathogenesis of these diseases. T regulatory (Treg) cells are a specialized subset of immune cells that have the capacity to control a variety of inflammatory responses. The goal of my Ph.D. project is to further elucidate the mechanism by which Treg cells control the expansion and activation of other immune cells that exacerbate inflammation and disease. These experiments will provide valuable insights into immune cell functional dynamics at mucosal sites offering new possibilities for the development of therapeutic strategies that aim at controlling inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Place and Immigrant Women's Sexual and Reproductive Health
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER; HEALTH GEOGRAPHY; IMMIGRANT HEALTH; MIXED METHODS; PLACE; POPULATION HEALTH; REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: New immigrants tend to be healthier than the general population, but their health declines the longer they spend in Canada.  This urges attention to factors that disproportionately affect immigrants' health.  Immigrant women are particularly vulnerable because of migration and gender-based disadvantages.  Sexual and reproductive health is one area where research has shown that immigrant women show worse outcomes and face barriers accessing care.  However, most research focuses on health care settings and neglects the potential impact of the broader environment on immigrant women's sexual/reproductive health.  In particular, features of the places in which people live, such as health services and social support, have been shown to influence sexual/reproductive health.  Place may be especially important to immigrant women's health because they bear a disproportionate burden of poverty and an increased risk of living in low-income neighbourhoods.    The objective of this research is to explore how immigrant women feel that the places in which they live impact their sexual/reproductive health.  This project moves beyond studies that describe health-related differences between places, to understanding how place affects health.  An approach will be used that combines two different research methods: qualitative interviews with recent immigrant women living in Ottawa, and geographic mapping of the health and immigration services in Ottawa neighbourhoods.  Ottawa is home to a significant and diverse immigrant community, but it is underrepresented in the migration and health literature.  Together, these multiple data sources will allow for an in-depth exploration of this issue.  The results of this study could inform community-based initiatives to improve sexual/reproductive health access and outcomes among immigrant women.  In addition, interventions based on the results of this study could help Canadian society to benefit from healthy new members of the population.

Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOTAXIN; CANCER; CELLULAR SIGNALING; GPCR'S; HYPOXIA; IN VIVO SCIENCE; INVADOPODIA; LYSOPHOSPHATIDIC ACID; METASTASIS; MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: The spread of cancer cells to distant sites in the body is the major cause of cancer patient death.  Growing evidence connects newly identified cancer cell protrusions, named invadopodia, to invasion of cancer cells and metastasis.  Oxygen deprivation of the tumour mass has also been shown to increase the invasiveness of tumour cells.  The oxygen deprivation is caused by the rapid and uncontrolled growth of the tumour where new blood vessels do not have time to grow properly. This project will investigate the implication of a protein called Autotaxin, which is known to increase invasion of tumor cells, in the formation of invadopodia and metastasis by tumor cells exposed to low concentrations of oxygen similar to what is found within tumours.  The results of this project may lead to the development of therapeutic targets to inhibit cancer metastasis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using Internet Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy with Older Adults: Is Age a Factor?
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; INTERNET; MENTAL HEALTH; OLDER ADULTS; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Depression and anxiety are prevalent, disabling, and under-treated conditions. To increase access to mental health services, researchers have begun delivering therapy via therapist-guided Internet-Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (I-CBT). Randomized controlled trials have consistently supported the efficacy of I-CBT for these conditions; however, use of I-CBT with older adults has not been evaluated. I-CBT may be particularly beneficial for this age group because it can be used by those with limited mobility, it allows for ongoing access to written therapy materials, and users can proceed at their own pace. Given that familiarity with the Internet is required to use I-CBT, it is important to address whether age affects access and receptivity to this form of therapy. Older adults constitute the fastest growing group of Canadian computer users and information seekers on the web. Yet, it is unknown whether they will utilize I-CBT if made available, how satisfied they will be with this service, what adaptations to existing I-CBT programs should be made for this age group, and, most importantly, whether it will be successful in reducing affective symptoms. The proposed study will address these topics by exposing 20 seniors to modules of I-CBT. Interviews will ask of their understanding and expectations of I-CBT and of ideas for improvement. Stage two will involve applying this feedback to existing I-CBT programs and recruiting 60 seniors to undergo either I-CBT for depression/anxiety, or be wait-listed to serve as a comparison group. Satisfaction with I-CBT and improvement of symptoms will be assessed and analyzed post-treatment. The proposed research has high potential to improve service delivery and the mental health of Canadians. Overall, research on I-CBT and its effectiveness in treating older adults will inform health care providers, policymakers, and the public of whether this is an acceptable avenue for offering mental health services to older adults in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Altered cardiovascular function during breast cancer treatment and implications for exercise
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CANCER TREATMENT; CARDIOVASCULAR; EXERCISE INTERVENTION; EXERCISE PHYSIOLOGY; EXERCISE PRESCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the leading cancer type among Canadian women. Exercise has been used successfully during and after breast cancer treatment to reduce the negative side effects and physical impairment caused by treatment. However, much more research is needed to determine the most beneficial exercise prescription for breast cancer patients. An exercise prescription is a detailed exercise plan or guideline that takes into account your current health status and goals. The exercise prescription currently used in cancer and exercise research does not take into account the cancer treatment's poisonous effects, which can affect the way the body reacts to exercise. When these effects are not considered, the exercise may not be appropriate and may not offer full potential benefits.   In my project I will first take several measurements to attempt to determine how the effects of breast cancer treatment affect the patient's body during exercise concurrent to treatment. I expect to find that the heart function of breast cancer patients will be lower than healthy women of similar ages and that some of the measurements can be used to determine exercise prescription more accurately. Then I will design an exercise rehabilitation program for breast cancer patients based on what was learned from the first study. This will be the first exercise program to use a prescription based on changes in the body that are cancer treatment-specific. I expect that this exercise program will be more beneficial than a typical exercise prescription.  My project is likely to create a more clear understanding of the way a cancer patient's body reacts to exercise during treatment and to identify a method for more accurate exercise prescription. This is important because current and future studies will attempt to determine the exercise prescriptions that deliver the most benefits to cancer patients. A clear understanding and high level of accuracy are imperative to attain the truly optimal benefits.

TitreApplicationTitle: Changing emotion with emotion: Testing a principle change mechanism in Emotion-Focused Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: EMOTION-FOCUSED THERAPY; PSYCHOLOGICAL ADJUSTMENT; PSYCHOSOCIAL ADJUSTMENT OF CANCER PATIENTS; PSYCHOSOCIAL ONCOLOGY; PSYCHOTHERAPY RESEARCH; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; STRESS AND COPING; TREATMENT OF DEPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Emotional distress is common in people with cancer, as the disease presents patients with numerous stressors, tests their coping abilities, and may trigger underlying psychological vulnerabilities. Some patients will have sufficient psychological difficulties to meet the criteria for a diagnosis of depression. Psychological difficulties are important to treat, not only because of the suffering they cause the patient, but also because they are associated with greater pain, less compliance with cancer treatment, and more distress in family members. The proposed study will test the effectiveness of a psychotherapy approach, Emotion-Focused Therapy, for treating depression in cancer patients who are experiencing coping difficulties. Emotion-Focused Therapy works by helping clients to come to terms with difficult emotions and to cope in healthy ways with difficult emotional experiences. It is a therapy approach that was developed in Canada, at York University, and is now used around the world. Previous research has shown Emotion-Focused Therapy to be effective at treating depression in physically well people.  Its effectiveness at treating depression in people with cancer has not been investigated before.  The proposed study will examine the effectiveness of this approach by recruiting 36 cancer patients who are also suffering from adjustment difficulties or depression.  They will receive 8 sessions of either Emotion-Focused Therapy or an already existing treatment. At the end of the study participants' scores on measures of depression, cancer-related anxiety and psychological adjustment will be compared, to assess which treatment was most helpful.  This research will assist clinical psychologists and others who work with cancer patients to make evidence-based decisions about which psychological therapies are the most useful for helping cancer patients who are experiencing psychological difficulties.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genome-wide RNA Interference Screens Identify Novel Regulators of Mitochondrial Morphology
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER; FISSION; FUSION; GENOME-WIDE SCREENING; MITOCHONDRIA; RNA INTERFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria are the main source of energy for the cell.  Interestingly, in the cell mitochondria exist as a network of individual mitochondria that fuse into long filaments and break apart into individual mitochondria. Evidence is accumulating that breaking apart the network of mitochondria can kill tumour cells.  We predict that finding new genes that can promote fragmentation of mitochondria will sensitize tumour cells to chemotherapeutic drugs such as paclitaxel and camptothecin and represents a promising approach to eradicate cancer cells. Here, we scan the entire set of human genes for those that can promote mitochondrial fragmentation and identify those that will kill tumour cells more efficiently when exposed to chemotherapeutic drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rôle de deux cyclines de type B dans la contractilité embryonnaire et la division cellulaire asymétrique.
Keywords-MotsClés: C. ELEGANS; CANCER; CONTRACTILITE CORTICALE; CYCLE CELLULAIRE; DIVISION CELLULAIRE ASYMETRIQUE; DEVELOPPEMENT EMBRYONNAIRE; MICROSCOPIE TEMPS REEL; POLARITE CELLULAIRE; PROTEINES PAR
Abstract-Résumé: Notre laboratoire s'interesse aux mecanismes qui permettent a la cellule de se diviser de facon asymetrique, un aspect fondamental dans la recherche sur le cancer. Une division asymetrique est une division inegale en termes de materiel acquis par chacune des deux cellules filles apres division de la cellule mere. Elle genere donc deux cellules differentes en devenir. La division asymetrique est importante puisqu'elle genere la diversite des types cellulaires qui constitue l'organisme. Elle est aussi utilisee par les cellules souches pour leur permettre de se renouveler et de se differentier. En effet, une cellule souche mere doit se diviser de facon a produire une cellule fille qui garde les proprietes de la cellule mere, c'est l'auto renouvellement, et une cellule fille qui se divise en adoptant les caracteristiques specifiques a type cellulaire, c'est la differentiation. La division asymetrique des cellules souches est  finement regulee et sa perte peu mener au cancer. La division asymetrique depend de la localisation specifique de facteurs ou determinants importants pour les futures cellules filles a un pole ou l'autre de la cellule mere. De cette facon, chacune des cellules filles issue de la division recoit des determinants cellulaires differents mais utiles a sa propre destinee. Nous etudions les mecanismes impliques dans la regulation d'une telle distribution polarisee des determinants au sein de la cellule mere en utilisant un organisme modele qui est le nematode C. elegans. L'avantage est que nos etudes se font dans le contexte d'un organisme a part entiere pour lequel de nombreux outils experimentaux sont disponibles. L'embryon de C. elegans est une cellule qui se divise de facon asymetrique grace a l'intervention de proteines PAR. Nous cherchons a determiner comment ces proteines PAR, qui sont conserves chez l'homme, controlent la division asymetrique pour comprendre comment la perte de ce mecanisme mene a la surproliferation des cellules et au cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying northern solutions to northern mental health and addictions problems: unraveling the lived experience of barriers to mental health and addictions care in the Yukon territory
Keywords-MotsClés: BRITISH COLUMBIA; DEINSTITUTIONALIZATION; HEALTH CARE SERVICES; HEALTH GEOGRAPHY; HOMELESSNESS; HOUSING POLICY; INSTITUTIONALIZATION; MENTAL HEALTH POLICY; PATIENT CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Canadians have long been concerned about the administration of mental health services due to the negative implications of inadequate treatment on society, families and the quality of life for patients themselves. Since the 1980s there have been significant efforts in all Canadian provinces to reform mental health services, known as the period of deinstitutionalization, which included reform measures to encourage treatment in the community and the building of life skills and social supports for patients. In recent years, however, there have been indications that a process of reinstitutionalization has started in selected provinces as a result of the need for government's to manage the negative externalities associated with deinstitutionalization, including rising rates of homelessness and growth in the number of persons with mental illness in the criminal justice system. This project will work to assess the factors that led to reinstitutionalization in British Columbia and it's implications on service providers, the organization of mental health care, and patients themselves. This research will determine whether reinstitutionalization is in fact improving access to services or reverting to the traditional institutionalized model of mental health service delivery that was dismissed in the 1980s as being insufficient. This project will stimulate a policy debate about the state of mental health services following deinstitutionalization, and determine whether reinstitutionalization is the appropriate model for organizing mental health services in British Columbia. The project will work to educate the research community, policy makers and the public about the past, present and future administration of mental health services, and provide the foundation for future research on reinstitutionalization in other Canadian provinces.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adolescent substance use and educational attainment as determinants of health in early adulthood: a longitudinal study of developmental trajectories
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL TRAJECTORIES; EDUCATIONAL ATTAINMENT; GROWTH CURVE MODELS; HEALTH OF YOUNG ADULTS; HEALTH RISK/PROTECTIVE FACTORS; INTER/INTRA-INDIVIDUAL CHANGE; MULTILEVEL MODELS; PROSPECTIVE LONGITUDINAL STUDY; SUBSTANCE USE; TRANSITIONS TO ADULTHOOD
Abstract-Résumé: There is strong research evidence for both a direct and indirect link between educational attainment and the health of young adults. Educational attainment is a key marker for future health mediated through work and economic resources and supports for healthy lifestyles. Substance use in adolescence is also an important risk factor for adverse health outcomes in adulthood. Early substance use is a risk factor for developing substance abuse and dependence in adulthood, which can affect ones health as well as their economic position. To date however, what we know about the links between education, substance use and health in young adults has mainly come from retrospective or cross-sectional studies. We know little about how particular substance use patterns and educational attainment in adolescence interact and determine physical and mental health in adulthood. While it has been shown that substance use and educational success in adolescence are inversely related with each other, few studies have examined their interrelationships in a longitudinal perspective. It is possible that substance use is just a marker for a host of risk and protective factors such as parenting styles or household income - or, alternatively, some patterns of substance use directly impair school performance. I have an opportunity to use a data set that has followed a group of young people age 12-16 through into adulthood (age 22-28). This data set will enable me to use advanced statistical analysis to clarify the unique role of substance use and educational pathways in the prediction of health outcomes in young adulthood. Further, this study will examine how substance use and education fit into the larger matrix of individual (i.e. healthy lifestyle) and contextual factors (i.e. peer group) that influence health in young adults. Understanding these relationships will contribute to the knowledge that is needed to guide services and policies that will support healthy transitions to adulthood.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparisons of CVD risk profiles in south Asian children in rural and urban India and Canada with Canadians of European origin
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOLOGY; CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; PEDIATRICS; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are the major contributors to global morbidity and mortality. South Asians have one of the highest risks for CVD in the world. This extremely high risk for CVD is also seen among migrants from the Indian subcontinent. We propose a study to document whether risk factors vary between children in rural and urban India compared to South Asian children and European children in Canada. The study aims to identify the cardiovascular risk profile of Indian children in three distinct settings (rural and urban India, and urban Canada) and compare the risk factors with European children in Canada. The study duration is 40 months and planned to be conducted simultaneously in India and Canada. The study population is 2400 school children in the age group of 9 -13 years. All children will be evaluated at the start of the study for cardiovascular risk factors by history, physical measurements, blood analysis as well as assessment for diet, physical activity and psychosocial factors. The children will be followed up for 24 months and re-evaluated at the end of the same. The information so collected will be utilized to develop culturally specific interventions that are relevant to each setting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vascular events In noncardiac Surgery patIents' cOhort evaluatioN study (VISION): Vascular Surgery Substudy and NT-proBNP Bio-bank Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BIO-BANK; BIOMARKERS; PERIOPERATIVE CARDIOVASCULAR MEDICINE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; VASCULAR EVENTS; VASCULAR SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide there are more than 200 million adults have major surgery every year, and millions of these patients will suffer a major vascular complication (i.e., death, heart attack, cardiac arrest, or stroke) in the first 30 days after their surgery.  Despite the magnitude of this problem, there are no known effective and safe interventions to accurately monitor, prevent or manage these events.            VISION is the world's largest international prospective perioperative cohort study including patients 45 years of age or older whom are undergoing noncardiac surgery that requires hospital admission.       The VISION Vascular Surgery Substudy will include approximately 5000 vascular surgery patients. The primary objectives of the VISION Vascular Surgery substudy are to determine the: 1) incidence of major vascular events at 30 days after surgery, 2) the optimal clinical model to predict major vascular events at 30 days after surgery; 3) proportion of patients 30 days after surgery with perioperative myocardial infarctions that may go undetected without troponin monitoring; and 4) relationship between postoperative troponin measurements and the 1 year risk of vascular death.         Secondly the VISION NT-proBNP Bio-bank Study will examine the prognostic capabilities of NT-proBNP in the postoperative period to predict cardiovascular events.  A recent small study has suggested that a postoperative elevation in the biomarker released from the heart called brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is able to identify patients who will experience major vascular complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental and social determinants of enhanced infectious mortality in HIV-Exposed but Uninfected (HEU) infants in South Africa.
Keywords-MotsClés: ***; ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL DETERMINANTS; HIV EXPOSED UNINFECTED; INFECTIOUS MORTALITY; PROSPECTIVE COHORT
Abstract-Résumé: One and a half million babies are born to HIV-infected mothers every year. Due to the worldwide expansion of  highly effective strategies to prevent the spread of HIV infection from mothers to their babies   the vast majority are not themselves infected. Nonetheless these HIV-Exposed but Uninfected (HEU) babies are at greatly increased risk of death during the first year of life and appear to suffer from more infections and die more often than babies born to HIV-uninfected mothers. South Africa has the highest burden of HIV in the world with almost twenty five percent of newborn babies being HIV-exposed but uninfected. Several theories have been offered to explain the very poor health of these HEU babies, but none has been proven to be the sole one responsible.  Putative immunodeficiency combined with other factors, including for example poor maternal health, absence of breastfeeding, exposure to a higher burden of infectious diseases and social insecurity logically conspire to result in the observed increased morbidity and mortality.   The goal of this series of proposed studies is to identify the environmental and social explanation for poor outcome of HEU babies in South Africa.  With information gained from these proposed studies, we hope to be able to subsequently test interventions to protect these very vulnerable children during the first year of life, when most of the fatal infections occur.

TitreApplicationTitle: Outcome toolkit for children who use power mobility
Keywords-MotsClés: OUTCOME MEASUREMENT; PAEDIATRIC; PARTICIPATION; POWER MOBILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Many children with disorders such as cerebral palsy, acquired brain injury, neuromuscular diseases, or spinal cord injury, have limited ability to move about (mobility). It is estimated that 25,000 children under 15 years in Canada have a mobility limitation. Many use manual wheelchairs or electric wheelchairs (power mobility). Although estimates are not available for children, it is believed that a large number of the >150,000 Canadians who rely on wheelchairs are children.       Providing power mobility at an early age for children who lack the ability to move on their own promotes healthy development, but the impact on participation is unknown. Participation in meaningful life activities (like play and learning) builds confidence, develops skill, helps with getting along with others, and ultimately increases growth and independence. Therapists help children choose equipment to assist them in doing the activities they want or need to do. Therapists use outcome measures to prioritize goals, monitor progress and evaluate success. It is unclear what outcomes are important, or what tools to use to assess the impact of power mobility on participation. The high cost of providing power mobility equipment ($5,000 to $50,000) requires decisions based on solid information to ensure resources are used appropriately.        A two-phase study will develop and evaluate a toolkit of measures that will assist all involved in determining how power mobility affects participation for children. Phase 1 will use a three-round process to identify and confirm the important factors and outcome measures to use. Phase 2 will determine the reliability and validity of those measures. Results will provide tools to evaluate the impact of power mobility on participation, helping people make informed decisions about power mobility use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the molecular mechanism in hereditary cytoplasmic body myopathy with early respiratory failure: implications for understanding ventilatory failure in muscular dystrophies
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS; HEREDITARY CYTOPLASMIC BODY MYOPATHY; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; NEUROMUSCULAR DISEASE; RESPIRATORY FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: Hereditary cytoplasmic body myopathy with early respiratory failure (HCBM) is a hereditary muscle disease which selectively affects muscles required for breathing, early in its disease course (among other select muscles). Respiratory dysfunction also occurs in other muscle diseases but it is not understood why some diseases involve the respiratory muscles more than others.  The genetic basis of HCBM has not yet been discovered, and will be studied from DNA samples and muscle tissue from patients with this condition. Once the gene is identified we will study the protein produced by this gene. We will explore to what extent different muscles contain this protein, and where the protein acts within the cell. Further study will be dedicated to understanding the role of this protein in other muscle diseases, to see if this protein is implicated in respiratory failure in other, more common muscle diseases. Using specialized techniques, the gene expression profile of HCBM will be studied and compared with other muscle diseases to see if this provides insight to the mechanism of respiratory muscle failure in these conditions.  Respiratory failure is the most important cause of mortality and morbidity in muscle disease. Potentially, the study of this condition will improve our knowledge of the development of respiratory failure in a number of muscle diseases, and identify targets for prevention and treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Influence of Environmental Contaminants on Human Reproduction
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMONITORING; COHORT STUDY; DISCRETE-TIME SURVIVAL ANALYSIS; ENVIRONMENTAL CONTAMINANTS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; FECUNDITY; FERTILITY; HUMAN REPRODUCTION; PRINCIPAL COMPONENT ANALYSIS; TIME TO PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: The consequences of exposures to environmental contaminants on human reproduction have become a key public policy issue, particularly given studies showing deleterious effects at levels considered low and experienced in general populations.  The fertility rates have declined during the last decades, which besides to social changes in desired family sizes and the use of contraceptive methods, may be attributed to the adverse effects of Environmental contaminants.  The goal of my research is to assess the potential of environmental contaminants to affect human reproduction.  The biological capacity for reproduction is known as fecundity. Fecundity will be measured by the time required for the women to achieve pregnancy. Women's who are unable to conceive within 6 months and within 12 months of trying will be identified and considered to have fecundity impairments. Fecundity impairments have been independently associated with increased risk of adverse perinatal outcomes such as low birth weight and preterm birth.  The primary groups of environmental exposures included in my research are: 1.) Metals, 2.) Plasticizers, surfactants, and flame retardants, 3.) Pesticides and persistent organic pollutants, and 4.) Passive exposure to tobacco smoke. A growing body of the literature suggest these compounds may exert effects on human reproduction; however, definitive data are lacking serving as the impetus for this research project. My research project will take advantage of the ongoing MIREC national pregnancy cohort study to address this issue.  Preconception exposure to the selected environmental contaminants will be estimated using a proxy measure based on questionnaires and biological measures performed on blood and urine samples obtained in the first trimester of pregnancy. Knowledge generated in this research project will allow policy makers to formulate sound strategies to reduce potentially harmful chemical exposures to women during their reproductive years.

TitreApplicationTitle: ED-directed interventions to improve guideline compliance after asthma exacerbations.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA EXACERBATIONS; COMPLIANCE; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; GUIDELINES; INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Despite improved understanding of asthma mechanisms and the risk factors associated with exacerbations, asthma continues to represent one of the leading causes of Emergency Department (ED) visits which result in significant health care costs. Our studies have suggested that most Canadian emergency physicians follow the recommendations contained within the current guidelines; however, follow-up care by primary care physicians (PCP) after ED visits for exacerbations is delayed (~30%). Ineffective reassessment, treatment adjustment and patient monitoring after an asthma exacerbation could leave patients at increased risk for future loss of asthma control.  The objective of this study is to determine if simple guidance provided to PCPs increases compliance with current ambulatory treatment guidelines and improve asthma control.   This randomized controlled trial will include asthmatics 18-55 years of age with no evidence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Patients will be eligible if they visit EDs in Edmonton and Calgary and receive treatment that results in discharge. All patients should have a PCP with whom to follow-up and will be prescribed systemic and inhaled corticosteroids (ICS). While in the ED patients will be divided into: Intervention group: PCPs will receive a personalized faxed letter signed by a local opinion leader describing their patient's ED visit for asthma and will be provided with guidance about the role of ICS, asthma education and regular follow-up. Standard care group: PCPs will receive a faxed ED patient record without advice. All patients will receive a Discharge Plan and will be told to review asthma management with their PCP. Phone calls will be performed at 30 and 90 days to compare relapses, symptoms improvement, follow-up and hospitalizations; and patients' health-related quality of life. This work will provide ED and PCP with an opportunity to decrease management gaps and base their practice on the highest level of evidence.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Immune Biomarkers that Predict Influenza in the Nursing Home Elderly
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOMARKERS; IMMUNOSENESCENCE; INFLUENZA; NURSING HOME ELDERLY
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza infection is a major threat to the health of residents of nursing homes. Ninety percent of deaths from influenza occur in the elderly and half of these deaths occur in residents of nursing homes. Despite high rates of influenza vaccination, outbreaks in nursing homes continue to lead to death and complications. It is hypothesized that the increased risk of infection stems from an aging immune system. It is known that immune system parameters change with age and these altered parameters (also referred to as immune biomarkers) can be used to predict frailty and death. However, it is unknown whether immune biomarkers can predict risk of influenza infection. The goal of this study is to identify immune biomarkers that predict influenza infection in nursing home residents. To accomplish this goal, we will enrol 1800 nursing home residents over three influenza seasons. Residents will be eligible to participate in the study if they are over 65 years, if they receive the seasonal influenza vaccine and if they are not taking medications that affect the immune system. Blood for immune cell analysis will be obtained in the fall, prior to the influenza season.  Residents will be closely monitored throughout the influenza season. In the event of respiratory symptoms, a nose swab will be obtained, and tested in the laboratory for influenza. The immune biomarkers of residents who acquire influenza will be compared to residents who do not acquire influenza. This study aims to establish an effective way of identify nursing home residents at highest risk for influenza infection. These residents may benefit from heightened surveillance for influenza and alternative prevention strategies such as preventative anti-influenza medications. In addition, this research will further our understanding of how the aging immune system predisposes the elderly to influenza infection; a critical step in developing more effective preventative strategies in the elderly.

TitreApplicationTitle: Do patients who exhibit serious bleeds on anti-platelet therapy have a previously undiagnosed defect in platelet function?
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIPLATELET THERAPY; ASPIRIN; BLEEDING RISK; CHRONIC KIDNEY FAILURE; CLOPIDOGREL; INDIVIDUALIZED TREATMENT; PERIPHERAL ARTERY DISEASE; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; PLATELET FUNCTION TESTING; THROMBOTIC RISK
Abstract-Résumé: Blood-thinning therapy is important among patients at an increased risk of acute ischemic events, such as a heart attack or stroke. Numerous studies have shown that responses to antithrombotic therapy are variable. Patients who are "resistant" to such drugs are at an increased risk of acute ischemic events, while those responding too strongly to the drugs may be at an increased risk of bleeding.  Platelet function testing holds the promise of individualizing antithrombotic treatment to the specific needs of individual patients, allowing precise dosing of medications so to prevent clot formation in blood without needlessly increasing the risk of bleeding.  However, how to interpret platelet function testing results remains an unresolved issue, particularly in patients suffering from peripheral artery disease, chronic kidney disease or diabetes, in whom the clinical efficacy of antithrombotic drugs remains largely understudied, despite a significantly increased risk of suffering from acute ischemic events.  This project aims to increase knowledge about antithrombotic therapy in peripheral artery disease, chronic kidney disease and diabetes, and the usefulness of point-of-care platelet function testing in the clinic to identify poor and pronounced responders to antithrombotic therapy. The efficacy of alternative treatments in selected patients with a poor response will be evaluated. Whether functional platelet testing can identify individuals at an increased risk of bleeding during antithrombotic therapy will be assessed.  As antithrombotic therapy involves balancing thrombosis (an insufficient effect) and bleeding (an excessive effect), testing of antithrombotic drug efficacy in order to individualize dosages is attractive. The outcomes of this project may provide means to improve the efficacy and safety of antithrombotic therapy in all patients, and most particularly in those at the highest ischemic and bleeding risks.

TitreApplicationTitle: Filaggrin and epidermal differentiation complex gene mutations in peanut allergy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANAPHYLAXIS; ATOPY; ECZEMA; FILAGGRIN; GENETICS; HYPERSENSITIVITY; IMMUNOLOGY; LOSS-OF-FUNCTION MUTATION; PEANUT ALLERGY; SKIN BARRIER
Abstract-Résumé: Peanut allergy can be a severe and life-threatening disease.  Peanuts and peanut derivatives are ubiquitous; peanut derivatives are not only present in food, but also in cosmetics, skin care products and even medication.  Prevalence of allergy in the general population may be increasing, and despite education and preventative measures, accidental peanut ingestions and use of epinephrine are still common.  Much of the research in peanut allergy has focused primarily on natural history, diagnosis, and management of this disease.  It is well known that allergic tendencies including asthma, eczema, and hayfever (allergic rhinitis) run in families, and that the prevalence of peanut allergy is increased in siblings and twins.  Our current project is investigating mutations in a gene encoding a protein called filaggrin.  A mutation in the gene, leading to a loss of its function, has been found in approximately half of studied cases of atopic eczema (also known as atopic dermatitis), and is involved in normal development and function of the skin.  People with defects in one or two copies of the gene for this protein often have dry skin, eczema, and also allergies to food and aeroallergens. This gene is a strong area of interest in peanut allergy and other food allergies, as people affected by peanut allergy often have eczema.  A defect in the skin barrier could potentially allow large protein molecules, such as the peanut allergen, to penetrate and cause the immune system to become sensitized.
