TitreApplicationTitle: Biomarkers of heart failure in adults with congenital heart disease: towards personalized medicine
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; GENOMICS; HEART FAILURE; MICROARRAY; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: With advances in surgical and procedural techniques, cardioprotection, and perioperative care in recent decades, increasing numbers of patients with congenital heart disease are surviving to adulthood. Many patients with congenital heart disease unfortunately develop heart failure, which is characterized by the inability of the heart to meet the body's demand for oxygen and nutrients. They can also have a reduced exercise tolerance and become short of breath with exercise. Studies have shown that these patients have a high mortality rate as well as poor quality of life. So far, there is no unified way to diagnose heart failure in adults with congenital heart disease, especially at an early stage. There is also no proven treatment for this disease. The goal of this project is to discover biomarkers which can help diagnose heart failure in this unique complex and growing population of patients with congenital heart disease. This will allow us to understand the unique pathways that lead to heart failure in this patient population. Understanding this disease is the first step toward developing personalized diagnostic methods and treatments for patients with congenital heart disease and heart failure. We will use two approaches to discover congenital heart disease and heart failure biomarkers. In the systems biology approach, we will search for key targets. Microarray technology will enable us to measure the activity of tens of thousands of genes simultaneously. We plan to compare gene expression of healthy individuals to those with different groups of congenital heart defects with heart failure using microarray analysis. This will allow us to find unique changes in gene expression and ultimately biological pathways related to heart failure in this adult population. Our second approach is candidate gene approach. From work previously done in our laboratory, there are a few targets that we suspect are important for heart failure in adults with congenital heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rx&D Renewal: Study of tumor dendritic cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER BIOLOGY; DENDRITIC CELLS; ONTOGENY; TUMOR IMMUNOLOGY; TUMOR VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: The failure of the body's immune system to kill cancer cells is a major factor in cancer development and progression. This problem of tumor tolerance also contributes to the poor success of cancer vaccines and cancer immunotherapy. Dr. Cattral's research team is studying a specialized population of white blood cells, called dendritic cells (DC).  Dr. Cattral's laboratory was the first to find and characterize the cells that become DC in mice. A similar cell population in humans has been isolated recently by his team.  These precursor cells, named pre-DC, originate in bone marrow and travel throughout the body and into tumors. The discovery of pre-DC has made it possible for the first time to study how tumors affect DC development. His team has made the exciting discovery that tumors cause pre-DC to develop into tolerogenic DC that block the immune system from killing tumor cells.    Dr. Cattral's laboratory is using tumor models in mice to study DC development from pre-cDC.  In the first aim, Dr Cattral's team will examine how the tumor causes pre-cDC to become tolerogenic DC.  Their previous studies have already provided important clues as to which molecules are important. They will perform studies to define more precisely how these molecules work inside the cell. In the second aim, Dr. Cattral's team will study how tolerogenic DC harm the immune systems ability to kill cancer cells.  They will examine ways to improve cancer therapy by blocking development of tolerogenic DC.  In the third aim, they will study the effects of human cancer on DC development.  This will allow them to confirm that the findings discovered in mice are translatable to humans.   The studies proposed are important for several reasons:  First, they will establish how DC develop in tumors; Second, they will help us understand which tumor DC cause tolerance; and third, they will allow us to identify new therapeutic targets and improve vaccines to treat and cure cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biomarkers of Disease Activity and Progression in IgA Nephropathy
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING : RHOA/AKT/ERK/EGF RECEPTOR; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; MESANGIAL CELL; PROTEINURIA; PROXIMAL TUBULE CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Over six thousand Canadians develop end stage renal disease (ESRD) each year requiring either dialysis treatment or kidney transplantation.  Diseases of the filter of the kidney (the glomerulus) account for the majority of cases of ESRD. The current proposal will focus on one of the most common diseases of the kidney filter: IgA Nephropathy (IgAN). The clinical course of IgAN is notoriously variable although almost 40% of patients will eventually develop ESRD. The goal of the proposed research program is to identify proteins in the urine that will enable doctors to more accurately predict the clinical course of IgAN and in particular to identify both "high risk" and "low risk" patients. The experimental approach is based on the measurement of gene expression in kidney tissue from patients with IgAN that we have already performed, and the proteins from two gene sets will be targeted for measurement in the urine of subjects with IgAN. The gene sets are linked to measures of kidney function. In order to perform these studies we will utilize a biobank of kidney tissue samples and urine samples linked to a database of long-term clinical data. Ultimately the identification of a set of proteins in the urine related to good clinical outcomes and bad clinical outcomes in our database should enable us to identify "high risk" and "low risk" at the time of diagnosis. The identification of "high risk" individuals will influence treatment decisions and facilitate early interventions designed to prevent progression to ESRD. Similarly, the identification of "low risk" individuals - those likely to have a benign course regardless of intervention - will also influence treatment decisions and spare patients from the toxicity of unnecessary therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: New Targets in Vascular Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; ENDOTHELIAL CELL; INFLAMMATION; RESTENOSIS; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELL; STENT; VASA VASORUM
Abstract-Résumé: Maintaining blood vessels in a state of health is an important ongoing process. Unhealthy blood vessels can block and prevent blood flow to vital organs such as the heart and brain, thereby causing heart attacks, strokes and sometimes death. Blood vessels to vital organs can often be re-opened by implanting a metal (scaffold) tube known as a stent. Most of the time, these stents also contains a drug that is slowly released into the blood vessel wall to try to prevent repeat blockages - but in some cases the drug is toxic and damages the blood vessel wall. In this proposal we will determine if a naturally occurring protein known as HSP27 can be loaded on a stent to provide a safer, long-term result. As well, we will examine how the deeper layers of the blood vessel wall respond to drug coated stents - as there is some concern that this layer is particularly susceptible to damage from the drug-coated stent. Finally, as new biodegradable stents (devices that "melt" in the blood vessel over time) are now being assessed in patients we will look towards devising new drug therapies that could be added to these stents in order to keep the blood vessel healthy after the stent has dissolved.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antithrombotics in atrial fibrillation: shared decision-making using incremental net-benefit analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICOAGULATION; ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; INCREMENTAL NET-BENEFIT ANALYSIS; RISK-BENEFIT ANALYSIS; SHARED DECISION-MAKING
Abstract-Résumé: The motive of this proposed research is to promote safe medication use and to advocate shared decision-making in medical practice. At the moment, we have plenty of data on emerging blood-thinning drugs in stroke prevention for patients with AF. However, clinical decisions on most appropriate therapy cannot be made because there has not been any direct comparison made among those drugs. This is potentially dangerous as the misuse of new therapies may lead to increased bleeding incidence without much benefit in stroke risk reduction. By utilizing novel statistical modeling, the result of this research will fill this knowledge gap and allow clinicians to communicate the expected risk and benefit with each of the new blood-thinning therapies to patients. This is crucial in the shared decision-making model (medical decision made jointly by physicians and patients together) as the result of proposed analysis will incorporate the patient's preference on benefit-harm trade-offs. The implication of having patients involved in choosing their medication regimen with physicians is a better quality of prescribing, improved compliance to the chosen therapy and decreased incidence of bleeding associated with blood-thinning drugs in patients with AF. The result of the proposed research will not only permit direct comparisons of different blood-thinning agents used for stroke prevention in patients with AF, it will also provide a unique opportunity to assess and evaluate a risk-benefit tool which has the potential to be applied to other therapeutic areas in cardiovascular diseases. It could provide the standard for assessing costly pharmacotherapeutic approaches by funders and decision-makers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modeling and mapping microbial diversity and function with marker genes, genomes and metagenomes
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; METAGENOMICS; MICROBIOMICS; MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Microbiomics is a new science, born of molecular ecology and metagenomics. Molecular ecology uses specific marker genes amplified from environmental DNA samples to tell the microbiologist "Who is there?" -- what species occupy a particular site on or in the human body, for instance. Metagenomics looks at all the genes in an environmental DNA sample, thus providing a wealth of information about metabolic process (and disease processes) that might be under way there -- an answer to "What can they do?"  Most large microbiomic projects will generate both kinds of information but our models for understanding one in terms of the other are as yet limited, and our ability to go from either to solid predictive knowledge -- "What will they do?" -- is limiting. Our project seeks to improve predictive ability through computational modeling and the bioinformatic analysis of available metagenomic data sets, and to produce a suite of software tools that should be of great use to many of the projects undertaken by the Canadian Microbiome Initiative.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; BACTERIA; BACTERIOPHAGE; COMMUNITY STRUCTURE; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; FUNGI; LUNG INFECTIONS; METAGENOMICS; NEXT-GENERATION GENOMICS; POPULATION DYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is the most common fatal genetic disease among individuals of European descent. One out of every 2500 babies are born with the disease, and 1 of 25 individuals carry a recessive CF allele. The most common cause of death for CF patients is due to respiratory problems associated with repeated episodes of bacterial infection of the airways. We will characterize the composition and dynamics of the microbial communities found in the CF lung during the progression of the disease and the initiation of antibiotic treatment via metagenomics and novel next-generation-genomics approaches. Our long-term goal is to establish guide-lines to assist clinicians in the design and selection of therapies tailored for individual patients based on their clinical status and the specific nature of the infectious community. We will do this via a longitudinal study focused on characterizing the community of bacteria, fungi, and viruses (bacteriophages) infecting the CF lung. We will also study much finer level population dynamics of two key bacterial and one fungal species commonly associated with clinical exacerbations, and monitor metabolic diversity and integron-associated antibiotic resistance through directed sequencing and genome sampling of total DNA isolated from the CF lung via and next-generation genomic sequencing.

Abstract-Résumé: Microbial colonization of the intestine during infancy influences the development of the immune system. Environmental factors that alter the composition or succession of the normal gut microbiota may increase the risk of childhood asthma and allergic disease. Compared to infants born in regions where atopic disease is uncommon, infants in countries with high prevalence rates of atopic disease have lower levels of intestinal bacteria, such as lactobacilli or bifidobacteria. Several studies including ours have linked antibiotic use in early infancy to the development of asthma and atopy in childhood. Antibiotic-induced gut dysbiosis is the proposed mechanism underlying these associations. Our team will use the Canadian Healthy Infant Longitudinal Development (CHILD) Study as a platform to assess the risk factors and outcomes from changes in gut microbiota based on fecal samples collected at 3 time points. Microbiota will be measured qualitatively by high throughput signature gene sequencing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of the Microbiota on Immune Development and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: 16S RRNA; ANTIBIOTICS; ASTHMA; ATOPIC DISEASES; COHORT STUDY; IMMUNE DEVELOPMENT; MICROBIOTA; NORMAL FLORA; TH1/TH2; WHEEZING
Abstract-Résumé: There is increasing evidence that intestinal microbiota impact on immune development and disease.  Allergic asthma is an ever-increasing problem in developed countries and affects up to 20% of all Canadians.  Although there are many theories about the potential cause of asthma, the actual causes remain undefined. Recent evidence suggests that shifts in resident microbiota (normal flora) may play a significant role in atopic diseases such as asthma (the so-called hygiene hypothesis. However, the role of the gastrointestinal microbiota in asthma has not been explored experimentally, and no attempt has been made to identify microbial populations affecting asthma. We propose to assemble a strong interdisciplinary team to explore the contribution of the microbiota to immune development and the atopic disease asthma in both murine and human hosts.  We will employ a well-characterized murine model of asthma to determine how the microbiota affects this disease by varying the microbiota using different antibiotics.  The murine immune responses will be monitored following these microbiota shifts.  Moreover, as part of the CHILD longitudinal cohort study, immune analysis will be performed on samples taken from children from birth until 1 year of age.  In correlation with these studies, the composition of the intestinal microbiota will be characterized, and correlated with atopic diseases, as well results from the murine studies. Applied ethical questions associated with these results will also be studied.  Collectively, these approaches will provide key information about the role of the intestinal microbiota in immune development and atopic diseases such as asthma. It will also bring together investigators with very different skills all working on a common problem.  Ultimately this information could be used to develop new ways of treating asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Vaginal Microbiome Project Team
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS; GYNECOLOGY; INFECTION; MICROBIOME; PRETERM BIRTH; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Recent advances in genomic sequencing and bioinformatics have provided adequate tools to investigate the human microbiome, and the opportunity for Canadian research teams to uniquely contribute to deciphering the role that microbes play in health and disease. Studies of the human vaginal microbiome represent a niche area where Canada has significant expertise, research capacity, and preexisting infrastructure upon which to build. The Vaginal Microbiome Project Team - VMPT - will place Canada at the forefront of research into the role of vaginal bacterial communities in health and disease. While our current collaboration represents an established scientific and clinical program, success in this competition will allow the extended team to not only identify the bacterial species present under various conditions over a woman's lifespan, but develop novel diagnostic tools and interventions to restore and retain health. Major research themes will continue with understanding of the core vaginal microbiome, but also explore the associations behind vaginal microbiota and preterm delivery, genital tract infection, and reproductive health.  Conditions associated with an imbalance in vaginal microbiota afflict several million Canadian women each year, and accumulate health care costs of billions of dollars annually. The Emerging Team Grant will lead to significant breakthroughs in the care of women in Canada and around the world.

Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affect more than 200,000 Canadians. The cause of IBD is thought to involve interactions between genetically determined immune responses to environmental challenges such as gut bacteria. We have started a prospective study of healthy people genetically at risk of developing Crohn's disease. This study will allow us to determine the differences in genes, environment exposure and gut bacteria that determine the cause of Crohn's disease. In collecting these healthy first degree relatives we will now be able to define the effect of genes on gut bacteria healthy people that carry the Crohn's disease risk genes. We think that the composition of the gut bacteria is influenced by genes. To understand this we propose to; 1- characterize changes in the gut bacteria i.e. the Microbiome in healthy subjects carrying genetic mutations known to increase the risk of CD; 2-define the gene content (metagenomic analysis) of these bacteria influenced by CD genes; 3- identify and isolate specific organisms related to the metagenomic signals. The proposal will focus on a very unique collection of healthy subjects carrying genes involve din the risk of developing Crohn's disease. The relationships between the host genes and gut bacteria are key to the maintenance of health and alterations may well be at the root of the cause of disease. The findings will be critical to developing strategies for prevention or treatment of IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Respiratory tract microbiome dynamics and the interplay of commensal bacteria with resident pathogens
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; HUMAN AIRWAY MICROBIOME; IMMUNOSENESCENCE; INNATE IMMUNITY; METAGENOMICS; PNEUMONIA; POLYMICROBIAL INFECTIONS; RESPIRATORY INFECTIONS; STREPTOCOCCUS
Abstract-Résumé: All exposed surfaces of the human body harbour a rich community of microorganisms such that there are more bacterial cells on or in the human body than there are human cells.  In general these are beneficial (commensal) bacteria that are essential for health.  When the normal balance of organisms in these communities is disrupted or when they get to body sites where they are not supposed to be, they can cause disease.  In addition, lurking among the commensal bacteria are pathogens.  Their numbers are held in check by the commensals and host defences, yet opportunities may present where they can cause an infection.  This is particularly true of the upper airways (nose, throat, mouth, pharynx and sinuses) that carry bacteria that are pathogens of the lower airways (lungs).  Many pathogenic bacteria such as Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Haemophilus and Neisseria are commonly found in healthy individuals without causing disease. The focus of this application will be to define the normal microbiota in the respiratory tract and investigate how these commensal bacteria inhibit or activate the pathogens.  Understanding these interactions may lead to new ways to control these pathogens.  In many chronic airway infections (such as in cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis) multiple bacterial species contribute to disease including pathogens missed by conventional clinical microbiology.  This study will also examine the microbiology of these infections.

Abstract-Résumé: Cancer cells have unusual metabolism of sugars, fats and amino acids that allows then to survive and grow rapidly into tumours.  This rapid metabolism of fat is proposed to allow cancer cells to make more membranes that are required for growth and cell division.  One such fatty molecule that makes up the majority of membranes is phosphatidylcholine or 'PC'. We will examine how cancer cells make PC compared to normal cells, and whether the altered metabolism of PC in cancer cells is responsible for their unusually rapid growth and ability to grow under conditions that kill normal cells.  These studies will provide fundamental insights into the relationship between fat metabolism and cell growth that could be used in the treatment or management of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: MIER1 alpha, a novel PPAR gamma co-regulator, and its role in adipogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTE FUNCTION; ADIPOGENESIS; CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT MICE; DIABETES; FAT METABOLISM; GENE EXPRESSION; MICROARRAY; PPAR GAMMA; PROTEIN INTERACTION; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATOR
Abstract-Résumé: The alarming rate of increase in obesity in Western society has led to a significant increase in obesity-related disorders including type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease and certain types of cancer. Society's approach to dealing with obesity requires multifaceted efforts at many levels, from public health and education to a complete understanding of fat metabolism at the cellular and molecular level. The fat cells in our body, the adipocytes, are the pivotal players in fat storage and metabolism. A molecule called PPAR gamma in these cells is a "master" regulator that controls adipocyte number, size and function.  We have discovered a critical modulator of PPAR gamma called mesoderm induction early response 1 alpha (MIER1 alpha) and our preliminary work provides evidence that knocking out MIER1 alpha significantly reduces the number of fat cells that form. Our hypothesis is that MIER1 alpha is crucial for adipocyte formation and function. This proposal outlines key experiments that will determine the role of MIER1 alpha in developing and mature human adipose tissue. We believe that MIER1 alpha has the potential to provide a novel target for the design of therapeutic drugs for the treatment of obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of genetic factors correlated with survival in colorectal cancer: Investigation of genetic markers from angiogenesis/lymphangiogenesis and metastasis pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS/LYMPHANGIOGENESIS; COLORECTAL CANCER; GENETIC MARKERS (SNPS); METASTASIS; PROGNOSIS AND SURVIVAL IN CANCER PATIENTS; SURVIVAL ANALYSES
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer survival is modified by a variety of factors, including genetic factors. Identification of these genetic factors plays a critical role in selection of appropriate treatment regimen and delivering the most effective medical care to patients. Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer in Canada and only 65% of the patients survive the first 5 years after the diagnosis. However, majority of the genetic factors influencing survival in colorectal cancer is currently unknown.  Generation of new blood and lymph vessels around tumors and tumor metastasis (i.e. spread to other parts of the body) are two main biological processes directly involved in tumor growth and its spread to distant sites in the body. In this study, we hypothesize that the genes involved in these processes are directly related to survival in colorectal cancer patients. Accordingly, here we aim to investigate the genetic correlation of genes involved in generation of new blood and lymph vessels as well as metastasis in relation to survival in colorectal cancer by obtaining genetic profiles in patients, followed by statistical analyses. Once confirmed, the results of this study may be used to select the best possible treatment for each colorectal cancer patient. Therefore, by expediting a personalized medicine approach, results of this study may improve the patient survival in colorectal cancer.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOTENSIN; ARRHYTHMIAS; CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW; HEMORRHAGIC STROKE; HYPERTENSION; RENAL FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of my research is to understand the mechanisms that are involved in producing hemorrhagic stroke and to try to develop treatment therapies that can be used to help prevent death and disability after this stroke develops.  There is a special breed of rats that I possess (SHRsp) that develop hemorrhagic stroke at a very young age.  Like humans, when these rats develop hemorrhagic stroke they end up dying within one and a half weeks.  I have found that if you treat these rats after stroke with drugs which either prevent the formation of a molecule call AII (captopril) or alternatively with a drug that prevents AII from acting on the cells (losartan) then the rats will not die.  They recover from stroke and look normal.  The drug that prevents AII from acting on the cells (losartan) works much better than the drug that prevents the formation of AII (captopril).  My research is aimed at trying to understand the role that AII plays in promoting stroke and death after stroke and to further understand how the two drugs act to prevent death and disability after hemorrhagic stroke.  In addition I want to understand why one drug works better than the other with the hope that I can develop the best therapy for this type of stroke.

Keywords-MotsClés: FAMILY AND POPULATION STUDIES; GENE MAPPING AND CLONING; GENE-GENE INTERACTIONS; GENETICS OF DEAFNESS; GENOTYPE-PHENOTYPE CORRELATION; ISOLATED POPULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Otosclerosis is a type of conductive hearing loss that affects adults in their 20s-30s and may progress to profound hearing loss. It is caused by abnormal overgrowth of the tiny bones in the middle ear, causing these normally mobile bones to "freeze". In some cases, this type of hearing loss runs in families and is passed on generation after generation.  For a diagnosis of otosclerosis, a doctor (ears, nose and throat specialist) has to exclude all other diseases that may cause the progressive hearing loss s/he observes in the patient. If the diagnosis is correct, a surgical procedure (a stapedectomy) can completely restore hearing. Genetic studies are underway in families with otosclerosis to identify the genes causing the abnormal bone growth in order to provide a genetic test that can quickly provide an accurate diagnosis and patients who would benefit from surgery and to understand why it happens so preventative therapies can be developed.

Keywords-MotsClés: CARE TRANSITIONS; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; GENDER ANALYSIS; INSTITUTIONAL ETHNOGRAPHY; LONG-TERM CARE; NURSING HOME RESIDENTS
Abstract-Résumé: There are a number of problems that are known to occur when residents of long-term care (LTC) facilities transfer to a hospital Emergency Department (ED) and later return to LTC. Assumptions about roles and miscommunicaton between staff of both care settings regularly occur and result in medical errors and fragmented care. These negative outcomes are of particular concern to women who comprise a large portion of the LTC care population and of the caregivers in both LTC and the ED.  Although our knowledge of older women's health is increasing, little is known about the role gender plays in the transitional experiences of older adults who move between settings of care.        In this research, a gendered analysis of resident transfers between LTC and a hospital ED will be conducted.  Findings from this study will help refine or develop new clinical practice strategies that will support older women and the health care providers who care for them during their care transitions.  Findings will contribute to a more efficient use of precious health care resources.  Because this research also involves a detailed examination of Institutional Ethnography, it will  strengthen our ability to understand the everyday experiences of people in a wide range of health situations, including, but not limited to, those who transition between other healthcare settings and providers.

Keywords-MotsClés: ATTITUDES AND BEHAVIOURS; COMPETENCY DEVELOPMENT; EDUCATIONAL REQUIREMENTS OF HEALTH CARE PROVIDERS; ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORD INTEGRATION; HEALTH INFORMATICS; HUMAN-COMPUTER INTERACTION; RESPONSIVENESS TO CHANGE
Abstract-Résumé: Health information technology (HIT) is a term used to describe the collection and management of information in a variety of healthcare environments. There is a rise in the use of HIT within health care settings.  An electronic health record (EHR) is one example of a HIT that is being introduced world-wide. The main goal of an EHR is to enhance the sharing of patient information and clinical practice knowledge amongst members of health care teams. Functions of an EHR will help to improve the quality, safety and efficiency of health care delivery systems. It is clear that education and training are key factors in smoothing the transition process for health care providers (HCP) who are preparing to work with a new HIT; however, there is litter research about how best to educate HCP. Another area where there is little research is the link between the HCPs' understanding of how technology benefits health care delivery and their motivation to learn about new technologies within their own working environments.   The primary goal of my research is to enhance what is known about the learning needs of HCP who are preparing to work with a new EHR. The objectives are: 1) to improve what is known about the impact that factors as age and computer experience and the impact they have on the learning needs of HCP, and; 2) to explore the relationship between the HCPs' understanding of the usefulness of an EHR and their engagement in the necessary learning activities. My research findings will help with the introduction and use of an EHR in a variety of health care settings. New knowledge will inform the development and implementation of education and training strategies that are evidence-informed, and will minimize unnecessary costs while improving the quality and safety of care delivery systems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the genetic determinants of hypertriglyceridemia in cardiovascular disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; GENETICS; GENOMICS; HIGH THROUGPUT RESEQUENCING; HYPERTRIGLYCERIDEMIA; MICROARRAYS; RARE VARIANTS; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISMS; TRIGLYCERIDE METABOLISM
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic analysis of patients with severe disorders of triglyceride metabolism will help to identify those genes and molecular pathways that contribute to poor triglyceride metabolism and increased CVD risk. We propose a study that will model the genetic factors which lead to the accumulation of triglycerides in our blood, through the study of a genetic disease called hyperlipoproteinemia (HLP). Patients with HLP have blood triglyceride concentrations that are higher than 95% of the population, resulting from increases in different particles that carry triglycerides through our blood. Elevations in triglyceride concentrations to this range are only caused by genetic contributions, impossible to reach through poor diet alone. We study patients with extreme disorders of triglyceride metabolism to identify those genes and molecular pathways that are defective, resulting in their extremely high blood triglyceride levels.  Identification and further understanding of genes and biochemical pathways that regulate blood triglyceride concentrations in normal subjects will provide clues for improved prevention and treatment of CVD. Ultimately, our objectives are to identify new genes that are responsible for increasing triglyceride concentrations in patients with HLP, which by extension will explain how normal genetic variation increases CVD risk in normal populations and provide potential drug targets for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the determinants of adiposity among newborns of Indian ancestry in Canada and India.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH COHORT; CARDIOVASCULAR; CHILDHOOD; CULTURE; ENVIRONMEN; FETAL; GENETIC; MATERNAL; OBESITY; SOUTH ASIAN
Abstract-Résumé: Globally, people of South Asian origin (people from the Indian subcontinent) are one of the highest risk groups for the development of type 2 diabetes.   Accumulation of abdominal obesity among South Asians is common, and is associated with the development of increased glucose, abnormal lipids, and increased blood pressure. The predilection of South Asians to develop abdominal obesity may be influenced by pregnancy-related factors. The accumulation of body fat of the growing infant may be "programmed" during the development of the fetus during pregnancy.  When the newborn leaves the in-utero environment and is exposed to a new environment, the interactions between the programmed newborns and the new environment influence the accumulation of adiposity during childhood. In order to understand the development of adiposity among South Asians, we propose to study detailed characteristics of the mothers, their offsprings, their household environments, as well as their genetic profiles.  Specifically we propose to create three birth cohorts with 250 babies per cohort  in Canada, in Bangalore city in India, and from rural regions outside Bangalore. The overarching objective of this study is to understand the effect of diverse environments on the development of adiposity among the growing offspring during the first three years of age.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of the RhoA-Rho kinase system in Regulation of Myosin Light Chain Phosphorylation in Human Uterine Myocytes.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM SENSITIZATION; CELL SIGNALING; IN-CELL WESTERN; MYOMETRIUM; MYOSIN LIGHT CHAIN; OXYTOCIN; PHOSPHORYLATION; RHO-KINASE; RHOA; SMOOTH MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: In the days prior to human birth, the uterine smooth muscle (myometrium) acquires a markedly enhanced ability to contract in order to expel the fetus from the uterus. A likely mechanism for this might involve an enhancement of signaling mechanisms in the uterine muscle cells. The correct timing of birth thus may depend on these changes. In Canada, 7 to 10% of pregnancies end with preterm birth (PTB), which is responsible for 50% of all long-term disability and 75% of neonatal mortality arising from the birth process. Current strategies to prevent PTB have been unsuccessful in improving neonatal outcomes. The focus of this project is to improve our understanding of uterine muscle cells to direct development of new strategies to prevent PTB. Normally when labour begins, the fetus has had sufficient time to grow and develop, and is physiologically prepared to be separate from the mother. However in some cases, the uterus becomes activated prematurely; this places the fetus at risk of being expelled prior to reaching full development. We currently do not fully understand the causes of premature labour, but it is possible that early activation of the myometrium is at fault. Specifically, we will address the potential that hormones such as oxytocin, are capable of activating key proteins (rhoA and rho-kinase) that cause biochemical changes to occur within the force producing smooth muscle cells of the uterus. In the laboratory, we will prepare muscle cell cultures from biopsies of uterine smooth muscle that are obtained from consenting full-term patients, and where possible, from patients in preterm labour. We will employ molecular techniques to measure biochemical changes indicative of muscle cell activation, and we will compare these events between the two patient groups. These experiments will help our understanding of uterine physiology and may ultimately help explain the conditions that bring about premature labour.

Abstract-Résumé: This proposed 5-year program under the leadership of a collaborative Canada-India translational research team intends to support action on the ground in the development of a breakthrough approach to prevent childhood obesity. The main objective of the proposed program is to examine the behavioral, body weight and nutritional risk for childhood obesity and associated chronic consequences, and to build capacity in both Canada and India research teams to build synergy in their respective strengths. This project will also examine the degree to which individual differences in genetics and biology and differences in the environmental exposures modulate the behavioral, body weight and nutritional risk over time. Another component of the research program is designed to contribute to childhood obesity research and policy-making, as well as to business and social innovation to mainstream health as a driver or change in everyday life of individuals and communities these serve. This work aims to advance our understanding of how childhood obesity in the specific context of each of the Canada and India local communities, as well as in efforts at the state/province, national and global level to promote. All of these findings will contribute to a new science to help preventing obesity and chronic diseases.

Abstract-Résumé: Obesity in Indians is a major health issue both because of the large global population of Indians and their increased risk for obesity-related health consequences like diabetes and heart disease. Rates of childhood obesity and its consequences including high blood pressure, high blood sugar and high cholesterol are rising with urbanization. Understanding the behavioural and social and physical environmental causes of childhood obesity in Indian children living in diverse settings is an essential step to reducing obesity and improving health in this population whose practices and beliefs may require different solutions than Europeans. This study will evaluate characteristics of individuals, families, schools and communities that are associated with obesity, blood pressure, glucose and lipids in 7-8 and 14-15 year old Indian children living in 3 different settings: rural India, urban India and urban Canada. The findings will be used to develop obesity prevention strategies that are in line with the priorities of the communities involved.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of the Filamin Signaling Network's Function in Cancer Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL CYTOSKELETON; CELL INVASION; METASTASIS FORMATION; MOLECULAR AND CELLULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN DYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Excessive cell locomotion and motile properties are among the earliest events by which cancer cells can spread and invade distant organs (referred to as metastasis formation). Invasive cancer cell's movement and migration beyond their primary sites are controlled by sophisticated and dynamic networks of signaling molecules. In particular, the cancer cell cytoskeleton plays a predominant role in creating and coordinating the autonomous contractile and motile properties of invasive cancer cells. We have screened a large number of non-invasive and invasive human cancer cells and identified a cytoskeleton protein called filamin A to be expressed at low levels in invasive cancer cells compared to normal or non-invasive cancer cells. We have used a combination of molecular and biological assays, as well as animal cancer models to demonstrate that high levels of filamin A prevents cancer cell migration and invasion, while low levels promote cancer invasion and metastasis formation. The correlation between low levels of filamin A and cancer progression was also confirmed in cancer tissues from patients with various stages of breast cancer progression. The overall goal of this proposal is to establish the mechanisms by which filamin A controls cancer invasion. This will be examined in cell lines and in a mouse model where filamin A is inhibited selectively in the mammary gland. The long-term goal of this research is to translate the basic finding obtained into discovery of biomarkers for early detection of invasive cancers, as well as identification of targets that can serve to develop novel therapeutics for invasive cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Body composition and breast cancer related biomarkers
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPONECTIN; BODY COMPOSITION; DUAL X-RAY ABSORPTIOMETRY; ESTRADIOL; INSULIN; MAMMOGRAPHIC DENSITY; POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMEN; TESTOSTERONE
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women.  Most breast cancer occurs in the postmenopausal years.  Women with larger body size have a higher risk of developing breast cancer after menopause, but the reasons why involve many different factors.  There are several factors related both to body size and to breast cancer that likely explain some of this increased risk.  These factors include hormones related to reproduction such as estrogen and also those related to blood sugar levels such as insulin.  Body fat has different effects depending on where it is located such as around the waist or in the upper or lower body.  We plan to test whether a common method of assessing bone density, dual x-ray absorptiometry, which can also detect amounts of body fat in different parts of the body, can be used to tell us more about the specific factors putting individual women at risk.  Postmenopausal women being screened in the Ontario Breast Screening Program who are not taking hormones will be invited to participate in the study.  We will look for relationships between amounts of fat and non-fat tissue in different areas of the body and factors related to both body size and breast cancer such as estrogen, testosterone, insulin, and adiponectin and also breast tissue patterns seen on mammograms.  Ultimately we hope to better determine what puts an individual woman at risk so that a more individual plan for prevention can be developed.  That is, more detailed information about an individual woman's body composition may help us determine the specific factors putting her at risk of getting breast cancer and allow us to develop a specific strategy to reduce her risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional characterization of the NIMA-related kinase 10 (Nek10) in development and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS OF CANCER; CANCER; KNOCKOUT MICE; NEK10; PHOSPHORYLATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: In 2006, the most frequently diagnosed women's cancer in Canada was breast cancer. Recent search for new breast cancer susceptibility genes, involving over 40,000 patients and as many healthy controls, pinpointed Nek10, a gene which is a subject of this grant proposal, as a strong candidate. Our preliminary work indicates that the product of the Nek10 gene participates in regulation of cellular growth and their response to envirionmental challenges.   Mice represent some of the most valuable tools in modern cancer research, as they have been developed as faithful and highly informative models of human cancer. Importantly, mice are amenable to elaborate manipulation mimicking complex disease states, as well as therapeutic regimens. By generating a mouse deficient for Nek10, we aim explore the function of Nek10 during mouse development. Moreover, by breeding our Nek10-deficient mice with other, breast cancer-prone mouse strains, we will determine the effect of Nek10 loss on breast cancer development. Ultimately, our work will advance our understanding of breast and other cancers and benefit diagnostic and therapeutic efforts aimed at tumors with Nek10 alterations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of Shank-interacting protein-like 1 (SIPL1)-mediated PTEN inactivation during breast tumorigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; PI3-AKT SIGNALING; PTEN; PTEN NEGATIVE REGULATOR
Abstract-Résumé: PTEN is a critical tumour suppressor that prevents breast cancer formation. Clinical observations have shown that a loss of PTEN occurs in high percentages (up to 50%) of HER2-positive and basal-like breast cancers, the two subgroups that are associated with a poor outcome. However, our knowledge on how PTEN is inactivated in breast cancer is incomplete. We propose here that although a large proportion of breast cancers contain PTEN, the protein may not function properly. Consistent with our hypothesis, we identified a protein (called SIPL1) that reduces PTEN function. Furthermore, we demonstrated that SIPL1 inactivates PTEN in breast cancer cells and importantly, associates with a loss of PTEN function in primary breast cancers obtained directly from patients. This strongly suggests that SIPL1 inactivates PTEN during breast cancer formation. In this study, we will closely examine the relationship between SIPL1 and the loss of PTEN function in breast cancer as well as how SIPL1 reduces PTEN function during breast cancer formation. As the loss of PTEN function is a major cause of therapeutic failure for breast cancer, this research may lead to the development of novel diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for patients with breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparisons of CVD risk profiles in south Asian children in rural and urban India and Canada with Canadians of European origin
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOLOGY; CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; PEDIATRICS; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are the major contributors to global morbidity and mortality. South Asians have one of the highest risks for CVD in the world. This extremely high risk for CVD is also seen among migrants from the Indian subcontinent. We propose a study to document whether risk factors vary between children in rural and urban India compared to South Asian children and European children in Canada. The study aims to identify the cardiovascular risk profile of Indian children in three distinct settings (rural and urban India, and urban Canada) and compare the risk factors with European children in Canada. The study duration is 40 months and planned to be conducted simultaneously in India and Canada. The study population is 2400 school children in the age group of 9 -13 years. All children will be evaluated at the start of the study for cardiovascular risk factors by history, physical measurements, blood analysis as well as assessment for diet, physical activity and psychosocial factors. The children will be followed up for 24 months and re-evaluated at the end of the same. The information so collected will be utilized to develop culturally specific interventions that are relevant to each setting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vascular events In noncardiac Surgery patIents' cOhort evaluatioN study (VISION): Vascular Surgery Substudy and NT-proBNP Bio-bank Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BIO-BANK; BIOMARKERS; PERIOPERATIVE CARDIOVASCULAR MEDICINE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; VASCULAR EVENTS; VASCULAR SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide there are more than 200 million adults have major surgery every year, and millions of these patients will suffer a major vascular complication (i.e., death, heart attack, cardiac arrest, or stroke) in the first 30 days after their surgery.  Despite the magnitude of this problem, there are no known effective and safe interventions to accurately monitor, prevent or manage these events.            VISION is the world's largest international prospective perioperative cohort study including patients 45 years of age or older whom are undergoing noncardiac surgery that requires hospital admission.       The VISION Vascular Surgery Substudy will include approximately 5000 vascular surgery patients. The primary objectives of the VISION Vascular Surgery substudy are to determine the: 1) incidence of major vascular events at 30 days after surgery, 2) the optimal clinical model to predict major vascular events at 30 days after surgery; 3) proportion of patients 30 days after surgery with perioperative myocardial infarctions that may go undetected without troponin monitoring; and 4) relationship between postoperative troponin measurements and the 1 year risk of vascular death.         Secondly the VISION NT-proBNP Bio-bank Study will examine the prognostic capabilities of NT-proBNP in the postoperative period to predict cardiovascular events.  A recent small study has suggested that a postoperative elevation in the biomarker released from the heart called brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is able to identify patients who will experience major vascular complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental and social determinants of enhanced infectious mortality in HIV-Exposed but Uninfected (HEU) infants in South Africa.
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL DETERMINANTS; HIV; HIV EXPOSED UNINFECTED; INFECTIOUS MORTALITY; PROSPECTIVE COHORT
Abstract-Résumé: One and a half million babies are born to HIV-infected mothers every year. Due to the worldwide expansion of  highly effective strategies to prevent the spread of HIV infection from mothers to their babies   the vast majority are not themselves infected. Nonetheless these HIV-Exposed but Uninfected (HEU) babies are at greatly increased risk of death during the first year of life and appear to suffer from more infections and die more often than babies born to HIV-uninfected mothers. South Africa has the highest burden of HIV in the world with almost twenty five percent of newborn babies being HIV-exposed but uninfected. Several theories have been offered to explain the very poor health of these HEU babies, but none has been proven to be the sole one responsible.  Putative immunodeficiency combined with other factors, including for example poor maternal health, absence of breastfeeding, exposure to a higher burden of infectious diseases and social insecurity logically conspire to result in the observed increased morbidity and mortality.   The goal of this series of proposed studies is to identify the environmental and social explanation for poor outcome of HEU babies in South Africa.  With information gained from these proposed studies, we hope to be able to subsequently test interventions to protect these very vulnerable children during the first year of life, when most of the fatal infections occur.

TitreApplicationTitle: Child Health and Mortality in India: action at the sub-national level to improve national child survival
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD HEALTH; COVERAGE OF INTERVENTIONS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GLOBAL HEALTH; INEQUITIES; NEONATAL HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Many countries have experienced rapid declines in infant and child mortality in the last decades. Nevertheless, progress towards neonatal and child survival in low and middle income countries has been rather slow and mortality rates remain ten fold greater than the rates observed in higher income countries. In India, efforts to reduce child mortality have intensified recently. The National Rural Health Mission of the Government of India has initiated several interventions to increase child survival. Efforts have also been made to monitor India's maternal and child health indicators using large scale surveys. This research proposal will leverage the work of the Registrar General of India in collaboration with the Centre for Global Health Research that is producing the first estimates of cause-specific child mortality at the sub-national level by combining it with information from large scale sample surveys such as National Family Health Survey and District Level Household Survey that for the last decades has been collecting data on sub-national coverage of health interventions and prevalence of key health practices. The innovative and unique combination of these three impressive surveys will help India in identifying priority areas for action by contextualizing the barriers to child survival according to prevailing socio-cultural practices; quantifying the impact of targeted interventions by estimating the annual number of lives saved and estimating the impact that local action could have on India's national neonatal and child survival rates.

TitreApplicationTitle: Trans-Disciplinary Team Research and Training Program in Sleep and Biological Rhythms
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR; CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; DEVELOPMENT; METABOLISM; NEUROSCIENCE; RESPIRATION; SLEEP
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately one in four Canadians are affected by significant sleep problems that can diminish their health, alertness and safety.  Also, up to one in five Canadians works shifts and can suffer the consequences of poor sleep because of disruption of their biological clock. Insufficient or disrupted sleep is associated with a number of prevalent acute and chronic health problems including difficulties in breathing (sleep apnea), cardiovascular diseases (such as heart attacks, hypertension, stroke and heart failure), obesity, diabetes, cancer and depression. Prioritizing optimum sleep and adequate rest is now recognized as an essential part of well-being and health. However, understanding the mechanisms underlying the associations of sleep and biological clock disturbances in acute and chronic health problems is relatively new science.  Major advances in understanding the biology of sleep and circadian rhythm disorders and their consequences to health is best achieved by collaborative trans-disciplinary programs to increase the capacity for research, education and knowledge transfer. Such capacity building needs to occur beyond the boundaries of established disciplines that traditionally do not consider sleep or body rhythms, despite their established influence on health. Currently, the training of basic science and clinical researchers, health care and education professionals in sleep and biological rhythms related to health and disease is inadequate, largely because of the lack of educational curricula, formal training programs and collaborative research. This application will establish trans-disciplinary team research and a superior training program to bring new science, technologies, researchers and trainees into the field, and so establish the fields of sleep and biological rhythms in the mainstream of other scientific and clinical disciplines to promote health and well-being, and the better recognition and management of sleep problems and their consequences.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Age and Apnea on Cognitive and Sensorimotor Processes During Sleep and Wakefulness
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITION; NEUROPROTECTION; PLASTICITY; SENSORIMOTOR; SLEEP; SLEEP APNEA
Abstract-Résumé: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (and other breathing disorders) result in a substantial decrease in oxygenation of the brain, which results in the degeneration of neurons and corresponding deficits in function.  Since there is an additional reduction in the delivery of oxygen to the brain simply due to the aging process, the consequences of OSA are exacerbated to a significant extent in the elderly.  This Team Grant will bring together four established researcher and their co-workers to determine the damage that occurs in various brain areas due to periods of apnea and also develop a therapeutic agent to reduce or prevent the consequences of apnea during sleep and waking states in adulthood and old age.

TitreApplicationTitle: Respiratory Sleep Disorders Research Team
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR; GENETICS; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH SERVICES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PUBLIC HEALTH; SLEEP APNEA
Abstract-Résumé: Team Mission: Our goal is to discover new knowledge about the causes, consequences, diagnosis, and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) so that the well-being, health, and safety of patients with this disease can be improved.  OSA is a major health problem affecting over 1,000,000 Canadians. The disease is characterized by recurrent asphyxia due to collapse of the upper airway during sleep. This leads to low oxygen levels and recurrent arousal from sleep. OSA can cause disabling symptoms, increase health care utilisation, lead to motor vehicle crashes and injuries, predispose to cardiovascular disease, and lead to premature death.   We have assembled a 17-person innovative multidisciplinary research team that will comprehensively investigate the causes and consequences of OSA. This Team will include core sleep researchers, and experts in a number of different fields (e.g., genetics, cardiovascular risk, physiology, inflammation, occupational injuries, dissemination of knowledge). We intend to identify the genetic and anatomic predispositions to disease, identify biochemical markers that might predict important future events (e.g., future heart attacks), and identify disease pathways by studying human and animal models of sleep apnea. We also want to tackle OSA from a larger societal level, and thus the public health consequences (e.g. economic consequences, public safety) will also be a key area of investigation. Eventually, we want to develop new therapies, and clinical guidelines that will improve the care of our patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Better Nights/Better Days: Improving Psychosocial Health Outcomes in Children with Behavioural Insomnia
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL INSOMNIA; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PEDIATRIC SLEEP; PSYCHOSOCIAL OUTCOMES; WEB-BASED TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Up to 25% of children suffer from sleep problems that are referred to as 'behavioural insomnia'; that is, they have difficulty settling, falling asleep, and staying asleep. This leads to inappropriate daytime sleepiness and negatively effects behaviour, mood, and school performance. It also has negative effects on parents' sleep and their daytime functioning. Although there are methods for treating these problems, few children receive these treatments, and many get inappropriate treatments like medications. Only about 1% of children with insomnia are treated with the behavioural approaches that have been shown to work. The main reasons for this are that most parents are unaware of what the right treatments are, and most health care providers they contact do not have the training to provide these treatments. The Better Nights/Better Days Pediatric Sleep Team will address these barriers by developing, putting in place, and testing the usefulness of a sleep treatment program for children aged 1-10 years with behavioural insomnia that will be delivered over the internet, with added telephone support. This approach will make the treatment program available to the majority of parents whose children have insomnia. We will test whether parents make good use of this program and whether it is effective in improving sleep among children. We will also study whether improved sleep results in better daytime functioning for children and for the sleep and functioning of parents. We will provide information to health care providers on how to use this treatment program. This approach will help ensure that the program will continue after the proposed research study ends. The proposed research program will therefore address an important public health issue by creating new knowledge and by turning this knowledge into a better way of delivering health care, thereby improving the health and well-being of Canadian children and parents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and environmental predictors of tobacco, drug and alcohol addiction in adolescence and young adulthood: a lifecourse twin and population approach
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ADOLESCENT; BIOMARKERS; ENVIRONMENTAL INFLUENCES; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENETICS; SMOKING; YOUNG ADULTS
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal will focus on identifying genetic and environmental predictors of the acquisition, development and persistence of drug addiction and the amount of a drug consumed. We will take advantage of the wealth of data available from three datasets in two countries including twin, longitudinal and family cohorts. The subjects have been followed since childhood and surveyed for a variety of potential influences on drug addiction throughout childhood and into young adulthood. Within the three cohorts we are able to examine environmental, genetic (using a genome wide approach, followed by a detailed examination of specific genes identified, and epigenetic assessments) and biochemical (for amount of drug use and the speed the body gets rid of the drug) predictors as well as their interactions. Of particular note is that among the three cohorts we have extensive data from an intensive study (4 survey's per year throughout youth), assessment of maternal drug use, evaluation in trios (parents and child), twin data sets as well as the ability to compare these results from two environmental settings (ie two countries) and extend into additional cohorts/countries for replication. In addition to outstanding data collection from a wide age range we have the ability to determine genetic variation in both twin pairs and in family groupings, extending our ability to investigate genetic and environmental influences. To complement these genetic and epidemiological approaches we can determine smoking quantity and rates of nicotine inactivation from biomarkers collected at multiple times within the cohorts. This allows biochemical validation of the survey measures, a more robust association with genetic predictors of amount consumed over time, and the ability to use the rate of nicotine inactivation as a predictor of acquisition of smoking behaviours - something we have done successfully on a pilot scale which can now be done in these large and informative longitudinal cohorts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Programming Brains across Generations: How early environment and genes shape the risk of addiction
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; BRAIN DEVELOPMENT; BRAIN IMAGING; COHORTS; GENES; PREGNANCY; SMOKING; TWO-GENERATIONAL FAMILIES; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: The probability of drug experimentation during childhood and adolescence, and the development of addiction later in life depend on genetic and environmental risk factors that program the brain from conception onwards. Recent studies in humans and experimental animals suggest, for example, that prenatal exposure to maternal smoking may lead to the modulation of reward systems and, in turn, drug-seeking behaviour later in life. In the proposed research, we will test the hypothesis that early environmental insults, such as prenatal exposure to maternal cigarette smoking, interact with individuals' genetic background to influence developmental trajectories and promote addiction later in life.   We will investigate the early environmental and genetic origins of addiction in adolescents and adults in two unique large population-based samples: The Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1986 (NFBC1986) and Saguenay Youth Study (SYS); we will study both the young members of these cohorts (n=1,800) and their parents (n=1,900). In addition to detailed information about addictive behaviour, psychopathology and cognition, we will also acquire intermediate brain phenotypes in all participants using magnetic resonance imaging. With the wealth of data available from these two unique family-based samples, we will build developmental models that seek to identify the exposures and outcomes underlying addictive behaviour.  The current proposal provides further opportunities to develop and refine novel cognitive and biologic interventions targeting youth at risk for addiction; we will be in a unique position to answer questions about the trans-generational transmission of early environmental and genetic factors that put an individual at risk for addiction. This, in turn, will allow policy makers and health professionals to develop effective strategies for early interventions and the prevention of addiction.

This new alliance of scientists proposes to explore and prevent this possible loss of mobility. The team will work together to propose interventions in different Canadian health care settings to maintain mobility and function after an injury in seniors.

TitreApplicationTitle: New Emerging Team: Gender differences in mobility: what we can learn about improving mobility in old age
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITION; GENDER; INFLAMMATION; INTERNATIONAL; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MOBILITY; MOOD; SOCIAL ENVIRONMENT; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Mobility, the ability to move through one's environment without assistance, is a fundamental feature of human functioning. However, mobility declines over time. Mobility disability is frequent after 50 years of age and is higher in women than in men of comparable age. Differences in mobility disability between older men and women are largely unexplained and increase with advancing age. In this research, we aim at better understanding the effects of sex (biological) and gender (social roles and identities) on mobility disability. We will assess the impact of potentially modifiable factors affecting mobility disability in later life. The most accepted factor is lack of physical exercise, but poverty, social isolation and living in violent environments or experiencing domestic violence seem also to increase the risk of mobility disability. These factors may act through biological pathways of inflammation and excessive response to stress or may induce an accumulation of chronic conditions.  The objectives of this research program are: 1) to examine the impact of life experiences on mobility of men and women in old age; 2) to increase knowledge on gender specific stress and inflammation responses during aging; 3) to identify sex-specific associations between selected chronic conditions and mobility limitations. We will conduct a three year longitudinal study (questionnaire, tests for blood and saliva samples) of people between 65 and 74 years of age at four sites, two in Canada (Kingston, Ontario and Longueil, Quebec) and two in Latin America (Natal, Brazil; Manizales, Colombia). We will also examine mobility difficulty in national representative populations over 50 years collected in 70 countries as part of the 2001 World Health Survey. This will answer the research questions related to social roles  and mobility disability. Our results will help to place mobility in old age as an important public health issue  in Canada and in the international scene.

TitreApplicationTitle: Walk the Talk: Transforming the Built Environment to Enhance Mobility in Seniors
Keywords-MotsClés: BUILT ENVIRONMENT; ECONOMIC HEALTH; HEALTH POLICY; MOBILITY IN AGING; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PSYCHO-SOCIAL HEALTH; SEDENTARY BEHAVIOUR; SELF EFFICACY; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOCIAL ISOLATION/EXCLUSION
Abstract-Résumé: We aim to promote and enable mobility of older Canadians. We define mobility as the physical capacity of humans to walk or move themselves within their communities.  Limited mobility predicts death in older adults and is a consistent risk factor for disability, social exclusion and poor quality of life. There is an increasing body of evidence linking the Built Environment (BE) (individual elements of how towns and cities are designed and the services and amenities they provide) with specific health problems in adults, but very few studies address these questions in seniors. Therefore, we propose research that evaluates how the BE is associated with mobility, social exclusion and quality of life in older adults. We have engaged key stakeholders  and continue to partner in an alliance to execute our research and implement and disseminate discoveries, tools and products. This proposal consists of 3 Research Themes. In Theme A, we gather and synthesize the existing knowledge related to our area of focus. In Theme B, we refine and create new tools to evaluate the 'walkability' (pedestrian-friendliness) and 'accessibility' (access to service and amenities) of different neighbourhoods in which older adults live. In Theme C, we evaluate the influence of the built environment on older adults' mobility and quality of life. In addition to these Research Themes, we have a 'key cross-cutting element' relating to knowledge translation and exchange. This refers to generating built environment research outcomes that have impact through creating new products, influencing policy, and effectively promoting mobility in aging.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANAIMAL MODEL; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; LOCOMOTION; LOCOMOTOR TRAINING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; PAIN; REHABILITATION; SPINAL CORD INJURY; STROKE; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injuries (SCI) after car accidents or others as well as stroke can have devastating effects on the lives of the individuals because the damages of the brain or spinal cord destroy parts of the central nervous system (CNS) essential to the control of movements such as walking. The costs to the individuals are enormous, physically, economically and psychologically and the costs to society are staggering especially when affecting young individuals with a normal life time expectancy, very often the case for SCI Any improvement in function (such as being able to cross a street in due time, in moving around in the house) should be seen as a gain for the individual and a reduction in the cost of Health Care. Is this possible? There are several evidence now (to which we have significantly contributed) showing that the nervous system has tremendous capabilities to adapt to lesions and can optimize the function of remaining intact CNS areas to regain function. But what should be done to rehabilitate these patients and on what scientific basis? The general goal of the Neurological SensoriMotor Rehabilitation team (NSMR) team is to focus specifically on this question. We form a multidisciplinary team of experts (juniors and seniors) who already have a recent history of productive interactions. Using cutting-edge approaches (force enhancement, sensory enhancement, magnetic resonance imaging), we will investigate sensorimotor mechanisms leading to functional recovery following CNS lesions in humans (spinal cord injury (SCI) and stroke) and in relevant animal models to understand the basic biological principles of plasticity. Thus we will provide a structured forum of interactions between clinicians and basic scientists working on complementary problems in patients and animal models leading de facto to concrete knowledge transfer to the benefit of scientists, therapists and patients.

Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer and atherosclerosis are major killers with huge health and socioeconomic costs.  This project will develop, and accelerate to clinical trial readiness, novel technologies based on nanoparticles (NP) that are targeted to these diseases, combined with optical imaging technologies.       For lung cancer, we will use gold NP coated with a 'reporter' molecule with a distinct optical signature. The metal surface hugely amplifies the optical (Raman) signal, so that it is bright enough to be imaged. The NP will be targeted by selected molecules that will attach to receptors on the surface of lung cancer cells. In parallel, we will develop a novel ultrathin endoscope and optimize it to detect the surface-enhanced Raman light. This combination will open a new era in bronchoscopy to detect/diagnose lung cancer at an early enough stage to be curable.        For atherosclerosis, the major challenges are to stabilize the plaques that block arteries and to reduce or prevent them recurring after treatment. We will use novel NP that mimic naturally-occurring lipoproteins. These will be loaded with existing clinically approved therapeutic drugs and delivered with high efficiency by targeting specific receptor molecules in the plaques. The ultrathin imaging system can then be used to guide the treatment and to monitor its effectiveness.     Our goal is to further develop recent advances from our nanotechnology efforts, to validate these through rigorous pathological assessment in clinically relevant models, and to test/optimize the corresponding advanced optical imaging platform for diagnosis and image-guided treatments.    Accelerating these discoveries to the clinic is enabled by a new Canadian NanoMedFab facility where we can prepare the NP-based agents under 'good manufacturing practice' conditions for patient use. The core intellectual property protection and further IP will support commercialization for adoption into clinical practice.

Abstract-Résumé: One of the major challenges of replacing or regenerating tissues using tissue engineering is the ability to obtain a functional blood supply following implantation of the construct or cells into the body. This team submission is focused on the biology of regenerating blood vessels and specifically endothelial cells (EC), the cells which line the internal surfaces of all blood vessels, in the context of modular tissue engineering - a novel approach to tissue engineering. Studies will examine the influence of EC interactions with other cell types, as well as the effects of blood flow. The new knowledge obtained on EC function during remodelling will be used to design novel therapies with a view to achieving improved/accelerated vascularization.

TitreApplicationTitle: Generation of Transplantable Beta-Cells from Human ES Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; HIGH-CONTENT IMAGING; MICRORNA; STEM CELLS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSPLANT
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is a chronic, debilitating disease characterized by high blood sugar levels that result from insufficient insulin production.  Insulin is a hormone that is normally produced by specialized cells that reside in the pancreas, called beta-cells.  In type 1 diabetes, these beta-cells are killed by the immune system, whereas in type 2 diabetes, beta-cells are not able to produce enough insulin to prevent blood sugar from rising.  The majority of patients with type 1 diabetes, and approximately one third of those with type 2 diabetes require daily insulin injections to survive.  Unfortunately this crude and inconvenient therapy seldom achieves optimal control of blood sugar levels and occasional high sugar levels result in long-term organ damage and reduced lifespan.  Transplant of a few milliliters of donor beta-cells represents a promising approach to cure diabetes, but is currently hampered by an insufficient supply of donor cells.  We have assembled a new Team of investigators with a diverse skill set that aim to directly tackle this major impediment to a broadly available cure for diabetes.  We have developed a protocol for the step-wise differentiation of human stem cells into cells that resemble the direct neighbour of beta-cells, the alpha-cells.  We believe that, with subtle refinements to this protocol, we will be successful in producing a differentiation protocol that will preferentially produce beta-cells that are capable of reversing diabetes.  To achieve this, we propose using both informed strategies and unbiased high throughput screening approaches.  Ultimately, we hope our efforts will result in the discovery of a method to produce larger numbers of beta-cells that will free patients from the burdens of insulin injections.

Keywords-MotsClés: HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA; HORMONE-REFRACTORY PROSTATE CANCER; LIPID NANOPARTICLES; NANOMEDICINE; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; RNA INTERFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer remains one of the greatest challenges of modern medicine. The ability to treat cancer is severely limited by the variability and complexity of the disease, where the genetic mutations that cause cancer in one patient are often not the same mutations that cause cancer in other patients. This unfortunately causes current cancer therapies to be ineffective in large subsets of patients and so these medicines are unable to cure the disease. However, exciting new diagnostic technologies have recently been developed that, for the first time, allow clinical researchers to identify the genetic mutations that are occurring in an individual patient's cancer. Further, advanced therapeutic technologies, known as nanomedicines, are for the first time, allowing scientists to rapidly and specifically target those genes that may be the cause of a patient's disease. This proposal seeks to combine these advanced diagnostic and therapeutic technologies to develop methods that will eventually allow physicians to prescribe nanomedicines that are most effective for an individual patient. To accomplish this, we have brought together expert investigators in advanced cancer genomics and advanced targeted nanomedicines to strengthen Canada's capacity to treat cancer in this promising way.

TitreApplicationTitle: Essential roles for Cdx2 in the intestine.
Keywords-MotsClés: AP PATTERNING; CDX; COLO-RECTAL CANCER; INTESTINAL CANCER; INTESTINE; KNOCKOUT; NOTCH; STEM CELL; TRANSGENIC; WNT
Abstract-Résumé: The intestinal tract begins life as a specialized group of cells, termed endoderm cells, that form early in development.  These cells, initially homogenous in nature, eventually give rise to all of the constituents of the digestive tract, including the esophagus, stomach and small and large intestines, as well as a number of ancillary glands and organs such as the pancreas and liver.  The development of the endoderm into this array of highly specialized structures relies on the coordinated activity of a number of signaling pathways, which allow cell-cell communication and regulated expression of various transcription factors which regulate the expression of genes which dictate the nature of a given cell.  A number of these signaling pathways and transcription factor networks continue to operate in the adult, where they are critical in order to maintain a constant supply of mature cells to replace those cells which the intestine constantly sheds off.  Lesions in the proper development of the endoderm can result a number of birth defects, typically with devastating consequence.  In addition, defects in the pathways dictating intestinal homeostasis in the adult can lead to intestinal cancers or other disorders such as Crohn's disease.  Our understanding of the pathways and processes involved in intestinal development and homeostasis is rudimentary.  Recently, two transcription factors, Cdx1 and Cdx2, have been implicated in both intestinal development and cancer, however, their precise roles in these events is poorly understood. Novel genetic models developed by our group hold strong propose for a better understanding of the gene networks and pathways that are dependent on Cdx function. The information forthcoming from these studies will have important bearing on our understanding not only of basic processes related to intestinal development, but may also shed light on the basis for certain congenital defects and cancers prevalent in the human population.
