TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Characterization of APIN/ODAM, a Novel Junctional Epithelium Protein
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; GENE TRANSFER; JUNCTIONAL EPITHELIUM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; ORAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The junctional epithelium is the portion of the gingiva that binds to the tooth surface. This specialized structure is important because it seals off the tissues supporting the tooth from the aggressive oral environment, and represents the first line of defence against periodontal diseases. A large segment of the adult population (~ 80%) is affected some forms of this disease and severe manifestation can lead to tooth loss in ~ 20% of cases; and jaw bone loss which complicates prosthodontic rehabilitation. Periodontal diseases have also been associated with systemic afflictions such as cardiovascular disease. By screening the genes encoding for proteins produced in teeth, we have unexpectedly identified a novel protein associated with the attachment of the gingiva to the tooth. We have also obtained initial data showing that absence of the protein replicates what happens in the human disease. We now propose to carry out a series of state-of-the-art molecular and functional analyses aimed at understanding the role of this protein. The information derived from these studies is expected to contribute to the understanding of how the gingiva attaches and holds onto teeth, and to the development of effective therapies for the prevention and treatment of periodontal diseases. This protein is also of interest since it is highly expressed in certain cancers and could therefore have diagnostic applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of skeletal muscle inflammation, fibrosis,  degeneration and atrophy in response to mycobacterium ulcerans  infection.
Keywords-MotsClés: BURULI ULCER; CONTRACTURE; INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGE; MUSCLE ATROPHY; MUSCLE FIBROSIS; MYCOBACTERIUM ULCERANS; MYCOLACTONE; NEUTROPHIL; REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Buruli ulcer (BU) caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans (MU) is an emerging disease of the wet tropical and subtropical zones that is closely related to tuberculosis and leprosy. The disease starts insidiously with a painless nodule, plaques or oedema that will lead to ulcer and formation of scar tissue. The release of mycolactone, a toxin produced by MU, appears to induce the necrosis and pathological processes. Because of the lack of simple, cheap, effective treatment modalities, BU is an extremely destructive and expensive problem in endemic areas. Our central hypothesis is that tissue damage following BU goes well beyond skin and underlying skeletal muscles are locally and possibly systematically affected by MU. Throughout this grant proposal, we will use in vitro and in vivo experiments to characterize and understand MU infection. More precisely, mice will be employed to characterize the inflammatory response and scarring in skeletal muscles following wild type MU and negative mycolactone mutant MU infection. In addition, we will evaluate muscle damage and repair after mycolactone injection. Interestingly, the presence of mycolactone not only causes muscle damage but also prevents muscle regeneration to occur. Finally, we will try to identify by which molecular pathways MU/mycolactone induce myotube atrophy in vitro. We strongly believe that this research proposal will provide additional insights into MU infection, which will pave the way to reducing muscle fibrosis and atrophy thereby promoting repair tissue.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of tumour suppressor ING1b in genomic stability upon replication stress
Keywords-MotsClés: CGH; CHK1; GENOMIC STABILITY; HISTONE ACETYLATION; ING1; MELANOMA; PCNA MONOUBIQUITINATION; SKIN CANCER; TISSUE MICROARRAY; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: The incidence of skin cancer has been increasing rapidly in the past few decades. Although it is well known that ultraviolet light is the primary environmental factor for skin cancers, the exact molecular mechanisms responsible for skin cancer development is still largely unknown. Recently, we have found that the tumour suppressor ING1b plays an important role in genomic stability upon replication stress including ultraviolet radiation. In this proposal, we will investigate the molecular mechanisms of ING1b in recovery of DNA replication and genomic stability. We will also use in vivo animal model to examine if ING1b-deficient mice are predisposed to UV-induced skin cancer development. This project will provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms on ING1 tumour suppressor in genomic stability, which may lead to novel strategies for cancer prevention and treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genes, Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Cardiovascular Disease Risk Factors.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE RISK FACTORS; FATTY ACIDS; GENE EXPRESSION; GENES; GENETICS; OMEGA-3
Abstract-Résumé: The effect of dietary changes on cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk profile differs significantly between individuals. Accordingly, we have shown that genetic variations in a gene encoding a nuclear factor that regulates many genes involved in lipid metabolism (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-alpha) interacts with fatty acids contained in the diet to modulate the CVD risk profile. However, PPAR-alpha is not the sole gene acting as a FA sensor to modulate CVD risk factors, but the approach developed with this gene is applicable to other genes. Indeed, several other nuclear factors are also thought to play a role as fatty acid sensors. In that context, we propose to investigate gene-diet interactions between genes acting as fatty acid sensors and dietary fat on CVD risk factors by focusing on PUFAs, in particular of the n-3 family of marine origin. To do so, 200 individuals (100 men and 100 women) will be subjected to a six-week supplementation of omega-3 fatty acids. At the end of the supplementation period, their CVD risk profile and gene expression levels will be compared in the presence and in the absence of omega-3 fatty acids. We will also verify whether genetic variations within genes encoding fatty acid sensors influence the CVD risk profile response to such a upplementation. Nutrition researchers recognized the potential offered by genomic tools to help understand the complex relation between the health of the individual, its genome, and the dietary exposure together with the potential to implement CVD prevention through better nutrition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sexual assault resistance education for university women: A trial in three Canadian universities
Keywords-MotsClés: INTERVENTION; PREVENTION; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SEXUAL ASSAULT/RAPE
Abstract-Résumé: More than one in six women will be sexually assaulted in their lifetimes, most by men they know. The risk of sexual assault by men is greatest for girls and women between the ages of 14 and 24 making this a critical time for intervention. Sexual assault has many immediate and long-term negative consequences for victims. Even a small increase in the ability of women to resist sexual assault will result in a substantial improvement in the mental and physical health of women. Recent research has suggested that many young women delay their resistance to unwanted sexual advances because they are not sure that they are reading the situation correctly, they do not want to hurt the man's feelings, or they are unsure whether they have the right to say no to some sexual activity and say yes to other activity. Earlier work from the applicants resulted in the development of a program affecting these critical areas. This program was shown to be effective in helping participants build skills and a knowledge base to help them resist sexual assault and to prepare them for better recovery following sexual assault. The proposed randomized controlled trial (RCT) builds on this prior work. We will establish whether the demonstrated short term effectiveness of this theoretically and empirically sound rape resistance intervention for university women extends to longer periods. We will determine whether the program can reduce the one year incidence of sexual assault by 30% among women attending Canadian universities. The results will also be used to indicate how long the effects of the program last and will indicate at which point in time refresher sessions may be necessary. A lay summary of the findings of the trial with a focus on application will be provided to all Canadian universities and to Provincial/Territorial Ministries of Education. This will be followed up with contact with those most likely to be involved in current campus education efforts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Subversion of Macrophage Signaling by the Protozoan Parasite Leishmania
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNE RESPONSE; INTERFERON; LEISHMANIA-MACROPHAGE INTERACTION; MYELOID RELATED PROTEIN S100A; NEGATIVE REGULATORY MECHANISM; NOD-LIKE RECEPTORS; PATHOGEN ASSOCIATED MOLECULAR PATTERNS; PROTEIN TYROSINE PHOSPHATASES
Abstract-Résumé: The protozoan Leishmania is an intracellular pathogen that invade macrophages of its human host infecting worldwide between 10-15 million people with 400 000 new cases every year.  Pathogens of this group can cause several clinical manifestations which varies from cutaneous and mucocutaneous lesions to visceral infections.  Infection of macrophages by Leishmania parasite leads to the inhibition of several important phagocyte immune functions bringing about an ineffective immune response development toward this pathogen.  We have reported that alteration of several macrophage signaling pathways by Leishmania are responsible for these functional inhibitions. In this project, we wish to discover the negative regulatory mechanisms used by Leishmania to dodge the host immune response.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms underlying atrial fibrillation in animal models
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIARRHYTHMIC; ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; ATRIAL REMODELING; CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIAS; CARDIAC CONDUCTION; CARDIAC ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a very common disorder of cardiac rhythm. It causes much disability in the population and increases the risk of dying from heart disease and stroke. The treatments now available for AF are inadequate. This project aims to develop new treatment options for AF by targeting the mechanisms that cause the problem. To do this, we will work with new animal models of AF that we have developed, such as a model of heart failure and a model of intense and sustained exercise training. We will study the changes in the molecular control of cardiac function that promote AF development. We will then examine new opportunities to prevent AF by normalizing specific molecular signalling pathways that we find to be disturbed. In this way, we hope to design improved treatment options to prevent AF and to suppress it once it occurs.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Replication of Telomeres
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; CHROMOSOME STRUCTURE; DNA REPLICATION; TELOMERE BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The genetic material in our cells consists in extremely long and linear structures called chromosomes. It is of vital importance that these linear entities are passed on unchanged from one cell to the next; any cases of alterations may cause a change in the behavior of the cells, quite often in a way that leads to cancer. In addition, we now know that a number of human genetic diseases as well as some premature aging syndromes are a consequence of such unwarranted and too frequent chromosomal changes. Therefore, research in our laboratory is aimed at understanding how cells do maintain these linear chromosomes in a stable fashion. This mentioned linearity in fact also implies that chromosomes do have ends, and as with the ends of shoelaces, chromosome ends need a special protective cap. If this protective cap fails, the genetic material next to it will be damaged or lost, with potentially dire consequences as mentioned above. The proposed experiments here use traditional as well as modern genetic and biochemical experiments to investigate the functioning of these caps. Because some of the projects goals are impossible or too expensive to achieve using human cells, we will use a simple yeast cell system. Nevertheless and as has been the case in the past, we expect our findings to be relevant to the functioning of these caps in human cells as well. Thus, the anticipated results may open unique and new opportunities for developing anti-cancer approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathogenesis and Etiology of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGENITAL; DEFECTS; DIAPHRAGM; EMBRYOLOGY; LUNG HYPOPLASIA; RETINOIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH) is a developmental disorder occurring in approximately 1 in 2500 live births (similar to the occurrence rate of Cystic Fibrosis). The primary characterization of CDH is that the diaphragm muscle fails to form properly during pregnancy. Normally, the diaphragm develops to form a continuous sheet that completely separates the space where the lungs develop. However, in the instance of CDH, a significant proportion of the diaphragm is absent. Consequently, the developing abdominal organs can invade the chest cavity, occupying space normally reserved to accommodate the growing lungs. As a result, newborns with CDH suffer from a combination of very small lungs and serious heart problems (approximately 50% die soon after birth and survivors often have life-long health concerns). Our laboratory uses a variety of animal models that very much mimic CDH in infants. Using these models, we will continue with our discoveries of why there is a hole in the diaphragm muscle, what stage of pregnancy the defect first occurs, what genes may be involved and the potential role of an abnormality of Vitamin A regulation in the embryo. We have made significant progress during past several years and have some novel targeted studies designed to advance our understanding of this serious birth defect.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating Brain and Behavioural Plasticity Following Self-Regulation Training in Children With Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONING; FETAL ALCOHOL SPECTRUM DISORDERS; INTERVENTION; NEUROIMAGING; SELF-REGULATION; SOCIAL COGNITION
Abstract-Résumé: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is a severe disabling disorder arising from prenatal exposure to alcohol. In adults, a high rate of mental health disorders is seen and in children, severe learning and behaviour problems. While early intervention helps prevent their later disturbances, few effective and validated therapies exist for children with FASD who show self-regulation deficits in controlling their impulses and understanding emotions; these deficits reflect common brain abnormalities. The Alert Program for Self Regulation® is effective in improving these skills in several pediatric populations including one limited study of FASD. We now propose to conduct a comprehensive study of 40 8-12 year olds with FASD and 20 normal controls (NC). Half of the FASD group will be randomly assigned to receive active treatment (Tx) and half will be on a waitlist for later treatment (WL). At Pretest, all groups will receive a comprehensive battery of executive function and social cognition tests and will undergo structural and functional MRI scanning to assess how treatment benefits are manifested in the brain. Tx will then receive the Alert intervention over a 4-month period. After this, the groups will be retested and rescanned (Posttest 1) and then WL will receive treatment. Six months later, Tx will undergo repeat testing and scanning as before (Posttest 2). We expect: (1) Alert training will lead to significantly improved behaviour and alterations in brain structure and function in Tx but not WL, (2) Tx will closely resemble NC after Alert, and (3) improvements in Tx will last. Because our findings will yield well-needed novel information on interventions for improving their core deficits and related brain function, our approach offers hope for alleviating the later mental health challenges these vulnerable children face.

TitreApplicationTitle: Does AMPK signaling regulate the pathological remodeling of sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins in diabetic muscle?
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; CALCIUM TRANSPORT PROTEINS; DIABETES; ENERGY HOMEOSTASIS; EXERCISE; HEART; SARCOPLASMIC RETICULUM PROTEINS; SKELETAL MUSCLE; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is a disease that causes blood sugar to be higher than normal and is a major public health issue in Canada. In fact, patients that have really high levels of blood sugar often develop heart problems or muscle weakness in their legs. Researchers have learned that these problems occur because at least two different proteins that move calcium (which are called sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins) within the heart and leg muscles are damaged by diabetes. Researchers have also learned that exercise training for 60 minutes per day, five days a week can protect these proteins so they are not damaged by diabetes, which helps to prevent heart problems and muscle weakness. However, researchers still do not understand how exercise causes this health benefit. Therefore, our research proposal will try to discover the biological machinery that are turned on by exercise in order to protect sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins within the heart and leg muscles of diabetic mice. We plan to use mice in our experiments because they develop diabetes in a way that is similar to humans. Also, by using mice we will be able to find out if problems with an energy sensing protein, which is called AMPK, are responsible for causing the damage to sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins in diabetes. Mice also appear to enjoy running, which will allow us to see if exercise can turn on AMPK and prevent sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins from being damaged by diabetes. In fact, this study is really interesting because it will be the first to find out if the AMPK protein controls the amount of damage that diabetes causes to sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins. This information may help researchers to understand why exercise is able to improve the health of diabetic patients. Someday, this information may also help researchers to develop new drugs that can prevent heart problems and muscle weakness in diabetic patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Finding new cellular factors of susceptibility/resistance to HIV-1 infection using a novel reporter virus and large-scale genomic/proteomic approaches
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; GENE EXPRESSION; HIV-1; MICROARRAY
Abstract-Résumé: Recent discoveries have shed some light on the mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of HIV-1/AIDS. Among these, a significant relationship between the depletion by the virus of Th17 cells, which are responsible for the integrity of the intestinal mucosal barrier, and the chronic and systemic immune activation seen in HIV-1-infected patients has been observed. The precise cellular factors involved in the relative susceptibility of these cells compared to others are as yet unknown. Moreover, the discrimination between the genetic program induced in an infected cell compared to another that has been only exposed but not infected, also called bystander cell, has still not been performed. Following the development of a unique and innovative molecular tool allowing the efficient separation of infected from bystander cells, large-scale transcriptomic and proteomic approaches will be used to characterize the gene expression profiles of both infected and bystander cells, identify specific CD4+ T cell subsets that are highly susceptible and others resistant to HIV-1 infection and then determine the exact cellular factors that are responsible for this different susceptibility. These approaches have the potential to provide as-yet unknown targets of intervention for the development of therapies seeking to either prevent HIV-1 transmission, or delay, perhaps indefinitely, the development of AIDS in infected patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Second generation cardiac cell therapy:  Combination and genetic tailoring of stem cells in ischemic heart disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGESTIVE HEART FAILURE; GENE THERAPY; REGENERATION; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a growing epidemic. While medical advances help people live longer, the number of patients with heart failure is increasing at a staggering rate. Currently over 400 000 Canadians are living with heart failure - but many will not survive for long. Heart failure is also the most serious killer in cardiovascular diseases.  Heart failure claims more lives than lung cancer, stroke, AIDs and breast cancer combined.  This study is designed to explore new ways to repair these broken hearts.  Currently, doctors are using techniques to re-implant a patients own blood and heart stem cells into these damaged areas.  Our early work has shown that while these cells strengthen the heart, improvements have limits.  Irregardless, doctors are starting preliminary studies exploring even these modest gains in small numbers of very ill patients.          This proposal will build upon our earlier work by exploring how these stem cells repair hearts.  We expect that understanding these mechanisms will help us to engineer new therapies that will allow a patients own heart to heal itself.  We will grow two different types of stem cells directly from blood samples (blood stem cells) and small pieces of heart tissue (heart stem cells).  Both samples will be donated by volunteer patients whose treating doctor has recommended they undergo cardiac surgery.  We will first study these cells in dishes to study increase our understanding about the specific cells and hormones that repair hearts.  Then, we will inject these cells into mice with weakened heart muscles to prove that findings in the dish heal the intact, but damaged, heart.   This work will provide us the knowledge and opportunity to enhance the genes within these cells that increase cell survival and regeneration.  These "enhanced" stem cells will be the next step in tailoring new stem cell sources for our patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vascular remodeling diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: I am a scientist studying basic mechanisms of vascular biology and translating my research to the treatment of patients with vascular remodeling diseases (VRD). The vessel wall in VRD including atherosclerosis, restenosis, pulmonary hypertension (PHT), is characterized by  vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, resistance to apoptosis and inflammation. Although VRD are important causes of morbidity and mortality, the current treatments are limited to slowing down the progression, as opposed to curing the disease. A Canadian Research Chair in vascular remodeling diseases will support my efforts to exploit basic mechanism, develop and apply effective VRD therapies.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Glial regulation and modulation of synapses in aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION; NEURON-GLIA INTERACTIONS; PERISYNAPTIC SCHWANN CELLS; SYNAPSES; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Communication and learning in the nervous system is executed by a group of structures called synapses. Although it was thought for a long time that only neuronal cells contributed to the communication process, recent work has shown that the other major cells in then ervous system,that is, the glial cells, are very active and are key elements in this fundamental process. Major changes in neuronal communication occur during aging. Here we will examine how the glial contribution to the communication and learning processes is altered during aging and what are the consequences of these age-related changes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing antiviral drug therapy and vaccines for influenza viruses
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUVANT; ANIMAL MODEL; ANTIVIRAL; IMMUNOGENICITY; INFLUENZA; MATHEMATICAL MODEL; NEURAMINIDASE INHIBITOR; RESISTANCE; REVERSE GENETICS; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Imfluenza viruses constitute a serious threat to mankind through yearly epidemics affecting 10-20% of the Canadian population and occasional pandemics as shown by the rapid spread of the pandemic 2009 H1N1 virus throughout the world. Besides public health measures, antivirals and vaccines are the only specific modalities that have shown benefits in decreasing the number and/or the severity of influenza infections. However, antiviral drug resistance and suboptimal immune response limit the efficacy of these modalities. In this research proposal, we seek to optimize both antiviral treatment through a better knowledge of the mechanisms of drug resistance as well as current inactivated influenza vaccines by assessing new adjuvants and routes of administration.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional characterization of the von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor gene product
Keywords-MotsClés: ACIDOSIS; HYPOXIA; NUCLEAR/CYTOPLASMIC TRAFFICKING; NUCLEOLUS; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Tumors of various tissue origins, such as breast, ovary or kidney occur because of mutations in very different genes.  However, cancers do shares some near-universal features including the fact that the center of tumors often lacks oxygen (termed hypoxia).  Our cells are programmed to produce energy exclusively from the degradation of sugar (glucose) in the absence of oxygen in a process that is called fermentation or anaerobic metabolism.  Yeasts produce alcohol when they ferment glucose in the absence of oxygen.  In the case of higher organisms, like humans, we produce lactic acid.  Therefore, the middle of tumors is often very acidic compared to normal tissues.  It is generally agreed upon that tumors that are hypoxic and acidic are likely to be more aggressive.  That is because cells in the middle of the tumors have been able to survive this particularly harsh environment whereas cells that did not are already dead. My laboratory is interested in the study of this process of cellular adaptation to anaerobic metabolism.  Our group has published papers that demonstrate that cells that engage in anaerobic metabolism are able to store or hide several proteins in a cellular closet (i.e. nucleolus) because they do not need them, or want them, in the absence of oxygen.  We also showed that when we prevent this hiding of proteins, cells cannot survive anaerobic metabolism an die.  This proposal is to continue studying this process in the idea of preventing the aggressive cancer cells to survive in the core of tumors as a way to treat cancer.

ResearchClassEN: ENDOCRINOLOGY; PROSTATE AND BLADDER CANCER THERAPY
ClasseRechercheFR: ENDOCRINOLOGIE; THERAPIE DU CANCER DE LA PROSTATE ET DE LA VESSIE
TitreApplicationTitle: In Vivo siRNA Knockdown of Androgen Receptors to Treat Advanced Prostate Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN RECEPTOR; DELIVERY; NANOPARTICLES; PROSTATE CANCER; SIRNA
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that more than 100,000 Canadian men are currently living with prostate cancer and that this year almost 25,000 will be newly diagnosed and over 4,000 will die of this disease, making it the most commonly diagnosed non-skin cancer in men and one of the leading causes of cancer-death. If caught early, it is frequently curable by surgical removal of the prostate or by radiation treatment. However, it often recurs with accompanying metastatic spread to bones. This advanced form of the disease is usually managed with treatments referred to as medical castration that prevent the synthesis of androgens like testosterone or obstruct their ability to bind and activate the androgen receptor in the prostate cancer cell. These treatments block the growth promoting effects of androgens and activate cell death processes in the cancer cells. Unfortunately, the cancers eventually become resistant and progress to the lethal, castration-resistant state with an androgen receptor that is now active despite very low levels of circulating androgens. With previous support from CIHR, we have shown that knocking down this androgen receptor using a specific RNA interference approach inhibits this progression and even causes complete regression of some castration-resistant tumours. We have also shown that we can package these RNA interfering molecules into liposomes, inject them into prostate tumour-bearing animals, and see a reduction of prostate tumour growth. Thus, the main objective of this renewal application is to develop better and more efficient ways to deliver these RNA interference molecules for targeting and knocking down the androgen receptor in castration-resistant prostate tumours. We anticipate that the combined strengths and expertise of the Cullis and Rennie labs will continue to perform synergistically to accelerate development of these delivery systems and have a major impact on the survival of men with advanced, castration-resistant prostate cancer.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
ClasseRechercheFR: VIEILLISSEMENT; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of senescence and aging by the axis STAT5-SOCS1-p53
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; INFLAMMATION; P53; SENESCENCE; STAT5; SUPPRESSORS OF CYTOKINE SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is strongly linked to chronic inflammation but the molecular basis of this relationship is poorly understood. Inflammation involves a family of molecules known as cytokines. At the cellular levels cytokine signaling can accelerate the aging process inducing cellular senescence. We have identified a molecular pathway mediating the senescent functions of cytokines. The transcription factor Stat5 which is activated by cytokines, can in turn induce an adaptor protein Socs1 that activates another transcription factor known as p53.  The result of activating this pathway is a lost of cellular renewal potential and the secretion of more cytokines. Now we propose to further investigate the molecular properties of these interactions, design assays to find drugs that modulate them and create an animal model to validate our findings in vivo and test for possible pharmacological or nutritional interventions against age-related diseases.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL DIGESTIF ET FOIE; SYSTÈME NERVEUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms sustaining abnormal peripheral sensory signaling in the abdomen in a model of post-infectious IBS: A dynamic interplay of peripheral and central factors.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABDOMINAL PAIN; DIARRHEA; DORSAL ROOT GANGLIA NEURONS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; INFECTIOUS COLITIS; IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a very common disorder for which there are currently no proven treatments. This proposal examines causes of pain in patients suffering from post-infectious IBS (IBS which onsets following an acute bacterial infection in the colon). Recent studies have shown that chronic stress is frequently associated with the development of IBS following an acute bacterial infection in the colon. Our hypothesis is that chronic stress releases mediators which in turn can signal to pain neurons innervating  the gut and this greatly exacerbate the abnormal pain signalling that occurs following infection. We have developed an animal model of post-infectious IBS which allows us to examine the interaction between a previous infection and chronic stress.  We have new data showing that chronic stress greatly exacerbates the pain signalling following resolution of an acute colitis and have identified several novel targets underlying these changes. We have also shown that the supernatant (fluid containing inflammatory mediators) obtained from human biopsies of the colon from post-infectious IBS sufferers can re-capitulate these findings when incubated with mouse pain neurons. The research plan is to use electrophysiological and molecular techniques to clarify the role of these new targets in animal and human models. Our ultimate goal is to identify the best targets for treating pain in this disorder and possibly new means of diagnosing this disorder.

ClasseRechercheFR: DIABETE SUCRE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Kinetic evolution of a diabetogenic CD8+ T-cell response
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE T-CELL TRANSFER; AUTOIMMUNITY; CYTOKINE ASSAYS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; IMMUNOGENETICS; IMMUNOPATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) results from immune dysregulation (autoimmunity) leading to destruction of the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas (B cells) by specific white blood cells (B cell-killer lymphocytes). It has been known for quite some time that development of overt autoimmune diseases, like diabetes, is preceded by prolonged periods of inflammation of the target tissues by white blood cells. We have discovered a mechanism that accounts for that puzzling observation. Namely, we found that evolution of inflammation to overt diabetes is driven by those inflammatory white blood cells that can most easily (faster and for longer periods of time) engage target cells. Importantly, these "strong" white blood cells are rare at the outset of the disease process but are selected for within the inflammatory lesions with time (the months or years it takes for inflammation to lead to overt disease). This process of selection is akin to the "survival of the fittest", where "strong" cells multiply more easily and kill their targets better than "weak" cells. An issue that remains unresolved is the molecular basis of this phenomenon. In aims 1 and 2, we will investigate how these "strong" white blood cells choose their antigenic targets, namely what makes specific proteins in B-cells preferable targets for these white blood cells. During the previous funding cycle, we have also discovered that the "weak" counterparts of these "strong" B-cell killer white blood cells function as active suppressors of disease progression. In aim 3, we will investigate why and how "strong" and "weak" white blood cells turn into aggressors and suppressors, respectively. Overall, this grant proposal is an effort to dissect, in detail, the mechanisms that govern competition among "gangs" of white blood cells for occupation of the intra-islet space. The information gained through these studies will further our understanding of autoimmunity, and identify new targets for therapeutic intervention.

ResearchClassEN: INJURY, REGENERATION; NONE OF THE ABOVE
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuron-glia interactions during synapse formation and competition
Keywords-MotsClés: GLIAL CELLS; MULTIPHOTON MICROSCOPY; SYNAPSE-GLIA INTERACTIONS; SYNAPTIC COMPETITION; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: Communication and learning in the nervous system is executed by a group of structures called synapses.  Although it was thought for a long time that only neuronal cells contributed to the communication process, recent work has shown that the other major cells in the nervous system, that is, the glial cells, are very active and are key elements in this fundamental process.  We will explore the role of glial cells during the dynamic establishment of synapses during postnatal development and following nerve injury.  In particular, we will test whether glial cells control and modulate the efficacy of synapses to communicate during these events to favour the establishment and consolidation of new synapses.

TitreApplicationTitle: The neural circuitry of executive functions in Parkinson's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; DOPAMINE; FRONTAL CORTEX; FUNCTIONAL IMAGING; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder. Current therapies for PD predominantly focus on relieving the motor deficits of the disease. However, many other non-motor symptoms of PD are not effectively managed by current therapies, a problem which is almost certainly due to the fact that the disease extends well beyond the nigrostriatal system. Among these non-motor symptoms, cognitive deficits have a significant impact on the quality of life and day to day activities of these patients. The main pattern of cognitive impairments seen in early stages of PD resembles that produced by frontal lobe damage and includes deficits of executive functions. The impairments in executive functions that characterize non-demented PD patients include deficits in planning and lost ability to alter a behavioral response in the face of a changing environment. Today, the possibility of investigating the contribution of cortical and subcortical areas, in vivo, in the human brain by using functional imaging provides us with a valuable probe of brain function that is unparalleled in its ability to study and dissect the prefrontal-striatal loops in awake behaving subjects. Using positron emission tomography (PET), the proposed studies are designed to explore in non-demented PD patients the relationship between executive deficits and dopaminergic receptor abnormalities in the striatum and prefrontal cortex.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanism of Intestinal Glycosidases: Nutritional Starch Digestion and Regulation of Blood Glucose Levels
Keywords-MotsClés: CARBOHYDRATE CHEMISTRY; DIABETES; GLYCOSIDASE MECHANISM; NUTRITIONAL STARCH METABOLISM; OBESITY; PROTEIN STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: As humans, we derive our nutrition from various sources. In many cases, including brain development, energy is delivered by glucose. We obtain much of our glucose from food starches, which have different structures depending on their sources.  The human intestinal system has evolved ways to deal with the many starches we eat. Two intestinal enzymes, maltase glucoamylase (MGAM) and sucrase isomaltase (SI), work together to digest many forms of starch. More resistant forms pass through to the colon, where they are acted on by symbiotic bacteria.    Each of MGAM and SI actually consists of two enzyme subunits. All four enzyme units are related structurally, members of a family called GH31, but have different substrate specificities to different starch forms. Our hypothesis is that the four enzyme units act in a complementary manner on different starch structures. Furthermore, regulating the enzymes' activities will be useful in controlling blood glucose levels. By studying the details of their mechanisms of action, we hope to understand how they work together in this complex process.    Specifically, our investigations will be applicable to developing modulators of these activities. These compounds will be used to turn on and off the individual activities of the four enzyme units, in order to investigate how each contributes to the digestion of nutritional starch in various conditions, for example conditions of starvation, gorging, physical activity and others.  Finally, if we can understand how the body generates nutritional glucose from starch, we can propose new forms of starch with high nutritional value.

TitreApplicationTitle: Copy number variation and expression in schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: COPY NUMBER VARIATION; GENETIC SYNDROME; GENETICS; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a serious psychiatric illness that affects about 1 in 100 people. Genetic changes are likely to cause many forms of schizophrenia. Changes in the structure of the human genome, such as copy number changes, are a newly discovered type of genetic change. The genetic code that makes up the human genome is like a recipe that tells the cells in every part of the human body how to develop and how to work throughout life. Copy number changes act like a paragraph missing, or a paragraph duplicated, in the genetic code (DNA).  Recent studies have shown that certain large copy number changes can be expressed as schizophrenia and other diseases related to changes in normal development. The research team will have recruited, assessed and obtained DNA samples from 600 people with schizophrenia. In this study, they will use these DNA samples and advanced genetic technology to find copy number changes that may cause schizophrenia. Information from the assessments of the people with schizophrenia, and their immediate family members, as well as software programs to analyze gene pathways, will be essential to help interpret the genetic changes found in the lab.  Results from this study should help improve understanding about the changes to genes that predispose to schizophrenia in the general population. Improved knowledge about these genetic changes and the gene pathways involved will shed light on the brain changes that lead to schizophrenia. Eventually this new knowledge will help us to develop improved treatments for those who suffer with schizophrenia.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
ResearchClassEN: ACCIDENTS, POISONING - VIOLENCE; PSYCHO-SOCIAL AND BEHAVIOURAL RESEARCH
ClasseRechercheFR: TRAUMATISMES, EMPOISONNEMENTS, VIOLENCE; RECHERCHES PSYCHOSOCIALES ET COMPORTEMENTALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental trajectories and pathways to recovery and resilience in children victims of sexual abuse
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE; INTERVENTION; RESILIENCE; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: The main objective of this research program is to document the health outcomes of children disclosing sexual abuse in regards more specifically to post traumatic stress symptoms. Our specific aims are first to test a conceptual model of outcomes linking characteristics of the sexual abuse experienced (duration, severity and identity of the perpetrator) with classic post-traumatic stress symptoms (re-experiencing symptoms, avoidance and hyperarousal) and complex post-traumatic symptoms (for instance, alterations in social relations, in regulation of affects and in self-perceptions). The longitudinal design of the study will allow for the exploration of distinctive trajectories of symptoms over a 24-month period after disclosure: chronic difficulties, delayed response to trauma, recovery and resilience. Our research program will also test the influence of two variables that may impact on symptoms over time: the child's coping strategies and the child's perception of security in regards to their relationhips with caregivers.  Questionnaires will be administered to children (6-12 years) and their mothers who are consulting following disclosure in five different facilities offering services to children victims of sexual abuse. This research plan will generate reliable and useful data to better understand the complex phenomenon of child sexual abuse and to provide needed cues for the design of efficient intervention programs. Documentation of consequences of sexual victimization will provide crucial information to health planning agencies in terms of needed services. This information will contribute to the implementation of adapted early intervention programs for vulnerable children that could be associated with a substantial reduction in health costs.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Vasculature-guided migration of neuronal precursors in the postnatal brain: From development to disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT NEUROGENESIS; ASTROCYTES; BDNF; BLOOD VESSELS; ISCHEMIA; NEURONAL MIGRATION; NEURONAL PRECURSORS; NOTCH; TIME-LAPSE VIDEOIMAGING; VEGF
Abstract-Résumé: The discovery of neuronal progenitors in the certain regions of the adult mammalian brain, including humans, raised the exciting possibility of using endogenous neuronal precursors to cure brain damage and neurodegenerative diseases. Yet, although promising, the use of adult neurogenesis to heal these devastating diseases is far from reach and depends upon a full understanding of the mechanisms that regulate production, migration and integration of new neurons into the adult brain tissue. This research program is aimed at investigating the mechanisms of neuronal migration in the postnatal brain under normal physiological conditions and following injury. The knowledge about molecular and cellular pathways orchestrating migration of neuronal precursors can be used to build up efficient cell replacement therapies by inducing neuronal recruitment into the diseased/damaged brain areas.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: TGFalpha/EGFR signaling in osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; CARTILAGE; CCL2; CCR2; CHONDROCYTE; EGFR; OSTEOARTHRITIS; TGFALPHA
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a serious and wide-spread disease causing severely reduced quality of life for millions of Canadians and enormous costs for our health care system and economy. There is virtually no treatment to stop or reverse the progression of OA. One reason for this lack of treatment is that we do not understand the causes of OA and the molecular and cellular processes that drive disease progression. We have shown earlier that a signaling pathway including the growth factor TGFalpha, its cell surface receptor EGFR and the pathways activated by these factors promote events associated with OA. Moreover, we have shown that blockade of this pathway slows OA progression in mouse and rat models. We will now study the mechanisms mediating these effects, and the role of TGFalpha/EGFR signaling in cartilage, both in health and in OA. We will use a combination of animal experiments (using genetic, surgical and chemical manipulations) and studies with cultured cartilage cells and tissue to address thee questions. Ultimately, our studies will yield important and novel insights into how OA develops and lead to improved therapies for OA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Basis of Ca2+ Release Termination and its Role in Cardiomyopathies
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM IMAGING; CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIAS; CARDIOMYOPATHIES; DISEASE MUTATIONS; EXCITATION-CONTRACTION COUPLING; RYANODINE RECEPTOR; SINGLE CHANNEL RECORDINGS; SR CALCIUM RELEASE; STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: In the heart, muscle contraction is triggered by the release of calcium from the internal calcium stores called the sarcoplasmic reticulum. To ensure stable muscle contraction and relaxation, calcium release, once initiated, is rapidly terminated to allow the released calcium to be pumped back to the internal stores and to set off for the next cycle of calcium release and reuptake. The mechanism underlying the initiation of calcium release has been extensively studied and is well defined, but how calcium release is terminated remains the least understood question in the field of muscle contraction. Recent studies have suggested that the calcium level inside the internal stores controls the opening and closing of the calcium release channel located in the internal calcium stores. It is this calcium release channel that determines the initiation and termination of calcium release. It is becoming increasingly clear that alterations in the initiation or termination of calcium release are major causes of many cardiac diseases. The objective of this research proposal is to investigate how calcium release is terminated and how defective termination of calcium release leads to cardiac abnormalities. Recent studies from Dr. Chen's laboratory have provided some important clues to these fundamental questions. It appears that the calcium release channel has its own calcium sensor that tells the channel to open or close depending on the level of calcium inside the stores. A variety of cutting-edge technologies will be employed to study the role of this putative calcium sensor in calcium release termination and how this process is affected by disease-causing mutations in the calcium release channel.  These proposed studies would shed novel and exciting insights into the molecular basis and regulation of Ca2+ release termination, and have profound implications for the prevention and treatment of various heart diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: SCHIZOPHRENIE; TROUBLE D'HYPERACTIVITÉ AVEC DÉFICIT DE L'ATTENTION (THADA)
TitreApplicationTitle: NMDA Receptors, Metaplasticity and Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR LEARNING; DOPAMINE RECEPTORS; HIPPOCAMPUS; NMDA RECEPTORS; PATCH CLAMP; SCHIZOPHRENIA AND ADHD
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is treated with drugs that inhibit one type of dopamine receptor in the brain and this help psychosis but fails to help learning and memory deficits. A new concept is that there is a chronic reduction in the excitation between neurons. New drugs are being tried clinically to correct this deficit in synaptic transmission; and, they do so by targeting the NMDA receptor.  We show that there are two different types of NMDA receptors in the hippocampus (a centre of learning and memory); and, each has very different effects on learning. We have found ways to selectively change the activity of each receptor subtype; and, to potentially use new drugs to restore the balance of activity between these receptors, rather that to arbitrarily boost NMDA, which can actually kill brain cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of the tumor suppression activity of the ERK pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; JAK/STAT SIGNALING; MAP KINASES; ONCOGENES; SENESCENCE; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENES
Abstract-Résumé: In normal healthy organisms cell proliferation is carefully controlled and the effects of oncongenic stimuli are neutralized by cellular tumor suppressor responses. We have discovered that a cellular signaling pathway known best for conveying proliferation signals in tumors can mediate antitumor responses as well. Here we propose to dissect the mechanisms of tumor suppression carry out by the extracellular regulated kinases 1 and 2 (ERK1 and 2). At the cellular levels the ERK pathway is essential to carry out the process of oncogene induced senescence, a permanent cell cycle arrest that prevents tumor formation. Senescence is the mechanism that keeps benign tumors harmless and can be activated in malignant tumors by chemotherapy. By unrevealing the molecular mechanisms by which ERK1/2 regulates senescence we can identify cellular targets for new cancer therapeutics.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; RETARD MENTAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Astrocyte-Secreted Factors in Synaptic Development and Brain Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN INJURY; DEVELOPMENT; DISEASE; GLIA; STROKE; SYNAPSE
Abstract-Résumé: Brain damage due to stroke and traumatic brain injury often has catastrophic consequences for patients and their families. Although current medical treatments have significantly improved the outcome of people who sustain these events, most individuals suffer lifetime impairments in bodily function and cognitive abilities. Thus, new therapies that can reduce the extent of damage to the brain following an injury and promote repair are greatly needed. A major contributor to brain damage following an injury is the neurotransmitter glutamate, which accumulates at sites of injury and is toxic to the surrounding cells. Hence, devising approaches to regulate glutamate and its receptors on neurons is important. The purpose of this grant is to identify and characterize new molecules that control the formation, stability, and strength of glutamate-based synaptic connections between neurons in the normal and injured brain. We have recently identified a new protein that is secreted by non-neuronal cells in the brain and plays a critical role in controlling the development and function of neural connections. Interestingly, the level of this protein is significantly increased at sites of brain injury. In this grant, we will utilize combined molecular, biochemical, imaging, behavioral and electrophysiological approaches to understand how this molecule regulates connections between neurons. These findings will help fuel proposed experiments which will directly investigate how this molecule regulates the function and health of neurons following brain injury. The ultimate goal is to reveal fundamental and new information that can improve the design and effectiveness of therapeutics that preserve the brain following an injury.

ClasseRechercheFR: LEUCEMIES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Assembly of domains in mammalian nuclei in development
Keywords-MotsClés: CROMATIN ORGANIZATION; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; NUCLEAR STRUCTURE; PROMYELOCYTIC LEUKEMIA; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Until recently researchers have viewed the cell nucleus simply as a bag full of DNA, the biopolymer that contains the genetic code. Our research program has replaced this model with one in which a high degree of internal structure exists within the nucleus. In fact, we think that the position of genes within the nucleus is critical. If a gene locates to the wrong sub-nuclear neighbourhood, its code may not be read-out, its information suppressed. For a gene, location (in the right place in the nucleus) is everything!  Importantly, this internal organization changes in dramatic ways during mouse development, between the stages of the fertilized egg through to the formation of distinct cells of the various tissues in the embryo. The goal of this application is to understand the mechanisms that dictate how the genome is organized as the embryo begins to develop, how genes are positioned in the right neighbourhoods. We will also study the process of cell differentiation in reverse, starting with very different types of differentiated cells such as skin cells vs. lymphocytes. By adding specific factors, we can turn these cells back into cells resembling the fertilized egg, in that this re-programmed cell can give rise to any cell type in the mouse. The question we want to ask is that as different cells are re-programmed, do they converge to a common genome organization, losing all memory of the cell type from which they were derived.  This re-programming technology has enormous potential for producing cells with precisely the correct properties for therapeutic applications to treat a variety of human conditions; but, at present, re-programming to obtain such properties is poorly understood. Our information will reveal the proper nuclear organization that is critically required in re-programmed cells that have the desired therapeutic characteristics.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of regulation of gene expression in the mammalian germline
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH DEFECTS; DISEASES:  CONGENITAL MALFORMATIONS; GAMETE TOXICITY; GROWTH DISORDERS; INFERTILITY; KEYWORDS:  EMBRYOGENESIS; OOGENESIS; SPERMATOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: The purpose of this research program is to understand how genes involved in the development of male and female germ cells are regulated. A better understanding of the normal development of sperm and eggs, in particular, could permit the development of specific means to interfere with the process, including contraception, and provide a better understanding of infertililty.  The chemical modification of genes, by DNA methylation, provides a way in which genes can be turned on or off at specific times.  Major differences in DNA methylation have been found between the testis and the ovary and provide a way of marking the mothers and fathers genes differently.  Differential marking of genes in the sperm and egg is being used to explain why genes responsible for human disease, such as growth disorders in children and cancer, may exert different effects depending on whether they come from an individuals mother or father.  The objective of our research is to determine the regulation and role of DNA methylation in programming gene expression in the germline and the resulting embryo.  The causes of approximately 70 percent of birth defects are unknown.  It is anticipated that our studies will help explain and prevent some of the as yet unknown causes of birth defects in children.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional control of adipose tissue by OcaB upon aging
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTES; ADIPOSE TISSUE; AGING; BONE MARROW TRANSFER; ENERGY METABOLISM; GENE EXPRESSION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LYMPHOCYTES B; MICE; NUCLEAR COFACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is associated with the development of metabolic disorders such as diabetes, obesity and atherosclerosis. The molecular pathways involved are not yet fully characterized. We have found a novel and possibly important gene that is robustly changed upon aging in fat tissue. The present grant application aims at determining the role of this gene, which is a protein found in the nucleus of cells that acts as a nuclear cofactor. We will study how this nuclear cofactor impacts on the biology of fat cells, adipose tissue, whole-body energetics and in the control of longevity. The project will use cellular models as well as mice with specific mutation by genetic engineering. The project is timely considering the important changes in the Canadian demography towards an older population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immune evasion by intracellular bacteria: The paradox of type I interferon.
Keywords-MotsClés: CROSS-PRESENTATION; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; INFLAMMATION; T CELL MEMORY; VACCINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Since pathogens proliferate rapidly (often doubling in minutes), the immune system must operate swiftly in order to combat the increasing pathogen burden.  Some of the specialized immune cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells handle the pathogens rapidly and solicit the help of other immune cells (T cells) to control the pathogen burden comprehensively.  However, some pathogens, such as Salmonella Typhimurium (ST), which induces a typhoid-like disease in mice and gasteroenteritis in humans, appear to escape this early recognition by the immune system.   This results in rapid fatality in susceptible hosts and establishment of a chronic disease in resistant hosts.  Outbreaks of such food- and water-borne pathogens are on the rise, and there are no efficient vaccines.  In this proposal we will unravel the fundamental mechanisms that are lacking during infection of the immune cells with ST.  We will modify the pathogen so that T cells are engaged early on and evaluate whether this modification makes the pathogen vulnerable to immune attack.  Our results indicate that ST induces rapid death of macrophages and this seems to be initiated by the key anti-viral cytokine, interferon (IFN)-I.  Thus, what protects us against viral infections seems to promote susceptibility against other pathogens.  How the expression of IFN-I upon ST infection leads to rapid death of macrophages, the quintessential immune cell is one of the key questions we will be unraveling.  These studies will lead to the identification of strategies that can be exploited for development of therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of postprandial fatty acid metabolism in the natural history of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D)
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES MELLITUS; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LIPID METABOLISM; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; POSTPRANDIAL LIPOPROTEIN METABOLISM; STABLE ISOTOPES
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes (adult onset diabetes) affects between 7 and 10 percent of the Canadian population and is a major cause of mortality and suffering from heart disease, stroke, amputations, blindness, and renal failure.  Its prevalence in our country is increasing due to the epidemics of obesity and aging of the Canadian population. We have shown that abnormal blood fat levels after meals may be implicated very early in the natural history of type 2 diabetes. This could lead to increased exposure of organs to dietary fats and contribute to the development of abnormal muscle, liver, and pancreatic function, the principal characteristics of this disease. Over the past years, we have established new investigation tools to study these processes in humans and have characterized the abnormalities of fat metabolism after meals in pre-diabetic individuals (with two parents with type 2 diabetes or with impaired glucose tolerance, who are at very high risk of developing diabetes). We have shown that fat in the diet is preferentially channelled into lean tissues of these individuals. We now want to determine whether this abnormality overwhelms capacity of lean tissues to burn fat and whether it could be reversed with short-term change in diet. The proposed studies may lead to a better understanding of the cause of type 2 diabetes and to more specific targets for prevention and early treatment of this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Curcumin to prevent perioperative complications after elective abdominal aortic anuerysm repair
Keywords-MotsClés: ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM; ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; CURCUMIN; PERIOPERATIVE COMPLICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a ballooning of the abdominal aorta, the major blood vessel of the body. AAA occurs in up to 2% of adults. Surgeons will plan an AAA repair when the aneurysm grows bigger than 5.5cm, because the AAA might burst without repair. Over 47,000 AAA repairs are performed around the world each year. Despite the benefits of AAA repair there are risks, and the kidneys can be severely injured. We will test whether the natural health product curcumin can prevent the development of kidney injury and other problems from AAA repair. Curcumin is found in a spice called turmeric, a member of the ginger family. Today, it is used most often as an ingredient in curry, and yellow food colouring; however it has been used for thousands of years in traditional East Indian medicine.  Curcumin appears to fight oxidation and inflammation, which are ways that the body can be injured during an AAA repair. We will perform a trial where we study 600 patients who have AAA repair. The patients will receive either curcumin or a placebo. We will recruit patients from nine centres in Canada. This trial will help us assess side effects and see if curcumin can help prevent kidney injury. If curcumin is beneficial and well-tolerated we will conduct the next stage of the trial. The next stage will have a total of 3600 patients and will look at outcomes most important to patients and their physicians.

Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MRNA TRANSPORT; PHOSPHORYLATION; RNA DECAY; RNA METABOLISM; STAUFEN; TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cellular processes require a coordinated expression of specific sets of genes that control cell growth, division and signalling. Perturbation of gene expression causes human diseases including cancer. In my laboratory, we are identifying and studying genes that, when disturbed, prevent the proteins from assuming their normal functions thereby causing the many symptoms characteristic of the diseases. The identification of such genes and the elucidation of their functions in normal and cancer cells are the first step in approaching these important health problems and are important since these studies may lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies for treating human cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessment of a Drama Workshop Program for Immigrant and Refugee Adolescents
Keywords-MotsClés: FRANCE; GESTION DE L'INFORMATION; H1N1; MEDIAS; QUEBEC; SERVICE D'INFORMATION SANTE; SECURITE
Abstract-Résumé: Helping youth immigrants and refugees adapt to the Canadian host society is a challenge that requires the development of school programs to meet their specific needs. Over the last 6 years, the transcultural psychiatry team (McGill University), working with  Montreal School Boards (high schools), has developed and qualitatively and quantitatively assessed a drama program aimed at helping such students adapt to their new environment through creative expression. At the request of a number of schools, the program was subsequently tailored to meet the needs of immigrant adolescents enrolled in special classes because of learning or behavioural problems. The main objective of the assessment of the drama workshop program for adolescents enrolled in special classes in multiethnic schools is to evaluate if the participation to this program decreases the impairment associated with emotional and behavioural symptoms (primary outcomes) and improves social adjustment as indicated by an improvement in peer relationships, and school performance (secondary outcomes). Our results will show whether the drama workshop program is beneficial to teenage immigrants and refugees with behavioural and learning difficulties that have been identified by their schools. They will also provide the basis for a discussion of high school programs designed for these young people and may prompt a rethinking of special education curricula to give greater consideration to the realities they face.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sensori-motor integration in neural circuits responsible for masticatory movements
Keywords-MotsClés: BURSTING PROPERTIES; CALCIUM IMAGING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MASTICATION; NEURON-GLIA INTERACTIONS; ORAL PHYSIOLOGY; REGULATION OF EXTRACELLULAR CALCIUM CONCENTRATION; RHYTHMOGENESIS; SENSORI-MOTOR INTEGRATION; SENSORY FEEDBACK IN CONTROL OF MOVEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Some of the most fundamental movements essential for survival, like breathing, chewing and walking are repetitive and rhythmic in nature. These movements are secured by neuronal networks that are similar in their organization and in their properties. One of the most important properties of these networks is the ability to generate a rhythmic motor command. In this project, we examine the cellular mechanisms underlying this property of "rhythmogenesis" in the masticatory system. Our previous results suggest that glial cells may be critical to enable the neurons of this system to generate a rhythmic activity by controlling the ionic composition of the extracellular fluid. Here we propose to dissect the mechanisms involved in this interaction and to explore how the pattern of activity generated by the "rhythmogenic" neurons is transmitted in a coordonated manner to the motoneurons controlling the various muscles involved in the behavior. We will also examine how the rhythmogenic neurons use sensry information from the oral region to adjust the pattern of the movements produced according to the prevailing conditions.  Many of the brain functions are based on the ability to generate a rhythm and we expect these findings to be of application to many other behaviors besides chewing.

Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM SIGNALING; CELL ADHESION; CYTOSKELETAL PROTEINS; INTEGRINS; MECHANICAL FORCES; PERIODONTIUM
Abstract-Résumé: The periodontal ligament is a highly specialized joint that attaches the teeth to the jaw bone and distributes chewing forces to the jaws. The periodontal ligament is essential for mastication and the health of the oral cavity. Specialized cells in the periodontal ligament (fibroblasts) maintain the proteins that attach the tooth roots to the jaw bone. Currently, the mechanisms by which cells in the periodontal ligament maintain their normal structure and function in spite of the high forces that are delivered to them as a result of chewing, are not understood. The purpose of this application is to determine how cells in the periodontal ligament respond to applied mechanical forces and maintain their ability to synthesize and remodel the attachment proteins that anchor the teeth to the jaw bone.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mitochondrial stress signalling: A target for drug development in cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG DEVELOPMENT; ETS-1; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; MITOCHONDRIA; MITOCHONDRIAL GLYCEROL PHOSPHATE DEHYDROGENASE; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; STRESS SIGNALING; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing evidence reveals that cancer has altered metabolism. The result of this change is an increase in metabolic byproducts, which in turn are responsible for signals that are unique in cancer cells. Identification and targeting the distinctiveness in cancer cells provides an opportunity to find novel targets and develop drugs that are selective for cancer cells and have negligible side effects for healthy cells. The focus of this project is to investigate the changes in the energy generating systems of tumour cells. The by-products of energy generation are breakdown of oxygen known as reactive oxygen molecules. These reactive oxygen molecules lead to abnormal signaling and may be associated with the cancer cell properties, such as uncontrolled growth and metastasis. We discovered in the energy producing sites of cancer cells a major protein source responsible for generating an abnormally high level of reactive oxygen molecules, called GPD2. We used sophisticated tools to identify inhibitors of this protein. Here we propose to further refine our inhibitor selection process and examine their biological consequences for cancer cells. This source of reactive oxygen molecules will be crystallized and its structure will be resolved. We will conduct sophisticated structure alterations and the potential mechanism(s) by which the inhibitors could block the production of reactive oxygen molecules will be determined. Limiting the ability of tumours to generate reactive oxygen molecules will reduce their ability to grow. This novel strategy would provide a new class of anticancer agents that target the energy producing sites of cancer cells and halt the abnormal processes in these cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: New Resources for Chemical Genomics, Metabolomics and Systems Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CHEMICAL GENOMICS; DRUG DISCOVERY; METABOLOMICS; NUTRIGENOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: We've all heard of the genome.  But have you ever heard of the metabolome?  The metabolome, which comes from the word metabolite, is the collection of all the small molecules that are found in the body.  These molecules include things like amino acids, fats and sugars as well as hormones, vitamins and minerals.  These compounds are the bricks and mortar of the body.  They also allow us to think, eat and breathe.  Over the past 3 years we have been identifying the 7500 metabolites, the 1500 drugs and the 3100 toxins or pollutants that can be found in our bodies.  In doing so we have assembled this information into a number of databases (DrugBank, The Human Metabolome Database, T3DB), spectral libraries and chemical libraries and made these publicly available.  These unique resources provide information about not only the chemicals themselves, but also the genes, the proteins and the diseases with which these compounds are associated.  This information is extremely important in diagnosing diseases, identifying drug targets and understanding the fundamentals of human biology.  These databases and libraries also contain key information, called "spectral fingerprints" that allow scientists to rapidly identify and quantify hundreds of chemicals at a time using special instruments called NMR and mass spectrometers.  For this project we are planning on expanding these resources and developing software to improve what they can do and what they can deliver to the biomedical community.  Over the next 5 years we plan on expanding the compound and spectral libraries, enhancing the content in the databases, creating new databases specific to foods and drug metabolites, developing novel software to improve the annotation of small molecule compounds, creating new computer programs to improve the identification of small molecules from blood and urine and developing novel software tools to model metabolic diseases on the computer.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the tumour suppressor PAR-4/LKB1 in cell polarity and asymmetric cell division
Keywords-MotsClés: ASYMMETRIC CELL DIVISION; C. ELEGANS EMBRYOGENESIS; CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL FATE SPECIFICATION; CELL POLARIZATION; DNA REPLICATION; GENETIC ANALYSIS; LIVE IMAGING; LKB1 SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Patients suffering from a disease called Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS) have a high risk (>90%) of developing tumors, mainly in the stomach and intestine. Tumors can also develop at various other sites, including lung, breast, pancreas, uterus, ovary, cervix and testis. Most PJS patients have mutations in a gene called LKB1, indicating that this is the gene that causes the disease and therefore that the normal function of LKB1 is to prevent the formation of tumors. However, how LKB1 performs this function is unknown. The goal of this research proposal is to understand how LKB1 functions in normal cells, to gain insights into its role during tumor formation. To do this, I am using a small worm called C. elegans. The advantage of using C. elegans as a model is that it is very easy to manipulate and its cells behave like human cells; therefore understanding a gene's function in this animal can help us to understand what it does in humans.  I am using modern cell biology, molecular biology and genetic tools to identify and characterize novel genes that can function with LKB1 to control the division of normal cells. This work will contribute to define the precise role of LKB1 in cell division. Because all of the genes that we study are conserved in humans, the discoveries that we make will help to understand how these genes function in human cells. As mutations in LKB1 are associated with a high risk of developing cancer, this work will also allow a better understanding of the molecular and cellular events that lead to the formation of tumors upon loss of LKB1 activity in PJS patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms through which ShcA integrates tyrosine kinase signaling to promote breast cancer progression
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; BREAST CANCER; ERBB2; RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASE; SHCA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSGENIC MICE; TUMOR STROMA
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer remains the most prevalent cancer in Canadian women and the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in this group. While targeted therapies have contributed to a decreased incidence of breast cancer mortality, the prevalence of this disease dictates that novel biomarkers and/or therapeutic targets are required to further improve disease-free survival.  The ShcA adaptor protein activates a critical signaling node in breast cancer cells to regulate diverse biological processes including tumor growth, survival and recruitment of a new blood supply, through a process termed angiogenesis.  We have previously demonstrating that ShcA signaling in breast cancer cells regulates each of these processes to favor a pro-tumorigenic state, which facilitates breast cancer progression.  We will mechanistically address how ShcA signaling induces tumor growth and angiogenesis using well-characterized breast cancer mouse models. This will lead to the identification of novel, ShcA-regulated genes that functionally contribute to the tumorigenic process and which may represent viable targets for disease intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional control of metabolism by the estrogen related receptors (ERRs)
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; METABOLISM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Energy homeostasis is the balanced regulation of fuel intake, storage and expenditure by a person. While a constant supply of energy is required to maintain the basal metabolic rate of the whole individual, energy is also differentially generated and utilized by individual cell types and organs in response to endogenous or exogenous signals specified by various developmental and physiological needs and stimuli. Regulated control of energy production and utilization thus allows the organism to function effectively in a broad range of environmental conditions. On the other hand, disturbance of energy homeostasis over a long period of time can contribute to the etiology of many diseases such as diabetes, obesity, heart failure and even cancer. Imbalance in metabolic homeostasis may originate from nutritional deprivation or overabundance, genetic variations and disorders as well as from gradual loss of efficiency in control systems during the aging process. Consequently, improving our knowledge of how metabolic homeostasis can be maintained through the life of the organism and defining, at the molecular level, control mechanisms that can be manipulated to prevent and treat metabolic-related diseases are of indisputable medical significance. Nuclear hormone receptors play a major role in controlling energy homeostasis, and this grant application is directed at increasing our knowledge of how one sub-family of nuclear receptors, referred to as the estrogen related receptors (ERRs), influences this process in normal physiology and diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Application of ultradeep sequencing technologies to study HIV compartmentalization and evolution
Keywords-MotsClés: CO-RECEPTOR USAGE; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNOCAPTURE; RESERVOIRS; ULTRADEEP SEQUENCING; VIRAL EVOLUTION
Abstract-Résumé: Although effective treatments have been developed to treat HIV infection, there remains no cure. Two major barriers to HIV eradication are the existence of viral reservoirs (specific cell types or anatomical sites where HIV can persist over time), as well as the virus' extensive capacity for mutation and evolution. This grant proposes to integrate two innovative laboratory techniques, viral immunocapture and ultradeep DNA sequencing, to address the fundamental challenges of viral reservoirs and HIV evolution. HIV transmission is characterized by "genetic bottleneck" whereby a single or few transmitted founder viruses initiate infection. However, these founder viruses quickly evolve to generate a diverse swarm of viruses within the patient. The seeding of cellular reservoirs of HIV (for example, latently-infected T-cells and other unknown cell types) also occurs early in infection. Using a technique known as "viral immunocapture", we can isolate individual HIV virus particles from patient plasma, and identify their likely cellular origin based on the detection of specific host-cell-derived proteins on the virus' surface. In this grant, we propose to examine the extent and timecourse of HIV evolution and diversification in different virus "lineages" - meaning, viruses originating from different types of infected cells within the body, including potential viral reservoirs.  We will use immunocapture to isolate viruses from different lineages and then use ultradeep DNA sequencing to study HIV diversification and evolution over time in these lineages. Our analyses will focus on a specific part of the viral envelope known as the 3rd hypervariable loop, which represents one of the most rapidly evolving sites in the virus as well as a major determinant of HIV pathogenesis.  In summary, this research is valuable because it will yield an improved understanding of HIV reservoirs and viral evolution, and thus represents a step forward towards efforts to eradicate HIV.
