TitreApplicationTitle: Autologous Bone Marrow-Derived Cellular Augmentation in Rotator Cuff Repair
Keywords-MotsClés: MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MECHANICAL TESTING; RADIOLOGY; ROTATOR CUFF TENDON TEAR; SHOULDER SURGERY; STEM CELL THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: The rotator cuff of the shoulder is the most commonly injured tendon in humans. Surgery is often needed to repair the tear.  However, the failure rate of this surgery is high. Long-term successful repair of the tear is achieved in only half of patients. Failed repairs cause pain, muscle wasting, weakness, decreased range of motion and poor shoulder function.  In the past, open surgery to repair rotator cuff tears created a bony trough, and sutures or tacks temporarily held the tendon onto the bone until the tear was healed. Cells from inside the bone were the major contributor to tendon healing. Currently, arthroscopic surgery has all but replaced open surgery. Arthroscopic surgery does not create a trough, and therefore cells from the bone marrow are not available to aid in the repair. The recruitment in large numbers of these bone marrow cells at the proper time could improve the success of current tendon surgery.  We aim to test this concept in both an animal model and a human trial. The distinguishing feature of this research is the unique timing for recruiting bone marrow cells to initiate the healing.  Our hypothesis is that the bone marrow cells will not only accelerate the healing but also increase the success of the surgery and the patient's shoulder function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cannabis and Motor Vehicle Crashes: A Multicentre Culpability Study.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANNABIS; MOTOR VEHICLE CRASHES
Abstract-Résumé: Marijuana is the most commonly used illicit drug in Canada and many drivers, especially young adults, report driving after using marijuana. Although there is abundant experimental evidence that marijuana, either alone or in combination with alcohol, impairs the skills required for safe driving, real world data on the contribution of marijuana to car crashes is mixed. This uncertainty hinders the ability of traffic safety policy makers to develop effective, evidence based, traffic laws or road safety campaigns targeting people who drive while impaired by marijuana. The primary objective of the study proposed here is to determine whether injured drivers who used marijuana before a car crash are more likely to have caused the crash than those who did not. Our aim is to improve traffic safety by providing current North American data that can be used to inform the development of evidence based road safety policy targeting people who drive while impaired by marijuana.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cholinergic enhancement of visual capacity in rodents
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; CEREBRAL CORTEX; FUNCTIONAL NEUROANATOMY; NEURONAL PLASTICITY; VISION RECOVERY; VISUAL DISCRIMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Because vision is not only a matter of eyes, the proposed research studies how the neurons in the brain could improve vision. The final objective is to find new pharmacological agents to alleviate visual deficits. The research particularly focuses on acetylcholine (ACh), a chemical substance secreted by certain neurons in the brain to communicate with each other. It is hypothesized that ACh could enhance the functioning of the region of the brain where visual information is first analyzed (named primary visual cortex or V1). The role of ACh in vision was examined because this neurochemical plays an active role in attention, learning and memory. The involvement of ACh in visual learning implies that this neurochemical facilitates the recognition of visual elements in a scene by increasing the rapidity and the efficiency of V1 to analyze these particular elements. We have already shown that ACh enhances the responses of the V1 neurons in rats to visual stimulation in a very persistent manner. Now the proposed experiments will examine the capacity of a repetitive exposition (during 2 weeks) of the rats to a visual pattern in combination to ACh circuit activation to improve permanently vision, electrical activity and neuronal circuits in V1. This is tested in normal animals as well as in animals with a retinal lesion to investigate whether a treatment with ACh contributes to the recovery of vision.   First, these groups of rats will be tested in a maze in order to recognize the pattern to which they have been exposed regularly. Electrical activity in V1 will be measured by a technique similar to electroencephalography and the neuronal circuits will be analyzed on brain slices by microscopy. Finally, cerebral imaging will be used to observe the changes induced by the training on the representation of the pattern in V1. This study should provide new findings in order to potentiate the rehabilitation therapy to recover visual capacities by low vision people.

TitreApplicationTitle: Saskatchewan Farm Injury Cohort Study: Phase 2
Keywords-MotsClés: AGRICULTURE; BIOSTATISTICS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; PEDIATRIC HEALTH; POPULATION HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH; RURAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Within Canada, injury remains a leading cause of mortality and morbidity.  Some populations are more vulnerable to injury than others.  Agricultural populations experience very high rates of injury, yet evidence surrounding underlying causes of agricultural injury remains limited. As part of an organized and long-term effort to understand more about the causes of agricultural injuries in Canada, in 2005 CIHR funded our research team to develop a cohort of farm families in Saskatchewan.  Phase 1 of this initiative was highly successful. The theoretical base for this study was population health theory; hence much of this research focuses on determinants of injury on farms. Because of our unique sampling frame and the breadth of our baseline survey, additional analyses allowed our group to understand other risk factors for injury, as well as other contributors to health in farm populations. The current grant application is for Phase 2 of this cohort study. The primary focus is to further understanding about physical, economic, and cultural environments and their effects on injury rates in agricultural populations.  We propose to follow our general cohort of 2,390 farms (5,502 people) for an additional 3 years.  We also propose an expanded focus on injuries experienced by members of vulnerable populations through the establishment of a child and young worker cohort.  Data from the two cohorts will also permit us to study potential causes of other health outcomes specific to agricultural populations, as well as their prevention. This project addresses multiple CIHR research priorities, and involves a strong research team. Our focus on vulnerable subgroups in the agricultural sector is timely. Our long-term goal is to provide useful evidence for this important segment of Canada's rural population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determination and inference of transcription factor sequence preferences across the eukaryotic kingdom
Keywords-MotsClés: EVOLUTION; GENE REGULATION; GENOMICS; MICROARRAYS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells read DNA using proteins that recognize specific sequences.  Knowledge of the sequence preferences of DNA-binding proteins is critical for understanding how genomes function.  We now have genome sequences from all major branches of the eukaryotic kingdom - that is, all non-bacterial life forms.  These sequences also provide lists of proteins, from which we can identify those that are likely to bind DNA.  My laboratory has implemented a high-throughput technique for determining the sequence preferences of DNA-binding proteins, and we also have a computational system for projecting these data among related proteins.  In the next five years we will endeavor to use these systems to determine or infer the sequence preferences of all eukaryotic DNA-binding proteins.  These data will be of widespread utility in biomedical research.

TitreApplicationTitle: ODF2 protein function in spermatozoa and embryo
Keywords-MotsClés: EARLY EMBRYO CELL DIVISION; MALE INFERTILITY; OUTER DENSE FIBER; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; SPERM MOTILITY; SPERM TAIL; SPERMATOGENESIS; TRANSGENIC AND KNOCKOUT MICE; ZYGOTE
Abstract-Résumé: Defects in spermatozoa, the cells that transfer the father's genetic material to an oocyte, underlie approximately half of all cases of infertility that are presented in the clinic. Spermatozoa are motile cells, and several unique structures in the sperm tail are believed to play important roles in motility. One of these structures is called the Outer Dense Fibers. Although these Outer Dense Fibers are present in sperm from fruit flies to man, their function is still unclear, but our recent evidence points to a role in sperm motility. However, several instances of abnormal sperm tail structures, including Outer Dense Fiber defects, have been reported in cases of human male infertility. It is not known what causes these defects. We had discovered and characterized many proteins in Outer Dense Fibers, as well as proteins that bind to these structures. For one of these, the abundant Odf2 protein, we recently developed two mouse models of male infertility. These mouse models show that this protein does not only play a role in sperm itself, but also -surprisingly- in the fertilized egg and embryo. Importantly, the mouse model shows sperm defects similar to what is observed in some cases of human male infertility. We propose to investigate these observations in detail, to establish the mechanisms of how this protein contributes to the normal Outer Dense Fibers and the sperm tail, and exactly how it contributes to the cell divisions in the fertilized egg. Our results may help explain the basis for some cases of human male infertility, and could be translated in future approaches to the clinic, by providing tools for diagnosis of male infertility involving ODF and axoneme defects and tests of a sperm's capability to fertilize an egg and support embryogenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Probing the circuits responsible for stroke recovery with light-mediated circuit monitoring and manipulation in mouse models.
Keywords-MotsClés: 2-PHOTON IMAGING; CALCIUM; CHANNELRHODOPSIN-2; DENDRITE; OPTOGENETICS; PLASTICITY; STROKE; SYNAPSE
Abstract-Résumé: Reductions in blood flow to the brain of sufficient duration and extent lead to stroke, which results in damage to neuronal networks and impairment of sensation, movement, or cognition. Although stroke damage can be devastating, many patients survive the initial event and undergo some spontaneous recovery which that can be further augmented by rehabilitative therapy. It becoming clear that the ability of patients to recover is in part mediated by the ability of the brain circuits to adapt in a process called plasticity. My lab will apply new light-based techniques to address how the brain's sensory and motor circuits adapt in response to stroke. The brain is organized much like a circuit diagram within a computer with discrete wires or connections. However, none of the brain circuits or cells have color-coding or labels which enable technicians to service them. Here, using new genetic technologies we will employ strategies, which label select mouse neurons with fluorescent proteins, which enable them to glow under particular wavelengths of light. Not only can the glowing neurons be found by light, but they can also be controlled by light using new light-sensitive protein ion channels, which transmit light energy into excitation or inhibition. Using these fluorescing neurons, which can be controlled by light, we plan to unravel how the brains sensory and motor system adapt following damage due to stroke. We hope that by understanding how the brain can partially cope with stroke damage that this knowledge can be exploited to help patients through innovative brain stimulation or rehabilitative strategies. We have now devised new strategies for both exciting and inhibiting the brains of mouse models of stroke damage to aid these studies. Overall, our goal is that through insight into natural sensory and motor system adaptation novel treatments will ensue, permitting better lives for those affected by diseases such as stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional analysis of the TGF-beta/Smad signalling pathway in regeneration.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR BIOLOGY; FIBROSIS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; REGENERATION; SMADS; TGF-BETA; TISSUE REPAIR; TRANSGENESIS; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: Regenerative medicine is the new frontier of biomedical sciences that promises to unlock the secrets of how the body generates and repair itself. The ability to regenerate lost of damaged tissues would greatly benefit people suffering from the loss of tissue function such as organ failure, amputation and burn victims. Fortunately for tissue regeneration research, there is a vertebrate model that can perfectly regenerate its tissues following amputation or injury which provides a unique opportunity to unlock the mechanisms of regeneration. Urodele amphibians (e.g. axolotls) are unique among vertebrates in their ability to regenerate tissues. In order to better understand the signals modulating the process of regeneration in urodeles, we have selected to study signalling molecules that are implicated in cell growth, differentiation and wound healing in other non-regenerating vertebrate models. A better understanding of how these animals can regenerate their tissues may one day lead to novel therapeutic approaches for treating loss of tissue function and organ failure in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Persistent Antipsychotic Polypharmacy: A Prevalent Practice Without Evidence
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIPSYCHOTIC POLYPHARMACY; GENDER AND SEX-BASED ANALYSIS; POPULATION-BASED LINKED HEALTHCARE DATABASE; SYSTEMATIC CHART REVIEWS
Abstract-Résumé: Persistent antipsychotic polypharmacy is the practice of prescribing more than one antipsychotic to a patient for an extended period of time. Presumably, physicians used this strategy to treat patients with schizophrenia that may be refractory to treatment with a single antipsychotic. However, the Canadian Psychiatric Association clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of schizophrenia state that antipsychotic polypharmacy should be the 'last strategy' used to treat patients with schizophrenia. Furthermore, there is very little evidence in the medical literature to support this practice that is known to be associated with excessive dosing and side effects. Using province-wide data, our research will determine the prevalence of persistent antipsychotic polypharmacy in both out- and inpatients in British Columbia. We will evaluate reasons physicians give for this prescribing practice as well as assess its associated benefits and risks. Our goal is to gain insight into this prescribing practice so that we can optimize antipsychotic treatment to improve mental health outcomes for patients affected with schizophrenia and related psychoses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the impact of a training and communication network program in nephrology to facilitate the detection and management of drug-related problems by community pharmacists: A multicentre cluster randomized controlled trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; COMMUNITY PHARMACISTS; DELPHI METHOD; DRUG RELATED PROBLEMS; MULTIDISCIPLINARY CARE INTERVENTIONS; PREDIALYSIS; QUALITY OF MEDICATION USE
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with chronic kidney disease are followed in predialysis clinic to slow down the progression of their disease and treat their co-existing health problems. These patients are usually elderly, have many diseases and take numerous medications prescribed by several physicians. Many problems related to their medication have been reported. Because community pharmacists are highly accessible and know all the medications taken by these patients, they are in a good position to help them. To optimise their work, the ProFiL program has been developed. It includes a web-training program and provides pharmacists with essential clinical information on their patients as well as access to a consultation service offered by clinicians with expertise in this field.   Six predialysis clinics will participate in this study and recruit 429 patients, about 144 community pharmacies, and about 288 pharmacists. Patients and pharmacists assigned to the ProFil program will be compared to those assigned to the usual care. Each patient will be followed-up for one year and the quality of their medication use will be evaluated at the beginning and at the end of the study. It is expected that the use of medication will improve in patients followed by a ProFiL pharmacists.  In our healthcare system, patients do not fully benefit from the professional competencies of community pharmacists even though they are among the most accessible primary healthcare providers. The ProFiL program is unique and designed to optimize the work of community pharmacists. It is simple and based mostly on resources that are already available. This model may be used as a reference model in the management of chronic diseases and may be applied to any other specialized clinics or medical clinics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innate Immune Pathways Involving Hemopoietic Progenitors in the Development of Allergy and Asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGY; ASTHMA; COHORT STUDIES; CORD BLOOD PROGENITORS; CYTOKINE RECEPTORS; CYTOKINES
Abstract-Résumé: Allergic diseases, including hayfever, food allergies and asthma, are increasing worldwide and sufferers of either of these airways diseases can become very ill. It is now clear that there is an inflammatory basis for these conditions in which specific white blood cells (eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells) are abundant. The reasons for variability among individuals to develop or not develop allergies and asthma, remain unclear.  Evidence directly implicating altered production of white blood cells, derived from mother ("stem") cells in the bone marrow, in ongoing allergic inflammation and disease pathogenesis has been well established, resulting in the "bone marrow hypothesis" of allergy and asthma, pioneered by the applicant. This proposal aims to continue to investigate the roles that blood stem cells play in determining the development of allergy and asthma in early infancy and childhood, based on several studies already conducted on mothers and their babies over the past few years, showing that there are differences in numbers and types of blood stem cells at birth in the cord blood, between infants at high risk (whose parents are allergic) versus those at low risk (whose parents are not allergic) for the development of allergy and asthma.  The cellular, molecular and genetic bases for these differences will be carefully explored, using novel tests and techniques developed by the applicant. Applying these methods to samples from a recently launched national birth cohort study will add important information on predicting, at birth, which babies will go on to develop allergies and asthma in the first years of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of the gene(s) predisposing to Chiari Malformation I using the Griffon Bruxellois dog model
Keywords-MotsClés: CANDIDATE GENES; CHIARI MALFORMATION I; COMPLEX TRAITS; DOG MODEL; FUNCTIONAL STUDIES; GENETIC STUDIES; LINKAGE DISEQUILIBRIUM MAPPING; MALFORMATION OF THE CRANIOVERTEBRAL JUNCTION; MUTATION SCREENING; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Chiari malformation I (CMI) represents a common abnormality of the lower region of the brain located at the junction with the spinal cord, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 1280. The lower portions of the brain called the cerebellar tonsils protrude into the vertebral canal causing a variety of clinical signs including headache, vision problems and dizziness. CMI is often associated with syringomyelia where a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) develops within the spinal cord. Most cases of CMI are congenital, meaning they are present at birth. The etiology of CMI is complex and thought to involve both genetic factors.  CMI in humans is similar to a condition in the dog called Chiari-like malformation (CM) that is particularly common in the Cavalier King Charles Spaniels (CKCS) and Griffon Bruxellois (GB) breeds. The dog model is the only known naturally-occurring animal model for CMI in humans and represents a powerful tool for understanding its complex genetic etiology. Our study aims at identification of the CM gene(s) in the dog which will provide an entry point for identifying equivalent genes involved in CMI in humans. We have conducted a scan of the whole dog genome using affected dogs from the GB and identified six potential CM candidate regions in the dog genome. We will investigate these candidate regions for true association to CM by additional genetic studies in a larger cohort. The confirmed candidate interval(s) will be further defined and will be sequenced to identify the defective CM gene(s)in the dog.  We will next identify the human equivalent(s) of the dog CM gene(s) and screen them for the presence of pathogenic mutations in a human cohort of CMI patients. Identification of a predisposing gene that contributes to the etiology of CMI may lead to the development of simple and accurate diagnostic tests for better clinical management of CMI patients and their relatives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring and improving the quality of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) care
Keywords-MotsClés: MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; OUTCOMES RESEARCH; PRIMARY PCI; REGIONAL VARIATION; REPERFUSION THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Heart attack survival rates vary dramatically in Ontario from 7% to 12% depending upon the health region in which one lives but the reasons for these variations are not known.  One factor that may explain these differences is the availability of emergency primary angioplasty, using a balloon to open a blocked heart artery, which can only be done in 14 hospitals in Ontario.  Emergency angioplasty is a more effective treatment than clot-busting drugs in improving heart-attack survival rates but clot-busting drugs have the advantage that they can be given in any emergency room.  Recently, doctors have been trying new strategies in some regions of Ontario whereby they arrange for paramedics to transfer heart attack patients by ambulance to the nearest angioplasty hospital to get emergency treatment rather treating the patients with clot-busting drugs at their local hospital.  However, it is uncertain if health regions that transfer patients for emergency angioplasty have better heart attack survival rates than regions where patients are treated at their local hospital.  In this project, we will determine the patient, treatment, and health system-related factors that explain variations in heart attack survival for 6,000 patients treated during 2008 to 2010 across Ontario's 14 health regions.  We will develop 'report cards' on the quality of care that heart attack patients received in each region in Ontario, and identify opportunities by which various health regions in Ontario, can improve their treatment and survival rates for heart attack patients.  We will share our findings with government, hospitals, and clinicians who treat these patients, so that the system can improve and reduce the number of patients who die from a heart attack.  We estimate that it may be possible to save up to 600 lives each year in Ontario, if all health regions could achieve the best heart attack survival rates currently observed in Ontario.

TitreApplicationTitle: The relationship between proteases, protease activated receptors and cytokines in mediating osteoarthritis pain
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CYTOKINES; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PAIN; PROTEASE ACTIVATED RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis affecting 1 in 10 Canadians. The number one concern for OA sufferers is the alleviation of joint pain; however, current analgesics are either ineffective or produce toxic side-effects. Thus, there is a pressing need to discover novel drug targets to manage OA pain. During OA, enzymes are released into the joint which cause destruction of joint tissues. In addition to their digesting effects, these enzymes can also signal pain by acting on a unique group of receptors called PARs. This proposal will examine how these enzymes activate PARs in diseased joints to cause pain and disability. This work will improve our understanding of joint neurobiology and has the potential to uncover new approaches to effectively relieve OA pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Central neuronal mechanisms underlying tactile roughness in the monkey
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION; PARIETAL CORTEX; PERCEPTION AND ACTION; SENSORIMOTOR INTEGRATION; SOMATOSENSORY; TACTILE ROUGHNESS; TACTILE SPEED
Abstract-Résumé: We are studying the central neural mechanisms that underlie the ability to perceive surface roughness using touch. Project 1 will examine the neuronal coding of roughness in somatosensory cortex. Project 2 will investigate the role of voluntary attention in enhancing neuronal responsiveness to touch at the level of the gateway for sensory inputs to the cortex, the sensory thalamus. Both projects examine neuronal discharge in relation to perception & action (sensory decision signaled by movement). Project 1 tests our hypothesis that roughness is encoded by the activity of small groups of specialized cortical neurones. The results will provide important insights into how the brain works & how it generalizes to form an invariant representation of tactile inputs. The results will have direct applications in the development of sensorimotor neural prosthetics: where to implant electrodes in the brain & what "language" to use. Project 2 is based on our pilot work showing for the 1st time that voluntary attention exerts substantial controls over neuronal sensitivity to tactile stimuli in the sensory thalamus. We will confirm & extend these observations.  Attention improves perception, focusing the brain's processing capacities on stimuli relevant to one's goals in the context of a CNS that is inundated with a steady stream of sensory inputs - information overload in our multi-tasking society. An example is using tactile search to quickly locate the car key, not the house key, at the bottom of a deep & cluttered purse. Our work challenges the old view that voluntary attention acts only at high levels of the CNS. Showing that attention is a global controller will provide new insights for interventions to re-educate attention, a major health issue affecting all ages. Moreover, we suggest - based on our previous work & that of others - that targeted strategies to rehabilitate tactile perception must include directed attention combined with sensory training + active movement.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of in utero-initiated benzene toxicity
Keywords-MotsClés: BENZENE; C-MYB SIGNALING; IN UTERO INITIATED LEUKEMIAS; OXIDATIVE STRESS; RECOMBINATION; TOPOISOMERASE
Abstract-Résumé: When a pregnant women is exposed to therapeutic drugs or environmental chemicals, her unborn child may be at increased risk for the development of cancer after birth.  Benzene is one of the most heavily used chemicals in the world and is known to cause toxicity to the blood system and has been associated with an increase in childhood leukemias.  Oncogenes are genes that have become altered in some way, leading to aberrant signalling pathways in cells, which ultimately may lead to cancer.  I am proposing to study the ways in which benzene disrupts the development of early hematopoiesis (blood cell formation) by looking at various oncogenes and pathways using a mouse model.  Using this model we have already shown that in utero exposure of pregnant mice to benzene leads to an increase in cancer incidence in the offspring.  We now want to use this model to determine how this occurs in order to understand the regulatory pathways involved. Understanding how drugs and environmental chemicals cause toxicity to the developing fetus will help us develop safer therapeutics and potential therapeutic approaches to treat pregnant who may have been exposed to toxicants.  In addition, results from this project will help guide policy for the use and exposure to benzene and other chemicals that might act the same way.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular biomarkers of antidepressant response
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIDEPRESSANTS; MAJOR DEPRESSION; MICRORNA; MRNA; NEUROBIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Antidepressants are commonly used treatments for major depression. While a significant proportion of patients treated with antidepressants respond to treatment, a large proportion (up to 60%, depending on the study) of patients do not respond. The proposed application aims to conduct a prospective study investigating molecular markers as predictors of antidepressant response to citalopram and venlafaxine, both commonly prescribed antidepressants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Introspection and insight in non-clinical and clinical populations
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; BELIEFS; CHOICE BLINDNESS; CONFABULATORY INTROSPECTION; DELUSIONAL DISORDER; IMAGINATION; INSIGHT; OBSESSIONAL DOUBT; OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER; REASONING
Abstract-Résumé: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) and Delusional Disorder (DD) are psychological disorders that are both characterized by faulty beliefs about reality which cause a considerable degree of distress and behavioral problems. Indeed, research over the past nine years has established that what is problematic for the person with OCD and DD is not what actually occurs, but what they imagine to be there. In particular, a tendency to arrive at false beliefs about reality appears strongly related to level of insight into our own reasoning. In particular, a critical mass of studies has shown that failures in introspection are 1) profound, 2) at the root of what appears to be insight, and 3) measurable in an experimental reasoning task (Johansson et al, 2005). Over the next four years, 140 adult patients will participate in a study to measure introspective ability and insight into their own reasoning (OCD, DD and Anxiety Disorder). An additional eighty participants from the general population will be tested for comparison purposes. After baseline assessment on questionnaire, clinical and experimental measures, those with OCD will be retested after 24 weeks of receiving specialized cognitive-behavior therapy. The key hypothesis is that those with OCD and Delusional Disorder will show systematic failures in introspection which leads to obsessional doubt and false beliefs about reality. It is also expected that improvements in insight and introspective ability will be associated with successful treatment outcome. The research program will provide crucial new information on reasoning and imaginative processes characterizing these debilitating psychological disorders, and assist in the development of much needed new treatment strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Electromechanical coupling in vascular smooth muscle: a novel signal transduction pathway involving the calcium-dependent tyrosine kinase, Pyk2
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM; CONTRACTION; DEPOLARIZATION; HYPERTENSION; MYOSIN LIGHT CHAIN PHOSPHATASE; PI 3-KINASE; PYK2; RHO-ASSOCIATED KINASE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: High pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to all tissues and organs of the body is a leading cause of illness and death through heart and kidney disease, hardening of the arteries, eye damage and stroke, and accounts for the deaths of more Canadians than any other disease (31% in 2005). Cardiovascular disease costs the Canadian economy more than $22.2 billion every year in physician services, hospitalization costs, lost wages and decreased productivity.  Blood pressure is controlled by "smooth muscle cells" in the walls of the blood vessels. When these cells contract (shorten), they reduce vessel diameter and increase blood pressure. Nerves, which terminate at the surface of smooth muscle cells, release chemicals, which act on the membrane (surface) of the smooth muscle cells to reverse the electric charge distribution across the cell membrane, allowing the entry of calcium, which triggers contraction (shortening). The molecular mechanism whereby calcium triggers contraction involves activation of an enzyme (a protein catalyst) called "myosin light chain kinase". We made the important discovery that this simple mechanism is only part of the story; the challenge now is to complete the story. We discovered that calcium also activates a pathway (a molecular cascade) leading to inhibition of the enzyme "myosin light chain phosphatase", which reverses the action of myosin light chain kinase. The objective of this project is to explain, at the molecular level, how calcium leads to inhibition of myosin light chain phosphatase, and how the pathway is altered in animal models of hypertension.  This work will lead to the identification of novel drug targets. Given the high incidence and serious impact of hypertension, combined with the side effects of existing blood pressure-lowering drugs, such as calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors and beta blockers, it is critical that such novel drug targets be identified.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strengthening Health Systems in Low Income countries through improving their Priority Setting processes: The case of H1N1, HIV and Prenatal conditions.
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPING COUNTRIES; EVALUATION OF QUALITY; PRIORITY SETTING; STRENGTHENING HEALTH CARE SYSTEMS
Abstract-Résumé: Improving priority setting would improve the sustainability of- and strengthen health care systems in low and middle income countries. However decision makers in these countries lack guidance and information relevant for making these decisions. The purpose of this study to use a framework, that was developed to evaluate priority setting in low income countries, to  evaluate a case of priority setting in Uganda. Using the examples of H1N1, HIV and Perinatal conditions, we will use the framework to assess the quality of the priority setting decisions. The framework will also enable us to assess the contextual factors that may facilitate/ inhibit quality priority setting, as well as the stakeholders that influence priority setting in LICs. The comprehensiveness of the framework will enable us to collaboratively identify specific areas where meagre resources for strengthening priority setting and health care systems in low income countries can be focused.The results will also provide an opportunity to reflect on the role of Canadian policy makers and non-government organizations in global priority setting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of iron and heme binding proteins in pathogenesis of Staphylococcus aureus
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG RESISTANT BACTERIA; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; IRON UPTAKE SYSTEMS; MICROBIOLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; STAPH AUREUS
Abstract-Résumé: Iron is an essential nutrient that is required for the survival and growth of all living organisms. This is no less important for disease-causing bacteria. In order to acquire sufficient iron to meet their needs, many bacteria have highly efficient systems to acquire iron. The bacterium Staphylococcus aureus is one of the most common causes of human infections. These infections range from mild (minor wound infections and carbuncles, for example) to more serious (endocarditis, osteomyelitis, arthritis, septicaemia, and toxic shock syndrome, for example). S. aureus is also the most common source of hospital-acquired infections and is frequently found as the cause of surgical wound and foreign implantation device infections. However, efforts to control this bacterium with antibiotics are becoming increasingly difficult due to its ability to acquire resistance to many different antibiotics. Our research is interested in studying the mechanisms that this bacterium uses to acquire iron in defining how this bacterium responds to iron limitation. Ultimately, our goal is to take advantage of our knowledge of the iron response in S. aureus to be able to find new avenues of treating infections caused by this bacterium. Our studies continue to provide novel information for how serious Gram-positive bacteria, like S. aureus, can obtain iron and thereby cause serious infections.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of Nuclear Entry of Parvovirus
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; MINUTE VIRUS OF MICE; NUCLEAR PORE COMPLEX; NUCLEAR TRANSPORT; PARVOVIRUS; VIRUS TRANSPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Viruses are responsible for many of the world's most serious diseases. In Canada, viral infections remain the single most common reason why people seek medical attention. In order to spread infection, many viruses replicate themselves in the nucleus of their host cells. To accomplish this, they transport their genome into the nucleus of their host cells. Today, many aspects of viral replication and cell entry are well understood at the molecular level; however, very little is known about how viruses deliver their genetic material into the nucleus. Interrupting the delivering of the viral genome into the nucleus could prevent the virus from spreading. Thus, a detailed characterization of the process of nuclear entry of viral genomes is an important step toward developing anti-viral therapy. In addition, because viruses are now used as vehicles in gene therapy in humans to deliver therapeutic genes to organs harboring disease, our work is critical for gene-delivery technology. The present research proposal plans to explore more in depth the mechanisms used by parvoviruses to deliver their genome into the nucleus of their host cells. Because of their ability to preferentially target and kill rapidly dividing cancer cells, parvoviruses are potential vectors for use in cancer gene therapy. Thus, our studies of nuclear import of parvovirus promise to bring significant insights for anti-cancer gene therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterisation and roles of isoprostanes in the pathophysiology of preeclampsia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIOXIDANTS; BLOOD; ENZYMATIC ACTIVITY / EXPRESSION ANALYSIS; ISOPROSTANES; LIPID PEROXIDATION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PLACENTA; PREECLAMPSIA; THROMBOXANE/ PROSTACYCLIN
Abstract-Résumé: Preeclampsia is a complex pathology diagnosed during the second part of the pregnancy. This disorder is characterized by hypertension (high blood pressure), proteinuria (high protein level in urine). This disorder occurs in 3 to 8% of all pregnancies. The only cure for preeclampsia is premature delivery, and this disorder is a leading cause of maternal and neonatal deaths. There are many evidences to support that oxidative stress plays an important role in preeclampsia. An oxidative stress is characterized by an excessive production of reactive oxygen derivatives that various antioxidant systems cannot eliminate, therefore leading to cell and tissue injuries. Some encouraging studies indicated that treatments with antioxidant supplements like vitamin E and C could be beneficial in the prevention of preeclampsia. In this research project, we will determine the role and the importance of lipid oxidation in preeclampsia.  In conclusion, this research project will improve our knowledge of the disease and determine the potential role of oxidized lipids as biochemical markers for the diagnosis of preeclampsia. This study will also help us to design new antioxidant therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of a brief motivational intervention on adherence behavior in asthmatics: A randomized controlled trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; ASTHMA CONTROL; ASTHMA QUALITY OF LIFE; BEHAVIORAL INTERVENTION; MEDICATION ADHERENCE; MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING; RCT; SELF-EFFICACY
Abstract-Résumé: The high personal and financial costs of asthma appear to be related to poor asthma control. The availability of effective treatments suggests that asthma can be well controlled in most patients, though most (53-58%) Canadians remain poorly controlled. Achieving optimal asthma control relies upon several behavioral factors, particularly daily taking one's medication as prescribed. However, research suggests adherence rates are as low as 32% in patients with asthma. Participation in education programs has increased patient knowledge about the importance of medication adherence, but recent reviews indicate that these programs have not significantly changed medication taking behavior. The purpose of this study is to assess the impact of a brief intervention that uses motivational interviewing (MI) techniques, on asthma medication adherence in sample of adult asthmatics. A total of 182 patients will be recruited, half of which will receive the intervention, and half of which will not. The primary outcome measure will be adherence to inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), a medication which must be taken daily to be effective. This will be measured at 6 and 12 months post-intervention by verifying how often patients fill their prescriptions. This is done by accessing pharmacy records and drug database files. Secondary outcome measures include: self-reported medication adherence, levels of asthma control, confidence in one's ability to manage asthma, and quality of life. Statistical analyses will compare adherence rates between the intervention and nonintervention groups, and statistical corrections will be made to ensure that other variables that could be associated with medication adherence (e.g., sex, age, asthma severity) cannot account for any post-treatment group differences. This study may provide support for the use of MI techniques to improve medication adherence and asthma outcomes, in order to improve asthma control and quality of life in asthmatics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Trajectories of Brain Development and Neurocognitive Outcomes in Children born Preterm
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN INJURY AND DEVELOPMENT; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; FUNCTIONAL MRI; HPA REPROGRAMMING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEONATAL STRESS; NEURODEVELOPMENTAL OUTCOME; PREMATURE NEWBORN; WHITE MATTER INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada preterm birth is the most important cause of infant death, illness and disability. Children born very early are at very high risk for developmental delays. This risk is increasing over time. In the first phase of our research program, we identified common patterns of brain injury and impaired brain development following preterm birth. How these brain abnormalities in the neonatal period relate to long-term brain changes and long-term outcomes is unknown. To our knowledge, ours is the only cohort of premature newborns serially studied with advanced brain imaging in the neonatal period and followed in early childhood with measures of stress system function that can be re-examined at 8 years of age with detailed advanced brain imaging and outcome measures to address these critical questions. The overall hypothesis of this research is that brain injury and altered brain development, in association with systemic illness, results in long-term changes in motor and cognitive function, and that this relationship is modulated by permanent changes in stress hormone levels. Building on the platform of our unique cohort, we are now positioned to address our overall objective of determining why and how children born very early are so developmentally vulnerable. A better understanding of the factors that effect long-term brain development will allow us to directly improve the neurodevelopmental outcome of preterm newborns by targeting those factors that promote good outcomes. The development of robust measures of brain development and injury in newborns will help parents and health care providers to care for newborns delivered preterm by providing important long-term prognostic information, and early identification of those children most in need of intervention to optimize neurodevelopment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nutritional status as a determinant of recovery after stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN-DERIVED NEUROTROPHIC FACTOR; CORTICAL STROKE; FOCAL ISCHEMIA; INFLAMMATION; NEUROPLASTICITY; NUTRITION; PHOTOTHROMBOTIC MODEL OF STROKE; PROTEIN ENERGY MALNUTRITION; RAT; STROKE RECOVERY
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a sudden loss of brain function caused when blood flow to the brain is interrupted.  Stroke is the number one cause of chronic disability, and many stroke survivors face physical and mental challenges. Treatment is inadequate to prevent disability and promote recovery after stroke.  Therefore, we are studying new treatments.  We will examine how poor protein-energy nutrition that develops as a result of the stroke interferes with the ability of the brain to recover. This is important for stroke patients because 20-35 percent of patients show poor nutritional status for protein and energy by 1 week after stroke.  Approximately 35-49 percent of patients are affected by the time they are admitted to a rehabilitation setting.  This happens to patents because of multiple problems such as difficulty in swallowing and feeding oneself. We will use a surgical procedure to cause a stroke in rats.  Animals will be fed varying diets after the stroke.  Brain damage will be measured both by the volume of the damaged area of the brain and by measuring brain function. Brain function is measured by observing the animals in specific behavioural tests.  For example, animals that have had a stroke are less able to use their front paw to reach for and obtain a tasty sugar treat.  We will also undertake chemical analyses on the brains of these animals at different times after the stroke to tell us how these nutritional conditions affect the function of brain cells. Our ultimate goal is to develop new approaches to nutritional care of patients after stroke that can improve recovery.

TitreApplicationTitle: mRNA localization in the regulation of genome stability and cell division
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DIVISION; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; DROSOPHILA GENETICS; GENOME STABILITY; HIGH-RESOLUTION IMAGING; MRNA LOCALIZATION; RNA-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells are highly organized entities that come in many different shapes and sizes. These characteristics allow different cells to carry out essential and specialized activities throughout our body. Loss of this organization, leading to abnormal cellular behaviour, is a hallmark of cancer. Traditionally, this organization has mainly been attributed to the ability of proteins and lipids to form cellular structures and organelles. However, in previous work we found that a distinct class of molecules, messenger RNA (mRNA), are also likely to play a major role in controlling cellular organization. We will investigate how the targeting of mRNA helps cells to divide properly and to protect their DNA from damaging toxins in their environment. These processes are extremely important, as their deregulation can give rise to cancer in humans. We will use a convenient and experimentally powerful model system, the common fruit fly, to investigate these questions. Studies in simple model organisms, such as flies, have contributed immensely to our understanding of many essential cellular processes and how these are disturbed in different diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism(s) of cigarette smoke-induced ovarian follicle loss
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; APOPTOSIS; AUTOPHAGY; CELL SURVIVAL; CIGARETTE SMOKING; FOLLICLE CULTURE; FOLLICULOGENESIS; INFERTILITY; OVARIAN REGULATION; STEROIDOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: The number of young women who smoke has increased in recent years posing a serious threat to their future health and reproductive capacity. Compared to non-smokers, cigarette smoking is associated with decreases in fertility, poor response to fertility treatment, decreased number of eggs in the ovaries, and an earlier age of menopause. The specific chemicals in cigarette smoke and the ways in which those chemicals injure the ovary have not been established. Furthermore, it is not known if the harmful effects of cigarette smoking on female fertility are permanent or reversible. Therefore, in this application we plan to determine the mechanisms through which cigarette smoke acts to hinder follicle growth and induce loss of ovarian follicles (eggs). It is also our goal to identify the most sensitive stage of follicle development and determine if the harmful effects of cigarette smoke are reversible and if the effects can be blocked by treatment with a protective dietary chemical. Finally, we will use a novel fractionation method to determine the chemical or chemicals responsible for the ovarian toxic effects of cigarette smoking. Results of our planned experiments will show how cigarette smoke causes follicle (egg) loss. These results will identify important processes in ovarian cells that could lead to new treatments to help preserve fertility in women who smoke or are former smokers. We also expect the results of these studies will provide physicians with much needed experimental evidence to support advice they give to patients concerning the time from smoking cessation before changes in fertility can be expected if at all.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and validation of MRI biomarkers for diagnosis and prognosis of prodromal Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; DIAGNOSIS; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; PREDICTION; PRODROMAL ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's currently affects approximately 0.5 million people in Canada, 5 million in North America, 25 million worldwide and will quadruple in prevalence by 2050 due to aging of the population. The social and financial costs are enormous.  At present, it is estimated that the disease will affect 1 in 14 people that live to 80 years old.  The aging baby-boomers are changing the population demographics, increasing the total numbers of people with AD. The good news is that the pharmaceutical industry is on the verge of a breakthrough in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.   As in most diseases, early treatment of patients, before they have too much irreversible degeneration of brain tissue, is likely to be more effective. However, it is currently almost impossible to test drugs in patients with early Alzheimer's disease, due to the fact that only about 10-15% of patients with symptoms of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) suggestive of possible Alzheimer's disease will actually go on to develop Alzheimer's per year. This percentage is too low to allow for reasonably sized clinical trials, and it is unlikely that regulators would approve a drug for a population of patients, most of whom will never get the disease.   We propose:   to develop sophisticated image analysis tools to detect patterns of brain atrophy characteristic of Alzheimer's disease,  to generate statistical models that will combine the image data with clinical data in order to predict which patients with MCI will  rapidly go on to develop Alzheimer's disease.    The tools we develop will substantially facilitate the development of therapies for early Alzheimer's disease.  They will make it feasible to perform drug trials in patients with MCI due to early Alzheimer's disease, and, looking forward, they will make it possible to select patients in the clinic for early treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Skeletal Muscle Drug Transporters in Statin-Induced Myopathy
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG TRANSPORTERS; MYOPATHY; PHARMACOKINETICS; STATINS
Abstract-Résumé: The cholesterol-lowering drugs called "statins" are important therapeutic agents used by over 2 million Canadians to prevent and treat heart disease and stroke. As with every drug, the benefits of statin use must be balanced by potential risks.  A common side effect of statins that affects 1 in 7 treated persons or 300,000 Canadians is skeletal muscle damage, which typically presents as muscle aches and pains (myopathy).  Rarely, statins cause severe muscle damage that is life threatening.  Importantly, these muscle side effects can be unpleasant enough to prevent continued drug therapy resulting in sub-optimal health benefit.  We are now beginning to better understand why some people are more susceptible to muscle damage by statins.  One theory that we are currently exploring proposes that a difference in the levels of statins in skeletal muscles contributes to interindividual variability in side-effect risk.  We believe that certain proteins called transporters that are found on the surface of cells act as gatekeepers that allow statins to gain access to and also prevent drug accumulation into muscles.  Certain drugs that are often used in combination with statins promote these side effects and may do so by blocking or enhancing the function of these transporters.  Moreover, patients may inherit non-functioning forms of muscle transporters or even express more transporter than others. We plan to use animal models and study patients with statin-associated myopathy to uncover the role of muscle transporters in the muscle distribution and toxicity of statins.  We will address specific genetic and environmental factors as well as the impact of drug-drug interactions on side-effect risk.  It is expected that these studies will provide the mechanistic basis for understanding why statins cause myopathies and form the foundation for strategies to predict, prevent and treat patients who experience the untoward effects of these important drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Poxvirus Anti-apoptotic Strategies
Keywords-MotsClés: BCL-2 PROTEINS; CELL DEATH; MASS SPECTROSCOPY; MITOCHONDRIA; UBIQUITINATION; VIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Everyday millions of cells within our body undergo cell death. Each cell contains a set of specific instructions that tells the cell when and how to committee cellular suicide, allowing unwanted cells to be efficiently eliminated. The ability to survive virus infections also depends on a rapid initiation of cell death that plays an essential role in eliminating virus-infected cells.  However, some viruses have developed strategies to inhibit cell death allowing the virus to efficiently replicate and cause disease. Our aim is to understand how viruses interfere with the cellular mechanisms of cell death. We anticipate that the knowledge gained from studying how viruses regulate cell death will provide important clues for the development of new therapeutic approaches that prevent viral illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of GABA-A receptors in postoperative memory deficits
Keywords-MotsClés: ANESTHESIA; BEHAVIORAL ASSAYS; COGNITION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HIPPOCAMPUS; LONG-TERM POTENTIATION; MEMORY; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Each year, more than 234 million patients undergo anesthesia and surgery worldwide. It is widely assumed that cognitive function rapidly returns to baseline in the early postoperative period. However, postoperative cognitive dysfunction, particularly long-term memory loss, is a frequent but poorly understood neurological complication after surgery. Postoperative memory loss is associated with a reduction in quality of life, early retirement, as well as premature death.     Our goal is to understand the mechanisms underlying postoperative memory deficits and to develop treatment and prevention strategies. In our previous CIHR-supported studies, we identified a "memory-blocking" receptor that, when activated, prevents the formation of new memories. Overactivation of these receptors disrupts communication in a region of the brain that regulates memory processes. General anesthetics can cause such overactivation, leading to profound memory blockade.     The prolonged time course of postoperative memory loss prompted us to look for an endogenous factor that activates the memory-blocking receptors. We discovered that one of the most important pro-inflammatory cytokines, interleukin 1 beta (IL-1b), increases receptor activity. This result is exciting because it is already known that IL-1b causes memory deficits, via mechanisms that remain unclear. Also, the levels of IL-1b in the brain increase after surgery. Thus, we hypothesize that IL-1b increases the activity of memory-blocking receptors, thereby causing postoperative memory deficits.     Using a mouse model, we will determine how IL-1b increases the activity of memory-blocking receptors. We will also determine whether inhibiting these receptors reduces the severity and/or incidence of postoperative memory deficits. If so, we anticipate developing a strategy for preventing postoperative cognitive dysfunction. Our results may have implications for the memory loss associated with anesthesia and inflammatory disease

TitreApplicationTitle: Distinct functions and therapeutic potential of tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) in myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury
Keywords-MotsClés: EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; ISCHEMIA-REPERFUSION; ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE; MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASES; MYOCARDIAL REMODELING; TISSUE INHIBITOR OF METALLOPROTEINASES
Abstract-Résumé: When and artery is clogged, the heart muscle normally supplied by this artery becomes deprived of ixygen and nutrition (ischemic). Re-opening the clogged artery is often a therapeutic solution, but that also triggers a number of cellular and molecular events leading to furhter damaging of the heart muscle, termed 'reperfusion injury'. Many therapies have been applied to prevent this type of injuyr, but they have been unsuccessful. A poorly studied aspect of reperfusion injury in the heart is the adverse remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM), the network that connects different cells and vessels in the heart, provides structural support, and also houses a number of signlaing molecules. When the ECM disrupted, these molecules are released and subsequently trigger damaging effects for the heart muscle. The structure of ECM is maintained by a balance in the function of matrix metalloproteases (MMPs) that degrade the ECM proteins, and their inhibitors, TIMPs. We have found that levels of TIMPs are generally reduced in myocardial reperfusion injury. We propose to use genetically modified mice that lack specific TIMPs to determine the function of these molecules in reperfusion injury in the heart. Subsequently, we will aim to prevent this type of injury by replenishing the specific TIMP (or a mixture of TIMPs) in the damaged heart muscle.

TitreApplicationTitle: Beyond VO2peak: Understanding exercise-induced changes in cardiovascular function after stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOLOGY; CHRONIC DISEASE; EXERCISE; REHABILITATION; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the leading cause of neurological disability in Canada; at age 55 there is a lifetime risk of stroke for 1 in 5 in women and 1 in 6 for men.  Stroke survivors have double the chance of a heart-related death compared to age-matched populations and one-third of stroke survivors will go on to have another stroke.  Up to 80% of people with stroke also have diabetes, obesity, and hypertension.  Exercise is one modality that has potential to reduce cardiovascular and stroke risk, as well as improve functional abilities.  However, no studies have determined whether exercise can actually improve function of the heart (and therefore reduce risk of cardiac and stroke events) in the stroke population.    This will be the first study in the stroke population to determine whether an aerobic exercise program can reduce the risk of heart disease and another stroke. Sixty participants living with stroke will be recruited and randomized to a 6 month aerobic exercise or control group (stretching and weight-bearing group).  Subjects will be measured at the beginning and end of the program, as well as 2 months after the program has ended.  We will measure resting blood pressure, in addition to other indices of cardiac function (e.g., glucose control, lipid levels, arterial stiffness which measures the thickening of the arteries and left atrial function). Stroke is a common condition in older adults and these individuals have known heart problems and severely compromised fitness.  Establishing whether aerobic exercise can reduce cardiovascular risk (and by how much) will be an important step towards determining the cost-benefits of aerobic exercise in stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of reproductive factors on ovarian cancer initiation and progression
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER INITIATION; ESTROGEN; HORMONES; MOUSE MODEL; OVARIAN CANCER; OVARIAN SURFACE EPITHELIUM
Abstract-Résumé: The majority of ovarian cancers arise from epithelial cells in the ovary, but the cellular and molecular events associated with early development of ovarian cancer are poorly understood. Epidemiologic studies have identified a number of reproductive factors that increase the risk of ovarian cancer, such as ovulation and certain hormones, notably estrogen. In addition, hereditary risk (family history) is associated with the more frequent incidence of pre- cancerous structures in the ovary. The mechanisms by which these factors increase the risk of ovarian cancer are unknown. The goal of this project is to address how ovarian cancers begin, with particular emphasis on reproductive factors, notably estrogen, that have been implicated in the initiation or progression of ovarian cancer. We hypothesize that these factors may promote the development of ovarian cancer by manipulating the behaviour of the epithelial cells of the ovary. The experimental strategies described in this proposal focus on a recently developed transgenic model of ovarian cancer that enables us to monitor tumour initiation and progression in a manner that is not possible in humans. We have shown that this model develops pre-cancerous changes and tumour responses that indicate its relevance to human ovarian cancer. The results of these experiments will significantly advance our knowledge about the origins of ovarian cancer, and have the potential to reveal possible explanations for the epidemiological studies that have linked ovulation and estrogen therapy to increased ovarian cancer risk. Perhaps more importantly, this study may identify processes or interventions that are protective against the initiation and/or progression of ovarian cancer leading to new strategies for disease prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidases in the pathogenesis of ankylosing spondylitis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS; ARTHRITIS; GENETIC PREDISPOSITION
Abstract-Résumé: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the most common form of inflammatory spine disease, and carries with it significant morbidity and cost. The cause of AS is not understood but there have been significant advances in understanding the genetic basis of this disease recently. It is now evident that two genes- HLA-B27 and ERAP- account for the major part of disease susceptibility. These findings have opened the door to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying this arthritis. In the current study, we address how the genetic discoveries can inform us about the cause and course of AS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Randomized controlled trial of the mass distribution of Nicotine Replacement Therapy to Canadian smokers
Keywords-MotsClés: MASS DISTRIBUTION; NICOTINE REPLACEMENT THERAPY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TOBACCO CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Smoking is the leading preventable cause of death in Canada. While the percentage of adult smokers decreased from 35% to 19% over the twenty years from 1985 to 2005, little further decline occurred in the years following. Large scale strategies are needed to further reduce the number of smokers in Canada.  One strategy generating interest is mass distribution of Nicotine Replacement Therapy to smokers. Research on Nicotine Replacement Therapy generated promising results, showing that it successfully helps many smokers quit smoking. However, no research study adequately addresses how effective mass distributions of Nicotine Replacement Therapy are in reducing smoking rates.   Telephone numbers will be randomly selected from across Canada in order to recruit adult smokers interested in completing a smoking survey and willing to be interviewed again in 8 weeks and 6 months time. Study participants will be asked about their smoking history and a hypothetical question: would they be interested in receiving the Nicotine Patch if this were to be provided to them free of charge? Participants expressing interest will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. One group will be offered the opportunity to actually receive a program of 5 weeks of the Nicotine Patch for free right away and the other group will not be offered the free Nicotine Patches.   The proportions of smokers in the two groups who quit smoking by the 6-month interview will be compared. Evidence that reduction in the number of smokers can be attributed to large scale distribution of free Nicotine Replacement Therapy will provide a strong argument that more initiatives of this type should be undertaken in Canada to further reduce the number of preventable deaths.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular analysis of genomic imprint maintenance during embryogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLELE-SPECIFIC EXPRESSION AND METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; GENOMIC IMPRINTING; IN VITRO EMBRYO CULTURE; MOUSE MODEL SYSTEM; PREIMPLANTATION DEVELOPMENT; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Infertility elicits an enormous physical, emotional, and financial toll on society, both nationally and internationally. With the rapid evolution of assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs), it is essential to monitor the consequences of manipulating embryos in an attempt to safeguard normal development. Recently, the efficacy and safety of human ARTs have come under intense questioning. Accumulating evidence suggests that children conceived by assisted reproductive technologies are at increased risk of intrauterine growth retardation, premature birth, low birth weight and certain genetic diseases. However, very little is known about the gene regulatory processes in the early embryo nor how they are deregulated by embryo culture. This study will identify biochemical factors involved in gene regulation, and will ascertain whether candidate factors play a role in stem cells and preimplantation development. The proposed study will help to elucidate the mechanisms behind embryo sensitivity to in vitro culture during assisted reproduction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term regulation of neuronal excitability and output
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM; CLONING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNELS; NEUROMODULATION; NEUROPLASTICITY; PHOSPHORYLATION; SECRETION
Abstract-Résumé: My research focuses on brain or nerve cells. I am interested in the control of bio-electric properties, which are governed by minute holes in nerve cells called channel proteins.  These proteins pass ions (such as calcium, sodium or potassium) in and out of the cell.  Because ions carry a charge, their movement constitutes the flow of very small electrical current. Nerve cells harness these electrical currents to receive and process information, as well as signal other nerve cells, muscles, or glands. Taking a reductionist approach, I study the brain of a sea snail, called Aplysia, which has large and identifiable nerve cells that control defined behaviours. My objective is to examine the channel proteins from those nerve cells that initiate reproduction in Aplysia. Essentially, these are motivational cells for a fundamentally important behaviour. I am particularly interested in understanding how, after only a very short stimulus, these nerve cells respond in a very prolonged manner. Changes in activity of this nature are essential for handling sensory information, learning, generating movement, and controlling behaviours like drinking, eating, ovulation, birth, and breast feeding. Studying the proteins responsible for the electrical properties of Aplysia's motivational nerve cells will provide a better understanding of how, in general, nerve cells trigger behaviour. The electrical changes that occur in Aplysia's cells are very similar to that observed in most animals, and these findings will apply to processes such as perception, memory, or certain basic and instinctual behaviours. Furthermore, because the channel proteins of interest allow a nerve cell to be active on its own, there may be implications for epilepsy.  Electric properties are inappropriately adjusted in epilepsy.  Given that some of the channel proteins implicated in this disease are related to Aplysia proteins, I will be able to examine their function in a well-defined system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Apoptosis of endothelial cells and extracellular matrix proteolysis: Roles in vascular healing and scarring
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CASPASE-3; CATHEPSIN L; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; NEOINTIMA; STEM CELLS; TRANSGENIC MICE; TRANSPLANT VASCULOPATHY; VASCULAR REMODELING; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: In transplanted organs, the vessels providing the blood supply to the organ become progressively narrowed due to rejection. This dramatically accelerates loss of function of the transplanted organ. Rejection increases the death rate of endothelial cells i.e. cells forming the inner lining of vessels within the transplanted organ. We have shown, with the support of the CIHR, that these damaged cells produce LG3, a novel mediator of importance in vascular repair and rejection. This mediator is produced by proteases released by dying cells that cleave the matrix surrounding the endothelial cells, therefore releasing LG3. We found that LG3 levels are increased in human renal transplant patients with rejection. Also, when injected in transplanted animals, LG3 increases the severity of vessel narrowing. In the present proposal, we plan to define the molecular pathways responsible for the production of LG3 by endothelial cells. We will also characterize the pathways activated by LG3 and leading to accelerated vessel narrowing. These experiments will provide insights into novel pathways of importance in rejection of transplanted organs in humans. A better understanding of these pathways will allow developing new strategies aimed at preventing rejection and prolonging the functional lifespan of transplanted organs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Class I MHC Receptors in Innate Immune Responses
Keywords-MotsClés: CLASS I MHC; GENE-KNOCKOUT; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTERFERON-ALPHA; LY49; MOUSE; NATURAL KILLER CELL; PLASMACYTOID DENDRITIC CELL; RECEPTOR; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Natural killer (NK) cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC) are necessary for anti-viral responses early after infection and against cancer induction. NK cells kill infected and cancerous cells, while pDC produce proteins that travel throughout the body to inhibit viral infection. Both cell types have receptors on their surface for class I MHC, a protein that is a marker of healthy, uninfected and non-cancerous cells. These receptors in mice are called Ly49. We have produced Ly49-deficient mutant mice and through these plus other molecular techniques will try to assess the importance of these proteins during immune responses to viruses and cancers mediated by the innate immune system.

TitreApplicationTitle: HIV-1 Viral protein U (Vpu) as an antagonist of Tetherin/BST2: molecular mechanisms and functional implications for viral replication and transmission
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-TETHERIN FACTORS; HIV-1 RELEASE; HIV-1 TRANSMISSION; HIV-1/AIDS; HOST CELL UBIQUITIN MACHINERY; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; TETHERIN/BST2/CD317; VIRAL PROTEIN U  (VPU)
Abstract-Résumé: AIDS is a slow degenerative disease of the immune and nervous systems resulting from HIV-1 infection. Despite considerable progress made in our understanding of HIV-1 infection, we still do not completely understand how the virus causes AIDS and how it maintains itself in infected individuals in presence of a vigorous immune response and highly suppressive antiretroviral regimens. Ultimately, our ability to control the AIDS pandemics, already destined to claim more than 33 million of lives world-wide, will depend on our ability: i) to interrupt effectively viral replication, transmission and persistence by developing novel antiviral strategies; ii) to render host antiviral immune responses more efficient at preventing viral infection by developing safe vaccine strategies. The HIV-1 vpu gene encodes a small integral membrane protein that is not found in HIV-2 and most simian immunodeficiency viruses. Vpu promotes the production of HIV-1 by antagonizing a newly identified interferon-regulated host restriction factor,called Tetherin/BST2, that retains newly formed virions at the surface of infected cells. The exact mechanisms underlying Tetherin antagonism by Vpu are yet to be elucidated. Furthermore, the role of Tetherin and Vpu in relevant cell targets of HIV-1 remains to be fully defined. Finally, given that the interaction of Vpu with Tetherin represents a potential therapeutic target, it is unclear whether HIV-1 can resist Tetherin restriction through Vpu-independent mechanism(s). The goal of this research project will be to continue our investigation on the function and mode of action of Vpu to develop a better understanding of key HIV-1-host interactions regulating virus release and transmission. Ultimately, elucidation of the interaction between HIV-1 Vpu and host innate defenses will lead to a heightened comprehension of viral replication and pathogenesis as well as suggesting additional targets for antiviral strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: TDAG51 in vascular calcification associated with chronic renal disease
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; END STAGE RENAL DISEASE; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; TDAG51; VASCULAR CALCIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the major cause of death in patients suffering from chronic kidney disease (CKD). Over half of all deaths in patients with end-stage renal disease result from CVD, with mortality rates 10 to 30-fold greater than in the general population. Calcification of the blood vessel wall is a major feature of CKD and is now recognized as an important predictor of cardiovascular disease. The purpose of these studies is to explain the role of TDAG51 in the development and progression vessel calcification. By better understanding how TDAG51 modulates vessel calcification, we will have a unique opportunity to develop novel drugs that decrease the accumulation of calcium in the blood vessel.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aboriginal Wellness in Alzheimer Disease: Intersections of Science and Tradition
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; CARE IN ALZHEIMER DISEASE; CULTURALLY RELEVANT RESOURCES; FIRST NATION; GENETIC PREDICTION OF ALZHEIMER DISEASE; GENETICS; INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOGY; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; REMOTE HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: In Canadian Aboriginal communities there are few culturally relevant resources dedicated to Alzheimer Disease (AD). Education about symptoms and disease progression can help people prepare for the life changes associated with AD. Without such information, Canadian Aboriginal people will be limited in their ability to plan for this disease and, overall, their health may suffer. We are working with a particular First Nation whose members are at risk for a familial AD that occurs around age 50.  Some members inherit a unique genetic mutation that leads to AD. In the face of predictive genetic testing, the need for culturally relevant information is even more pressing. Most Canadian resources explain AD as a brain illness, but this explanation does not align with Indigenous worldviews that balance physical, emotional, mental and spiritual wellness. We anticipate that culturally relevant informational resources based on Indigenous concepts of wellness and illness will improve the understanding of AD prediction, diagnosis, and care. We will work with members of this Nation to: 1. Elucidate how members explain AD within a holistic framework that values both scientific knowledge and traditional teachings. To do this, we will facilitate Sharing Circles and Family Interviews with members of this Nation, and we will interpret the findings in collaboration with the research participants. 2. Synthesize the findings in a preliminary report and, through an iterative process with the community, discuss and further interpret the results.  3. Create a final resource report that leads to improved understanding of AD prediction, diagnosis, and care for members of the Nation, clinicians, academics and policy makers. Our research will bring together traditional teachings and scientific understandings.  It will contribute to Canadian knowledge of Aboriginal health and wellness, rural and remote health, AD, and intersecting challenges in the science of the brain, genetics, and ethics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetic disruptions in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: COPD; DNA METHYLATION; GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Smoking is a major cause for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). While smoking induces changes to gene expression pattern in the lungs, some of the affected genes return to normal levels of expression upon smoking cessation and some do not. Increasing evidence suggests that smoking introduces reversible DNA modifications (called methylation), which impact the regulation of genes. Aberrant DNA methylation is implicated in a vast spectrum of diseases, however little is known about how the change in DNA methylation relates to the clinical features of COPD. The overall goal of our study is to determine the biological pathways affected by DNA methylation changes associated with COPD. As therapies that prevent or treat COPD are limited, a better understanding of the molecular alterations that drive this disease will be the foundation for effective treatments that improve survival rates.
