TitreApplicationTitle: Functional analyses of molecularly-defined spinal interneurons in regulating motor activity
Keywords-MotsClés: CENTRAL PATTERN GENERATOR; EXCITATORY COMMISSURAL INTERNEURONS; LOCOMOTION; LOCOMOTOR CIRCUITS; MOLECULARLY DEFINED INTERNEURONS; NEURONAL CONNECTIVITY; PATCH-CLAMP RECORDINGS; SPINAL CORD INJURY; TRANSGENIC MOUSE; V3 INTERNEURON
Abstract-Résumé: Locomotor movements, such as walking, running and swimming, come to us so naturally that most people may not realize that such activities are very complex and require a high degree of coordination of many limb and body muscles involved. The neurons that control the muscles that generate locomotion are located in the spinal cord. Motor neurons are the commanders that directly innervate different muscles. The activity of these motor neurons in turn is strictly and precisely controlled and regulated by interneuron circuits mainly located in the ventral spinal cord. Up until very recent research, the components and structure of the neural circuits that ultimately control locomotion have remained largely unknown. New discoveries of the molecular codes of different neurons in the spinal cord have allowed us to identify several groups of interneuons there and have also provided us with powerful genetic and molecular tools to manipulate the activity of these neurons. In my laboratory, we will take advantage of these breakthroughs and combine anatomical, behavioral, electrophysiological and optical recording technologies to study the functional roles that different spinal interneurons play in the locomotor circuits. This will allow us to better understand how they regulate the motor neuron activity that generates a balanced and stable gait. Such knowledge will be the foundation for further explanation of the roles that different spinal neurons play under pathological conditions, such as spinal cord injury and degenerative diseases, and this in turn will potentially enable us to find new treatments for these conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of frontal cortical projections to the superior colliculus in saccade suppression and task switching in primates
Keywords-MotsClés: EYE MOVEMENTS; FRONTAL CORTEX; LESION; MONKEY; SINGLE NEURON RECORDINGS; SUPERIOR COLLICULUS
Abstract-Résumé: Diseases or damage to the frontal part of the brain, including psychiatric disorders, stroke, and head trauma, often result in profound cognitive disabilities. These problems can be seen in a reduced attention span, difficulties to memorize things, poor judgment skills, and in difficulties to plan and prioritize everyday life. These symptoms place an enormous physical, mental and social burden on patients, their families, employers and the public health care system.   Cognitive deficits can easily be tested with simple eye movement tasks. Brain researchers have long known that people who suffer from certain psychiatric disorders or brain trauma to the frontal cortex show telltale eye movements under certain conditions. Told to fix their gaze on a visual target, for example, they are unable to resist the reflexive urge to glance away at a peripheral stimulus, like a flash of light. Subjects without the disorder or damage can override the impulse. In our research program, we will systematically investigate the role of different frontal brain areas in monkeys while they perform this type of task. We will cool these brain areas to see test whether a disruption of neural activity in one of these areas will make it impossible for the monkeys not to glance towards the stimulus. We will then study how cooling of a frontal brain area affects the activity of other brain areas in monkeys.   We aim to understand how frontal brain areas influence cognitive functions in the primate brain. By better understanding which areas underlie which cognitive functions, we hope to identify brain areas that can serve as targets for future treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Does food labelling influence long-term food intake and eating-related variables in women?
Keywords-MotsClés: APPETITE SENSATIONS; EATING BEHAVIORS; FOOD INTAKE; FOOD LABELLING; FOOD-RELATED ATTITUDES; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: A majority of Canadians know that they should adopt healthier food habits, and that physical activity is good for their health. In fact, much effort has been invested to educate the population about healthy behaviors. Different food labels can be used by consumers to identify healthier foods in the market, so that they can make informed food choices and have better eating habits. But, does nutritional information on food labels really contribute to improve what we eat? While it could improve consumer's choices and purchases, food labels can also be confusing and difficult to understand for many of them. It is also not clear whether food labelling has always beneficial impacts on food intake, as overeating can be observed when foods are perceived as healthy. The general objective of the present research proposal is to better understand the long-term effects of different food labelling strategies on the regulation of food intake among women. Because the popularity and demand for nutrition information is increasing, results from this study will help health professionals and public health organizations to identify better tools that promote healthy weight and eating habits among Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bacterial glyco-ABC transporters
Keywords-MotsClés: ABC TRANSPORTERS; BACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; CAPSULAR POLYSACCHARIDES; CELL SURFACES; EXPORT SYSTEMS; LIPOPOLYSACCHARIDES; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; MICROBIOLOGY; VIRULENCE FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The surfaces of bacteria contain a complex and dynamic array of polysaccharides (sugar-containing polymers) that are linked to the surface by a variety of anchoring processes. Cell-surface polysaccharides play diverse functional roles in bacterial pathogens but are generally associated the ability to avoid components of the innate immune system. They are therefore vital for the survival of those bacteria that produce them and influence their ability to cause infection. Polysaccharides are synthesized from building blocks available inside the cell and they must be exported to their final location on the bacterial surface. The goal of this research is a detailed investigation of specific export pathways, as these represent the least understood elements of the polysaccharide-assembly assembly processes. The proposed research addresses fundamental questions concerning how complex molecules pass across biological membranes in a rapid coordinated and specific manner, without compromising the essential barrier functions of the membrane. The exporters are part of a large family called "ABC transporters", whose representatives are found in all forms of life. The two selected prototype systems are relevant for a range of important bacterial pathogens and may also provide insight into related processes in higher organisms. It is conceivable that elucidation of key elements of the export pathways could be exploited for therapeutic intervention strategies. In such a strategy, specifically targeted disruption of polysaccharide export pathways by small molecule inhibitors would yield a bacterium that is easily eradicated by existing host defenses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interaction of cancer initiating cells with the tumor microenvironment during leukemogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE THERAPY; ERYTHROLEUKEMIA; FACS ANALYSIS; GROWTH FACTOR AND CYTOKINES; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; IN VITRO CELL PROLIFERATION ASSAYS; IN VIVO TRANSPLANTATION; TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: It is widely accepted that cancer is a multistep process associated with the activation or inactivation of certain cancer genes. In our laboratory, we are using multistage erythroleukemias induced by Friend virus as a model to identify and characterize genes associated with leukemia development. Toward this goal, we have previously isolated several genes whose activations or inactivations have been shown to be involved in the induction and progression of erythroleukemia (cancer of red blood cells). These genes have also been shown to be involved in other types of human cancers. In a recent development, we have also discovered that the spleen, a site of tumor migration, supports proliferation and expansion of leukemic cells. Moreover, we have shown that a unique population of primitive blood cells can delay tumor progression when injected into the leukemic mice. We provide evidence to suggest that these unique blood cells inhibit leukemia progression through the induction of changes in the tumor microenvironment. The experiments described in this research proposal are designed to characterize the components of the microenvironment capable of inhibiting tumor progression and identify strategies to promote a tumor inhibitory niche toward the clinical treatment of leukemia. Therefore, we plan to first characterize the leukemic inhibitory cells from both mouse and human by isolating them using advanced cell culture methods. We will also examine whether injection of various factors into mice is capable of expanding these leukemic inhibitory cells. Overall, these studies should provide important insight into the role of the microenvironment in the progression of leukemia that can eventually be used for the development of more efficient treatments for leukemia and other cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preclinical Assessment of Rho-kinase Inhibitors for Chronic Pulmonary Hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; FASUDIL; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION; RHO-KINASE; RIGHT-VENTRICULAR DYSFUNCTION; VASCULAR REMODELING; Y-27632
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pulmonary hypertension is a rare but debilitating and lethal disease characterised by high blood pressure in the lung, causing low oxygen levels in the blood, breathlessness and heart failure.  The ability of the heart to compensate for increased workload (and thus provide the body with sufficient blood and oxygen) is the main determinant of survival in this condition.  Unfortunately, when compared to adults, efforts to treat chronic pulmonary hypertension in newborns, infants and children are hampered by a rapid and apparently irreversible progression toward end-stage disease and death, despite an expanding range of available treatments.  Until more effective treatments are developed, the outlook for children with this condition will remain poor.  With the funding received to date, our laboratory has made the important and novel observation that severe chronic pulmonary hypertension is reversible in young animals using drugs that inhibit Rho-kinase (ROCK).  In this application, we propose to build upon these observations by targeting ROCK inhibitors to the lung as a means of avoiding effects on other tissues, by further defining the mechanisms by which ROCK inhibition reverses chronic pulmonary hypertension and by exploring the mechanisms behind heart failure in the context of chronic pulmonary hypertension and its therapy.  Our ultimate goal is to translate this promising therapy to humans, with the hope of achieving improved outcomes from an otherwise devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Action Seniors! An RCT of Secondary Falls Prevention in Community-Dwelling Senior Fallers.
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; ECONOMIC EVALUATION; EXERCISE; FALLS
Abstract-Résumé: Falls are a common geriatric syndrome and are the third leading cause of chronic disability worldwide. About 30% of community-dwellers over the age of 65 experience one or more falls every year. Although not all falls lead to injury, about 20% require medical attention and 5% result in fracture, with one-third of those being hip fractures. In particular, about half of the 30% of community-dwelling seniors who fall experience recurrent falls and are at significant risk for fall-related injuries. Currently, the evidence strongly suggests that an exercise program of strength and balance training reduces falls in the general population of community-dwelling seniors. However, to date, very few studies have specifically evaluated whether these types of exercises can also reduce falls in seniors with a significant history of falls. Yet, given the significant impact of falls on both the health care system and the individual, effective prevention strategies need to be identified for this high-risk population. We propose that it is logical to target simple prevention strategies to persons at high-risk for falls and fall-related injuries.   Therefore, we aim to carry out a 12-month study of 344 community-dwelling senior fallers aged 70 years and older to evaluate the effect of a home-based strength and balance exercise training program on falls. We will also conduct an economic evaluation of this home-based exercise program as a falls prevention strategy for high-risk seniors compared with standard of care. Our economic evaluation will enable us to assist health care decision makers in allocating scarce resources.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards closing the gap: using evidence to identify the need for investments in primary health care services on BC First Nation reserves
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS; AMBULATORY CARE SENSITIVE CONDITIONS; EQUITY; FIRST NATIONS; GEE MODELING; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE
Abstract-Résumé: The objective of this study is to document the relationship between access to primary healthcare services available on First Nations reserves in British Columbia, community control and avoidable hospitalizations (that is hospitalization for conditions that could be in a primary healthcare setting if services were available). Communities in which avoidable hospitalization rates are higher than those of other British Columbia rural and remote communities are those in which one would expect additional investment in primary healthcare to be especially necessary. We will examine the rates of avoidable hospitalization by community to determine whether there appears to be any relationship between these rates, and (1) models of community control over the administration and delivery of health services (transfer, integrated, others), and (2) models of service delivery (services limited to public health versus primary care services provided by nurses with an expanded scope of practice). This project will make four broad contributions. (1) It will identify communities with particular needs for primary health care investments. (2) It will build on the methodology developed in the context of the Manitoba study and attempt to replicate findings to ascertain their generalizability nationally. (3) The results of the study will be used as a step forward towards identifying essential primary healthcare services necessary to address existing primary healthcare needs; and inform the development of services provided via telehealth. (4) It will bring evidence to the relationship between community control and outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of dietary interventions on disease progression in orthologous models of polycystic kidney disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CAMP; EICOSANOIDS; KIDNEY DISEASE; KIDNEY PATHOLOGY; LIPID SOURCE; NUTRITION; POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE; PROTEIN SOURCE
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 5-10% of patients with chronic kidney disease have a type of inherited kidney disease that is one of a number of diseases that are collectively referred to as polycystic kidney disease (PKD).  Studies in some models of PKD have demonstrated that dietary interventions such as soy protein and oils rich in omega-3 fatty acids (e.g fish and flax oils) significantly retard the development of disease.  Dietary effects are not always the same in different models, however, reflecting the fact that different types of PKD respond differently to dietary interventions.  In addition, studies in models have been limited to those that do not have the same mutation as human forms of PKD.  One of the ways in which these dietary changes may affect PKD is via their effects on kidney molecules, called cAMP and eicosanoids, which regulate various functions and disease progression in the kidney.    The development of models which have the same genetic mutations as the human forms of PKD now provides the opportunity to test nutritional strategies in specific PKD disorders.  We hypothesize that dietary soy protein and oils containing omega-3 fatty acids will slow the development of disease and affect kidney signaling molecules in three of these true PKD models.  These models represent more than 99% of human PKD disorders.  They will be given diets containing either casein or soy protein as the protein source and either soy oil, fish oil or flax oil as the fat source.  The effect on kidney damage, function and on signaling molecules will be determined.  The results of these studies will provide novel information that will enhance our understanding of diet effects on disease and on signaling molecules in specific PKD disorders.   This information is an important step before engaging in human clinical trials of dietary interventions in PKD.  This information is needed to provide accurate information to patients so that they can take an active role in their own health care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Early prediction of patient-related and radiological outcomes in patients with recent-onset inflammatory polyarthritis (EPA) using established and novel independent predictors
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOANTIBODIES; DISEASE COPING; EARLY INFLAMMATORY POLYARTHRITIS; GENETIC MARKERS; IMMUNE DYSREGULATION; LONGITUDINAL OBSERVATIONAL STUDY; OSTEOCLASTOGENESIS; PAIN; TELOMERE LENGTH; ULTRASOUND JOINT EXAMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Early inflammatory polyarthritis (EPA) describes recent-onset disease with signs of inflammation in at least 3 peripheral joints, typically starts between 40 and 55 years of age, affects up to 5% of adults over their lifetime, and results in persistent inflammatory arthritis in close to 2% (30-50% of EPA). EPA patients are clinically very similar at onset, and their prognosis remains ill-defined and frequently poor, despite the availability of effective medications and the use of remission-targeted strategies. The lack at baseline of effective prognostic markers to identify patients needing these interventions is in part responsible for missing the window of opportunity for treatment in many patients. Based on previous observations that individuals segregate into poor and good in vitro activators of bone cells called osteoclasts (OC), we propose to identify characteristics of OC precursors and of OCs formed in vitro from patients' blood cells to correlate these characteristics with severe joint damage. As RA patients have short-for-age telomeres (i.e. DNA sequences at the ends of chromosomes), we propose to determine whether short telomeres at baseline (and rapidly shortening telomeres soon thereafter) are independent predictors of severe RA-like disease in EPA patients. We will also define the role of ultrasound joint evaluation in patients who do not have bone erosions on Xrays to predict which ones will develop severe joint damage. Finally, we will look at variants of immune-related genes and at the psychosocial characteristics (e.g. depression, coping strategies, pain perception) that may predict poor pain improvement and poor outcomes. The combination of these prognostic markers will lead to a prognostic tool that may guide early treatment (both biomedical and psychosocial) targeted to those patients most likely to benefit (cost-saving) and avoid unnecessary exposure to expensive and potentially toxic drugs when these are not needed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuron-Microglia-Astrocyte interaction in the pathogenesis of neuropathic pain
Keywords-MotsClés: ANATOMICAL STUDIES; BEHAVIORAL STUDIES; GLIAL CELLS; IMMUNE RESPONSE; PAIN
Abstract-Résumé: Neuropathic pain is a prevalent condition for which no effective treatment is available.  For decades, pain has been viewed as being mediated solely by nerve cells.  However this view has been challenged by highlighting the active participation of other type of cells, called "Glia" in the initiation and/or maintenance of this hypersensitivity in different pathological conditions.  Microglia and astrocytes are two major types of glial cells in the central nervous system.  While ample evidence support the role of microglia in the regulation of chronic pain, much less is known about the importance of astrocytes.  In this proposal I will focus on the involvement of this specific type of glial cells in the pathogenesis of neuropathic pain.  Our previous studies revealed that nerve injury activated both microglia and astrocytes within the spinal cord and this glial cell activation is characterized by an early, transient response of microglia, followed by a late, persistent astrocyte activation.  I will use pharmacological and molecular tools to disrupt locally astrocyte activation within the spinal cord to verify whether the astrocyte activation is necessary and to what extent it is important for the maintenance and the progression of the disease.  Then I will investigate the mechanisms by which astrocytes modulate pain signal processing by targeting a specific protein located on astrocytes-Cx43 gap junction hemichannels.  I will also examine the relationship of microglia and astrocyte activation to see whether early microglial activation is necessary for the subsequent astrocyte activation and what is (are) the signalling molecules involved in the crosstalk between two types of glial cells.  Elucidating how spinal cord glia interact with nociceptive processing will advance our understanding on the etiology of chronic pain.  Identification of new strategies and targets involved in neuropathic pain is likely to open new avenues to effective treatment of chronic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: The transcriptional control of caudal neurogenesis: the role of the Cdx homeodomain proteins.
Keywords-MotsClés: CDX HOMEODOMAIN PROTEINS; CONDITIONAL KNOCKDOWN; GENETICALLY MODIFIED MOUSE MODELS; NEURAL CREST AND NEURAL TUBE FORMATION; NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS; NEUROCRISTOPATHIES
Abstract-Résumé: During embryonic development, the process of neurulation is the first step toward establishment of the nervous system. It involves specific determinants of anterior (brain) and posterior (spinal cord) fates. In the posterior embryo, the first step of neurulation involves the generation of a sheet of cells called the neural plate. Through different processes, the neural plate is then shaped in a closed neural tube, the spinal cord precursor. From the dorsal neural tube, a specific subpopulation of cells, called the neural crest cells, emigrate to generate the peripheral nervous system. These cells have stem cell properties allowing them to also contribute other specialized cell types such as pigment cells (melanocytes), some hormone-producing cells and some muscle cells of the cardio-vascular system. Problems affecting neural tube closure as well as neural crest cell development are the cause of many birth defects or genetic syndromes, such as spina bifida and aganglionic megacolon. Misregulations of neural crest cell development are also responsible of many cancers from childhood to adulthood such as neuroblastoma and malignant melanoma. A better understanding of neural tube formation and neural crest cell function at the molecular level is therefore required to allow identification of predisposed individuals as well as facilitating diagnosis and treatment of the related illnesses. Members of the Cdx protein family (Cdx1, Cdx2 and Cdx4) are specific determinants of posterior fates and they are active in the early developing spinal cord, starting well before the formation of a neural tube. They are also active in pre-migratory and early migratory neural crest cells. However, the Cdx function in these cells is still not clear because of a lack of a good experimental model. Using innovative approaches, the purpose of this project is to determine Cdx function in the process of neural tube formation as well as in the specification of neural crest cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: A mechanistic study of G-protein coupled receptor binding and activation by apelin.
Keywords-MotsClés: APELIN-RECEPTOR INTERACTIONS; BIOPHYSICAL CHARACTERIZATION; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; PEPTIDE-GPCR INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The peptide molecule apelin is used as a messenger in the cardiovascular system, brain, and in response to blood glucose. Its involvement has been specifically implicated in cancer progression and atherosclerosis. Apelin functions by interacting with a specific receptor protein. This receptor is located in membranes of many cells in the body. As a whole, proteins found in the membranes of cells such as heart muscle cells and neurons have important roles in controlling proper cellular and body function and are frequently used as drug targets. The activation of the apelin receptor, which occurs upon apelin binding, can cause dramatic physiological effects. These include changes in blood pressure and heart muscle contraction, changes to levels of blood insulin or other circulating hormones, and changes to behavior and neurological function. The molecular-level basis of the interaction between apelin and its receptor is not understood. Using the technique of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR), which allows us to locate and study individual atoms in a molecule, the atomic arrangement and motion in both apelin and its membrane-bound receptor will be studied. These NMR studies will be correlated to information obtained using other biophysical methods. By developing this type of atomic-level understanding, specific drugs can be designed to target either apelin or its receptor, increasing therapeutic treatment options for cancer and a variety of cardiovascular, central nervous system and metabolic disease conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antecedents of persistent antisocial behaviour and psychopathy: A developmental follow-back study of Canadian men using prospectively collected data from age 6 to 30
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTISOCIAL DISORDERS; ETIOLOGY; FOLLOW-BACK; LONGITUDINAL STUDY (AGE 6 TO 30); PROSPECTIVE; SOCIETAL BURDEN; TREATMENT NEEDS IN CHILDHOOD; USE OF HEALTH SERVICES
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 5% of males display antisocial and aggressive behaviour that emerges in childhood and remains stable throughout life. They commit more than 50% of all violent crimes. In addition, they assault others, participate in the illegal drug trade, do not work or pay taxes. The first goal of the proposed project is to estimate the burden this small group of males places on Canadian society in order to inform policy decisions regarding investment in child and family focused prevention programmes. The second goal is to identify distinctive sub-types within the population of males who display stable antisocial behaviour. These sub-types, we propose, differ as to the traits of psychopathy and symptoms of anxiety. This evidence is needed in order to investigate the mechanisms that initiate and maintain antisocial behaviour and to develop childhood intervention programmes that are tailored to the needs of different sub-types of boys presenting antisocial behaviour. There is presently no effective treatment for persistent antisocial behaviour. Interventions in childhood present the greatest potential for success. The present project will provide evidence about the treatment needs at different ages of each sub-type of males who engage in persistent antisocial behaviour.  To achieve these goals, the proposed project will examine 2631 men, aged 30-33, who have been participating in a study since they were 6 years old. We will collect official records to identify all those who have a criminal conviction (~376) and a random sample of 350 with no record of criminality. We will interview these 726 men in order to assess mental health, psychosocial functioning, and aggressive behaviour, and collect their health files. This new information will be combined with parent, teacher, and self-reports of behaviour, symptoms, and parenting, and official reports of maltreatment, delinquency and social service interventions collected since age 6.

TitreApplicationTitle: Natural Killer (NK) cell mediated anti-viral activity in HIV infected slow progressors: Killer Immunoglobulin like receptor (KIR)/HLA genotype as a determinant of NK function.
Keywords-MotsClés: FLOW CYTOMETRY; HIV/AIDS; HLA; INNATE IMMUNITY; KILLER IMMUNOGLOBULIN-LIKE RECEPTORS; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; NK FUNCTION; SLOW PROGRESSORS
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 5% of HIV-infected individuals can be classified as slow progressors (SP) because they remain healthy with normal CD4 counts for >7 years and/or control HIV viral load without treatment. Disappointing results from recent HIV vaccine trials has led to increased interest in studying how SP control HIV infection. This information may suggest therapies for HIV infected progressors so that they too can better control their infection. This knowledge may also suggest strategies for improving the design of effective vaccines for HIV. To this end a Canadian-wide cohort of HIV infected SP was recently set up with funding from CIHR and is currently recruiting and following SP. This cohort will be the source of samples for the research project submitted here. The project will study mechanisms underlying how Natural Killer (NK) cells influence the rate of HIV disease progression. NK cells are key players in innate immune responses to viruses such as HIV. Epidemiological studies have found that the co-expression of certain NK receptors called KIR and the molecules they recognize on neighboring cells (HLA) is associated with slower time to AIDS and viral load control. Indeed, certain KIR/HLA combinations are over-represented among SP. Our hypothesis is that the association between KIR/HLA and rate of HIV disease progression is related to how various KIR/HLA interactions determine the potency of NK activation. We have the expertise and tools to measure features of NK activation such as killing HIV infected targets and secreting factors called cytokines that suppress HIV replication. We will assess the requirements for activation of NK anti-viral function at the level of KIR/HLA interactions and how this translates into the distribution and potency of NK subsets with anti-viral activity when NK cells are stimulated with HLA negative target cells or autologous HIV infected CD4+ T cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: The tumor suppressors, p53 and PTEN, are also suppressors of  vascular smooth muscle cell migration and invasion.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; CELL MIGRATION AND INVASION; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; TUMOR SUPPRESSORS
Abstract-Résumé: Atherosclerosis is a vascular disease that is a primary cause of heart attack and stroke. It is becoming clear that abnormal migration of smooth muscle cells from their normal locations in the interior of the arterial wall to the inner layer close to the lumenal surface and subsequent division of newly accumulated smooth muscle cells are key events in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis and arteriosclerosis.  The long-term goal of this proposal is to study the mechanisms by which vascular smooth muscle cell migration is inhibited in healthy arteries, but stimulated under pathological conditions. Recently, we have found that the cancer cell suppressors, p53 and PTEN, also play a crucial role in inhibiting smooth muscle cell movement and may regulate pathogenesis of atherosclerotic plaques. This finding suggests a commonality in the mechanisms regulating cancer cell and vascular smooth muscle cell migration.  Knowledge gained from this research will help us define the mechanisms by which vascular smooth muscle cell migration is regulated at the molecular level and will provide information for future designs of drugs to combat atherosclerosis and arteriosclerosis

ClasseRechercheFR: SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL; RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the Accuracy of New Methods of Pharmacosurveillance: Computerized Administrative Data and Electronic Prescribing and Drug Management Systems
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE DRUG EVENTS; COMPARATIVE EFFECTIVENESS OF DRUGS; ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORDS; PHARMACOSURVEILLANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Prescription drugs play a rapidly expanding and important role in the prevention and treatment of common health problems. Over 60% of adult Canadians have used at least one prescription drug in the past 6 months, and six or more drugs are taken by 18% of the older population. While there are considerable benefits from modern drug therapy, the frequent occurrence of adverse drug-related events and the uncertainty about effects of drugs after they enter the market have highlighted fundamental shortcomings in the ability to actively monitor drugs after their approval.  Electronic health records, computerized prescribing and automated patient follow-up systems are health information technologies that are being increasingly used to improve the quality of care around the world. These new health information technologies provide an unprecedented opportunity to develop an active surveillance system that will monitor and provide patients and physicians with real-time feedback on the comparative safety and effectiveness of new drugs.  Conducting active surveillance on a collaborative international scale will provide more rapid information about drug safety and effectiveness from users around the world as well as permit more personalized risk/benefit analysis for subgroups where drugs may have a different risk/benefit profile. The purpose of this project is to develop state-of-the-art methods of i) monitoring, and  ii) analyzing the comparative risk and benefit of new drug therapies, in real-time, through an international prospective surveillance system, and iii) communicating this information to clinicians to inform treatment decision-making at the point-of-care.

TitreApplicationTitle: miR-17-5p in Tissue Development, Regeneration and Angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CELL BIOLOGY; GENE EXPRESSION; MICRORNA; SIRNA; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: Different kinds of heart diseases are the leading cause of death in developed countries.  Among them, vascular disease is the most important manifestation resulting from extensive inflammation and fibrosis due to blood vessel injury. Cell self-renewal is an integration of growth control. It is important to maintain organ integrity and functions. We are interested in studying regulation of tissue regeneration and blood vessel formation by microRNAs. MicroRNAs are a group of newly discovered tiniest genetic materials. MicroRNA is known to play important roles in physiological and pathological conditions, including heart disease-associated formation of new blood vessels. We will study the role of a microRNA named miR-17-5p in regulation of the expression of a number of proteins associated with tissue regeneration and blood formation. We will develop an anti-sense construct (to combat against miR-17-5p) and to promote new blood vessel formation for the recovery of heart diseases. With such an approach, it is possible to inhibit the function of a particular microRNA by producing an anti-sense construct against that microRNA. Since chemically synthesized RNAs are unstable and it always produces off-target results (side-effect), body-expressed microRNAs are under strict control of the body system and can exert normal physiological functions. Fulfillments of the proposed experiments will provide new information in understanding the regulatory roles of miR-17-5p in factors associated with blood vessel formation and wound repair. This could lead to the development of a new method to treat vascular diseases, which could increase the chance of survival and recovery in patients with myocardial ischemia, cerebral ischemia myocardial infarction and stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: The genetic determinants of human anti-mycobacterial immune reactivity
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEX TRAIT; FUNCTIONAL VALIDATION; GENE CLONING; GENETIC ANALYSIS; QUANTITATIVE TRAIT; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Identification of human genes controlling resistance and susceptibility to tuberculosis is crucial to developing new treatments and vaccines as well as preventing transmission. Many genetic studies in tuberculosis have been inconclusive due to small datasets and/or inexact clinical phenotypes. Over the last several years, we have successively targeted three areas to identify genetic risk factors. First, we have built up large family datasets in different endemic areas of disease. Second we have designated for study phenotypes only immune tests that are clinically relevant. Third, we have established robust genome wide methods designed for immunological responses. These resources are now being used to identify genes that impact on the quantity of the anti-mycobacterial immune response. Specifically, the present application will focus on the molecular isolation of gene variants that make a person innately resistant to infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Innate resistance to infection is the holy grail of tuberculosis research since without infection no tuberculosis disease can develop.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular genetic analysis of adenovirus E1A function
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRUS E1A; CANCER; EPIGENETICS; GENETICS; ONCOGENIC TRANSFORMATION; TRANSCRIPTION; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites.  The absolute dependence of viruses on their host makes viruses incredibly useful for identifying critical regulators of host cell function.  The proteins encoded by Early Region 1A (E1A) of human adenoviruses are powerful tools for investigating the relationship between gene regulation and aberrant cell growth because of the large number of gene and growth regulatory activities they perform. Although studied extensively, much remains to be learned about the mechanisms by which E1A reprograms cell growth and differentiation. The information we obtain regarding the mechanisms regulating cell growth and development may help define novel targets for cancer therapies or suggest strategies to prevent cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of renal tubular epithelial cell injury to promote kidney allograft survival
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CYTOKINES; EPITHELIAL CELL; INFLAMMATION; ISCHEMIA REPERFUSION; KIDNEY; MOUSE MODELS; NECROPTOSIS; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic injury and premature loss of transplanted kidneys has emerged as our greatest current clinical challenge.  The premature failure of kidney transplants is related to both early rejection and chronic injury of kidney cells by inflammation.  This inflammation may be regulated within the transplanted kidney itself.  Kidney cells can be eliminated by different "forms" of cell death.  We have discovered that a unique form of kidney death termed "necroptosis" differs from more typical cell death (apoptosis) in that it may lead to increased inflammation within the kidney and contribute to long term injury.  Furthermore this inflammation can activate harmful Natural Killer cells which injure the transplant and are not affected by current anti-rejection drugs.  In this grant, we will study how the form of kidney cell death regulate kidney transplant inflammation and rejection.  These studies will determine how the form of kidney cell death affects immune responses and chronic transplant kidney injury.  These studies will guide future clinical therapy of kidney inflammation and may translate to truly new approaches to preventing kidney transplant injury in patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding how the HIV-1-dependent ribonucleoprotein counters host stress responses
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV-1/AIDS; LASER SCANNING CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; MAMMALIAN TARGET OF RAPAMYCIN; MOLECULAR & CELLULAR BIOLOGY; MTOR; PROTEOMICS AND MASS SPECTROMETRY; RIBONUCLEOPROTEINS; STAUFEN1; STRESS GRANULES; VIRAL EVASION STRATEGIES; VIRUS-HOST INTERACTION
Abstract-Résumé: HIV-1 is the causative agent that causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome or AIDS. Since 1981, more than 25 million people have died of AIDS. It is estimated that close to 40 million people worldwide are infected (United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS) and in Canada, recent data released by the Public Health Agency of Canada show that there are about 4000 new HIV-1 infections per year. Without effective treatments or a cure, the socio-economic impact will continue to be disastrous. Several drugs have been developed to target specific processes of the virus replication cycle and have been instrumental in maintaining and enhancing the quality of life and life expectancy of infected individuals. However, HIV-1's ability to adapt leads to sequence variation in the viral genetic material and the inevitable development of resistance to most current drug therapies. This is an all-to-common occurrence that leads to treatment failure and juggling of alternative drug regimens. Without a cure, there is an urgent need to identify new therapeutic targets for drug design to block HIV-1 infection and replication. The proposed projects described in this application represent our efforts to further our understanding on how HIV-1 co-opts some of the cell's major machineries to ensure an environment that allows for efficient viral gene expression. With this knowledge, we can envisage the development effective and new drugs with potent anti-viral activities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurochemical Aspects of Depression in Women: Monoamine Oxidase A During Perimenopause
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL DEPRESSION; MOOD; PERIMENOPAUSE; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; SEROTONIN
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is an important problem for women in the perimenopausal period with an incidence rate of 17% for full clinical depression and 16% having significant symptoms. This study will examine brain changes during perimenopause that may relate to greater risk for clinical depression and clinical symptoms. Social factors like stressful life events elevate the risk of a depressive episode, and it may be that drops in estrogen may also contribute to the risk of a depressive episode. This study will measure a brain protein called monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) which increases after estrogen drops. MAO-A breaks down chemicals that maintain normal mood like serotonin. This study will use a brain imaging method to measure MAO-A levels in women in perimenopause. It will compare MAO-A levels during perimenopause to levels prior perimenopause and after perimenopause. It will determine if MAO-A levels are higher in women with full clinical depression with onset in perimenopause. It will also determine whether MAO-A levels are higher in women with some clinical depression symptoms during perimenopause. Should the results of the study show that MAO-A levels elevate more in perimenopause, particularly in those who have sad mood, and in those with clinical depression, it would argue that future treatments of clinical depression with perimenopausal onset should consider targeting MAO-A or compensating for effects of overly active MAO-A. In the case of people experiencing some mood symptoms but not a full clinical depression, this could involve dietary recommendations or natural health food products that contain the nutrients which become the mood maintaining chemicals like serotonin.For full clinical depression, it may be that MAO-A inhibiting treatments are superior but the clinical trial to test such treatments has not yet been done in clinical depression. The current research would guide selection of new treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of LKB1 in beta cell biology
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; BETA CELLS; GENE EXPRESSION ANALYSIS; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; INSULIN SECRETION; ISLETS; LKB1; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TYPE 1 DIABETES; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing our understanding of how beta cells function and survive is critical to the improvement of treatment of type I and type II diabetes. While islet transplantation offers a promising treatment for Type I diabetes, this approach is limited by graft immune rejection and impaired function and survival of transplanted islets. We have found that the Lkb1 gene regulates many central beta cell functions, including insulin production and secretion. Loss of Lkb1 leads to beta cell proliferation, cell growth, and consequent protection from high fat diet induced diabetes due to an increase in the overall amount and fitness of the beta cell population. Lkb1 controls the activity  of a family of 12 downstream 'switch' proteins, the so-called Ampk kinase family. We hope to delineate which Ampk family member(s) control which specific beta cell functions downstream of Lkb1, with a view to designing specific therapeutics for improving beta cell function (i.e. insulin secretion) and beta cell growth and survival. The knowledge gained will be applied to preserve islet cell survival during islet transplantation for children with Type I diabetes, and to improve islet cell function in Type II diabetes patients who display impaired glucose control.

Abstract-Résumé: The principal goal of this project in to understand how iNOS, a pro-inflammatory mediator, promotes insulin resistance which can lead to diabetes in obese individuals. We hope that the proposed research will unravel the molecular and cellular mechanisms behind iNOS-driven insulin resistance and thus help develop novel treatments for obese diabetic individuals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing mutations in the a3 V-ATPase subunit in osteoclasts: A key player in bone loss due to inflammatory arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE RESORPTION; INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIS; ION TRANSPORT; OSTEOPOROSIS; PROTON PUMPS; V-ATPASES
Abstract-Résumé: The theoretical "silver-bullet" therapy for pomoting healthier bone is to reduce osteoclastic bone resorption while increasing osteoblastic bone formation.  To date, the "gold standard" treatment to prevent bone loss are the bisphosphonates, which do indeed eliminate osteoclasts, but they also prevent the effectiveness of PTH therapies aimed at increasing bone formation.  We hypothesize this is due to bisphosphonates eliminating the osteoclast-osteoblast signaling essential for bone formation.  By trying to understand the various roles V-ATPases play in osteoclastogenesis and activity, a therapeutic can be developed that would prevent V-ATPases from pumping acid onto bone but would not affect osteoclastogenesis.  Osteoclast-osteoblast signaling would remain unaffected and bone formation therapies such as PTHrP could be used in conjunction, allowing for the first time inhibition of bone loss and concurrent stimulation of bone formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanistic insights into the invasion of human erythrocytes by the malaria parasite.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; IMAGING; INVASION OF ERYTHROCYTES; MALARIA; PHOSPHORYLATION; REVERSE GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Malaria is a major public health problem caused by the infection with apicomplexan parasites of the genus Plasmodium. These obligatory intracellular parasites infect an estimated 500 million people annually, resulting in over 1 million deaths seach year. A vaccine is not available and resistance to antimalarial drugs is widespread. It has been estimated that the number of cases will double in the next 20 years unless new methods of treatment and control are developed. The publication of genome sequences for Plasmodium falciparum, the analysis of its transcriptome and proteome provides the research community with exciting new possibilities in the fight of this disease. However, new treatments arising from genomic targets remain some way off and there are still multiple black boxes in the complex life cycle of the parasite that are beyond our current knowledge. This is one of the biggest hurdles in the fight against this disease. The malaria parasite spends much of its time within the human erythrocyte. All the symptoms of malaria occur during erythrocytic development and consequently most anti-malarial therapies target this developmental stage. The objectives of this proposal are to identify and validate novel key players in erythrocyte invasion in order to deepen our understanding of this fundamental biological process and to identify novel therapeutic targets. It will concentrate on (1) the functional characterization of novel proteins implicated in invasion and (2) the assessment of phosphorylation as a suitable therapeutical target. These two approaches on its own will significantly contribute to the field of host-parasite interaction but their synergistic effects will facilitate and accelerate the understanding of human red blood cell invasion on the molecular level.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cell polarity and generation of the first distinct lineages in the mouse embryo
Keywords-MotsClés: ASYMMETRIC DIVISION; BLASTOCYST; CELL ADHESION; CELL POLARITY; CELL SORTING; CORTICAL TENSION; DEVELOPMENT; LINEAGE; LIVE IMAGING; MOUSE EMBRYO
Abstract-Résumé: How does our body form from a tiny simple fertilized egg? Current methodology used to study early mammalian embryonic development limits our understanding of what is an extremely complex and dynamic process. I have developed unique tools and methods to observe living mouse embryos in real-time in test tubes. Now changes in embryonic structure, cell shape and cell movement can be observed directly. We will document the processes generating complexity in embryos and address its mechanisms. Through focused experimental disruption of important variables such as chemical cell-cell communication and physical cell-cell contacts, we can both document their relative importance in development, and observe the dynamic responses in living embryos to such insults. The knowledge we obtain from this work, how the embryo works, will serve as a basic foundation to devise strategies to generate various types of cells in our body in test tubes, such as neuron, cardiac cells and hepatocytes. This will allow us doing drug screening and toxicology in test tubes as well as generating repair parts for diseases or injuries such as pancreatic beta cells for diabetes or red blood cells for blood transfusion in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring and Enhancing Access to In-Home Health Services for Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual and Transgender Communities in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: DIVERSITY; GENDER IDENTITY; GENDER-BASED ANALYSIS; HEALTH SERVICE ACCESS; HOME CARE; INTERPROFESSIONAL CARE; MIXED METHOD; ORGANIZATIONAL POLICY; SEXUAL ORIENTATION; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research, the second phase in a comprehensive, multiphase project exploring access and equity issues within the home care sector for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) populations, will use a mixed method design and a gender-based diversity sensitive approach to: 1) foster the development of an evidenced-informed home care-specific LGBT access and equity tool that will enable Community Care Access Centres (CCACs) and contracted service provider organizations to evaluate their policy and practice in relation to LGBT populations; and 2) address the process of translating LGBT policy into practice. Data obtained from the proposed study will be used to further refine a home care-specific LGBT access and equity tool, developed in phase one of the longitudinal project, by integrating the knowledge and experiences of key informant referral sources, service users, service providers and CCAC managers. The proposed study offers opportunity to address: 1) a gap in the LGBT health services access literature by providing evidence-informed knowledge about service access barriers for LGBT populations that are unique to the home care sector; and, 2) the process of translating LGBT policy into practice, therefore, this phase two will address CCAC organizational readiness in preparation for a Phase 3 piloting of the LGBT access and equity tool. In addition, findings from the proposed study will contribute to the development of fact sheets that 1): provide educational information to LGBT communities about the scope of home care services, accessing home health services and client rights; and 2) provide information to interdisciplinary home care service providers that provide information about the provision of home care services to LGBT communities in relation to their unique service needs and barriers to accessing home care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determinants of 25-hydroxyvitamin D in a multiethnic Canadian population
Keywords-MotsClés: 25-HYDROXYVITAMIN D; DIET; ETHNICITY; GENETICS; SEASON; SUN EXPOSURE; SUPPLEMENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Vitamin D is important in bone health and has been linked to many diseases including cancer and heart disease, but studies are difficult because we do not have a very good understanding of what determines the average levels of vitamin D in people over time.  The sun is a major source of vitamin D and levels can vary over the seasons.  They also vary in people from different ethnic backgrounds.  Genetic and other factors can also contribute to the amount of vitamin D and we do not completely understand what factors are the most important.  We plan to recruit volunteers aged 18 to 59 from different ethnic groups in the Toronto area and ask them to provide a DNA sample and to complete a diary about factors that might contribute to vitamin D levels every two months over the year.  We have already had 53 people participate in a pilot study.  A blood sample will be taken each time to measure blood indicators of vitamin D.    We can use this information to develop better ways of assessing vitamin D in large population studies to study vitamin D and health and to create better public health messages and clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transferring a rural community-based HIV treatment program in Uganda from researchers to local stakeholders :  can program successes be maintained?
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED TREATMENT; GLOBAL HEALTH; HIGHLY ACTIVE ANTIRETROVIRAL TREATMENT; HIV/AIDS; UGANDA
Abstract-Résumé: Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) has transformed the lives of HIV-infected persons and their families in sub-Saharan Africa.  However, access to HAART is still low in sub-Saharan Africa, where only 33% of those who need it can access it.  One of the challenges is access to HAART by those living in rural areas located at a distance from existing hospital-based program.   The purpose of this study is to evaluate the long-term sustainability of a community based antiretroviral treatment (CBART) program that was established by our research team in western Uganda in 2005 in order to provide access to HAART to the rural population in this area.  We will undertake a process to effectively hand over the program to the local health care system and community and evaluate their ability to sustain the activities and treatment outcomes of this program.  If our community-based approach to HAART delivery can be maintained successfully over a two-year period by the local stakeholders this model could be confidently recommended for replication in Uganda and elsewhere in Africa as truly viable and locally sustainable with desirable outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Controlling epithelial cell polarity in Drosophila: Regulation of adherens junctions by Bazooka/PAR-3
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL ADHESION; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL POLARITY; CYTOSKELETON; DROSOPHILA; EPITHELIA; GENETICS; MICROSCOPY; MORPHOGENESIS; PAR COMPLEX
Abstract-Résumé: My lab studies how epithelial tissue structure is regulated. Epithelia are the sheets of adherent cells that form our skin and separate our body compartments. Each side of an epithelial sheet has distinct molecular properties. This epithelial polarity guides embryo development and directs adult functions (e.g. nutrient uptake in the gut). Its loss is associated with cancer. We are studying how epithelial polarity is established and maintained, focusing on polarity-organizing machinery operating in each epithelial cell. We are identifying the proteins making up this machinery, and determining how they function together to establish and maintain epithelial polarity in the Drosophila embryo. Because the same polarity proteins function in Drosophila and humans, this fundamental research will provide an important foundation for understanding cancer and developing regenerative medicine. By defining the molecular machinery that controls normal tissue development, we can devise strategies to (1) control tissue breakdown and metastasis during cancer progression and (2) guide tissue engineering for treating diseases and disabilities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Liposomal nanoparticle formulations of difficult to formulate drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICANCER DRUGS; CANCER CHEMOTHERAPY; DRUG DELIVERY; IMMUNOSUPPRESSIVE DRUGS; LIPOSOMES; MEMBRANE ANTIGEN TARGETING; PRODRUG
Abstract-Résumé: Liposomes or liposomal nanoparticles (LNP) are small vesicles within which drugs such as anticancer drugs can be encapsulated. The therapeutic benefits of LNP as drug carriers rely on their ability to efficiently load and retain the drug in the carrier so that it is delivered to the disease site. This is readily achieved for drugs that are weak bases, which can be loaded into LNP at high concentrations in response to a transmembrane pH gradient. However, there are important drugs that do not have the weakly basic amino groups that are required for drug loading and cannot be stably encapsulated and retained in liposomes. We have recently developed a way to efficiently encapsulate hydrophobic, poorly water-soluble drugs into LNP and have demonstrated the validity of this approach for docetaxel, a major anticancer drug. This approach involves synthesis of weak base derivatives of the drug that can be loaded into, and retained by, LNP but which is converted back to the parent drug on release. The work to be conducted under the present grant will extend this approach to develop LNP formulation of the anticancer drug etoposide and immunosuppressive drugs. In addition, targeting information will be incorporated into the LNP to achieve LNP uptake into prostate cancer cells. It is anticipated that the targeted LNP formulations of docetaxel and etoposide will result in improved modalties for the treatment of prostate cancer, whereas LNP immunosupressants will have an improved therapeutic profile as compared to drugs currently used to prevent transplant rejection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of NLRP7 in the spectrum of reproductive wastage
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEUPLOIDIES; FOETAL LOSS; GENETIC MAPPING; INFLAMMATION; MATERNAL DEFECT; MOLAR PREGNANCIES; POSITIONAL CLONING; POSTZYGOTIC CLEAVAGE ABNORMALITIES; SPONTANEOUS ABORTIONS; STILLBIRTH
Abstract-Résumé: Hydatidiform mole is a human pregnancy with no embryo. The paradoxical nature of this condition has fascinated and puzzled scientists in all civilizations. The common form of hydatidiform moles is not recurrent and affects one in every 1000 pregnancies in western countries, but up to 10 in 1000 pregnancies in the Far East. Hydatidiform mole or molar pregnancy is also a benign tumour of the placenta that may persist after dilatation and curettage evacuation and require chemotherapy or degenerate into a choriocarcinoma, a malignant, aggressive, and metastatic cancer and lead to death in the absence of appropriate management. By studying rare families with moles, our group identified a first gene, NLRP7, for this condition. The goal of the current application is to understand more the role of the new gene and investigate its role in the common form of moles and in other forms of reproductive wastage and prenatal morbidities frequently found in patients with moles.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CHROMATIN; CHROMOSOME CONFORMATION CAPTURE; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; EPIGENETICS; FLUORESCENCE IN SITU HYBRIDISATION; NUCLEAR ORGANISATION; REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Embryonic stem cells have the potential to become any cell type in an adult organism. These cells may be used to treat diseases by replacing diseased cells with healthy (differentiated) cells generated from stem cells. Scientists believe that the potential of stem cells to become any other type of cell is accomplished by maintaining the expression of a specific set of genes and by preventing the complete inactivation of genes that need to become activated in differentiated cells. The DNA that makes up our genome is folded and organised in the 3-dimensional space of the cell nucleus. The importance of this organisation in regulating gene expression has recently been revealed for differentiated cells. The genome is organised differently in stem cells than it is in adult differentiated cells and this appears to be necessary to maintain their unique states. Although this has been seen at a basic level, little is known about the specifics of genome folding in stem cells and how this folded organisation regulates gene expression. This project will use advanced new techniques to identify the genetic elements that regulate genes in embryonic stem cells and explore how the genome is folded differently in these cells compared to differentiated cells. Through a better understanding of how embryonic stem cells maintain their potential we will be able to generate cells with the same potential which can then be used to replace diseased and damaged cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of mechanisms and efficacy of neuroprotection by water-soluble coenzyme Q10 in a cellualr an animal model of Parkinson's Disease and its effects on behavioural changes
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; ASTRO-GLIAL ACTIVATION; BEHAVIOURAL CHANGES; COGNITION; LEARNING; NEURONAL CELL DEATH
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neuro-motor disease associated with the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the brain. PD is the second largest neurodegenerative disease in Canada. Other than treatments for symptomatic relief, at present there is no therapy for prevention of further loss of brain cells in PD patients. Furthermore, the exact cause of PD is also not known. Recent research suggests that exposure to environmental toxins may be a factor in the development of PD. Recently it has been shown that exposure to paraquat, an herbicide, is correlated with increased risk of PD. We have developed a cellular (in vitro) and animal (in vivo) model of paraquat-related PD. We have demonstrated that a water-soluble formulation of coenzyme Q10 (WS-CoQ10), developed by our collaborator Dr. Sikorska, shows near-complete protection against  paraquat-induced death of cultured neurons. On-going research in our laboratory has indicated that feeding rats WS-CoQ10 in their drinking water prevents behavioural and neurological deficits when they are exposed to paraquat in contrast to paraquat-exposed rats that have received only water.  It is noteworthy that other CoQ10 formulations are only similarly effective at very high dosages, whereas WS-CoQ10 is so at clinically appropriate low dosages. Results of our research may lead to a therapy that can stop the progression of PD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Branched O-glycan expression and lymphocyte function
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS OF DISEASE; CELL TRAFFICKING; GLYCOSYLTRANSFERASES; SELECTINS; T CELL HOMEOSTASIS; THYMUS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells in the body travel continuously through the blood vessels ready to seed new tissues replacing older cells in blood cell formation or to repair injury or defend against infectious agents in immune response. If an infection occurs many different cells are mobilised to fight the infectious agents. Some of these cells (dendritic cells) will ingest bacteria or virus at the site of infection and then travel to centres in the body (the lymph nodes) that are designed to instruct lymphocytes to fight the invading infectious agents. Lymphocytes continuously enter lymph nodes where they interact with the dendritic cells. If they encounter dendritic cells that have ingested an infectious agent that matches their receptor the lymphocytes become activated and multiply in the lymph node. (This is the reason that the area under the chin becomes swollen when people have a sore throat). In order to fight the infectious agents these activated lymphocytes need to receive directions where to go. To this end, dendritic cells also induce specific antennae shaped homing receptors on the lymphocytes surface that will then direct them to enter the inflamed tissues that bind these antennae.  There are several ways for lymphocytes to regulate these antennae. The cells can stop expression of the antennae or express functional/non-functional antennae by adding or removing sugar molecules that are attached to these antennae. We are interested in understanding the signals and mechanisms that alter the sugar molecules on these antennae and thus program directions into immune cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional and Metabolic Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Lung Inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY; BICARBONATE; CARBON-13; INFLAMMATION; LEUKOCYTES; LUNG; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; PYRUVATE; XENON GAS
Abstract-Résumé: Lung diseases, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma and acute lung injury (ALI), are the fourth leading cause of death of Canadians and are expected to result in a third of all deaths by 2020, placing an enormous societal and economic burden on Canadians.  In 2010, COPD alone accounted for the highest rate of hospital admission among major chronic illnesses in Canada, at a cost of more than $1.5 billion.  The prevalence of asthma in Canada is 7.5% for adults and is responsible for almost 50,000 hospitalizations, over 2 million missed school and work days at a cost of over $1 billion in direct and indirect costs annually. ALI, and its more severe form; acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), is currently one of the largest contributors to mortality and morbidity in the intensive care unit (ICU) with a  mortality rate of approximately 40%.  Central and immediate to all these diseases is lung inflammation which triggers a cascade of events leading to organ failure and mortality.  In this project, we will develop novel Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) methods sensitive to the earliest stages of lung inflammation based on hyperpolarized nuclei (xenon-129 and carbon-13)  in combination with labelled inflammatory cells. These methods will reveal changes in: ventilation, blood flow, gas exchange, metabolism and cell trafficking associated with lung inflammation and subsequent disease progression, both longitudinally and regionally, and are expected to provide: (i) earlier detection, (ii) fundamental insight into disease mechanisms and (iii) novel measures of therapeutic response to aid drug development. As well as having a strong impact on preclinical research, these imaging approaches can be directly translated to the clinic and should significantly impact understanding and management of human lung diseases. Furthermore, it is expected that this research will also have relevance to cardiac and metabolic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Host microRNA Response and Cytomegalovirus Infection after Transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOMEGALOVIRUS; TRANSLATIONAL STUDIES; TRANSPLANTATION; VIRAL INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Organ transplantation is the treatment of choice for end-stage organ disease including kidney failure, severe lung and liver disease.  Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common viral infection after transplantation. It can cause serious disease including pneumonia and hepatitis.  Recently novel small molecules called microRNAs have been found to play an important role in a number of cellular processes including the patient's response to viral infection. The goal of this set of studies is to analyze the immune response to CMV in transplant patients and to discover how the patient's miRNAs affect CMV replication. We will perform a number of clinical studies to look at their role as potential biomarkers in transplant patients. This study will be performed accross two of the largest Canadian transplant centers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Alveolar epithelial integrity after acute lung injury: control of repair mechanisms by K+ channels
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY/ACUTE RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME; ALVEOLAR EPITHELIAL INJURY AND REPAIR; CELL DIVISION AND MOTILITY; CELLULAR AND ANIMAL MODELS; K+ CHANNELS; LUNG PHYSIOPATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: A common feature of several lung diseases is extensive damage to alveoli. Acute lung injury (ALI) and its more devastating form, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), secondary to pneumonia, sepsis or trauma, for example, are characterized by severe injury to the alveolar epithelium, leading to lung oedema and respiratory failure. With a mortality rate of about 30%, ARDS is a common cause of mortality in hospital intensive care units. It has been established that alveolar regeneration is crucial for rapid recovery from ALI/ARDS, and it is clear that a better understanding of the alveolar repair mechanisms is necessary for the development of novel therapeutic strategies to improve survival in ARDS patients. Interestingly, our results show that proteins transporting K+ ions, called K+ channels, play a key role in the control of alveolar repair processes.   Our main goal is to better understand the mechanisms of alveolar regeneration and, in particular, the role of K+ channels in repair processes, using cellular and animal models.  In a first step, we will further study the role of K+ channels in cell migration and proliferation processes, crucial components of alveolar repair.  Our second objective is to clarify the mechanisms and intracellular signals whereby K+ channels control alveolar repair.  Our third objective is to explore the function of K+ channels in alveolar repair and secondary resolution of lung oedema in a mouse model of lung injury.   In summary, our project aims to demonstrate that K+ channels are key elements of alveolar repair and could be identified as a promising strategy for the resolution of alveolar injury and secondary lung oedema in ARDS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Moonlighting intracellular proteins in the extracellular matrix
Keywords-MotsClés: AMINOACYL TRNA SYNTHETASES; CLINICALLY RELEVANT STUDIES IN ARTHRITIS AND DERMATOLOGY; CONNECTIVE TISSUE; ECM PATHOLOGY; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; HEAT SHOCK PROTEINS; HIGH MOBILITY BOX GROUP PROTEINS; INFLAMMATION; RHEUMATOLOGY; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: . In inflammation the tissue proteins are dissolved by enzymes termed "proteases" causing loose teeth in gum disease and swollen, sore joints in arthritis. To do this most tissues and white blood cells that fight infection make important enzyme proteases called MMPs. These destroy tissue by dissolving collagens found in joints and gums, which normally are rope-like structures that add strength to these tissues.  We have found that MMPs do much more than just dissolve tissue. By cutting a cells signal molecules, MMPs also orchestrate healing and the way white blood cells protect the body from infection. Signal molecules are like traffic signals. Cells go differently when the signals are in the "on" or "off" position. So proteases are like light switches as they turn signals on and off. However, if important ones are left on, then disease can result.  We first developed new techniques (proteomics) to identify 1000s of proteins in inflamed tissues and so obtain an overall picture of the disease. Our methods specifically detect the dissolved protein stubs left after proteases work and by knowing these we can decipher which signal molecules that proteases are leaving on or off. Surprisingly, we found that certain proteins that are normally inside the cell can on occasion occur outside the cell and some of these play important signaling roles in inflammation. We call these proteins "moonlighting proteins" as they have different activities depending on when and where they  go to different places.  Understanding these moonlighting proteins is important in order to fully understand the ways inflammation destroys tissues and gives disease. Luckily, the dissolved protein stubs leave important tell tale signs of the disease called biomarkers. We hope that these biomarkers will improve disease diagnosis. We trust our research will also discover new drug targets to fight inflammation in disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; MONOCYTES; POLYMERIC-BIOMATERIALS; TISSUE ENGINEERING; VASCULAR GRAFTS; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: A conservative estimate reports that approximately 1.6 million Canadians suffer from vascular disease or live with the effect of stroke, costing $22B annually and accounting for approx. 32% of deaths in Canada. Vascular bypass remains a critical intervention to the repair of diseased blood vessels, where the need for coronary artery replacements remains elevated in Canada and in the world (in the US ~400,000 coronary artery by-passes annually).  Peripheral arterial disease occurs when blood flow to the limbs is damaged or blocked.  It is estimated that 4.3% of the population over 40 suffer from peripheral arterial disease and 14.5% over the age of 70, and the numbers are increasing due to shifting demographics and the rise in type II diabetes (~27 million people in Europe and North America). A person with Peripheral vascular disease is 2-6 times more likely to die from a heart attack or have a stroke than a person without peripheral vascular disease. The need for non-occluding small diameter vessel replacements is increasing since the current standard for vessel replacement is still to use healthy vessels from the patients themselves (which is difficult to find in this patient group). The principal investigators have synthesized a degradable polymer that is non-toxic to human blood vessel cells, produces low-inflammation and good wound healing characteristics, and yields healthy connective tissue integration within the material. This grant will establish the methods needed to use this novel polymer to regenerate replacement vascular grafts and the research will be validated with an animal model. The research will impact peripheral vascular disease by introducing a new approach to generating life-saving by-pass vessels.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proteolytic Signatures in Breast Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CANCER BIOMARKERS; CANCER PREVENTION; CARCINOGENESIS; DEGRADOMICS; HOST DEFENSE; MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASES (MMP); PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: . Death from cancer mainly occurs after cancer growth (carcinogenesis) by spreading (metastasis). In breast cancer the tissue is dissolved by enzymes termed "proteases" causing malignant cells to spread and then enter blood vessels and finally go to organs like lung.  We found that highly malignant breast cancer cells make important proteases called matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and others called "matriptases". We discovered that these proteases do much more than just dissolve tissue. By cutting signaling molecules they act like molecular cell phones: the cancer cell changes its behaviour, usually for the worse.  We first developed new techniques (gene chips and "proteomics") to identify 1000s of proteases and dissolved proteins and so obtain an overall picture of the disease. Doing so uncovers the different changes as proteolytic signatures that occur in breast and lung cancer. Our proteomics methods specifically uncover the dissolved proteins and by knowing these we can decipher the circuits that proteases use to "call in" on tumors, making them more cancerous. The dissolved protein stubs also form important telltale signs of cancer called biomarkers.  Tumors in mouse mammary glands are a good model for human breast cancer. We found certain proteases that are only in those primary tumors in mice that spread. It is important to know what they do at this stage in helping cancer grow and spread. Some of the proteins cut by these key proteases might become tumor biomarkers to help diagnosis and others identify the ways the body prevents cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functions of the tumor suppressor PALB2 in DNA double-strand break repair and tumorigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL AND CELLULAR ASSAYS; BRCA2; BREAST CANCER RESEARCH; DNA REPAIR; DOUBLE-STRAND BREAKS; FANCONI ANEMIA; PALB2; PANCREATIC CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes strongly predispose to breast cancer. PALB2 is a BRCA2 interacting protein that has been newly identified. Individuals who inherit PALB2 alterations have a risk of developing breast cancer. For instance, a novel truncating mutation in PALB2 was found in approximately 0.5% of unselected French-Canadian women with early-onset breast cancer. Interestingly, defects in BRCA2 and PALB2 cause a defect in homologous recombination, an important process to repair DNA damage within the cell. We aim to understand how the DNA repair proteins affect the cell ability to repair DNA by homologous recombination and then use this knowledge to design new therapies to reduce cellular viability of cancer cells.
