TitreApplicationTitle: Retrovirus silencing and chromatin reorganization in stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN REORGANIZATION; EPIGENETIC REPROGRAMMING; INSULATOR ELEMENT; PLURIPOTENT STEM CELL; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; RETROVIRUS SILENCING; SUICIDE VECTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Induced Pluripotent Stem (iPS) cells are generated by inducing skin cells to change into stem cells in culture. This cell induction is called "reprogramming" and is performed by using viruses to deliver a combination of four genes that normally control the stem cell state. Once the induction is complete the viruses are turned off, and the stem cells can make any cell type of the body. iPS cells therefore have the potential for rejection-free transplantation back into the original patient. We have made mouse and human iPS cells using these four genes, and have developed a method that signals when the skin cells have become iPS cells. We find that induction of reprogramming is often incomplete, and the viruses stay on in these partially reprogrammed stem cells making them inefficient at differentiating into the desired mature cell types. If these cells are used to repair injuries in a patient, they are likely to form tumours. We hypothesize that virus silencing is a crucial final step in the establishment of fully reprogrammed iPS cells, and that a better understanding of this process will help develop safe iPS cell lines for use in cell therapies. Our first aim is to characterize partial iPS cell lines to identify genes that induce virus silencing in stem cells, and evaluate their ability to promote full reprogramming compatible with efficient differentiation. Our second aim is to employ a new virus that resists silencing to prevent tumour formation after transplantation of iPS-derived cells. This virus will turn on a suicide gene only in stem cells. After differentiation into nerve cells, contaminating stem cells that could form tumours will be killed by the suicide gene. The effectiveness of this approach will be tested in mice. Overall, these studies will address the basic mechanism of virus silencing and its role in stem cell reprogramming, and apply this knowledge towards the development of safe iPS cells for transplantation therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the calcium-binding protein, S100B, in cardiovascular disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM-BINDING PROTEINS; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: A specific protein is found in heart and blood vessels in quantities that are altered in disease.  These alterations contribute to changes in heart structure and function and may even be important for the development of the heart.  This protein, S100B, acts both inside the cells of the heart and can be released from these cells to affect the function of neighbouring cells.  In this project we will study the role of this unique protein in isolated heart cells and in genetically modified mice (as models of human heart disease by creating heart attacks, high blood pressure, and diabetes in these animals). The role of S100B in the heart makes it a very attractive target for the development of new treatments for numerous diseases including heart attacks, heart failure, high blood pressure, hardening of the arteries, and the consequences of diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical search retrieval from, and comparative usefulness of, large unfiltered internet databases and smaller filtered internet databases
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH INFORMATICS; INFORMATION STORAGE AND RETRIEVAL; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION AND DISSEMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: The projects in this proposal are part of a series of studies seeking ways to improve retrieval and dissemination of scientifically sound and clinically relevant studies, especially to answer this question: What are the current best treatments or diagnostic tests for a given health problem?. The retrieval studies in the project focus on the large, general, medical literature databases such as MEDLINE. The purposes of the search filters developed for use in these large databases are 1) to assist clinicians to do their own searches; 2) to help reviewers of published evidence retrieve all relevant citations; and 3) to provide resources for librarians to help clinicians construct their own searches. Improved search filters are highly important given the problems of indexing and retrieval in large databases, and the widespread and rapidly increasing direct use of these databases by clinicians, patients, the public, researchers, educators, lawyers, and journalists, whose interests are primarily directed towards a small subset of the research literature that is of most direct relevance to the management of health care problems. Our dissemination projects focus on developing and testing systems for the delivery of best research evidence to clinicians. Our long-term objective is to harness the most clinically relevant content to test effects on clinical practice - a target of several objectives in this proposal. The questions in this proposal are related to determining the robustness of the search filters we have already developed and that are currently in use in PubMed and Ovid MEDLINE; developing search filters to retrieve other types of studies; developing and testing more efficient and effective methods of disseminating the most clinically important research evidence to practitioners; and comparing these approaches with the current, exhaustive and expensive methods for research evidence retrieval, appraisal, and synthesis in practice guidelines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the internal and the external pore of  Nav1.5 Voltage-gated sodium channel
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIARRHYTHMIC DRUGS; ARRHYTHMIAS; BIOPHYSICS; EXPRESSION; MUTAGENSESIS; NAV1.5; PATCH CLAMP; SODIUM CHANNELS; STRUCTURE-FONCTION STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: Sodium channels are pores present at the surface of every cardiac cells, they allow exclusively sodium ions to enter the cell, they are very crucial for initiating heart beats and its regular rhythmicity. These sodium selective pores are blocked by antiarrhythmics, drugs used to treat heart rhythm disturbances especially when heart rhythm is out of control. Indeed, sodium channel blockade has been the foundation of the therapy of cardiac arrhythmias in several cardiovascular diseases. Despite the addition of new drugs to the older drug arsenal, they failed to completely suppress arrythmogenesis and the presence of adverse side-effects of the drugs still limit their therapeutic usefulness. The molecular components that form the intracellular pore, where these drugs bind are not well elucidated. Using molecular biology techniques we will introduce amino-acid replacement of key residues and test their role in forming the pore. To achieve this goal it is necessary to alter the structure of cardiac sodium channels and evaluate the effects of those alterations on function. Cardiac sodium channels will be expressed in cells; this is an advantageous system to perform experiments which help us to better understand the structure and function of the human cardiac sodium channels. This will provide us with some extremely important information on the structure of the pore and finding the means of treating heart rhythm disorders. Finally, study of cardiac sodium channel pore, hopefully, will lay the groundwork for the design of new drugs targeted more specifically at maintaining cardiac sodium channels in nonconducting state.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of Vascular Injury by the Motility Regulators, Slit and Roundabout
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERIES; CELL CULTURES; CIRCULATION; IMMUNE SYSTEM; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease and stroke are the leading causes of major illness and death in the Western world and result from atherosclerosis, which occurs when blood vessels become inflamed and narrowed. Progressive narrowing occurs when white blood cells from the bloodstream and muscle cells from the outer vessel wall migrate into the inner layer of the blood vessel where they cause injury and scarring. In heart attack and stroke, blood vessels supplying the heart and brain become critically narrowed and blocked by blood clot formation.  Clot formation itself worsens inflammation in the blood vessel wall, fueling the entire process.  At the cellular level, each event described above contributes to atherosclerosis.  Traditional therapies and preventative strategies focus on targeting individual events.  Recent work from our laboratory suggests that Slit2, a molecule originally described in the developing brain, can potentially block each of these harmful events at the same time.  Our studies further suggest that, unlike many medications currently used, Slit2 does not cause side effects harmful to the immune system, but rather, leaves immune functions completely intact.  Indeed, Slit2 is not a synthetic medication, but rather, a molecule normally produced by blood vessel cells in the body, whose levels fall when vessel injury has occurred.    We will use a combination of cutting-edge biochemical, molecular, and cell biology techniques to define how Slit2 prevents blood vessel injury in atherosclerosis.  We will use animal models of blood vessel injury and clot formation to test Slit2's ability to prevent blood vessel damage in the living organism.  By understanding the molecular details, these studies will allow development of completely new strategies for preventing and minimizing the damage from heart attack and stroke.  The proposed studies are designed to adopt a rational approach for developing new strategies that can complement the existing treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting seizure onset.
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD FLOW; EEG; EPILEPSY; FUNCTIONAL MRI; HIGH FREQUENCY OSCILLATIONS; SEIZURE ANTICIPATION
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is one of the most common and serious neurological conditions, affecting up to 300,000 Canadians. About 30% of these patients have seizures that cannot be controlled by any available therapy. One devastating aspect of seizures is their seemingly unpredictable nature, which precludes driving and many types of employment. If it was possible to predict seizures before they occur, then preventative action could be taken to avoid them, thereby opening new treatment options. For example, patients could have implantable devices (e.g., deep brain stimulators or drug delivery devices) that would be activated during the transitional period leading into seizures, known as the pre-ictal period. In this proposal, we plan to identify and characterize markers of the pre-ictal period in persons with epilepsy.       Increasing evidence suggests that seizures are preceded by changes in overall brain activity, increased blood flow, and changes in the activity rate of cells in different brain regions. We hypothesize that these changes are reliable predictive markers for seizure onset. We will test this hypothesis by identifying pre-ictal changes in i) brain activity levels using functional magnetic resonance imaging, ii) synchronization of brain activity, and iii) brain blood flow.       Overall, the proposed research will lead to a better understanding of how seizures begin and how to predict them. It is important to note that the technology is currently available to monitor some of these markers in freely moving patients who have measuring devices of these markers surgically implanted. Because our centre uses this technology, we will be uniquely positioned to begin clinical trials using these markers to predict seizures and deliver therapies to prevent the onset of seizures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of alternative splicing in C. elegans by RRM-containing proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: IN VIVO SPLICING REPORTER; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; SPLICING; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins are the workhorses of the cell and each protein is encoded by a gene. The human genome contains ~25000 genes, yet there are several hundred thousand different proteins. One gene must encode many proteins - how can this be? The answer is a process called splicing.  Each gene is made up of blocks, or 'exons'. Splicing allows one gene to encode many proteins by using different combinations of exons. Imagine each protein is a word and that each exon of a gene encodes a letter. If a gene contained 8 exons, e.g. the letters S-P-L-I-C-I-N-G, then these letters can be used in different ways. They can be used to make full-length protein, SPLICING, or a shorter form like ICING. Crucially, more complex combinations like SPIN or SLICING can be made by skipping internal blocks.  Each example here is a meaningful combination but there are other nonsensical possibilities like SPLG.  How does the cell make only the meaningful splice forms and never the nonsensical ones? How do different tissues make different meaningful forms? This is what we want to examine. Surrounding each exon are signals that tell the cell whether to use the exon or not. These signals are seen by splicing factors but we do not know which factor sees which signal. Splicing in nematode worms is very like that in human but the genome is simpler and we can do direct experiments. We have already used cutting edge tools to find all the ways that exons are combined in normal worms. What we propose to do now is to remove each splicing factor in turn and see the effect on the pattern of splicing. In this way we will see which splicing factor is required for which splicing events. By examining the signals present around the affected exons, we can predict which factor sees which splicing signals. Finally, we confirm this by examining which signal each factor sees in a test-tube. Together, this will give us a deep understanding of how splicing is regulated, and how errors in splicing lead to human disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mucopolysaccharidosis IIIC as a protein folding disease: using animal models to study pathophysiology and explore potential therapeutic solutions
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ENZYME REFOLDING THERAPY; LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISEASE; LYSOSOME; MOLECULAR CHAPERONS; MUCOPOLYSACCHARIDOSIS; MUTATION ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Sanfilippo disease belongs to a group of devastating inherited diseases of children affecting the lysosome, a cellular compartment responsible for degradation and recycling of big biological molecules. It causes rapid mental retardation in infants and children, accompanied by variable problems of the eyes, skin and bones. Most of patients become demented and die before the adulthood. Previously we identified defects in the patient's genes that cause Sanfilippo disease. Now we want to produce and study a colony of mice that will have the same defects in their genes which will allow us to understand how exactly the disease affects human patients. We also want to use these mice to verify different drugs that can potentially cure the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Angiopoietin/Tie-2 signaling in endothelial cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ENDOTHELIUM; HDACS; IMMUNOBLOTTING; INFLAMMATION; MAPKS; NADPH OXIDASE; PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Maintenance of endothelial cell integrity represents a very important aspect of normal vascular function. Understanding of mechanisms influencing endothelial cell viability has, therefore, very wide implications to normal vascular biology and pathological conditions of the vasculature. Recent studies have identified the Angiopoietin/Tie-2 receptor system as a major regulator of endothelial cell integrity and survival. This system consists of endothelial cell-specific receptors (Tie-2) and a group of ligands (angiopoietins). Upon Tie-2 receptor activation, endothelial cells undergo several changes designed to enhance angiogenesis. These changes include increased migration, sprouting, adhesion and proliferation.  In our previous grant, we have discovered that Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinases (MAPKs) are important signaling pathways through which Tie-2 receptors modulate endothelial cell growth and differentiation. In this proposal, we will investigate who MAPK activity is finely tuned by various signaling pathways. We will first evaluate how the  NADPH oxidase regulates individual components of the MAPKs when the Tie-2 receptors are activated. We will then test how MAPK signals that are elicited by Tie-2 receptor activation are being terminated by dual-specificity phosphatases. We will also assess whether MAPKs induce two transcription factors, namely, AP-1 and Nur77 and whether these factors regulate inflammation on endothelial cells. Finally, we will evaluate in the final project whether modification of histones by histone deacetylase 7 is a signal pathways through which Tie-2 receptors modulate endothelial cell survival and angiogenesis responses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel mechanisms underlying ciliogenesis, planar cell polarity, and polycystic kidney disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELL POLARITY; CILIOGENESIS; DEVELOPMENTAL GENETICS; EMBRYONIC MORPHOGENESIS; EXPERIMENTAL EMBRYOLOGY; LIVE IMAGING; POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is the most common life-threatening syndrome that can be inherited from generation through generation. It afflicts approximately 1 in 500 people, and 50% of these individuals will ultimately lose all kidney function. Treatments for cystic kidney diseases are exceedingly costly (patients often require dialysis and kidney transplantation), and there are no current therapeutic drugs or preventive strategies. PKD therefore represents a critical target for clinical and experimental research.  Mutations in many different genes can cause cystic kidney disease. However, each gene appears to control the formation or function of cilia - small antennas that are present on most every cell, and which allow cells to sense and respond to their surroundings. Mutations in these genes also appear to disrupt cell "polarity". Polarity allows cells to distinguish up from down, left from right, and back from front - essential information when cells need to come together to form complex organs like the kidney. One of the outstanding challenges in the field of PKD lies in understanding this apparent link between cilia and cell polarity.  My lab uses zebrafish, a small aquarium fish, as an experimental organism for determining how genes control cilia and cell polarity. Zebrafish embryonic development is remarkably similar to humans. However, zebrafish embryos are transparent, easily grown and manipulated under a microscope, and we have developed powerful techniques for watching, in real time, how mutations in genes that cause PKD affect kidney formation. Recently, we discovered a new gene that could provide the missing link between cilia, cell polarity, and PKD. In the proposed studies, we combine cell biology, experimental embryology, and classic genetic approaches to fully define this gene's function. Results will provide fundamental new insights into what causes cystic kidneys, and how we might ultimately treat human disease.

Abstract-Résumé: Evidence supports the use of gangliosides to improve aspects of IBD. Gangliosides are dietary fats found in milk and are important constituents of the intestinal surface. We propose that ganglioside in the diet can replace ganglioside that is degraded in the gut of IBD patients to restore proper structure and function to the diseased intestine, resulting in disease remission. IBD is a lifelong struggle for patients. Insight into new non-invasive, diet-based treatment strategies would allow patients to live productive, healthy and happy lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Gap Junction Proteins in Immune Cells and Tumors
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER CELL MIGRATION; CELL:CELL INTERACTIONS; CYTOSKELETON; GAP JUNCTION COMMUNICATION; LYMPHOMAS; MYELOMAS; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: In this proposal we will study the modes of intercellular communication among cells of the immune system and explore the roles of gap junction proteins. The immune system is an important avenue of protection against invading pathogens. The proper regulation of this system is key. Dysfunction and blocks in normal developmental processes can lead to infection, immune disorders, as well as cancers of the immune system, including lymphomas, leukemias and myelomas. The gap junction proteins form pores or channels in cell membranes and facilitate the transfer of material from cell to cell and the exchange of material from the cell with the environment. Importantly these proteins are associated with tumor suppression and it has been proposed to use them as markers for tumor status in other types of tumors. Recent evidence has highlighted the importance of gap junction proteins in regulating cell shape and cell movement, important processes involved in tumor invasion and metastasis. Thus a better understanding of how gap junction proteins work will help us understand the fundamental mechanisms used to regulate these channel proteins during development, as well as insight into how they can influence the formation and spread of cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: A randomized trial to compare effectiveness of 4 months Rifampin (4 RIF)  with 9 months Isoniazid (9 INH) in the prevention of active TB in children: The P4v9 Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD HEALTH; GLOBAL HEALTH; LATENT TB INFECTION; RANDOMIZED TRAIL; TUBERCULOSIS PREVENTION; TUBERCULOSIS TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) is spread by airborne transmission from adults with active contagious TB to children, especially those living in the same household. Once children are exposed and infected they are at very high risk to develop active TB - which can be lethal if not detected and treated promptly.  This makes it very important to detect TB infection as soon as possible, and treat this while it is still latent or dormant.  Current therapy for latent TB infection is 9 months of Isoniazid; this is very effective if taken properly but because treatment is so long many children do not finish this.  4 months Rifampin is a recommended alternative. In adults this has been shown to be safer with much better completion. However the effectiveness of this treatment is unclear, and is being studied in an ongoing study.  We plan to compare the safety as well as the acceptability and effectiveness of 4 months Rifampin with 9 months Isoniazid (standard treatment) in children in several sites in Canada and other countries.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tissue Engineering of Intervertebral Discs
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLAGENS; DISC DEGENERATION; INTERVERTEBRAL DISC; LINK N PEPTIDE; MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS; PROTEOGLYCANS; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: The long-range goal of this research is to develop a biological repair strategy for intervertebral disc degeneration, a disorder which affects the majority of adults and often results in debilitating low back pain. Low back pain affects about 60% of the population by age 70, and although the origin of low back pain is often unclear, it is believed that degeneration of intervertebral discs plays a major role. As disc repair does not occur spontaneously, surgical intervention is often needed for treating chronically painful disc degeneration. Currently, the two major clinical procedures are disc excision and spinal fusion, which have a failure rate of up to 40% after 5 years. The hypothesis of this proposal is that new disc formation essential for repair can be induced by injecting a growth-promoting molecule and additional cells into the center of the degenerate disc. We believe that using this approach, it will be possible in the future to avoid or at least delay the need for surgery by promoting repair of the degenerate disc. This approach is relatively cheap and would therefore not only be beneficial to the patients but would also result in a major saving to the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ultra high field MRI measurements of tissue magnetic susceptibility in Multiple Sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MRI; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NEURODEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Canada's multiple sclerosis (MS) prevalence rate is amongst the highest in the world at 240 per 100,000 population for reasons we don't understand. Fortunately, there are drugs that can reduce the symptoms and slow the progression of the disease, but these drugs are very expensive. The lifetime cost of these drugs for a single MS patient is about $1.6 million, and the cost to treat all 70,000 patients for their lifetimes is a staggering 88-120 billion dollar obligation (in 2007 dollars). If we could come up with a way to decide when, and what dose of drug to deliver to each patient, we could save the health care system billions of dollars. The long-term goal of our research program is to develop and use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) methods to inform such decisions, by measuring biomarkers of the disease. MRI has been used for many years as part of the diagnosis of MS. However normal MRI findings have not correlated well with clinical symptoms and have not demonstrated significant ability to predict the course of the disease. This may be related to the fact that conventional MRI visualizes only some of the lesions and damage seen by pathologists. Ultra high magnetic field MRI systems have the potential to be more sensitive to the microscopic changes in tissue properties that occur as MS progresses. MRI machines at such magnetic field strengths are very expensive and relatively rare. Using a 7 Tesla (140,000 times the earth's magnetic field) human MRI system, we will develop MRI techniques that can characterize MS in patients on a microscopic scale. This could lead to earlier diagnosis of MS, and therefore the ability to intervene sooner with drug treatments. Earlier intervention results in better patent outcomes and lower treatment costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: MODULATION OF PHASE II DRUG METABOLISM: Role of a novel class of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; CARCINOGEN METABOLISM; CONJUGATION; DRUG METABOLISM; UDP-GLUCURONOSYLTRANSFERASES
Abstract-Résumé: There are considerable compounds from environmental and dietary sources that humans have to cope with every day. Glucuronidation, mediated by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) is the prevailing conjugative pathway for both xenobiotics, including drugs, and endogenous compounds.  This process is involved in their inactivation and elimination from the body and is particularly active in liver, but also in other excretory organs, such as kidney, small intestine, and colon. Understanding the mechanisms for regulation of these enzymes has importance implications for safe and effective drug therapy as well as for carcinogenesis. Our recent research has led to the discovery of a new regulatory mechanism of the UGT pathway involving nine novel proteins produced by alternative splicing. This discovery clearly represents a new paradigm for the regulation of drug-metabolizing enzymes. Our goal is now to demonstrate the pharmacological and toxicological relevance of this new mechanism through various functional studies. We will use complementary approaches to study human tissues involved in drug metabolism as well as cellular models that will be exposed to drugs and carcinogens. We will use complementary approaches to study human tissues involved in drug metabolism as well as cellular models that will be exposed to drugs and carcinogens. This emerging project is highly focused and its clinical relevance is likely to be substantial because of the importance of this metabolic pathway for drugs, carcinogens and hormones.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diet and weight in childhood: a longitudinal analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH COHORT; CHILDREN; GENDER; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; NUTRITION; OBESITY; POPULATION HEALTH; QUEBEC
Abstract-Résumé: The ultimate goal of this research project is to determine the factors underlying weight trajectories and the development of overweight and obesity in boys and girls, at the population level. More specifically, the research project will study the roles of the social environment and behaviours (diet and physical activity) on weight change in primary school children, taking into consideration birth, infancy, and preschool and primary-school factors. Such research is important because, to date, current weight-reduction and -maintenance interventions at both the individual and population levels have proven to be ineffective. The factors involved in the development of obesity must be considered simultaneously in order to better understand the etiology of this condition, and a gender-based approach is essential to study the situation. As the roots of adult obesity can be traced to childhood, it is thus essential to identify the factors associated with the maintenance of a healthy weight and with the development of overweight and obesity in boys and girls in childhood. The 3 primary objectives of this project are: (1) To study the process of weight change in a population of primary school children (aged 5 to 12 years); (2) to identify the main factors in the social environment and among behaviours (diet, physical activity) that contribute to the maintenance of a healthy weight and the development of overweight and obesity; and, (3) to analyze interactions between the social environment and behaviours in relation to different weight trajectories for boys and girls. Analyses will be done on a large birth cohort of singletons, the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Child Development. The project will be innovative in presenting a gender-based analysis at the population level.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pain in Older Cancer Patients with Delirium: Development of an Observational Measure
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER PAIN ASSESSMENT; DELIRIUM; MEDICAL DECISION MAKING; OBSERVATIONAL METHODS; OLDER PATIENTS; PALLIATIVE CARE; SCALE DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Over 40,000 older Canadians die of cancer each year, a number that will grow as the population ages. Many of these patients will experience pain and delirium, a brain dysfunction that makes it difficult to report pain. At present, we do not have a tool to measure pain in older people with delirium at the end of life, and we know very little about pain control for these vulnerable patients. Our primary objectives are to develop a tool to measure their pain and to advance our understanding of how patient factors (like gender) and healthcare worker factors (like clinical experience) impact on judgments and treatment decisions about pain. We propose two studies. In the first, healthcare workers will be asked about pain in these patients and how they can tell if a patient is in pain. This information will be used to develop a checklist of cues for pain that can be completed by observing patients. A questionnaire about their beliefs about pain will also be developed. In the second study, we will test the checklist. Healthcare workers will complete it as they watch videos of elderly cancer patients with delirium who might be in pain. We will also measure factors like clinical experience, beliefs, and empathy and test how these factors are related to pain judgments. This study is important for end-of-life care of cancer patients. The majority of cancer patients are over 60 years old, and most of them will experience pain and delirium. The results of this study will lead to better pain detection in elderly cancer patients with delirium. They also will make it possible to study which treatments provide the best pain control. The results will also help us develop educational workshops for healthcare workers to improve their knowledge about and management of pain. In this way, the results of these studies will improve pain control for elderly people at the end of life. Good pain control will relieve the burden of cancer both for patients and their families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Single-plane dynamic radiography for quantification of bone and joint motion
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; DYNAMIC DIGITAL RADIOGRAPHY; OSTEOARTHRITIS; TOTAL JOINT REPLACEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: We depend on healthy bones and joints for life-long mobility, but trauma and diseases of moving joints (like osteoarthritis) can cause pain and loss of function, leading to decreased quality of life for more than 2 million Canadians. The economic burden is high, costing the Canadian economy more than $6 billion per year.  To help us understand the causes of joint disease, and to select the best treatments, we need to analyze moving bones and joints under their normal loads. While it is relatively easy to acquire a single x-ray of a stationary joint, it is not commonly possible to obtain a 3D movie of a moving joint.  This can be done using simultaneous imaging with two x-ray systems (similar to binocular vision), but few hospitals have two identical x-ray systems to use for this purpose.  Because of this lack of routinely available dynamic imaging systems, physicians are often not able to obtain the information that they need to evaluate the effectiveness of new treatments for joint failure.  Recent advances in digital x-ray imaging technology, combined with much faster computers and new software, will allow us to develop a new system for dynamic imaging of moving joints (such as the knee, shoulder, elbow, and wrist) during normal activities.  The advantage to our approach is that the hardware and software that we develop will be designed to work with a standard digital x-ray imaging system, which is already available in most hospitals.  By taking this approach, we will ensure that our new system will be implemented more quickly by other researchers and clinicians. The final stage of our project will involve studies of patients who have had knee surgery, to demonstrate that we can make accurate measurements of joint motion with an existing hospital x-ray system.  The result will be novel techniques for routine evaluation of new orthopedic surgical devices and techniques, ensuring that the best treatment becomes available as soon as possible.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Vascular G Protein-coupled Receptor Signal Transduction
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOTENSIN; DESENSTIIZATION; GRK; HYPERTENSION; PHARMACOLOGY; PHOSPHOLIPASE; RAB GTPASE; RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The objective our project is to understand how hormones that circulate in the blood to regulate blood pressure alter the activity of the receptors that are expressed on vascular smooth muscles cells (VSMCs) of blood vessels to control blood pressure.  The hormones that we are interested in are adrenaline and angiotensin II.  Adrenaline activates adrenergic receptors and works to dilate blood vessels and angiotensin II works to constrict blood vessels.  However, the activity of the receptors for adrenaline and angiotensin II is changed in both hypertension and congestive heart failure.  Our goal is to better understand how other proteins expressed in VSMCs regulate the activity of these receptors under normal conditions and how changes in this regulation of receptor activity might lead to disease.  To do this, we propose three sets of experiments.  First, we will examine the mechanism by which an enzyme called phospholipase Cdelta1 is activated by the angiotensin receptor to alter VSMC responsiveness Second, we will examine how a loss of expression of a protein called G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (GRK2) results in altered angiotensin and adrenergic receptor signaling in VSMCs and leads to the development of hypertensive mice.  Third, we will study a protein called Rab4 that is upregulated in cardiac failure.  Rab4 controls the movement of receptors between different compartments of the cell and overexpression of a mutant Rab4 in the heart results in cardiac failure.  Therefore, we will assess the effect of reducing Rab4 protein expression on angiotensin and adrenergic receptor signaling in VSMCs and will test whether the overexpression of a mutant Rab4 protein in VSMCs will generate mice that become hypertensive.  Understanding the mechanism(s) by which angiotensin and adrenergic receptor signaling is regulated is essential for the development of novel and selective approaches for the treatment of cardiovascular disease.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Syncope: Pacing or Recording in the Later Years (SPRITELY)
Keywords-MotsClés: BUNDLE BRANCH BLOCK; HEART BLOCK; IMPLANTABLE LOOP RECORDER; PACEMAKER; PRAGMATIC RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; SYNCOPE
Abstract-Résumé: Fainting affects about half of Canadians, is the cause of 1-2% of emergency room visits, and probably causes $250 million in health care spending each year. It is a particular problem for older people, because of their increased frailty and because it has several possible causes. One of these causes is intermittent heart block. The heart has 3 cables that conduct impulses from the pacemaker in the top of the heart to the pumping chambers in the bottom, and then the heart does not beat. This stops blood flowing to the brain, and people faint. Heart block occurs when all 3 cables fail to conduct at the same time. If this is seen, treatment is easy: insert a pacemaker. However doctors often only see that 2 of the 3 cables are missing on the patient's ECG. There are 2 ways to treat fainting in people who have ECGs that show 2 cables are missing: put a pacemaker in everyone, or insert a small ECG recorder under the skin, see what happens with the next faint, and then insert a pacemaker in those patients who have all 3 cables temporarily shorted out. No one knows which approach best balances risk and benefit. We will study 120 patients over 50 years old who have fainted recently, and who have ECG evidence of 2 cables missing. They will enroll in a randomized clinical trial, which is designed to give practical information to doctors and administrators. Consenting patients will be assigned randomly to receive either a pacemaker or an implantable ECG recorder, and we will follow them for 2 years. We then will compare the number of faints, the number of severe light headed spells associated with all 3 cables shorted out, and the number of complications related to the implanted devices, in each arm of the study.  This is the only study of its kind in the world. It will have centres in Canada, Europe and South America. There is no "right" answer to the study; it will simply help us make sounder judgments in the care of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of endogenous stem cells during spinal cord disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES/GROWTH FACTORS; EPENDYMAL CELLS; INFLAMMATION; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; OLIGODENDROCYTES; SPINAL CORD INJURY; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury (SCI) and multiple sclerosis (MS) are just some of the devastating conditions that can affect the adult spinal cord. There are currently few to no treatment options or cures for such disorders. Clinically, they are diverse in terms of functional losses, rate of progression and severity. For  example, mild SCI patients can have partial loss of locomotor ability and yet have nearly normal life-spans, whereas MS patients begin with bouts of relatively mild sensori-motor symptoms that recur with increasing intensity and duration. Beyond the motor losses, spinal cord diseases and injury are also associated with important sensory and autonomic consequences that further reduce patient quality of life.  The recent discovery of stem cells within the adult spinal cord may offer a novel way for improving the outcome following such diverse spinal cord conditions. We propose to use these spinal cord stem cells to improve the spinal cord's innate self repair capabilities. Before being able to achieve this, however, we must answer fundamental questions about spinal cord stem cells, including: what do they normally do? How do they react during different types of spinal cord diseases? And how are these reactions controlled by processes such as inflammation, a major and complex component of the wound healing process? In this research proposal, we tackle these key questions using animal models of SCI and MS. This project is a novel collaboration between the laboratories of Dr. Karl Fernandes (stem cell and spinal cord researcher, Montreal) and Dr. Steve Lacroix (neuroimmunologist and spinal cord researcher, Quebec City). We hope that this work will ultimately contribute to the development of innovative stem cell-based therapies for spinal cord repair.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of secretion of cardiac endocardial endothelial cells by neuropeptide Y. Régulation de la sécrétion des cellules endothéliales endocardiques par le neuropeptide Y.
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOCARDIAL ENDOTHELIUM; ENDOTHELIN-1; HYPERTROPHY; LEFT AND RIGHT VENTRICLES; NEUROPEPTIDE Y
Abstract-Résumé: The endocardial endothelium is a monolayer of hormone secreting cells that line the cavities of the heart. It has a strategic localization between the circulating blood and the cardiac contractile muscle. It was reported that dysfunction of the endocardial endothelium is 100% implicated in many cardiac diseases such as hypertrophy and heart failure which leads to sudden death. Recently, our group clearly showed that endocardial endothelial cells release various hormones towards the cardiac contracting cells and alter their function. In addition, our group demonstrated that these special types of cells also secrete a neuronal hormone called neuropeptide Y. The goal of this proposal is to test the general hypothesis that endocardial endothelial cells secrete a neuronal hormone neuropeptide Y which in turn triggers the secretion of an important hormone endothelin-1. This secreted hormone will promote the development of heart diseases such as cardiac hypertrophy. Thus, this work will help to better understand the normal and pathological roles that endocardial endothelial cells play in cardiac diseases such as arrhythmia, hypertrophy and other heart diseases. Such knowledge will help to develop drugs that target endocardial endothelial cells in order to better control their abnormal secretion of cardiac hormones.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural mechanisms of osmosensing and transport for proton-osmolyte symporter ProP of Escherichia coli
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR OSMOREGULATION; CYSTEINE REACTIVITY; CYSTEINE SCANNING; EPR AND FLUORESCENCE SPECTROSCOPIES; ESCHERICHIA COLI; KINETIC MECHANISM; OSMOSENSORY TRANSPORTER PROP; PEGYLATION ASSAY
Abstract-Résumé: Living cells are perturbed by "osmosis", the flow of water into or out of cells in response to changes in the osmotic pressure of their environment. Cells must sense and respond to this osmotic stress because hydration changes perturb many cellular processes, threatening survival and growth. When faced with dehydration, cells take up benign compounds called osmolytes, water follows and cell functions resume.  Transporters are protein molecules with dimensions of nanometers that function as pumps to select specific chemicals and move them into or out of cells. We were the first to show that a single protein, osmosensory transporter ProP of bacterium Escherichia coli, could detect changes in osmotic pressure and respond by transporting osmolytes into the cell.  Our work suggests that the rate at which ProP pumps osmolytes depends on the osmotic pressure because ProP, itself, must be correctly hydrated to function effectively. We will test that hypothesis by probing the structure and transport mechanism of ProP, thereby determining how they are altered by osmotic pressure changes. Exploiting our current structural model for ProP, we will experimentally modify ProP structure, determine what steps in the transport process are affected by the osmotic pressure and monitor interactions of electromagnetic radiation with ProP to determine how its structure changes over time (its structural dynamics).  Our work is important to human health because osmoregulation promotes the survival and health of disease-causing bacteria. Osmoregulation is also critical for the survival and health of human cells, particularly those in the kidneys and the brain. Many biological principles are universal, so knowledged gained through the study of bacterial protein ProP will help us to understand the functions of corresponding proteins in other organisms, including humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of strategies to curb the HIV epidemic based on molecular epidemiological surveillance
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV TRANSMISSION; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; PHYLOGENETICS; PRIMARY HIV INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: While antiretroviral therapy has prolonged and improved the lives of persons infected with HIV/AIDS, the onward spread of regional epidemics in most-at-risk populations shows no evidence of decline. Phylogenetic approaches, using large viral sequence datasets from genotyping programs, provide an important tool to identify HIV transmission networks. Our findings show half of the male-sex-male (MSM) epidemic in Quebec is driven by newly infected persons, often unaware of their status. Transmission networks arise wherein one infection is associated with 10 onward transmissions. Our study will combine phylogenetic,epidemiologic and cohort approaches to ascertain the driving forces of the provincial MSM and heterosexual epidemics with a view to improving testing, treating, and prevention paradigms so as to avert and ideally eradicate onward spread of HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: A molecular genetic study of autism and related Phenotypes in extended pedigrees
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; GENETICS; GENOME SCAN; PHENOTYPES
Abstract-Résumé: Autism is perhaps the most handicapping disorder of childhood.  It is caused largely by genetic factors but few of the many genes that lead to the disorder have been discovered.  Most studies investigating the genetic etiology of autism have focused on affected sibpairs or singletons, but these approaches are limited by the amount of genetic information available.  New and innovative genetic studies are needed that can account for the missing heritability associated with autism. We are studying extended multi-generation pedigrees where there are several members that either have autism or some milder, genetically related, trait.  So far, we have collected 26 such pedigrees and are collaborating with an American team who have another 13.  In this renewal, we propose to complete data collection of both clinical information and DNA from key members of these families.  We have developed new methods of linkage analysis that will allow us to take full advantage of all the clinical information available.  We feel that this design is much more likely to lead to the discovery of the genes that cause inherited forms of autism than traditional designs for studying complex genetic disorders.  Discovering these genes will go a long way towards developing novel and effective biomedical treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural stem cells and the promotion of healthy brain aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; MICROSCOPY; NEURAL STEM CELLS; TISSUE CULTURE; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Aging and Alzheimer's disease have developed into major social and economic burdens throughout the developed world. They are associated with an abnormally rapid deterioration in cognitive functions, termed dementia. In North America, for example, the incidence of Alzheimer-associated dementia rises from 10% at 60 years of age to 50% by 85 years; hence, understanding how aging and Alzheimer's alter brain function is of growing importance.   Our recent work indicates that stem cells within the adult brain are a major target of both aging and Alzheimer's disease. The normal function of these stem cells is to produce new brain cells that are required for multiple types of learning and memory processes. However, the numbers and activity of brain stem cells steadily decline as we age, and since human lifespans have been steadily increasing, this means that more of us are likely to develop learning and memory defects as we get older. This problem is compounded in Alzheimer's disease, which accelerates the loss of brain stem cells.   We believe that maintaining youthful levels of brain stem cell activity is one of the keys to promoting healthy brain aging. In this research proposal, we focus on identifying the cellular and molecular processes by which the brain stem cell system is suppressed during normal aging and during Alzheimer's disease. Our experiments will be carried out using innovative and powerful animal models, which will provide us with fundamental new insights into how stem cells can be activated within the aging brain. It is our hope that this will contribute to the development of therapeutic approaches for using the brain's own stem cell system in order to promote healthy brain aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Corticosteroid-binding globulin: key regulator of glucocorticoid action during development and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE EXPRESSION/TRANSCRIPTION; GENETIC POLYMORPHISM; GLUCOCORTICOIDS; HYPOTENSION AND CHRONIC FATIGUE; INFLAMMATION; PLASMA STEROID BINDING PROTEIN; PROTEIN STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Cortisol is a natural steroid hormone that controls the growth and development of most of our vital organs, and it helps us deal with stress, fight off infections, and recover after illness. It is also used extensively as a drug that is commonly known as hydrocortisone. The way cortisol acts as a hormone inside cells has been well studied but how it gets to these cells is less well understood. Our studies of the plasma binding protein for cortisol, known as Corticosteroid Binding Globulin or CBG, have shown us that - in addition to transporting cortisol in the blood - CBG influences how cortisol gains access to specific cells during normal development and diseases like inflammation. There is evidence that defects in the production or function of CBG in humans are associated with hypotension, chronic fatigue, and our ability to respond to acute inflammation. We propose that a greater understanding of how CBG is produced and functions, and how CBG deficiencies might contribute to disease states, could improve and personalize steroid and other drug treatment regimens, especially during life-threatening events. With this as the ultimate goal, our priority is to: (1) Further define the structure and function of CBG and to use this knowledge to design novel therapeutic strategies; (2) delineate how plasma CBG production is regulated under both normal and pathological conditions, and (3) define how abnormalities in human CBG production or function contribute to adverse clinical outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Multicentre Osteoporosis Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MINERAL DENSITY; FRACTURES; OSTEOPOROSIS; OSTEOPOROSIS TREATMENT; POPULATION HEALTH; QUALITY OF LIFE; RISK FACTORS; SECCULAR EFFECTS; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Multicentre Osteoporosis Study (CaMos), which was established in 1995, is an ongoing population study being carried out in nine cities across Canada. CaMos has helped to shape our understanding of osteoporosis, both in Canada and internationally. Continued follow-up of the participants in CaMos will provide data to address critical questions by clinicians, health care policy makers, and the general public. We will collect five additional years of follow-up data to examine changes over time in fracture rates in women and men (particularly hip and back fractures) as well as changes over time in the major risk factors for fractures (such as bone mineral density, and serum vitamin D levels). We will evaluate the effectiveness of therapy on the prevention of first and subsequent fractures, the long-term effectiveness of therapy, the factors predisposing to loss of effectiveness of therapy, and how therapy impacts on quality of life. We will also examine  the quality of life of participants who have a diagnosis of osteoporosis but have not yet fractured and in those with osteoporotic fractures. Annual follow-up will continue through the period of this grant, with complete reassessment of the participants once during the study. This will include an interviewer-administered questionnaire; measurements of height, weight, bone densitometry; spine x-rays; and blood samples. Participants who report a fracture on the annual mailed follow-up questionnaire will complete a telephone interview on fracture and health-related quality of life. We will also recruit an additional group of men and women ages 60-75 years, using the same methods as were employed originally, in order to facilitate interpretion of the  observed changes in fracture rates and risk factors.  Our study should provide new and important information on both prevention and treatment of a common debilibitating disease of both Canadian and international significance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Distinctive contribution of epithelial and mesenchymal Bmp signaling in intestinal homeostasis.
Keywords-MotsClés: BMP SIGNALING PATHWAY; CELL CULTURE; CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT/CRE-LOXP SYSTEM; EXPERIMENTAL COLITIS; GASTRO-INTESTINAL EPITHELIAL-MESENCHYMAL CROSSTALK; GASTRO-INTESTINAL PROLIFERATION AND DIFFERENTIATION; GATRO-INTESTINAL  CANCER; IBD; MOLECULAR GENETICS; SMAD TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The functional complexity of a multicellular organ such as the intestine involves a high degree of coordination among diverse specialized cell types. Maintaining this organization as well as regulation of intestinal cell functions requires a permanent and dynamic crosstalk between epithelial and underlying stromal cells. This crosstalk is mediated by crucial soluble factors such as the Bone Morphogenetic Proteins (Bmps). Bmp signaling within the intestine is complex:  Bmps and their receptors are expressed in both epithelial and mesenchymal compartments, suggesting bidirectional signaling between the mesenchyme and the epithelium. The use of genetically modified mice is a powerful tool to establish significant advancement in the understanding of the in vivo function of a molecule of interest, especially in the context of intestinal epithelial-mesenchymal interactions. The main objective of this research proposal is to explore the distinct and specific contribution of mesenchymal and epithelial Bmp signaling components on intestinal epithelial functions and pathologies. This research proposal will unravel the mechanisms underlying the distinctive contribution of both the mesenchyme and epithelium to the homeostasis of the intestinal mucosa in health and disease Improving our knowledge of the spatial and temporal control of gastrointestinal cell functions might ultimately contribute to developing cell-based therapies for pathologies such as the inflammatory bowel diseases and colorectal cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Auditing:  An Evaluation of Tissue Specimen Misidentification
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPSY; DNA FINGERPRINT; LABORATORY ERROR; MISIDENTIFICATION; MISMATCH; MOLECULAR AUDITING; PATIENT SAFETY; TISSUE SPECIMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Laboratory errors, including specimen misidentification, can have catastrophic impact to patients.  It is not uncommon for such errors to be recognized by the laboratory or submitting physicians, and the errors can then be corrected.  Some specimens may be at higher risk for misidentification errors, such as gastrointestinal biopsies or prostate and breast needle biopsies, which are accrued and submitted in high numbers by busy clinicians,.  We seek to test the hypothesis that there is a background rate of unsuspected specimen mismatch/misidentification in tissue biopsies submitted for microscopic examination to a pathology laboratory.  If our hypothesis is correct, we will have identified a significant source of potential adverse affects for patients which may justify changes to the current processes used to submit and evaluate small tissue biopsies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of parasite drug metabolism as a mechanism of anthelmintic resistance and the identification of novel resistance genes.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTHELMINTICS; GENOMICS; HPLC-MS; NEMATODES; PARASITES; XENOBIOTIC RESPONSES
Abstract-Résumé: Parasitic worms infect over a billion people worldwide and are a major cause of suffering in the developing world. As with other types of infectious disease, parasites are developing resistance to the few available drugs. We need to understand the mechanisms by which parasites become resistant to drugs in order to diagnose, treat and manage the problem. This project will investigate the processes by which parasites modulate the activity of drugs and become resistant to them. The identification of the molecules involved is an important step in the development of sensitive and accurate tests for the diagnosis of resistance. It may also allow the design of new pharmaceutical agents which block these processes which would provide new powerful approaches to the treatment of drug resistant parasites.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rhinovirus induced exacerbations of asthma and COPD
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRALS; ASTHMA; CHEMOKINES; CIGARETTE SMOKE; COPD; EPITHELIAL CELLS; GENE REGULATION; HOST DEFENSE; INFLAMMATION; RHINOVIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD - sometimes called smoker's lung) and asthma are two of the most common chronic diseases in the world. There are well over 1 million Canadians who are affected either by COPD or asthma. These two diseases can severely limit quality of life and represent a major burden on the health care system. Acute attacks of asthma and COPD can be life threatening and also account for the majority of the costs of treating these diseases.  Human rhinoviruses (the common cold viruses) are now known to be among the most frequent triggers for acute attacks of asthma and COPD, but we do not fully understand how rhinoviruses cause such attacks. We do know that these viruses infect the epithelial cells that line the airways and cause the release of chemicals that can increase airway inflammation. Interestingly, these cells can also produce antiviral molecules that can fight the virus and could prevent attacks of asthma and COPD.  As yet, we do not know which antiviral molecules are the most important. This grant aims to find out which antiviral molecules may be most important and how they may affect the virus. We are also trying to understand how cigarette smoke, the main cause of COPD, alters responses to rhinovirus infection.  Patients with COPD, and asthmatic subjects who smoke, have worse outcomes to viral infections than non-smokers.  If we can understand why this happens we may be better able to reduce rhinovirus-triggered attacks of asthma and COPD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolic and genetic determinants of obesity and obesity-related phenotypes
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE TISSUE; CANDIDATE GENES; GENE EXPRESSION; GENETICS; GENOME WIDE ASSOCIATION STUDIES; INSULIN SENSITIVITY; LIPOPROTEINS; OBESITY; OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is an important risk factor for hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, cardiovascular disease and various cancers and has become one of the most serious health problems in Canada.  In 2004, approximately 6.8 million Canadian adults ages 20 to 64 were overweight, and an additional 4.5 million were obese. Current guidelines recommend the initial use of diet, exercise and behavioral therapy, with judicial use of a very limited repertoire of pharmaceutical products as part of a comprehensive weight loss program.  Overall, current treatments are inadequate. Surgery is an effective option for selected patients with clinically severe obesity.   Obesity results from a combination of environmental and genetic factors, with the genetic contribution being at least as large as the environmental contribution and both lifestyle and genetic factors interacting to increase obesity risk. The goals of these studies are to determine the contribution of rare and common genetic variants to obesity, obesity-related medical complications and individual differences in the capacity to lose weight in response to diet.  Ultimately, a better understanding of the diverse genetic, metabolic and environmental contributors to this disease may permit more rational and individualized prevention and treatment strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modes d'action des résolvines et des époxy-éicosanoides dérivés des Omégas 3 dans les bronchioles humaines.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-INFLAMMATOIRES; ARN INTERFERANT; CONDUCTANCES IONIQUES; CPI-17; CULTURE ORGANOIDE ET CELLULAIRE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGIE; MODE D' ACTION; MUSCLES LISSES BRONCHIQUES; SIGNALISATION ET RELAXATION; EICOSANOIDES
Abstract-Résumé: Plusieurs maladies des voies respiratoires, comme l'asthme et les maladies pulmonaires obstructives chroniques resultent d'une inflammation et d'une constriction bronchique severe. Nous avons obtenu des evidences tres serieuses que de nouvelles substances produites par les cellules de la paroi des bronches (et des arteres pulmonaires) pouvaient dilater ces structures vitales et avaient des effets anti-inflammatoires. La production de ces substances serait largement diminuee chez de nombreux patients presentant des maladies  inflammatoires. Un apport exogene de ces substances est toujours envisageable, mais une meilleure comprehension de leur mode d'action et de la regulation de leur metabolisme (production / degradation) est primordiale. Dans ce projet novateur nous proposons d'etudier aux niveaux tissulaire et cellulaire le mode d'action de ces nouvelles substances anti-inflammatoires biologiques que sont les epoxy-eicosanoides, derives des acides gras polyinsatures. Nous analyserons dans le poumon humain comment ces substances modulent les proprietes fonctionnelles de la paroi des bronches et des arteres pulmonaires. Plusieurs types de mecanismes seront donc analyses, notamment ceux qui controlent le transport des ions a travers les membranes des cellules, les regulations biochimiques intracellulaires et l'expression des genes pro-inflammatoires. L'originalite de notre approche repose sur l'utilisation de petites sections de poumon humain maintenues vivantes et de techniques complementaires sur des tissus et des cellules mis en culture. Les modeles biologiques utilises permettront de determiner le role fonctionnel de differents systemes cellulaires qui sont susceptibles d'etre regules par ces substances endogenes derive des lipides connus sous le nom d'acides gras de type omega trois. Nous analyserons egalement comment ces nouveaux eicosanoides exercent des effets regulateurs sur l'expression des proteines qui controlent leur production et leur degradation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessment of cerebral hemodynamic abnormalities in children with sickle cell disease using quantitative non-invasive MRI measures of vascular reactivity and their relationship to stroke risk
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOREGULATION; CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; CHILDREN; PHYSIOLOGY; QUANTITATIVE MRI; SICKLE CELL DISEASE; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a genetic disease that leads to deformation of red blood cells to the sickle shape, which reduces the flexibility of the red cells and causes them to stick together and clump within the inner surface of blood vessels. This narrows the vessels in the brain and makes smooth flow of the blood cells difficult. The risk of stroke in children with SCD is considerable, with approximately 11% of these children suffering a stroke before their 14th birthday. Survivors of childhood stroke continue to suffer lifelong neurological challenges, which can place an enormous burden on both the child and his/her family. Currently, physicians use ultrasound to identify SCD patients who are at greatest risk. These high risk patients will then undergo blood transfusion treatment to help prevent stroke. Unfortunately, ultrasound is not a very reliable tool for this. To better assess the risk of stroke in children with SCD, we require tests capable of assessing and visualizing blood vessel function as this parameter is associated with the increased risk of stroke. Our team of imaging scientists and physicians recently developed a sophisticated method to investigate brain blood vessel function using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We have used this method in both adults and children to demonstrate its reliability, its ability to help assess other diseases affecting blood vessels in the brain, and its ability to monitor the success of treatment. We want to use similar methods to determine the risk of stroke in SCD. If our method proves to be useful, then we can use it to help identify children who are at greatest risk for stroke and who are in need of treatment. This will help reduce the burden of stroke in SCD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Augmenting cerebral blood flow during stroke via partial aortic occlusion: Defining mechanisms and neuroprotective efficacy in clinically relevant models of stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD PRESSURE; CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW; HYPERTENSION; ISCHEMIA; NEUROIMAGING; NEUROPROTECTION; STROKE; THROMBOLYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the leading cause of chronic disability and the third most common cause of death in Canada. Death and disability result from the death of brain cells during stroke. It is believed that early treatment can protect brain cells in areas of reduced blood flow from death and improve the recovery of stroke patients. Unfortunately, while many treatments have been proposed, few have been successful in protecting brain cells from death due to stroke in human patients. This grant proposal explores an exciting new technique for saving brain cells during stroke by increasing blood flow to the whole brain. Early evidence suggests this strategy may save brain cells and drastically improve recovery after stroke, but relatively little is known about the effectiveness, mechanisms, and safety of the treatment. We will use animal models of stroke to learn more about the mechanisms and benefits of this procedure to augment cerebral blood flow during stroke. At early time points after the onset of the stroke, animals will undergo the cerebral flow augmentation procedure. The effects of augmentation alone, or combined with drugs that try to break the blood clot to restore blood flow (the only treatment currently used clinically for stroke), will be assessed in the two weeks after stroke. Live animal imaging will be used to assess whether increasing cerebral blood flow can save normal brain function and determine how blood flow is restored to brain tissue. The mechanism of action will be important in order to understand whether flow augmentation can be used in conjunction with current therapies to improve recovery. We will also investigate if increasing blood flow to the brain damages blood vessels that are already injured by stroke and increases the risk of bleeding in the brain after stroke. Our research project will define the mechanisms and efficacy of a completely new method for early treatment of stroke, and ease the transfer of the procedure into human stroke care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interdisciplinary Study of Inequalities in Smoking (ISIS)
Keywords-MotsClés: LONGITUDINAL; NEIGHBOURHOOD; SMOKING; SOCIAL INEQUALITIES IN HEALTH; SOCIAL THEORY
Abstract-Résumé: While smoking rates in Canada as a whole are on the decline, not all groups of people are enjoying the same decreased rates of smoking as others. The reasons behind these distinctions in smoking rates remain unclear. Recent research has found particularly stark differences in smoking rates based on where people live. This research project aims to better understand what it is about people's neighborhoods that lead to differential rates in smoking. The study examines the case of the Metropolitan area of Montreal. The objectives of this study are both to understand why these inequalities in smoking rates come about, but also aims to address which aspects of neighborhoods most influence smoking in order to begin to develop new ways that smoking prevention might be addressed based on people's place of residence.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure, dynamics and contingency in nuclear regulatory networks
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL REGULATORY NETWORKS; CELL CYCLE; CHIP-CHIP; DNA REPLICATION; GENE REGULATORY NETWORKS; PROTEIN-FRAGMENT COMPLEMENTATION ASSAYS; PROTEIN-NUCLEIC INTERACTIONS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; REPLICATION; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: If you wanted to understand an electronic device like an iPhone, you would likely look at the individual electronic components, see how they are wired together and then figure out how individual and groups of components dynamically respond to inputs and what signals come out as a result.  You'd start with individual components and then look at hierarchically more complex two, three or more component relationships.  Along the way, you'd make lists of motifs, groups of different components that behave the same way, to try to figure out the modular organization of the whole.  Can the same logic be applied to life?  The Nobel laureate Sir Paul Nurse recently argued that we can do just this.  But it is an arduous task and some aspects of regulatory organization, such as structure and dynamics, are not easy to study.  We have developed novel experimental strategies that allow us to study, en masse, the structure and dynamics of regulatory circuits in cells and to dissect the relationships between individual components. The central aim of our proposal is to build on evidence for the organizing principles of chromosome structure, the DNA fibers that encode genes, to understand how the DNA is organized and modified by proteins in order that genes can be turned on or off and that the faithful replication of our DNA is achieved.  We will perform our studies in baker's yeast, which has the advantage that they are simpler, but share many genes with humans including those that are most primordial and become dysfunctional with age and in diseases such as cancers. The results of our efforts will help us to more generally define how cell regulation is most vulnerable to dysfunction and what kinds of strategies could re-stabilize them.  We will create new opportunities for researchers to address the most fundamental questions of life including how genes are constrained by how they are organized and whether structural constraints affect gene function and genome evolution.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Tool to Assess Decisional Capacity to Consent for Clinical Treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS; COGNITIVE ASSESSMENT; CONSENT FOR TREATMENT; DELIVERY OF HEALTH CARE; MARGINALIZED POPULATIONS; SUBSTANCE ABUSE
Abstract-Résumé: Determining a persons ability to make reasoned and authentic decisions surrounding health care can present ethical challenges especially when caring for clients suffering from addiction to substances such as alcohol or drugs.  Public health care frequently involves engaging individuals whose capacity to consent may be impaired.  Clinical assessments of decisional capacity have shown poor reliability and there is a need for reliable validated tools to ensure clients are providing informed consent for treatment and care.  This study is aimed at developing, validating, and piloting a brief and easy-to-use tool to assist public health clinicians in making ethical decisions when delivering public health care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissection of the molecular mechanism controlling the establishment of neuronal circuitry during development
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CULTURE; DROSOPHILA GENETICS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; TILING AND SELF-AVOIDANCE
Abstract-Résumé: One key issue in treating nerve injuries is how to restore the appropriate neuronal circuitry for functional recovery. In this application, I propose to utilize fruitfly as a model system to study the molecular mechanism by which neuronal circuitry is  initially established during development. We will investigate the mechanism by which two evolutionarily conserved genes Semaphorin and Turtle regulate the assembly of neuronal circuitry in the developing nervous system. By taking a combination of molecular and genetic approaches, we will determine how these genes interact with other genes to facilitate the wiring of neural networks. The proposed research will provide invaluable clues to the development of new therapeutical approaches to treat neurological diseases and nerve injuries in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of natural killer T (NKT) cell development, homing, and activation
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMOKINE RECEPTORS; DENDRITIC CELLS; GPCR SIGNALING; LEUKOCYTE HOMING; METASTASIS; NKT CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The ability of the body's immune system to recognize and destroy abnormal or cancerous cells depends on the proper localization and function of each component. Natural Killer T (NKT) cells are a population of white blood cells that have been shown to induce potent anti-tumour responses and prevent the spread of cancer cells. The infiltration of NKT cells into tumours has been associated with greater survival in patients with certain cancers, while reduced NKT cell numbers in the blood have been associated with poor outcomes. However, the mechanisms that regulate the development, localization and activation of NKT cells are not well understood. One class of molecules that could regulate the tissue distribution and activation of NKT cells are the chemokine receptors. These molecules belong to a family of proteins that have been shown to direct different types of white blood cells to specific locations in the body. We have found that one of these proteins, CXCR6, is expressed on NKT cells and mediates accumulation of NKT cells in the liver and lungs. However, CXCR6 also seems to be important for NKT cell development and activation.  NKT cells in mice lacking this protein do not generate normal levels of anti-cancer molecules and are more susceptible to the spread of cancer cells. In this study, we will examine the role that CXCR6 plays in NKT cell development. We will also examine the role that CXCR6 and other chemokine receptors play in NKT cell infiltration into tumours, and how they regulate activation of tumour responses by NKT cells. We will use this knowledge to try to direct NKT cells to cancerous tissues sites more efficiently, and/or activate NKT cells to make better responses to tumour cells. Any potential therapy that can be developed to reduce the burden of cancer will be an important addition to our current arsenal of treatments.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DES TUMEURS CEREBRALES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Prediction and Prevention of glioma recurrence by targeting telomere dependent self-renewal capacity of tumor initiating cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: EXPRESSION PROFILE; GLIOMA; SNP ARRAY; STEM CELLS; TELOMERASE; TELOMERES; TUMOR INITIATING CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Pediatric neural tumors (neuroblastoma and brain tumors) are the main cause of death from childhood cancer. Death is almost always a result of their ability to relapse after maximal therapy with chemotherapy and radiation. New approaches are crucial for these devastated children.  We have discovered that an enzyme called telomerase is active in a small population of cells in these tumors, tumor stem cells. It gives these cells endless self renewal and enables these cancers to recur. Strikingly, normal stem cells do not require telomerase for their survival. We then demonstrated that inhibition of telomerase using a novel drug causes exhaustion of tumor but NOT normal stem cells.  In this proposal, we will find which children require less toxic treatments and which are candidates for our novel therapies. We will build on these exciting findings to explore the causes of telomerase activation and inactivation in normal stem cells during development and how tumor stem cells reactivate this enzyme. Finally, we will use that to develop combination therapies with novel drug screens available to our group.  These combinations will specifically target tumor stem cells for exhaustion to prevent relapse.  We believe that this new concept of tumor stem cell exhaustion can transform the treatment and survival for children with neural tumors specifically and may open a new window to prevention of relapse in cancer.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of GPR40 in pancreatic beta-cell function
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; G-PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTORS; GPR40; INSULIN SECRETION; ISLETS OF LANGERHANS
Abstract-Résumé: The secretion of insulin by the beta-cells of the pancreas is a tightly controlled process that enables the maintenance of blood glucose levels within a very narrow range. Abnormalities in these control mechanisms cause type 2 diabetes, a disease affecting over 2 million Canadians. One of the therapeutic approaches to treat type 2 diabetes consists of increasing the secretion of insulin by the beta-cell with pharmacological compounds. The prerequisite to developing such novel compounds is to understand the molecular and cellular events that regulate the secretion of insulin, so that new drug targets can be identified.  The cell surface receptor GPR40 is present on the beta-cell plasma membrane and binds fatty acids. Binding of fatty acids to GPR40 enhances insulin secretion, suggesting that it could represent a novel drug target. However, the mechanisms by which fatty acid binding to the receptor augment the secretion of insulin are still poorly understood. The objective of this proposal is to better define the role of GPR40 in the regulation of insulin secretion. First, we will examine how expression of the receptor is regulated by glucose and fatty acids. Second, we will attempt to identify the cascade of intracellular signals that is activated upon binding of fatty acids to the receptor. Third, we will characterize the mechanisms by which this receptor stimulates insulin secretion.  This work will be carried out by using a combination of experimental approaches, including the use of pharmacological agents, molecular tools, and genetic mouse models. By contributing to the understanding of the mechanisms of action of GPR40 and its role in the regulation of insulin secretion, this project will help identify novel drug targets for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.
