TitreApplicationTitle: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Renal Hypothermia during Partial Nephrectomy
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL TRIALS; COHORT; PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMY; RANDOMIZED; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; RENAL CANCER; RENAL FUNCTION; RENAL HYPOTHERMIA; WARM AND COLD ISCHEMIA
Abstract-Résumé: ABSTRACT  Background/Hypothesis:  The incidence of renal cell carcinoma is increasing and in 2008 it is estimated that over 51,000 new renal cancers will be diagnosed in the United States.  To preserve renal function, urologists commonly remove the diseased segment of the kidney (partial nephrectomy) instead of removing the entire kidney (radical nephrectomy).  While the benefit of preserving function in patients with renal cell carcinoma has become clear, optimal preservation techniques are yet to be determined.  Specifically, the role of hypothermia during partial nephrectomy has been inadequately studied despite theoretical benefit.  Our objective is to assess the effectiveness of renal hypothermia during partial nephrectomy. Our hypothesis is that renal hypothermia during partial nephrectomy results in improved post-operative renal function compared to warm ischemia.    Methods:  To test our hypothesis, 180 partial nephrectomy patients will be randomized to cold or warm ischemia.  Global and side-specific renal function will be assessed pre-operatively and 12 months post-operatively using radionucleotide clearance and renal scintigraphy.    Significance:  To our knowledge, this study will be the first prospective trial to evaluate the clinical impact of renal hypothermia during partial nephrectomy.  Since renal function preservation is the primary purpose of partial nephrectomy, these findings will have an important impact on surgical technique and patient outcome.

NomDuComitéFR: Déterminants psychosociaux, socioculturels et comportementaux de la santé
TitreApplicationTitle: Psychological burden and pathological aging in individuals with and without cardiovascular disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BLOOD SAMPLES; PROSPECTIVE STUDY; PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; QUESTIONNAIRES; TELOMERES
Abstract-Résumé: The number of individuals reaching 65 years and older is increasing significantly. With aging often come a number of illnesses, including heart disease. The costs of treatment and loss of productivity are great, and likely to worsen. It is critical that we better understand the factors that contribute to ill health with aging, and the mechanisms by which they do so.  One biological marker of aging is telomere length. Telomeres are found at the end of chromosomes and are important in assuring that chromosomes remain healthy. However, telomeres shorten with age, which is why telomere length can be used as an index of how the cells age within an individual. The shorter the telomere, the more likely the individual is to suffer from disease or to die early. Psychological factors, such as depression and chronic stress, impact on how a person ages. The more a person is (di)stressed, the more he/she is likely to suffer from physical ailments or to die prematurely. A few small studies suggest that depression or stress can shorten telomeres.  We will examine the relation between psychological factors and telomere length in 1518 adults recruited for the Montreal Heart Institute Hospital Cohort. Participants will be healthy or suffering from heart disease, and will be seen once at recruitment and every 2 years afterwards. We will see whether telomeres get shorter faster (and therefore, age earlier) when individuals are more distressed psychologically, and whether this increases risk for adverse events (hospitalizations, mortality). Those who suffer from heart disease may age even faster because of the added stress of being ill. This project will help us understand why a person ages worse than others. To the extent that psychological factors are important, their effect on aging can be minimized by addressing (or even better, preventing) the distress. Medications or other interventions that protect the telomeres from stress could also be developed.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional regulation of the tRNA genes
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE CHECKPOINTS; GENOME STABILITY; REPLICATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: The tRNA genes make molecules called tRNAs. tRNAs are important because they are essential for protein production. In general the tRNA genes are very active in rapidly growing cells. Most cancer cells, for example, grow rapidly and make tRNAs at a high rate. On the other hand, the slower growing cells from which such cancers develop make the tRNAs at a low rate. Because of these relationships, we are interested in understanding how the rate of tRNA synthesis is controlled.  We study the regulation of tRNA synthesis in yeast, which is easy to manipulate experimentally and uses many of the growth control methods that are used by human cells. We recently discovered a new mechanism for controlling the tRNA genes. This mechanism turns off tRNA genes if the cell is having difficulty copying its DNA. Most importantly, this mechanism becomes highly active when DNA copying is inhibited by some cancer-causing chemicals. Why turn off the tRNA genes when DNA copying is perturbed? The reason is likely related to the fact that tRNA genes themselves interfere with DNA copying when they are active, i.e. how better to improve DNA copying than to turn off natural barriers to copying (i.e. turn off the tRNA genes)?  Because of the implications of our findings for cancer, we are interested in exactly how the cell turns off the tRNA genes when DNA copying is perturbed. Cells can turn off the tRNA genes by many different methods. Our discovery of how they do it when treated with cancer-causing chemicals is particularly exciting: they actually use regulatory proteins that are frequently mutated in cancer cells.   We now propose to determine the molecular mechanism by which these regulatory proteins turn off tRNA genes. In the longer term, our discoveries concerning the control of tRNA synthesis in yeast are expected to guide studies aimed at understanding how the activity of these genes is controlled in human cells, particularly during the development of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Neuroligin 1 in Sleep Homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION PROTEINS; CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; NEURONAL PLASTICITY; QUANTITATIVE EEG; SLEEP HOMEOSTASIS; SYNAPSE
Abstract-Résumé: In developed countries, there is a drastic rise of chronic sleep loss, as exemplified by reduced sleep duration in children and adolescents, and increasing prevalence of insomnia and night work. However, the mechanisms underlying its adverse effects on mental health, vigilance, learning, and mood are poorly understood. It is known that sleepiness increases with the duration of wakefulness. Moreover, the longer the duration of wakefulness, the more intense/deep the subsequent sleep. Recent work supports the involvement of synapses, the functional unit of communication between neuronal cells, in this process. Neuroligin 1 is an adhesion protein binding to other adhesion molecules and holding the two sides of the synapse together. Importantly, this protein controls the type of excitatory synapses that predominates in the brain, which type is also linked to both deleterious effects of sleep loss and sleep intensity regulation. In this project, the contribution of Neuroligin 1 to sleep regulation will be investigated. First, markers of sleep intensity (i.e., brain electrical activity and gene expression) will be evaluated in mice where Neuroligin 1 is absent or decreased. Second, the effect of the duration of time awake on Neuroligin 1 will be examined by measuring gene and protein expression in the mouse brain after sleep deprivation (i.e., preventing sleep for different duration). Lastly, because we observed that Neuroligin 1 expression could be modulated by specific factors driving transcription (i.e., the reading of a gene expressed as a transcript), we will identify the functional DNA sequences within its gene by in vivo (in mice) and in vitro (assays with cells in culture) methodologies. The results of the project will advance our understanding of neuronal functions, and assist in the prevention and in the development of interventions for people suffering from sleep debt accumulation, including age-related disturbances and insomnia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural properties of glutamatergic neurons in major depression and suicide
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON TERMINALS; BDNF; CELLULAR NEUROANATOMY; CEREBRAL CORTEX; DENDRITES; GLUTAMATERGIC; HIPPOCAMPUS; MAJOR DEPRESSION; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: According to the World Health Organization, major depression affects approximately 121 million people worldwide and is ranked as one of the leading causes of disability. Many studies have suggested that the structure of some brain regions, namely those involved in processing emotions, is altered in the depressed brain. Surprisingly, none of these studies have examined the structure of nerve cells (neurons) in these regions. Here, we propose a project that will describe the state of both types of neuronal extensions (dendrites and axons) in cortical and hippocampal tissue samples from depressed suicides and matched control subjects. Postmortem brain tissues will be obtained from the Quebec Suicide Brain Bank (Douglas Institute). Studying these microscopic structures which are crucial for neuronal communication should lead to a better understanding of the biological underpinnings of depression and suicide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Shift work and cardiovascular risk in working women:  A process model linking physiological, behavioural and social pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR RISK; GENDER; MECHANISMS; SHIFTWORK
Abstract-Résumé: Recent national reports raise concern about the growing risk of heart disease in younger and middle-aged adults.  The face of heart disease is changing such that young adults are entering adulthood with a number of cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors and older adults have lived longer with their unhealthy habits and are developing heart disease at an earlier age.  A recent Heart and Stroke Foundation report identified adult women as a population at risk.  Given that adults spend a significant amount of time in the workplace, the potential influence of the work environment on CVD risk requires careful examination.  In this study we are focusing on one aspect of the work environment (shift work) and an identified at risk population (adult females) as approximately 28% of employed women have worked at some time in a shift work pattern, and this proportion of female shift workers is the highest among hospital workers.  Current studies, predominantly completed among male workers, suggest that individuals working night shift may be at increased CVD risk; however, the mechanisms linking shift work and CVD risk are unclear. The purpose of this study is to empirically test a mechanistic model that postulates that shift work is associated with increased CVD risk through its influences on 3 different but interactive physiological, behavioural and social pathways.   We will conduct an observational study and recruit 300 female hospital employees who have been in the workforce for at least 10 years. Information will be obtained through clinical assessment, biochemical measures, continuous actigraphy and self-report.  Our analysis plan is designed to elucidate the different hypothesized pathways linking shift work to CVD risk in working women.  The findings from this study will contribute novel findings to our understanding of the harmful and protective characteristics of shift work, and will inform the development of healthy workplace policies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of endothelial VEGF receptor-2 signaling by ubiquitination and HSP90 activity in angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL SIGNALING; CHAPERONES; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; GROWTH FACTORS; NITRIC OXIDE; RECEPTORS; UBIQUITIN; VEGF
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding the intracellular mechanisms by which growth factors produce their effects in endothelial cells is an important aspect of vascular biology. Endothelial cell are intimately involved in formation of new blood vessel, termed angiogenesis, and in the control of vascular tone. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is an important factor for endothelial cells as it promotes their proliferation, survival and angiogenesis. Angiogenesis is deregulated in several cardiovascular pathologies such as atherosclerosis and cardiac infarct. In this proposal, we will attempt to modulate the ability of VEGF to control angiogenesis by altering cellular processes that affect the degradation and stability of VEGF receptors in endothelial cells. Furthermore, we will investigate how the release of nitric oxide, a critical factor produced by endothelial cells in response to VEGF, is affected by the modulation of VEGF receptor degradation. Defining new approaches to modulate the effects of an essential factor for the formation and maintenance of blood vessels will hopefully open the way to the identification of novel therapeutic targets in cardiac and vascular diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: MicroRNA-mediated gene regulation as a determinant of tissue tropism and pathogenesis in coxsackievirus infection
Keywords-MotsClés: HEART DISEASE; HEART MUSCLE CELL INJURY; ORGAN SPECIFIC INFECTION; VIRUS INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide, heart disease is the leading cause of death, particularly in developed countries. Virally caused heart disease called myocarditis (heart muscle cell injury) is one of the common heart diseases, particularly in children, young adults and pregnant women. Coxsackie virus, a virus that was discovered in a small town called Coxsackie near New York City, is ranked the #1 virus that can cause this heart disease. This virus can infect multiple organs of humans, but the degrees of infection are different. For example, heart and pancreas can be easily infected by this virus and develop deadly diseases shortly after infection, particularly in the heart. However kidney and lung are hardly infected by this virus and thus no disease is developed. This phenomenon can not be explained very well with the current knowledge. Therefore, the goal of this grant is to search for the genes or molecules in the body that determine why Coxsackie virus can easily infect the heart but not the kidney. Recently, a group of small genetic molecules called microRNAs (miRNA) has been found to play an important role in controlling virus infection in other diseases. Based on this finding, we hypothesize that this newly discovered group of miRNAs may control the degree of easiness of infection in different organs, such as the heart and kidney. To test this hypothesis, we will first search for and evaluate the miRNA production in different cell cultures or in different organs of mice. Then we will select several important miRNAs that either produce a lot or produce a little and test their functions in controlling viral infection and growth in the heart muscle cells using culture dishes. At the same time, we will use kidney cells to perform the same experiment for comparisons. Finally, these experiments will be verified by using mice, an established animal model mimicking human heart disease. These experiments are aimed to find a strategy to block virus infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functions of the pulvinar in normal vision: role in transthalamic cortico-cortical communication
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTICO-THALAMO-CORTICAL LOOPS; DRIVER AND MODULATORS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EXTRAGENICULATE THALAMIC NUCLEI; NEUROANATOMY; OPTICAL IMAGING; PERCEPTION; RESIDUAL VISION; REVERSIBLE INACTIVATION; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: It is generally considered that the visual images that we are seeing are analysed by a number of areas of the cortex, leading to a coherent perception of the external world. This dogma has been challenged in recent years. There is now evidence that subcortical structures located in the thalamus are also involved in the complex processing yielding the perception of the visual world. My laboratory explores the possibility that neurons in the largest thalamic nucleus, the pulvinar, contribute to our capacity to analyse the various aspects of the visual environment, in close relation with cortical areas. This work is important not only to understand how our brain can recognize an image (yielding the appropriate behaviour) but also to understand pathologies which affect the communication between the cortex and the thalamus, such as in schizophrenia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Early relational, cognitive, and neural manifestations of social dysfunction after preschool TBI
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY/OPTICAL IMAGING; EMOTION; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; LONG-TERM OUTCOMES; MILD BRAIN INJURY; MIRROR NEURONS; PARENT-CHILD INTERACTION; SOCIAL COGNITION; THEORY OF MIND; TODDLERS AND PRESCHOOL CHILDREN; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Brain injuries are the most frequent cause of death and disability in children, and those under the age of five are at particularly high risk. Studies in older children have shown that brain injuries can cause serious mental, psychological, social, and behaviour problems. For example, teenagers with brain injuries often have difficulties making friends or participating in group activities, which can cause feelings of loneliness and rejection. Some may also participate in socially inappropriate acts, which can have legal consequences. Even mild injuries have the potential to cause lasting problems in young children because of subtle changes to the way the brain works, but no one has yet looked into this. For instance, we do not know how social problems first appear in the early years after brain injury in preschool children, or what initial signs and symptoms might help us predict the development of social problems in later years. This study will investigate the appearance of social problems after young children have a mild brain injury. We will also see whether these problems are associated with changes in the way the brain processes information during social situations. Children (1.5-5years) and their parents will be invited back to the hospital six and eighteen months after an accidental brain injury. During these meetings, parents will play games and complete tasks with their children, which will help us measure their social interactions. We will also look at what is happening in the brain while children participate in social tasks by measuring their electrical brain activity using non-invasive and non-harmful techniques. The results will help us better understand how social problems develop after brain injuries in children.  We will also be able to quickly identify preschoolers who are at-risk for developing social problems and provide them and their families with support and resources to improve their social development and prevent problems before they appear.

ClasseRechercheFR: APOPLEXIE, INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE; METABOLISME ET NUTRITION
TitreApplicationTitle: Pathophysiology and Treatment of Stroke Recurrence
Keywords-MotsClés: NEURONAL PROTECTION; NUTRITIVE SUPPLEMENT; RECURRENT STROKE; RESVERATROL; VASCULAR PROTECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Strokes are a leading cause of disability and death.  The majority of strokes are caused by a blockage of blood flow through a cerebral artery.  Patients who have a major stroke often have had one or more mini-strokes days to weeks prior to the disabling insult.  Our knowledge is very limited as to how the mini-stroke affects the health of the brain.  It is possible that if there is sufficient time for the brain to heal after the first mini-stroke and prior to the second stroke (recurrent stroke), then brain damage will be less.  To study this we have developed a unique model of recurrent stroke in the rat. We currently propose to use our unique rat model to study the recovery of the brain from a mini-stroke and see if magnetic resonance imaging methods can be improved to better detect mildly injured brain.  We will also investigate whether the timing between strokes affects brain damage.  Then, we will examine whether resveratrol, a beneficial component in red wine, helps the brain heal after a minor stroke.  The results of these studies will provide highly original insights into the recovery of the brain from a mini-stroke and its susceptibility to damage should its health status remain compromised.  This will improve our ability to manage patients with mini-strokes or recurrent strokes and provide readily translatable treatment options leading to improved outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cathepsin D Activation: A Target to Reduce Alpha-Synuclein Pathology in a Parkinson's Model
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA-SYNUCLEIN; AUTOPHAGY; CATHEPSIN; LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISEASE; NEURODEGENERATION; SYNUCLEINOPATHY
Abstract-Résumé: Increased levels of a nerve cell protein named alpha-synuclein are linked to two common brain conditions: parkinsonism and dementia. To the detriment of >1.1 Mill Canadians and Americans, these alpha-synuclein-linked brain diseases remain incurable and progressive due to the lack of cause-directed therapy. Such targeted therapy involves - for example - the use of statin drugs to lower cholesterol levels to minimize the risk of stroke and heart attacks. Few biological 'scissors' (enzymes) have been explored for their ability to remove excess alpha-synuclein, which acts like the 'bad cholesterol of Parkinson disease' in the statin analogy. Two teams (one led by the applicant) recently identified a first "target", in the form of a protein-degrading enzyme called cathepsin D. Cathepsin D contributes to the elimination of alpha-synuclein in nerve cells grown in tissue culture dishes and seems to act similarly in brains of flies, mice, sheep, and humans.  This proposal seeks to carry out the next step in translational research following the identification of the target; it is called 'target validation'. We will test the hypothesis that enhanced cathepsin D activity in the adult nervous system is capable of lowering excess amounts of alpha-synuclein in the brain of mice. We will cross an existing, human alpha-synuclein-expressing Parkinson's mouse model, which was recently published by a collaborator, with a second mouse strain which we have created; the latter carries extra copies of the human cathepsin D gene. In a related step of target validation, we seek to better define the conditions under which cathepsin D operates and by which we can pharmacologically manipulate the target. The successful demonstration that alpha-synuclein pathology in mice can be modified by cathepsin D activation would represent an essential step forward to ultimately treat alpha-synuclein-related diseases at their root cause.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTÉ; SANTÉ DES POPULATIONS

TitreApplicationTitle: The Vancouver Interdisciplinary Collaboration on Supervised Drug Consumption Research
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG CONSUMPTION FACILITIES; ETHNOGRAPHIC RESEARCH; HEALTH SERVICES EVALUATION; INTERDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MIXED METHODS RESEARCH; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Increasingly, health policy is driven by scientific evidence. However, gaps persist between best evidence and public policy, particularly in response to the illicit drug problem.  In light of the growing harms associated with illicit drug use, many municipalities internationally have implemented drug consumption facilities (DCFs): controlled settings where drug users can inject or smoke illicit drugs under medical supervision. While recent research has shown benefits associated with DCFs, currently evidence is insufficient to recommend including them in programming for drug users. Despite this, the number of DCFs has increased steadily over the past decade.  Researchers at the BC Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS (BC-CfE) have conducted research on DCFs for over a decade and led the scientific evaluation of North America's first supervised injecting facility. This evaluation has led to more than 35 papers in top peer-reviewed journals (e.g., Lancet, British Medical Journal, New England Journal of Medicine, Canadian Medical Association Journal) which show several short-term impacts, such as reduced syringe sharing and increased enrolment into addiction treatment. Building on this work, BC-CfE researchers recently were awarded partial funding from CIHR to conduct a pilot study of an inhalation room for crack cocaine smokers. Despite these developments, DCFs remain highly controversial and have been the subject of legal proceedings in Canada and elsewhere.  This proposal seeks funding for a continuing program of interdisciplinary DCF research which will build on past work by assessing the long-term impacts of DCFs on patterns (including cessation) of drug use and on street-level violence, and by assessing the impact of a targeted knowledge translation program on the knowledge, attitudes and practices of stakeholders. The requested funding would also maintain ongoing interdisciplinary research on emerging models of supervised consumption.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of G protein-coupled receptor function by ARF6
Keywords-MotsClés: ADP-RIBOSYLATION FACTOR; ANGIOTENSIN; CELLULAR MODEL SYSTEMS; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; MIGRATION; MOLECULAR AND CELLULAR BIOLOGY; PROLIFERATION; SIGNALING MECHANISMS; SMALL GTP-BINDING PROTEINS; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The development of cardiovascular diseases such as atherosclerosis has often been associated with impaired function of cell surface proteins named receptors. These are the targets of more than 50% of all drugs sold today. Receptors are activated mainly by stimuli such as circulating hormones, which initiate a broad variety of intracellular signaling cascades leading to a subset of cellular responses such as cell migration and growth. Blocking the activation of the receptor often results in important sides effects. The identification of new intracellular pharmacological targets will allow us to design more effective and specific drugs. For the last 8 years, we have engaged, through funding by CIHR, the study of an intracellular protein that is activated by hormone stimulation. We have shown that this protein named ARF6 is a central regulator of several cellular responses. Here, we propose to study its role in cellular as well as tissue responses of the cardiovascular system. First, we will examine how exactly these proteins are activated following angiotensin II stimulation, a potent vasoactive hormone. Next, we will examine the role of ARF6 in regulating cell migration, invasion, proliferation and contraction in cells of the vascular wall as well as tissue responses. Altogether, our findings will further our understanding of the role of ARF proteins but, most importantly, will help us develop more specific new drugs and directly contribute to improve health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of Protein Ubiquitination by Human Ubc13-UEV Protein Complexes
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA REPAIR; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; PROTEIN UBIQUITINATION CYCLE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Living organisms must be able to respond to changes in their environment. At the cellular level, part of the adaptation to environmental changes involves regulating various protein and enzyme levels. This regulation is accomplished by a set of enzymes that tag specific proteins with the small protein ubiquitin, in a process known as the protein ubiquitination cycle. Proteins that are regulated by this cycle are involved in life processes such as growth, division, immunity, and DNA repair. Thus, the ubiquitination cycle has been targeted for development of therapeutics for the treatment of cancer. The objectives of our research are to determine the chemical principles underlying the attachment of ubiquitin to other proteins by applying the tools of modern biochemistry and computational chemistry. In addition, we use magnetic resonance spectroscopy to determine how proteins specifically recognize the ubiquitin tag. The basic knowledge we gain through this research is a fundamental requirement not only for understanding the cellular function of the ubiquitination cycle, but to also help develop rational therapies, in the long term, for associated diseases such as cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of autocrine motility factor as a targeted delivery agent for cancer therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-CANCER AGENT; CANCER METASTASIS; CYTOKINE RECEPTOR; DRUG DELIVERY; ENDOCYTOSIS; TUMOR CELL MOTILITY; XENOGRAFT MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Autocrine motility factor (AMF) and its receptor, gp78/AMFR, promote tumor cell motility and metastasis and are closely associated with malignancy in various cancers. When AMF binds to gp78/AMFR it is efficiently and selectively taken up by cancer cells. We are exploring whether internalization of AMF can be used to deliver chemotherapeutic agents selectively to cancer cells. We have developed a novel targeted therapeutic for cancer, called AMF-paclitaxel. By linking AMF to paclitaxel (an anti-cancer drug used clinically for cancer treatment) we expect to deliver this chemotherapeutic drug more selectively to cancer cells, but not normal body cells. This should increase the efficacy and reduce toxic side effects of cancer treatment with paclitaxel.    In this grant, we propose to link AMF to the clinically relevant isotope (99m-Technetium) and determine whether it can be used to visualize cancer cells in the body. We will assess whether AMF-paclitaxel prevents tumor growth, induces tumor regression and prolongs survival in mice bearing human tumors. We will also generate cancer cells expressing reduced levels of gp78/AMFR to test the effect of gp78/AMFR expression on tumor growth and metastasis and also for AMF-mediated tumor cell targeting. If successful, these studies will suggest that AMF is an effective delivery agent for human cancers and lead to its development for clinical application.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rôle de sFRP2 dans la régénérescence du muscle squelettique vieillissant
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTAGONISTE SFRP2; CELLULES PROGENITRICES ADULTES; FONCTION MUSCULAIRE; MODELES MURINS; MUSCLE SQUELETTIQUE; NICHE DES CELLULES SATELLITES; PROFIL D'EXPRESSION GENIQUE; PROMOTEURS ET TRANSCRIPTION DES GENES; VIEILLISSEMENT; VOIE DE SIGNALISATION WNT
Abstract-Résumé: La perte de masse musculaire chez la personne agee, communement appelee sarcopenie, se traduit par une diminution de mobilite et un risque eleve de chute et de fracture. Compte tenu de la forte croissance de la population vieillissante et des frais d'hospitalisation s'y rattachant, la comprehension des mecanismes responsable de la sarcopenie revet un caractere urgent. Une abondante litterature decrit les differences physiologiques entre les muscles d'individus jeunes et ages sans toutefois percer les mecanismes moleculaires qui en sont responsables. Nos recents travaux ont permis d'identifier differentes cibles dont une proteine clef inhibant la voie Wnt canonique. Notre hypothese de recherche est de montrer la contribution cette voie de signalisation lors du vieillissement par laquelle les cellules progenitrices perdent leur(s) propriete(s) regenerative(s). Plus specifiquement, nos travaux permettront d'identifier la contribution d'un inhibiteur naturel de cette voie sur les mecanismes regeneratifs du muscle squelettique jeune et adulte. Les resultats decoulant de cette etude permettront eventuellement de mettre en place de nouvelles strategies preventives pour ralentir la sarcopenie ce qui contribuera a ameliorer la qualite de vie d'une grande partie de la population au Canada et dans les autres pays industrialises.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving early childhood growth and development in resource-poor LMICs by incorporating deworming in integrated child health care
Keywords-MotsClés: DEWORMING; GLOBAL HEALTH; GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT; INTEGRATED HEALTH INTERVENTIONS; PRESCHOOL-AGE CHILDREN
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide, over 2 billion people suffer from worm infections in developing countries. These infections are especially damaging to the health of children, resulting in both short-term and lifelong disability. Older children with worm infections are more likely to be stunted, underweight, vulnerable to other illnesses and perform poorly in school compared to non-infected children. Large-scale deworming programs in school-age children are therefore recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). WHO also recommends deworming of preschool-age children (as of 12 months of age) in these areas; however, the benefits of deworming, especially in the 12-24 month age group, have been inadequately studied. This knowledge is urgently needed as studies show that all children have a similar potential for healthy growth and development, provided that appropriate nutrition and health interventions are given in the critical window of opportunity before the age of two.    Therefore, we are proposing to undertake a randomized controlled trial to determine the optimal deworming program for improving growth and development in children between 12 and 24 months of age. Our results will provide solid rigorous evidence on if, and when, deworming should be integrated into routine child health care packages provided by Ministries of Health in the 130 countries in the world where worm infections are endemic.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Antidepressant effects of deep brain stimulation and the serotonergic system
Keywords-MotsClés: DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; DEPRESSION; MOOD DISORDERS; SEROTONERGIC SYSTEM; SEROTONIN
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, 5-6% of the population (~1.75 million people) have symptoms consistent with depression on a yearly basis. Though most patients respond to medications and/or psychotherapy, 10-15% are considered to be resistant to treatment. For this population, surgical therapy has been proposed, including a technique called deep brain stimulation or DBS. This consists of the implantation of wires into the brain for the delivery of electrical current. Overall, 50-60% of patients undergoing DBS have a substantial improvement after surgery.  We have recently applied DBS to rats and observed a significant antidepressant effect in behavioral tests. We have also found that a molecule called serotonin was very important for the efficacy of this treatment. This is of interest as various therapies currently used in depression increase serotonin levels in the brain. In this proposal, we will address 1) how DBS given for a long period of time changes serotonin brain levels, 2) whether medications that increase serotonin levels potentiate the effects of DBS, and 3) whether mice with a specific mutation in a protein that regulates serotonin levels respond to DBS.  Results from these studies may not only increase our knowledge on the mechanisms of DBS but also provide clinical insights. As an example, we may recognize that certain changes in the systems that produce or degrade serotonin are necessary before the full clinical effects of DBS are observed. Characterizing medications that potentiate the effects of DBS may pave the way for future clinical trials using these agents in patients receiving stimulation. In the clinical scenario, 40-70% of patients with depression bear specific genetic features that resemble to some extent those in the mice to be used in our study. These patients do not respond well to some of the most commonly used antidepressant medications and DBS could be an important treatment alternative for these individuals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the role of FSH in oocyte development: an essential prerequisite to treat infertility
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTED REPRODUCTION; INFERTILITY; OOGENESIS; OVARY
Abstract-Résumé: More and more Canadian women are turning to in vitro fertilization (IVF) to help them have children, but many are frustrated by its poor success rate - only about 30%. Although women undergoing IVF cycles usually receive multiple injections of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), some researchers are now questioning whether lower doses might be better. Unfortunately, because we do not know what role FSH plays in the normal development of a healthy egg, we cannot answer the question. We will study the role of FSH using mice that are unable to produce this hormone. Our preliminary results indicate the eggs of these mice seem to develop normally, but that following fertilization they cannot develop as embryos. We will study these eggs more closely to find out what goes wrong during their development and will attempt to find conditions that will rescue them so that they can produce healthy embryos. We hope that the results will allow women to enjoy a higher rate of successful IVF without the need for stressful and costly injections of FSH and repeated trips to the hospital for egg collection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intravaginal Ring for the Prevention of HIV Transmission
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODIES; CYTOKINES; HIV / AIDS; IMMUNOTHERAPY; IN VIVO RABBIT STUDIES; INTRAVAGINAL RING; POLYMERS; PROTEIN DELIVERY; VACCINES; VIRUS NEUTRALIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Women's susceptibility to HIV infection via male-to-female transmission is in part due to the fact that current preventative methods such as abstinence, condoms, and monogamy are often outside a woman's control. As a result, there is a desperate need to develop methods which provide women-controlled prevention of HIV infection. We propose to develop a novel intravaginal delivery system which can locally induce mucosal immunity for extended periods of time. To date, there are currently no vaccines that can successfully protect an individual from HIV infection. In the case of HIV vaccines, it is ideal to elicit mucosal immunity at the site of transmission (ie. vagina). To our knowledge, there are currently no vaccines designed for local administration via the vagina and most importantly there are no studies examining the impact of sustained induction of mucosal immunity on the prevention of HIV type I infection (HIV-1). To accomplish this, we will develop a novel intravaginal ring formulation composed of medical-grade polyether urethane (PU). The inexpensive cost along with the ability to control the physical and chemical properties of the PU make it a suitable material for the delivery of proteins. We are interested in delivering the proteins gp120 (a component of the envelope glycoprotein of HIV-1) and IL-12 (cytokine used as an adjuvant) for inducing mucosal immunity. Studies have shown that administration of both gp120 and IL-12 can elicit the production of neutralizing antibodies against HIV-1. We hypothesize that by administering low, continuous doses of gp120 and IL-12 over extended periods of time (>30 days), the continuous elevated levels of mucosal antibodies will provide a more effective method of protecting against HIV-1 infection. If we are successful, this system could be a breakthrough platform for inducing mucosal immunity to a variety of sexually transmitted pathogens and could be a significant breakthrough in women's health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Duration of Changes in Intracortical Excitability and Diffusion Abnormalities after Transient Ischemic Attack
Keywords-MotsClés: MRI; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION; TRANSIENT ISCHEMIC ATTACK
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 25% of strokes are preceded by a mini-stroke, or transient ischemic attack (TIA). A TIA occurs when people experience stroke-like symptoms that rapidly disappear and the risk of future stroke after a TIA is very high. However, TIA is very difficult to accurately diagnose, since the symptoms of TIA disappear so rapidly and there are several conditions that have similar symptoms, but are not TIA (e.g., TIA-mimic). Information from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be used to help identify TIA, but only a percentage of people with TIA have abnormal MRIs. A brain stimulation technology, called Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS), provides information about the activity of different types of cells in the brain. Disruptions in brain activity have been shown to occur shortly after TIA, but it is not known whether these disruptions are related to abnormal MRIs after TIA, if these disruptions are permanent, or if they differ in people with TIA compared to people with TIA-mimic. The purposes of this study are 1) to test if disruptions in brain activity are related to abnormal MRIs after a TIA, 2) to test how long brain activity remains changed after a TIA, and 3) to test if these changes can help distinguish TIA from a TIA-mimic. We will use both TMS and MRI in individuals with TIA and TIA-mimic. Participants will complete the first session of TMS and an MRI within two weeks of their symptoms and several follow-up sessions within the following two months. This will allow us to test how long changes in brain activity last after a TIA. The results of this study will provide information about new ways to identify people at high risk of stroke and have the potential to improve stroke prevention strategies after TIA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of cerebellum cell specification, migration and organization by SUFU
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CEREBELLUM; GLI3; MALFORMATION; MOUSE MUTANTS; SONIC HEDGEHOG; SUFU
Abstract-Résumé: The cerebellum is the primary centre for motor control in the nervous system. It is composed of several different cell types, called Purkinje, granule and glial cells, each of which arises from stem-like cells in the embryo. These cells are organized into distinct layers the organization of which is critical to cerebellar function. Abnormalities in cell identity and organization are characteristic of congenital cerebellar malformations. Loss of control over granule cell number underlies medulloblastoma, the most common childhood brain cancer. Despite the importance of the cerebellum to health and disease, the mechanisms that control cerebellar cell identity, organization and number are not well defined. We are investigating how a molecule called SUFU controls how cerebellar cells establish their identity and proliferate. In non-cerebellar tissues, SUFU controls a pathway of molecules, the Hedgehog-GLI signaling pathway, that controls the number and identity of cerebellar cells, in part via the generation of a molecule called GLI3 repressor. We generated mice with SUFU deficiency in the cerebellum. These mice have abnormal gait, disruption of cerebellar structure, delayed differentiation of all cerebellar cell types, and near-absent levels of GLI3R. Remarkably, expression of GLI3R in SUFU-deficient cerebellar tissue almost totally corrects all these abnormalities. Since different types of cerebellar cells influence the behaviors of other cell types during development, we have begun to study SUFU functions in each cell type individually. Our new work using genetic mouse models and novel cell culture systems will define how SUFU and Hedgehog signaling control cell identity and will provide a basis for understanding human cerebellar diseases and developing treatments aimed at controlling abnormal cell behavior.

OrgNm: CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Jewish General/CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Hôpital juif
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; LEUCEMIES
TitreApplicationTitle: c-Abl-directed molecular re-engineering of chlorambucil to offer new therapeutic options to patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) has improved with combinations  of different drugs and antibodies, but cure of CLL remains elusive.  One of the standard drugs used in the treatment of CLL is a nitrogen mustard analogue (cyclophosphamide or chlorambucil), but resistance to these therapies develops.   My laboratory  has been investigating the mechanism of resistance to  chlorambucil in  CLL  for many years.  Our results suggest that this resistance is due to accelerated repair of  chlorambucil-induced lesions in the DNA of CLL malignant lymphocytes. Moreover, this resistance to therapy is associated with specific DNA repair systems.   In recent years, we have demonstrated that specific inhibitors of these repair systems can improve the ability of chlorambucil to kill malignant CLL lymphocytes.  One class of these inhibitors includes c-abl inhibitors such as imatinib, as well as the more potent inhibitors, nilotinib and dasatinib.  While imatinib sensitizes CLL lymphocytes to chlorambucil-mediated killing of these cells,  nilotinib and dasatinb are better sensitizers.  We have now synthesized a combi-molecule incorporating imatinib and a  chlorambucil-like moiety into one molecule called ZRF-4.  This compound is better at killing CLL lymphocytes than the individual components. We propose to:  (1)Synthesize combi-molecules incorporating  more potent c-abl inhibitors, such as  nilotinib or dasatinib-like moieties, plus a chloambucil-like moiety   (2)Compare these new combi-molecules to ZRF-4 and the individual components of each combi-molecule in their ability to kill CLL lymphocytes, as well as their effect on important signaling pathways in the CLL lymphocytes in test tubes. (3)Select promising combi-molecules for in-vivo studies in  CLL mouse models.     The best combi-molecule will be selected for clinical development.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE DE PARKINSON; MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Function of Parkinson Disease Genes in Mitochondrial Quality Control
Keywords-MotsClés: MITOCHONDRIA; NEURON; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; SIGNALING; TRAFFICKING; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects over 100,000 people in Canada and the numbers will only grow as the population ages. PD involves the death of dopamine neurons in the midbrain, which leads to devastating motor and functional impairment. Although treatment is available, its effectiveness diminishes over the long term. Hope for a more definitive treatment lies in basic biomedical research. Already, important advances have been made using molecular and genetic approaches. Not very long ago, genetics was not thought to be important in PD. However, in the past 15 years, several genes have been identified which cause familial forms of PD. My laboratory has a longstanding interest in understanding the normal function of these PD genes and how defects in the genes lead to PD. A convergence of work over the past few years has led to the discovery that mitochondria, the cell's energy power plant, are a focal point of the degenerative process in PD. The aim of this application is to decipher how the PD genes impact mitochondrial function normally and what goes wrong in disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Glia and the purinergic modulation of inspiratory rhythm generating networks
Keywords-MotsClés: GLIA; OPTOGENETICS; PURINE RECEPTOR; RESPIRATORY DISEASE; RHYTHM GENERATION; WHOLE-CELL RECORDING
Abstract-Résumé: There are two main types of cells in the central nervous system, glial cells and neurons. Until recently, glial cells were primarily considered to play a supportive role, maintaining a stable environment and supplying nutrients and essential metabolites for the neurons, which were considered to be solely responsible for the integrative, information processing functions of the brain. However, we are now learning that glial cells, which greatly outnumber neurons, can receive and send chemical signals called gliotransmitters to other glia cells and neurons and are actively involved in determining how information is processed. ATP features prominently in glial signaling. A significant challenge facing efforts to understand the functional significance of glia for neuronal networks in health and disease is the difficulty of selectively manipulating and measuring the activity of neuronal vs glial cell populations.      The aim of this proposal is to understand the respective roles of neurons and glia, and the transmitter ATP, in producing adaptive breathing responses to periods of low oxygen (hypoxia), which are common in many types of sleep-disordered breathing, and potentially life threatening in premature and newborn infants.We will apply high resolution electrophysiological, pharmacological and imaging methodologies to discretely monitor the responses of neurons and glia to specific stimuli in a region of the brain critical for generating breathing. Importantly, we will also employ novel optogenetic approaches (which combine genetic engineering with light to control specific groups of cells) to selectively activate glial cells to understand how these previously neglected cells contribute to such basic homeostatic processes. These studies will provide invaluable insight into the role of ATP signaling, neurons and glia in modulating respiratory network activity, and how these different elements might be manipulated to stimulate breathing during periods of low oxygen.

TitreApplicationTitle: Polymeric Nanospheres Designed for Targeted Delivery in Breast Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODIES; BIODEGRADABLE; BREAST CANCER; CHEMOTHERAPEUTICS; DRUG DELIVERY; ENGINEERED FABS; POLYMERIC NANOPARTICLES
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer affects 1 million women worldwide and is the leading cause of death among women due to cancer.  Of these women, 20-30% of them will have the most deadly of breast cancers, where the breast cancer cells express the human epidermal growth factor receptor, HER2.  These HER2-positive tumors can be treated with an antibody, trastuzumab, in combination with chemotherapeutic therapy; however, relapse is common, in part because the doses administered are limited by severe systemic side effects.  We have synthesized a drug delivery system designed specifically to target tumour cells for greater efficacy and decreased systemic toxicity.    The drug delivery system is comprised of an innovative polymer that self-assembles to tiny beads, called nanospheres, which are able to penetrate the leaky blood vessels that surround the tumor site.  The spherical beads themselves are composed of a non-toxic, biodegradable polymer that will dissolve over time, after releasing its payload at the targeted, cancerous tissue.  This system of localized delivery is particularly compelling for metastatic cancers where the cancerous cells have spread through the body and are not easily removed.  These nanospheres will encapsulate the potent chemotherapeutic, docetaxel, which is used clinically to treat breast cancer.  Using elegant chemistry, the nanospheres will have targeting molecules attached to their outer shell such that once they accumulate at the tumour site, they will selectively bind with and kill the tumour cells.    Our team has the complementary expertise required for success in the complex race to overcome cancer.  By combining novel bioengineering strategies with innovative targeting ligands and fundamental pharmacodynamics, the team will provide a superb environment for training of HQP while advancing knowledge to practical application.  Ultimately, we aim to defeat cancer.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Point of care diagnostic and analytical metabolomic testing.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL CHEMISTRY; CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS; DIAGNOSTICS; INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY; MASS SPECTROMETRY; METABOLOMICS; MICROFLUIDICS; MULTIVARIATE ANALYSIS; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; POINT OF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Blood and urine tests are the front line in screening and diagnosis of disease. For example they are used to help diagnose diabetes and to monitor its treatment (blood glucose testing). They are also used to identify people most likely to develop heart disease (cholesterol testing). The main purpose of this proposal is to develop new tests that would benefit two large groups of patients through more rapid and accurate diagnosis. Such tests could also save the Canadian health care system an enormous amount of money.  The first test would provide rapid diagnosis of the 800,000 Canadians who visit hospitals every year with chest pain. There is no fast way to rule out heart attacks in the 90% of patients whose EKG's are inconclusive. A large fraction of them (typically 70%) are admitted to the hospital for tests that can take several hours or days to confirm a heart attack. More than half will ultimately be discharged with heart attack ruled out. The new test would quickly rule out heart attacks in these individuals and allow their rapid discharge from hospital. Cost savings would be $2,000 per patient, or $600,000,000 annually in Canada alone. Equally important would be faster treatment for those who require it, sparing the loss of heart function - or worse - associated with treatment delays or misdiagnosis.  The second test would benefit patients with chronic kidney disease by forecasting the rate at which their disease would progress if untreated. The test result would be used to trigger aggressive preventive therapy for those patients who would otherwise deteriorate rapidly, and spare such interventions for those (the majority) who remain clinically stable. Discovery of such a test has been declared by the U.S. National Kidney Foundation to be the most urgent priority in chronic kidney disease research. The potential impact can be appreciated by estimates that up to 10% of the general population suffer from chronic kidney disease.

CommitteeNameEN: Social & Developmental Aspects of Children's & Youth's Health
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional neuroimaging, cognitive testing and postural stability assessment in children with mild traumatic brain injury
Keywords-MotsClés: BALANCE AND POSTURE; CHILD HEALTH; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MILD TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY; NEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL TESTING; PAEDIATRIC; POST CONCUSSION SYMPTOMS; RECOVERY; VOXEL-BASED MORPHOMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last decade, awareness of the problems associated with mild traumatic brain injury (MTBI) in children has grown significantly. Although cognitive, behavioural and physical symptoms are reported by the families as well as by the children with mTBI, the results of conventional clinical tests are often negative making their sensitivity questionable. Clinical studies by our team have revealed that children can present with balance and visual perceptual deficits after a MTBI in addition to decreased self confidence at the time of returning to regular activities. Attempts to link these deficits to the results of the imaging examinations have up to now failed. In the first part of the present study, we will ask children with and without a MTBI to perform memory tasks while undergoing a functional magnetic resonance imaging test. This procedure will allow us to examine each subject's brain in activity while they are performing the task. We will also evaluate balance, overall cognitive abilities and variables pertaining to the trauma (severity scores, duration of loss of consciousness, duration of post-traumatic amnesia, characteristics of the head injury sustained). In the second part of the study, one month later, we will reexamine brain function of those children who did not recover from the MTBI with the aim to compare to those who recuperated. We will then be able to compare each profile to its own obtained immediately after the trauma. We believe this study has the potential to provide a powerful diagnostic and prognostic method to document the degree of disability and recovery in children having sustained a mild head injury.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - A: Reproduction, Maternal, Child and Youth Health
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms underlying the in utero origins of hypercholesterolemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CHOLESTEROL; CHOMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION (CHIP); EPIGENETICS; FETAL PROGRAMMING; INTERVENTION STUDY; LIVER; LIVER X RECEPTOR (LXR); NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; POSTTRANSLATIONAL HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; SEXUAL DIMORPHISM
Abstract-Résumé: While genetics,lifestyle, and diet contribute to the development of impaired liver function, elevated cholesterol, and cardiovascular disease (CVD), emerging epidemiological evidence also suggests that these abnormalities are also inversely related to impaired birth weight as a result of an adverse in utero environment. This can include under nutrition in pregnancy. Understanding the overall role of transcription factors in mediating these developmental events would provide us with a better understanding of the mechanisms controlling normal and abnormal liver development and cholesterol homeostasis. In this proposal, we will use a 'candidate transcription factor' approach to examine the role of one lipid-sensing nuclear receptor, the Liver X Receptor (LXR), in an intrauterine model of protein restriction in rats, which leads to impaired birth weight and offspring growth, decreased liver to body weight ratio, and augmented circulating cholesterol. With this model, we plan to examine how the timing in protein restoration and/or LXR agonists in early postnatal life could diminish the long-term adverse effects leading to hypercholesterolemia.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms regulating the outgrowth of initiated cells in the mammal
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER INITIATION; CELL COMPETITION; CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUTS; E2F; HIPPO/WARTS PATHWAY; NEUROGENESIS; P107; RB
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer arises when a cell acquires a gene defect that allows it to grow abnormally. The mutant cell divides to produce more mutants increasing the chance of a cell acquiring a second defect, making it more aggressive. This process can continue until a lethal tumor arises.  Few models exist to study the early events that trigger the whole process.  We developed such a system to study retinoblastoma, a childhood cancer that arises from mutant cells in the embryonic retina.  We found that a mutant cell starts to generate more cells than normal cells, yet strikingly mutants are pruned to normal numbers through cell death.  Yet the cell types preserved include an excess of one type thought to give rise to retinoblastoma.  Thus, while there are constraints on abnormal growth, they carry risk.  Our goal is to understand where the constraints emanate from, and to define the changes that allow cancer to emerge.  Work in fruit flies suggests that mutant and normal cells compete for survival.  To test whether normal cells block mutant cell expansion we will ask if a mutant cell grows better amid mutant cells.  To test the function of cell death in sculpting groups of mutant cells we will block the process.  Third, we showed that the protein E2f1 is required to drive division, death and cell type changes in mutant cells.  We will examine if E2f1 uses distinct or common molecular activities to drive these effects.  Finally, the Hippo pathway is critical to limit mutant clones in fruit flies and is important in human cancers.  We have evidence that it may regulate the early stages of retinoblastoma.  We will ask whether perturbing or enhancing this pathway's activity helps or hinders the growth of mutant cells.  Understanding the early stages of mutant cell growth in a mammalian context is critical to develop new ways to detect cancer sooner and to prevent and treat the disease.

Understanding the early stages of mutant cell growth in a mammalian context is critical to develop new ways to detect cancer sooner and to prevent and treat the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: CAR-engineered CD4+ T cells for tumor immunotherapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CD4+ T CELLS; CHIMERIC ANTIGEN RECEPTORS; GENE TRANSFER; MELANOMA; ONCOLYTIC VIRUSES
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic methods will be used to direct white blood cells against targets that are present on tumors. This strategy allows scientists to harness the robust tumor-fighting properties of white blood cells and direct them selectively against the tumor.  Given the power of the white blood cells, there is some concern of that the white blood cells may also attack healthy tissues.  We have developed a novel method that produces a white blood cell which selectively attacks tumor tissue while leaving healthy tissue unaffected. We propose to use the funds provided by this grant to confirm our new technology with the intention of moving it into clinical trial. We also propose to investigate the outcome of combining our white blood cell therapy with a novel class of specially-modified viruses which selectively infect and kill tumors.  The combined treatment is expected to provide a powerful immune stimulation that will provide long-term control of future tumor outgrowth.  Our research program employs cutting-edge technologies that are unique in Canada and offers an excellent opportunity for training young scientists.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of the role of genetically-defined interneurons in the operation of the locomotor CPG.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTEROGRADE TRACING; INTERNEURON; INTRACELLULAR RECORDING; LOCOMOTION; SPINAL CORD
Abstract-Résumé: Neural networks located entirely within the spinal cord are responsible for generating much of the timing and pattern of muscle activation required for locomotor movements. These neural networks are known as central pattern generators (CPGs) and are composed of multiple interneuron cell types. Little is known about the structure or mechanism of function of the locomotor CPG in walking mammals, primarily because of our inability to identify their intrinsic interneuronal components. Recently, a genetic approach has been used to identify distinct populations of interneurons in the spinal cord based on transcription factor expression. Preliminary work has shown that some of these populations comprise essential components of the locomotor CPG. Work in my laboratory will use this approach to characterize and assess the function of a specific interneuronal population that we believe to be important for locomotor rhythm generation. These studies will help us to understand how locomotor CPGs are assembled and function and may help to devise therapies aimed at enhancing functional recovery of movement after spinal cord injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining Myt3's role in beta-cell maturation, function and inflammatory response.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; DIABETES; GENE REGULATION; GLUCOSE-STIMULATED INSULIN SECRETION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 Diabetes is an autoimmune disease caused by a patients own immune cells killing the insulin producing cells in the body. This life-long disease typically occurs in children and is a major health concern in Canada. The transplantation of donor islets can cure patients with Type 1 diabetes; however, the recipient needs to take immunosuppressive drugs that have serious side effects, and the transplanted islets typically fail within a few years. A great deal remains unknown about how and why immune cells kill the insulin-secreting cells in patients with Type 1 Diabetes, and a better understanding of these processes is essential for developing a cure for this disease. When immune cells start to kill insulin-secreting cells the genes expressed within the insulin-secreting cells change dramatically. For example, we have identified a gene, called Myt3, whose expression is dramatically lowered in insulin-secreting cells when immune cells attack. Interestingly, Myt3 is almost exclusively expressed in the body's insulin-secreting cells, and is a member of a family of genes called transcription factors that are master regulators of gene expression.  We have shown that reducing Myt3 expression causes insulin-secreting cells to stop producing insulin efficiently, and to start to die. Based on our research thus far, we believe that Myt3 regulates genes that control insulin production and secretion, while at the same time preventing the expression of genes that induce insulin-secreting cells to die.  We propose that by preventing immune cells from reducing Myt3 expression we can improve the number of healthy functional insulin-secreting cells in patients with Type 1 Diabetes. The work in this grant is aimed at testing these hypotheses. We believe that this will bring us one step closer to a cure for Type 1 Diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dose dependent role of Gfi1 in the initiation and maintenance of T-cell leukemia and lymphoma
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHROMATIN; HEMATOPOIESIS; PROTEIN COMPLEXES; TRANSCRIPTION; ZINC FINGER DOMAINS
Abstract-Résumé: Many patients with blood cancer die despite intensive chemotherapy. One particular subtype of blood cancer is called T-cell Acute lymphoblastic leukemia and is one the most common forms of cancer in children. Leukemia usually arises, when the genetic system controlling normal blood forming cells in the bone marrow is not working properly and these cells become cancer cells. This cancer cells then multiply in an uncontrolled manner, enter the bloodstream and cause leukemia with the consequence that the function of the red blood cells (oxygen transport) and the white blood cells (immune defense) are compromised leading to a severe illness and death. Different causes have been described for leukemia, one is the malfunction of a protein called Notch1 caused by a mutation in the Notch1 gene. We have observed that another regulatory protein called Gfi1 can influence the function of Notch1 and we found that if we turn the Gfi1 gene off in a mouse, the mutated form of Notch is no longer able to cause leukemia in this animal. Moreover, if the Gfi1 gene is turned off in a mouse that already has leukemia, the cancer shrinks and disappears. In addition we have also found that if the Gfi1 gene is not completely switched off but just turned down the development of leukemia in our mouse models is markedly accelerated. We conclude that blood cancer cells need the Gfi1 gene and without Gfi1 they cannot proliferate and cause the leukemia, but rather regress and die off. However, we must also conclude that cancer cells develop fastest into a very aggressive form when they have reduced Gfi1 gene activity. In the present study, We wish to investigate the mechanisms that are responsible for these functions of Gfi1 in more detail. The result of this work would enable us to design a therapy, which would involve the elimination of Gfi1 in cancer cells with the final objective to improve therapy in leukemia patients

TitreApplicationTitle: Therapeutic potential of surfactant protein D (SP-D): Enhancing neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) function and subsequent NET-immune complex clearance by macrophages
Keywords-MotsClés: INNATE IMMUNITY; LUNG INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGES; MICROBIAL INFECTION; MOUSE MODELS; NETS; NEUTROPHIL EXTRACELLULAR TRAP; RECOMBINANT PROTEIN; SURFACTANT PROTEINS A AND D; THERAPEUTIC MOLECULE; THERAPEUTIC POTENTIAL
Abstract-Résumé: .           Bacterial infections of the airways cause severe sickness and death in children and immunocompromised individuals. A large proportion of healthcare dollars (~6.5%; $12 billion/year) is used for treating respiratory diseases in Canada. We face challenges in successfully treating many of these diseases due to the emergence of drug-resistant pathogens and the side effects of synthetic drugs. An antibody-like immune protein (pulmonary surfactant protein D or SP-D) has the potential to become an important therapeutic molecule in treating some of these diseases. SP-D binds, clumps and kills germs for effective killing and clearance by white blood cells.             Recent studies show that one of the important white blood cells (neutrophils) die by a unique suicidal death. This process leads to neutrophil extracellular trap or NET formation. Literally, NETs are physical nets formed by toxic material-coated DNA threads of suicidal neutrophils. NETs catch and kill germs.            We have previously reported that SP-D binds DNA very well. We believe that SP-D will catch the germs and stick them to NET DNA for effective trapping. Our new data indeed suggest that SP-D binds bacteria and NET DNA at the same time. We have also identified that SP-D could recognize alpha-2-macroglobulin, a surface receptor (anchor)-binding protein (similar to the Venus fly trap).  We hope to use this data to figure out new ways to treat lung infections.            In summary, the overall objective of this study is to establish how SP-D eliminates germs and dying immune cells while maintaining minimal lung inflammation. This knowledge is essential for establishing the therapeutic potential of SP-D in treating or preventing many infectious and specific inflammatory lung diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Placental mesenchymal stem cells in regenerative therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; CEREBRAL ISCHEMIA; DIABETES; INSULIN-LIKE GROWTH FACTORS; MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS; PLACENTA; REGENERATIVE THERAPY; TISSUE ENVIRONMENT; TUMORIGENESIS; UMBILICAL CORD BLOOD
Abstract-Résumé: Insulin-like growth factors are the most prevalent and important growth factors that are synthesized by the developing embryo at the earliest stages of development when stem cells are dividing (self-renewing) or forming specific cell types (differentiating). This study proposes to investigate the mechanisms by which insulin-like growth factors regulate the processes of self-renewing or differentiating into specific tissues via different intracellular signaling pathways in stem cells derived from the placenta. This information will be crucial in establishing conditions of culture of placental stem cells in serum free conditions for in vivo regenerative therapies and prevent these cells from forming cancer cells within the recipients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sustainability of a multidimensional knowledge translation intervention to improve paediatric pain practices and outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PAIN; SUSTAINABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Recent studies show that hospitalized children undergo many painful procedures such as heel lances and finger pricks daily. Although there has been some improvement in pain management over the past two decades, regular pain assessment and management remains sub-optimal. The main issue is that the knowledge from research on pain in children has not been effectively translated into every day clinical practice. The CIHR Team in Children's Pain (Stevens et al, 2006-2011) is currently evaluating the effectiveness of a 2-year multidimensional knowledge translation (KT) intervention, Evidence Based Practice for Improving Quality (EPIQ), to improve pain practices and clinical outcomes across 8 Canadian paediatric centres. We have made important advances in improving pain practice changes through EPIQ; however, we have little knowledge about the sustainability of practice changes or individual or organization factors influencing sustainability over time. In this grant we propose to: 1) compare the sustainability of pain practices of the EPIQ units who receive a practice change booster with units who receive standard care; and 2) to explore factors that could influence sustainability of practice changes over time.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian fathering and child unintentional injury prevention
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD INJURY PREVENTION; FATHERS; GENDER; MASCULINITY; QUALITATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Unintentional injuries, such as car crashes and falls, are the leading health concern - more Canadian children and youth die of injuries than from all other causes combined. Gender and geography have a significant impact on injury rates, with males and rural residents at greater risk. Parents play a large role in limiting children's injury risks. Fathers and mothers parenting roles are different in ways that may influence their attitudes and practices regarding child injury prevention. For example, fathers may allow children to engage in activities that mothers may consider dangerous. Fathers' unique role in encouraging exploration and risk taking requires investigation. Fathering is impacted by notions of masculinity, which is in turn influenced by broader contexts such as geography, society, and family. Our research questions address how fathering as it relates to childhood unintentional injury prevention is influenced by perceptions of masculinity, gender roles and contextual factors. We will be interviewing fathers and mothers of children aged 2 to 7 years to better understand fathering related to child unintentional injury prevention. The places we will be studying include rural and urban areas in British Columbia and Quebec. The results will help build theory, and guide research and prevention efforts. Findings will be applied to parenting programs, will help target prevention efforts and develop evidence-based policies and programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Arf-dependent traffic to and through the Golgi complex
Keywords-MotsClés: ARF GTPASES; GOLGI COMPLEX; IMMUNO-FLUORESCENCE; LIVE IMAGING; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN TRAFFIC
Abstract-Résumé: Human cells contain a variety of compartments with specialized functions.  Some like the nucleus store genetic information while others generate energy.  This application concerns a set of such compartments implicated in the modification, sorting and delivery of various cargoes both within the cell, as well as to and from the cell surface. Carriers that often appear as small spheres, or vesicles, move important cargoes with great precision between these various compartments.  The Golgi, like a hub or airport, lies at the center of this network and acts as a central sorting station. Nearly a third of proteins encoded by the human genome must pass through this hub for important modification and sorting to their ultimate destination. Therefore, mutations that compromise this process often cause disease or are sometimes lethal. Furthermore, many human pathogens hijack this pathway to ensure successful infection. Formation of carrier vesicles is mediated by the recruitment of proteins that form coats on flat membranes and facilitate their deformation into vesicles. A group of proteins called Arfs control assembly of these coats (the ground crew at the airport), while GEF proteins activate Arfs and regulate this process (air traffic controllers). Together, these proteins provide the necessary regulatory mechanism required for protein traffic and maintenance of the Golgi. While much research has focused on the Golgi, many aspects of how Arfs and GEFs perform their central roles remains unclear.  Here we propose to identify the specific function of several type of Arfs and GEFs to better define their unique contribution to protein traffic. Our approach to tease these complex pathways apart relies heavily on microscopy and expression of fluorescent proteins in animal cells. Using live cell imaging we examine how each of these proteins is recruited to unique sites of action and thereby maintains the intricate organization/function of the Golgi and associated compartments.

TitreApplicationTitle: RAD Study Phase 2: Validation of the Canadian HF and COPD Risk Scores for Respiratory Distress in the Emergency Department
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; CLINICAL DECISION RULES; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; HEART FAILURE; HOSPITAL ADMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: Shortness of breath is a common problem in the emergency department (ED) and is associated with important conditions like heart failure (HF) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). These conditions have high rates of death and serious outcomes, particularly in older patients who often require hospital admission. Because there is a significant shortage of hospital beds, physicians in Canadian EDs are under great pressure to send home HF and COPD patients. Many such patients discharged from the ED suffer poor outcomes or return to the ED and require admission. Hence, the decision to admit or discharge a patient from the ED is very important. There is, however, little evidence to guide decisions on patient admission. In our CIHR-funded RAD Study Phase 1, using careful data collection and statistical analysis of 1,500 patients, we developed risk scoring systems to predict poor outcomes. These Canadian HF and COPD Risk Scales, consisting of 10 clinical findings each, will allow physicians to estimate the risk for poor outcomes as high, medium, or low and to make better admission decisions. The HF and COPD Risk Scales must now be tested in new patient populations before they can be applied in clinical practice.   There are two goals for this renewal application (RAD-2 Study). First, we wish to prospectively test the accuracy, reliability, and acceptability of the HF and COPD Risk Scales in ED patients. Second, we wish to evaluate in detail the safety of current admission practices. This study will take place in the EDs of five Canadian hospitals and involve 2,500 adults aged > 50 years, who are diagnosed with HF or COPD. Patients will be assessed for the two new scoring systems as well as for standardized clinical and laboratory variables. We expect these guidelines, once tested, will be widely used and will improve and standardize admission practices for these patients, diminishing both unnecessary admissions as well as unsafe discharge decisions.
