TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of human embryonic stem cell- and adult pancreatic multipotent precursor-derived beta cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT PANCREATIC DERIVED STEM CELLS; BETA CELLS; GENE ARRAY; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; HUMAN EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; INSULIN SECRETION; ISLET; PROTEOMICS; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 diabetes is a devastating disease that causes reduced quality and length of life in humans. Treatments that aim to correct the loss of insulin-secreting pancreatic beta cells in type 1 diabetes traditionally involve multiple daily injections of insulin and recently transplantation of cells from donors. However, both regimens have their drawbacks as they are invasive and supply of donor tissue is limited. Therefore the generation of beta cells from human stem cells from either embryonic or adult tissue, represents a potentially unlimited supply of beta cells to treat this debilitating disease. Our collaborators have successfully generated beta-like cells from human embryonic and adult human pancreatic tissue but these cells have yet to be fully characterised for their insulin secreting potential. Therefore, this grant aims to determine the expression profile of hormones, including insulin, in these two stem cell populations and see whether they secrete insulin normally when stimulated with glucose. Beta cells contain very specialised glucose sensing machinery within them and we propose to establish which parts of this machinery are defective in the stem cell-derived beta cells. Finally we will examine the pattern of genes and proteins that are expressed in pure populations of stem cell-derived beta cells. The information gained from these studies will help to generate strategies to improve the production of beta cells from different sources of stem cells to be used in the treatment of type 1 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing risk with E-based support for Adherence to lifestyle Change in Hypertension: REACH
Keywords-MotsClés: DIETARY SALT RESTRICTION; EXERCISE; HYPERTENSION; INTERNET; LIFESTYLE COUNSELLING
Abstract-Résumé: Population research indicates that 21% of Canadian adults are diagnosed with clinically high blood pressure (hypertension). Community-based programs that provide lifestyle counseling significantly reduce blood pressure and the risk for cardiovascular disease. However, a major challenge for these programs is to extend lifestyle counseling, to persons with hypertension or high risk for cardiovascular events, without burdening available resources. Internet programs of preventive e-counseling may be well-suited to meet this challenge.   This proposed clinical trial builds upon the findings of 2 previous trials by our team. In COHRT, we reported short-term improvements in blood pressure and self-reported diet and exercise following preventive telehealth counseling for persons at high risk for cardiovascular disease. In I-START, short-term improvements in blood pressure and self-reported exercise and diet were associated with preventive e-counseling for subjects with hypertension.  This proposed clinical trial, REACH, will enroll 624 persons with hypertension. All subjects will continue with their prescribed medications. Our main objective is to assess whether  preventive e-counseling (provided through a website of the Heart and Stroke Foundation) improves blood pressure and lifestyle behaviors over a long-term, 12-month interval. REACH will also evaluate improvement in lifestyle behaviors (diet, exercise, smoking, and compliance to prescribed medications) using objective and validated measures. Finally, we will quantify the amount of e-counseling support that is required during REACH to evoke a significant reduction in blood pressure.   The findings of this trial will provide information that is critical to our understanding of how internet-based programs can help to improve blood pressure and to reduce the risk for cardiovascular disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurovascular Adaptation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; BIOPHYSICAL MODELLING; IMAGE ANALYSIS; INTRAVITAL TWO-PHOTON CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MICROCIRCULATION; MOUSE
Abstract-Résumé: The brain responds to not receiving an adequate supply of oxygen by growing more of the small blood vessels that permeate all brain tissue. This process of adding new blood vessels can be induced by prolonged intense exercise or exposure to high altitude (low oxygen) environments. In disorders such as stroke and traumatic brain injury, growth of new blood vessels is considered critical to recovery; whereas in Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia, new vessels either do not grow or grow abnormally. A challenge of understanding how growth of new vessels affects health is that blood vessels are all connected. This means that adding a new vessel affects the whole blood vessel network and that not all such additions improve the delivery of oxygen. This is further complicated by the ability of existing vessel to grow, shrink, or even split in two. The goal of the present proposal is to understand how structural changes in the vessel network of the brain lead to improvements in blood and oxygen delivery. This question will be addressed by experiments using advanced 3D imaging techniques that can visualize the changing blood vessels within the brains of mice that complete a regime of voluntary exercise. The response of the healthy brain to exercise will be contrasted against that of animals where sprouting of new blood vessels has been impaired by drug treatments and to mice that show a form of Alzheimer's disease. Taken together these experiments will interrogate the mechanisms by which structural changes in the blood vessel network support the survival of brain tissue in health and disease. Understanding the mechanisms by which a network of blood vessels is reorganized with corresponding gains or loses in capacity to deliver blood is critical to treating the many disorders where this reorganization plays a crucial role.

TitreApplicationTitle: Food intake control in children
Keywords-MotsClés: APPETITE REGULATION; BODY COMPOSITION; CHILDHOOD OBESITY; FOOD INTAKE; GASTROINTESTINAL HORMONES; GLUCOSE SATIETY
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity among children has increased dramatically in the past 15 years. Obesity in childhood predicts obesity and chronic diseases such as heart disease and diabletes in adulthood.  A vulnerable time in the setting of systems controlling appetite and eating behaviours and risk of obesity is during the ages of 9-14 when many physiological and social factors impact on the development of eating behavour and appetite control.  The goal of this research is to understand the physiological and environmental forces that contribute to a life-long habit of overeating. The subjects will be 9-14 year old normal weight, over weight and obese boys and girls. Their food intake at test meals will be measured after exercise, TV watching, stress, protein and sugar drinks and other beverages, foods/snacks and at different stages of puberty.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mitigation of Radiation-Induced Lung Damage.
Keywords-MotsClés: LUNG SPECIFIC STEM CELLS; PROTECTORS/MITIGATORS OF DAMAGE; RADIATION PNEUMONITIS; RADIATION-INDUCED FIBROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Radiation-induced lung injury (pneumonitis and fibrosis) is a potentially serious and dose-limiting complication following conventional radiation therapy (RT) for thoracic cancers. The mechanisms involved in the initiation and perpetuation of such injury are poorly understood. The current project will use mouse models to investigate three new approaches to protecting/mitigating against radiation-induced lung injury without affecting the response of thoracic cancers. The first two approaches will address the development of radiation-induced fibrosis. These studies will focus on blocking the activity of specific proteins which appear to be involved in the development of radiation-induced fibrosis in other tissues and in the development of lung fibrosis following other types of damage. The third approach will examine whether transplanting specific lung precursor cells (derived from the bone marrow) into irradiated lungs can protect against the development of pneumonitis and fibrosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of Microtubule Architecture by Doublecortin
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICS; CORTEX; DOUBLECORTIN; LISSENCEPHALY; MICROTUBULE; NEURON; NUCLEATION; SINGLE MOLECULE
Abstract-Résumé: The outermost layer of the brain, just below the skull, is the cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex is the seat of our intellect, and in healthy people it has many deep folds. In unfortunate cases, however, a genetic mutation causes a loss of these folds, a disease known as "smooth brain," or lissencephaly. The mutations occur in a protein called doublecortin (DCX). DCX works inside of brain cells, or neurons, to control where neurons are located in the brain and how neurons connect to one another. In humans with DCX mutations, neurons are not located properly in the brain and do not make correct connections, causing mental retardation and epilepsy. We know that DCX works by controlling the shape of the "cytoskeleton," a scaffolding system inside of cells that give them structure, much like the scaffolds used at construction sites. The goal of this grant is to understand precisely how DCX controls the shape of the cytoskeleton and to explain why DCX mutations cause disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the Inhibitors of Apoptosis (IAPs) in cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ABLATION; ANTAGONISTS; CANCER; CASPASES; INHIBITORS OF APOPTOSIS (IAPS); MECHANISM; PROTEASOME DEGRADATION; SIGNALING; THERAPY; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Our research program involves the study of apoptosis and its relevance to cancer progression and therapy.  Apoptosis is a normal process by which cells initiate a genetic program to commit cell death.  Apoptosis can contribute to the development of many diseases, including AIDS, diabetes, blindness, muscular dystrophy, neurodegeneration and cancer.  Inducing cancer cells to die is a major goal of cancer therapy.  However, cancer cells often become resistant to therapy and apoptosis, eventually leading to patient relapse and morbidity.  We have identified a family of several highly conserved mammalian genes called the IAPs, for Inhibitors of Apoptosis, which are now well-established oncogenes, biomarkers and cancer drug targets. A major focus of our research is to study the regulation of the IAPs and their protein products, and to investigate their role in apoptosis in normal and cancer cells. We plan to study the specific cellular signaling pathways that affect IAP expression and function, as well as the pathways affected by small molecule drugs that antagonize IAP function. We will investigate how the IAPs interact with one another and with other cellular partners, as well as with IAP antagonists.  The study of IAP mechanism of action will allow us to gain a better understanding of how these proteins promote cancer and induce resistance to therapy.  In addition, our studies will allow for the design, refinement and implementation of novel therapeutic approaches for the treatment of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fetal Origin of Endocrine Dysfunction: The Phthalate Model
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRENAL FUNCTION; ENDOCRINE DISRUPTORS; ENVIRONMENTAL EXPOSURES; EPIGENETICS; HYPOGONADISM; METABOLIC SYNDROME; STEROID BIOSYNTHESIS; TESTICULAR FUNCTION; TRANSCRIPTION REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Epidemiological and experimental studies suggest that disruption of embryonic programming and fetal gonadal development can result in undescended testis, hypospadias, poor semen quality, or testicular cancer. Among these conditions, some appear only later in life. Phthalates are plasticizers that are ubiquitously found in the environment and shown to alter male sexual organ development and to decrease testosterone production in the fetus. Di-(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) is among the most prevalent of the plasticizers, and its active metabolites are present from fetal development to adulthood. In men, there is an inverse correlation between DEHP metabolites and circulating androgen levels. In rats, we have shown that fetal exposure to DEHP results in reduced circulating testosterone and aldosterone levels in the adult offspring. It is our hypothesis that in utero exposure of rats to DEHP leads to changes in testis and adrenal function, and that it is the interaction of the testes and adrenals in the adult that results in reduced testicular testosterone production. Using a combination of in vivo, ex vivo and in vitro experiments together with morphological, biochemical, pharmacological, genetic and epigenetic tools, we propose to determine the endocrine and metabolic changes occurring in the adult male following in utero exposure to environmentally relevant concentrations of DEHP, and to identify the mechanisms underlying the long-term effects of DEHP exposure leading to inhibition of steroid biosynthesis. Reduced testosterone (primary hypogonadism) has been linked to infertility, erectile dysfunction, obesity, osteoporosis and cardiovascular diseases. Moreover, changes in adrenal function could lead to changes in blood pressure, a common disease for which the origins remain unknown in most cases. It is critical to determine whether exposure to a highly prevalent environmental toxicant such as DEHP could be a risk factor in the origin of these disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nox homologues, redox signaling and vascular biology in hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL PHYSIOLOGY; FREE RADICAL; HYPERTENSION; MOLECULAR AND CELL BIOLOGY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; REMODELING
Abstract-Résumé: High blood pressure (hypertension) affects 30% of adult North Americans, is the most frequent reason for consultation of family physicians in Canada and is the leading cause of heart disease, kidney failure and stroke worldwide. Despite the fact that this condition is so common and is a major killer, we still do not know exactly what causes high blood pressure.  Factors that have been suggested include increased production in the body of free radicals, called reactive oxygen species. High levels of free radicals cause damage to blood vessels, the heart, brain and kidneys and could promote an increase in blood pressure. Processes responsible for increased production of dangerous free radicals are unclear, but special proteins, called Noxs, may be important. The present proposal will focus on understanding how Noxs are regulated, how they produce free radicals in vessels and how they can contribute to blood pressure elevation. The clinical significance of our studies relates to the fact that these Noxs may be important targets for new therapies. In fact, there are a number of biotech companies in Japan and Switzerland, which are actively developing inhibitors of Noxs for the treatment of hypertension. By learning more about the Nox system through research, such as that supported here by the CIHR, new and better drugs and strategies for treating, and perhaps even preventing, hypertension may be developed. Considering that hypertension is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in Canada, this would impact significantly on the overall well-being and health of the Canadian population at large.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of genome mutators governing adaptive immunity and lymphomagenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; DNA MUTATIONS; ENZYMES; IMMUNE SYSTEM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: A unique way that the body enhances immunity to pathogens is through introducing subtle changes at the genetic level in some cells of the immune system.  B cells are the white blood cells which produce antibodies necessary to neutralize pathogens and toxins.  The genetic changes in B cells are carried out by Activation induced cytidine deaminase (AID), an enzyme that makes changes to the antibody genes, leading to the production of stronger and better antibodies. Overall, genetic alterations are an effective means to boost immunity, with the caveat that these processes are not perfect and can be misdirected to the wrong genes.  Such unwanted genetic changes have been shown to be a leading cause of cancers of immune cells, namely lymphoma/leukemia.  Thus, these processes are a double-edged sword. The focus of my research is to understand the mechanisms of processes which introduce genetic changes in the immune system, the facets through which they modulate immunity, and how they are regulated and targeted to certain genes. These studies are essential in order to understand how a system that is there to help immunity can actually result in the generation of cancer. Our results and future studies outlined in this proposal have direct implications on strategies for treatment of leukemia/lymphomas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study of the pathophysiology of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: NEPHROTIC SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome (INS) is an immune-mediated disease that targets the kidney. At present, there is no murine model and no cellular in vitro model suitable for the study of INS mechanisms. We have succeeded in developing a new murine model of the disease by injecting immunocompromised mice with patients' cells. By analyzing this new models, we could develop in vitro condition with patients cells in which the supernatant of the culture could induce proteinuria when injected to mice. Our objective is to use this new in vitro model to precisely identify and characterize the responsible cells and to identify the factor that is present in the supernatant that is responsible for proteinuria. These advances would constitute a major progress in the understanding of the physiopathological mechanisms of INS.  Moreover, this could provide a solid basis for the implementation of innovative therapeutic strategies for this disease, that has so far been extremely frustrating from a therapeutic point of view.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Immunology and Neuroscience of Diabetes Mellitus.
Keywords-MotsClés: B6 MOUSE & CONGENICS; DIET INDUCED OBESITY (DIO); NOD MOUSE; PRIMARY SENSORY AFFERENT NEURONS; T1D & T2D PATIENTS; TRPV1; TRPV1 ALLELIC VARIANTS; TYPE 1 DIABETES (T1D); TYPE 2 DIABETES (T2D); VISCERAL FAT-RESIDENT LYMPHOCYTES
Abstract-Résumé: Lay abstract: This proposal continues a research program focused on neuronal and immunological elements of Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) and since expanded to Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) and Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Based by now on four published high-profile CELL and Nature Medicine papers, two more in the review process at Nature-type journals. Our publications gathered >400 citations over the last granting period and altered our views of T1D, T2D and MS. The program is based on our recent discovery of neuronal targets of T1D, with a major role for sensory afferent neurons in the initiation and progression of NOD mouse T1D: these papers were funded by CIHR. The present application is to fund the next logical research steps in the decade of program evolution, stud-ies aimed to mechanistically define new therapeutic strategies in T1D and T2D rodent models, and human pre-clinical studies to begin the process of translating our findings to the human system. In T1D, we aim to reverse new onset diabetes and re-establish normal, physiological insulin/glucose homeostasis with exogenous insulin. We establish neuropeptide deficiency as a fundamental T1D abnormality, our new strategies aim to up-regulate endogenous neuropeptide secretion in the pancreas. Insulin overproduction, insulin resistance and glucose intolerance are, in our view, the disease-driving abnormalities for both, T1D & T2D, both have secondary, but major immune elements that drive disease progression, and, it now appears, both can respond to the nervous system thera-peutic targets discovered in this program and pursued with sophisticated, tried experimental tools that already have begun expanding into the human system as necessary preludes to translation of these treatment strategies to our patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathways of lipid antigen presentation in B cells
Keywords-MotsClés: APOE; APOLIPOPROTEINS; B CELLS; CD1; LDL-R; NKT CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: B cells are the antibody producing cells of the immune system and require "help" from other cells in order to generate a productive antibody response. This help classically comes from T cells, which must recognize peptides presented by the B cells.  It has recently been found that another class of T cells exist called NKT cells that are innate-like T cells which, instead of recognizing peptides, recognize lipid antigens. We will explore how B cells can present lipid antigens to NKT cells and how this affects B cell function. We will follow up on our previous work which demonstrated the role of lipid transport molecule, apoE, and its receptor, LDL-R in lipid presentation. This lipid transport has not been explored in B cells, and we will determine the requirements for these molecules in allowing B cells to present lipids to NKT cells, a process which we call "innate help". The work will improve our understanding of how B cells function and allow us to enhance immune responses to vaccines or prevent autoimmune responses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing treatment outcomes for women with stress urinary incontinence through the identification of factors contributing to successful interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; PELVIC FLOOR MUSCLES; PHYSIOTHERAPY; STRESS URINARY INCONTINENCE; TRANSVAGINAL TAPE; ULTRASOUND IMAGING; URODYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Urinary incontinence (UI) affects up to 50% of adult populations and stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is the most common form of UI, accounting for approximately 60% of patients.  Women are affected by SUI much more often than men.  Urine leakage in women with SUI occurs on exertion or during tasks that increase pressure on the bladder such as sneezing or coughing. SUI has been shown to be a barrier to physical activity in women, and as such can contribute to the development of diseases and disorders associated with inactivity.    SUI appears to have many contributing factors such as structural damage (eg. tears in the pelvic organ supporting tissues), muscle weakness related to nerve injury or aging, or thinning of the urethral wall and/or its surrounding muscular sphincters. Currently the most common treatments for SUI are conservative therapy, which normally takes the form of exercise therapy provided by specialized nurses or physical therapists, and surgery, which is aimed at enhancing urethral support.  Exercise therapy is effective, resulting in complete cure in 50% of cases, and surgery is effective for approximately 80% of patients but carries risks such as the development of urinary retention.  It is currently not clear which treatment approach is better for which women.    Through the proposed research, we aim to determine how to predict which patients will improve or be cured with exercise therapy such that surgery can be avoided.  Specifically we will determine what is different between patients in whom exercise therapy succeeds and in whom exercise therapy fails.  We will also determine whether physiotherapist-supervised training of the pelvic floor muscles before surgery improves surgical outcomes.  The proposed research will enable us to better understand the female continence system and how it responds to physiotherapeutic intervention.  It will help us to develop improved assessment procedures that can streamline patient management.

TitreApplicationTitle: Plasticity in the undamaged hemisphere following motor cortical infarct in a primate model
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNECTIONS; CONTRALESIONAL HEMISPHERE; HAND CONTROL; ISCHEMIC LESION; MONKEY; MOVEMENT RECOVERY; PLASTICITY; SINGLE-NEURON ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: A stroke is a vascular lesion within the brain. Following a stroke located in the motor cortex, patients have several deficits including loss of upper extremity function. However, patients undergo substantial motor recovery in the weeks and months following the lesion. One hypothesis, for which there is now remarkable support, is that the recovery is dependent upon adaptive reorganization of intact, remaining brain structures. The changes in the hemisphere that had sustained the lesion (ipsilesional) are generally believed to be beneficial to the recovery. Conversely, the role of the reorganization that occurs in the hemisphere opposite to the lesion (contralesional) is controversial. Some studies conclude that plasticity in that hemisphere supports recovery, while others conclude that it actually interferes with it. The goal of the present project is to study the nature of the reorganization in the contralesional hemisphere in order to understand how it can either participate or interfere in recovery. We will record neurons in various contralesional cortical areas in monkeys using electrode arrays while they perform a motor task. We will identify changes of the neural activity that are related to the recovery of the impaired limb. This information will be of great value for the development of experimental protocols modulating brain activity to favor beneficial plasticity in humans after stroke. Because the greatest contralesional plasticity is often observed in individuals with the highest impairments after stroke, understanding this reorganization will be particularly useful for our care of these patients, for whom we currently have the fewest treatment options to offer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Risk factors for influenza infection in hospital-based healthcare workers
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT; HEALTHCARE WORKER; INFLUENZA; VIRAL RESPIRATORY ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: This study will follow a group of hospital workers over three influenza seasons to idenfity risk factors for influenza transmission in acute care hospitals. This information will provide a better estimate of the risk of influenza for healthcare workers, and assist in the development of programs to better protect workers from this risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Addressing the Consequences of Violence and Trauma: A Health Intervention for Women in an Indigenous Context
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL WOMEN; CHRONIC PAIN; INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE; INTERVENTION; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SUBSTANCE USE; TRAUMA; TWO GROUP CROSS-OVER DESIGN; VIOLENCE; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The burden of illness experienced by Aboriginal people in Canada has been directly linked to colonization. However, health problems and possible "interventions" for Aboriginal people are often studied without taking socio-historical contexts into account. Despite extensive evidence of the connections among childhood trauma, violence and myriad health problems, including chronic pain and substance use, mainstream approaches to "treatment" rarely address the historical and social roots of such issues. Often, interventions are designed at an individual level, focus on single-issue problems, and do not account for social determinants of health. In contrast, current thinking about public health issues emphasizes the need for complex interventions. Based on long standing research partnerships among leaders in Aboriginal health, service providers and researchers, the study will build on several research programs to develop and test a complex intervention that addresses the intersecting issues of trauma, violence and pain for women in an indigenous health care context. The study aims to: a) articulate an indigenous lens for use in developing and testing interventions, b) adapt a health promoting intervention (developed for women who have left abusive partners) for Aboriginal women in an inner city context who have experienced intimate partner violence (IPV), and c) test the feasibility and efficacy of the revised intervention. In Phase I, the existing intervention will be adapted to three interrelated conditions: an Aboriginal health care context, the fact that women may, or may not have left abusive partners, and an urban, low income inner-city context. In Phase 2, a pilot test will be conducted with a sample of 20 women to assess feasibility, identify strengths and weaknesses and assess effects on selected study outcomes. In Phase 3, efficacy will be examined with a sample of 130 women using a two-group cross-over design. We will engage in knowledge translation througout.

TitreApplicationTitle: Barriers and Facilitators to Recovery from Severe Mental Illness: a Socio-Cultural Analysis.
Keywords-MotsClés: CULTURE; ETHNICITY; GENDER; MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES; PSYCHOSOCIAL; QUALITATIVE; RACE; RECOVERY; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SEVERE MENTAL ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: The Mental Health Commission of Canada recently announced that mental health services must become more focused on helping people recover from their illness. This is because previous models of mental health care were often based on a belief that people with mental illness were scarred for life and could not recover. This belief has been refuted by scientific evidence. The policy change to recovery is welcome. However there is no agreement as to what 'recovery' actually means in practice, and how it can be integrated into routine care for people with mental illness. In this study, we propose to ask the people who really matter what recovery means to them, and how it can be integrated into the day-to-day practice of mental health services. Specifically we will ask (i) patients with severe mental illness; (ii) family members of patients with severe mental illness; and (iii) clinicians working with people with mental illness. We will ask 60 patients to partake in a one-to-one interview with researchers to understand their perspectives. We will ask family members and clinicians to partake in focus groups. We will deliberately sample patients from different ethno-racial backgrounds, and also ensure we have a balance of men and women. This will allow us to compare and contrast experience between ethno-racial groups and by men and women. These factors have previously been shown to influence use and satisfaction with health services. During the discussions we will ask people (i) their own definitions of recovery, (ii) what personal characteristics help or hinder recovery; (iii) what aspects of the mental health system influences recovery; (iv) what factors in wider society help or hinder recovery. Once we have completed these tasks, we will assess what needs to be done to transform existing mental health services to become truly 'recovery-oriented'. This will lead us to make recommendations regarding procedures, policies and guidelines that can be implemented into practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Genome-Wide Analysis of Brain Regions Involved in Cognition
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN MAPPING; C-FOS; EXPLORATION; GENOME; MICROARRAY; NCS-1
Abstract-Résumé: Neuronal Calcium Sensor-1 (NCS-1) was first discovered in a Drosophila mutant with elevated NCS-1 levels that resulted in increased transmitter release at neuromuscular junctions. We have found that an increase in NCS-1 in the DG causes an increase in rearing in dimly lit, but not well lit, environments. This difference has been suggested to represent exploratory-driven (vs fear-driven) behaviour. We have also found that an increase in DG-specific NCS1 causes an increased sensitivity to LTP (an electrophysiological readout of neural plasticity/learning) and enhanced spatial memory. In this grant we propose three different ways of reducing ncs-1. If we find reduced exploration this will provide a causal relationship. One of the main hypotheses underlying this proposal is that exploratory-driven behaviour is a prerequisite to efficient learning and memory. We will analyze all of the brain regions and genes activated by exploration behaviour. This work may have relevance to diseases such as cognitive impairments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chondrocyte mechanics and biology in the intact joint: towards an understanding of osteoarthritis development in vivo
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; CELL SIGNALLING; CHONDROCYTES; JOINT DEGENERATION; OSTEARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a debilitating disease of the joint. It affects approximately half of Canada's population aged sixty and older. It is associated with pain, joint stiffness, loss of muscle mass, impaired mobility, and it harms the quality of life of the elderly more than any other single disease. The causes leading to osteoarthritis remain unknown. However, it is generally believed that mechanical loading of the joints deforms articular cartilage cells, and that these cells provide the biological signals for maintaining healthy cartilage. If the mechanical loading of the cartilage and cells becomes non-physiological, cells are unable to maintain the cartilage matrix, the cartilage becomes soft and cell deformations increase, thereby disturbing equilibrium conditions, leading to joint degeneration and osteoarthritis. The purpose of our research is to understand the relationship of cartilage loading, cell deformations, and associated biological signaling of the cells. We developed sophisticated techniques to perform such studies for the first time with the cells fully embedded in the cartilage and with the cells in the intact joint, thereby guaranteeing that experimental artifacts associated with cartilage or cell isolation, approaches that have been used in the past, are eliminated. Pilot work has shown that cell mechanics and biology differ vastly between the traditional approaches and the more physiologically relevant approaches proposed here, suggesting that much of our present understanding of osteoarthritis may not hold for the intact joint.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of VEGF Signaling in Glomerular Development and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT; GENE TARGETING; GLOMERULAR DISEASE; KIDNEY DEVELOPMENT; NEPHRIN; PODOCYTE; TRANSGENIC; VEGF; VEGF RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of our research is to understand what genes lead to scarring of the kidney filters, and how we can reverse this scarring. Kidney is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Canada and worldwide. Unfortunately, damage to the kidney due to high blood pressure, diabetes (sugar disease) and other causes, often leads to irreversible scarring and kidney failure. The treatments available to treat the kidney filter are imperfect and also toxic. Thus, it is critical that we develop new therapies. As a first step, we have generated a powerful genetic toolbox that allows us to snip out or add in genes ONLY in the kidney filters in living organisms. Using these tools, we snipped out a gene called VEGF (a gene that affects blood vessel growth and survival), and showed that the mice develop an important and severe glomerular disease that resembles the kidney failure seen in preeclampsia, a serious illness of pregnancy. When we add back too much VEGF, the mice also get sick and develop the kidney disease seen in AIDS. Most recently we showed that loss of the VEGF receptor (VEGFR1) from podocytes results in massive glomerular leak and kidney failure.  From our results, it is clear that VEGF and its receptors play a critical role in health and disease of the kidney. We will continue to dissect the role of VEGF and its receptor, VEGFR1, in kidney disease, with an ultimate goal to develop new therapies for our patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolic and Functional Correlates in Spinal Cord Compression Measured by Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY; PLASTICITY; SPINAL CORD COMPRESSION; SPINAL CORD INJURY; SPINAL CORD REORGANIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Arthritic degeneration of the spine (spondylosis) is a natural part of human aging, affecting 51% of adults. In its mildest form, arthritis in the neck (cervical spondylosis) can cause symptoms such as stiffness, restricted movement as well as neck and arm pain. In advanced cases, however, it can lead to debilitating paralysis in the arms and legs with loss of dexterity, balance, and bladder control. Left untreated, patients ultimately become wheel-chair bound. To prevent paralysis, each year thousands of Canadians undergo spine surgery to relieve spinal cord and nerve compression. Spinal cord compression has a profound affect on individuals, their families and society, with the direct and indirect costs estimated to be in the hundreds of million of dollars. Unfortunately the outcomes of surgery can be somewhat unpredictable, depending on whether the spinal cord has undergone reversible or irreversible damage. Unfortunately, there is no current imaging modality or blood test that can help predict which patient will respond to surgery.   The purpose of our study is to explore the role and inter-relationship of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) in evaluating patients with reversible spinal cord compression. We predict that patients who experience the greatest clinical recovery will also demonstrate the greatest ability for adaptation in both the brain and spinal cord following surgery. Patients that have the best response to surgery will also have a significant recovery of neuronal activation, metabolites and fiber tracts when tested with these newly developed imaging tests. With arthritis of the spine increasing in both prevalence and severity in our aging population, a precise and accurate tool is required to tailor the treatment of spinal dysfunction on a patient-by-patient basis to ensure appropriate and efficient use of medical resources and technology.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of structural plasticity in dendritic spines
Keywords-MotsClés: 2-PHOTON MICROSCOPY; LEARNING AND MEMORY; LIVE IMAGING; OPTICAL MOLECULAR MANIPULATION; STRUCTURAL PLASTICITY; SYNAPSE
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how learning and memory information is stored in the brain is essential for elucidating human brain disorders such as Alzheimer disease. Here we propose to study the novel role of a unique protein called CaMKII beta in learning and memory. CaMKII beta serves as both an enzyme and a structural protein in the brain, however, little is known about its role in learning and memory. To study the role of CaMKII beta, we will develop new laser microscopy technologies to visualize and control CaMKII beta activity in living brain tissues. Utilizing these technologies, we will reveal how CaMKII beta is involved in learning and memory in the brain. Moreover, the developed technologies will provide valuable tools for elucidating the role of other proteins in various research fields.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dysferlin in endothelial dysfunction and atherogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; ENDOTHELIAL DYSFUNCTION; ENDOTHELIUM
Abstract-Résumé: Blood vessels are well known to be the target of various physical insults.  High blood pressure, high fat diet and smoking cause injuries to blood vessels and this has been known for quite some time.  What is not known is how blood vessels repair after injury.  We found in blood vessels several members of the Ferlin family of proteins, which are well known to promote repair after physical injury in skeletal muscle. Hence these proteins are likely candidate to explain how blood vessels undergo repair after physical stresses and insults.  We propose to use animals with deficient repair machinery and determine how cardiovascular disease develops.  This will shed a new light on how vessel repair prevents vascular disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Is the improvement in survival for HPV associated head and neck cancer due to the addition of chemotherapy to radiotherapy or to a more treatment-sensitive cancer?
Keywords-MotsClés: HPV; OROPHARYNGEAL CANCER; OUTCOME; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Cancers of the mouth and throat have traditionally been caused by and associated with individuals who abuse tobacco and alcohol. It has however become apparent over the past 10 years that a new subpopulation of patients is emerging at an epidemic rate. The new patient group was born after the 1940's, were part of the sexual revolution and their cancers are caused by sexually transmitted HPV virus. Over the same 10 years clinical trials have shown that combining chemotherapy with radiation treatment improved survival compared to the traditional treatment of radiotherapy (with or without associated surgery) for patients with cancers of the mouth and throat but carries a huge increase in the incidence of acute and late side effects. More recently it has been shown that the prognosis for those with HPV associated cancer is better than those without the virus association, but we do not know if the improvement in survival is due to a more treatment sensitive tumor or to the newer treatment. Patients need to know this information to balance the potential of side effects and complications to the potential for survival, and oncologists need to know this information to efficiently and effectively use resources as the incidence of this cancer increases. A clinical trial will not be done on this question due to the belief that more intensive treatment is always better but the question can be answered using carefully designed population-based research. The Cancer Care and Epidemiology group at the Queen's Cancer Research Institute has the expertise and experience to complete the study.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physiologic role of CD248 in inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; ASTHMA; COLITIS; GROWTH FACTOR; INFLAMMATION; PERIVASCULAR; SEPSIS; STROMAL CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory diseases are common and debilitating and involve all parts of the body. For example, inflammation of the joints is called arthritis and causes pain and loss of mobility. Inflamed or infected intestines occurs with colitis and is manifest by pain, diarrhea and weight loss. Asthma features inflamed lung airways. Blood vessels are inflamed in atherosclerosis and causes heart attacks, strokes, blindness and poor circulation. In fact, any organ may become inflamed for a short or long time and this affects the well-being of millions of people. There is an urgent need for effective treatments for these diseases.  In our lab, we identified a protein known as CD248, that is made by cells (stromal and perivascular cells) that are normally resident in all tissues. These cells only make CD248 when inflammation is present, suggesting that CD248 might make the inflammation worse. We tested this by generating mice that lack CD248. These CD248 "knockout" mice are resistant to inflammation in a model of arthritis, i.e. the inflammation was much less severe.  This is a very important finding: With this information, drugs may eventually be designed that decrease the effect of CD248, which in turn will decrease the arthritis and hopefully other inflammatory disorders. Our goal is to learn how CD248 decreases inflammation. To do this, we will use various biochemical methods to determine what proteins attach to different parts of CD248 and how the cells switch from being normal to inflamed. The studies will help us figure out how to better turn off the pro-inflammatory effects of CD248. We will also use mice models to determine which diseases are affected by changes in CD248 so that we can better devise therapies for the different diseases. We are confident that with the information gained, scientists will be able to design better ways to decrease the severity of the many diseases associated with inflammation, thereby improving health and quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure/function of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor in its lipid environment
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTORS; BACTERIAL ION CHANNELS; BRAIN FUNCTION; GLIC; LIPID RAFTS; LIPID-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; NEUROTRANSMITTER RECEPTORS; STRUCTURE/FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: We are interested in understanding how nerve cells, or neurons, communicate with each other within the brain.  Neurons communicate at junctions called synapses.  Modification of synaptic communication underlies fundamental processes, such as memory and learning.  Synaptic commiunication is also affected by neurodegenerative disease.  We believe that lipids, the molecules found in the membranes that surround neurons, influence the strength of synaptic communication.  We have also discovered a new inactive structure of one neurotransmitter receptor, called an uncoupled state.  We believe that nerve cells control the proportion of uncoupled versus functional receptors to fine tune communication at synapses.  We also believe that these uncoupled receptors may form under neurodegenerative conditions.  The goal of this research is to characterize this new uncoupled structure, understand the mechanisms by which lipids influence uncoupling, and ultimately synaptic communication, and thus achieve a better understanding of fundamental brain function during both normal and pathological conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proteins that are important for the biosynthesis of lipopolysaccharide, capsules, and other glycoconjugates in pathogenic bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIALS; CAPSULE; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; GLYCOSYLTRANSFERASE; LIPOPOLYSACCHARIDE; NUCLEOTIDE DIPHOSPHATE SUGAR; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA; SUGAR METABOLIC PATHWAYS
Abstract-Résumé: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an important opportunistic pathogen that can cause fatal infections in individuals compromised by burn wounds, cystic fibrosis, and other conditions. This bacterial species produces two forms of lipopolysaccharides (LPS) on its cell surface, one contains an O antigen (called B band, serotype specific), and the other contains a common polysaccharide antigen (called A band). B band is a major virulence factor, while A band is important for P. aeruginosa to adhere to human airway epithelia.  Interestingly, LPS and capsules from P. aeruginosa and a host of other bacterial pathogens are composed of rare sugars not found in humans. My laboratory has been using genetic and biochemical methods to investigate how this LPS coat is made. This line of research has high translational potential because the knowledge derived from our work could lead to the identification of specific targets that can be used for high throughput screening to identify novel antibiotics against bacterial pathogens. Our Specific Aims in this proposal include: 1) To perform functional characterization of each of the genes in the 5-gene operon (pa5455-pa5499) and to determine their role in A-band biosynthesis.  2) To test the hypothesis that the catalytic activities of GMD and RMD can switch from dehydratase to reductase or vice versa by amino acid switches in the catalytic triad.  3) To characterize hisH2, hisF2 and wbpG that are important for O-specific polysaccharide biosynthesis and production of rare acetamidino sugars in P. aeruginosa.  4) To use cutting edge super-resolution 3D-structured illumination microscopy for live-cell imaging to investigate the spatial localization of A-band and B-band LPS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurocognitive Correlates of Hypertension and Type 2 Diabetes in Older Adults
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE RESPONSES; BRAIN AGING; COGNITIVE FUNCTION; FMRI; HYPERTENSION; TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS
Abstract-Résumé: Numerous factors contribute to the fact that some adults retain their cognitive function with aging while others show increasing degrees of losses. Both hypertension and type 2 diabetes are among these risk factors. This proposal will explore changes in brain blood flow and brain activity in individuals with and without hypertension, type 2 diabetes and 'pre-diabetes'.  Participants will perform a variety of tasks reliant on different brain regions while in an MRI so that we can explore how brain activity changes as an individual engages in  task performance. This will allow us to determine the contribution of altered brain blood flow and changes to brain activity which may underscore the decrements in brain function observed in these patient populations.  Subjects will attend two sessions, one to assess globally their cognitive function and the other to undergo brain imaging. Our goal is to understand how underlying metabolic disturbances and diseases, common in older adults, contribute to loss of cognitive function with aging. Through this understanding, we would hope to ultimately develop strategies to promote cognitive retention with aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: The interplay of genotype and maternal care in the moderation of the risk for anxious and depressive psychopathology in preschool children with prenatal adversity: low birth weight, maternal prenatal depression and the prenatal programming of development
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT CHILD PSYCHOPATHOLOGY; ENDOPHENOTYPES; FOETAL PROGRAMMING; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; MATERNAL CARE; POST NATAL MODERATORS; PRENATAL ADVERSITY
Abstract-Résumé: Anxiety and depression are only partially predicted by such risk factors as prenatal developmental history (e.g. low birth weight) and familial history of anxiety and depression. Such findings suggest the influence of intervening factors. We suggest that early maternal care influences these outcomes. In a population of 600 children followed in the community since the prenatal period, we will measure maternal care at 6 months and see how the mother-child interaction changes the risk for anxiety and depression in 6 year old children with risks from prenatal adversity and genes that associate with anxiety and depression. Our project will make 5 novel contributions: (i) We will examine children with 2 common prenatal adversities: low birth weight (observed in 8% of births in Canada, higher in lower income neighbourhoods); and, prenatal maternal depression (formally diagnosed in 9% of pregnant women, and experienced in lesser intensity by as many as 50%); (ii) We will examine the role of maternal care. While there is good evidence that the environment and genes act together to influence the emotional development of children, traumatic experiences have been the main environmental factor studied; (iii) We will focus on early emotional difficulties because these are the first emerging signs of possible later problems and their rates in toddlerhood (15-25% of children) are similar to those in older children. Focusing on early manifestations also allows for early identification and intervention; (iv) We will pay special attention to anxiety and depression since it is less studied in this age group and since both low birth weight and maternal depression are associated with depression in early childhood; (v) We will measure comprehensively childhood psychopathology by using reports by parents, teachers, children as well as a investigator-based parent diagnostic interview.

TitreApplicationTitle: Acute modulation and chronic remodelling of intrinsic cardiac nervous system properties during myocardial ischemia, atrial tachyarrhythmias, and spinal cord stimulation.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL/VENTRICULAR ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL PROPERTIES; ATRIAL/VENTRICULAR TACHYARRHYTHMIAS; AUTONOMIC NERVOUS SYSTEM; INTRINSIC CARDIAC NEURONS; MYOCARDIAL ISCHEMIA; THORACIC SPINAL CORD SEGMENT STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiac arrhythmias, which include heart beat irregularities and excessively rapid or slow heart rate, are major causes of cardiac morbidity and mortality. In particular, atrial fibrillation is the most common arrhythmia in adults and its prevalence increases with ageing. It has been suggested that targeting cardiac nerves, in addition to cardiac muscle, might allow interventional cardiologists and surgeons to improve the effectiveness of ablation therapy, particularly to reduce the risk of arrhythmia recurrence.  The 'intrinsic' cardiac neurons form about 6 cellular aggregates called 'ganglionated plexuses' that are nested in fatty tissues at specific locations on the surface of the heart. Herein, we hypothesize that the activity of the intrinsic cardiac nervous system is enhanced in cardiac pathologies such as cardiac arrhhythmias and coronary artery disease, leading to further exacerbation of the disease, and that the system can be stabilized by stimulation of the upper thoracic segments of the spinal cord. In fact, spinal cord stimulation via chronically implanted electrodes is in clinical use, especially in Europe, for the treatment of symptomatic coronary artery disease refractory to pharmacological and surgical therapy, but the mechanism of this therapy is not known. The general objective of the proposed research is to elucidate the mechanisms for therapeutic modulation of the intrinsic cardiac nervous system.  These clinically-relevant issues will be investigated in canine models of atrial fibrillation and coronary artery disease using elctrocardiographic recording in situ and intracellular recording of neuronal activity in vitro. Corroborative data will be obtained in a pilot study of the properties of intrinsic cardiac neurons contained in atrial fatty tissues collected from patients undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural and Behavioral Mechanisms of Conditioned Sexual Excitement and Inhibition: Sex Differences and Similarities
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS OF SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION; CONDITIONING; IMMUNOCHEMISTRY; IN-VIVO MICRODIALYSIS; INHIBITION; NEUROPHARMACOLOGY; PARTNER PREFERENCE; REWARD; SEXUAL AND REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH; SEXUAL DESIRE
Abstract-Résumé: Sexual dysfunctions affect a substantial number of people worldwide, with North American estimates ranging from 10-60% of men and women, depending on the particular type of dysfunction.  Unlike sexual arousal disorders such as erectile dysfunction or lack of vaginal blood flow, sexual desire and orgasm disorders are more complex and involve experience and expectation, processes that are controlled by the brain. At present, very little is understood about the neural mechanisms involved, although a growing body of evidence from animal models has identified excitatory and inhibitory systems in the brain that likely play a role. Our previous CIHR-funded studies revealed a strong link in both male and female rats between the experience and expectation of sexual reward and behaviors aimed at sexual contact.  Such behaviors are analogous to human sexual desire. Sexual reward states are critically dependent on the activation of endogenous opioid systems. We will utilize these models of sexual reward in the present proposal to study the ability of odor and tactile cues to be associated with sexual excitation or inhibition, and then to use the cues as "priming stimuli" to examine whether they activate or inhibit neurotransmitter systems in the brain associated with exitation (e.g., dopamine, oxytocin) or reward (opioids like endorphin). We will also examine how experience with sexual nonreward comes to induce conditioned sexual inhibition, and how the cues stimulate a pattern of brain activation that is different from the patter induced by the same cue associated with sexual excitation.  Finally, we will examine how excitatory and inhibitory cues interact, and whether a cue that primes excitation in the brain can override the reaction to an inhibitory cue. These studies will have important implications for our understanding of the etiology and maintenance of sexual dysfunction, and for the design of drug therapies to treat sexual desire and orgasm disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular Mechanisms underlying vascular dysfunction & aortic aneurysm in Marfan syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: AORTIC ANEURYSM; CELL & MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; DISEASE BIOMARKER; HISTOPATHOLOGY/PATHOPHYSIOLOGY; HUMAN AORTIC EXPLANTS; IN VIVO PHARMACOLOGY; SIGNALLING PATHWAY; WHOLE ORGAN &CELL CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Marfan syndrome (MFS) is a genetic disease of the connective tissue, which provides material and support for our skeleton, muscles, blood vessels and other parts of our bodies. People may be tall and thin with slender, tapering fingers, long arms and legs, and spine curvature. They often have heart and eye problems. In some patients, the condition is very mild and the person has few or no symptoms. Others are always at risk of life-threatening problems, which usually involve damage to the valves in the heart or weakening of the large blood vessels leading from the heart (e.g. aorta). If the blood vessels become weak, they can balloon out (dilate) and break (rupture), which might cause the person to die suddenly. We have only a limited ability to stop the progression of disease in Marfan syndrome. Typically we use medicines that lower heart rate or blood pressure (or both). But this does not prevent the disease and very few drugs work well enough to keep patients from needing surgery or dying suddenly because a blood vessel has torn open.   Our objective is to understand intra and extra cellular events within the walls of the blood vessels that occur during the early stage of disease using a well-established mouse model of Marfan syndrome that mimics human disease. Our previous findings using the mouse model have shown that a blood lowering drug called Losartan improves the blood vessel function and delay the dilatation of the blood vessel. We would like to understand the mechanism underlying such effects. We also intend to find new indicators of disease progression in blood samples of human subjects and MFS mice in both treated and non-treated groups.  This study will help us to find better ways to treat people with Marfan syndrome and find early indicators (bio-markers) as a tool to detect early changes in blood vessels. If we can do this, fewer people will need emergency surgery for torn blood vessels and fewer will die suddenly.

TitreApplicationTitle: CD123-Targeted Auger Electron Radioimmunotherapy of Acute Myelogenous Leukemia (AML)
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE MYELOGENOUS LEUKEMIA; AUGER ELECTRONS; CD123; INDIUM-111; LEUKEMIA STEM CELLS; MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES; NUCLEAR LOCALIZATION SEQUENCES (NLS); RADIOIMMUNOTHERAPY; STARBURST DENDRIMERS
Abstract-Résumé: Acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) is thought to be caused by a primitive leukemia stem cell in the bone marrow which maintains the disease and prevents cure due to its survival after chemotherapy and bone marrow transplant. This malignant stem cell has a unique feature in that it displays on its surface, a protein called CD123. We have been studying a new approach to eliminating these leukemia stem cells using antibodies that bind to CD123 that are linked to a radioisotope called indium-111. This radioisotope is very toxic to the leukemia cells if it is transported to the nucleus of the cells. We have taken advantage of the fact that the radioactive antibodies are naturally taken up by cells displaying CD123 and also that they can be encouraged to localize in the nucleus of the cells by modification with small peptides that have nuclear localization signals. Already, we have shown that these radioactive antibodies are indeed taken up by leukemia cells and transported to the nucleus where the indium-111 has proven moderately toxic to the cells. We have also shown that these radioactive antibodies localize specifically at sites of leukemia in mice inoculated with AML cells. In the proposed research, we will study approaches to enhance the toxicity of these radioactive antibodies towards leukemia cells, and examine their ability to decrease leukemia in AML engrafted mice as well as study their normal tissue toxicities. If successful, our research will lead to a new targeted radiation treatment for leukemia which could be tested in a Phase I clinical trial. Ultimately, our goal is to improve the long-term outcome for 4 out of 5 patients with AML who cannot currently be cured and rarely survive more than a few years.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of EPI-001 for the treatment of prostate cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN RECEPTOR; COMBINED THERAPIES; DRUG TARGET; MECHANISMS OF RESISTANCE; PROSTATE CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Once prostate cancer becomes castrate-recurrent there are no effective therapies that can be offered and the patient will succumb to his disease in approximately two years.  There is mounting evidence supporting the concept that development of castrate-recurrent disease is causally related to molecular changes affecting the function of the androgen receptor. All current hormonal therapies target the C-terminus ligand-binding domain of the androgen receptor and include androgen ablation and antiandrogens. We have identified EPI-001, a specific small molecule inhibitor to the N-terminus of the androgen receptor which represents a new mechanism of pharmacologic specificity.  EPI-001 causes regression of prostate cancer tumours without any significant toxicity in preclinical animal models. The mechanism of action has been characterized for EPI-001. Here we propose to examine known mechanisms of resistant for current antiandrogens to determine if EPI-001 could be used in patients that develop resistant to current therapies. In addition, EPI-001 will be tested in combination with other therapeutic approaches used clinically.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
TitreApplicationTitle: Oncogene-containing microvesicles as mediators and messengers of tumour progression
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ANTIANGIOGENESIS; BIOMARKER; EGFR; GLIOMA; INTERCELLULAR COMMUNICATION; MICROVESICLES; ONCOGENES; ONCOSOMES; TARGETED AGENTS
Abstract-Résumé: We have previously discovered that cancer causing genes (oncogenes) are responsible for the ability of tumor cells to attract blood vessels (angiogenesis), which they need to grow and spread (progression). Recently we have identified a completely new mechanism that may facilitate such communication between cancer cells and blood vessels. Thus, cancer cells containing active oncogenes produce myriads of tiny bubbles (vesicles, microvesicles or oncosomes), which contain the oncogenic proteins themselves, and can transfer them from cell to cell, causing angiogenesis and cancer progression. We have preliminary data to suggest that oncosomes can also be easily collected from blood of cancer patients, and their content decoded to inform us how to treat the tumour (what oncogenes are present) and whether the treatment actually works in a given patient.   It is essential that we understand exactly how this works: How do cancer causing oncogenes trigger cellular bubbling (oncosome formation), and how different are oncosomes from bubbles produced by some agitated normal cells (e.g. blood vessel cells). None of this is known, especially whether oncosomes mainly come from within the cancer cell (exosomes) or from the cellular surface (ectosomes), or both/neither. We will examine the molecules that control these processes, and how their actions are altered in cancer cells (neovesiculation). Knowing this would allow us to devise drugs that block formation of oncosomes, or inhibit their interactions with blood vessels. We already found one (Diannexin).   We will use advanced technology to study active molecules present within oncosomes and we will assess how they change when tumors are treated with various drugs. We will use this information to explore ways to block cancer-promoting effects of oncosomes. This knowledge will also serve to develop a new oncosome-based blood test, to follow and modulate anticancer treatments and improve their results.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endocytic degradation of hERG potassium channels in cardiac function and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HERG; ION CHANNEL EXPRESSION; ION CHANNEL TRAFFICKING; LONG QT SYNDROME; PATCH CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Heartbeats are controlled by electrical impulses generated by specialized proteins in the cell membrane called ion channels. Dysfunction of ion channels causes irregular heartbeats (cardiac arrhythmias) which can lead to sudden death. Therefore, ion channels are primary targets for anti-arrhythmic therapies.    The overall activity of a type of ion channel in a cell is determined by the function of a single channel and the total number of channels. While the function and modulation of existing ion-channels have been extensively studied, little is known about how the number of ion channels on the cell membrane is regulated. The number of channels in a cell (channel density) is determined by both degradation (destruction) and synthesis (construction). This application will study how cells degrade ion channels and what diseases are caused by over-degradation of ion channels in the heart. We will focus on one type of channel in the heart called HERG which passes potassium ions. The HERG channel will be expressed in a cell line for detailed studies to find which cellular molecules are critical for the channel degradation. We will test a novel idea that genetic defects (mutations) in an HERG-interacting protein called caveolin-3 reduce hERG density and cause cardiac disorders. We will also study the channels in heart cells to test our hypothesis.    This proposal is based on our ongoing research. We recently discovered that the HERG channel density is regulated by blood potassium concentrations. The present research will extend our research program by addressing how HERG channels are degraded under normal (physiological) and abnormal (pathophysiological) conditions. We have obtained substantial preliminary data to support our proposed research. Thus, we have both experience and techniques to accomplish the proposed work, which will generate information important for developing new strategies to treat cardiac arrhythmias by regulating ion channel density.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mapping the microcircuits of attention in the primate brain
Keywords-MotsClés: AREA MIDDLE TEMPORAL; ATTENTION; BIASED COMPETITION; CORRELATIONS; FEATURE SIMILARITY; MACAQUE MONKEYS; MICROELECTRODE ARRAYS; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; SINGLE CELL RECORDINGS; SINGLE NEURONS
Abstract-Résumé: Attention can be defined as the filtering and modulation of information processing in the brain. It protects sensory systems from signal overload determining the organism's performance in many tasks. Disorders of attention affect 4-8% of school age children and are a main cause of learning disabilities. The neural mechanisms underlying attention are poorly understood, hindering our search for the cause and treatment of attentional disorders. Over the last years, we have recorded the activity of single neurons in extrastriate visual cortex of macaques. We have found that when two stimuli fall inside a cell's receptive field instructing the animal to attend to one of them causes the cell's response to selectively represent the features of that stimulus, as if the receptive field contracted around it excluding the distracter. This filtering effect became weaker as the contrast of attended and distracter stimuli increased. In the experiments proposed here we will test the hypothesis that attentional filtering by extrastriate neurons results from a modulation in the activity of different populations of striate (V1) units with small receptive fields including attended and unattended stimuli and projecting toward a recipient extrastriate cell. We will further test whether this modulation occurs through competitive interactions between populations of V1 units with different selectivities for stimulus features and receptive field locations, and whether such interactions are triggered by changes in activation strength within one population. We will finally test whether prefrontal neurons encoding the stimuli spatial location competitively interact to produce trigger signals during attention. We will record the activity of neurons within a given brain area in macaques performing attentional tasks and measure changes in the units' activation as well as interactions between them. Our results will provide new and important insights into the brain mechanisms underlying attention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pregnancy and Subsequent Cardiovascular Risk in Women with Heart Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTORS; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: It is important to find out who is at high risk for developing high blood pressure or diabetes as these conditions are leading causes of death and disability.  There are early reports that premature birth, low birth weight, diabetes, or high blood pressure during pregnancy increases the mother's risk of developing high blood pressure or diabetes later in life.  Women with heart conditions prior to pregnancy are known to be at increased risk for premature birth, low birth weight, or heart complications during pregnancy, and thus may be at even higher risk than the general population for developing diabets, high blood pressure, or premature heart attack/stroke late after pregnancy.  The objective of our study is to find out if, and understand how, pregnancy in women with heart conditions affects the later development of diabetes, high blood pressure, and premature heart attack/stroke.  We will be studying 1400 women with preexisting heart disease who delivered from 1994 to 2013 and are part of our ongoing research study in which we systematically enter the results of pregnancy in all women with heart disease who receive care at our centres. In women with heart disease who delivered or will deliver between 1994 and 2011, we will determine how many of them will develop new high blood pressure, diabetes, heart attack, or stroke late after pregnancy.  The rate of the same health problems in Ontario women delivered during the same time period, will serve as  a comparison. In those pregnant women with heart disease who will be delivering from 2011 onwards, we will be obtaining additional measurements during and after pregnancy to better understand how pregnancy or its complications affect the future chance of having high blood pressure and diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bridging the Gap Between Infant Mental Health and Infant Health: Bringing Attachment Theory into the Infant Acute Pain Context
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTACHMENT; DEVELOPMENTAL TRAJECTORIES; INFANT ACUTE PAIN BEHAVIOUR; LONGITUDINAL GROWTH MODELING; PARENTAL SOOTHING BEHAVIOUR
Abstract-Résumé: Over forty years of research has demonstrated that insecure infant attachments (to parents) predict poor health outcomes across the lifespan, such as being diagnosed with serious psychiatric illnesses or chronic pain conditions.  Being able to help lessen the impact of insecure infant attachments before they are set, would have a high potential for significantly impacting the health of Canadians. This grant aims to take the first step in this process by generating knowledge regarding how parents and infants interact over the first year of life during immunizations.  Immunization pain triggers infant attachment behaviours because it triggers infants sense of danger and thus, the infants' need for parent.  Caregivers and infants who have taken part in an ongoing research project will be invited to participate in the current study after infants attend their 12-month immunization appointments. During the original study, immunization procedures at 2, 4, 6 and 12 months were videotaped to capture infant pain-related behaviour as well as the way they interacted with their caregiver; these data will be utilized in the current analyses. The current study will then invite these caregiver-infant dyads to take part in a wellknown attachment assessment procedure called the Strange Situation Paradigm. By examining how an infant's relationship with his or her caregiver is related to how an infant reacts when in pain, this project will help us better understand how insecure infants act in a commonly occuring stressful situation. Ultimately, it is hoped that information created in this grant will be able to be used by health professionals, in the immunization context, to help lessen the occurence of insecure attachments and improve the health of Canadians at all ages.

TitreApplicationTitle: Suppression of DNA mismatch repair by the oncoprotein NPM-ALK
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA MISMATCH REPAIR; LYMPHOMAGENESIS; MICROSATELLITE INSTABILITY; NPM-ALK; TYROSINE KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: There are many mechanisms known to contribute to cancer formation, one of which is related to a group of enzymes called tyrosine kinases. In normal cells, tyrosine kinases are known to play key roles in regulating many important cellular functions. In some cancer cells, tyrosine kinases are known to be over-active, thereby deregulating a wide range of cellular processes and often leading to uncontrolled cell growth and tumor formation. Our research group has been studying such a cancer-forming tyrosine kinase called NPM-ALK for the past 9 years. Recently, we discovered that NPM-ALK can induce genetic instability, by interfering with a critical cellular function called DNA mismatch repair, a mechanism normally used to safeguard the integrity of our genes. The main purpose of this study is to further investigate this novel mechanism by which cancer formation is promoted. We aim to develop new therapeutic approaches based on the new information derived from this study.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Strategies to Enhance BCG Vaccine-induced Mucosal Immunity against Pulmonary Tuberculosis
Keywords-MotsClés: DESTRUCTIVE LUNG DISEASE; LUNG INFLAMMATION; LUNG MUCOSAL IMMUNITY; PULMONARY TUBERCULOSIS; T CELL RESPONSES; VACCINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic destructive lung disease and remains one of the top infectious causes of death worldwide. While the current vaccine, BCG, is effective in protecting from disseminated forms of childhood TB, it fails to protect from pulmonary TB, the major global TB burden. There is an urgent need to understand the immune mechanisms underlying the failure of BCG vaccination and develop safe and effective strategies to enhance protective immunity by BCG. Built on the progress that we have made, our current proposal aims to investigate the mechanisms of BCG vaccine-induced lung mucosal immunity and develop novel strategies to improve such protective immunity against pulmonary TB in animal models. Our proposed studies will provide much needed knowledge and solutions for the fight against global TB epidemic.

OrgNm: CIUSSS de l'Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Douglas Hospital/CIUSSS de l'Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Hôpital Douglas
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the Dopamine Transporter functional activity. Identification of new targets.
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE TRANSPORTER; PROTEOMIC
Abstract-Résumé: Synthesized in only a few restricted places in the brain, dopamine (DA) is a major chemical transmitter of motor and cognitive functions. The importance of DA neurotransmission is highlighted by its direct implication in neurological and psychiatric disorders, such as Parkinson disease, Tourette syndrome, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorders, Schizophrenia or addiction to drugs of abuse, to refer to the most established. All these disorders share in common a disturbance of DA transmission. It therefore appears that a key to restore the deficits of these disorders, as well as to understand the normal functioning of DA, would be to have a comprehensive knowledge of the various processes that are regulating the quantity of DA at the synapse (the synapse is the small space between two neurons, where the chemical dialog takes place).  The dopamine transporter (DAT) is the key protein that terminates DA in the synaptic space, once it is released from the DA neurons. The DAT controls DA availability both in time and space. The importance of this reuptake process is established by the effects of psychostimulant drugs (amphetamine, cocaine, methylphenidate) that actually works by blocking the DAT function.   The main objective of this project is to study DAT regulation at the molecular and cellular level, and to understand how this regulation is achieved through interactions with other protein located at presynaptic terminals. To achieve our objectives, we will use technologies ranging from molecular biology (to identify precisely the sequence of new presynaptic proteins), cellular biology (functional assays of DA uptake), biochemistry and mouse genetic.  Understanding of these mechanisms and characterization of the main interacting proteins will not only  represent important advance for our current understanding of brain functioning, but also identify novel targets for therapeutics approaches for brain disorders.
