NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Early-life origins of visceral adiposity
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE TISSUE GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT; CELLULAR AND MOLECULAR MECHANISMS; EARLY-LIFE PROGAMMING; KNOCKOUT MOUSE MODELS; MATERNAL PROTEIN RESTRICTION; VISCERAL ADIPOSITY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, obesity is becoming a leading health problem not only because of its high prevalence but also because it substantially impairs quality of life and increases the risk of developing metabolic diseases, such as hypertension, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes. Obesity is characterized by excess fat accumulation in all or certain fat depots in the body. This research program will specifically address central obesity because it is the best predictor of the obesity-associated metabolic disorders. Although its causes remain largely unknown, increasing epidemiological studies indicate that low birth-weight is associated with an increased risk of central obesity in adult life, suggesting that fetal life may be a critical period in the development of this disorder. However, the mechanisms that underpin this relationship are unclear. The objectives of this research program are therefore to study the fetal origins and the molecular mechanisms of central obesity. An experimental rat model of low birth-weight with subsequent development of central obesity as well as two genetically modified mouse model will be utilized. This project is expected to uncover the critical periods during development when offspring are most vulnerable to the central obesity-inducing effects of mother's low protein diet. It is also expected to show whether supplementation of mother's low protein diet with a key protein component can prevent the development of central obesity in her offspring, and if the female hormone estrogen has a protective role in protecting females from developing central obesity. In addition, we expect to find a cause and effect relationship between overproduction of two growth factors by fat tissue and development of central obesity. Information generated from these studies will advance our understanding of the causes of central obesity, and it will be of value in developing novel therapeutic interventions aimed at preventing and, or reversing this disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the role of Serpin antiproteases in resistance to HIV-1 infection in the female genital tract to aid in the development of novel vaginal microbicide candidates
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV REPLICATION; HIV-RESISTANCE; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNE ACTIVATION; MICROBICIDES; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; PROTEASE INHIBITORS; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: HIV infects over 40 million people worldwide, with over 60 million individuals infected or dead since the 1980's.  HIV disproportionately infects women due to social and biological factors, and thus there has been an effort to develop female-controlled preventative technologies for women, such as vaginal microbicides. Such technologies would be extremely beneficial as it would give women the ability to protect themselves independent of partner consent, especially when partners do not wish to use condoms.  However, a lack the knowledge of what provides natural protection from HIV infection in women has prevented progress in this area.  Clues of what provides protection from HIV may come from studying a group of women Pumwani Sex Worker cohort in Kenya who have shown a natural protective immunity to HIV.   Even after repeated exposures to HIV, from multiple infected sexual partners, they remain infection-free, some for more than 25 years.  These 'HIV-resistant' individuals represent a model of protection and understanding their unique immune systems may provide us with information on how to design an effective microbicide.  Our research has shown that HIV-resistant women secrete higher amounts of novel protein factors in their genital secretions, called Serpins.  Serpins are known to be involved with host defense against bacteria/viruses and have shown direct anti-HIV activity, as well as have general anti-inflammatory capabilities, which is a known risk factor for infection in women.  For these reasons we believe Serpins are contributing to natural protection against HIV-infection.  We wish to study their biological function in the female genital tract with respect to HIV-infection. This proposal will further our understanding of their biological role against HIV-infection and may allow us to use them in a novel microbicide formulation.  This may lead to the development of novel female-controlled protection technologies.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: PTP1b as a target in human cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPIES; ONCOGENE; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; TISSUE MICRO ARRAY; TRANSGENIC ANIMAL MODELS; TYROSINE PHOSPHATASE
Abstract-Résumé: PTP1B is a gene that my laboratory and others showed in previous work to be an important target for type II diabetes and obesity. From these observations several companies developed, or are in the process of isolating PTP1B inhibitor. Indeed, at least one company (ISIS Inc) has already entered clinical trials for the treatment of those metabolic diseases with their PTP1B inhibitors. We have found in the past funding period that PTP1B is also an oncogene in breast and other cancers, where metabolic syndrome, and in particular obesity, are risk factors. We propose to pursue our analysis of this gene and identify how PTP1B causes cancer. We also propose to examine what is the relationship between its pro-obesity and type II diabetes action with its cancer promoting activity.  Moreover, since there are already PTP1B inhibitors treatments and more will eventually be developed, we want to gather important information on: Which cancers can be treated with existing and future PTP1B inhibitors? What is the genetic profile that defines subgroups of patients that will most benefit from such treatments?  And finally, can we use PTP1B inhibitor in conjunction with existing cancer therapies to better treat cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of Organellar pH-regulating Transporters in Cellular Homeostasis and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALKALI CATION/PROTON EXCHANGERS; DNA TRANSFECTIONS; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; GENE CLONING; MAMMALIAN CELL CULTURE; MUTAGENESIS; ORGANELLAR ION HOMEOSTASIS; PROTEIN PROCESSING & MEMBRANE TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: The conversion of fuel molecules such as glucose into the main source of biochemical energy, adenosine 5'-triphosphate (ATP), generates waste products such as carbon dioxide, protons and other weak acids (i.e., lactic acid) or bases (i.e., bicarbonate) that must be efficiently removed or buffered to sustain a suitable acid-base (pH) milieu for stable protein activity and interactions, and ultimately the function and survival of all living organisms.  Regulation of pH is mainly achieved by a variety of ion transport proteins present in cell membranes that can selectively move these waste products from one side of the membrane to the other for disposal or for reuse in other cellular processes.  This research proposal is focused on the study of one specific group of pH-regulating transporters called sodium/proton exchangers (NHEs). The NHE gene family contains 11 structurally-related members.  Disruptions in the normal functioning of some of these genes have previously been linked to different human diseases, including hypertension, heart attacks, stroke, and chronic diarrhea.  In this particular proposal, we are focusing on two poorly studied members NHE6 and NHE9 that are located inside most cells in small membrane vesicles called recycling endosomes.  Recent studies have identified mutations in these genes that cause mental retardation, autism and attention deficit disorders. We have isolated the NHE6 and NHE9 genes and are currently studying the effect the mutated genes have on recycling endosomal function.  We hypothesize that these defects impair the pH and movement of recycling endosomes that carry neurotransmitter receptors to synapses of neurons, which in turn affects brain electrical activity and function.  This research proposal will test this assumption using sophisticated techniques in molecular & cellular biology as well as electrophysiology; thereby shedding new insights into their physiological contributions to human health, disease and treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Experimental reversal of retinal defects in murine models of CSNB2A
Keywords-MotsClés: CSNB; ELECTRORETINOGRAPHY (ERG); GENE THERAPY; GENETICS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; KNOCKOUT AND CONDITIONAL MOUSE MODELS; OPTOKINETIC TESTING (OKR); PHOTORECEPTORS; RETINAL DISEASES; RIBBON SYNAPSES
Abstract-Résumé: Can normal vision be restored to animal models of CSNB?  Mutations in more than 180 human genes are known to be cause heritable retinal diseases that often lead to blindness. The gene called CACNA1F produces a protein that mediates the entry of calcium into photoreceptor cells in the retina, which is essential for transmission of visual signals from rods and cones to the brain.  Mutations in CACNA1F cause a disease called congenital stationary night blindness (CSNB), in which patients have impaired night vision, short-sightedness (myopia), and a substantial loss of visual acuity that cannot be corrected.  The major focus of our research is to determine whether photoreceptors can be made to establish functioning synaptic connections after they have failed to form during the normal period of retinal development. In studying the retina of a novel mutant mouse (G305X-CSNB) that models or mimics CSNB, we found that rod and cone photoreceptors fail to form the synaptic connections needed for sending visual signals to other retinal nerve cells. This failure causes the remaining cells in the retina to undergo characteristic changes and rearrangements. Such cellular remodeling is also observed in many other retinal diseases including retinal detachments. We want to know whether we can reverse these abnormal retinal features and restore normal function to the CSNB retina. This problem will be investigated using a genetic-engineering approach and by transferring a normal calcium channel gene (CACNA1F) into the retina of G305X-CSNB mice.   Our research involves far-reaching collaborative efforts that will bring together the required expertise for achieving our research goals. Establishing that rod and cone photoreceptors can make functional synapses after long-standing retinal disease or injury will further encourage the development of therapeutic strategies for human retinal diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; ANOMALIES CONGENITALES
TitreApplicationTitle: TGFbeta Family Signalling in Mammalian Development
Keywords-MotsClés: BMP; CELL FATE DECISION; MOUSE MODELS OF MAMMALIAN DEVELOPMENT; SIGNALLING; TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR-BETA
Abstract-Résumé: The development of all organisms, including humans, from the fertilized egg until birth is an extremely complex process.  Cells grow and selected cells become highly specialized to form different tissues, such as the skeleton, which shapes our body.  Instructing these cells on where to go and how to behave thus becomes an enormously complex process.  My lab works on a family of small proteins called Transforming Growth Factor-beta, which act like a set of instructions on how to make the body. Little is known of how the same signal can be used in so many different contexts, so one aim of this research proposal is to study how some factors that are related to TGFbeta, called the Bone Morphogenetic Proteins (BMPs) control the fate of cells and thereby the development of mammals.  Since many of these BMPs also have important functions in adults (for example in controlling bone formation), these studies will help us understand certain developmental abnormalities.  In addition, derangement of instructive signals like BMPs contribute to a wide range of human cancer and we expect our work could also yield important information about this and other disease processes.

ClasseRechercheFR: DYSTROPHIE MUSCULAIRE; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Signals from diacylglycerol kinases to the actin cytoskeleton regulate membrane ruffling, blebbing and macropinocytosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN CYTOSKELETON; CULTURED CELLS; DIACYLGLYCEROL KINASES; LIPID SIGNALING; MACROPINOCYTOSIS; MEMBRANE BLEBBING; RHO GTPASES; SYNTROPHIN
Abstract-Résumé: Specialized lipid molecules in the plasma membrane called second messengers can relay signals to the cell's cytoskeleton. Diacylglycerol kinases (DGKs) are a family of enzymes that phosphorylate the lipid second messenger diacylglycerol to yield another second messenger called phosphatidic acid. By regulating the balance of these two important signaling lipids, DGKs occupy a central position in lipid signaling pathways. One DGK family member called DGKz is a component of several distinct signaling pathways that underpin different biological functions in several cell types; however, the full spectrum of its function remains to be identified. This application is focused on understanding the molecular mechanisms that underlie the regulation actin cytoskeleton reorganization by DGKz signaling complexes. The actin cytoskeleton is critically important in the tissue morphogenesis events required for the normal development of multicellular organisms. Using cells genetically deleted for DGKz and a combination of cell and molecular biological techniques, we hope to tease apart the signaling pathways that DGKz uses to regulate actin organization.

NomDuComitéFR: Déterminants psychosociaux, socioculturels et comportementaux de la santé 2
TitreApplicationTitle: The life course approach to studying the aetiology of head and neck cancer: HeNCe Life study
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; HEAD AND NECK CANCER; LIFE COURSE; PSYCHOSOCIAL; SOCIOECONOMIC
Abstract-Résumé: Certain adult chronic diseases such as cancer may be influenced by circumstances during birth, childhood, adolescence and adult life instead of only circumstances that happen at one point in life. We developed the HeNCe Life study to investigate the relationships between genetic, biological (e.g., viral infections), social, psychological and behavioural factors along people's life and the occurrence of mouth and throat cancers. We want to determine which factors influence this disease other than the known behavioural risk factors (e.g., smoking and alcohol habits) and to understand how these and other risk factors like viral infections are linked and interact with the environments in which one grows, develops and lives. The HeNCe Life study aims to investigate these factors in residents of Canada, Brazil, USA and India. This will allow us to compare people who have mouth and throat cancers to people who do not have this disease. We interview people using a technique which is specially designed to help them remember their past life events and ask them many questions about their living and working conditions and several behaviours. We also collect saliva samples to look for genetic abnormalities related to alcohol and tobacco habits and to test for viral infections. This unique study investigates several characteristics of different populations while taking into consideration their social and cultural diversity. This study will contribute to explain how certain events may put people into life trajectories that are either conducive to good health or not. Also, we will help to clarify if there is a specific life period where certain conditions or events (infections, poor nutrition) have a bigger impact than other time periods. This will assist health care providers to set policies and intervention programs (e.g., vaccinations, screening tests) that are more effective for a particular stage of life, minimizing the occurrence of these cancers globally.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; MALADIES A VIRUS
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and Engineering Studies of Ribozymes and Riboswitches
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICS; ENZYMOLOGY; HETERONUCLEAR NMR; LIGAND BINDING; RIBOSWITCHES; RIBOZYME; RNA ENGINEERING; RNA TARGETING; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: RNA controls gene expression through a number of different mechanisms, and disruption of RNA-dependent events are associated with several human diseases, including developmental aberrations, pathogenic infections and cancer. Over the last several years, we have focused on structure-function studies of two types of functional RNAs: ribozymes and riboswitches. Ribozymes are RNA enzymes that cleave specific RNA sequences and, thus, have the potential to be engineered to inactivate target genes. Riboswitches are RNA regulatory elements that modulate gene expression in response to metabolite binding. Most riboswitches have been found in bacteria and, thus, represent ideal targets for the development of new antibiotics against pathogenic bacteria. The overall objective of this proposal is to continue our structure-function studies of ribozymes and riboswiches in order to help develop RNA-based therapeutics and diagnostic agents. More specifically, we propose to 1) Structurally investigate the Neurospora VS ribozyme; 2) Engineer VS-derived ribozymes; and 3) Structurally investigate the interaction between purine riboswitches and agonists with antibiotic properties. Our proposed investigations will reveal important structure-function aspects of both purine riboswitches and the VS ribozyme. In addition, they will assist in the development of novel antibiotics that target RNA and help derive principles of RNA engineering that will be valuable in the development of RNA-based tools for biochemical and biomedical applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proteolytic regulation of mitochondrial dynamics in health and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALLING; GENETICS; MEMBRANE DYNAMICS; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; OPA1; PARL; PROTEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria are bean-shaped organelles that evolved from the symbiotic relationship of aerobic bacteria living inside the primordial animal cell. They were discovered over 50 years ago as the power plant of the cell: primary energy-generating systems that converts sugars into ATP. In the past 10 years, however, the study of mitochondria in laboratories across the world has become very intense, mainly because mitochondria have been found to be also a major store of calcium and the gatekeepers of programmed cell death, a process that when activated can cause neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson's and blindness, and when inhibited can cause cancer.  But how mitochondria regulate so many and diverse cellular functions?   Recent studies have shown that much of the way this organelle can do that is by changing its shape: becoming elongated like a "spaghetti", or fragmented in small units like "lentils", renders the mitochondrion competent to execute specific cellular programs, but not others. Since this breakthrough discovery, an increasing number of human diseases and metabolic disorders have been found to be caused by the inability of mitochondria to shift their shape in order to respond to the ever changing energetic and physiological needs of the cell.  Our laboratory has pioneered some of the main aspects related to the regulation of these mitochondrial dynamics. Thus, the research program illustrated here starts from our previous discoveries to explore, next, how mitochondrial enzymes that degrade proteins that execute the "spaghetti-to-lentil" transition control the various functions of this unique organelle. This is necessary in order to discover which of the many still uncharacterized "mitochondrial diseases" are specifically caused by a deficit in the activity of these enzymes, so that we can designed therapeutics that can treat them.

ResearchClassEN: MULTIPLE DISEASE RELEVANCE; NONE OF THE ABOVE
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES
TitreApplicationTitle: Map of cis-regulatory variants in human genome
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETICS; FUNCTIONAL VARIATION; GENE ANNOTATION; GENOMICS; HUMAN GENE EXPRESSION; POLYMORPHISMS
Abstract-Résumé: Studies of human genetic variation have in the past largely focused on rare genetic variants which alter protein structure, also known as coding variants. Contemporary genetic studies have indicated that genetic susceptibility to common diseases (such as asthma, diabetes or cardiovascular disease) can be due to common genetic variants (present in over 5% of population) that do not alter protein structure and these non-coding variants, sometimes also called regulatory variants, are presumed to influence how human genes are regulated in cells and tissues. Non-coding DNA accounts for over 95% of human genome sequence. A challenge to understand the non-coding genetic variation is that as compared to coding variation we do not understand the genetic code underlying human gene regulation. We have developed new approaches to directly measure impact of non-coding genetic variation in panels of human cells derived from healthy donors. As opposed to previous studies we can separately assess the maternal and paternal influence on gene expression or regulatory protein - DNA interaction based, this allele specificity provides noise-free assessment of regulatory function. Using these sensitive and comprehensive assays in multiple cell type we are able to uncover 5-10x more genetic variation directly involved in regulation of human genes than realized to date. This functional map of inter-individual regulatory variation forms the basis of understanding how genetic susceptibility to common disease can be coded in our DNA and consequently we can show that genetic susceptibility to common diseases can be mediated by these DNA variants altering gene regulation.Our approach offers the promise for global understanding genetic variation in the "dark matter" of human genome in health and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gfi1b regulates hematopoietic stem cell dormancy and blood mobilization
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; HEMATOPOIESIS; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; PROTEIN COMPLEXES; TRANSCRIPTION; ZINC FINGER DOMAINS
Abstract-Résumé: In leukemia, a form of blood cancer, cells from the bone marrow multiply without control and invade the bloodstream and other organs. This compromises the function of the red blood cells (oxygen transport) and the white blood cells (immune defense) and leads to severe illness and death. Patients with leukemia cannot always be cured by chemotherapy and have to undergo stem cell therapy. During this therapy, the entire blood producing system (and with it all cancer cells) of a leukemia patient are killed off by irradiation and is then replaced by a new and healthy blood producing system by giving patients blood stem cells from a healthy donor by infusion. These blood stem cells are then capable of regenerating the entire blood producing system. However this therapy still fails in about 20% of all cases and the leukemia patients die during the procedure mostly because the transplanted blood stem cells do not give rise to enough new blood cells in the patient. One reason is that blood stem cells are normally very passive and are dormant in a defined place in the bones (called the endosteal niche). After transfusion, the transplanted done stem cells go again back to their niche this time in the patient, where they are kept in a dormant state. We have observed that a protein called Gfi1b regulates where the stem cells reside in the bone and whether they are active or not. We have generated a mouse model enabling us to switch the Gfi1b gene off, and when we do this, suddenly the stem cells become activated, start to expand drastically and also leave their niche but do not loose their function. We wish to study, how this regulatory protein (Gfi1b) works and in particular, how it can determine where blood stem cells are localized and how it restricts their activation. The ability to activate and mobilize stem cells by antagonizing Gfi1 would certainly be beneficial for leukemia patients that undergo a stem cell therapy and have received a stem cell transplant.

TitreApplicationTitle: In vivo imaging of visual stimulation-evoked dendritic arbor growth and synaptogenesis in the CNS: Role of synaptic transmission and downstream signaling in brain circuit development
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY-DEPENDENT GROWTH; CALCIUM IMAGING; DENDRITIC ARBOR GROWTH; ELECTROPORATIVE TRANSFECTION; GLUTAMATERGIC TRANSMISSION; IN VIVO IMAGING; METAPLASTICITY; PKMZ; PLASTICITY; TWO-PHOTON IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: It is becoming clear that numerous common and devastating neurological disorders, like Autism Spectrum Disorders, Schizophrenia and Epilepsy can be caused by abnormal brain development. Here, we propose to employ advanced imaging techniques to directly image brain structural growth during critical periods sensitive to disruption, in order to understand normal and pathological brain circuit development. These imaging techniques provide high-resolution 3D images of brain neurons and movies of neuron growth as brain circuits are formed. In addition, using fluorescent dyes sensitive to neuronal firing, we propose to directly image network activity in the awake brain.  By controlling activity and gene expression of individual brain neurons, we are able to test the roles of external and intrinsic factors in regulating structural and functional growth. Results will identify novel proteins involved in developmental brain plasticity that may offer new targets for developing therapeutics or preventative treatments to counter developmental neurological disorders.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of anaplerosis in glucose-stimulated insulin release.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; INSULIN SECRETION; ISLET FUNCTION; METABOLISM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PANCREATIC BETA-CELL
Abstract-Résumé: A primary defect in type 2 diabetes mellitus is the inability of the insulin-secreting beta-cells to sense and respond to changes in blood sugar levels. How insulin-secreting beta-cells sense glucose is incompletely understood. This lack of understanding hinders development of new cell-based and drug therapies for both major forms of diabetes. Our group has developed a modern set of tools that provide a unique opportunity to gain major new insights in this area. The goals of the laboratory are to apply these newly developed tools to study stimulus/secretion coupling mechanisms in insulin-secreting beta-cells. These studies will provide new insights into relevant pathways involved in sensing sugar levels in the blood by insulin-secreting beta-cells and will have important applications for therapy of both major forms of diabetes. More specifically, since the demand for human islets for transplantation far exceeds the supply, our findings may influence genetic engineering approaches for creation of cells or cell lines that can be used for transplantation therapy to treat diabetes mellitus.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Exploration of global control mechanisms of endosomal and phagosomal chemistries and their consequences to macrophage and dendritic cell function in health and disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTATION; CELL BIOLOGY; ENDOSOME; FLUOROMETRY; IMMUNOLOGY; MACROPHAGE; MICROSCOPY; PHAGOSOME; PROTEOLYSIS; REDOX
Abstract-Résumé: Macrophages and dendritic cells are cells of the immune system known as phagocytes (meaning "eating cells").  They are named for their ability to engulf particulate material by a process called phagocytosis.  Following phagocytosis, the engulfed material is broken down within compartments known as phagosomes.  This process has a diverse range of functions in normal growth and development, but also has a critical role in our body's immune defense system.  When macrophages and dendritic cells phagocytose (eat) microorganisms, they break down their proteins (also called antigens) in their phagosomes into small pieces that can be recognized by other cells.  The macrophages and dendritic cells then show these pieces of antigen to T-cells, triggering a powerful immune reaction that our body can remember.  This is important in our defense against foreign organisms, as well as in disease where our immune system mistakes our own cells as invaders (such as in autoimmunity).  Despite their pivotal role, there are fundamental gaps in our understanding of how phagosomes function.   We have evidence that a particular chemistry within the phagosome, known as the redox potential, influences how macrophages and dendritic cells digest protein antigens.  We think that this can control which parts of an antigen are presented and could have consequences to subsequent events in acquired immunity.  In particular, in many autoimmune diseases, which piece of an antigen is presented is critical to how our body reacts.  This proposal aims to further understand how the redox potential affects the way phagosomes process antigen, and in turn, how it influences which parts of the antigen are presented.    This basic scientific research is broad reaching as it has the potential to profoundly impact human health.  In addition to better understanding how our immune system works, this work may lead to different strategies in the management of autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of CRTh2 and its role in allergic disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGY; CELL CULTURE/TRANSFECTION; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE REGULATION; HUMAN TH2; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISM
Abstract-Résumé: Allergic diseases such as asthma are mediated by a number of cell types, particularly T helper type 2 (Th2) cells and eosinophils. Both these cell types express a protein called CRTh2, which helps them enter the site of allergic inflammation, such as the lung, nose or skin. CRTh2 also regulates the production of pro-allergy mediators like the Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13. This proposal is focused on understanding expression of CRTh2. Since genetic variation in CRTh2 is associated with higher risk of developing allergic asthma, we will also examine whether these single changes in DNA sequence change expression of CRTh2 and/or are more frequent in certain types of asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Randomized Ablation-based atrial Fibrillation rhythm control versus rate control Trial in patients with heart failure and high burden Atrial Fibrillation (RAFT-AF)
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; CATHETER ABLATION; HEART FAILURE; MORBIDITY; MORTALITY; MULTICENTRE; OPTIMAL MEDICAL THERAPY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation and heart failure are two common heart conditions that are encountered with an increase in death and suffering.  When both these two conditions occur in a patient, the patient's prognosis is poor with a reduced quality of life. These patients are frequently admitted to the hospital. The treatment of atrial fibrillation, in heart failure patients, is extremely challenging. Two options for managing the atrial fibrillation are permitting the atrial fibrillation to continue but controlling the heart rate, or to convert the atrial fibrillation rhythm back to normal and try to maintain the heart in sinus rhythm. Until now, the method to keep the patient in normal sinus rhythm is with antiarrhythmic drugs. Studies using anti-arrhythmic drugs to control the rhythm failed to show any survival benefit when compared with permitting the patient to be in atrial fibrillation. In the last few years, new development in techniques and technologies now enable catheter ablation (cauterization of tissue in the heart with a catheter) to be a successful treatment in abolishing atrial fibrillation and that this approach is better than antiarrhythmic drug to control the rhythm. However, there has not been any long-term study to determine whether catheter ablation to abolish atrial fibrillation in heart failure patients would improve mortality. This study is to compare the effect of catheter ablation-based atrial fibrillation rhythm control to rate control in patients with heart failure and high burden atrial fibrillation on cardiovascular mortality. We will also be assessing the cost-effectiveness of this treatment strategy and the life quality for these patients. This study may have a dramatic impact on the way we manage these patients with atrial fibrillation and heart failure and may improve the outlook and well being of these patients.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Myocardial Production of Erythropoietin and hemoglobin variants
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC; CYTOKINES; ERYTHROPOIETIN; HEART FAILURE; HEMOGLOBIN; RODENT
Abstract-Résumé: Although the kidney, and to a lesser extent the liver, can increase serum EPO levels in response to hypoxia, it is unclear if they are the sole or primary contributor of serum EPO levels. Recently, EPO production has been reported in several non-renal tissues of mammals (e.g., brain, skeletal muscle, hair follicles, and uterus).  While EPO's role was thought to be related strictly to erythropoiesis, it was the discovery of the presence of the EPO receptor in other tissues (e.g., heart, limb muscle and brain) that raised the possibility of EPO signaling unrelated to erythropoiesis, i.e., extrahaematopoietic effects.  Exogenous EPO administration has been reported to reduce infarct size and prevent remodeling after acute myocardial infarction.  We have recent preliminary evidence establishing that the heart produces EPO even during normoxia which increases with hypoxia.  Furthermore, we have establish that induction of cardiac EPO helps to markedly reduce left ventricular hypertrophy and preserves cardiac function in response to chronic hypertension, suggesting that endogenous EPO plays an important role in enabling the heart to adapt to chronically working at high workloads without leading to the development of heart failure.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - C
ClasseRechercheFR: GLAUCOME; TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: The Polygenic Nature of Open-Angle Glaucoma: Dissecting the Roles of Modifier Genes for the Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: BLINDNESS; GLAUCOMA; LINKAGE AND ASSOCIATION STUDIES; MOLECULAR GENETICS; PHENOTYPE/GENOTYPE CORRELATION STUDIES; POLYGENIC - MODIFIER GENES; QUANTITATIVE TRAITS; STATISTICAL GENETICS; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: The term "glaucoma" encompasses a large group of eye diseases characterized by a special type of blindness that starts from the periphery of our vision. The most common form of glaucoma is primary open-angle glaucoma. It affects 2 % of the Canadian population aged over 40 years old, or about 300,000 Canadians. Because primary open-angle glaucoma is painless and progress very slowly, almost a third of the persons who are sick, do not know that they have the disorder and are becoming blind. At least 30 genes cause glaucoma but only a few of them have been identified. They have names like myocilin, optineurin, WDR36, NTF-4 and FOXC1. During the past 10 years, our research group has been following a large number of glaucoma families. Our team discovered a few years ago that many old individuals have still their vision healthy despite the fact that they were carrying mutations in the myocilin gene which is causing aggressive forms of glaucoma. These elders should be severely affected but they showed no signs of glaucoma. Our finding raised the interesting hypothesis that "good" glaucoma genes, named protective modifier genes, maintain our vision healthy by preventing the effects of the "bad" glaucoma genes, like myocilin. The goal of our research project is to identify these "good" modifier genes using two very large glaucoma families. We will first localize these modifier genes within small regions of our DNA. Once this mapping is done, we will characterize these good genes by exploiting the new science of genomics. Identification of these 'good' glaucoma genes will offer powerful approaches for discovering novel drugs to treat and perhaps prevent glaucoma effectively. Their identification will also help to understand how the "good" glaucoma genes prevent blindness in people who should have been affected.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Structure and function of neuronal calcium channels - contributions of splice variation to physiology and pathophysiology
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM CHANNEL; CDNA CLONING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EPILEPSY; MIGRAINE; MUTATION; SPLICING
Abstract-Résumé: The entry of calcium ions into cells is mediated by a class of protein that responds to electrical signals by opening a calcium selective pore (called calcium channels). Calcium channels are involved in a large number of normal physiological processes including muscle contraction, hormone secretion and all electrical signaling in the nervous system. The alteration of calcium entry into cells is highly detrimental and some human diseases can be treated by drugs that inhibit calcium channels including, migraines, chronic pain, epilepsy, hypertension and heart failure. Utilizing gene cloning techniques we have isolated a family of ten genes encoding calcium channels. To characterize the channels outside of the body we introduce the cloned genes into cultured cell lines. By determining the electrical and pharmacological properties of the cloned calcium channels the work has accounted for many of the properties of calcium channels found in nerve, smooth muscle and heart. We have found that in addition to the ten calcium channel genes, many more functional channel subtypes can be generated by a process known as "splicing". The recent work shows that in genetic animal models of human disease only certain calcium channel splice variants contribute to the disease pathophysiology. The results suggest that genetic mutations preferentially affect only a fraction of the possible channel subtypes and the proposal aims to investigate the underlying basis for where each of the variants is expressed in cells and tissues, when during development each is expressed, and how particular genetic mutations selectively affect channel properties to cause physiological aspects relevant to disease. By identifying the specific calcium channel slice variants involved in disease the work will provide the pharmaceutical industry with new and valuable tools for the design and testing of new drugs predicted to be more specific and to have less side-effects than current treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Project Ice Storm: Continuing Effects of Prenatal Stress on Children's Physical, Cognitive and Behavioural Development in Adolescence.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; CHILD DEVELOPMENT; COGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT; OBESITY; PRENATAL STRESS; PSYCHOEDUCATIONAL ASSESSMENT; PSYCHOPATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Retrospective studies show that exposure to prenatal maternal stress (PNMS) increases risk for learning and behaviour problems that emerge in adolescence when dramatic brain changes occur; but little is known about how this works. The peak age at onset of psychiatric disorders is 14 years. Prospective, longitudinal studies are needed to understand how PNMS contributes to problems in adolescence. However, since researchers cannot stress pregnant women, most studies rely on non- randomly distributed maternal anxiety or life events during pregnancy. Without randomization, the effects of the objective exposure and subsequent subjective reaction to an event cannot be separated. Project Ice Storm is the world's largest prospective study of PNMS from a natural disaster. Data on pregnant women's objective exposure and subjective reactions to the 1998 Quebec ice storm was collected, and their children have been assessed regularly since the age of 6 months. Longitudinal analyses show that, the higher objective and subjective PNMS levels are associated with more childhood behavioural problems, and poorer cognitive, motor, and physical outcomes through the age of 11½ years, and perhaps beyond. The goal of this renewal is to determine the extent to which PNMS continues to explain individual differences in the children's development in adolescence, and to determine how the hormonal changes of puberty might influence this development. Children will be seen and assessed at the ages of 13½, and mothers will complete ratings of their children at these same times. This unique study will allow us to determine the extent to which PNMS influences problems that emerge during adolescence. Our data will show how PNMS predicts long-term trajectories of cognitive, behavioural and physical development. This knowledge will aid us in developing recommendations for limiting harm to the foetus following stress in pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Managing the Dysexecutive Syndrome following traumatic brain injury: An ecologically valid rehabilitation approach.
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN INJURY; COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION; EXECUTIVE COGNITIVE FUNCTION; REHABILITATION; SELF-REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Successful community participation following acquired brain injury (ABI)continues to be an elusive goal for patients, clinicians and researchers.  Our pilot work on a strategy training approach (Cognitive Orientation to Occupational Performance) shows that community dwelling survivors of ABI can significantly improve performance on self-identified real-world performance problems and that they can transfer this learning to improve goals not trained in the treatment sessions.  We will compare this experimental treatment with treatment as usual using a randomized controlled trial.  We will also interview survivors, their significant others and clinicians regarding their experiences with each intervention to help us discover what works best.

TitreApplicationTitle: Kawasaki Disease: On our way to unraveling the pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; AUTOIMMUNITY; CYTOKINES; MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASES; SUPERANTIGENS; T-CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The overall objective of our project is to understand why the body damages the blood vessels in Kawasaki disease (KD), the number one cause of acquired heart disease in Canadian children. In KD our body's defense system, the immune system, responds to an infectious trigger and somehow this response gets out of hand and leads to a battle against both the infection and also against our own blood vessels, specifically the coronary arteries. An infection-triggered immune response directed against our own bodies is a common theme in many autoimmune diseases including arthritis. We have identified a final common pathway resulting in production of enzymes (Matrix Metalloproteinases-MMPs) which eat away the blood vessel walls leading to aneurysm formation in KD. Many different cell types, including blood cells and cells in the heart and blood vessels are able to make MMPs via different pathways. Very young children are affected with KD, with 18 months being the most common age. To answer questions about the immune system and heart damage, we must have immune cells and affected heart tissue, this is not possible in children with KD, thus necessitating an animal model. Our model of KD is the model best suited to answering these research questions. This project will identify which cells, molecules and pathways govern the production of MMPs and destroy blood vessels, and how these cells and pathways interact. Understanding these mechanisms will allow us to stop them by blocking the molecules, pathways or enzymes responsible for disease. Our work in the animal model will be used to identify possible new biomarkers, to help predict which children are prone to more severe disease, thus identifying who will need more treatment. We will confirm our findings by studying the relationships between biomarkers from a blood test with coronary disease in affected children. Ultimately, our work will help improve treatment, outcome and quality of life in affected children and their families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Drivers and Consequences of Immune Quiescence in HIV Exposed Seronegative Individuals from Nairobi, Kenya
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES/CHEMOKINES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HIV EXPOSED SERONEGATIVE; HIV INFECTION; IMMUNE QUIESCENCE; IRF-1
Abstract-Résumé: One of the hallmarks of HIV disease is the inappropriate over-activation of the immune response which can lead to serious detrimental effects to the infected person including providing more targets for the HIV virus to infect.  Our research group has identified commercial sex workers from Nairobi Kenya who, despite counseling and provision of condoms, are highly exposed to HIV.  Amazingly, despite years of such high risk activity they remain HIV uninfected.  We have recently determined, quite unexpectedly, that a common feature of these women is that their immune systems remain calm and are not as highly activated as women who do become HIV infected.  We have termed this phenomenon Immune Quiescence. This study proposes to investigate the factors that are unique in the HIV exposed uninfected women that cause their immune systems to resist inappropriate activation and assess the consequences of that lower immune activation.  As sex work is a power immune stimulant itself, we will study the effect on the immune system of stopping sex work for a period of time.  If we can understand what is driving the state of Immune Quiescence perhaps we can determine how to mimic that state in other at-risk individuals and thereby protect them from acquiring HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optical Coherence Tomography for Intraoperative Imaging During Skull Base Neurosurgical Procedures
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL ANEURYSM; DOPPLER MICROVASCULAR IMAGING; INTRAOPERATIVE IMAGING; NEUROSURGERY; OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY; PITUITARY TUMOR
Abstract-Résumé: Newly diagnosed and mortality rates from pituitary tumors and cerebral aneurysms occur at a rate of ~325 (~220 deaths) and ~3,300 (~2,200 deaths) per year, respectively. Combined these central nervous system diseases present a significant health care burden to Canada. This research proposal focuses on the development and feasibility testing of a high-resolution hand-held imaging probe that may be beneficial to guide interventional surgical procedures, such as identifying tumor boundaries during pituitary tumor removal, defining risk factors associated with aneurysm rupture or guide the placement of aneurysm clips used to stop bleeding in the brain.  Specifically, we will compare our high-resolution images to that of real pituitary and aneurysm samples to create an atlas of images for use in identifying important disease related features, such as blood vessel wall thickness or the presence of tumor related tissue structures. In addition, pre-clinical animal imaging of both aneurysms and pituitary tumors will be required to test the accuracy of disease detection and to determine clinical utility prior to use in humans.  We expect this high-resolution imaging innovation will not only aid in surgical guidance for pituitary and cerebral aneurysm procedures, but the groundwork established by this research may also be extended into additional areas of surgical guidance, including carotid artery imaging for stroke prediction or cancer therapy monitoring.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analyses of Polycomb group (PcG)/trithorax group(trxG) dependent mechanisms governing vertebrate neural development
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHROMATIN REMODELING; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; DEVELOPMENTAL NEUROBIOLOGY; EPIGENETICS; MOUSE GENETICS; NEURONAL DEVELOPMENT; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: As we develop from embryos to adults and throughout our adult lives as our tissues (such as skin or blood) regenerate, our cells must remember precisely what, where, and who they are, but also who they are not.  Cells, like people, pass through different stages of development and in order to develop normally they cannot get stuck or slip backwards.  To assure that they stay on the right developmental track cells use " cellular memory".   Cellular memory can be achieved by wrapping genes that should be turned off very tightly so that they are difficult to unravel and turn on .  The proteins that do this are called "Polycomb Group" regulators.   Alternatively, the genes, that a cell really needs, can be left unwrapped so that they will stay on.   The proteins that leave genes unwrapped belong to the "trithorax group".   How these regulators recognize which genes should be wrapped up ( turned off) or unwrapped is still largely a mystery.  Recently we identified a cue, known as a Polycomb response element (PRE)- that allows these regulators to wrap or unwrap a gene important for neural development.  Using this PRE we will analyze how genes are turned off or on so effectively.  What happens when cellular memory fails? One of the most dramatic and tragic examples of what happens when nerves stop developing normally is seen in children with autism.  These appear normal until ~2 years of age, when they not only stop reaching normal developmental landmarks, but they regress.  Another example can be seen in cancer.  For example, when cells that would normally develop into mature blood cells stall and instead become an immature population that begins to expand and overgrow, this can cause leukemia.  Thus, understanding how cellular memory works (and so, in future, how it may be corrected)  may help us develop approaches to restabilize cellular memory,and, thereby, possibly reverse or arrest some neurobiological disorders and cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: SR-related proteins and the regulation of gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; ANIMAL MODELS; BIOINFORMATICS; GENE REGULATION; HIGH-THROUGHPUT RNA SEQUENCING; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION SCREENS; SPLICING ASSAYS; SR PROTEINS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Alternative splicing (AS) is an essential step in the regulation of gene expression and allows a single gene to specify multiple genetic messages (mRNAs) and corresponding protein products encoded by these mRNAs. Approximately 90% of human genes produce multiple mRNAs by AS and it is estimated that this process can result in generation of orders of magnitude more proteins than there are genes. Alternative splicing is therefore one of the main processes responsible for the generation of protein diversity required for the development of complex metazoan organisms. In the last funding period we discovered and characterized a new protein (nSR100) that regulates the splicing process, specifically in the nervous system. In the present proposal, we describe experiments directed at developing a more detailed understanding of the role of nSR100 in the regulation of genes required for the formation of neurons and the fully developed adult nervous system. These studies will pave the way for a more detailed understanding the molecular basis of complex neurological diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of HDL induced signaling and role in protection against coronary artery atheroscelrosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION; CORONARY ARTERY; HDL; HEART DISEASE; MACROPHAGES; SCAVENGER RECEPTOR; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: High density lipoproteins are called "good cholesterol" because high levels of HDL in blood protect against heart disease. This protection is due to the ability of HDL to prevent the accumulation of fat that clogs arteries and leads to heart attacks and stroke. The research we are proposing in this application aims to understand how HDL interacts with cells in the artery wall to bring about this protection. We are proposing to analyze the molecular events that are triggered by the interaction of HDL with different cells in the artery wall, and will test the roles of some of the cellular machinery that is either involved in the interaction or which is activated by it. We will then test the roles of the key cellular factors in a unique mouse model of coronary artery disease and heart attack. These mice lack the HDL receptor and develop blocked coronary arteries and heart attack when fed a high fat diet. We showed that we can prevent this by transplanting stem cells containing the intact HDL receptor gene--these stem cells go on to give rise to all blood cells including macrophages, which play a key role in the formation of blocked arteries. This model system will allow us to test the roles of other genes that might be involved in this pathway, downstream of the HDL receptor. The results from this study will give us important information on the molecular and cellular pathways that underlie how HDL protects against hardening of the arteries and will lead to new targets for drug development and new ideas for treatment of disease in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Neonatal Critical Care through Real Time Analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH INFORMATICS; HEART RATE VARIABILITY; NEONATAL INTENSIVE CARE; NOSOCOMIAL INFECTION; REAL-TIME PATIENT MONITORING
Abstract-Résumé: Premature birth, defined as birth before 37 completed weeks estation, has been identified as one of the most important health problems for babies in developed nations. Immature newborn babies often have quite complex medical conditions that require the sophisticated care provided within level III Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs). In 2009, the March of Dimes Foundation released a report that shows that premature birth is actually on the rise.  Doctors and nurses who look after these babies within NICUs need to quickly and accurately analyse and interpret data shown on a number of medical devices to provide optimal care for these babies while they grow and develop. Despite the availability of newer information technologies in the NICU, most tasks performed by neonatologists, nurses, and other healthcare providers are manual as there is no system which integrates the data from all the different medical devices used on a baby on an ongoing basis. Recent medical research has discovered that nosocomial infection and other conditions of the premature and/or critically ill newborn may have common early indicators in aspects that are seemingly unrelated such as heart rate and breathing rate. In our research we have created a system that is capable of receiving and analysing a range of data from the babies and looking for patterns in a flexible way. We have begun initial testing for nosocomial infection in real-time. Within this application we will use retrospective analysis of historical data to look for early onset indicators for two other conditions and then test algorithms that watch for these behabiours in real time.

TitreApplicationTitle: Synaptic organisation of dorsal horn modulatory circuits
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL BEHAVIOUR; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; NERVE LESIONS; PAIN
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain is a major health concern which affects all Canadians. From whatever cause, all of us either experience it ourselves or have friends and loved ones which do. Chronic pain is responsible for considerable suffering which is not always well-managed by our healthcare system. One of the reasons for this is that we are still ignorant about the mechanisms that contribute to its initiation and maintenance. The research proposed in this grant aims at studying these mechanisms at the level of the spinal cord in two animal models of chronic pain. These models reflect the two types of pain most frequently encountered by Canadians, pain following nerve lesions (neuropathic pain) and pain associated with chronic inflammation and arthritis. In our research, we will focus on the region of the spinal cord where pain-related fibres terminate.  This region is of interest as it is the area of the central nervous system where the first modulation of pain-related information takes place, before being forwarded to the brain. Our objective is to study the connections in the spinal cord and function of the two main populations of nerve fibres which transmit pain-related information from the source of injury to the spinal cord. Our studies will assess the participation of each nerve fibre population in these two models of chronic pain. For this, we will use a combination of methods, including advanced microscopy techniques, the latest means to label the connections of neurons and a technique that will selectively destroy the nerve fibre populations involved in pain processing.  We will identify the substances, called neurotransmitters, which are released from these neurons, and will assess the changes in animal pain-related behaviour. The research under this grant should provide important clues that will be of use in the future management of chronic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanism of Self-renewal and Mesoderm Development of Human Pluripotent Stem Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFERENTIATION; E-CADHERIN; HUMAN PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; L1TD1; OCT4; REPROGRAMMING; SELF-RENEWAL; WNT
Abstract-Résumé: Embryonic stem (ES) cells hold strong therapeutic promises. To realize their application potentials, it is essential to understand what makes them self-renew (unlimited division) and what drives them to differentiate (becoming adult tissues for cell-based therapy). Our current studies suggest that one cell-cell binding protein contribute to the self-renewal and subsequent differentiation of ES cells. This cell-cell binding protein requires and connects to an adaptor protein inside the cells, which is essential for making cells stick together. Interestingly, this adaptor protein is also a key player of Wnt pathways. Wnt is a complex network of proteins and has been shown to play crucial roles in both self-renewal and differentiation of stem cells. However, it remains unclear how one signaling pathway can exert two opposite functions. In this proposal, we will attempt to study the underlying molecular mechanism. It is expected that successful completion of this project will enable efficient differentiation of embryonic stem cells into a given cell type for stem cell-based therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tissu adipeux humain reconstruit par génie tissulaire: substituts endothélialisés et compatibles avec la clinique
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOGENESE; ANGIOGENESE; CELLULES ENDOTHELIALES; CELLULES MESENCHYMATEUSES; CELLULES SOUCHES POSTNATALES; GREFFE; GENIE TISSULAIRE; TISSU ADIPEUX
Abstract-Résumé: Le genie tissulaire permet de recreer en laboratoire plusieurs types d'organes qui peuvent etre greffes afin de remplacer les tissus malades. Les tissus reconstruits en laboratoire permettent aussi de mieux connaitre et comprendre plusieurs phenomenes biologiques. L'objectif principal de ce programme de recherche est de produire, a l'aide de techniques de genie tissulaire, des tissus adipeux humains reconstruits (TAR) qui seront compatibles avec de futures applications cliniques. Il s'agit de prendre des cellules souches adultes extraites d'un petit morceau de gras humain, puis de cultiver ces cellules en laboratoire dans des conditions qui permettent de produire un tissu adipeux de rechange qui a une certaine epaisseur. Ces conditions de culture permettent de reconstruire in vitro un tissu adipeux qui ressemble au tissu original (cellules entourees de matrice extracellulaire, sans ajouter de biomateriau ou de produit synthetique ou animal). Ces tissus sont donc de meilleurs modeles que les cellules en culture conventionnelle. L'incorporation de cellules endotheliales durant la production des tissus va determiner si l'ajout d'un reseau de petits capillaires sanguins va permettre aux greffons de mieux survivre et garder leur volume a long terme chez l'animal. Du point de vue clinique, reconstruire des tissus adipeux par auto-assemblage a partir des cellules du patient lui-meme et en utilisant des milieux ne contenant aucune proteine animale sera tres avantageux et securitaire. En effet, ces tissus pourraient ainsi etre utilises dans le futur pour remplacer les tissus perdus ou endommages suite a des accidents, a la resection de tumeurs ou a cause de maladies hereditaires ou acquises (lipoatrophies). Ces tissus serviront aussi de modeles originaux pour etudier en laboratoire les effets de l'inflammation sur les capillaires sanguins et les cellules du gras humain. Ultimement, ces resultats aideront a mieux comprendre et ameliorer la survie des tissus greffes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanical and epithelial cell regulation of airway smooth muscle contractile function
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY EPITHELIAL CELLS; AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; BIOMEDICAL INSTRUMENTATION; CELL PHENOTYPE; CONTRACTILE TONE; CONTRACTION; CYTOSKELETAL IMAGING; MECHANICAL STRESS; SUBSTRATE STIFFNESS; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: It is the airway smooth muscle that surrounds the airways in the lung that ultimately causes constriction leading to difficulty breathing in asthma. Asthma alters the airways in ways that can grow more smooth muscle and make the muscle contract more. These changes include changes in the tissue that surrounds the smooth muscle, changes that increase the constant, baseline contraction of the muscle, as well as changes in the airway epithelial cells that line the inside surfaces of the airways. We think that some or all of these changes can lead to changes in the proteins inside smooth muscle cells that can cause more smooth muscle to grow or to become more contractile. Both of these changes can lead to worsening of airway function in asthma, leading to more narrowed airways during an asthma attack. We will do experiments to examine these effects, using airway smooth muscle and airway epithelial cells, grown on special surfaces and in special gels. We will measure the changes in the growth of airway smooth muscle and changes in the ability of the airway smooth muscle to contract, as well as changes in the structure of the cells. In this way we will determine which of these changes outside the smooth muscle, are more important to changing how smooth muscle contracts, and which are most important for worsening airway constriction. This will help us decide how best in future to develop methods to stop these changes in the airway smooth muscle, and improve the health and quality of life of patients that suffer from asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies of hepatitis C virus infection using activity-based protein profiling
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; HOST-VIRUS INTERACTIONS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; REPLICATION; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a serious health issue affecting more than 250,000 Canadians, with no cure currently available and limited treatment options. Thus, there is a strong interest in elucidating the role of human and viral proteins to better understand the cellular pathways essential for the life cycle of this virus and thereby develop novel diagnostic markers and new therapeutic drugs against HCV. While many proteins have functions that are well characterized and understood, little is known of the complex interactions of the entire cellular protein pool. Recently, we developed molecular tools, activity-based probes, aimed at understanding the protein functions of entire enzyme families. By applying these tools on human cells and HCV-infected mouse models, we have shown that the activity of the liver enzyme carboxylesterase 1 (CES1) is influenced by HCV and is necessary for efficient viral infection. In the current proposal, we intend to use activity-based probes to understand how the activity of CES1 correlates with HCV infectivity in human liver biopsies and if CES1 activity can be used as an activity-based marker of HCV infection. As HCV modifies the lipid metabolism of the liver, novel activity-based probes will also be used to analyze the effects of HCV on lipid enzymes such as fatty acid synthase (FAS). Using our mouse model for HCV infection, we will assess and visualize the effects of known CES1 and FAS inhibitory drugs on cellular lipids and HCV levels using modern microscopes. If proven successful, these inhibitors could be developed into new drugs against HCV infection.

Abstract-Résumé: The overall objective of the proposed study is to evaluate timeliness and appropriateness of care for patients with possible and definite breast cancer. We will account for the patient care experience from pre-diagnosis to completion of treatment in order to identify and quantify the current roadblocks in the health care system to timely access to quality cancer care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Behavioural and neural examinations of disgust in healthy individuals and obsessive compulsive disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFECTIVE NEURSOCIENCE; COGNITION; COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE; EMOTION
Abstract-Résumé: The capacity for higher order cognition and ethical behaviour are pointed to as the pinnacle of human evolution. The present research program will consider how evolutionarily older parts of the brain associated with primitive emotional responses also play a critical role in higher order cognition. Using multiple approaches, including reports of emotional experience, facial expression analysis, and functional magnetic resonance imaging, we will examine how emotions and evolutionarily older biological systems have a pervasive influence on cognition. To do so will focus on disgust, examines its basis in oral distaste and extension in the moral domain. Further we will examine whether, Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, a disorder characterized by pathological disgust, increases the role emotions play in moral judgment. Findings from this research may aid in understanding how emotions can both enhance cognition but also render it dysfunctional, resulting in cognitive impairments central to mental health disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chaperone-mediated protein quality control in mitochondria
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CHAPERONE; FRIEDREICH ATAXIA; MITOCHONDRIA; MITOCHONDRIAL DISEASES; PROTEIN QUALITY CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria play many important roles in cellular homeostasis. They are involved in energy production through oxidative phosphorylation and beta-oxidation of fatty acids, in initiation of the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis and in calcium homeostasis modulation. Recently, the importance of maintaining protein quality control in this organelle has been demonstrated by the identification of diseases associated with members of this control system. Interestingly, organisms having an enhanced protein quality control system tend to have an increased longevity and an enhanced resistance to stress. As mitochondria are key players in different important cellular processes and since the lost of their integrity can have severe cellular consequences and is linked to aging and neurological disorders in human, we will investigate the modulation and the mechanisms of the mitochondrial protein quality control system during lifespan and validate them in a disease model, Freidreich ataxia. In addition to unveiling hidden facets of protein maintenance in mitochondria, the work should highlight new ways to fight against diseases involving mitochondrial dysfunction defective protein folding and suggest alternative therapeutics for slowing of the aging process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Behavioural and Functional Neuroimaging Studies of Recent and Remote Spatial Memory in Humans
Keywords-MotsClés: AMNESIA; BRAIN LESIONS; DEMENTIA; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; HIPPOCAMPUS; PARIETAL LOBES; RECENT SPATIAL MEMORY; REMOTE SPATIAL MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Memory of our spatial environment is crucial for daily life. We rely on spatial memory to get around at home and in the world, and to locate objects, buildings, and other landmarks.  Without spatial memory we literally would be lost. This proposal is concerned with brain structures implicated in the acquisition and retention of spatial memories of large scale environments, such as downtown Toronto, and the possible transformation of these memories with time and experience. The acquisition and retention of spatial memories are dependent on the hippocampus, a structure deep in the temporal lobes. Damage to it impairs newly-acquired spatial memories. Once one has become very familiar with a spatial environment, retaining and retrieving such memories for the purpose of navigation is preserved after hippocampal damage, suggesting that the memories are now dependent on other structures. The question we are asking is whether spatial memories of highly familiar environments that are not dependent on the hippocampus are fundamentally different from memories which are, and if so, what is the nature of that difference. Some of our research suggests that spatial memories are highly detailed and precise if they are dependent on the hippocampus, but more schematic and coarse if they are not. Experiments are designed to test this hypothesis by having people make decisions about distances and direction between landmarks, as well as the configuration and appearance of landmarks, and the spatial context around them. By imaging the activity of the brain of healthy people while taking these tests, we will be able to see whether activity in the hippocampus, and other brain regions, is influenced by the precision required in these tests, and whether that varies with the individual's familiarity with the environment. We also plan to test people with brain damage due to trauma or disease, such as Alzheimer's, to see if spatial memory of new and familiar environments is affected.

Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH DISPARITY; IMMIGRANT HEALTH; NEIGHBOURHOOD EFFECT; PERINATAL HEALTH; SOCIOECONOMIC POSITION
Abstract-Résumé: Despite marked reductions in infant mortality over the past several decades, the rate of premature birth, a key determinant of infant mortality and morbidity, has remained the same or even increased over the same period in many countries. Moreover, socioeconomic disparities in pregnancy outcomes such as preterm birth and stillbirth persist in many developing and developed countries, including Canada. The magnitude and patterns of socioeconomic disparities are known to differ across ethnic and cultural sub-groups. Such differences have important implications for the health of Canadians, because approximately one in five Canadians are immigrants, making Canada highly multi-ethnic. Pregnancy and birth outcomes such as the infant mortality rate are not only good measures of current population health but are also predictive of the future health of the population, because health in early life predicts health later in life. Therefore, achieving socioeconomic equity in pregnancy outcomes is an important public health goal. However, existing scientific evidence on socioeconomic disparities in pregnancy and birth outcomes is limited, owing to the lack of detailed socioeconomic and ethno-cultural background information in routinely collected data. Our research will create a national database by linking the national database of pregnancy and birth outcomes (the previously-linked Canadian stillbirth, live birth, and infant death database) with detailed characteristics of parents ascertained in the censuses of 1996 and 2006, so as to be able to systematically examine the patterns of perinatal health in Canada across social, racial, and ethnic groups and over time. This study will provide nation-wide assessment of perinatal health disparities not previously possible in Canada, including robust results of socioeconomic differences in perinatal health for immigrants, visible minorities and Aboriginal people, at both the individual and neighbourhood levels.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Towards a better understanding of Kawasaki Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; CO-STIMULATION; CORONARY ARTERY; DISEASE MODELING; GENETICS; INFLAMMATION; KAWASAKI DISEASE; T-CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The overall goal of this project is to understand how the immune system turns on and stays on and attacks parts of our body in Kawaski Disease (KD). The battle between the immune system and the blood vessels leads to vasculitis and in the case of children the most common cause of vasculitis is KD. The blood vessels most commonly damaged are the coronary arteries, making KD the number one cause of acquired heart disease in Canadian children. There is much evidence from a disease model and from affected children that molecules controlling the immune system are dysfunctional in KD. The goal of my research is to understand what is defective (the genes and molecules), how (the mechanisms) these defects lead to an uncontrolled immune response. Very young children are affected with KD, with 18 months being the most common age. To answer questions about the immune system and heart damage, we must have immune cells and affected heart tissue, this is not possible in children with KD, thus necessitating an animal model. Our model of KD is the model best suited to answering these research questions. This project will identify which genes, molecules and pathways govern the uncontrolled immune response in KD. We will use the animal model to find new biomarkers to help predict which children are at risk for developing more severe disease and confirm these findings in affected children by studying the usefulness of these biomarkers from blood to predict coronary disease in affected children. Our overall objective is not only to understand why blood vessels are damaged in KD, but more importantly, to improve treatment, outcome and quality of life in affected children.
