TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular basis of memory defects in Drosophila Fragile X mutants
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOR STUDY OF FRAGILE X DROSOPHILA MODEL; GENETIC INTERACTION STUDIES; GENETICS OF LEARNING AND MEMORY; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; PHARMACOLOGICAL RESCUE; TRANSLATIONAL CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: More than 500 000 Canadian children under 14 years of age suffer from intellectual disability (ID).  1.3 billion dollars is spent each year in Canada for schooling and specialized medical services for these children.  An increasing number of cases of ID are now known to be caused by genetic defects. The most common cause is a defective gene called Fmr1, which causes Fragile X syndrome (FX). Children with FXS suffer from ID, and may also suffer from autism and/or epilepsy. Unfortunately, no treatment option is available for FX.  Thus, it would be useful to have an animal model system for experiments to learn how a defect in the Fmr1 gene leads to ID and the other problems associated with FX.   FX is a complex disease, but mice and fruit flies (Drosophila) with defective Fmr1 genes have learning problems like those observed in human FX patients.  Fruit flies have been used for decades to study the genetic mechanisms of memory.  I have found that FXS flies have a profound memory defect.  When normal flies are subjected to two odors, with one odor accompanied by a mild electrical shock, the flies quickly learn to avoid the odor with the shock.  However, FX flies do not.  I observed high levels of protein expression in the brains of FX flies, and, most interestingly, memory was improved by feeding the flies drugs that block protein production.  Protein excess is also observed in FX patients and in those with other ID syndromes.  I propose to use the FX flies and our memory assay to uncover the specific reasons why too much protein is being produced in the FX brain and then reverse the excessive protein synthesis using genetics and medication. Our findings have the potential to help treat children with FX, as well as those with other ID syndromes, epilepsy and autism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of RGS2 in the response of cells to stress
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTE DIFFERENTIATION AND FUNCTION; CARDIOMYOCYTE HYPERTROPHY; G PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTORS; G PROTEINS; RGS2 (REGULATOR OF G PROTEIN SIGNALING PROTEIN 2); SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Cellular stress contributes to human illnesses such as diabetes, heart disease, and neurodegenerative disorders. Typically, stressed cells undergo a coordinated series of changes known as the integrated stress response. While not completely understood, this responce involves a sharp decrease in the overall rate at which new protein molecules are formed, with the production of key proteins maintained at normal or elevated levels. This lets cells conserve energy and nutrients, and promotes survival. We hypothesize that RGS2 (regulator of G protein signaling 2) may play a novel role in cell stress. RGS2 is best known for its ability to decrease receptor signals that are mediated through G proteins. RGS2 can be increased in response to receptor signals, thus leading to receptor desensitization. However, some studies indicate that RGS2 increases under conditions that are not clearly related to receptor signaling, particularly various forms of environmental or internal stress. We have found that RGS2, unexpectedly, can bind to the protein-producing machinery within the cell to inhibit protein synthesis. It appears to do this by blocking the function of a protein called eIF2B (eukarytotic initiation factor 2B), which plays an essential role in initiating protein synthesis. Therefore, RGS2 may be a previously unrecognized component of the integrated stress response, wherein it is increased by stressful stimuli, resulting in the inhibition of eIF2B activity and therefore diminished rates of protein synthesis. In the proposed studies, we will explore this hypothesis by 1) mapping the RGS2 binding domain of eIF2B to determine how these two proteins interact with one another and 2) studying how RGS2 is increased in response to stress by investigating the mechanisms by which it is upregulated at the genetic level. This work may lead to improved therapies for stress-related diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: O-antigen synthesis in intestinal pathogens
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; BIOSYNTHESIS; GLYCOSYLTRANSFERASES; INHIBITORS; LIPOPOLYSACCHARIDES; O-ANTIGENS
Abstract-Résumé: Shigella bacteria can cause severe intestinal infections and death, especially in children. These bacteria are highly infectious; they protect themselves with an outer coat of complex polysaccharides (O-antigens) that determines the infectious and antigenic properties of bacteria. Many of the genes responsible for the assembly of these polysaccharides are known but the enzymes involved have not been identified. Thus, the biosynthesis of these complex polysaccharides is still not understood, mainly due to the lack of appropriate methods. We have recently developed these methods and synthesized enzyme substrates that resemble the natural substrates. In this proposal we will use the Shigella strain B14 as a model to study the enzymes that sequentially assemble O-antigen polysaccharides. Having the methods and expertise to study the bacterial enzymes, as well as collaborators that are experts in bacterial genetics and protein structure determination, we propose to unravel the sequence of events in O-antigen assembly in Shigella. Using new synthetic compounds and methods based on previous success, we will identify and purify the enzymes required to assemble the O-antigen and thoroughly characterize their properties. The protein structures will be determined in order to understand the molecular mechanisms of their action and to design specific enzyme blockers. We will thus gain a better understanding of the functions of genes and enzymes in Shigella, as well as in other intestinal bacteria. This work is hoped to result in new anti-bacterial strategies. Knowledge of these enzymes will allow the synthesis of specific bacterial carbohydrates for the purpose of vaccines, and will reduce bacterial virulence.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DES TUMEURS CEREBRALES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of protein kinase C iota as a target for glioblastoma therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOURS; PROTEIN KINASE; RNA INTERFERENCE; TUMOUR XENOGRAFTS
Abstract-Résumé: Glioblastoma is an incurable and aggressive form of brain cancer. The goal of my research is to determine whether inhibition of a molecule known as "protein kinase C iota" would be an effective way to treat glioblastoma. Previous data from my lab has shown that inhibition of protein kinase C iota decreases the growth and invasiveness of glioblastoma cells in culture, and sensitizes them to chemotherapy. The aims of this proposal are: (1) to determine how protein kinase C iota inhibition prevents tumour cell growth. This knowledge will be used to identify chemotherapy agents that work in combination with protein kinase C iota inhibition;(2) to determine the effects of protein kinase C iota inhibition in animal models of glioblastoma. Brain tumours kill approximately 1500 patients a year in Canada and the majority of these deaths are due to the aggressive type of glioblastoma we are studying with this project. The proposed work has the goal of developing new treatments for glioblastoma that will reduce morbidity and mortality due to this disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: SUBSTANCES CANCERIGENES (ET ENVIRONNEMENTALES); MALADIES DU FOIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Inducible metabolism of xenochemicals and endogenous toxic compounds: nuclear receptors and the CYP2B paradigm
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CYP2B GENES; CYTOCHROME P450; INDUCIBLE DRUG METABOLISM; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; PHENOBARBITAL
Abstract-Résumé: Cytochrome P450s are key enzymes in the modification of drugs and other foreign small molecules within the body. They form an essential part of a system that modifies an extraordinary diversity of substances. The normal biological role of cytochrome P450s is believed to be one of detoxication. However, in the case of certain foreign small molecules, the immediate product is a chemically reactive form, capable of combining with and damaging cellular target molecules, such as proteins and DNA. One consequence of the formation of such reactive intermediates may be cellular toxicity or adverse drug reactions. Another may be to cause mutations in cellular DNA and yet another may be to cause cancer. Thus cytochrome P450s are implicated in reactions leading both to detoxication and to toxicity. Much remains to be learned at the molecular level concerning how the levels of the different cytochrome P450s present in humans and in experimental animals are regulated. The major objective of the present project is to analyze the regulation of specific P450 genes in mouse and rat liver. This work will provide an indication as to how cytochrome P450 genes are regulated and how they vary from one individual to another. It may also contribute to an understanding of why there is interindividual variation in drug metabolism in humans and perhaps suggest reasons why individuals might vary in their susceptibility to cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: A protein on the edge: balancing structural order and disorder in the assembly of elastin. Implications for vascular pathology.
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYLOID; AORTA; ASSEMBLY; ELASTIN; STRUCTURE; VASCULAR
Abstract-Résumé: Elastin is the protein responsible for the elastic properties of tissues. These properties are particularly important for vascular tissues, especially the large arteries, which have to undergo repeated stretching and elastic recoil as a bolus of blood is ejected with every beat of the heart. Several vascular diseases which manifest themselves later in life (e.g. atherosclerosis, hypertension, aneurysms) are preceded/accompanied by premature fragmentation of this elastic network. Once elastin is laid down in the vascular tissue, it remains for life. Therefore the elastic network must have the structural integrity to undergo literally billion of cycles of stretch and recoil without mechanical failure, dramatic evidence of the remarkable durability of this protein. Such durability is dependent on correct assembly into the proper architecture in the vessel wall. The consequence is that subtle imperfections in the architecture of this assembled network may be manifested later in life by an increased susceptibility for mechanical failure of this elastic network, leading to later onset vascular diseases. The rubber-like properties of elastin dictate that the structure of the protein  must remain disordered. Thus, the structure of elastin must remain balanced on the edge of disorder/order. This is a precarious state, with growing evidence that subtle changes in the sequence of elastin will tip this balance towards the kinds of ordered structure that could affect the long-term durability of the elastic network. Our objective is to use biochemical, biophysical and computational techniques to understand how the sequence of elastin achieves the crucial balance between disorder and order required for proper assembly and architecture of the polymeric elastic matrix, and how subtle mutations and polymorphisms (sequence variations) in elastin may influence that balance, resulting in architectural imperfections leading to increased susceptibility to later-onset vascular pathologies.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Infantile Spasms in Down Syndrome: Correction of the Epileptic Phenotype
Keywords-MotsClés: CATASTROPHIC EPILEPSY; DOWN SYNDROME; ENVIRONMENTAL ENRICHMENT; GLUR5; INFANTILE SPASMS; SEIZURES; TS65DN
Abstract-Résumé: Down syndrome (trisomy of chromosome 21) is the most common genetic cause of mental handicap. Children with Down syndrome are particularly susceptible to a particularly horrific form of epilepsy known as infantile spasms. The typical clinical story of infantile spasms is that of an infant who is on track with his/her development when the child begins to have clusters of spasms, which are really myoclonic seizures, that consist of the head coming forward, the arms coming up, and flexion at the abdomen, often associated with a cry. The clusters may last minutes and may occur over 100 times per day. Soon, the child becomes less visually responsive and loses all developmental milestones. If the seizures are not treated in a timely fashion or fail to respond to treatment, the child will become severe mentally handicapped. Recently, we have been able to create an animal model of infantile spasms in Down syndrome using a genetic mouse model of Down syndrome. We propose to investigate the mechanism by which this phenomenon occurs by focusing upon a particular ion channel - a potassium channel - in the brain that is over expressed in the brain of the Down syndrome mutant mouse. We hypothesize that over expression of this particular potassium channel in the brain of the Down syndrome mouse is responsible for the infantile spasms phenotype. We propose to use the power of mouse genetics to both rescue the infantile spasms phenotype in the Down syndrome mutant mouse both to rescue the infantile spasms phenotype in the Down syndrome mouse as well as to recreate the infantile spasms phenotype in a wild type mouse, and thus elucidate the mechanism by which this phenomenon occurs. These studies have broad ramifications for Down syndrome, infantile spasms, and epilepsy in general. They will allow us to understand the basic mechanisms of Down syndrome and lead to more effective treatments of Down syndrome, infantile spasms, and other malignant epilepsies of childhood.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of CNK in RTK-dependent signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL ADHESION; DROSOPHILA GENETICS; MAPK MODULE; PROTEIN KINASE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Receptor Tyrosine Kinases (RTKs) are cell surface proteins that perceive and transmit chemical messages from outside the cells. The relay of RTK signals within the cells is accomplished by distinct proteins complexes that form so-called signaling pathways. One such pathway is known as RAS/MAPK and plays a central role in the control of cell division. Consistent with this, over 30% of all human cancers have mutations in genes encoding factors that directly or indirectly affect this pathway. Therefore, a thorough description of the events governing RAS/MAPK signaling should provide novel targets and strategies for anticancer therapies. RAS governs cell division primarily by sending signals through a module of three core proteins (RAF, MEK and MAPK). The mechanisms and the proteins required for RAS/MAPK function have been remarkably well-conserved during evolution. Therefore, the use of simpler models, such as Drosophila fruit flies, is accelerating the identification and characterization of novel proteins influencing RAS/MAPK signaling. For instance, we have previously identified several new factors required for the RAS/MAPK pathway using genetic screens in Drosophila. One of these is CNK, which we initiated the characterization a few years ago. To our surprise, we found that CNK physically links together several of the keys players composing the RAS/MAPK pathway and therefore appears to work as a molecular scaffold. In this proposal we want to further explore the scaffolding property of CNK. A better understanding of CNK action may lead to the development of drugs that reduce the activity of cancer-causing mutations affecting the RAS/MAPK pathway. Moreover, our preliminary data suggest that CNK influences another pathway, which governs the ability of cells to contact each other or to move around. We now plan to explore this possible new role for CNK, which may shed light on some of the early events leading to cancer cell detachment; a prerequisite for metastasis.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Multi-Site Trial of the Impact of Assistive Technology with Individuals with Mobility Limitations and their Caregivers.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTIVE TECNOLOGY; CAREGIVER BURDEN; DISABILITY; INDEPENDENT LIVING; INFORMAL CAREGIVERS; MOBILITY AGING; OUTCOME ASSESSMENT; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Many people with mobility limitations use assistive technology, such as wheelchairs and bathroom grab bars, to help them perform daily activities. However, scant attention has been paid to the impact of these devices on their caregivers. This neglect produces an incomplete portrayal of the outcomes of assistive technology provision, which has significant implications for policy and practice. In order to address this deficiency an assistive technology intervention has been developed that is inclusive of assistance users and their caregivers. This intervention involves a detailed in-home assessment of the person's current assistive technology, the negotiation of a personal assistive technology plan with the person and his/her caregiver, and the timely provision of devices and training. To test the effectiveness of this intervention we will perform an experiment. We will enrol 120 individuals with mobility limitations and 120 of their caregivers in the study. Participants will be assigned to either the experimental or the standard care group. Outcomes for individuals with mobility limitations and their caregivers will be measured before and after intervention using a variety of standardized instruments. We expect this experimental intervention will 1) increase the daily activity and social participation of assistance users; 2) reduce the amount of caregiver assistance required; and 3) decrease the physical and psychological demands on caregivers. The evidence produced by this study will enable service providers to offer assistive technology interventions that are more attuned to the needs of both individuals with mobility limitations and their caregivers and enable providers to lobby for better funding for equipment and follow-up intervention services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Progesterone Signalling During Pregnancy and Labour
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE RNA SPLICING; GENE TRANSCRIPTION; MYOMETRIUM; PREGNANCY; PROGESTERONE
Abstract-Résumé: Preterm birth occurs in only 5-10% of all pregnancies but is associated with 70% of all neonatal deaths and up to 75% of neonatal related disability. Progesterone has recently been proposed as a therapy to prevent preterm birth however the mechanisms by which progesterone acts are poorly understood.  Our studies will investigate novel signalling pathways by which progesterone regulates the expression of genes and proteins in human myometrial tissues during pregnancy and labour.

TitreApplicationTitle: Specific inhibitors of deubiquitinating enzymes
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALLING; DEUBIQUITINATION; INHIBITION; NOVEL SCAFFOLD; PHAGE DISPLAY; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: The task which each eukaryotic cell has to accomplish dictates the levels of enzymes and proteins it produces at any given stage of its live cycle. This equilibrium of protein expression and degradation is in part regulated by a process called ubiquitination. During this process the small protein ubiquitin is attached to other proteins in the cell which determines their intracellular fate. Ubiquitination plays important roles in controlling protein degradation, protein localization and cellular signalling. Deubiquitination counteracts the effects initiated by ubiquitination and by that regulates and modulates these effects. The human genome encodes approximately 100 deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs); each DUB deubiquitinates a specific set of proteins and thereby modulates specific biological functions. Because Dubs are enzymes with well-defined catalytic sites, they have attracted considerable attention as therapeutic targets for cancer treatment. As has been the case with kinase inhibitors, specific inhibitors of Dubs would be invaluable tools for understanding normal and cancer biology and they could be developed into anti-cancer drugs. Our overall goal is to break new ground to generate the first-ever specific inhibitors of enzymes in the deubiquitination pathway.  These inhibitors will be used as tools to probe biology and for the validation of Dubs as potential targets for cancer therapeutics.  Furthermore, structural analyses will elucidate the roles of critical contacts that mediate specificity and affinity, and this information will aid the design of small molecule inhibitors. Importantly, the general strategy will be extendable beyond the USP family to other DUBs, and also, to enzymes involved in the ubiquitination pathway.  The tools and knowledge acquired through our research will greatly enhance our understanding of deubiquitination and will drive many additional experiments that may eventually lead to novel therapeutics for unmet medical needs.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; AUCUNE DE CES CATÉGORIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator Selection to Improve Survival in Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction: ISIS-LVSD Study (Ontario ICD Database Phase 2)
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLICATIONS; IMPLANTABLE CARDIOVERTER DEFIBRILLATORS; LEFT VENTRICULAR DYSFUNCTION; OUTCOMES; SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH; VENTRICULAR ARRHYTHMIAS
Abstract-Résumé: Implantable cardioverter defibrillators are small devices that are implanted under the skin to detect and treat serious, life-threatening heart rhythm disorders that can lead to sudden cardiac death. Although implantable defibrillators are now commonly used, questions remain about their use in patients with abnormal heart pump function. Many patients with abnormal heart pump function may not be implanted with a device but may suffer sudden cardiac death. Conversely, many patients who undergo defibrillator implantation do not receive any form of electrical (e.g., device shock or pacing) therapy from their device. Improved ability to determine the risk of serious rhythm problems and death may allow for more optimal use of implantable defibrillators and improved outcomes.  We have developed a model that identifies those who are low or high risk of developing serious heart rhythm problems that require treatment. Our model also identifies factors that increase risk of death despite having a defibrillator already implanted. In this proposal, we will test our risk model in 2 groups of patients. First, we will study those who have never had any symptoms of life-threatening arrhythmia, but have been referred for possible defibrillator implantation as a preventative measure. Second, we will study those who have not been referred for a defibrillator, but have evidence of abnormal heart pump function. We will consider different types of events that could occur in these 2 study groups, and we will compare how well the models perform vs. physicians' best estimate of patient risk.  Once the decision has been made to implant a defibrillator, subsequent events may influence patients outcomes. In prior work, we found that many patients experience complications soon after the defibrillator has been implanted, and 1 in 5 patients are hospitalized. Therefore, we will examine the complications and patterns of hospitalization in the year following defibrillator implant.

ClasseRechercheFR: ANOMALIES CONGENITALES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms that Regulate Peroxisome Turnover and their role in Neurodegenerative Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CHILD HEALTH; CHRONIC DISEASES; DEVELOPMENTAL ORGINIS OF CHRONIC DISEASE; KIDNEY DISORDER; LIVE CELL IMAGING; LIVER DISORDER; METABOLIC DISORDER; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES; PEROXISOME TURNOVER
Abstract-Résumé: The peroxisomes are essential organelles involved in both the breakdown and formation of various fats.  They are also one of the key players involved in maintaining cellular level of reactive oxygen species (ROS).  Disruptions in ROS levels have many dire affects on cells including cell death. Peroxisomes contain the highest concentration of proteins that breakdown ROS and its numbers increase in response to elevated cellular ROS levels.  However, a loss of peroxisome numbers during neuroinflammation have been observed in a several  neurodegenerative diseases including cerebral palsy, Zellweger's syndrome, congenital muscular dystrophy, Alzheimer's and most leukodystrophies.   The mechanism(s) that causes the decrease in peroxisome numbers is not known. We believe that there is an increase in peroxisome destruction during neuroinflammation resulting in an unregulated increase in ROS levels. Therefore preventing peroxisomes loss may prolong the life of brain cells in individuals with these various neurodegenerative disorders.  To test this theory, we will decipher how peroxisomes are degraded using biochemical and cutting-edge microscopy techniques, and then examine whether these mechanisms are altered in neurodegenerative disorders.  Understanding the mechanism of peroxisome degradation may provide valuable therapeutic targets to prevent the destruction of these organelles and thus protect brain cells from neuro-degradation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chemical inhibitors of androgen receptor splice variants lacking the ligand-binding domain as novel agents for castration-resistant prostate cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN RECEPTOR; ANTIANDROGEN; AR VARIANT LACKING THE LBD; CASTRATION-RESISTANT PROSTATE CANCER; CHEMICAL OPTIMIZATION; INHIBITOR OF AR VARIANT
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer cell growth is critically dependent on the androgen receptor (AR) signaling. Current treatment strategy for advanced prostate cancer is to reduce level of androgens (via castration) and compete with androgens for binding in the AR ligand-binding domain (LBD) by antiandrogens. Despite of initial response, lethal 'castration-resistant' prostate cancer (CRPC) arises as a result of AR reactivation. All current hormonal modalities are assuming the dependency of prostate cancer cells on the LBD of AR. However, recent study indicated this assumption may be premature. Several AR splice variants lacking the LBD, such as AR-v7, were recently characterized from tissue specimen of advanced prostate cancer. Significantly, AR-v7 is constitutively active in the absence of androgens, and it is thus no longer possible to be inhibited by reducing the level of androgens or by antiandrogens that target the LBD. This provides a novel mechanism for the development of CRPC and represents a considerable threat to the efficacy of currently used antiandrogens, all of which target the AR LBD.   Our preliminary work has identified an organic molecule that inhibits transcriptional function of AR-V7. This AR-V7 inhibitor is also active against full-length ARs, including the wild type and multiple clinically relevant mutant ARs. Our study indicated this AR-v7 inhibitor binds to the AR in the region not involved with androgen binding. We hypothesize this novel AR-v7 inhibitor may be particularly effective against CRPC, and could delay or prevent the progress of prostate cancer to CRPC. We propose to further characterize and chemically optimize this AR-v7 inhibitor, identify additional AR-v7 inhibitor, and evaluate their therapeutic potential against CRPC in cellular models. This project could lead to novel AR inhibitors effective against CRPC patients who have acquired resistance to LBD-targeting antiandrogens and androgen-depleting agents, including MDV3100 and Abiraterone.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the neuronal circuitry controlling voluntary and automatic saccade generation
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; CAUDATE NUCLEUS; COGNITIVE CONTROL; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; EYE MOVEMENTS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; SACCADES; SUBTHALAMIC NUCLEUS; SUPERIOR COLLICULUS
Abstract-Résumé: One of the most important functions of the central nervous system is the generation of coordinated movement in response to, and in expectation of, the changing environment around us. The rapid movements of our eyes from one interesting visual object to another represents a simple sensory-to-motor transformation that has provided many significant insights into our understanding of how the brain controls movement. These eye movements, called saccades, can be triggered automatically, such as how fireworks can cause us to quickly orient toward them, or can be initiated voluntarily, such as when we are looking for a friend on a busy street corner. We can measure saccades very precisely in the laboratory. In human experiments, we investigate behaviour of control participants and patients with neurological and psychiatric disorders to identify specific deficits in eye movement control. In animal experiments, we measure the activity of individual neurons in different brain areas while animals make saccades and we use this information to infer how the system works in normal humans and patients. Many brain areas are interconnected to control eye movements. By combining the knowledge we gain from the human and animal experiments we hope to better understand how problems within this neural network lead to deficits in neurological and psychiatric patient groups. The purpose of this proposal is to further our knowledge of how these brain areas contribute to the initiation and suppression of saccades by recording from, and manipulating, neurons in key brain regions while animals perform sophisticated eye movement tasks that mimic human clinical experiments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Perception of Audiovisual Communication Signals
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; BRAIN DEACTIVATION; BRAIN IMAGING; COMMUNICATION; HEARING; HUMAN; MULTI-SENSORY INTEGRATION; NERVOUS SYSTEM; SPEECH PERCEPTION; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Grasping the full meaning of a message during face-to-face conversation requires the perception of auditory and visual information. When we listen to someone speaking, we are not only processing the speech sounds but also visible speech movements, facial expression, body posture, manual gestures and the tone and timing of the voice. While we can comprehend someone's auditory speech by itself - for example, on the telephone - human communication in its most natural form is multi-sensory and multi-dimensional: when vision is available, speech intelligibility increases dramatically. The gains resulting from audiovisual integration are, however, not uniform across individuals and over our lifespan. Communication degrades with deficits in vision and audition, and these sensory deficits are common factors in communication problems associated with aging.  The goal of the proposed research is to elucidate how auditory and visual speech information is combined to gain greater speech intelligibility. A series of experiments are designed to investigate how visual and auditory signals interact, how this interaction is subject to learning, and what are the underlying brain processes. This work is anticipated to provide new insights into the communication processes that giving us a social life, which could guide both the diagnosis of those eventually afflicted by communication disorders and the development of therapeutic methods to improve their social life quality, which is key to healthy aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of developmental deficiency of Lgl1 on longterm respiratory risk
Keywords-MotsClés: BRONCHOPULMONARY DYSPLASIA; CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; EMPHYSEMA; LUNG DEVELOPMENT; MOLECULAR DETERMINANTS OF RESPIRATORY RISK; NEONATAL LUNG INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing evidence suggests that events that lead to impaired lung function during development influence risk for respiratory diseases in adult life. We are studying a gene called Lgl1, cloned in our laboratory, that regulates aspects of lung development. Deficiency of the Lgl1 gene leads to some features characteristic of lung injury in the newborn period. Deficiency of Lgl1 also leads to changes in lung function in mature animals. We propose to study whether Lgl1 is important in determining risk for respiratory disease in adult life by analyzing mice which are Lgl1 deficient and lung tissue samples from patients with chronic obstructive lung disease or emphysema. Improved understanding of how genes important in development contribute to risk for adult lung disease may be of value in the development of new strategies for treatment and prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional interactions between PI3K-Akt and eIF2alpha phosphorylation pathways: Implications in cell signaling and tumor treatment.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CHEMOTHERAPEUTIC DRUGS; EIF2ALPHA PHOSPHORYLATION; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM STRESS; MRNA TRANSLATION; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PI3K-AKT PATHWAY; PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION; TUMORIGENESIS; XENOGRAFT TUMOR ASSAYS
Abstract-Résumé: Synthesis of proteins within cells is a complicated process, which is affected by signals that the cells receive from their environment. Deregulation of the machinery that synthesizes proteins is often associated with uncontrolled cell proliferation, induction of tumorigenesis as well as development of metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes. We study the function of an important component of the protein synthesis machinery, which is known as translation initiation factor 2 (eIF2). Modification of this protein by phosphorylation has a serious impact on protein synthesis in cells. Modification of eIF2 is mediated by enzymes, known as eIF2 kinases, which respond to various forms of environmental stress.  The phosphoinositol 3 kinase (PI3K) pathway plays an essential role in tumor development because it helps cells to survive from stress that leads to carcinogenesis. This important function of the PI3K pathway is highlighted by the frequent activation of its components by mutations in many human cancers. As such, the PI3K pathway remains a primary target of pharmaceutical intervention. We have found a novel link between the PI3K pathway and protein synthesis via eIF2 phosphorylation. We provide evidence that this link is involved in insulin signaling, with possible implications in metabolic diseases, such obesity and diabetes, which also predispose humans to cancer. We also show that the link is implicated in tuberous sclerosis, a tumor predisposition syndrome in humans connected to insulin action and diabetes. Furthermore, our work indicates that the novel link is involved in the treatment of tumor cells with chemotherapeutic drugs. We wish to thorough analyze the molecular basis of the link between eIF2 and PI3K in the hope to improve the current strategies for the treatment of cancer and metabolic diseases that lead to cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and signaling roles of the cytoskeleton in neuronal survival
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS; CALCIUM SIGNALING; CYTOSKELETON; MICROTUBULE-ASSOCIATED PROTEIN; NEURODEGENERATION; NEURONAL SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: What happens in the aging and degenerating brain? This is the question that has driven the research of my laboratory since September 2005. The main goal of my research program is to understand the mechanisms involved in the aging of the brain and in such neurodegenerative disorders as Alzheimer's disease. We focus mainly on the cytoskeleton, the internal building blocks of neurons in the brain. Composed of thread-like structures made of protein, the neuronal cytoskeleton serves three different purposes:  it provides structure for the cell, as well as transports materials and sends signals to other parts of the cell. Dysfunctions in the neuronal cytoskeleton can lead to such neurodegenerative disorders as Alzheimer's disease, Frontal Temporal Dementia, Parkinson's disease, ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease), and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.   One unique feature of neurons is their capacity to communicate with each other by electrochemical activity. However, when neurons are hyperactivated (hyper-depolarized), they can't talk to each other and instead, undergo demise associated with collapse of the cytoskeleton. The present grant aims to understand how the cytoskeleton behaves and copes with an excess of neuronal activity. Ultimately, my laboratory is looking for ways to protect nerve cells from the damage that results from alterations in the cytoskeleton.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transfusion Requirements in Cardaic Surgery II (TRICSII)
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC SURGERY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; RED CELL TRANSFUSION
Abstract-Résumé: A high proportion of patients having cardiac surgery receive red blood cell transfusions. Yet, we are not certain of when to transfuse these patients as there have not been any randomized controlled trials of red cell transfusions that can be used to guide transfusion practice. There is a risk associated with transfusing patients because of transfusion reactions and there is a risk of morbidity if a transfusion is needed and is not administered. It is thus essential to determine when to transfuse red cells to thes patients. However, as any definitive trial will require thousands of patients, and as there is variability in transfusion practices, pilot studies need to be conducted to ensure adherence to proposed transfusion strategies. We will conduct a multicentred randomised controlled pilot study of two red blood cell transfusion strategies in 200 cardiac surgery patients who are at high risk of receiving a red cell transfusion. The primary outcome is to determine adherence to transfusion strategies.  The results of this study will be used to design a large definitive multicentered trial of these transfusion strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian HIV Women's Sexual and Reproductive Health Cohort Study, a Canadian Observational Cohort (CANOC) Affiliated Study
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; HIV; MULTI-CENTRED; NATIONAL; REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Women represent one of the fastest growing groups at risk for HIV, comprising over half of all adults living with HIV globally and 22 percent of cases in Canada. However, little is known about HIV epidemiology, management and response in HIV positive women living in different areas of Canada, nor the impact of women-specific HIV/AIDS services on sexual, reproductive, mental and women's health. This study aims to assess the proportion, distribution and pattern of women-specific HIV/AIDS service use, and the effect of such use on reproductive health (e.g. fertility intention, contraceptive use, pregnancy experience), sexual health (STI risk, sexual satisfaction and functioning), mental health (depression, anxiety, PTSD) and women's health (e.g. menstruation, menopause, cervical dysplasia, breast cancer) among women living with HIV in Canada.  It is hypothesized that women-specific HIV/AIDS service use will be lowest in rural areas and among younger, Aboriginal and new immigrant women and those who report high levels of stigma; and that HIV positive women who report higher use and uptake of women-specific HIV/AIDS service will report better sexual, reproductive, mental and women's health outcomes.  This multi-site, community-collaborative, prospective cohort study will enroll 1,050 HIV positive women from British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec. Peer research assistants (PRAs) will provide participant outreach and recruitment. Participants will complete a PRA-administered survey at baseline and two years, with a phone call and brief survey at one year to ensure continuity of contact. Survey data will be linked to existing national and provincial cohorts. Further funding will be sought to follow the cohort longitudinally and include other provinces. This study will yield critical information to help fill knowledge gaps about women and HIV, and will enable an assessment of services aimed at improving the health and wellbeing of HIV positive women in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Subclinical cardiovascular health benefits of interventions to reduce exposure to combustion-derived particulate air pollution
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTION; CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; ENDOTHELIAL FUNCTION; INFLAMMATION; INTERVENTIONS; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Although persuasive evidence links exposure to air pollution with cardiovascular illness and death, there are few exposure reduction interventions that are known to effectively reduce the health risks.  This study will explore the cardiovascular health benefits of two interventions: the use of portable air filters in residences and the exchange of old residential wood-burning stoves with cleaner-burning alternatives.  In addition, by studying individuals living in specific locations, this study will provide information on the health impacts of different pollution sources, thus providing information necessary for the development of air quality management strategies that more effectively protect public health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural alterations in the hippocampus in major depression: contributions of disease and treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIDEPRESSANT TREATMENT; HIPPOCAMPUS; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER; NEUROGENESIS; NEUROIMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Discovering the neurobiological basis of major depression is one of the main challenges for today's society. Severe forms of depression affect 2-5% of the population, and rank among the top ten causes of disability. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies of patients with major depression have consistently shown a reduction in hippocampal volume relative to healthy subjects. Animal studies have also shown that antidepressant treatment can protect hippocampal structure and blocks the effects of stress. However, the information from most previous MRI studies in major depression has been inadequate to allow measurement of any such effects due to limited spatial resolution. The major advance in high field strength (4.7T) MRI by our research group has enabled a 5-fold improvement in the spatial resolution and quantification of specific cellular subfields of the hippocampus directly in depressed patients for the first time. The purposed study will investigate whether particular subfields of the hippocampus may be responsible for reductions in hippocampal volume in depression and to determine whether antidepressant treatment can reverse these changes. We will compare healthy adult controls with 2 groups of depressed patients: unmedicated depressed patients and patients on long term antidepressant treatment. All participants will undergo a high resolution MRI scan and the hippocampal subfields will be measured using a reliable protocol established by our group. In addition to MRI procedure, assessment of memory function and salivary cortisol will be conducted. A prospective follow up program for unmedicated patients will be initiated to repeat MRI scans after 16 weeks and after 12 months of continuous antidepressant treatment. The study will provide the first evidence of whether hippocampal structural plasticity in major depression is progressive and whether antidepressants are protective.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic architecture of cardiometabolic risk in families and communities.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; DIABETES; GENETIC ASSOCIATION ANALYSIS; LIPIDS; METABOLIC SYNDROME; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The metabolic syndrome is a cluster of risk factors for cardiovascular disease, namely obesity, high blood pressure, abnormal blood lipids and abnormal blood sugar that occur together in the same person.  When it is present, a person's risk over the next 10 years of developing a stroke or a heart attack is doubled and of developing type 2 diabetes is increased by up to 5 times.  Our lab was the first in the world to identify the causative genes in Canadian families with a severe inherited form of the metabolic syndrome.  These earlier findings indicated that the metabolic syndrome, rather than being simply related to over-eating and lack of exercise, has an inherited biological basis in some people.  Furthermore, there are likely certain people who are genetically susceptible to develop the syndrome even when caloric intake and expenditure are taken into account. These genetic aspects of metabolic syndrome remain incompletely understood.  This project has four main components.  First, we will study rare patients who have an inherited form of the metabolic syndrome, but with no gene yet identified, and will use state-of-the-art next-generation DNA sequencing technology to find the causative genes.  Second, we will study clinic patients with metabolic syndrome using targeted DNA sequencing to determine whether genetic variants accumulate in their genomes.  Third, we will study the variants discovered in the first two aims to understand the mechanisms in the cell that explain how they lead to the syndrome. Finally, in collaboration with a global network of scientists, we will comprehensively evaluate the genes that underlie metabolic syndrome across a range of populations and ethnic groups.    The project brings together unique families and populations, excellent scientific collaborators, a laboratory with world class experience in finding genes and new state of the art genetic technologies directed towards a medical problem that threatens the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the function and regulation of the new metastasis suppressor gene Growth Arrest Specific 1 (GAS1)
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CANCER PROGRESSION; CELL CULTURE; GAS1; MELANOMA; METASTASIS; METASTASIS SUPPRESSOR GENE; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Metastasis occurs when cancer cells leave the primary tumor and colonize other sites in the body to form new tumors. Over 90% of deaths arising from solid tumors are caused by metastasis. Clinical aspects of metastatic progression are well established. However, changes happening inside a cancer cell - at the molecular level - causing it to become metastatic are poorly understood. Characterizing the molecular basis by which a primary tumor develops the ability to metastasize will help developing more efficient treatments. The loss of certain genes, known as metastasis suppressor genes (MSGs), has been associated with cancer progression. These genes act as a break pedal on cancer cells and stop them from forming tumors throughout the body. However, metastatic cells are using tricks to get rid of these genes, which allow them to establish outside the primary tumor and survive. Melanoma is a skin cancer, which metastasizes very quickly and is often lethal. We recently discovered 22 new genes that suppress melanoma metastasis. Among the novel MSGs identified is the Growth Arrest Specific 1 (Gas1) gene. We have shown that melanoma cells specifically block the expression of Gas1, which allow them to metastasize. Normally, a gene like Gas1 would help the body to kill tumor cells before they become metastatic. Therefore, the loss of Gas 1 creates signals inside the cancer cells that allow them to go through the many changes of becoming metastatic and to survive on their own, outside of the primary tumor. We identified a chemical, SD-208, that can force melanoma metastatic cells to re-express Gas1. Our results suggest SD-208 can block melanoma metastasis. How can metastatic cells block the expression of Gas1? How does Gas1 suppress the metastatic potential of cancer cells? Could SD-208 be used to treat patients with melanoma metastasis? Our research proposes to study these questions with the ultimate goal of developing more efficient anti-metastatic therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Scaling,plasticity and the tripartite synapse
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOSY; GLIA; HYPOTHALAMUS; PLASTICITY; SYNAPSE; SYNAPTIC PHYSIOLOGY; TRIPARTITE
Abstract-Résumé: Conventional wisdom suggests that the electrical and chemical signals relayed from one nerve cell to another are the essence of every breath, every movement, every thought. Nerve cells, however, cannot perform these functions in isolation and new findings now suggest that glial cells are active participants in this ongoing dialogue in the brain.  Classically relegated to secondary status as 'helper' cells, glia are now front and centre in theories suggesting they are essential facilitators that allow nerve cells to communicate more effectively and may even be pivotal in helping the brain learn and remember.Definitive evidence to support these theories, however, has been sparse and not without significant challenge. We will examine closely glial-neuron interactions in an effort to understand how this partnership facilitates the processing of multiple chemical signals in the brain. In particular, we will focus on how glia can process different signals through independent, but parallel mechanisms. Our experiments seek to proved the first unambiguous demonstration that this parallel processing of information ensure neural networks function effectively and are able to learn and remember physiologically salient information.

TitreApplicationTitle: High-Resolution OCT Imaging of Bronchial Epithelium
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOFLUORESCENCE BRONCHOSCOPY; CHEMPREVENTION; LUNG CANCER; OCT
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer death world-wide. More than 1.3 million people die annually and the 5-year survival rates have improved only marginally in the last three decades. We propose to combine autofluorescence bronchoscopy and optical coherence tomography (OCT) to manage this disease through earlier detection and treatment. Autofluorescence bronchoscopy is a technique that uses blue light illumination in an endoscope to excite natural tissue fluorescence (a healthy green glow) in the lung. This technique has dramatically improved the early detection of lung cancer by identifying high-risk areas where biopsies should be collected. Although this method improves detection, a biopsy is still required to verify the presence or absence of a precancer. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a new imaging technique that can be used to study these high-risk tissue sites at high resolution without removing tissue (no biopsy required). It is the optical equivalent of ultrasound. It uses light waves instead of sound waves to build a high-resolution map of structures below the tissue surface. Our team was the first to use OCT in conjunction with autofluorescence bronchoscopy. We found that OCT does have promise for the differentiation of early lesions and for determining if the lesion has invaded. Over the last 10 years, we have made 1000's of quantitative measurements on surgical specimens (biopsies) removed from the lung. We believe that we can use these measurements to improve current OCT instruments to help identify precancerous lesions in the lung.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mapping eQTLs that affect susceptibility to bacterial infections.
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL INFECTIONS; CELLULAR BIOLOGY; EVOLUTIONARY GENETICS; GENE EXPRESSION; GENOMICS; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; HUMAN GENETICS; IMMUNOLOGY; POPULATION GENETICS; QUANTITATIVE TRAITS
Abstract-Résumé: Infectious diseases have always been a major health problem throughout the world, imposing a strong selective pressure on the human genome. Despite the recent advent of vaccines and antibiotics, there are still nearly 15 million deaths every year attributable to the effects of infectious diseases. Although a significant proportion of inter-individual variation in susceptibility to particular microbes can be attributed to environmental factors such as malnutrition or poor hygienic conditions, a substantial portion is thought to be due to host genetic factors. The importance of host genetic factors on susceptibility to infectious diseases has been shown by comparative studies involving twins and adopted persons. In addition, multiple rare single-gene mutations leading to severe immunodeficiencies have also been linked with susceptibility to different infectious agents. Although genetic studies of infectious diseases have identified important pathways involved in protective immunity, very little is known about the underlying genetic factors contributing to differences in susceptibility to infectious diseases at the population level. Here, we propose to use a combination of genomic and statistical approaches, including gene expression profiling and eQTL mapping in infected primary cell cultures, to identify genes and regulatory pathways that contribute to inter-individual and inter-population variability in susceptibility to bacterial infections. Our work may lead to the implementation of novel preventive strategies against infectious diseases and other immune-related disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strengthening Parent-Teen Relationships to Reduce Risk and Enhance Healthy Development: A Sex and Gender Framework in Translating Research into Practice
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; AGGRESSION AND VIOLENCE; GENDER AND SEX; HEALTHY DEVELOPMENT; INDICATORS OF CHANGE; INTERVENTION; PARENT-TEEN RELATIONSHIPS; RISK AND PROTECTIVE FACTORS; TREATMENT OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: The social and economic costs of teen violence and aggression are substantial and rising. Despite recent progress, further research is needed to develop interventions for pre-teens and adolescents, particularly those at the highest level of risk. Few programs have addressed the relevance of gender differences in risk and protective factors, and important questions remain regarding the need for 'gender sensitive', 'gender tailored' or 'gender specific' programming. To be effective interventions must be research driven; based on established knowledge about risk and protective factors; and targeted to sensitive developmental transitions which present different risks for girls and boys. Programs that promote and strengthen relationships between youth and their parents offer considerable promise in enhancing healthy development, and reducing violence, aggression and related mental health and social problems. Building on our eight-year longitudinal study of adolescent girls and boys at high risk for violence, aggression, and poor social and mental health, we developed an attachment focused intervention designed to strengthen parent-teen relationships. The proposed research evaluates the short and long term effectiveness of this program for girls and boys; examines the role of risk and protective factors as determining treatment outcomes; and investigates shared and gender specific social, psychological, genetic and biological factors that underlie change in therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic mechanisms underlying immune escape in malignant lymphomas
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNOLOGY; LYMPHOMA BIOLOGY; MOLECULAR GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Primary lymphoid cancer (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas) is the fifth most frequent cancer in humans and affects patients of all ages. These cancers are diverse in their biological and clinical behavior and thus subgroups of lymphomas have been defined. In some of these subgroups many normal cells of the immune system are in direct contact with the malignant cells, yet are unable to kill the cancer cells. Our research group has recently identified that in a subgroup of lymphomas rearrangement of chromosomes (translocations) leading to gene fusions (with genes called CIITA, PDL1 and PDL2)  appear to explain some of the mechanisms by which the malignant cells are able to escape the surveillance of the immune system. In the present study we propose to investigate these mutations of the genome in more detail to determine how often these events occur, exactly which genes are involved and by which mechanisms the cells achieve their goal and prevent immune system destruction. We will use staining techniques in lymph node tissue sections and molecular genetic methods to detect changes of the previously identified genes in a large number of cases, and find out if these changes are correlated with the presence of certain immune cells in the direct vicinity of the cancer cells. Furthermore, we will learn if these findings are helpful to predict the prognosis of patients treated with chemotherapy. We will also use modifications to the genome of cultured lymphoma cells to study the mechanistic consequences of our novel findings. Overall, this study will improve our understanding of how lymphoma cells and, likely in more general terms, cancer cells develop into a malignant disease and resist being killed by the patient's immune defence mechanisms. Finally, the results will likely provide cellular targets that can be used for future therapies for patients with malignant lymphoma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dynamic Striatal/Cerebellar interactions in Parkinson's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; CEREBELLUM; FUNCTIONAL MRI; PARKINSON'S DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) has been considered a "classic" basal ganglia disease, and dominant models of the last two decades have examined the role of altered basal ganglia function in PD. However, it is becoming increasingly clear that solely focusing on abnormal basal ganglia function cannot explain many disease features that are vitally important to those affected: the significant variability in the progression of the disease, why PD subjects with tremor tend to have a more benign prognosis and reduced motor complications of treatment, and why tremor often does not respond to dopaminergic therapy. This work proposes to answer these questions by investigating the complementary role the cerebellum plays in PD. By using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and manual tracking tasks, we will determine how cerebellar function becomes altered when the basal ganglia are affected by PD. In addition to explaining many features of PD, this work may spawn new rehabilitation strategies, and provide novel targets for future drug therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Living in "transnational spaces": Gendered vulnerability to HIV of Chinese immigrants in Canada and the implications for future interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADA; CHINA; GENDER; GLOBAL HEALTH; HIV/AIDS; MULTIDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH; TRANSNATIONALISM
Abstract-Résumé: This proposed study is an extension of a CIHR-funded pilot project that revealed a sharp contrast between Chinese immigrants' risky sexual behviours on the one hand and silence surrounding sex and HIV on the other. Since the early 1990s, China is the largest source of immigrants to Canada. Through the internet, Chinese mass media, and frequent travel "home", these recent immigrants commonly live in what are increasingly recognized as "transnational spaces", ones where the territorial borders of Canada and China are reduced in importance when it comes to sexual health. It appears that, unlike in earlier generations, China continues to play an important role in the lives of recent immigrants, affecting their health risk (including risk for HIV). Aiming to understand the specific vulnerability to HIV faced by the current generation of Chinese immigrants in a transnational context, the study has three main objectives: a) to understand how such "transnational spaces" have had differential impacts on Chinese immigrant men and women's exposure to HIV risk and their capacity to respond to such risk; b) to compare the ways in which HIV/AIDS related responses (such as knowledge construction, education, service delivery, involvement of civil society organizations [CSOs] and policy-making) have taken account of these gender-based differences in Canada and China; and c) to explore the implications of transnationalism and globalization on HIV interventions, as well as on inequalities, including gendered ones, in health outcomes and services. The data will be collected through qualitative interviews with Chinese immigrants, CSO workers, service providers and governmental officials in the two countries. The findings will help develop more responsive education programs, services and policies that take account of the transnational spaces and lay a foundation for strengthening future global health collaborations and governance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Facilitating the Development of New Therapeutics for Diabetes, Pre-Diabetes and Obesity by Inhibition of Human Pancreatic Alpha-Amylase: A Structural and Mechanistic Approach
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; ENZYME KINETICS; INHIBITOR DESIGN AND OPTIMIZATION; INHIBITOR IDENTIFICATION AND CHARACTERIZATION; MECHANISM BASED INHIBITOR SYNTHESIS; MECHANISTIC STUDIES OF ENZYMATIC CATALYSIS; OBESITY; PROTEIN STRUCTURE - FUNCTION RELATIONSHIPS; PROTEOMIC APPROACHES; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes and obesity are serious chronic diseases that lead to significantly reduced life expectancy and associated life-threatening complications such as heart disease, stroke, blindness, kidney failure and lower limb amputation. The incidence of diabetes is increasing rapidly and currently afflicts 6% of the population throughout the Western World (approximately 3 million Canadians), ranking it as the third most prevalent disease. Likewise, obesity is approaching epidemic proportions, with an estimated 25% of adults in Canada being obese. A major challenge in treating diabetes or obesity is reducing excessively high patient blood glucose levels. Human alpha-amylase is a particularly compelling target for the development of therapeutics for these diseases, being the first enzyme in the pathway of starch digestion, the principal source of dietary glucose. Unfortunately, previously identified inhibitors of human amylase exhibit limited specificity, and the effectiveness of those in medical use is severely limited by deleterious side effects (diarrhea, flatulence). To alleviate these problems we have pursued a targeted screening program of natural extracts and thereby developed a portfolio of novel human amylase inhibitors of exceptional affinity and exquisite specificity. We have further advanced the first of these uniquely active inhibitors, Montbretin A, through the proof of concept phase in a diabetic rat model system, demonstrating both the ability to significantly reduce blood glucose levels without adverse events and to delay the onset of diabetes in these animals. Future research will focus on two essential areas. Firstly, determining the modes of inhibition of Montbretin A and the other potent inhibitors that we have identified. Secondly, attaining a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of the catalytic function of human amylase, along with its mode of attack on polymeric starch and its relationship to alpha-glucosidases in the gut microbiome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of poor sleep on children's emotional, attentional and behavioural functioning
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIGRAPHY AND POLYSOMNOGRAPHY; ATTENTION-DEFICIT/HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER; CHILD PSYCHOPATHOLOGY; DAYTIME SEQUELA OF SLEEP DISRUPTION; SLEEP DISTURBANCES; STIMULANT MEDICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Poor sleep has been reported to disrupt daytime functioning in adults, but there is limited research in children. The research that does exist suggests that children who sleep less have lower academic achievement, act out more, and are more emotional. The majority of studies have used correlational designs, which demonstrate that sleep and daytime functioning are related but does not prove that one causes the other. The few studies that have tried to demonstrate a cause and effect relationship have had a number of problems related to their design and interpretation, so the question remains open as to whether sleep loss actually causes daytime problems. Our study will use an experimental approach to determine if short sleep causes problems with children's daytime functioning and if more sleep improves daytime functioning. We will manipulate sleep by asking our participants to go to bed one hour later for one week and to go to bed one hour earlier for one week. We will measure the children's performance on tests of attention and emotional regulation, as well as their general behavioural functioning.  Information will be collected after their typical sleep, after they have had more sleep than usual, and after they have had less sleep than usual. We will study both typically developing children and children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and the effects of sleep loss and additional sleep will be compared between these two groups of children. Our results will help to determine the cause and effect relationship between sleep and daytime functioning in children. The findings from this study will have implications for the assessment and treatment of children with cognitive, emotional, and behavioural problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of conformationally defective membrane proteins removal from the cell surface in health and diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFORMATIONAL DISEASE; ENDOCYTOSIS; PROTEIN PROCESSING; PROTEOLYSIS; QUALITY CONTROL; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: To preserve cellular homeostasis, proteins with impaired architecture have to be repaired or eliminated from living cells in a timely manner. Since structural errors are frequently incorporated in newly synthesized proteins, as well as imposed by various environmental stresses (e.g. thermal, oxidative and osmotic stress) during the lifespan of polypeptides, sophistical mechanisms have evolved to eliminate impaired proteins from the cell. Surprisingly, the removal mechanism of damaged proteins from the cell surface, termed peripheral quality control, is not known. We designed model systems to investigate the cellular fate of damaged membrane protein from the cell surface. Using biochemical, genetic and proteomic techniques, we showed that ubiquitination plays a central role in the degradation of damaged protein from the cell surface. Remarkably, our pilot studies suggest that similar mechanism appears to be responsible for four other mutant receptors and transporters degradation from the cell surface, associated with various genetic disease. The present application aims at elucidating three specific steps in the degradation pathway of damaged membrane proteins from the cell surface: the internalization, the endosomal sorting and the lysosomal delivery. The proposed experiments will identify components and mechanism of each of these sorting steps. The results will potentially identify novel drug targets that may be utilized to rescue the membrane protein stability defect in certain conformational diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Peer victimization, mental health, and academic achievement: A multi-informant, multi-method longitudinal study
Keywords-MotsClés: ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT; ADOLESCENTS; CHILDREN; LONGITUDINAL; MENTAL HEALTH; PEER VICTIMIZATION; TRANSITION
Abstract-Résumé: Few topics in child and adolescent development have united researchers, parents, teachers, and health professionals in the way that the study of peer victimization has over the past three decades. The motivation of this work is the underlying belief that peer victimization is an extremely difficult life experience that has lasting and serious negative ramifications in the lives of young people and as such should be stopped (or at least reduced) through intervention and prevention efforts. A review of the scientific research on peer victimization reveals that the introductory paragraphs in much of the published literature include a common script with three key premises: (1) victimization is prevalent in schools, (2) victimization is tied to a host of negative social and emotional adjustment indices, and (3) victimization is largely stable and the consequences of victimization are lasting. There is certainly considerable cross-sectional evidence to support the first two premises. What remains much less clear however, is the question of whether peer victimization and the concurrent correlates of these negative peer experiences are in fact long-term.  The proposed study is unique in that we plan to continue to follow our large cohort (n= 600) of Canadian children as they transition into and out of high school with a focus on the interplay between peer victimization, mental health, and academic achievement. To date, we have collected annual data from participants, their families, and their schools from the time they were in Grade 5 until now, Grade 8.  Using a "pathways approach", our multi-disciplinary team has and will continue to examine typical and atypical outcomes as well as divergent pathways by which outcomes are manifested by different children. This research will helps us begin to untangle the complex system of personal attributes, risk and protective factors, conditions, and processes that characterizes the long-term consequences of peer victimization.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the dynamics of transcription regulation at a single cell level
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICS; DRUG RESISTANCE GENES; GENE EXPRESSION NOISE; GENETICS; LIVE CELL IMAGING; MODELING; NON CODING RNAS; SINGLE MOLECULE IMAGING; TRANSCRIPTION; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: All life forms are assembled around a basic unit, the cell. Multicellular organisms have organized these unites into tissues and ultimately into even more complex structures like the human body. From beginning to end, all life depends on proper functioning of these single unit. Every human starts life as such a single cell, but during development, cells divide and differentiate to form specialized structures. To achieve this, different genes characteristic for the development of a specialized organ, such as the liver, must be activated. Misregulation of such gene activation programs can have severe consequences, causing developmental problems or serious diseases such as cancer.  For instance, a tumor can be formed simply because a gene activation program is incorrectly executed within a single cell. Thus, to understand why such defects can occur and to be able to correct or prevent them, we have to understand how gene activation is achieved within a single cell.  Yet paradoxically, to date most of what we understand about gene control has been achieved only by studying average behaviors of cells, not the individuals from which ha tissue develops or a rogue cell that madly divides to form a tumor. I have developed unique and powerful methods to study gene activation in single cells. These methods allow us to directly visualize how individual cells change their gene acitvation programs in real time, with a precision of seeing individual molecules being produced. Using these tools, I aim to determine what elements in the genome are responsible for precise control of normal gene expression within single cells and how, where and when such control breaks down.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular dissection of valve and outflow tract development
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL EXPERIMENTATION; CELL AND MOLECULAR BIOLOBY; CELL CULTURE; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; DNA  CLONING; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSCRIPTION REGULATION IN THE HEART; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: In humans, congenital heart malformations represent the single largest class of birth defects with an estimated frequency of 4-5 percent of live births.  Defects of the septa and valves account for the majority of congenital heart disease.  Thanks to advances in surgical repairs, over 1 million adults in North America are living with CHD but face a lifetime of problems including arrhythmias, ventricular dysfunction, one or more re-operations and premature death from myocardial infarction, sudden death or stroke.  Late referral and intervention have a deleterious effect on  long term and event free survival.  For example, the more subtle defects like atrial septal defects or subclinical valve defects, cause progressive degeneration leading to early adult requirement for valve replacement and other major interventions.  Even benign defects like persistent foramen ovale , a form of ASD affecting 25 per cent of the population are associated with significant cardiovascular risks including a 3 to 6 fold increase in stroke, the major cause of morbidity in industrialized countries.  Identification of the genes responsible for CHD will enhance early diagnosis, care and follow up of patients which will significantly decrease cardiovascular complications.  It is the objective of the present grant proposal to identify the regulatory circuits and genes essential for valve and septal formation and test the consequences of their dysfunction on heart development using molecular genetics and biochemical studies. The experiments proposed are likely to identify potential disease causing genes and to produce animal models of human birth defects that will accelerate development of preventive and therapeutic approaches of heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Early Events In BRCA1 tumorigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BRCA1; BREAST CANCER; CELLULAR SENESCENCE; P53; REACTIVE OXYGEN
Abstract-Résumé: Mutations in BRCA1 are the major known cause of familial breast cancer.  Unfortunately, tumors that form in BRCA1 mutation carriers grow quickly, show aggressive behavior, and are uncommonly diagnosed at early stage. Our inability to detect, diagnose, and treat these tumors at an early point in time is, in part, due to a lack of understanding of events that occur shortly after the function of BRCA1 goes awry. Our proposed studies seek to understand these "early events" in BRCA1-associated breast cancer by studying human breast cells donated from volunteers with and without BRCA1 mutations.  Our preliminary findings uncover new knowledge about how BRCA1 works and how mutations in BRCA1 may lead to familial breast cancer.  If funded, these studies will deepen our understanding of familial breast cancer and provide candidate "biomarkers" to detect tumors early and predict risk for future tumor formation in women who carry a mutation in the BRCA1 gene.

TitreApplicationTitle: The urban built environment and health: Implications for diabetes prevention
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; BUILT ENVIRONMENT; DIABETES MELLITUS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; FOOD ENVIRONMENT; NEIGHBOURHOOD CHARACTERISTICS; OBSERVATIONAL STUDIES; PUBLIC/POPULATION HEALTH; RISK ALGORITHMS; WALKABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic diseases caused by overweight and obesity are rapidly growing health problems. A host of environmental factors have contributed to the obesity epidemic, including trends toward larger portion sizes, the ubiquity of high-calorie convenience foods, and changes in zoning laws and urban design that discourage walking and increase our reliance on cars for transportation. Hence, neighbourhoods may have a profound influence on the risk of diabetes through the opportunities they provide for achieving a healthy lifestyle.  We propose a series of studies using linked neighbourhood, survey and health data from Ontario to evaluate the relationship between environmental factors that are contributing to the obesity epidemic and the risk of diabetes. Specifically, we will examine whether the prevalence and incidence of diabetes is rising at a faster rate in urban neighbourhoods in Southern Ontario that discourage physical activity and healthy eating compared to areas that encourage these behaviours; and whether individuals living in areas that discourage physical activity and healthy eating have a higher risk of developing diabetes that those living in areas that encourage a healthy lifestyle.  Strategies to halt the diabetes epidemic are critically needed. This research will advance our understanding of the role that neighbourhoods play in shaping our risk of diabetes. Modifiable factors within the urban built environment may be ideal targets for interventions aimed at preventing obesity-related diseases like diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modelling T cell leukemogenesis in mice
Keywords-MotsClés: FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENETIC COLLABORATION; HEB TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; LEUKEMIA; LMO1 ONCOGENE; T-ALL; THYMOCYTE; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common childhood cancer and 25% of those are of T cell origin (T-ALL). The latter is considered a high risk group in ALL and approximately 20% of childhood and 60% of adult ALL patients succumb to this disease.  We have previously shown that the aberrant activation of three oncogenes, namely SCL, LMO1/2 and Notch1 together with a normal signal from a cell surface receptor might be sufficient to induce T-ALL in mouse models. T lymphocytes are produced in the thymus and these thymocytes normally proliferate and differentiate in response to the pre-TCR and to their environment in the thymus. Surprisingly, these normal responses accelerate leukemia onset. In the present research proposal, we will define how oncogenes confer the capacity for extended division to thymocytes that have a finite life span and how tumor suppressors restraint this oncogenic activity.  In the long term, our observations may improve the capacity to direct clinical intervention towards thymocytes that are transformed by the oncogenes.  The high cure rate in childhood T-ALL is a success story in oncology. However, treatments have sequelae and cure is not always assured. For example, dexamethasone is a drug which is successfully used in T-ALL. However, dexamethasone may later cause osteonecrosis, due to loss of some sites in the bones.  Therefore, understanding the root of the disease in specific subpopulations in the thymus may allow investigators to specifically focus their efforts to develop therapies that are directed towards abnormal processes in these thymocytes, thereby minimizing general drug toxicities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular lipids in Huntington's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL STUDIES; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL SIGNALING; GANGLIOSIDES; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; LIPID METABOLISM; NEUROBIOLOGY; PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington's disease (HD) is the most common inherited neurodegenerative disorder. It is characterized by progressive motor dysfunction, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbances. There is currently no cure for this disease. The production of certain lipid molecules that are important for normal functioning of brain cells is impaired in HD. The aim of this proposal is to investigate the consequences of reduced lipid synthesis in HD brain and to test whether restoring normal levels of these important neural molecules improves HD symptoms and slows down disease progression. Supported by encouraging preliminary results, our studies will potentially identify new therapeutic interventions for the cure of HD.
