TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the role of dermal stem cells in wound healing and the influence of niche-derived factors that govern their behavior.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; HAIR FOLLICLE; LINEAGE SPECIFICATION; NICHE REGULATION; REGENERATION; SKIN; STEM CELL BIOLOGY; TRANSGENIC MICE; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: In 2005, more than 11 million skin wounds (burns, trauma) were treated in emergency departments in the North America. In addition, at least 3 million adults are reported to have pressure ulcers yearly. The result is chronic pain, immobility, disfigurement and in many cases infection leading to further medical complication or death. The physical and emotional recovery can often require years of treatment and have devastating impact on quality of life. Moreover, the cost of chronic wound care alone in North America is estimated at $10 billion annually. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms involved in skin regeneration and wound healing and the potential for stem cell-based therapies to improve repair are of tremendous importance. Unlike other adult tissues, the mammalian hair follicle repeatedly regenerates itself, without formation of scar tissue. This remarkable regenerative capacity is due to the presence of stem cells that are maintained within the hair follicle throughout life. We have recently identified a multipotent dermal stem cell from adult hair follicles that functions to regulate hair follicle regeneration and growth. We have also obtained evidence to suggest that these cells may play a role in skin wound healing. Therefore, the objectives of the proposed studies will be to understand: 1) how dermal stem cells contribute to wound healing, 2) whether supplementing wounds with dermal stem cells improves healing, and 3) how the hair follicle micro-environment regulates the behavior of these stem cells throughout adulthood. These studies will provide important insights into adult stem cell biology and tissue regeneration. Dermal stem cells may provide a novel source of cells for hair follicle restoration and improved skin repair for burns and chronic ulcerations. Understanding how these cells are regulated may also provide clues as to the cause of skin disorders such as keloid, Neurofibromatosis and alopecia areata.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical Outcomes and Tissue Changes in Knee Osteoarthritis: A Novel Approach Using Cumulative Knee Loading
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOMECHANICS; GAIT; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Knee osteoarthritis causes chronic pain, limits mobility and reduces quality of life for thousands of Canadians.  The magnitude and repetition of mechanical loads placed on the knee during daily activities are very important to understanding why knee osteoarthritis worsens over time.  Unfortunately, studying the loads in a laboratory setting does not provide a complete understanding of the pain and mobility limitations people with this condition experience.  We need fresh approaches to understanding and correcting these joint loads to improve health for people with knee osteoarthritis.  Our innovative approach, which measures the magnitude and repetition of knee joint loads that occur during every day activity, is called "cumulative knee load."  To identify magnitude, we will measure the loads a person places on their knees during walking in a laboratory.  To identify repetition, we will use a device like a pedometer to count a person's activities over one week.  Cumulative load will be calculated by multiplying the loads by the week-long activity count.  The relationships between cumulative load and knee alignment, obesity and muscle strength will be investigated.  We will also investigate the link between cumulative knee load and damage of knee cartilage and bone using magnetic resonance imaging.  Ultimately, our goal is to predict knee osteoarthritis progression and cartilage damage over 3 years by evaluating the magnitude and repetition of loads experienced throughout daily activity.  Clinicians can use cumulative load to facilitate early detection of knee osteoarthritis by identifying overuse due to physical activity in people at risk.  Clinicians can also use cumulative load to track the progression of this disease and to tailor exercise programs for each person.  As a result, cumulative load is a novel approach with great potential to advance care for people with knee osteoarthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pain at Home in Children Following Major Surgery: Physical, Psychological, and Economic Consequences
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTION; PAIN; PSYCHOLOGICAL; RECOVERY; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Pain has long-term negative consequences for children. Early experiences with medical pain are related to a host of negative outcomes including heightened pain sensitivity, medical fears, and even avoidance of future health care. Pain in childhood may also lead to declines in learning ability and can affect physical and mental health and quality of life. For thousands of children across Canada each year, surgery is an excessively painful experience. Literature on minor surgery suggests that postoperative pain in children is not well managed, especially at home, where children often receive less than prescribed doses of analgesia and non- pharmacological strategies are underused. Children undergoing major surgery are at a particularly high risk of suffering significant pain because these procedures are typically highly invasive, cause significant tissue damage, and require long recovery periods at home. Literature from adult studies suggests that postoperative pain and associated physiological processes may interfere with physical recovery, return to function, quality of life, and may be associated with the development of chronic pain. Despite evidence from adult studies, there has been little research on postoperative pain in children following major surgery. In particular, there has not been systematic prospective research examining the severity, trajectory, and treatment of children's pain at home following major surgery. There has also been little research examining the physical, emotional, and economic consequences of children's postoperative pain. Thus, the purpose of this research is to examine the prevalence, treatment, and impact of postoperative pain following children's major surgery This project brings together a team of scientists and practitioners from psychology, surgery, anesthesia, nursing, and biostatistics who have the interests and skills to carry out the research and translate the knowledge gained.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR/SME Chair Renewal in Bioelectromagnetics: examining the biological, behavioural, diagnostic, and therapeutic effects of exposure to low frequency electromagnetic fields
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOELECTROMAGNETICS; HUMAN MOVEMENT AND COGNITION; MAGNETIC FIELD DIAGNOSTICS; MAGNETIC FIELD HEALTH EFFECTS; MAGNETIC FIELD SAFETY; MAGNETIC FIELD THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: The Bioelectromagnetics Program at the Lawson Health Research Institute (LHRI), St. Joseph¹s Hospital, and University of Western Ontario (UWO) has contributed substantially to scientific knowledge, medical applications, and public health. Bioelectromagnetics is the study of the biological and behavioural effects of exposure to magnetic fields (MF), such as those produced by: power lines, industrial equipment, residential appliances, medical equipment such as magnetic resonance imaging, and other medical devices used for diagnostics and therapeutics. Until 1995, the study of bioelectromagnetics in London ON was a part-time endeavour by Dr. Frank Prato (one of the world¹s most respected and senior bioelectromagnetics scientists) and a graduate student. After obtaining an MSc (Neuroscience) and PhD (Medical Biophysics) as a mature student, this graduate, Dr. Alex Thomas, was subsequently recruited by the LHRI and UWO as the Director of the Bioelectromagnetics Program with funding from the Ontario Research and Development Challenge Fund, the Canadian Foundation for Innovation, and the St. Joseph¹s Health Care Foundation. Dr. Thomas quickly grew the program from a part-time basic research platform into one of the top bioelectromagnetics research laboratories in the world with excellent facilities, student recruitment, scientist development, intellectual property, and a successful spin-off company. The Bioelectromagnetics Program continues to grow and flourish, and has attracted considerable attention and interest from around the world, including electric power companies such as Hydro-Quebec, Electricite de France, and Reseaux Transport Electricite (France). Here, we propose the renewal of an Industry-Partnered CIHR/SME Chair in Bioelectromagnetics to investigate and freely publish any health-related and potentially subtle effects of power line frequency MF exposure (50/60 Hz), medical applications of MF, and validate new international electromagnetic exposure standards.

ClasseRechercheFR: VIEILLISSEMENT; TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Age-related cognitive decline: basic mechanisms and role of sensory experience
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE-RELATED COGNITIVE DECLINE; AUDITORY SYSTEM; BEHAVIOR; CORTEX; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; INHIBITION; OPERANT CONDITIONING; PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Perceptual and cognitive decline are near-universal aspects of normal aging. The neurophysiological bases of age-related cognitive decline are complex and piece-meal, resulting in a near absence of specific effective treatment for this growing health problem.  In this line of experiments aimed at determining the role of sensory experience in the emergence and remediation of age-related cognitive decline, I will examine in depth the impact of two exaggerated types of sensory experiences on sound processing in the rat primary auditory cortex (A1). As a first step, I will test the hypothesis that chronically degraded sensory inputs will result in A1-specific functional and structural changes comparable to what is observed with aging. This will be achieved by exposing young adult rats to moderate intensity noise during two months. In a second step, I will measure in aged rats the impact of a newly designed auditory training strategy aimed at restoring A1 noise immunity on specific elements of the cortical machinery involved in noise suppression. The identification of specific neurophysiological and cytochemical correlates of age-related perceptual deficits will provide a better understanding of its pathogenesis and will help differentiating normal aging from pathological brain aging (dementia). Studying the impact of targeted perceptual training on these age-impaired processes will teach us how cognitive training could delay or perhaps even reverse the cognitive deficits that we normally associate with aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Medical Decision Science
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Motor vehicle crashes kill one Canadian every 3 hours, disable one Canadian every 7 minutes, and cost all Canadians $27 billion annually.  Increasing driver safety would yield major immediate benefits to society, yet the scientific literature provides little information on what is effective, affordable, and acceptable for reducing traffic risk.  Dr. Donald Redelmeier proposes to apply the fundamentals of Decision Science using the methods of Clinical Epidemiology to explore the problem of driver error and traumatic injury.  The research promises to yield important new insights for drivers to avoid a crash, policymakers to maximize traffic flow, and health providers to reduce the demands on medical care.

Abstract-Résumé: This research program examines the role of culture in health, specifically with respect to the health and wellness of Aboriginal Peoples in Canada. Dr. Abonyi and her team have developed a conceptual framework and measures of culture in population health (a Community Health Indicators Tool Kit), and a more comprehensive and critical perspective on the role of culture in the health of Aboriginal peoples. Her research findings are already being adopted in at least 25 Aboriginal communities across Canada to plan programs and track progress on indicators of community health that are culturally relevant and reflect local contexts and priorities.

Abstract-Résumé: The research being proposed will extend some of the Chairs seminal work in the area of dignity and palliative care. Dignity studies will take place amongst cancer and non-cancer populations (COPD, ALS, ESRD and the Frail elderly) facing end-of-life challenges. These studies will further explore the nature of dignity related distress, along with ways it can be mitigated and how this might be facilitated by health care providers. The Chair will also continue a line of research and knowledge translation, utilizing web-based technologies to meet a variety of palliative care needs for patients, families, volunteers and their care providers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancing mental health services for vulnerable and underserved groups: the importance of recovery.
Keywords-MotsClés: CRIMINAL JUSTICE INVOLVEMENT; ETHNICITY; GENDER; MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES; MENTAL ILLNESS; QUALITATIVE; RACE; RECOVERY; RELIGION; STIGMA
Abstract-Résumé: People who use mental health services come from different backgrounds. Some come from especially vulnerable groups. Many people who use mental health services are immigrants or ethnic minorities. Others may have come to services after contact with the criminal justice system. Some low-income women use services after childbirth if they are diagnosed with post-natal depression. Evidence suggests that these groups are less likely to use services in the first place and more likely to drop out of services. This leads to a significant number of people with untreated or undertreated psychiatric illness. This is to the detriment of individuals, their families and society as a whole. Researchers, policy-makers and other key groups agree that action must be taken to improve the sysstem for these vulnerable groups, so that it can better help people recover. In the proposed research, I intend to investigate how services can be improved to help especially vulnerable groups recover from mental illness. The term 'recover' is here defined broadly, and refers not just to reducing symptoms. It also refers to things like community integration, finding work, completing an educational course, or improving physical health; in short leading a productive and fulfilling life. Evidence shows this is possible for people with a severe mental illness, if only they are given the right supports. Unfortunately, there is a lack of data on the right supports for vulnerable groups. In my planned research, I will begin four new projects focusing on recovery in vulnerable groups. These are (i) a study comparing recovery among six ethno-racial groups; (ii) a study of recovery among those in contact with the judicial system but found not criminally responsible for actions on account of mental illness; (iii) a study of recovery comparing immigrant women to Canadian born women with Post Natal Depression; (iv) a study of the role religion and spirituality can play in enhancing recovery in vulnerable groups.

TitreApplicationTitle: Self-Conscious Emotions and Alcoholism
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ALCOHOLISM; CAUSAL ATTRIBUTIONS; EMOTIONS; GUILT; LONGITUDINAL METHODS; PRIDE; SHAME
Abstract-Résumé: Alcoholism poses major financial, social, and health burdens on Canada, so understanding why some alcoholics recover and maintain sobriety, whereas others do not, is a critical national priority. The proposed research will test whether "self-conscious" emotions (i.e., emotions that require self-evaluations, such as shame, guilt, and pride), and the cognitive processes that elicit them, influence alcoholics' recovery and long-term health. Studies have shown that while shame promotes maladaptive social and mental-health outcomes (e.g., aggression, depression), guilt has generally beneficial effects (e.g., increased empathy, high self-esteem). Correspondingly, two distinct kinds of pride ("hubristic" and "authentic") have similarly divergent effects, with hubristic pride promoting anti-social behavior and psychopathology, and authentic pride promoting pro-social behavior and mental health. The proposed research will test whether recovering alcoholics who experience guilt and authentic pride, rather than shame and hubristic pride, in response to major life events, demonstrate greater health and recovery benefits over time. We will also test whether the distinct cognitions underlying these emotions contribute to outcomes, and, if so, whether self-conscious emotions account for the effects of cognitions on health. We will address these aims by studying emotions, cognitions, and health and recovery outcomes over time in newly sober alcoholics, and comparing these individuals with long-term sober, recovered alcoholics. Our emphasis on self-conscious emotions is highly novel; despite longstanding assumptions that shame lies at the core of addiction, previous studies have not examined whether regulating shame, and experiencing guilt instead, promotes recovery. Furthermore, no previous research has examined the role of pride in addiction. The proposed research is likely to pinpoint new treatment methods (e.g., targeting emotions) for those seeking recovery from addiction.

TitreApplicationTitle: The use of Next Generation Exome sequencing in the identification of genes responsible for rare childhood neurologic disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS; HOMOZYGOSITY MAPPING; MENTAL RETARDATION; NEUROPATHY; PEDIATRIC NEUROLOGY; WHOLE-EXOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic childhood neurologic disorders are rare if considered individually, however as a group, they represent a significant burden to the population and the health care system. Identification of causative genes is critical as it allows genetic counseling to the family, better characterization of patients and insight into the pathophysiology of disease. Unfortunately, the underlying genetic cause of many rare heritable neurologic disorders remains unknown. Because, by definition, they affect only a small number of individuals and families, rare hereditary childhood neurologic disorders are not easily amenable to the typical methods used to identify causative genes (i.e. linkage analysis or association studies). Powerful new sequencing technologies have the potential of revolutionizing the study of these conditions by allowing 'whole exome mutation analysis', which essentially scans all the genes for mutations . We propose to evaluate the feasibility of this method to identify genes responsible for rare childhood neurologic disorders in two groups of patients: those from  consanguineous (i.e. parents are related) and non-consanguineous families. A systematic approach will be carried out to validate mutations.  The applicant will examine and characterize the genetic conditions.  In addition, the applicant will carry out the analysis of the whole-exome sequencing results as well as all the mutation validation steps.  These studies will allow us to identify several disease-causing genes and novel pathways that are important for increasing our understanding of human neurologic development and developing new treatments for these devastating neurologic disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Do rhinovirus infections contribute to airway remodeling in asthma?
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY EPITHELIAL CELL; AIRWAY REMODELING; ASTHMA; CELL BIOLOGY; CLINICAL TRIAL; INTERCELLULAR SIGNALING; RHINOVIRUS; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Infections with the common cold virus (human rhinovirus) are a frequent cause of wheezing illnesses during early childhood. Studies indicate that wheezing illnesses due to human rhinovirus (HRV) infections are associated with an increased risk of developing asthma by the age of 6 years. Asthma symptoms are due to an underlying abnormality of the airways, termed airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR), in which the airways contract too much and too quickly in response to stimuli that have little or no effect on healthy subjects. The airways of asthmatic patients have chronic structural changes (scarring) present, which is termed airway remodeling, and there is now good evidence that this airway remodeling contributes to AHR. Airway remodeling changes are seen in childhood, and may predate the onset of asthma symptoms. Given these observations, and the association between childhood HRV infections and the subsequent development of asthma, we hypothesize that HRV infections play an important role in the development of airway remodeling. We have shown that HRV infection of the cells lining the airways, known as airway epithelial cells, results in increased production of mediators involved in the development of airway remodeling. We now plan to build on these published observations by studying the effects of commonly prescribed asthma medications on HRV-induced remodeling mediators. We will also study how these mediators affect other types of cells in the airways that are also involved in airway remodeling. Finally, we will perform a clinical study in which we will give experimental cold infections to asthmatic and healthy volunteers to see whether there are differences in airway remodeling mediators in these subjects before and after infection. These studies should lead to a better understanding of how common cold virus infections lead to the development of asthma.   See also: http://www.cihr-irsc.gc.ca/e/41658.html

TitreApplicationTitle: Comprendre les enjeux d'implantation et d'intégration des meilleures pratiques de réadaptation au Québec pour les personnes atteintes de schizophrénie et autres troubles mentaux graves
Keywords-MotsClés: APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES; RECHERCHE PARTICIPATIVE; RECHERCHE EVALUATIVE; SCHIZOPHRENIE; SERVICES ET PRATIQUES DE READAPTATION; SYSTEME ET SERVICES DE SANTE; TROUBLES MENTAUX GRAVES
Abstract-Résumé: Le present projet vise a comprendre, pour 3 regions du Quebec, comment chacune d'elle met en place un programme qui repond a l'ensemble des besoins de readaptation de sa population atteinte de troubles mentaux graves (particulierement les personnes atteintes de schizophrenie). Le projet propose de: 1.decrire les services et les pratiques de readaptation offerts dans ces regions du Quebec aux personnes atteintes de troubles mentaux graves (TMG) afin de comprendre comment ils sont deployes; 2.analyser les facteurs qui soutiennent ou limitent l'implantation et l'integration des meilleures pratiques de readaptation dans ces quelques regions du Quebec; 3.identifier les actions a entreprendre pour soutenir les cliniciens et les gestionnaires dans l'amelioration des pratiques de readaptation. Les actions a entreprendre tenterons d'interpeller a la fois les acteurs locaux, provinciaux que nationaux. Des journees de reseautage avec l'ensemble de ces partenaires sont prevues en fin de projet.

TitreApplicationTitle: Making unbiased estimates of treatment effect using observational data in uncommon disease. The scleroderma-pulmonary hypertension model.
Keywords-MotsClés: BAYESIAN; CONFOUNDING; OBSERVATIONAL; PROPENSITY SCORE; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION; SCLERODERMA; SURVIVAL; SYSTEMIC SCLEROSIS; WARFARIN
Abstract-Résumé: Studies of uncommon diseases are challenged by small numbers of patients available for recruitment, and studies are often too small to detect important treatment effects. The Bayesian paradigm allows us to draw inferences with the data at hand, and has the ability to incorporate previous knowledge into estimates of treatment effects. This paradigm is useful in the study of uncommon diseases. An example of an uncommon disease is systemic sclerosis (SSc). SSc is a disease that can affect the skin, joints and lungs. There is no cure. The leading cause of death for Canadians with SSc is high pressure in the lungs called pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Experts suggest use of a blood thinner called warfarin for patients with PAH. A major side effect of warfarin is that it can cause severe bleeding. Whether this drug improves survival is not known. Using a novel research approach, this series of studies will evaluate if warfarin improves survival in SSc-PAH. We will use innovative techniques to study if warfarin improves survival by comparing the survival of SSc-PAH patients who did and did not take warfarin. This research will be the first to study if warfarin improves survival in this deadly disease, and will develop innovative research methods for all researchers who study uncommon diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The central role of the vagus nerve in diet-induced obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ENERGY EXPENDITURE; GENE REGULATION; HIGH-FAT DIET; LIVER; NUTRITION; VAGUS NERVE
Abstract-Résumé: The incidence of obesity in Canada is increasing at a staggering rate. The number of Canadians afflicted by Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus continues to grow, and we know that increased body mass is associated with the development of this disease. The rate of heart disease and stroke, the largest cause of death and disability in Western Society, is significantly elevated in those with obesity and Type 2 Diabetes. Consequently much effort has been spent on understanding how our bodies respond to excess dietary fuel and the mechanisms involved in diet-induced obesity.  The body controls fuel usage, in part, through the communication of metabolic information between organs. It is becoming apparent that this communication consists of factors secreted into the blood and neuronal connections between tissues. The main objective of this project is to explore the role of neuronal connection between the brain and liver in controlling whole-body energy usage. The vagus nerve, one of the most important nerves in the body, is a two-way highway of communication between the brain and many organs. The liver-branch of this nerve controls many aspects of food intake and energy metabolism, though exactly how remains largely unknown To investigate the role the vagus nerve plays in the development of obesity, we will surgically disrupt the action of this nerve in mice. Following surgery, mice will be fed a high-fat diet for 10 weeks which normally causes weight gain and impairs insulin action. Our subsequent experiments will allow us to elucidate the role of the brain-liver axis in the development of obesity. We believe that by understanding the mechanism by which these neuronal signals alter weight gain, hormone action and fuel partitioning we will discover new targets for the prevention/treatment of obesity, diabetes and heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immune regulatory role of host lipid mediators in pulmonary influenza infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNITY; ANIMAL MODEL; INFLUENZA; INNATE IMMUNITY; LIPID MEDIATORS; PULMONARY INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza virus remains a persistent threat to humans causing 3-5 million cases of severe illness and around 500,000 deaths during a non-pandemic year. However, during pandemic influenza virus-associated mortality is drastically increased. For instance, the 1918 "Spanish" influenza pandemic killed 40 million people in just one year, the single greatest loss of human life in history. Intriguingly, most influenza-related mortality results from the host immune response rather than influenza virus itself. This highlights the importance of immune regulation in determining who is protected from the consequences of influenza infection. We have recently demonstrated that lipids produced by the host play a critical regulatory role in pulmonary tuberculosis infection. In the present proposal, we aim to investigate the immune-regulatory mechanism of host lipid mediators during pulmonary influenza infection. Considering the availability of pharmacologic interventions to manipulate levels of these lipids, our findings can translate directly into clinical interventions to selectively modulate proinflammatory cascade and its associated pathology. This may potentially be important during the influenza outbreak as an adjunct to anti-viral therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of the Retinoblastoma gene using fruit flies as a model organism
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER; CELL CYCLE; DROSOPHILA GENETICS; RB/E2F
Abstract-Résumé: Accumulation of hazardous mutations is responsible for cancer development. Many genes prone to mutation in cancer are evolutionarily conserved, and their homologs have been identified in different species. Rb was the first identified tumor suppressor gene whose mutations were found in a childhood cancer, Retinoblastoma. Most cancer cells possess inactive Rb, which is targeted by various oncogenic events. Therefore, if one can find genes that can control the survival and/or proliferation of Rb deficient cells, they can be potentially used to specifically target cancer cells.  The homolog of Rb, rbf1, was identified in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, and its biological activity is found to be well conserved. Recent advance in genetic tools and techniques has made Drosophila an attractive model organism to study human cancer genes. Using Drosophila, I propose to investigate genes that can cooperate with the loss-of-Rb to promote cell death. I have recently discovered that another tumour suppressor gene, tsc1, cooperates with rbf1 to regulate cell death, and conducted a genetic screen to identify novel genes that can specifically promote cell death in rbf1 mutant cells. In this proposal, I describe experimental plans to further characterize these findings.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing trauma centre performance indicators for nonfatal outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: NONFATAL OUTCOMES; PERFORMANCE INDICATORS; QUALITY OF CARE; RISK ADJUSTMENT; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW; TRAUMA SYSTEMS
Abstract-Résumé: Injury is the leading cause of death in Canadians under 45 years of age, the leading cause of loss of active life years in Canadians under 70 years of age, and costs approximately $20 billion per year in Canada. The introduction of trauma systems, comprising a network of designated trauma centers, has been shown to improve patient survival. However, it has been estimated that up to 50% of patients do not receive optimal care and there still exists great variation in injury mortality between hospitals and across health systems. To improve the quality of trauma care, the performance of trauma centers in terms of patient outcome, defined as the status of the patient following a given set of interventions, must be evaluated. In order to evaluate outcome performance, we must be able to accurately measure patient risk factors such as age and injury severity. Currently, valid methodology is only available for the evaluation of mortality despite the importance of nonfatal outcomes such as morbidity. Long term outcomes such as functional status or quality of life are of interest but require long and costly data collection. This project aims to develop performance indicators for a series of nonfatal outcomes that can be measured using routinely collected data. To do so, we will review current literature to identify nonfatal outcomes and describe how they are being used to evaluate trauma care presently. We will then build a risk adjustment model to describe patient risk for selected nonfatal outcomes which will enable us to compare hospitals that receive different kinds of patients. Finally, we will develop risk-adjusted indicators for selected nonfatal outcomes that can be used to identify trauma centers that perform better or worse than expected and to monitor performance over time. The results of this study should facilitate the improvement of the quality of hospital care provided to victims of injury and may be applied to other areas of the health service.

TitreApplicationTitle: A program of research in knowledge translation in child health
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD HEALTH; CLINICAL PATHWAYS; CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES; EVIDENCE-BASED PRACTICE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Canada is among the most prosperous nations in the world, yet the health and wellness outcomes of Canadian children, when compared to children from other developed nations, are surprisingly poor. There is some evidence to suggest that these poor health outcomes are partly due to variation in health care treatment (clinical practice variation), which stems from a failure to apply the best available research evidence in clinical practice, otherwise known as knowledge translation (KT).   Surprisingly, clinical practice variation, even for everyday acute child health conditions, is common.  Clinical practice variation results in unnecessary medical treatments, increased suffering, and increased health care costs. My child health services research program focuses on improving health outcomes for common child health problems by developing strategies that improve KT and reduce clinical practice variation. The largest improvement in outcomes for both patients and the health care system will be achieved by decreasing clinical variation in those conditions that most commonly present to Emergency Departments or Urgent Care Centers. The purpose of the research project discussed is to explore the factors that influence how research-based guidelines for croup and gastroenteritis (two common child health problems) are implemented.  The application of research findings in policy is a strategic value of many provincial and national health care agencies, yet the KT science specific to child health settings is lacking. Canada has the capacity to become a world leader in child health research however achieving that goal requires commitment and strategic investment in child health research focused specifically on knowledge translation. The research program proposed here will generate new knowledge to capture the distinct characteristics and nuances of the delivery of health care to children -- new knowledge that can facilitate successful future research implementation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging the impact of diabetes on brain function and recovery from stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CEREBRAL CORTEX; DIABETES; PLASTICITY; STROKE; VASCULAR SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: It is now estimated that a North American child stands a 1 in 3 chance of becoming diabetic. This staggering figure has an enormous cost, both for the general population that must cover diabetes related health care costs (15.6 billion per year in Canada) and for the individual that will likely suffer complications such as blindness, heart failure, impaired cognition and stroke. At the present time, very little is known about how diabetes affects the brain, perhaps owing to the fact that diabetes has long been thought of as a disease that targets the heart, kidney and peripheral nerve networks. The goals of the current research proposal will be threefold. First, new imaging technologies will be used to visualize how diabetes (using an experimental model of type I diabetes in mice) alters the brain's circulatory system and its functional consequences. Understanding how diabetes affects the brain will generate new insights into why diabetics are at greater risk for cognitive impairments and stroke. Second, the present research proposal will determine how the diabetic brain reacts to, and adapts to stroke (ie. forms new vascular and neuronal circuits). This aim will help determine why the prognosis for successful stroke recovery in diabetics is, at the present time, relatively dismal. A final goal will be to explore the possibility that enhancing angiogenic signaling pathways through the administration of statins will reduce stroke damage and promote brain plasticity that is essential for stroke recovery. Ultimately, the proposed project will generate new information regarding the effects of diabetes on the brain, which will stimulate new treatment options for those Canadians suffering from diabetes related sequeleae.

TitreApplicationTitle: Consequences of Suicide Bereavement: A Population-Based Study in Manitoba
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; BEREAVEMENT; DEPRESSION; EPIDEMIOLOGY; MENTAL DISORDERS; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Suicide often has a devastating effect on the surviving family members. Those who are bereaved by suicide (suicide survivors) frequently experience major emotional problems such as depression. Even more worrisome is that family members who lose a relative to suicide are at risk of suicide themselves. Not surprisingly, suicide survivors say they need help. Unfortunately, the type of help they need is not known. Suicide survivors are not well studied and therefore there is a poor understanding of the problems they experience. There is disagreement among experts about the emotional consequences of suicide bereavement. There are no studies examining the physical problems that may affect suicide survivors, such as heart disease or high blood pressure, even though it is known that these diseases are common among people bereaved from other causes of death. Although they express a need for help, there is no knowledge of whether they see doctors regularly or use medications when needed. It is thus extremely important to carefully study people bereaved by suicide in order to understand their difficulties. This study will investigate the emotional, physical, and social consequences of suicide bereavement in the entire population of Manitoba, providing the first ever large-scale perspective of suicide's effects on surviving relatives. It will also look at vulnerable groups including children who have lost a parent to suicide, as well as parents who have lost a child to suicide, to see if these groups suffer in different ways. Findings from this study will help identify the problems faced by suicide survivors, leading to better resources and treatment for these people in need.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms through which ShcA integrates tyrosine kinase signaling to promote breast cancer progression.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; ERBB2; RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASE; SHCA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSGENIC MICE; TUMOR ANGIOGENESIS; TUMOR IMMUNITY; TUMOR STROMA
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer remains the most prevalent cancer in Canadian women and the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in this group. While targeted therapies have contributed to a decreased incidence of breast cancer mortality, the prevalence of this disease dictates that novel biomarkers and/or therapeutic targets are required to further improve disease-free survival.  The ShcA adaptor protein activates a critical signaling node in breast cancer cells to regulate diverse biological processes including tumor growth, survival and recruitment of a new blood supply, through a process termed angiogenesis.  We have previously demonstrating that ShcA signaling in breast cancer cells regulates each of these processes to favor a pro-tumorigenic state, which facilitates breast cancer progression.  We will mechanistically address how ShcA signaling favors a pro-tumorigenic and pro-angiogenic state using well characterized breast cancer mouse models. This will ultimately lead to the identification of novel, ShcA-regulated genes that functionally contribute to the tumorigenic process and which may represent viable targets for disease intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and functional characterization of NPHP5, a novel centrosomal protein implicated in human ciliary disease and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CYCLE; CENTROSOMES; CEP290; CILIA; CILIOPATHIES; NPHP5; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: The centrosome is the major microtubule-organizing center of animal cells. It is best known for its role in cell division (in forming the mitotic spindle) and in templating the formation of cell cilia important for proliferation, differentiation, and development. Centrosome aberrations are implicated in wide variety of disorders including cancer, and the presence of supernumerary centrosomes is a distinguishing feature of cancer cells. Ciliary defects can also mediate tumorigenesis and induce disorders such as polycystic kidney disease. Although centrosomes were identified over a hundred years ago, their molecular structure and composition are not fully understood, and the functions of many individual centrosomal components remain elusive. Our research focuses on one novel protein, NPHP5, whose de-regulation is implicated in human ciliary disease and cancer. Through four specific aims, we will examine the function of NPHP5 at the molecular, cellular, and organismal level, and evaluate its contribution to disease. These study results will serve as an important step towards understanding the pathological mechanisms of centrosome dysfunction, and in guiding the development of novel diagnostic and therapeutic applications for diseased patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cell migration and invasion by novel beta-arrestin interacting proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-ARRESTIN; BREAST CANCER; CELL MIGRATION; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; CYTOSKELETON; EXPERIMENTAL ANIMAL MODELS OF METASTASIS; G PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTORS; INVASION; METASTASIS; MOLECULAR IMAGING; SMALL GTPASES
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is one of the most common causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide. The high mortality rate from breast cancer is largely due to the metastatic spread of the disease. Metastasis is the ability of a cancer to spread from where it starts to other parts of the body. Therefore suppression of dissemination is an important issue in the treatment of the disease.  We have identified proteins namely 'arrestins' that are highly expressed breast tumor cells and stimulate their ability to migrate and invade, two processes required for metastasis. We will now assess the ability of arrestins to regulate metastasis, using animal models of metastasis. We will deplete arrestin proteins from breast cancer cells, and evaluate the effect on tumor formation and growth. The tumors in animals will be tracked using fluorescent (glowing) tags, which will allow us to monitor their growth and number. We will determine if less tumours develop and if cancer spread is reduced if arrestins are depleted from the breast cancer cells. This will establish for the first time a direct role for arrestin proteins in regulating metastasis.  We will also determine how the expression of arrestin and downstream signaling molecules changes in patient breast tumors compared to normal breast tissues, and use cell model systems to understand how arrestin proteins signal in breast tumor cells to regulate cell invasion. These 'bench-to-bedside' translational studies will enable us to identify specific small molecule inhibitors that interfere with arrestin signaling in tumor cells. This work will provide a better understanding at the molecular events regulating breast cancer metastasis, and may reveal novel drug targets for the treatment and prevention of this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diesel Exhaust and Mechanisms of Asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTION; AIRWAY REACTIVITY; ALLERGEN; ASTHMA; CONTROLLED EXPOSURE; DIESEL EXHAUST; HUMAN; METHACHOLINE; OXIDATIVE STRESS; SYNERGY
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is common, within Canada and worldwide, and has major health and economic consequences. The airways ("breathing tubes") of people with asthma are inflamed and will react to irritants by narrowing and making it more difficult to breathe. This typically results in an "asthma exacerbation" whereby the asthmatic will notice shortness of breath and may need urgent medical attention.    Diesel exhaust (DE) is associated with asthma exacerbations, but how and why this occurs is unclear. One hypothesis (or "educated guess") has been that DE causes "oxidative stress", which is damage to cells and body tissues due to certain chemical characteristics classically, this is due to an "unpaired electron"). Therefore, we want to test the idea that DE creates oxidative stress and that this is responsible for airway narrowing in human asthmatics. We also want to know if this is made worse by the addition of a typical allergen (for example, pollen from the alder tree).     In our laboratory, we create DE and we finely control its concentration while volunteers inhale it for 2 hours. The concentration of DE is typical of that in a mining operation or on the streets of Mexico City. Such a short exposure time has no permanent effects but should show mild changes in the airways and blood (which return completely back to normal within hours) to help us decide if our hypothesis is correct. Each volunteer subject is exposed, on different days, to DE and to clean air. Before and after each exposure, we perform tests to see how much oxidative stress and airway narrowing is occurring. In some subjects, we add alder pollen to see if that worsens the effect of DE.     This research will allow a better understanding of DE-related airways disease, and this may should lead to measures to protect Canadians exposed to traffic-related pollution. This research may support a recommendation for or against changes in fuel composition or personal measures to bolster anti-oxidant levels.

TitreApplicationTitle: The British Columbia Adolescent Substance Use Survey
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT TOBACCO; INTERNET-BASED WEB SURVEY; LATENT GROWTH MIXTURE MODELING; MARIJUANA AND ALCOHOL USE; PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY; TIME-DEPENDENT PSYCHOSOCIAL DETERMINANTS; TRAJECTORIES OF SUBSTANCE USE
Abstract-Résumé: The use of tobacco, alcohol and marijuana by teenagers continues to pose a significant threat to the health and safety of many young Canadians. Recent national surveys indicate that 15 percent of Canadian teens smoke tobacco; one third of all teens have tried marijuana more than once with about 8 percent of teens reporting marijuana use of at least once a week. Just over 44 percent of teens reported drinking 1 to 3 times per month with an additional 17 percent of teens aged 15 to 17 drinking 1 to 3 times a week or more. Despite extensive prevention efforts, the use of these substances appears to have become a normalized part of adolescence. The goal of this study is to investigate patterns in the progression of substance use, using an internet-based web-survey, in approximately 5,000 adolescents as they progress through the first 3 years of secondary school. We plan to group adolescents into different trajectories of alcohol, tobacco and marijuana use and then examine how the level and influence of known risk factors (e.g., sensation seeking and peer substance use) change as adolescents enter and then progress through high school. The information gained from this study will improve our understanding of the determinants of individual differences in the development of alcohol, tobacco, and marijuana use. The findings will be shared with health promotion experts and school district supervisors to inform local drug education and health promotion activities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the formation of protein aggregates induced by the inhibition of the ubiquitin proteasome system
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMICAL BIOLOGY; HUNTINGTON DISEASE; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MISFOLDING; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; PROTEASOME; PROTEIN AGGREGATE; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Protein aggregation is a pathological feature of a large number of diseases with a strong preponderance in age-related neurodegenerative disorders like Huntington's disease. Failure to eliminate aberrant proteins plays a major role in these pathologies and is often linked to the impairment of the ubiquitin proteasome system, which degrades proteins labeled (or modified) with ubiquitin. The overall goal of this proposal is to further define the involvement of this system in aggregation diseases using proteomic and chemical biological approaches.   We developed a new assay to monitor the formation of aggregates induced by proteasome inhibition and we identified several new proteins that localize in these structures. We will determine whether these newly identified proteins are also involved in the formation of the aggregates. We also identified several small molecules that perturbed the aggregate formation in the cell and will further characterize them.  Current treatments for most aggregation diseases are primarily based on symptom management instead of directly treating the cause. A major endeavor is to identify small molecules that block the cause of the disease progression and identify which cellular pathways are involved in aggregation. Our work may potentially lead to better understanding of aggregation mechanism and identify new targetable pathways to prevent formation or favor clearance of proteins aggregates.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing Stroke Family Caregiver Support across the Care Continuum by Improving the Timing of Intervention Delivery
Keywords-MotsClés: CARE-GIVING; HOME CARE; MIXED METHODOLOGY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; STROKE; SUPPORT INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: About 50% of stroke survivors have limitations in their activities of daily living on return to the community.  Family caregivers provide invaluable support to these individuals during their recovery and rehabilitation. Unfortunately, there is no standard clinical practice to prepare caregivers for this role and, as a result, many experience stress and poor health that can compromise stroke survivor recovery and threaten the sustainability of the care needed to thrive in their home.  To address this gap, we have developed the Timing it Right Stroke Family Support Program that aims to meet the evolving needs of caregivers. The objective of this multi-province randomized controlled trial is to determine if this program delivered across the stroke care continuum improves caregivers' sense of being supported and emotional well-being. Ultimately this program could be used by stroke care programs from across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: The social and structural contexts of HIV/STIs among women and youth working in the sex industry in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER; HIV/STI PREVENTION; SEX WORK; SEXUAL HEALTH; SOCIAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; VIOLENCE; WOMEN; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: This new investigator award application aims to investigate the social (violence, work conditions) and structural (laws, regulations, urban renewal) contexts of HIV/STIs among youth and women working in the sex industry in Vancouver, BC. The persistently high rates of health-related harms, violence and mortality among sex workers both in Canada and globally highlight a desperate need for renewed public health interventions targeting the reduction of harms in the sex industry. Building on international guidelines and the CIHR priorities for sex and gender-based analyses, we will aim to evaluate longitudinally the broader risk environment that shapes gendered negotiation of partner-level risk and HIV/STI acquisition among youth and adult women in sex industry work.  To meet these objectives, the proposed research will be based upon the assembly and follow-up of a real cohort consisting of: 1) 500 existing and new adult women working in both the street and indoor sex industry in the AESHA (An Evaluation of Sex Workers' Health Access) I cohort; and 2) 500 female youth aged 14-20 years who have exchanged sex for money, drugs, gifts, shelter or other commodities in the previous 30days in the AESHA II cohort (youth arm).   The novel integration of individual mapping data and neighborhood environment data from publicly- available data sources (such as, housing, violence) will increase the potential for directly informing interventions to reduce harm. To our knowledge this study is among the first prospective studies of sex work in North America. The team I have assembled brings a wealth of expertise in observational and intervention research, policy and sex work, and as such, is uniquely positioned to conduct this study, which aims to directly improve the health of some of the most marginalized youth and women in Canadian society.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS; ANTIVIRAL DRUGS; CHEMOTHERAPY; CHILDREN; CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY; CORTICOSTEROIDS; DRUG SAFETY; OPTIMAL THERAPEY
Abstract-Résumé: Serious drug side effects (Adverse Drug Reactions or ADRs) are both common and important problems in treatment of children. How these reactions occur is poorly understood.  The goal for the CIHR-GSK Chair in Paediatric Clinical Pharmacology is to study the question of how ADRs occurs in order to better understand how to treat serious side effect and develop strategies to predict which patients are at risk for these side effects before the drug is administered.  These studies have not been possible to date because of problems in identifying patients and in finding suitable control patients.  The CIHR-GSK Chair will undertake these studies by using a new and unique Canadian resource, the Canadian Pharmacogenomic Network for Drug Safety, a unique cross-Canada national network to collect large numbers of children who have had serious ADRs and control patients who have tolerated these drugs. .  The CIHR-GSK Chair will undertake studies of the mechanisms responsible for serious ADRs, the genetic factors that may change risk and the validation of these findings in pursuit of the goal of the CIHR-GSK Chair safer drug therapy for children in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Introspection and insight in non-clinical and clinical populations
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; BELIEF FORMATION; CHOICE BLINDNESS; CONFABULATORY INTROSPECTION; DELUSIONAL DISORDER; IMAGINATION; INSIGHT; OBSESSIONAL DOUBT; OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER; REASONING
Abstract-Résumé: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) and Delusional Disorder (DD) are psychological disorders that are both characterized by faulty beliefs about reality which cause a considerable degree of distress and behavioral problems. Indeed, research over the past nine years has established that what is problematic for the person with OCD and DD is not what actually occurs, but what they imagine to be there. In particular, a tendency to arrive at false beliefs about reality appears strongly related to level of insight into our own reasoning. In particular, a critical mass of studies has shown that failures in introspection are 1) profound, 2) at the root of what appears to be insight, and 3) measurable in an experimental reasoning task (Johansson et al, 2005). Over the next four years, 140 adult patients will participate in a study to measure introspective ability and insight into their own reasoning (OCD, DD and Anxiety Disorder). An additional eighty participants from the general population will be tested for comparison purposes. After baseline assessment on questionnaire, clinical and experimental measures, those with OCD will be retested after 24 weeks of receiving specialized cognitive-behavior therapy. The key hypothesis is that those with OCD and Delusional Disorder will show systematic failures in introspection which leads to obsessional doubt and false beliefs about reality. It is also expected that improvements in insight and introspective ability will be associated with successful treatment outcome. The research program will provide crucial new information on reasoning and imaginative processes characterizing these debilitating psychological disorders, and assist in the development of much needed new treatment strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanism(s) of Lung Protection from Acute and Ventilator Induced Lung Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY; ACUTE RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME; ADENOVIRUS VECTORS; CYCLIC STRECH; DIFFERENTIAL EXPRESSION; GENE THERAPY; INTERFEARING RNA; KNOCKOUT MICE; MECHANOTRANSDUCTION; VENTILATOR INDUCED LUNG INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a common and devastating problem affecting many patients in the intensive care unit. This syndrome is characterized by severe lung inflammation which prevents patients from breathing independently, so most patients need to be placed on life support. Although mechanical ventilation in these patients can be life saving, studies have shown that repeated lung stretch that occurs during artificial ventilation can also increase lung injury and promote further inflammation. This is called ventilator induced lung injury (VILI). VILI contributes significantly to the mortality and long term morbidity of ARDS patients.  There are no known specific treatments for ARDS. The only strategy shown to decrease mortality in these patients is the use of lower tidal volumes - which minimizes lung stretch. My lab is dedicated to understanding how inflammation and mechanical ventilation cause injury and to use this knowledge to develop new therapeutic approaches to reduce lung injury. Using novel genomic technology we have identified a new transcription factor (a molecule that regulates the function of other molecules) that we believe may be important in protecting the lungs from mechanical injury. The mechanism of this protection is unknown. Therefore, in this grant we propose identify the mechanisms by which ATF3 may protect lungs from VILI. We will use both in-vivo (animal) and in-vitro (cell) models to determine which cells (circulating vs. tissue) play a major role; and which mechanisms (inflammation, cell death (apoptosis) and oxidative stress) enable ATF3 to protect lungs from lung injury. This is very important because identifying and understanding novel mechanisms of lung protection is fundamental to developing novel treatment approaches for these and possibly all other patients on life support.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oligodendrocyte Genes, White Matter Disconnectivity, and Cognition in Schizophrenia: An Imaging-Genetics Study
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; GENETICS; OLIGODENDROCYTES; SCHIZOPHRENIA; WHITE MATTER
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness affecting nearly 1% of all Canadians. Although schizophrenia is primarily a genetic disorder, it has been hard to discover genes that may be related to this illness. To help overcome this difficulty, we are using an alternative strategy called imaging-genetics, where we examine the relationship of genes with brain structure and function, to better understand disrupted mental functions (i.e. cognitive deficits) in schizophrenia. This approach may tell us more about how schizophrenia vulnerability genes act in the brain ultimately leading to impaired mental function. Furthermore, this approach may help us understand how risk genes predict disrupted relationships between the brain and mental (cognitive) functions that are impaired in this disorder. The brain imaging technique that we are focusing on is an MRI technique called diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) that allows us to examine the connections between brain regions, known as white matter tracts. Disruption of these brain connections in schizophrenia may lead to impairment of certain mental functions that are impaired in schizophrenia, thus making it difficult for many schizophrenia patients to work and function in daily life. Using a combined genetics and brain imaging approach, we hope to discover the genes related to impaired brain circuitry and mental functions in schizophrenia, and an improved understanding of, and better treatment for cognitive deficits in this debilitating disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of eIF4E in stress granules formation and the associated resistance to chemotherapy
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; EIF4E; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; MRNA EXPRESSION; MTOR SIGNALING; RNA FISH; RNA INTERFERENCE; STRESS GRANULES; TUMOR XENOGRAFTS
Abstract-Résumé: In response to environmental stresses such as exposure to toxic components, to high or cold temperature, and to low oxygen conditions, the cell uses a defense mechanism to fight the stress and survive. Stress can also be produced during anti-cancer treatment. Exposure to patients to prolonged chemical or radiation treatment can induce stress conditions to which cancer cells will respond by mobilizing a defense mechanism. This will allow cancer cells to resist to treatment and grow. The resistance of cancer cells to anti-cancer treatment is one of the major obstacles in treating patients suffering from cancer. Our objective is to understand how cancer cells managed to resist treatment I have been investigating the role of a novel cellular bodies recently identified as important players in mediating the resistance of the cell to stress. These cellular bodies, named stress granules, form within the cell only under stress conditions and their formation promotes cell survival and cancer cells resistance to treatment. We believe that these cellular bodies are sites where specific gene products that are essential for cell survival and growth are protected during treatment. My research focuses its activities on defining the molecular mechanisms that lead to the formation of these cellular bodies, mediating cancer cell resistance to therapy. To achieve our goal, my team is using cancer cells in culture as well as mice models. We investigate how stress granules are formed and how their formation aids cancer cells to resist treatment. Our first objective is to identify the genes involved in their formation. Our second objective is to determine whether targeting these genes can prevent cancer cells resistance to treatment, reducing tumor growth. Our studies will contribute to establish specific strategies to prevent the formation of stress granules, reducing the occurrence of cancer cell resistance when used in combination with conventional cancer therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of language proficiency on stroke care
Keywords-MotsClés: DATA BASE ANALYSIS; LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY; OUTCOMES OF CARE; QUALITY OF CARE; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a common and debilitating medical problem, and a frequent cause of disability and death. Unlike many other medical conditions where the diagnosis and treatment decisions are based largely on laboratory or other diagnostic tests, diagnosis and treatment of stroke are strongly influenced by the symptoms patients describe. Therefore, the ability to communicate effectively with health care providers may influence stroke care. As Canada's population evolves, the proportion of the population that does not speak English or French continues to increase. Any disparities in stroke care due to language proficiency will have an increasing impact at a population level.  The objective of this study is to compare the quality of care and clinical outcomes for Ontario stroke patients who are proficient in English and those who are not.  We will use the Registry of the Canadian Stroke Network, which was established in 2001 to collect data about stroke care for people across Canada. The database includes detailed clinical information not available from other data sources, including language preferences. We will use these data to examine associations between language and stroke care and long-term outcomes.  There is very little previous research studying stroke diagnosis and treatment for people with language barriers, even though stroke care is probably much more affected by communication than other diseases. Most of the previous studies on the impact of language on health care took place in the United States, where the language mixture is very different than in Canada, so the results of those studies are probably not applicable here. The results of this study will lead to greater understanding of the impact of communication and language on health care, which will lead to further research in this important area.

TitreApplicationTitle: CIHR/GSK Chair of Diabetes: abnormal lipid metabolism in the development of type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CHYLOMICRONS; DIABETES MELLITUS; FATTY ACID METABOLISM; INSULIN RESISTANCE; INTEGRATIVE PHYSIOLOGY; LIPOPROTEINS; NUTRITION; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; POSTPRANDIAL METABOLISM; STABLE ISOTOPIC TRACERS
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes (adult onset diabetes) affects between 7 and 10 percent of the Canadian population and is a major cause of mortality and suffering from heart disease, stroke, amputations, blindness, and renal failure.  Its prevalence in our country is increasing due to the epidemics of obesity and aging of the Canadian population. We have shown that abnormal blood fat levels after meals may be implicated very early in the natural history of type 2 diabetes. This could lead to increased exposure of organs to dietary fats and contribute to the development of abnormal muscle, liver, and pancreatic function, the principal characteristics of this disease. Over the past years, we have established new investigation tools to study these processes in humans and have characterized the abnormalities of fat metabolism after meals in pre-diabetic individuals (with two parents with type 2 diabetes or with impaired glucose tolerance, who are at very high risk of developing diabetes). We have shown that fat in the diet is preferentially channelled into lean tissues of these individuals. We will now determine whether this abnormality overwhelms capacity of lean tissues to burn fat and whether it could be reversed with short-term change in diet. The proposed studies may lead to a better understanding of the cause of type 2 diabetes and to more specific targets for prevention and early treatment of this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epidemiology of sexually-transmitted co-infections among HIV-infected persons in care in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: BURDEN OF DISEASE; COHORT STUDIES; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIV/AIDS; INCIDENCE; OBSERVATIONAL STUDIES; RISK FACTORS; SCREENING; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: When people living with HIV acquire a sexually transmitted infection (STI), there are critical implications. First, such coinfections may increase the chances that people will pass on the HIV virus. Acquisition of an STI suggests that sexual risk behaviour is occurring. Moreover, STIs may increase HIV infectiousness. Second, STI co-infections may worsen the health of persons with HIV. Untreated syphilis may lead to neurosyphilis, in which neurological symptoms such as meningitis or dementia may develop. Cancer-causing STIs such as hepatitis viruses lead to far greater risk of progression to cancer than among HIV-uninfected persons.  We propose to study STIs among persons living with HIV in Ontario. We will determine how many were tested for STIs, describe those diagnosed with STIs, and report rates of and risk factors for infection. This project will be carried out in collaboration with the Ontario HIV Treatment Network Cohort Study (OCS). Since the mid-1990s, the OCS has recruited over 5,000 HIV-infected persons from HIV and family practice clinics. The OCS then follows people over time by monitoring their medical charts and interviewing participants annually. We will obtain information on tests done by the participant's regular doctor, as recorded in patients' medical charts. Next, we will obtain data on STI tests submitted to the Ontario Public Health Laboratories, which provide testing for chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, herpes viruses, and hepatitis viruses.   Rates of STIs are on the rise in Canada. Syphilis outbreaks have been reported in Toronto and Ottawa, with many cases among homosexual men who were co-infected with HIV. It is crucial to monitor STIs among the HIV-infected. We will be the first in Canada to report on STIs in a large number of persons living with HIV. The results can be used to improve STI test guidelines, HIV/STI prevention, and the health care and quality of life of those living with HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunotherapy of leukemic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE MYELOID LEUKEMIA; IMMUNOTHERAPY; LEUKEMIC STEM CELL; NATURAL KILLER CELL
Abstract-Résumé: The five year survival of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is less than 40%.  The discovery of leukemic stem cells (LSCs) in AML changed the previous dogma that all cancer cells had equivalent unlimited ability to divide and established that only a small minority of leukemic cells can actually perpetuate the cancer.  Therefore, the development of therapies that target LSCs is of utmost priority to cure patients of their disease. Most patients with AML can achieve a remission with chemotherapy, but many relapse because of minimal residual disease containing LSCs.  The most effective therapy for AML is bone marrow transplantation which allows for high dose chemotherapy and a form of immune therapy from the donor's immune system which consists of T cells and Natural Killer (NK) cells.  Our preliminary work has examined the role of therapeutic NK cell lines to treat AML.  We have found that there is variation of our NK cell lines ability to kill leukemia samples and predict that this may be related to receptors expressed by NK cells which recognize molecules called HLA present on leukemic cells.  We propose here to test if we can predict the sensitivity to killing by NK cell lines based upon a patient's unique HLA type allowing us to potentially personalize therapy by selecting NK cell lines that are most effective for a given patient.  We will also test how effectively the NK cell lines kill the LSCs from leukemia samples.  Our preliminary data shows that one NK cell line, NK-92, can kill LSCs and we are investigating a second one called KHYG-1.  Further, we have been able to treat mice with human leukemia successfully using infusions of NK-92 and propose here experiments to optimize the dose of NK-92.  It is also known that LSCs express a marker on their surface called CD123.  We will test a genetically modified NK-92 cell line that can bind to antibodies and use this in combination with an antibody that can bind CD123 to enhance NK cell killing of LSCs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sleep, Learning, Education, hEalth Project - Edmonton (SLEEP-E at 2 years of age
Keywords-MotsClés: LONGITUDINAL BIRTH COHORT; POLYSOMNOGRAPHY; POPULATION REPRESENTATIVE STUDY; PRESCHOOL BEHAVIOUR AND EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; PRESCHOOL NEURODEVELOPMENT; SLEEP DISORDERED BREATHING
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood sleep disordered breathing (SDB), from habitual snoring to obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, is associated with academic difficulties and ADHD-like symptoms long after the SDB has resolved. SDB in pre-school children, a period of significant brain development, is under-studies and consequently, the long-term impact on growth and development may be under-appreciated. We hypothesize that children with SDB in the first two years of life are more likely to present with learning difficulties at 2 years of age. We are currently recruiting 1000 pregnant women in Edmonton for a new longitudinal birth cohort study. Cognitive development will be assessed by the Bayley Scale of Infant Development (BSID-III) at age 1 and 2 years. Childhood behaviour and executive function will be assessed by the Child Behaviour Checklist (CBCL) and the Behaviour Rating Inventory of Executive Function®-Preschool Version (BRIEF-P) at age 2 years. To identify children with SDB, we will administer the Paediatric Sleep Questionnaire to all 1000 children every 3 months, complete a laboratory sleep study on all children at age 1, and a sleep study at age 2 years in children previously identified as having SDB or developmental delays. This proposal describes a unique opportunity to address questions of critical importance to human development in the context of a new longitudinal birth cohort study.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of CRTh2 and its Role in Allergic Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; CELL CULTURE; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE REGULATION; HUMAN TH2 CELLS; MECHANISMS OF ALLERGIC DISEASE; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISM; TRANSIENT TRANSFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Allergic diseases such as asthma are mediated by a number of cell types, particularly T helper type 2 (Th2) cells and eosinophils. Both these cell types express a protein called CRTh2, which helps them enter the site of allergic inflammation, such as the lung, nose or skin. CRTh2 also regulates the production of pro-allergy mediators like the Th2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13. This proposal is focused on understanding expression of CRTh2. Since genetic variation in CRTh2 is associated with higher risk of developing allergic asthma, we will also examine whether these single changes in DNA sequence change expression of CRTh2 and/or are more frequent in certain types of asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Applying a theory-based approach to identify the psychosocial determinants of the intention of dietitians to engage in shared decision making behaviours
Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NUTRITION; SHARED DECISION MAKING
Abstract-Résumé: Enormous scientific advances have been made in the area of nutrition, and several diets are now advocated for the management of chronic diseases including cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and obesity. Patients have also become reliant on the unregulated nutrition information emerging in cyberspace, television and magazines to base their diet-related decisions. As a result, the need for patient guidance and decision support from dietitians is expected to increase in the near future. Shared decision making is defined as a decision-making process jointly shared by patients and their health professional. It aims at helping patients play an active role in decisions concerning their health and fosters the establishment of a context in which the preferences of the patient are sought and his/her opinions valued. To date, few studies have explored shared decision making in health professionals other than physicians. Therefore, this research program proposes to identify the determinants of the intention of dietitians and patients to adopt selected behaviors necessary to engage in shared decision making. Studying shared decision making in nutrition has the potential to contribute to the acquisition of skills that will allow patients to make decisions that are best for them in interaction with their dietitians, which will result in an overall improvement of the quality and effectiveness of health services and care of patients facing nutrition-related decisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gait variability as predictor of cognitive decline and risk of falls in MCI: A cohort Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGES; DEMENTIA; FALLS; GAIT; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; VASCULAR RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: A decrease in walking speed (gait slowing) is a common problem in older persons and is frequently overlooked though it is a strong predictor of future disability and adverse events. Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a transitional state between normal cognition and mild dementia, however, not all older people having MCI will develop dementia. Recently, a Canadian consensus on dementia called for better characterization of MCI emphasizing the need to identify potential clinical, imaging, and biological changes that may serve as predictors of further dementia. To date, such a predictors have not been identified. However, since an association between gait slowing and dementia has been established, gait itself might be able to serve as such a predictor.  This study plans to assess the ability of quantitative gait analyses, specifically gait variability under a dual-task condition (e.g.walking while counting backwards), to predict time to progression to dementia in older persons with MCI. A secondary objective is to determine if there are particular physical changes in the brain that are associated with gait variability and slowed gait velocity.  Our hypotheses: 1) High gait variability in people with MCI will predict future progression to dementia. 2) Further gait variability during dual-task conditions is an independent predictor of dementia. 3) Gait variability and a faster progression to dementia will be associated with specific physical changes in the brain.  If the hypotheses are confirmed, conducting practical assessments of gait in people with MCI may help determine who may eventually progress to dementia. Since dementia is a prevalent and important public health problem, improved detection of those at higher risk is a priority. Better detection will help the Canadian health system to optimize available resources and strategies to implement early interventions to preserve function and to improve the quality of life of seniors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Detrimental dialogue between the immune system and the central nervous system: roles of CD8 T lymphocytes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; AUTOIMMUNITY; CYTOKINES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; LYMPHOCYTES; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis is the most common disease of the brain in young adults: between 55,000 and 75,000 people are affected by this disease in Canada. Despite many years of research, the cause of this illness is still unknown. The immune system usually provides protection against microbes. However, the immune system in multiple sclerosis patients shows abnormalities and it attacks components of the brain as if they were foreign microbes. The purpose of our study is to identify molecules present in the brain of multiple sclerosis patients that are used by the immune system to attack it. A particular type of white blood cells bears the capacity to kill other cells and was observed in the brain of multiple sclerosis patients at the site of tissue destruction. The goal is to analyze these killing cells and determine what potentiate their capacity to be toxic in the brain of multiple sclerosis patients. We hope to identify new molecules and cells that could eventually be targeted by future treatments.
