TitreApplicationTitle: Structure and dynamics of the cardiac troponin I - troponin C complex by solution NMR spectroscopy: Implications of phosphorylation of troponin I Ser22 and Ser23
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC PROTEIN; DRUG BINDING SITES; DYNAMICS; FUNCTION; HEART FAILURE; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; STRUCTURE; TROPONIN COMPLEX
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a major problem in people who have had heart attacks or who suffer from other diseases affecting the heart. People with heart failure cannot pump enough blood forward to meet the metabolic needs of the body. The back pressure from the pump failure also causes fluid to collect in the lungs and the rest of the body, making it difficult to breathe and to move.  Understanding heart function at the molecular level is essential to developing new drugs to prevent and treat heart failure. Some drugs reduce the stress on the heart. Others help the heart to pump harder. All drugs work by binding to proteins to change how they function. Proteins are the molecular machines that carry out all biological functions.  Two proteins important to heart function are called troponin I and troponin C. Troponin I prevents the muscle cell from contracting when it is not supposed to. (The "I" is for inhibition.) When a muscle cell receives an electrical signal telling it to contract, the signal causes calcium channel proteins to open, flooding the cell with calcium. The calcium binds to troponin C (the "C" is for calcium). This triggers a conformational change in troponin C so that it neutralizes troponin I and allows heart muscle contraction to occur.  Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a powerful technique that allows scientists to "see" proteins at the atomic level. We will use NMR to visualize the complex between troponin I and troponin C.  When the body becomes stressed, adrenaline causes the heart to pump harder. One of the ways this happens is troponin I becomes "phosphorylated" - this means that extra phosphate groups are attached to it. We will also use NMR to see how phosphorylation affects the troponin I - troponin C complex and how this changes heart function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Monoamine Oxidase A Binding in Impulsive Aggressive Individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder and Antisocial Personality Disorder: A Carbon 11-labeled Harmine PET Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTISOCIAL PERSONALITY DISORDER; BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER; HARMINE; IMPULSIVE AGGRESSION; MONOAMINE OXIDASE-A (MAO-A); POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; SUICIDALITY; VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Human aggression and violence represent significant public health concerns in Canada and worldwide.  The World Health Organization provided a one-year, worldwide estimate of 1.43 million deaths due to self-inflicted or interpersonal violence (excluding armed conflict), with most fatalities resulting from unplanned or impulsive acts of aggression (WHO, 2007).  Borderline personality disorder (BPD), which affects 2% of the population, and antisocial personality disorder (ASPD), found in 6.5% of Canadian males, are two common psychiatric conditions often seen in people who act aggressively on impulse.  These individuals undermine the health of the population through their repeated acts of aggression toward themselves and others.  Certain animals lacking a brain chemical called monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) act very aggressively compared with animals that have normal brain levels of MAO-A.  MAO-A is a brain protein that affects brain development.  Levels of MAO-A are low in healthy people who report more impulsive behavior.  At present, we do not know whether MAO-A is low in people who are extremely impulsive and aggressive and have BPD or ASPD.  We propose using a well-developed brain scanning technique called [11C] harmine positron emission tomography (PET) to study MAO-A levels in the brains of aggressive and impulsive people with ASPD or BPD.  We will also use [11C] harmine PET to study brain MAO-A levels in healthy people without personality disorders who do not act aggressively.  We hypothesize that brain MAO-A levels will be lower in people with ASPD or BPD compared with healthy people.  Our anticipated results could have important implications for the prevention and treatment of maladaptive aggression and impulsivity.  For example, lower brain MAO-A in aggressive people with BPD or ASPD may mean that treatments which raise MAO-A or perform the same function as MAO-A could lower impulsivity, aggression, and violence.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of G-protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (Gprk2) in Hedgehog signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; DROSOPHILA; G-PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; HEDGEHOG SIGNALING; MOLECULAR GENETICS; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Hedgehog (Hh) proteins are an evolutionarily-conserved family of growth factors that are secreted from cells and convey information to neighbouring cells within tissues. These proteins play a critical role in controlling the growth and organization of embryonic and fetal tissues in species ranging from flies to man. They are also important for stem cell function, and consequently for maintenance of adult tissues. Due to their central role in these processes, misregulation of Hh activity can result in congenital birth defects and cancer. Much of our understanding of how Hh proteins work comes from studies in the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster. The main initiator of intracellular signaling in response to Hh is a protein called Smoothened (Smo). Upon exposure of cells to Hh, Smo moves to the cell surface and becomes active, sending a signal that is relayed to the nucleus to change patterns of gene expression. We have shown that a protein called G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (Gprk2) is involved in Hh signaling in flies, as loss of this protein affects Smo regulation and blocks changes in gene expression in response to Hh. Our studies are aimed at identifying how Gprk2 regulates Smo, and how this contributes to the relay of the Hh signal to the nucleus. Gprk2-related proteins in mammals have also been implicated in Hh signaling. Thus, we expect that our studies in flies will provide important basic insights into how Hh proteins normally signal in humans, and how this can be misregulated in disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the Dynamics of Large Ribonucleoprotein Complex Maturation
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY CHROMATOGRAPHY; BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL BIOLOGY; FLUORESCENT MICROSCOPY; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEOMICS; RIBONUCLEOPROTEIN MATURATION PATHWAYS; RIBOSOMES; RNA; RNOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: One of the central tenets of biology is that DNA makes RNA, which then makes protein. The DNA sequence in genes is copied into a messenger RNA, whose encoded information is then read by ribosomes, the cellular protein translation machinery, and used to produce proteins. Ribosomes consist themselves of RNA and proteins, and the communication of correct DNA-encoded information, does not only depend on proper conversion of a genes sequence into messenger RNA, but also on the presence of functional ribosomes within cells. Ribosome biogenesis is the process of making ribosomes and involves the coordinated function of over 200 proteins in the synthesis and processing of four ribosomal RNAs, as well as assembly of those ribosomal RNAs with the ribosomal proteins. Incorrect processing and assembly of ribosomal RNAs, which comprise the catalytic part of the protein translation machinery, can result in serious diseases such as various cancers, hematopoietic diseases, and even Altzheimer's Disease. Understanding the molecular mechanisms that define the order of maturation events during ribosome biogenesis is therefore of great interest and importance. The main aim of the proposed research is to study the dynamic changes that take place during the maturation of ribosomal RNA-protein complexes in the unicellular eukaryotic model systems Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which will allow us to gain insight into how the ordered assembly of molecular interactions controls the regulation of ribosome maturation. Since ribosomes and their biogenesis have been highly conserved during evolution, the results from this study will be used in the future to understand how ribosome biogenesis events can affect the development of certain diseases as well as the fate of cells and organisms as a whole.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying regulators of alpha-synuclein toxicity in dopaminergic neurodegeneration using a novel in vivo assay
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA-SYNUCLEIN; C. ELEGANS; GENETIC SCREEN; LEWY BODIES; MOLECULAR SIGNALLING; NEURODEGENERATION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a debilitating movement disorder which is increasing in prevalence and thus having a growing impact on the Canadian population. The clinical symptoms of PD include tremor, rigidity, slowness of movements, and postural instability. It has long been recognized that these symptoms are a consequence of the death of specific groups of cells in the brain. There are drugs which treat the clinical symptoms of PD by replacing the neurotransmitter that is lost with the death of these brain cells. However, there are currently no treatments available to slow or stop the disease process itself. A growing body of evidence implicates a protein called alpha-synuclein in the death of brain cells in PD. It is believed that early in the disease alpha-synuclein accumulates in brain cells and, by mechanisms not yet fully understood, leads to the death of these cells. The goal of this research project is to identify molecules that may influence alpha-synuclein-mediated cell death. To accomplish this, I propose to develop a novel assay using the nematode C. elegans as a non-mammalian model system. This C. elegans assay will be used to perform a large screen for genes responsible for modulating alpha-synuclein. The candidate genes will be further characterized using biochemical techniques to assess for physical interactions with alpha-synuclein in vitro as well as functional interactions in live cells. I plan to continue to further characterize these modifiers of alpha-synuclein as I transition to independent investigator. It is hoped that new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of PD will evolve from this project. In particular, therapies that increase the action of molecules which inhibit alpha-synuclein or, conversely, treatments that decrease the activity of molecules which increase alpha-synuclein may be strategies that could prevent neurodegeneration in PD. This is an avenue of investigation that I plan to pursue in future studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation and Dynamics of Mitotic Spindle Assembly
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DIVISION; CHEMICAL BIOLOGY; FLUORESCENCE LIGHT MICROSCOPY; KINESIN MOTOR PROTEINS; LIVE CELL IMAGING; MITOTIC SPINDLE ASSEMBLY
Abstract-Résumé: When a cell divides, a complex machine is built to accurately separate genetic material (DNA) into two daughter cells. This machine is called the mitotic spindle, due to its shape: a broad barrel, pointed on both ends.  The spindle composed of mainly cable-like polymers called microtubules, which can connect to and move the DNA. Dr. Kwok's Laboratory will study key protein molecules that interact with these polymers and understand how they are coordinated to build this DNA-segregation machine. Improper segregation of DNA can cause cells to have an abnormal amount of genetic material, an outcome often associated with cancer. Our cells have surveillance systems to monitor whether this DNA-segregating machine is properly assembled, they will not divide until the spindle is properly formed and connected to DNA. Since cancer is a disease of uncontrolled cell divisions, inhibiting spindle formation thus provides a way to block cells from dividing. Understanding how this DNA-segregation machine is built could help us to identify new targets for developing improved anti-cancer drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exome Sequencing of Familial Colorectal Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENETICS; EXOME CAPTURE; GENOMIC ANALYSIS; GERMLINE; HEREDITARY CANCER; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is common and kills over 60,000 men and women each year in North America.  Up to a third of cases can be attributed to the genes you inherited from your mother and father. In five to ten percent of cases the strong predisposition to CRC is thought to be due to mutations in single genes. Thus if, the causative gene is identified in a family, family members can be tested for the gene and if they have it, undergo regular screening or alternatives like prophylactic surgery to remove the organ where cancer is likely to occur.   Many families with familial CRC are not found to carry genes known to predispose to cancer. Identification of further cancer genes would greatly benefit these families. Recently, advances in ways of quickly analyzing all of the genes in a family have enabled us to see which genetic variations correlate in a family with susceptibility to CRC.  By identifying genes that predispose to cancer, we might also find out more about how to prevent or cure cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health Outcomes and Physical activity in Preschoolers: The "HOPP" Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCELEROMETRY; HEALTH  OUTCOMES; HEALTH-RELATED FITNESS; MOTOR PROFICIENCY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PRESCHOOL CHILDREN
Abstract-Résumé: The preschool years are a period of growth for which we know the least about the impact of physical activity. Since society has traditionally thought of little kids as "active enough", important questions regarding physical activity and health in preschoolers have gone unanswered. Because Canada is facing a childhood obesity epidemic, there has never been a greater need to understand how physical activity during the early years is related to health. If we do not fill this gap in our knowledge, it will be impossible to develop evidence-based policies to promote physical activity for preschoolers. The goal of our study is to measure physical activity in preschoolers and determine how activity levels relate to key health outcomes, including body composition (obesity), how well blood vessels work (heart health), fitness levels, and information related to quality of life. To know if active preschoolers are really healthier preschoolers as they grow up, we will make these assessments in 408 children ages 3 to 5 years (equal number of boys and girls) who will be tested once per year for 3 years, until the 3-year-olds are 5 and the 5-year-olds are 7. Since preschool children are still developing movement skills, we will also test their ability to perform basic movement skills at each yearly assessment along with their parents' beliefs about physical activity for their preschooler - two pieces of information that could be used to help influence preschooler physical activity. In preparation for this study, we have adapted existing tests and even developed new ones for use with preschoolers, and our research team is involved in several initiatives related to physical activity for preschoolers including the possibility of developing physical activity guidelines. Canada could be a leader in this area. Our study will provide the evidence to create public policies that work and optimize the spending of precious public funds for physical activity promotion during the early years.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional regulation by a novel deubiquitinase multi-protein complex
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; DEUBIQUITINASE; GENE EXPRESSION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN INTERACTION; RNAI; TRANSCRIPTION; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Ubiquitination is an essential biochemical reaction which occurs in all cells of our body. This process consists of the attachment of a small protein, called ubiquitin, to various cellular proteins. This labeling system marks the target proteins as unwanted (or no longer needed), and induces their degradation by a molecular machine called the (proteasome). Interestingly it has recently been realized that ubiquitination can also cause changes in the function and properties of the targeted protein without any degradation. Moreover we have now started to appreciate that ubiquitination is a dynamic process and that certain enzymes, called deubiquitinases (or DUBs for short), ensure the timely removal of ubiquitin from proteins. In fact, the functional interaction between ubiquitination and deubiquitination allows cells to tightly regulate protein function. With this capability, the ubiquitin system executes and/or regulates many cellular processes, and these include cellular proliferation. It is therefore not surprising that alterations in components of the ubiquitin system have been causally linked to cancer. The goal of my research is to determine how DUBs regulate gene expression, a subject about which very little is currently known. I plan to use molecular and cellular biology approaches to characterize the biological function and mechanism of action of a DUB called BAP1. This will not only shed new light on the mechanisms that govern normal cellular processes, but will also help in furthering our understanding of disease development and treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of antiviral immunity and eradication rates after modulating immunoregulatory mechanisms in chronic Hepatitis B virus infection
Keywords-MotsClés: HEPATITIS B VIRUS; HIV; IMMUNOLOGY; TREATMENT RESPONSE; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) affects 350 million people worldwide and is a leading cause of liver cancer and liver disease, particularly in HIV co-infected populations.  People who develop chronic infection most often become lifelong HBV carriers, with current therapies failing to eradicate the virus in most cases. The reason why the immune system does not clear the infection is unclear, however exhaustion or inhibition of immune cells that act against the virus are possible explanations. In chronic HBV infection, previous studies have shown high levels of an immune system inhibiting receptor, programmed death (PD)-1. We hypothesis that blocking the PD-1 receptor in HBV-infected individuals, whether HIV co-infected or not, will promote more effective cell mediated immune responses, and lead to higher cure rates than current HBV therapies alone. Our study will assess the effect of blocking PD-1 on HBV-specific and non-specific immune responses in HBV mono-infected and HBV/HIV co-infected individuals. In addition to providing further information on immune responses in chronic viral infection, this study will provide vital information about the potential for directly harnessing the immune system to cure HBV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Étude de la prévalence et des déterminants de la boue intra-amniotique en relation avec la grande prématurité
Keywords-MotsClés: GROSSESSE; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; LIQUIDE AMNIOTIQUE; MALADIE PARODONTALE; PREMATURITE; RUPTURE PREMATUREE PRETERME DES MEMBRANES; TRAVAIL PRETERME; VAGINOSE BACTERIENNE; ECHOGRAPHIE
Abstract-Résumé: L'infection et l'inflammation du liquide amniotique sont associees a la majorite des naissances prematurees avant 32 semaines et aux complications chez la mere et l'enfant qui en resultent. Les connaissances actuelles semblent demontrer que la contamination du liquide amniotique aurait lieu bien avant que les symptomes de travail premature ne soient detectables. Nos travaux preliminaires suggerent que la presence d'agregats (communement appeles « boue ») dans le liquide amniotique pourrait etre un des signes precoces d'infection du liquide amniotique. L'identification de cette «boue» par echographie serait une technique non-invasive prometteuse pour depister les femmes presentant une infection et/ou une inflammation intra-amniotique pouvant mener a la prematurite. Par la presente etude, nous proposons d'evaluer l'association entre la presence de boue intra-amniotique au 2ieme trimestre de la grossesse et la grande prematurite dans la population generale ainsi que les facteurs associes a la presence de cette « boue » dans le liquide amniotique.

Keywords-MotsClés: BONE DENSITY; BONE QUALITY; BONE STRENGTH; COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; FRACTURE; MECHANICAL UNLOADING; NEUROLOGIC INJURY; OSTEOPOROSIS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis-related fragility fractures impose a substantial burden on patients, their families and the health care system. Vertebral and hip fractures are associated with higher mortality rates and reduced quality of life. Individuals with neurologic impairment (e.g. stroke or spinal cord injury), experience dramatic losses of bone and a high fracture risk, but there are no guidelines for assessment and treatment of osteoporosis for these individuals.  The current proposal outlines research that will: 1) improve the identification of individuals at high risk of fracture; 2) evaluate the effectivness of new treatments, including non-drug strategies like exercise; and 3) integrate the knowledge learned into practice.

Abstract-Résumé: Adult-onset diabetes frequently occurs in family members as a result of inherited changes in the sequence of their genes. We have discovered a number of changes in DNA can make people more prone to developing diabetes. In the current project, we will study the physiologic effects of one of these these DNA changes to determine how it increases a person's risk of developing diabetes. In particular, we will determine how a genetic change on human chromosome 2 affects insulin's ability to alter cellular metabolism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathways to pediatric mental health care: A distance support program for parents following pediatric emergency mental health care
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN'S MENTAL HEALTH; DELPHI CONSULTATION; INTERVENTION DEVELOPMENT; INTERVENTION EVALUATION; PARENT-BASED SUPPORT; POST-EMERGENCY CARE; QUALITATIVE METHODS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TELEHEALTH; WAITING LISTS
Abstract-Résumé: Currently, in times of acute crisis, immediate mental health care options for families with children with mental illness are limited. While hospital emergency departments (EDs) are recognized as a critical health care access point, most children are discharged from the ED without access to appropriate, urgent follow-up care. A failure to provide urgent care can result in: increased emergency service demands through repeat visits for same events, increased stress for families, and increased economic costs through use of expensive emergency services. These outcomes suggest a need for follow-up support for families that includes support for parents who care for their child after an acute crisis. Through national collaborations with researchers, health care providers and administrators, and Canadian families, we propose to develop and evaluate a potentially groundbreaking telehealth intervention that can provide Canadian parents of vulnerable children timely access to evidence-based care and critical support while they are waiting for services. This intervention, Family Pathways, will bridge emergency and community-based services addressing the current urgent care gap. We will conduct a multi-phase study. Phase 1 will focus on intervention adaptation, refinement and pre-testing using the Delphi process with a nationally representative group of clinical experts, and qualitative interviews with intervention stakeholders (parents, clinicians, and administrators). In Phase 2, Family Pathways will be compared to a wait-list, control group in a multi-site demonstration trial (randomized controlled trial; RCT) to assess intervention acceptability and feasibility, and to establish processes for a full-scale, nation-wide RCT. This study will result in a robust, clinical intervention that can provide parents with timely access to evidence-based care and, if effective, will be a critical support while families are waiting for services after a mental health crisis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Composition, Structure and Function of Human Acquired Enamel Pellicle
Keywords-MotsClés: ACIDIC PRP; ACQUIRED ENAMEL PELLICLE; AFM; ENAMEL HOMEOSTASIS; HISTATIN; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEOMICS; SALIVA; SALIVARY PROTEINS; STATHERIN
Abstract-Résumé: The acquired enamel pellicle (AEP) is a protein film with unique composition and properties which is formed in a selective manner on tooth enamel surfaces. The composition and the structure of this protein film are still mainly unknown but play functionally a vital role with important physiological/clinical implications. Its presence has important consequences both with respect to the protection of tooth enamel mineral and with respect to the nature of oral bacteria which colonize this tooth integument leading ultimately to bacterial colonization and the formation of dental plaque. The overall goal of this project is to gain insight into the biologic formation and function of the human acquired enamel pellicle. A major driving force of this application is therefore to use state-of-the-art proteomics to better characterize the components of the in vivo formed pellicle. It is also planned to explore the structural and functional properties of those in vivo AEP components by in situ and in vitro experiments. The results of the work proposed herein will contribute significantly to the characterization of human AEP in vivo, and to our understanding of the biological functions of its components. In addition, this study may provide insights into the pathological processes underlying the initiation of dental caries and periodontal diseases. Moreover, the functional characterization of novel proteins and peptides may lead to the development of therapeutics aimed at controlling biofilm growth, remineralizing early carious lesions and providing new salivary substitutes.

Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is an idiopathic condition involving the gut that leads to many complications unrelated to the bowels - blood clots being among the most deadly.  IBD patients who develop blood clots require the use of blood thinners. Being on these medications reduces the risk of death from blood clots but also increases the risk of bleeding.  Currently, it is not clear how long IBD patients with blood clots should receive blood thinners since we do not have enough information on the long-term risks of recurrent blood clots and death.  This current study seeks to obtain this vital information by reviewing the medical records of IBD patients in Ontario who have developed blood clots.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing Healthcare-Associated Infections in the Vancouver Metropolitan Region
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH BEHAVIOR; HEALTHCARE-ASSOCIATED INFECTIONS; INFECTION CONTROL; POLICY REFORMS; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Healthcare-associated infections (HAI) are an increasingly serious threat to the well-being of Canadians and the health care system. Despite the severity of the threat, evidence-based infection control programs can reduce HAIs. Researchers estimate that between 30% and 50% of health-care associated infections are preventable. While research has focused on modifying behaviour of healthcare workers, more research is needed on structural barriers to implementing infection control programs, policies, and practices. My previous research with hospital housekeepers and support workers in the Vancouver region uncovered some issues with understaffing, work stress and inadequate training among these workers after their jobs were privatized and outsourced. The proposed research builds on these findings to use qualitative research methods - including interviews with scholars, expert and stakeholder - in order to identify structural barriers to improving infection control and reducing HAIs, with a focus on MRSA and C.difficile in acute care settings, in the context of Vancouver metropolitan region. These interviews and regular think tank meetings that bring together experts and stakeholders will focus on identifying barriers and strategies to improve infection control and reduce HAIs with the goal of improving patient safety and quality of healthcare.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reversibility of Neurobehavioral Deficits Associated with Manganese Exposure from Drinking Water
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; COGNITION; COHORT; DRINKING WATER CONTAMINATION; ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; MANGANESE NEUROTOXICITY; MEMORY; NEUROMOTOR FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Manganese is an essential nutrient in small dose, but in excess, this metal can be neurotoxic for humans. In several regions of Canada, drinking water can contain a high concentration of manganese. Yet, the risks for children's health are largely unknown. Our research team carried out a study on 362 children showing that higher manganese concentration in home tap water was associated with significant deficits on tests of intelligence and memory. For instance, there was a drop of six intellectual quotient points in children exposed to the higher levels of manganese in water compared to those exposed to the lower levels. For approximately half of the children in the study, exposure to manganese from drinking water has dramatically diminished since the initial study because the water is now treated to remove manganese. A key-question is whether the cognitive deficits are permanent or reversible. This cohort of children represents a unique opportunity to answer important questions on the effects of manganese on children's health.  We propose to follow-up these children to examine whether children who benefited from a reduction of water manganese concentration improved their cognitive performance, compared with children whose exposure did not change. In order to do this, we will assess children's cognitive function with the same tests used in the initial study, and we will re-measure manganese concentration in their home tap water. The analysis will also take into account a series of variables determinant for children's cognitive abilities, such as the socioeconomic status. Our hypothesis is that reducing children's exposure to manganese might reverse cognitive impairment, or at least prevent further deterioration in children who were exposed to high levels in the past.   The prevention of cognitive deficits is of upmost important, as cognitive abilities are predictive of many outcomes later in life, including health and future earning capacity.

TitreApplicationTitle: The prevalence and severity of asthma among children in a north-central Saskatchewan region
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; ASTHMA; EPIDEMIOLOGY; LUNG FUNCTION; OBESITY AND HEALTH BEHAVIOURS; PEDIATRIC; POPULATION-BASED; RURAL; SKIN PRICK TESTING
Abstract-Résumé: The purpose of this study is to investigate the prevalence and severity of asthma among children in a north-central Saskatchewan region. The indoor environment, including tobacco smoke and home mold, has been suspected to play a role in asthma development but the contribution of obesity and health behaviours has been studied less frequently. Two understudied populations with regard to asthma are rural dwellers and Aboriginal persons. Obesity, health behaviours, and environmental exposures in these groups have been shown to differ from urban populations and may help explain recent geographic and temporal variation in asthma prevalence. Finally, it is becoming apparent that there are differences in the association between various exposures and asthma by sex. We aim to determine if there are differences in these outcomes by area of residence (urban vs. rural) and by Aboriginal ancestry. We will also investigate associations between determinants of asthma including obesity, health behaviours (eg. physical activity, diet and sedentary behaviours), and the indoor environment with asthma presence and severity. Finally, we will investigate potential effect modification by area of residence, Aboriginal ancestry, and sex with these determinants. We will use a cross-sectional study of Grades 1-6 children attending school in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan that includes a questionnaire phase and a clinical phase (lung function testing, anthropometric measures, and skin prick testing). Investigation of asthma prevalence and severity and their determinants among these populations will help establish the level of disease burden, which has not yet been studied in this region, identify groups at higher risk of asthma, and will aid in addressing gaps in asthma etiology. This knowledge can help focus initiatives to prevent asthma and reduce asthma morbidity, resulting in better quality of life for children with asthma and lower health care costs in Saskatchewan and, more broadly, Canada.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse nouveau chercheur - Annonce de priorités : recherche biomédical/clinique sur le HIV/SIDA
TitreApplicationTitle: The virus infectivity factor (Vif) of HIV-1: mechanisms of inhibiting APOBEC3 immune factors
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CYTOSINE DEAMINASES; ENZYME MECHANISMS; HIV; HIV ACCESSORY PROTEINS; HIV RESTRICTION FACTOR; MOLECULAR IMMUNOLOGY; MUTAGENESIS; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; VIRUS-HOST INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), the causative agent of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), currently infects 33 million people worldwide, 58 000 of which are Canadian. Presently, HIV treatments have made the disease one that is chronic, but manageable, for people who have access to proper medical care. However, the current therapy has significant long term side effects in patients, such as lipid abnormalities and cardiovascular risks. An alternative route for developing HIV therapeutics is to take advantage of human enzymes, naturally present in the immune cells that HIV infects, which have the the ability to restrict HIV replication. These 'host restriction factors' can block the HIV lifecycle at specific steps, but are often thwarted by HIV accessory proteins designed to overcome these barriers. My laboratory's research focuses on the APOBEC3 family of human enzymes that can restrict HIV replication by causing chemical modifications in the HIV genetic material (DNA), which makes the virus non-functional. However, APOBEC3 enzymes can only act in the absence of the HIV virus infectivity factor (Vif) protein, which inhibits APOBEC3 enzymes by a number of mechanisms. If we can enable APOBEC3 enzymes to work better for humans, by designing molecules the block Vif from doing its job, it is possible that the human immune system will be able to manage HIV infection. To this end, my research takes a fine-tuned look at the interactions between Vif and APOBEC3 enzymes by purifying the relevant components from cells and conducting experiments in a test tube. There are many gaps in our understanding of these molecular battles that human APOBEC3 enzymes and HIV Vif wage against each other. Understanding this relationship is the first step for designing APOBEC3-based therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Social Exclusion and the Health and Well-Being of Gender and Sexual Minorities
Keywords-MotsClés: GAY AND BISEXUAL YOUTH; HEALTH AND HIV; HEALTH CARE ACCESS BARRIERS; HIV; LESBIAN; LGBT; RESILIENCY; SEXUAL AND GENDER MINORITIES; SOCIAL EXCLUSION; TRANSGENDER; TRANSGENDER HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: HIV has been shown to disproportionately affect groups that experience social exclusion, and in Canada, a strong case has been made to understand HIV in its social context. The Canadian Public Health Association notes that poverty, homelessness, stigma, addiction, violence, untreated mental health problems, lack of employment opportunities, powerlessness, lack of choice, lack of legal status and lack of social support create environments in which HIV and other illnesses flourish and spread.  Very little Canadian health research has focussed on understanding the health issues and health care needs of two marginalized populations,  transgendered and transsexual individuals as well as lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender youth.  Drawing on a social determinants of health framework, this five year program of research will focus on exploring the role that social exclusion plays in shaping health outcomes, and healthcare access barriers for gender and sexual minorities.  Given the dearth of information addressing the needs of these populations in the Canadian context, a significant emphasis of this research program will be on identifying factors that will 1. lead to improved health outcomes, 2. help to ameliorate service access barriers, and 3. help to overcome vulnerability by fostering personal resiliency.  The program of research will be community based and collaborative, involving a number of community agencies and service providers as partners.  In addition, this research program will include significant opportunities for student mentoring.  This will help to support the development of a new generation of researchers in Ontario able to work collaboratively with community partners and other stakeholders to impact this epidemic.  A key goal of the research program will be to prioritize knowledge transfer and exchange initiatives that get data into the hands of decision-makers who need them.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hearing Loss as a Contributor to Excess Disability among Long-term Care Residents with Dementia: Effects of an Intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS AND ADAPTATION; ALZHEIMER DISEASE; CAREGIVING; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; COMMUNICATION; EXCESS DISABILITY; HEARING LOSS; LONG-TERM CARE; NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Hearing loss is common among older adults and has a negative effect on communication. However, hearing loss often goes unrecognized or is accepted as a normal part of aging and disregarded. In Alzheimer disease, the most frequent cause of dementia, hearing loss makes cognitive deficits seem worse. Specifically, when people cannot hear normally, they may seem more confused than they really are because many of the behaviours caused by hearing loss (e.g., not paying attention, often asking people to repeat what they say, not staying on topic) are also behaviours caused by dementia. These added negative effects of hearing loss are referred to as excess disability. Excess disability is a particular problem in long-term care settings, where the majority of the residents have dementia. Interventions to reduce excess disability are necessary to improve the  quality of life and the quality of care of individuals with dementia.  In this study, we plan to evaluate the hearing of people with dementia who live in long-term care facilities and to determine the impact of an assistive listening device on communication during specific tasks. We will also interview long-term care staff members about their views on hearing loss and how it is identified and treated. This project will lay the groundwork for future research to improve the hearing, communication and, ultimately, the overall care of long-term care residents with dementia.

Abstract-Résumé: Using novel computational techniques and magnetic resonance imaging, this project aims to identify specific changes to structural and functional brain networks in patients with Alzheimer's disease. Such patterns might be used to identify and clinically treat this disease at an early stage, as well as help understand its causes and its progression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidation of novel regulators of invadopodia formation and function
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN POLYMERIZATION; ACTIN TAILS; CELL MOTILITY; HIGH THOUGH-PUT MICROSCOPY SCREENS; INVADOPODIA; INVASION; LIVE CELL IMAGING; METASTASIS; SIRNA LIBRARY SCREEN; VACCINIA VIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Metastasis, the spread of cancer cells to distant sites in the body, represents the major cause of death in cancer patients.  The ability of cancer cells to undergo metastasis and establish new tumours is critically dependent on their capacity to move and invade their surrounding tissue.  Cell movement and invasion however, are also involved in many normal processes such as the immune response and wound healing. Many proteins that regulate these key processes are also altered in tumour cells, which undergo metastasis.  It is therefore important that we understand what signals regulate normal cell movement and secondly, what happens to these signals when they cause cells to metastasize.   In 1989, a structure termed an invadopodia was identified to protrude from the surface of cancer cells isolated from tumours. Since this initial discovery, researchers have been able to show that invadopodia, function to degrade the surrounding environment to create a path that is easier for cells to move along. To date however, very little is known about the mechanisms regulating how invadopodia are formed. My proposal aims to identify new proteins required for invadopodia formation and function. I will examine if the loss of function of over 300 proteins, can alter or inhibit the ability of cancer cells to form invadopodia.  I will carry out this large-scale screen using an automated microscope to access the ability of treated cancer cells to make invadopodia. Candidate proteins identified in this screen will then be validated for their role in cell movement and tumour cell metastasis in mice. This work will provide important information on cancer cell movement and invasion and may lead to development of new therapeutic strategies to target cancer cell metastasis.  Moreover, since invadopodia are not required for cell viability, treatments developed to inhibit their formation have the potential to cause far fewer side effects than current therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and characterization of the factor Va binding site on platelets
Keywords-MotsClés: COAGULATION; FACTOR VA; IN VIVO; INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY; MICE; PLATELETS; PROTHROMBINASE; RECEPTOR; SDPR; THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Blood clots are the basis for most heart attacks and strokes, the number one cause of death and disability in Canada and worldwide. Blood clots are composed of clumps of platelets that are held together by a mesh-like network of fibrin fibres. Formation of these platelet/fibrin clots is effected by thrombin, the enzyme that is generated once the coagulation system is activated. Thrombin generation is effected by an enzyme complex, known as prothrombinase, which assembles on the surface of platelets. The prothrombinase complex consists of activated factor X, which binds to activated factor V on the surface of platelets. Localization of this complex on the surface of platelets enhances its activity over 1000-fold. Although activated factor V serves as the glue to localize activated factor X onto the platelet surface, the binding site for activated factor V on the platelet surface is unknown. We have preliminary evidence that activated factor V binds to SDPR (serum deprivation protein response), a platelet protein that is expressed on the surface of activated platelets. The purpose of this project is to a) confirm these findings, b) characterize the activated factor V/SDPR interaction and c) determine whether soluble SDPR will inhibit the activated factor V/SDPR interaction by competing with platelet SDPR for activated factor V. These studies are important because a better understanding of how platelets and the clotting system interact to form the clots that cause heart attacks and strokes will help us to develop rational strategies for their prevention.

Abstract-Résumé: Bone cells are responsible for making strong healthy bones. In patients experiencing osteoporotic disease, the amount of bone made is reduced resulting in a higher incidence of fractures.  The number of bone-forming cells and their activity levels are controlled by genes and proteins.  A mouse model that makes high levels of DFosB proteins (or its close relative D2DFosB)builds larger bones than normal mice. It is still unclear exactly how DFosB and D2DFosB causes this enhanced bone-building effect.  Preliminary evidence suggests that FosB might interact with another bone building protein known as B-catenin. B-catenin is a major regulator of bone cell activity. In this project, we propose to use in-vitro and in-vivo experiments to understand the mechanism of FosB and B-catenin interactions and the role these interactions have on bone formation. Understanding the mechanisms by which DFosB and D2DFosB enhance bone formation might reveal possible drug targets for the therapeutic management of osteoporotic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Src/ezrin signalling in tumour-induced angio and lymphangiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; BREAST CANCER; GROWTH FACTORS/CYTOKINES; INVASION; LYMPHANGIOGENESIS; METASTASIS; SRC/EZRIN; TUMOUR MICROENVIRONMENT; TUMOUR XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Metastasis, the spread of tumour cells to other organs, is the cause of death in breast cancer patients. Tumour cells can spread through two main routes, blood vessels and lymphatic vessels. The new formation of these vessels is associated with poor disease outcome in breast cancer. Recent studies have revealed that tumour cells can stimulate the formation of new lymphatic vessels in their local environment. Our group has previously demonstrated that interaction between signalling molecules Src and ezrin regulates the local invasion and spreading of aggressive breast cancer cells. Interestingly, preliminary data indicate that Src/ezrin can also induce the production of growth factors responsible for stimulating the formation of new blood vessels. We propose that breast cancer cells exploit the Src/ezrin signalling pathway to stimulate the production and release of factors that function to stimulate the formation of new blood and lymphatic vessels in the tumour's environment and accelerate the metastasis process.

TitreApplicationTitle: N. Meningitidis-inspired stealthiness: Prolonging the circulation times of anticancer nanocarriers by scavenging endogenous complement-inhibitors.
Keywords-MotsClés: APTAMERS; BIODISTRIBUTION; CANCER THERAPY; COMPLEMENT SYSTEM; DRUG DELIVERY; NANOCARRIERS; PHAGE DISPLAY; PHARMACOKINETICS; TARGETING
Abstract-Résumé: Through evolution, bacterias have found various ways to circumvent the human defence mechanisms. One recent discovery in microbiology involves a pathogen that recruits host proteins on its surface to imitate healthy cells and avoid detection by the immune system. This project proposes to use the same approach to prolong circulation times of therapeutic nanocarriers (NC) in the blood, and enhance their efficiency to treat cancer. NC are particularly promising in cancer treatment because they are multifunctional; they can be loaded with multiple actives, can specifically target diseased cells and can elude resistance mechanisms which develop in cancer cells. However, their efficiency is limited by rapid clearance from the bloodstream and non-specific sequestration in the liver and spleen. In this project, the surface of NC will be functionalized with recognition patterns for host proteins implicated in the discrimination between "self" and "non-self". Upon injection of the NC, the ligand will sheath their surface by binding its target in the plasma, and protect it from recognition by the traditional defence mechanisms. Using state-of-the-art ligand synthesis techniques to mimic this bacteria-inspired mechanism will translate into less capture in the liver and the spleen, and higher doses delivered to the diseased cells. During this project the candidate will synthesize the ligand, attach it to the surface of NC and study its ability to prolong the NC circulation time in the bloodstream. Lastly, the ability of drug-loaded NC to induce tumour regression will be evaluated. The results obtained in this work will result in better fundamental understanding of one of the challenges faced in contemporary chemotherapy and nanomedicine. We believe these innovative ligands will allow the improvement of a variety of drug delivery systems, and open the door to the development of a number of other applications in tissue engineering and immunology.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Prion Protein's Role in Brain Metal Homeostasis.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINORGANIC CHEMISTRY; BIOMETAL SPECIATION; COMPUTATIONAL CHEMISTRY; METALLOPROTEINS; MOLECULAR DYNAMICS; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; PRION DISEASE; SYNCHROTRON IMAGING; TRACE METAL HOMEOSTASIS; X-RAY ABSORPTION SPECTROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Prion diseases are fatal neurodegenerative diseases which affect both humans and animals. Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), also known as Mad Cow Disease, is the most widely known of this family. These diseases are caused by the prion protein (highly abundant in the central nervous system) which has been altered from its normal form, which does not cause disease, into a disease-causing form. Part of the prion protein's normal function in healthy individuals is regulating vitally important trace metals in the brain and nervous system.  We have demonstrated, using synchrotron-based imaging, that changing how much prion protein is produced disrupts levels of naturally-occurring copper, iron and zinc in the brain - indicating that the prion protein is part of the integral cellular machinery for regulating metals in the nervous system. We hypothesize that similar disruptions are likely present in individuals with prion disease and that disrupted brain metal content could be an exacerbating factor of other neurodegenerative diseases.  Using a combination of synchrotron-based X-ray techniques (such as those available at the Canadian Light Source synchrotron at U. Saskatchewan) to map metals in the brain, as well as computational chemistry and positron emission tomography (PET) we are developing detailed pictures of how changes in metals at the molecular and atomic level influence the anatomic level.  Altered trace metal levels in the brain are a common feature in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases as well as metal storage disorders such as Wilson's disease and hemochromatosis. Understanding how metals are disrupted in prion disease may be beneficial for understanding how disrupted metal levels affect neurodegeneration in general. Detailed molecular and anatomic knowledge of which metals and regions of the brain are preferentially affected in individuals is vital to devise custom therapies and individualized treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expanding access to HIV treatment within vulnerable populations
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; HIV/AIDS; ILLICIT DRUG USE; LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Outside of sub-Saharan Africa, at least one in three new HIV infections occurs among individuals who use illicit drugs, their sexual partners and other members of indigent and vulnerable populations. In the United States and Canada, HIV-positive members of these groups suffer from high levels of AIDS-related morbidity and mortality, even in areas where HIV treatment is delivered free of charge. Thus, medical evidence is urgently needed to identify the barriers to accessing and adhering to HIV treatment among members of these groups. In this research project, I will build on my doctoral research which identified strong links between social and environmental aspects of HIV treatment delivery among drug users, such as incarceration and homelessness, on treatment outcomes in British Columbia. My proposed post-doctoral research at Harvard University with Dr. David Bangsberg, an internationally-recognized expert in the provision of HIV treatment to vulnerable groups in the United States and Africa, will investigate the barriers to effective HIV treatment using data from a study involving indigent HIV-positive individuals in the United States. Focusing on the interrelated effects of poverty, illegal drug use and mental illness on HIV treatment outcomes in a setting without universal access to care, the findings from this research project will have implications for the effective scale-up of HIV treatment and care among vulnerable populations. Expanding access to HIV treatment not only holds the promise of reducing high levels of AIDS-related morbidity and mortality within these groups but also curbing the number of new infections and controlling the HIV/AIDS pandemic. Emerging research suggests that individuals receiving effective HIV treatment are far less likely to transmit the virus to uninfected individuals. Thus, my research seeks to contribute to the global efforts to address the ongoing HIV/AIDS pandemic.

Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOSTERIC RAF INHIBITORS; C-RAF; CELL PROLIFERATION/DEATH ASSAYS; CELL SIGNALING / TUMORIGENIC MECHANISMS; CILENGITIDE; GLIOBLASTOMA MULTIFORME; HOST-TUMOR INTERACTIONS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INTEGRIN ALPHA V BETA 3; ORTHOTOPIC BRAIN TUMORS
Abstract-Résumé: The most common form of brain cancer, glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), is highly aggressive, virtually untreatable and most often fatal.  This is reflected in the median survival time of GBM patients which is in the range of 14 months with surgery and currently available treatments.  Encouragingly, Cilengitide, a drug discovered over 15 years ago by my mentor David Cheresh in collaboration with scientists at Merck KGa, is showing promise in patients with this form of cancer.  Cilengitide targets a cell adhesion receptor, integrin (alpha)v(beta)3, on the surface of these tumor cells.  Importantly, Cilengitide has been significantly extending the lifespan of GBM patients in clinical trials.  While some patients respond exceptionally well to this drug others fail to respond.  Therefore I plan to study in detail how Cilengitide works at the molecular level.  These studies should help us better understand why this drug works in some patients and identify ways of improving its activity in others.  Recently I discovered that integrin (alpha)v(beta)3 activates c-Raf, another molecule implicated in GBM tumor cell survival and proliferation.  As a result of these findings, I propose to delineate how integrin (alpha)v(beta)3 and c-Raf contribute to GBM tumor growth both in cellular and in animal models.  In fact the Cheresh laboratory has already begun to develop a new class of Raf inhibitors that are effective in treating certain cancer types in mice.  It is my hypothesis that by combining these c-Raf-targeted drugs and Cilengitide it will be possible to observe a more potent anti-tumor effect in a wider range of patients with GBM.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidation of the role of ULK1 in the regulation and initiation of mammalian autophagy
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; AUTOPHAGY; MTOR; NUTRIENT SENSING; ULK1; VPS34
Abstract-Résumé: Autophagy or 'self-eating' is a regulated process that generates nutrients for maintenance of essential cellular functions in times of nutrient starvation.  Autophagy is also responsible for the removal of protein aggregates, infectious pathogens and damaged organelles.  Autophagy may also have a role in promoting cell death, although the lines between enhancing survival and promoting death have not been clearly drawn.  It has been observed autophagy that is suppressed and is implicated in many diseases including  cancer and neurodegeneration.  Autophagy promoting genes Beclin1 and UVRAG have been described as tumour suppressors and are found to be deleted in breast and colorectal cancer, underscoring the role of autophagy in cancer.  Despite being a well conserved process from yeast to man, the mechanisms of autophagic initiation in man remain to be determined.  There are two kinases that lie at the top of the autophagy pathway.  These two proteins likely link the signals promoting autophagy to the downstream machinery responsible for its execution.  This proposal outlines a detailed study of how these kinases are regulated by cellular cues and pass the message along to the downstream pathway.  Successful completion of this study will further our knowledge of this important process and offer additional insight into its dysregulation in disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Power Wheelchair Use Among Older Adults: A Longitudinal Study
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MOBILITY DISABILITY; OLDER ADULT; POWER MOBILITY; POWER WHEELCHAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Mobility impairment is the number one form of disability for Canadians 50 years of age and older.  The use of a power wheelchair is often used to compensate for mobility impairment and prevalence of use increases with age.  Although there is evidence that power wheelchairs can have a profoundly positive impact on the quality of life of older adults, wheelchairs are also among the most commonly abandoned assistive technology devices.  To date, we have little comprehensive understanding of power wheelchair use among older adults and its impact on health and quality of life.  The aim of this research is to describe the natural history of power wheelchair use over a two year period in older adults.  This longitudinal study will take place at six sites across Canada.  Three cohorts of power wheelchair users (experienced power wheelchair users not receiving new chair within study timeframe, experienced power wheelchair users receiving new chair within study timeframe, and new power wheelchair users) will be followed for 24 months.  Data will be collected at baseline and 1, 3, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months post baseline.  The primary outcomes assessed include measuring wheelchair skills performance, confidence with power wheelchair use, and the impact of power mobility use on activities and participation.  Results of this longitudinal study will advance our knowledge of power mobility use among older adults and build upon previous cross-sectional studies.  It will enhance our understanding of the impact of provision of power mobility on the participation and quality of life of older adults.

Keywords-MotsClés: HIF SIGNALING; HYPOXIA; MESENCHYMAL PROGENITOR CELLS; MOUSE MODELING; OSTEOCHONDROPROGENITORS; PROGENITOR CELL LINEAGE COMMITMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The functions of bones include providing mechanical support to soft tissues, supporting blood development, and housing the brain and the spinal cord.  Cartilage functions to mechanically support bone and skeletal growth and to serve as a cushioning layer, preventing bones from rubbing against each other. Not surprisingly, given these broad range of responsibilities, the loss of proper function of skeletal cells or an inability of these cells to repair themselves results in a wide range of degenerative bone and joint disorders, such as osteoarthritis and osteoporosis.   During development, cells referred to as osteochondroprogenitor cells, have the potential to become either cartilage or bone elements within the skeleton.  Surprisingly, little is known about the events that govern this decision making process in adult osteochondroprogenitor cells. Using mouse models, we will determine if over-expression of certain genes within these cells will result in aberrant cell fate decisions, such as the overproduction of either bone or cartilage. We will access the impact of our genetic modifications by observing the skeletal development of these animals, isolating osteochondroprogenitors, and studying their behaviour in cell culture systems. In parallel to these experiments, we will pharmacologically block signaling events discovered in our mouse studies to determine if we can modulate the behaviour of the human cell equivalents using specific chemical inhibitors. Specifically, we seek to determine if we can force osteochondroprogenitor cells to become either bone or cartilage cells. Manipulation of this signaling pathways to control the fate of these cells will be important in not only understanding the fundamental biology of skeletal development, but will also provide potential therapeutic modalities for a wide range of bone pathologies and potentially improve health care for individuals suffering with degenerative bone and joint disorders.

Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CO-REGULATORY FACTOR; INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGE GENE REGULATION; NUCLEAR RECEPTOR; QUANTITATIVE MASS SPECTROMETRY; REVERSE CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT; SRM TARGETED MASS SPECTROMETRY; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in the Western world and therefore represents a significant health care concern and a major burden on resources for Canadians.  For atherosclerosis, plaque formation in arterial walls occurs as an inflammatory response to high cholesterol, with mature plaques at significant risk for rupture, which not only releases destructive inflammatory mediators into the circulatory system, but can also occlude major arteries resulting in heart attack or stroke.  Prior attempts to treat atherosclerosis by preventing cholesterol accumulation in these immune cells, namely macrophages, have produced potentially lethal side effects due to the nature of the protein specifically targeted by these drugs.  However, by defining additional regulatory mechanisms responsible for preventing cholesterol accumulation, new therapeutic targets could be identified.  We therefore propose to identify and characterize the molecular regulatory mechanisms controlling cholesterol removal from macrophages.  This will provide important insights into the pathways involved in cholesterol regulation and lesion development, and will allow for the design of therapeutics for the treatment and prevention of atherosclerosis in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: L'effet de l'entraînement physique sur les capacités d'attention de consommateurs âgés de benzodiazépines
Keywords-MotsClés: BIEN-ETRE PSYCHOLOGIQUE; CONSOMMATION DE BENZODIAZEPINES; ENTRAINEMENT COGNITIF; ENTRAINEMENT PHYSIQUE; INTERVENTIONS PSYCHOSOCIALES; PREVENTION DU DECLIN COGNITIF
Abstract-Résumé: Les calmants de type benzodiazepines (BZD) sont des medicaments prescrits pour traiter les problemes d'anxiete et d'insomnie. Il est preferable de ne pas en consommer sur de longues periodes (pas plus de trois mois selon le College des medecins du Quebec) etant donne qu'ils provoquent une accoutumance et une dependance. Il est alors plus difficile d'arreter le medicament a cause des effets de sevrage. Une consommation prolongee de BZD, surtout si elle excede 1 an, peut aussi occasionner des problemes cognitifs et de concentration. En etant moins concentre ou plus distrait, le consommateur age de BZD est alors plus a risque de se blesser en chutant ou d'etre responsable d'accidents de la route lorsqu'il conduit. Outre l'option d'arreter completement son medicament, le consommateur age qui desire ameliorer ses fonctions cognitives et sa concentration peut se tourner vers l'activite physique. Des etudes ont effectivement demontre que l'entrainement physique pouvait ameliorer les capacites d'attention de patients ages. Or, pour plusieurs personnes agees, le simple fait de penser qu'ils devront investir temps et argent dans un programme d'entrainement physique, les decouragent et les empechent de passer a l'action. La psychoeducation, c'est-a-dire le fait d'informer les gens sur les bienfaits de l'activite physique, serait un motivateur a considerer. Realisee aupres de consommateurs ages de BZD, faisant peu d'activites physiques au depart, la presente etude a comme objectif de verifier si des seances d'informations sur les effets positifs de l'activite physique pourraient les encourager a passer a l'action et a demeurer actifs. Aussi, la presente etude vise a savoir si l'entrainement en gymnase pourrait ameliorer les fonctions cognitives et la concentration de consommateurs ages. Cette recherche est hautement pertinente puisqu'elle permettra d'ameliorer la qualite de vie des consommateurs ages de BZD exposes, bien malgre eux, aux effets indesirables du medicament.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of protein arginine methyltransferase 7 in breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER BIOLOGY; BREAST CANCER TREATMENT; CHEMORESISTANCE; INVASION; METASTASIS; NOVEL PRMT7 SUBSTRATES; PROTEIN AGININE METHYLTRANSFERASE 7 (PRMT7); PROTEIN METHYLATION; TARGETED THERAPEUTICS; XENOGRAFTS
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the second most common cancer affecting Canadian women today.  In 2010, an estimated 23 200 women will be diagnosed with and 5 300 will die from breast cancer in Canada (Canadian Cancer Society). The optimal treatment for breast cancer depends on how advanced the disease is, with highly advanced disease typically requiring invasive surgery, radiation and/or chemotherapy. Despite these aggressive treatments, tumours often recur. The new tumour oftern is resistance to previous therapies and can be more aggressive than the original tumour, potentially spreading to different parts of the body.  Research into specifically what makes breast tumours develop, grow, and spread within the body suggests that more specific treatments targeted to distinct characteristics within each tumour may increase disease responsiveness.  For example, it has been shown that certain proteins within breast tumour cells are not properly regulated.  Examination of these proteins may allow for the development of novel treatment strategies and ultimately a cure. My current research focuses on a protein called protein arginine methyl transferase 7 (PRMT7) which may be a critical player in breast tumour development and growth.  My preliminary studies show that, compared to normal breast cells, breast cancer cells have higher amounts of this protein. PRMT7 is known to be important in keeping cells alive when they are exposed to toxic agents. Therefore, because there are higher amounts of PRMT7 in breast cancer cells, it may allow them to survive in the body when a patient is undergoing chemo or radiation therapy.  The primary goal of my research is to examine the role that PRMT7 plays in breast cancer cells by performing experiments which will show how important it is to the survival of these cells. Further understanding of how PRMT7 behaves in breast cancer cells may lead to more effective treatment options for the 1 in 9 women that will develop breast cancer in their lifetime.

TitreApplicationTitle: Horizontal transfer of antibiotic resistance in polymicrobial communities
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; EVOLUTION; GENETICS; HORIZONTAL GENE TRANSFER; MICRO-DROPLET PCR; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; SOIL MICROBIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Antibiotics like penicillin are often thought of as 'miracle drugs' that are able to cure all infectious disease. However, many of the antibiotics we used 10 years ago are no longer effective against the bacteria that threaten human health today. When a bacterium is not killed by a particular antibiotic, it is said to be 'resistant' to that antibiotic (i.e. the antibiotic is no longer effective as a medical solution).  Most antibiotic resistance happens when bacteria pick up DNA carrying antibiotic resistance genes from other bacteria living in the same environment.  We know this happens often in hospitals, where 'superbugs' like methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (known as MRSA) have become a global health problem.  But where do antibiotic resistance genes come from in the first place? While some bacteria cause infections in animals and people, most bacteria are completely harmless, and some are even useful; for example, many bacteria found in the soil are used to manufacture the antibiotics which are currently prescribed to fight human infections.  Since bacteria in the soil live in large communitites with other bacteria, they are often exposed to the antibiotics their neighbours produce.  As a result, many have evolved resistance to antibiotics long before those drugs are used therapeutically in hospitals. Our lab has previously shown that antibiotic resistance genes are widespread in soil bacteria. However, there is no research to date to show how these genes end up in bacteria that cause disease. Our goal is to track the spread of resistance genes to the antibiotic erythromycin from soil bacteria to bacteria that cause disease in people like Acinetobacter baumannii. This project is important for the health of Canadians, since if we know where antibiotic resistance genes come from, we may be albe to predict what bacteria will next become resistant and design antibiotics that are more effective in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and metagenomic study of digoxin metabolism by Eggerthella lenta and other members of the human gastrointestinal microbiota.
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN MICROBIOME; METAGENOMICS; THERAPEUTIC DRUG METABOLISM; TRANSCRIPTOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Within recent years, there has been an increasing appreciation for the role played by the microorganisms living in, and on the human body. This includes the "gut microbiota", the diverse and abundant group of microorganisms that colonize the human gastrointestinal tract. Collectively, the genes of the microbiota are referred to as the "microbiome". Recent technological advancements have made it possible to begin studying the microbiome, and its role in human health and disease states. The gut microbiota prevent the growth of disease-causing bacteria, help extract nutrients from our diet, and also play a role in certain intestinal diseases. It has become abundantly clear that in order to fully understand human metabolism, we must consider the contributions of the gut microbiome. One such contribution is the chemical modification of orally ingested therapeutic drugs from active, to inactive forms. Importantly, the unexpected alteration of drug concentrations by the microbiota can adversely affect treatment. As such, this study will examine the metabolism of a commonly prescribed heart medication named "digoxin" by a member of the gut microbiota, Eggerthella lenta. We will harness cutting-edge techniques to identify the genes involved in the metabolism of digoxin by E. lenta. These findings will then allow us to identify other members of the gut microbiota able to carry out this same chemical reaction. Additionally, using mouse models, we will investigate whether dietary changes affect the ability of the gut microbiota to metabolize digoxin. By providing a more complete understanding of digoxin metabolism, this work will lead to improved therapeutic strategies for treating heart disease. Our investigation will also serve as a landmark study, the findings of which will be broadly applicable to future drug discovery protocols incorporating the role of the gut microbiota.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the role of hepatitis C virus core protein in the production of infectious virus particles
Keywords-MotsClés: HEPATITIS C VIRUS; MOLECULAR VIROLOGY; RNA PACKAGING; VIRUS ASSEMBLY; VIRUS EGRESS; VIRUS REPLICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Current estimates indicate that 130-170 million people worldwide are infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV), a pathogen that targets hepatocytes within the liver of those it infects. Many individuals are unable to clear the virus post-infection, often leading to the development of liver cirrhosis and/or liver cancer within these patients. Accordingly, hepatitis C virus in now the main cause for liver transplantation in the USA and Europe. Unfortunately, no HCV vaccine exists and current treatments are poorly tolerated and frequently ineffective.  The production of infectious hepatitis C virus in cell culture has only recently become possible, permitting investigation into how the virus is assembled and released from infected hepatocytes. Studies utilizing this novel system highlight the importance of several virus-encoded proteins to this process. One virus protein, core, is thought to self-interact to form the virus capsid - the protein shell into which the viral genetic code is packaged. Evidence suggests that core may also interact with other viral proteins in order to facilitate the capsid assembly process. However, the core-core interaction regions and the role of other viral proteins in capsid assembly are poorly characterized.   In this project, we have identified a small region of core that is essential for the production of infectious virus. We possess the necessary systems to determine whether this region is (i) important for assembly of the viral capsid, or (ii) required for a step that is subsequently important for virus infectivity. We can also detect any other mutations within the viral genetic code that may arise and restore virus production from this deleterious core mutant. Such studies could identify novel protein-protein interactions that are essential for the generation of infectious HCV and ultimately, identify targets for improved HCV therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Function of cis-acting long non-coding RNAs in colorectal tumorigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; DEVELOPMENT; DNA METHYLATION; EARLY DETECTION; FORMER SMOKERS; GENOMICS; LUNG CANCER; ONCOGENE; SMOKING; TUMOUR SUPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer represents one of the largest health burdens worldwide.  Tobacco smoke is a well recognized cause of lung cancer.  However, even with smoking cessation, former smokers sustain an elevated risk of developing lung cancer.  In Canada alone, the population of former smokers is well over 7.5 million individuals and growing.   Therefore, cancer in former smokers will remain a significant health concern for decades to come.  Recent studies have discovered that while the majority of smoking-induced gene expression return to normal levels after quitting smoking, some genes are permanently damaged.  Some of these irreversible genes are tumor suppressors which serve as gatekeepers of cancer development.  In this study, I will first compare lung tissue from former smokers to those of current and never smokers, to identify smoke induced effects.  Secondly, I will identify those genes that do not return to normal state after quitting smoking that are specific to lung cancer in former smokers.  I propose that genes that are irreversibly disrupted in former smokers with lung cancer may have biological role in lung cancer development in this population.  The identification of these irreversible genes will yield novel molecular targets for developing anticancer therapeutics or serve as diagnostic markers for early detection of lung cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolic Role of Nrf2 in Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; ER STRESS AND SIGNALLING MECHANISMS; GENETIC AND DIETARY MOUSE MODELS; GLUCOSE TOLERANCE; INFLAMMATION AND LIPID MEDIATORS; INSULIN ACTION AND BETA CELL FUNCTION; OBESITY AND TYPE 2 DIABETES; PHYSIOLOGY AND METABOLIC SYSTEMS
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) affects millions of Canadians by causing debilitating conditions such as blindness, kidney failure and cardiovascular disease, yet the means of its cure remains unknown. T2D is often linked to obesity. However, it is not obesity per se that causes T2D but an insufficient adaptation of metabolic systems to chronic obesity that result in T2D by causing insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction. An understanding of how metabolic adaptations go awry in chronic obesity may reveal a means to reverse this worsening epidemic.  In metabolic tissues, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) plays a central role in sensing and coordinating responses to obesity via signalling branches collectively known as the unfolded protein response (UPR). During ER stress, the UPR relays messages to various cellular centres to generate responses that restore homeostasis. However, when ER stress is chronic and excessive such as in chronic obesity, the UPR relays a different message that impairs cell function and worsens the metabolic state. These differential relays remain obscure but revealing its nature may identify a means for its manipulation to restore metabolic systems in chronic obesity and T2D. For our studies, we propose to investigate the molecular interface from which the ER coordinates stress responses to obesity. Our hypothesis is that a nuclear receptor linked to ER stress, called Nrf2, functions to moderate ER stress in obesity, thereby preventing the build-up in ER stress that leads to T2D. To test this, we will 1) utilize gain- and loss-of-function models of Nrf2 to examine its role in metabolic systems, ER stress and T2D development in obese mice, 2) characterize the mechanistic links between ER stress and Nrf2 function, and 3) determine the anti-diabetic potential of Nrf2 activators. Overall, these studies will interrogate the metabolic role of Nrf2 in ER stress and chronic obesity, and may reveal Nrf2 as a promising drug target for T2D

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Studies on the Rhomboid Family of Membrane Proteins Involved in Human Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: DERLIN; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM ASSOCIATED DEGRADATION; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; RHOMBOID PEPTIDASES; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Many of the proteins that malfunction in human disease are associated with the outer surface of the cell. Although these proteins are among the most important players in disease, very little is known about their 3D structure.  Using a technique called X-ray crystallography, we aim to determine the 3D structure of several of these proteins. We have determined the structure of one class pf proteins, and this structure has provided us with invaluable information regarding their function. We now propose to solve the structure of another set of membrane proteins who play a role in cancer and heart disease.
