TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the immune cascade leading to NLR mediated Type2 immune responses
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNE RESPONSE; IBD; INFECTIONS; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNE RECOGNITION; MICROBIOLOGY; NOD-LIKE RECEPTORS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; STROMAL CELLS; TYPE 2 IMMUNITY
Abstract-Résumé: The re-emergence of infectious disease in both, the developed and the developing worlds are a global health problem that accounts for over 25 % of the mortality. Progress can only be achieved on the basis of our increasing insights into the complex host defence mechanisms, which will enable us to tailor novel medical intervention strategies. Therefore, my research study focuses on deciphering the mechanisms of how the mammalian immune system recognizes pathogens, leading to the subsequent instruction of long-lived immune responses. Recent observations have led to the discovery of several host protein families, referred to as pattern recognition molecules (PRM), which specifically detect molecular patterns of pathogens as well as infection-induced physiological changes of infected host cells, suggesting a critical role fort he function of PRM in antimicrobial immunity. Indeed, this concept has been further fueled by observations that polymorphisms and mutations in the human genes of PRM, particularly in members of the Nod-like receptor (NLR) family such as Nod1 and Nod2 are linked to both impaired antimicrobial resistance. Thus, the focus of my study is to investigate the cellular and molecular mechanisms induced upon recognition of pathogens by the PRM Nod1 and Nod2 for the elicitation of potent antimicrobial long-lived immunological memory. Within the excellent research environment of Montreal by using highly developed and advanced methods and tools, we hope to make highly significant contribution in this research field. The scientific insights gained from the proposed research program will advance our medical and scientific understanding to enable us to tailor preventive vaccination strategies as well as therapies for the intervention of chronic inflammatory disorders to improve the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neighbourhood, Familial, and Individual-level determinants of inequalities in blood pressure: identifying weight status as a mediator.
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD PRESSURE; NEIGHBOURHOOD HEALTH; OBESITY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SOCIAL AND HEALTH INEQUALITIES; SOCIAL CAPITAL; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOCIAL EPIDEMIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Individuals from underprivileged groups living in economically deprived neighbourhoods are more likely to experience morbidity and mortality in comparison to individuals from privileged backgrounds. High blood pressure is one such example.  More specifically, individuals from underprivileged backgrounds are more likely to experience high blood pressure in comparison to their counterparts from privileged backgrounds. Little is known about the sociocultural processes through which the complex milieu of individual and neighbourhood factors either supports or weakens health. The proposed project aims to conduct analyses to disentangle the role of economic deprivation, familial and cultural factors, and ethnicity on blood pressure. The role of overweight and obesity will also be investigated.  The Boston Area Community Survey is a cohort study with a randomly sampled population of 6,000 ethnically diverse men and women from economically diverse neighbourhoods will be used to gain a better understanding of the relationship between income and blood pressure. The Framingham Heart Study is a multigenerational study that follows individuals, their children and grandchildren. Analyses will involve looking at social inequalities, such as poverty and neighbourhood economic deprivation, familial characteristics, and cultural attributes and how they influence change in blood pressure across time and generations. This project will provide much needed information on patterns and trends in the likelihood of experiencing high blood pressure over time and the significance of the individual, the family, and the community. Results can also help to guide health practitioners and policy makers to develop and implement public health policies to decrease inequalities in blood pressure.

TitreApplicationTitle: The built environment and risk of cardiovascular disease: a population-based study in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH CARE AND HEALTH SERVICES; POPULATION HEALTH; RACE/ETHNICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death among Canadians. Although individual-level risk factors for CVD are well established, the effects of community-level factors, such as the built environment, are not well understood. The overall objective of the proposed research project will be to examine the association between the built environment and the prevalence of CVD in Ontario. I will also examine whether there are interactions between ethnicity, immigration status, and the built environment in determining CVD prevalence. I hypothesize that there will be a significant association between the built environment and CVD prevalence even after controlling for individual risk factors. The study population will include approximately 160,000 individuals who participated in the Ontario components of Statistics Canada's National Population Health Surveys (1996) and Canadian Community Health Surveys (2001-2007). Prevalence of CVD will be defined as self-reported heart disease or stroke obtained from survey data. Community-level factors will include area-based socioeconomic status, and three measures of the built environment: neighbourhood-level physical activity friendliness; access to healthy resources (e.g. grocery store, park, or public recreational space); and exposure to healthy vs. unhealthy foods (e.g. grocery stores vs. convenience stores or fast food restaurants). These community-level factors have been developed and validated for discrete neighborhoods in Ontario. The mandate of CIHR is the creation and translation of new knowledge to improve the health of Canadians. The results of this study will be of great value in identifying high-risk communities, informing public health policy, and designing effective population-level prevention strategies in an effort to reduce the significant burden of CVD among Canadians. Study findings will be disseminated widely through peer-reviewed publications and presentations at scientific and community conferences.

TitreApplicationTitle: The use of dietary nitrate to attenuate skeletal muscle anabolic-resistance with aging.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BEET ROOT JUICE; EXERCISE; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MUSCLE BIOSPY; MUSCLE STRENGTH; NITRATE; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; SATELLITE CELLS; STABLE ISOTOPE TRACERS
Abstract-Résumé: Sarcopenia, is an unavoidable age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength causing impairment in muscle function. Ultimately, this muscle loss will lead to disability and the loss of personal independence, in addition to increasing the risk of developing chronic metabolic disease(s) such as type II diabetes and obesity. The causes of muscle-wasting are not completely understood, however it has been demonstrated that aging muscles are not as responsive to the health benefits of exercise. One faulty mechanism that may be partly responsible is the broken signal of the hormone insulin with age, to cause the release of nitric oxide which acts to enlarge blood vessels. Blood vessel dilation is important as they carry nutrients and hormones to our working muscles. Using drugs, it has previously been shown that restoring insulin's ability to release nitric oxide increases the potential for muscle growth. Interestingly, daily diet is a major source of nitrate, which can be converted to nitric oxide once digested. Therefore, ingesting extra nitrate through dietary products such as beet root juice may potentially repair the damaged muscle response to exercise, increasing muscle strength and overall muscle health. This research aims to test whether ingested dietary nitrate, in combination with exercise, will increase muscle strength and function in the elderly population. This type of research is extremely important as in Canada alone, the next 30 years will bring about a significant rise in the aging population, as the proportion of persons over the age of 65 will have increased from 13 to 22% by the year 2031, causing a major strain on the health care system. This research aims to improve through diet and exercise, the overall health of an aging population which will ultimately decrease the risk of developing chronic metabolic disease(s) but also restore personal independence in the elderly, therefore increasing their overall quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fear Conditioning in Social Phobia
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL NEUROSCIENCE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EXTERNALIZING; MENTAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Psychiatric conditions such as substance dependence, antisocial deviance and conduct disorder share a common risk factor known as externalizing. This factor is heritable and influences the function of brain regions that are involved in self-control of behavioural impulses. It is important to gain a greater understanding about the nature of brain processing deficits that contribute to increased risk for the externalizing class of psychiatric disorders. A better understanding would inform us about the origins of these disorders and potentially help identify at-risk individuals before they manifest more chronic psychiatric problems. A promising way to meet this research challenge is by recording brain electrical activity while individuals perform tasks that require withholding inappropriate behaviours. The Clinical Neuroscience Laboratory of Dr. Edward Bernat has collected such neurophysiological data from large community samples of adults. I propose to use these data to study how the brain circuits for inhibiting inappropriate behaviour malfunction among individuals who are high in externalizing risk. I will use a combination of electrophysiological measures that track brain changes in real time and imaging data that provides information about the tissues connecting the different brain regions that must communicate during impulse control. This research will identify the specific aspects of brain processing that are deficient in people who are prone to externalizing problems. In addition, we will extend the research to see how these same brain circuits operate in incarcerated offenders who have committed violent crimes. Together, the findings will help us to better understand how and where the brain's circuits break down to influence the development of socially costly psychiatric disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Explaining the occurrence and role of depression in the process of care and outcome after acute coronary syndrome in young adults
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOLOGY; DEPRESSION; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENDER; HEALTH CARE UTILISATION; MEDIATION EFFECT; NATIONAL MULTICENTRE STUDY; OUTCOME; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Studies have showed that patients suffering from depression following a cardiac event (e.g. heart attack) were at greater risk of mortality. An explanation for this might be that depressed patients tend to poorly manage their health, for example by not taking their medication, not perceive the need for medical help, or by being physically inactive. In addition, depression is found in 40-65% of patients who have suffered a heart attack and, thought it increases the risk of a cardiac event in both men and women, a number of sex differences in the rates and impact of depression in cardiac patients exist. In fact, depression is more common in women than in men in the general population, as well as among women with heart disease. Moreover, depression would have worse cardiac consequences in women than in men. However, we do not know if these differences are due to a pure biological phenomena (sex differences), or if it is rather explainable by gender-related variables, including the effects of social norms and expectations for women and men (e.g. family role, job situation). This project therefore aims to assess the possibility that specific gender variables would cause depression, which would in turn influence the way men and women manage health cares, and therefore influence their health. We will evaluate gender characteristics and depression, as well as the use of health care services during one year, in patients from 30 hospitals across Canada, after their admission for a heart attack. This project will improve population's health and health delivery system by allowing more adapted ways to assess and treat men and women with heart disease. More specifically, by identifying factors responsible for the sex differences in health care management, and therefore sex differences in mortality rates, we will be able to intervene directly on these factors (e.g. by the modification of cardiac women's family roles), and prevent their harmful consequences on cardiac health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sleep and circadian disruptions in early Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIGRAPHY; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; CIRCADIAN RHYTHM; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; MINI-MENTAL STATE EXAM; QUESTIONNAIRES; SLEEP
Abstract-Résumé: Sleep and circadian disruptions are a common complaint in patients with early Alzheimer's disease (AD). A fragmented sleep/wake pattern, characterized by increased daytime activity and disrupted nighttime sleep, is frequently observed. Sundowning, or the presence of certain psychological symptoms and behaviour at specific times of the day, has also been noted in AD patients. Because individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) often develop AD, it is important to understand the disturbances that occur in both of these populations to determine the patterns of change over time. The sleep habits of healthy aged adults, those with MCI, and early AD patients, will be assessed in this study via questionnaires. A caregiver version of the questionnaire will also be given, where appropriate. Their sleep/wake activity will be analyzed using actigraphy, a wrist-watch-like measure of motor activity that corrects with sleep recordings. Participants will also be screened for cognitive impairments with the mini-mental state exam. Combining this information will help determine targets for clinical intervention in those with MCI and early AD. Specifically, understanding the changes in sleep and circadian rhythms that occur in individuals with MCI and early AD will aid in structuring a day/night regimen that may slow disease progression, as well as delay institutionalization.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel investigation of functional pathoanatomy and outcomes of lumbar spinal stenosis 5 years following diagnosis
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT; LONGITUDINAL; LOW BACK PAIN; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; PROGNOSIS; SPINAL CORD; SPINAL STENOSIS; VASCULAR
Abstract-Résumé: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis is a condition that is believed to primarily have a degenerative aetiology in which narrowing of the spinal canal results in entrapment and compression of neurovascular structures. The prevalence of spinal stenosis has increased with the aging of the population, yet limited information is available to determine prognosis and guide effective management. Although a narrowing of the spinal canal or neural foramen identified on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a defining feature for the diagnosis of spinal stenosis, it is unclear why the clinical syndrome develops in some, but not others with similar imaging findings. A study with repeated standard MR imaging could provide insight into this variability in patient outcomes. Furthermore, one of the main drawbacks of traditional MRI is that patients are imaged in a neutral spinal position and patients' symptoms are commonly aggravated by direction-specific posturing of the lumbar spine. Therefore, positional MRI could provide new information regarding the stage and severity of the stenosis and provide explanatory or prognostic information for patients outcomes. Thus, the proposed study aims to identify novel prognostic factors, focusing on imaging findings and to gain further insight into the variability in patient outcomes. These aims will be accomplished through acquisition of repeated imaging and positional MRI from patients with lumbar spinal stenosis. We will recruit a subgroup of patients from a prognostic study that followed over 500 patients with spinal stenosis over a 5 year period. Innovative research methods and cutting edge technologies in imagery will be used to gain a better understanding of associated anatomical changes on the site of the spinal stenosis and its role in symptom progression. The new information acquired will inform health care decision-making of affected patients, health care providers and policy makers, and guide the development of more effective interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of adherent invasive Escherichia coli in the development and progression of intestinal fibrosis associated with Crohn's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CROHN'S DISEASE; CYTOKINES; FIBROSIS; HISTOLOGY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INFLAMMATION; ISOGENIC MUTANTS; MURINE MODELS; PATHOGENIC E. COLI; VIRULENCE FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) such as Crohns disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) are chronic inflammatory diseases that occur primarily in the gastrointestinal tract. CD is characterized by chronic inflammation, fibrosis and intestinal obstruction that causes diarrhea, vomiting and abdominal pain. CD afflicts both men and women of all age groups, however, the usual onset typically occurs between the ages 15 and 30 years of age. In Canada, more than 200,000 individuals have CD and of these, approximately more than two thirds will have intestinal fibrosis, which requires hospitalization and surgery. Recent reports have shown that people with CD are at an increase risk of developing colon cancer. Being a lifelong disease, CD significantly impacts quality of life through social and economical challenges. Treatment can help with the better control and management of the disease, but presently there is no cure. Several investigators have implicated intestinal bacteria in development of CD. For example, certain pathogenic strains of Escherichia coli have been detected frequently in the intestine of CD patients. Taken together, there is an urgency to gain better insight into the complications associated with CD. In our proposed study, we will investigate the role of a highly pathogenic strain of E. coli in the development and progression of intestinal fibrosis in mice. We believe that this research will enhance our understanding of the underlying mechanisms by which intestinal bacterial pathogens could alter the host's immune defense and cause significant complications in susceptible individuals. CD is notorious for reducing the quality of life for thousands of people annually, thus this research will bring us a closer to the development of better treatment management and control of such debilitating inflammatory bowel diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nuclear receptors and control of organogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; C. ELEGANS GENETICS; CANCER; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; LIGAND IDENTIFICATION; NUCLEAR HORMONE RECEPTORS; ORGANOGENESIS; SF-1/LRH-1; SUMOYLATION; TRANSCRIPTION/GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Hormones work by binding to specific molecules in cells known as receptors. Like a lock and key, specific hormones bind to specific receptors. Changes in how these hormones and receptors work have dire consequences for human health. In humans, two receptors named SF-1 and LRH-1 are important for the development of our organs, reproduction, and control of our metabolism. Alteration in how SF-1 and LRH-1 work leads to breast and adrenal cancer, and cardiovascular disease. The lock and key biology that is typical of molecules like SF-1 and LRH-1 is very amenable to manipulation with drugs, therefore making them promising targets for cancer and cardiovascular disease therapies. My work uses a simpler animal, the worm C. elegans, to explore this biology. The worm is only 1 mm long, consisting of 959 cells, and goes from egg to adult in three days. It has elementary organs and has a single protein doing the work of SF-1 and LRH-1. I plan to use one of the simplest organs known to scientists, the worm vulva, to understand how these receptors orchestrate organ formation. Though only comprised of 22 cells, worm vulval development uses many of the same processes and pathways required to form human organs and alteration in many of these processes leads to human cancers. In particular, I am focusing on how small molecules and proteins can be used to subtly change the function of these receptors and how this impacts on organ shape and function. By establishing the worm as a model to study these receptors we can gain fundamental insight into how these proteins work and spur new therapies for breast and adrenal cancer, and cardiovascular disease. Further, the simplicity of the worm makes it a powerful tool to quickly screen new drugs designed to turn SF-1 and LRH-1 on or off.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of postsynaptic complexin in long-term potentiation of synaptic transmission
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN CIRCUITRY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IN VIVO; LONG TERM DEPRESSION; LONG TERM POTENTITATION; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; TWO PHOTON IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: The brain is comprised of complex networks of nerve cells that communicate at specialized physical contacts called synapses. The process of communication, termed synaptic transmission, is initiated when a neurotransmitter, a chemical messenger, is released from a specialized site called a presynaptic terminal. The neurotransmitter then activates proteins called receptors, which modify the electrical properties of the postsynaptic cell. The majority of excitatory synapses within the brain are formed on dendritic spines, specialized structures containing the receptors important for synaptic transmission. A remarkable feature of synaptic transmission is that it is plastic and can be modified by the brain's own activity.  This synaptic plasticity results in changes to neuronal circuitry and is responsible for the ability to learn and remember. In this project, I will investigate whether a protein called complexin, which plays a critical role in the release of neurotransmitters, also plays a mandatory role in the plasticity of synaptic transmission by influencing the trafficking of specific receptors to synaptic sites. This will involve using tools to molecularly manipulate complexin in nerve cells in living animals and then determine the consequences on synaptic transmission. In addition, using a special microscope, I will examine the role of complexin in the structural changes in synapses that can occur when brain activity changes. As abnormalities in synaptic transmission are linked to neurological disorders involving learning and memory, my research will lead to a better understanding of diseases such as Alzheimer's disease. It will also have important impact on current thinking concerning the pathophysiology and treatment of the large number of brain disorders that are involved in maladaptive or dysfunctional synaptic plasticity at excitatory glutamatergic synapses. These include addiction, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, autism, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Single-cell analysis of mesenchymal stem cells lineage hierarchy and interactions with hematopoietic cells
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFERENTIATION; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; LINEAGE HIERARCHY; LINEAGE TRACING; LIVE ANIMAL IMAGING; MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS; MICROENVIRONMENT; NICHE; SINGLE CELL ANALYSIS; TIME-LAPSE MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Long bones (bones containing marrow) are home to two types of stem cells: 1)bone-forming stem cells (also called mesenchymal stem cells, MSCs), and 2)blood-forming stem cells (hematopoietic stem cells or HSCs). HSCs are rare cells residing in the marrow and produce each day billions of blood cells that constitute blood and immune systems. They are the cells needed in bone marrow transplants, the first clinically effective stem cell therapy used for nearly 6 decades today. We can now identify HSCs and their progeny well in the laboratory. However we cannot control their fate, growth or differentiation in the laboratory. This is because we do not know where HSCs reside in bone marrow, thus the signals necessary to guide HSCs toward a desired fate are unknown. This represents an unmet clinical need as HSCs are desperately needed for transplantation. Marrow is a liquid organ encased in a hard ceramic structure: bone. Although long thought of as static and boring organs we now know that bones are highly dynamic, with exceptional regenerative properties and are under constant remodeling (fine balance between bone formation and removal). Although the existence of bone-forming stem cells (MSCs) has been acknowledged since 1971 we are only beginning to understand how the various bone cells are created, how they move from one location to another, and how they create environments within the marrow capable of orchestrating the formation of blood and immune systems by HSCs. In the proposed project we will use innovative technology to study interactions between bone cells and blood cells at the single cell level. This means we will study each bone stem cell individually and observe what controls its fate, how it divides and how it interacts with HSCs and influences it. We will first observe these phenomena in test tubes using existing technology we developed. We are currently developing the technology to observe individual stem cells in their native bone environment.

Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide, cases of type 1 and 2 diabetes are reaching epidemic numbers. Diabetes is associated with nerve complications known as diabetic peripheral neuropathy, also known as DPN. DPN affects approximately 30% of individuals with diabetes. Symptoms include incapacitating pain, loss of certain sensations, foot ulceration, infection and amputation. No effective treatment currently exists to reverse or even slow the progression of DPN. We have recently shown that mitochondria, the powerhouse of cells, have reduced function in neurons from diabetic rodent models. This is significant as the neuron requires substantial amounts of energy to fuel its processes. In this proposal, we aim to study the role of a specific protein, PGC-1alpha. PGC-1alpha has been shown to regulate both the number of mitochondria within a cell as well as their function. The level of PGC-1alpha protein is lower in neurons from diabetic models. Firstly, we aim to understand how the expression of PGC-1alpha protein is regulated in diabetic neurons. Secondly, we propose to induce diabetes in our rodent model and enhance PGC-1alpha activity following the development of neuropathy. If increased PGC-1alpha activity restores mitochondrial function and this improves or reverses the diabetes-induced neuropathy, we will have shown the importance of maintaining mitochondria health in neurons in diabetic individuals. If a positive link between PGC-1alpha and diabetic neuropathy is found, these studies could lead to potential targets for therapeutic avenues in diabetic neuropathy. In addition, these findings could be extended to a number of neurodegenerative diseases that share common pathological features with diabetic neuropathy, such as Alzheimer's disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; HEALTH INFORMATION; IMMUNIZATIONS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PAIN MANAGEMENT; PARENT EDUCATION
Abstract-Résumé: Immunization injections are a common source of pain in childhood. Unfortunately, even though previous research has identified a number of strategies that parents can use to reduce children's pain during immunizations, these techniques are not used in practice. Parents are recognized as the primary targets for education regarding healthy child development since they are responsible for all aspects of the care of their child. Parents reported that they are largely unaware of effective pain relieving strategies for immunization and that they would use pain relieving strategies if educated about them. This pilot study will compare three teaching modules to educate parents about strategies they can use to alleviate pain during their child's immunizations. The objective is to determine the optimal strategy to translate knowledge on proven pain management techniques into use in practice. The results of this research will indicate the best way to educate parents and thereby improve pain management for children receiving immunizations. Better pain management during these common procedures will not only reduce children's immediate suffering, but may also avoid long term sequelae that can arise from poorly managed pain during medical procedures, such as needle fears and healthcare avoidance, including non-adherence with immunization schedules.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of VARP in endosomal sorting
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; ENDOCYTIC RECYCLING; ENDOSOME; LYSOSOME; MAMMALIAN CELL CULTURE; MEMBRANE TRAFFICKING; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; RNAI; SNARE
Abstract-Résumé: Living organisms are made up of cells, which serve individual functions to support the life of the organism. To serve these functions, cells must precisely orchestrate complex internal processes, which when perturbed may alter the function of the cell. In some cases this may lead to disease in the organism. For example, if something changes within a cell that causes it to multiply uncontrollably, cancer may occur. The majority of human diseases can be explained in terms of one or more cell types either doing something that they shouldn't be doing, or not doing something that they should be doing. Our understanding of human disease is therefore limited by our understanding of cell function. It is the goal of basic cell biological research to uncover the fundamental mechanisms of cell function, and learn how these mechanisms contribute to the productive life of an organism. One important cellular function is the regulated transport of molecules from one place to another. This is primarily achieved by packaging molecules into small sacs (called vesicles), which are carried to specific spots in the cell to deliver their contents. These vesicles are formed, loaded with the correct cargo, and transported around the cell by machinery (mainly proteins) specifically devoted to these transport processes. It is critical that cells transport the right molecules to the right places at the right time for the cell to function correctly. The research proposed in this application aims to characterize the role of one particular protein, called VARP, that we hypothesize plays an important role in cellular transport processes. The function of VARP is not yet known, and therefore the direct medical relevance of this research is currently unclear. However, although a direct medical application of cell biological research is not always immediately apparent, all disease starts at the level of the cell, and until we fully understand cells, we cannot fully understand disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Directed differentiation of human embryonic stem cells towards thymic epithelium for the purpose of inducing immune tolerance to stem cell-derived tissue upon transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: EPITHELIAL THYMIC CELLS; IMMUNE TOLERANCE; PANCREATIC BETA CELLS; STEM CELL-DERIVED TISSUE; STEM CELLS; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Numerous efforts are currently underway to use stem cells to treat patients suffering from prevalent diseases, including diabetes, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease. For example, pancreatic insulin-producing beta cells derived from stem cells could be transplanted to replace lost cells in Type 1 Diabetes as well as in some Type 2 Diabetes patients who have lost the ability to generate sufficient amounts of insulin. However, an important barrier to bringing stem cell therapies to the clinic is the activity of the immune system that is primed to reject the genetically foreign transplanted cells. One strategy that could be used to overcome that problem would be to teach the immune system to accept the foreign stem cell transplants. The objective of the proposed work is thus to generate pancreatic beta cells from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), a process that is being optimized in Dr. Hebrok's laboratory, but to also generate thymic cells from the same stem cells. The reason for this is that thymus cells are normally involved in excluding cells from the immune system that have the ability to attack cells of their own body. By generating thymic cells from the same hESCs that will form insulin-producing cells, we anticipate that these hESC-derived thymic cells will instruct the immune system not to attack the hESC-derived beta cells.  If this strategy proves successful, this work will help improve treatment for many diseases by increasing our ability to put a break on the immune system when transplanting cells or tissue derived from stem cells. This represents an appealing alternative to the current strategies that involve exposing patients to long-term immunosuppression therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Drug design principles for nicotinic acetylcholine receptor-channels
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTOR; CHANNEL GATING; DRUG BINDING; DRUG DESIGN; KINETIC ANALYSIS; LIGAND-RECEPTOR INTERACTIONS; MOLECULAR MODELLING; MONTE CARLO-ENERGY MINIMIZATION; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; SINGLE-CHANNEL ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Synapses are the primary points of communications in the nervous system. Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor-channels (AChRs) are involved in the fast transmission of signals at nerve-nerve and nerve-muscle synapses. Small molecules, called agonists, bind to and activate AChRs causing them to open and conduct ions across the cell membrane, which eventually initiates a physiological response. Nicotine, an AChR agonist, is responsible for the addictive properties of tobacco smoking, which leads to cancer, heart disease, and stroke. Over 5 million smoking-related deaths worldwide annually are the largest source of preventable mortality. AChRs contain binding sites for drugs that potentially could treat nicotine addiction, epilepsy, muscle weakness disorders, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and autism. The key to designing efficient drugs for AChRs is to understand the detailed mechanism by which agonists bind to and activate AChRs. However, previous studies with AChR agonists encountered technical problems and where unable to measure the full action of the drugs. Recently, we developed a new experimental approach to overcome these problems and, for the first time, to allow us to precisely and directly measure the action of AChR agonists. Using this new electrophysiology technique, we will measure and compare the binding and activation properties of novel AChR agonists. We plan to test these molecules on both the native and mutant AChRs. This will provide us with a map of specific atom-atom interactions (between the drug and AChR) as related to drug binding or AChR activation. To visualize the site of drug action, we will build a model of the AChR using sophisticated molecular modelling methods and supercomputers, which will guide further experiments and explain our findings. Our study will help improve the design of new pharmaceuticals by providing valuable information about the molecular events occurring at the drug binding site of AChRs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving the immune response to spinal cord injury using galectin-1
Keywords-MotsClés: ANATOMICAL OUTCOMES; AXON REGENERATION; BEHAVIOURAL OUTCOMES; CNS DISEASE; IMMUNOLOGY; MACROPHAGES; NEUROIMMUNOLOGY; NEUROPATHOLOGY; POTENTIAL THERAPY; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: The earliest documented cases of spinal cord injury (SCI) are in ancient Egyptian texts. 2500 years later, we are beginning to understand events that prevent repair after SCI. SCI permanently disconnects nerve cells (neurons) from other neurons in the spinal cord. Invading immune cells called macrophages worsen the situation by releasing toxic chemicals after SCI that kill nearby cells. We aim to improve how macrophages respond to SCI by treating animals with galectin-1 (Gal1), which changes macrophages so they release chemicals that protect, not kill, spinal cord cells. Gal1 could aid cell survival in the spinal cord and improve SCI animals' movement and sensation.   Why use Gal1? Gal1 causes macrophages to release helpful chemicals. Gal1 also benefits other cells after SCI. Gal1 causes spinal cord cells called astrocytes to release chemicals that aid survival/growth of neurons. Gal1 also promotes blood vessel growth.  To discover if Gal1 could benefit humans after SCI, we will use a clinically-relevant rodent SCI model . We expect that Gal1-treated SCI rats will recover walking/sensation better than normal SCI rats. We will also study mice that lack Gal1 (Gal1- mice). Gal1 likely improves repair after SCI, so we expect that Gal1- mice will not recover as well as Gal1+ mice.  To determine how Gal1 improves function after SCI, spinal cord cells will be studied. We expect that Gal1-treated SCI rats will have reduced injury size and more protective macrophages vs normal SCI rats. We expect that Gal1- mice will have larger injury sites and more toxic macrophages vs Gal1+ mice. These results would show that Gal1 protects spinal cord cells after SCI.  Gal1 benefits many different cells, so it could improve recovery significantly. These studies would show that Gal1 aids mobility and sensation after clinically-relevant SCI, and how Gal1 improves function at the cellular level. This work could identify Gal1 as a potential therapy that limits damage after SCI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mutational drivers of metastatic colorectal cancers
Keywords-MotsClés: COLORECTAL CANCER; COPY NUMBER VARIATION; GENOMICS; METASTASIS; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE VARIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Each human cell contains instructions, called the genome, that direct its growth, function, and death. The genome is made up of 3 billion molecules, called nucleotides. Nucleotides are joined in a specific sequence, but sometimes that sequence becomes mutated and causes cancer and metastasis. Metastasis is the spread of cancer to other parts of the body; it is the main cause of death from cancer. A new technology, called next-generation sequencing, allows researchers to rapidly 'read' the 3 billion nucleotide sequence of a cancer genome. With this technology, we will discover new cancer-specific mutations that drive the progression of noncancerous tissue, to primary tumor tissue, to metastatic tissue. Our aim is to identify genes that when mutated predict or promote metastasis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Therapeutic Manipulation of Glioblastoma Microenvironments using Tumor-derived Exosomes
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMORS; CANCER; EXOSOMES; GENE THERAPY; GLIOBLASTOMA; GLIOMA; LENTIVIRUS; MICROVESICLES; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PRODRUG
Abstract-Résumé: Glioma is the most prominent type of CNS tumour and accounts for more than 65% of all primary brain tumors.  Between Canada and the United States, more than 100,000 patients are diagnosed with a brain tumor annually, representing a major health burden on the individual as well as society. Furthermore, therapeutic strategies often pose a high risk of side effects to glioma patients due to its occurrence in the brain, and invasive gliomas frequently recur after treatment, resulting in death in nearly all cases.  Many types of tumors including gliomas modify normal cells in their environment to bestow upon themselves malignant properties such as increased tumor growth, invasion and metastasis. Recently, we discovered that glioma cells have an insidious means of manipulating cells in their environment to gain cancerous advantages for themselves: exosomes (microvesicles). Exosomes are small vesicles produced in abundance by glioblastomas (GBMs), the highest grade of gliomas, and contain cellular proteins and genetic information designed to "take over" the surrounding recipient cells, making them to acquire pro-cancerous properties and consequently facilitate tumor progression.  In this study, I will reversely employ GBM exosomes as a novel therapeutic gene vehicle to manipulate tumor environments in order to suppress tumor oncogenicity, and thereby turning the tumor cells into their own worst enemy. To develop this novel therapeutic paradigm, I will genetically engineer a subset of tumor cells to produce exosomes containing therapeutic "suicide genes" and subsequently investigate their effect in eradicating the tumor. Importantly, this devised "exosome therapy" also aims to destroy the tumor's surrounding cells which provide nutrients to propagate tumor development, as well as to kill peripheral cancer cells that often infiltrate into neighboring tissues.   Altogether, this innovative project will open a new dimension to gene therapy against gliomas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular dissection of the roles of the Hippo pathway in embryonic stem cell fate decision
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CELL BIOLOGY; CHIP-SEQUENCING; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; GENE REGULATION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MOUSE MODELS; PLURIPOTENCY; TISSUE REGENERATION; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATORS
Abstract-Résumé: While the adult body is composed of differentiated cell types specific to each organ, the cells of the developing embryo or embryonic stem (ES) cells, are still in an undifferentiated state (pluripotency), where they still have the potential to differentiate in almost any cell type of the body. In the past few years the concept of regenerative medicine, a promising therapeutic approach based on our ability to repair damaged organs, has emerged as a potentially viable method to improve a variety of human health issues such as diabetes, leukemias, muscular dystrophy or nerve injuries. Our ability to successfully bring this approach to the clinic is directly linked to our understanding of how these pluripotent ES cells undergo cellular lineage fate decisions to become a specific cell type. Recently, a cellular pathway involved in the control of organ size in mice, the Hippo pathway, has been associated with the maintenance of the pluripotency state of ES cells. This pathway is acting mainly via two essential proteins, Yap and Taz. We believe that these regulators of gene expression are potential candidates for the development of ES-cell based therapies. The goal of the proposed project is to decipher the precise mechanisms by which Yap and Taz control the ES cells switch from pluripotency to a more specialized state. The findings generated from this study will increase our understanding of the ES cells commitment process and potentially extend our ability to eventually manipulate ES cell fate for the achievement of successful regenerative medicine therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Save the Virus, Kill the Cancer: Selective Inhibition of Anti-Viral Immune Response to Establish Anti-Tumor Immunity and Complete Cancer Regression
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN-SPECIFIC IMMUNOMODULATION; IMMUNOTHERAPY OF CANCER; KILLER DENDRITIC CELLS; VIROTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: According to the Cancer Statistics Canada 2008 Report, last year 24,700 new cases and 4300 deaths were attributed to prostate cancer in Canada. Unfortunately, currently available treatment options fail to manage this disease. Such unavailability of effective treatment options have led to the development of a novel class of anti-cancer therapeutic therapies as reovirus-based virotherapy.  Reovirus is a benign, naturally occurring virus has an ability to specifically target cancer cells of various origins including prostate cancer, while leaving healthy, non-cancerous cells unaffected.  Additionally, reovirus virotherapy educates the patient's immune system to mount attack on cancer cells.    Unfortunately, the implementation of this novel treatment has not been completely successful due to the hindrance caused by patients' immune system.  During the administration of reovirus, immune system identifies reovirus as a pathogen and promptly removes it from the body.  Such an anti-reoviral immune response purges reovirus before it can spread and kill enough cancer. So far, this problem has only been partially addressed by shutting down the patient's immune system using immuno-suppressive drugs.  However, these harsh immuno-suppressive drugs have non-specific effects on immune system that render patients susceptible to infections, and more importantly avoid the development of reovirus-mediated initiation of beneficial anti-prostate cancer immunity.  Therefore, it is believed that the success of the reovirus cancer treatment will ultimately depend on acquiring an exclusive inhibition of anti-reovirus immune response, without affecting immunity against prostate cancer.     In this study, we propose a safe, practical, least invasive and clinically applicable immuno-modulatorynovel approach that will exclusively shut down anti-reovirus immunity temporarily and thus allow reovirus to persist longer and induce complete cancer regression.

Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER CELL INVASION; CANCER CELL MIGRATION; NONCANONICAL WNT SIGNALING; PLANAR CELL POLARITY; TUMOR PROGRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: In approximately one-third of breast cancer patients, breast cancer tumors display strong resistance to conventional treatments, such as hormone-based therapies. Coincidently, these breast cancer tumors have an unusually strong ability to quickly spread to other organs.  This project aims to tackle the question of how breast cancer cells migrate within organs and eventually transform into invasive tumors. To address this question, we aim to (1) study the function of "molecules" that help in cell migration and (2) identify new factors that control the function of these migration molecules.  We will then manipulate these newly identified factors and examine how breast cancer cell migration is affected. Expanding our knowledge in breast cancer cells migration is very important since it may help in the discovery of new ways to inhibit their invasive properties.  This, in turn, could save the lives and reduce the suffering of at least the one-third of breast cancer patients with the highly aggressive tumor types.  We aim to openly share our findings with other scientists though publications and conferences and we hope that this will lead to the discovery of new treatment options.

Abstract-Résumé: High blood pressure (hypertension) is a major factor in the occurrence of stroke and heart attacks.  Over the last two decades there is increasing evidence to implicate the brain in control of cardiovascular function though the sympathetic nerves and secretion of powerful hormones into the blood stream.  Many chemical messengers have been identified within the brain that control cardiovascular function but their precise role and mechanism of action is less clearly understood.  The studies outlined in this proposal focus on two peptides, Neuropeptide FF (NPFF) and prolactin-releasing peptide (PrRP), which have recently been identified within brain areas important for cardiovascular control.  This work will provide novel and important information on how these peptides are involved in the control of blood pressure.  It is possible that newer compounds based on NPFF and PrRP have the potential to be used in the treatment of hypertension, which is a major risk factor for stroke and heart disease.  Since both NPFF and PrRP are also implicated in feeding behaviour, there are also prospects to develop drugs based on these peptides to treat obesity, also a risk factor for atherosclerosis.  Our research program will train the next generation of scientists and clinicians, who will be intimately involved in the care of heart attack and stroke patients.  These elements collectively will improve the quality of life for all Canadians with heart disease and stroke.

Abstract-Résumé: The construction, development and consistent use of biomedical standards to regulate health risks (standardization) are essential to the health and safety of Canadians. We aim to investigate how different types of engagement affect knowledge translation when stakeholders come together to create and negotiate standards. Our interdisciplinary team proposes to study how knowledge is communicated in the negotiation of standards in three case studies: 1) the international Human Proteomics Organization (HUPO) and its Proteomics Standards Initiative (PSI) which creates human proteomes research standards for the development of personalised medicines; 2) the implementation of global vaccine safety standards and their uptake in a developing country; and 3) negotiations for biomedical standards that will recognize the environmental and health consequences of pollutants in the Walpole Island First Nation. Using qualitative ethnographic methods including interviews, observations and document analysis, this comparative study represents the continuum of standards development and stakeholder engagement from lab to public: before a biotechnology reaches society-wide application and is integrated into public discourse (HUPO); during the implementation of global vaccine safety standards; and after technical standards of health risks have failed and been challenged in public discourses (Walpole Island). We will evaluate knowledge translation between scientists, clinicians, industry, regulators and communities, producing accounts of systematic patterns of communication and mis-communication between stakeholders engaged in standardization. Targeted areas will be identified to facilitate more effective engagement and knowledge translation between stakeholders in future, and produce a model of participation in biomedical standardization which will aid regulators, policy makers, researchers and practitioners involved in assessing and implementing new standardized health technologies.

ProgramNameEN: Operating Grant - Priority Announcement: HIV/AIDS Research Initiative - Biomedical/Clinical Research Stream
NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de fonctionnement - Annonce de priorités : VIH/sida Initiative de recherche - volet recherche biomédicale/clinique

TitreApplicationTitle: Reconstructing within-host evolution of HIV-1 from next-generation sequencing data
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CYTOTOXIC T-LYMPHOCYTES (CTL); HIV/AIDS; HUMAN LEUKOCYTE ANTIGEN (HLA); IMMUNE ESCAPE; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; PHYLOGENETICS; POPULATION GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Many pivotal advances in HIV research have relied on our ability to interpret genetic sequences of the virus.  Using a model of how sequences evolve over time, for example, others have reconstructed the history of the HIV epidemic as it crossed over from non-human primates into human populations, and subsequently spread throughout the world.  Similar models are now being used to estimate the rates that HIV is being transmitted in different populations.  This task is a central component of a global effort to find and assist populations that are at greater risk of infection, and to identify the factors that can decrease the risk of infection, such as highly-active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).  Estimating the transmission rates of HIV at a large scale relies on comparing how much HIV sequences have evolved between different patients.  Therefore, it is crucial to have a detailed understanding of what influences the pace of evolution of HIV within a patient.  A great deal of this evolution is driven by the adaptation of HIV to a patient's immune system.  For instance, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules are an important component of our immune systems that exerts significant pressure on HIV to evolve, by attacking specific sequences in the virus genome.  Because different HLA molecules are expressed by different people, the sites and rates of evolution in the HIV genome are unique to each patient.  One of the most important advances in biological research in the past few years, called next-generation sequencing (NGS), is making it possible to study the evolution of HIV within patients to an unprecedented level of detail.  This proposal presents the first large-scale study of patient-specific adaptation of HIV to the HLA using NGS technology.  We are developing a new generation of analytical models to reconstruct patterns of evolution of HIV within patients, which will enable us to assess more accurately the impact of HAART on the transmission rate of HIV.

ProgramNameEN: Operating Grant - Priority Announcement: HIV/AIDS Research Initiative - Biomedical/Clinical Research Stream
NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de fonctionnement - Annonce de priorités : VIH/sida Initiative de recherche - volet recherche biomédicale/clinique
TitreApplicationTitle: The virus infectivity factor (Vif) of HIV-1: mechanisms of inhibiting antiviral APOBEC3 immune factors
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CYTOSINE DEAMINASES; ENZYME MECHANISMS; HIV; HIV ACCESSORY PROTEINS; HIV RESTRICTION FACTOR; MOLECULAR IMMUNOLOGY; MUTAGENESIS; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; VIRUS-HOST INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), the causative agent of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), currently infects 33 million people worldwide, 58 000 of which are Canadian. Presently, HIV treatments have made the disease one that is chronic, but manageable, for people who have access to proper medical care. However, the current therapy has significant long term side effects in patients, such as lipid abnormalities and cardiovascular risks. An alternative route for developing HIV therapeutics is to take advantage of human enzymes, naturally present in the immune cells that HIV infects, which have the the ability to restrict HIV replication. These 'host restriction factors' can block the HIV lifecycle at specific steps, but are often thwarted by HIV accessory proteins designed to overcome these barriers. My laboratory's research focuses on the APOBEC3 family of human enzymes that can restrict HIV replication by causing chemical modifications in the HIV genetic material (DNA), which makes the virus non-functional. However, APOBEC3 enzymes can only act in the absence of the HIV virus infectivity factor (Vif) protein, which inhibits APOBEC3 enzymes by a number of mechanisms. If we can enable APOBEC3 enzymes to work better for humans, by designing molecules the block Vif from doing its job, it is possible that the human immune system will be able to manage HIV infection. To this end, my research takes a fine-tuned look at the interactions between Vif and APOBEC3 enzymes by purifying the relevant components from cells and conducting experiments in a test tube. There are many gaps in our understanding of these molecular battles that human APOBEC3 enzymes and HIV Vif wage against each other. Understanding this relationship is the first step for designing APOBEC3-based therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring Novel Inhibitors of HIV-1 Replication
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV-1; HNRNPS; RNA PROCESSING; RNA SPLICING; SR PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Although current drug treatments have proven effective in preventing the progression of patients to AIDS, they are not a cure. This fact, coupled with the toxic side effects of the drugs and the increasing appearance of drug resistant forms of HIV-1, calls for continued investment in the discovery and evaluation of new treatment strategies. Our laboratory has recently identified a number of compounds that block expression of the virus through a novel mechanism, altering the metabolism of the viral RNA. Understanding how these compounds act and exploring alternative forms of the current compounds for their antiviral potency will allow development of these initial finding towards a novel therapy for this infection. Use of the drugs in conjunction with existing therapies offers the promise of improved control of this infection and extended life span for those affected.

TitreApplicationTitle: Heteroclitic Stimulation and CD5 Modulation as Strategies to Expand Human Immunodeficiency Virus-specific CD8+ T cell Recognition Breadth
Keywords-MotsClés: CD5; CD8; HETEROCLITIC; HIV; HLA; IMMUNOLOGY; PEPTIDE; T CELL
Abstract-Résumé: One of the biggest obstacles to developing an effective vaccine against human immunodfeficiency virus (HIV) is the tremendous diversity of the virus.  This allows the virus to rapidly evade both antibody and T cell-mediated immune responses.  The most common approach to addressing viral variablilty in vaccine development has been to focus on identifying conserved sequences or structures within virus variants. There may also be ways to alter the nature of the immune response so that more viral variants are recognized.  This research project involves two methods of expanding the capacity of the immune response to recognize variants of HIV.  One method focuses on using specialized antigens to recruit a greater variety of immune cells to fight the virus.  The other method focuses on using a greater variety of antigens so that those cells that are recruited recognize more variants of HIV.  Together, these two approaches have the potential to expand the breadth of immunity to cover more variants of HIV and thus, increase the effectiveness of HIV vaccines.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Causal Role of Acute Alcohol Consumption in Unprotected Sex among MSM at Risk for Acquiring HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; ALCOHOL; CONDOMS; HIV; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN (MSM); RISK; SEX
Abstract-Résumé: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) remains a public health issue in Canada, and particularly affected by the Canadian HIV epidemic are men who have sex with men (MSM), who comprise over half of all HIV diagnoses in Canada to date. Unprotected sexual intercourse is the primary method through which HIV is spread in Canada, and this is especially true for MSM populations. Although it has often been suggested that consuming alcohol causes people to engage in unprotected sex, research has tended to provide mixed support for this link. Our understanding of the alcohol-risky sex link is further limited by the fact that there has been no research to date that has directly examined alcohol's causal role in condom use decisions among populations who are at an elevated risk for acquiring HIV, including MSM. Building on the previous work in this area and addressing these limitations, the present investigation will involve an innovative experimental approach to identify the causal role of alcohol consumption in MSM's intentions to engage in unprotected sex, taking into account risk-relevant personality traits, partner characteristics, and alcohol-related expectancies. In this study, 130 sexually active MSM will be recruited from a clinical care facility to take part in an experimental session in which they will 1) complete measures assessing personality traits and expectancies, 2) undergo an alcohol manipulation, and 3) indicate their intentions to engage in a variety of protected and unprotected sexual acts with a series of hypothetical sexual partners. Results yielded through this comprehensive experimental approach will help identify the extent to which alcohol plays an independent role in condom use decisions, which, in turn, could guide the development of future HIV prevention initiatives that target unprotected sex among at-risk populations. Such initiatives could ultimately impact large-scale public health campaigns aimed at reducing HIV incidence in Canada over time.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the Impact of HIV/AIDS Service Delivery in Zomba District, Malawi: The Zomba District Observational Cohort Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL TREATMENT; COHORT STUDY; HEALTH SYSTEMS STRENGTHENING; HIV/AIDS; OBSERVATIONAL DATABASE; PRIMARY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Our proposed research aims to assess the effectiveness of decentralization of antiretroviral treatment (ART) in Zomba District, Malawi on access to and equity of care. ART decentralization is an example of a complex, multi-faceted public health intervention in a health district in a low-income country. We believe that the results of this study will provide valuable insight for policy makers and program implementers for strengthening and expanding HIV/AIDS services in Malawi and other middle- and low-income countries.  We propose to establish the Zomba District Observational Database, a longitudinal, integrated population-based observational database in Zomba District, Malawi for HIV/AIDS, TB and maternal and child health using inventive, low-tech methods that are compatible with the context of a low-income country with weak infrastructure across all sectors (health, education, transportation, agriculture, etc.).

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of EGFR-mediated Cell Signaling and Endocytosis during Mitosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; DIMERIZATION; EGF RECEPTOR; ENDOCYTOSIS; ENDOCYTOSIS MOTIF; KINASE ACTIVITY; MITOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Cell growth is controlled by various growth factors. Growth factors bind to their receptors at cell surface to stimulate cell growth by activating these receptors. Over-activation of these receptors will cause the over-growth of the cells, leading to cancer development. The growth factor and its receptor involved in this grant are called epidermal growth factor (EGF) and EGF receptor (EGFR). EGFR over-activation happens in many cancers especially in breast cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer and lung cancer. EGFR over-activation correlates to poor prognosis, drug resistance, cancer metastasis and lower survival rate. All these make EGFR the top choice as a target for developing cancer therapies. Cell division is the most dramatic period of the cell cycle, involving a major reorganization of virtually all cell components. A major difference between cancer cells and normal cells is that the cancer cells are much more mitogenic and frequently enter mitosis for proliferation. Therefore, most cancer drugs are designed to specifically target the mitotic cells. However, the role of growth factor receptor during cell division is very rarely and poorly studied. In this proposal we plan to study how the growth factor receptor controls cell signalling during cell division, what is the molecular mechanism regulating the internalization and trafficking of the receptor during cell division, and how the internalization of the receptor controls the receptor activity during cell division. The results generated from our research will certainly strengthen our ability to develop better therapeutic treatment for various cancers.

Keywords-MotsClés: CELL POLARITY; ERBB2; JUNCTIONAL ADHESION MOLECULE; MAMMARY EPITHELIA; MOUSE MODELS; TIGHT JUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The role cell-cell junctions play during cancer is not well understood. In this proposal we investigate the role played junctional adhesion molecule-A (JAM-A) during ErbB2 mediated tumorigenesis. Our study has strong clinical significance because previous studies have demonstrated that JAM-A is overexpressed in breast cancer and the overexpression correlates with poor clinical prognosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: A comparative study of assisted human reproduction patients' views about the donation of eggs and embryos for scientific and clincal research
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTED REPRODUCTION; BIOETHICS; COMPARATIVE RESEARCH; EMPIRICAL RESEARCH; HUMAN EGG RESEARCH; HUMAN EMBRYO RESEARCH; INTERDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH; PHILOSOPHICAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: To date, much has been written, globally, about the views of women and couples in various jurisdictions concerning the disposition of both excess human eggs and embryos for therapeutic or research purposes (in either an altruistic or a commercial context).  Canadian contributions to the theoretical literature are noteworthy, but contributions to the empirical literature are scarce.  The proposed research has three objectives: (i) to generate much-needed Canadian data on the perceptions, views and understandings of women and couples in Canadian IVF programs who have been asked to donate their eggs or embryos for research; (ii) to analyze the potential social and ethical costs associated with egg and embryo donation for research from a feminist perspective, with particular attention to similarities and differences between (a) donors and non-donors, (b) egg donors and embryo donors, and (c) supporters of altruistic donation as compared with those who would prefer a commercialized system; and (iii) to transfer the knowledge gained from Projects 1 and 2 to clinicians, researchers, and policymakers with a view to improving informed decision-making by potential donors and improving existing legislation, regulations, and guidelines governing egg and embryo donation for research.   In brief, this research will generate Canadian data on the acceptability of egg and embryo research to potential donors. This data will inform our analysis of the social and ethical costs associated with egg and embryo donation for research. Together, the empirical data and philosophical reflections will provide practical feedback to researchers, practitioners and policymakers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Animals, Humans, and the Continuity of Evidence: A Study of Clinical Translation
Keywords-MotsClés: DISEASE MODELS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MEDICAL EVIDENCE; PHARMACEUTICAL DEVELOPMENT; PHASE 1 TRIALS; PRECLINICAL RESEARCH; RESEARCH INTEGRITY; SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH; VALIDITY
Abstract-Résumé: In the last two decades, researchers have made enormous progress in understanding the causes of human disease.  Yet many important discoveries have not yet had an impact on the practice of medicine.  This grant aims to understand some of the reasons why therapies that show promise in animals never make it to the clinic.  We believe one of the reasons is that animal studies are often not as well designed  as they should be.  This grant will look at a large group of animal and human studies to see whether this is the case. Our study will further allow us to see whether certain research practices might improve chances that a new drug will have a clinical impact, and whether patients benefit or are harmed by participating in first in human drug studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study of the determinants of nurses' and physicians' intention to practice an act of euthanasia in a context of palliative care.
Keywords-MotsClés: APPLIED ETHICS; EUTHANASIA; HEALTH BEHAVIOURS; HEALTHCARE PRACTICE; INTENTION; PALLIATIVE CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Euthanasia is still a controversial topic in Canada to this day, highlighting the clash between fundamental values and impassioned debates. Some groups are exercising more and more pressure to legalize its practice. Closely linked to the context of palliative care, euthanasia generates support which is far from unanimous among the health professionals taking care of persons at the end of life. The practice is criticized because it represents an act aimed at deliberately causing death, something which runs counter to the philosophy of palliative care. When supported, it is because it helps to relieve "inhuman" suffering or to support the sick person's autonomy. Thus, if euthanasia were to be legalized, what would that mean for the autonomy of the caregivers requested to apply it? Current researches still provides little explanation of their intentions when faced with carrying out an act of euthanasia. This is why our project aims at studying the determinants of intentions of nurses and physicians eventually invited to perform an act of euthanasia in palliative care. It could enlighten decision-makers as to its possible impact on the practices of health professionals and caregivers themselves. It includes four objectives: 1. Identify the determinants of nurses' intention to practice an act of euthanasia or not; 2. Identify the determinants of physicians' intention to practice an act of euthanasia or not; 3. Identify the significant differences between the determinants in the predictability model of nurses compared to that of physicians; and 4. Measure the impact of the presence or absence of the person's wishes on the intention of the nurses (4a) and of the physicians (4b). The project is based on Triandis's psychosocial theory (1980) which permits, through a questionnaire, to study the determinants of the healthcare professionals' intention (Godin et al., 2008a).

Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; DUAL INHIBITOR OF IGF-1R AND IR; PATIENT-DERIVED HUMAN TUMOR XENOGRAFTS; PREDICTIVE MARKERS; TARGETED AGENTS; TARGETED SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed in Canadian women (excluding non-melanoma skin cancer). Despite advances in early detection and treatment, breast cancer remains the second-leading cause of cancer death in Canadian women. There is an urgent need to develop improved therapies for women with advanced breast cancer. OSI-906 is a promising new drug that blocks two critical pathways involved in breast cancer growth and resistance to existing treatments, the Insulin Growth Factor-1 Receptor (IGF-1R) and the Insulin Receptor (IR). The aim of this project is to test OSI-906, either alone or in combination with other promising new drugs, in mouse models implanted with samples of breast tumors donated by women with advanced breast cancer. This will provide a better understanding of which types of breast cancer are likely to benefit from treatment with OSI-906 either alone or in combination with other promising new drugs that can be tested in future clinical trials involving patients with breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pregnancy Outcomes and Patterns of DMARD Use Longitudinally Among Rheumatoid Arthritis Subjects (POPULAR) Study
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; PREGNANCY; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is the most common autoimmune disease.  It affects 2% of the general population (~700,000 Canadians) and disproportionately affects women of reproductive age. Medical therapy with disease modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) is recommended to halt joint destruction and disability and maintain quality of life.   A great deal of uncertainty surrounds the use of RA treatments around the time of pregnancy because no clinical guidelines exist for doctors to follow. On one hand, controlling disease improves the chance of a successful pregnancy.  On the other hand, exposure may pose risk to the fetus. Many physicians advise stopping treatment once pregnancy is confirmed, while others advocate continued use throughout pregnancy to prevent disease flares. Of concern is the observation that some DMARDs may be associated with poor pregnancy outcomes.  However, no large-scale studies have been done to determine to ascertain the true risk.  Furthermore, no studies have looked at how women with RA are actually being treated in real-world practice and whether treatment patterns have changed over time as new drug therapies become available.   Our study proposes to describe the frequency and type of RA treatments prescribed during pregnancy.  We will also estimate if exposure to DMARDs during pregnancy affects the success of  pregnancy outcomes by examining rates of spontaneous abortions, therapeutic abortions, live births, pre-term births and congenital anomalies.    A better understanding of these treatment patterns will assist the creation of clinical practice guidelines for RA treatment during pregnancy. It may also help drug funding agencies understand which medications are essential or which may be more/less cost-effective.  More importantly, knowledge of the risk/safety profile of medications will inform treatment decisions between physicians and patients so that the best and safest choice for a woman and her future child can be selected

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical supervision during acute resuscitation: how to balance patient safety and resident learning.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL LEARNING; CLINICAL SUPERVISION; CRITICAL CARE; HIGH-FIDELITY SIMULATION; MIXED METHODS; PARTICIPANT OBSERVATION & INTERVIEWS; PATIENT SAFETY; POSTGRADUATE TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing attention to patient safety, combined with higher level of patient acuity and complexity, is reshaping post-graduate medical training. Attending physicians supervising trainees' clinical activities are strongly encouraged to more closely oversee patient care. Direct supervisor involvement in care delivery could affect learning opportunities by changing the nature of trainees' participation in patient care and their interactions with the supervisors. The main objective of this program of research is to better understand how a closer level of supervision during acute resuscitation episodes affects trainees' learning. More specifically, we will observe the interactions between the physicians-in-training, their supervisors, and their clinical environment during acute resuscitation episodes encountered under different levels of clinical supervision. In addition, we will measure trainees' understanding of specific resuscitation episodes and their future ability to independently resuscitate critically ill patients. This program of research includes one systematic review of the literature on participation and learning and two observational studies. The first observational study will be completed in a simulated setting, whereas the second study will occur in real critical care environments. Our findings will allow us to identify factors related to the level of clinical supervision that can be targeted by educational interventions in order to optimize learning during postgraduate clinical training. Understanding how to best optimize learning opportunities while maintaining a safe clinical environment for the patients is essential to preserve the quality of medical training and patient care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery of clinical and metabolic genetic syndromes manifesting as neuropsychiatric disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL GENETICS; GENETIC VARIANTS; GENOTYPE-PHENOTYPE; HIGH-THROUGHPUT SEQUENCING; METABOLIC GENETICS; MICROARRAY; NEUROPSYCHIATRY
Abstract-Résumé: Many clinical and metabolic genetic syndromes are known to present with psychiatric disorders or features.  While much of ongoing psychiatric genetic research has been dedicated to the identification and characterization of genes involved in psychiatric disease, little research has been done to determine the extent to which clinical and metabolic genetic syndromes contribute to the psychiatric disease load in the population.  Significantly, many of these conditions require surveillance for other, sometimes preventable or treatable, clinical manifestations, such as hormonal disturbances, heart disease, or neurodegenerative processes.  Additionally, many metabolic conditions are treatable by adjustments in diet, medication and/or enzyme replacement therapy.  The shorter-term goals of this study will be to identify the prevalence of clinical and metabolic genetic syndromes amongst large populations of psychiatric patients, with or without secondary diagnoses, allowing insight into the underlying disease-causing mechanisms of psychiatric disorders.  This would lead longer-term to the development and refinement of diagnostic, management, surveillance and therapeutic protocols for the assessment of such patients, the characterization of clinical features amongst groups of patients found to have underlying genetic syndromes, as well as the education of primary care physicians, such as family physicians, psychiatrists and neurologists, so that appropriate and timely referrals can be made in the future.  This would contribute to the improvement of physical and mental health outcomes, and ultimately to a better use of health care resources.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prediction of clinical improvement by deep brain stimulation surgery in primary generalized dystonia using clinical, genetics and neurophysiologic measures
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTICAL PLASTICITY; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; INTRACORTICAL CIRCUITS; LONG TERM POTENTIATION; PAIRED ASSOCIATIVE STIMULATION; PAIRED PULSE PARADIGMS; PRIMARY GENERALISED DYSTONIA; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Dystonia is a common movement disorder characterized by excessive muscle contraction and severe refractory cases can be effectively treated with deep brain stimulation (DBS) of one of the deeper brain structure viz., globus pallidus internus. Previous studies found that dystonia is associated with abnormal motor cortical functions as measured by plasticity and DBS corrects this abnormality through basal ganglia-motor cortical connections. However, the effects of DBS on motor cortex have not been investigated before and after the surgery to assess the changes in motor cortical plasticity. In this study, we plan to investigate the effects of DBS on motor cortex before and at different time points after the surgery. We also plan to study the single nucleotide polymorphisms of brain derived neurotrophic factor (genetic factor associated with changes in cortical plasticity) and clinical dystonia scores. Based on these neurophysiologic measures coupled with genetic and clinical profile, we propose to derive the prediction of improvement following DBS surgery in patients with dystonia.
