TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Enzymatic Removal of Major Blood Antigens
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD ANTIGENS; BLOOD GROUPS; CARBOYHYDRATES; DIRECTED EVOLUTION; ENZYME ENGINEERING; ENZYMOLOGY; GLYCOSYLHYDROLASES; PHAGE-DISPLAY; RED BLOOD CELLS; TRANSFUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Blood transfusion is a critically important medical procedure, used to treat blood-loss due to trauma or during surgery, and also in the treatment of chronic blood disorders such as thalassemia, sickle-cell disease, or other forms of anemia. Over 15 million units (approx. 450mL per unit) are collected per year for preparation of blood products in Canada and the United States alone. Due to the presence of blood antigens, however, careful blood-typing is necessary to avoid adverse and sometimes fatal reactions that may result from a mismatched blood transfusion. The A and B blood antigens are considered the most clinically important blood antigens. People of blood-type O lack the A and B antigens on their red-blood-cells and thus are often considered "universal donors" (not accounting for minor antigens), yet units of type-O blood are frequently in short supply due to high demand. The use of enzymes to remove A and B antigens is a potential means of generating universal blood donor cells from blood types other than O. The recent discovery of an enzyme (of microbial origin) capable of removing both A and B antigens from red-blood-cells opens up a new approach for generating universal blood donor cells. The goal of this project is to develop the use of this enzyme, known as EABase, as a means to remove A and B antigens from red blood cells. Enzyme engineering, using "directed evolution" techniques, will be carried out to improve the efficiency of EABase in removing blood antigens. The ability to generate universal blood donor cells in such a way would be a breakthrough development, allowing transfusion without the need to find a positive match thus tremendously improving the supply of blood while increasing the safety of blood transfusions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genome Variations that Drive Increased Fitness in MAD1 and FANCJ-Defective C. elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: CAENORHABDITIS ELEGANS; CANCER; DOG-1/FANCJ; FANCONI ANEMIA; GENETIC INTERACTIONS; GENOME STABILITY; GENOMICS/BIOINFORMATICS; MDF-1/MAD1; MOLECULAR PATHWAY; SPINDLE ASSEMBLY CHECKPOINT
Abstract-Résumé: The majority of tumours exhibit changes in chromosome number or structure, a phenomenon called Chromosomal INstability (CIN). Genes contributing to the proper chromosome transmission are mutated in cancer. My project has been focused on analysis of two genome-guardian genes using the model organism, C. elegans. mdf-1/MAD1 is a conserved component of the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC), a surveillance mechanism that prevents CIN. In C. elegans, loss of MDF-1 leads to accumulation of defects and death. The second gene, dog-1/FANCJ, is a conserved gene, discovered in C. elegans, with unique task to protect stretches of guanines from being deleted. In human, mutations in the FANCJ have been identified in Fanconi Anemia (FA) patients. When I introduced mdf-1 mutant gene into the dog-1 mutant background (a strain nicknamed MAD_DOG), I isolated a dog-1 induced tandem duplication that allowed the mdf-1 animals to survive. Recently, I found that this duplication suppresses mdf-1 lethality via a dosage effect of cyb-3 (Cyclin B3). Then, I cultivated MAD_DOG animals for more than six years, and have found that the fitness of these animals has further improved (beyond cyb-3 dosage suppression) over time. Thus, I hypothesize that multiple dog-1-induced suppressors of mdf-1 lethality have accumulated in this strain. The overall goal of my research is to identify all of the mutations that have accumulated in the absence of dog-1 over 6 years using next-generation sequencing methods and to identify and understand all of the dog-1 induced lesions that suppress mdf-1 lethality. Considering the fact that both MAD1 and FANCJ are misregulated/mutated in human cancers, this research is particularly relevant to understanding of FANCJ targets and mutational events that may contribute to aetiology of FA, as well as causation and development of cancer in general, providing a possible foundation for prevention and treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Allele-specific silencing of the mutant huntingtin gene in a mouse model of Huntington's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLELE-SPECIFIC SILENCING; ANTI-SENSE OLIGONUCLEOTIDE; GENE SILENCING; GENE THERAPY; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INTRACRANIAL DELIVERY; MOUSE BEHAVIOR; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROPATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington disease (HD) is an inherited, fatal, neurodegenerative disease characterized by chorea, dementia and psychiatric disturbance. Death usually occurs 15-20 years after onset of symptoms, and there is currently no effective therapy. Huntington disease is caused by a mutation in a protein called huntingtin. Preventing the generation of this mutant protein by gene silencing could prevent or delay HD. The normal huntingtin protein is important for neuronal health and disrupting or silencing of this gene could have detrimental effects. We are developing a strategy of silencing only the mutant copy of a patient's huntingtin gene as a novel treatment for HD. Our lab has identified DNA sequence variations that are more common in human mutant huntingtin genes than normal huntingtin genes. We have generated reagents targeting these variations that reduce expression of the mutant but not the normal protein in cellular models of HD. We have also generated a humanized mouse model of HD that recapitulates these DNA variations. I will deliver candidate therapeutics to the brains of these mice and evaluate them for efficacy in reducing expression of the mutant protein in the living brain and for benefit to the abnormal behavior and brain pathology of these mice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetic regulation of CD4+ T cell dependent immunity and inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: CONDITIONAL DELETION MOUSE MODEL; CYTOKINE BIOLOGY; EPIGENETICS; HELMINTH IMMUNITY; HELPER T CELLS; IMMUNOPARASITOLOGY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; LYSINE-METHYLTRANSFERASE (G9A AND SET7); MUCOSAL IMMUNITY
Abstract-Résumé: The human body fights off infections using several types of white blood cells, such as helper T cells (Th), to kill invading germs. Once Th cells encounter an infectious microbe, they can develop into one of several types of activated cells including Th1, Th2 or Th17 cells. This choice is absolutely critical as each type of cell has a different function in the body. Th1 cells kill bacteria and viruses, Th2 cells attack worm parasites and Th17 cells control fungal infections. However, uncontrolled or inappropriate Th cell responses can also cause autoimmune disease like arthritis, Multiple Sclerosis, asthma and allergies. Thus, appropriate control of helper T cell development is critical for preventing infection and autoimmune disease.    The gut is a unique environment that must simultaneously tolerate an endless variety of foods and billions of helpful bacteria, while retaining the ability to recognize and respond to dangerous infectious diseases. In Canada, over 200,000 people suffer from inflammatory bowel disease (one of the world's highest incidence rates) and each year over 20,000 Canadians will be diagnosed with colorectal cancer, a disease linked to inflammation. The focus of this proposal is to understand how helper T cell development choices are made in the gut. We have identified two molecules, G9a and Set7, which play important roles in this decision process. In the absence of G9a, Th cells cannot become Th2 cells. This is a good thing for preventing asthma and ulcerative colitis but a bad thing if you are infected with an intestinal worm parasite. On the other hand in the absence of Set7, Th cells preferentially become Th2. Although this could prevent chronic infection with a worm parasite, it may make asthma worse. How G9a and Set7 control this choice is completely unknown. Our research will answer this important question and may identify new drug targets that could aid in the treatment of infections and autoimmune disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the Role of NADPH Oxidases (NOXs) in the Development of Crohn's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CROHN'S DISEASE; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; INFLAMMATION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INNATE IMMUNITY; MOUSE MODELS; NADPH OXIDASES
Abstract-Résumé: Crohn's disease is a life-long disorder that affects the gastrointestinal tract. It is a major health concern across the globe and currently affects nearly 100,000 Canadians, with over 5,000 new cases diagnosed every year in Canada alone. Although we now understand that Crohn's disease involves an inappropriate and exaggerated immune response against the bacteria that are normally present in everyone's intestines, why this response happens in only some and not in the large majority of people is still not known. Many lines of evidence suggest that, at least in some cases, genetic factors (i.e. defects/alterations in genes) may promote the development of this disease. In fact, genetic studies are beginning to identify alterations in a number of genes in people afflicted with Crohn's, many of which are known to be critically involved in the immune system. Our studies will focus on a group of genes that code for a specialized family of proteins called NADPH Oxidases (or NOXs). The NOX family of proteins is dedicated to the formation of highly toxic molecules called reactive oxygen species (or ROS) that are used by our immune system to fight off and kill any invading microbes. Previous genetic studies in humans have identified an alteration in the gene of a NOX2 protein subunit of some Crohn's patients that we predict will make this protein non-functional. Moreover, we think that a defect in one or more members of the NOX protein family may weaken the immune system's ability to fight off bacteria in the gut, leading to prolonged immune responses and, eventually, disease. Using a variety of methodologies we seek to uncover how a defect in the gene of a NOX2-subunit will impact the ability of the immune system to fight off bacteria and how this may influence the development of Crohn's disease.  We think that this research will provide important insights into the factors that cause Crohn's disease, and yield new avenues from which better treatments can be developed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Gene-Environmental Interactions in the Pathogenesis of Inflammatory Bowel Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; DENDRITIC CELLS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTESTINAL PERMEABILITY; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The mucosal immune system is constantly exposed to an immense load of antigens from ingested food, resident microbes to invading viruses, yet remarkably discerning between harmful invaders from digested food antigens and the symbiotic microbes. However in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, the intestinal mucosa is disrupted resulting in chronic intestinal inflammation. The current paradigm for the pathogenesis of IBD is an inappropriate intestinal immune response to luminal microbes in genetically susceptible individuals. The number of individuals suffering with this condition has been gradually increasing in Canada. This trend has also been observed in developing countries and has recently been attributed to air pollution. Recently a new paradigm has emerged suggesting that IBD, especially Crohn's disease, results from an innate immuno-deficiency. Data from our laboratory supports this concept where colonic epithelium from healthy individuals responded to isolated DNA from pathogen while epithelium from CD patients did not. The aims of this fellowship are to investigate the mechanisms behind the dysfunctional response to bacterial DNA in Crohn's disease patients and determine how air pollution particles might be modulating these immune responses. Experiments will be done on cell culture systems, animals models of IBD and biopsies from IBD patients. Additionally an in silico method using Computational Systems Biology will be used to visualize network systems produced during the complex gene-environment interactions. It is expected that this powerful tool will not only open new avenues to examining complex biological systems, but will also lead to a more comprehensive understanding of IBD and the eventual hope to preventing the diseases altogether.

TitreApplicationTitle: VHL-mediated regulation of JAK/STAT pathway in kidney cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: E3 UBIQUITIN LIGASE; JAK2; JAK2-STAT5 SIGNALING; RENAL CELL CARCINOMA (RCC); SOCS1; VON HIPPEL-LINDAU TUMOR SUPPRESSOR PROTEIN (PVHL)
Abstract-Résumé: Our research team recently discovered a novel link between two genes, the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) and the Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) that have important roles in the development of cancer. The VHL gene is a tumour suppressor gene that helps to control cell growth and proliferation. Abnormalities or mutations of the VHL gene result in the development of numerous cancers, including those of the brain, eye, and kidney. In the general population VHL gene mutations are very common in the development of kidney cancer, one of the most resistant cancers to conventional anti-cancer therapies. The significant discovery made by our research team is that the two proteins are physically linked, and that VHL actually regulates the activity of JAK2. My research objectives are to elucidate the precise molecular mechanisms by which VHL regulates JAK2 in kidney cancer with the supposition that the lessons learned from my research will provide better understanding of kidney cancer development and progression, and ultimately aid in the development of novel cancer therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development of a theory-derived intervention for increasing the use of standardized outcome measures in rehabilitation
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR CHANGE; INTERVENTION DESIGN AND EVALUATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OCCUPATIONAL THERAPISTS; PILOT TEST; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW; THEORY APPLICATION
Abstract-Résumé: The use of objective methods or instruments for evaluating improvements in patients has been encouraged for decades with little success.  Many health care practitioners, including occupational therapists, prefer to use more informal and subjective methods of determining if their patient has improved; unfortunately, these methods are much less accurate. Using an objective approach to measuring improvements in patient care in combination with subjective determination is believed to help health care practitioners to provide better care and ultimately will improve patient outcomes.  Strategies that have previously been tried to increase the use of outcome measures have largely failed; however, they have not been designed using theories specific to behaviour change.  This project will develop an evidence-based intervention using appropriate theory to increase the use of standardized outcome measures in occupational therapy.  This project has 3 theory-driven phases.  The first is to review and summarize the methods examined to date and establish if any components have been effective. Second, occupational therapists will be interviewed to better understand the drivers of outcome measure use and to identify what factors might encourage or discourage use.  These factors will be organized using proven theories relevant to behaviour change.  Third, potential interventions for behaviour change will be mapped to these drivers to ascertain the best behaviour change strategies for this particular issue. The resulting theory-based intervention will be piloted in a rehabilitation hospital. This research has implications for the role of patient measurement in occupational therapy practice and health care practice in general. Through increased use of standardized outcome measures the quality of care will be advanced, patient outcomes will be improved, ultimately improving the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sitting Pivot Transfers in Individuals with a Spinal Cord Injury: Minimizing Upper Extremity Risk Exposure and Maximizing Performance
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; INJURY PREVENTION; JOINTS; MODELISATION; REHABILITATION; SITTING TRANSFERS; SPINAL CORD INJURY; UPPER LIMBS
Abstract-Résumé: Most individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI) who use manual wheelchairs as their primary source of mobility perform sitting pivot transfers (SPTs) numerous times per day. The upper extremity (U/E) is exposed to substantial mechanical/muscular stress while carrying out SPTs that may contribute to the development or perpetuation of secondary U/E impairments. These secondary impairments may reduce functional capacity and hamper societal participation. Surprisingly, SPT tasks have not been extensively studied among long-term manual wheelchair users. Physical and occupational therapists still rely almost exclusively on qualitative measures for the assessment of SPTs. Moreover, SPT techniques taught by therapists during task-specific training still primarily rely on an intuitive hands-on, trial-and-error clinical process influenced by their knowledge, clinical experience and ingenuity. For these reasons, we now propose a comprehensive biomechanical study that aims to identify the most effective and safest SPT technique(s) in 45 individuals with a SCI. More precisely, the proposed project aims (1) to compare U/E mechanical strain, U/E muscular demand and dynamic stability requirement for various SPT techniques performed between surfaces of even and uneven heights, without and with a gap between surfaces and (2) to provide a thorough understanding of the impact of the individual's characteristics on the U/E mechanical strain, U/E muscular demand as well as dynamic stability requirement of SPTs. This highly relevant study will be the first to rigorously assess SPT performance and compare various SPT techniques among a large group of individuals with a SCI. The identification of the best SPT technique and of the best predictors of SPT performance will rapidly translate into clinical practice. In fact, new assessment protocols and innovative therapeutic interventions aimed at minimizing U/E risk exposure and maximizing performance during SPT will be proposed to clinicians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization and Modulation of the Immune Activation during HIV Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUNCT THERAPY; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNITY; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALING; LYMPHOCYTES; MONOCYTES/MACROPHAGES; PKR; PRIMARY HIV INFECTION; WESTERN BLOTS
Abstract-Résumé: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is a disease caused by a virus called the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The patients have a reduced effectiveness of the immune system and become highly susceptible to other infections. About 33.4 million people worldwide are now living with HIV/AIDS. HIV infects vital cells of the human immune system such as lymphocytes. Without lymphocytes, the body cannot fight infections or kill cancerous cells. HIV causes AIDS by directly and indirectly destroying lymphocytes. The bulk of lymphocytes loss occurs during the first weeks of infection, especially in the intestinal mucosa, which harbors the majority of the lymphocytes found in the body. HIV-infected patients are currently treated with antiretroviral therapy (ART), which consists of the use of at least three antiretroviral drugs. ART achieves a remarkable decrease in viral load, leads to recovery of lymphocytes in most individuals, and improves patient life expectancy. However, about 30% of ART treated patients have chronic HIV infection, which results in increased levels of activation, a continuous decline of lymphocytes correlated with disease progression and additional infections. A clinical priority is to discover therapeutic strategies to attenuate chronic immune activation and improve lymphocytes recovery in such individuals. This persistent immune activation might be mediated by microbial products that go from the gastrointestinal tract to the bloodstream and recent data show that treatment with chloroquine, an anti-malaria product, reduces the immune activation in some patients, but its mechanism is not understood. We will evaluate the consequences of HIV infection and stimulation by microbial products on immune activation, the molecular pathways involved and the biological consequences of chloroquine treatment as adjunct therapy. This project should identify more efficient therapeutic strategies to reduce the risks of AIDS.

Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; HIV; HUMAN INNATE IMMUNE SYSTEM; NOVEL ANTIVIRAL THERAPEUTICS; RESTRICTION FACTORS; VIRAL INFECTIVITY FACTOR; VIRAL PATHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: HIV-1 poses a critical threat to humankind all around the world.  The Joint United Nations program on HIV/AIDS and the World Health Organization recognize HIV-1 as a global pandemic, with an estimate of ~2.5 million new HIV-1 infections each year.  In 2005, 16-40% of new HIV-1 infections were resistant to one or more existing forms of antiviral therapy.   There is pressing need for radically different therapeutics.  The infectivity of HIV-1 is largely influenced by a protein called Viral Infectivity Factor (VIF).  This proposed research aims to uncover how VIF counteracts proteins of humans' immune system, specifically the apolipoprotein B mRNA-editing catalytic polypeptide 3 family of proteins.  Our findings will drive the development of novel therapeutic agents that will hinder the spread of HIV among individuals, as well as the progression of HIV to AIDS in infected patients.

The renewal of this CRC will allow the investigation of the impact of these mechanisms in neurological diseases such as stroke, migraine, vascular dementia and epilepsy. TitreApplicationTitle: Appraising local HIV epidemics for prevention strategies: insights from mathematical modeling
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOBAL HEALTH; HIV EPIDEMIOLOGY; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; TRANSMISSION DYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: The global HIV epidemic continues to outpace our response and the world health community is calling for a 'prevention revolution'. Key to our prevention response is an understanding of local HIV epidemics - how they begin and how they persist. But traditional methods of appraising epidemics do not take into account pathways of HIV transmission - that individuals with seemingly several degrees of separation can be linked by current or prior sexual partnerships. The links between people who participate in different sexual activity groups (for example, women or men who sell sex) and their partners' partners and individuals without any apparent direct sexual connection to a higher-risk network, are key to understanding how HIV may spread within a community and how prevention efforts along the pathways can impact on the epidemic as a whole. We recently showed that when applied to Indian districts, results of traditional epidemic appraisals developed by UNAIDS did not coincide with the prevention strategies already in place - strategies developed by local public health teams and community based organizations who understood the sexual structure of the population. We therefore proposed a modified framework based on key transmission pathways observed in India. But how does this framework compare with the traditional methods, and how can it be used rapidly and reliably by policy-makers? We aim to address these questions with the use of mathematical models to simulate observed epidemics at a district-level in India. We will test the short and long-term impact of prevention strategies allocated based on traditional epidemic appraisals as compared with the modified framework. We will then determine the key features of a district that help distinguish local epidemics within the framework so districts may be reliably classified based on where and how prevention resources should be allocated to not only prevent infections in the short-term, but also control the epidemic.

Abstract-Résumé: Retroviruses (e.g. HIV) and retrotransposons constitute a unique threat to human health because they have the capability of stably and permanently integrating their DNA into their hosts genome. This can result in gene disruption and misregulation, which could ultimately lead to disease and death. Also, if integrations occur in the genomic DNA of germinal cells, these retroelements could be passed down to further generations. Luckily our cells express innate restriction factors, such as the APOBEC3 proteins, that help protecting them against these pathogens. My research will focus on determining how these host-encoded restriction factors protect us against retroelements and how, in some instances, these pathogens find ways to get around this innate line of defense.

Abstract-Résumé: Genetic variation among individuals controls many important phenotypic traits, such as susceptibility to disease and complex disorders. We, and many others, have demonstrated that some of the most immediate effects of common genetic variation involve alterations in the regulation of gene expression. More recently, our group has shown that genetic variants affect pre-mRNA splicing, a process which allows the production of several functional products  isoforms  of the same gene. We expect that DNA-level variations that influence splicing will have significant effects on gene function. Our research aims to catalogue, understand, and determine the functional consequences of polymorphisms controlling the splicing process.

Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian population is aging; while individuals aged 65 years or older now constitute 14% of the population, this is projected to increase to 21% by the year 2026. Although seniors of today are healthier and live more independently than seniors of the past, the rates of chronic health problems have been increasing. Health care use (and cost to the health care system) also increase with age. As the senior population grows, it is therefore more important than ever to examine how to promote healthy, active aging into old age. Dr. Menecs research focuses on how the physical and social environment that people live in can promote health and activity participation in later life. The research is designed to help communities become more age-friendly in order to foster healthy, active aging.

Abstract-Résumé: The discovery of antimicrobial agents was one of the great triumphs of the 20th century. In less than 50 years, however, we have moved to the age of antimicrobial resistance which has snowballed into a serious public health problem with immense costs. This Chair program proposes to use powerful genomics methods to identify the factors contributing to drug resistance for a better management of resistant organisms. The Chair research program proposes work with the protozoan parasite Leishmania and the bacteria Streptococcus pneumoniae. These organisms display high levels of resistance and incur great economic and social costs throughout the world.

Abstract-Résumé: This project involves a highly interdisciplinary approach to the study of vision and visually-guided behaviors.  We will use electrophysiological techniques to record the activity of individual neurons, and computational methods to characterize the response properties of these neurons during naturalistic visual stimulation.  The resulting mathematical models will be used to make predictions that can be tested during psychophysical experiments on visual perception and eye movements.  These perceptual results will guide experiments that use transcranial magnetic stimulation to influence brain activity in a manner that will potentially improve visual acuity for clinically relevant populations.

Abstract-Résumé: Neuronal circuit development relies on developmental sculpting of axons, dendrites, and the synaptic connections that link them.  Modern imaging has revealed that neurons continuously add and retract branches throughout development in response to sensory experience and local molecular cues.  This research program will dissect the signaling that remodels neuronal connectivity  by combining electrophysiology and in vivo time-lapse imaging of neuronal development with targeted manipulation of genes involved in neurite outgrowth, synaptogenesis, and synaptic plasticity. Understanding the cellular mechanisms of circuit construction will provide insights into normal development and may suggest approaches for recovery of circuit function after injury in adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving the Pandemic Response in Remote First Nation Communities of Sub-Arctic Ontario Using A Community-based Approach (Including Collaborative Geomatics and Mathematical Modeling)
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATIVE GEOMATICS; COMMUNITY-BASED APPROACH; FIRST NATIONS; H1N1 PANDEMIC; HEALTH SERVICES; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; QUALITATIVE ANALYSES; QUANTITATIVE ANALYSES; SEMI-DIRECTED INTERVIEWS; SUB-ARCTIC
Abstract-Résumé: The 2009 H1N1 pandemic disproportionately affected Canada's First Nation populations living in remote, northern communities, inferring that their unique needs were not being addressed. Existing pandemic plans do not offer many mitigation strategies which are culturally-sensitive and feasible in remote First Nation communities. The proposed Ph.D. research objectives aim to improve the pandemic response capacity by remote First Nation communities by using a community-based approach to ascertain information to create the most feasible, culturally-appropriate, community-level pandemic plans. The first objective is to revise the community-level pandemic plans of three remote First Nation communities of Ontario, Canada (i.e., Fort Albany, Attawapiskat, and Kashechewan), after the anticipated amalgamation of federal and provincial health care services. Secondly, via semi-directed interviews of First Nation-based health care personnel, a list of recommended public health measures specific for remote communities will be created, which can be incorporated into future pandemic plans. Thirdly, using mathematical modeling, the spread of diseases in remote communities will be modeled and the effectiveness of recommended public health interventions will be examined quantitatively. Lastly, collaborative geomatics, a web-based informatics mapping tool with real-time capability, will be adapted specifically for disease monitoring and distribution of information in remote communities. The main outcomes of this study are to empower First Nations by encouraging their involvement and to provide data for community leaders to make informed decisions. These outcomes will have a broader impact by incorporating First Nations' concerns into future pandemic plans, which will assist these and similar communities to be better prepared for the next public health emergency and in turn decrease the impact of communicable diseases and protect the health of Canadian First Nations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Community-based mixed method study of the association between HIV status and Aboriginal self-identification, men who have sex with other men (MSM) behaviour, and sexual scripts within and between Canada and New Zealand
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLE; FOCUS GROUP; HIV AND AIDS; HIV TESTING; INTERVIEWS; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN (MSM); SEXUAL BEHAVIOUR AND ATTITUDES; SEXUAL SCRIPTS; THEMATIC ANALYSIS; TWO-SPIRITED
Abstract-Résumé: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), which leads to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS), is a major global health epidemic with no known cure. Men who have sex with men (MSM) and Aboriginal people were identified as key populations at increased risk of HIV infection in Canada's Federal Initiative to Address HIV/AIDS.   This research will improve the understanding HIV infection and testing, which is needed to support evidence-based prevention programs. The objective of this research is to determine the association between HIV status and Aboriginal self-identification, MSM behaviour, and sexual scripts within and between Canada and New Zealand using quantitative and qualitative methods. The research hypothesizes that Aboriginal MSM compared to non-indigenous MSM and indigenous non-MSM are at increased risk for HIV, have lower HIV testing patterns and engage in more risk sexual script.   This research will use both qualitative and quantitative methods and will be conducted through community-based partnership with indigenous groups. As internationally recommended for studying HIV in minority populations, a behavioural and attitudinal survey will be paired with a participant's biological sample, which will be tested for HIV. Statistical analyses will determine associations between HIV status and factors including sexual behavior, drug use and HIV testing. Participants will also be invited to participate in a confidential interview or focus group, which will be used to determine the sexual scripts for indigenous MSM in each country, which can be used to help understand and predict sexual beheaviour.  Understanding the HIV epidemic in these minority groups at increased risk for HIV infection will provide the necessary foundation for community groups and health care providers to effectively develop and deliver culturally-relevant campaigns, programs and services. Ultimately, this research will contribute to battling the HIV epidemic in Canada and in New Zealand.

TitreApplicationTitle: Caractérisation des protéines de la recombinaison homologue et de la stabilité du génome chez Leishmania infantum
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITES BIOCHIMIQUES; BRCA2; CANCER DU SEIN; CASSURE DOUBLE-BRIN; DMC1; INTERACTIONS MOLECULAIRES; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES; RAD51; RECOMBINAISON HOMOLOGUE; REPARATION DE L'ADN
Abstract-Résumé: L'acide desoxyribonucleique (ADN) possede une structure instable continuellement confrontee a plusieurs menaces qui peuvent atteindre son integrite. C'est pourquoi la cellule a besoin, lors de sa replication, des processus de reparation par lesquels les dommages a l'ADN seront corriges. La recombinaison homologue represente un des systemes de reparation fidele capable de restaurer l'ADN endommage.  Durant mes travaux de maitrise, la purification de BReast CAncer gene 2 (BRCA2)  de Leishmania infantum a ete effectuee et ce, dans le but d'etudier son role et ses interactions avec les autres acteurs essentiels de la recombinaison homologue dont RAD51 et DMC1. Notons que la taille de BRCA2 chez l'humain est tres grosse et sa purification est tres complexe. La necessite d'isoler une BRCA2 plus petite dans un autre organisme vient alors justifier l'utilisation du parasite Leishmania infantum qui possede une BRCA2 trois fois plus petite que celle de l'humain. En fait, l'etude de BRCA2 est essentielle pour une meilleure comprehension de la reponse aux cassures double-brin qui se produit dans les cancers. En considerant le fait que BRCA2 est impliquee dans dix pourcent des cancers du sein provenant de causes hereditaires, cette proteine represente une cible ideale dans l'etablissement de strategies pour contrecarrer la progression de la maladie. De meme que selon des etudes epidemiologiques, il y aurait deux millions de nouveaux cas de leishmaniose par annee pour un total de 12 millions de personnes infectees dans le monde. En caracterisant bien les principaux acteurs de la recombinaison homologue necessaires a la replication de Leishmania infantum, il sera possible d'inhiber sa reproduction et ainsi limiter les cas de leishmaniose chez nos soldats canadiens. Mes objectifs pour le doctorat seront d'etudier structurellement et fonctionnellement la proteine BRCA2 a travers ses relations sequentielles entre les principaux elements de la recombinaison homologue.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sucrose-Fed Model of Gestational Insulin Resistance: Mechanism, Modulation and Impact on Pregnant Rat
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; ANTI-OXIDANT COCKTAIL; EUGLYCEMIC CLAMP; GESTATIONAL DIABETES; HEPATIC INSULIN SENSITIZING SUBSTANCE (HISS); INSULIN RESISTANCE; METABOLIC SYNDROME; RAPID INSULIN SENSITIVITY TEST (RIST)
Abstract-Résumé: Pre-diabetes in pregnancy is a natural phenomenon that only results in diabetes if the insulin levels are incapable of regulating post-meal blood sugars. Diabetes in pregnancy causes increased risk to mother and fetus for development of diabetes and obesity, as well as long-term health complications for the mother (high blood pressure, blindness, limb loss, etc). The pre-diabetic state in pregnancy is resistance to the hormone insulin, which is proposed to be related to a recently characterized molecule called Hepatic Insulin Sensitizing Substance (HISS). This condition is typified by the inability of muscle to respond to insulin, creating a state whereby nutrients are converted to and stored as fat in fatty areas (instead of sugar chains in muscle). In normal animals both a high sugar diet and chronic alcohol consumption result in insulin resistance due to HISS. The impact of a high sugar diet will be examined for its effect on a pregnant female rat (using a metabolic blood sugar test) and pregnancy outcomes (such as fetal loss and pup number). By studying an animal model of diabetes in pregnancy, the mechanism of this pregnancy-induced pre-diabetes may be understood. An antioxidant cocktail S-adenosyl methionine, Vitamin E and Vitamin C (Samec) shown to additively protect against diet-induced insulin resistance associated with the HISS molecule will be tested on the pregnant females to see if it is able to prevent and/or treat diabetes during pregnancy.  Samec will present a novel therapeutic in the treatment of diabetes in pregnancy and these studies will determine the suitability of a randomized control trial in the pregnant population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Public Health Interventions and Unintended Harm:  A Theoretical Framework for Intervention Evaluation and Knowledge Translation.
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOBAL HEALTH; INTERVENTIONS; META-ANALYSIS; MIXED METHODS; PUBLIC HEALTH; SCOPING REVIEW; THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK; UNINTENDED HARM; WHO PRESUMPTIVE TREATMENT OF MALARIA POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: Public health interventions are designed to improve health and reduce health inequalities.  Despite good intentions and the historical premise that public health interventions are acceptable as long as they do good in general, evidence of harmful unintended consequences are emerging in a number of public health areas.  Consequently, it is now important that interventions demonstrate proven benefits that outweigh any potential harms.  The difficulty is that harm as related to public health interventions is not well defined, with harm evaluation and reporting often absent or incomplete.    This research responds to this problem by developing a new framework that will guide public health professionals and researchers when identifying, evaluating and communicating intervention-related unintended harms.  Design and evaluation of a framework to assist researchers and public health professionals is an important step towards the reduction of unintended harms for all.  This framework will be an important advance and will provide a starting point for future research as it is employed in a variety of settings to anticipate or evaluate unintended harm associated with public health interventions.  The framework designed by this research will be useful for interventions implemented in Canada, especially for aboriginal communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering the function of alpha B-crystallin in oligodendrocytes and its possible role in multiple sclerosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA B-CRYSTALLIN; CELL CULTURE; DEMYELINATION; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; IMMUNOLOGY; LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; OLIGODENDROCYTE; TUNEL STAINING; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Canada has one of the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) worldwide. MS is a neurological disease in which self-reactive immune cells target and destroy oligodendrocytes. Oligodendrocytes produce myelin that insulates and supports neurons in the central nervous system (CNS). Studies suggest that prolonged oligodendrocyte injury and death may contribute to neuron degeneration. Therefore, oligodendrocyte protection and replacement are fundamental issues in MS to enhance therapy and disease perception. Alpha B-crystallin (alphaBC) is the highest up-regulated gene in oligodendrocytes and other CNS cells in active MS lesions. Also, the level of alphaBC increases as oligodendrocytes mature and myelinate. AlphaBC is a small heat shock protein that possesses a number of protective functions including pro-survival and anti-neurotoxic. Studies have shown that alphaBC promotes the survival of other CNS cells such as astrocytes and suppresses symptoms of the animal model of MS known as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. We hypothesize that alphaBC may modulate the maturation, myelination and/or survival of oligodendrocytes. To investigate the role of alphaBC in myelination by oligodendrocytes the immune-mediated demyelinating agent, lysophosphatidylcholine, will be injected into the spinal cord of normal wild-type mice and mice lacking the alphaBC protein. The myelin content within the injured area will be quantified post-injection to analyze the demyelination and remyelination process. The number of immune cells as well as immature and mature oligodendrocytes will also be measured post-injection. The survival capability of oligodendrocytes is a crucial concern in MS research. Cell survival will be assessed in mature oligodendrocytes from normal wild-type and alphaBC-deficient mice that are grown in the presence of tumor necrosis factor to mimic the MS environment. This research will solidify a role for alphaBC in oligodendrocyte function and multiple sclerosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Electrophysiological and Regulatory Properties of Voltage Gated Calcium Channels in The Cerebral Vasculature
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM CHANNELS; CEREBRAL ARTERIES; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; STROKE; VASOSPASM
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease and stroke are leading causes of death in Canada. Six percent of all annual deaths in Canada are due to stroke. Blood flow in the brain is mediated through a network of blood vessels. The tone of these vessels (cerebral arteries) is controlled by factors arising from changes in tissue metabolism, nerve activity, blood flow and pressure. The ability of arteries to narrow in response to such stimuli depends on the availability of calcium ions inside the cells. Extracellular calcium enters the cells through cell membrane proteins that only allow the passage of this particular ion. Given the importance of calcium channels, it is essential to define the events that control these particular proteins in health and disease. Indeed, inadequate function of calcium channels during stroke and vessel spasm gives rise to devastating problems in brain function.  Recent reports, including our own, have highlighted the possibility that there is a new unknown type of calcium channels (T-type) in brain arteries. Using a range of physiological and biochemical techniques, we plan to investigate the role of these newly identified calcium channels in cerebral arteries. More specifically, this study will carefully distinguish the different types of calcium channels and define which signals control their biological functions. Through knowledge building, this work will help advance new therapeutic strategies that could potentially alleviate the debilitating effects of cerebral vessel dysfunction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating relationships among RAI-MDS quality indicators for residents in long-term care
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTINUING CARE; ELDER CARE; FOCUS GROUP; LONG-TERM CARE; MULTIVARIATE ANALYSIS; QUALITY INDICATORS; QUALITY OF CARE; RAI-MDS 2.0; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: The care that older adults receive in nursing homes has been a serious concern for many reasons.  One reason is that, until relatively recently, there was no standard for assessing nursing home residents and documenting the care that they receive. In many nursing homes, only minimal records were kept of the care given to residents. One major initiative to improve resident care has been to standardize approaches to assessing nursing home residents. In Canada, a single assessment tool is mandatory in most jurisdictions, called the Resident Assessment Instrument, or RAI version 2.0. The RAI 2.0 instrument collects information on the resident, allowing providers to develop comprehensive plans to provide care. RAI 2.0 data is also used to compare care across nursing homes by combining RAI 2.0 information for all residents within a unit or facility to construct 25 quality indicators. Quality indicators provide information on certain resident health characteristics that can be affected by the quality of care provided by that facility. For example, one RAI 2.0 quality indicator is the proportion of residents in a facility with pain. Past research has shown that presenting a long list of quality indicator scores to care providers does not always change the quality of care. The reason for this is partly because the large number of quality indicators makes it difficult to decide which quality area to focus on and invest resources into. I propose to address this problem by developing statistical quality indicator models that show which indicators influence each other and by how much. My work will illustrate which indicators may have the greatest influence on the quality of life of nursing home residents. It will also assist decision-makers such as unit managers to determine priorities among indicators. My research will contribute to our understanding of how the information from RAI 2.0 can be used to improve the care that nursing home residents receive.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endothelial progenitor cells in heart failure patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIAL PROGENITOR CELLS; FUNCTIONAL CAPACITY; HEART FAILURE; MORTALITY; PROGNOSIS; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a serious and common disease in Canada. The adequate management of patients with heart failure relies on appropiate prognostic assessments and adequate treatment. Despite the diverse availability of prognostic markers,  the progression of this disease is difficult to predict. Therefore, new factors associated to disease stage need to be identified in order to optimize the clinical management of these patients. In the past decade, the existence of bone marrow-derived cells in peripheral blood has been demonstrated. These cells are capable of forming new vessels and repairing dysfunctional ones. These cells have received the name "endothelial progenitor cells". In patients with ischemic heart disease, these cells are associated with the number of cardiovascular risk factors, disease severity and mortality. These findings have opened alternative lanes to understand the complex mechanisms of heart failure and identify new prognostic markers and therapeutic targets. As such, this research proposal will evaluate the relationship between endothelial progenitor cells and clinical characteristics and outcomes in patients with heart failure. Hence, we will explore whether there is an association between the levels of these cells and the functional capacity in 140 patients with heart failure seen at the Toronto General Hospital. Functional capacity will be measured through an exercise test known as a cardiopulmonary study. In addition, we will analyze whether an association exists between the levels of endothelial progenitor cells and outcomes in patients with heart failure. As outcomes, we will evaluate death, heart transplantation, mechanical heart implantation, the development of potentially lethal arrhythmias and hospital admissions due to decompensated heart failure. Our study will help to better characterize the association between these cells and heart failure stage and potentially identify new prognostic markers and therapeutic options.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Shared Neurobiology of Autism and Fragile X Syndrome through the Neuroligin Gene Family
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL NEUROSCIENCE; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MOLECULAR NEUROBIOLOGY; NEURODEVELOPMENT DISEASE; PATCH CLAMP PHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) are characterized by impairments in social interaction, communication, and repetitive behaviour. The impact of ASDs on individuals and their families is life-changing. Diagnosis has risen considerably in the last 20 years, yet very little is known about this complex disorder. The annual costs related to caring for a patient is up to five times the amount for an individual without the disease. The lifetime public expenditure per patient is in the millions of dollars. Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited mental disorder. Studies report that 25% of males and 6% of females with Fragile X have a form of ASD. Understanding the reasons behind the overlap between these two disorders will be key to improving our understanding of both conditions and greatly enhance the development of treatment. This study will examine brain development in mouse models of these two disorders. The two models are the valproic-acid (VPA) model of autism and the Fragile X knockout. When pregnant mothers (both human and mouse) are exposed to VPA, their offspring's behaviour mimics the symptoms of autism. In the latter model, the mice lack the same protein that is lacking in human cases of Fragile X. In these mice, I will examine molecules that regulate signalling between brain cells that are risk genes for ASDs. Disruptions in these molecules change the connectivity between cells, resulting in impairments in behaviour. Using techniques to determine when brain circuitry matures, I will compare these mouse brains during the first month of development, which correlates to the period of infancy and childhood in humans. This study will address how connectivity in the brain occurs, which is a component implicated in developmental brain disorders. Understanding this is paramount in our knowledge of what causes these two disorders and for developing new therapeutic targets, allowing improvements to the current treatment regimes for these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hope-Focused Group Interventions for People Limited by Chronic Pain: A Grounded Theory Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUSTMENT TO CHRONIC PAIN; CHRONIC PAIN; GROUNDED THEORY; GROUP THERAPY; HOPE FOCUSED INTERVENTIONS; INTERPERSONAL PROCESS RECALL
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain can impose significant limitations on one's ability to engage in day-to-day activities. Undeniably, it is difficult for people to accept that pain may become a permanent part of their reality, and a lot of energy is invested seeking a cure for their pain. Unfortunately, the needed technology to resolve pain is often unavailable. Incurable pain that impairs a person's ability to function in daily life can result in feelings of despair and hopelessness. Tang and Crane (2006) report that up to 50 percent of people participating in chronic pain support groups have seriously contemplated suicide due to difficulties coping with pain and related challenges.  Although hope-focused psychotherapy interventions are expected to provide broader possibilities for achieving desired and meaningful futures for those limited by pain, there are currently no studies on the experiences of people participating in such therapeutic groups.  This study will explore clients' experiences of a hope-focused therapy group with particular attention to participants' individual accounts of hope. The results of this study will contribute to the research literature on psychotherapy, may be used to enhance therapeutic practice, and will benefit other care professionals working with people who experience chronic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Étude des processus mnésiques sous-tendus par le cortex préfrontal qui contribuent aux déficits de la mémoire dans la schizophrénie.
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTEX PREFRONTAL; IMAGERIE PAR RESONNANCE MAGNETIQUE FONCTIONNELLE; MEMOIRE DE TRAVAIL; MEMOIRE EPISODIQUE; SCHIZOPHRENIE
Abstract-Résumé: Une personne sur cent recevra un diagnostic de schizophrenie au cours de sa vie et les couts directs de cette maladie au Canada sont estimes a 2,35 milliards de dollars par annee (Societe Canadienne de la Schizophrenie).   Il est maintenant bien etabli que la schizophrenie est associee a plusieurs troubles cognitifs. De plus, les schizophrenes qui possedent de plus fortes habiletes cognitives demontrent une meilleure evolution de la maladie et ont plus de chances de bien s'integrer a la societe. Il est donc primordial de bien comprendre ces deficits cognitifs et d'etudier les processus cerebraux qui les sous-tendent.   La memoire est un des processus cognitifs les plus affectes dans la maladie. Les deficits de memoire sont aussi de meilleurs indicateurs du fonctionnement dans la communaute et des habiletes psychosociales des patients que les autres dysfonctions cognitives et symptomes cliniques. Mes recherches porteront donc sur l'etude des processus neuronaux qui sont associes aux troubles de la memoire dans la schizophrenie. Nous comparerons l'activite cerebrale deployee lors de la realisation de taches de memorisation dans un groupe de schizophrenes, avec celle observee dans un groupe controle. Nous ferons aussi des liens entre les deficits observes et les symptomes presents chez les patients.  Les resultats que nous pourrons tirer de cette etude nous permettront d'ameliorer nos connaissances quant a l'activite cerebrale reliee aux troubles de la memoire presents dans la schizophrenie. Une contribution plus importante encore des resultats consiste au fait qu'ils permettront la mise en place de techniques de therapies cognitives plus efficaces et le developpement de nouvelles methodes d'intervention. Ils permettront aussi de cibler les regions d'interet dans le cadre des traitements deja existants qui stimulent directement les regions du cerveau reliees au mauvais fonctionnement des processus cognitifs concernes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effets neurotoxiques du méthylmercure et des biphényles polychlorés sur l'attention visuospatiale : une étude électrophysiologique réalisée chez des enfants inuits du Nunavik
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION VISUOSPATIALE; BIPHENYLES POLYCHLORES; CONTAMINANTS ENVIRONNEMENTAUX; ENFANT; INUIT; METHYLMERCURE; PROCESSUS CEREBRAUX; PERIODE POSTNATALE; PERIODE PRENATALE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGIE
Abstract-Résumé: Les Inuits du Nunavik se nourrissent principalement d'aliments issus de la peche, s'exposant ainsi quotidiennement a de fortes concentrations de methylmercure (MeHg) et de biphenyles polychlores (BPCs), presents dans le poisson et les mammiferes marins. La communaute inuite est ainsi l'une des plus exposees aux contaminants environnementaux en Amerique du Nord. Cette exposition est particulierement preoccupante pour les enfants inuits dont le cerveau en developpement est plus sensible aux agents toxiques. Plusieurs etudes ont identifie chez l'enfant des difficultes attentionnelles associees a l'exposition pre et postnatale au MeHg et aux BPCs. Toutefois, les processus cerebraux de l'attention qui sont affectes par les contaminants demeurent a ce jour inconnu.  La disponibilite des donnees d'exposition des enfants inuits, de la periode prenatale a l'adolescence, fait de cette etude longitudinale une opportunite exceptionnelle pour examiner les effets a long terme des contaminants environnementaux sur le fonctionnement du cerveau. L'objectif principal de mon projet de doctorat est d'identifier les alterations dans le traitement cerebral qui sont causees par les contaminants et qui sont a l'origine des deficits d'attention repandus dans la communaute inuite. L'electrophysiologie est une technique non-invasive qui me permettra d'enregistrer l'activite cerebrale des enfants inuits durant une tache attentionnelle. L'identification des processus cerebraux affectes s'avere essentielle pour developper des interventions appropriees chez les jeunes inuits qui presentent des difficultes d'attention.  Les hauts niveaux d'exposition au MeHg et aux BPCs du Nunavik constituent une preoccupation majeure de sante publique. Ce projet est d'une grande importance pour la sante et le developpement des enfants du Nunavik, mais egalement ceux du reste du Canada qui sont eux aussi exposes aux contaminants a des niveaux variables.

TitreApplicationTitle: Asymétrie locomotrice réelle et perçue lors de différentes conditions sur tapis roulant chez le sujet hémiparétique.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASYMETRIE LOCOMOTRICE; BIOMECANIQUE; HEMIPARETIQUE; PERCEPTION DE L'EFFORT; PHYSIOTHERAPIE; READAPTATION; ELECTROMYOGRAPHIE
Abstract-Résumé: Le vieillissement de la population est associe a une croissance des maladies et de leurs consequences. Chaque annee, quelques 50 000 Canadiens sont victimes d'un accident vasculaire cerebral (AVC) et plusieurs d'entre eux ont des deficits persistants (hemiparesie, problemes d'equilibre et sensitifs, fatigue, etc) qui les empechent d'executer efficacement leurs activites quotidiennes et d'etre socialement actifs. La difficulte a marcher est caracterisee par une diminution de la vitesse de marche, de l'endurance et une asymetrie dans l'execution du mouvement. Rares sont les chercheurs qui ont tente d'expliquer l'asymetrie (difference entre les deux jambes) des personnes hemiparetiques autrement qu'en la liant aux deficits physiques  (faiblesse musculaire, perte de sensibilite, etc.). De recents travaux suggerent que les personnes hemiparetiques utilisent l'asymetrie pour rendre semblables les efforts a produire aux deux membres inferieurs. Le present projet vise, d'une part, a etudier les effets de differentes conditions de marche sur tapis roulant instrumente a double courroie sur l'asymetrie reelle et percue du patron de marche chez le sujet hemiparetique et a en etudier les liens avec les efforts produits au niveau des deux jambes. D'autre part, il vise aussi a tester chez un petit groupe de sujets hemiparetiques un entrainement visant a reduire l'asymetrie locomotrice. Trente sujets ayant une hemiparesie consecutive a un AVC seront recrutes pour la premiere partie de l'etude et un sous-groupe de 15 sujets fera l'entrainement experimental. Ces personnes seront evaluees cliniquement et en laboratoire avec des equipements a la fine pointe de la technologie. A notre connaissance, aucune etude n'a evalue de facon aussi explicite l'asymetrie lors de diverses conditions (differentes vitesses, marche prolongee etc.). Ces etudes nous guideront vers de nouvelles pistes de traitement afin d'ameliorer le succes de la readaptation a reduire l'asymetrie locomotrice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Visual-Auditory Connectivity After Deafness
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY CORTEX; COCHLEAR IMPLANT; CONNECTIVITY; CROSS-MODAL; DEAFNESS; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEUROPLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: The capacity of the brain to change itself provides countless advantages in human adaptation. This potential, known as neuroplasticity, can also be disadvantageous when it interferes with rehabilitation after sensory loss, as can occur with the restoration of hearing in deaf people through cochlear implantation. After deafness, the brain can become re-wired so that vision is processed in the auditory cortex, a region of the brain that normally responds to sound. Our research will use state-of-the-art neuroimaging techniques to examine how visual information reaches the auditory cortex of deaf people, how these connections are different between deaf and hearing people, and the impact of these differences on the ability to hear with a cochlear implant. By better understanding the neuroplasticity associated with deafness, this research advances our basic knowledge of brain organization. This knowledge can be applied to improving procedures for cochlear implantation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adiposité cardiaque et facteurs de risques cardio-métabolique liés à l'obésité ou au diabète de type 2: rôle du gras épicardique
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOKINES; COMPOSITION CORPORELLE; CULTURE CELLULAIRE; DIABETE DE TYPE 2; EXERCICE PHYSIQUE; GRAS EPICARDIQUE; OBESITE; RESTRICTION CALORIQUE; RISQUE CARDIO-METABOLIQUE; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIE
Abstract-Résumé: Le nombre de personnes souffrant d'exces de poids et de diabete de type 2 (DT2) est en progression constante au Canada. Cela constitue un fardeau tres couteux pour le systeme de sante publique. En effet, l'obesite augmente le risque de maladies chroniques telles que le DT2,  l'hypertension et les maladies cardiaques, que l'on regroupe sous le terme de « risque cardio-metabolique ». Par ailleurs, le DT2 augmente les risques de maladies cardiaques. Il est maintenant urgent de trouver des methodes efficaces qui permettent d'identifier rapidement les personnes obeses qu'elles soient, diabetiques ou non, et qui sont a risque de developper des complications. Le gras retrouve autour des organes de l'abdomen (gras visceral) est un excellent indicateur du risque cardio-metabolique chez la personne obese diabetique ou non. Il en est de meme pour le gras retrouve dans le foie (gras hepatique). Mais, les methodes existante pour mesurer ce gras sont soit invasives (biopsie du foie) ou comportent des risques lies a la sante du patient (exposition au rayon X lors de l'examen de tomographie axiale pour la mesure du gras visceral) ou coutent trop cheres pour etre utilisees comme examen de routine. Des equipes de chercheurs ont suggere que l'epaisseur du gras autour du cur (gras epicardique) mesuree par echographie simplifiee pourrait etre un bon indicateur de risque des maladies liees a l'obesite ou au DT2 et pourrait donc remplacer certaines methodes plus invasives. Le but de notre projet est de tester cette hypothese. Pour ce faire, nous proposons trois etudes incluant une avec deux programmes d'intervention de 4 mois axes sur la diete et l'exercice physique chez les personnes obeses diabetiques ou non. A la fin du projet, nous obtiendrons un outil de prediction simple et valide. Son utilisation permettra d'identifier plus tot les sujets a risque de developper des complications incluant les maladies cardiaques liees a l'obesite ou au DT2, et donc de les traiter plus rapidement.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation du système d'inhibition intracortical GABAergique chez l'athlète commotionné
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMOTIONS CEREBRALES; CORTEX MOTEUR; INHIBITION INTRACORTICALE; NEUROPHYSIOLOGIE; SPECTROSCOPIE PAR RESONANCE MAGNETIQUE; STIMULATION MAGNETIQUE TRANSCRANIENNE; TRANSMISSION GABAERGIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: Le phenomene des commotions cerebrales dans les sports prend de plus en plus d'importance tant dans la communaute scientifique que dans les medias. En effet, cet engouement est du au fait qu'il y a de plus en plus d'etudes qui demontrent les effets deleteres des commotions cerebrales. Il est donc primordial de bien comprendre leur impact sur le cerveau afin de mettre sur pied des programmes de sensibilisation aupres de la population geerale et ce, particulierement aupres des jeunes qui ne sont pas toujours conscients de la gravite des consequences que ces blessures peuvent engendrer au niveau cerebral. Par ailleurs, une meilleure comprehension des alterations qui peuvent survenir suite a celles-ci pourra permettre d'etablir des programmes de rehabilitation et des traitements mieux adaptes.  Suite a une commotion cerebrale, les troubles moteurs, tels que des troubles de l'equilibre et de la coordination, font partie des principaux symptomes qui tendent a persister. Malgre le fait que ceux-ci tendent a se resorber apres quelques semaines, des etudes ont demontre que de legeres alterations persistent plusieurs mois apres l'incident. Il semblerait meme que les effets deleteres des commotions cerebrales se font ressentir des decennies apres ce dernier. En effet, de recentes etudes suggerent que les personnes qui ont subi une commotion cerebrale ont onze fois plus de chances de developper la sclerose laterale amyotrophique, une malade degenerative qui affecte specifiquement les cellules des regions motrices du cerveau. Ainsi, le but de la presente etude est d'investiguer les effets a long terme des commotions cerebrales sur les regions motrices du cerveau chez des jeunes athletes de niveau universitaire qui ne presentent aucun symptome. A l'aide de techniques d'imagerie medicale a la fine pointe de la technologie, nous allons evaluer s'il y a presence d'alterations au niveau des interactions entre les neurotransmetteurs au sein des regions motrices.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Lipid Phosphate Phosphatases in Attenuating Cancer Cell Survival and Migration
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRAL VECTORS; APOPTOSIS; CHEMORESISTANCE; CHEMOTHERAPY; CONFOCAL ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; LIPID PHOSPHATE PHOSPHATASES; LYSOPHOSPHATIDATE; LYSOPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE; REVERSE-TRANSCRIPTASE PCR; WESTERN BLOTS
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common malignancy in Canadian women and about a third of women will develop metastases and die, despite treatment by both surgery and chemotherapy. This is explained in two ways. First, cancer cells spread (metastasize) to other organs and establish secondary tumors.  Second, the ability to treat patients and kill cancer cells with chemotherapeutic agents is compromised by the development of resistance to these agents through the activation of cell survival signals by bioactive signaling molecules.  Hence, there is an urgent need to identify the signal pathways that lead to these problems. Such molecules are known to be degraded by a group of three lipid mediators called lipid phosphate phosphatases (LPPs). It has been hypothesized that abnormal expression levels of LPPs make cancer cells hypersensitive to the signal effects of bioactive signaling molecules, promoting tumor growth.  However, the relative function of the three LPPs in attenuating cancer cell survival signaling is poorly understood. To study these roles, I will alter LPP activity in breast cancer cell lines to determine how these changes modify the activation of cell survival signals that are normally upregulated in cancer cells and the ability to kill the cancer cells upon treatment of common chemotherapeutic drugs. Overall, this knowledge should help to develop new strategies and treatments for improving the effectiveness of surgery and chemotherapy, particularly for cancers that show resistance to conventional treatment regiments. These developments should lead to increased survival rates and cures for cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: External validity of the cold pressor task in pediatric pain research.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE PAIN; CHILDREN; CLINICAL PAIN; EXPERIMENTAL METHODS; EXPERIMENTAL PAIN; EXTERNAL VALIDITY; PEDIATRIC PAIN
Abstract-Résumé: The cold pressor task (CPT) is a commonly used experimental method of inducing pain requiring a child to submerse his/her hand or forearm in cold water for as long as can be tolerated, lasting several minutes. Use of the CPT has led to numerous critical advances in our understanding of children's pain. Lab-based methods, such as the CPT, are particularly valuable because they provide greater control over the environment, allowing researchers to investigate important research questions that cannot be adequately addressed in a clinical setting. Although the CPT is thought to produce pain similar to that of a medical procedure such as a needle, the extent to which this lab-based task produces a similar experience to clinical pain has surprisingly never been tested. To address this knowledge gap, the proposed study will examine the extent to which pain experienced by a child during a lab-based CPT corresponds to their pain experiences during a Hepatitis B immunization received during a school-based clinic. It will also determine whether child characteristics known to negatively impact pain experience (e.g., sex, anxiety, medical fears, previous pain experiences, coping style) have a similar impact on pain in both contexts. One hundred children (50% boys) aged 12-14 years will be video-recorded completing the CPT and the immunization. Children will report on the intensity, unpleasantness, and quality of their pain. Behavioural and physiological indicators of pain will also be obtained. Children and parents will complete questionnaires to assess the influence of child characteristics on the child's pain experiences. This study will contribute critically to our understanding of how well knowledge obtained from CPT studies can inform us about children's pain experiences in clinical contexts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intestinal microbiota and child health: Does supplemental feeding, improved environmental hygiene and sanitation in resource limited settings improve child growth by restoring the composition of microbes in the human intestine and preserving the intestinal barrier?
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD GROWTH; INFANT HEALTH; INTESTINAL MICROBIOTA; TROPICAL ENTEROPATHY
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Early childhood under nutrition significantly reduces child growth, resulting in poor mental and physical development, and causes about one-third of under-5-year mortality worldwide. Supplementary feeding and sanitation/hygiene interventions only reduce impaired growth by 30% and 2.4%, respectively.  Tropical enteropathy (TE) is another potential contributor. In TE, the small bowel surface area decreases and the gut wall becomes 'leaky', allowing microbes to enter the bloodstream. In addition to decreasing nutrient absorption, these changes may result in chronic immune activation, which may impair child growth by diverting resources needed for growth to immune stimulation. The assembly and composition of intestinal microbiota (micro-organisms that live normally in the intestine) is thought to be critical to the development of TE and to growth. Methods: We will test the hypothesis that poor child growth is the result of: altered intestinal microbiota, development of TE, decreased nutrient absorption, a 'leaky gut', and growth-suppressing immune stress. We will test this in the context of the ZVITAMBO trial. ZVITAMBO is a cluster-randomized trial of 2,800 non-HIV-exposed infants in Zimbabwe. It aims to determine whether TE is prevented in infants by household sanitation, complementary feeding, or both. Fecal and blood samples will be collected from a random subsample of 600 infants at 3, 6, 12, and 18 months. To test the causal pathway, changes to the microbiota will be characterized from stool specimens using DNA sequencing methods. Biological markers of immune response (calprotectin in feces) and intestinal microbes in the blood (serum endotoxin) will also be measured. A 'leaky' gut will be defined by measures of intestinal permeability and absorptive capacity of the bowel. A more meaningful understanding of the causal pathway leading to growth impairment in infants may have profound implications for improving child health and quality of life worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: The neural basis of first-language loss in minority-language speakers who are dominant in their second language: New light on the Critical Period Hypothesis
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE EFFECTS IN LANGUAGE ACQUISITION; BILINGUAL BRAIN; BILINGUALISM; BRAIN PLASTICITY; CRITICAL PERIOD HYPOTHESIS; EVENT-RELATED POTENTIALS; FIRST LANGUAGE ATTRITION; NEUROLINGUISTICS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; SECOND LANGUAGE ACQUISITION
Abstract-Résumé: In a linguistically and culturally diverse country such as Canada, second language learning is an extremely relevant topic for many of us. The idea that there may be an optimal period early in life for successful language learning is one that many bilingual speakers are intuitively familiar with, based on their own experience. It follows that one's mother tongue seems to be "privileged", whereas bilingual speakers' proficiency level in a language acquired at a later age typically falls short of being "native-like", especially in complex and subtle aspects of grammar.  The question of whether such a neurobiological "critical period" exists is the subject of much controversy in language research. There is unresolved debate about how age of acquisition and other environmental factors affect the way the human brain organizes and processes a second language compared to the mother tongue.   Minority-language speakers are a unique group of second language learners, as they experience reduced exposure and practice with their minority-status mother tongue in favour of the more widely-spoken second language. This unique population of bilinguals, though considerably prevalent in our Canadian society, is largely under-investigated and allows us to clarify the controversial notion of an early critical period for language acquisition.  Using highly sensitive electrophysiological measures of brain activity, this innovative research investigates how language-related brain processes change in cases where a late-learned second language becomes increasingly stronger than one's mother tongue acquired in infancy. Are minority-language speakers still native-like in their first language, even despite their "loss" of proficiency in this language? Or is early language exposure not sufficient to guarantee native-like processing, making them more native-like in their more proficient second language? In other words, could their second language replace their mother tongue in their brain?

TitreApplicationTitle: Unravel the silence within: probing the initial steps of endoRNAi
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; C.ELEGANS; ENDORNAI; GENE REGULATION; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; RNA INTERFERENCE; RNA-DEPENDENT-RNA-POLYMERASE
Abstract-Résumé: Nucleic acids, such as DNA and RNA, have been known since the 1950s for their roles as carriers of genetic information. In the 1990s, a ground-breaking discovery revealed that nucleic acids, such as certain kinds of RNA, can play a much more active role in the control of genetic information. Indeed, a new class of tiny nucleic acids later named small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) can shut down the expression of genes. It is now known that a group of related mechanisms, altogether termed RNAi, plays a major role in development, and is required for the healthy maintenance of genetic material in living cells of all animals. The discovery of RNAi opened an entire new field of biology. siRNAs and the related nucleic acids microRNAs, are absolutely essential for a wealth of normal biological processes, but they are also deeply implicated in the genetic alterations that occur in cancers. As such, RNAi represents a potential therapy for many kinds of diseases, as one can use RNAi to target ''bad'' genes, but it also represents a new aspect of the biology waiting to be explored.   This project relates to one such phenomenon, named endoRNAi, where siRNAs are produced from many of the genes in animals, and converge back onto that gene to shut it down. We now know that an important fraction of genes in animals are subject to such a phenomenon, but how this process happens, and how the target genes are chosen is completely unknown. With this project, I will study the different mechanisms responsible for the production of siRNAs in endoRNAi, and find what defines the very first steps of their production using various molecular approaches, and a powerful model organism named C. elegans.  This work will bring us closer to understanding this new class of small interfering RNAs and their role in biology. It will also improve the knowledge we have of this new field of biology that opened with the discovery of these nucleic acids.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating axon guidance by Shh at the midline of the visual system and spinal cord
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; CANCER; LKB1; MODEL ORGANISM; NOTCH; PEUTZ-JEGHER SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a disease that starts when our cells divide inappropriately, often because they have lost an essential "tumour suppressor" gene that normally keeps them from dividing. An example of a tumour suppressor is LKB1, a gene which is lost in patients with Peutz-Jegher syndrome, who are 100 times more likely to get cancer during their lifetime compared to the average person. Understanding how these tumour suppressor genes work will enable us to develop newer, more effective treatment methods for cancer.  Because of practical and ethical constraints, it is often easier to study these genes in another organism. Because all animals are evolutionarily related, about 80% of human cancer genes are found even in an animal like C. elegans, a microscopic worm! In C. elegans, loss of LKB1 means that they have trouble remaining in a dormant larval stage. While all the cells in normal worms stop dividing during this dormant stage, some cells divide inappropriately in worms that lose the LKB1 gene.  Because C. elegans is a small animal that reproduces very quickly, we can use various genetics techniques to go through each gene and ask whether their loss results in the same inappropriate division of cells. This way, we can find genes that work alongside or directly with LKB1, both in worms and humans too. Increasing our understanding of how cancer genes function is the first step into one day finding a cure!

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards detection of grey matter lesions in multiple sclerosis using high-field magnetic resonance imaging techniques
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; HIGH-FIELD MRI; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NEURODEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a debilitating neurological disease that affects between 55,000 and 75,000 Canadians; moreover, Canada's prevalence of MS is among the highest in the world. Currently, diagnosis of MS and monitoring of disease status rely on Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) techniques to visualize disease-induced damage in the white matter of the brain. However, this damage does not correspond well with the observed clinical symptoms. Post-mortem observations indicate that damage in the grey matter of the brain is a better indicator of disease status. Unfortunately, there are currently no efficient methods to visualize this grey matter damage. The goal of this project is to develop methods by which gray matter damage can be quantified using MRI. We will optimize MRI techniques that are sensitive to microscopic changes in tissue that are characteristic of MS. Following this, we will apply these techniques in a cohort of patients who may have MS. The ability to visualize grey matter damage would facilitate an earlier diagnosis of MS earlier than is presently possible. Drugs exist that can dramatically improve the quality of life of MS patients. An earlier diagnosis would allow these drugs to be initiated earlier on in the course of the disease, thus delaying severe disability by years. These methods could also be used to better classify patients with MS, allowing for improved patient management. The total cost of just the drugs for the existing MS population in Canada is a staggering 88-120 billion (2007) dollars. The findings of our research will help clinicians to make more informed decisions regarding when and at what dosage drugs should be administered. This has the potential to save the health care system billions of dollars.
