TitreApplicationTitle: The Implementation and Evaluation of an Alberta Childhood Asthma Clinical Pathway.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; CHILDHOOD; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; WEB-BASED TEACHING MODULES
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is the most common chronic disease in children. Unfortunately many children do not receive optimal therapy based on best evidence. One way to optimize management is to develop clinical pathways which help guide clinicians. A provincial clinical pathway for the management of chronic and acute childhood asthma is being developed. We propose a three year project to implement the asthma pathway in two former Alberta health regions (Peace Country and Palliser) and evaluate its overall impact.   Our specific objectives will be:  1. To assess potential barriers to implementing the provincial pathway to facilitate our implementation strategy.  2. To implement the provincial pathway using 'local champions' identified at hospitals within the former Peace and Palliser Regions, an interactive web-based teaching module designed for primary care clinicians, and customized physician order sheets that will serve to remind clinicians of best practice.  3. To evaluate whether the asthma pathway increases the proportion of children treated in emergency departments and primary care clinics with evidenced-based therapies.  4. To evaluate whether the asthma pathway reduces emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and total health system expenditures per child with asthma.  5. To evaluate how many health care workers use the web-based module and what they learn from it.  6. To conduct focus groups of health care workers from a representative sample of Peace Country and Palliser hospitals to elicit a better understanding of why implementation was more successful in some sites than others.  7. To create a continuous quality improvement cycle that will extend indefinitely after the life of this project. This will be possible because decision makers and clinician leaders have been involved in this project from its inception, and it responds directly to their needs and priorities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of clinical outcomes and costs of a transferable interdisciplinary lifestyle intervention pre-and per-pregnancy in obese infertile women
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH SYSTEM IMPROVEMENT; INFERTILITY; LIFESTYLE MANAGEMENT; OBESITY; POLYCYSTIC OVARY SYNDROME; PREGNANCY OUTCOMES; RANDOMIZED-CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Infertility affects approximately 10-15% of couples and is one of its modifiable risk factor is overweight. In Canada, 43% of women in their reproduction age are overweight or obese. Moreover, obesity increases the costs of fertility treatments and reduces its efficiency. In addition, obesity increases significantly the risks of many complications of pregnancy. Even a modest loss of 5-10% of body weight can restore ovulation and improve pregnancy rates. Our general objective is thus to design, implement and evaluate a transferable cost-effective program for lifestyle management of obesity in infertile women in the Canadian context. The program will be developed and its implementation closely monitored by our research group with our expert and decision-maker collaborators. The design and implementation phase will include a quantitative and qualitative evaluation of health professionals' and patients' satisfaction, perceptions and impact of the program on their life. In order to evaluate lifestyle benefits of this program and assess its impact on fertility, pregnancy and neonatal outcomes, and cost, 128 obese women (BMI >= 30 kg/m2), or overweight women with polycystic ovary syndrome (BMI >= 27 kg/m2), consulting at the CHUS fertility clinic will be randomized into 2 groups: the intervention group will participate to our program and will suspend fertility treatments for six months, while the control group will receive standard fertility treatments. The results obtained will also be compared to those of women with the same criteria who will consult in 3 tertiary IVF clinics (with access to IVF at the clinic) not offering a similar lifestyle management program. This project is very important as it will generate new knowledge about the implementation, impacts and costs of a new lifestyle management program in obese infertile women. Our results may therefore accelerate public financing of such programs integrated to fertility clinics in Quebec and Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dynamic case studies and the impact on health policy decision preparedness
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DECISION PREPAREDNESS; DECISION PRINCIPLES; DYNAMIC CASE STUDIES; HEALTH POLICY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NON-SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Building upon a previous research grant from the Canadian Centre for Applied Research in Cancer Control, this project brings together a diverse team of health care decision makers and researchers to develop and evaluate a new tool that better prepares decision-makers for making complex decisions.    This tool will be based on a web-site where interested individuals can interact and contribute to a discussion related to specific and topical health care decisions.  The intention is to clarify the key questions that need to be answered and then identify relevant and trustworthy sources of research and non-research evidence that would best position decision-makers to make good decisions.    Focusing on six complex decisions that decision-makers in cancer systems routinely face, this project will involve interviews with these decision-makers, surveys of individuals who use and/or contribute to the website discussion and analysis of website usage data.  Ultimately, this project will contribute to a better understanding of the key factors that help decision-makers make better decisions and will provide a useful tool to guide future decisions on challenging topics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Collaboration familles/organismes communautaires dans la création et l'implantation d'une formation novatrice sur la gestion de l'agressivité de leur proche atteint de troubles mentaux : évaluation du processus, des effets et de l'empowerment
Keywords-MotsClés: FAMILLES; GESTION DE L'AGRESSIVITE; METHODES MIXTES; ORGANISATIONS COMMUNAUTAIRES; EVALUATION DE PROGRAMMES; EVALUATION DES SERVICES EN SANTE MENTALE
Abstract-Résumé: Soixante pourcent des familles de personnes atteintes de maladie mentale grave ont la responsabilite d'assurer les soins primaires et plusieurs sont amenees a jouer un role d'aidant naturel sans toutefois beneficier des conseils, du soutien ou du repit dont elles auraient besoin. Or, les ecrits rapportent qu'entre 10% et 40% des proches atteints ont presente des comportements agressifs et qu'entre 50% et 65% de ces comportements sont perpetres envers les membres de la famille. De plus, lors d'un des projets menes actuellement par notre equipe (Bonin et Lavoie-Tremblay, 2008-2011), il a ete souligne que les familles eprouvaient des difficultes avec leur proche atteint, particulierement, lorsqu'elles devaient obtenir un ordre de cour pour une ordonnance d'evaluation psychiatrique. Notre projet se situe dans une perspective d'implication active des familles et des decideurs dans ce probleme de gestion de l'agressivite du proche atteint. En effet, Entwistle (1998) soutient qu'il importe, afin de realiser des recherches de qualite, d'etablir un partenariat ou la perspective des utilisateurs et de leur famille est au centre du projet. Il s'agit d'une recherche action participative qui implique des decideurs institutionnels, communautaires et des membres de familles. Le projet porte precisement sur la gestion de l'agressivite des proches atteints de troubles mentaux par leur famille. Concretement, des membres de familles vont se former a l'approche Omega, qui est actuellement implantee dans plusieurs hopitaux du Quebec pour les intervenants. Ils vont aussi adapter cette approche pour qu'elle corresponde mieux aux besoins et situations des familles, appliquer cette approche comme formateurs et, enfin, devenir eux-memes des formateurs de formateurs. Cette recherche utilise une methode mixte, soit qualitative et quantitative et repose sur le modele d'evaluation de programme de Damschroder et al. (2009).

TitreApplicationTitle: Empowering Patients as Active Partners in Their Care:  Lupus Interactive Navigator (LIN)
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SYSTEM IMPROVEMENT; INTERACTIVE NAVIGATOR; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; LUPUS; PATIENT CENTERED CARE; PATIENT EMPOWERMENT; PSYCHOLOGICAL STRESS; QUALITY OF LIFE; SOCIAL SUPPORT; SYSTEMIC AUTOIMMUNE RHEUMATIC DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Lupus is a disease with no cure with chronic fatigue and inflammation and a greater risk of disability. A typical person with lupus is a young woman taking on average 5-8 medications, with doses that may vary from visit to visit.  The risk of confusion is great and there has not been, to date, much effort to simplify this for the patients. In addition, there are other issues that need to be addressed such as the importance of taking medications as prescribed and to follow strategies to prevent osteoporosis, heart disease, coping, mental health and social needs like work adaptation. There are 17,000 Canadians with lupus and only 13% are seen in academic centers or participate in research studies. These subjects may not be representative of the whole lupus population in Canada. Lupus research should therefore include a larger group of patients from across Canada. The Oncology Interactive Navigator (OINTM) developed by Jack Digital Production (JDP) Inc. is a new web-based tool which provides support to people with cancer. It uses an approach that focuses on the person-centered model, which integrates psychosocial elements of, education and self-management focusing on wellness as part of the standard care. We will use JDP expertise to develop the Lupus Interactive Navigator (LIN).  The LIN will not only be a knowledge transfer tool, it will also allow the inclusion of a larger Canadian lupus population in research studies. Our objectives are as follow: 1)we will evaluate needs to identify care gaps in lupus and build the web-based LIN with JDP Inc. after consultation with various stakeholders; 2)we will further test and make revisions to the LIN; 3)we will work with patient organizations such as Lupus Canada, the Canadian Rheumatology Association and Consumer Groups, to develop the guidelines for broader use of the LIN.   Ultimately, we will test if the LIN contributes to a better quality of life and if it should be adopted as a standard of care for lupus patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of an Integrated Internet-based Testing Program for HIV and Sexually Transmitted Infections in British Columbia.
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV SCREENING; INTERNET STI TESTING; STI SCREENING; STI SERVICE DELIVERY; STI/HIV PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: The number of people who get a sexually transmitted infection or HIV in Canada continues to increase despite the efforts of public health efforts to prevent the spread of these infections.  Many people who are infected with a sexually transmitted infection or HIV do not get tested right away, for a variety of reasons, including stigma or being unable to access testing services.  We need to find new and innovative ways to improve these trends.  We are living in the internet age and health services over the internet are acceptable and have the potential to reach many people and break down barriers to accessing services.  This study will evaluate a program that allows people to get tested for sexually transmitted infections and HIV through the internet, called iTEST, to see what impact this program has on the health of people and on the Canadian health care system.  This study will be focused on the first phase of iTEST, which will be focused on Vancouver, and the results of this study will be used to expand iTEST so that it is offered at more places in the province of British Columbia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a Framework for Information Needs at Diagnosis in Young-Onset Parkinson's Disease: A Patient-Centered Approach Using Grounded Theory Methodology
Keywords-MotsClés: CONSTRUCTIVIST PERSPECTIVE; COPING; DIAGNOSIS EXPERIENCES; GROUNDED THEORY; INFORMATION MATERIAL DEVELOPMENT; INFORMATION NEEDS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION PRACTICE; PATIENT-CENTERED; PSYCHOSOCIAL HEALTH; YOUNG-ONSET PARKINSON'S DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada there are 100,000 people living with Parkinson's disease (PD). The average age of onset of PD is 60 years, but a significant number of people will develop the disease in their 50s or younger when social responsibilities like employment and family are paramount. Often the psychosocial stress of the diagnosis rather than any physical impairment is what impedes their ability to remain active in society, and so dealing with psychosocial stressors at the time of diagnosis is therefore essential. It is clear that the needs and concerns of people developing PD at this age will be much different from those diagnosed later in life. Unfortunately, information programs are not currently in place to address the needs and concerns of this group of PD patients.   The goals of the proposed research are two-fold: 1) to identify the unique needs and concerns of younger adults newly diagnosed with PD and 2) to utilize this information to develop educational materials for health professionals caring for this population. This information will be gathered and analysed by way of a qualitative research methodology called constructivist grounded theory. Information will be gathered through multiple semi-structured interviews with individuals recently diagnosed with PD who are less than 60 years of age. The resulting data will guide the development of educational materials designed for this population's needs and concerns. The educational materials will then be tested with a larger sample of younger individuals with PD to assure the wider applicability of the content.    With a focus on the translation of knowledge from research to practice, the end goal of this project is to develop materials that health professionals can provide to newly diagnosed patients to assist with coping and transitioning into a life with PD. Providing these individuals with information to better cope with their diagnosis may help them to remain active and productive members of society for many years.

TitreApplicationTitle: Childhood Obesity and Inadequate Nutrition: An Exploration of Meal Time Consistency as a Potential Protective Factor
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD NUTRITION; CHILDHOOD OBESITY; LONGITUDINAL DESIGN; MEAL PATTERNS
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is a major health concern in Canada, and prevention during the childhood years is key. Previous research on childhood obesity has shown that meal patterns, including how frequently children consume meals and whether or not children eat breakfast, have an impact on children's eating habits, nutrition, and weight status. However, little is known about meal time consistency, or the extent to which an individual eats meals at the same time everyday. The purpose of this study is to explore whether or not meal time consistency is related to (a) children's eating habits, (b) children's weight status (i.e., whether or not a child is overweight or obese), and (c) other factors known to influence child eating behavior and weight status (such as breakfast skipping). Participants will include approximately 80 children, aged 10 to 12, and their parents. Questionnaires will be used to assess study variables. Children's height, weight, and body fat will be measured in order to assess weight status. If meal time consistency is related to child weight status, this study will have important implications for the treatment and prevention of childhood obesity.

Abstract-Résumé: In January 2010, the Ontario Ministry of Education (MOE) introduced a School Food and Beverage Policy which defines what healthy foods can be sold at school. This policy is to be fully implemented by September 2011. The proposed research, within Region of Waterloo schools, will 1) describe opportunities for and barriers to successful policy implementation from the perspectives of teachers, parents and students from schools at early, middle and advanced stages of policy implementation; 2) assess food behaviours of a representative sample of grade 6 - 10 students over the course of policy implementation; 3) appraise the food environment of a sample of schools in Spring 2011 and 2012; and 4) effectively share 'lessons learned' from the above within and beyond Region of Waterloo.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of family and school nutritional-related factors on dietary behaviour change in teens participating in a lifestyle modification intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH BEHAVIORS; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; NUTRITION; OBESITY; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood obesity is a major public health concern in Canada. Increasingly, it is important to determine what puts youth at risk for becoming overweight or obese, how to improve prevention efforts, and how to develop more effective interventions. Diet has been identified as an important lifestyle factor that contributes to weight gain and obesity. The family and school environments are known to influence adolescent's eating behaviours but little is known about the combined influence of factors in these environments on changes in eating habits as adolescents participate in an intervention to improve healthy eating and physical activity.  The purpose of this study is to investigate how factors in the family and school environments influence dietary behaviours in adolescents. It is hypothesized that access and availability of unhealthy foods in the family and school environment, unhealthy food modelling, and frequency of purchased meals will be associated with poorer dietary habits and will impede dietary behaviour change as adolescents progress through the intervention.  Data will be collected from 150 overweight or obese adolescents and one of their parents over an 8-month period in 2010/2012. A combination of web-based surveys and 24-hour recalls will be used to collect information from adolescents and parents about their dietary behaviours. Results from this research will provide timely evidence that informs obesity prevention efforts and the development of more comprehensive public health interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of energy balance in age-dependant neurodegeneration and stress response in C.elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; C. ELEGANS; CELLS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES; PROTEOTOXICITY; STRESS RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: The world and Canadian population shift to an older demographic and and we see an increase in neurological disorders, especially neurodegenerative diseases that result in the progressive death of neurons. There is currently no effective treatment for patients with these disorders. The neuron is a complex cell that has a high energy demand. Often, in brain diseases, the metabolism is disrupted and it is possible that restoration of energy balance may help neurons. Although it was shown that caloric restriction has the effect of lengthening life expectancy, we believe that this mechanism is not the most suitable in the treatment of diseases of the nervous system. In this project, we have shown that a diet rich in energy, mainly glucose, the sole supplier of energy in the brain, results in better survival of neuronal cells. If this mechanism is conserved in humans, it is possible that a diet enriched with glucose can slow the symptoms associated with brain diseases like Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington disease and perhaps several others. The project proposed here will explore the different pathways involved in the beneficial effect of glucose. To do this we will use C. elegans, a simple organism that has proven his value in the study of cell survival.

TitreApplicationTitle: Does a school-based mental health curriculum for grade 9-10 youth improve knowledge, reduce stigma and enhance help seeking behaviors?
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY HEALTH; INTERDISCIPLINARITY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MEASUREMENT; MENTAL HEALTH LITERACY; PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT; RESEARCH METHODOLOGY; SCHOOL MENTAL HEALTH; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW; YOUTH HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, approximately ten to twenty per cent of children and adolescents suffer from some form of mental disorder. However, only one in five adolescents requiring specialty care receives it. Many youth do not receive needed care because of their insufficient knowledge for early identification, stigma about mental disorders, and lack of help resources. There is a need to effectively address these issues. My PhD research will focus on understanding effective mental health literacy programs that will address youth mental health for Canadian secondary schools. The fundamental assumption of mental health literacy programs is that increasing knowledge and awareness can lead to positive health improvements such as decreased emotional and behavioral problems, improved clinical and functional outcomes, and improved school performance among youth. The study will evaluate a mental health literacy program, Mental Health and High School Curriculum Guide. The program addresses brain functions, specific mental disorders, stigma about mental illness, help seeking resources and the importance of positive mental health. It will be evaluated among grade nine to ten students in Nova Scotia high schools with a cluster randomized controlled trial study design. The study will include the integrated knowledge translation component through the engagement of related stakeholders in each phase of the study. Should the program be effective, it will potentially enable both youth and educators to achieve better understanding about mental health, to reduce stigma about mental illness, and to appropriately recognize and respond to signs of mental disorders and therefore link with health care providers for treatment, and ultimately promote mental health in youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Young men and online STI/HIV testing services
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS/FACILITATORS TO STI/HIV TESTING; FOCUS GROUPS; HEALTH EQUITY; IN-DEPTH QUALITATIVE INTERVIEWS; MASCULINITIES AND MEN'S HEALTH; ONLINE HEALTH SERVICES; POPULATION HEALTH INTERVENTION RESEARCH; STI/HIV; VULNERABLE SUB-GROUPS; YOUNG MEN
Abstract-Résumé: Rates of sexually transmitted infections (STI) and HIV are high among young people in Canada. However, young men's engagement with STI/HIV testing remains disproportionately low. The British Columbia Centre for Disease Control's (BCCDC) new Online Sexual Health Services Program (OSHSP) is developing online STI/HIV testing services in the hopes that it will improve young men's participation in STI/HIV testing. Understanding the processes by which the OSHSP can create new opportunities to meaningfully engage men in accessing STI/HIV testing services is therefore the fundamental aim of the proposed study. The findings from the proposed study will provide recommendations for tailoring the OSHSP to meet the needs of young men in BC to improve young men's sexual health services. This study will: (1) Examine young men's perspectives on the saliency, credibility and value of the emerging OSHSP; (2) Describe and examine how men are represented (e.g., gender norms; sexuality) within the OSHSP; (3) Use these perspectives to facilitate the development of recommendations for tailoring the OSHSP to accommodate the needs of young men; (4) Explore the differential effects of the OSHSP across potentially vulnerable subgroups of men and use this information to respond to their needs. The study will use a purposive sampling strategy to recruit participants (men ages 15-24) from a variety of socio-cultural backgrounds to ensure a wide variety of perspectives. There will be a particular emphasis recruiting young men who may be most vulnerable to the health and social impacts of STIs/HIV (e.g., economically disadvantaged; men who have sex with men). A variety of qualitative data collection techniques will be used, including: in-depth, qualitative interviews (n=40); focus groups (4 groups with n=5 men); and a one-day Participatory Planning Summit (n=12 men).

TitreApplicationTitle: Violence and HIV prevention among young women who exchange sex for survival in post-conflict Northern Uganda
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFLICT AND HEALTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE; GLOBAL HEALTH; HIV/AIDS; TRANSACTIONAL SEX WORK; VULNERABLE POPULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Hindered by social stigma and lack of access to health resources, sex workers experience inordinate amounts of gender-based violence (GBV) and represent the group with the highest rate of new HIV infections in Africa. Young women remain educationally and economically disenfranchised, increasing their risk of exchanging sex for survival. Elevated rates of HIV infection commonly accompany the post-conflict phase, emphasizing the need for evidence-based strategies to intervene as Northern Uganda transitions to post-conflict after 20 years of war. Within a longitudinal study of HIV prevention and care among female youth who exchange sex for survival in Northern Uganda, this proposal aims to:  1) Estimate the prevalence of historical GBV among youth and relationship to HIV prevalence; 2) Examine how historical violence shapes patterns of condom use with clients and incidents of interpersonal violence; 3) Estimate the incidence of HIV infection among youth mediated by historical and current experiences of GBV.  Methods: Participants (n = 500 women engaged in sex for survival; 14-29 years) will be recruited through The AIDS Support Organization (TASO), the most well-established indigenous AIDS organization in Africa. This study will use participatory mapping and time-location sampling to identify young women and the places where they congregate. We will use Logistic regression to examine the relationship between violence and the biological and socio-cultural associations with HIV status. Survival analysis will be used to determine the gendered predictors of sero-conversion over a 2-year follow-up period.  Outcome: The post-conflict moment in Uganda is a critical time to address the needs of young women and combat the further escalation of Uganda's HIV epidemic. Results from this research will inform evidence-based HIV prevention among one of the most at-risk groups and contribute to TASO's intervention efforts, both in Northern Uganda and other branches across Uganda.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical and immune correlates of isolated semen HIV shedding
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL INVESTIGATION; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENITAL MUCOSA; HIV; IMMUNOLOGY; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; SEMEN; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASE; T CELLS; TISSUE CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: The global prevalence of HIV-1 is 0.8% with the number of persons living with HIV continuing to increase as a result of global population growth, continued transmission, and antiretroviral-associated reductions in mortality. With no cure or vaccine likely in the short term, understanding factors that affect HIV transmission is pivotal to the design of new prevention and treatment strategies.    The advent of antiretroviral therapy had a dramatic effect on the HIV community through its ability to suppress HIV replication to often-undetectable levels in blood (effective ART). However, it has been estimated that even with effective antiretroviral therapy, transmission still occurs roughly 10% of the time. Previous work by our lab has identified a subgroup of men, who despite effective ART with no clinical STI or urethritis, shed High-level HIV in their semen, leaving them in a potentially infectious state.   Various studies have shown that while ART compounds penetrate into the semen, many of them only do so to low levels. We propose to investigate whether an "intensified" drug therapy (standard therapy + two additional drugs of differing mechanistic class), can prevent the occurrence of isolated semen shedding. In addition we plan to investigate whether an unidentified infection localized to the male genital tract is responsible for the inability of therapy to suppress viral replication. Preliminary data has shown evidence of immune activation in semen but not blood in those men shedding.   Finally we plan to investigate the phenomenon of disproportionate semen HIV shedding. A situation where a ART drug naive person has higher HIV levels in semen then blood. We will investigate various immunological correlates to determine potential immune mechanisms for this occurrence.

TitreApplicationTitle: Drug Resistance of HIV  to Second Generation Integrase Inhibitors
Keywords-MotsClés: DOCKING; DOSE RESPONSE CURVES; DRUG RESISTANCE; HIV/AIDS; HOMOLOGY MODELLING; IN SILICO; INTEGRASE; SELECTION PRESSURE; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; SUB-TYPE VARIABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Insertion of reverse-transcribed DNA of Human Immunodeficiency virus (HIV) into human DNA; ultimately leading to translation of viral proteins by human proteins is catalysed by HIV integrase. Un-integrated viral DNA would otherwise be degraded. Inhibition of integration is thus critical in fighting HIV/AIDS and HIV integrase is an important target. Drug resistance development, upon treatment with Raltegravir (Isentress®), the only integrase inhibitor (INI) approved for early and later stage anti retroviral therapy, also confers resistance to Elvitagravir (EVG) (GS-9137, Gilead), another first generation integrase inhibitor in phase III clinical trials; second generation INIs are thus needed to treat patients with RAL or EVG resistant virus. Additionally, current INIs are designed primarily for HIV-1 subtype B viruses, though our laboratory has evidence that drug resistance development to RAL and EVG differ in non sub-type B viruses which represent most worldwide infections; subtype variability should be considered in testing drug  resistance to design treatment regimes which would have global relevance.  Two second generation INIs, MK-2048 (Merck) and S/GSK-1349572 (Shiniogi/ GlaxoSmithKline) are in stage II and IIb clinical trials respectively. These two integrase inhibitors are expected to improve resistance profiles of INIs ultimately better the treatment outcomes of patients undergoing treatment with INIs.  The Wainberg lab therefore deems it necessary to determine the sub-type specific effect of second generation inhibitors on RAL/ EVG resistant HIV integrase as well as the effect of EVG and RAL on HIV integrase with resistance to MK-2048 and S/GSK-1349572. Our proposed biochemical analysis, in concert with computer modeling simulations would potentially lead to design of sub-type and situation specific INI treatment regimes and also provide insights for design of third generation INIs to treat patients who with resistance to previous INI generations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanism of Nutritional Starch Digestion by Family 31 Glycoside Hydrolases
Keywords-MotsClés: CARBOHYDRATE BIOCHEMISTRY; DRUG DISCOVERY; METABOLISM AND NUTRITION; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NUTRITIONAL BIOCHEMISTRY; PROTEIN OVEREXPRESSION; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding the molecular mechanism of starch digestion will allow researchers to gain a better understanding of diet-associated disorders such as Type II diabetes and obesity. Despite the importance of carbohydrates and glucose in the human diet, the mechanism of starch digestion at the molecular level in the human gastrointestinal tract is not fully understood, especially in terms of the specific role each enzyme plays in the process. This project aims to more fully understand the enzyme activity involved in starch digestion, as well as the actual structure of the enzymes at the atomic level through crystallographic and kinetic studies. The enzymes that will be studied in detail are the C-terminal domain of maltase-glucoamylase (MGAM) and sucrase-isomaltase (SI). In the future, this knowledge can be applied to studies in animal models in which the enzyme activities can be toggled on and off in various combinations as well as individually. This will ultimately lead to the development of novel classes of glycosidase inhibitors to be used in treatment of diet-related disorders such as Type II diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of CD45 on dendritic cells in the intestinal immune system
Keywords-MotsClés: COLITIS; CYTOKINES; DENDRITIC CELLS; HELMINTHS; IMMUNOLOGY; LYMPH; MICROBIOTA; PROTEIN TYROSINE PHOSPHATASES; T CELLS; TOLERANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is an unexpected inflammatory response in the gut. The incidence of IBD is steadily increasing in western populations; therefore it is necessary to study this disease since there is still no definitive cure. Immune cells such as dendritic cells (DC) have been implicated in the development of IBD. These cells are thought to recognize the commensal bacteria through pattern recognition receptors but instead of producing an anti-inflammatory response to the beneficial flora, a pro-inflammatory response is initiated. Although the inflammatory response is thought to occur when immune cells in the intestine recognize the normal bacteria in the gut as foreign, why this occurs is still unclear.  Helminths (worms) are another interesting infection of the intestinal immune system. While there are effective treatments for worms, curing people of worms has resulted in the increase of IBD. Recently, there has been evidence that a worm infection in the gut results in decreased expression of pattern recognition receptors on DCs specific to that parasite. As a result, the worm is able to persist and survive while causing various complications to its host.  Our lab has shown that the absence of the protein CD45 on DCs increases the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines when certain pattern recognition receptors on DCs are stimulated. We have already shown that in an animal model of chronic IBD, the absence of CD45 decreases the severity of systemic disease. We will continue to study the role of CD45 in other models of IBD to best mimic all aspects of human IBD. We predict that in these acute models, the severity of IBD will be more severe in CD45 deficient mice. We will also study the role of CD45 on innate immune cells in helminth infection and predict that CD45 deficient mice will be more resistant to helminthes due to a protective T cell response in the mucosa of these mice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of Genetic Loci Controlling Susceptibility to Colitis-Associated Colorectal Cancer in Mice
Keywords-MotsClés: AZOXYMETHANE; COLITIS-ASSOCIATED COLON CANCER; DEXTRAN SULFATE SODIUM; FAMILIAL COLON CANCER; GENE MAPPING; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer related deaths in Canada. My current research involves the use of mouse models to identify and characterize predisposing CRC risk factors in the form of low penetrance tumor susceptibility genes. The premise of my research is that a better understanding of these genes will help to identify those at risk of developing CRC and assist researchers in understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms mediating CRC development. The mouse model used in my research mimics colitis-associated (CA)-CRC in humans and allows me to study these gene effects independently of diet and lifestyle risk factors, which often complicate human studies. My initial studies have identified two genetic regions (loci) that interact with each other to regulate susceptibility to CA-CRC in A/J (susceptible) and B6 (resistant) mice. My ongoing studies are designed to define the specific gene effects and mechanisms underling this differential susceptibility. This will involve further testing of different mouse strains and subsequent gene sequencing to identify the causative mutations. To understand the mechanism underlying increased tumor development in A/J mice I will first focus on identifying differences in the immune cells and inflammatory mediators released into the colon at various experimental time points. The long-term goal of my project will involve validation of these loci in human CRC association studies and tumor samples. Multi-gene interactions associated with CRC susceptibility have yet to be identified in humans and therefore this model provides a starting point to search for such interactions. Recently, inflammation has been referred to as the seventh hallmark of cancer, suggesting that the underling genes and mechanisms associated with differential CA-CRC in this model may have relevance to other cancers. Therefore, it is hoped that this knowledge will assist in the detection and treatment of CRC and other cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using proteomics to investigate the role of TDP-43 (TAR DNA-binding protein 43) in the pathogenesis of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; MOTOR NEURON DISEASE; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; STABLE CELL LINE; TAR DNA-BINDING PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), commonly known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is an adult-onset neurodegenerative disease caused by degeneration of motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord. This devastating disease, with no cure and only one FDA-approved treatment to date, affects 1 in every 100,000 Canadians per year and causes muscle paralysis and eventual death, typically within 3-5 years.   Mutations in the TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) have been linked to both sporadic and familial forms of ALS, and studies have shown that TDP-43 is present in the ubiquitinated inclusions found in affected motor neurons of ALS. Very little is known about the role of TDP-43 under physiological conditions and how it contributes to disease, therefore this project aims to elucidate the disease mechanism underlying motor neuron degeneration by identifying TDP-43 interacting proteins. A proteomic approach will be used, which involves the use of chemical crosslinking of TDP-43 to its interacting partners both in vitro and in vivo, immunoprecipitation of these complexes using TDP-43 antibody, and mass spectrometry to identify interacting proteins of TDP-43. This will be performed on human control and ALS brain and spinal cord tissues, as well as stable cell lines expressing wildtype and various pathological forms of TDP-43. Identifying TDP-43 interacting proteins will uncover specific biochemical pathways that underlie motor neuron degeneration, and will identify biomarkers for early diagnosis and potential candidates for therapeutics and genetic analyses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prion-like intermolecular transmission of superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) misfolding in embryonic spinal cord cultures of an amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) mouse model.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALS; IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; MOUSE MODEL; NEURODEGENERATION; PROTEIN MISFOLDING; SOD1; SPINAL CORD CULTURES; TEMPLATE DIRECTED MISFOLDING
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a common and incurable disorder that affects the nerve cells in the central nervous system (CNS) that control voluntary muscle movement. There is currently no cure for ALS, which afflicts 2,500-3,000 Canadians, and ~30,000 people in North America. The survival after diagnosis is bleak, with 80% of patients dying within 2-5 years. Hereditary forms of ALS can be caused by genetic mutations that alter a cellular defense protein called superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1). SOD1 normally functions to help protect cells from damage, but when the three-dimensional shape of the protein changes, it can take on an opposite role and contribute to cell death. There is growing evidence that ALS is associated with  abnormal changes in the three-dimensional shape of SOD1. Our  laboratory has evidence that altered SOD1 can change normal SOD1 to a toxic form that can then go on to change other normal forms of the protein. This "chain reaction" can occur inside cells and can travel from one cell to another. We predict that this process is how ALS  spreads throughout the nervous system. I aim to test this disease process in systems that more reflect the nervous system of humans. We will study this mechanism in mouse nerve cell models of ALS, which will allow us to see if diseased SOD1 can be passed from one nerve cell to another, and test molecules that could block the toxic chain-reaction of altered SOD1, thereby stopping the spread of the disease. It is essential that we understand the biological mechanism of this disease so new treatment strategies and/or vaccines can be developed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Informed Decision Making in Health Care: the Impact of Research Methods on Treatment Recommendations
Keywords-MotsClés: EFFECT SIZE ESTIMATES; EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE; EVIDENCE BASED PRACTICE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; META-ANALYSES; META-EPIDEMIOLOGICAL RESEARCH; METHODOLOGICAL QUALITY ASSESSMENT; PHYSICAL THERAPY RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS; RISK OF BIAS; SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS
Abstract-Résumé: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and systematic reviews (SRs) of these trials are used to make policy and clinical decisions regarding health care. These types of studies are considered the highest quality of evidence, but they can sometimes provide misleading information depending on how they are done. Healthcare workers and other decision-makers need the highest quality of evidence to make decisions about which treatments should be used. However, the way to determine what is good quality evidence has been controversial and most of the tools used to decide which are good or bad trials have not been well tested. We know from scientific studies that research should be done in a certain way to provide accurate information about the effectiveness of treatments. For instance, studies where the researchers and participants do not know what intervention they are getting provide more accurate results than other studies. Much research has been conducted in recent years to help guide how studies are done. However, most of this research has been done in the field of medicine and now needs to be expanded to other health areas, in particular the allied health professions such as physical therapy. This project will identify how to design randomized trials in physical therapy so that they provide the most accurate information about the effectiveness of different interventions. This information is particularly important for researchers, healthcare workers, decision-makers, and patients. Physiotherapists and other decision-makers need solid evidence to decide which treatments will help their patients so that they can provide the best healthcare possible. Patients need to be sure that decisions regarding their clinical care are based on solid information. Thus, more informed decision making regarding clinical care will ultimately improve patient outcomes and will increase efficiency in the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: N-acetylcysteine as a novel prophylactic treatment against nephrotoxicity caused by ifosfamide.
Keywords-MotsClés: IFOSFAMIDE; N-ACETYLCYSTEINE; NEPHROTOXICITY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PEDIATRICS; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Ifosfamide is a chemotherapy drug commonly used to treat solid tumours in children. While it is an effective antineoplastic agent, it has a number of well known side effects including kidney toxicity. Up to 30% of children who are treated with ifosfamide will suffer some degree of kidney dysfunction, with 5% of these patients suffering from the most severe form of kidney toxicity, Fanconi's syndrome. This may result in hypophosphatemic rickets and/or the need for renal dialysis or kidney transplant. Therefore, while the use of ifosfamide may provide successful treatment of cancer, many children will continue to suffer a diminished quality of life due to kidney damage caused by their chemotherapy. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is an antioxidant which has been shown to prevent ifosfamide-induced kidney toxicity in both a kidney cell line (LLC-PK1) and in an animal model (rat). These results demonstrate the potential therapeutic role for NAC in a patient population against such kidney toxicity. Furthermore, NAC is currently used clinically in children as an antidote for acetaminophen overdose. This fact becomes extremely important as it demonstrates the safe use of NAC in children, a population for which the safety data of most drugs is not well known and is difficult to obtain. We plan to continue to add support to the use of NAC in kidney protection during ifosfamide therapy through completion of the following research:  1) demonstration that NAC does not affect the efficacy of ifosfamide in its ability to treat cancer using an animal model and 2) demonstrating the efficacy of NAC to prevent kidney toxicity caused by ifosfamide in a pediatric population with a randomized controlled clinical trial. This will show that N-acetylcysteine is a clinically a relevant and effective choice in the prevention of ifosfamide-induced kidney damage, which will allow for the continued administration of ifosfamide in children without the associated risk of kidney dysfunction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Traitement des symptômes dépressifs dans le contexte du cancer : Comparaison de la luminothérapie et de la thérapie cognitive
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETE; DEPRESSION; FATIGUE; GROUPE CONTROLE; LUMINOTHERAPIE; PSYCHO-ONCOLOGIE; QUALITE DE VIE; RANDOMISATION; SOMMEIL; THERAPIE COGNITIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Le diagnostic de cancer et les traitements oncologiques s'accompagnent souvent de symptomes depressifs, qui peuvent avoir des consequences considerables sur la qualite de vie des patients et leur adherence aux traitements. Cette etude menee aupres de personnes atteintes de divers types de cancer vise a evaluer l'efficacite de la luminotherapie pour traiter les symptomes depressifs comparativement a une condition placebo et a comparer l'efficacite de la luminotherapie a celle de la therapie cognitive pour traiter les symptomes depressifs. Pour ce faire, deux groupes de 30 patients atteints de cancer seront recrutes a L'Hotel-Dieu de Quebec du CHUQ. Les participants admissibles seront assignes aleatoirement a l'un ou l'autre des deux groupes experimentaux (i.e., luminotherapie ou therapie cognitive). Les participants du groupe luminotherapie recevront d'abord un traitement de luminotherapie placebo lors duquel ils s'exposeront 30 minutes par jour a une faible lumiere rouge de 0,5 lux pour une duree de 4 semaines. Ils recevront ensuite un traitement de luminotherapie active, lors duquel ils s'exposeront a une lampe de 10 000 lux a la meme frequence et pour la meme duree. Les participants du groupe therapie cognitive recevront 8 seances hebdomadaires de psychotherapie de 50 minutes. Une batterie d'evaluation sera completee au pre-, mi- et post-traitement, ainsi que 3 et 6 mois apres l'intervention. A chaque temps de mesure, les participants completeront des questionnaires (p. ex. : Echelle hospitaliere d'anxiete et de depression), un auto-enregistrement quotidien du sommeil et porteront un actigraphe pour fournir des indices objectifs du sommeil. Ce projet permettra de verifier si la luminotherapie peut etre aussi efficace que la therapie cognitive pour attenuer les symptomes depressifs chez les personnes atteintes de cancer. Si tel est le cas, il sera alors possible de fournir un traitement alternatif aux patients pour qui une therapie cognitive n'est pas accessible.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of drug transporters in rivaroxaban disposition: molecular determinants of kinetics and clinical drug response
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY; DRUG METABOLISM; DRUG TRANSPORTERS; GENE EXPRESSION; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; PHARMACODYNAMICS; PHARMACOGENOMICS; PHARMCOKINETICS; TRANSLATIONAL MEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: Blood clotting disorders are a significant source of mortality and morbidity. Warfarin has been the mainstay of blood thinning therapy for the last 60 years. However, its clinical use is associated with unpredictable responsiveness and bleeding events, resulting in emergency room visits and potential hospitalization. Thus, new therapeutic agents have been developed to alleviate the problems of warfarin therapy. The new blood thinning agent, rivaroxaban, has recently been approved for use in Canada. Although rivaroxaban requires less monitoring and is deemed as a "one size fits all" dosing paradigm, elevated risk for minor or life-threatening bleeding event in patients with lowered ability to excrete the drug is still a major concern. In this proposal, we plan to examine how rivaroxaban exits the bloodstream. We believe that proteins called transporters, found on the cell surface, can act as gatekeepers that allow rivaroxaban to gain access to, or prevent drug accumulation in the bloodstream. Drugs that are used in combination with rivaroxaban therapy are expected to increase bleeding risk by blocking the function of gatekeeper transporters. Moreover, patients with more non-functioning forms of transporter proteins due to genetic variations could play an important role in determining rivaroxaban disposition. The ultimate goal is to determine how transporter proteins influence rivaroxaban kinetics and response. In addition, we plan to elucidate how drug-drug interactions and genetic variations may further increase adverse events. Personalized medicine is an emerging field that seeks to understand interindividual variability in drug response and utilizes individual genetic makeup when choosing appropriate drug therapy and dosages. It is expected that our studies will provide the basis for understanding rivaroxaban disposition, and in turn form the foundation for strategies to predict and prevent life-threatening bleeding events while maintaining therapeutic efficacy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a Platform for Data Harmonization to study Pediatric Multiple Sclerosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; HARMONIZATION; PEDIATRIC MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding the causes of Multiple Sclerosis has tremendous implications for Canadians. Worldwide, Canada is one of the countries with the highest number of people living with Multiple Sclerosis - most Canadians know someone who suffers from this disease. In the past, Multiple Sclerosis was considered a disease of adulthood, however, in recent years Multiple Sclerosis in children is being increasingly recognized. Children are an excellent population to study the causes of Multiple Sclerosis as the number of potential exposures that can cause the disease are fewer in children than in adults, because they are younger, making it easier to identify correct causes. This project will be led by researchers at McGill University. However, it will also bring together Canadian and International experts interested in Multiple Sclerosis in children. The objective of this project is to establish a tool that will enable the integration of information collected through ongoing studies of childhood Multiple Sclerosis. The tool will include clinical, genetic, biological and medical imaging information that is important to collect when studying patients with the diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis. This tool will be created in collaboration with Dr. Isabel Fortier, responsible for the International Public Population Project in Genomics (P3G). The tool created in this project will be used to understand the relationships between certain genes and the environmental and biological risk factors that have been shown to be associated with Multiple Sclerosis. This study will focus on children, and will be the largest study to assess gene-environment relationships, as information will be pooled from many ongoing studies. This project will provide insight into why certain individuals get Multiple Sclerosis; a better understanding of this disease will translate into benefits for many affected Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating Mechanisms of Resistance to HIV-1 Integrase Inhibitors
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; ENZYME KINETICS; HIV-1; IN SILICO STUDIES; INHIBITION STUDIES; INTEGRASE; PRE-CLINICAL; PROTEIN-NUCLEIC ACID INTERACTIONS; RESISTANCE MECHANISMS; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: HIV-1 encodes three enzymes: reverse transcriptase, protease and integrase, all of which are crucial for viral replication. Until recently, only two of these had been characterized and extensively utilized as therapeutic targets. Although combination therapy against reverse transcriptase and protease can reduce viral burden to levels below the limit of detection, the emergence of mutations in the viral genome can compromise treatment. As a result, the search for new antiretroviral targets has lead to the development of integrase inhibitors. HIV-1 integrase catalyzes the insertion of viral DNA into the host chromosome where it can persist. Raltegravir is a potent, first-generation integrase inhibitor; however, the inhibitor is also vulnerable to the development of resistance. A better understanding of how mutations in the integrase enzyme confer resistance to raltegravir is necessary in order to establish a basis for developing new inhibitors. We have used recent structural data from a related retroviral integrase to analyze with computer-based software how resistance mutations can affect inhibitor binding. We propose to compare the computer-based predictions to data obtained with the purified HIV integrase enzyme. A correlation between the prediction and actual data would validate the structural model. Success in this research would facilitate the development of new integrase inhibitors that are active against both wild-type and resistant mutant viruses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phenotypic and Functional Characterization of Two New Th17 Cell Subsets Permissive versus Resistant to HIV-1 Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: CCR6; CD4+ T-CELLS; CELL DIFFERENTIATION; ELISA; FLOW CYTOMETRY CELL SORTING; GENOME WIDE ANALYSIS OF GENE EXPRESSION; HIV-1; HOST CELL RESTRICTION AND PERMISSIVENES FACTORS; REAL TIME PCR; TH17 POLARIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: The HIV/AIDS epidemic remains a major challenge for medicine, public health and biomedical research, with >25 million people killed by AIDS throughout the world since 1981. More than 60,000 people are currently living with HIV in Canada, with an increasing portion of HIV infections occurring in young Aboriginal women. Despite the key advances made in the HIV field in the past years, an HIV vaccine does not exist yet and eradication has not been achieved with current antiretroviral therapies. Difficulties in solving HIV epidemics are, in part, related to the fact that HIV infects and persists in a small fraction of CD4+ T-cells, with phenotypic and functional characteristics that are still not clearly understood. Therefore, a better understanding of CD4+ T-cell heterogeneity is imperative to allow the design of successful vaccines and/or cell-targeted eradication strategies. The present proposal will provide an in depth characterization of CD4+ T-cell phenotypic and functional heterogeneity under homeostatic conditions and HIV pathogenesis. Our objective is to characterize the contribution to immunity and HIV pathogenesis of two new memory T-cell subsets expressing the gut homing chemokine receptor CCR6 and markers of Th17 polarization. The proposed studies will provide a new understanding of the functional heterogeneity of Th17 cells in the context of HIV pathogenesis and will identify biomarkers for T-cell subsets fuelling HIV replication/persistence in vivo. This knowledge will be critical for purging HIV reservoirs from discrete T-cell subsets and will identify new targets for the development of drugs that interfere with molecular mechanisms of HIV permissiveness versus resistance in primary T-cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Perceived HIV risk and condom use among men who have sex with men in the STI/HIV Co-Infection Study.
Keywords-MotsClés: CONDOM USE; CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY; HIV/AIDS; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; MULTIVARIATE LOGISTIC REGRESSION; PERCEIVED HIV RISK
Abstract-Résumé: Background and rationale: In 2008, Men who have sex with Men (MSM) comprised the greatest proportion of new HIV infections at 44% <1>. The estimated HIV prevalence for MSM in 2008 in Toronto was 21% and the annual HIV incidence was 1.4%, indicating that MSM in Toronto are still seriously affected by the HIV epidemic <2>. Unprotected anal intercourse (UAI) among MSM has increased among susceptible MSM with HIV-infected partners and partners of unknown HIV status <3>. However, perceived HIV risk as a potential determinant of safer sex practices (i.e. using condoms) has yet to be fully characterized. Study population: The population recruited by the CIHR-funded and REB-approved STI/HIV Co-infection Study which is an ongoing cross-sectional study of sexually active MSM 16 years of age or older. Hypothesis: Increasing perceived HIV risk is associated with increased condom use. However, HIV positive and HIV negative men perceive their risk differently, and therefore, prevention intervention programs should be directed at these separate populations.  Aims: (1) To characterize perceived HIV risk among study subjects, and (2) To examine the association between perceived HIV risk and condom use.  Recruitment and methods: 300 HIV-negative and 300 HIV-positive MSM are being recruited from the Maple Leaf Medical Clinic in Toronto, Ontario. Data are collected using a computer based self-administered questionnaire (ACASI). Blood, anal swab and urine specimens are being collected. We will analyze the data using STATA 10.0. Perceived HIV risk will be categorized. This measure will then be stratified by known confounders and effect modifiers (Aim 1). We will use multivariate logistic regression to examine the relationship between perceived HIV risk and condom use (Aim 2). Contribution to knowledge: New insights concerning the relationship between perceived HIV risk and condom use will allow public health personnel to develop better, more focused preventive intervention policies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intimate partner violence and HIV risk: exploring the impact of a male-targeted, violence prevention intervention on household gender equality, violence and HIV risk behaviours in Cote d'Ivoire
Keywords-MotsClés: CLUSTER RANDOMIZED TRIAL; GENDER VIOLENCE PREVENTION INTERVENTION; HIV/AIDS; HOUSEHOLD SURVEYS; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; MEASURES OF GENDER EQUALITY; POST-CONFLICT COUNTRY; PROCESS AND IMPACT EVALUATIONS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOCIAL SCIENCE QUALITATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: BACKGROUND: strong evidence demonstrates links between intimate partner violence (IPV) and HIV. HIV rates have been particularly high among women who report IPV. Rising levels of sexual violence in conflict zones have been associated with increased HIV risk. HIV and violence-prevention interventions have been trialed to influence men to adopt more gender equitable attitudes and behaviours about gender equity. These interventions have begun to show positive results. AIM: to explore whether a male-targeted violence-prevention intervention can reduce IPV levels and HIV risk behaviours, and improve household gender equality in post-conflict Cote d'Ivoire. OBJECTIVES: to document household decision-making roles, attitudes about gender equity, IPV, and HIV risk behaviours. METHODS: A Men's Dialogue Group (MDG) intervention was created by South African NGO 'Sonke Gender Justice Network' to influence men's attitudes and behaviours about gender equity. International Rescue Committee (IRC), a global leader in humanitarian services for sexual violence, will implement the intervention. Male volunteers in 6 treatment communities will participate in the MDGs and will also be exposed to community-level violence-prevention activities. Six control communities will receive community violence-prevention activities alone. Outcomes will be compared across treatment and control communities before and after the intervention. The following quantitative and qualitative methods will be used: men and their partners will be surveyed; interviews will be conducted with men, their partners, intervention facilitators, and community leaders; and focus groups will be held with men participating in the MDG intervention. The majority of this research project comprises the last two phases of a 5 phase intervention evaluation. HEALTH IMPLICATIONS: if we can encourage men to adopt more gender equitable attitudes and behaviours, we may observe reduced household IPV levels and HIV risk behaviours.

TitreApplicationTitle: Black, Female, Poor, and Powerless: An Intersectional Analysis of HIV/AIDs Policy in Mozambique
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNICABLE DISEASE; GENDER; HEALTH SERVICES; HIV/AIDS; INTERSECTIONALITY; POLICY; POPULATION HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The HIV/AIDS crisis in sub-Saharan Africa is staggering, and though only 10% of the world's population live there, it is home to over two-thirds of the world's HIV-infected people. The region has suffered over 80% of AIDS-related deaths, yet despite efforts, the epidemic continues. Not only are countries devastated by the epidemic, but their development status and high proportion of other vulnerabilities among their populations compromises whatever defences they have. Mozambique, for example, has prevalence rates ranging from 3-35%, with a national estimate of 16%, predominantly heterosexual infections. Mozambique is characterized by poor knowledge of HIV/AIDS, lagging access to preventive and therapeutic services relative to the rest of southern Africa, compounded by the world's most severe health worker shortage. Exacerbating factors include inadequate education systems, poverty, and gender inequality. HIV/AIDS disproportionately affects women, through infection and social role, rendering the epidemic a women's issue. What remains unclear is exactly how these multiple factors interact to make HIV/AIDS both a sociocultural and epidemiological problem in Mozambique. To explore the complex mix of factors influencing HIVAIDS among women in Mozambique, I will use grounded theory, informed by situational analysis methods of mapping relationships, discourses, and action, to identify how the intersections between and among factors such as gender, colonization, race, poverty, politics, food insecurity, health policy, economics, culture, and globalization impact HIV/AIDS in Mozambican women. Study findings will inform programming and care for women affected by HIV/AIDS, and can further inform donor, NGO, and national policies on prevention and planning of health and social service delivery for vulnerable women in Mozambique.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of peripheral macrophage-derived immune mediators on nociceptors and the evolution of inflammatory pain
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM IMAGING; CELL DEPLETION MODELS; CYTOKINES AND CHEMOKINES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; MACROPHAGE; NEUROIMMUNOLOGY; PAIN; PROTEOMICS; SENSORY NEURON
Abstract-Résumé: Pain is one of the major complaints of patients suffering from various neurological and non-neurological conditions, such as infections, tissue injuries and autoimmune diseases like arthritis and multiple sclerosis. Recent advances have shown that the immune response is a major contributor to pain outcomes. Immune cells, including macrophages, neutrophils and T cells (collectively known as white blood cells), release factors during the immune response. The action of these factors on sensory neurons, those that help us "feel" pain, is a prominent feature of pain caused by inflammation. Several candidates have been studied thus far, though this research has largely been limited to either an immunological or neurobiological perspective. Furthermore, there has never been a systematic, unbiased search for such targets. In this study, we aim to identify all factors produced by macrophages and identify those that have an effect on sensory neurons. This work may reveal novel targets for the development of new therapeutic options for the treatment of pain caused by inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Old and new environmental exposures: focus on flame retardants mixture as a potential risk factor for neurodevelopmental impairment. Follow up of GESTE birth cohort.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARQUEURS D'EFFETS; CHIMIE ANALYTIQUE; HYPERACTIVITE ET DEFICIT DE L'ATTENTION; NEURODEVELOPPEMENT; POLLUANTS EMERGEANTS; POLY-EXPOSITION ET INTERACTION; SANTE DES ENFANTS; SANTE ENVIRONNEMENTALE; EPIDEMIOLOGIE; EVALUATION DES RISQUES
Abstract-Résumé: The potential for environmental contaminants to produce neurobehavioral deficit as a result of in utero exposure has received increasing attention. Emergent pollutants such as polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE), hexabromocyclododecanes (HBCDs) and tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) are of concerns for their potential risks to human health. They are used as brominated flame-retardant (BFR) additives in the manufacture of household items (eg TV sets, toys...). Recently, data showed that PBDE levels in breast milk of North American women are doubling every 5 years. In addition, PBDE levels in pregnant women's plasma are 20 to 106 fold higher than those of Swedish women. HBCDs and TBBA levels have never been monitored in Canadian women.   Foetal brain is more susceptible to toxic exposure due to blood-brain barrier immaturity. In rodents, low doses exposure to BFR during development leads to hyperactivity and neurobehavioral impairments. In addition, foetus is usually exposed to a mixture of pollutants. When mixed, even at low doses, these substances can have additive adverse effects. Animal studies showed that PBDE, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB) and mercury, all present in cord blood, can interact to enhance neurobehavioral defects.  In spite of these observations, there are still no data on combined effect of BFR and other pollutants on neurodevelopment.     I propose to conduct a follow up study which is the first who addresses exposure to PBDE, TBPPA and HBCDs in relation to psychomotor skills and behaviour in childhood. Pre- and post-natal BFR exposure as well as interaction between BFR and known neurotoxic pollutants will be studied. This study is a part of an ongoing study including 800 pregnant women and their babies. We now are processing with the 2-year old follow up. A complete biobank and a database are available to test my hypothesis. The biobank will be used to analyse BFR levels which will be correlated to neurobehaviour skills at 2 and 4 years old.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Firefighter Injury Reduction Enterprise: Wellness Enabled Life & Livelihood  (FIRE-WELL)
Keywords-MotsClés: FIREFIGHTING; FITNESS; MUSCULOSKELETAL; RETURN-TO-WORK; SCREEN; WORK-LIMITATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Firefighters are exposed to significant personal risk while providing essential services. Musculoskeletal (MSK) injuries, poor fitness & cardiovascular health are common problems. Firefighters, their union and employer approached researchers to develop, implement and evaluate an evidence-based "wellness" program to prevent injuries, optimize safe return to work and reduce rising health care costs. The research program has 2 phases. The goal is to evaluate the impact of community-based medical, fitness and MSK injury screening. Phase 1 will examine and characterize health problems identified by a doctor specialized in occupational medicine in a series of 300 firefighters and monitor the health services they require.  In preparation for Phase 2, we will define job demands using motion analysis of firefighting tasks. Then we will conduct a screen of MSK injury and fitness of 150 firefighters with identified signs of emerging MSK problems. From these, 75 will be assigned to a personal education intervention within their fire station about how to perform their work in a manner that reduces risk of injury. We will evaluate our success by measuring health and work indicators at the start, and 6 & 12 months later. Outcomes include; number/type and cost of injuries, lost work, self-reported overall health status, change in fitness and at-work limitations. They will be measured by trustworthy methods. Mathematical models will help us know if this approach reduces the illness and disability burden experienced by firefighters. Cost savings will be put back into the wellness program to enable program expansion and long-term sustainability. Firefighters intend to lead the project and share it with other groups.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the gene-environment interaction in temperamental vulnerability to depression: The role of psychophysiological reactivity to stress.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD; CORTISOL; DEPRESSION; DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOPATHOLOGY; ETIOLOGY; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTION; HPA AXIS; LONGITUDINAL; MULTI-LEVEL MODELING; PSCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL REACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Research indicates that the onset of depression occurs earlier than believed in past decades and it is being increasingly recognized that heterogeneity in the disorder's expression poses the need for re-analysis of a problem once thought to manifest only in adolescence in adulthood. Early detection has the potential to lessen both individual suffering and financial burden on families, businesses, and the economy as preventative strategies are a cost-effective way of potentially stopping a life-persistent problem from developing. Because depression is etiologically heterogeneous and likely rooted in both biological and environmental factors, studies should attempt to reflect this complexity by including measures that tap these domains which is what this research aims to do. The proposed study will be conducted in a sample of 410 three-year-old children from Southwestern Ontario. Each child and their primary caregiver attends a laboratory visit comprised of episodes taken from the Laboratory Temperament Assessment Battery (Lab-TAB), an observational measure of child temperamental emotionality during which time non-invasive DNA collection is conducted. Within a few weeks of the laboratory visit, a home visit is conducted where observational measures of parent-child interactions, and biological measures (salivary cortisol samples) of psychophysiological stress reactivity, are collected. Parent-report measures of child temperament, marital satisfaction, parent personality and parenting behaviors are collected from both parents when possible. At 30 month follow-up, children participate in an adaptation of the Lab-TAB for slightly older children. Also, the primary caregiver and/or co-parent participate in structured interviews at this follow-up to assess chronic stressors and life events occurring over the course of the follow-up period, and for lifetime psychopathology history.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidation of KLF13 role in the genetic circuits that pattern the embryonic heart.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC GROWTH AND DIFFERENTIATION; GENETICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; RECOMBINANT DNA TECHNOLOGY; REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Congenital heart malformations (CHD) represent the single largest class of birth defects in humans with an estimated frequency of 1%. Moreover, they are the leading cause of mortality in infants under one year of age. Accumulating evidence points to a major role for genetic determinants in CHD. Despite remarkable progress over the past decade, CHD-causing gene mutations in humans have only been identified in a minority of cases. Proper function of the heart requires a formation of the four chambered heart in which blood flow is unidirectional. To ensure this, membranous walls - known as septa - separate the left and right atria and ventricles and specialized valves allow normal blood flow. Defects in septa and valves represent the major heart malformations in humans. Previously, we have used genetic and biochemical approaches to further define the role of newly discovered regulatory proteins in heart development and function, and their interactions with each other. In addition, several genes were identified and they were shown to be essential for heart formation and their studies provided the rationale to screen for a linkage between mutations in these genes and human CHD, which in turn identified them as disease causing genes. We have also developed new animal models of human heart disease that will be invaluable in pre-clinical studies aimed at identifying new preventive and therapeutic approaches to heart disease. The overall objectives of this proposal are to identify the genetic circuits that control the gene encoding atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), the heart major secretory product, during embryonic and postnatal development; this in turn will shed light on the temporal and molecular events that pattern the embryonic heart and are essential for proper heart development. These studies will provide further insight in understanding the molecular basis of heart disease and will likely identify potential new candidates for CHD causing genes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translational neuroimaging in alcoholism: identification of altered brain connectivity and treatment efficacy predictors
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOLISM; TRANSLATIONAL NEUROIMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Alcoholism is a common pschiatric disorder with largely unmet treatment needs.  Excellent animal models for this disorder have put forward a number of promising molecular targets for medication development.  Yet, clinical trials aimed at exploiting this potential often fall short of expectations.  We aim to improve the predictive validity of animal tests by means of functional connectivity analysis using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to identify brain response patterns to pharmacotherapy that are comparable between patients and animal models of alcoholism.  To this end we have formed an international consortium with highly complementary expertise in the field of alcoholism and neuroimaging research.  This project will reveal alcoholism specific connectivity maps and knowledge of their modification by clinical reference compounds, i.e. acamprosate and naltrexone, in humans and animals.  Based on this information we expect to predict better the effects of experimental drugs proposed for treatment of alcoholism in human patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Describing pathophysiology to promote focal therapy in treatment of schizophrenia - an animal experimental study
Keywords-MotsClés: SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is characterized by profound disruptions in cognition and emotion.  Despite pharmaco-therapeutic progresses, a considerable percentage of patients has no or only partial response to treatment.  Development of more efficacious treatments is indispensible but crucially depends on an advanced elucidation of the progressive pathophysiological mechanisms underlying schizophrenia.  Given methodological and ethical limitations of human studies, the use of appropriate and valid animal models of schizophrenia is a promising tool for such endeavours.  The present project uses the maternal immune stimulation rat model of schizophrenia and deep brain stimulation (DBS) as an investigative tool to modulate neural activity of selected brain areas and associated networks in order to i) correlate the emergance of a schizophrenic phenotype with the development of dysfunctions at different levels of neurobiological integrity; ii) study bi-directional consequences of DBS and iii) study the preventive potential of pre-symptomatic activity-modulation on the emergence of behavioral and neurobiological abnormalities.  The project will foster our understanding of dysfunctional neural circuitries in schizoprenia and set a strong interdisciplinary foundation for the translational application and advancement of DBS as a novel focal and causative strategy in the treatment of therapy-resistant schizophrenia.

Keywords-MotsClés: IMPULSE CONTROL DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: The lack of control of impulsivity (i.e. Impulse Control Disorders; ICD) can lead to various disorders that encompass drug addiction, pathological gambling, compulsive shopping, binge eating, hypersexuality.  In the past years, the role of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in impulsivity has been highlighted.  The STN is the current target for the surgical treatment of Parkinson's Disease using Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS). Interestingly, PD is a disease often associated with ICD.  The aim of the present project is thus to characterise the effects of STN DBS in various forms of ICD in intact rats and assessed in various behavioural tasks measuring impulsive choice, gambling and addiction.  The studies carried out in rats will be paralleled by clinical studies characterizing the effects of STN DBS applied in PD patients on ICD, measured in various tasks such as Go/NoGo and the Iowa gambling task.  This project, bringing together experts in rat STN, impulsivity and clinical experts of STN DBS in patients, should lead to a better understanding of STN contribution in ICD processes and may also lead to a more refined prescription of STN DBS for the treatment of ICD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Omega-3 Fatty Acids for Treatment of Intestinal Failure Associated Liver Disease: A Translational Research Study
Keywords-MotsClés: INTESTINAL FAILURE; INTESTINAL FAILURE ASSOCIATED LIVER DISEASE; LIVER DISEASE; PARENTERAL NUTRITION; POLYUNSATURATED FATTY ACIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Liver disease is the main cause of death in babies and children who depend on intravenous nutrition because their bowel is not adequate to absorb nutrients from food. The most common cause of this so called intestinal failure is short bowel syndrome, when babies are born without part of the bowel or lose bowel length with surgeries needed after birth. Early studies we conducted in piglets in our institution suggested that using a fish based intravenous fat rather then a soy based intravenous fat might improve this liver disease. Soy is the most common intravenous fat used in Canada. Many childrens hospitals around Canada have since started using the fish oil for intestinal failure and other conditions even though we don't fully understand how it works or what the risks might be for babies who depend on fat to grow. We can help provide some answers by going back to our original baby piglet model. It is not possible to undertake some kinds of research studies in sick human babies to answer these questions. We cannot always do studies in sick babies quickly to gain answers, but we can do this with animal studies. Our research group includes frontline clinicians, who care for these babies, as well as senior nutrition scientists, who are motivated to undertake this research to advance and improve how we are currently looking after sick babies with intestinal failure.
