TitreApplicationTitle: Risk of brain cancer from exposure to radiofrequency fields from wireless telecommunication devices in childhood and adolescence
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOURS; CASE-CONTROL; CHILDREN AND ADOLESCENTS; ENVIRONMENTAL EXPOSURES; MOBILE PHONES
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, the widespread use of mobile phones has drawn public attention to their possible human health and safety effects. A substantial body of experimental evidence has demonstrated that radiofrequency (RF) radiation affects biologic processes that are believed to influence the development of cancers.  The few epidemiologic studies evaluating the association between mobile phone use and cancers have been limited to an adult population and also by several factors particularly insufficient exposure times. With many unanswered questions regarding children and adolescents, the European Commission funded an international multi-centre case control study including 13 countries. The present Canadian study is to conduct a national epidemiologic case-control study in major Canadian metropolitan cities of brain tumours (malignant and benign) diagnosed in young people aged 10 to 24 years in relation to EMF exposure from mobile telephones and other environmental exposures. Such a study would be timely and cost-effective since it could benefit from expertise of the EU members and adapt the protocol and questionnaire developed by the EU consortium. Results of this project are expected to be of great importance in the assessment of potential health risks from mobile telephones as well as from EMF in general.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vascular Health and Disease: New Concepts & Therapeutic Opportunities
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERY; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; RESTENOSIS; STENT
Abstract-Résumé: Maintaining blood vessels in a state of health is an important ongoing process. Unhealthy blood vessels can block and prevent blood flow to vital organs such as the heart and brain, thereby causing heart attacks, strokes and sometimes death. To reduce the development of blockages in arteries the human body can activate defense mechanisms. One mechanism is to prevent the build-up of cholesterol in the artery wall. Another mechanism is to enlist the services of somewhat magical cells (in that they can change into various forms) to either repair arteries that are foming blockages or prevent their occurrence. However, both of these defense mechanisms are typically reduced in those very patients who develop blockaged arteries. In this research proposal we will address new and exciting ways of improving blood vessel health with the aim of limiting the serious problems that patients may suffer when an artery is unhealthy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of antiviral drug resistance in seasonal and pandemic influenza strains and evaluation of new therapeutic modalities
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; ANTIVIRAL; IMMUNOMODULATOR; INFLUENZA; MATHEMATICAL MODEL; NEURAMINIDASE INHIBITOR; RESISTANCE; REVERSE GENETICS; VIRAL FITNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza viruses constitute a serious threat to mankind through yearly epidemics affecting 10-20% of the Canadian population and occasional pandemics as shown by the rapid spread of the pandemic 2009 H1N1 virus throughout the world. Besides general public health measures and vaccines, antivirals have an important role in the management of influenza infections by decreasing the number and/or the severity of influenza cases. However, antiviral drug resistance can seriously limit the efficacy of prophylactic or therapeutic antiviral interventions. In this research proposal, we seek to optimize antiviral treatment through a better knowledge of the mechanisms of drug resistance as well as to assess new therapeutic modalities for influenza infections including combination antiviral therapy and agents that modulate the immune response to influenza viruses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Cohort Obstructive Lung Disease (CanCOLD)
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; COHORT STUDY; COPD; PROSPECTIVE LONGITUDINAL STUDY; TISSUE BANK
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the fourth leading cause of death in Canada. People with COPD, the umbrella term for chronic bronchitis and emphysema, often don't get the care they need because of a lack of knowledge of the diseases among both physicians and patients in addition to a lack of awareness and of appropriate diagnosis.  Epidemiological research (in association with basic research) is needed to develop a framework to combat this major health problem, by better characterization of the population of men and women at risk and patients with early disease, by better understanding which factors modifiable through health interventions are related to disease severity and progression of COPD. This will be possible through the Canadian Cohort Obstructive Lung Disease (CanCOLD), a pan-Canadian longitudinal study involving approximately 2,000 participants at nine sites. CanCOLD will be the first study to assess COPD consequence in men and women, and to evaluate a conceptual model of disease severity based on patient's health perception (health-related quality of life) and disease evolution. This project will extend to a longitudinal follow up (5 years or beyond) and will allow to have a better understanding of the lifestyle risk factors, not only smoking but also diet, physical activity, environmental exposures and co morbid conditions. The results of the study will greatly help to assist decision makers in developing policies and new solutions to improve the diagnosis, the management of COPD and the organization of care related to chronic diseases, to optimize health care service use and reduce the burden on the society. Furthermore, this Canadian study will enable the resource intensity and research capacity in COPD to address challenging and important research questions in a more concerted and high-impact fashion.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of S1P receptor directed pharmaceutical agents on central nervous system myelination
Keywords-MotsClés: CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; MYELIN; OLIGODENDROCYTES; S1P RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The neurologic disorder multiple sclerosis (MS) involves injury and destruction of the myelin membrane that ensheaths nerve fibers (axons) and is required for efficient electrical conduction with the central nervous system (CNS). We postulate that the overall extent of neurologic dysfunction in MS patients reflects both the extent of injury of myelin and its cell of origin the oligodendrocyte (OL) and the extent of repair mediated by OL progenitor cells (OPCs). FTY720 is a sphingosine-1phosphate receptor (S1PR) agonist about to enter clinical use in MS because of its effects on the peripheral immune system. As this agent can access the central nervous system (CNS) and S1PRs are expressed on all cells of the CNS, we ask what effects FTY720 and related SIPR directed agents will have on protecting OLs from injury in MS and on the capacity of OPCs to contribute to repair.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel in vivo Mechanisms of Neutrophil Mediated Host Defense
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNITY; ADJUVANTS; DENDRITIC CELL BIOLOGY; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; MONOCYTES; SEPSIS; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS TLR; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Endotoxin from microbes has been implicated in the pathogenesis of severe life-threatening infections and septic shock through the activation of innate receptors (Toll-like receptors, TLR). Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is well known to activate the innate immune system through TLR4, and inhibitors of TLR are in clinical trial for treatment of sepsis.  In contrast, stimulants of the TLR are being used to activate specific immune responses to improve vaccines. A new synthetic TLR4 agonist gluco-pyranosylphospho-lipid A (GLA) is been developed as a potential adjuvant.  Therefore in one situation TLR4 activation is detrimental while in the other TLR4 stimulation is desired. Clearly large knowledge gaps exist in our understanding of TLR4 mediated inflammation and immunity and these gaps need resolution as we attempt to manipulate the human immune system. Dendritic cells (DC) are highly specialized immune cells that express multiple Toll-receptors including TLR4, and act as a bridge between the innate and adaptive systems.  Depending on the initial inflammatory stimuli DC directly influence the type of T cell response, which can either positively or negatively impact the host.  Monocytes and monocyte subsets are also important immune cells that are activated through TLR4.  They are intimately related to DC, but many unresolved issues remain concerning the relationship and contribution of each of these cells to inflammation and immunity. We are interested in determining how molecules that stimulate the innate inflammatory immune response through TLR4 (LPS, and GLA) alter the function of DC subsets, monocytes and monocyte subsets in mice and humans.  We will determine the effects of both GLA and LPS on these cells in mice and use this information to provide scientific direction to aid a phase I randomized human trial evaluating the immunogenicity and safety of the TLR4 agonist GLA.  Key concepts of human immunology will be gained for both vaccine science and host defence.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: VIEILLISSEMENT; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancing Participation In the Community by improving Wheelchair Skills (EPIC Wheels): A randomized controlled trial.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY; COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION; MIXED METHODS; MOBILITY; OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY; OLDER ADULTS; WHEELCHAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Canada's population is aging rapidly and maintaining independence among older adults is a critical factor from a health, social and economic perspective. Mobility impairment is the most common issue for older adults in Canada, and threatens their independent participation in community-based activities such as shopping, social events and attending appointments. When the ability to safely and independently walk is compromised, a manual wheelchair is commonly prescribed. However, using a wheelchair is a highly skilled activity and older adults typically receive little, if any, training. Current research indicates those who use a wheelchair participate less in community activities; however, it is unclear how much the skill of operating a wheelchair contributes to this restriction. The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether providing comprehensive and standardized wheelchair skill training program will increase community participation among older adults and identify which skills are most critical. Participants receiving the training program will be compared to those who receive the typical prescription with limited training. In addition, a select group of participants will be interviewed to solicit their experience and identify which skills they found most important to their success. This information will provide valuable input for health care at many levels. Older adult consumers will learn about a service that can improve their ability to maintain a healthy and active lifestyle in their community. The research findings, including the unique experience of older adults and their priorities, will translate into concrete guidelines for rehabilitation professionals, and direct changes in healthcare policy and provision of rehabilitation care. Ultimately, this knowledge will educate wheelchair consumers, impact clinical practice among rehabilitation professionals, and inform government and stakeholders who fund and create policies for healthcare provision.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanistic study of the anti-dyskinetic action of the dopaminergic D4 receptor antagonist L-745,870 in the 6-OHDA-lesioned rat model of Parkinson's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: 6-OHDA; 870; D4 RECEPTOR; DOPAMINE; DYSKINESIA; GLUTAMATE; IN VIVO MICRODIALYSIS; L-745; L-DOPA; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; RAT
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is caused by a deficiency of the chemical substance dopamine in the brain and the treatment of PD aims at restoring brain dopamine levels. However, long-term treatment is associated with the emergence of abnormal movements called dyskinesia, which affect virtually all PD individuals, if they are treated long enough. We have recently demonstrated that blocking a receptor by which dopamine exerts its effects, called the dopaminergic D4 receptor, alleviates the severity of dyskinesia, in both the rat and macaque models of PD. However, the mechanisms by which D4-receptor blocking agents exert their beneficial effect remain unknown. We hypothesise that blocking dopaminergic D4 receptors modulates the release of dopamine and another chemical substance called glutamate, in the striatum, an area of the brain involved in the emergence of dyskinesia. The proposed study therefore aims at verifying this hypothesis in the rat model of PD. Rats will rendered parkinsonian by the injection of a toxin and will then be treated until they exhibit dyskinesia. The levels of both dopamine and glutamate will be measured by a technique called in vivo microdialysis, in the striatum of rats following the exposition or lack thereof to a dopaminergic D4-blocking agent. We believe that the levels of glutamate and dopamine will be reduced in the striatum of rats treated with a D4-blocking drug. The goal of the proposed study is to improve the understanding and the treatment of dyskinesia. Ultimately, the findings of the proposed study could lead to the development of new, more selective therapies against dyskinesia, with potentially less adverse effects. The development of new therapies against dyskinesia is likely to benefit a great number of people suffering from PD, especially with the ageing of the population in the Western hemisphere.

TitreApplicationTitle: Therapeutic Hypothermia:  Exploring the Association of Processes of Care with Outcomes of Cardiac Arrest
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ARREST; LOGISTIC REGRESSION; POST-RESUSCITATION CARE; PROCESSES OF CARE; THERAPEUTIC HYPOTHERMIA
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiac arrest is a common and deadly medical emergency.  Up to 45,000 out of hospital cardiac arrests occur each year in Canada and of these only 6% survive.  Many patients who do not die immediately and develop a complex disease called post-cardiac arrest syndrome, which often proves fatal.  Until recently, treatment options have been limited.  Two studies showed cooling the body and brain after cardiac arrest improved survival rates and brain function.  However, there are many questions about how to best cool patients that remain unanswered, particularly when to cool, how to cool and how long to cool.  Our objective is to answer these questions about how best to cool the body and the brain.  Based on what we know to date, we think that starting early and cooling longer as well as using medication to help patients be comfortable during cooling will improve their survival and brain function.  A network of 37 rural and urban hospitals throughout the southern Ontario regions of Durham, Hamilton, Halton, Muskoka, Peel, Simcoe, Toronto and York are participating in research studies to improve the care of patients who arrive at one of these hospitals after surviving an out of hospital cardiac arrest.  This network has been working together for 3 years and has an active and helpful website encouraging the use of cooling in post arrest patients (www.sparcnetwork.ca).  From the data collected on these patients, we plan to construct a statistical model that will use improved survival and brain function to identify the best way to cool the body and brain.  Finding the answers to these important questions may potentially improve the quality of care provided in all hospitals and increase the number of patients that survive with improved brain function after out of hospital cardiac arrest.

TitreApplicationTitle: Connective Tissue Growth Factor and fibrocyte recruitment to the myocardium
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMYOCYTE; COLLAGEN; CTGF; FIBROBLAST; FIBROCYTES; FIBROSIS; HEART FAILURE; TGFBETA
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is considered to be the number one killer of Canadians. An important part of many heart diseases is a process of heart scarring also called fibrosis that occurs in response to injury. Unfortuntely, while this process is benneficial initialy it can lead to replacement of heart muscle and worsening heart function. This means that when fibrosis occurs it can result in difficulty for the heart to pump blood into the body, a condition that is called heart failure and is associated with a high mortality rate. The mechanisms that results in fibrosis are not well characterized.  Our laboratory is interested in studying the mechanisms that lead to heart muscle fibrosis, including why and how particular cells are attracted to the heart and participate in this process. In the present project we will study the role of a specific protein called connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) in the development of heart fibrosis. We will use an established animal model of heart fibrosis in which animals are given Angiotensin II (AngII). Using this model we will look at the levels of CTGF produced in heart tissue and characterize the possible mechanisms by which this molecule can recruit cells from the circulation that have recently been shown to be important in the eventual development of fibrosis. What is unique about our project is that we will be investigating role of CTGF in recruiting a novel cell that is now believed to come from the bone marrow and be responsible for the development of fibrosis. The name of this specialized cell is a fibrocyte or a fibroblast progenitor cell. We believe that knowledge gained from this study will lead to important treatment options for patients with heart fibrosis and heart failure. The only treatment of end stage heart failure remains heart transplantation but is limited to approximately 10 patients per year in Nova Scotia largely due to donor shortage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the role of BRK in breast cancer formation and metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; BREAST TUMOR KINASE; CELL INVASION; EPITHELIAL-TO-MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION; METASTASIS; MIGRATION; PROLIFERATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TYROSINE KINASE; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women worldwide and a serious public health issue in Canada with 1 in 9 women at risk. Statistics Canada reports more than 22,000 new diagnoses in Canada every year and over 5,000 deaths. Elevated expression of BReast tumor Kinase (BRK) occurs in about 60% of breast tumors, but the oncogenic, prognostic, diagnostic and physiological roles of BRK overexpression have not been clarified. The human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), overexpressed in about 25-30% of breast cancers, is targeted for breast cancer treatment with the drug Herceptin. We have previously established that BRK contributes to the oncogenic effects of HER2 in breast cancers. In this proposal we intend to determine the oncogenic properties of BRK. We will knockdown BRK in breast cancer cells and introduce BRK into normal cells and determine the effect on tumor formation, breast cancer cell morphogenesis and metastasis using in vitro and in vivo assays.  We will also assess if BRK is associated with specific breast tumor subtypes and/or tumor grades, by analyzing the expression of BRK in a panel of clinically classified breast cancer cell lines, human breast tumors and tissue microarrays. Together, these studies will define the physiological role of BRK in mammary tumorigenesis and validate BRK as a possible new target for breast cancer therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term consequences of prenatal infection on behaviour and brain: Role of glycogen synthase kinase 3.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; BEHAVIOURAL TESTING; BRAIN; DEVELOPMENT; IMMUNE SYSTEM; IN VIVO ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; PROTEIN ANALYSIS; PSYCHIATRIC ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Psychiatric illness severely affects many thousands of Canadians. Increased understanding of the causes of psychiatric illness may aid in the goal of developing improved treatments or preventative therapies. Adverse events early in life are strongly associated with psychiatric illnesses such as schizophrenia and autism. Recent evidence provides direct support for the role of prenatal infection (i.e., exposure to an infection while in utero) as a predisposing factor for psychiatric illness in the offspring. The present research seeks to further understand the specific consequences of prenatal infection using a rat model of viral infection. Discrete measures related to learning and memory and their underlying neural circuits will be taken from rats whose mothers were exposed to either a viral mimetic compound or a control treatment while pregnant. In addition, the potential benefits of a novel strategy aimed at reducing the negative consequences of the infection will be tested. These experiments will significantly increase understanding of the consequences of prenatal infection and potentially provide novel avenues for prevention of psychiatric illnesses such as schizophrenia and autism.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse salariale pour nouveau chercheur - Annonce de priorités : programme de partenariats régionaux - Saskatchewan
ClasseRechercheFR: INFACTUS DU MYOCARDE; APOPLEXIE, INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Heart Protection from Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury by Multidrug Treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR; CONTRACTILE PROTEINS; FUNCTIONAL PROTEOMICS; ISCHEMIA-REPERFUSION; ISOLATED CARDIOMYOCYTES; ISOLATED HEART PERFUSION; MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASES; MULTIDRUG TREATMENT; MYOSIN LIGHT CHAIN; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: The development and progression of heart disease has been associated with the generation of toxic oxygen compounds, known as reactive oxygen species (ROS). These ROS can be produced in every cell of the heart and cause a high degree of damage to the cells and even death. The process by which damage to the cells and the heart occurs remains unknown. ROS can act on proteins responsible for contractility (contractile proteins) of the heart and modify them. I hypothesize that these contractile proteins will be more likely to be broken down by other proteins (proteolytic enzymes) and this break down of contractile proteins is responsible for the abnormal contraction (contractile dysfunction) of the heart after a heart attack (myocardial infarction). The major objectives are: (1) Determine if the use of drugs that prevent modification of proteins by toxic oxygen compounds (ROS) or inhibit the proteins responsible for protein break down (proteolytic enzymes) can protect the heart against cardiac contractile dysfunction (abnormal heart contractility. (2) Determine if using a combination of these drugs in sub-protective doses will show an additive effect.  The research proposed in this application will provide new and very important information that will help us understand the processes responsible for abnormal heart contraction observed in several heart diseases. Also, combining drugs that prevent generation of ROS, modification of proteins and activation of proteolytic enzymes will be a very important strategy for treating heart disease.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de fonctionnement - Annonce de priorités : Programme de partenariats régionaux - Terre Neuve et Labrador
TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of novel genes causing pulmonary fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: BENCH TO BEDSIDE; INHERITED DISEASE; NEXT GENERATION DNA SEQUENCING; PULMONARY FIBROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is an adult-onset lung disease. In Canada, about 20,000 individuals are affected by IPF and its prevalence is expected to double in the next 20 years. The same number of individuals die from IPF each year as from breast cancer. The only treatment that improves survival is lung transplant. Without treatment, mean survival ranges from 2 to 4 years. Sporadic and familial (FPF) forms of IPF have been recognized.  Preliminary Data: Over the past five years, we have generated much preliminary data regarding FPF. Thus far, we have recruited 43 affected sporadic patients and 63 patients belonging to 17 FPF families, and performed genetic analyses to rule out the known causative genes. We have estimated the prevalence of IPF in Newfoundland is over 20 times that reported in other northern European derived populations. Objective: The goals are (1) to identify mutations in novel genes that cause FPF; (2) to offer the families participating in the study important genetic information in order to provide better clinical management. Research Plan: In order to identify novel genes causing FPF we will: (1) continue to recruit additional families to obtain a large population-based cohort of IPF patients that can be used to identify novel genes and to validate these discoveries; (2) to sequence the DNA in families using a state-of-the-art technology, called next generation sequencing, in order to identify gene mutations. Relevance: Although the familial form of PF is relatively rare, identifying gene(s) that are mutated in these families will improve our understanding of the biologic pathways that are altered in patients with the more common sporadic form of IPF, eventually leading to improved therapeutic management. Gene discovery could potentially reduce the cost to the health care system, because of reduced clinical screening, since we will be able to identify individuals who are at-risk of developing the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: ARRT: Adaptive and Robust Radiation Therapy treatment planning for lung cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: RADIATION THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in Canada and worldwide. Improving current methods of treatment is paramount to increasing survival and reducing the rising costs of managing this disease. Radiation therapy is a core technology used to treat lung cancer. Radiation is delivered to the patient using external beams of high energy x-rays aimed at the tumor. However, there are several challenges associated with delivering high quality treatments. First, since radiation damages healthy tissue, the amount of radiation delivered to the tumour is limited by the radiation tolerance of nearby organs such as the lung, heart, and spinal cord. Second, lung tumours are subject to irregular movements caused by patient breathing. As a result, the radiation beam may miss part of the target or may end up delivering increased dose to the healthy tissue. Third, the tumour's size, geometry and metabolic activity will change over the course of a typical multi-week treatment. Current clinical protocols typically do not adapt to these changes. The goal of our research is to improve the efficacy of radiation therapy treatments for lung cancer. In this project, we will address current limitations by developing a new treatment planning method based on sophisticated mathematical techniques. We will develop a mathematical model that optimizes treatments and, in comparison to traditional methods, allows more dose to be delivered to the tumour while keeping dose to the healthy tissues low. Our model will account for the presence of healthy lung tissue, the motion of the tumour during treatment, and the evolution of the tumour's characteristics over multiple weeks. We will test our methodology on clinical data, and we will develop protocols to ensure such advanced treatments can be delivered within the clinical constraints under which hospitals currently operate. Our collaborative team brings together researchers from both engineering and health sciences to pursue this innovative research project. In the long term, our technology has the potential to impact therapies for many types of cancer and to improve the health of cancer patients in Canada and worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engineering low-cost nanotechnology based molecular diagnostics using paper
Keywords-MotsClés: DIAGNOSTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Emerging infectious diseases continue to pose threats to hospitalized patients, individuals made vulnerable by immune compromise, and residents of long-term care facilities, as well as otherwise healthy community residents. The dynamic nature of microbial populations necessitates a nimble, dynamic, and creative approach to disease control, and requires continuous evolution of public health policy and practice. Here our objective is to create a simple, low cost device capable of detecting multiple microbial targets in a rapid manner. The successful creation of such a device would enable identification, assist in timely proper treatment, and could prevent their spread. Because of the short-timeframe of the project, we selected to focus on highly prevalent genital tract and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and leverage our collaboration with the Ontario Public Health Laboratory, a high volume clinical testing facility with established experience in assay development, evaluation and clinical interpretation that also houses an extensive repository of archived clinical specimens and isolates. This project will provide the proof-of-concept for the feasibility of the technology and once established we should be able to adapt our methodologies to other infectious disease panels (e.g., blood-borne infection, respiratory, food-borne and gastro-enteric) into our device.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hydrogel-based microfluidic cell culture system for controlled drug dosage effects
Keywords-MotsClés: MICROFLUIDICS
Abstract-Résumé: OBJECTIVE: This project will develop a microfluidic system to culture, characterize, image, and screen cells within a single automated, portable platform, with large potential impact to improve cell-based drug screening. BACKGROUND: The 2-D monolayer-based method of cell culture is well established in molecular and cell biology. Recently, there has been increased interest in 3-D cell culture, in which cells are embedded in a material that mimics the ECM. Interaction between cells and the ECM in vivo regulates differentiation, migration, and many other functions. As a cancer model, the tissue culture environment can have a dramatic influence on cell behaviour, such as modified morphology, gene expression, and proliferation. This phenomenon will have a crucial impact in the pharmacological response of a tumour cell to therapeutic agents. Thus, drugs developed using a 2-D screening system may not subsequently have the same activity against solid tumours, contributing to the high attrition rate in drug development. APPROACH: As a new paradigm for cell-based testing, this microscale platform will address a gap between in vitro and animal models by providing a simple, scalable tool to apply standardized protocols used in cellular response assays. This research will combine a hydrogel-based method 3-D of culturing cells with on-chip microfluidic flow control for precise fluid handling. Breast tumour cells will be seeded into an array of chambers where they can form tumour-like aggregates. We will use this system will to conduct controlled, repeated treatments and monitoring of the effects of therapeutic drugs and drug combinations on the cells. We will use the on-chip mixing and fluid handling capability to recreate more realistic pharmacokinetic profiles of compounds to examine the relationship between dose and concentration with response. The use of transparent materials allows the integration of these chips onto high-throughput imaging systems, with advantages in speed, cost, and efficiency. This platform will thus provide a means to assess the impact of treatment standards as well as new treatments designed to achieve more personalized therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implantable telemetric devices for electrophysiological and behavioural research using rodent disease models
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Mice and rats are the workhorses of basic biomedical research. Numerous disease models have been created in mice by modification of specific genes that when disrupted lead to symptoms similar to those seen in humans. Mice are small, which is advantageous for housing and breeding, but presents challenges to physiological and behavioural studies. Evaluating neural activity or movement of awake and freely moving mice is hampered when the animal is tethered to the recording apparatus by power and data transmission lines. The exponential pace of wireless technology development microelectronics and microprocessor miniaturization during the last 5 years has enabled telemetry (wireless radio) based devices to record neural signals and one can find some of these solutions commercially available for large rats. Devices that can electrically stimulate and record neural activity in mice are not commercially available. Another identified need for research and drug development is for routine and long-term monitoring of activity levels and movement characteristics in rats and mice. We have developed a prototype telemetric neural recording and nerve stimulating device which is remotely powered by radio frequency waves, small enough to be for long term (> 4 weeks) subcutaneous implantation in animals as small as mice or young rats. In this project we will improve device powering, add capability to simultaneously monitor/stimulate 4 animals/cage and refinethe fabrication process by application of ASICs and/or microfab/MeMs technologies. We will add a rechargeable energy storage element that will allow it to continue to function briefly outside the radio frequency power field. We will also create a telemetric 3-axis inertial motion unit which will monitor locomotion, rearing tremor, abnormal breathing patterns and other movements which are used to evaluate activity levels, disease progression and treatment efficacy in a number of behavioural models. During the funding period devices that we develop will be applied in experimental situations to try to improve recovery from stroke, spinal cord injury, monitor disease progression in Rett model mice and evaluate therapies to improve outcome in fetal alcohol syndrome rats.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Phone Oximeter: A simple, mobile device for respiratory disease management in the community
Keywords-MotsClés: PULSE OXIMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: Respiratory disease is a major health problem in Canada. Over 3 million Canadians have to cope with serious respiratory conditions. Effective diagnosis and monitoring requires ready access to clinical expertise and technologies that can assess lung function accurately. The capability of pulse oximeters to non-invasively measure oxygen saturation in the blood (SpO2) through a sensor placed on the fingertip has already greatly improved patient safety in hospitals (a reduction in SpO2 strongly predicts abnormal lung function). The extension of this medical device into homes will greatly improve the management of respiratory disease in non-hospital settings. Our goal is to develop the "Phone Oximeter", an intelligent, mobile device for the diagnosis and management of respiratory disease in the community. Current portable pulse oximeters are limited in use because of their cost, cumbersome nature and inability to communicate with clinicians in real-time. Our innovative tool will overcome these limitations by integrating a pulse oximeter with a cell phone. In addition, it will improve the accuracy of a standard pulse oximeter; the inherent processing power of a cell phone will be used to extract additional information about other key signs of respiratory disease from the pulse oximeter's raw data, such as respiratory rate and heart rate variability. Via an easy-to-use, intuitive display, the Phone Oximeter will convert this information into real-time clinical advice that is accessible even to patients. When connected to a network, the Phone Oximeter will readily transmit critical information to and from central support and referral locations. This research will support the full time training of two types of student (engineering graduate and summer students), as well as clinical research fellows, residents and medical students. This healthcare service will be available to all Canadians, regardless of where they live. Prompt, appropriate action for disease management will reverse clinical deterioration. Early intervention will reduce unnecessary procedures, improve health, save lives and reduce long term costs by minimizing resource wastage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Muscle rehabilitation of cerebral palsy patients recieving botulinum toxin type-A (Botox) treatments
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL PALSY
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Cerebral Palsy (CP) is an umbrella term designating a group of non-progressive neurological disorders. One common treatment in CP is chemical denervation of spastic muscles using botulinum toxin type-A (BTXA). However, in pilot work we demonstrated that BTXA injections cause atrophy, fat invasion and loss of structural integrity in target and non-target muscles, thereby severely compromising the strength and function of these muscles. We hypothesize that much of the deterioration of BTXA-injected muscles could be prevented with direct electrical stimulation of the target muscles. Objectives: The primary purpose of this project is to test the hypothesis that direct muscle stimulation training prevents BTXA-induced muscle atrophy, fat invasion and structural degeneration of target and non-target muscles in patients with CP and in a rabbit model of BTXA injections. A secondary purpose is to develop a small and easy to operate functional muscle stimulation unit for safe use by patients at home. Scientific Approach: This study consists of three parts: (i) a controlled animal study of BTXA injections with and without direct muscle stimulation training; (ii) a clinical study with CP patients receiving/not receiving direct muscle stimulation training during the BTXA intervention period; and (iii) a design study aimed at developing a cheap, safe and easy to use direct muscle stimulation device for training at home. Significance: BTXA treatments are a frequently used modality to chemically ablate muscles in CP patients to restore joint excursion and function. Following BTXA treatment, muscles should be strong and allow for mobility and improved functionality. However, this is not the case, because of the loss of strength and structural integrity of the target musculature. Here, we will test an approach that will retain all advantages of the BTXA treatment while simultaneously protect the target muscles thus provide for a better patient outcome. If successful, the results of this study will have a direct and profound impact on BTXA treatments in CP patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Risk factors and optimization model for breast cancer screening
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among Canadian women. One in 9 women is expected to develop breast cancer during her lifetime, and of these, one in 28 will die. Although the causes have not yet been completely identified, a woman can minimize the chances of developing breast cancer and possibly dying from it, as some factors are known to increase the risk of formation and development of a cancer cell. The main objectives of the proposed project are summarized as follows: (1) Identify, study and describe the effects and associated costs of factors that have the potential to influence breast cancer incidence and mortality rates: We aim to investigate breast cancer incidence and/or mortality in Canadian society, considering risk factors, as well as screening and treatment policies. We will build a risk model to estimate the chance of developing breast cancer and the risk of dying from it over a specific period of time for age-based population groups. (2) Develop an evidence-based tool for policy-makers to evaluate the long-term effectiveness of various screening strategies: The results will enable decision-makers to evaluate which screening strategies work best, thus decreasing death rates and eliminating unnecessary costs. To this end, we will first model breast cancer progression using appropriate stochastic processes. We will then use the model to find the optimal initial and ending screening ages and screening schedules for different age and risk based population groups.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel technologies for cognitive repair
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: The Problem: Neurological disease such as stroke, Parkinson's disease and even neurological changes underlying normal aging are commonly associated with cognitive impairments (problems with attention, memory and thinking) that are difficult to treat and result in chronic disability, dependence on family resources and chronic need for continued health care resources. Given the high prevalence of these diseases, there is great need for better treatments. The current challenge is that current health care resources and effective treatments for cognitive impairment are limited. With the advances and availability of flexible and powerful computer software and hardware, there is now an opportunity to translate current knowledge in cognitive neuroscience into novel, evidence-based, computerized technologies that can provide intensive and accessible treatment in home or hospital. The Solution: Our proposed multi-disciplinary project includes cognitive scientists, neuro-rehabilitation specialists, biomedical engineers and human computer interface designers to develop novel computerized, game-like technologies for the assessment (Dalhousie Computerized Attention Assessment Battery, DalCAB) and targeted treatment (Cognitive Repair Kit) of cognitive dysfunction. The goal of the proposed CHRP project is to conduct iterative usability studies on computer prototypes currently available. These studies will ensure that our products will be flexible enough to be usable by a range of end-users, many of whom will have functional limitations (e.g., sensory-motor deficits) due to the neurological involvement. These sensory and motor limitations need thorough consideration in an iterative prototype design and testing cycle in order to identify hardware and/or software innovations so that intended clients will not experience any significant impediments to their use. The ultimate goal of our research program is to develop a flexible, commercializable computer-based cognitive assessment and intervention package for improving the adaptive functioning and quality of life for individuals who have cognitive deficits

TitreApplicationTitle: Signal analysis of T-wave alternans for predicting sudden cardiac deaths
Keywords-MotsClés: SUDDEN CARDIAC EATH
Abstract-Résumé: T-wave alternans (TWA) refers to the changes in T wave shape or amplitude appearing every second heart beat on a surface electrocardiogram (ECG). The magnitude of TWA signal is very small, in the microvolt range, but some clinical trials have recently suggested that its presence can predict sudden death in patients with heart disease. From a signal analysis perspective, the accurate measurement of the TWA signal is challenging due to very low signal to noise ratio (SNR), and signal non-stationarity. Several noise sources can potentially confound TWA signal detection, including periodic noise from movement or respiration, and non-periodic/spurious noise. The primary objective of this proposal will be to develop a more accurate TWA detection algorithm that tackles the signal non-stationarity and provides robust measurement of TWA signal parameters even in low SNR conditions.In the proposed techniques the non-stationarity of the TWA signal is handled by transforming the signal to a joint time-frequency representation (TFR) which provides the time-varying spectral representation. The marginals computed as first-order and second-order moments along time or frequency direction in a proper TFR will provide features such as instantaneous frequency (IF) and instantaneous bandwidth (IBW). IF and IBW could be used to characterize the non-stationary TWA and thereby lead to better detection and estimation of TWA. The secondary objective will be to evaluate the accuracy of the proposed techniques in risk stratifying patients with heart disease. This will be achieved by measuring TWA every 6 months from a 24-hour ambulatory ECG recording in 450 patients with heart disease, and then following these patients prospectively for 2 years to determine whether TWA predicts subsequent death or nonfatal ventricular arrhythmias. Developing accurate risk assessment algorithms is essential to identify patients at highest risk of sudden death who will derive the greatest survival benefit from costly medical device therapy, such as implantable defibrillators.

TitreApplicationTitle: Detection and simulation of femoroacetabular impingement
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTER SIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) of the hip is the main reason that total hip arthroplasty is required. In the past decade, a growing body of literature suggests that up to 80% of adult idiopathic hip OA cases are caused by a condition known as femoracetabular impingement (FAI). FAI occurs as a result of abnormalities in the femoral head and/or acetabulum. These problems lead to significant articular damage. An experienced surgeon determines the location and the amount of bone that requires cutting in order to remodel the bone shape to remove the impingement. If too much bone is removed the hip may be weakened resulting in a possible bone fracture. Conversely if too little bone is removed, the surgery may be unsuccessful and further surgery may be required. The development of computer assisted guidance software is required to help clinicians to perform the process in a more precise manner. We propose to (i) make technical enhancements (in image processing, computer visualization, 3D reconstruction, and statistical analysis) and (ii) build basic components that will be used for a computer-assisted system to help diagnosis, pre-operative planning, and visualization. In the future, through the development of these improved diagnostic tools, as well as surgical planning/guidance software, clinicians will be better suited to treat this deformity in a more precise manner as well as in a less invasive way facilitating and optimizing patient recovery and function; this will lead to the overall improved wellbeing of patients, less stress on the system due to repeated surgery, and a lower cost to the Canadian healthcare system. This research brings together a team of nationally and internationally recognized researchers and clinicians, and will place Canada at a strategic position in this critical area of research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pulsatile displacement of the lamina cribrosa in the pathogenesis of glaucoma: development of a novel device and preliminary clinical testing
Keywords-MotsClés: LASER OPTICS
Abstract-Résumé: CONTEXT: The pathogenesis of open angle glaucoma is poorly understood. While intraocular pressure (IOP) is confirmed as a major factor, ocular blood flow and the elasticity of the sclera and lamina cribrosa may play a role. We propose a new theory uniting these three factors. We propose that the lamina cribrosa moves backwards with each cardiac cycle, driven by the pulsatility of the choroid, while the retina moves in the opposite direction. These counter-directional movements could lead to stretch damage of axons that form the optic nerve, which run from the retinal nerve fibre layer through the lamina cribrosa. This hypothesis is based on our recent studies, which suggest that the biomechanical compliance of the lamina cribrosa differs dramatically between patients at risk of aggressive glaucoma and patients with stable glaucoma [Lesk et al., Arch Ophthalmol, 124, 1568 (2006)], as well as on recent literature on the pulsatile movements of the retina. To test this hypothesis, we have developed a prototype of a novel non-invasive device based on Low Coherence Interferometry (LCI), which measures with high spatial (400 nm) and temporal resolution (0.01 sec) the movement of intraocular tissues, such as the retinal inner limiting layer and the lamina cribrosa [Singh et al Exp Eye Res (April 14, 2010)]. This device has recently been successfully tested on human volunteers. OBJECTIVE: The objectives of this project are (A) to evaluate our theory on actual glaucoma patients at Hopital Maisonneuve-Rosemont (HMR) using the developed non-invasive device; (B) to improve the prototype device for better data acquisition and stability; (C) to develop image analysis protocols that permit the efficient and reliable extraction of meaningful data; (D) to develop a complementary system with greater lateral resolution on the platform of a commercially availible device. CONCLUSION: This project could lead to the first method to ascertain whether a patient with early glaucoma is at high risk for rapid loss of vision, and thus requires early aggressive therapy.Ultimately, improved understanding on the pathophysiology of glaucoma could lead to new therapeutic modalities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Microfluidic enrichment of circulating tumor cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CIRCULATING TUMOR CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are malignant cells shed by a primary tumor. They circulate in the bloodstream and have the potential to establish metastases in anatomically distant tissues. The capture and enumeration of CTCs has gathered considerable attention because of the potential to use the number and status of these cells (1) as a prognostic marker for tailoring systemic therapies to the needs of individual cancer patients, (2) as a rapid surrogate for evaluating the clinical benefit of new drugs, and (3) as a fluid biopsy of a particularly invasive subpopulation of the original solid tumor. The key challenge in working with CTCs has been their extreme rarity. Existing technologies overcome this problem by first enriching the concentration of CTCs by using the cell surface maker, EpCAM to select for cells with epithelial characteristics. The effectiveness of this selection technique has come into question since one of the key steps of invasion and metastasis is epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition where tumor cells initiate a phenotype switch that is accompanied by a loss of epithelial antigens (e.g. EpCAM). As a result, the aggressively metastatic CTCs are actually the most likely group to evade capture by current methods. We propose to develop a new method for enumerating CTCs by initially depleting leukocytes from a blood sample using CD45 magnetic beads and then developing a microfluidics device to separate CTCs from the remaining CD45-negative leukocytes based on their morphological differences. Since CTCs originate in the primary tumor, they are mechanically distinct from normal hematological cells. Our microfluidics device is designed to separate cells based on differences in cell size and cell rigidity with a high degree of specificity. Our hypothesis is that after these two leukocyte-depletion steps, the concentration of CTCs in the sample is sufficiently enriched to be identified by staining and manual selection. The key advantage of the proposed approach over existing methods is the preservation of relevant CTCs that may have lost their expression for EpCAM due to epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Co-Registered Autofluorescence and OCT Imaging of the Airways
Keywords-MotsClés: OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY (OCT)
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the most common cause of cancer death world-wide. More than 1.3 million people die annually and the 5-year survival rates have improved only marginally in the last three decades. We propose to combine autofluorescence imaging and optical coherence tomography (OCT) to manage this disease through earlier detection and treatment. Autofluorescence imaging is a technique that uses blue light illumination in an endoscope to excite natural tissue fluorescence (a healthy green glow) in the lung. This technique has dramatically improved the early detection of lung cancer by identifying high-risk areas where biopsies should be collected. Although this method improves detection, a biopsy is still required to verify the presence or absence of a precancer. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a new imaging technique that can be used to study these high-risk tissue sites at high resolution without removing tissue (no biopsy required). It is the optical equivalent of ultrasound. It uses light waves instead of sound waves to build a high-resolution map of structures below the tissue surface. Our team was the first to use OCT in conjunction with autofluorescence bronchoscopy. We found that OCT does have promise for the differentiation of early lesions and for determining if the lesion has invaded. Over the last 10 years, we have made 1000's of quantitative measurements on surgical specimens (biopsies) removed from the lung. We believe that we can use these measurements to improve current OCT instruments to help identify precancerous lesions in the lung.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improved membrane permeation assays for drug bioavailability assessment
Keywords-MotsClés: ORAL DRUG BIOAVAILABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Poor intestinal absorption is a major bottleneck in drug discovery as promising new chemical entities often lack suitable amphiphilic balance required for absorption. No one knows how many acceptable candidates have been discarded from the discovery pipeline although their bioavailability could have been significantly improved. Inappropriate in vitro prediction of drug bioavailability is suspected as one of the reasons explaining the rejection of many promising drug candidates from development after time and millions invested in research. The challenge is, thus, to provide just-in time information about drug-like properties to orient the medicinal chemistry lead optimization effort. Parallel artificial membrane permeability assay (PAMPA) is a well-established and simple in vitro model that however lacks biological relevance and reliability. It assesses passive intestinal permeation - the principal route for drug absorption. The objectives of our project are (1) to enhance the PAMPA technology by developing new membranes more representative of the gut cell lipid walls and (2) to make it amenable to HTS and non-specialized lab personnel. We will thus develop phospholipid floating membranes on polymer cushion amenable to Franz cells and multi-well plate setup. This project, in collaboration with an industrial partner, combines a robust technology well-known in the pharmaceutical field to a recent advance in bilayer fluidity devices (polymer-supported membranes) to develop a new assay of drug permeability. It is enabled by the combination of expertises in lipid physicochemistry, polymer science and biopharmacy. The use of this new PAMPA in R&D labs should accelerate the discovery of new drug therapies, reduce the number of discarded promising drugs, and provide more drugs with improved bioavailability and reduced risks of side effects due to too high dosage. The impact on the health of the Canadians should be major - less people should suffer of side effects, and more drug therapies should be available for the treatment of diseases that are affecting the population. Economically, our project will have a positively impact the Canadian pharmaceutical industry and health system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing technologies to assess long-term exposures of the Canadian population to air pollution: research leading to knowledge-transfer to reduce health effects
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTION
Abstract-Résumé: Epidemiological studies that juxtapose high quality information on health with that of exposures to ambient air pollutants have shown that air pollution adversely affects human health. It is now clear that there are health impairments at very low levels of air pollution. An improved understanding of these effects requires very large studies that are capable of characterizing ambient exposures at small spatial scales. These studies are needed to make appropriate public health actions. Indeed, the Canadian government is considering developing annual ambient air pollution standards to address health effects from long-term exposures (annual to multi-year). There has been reluctance to develop these, owing partly to a lack of Canadian evidence of these effects, but also due to a lack of high quality studies that link chronic diseases, such as lung cancer and cardiovascular diseases, with levels of exposure at relatively small spatial scales. Traditional observations from fixed-site monitoring stations, which are used mainly for the purposes of ensuring compliance to regulations, provide only sparse coverage of the country. In this proposal, we will develop technologies to assess the health impacts from long term exposure to air pollution throughout Canada by 1) exploiting recent advances in satellite observations and modeling to produce a complete national characterization of outdoor air pollutant exposures (i.e. PM2.5 and O3); 2) linking these exposures with two large Canadian population cohorts to quantify the impact of long term air pollutant exposure on important adverse health outcomes (i.e., mortality, cancer); and 3) applying this information to contribute to science-based ambient air quality regulations and decision making. These research activities would constitute an important body of evidence as to whether annual average standards should be developed in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Robotic assisted transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: During the acute stage after stroke, 80% of individuals suffer from hemiparesis, while in the long-term more than 40% have chronically impaired arm function. Many have attempted to define neural mechanisms for stroke recovery in the hope that understanding these processes will improve rehabilitation interventions and enhance function. Though not insignificant, the main complaint of individuals with stroke is poor hand and wrist function, and integration of movements across all the joints of the upper extremity (UE). Recent efforts have focused on the possibility of promoting recovery from stroke using emerging brain stimulation technologies, which can facilitate cortical excitability, paired with skilled motor practice. On the other hand, the development of robotic devices that can assist with functional movements and direct movement towards more normal patterns is one new approach, which demonstrated to reduce rehabilitation costs while aiding recovery after stroke. Based on this evidence, the applicants propose to develop a novel method that combines cutting edge brain stimulation and rehabilitation robotics to facilitate active UE movements, improve joint range of motion, and promote functional recovery. Recovery will be indexed by changes in muscle contraction and activity, brain plasticity as indexed with TMS paired-pulse mapping, and functional outcome measures of motor recovery. Taken together the proposed research will focus on expanding our understanding of how to optimally stimulate neural plasticity and facilitate UE motor recovery after stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and potential mechanisms in bifunctional lanthanide compound enhancement of deteriorating bone structures
Keywords-MotsClés: LANTHANIDES
Abstract-Résumé: Bisphosphonates are a class of drugs used to treat metabolic bone disorders such as hypercalcemia, Paget's disease and, in oral form, for the treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis. Due to their poor lipophilicity and polarity they possess very low bioavailability, typically less than 1%. Two recent (2008, 2010) case studies have suggested a link between prolonged bisphosphonate therapy and atypical fractures. It is evident that though effective, due to their adverse side effects, cost, and low patient compliance, more effective medications are necessary for the treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis. The chemical elements the lanthanides (Ln) share many similar biomolecular binding attributes with calcium, Ca, including a high affinity for the bone matrix; Ln(III) also share with Ca(II) similar ionic radii, donor atom preferences, and almost identical coordination numbers in protein binding sites. Our hypothesis is that chemical compounds of the lanthanide elements with designed ligands have potential as therapeutic agents for bone disorders in humans; bone disorders in which the bone remodeling cycle is disrupted include osteoporosis, osteomalacia, osteoarthritis and periodontal disease. In preliminary published work (Dalton Trans. 2007), we identified one preliminary lead compound (La(dpp)3) based on preliminary in vitro and cell studies. The proposal concerns the design, synthesis, characterization and testing of a series of lanthanide compounds with ligands of varying lipophilicity. Our goal is to translate the results of our early stage lanthanide hydroxypyridinone discovery into drug candidates for the treatment of a number of bone density disorders. By incorporating phosphorylated substituents into some ligand candidates, so they can bind to both bone and lanthanides, it is possible that an active agent may also be discovered which works in the absence of an added lanthanide, diversifying the design paradigm. Two lead compounds of interest are expected to result from this work, at the conclusion of which we should be ready for advanced preclinical and early human studies. As the Canadian population ages, more and better drugs for such aging conditions as osteoporosis are required.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel daptomycin-derived lipopeptide antibiotics for overcoming resistance in gram-positive bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICS
Abstract-Résumé: The acquisition of bacterial resistance to conventional antibiotics represents a major threat to human health. Daptomycin (DAP) is a cyclic lipopeptide antibiotic (LPA) that kills bacteria through membrane damage. It is used to treat a broad range of infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria, including ones that have become resistant to other types of antibiotics. As the development of DAP resistance in certain Gram-positive bacteria has been reported, concerns about decreasing clinical effectiveness of DAP have to be addressed. Another issue with DAP is that it is inhibited by lung surfactant, which compromises its effectiveness for treating pneumonia. The objectives of the proposed research are to prepare DAP analogs with increased potency and to learn more about the mechanism of action of DAP. The 3-D structure of membrane-associated DAP will be determined by high resolution NMR spectroscopy (Dieckmann). Multimeric forms of DAP will be prepared (Dmitrienko), and combinatorial total synthesis will be used to prepare libraries of DAP analogs (Taylor). Analogs that are active against a model Gram-positive bacterium, Bacillus subtilis will be tested against a broad range of DAP-susceptible and DAP-resistant Gram-positive pathogens (Pillai). Functional studies on DAP interaction with membranes will be performed by cross-linking and fluorescence (Palmer). The results from these studies will provide crucial information on the mechanism of action of DAP and hopefully provide DAP analogs with superior potency in both the absence and presence of surfactant and good potency against resistant strains.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel platform for minimally invasive tumor localization and treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: TUMOUR LOCALIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer remains the most common cancer and the most common cause of death from cancer in North America. Secondary effects of treating cancer may be mitigated through a minimally invasive approach. While promising, all minimally invasive surgery and therapy (MIST) methods suffer from the same problem: without direct access to the target tissues, reliable and accurate tumour localization remains a formidable challenge. The objective of this research is to develop and validate a system for MIST, with particular emphasis on lung cancer, which provides accurate tumour localization through the integration of tracked and fused kinesthetic, tactile, ultrasound (US), and computed tomography (CT) data, and enables accurate delivery of ablative therapies. The proposed research will consist of the following steps: 1. Develop a minimally invasive mechatronic tool capable of performing multi-modal tumour localization. This device will collect data from tactile, force, position and US imaging sensors that will be fused to provide robust and accurate localization data. 2. Develop patient-specific procedures that allow tracking of lung tumours with respect to known anatomical landmarks using preoperative CT and intraoperative US in order to compensate for the effect of insufflation, lung deflation, respiration, and patient motion. 3. Develop a sensor fusion strategy that combines the intraoperative multi-sensor data from the tumour localization instrument with patient-specific preoperative CT. 4. Develop modular minimally invasive "smart" instruments for image-guided tumour ablation. These instruments will allow precise delivery of probe- and needle-based ablative therapies, and will incorporate real-time position tracking and provide active tremor compensation. 5. Integrate the above elements into a complete surgical platform that presents the information effectively for increased safety and reliability. The outcomes of procedures performed with the proposed system will be compared to those performed using current MIST techniques to assess the effectiveness of the system. Evaluation will progress through tissue phantoms, ex vivo tissue and in vivo animal trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advanced real-time 3D imaging, planning and navigation of fracture surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: IMAGE-GUIDED SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Tremendous advances have occurred in fracture management, due in part to new implants that internally fixate many fractures with minimally invasive techniques. For example, complex femoral fractures are now treated by sophisticated 'locking' nails that require only a few small incisions to insert, giving better outcomes. Despite these advances, articular fractures - which occur near joints - are still challenging even when using specialized locking plates, in part because of the difficulty in achieving anatomic reduction of the joint surface (articular surface fractures that heal with 2 mm or more of residual displacement are at high risk of causing arthritis). To better exploit these new fixation devices we need better minimally invasive surgical techniques, but there currently is no efficient intraoperative means of visualizing bone fragments in 3D. In particular, complex multi-fragment articular fractures are routinely reduced using surgical exposures that may increase scarring, devascularize bone or joint surfaces, and dislodge previously undisplaced bone fragments. Less invasive techniques often involve liberal usage of conventional 2D X-ray fluoroscopy that often provides suboptimal images, and that also exposes the patient and surgical team to significant doses of radiation. Image-guided surgery uses preoperative and intraoperative images to aid the surgeon in performing tasks for which direct vision is impossible or inappropriate. Current commercial navigation systems use 2D fluoroscopy, and a tracking device affixed to the fracture fragment, to estimate a 3D registration transformation between the segmented images and the patient. Such a technique cannot be used for small fracture fragments - particularly articular fractures - because: (1) fixation of a tracking device could damage articular surfaces; (2) the registration of 2D X-ray images to the 3D anatomy is a challenging task under operating room conditions; (3) no automated segmentation algorithms exist for fractures, and (4) manual segmentation of imaging data is time and labour intensive, requiring skilled technical staff. The associated costs significantly limit the clinical utility and availability of current navigation interfaces for fracture reduction

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a protocol for the renewal of housing to improve the health of First Nations residents
Keywords-MotsClés: HOUSING
Abstract-Résumé: Extreme weather and social conditions create many challenges that affect the conditions of homes and the health of their inhabitants. First Nations housing has been characterized as "substandard", "Third World", "inadequate", "unsuitable", "overcrowded", "mouldy", "unhealthy", "in need of major repairs", "of poor quality", and more. The demand for engineered solutions for northern housing is of high priority. The objectives of the proposed community-based research project are to: (a) develop a protocol for assessing First Nations housing; (b) use this protocol to develop a Best Practice Process for First Nations housing renewal; and (c) develop a Healthy Housing Index (HHI) which will serve as a tool to measure the link between housing conditions and health, using both medical and building sciences. The proposed research project fills a serious gap in the evaluation tools available in assessing the housing conditions as determinants of health of First Nations people. The interdisciplinary research is designed to draw from the expertise of professionals from engineering, medicine and education that will lead to knowledge and technologies useful in improving the health of First Nations Canadians. The proposed Protocol and the Best Practice Process will ensure uniformity in the renewal process, allow only qualified personnel to carry out renewal projects, guarantee the quality of the work, result in quantifiable levels of success, prevent "patch work" by non-qualified contractors, and lead to the development of appropriate design and construction guidelines for sustainable healthy housing for First Nations communities. Home remediation can be incorporated as part of an overall intervention strategy in the treatment and control of respiratory and other associated medical problems. The HHI will allow healthcare officials to evaluate health outcomes with reference to housing conditions, help community leaders more effectively address housing conditions in their community to improve the health of its residents, assist provincial/federal housing and health authorities to identify areas in which housing rehabilitation programs can yield the greatest gains in residents' health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analyses de polyphénols issus d'écorces d'essences canadiennes pour le traitement du psoriasis

Abstract-Résumé: Psoriasis is an incurable skin disorder characterized by abnormal differentiation and inflammation. Taking into account that clinically approved anti-psoriatic treatments present many undesirable effects, it has been estimated that 51 % of patients use natural health products. Natural polyphenols are multifunctional molecules that can act through the modulation of multiple signaling pathways. This characteristic could be advantageous for the treatment of multi-causal diseases, such as psoriasis. So far, in vitro studies using natural polyphenols have been conducted on isolated enzymes and on normal or immortalized keratinocytes, which show significant differences regarding psoriatic samples. Thus, in this project, it is proposed to study the polyphenolic extract from black spruce bark on psoriatic cells and on a new psoriatic skin model produced by tissue engineering. TitreApplicationTitle: Development of SPARC mimetic peptides for targeting peritoneal metastasis of epithelial ovarian cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: EPITHELIAL OVARIAN CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 2500 women in Canada are diagnosed with ovarian cancer each year and about 1700 of these women die of their disease. This high mortality rate is due to a lack of early detection and to the development of chemotherapy-resistant disease. Since most women present with advanced disease, there is a desperate need for more effective therapies targeting metastatic disease. The matrix surrounding cells plays a central role in promoting or inhibiting tumor progression. Our laboratory is interested in how proteins in the extracellular matrix regulate cell behaviours. A prime focus of my laboratory is a small mobile extracellular matrix protein called SPARC. Studies have indicated that SPARC serves as a tumor suppressor and impedes metastasis of ovarian cancer. Work in my laboratory on model organisms supports a role for SPARC in stopping cell proliferation and migration. Moreover, I have found that a small part of the SPARC protein (peptide 4.2) can elicit these effects. My lab has joined with two molecular biology and one protein biochemistry laboratories working in ovarian cancer to test the ability of this small peptide to inhibit ovarian cancer progression. We will develop stable analogues of peptide 4.2 with enhanced biological function, which we will test using a variety of cell line models. We will also use a powerful mouse model of ovarian cancer to test the efficacy of promising analogues to inhibit cancer progression. This work will establish the potential of these analogues for further development as therapeutics in the treatment of advanced ovarian cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Thymoproteasomes in T-Cell Development
Keywords-MotsClés: FETAL THYMIC ORGAN CULTURE; FLOW CYTOMETRY; KO MICE; MAJOR HISTOCOMPATIBILITY COMPLEX; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEASOME; PROTEOMICS; T-CELL DEVELOPMENT; TRANSCRIPTOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: The differentiation of T lymphocytes takes place only in the thymus, largely because the thymus produces a unique protein called the thymoproteasome.  The goal of this project is to understand the biochemical and biological roles of the thymoproteasome. As thymic function progressively diminishes with age in all individuals, and decreased thymic capacity causes impaired resistance to infections and cancer, understanding (and enhancing) thymic function could have an important impact on  health management in elderly subjects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Membrane Receptors and Hormone Action: Proteinase-mediated signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; INFLAMMATORY DISEASE; INFLAMMATORY PROTEASES; LIGAND-BIASED SIGNALING; MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY; PROTEASE ACTIVITY-BASED PROBE IDENTIFICATION; PROTEASE-ACTIVATED RECEPTORS; RECEPTOR STRUCTURE-ACTIVITY; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Certain digestive enzymes (proteinases), notably the blood-clotting enzyme thrombin and the digestive enzyme, trypsin, can act like hormones to regulate inflammation by activating a unique family of cell surface G-protein-coupled proteinase-activated receptors (PARs: Fig. 1).  Our CIHR-funded project and work by others has shown that PARs play important roles in diseases like arthritis and asthma.  The next frontier is to understand in depth, the molecular pharmacology of these intriguing receptors and to identify the endogenous and pathogen enzymes that regulate the PARs in vivo.  The central hypothesis of this proposal is that both endogenous and pathogen-derived proteinases act like hormones, via the PARs, to play an inflammatory role in vivo.  Questions that drive the main aims of this proposal are: (1) What receptor mechanisms are involved in signaling via the PARs? (2) Are distinct signals activated by the different PARs in the same cell and can these pathways be selectively activated by newly designed drugs, (3) What are the tissue or pathogen-derived proteinases that might regulate PARs in vivo? and (4) Can the PARs or the PAR-activating proteinases play an inflammatory role in vivo? Using newly developed tools, the proposal will deal with the four questions with the following aims:  Aim 1: Assess the molecular pharmacology of PAR signaling with a focus on the structure-function properties of PARs 2 and 4. Aim 2: Determine structure-activity relationships (SARs) for PAR stimulants that can selectively activate unique PAR-triggered signals.  Aim 3: Evaluate differential signaling by PARs 1, 2 and 4 and their site-mutated isoforms in a common cell background (e.g human airway or kidney epithelial cells)  Aim 4: Evaluate the role of PAR2 and its pathogen-derived activating proteinases in an in-vivo model of allergen-induced airway inflammation.  The data will  surface new therapeutic targets for treating inflammatory diseases like asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunoregulatory nanovaccines: Optimization of physical, chemical, pharmacokinetic and immunological properties for bench-to-bedside translation
Keywords-MotsClés: PEPTIDE-MHC
Abstract-Résumé: The current proposal is founded on the discovery of a new paradigm in the treatment of type 1 diabetes (caused by the white blood cells of the immune system) of potential groundbreaking significance. Traditionally, vaccines have been used to expand white blood cells capable of affording protection against viruses, bacteria or cancer, or to delete white blood cells capable of causing autoimmune diseases (such as T1D). We have developed a 'vaccine' that can cure diabetes by selectively expanding what we call 'autoregulatory' white blood cells. These constitute a new type of 'autoreactive' white blood cells (like their diabetes-causing counterparts, they specifically recognize pancreatic B-cells) whose function is to put the brakes on the diabetes-causing autoimmune attack. These cells become activated when they sense the attack on the pancreas and engage into a competitive tug-of-war with the B-cell killer white blood cells, often unsuccessfully. Our vaccine can expand this population of white blood cells, enhancing their diabetes-countering effects. This vaccine can blunt disease progression in pre-diabetic animals and restore normal blood sugar levels in diabetic mice without causing generalized suppression of the immune system. The current vaccine platform is based on tiny particles of a metal (many times smaller than a cell; also referred to as nanoparticles -NP-) coated with antigenic targets of beta cell-killer white blood cells (pMHC-coated NPs). The objective of this proposal is to synthesize optimized clinical-grade pMHC-coated NPs to maximize therapeutic efficacy while reducing the potential for toxicity. This work, which will be done by an interdisciplinary team of established scientists and trainees spanning the spectrum of nanotechnology, biochemistry, immunology and autoimmune disease will pave the way for human clinical trials.
