TitreApplicationTitle: Microfluidic high-throughput screening device for C. elegans movement based assays
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROTAXIS
Abstract-Résumé: C. elegans is one of the most widely studied organisms that is of great importance in the study of molecular mechanisms underlying numerous biological and disease processes. Because C. elegans carries more than half of human disease genes and utilizes many of the same mechanisms, the findings in this model can be successfully translated to humans. Furthermore, due to its small size (~1 mm, ~1,000 somatic cells), short generation time (~2.5 days), and transparent body, C. elegans (worms) serves as an ideal laboratory model for understanding the role of human genes in diseases as well as an effective screen to determine the effect of drug candidates in mitigating these diseases. However, current methods of screening worms involve observation of their movement and imaging them following exposure to chemicals. These methods are qualitative, labor-intensive prone to human errors, time consuming, costly and not amenable to high throughput. Automation, standardization and parallelization of screening processes for model organisms is crucial in lowering their cost and enabling their widespread use in drug discovery. We propose to take a novel approach to develop microfluidic devices to study the response of worms to various chemicals. This is based on our recent promising discovery that C. elegans respond to electrical signals and move in a directed manner inside microfluidic channels. This discovery has allowed us, for the first time, to induce movement behaviour on demand and quantitatively measure its response. Here we propose to combine electric stimuli based movement response of the worms with microfabrication and microfluidic technology to develop devices that will screen for drug candidates for Parkinson's disease in a high throughput manner. The successful outcome of this project will be a low cost device that can be used by biologist and pharmaceutical researchers for drug candidate screening using animal models for Parkinson's disease. The technology developed can also be applied with suitable modifications for any movement based disorders, neurological diseases and even obesity and hypertension if expressed in C.elegans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bioengineered cell delivery system
Keywords-MotsClés: INJECTABLE HUDROGELS
Abstract-Résumé: Traumatic spinal cord injury is often described in terms of the primary injury, which results from a mechanical insult such as a motor vehicle or sports-related accident, and the secondary injury, which results in a cascade of events, resulting in an inhibitory environment. The latter limits regeneration by forming a scar-like tissue which can be degraded. The environment in the injured spinal cord is not conducive to cell growth; however, cell transplantation holds promise for regeneration. Here we propose to both degrade the scar-like tissue that forms after injury and deliver stem cells that will promote regeneration. Critical challenges in the development of stem cell based therapies, are the survival of transplanted cells and tissue integration within the host. By addressing both with novel bioengineering strategies in combination with advanced stem cell biology and animal models, we anticipate developing platform strategies that will impact spinal cord injury repair strategies and be broadly applicable to other traumatic or neurodegenerative diseases of the central nervous system, such as stroke and retinal degeneration. Our team has the collective expertise required for success. By bringing together world-leading experts in bioengineering, stem cell biology, cellular microenvironment and spinal cord injury models, we aim to overcome injury in one of the most challenging frontiers in medicine - the central nervous system. We will provide a superb training environment for our researchers, taking advantage of the multidisciplinary approach to overcome spinal cord injury. Our team is strengthened by our three industrial collaborators with expertise in commercialization of research, scar tissue degradation, and stem cell delivery. Together, we aim to advance knowledge towards commercial products in the fields of regenerative medicine and neuroscience - two focus areas identified by the Federal government for funding.

TitreApplicationTitle: High-throughput sperm motility assay and automated selection for clinical in vitro fertilization
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SORTING
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal describes the development and application of a high-throughput sperm physiological motility measurement to: (1) quantify the correlation between sperm motility and DNA integrity; (2) correlate the tendency of sperm to swim near vessel walls with sperm viability; and (3) apply these findings to screen candidate sperm for the clinical application of in vitro fertilization (IVF). The project contains three iterative segments of device development, initial testing, and human sperm based testing, followed by implementation at the OVO Fertility Clinic. In Canada, one in six couples experience fertility issues and each year an estimated 3500 live births involve assisted reproductive technologies, most notably IVF. Current techniques of semen processing and sperm selection are crude and differ greatly from the natural process in vivo. Moreover, these techniques may be ineffective in selecting the best spermatozoa and, may result in iatrogenic damage to the sperm, including the sperm DNA. Sperm DNA damage is associated with reduced IVF pregnancy rates, increased risk of pregnancy loss after IVF, and compromised health of offspring. This project addresses the critical need for a clinically-viable, sperm selection method that avoids technician error, cell trauma, oxidative stress, and DNA damage while reflecting as much as possible the natural in vivo process. This project is a new collaboration enabled through the CHRP opportunity. The project brings together engineering and male and female fertility health researchers, and IVF treatment providers at the OVO Fertility Clinic. This work will lead to: (1) a new understanding of the fundamental characteristics of human sperm motility; (2) sperm transport modes and metrics as indicators of sperm viability; (3) the application of these findings at the clinical-level to the benefit of infertile couples and offspring; (4) new commercialization opportunities for Canadian industry; and (5) highly qualified personnel with the multidisciplinary skills needed to develop next-generation fertility treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effective estimation of second cancer risks and resultant possible improvements of treatment protocols
Keywords-MotsClés: ONCOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that 3.5% of the population are cancer survivors, a prevalence that has tripled in North America since 1971. For many patients cured of their initial cancer, their treatment can give rise to significant delayed morbidity, and those originally diagnosed at young ages have a particularly high burden of late effects including second cancers (SC), and cardiovascular disease (CVD). For example, recent research suggests that childhood cancer survivors in particular face significant late morbidity or mortality during adulthood, with excess risks reducing life expectancy by as much as 28%. Much of the late toxicity is related to exposure to radiation therapy as part of initial treatment. The development of new therapeutic strategies that reduce long-term treatment related toxicity is a major theme in pediatric oncology. A major obstacle to the rational development of less toxic but effective new treatment strategies is that most published estimates of the risks late toxicity are based on outdated therapy, and conceal large variation in risks among individual patients. These limitations make it difficult to use these risk estimates to develop new treatments intended to reduce the occurrence of late effects. Simply eliminating radiation therapy without an understanding of the magnitude of the potential benefit has resulted in poor outcomes and in some clinical trials led to unacceptably high relapse rates. The overall aim of this study is to utilize recent advances in image processing, radiation dosimetry and biomathematical modeling to develop robust and flexible models of the treatment-related risks of SC and CVD for children with Hodgkin Lymphoma. With collaborators in the Children's Oncology Group (COG), we will work towards developing tools that will allow clinicians and clinical trialists to prospectively estimate the reduction in the risks of SC and CVD that would be expected with new changes in HL treatment. These models could be applied to individuals, to optimize the treatment for specific patients, or to groups, to aid the design of clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optical mapping of the neonate heart to determine the etiology of Junctional Ectopic Tachycardia
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Junctional Ectopic Tachycardia (JET) is a supraventricular tachycardia that occurs post-operatively after open heart surgery in young children. JET can occur in >20% of patients undergoing correction for specific congenital heart defects and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Since the etiology of JET is not understood, clinical treatment often lacks efficacy and often results in poor patient outcomes. Cardiac synchrony is maintained by a complex arrangement of primary and secondary pacemaking foci. These foci communicate with the rest of the myocardium through electrical conduction pathways and it is this co-ordinated communication that ensures cardiac synchrony and adequate blood flow to the brain and to the rest of the body. Electrical propagation in the heart is directional: electrical wave fronts do not spread evenly in all directions but rather follow electrical pathways formed by various heart tissues. Electrical conduction follows the myofibril alignment of the heart muscle and surgery may disrupt these conduction pathways. In the absence of primary pacemaker activity, secondary and or ectopic pacemaking sites may further disrupt cardiac synchrony. However, neither electrical conduction nor myofibril alignment is easily detected. An instrument that can visualize both electrical conduction pathways as well as the cardiac tissue that delineates these conduction pathways is required to minimize dyssynchrony. Two separate technologies exist that can visualize these respective attributes. Fluorescent optical action potential mapping (APM) can resolve electrical conduction pathways and optical coherence tomography (OCT) can resolve myofibril alignments. Optical mapping is a fluorescent imaging technique that replaces the traditional microelectrode with a voltage-sensitive dye and a high performance digital camera. The fluorescent dye encodes changes in cellular membrane potential into changes in cellular fluorescence and provides non-contact action potential recordings. Optical coherence tomography utilizes back-scattered light, similar to the acoustical reflections used in ultrasound imaging devices, and creates a depth-resolved image indicating tissue type and myofibril direction as a function

TitreApplicationTitle: Antibody-nanoparticle conjugates as molecular imaging agents for solid brain tumour (glioma)
Keywords-MotsClés: MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI)
Abstract-Résumé: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) (WHO grade IV) is a highly aggressive tumour with distinct histopathological features including high proliferation, necrosis, and considerable neo-vascularization. GBM remains one of the most devastating cancers and is among the most common solid tumours in children. Radiographic and histological evidence have determined that increased tumour vascularity is correlated with the clinical grade of gliomas. At present, tissue samples are required for absolute classification, from which the outcome may be predicted and adjuvant therapies, such as radio and/or chemotherapy, may be determined. Therefore, there is an unmet clinical need to develop a non-invasive method to assess the degree of glioma vascularity and determine the associated clinical aggressiveness. Such a molecular imaging method could significantly improve the clinical management of gliomas. The application of molecular imaging to CNS neoplasms would ensure more accurate diagnosis if an appropriate targeted contrast agent were developed. Previously in our laboratory, the insulin-like growth factor-binding protein-7 (IGFBP7) has been discovered to be a highly up-regulated biomarker specific for GBM vessels and a single domain antibody (sdAbs) that target against IGFBP7 has been developed. Bioconjugation of sdAbs to magnetic resonance (MR) and near-infrared (NIR) imaging contrast agents is a novel method that has the potential to provide accurate molecular imaging of GBM vessels in the clinic. MRI is an advanced 3D non-invasive imaging modality, but the lack of molecular MR imaging contrast agents with sufficient specificity and high relaxivity, and thus MR contrast sensitivity, is a major impediment. We propose to make antibody-nanoparticle conjugates, more specifically to make MR molecular imaging agents consisting of anti-IGFBP7 sdAb targeted FeCo nanoparticles, which are predicted to have a 3 times stronger magnetic moment than 20 nm SPIO (superparamagnetic iron oxide) thus providing better targeted tissue contrast. In addition, it has a turn-on near-infrared optical probe.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advanced tissue engineering strategies for generating replacement tracheal tissues
Keywords-MotsClés: REGENERATIVE MEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: Malignancy, subglottic stenosis, and traumatic injury to the trachea require surgical resection. When short segments are involved, primary re-anastomosis affords excellent results. Longer lesions, however, have no currently acceptable solution. Some patients need permanent tracheostomies or receive only palliative treatment. Recent progress in airway transplantation has provided renewed optimism for potential solutions to these problems, however much remains to be done. Tissue engineered solutions, using constructed substrates, offer the best hope for a far simpler approach with much reduced risk of immunogenicity. Substantial work to date has provided exciting progress but has largely focused on chondrocyte regeneration and structural integrity. The epithelial layer of the airway has several functions: a barrier function, secretion of mucous, and mucociliary clearance of inhaled pathogens yet it has received much less attention. This latter role requires the synchronized, aligned beating of the cilia of the many millions of epithelial cells comprising the entire airway tree. The factors controlling optimal epithelial maturation and organization have barely been explored let alone defined. The present collaborative proposal will bring together a team of engineers and clinicians to enhance our understanding of physical factors that can be engineered to control epithelial organization and tissue functionality. Specifically, we will expose developing epithelium to controlled physical forces and examine the resulting effects on epithelial organization in two and three-dimensional epithelial layers. We hypothesize that physical forces will influence the growth, organization and functional maturation of the epithelial cells, grown from local progenitors on engineered basement membrane, and that engineering specific physical forces during tissue development will provide a novel strategy for improving the quality and clinical utility of engineered epithelial tissues. Our ultimate goal is to create highly functional epithelial monolayers with ciliary alignment and coordination, suitable for immediate clinical use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Specific and cell-permeable molecular probes of capital function
Keywords-MotsClés: CYCLIC PEPTIDES
Abstract-Résumé: The Calpain family of Ca2+-dependent proteases is involved in many physiological functions. Calpain dysfunction is implicated in many diseases. The greatest impact of Calpain proteases lies in their involvement in stroke, the third leading cause of death in Canada (source: Heart and Stroke Foundation). In addition to the damage done during hypoxic conditions of an ischemic stroke, the ischemic cascade contributes to a number of downstream effects even after the restoration of blood flow. The fact that over 88% of stroke survivors end up with some form of impairment or disability stresses the importance of battling this affliction and the need for new therapies. The low energy state of cells under anaerobic conditions shuts down the ATP-dependent ion exchange pumps, creating a large influx of Ca2+, thereby over-activating calpain. One of the targets of calpain is the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger which is cleaved during ischemia. The positive feedback loop rapidly pushes the cell down the death pathways of necrosis or apoptosis. Calpain inhibitors such as AK295 and SNJ1945 have been shown to reduce tissue damage upon experimental brain injury and stroke but have not been pursued further due to modest specificity. The grand challenge is to identify specific and potent calpain inhibitors that will not affect other cysteine proteases. Using the cyclic peptide methods developed recently in the Yudin lab, we will address the challenge of finding specific inhibitors for Calpains 1&2. Driven by a ground-breaking study published by Peter Davies (Nature 2008), we recently synthesized cyclic peptides for the unprimed area of the active site of the protease. This chemistry is based on a breakthrough disclosed by the Yudin lab in 2010 (JACS 2010, Chemical and Engineering News 2010, Faculty of 1000). Our cyclization technique allows facile incorporation of end-of-synthesis modifications to a key part in the structure, which we will use in order to fuse cyclic peptide inhibitors targeting both the primed and unprimed site of the calpain active site.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the process of how expert-consult teams deliver home-based palliative care in 2 provinces
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CARE UTILIZATION; EXPERT CONSULT-TEAMS; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HOME AND COMMUNITY CARE; PALLIATIVE CARE; QUALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Palliative care is an approach that relieves symptom issues and improves quality of life for patients who have terminal illness. The rapidly aging population is pressuring health systems to provide palliative care outside the hospital that is high-quality and cost-effective. A lot of research has investigated "expert-consult teams" that deliver palliative care in the home. These teams consist of a nurse, palliative care physician, and involvement with family physicians. Expert-consult teams vary considerably in communities and regions across Canada, particularly in their processes of care delivery. Processes of care delivery include assessment and monitoring, coordination, and care-planning, all of which directly affect patient and family outcomes. Yet, there is a little research that describes and compares the various processes of care within multiple team models, and assesses how processes of care link to healthcare use and costs.  To address this gap, this study will examine 6 palliative care, expert-consult teams across Ontario and Alberta. It will investigate whether patients who received care from an expert-consult team compared to patients who received "usual care" had reduced use of hospital days, emergency department visits, and lower costs. It will also interview the teams to compare the similarities and differences between team's processes of care, and understand which processes are important to lowering healthcare use and costs. In the end, this study will generate new knowledge about effective models to deliver palliative care in the community. The results are relevant to decision-makers across Canada and other countries, who have implemented different models of expert-consult teams in their communities, but lack evidence about which models are optimal. Ultimately, the knowledge generated will be essential to spreading effective models so that all Canadians can access high-quality palliative care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Colonic mucin biosynthesis, secretion and function in infectious diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: COLONIC CELLS; ENZYMES; INFLAMMATION; MUCIN; PARASITE
Abstract-Résumé: The parasite Entamoeba histolytica causes the disease amebiasis, which results in 100,000 deaths/year. How the parasite cause disease is not known but it has to overcome the protective mucus barrier to invade intestinal cells. The parasite attaches to colonic mucins (proteins in mucus) and the gut lining via a surface protein prior to causing disease. This proposal examines the hypothesis that E. histolytica secreted cysteine proteinases (enzymes) and prostaglandin (PGE2, an inflammatory mediator) play major roles in altering the protective mucus barrier in the pathogenesis of intestinal amebiasis. The study will characterize how the enzymes released by the parasite break down the protective mucus proteins and dissolve the mucus barrier. In addition, the parasite also produces PGE2 that not only cause depletion of mucus but also stimulate inflammation in the gut which help the parasite to cause disease. We are proposing to study how cysteine proteinase and PGE2 together can synergize to help the parasite cause disease.  By studying both these virulent factors, the results of this study will define the mechanisms of how disease is initiated by this parasite and in the identification of novel strategies to control this medically important pathogen.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Bk channel in sensory filtering
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; BK CHANNEL; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HABITUATION; ION CHANNEL; MENTAL DISORDERS; SENSORY FILTERING; STARTLE; SYNAPTIC PLATICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Our brain is constantly bombarded with sensory information reaching the brain through the senses (eyes, ears, smell, touch, taste). In order to cope with this vast amount of information and to extract the really important pieces, unimportant information needs to be suppressed. In a whole group of mental disorders (schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease, autism, and others) this sensory suppression, which acts like an information filter, does not work properly. Hence, the brains of affected people are flooded by sensory information, leading to difficulties of thought, concentration, memory, and learning. Current medications in any of these disorders do mostly not improve sensory filtering. We recently discovered that a specific ion channel plays a crucial role in sensory filtering in worms, mice and rats. These channels sit in the membrane of nerve cells close to their connection to other cells and regulate the excitability of the cell. When the ion channel is not functioning, sensory filtering is impaired. We here want to further explore 1. the role of this ion channel in sensory filtering, learning, and memory; 2. how this ion channel regulates sensory filtering and 3. if drugs that act on this ion channel can enhance sensory filtering, learning and memory.  We will use common models for sensory filtering in rats and mice (changes of acoustic startle responses) and we will also record tiny signals directly from single nerve cells for this purpose. We will use different substances that block this specific ion channel or enhance its activity, and we will also use mice which lack this ion channel due to a mutation.  Once we understand the mechanism of sensory filtering in more detail, specific drugs can be developed for improving sensory filtering and ameliorating the symptoms associated with this deficit. This will increase the quality of life of patients suffering from e.g. schizophrenia or Alzheimer's disease, and help them to live more independently.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of DJ-1 in an aging model of PD
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CELL DEATH; DJ-1; DOPAMINE; NEURONS; PARKINSON DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is a critical factor in the incidence of Parkinsons disease (PD).  However, the initial causes of the disease are mostly unknown.  One impediment to understanding the disease has been the lack of animal models of PD.  Here we propose to generate one such chronic degenerative model based upon the loss of a gene, DJ-1, known to cause rare forms of PD.  We propose to examine how loss of this gene sensitizes animals to environmental toxins known to cause the same loss of neurons as in PD.  We will also explore how DJ-1 loss itself may cause spontaneous death of these neurons in the live animal.  These studies will provide important new insights into how PD progresses and provide new potential avenues of therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of cell cycle signals in neuronal death
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL CYCLE; CELL DEATH; NEURON; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Neuronal cell death is an important event during brain development and in diseases related to the brain such as stroke.  Recent efforts in this field have focused on understanding the regulatory processes which control one type of death known as apoptosis.  Previous evidence indicated that certain signalling elements play a key role in controlling the apoptotic death of neurons and that these events are uniquely arranged depending upon cell type and the initiator of death.  We have recently made the exciting observation that dying neurons utilize cell cycle components to signal for death.  The present research is designed to uncover how these abnormal cell division signals actually cause death following ischemia and stroke.  In understanding these pathways, we hope to, not only gain an appreciation for an important basic biological process, but also devise therapeutic strategies to treat brain injury conditions such as stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and cellular characterization of phagosome and autophagosome biogenesis and their role in antigen presentation
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNITY; AUTOPHAGY; CELL BIOLOGY; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; INNATE IMMUNITY; PHAGOCYTOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Our ability to fight infectious diseases relies on the triggering of an efficient immune response.  This response involves several cell types and a variety of organelles within these cells.  For example, during infection with the Herpes virus, infected cells will generate viral peptides through proteolytic degradation that will be presented at the cell surface on MHC class I and class II molecules.  Our research program will highlight the molecular mechanisms that allow two key organelles (the phagosomes and autophagosomes)to promote the processing of viral peptides for antigen presentation.  These studies will highlight cellular mechanisms and specific molecules that could be targeted to stimulate the immune response.

TitreApplicationTitle: RNA Helicases in Tumorigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: DDX28; DDX3X; EU-MYC LYMPHOMA MODEL; RNA HELICASE; RNA-INTERFERENCE BASED SCREENING; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Helicases are molecular machines that utilize energy to remodel DNA and RNA. Based on similarities among members of this family of proteins, they can be divided into several superfamilies. One of these, called Superfamily 2, consists of a group of proteins that are thought to be involved in regulating many aspects in the flow of genetic information from DNA to protein. Despite this central role in biology, little research has been done on this class of gene expression regulators to systematically investigate their deregulation in cancers or to explore their potential as anti-cancer drug targets. My lab has performed a genetic screen to identify new tumor suppressors among RNA helicases. This screen was performed in vivo in a pre-clinical mouse lymphoma model by decreasing the expression of each helicase and we identified two proteins, DDX3X and DDX28, as novel tumor suppressor genes. We propose herein to unravel the molecular mechanism by which DDX3X and DDX28 act to suppress cell growth. We also propose to validate our results in human tumors. Our preliminary results have identified novel tumor-specific vulnerabilities and pathways against which molecular-targeted therapeutics could be developed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessment of Midodrine in the Prevention of Vasovagal Syncope (POST 4)
Keywords-MotsClés: HYPOTENSION; MIDODRINE; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; SYNCOPE; VASOVAGAL
Abstract-Résumé: Fainting affects about 50% of Canadians, is the cause of 1-2% of emergency room visits, and probably causes $250 million in health care spending each year. Frequent fainting causes a poor quality of life, and problems at work, at home, and while driving.  The most common cause is reflex fainting. This occurs in people of all ages, and while many people only faint once or twice there are hundreds of thousand of Canadians who faint many times, and often more than once a year. Reflex fainting is due to abrupt drops in blood pressure and often drops in heart rate, and these reduce blood flow to the brain enough to make people lose consciousness. There is no known medical treatment for frequent fainting.   One possible treatment would be to prevent the blood pressure drop by increasing the pressure in the veins and arteries. A drug called midodrine does this, by increasing blood flow to the heart and increasing blood pressure. It prevents lightheadedness and fainting in elderly people with damaged nerves around their blood vessels, and it might prevent reflex fainting. However there is no solid evidence of its effectiveness, and we will test whether midodrine prevents moderate to severe reflex fainting.   We will study 128 patients who have fainted recently, have reflex fainting, and are at high risk of fainting again. They will enroll in a randomized clinical trial. Consenting patients will be assigned randomly to receive either midodrine or a dummy pill called a placebo, and we will follow them for 1 year. We then will compare the number of people who faint in those taking midodrine compared to placebo. We will also compare the frequency of fainting, quality of life, and health costs, in each arm of the study.   This study will have centres in Canada, Europe and South America. It is the only study of its kind and it will be pivotal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms of Phagocyte Activation
Keywords-MotsClés: DIGITAL IMAGING; MEMBRANE TRAFFIC; PHAGOCYTOSIS; PHAGOSOME MATURATION
Abstract-Résumé: White blood cells of the innate immune system protect the body against invading microorganisms.  These white cells have the unique ability to engulf and destroy the microorganisms.  The engulfment phenomenon, known as phagocytosis, is initiated by specialized molecules on the cell surface, called receptors, which detect the microorganisms and trigger their uptake.  Once internalized, the microorganisms are killed and degraded inside vacuoles (phagosomes) by digestive enzymes delivered by a process called phagosomal maturation.  In some instances, pathogenic microorganisms thwart the ability of the immune cells to engulf and kill them, resulting in widespread, life-threatening infection.  To avoid such infections, it is important to understand the mechanisms underlying the engulfment and maturation of phagosomes, and how some microbial species interfere with these processes.  The proposed research has two main objectives:  1)Understand how the receptors on the surface of the immune cells detect microorganisms and drive their engulfment and  2)Define the early stages of the phagosomal maturation process, which are often co-opted and impaired by infectious microorganisms

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of heterochromatin by the Retinoblastoma protein in cell cycle control and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; CHROMATIN; CONDENSIN; GENE-TARGETED MICE; MITOSIS; SENESCENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Deregulated cell proliferation is one of the fundamental characteristics of cancer.  In addition to unwanted cell growth, the genetic make-up of cancer cells is often unstable.  This allows them to acquire new characteristics that promote increased aggressiveness and accelerated disease progression.  All cells possess the ability to alter the way they package their DNA, making it inaccessible for replication and instability.  This inaccessible state is called "heterochromatin".  Heterochromatin can block cell growth and prevent instability, allowing a cell to protect itself from becoming cancerous.  Despite its importance in cancer, there is relatively little known about how heterochromatin is packaged.  Our research has recently revealed that a key regulator of cell proliferation called pRB also controls the packaging of DNA into heterochromatin.  Our initial work shows that a partially active form of pRB that is defective for making heterochromatin allows cells to proliferate inappropriately and acquire instability.  In this proposal we plan to study how heterochromatin is assembled and where pRB functions in this process.  Using mice we also plan to investigate how defective assembly of heterochromatin influences cancer incidence.  For example does defective heterochromatin cause cancer, or only accelerate its progression when caused by another means. Understanding how heterochromatin assembly affects cancer incidence and progression will allow us to find treatments that best suit patients whose cancer exhibits heterochromatin defects.

ClasseRechercheFR: INFACTUS DU MYOCARDE; APOPLEXIE, INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Characterization of the Na+/H+ Exchanger Protein
Keywords-MotsClés: CYSTEINE SCANNING MUTAGENESIS; MEMBRANE PROTEIN; NA+/H+ EXCHANGER; PROTEIN EXPRESSION; SITE SPECIFIC MUTAGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Our study investigates the protein that is responsible for removal of acid from cells. As a byproduct of cell metabolism, acid is produced. Too much acid has detrimental effects on many cellular tissues including the heart. The protein that removes the acid from cells is called the Na+/H+ exchanger. This protein removes the excess inside acid in exchange for an outside sodium (salt). Through a series of reactions, too much salt inside a cell leads to too much calcium inside and this damages cells, especially heart cells during heart disease. Thus, the Na+/H+ exchanger protein is critically involved in heart disease.  Several companies have developed drugs to inhibit the activity of this protein - which results in improved outcome in heart disease in animal models. However, when used in humans, those drugs had detrimental side effects that outweighed their beneficial effects. Similar to a complicated car, if you can't understand how something works, it is difficult to fix. Our study therefore investigates how the protein works, and what parts of the protein are important in function. We change parts of the protein to determine how they function. We measure how the changed protein works in cells. We are also expressing the protein in large amounts, to essentially get a good quality picture of the protein through high resolution imaging techniques for small molecules. Reaction with specific chemicals also gives us a picture of what parts of the protein are facing outside of the cell, and what parts are facing towards the inside of the cell. Our study will give new information on this physiologically important protein. A better picture and understanding of the protein will ultimately lead to better design of drugs that inhibit the protein. We will also provide valuable fundamental knowledge on how this human membrane protein functions.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Differential control of E2F transcription factors by pRB in  normal and cancer cells
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL CYCLE; DNA DAMAGE; GENE-TARGETED MICE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Human cancer arises when normal cells sustain damage to their DNA, acquire permanent change to their genes, and as a result proliferate uncontrollably. The study of cells derived from human tumors has revealed that mutations disrupting cell proliferation control mechanisms are found in virtually all cancers. Some of the same molecules that control cell growth also control a process that can kill cells known as programmed cell death or apoptosis. This proposal seeks to investigate how these molecules control programmed cell death in hopes of learning how to kill cancer cells.      On a molecular level, specific genes are involved in sensing DNA damage and instructing cells to die. Dr. Dick's laboratory has found a unique mechanism that regulates the response to DNA damage induced cell death. They have found a mechanism that works much like a lock and key where one position of the key causes cells to die and the other helps to keep them alive and grow.      DNA damage causes a protein called pRB to stop inhibiting the programmed cell death process. When pRB is turned off it allows another protein called E2F1 to become active and instruct the cells to die. Dr. Dick's lab will investigate the molecular mechanism that induces the release of E2F1 from pRB's control. In addition, genetically engineered mice where pRB can't control E2F1 will be created. These mice will be examined to determine how E2F1 instructs cells to die when tumors are forming. These experiments will evaluate how the E2F1 mechanism kills cells and how this can be harnessed in new cancer treatments.      Understanding how programmed cell death kills cancer cells holds tremendous potential for improving cancer treatment. The molecular mechanisms that underlie how DNA damage works in cancer treatment are important to understand because they can be manipulated to improve treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health Coaching to Effect Lifestyle Behaviour Change: A Randomized Trial of Individuals with Pre-disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CARDIOVASCULAR LIFESTYLE; LIFESTYLE MODIFICATION; NURSE COACHING; PRE-DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease related to lifestyle (in particular, a person's diet, exercise habits, smoking status, stress levels, and alcohol consumption) is on the rise in Canada, especially in Newfoundland. Interventions aimed at promoting lifestyle change without addressing an overall change in how people think are less likely to be successful in the long run. Using a nurse coaching delivery model, we hope to determine whether people with pre-diabetes and pre-hypertension will change the way they think about their health and change their unhealthy lifestyle behaviours. The primary outcomes of the study are change in thinking and change in lifestyle. The intervention will last for 6 months and the outcomes will be measured at the end of the intervention and again at 12 months. We hope to prove that the intervention will be effective at changing lifestyle at 6 months and that those people who also changed their thinking will continue to have improved lifestyle at 12 months.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Vangl proteins in normal development and in neural tube defects
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENT; GENETICS; MEMBRANE PROTEIN; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NEPHROLOGIE; NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS; RETINAL DEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Vangl proteins form multi-protein membrane complexes that provide positional information to cells. These Vangl complexes play a critical developmental role in establishing cell polarity in the plane of epithelia, in the positioning of cellular appendages such as motile cilia, in the formation of three dimensional structures such as tubules, and in cell movement and migration. These fundamental processes are essential to organogenesis. We have shown that mutations in Vangl genes cause neural tube defects such as spina and excencephaly in the Lp mouse mutant, and we have detected mutant VANGL1 and VANGL2 variants in clinical cases of human neural tube defects. We wish to study the mechanism by which mutations in VANGL1 and VANGL2 cause neural tube defects in humans; We also propose to identify the Vangl protein determinants responsible for different aspects of protein functions such as membrane targeting and assembly into membrane signaling complexes. We have created a conditional Vangl2 mutant that can be inactivated in a tissue and time-dependent fashion. We will use this mutant to study the role of Vangl2 in the structure and function of the retina and of the kidney, including a possible association with retinal degeneration and cystic kidney disease. We also propose a genetic approach in mice to identify genes in the Vangl2 pathway that may also be associated with NTD in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of caspases in human neuronal cell death and in Alzheimer's disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; ANIMAL MODELS; CASPASE-6; CASPASES; GENE EXPRESSION; INFLAMMATION; PRIMARY CULTURES OF HUMAN NEURONS; SYNAPTIC STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Current therapies against Alzheimer disease are very limited. One possible reason for failure to achieve efficient therapies against Alzheimer disease is that we do not have a thorough understanding of the earliest degenerative events that occur in the brain to lead to Alzheimer disease. The research of my team is dedicated at identifying the earliest degenerative processes that occur in aging brains.  We have identified that Caspase-6, an enzyme that causes neurodegeneration, is activated in some aged individuals but not in younger individuals.  The Caspase-6 is activated in the area of the brain first affected by Alzheimer disease. Caspase-6 is also abundantly active in brains of Alzheimer disease patients at all stages of the disease and is present in all areas that are affected by Alzheimer disease. In this proposal, we will try to further understand how Caspase-6 is activated in neurons, attempt to develop a mouse model with Alzheimer disease by expressing Caspase-6 in the brain of mice, and assess the effects of Caspase-6 on neuronal function. The results of these experiments could indicate that Caspase-6 is an important therapeutic target against Alzheimer disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Isolation of a novel human retrovirus associated with primary biliary cirrhosis and fulfillment of koch's postulates in vitro
Keywords-MotsClés: KOCH'S POSTULATES IN VITRO; MITOCHONDRIA; PRIMARY BILIARY CIRRHOSIS; RETROVIRUS INFECTION; VIRUS ISOLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) develop progressive liver disease and often require liver transplantation. The cause of disease is unknown. It is thought to occur as a result of an infection in subjects that are more susceptible to disease than others. We found evidence of virus infection in patients with primary biliary cirrhosis. We saw virus like particles by electron microscopy in patients liver tissues and then obtained the viral genomic DNA sequences. We found that most patients with PBC have evidence of viral infection. Since then we have conducted clinical studies using anti-viral therapy. We found that PBC patients treated with combination anti-retrovirus therapy experienced significant reversal of the disease process. This provides some circumstantial evidence for a retroviral infection. Although we could show significant improvements, the changes were not substantial and we are now looking for better antiviral regimens. Now we have found a mouse model with a similar virus infection that develops a similar biliary disease. Importantly, we found that antiviral therapy blocks the development of the disease in this mouse. Now we are using this model to find antiviral treatments for patients with PBC. In the laboratory, we have isolated the virus in culture as a proof that patients are infected. Now we are now trying to find diagnostic tools to detect viral infection and monitor response to antiviral treatment. We are also trying to find out how the virus triggers specific aspects of the disease to find better therapies.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Xin, an actin-binding protein, in satellite cells and muscular dystrophies
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE EXPRESSION; MUSCLE FUNCTION; MUSCLE REGENERATION; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; SATELLITE CELLS; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Mutations to many of the proteins that compose the 'skeleton' of muscle cells lead to the development of disease states such as the muscular dystrophies.  These proteins are, however, part of a large network involving other proteins whose roles are less well-defined. My lab has demonstrated that one of these poorly understood proteins, Xin, is expressed in muscle stem cells during regeneration and plays a vital role in maintaining muscle stem cell function during the repair process. The studies proposed herein build on our previous work and have two main goals: 1. Uncover the roles and regulation of Xin within skeletal muscle.  To undertake these studies we will use a novel mouse model which lacks Xin expression. We hypothesize that Xin is critical for the structural integrity of muscle cells during contraction and is essential for promoting the activation of muscle stem cells in response to injury. 2.  Define the expression pattern of Xin in human dystrophic muscle of known and unknown etiologies.  Approximately 20% of people diagnosed with muscular dystrophy do not know the mutation causing their condition. We hypothesize that mutations in Xin will account for at least a subset of these cases.  Furthermore, we hypothesize that the degree to which Xin is abnormally expressed in known dystrophic conditions (e.g. limb-girdle muscular dystrophies) contributes to the variability in onset, progression and severity that is observed in these diseases. We believe the findings of the research undertaken by myself and my trainees will uncover novel information pertaining to the regulation of muscle stem cells and has a strong potential to discover an novel form of muscular dystrophy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and genetic analysis of estrogen-related receptors (ERRs) function in breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CHIP-SEQ; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most frequent cancer in women. The estrogen receptor and the oncogene ERBB2 have been known to play a major role in the initiation and progression of the disease. Consequently, these two proteins have been the subject of intense investigation during the last 20 years, and drugs inhibiting their activity such as Tamoxifen, Anastrozole and Herceptin have been developed and successfully used to treat breast cancer. However, not all patients respond to these drugs or patients that initially respond to tem develop resistance during the course of the treatment. Thus, we must continue to search for complimentary and alternative therapeutic avenues. The estrogen receptors belongs to a large family of functionally related proteins. Among this family exist a group of very closely related orphan receptors referred to as the ERRs. Orphan receptors are members of the family for which an association with a known natural hormone has yet to be found. Recently, we have found that the ERRs play an important role in controlling breast cancer cell growth and proliferation. The ERRs do so by directly interacting with the estrogen receptor and the ERBB2 oncogene. The goal of our research project is thus to understand how the ERRs promote the growth and proliferation of breast cancer cells. Our laboratory employs the most up-to-date technologies to probe the genome of breast cancer cells for answers as well as to transfer this knowledge to the clinic as rapidly as we can. We hope that our research program will lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies to treat the disease and prolong the life of breast cancer patients in a significant manner.

TitreApplicationTitle: Shaping the direction of youth health by evaluating how Changes in policies, programs and resources in the school environment impact Obesity, Marijuana use, Physical activity, Alcohol use, Smoking and Sedentary behaviour of students over time: The COMPASS Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL AND DRUG USE; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; NATURAL EXPERIMENT; OBESITY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY / SEDENTARY BEHAVIOUR; POLICY AND BUILT ENVIRONMENT; PROGRAM; QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN; SCHOOL-BASED; SMOKING; YOUTH/ADOLESCENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Research suggests that school-based prevention strategies targeted at individual students have limited impact on preventing the development of risk behaviours among youth, whereas population-level intervention strategies that change the school environment may have greater impact. As such, the purpose of this study is to establish a longitudinal study which follows a cohort of 6,500 students (Grade 9 at baseline) attending 115 Ontario secondary schools for 4 years to understand how changes in school environment characteristics (policies, programs and resources) are associated with smoking, physical activity, healthy eating behaviour, obesity, marijuana use, alcohol use, sedentary behaviour and educational outcomes among students. Each year, student- and school-level data pertaining to the 8 behavioural outcomes and their correlates will be collected using the School Health Action, Planning and Evaluation System (SHAPES). We will also provide annual feedback reports to schools that provide a school-specific understanding of what is happening in their school (i.e., student behaviours and existing programs and policies), and a list of evidence-based ways to intervene at the school-level. We will then evaluate how changes in school characteristics over time are associated with student behaviours; valuable insight for understanding how to best tailor and target future school-based interventions so that they have impact.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of human neutrophil peptides in lung inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY; ARDS
Abstract-Résumé: Acute lung injury is known to be related to white blood cell invasion into the lung. However, how exactly the white blood cells cause lung injury remains unclear. We found that the proteins named human neutrophil peptides (HNP) released from white blood cells during infection can induce lung injury. The present research proposal will identify the proteins that can recognize HNP by lung cells so that we will design medications to block those proteins interacting with HNP thus reduce and prevent lung injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Déterminants de l'adéquation de l'aide aux besoins des personnes avec des troubles de santé mentale dans le contexte de transformation (Phase 2)
Keywords-MotsClés: ADEQUATION DE L'AIDE A REPONDRE AUX BESOINS; ANALYSES QUANTITATIVES ET QUALITATIVES; BESOINS DES PERSONNES AYANT DES TROUBLES DE SANTE MENTALE; DETERMINANTS DE L'AIDE ET DE L'ADEQUATION DES SERVICES; PERFORMANCE DU SYSTEME DE SANTE MENTALE; PERSPECTIVE DES PATIENTS; REFORMES DES SERVICES DE SANTE MENTALE; RETABLISSEMENT ET QUALITE DE VIE; TROUBLES DE SANTE MENTALE; UTILISATION DES SERVICES DE SANTE (TRAJECTOIRE/DETERMINANTS)
Abstract-Résumé: Ce projet vise a mieux comprendre les determinants de l'adequation de l'aide aux besoins des adultes presentant des troubles graves de sante mentale, et specifiquement dans le contexte de l'implantation de la reforme en sante mentale au Quebec, et des orientations soutenues par le comite senatorial canadien. L'adequation de l'aide aux besoins impose que soient atteintes les conditions necessaires a offrir pour qu'une personne atteigne, maintienne ou restaure un niveau acceptable d'independance sociale ou de qualite de vie. Les determinants referent a differentes dimensions en interaction influencant la reponse aux besoins en sante mentale: sociodemographiques, economiques, cliniques, psychologiques et environnementales. Tant au Quebec qu'au Canada, les politiques de sante mentale visent a optimiser la qualite des services par un accroissement de leur dispensation dans la communaute, une meilleure integration du dispositif de soins et la promotion du retablissement des personnes. A cette fin, une nouvelle equipe locale de sante mentale dans les centres de sante et de services sociaux a ete creee au Quebec, et d'importantes cohortes de ressources humaines et d'usagers presentant des troubles graves stabilises de sante mentale ont et seront transferees des hopitaux psychiatriques a l'equipe des CSSS. Tout en contribuant au suivi de ces transformations et de leurs impacts sur les usagers, cette etude permettra de mieux comprendre les determinants de l'adequation de l'aide aux besoins. Cette derniere a fait l'objet de peu d'etudes, pourtant elle est au cur du retablissement des usagers et de l'amelioration des services. Les usagers sont aussi souvent absents de l'interpretation de ce qui repond a leurs besoins, or leur adhesion a la planification de leur soin est une composante cle dans leur retablissement.

TitreApplicationTitle: Compartment specific cyclic nucleotide signaling and control of mural cell vascular functions
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERY; CAMP; PHOSPHODIESTERASE; RESTENOSIS; STENTING; THERAPEUTIC ANGIOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Placement of a stent is an effective way to unblock clogged arteries. However, this procedure can sometimes result in damage to the artery and promote growth of cells that eventually re-block the artery. In part to reduce this problem, most stents currently in use release drugs that act to inhibit the growth and movement of the cells that might block the artery. Although this approach can reduce this problem, it also can promote the formation of blood clots on the stents, a process called in-stent thrombosis. Thrombosis on the stent is often fatal since it can spread to the heart to cause a heart attack, or to the brain and cause a stroke. Our work aims to uncover new methods of inhibiting artery re-blockage after stenting that will not promote clotting.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; CANCER DU POUMON
TitreApplicationTitle: Surviving the break-up in DNA damage response with a novel partner: TPX2
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCERS; CELL CYCLE; CELLULAR BIOLOGY; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR; MITOTIC CELLS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NEUROLOGICAL DISORDERS; NEURONS; SPINDLE
Abstract-Résumé: Our genetic material (DNA) is constantly exposed to toxic metabolites and deleterious environmental agents. Thousands of DNA lesions can occur per day in one single cell. To avoid cancers, the damaged DNA has to be repaired. Human cells possess a very sophisticated system called the DNA damage response system (DDR) that allows them to sense and repair the damage. Humans with defective DDR often develop cancers. My laboratory has discovered a unique protein to impact the DDR of cancer cells and consequently, to affect their proliferation and survival behaviors. We propose to further study this protein known to be upregulated in cancers in order to establish it as a marker and target for cancer research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adding Motivational Interviewing to Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Severe Generalized Anxiety Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: AUGMENTING TREATMENT RESPONSE; COGNITIVE BEHAVIORAL THERAPY; ENGAGEMENT IN TREATMENT; GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER; INTERPERSONAL PROCESS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SEVERE ANXIETY; TREATMENT RESISTANCE & NONCOMPLIANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Although effective treatments have been developed for anxiety and depression, nonresponse or partial treatment response remain common occurrences. This limited response is at least partly a function of low patient motivation for adhering to recommended treatment procedures. That is, clinicians who are knowledgeable about methods of facilitating change will often find themselves ineffective if they are unable to build client motivation and help clients work through their conflicting and often powerful feelings about change.     Motivational Interviewing (MI) is a brief treatment that is strongly supported in increasing internal motivation and commitment to change for substance abuse. But despite widespread calls to add MI to the treatment of anxiety, and promising preliminary data supporting its potential to reduce resistance to change among those with anxiety, no previous study has systematically and rigorously tested its value in augmenting existing anxiety treatments. The proposed project provides a powerful test of the value of adding MI before and during the recommended therapy for excessive worry (Cognitive Behavioural Therapy), among those with severe symptoms who typically do not respond to existing therapies. Moreover, the study also seeks to identify exactly how and why adding MI to existing therapy for anxiety augments treatment response.    If successful, the study findings will have significant public health implications by demonstrating that by adding brief interventions to enhance motivation, we can improve adherence and outcomes with existing treatments for the substantial number of individuals living with anxiety disorders. Such findings would also suggest the possibility that MI might enhance treatment response for other problems and other treatments (eg., medication). Finally, we will integrate state of the art methods for translating knowledge into practice throughout the project (including methods for informing training in these treatments).

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; RECHERCHE SUR LES MÉDICAMENTS
TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibition of calcium overload: Harnessing its therapeutic potential to limit post-ischemic myocardial dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM OVERLOAD; CARDIAC MECHANICAL FUNCTION; GLUCOSE METABOLISM MODULATORS; INFARCTION; ISCHEMIA-REPERFUSION THERAPY; LATE SODIUM CURRENT INHIBITORS; PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: A reduction in blood flow to the heart (termed cardiac ischemia) or an imbalance between oxygen supply and oxygen demand (workload) causes anginal pain and depresses the normal contractile activity of the heart.  Severe reductions in blood flow may cause a heart attack (termed myocardial infarction).  Following a heart attack, the heart cells can be saved from dying by the speedy restoration of blood flow (termed reperfusion).  Although restoration of blood flow is beneficial and prevents heart cells from dying, there may be a delay before the heart is able to pump normally.  There has been a major research effort aimed at enhancing the recovery contractile function, and we have determined that one of the factors that contribute to poor recovery is a high rate of acid production within heart cells that causes excessive and deleterious accumulation of calcium ions that worsen mechanical function and promote cardiac cell death.  We have already discovered some drug targets in the pathways of glucose metabolism that reduce acid production inside of heart cells, and that this limits calcium accumulation and improves recovery of heart mechanical function.  Using our novel experimental system in which we can measure glucose metabolism, intracellular calcium levels and mechanical function in hearts under carefully controlled conditions of energy supply and demand, we plan additional and detailed studies on the pharmacological regulation of new, as yet unexplored, targets that we hypothesize will regulate glucose metabolism and calcium accumulation.  We anticipate that these approaches will be beneficial and will facilitate an improved return of normal pumping activity, as well as reduce irreversible injury and cell death (infarction).  We expect our planned investigation will help identify new drug strategies that will ultimately translate into clinical practice to enhance recovery of the heart from potentially lethal reductions in blood flow.

NomDuComitéFR: Programme conjoint de recherche en santé Canada-R.-U. sur l'antibiorésistance

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Novel antibacterial targets, assays, probes and opportunities in bacterial cell wall biogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBACTERIAL PEPTIDES; BACTERIAL CELL WALLS; BIOSYNTHESIS; ENZYME SUBSTRATES & ASSAYS; HIGH THROUGHPUT  SCREENING; INHIBITORS; MATURATION; PEPTIDOGLYCAN; SYNTHESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Millions of people die each year from bacterial infections and tens of millions suffer from the consequences of these infections. The discovery of the antibiotic penicillin once opened the door to treat these infections by stopping bacteria making the polymer in the cell wall that holds them together. This polymer, called peptidoglycan, is made up of an interlocking network of sugars and strings of amino acids (peptides). Specialised proteins (called PBPs), with the ability to stitch together these sugars and peptides are the targets inhibited by penicillin, stopping cell wall synthesis and killing the bacterium. Many important bacteria are no longer killed by penicillin and other antibiotics that attack other stages in the production of peptidoglycan. Bacteria have changed, evading the action of these antibiotics. We need to fight back. Our progress until recently has been hampered by our inability to routinely synthesise the key chemical components that make this polymer. We can now do this. This is exciting, as we develop the capability to explore important unanswered questions about how bacteria grow and control the production of peptidoglycan. As leading researchers in peptidoglycan metabolism in Canada and the UK with complementary facilities and expertise, Team CanUK proposes to consolidate established collaborations and further the development of a research network to increase our understanding of the fundamental biology of this process. All of this will open fundamentally new biological insights, and opportunities to use these for the future development of new antibiotics that will work against multiply antibiotic resistant bacteria like MRSA and TB.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: The contribution of extracellular tau to the propagation of neurodegeneration in Alzheimer disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; FRONTO-TEMPORAL DEMENTIA; MICROTUBULES; NEURODEGENERATION; PHOSPHORYLATION; SECRETION; TAU PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Tau protein is believed to normally stabilize microtubules, the railways responsible for the transport of proteins within a neuron. During the course of Alzheimer disease and other neurodegenerative disorders termed frontotemporal lobar degeneration, tau protein detaches from microtubules and forms toxic aggregates that are associated with neuronal cell death. The formation of tau aggregates begins in a discrete region of the brain and propagates to larger areas at later of stages of the disease. A new concept has emerged to explain this specific pattern of the propagation of tau aggregation in the brain. Tau aggregates would be released from neurons and taken up by neighboring neurons. The uptake of tau aggregates would induce the formation of aggregates by normal endogenous tau. These newly formed aggregates would be released by neurons and then would initiate a new cycle of propagation. Our research program aims to define how and where tau aggregates are released by a neuron and how and where tau aggregates are taken up by a neuron using diverse cellular and molecular biology techniques. Our research will have direct impact on the elaboration of new therapeutic strategies to slow down the progression of the Alzheimer disease and frontotemporal lobar degeneration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cadherin Adhesion Complexes in Synapse Development and Plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; BETA-CATENIN; CADHERIN-BASED ADHESION; DELTA-CATENIN; DOPAMINERGIC PATHWAY; PALMITOYL-ACYL TRANSFERASE; PALMITOYLATION; PRIMARY HIPPOCAMPAL CULTURES; SYNAPSE PLASTICITY; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Synapses are highly specialized regions of cell-cell contact designed to rapidly and efficiently relay signals from one neuron to another. By establishing a dynamic yet precise network of synaptic connections, the brain is able to attain a level of functional complexity that enables not only simple motor tasks, but also sophisticated emotional and cognitive behaviours. Previous work has implicated cadherin adhesion molecules in the appropriate development of neural circuitry. This proposal aims to understand how cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion is modified in response to neuronal activity, and how regulation of cadherin-based adhesion impacts synapse function. We will specifically examine the role of two cadherin intracellular binding proteins, delta-catenin and beta-catenin, in regulating cadherin-based adhesion and synapse function. Perturbations in the function of cadherin and their associated catenins are closely tied to many neurological and psychiatric diseases including Alzheimer's and Huntington's diseases, schizophrenia and drug addictions. This underscores the importance of studying this adhesion complex in the context of brain development and function.

CommitteeNameEN: Canada-UK Joint Health Research Program on Antibiotic Resistance
NomDuComitéFR: Programme conjoint de recherche en santé Canada-R.-U. sur l'antibiorésistance
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada-UK Team in Bacterial Resistance to Beta-Lactam Antibiotics
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Hospital-acquired infections (HAIs) are increasing with growing numbers of susceptible individuals in aging populations.  Antibiotic-resistant HAIs are more dangerous and difficult to treat.  So-called Gram-negative bacteria like Escherichia coli cause many thousands of HAIs each year.  The beta-lactams, such as penicillin, are the most important antibiotics for HAIs caused by these organisms. Since Gram-negative bacteria have become resistant to most other antibiotics, carbapenems (the most powerful beta-lactams) are now the most important treatment for these infections. Carbapenem resistance in Gram-negative bacteria has been relatively rare, and has usually arisen in species that cause relatively few HAIs.  However, this situation has now changed: carbapenem-resistant strains of several Gram-negative bacteria, including E. coli, (many carrying a gene called NDM-1) are spreading rapidly worldwide.  As there are no new drugs for antibiotic-resistant Gram-negative bacteria, infections by these organisms are consequently very hard to treat.We aim to develop a new treatment for HAIs caused by carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria.  Penicillin-resistant Gram-negative bacteria can be treated by combining penicillin with a drug that blocks the resistance mechanism, but it is not yet possible to block NDM-1 (or related genes). We will design, make and test molecules that will block carbapenem-resistance mechanisms like NDM-1 and so enable carbapenems to kill resistant Gram-negative bacteria.  A reliably active antibiotic against these organisms will transform the outlook for many patients with HAIs.  We will also monitor the spread, particularly in hospitals, of bacteria carrying NDM-1 and similar genes, and identify the most important types to use in our testing programme.  We will further develop new methods to measure how molecules block NDM-1 function.  These new methods and resources will benefit other efforts to overcome carbapenem-resistant HAIs

TitreApplicationTitle: On-line and on-the-ground: bridging the gap between vulnerable populations and public health.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO SERVICES; BEHAVIOUR CHANGE; BLOODBORNE PATHOGENS; COMPUTER TECHNOLOGY; HEALTH EDUCATION; HEALTH PROMOTION; MOBILE PHONE TECHNOLOGY; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The global health community continues to struggle to lower the number of new cases of HIV.  Although the prevention and control of HIV should be relatively straightforward, it has proven to be anything but.  Despite having all the tools necessary to stop the spread of disease, those populations most vulnerable to HIV continue to suffer from a lack of access to testing and treatment.  The issue largely comes down to marginalization; those individuals most at risk of HIV, tend to be those who are most marginalized in society and have the poorest access to and ability to find health care resources and services.  Therefore, HIV prevention does not necessarily need new or better diagnostic or treatment options, rather, the degree of marginalization of those populations most vulnerable to disease must be reduced, such that they are aware of and can take advantage of the services available.  In this proposal we use the latest technological innovations in eHealth approaches to health promotion to better bridge the gap between marginalized populations and health care providers.  The work will take place in Canada, Colombia, and Kenya.

TitreApplicationTitle: Trifunctional folate-metabolizing enzyme MTHFD1: impact on birth defects and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CONGENITAL HEART DEFECTS; FOLATE; GENETICS; MTHFD1; NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS
Abstract-Résumé: Low dietary folate has been well-established as a risk factor for the development of birth defects and cancer. Variations in folate pathway genes have been identified that also increase the risk for these disorders. Folate is required to provide the building blocks for DNA and protein synthesis. The relationship between folate, birth defects and cancer may reflect the increased demand for folate pathway products in rapidly dividing cells. The MTHFD1 R653Q variant is a sequence change in an important enzyme of folate metabolism and may be a risk factor for neural tube defects (NTD), pregnancy complications and gastric cancer. We have found that the R653Q variant decreases the stability of the protein and disrupts folate metabolism in cells. The effects of the variant may be modulated by the diet or by the presence of other folate pathway variants. In this project we propose to use a mouse model to investigate the effects of MTHFD1 variants on the development of birth defects and cancer. This mouse model will allow the investigation of dietary and genetic factors not possible in human studies. Our work will further the understanding of folate metabolism and the mechanisms of the development of folate-related birth defects and cancers. This work may produce recommendations for diet and/or genetic screening for birth defects and cancer prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stimulation cérébrale dans la maladie de Parkinson: mécanismes d'action et implication clinique
Keywords-MotsClés: INFLAMMATION; INTERVENTION THERAPEUTIQUES; MALADIE DE PARKINSON; MODELES ANIMAUX; NEUROGENESE; STIMULATION CEREBRALE PROFONDE; STIMULATION MAGNETIQUE TRANSCRANIENNE; TRANSGENE
Abstract-Résumé: La stimulation cerebrale profonde (appelee chirurgie DBS) - qui consiste a stimuler electriquement des structures ciblees du cerveau - est une approche therapeutique de plus en plus utilisee dans le traitement de la maladie de Parkinson. Bien que les effets rapportes sur les symptomes cliniques de la maladie soient en grande partie benefiques, certains patients experimentent des effets secondaires importants. Les effets a long terme de ce traitement, qui cible actuellement les patients de stade avance, font encore l'objet de debats au sein de la communaute scientifique. Malgre le nombre croissant de chirurgies DBS chez les patients parkinsoniens a travers le monde, on ne sait toujours pas si le DBS represente simplement une mesure palliative ou s'il peut constituer un traitement capable de modifier le decours/profil de la maladie. Pour adresser ces questions fondamentales qui demeurent sans reponse, notre groupe de recherche a developpe un tout premier prototype de microstimulation permettant la stimulation a long terme chez le rongeur, lequel replique les methodes utilisees chez l'humain. Grace a cette percee technologique, nous proposons d'investiguer les mecanismes d'action de cette approche therapeutique ainsi que la fenetre d'applicabilite selon les changements observes dans le cerveau de rongeurs rendus parkinsoniens. Les resultats generes permettront de mieux comprendre les mecanismes d'action de ces traitements, d'en evaluer les impacts cliniques et ainsi d'adapter les therapies aux divers stades de la maladie.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: Neural markers of Depressive Relapse Vulnerability and their Modification
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION; DEPRESSION RELAPSE; EMOTION; FMRI; MAJOR DEPRESSION; MINDFULNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a chronic disabling disorder, where each new episode of depression significantly increases a patient's risk for falling into depression again, this is called relapse. Preventing depression relapse is a fundamental challenge in the care of formerly depressed patients. At present it is unclear why, following successful treatment, depression returns. The present proposal intends to examine the underlying cognitive and associated brain events that predict depression relapse in formerly depressed individuals. To do so we will measure brain activity in formerly depressed individuals' with functional magnetic resonance imaging to visualize these vulnerabilities, presently invisible to us. We will examine if a brain and a behavioural bias in how people pay attention to depression-relevant events predict relapse. To that end, we will employ treatments to see if these presumed abnormal biases can be undone, protecting individuals from the return of depression.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - C : Systèmes digestif, endocrinien et excrétoire
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of gut microbiota in Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY AND DEPRESSION; GASTROINTESTINAL MICROBIOTA; GASTROINTESTINAL MOTILITY; INFLAMMATION; IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME; METAGENOMICS; MOUSE MODELS; VISCERAL SENSITIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Gut bacteria are known to shape the body immune system and to affect the function of the gut. Many studies have shown that patients with chronic gut diseases, such as Irritable Bowel Syndrome, have either abnormal or unstable balance of gut microbes. We believe that this abnormal balance of bacteria, that normally reside harmlessly in our gut, can produces abdominal cramping and diarrhea, and also lead to altered mood. We propose to collect and examine the bacteria from stool samples in patients with Irritable Bowel Syndrome during 6 month period, and investigate whether alteration in bacteria correlate with changes in gut symptoms and mood. We plan then to colonize germ-free mice with gut bacteria from symptomatic patients and investigate possible mechanisms causing gut dysfunction and mood changes.  If there is indeed a difference in the bacterial population in symptomatic individuals, this information could lead to new treatments, such as prebiotics or probiotics, to cure this chronic problem.
