TitreApplicationTitle: Atrial Substrate Modification with Aggressive Blood Pressure Control to Prevent Atrial Fibrillation
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; BLOOD PRESSURE; CATHETER ABLATION; CLINICAL TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is an abnormal heart rhythm that comes from the upper chambers of the heart. Atrial fibrillation causes the main pumping chambers of the heart to beat in an irregular and sometimes very rapid fashion. Some people with atrial fibrillation feel completely well. Others feel unwell, with palpitations, a feeling of shortness of breath, reduced exercise ability,  lightheadedness or chest pain. Atrial fibrillation is not usually a dangerous rhythm but can cause you to feel unwell and can reduce your quality of life. If atrial fibrillation causes signficant symptoms, catheter ablation is often used to try to prevent it from coming back. Catheter ablation involves putting special wires up through the veins of the legs to record the electrical signals of the heart and to cauterize the areas of the heart that cause this abnormal rhythm. The cure rate is between 50 and 60% for those patients who are in AF persistently. Aggressive blood pressure control may improve this cure rate significantly, reducing the need for second and third procedures for this problem. With each procedure, the risks for major and minor complications is up to 6%, with a risk of death of 1 in 1000. Objective: We propose to determine if aggressive blood pressure lowering reduces the recurrence of atrial fibrillation after a catheter ablation procedure for atrial fibrillation. Methods: This objective will be accomplished by performing a clinical trial whereby patients with persistent AF who will be undergoing catheter ablation to treat their AF will be randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups: 1) aggressive blood pressure control versus 2) standard therapy. There will be 184 patients required for the entire study. This is the first trial to study the effects of blood pressure lowering on atrial fibrillation in a randomized fashion.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and cellular biology of T regulatory cells
Keywords-MotsClés: T CELL SIGNALLING; T REGULATORY CELLS; TOLERANCE
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system has a remarkable ability to specifically recognize "danger". The mechanisms by which the immune system discriminates between dangerous or non-dangerous proteins are highly complex and are not foolproof. When the immune systems starts to react against non-dangerous proteins, pathologies such as autoimmune diseases and allergies result. On the other hand, failure to recognize truly dangerous proteins, such as those present in tumour or virally-infected cells, can result in loss of tumour immunity or an inability to clear infections. A better understanding of how the immune system learns to accept certain proteins, and to eliminate others, will lead to the development of more rational therapies for the diseases which result when these natural mechanisms go awry. A type of white blood cells, known as T regulatory cells, represents an ideal candidate for an innovative therapy that could specifically control undesired immune responses, without affecting other aspects of the immune system. This proposal aims to address basic questions about the biology of these T regulatory cells. The studies will increase our understanding of how T regulatory cells arise naturally, how they suppress immune responses, and how they differ from normal T cells. Ultimately, the work will contribute to the application of T regulatory cells as a "cellular therapy" to control immune responses in the clinic.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Distinct Role of PI3K isoforms in Signaling and Heart Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC TOXICITY; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; HEART FAILURE; KNOCKOUT MOUSE MODEL; MYOCARDIAL ISCHEMIA; PRESSSURE-OVERLOAD; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a common and devasting condition with high morbidity and mortality. Pressure-overload occurs in common clinical scenarios such as hypertension and coronary artery disease leads to heart attacks which are the major causes of heart failure. Our research will tackle and elucidate the precise role of PI3 kinase (PI3K) isoforms in the control of the heart under these stressors. PI3K is an enzyme that adds a phosphate group to a lipid molecule involved in signalling to generate an active chemical called phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (abbreviated PIP3). There are three major isoforms of PI3K: alpha, beta and gamma. Changes in PI3K signaling are a key finding in heart failure. Previous studies in this field of investigation have utilized non-specific pharmacological blockers of PI3K which coupled with the fact that they can only be used on a short-term basis limits the conclusions that can be drawn from these studies. We will for the first time appreciate the unique and distinct roles of the different classes of PI3K in heart disease. We have the unique opportunity to combine the findings obtained from four genetically engineered murine models with a thorough set of in vivo and in vitro investigations. Our studies employ in vivo experimental models (pressure-overload and heart attacks) and functional assays and thus provide pre-clinical data for novel therapeutic interventions in heart disease. We can begin to explore the potential therapeutic and/or toxic effects of blocking or enhancing specific isoforms of PI3K in heart disease. Indeed, the pharmaceutical industry has successfully targeted these specific isoforms as novel anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory agents. These agents may indeed have important cardiac toxicity.

OrgNm: Ottawa Hospital Research Institute/Institut de recherche de l'Hôpital d'Ottawa
CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - A: Reproduction, Maternal, Child and Youth Health
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Cell volume regulatory mechanisms in oocytes and preimplantation embryos
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTED REPRODUCTION TECHNOLOGIES; CELL VOLUME REGULATION; EGGS; EMBRYOS; INFERTILITY; OOCYTES; TRANSPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Increasingly, infertile couples are treated by assisted reproduction technologies that include in vitro fertilization and the extended culture of eggs and embryos outside the woman's body. Recently, this is being extended to "in vitro maturation" (IVM) of eggs. In IVM, immature eggs are taken from the ovary and matured to fertilizable eggs in the clinic. IVM would avoid the serious side effects and expense of using hormones to stimulate egg production in women. However, it is still experimental, and there are serious concerns about safety and success rates. Early embryos are extremely sensitive to perturbations of their cells' size, indicating that cell volume regulation is critical to early embryo development. We previously found, using the mouse as our model, that  early embryos have a unique mechanism for maintaining cell size that relies on accumulation of the amino acid glycine inside embryonic cells. We propose that what glycine does is to replace some of the salts that the embryos, like other cells, routinely take up to quickly correct deviations from their preferred size. Embryos appear to be very sensitive to having too much salt inside them, and need to replace it with something more benign like glycine. This implies that embryos have mechanisms that import ions in response to decreased cell volume, which must be carefully regulated to allow glycine to replace salts. In this project, using the mouse model, we will determine their identity, how they are regulated during embryo development, and when they develop during the growth of the egg in the ovary. Finally, we will investigate how the egg switches to the mechanism that uses glycine, and turns off the ones that use salts, during egg maturation. We propose that dysregulation of this process is one major reasons for problems with current IVM. Therefore, finally, we will use our findings to improve the conditions for IVM, with the aim of making it safer and more effective.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Control of herpes simplex virus infection: viral regulators of host signaling pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: HOST SIGNALING PATHWAYS; INNATE AND ADAPTIVE IMMUNE SYSTEMS; PROTEIN KINASES; TRANSLATION; VIRAL GENE EXPRESSION; VIRUS INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Many viruses alter host cell functions to promote virus replication and evade host antiviral responses, for example by activating the PI3-kinase/Akt pathway to enhance cell survival and translation of viral mRNAs while inhibiting pathways that detect and control pathogens. We and our collaborators have discovered that the herpes simplex virus protein VP11/12 plays key roles in modulating host signaling: it is essential for virus-induced activation of Akt, and it is also able to disarm signaling through the T cell receptor, thereby dampening antiviral immunity. This research project focuses on determining exactly how VP11/12 achieves these remarkable effects, and delineating their impact on virus replication. The results will increase our understanding of viral replication strategies, and perhaps point to new approaches to controlling virus infection.

ResearchClassEN: SKIN AND SUBCUTANEOUS TISSUS; MUSCULO SKELETAL
ClasseRechercheFR: PEAU ET TISSUS SOUS-CUTANES; MUSCLES ET OS
TitreApplicationTitle: Skin-derived precursors: their role in tissue maintenance, repair and regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DERMIS; REGENERATION; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: We now know that most mammalian tissues contain adult stem cells that are capable of generating the cell types present in that tissue.  In addition, increasing evidence indicates that these adult stem cells play key roles in the maintenance, repair and regeneration of those tissues, and that when they are perturbed, this causes  premature tissue and organismal aging.  In this regard, our laboratory previously identified an adult stem cell from the skin and recently showed that they derive from resident stem cells for the dermis, the second skin layer.  Here, we propose to ask how these stem cells function to maintain, repair and regenerate the skin and in so doing prevent premature skin aging.  In addition, we propose to ask whether similar stem cells can participate in the regeneration of fingertips, something that occurs in children, with the hopes that if we could understand this process, then perhaps we could promote other types of regeneration in humans.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - C: Digestive, Endocrine and Excretory Systems
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - C : Systèmes digestif, endocrinien et excrétoire
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES DU FOIE; MALADIES A VIRUS
TitreApplicationTitle: Pilot study of highly active anti-retroviral therapy for patients with primary biliary cirrhosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-RETROVIRAL THERAPY; PRIMARY BILIARY CIRRHOSIS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; RETROVIRUS INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) develop progressive liver disease and often require liver transplantation. The cause of disease is unknown. It is thought to occur as a result of an infection in subjects that are more susceptible to disease than others. We found evidence of retrovirus infection in patients with primary biliary cirrhosis. We found that most patients with PBC have evidence of viral infection. Since then we have conducted clinical studies using anti-viral therapy. We found that PBC patients treated with combination anti-retrovirus therapy experienced significant reversal of the disease process. This provides some circumstantial evidence for a retroviral infection. Although we could show significant improvements, the changes were not substantial and we are now looking for better antiviral regimens. Now we have found a mouse model with a similar virus infection that develops a similar biliary disease. Importantly, we found that antiviral therapy blocks the development of the disease in this mouse. We have used this model to find safer and more effective antiviral treatments for patients with PBC. We have now found out that a combination of highly active antiretroviral therapy with Truvada and Kaletra stops disease in the mouse and plan to use this combination to see if it works in patients with PBC. Of interest, a recent case report shows that this combination is associated with normalizing liver tests in a patient with PBC and retrovirus infection.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Mathematical modeling of fitness and frailty in relation to biological age in individuals and populations
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DISABILITY; FRAILTY TRAJECTORIES; HEALTH CHANGES; MATHEMATICAL MODELING IN BIOMEDICAL DATABASES; MORTALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Chronological age is often used as a rough measure of the aging process. But individuals do not die from old age. They die because they become more vulnerable, and this occurs with age. We have developed a better measure of aging than chronological age - a measure that takes individual health vulnerability into account. This 'frailty index' represents a person's biological age by integrating various characteristics of health and social-demographics. The frailty index is used to predict individuals' future health status and their risk of adverse outcomes (the chance of entering a nursing home or of dying). Because the frailty index summarizes health status as a single number, we can analyze the trajectories of how individual people's health changes over time. This has the potential to open up exciting opportunities, such as to describe the conditions under which biological aging (deficit accumulation) might become slower. In this project, we seek to further develop our modeling technique to analyze individual trajectories of changes, and to identify the factors influencing these changes. We aim to apply an advanced analytical technique to detecting such factors, even when their influence is seemingly small. Even small changes in individual's chances of health improvement may result in a considerable improvement in population health. We will conduct these studies using large databases of health data from Canada and other countries, on tens of thousands individuals followed for up to 20 years. This gives us the resources to validate novel techniques that are sensitive to small but important factors, including biological, social, environmental characteristics and lifestyle variables. In addition, we aim to make our research findings useful for clinical practice, to help improve health care for older people. Our multidisciplinary team will provide a good account of not only how health changes occur in older adult but at what extent the process of changes can be reversed.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Hematopoietic Transcription Factor Ikaros As a Metabolic Sensor in Neuroendocrine Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRENAL; CHROMATIN REMODELLING; IKAROS; PITUITARY
Abstract-Résumé: We have discovered that the nuclear protein Ikaros which is known to be involved in immune stem cell development is also present in some hormone-producing glands. With funding from CIHR we identified that Ikaros is essential for the development of cells that produce hormones allowing the body to fight infections and promote growth. In its absence, animals succumb to stressful demands and fail to grow. In this grant renewal we propose to examine (1) how the hormone system is able to sense increased stressful demands through Ikaros and (2) how Ikaros is able to control hormonal responses. Our findings will provide new insights on how the immune and hormone systems are inter-connected during development and throughout the stressful demands of life.

OrgNm: Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM)
NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
DomainesScientifiquesFR: MÉTABOLISME/DIABÈTE; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Glucose regulation of insulin secretion and metabolic enzymes' gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: ANAPLEROSIS/ CATAPLEROSIS; GLYCEROLIPID/FREE FATTY ACID CYCLING; INSULIN SECRETION; LIPID METABOLISM; MONOACYLGLYCEROL; PANCREATIC BETA CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Insulin is a hormone produced by pancreas in our body. It controls the levels of sugar in blood and its utilization by other tissues. Either a lack of enough insulin in the blood or reasons that interfere with its function, cause diabetes. In order to understand how our body produces and releases insulin under different dietary conditions and the regulation of this process, we are proposing the present research. Specifically, the primary goal of our proposal is to identify both the positive and negative signals within the pancreatic beta cell that mediate the link between the metabolism of glucose and fats and the release of insulin. A better knowledge of the molecular basis of the insulin secretion process is necessary to develop novel therapeutics against diabetes that work efficiently and without any unwanted side effects.

ResearchClassEN: CANCER THERAPY GENERAL; BREAST CANCER THERAPY
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: Structure/Function of the DNA Repair Enzyme, Polynucleotide Kinase/Phosphatase
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPY; DNA REPAIR; INHIBITOR DESIGN; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: All cancers initiate through genetic mutations that arise as a result of damage to DNA. Our cells contain elaborate mechanisms that have evolved to recognize and repair damaged DNA, thereby protecting our genetic information. Our lab studies the proteins that are involved in detecting DNA damage and repairing the damage. This grant focuses on the DNA repair enzyme polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP), which is a critical enzyme in the repair of broken DNA ends. Mutations in PNKP make human cells highly sensitive to DNA damage, and also are associated with a form of a developmental neurological disorder called MCSZ. This grant aims to understand how PNKP recognizes and repairs broken DNA ends, and how it interacts with other proteins to help in the DNA repair process. This work will provide insights that will help us to develop molecules that inhibit PNKP function that could provide leads in the development of new cancer therapies.

ResearchClassEN: METABOLISM AND NUTRITION; MULTIPLE DISEASE RELEVANCE
ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: New roles for copper metabolism proteins in meiotic differentiation.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHAPERONES; COPPER METABOLISM PROTEINS; COPPER TRAFFICKING; MEIOTIC DIFFERENTIATION; METALLOPROTEINS AND DISEASES; YEAST AS A MODEL SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Yeasts are organisms that are closely related to mammals at the cellular level. Both fungal and mammalian cells are eukaryotic, which means that they carry genes on chromosomes in a nucleus and divide their cells up into different functional compartments. This similarity implies that one-celled fungi are important models for studying processes that occur in our own (mammalian) cells. Meiosis is a specialized cell division process, common to sexually reproducing eukaryotes. During meiosis the chromosome number is reduced by half to generate haploid gametes. In humans, meiotic defects are the leading causes of infertility, pregnancy loss, congenital birth disorders and mental retardation. Despite essential roles for copper-dependent proteins during meiosis, the function and mechanisms of action of these proteins in this biological process remain poorly understood. Our research model is based on the unique biology of the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe. In this organism, meiosis can be induced in a highly synchronous manner, thereby allowing meiotic steps to be monitored and dissected directly. This unique property makes S. pombe particularly powerful in the elucidation of basic principles that govern meiosis. Moreover, S. pombe is one of the best-understood models for chromosome behaviour, and has a complete collection of tools and technology. The goal of this research is to provide a better understanding of key mechanistic aspects of copper-requiring proteins that are required for faithful and healthy reproduction (fertility) and to understand how aberrations can lead to diseases such as aneuploidy, infertility and developmental defects.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
ClasseRechercheFR: PNEUMONIE; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Dissection of Murine Radiation-Induced Lung Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALVEOLITIS; CONGENIC; FIBROSIS; GENETICS; LUNG; MOUSE MODELS; RADIATION
Abstract-Résumé: The common cancer treatment modality of radiotherapy could be used more effectively if the side effect it produces, normal tissue damage, could be eliminated or treated. Up to 30 percent of patients receiving radiation treatment of the thorax, breast, lung and oesophageal cancer; Hodgkins disease patients, develop alveolitis and fibrosis in the lungs. Genetic differences among people likely contribute to who develops this response and who does not. In the proposed research we will study animal models which present the same lung damage as cancer patients may suffer after radiation exposure, to identify specific genes which predispose to the development of these side effects. Such genes are more easily detected in animal models (than in the clinic) as breeding permits the needed number of animals to be created.  The proposed investigations will use the latest advances and approaches of genomics research, related to the Human Genome project, to uncover specific lung response genes for later testing in a cancer patient population. This research would enable a therapeutic plan including a pretreatment marker to be developed from knowledge of specific genes of lung disease response, which would directly produce a reduction in morbidity & mortality from cancer, by sparing side effects and increasing the dose to the tumour, which may, in turn, increase cure rates.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of AMP-activated protein kinase in regulating inflammation in obesity:  implications for the treatment of insulin resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYL-COA CARBOXYLASE; AMP-ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASE; FATTY ACIDS; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; INSULIN RESISTANCE; MACROPHAGE; MOUSE MODELS; OBESITY; PGC1 AND MITOCHONDRIA
Abstract-Résumé: Nearly 50% of Canadian are overweight or obese. Obesity is strongly associated with inflammation and defects in fat metabolism which contribute to insulin resistance (pre-diabetes).   In the current proposal we will examine the role for a metabolic sensing molecule, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), in regulating inflammation and fat metabolism in immune cells.  We believe that activation of this molecule in immune cells will reduce inflammation and fat accumulation preventing the development of diabetes.

ResearchClassEN: DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS; INFECTIOUS AND PARASITIC
ClasseRechercheFR: DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Overcoming Aminoglycoside Resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLTRANSFERASE; AMINOGLYCOSIDE; INHIBITION; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: The World Health Organization (WHO) has recently classified antibiotic resistance as one of the three greatest threats to human health. Amongst antibacterial agents, aminoglycosides occupy a special niche due to their effectiveness against most bacteria, including the causing agent of tuberculosis. The long term goal of this project is to find agents to overcome aminoglycoside resistance. To achieve this, our efforts will focus on 3 streams: 1) study one of the most common determinants of aminoglycoside resistance, aminoglycoside N-6'-acetyltransferase (AAC6'); 2) design molecules that block resistance caused by AAC(6'); and 3) design new antibacterial agents active against resistant strains. A better understanding of resistance-causing mechanisms is critical to the development of resistance inhibitors and of antibacterials active against resistant strains. We have made significant progress in this area. We have also reported the first AAC(6') inhibitor able to block aminoglycoside resistance in cells as well as the first prodrugs with such an activity. Finally, we have recently reported some molecules with activity against antibiotic resistant bacteria. One of these is especially active and will be studied further. The main goal of this research project is to improve the potency and pharmaceutical properties of our most active molecules. To this end, medicinal chemistry studies will include the synthesis of multiple derivatives, followed by biological studies with purified enzymes, in cells or in animals.

NomDuComitéFR: Soins palliatifs et soins de fin de vie
TitreApplicationTitle: Les soins palliatifs et de fin de vie dans la démence: Évaluation d'un programme interdisciplinaire et multidimensionnel d'organisation des soins en milieu d'hébergement.
Keywords-MotsClés: DEMENCE; MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; RECHERCHE EVALUATIVE; SOINS DE FIN DE VIE; SOINS DE LONGUE DUREE; SOINS PALLIATIFS; VIEILLISSEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Au Canada la maladie d'Alzheimer et les autres types de demence affectent un nombre croissant de personnes agees. Au stade avance, les personnes atteintes sont la plupart du temps admises dans un Centre d'hebergement et de soins de longue duree ou elles vivront les derniers moments de leur vie. L'approche de soins palliatifs est de mieux en mieux integree aux soins offerts aux personnes atteintes de cancer mais elle n'est souvent pas accessible aux personnes atteintes de demence en phase avancee. Ces soins visent notamment a offrir aux patients et aux familles une meilleure detection et prise en charge de la douleur et des autres symptomes physiques et psychologiques qui accompagnent la fin de vie. Ils visent egalement a ameliorer les communications entre les patients, leurs familles et les soignants tout particulierement en ce qui a trait aux niveaux de soins et aux directives anticipees. L'objectif general de la presente demande est d'implanter et d'evaluer un programme d'organisation de soins palliatifs et de soins en fin de vie adapte aux personnes souffrant de demence terminale hebergees dans les centres d'hebergement. Le programme d'interventions comporte les composantes suivantes: (a) implication d'une infirmiere de l'etablissement comme agent de changement; (b) sensibilisation des gestionnaires et des soignants a l'importance des soins palliatifs dans la demence, (c) programme de formation pour les medecins et les membres du personnel soignant, (d) rencontres de famille et distribution d'un livret d'information aux familles, (e) suivi clinique systematique pour le controle des symptomes. Le programme sera implante pendant une periode de 12 mois dans 2 centres d'hebergement experimentaux (un a Quebec et un a Sherbrooke) et les effets seront evalues en comparaison avec deux autres etablissements temoins comparables (un a Quebec et un a Sherbrooke) ou les soins usuels continueront de s'appliquer pendant la meme periode mais sans l'implantation du programme.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN; CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting the YB-1 pathway to overcome breast cancer recurrence
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CD24; CD44; CHIP-SEQUENCING; EXPERIMENTAL THERAPEUTICS; KINASE INHIBITORS; RSK; TUMOUR TISSUE MICROARRAYS; TUMOUR-INITIATING CELLS; YB-1
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide there are 1 million new cases of breast cancer and the greatest challenge is tumours that are resistant to conventional therapies. This is not all that uncommon given that 30% of women will experience breast cancer recurrence following their initial treatment. Further complicating matters, once the cancer returns womens are 100 times more likely to die from the disease. We discovered a protein referred to as YB-1 and its activated form P-YB-1S102 are expressed in ~50% of all breast cancers based on measuring it in ~5500 cases. It holds promise as a therapeutic target for this disease because it mediates resistance and further breast cancer cells continue to depend on it even when they have developed drug insensitivity. In this proposal we will explore the possibility that we can inhibit YB-1 using drugs that block its activation. In order to translate this quickly we will screen drugs that are currently in clinical trials in the hope that there may be agents "in the pipline" that could be used to tailor treatment.

ResearchClassEN: DENTAL DISEASE (INCL. ORAL BIOLOGY); INFECTIOUS AND PARASITIC
ClasseRechercheFR: AFFECTIONS DENTAIRES (ET BIOLOGIE BUCCO-DENTAIRE); MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional genomic analyses of a peptide antibiotic-sensing and response regulon in Streptococcus mutans
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTATION TO PEPTIDE ANTIBIOTICS; ANALYSES OF PROTEIN-DNA INTERACTIONS; ANIMAL MODEL ANALYSIS; ANTIBIOTIC-SENSING & RESPONSE REGULON; BIOFILMS; CELL ENVELOPE STRESS RESPONSE; FUNCTIONAL GENOMIC ANALYSIS OF A REGULON; GENETIC ANALYSIS; MICROARRAY ANALYSIS; STREPTOCOCCUS MUTANS
Abstract-Résumé: Tooth decay or caries is one of the most common human diseases, affecting over 80% of young people worldwide. By the age 70, more than 25% of populations may have lost some or all of their natural teeth due to tooth decay. Children and adults receiving chemotherapy for cancer, AIDS or other systemic diseases are notably at higher risk for caries. Although caries is not a life-threatening disease, diagnosing, treating and retreating caries and caries-related diseases is still a major financial burden to the public health systems worldwide. In many undeveloped regions and countries, tooth decay remains a "silent epidemic" left untreated.   Tooth decay is caused by bacteria living in the oral cavity. One bacterium called Streptococcus mutans is considered as a leading cariogenic pathogen worldwide, because this bacterium is highly efficient to express several virulence-associated traits, of which the ability of this bacterium to survive and adapt to killing by host defense peptides or by antibiotics is a prerequisite for its persistence in the oral cavity. Such an ability may provide this bacterium with an overwhelming ecological advantage, resulting in an emergence of significant number of this bacterium that may initiate tooth decay. Our understanding of molecular mechanisms of how this bacterium adapts to antibiotics and initiates tooth decay is still lacking. This requires new knowledge and experimental approaches to explore these questions.   In this project, we propose to develop innovative approaches to investigate these questions. The data obtained from this project will contribute to the body of knowledge that facilitates our understanding of how this bacterium adapts to peptide antibiotics and the mechanisms in which the bacterium initiates tooth decay. The knowledge obtained from this research will allows us to develop new strategies to prevent tooth decay.

TitreApplicationTitle: External regulation of Start in C. albicans
Keywords-MotsClés: CANDIDA ALBICANS; CELL CYCLE; MATING RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: Fungi such as molds and mushrooms often attack and destroy crop plants and stored food, but luckily not that many fungi directly attack humans.  One of the most common of the fungi that do cause human disease is the yeast Candida albicans, which is the source of most yeast infections in women, and of thrush in infants and patients suffering with AIDS.  Because the fungi that cause human disease have cells that work very similarly to human cells, they are hard to treat, because drugs that kill the fungi tend to also damage the human patient.  As part of a long-term goal of finding new ways to treat Candida infections, we are investigating how these cells chose whether or not to divide to make new cells when they receive signals from outside the cell.  Both human and fungal cells have similar motors that control the production of new cells, so we hope that by finding out the details of how Candida cells make the decisions to turn the division motor on or off we can find unique processes that the fungus uses that human cells do not.  Because we can manipulate the genetic information of Candida cells very precisely, we can ask very specific questions about how controls of the division machinery work. If these processes are needed by the Candida cells to live, we may be able to block them and prevent the growth of the disease-causing organism without hurting the patient.  While it would be nice to be able to cure yeast infections and thrush, Candida can cause even more serious, often fatal infections if it gets into the bloodstream of a patient.  Thus identifying new ways to cure Candida infections by studying the way the cells control the production of new cells may help us save lives.

ResearchClassEN: DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS; CANCER THERAPY GENERAL
ClasseRechercheFR: DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting topoisomerase II
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICANCER DRUG; BREAST CANCER; CANCER; DRUG DESIGN; DRUG SYNTHESIS; MOLECULAR MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Anticancer drugs that target DNA topoisomerase enzymes are the most effective and widely prescribed anticancer drugs in current use. More than half of all current cancer chemotherapy treatments use topoisomerase II-targeted drugs. However, the currently used anticancer drugs have a number of properties that must be improved. The use of the widely used anthracycline class of anticancer drugs results causes a potentially fatal cardiotoxicity. The problem of serious cardiotoxic side effects appearing later in life is particularly acute for children treated with the anthracycline class of anticancer drugs for childhood leukemias which are highly curable. The goals of this project are to develop structurally novel potent anticancer drugs that target topoisomerase II that are not cardiotoxic. This goal will be achieved by using structure-based drug design to discover and synthesize new anticancer drugs that specifically target topoisomerase II at a newly characterized binding site on the enzyme. Molecular modeling and docking of candidate drugs into the topoisomerase II binding site and also its DNA substrate will be used to identify and develop new non-toxic anticancer drugs. Drugs discovered using these methods will be tested for their ability to kill various types of cancer cells. With the development of these new anticancer drugs the health of Canadians with cancer will benefit with higher cure rates and an improved quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and epigenetic control of the ZPBP2/ORMDL3/GSDMB domain and susceptibility to asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN STRUCTURE; CILDHOOD ASTHMA; EPIGENETICS; GENETIC VARIATION; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: In living cells, DNA exists in a packaged form: it is wrapped in proteins. Depending on the packaging, DNA is either easily accessible for transcription factors (proteins that help reading the information stored in DNA) and actively functioning, or is not accessible and is silent. DNA packaging is also termed "epigenetic state". An abnormal epigenetic state may silence an important gene, and thereby cause disease. We will test the role of epigenetic states in predisposition to asthma. Asthma is an autoimmune disorder that affects about 300 million people worldwide, a large proportion of whom are children. It has a strong hereditary component and is thought to result from interaction between genes and environment. During the last 20 years, asthma has been on the rise with a steeper increase in children. This is attributed to environmental factors, such as allergens and pollution. Genetic studies found that the DNA sequence in a region of chromosome 17 increases the risk of developing asthma. However, the exact mechanism underlying the relationship between DNA sequence change and risk to develop asthma remains unclear. Our work shows that epigenetic states are being also affected in this region. We hypothesize that changes in the DNA sequence of this specific region of human chromosome 17 provoke changes in DNA packaging that in turn lead to abnormal functioning of neighboring genes and cause predisposition to asthma. To test this hypothesis we will study gene regulation in the asthma-associated region of human chromosome 17. This work will help to better understand how common genetic variants lead to disease susceptibility in humans; clarify the pathogenesis of autoimmune disease, including asthma; and eventually help the treatment and management of autoimmune disorders.

ResearchClassEN: CANCER THERAPY GENERAL; BREAST CANCER THERAPY
ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: Remodeling of the tumor microenvironment by CD73: a therapeutic target
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOSINE; BREAST CANCER THERAPY; CD73; CHEMORESISTANCE; PURINERGIC SIGNALLING
Abstract-Résumé: CD73 is a cell-bound enzyme overexpressed in breast cancer. Recently, my work has shown that the expression of CD73 in breast cancer is associated with increased tumor growth and metastasis. Furthermore, I have shown that CD73 inhibition can significantly delay the progression of breast cancer. It remains unknown, however, whether anti-CD73 therapy can be effectively combined with other forms of breast cancer treatment, such as chemotherapy and new forms of targeted treatments. This project proposes to investigate the therapeutic effect of combining anti-CD73 therapy with chemotherapy and treatments that act through the immune system, such as trastuzumab (anti-HER2 therapy) and immune-modulators.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting reduced stress responsiveness in the postpartum: role of stress appraisal mechanisms, metabolic factors and parity
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION; COGNITION; LACTATION; METABOLIC HORMONES; MULTIPARITY; POST-PARTUM; REPRODUCTIVE HISTORY; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: In the initial postpartum period, mothers are faced with important challenges in order to cope with novel stimuli and demands that are presented by the offspring.  The fact that 10 to 15 percent of new mothers suffer from postpartum depression is an index of how demanding this phase of the life cycle can be. Physiological and behavioral adaptations occur during this period, including a reduction in the neuroendocrine response to stress observed in rodents and in human breastfeeding mothers. We propose that post-partum depression is associated with a failure to adequately filter relevant from irrelevant stimuli, leading to exaggerated stress responsiveness and anxiety in this period.  Our proposal will attempt to understand some of the mitigating mechanisms. In particular, we hypothesize that stress responses in the postpartum are governed by 1) the perception of a threat specific to the infant and increased vigilance; 2) the metabolic demands placed on the mother and 3) the number of previous pregnancy/lactation episodes (i.e. parity). We will use physiological and metabolic manipulations in lactating dams during the early and late postpartum period and measure activation of cellular and neuroendocrine responses in the brain as well as behavioral responses.  This work should help understand some of the underlying mechanisms of postpartum depression and design effective preventive treatment for this disorder.

ClasseRechercheFR: VIEILLISSEMENT; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of longevity in C. elegans mutants with defective mitochondria.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; C. ELEGANS; GENE EXPRESSION; MITOCHONDRIA; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; REVERSE GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: It has been observed that aging, which is the main risk factor for many diseases, is systematically accompanied by increased production of reactive oxygen species (also called free radicals), which are molecules that can be toxic at high concentration. It has therefore been suggested that these free radicals might be the cause of aging, and people have tried to combat their production or their effects with so-called anti-oxidants, although the efficacy of anti-oxidants in slowing down aging has never been clearly demonstrated. Recently, we and others have shown through genetic experiments in animals that free radicals are almost certainly not the cause of aging. It remains very important however to explain why increased free radical production accompanies aging. For this we are proposing to use a model animal, the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, and to study several long-lived mutants that we have previously identified. These mutants have dysfunctional mitochondria, which are the energy producing parts of the cell and are the main site of free radical production. We have found that these mutant mitochondria generate high levels of free radicals, yet age slowly and are protected from free radical toxicity. We hypothesize that free radicals can function as a cellular stress signal that induces a protective response. This hypothesis suggests that aging is accompanied by increased free radical production because, with time, the organism sustains ever greater stresses due to aging. We will try to understand the mechanisms that link mitochondrial function, free radical production, protection from free radical toxicity, and aging in the mutant animals. Understanding these links should shed light on these processes in non-mutant animals and in people. We believe that our results could help to understand the nature of the aging process and when and why antioxidants could, or would not, be beneficial.

ClasseRechercheFR: MUSCLES ET OS; AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES
TitreApplicationTitle: Development of better and more effective treatments for patients suffering of hyperkalemic periodic paralysis (HyperKPP)
Keywords-MotsClés: CHANNELOPATHY; CHLORIDE CHANNEL; MEMBRANE EXCITABILITY; POTASSIUM CHANNEL; SKELETAL MUSCLE; SODIUM CHANNEL
Abstract-Résumé: Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis (HyperKPP) is a disease that is primarily characterized by uncontrolled contractions of skeletal muscles with periods of complete paralysis that mainly affect limb muscles. The paralysis completely incapacitates patients because they are unable to move, often confined to bed for a period of time varying from a few hours to days. Past the age of 30, uncontrolled contractions and paralysis may cease, but patients suffer of muscle weakness such that walking becomes a difficult task; in some cases, patients become wheelchair bound. None of the present available treatments for HyperKPP are fully effective.  Muscle contraction is initiated by the generation of an electrical signal, i.e., action potential, on the cell membrane. In turn, the action potential starts with the entry of sodium into muscle fibers via a pore made by a protein called the sodium channel. HyperKPP results from mutations of this sodium channel that is primarily expressed in skeletal muscle. The mutation results in uncontrolled sodium influx at rest giving rise to the uncontrolled contractions and then paralysis. One common gene defect for this disease is a missense mutation where valine replaces methionine at residue 1592 (NaV1.4/M1592V).   The overall objective of this study is to document the mechanism of the disease and to develop new and more effective therapeutic approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-Term Potentiation in the Motor and Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex of Patients with Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; MENTAL ILLNESS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; NEUROPLASTICITY; PAIRED ASSOCIATIVE STIMULATION; SCHIZOPHRENIA; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is among the most debilitating disorders. Most of its burden is due to associated memory deficits. Weakening of frontal brain cell connections is considered to underlie these deficits. However, this has not been directly demonstrated in patients yet. Paired associative stimulation (PAS) is a novel brain stimulation method that assesses the strength of brain cell connections in humans. PAS has been mostly applied to the motor brain region that controls hand movements, in which case, the strength of brain connections can be measured using the electrical activity of the hand muscles.   PAS has yet to be applied to the frontal brain region of patients with schizophrenia. The challenge has been in the ability to measure the strength of frontal brain cell connections since there is no direct output measure such as the electrical activity of the hand muscles when PAS is applied to the motor brain region. This challenge can now be overcome using our technique of combining brain stimulation with the direct measurement of electrical activity from the brain. Using this technique, the strength of brain cell connections can be directly measured from the brain. We propose to use PAS in combination with the direct measurement of brain electrical activity to compare in 30 participants with schizophrenia and 30 age and sex matched healthy participants the strength of brain cell connections in the frontal brain region and how it relates to memory.  The originality of this proposal lies in the fact that it aims at directly assessing the strength of brain cell connections in patients with schizophrenia. It also uses innovative methodology that is based on brain stimulation. Finally, it intends to advance current knowledge on the cause of schizophrenia and associated memory deficits. Such knowledge will lead to novel treatments that strengthen brain cell connections, enhance memory, and improve the quality of life and function of hundreds of thousands of Canadians.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS CEREBRALES (ET RETINIENNES); THERAPIE DES TUMEURS CEREBRALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting Paediatric Brainstem Glioma Using Integrated Whole Genome Analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSE INTRINSIC PONTINE GLIOMA; GENOMICS; PAEDIATRIC; THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumours are the leading cause of cancer-related death in children and the most deadly of these are those involving the brainstem. Current therapy for childhood brainstem cancer, including radiation and chemotherapy, has had little impact on the survival of these children. This is because current therapies are largely based on studies of adult brain tumours, which we have shown bear little genetic resemblance to the childhood disease. We were the first to undertake a detailed study of the genetics of childhood brainstem cancer. We found interesting genetic changes pointing to new potential therapeutic targets. Here, we will use state-of-the-art, high-resolution techniques to examine the genetic alterations at multiple levels. These will then be combined to provide a complete view of tumour gene and pathway alterations. Further, we will undertake pre-clinical testing of the therapeutic targets we have already uncovered. Given the devastating outcome for the majority of these children it is imperative that new treatment strategies be attempted as rapidly as possible. The knowledge of the biology of these tumours amassed through this study will allow us to rapidly screen for agents already in use or in early clinical trials in adults which could be swiftly moved to trial in paediatric brainstem cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protective Factors Against HIV Risk Behaviour Among Gay and Bisexual Men: A Longitudinal Study
Keywords-MotsClés: GAY AND BISEXUAL MEN; HIV; HIV PREVENTION; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; PROTECTIVE FACTORS; SEXUAL BEHAVIOUR
Abstract-Résumé: Gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) bear a disproportionate burden of the epidemic in Canada, and HIV incidence appears to be rising among Canadian MSM. There is therefore clearly a need for new thinking to improve HIV prevention efforts for HIV-negative MSM. The research literature tends to use a risk factor/deficit model. This model does not adequately explain why most MSM manage to consistently practice protected sex. The lack of knowledge on protective factors limits the ability of public health agencies and AIDS service organizations to prevent the spread of HIV. The present study aims to examine how HIV- MSM rely on to reduce their sexual risks. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study will identify protective factors and sexual strategies among MSM that lead to higher or lower sexual risk outcomes. The research team includes university researchers from multiple disciplines, researchers from the AIDS Committee of Toronto and OHTN-based researchers. This study intends to build capacity of AIDS service organizations (ASOs), support evidence-based practice, support research, and build, support, and enhance community-academic-policy partnerships.

TitreApplicationTitle: Learning From the Voices of Youth: A Participatory Research Study Exploring the HIV and HCV Prevention Needs of Youth who Smoke Crack
Keywords-MotsClés: HEPATITIS C PREVENTION; HEPATITIS C RISK; HIV PREVENTION; HIV RISK; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; PEOPLE WHO SMOKE CRACK; QUALITATIVE INTERVIEWS; QUANTITATIVE STUDY; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: This research is driven by the expressed need of community partners for age-specific data relating to the HIV- and HCV-related prevention needs of youth who smoke crack. The lack of targeted health care and HIV and HCV prevention support services for people who smoke crack is particularly concerning considering the epidemiologic evidence demonstrating escalating engagement in crack smoking and virologic evidence documenting the HIV- and HCV-related risks associated with this practice. Street-involved youth are particularly vulnerable to crack use initiation.  In Ottawa, 64% of street-involved youth reported using crack and/or cocaine without injecting.   Youth engagement is an essential component of this project, as it is through the knowledge provided by youth that we will create the research tools, develop effective recruitment strategies, appropriately understanding the research findings and design a targeted plan for the dissemination of findings. As such, youth under 25 who have experience with crack (direct or indirect) will be recruited to join the Project Team, which will serve as a working group to inform the research process and ordering of priorities.  As a component of each Project Team meeting, youth will participate in a guided debriefing session in order to provide them with a safe space to share their feelings, reflect on their experiences in the meetings and make suggestions for ways of improving the process. This study will employ a sequential mixed methods design. We will use qualitative interviews to gather the perspectives of youth who have been identified as holding insight into the particular risk environments occupied by certain groups of youth who smoke crack. This data will inform the development of the quantitative analysis plan and survey tool.   We will then carry out a quantitative survey to document engagement in HIV- and HCV-related risk behaviours and practices that may place youth who smoke crack at risk of HIV and HCV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Community Champion HIV/AIDS Advocates Mobilization Project: A community-based intervention study
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCEPTANCE COMMITMENT THERAPY; COMMUNITY MOBILIZATIONS; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; ETHNO-RACIAL COMMUNITIES; HIV/AIDS; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; VULNERABLE COMMUNITIES
Abstract-Résumé: Ethno-racial communities, a growing proportion of Canada's population, experience disproportionately higher rates of HIV. CAAT's multi-disciplinary community-academic research team engaged PHAs and faith, media and social justice leaders from Black, Asian and Latin American communities in Toronto to study this problem. We found that homophobia and the lack of visible presence of PHAs within these communities sustain stigma and denial.  This undermines HIV/AIDS prevention efforts and heightens discrimination against ethno-racial PHAs. It also highlights the need to mobilize PHA and other community champions to address HIV/AIDS-related stigma within these communities. This study will pilot and test two interventions with potential to mobilize community champions as key agents to advance HIV/AIDS work. Social Justice Capacity Building training (SJCB) is based on the principles of empowerment education and skills development and has been used widely to engage communities in addressing their health issues. However, since HIV/AIDS-related stigma impedes the extent to which affected communities can fully utilize SJCB to address HIV issues in their communities, this project will also pilot and test the use of SJCB in conjunction with Acceptance Commitment Therapy (ACT). ACT is a psychological intervention which has shown potential for addressing stigma, but it has not been tested in the context of HIV/AIDS-related stigma. Using a pre- and post-test design, 30 PHAs and 30 community leaders will participate in one of two intervention programs: (1) SJCB only; or (2) ACT plus SJCB. This study will test the effectiveness of using SJCB and ACT to increase participants' readiness to act as champions to reduce HIV/AIDS-related stigma in the target communities. Study results will inform HIV prevention efforts in the target ethno-racial communities disproportionately affected by HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Facilitators and Barriers to Engagement in HIV health research: Key communities affected by HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HIV/AIDS; POPULATION HEALTH RESEARCH; RESEARCH ETHICS
Abstract-Résumé: With the growing focus and investment in population/public health research and community-based research in HIV/AIDS in Canada, there is an need to be able to recruit and enroll representative samples of the population under study if the results from these studies are to have good generalizability and broad application/policy impact to get ahead of the epidemic. However, results from recent studies have raised some concerns around if certain individuals or subgroups, by virtue of being "vulnerable" and having a potentially stigmatizing condition or issue (e.g. person living with HIV, being Aboriginal, men who have sex with men, HIV positive mother from a country where HIV is endemic, persons using injection drugs), may be less likely to participate in research because of their vulnerable situation, individual characteristics and/or concerns of being further stigmatized by how their data may be used. The aim of this study is to examine the factors that impact on the attitudes and willingness of people to participate in HIV-related health research. We will: 1) ascertain the attitudes and beliefs of people living with and at risk of HIV towards their consent for their personal health information to be used in various types of health research (e.g. clinical trials, cohort studies, administrative data) and research uses (e.g. market research, help to improve care, examination of the relationship between health); 2) determine the key facilitators and barriers which are related to a person's willingness to consent to different types of health research; and 3) determine the key factors about "community-based research" that may help facilitate the consent and participation of people living with and at risk for HIV/AIDS in health research. Through this study, we hope to be better able to suggest how we can ensure the broadest and most representative participation in research studies so that the work that is done will have the most impact.

TitreApplicationTitle: Taking Action II: Fostering Aboriginal Leadership in HIV Prevention Using Arts-Based Methods
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL YOUTH; ARTS-BASED; DIGITAL STORYTELLING; HIV PREVENTION; QUALITATIVE; SEXUAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: OBJECTIVES:(1) To understand what inspires some young people to become active around HIV prevention in their communities. (2) To explore digital storytelling as a strategy for increasing Aboriginal youth activism in HIV prevention. (3) To develop and disseminate community-specific "by youth for youth" HIV prevention and support materials.   METHODS: Stage 1: We will invite Aboriginal youth from across Canada to apply to "tell their stories" about HIV leadership, activism and engagement. We will select youth (n=20; ages 16-25) to ensure representation from all regions of the country. These youth will be welcomed to a week-long workshop at which they will be taught digital story-telling skills and provided assistance to create short (3-5 minute) films that tell their unique stories (in their own words and languages) about how and why they became involved and engaged in HIV prevention.   Following the creation of these stories, each youth will be interviewed about their film and why they became HIV leaders and activists. Stage 2: Each youth leader/film maker will be asked to organize a screening of their film in their own community with other youth, elders and community members. Following the film, a facilitated discussion will ensue about the impact of HIV on Aboriginal communities, why it is so difficult to talk about, and what might inspire others to become leaders.   ANALYSIS: We will analyze all of the digital stories collected, and all of the interviews and facilitated discussions.   DISSEMINATION: In addition to disseminating findings through traditional academic media, youth productions will also be shared online. We will create community-friendly packages with a copy of the DVD that has all the stories, a manual and a discussion guide for others seeking to screen the stories.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multilevel social determinants of risky sexual behavior among Nunavik young adults
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; COMMUNAUTES VULNERABLES; EMPOWERMENT; PROMOTION DE LA SANTE SEXUELLE; PREVENTION DES ITS ET DU VIH-SIDA; RECHERCHE COMMNAUTAIRE; SANTE DES AUTOCHTONES; SERIES CHRONOLOGIQUES; EPIDEMIOLOGIE; EVALUATION
Abstract-Résumé: Au Canada, le VIH dans les communautes autochtones ne cesse de croitre. Les adolescent(e)s de ces communautes sont particulierement a risque pour le VIH et les infections transmises sexuellement (ITS). Chez les Cris, certaines ITS se retrouvent en proportion beaucoup plus grande que dans le reste du Quebec. Pour ces raisons et pour repondre aux preoccupations des communautes cries a cet egard, les instances des Terres-Cries-de-la-Baie-James ont decide d'elaborer un programme culturellement adapte sur les relations interpersonnelles et la sante sexuelle, que l'on nomme le Chii kayeh iyaakwaamiih. Ce programme de promotion de la sante sexuelle et de prevention du VIH/sida qui se base sur des theories demontrees efficaces, a ete cree en collaboration avec les communautes cries et suite a plusieurs consultations avec ces dernieres. Depuis l'automne 2008, le «chi » comme l'appelle les jeunes, fait partie du curriculum scolaire de la majorite des ecoles secondaires du territoire cri. Etant donne le caractere unique de ce programme, il est desormais necessaire de proceder a son evaluation pour ainsi connaitre les effets qu'engendre la participation au Chii kayeh iyaakwaamiih. Pour ce faire, plusieurs eleves du programme seront suivis sur une periode de trois ans. Plus precisement, le projet de cette these consiste, en premier lieu, a evaluer si les objectifs du programme ont ete atteints, et ce grace, entre autres, a la comparaison de reponses a des questionnaires administres a tous les eleves avant et apres leur participation au programme. En second lieu, cette etude permettra de connaitre quels sont les impacts du programme sur la sante sexuelle des jeunes cris a partir de donnees disponibles sur la sante sexuelle. Etant donne les qualites novatrices d'un tel projet de recherche, des resultats d'evaluation favorables pourront permettre de reproduire cette demarche tant dans des disciplines variees que dans d'autres communautes et ainsi ameliorer la sante des populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Les trajectoires addictives et d'utilisation de services: l'expérience des hommes ayant des relations sexuelles avec d'autres hommes (HARSAH).
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPORTEMENTS; HARSAH; RECHERCHE COMMUNAUTAIRE; SERVICES DE SANTE; TOXICOMANIE; VIH
Abstract-Résumé: Les hommes ayant des relations sexuelles avec d'autres hommes (HARSAH) consommeraient davantage de substances que leurs pairs heterosexuels et leur consommation aurait augmente au cours des dernieres annees. La consommation abusive de substances dans cette population semble associee a certains determinants lies a leur vecu homosexuel, notamment: la difficulte d'acceptation de son orientation sexuelle, le vecu de la discrimination, l'importante presence d'alcool et de drogues dans plusieurs endroits de socialisation gais, etc. Le statut serologique semble etre un autre determinant de la consommation problematique, qui est plus importante chez les HARSAH seropositifs. De plus, les HARSAH initieraient des therapies en toxicomanie plus tardivement que les hommes heterosexuels et ces therapies ne seraient pas toujours adaptees a leur contexte de consommation, a leurs experiences de vie, ou a leur statut serologique. En outre, on sait que les prevalences du VIH chez les HARSAH au Canada et a Montreal seraient respectivement de 15,3% et de 12,5% et que la consommation de drogues serait associee a certains comportements sexuels a risque. En raison de ces nombreux enjeux, cette recherche vise a: 1) Decrire l'experience au cours de la trajectoire addictive des HARSAH et comprendre comment celle ci s'inscrit dans leur vecu homosexuel; 2) Identifier les besoins de sante specifiques decoulant de cette interaction (addiction/vecu homosexuel), notamment en rapport avec le VIH; 3) Documenter l'experience des HARASH, seropositifs et seronegatifs, en rapport avec leur utilisation des services et examiner dans quelle mesure les services repondent a leurs besoins de leur point de vue. En plus de l'avancement au plan des connaissances, ce projet permettra d'obtenir des donnees scientifiques sur la trajectoire de consommation problematique de substances des HARSAH afin de developper ou d'adapter des interventions appropriees.

TitreApplicationTitle: The cellular electrophysiology of neuropathic pain
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CALCIUM CHANNEL; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NERVE INJURY; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; NEUROTROPHIN; ORGANOTYPIC CULTURES; SPINAL CORD INJURY; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: 100,000,000 people worldwide suffer from the 'disease of pain'. This frequently reflects the presence of chronic, 'neuropathic' pain that can be initiated by traumatic nerve injury, diabetes or by infections such as AIDs or 'shingles'. Because this type of pain is resistant to most types of pain killers, there is an urgent need to understand the changes in the nervous system that accompany its onset, as only this can lead to the rational development of effective therapies. We study neuropathic pain in two ways. First, using procedures approved by the International Association for the Study of Pain, we subject rats to experimental nerve injury and study the changes in the electrical activity of nerve cells associated with pain processing in the spinal cord. These neurons become more prone to generate nerve impulses and this leads to a phenomenon known as 'central sensitization'. Secondly, we use 'organotypic' cultures where we maintain small slices of spinal cords in tissue culture for many weeks. Cultures are treated with known mediators of neuropathic pain to produce 'pain in a dish' and we again analyze neuronal electrical properties as signs of pain develop. We have found that brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) may be responsible for many aspects of 'central sensitization' and hence for the onset of neuropathic pain. BDNF produces a complex array of changes in spinal cord physiology and we plan to determine the molecular basis for these changes. It is also likely that 'central sensitization' leads to increased release of neurotransmitters from the nerves that carry painful information into the spinal cord and brain. This likely involves changes in 'calcium channels' that regulate the tendency of nerves to release neurotransmitters. This process is incompletely understood and requires further analysis.  By understanding such changes we will provide the theoretical basis for the development urgently needed new drugs for neuropathic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of potential biomarkers of successful treatment of latent tuberculosis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; LATENT TUBERCULOSIS; TREATMENT OF TUBERCULOSIS; TUBERCULOSIS; TUBERCULOSIS PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) infects about a third of the world's population and is the most important infectious cause of death in adults' worldwide. A cornerstone of TB control is treating TB while it is still dormant or latent, before it causes illness. The current standard treatment of latent TB is isoniazid for 9 months (9INH). This lengthy treatment is burdensome, and can sometimes cause serious side effects, so is often not taken. A potential alternative is 4 months of rifampin (4RIF), which is more rapidly effective than isoniazid - allowing the shorter duration of treatment.  A blood test that tested whether treatment of latent TB infection was effective could make it much easier to study new drugs or combinations of drugs to prevent TB, and to indicate when an individual could stop latent TB treatment. The blood tests that are most promising are measures of the immune response to TB.  We have begun a randomized trial to compare 9INH with 4RIF for the treatment of latent TB infection in almost 6,000 adults. We propose to measure results of immune response tests before, and at the end of 4RIF and 9INH. We will determine whether reduction in these immune responses is greater in persons who complete the standard treatment (9INH), or complete 4RIF, and if changes occur more rapidly with 4RIF. These results in turn will be compared to the effectiveness of the two drugs for preventing TB. Finally the most promising results will be re-tested in stored samples of blood that were gathered in an independent study of INH treatment of LTBI. This will act to confirm (validate) our results. This proposal is a unique, cost effective opportunity to compare the effect of each of these two drugs on the immune responses to TB. If these results can be correlated with the effectiveness of treatment, it could be used as a measure of treatment effectiveness for future clinical studies, allow them to be conducted more quickly, with fewer patients, and much lower costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epithelial cell-fibroblast interplay a key pathway to understand airway remodelling in asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY REMODELLING; APOPTOSIS; ASTHMA; BRONCHIAL EPITHELIAL CELLS; BRONCHIAL FIBROBLASTS; CYTOKINES; EPITHELIAL CELL PROLIFERATION; GROWTH FACTORS; KGF REGULATION; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a bronchial disease characterized by inflammation and changes in the structure of the bronchi. These changes are termed airway remodeling. Bronchial cells (epithelial cells) are considered as a key player in coordinating these airway changes. The function of these cells can be modulated trough different mechanisms. In asthma repeated damage to epithelial cells perturbs the structure of the bronchi Our group has developed a unique expertise to isolate bronchial cells (epithelial cells and fibroblasts) from very well characterized asthmatic and healthy patients. These cells put us in valuable position to study communication between these cells. Moreover we developed an attractive engineered bronchial mucosa that will allow evaluating this communication in a way that imitates in vivo situation. Our studies and those of others have shown that structure and function of epithelial cells and fibroblasts are changed in asthma. These changes may have an important impact on the structure of the bronchi. The goal of this renewal proposal is to evaluate the impact of these changes and develop new therapeutic approaches that will specifically target this aspect of asthma pathogenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of the anti-platelet functions of endothelial progenitor cells by sCD40L
Keywords-MotsClés: CD40L; ENDOTHELIAL PROGENITOR CELLS; PLATELETS; THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in Canada. It can be caused by multiple risk factors, which cause inflammation by activating blood cells, and damage blood vessels that supply the heart with oxygen. Such damage causes hardening of the arteries by plaque formation (atherosclerosis) and symptoms such as chest pain. This may cause complete blockade of the artery by a blood clot (thrombus) composed of blood cells and proteins. Unfortunately, current drug treatments do not prevent completely or limit the progression and the occurrence of narrowed and blocked heart blood vessels. Actually, a subset of progenitor cells called endothelial progenitor cells have shown promising results in repairing the damaged arteries and in limiting the reactions of platelets, the principal blood cells involved in blood clots. However, some inflammatory molecules in blood, such as CD40 ligand, may affect the function of endothelial progenitior cells and their capacity to reduce blood clot formation.   The objectives of our research program are:  1) Determine that CD40 ligand reduces the anti-platelet activities of endothelial progenitor cells; 2) Identify the biochemical reactions involved in the action of CD40 ligand on endothelial progenitor cells; and 3) Demonstrate that the anti-blood clot potential of endothelial progenitor cells is impaired by elevated blood levels of CD40 ligand in an animal model of blood clot formation.  Our experimental approaches include molecular and pharmacological tools which involve in vitro experiments with isolated blood cells, as well as in vivo studies with a clinically relevant animal model of heart vessel disease.    This project is very important for many fundamental and clinical reasons. We intend to identify new mechanisms linking blood and progenitor cells and damaged vessels. These insights should enable us to identify new drugs and to propose innovative approaches in the clinical management of heart diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dorsal ventral pancreas development
Keywords-MotsClés: BRUNOL1; CELL PROLIFERATION; EIF3; ENDODERM; PANCREAS DEVELOPMENT; RNA BINDING PROTEIN; TM4SF3; TRANSLATIONAL REGULATION; XENOPUS
Abstract-Résumé: The main goal of the research from my lab is to identify how the pancreas develops from separate dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds. Many of these same genes involved in early development are also implicated in controlling pancreatic tumor cell motility and growth. We recently identified two new genes that are directly involved in controlling pancreatic cell growth and fusion. The main goals of this research proposal are to define how one of these genes, BrunoL1 regulates cell proliferation and how another, Tm4sf3, controls fusion of the pancreatic buds. In the end, the results obtained will help elucidate the molecular pathway used by pancreatic cells during development, and may have implications for both diabetes and pancreatic cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Step Monitoring to improve ARTERial health (SMARTER)
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERIAL STIFFNESS; BEHAVIOUR; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE RISK FACTORS; DIABETES; HYPERTENSION; OBESITY; PEDOMETERS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Many people with diabetes and/or high blood pressure (hypertension) carry more weight than is healthy for them and are not very active. When people are more active, they can reduce the chances of having a heart attack or stroke. Walking more is a cheap and effective way to be more active and to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes. The problem is that many people do not walk enough! We will study if people with diabetes and/or hypertension walk more when the doctor gives them a prescription with the number of steps they should be walking every day. We will compare this group, called 'active', to another group, called 'control', in which doctors and their patients do what they usually do, over a period of one year.   We will measure the number of steps we walk everyday with a step counter or pedometer. In the step count prescription group, the doctors will give to the 'active' group a pedometer, a step count record book, and step count prescriptions. The overall goal is to gradually increase daily steps. The speed of the increase in step count will be slower for less active people. At each visit the doctor will look at the step count record book. The doctor will then give a new step count prescription to the patients. Patients of the two groups will see their doctor about four times during the year, which is how often they usually see their doctor.   At the end of one year, we will see the difference in the hardness of the arteries between the 'active' and the 'control' groups, using simple and safe measurements, similar to ultrasound in pregnant ladies. People with hard arteries are more likely to have a heart attack or stroke.   We suspect that patients who get the step count prescriptions will walk more and their arteries will be less hard than the control group. Our study will help decide if this is true. In that case, doctors should take the time to prescribe steps for all their patients with diabetes and/or hypertension.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolic Determinants of the Progression of Aortic Stenosis - PROGRESSA Study - Phase II
Keywords-MotsClés: AORTIC STENOSIS; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARDIAC RESONANCE IMAGING; CARDIOMETABOLIC RISK; DOPPLER-ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; HEART VALVE DISEASE; TOMODENSITOMETRY; VISCERAL OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Aortic stenosis (AS) is a cardiac disease that is characterized by the progressive obstruction of the aortic valve, which is one of the 4 valves present in the heart. AS is one the most frequent heart disease and there is no drug to slow its progression. The only efficient treatment for this disease is to perform a heart surgery to replace the diseased valve by a prosthetic valve. In the past, AS was thought to be a degenerative disease because of time-dependent wear and-tear of the valve. There is now substantial scientific evidence that AS is caused by the accumulation of lipid and inflammation within the valve, a process called: atherosclerosis. Recently, we obtained preliminary data, suggesting that the progression of AS is accelerated in patients with excessive amount of intra-abdominal fat. The accumulation of fat in the abdomen indeed causes several metabolic abnormalities including the release of small particles of "bad" cholesterol into the blood. This may predispose to the penetration of bad cholesterol into the aortic valve and to the development of inflammation and mineralization. Moreover, these metabolic abnormalities may also have harmful effects on the cardiac muscle therefore further increasing the risk of adverse events. The objective of this study is to elucidate the mechanism responsible for the progression of AS and, more specifically, to determine which are the key metabolic factors responsible for faster progression in the AS population. Our study will be the first of its kind, as it will measure, in parallel, the metabolic disturbances linked to abdominal obesity, the progression AS by echocardiography, tomodensitometry, and cardiac resonance imaging, and the occurrence of adverse events in a cohort of 260 patients with AS. The new knowledge provided could lead to the development of new approaches for the prevention or treatment of AS. This could contribute to substantially reduce the number of valve replacements and deaths related to A

TitreApplicationTitle: Satellite Stem Cells from Skeletal Muscle for the Treatment of Neuromuscular Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MUSCLE STEM CELLS; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; REGENERATIVE MYOGENESIS; WNT SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: The growth and repair of skeletal muscle in adults is accomplished by a population of cells called satellite cells that are found closely associated with muscle fibers in tissue. We have found that within this population there exists a subpopulation that exhibit the character of stem cells. These have been named satellite stem cells. Moreover, we have identified a secreted protein called Wnt7a that stimulates the activity of these stem cells. In this application, we aim to identify new components involved in regulating Wnt7a activation of these stem cells and to conduct experiments to understand the function of these components. We will next investigate the ability of Wnt7a-treated satellite stem cells to contribute to the formation of healthy muscle after transplantation into regenerating and diseased muscle. Lastly, we will explore whether similar cells can be isolated from human muscle tissue and whether these cells also exhibit a stem cell character following transplantation. Together these experiments will provide important new information about the mechanisms that control muscle stem cell function and provide insights into how stem cells contribute to the regeneration of skeletal muscle. Potentially, such experiments will open new avenues for the treatment of human diseases such as muscular dystrophy.

Abstract-Résumé: Dr Piche is working to characterize the effects that ovarian cancer ascites, a peritoneal fluid that accumulates during ovarian cancer progression, may have on enhancing drug resistance and disease-free progression. This work will identify soluble factors in ascites that affect tumor cell sensitivity to drugs, will define the intracellular mechansims involved, will identify new biomarker for early relapse and potential new therapeutic targets.
