TitreApplicationTitle: Strategies to Improve Diagnosis and Treatment of Asthma in Canadians
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; CLINICAL RESEARCH; HEALTH SYSTEMS RESEARCH; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: It is not currently known if physicians in Canada are ordering the appropriate diagnostic lung function tests necessary to make correct diagnoses of asthma in Canadians.  Our study will enroll 644 randomly-selected Canadians who have been diagnosed with asthma by a physician within the previous five years.  We will determine whether lung function tests were originally ordered in these patients to establish their initial diagnosis of asthma.  We will also test these patients over a 6-8 week period to determine if they truly have asthma.  Those patients in whom the diagnosis appears to have been incorrect will have their asthma medications stopped and we will follow them for one year.  The primary outcome of the study will be the proportion of patients in whom the diagnosis of asthma is excluded after one year of follow-up.  Should our study determine that diagnostic tests are not being properly employed, or that asthma is commonly misdiagnosed amongst Canadians, then this will provide an impetus for us to develop better strategies to promote more rigorous, objective methods to diagnose asthma in the community.

TitreApplicationTitle: Simvastatin Therapy for Moderate and Severe COPD (STATCOPE)
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; MULTI-NATIONAL; RANDOMIZED DOUBLE BLIND PLACEBO CONTROLLED TRIAL; STATIN THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) often experience frequent exacerbations which are of major importance since they have a long-lasting adverse influence on health status. COPD exacerbations are associated with increased lung inflammation that may contribute to other health problems such as muscle weakness, cognitive impairment,depression, stroke, and heart conditions. Statins are effective medications that have been shown to significantly reduce heart attacks and strokes and they also have anti-inflammatory effects. Observational studies suggest statins can reduce COPD exacerbations, but this has not been studied in a clinical trial. The purpose of this study is to determine whether patients treated with a statin medication have fewer exacerbations of COPD in comparison to patients who receive placebo therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term renal outcomes of critically ill children with and without acute kidney injury: a multi-centre Canada-USA study
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; CHILDREN; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; CRITICAL ILLNESS; DIAGNOSIS; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: Many children admitted to intensive care experience injury to their kidneys. This occurs because of the condition that affects them or the interventions they undergo, for example open heart surgery. Severe kidney injury in the intensive care unit leads to many problems, like fluid retention and heart failure and sometimes requires dialysis. Although we know that kidney injury  has effects on various short term outcomes (length of hospital stay and risk of death) we know very little about how this kidney injury occurring in hospital affects children in the long term. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a significant burden of illness in populations across the world including those in Canada. Early lifetime events such as kidney injury during critical illness may be an important risk factor for CKD. Early treatment and prevention of this injury could lead to significant improvements in outcomes for individuals and decrease burden of this  condition to the health care system. We therefore need to clarify if children admitted to the intensive care unit with kidney injury develop CKD. We also need to determine if traditional tests of kidney function are useful for detecting CKD in children who have recovered from kidney injury in the intensive care unit. We will follow-up children from 3 previously-studied North American groups of children who were admitted to the intensive care unit.  We will evaluate if they have developed signs of CKD at 6 year follow-up. We will also explore new and hopefully better tests for detecting CKD at follow-up. By showing the long term effects of acute kidney injury in children and evaluating possible risk factors for these outcomes, this study will help direct future treatment studies. Our results will also allow us to make recommendations on how to follow-up kidney function in children after they have been critically ill.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dietary manipulation of gut microbiota to manage obesity and insulin resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: GUT MICROBIOTA; INSULIN RESISTANCE; MATERNAL HEALTH; OBESITY; PRE-CONCEPTION; PREBIOTIC FIBER; SATIETY HORMONES; SITAGLIPTIN
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is highly prevalent among Canadian women. Obesity can lead to gestational diabetes as well as other complications during pregnancy. Maternal obesity also increases the risk of obesity in the child. Thus, it is essential to help women achieve a high level of health prior to conception. Modification to diet is a valuable intervention strategy for improving maternal metabolism and body weight. Research has shown that dietary fiber can help with weight and specifically body fat loss. Sitagliptin, a novel anti-diabetic drug, improves glucose control without promoting weight gain. Sitagliptin helps preserve levels of a specific hormone in the body that controls appetite and blood glucose called GLP-1. We thus propose to use a combination therapy of dietary fiber with sitagliptin to treat obesity in female rats in the period just prior to pregnancy. In addition to examining this combination of diet and drug therapy we will also determine whether altering the profile of bacteria in the intestine can help with weight control. We will enhance healthy bacterial levels with probiotics and selectively remove bacteria with an antibiotic. These studies will help us determine how bacteria in the intestine help dietary fiber improve metabolism and health. Ultimately this work has the future potential to improve the health of expectant mothers and their children in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diagnosis Of Uncertain-origin Benign Transient neurological symptoms.  (DOUBT)
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; MINOR STROKE; MRI; NEUROLOGY; STROKE; TIA
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke and transient ischemic attacks (TIA) are both due to a blockage in an artery in the brain. When it occurs, part of a patient's brain does not work properly giving them symptoms such as an inability to move one side or to speak. In the best case, this resolves quickly and we call this a TIA. In less fortunate patients the deficits may remain in mild form (minor stroke). Having a TIA or a minor stroke is a serious event because it is a warning that a second more severe stroke might happen. There are medicines that can reduce the risk of a second stroke. Because of this, patients are advised to go immediately to the emergency room if they present symptoms such as weakness, numbness, loss of vision or dizziness, as these may be symptoms of a TIA or minor stroke. Many patients with symptoms of dizziness or numbness have not actually had a stroke, but have a different disease that needs another treatment such as migraine or carpal tunnel syndrome. Even for experts the clinical history and examination are frequently not enough to decide exactly what just happened. MRI is one way to confirm the diagnosis of stroke. Even if the symptoms have resolved, in many patients we can see damage on an MRI scan of their brain proving that there was a blood clot in their brain. This finding confirms the diagnosis of TIA or minor stroke and can allow us to treat patients correctly. Patients with transient deficits that are not currently considered high risk (patients without symptoms of weakness of speech difficulties) will be enrolled and have an MRI scan of their brain completed within 7 days of the event to look for signs of brain damage (i.e a stroke). Patients will then be followed to see if they have complications such as a second stroke or a heart attack. When the study is complete we will then look back at exactly what symptoms put patients at risk for damage on their MRI scan. This will allow more precise diagnosis for patients and better use of stroke treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and characterization of genes involved in the genesis and progression of pediatric astrocytomas.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTOMAS; BIOMARKERS; DNA METHYLATION; EXOME SEQUENCING; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; INTEGRATED GENOMICS; MAPK SIGNALLING; MOUSE MODELS; PEDIATRIC BRAIN TUMOUR; SENESCENCE
Abstract-Résumé: While overall survival for children with cancer has improved substantially over the last 3 decades, significant challenges remain. Specifically, a considerable proportion of childhood cancers remains incurable, or can only be cured with treatments that leave a child with life-long mental or physical disabilities. In order to further improve survival, and the quality of life of children surviving high-grade astrocytomas, a particularly lethal and maiming form of brain cancer, it is important to understand what is driving this tumour type and inducing resistance. We identified Y-Box Protein 1 (YB-1) and Sorting nexin 3 (SNX3) to be abnormally highly present in these tumours and to be associated with worse outcome when present together. The ultimate aim of this comprehensive project is to gain insight into the function of YB1 and SNX3 and how they help drive tumour formation. We aim to identify targets and new therapies that may be developed for this particularly challenging disease.  We will determine the gene signatures driven by aberrant YB-1 expression based on where it is present in the cell and uncover targets driven by this factor for new drug therapies.  We will also uncover how SNX3 and YB-1 work together ad enhance tumour formation. These studies will provide an unprecedented view of YB-1/SNX3 functions and how best to counterbalance their effects. They will enable the development of new drugs, and offer the potential for tailored therapies for children with these presently lethal cancers who currently have limited options for clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Nitric Oxide Delivery System for Wound Healing
Keywords-MotsClés: CRITICAL DESIGN PARAMETERS AFFECTING NO DELIVERY PROPERTIES; ENHANCED WOUND HEALING IN A DIABETIC ANIMAL MODEL; MECHANISMS OF NITRIC OXIDE RELEASE FROM THE PRESENT SYSTEM; NEW SUPRAMACROMOLECULAR COMPLEXES FOR EXTENDED RELEASE OF NO; OPTIMIZATION OF NITRIC OXIDE LOADING AND RELEASE; STUDY OF VARIOUS PHYSICAL FORMS OF THE PRESENT COMPLEXES
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetic foot ulcers are a leading cause of amputations in diabetes patients. An effective therapy for treating chronic diabetic foot ulcers is still lacking. Nitric oxide (NO), a critical mediator in normal tissue repair, has been shown to play a pivotal role in the overall wound healing process. Several studies have linked impaired wound healing in diabetic ulcer patients to NO deficiencies at the wound site. Topical administration of NO or NO donors has been shown to promote tissue repair and healing of diabetic ulcers in animal models. However, existing avenues for NO delivery have major challenges regarding the safety of the nitric oxide donor system. Also, the short half life of NO makes it is necessary to deliver NO at optimal concentrations over a long enough period of time to maximize therapeutic effectiveness. Most systems exhaust their NO load in hours, too quick for optimal wound healing in diabetic ulcers. To overcome these, we have developed a simple, stable and biocompatible system which can release NO over an extended period of time (>9 days). This is based on the discovery that immobilizing S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO), a short-lived endogenous NO donor, onto a polymer complex greatly enhances the stability of GSNO and provides controlled NO release for an extended time not achieved by most existing systems. Preliminary test in a diabetic rat model suggests that a single topical application of this system can potentially accelerate wound closure. We propose to further study critical design parameters affecting the performance of this delivery system. Animal studies will be carried out in a diabetic animal model to demonstrate efficacy and improved quality of healed wound through histology assessment. Results obtained will help the design of more effective NO delivery systems for enhancing diabetic wound healing and should have a significant impact on the health care system by reducing the need for amputations in millions of diabetic ulcer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The design and planning of a randomized controlled trial to evaluate a tailored cardiovascular surgical patient education intervention in reducing post-hospital discharge complications and readmission rates
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR SURGERY; LEADER IN RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS DESIGN; PATIENT EDUCATION; TRAINING AWARD; TRIALS RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Educating patients following coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) and valve replacement (VR) surgery is carried out to provide the necessary information needed to promote performance of self-care behaviours during the home recovery period. In spite of this, approximately a quarter of all patients in Ontario are being readmitted to hospitals with post-operative complications, specifically the onset of infections (28%) and heart failure (22%), experienced during the first 3 months of recovery. A possible reason for the high rate of readmission is the quality of the patient education intervention. Particularly, the mode, dose, and timing of delivery of the educational intervention may not be effective in promoting the performance of self-care behaviours, resulting in the development of complications and hospital readmissions. The purpose of this training experience will be to develop the skills and expertise to be able to design and plan a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate a tailored cardiovascular surgical (CVS) patient education intervention that will reduce the number of complications as well as hospital readmission rates following heart surgery. A mentor-mentee relationship will be established in which diverse RCT training opportunities, scientific collaboration, and career development will be provided over the course of 2 years. During the course of the training period, a systematic review will be carried out to identify the specific attributes of CVS patient education most likely to contribute to a decrease in the rate of development of post-operative complications, along with reduced hospital readmission rates. This review will be submitted for consideration to the Cochrane Heart Group. The findings from this review will guide the formulation and conceptualization of a tailored CVS patient education intervention which will be incorporated into a RCT full application that will be submitted to CIHR before the end of the training period.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural studies of the fungal mannan biosynthesis pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: ENZYMOLOGY; FUNGAL INFECTIONS; GLYCOBIOLOGY; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; VIRULENCE FACTORS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; X-RAY SCATTERING
Abstract-Résumé: Fungal infections can be extremely dangerous, especially for the elderly, infants and the critically ill.  Even with our current collection of antifungal drugs, we are unable to effectively treat some infections, and as a consequence the mortality rate for fungal infections such as invasive candidiasis and aspergilosis is unacceptably high (e.g. up to 50% for patients with compromised immune systems).  This implies that research on fungal infections is needed.  In this proposal, we will examine how fungi make a major component of their cell wall known as mannan. Mannan is one of the main components of fungi that first interact with us (fungal-host interaction), and this interaction impacts how our immune system responds to the fungal infection.  Moreover, the amount of mannan modulates how dangerous fungi are (virulence).  Because of the importance of mannan for fungal-host interactions and virulence, we will study the enzymes that synthesize mannan, by elucidating their three-dimensional shape and how they facilitate chemical reactions.  This information can be exploited for antifungal therapy development that reduces the virulence of fungal infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural biological studies of antibiotic resistance mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: ENZYMOLOGY; FUNGAL INFECTIONS; GLYCOBIOLOGY; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; VIRULENCE FACTORS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; X-RAY SCATTERING
Abstract-Résumé: Due to the extensive use and abuse of antibiotics, bacteria have increasingly acquired resistance mechanisms against these drugs.  In turn, this rise in antibiotic resistance has dramatically compromised our ability to treat infections caused by "superbugs".  The situation is currently such that there are no antibiotics available to which bacteria have not found a resistance mechanism and many bacteria have multiple resistance mechanisms, making infections caused by superbugs exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, to cure.  To address this pressing healthcare problem, multiple strategies must be employed.  In addition to judicious use of antibiotics, one important strategy to pursue is to study the mechanisms by which bacteria resist the effects of antibiotics.  This information can subsequently be exploited for the development of antibiotic therapies that are impervious to the bacterial resistance mechanisms.  We have been examining, at the level of the atom, how certain bacterial enzymes confer resistance to antibiotics.  In addition to better understanding the intricate details of what enables these enzymes to provide protection against numerous drugs, our studies have also contributed to the design of next-generation antibiotics with improved efficacy, as well as the exploration of adjuvant therapies.  In the next five years we will continue and expand our studies, so as to further contribute to combating antibiotic resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancing Breast Milk Production with Domperidone in Mothers of Preterm Neonates (EMPOWER Trial)
Keywords-MotsClés: DOMPERIDONE; LACTATION; RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIALS
Abstract-Résumé: Recent advances in Perinatal and neonatal care have enhanced the survival of the extremely preterm infant. Breast milk is the most optimal form of nutrition for these infants. The mothers of these infants begin pumping breast milk soon after delivery but face many challenges in achieving and maintaining a volume felt to be adequate for their infants during and after hospitalization. Many mothers who have difficulties require medications to help enhance breast milk production. However, it is not known how these medications should be used. Domperidone is the most commonly used medication used in Canada. The idea behind this medication is that it helps with increasing milk supply through increasing a hormone, prolactin. The goal of this study is to evaluate whether using a medication like domperidone in a mother who is pumping expressed breast milk for her preterm infant is safe and effective for both her and her infant. Mothers will be randomized into one of two groups to evaluate safety and efficacy of domperidone. The results of this trial will inform both mothers and clinicians about the choices available to increase and maintain an adequate milk supply. Mothers will also have better information as to what are the potential risks and benefits of domperidone and enable more informed choices.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms of ApoA-I Interactions with Membrane Microdomains and Regulation of HDL Biogenesis and Function
Keywords-MotsClés: ABCAI TRANSPORTER; APOLIPOPROTEIN AI; CELL-SURFACE BINDING; CHOLESTEROL; HIGH DENSITY LIPOPROTEINS; LIPOPROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: One of the principal research interests of our laboratory over the last decade has been the investigation of the mechanisms by which a specific protein, the ABCA1 transporter, plays a key role in the formation of HDL. During the previous funding period (CIHR grant MOP 15042, 2006-2011), our group has documented several novel mechanisms, including the identification of a binding site on the cell surface, created by the ABCA1 transporter. This site allows the formation of HDL (hence, the term "HDL Biogenesis") and permits the removal of cholesterol, the first step in reverse cholesterol transport. This mechanism, reverse cholesterol transport, is the way by which the body removes cholesterol from cells and prevents build up, leading to atherosclerosis and heart disease. We believe that a complete understanding of the mechanisms underlying the regulation of HDL biogenesis will lead to novel information concerning the early stage of  HDL formation that may have important implications in the translation of the basic research in this field to the development of clinically relevant assays and biomarkers of HDL function, as well as novel HDL-based therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing Inhibitors of Bacterial and Trypanosomal CTP Synthases
Keywords-MotsClés: ATOMIC FORCE MICROSCOPY; COVALENT MODIFICATION; ENZYME ASSAYS; ENZYME INHIBITION; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; STRUCTURE-ACTIVITY STUDIES; T. BRUCEI & E. COLI CTP SYNTHASES
Abstract-Résumé: Trypanosomal infections present major health problems for humans and livestock in sub-Saharan Africa.  In 2008, African trypanosomiasis (or sleeping sickness) killed ~48,000 people.  In addition, the disease in domestic animals, particularly cattle, poses a serious impediment to the economic development of affected rural areas.  Another trypanosomal infection, known as American trypanosomiasis or Chagas disease, occurs mainly in Latin American countries.  It causes heart disease and digestive problems in chronic cases and is a concern for tourists.  Unfortunately, treatments for these infections suffer from several problems including failure, adverse reactions, and continued availability.  Consequently, there exists a need for well-tolerated and easy to use medications to treat these infections.  The enzyme cytidine 5'-triphosphate (CTP) synthase (CTPS) catalyzes the production of CTP, which is utilized in cells for many functions including the manufacture of genetic material and cell membranes.  The trypanosome parasite that causes African sleeping sickness (T. brucei) lacks the ability to salvage old cytidine/cytosine from broken down CTP to make new CTP and must make CTP "from scratch".  Hence, the parasite CTP synthase is a target for drug development.  Guanosine 5'-triphosphate (GTP) activates CTPS activity; however, our laboratory recently discovered that in some organisms elevated concentrations of GTP actually inhibit the action of CTPS.  For example, human CTPS is not inhibited by GTP but the enzymes from bacteria and T. brucei are inhibited by GTP and related compounds.  We will extend our discoveries through studies to identify the inhibitor binding site on CTPS and the molecular features of the inhibitor required for its binding to CTPS.  Using this information, we will design and synthesize more potent CTPS inhibitors to serve as lead compounds for the development of new drugs directed against African sleeping sickness and other trypanosomal infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Systematic Proteomic Analysis Strategy for Biomarker Discovery in Head & Neck Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; CANCER; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: A biomarker is a biological substance that is used to evaluate the presence, progression, or treatment-response of a disease. To be clinically useful, a biomarker should be readily accessible (i.e. body fluids) and provide sufficient sensitivity and specificity by minimizing false negatives and false positives. Owing to recent technical advances in protein mass spectrometry, large international efforts have been expended on the discovery of disease biomarkers. To the best of our knowledge, no clinically useful biomarker for the accurate detection or prognosis of HNC exists. The main reasons for this include technological challenges faced by biomarker discovery, the lack of adequate and well-defined clinical samples, and the time consuming process of validation. Here, we will initiate a series of crucial pilot experiments, using an integrated, candidate-driven proteomics analysis strategy, to discover novel biomarkers, focusing on secreted and glycosylated proteins, with a clear focus on identifying prognostic biomarkers for patient risk categorization.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of collective cell migration by the recycling endosome
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL MIGRATION; CELL POLARITY; CELL SIGNALING; DROSOPHILA; RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASE; STEM CELLS AND CANCER; VESICULAR TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: In the ovary of the fruitfly, the so-called border cells migrate in a similar way to the cancerous cells inducing metastasis. They migrate as a group of cells and are attracted by the same signals as metastatic cells, and finally they stop moving at a specific place. We are studying how different trafficking routes within the cells regulate this migration. We have found in previous work, that a specific trafficking circuit regulates the spatial position of the receptors sensing the direction of migration. Interestingly, the key regulator of this transport route has been involved in the migration of metastatic cells in human. In this project we want to detail our understanding of this mechanism by studying new constituents of the machinery regulating metastasis-like migration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intradermal Influenza Vaccine Evaluation in Organ Transplant (InVEnT)
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR IMMUNITY; HUMORAL IMMUNITY; INFLUENZA VACCINE; REJECTION; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza is an immensely important public health problem as underscored by the recent pandemic. A key difference between pandemics of the past is the ever-increasing population of immunocompromised people. This is important because this population may serve as highly contagious nodes of spread (i.e. 'super-spreaders') thereby hampering public health efforts. Among the most immunosuppressed are organ transplant recipients and current vaccine strategies lead to sub-optimal effectiveness in these patients. Therefore, it is essential to develop more effective and novel ways to immunize them. Intradermal vaccination takes advantage of local immune cells and may therefore be more effective than standard intramuscular vaccine.  In order to test this, we enrolled 240 organ transplant patients and randomized them to receive either the standard intramuscular vaccine or novel high-dose intradermal vaccine.  We have saved all the necessary blood samples needed for testing.  Our primary outcome will be a protective antibody response to the vaccine.  We will also examine cellular immune responses in these patients.  In addition, all patients will have testing for antibodies directed against the transplanted organ to determine whether immunization can contribute to organ rejection.    Importance of the Study:  This will be a unique study and the largest ever randomized trial of influenza vaccination in this patient population. The results will have immediate clinical relevance and may lead to important improvements in patient care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stabilization of blood vessels by a genetic pathway downstream of Sonic Hedgehog
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; DEVELOPMENT; HEMORRHAGE; SONIC HEDGEHOG; VASCULAR STABILIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Blood vessels are functional at an early stage of development and therefore rapidly need to develop a structure that can withstand the pressures of the circulatory system so that they do not hemorrhage. We use the zebrafish model to identify genes that function in the genetic pathway to stabilize blood vessels. In this work we have identified more than 50 genes that are misregulated in a model of embryonic hemorrhage. We will characterize the functions of three genes in this work, Nkx3.2, FoxF2 and Pim1. We hope to identify genes that would be useful diagnostic markers for human vascular stability defects, or that would be therapeutic targets to improve the outcome after hemorrhage.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of sarcomere disruption and structural proteins in skeletal and cardiac muscle injury
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC MYOPATHIES; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHIES; MYOFIBRILS; SARCOMERES
Abstract-Résumé: When active muscles are repeatedly stretched, they become injured and lose the ability to produce force. Although observations on stretch-induced muscle injuries are abundant, the origin for these injuries remains a matter of debate. The most prominent theory is the idea that the smallest contractile units in muscles (the sarcomeres) become over-stretched (disrupted), thereby loosing the ability to produce force. This is thought to occur because sarcomeres are either over-stretched or not activated properly and thus fail. In skeletal muscles, the first theory prevails, while in heart muscle the second does. In the proposed research, we will study sarcomere disruption and contraction failure systematically in skeletal and heart muscles for the first time on the individual sarcomere level, thereby gaining novel information about the sub-cellular mechanisms of skeletal muscle injury and heart failure. We can perform these unique experiments because we have refined an approach to work with single myofibrils and mechanically isolated sarcomeres, and have invented a completely new approach to simulate contraction failure in selected sarcomeres of a myofibril. The results of this study will not only add basic knowledge to our understanding of how muscles contract and produce force, but will also provide first direct information on the effects of sarcomere disruption and contraction failure on skeletal muscle injury and heart failure.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES DU FOIE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the E2F1 transcription factor in TGFß-mediated signal transduction
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL GROWTH; CELL IMMORTALIZATION; TELOMERASE; TGFB/SMAD SIGNALING; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; TUMOR SUPPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Growth factors from the transforming growth factor-B (TGFB) induce cell death, block cell proliferation and prevent cell immortalization in most human tissues. Thus, they block the growth of the cells and their main role is to act as safeguards to prevent tumor formation. As a result, any defect in their mechanism of action lead to increased cell survival and proliferation and many human diseases are due to such a defect. Our main research goal is to understand how these growth factors exert these tumor suppressive effects at the molecular level. These TGFB effects depends on specific proteins expressed inside the cells. One of these protein is the transcription factor E2F1. In this application, we propose to study the mechanism by which TGFB regulates E2F1 expression and to investigate what is the role and contribution of E2F1 in the mediation of the TGFB effects leading to cell death and prevention of cell immortalization. Overall, our research aims at understanding how to block hyper-proliferation of the cells and how to prevent cell immortalization of diseased tumoral cells. Such understanding of those mechanisms that control cell growth and immortalization will help us develop new therapies to prevent tumor cells to further grow and spread to distant tissues.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of a new cognitive therapy (inference-based therapy) for the treatment of obsessional compulsive disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE BEHAVIOR THERAPY; INFERENCE-BASED THERAPY; OBSESSIVE COMPULSIVE DISORDER; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Obsessional compulsive disorder (OCD) is a very debilitating psychiatric problem which affects around one million Canadians and their families. Obsessions are intense preoccupations about bad, harmful, dangerous, shocking or unlucky events which 'may' occur and which drive sufferers to perform time consuming and distressing compulsive rituals to prevent the possible event occurring.  The current psychological treatment of choice is cognitive behavior (CBT) therapy which focuses on treating OCD by reducing obsessional anxiety about the likelihood and the consequences of the preoccupying event. A rival cognitive model termed the inference-based therapy (IBT), developed by the principal investigator and co-workers, considers that the OCD begins with the initial doubting inference 'maybe something is wrong' and focuses on changing the reasoning behind this doubting inference which often trumps the common sense conviction that there is no reason to doubt.  This clinical trial randomly allocates participants to either IBT or CBT treatment condition or to a third generic mindfulness condition. The latter condition is a non-specific meditational-based training which has shown evidence of reducing stress and anxiety across a number of psychiatric problems including OCD. Two hundred and forty people will be recruited over a 5-year period from two principal sites (Montreal and Gatineau/Ottawa) with which the principal investigator and co-investigators have clinical links. Therapy will be administered by trained professionals following a treatment manual specific to each approach. The therapy will last a maximum of six months or until the point when the person achieves a non-clinical status. The patients will be assessed pre, post, and at six months following treatment on standard evaluation instruments as well as on subjective measures. We expect the IBT to be superior in terms of number of participants responding to treatment, rapidity of improvement and gains at follow-up.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of maternal iron deficiency during pregnancy on the offspring's CNS development
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY BRAIN STEM RESPONSES; DIETARY IRON DEFICIENCY; EICOSANOIDS; FATTY ACIDS; GESTATION; LEARNING AND MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: In developed countries such as Canada, iron deficiency (ID) remains a nutritional problem. Although there is enough evidence to indicate that ID during gestation has an impact on the progeny, the biochemical, physiological and cognitive effects on the offspring are not well characterized. Iron is known to play an important role in central nervous system(CNS)development. Indeed, brain iron uptake is maximal during rapid brain growth which coincides with the peak of myelinogenesis. In fact, ID induced in young rats has been associated with hypomyelination. Furthermore, ID during early postnatal life results in learning deficits in rodents and in children. The possible mechanism(s) responsible for the CNS hypomyelination may be related to an alteration of polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) metabolism. These long chain PUFA are precursors of the eicosanoids, potent metabolites involved in numerous biological functions. It is hypothesized that ID during gestation has a negative impact on CNS myelination resulting from an alteration in fatty acid and eicosanoid metabolism in the offspring's brain. This research program aims to investigate the impact of mild ID during gestation in guinea pigs on the offspring's learning and memory processes, auditory functions and CNS fatty acid and eicosanoid metabolism. The proposed research program should characterize some of the biochemical, physiological and cognitive effects of ID during gestation on the progeny.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving tuberculosis diagnosis in vulnerable populations: impact and cost-effectiveness of a novel, rapid molecular assay
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINALS; COST-EFFECTIVENESS; DIAGNOSIS; TEST ACCURACY; TUBERCULOSIS; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a severe global public health threat, with over 9.4 million cases each year. TB is an important public health problem in Canada among immigrants and Aboriginal populations. Currently, Nunavut is facing the largest TB outbreak in the territory's 10 year history. One of the biggest challenges for TB control is early diagnosis. Many TB cases are detected late and this results in the spread of the infection in the community. Currently used TB tests are either inaccurate or not rapid enough. Better diagnostic options are urgently required, so that the spread of TB can be contained. Recently, the World Health Organization announced its endorsement of a novel molecular test for TB - the Xpert MTB/RIF test, a cartridge-based, completely automated test, which can accurately detect TB and drug resistance in less than 2 hours, and can be performed at the point-of-care (clinic) setting without laboratory expertise. We are proposing the first evaluation of Xpert MTB/RIF in Canada and one of the first studies to evaluate its impact at the point-of-care, to assess reduction in diagnostic and treatment delays, and cost-effectiveness. Our study will be conducted in Montreal, Quebec, and Iqaluit, Nunavut, and will generate data that will enable agencies such as the PHAC, Health Canada, and the Canadian TB Committee to develop evidence-based Canadian guidelines on this novel TB test.

TitreApplicationTitle: Acute bacterial infection promotes cancer metastasis through toll like receptor signal transduction
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY; LUNG CANCER; METASTASIS; MICE; PNEUMONIA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TOLL LIKE RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer related death in the world. Surgery is the cornerstone of curative treatment but is associated with a high rate of infectious complications including pneumonia. There is emerging clinical data to suggest that complications after surgery may increase cancer recurrence. This present study investigates the relationship between bacterial infection and cancer progression, with a particular focus on specialized bacteria recognition proteins, the Toll Like Receptors. Results from this proposal will identify Toll Like Receptors as a potential target in the treatment and prevention of cancer progression.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Heart-Mind Connection: Evaluating the Association between Ceramides and Cognitive Decline in Coronary Artery Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CERAMIDES; COGNITION; CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE; INFLAMMATION; LIPID METABOLISM; MEMORY DECLINE; NEURODEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Coronary artery disease (CAD) involves hardening and clogging of the arteries supplying blood to the heart. Many studies have shown that those with CAD have a more rapid decline in memory than expected and that they are at an increased risk of developing dementia. In patients with CAD, memory changes also have important immediate consequences: they are associated with physical disability, unemployment, poorer quality of life and more medical complications causing dropout from cardiac rehabilitation. It is not understood how memory decline is linked to CAD; however, it has recently been discovered that certain byproducts of fat breakdown involved in the development of CAD, called ceramides, can harm brain cells. Ceramides are overproduced in response to inflammation, a key feature of CAD. Also, inflammation has been associated with poorer memory performance in those with CAD. Taken together, this evidence suggests that ceramides may be the link between CAD and memory decline. We hypothesize that ceramide production will be associated with more memory decline over 1 year in CAD patients. To test this, we will recruit 129 CAD patients from a cardiac rehabilitation facility and measure memory performance and blood ceramide concentrations at baseline, 6 and 12 months. We will also measure important blood messengers of inflammation and assess whether they are associated with ceramide production. In addition, relationships between ceramides and other aspects of brain function, such as thinking speed and the ability to plan and sort information will be explored. As a greater proportion of Canadians reach older ages, there is a pressing need to maintain cognitive function later in life. The knowledge from this study may be the key to developing new treatments targeting memory decline in patients with CAD. New treatments based on relevant mechanisms might not only improve memory and quality of life, but also reduce mortality and the odds of developing dementia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intravesicular nanoparticulate drug delivery systems for application in bladder cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICANCER DRUGS; BLADDER CANCER; BLOOD AND TISSUE DISTRIBUTION; DRUG DELIVERY SYSTEMS; HYPERBRANCHED POLYMERS; MUCOADHESION; NANOPARTICLES
Abstract-Résumé: Bladder cancer is the fifth most common cancer in Canada and the incidence is increasing. Superficial disease is treated by surgical removal of tumors and the intravesical instillation of chemotherapy agents, usually mitomycin C, directly into the bladder via a catheter. However, the highly impermeable barrier presented by the superficial umbrella cells of the bladder wall seriously limit drug uptake and effectiveness of intravesical chemotherapy and patients require life-long surveillance, usually with repeated interventions. New therapeutic approaches are urgently needed. We have developed tiny, spherical nano-sized particles that are very highly branched and possess a core that can carry a payload of docetaxel and a surface that can be modified with positively charged amine groups. These nanoparticles show markedly superior bladder tissue drug levels and efficacy in a mouse model of superficial bladder cancer and we believe this may be explained by the amine coated nanoparticles causing shedding of the surface barrier cells. We also found that, following removal of the nanoparticles and washing of the bladder tissue, the superficial cell layer was regenerated extremely rapidly, within hours. The goal of this translational research is to develop these unique drug nanoparticles for potential treatment of patients receiving intravesical chemotherapy after surgical resection of tumors. The objectives are to investigate the processes leading to superficial cell shedding and recovery, to determine the uptake and distribution of the drug and nanoparticles in bladder and tumor tissue and to evaluate the efficacy and toxicity of the drug loaded nanoparticles in mouse models of superficial bladder cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of LTB4 action on innate immune pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: HOST DEFENSE; INNATE RECEPTORS; INNATE RESPONSE; LEUKOTRIENES; TYPE 1 IFN; VIRAL INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Leukotriene B4 (LTB4) is a natural mediator of host, recognized as a regulator of leukocyte functional responses. We have recently demonstrated that LTB4 can inhibit viral infection in "in vitro" and "in vivo" models. During the course of a phase I clinical study, we observed that administration of LTB4 to humans caused a dose-dependent plasmatic increase in antimicrobial peptides and our preliminary observations indicate that LTB4 induces the release of interferon alpha, a well-known mediator essential for viral clearance. The recent discovery of molecules named pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) has established a major mechanism for innate immune recognition of pathogens, including viruses. New molecules that activate the PRR system were then developed for their potential therapeutic use, including protection of host defense against infectious pathogens. Our research has previously demonstrated that LTB4 can trigger PRR receptors expressed on different populations of human cells to induce the production of antiviral factors including interferon alpha. The present study is then a follow-up of our research. We propose to investigate the action of LTB4 on other classes of PRR and to evaluate whether LTB4 can exert its action through this system to reduce the severity of respiratory illness during influenza infection and also to determine whether LTB4 can restore normal lung functions. These studies will therefore significantly forward our knowledge of the mechanism of LTB4 against viruses and will indicate new directions and approaches for more efficient pharmacological interventions in the treatment of viral infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strategies for therapy of respiratory muscle failure in muscular dystrophy.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMOKINES; DIAPHRAGM FUNCTION; DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; INNATE IMMUNITY; MACROPHAGES; MUSCLE PHYSIOLOGY; MUSCLE REGENERATION; TOLL LIKE RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most frequent X-linked lethal disorder in man, affecting approximately 1 in 3500 males.  Patients most often die of respiratory failure caused by involvement of the diaphragm and other respiratory muscles by the pathology.  The disease is characterized by progressive muscle fiber destruction and a failure of adequate compensation by muscle repair mechanisms. Therefore, a better understanding of the factors which regulate muscle damage and repair in this disease could offer new therapeutic avenues.  In this proposal, we will explore the role of the host immune system in this process.  We believe that activation of innate immunity through chemokine and Toll-like receptors plays an important role in regulating the balance between muscle damage and repair in the dystrophic diaphragm. We will use genetically modified dystrophic mice and test a novel therapeutic agent to determine whether manipulation of innate immunity could be a new and promising therapeutic strategy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure, Production and Mechanisms of Neopetrosiamides, Antimetastatic Agents That Prevent Human Tumor Cell Invasion
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMETASTATIC AGENT; DRUG TARGETS; METASTASIS; PEPTIDE PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PEPTIDE SYNTHESIS; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; STRUCTURE-ACTIVITY RELATIONSHIPS
Abstract-Résumé: According to the Canadian Cancer Society, 40% of Canadian women and 45% of men will develop cancer during their lifetimes, and 1 out of every 4 Canadians will die of cancer. A major problem that increases mortality is the spread of cancer cells from the primary tumor site to other organs and tissues in a process known as metastasis. Recently two closely related compounds named neopetrosiamide A and B were isolated from a sponge off Papua New Guinea and shown to convert metastatic cells to a seemingly normal state and prevent their invasion of human tissues. Our group recently revised the chemical structures assigned to neopetrosiamides and made them in the laboratory together with few active analogs. As collection of sponge cannot supply the amounts of neopetrosiamides needed for biological studies or clinical use, we propose to develop synthetic methods to make improved analogs and simpler, more accessible, derivatives. In addition, we propose to make derivatives bearing handles for attachment of fluorescent labels and to use these to study the mechanism of action of such potential drugs on metastatic tumor cells. The results will provide significant amounts of this drug candidate for study and will allow its assessment as a possible therapeutic agent. It should also reveal new cellular targets to prevent invasion of healthy tissue by tumor cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of the Autism Classification System of Functioning: Social Communication
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER; FUNCTIONAL CLASSIFICATION; MEASUREMENT; SOCIAL COMMUNICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) are a huge challenge in the field of childhood developmental disability. The wide 'spectrum' of these conditions means that people's functional capacities and limitations vary enormously. Thus, it makes little sense to talk about ASDs as if they were a single disorder.  A challenge in the field of ASDs is how to categorize children's functional difficulties meaningfully. There are many tools that assess the functional status of children with ASD, but no valid and reliable functional classification system exists with which to group children with apparently similar functional status. Such a system (the GMFCS), developed by the PI's group for Cerebral Palsy (CP), is used around the world. This makes it possible to talk about and study groups of children who are similar with respect to the characteristic(s) being classified. This kind of categorization allows clinicians to answer parents' key questions ("How bad is our child's condition?" "What does the future hold for our child?"). In CP, gross motor function is the GMFCS domain by which to group ability levels. The hallmark domain that impacts on function of children with ASD, identified in our pilot work, is social communication and a spectrum of levels of this ability must be categorized.   This study will develop and evaluate an Autism Classification System of Functioning: Social Communication (ACSF:SC) modelled on the GMFCS. The ACSF:SC is NOT a new measure; rather it will provide a consistent, valid and reliable way to identify functionally similar children with ASDs. The ACSF:SC, complementary to clinical assessment and outcome tools, will enrich the field by facilitating communication among parents and professionals, and providing a way to stratify children for clinical and research purposes. We are purposely focusing first on preschool children. Once an ACSF:SC has been developed this research program will expand the work downward to infants and upward to older children.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; APOPLEXIE, INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation into the molecular mechanisms mediating excitotoxicity - developing novel post-stroke therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: EXCITOTOXICITY; ISCHEMIC NEURONAL INJURY; NMDA RECEPTOR; PTEN; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the third leading cause of death in North America, and the leading cause of disability and represents a huge economic and social cost.  Stroke is a brain attack from a sudden loss of blood supply to the brain that occurs when the blood supply to a specific part of the brain is suddenly interrupted (ischemic) or when a blood vessel in the brain either bursts or is blocked.  Cells in the affected brain die when they no longer receive oxygen and nutrients from the blood, leading to the symptoms and disabilities of stroke patients.  However, effective pharmacotherapy that directly protects brain cells from stroke insults is still lacking.   Our objectives are to achieve a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms by which stroke insults produce brain cell damage, and thereby develop novel pharmacotherapies.  Using cellular models of stroke, we have identified a molecule called PTEN (a lipid phosphatase) as an essential step in the signaling cascade initiated by stroke insults that causes brain cells to die.  By understanding the mechanisms by which stroke insults causes the PTEN nuclear translocation, we have been able to devise a novel drug to specifically disrupt this stroke-induced PTEN nuclear translocation, and thereby to reduce stroke-induced brain cell death.  We propose further validation using several animal models of stroke if the new drug we developed can be used as a new and effective post-stroke pharmacotherapy.  We expect that the completion of our proposed study will help to bring this drug to the point where it can be tested in human stroke patients.  Because this therapeutic is specifically designed to target the stroke-related neuronal death process, without affecting normal function of the brain cells in affected areas, it is expected to have minimal side effects.  Studies as such can be expected to lead to better stroke therapies and hence, will directly impact the health of Canadians and reduce mortality and morbidity from stroke.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Aminopeptidases of malaria parasites: understanding their biochemistry, structure and function for new drug development
Keywords-MotsClés: AMINOPEPTIDASES; BIOCHEMISTRY; CELLULAR BIOLOGY; ENZYMOLOGY; MALARIA; PROTEIN CHARACTERISATION
Abstract-Résumé: Malaria remains one of the most serious infections of humans worldwide. Over 3 billion people are at risk of infection with this parasite and 2-3 million die each year, mainly children under the age of five. Due to the global spread of drug resistant malaria our armoury of drugs available to combat this disease is seriously reduced. Moreover, there is no vaccines available or in sight. Accordingly, there is an urgent need for us to identify and characterise new parasite targets at which we can develop new drugs. We have identified enzymes called 'aminopeptidases' in malaria parasites have great potential for new drugs. Here we will study the biochemistry, structure and function of these enzymes to learn more about the mechanism of protein anabolism/catabolism, growth and development in malaria which will forge a new path towards the design of a new class of anti-malarial treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engineering of Irradiation-Sterilized Musculoskeletal Allografts for Improved Biomechanical Performance
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOGRAFTS; BIOMATERIALS ENGINEERING; COLLAGEN; DURABILITY; FATIGUE RESISTANCE; FRACTURE; MECHANICAL TESTING; MUSCULOSKELETAL; STRENGTH; TOUGHNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Musculoskeletal allografts are pieces of tissue, such as bone or tendon, from an individual who has donated their body to medicine and this tissue is used in surgery to repair injuries and problems in orthopaedic patients. In order to reduce disease transmission from the donor to the patient, radiation is used to kill bacteria and viruses which may exist in/on the donated allograft tissue. Unfortunately, the radiation also damages the tissue making it weak and less able to perform in mechanically demanding roles. We propose to investigate a method by which the mechanical performance of bone and tendon allografts will be improved by including special additives during the radiation sterilization step. The mechanical behaviour and performance will then be evaluated using established biomechanical testing and biomaterials science methods and compared to normal tissue and allografts sterilized by the current method. This new method of radiation sterilizing of allografts is under-studied and, if successful, should enable the production of radiation-sterilized allografts with improved biomechanical performance and therefore improve patient outcomes. The tissue banking industry is growing rapidly while trying to fill an enormous and immediate demand from our health care system. At the same time, it is searching for solutions to serious graft quality and performance issues. This work should greatly help solve these problems.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Regulation of E2F-1 Dependent Gene Transcription and Cell Death Signaling Pathways in Ventricular Myocytes
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL SIGNALING; E2F-1; GENE TRANSCRIPTION; HYPOXIA; MITOCHONDRIA; VENTRICULAR MYOCYTES
Abstract-Résumé: A delicate balance exists between cell growth and cell death. In the context of the adult myocardium inappropriate or inordinate cell loss through an apoptotic process may profoundly influence cardiac structure and/or function given the limited and meager ability of the heart for repair after injury. The ability to prevent or modulate inappropriate cardiac cell death would be of significant therapeutic value in maintaining cardiac function after injury. These studies will provide new information and advance our current understanding regarding the mechanisms that govern cell death in the heart. The long-term goals of these studies are directed towards understanding the mechanisms that underlie aberrant apoptosis in hypertrophic and failing hearts. This will lead to the development of new more effective treatments for patients with heart disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: Refining a Decision-Support Model for Siting Palliative Care Services in Rural Canadian Communities
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADA; DECISION-MAKING; HEALTH SERVICES; MIXED-METHOD; PALLIATIVE CARE; RURAL; SERVICE SITING; SITING MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Palliative care comes in many forms, but in general refers to support provided to maintain quality of life for individuals living with chronic conditions at end-of-life, and the facilitation of quality of death for persons in the end stages of disease or infirmary. Rural and remote Canadian communities face particular challenges in providing diverse and specialized forms of palliation, along with other health services. For example, sparse populations in rural and remote areas make it difficult to attract a broad array of primary care providers and specialists, thus narrowing the range of palliative care expertise available to residents. At the same time, such communities are home to rapidly aging populations and therefore have a pressing need to enhance palliative care service provision. Meanwhile, little research attention has been given to this issue. In this proposal, we address the question: how can we best determine which rural and remote Canadian communities are most in need of and most suitable to enhance their palliative care service provision (based on factors such as need, vulnerability, and readiness)? In addressing this question we are advocating for a thoughtful approach to palliative care resource allocation and service siting, one informed by the best science available. Based on the successfull completion of three-years of pilot research focused on rural and remote British Columbia, we specifically propose to refine and test a pan-Canadian decision-making framework that can assist in determing where to site new, or enhance existing, services in rural and remote communities in order to address this pressing health service need. This framework can be used to inform evidence-based decision-making and may be extended in the future to include other health services, with further research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies on the molecular pathogenesis of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; DROSOPHILA; ER STRESS; MOUSE; NEURODEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder caused by progressive loss of motor neuron function in the brain and spinal cord.  Eventually patients will not be able to stand, walk, or use their hands and arms.  Most people with ALS die of respiratory failure or pneumonia caused by weakness of the respiratory muscle within two to five years after onset.  There is no primary therapy for ALS.  It is therefore important to understand the mechanism by which this disease occurs, as this may allow us to develop a future therapy for ALS.  One approach is the use of genetic analysis in Drosophila (commonly known as fruit flies) to identify the genetic pathways leading to pathology of ALS. The information gained from this work has also been applied to studies in mice and human.  A large body of work has convincingly demonstrated the great degree to which genes and genetic pathways are conserved between Drosophila and mammals, and recent studies indicate that this conservation of molecular mechanisms also makes Drosophila an excellent system in which to model human diseases. For example, our preliminary studies have shown that flies expressing the mutant protein identified in a familial form of ALS (ALS8) recapitulate many of the characteristic features of the disease.  Importantly, based on the data from Drosophila studies, we have discovered that a novel hormone derived from ALS8 protein (VAP MSP) is secreted into the blood and that the serum levels of VAP MSP in ALS8 patients are decreased.  This hormone might contribute to the pathogenesis of ALS, just like decreasing insulin levels cause diabetes mellitus.  Hence, studies in Drosophila and mice provide a productive approach to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of ALS. We believe that this project will enable us to advance our understanding of the mechanisms of ALS and provide insight towards developing more effective treatment.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: The structure of excitation-contraction coupling in ventricular and atrial muscle.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM REGULATION; CELL PHYSIOLOGY; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ELECTRON TOMOGRAPHY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; MOLECULAR ARCHITECTURE; SUPER-RESOLUTION IMAGING; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS; VENTRICULAR FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The force with which the heart contracts depends on a number of variables, the most important of which is the way two key proteins interact with each other. Our preliminary evidence indicates that this arrangement is malleable, and controlled by local factors. The second area of investigation is in how the force of contraction might be regulated. My lab has evidence that there is a small domain inside the ventricular cells that could alter the force of contraction, up or down,depending on what signals the heart is receiving from the nervous system and the body's hormonal state. The third avenue of investigation is to look at human cells to see if they are organized the same way as the animal models that we're studying. This is very basic research dedicated to understanding how the normal cell operates. My lab, if funded, would continue to train people who work in both industry and academia, and the findings from this grant might open up new ways of thinking about future treatment if the hypothesis about the signaling microdomain proves true.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal and chemosensory basis of respiratory rhythm generation in a model system
Keywords-MotsClés: CA2+ IMAGING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HYPOXIA; NEURAL CONTROL OF BREATHING; RESPIRATORY CHEMORECEPTORS; RESPIRATORY PATTERN GENERATOR; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: In mammals, either direct or indirect perturbations of both peripheral and central respiratory control centres result in drastic breathing disturbances leading to cardiovascular and respiratory disorders (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease-COPD, heart failure, sudden infant death syndrome-SIDS, persistent hypertension etc). Despite recent advances in our understanding of neural and chemosensory basis of respiratory control, the fundamental mechanisms that regulate breathing remain however largely unknown. A number of questions regarding the identity, location and the organization of mammalian respiratory pattern generating neurons (CPG) and their chemosensory counterparts in both adults and newborns remain unanswered. In this context, our approach is to develop a simple model system where cellular and molecular mechanisms by which hypoxia modulates respiratory activity in both in vitro reconstructed networks and intact animals can be elucidated at the level of individual neurons. In our snail model system, we have not only identified CPG networks that control its respiratory behaviour, but also the peripheral chemosensory cells that regulate hypoxia-driven breathing. We will now use our novel brain-chip recording technologies to define mechanisms of neural control of respiration - from ion channels to single genes. This research would also help design future implantable, bionic devices for the respiratory dysfunction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Activation, Expression and Hormonal Regulation of the Human Pituitary Growth Hormone Gene
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN REMODELING/GENE ACTIVATION; DISORDERS RELATED TO DYSREGULATION OF GROWTH HORMONE; HORMONAL (GLUCOCORTICOID AND INSULIN) REGULATION; HUMAN PITUITARY GROWTH HORMONE GENE; TISSUE-SPECIFIC REGULATION; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION/GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: The organization of genes in the human genome, the genetic blue print for a human being, has been described. There is evidence that this organization, which has occurred during evolution, has likely resulted in some cases where DNA sequences associated with one gene influence the use (expression) of a nearby gene. In simple terms, we are more than the sum of our individual genes and their expression. This has implications at a time when changes to the genome are being considered either as a research tool or for what is referred to in medicine as corrective gene therapy. We are using the human growth hormone gene family as a model system to understand the influence of nearby immune system-related and muscle-related gene sequences on the "normal" production of pituitary growth hormone. We are interested in how these sequences have come to be used to control when the growth hormone gene is opened up before we are born, why it is switched on only in the pituitary, and how it is able to respond to other hormones including steroids and insulin at different times. This certainly involves recognition of these DNA sequences by protein factors that interact with other proteins and are capable of changing the structure of specific regions of the chromosome. Identification and study of these sequences and associated proteins will increase our understanding of these processes, as well as when things start to wear out as with aging or go wrong as in conditions where insulin levels are high as with overeating or obesity. This is particularly important at a time when the growth hormone producing cell is being considered as a sensor for changes in our metabolism.

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of cell-fate choice in the developing mammalian retina
Keywords-MotsClés: ASYMMETRIC CELL DIVISION; CELL CULTURE; CELL-FATE; DEVELOPMENT; LINEAGE; LIVE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Neural stem cells have the potential to generate any cell types in the nervous system, providing a promising new avenue for replacing lost cells after injury, stroke or disease. Disappointingly, when neural stem cells are transplanted into a damaged region of interest in the brain, or the retina, they do not always become the appropriate cell type for that region. These findings indicate that there is great potential for stem cell therapies, but that a better understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms controlling how neural stem cells choose to become a particular cell type or another during normal development will be crucial in designing efficient stem cell therapies. Here, we propose experiments to study the molecular mechanisms that lead to the generation of different cell types during development of the vertebrate retina, with a particular emphasis on the production and function of the light-sensing cells of the retina: the photoreceptors. We reason that a deeper understanding of the mechanisms regulating normal retinal development will be critical in designing efficient cell replacement therapies for diseases leading to photoreceptor degeneration and vision loss.

TitreApplicationTitle: Direct current stimulation modulation of hyperphagia in Prader-Willi syndrome.
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGING; GENETICS; GENOMIC IMPRINTING; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; SOCIAL COGNITION; TURNER SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Turner syndrome (TS) is a complex genetic disorder associated with complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome and is one of the most common sex chromosome abnormalities, affecting 1/2000 live born females. Individuals with TS present a particular cognitive profile, among which social impairments are prominent. While the cognitive profile of TS is reasonably well understood, the neural underpinnings of this profile are only beginning to emerge. Namely, functional and structural abnormalities documented in TS have been suggested to contribute to the cognitive profile observed in this population. Interestingly, these neuroanatomic and cognitive- behavioral outcomes in TS may be influenced by epigenetic factors in the form of genomic imprinting, a process by which certain genes are expressed in a parent-of-origin-specific manner. Indeed, TS who retain the paternal (Xp) X chromosome seems to show less cognitive deficits than individuals with an X from maternal origins (Xm). The specific aims of this study are designed to examine the gene-brain-behavior associations in a large, pre-estrogen TS cohort. The two main objectives are (1) to elucidate the neuroanatomical/functional substrates of face/emotion processing impairments in TS; and (2) to characterize neuroanatomical and brain function differences in Xm and Xp girls. Establishing the neural underpinnings of cognitive deficits in TS, as well as their developmental course, will greatly improve our understanding of the pathogenesis of the TS phenotype and provide a foundation for the development of specific and effective interventions. Moreover, potential differences between girls with Xp and Xm in brain and cognitive/behavioral function will provide important clues for targeting individuals in particular need of social, behavioral, educational or pharmacological interventions early in development.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: REPRODUCTION/GROSSESSE; RECHERCHE SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Socioeconomic status as a predictor of prenatal mental health, use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors during pregnancy, and infant outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: INFANT OUTCOMES; MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH; PERINATAL HEALTH; PRESCRIPTION DRUG USE; SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS
Abstract-Résumé: Depression and anxiety during pregnancy have been linked with adverse birth outcomes. However, managing maternal mental illness during pregnancy with prescription medicines is not without risks. For example, the use of some types of antidepressants during pregnancy has been associated with increased risk of preterm birth, small for gestational age (SGA) birth, respiratory distress, septal heart defects, and persistent pulmonary hypertension. However, being of low socioeconomic status (SES) during pregnancy has also been associated with poor outcomes for the newborn, including increased risk of preterm birth, SGA birth, still birth and neonatal and infant death, and, while it has not been adequately studied in Canadian populations, American literature suggests that low SES also increases the risk of the mother experiencing depression and/or anxiety during pregnancy. Finally, preliminary studies examining the relationship between SES and the use of antidepressant medicines during pregnancy in British Columbia indicate that pregnant women of low SES are significantly more likely to be using these medicines. These relationships suggest that some of the negative infant outcomes that were previously thought to be caused by use of antidepressants during pregnancy may partly, or even primarily, result from the effects of being of low SES during pregnancy. I aim to clarify the relationship between SES, maternal depression and anxiety during pregnancy, use of antidepressants during pregnancy and infant outcomes. Clearly understanding these relationships will lead to a more accurate understanding of the risks associated with antidepressant use during pregnancy. A clearer picture of these risks will enable providers to make the safest and most effective decisions for both mother and newborn when treating pregnant women with depression or anxiety.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modeling the relationship between genotypic configurations and traits
Keywords-MotsClés: AGGREGATION METHODS; CONDITIONAL MODELING; GENE-LEVEL SUMMARY; MIXTURE MODELS; MULTIVARIATE PHENOTYPES; PARTIAL LEAST SQUARES REGRESSION; PLEIOTROPY; RARE VARIANTS; RESEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Rare genetic alterations or variants have been shown, in some cases, to have large influences on disease risks or disease-related traits.  However, due to the rarity of these events, finding DNA variants that influence diseases or traits is very difficult.  Instead of focusing on each variant alone, methods are being developed to examine all the variation in a candidate gene simultaneously.  A series of methods have been recently proposed that count the number of rare variants carried by each individual, however, these approaches do not perform well when there are only a few DNA variants that influence disease, and many that have no effect.  Here we propose to develop new approaches for identifying patterns of DNA variation that influence disease-related traits.  Our approaches will examine changes in the variance of the traits instead of counting the rare variants.  We are also proposing to adapt a flexible method called partial-least-squares analysis to our goal of identifying associations between traits and genetic variation.  Our adaptation ensure that this flexible approach optimally uses the rare DNA configurations.  Our new methods will be assist in finding genetic variation that influences lipid-related traits, pain, insulin resistance, osteoporosis and colorectal cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the functions of the Bub1 and BubR1 kinases during mitosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMOSOME CONGRESSION; HIGH RESOLUTION MICROSCOPY; MITOTIC KINASES; PEPTIDE ARRAYS; PHOSPHOPROTEOMICS; SPINDLE CHECKPOINT; VIDEO-MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Aneuploidy is a genetic state defined by an abnormal number of chromosomes. It is caused by aberrant cell division and is the most common genetic affliction in man. It is the primary cause of miscarriage, with approximately 30% of spontaneous miscarriages exhibiting aneuploidy.  Aneuploidy is also linked to mental and physical anomalies in newborns. In cancers, aneuploidy is the most common genetic trait. Although the detrimental effects of aneuploidy to foetal and human health have been long recognized, the molecular mechanisms that result in aneuploidy remain poorly understood. Aneuploidy is prevented by cell cycle checkpoints that detect errors in, and halt cell division processes until these errors are corrected. One such mechanism, known as the SAC or Spindle Assembly Checkpoint functions during mitosis to ensure equal segregation of chromosomes to daughter cells, thus preventing aneuploidy. This project aims to understand the regulation of a small but essential group of enzymes that control both the SAC itself, as well as the chromosome segregation machinery of the cell, and thus play a pivotal role in preventing aneuploidy. In particular, the catalytic function of these enzymes is poorly understood, and how they are regulated during the different stages of cell division remains unclear. Importantly, misregulation of this activity is a known cause of chromosome segregation errors and thus aneuploidy. Determining how these enzymes regulate targets and are themselves regulated by the fundamental biological process of cell division is critical for understanding the basis of wide range of chromosome-based genetic diseases ranging from spontaneous abortions and infertility, to cancer and aging. Moreover, there has been increasing interest recently in targeting these enzymes as for cancer therapy. The work proposed here will facilitate the discovery of both biomarkers and novel targets for aneuploidy based diseases, as well as the generation of novel therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: The neuro-circuitry of terror: High resolution SPECT imaging of REM sleep in PTSD and Nightmare Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: DREAMING; FEAR; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; NIGHTMARE DISORDER; POST TRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER (PTSD); REM SLEEP; SLEEP DISORDERS; SPECT IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Nightmares are fearful, frequently terrifying, sleep experiences that afflict patients who suffer from either post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) or Nightmare Disorder. Yet it remains unknown if the brain circuits responsible for nightmares are similar in the two conditions or even if Nightmare Disorder may be a form of partial PTSD brought on by accumulation of past adverse events. The goal of this research is to comparatively study PTSD and Nightmare Disorder patients to clarify the dysfunctional brain circuits underlying the two conditions, to determine whether or how the circuits differ and to evaluate if they are unique to REM sleep. We will use high resolution SPECT (single photon emission computed tomography) neuroimaging to assess brain activity during both a fearful picture viewing task and REM sleep periods that have been experimentally 'intensified' to contain emotionally negative dreams. We will test our neural model of nightmares that implicates a fear memory processing circuit consisting of the amygdala and 3 other modulator brain regions (hippocampus, medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortexes). We expect that PTSD and Nightmare Disorder patients will have similar dysfunctions in this circuit when compared with healthy subjects, i.e., more amygdala activation and less activation in some modulator regions, but that the dysfunction will be more severe for PTSD than for Nightmare Disorder patients, will differ for men and women, and will exceed waking state dysfunctional activity. We also expect that the dysfunctional activity will correlate with other measures of pathology: intensity of dream fear, levels of stress hormones, and a lifetime history of exposure to adverse events. Our procedure for altering REM sleep may prove useful in laboratory-based diagnoses of PTSD and other nightmare disorders, while brain scans are expected to advance medical understanding of fear pathology and lead to more varied, faster-acting and efficacious treatments.
