TitreApplicationTitle: Lipid droplets: a link between hepatic production of Hepatitis C virus and very low density lipoprotein
Keywords-MotsClés: APOLIPROTEIN B; HEPAITIS C VIRUS; SCID-ALB/UPA ANIMAL MODEL; VERY LOW DENSITY LIPOPROTEIN LIPID
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a global health threat with substantial risk of end-stage liver disease causing death or a need for liver transplant. The majority of HCV circulating in blood of infected patients is in association with entities called lipoproteins that transport fat to be used by various tissues. Lipoproteins are classified by density attributed by their fat content. The most infectious populations of HCV are in the form of very low density lipoprotein (VLDL). VLDL is assembled only in liver and they get their cargo from fat stored in lipid droplets. Interestingly, agents that disrupt VLDL production also disrupt HCV production and lipid droplets appear to have an essential role in HCV production perhaps by acting as scaffolding for viral assembly. Fat retention in liver is a predominant clinical feature of HCV infection that enhances liver disease, and impaired VLDL assembly is a leading cause of lipid retention in liver. Our objective is to explore the possibility that decreased fat export with VLDL, causing fat retention, is essential for HCV production. The outcomes are expected to provide important insight regarding how infectious HCV is produced and why it causes liver disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Génomique: Biologie computationnelle et biologie des systèmes
TitreApplicationTitle: Endosymbiosis, parasitism, and genome evolution
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOSYMBIOSIS; GENOME REDUCTION; GENOME SEQUENCING; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PARASITISM; TRANSCRIPTOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Microorganisms thrive in virtually every habitat imaginable. Understanding how they adapt to changing environments is a fundamental problem in biomedical research. The genetic makeup of endosymbionts -- cells that live inside other cells -- often differs significantly from free-living organisms, and while endosymbiosis can be an important first step in the evolution of an intracellular parasite, little is known about the molecular processes underlying this transition.   We propose to use advanced molecular and cell biological techniques, ultra-modern DNA sequencing, and computational methods to improve our understanding of how the genomes of single-celled, nucleus-containing organisms change in response to intracellular life. Specific questions to be addressed include examining how non-essential DNA is removed from an endosymbionts genome, and determining how (and how often) genes move from an endosymbionts genome to that of the host cell in which it resides. We will study the genomes of recently established endosymbionts as well as those more anciently evolved in order to gain perspective from both ends of the continuum between transient endosymbiont and permanent intracellular resident.  Although fundamental in nature, the research we propose has a number of practical benefits. The endosymbionts we will study live inside single-celled amoebae that are animal pathogens; elucidation of host-endosymbiont interactions will provide a framework for understanding the genetic basis of this pathogenicity. The endosymbionts themselves are also related to important human disease-causing parasites. Determining their genetic blueprint will improve our knowledge of how the causative agents of Chagas disease and African sleeping sickness first evolved and the genes they share with their endosymbiotic, but non-pathogenic, relatives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibitory interneurons in hippocampal long-term synaptic plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: CRE-LOX SYSTEM TRANSGENIC MICE; HIPPOCAMPAL NETWORK; HIPPOCAMPAL-DEPENDENT MEMORY; INHIBITORY INTERNEURONS SUBTYPES; LONG-TERM SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MULTIPHOTON CALCIUM IMAGING; PATCH CLAMP RECORDING IN BRAIN SLICES; SYNAPTIC PHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: GABAergic interneurons are the major inhibitory cells in the brain and they play a crucial role in controlling the excitability of projection cells in neuronal networks. They are multiple types of inhibitory interneurons which regulate neuronal activity in distinct ways. They are essential for normal brain function and are implicated in many CNS disorders, including epilepsy, autism, Rett syndrome, anxiety disorder, Tourette syndrome, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. However the distinct role of the different subtypes of inhibitory interneurons has been difficult to define because of the large diversity of cell types. The hippocampus is an excellent model system to determine the role of inhibitory interneurons in cortical networks because of its highly ordered and well-defined anatomical architecture. We propose to take advantage of new transgenic mice and molecular biological approaches that allow manipulations specifically in certain subtypes of interneurons. We will build on our previous work and carry out a comprehensive study of the function of identified GABA interneuron in the hippocampal network underlying memory consolidation.  Identifying and elucidating the network contributions of identified interneurons will shed new light on the inhibitory control of neuronal networks in the brain at the molecular, cellular, network and system levels. These are necessary first steps in developing new approaches to tackle the important health problems associated with CNS disorders implicating GABAergic interneurons.

TitreApplicationTitle: System Identification of Intrinsic and Reflex Stiffness Contributions to the Control of Posture and Movement.
Keywords-MotsClés: JOINT MECHANICS; MUSCLE MECHANICS; NEUROMUSCULAR  CONTROL; POSTURE; STRETCH REFLEX; SYSTEM IDENTIFICATION; VOLUNTARY MOVEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The mechanical behavior of a joint is important to the control of posture where it determines the automatic resistance to disturbances before voluntary intervention. It it is also important  during movement since it defines the properties of the  actuator that the nervous system uses to control movement as well as determining how disturbances will alter movements. This research will use novel quantitative methods to measure overall mechanical behavior and the relative contributions of intrinsic and reflex mechanisms. It will also  determine how the central nervous system changes these to meet different functional requirements. The results of this research will provide a better understanding of how the nervous system controls posture and movement. This will have  applications to the diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation of individuals suffering from neuromuscular disease.  Important application areas include the objective measurement of motor function, the design of devices to restore function to paralyzed muscles, robotic aids for the disabled, and the prediction and prevention of falls in the elderly.

Abstract-Résumé: The Public Health Agency of Canada reports between 2000 and 8000 Canadian deaths each year from the seasonal flu and its complications. The seasonal flu is caused by the influenza virus. After initial infection, the virus starts to multiply inside human cells, and then leaves those cells to infect more. We are studying how the virus can leave human cells because that is an important part of the spreading infection. Studying a virus at the moment it leaves a cell is technically challenging, and our strategy is to use a computer-based technique to watch a virus exit a cell and figure out how this happens and how we might prevent it to curb the infectious process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurofibrillary pathology and amyloidogenesis in Alzheimer's disease: mechanistic insights
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BACE-1; BETA AMYLOID; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; EGR-1; KINASE ASSAYS; NEUROFIBRILLARY TANGLES; PRIMARY NEURONS IN CULTURE; TAU PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia and afflicts 10 percent of population over age 65, 20 percent over age 75 and 50 percent of those age 85 and over. In Canada, more than 300, 000 people currently suffer form AD. This figure is projected to rise to over 500, 000 in 2031. The current yearly economic cost of AD is 10 billion dollars. This tag is estimated to grow to 17 billion dollars in 2031. Currently there are no effective treatments. To develop effective therapies, its cause must be determined.  The neuropathological features of AD are progressive neuronal and synapse loss in brain regions associated with cognitive dysfunction and deposition of two defining pathological hallmarks, senile plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. senile plaques contain beta-amyloid peptide and neurofibrillary tangles are composed mainly of microtubule-associated protein tau. The tau protein becomes abnormally hyperphosphorylated and accumulates leading to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles. Current studies suggest that therapies targeted against both beta-amyloid and tau are essential for treating AD. We have discovered a signaling pathway that controls both beta-amyloid synthesis and tau phosphorylation in the normal brain. This pathway involves a transcription factor called Egr-1. Our studies have shown that the Egr-1 is abnormally increased in AD brain and plays role in the development of pathology. In this proposal, we wish to examine how upregulated Egr-1 in AD brain causes nerve damage and dementia. We will use rat primary neurons and mice expressing human Egr-1 for our studies. Results of our proposed studies will determine step-by step mechanism by which beta-amyloid and tau accumulate leading to the formation of senile plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in AD patients. Determination of such mechanism will open new windows for the development of novel therapies against AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Selectivity for complex stimulus features in extrastriate visual cortex
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTATION; CORTEX; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MODELING; MULTI-ELECTRODE; NEURONS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PERCEPTION; VISION; VISUAL SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Our brains are capable of recognizing a face in a crowd or calculating the velocity of a moving object, and in this regard our abilities far exceed those of even the most sophisticated computers.  Underlying these abilities is a complex network of neurons and connections that are still not well understood. In this research we will study the neural pathways responsible for vision, with the goal of obtaining a detailed mathematical characterization of their function. In particular, we will focus on the interactions that occur among nearby neurons within the visual cortex. These local connections have the function of placing isolated visual signals into a more global context. This function is crucial for accurate vision and is often impaired in a number of sensory dysfunctions. Our work will therefore advance the basic understanding of the visual system while providing a foundation for interpreting and treating neurological disorders.

Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENETICS; CHROMOSOME INSTABILITY; CROSS-SPECIES APPROACHES; HIGH-CONTENT ANALYSIS; NOVEL THERAPEUTIC TARGETS; POST-TRANSLATIONAL HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; REVERSE GENETICS; RNF20; SYNTHETIC LETHALITY; TUMORIGENIC MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that in 2008, ~7.6 million deaths worldwide were attributed to cancer. In Canada, the number of cancer-related deaths in 2010 was estimated at ~76,200. Despite the wealth of cancer research conducted each year and the various drugs available to combat cancer, the WHO forecasts that cancer-related deaths will continue to increase and claim ~12 million lives in 2030. What's more, many of the current drugs used to treat cancer are linked to a variety of side effects stemming from the nonspecific nature of the drugs employed. Accordingly, new treatment approaches and new drug targets must be identified that will not only enhance the specificity and effectiveness of those treatments, but eliminate or minimize many of the current side effects.     Defects in specific genes cause genome instability which is a common step required to convert normal cells into cancer cells. This instability most often results in the abnormal chromosome numbers which is a hallmark frequently found in nearly all tumor types. We believe the presence of abnormal chromosome numbers is an effective way to distinguish cancerous from normal cells and therefore is an attractive therapeutic target. As a result, we believe that the instability, or the defective genes causing the instability, can be used as a homing beacon to selectively and specifically target and kill cancerous cells while leaving normal cells unaffected. Thus, our major goal is to identify and characterize genes that regulate genome stability, and use this information to identify new drug targets that can specifically kill cells with defects in those genes. Using state-of- the-art approaches, we seek to uncover new and highly selective drug targets. The result of this work will dramatically impact the future development of cancer therapies, by increasing the specificity of cancer treatment while minimizing the adverse side effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of valproic acid induced teratogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA RECOMBINATION; EMBRYO CULTURE; OXIDATIVE STRESS; TERATOGENESIS; VALPROIC ACID
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory studies the ways in which environmental chemicals and drugs produce birth defects.  We have shown that the overproduction of certain chemically reactive forms of oxygen, called reactive oxygen species, produce DNA damage within the developing embryo. Valproic acid is a commonly prescribed antiepileptic drug, used to treat a wide variety of seizure disorders. Despite its effectiveness and widespread use, valproic acid can cause birth defects when taken during pregnancy.  Since it is well known that uncontrolled seizures are also harmful to the developing fetus, a pregnant woman with epilepsy will be advised to continue to take her anticonvulsant therapy during her pregnancy.  It is therefore important to learn how drugs like valproic acid cause birth defects, and how to prevent this from occurring.  We have shown that metabolism of valproic acid generates reactive oxygen species, which causes breaks to occur in the DNA in cells, and this in turn causes the DNA to become rearranged in a process called DNA recombination.  DNA recombination can lead to genetic changes that can kill cells in the fetus and stop important developmental genes from functioning properly. We hypothesize that an increase in chemical-initiated DNA recombination is responsible for at least some of the birth defects seen in children born to mothers who are exposed to toxic chemicals during pregnancy.  We propose to test this hypothesis using both in vitro (cell cultures) and animal models.  Ultimately, the understanding of how this drug causes birth defects will lead to the design and development of safer therapeutic strategies to reduce birth defects.

TitreApplicationTitle: BMI1 as a mutlifunctional protein master regulator of stem cell activity
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION; DNA REPAIR; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELL SELF-RENEWAL; LEUKEMIA; MOUSE GENETICS; POLYCOMB GROUP PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: Stem cell are characterized by their ability to self-renew, a process which implies the coordination between cell division and cell differentiation. Understanding the basis which underly self-renewal has relevance in regenerative medicine (e.g., stem cell expansion for bone marrow transplantation) and in cancer. Indeed, most cancer analyzed to date include a rare population of self-renewing cells termed cancer stem cells. We showed before that the Bmi1 gene is a master regulator of normal and leukemia stem cells. In its absence, these cells loose their ability to self-renew. Over the years we have identified numerous co-factors which help Bmi1 accomplish its role in stem cells. In this project we will study the function of these partners and hopefully decipher the network through which Bmi1 controls self-renewal. This could lead to novel therapies which specifically target self-renewal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Computation in Sensory Systems: Information Transfer and Decoding by Neural Networks
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBELLUM; FEEDBACK; NEURAL CODING; NEURAL COMPUTATION; SENSORY PROCESSING; WEAK SIGNAL DETECTION
Abstract-Résumé: We navigate through our everyday environment with ease. Yet, in a completely unconscious manner, we are successfully solving some very difficult problems. We easily recognize a friend's voice even though they may be far away and their voice faint. Once having recognized their voice, we can quickly determine where it is coming from and move towards them. Remarkably, this is all happening in a noisy environment with other speakers and traffic noise presenting a potentially confusing mix of sounds. The human nervous system is so complex and powerful that we have no idea of how we can so readily perform these amazing feats. And, when disease or age cause some detioration in this wonderful abilities, we do not know how to mitigate their effects. Our research has used a special model system- the weakly electric fish- to investigate these problems. These fish can detect weak inputs emanating from prey and swim towards them; and they can do this in the presence of noise that masks the prey signals. In the small and relatively simple fish brain we have been able to identify key principles of sensory processing relevant to the human condition. For example, we have found that a  special part of the brain- the cerebellum- can act to cancel background noise. In fact, we have found that it acts in much the same way as the commercially available noise cancelling headphones  popular with air travelers. Our brains also contain a large cerebellum and our work suggests that enhancing its function might be a good strategy for improving attentional focus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advancing gel dosimetry for clinical radiation therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE RADIATION THERAPY; INTENSITY MODULATED RADIATION THERAPY; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE; OPTICAL COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY IMAGING; POLYMER GEL DOSIMETERS; POLYMER REACTION ENGINEERING AND MODELLING; RADIATION DOSIMETRY; RADIOCHROMIC GEL DOSIMETERS
Abstract-Résumé: The major advance in modern radiation therapy has been the development of techniques to better shape radiation dose to tumor volumes, while minimizing the dose to surrounding normal tissue. The verification of such delivery with traditional measurement methods is difficult, since the doses need to be determined in three dimensions (3D). A promising technique for volumetric 3D dose measurement is gel dosimetry, based on the imaging of certain gel systems which change under irradiation.  Despite its promise, gel dosimetry has not come into widespread clinical use, mainly because of difficulties in reproducibility during gel preparation and readout, toxicity of gel components in certain gels, and limited access to imaging modalities (e.g., magnetic resonance imaging) for dose readout.    In the last few years we have used CIHR funding to advance clinical gel dosimetry by: 1) developing recipes for new dosimeters using knowledge gained from fundamental physical experiments and mathematical modeling, 2) developing less-toxic polymer-based dosimeters, and 3) characterizing and optimizing optical computed tomography (optical CT) imaging to achieve accurate and reproducible 3D gel dosimetry.   In this application we propose to 1) continue to invent, characterize, and test formulations for gel dosimeters, 2) develop standard protocols by which specific gels can be used with specific readout schemes, 3) evaluate the dose measurement integrity of gel dosimetry by comparing to standard techniques, and 4) develop standard software to evaluate and compare gel-measured doses to the planned dose delivery and to dose measurements using conventional tools available in the clinic.   Objectives 1) and 2) provide the basic information required to develop the rigorous protocols for gel dosimetry (including preparation, handling and readout) required for good dosimetry, while objectives 3) and 4) are necessary steps towards translating the dosimetry to clinical use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of statistical methods for meta-analysis of tuberculosis diagnostic studies
Keywords-MotsClés: BIAS; HETEROGENEITY; INCREMENTAL VALUE; META-ANALYSIS; SENSITIVITY/SPECIFICITY; TUBERCULOSIS DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
Abstract-Résumé: Availability of an accurate diagnostic test has been identified as an urgent need in the global battle against tuberculosis (TB). The last two decades have seen a steady growth in research studies on the accuracy of rapid tests for TB screening in vulnerable populations. Systematic reviews and accompanying meta-analyses have played a key role in synthesizing the results of this diverse literature. They have aided in directing medical research towards more promising technologies, and also in identifying failed technologies that have proved detrimental to public health.  The last decade has also seen a growing recognition of the need for more sophisticated statistical modeling to support meta-analyses. This proposal describes development of new tools to improve meta-analyses of tuberculosis diagnostic studies. Building on our earlier work in this area, we propose methods for addressing three principal concerns: i) Quantifying and modeling variation across diagnostic studies, ii)Studying the impact of common biases in diagnostic studies, and iii) Estimation of the incremental value of a new test over and above a standard test. Our methods will be applied toe data from published meta-analyses of TB tests. We anticipate that our research will lead to improved methods for evaluating available evidence and aid in policy making. For all models we will develop user-friendly software to permit easy application. The methods we propose will also find application in areas besides tuberculosis where diagnostic meta-analyses are needed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bone marrow-derived stem cell-based gene therapy to accelerate fracture healing
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW STEM CELL; CELL BASED GENE THERAPY; EPC MSC; PROMOTE BONE HEALING; RAT FRACTURE; VEGF ENOS GENES
Abstract-Résumé: Bone fractures often damage the local blood vessels and soft tissues impairing the delivery of sufficient nutrients required for fracture repair. The healing of severe fractures can thus be delayed or completely stopped, leading to significant patient morbidity. Bone regeneration following a fracture requires the presence of pluripotential cells and specific growth factors.  Here we propose a new technique involving bone marrow cell-based gene therapy to promote blood circulation and fracture healing. Endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) and mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) will be isolated from the bone marrow and transfected with genes encoding for vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS). These modified EPC and MSC will then be delivered to a fracture site in an animal model so that they can produce VEGF and eNOS proteins. These proteins will aid in new blood vessel formation and/or osteogenesis. We hypothesize that the bone marrow cell-based gene therapy is effective in stimulating new blood vessel and bone formation. It is hoped that this work will result in a more effective strategy for improving fracture healing.

TitreApplicationTitle: The use of flaxseed as a dietary intervention to modify cardiovascular disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; NUTRITION; VASCULAR FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Blockages in the arteries are the primary cause of both stroke and heart disease, the leading causes of death and disability in the world today. The more that we can understand about how the vessels get blocked, the better we will be able to treat, prevent and/or delay their occurrence. Recent data would suggest that dietary interventions may be far more powerful to protect the body from cardiovascular disease than any drug treatment available. Dietary interventions, however, not only treat a pre-existing disease but also delay or prevent the occurrence of atherosclerotic disease. Supplementation of the diet with omega-3 fatty acids found in fish has been used to alter cardiovascular disease. However, dietary compliance for fish supplementation has been a problem. Fortunately, an alternative, tasty source of omega-3 fatty acids exists in flax. The purpose of this study is to determine if flax supplementation of the diet will retard the development of blockages in arteries that lead to heart attacks and stroke. Alternatively, we will also investigate if a different kind of fat, trans fats, can induce these blockages. Our study, therefore, will identify two compounds that may directly protect or advance heart disease. The data will directly address the need for further work to advance our dietary recommendations for the prevention of heart disease and stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional regulation by a novel deubiquitinase multi-protein complex
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; CHROMATIN; EPIGENETICS; PROTEOMICS; TRANSCRIPTION; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Ubiquitination is an essential biochemical reaction which occurs in all cells of our body. This process consists of the attachment of a small protein, called ubiquitin, to various cellular proteins. This labeling system marks the target proteins as unwanted (or no longer needed), and induces their degradation by a molecular machine called the "proteasome". Interestingly it has recently been realized that ubiquitination can also cause changes in the function and properties of the targeted protein without any degradation. Moreover we have now started to appreciate that ubiquitination is a dynamic process and that certain enzymes, called deubiquitinases (or DUBs for short), ensure the timely removal of ubiquitin from proteins. In fact, the functional interaction between ubiquitination and deubiquitination allows cells to tightly regulate protein function. With this capability, the ubiquitin system executes and/or regulates many cellular processes, and these include cellular proliferation and differentiation. It is therefore not surprising that alterations in components of the ubiquitin system have been causally linked to several human diseases. The goal of my research is to determine how DUBs orchestrate the function and stability of the genome, a subject about which very little is currently known. I plan to use molecular and cellular biology approaches to characterize the biological function and mechanism of action of a DUB multiprotein complex. This will not only shed new light on the mechanisms that govern normal cellular processes, but will also help in furthering our understanding of various human diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The evolution of Mycobacterium tuberculosis virulence - not all strains are created equal.
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; MICROBIOLOGY; MOUSE MODELS OF INFECTION; STRAIN VARIATION; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) in humans is an extremely complex infection that is spread from individuals with active lung disease to uninfected individuals via air droplets containing the bacteria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis.  Despite the availability of effective drug treatment for more than half a century, 2 million people still die as a result of this devastating disease each year.  Recent evidence indicates that M. tuberculosis has evolved into several large, genetically diverse families of strains that possess unique attributes potentially related to the development and spread of disease.  One family of TB strains that has gained considerable notoriety over the past decade is known as the "Beijing" or "W/Beijing" family.  In many parts of the world, the number of TB cases due to W/Beijing strains is found to be increasing in an epidemic fashion and these strains are frequently associated with the development of drug resistance.  The research in this proposal aims to characterize the unique attributes of the W/Beijing family that contribute to their global success as an emerging pathogen.  Understanding the contribution of strain variation to the overall disease process will greatly increase our knowledge of the range of strategies employed by M. tuberculosis to cause infection.  Moreover, this may ultimately shed light on important new ways to diagnose and prevent TB transmission and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a targeted drug delivery and high-throughput drug screening technology using droplet-based microfluidics and functionalized nano-structured materials
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICANCER; DRUG CONTROLLED RELEASE; DRUG DELIVERY; DRUG TARGETING; DRUG TOXICITY; MICROFLUIDICS; SINGLE CELL STUDY; SYNTHESIS OF NANOMATERIALS
Abstract-Résumé: Personalized treatment approaches improve therapeutic safety and efficacy by tailoring therapies to the unique requirements of each patient's illness, physiology, and tolerability. The current project aims to develop a high-throughput drug screening platform using droplet-based microfluidic technology developed by a proposed supervisor for this project, Prof. David Weitz of Harvard University. Using this system, an individual cell (such as tumour cell isolated by biopsy from a patient or from an experimental animal, rat) can be encapsulated in a picoliter-sized droplet, and introduced to a similarly-encapsulated drug or drug combination within droplet micro-reactors. Using this approach, cellular responses towards a suite of drugs can be assessed for effectiveness at the single cell level within very short intervals, dramatically improving patient outcomes by identifying effective treatments among a suite of potential therapeutics. Relative to traditional approaches, microfluidics promises rapid assessment of physiological responses to each drug, at a known dosage, with toxicity of the drug/drug combination evaluated on healthy cells from the same patient. The efficiency (up to 2000 cells/second) of the screening procedure would also be of tremendous benefit to the pharmaceutical industry in developing and assessing novel therapies. A further aspect of the proposed project is improving therapeutic effectiveness and reducing side effects by restricting drug delivery to target tissues. Such a strategy would result in less frequent dosing (and fewer pills) which will improve convenience and compliance while reducing the potential for overmedication. By targeting the drug (using antibody, synthetic antibody with molecule imprinted polymer, folate targeting, or aptamer labelling technique) to a specific region of the GI tract or other tissues, optimal absorption and efficacy, with a lower peak drug concentration should result in improved patient tolerability.

TitreApplicationTitle: Models of Human Salivary Enzymes and Oral Biofilms to Study the Dentin-Composite Interface Breakdown
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; BIODEGRADATION; COMPSITE RESIN; CONFOCAL LASER MICROSCOPY; ESTERASES; FRACTURE TOUGHNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Tooth-coloured resin-composite based restorations are currently the most popular restorative materials in the dental field; their applications include direct and indirect restorations of the teeth, dental adhesives and cements. Bacterial penetration and proliferation along the tooth-resin dental restoration interface contributes to postoperative sensitivity, recurrent caries and pulp inflammation. Recurrent caries at the tooth-restoration interface margin is regarded as the major cause of restoration failure.  Therefore, the success of a resin- based dental restoration is highly dependent on the formation, and the maintenance of impermeable seal to bacterial penetration to prevent ingress of bacteria and bacterial by-products. Our group developed a laboratory model, consists of continues media system in combination with fluorescent dyes and confocal laser microscopy, optimizing the conditions for bacterial microleakage and biofilm formation studies of dental plaque bacteria.  This system provides a valid laboratory model which is physiologically relevant to pathogenic intra oral conditions.  Using this system, the PIs' research group has revealed that human saliva induced biodegradation, compromising the restoration-tooth marginal interface, leading to bacterial penetration and proliferation along the restoration-tooth interfacial gap, as well as reducing the bond strength between the restoration and the tooth.  The model developed by the PIs allows for testing of different strategies to inhibit degradation of the bonded interface, with the potential to increases its resistant to bacterial invasion and proliferation, ultimately leading to increase in the restorations service life.  This model is novel to the dental health care community and its clients, and merits attention since it has the potential to change the way composite resin materials adhesives are formulated and tested.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adaptive regulation of sensory processing
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBELLUM; COMPUTATIONAL NEUROSCIENCE; FEEDBACK; INHIBITION; NEURAL CODING; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; NMDA RECEPTORS; SENSORY PROCESSING; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: The nervous system must detect very weak signals in the presence of noise. For example, we must attend to and comprehend conversation even when traffic and other noise source might be louder than the speech we are trying to understand. This subject is of great importance for both normal function and may be perturbed in some individuals.  However it is very difficult to study in humans because of the great complexity of speech and other signals important to us and, also, because of the overwhelming complexity of the human brain. We work on a simple model system- the electric fish- that specializes in the detection of weak electric signals that occur in the presence of strong noise. Our studies reveal how the same biological mechanisms found in our brain can be organized so as to reject noise and detect the weakest of signals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining regulatory landscapes within Hox clusters
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN CONFORMATION; CHROMOSOME ENGINEERING; CONGENITAL MALFORMATIONS; ENHANCER; GENE REGULATION; HOX GENES
Abstract-Résumé: Between 3 to 5% of births are affected by congenital malformations and 20 to 30% of infant deaths are due to genetic disorders. Understanding genetic traits associated with congenital disorders is critical for early diagnosis and improving treatments. This represents an enormous task and major efforts should be dedicated to defining the genetic anomalies responsible for congenital malformations. One of the major difficulties is that genetic anomalies are not restricted to the genes themselves and can affect regulatory elements that control gene activity. These regulatory elements can be located far from the gene(s) they control. Understanding mechanisms that control gene activity is essential to help unraveling the etiology of congenital disorders. Mutations affecting the Hox gene family were previously identified in numerous congenital disorders and it is assumed that much more disorders are linked to improper Hox genes activity. The aim of this research proposal is to identify genetic parameters that are critical for ensuring stringent control of the activity of Hox genes, which in turn should be valuable to improve diagnosis and help improving treatments of Hox related genetic disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exome capture in severe early onset Essential Tremor families.
Keywords-MotsClés: ESSENTIAL TREMORS; FUNCTIONAL VALIDATION; GENE IDENTIFICATION; GENETIC VARIATIONS; WHOLE EXOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Essential Tremor (ET) is a chronic brain disease characterize by tremors occurring during volitional movement of the arm. As the disease advances, patients may also experience head tremor and difficulties with coordination, gait and balance. The disease is present in 4.0% of individuals aged over 40. ET is the most common cause of tremor in humans and is among the most common neurological disorders. Although the causes of ET are poorly understood, the disease is known to have a strong genetic component. However, none of the existing results have been replicated. We propose to sequence the entire coding region of the genome (known as the exome) of individuals with ET in order to identify genetic variations associated with the disease. Identifying such genes will help understand the pathological mechanisms of ET and open new avenues for the development of a treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Why are women at increased risk of COPD?
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL STUDIES; COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; COPD; FEMALE SEX HORMONES; OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past 20 years, the number of women with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (which was in the past called "chronic bronchitis", "emphysema" or "smokers' lung") in Canada has more than doubled such that in 2011 the number of women with COPD exceeds the number of cases in men. When women develop COPD, they are more short of breath, have poorer quality of life and experience more frequent hospitalizations and exacerbations than male patients even though female smokers on average smoke less than male smokers. In the proposed research program, we will figure out why women are at increased risk of COPD and how female sex hormones may affect in the breathing tubes that may lead to lung disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of forgetting: Neural representations for memory and perception
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMNESIA; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; INTERFERENCE; MEDIAL TEMPORAL LOBE; MEMORY; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; PERCEPTION; PERIRHINAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Memory disorders are on the rise: An estimated 500,000 Canadians and 35 million people worldwide are currently living with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia. Barring a medical breakthrough, the number of people with dementia will double every 20 years. The disease is not limited to the oldest members of society. In Canada alone, 71,000 people under the age of 65 have the disorder, with 50,000 of these 59 years or younger. But age is the number one risk factor for dementia, and as developed societies age rapidly, there will be a drastic increase in memory disorders. This is a ticking time bomb - an enormous future burden for health care systems, afflicted individuals, their families and caretakers.   In order to treat those with memory disorders more effectively, we must gain deeper insight into how memory is organized in the healthy brain, and how this organization deteriorates with brain damage. Studies of people with memory impairments (e.g., from dementia, stroke, infection, alcohol abuse, or head injury) have shown that a specific set of structures deep inside the brain, called the medial temporal lobe (MTL), is vital for memory. However, the specific contribution of different MTL structures to memory remains the subject of intense debate. The proposed research will provide evidence that these brain structures support aspects of perception in addition to memory. These findings will reshape our understanding of the origin of memory deficits in patients with MTL damage: impaired memory retrieval may not simply indicate a breakdown in memory functions per se, but may also be due to perceptual problems at encoding. In other words, if a stimulus cannot be perceived correctly, it cannot be stored and retrieved correctly. This has major implications for therapeutic approaches in individuals with memory disorders: instead of focusing only on memory-based strategies, it may also be beneficial to enhance perceptual processes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Heterotopic ossification following traumatic skeletal muscle injury: alteration of the stromal cell micro-environment and induction of the osteogenic differentiation program
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MORPHOGENIC PROTEINS; CELLULES STROMALES; CYTOMETRIE DE FLUX; FACTEURS CIRCULANTS; HYPOXIE; MODELES MURINS; MUSCLE SQUELETTIQUE; OSSIFICATION HETEROTOPIQUE; TRAUMATISME CRANIENS; WNT CANONIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: A la suite d'une blessure, le muscle squelettique se repare normalement. Toutefois lors d'un accident grave, ou encore, apres certaines chirurgies, le processus de reparation peut etre compromis et favoriser la formation d'os mature a l'interieur du muscle. La formation d'os dans les muscles peut avoir de graves consequences pour le patient notamment une douleur vive et une perte de fonction du membre atteint. Les causes de cette maladie ne sont pas connues. Selon nos recents travaux, il semblerait que des facteurs presents dans le muscle endommage conduisent les cellules souches a l'interieur du muscle a former de l'os. Dans cette proposition de recherche, nous souhaitons mettre en evidence ces facteurs et les tester sur des cellules cultivees en laboratoire. De plus, nous examinerons les constituants presents dans le sang de patients qui, suite a un traumatisme, ont une predisposition a former de l'os dans leur muscle. Les resultats qui decouleront de ces travaux, permettront d'identifier des cibles therapeutiques pour prevenir cette maladie, ce qui contribuera a ameliorer la qualite de vie des patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Needle Guidance System for Neuraxial Analgesia and Anesthesia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANESTHESIOLOGY; AUGMENTED REALITY; EPIDURAL INJECTIONS; FACET JOINT INJECTIONS; IMAGE REGISTRATION; MEDICAL IMAGE ANALYSIS; PAIN MANAGEMENT; REAL-TIME VISUALIZATION; STATISTICAL SHAPE MODELS; ULTRASOUND GUIDANCE
Abstract-Résumé: The purpose of this research is to develop an innovative, robust, intuitive and affordable system for guiding needle insertion into the lumbar spine. Ultrasound imaging will be the basis for guidance before and during needle insertion. The main application is facet joints and epidural/steroid injection for the relief of chronic back pain, and labour/analgesia. The anesthesiologist is expected to use the system to choose a suitable puncture location, insert the needle at an appropriate angle and stop when the needle reaches the desired depth. The goal is to increase the confidence level by enabling an accurate needle placement on the first attempt, and hence reduce complications and pain for the patient. In current practice, the needle insertion is either done blindly, using palpation to choose a puncture site, or under fluoroscopy/CT guidance, which carry a high radiation dose risk to both patient and anesthesiologist. We will develop and validate a system that adds real-time ultrasound capability to these procedures by using an augmented reality environment that displays the ultrasound, pre-procedure CT and needle trajectory to the anesthesiologist. The system will integrate new ways of aligning ultrasound images with pre-procedure data in an innovative guidance interface for the anesthesiologist to interpret the images and relate them to the patient's anatomy. This includes incorporation of spine statistical atlas information. The tools and techniques will be validated in a number of patient studies. The proposed system is timely as ultrasound has enjoyed a recent resurgence for spinal needle placement among clinicians. The development of the system will uniquely combine recent technological and medical advancements at the University of British Columbia and University of Western Ontario, and their affiliated hospitals, on image-guided interfaces for needle placement in the lumbar spine.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES PARASITAIRES; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Pathogenesis and interventions for severe malaria
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOBAL HEALTH; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; INNATE IMMUNITY; MALARIA
Abstract-Résumé: STATEMENT OF THE PROBLEM: Millions of individuals acquire malaria each year but relatively few develop life-threatening illness. The current inability to identify the small proportion of individuals who will progress to life-threatening illness is a major barrier to effective treatment of severe infections. Moreover, once initiated, severe malaria is associated with a high death rate despite the use of potent antimalarial drugs. The ability to rapidly identify individuals at risk of critical illness and deliver novel treatments to improve survival would represent a significant advance in management.  PROPOSED SOLUTION: The endothelium lines our blood vessels and is the largest organ in the human body, linking all other organs. Endothelial activation is a common pathway of injury in a number of life-threatening infections including severe malaria, toxic shock syndrome, dengue shock syndrome, sepsis etc. Endothelial activation and injury are associated with critical illness and death. This research proposal focuses on the discovery of endothelial-based "biomarkers" (e.g. genes and proteins) that control endothelial activation and that might reliably identify individuals at risk of severe disease. We are also focusing on using this knowledge to design new endothelial-based therapies to improve survival in these individuals. Collectively this approach will facilitate the identification of biomarkers enabling risk prediction and may suggest new interventions for severe malaria and other life-threatening infections for which no therapy currently exists.

TitreApplicationTitle: Automatic Motion Correction for Dynamic Contrast Enhanced MRI
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSESSMENT OF THERAPEUTIC RESPONSE; CONTRAST-ENHANCED IMAGING; IMAGE PROCESSING; IMAGE REGISTRATION; MRI; TUMOUR CHARACTERISATION
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that 75,300 Canadian deaths occurred from cancer in 2009. Currently the major treatment options are radiotherapy, surgery and chemotherapy but survival rates are still poor and these therapies are all associated with serious side effects. Recently there has been an explosion of interest in new anti-cancer drugs that target the growth of new blood vessels feeding the tumour. Before these drugs can be approved for routine clinical use, trials are needed to determine whether they provide benefit over existing therapies. Medical imaging has an important role in assessing how well patients are responding to therapy. The most widely used method of measuring response is to make a simple measurement of tumour size from a CT or MRI image. Although this method has worked well for assessing drugs that have the effect of shrinking tumours, it does not help us to see whether we have successfully stopped the blood supply to the tumour. Dynamic Contrast-Enhanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (DCE-MRI) does provide information about tumour function as well as size and has been shown to provide useful clinical information about tumour grade and likelihood of recurrence in a variety of cancer types. DCE-MRI involves injecting a dye into the patient that can be tracked using MRI. By measuring how quickly the dye travels into and out of a tumour we can gain valuable information for diagnosis and therapy planning. When a patient is lying in the scanner a series of images are taken and it is important that there is no movement between each image. Unfortunately it is impossible to stay completely still and some motion, for example movement due to breathing is inevitable. We are developing a computer technique to correct for this motion which will provide more accurate images and reduce the need to rescan patients. The new methodology is expected to improve the value of DCE-MRI for drug design and evaluation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Retinal Stem Cells As Potential Treatments for Blindness
Keywords-MotsClés: BLINDNESS; PHOTORECEPTORS; RETINAL STEM CELLS; TRANSPLANTATION; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Permanent vision loss caused by damage or degeneration of the retina is a severely debilitating condition, and its burden on both society and the health care industry will only increase as the average world population continues to age.  We have characterized a stem cell population within the adult mammalian eye (including the eyes of humans) that shows fantastic potential for the treatment of these conditions.  These adult retinal stem cells have the capacity generate new photoreceptors, the light-sensing cells of the retina, and therefore could be used to replace those cells lost due to retinal disease or injury.  The present proposal builds upon our current understanding of these cells in order to improve their ability to successfully treat a variety of forms of vision loss.  We will be approaching this problem from two distinct directions, both by investigating ways of activating the stem cells already present within the eye (thus minimizing the need for invasive surgery) and in a more classical cell culture and transplantation model.  By taking both of these approaches, we can improve our understanding of adult retinal stem cell biology from a basic science perspective; while at the same time develop techniques that have significant therapeutic potential.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms and regulation of ribosomal RNA synthesis in health and disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHROMATIN REMODELLING; GENE KNOCKOUT AND TRANSGENESIS; GROWTH REGULATION; HUMAN; MOUSE; RIBOSOMAL RNA GENES; RIBOSOME BIOGENESIS; RNA POLYMERASES I AND II; TRANSCRIPTION REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: The form that cancers take can be extremely varied, ranging from solid tumours that can affect almost any part of the body, to the overgrowth of blood cells. These differences are related mainly to the origins of the cancer cells. However, regardless of its origin cancer is fundamentally the result of unrestricted growth. It was recognized many years ago that, to improve the effectiveness of cancer treatments, we need to understand how cells regulate their growth and what exactly goes wrong with this process in cancer. Each cell uses a complex network of signals in order to decide how rapidly it should grow. Our work aims to understand this growth network and how it is changed in cancer cells. The ribosome, the large and complex "machine" that makes all the proteins of the cell, is at the heart of this network. Manufacture of the ribosome requires many hundreds of components and is an endeavour that occupies between 50 and 80% of the cell's efforts. We have found that growth factors, oncogenes and tumor suppressors directly control ribosome manufacture. Further, bottle-necks in production of ribosomes cause a range of degenerative diseases, but have been also been correlated with an inability to activate the most important tumour suppressors. Our aim is to understand how the earliest steps of the manufacture of ribosomes occur and how this relates to cancer and other diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: New Statistical Methods for Population-based Studies of Comparative Effectiveness and Safety of Medications: Development, Validation and Applications
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; COMPARATIVE EFFECTIVENESS; COMPETING RISKS; CONFOUNDING BIAS; CUMULATIVE EFFECTS; DRUG INTERACTIONS; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; SIMULATIONS; STATISTICAL MODELING; TIME-VARYING COVARIATES
Abstract-Résumé: Medication use and health care costs increase steadily with the aging of Western societies, and the ever increasing number of drugs available on the market. Overall, new drugs and treatments contribute to the improvement of the population health and increasing life expectancy. However, there are concerns about potential adverse effects of some medications and it is not always clear which of the alternative drugs that are currently used to treat a given disease are the most effective. Thus, evaluation of comparative effectiveness and safety of treatments is a top priority for both the health research and the society at large.   Evaluations of the effects of treatments on the health outcomes typically rely on large long-term studies and have to account for differences in both the characteristics of the patients and the dose and duration of treatment. Scientific validity of the results and conclusions of such studies depends critically on the accuracy of statistical methods used to analyze such complex data.  The overall objective of our proposal is to develop new statistical methodology for analyzing large studies of comparative effectiveness and safety of medications. The proposed new methods will account for the changes over time in drug use and doses, and for the complexity of biological processes linking medication use and the clinical, socio-economic, behavioral and environmental characteristics of the patients with the clinical outcomes such as mortality, infections or hospitalizations. These new methodological developments will build on our ongoing research on flexible statistical methods for analyzing effects of treatments and risk factors that change over time.   Our new methods will help efficient identification of adverse effects and accurate comparison of therapeutic effectiveness of alternative drugs used to treat many diseases. This, in turn, will permit optimizing drug prescribing practice, to minimize the risks and maximize therapeutic benefits.

TitreApplicationTitle: In vivo regulation of mitosis in stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CAENORHABDITIS ELEGANS; CANCER STEM CELLS; GERMLINE DEVELOPMENT; LIVE IMAGING; MITOSIS; POLARITY; STEM CELL DIVISION
Abstract-Résumé: Stem cells are the basis of life.  As an embryo, stem cells develop into the multitude of diverse tissues in the body.  In adults, stem cells are critical for maintaining the body; for instance the red blood cells in your body (about 4% of your body mass) now will be 100% different in about a month.  On the other hand, misregulation of stem cell divisions leads to cancer.  In this proposal, we will work to understand the fundamental properties of stem cell divisions in a living organism. Our well will identify new pathways to regulate stem cell proliferation as well as means to stop cancer stem cell divisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of pancreatic beta-cell exocytosis and insulin secretion by SUMOylation
Keywords-MotsClés: EXCITOSOME; EXOCYTOSIS; INSULIN; ION CHANNELS; SENP; SNARE PROTEINS; SUMO; UBC9
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes affects more than 2.5 million Canadians and costs our healthcare system nearly $15 billion dollars annually in direct and indirect costs. An inability of the pancreatic islet of Langerhans to secrete sufficient amounts of insulin is central to the development and progression of type 2 diabetes. It is therefore essential that we gain a further understanding of the mechanisms and processes regulating insulin secretion in order to understand potential defects that occur in type 2 diabetes, and to develop improved strategies for the treatment, prevention and ultimate cure of the disease.  In the present study we will examine the role of a novel cellular signaling pathway, known as SUMOylation, in the acute regulation of insulin secretion from islet beta-cells. Recent work from us and others suggests that this pathway, thought to function primarily in gene transcription, may be an important and regulator of cellular electrical activity. New data from our lab also supports a role for SUMOylation in controlling the cellular machinery responsible for the actual release of insulin (the 'exocytotic' machinery) in response to increases in blood sugar. Thus, we hypothesize that SUMOylation represents an important new pathway for the regulation of insulin secretion. We will therefore examine the role of this pathway in regulating the cellular function of mouse and human pancreatic islet cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Self-Employment and Immigrant Health:  Job Stress and Health Among Asian Immigrant Micro Business Owners
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCULTURATION STRESS; ASIAN IMMIGRANTS; IMMIGRANT HEALTH; JOB STRESS; MICRO BUSINESS; SELF EMPLOYMENT; STRESS PROCESS
Abstract-Résumé: By 2031, more than 1 in 2 Canadians aged 15 and over will be immigrants, and Asians will comprise the largest proportion of all immigrants. The socio-cultural and economic integration of immigrants has an increasingly large impact on the health and well-being of the Canadian population. Although a growing number of immigrants have turned to self-employment or micro business ownership, there has been virtually no research on the psychosocial factors affecting the health of self-employed immigrants or immigrant micro business owners. Considering that micro businesses account for more than 50% of Canadian businesses and generate over 25% of all jobs in Canada, it is important to determine factors that affect the health of micro business owners, especially among immigrants. Immigrant micro business owners typically manage heavy workloads and endure high levels of physical and mental labour without receiving extra health care benefits or pensions. In the proposed study, the health of immigrant micro-business owners will be examined by comparing micro business ownership to paid employment. The findings of the study will be used to suggest bases for further research on the health implications of other types of self-employment among immigrants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brain mechanisms of human colour and form vision
Keywords-MotsClés: COLOUR VISION; CONTRAST SENSITIVITY; FMRI; SPATIAL VISION; VISION; VISUAL PSYCHOPHYSICS
Abstract-Résumé: The understanding of colour vision is a challenge that has interested scientists for over 300 years, since the time of Sir Isaac Newton. The core of the problem is to understand how the spectral differences in the physical world are translated by the brain into the neural signals that represent the wide array of colours we see in our perceptual world. This research investigates how the human brain sees colour. In particular, my experiments investigate which pathways and areas in the brain are used to respond to colour and which to black and white, whether our colour and form vision are combined in the brain, and why, of all the mammals, only old world primates (including humans) have developed colour vision that allows discrimination in the red-yellow-green regions of the spectrum.  The research uses the latest techniques, including fMRI of the human brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Colonic Goblet Cell Mediators: Active Players in Host Defense and Mucosal Protection?
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELING; ATTACHING/EFFACING BACTERIA; EPITHELIUM; GASTROENTEROLOGY; GOBLET CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The colonic epithelium consists of both absorptive cells as well as secretory goblet cells that produce mucus. While many damaging agents, including bacterial pathogens target the epithelium, bacteria must first cross the sticky mucus layer that covers and protects these cells. It is currently unclear if the host immune system changes goblet cell function, in order for these cells to play a more active role in host defense. Considering that certain diarrhea causing bacterial pathogens, like enterohemorrhagic E. coli, (EHEC) colonize the gut epithelial surface, and thus reside within the mucus layer, we will address the impact of goblet cells and mucus on host defense using this family of pathogens. Since EHEC is human specific, we are using a related bacterial pathogen called Citrobacter rodentium that causes diarrhea and colitis in mice. Muc2 deficient mice lack an intestinal mucus layer and are highly susceptible to infection, carrying heavy C. rodentium burdens that are only loosely bound to the gut surface. As a result, these mice suffer excessive inflammation and bacterial translocation, leading to sepsis and death. In contrast, wildtype mice show increased mucus release during infection, which appears to protect the gut by flushing away loosely bound bacteria. Based on these studies, we will now examine how mucus actually protects the host. Since we also found that infection elevates the expression of RELM-B, another goblet cell derived mediator, and since RELM-B deficient mice suffer worsened infections, we will also explore RELM-B's role in host defense. Lastly, since subpopulations of C. rodentium do manage to cross the mucus barrier and colonize the intestinal surface, we will define the virulence strategies utilized by C. rodentium to overcome this host barrier. Taken together, our proposed studies will explore an important but understudied aspect of pathogen-host interactions at the mucosal surface that should aid in identifying new therapeutic targets.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural and biochemical correlates of resting state activity and emotional processing in major depressive disorder - Multimodal imaging (fMRI, MRS and PET) during gaba- and glutamat-ergic intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGING IN HUMANS; DEPRESSION; GABA; GLUTAMATE; PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prominent psychiatric disorder which is projected to be the second most often occurring illness (after cardiac disorders) in about 10 years, world-wide. Clinically, MDD can be characterized by strong ruminations, enhanced feelings of guilt and self-blame, abnormally negative emotions, and increased attention to one's self, e.g., increased self-focus [1-3]. These symptoms can be treated with serotoninergic drugs as well as with GABAergic and glutamatergic drugs like lorazepam and ketamine. While there has been much research about the serotoninergic system, the mechanisms underlying GABA- and glutamatergic dysfunction in MDD remain to be explored and are the target of our study proposal.

TitreApplicationTitle: The nature of repulsion during axon guidance
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; CHIMERIC RECEPTORS; DROSOPHILA GENETICS; DROSOPHILA IN VITRO CULTURE SYSTEM; EFFECTS OF PURIFIED WNT5 PROTEINS ON GROWTH CONE; GAL4-UAS SYSTEM; GROWTH CONE TURNING ASSAY; NETRIN AND UNC5; REPULSIVE GUIDANCE CUES AND THEIR RECEPTORS; WNT5 AND DRL
Abstract-Résumé: One of the outstanding questions in the neuroscience field is how nerve cells are precisely wired during development. An answer to this question is key to finding ways to restore the functional neural circuits after brain or spinal cord injury. During development, nerve cells elongate long processes, axons, which are guided to other nerve cells with which they make connections, thus forming neural circuits. Several molecules have been discovered that guide axons to their target nerve cells. These guidance molecules are grouped into two categories: attractive cues that attract axons and repulsive cues that repel them. Our lab at the Salk Institute discovered a repulsive molecule, called Wnt5, and the receptor on the axons through which it signals, called Derailed (Drl). Wnt5 activates Drl on the axons of certain nerve cells and repels them away from the Wnt5 source. The inappropriate upregulation of Wnt-Drl repulsive signaling appears to contribute to the failure of axon regeneration after spinal cord injury. Our preliminary work suggests that in addition to being repelled, axons display increased growth to Wnt5. This is surprisingly different to the "collapse and stall" response of axons to other repulsive guidance molecules. We hypothesize that different repulsive cues have different effects on axons. The experiments in this proposal will test this hypothesis. Specifically, I will 1) examine the dynamics of the repulsive response of Drl-expressing axons to Wnt5, 2) understand how Wnt5 simultaneously repels and increases the growth of axons, and 3) compare these responses to those of other repulsive molecules that appear to induce collapse. The studies in this project will provide new insight into how nerve cells become properly wired during development, as well as provide a better understanding of axon regeneration potential after spinal cord injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the Mechanism of Surface Lipoprotein Translocation in Gram Negative Bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: LIPOPROTEIN SECRETION; NEISSERIA MENINGITIDIS; PROTEIN CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; PROTEIN TRANSLOCATION
Abstract-Résumé: Health practitioners throughout the world are fighting a losing battle against multi-drug resistant strains of bacteria that are the leading cause of hospital-acquired infections. We are investigating proteins that are anchored onto cell surface of these bacteria via a lipid - thus called a "lipoprotein". These lipoproteins have essential roles in acquiring nutrients and evading the host's immune system.  Since these mechanisms are required for the bacteria to survive within the host, the lipoproteins have become attractive targets for the development of vaccines and antibiotics. This research program is focused on understanding how lipoproteins are exported to the cell surface of pathogenic bacteria. We will obtain molecular details and delineate the mechanism of lipoprotein export, and explore various ways to inhibit lipoprotein secretion to the cell surface.  Information on the lipoprotein export apparatus will aid in the development of novel antibiotics and vaccines.  Taken together we will help specifically eradicate these pathogenic bacteria and aid in the global crisis of infections caused by multi-drug resistant strains of bacteria.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cortical underpinnings of speech segregation and comprehension in aging: influence of acoustic and knowledge-based cues
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; AUDITORY; COMPREHENSION; NEUROIMAGING; SEGREGATION; SPEECH
Abstract-Résumé: Segregating a target voice from concurrent sounds in a «cocktail party» environment is one of the most complex operations performed by the auditory system. Older adults very often report difficulties understanding speech in such challenging situations and this can enhance their experienced level of social handicap. Although age-related changes in hearing sensitivity clearly affect speech comprehension, impairments in the ability to segregate and identify a target sound are also associated with age-related changes at the central, or cortical, level. In challenging auditory situations, listeners can rely on various cues to improve their ability to segregate and understand speech sounds. For instance, listeners can more easily separate sounds at different frequencies (acoustic cue) or sounds with which they are familiar (knowledge-based, non-acoustic, cue). The proposed project includes both behavioral and neuroimaging experiments designed to investigate how acoustic and non-acoustic cues improve speech segregation and comprehension in younger and older listeners. Listeners will be asked to segregate and identify a target voice presented concurrently with a masker voice. The acoustic (i.e., fundamental frequency) and non-acoustic (i.e., familiarity) properties of the target voice will be independently manipulated. This project will explore how these different, very common cues improve speech segregability and how this is reflected within the cortical network subserving auditory and speech perception. This project will be the first investigation of how acoustic cues interact with knowledge-based cues to improve speech segregation and comprehension in younger and older adults. This research question is particularly relevant in aging considering the negative consequences of impaired communication in social situations on older listeners.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms and optimisation of marrow stimulated cartilage repair
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; BIOMATERIALS; BONE-MARROW STIMULATION; CARTILAGE REPAIR; GENE DELIVERY; MICROFRACTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Articular cartilage covers the ends of bones in joints and provides lubricating surfaces for painless joint movement. Cartilage lesions can develop from trauma or other predisposing conditions and progress to arthritis where cartilage is destroyed. Cartilage lesions are difficult to treat before joint destruction occurs. One method to treat them is practiced by orthopaedic surgeons where they pierce the bone underneath the cartilage to induce a healing response. Very little is known about how healing occurs in these procedures or what determines successful healing versus failure. Our studies examine the parameters that can influence repair in order to design procedures that maximise successful regeneration of articular cartilage.  We will be studying the way specific surgical techniques influence the success of cartilage repair procedures and how the implantation of biomaterials on top of a surgically prepared cartilage lesion can further improve outcome. Potential outcomes include novel surgical instrumentation and new biomaterials to aid the regeneration of articular cartilage and reduce the development of arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multidrug Resistance in the Developing Blood Brain Barrier: Fetal Brain Protection
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER RESISTANCE PROTEIN (BCRP); CYTOKINES; DRUG THERAPY; EPIGENETICS; FETAL BLOOD-BRAIN-BARRIER; GLUCOCORTICOIDS; MULTIDRUG RESISTANCE; P-GLYCOPROTEIN (P-GP); PREGNANCY; SELECTIVE SEROTONIN REUPTAKE INHIBITOR (SSRI)
Abstract-Résumé: P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and Breast Cancer Resistance Protein (BCRP) were first discovered in drug resistant cancer cells. More recently, P-gp and BCRP have been discovered in normal cells of the blood-brain-barrier. Here, P-gp and BCRP act to prevent passage of xenobiotics from the blood into the brain. These multidrug resistance pumps are unique in that they can exclude a wide range of compounds, including anticancer drugs, HIV protease inhibitors, cardiac glycosides, antibiotics, herbicides and pesticides. In addition to excluding drugs, P-gp and BCRP can also exclude a number of steroids, suggestive of an important role in normal physiology. We have shown that high levels of P-gp and BCRP are located in microvessels of the fetal brain, which constitute the primary blood-brain-barrier. Here, they actively prevent xenobiotics and some hormones from entering the brain. The fetal brain is extremely susceptible to the teratogenic effects of several substances found in the environment and therefore the maternal circulation (i.e. pesticides and herbicides) as well as drugs administered to the mother in pregnancy (including anticancer drugs and steroids).  While the blood-brain-barrier is developed early in fetal life and P-gp and BCRP have been localized to endothelial cells of the brain vasculature, little is known about their regulation at the fetal blood-brain-barrier. This is clearly important as alterations in P-gp and BCRP mediated efflux will have significant effects on transfer of xenobiotics into the fetal brain. A large number of these substances adversely affect the developing brain. This project is designed to determine the function and regulation of the multidrug resistance genes and their products, P-gp and BCRP in the fetal blood-brain-barrier. Understanding the role and regulation of P-gp and BCRP during normal development and disease will enable us to begin to develop therapeutic strategies focused towards optimizing brain health in the fetus and infant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Membrane and submembrane targeting of lipid-modified proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; EPITHELIAL CELLS; LIPID-MODIFIED PROTEINS; MEMBRANE MICRODOMAINS; MEMBRANE ORGANIZATION; MEMBRANE TRAFFICKING; PROTEIN-MEMBRANE INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The proper functioning of many cellular proteins depends on their proper localization within the cell, which may include their controlled movement between multiple cellular locations (a process termed "trafficking"). Our research seeks to understand how cells control the localization and trafficking of a broad and diverse group of cellular proteins known as glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored proteins ("GPI-proteins"). These proteins play important biological roles, ranging from control of immune reactions to cellular uptake of nutrients like folic acid. They also serve as targets for several important bacterial toxins, including Clostridium and Pseudomonas toxins, and other pathogenic agents. Both the physiological and pathological functions of GPI-proteins are intimately linked to their location and their trafficking within cells.  This project will investigate how GPI-proteins are localized and trafficked in cells that form the lining of tissues like the intestines and the urinary system, which are "front-line" sites for uptake of nutrients, excretion of materials and defense against infections. By understanding how cells control the locations and intracellular movements of these proteins, we can identify novel therapeutic possibilities to treat diseases in which GPI-protein functions are compromised by mutations or subverted by infectious organisms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Natural history and treatment of insomnia
Keywords-MotsClés: BURDEN; COMORBIDITY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; INCIDENCE; INSOMNIA; LONGITUDINAL; NATURAL HISTORY; REMISSION; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Insomnia is a very frequent health complaint in the general population and among patients with medical and psychiatric conditions. Chronic difficulties initiating and maintaining sleep are often associated with significant psychosocial and occupational impairments such as daytime fatigue, mood disturbances, performance impairments, more frequent absences from work, and reduced quality of life. The financial costs associated with having insomnia is also very elevated, both at the individual and societal levels. For many individuals, this problem occurs nightly and can last for many years. Yet, only a small percentage of individuals with insomnia seek professional advice and treatment for their difficulties. The reasons for this remain unknown and, although many factors associated with insomnia have been identified, little is known about its causes or about the factors associated with its persistence or remission. Moreover, although chronic insomnia has been linked to psychological and physical health problems, such as depression and hypertension, for example, the long-term consequences of chronic insomnia are still poorly understood. What are the risk factors for developing insomnia? How long does it last if it remains untreated? What are the factors associated with its remission? What are some of the reasons which motivate help-seeking? These are some of the questions this longitudinal study will examine by monitoring the sleep patterns and the psychological and health characteristics of nearly 4000 adults over a 10-year period. This study is likely to yield new information to improve our understanding of the natural course, risk factors, and consequences of insomnia, which may lead to the development of more effective intervention and prevention programs for this important public health problem.

TitreApplicationTitle: Use of laboratory and diary methods to clarify the link between social anxiety and risk for university student problematic drinking
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE PROCESSES; DRINKING MOTIVES; ECOLOGICAL MOMENTARY ASSESSMENT; MEDIATED MODERATION; MOOD MANIPULATION; MULTILEVEL MODELING; MULTIMETHOD; SOCIAL ANXIETY; UNIVERSITY PROBLEMATIC DRINKING
Abstract-Résumé: More than one-third of university students in Canada drink at harmful levels. This behaviour is a major public health concern because of the costs to individuals and society, such as unplanned sex when drinking and drunk driving accidents. The development of effective prevention programs need to be based on an understanding of why students drink so heavily. Despite the typical image of a "party animal", students who are socially anxious and experience extreme discomfort in social situations may also be at risk for heavy drinking. At university, alcohol use often occurs at social events, like parties, which cause great distress for some students. As a way to tolerate these difficult social situations, socially anxious students may be inclined to drink heavily, since alcohol has beneficial tension relief effects. Conversely, social anxiety could protect students against heavy drinking because students may worry that they will embarrass themselves if they are intoxicated. In light of inconsistent findings about the association between social anxiety and alcohol use, the proposed research aims to determine the role of social anxiety as a risk factor for problem drinking in university students. Factors that affect social anxiety and lead to attitudes (alcohol has positive effects) and motives (alcohol helps me cope) that support drinking will be evaluated. Two studies are proposed. First, in a realistic 'bar-lab' setting, students' moods will be modified and real-time effects on alcohol attitudes will be examined. Second, students will use cell phones to report real-time information while drinking, including motives for drinking. This research will help clarify the mixed findings in the literature. The findings will sustain key stakeholders on campus to better develop comprehensive university prevention programs/campaigns. Further, this work may have important clinical implications by identifying specific targets (e.g., attitudes and motives) for clinical intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Molecular and Mechanistic Investigation into the Benefits of  Breastfeeding in Women's Health
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; BREASTFEEDING; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: While it is known that breastfeeding is beneficial to the newborn, the contribution of breastfeeding/lactation to women's health is less acknowledged and has been largely ignored. Epidemiological studies have suggested that extended periods of breastfeeding/lactation produce protective effects to the mother against breast cancer independent of age, menopausal status or ethnic origin. It is also suggested that women in developed countries who in general have no or short lifetime duration of breastfeeding makes a major contribution to the high incidence of breast cancer in these countries. Therefore, it is essential to define at the molecular level how breastfeeding produce these protective effects against breast cancer. Unravelling the role of the lactation hormone prolactin (PRL) is the focus of our research program and this application. PRL is a primary factor required for mammary gland growth leading to induction and maintenance of lactation. We have made several important contributions in molecular cloning of the PRL receptor and characterizing downstream signaling mechanisms. Moreover, we have recently provided a new concept in PRL regulation of breast carcinogenesis. Most interestingly, our results indicate that PRL regulates plasticity of breast cancer cells leading to suppression in their invasive capacity (Cancer Research, 2006) and that mammary cells exposed to PRL become resistant to the proliferative effects of EGF, a factor implicated in mammary carcinogenesis (Molecular and Cellular Biology, 2009). In this proposal we plan to determine the role of PRL target genes in mammary epithelial differentiation and study their role in suppression of breast carcinogenesis. Such information will significantly accelerate progress into how breastfeeding/lactation may provide protective effects against breast cancer and will help in applying interventions to improve women's health and reduce breast cancer incidence and mortality.
