TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting the Integrin-Linked Kinase Pathway in Rhabdomyosarcoma
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMORADIOSENSITIVITY; INTEGRIN-LINKED KINASE; MASS SPECTROSCOPY; ONCOGENE; RHABDOMYOSOSARCOMA; SIRNA; SMALL MOLECULE INHIBITORS; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENE
Abstract-Résumé: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common soft tissue tumor of children. It is classified into embryonal (ERMS) and alveolar (ARMS) subtypes, based on appearance under the microscope. While research has led to a greater basic understanding of how RMS tumors grow, the survival of patients with metastatic disease is less than 20%. We are exploring a new target, termed integrin-linked kinase (ILK), which we believe is involved in RMS tumor growth, with the hopes of identifying a treatment which eventually will be used clinically to improve survival.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of IgE/FceRI pathway in Airway Smooth Muscle Function in Allergic Asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY REMODELING; AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; ASTHMA; FCEPSILON RECEPTOR; IGE; INFLAMMATION; REAL-TIME PCR; SHRNA; SYK; THYMIC STROMAL LYMPHOPOIETIN; TSLP RECEEPTOR KNOCK OUT
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is chronic inflammation of airways which is widespread worldwide. Asthma is the most common chronic disease among children and it currently affects 300 million people worldwide with 250,000 annual deaths attributed to the disease. It is also estimated that there may be an additional 100 million more asthmatics by 2025. About 12% of Canadian children and 8% of the population aged 12 or older have been diagnosed with asthma. Because of economical and social issues associated with asthma, understanding the mechanisms involved in this disease is necessary to develop effective strategies to fight it.  It has been shown that protein called, immunoglobulin-E, plays an important role in allergic asthma. However, its effect on airway smooth muscle cell has not been clearly understood. In this project, we want to study the role of immunoglobulin E in modulating airway smooth muscle cell function. Determining the functional outcome of immunoglobulinE in airway smooth muscle cells and signaling pathway(s) behind it, will pave the way to fully understand the role of this molecule in the pathogenesis of asthma and better therapeutic design in the near future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Calcium signaling in astrocytes in neurovascular control
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTE; BRAIN SLICE; CALCIUM IMAGING; CALCIUM UNCAGING; CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW; NITRIC OXIDE; TWO PHOTON LASER SCANNING MICROSCOPY; VASCULATURE
Abstract-Résumé: There has been a revolution in our understanding of the regulation of both brain function and cerebral blood flow. Over the past 10 years it is clear that astrocytes, the support cell of the brain that outnumber neurons, can modify neuronal activity and directly alter blood flow through cerebral blood vessels. The maintenance of cerebral blood flow at levels to match the metabolic demands of the brain is critical for a healthy brain. Inappropriate decreases in cerebral blood flow can lead to dementia and in severe cases neuronal damage. Work from the previous grant has shown the mechanisms by which astrocytes modulate cerebral blood vessels. Under conditions of increased metabolic demand and lower oxygen astrocytes causes arteriole dilations.  In contrast when brain tissue is well oxygenated constrictions are triggered. The work in this grant will investigate the mechanisms in addition to metabolism that control whether astrocytes cause constrictions or dilations.  Understanding these mechanisms may provide therapeutic avenues to prevent pathological changes in cerebral blood flow.

TitreApplicationTitle: L'analyse spectrale des enregistrements intracrâniens dans l'exploration des réseaux fonctionnels cérébraux chez l'enfant épileptique
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYSE SPECTRALE; DEVELOPPEMENT COGNITIF; ENREGISTREMENTS INTRACRANIENS; MEMOIRE; NEUROANATOMIE; NEUROPHYSIOLOGIE; PLASTICITE CEREBRALE; POTENTIELS EVOQUES; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGIE; EPILEPSIE
Abstract-Résumé: La neurochirurgie est le traitement de choix contre l'epilepsie lorsque la medication anticonvulsive n'est pas efficace. Une telle operation requiert une evaluation rigoureuse afin d'identifier la source cerebrale des crises et de s'assurer que sa resection n'entrainera pas de deficits (ex. langage, memoire). Cette evaluation peut necessiter des enregistrements de l'activite electrique du cerveau a l'aide d'electrodes intracerebrales (iEEG) pour definir la zone epileptogene. Des etudes recentes menees aupres d'adultes demontrent que l'iEEG peut aussi etre utilise pour localiser les regions cerebrales impliquees dans des fonctions comme la memoire et le langage, a l'aide d'analyses des types d'activite enregistree. Toutefois, aucune etude n'a utilise cette technique pour localiser ces fonctions chez l'enfant. Or, l'immaturite cerebrale de l'enfant permet une certaine reorganisation des fonctions du cerveau lorsqu'une region est affectee, modifiant l'architecture fonctionnelle typique. La localisation pre-chirurgicale des fonctions cerebrales est donc d'autant plus importante dans cette population. Nous proposons d'utiliser l'analyse de l'activite iEEG chez des enfants epileptiques candidats a la neurochirurgie (N = 20; 3 a 18 ans) pour etudier les substrats neuro-anatomiques de fonctions cognitives chez ces enfants. Pendant les enregistrements iEEG, l'enfant sera evalue a l'aide de taches sollicitant differentes fonctions cognitives. Des analyses permettront d'identifier les regions cerebrales activees pendant chaque type de tache. Cette etude permettra d'etablir l'applicabilite de l'analyse de l'iEEG pour localiser les fonctions cognitives chez l'enfant, une technique ayant un grand potentiel d'application clinique dans la prediction des impacts fonctionnels de la neurochirurgie. L'etude permettra de documenter la localisation de diverses fonctions cognitives avec precision et d'en examiner les differences selon l'age et la localisation du foyer epileptique.

TitreApplicationTitle: The socio-cultural and structural context of mobility and HIV risk among female sex workers
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV/AIDS; MIGRATION; MIXED METHODS; POPULATION MOBILITY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; RISK ENVIRONMENT; SEX WORK; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS; SOCIAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Globally and in Canada, women in the sex industry experience unacceptably high rates of HIV, sexually transmitted infections (STI), and violence. Population mobility has been implicated as a key determinant of HIV transmission in Asia and Africa; however, its role in the Americas is poorly understood. Women seeking a better livelihood often migrate to improve their economic situation. Though some intentionally migrate for sex work, many engage in sex work to meet subsistence or remittance needs, while others are trafficked. While most research suggests that mobility may increase the risk of HIV/STI infection and poses barriers to accessing health services, mobility may also offer an avenue for mitigating risk. However, few studies have explicitly studied how different forms of mobility (e.g., international migration; rural-urban mobility) may have differential impacts on HIV/STI vulnerability. This project will explore how mobility may have dynamic roles in shaping HIV risk among women in the sex trade in two distinct settings: Vancouver, BC, where the risks associated with mobility are shaped by the city's large, concentrated illicit drug scene, heavy policing, and violence; and the Mexico-Guatemala border city of Ciudad Hidalgo, Mexico, where undocumented migration, exploitation of migrants by authorities, and abuse of sex workers' rights are commonplace. This fellowship will be nested in two larger studies in Vancouver and Cd. Hidalgo.  I will use fieldwork, interviews, and statistical analyses of survey data to investigate the prevalence and context of mobility, migration, and trafficking among women and youth in the sex industry in Vancouver and Cd. Hidalgo. This fellowship will provide training in HIV prevention among vulnerable women, and will equip me with the skills and experience to emerge as an independent investigator with a focus on mobility and HIV, which is a pressing public health issue in Canada and internationally.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the role of Musashi 2 (Msi2) in neural stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHEMOKINES/CYTOKINES; CHEMOTHERAPY; HOST-RESPONSE; PLATELETS; STROMAL CELL-DERIVED FACTOR-1 (SDF-1); TARGETED THERAPY; TUMOUR ANGIOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Despite major advances in basic cancer research the treatment of cancer particularly advanced metastatic disease remains a formidable challenge. This is partly due to the fact that although treatment of many types of cancer with conventional chemotherapy regimens often results in partial or complete tumour shrinkage, this is almost always followed by rapid tumour regrowth. In this regard, studies from our laboratory have been particularly relevant.  For example, we have shown that the overall anti-tumour impact of certain commonly used anti-cancer drugs is accompanied by a rapid reaction and systemic host response that acts to reduce anti-tumour effects.  This response includes induction of a number of tumour growth promoting factors and circulating bone marrow-derived cell populations, in such a way as to increase the tumour's ability to 'recover' more quickly from the anti-cancer therapy.  Objectives of the Research Proposal: The overall aim of my research is to identify the mechanisms involved in this 'counter-active' host response leading to accelerated tumour regrowth, such that we can develop better ways to enhance the impact of anti-cancer treatments.  Brief Description of the Research Proposal: With respect to the growth factors that are induced by chemotherapy, we are studying the sources of such factors, e.g. what cells are responsible for rapidly releasing these factors when exposed to chemotherapy drugs. In order to accomplish this, we will use preclinical models in conjunction with the same chemotherapy drugs used to treat cancer patients.  We will monitor the effects of these anti-cancer agents in the models and employ treatment strategies to enhance their anti-cancer effect while reducing the negative 'counter-acting' response. These approaches will include reducing the doses of chemotherapy drug administered and combining conventional chemotherapy with drugs that target the growing tumours blood vessel supply.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Oxidative / Nitrosative Stress and Aging on Cholinergic Neuron Function
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYLOID PEPTIDE; BRAIN AGING; NEUROTRANSMISSION; OXIDATIVE - NITROSATIVE STRESS; PROTEIN MODIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed studies investigate changes that occur in nerve cells due to chemical alterations in the aging brain caused by neurodegeneration, hypertension, blood vessel disease that leads to decreased oxygen and blood flow, or due to stroke. A consequence of these pathological changes is inability of nerve cells to effectively communicate information to fulfill their physiological functions. Cholinergic nerves in brain are particularly susceptible to damage by these pathological conditions, and dysfunction of these nerves can lead to memory loss, dementia, changes in control of blood vessels and blood flow. This could arise if cholinergic neurons are vulnerable to changes in the brain microenvironment that are increased during aging. To illustrate this, amyloid peptide levels increase before cognitive deficits begin and are likely responsible for at least some of the oxidative stress that occurs very early in mild cognitive impariment or in AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Skeletal muscle endurance and wasting in COPD
Keywords-MotsClés: CACHEXIA; COPD; DIAPHRAGM; EMPHYSEMA; EXERCISE; MUSCLE BIOPSY; QUADRICEPS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common problem and it includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema. The most important risk factor for COPD is tobacco smoking. COPD originates within the lung but eventually, in the course of the disease, it affects other organs such as the muscles of respiration and of the limbs. This is important because muscle impairment in this disease is associated with poor quality of life, exercise intolerance and even premature mortality. This research proposal is intended to study why patients with COPD are susceptible to the development of muscle fatigue during physical activities. We will also study the mechanisms that are responsible for the progressive  loss in muscle mass that is often seen in COPD. This human research program involves obtaining biopsy of the quadriceps in patients with COPD and in healthy controls in order to identify the abnormalities responsible for the loss of muscle mass in COPD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Statistical Methods for Multiple Event Processes: Application to Emergency Department and Physician Visits for Pediatric Mental Health Care
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATABASES; BIOSTATISTICAL METHODS; CHILD AND YOUTH; EMERGENCY SERVICES; MARKED POINT PROCESSES; MENTAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: While 1.2 million Canadian children and youth live with a mental illness, only 1 in 6 receives necessary health services. Without formal mental health care, children and youth are vulnerable to illness deterioration that can escalate to crises involving aggressive or life-threatening behaviours and emotional distress. For acute crises, there are limited immediate unscheduled mental health care options. On any given day, Emergency Departments (EDs) are a key service point for families hoping to access care, and are considered a 'safety net' in response to the lack of inpatient and outpatient services.  To create health care improvements, a better understanding of the nature of ED visits for pediatric mental health issues is needed. Canada's public health system provides an opportunity to examine a variety of health care services through administrative data sets. Using different data sources, we can get a comprehensive picture of patient needs, if the statistical and computational techniques exist to turn these data into usable information for stakeholders. In this project, we will develop new statistical analysis methods. We will apply these new methods to Alberta administrative data sets on children and youth presenting for mental health care between April 2002 and March 2008. We will invent new methods, called multivariate marked point processes, that will allow us to combine data in a novel and more accurate way. Estimates from the methods will quantify the extent and direction of the relationships between ED visits and physician visits in non-ED settings. In addition, we will conduct extensive simulation studies (computer experiments) to investigate the properties of our new methods. With our results, we will be able to inform health services planning and ultimately help improve the care of children and youth with mental health concerns. In addition, our methods will be more widely applicable for researchers modeling different illness processes.

Abstract-Résumé: La pauvrete represente l'un des plus grands risques pour la sante. Les systemes de soins et les professionnels de la sante rencontrent des defis importants et sont appeles a ameliorer l'equite dans les soins. Peu d'etudes impliquent la participation des usagers en situation de pauvrete, en collaboration avec l'equipe de soins. Cette etude vise a comprendre comment les equipes interprofessionnelles peuvent mieux repondre aux besoins des personnes confrontees a la pauvrete.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of mast cells in early immunity to viral infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGY; CHEMOKINES; DENDRITIC CELLS; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; MAST CELLS; NK CELLS; VIRAL INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Mast cells are an immune cell type found throughout the body and particularly common at sites of potential infection such as the airways, skin and intestine. Most mast cell research has focused on their important role in allergic disease. However, they also help to fight infection. In the current proposal we are seeking to better understand how mast cells might help us to fight virus infections. This area has not been widely studied previously and our recent research suggests it is very important. For these studies we will be doing experiments using two virus models. The first, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common infection of the airways which is a major cause of hospital admissions in young children and to which our immune response is thought to often be inadequate. The second is reovirus a common infection to which we develop a very vigorous and effective immune response. This virus is being used in new cancer therapies.  We propose to examine the importance of mast cells in producing anti-viral substances and helping the body recruit natural killer cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells at the sites of early viral infection. Natural killer cells  have the ability to directly kill virally infected cells, even very early in infection. Plasmacytoid dendritic cell responses are important since these cells produce large amounts of proteins, known as interferons, which can protect neighbouring cells from viral infection. Overall, these studies will greatly increase our understanding of the importance of mast cells in viral infection. An increased understanding of these processes will allow us to develop strategies to modify mast cell function appropriately to enhance effective anti-viral responses

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of neurogenesis by Cux factors and their interacting proteins.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT NEUROGENESIS; CELL FATE; CUX2; DIFFERENTIATION; HIPPOCAMPUS; LATERAL VENTRICLE; NEURAL PROGENITORS; PROTEOMICS; SUBVENTRICULAR ZONE; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, Multiple Sclerosis, and Amyotropic Lateral Sclerosis, along with brain injury are devastating conditions that are associated with the decline of the brain function. Due to our aging population, the frequency of these illnesses is rapidly increasing in Canada. We have very limited treatment options for these conditions, thus there is an urgent need to develop new therapeutics to overcome neurodegeneration. A common feature of neurodegenerative diseases is the severe loss of neurons in affected individuals. One exciting avenue for therapeutics is to stimulate the brain to make new neurons to replace those lost to injury or illness. The adult brain has considerable plasticity and continually generates neurons from neural stem cells in two principal regions: the hippocampus, and the subventricular zone, which supplies neurons to the olfactory region. If we wish to use the brain's endogenous ability to make new neurons, we must first seek to understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms that regulate the formation of new neurons. To that end I have identified a group of regulatory proteins called Cux factors that are expressed in neural stem cells of the embryonic and postnatal brain. It is currently unclear whether these proteins play a role in regulating the formation of neurons in the postnatal brain. Thus a primary objective of this proposal to explore the roles of Cux genes in the formation of neurons in the adult brain using mice that have been engineered to lack these proteins. I have also identified a network of proteins that interact with Cux factors and will examine their roles in the formation of neurons. The goal of the research described in this proposal is to understand how the formation of new neurons in the adult brain is regulated by these Cux factors. This in turn will lead to ways in which we can stimulate neuronal repair in diseased and injured brains.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of netrin-1 in the organization and function of dopamine circuitry
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; NEURAL DEVELOPMENT; NEURAL PLASTICITY; NEUROANATOMY; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Abnormal functioning of the brain dopamine (DA) system causes or contributes to the symptomatology of schizophrenia and related disorders. Studies conducted in humans and in laboratory animals suggest that this DA dysfunction results from disruptions in normal brain development caused by exposure to complications during the perinatal period and/or genetic predisposition. The aim of my research is to identify how such disruptions of the normal course of brain development bring about dysfunction of DA and DA-mediated behaviors in the adult. Recently, I have shown that netrins, a family of guidance cues that organize neuronal connectivity during development, are implicated in the development and function of DA systems. I propose to conduct molecular, neuroanatomical, electrophysiological and behavioral experiments to address the hypothesis that disruption in brain development leads to abnormal DA function and DA-related behaviors in the adult by altering the function of netrins. These alterations, in turn, induce 'rewiring' of the DA circuitry, rendering the brain more prone to disease. The proposed work could potentially define a causal link between exposure to adverse events early in life and psychopathology. Therefore they will have important implications for prevention and therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroprotection in models of retinal ganglion cell death
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG DEVELOPMENT; GLAUCOMA; IN VIVO MODELS OF DISEASE; NEUROPROTECTION; NEUROTOXICITY; NEUROTROPHIN; RECEPTOR; RETINA; TARGET VALIDATION
Abstract-Résumé: Glaucoma is defined as a special form of death of specialized neurons in the retina, called retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). Glaucoma is often associated with high pressure in the eye. The RGCs die in a progressive manner. These neurons transmit visual signals to the brain, and therefore their death results in progressive blindness.  The only approved pharmacological therapy is to reduce the high intraocular pressure. However, this treatment often fails to stop the disease from progressing. Moreover, there are a significant number of glaucoma cases with no increased pressure in the eye. Hence, there is a significant medical need to improve therapy. We have studied the mechanisms by which RGCs die during stress in the retina. We have learned that there are at least two paths for neuronal death: the loss of the factors that provide protection to neurons, and an increase in the factors that cause toxicity. We will utilize pharmacological tools to promote protective signals; and to block the toxic signals. Together these approaches could result in the prevention of the neuronal death that leads to blindness. This work may yield a rationalization towards the therapy of diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and characterization of novel substrates of the mammalian target of rapamaycin complex 1 (mTORC1).
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL PROLIFERATION AND GROWTH; MAMMALIAN TARGET OF RAPAMYCIN; MASS SPECTROMETRY; METABOLISM; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: The activity of the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) is frequently dysregulated in human diseases characterized by abnormal metabolism and proliferation such as diabetes, cancer and heart disease. Accordingly, compounds modulating the activity of mTORC1 hold great promise for treatments of these diseases. In recent years several of the factors, which mediate the activity of mTORC1 on cellular processes have been uncovered. Notwithstanding these recent advances in the understanding of the mTORC1 pathway, many of the cellular effects of mTORC1 cannot be accounted for by the actions of its known substrates. Thus, to better apprehend the intricate molecular mechanisms underlying the actions of mTORC1, in this proposal we will set out to uncover unknown substrates of mTORC1. To achieve this we will deploy a strategy in which the standard biochemistry and molecular biology techniques will be combined with mass spectrometry. We will further assess how these factors mediate the effects of mTORC1 signaling in normal versus cancer cells using the standard cell and molecular biology and biochemistry techniques. These findings should improve our knowledge of how are mTORC1 signals relayed to cellular processes, which in long-term should open new therapeutic avenues to curb dysregulated mTORC1 signaling in cancer and other human diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Population-based Study of Cancer Incidence and Mortality in Patients with Solid Organ Transplants
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER INCIDENCE; CANCER OUTCOMES; CANCER TREATMENT; IMMUNOSUPPRESSION; NON-RANDOMIZED DESIGN; POPULATION-BASED DATA; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Solid organ transplantation is life-saving for patients with organ failure. However, transplant patients are known to be at a higher risk of developing cancer because their immune system needs to be suppressed. This study will use information from the CORR registry - a registry of all patients having a solid organ transplant in Ontario linked to information from the Ontario Cancer Registry, a registry of people developing cancer in Ontario. We are interested in evaluating if transplant patients develop cancer over time, if some cancers occur more frequently, and in patients who develop cancer, if the outcomes of these patients are worse than non-transplant patients. Very little is known about how cancer is treated in transplant patients and we will perform a review of the medical charts of 600 transplant patients with cancer and 600 non-transplant patients with cancer (control patients) to help determine if there are differences in how cancer is detected and/or treated in transplant vs. control patients. If we identify differences that have an impact on survival, we can then develop strategies to improve outcome. For example, if cancer tends to be diagnosed late in transplant patients a greater focus on screening and early detection of cancer would be an important strategy to improve cancer survival in this group of patients. We will gather together experts in the field of cancer care and transplantation as well as groups representing transplant and cancer patients. These individuals and organizations have input into our study so that the results of our research are maximally useful and have an impact.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analyzing the significance of policies that restrict men who have sex with men (MSM) as eligible donors of human biological materials for transplantation and assisted reproduction
Keywords-MotsClés: AND CELL DONATION; BIOETHICS; HEALTH POLICY; LGBT COMMUNITY; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; ORGAN; POLICY DEVELOPMENT; PUBLIC HEALTH; QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS; SOCIAL JUSTICE; STIGMATIZATION; TISSUE
Abstract-Résumé: Biomedical innovation has made human organs, tissues, and cells valuable tools in treating a variety of diseases, ranging from cancer to infertility. However, as human biological materials grow in medical importance, the supply of many of these materials remains severely limited, making donor eligibility criteria an important issue for analysis and debate. This post-doctoral project will analyze North American policies that ban all sexually active gay and bisexual men from being eligible donors of human biological materials for transplantation and assisted reproduction. Analysis will centre on issues of social justice and stigmatization in public health policy development. While MSM donor bans have created much media attention in the past, to date, few academic publications have analyzed the political and ethical legitimacy, or the social and public health ramifications of these regulations. The proposed post-doctoral project aims to remedy this deficiency in academic knowledge. This project will involve an ethics and policy analysis of regulatory documents. Critiques and assessment of these regulations will develop from a literature review of biomedical publications concerning organ and tissue transplantation, transmission and screening methods for viral pathogens, and biomedical application of human materials in medicine and research. The final aim of this research is to provide a knowledge foundation to draft new donor eligibility guidelines that are both ethically sound and best serve the health and well-being of patients in need of a transplant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Small molecule control of the functional dynamics in cardiac potassium channels.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; CARDIAC POTASSIUM CHANNELS; CARDIOTOXICITY; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; MOLECULAR BIOPHYSICS; MOLECULAR MODELING; MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Malfunctioning of membrane proteins, known as potassium channels, is associated with a broad spectrum of cardiac arrhythmias. The exact mechanism that governs arrhythmias and how it is determined by proteins involved is yet to be understood. The focus of the current proposal is on the detailed understanding of molecular mechanisms governing formation of cardiac arrhythmias. The information obtained from theoretical and experimental studies will be used for creation of small-molecules that can restore normal function of the channel directly involved in the formation of a clinical condition known as long QT syndrome II type (LQTS-2). Another dimension of the submitted proposal is on the evaluation of cardiotoxicity of novel and existing drugs. A combined strategy to optimize drug-like compounds by targeted chemical synthesis has been developed by our group in the last three years of studies. The current submission proposes to extend this strategy to a broad range of drugs that are currently removed from the market because of their cardiotoxic and arrhythmogenic properties.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of Metacognition in Bipolar Disorder and its Association with Functional Outcome and Quality of Life
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; COGNITION; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; FUNCTIONAL OUTCOME; MEMORY; METACOGNITION; NEUROCOGNITION; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing understanding of the specific cognitive impairments that affect patients with bipolar disorder is critical as these difficulties are likely to identify patients who show poorer everyday functioning and quality of life. Knowledge of these core cognitive deficits can also facilitate development of treatments that improve these specific impairments as well as overall patient functioning and quality of life. To date, research in bipolar disorder has determined that many patients show difficulties in traditional cognitive abilities such as attention, memory, and executive functioning. One thing that all these skills have in common is that they evaluate how well an individual is able to process external information about the world (e.g. words, stories, pictures, etc.). In contrast, the field of metacognition involves the study of a person's ability to reflect on their internal world, namely their own thinking skills. Thus, whereas traditional skills measure a person's performance on a task, metacognitive tasks measure a person's ability to evaluate their own cognitive skills and performance. Despite the fact that metacognitive deficits are strongly implicated in bipolar disorder, such methodologies have not been integrated into bipolar research. The goal of the present research is to investigate whether patients with bipolar disorder show abnormalities in metacognition characterized by poor awareness of their own cognitive performance. A secondary goal is to assess whether these metacognitive abnormalities predict poorer everyday function and quality of life in patients. Finding such a connection would be important because it would 1) alert clinicians to assess an important symptom in patients with bipolar disorder, and 2) provide new direction for development of novel treatments that target the metacognitive abnormalities and also improve daily functioning and patient quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Thrombospondin-1 as a potent anti-tumor and anti-angiogenic factor in ovarian cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ANIMAL MODEL OF OVARIAN CANCER; ANTI-ANGIOGENIC THERAPY; CHEMOTHERAPY; OVARIAN CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Epithelial ovarian cancer is the most lethal gynecologic cancer in women. In order for ovarian tumors to grow, they must recruit new blood vessels through a process called angiogenesis. We have shown previously that an effective treatment against ovarian tumor development is to inhibit this new blood vessel formation. Thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) is a potent inhibitor of ovarian tumor vessel growth and slows growth of new tumors and can cause regression of established disease. In addition to preventing blood vessel growth, TSP-1 also directly kills tumor cells, while leaving healthy cells intact. We plan to evaluate the ability of TSP-1 treatment to synergize with, and increase the effectiveness of chemotherapy drug treatmet. In this application, we propose to increase the effectiveness of TSP-1 mediated therapy in ovarian cancer and to devise novel therapeutic approaches that may significantly improve our ability to treat this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory role of NK cells in the hepatic innate immune response
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE TRANSFER; CHEMOKINE RECEPTORS; CHEMOKINES; CYTOKINES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HEPATITIS; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY; NK CELLS; NKT CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The innate immune system is the first line of defence our bodies have against many infections and cancers. The innate immune system responds quickly, and its' classical job is to destroy infected or cancerous cells. More recently it has become apparent that the innate immune system may also play a significant role in regulating inflammation and the development of autoimmune diseases. Natural killer (NK) cells are an important component of the innate immune system and they are enriched within the normal liver. NK cells accumulate significantly within the liver during activation of the hepatic innate immune response, which often occurs in the setting of liver inflammation and liver autoimmunity. Although we know that NK cells are rapidly recruited to, and activated within the liver in response to many pathological insults, the mechanism driving their recruitment and accumulation within the liver during an innate immune response is poorly understood. Furthermore, it is becoming increasing clear that different types of NK cells exist, and some of these NK cell types may actually suppress liver inflammation and help the liver recover from damage which has occurred in response to an inflammatory insult. Therefore, the series of experiments outlined in this proposal will help us to establish a better understanding of the mechanisms which lead to the hepatic accumulation and activation of NK cells, as well as determine the regulatory roles played by NK cells in suppressing the hepatic innate immune response. This work may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies, involving the manipulation of hepatic NK cell numbers or subtypes, for the treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory liver diseases. Moreover, these findings may have broader implications for therapeutic approaches to autoimmune diseases in general.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sleep and circadian rhythms in moderate and severe traumatic brain injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIGRAPHY; CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; CRITICAL CARE; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MELATONIN; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; POLYSOMNOGRAPHY; SLEEP; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major public healthcare concern. TBI is the leading cause of mortality in children and young adults in industrial countries and its incidence is higher than the annual diagnosis of breast, lung, prostate, brain, and colon cancer combined. TBI can result in short and long-term cognitive, physical, neurobehavioral and psychological impairments known to interfere with daily living activities and return to work or school. Chronic sleep-wake disturbances, particularly fatigue, hypersomnia, and insomnia, are among the most severe, the most persistent and the most disabling symptoms after TBI. They affect at least 50% of this population and are present across the range of TBI severity. Despite the high prevalence of post-traumatic sleep-wake disturbances and their consequences on quality of life, their emergence and their evolution are still poorly understood. This research program proposes to objectively measure sleep and circadian rhythms in the acute stage after a TBI, to investigate factors contributing to sleep-wake disturbances and the association between acute sleep-wake disturbances and brain recovery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of Translation Initiation Indepedent of Initiator Met-tRNA
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL STRESS; INFECTION; INTERNAL RIBOSOME ENTRY SITE; POLYSOME; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; RIBOSOME; RNA; TRANSLATION; TRNA; VIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Viruses have evolved strategies to infect host cells and disrupt normal cellular functions while hijacking critical host machinery to express viral genes. All viruses proceed through an important stage during their life cycle called translation where viral proteins are expressed from a viral RNA. Some viruses such as poliovirus and Hepatitis C use a translation mechanism called an Internal Ribosome Entry Site or IRES for expressing their proteins. This IRES mechanism is not only important for viruses but also for cellular genes, including those involved in cancer. Therefore, elucidating IRES mechanisms is crucial for understanding a fundamental process of gene expression. Currently, IRES mechanisms are poorly understood. To gain insight, we will characterize the simplest IRES found to date, within the dicistroviridae family. Using biochemical techniques, we will identify how this IRES interacts with and hijacks the host cell's machinery. This IRES is functional in many systems including yeast and human cells, indicating that this unprecedented mechanism is conserved and that specialized cellular genes may also use this mechanism. Using genomic methods, we will identify cellular conditions when this viral IRES mechanism is used, thus revealing situations that are conducive for viral expression. Moreover, using this knowledge, we can search for cellular genes that also use this mechanism for gene expression. This proposal will not only shed light into the biological significance of this novel viral IRES mechanism but also provide a framework for understanding other viral and cellular IRES mechanisms in general.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Pre-conception Cohort to Study Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: Pre-gravid Determinants, Early Pregnancy Bio-markers and Postpartum Cardio-metabolic Risk Factor Profile
Keywords-MotsClés: BIO-MARKERS; CARDIOVASCULAR RISK; CLINICAL RESEARCH; COHORT STUDY; GESTATIONAL DIABETES; PREGNANCY; RISK FACTORS; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Women that develop gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or temporary diabetes in late pregnancy have an increased risk of ultimately developing type 2 diabetes and heart disease later in life. Recently, it has emerged that these women exhibit abnormalities associated with type 2 diabetes and heart disease by as early as 3 months after their pregnancy. These abnormalities or risk factors include resistance of the body to the action of insulin and abnormal levels of certain proteins in the blood. Given their presence by 3 months after delivery, it has been postulated that these factors may exist prior to the pregnancy and hence could provide a means for the early detection of those women who are at risk of developing GDM. To address this question, we propose to recruit a large cohort of women in the Chinese province of Hunan who are planning to become pregnant in the near future. In the women comprising this 'pre-conception cohort', we will measure these factors before, during, and after pregnancy. We will determine whether the presence of these factors either before or in the early stages of pregnancy can identify those women who will go on to develop GDM. We will also determine whether the levels of these factors after delivery are similar to those before the pregnancy or if they are worsened by GDM itself. Ultimately, this study might suggest ways in which healthcare providers can identify high-risk women prior to the development of GDM. Furthermore, the work may lead to ways in which to treat these factors either before or in the early stages of pregnancy and thereby prevent GDM and its associated future complications of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advanced techniques for image assisted cardiac interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: 3D IMAGING; CONE-BEAM CT; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IMAGE GUIDED INTERVENTION; IMAGE REGISTRATION; MINIMALLY INVASIVE THERAPY; PERSONNALIZED INTERVENTIONAL DEVICES; RADIOFREQUENCY ABLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Motivation: Heart rhythm disorders (such as atrial fibrillation) are often treated using procedures that destroy the abnormal heart tissue - radiofrequency (RF) ablation.  RF ablation treatment is usually performed using a catheter that is maneuvered in the left atrium and requires tremendous expertise; procedure times are long - 3 hours or more.  Although the treatment is effective in approximately 65-70% of patients, many must return for repeat procedures because the ablation of the tissues did not completely resolve the rhythm disorder.  Most often this happens because some tissues were not completely ablated and some regions were missed entirely.  The goals of this proposal are to develop techniques that will reduce procedure times and the requirement for repeat ablations.  Proposal: To achieve this we propose to design, fabricate and evaluate a series of ablation-guidance devices that will be made specifically for each patient.  Because the left atrium anatomy varies a lot, the patient's 3D images will be used to design flexible "guide rails" that can be inserted into the left atrium during the procedure; ablation catheters can then be pulled along these guide rails to ensure contact at every position.  Fabrication of these personalized devices is now possible using new 3D "metal printing" technology that can fabricate any shape out of biocompatible materials rapidly - making personalized devices possible.  In addition to the devices, we will develop methods to integrate 3D imaging during the ablation procedure, instead of the currently used 2D x-ray imaging.  All devices and imaging developments will be evaluated experimentally and compared directly with current techniques before they become ready for patient trials.  Significance: When translated into clinical practice, the technical innovations proposed in this grant will lead to improved ablation success rates, reduction of procedure times, and reduced healthcare costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evolution and genetic variation of microRNA regulatory network in humans
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPARATIVE GENOMICS; EVOLUTION; FOXP2; HUMAN GENETICS; MICRORNA; PIGMENTATION; POPULATION GENETICS; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISM
Abstract-Résumé: What makes human different from chimpanzee? Almost all of the phenotypic differences between human and other primates and between human individuals are caused by genetic factors. These genetic factors include differences in protein sequences, the building block of our body, or difference in how genes are regulated, e.g. how much and when and where specific types of protein are made. It is fundamentally important to identify and characterize these genetic factors since they either directly contribute to our "humanness" or cause physiological and morphological differences between human individuals. Such genetic differences between human individuals can often result in difference in disease susceptibility and in response to therapeutic treatments. In this proposal we focus on studying the evolution and genetic variation of one type of genetic regulators: microRNAs. MicroRNAs are a class of small regulatory RNAs that are usually 22 nucleotides long and post-transcriptionally repress their target genes. It is estimated that human genome has 1000 microRNAs and about one-third of the genes are under their regulation. We have identified a list of microRNAs that only arose in the human lineage and are absent in other primates; we will use a combined experimental approach to investigate the genes and biological processes that are regulated by these human-specific microRNAs. We will also apply the same computational and experimental methods on a list of microRNAs who target different genes in different human populations (e.g. Caucasians versus Africans). Such knowledge is very valuable in understanding human genetic variations and in designing and implementation of personalized medicine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tumour suppressor mediated mechanisms of angiogenesis inhibition
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ANGIOGENESIS INHIBITORS; CANCER BIOLOGY; CANCER THERAPEUTICS; P53; TUMOUR SUPPRESSORS
Abstract-Résumé: In order for tumours to become large and life threatening they must first develop a network of blood vessels in order to deliver oxygen and nutrients to cancer cells.  The process of blood vessel formation, called angiogenesis, is an absolutely necessary step in the formation of solid tumours and an ideal point at which novel therapeutic agents can be developed.  Our previous work demonstrated that the natural mechanisms of the human body that prevent cancer do so by inhibiting angiogenesis.  We showed that the p53 tumour suppressor, which is mutated in half of all human cancers, stimulates the production of a natural anti-angiogenic factor called Arresten.  When p53 becomes mutated in tumours, levels of Arresten are decreased and cancer growth accelerates.  In this current application we propose to study the levels of Arresten circulating in the bloodstream of patients with ovarian, breast and prostate cancer.  It is our hope that the development of this form of test can provide a new and powerful tool for the diagnosis of these cancers and possibly indicate when events such as metastasis have occurred.  In addition, we will study the biochemical pathways in human cells by which Arresten is produced in the hopes of learning how production of such factors can be enhanced in the fight against cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploiting KIM-1 signalling to ameliorate acute kidney injury through clearance of apoptotic cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; APOPTOTIC CELL CLEARANCE; CYTOSKELETAL REORGNIZATION; FLOW CYTOMETRY; G PROTEINS; INFLAMMATION; PHAGOCYTOSIS; PROTEIN TYROSINE PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; RENAL ISCHEMIA REPERFUSION INJURY MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Acute kidney injury (AKI) affects about 5-10% of all hospitalized patients and is associated with a mortality rate of over 50% in critically ill patients that require renal replacement therapy (e.g. dialysis). Despite considerable advances in diagnosis and treatment of AKI, mortality rates remain largely unchanged. Severe AKI caused by circulatory collapse or medications that are toxic to the kidney can result in massive death of kidney epithelial cells. The rapid removal of dead cells occurs through a process known as "phagocytosis" that is vital to preventing further inflammation and for hastening tissue repair. Recently, we and other scientists discovered that injured kidney epithelial cells express KIM-1, a gene product that transforms surviving kidney epithelial cells into phagocytes that are able to clear the dead or dying cells from the injured kidney. Emerging experimental evidence suggests that genetically engineered mice lacking the ability to remove dead cells owing to a mutation in the KIM-1 gene are more susceptible to inflammation and kidney dysfunction after AKI. Our research aims to understand the complex cell signalling pathways that govern how KIM-1 enables kidney epithelial cells to perform phagocytosis and regulate inflammation during AKI. Our studies will culminate in the development and testing of a novel therapeutic strategy aimed at enhancing this (KIM-1 dependent) kidney protective mechanism that already exists in all humans. On the whole, the studies supported by this grant will help us to gain detailed mechanistic understanding of how KIM-1 protects us from AKI and inflammation so that we can translate this knowledge into development of therapies aimed at improving outcomes in patients with AKI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Function of the BTB/POZ domain transcription factor Miz-1 in the activation of lymphoid cells and in lymphoid leukemia and lymphoma
Keywords-MotsClés: HEMATOPOIESIS; LYMPHOCYTE ACTIVATION; LYMPHOCYTE MATURATION; MALIGNANT TRANSFORMATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSGENIC AND KNOCKOUT MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Lymphoma and leukemia are both cancers of blood cells, blood cell precursors or even blood stem cells that are programmed to form blood cells. While a lymphoma is present as a solid tumor mass in lymph nodes, spleen or thymus, leukemia is characterized by a massive expansion of malignant cells in the bloodstream. Both leukemia and lymphoma are fatal diseases. Therapies exist, but are a heavy burden on patients and in many cases cannot prevent relapse of the disease. In cancer research, one of the major objectives is to render current therapies more efficient and more tolerable to patients. To be able to do this, the molecular mechanisms behind the emergence and maintenance of blood cancers and the intricacies of the cells that form blood cancers have to be known. We have identified a group of three proteins (called Miz-1, c-Myc and Bcl-6), which control the transcription of genes in normal blood cells and their precursors and which seem to be critical for the development of specific types of lymphoma and leukemia. How these proteins work together in blood cells and whether they represent a suitable target structure on which future therapies can be built on is the goal of the present project. We will use mouse models, in which the genes for these proteins can be switched on or off under conditions where lymphoma and leukemia develop. We expect to generate important information that will pinpoint the function of the Miz-1/c-Myc/Bcl-6 complexes and the molecular pathways that they control as a critical element that could be targeted in future therapies against leukemia and lymphoma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the Ubiquitin System in Sperm Development and Function
Keywords-MotsClés: GONADAL DEVELOPMENT; INFERTILITY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN METABOLISM; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; PROTEOLYSIS; SPERM MOTILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Infertility is a common problem that is increasing, particularly in Western societies. Approximately 20-25% of infertility cases are due to the male partner and ~30% of additional cases are due to abnormalities in both partners.  The causes of male infertility remain largely unknown.  In order to fertilize eggs, sperm must undergo normal development and maturation.   This involves the conversion of undifferentiated stem cells in the testis into mature elongated spermatids.  These spermatids undergo further maturation in the epididymis and activation upon ejaculation into the female reproductive tract.  Here the activated sperm acquire the necessary motility to move through the reproductive tract and then penetrate the outer layers of the egg structure to fuse with the egg.  In order for proper development and maturation of spermatids to take place, proteins that are not required in the final sperm cells must be destroyed. My laboratory is studying the mechanisms by which the non-required proteins are degraded in developing spermatids.  Defects in this breakdown of proteins may lead to abnormal development of sperm and infertility.  Indeed we have recently observed that mice lacking USP2, an enzyme in this pathway of protein breakdown, are almost completely infertile. Their sperm have defects in motility and in ability to penetrate the coatings around the egg.  Therefore, we will compare the sperm from mice lacking USP2 with normal sperm to determine the cellular and molecular mechanisms for these abnormalities. Defects in sperm motility are found in the majority of infertile men and so this research may lead to new approaches to treating infertility or new contraceptive methods in men. Indeed, we will begin exploring in this project whether there are abnormalities of the USP2 gene in infertile men.

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging genotype-phenotype relationships in post-stroke recovery
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC RISK FACTORS; MRI; PET; STROKE RECOVERY; TMS
Abstract-Résumé: The capacity of a patient to recover from stroke depends on many factors. One of them, the amount of rehabilitation, can be influenced within certain practical and economical limits. It is just recently, with our more advanced understanding of the extent to which even the adult brain can regenerate, that certain genetic factors were brought into the focus of stroke recovery research. Such genetic factors (so called genetic polymorphisms)can not be influenced but they may put patients at risk for prolonged or incomplete stroke recovery.The mechanisms, how these genetic factors actually interfere with the recovery processes in the brain are not well understood. It is known from animal experiments, that the amount of inflammation in the brain after a stroke might represent one link between certain genetic factors and recovery. Another possibility is the lack of certain growth factors which facilitate the repair of nerve cells. We have developed methods to directly image the amount of inflammation in the living human brain after stroke and to measure changes in the nerve-cell composition of the brain. With this project we plan to investigate the possible link between inflammation, growth factors and recovery in the living human brain during after stroke using these advanced imaging methods. If successful, we will be able to identify patients at risk for pro-longed stroke recovery immediately after the event and may thus be able to allocate more resources to those patients. We furthermore will be able to directly image the effect of possible therapies on e.g. inflammation and thus be able to more rapidly and easily evaluate possible new treatment approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using A Novel Conditional Gene Knockout Strategy To Examine The Role Of VEGF Signaling In The Cellular And Behavioral Actions Of Antidepressant Treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANTIDEPRESSANTS; BEHAVIOUR; CONDITIONAL GENE KNOCKOUT; DEPRESSION; HIPPOCAMPUS; NEUROTROPHIC FACTORS; RECOMBINANT VIRUSES; STRESS; VASCULAR ENDOTHELIAL GROWTH FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a debilitating illness affecting 1 in 7 Canadians at some point in their life. Because of its high prevalence and economic cost, depression imposes a profound health care burden that not only affects the individual but permeates throughout all avenues of social, work, and family life. Although several antidepressant drugs are available, chronic administration is necessary for therapeutic effects to be achieved and only some patients (<50%) show improvement. However, despite these limitations, significant progress has been made in identifying molecules and genes important in antidepressant action. One promising candidate in this regard is vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Several studies have found that various antidepressant treatments increase VEGF expression in brain regions involved in depression, and that the induction of VEGF appears to be important in producing the therapeutic effects of these treatments. Although these findings suggest a role of VEGF in antidepressant action, it is presently unclear if the loss of VEGF actually results in the development of depression. In this study, a novel strategy involving genetic and viral manipulations will be used to selectively delete the VEGF gene in neurons (or other cell types) within brain regions important in depression (e.g. hippocampus, medial prefrontal cortex). These genetically modified mice will be tested for depressive and anxiety behavior and the effects of various antidepressants examined to determine which specific source of VEGF (e.g. neuron, astrocyte, endothelial) is necessary for producing the behavioral and cellular effects of these treatments. It is anticipated that these studies will provide important information about the role of VEGF-signaling in the cellular and molecular mechanism action of antidepressants that one day could help identify new antidepressant compounds that can rapidly and safely act in high proportion of patients with depression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development & Evaluation of a Mobile Patient Monitoring Device for Nurses in the Intensive Care Unit
Keywords-MotsClés: ALARMS; BIOMEDICAL INSTRUMENTATION; COMMUNICATION; DECISION SUPPORT; HUMAN FACTORS; INTENSIVE CARE UNIT; INTERDISCIPLINARY WORK; MOBILE APPLICATION; NURSING
Abstract-Résumé: Devices used to monitor patients' vital signs are a crucial part of safe care in the intensive care unit (ICU). While these monitors have been available at the bedside since the early 70s, they have not been designed with their main user, nurses, in mind. Additionally, these devices are not particularly user-friendly, showing three key problems: a high false alarm rate, the lack of integration of information between devices, and that they can provide information for only one patient at a time. Alarms, such as a low heart rate alarm, can notify bedside nurses of deleterious changes in a patient's condition, allowing for rescue before harm occurs. However, false alarms are frequently caused by things like patient movement in bed. These alarms add to the noise in the ICU, disturb the patients' sleep, delays recovery, and contribute to the high burnout rate in nurses. The solution is "smart alarms" that can use additional information about the patient and the environment. Information from a number of bedside devices commonly used for a patient in the ICU, such as infusion pumps or mechanical ventilators, is not integrated. This prolongs the time until changes in a patient's condition are detected. Combining these displays into a single hand-held device is an attractive solution as it moves the alarms away from the bedside and into the hands of nurses wherever they are. An intelligent computer system can also improve their ability to detect potentially life-threatening conditions more correctly and rapidly. The mobile device will improve communication and information exchange between members of the health care team. Finally, by providing information about the condition of patients anywhere, nurses can cut the time needed to look for information and spend more time caring for their patients. Reducing the false alarm rate, improving the quality of information and its exchange, and providing it wherever the nurse might be, has a high potential for improving patient safety

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the impact of translation inhibitors on the intrinsic apoptosis machinery in lymphomas
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER; LYMPHOMA; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS INHIBITORS
Abstract-Résumé: In the western world, cancer accounts for one in three deaths as well as causing significant social and economic impact. This Fellowship proposal seeks to decipher how drugs that act to inhibit protein synthesis can kill cancer cells. Recently, there has been much interest in this class of drugs especially for treating cancers of the blood. One, homoharringtonine has successfully undergone clinical trials and another, silvestrol, proved to be efficacious in mouse models of multiple cancer types. I plan to investigate whether these drugs trigger cell death by causing apoptosis, an evolutionarily mechanism of cell suicide that is deployed to remove damaged or unwanted cells. Pertinently, this pathway is often defective in cancer cells which accounts for the persistence of tumor cells. I shall also explore if the combination of drugs that act to inhibit protein synthesis with those directly activating cell suicide could be effective in mouse cancer models. These studies will provide a greater understanding how these anti-cancer agents act and will critically presage how they can be tested and used in the clinic for treating patients with cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the dynamics of CD28-mediated costimulatory signaling in T cell activation by quantitative proteomics
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNOLOGY; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEOMICS; SIGNALING TRANSDUCTION; T CELL SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Proper T-lymphocyte activation is critical in controlling immune response against infection and cancer. This activation requires the signals received by both the T-cell receptor (TCR) and a series of costimulatory receptors. CD28-mediated costimulatory signaling provides the most prominent one for regulating a broad range of T cell functions. Inspiringly, an inhibitory polypeptide targeting CD28 has been applied for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis in clinical trials. However, as compared with its prominent consequences on T cell functions and its potential for therapeutic intervention, current understanding of the CD28-mediated signaling and its connection with TCR signaling is still very limited. Here we propose to apply quantitative proteomics approaches for studying the global phosphorylation events and CD28 interactome as this will help to develop a precise and dynamic map of CD28-mediated costimulatory signaling cascades. The outcome of this study will provide insight into the mechanisms about how CD28 costimulation regulates T cell activation. Potentially, these understanding will help to find new targets and strategies for clinic treatment of related diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Food reservoir for Escherichia coli causing human extraintestinal infections
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE; ANTIMICROBIAL USE IN ANIMAL FOOD PRODUCTION; COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED BACTERIAL INFECTIONS; COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS; ESCHERICHIA COLI; FOOD SAFETY; FOODBORNE INFECTIONS; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: There is strong new evidence in Canada that a link exists between the E. coli recovered from retail meat, specifically chicken, and the E. coli that cause urinary tract infections (UTIs) in healthy women.  This proposal seeks to demonstrate whether chicken meat may be a source for the E. coli that cause infections in people.  Our hypothesis examines whether there are genetically indistinguishable or closely related E. coli found in retail chicken, but not beef or pork, that cause UTIs in humans.  The study has two research aims.  First, the project will compare the DNA fingerprints (or genotypes) of E. coli collected by the Public Health Agency of Canada, which monitors antimicrobial resistance in bacteria from meat obtained from grocery and other retail stores, to E. coli recovered from cases of community-acquired UTIs at four sites across Canada (2011 - 2014).  Second, the study will determine whether food animals (chicken, cows and pigs) themselves are infected with E. coli that cause infections in humans at the time they are slaughtered.  There are significant public health implications to this research. First, E. coli that cause diseases other than diarrhea may be transferred via food.  Second, the use of antibiotics during food animal production (e.g., for growth promotion) may contribute to the development and selection of drug-resistant E. coli in food animals, these drug-resistant E. coli can then be transmitted from retail meat to humans, where they can cause difficult to treat infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: A trial of adjunctive prednisolone and mycobacterium w Immunotherapy in Tuberculous Pericarditis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUNCTIVE CORTICOSTEROIDS; CLINICAL TRIAL; MYCOBACTERIUM W IMMUNOTHERAPY; TUBERCULOUS PERICARDITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection puts people, especially the young, at risk of opportunistic infections, such as tuberculosis. In Africa, the HIV epidemic has resulted in an increase in the number of cases of tuberculosis affecting various parts of the body, including the membrane surrounding the heart (i.e., pericardium). Pericardial tuberculosis is a serious form of tuberculosis that results in the death or serious complications for 1 in 2 people affected despite the use of anti-tuberculosis medication. The addition of corticosteroids to the anti-tuberculosis medication could result in the reduction of the number of deaths, but this hypothesis remains to be confirmed in appropriately designed clinical trials. Vaccination with the Mycobacterium w injection may also reduce the damage caused by the tuberculosis infection of the heart. We propose to conduct a randomized clinical trial in people with pericardial tuberculosis treated with anti-tuberculosis drugs. Patients will be randomly allocated to receive either prednisolone or a matching placebo tablet, and Mycobacterium w injection or placebo injection. The number of people who die or who develop hardening of the pericardium with compression of the heart (called pericardial constriction) or who need emergency evacuation of the pericardial fluid from pericardial sac for severe compression (called tamponade) will be compared in each group. If these therapies are proven to be effective, they could potentially benefit several tens of thousands of patients every year.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of ectonucleotidase in the calcification of the aortic valve
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIFIC AORTIC VALVE DISEASE; CALCIFICATION; DIABETES; ECTONUCLEOTIDASE; HYPERTENSION; INSULIN RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (AS) is the most common heart valve disease and the third cause of cardiovascular death. AS is a progressive disorder in which a chronic mineralization of the aortic valve leads with the years to an obstruction and a narrowing of the aortic valve orifice. In the late stage of the disease process when AS is severe, the life expectancy is shortened drastically and the only hope for a cure is an open-heart surgery, which consists in the replacement of the diseased valve. It is important to underline that, for a vast majority of patients, AS can be diagnosed early in its evolution and could thus be treated with a pharmaceutical agent. However, so far, no medical treatment has shown efficacy in preventing the progression of AS once diagnosed. This is largely due to the absence of specific molecular target to AS, which could, in turn, be used to develop novel pharmaceutical agents. To this effect, we have recently discovered such an important target, which is playing a key role in the calcification of aortic valve and the clinical progression rate of AS.  Ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase-1, or in short ENPP-1, is one of 700 genes or so found differentially regulated in AS, but which plays a fundamental role in the disease process. In fact, we have found that ENPP-1, by its ability to hydrolyze nucleotide to phosphate, promotes the calcification of the aortic valve. In the next several years, the goal of our studies will be to further understand the role of ENPP-1 in the development of AS and to characterize the potential implication of this gene in diabetes and hypertension, two important risk factors for the development of AS. These experiments will, for the first time, give several important insights into the pathophysiology of AS and will certainly help to translate those findings into the clinical practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oxytocin in the maternal circulation influences the effects of birth hypoxia on the neonatal brain
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BIRTH; CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM; HYPOXIA; NEUROPROTECTION; OXYTOCIN
Abstract-Résumé: A lack of oxygen during birth, or birth hypoxia, can often result in lifelong neurological consequences such as learning problems, lower IQ and increased vulnerability for disorders such as cerebral palsy, epilepsy or schizophrenia.  Despite many years of research, there are no available drug therapies to protect brain neurons from ongoing damage once birth hypoxia has occurred.  Therefore it is important to understand the physiology of the birth process and to minimize practices which might aggravate effects of birth hypoxia.            Oxytocin is a hormone very often used to induce or speed up labor in pregnant women.  In fact, in North America and Europe, approximately 50-70% of women giving birth to their first child are given oxytocin during birth.  There is some evidence that oxytocin use at birth is associated with reduced oxygenation of the newborn's blood.  In this research project, we will use animal models to test if giving oxytocin to a pregnant mother will aggravate the effects of birth hypoxia on brain function in the newborn.  We will examine markers of brain injury and brain function in the newborn both at the time of birth, and later on in life. We will also carry out experiments attempting to understand the mechanism by which oxytocin might worsen the effects of birth hypoxia on the newborn brain.             These studies should give us a better understanding of how oxytocin use might interact with birth hypoxia to impact the newborn brain.  It is anticipated that these studies may also lead to suggestions for optimizing birth practices for healthy brain function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modelling of Radiotherapy Induced Damage in Locally Advanced Lung Cancer by a Novel System Radiobiology Approach
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; MEDICAL PHYSICS; NORMAL TISSUE TOXICITIES; PROTEOMICS; RADIATION THERAPY; RESPONSE PREDICTION; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TREATMENT PLANNING
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is a leading cause for death among men and women with 5-year survival rate of only 15%. Patients at advanced stages suffer from further poorer prognosis and dire socioeconomic consequences for them, their relatives and the healthcare system. The majority of these patients is diagnosed with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and receives radiation therapy as their main treatment. However, radiation hypersensitivity, which manifests as inflammatory response known as radiation pneumonitis, is a major limiting factor to treatment success and a main obstacle to applying new promising radiation modalities. This is a potentially fatal condition that damages normal lung tissues, therefore, a key goal of modern radiotherapy research is to predict at the time of treatment planning, the risks of pneumonitis for each individual patient. However, because of the inherent complexity and variability of the biological response to radiation therapy, current physical or biological models separately are insufficient to accurately predict this risk. Therefore, in this proposal we plan to investigate a novel system-based approach that would integrate relevant biological information while controlling for physical variations in the same population using artificial intelligence and bioinformatics techniques. We plan to conduct a prospective study in a cohort of locally advanced NSCLC patients who receive radiotherapy at McGill University Health Centre. The data collected in this study and developed methodology would provide new insights into radiation pneumonitis signaling mechanisms and allow for better predictive models of its onset. The findings can be used clinically to personalize patients' treatment plans, reducing the risk of complications or supporting therapy that is more intensive for those patients likely to benefit. This could potentially improve outcomes, provide greater quality care for patients, and reduce associated healthcare costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mutational and Functional Analysis of Genes Identified by GWAS Studies of Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; GENETICS; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROSCIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer disease (AD) is an incurable neurodegenerative disorder which, as the 4th leading cause of death in adults, is a growing unmet medical need worldwide. Epidemiological studies have identified age and family history as principal risk factors, with genetic factors contributing ~40% of this risk. Half of the genetic risk is attributable to variants in APP, PS1, PS2 or APOE. We have shown that mutations in these genes cause AD by inducing accumulation of Abeta - a neurotoxic aggregation-prone proteolytic fragment of APP. Although the accumulation of Abeta is a widely accepted pathophysiological hallmark of AD, it does not explain several other features of AD (e.g. changes in lipid metabolism, defective autophagy, and progressive spreading of pathology across the brain). To identify other genes potentially involved in these unexplained aspects of AD, we have used a hypothesis-free GWAS approach. This has revealed that AD is associated with SNPs in 9 loci. The current program will focus on 4 of these loci because analysis of their genomic architecture reveals that: i) they each contain only a single gene (making them TRACTABLE GENETIC TARGETS); and ii) these genes had NOT PREVIOUSLY BEEN PREDICTED to play a causal role in AD. Significantly, we have also shown that these genes do not affect Abeta production (indicating that they constitute PROMISING LEADS INTO NOVEL ASPECTS OF AD BIOLOGY). We will identify: a) the disease-causing variants; b) the molecular effects of these variants; and c) the pathways within which these genes work to cause AD. This experiment is TRACTABLE BECAUSE WE HAVE ASSEMBLED NOVEL, CUTTING-EDGE biophysical, molecular, cellular and animal model tools. We will use these tools to assess the impact of these genes on currently unexplained features of AD. The discovery of AD-causing variants and understanding their role in AD will have MAJOR TRANSLATIONAL IMPACT by providing the previously unavailable basis for novel diagnostics and treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Muscle-Related Side Effects of Statins: Functional Impact, Mechanisms, and Potential Relief with Vitamin D Supplementation
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPSY; FATIGUE; MUSCLE; SIDE EFFECTS; STATINS; STRENGTH; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Statins are a class of drugs that are widely prescribed to lower blood cholesterol levels. Although they have few side effects, many patients report muscle pain, cramps, and weakness when using these drugs. We know very little on the real impact of these muscle symptoms on patient quality of life, especially in relation to muscle strength and endurance. Even less is known on how to prevent or treat these symptoms, short of stopping statin use.  This proposal will explore muscle function (strength and endurance) in men and women suffering from statin-induced muscle symptoms. The mechanisms responsible for these muscle symptoms will also be explored.  Also, since some data suggest that vitamin D supplementation could alleviate statin-induced muscle symptoms, we will assess the potential usefulness of this supplement in a randomized control trial.   Together, the results from this project will provide real information on the effects of these drugs on muscle-related function, how they come about, and potentially how to palliate them.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel anti-angiogenic therapy for endometriosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ANTI-ANGIOGENIC THERAPY; CHEMOKINES; CYTOKINES; ENDOMETRIOSIS; ENDOTHELIAL PROGENITOR CELLS; HAEMATOPOIETIC PROGENITOR CELLS; IMMUNODEFICIENT MICE; LASER CAPTURE MICRODISSECTION; STROMAL CELL DERIVED GROWTH FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Endometriosis is characterized by the growth of endometrial tissue (normal uterine lining) outside of the uterus.  It affects more than 8.5 million women and teens in North America alone, with 176 million more worldwide. The disease can only be diagnosed definitively through invasive surgery, and there is no absolute cure. Similar to cancer, endometriosis lesions require establishment of blood supply for survival and growth. This has led to the idea that suppression of blood vessel growth (anti-angiogenic therapy) may be a successful approach. One of the key components of new blood vessel formation is recruitment of specialized blood vessel growth promoting cells called endothelial and hematopoietic progenitor cells from bone marrow. These cells are recruited by stromal-cell derived factor-1 protein. We confirmed abnormally high expression of stromal-cell derived factor-1 protein and corresponding increase in the progenitor cells in the lesions from endometriosis patients. The goal of this study is to test the hypothesis that endothelial and hematopoietic progenitor cells are recruited at the lesion sites by stromal-cell derived factor-1 and that blocking of this protein in combination with anti-angiogenic drug, ABT-898 prevent new blood vessel development and ultimately survival of endometriosis lesions. We will test this hypothesis using a combination of molecular biology approaches, patient-based studies and animal models. These innovative and clinically relevant research studies will allow us to gain a greater understanding of endometriosis progression and identify new treatment for this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Secondary Immunity in Cutaneous Leishmaniasis by Leishmania Phosphoglycans
Keywords-MotsClés: CUTANEOUS LEISHMANIASIS; HOST DEFENSE AND IMMUNITY; HOST-PARASITE INTERACTION; IMMUNOLOGIC MEMORY; INFECTION-INDUCED RESISTANCE; MICROBIAL PATHOGENESIS; REGULATION OF IMMUNITY; VACCINE AND VACCINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Infectious diseases including those caused by parasites remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality throughout the world, particularly in developing countries. With climate changes, increased traveling, immigration and military operations in endemic countries, Canadians are increasingly in contact with novel infections. Currently, about 350 million people the world are at risk of contracting Leishmaniasis, with 2 million new infections per year. Several species of th e parasite cause clinical disease manifestations ranging from self-healing cutaneous, disfiguring mucocutaneous, to fatal visceral leishmaniasis. In endemic areas, Leishmania is also found to be an opportunistic pathogen in HIV-1-infected patients. Indeed, it was estimated that AIDS increases the risk of visceral leishmaniasis by up to a 1,000-fold. There are no effective vaccines against leishmaniasis because we still do not fully understand the mechanisms of protective immunity, particularly those associated with secondary (memory) response. While recovery from natural or experimental infection results in development of long-lasting immunity to re-infection, vaccination with heat-killed L. major (as is currently practiced in some areas) induces only short-term protection. We have discovered that persistence of parasites at the site of primary infection is important for maintenance of immunity. We have engineered a non-pathogenic Leishmania that persists after infection, does not induce overt disease and protects mice against virulent challenge infections. The work proposed here will investigate the mechanisms of secondary anti-Leishmania immunity in mice. The results would define the factors that regulate the generation, maintenance and loss of secondary anti-Leishmania immunity. The findings may suggest new strategies for vaccine designs and vaccination against this other important diseases caused by intracellular pathogens including Malaria, Tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS.
