Abstract-Résumé: We will assess participants' causal attributions regarding the co-occurrence of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms, as well as functional impairment. Consistent with research suggesting that anxiety disorders may play causal (aetiological) roles in clinical depression, we hypothesize that depressed individuals will report strong causal associations between their anxiety symptoms and their symptoms of depression. We will test our hypotheses using an innovative psychological assessment method that we have developed that we call a Perceived Symptom Causal Relationship (PSCR) scale. Our research will provide insight into the causal interactions between anxiety disorders and depression, and how these disorders influence impairment in social and occupational functioning.

TitreApplicationTitle: Risk Stratification of Adult Emergency Department Syncope Patients to Predict Short-term Serious Adverse Events after Discharge (RiSEDS study)
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIA; CLINICAL DECISION RULES; DEATH; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; HOSPITAL ADMISSION; SERIOUS ADVERSE EVENTS; SYNCOPE
Abstract-Résumé: Syncope (fainting) is a common problem in the emergency department (ED). Annually about 100,000 patients visit Canadian emergencies and about 10,000 of them will have serious underlying problems such as blood clots in the lung (pulmonary embolism), heart attack, or irregular heart rhythm requiring pacemaker/defibrillator, or will die. About half of these conditions are not evident during the ED visit. Because of a significant shortage of hospital beds, most patients will be discharged home including one-third with serious conditions. Among those who die after the ED visit; two-thirds will die outside the hospital. There is little evidence to guide emergency physicians to risk-stratify ED syncope patients. A previous study conducted by our team showed that it is feasible to identify those at risk for serious events.  The goal of this study is to develop a decision tool to accurately risk-stratify adult ED syncope patients for serious events after ED discharge. We are presently conducting a pilot study and with funding from this application, we intend to enroll a total of 4,000 consenting syncope patients at six Canadian EDs. We will collect patient characteristics, medical information and test results. Treatment will not differ for enrolled patients. We will conduct a 30-day telephone follow-up to assess for occurrence of serious events. Based on the information collected, we will develop a new risk scale to risk-stratify patients as low-risk who can be discharged; medium-risk who need urgent specialist follow-up and high-risk who need to be admitted. We will undertake subsequent research to validate this decision tool. This tool will help emergency doctors, cardiologists, neurologists, medicine specialists and family doctors to improve and standardize the care of syncope patients; improve patient safety by admitting those at risk; and help doctors quickly decide treatment thereby improve emergency wait times.

TitreApplicationTitle: Paying for primary care: Relationship between incentives and patient/provider characteristics
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS; DISTRIBUTION OF HEALTH EXPENDITURES; PHYSICIAN PAYMENT; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Primary care reforms, in Canada and internationally, have introduced different models of remuneration for primary care providers. These models differ in how they address variability in both patient and provider characteristics. How best to pay for primary care has major policy implications, because health costs are not homogeneous; most health costs are incurred by a small proportion of the population. Primary care physicians may also vary in how they prefer to practice. The proposed research will examine the characteristics of different reform models in Ontario and Manitoba, with an emphasis on how payment varies. It will examine the distribution of health expenditures in the populations of each province, overall, by age-sex group, and by sub-category of expenditures. It will then examine the relationship of both patient and provider characteristics to the primary care model with which they are associated, the extent to which the fiscal incentives to select into different models appear to be realized, and the implications for costs and access.  The results should help ensure a better match between payment models and costs of caring for particular sub-groups of patients, and reduce the likelihood of such unintended consequences as providing financial disincentives to care for vulnerable populations.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of epidermal growth factor receptor signaling in the Drosophila ovary.
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; DROSOPHILA GENETICS; EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; EPITHELIAL PATTERNING; GENETIC MOSAICS; OOGENESIS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: We study how signals in a tissue environment govern the proliferation and behavior of the cells within the tissue. We focus on a molecule called the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), whose excessive activity is associated with tumor growth. These studies, carried out in the fruit fly model system, will help us to understand the factors that influence whether cells can respond to EGFR activity, thus improving our understanding of cancer mechanisms. For example, identifying a molecule that makes cells resistant to EGFR activity in the fruit fly may provide useful insight for the development of strategies to block this activity in tumor cells.  Previous work in the fruit fly ovary has shown that certain cell behaviors are restricted to specific regions of the tissue where EGFR is activated. However, later work showed that switching on EGFR activity parts of the tissue where it is not usually active does not necessarily result in the expected changes in cell behavior. These findings prompted the hypothesis that some cells in this tissue are naturally resistant to EGFR activity. To investigate the cause of this resistance, we will study these cells further by using a variety of experimental tools to artificially activate EGFR and observe the effect on cell behavior. In addition, we will study a mutant strain of fruit flies in which this tissue seems to be inherently more sensitive to EGFR activity; by identifying the gene that is mutant, we will learn which more about why normal cells can be resistant.  This work will advance our knowledge of how sensitivity to EGFR activity is regulated. Increased EGFR activity is found in a variety of human tumors and is one of the most common defects associated with breast cancers. Since fruit fly genes are so similar to human genes, understanding the factors that inhibit or promote responsiveness to EGFR in this system may provide important targets for therapies, complementing those that target EGFR activity.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of a nuclear protein, Bat3, in oncogenic signaling networks
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MOUSE MODEL; P53; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATION; PTEN; STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Tumorigenesis is a multi-step process where healthy cells gradually acquire the characteristics of cancer cells, and start unlimited and increased proliferation.  This transformation involves the activation and/or inactivation of genes which regulate cell growth, programmed cell death (apoptosis) and cell survival.  p53 is a well-known regulator of apoptosis and cell growth, of which mutations are observed in over half of human cancers. We have recently discovered that Bat3 is a positive regulator of p53 functions, thus regulates apoptosis and cell growth. In support of our findings, Bat3 mutations have been identified in colon, lung, and breast cancers.  Dysregulation of apoptosis and increased cell survival are hallmarks of cancer, and ultimately affect therapeutic response. Thus, evidence from our studies will aid in developing fresh strategies to restore proper apoptotic signaling pathways in cancer cells and identifying novel therapeutic targets for anti-cancer therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The gut microbiota in pediatric inflammatory bowel diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; CROHN'S DISEASE; GUT MICROBIOTA; METAGENOMICS; METAPROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; ULCERATIVE COLITIS
Abstract-Résumé: There are currently hundreds of thousands of Canadians that are suffering from chronic incurable conditions known as Inflammatory Bowel Diseases (IBD). Canada has one of the highest incidence rates of IBD in the world and approximately 25% of these cases are diagnosed in childhood. Canadian physicians have noted with great concern that the number of children diagnosed with IBD increased by 50% between the mid 1990's and 2005. Moreover, there is currently no medical cure for IBD and the cause of IBD is uncertain. Recent work has made great strides in identifying the large number of human genes involved in IBD, but how these genes relate to IBD presentation and disease course remains largely unknown. There is a huge diversity of bacterial microbes situated at the surface of the digestive tract. Recent studies suggest that the types of bacteria that are present in the intestinal tract of healthy people may be important in maintaining proper health. Conversely, an imbalance in the types of these bacteria is associated with the development of diseases or pathological conditions such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Determining the identities of these different types of bacteria and how they interact with human genes in the context of pediatric IBD is the goal of this project. This proposal is unique in combining the expertise and experience of both top Canadian pediatric IBD physicians and world renowned research scientists. This study will have important implications for understanding the cause and mechanism of IBD and could provide us with the required knowledge to develop novel treatments. The role of these intestinal bacteria in causing IBD or maintaining inflammation will be determined. Improved understanding of these microbes and their activities is essential to design novel therapeutic interventions aimed at manipulating these intestinal microbial communities (for example with specific diets) or their interactions with the host immune system.

TitreApplicationTitle: A cluster randomised trial investigating the effects of delaying onset of substance use on adolescent cognitive development.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ALCOHOL AND DRUG ABUSE; COGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT; NEURO-TOXIC EFFECTS OF SUBSTANCES; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Empirical studies indicate that early onset substance misuse is associated with long-term negative outcomes, including greater risk for addiction, school drop-out, mental illness and poor physical health. However, it is unclear how early onset substance use translates to future risk. This proposal uses a randomised trial with developmentally sensitive neuropsychological measures to examine whether preventing or delaying onset of alcohol and drug misuse can positively impact on adolescent cognitive function or development, which, in turn, has future implications for risk for addiction and other mental health problems. This cluster randomized trial will use a selective youth alcohol and drug prevention programme with well-established efficacy in terms of delaying onset of substance use and reducing rates of adolescent substance use by 30-80%, (23-29, 70). Thirty-two schools will be recruited in Montreal of which half will be randomized to deliver a personality-targeted selective prevention programme. Consenting Year 7 students in each school will be screened and interventions will be delivered to those scoring one standard deviation above the grade-level mean on one of four personality risk factors for substance misuse:  anxiety sensitivity, hopelessness, impulsivity and sensation seeking. In total, over 1000 high risk students will receive interventions in this trial and will benefit from this evidence-based intervention.  Participants will be followed every 12 months for 5 years to test the effects of the intervention on the causal pathway from substance use to poor cognitive and addiction outcomes. This investigation provides a unique opportunity to answer an imperative research question on the possible neuro-toxic effects of early onset substance use and their role in the development of addiction and mental health problems. Findings will also address public policy questions on the need to intensify drug prevention resources in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of novel genomic and proteomic signatures to predict imminent preterm birth
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; DIAGNOSTICS; GENOMICS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MICROARRAY; PREDICTION; PREGNANCY; PRETERM LABOUR; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Two million women are admitted annually to North American hospitals with a clinical diagnosis of threatened preterm labour (TPTL). However, only <100,000 (5%) will deliver a premature baby within two to ten days (true PTL), 80% will continue their pregnancies to term. Currently, there is no effective means to determine which of these two million women will progress to true PTL and have a preterm delivery. Those 80% of women who present with TPTL will be hospitalised unnecessarily, causing psychological stress on the families and significant costs to the healthcare system. These women are also candidates for drug treatments in an attempt to delay labour or mature the babies' lungs with adverse side effects to the mother and baby.  There is an abundant of evidence that white blood cells (leukocytes) can be used to monitor a variety of biochemical and physiologic processes occurring in the body. Previous studies, including convincing data from the candidate's present laboratory (Lye Lab), have shown that leukocytes contain biomarkers that are present in the uterus and that these biomarkers can be used to monitor the progression of labour.  The aim of Dr Heng's postdoctoral fellowship is to investigate gene and protein expression signatures of white blood cells collected from women admitted for TPTL; and distinguish between women with true PTL and those whose pregnancies will continue to term. The goal is to develop a diagnostic test to accurately diagnose women in TPTL who will progress and deliver within two to ten days (true PTL) after performing the test. This will spare unnecessary medical intervention on the remaining women whose pregnancies will continue to term, thereby reducing the cost to the healthcare system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the 'Functioning, Disability and Health' of Women and Men Living with HIV in Zambia: Shifting Perspectives for a Longer-Term Approach to HIV Care in Southern Africa
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; CRITICAL SOCIAL SCIENCE; DISABILITY; GENDER; HIV; ICF; QUALITATIVE; REHABILITATION; SOUTHERN AFRICA; ZAMBIA
Abstract-Résumé: One-third of all people living with HIV worldwide and 40% of all HIV+ women live in the ten countries in Southern Africa, which includes Zambia.  The recent arrival of effective HIV drugs in that region marks a new era in the history of HIV as vast numbers of people living with HIV may expect improved health and far longer lives.  HIV in these poor countries is becoming a chronic illness.  Thus, research is needed that moves beyond the medical challenges of treatment roll-out and embraces a longer-term approach to HIV as a chronic condition.  Rehabilitation is an approach used in Canada with great success ever since treatment turned HIV into a chronic illness here in the 1990's.  The leading rehabilitation lens has been the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disablity and Health.  But these ideas have not yet been considered for people living with HIV in Southern Africa.    The purpose of our research is to use the WHO framework to explore the experiences of "functioning, disability and health" among women and men living with HIV in Lusaka, Zambia who are on HIV treatment.  We plan to have in-depth discussions with 15 men and 15 women at 3 points over the course of 12-18 months to find out about their lives.  We want to learn about them as individuals and how context shapes their experiences.  In Canada, people living with HIV have described their experience as episodic disability whereby life with HIV is highly unpredictable.  We plan to explore how episodic disability might be playing out for people in Lusaka.  Along with challenges, we know that people living with HIV can be amazingly resilient, so we plan to explore not just problems but also the successes achieved by our participants in managing their obstacles.  Finally, for each of these issues, we will use a gender lens to explore how experiences are the same or different for women vs men.  These insights will help inform practice, policy, education and research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory mechanisms of the cell response to proteotoxic stress
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL DEATH; MITOSIS; MOLECULAR CHAPERONES; PROTEIN CONFORMATIONAL DISEASES; PROTEIN FOLDING AND DEGRADATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cells have developed early during evolution very sophisticated mechanisms to detect, to respond and to adapt to stressful environment. Resistance and adaptation to stress are key factors in the etiology of many human diseases and also in the success of therapies that make use of cytotoxic drugs. The general objective of this research program is to delineate the mechanisms of the mammalian cell response to proteotoxic stress, i.e. stress that affects the integrity of the proteins.  We are studying a family of protein, called the HspB family, which have the capacity of chaperoning damaged proteins, detecting their presence, isolating them from the rest of the cells and preparing them for either repair or degradation. A better understanding of the function of these proteins is of utmost importance considering that defects at their structures have already been associated with a number of degenerative diseases in human.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Profiling cell activation in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNITY; FIBROCYTES; LEUKOCYTE ACTIVATION; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Rheumatoid arthritis is a complex disease that progressively affects many joints. It is unclear how the disease spreads from one joint to the next. In preliminary studies we have identified a cell population in the blood of rheumatoid arthritis patients that is abnormal and may migrate to joints to cause disease. Indeed, these cells may be the precursors that determine the bone and cartilage destruction in rheumatoid joints. Using a mouse model of rheumatoid arthritis, we will follow the fate of these cells to determine whether they promote disease. In parallel, we will analyze blood specimens from rheumatoid arthritis patients to see whether these cells may be markers of disease severity for arthritis sufferers.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Cerebral Arterial Myogenic Response in Health and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW AUTOREGULATION; CYTOSKELETON REORGANIZATION; GOTO-KAKIZAKI TYPE 2 DIABETIC RAT; MYOGENIC RESPONSE; MYOSIN LIGHT CHAIN PHOSPHATASE; RHO KINASE PHOSPHORYLATION; SPONTANEOUSLY HYPERTENSIVE RAT; STROKE-PRONE HYPERTENSIVE RAT; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE; VASOCONSTRICTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Control of blood flow to the brain relies on appropriate contraction and relaxation of muscle cells within the walls of blood vessels. Inappropriate contraction of these muscle cells is observed in serious disease conditions, such as hypertension, stroke and diabetes. This abnormal behaviour can result in low blood flow to the brain and/or death or disability by causing stroke. The molecular mechanisms that underlie the abnormal contraction of blood vessels in the brain in these conditions are not known. Accumulating evidence indicates that the regulation of the contractile apparatus and cellular skeleton of the muscle cells are altered. These changes cause too much contraction in the vessels leading to increased vessel narrowing and low blood flow. The proposed experiments will investigate this possibility using rat models of hypertension, stroke and diabetes. Small blood vessels of 0.2 mm in width will be removed from the brain of normal and disease rats and studied by pressurizing the inside of the vessels as occurs in the body. The muscle cells contract in response to pressure, but the contraction is too large in the disease models. We will prepare these vessels to detect the changes in contractile apparatus and cytoskeleton proteins associated with the abnormal contraction in hypertension, stroke and diabetes. These experiments will provide novel, important information about how brain blood vessel contraction is regulated in health and disease. The long-term goal is to identify the changes so that we may find ways to restore normal contraction and regulation of brain blood flow.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prenatal infection as a risk factor for schizophrenia: studies using animal models
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; BEHAVIOR; CYTOKINES; DNA METHYLATION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; LONG TERM DEPRESSION; N-METHYL-D-ASPARTATE RECEPTORS; PRENATAL INFECTION; REELIN; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Studies have shown that a person has an increased risk for developing schizophrenia if their mother had an infection during pregnancy. However we do not know if an infection during pregnancy can actually cause abnormal brain development, and if so, how does it do this? This project uses animal models to study how an infection during pregnancy affects brain development. We have already found that rats, born from mothers exposed to bacterial infection during pregnancy, show some changes in brain function and behavior when tested as adults. These changes include reduced levels of a protein called reelin which guides neurodevelopment and changes in the electrophysiology of the hippocampus, a brain region implicated in schizophrenia.      In this grant we will study how prenatal infection produces these long term brain changes in offspring. To help defend against infection, the body produces a class of chemicals, called cytokines. Interestingly, it has been discovered that cytokines also affect brain development. In this project, we will study if an infection in rat mothers during pregnancy changes brain development in her pups, through effects of cytokines released at the time of the infection. To understand how an infection early in fetal life could produce lasting changes in brain function much later at adulthood, we will test if prenatal infection affects the DNA mechanisms regulating whether or not the reelin protein is produced, resulting in changes in hippocampal electrophysiological function and behavior of the animal.      These studies may identify how a known risk factor for schizophrenia, namely maternal infection, alters brain function later in life. It is hoped that understanding this process will lead to preventive strategies to reduce the risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Alveolar fluid secretion - a novel mechanism of pulmonary edema
Keywords-MotsClés: ALVEOLAR FLUID CLEARANCE; CFTR; EPITHELIAL ION TRANSPORT; INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY; ISOLATED PERFUSED LUNG; NITRIC OXIDE; NKCC1; PULMONARY EDEMA
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary edema describes an excess accumulation of fluid in the lungs. With increasing amounts of fluids in the lungs, gas exchange becomes impaired and patients ultimately die of respiratory failure. The current concept of pulmonary edema differentiates between two forms: In one case ("cardiogenic edema"), high blood pressure in the lung "squeezes" out fluid from the blood vessels into the air space. In the other case ("non-cardiogenic edema"), the blood vessels of the lung become "leaky" due to ongoing inflammatory responses, allowing fluid to leak from the blood vessels into the airspace. Here, we propose a third mechanism how pulmonary edema may evolve. We know that the epithelial cells outlining the air spaces can actively transport ions such as Na+ and Cl-. For osmotic reasons, this ion transport will be accompanied by a movement of fluid into the same direction. In healthy lungs, the epithelial cells of the distal air spaces absorb ions and thus, fluid, out of the airspace back into the blood. Here, we propose that in some disease conditions, the direction of this ion transport may reverse. As a result, the epithelial cells will start to move ion and thus, fluid, into the airspaces. Ultimately, this flooding of the airspaces will fatally impair breathing. In this proposal, we aim to i) consolidate this novel concept and test its validity for different forms of cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic edema, ii) elucidate the cellular mechanisms which cause the proposed reversal of ion and fluid transport, and iii) exploit this knowledge for the development of new treatment strategies for pulmonary edema. The results of this project are expected to profoundly change our understanding of one of the basic mechanisms of lung disease, i.e. pulmonary edema. They will provide new insights into the cellular mechanisms regulating the movement of ion and fluid. Importantly, we anticipate our findings to provide the basis for a better treatment of pulmonary edema.

TitreApplicationTitle: Contrôle et stabilité des régulations épigénétiques dans les cellules souches pluripotentes humaines: le paradigme de l'inactivation du chromosome X
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULES SOUCHES HUMAINES; IMMUNOPRECIPITATION DE LA CHROMATINE; INACTIVATION DU CHROMOSOME X; MEDECINE REGENERATIVE; PLURIPOTENCE; REPROGRAMMATION; THERAPIE CELLULAIRE; TRANSCRIPTION; XIST; EPIGENETIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: Les regulations epigenetiques se definissent comme des changements transmissibles et reversibles de la fonction des genes sans alteration de la sequence genomique, un des fondements de la diversite biologique. Ces regulations peuvent etre influencees par l'environnement et nous savons maintenant que des anomalies d'ordre epigenetique participent a l'etiologie d'un nombre important de pathologies humaines dont les cancers. L'inactivation du chromosome X chez les mammiferes represente un exemple fondamental de regulation epigenetique precoce liee au developpement et a la differentiation. Mise en place au cours de l'embryogenese, l'inactivation aleatoire donne naissance a des individus mosaiques dont une partie des cellules aura inactive le chromosome X paternel et l'autre partie, le chromosome X maternel. Cette caracteristique a des consequences importantes sur les manifestations phenotypiques des maladies liees a l'X chez des femmes porteuses de mutations. Le projet que nous proposons vise a rechercher les acteurs et etudier les mecanismes controlant l'initiation de l'inactivation dans les cellules ES humaines. Ce projet est essentiel pour connaitre les acteurs controlant la mise en place de l'inactivation dans les ES humaines et comprendre leur mode d'action. Une comprehension detaillee de ces mecanismes peut nous permettre d'envisager d'influencer cette etape d'initiation, en particulier au niveau du choix du chromosome a inactiver, et de compenser ainsi des defauts dus a des biais d'inactivation en faveur d'un chromosome X portant une mutation deletere. De plus, comprendre la regulation de l'inactivation et des processus epigenetiques dans leur ensemble apportera certainement des donnees sur les mecanismes controlant la stabilite des regulations epigenetiques dans les cellules ES humaines, aspect fondamental pour la realisation du plein potentiel therapeutique de ces cellules.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic dissection of taste circuits and feeding behaviour in Drosophila
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL GENETICS; CHEMOSENSATION; DROSOPHILA; IMAGING; INGESTIVE BEHAVIOUR; MODEL SYSTEM; NEURAL CIRCUITS; NEUROANATOMY; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; TASTE/GUSTATION
Abstract-Résumé: The sense of taste plays a critical role in determining what animals decide to eat.  For example, sweet taste guides us towards calorie-rich sources of carbohydrates and bitter taste steers us away from potential toxins.  While this drive for calories evolved as an effective survival strategy, it has created an increasing problem for modern human populations - obesity.  Understanding the mechanisms by which the brain processes taste information and controls feeding behaviour is an important step in developing strategies to control food intake and prevent obesity and its associated diseases.  These mechanisms are not understood in any animal.    Our work uses the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a well established and powerful genetic model system, to investigate the neural pathways controlling taste perception and feeding behaviour.  We use the fly because the size of its brain is more manageable (about 1 million times fewer neurons than ours), and because decades of research have established unparalleled genetic tools for investigating the neurons and genes that control behaviour.  Moreover, flies and humans share remarkable similarities in how they process information from their environment, suggesting that what we learn in flies will help us understand our own brains.  The studies proposed here will provide insight into the complex question of how neurons and genes interact in the fly brain to guide their decisions on what - and how much - to eat.  In the long-term, we would like to understand whether similar systems operate in mammals, and how they contribute to food consumption and obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Rab GTPases during endocytic trafficking
Keywords-MotsClés: CAENORHABDITIS ELEGANS; ENDOCYTIC TRAFFICKING; RAB GTPASES; RABGAP/TBC DOMAIN PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: Endocytosis is one of the mechanisms by which cells can internalize proteins on the cell membrane and extracellular molecules into cytoplasmic membrane bound vesicles.  Switch-like proteins called Rab GTPases, regulate the formation of membrane vesicles as well as their trafficking to different destinations such as back to the outer membrane (recycling) or to the lysosome for degradation.  Our research aims to identify and characterize regulators of the Rab GTPases and thus vesicle trafficking.  Endocytosis is an essential cellular process with important implications for human health.  Endocytosis is important for lipid and protein homeostasis, clearance active membrane receptors that can contribute to oncogenesis when left activated, and it is used by certain viruses and bacteria for cell infection.  Understanding the mechanisms regulating endocytosis and vesicle trafficking will provide insights for the development of therapies for cancer, lipid storage diseases, infection, and much more.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effects of mechanical ventilation on the biophysical properties of pulmonary surfactant
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY; ANIMAL MODELS; PULMONARY SURFACTANT; SURFACTANT BIOPHYSICS; VENTILATOR INDUCED LUNG INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with a variety of lung injuries require mechanical ventilation to help with inflation of the lungs thereby promoting gas exchange. Unfortunately, mechanical ventilation can also cause damage to the lung. To improve the outcome of mechanically ventilated patients we need to understand the mechanisms by which this clinical intervention causes lung damage. Our research focuses on a material in the lung called pulmonary surfactant which is important for maintaining normal lung function. Our previous studies have demonstrated that surfactant function is impaired during mechanical ventilation. Our current proposal investigates how the dysfunction of surfactant occurs. This information will be essential to develop therapies to avoid or treat the ventilation induced lung damage occurring in patients requiring this intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: ACUTE Study: Acute Congestive Heart Failure Urgent and Transitional Care Evaluation
Keywords-MotsClés: EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEART FAILURE; HOSPITAL DISCHARGE; TRANSITIONAL CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a common condition that occurs when there is excessive fluid in the lungs causing patients to feel shortness of breath, often resulting from prior heart damage. It is one of the leading reasons for hospitalizations, emergency department visits, and cardiovascular death. It is estimated that over 3.3 million Canadians have or will develop heart failure since approximately 1 in 5 adults will be affected. The emergency department is the point of first contact for patients with heart failure, but there are few tools to guide physicians who care for such patients. As a result, some patients who are considered safe to discharge home may die shortly after leaving the emergency department, and conversely, some patients who could be safely discharged home may be admitted to hospital unnecessarily.   We have developed a tool to guide physicians to better assess the risk of the heart failure patients that seek care in the emergency department: the Emergency Heart failure Mortality Risk Grade (EHMRG). In this grant, we will test and optimize the EHMRG and examine how it performs in the real world practices of busy emergency department physicians. We will also examine how using the EHMRG could potentially affect overall admissions or discharges for HF patients in the ED.   We have also found that the type of care received by heart failure patients soon after discharge from the emergency department (e.g., discharge transitional care) has a major impact on whether patients will die, need to revisit the emergency department or require hospital admission. We will conduct a detailed examination of factors that predict whether patients will be more likely to require repeat emergency department visits and hospitalizations. We will determine the impact of different levels of care provided after emergency department discharge, and who might most benefit from such care to reduce the burden of heart failure on the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and mechanistic studies of non-ribosomal peptide synthetases
Keywords-MotsClés: ACV SYNTHETASE; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; NON-RIBOSOMAL PEPTIDE SYNTHETASES; NOVEL THERAPUETICS; PENICILLIN; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) are large macromolecular machines that produce a vast variety of small molecules with important and diverse biological activity. Many anti-fungals, anti-microbials, anti-virals and anti-immunosuppressants, including the important therapeutic compounds penicillin and cyclosporin, are produced by these NRPSs. There is huge potential for engineering NRPSs to produce new, or modified bioactive molecules, making them an excellent source of novel therapeutics and chemicals. However, in order to fully harness this potential, an increased understanding of the structure and mechanisms of NRPSs is required.  The structural techniques of X-ray crystallography and electron microscopy will be used to determine detailed structures of NRPSs at various stages of their reaction cycle. Such structures will reveal the modular architecture of NRPSs and elucidate the large-scale conformational changes that facilitate their function. This knowledge will form a framework for future efforts to re-engineer NRPSs to produce new or modified products.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of a low glycemic index (GI) diet on maternal glycemic control and maternal and neonatal markers of postpartum diabetes risk in women with gestational hyperglycemia.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL TRIAL; DIETARY CARBOHYDRATES; GESTATIONAL DIABETES; GLYCEMIC CONTROL; GLYCEMIC INDEX; HUMANS
Abstract-Résumé: Women who develop gestational diabetes (high blood sugar during pregnancy) are treated with diet, exercise and/or medication. Managing blood sugar reduces risk for the mother and the baby. The glycemic index (GI) is a way of ranking the ability of food to raise blood sugar after eating. Recommending low GI foods may improve treatment of gestational diabetes, but has not been tested in this population. The main objective of this study is to see if using low GI food will result in better blood sugar 2 hours after meals. Blood sugar before breakfast, medication dose, inflammation and stress, complications of pregnancy, and maternal diabetes risk after pregnancy will be measured. Infant growth and mother's weight change post delivery will be measured. Information on participants' opinion of low GI will be collected. Women with gestational diabetes who volunteer will receive usual treatment, but will also be randomly assigned (like flipping a coin) to follow regular treatment or add low GI foods. Most study outcomes will be taken from participants' medical chart. In addition, diet records and questionnaires will be collected when the study starts, 4 weeks after the study starts, and 8 weeks and 1 year after delivery. An extra tube will be collected during regular blood work to measure inflammation and stress and if genetic makeup effects how the GI works. Results may help improve treatment of gestational diabetes. This study will collect information on perception of low GI food and how it affects blood sugar control.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protective signaling by PPARs in cardiac hypertrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: 2-PHOTON LASER SCANNING MICROSCOPY; CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CARDIAC MYOCYTES; DIACYLGLYCEROL KINASE (DGK); HISTONE DEACETYLASES (HDAC); PEROXISOME PROLIFERATOR-ACTIVATED RECEPTOR (PPAR); PRESSURE OVERLOAD MODEL OF HYPERTROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Conditions such as hypertension, heart attack or heart valve disease, increase the risk of heart failure. An intermediate step between these conditions and heart failure is cardiac hypertrophy, or abnormal growth of the heart. Finding ways to avert hypertrophy has emerged as a research priority.    Our focus is on Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptors (PPARs). Drugs that activate PPARs block hypertrophy. We hypothesize that PPARs protect against hypertrophy by activating an enzyme called diacylglycerol kinase (DGK); DGK then inhibits critical signals that promote hypertrophy.     We will study the mechanisms that mediate the ability of PPAR-DGK signaling to inhibit hypertrophy. We will use a well-established model of hypertrophy - rat heart muscle cells that are treated with a growth stimulus. We have identified targets within hypertrophy pathways at which PPAR-DGK signaling might be interfering. The effects of PPAR-DGK signaling on these targets will be pursued by genetic, biochemical, and imaging techniques. We will next determine the effects of PPAR-DGK signaling on hypertrophy in intact animals. We will switch to mice so we can take advantage of relevant genetically-manipulated mice. We will generate hypertrophy in normal mice, and in mice that do not express DGK or PPARs, by placing a band on the aorta. We will treat mice with PPAR-activating drugs and assess PPAR-DGK signaling.    There is major interest in regulation of cardiovascular function by PPARs. PPARs act directly on heart muscle cells to block hypertrophy, and we know that DGK is important in this process. We will be the first to study how PPAR-DGK signaling ultimately blocks cardiac hypertrophy.     The incidence of heart failure is predicted to double by 2025, so we are striving to block the transition from hypertrophy to heart failure. By learning how PPARs control this transition, we may discover molecular targets that can be manipulated for therapeutic gain to treat heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Tailored Myocardial Protection Strategy for Aged Hearts
Keywords-MotsClés: AGEING; CALCIUM; CARDIAC SURGERY; CARDIOPLEGIA; ISCHEMIA REPERFUSION INJURY; ISOLATED CELLS; ISOLATED HEARTS; LANGENDORFF APPARATUS; MYOCARDIAL PROTECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Canada's population is ageing and the number of elderly patients requiring heart surgery is increasing.  However, older patients face higher risks during heart surgery, in part due to age related changes in the heart cells that can cause potentially damaging calcium to accumulate during surgery.  We have found that a cardioplegia solution used to protect children's hearts during cardiac surgery also shows some potential benefits when tested in cells isolated from elderly rat hearts.  We are now proposing to further test this solution to determine if it is superior to standard cardioplegia at protecting old hearts.  We have also been studying a calcium blocker SEA0400 that is designed to prevent calcium accumulation in the heart muscle.  We plan to add SEA0400 to the cardioplegia solution we are developing for elderly patients and determine if it might be of further benefit.  Our proposed studies would be performed using hearts and heart muscle cells isolated from very old rats.  We will begin by testing cardioplegia solutions in whole hearts to determine if they prevent damage and result in improved cardiac function in elderly hearts.  We will then use single heart muscle cells to study the mechanism of action of the cardioplegia solutions and adjust the formulation to optimally prevent accumulation of calcium in the cell.  It is our goal to optimize a cardioplegia solution specifically designed for elderly patients that could be tested in a group of patients undergoing cardiac surgery who are at very high risk of complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Central effects of stress
Keywords-MotsClés: COPING; DOPAMINE; GLUTAMATE; MEDIAL PREFRONTAL CORTEX; MICRODIALYSIS; RATS; STRESS; VOLTAMMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: The focus of this research project is on the brain circuitry that controls how we cope with stress.  I am particularly interested  in the role played by the medial prefrontal cortex (PFC), a brain region that reaches its full development relatively late in life,  that is during late adolescence/early adulthood.  This brain region is interesting for several reasons.  First, it controls several  complexe tasks such as decision making and planning.  Second, in part because it matures slowly, the PFC is particularly vulnerable to a host of traumatic events, including stressors, which can cause it to develop abnormally and lead to a number of mental disorders. Third but not least, the PFC is extremely sensitive to stressors and plays an important role in mounting the appropriate coping responses. Interestingly, the left and right PFC appear to control different aspects of our responses to stressors.  My research is aimed at understanding the mechanisms by which the PFC is activated by stressors and in particular how the left and right PFC communicate with each other when coping with stressors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic dissection of aneuploidy tolerance
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEUPLOIDY; CELL CYCLE CHECKPOINTS; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; GENOME-WIDE RNAI SCREEN; GENOMIC INSTABILITY; HUMAN CELLS; LIVE-CELL IMAGING; P53; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Our genetic information is stored within DNA and organized into chromosomes. Losses or gains of chromosomes (also called aneuploidy) is a hallmark of most cancer cells. Aneuploidy leads to genetic imbalances and has been linked to the development of malignancies. Although aneuploidy has been shown to hamper cellular fitness, cancer is a disease of malfunctioning cells that multiply in an uncontrolled fashion. This paradox implies that cancer cells have escaped the normal regulatory mechanisms responsible for limiting the proliferation of aneuploid cells.  Our understanding of the mechanisms limiting the proliferation of aneuploid cells is sparse and it is thus of pivotal importance to identify the factors responsible for this effect. My research plan involves the systematic inactivation of genes in normal human cells followed by the selection of those genes which, upon inactivation, allow aneuploid cells to multiply and thrive. Subsequently, I will characterize the function of the genes identified in order to understand how human cells sense and respond to the challenges of genetic imbalances. These genes are likely to be inactivated in human tumors.  Efficient cancer therapies aim at selectively targeting tumor cells. It is thus essential to characterize the fundamental differences between normal and cancer cells, one of which is the ability of cancer cells to outcompete normal cells despite often being aneuploid. Identifying the mechanisms determining whether or not aneuploid cells multiply and how these processes are deregulated in cancer will offer new avenues to selectively attack cancer cells in future therapeutic approaches. Genes identified in this study might also become useful for their prognostic value, since it is estimated that 90% of human solid tumors become aneuploid.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tumor necrosis factor receptor mediated signaling dynamics and the determination of cancer cell fate
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; COMPUTATIONAL BIOLOGY; LIVE CELL IMAGING; NF-KB; P65; SIGNAL DYNAMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION MICROSCOPY (TIRF); TUMOR NECROSIS FACTOR (TNF); TUMOR NECROSIS FACTOR RECEPTOR (TNFR)
Abstract-Résumé: In the human body, the fate of each cell is determined by a decision process that integrates multiple signals or cues from the environment and surrounding cells. One such cue, Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF), is of particular interest to me because it can induce several different cell fates. In healthy cells, TNF induces proliferation or death in a context dependent manner. Each cell must evaluate the cue and react appropriately; damage to the decision 'circuit' can lead to diseases such as cancer if cells fail to die when they should. TNF has a pro-death effect on cancer cells; however, cancer cells display marked variability in response to TNF-induced death which limits its use as a stand-alone treatment. This variability is intriguing because one would presume that seemingly identical cancer cells should all be capable of committing to death, yet subtle differences lead some cells to interpret this cue differently and survive. Cells recognize TNF in their environment by a protein that moves along on the cell surface, the TNF-receptor (TNFR). TNFR is activated when it captures TNF causing it to form into larger clusters which successively activate the pro-life and pro-death decision 'circuits'. We hypothesize that the dynamics of activated receptors, such as their location, mobility and clustering on the cell surface determine if pro-life or -death circuits dominate. Here, I will address this directly by monitoring TNFR1 mobility and clustering in living cancer cells with cutting-edge single-molecule time-lapse microscopy. I will take advantage of variability within cell populations to associate receptor behavior with decision signals and cell fate. Ideally, this knowledge could lead to the design of drugs that target the clustering and mobility of TNFR in ways that uniformly kill TNF-sensitive cancer cells. More broadly, the relationship between receptor dynamics and fate will be relevant to understanding why some tumors form and how they evade the immune system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of invariant Natural Killer T cell development and function
Keywords-MotsClés: CD1D; IMMUNOMODULATION; LIPID ANTIGENS; NATURAL KILLER T CELLS; NKT CELL DEVELOPMENT; OP9-DL1; TCR RETROGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells are lymphocytes that respond to lipid antigens presented by a molecule named CD1d. Activated iNKT cells rapidly produce large amounts of various solubles mediators that influence ensuing immune responses. Consistent with this, iNKT cells have protective or deleterious functions during the immune responses associated with cancer, inflammation, autoimmunity and infection. Understanding the mechanisms controlling the activation and functional plasticity of these cells constitutes a major challenge. iNKT cells express particular T cell receptors (TCRs) that are able to recognize a variety of host- (self) as well as microbe-derived lipids presented by CD1d. Self-lipid recognition is important for the development and activation of these cells, although the relevant CD1d-binding self-lipids remain poorly defined. Recent work, including from our group, demonstrated that iNKT TCRs recognize CD1d-lipid complexes in a one-size-fits-all strategy, suggesting that iNKT cells are devoid of antigenic specificity. We further demonstrated that the lipids as well as the TCR composition modulate the affinity between CD1d and iNKT TCRs. Whether the strength of CD1d-lipid-TCR interactions controls iNKT cell responses quantitatively and qualitatively remains an open question. In this proposal, we will address these questions that are a direct extension of our previous work. Our specific goals are to identify CD1d-binding self-lipids and define their regulation of expression in health and disease, as well as their role in iNKT cell development and response. We will also investigate whether the strength of CD1d-lipid-TCR interactions translates into differential biological responses from these cells. The results from the proposed studies will shed light into crucial aspects of iNKT cell biology, and will ultimately help the rational design of novel immunotherapies that target iNKT cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bioavailable plasmalogen precursors in models of Parkinson's disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTORADIOGRAPHY; BEHAVIORAL MEASURES; DOPAMINE; DOPAMINOMIMETIC-INDUCED DYSKINESIAS; HPLC; MONKEY; MPTP; PARKINSON; PLASMALOGEN; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson disease (PD) is a progressive neurological condition affecting 100,000 Canadians and will likely increase due to the aging population. The primary biochemical deficiency in PD is lack of the neurotransmitter dopamine, which is caused by loss of brain cells producing this neurotransmitter. There is no cure for PD. Preventing or protecting against brain dopamine cell death is not yet available for PD but laboratory studies have found promising agents. The most common medication used in PD, levodopa, is converted into dopamine in the brain. While this is an effective treatment, PD is a progressive disease and with time motor complications such as dyskinesias can develop. Dyskinesias are twisting and turning movements that may be quite disabling and can be very difficult to manage. Dr. Di Paolo has previously reported that DHA (omega-3) inhibits levodopa-induced dyskinesias in the MPTP monkey model of PD. Moreover DHA was reported to be neuroprotective against MPTP toxicity in mice. Dr. Wood has designed orally bioavailable plasmalogen precursor analogs that effectively increase steady-state DHA and lipoic acid levels in plasma. Lipoic acid also replenishes brain glutathione and thereby acts as a neuroprotectant. This project will determine if a plasmalogen treatment can reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesias in MPTP monkeys and will investigate the neuroprotective drug effects in MPTP mice. Brain dopamine, DHA and plasmalogens will be measured. This treatment could protect dopamine neurons from degeneration, delay progression of the disease as well as the use of levodopa and reduce clinical doses thus delaying the onset of dyskinesias. Moreover, if dyskinesias are already established the treatment may reduce their expression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Visceral obesity/ectopic fat and non-invasive markers of atherosclerosis: A cardiometabolic-cardiovascular imaging study
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARDIOMETABOLIC RISK FACTORS/MARKERS; CARDIORESPIRATORY FITNESS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE AND TYPE 2 DIABETES; VISCERAL ADIPOSITY/ECTOPIC FAT
Abstract-Résumé: Although it is frequently mentioned in the media that overweight and obesity have reached epidemic proportions worldwide and in our country, some Canadians are perplexed and sometimes confused about the role of obesity in diabetes and heart disease. In fact, we even hear from time to time that there could be "healthy" obese individuals. In clinical practice, assessment of obesity as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a challenge as even some physicians are confused. However, studies conducted in our laboratory and by other research teams around the world over the last 20 years have clearly shown that body shape is more important than body size when evaluating the risk of overweight/obesity and that high accumulation of abdominal fat (excess belly fat) increases the risk of diabetes and CVD.  We now need to better understand the link between excess belly fat and atherosclerosis (the thickening of artery walls by fatty deposits, also referred to as atherosclerotic plaque), leading to complications such as angina (chest pain) and myocardial infarction (heart attacks). Using non-invasive imaging techniques such as magnetic resonance imaging, we therefore propose to examine the relationships between measures of fatness and of abdominal fat and the size of atherosclerotic plaque in large blood vessels of apparently healthy human subjects. This study is also a unique opportunity to look, for the first time, at the relationship between belly fat, blood sugar, several well-known risk factors for heart disease (cholesterol, blood pressure, cardiorespiratory fitness, etc.) and the size of atherosclerotic plaques. This research program should pave the way to the development of new improved preventive/therapeutic approaches focussing not on body weight but rather on abdominal fat and associated blood abnormalities which are predictive of the development of atherosclerotic plaques leading to the premature development of heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of skeletal growth and patterning.
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGENITAL MALFORMATIONS; DIFFERENTIATION; GENE REGULATION; SKELETOGENESIS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal is aimed at understanding the molecular pathways that coordinate the growth and development of the skull.  Defects in the formation of the skull account for a large number of congenital malformations (i.e. present at birth) in Canadian children.  Development of the skull is a complex process. Growth of the skull (or cranium) must occur in concert with the growth of the brain.  As the brain rapidly increases in size early in postnatal development, the skull must remain plastic to accommodate these changes.   Such plasticity is achieved by cranial sutures, which are fibrous joints that form at the interface of opposing cranial bones.  These sutures remain unfused  during early childhood in what is commonly referred to as the "soft spot" of the skull.  The premature fusion of the cranial sutures causes craniosynostosis and occurs at a frequency of 1 in 2500 live births.  Unless surgically treated, this disorder can impede brain growth and impair a child's intellectual development. The molecular and cellular mechanisms that regulate cranial growth are poorly understood. The gene FOXC1 is essential for normal craniofacial(i.e. skull and face) development in humans and mice. We will utilize genetic and biochemical approaches to dissect the role of FOXC1 in the formation of the skull. These experiments will improve our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms that control cranial bone formation. Such research will be instrumental in understanding how dysregulation of developmental pathways contribute to the pathologies of craniofacial malformations. Furthermore, these studies are essential if we wish develop safer and more effective means to treat craniofacial malformations.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Response in Pancreatic beta-Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CELLULAR STRESS RESPONSE; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM STRESS; PANCREATIC BETA CELLS; PRIMARY CULTURED CELLS; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal plans to study how insulin secreting pancreatic cells deal with the stress of producing large amounts of insulin and how this stress may eventually cause the cells to fail or die. The dysfunction or death of these cells is a direct cause of hyperglycemia that defines type 2 diabetes. Understanding the impact of this stress on insulin producing cells, as well as the mechanisms that these cells use to protect themselves from this stress may lead to novel strategies to preserve insulin cell function as a treatment for type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Untangling the Web: Understanding the Abrupt Increase Chlamydia Risk in Ontario through Applied Epidemiology and Mathematical Modeling
Keywords-MotsClés: CHLAMYDIA TRACHOMATIS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; LABORATORY SERVICES; MATHEMATICAL MODELING/SIMULATION; PUBLIC HEALTH POLICY; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS; SURVEILLANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Chlamydia is the most common infectious disease in Canada, and Chlamydia infection can lead to infertility, pain, and risk of pregnancy in the tubes in women.  Because people with Chlamydia often don't know they have it, people get tested for this infection and treated if they test positive.  However, even though testing programs have grown greatly over the past 20 years, Chlamydia rates still seem to be going up, rather than down.  This increase could be real (and related to unexpected effects of antibiotic treatment, or changes in behaviour), or it could simply be a result of us finding more infections because we're looking for them.  We propose to analyze information on Chlamydia reports, laboratory testing rates, and rates of Chlamydia complications, in order to figure out whether or not rates of Chlamydia infection are truly rising in three major Ontario jurisdictions: Hamilton, Toronto, and York Region.  If they are truly rising, we will try to find out why using statistical models.  We will also use this information to create mathematical simulations that can be used to better understand how Chlamydia is being spread, and to pinpoint the best and most efficient ways to reduce the spread of Chlamydia, using the limited health resources at our disposal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of novel FFA1 and GPR120 ligands and their use in elucidating the pharmacology, function, and clinical utility of these receptors in the treatment of obesity and diabetes.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; FFA1; FREE FATTY ACID; G PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTOR; GPR120; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: G protein coupled receptors are a large family of proteins responsible for producing many different biological effects.  Not only are these receptor proteins the most common target for currently available drugs, but they are also known to respond to a great variety of different stimuli including: light, odor, neurotransmitters, and hormones just to name a few.  One recently identified family of these receptor proteins has been shown to generate its biological effects in response to free fatty acids, chemicals that are critically involved in metabolism.  Interestingly, two of these proteins that respond to fatty acids have also shown promise as potential targets for the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes.  In the proposed work, the basic biological functions of these two free fatty acid sensitive receptor proteins will be probed, specifically with the aim of identifying new chemical compounds that will produce different effects on each of the two receptor proteins.  The identification of such chemicals will then be critically useful in determining any role that these two proteins will ultimately have in the treatment of obesity and diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the tissue specific role(s) of Glucose-Dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide on whole body glucose metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE TISSUE; ADRENAL; BETA-CELL; DIABETES; GENETIC MODELS; GIP; INCRETINS; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: The current epidemic of obesity is leading to a greater incidence of metabolic complications including Type 2 Diabetes. Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) is a hormone made by the gut that can potently increase pancreatic insulin secretion. However, administration of GIP in animals causes insulin resistance and may contribute to the development of Type 2 Diabetes. One theory that explains these contrary findings is that GIP effects tissues other than the pancreas in a negative manner. Besides the pancreas, GIP action has been shown to take place in both adipose tissue and the adrenal glands, suggesting these are potential sites for GIP to cause insulin resistance. In adipose tissue, GIP increases the production of harmful adipokines, hormones that can cause insulin resistance. In the adrenals glands, GIP causes corticosterone release, a hormone that also causes insulin resistance and increases fat mass. It is hypothesized that a loss of GIP action in either of these tissues will improve insulin sensitivity. To test this, mice will be genetically created so that they lack GIP action exclusively in either adipose tissue or the adrenal glands. These mice will be compared to normal mice that have functional GIP action. In all mice, induction of insulin resistance will be accomplished with either high-fat feeding or pharmacological destruction of beta-cells. An insulin resistance phenotype will be tested for by measuring blood glucose and insulin levels, circulating triglycerides and free fatty acids, monitoring body weight and fat mass, and challenging with glucose and insulin sensitivity tests. It is expected that selective inhibition of GIP action in either adipose tissue or the adrenal glands will result in a similar phenotype of improved insulin action and resistance to diet-induced obesity. Overall, these studies will add to our understanding of the importance of GIP in the development of Type 2 Diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nogo, the ER-mitochondria unit and the vascular remodeling of pulmonary hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: VASCULAR REMODELING OF PULMONARY HYPERTENSION
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary hypertension is a deadly and relatively common disease that kills patients within three years from the time of diagnosis.  While existing therapies improve the quality of life and improves some symptoms, they do not appear to prolong life and they do not reverse the condition.  Pulmonary hypertension is caused by excessive growth of cells that eventually occlude the lumen of the blood vessels in the lung, putting strain on the right chambers of the heart which eventually fail, killing the patients.  In this work, we proposed that a newly discovered protein that regulates the communication between different organelles within the cell is expressed at much higher levels in the diseased lung arteries compared to the healthy ones, both in humans and animals.  We proposed to show that this increase in protein levels (this protein is called "nogo") explains a number of unresolved abnormalities that have been described in this disease.  This might open a new window in approaching this mysterious disease.  In addition, we aim to show that decreasing or preventing the increase of this protein may be a new therapy for this disease.  Because this protein is increased selectively in the lung vessels, sparing the rest of the vessels in the body, such therapies might have less adverse effects and offer better quality of life to the treated patients.

Keywords-MotsClés: DETERMINANTS DE LA SANTE MENTALE; DETERMINANTS DES TROUBLES MENTAUX; DETERMINANTS ENVIRONNEMENTAUX; DETERMINANTS PSYCHOSOCIAUX; ENQUETE DANS LA COMMUNAUTE; EPIDEMIOLOGIE SOCIALE ET PSYCHIATRIQUE; INSTRUMENTS STANDARDISES; ETUDE  PROSPECTIVE; ETUDE LONGITUDINALE
Abstract-Résumé: En 2006, nous avons recu des IRSC une subvention d'equipe pour creer la premiere zone d'etudes epidemiologiques au Canada pour determiner l'etat de sante mentale de la population. La subvention que nous demandons permettra de poursuivre ce programme de recherche qui vise a evaluer la prevalence des troubles mentaux et les besoins en termes de services de sante mentale. Nous suivons un echantillon de 2400 personnes du Sud-ouest de Montreal a travers le temps que nous interviewons aux deux ans. Nous examinons ce qui change dans leur vie et ses effets sur leur sante mentale. Cette etude permet donc de mieux connaitre les determinants psychosociaux et environnementaux qui affectent la sante mentale et la qualite de vie de la population. Une equipe multidisciplinaire composee de psychologues, psychiatres, epidemiologistes, anthropologues, sociologues, administrateurs de la sante et de geographes permet d'etudier et de comprendre la sante mentale dans sa globalite. Nos resultats servent a adapter les services de sante mentale aux besoins de la population et a mettre en place des programmes de prevention et de promotion de la sante mentale.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chemokine Network and HIV-1 Pathogenesis: Phenotypic and Functional Characterization of New Th17 Subsets Permissive versus Resistant to Viral Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRAL IMMUNITY; CHEMOKINES/CHEMOKINE RECEPTORS; GENOME WIDE ANALYSIS OF GENE EXPRESSION; HIV REPLICATION AND VIRAL RESERVOIRS; HIV RESTRICTION AND PERMISSIVENESS FACTORS; POLYCHROMATIC FLOW CYTOMETRY ANALYSIS AND SORTING; REAL TIME PCR AND RT-PCR; RNA INTERFERENCE; T CELL SURVIVAL AND DEATH; TH17 CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV) establishes a lethal infection by mechanisms that are not clearly understood and viral eradication is not achieved under the current antiretroviral therapies (ART). HIV infection is associated with a rapid depletion of memory CD4+ T-cells from the gut-associated lymphoid tissues (GALT), impaired mucosal integrity, and microbial translocation from the gut. These alterations are a cause for chronic immune activation and disease progression in HIV-infected individuals, including subjects with slow disease progression. Among CD4+ T-cells, Th17 cells play a critical role in maintaining mucosal barrier integrity and immunity against bacterial pathogens. Th17 cells are preferentially depleted from the GALT of HIV-infected individuals and their functional restoration under long-term ART is only partial. We and others demonstrated that Th17 cells are highly permissive to HIV infection. However, in preliminary studies we identified a new Th17 subset that is preserved during disease progression and is potentially resistant to HIV infection. Our hypothesis is that HIV infects some but not all Th17 subsets. We propose to identify molecular mechanisms underlying differences in immunological function and viral permissiveness between Th17 subsets. This research proposal will reveal new therapeutic strategies to prevent HIV replication in Th17 cells, while improving their role in mucosal immunity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Eye Disease, Mobility Restriction,and the Risk of Subsequent Health Problems:  A Longitudinal Study
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION; AGING; EYE DISEASE; GLAUCOMA; LIFE SPACE; MOBILITY; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: The loss of eyesight at an older age can profoundly disrupt a person's life in many ways. This project focuses on how age-related eye disease affects a person's ability to move around independently in the environment. There is a concern that people with eye disease may overly restrict their mobility and therefore will enter a stage of decline in physical and mental health. We will examine this process by extending our current study into a 4 year study. At Maisonneuve-Rosemont Hospital in Montreal, Quebec, we are in the process of recruiting people who have either age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, or corneal disease. We will compare them to older adults who do not have significant eye disease (440 people total). We will collect data from them 2 more times over a 4 year period and will measure vision, perform mobility tests, and ask questions about driving behaviours, falls in the last year, fear of falling, geographic extent of mobility (life space), exercise habits, and health status. This research will be important to understand the process of how eye disease affects mobility difficulties and subsequent health problems in older adults. This information will help us to more effectively design interventions to help people with eye disease to stay active and healthy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multigenic analysis and chemical drug screening using in vivo zebrafish models of motor neurodegenerative disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; ATAXIA; ATX2; CHEMICAL SCREEN; FUS; GENETIC INTERACTION; SMN1; SPINAL MUSCULAR ATROPHY; STABLE TRANSGENIC MODELS; TARDBP; THERAPEUTIC COMPOUNDS; ZEBRAFISH MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: The concept of genetic networks spaning neurodegenerative diseases has been emerging, with some genes playing pivotal roles, such as the TDP-43 encoding TARDBP gene which is mutated in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). ALS is a genetic neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the death of large motor neurons in the cerebral cortex and spinal cord. Mutations in the TARDBP and FUS genes account for nearly 3% of cases. The Drapeau lab has extensive expertise in zebrafish spinal cord neurobiology and models of hereditary neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS. They showed that TARDBP and FUS genes interact in a common pathogenic pathway. Moreover, they have created a stable inducible transgenic zebrafish which displays a progressive motor neuron disorder mimicking disease progression.  In this research project, we propose to do multigenic analyses using zebrafish model in order to delineate the genetic network of the ALS-associated TARDBP gene. This will allow characterization of molecular pathways shared by the broad spectrum of neurodegenerative disorders. We also propose to develop new transgenic zebrafish models of ALS, which will be uniquely useful to better understand the disease mechanism. In addition, we plan to screen libraries of several thousand small chemicals, including clinically approved drugs, for their ability to suppress the pathogenic phenotypes in order to discover molecules with therapeutic potential. As the molecular mechanism leading to neuronal degeneration is still unknown, it is not yet possible to perform direct chemical in vitro screens. Large scale chemical genetic screens in zebrafish models of human diseases have already led to the identification of several molecules which are currently in clinical trials; thus, we believe that these in vivo zebrafish models are the best starting point to develop a pharmacological screening approach to discover therapies for this devastating disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Establishing annulus fibrosus interfaces:  towards tissue engineering an intervertebral disc
Keywords-MotsClés: IN VITRO; IN VIVO; INTERFACES; INTERVERTEBRAL DISC; PHENOTYPE; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Degeneration of the intervertebral disc, a poorly understood disease, can result in pain and neurological symptoms. The disease is so common that approximately 1 in 50 Canadians become disabled by neck/back pain. Currently, there is no optimal treatment for these individuals. Although the pain is rarely life threatening, the cost in terms of lost productivity and suffering is enormous. There is a growing consensus that surgical treatments used currently are not effective and cannot be further optimized. Thus, there is a great need to develop an entirely new approach to treat this disease. The long term goal of our research is to generate, using a regenerative medicine approach, an intervertebral disc in culture composed of tissue which structurally and functionally approaches that which occurs in the human body and is suitable to use as a replacement for a damaged disc. The intervertebral disc is composed of three different tissue types, a centrally placed nucleus pulposus surrounded by annulus fibrosus which is integrated to bone, in part, through cartilage endplate. In previous studies we developed the methodology to make almost all the components of the disc. We are now focusing on making the remaining tissue, the annulus fibrosus. The proposed experiments are directed towards characterizing the native annulus tissue and forming annulus fibrosus tissue in vitro (in the lab) whose organization mimics the annulus fibrosus tissue that occurs in vivo. This tissue will be used to form a model of the disc. Developing interfaced tissues will not only facilitate progression to generating a functional biological disc replacement but also lead to an in vitro model suitable to use to study mechanisms regulating tissue regeneration and degeneration. The proposed research will enable development of personalized treatments for those disabled by chronic neck/back pain and facilitate healthy aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Building knowledge on determinants of health of immigrants in smaller cities: A Photovoice Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNICITY; GENDER; HEALTH; IMMIGRANT SETTLEMENT; IMMIGRANTS; MARGINALIZED POPULATIONS; MENTAL HEALTH; PHOTOVOICE; SMALL CITIES; SOCIAL-GEOGRAPHIC FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed study will develop knowledge about the impact of immigration and settlement on the health and wellbeing of immigrants in Canadian small cities. The increased number of immigrants to smaller cities is expected to benefit the social and economic progress of these cities. However, the benefits to immigrants' health and wellbeing are unknown when smaller cities are unprepared to meet their needs in the context of financial cuts to essential services and immigrant settlement services. Therefore, this study seeks to understand: 1) What are the roles of settlement experiences in shaping recent visible ethnic minority immigrants' health and wellbeing in the social-geographic context of smaller cities?  2) How do recent ethnic minority immigrants conceptualize an understanding of their health and wellbeing in their social-geographical context?  3) What are the strategies that recent visible ethnic minority immigrants develop and use to maintain their health and wellbeing in smaller cities?  The study seeks to illuminate the experience of immigrants in small cities by making their existence and life conditions visible by using Photovoice, a Participatory Action Research (PAR) method.  A sample of 72 eligible participants ages 24 to 44 will be drawn from Kelowna, British Columbia, Red Deer, Alberta, and Brandon, Manitoba.  The perspectives and stories of immigrants' health and wellbeing will be collected at each site.  Participants will be provided cameras to take pictures that represent their perceptions and experiences of their settlement experience, health, and wellbeing from their point of view.  Photo-elicitation interviews will provide dynamic insights for building better understanding of immigrants' experiences in smaller cities.  An in-depth understanding of these factors is critical to developing appropriate forms of clinical care to prevent poor health outcomes among new and not-so-new immigrants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Déterminants moléculaires responsables de l'implication de protéines du cycle visuel dans la dégénérescence des photorécepteurs
Keywords-MotsClés: CYCLE VISUEL; LIAISON MEMBRANAIRE; LECITHINE RETINOL ACYLTRANSFERASE; PHOTORECEPTEURS; RETINITE PIGMENTAIRE; RETINOL DEHYDROGENASE; STRUCTURE DE PROTEINE; VISION; EPITHELIUM PIGMENTAIRE RETINIEN
Abstract-Résumé: La lecithine retinol acyltransferase (LRAT) et les retinol dehydrogenases (RDH) sont des enzymes impliquees dans la regeneration du pigment visuel des photorecepteurs. Des mutations de la LRAT et de la RDH sont responsables d'un certain pourcentage de degenerescences des photorecepteurs. Ces mutations menent a la production d'enzymes inactives. L'objectif de ces travaux de recherche est d'identifier les determinants moleculaires responsables de la fonction normale et aberrante de ces enzymes. Nous proposons donc de determiner la structure de ces proteines normales ainsi que celle de ces enzymes portant une mutation afin de comprendre pourquoi les proteines mutees menent a la degenerescence des photorecepteurs. Nous proposons aussi de determiner si une liaison membranaire inappropriee de la RDH pourrait etre responsable de la perte de sa fonction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Granzyme B in Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEURYSM; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; GRANZYME; PROTEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a disease that occurs in the main blood vessel (aorta) that supplies blood to the lower extremities. During AAA, weakening of the wall of the aorta causes it to balloon outwards. When the vessel expands to a certain point, it can rupture leading to abdominal bleeding. If not treated immediately, there is a 90% chance of death. AAA is a silent disease and rupture is often the first sign of disease. As such, AAA is the 13th leading cause of death in North America. Unfortunately, the only treatment for AAA is at later stages when the risk of dying from surgery outweighs the risk of rupture. There are no pharmacological treatments for small aneurysms. We have identified a protein degrading enzyme (GrB) that breaks down the proteins responsible for maintaining the structural integrity of the aorta wall. When this enzyme is blocked, AAA progression and rupture are reduced. The current proposal will determine how GrB attacks and weakens blood vessels and whether inhibitors targeted to this protein can prevent the disease from occurring or advancing further if the disease is already present. Due to early screening programs that have been implemented, it is expected that there will be increasing demand for new, non-surgical treatment options that can be used early after detection to prevent AAA growth and rupture. Such treatments would ultimately reduce both the patient's sense of helplessness and the need for surgery.
