TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and functional characterization of NPHP5, a novel centrosomal protein implicated in human ciliary disease and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CYCLE; CENTROSOMES; CEP290; CILIA; CILIOPATHIES; NPHP5; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: The centrosome is the major microtubule-organizing center of animal cells. It is best known for its role in cell division (in forming the mitotic spindle) and in templating the formation of cell cilia critical for proliferation, differentiation, and development. Centrosome aberrations are implicated in a wide variety of diseases including cancer, and supernumerary centrosomes are a distinguishing feature of many cancer cells. In addition, ciliary defects can also mediate tumorigenesis and induce ciliary disorders such as polycystic kidney disease. Although centrosomes were identified over a hundred years ago, their molecular structure and composition are not fully understood, and the functions of many individual centrosomal components remain elusive. Our research focuses on one novel centrosomal protein, NPHP5, whose de-regulation is implicated in human ciliary disease and cancer. Through three specific aims, we will examine the function of NPHP5 at the molecular, cellular, and organismal level, and evaluate its contribution to disease. These study results will serve as an important step towards understanding the pathological mechanisms of centrosome dysfunction, and in guiding the development of novel diagnostic and therapeutic applications for diseased patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism(s) of autophagy regulation by the Rab1 GTPase
Keywords-MotsClés: ATG5-ATG12 CONJUGATION; AUTOPHAGY; CO-IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; GENE KNOCKDOWN BY SIRNA; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; PULSE-CHASE; RAB1 GTPASE; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: When cells are under stress conditions, such as starvation or infection, a cellular process called autophagy (meaning "self-eating") is activated as a survival mechanism.  This process plays a very important role in many human diseases, such as cancer, neurodegenerative disease and muscle disease. We recently identified a new cellular regulator of autophagy, called Rab1.  In our proposed research project, we will determine how Rab1 affects the machinery that controls the autophagy process.  Our study will provide new insights into the understanding of autophagy and may lead to new ways to control autophagy as a means to prevent disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: DOIT Trial: vitamin D Outcomes and Interventions in Toddlers
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA EXACERBATIONS; CHILD HEALTH; PEDIATRICS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SUPPLEMENTATION; UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTIONS; VIRAL INFECTIONS; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Vitamin D can be made in the skin by exposure to sunlight and can be found in certain foods. Vitamin D levels are alarmingly low in many North American children. Several health issues have been linked with low vitamin D. These include colds caused by viruses and asthma attacks. However, no study has determined whether vitamin D supplementation can reduce the risk of these conditions in young children where they are most common and most severe.  The goals of this study are to determine whether wintertime 'high dose' vitamin D supplementation of preschoolers can prevent colds and asthma attacks. We also aim to work out how much money would be saved by the health care system and society if preschoolers were routinely supplemented with Vitamin D during the winter.  We believe that preschoolers receiving 'high dose' vitamin D supplementation during the wintertime will  be less likely to have colds, asthma attacks, and low vitamin D levels and will be less likely to use the medical system and keep their parents away from work.  Exposure to sunlight to make vitamin D is limited for much of the year in Canada. Therefore, understanding whether vitamin D supplementation can decrease common child health issues like colds and asthma attacks is of critical importance and may offer a large reduction in suffering and economic costs. This information would be very important to parents, doctors, employers and policy makers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autophagy in skeletal muscle
Keywords-MotsClés: ATROPHY; AUTOPHAGY; DENERVATION; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; MUSCLE DISUSE; NEUROMUSCULAR DYSFUNCTION; PGC-1; SKELETAL MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: The muscles that we use for movements and locomotion are highly adaptable.  For example, muscles can undergo enlargement (hypertrophy) in response to exercise, and they can shrink, or atrophy, when they are not used for prolonged periods of time.  This adaptability has been studied for many years, but recently it has become known that a cellular process known as "autophagy" may be very important in the adaptive process.  Autophagy, or "self-eating", is a series of events within the cell that leads to the breakdown of damaged cellular components, like internal organelles.  We are particularly interested in the mitochondria within cells, because they are the organelles that generate energy for cell survival.  Mitochondrial number within muscle cells is markedly reduced, and the remaining organelles do not function well, during conditions of chronic muscle disuse, leading to increased muscle fatigue and the production of damaging molecules called "reactive oxygen species", or ROS.  An increase in the formation of ROS can lead to cell death, and to the degradation of DNA.  The role of autophagy appears to be to remove, or digest, these damaged organelles, in order to minimize the consequences to the cell of having mitochondria that function poorly.  The importance of autophagy has only recently been recognized in muscle.  Therefore, the processes involved in the regulation of autophagy are still poorly understood.  This is important for our understanding of muscle health, and our comprehension of how muscle adapts to exercise, or particularly the lack of exercise.  The purpose of this research proposal is to clearly identify some of the important regulatory features of autophagy in our muscles, using animal and cell culture models of chronic muscle disuse.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Accelerated Partial Breast Irradiation
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCELERATED PARTIAL BREAST IRRADIATION; BREAST CANCER; RADIATION THERAPY; RANDOMIZED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Breast irradiation is normally given following breast conserving surgery to reduce high risk of cancer recurrence and to prevent the need for mastectomy. Breast irradiation is currently given for 3 to 5 weeks and is associated with fatigue, irradiation of the skin, firmness of the breast, and pain, which can have a significant impact on quality of life. In order to improve the convenience and quality of life for patients who receive breast irradiation, investigators have evaluated short accelerated radiation therapy schedules lasting only one week. Radiation is delivered only to the surgical site and appears to be well tolerated. The purpose of this study is to determine if this approach called accelerated partial breast irradiation (APBI) delivered in one week is as effective as whole breast irradiation (WBI) delivered in 3 to 6 weeks in women with early breast cancer. The primary outcome of the study is recurrence of cancer in the breast. Important secondary outcomes are treatment morbidity and quality of life. As of 25Feb2011, 1938 of a total 2128 patients have been entered at 28 centres across Canada, 4 Australian Centres and 1 New Zealand centre. If APBI is equally effective to current techniques, this will permit Canadian women with breast cancer to be treated in a short period of time at similar or less cost. Such an approach will benefit both women with breast cancer and the cancer system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of RanBPM function in apoptosis and cell transformation
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER; CELL TRANSFORMATION; DNA DAMAGE; DOUBLE STRANDED DNA BREAK RESPONSE; ERK; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; SIRNA
Abstract-Résumé: Damage to the cells genetic material (DNA) can lead to the development of cancer if not repaired properly. Cells respond to DNA damage by using a variety of pathways to repair the DNA lesions. If repair cannot be completed, cells commit to pathways leading to cell death by suicide, a process called apoptosis. Disruption of the mechanisms that control the repair of DNA and apoptosis results in genomic instability, the underlying cause of carcinogenesis. Moreover, defects in pathways that lead to apoptosis also lead to resistance of cancer cells to therapeutic agents.  We recently identified RanBPM as a factor that induces cell death when over-expressed in cancer cells. Moreover, we found that RanBPM was necessary for the activation of cell death pathways induced by DNA damage. We have also determined that RanBPM controls the levels of Bcl-2, a critical regulator of the apoptotic machinery that is over-expressed in many types of cancer. Our recent results suggest that RanBPM inhibits the extracellular regulated kinases (ERK) pathway which is often found over-activated in many cancer types. The aim of this project is to elucidate the means through which RanBPM promotes cell death and investigate its potential role in preventing tumorigenesis. In particular, we will characterize the determinants of RanBPM that mediate its ability to induce cell death in response to DNA damage. We will investigate how RanBPM functions to inhibit the ERK pathway and determine whether RanBPM functions as a tumour suppressor to prevent tumour formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modular Tissue Engineering for Islet Transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; FAT TISSUE; ISLETS; MICROFLUIDICS; REMODELING; TISSUE ENGINEERING; VASCULARIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: While islet transplantation is a promising treatment for the 1% of Canadians who live with insulin dependent (type 1) diabetes, the majority of islets (perhaps 60%) in current protocols are lost almost immediately upon transplantation. This is due to inflammatory responses and a failure to make intimate connections between the beta cell (the glucose sensing and insulin making portion of the islet) and the blood vessels of the host. The absence of these vessels near and in the islet impairs islet survival and function. Our approach ("modular tissue engineering") enables the creation of uniform, scalable and most importantly vascularized constructs. Small collagen rods ("modules") are embedded with functional cells (here, pancreatic islets) along with support cells derived from fat tissue and surface seeded with endothelial cells, the cells that line blood vessels.  Random packing of many modules creates a porous construct (a "pseudo-fat pad") where the gaps among modules form interconnected channels lined with endothelial cells. Once implanted, the endothelialized channels connect with the host vessels (through a remodelling process) and enable blood flow to nourish the transplanted islets and thereby maintain their viability and function. We expect that this engineered vasculature will also provide at least some of the required intimate contact between the beta cell and the vessels of the host. The specific aims address the fate of modules and islets in diabetic mice and in vitro, the latter using advanced optical imaging methods and custom designed microfluidic chambers made by photolithography as adapted from the processes used to make microelectronic chips. The long-term objective is to enable islet transplantation to be successful.

TitreApplicationTitle: Teens Taking Charge: An Internet-based Self-management Program for Adolescents with Arthritis: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; E-HEALTH; INTERNET INTERVENTION; JUVENILE IDIOPATHIC ARTHRITIS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SELF-MANAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is a chronic childhood illness that negatively impacts quality of life. While activities to manage JIA are shared by the child and family, adolescents are expected to assume a greater role in disease management. Better management early on could help prevent worsening of the disease and symptoms. Therefore, it is important to develop programs to make it easier for adolescents to manage their disease. A trial design will be used to determine whether a web-based home management program is effective in reducing symptoms and improving quality of life in adolescents with arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Acquired abnormalities in the hemostatic system in obese children prone to Type 2 diabetes:  Mechanisms and interventions for risk of cardiovascular disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BLOOD PROTEINS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CELL SIGNALLING; CLINICAL STUDIES; COAGULATION/FIBRINOLYTIC CAPACITY; GENE EXPRESSION; OBESITY; PEDIATRICS; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Almost 2,000,000 Canadian children are obese and meet criteria for needing weight management.  The main health concern is that obese children can develop Type 2 diabetes putting them at risk for blood clots.  Blood clots lead to low blood flow to important body organs, for example, if blood clots lodge in the brain they can cause a stroke. We know that obese children are at increased risk for blood clots including strokes.  We also know that obese children, even if they do not have a blood clot when young, that when they grow up, they will have an even bigger risk for blood clots when they are young adults.  The experts believe the best way to ensure you are not at a big risk for blood clots as a young adult is to minimise the risk when you are a child. We would like to learn why obese children are at risk for blood clots. We think the risk is associated with Type 2 diabetes disease components called insulin resistance and inflammatory response.Also, we want to see if we can prevent blood clot risk by diet or lifestyle interventions.   First, we will test the blood clotting system in obese children compared to normal weight children to see why they are at risk of having blood clots.Secondly, we will see what will happen when these children participate in a lifestyle management program as we think the program will decrease their risk for blood clots. Third, we will watch how blood clot risk develops in a juvenile obese animal model.We will see relationships of risk for blood clots with insulin resistance and inflammatory response as these animals develop obesity in their teenage years.Finally, we will try to minimize blood clot risk by changing the animal diet to include fish oil. We already know that eating fish oil stops the inflammatory response so we think it will decrease blood clot risk. If we can learn why obese children are at risk for blood clots we could prevent stroke in childhood and prevent stroke and heart attacks when they become adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Ethics of End-of-Life Care: Understanding the Moral Landscape of Medicalized Dying in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: EMPIRICAL BIOETHICS; END-OF-LIFE CARE POLICY; ETHICAL ANALYSIS; MEDICALIZED DYING; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SOCIAL WORLDS THEORY
Abstract-Résumé: Since the report of the Special Senate Committee on Euthanasia and Assisted Suicide was published in 1995, end-of-life care continues to be an important issue for many Canadians. Quebec, for example, recently revisited this issue with its own Select Committee on Dying with Dignity in 2009-2010. There are five medical practices in end-of-life care that remain ethically controversial among various stakeholders that include bioethicists, health care providers, policy makers, and individuals from vulnerable and marginalized communities. These practices are: withholding of treatment, withdrawal of treatment, terminal sedation, euthanasia, and physician-assisted suicide. The fact that various governments continue to repeatedly consult the public on these issues suggests that we still lack a comprehensive understanding of Canadians' moral beliefs on these practices and the values that underpin those beliefs. This lack of understanding has resulted in discrepant, and at times contested, end-of-life treatment and policies throughout Canada, creating ethical dilemmas for various stakeholders and undermining the accessibility provision of Canada Health Act. This three-year research project is designed: 1) to describe and analyse the diverse moral beliefs of Canadians through an examination of media reporting of these issues from 1995 to present; 2) to gain an ethical understanding of key stakeholders' reasons for holding particular positions on these issues through in-depth interviews; 3) to present a comprehensive analysis of these issues to policy makers so that they may engage the public more effectively in the future. We are a team of social scientists and bioethicists trained and knowledgeable in end-of-life care issues and qualitative research methods. Our analysis will inform the development of meaningful end-of-life care policy for Canadians and contribute to improving clinical end-of-life care for patients.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE; TUMEURS CEREBRALES (ET RETINIENNES)
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of AP2delta in Retina
Keywords-MotsClés: AP2; AXONAL OUTGROWTH; GANGLION; RETINA; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Molecular neurobiology is a rapidly expanding field that promises to make a major impact on our understanding of both the central nervous system and neurological disorders. A major drawback to the treatment of central nervous system injuries and disorders is our lack of understanding of nerve regeneration. It is important that we gain a better understanding of the molecules involved in nerve regeneration if we are to make inroads in the treatment of diseases or injuries characterized by nerve degeneration.  We are using the retina as our model system to carry out molecular neurobiological investigations. We have identified a protein (called AP2delta) which has the ability to: (i) promote the formation of the structures required for nerve regeneration and (ii) induce the production of molecules associated with nerve regeneration. We have three major objectives. First, we will pursue the biochemical analysis of this protein in order to understand its mechanism of action. Second, we will establish a mouse model in order to carry out a detailed analysis of how expression of AP2delta affects retina function. Third, we will determine whether AP2delta can alter the course of optic nerve injuries (such as those caused by glaucoma) in an animal model. Glaucoma, a neurodegenerative disease that affects 60 million people worldwide, is a leading cause of blindness. Glaucoma is caused by raised pressure inside the eye which results in damage to the nerve cells of the eye. Our long-term goal is to replace the damaged nerve cells with AP2delta-expressing cells in order to reverse the progression of this disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of Nodal signaling pathway by microRNAs and their involvement in preeclampsia
Keywords-MotsClés: HYPOXIA; MIRNA; NODAL; PREECLAMPSIA
Abstract-Résumé: Preeclampsia is a serious pregnancy complication associated with 10% of perinatal and neonatal mortality worldwide.  It is also a leading cause of maternal and fetal death, and a significant burden to the health care system as preeclamptic pregnancies result in the preterm delivery of babies. Currently, there are no early diagnostic markers available to predict preeclampsia and the only effective intervention is delivery.    MicroRNAs are small RNA molecules that play important roles in gene regulation. We have recently identified a group of microRNAs that have abnormal levels in placentae otained from patients with preeclampsia, when compared to placentae from women with healthy pregnancies. This suggests that abnormal expression of microRNAs may be linked to preeclampsia. The objectives of this study are to investigate the function of these microRNAs during normal placental development and to determine how their abnormal expression may contribute to the development of preeclampsia. We will use cell culture and organ culture with placentas from normal and preeclamptic pregnancies to study the function of these microRNAs and their target genes.  The proposed project will provide novel information on the role of microRNAs in the development of preeclampsia.  It may ultimately result in the development of novel strategies for diagnostic, prevention and treatment of preeclampsia, and consequently improve the health and quality of life in pregnant women and infants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rôle des cytokines inflammatoires dans l'obésité et le syndrome métabolique
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; FACS; GLUCOSE; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; INFLAMMASOME; LEUKOTRIENE; LIPID MEDIATORS; MICROVASCULAR CELLS; PLATELET-ACTIVATING FACTOR; RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The organism is normally programmed to turn off inflammatory and/or immune reactions. If a dysbalance between pro- and anti-inflammatory factors takes place, this 'auto' anti-inflammatory response fails, leading to chronic inflammation, and further major associated-disorders like arteriosclerosis or ischemic stroke. Chronic inflammation occurs in type 2 diabetes (T2D), which associates hyperglycemia and various lipid disorders. Additionally, elements of the immune system have been shown to be altered in obesity/T2D, with elevated circulating levels of pro-inflammatory molecules. These changes occur in the adipose tissue, the liver, and the pancreas as well as in blood vessels and immune cell populations. Generation of inflammatory factors depends on the activation of a multi-protein complex termed the inflammasome. Inflammasomes sense various stressor or danger signals, including high glucose concentrations or free fatty acids. Lipid mediators may also play a role in inflammasome activation. They have privileged interactions with cytokines and some of them can promote inflammation, while others lower it. As a potent novel therapeutic strategy for cardiovascular disease, inducing some of those peculiar lipid mediators may improve cardiovascular disorders during obesity-related disease like T2D in human and potentially lead to enhancement of cardiometabolic therapeutics. We hypothesize that lipid mediators play a crucial role in inflammasome regulation at the vascular level in the context of obesity/T2D. Hence in this project, we aim at investigating first the inflammasome activation/deactivation pathways in research model of human vascular cells and its potential underlying mechanisms during metabolic stress (mimetic of diabetic milieu). In a second study, we will evaluate the effects of blocking lipid mediator activity on inflammasome activation. Future directions will include in vivo validation of these findings.

ClasseRechercheFR: CATARACTES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the invisible state structure of a mutant gS-crystallin involved in cataract formation
Keywords-MotsClés: CATARACTS; EXCITED PROTEIN STATES; HIGH RESOLUTION STRUCTURE; INVISIBLE PROTEIN STATES; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; PROTEIN AGGREGATION; PROTEIN MISFOLDING DISEASE; RELAXATION DISPERSION
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins are vital for life and generally have a well-defined three-dimensional structure (the native state). It is recognized that some proteins are highly dynamic and can assume different shapes or structures, with some shapes having higher energies than others. These high energy shapes are referred to as excited states. Excited states are critical for protein function but may also may lead to deleterious protein aggregation, which has serious biological consequences. Protein aggregation is implicated in common and debilitating diseases, like neurodegenerative disorders (eg. Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases), Type II diabetes and cataract formation. Despite their biological importance, protein excited states are difficult to study because they are short-lived and present in trace amounts, hence they are invisible. Relaxation dispersion NMR (RDNMR) spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful tool to study such invisible excited states and recent breakthroughs in this methodology have enabled the first structure of a protein excited state to be solved at atomic resolution. gS-crystallin is the protein responsible for the structure and transparency of the eye lens. A mutant of gS-crystallin (Opj) is aggregation-prone, leading to cataracts in mouse models. It populates an invisible excited state, which potentially nucleates aggregation. We propose to determine the structure of this excited state using RDNMR. We anticipate our research to further therapeutic strategies to not only combat cataract formation, which is a leading cause of blindness worldwide, but also other diseases associated with protein aggregation.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES DU FOIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional characterization of new regulators of the innate antiviral immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLUMINESCENCE RESONANCE ENERGY TRANSFERT; CHEMOGENOMICS; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; HIGH-THROUGHPUT SCREENING; HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS; INNATE ANTIVIRAL IMMUNITY; MOLECULAR INTERACTION NETWORKS; RNA INTERFERENCE; VIRAL REPLICATION AND INFECTION; VIRUS-HOST INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The innate immune system is the first line of host defense for organisms that possess an adaptive immune system. It allows discrimination between self and non-self, restricts pathogens dissemination, eliminates pathogens and instructs pathogen-specific adaptive immune response. In order to establish infection, viruses need to either suppress or escape from host immune defense systems. An effective way to treat viral infection is to restore immunity upon virus evasion strategies by modulating the host innate immune response. In a genome-wide lentiviral-based RNA interference (RNAi) screen designed to silence expression of the 16,000 human genes, one at a time, in cells subsequently infected with Sendai Virus (SeV), we identified 235 candidate genes that regulate the virus-mediated early antiviral immune response. This study represents a first step to the extensive understanding of pathogen recognition molecule-mediated antiviral signaling pathways, and paves the way to the development of immunomodulatory pan-therapies for a broad spectrum of viral infections. By elucidating the mechanism of action of new regulators of the innate antiviral immunity and validating the modulatory role of candidate genes for selected RNA viruses, a chemical high throughput screening approach will be used to validate novel antiviral pan-targets. The ultimate goal is to identify lead therapeutic molecules for established and emergent RNA diseases such as hepatitis C virus (HCV), human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV-1) and may come to include Avian influenza (FLU) H5N1 virus infection.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroimaging biomarkers of cognitive aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITION; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; HIPPOCAMPUS; LIMBIC SYSTEM; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MEMORY; NEUROGENESIS; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; WHITE MATTER
Abstract-Résumé: At the start of this new century, Canada faces significant aging of its population as the proportion of seniors increases more rapidly than that of all other age groups. By 2026, one Canadian in five will be 65 years or older. Aging has a pronounced impact on mental abilities, particularly on learning and memory. Success in identifying and treating age-related brain diseases depends on understanding normal and optimal aging. Non-invasive neuroimaging is a vital tool in advancing towards this goal. The current proposal will use the most recent advances in neuroimaging to illustrate neural processes that accompany cognitive changes in normal aging. Thus, we will combine anatomical and behavioural measures to reveal if and how the normally aging brain causes age-related reductions in cognitive functions. In addition, we will test whether select genetic polymorphisms contribute to brain changes associated with aging. As a first step, we will validate our imaging predict cognitive aging in a large group of healthy adults spanning 18 to 90 years of age. All participants will undergo high-resolution Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) scans together with comprehensive neuropsychological examination and genetic tests. The second step is to follow-up older participants (>60 years of age). These will have repeated brain scans and neuropsychological tests 3-years after their first visit. This will show us who will remain cognitively stable and who will develop cognitive deficits. In this subgroup we will also examine the long-term relationships between changes in frontal and temporal brain regions, individual cognitive changes, and genetic profiles. Studying neurocognitive aging will help us better characterize pathological and non-pathological changes in the brain throughout the lifespan and identify preclinical markers for cognitive decline.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of novel pathways essential for blood cell formation
Keywords-MotsClés: BAC COMPLEMENTATION; CHIMERIC MOUSE; CHROMOSOME ENGINEERING; COMPARATIVE GENOMIC HYBRIDIZATION ARRAY; ES CELLS; HEMATOPOIESIS; IN VITRO DIFFERENTIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Stem cells have received considerable public attention in part because of their potential application in regenerative therapies. Stem cells can be operationally defined as cells that have the unique property to self-renew as well as to generate more differentiated progeny (differentiation). However, much remains to be learned about the genes regulating stem cell differentiation and renewal, their relationship to each other, and the signalling pathways that control their expression and/or activity. In this application, we propose to use a new resource developed in our laboratory to efficiently identify novel genes and other elements which are essential for the generation of (adult) blood cells from embryonic stem cells. A particular emphasis is put on genes involved in ribosome biogenesis. They are becoming key players in blood cell formation and cancer development.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: The promyelocytic leukemia protein and nuclear domain function in DNA damage signalling and tumour suppression
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE AND REPAIR; LIGHT MICROSCOPY; MECHANISMS OF ONCOGENESIS; MRNA TRANSLATION; NUCLEAR STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION; PROMYELOCYTIC LEUKEMIA NUCLEAR BODIES; SUMOYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer arises when cells accumulate genetic changes (mutations) that result from damage to our DNA.  These mutations alter the normal regulation of cell growth and division, allowing cancer to develop. A cell normally prevents these mutations by efficiently detecting and repairing damaged DNA. Ironically, DNA damage is also used to kill cancer cells during radiation and chemotherapy. Therefore, it is essential to understanding how a cell responds to and repairs DNA damage if we are to develop better ways to prevent and treat cancer.   DNA is found in the nucleus of the cell, which is organized into specialized compartments. One of these compartments is the promyelocytic leukemia nuclear body (PML NB). These bodies are made of a number of different molecules (proteins), and are believed to help prevent cancer from developing because these bodies are disrupted or absent in many types of cancer. For example, PML NBs are disrupted in a type of cancer called acute promyelocytic leukemia, and PML NBs are often absent in the cancer cells that arise in many organs of the body, including the brain, breast, lung and prostate. PML NBs are important to the cell because they help regulate the cell's response to DNA damage but how these bodies carryout this important job is unclear. However, we do know that the different proteins that make up PML NBs can change in response to DNA damage. In addition, we have shown that more PML NBs are produced in response to DNA damage, and that damaged DNA can associate with PML NBs. With these findings in mind, we plan to determine how the association of proteins and damaged DNA with PML NBs is regulated, and what effect this association with these bodies has on the cell's response to DNA damage. These studies will improve our understanding of the role of PML NBs in DNA repair, and will clarify how PML NBs prevent cancer growth. This information will ultimately aid in the development of more effective and safer cancer therapies.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: CHIPS-Child: Testing the developmental origins hypothesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIHYPERTENSIVE THERAPY; CHILD; DEVELOPMENTAL ORIGINS OF DISEASE; DIFFERENTIAL CONTROL OF MATERNAL BLOOD PERSSURE; EPIGENETIC CHANGE; POSTNATAL GROWTH; PREGNANCY HYPERTENSION; RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIAL - ANCILLARY STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: There is now solid evidence that a reduced rate of growth before birth is associated, in adulthood, with more cardiovascular disease (like heart attack or stroke). The information comes from different populations around the world, and is true even when babies are born with birthweight that is within the 'normal' range. At present, the 'Developmental Origins Hypothesis' provides the best explanation. In response to a decrease in nutrition during in utero life, the fetus makes changes to how he/she 'reads' his/her genes. These changes are permanent and after birth, set up the child's metabolism in a way that may be harmful in the long-term (e.g., predispose to diabetes or high blood pressure). CHIPS-Child is a follow-up study of CHIPS, a multicentre CIHR-funded randomised controlled trial that will recruit 1,028 women internationally (2008-14). CHIPS is designed to determine whether allowing blood pressure to be higher than normal during pregnancy may be better for the baby without increasing risk to the mother. CHIPS-Child is designed to determine whether the way that a mother's blood pressure is managed during pregnancy may have long-lasting effects on the child. Children will be seen at 12 months for basic body measurements, a painless swab of cells from the inside of their cheek, and a hair sample; mothers will complete a questionnaire about infant feeding practices and their years of education. Contact will be maintained with families on an annual basis, by mail, until CHIPS-Child concludes and the necessity of ongoing follow-up is determined. All women who have been enrolled in CHIPS so far are aware of the potential for follow-up through the current 'Information and Consent Form'. We anticipate that we will follow-up 626 children (313/group) to the age of 12 months. CHIPS-Child will help us to understand how therapies for the women during pregnancy may have long-lasting effects on the baby.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the epileptic network in epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; EPILEPSY; HISTOLOGY; IDIOPATHIC GENERALIZED EPILEPSY; LIMBIC SYSTEM; MAGNETIZATION TRANSFER RATIO; MESIAL TEMPORAL SCLEROSIS; MYELIN WATER FRACTION; TEMPORAL LOBE EPILEPSY; WHITE MATTER
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is one of the most common neurologic disorders.  While 75% of patients respond to medical therapy, the remainder often experience severe disability due to uncontrolled seizures.  Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)has recently demonstrated that structural abnormalities in patients with epilepsy are far more extensive than previously believed.  How these structural abnormalities relate to the development of epilepsy, associated conditions such as memory impairement or depression and surgical outcome remains unknown.  The purpose of this proposal is to characterize the anatomical abnormalities in epilepsy patients and to determine the relationship between anatomical abnormalities, seizures and associated conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stress Hormones, Mood and Women's Sexual Desire
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD MALTREATMENT; CORTISOL; DEHYDROEPIANDROSTERONE; DEPRESSIVE SYMPTOMS; FINGERNAIL ASSAYS OF STRESS HORMONES; QUESTIONNAIRES; SALIVARY ASSAYS OF STRESS HORMONES; STRESS HORMONES; STRUCTURED INTERVIEWS
Abstract-Résumé: Many women worry that they have too little sexual desire and some find this very distressing. Although men's sexual desire is related in part to the testosterone in their bodies, this has not been shown to be true for women. We have found in women who are distressed with a low sexual desire, lower levels of certain hormones that can produce testosterone. But these hormones have other actions as well, for instance they are also stress hormones. Additionally, they can affect our mood and tendency to be depressed. This study is to investigate stress hormones (measured in the saliva and nail clippings), and stresses that occurred in childhood including abuse or other negative experiences in women with and without low sexual desire. As well we will carefully measure symptoms of low mood, for example unhappy thoughts, feeling irritable or sad, in women with and without low desire problems. We will need to exclude women who have  current depression. In conclusion, we want to understand the meaning  of these lower hormones (like DHEA) in women with low sexual desire so that we can better focus our treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translational Research on the Role of Tubular ACE2 in Kidney Disease Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: ACE2; ADAM-17; ANGIOTENSIN 1-7; CELL SIGNALING; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; HUMAN SUBJECTS; KIDNEY FIBROSIS; PROXIMAL TUBULE; RENIN ANGIOTENSIN SYSTEM; TUBULE PERFUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic kidney disease is a growing health care problem in Canada, and there are few treatments. Many kidney diseases eventually lead to the need for life-saving dialysis treatments or transplantation. Our laboratory is interested in finding the mechanisms causing kidney failure. With funding from the CIHR, we have studied the role of a protein called ACE2, which is produced in the kidney and may protect against kidney damage by removing a substance called angiotensin II.  ACE2 also results in the formation of a substance called angiotensin-(1-7), which we found can block damaging effects of diabetes or angiotensin II on kidney tubular cells. We recently showed that blocking ACE2 in mice with kidney disease caused increased urinary loss of protein, which is a sign of worsening kidney damage. Furthermore, our preliminary data show that urinary ACE2 levels are high in people with kidney transplants, compared to people with normal kidneys. This suggests that in kidney disease, ACE2 may be released into the urine from the tubule, and its protective effects may be lost.  In our grant to the CIHR, we will use a multi-disciplinary research approach involving a mouse model of kidney injury, isolated kidney cells and tubules, and studies in humans, to examine the potential protective effects of ACE2 in kidney disease.  We will determine if ACE2 is shed into the urine in kidney disease, by a specific enzyme reaction in the tubular cell. We will also study the effect of loss of ACE2 on the development of kidney scarring, which is a feature of all chronic kidney diseases.   Finally, we will learn more about angiotensin-(1-7) as a potential protective factor.  Our research may lead to strategies to prevent the loss of ACE2 from kidney tubular cells in chronic kidney disease, which may improve kidney function.  Our studies may also lead to new methods to identify people at risk for kidney disease progression, via measurement of urinary ACE2.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Mitochondrial Dynamics by Eicosanoids: Novel Mechanisms for Limiting Cardiac Dysfunction Caused by Ischemia Reperfusion Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: CAVEOLIN-1; CYTOCHROME P450; EPOXYEICOSATRIENOIC ACID; HEART FAILURE; ISCHEMIA REPERFUSION INJURY; MITOCHONDRIA; MITOCHONDRIA FUNCTION; MITOCHONDRIA PERMEABILITY TRANSITION; MITOCHONDRIAL DYNAMICS; SOLUBLE EPOXIDE HYDROLASE
Abstract-Résumé: Heart damage begins to occur after it has been deprived of oxygen (ischemia) for an extended period of time. While the immediate return of blood flow (reperfusion) to the heart is important, it too can damage the heart. Ischemia-reperfusion injury can significantly affect key components of the cell, such as mitochondria. In the heart, mitochondria provide about 90% of the energy for cardiac function. These dynamic organelles undergo continuous elongation and fragmentation processes to maintain proper function and meet cellular demands. Significant disruption in these processes caused by ischemia-reperfusion injury can impact the energy production of the cell resulting in dysfunction and death.   Arachidonic acid (AA) is a molecule found in cell membranes that can be released in response to several stimuli such as hormones and cellular stress. Proteins within a cell break it down into active molecules called epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs). These EETs are involved in regulating different functions in the body.  Our reseach has demonstrated that EETs can limit mitochondrial injury.  Thus, the objective of these studies is to advance our understanding of the EET-pathway targeting mitochondria and limiting injury.  We propose targeting this pathway as a viable therapeutic strategy to prevent and/or treat mitochondrial damage caused ischemia-reperfusion injury.  Results from this study will identify new regulatory mechanisms and advance our understanding of mitochondrial function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of elongation factor 1A-1 in apolipoprotein B metabolism and the pathogenesis of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
Keywords-MotsClés: APOLIPOPROTEIN B; CELLULAR STRESS; LIPID; LIVER; NONALCOHOLIC FATTY LIVER DISEASE; OBESITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity and adult onset (type 2) diabetes have become epidemic in North America and are associated with multiple organ complications, including liver disease.  Research suggests that the elevated blood lipids (fats) in obese diabetic individuals accumulate in the liver causing dysfunction and/or death of the cells that make up this organ.  This can lead to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, a disease which has recently become a common cause of liver transplantation.  The liver of a healthy individual can export excess fat.  However, clinical studies have shown that liver fat export is impaired in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.  This is because of the increased breakdown of a protein critical for fat export from the liver, apoB.  Another protein, eEF1A-1, which we have shown to be increased in cells exposed to excess fat, may be involved in this increased breakdown of apoB.  For this project we will use cellular and molecular biological techniques in cultured liver cells and in obese diabetic mice to determine whether increased eEF1A-1 protein levels in the liver contribute to increased apoB breakdown during nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.  If this is the case, developing medications to inhibit eEF1A-1 in the liver might improve nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural, biophysical, and genetic studies on bacteriophage morphogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIOPHAGE LAMBDA; BIOINFORMATICS; BIOPHYSICAL ASSAYS; EVOLUTION; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; VIRAL ASSEMBLY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Most of the fundamental processes occurring within living cells are mediated by large complexes of different proteins. The assembly of these complexes requires the simultaneous interaction of large numbers of protein, and (often) nucleic acid subunits. To gain a full understanding of cellular events, we must determine in atomic detail how the specific interactions between proteins are mediated and how these interactions are controlled in the assembly pathways of large complexes. Our research is directed at understanding the assembly of viruses that infect bacteria, which are known as bacteriophages. The intensive study of these types of viruses, which has been under way for more than 60 years, has led to many of the major breakthroughs in molecular biology. In this proposal we address the problem of how bacteriophages assemble their complex structures, which comprise hundreds of copies of many different proteins. Bacteriophages are very attractive for these studies because they are well characterized, we can study their assembly in a test tube, and we have recently determined the atomic structures of several of the proteins required for the assembly process. In the long term, these studies will increase our knowledge of how large protein complexes, like viruses, can assemble in a regulated fashion. Understanding this process will help us design drugs to inhibit viral growth, and will contribute to our basic understanding of how cells function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional characterization of microRNAs in acute myeloid leukemia stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; FLOWCYTOMETRY; IMMUNO DEFICIENT MICE; LENTIVIRUS; LEUKEMIA STEM CELL; MICRORNA
Abstract-Résumé: Leukemic tissue is arranged in a hierarchy and is thought to be sustained by a rare subpopulation of leukemia stem cells (LSC). LSCs distinguish themselves from the rest of the cells by their ability to generate functionally identical copies of themselves, a process termed self-renewal. Emerging evidence is pointing to LSC having unique biological properties (dormancy, drug/radiation resistance) that could permit them to survive current therapies and eventually lead to relapse of the disease. It is generally accepted that genetic changes underlie cancer initiation and progression. Although most studies have focussed on coding genes, there is increasing recognition that non-coding RNAs play a role. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs and they function as important negative regulators of gene and protein expression via the RNA interference machinery. There is emerging evidence that miRNAs play important roles in cancer stem cell biology. Moreover, a number of miRNAs have been identified within cancer to function as oncogenes or tumorsuppressor genes. Therefore, the aim of this research proposal is to functionally characterize miRNAs in leukemia stem cells by in vitro and in vivo assays and to identify specific target genes for each of the candidate miRNAs. This work will establish the role that miRNAs play in the generation and maintenance of leukemia stem cells, and thus, a greater knowledge of how leukemia develops and progresses into malignant tumor formation. Also, these miRNAs and their regulated target genes will offer great promise as drug targets for leukemia therapy if they are differentially expressed between normal hematopoietic stem cells and leukemia stem cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: A randomized controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of the Making It Work program at preventing work loss and improving at work productivity in employed people with inflammatory arthritis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS; EFFECTIVENESS STUDY; EMPLOYMENT; EMPLOYMENT INTERVENTION; INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIS; PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS; SELF-MANAGEMENT PROGRAM; VOCATIONAL PROGRAM
Abstract-Résumé: People with inflammatory arthritis, commonly have to stop working, with major consequences to their quality of life. Yet, few services exist to deal with employment. We have developed and pilot tested a novel intervention to help people with inflammatory arthritis remain employed. Results were very favourable. For the program to become widely available and health policy planners to agree to fund it, we need to demonstrate its effectiveness. In a randomized controlled trial, we will compare work outcomes in 263 employed people receiving a web-based version of our program compared to 263 receiving usual care, along with printed material about work and arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Involvement of PDB3 and PDB4-related genes in bone diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; BONE RESORPTION; GENE EXPRESSION; METABOLIC BONE DISEASES; MUTATION; OSTEOCLAST; OSTEOCLAST SURVIVAL; PAGET'S DISEASE OF BONE; SOMATIC MOSAICISM; SQSTM1/P62 PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: Paget's disease of bone (PDB) is the second most frequent bone disorder after osteoporosis, affecting approximately three percent of people over 55 years of age. Disabling complications of PDB, such as bone deformity, bone pain and fractures occur in about 30% of patients. PDB is caused by an excess activity of osteoclast cells, which are responsible for removing bone tissue. A genetic component of this disease is well-known and a mutation in a gene linked to PDB has been described in the French-Canadian population. Experiments have shown that this genetic mutation may predispose a person to PDB, although other factors are likely required to be present for the complete development of the disease.  In this study, we aim 1) to investigate the role of other relatively-unstudied osteoclast-related genes in PDB, 2) to assess whether the already-known genetic mutation occurs in cells after conception and 3) to better characterize the consequences of a new genetic mutation on bone cell functions.  By gaining more knowledge on the impact that specific genes may exert on osteoclast function in PDB, a better understanding is also gained regarding the molecular mechanisms of this and other similar bone diseases which are increasingly prevalent in our aging Canadian population, such as osteoporosis and bone metastases.  By better understanding the factors that turn on and off bone diseases the development of new targeted treatments designed to regulate or suppress bone resorption becomes increasingly possible. Preventing and appropriately treating bone diseases would be of a major impact on public health by decreasing the direct and indirect costs associated with chronic bone diseases.

Abstract-Résumé: The research proposed in this grant will investigate novel types of interactions between neurons that are important for generating the aura of migraines, in causing the neuronal swelling underlying cytotoxic brain edema and in allowing the immune cells of the brain, called microglia, to sense when intense activation and damage occurs in nearby neurons.  Each of these pathways involves a new form of transmitter release and reveals the potential cytotoxic impact of ionic disruptions in nerve cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bisexual Identity: Implications for Mental, Behavioural, and Physical Health
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL HEALTH; BISEXUAL IDENTITY; HIV; MENTAL HEALTH; STIGMA; SURVEY/CORRELATIONAL METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Bisexual men, despite belonging to a group at high risk for HIV, have received little empirical scrutiny. The limited data available suggest that, relative to gay men, bisexual men are at increased risk for HIV. However, research exploring HIV risk determinants in men who have sex with men has failed to explore the unique psychosocial issues of bisexual men and how those factors are related to HIV risk. Using minority stress theory and syndemics as theoretical frameworks, this project will explore the associations between various aspects of minority stress specific to bisexual men (i.e., internalized binegativity, feelings of illegitimacy, anticipated binegativity, lack of bisexual identity affirmation, and anti-bisexual prejudice), mental health (i.e., anxiety, depression, psychological distress, and self-esteem), substance use, and risk factors for HIV (i.e., multiple sexual partners and unprotected anal and/or vaginal intercourse). The results will shed important light on the unique determinants of HIV risk among bisexual men and have implications for developing HIV prevention methods targeted specially at this high-risk population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Computational studies of lipid-protein and helix-helix interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: HELIX-HELIX INTERACTIONS; LIPID-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; MEMBRANE PROTEIN STRUCTURE; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; MOLECULAR DYNAMICS SIMULATION; THERMODYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells are surrounded by a thin barrier of lipids and proteins called the cell membrane. Membranes separate the inside of a cell or a cellular compartment from the outside, which makes it possible to maintain different conditions inside the cell. Membranes have amazing mechanical and electrical properties despite being only a fraction of a micrometer thick. They are responsible for transporting nutrients, waste products, and information to and from the cell. In recent years our view of membranes has changed from a relatively homogeneous sheet of molecules to a patchwork with distinct properties in different areas of the membrane. This project examines some of the most fundamental interactions between the molecules that make up a membrane. In particular, we study the interactions between protein structures that are essential in transmitting information, a membrane thermometer that regulates membrane structure when the temperature changes, and a small protein from the flu virus that is essential in replicating viral particles for further infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transformation de la psychopathologie de la vie quotidienne: des anciennes névroses aux anxiodépressions contemporaines
Keywords-MotsClés: ASPECTS SOCIAUX; DEPRESSION; ENJEUX ETHIQUES; MEDICAMENT; SANTE MENTALE; EVOLUTION HISTORIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: La depression et les troubles anxieux apparaissent de plus en plus, chez les experts, les medias et le public, comme des maladies qu'on peut controler ou guerir grace a un traitement approprie. Pourtant, malgre l'efficacite proclamee des nouveaux antidepresseurs et anxiolytiques, la prevalence de troubles anxieux et de l'humeur ne cesse de s'accroitre. Elle genere depuis quelques annees des discours epidemiologiques assez alarmistes et pose egalement des dilemmes ethiques. Pourtant la tendance a s'inquieter de la prevalence grandissante des troubles «nerveux» au sein de la population ne date pas d'hier. Deja au XIXe siecle, la prevalence des «affections nerveuses» en Europe et en Amerique du Nord etait vue comme ayant atteint des sommets jusque-la inegales. Dans les annees 1950, les «nevroses freudiennes» allaient prendre le relais en tant que problemes de sante mentale affectant des populations de plus en plus larges. Des annees 1980 jusqu'a aujourd'hui, le constat d'un accroissement considerable des cas de depressions et de troubles anxieux est au coeur de la reforme de la sante mentale au Quebec. Cerner l'evolution des psychopathologies du quotidien depuis les annees cinquante, de leur accroissement, de leur classification et de leur traitement revient a poser une question fondamentale qui est celle des ruptures et des continuites entre hier et aujourd'hui. Ce projet a pour objectif d'analyser la transformation de l'univers de la psychopathologie de la vie quotidienne depuis les annees 1950 jusqu'a aujourd'hui au Quebec, et ce, a travers l'analyse 1) des modes d'intervention medicaux, paramedicaux, psychologiques et alternatifs auquel on a eu, et on a, recours et 2) les representations scientifiques, profanes et alternatives des maux psychiques fort generalises au cours de la periode. Nous visons a poser un regard a la fois documente et neuf qui puisse apporter un eclairage retrospectif et multidimensionnel sur la reforme actuelle de la sante mentale au Quebec.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Proteomics of Host-Pathogen Interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: EFFECTORS; GENE KNOCK-OUT; GENOME-WIDE RNAI SCREENING; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; PROTEIN CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; PROTEIN NMR; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; STRUCTURAL PROTEOMICS/GENOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Pathogenic bacteria cause infection and illness in many ways, including injecting bacterial proteins into human cells so that our cells do not work properly. The proteins that these bacteria inject make people sick by interfering with the normal functioning of human cells. To combat these pathogens, we need to understand how these bacterial proteins bind to human proteins and interfere with normal cell functions. Structural biology allows us to 'see' the microscopic details of how proteins interact. If we can understand this process at the level of molecules, we can develop novel therapies for treating bacterial infections. As part of our proposed research, we have cataloged a list of secreted bacterial proteins, called effectors, from three disease-causing bacteria, Salmonella, Legionella and E. coli, and made a list of which proteins they interact with in human cells. As many of the bacterial proteins do not have a known binding partner, we will use specific experiments to identify the corresponding human protein(s) that interact with the bacterial proteins. These experiments will be performed both in cells (in vivo) and without cells (in vitro). Together these experiments will tell us which combinations of proteins interact with one another so that we can focus protein structural studies on these pairs of proteins. Various methods of structural biology (X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, small-angle X-ray scattering and electron microscopy) will be employed to see how these protein molecules interact. Together, the results of these experiments will provide details on how bacterial and human proteins bind to each other and help in the design of novel treatments to fight bacterial infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genomic Disruption in High-Grade Serous Ovarian Carcinomas: Steady State or Continuous Drift?
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMOSOMAL STABILITY; EARLY LESIONS; HIGH-GRADE SEROUS OVARIAN CANCERS; INTRATUMOURAL HETEROGENEITY; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: In North America, ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death due to gynecological malignancies and 75% of women with advanced ovarian cancer are not expected to survive beyond five years. High-grade serous ovarian cancers account for 70% of ovarian cancer cases. These cancers are thought to be chromosomally unstable, which means their genomes are highly susceptible to the introduction of large-scale genetic mutations and rearrangements on a continual basis. This assumption stems from the observation that the chromosomal makeup (karyotype) of ovarian cancers is extremely abnormal. Recent results from our group suggest that this presumption is incorrect. It seems that ovarian cancers undergo a period of chromosomal instability very early on as the cancer is being established which leads to the abnormal karyotype. At the time of disease diagnosis, however, these cancers have already reached a state of chromosomal stability. Thus, with respect to large-scale genomic changes, recurrences and metastases are almost identical to the original tumour. We have found, however, that small-scale changes corresponding to single letter DNA alterations continue to occur as tumours evolve. This finding represents a moment of recognition that 'the emperor has no clothes' with respect to the study of ovarian cancer. For this project, we will conduct an in-depth study of multiple tumour samples from 10 cases of high-grade serous ovarian cancer to determine the extent of genetic variability between tumours and try to discover how these cancers acquire chromosomal stability. We will also compare these results to early precursors of ovarian cancer from the fallopian tubes, to identify when chromosomal instability occurs in cancer evolution. The results of this work could reveal why a large proportion of ovarian cancers do not respond to treatment or develop treatment resistance and has important implications for the development of new treatments for this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: 'From Crying to Shaking': Reducing the Chances of Infant Abuse
Keywords-MotsClés: ABUSIVE HEAD TRAUMA; CRYING; CRYING DOLL; ELECTRONIC DIARIES; FRUSTRATION; INFANT ABUSE; INFANT SOUNDS; SHAKEN BABY SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Shaken Baby Syndrome (or SBS; also known as Abusive Head Trauma) and infant abuse in general is an individual, family and societal tragedy.  New evidence has clearly demonstrated that caregiver frustration with normal increased early infant crying in completely healthy newborns tiggers SBS in the vast majority of cases.  New community-based efforts have targeted caregiver understanding of early increased infant crying as a way of preventing these tragic occurrences.  In this project, we examine how prolonged bouts of infant crying generate such frustration in caregivers that it can lead to abuse.  In a series of studies, we use 'crying sounds' and 'crying dolls' as subjects, and parents-to-be, adolescents and  parent adults as participants.  In ethically sound experiments, we elicit affective and emotional responses to crying behavior in a variety of forms under a variety of conditions.  The results will provide for the first time empirical descriptions of how caregivers get from inconsolable infant crying to frustration as the precursor of shaking in rigorous trials.  The results will contribute to new efforts to prevent the devastation of infant SBS and abuse.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of carcinoma associated fibroblasts and tumor stromal genes in lung cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER STROMA; CARCINOMA ASSOCIATED FIBROBLAST; GENE EXPRESSION; LUNG CANCER; MICRORNA; MOLECULAR PATHOLOGY; MOUSE MODEL; SHRNA; TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the leading cause of death worldwide. There have been recent notable successes in developing new therapies that target mainly the genetic aberrations crucial for the growth and survival of lung cancer cells. However, the overall impact on patients survival has been minimal. Strong evidence has recently emerged that non-cancer cells and tissue surrounding the tumor cells also play important role in cancers including lung. Tumor microenvironment including extracellular matrix molecules and stromal fibroblasts (carcinoma associated fibroblast or CAF) have strong influences on cancer cell growth, survival, invasion, metastasis, and resistance to chemotherapy. The fact that the stromal cells are genetically more stable in contrast to the cancer cells themselves, suggest that they could be targets of novel treatment strategies. This project will examine the functional importance of stroma/CAF genes in the biology and behavior of lung cancer cells and explore them as potential new targets to improve the treatment of lung cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Community-Based Intervention to Prevent Fall Injuries to Young Children in the Home
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY INTERVENTIONS; IDENTIFYING BEST PRACTICES; PARENT SAFETY PRACTICES; PREVENTING CHILDHOOD FALLS AT HOME; PROGRAM EVALUATION; RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Falls are the leading cause of injury hospitalizations for young children in Canada. Although we now know the primary causes of these falls, very little has been done to identify ways to prevent such falls. The proposed research represents a unique collaboration between child-injury prevention researchers and public health units and aims to address this important child health issue. In this research we will compare the impact of two community-based interventions in an effort to identify 'best practices' for preventing falls to young children (1-4 years) in the home. Drawing on findings from systematic reviews on effective child-injury prevention approaches,one intervention approach focuses on social marketing using the media and the other adds two additional components that more directly target parent behaviors relevant to fall prevention in the home. Comparing pre-intervention with post-intervention incidence of falls will reveal the relative success of each intervention approach. In addition, we will assess for changes in parents' awareness of fall injuries, knowledge of fall risks, attitudes towards prevention, and fall-prevention practices to determine which are the key factors that predict any resulting reduction in the incidence of falls. The findings from this research will provide important information on ways that communities can take action to prevent falls in the home to young children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Characterization of UBE4B and Its Role in Cancer.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENETICS; DISEASE; E3/E4 LIGASE; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE REGULATION; ONCOGENE; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENE; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: The importance of p53 in the prevention of cancer is highlighted by the fact that p53 is inactivated in more than 50 % of all human tumors. Regulation of p53 expression and stability is essential for maintaining normal cell growth. The research team of Dr. Leng is interested in understanding how molecules promote or inhibit the growth of tumors. Dr. Leng is particularly interested three molecules called UBE4B, p53 and MDM2, which appear to regulate the growth of tumors. They propose to study the role of UBE4B in regulating of p53 in tumors. They are using cell culture, mouse model to study the mechanisms of how UBE4B regulates p53, and define the correlation of the UBE4B expression and p53 statues in tumors. Thus, the outcome of this proposal has significant implications regarding an important role for UBE4B negatively regulates p53 and the possible effect in cancer therapy. Successful completion of the proposed experiments could lead to novel anti-cancer therapies that could potentially improve the prognosis for cancer patients and reduce the public health burden from cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Value and Limitations in Hospital Utilization and Expenditures (VALHUE)
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY-BASED FUNDING; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES; HEALTH STATUS
Abstract-Résumé: In most provinces, hospital funding is currently allocated through global budgets.  While this funding policy has been perceived as being effective at constraining expenditure growth, 2010 marked a significant shift in hospital funding policy for British Columbia (BC), announcing a move towards activity-based funding (ABF).  ABF is a policy wherein hospitals are partially remunerated based on the volume and characteristics of the patients they treat.  The incentives of ABF induce hospitals to reduce lengths of stay and increase the number of hospitalizations per bed, potentially reducing waits of stay.  Clearly, reduced wait times is an important outcome to policymakers, but this policy does not take into account the effect of incentives to increase the amount of hospitals care on the health of its residents.  While an important body research suggesting that increasing the supply of care does not translate into significant gains in health, the relationship between hospital funding policies designed to increase the 'volume' of hospital care and patients' health have yet to be specified.  The objectives of this study are to determine the relationship between volume-driven hospital funding policies being pursued in BC and gain in health, an important issue which represents a serious gap in the current knowledge-base.  The direction and magnitude of this relationship will inform hospital funding policy and will be immediately relevant to policymakers in BC, Alberta and Ontario, other provinces having announced ABF policies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating higher mental functions using real-time fMRI
Keywords-MotsClés: DEFAULT NETWORK; EXECUTIVE NETWORK; FUNCTIONAL NEUROIMAGING; META-COGNITIVE AWARENESS; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; REAL-TIME FMRI TRAINING; SELF-REFLECTIVE THOUGHT; SPONTANEOUS THOUGHT
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to reflect upon our own thoughts and emotions represents one of the highest mental processes in humans. Recent neuroimaging studies have begun to identify the neural correlates of such processes. At the same time, recent technological advances have resulted in the emergence of real-time fMRI, a technique which allows individuals to view feedback about their own brain activity and use it to improve their ability to regulate their own brain. This research program aims to improve our understanding of the neural basis of human thought and self-reflection by employing recent developments in real-time fMRI.  To do this, the present research program will undertake a number of investigations with healthy volunteers in order to examine different aspects of their ability to achieve increased brain self-regulation through viewing real-time feedback about their own brain activity and engaging in self-reflection. First, a longitudinal study will examine the effects of increased duration of training on one's brain-regulation ability. A second, separate study, will examine whether individuals can learn to enhance the connectivity between two brain regions. A third study will examine whether fluctuations in medial prefrontal activity predicts qualities of spontaneous thought, such as stimulus-oriented versus stimulus-independent thought contents.  A fourth study will examine whether it is possible to predict the quality of one's mental experience based on the level of activity in particular brain regions.  The results from these investigations will lead to improved scientific understanding of higher cognition and brain functions, as well as a better understanding of mental disorders such as depression and addiction that are specifically characterized by dysregulation of emotional self-regulation and self-reflective thought.  This improved understanding could lead to novel treatments, thus improving patients' well-being and benefiting our society as a whole.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of hair cycle and wound healing by alpha-v-beta-6 integrin
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA-V-BETA-6 INTEGRIN; EPIDERMIS; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; HAIR CYCLE; HAIR FOLLICLES; INTEGRINS; KERATINOCYTE PROLIFERATION; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: More than 30 million patients in North America receive steroid drug treatment. The therapeutic indications are widespread but side effects are common and of great importance to patients. Chronic glucocorticoid therapy induces detrimental effects in several tissues including the skin where it causes skin atrophy. When encountering an accidental or surgical trauma, impaired tissue repair is one of the serious complications of glucocorticoid therapy. Glucocorticoids affect almost every phase of wound healing due to their inhibitory effects on gene expression in various cells involved in healing. Transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-B1) is a naturally-occurring molecule which regulates skin inflammation and tissue maintenance. It serves as a strong inhibitor of hair follicle stem cell growth and has been directly implicated as a significant factor in hair growth regulation. TGF-B1 is produced as an inactive molecule and needs to be activated to function. One of the main activators of TGF-B1 is an integrin that is expressed on the epithelial cell surface. We have recently demonstrated that this integrin is localized in hair follicle stem cells where it could keep these cells quiescent via TGF-B1 activation. Our work has also demonstrated that mice engineered to lack this integrin (B6-/-) have accelerated hair growth and delayed hair regression. In addition, steroid-impaired wounds heal significantly better in B6-/- mice than in normal mice. The aim of this research proposal is to further investigate the role of this integrin in hair stem cells and healing of steroid-impaired wounds. Our hypothesis is that this integrin naturally suppresses stem cell proliferation in hair follicles. When patients receive corticosteroids, these drugs further inhibit stem cells delaying reepithelialization of wounds. Use of inhibitors of this integrin could potentially reduce stem cell suppression and provide a useful therapeutic tool to improve outcomes of steroid-impaired wound healing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of IL-1alpha in cigarette smoke-induced inflammation and microbial exacerbations.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CLINICAL SAMPLES; COPD; INFLAMMATION; TOBACCO SMOKE; VIRAL AND BACTERIAL INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The devastating impact of cigarette smoking on human health is well known. Despite this, over 1.1 billion people continue to smoke, representing one-sixth of the world's population. About half of these smokers will develop severe smoking-related illnesses, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), stroke, and cancer. The proposed research focuses on mechanisms that contribute to the pathogenesis of COPD; a chronic inflammatory lung disease. We will investigate mechanisms by which cigarette smoke elicits lung inflammation and how these inflammatory processes affect viral infections. Ultimately, we hope that this knowledge will allow us to design novel therapies to prevent and control this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Methods to measure (and measures of) the (actual) mortality reductions produced by cancer screening.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; CANCER; DATA EXTRACTION; LIKELIHOOD METHODS TO COMBINE DATA; NEW STATISTICAL METHODS; PARAMETER-ESTIMATION; SAMPLE SIZES; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: We spend a lot on screening. We can count the dollars and document the harms to individuals. Sadly, despite many long costly trials involving large numbers of people, policy makers, funders and the public do not confidently know how much these programs have (or would) cut the numbers of breast, colon, prostate, and lung cancer deaths. One reason is the metric used, which averages over the full (but arbitrary) period of follow-up. This metric is suitable for interventions that result in virtually immediate and long-lasting reductions in sickness and death rates, such as adult circumcision, HPV/polio vaccine, or screens for abdominal aneurysms. However, it mis-measures the delayed effect of screening. The benefit of screening seen in 2011 is not due to  screens done in 2011, but earlier ones. Returns on 2011 screens will emerge in mid, but mostly the late 2010s. The usual metric ignores critical timing information and badly underestimates the impact of a screening program. Naively pooling results from several trials further dilutes it.  We will extend the method we developed to re-analyze data from the European  Prostate Cancer Screening trial. Our method estimates the yearly benefit of a screening program by summing returns on past financial investments. Using this method, we estimated that the reduction in mortality was 50% beyond year 7, much lower than the  20% reduction first reported.  We will refine our method to handle data from trials with varying schedules, thus making proper use of all available data. We will test the methods on simulated situations where we know the correct answer. We will also apply it to data from all completed trials on breast, colon and lung cancer and report the results in a meaningful way. We will also develop methods for planning the size of new screening trials. The methods described in this proposal will give policy makers and funders more accurate and relevant data on how effective cancer screening programs are/could be.

TitreApplicationTitle: Free radical determinants of neurodegenerative disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIOXIDATIVE ENZYMES; FREE RADICALS; NEURODEGENERATION; OXIDATIVE DNA DAMAGE; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES
Abstract-Résumé: Amphetamines such as ecstasy and speed are used as recreational drugs at parties or raves by college and high school students, and cause severe toxicities. Amphetamine itself and related drugs are widely prescribed to children with attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder.  In animal models, amphetamines cause the destruction of particular nerves in the brain, leading to neurodegenerative disorders, and a similar process has been implicated but not proven in humans.   Evidence from a number of laboratories including ours suggests that reactive oxygen species (ROS) formed during normal body metabolism may cause neurodegeneration, and that this process is substantially enhanced by drugs like amphetamines that increase ROS formation, which can damage critical components in the brain.  We are using several mutant, transgenic and knockout mouse models to elucidate both the neurodegenerative role of ROS and the protective pathways that detoxify ROS or repair the brain damage, with imbalances among these pathways determining individual risk.  The lack of such knowledge, together with the growing use of amphetamine abuse and therapeutic use, heighten the clinical importance of such studies, which may facilitate the identification of high-risk individuals and therapeutic strategies to minimize neurodegeneration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of TGF-beta action in chondrocytes: Role of ALK1-endoglin interplay
Keywords-MotsClés: ALK1; ANIMAL MODEL; ARTHRITIS; CARTILAGE; CARTILAGE REGENERATION; CHONDROCYTES; ENDOGLIN; OSTEOARTHRITIS; RECEPTORS; TGF-BETA
Abstract-Résumé: Arthritis is a serious medical problem affecting a large majority of the population and has limited options for treatment. Symptoms including pain, joint inflammation and swelling have adverse effects on joint mobility and a significant impact on quality of life. Although the cause of arthritis in not known, several studies suggest that abnormal transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) is involved in arthritis. TGF-beta is produced by most cells of the body and plays an important role in the development and maintenance of healthy cartilage. However, abnormal TGF-beta action in the joints can lead to several problems including cartilage destruction leading to osteoarthritis or other joint diseases. Our research goals are to understand the biology of TGF-beta in human cartilage cells (chondrocytes) and to uncover how deregulated TGF-beta action is involved in arthritic conditions. The proposed research may lead to the development of new therapies for the treatment these conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proteins of iron homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEMIA; IRON METABOLISM; METALLOCHAPERONE PROTEINS; PANCREATIC ISLETS; RECOMBINANT PROTEINS; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Because humans have no way of removing iron from the body, iron uptake from the diet must be very strictly controlled; however, our understanding of this complex process is incomplete.  Iron is absorbed in the gut by specialized cells lining parts of the small intestine.  The iron is then transported through these cells to the blood where the iron is distributed throughout the body.  In this application, we propose to study the proteins involved in iron transport through the intestinal cells.  We also propose to study the mechanism whereby iron leaves the intestinal cell and enters blood. We also propose to investigate why insulin-containing cells in the pancreas have high levels of a protein that keeps iron in its oxidized state.  These studies will increase our understanding of diseases such as anemia and may lead to the identification of targets for drugs to control iron distribution in the body.
