TitreApplicationTitle: MAG-CP: Magnesium sulphate for fetal neuroprotection of the preterm infant
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL PALSY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEALTH SURVEILLANCE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MAGNESIUM SULPHATE; PRACTICE VARIABILITY; VERY PRETERM BIRTH
Abstract-Résumé: Preterm birth is the most important cause of infant death and disability in Canada and worldwide. Survival rates of preterm infants are improving but these infants are at substantial risk of medical and neurodevelopmental impairment, including cerebral palsy (CP). MgSO4 given before birth improves the motor outcomes of preterm infants. MgSO4 is inexpensive and used routinely for women with seizures in pregnancy. However, there are ongoing controversies about side effects (such as whether MgSO4-exposed newborns require more resuscitation at birth), inadequately studied outcomes (such as developmental follow-up), and cost. MAG-CP aims to actively manage the national implementation of MgSO4 into clinical practice, explore barriers to change and resolve controversies. MgSO4 use and clinical outcomes will be monitored through the existing Canadian Perinatal Network (CPN) and Canadian Neonatal Follow-Up Network (CNFUN). MAG-CP will include all babies born at <29 wk. These babies are at highest risk of CP and are those with linked data between CPN and the CNFUN. The primary outcome will be use of MgSO4 for neuroprotection as a proportion of eligible women, with a target utilization rate of 80% by the end of 4 years. Other outcomes will include CP, death or CP as a combined outcome, maternal adverse effects, paediatric death, and neurodevelopmental outcomes at 3 years of age. A Data Monitoring Committee will review outcomes and given annual feedback to centres about how they are doing relative to both other centres and rates of outcomes in the published trials. Over 4 yr of managed KT, we anticipate recruitment of 3752 mothers with 2497 children evaluated at 18 mos. This is based on CPN enrollment of 940 babies/yr born at <29 wk, their 83% survival to 18 mos, and 80% parental consent to 18 mos follow-up. This will give us ample power to detect anticipated or important changes in CP and adverse outcomes, even if MgSO4 use reaches only 50% by the end of year 4.

TitreApplicationTitle: Risk factors for HIV-1 infection and access to treatment among boys and men in Uganda
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER; HIV/AIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Boys and men are likely to behave in risky ways that increase their likelihood of infection with HIV/AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases. We aim to understand what perceptions of risk place boys and men at an increased risk so that we can target interventions to reduce their risk taking behaviours. We intend to develop a cohort of HIV negative boys and men in Uganda and assess their perceptions of masculinity, quantify the extent of their risk taking behaviours, and then assess the likelihood of HIV seroconversion over the study period.

TitreApplicationTitle: Working Memory Training in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Neural Mechanisms of Change.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHD; ADULT; EVENT RELATED POTENTIAL (ERP); INTERVENTION; LEARNING DISORDERS; NEUROIMAGING; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Working memory (WM) is a key cognitive function that allows individuals to hold and manipulate information in one's mind for a few seconds. It is essential for many daily tasks, like following directions, comprehending what you are reading, complex reasoning, and staying focused on a problem. Individuals with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) seem to have particularly poor WM, making it difficult for them to pay attention and learn from experience. Scientists have recently discovered that WM capacity depends in part on the ability to exclude (inhibit) irrelevant information - which could clog up WM - and thereby control what is held in mind. Excitingly, a brain imaging technique has been developed that can identify the brain processes responsible for filtering out (inhibiting) irrelevant information from WM. What's more, scientists believe that WM performance, and perhaps even some other types of brain processes and ADHD symptoms in children with ADHD, can be improved by a 5-week intensive, individualized, and progressive computerized training program. However, scientists don't know whether the WM problems in ADHD arise from poor filtering ability, or whether the WM training program would be effective for adults with ADHD. So our plan is to use this brain imaging technique with young adults with and without ADHD to first determine whether WM problems in ADHD are related to poor filtering abilities or other brain processes. Then we will examine the effects of the WM training program on young adults with ADHD to see if it does produce long-lasting improvements in WM and other aspects of daily functioning. To do so we will compare the effects of the individualized, progressive and high-intensity WM training program with those of a low-intensity and non-progressive version. Findings will increase our understanding of brain mechanisms underlying WM problems in ADHD, and thereby help fine-tune the WM training approach so that it can be maximally effective.

TitreApplicationTitle: In vivo quantification of glutamatergic abnormalities in patients with Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID-BETA; BIOMARKERS; CSF; IMAGING; PET
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia after 65 years old. AD dementia is characterized by a silent period followed by a progressive deterioration of cognitive function.  Loss of neuronal contacts, accumulation of abnormal proteins progress asymptomatically for many years and dementia symptoms indicate a severe brain damage caused by these events. Although advanced imaging methodology is capable to demonstrate the presence of dementia secondary to AD, it is currently impossible to diagnose individuals with incipient AD.  The imaging diagnosis of incipient AD is crucial for therapeutic interventions during phase of the AD in which the cortex remains functional.  Thus, the cure of AD depends on the early diagnosis of this condition.  We propose a novel imaging technique to diagnose insipient AD using Positron Emission Tomography (PET).  This novel imaging technique relies on the quantification of a protein that mediates neuron-to-neuron communication.  This protein is present in the neuronal contacts lost during the "clinically silent" phase of AD.  In normal persons, this protein mediates important cognitive processes such as memory.    We hope that this novel PET tracer will also allow monitoring progression of AD.  It is expected that the results of this study will indicate whether medications targeting brain glutamate can be useful to treat for AD patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Abnormal Activation of Thymocytes High-Mobility Group Box Protein (TOX) in Cutaneous T Cell Lymphomas: Pathogenic Significance and Clinical Applications
Keywords-MotsClés: CUTANEOUS T CELL LYMPHOMA; EPIGENOMICS; MOLECULAR DISEASE MARKERS; SEZARY CELLS; SEZARY SYNDROME; T CELL DEVELOPMENT; TOX
Abstract-Résumé: Cutaneous T cell lymphomas (CTCL) are cancers that are developed from the CD4+ subset of the mature T lymphocytes in the skin. Although rare, these cancers are highly aggressive in advanced stages, causing high mortality because there are no curative therapies at present. These cancers are difficult to diagnose because of lack of sensitive and specific markers.  Further the molecular events leading to the initiation and progression of skin lymphoma cells remain unclear.    Our laboratory recently discovered a previously unrecognized marker, TOX (which stands for thymocytes high mobility group box protein), that is abnormally activated not only in late stage disease but also in the earliest form of skin lymphomas. In the current study, we will perform a series of experiments to answer two questions:  (1) Can TOX protein serve as a sensitive and specific diagnostic marker for skin lymphoma cells?  Currently, the lack of such a marker is a major bottleneck in the treatment and research of skin lymphomas; and (2) Is TOX abnormal activation a cause for the development of skin lymphomas? Not only does this study have the potential of identifying a specific diagnostic marker for skin lymphomas, it also offers the unique possibility of clarifying how skin lymphomas develop, thus facilitating therapeutic development for skin lymphomas, which remain incurable at present.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of the molecular pathways controlling the development of functional CD8+ memory T cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC INFECTION; IMMUNOLOGICAL MEMORY; KNOCK-OUT MICE; NOTCH SIGNALING; T CELLS; VACCINATION
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system of an individual is devoted to figth infectious agents. This is achieved by white blood cells that patrol the organism to eliminate pathogens. T cells, a type of white blood cells, are the central player allowing to mount an efficient immune response. These T cells recognize specifically the foreign materials via a cell surface receptor, the T cell receptor(TCR). This recognition allows for the expansion and differentiation of T cells that are specific to the infectious agent. The differentiation of T cells is crucial to allow them to acquire the ability to eliminate the infectious agent. After pathogen clearance, most of the differentiated T cells will die to reset the system. A few of these T cells will survive as long-lived memory T cells. These memory T cells remember their previous encounter with the infectious agent and will therefore respond much more efficiently to a second infection by the same pathogen. The generation of these memory T cells form the basis of vaccination. Therefore, it is critical, to ameliorate vaccination, to better understand how these memory T cells are generated. The overall goal of this proposal is to define the signals that are required for the generation of memory T cells. To do so, we will immunize different mouse mutant models and we will identify the genes controlling memory T cell formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: cyclin G2 in ovarian cancer development
Keywords-MotsClés: CYCLIN G2; EPITHELIAL OVARIAN CANCER; GROWTH FACTORS; METASTASIS; MICRORNA
Abstract-Résumé: Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC), which is the most common form of the ovarian cancer, has the highest mortality rate of female cancers.  The low survival rate for women with EOC results from an inability to detect the disease at an early, curable stage, from the lack of effective treatment for the advanced cancer, and from our incomplete understanding of how the EOC develops.    Recently, we discovered that a protein named cyclin G2 exerts potent anti-tumour effects in ovarian cancer.  We also observed that several growth factors, which promote ovarian cancer metastasis, decreased cyclin G2 levels. These novel findings suggest that cyclin G2 plays important roles in inhibiting ovarian metastasis. In this study, we will further investigate the functions of cyclin G2 in preventing ovarian cancer development. We will also determine how cyclin G2 exterts anti-tumor effects.  Finally, we will evaluate how oncogenic signals inhibit cyclin G2 expression.  This study will lead to a better understanding of ovarian epithelial carcinogenesis and may ultimately provide a potential screening and/or therapeutic approach for EOC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation on cigarette smoking and cognitive function in smokers with schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; BRAIN STIMULATION; CIGARETTE SMOKING; COGNITION; CRAVING; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Cigarette smoking rates are extremely high in persons with schizophrenia and this increases the risk of disease and death due to tobacco-related disorders. One of the features of schizophrenia is reduced cognitive abilities, such as poor attention and memory. It is thought that people with schizophrenia smoke cigarettes to reduce these cognitive problems, as nicotine can improve cognitive function in these people. When people with schizophrenia stop smoking it causes further cognitive difficulties, which makes quitting harder for them compared to people without schizophrenia.    A method called repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) allows clinicians to give repeated magnetic pulses through the scalp to cause changes in brain activity and behaviour. rTMS can improve cognitive function in people with schizophrenia. Studies have also shown that rTMS can reduce tobacco craving and consumption of cigarettes. Therefore, we believe that rTMS will improve the cognitive deficits observed during cigarette smoking abstinence and help reduce cravings for cigarettes. Ultimately, rTMS may help smokers with schizophrenia who can't quit smoking with available treatments.  This study will examine the effect of rTMS on tobacco cravings and cognitive problems produced by overnight abstinence from cigarette smoking in persons with schizophrenia in comparison to people without mental illness who smoke. Important information about the potential of rTMS for the treatment of cognitive deficits and tobacco addiction in schizophrenia will be obtained. Providing more effective smoking cessation treatments in people with schizophrenia may lead to improved physical and mental health for these patients, who are extremely susceptible to tobacco addiction and tobacco-related illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expanding Antimicrobial Chemical Diversity
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTINOMYCETE; ANTIBIOTIC; DRUG DISCOVERY; NATURAL PRODUCT
Abstract-Résumé: Antibiotics are vital to the health of Canadians yet the remarkable success of these drugs over the past half century is under threat.  There are two main reasons for this state of affairs.  First the microbes targeted by antibiotics have developed resistance to all classes of available drugs.  Second, the pharmaceutical industry has largely fled the antibiotic discovery field and is focusing on mature compounds with proven efficacy.  The role of academe in contemporary antibiotic discovery is therefore paramount.  In this renewal application we propose to expand our research on engineering antibiotic producing bacteria in the search for new methods to expand our antibiotic repertoire. By leveraging our expertise in bacterial genetics, enzyme function, and chemical purification and synthesis, we will contribute significantly to the development of new antimicrobial strategies that have the potential to prime the antibiotic development pipeline.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of matrix metalloproteinase 12 in trophoblast-directed uterine vascular remodeling
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR INVASION; FOCAL ADHESION KINASE; IN VITRO CELL MODELS; IN VIVO LENTIVIRAL GENE TRANSFER; PLACENTA; PREGNANCY; TROPHOBLAST; VASCULAR REMODELLING
Abstract-Résumé: Preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction (FGR) are leading causes of hospitalization, preterm birth, and death in pregnant mothers and their babies in Canada and worldwide. A recent Canadian Institutes of Health Information survey found that babies born small for gestational age or preterm, constituting 1 in 7 births in Canada, had hospitalization stays up to twelve weeks longer than normal births, costing up to $107,000 more in health care costs per birth. Moreover, babies born from these complicated pregnancies often exhibit significant physical and cognitive disabilities and chronic health problems later in life. Therefore, studying the causes of preeclampsia and FGR is of utmost importance. The primary pathologic feature of preeclampsia and FGR is reduced blood flow through the uterine blood vessels that supply the placenta. Normally, placental cells migrate into the uterus and actively cause expansion of uterine blood vessels to increase blood flow to the placenta. In particular, expansion is mediated by breaking down the elastic layer surrounding the blood vessels. Our lab and others have recently identified abundant and specific expression of matrix metalloproteinase 12 (MMP12), an enzyme with potent and specific elastase activity, within migrating placental cells. However, the regulation of this protease in migrating placental cells, as well as the biological significance of its expression, is unclear. Therefore, using in vitro and in vivo models, we will determine the role of MMP12 in placental cell-mediated expansion of uterine blood vessels. This project will have important diagnostic and therapeutic implications for women's and children's health, which is certainly within the goals of the CIHR.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the purinosome and the cellular milieu that drives its formation and function
Keywords-MotsClés: ENZYME COMPLEXES; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; FRET; PURINES; PURINOSOME
Abstract-Résumé: Purines are molecules that are essential for all life and, among other important functions, provide the building blocks for RNA and DNA.  Because of the high demand for purines in rapidly proliferating cancer cells, the purine biosynthetic pathway has attracted considerable attention as a target for cancer chemotherapy.  Recent work on the biosynthesis of purines has shown that the enzymes in this pathway colocalize into a multi-enzyme complex termed the purinosome.  Using a variety of in vivo and in vitro methods, we will characterize the components of the purinosome and the protein-protein interactions that control its formation.  We will also identify non-pathway proteins and post-translational modifications that are necessary for purinosome formation or function.  In addition, we will optimize conditions to reconstitute the purinosome in vitro in order to characterize the molecular structure.  Investigation of how this macromolecular assembly forms and functions will provide valuable insights into the biosynthesis of purines and will shed light on the role that these types of multi-enzyme complexes play in biosynthetic pathways in general.  In addition, characterization of the components and essential interactions of the purinosome will provide a novel strategy for the development of anticancer chemotherapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: MicroRNA mediated effects on macrophage activation and disease pathology in steroid-resistant asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY EPITHELIUM; ANTAGOMIRS; ASTHMA; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGES; MICRORNA; RESPIRATORY HEALTH; STEROID RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: In severe asthma, patients often respond poorly to steroid-based therapies.  While this subset of patients represents a small portion of asthmatic patients, they account for around 50 percent of all health care expenses associated with asthma in many developed countries (including Canada and Australia).  Further, the numbers of patients and the severity of disease has increased dramatically in recent years, resulting in increased health care costs, and decreased quality of life for severe asthmatic patients.  The lack of steroid-mediated control of both inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) in these patients suggests a fundamentally different mechanism of disease, compared to the more common moderate for of asthma.  However, the direct mechanisms underlying steroid-resistant asthma pathology remain poorly understood and no effective therapies currently exist to treat this population.    Release of the small molecule cytokines interferon (IFNg) and IL-27, activation of bacterial (LPS)-induced inflammatory pathways and macrophage activation play key roles in the development of AHR in severe steroid-resistant asthmatics.  Dr. Paul Foster's lab recently demonstrated that administration of IFNg and LPS can also induce steroid-resistant neutrophilia and AHR in mice, as a model of human asthma.  MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are also molecules that are emerging as regulators of inflammation and preliminary studies suggest they may play a key role in the regulation of airway disease.   In my research proposal, I will characterize miRNA expression profiles in the steroid-resistant mouse model, focusing on responses in airway cells and activated immune cells. I will then selectively block specific miRNAs to determine effects on disease severity and cell function, with the aim to identify novel therapies for asthma treatment.  Ultimately, our aim is to bring these findings into the clinic and provide a new therapy to treat patients suffering from steroid-resistant asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of cardiac-specific knockout of GSNOR in cardioprotection following myocardial infarction (MI): Focus on gender differences
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER; GSNOR; HEART; MOUSE; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; NITRIC OXIDE; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PHYSIOLOGY; S-NITROSYLATION; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: There are considerable epidemiological data showing that pre-menopausal females have reduced risk for cardiovascular disease.  Compared to age-matched males, pre-menopausal women show lower incidence of left ventricular hypertrophy, coronary artery disease and cardiac remodeling following myocardial infarction.  The incidence of cardiovascular disease increases in post-menopausal women.  Studies in animal models have also suggested that females have reduced injury following myocardial infarction.  A large body of evidence suggests that estrogen working through the nitric oxide pathway is involved in this gender-related cardiac protection, but the exact mechanism involved remains largely unknown.  Nitric oxide is a highly versatile signaling molecule, and S-nitrosylation is thought to be one of the major signaling pathways through which it exerts its action.  S-nitrosylation is regulated by S-nitrosogluathione reductase (GSNOR) and mice lacking the GSNOR gene show more favorable outcome following myocardial infarction, yet the mechanisms involved are not well understood.  Thus, in this current study, I hypothesize the females with cardiac-specific knockout of the GSNOR gene will have more favorable outcome following myocardial infarction due to reduced myocyte apoptosis and left ventricular remodeling and improved angiogenesis.  The results from these study will provide an integrated view of the role of nitric oxide and GSNOR in cardiovascular pathophysiology and also allow us to assess the role of S-nitrosylation in gender-related cardioprotective effects against ischemic injury.  Our findings will also help to identify new drug targets and help to optimize treatment of heart disease in women and men.  In the long term, our findings will have implications for developing new therapeutic strategies for myocardial infarction and other related cardiovascular diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional significance of calcium channel properties in cochlear hair cells and spiral ganglia neurons
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR IMAGING; COCHLEA HAIR CELL; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EPIFLUORESCENCE; ION CHANNELS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; REGENERATION; SPIRAL GANGLIA NEURONS
Abstract-Résumé: Cochlear Hair cells (HCs) in the inner ear convert sound and balance signals into electrical impulses, which are then transmitted to spiral ganglia neurons (SGNs) with remarkable precision and sensitivity. Our long-term goal is to understand how calcium (Ca) channel proteins and Ca ions regulate the electrical activity and biochemistry of HCs and SGNs. Studies from our group and others have demonstrated that Ca-mediated changes underlie electrical activity of HCs and SGNs and indeed, Ca may turn on genes that are responsible for neuronal survival. We know very little about the different Ca channels that confer Ca-dependent changes in HCs and SGNs, despite their potential therapeutic ramifications. Strong evidence from data in developmental cell biology and electrophysiology motivates our overall hypothesis that multiple Ca channels in HCs and SGNs regulate distinct functions ranging from short-term membrane excitability to long-term developmental processes and gene expression. For example, we predict that the channel Cav1.2 is expressed in SGNs, serving as a channel as well as a transcription factor. These studies will reveal how HCs and SGNs coordinate and regulate their electrical and bichemical machinery, and this information can be exploited to induce HC and SGN survival after damage.

TitreApplicationTitle: The influence of targeted genetic polymorphisms on emotionally enhanced attention and episodic memory: an Endophenotopic approach
Keywords-MotsClés: EMOTION; FMRI; MEMORY; NEUROGENETICS; PTSD; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: Some people can remember important past events much more easily and vividly than others. Such a capacity for emotional memory may be linked to anxiety, and can influence susceptibility to posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Recent research suggests that some of this difference in memory capacity may be genetic. Understanding genetic influences on the capacity for emotional memory has tremendous implications for understanding normal human memory as well as pathological reactions to traumatic stress, which can differ across individuals even when they are exposed to the same events. Certain genetic polymorphisms, or commonly found variations in genes, have been found to influence brain processes linked to differences in emotional memory, and may render individuals more vulnerable to negative life experiences. However, it is still not known what aspects of memory formation and recollection are influenced by those genetic variations, nor how they interact with life experience to influence emotional memory. In this study, we propose to use state of the art genotyping techniques to probe links between genotype and brain activity while laying down and reinforcing memory for emotional events. This work will provide new data on how genetic variability in neurochemical activity alters both behavior and brain activity underlying emotional influences on perception and memory. In this way we can better understand how genetic differences, in interaction with life experience, may influence aspects of attention and emotion that lead to healthy and pathological responses to stressful events.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brainstem and spinal cord mechanisms for control of locomotion
Keywords-MotsClés: INTRACELLULAR OR PATCH CLAMP RECORDING; ISOLATED NEONATAL RAT AND MOUSE BRAINSTEM-SPINAL CORD PREP; LOCOMOTION; SPINAL CORD INJURY; SPINAL CORD SLICE PREPARATION; SPINAL INTERNEURONS
Abstract-Résumé: According to the Canadian Paraplegic Association, 35 persons/million or 1,050/year in Canada suffer spinal cord injuries. Approximately 36,000 Canadians are currently living with spinal cord injury. A major goal for spinal cord injury research is the restoration of locomotion. My research focuses on defining of the neural pathways descending from the brain that are responsible for initiation of locomotion, and on identification of the nerve cells of the spinal cord that are activated by these pathways. This knowledge is required for development of new strategies for restoring walking after spinal cord injury. We have defined a pathway from the brain to the spinal cord of rodents that is involved in the initiation of locomotion, and we have shown that this pathway activates spinal neurons via specific receptors for 5-hydroxytryptamine. This research is designed to define the anatomical details of this pathway, to characterize the properties of the neurons that make up this pathway so that they can potentially be controlled with drugs or other interventions. I will also determine the properties and roles in locomotion of the target neurons that are activated by this pathway in the spinal cord. In spinal cord injury, these cells can be targeted for control by interventions such as drug applications and electrical stimulation to aid in the restoration of locomotion.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of SHP-2 in Prolactin Hormone Signaling in Mammary Epithelial Cell Differentiation and Morphogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; HORMONE ACTION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The growth and development of the mammary gland is a complex process that begins during embryogenesis and continues postnatally through puberty, pregnancy and lactation and finally involution. During lactation the mammary epithelial cells are growth arrested and functionally mature to produce milk. Multiple growth factors regulate the various stages of mammary gland development. The hormone prolactin (PRL) is critical for the induction and maintenance of differentiation of mammary epithelial cells during lactation. Furthermore, recent evidence generated in our lab has highlighted the role of PRL as a suppressor of breast cancer aggressive phenotype. The signaling pathways operating downstream of PRL to regulate mammary gland development are not fully elucidated. We have previously shown that the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2 plays an important role in PRL signaling leading to activation of the Jak2/Stat5a pathway, a critical pathway implicated in mammary epithelial cell differentiation. The objective of this proposal is to characterize further the role of SHP-2 in mediating PRL functions in the mammary gland and also define its role in breast cancer. In this proposal we expect to identify new signaling networks operating downstream of PRL/SHP-2 with important implications for the normal growth and Differentiation of the mammary gland.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the Adaptor Protein Nck in the Pathogenesis of Insulin Resistance and Type 2 Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTOR PROTEINS; DIABETES; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM STRESS; GLUCOSE AND LIPID METABOLISM AND HOMEOSTASIS; HEPATIC GLUCONEOGENESIS; INSULIN SIGNALING AND RESISTANCE; NCK KNOCK OUT MICE; OBESITY; PRIMARY HEPATOCYTES; UNFOLDED PROTEIN RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: When obese people develop type 2 diabetes, it could be because the cells that produce insulin make less insulin, and their body cannot use the insulin it makes as effectively, a condition called insulin resistance. Obesity puts stress on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), a compartment of all the cells in our body. Normally when the ER is stressed, it protects the cells by elaborating a process called the unfolded protein response (UPR). In obese mice, the UPR is excessively activated. This makes the cells less sensitive to insulin, thereby it is harder for the body to lower blood glucose levels.  We have discovered that a protein called Nck is involved in the regulation of the UPR. Recently, we have provided strong evidence that Nck is important in the development of insulin resistance in obese mice through its role in regulating the UPR. More importantly, we have identified Nck as a negative regulator of insulin action in liver. Therefore, during the next 5 years, we will determine how Nck counteracts insulin action in liver. By learning more about Nck related to the UPR and insulin signaling, we will be able to find new ways of treating or preventing type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: HCV genetic variability and resistance to antiviral drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRAL DRUGS; BIOCHEMICAL MECHANISMS; DRUG RESISTANCE; ENZYME KINETICS; FIDELITY; GENOTYPE; HCV REPLICONS; HEPATITIS C VIRUS (HCV); JFH-1; RNA POLYMERASE
Abstract-Résumé: The hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a major human pathogen. Infection with the virus can cause severe liver disease, including cancer. Unfortunately, by far not everyone benefits from available therapies. Although several new antiviral agents have been developed, many of these drugs lose their activity over time. The virus changes rapidly and certain genetic variants can survive in the presence of literally any given drug. Here we hypothesize that a complex interplay between the frequency with which these mutations emerge and the efficiency with which the resistant viruses can replicate can determine success or failure of a given antiviral drug. We propose to employ a combination of biochemical experiments and cell-based assays to tackle this problem. Success in the proposed research will likely contribute to the design of drugs and drug combinations that are associated with a high barrier to the development of resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms involved in abnormal differentiation of osteogenic mesenchymal stem cells in osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTES; HUMAN MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS; LEPTIN; OSTEOBLASTS; STR/ORT MOUSE; WNT PATHWAY
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most frequent form of arthritis yet our capacity to treat OA is limited since we still do not know the causes of OA.  In recent years, it became evident that OA cannot be limited to a disease of articular cartilage, although articular cartilage loss is the clinical hallmark of OA.  We now know that multiple tissues are affect in OA and it is interesting to note that all tissues affected share a common precursor cell type, the mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) present in the bone marrow.  These MSC can proliferate into a number of different cell types, namely osteoblasts (Ob), adipocytes (Adipo), and chondrocytes.  Most importantly, the capacity to form Ob from bone marrow of OA patients is increased whereas the capacity to form Adipo or chondrocytes is reduced.  MSC can form these multiple cells in response to local factors promoting one or the other cell type.  In particular, the Wnt signaling pathway, a very important pathway for cell proliferation, differentiation and commitment to a specific lineage, is responsible to control the balance between Ob and Adipo in bone marrow.  We recently reported that the Wnt signaling pathway is reduced in Ob from OA patients which could explain the altered capacity to form mature Ob and Adipo in OA patients.  Indeed, local factors produced by Ob from OA patients inhibit the normal function of chondrocytes, hence could also influence the recruitment of MSC from the bone marrow.  Our proposed studies will explore the role and impact of the Wnt signaling pathway in human OA MSC, and in mouse MSC from an animal model of OA to test new avenues of treatment to correct the altered mechanism that leads to abnormal recruitment and proliferation of Ob and Adipo from human OA MSC.  This approach could then be translated into new clinical intervention in human OA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functions of Nod1 and Nod2 in host resistance.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGIC LUNG INFLAMMATION; HOST RESISTANCE TO INFECTION; INTERFERON; MOUSE MODEL; MUCOSAL INFECTION; NOD-LIKE RECEPTORS; NOD1; NOD2; PRIMING OF T AND B CELL IMMUNITY; SKIN INFLAMMATION; TNF-ALPHA
Abstract-Résumé: My research program focuses on deciphering the mechanisms of how the human immune system recognizes pathogens, leading to the subsequent instruction of long-lived immune responses to fend off infectious microbes. Recent advances in our understanding of the human immune system have led to the discovery of several host protein families that specifically detect molecular patterns of pathogens for the instruction of antimicrobial immune responses and the regulation of local and systemic immune-homeostasis. This concept has been further fueled by observations that polymorphisms and mutations in the human genes of the Nod-like receptor (NLR) protein family members encoding host proteins involved in detecting pathogens (e.g. Nod1, Nod2) are linked to both impaired antimicrobial resistance as well as to chronic inflammatory barrier disorders. Thus, the focus of my laboratory is to investigate the cellular and molecular mechanisms induced upon recognition of pathogens by Nod-like receptors, in particular Nod1 and Nod2. The scientific insights gained from the proposed research program will advance our medical and scientific understanding to enable us to tailor preventive vaccination strategies as well as therapies for the intervention of chronic inflammatory disorders to improve the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Knowledge to Action Intervention for Long-term Care: A Feasibility Study Focusing on the Uptake of Osteoporosis and Fracture Prevention Best Practices
Keywords-MotsClés: FALLS; FRACTURES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LONG-TERM CARE; OSTEOPOROSIS; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: In the long-term care (LTC) setting, more research is needed on how health care professionals can be kept up to date on the latest medical evidence for providing care to elderly residents. The LTC environment differs from other health care settings. We need to examine what types of strategies can be used to effectively educate LTC physicians, nurses, and other care professionals about the best care practices.   In this study, we will deliver and evaluate a multi-component educational strategy that builds on research in LTC by our team. In order to evaluate its success, 20 homes will receive the intervention and 20 homes will receive usual care. In the intervention homes, a team of experts will give educational sessions at the LTC home, delivering key messages about "best practices", helping LTC professionals to plan changes for delivering better care, giving feedback about performance, and providing materials (e.g., DVD, treatment plans). We will also train a professional in the home to "champion" the cause after the experts are gone.   The specific "best practices" topic we have chosen to test our model is osteoporosis and fractures. These conditions are very common in the elderly living in LTC and negatively impact quality of life. For example, an individual with a hip or other fracture may experience unnecessary pain and suffering and even pre-mature death. There are effective treatments that can be used to reduce fractures, including vitamin D, which is a low-cost, well-tolerated and easy treatment to deliver. Unfortunately our previous studies have shown that most LTC residents are not receiving effective fracture-prevention treatments. To determine our intervention's success, we will examine whether the rate of vitamin D use and other treatments increases, and whether fewer LTC residents fall and fracture. We are also interested in studying the strategy's format and feasibility and what future changes should be made.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cannabinoid and Dopamine Modulation of Emotional Memory Plasticity in the Amygdala-Prefrontal Cortical Circuit
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYGDALA; CANNABINOIDS; DOPAMINE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EMOTIONAL MEMORY; FEAR; LEARNING; PLASTICITY; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: The primary goal of our research project involves the characterization of brain pathways responsible for emotional learning and memory encoding at the level of the single neuron, and at the behavioural systems level. We use an integrative combination of in vivo electrophysiology and behavioural pharmacology techniques to determine how the brain perceives and encodes this emotionally salient information and specifically, how a specific neural circuit comprising the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), basolateral amygdala (BLA) and ventral tegmental area (VTA) encodes and expresses conditioned emotional associations and memories. To study emotional memory formation and expression, we use a well established olfactory 'fear-conditioning' procedure that simultaneously allows us to measure behavioural outputs of emotional memory processing, and also how either single neurons, or neuronal ensembles within specific brain regions may encode this information in terms of associative neuronal activity patterns. Our research focuses on functional interactions between two specific neurotransmitter systems, the endocannabinoid system, which is regulated via CB1 receptors, and the dopamine (DA) system. Functional disturbances in both systems are implicated in the psychopathology and etiology of schizophrenia and other neuropsychiatric disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: From Birth to Adolescence: The Developmental Trajectories Leading to Mental Health Problems in a Representative Population Sample.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; CHILDHOOD; CONTINUITY AND CHANGE; DEVELOPENTAL TRAJECTORIES; ETIOLOGY; HUMAN DEVELOPMENT; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MENTAL HEALTH; POPULATION SAMPLE; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: While physical illnesses account for most of the social and economical burden among adults, mental health problems are the first cause of disability among youths. The prevalence of mental health problems in children and adolescents is higher than previously thought. Point estimates in the past decade suggest that at least 20% of children will have a mental health problem in any given year, and the rates are as high as 36.7% when considering the risk of having at least one disorder by age 16 years. Preventive measures are less costly and intrusive than curative ones, which explains why prevention has been adopted in many societies. Recent research has shown that most mental health problems have their roots early in life. But most studies have not searched for the roots of mental health problems as early as the preschool years. This research project will examine the development of Mental Health Problems (MHPs) from birth to adolescence (14-16 years) among a population cohort (the Quebec Longitudinal Study on Child Development, N=1979). The study is likely to fill a significant gap in health research as it will provide unique information on the relative role of the first 5 years (versus later years) of life in the development of mental health problems among a representative population cohort. The project will address 2 main questions: (1) Are symptoms of mental health problems during early and middle childhood predictive of mental health problems in adolescence? (2) What are the contributions of risk and protective factors to the prediction of mental health problems in adolescence? The study, with its focus on the comparison of the timing of risk factors, will generate knew knowledge on how risk and protective factors work together over the first 16 years of life. The result will refine our knowledge of the factors that should be the target of preventive intervention at specific developmental periods and for specific mental health problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Shb in EphB2-ephrinB1 Signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTORS; CANCER; CELL SIGNALLING; IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PHOSPHORYLATION; RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASES; SIRNA; TISSUE DEVELOPMENT/REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Cell contact-dependent binding of Eph receptors by their cognate ephrin ligands initiates bi-directional signalling into the cell expressing the receptor and the cell expressing the ligand.  This process plays a key role in disease pathogenesis as well as healthy tissue development and repair. Our lab recently developed an assay qBids (quantitative analysis of bidirectional signalling), which allows us to investigate signalling events in distinct cell types (EphB2 or ephrinB1 expressing cells) within a mixed culture of interacting cells.  This approach uses quantitative mass spectrometry to measure signalling events such as protein-protein interactions and tyrosine phosphorylation in combination with SILAC (stable isotope labelling by amino acids in cell culture) to distinguish between the proteins of the two cell types.  Using this approach, an adaptor protein, Shb demonstrated increased and decreased levels of tyrosine phosphorylation in EphB2 and ephrinB1 cells, respectively. An siRNA screen also demonstrated that Shb is required for EphB2-ephrinB1 mediated cell sorting. These results suggest that Shb is a critical effector in EphB2 and/or ephrinB1 signalling.  Shb is a poorly characterized signalling scaffold. Mounting evidence from the Welsh group (Uppsala, Sweden) has implicated Shb in signalling downstream of focal adhesion kinase, growth factor receptors and T cell receptor, and in biological processes such as tumour survival, vascularisation, and oogenesis. The reported binding partners of Shb vary between pathways, suggesting that the crucial signalling function(s) of Shb have yet to be defined. Using the cutting-edge qBids technology, I expect to elucidate Shb's most essential function(s) in EphB2-ephrinB1 signalling. This work has the immediate potential to impact the treatment of physiological processes influenced by EphB2 signalling including peripheral nerve regeneration, neuronal dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease, and tumour vascularisation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Dissection of Primary Biliary Cirrhosis
Keywords-MotsClés: FINE-MAPPING STUDIES; GENETICS OF LIVER DISEASE; GENOME WIDE ASSOCIATION STUDIES; GENOTYPE-PHENOTYPE CORRELATION
Abstract-Résumé: Primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) is a disease of the small bile ducts, in which the immune system attacks and destroys bile duct cells.  This can ultimately result in significant scarring of the liver, and the need for liver transplantation.  As many as 1 in 1000 women over the age of 40 have this disease, with many living for 20-30 years with disease, including its symptoms.  To date no specific therapy exists.  The causes for PBC are not known but it is thought factors in the environment are triggers for disease, in patients predisposed by their genetic "make up".  We have led the world in discovering some of the genes responsible for disease, which has been an exciting project, from which for the first time new approaches to treatment have been suggested.  We propose to continue this pivotal Canadian led study of PBC by further unraveling the genetic "make up" of disease in patients, and elucidating how genetic changes in particular genes ultimately lead to disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of kindlin-2 in myofibroblast differentiation and mechanotransduction of fibroblasts
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNECTIVE TISSUES; CYTOSKELETON; FIBROBLAST; FIBROCONTRACTIVE DISEASES; FOCAL ADHESIONS; GROWTH FACTORS; KINDLINS; MECHANO-SENCING; TISSUE ENGINEERING; TISSUE REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Fibrosis is a major cause for heart failure and death with no effective therapies available to date. When an infarct destroys parts of the heart muscle or in response to cardiac hypertrophy, local fibroblasts become activated to differentiate into contractile and matrix secreting myofibroblasts with the intention to repair the tissue. Frequently however, chronic activation of myofibroblasts results in the development of pathological fibro-contractures that severely impede the heart pumping function. To halt the progression of fibrosis we aim to understand the molecular mechanisms regulating myofibroblast evolution. The stiff mechanical environment of fibrotic scars is one of the most crucial factors promoting harmful myofibroblast differentiation. Recent advances have provided a more detailed understanding of how cells sense the stiffness of their environment by pulling on the matrix using transmembrane integrins. It is the aim of my research to control mechanical stress-mediated differentiation of myofibroblasts to fight fibrosis. Kindlins are a recently identified group of proteins that mediate the link of integrins to the cell's contractile actin cytoskleton within cell-matrix junctions that are important signalling and mechano-transducing cell compartments. Kindlin defects have been associated with a variety of acquired and inherited human diseases. The role of kindlins in fibrotic diseases is poorly studied. We hypothesize that kindlin-2 acts as mechanosensor within the myocardium, contributing to the tissue contractures upon in heart fibrosis. Our preliminary observations suggest a central role for kindlin-2 in cardiac fibroblast activation. It is my aim to examine the molecular mechanisms of kindlin-2 action in cardiac fibroblast mechanosensing and myofibroblast differentiation. Understanding of kindlin-2 function is particularly relevant for cardiac fibrosis and our findings may reveal new targets and therapeutic approaches to prevent cardiac dysfunction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Incidence of Asthma and Outdoor Ambient Air Pollutants: A population-Based Birth Cohort Study
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTANTS; ASTHMA; CHILDREN; ENVIRONMENTAL EXPOSURE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; INCIDENCE; INDUSTRIAL EMISSIONS; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is the most common chronic disease of childhood in Canada. It creates a huge burden of increased morbidity and costs. Risk factors contributing to asthma development include genetic, host and environmental factors. There are controversies about the association between exposure to ambient air pollutants and the development of asthma. Nonetheless, one recent study suggests that a large proportion of the geographic variation in asthma incidence in children could be explained by exposure to on-road traffic-related pollutants. Given the importance of this observation to orient public health interventions, studies are needed to confirm or refute these results. Furthermore, few cohort studies have assessed the association between community exposure to industrial emissions of air pollutants and the development of asthma. We propose the construction of a population-based birth cohort using Quebec Health Care administrative databases to i) describe the geographic variation of asthma incidence in Quebec; ii) assess whether new cases of asthma in children are associated with long-term residential exposure to local on-road traffic, with industrial air pollutant emissions and, with secondary air pollutants such as ozone and fine particles; iii) relate geographic variations in occurrence of new cases of asthma in children through Quebec's regions to children's long-term exposure to air pollutants. This project will contribute to our understanding of the effects of air pollutants on asthma onset in children. It will provide information to calculate incident cases attributable to air pollutant exposure for environmental health and chronic disease surveillance in Quebec and in Canada; this will help target best interventions to reduce health impacts of air pollutants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antiandrogenic and antiproliferative effects of diindolylmethane (DIM) and ring-substituted analogs (ring-DIMs) in androgen -ependent and -independent human prostate cancer cells in vitro, and in vivo using real-time imaging technology.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN DEPENDENT; ANDROGEN INDEPENDENT; ANDROGEN RECEPTOR SIGNALING PATHWAYS; ANTIANDROGENS; APOPTOSIS; DIINDOLYLMETHANE DERIVATIVES; HUMAN PROSTATE; IN VIVO IMAGING AND REDUCTION OF ANIMAL USE; LNCAP AND PC-3 CELL CULTURE; STEROIDOGENESIS AND ENZYME KINETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Numerous studies have shown the protective effects against cancer of high vegetable consumption, particularly that of cruciferous vegetables of the Brassica family (broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage). These vegetables contain high amounts of the compound indole-3-carbinol (I3C), which is converted in the body to a metabolite, diindolylmethane (DIM). DIM has more potent anti-cancer properties than I3C, and studies have shown that it is effective against a variety of cancers, including that of the prostate. Hormone-dependent prostate tumors grow under the influence of the potent male sex hormone dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Current treatment of these prostate tumors involves drugs that block the action of DHT on the androgen receptor (AR antagonists), or those that prevent the production of DHT by inhibiting the enzyme, steroid 5-alpha-reductase (SRD5A inhibitors). DIM acts as an AR antagonists and this is thought to be one possible way in which it inhibits prostate cancer growth. Preliminary results using cancer cell lines (in vitro) suggest that a group of synthetic derivatives of DIM, called ring-DIMs, have more potent anticancer properties than DIM. Furthermore, these ring-DIMs appear to be effective against hormone-dependent as well as -independent prostate cancer cells. This suggests that they are excellent candidates for detailed studies of their mode of anti-prostate cancer action and biological effectiveness in vivo. The present research proposal wishes to determine whether ring-DIMs are effective in vivo by testing their anticancer activity in mice that carry bioluminescent human prostate tumor cells (xenografts). These cells produce light, so the location and growth of the tumor can be easily monitored using an imager, without the need to sacrifice the animals periodically to assess tumor progression. Experiments using prostate cancer cell lines in culture will assess various mechanisms of anticancer action to better understand how ring-DIMs work in tumor cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the clinical and immune causes of disproportionately high HIV levels in semen.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; COHORT STUDIES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HIV TRANSMISSION; MICROBIOME; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; PHARMACOKINETICS; SEMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Globally most HIV is transmitted through the semen of an infected man. However, virus levels in semen are very variable and difficult to predict, even if a man is taking effective HIV medications and has an undetectable level of HIV in the blood. We propose to expand a productive and long-standing research collaboration within the Toronto HIV community to understand this phenomenon better. Specifically, we will examine how semen HIV levels are affected by local immune factors, different HIV medications and other bacteria/viruses that may be present in semen. We believe that this work will lead directly to new strategies to reduce or prevent HIV sexual transmission.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diet induced obesity downregulates gastrointestinal vagal afferent satiety signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EXTRACELLULAR RECORDING; NODOSE GANGLION; OBESITY; VAGAL AFFERENT; WHOLE CELL PATCH CLAMP RECORDING
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is poised to be one of the major health threats to the current generation of Canadians. Nearly 1/2 of Canadians are overweight and 1/3 are obese. The health consequences of obesity such as heart disease, diabetes and cancer have a significant impact on the life of Canadians. Obesity results when more energy is consumed than is used in day to day life. All animals including humans have systems designed to signal when one has eaten enough - this is termed "satiety". Many of these satiety signals are transmitted from the gut to the brain through sensory nerve fibres known as vagal afferents. These nerves can detect the presence of food in the gut two ways; the first is through stretch of the gut as it fills with food. The second is through the release of so called "satiety hormones" and other chemicals that then activate these nerves, sending a message to the brain telling it to stop eating. Why can individuals eat in excess of their daily requirements resulting in the development of obesity? We hypothesize that overconsumption of high fat foods results in "desensitization" of these satiety signaling vagal afferents. The result of this is that the number and strength of signals sent to the brain telling the individual to stop eating are decreased. We plan to test responses of these nerves to satiety hormones using electrical recording techniques. We will compare responses in obese mice (fed a diet with 60% calories from fat) and lean mice (fed a diet with 10% calories from fat). We expect that responses to these satiety signals will be decreased in obese mice. If we do find these differences,we will then attempt to determine: 1. Are the changes specific to satiety, or are the nerves less sensitive overall? 2.Are the changes due to decreases in levels receptors for these hormones, or alternatively the way in which the cells respond to to these hormones. It is hoped that this may lead to new treatments for this important health problem

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Cytochrome P450-dependent Arachidonic Acid Metabolites in Hypertrophy and Heart Failure
Keywords-MotsClés: ARACHIDONIC ACID; CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CELLULAR MECHANISMS; CULTURED ADULT VENTRICULAR MYOCYTES; CYTOCHROME P450/EPOXYGENASE; EETS; HEART FAILURE; RAT CORONARY LIGATION
Abstract-Résumé: Arachidonic acid is what is known as a polyunsaturated essentially fatty acid which is found in limited amounts in the diet and therefore needs to be produced by the body. Normally, arachidonic is found in the membranes of cells but can be released from these membranes under stimulation by an enzyme called phospholipase A 2. When arachidonic acid is released it can be metabolized to potent compounds having diverse effects on various tissues. These include the prostaglandins which have a myriad of effects and the leukotrienes whose best known effects are to constricts the airway passages in the lungs and thus contribute to asthma. A third, more recently discovered pathway produces compounds called epoxides whose functions are not well understood but they are produced by the heart and studies from my laboratory and those of others have shown that they protect the heart from damage when there is a reduction in blood flow. Our hypothesis is that epoxides also reduce abnormal excessive heart growth when the heart is subjected to stress (hypertrophy). In initial experiments we found that when we add epoxides to isolated heart cells or prevents the breakdown of epoxides that are produced in the cell, hypertrophy can be ompletely prevented. In the proposed studies we will use isolated cultured cells as well as an established animal model of heart failure to study the role of epoxides in hypertrophy and heart failure. We will determine what regulates the production of epoxides in the heart in response to distinct hypertrophic stimuli and clearly establish whether manipulation of epoxide production alters hypertrophy. We will also determine the direct effects of epoxides on the hypertrophic response in vitro and in vivo and will study mechanisms for these effects. Taken together it is envisaged that this study will advance our knowledge of how heart failure and hypertrophy are modified by endogenous factors and help to establish new therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Kungatsiajuk: Supporting the healthy smiles of NunatuKavut children
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL YOUTH; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; DISEASE PREVENTION; HEALTH PROMOTION; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; MIXED METHODS; ORAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: A child's smile is a beautiful thing. But when a child suffers from oral disease and decay a smile can be a source of pain and embarrassment.  Poor oral health can affect children's self-esteem, their eating and sleeping habits and eventually their overall health. Aboriginal children in Canada have much higher rates of tooth decay than non-Aboriginal children. The children of NunatuKavut, who live in Inuit communities located in the isolated south coast region of Labrador, face many difficulties that prevent them from having 'kungatsiajuk' (a healthy smile). Many of these difficulties are related to the high cost of travelling to access specialized oral health care outside of their communities, along with very few opportunities to learn about how to prevent oral health problems from happening in the first place. We are proposing to work with the people of NunatuKavut to identify oral health needs of children (ages 0-17). With an understanding of these needs, we will create and implement culturally appropriate oral health promotion and oral health-care service delivery interventions for children. Our research team is made up of health researchers, community members and health-care providers, who hold an interest in the oral health of NunatuKavut children. The success of this program will inform policy recommendations regarding oral health in NunatuKavut and other Aboriginal communities across Canada, and importantly, it will ensure our Inuit children have 'kungatsiajuk'.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the Role of Metabolism in Cell State Reprogramming:  Systems and Synthetic Biology Approaches.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL STATE TRANSITIONS; CELLULAR REPROGRAMMING; CHEMICAL BIOLOGY; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; GENE REGULATION/EXPRESSION; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; METABOLOMICS; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; REGULATORY NETWORKS
Abstract-Résumé: The history of medical research is punctuated by key discoveries that have transformed the course of human health.  In the 1960s, Canadian researchers identified the first stem cells in bone marrow, and since this first discovery, stem cells have been found throughout the body.  During embryonic development, stem cells serve as the "seeds" for organ growth and later, adult stem cells serve to repair and maintain the body.  Recent work has shown that adult skin cells can be "rebooted" back to a state virtually identical to embryonic stem cells.  Such cells have the potential to be redirected into any other cell type in the body, such as neurons or heart muscle.  This breakthrough demonstrates that cell state can be engineered, and promises to bring revolutionary changes to human health.  While these techniques have been successful in the lab, there are several technical barriers to the safe and reliable use of these cells in medicine.  In their current state, these methods are inefficient and slow, and use a viral method that increases the risk of cancer.  This project aims to improve the speed and efficiency of the methods by mapping cell regulatory pathways before, during and after reprogramming.  This map will then be used as guide to find more direct routes between cell states.   Drawing further inspiration from nature, we are replacing the current method with a virus-free approach using molecules that naturally direct cell fate during development, mRNA and metabolites.  These molecules leave the genome untouched and thus do not increase the risk of cancer.  Results from early trials of our virus-free protocols have been successful, and, when combined with the more direct routes described above, promise to advance the next generation of reprogramming technology.  Such stem cells would open the door for incredible medical advances, including patient-specific regenerative medicine, more relevant drug discovery and research into complex disease processes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating skeletal muscle oxidative stress in weight loss variability in obese humans
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LIPOLYSIS; MITOCHONDRIA; OBESITY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; SKELETAL MUSCLE; UCP3
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, and it is increasing by epidemic proportions. Weight loss through diet is possible, but often occurs at varying rates, even in highly controlled weight loss programs. This may be due to factors in the muscle that change how we use fats and sugars as energy.   Objectives: We will investigate if there are differences in the muscle cells of individuals who lose weight quickly compared to those who lose weight slowly. The Harper laboratory proposes that the different rates of weight loss are due to differences in how the mitochondria (powerhouse of the cell) inside muscle cells use fats and sugars to make energy. Based on previous studies, the Harper laboratory believes that these factors cause the cell to produce molecules, called ROS (reactive oxygen species), that can be harmful to the cell, and this contributes to the variability in weight loss.  Experiments:  Muscle samples will be collected from women who participate in the professionally supervised Ottawa Hospital Weight Loss Program. We will measure if there are differences in the amount and the function of important proteins that breakdown sugars and fats in the mitochondria and in the amount of ROS between patients who lose weight more or less quickly. We will also grow muscle cells from the collected muscle samples to see if the cells from those who lose weight more slowly break down sugar and fat differently.   Significance: This research will help us understand why people lose weight differently. Understanding what biological factors contribute to weight loss is important in developing successful treatment strategies for obesity and type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multi-sensory integration for motor control
Keywords-MotsClés: FEEDBACK CONTROL; MOTOR CONTROL; MULTI-SENSORY INTEGRATION; NEURAL CONTROL OF MOVEMENT; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; NEUROSCIENCE; SENSORIMOTOR COORDINATION; SENSORY SYSTEMS
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to control ongoing movements is a critical component of brain functions allowing us to interact with the world. In general, such control depends on the state of the body perceived from visual information and proprioceptive feedback provided by muscles afferents. While the integration of vision and proprioception has been thoroughly investigated during movement planning, their integration during the execution of motor actions remains largely unexplored. In particular, the two sensory systems do not reach the motor cortical regions at the same time, which complicates multi-sensory integration substantially. We will investigate this issue by using a robotic exoskeleton that allows planar movements of the upper limb and can apply loads at the shoulder and elbow joints. The full system, mounted with a virtual reality display, will allow us to selectively perturb the limb mechanics and/or alter the visual information given to the participants about the location of their limb and target goals. We will quantify the timing and contribution of each sensory system by measuring their effect on motor commands from movement and electromyography recordings. The role of specific brain regions in this multi-sensory integration process will be addressed by means of transcranial magnetic stimulation. The control mechanisms underlying multi-sensory integration for motor control are of prime interest, as we constantly need to interact with a non-static world and respond to changes in the environment that we perceive from the visual and proprioceptive sensory systems. The expected results will impact our fundamental understanding of the neural control of movement and support clinical research on the neurological disorders affecting sensorimotor coordination.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physiological Responses to Public Displays of Affection in Stigmatized and Non-Stigmatized Couples
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSIOLOGICAL MEASUREMENT; HEALTH PSYCHOLOGY; LGBTQ PSYCHOLOGY; MINORITY STRESS; PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL RESEARCH; PSYCHOSOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; RELATIONSHIPS & HEALTH; SEXUALITY & SEXUAL FUNCTIONING; STIGMA & PREJUDICE
Abstract-Résumé: "Love is what makes two people sit in the middle of a bench when there is plenty of room at both ends." Physical affection and contact between romantic partners has been consistently linked with positive health outcomes, yet very little research has investigated the health outcomes of public displays of affection (PDAs). Affection between partners can reduce hormonal stress responses, lower cardiovascular reactivity, improve mood, provide pain relief, and reduce blood pressure, but no research to date has examined whether or not PDAs provide these same benefits.  If PDAs do indeed offer couples similar health-protective benefits, doctors and therapists alike may need to prescribe a healthy dose of hand holding or sharing a hug while waiting in line.  But what are the physiological effects of PDAs in couples whose relationships are stigmatized, such as same-sex couples or interracial couples? What happens if a stigmatized couple avoids PDAs for fear of encountering negative social responses? The present study seeks to examine the physiological responses to PDAs in private and in public, in same-sex and in mixed-sex couples using a multi-method design. The results of this study will contribute to our understanding of how relationships influence our health, and will shed light on what individuals can do to improve both their relationships and their health. If the results indicate that stigmatized couples are more likely to avoid PDAs, or encounter negative responses more frequently when they do publically display their affection, this will shed light on some of the existing health discrepancies within the sexual minority community. Sexual minorities report poorer mental and physical health, which is often attributed to the chronic experience of minority stress, but it may also be due to the inability of individuals in same-sex couples to access the health-protective factors of socially accepted displays of affection that are available to non-stigmatized couples.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optogenetic dissection of hypothalamic regulation of sleep states.
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC ENGINEERING; HOMEOSTASIS; HYPOTHALAMUS; METABOLISM; NEURAL CIRCUIT; OPTOGENETICS; SLEEP; WAKEFULNESS
Abstract-Résumé: The prevalence of sleep curtailment is increasing worldwide, particularly in industrialized countries. Sleep disturbances are associated with hormonal imbalances that often results in obesity, diabetes, decreased attention and cognitive performance. In addition, sleep perturbations have been identified as early symptoms of dementia in Alzheimer's Disease and schizophrenia. Thus, understanding the neurobiological mechanisms of the sleep-wake cycle in normal and pathological conditions represents a major challenge of biomedical research. Our goal is to identify and characterize the neural circuits of the brain that control the sleep-wake cycle. In particular, we investigate the properties of wake- and sleep-promoting neuronal populations that are restricted to the hypothalamus. We previously found that selective activation of hypocretin/orexin (Hcrt/Ox)-expressing neurons increases the probability of sleep-to-wake transitions. In this project, we hypothesized that melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH)-producing neurons - a functional counterpart to the Hcrt system - promotes sleep states and stabilizes sleep in mammals. Since the MCH system also regulates food intake and energy expenditure, we will ultimately investigate whether MCH neurons integrate inputs from sleep and metabolic homeostats to consolidate sleep. To achieve our goal, we use in vitro and in vivo optogenetics combined to mouse genetic engineering and electrophysiology. Optogenetics is a new technology that allows optical control of the activity of genetically-targeted neurons with unprecedented temporal and spatial resolutions.  This project will identify new neurobiological mechanisms underlying sleep and sleep-dependent fonction. Long-term perspectives envision alternative therapeutical strategies for significant improvement of sleep induction and sleep maintenance in sleep disorders and pathologies associated with sleep disturbances.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies concerning chronic precoditioning: Development of a new therapeutic paradigm
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIUM; FLOW-MEDIATED DILATION; ISCHEMIA; PRECONDITIONING; REMOTE PRECONDITIOING; REPERFUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease reamins the most common cause of death in our society affecting adults both young and old. A very common form of heart disease is the development of an acute heart atteack where part of the heart muscle dies because of an interruption of blood flow to heart muscle. For decades a great deal of research has been done to develop treatments that reduce the death rate and long-term illness associated with this common condition. It is now recognized that the heart (and other tissue) has the ability to protect itself from the adverse effects of an interruption in blood flow if it experiences less severe reductions in blood flow before a true heart attack occurs. This phenomenon has been termed preconditioining and provides a potential opportunity to develop new therapies for those suffering a heart attack. The current proposal explores  approaches to the development of such preconditioning as new forms of therapy to help reduce the adverse effects of heart attacks.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toward Designed Antibiotics: Mechanisms and Inhibition of PEP Utilizing Enzymes
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL INFECTION; CARBOXYKETOSE SYNTHASE; CARBOXYVINYL TRANSFER; ENZYME INHIBITION; ENZYME MECHANISMS; INHIBITOR DESIGN; KINETIC ISOTOPE EFFECTS; PROTEIN STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Antibiotic resistance is a serious and rapidly escalating health care problem.  We are faced with the prospect of growing numbers of pan-resistant bacteria - bacteria resistant to every known antibiotic.  We study two types of enzymes that bacteria need to survive.  The carboxyvinyl transferases synthesize the aromatic amino acids and components of the cell wall.  The carboxyketose synthases are a group of three enzymes which produce unusual sugars that bacteria require.  One sugar is a building block for aromatic compounds, another forms part of the bacterial cell's outer surface, and the third helps bacteria evade the immune system.  We use a variety of techniques to gain a detailed understanding of the reactions catalyzed by our target enzymes, including determining the structures of the high-energy species by measuring kinetic isotope effects, determining reaction rates, determining the enzymes' structures, and designing and testing new enzyme inhibitors.  Having a thorough understanding of how the enzymes work allows us to design new inhibitors.  These inhibitors will have the potential to become new antibiotics to treat bacterial infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Contextual modulation of Wnt/betacatenin signalling by the Hippo pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CANCER; COLON CANCER; DIFFERENTIATION; HIGH-THROUGHPUT SCREENS; HIPPO PATHWAY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; WNT SIGNALLING
Abstract-Résumé: The proper development of an organ requires the coordination of two distinct sets of instructions or signals.  One signal, exemplified by a family of proteins called Wnts, is important for establishing the type of cell that is formed and its function.  Disruptions in Wnt signalling are associated with colorectal, breast and other cancers.  Equally important are signals, like those of the Hippo pathway, that indicate when there are enough cells present and that the tissue has reached an appropriate size.  These distinct types of signals must cooperate and disruption of either signal leads to defects in development or cancer.  Using a novel highthroughput, robotics-based screening method we developed, we identified a protein that is key in coordinating the activities of these two pathways.  Here we propose to gain a molecular understanding of how the talk between these two pathways occurs and establish what aspects of this communication promotes tumorigenesis.  This work will suggest novel approaches to therapeutic intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: The vitamin D receptor (VDR) is a target for cholesterol lowering
Keywords-MotsClés: 1; 25-DIHYDROXYVITAMIN D3; APOE; CHOLESTEROL; CYTOCHROME P450 7A1; FARNESOID X RECEPTOR; FGP15 KNOCKOUT MICE; FXR; LDLR; LITHOCHOLIC ACID DERIVATIVES; MOLECULAR MODELING AND DESIGN; REGULATION; SHP; SMALL HETERODIMER PARTNER; VITAMIN D RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: We have uncovered an exciting new application of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (1,25VD3), the active component arising from vitamin D intake, towards cholesterol lowering in mice. We observed that 1,25VD3, when administered for binding to the vitamin D receptor (VDR), resulted in suppression of a repressive receptor known as the small heterodimer partner (SHP). Suppression of the SHP led to removal of repression of cholesterol 7alpha-hydroxylase (CYP7A1), the key enzyme responsible for cholesterol degradation  and lowering of cholesterol in serum and liver. We plan to study the mechanism of action of the VDR on other nuclear receptors:  FXR (farnesdoid X receptor, normally a stimulator of SHP and/or intestinal FGF15, another repressor of CYP7A1), SHP, or other nuclear receptors in cholesterol lowering. We plan to use gene knockout mice that lack FXR or SHP and the cholesterol transport genes - the low density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) and apolipoprotein E (apoE), an enzyme essential for normal catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein constituents.  In our planned studies, mice will be given a high fat/high cholesterol diet for us to assess the effectiveness of 1,25VD3 treatment on altered SHP and CYP7A1 levels in cholesterol lowering. We will identify the molecular mechanism and show that 1,25VD3 and the VDR regulate CYP7A1.  We further plan to synthesize nontoxic, new compounds that bind to the VDR with optimized cholesterol lowering properties, including lithocholic acid derivations as alternates of 1,25VD3, via computer design (molecular modeling). Ideally, these compounds would bind strongly to the VDR and not to FXR and are nontoxic. We plan to examine the properties of 1,25VD3 and these new agents (lithocholic acid derivatives) in vivo with the statins (cholesterol lowering medication) to appraise their usefulness when these are used singly or in combination.  Our work will firmly establish that the VDR is a target for cholesterol lowering.
