TitreApplicationTitle: Phosphoregulation of Disordered Protein Interactions in Neurobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: 4E-BP2; DISORDERED STATE STRUCTURE; DYNAMIC COMPLEXES; EIF4E; NMDA RECEPTOR; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY (NMR); PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; SAXS; SRC
Abstract-Résumé: The brain is very complex and how it functions is currently not understood. We are studying specific mechanisms for controlling normal learning and memory that go awry in seizures, stroke, schizophrenia, chronic pain, autism, and brain cancers. This control involves interactions of intrinsically disordered proteins. Proteins are composed of a chain of amino acids, like a chain of beads, with each bead having one of 20 different chemical groups. When proteins are first made, they are disordered and flexible, exactly like a chain of beads. Many proteins then fold or form a compact shape to precisely position the different chemical groups. However, ~20% of human proteins do not fold and remain disordered; an additional 30% have long stretches of disorder in them. These disordered proteins have an important function in biology but are hard to study with conventional methods due to their flexibility. Our group has developed a new approach to study disordered proteins and their binding interactions. Phosphorylation, which is a modification of specific amino acids within proteins that can have important functional effects, often occurs in disordered regions. The two disordered brain proteins we are studying, 4E-BP2 and the Src unique domain (Src UD), both have sites of phosphorylation. 4E-BP2 binds to eIF4E, which controls the synthesis of proteins in the cell. The Src UD binds to a part of the NMDA receptor, which is critical for many brain functions. These binding events are thought to be switched on and off by phosphorylation of 4E-BP2 or Src UD. Our studies will reveal information about the effects of phosphorylation in regulating binding of 4E-BP2 and Src UD to their partners. Importantly, they will provide molecular insights into brain function in memory and learning, as well as enable development of drugs for multiple disorders of the brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intestinal lipid and lipoprotein metabolism in relation with insulin-resistant and diabetic states in humans.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOLIPOPROTEIN; CHOLESTEROL; INSULIN RESISTANCE; INTESTINE; LIPID; LIPOPROTEINS; ORGAN CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Incidence of type 2 diabetes shows a rapid and continuous rise in industrial societies such as Canada. Insulin resistance is the central feature of this pathology, but is also commonly associated with dyslipidemia. Exaggerated hepatic lipid production and impaired clearance by peripheral tissues are believed to play key roles in the development of dyslipidemia. Recent studies have also pointed out the intestine, which is usually cited as a simple absorptive organ, as an important regulator of lipid homeostasis. The study of mechanisms underlying the contribution of intestine to the development of diabetic dyslipidemia is limited by technical issues in humans. Therefore, most cellular and molecular data are from studies in animal models. These studies clearly suggest that, at least in animal models, intestine is an important contributor to the development of dyslipidemia in insulin-resistant state. This study was designed to test the hypotheses that intestine may develop insulin-resistance and inflammatory states and represents a major contributor to diabetic dyslipidemia. The project will characterize the presence of insulin resistance and inflammation in intestine as well as precise mechanisms of lipoprotein overproduction by the intestine. Experiments will be carried out on intestine samples obtained from massively obese men who experience a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with normal glycemia and insulinemia, with insulin resistance or with type 2 diabetes. Measures of insulin signalling, inflammatory state, lipid and apolipoprotein synthesis will be performed to identify the precise mechanisms involving intestine in dyslipidemia. Outcomes of this study are expected to reinforce the role of intestine in the development of atherogenic dyslipidemia in insulin-resistant subjects. Increased knowledge on the mechanisms involved in the development of dyslipidemia may help identify treatment strategies to reduce cardiovascular disease risk in diabetic patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of compensatory mechanisms in locomotor recovery and spinal plasticity after partial spinal cord injury : dual spinal and cortical lesion paradigm
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; FICTIVE LOCOMOTION; FUNCTIONAL RECOVERY; KINEMATIC ANALYSES; LOCOMOTION; MICROSURGERY; MOTOR CORTEX; NEUROPLASTICITY; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: In North America, more than 250,000 people live with a spinal cord injury (SCI), and more than 10,000 new cases arise every year. For SCI patients, severe limits of such basic capacities as walking and controlling posture are a fact of life, and a crucial goal for the scientists is to find effective means of helping these individuals recover and lead active and productive lives. Following incomplete SCI, whose incidence is greater than complete lesions in humans, some recovery of function can occur depending on the severity of the lesion as well as on the intrinsic capacity of the central nervous system to reorganize itself. While significant progress has been made in the last 25 years, the mechanisms of locomotor recovery -and the optimum conditions to enable these mechanisms within the spinal cord and thus improve treatment- remain unclear. The laboratory has recently developed an animal model based on a dual-lesion paradigm that enables us to better understand the physiological mechanisms sustaining locomotor recovery after incomplete SCI. This model allowed us to demonstrate that, after incomplete SCI: 1) the spinal cord itself can reorganize and play a key role in locomotor recovery; 2) intact structures projecting to the spinal cord probably participate actively in reshaping the spinal cord functions. In this postdoctoral project, we will try to determine more precisely the role that specific structures which were undamaged by the SCI may play in optimizing recovery of locomotor functions. We hope that our research will enable us to determine how intact structures contribute to the functional reorganization of the spinal cord after SCI. This comprehensive and integrative approach addresses questions of great clinical significance and such a proof of principle is necessary to design adapted rehabilitative procedures aimed at promoting the recovery of walking in SCI patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Efficacité des traitements pour la vestibulodynie provoquée: un essai clinique randomisé comparant la physiothérapie multimodale et l'application de lidocaïne topique
Keywords-MotsClés: DOULEUR GYNECOLOGIQUE; DYSPAREUNIE; MUSCLES DU PLANCHER PELVIEN; PHYSIOTHERAPIE; READAPTATION; RETROACTION BIOLOGIQUE; SANTE DE LA FEMME; TRAITEMENTS CONSERVATEURS; VESTIBULODYNIE PROVOQUEE; VULVODYNIE
Abstract-Résumé: La douleur recurrente lors des relations sexuelles est un probleme medical important, affectant jusqu'a 21% des femmes nord-americaines. Cette problematique peut entrainer des impacts majeurs sur la vie sexuelle et conjugale des femmes atteintes et devenir une source de detresse psychologique. En effet, ces femmes presentent une augmentation de la depression ainsi qu'une diminution de la qualite de vie. Cette pathologie demeure cependant encore peu comprise. La lidocaine (onguent anesthesique) est le traitement medical le plus utilise actuellement pour les douleurs lors des relations sexuelles. Les muscles du plancher pelvien ont ete identifies recemment comme acteurs importants dans cette pathologie. Un traitement de physiotherapie ciblant les deficits de ces muscles pourrait etre efficace pour diminuer et enrayer la douleur chez ces femmes. Aucune etude n'a evalue l'efficacite de la physiotherapie pour ce probleme ni compare cette intervention au traitement conventionnel de lidocaine. L'objectif de l'etude est de comparer l'efficacite de ces deux traitements chez 224 patientes (de 18-45 ans) souffrant de douleur lors des relations sexuelles recrutees dans 4 hopitaux (CHUS, Hopital general Juif, Hopital Royal-Victoria et CHUM St-Luc). Le premier est un traitement de physiotherapie reparti sur 10 seances hebdomadaires de 60 minutes comprenant, entre autre, des techniques de relaxation, d'etirement et de controle des muscles du plancher pelvien. Le deuxieme traitement consiste en l'application quotidienne de lidocaine au niveau de la vulve pendant 10 semaines. Les physiotherapeutes pourront evaluer les douleurs ainsi que la fonction sexuelle des patientes tout de suite apres le traitement et 6 mois plus tard. Compte tenu de la prevalence et des repercussions, la presente etude pourra contribuer de maniere significative a ameliorer la sante des femmes aux prises avec ce probleme gynecologique pour lequel peu d'options therapeutiques ont ete validees.

TitreApplicationTitle: A new role for CCAAT/Enhancer Binding Protein beta: inhibition of muscle satellite cell differentiation in cancer cachexia.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER CACHEXIA; CCAAT/ENHANCER BINDING PROTEIN BETA; MUSCLE REGENERATION; MUSCLE WASTING; MYOD; SATELLITE CELLS; SELF-RENEWAL
Abstract-Résumé: Many cancer patients lose a lot of weight while sick. They lose not only body fat but also muscle mass, and when this happens, they do not heal as well and cancer treatments are less effective. It is therefore of great importance to identify cancer patients that will suffer from muscle wasting early and to develop treatments that will help preserve body weight and muscle mass. To do this, scientists must first understand what causes some cancer patients to develop muscle wasting. Our research focuses on understanding how a tumour damages the muscle. We have found that some tumours release products which stimulate the immune system and in muscle cause a protein called C/EBPbeta to persist in muscle stem cells. This expression prevents these satellite cells from acting to repair muscle and so muscle damage is not repaired. Over time, the muscle becomes weaker and smaller. The objectives of this proposal are to explore the mechanisms by which C/EBPbeta regulates muscle stem cell function in healthy muscle and to understand how tumours prevent normal stem cell function.

TitreApplicationTitle: A DNA-Based Universal Seasonal Influenza Vaccine Phase I Safety and Immunogenicity Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNE RESPONSE; DNA-BASED VACCINE; ELECTROPORATION; ELISPOT; HEMAGGLUTINATION INHIBITION; INFLUENZA VIRUS; PHASE I SAFETY TRIAL; T AND B CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Seasonal Influenza infection is an important medical problem. Each year many Canadians become ill with the "flu", resulting in economic loss and a substantial number of hospitalizations and deaths. The current flu vaccine is produced in chicken eggs and requires the identification of each season's new circulating flu viruses, followed by development and testing of a perfectly adapted vaccine. This is a timely and costly procedure that often results in under vaccination due to prioritization using limited stock supplies and inefficient vaccines developed against flu viruses no longer circulating. There is therefore a great need to develop new vaccination approaches for achieving long-term protection against different flu viruses. This application proposes to evaluate a novel universal seasonal influenza vaccine in 22 healthy human volunteers. We will use a new DNA technology that eliminates egg-based virus culture entirely and potential allergic reactions. The DNA-based universal influenza vaccine has already been shown to be safe and efficacious against a broad range of flu viruses in several animal studies and is further supported by a promising Phase I clinical study focusing on avian influenza currently ongoing in the US. Such a vaccine is easy to produce in large quantities, will eliminate the need for yearly flu shots and will be available to the entire population at any given time. A synthetic vaccine made of selected and optimized influenza proteins (parts of the virus) has been designed to focus on stimulating protection against many existent and emerging seasonal flu viruses. The main objective of this project, a Phase I clinical trial in healthy volunteers will confirm safety and compare the range of protection against flu viruses obtained with this novel vaccine. Protective antibody levels will be evaluated in this pilot safety study using the developed universal DNA vaccine when delivered in a highly tolerable and safe fashion to 22 healthy volunteers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Addressing community concerns about health risks from Helicobacter pylori infection in Northern Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; CIRCUMPOLAR HEALTH; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; DIGESTIVE DISEASES; HELICOBACTER PYLORI
Abstract-Résumé: Despite limited systematic data on its presence in northern Canada, Helicobacter pylori infection has been an emerging health concern in northern Aboriginal communities, where people are becoming aware of its health risks. In many such communities, people worry about the link between H. pylori and stomach cancer, a cancer that occurs more frequently in this region than on average across Canada. Physicians in the north view this infection as a major problem because it is found in many patients with common stomach complaints and standard treatment is often ineffective in this setting. Health authorities have identified the need for research aimed at developing H. pylori control strategies appropriate for the north. The proposed research seeks to generate knowledge about how health care decision makers can effectively manage H. pylori infection in a manner that addresses community concerns. To begin working toward these goals, the applicants formed the Canadian North Helicobacter pylori (CANHelp) Working Group, a collaborative team that links the University of Alberta with northern health authorities and community organizations. While the research goals require data from multiple northern settings, the team conducted a pilot project as a starting point in Aklavik, NWT, where they found that 62% of 355 participants had H. pylori infection, and among those infected, there was a high prevalence of precancerous stomach conditions. The objectives of the current proposal, developed at the request of northern communities are to: 1) Expand the research to additional communities in the NWT and Yukon to obtain representative data for informing regional public health strategies pertaining to H. pylori infection; 2) Identify cost-effective H. pylori management strategies for northern communities; 3) Create knowledge exchange strategies to help community members understand H. pylori health risks and currently available solutions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel bivalent hybrid molecules with retinoic acid receptor agonistic and histone deacetylase inhibitory activity for cancer treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; HISTONE DEACETYLASE INHIBITORS; HYBRID MOLECULES; RETINOIC ACID RECEPTOR AGONISTS
Abstract-Résumé: An effective way to combat cancer and other diseases is through combination therapy - the use of more than one therapeutic agent at a time in order to simultaneously target more than one biochemical process that may be responsible for a disease. In most cases, this is accomplished by administration of two separate drugs. In this research project, we attempt to combine two therapies in a single drug by making it bifunctional, able to interact with two separate biological targets. We have found that drugs which simultaneously target two particular biomolecules, a hormone receptor and an enzyme, histone deacetlase, that is important for regulation of expression of genes, are more effective against certain types of breast cancer. This project will optimize these drugs so that they may eventually enter clinical trials.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
ResearchClassEN: LIPOPROTEINS, LIPID TRANSPORT; METABOLISM AND NUTRITION
ClasseRechercheFR: LIPOPROTEINES, TRANSPORT LIPIDIQUE; METABOLISME ET NUTRITION
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and cellular determinants of hepatic apolipoprotein B metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: APOLIPOPROTEIN B; DEGRADATION; EXPRESSION; LIVER; METABOLISM; PROTEASOME
Abstract-Résumé: Lipoproteins are complexes of protein and dietary fats that are important in the distribution of food energy through the bloodstream to the distant sites where energy is needed. The liver produces a protein, called apolipoprotein B, which binds and transports cholesterol and dietary fats in the liver and delivers them to sites in the body where they are needed. However, when fats are consumed in excess, they can cause the liver to produce even more lipoproteins and these may accumulate in the blood where they can cause atherosclerosis, or "hardening", of the blood vessels. On the other hand, if these lipoproteins cannot be made fast enough, the fat can accumulate to high levels in the liver. My research is trying to understand how the liver controls how much lipoprotein is made in the liver and transported into the blood and how the natural breakdown of apolipoprotein B can affect this control. We want to identify the components of this removal system that might be specific for the apolipoprotein B, and study how this system fails with aging or with dietary excess. The fat binding properties of this protein may be important in determining how the liver responds to and complexes with dietary fat, as well as how the protein is destroyed when fat is not present. We are working to understand how the structures in the apolipoprotein B interact with dietary fat and other proteins in the liver, in an effort to understand how some foods and drugs might be used to reduce the blood levels of lipoproteins and the progression of vascular diseases.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the hypothalamo-pancreatic axis in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA CELL FUNCTION; BETA CELL MASS; HYPOTHALAMUS; INSULIN SENSITIVITY; INTRACELLULAR METABOLISM; NEURONS; NEUROPEPTIDES; NUTRIENT SENSING MECHANISMS; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Excessive consumption of nutrients with high caloric density and obesity negatively affect insulin action in peripheral and central insulin-sensitive tissues including muscle, liver and the central nervous system (CNS) which in turn promote type 2 diabetes (T2D). The normal pancreatic beta-cell response to nutrient surfeit and insulin resistance is compensatory insulin hypersecretion to maintain normoglycemia. This response involves expansion of beta-cell mass, increased insulin biosynthesis and heightened glucose-induced insulin release. T2D develops in subjects that are unable to sustain the beta cell compensatory response. In the CNS, the hypothalamus plays a critical role in the maintenance of energy balance by modulating food intake as well as the metabolic and endocrine activity of peripheral tissues via the autonomic nervous system (ANS), including the liver and the pancreas. The hypothalamus is able to detect changes in nutrient levels ("nutrient sensing" mechanisms) and activates neuroendocrine reponses to maintain energy homeostasis. Glucose and fatty acids(FAs) act centrally to control food intake and glucose homeostasis via the ANS. Although the involvement of the ANS in insulin secretion is well accepted, whether the hypothalamus is involved in the beta-cell compensatory responses to nutrient surfeit is still unknown. The proposed research program will investigate the signaling mechanisms by which glucose and FAs are detected in the hypothalamus to modulate insulin secretion. We will study these mechanisms under normal nutritional conditions and, study how nutrient excess modulates hypothalamic nutrient-sensing mechanisms to participate in the beta-cell compensatory responses. This project will determine the role of hypothalamic nutrient-sensing mechanisms in beta-cell function and addresses a fundamental issue in human physiology which is directly relevant to the mechanisms of T2D, a disease which affect over 2M Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oscillatory networks for rhythmic timing in auditory and motor regions:  Interaction, development and plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY SYSTEM; DEVELOPMENT; EEG; HEARING; MEG; MOTOR SYSTEM; MULTISENSORY; MUSIC; NEURAL PLASTICITY; TMS
Abstract-Résumé: Deficits in the ability to process auditory rhythms or to perform rhythmic movements have been implicated in a number of disorders and diseases including dyslexia, specific language impairment, Down syndrome, Autism, and Parkinson's disease. Here we investigate how the brain processes auditory rhythms and interactions between hearing rhythms and moving rhythmically. In this context, it is interesting that music is universal across human societies. Its presence at all important social gatherings, including weddings, parties, funerals, and religious ceremonies, attests to music's ability to promote social bonding and common emotional feelings among people. Yet it remains mysterious as to why music has this powerful effect on people. One possibility relates to the fact that people produce music in rhythmic synchronization with each other, in contrast to speech interactions, which typically involve turn taking. In order for synchronization to occur, people must be able to entrain to beats at different tempos. They also need to be able to coordinate between hearing and movement in order to sing and play instruments in time with other people.  Here we investigate how auditory and motor areas of the brain communicate. Specifically, we will measure the activity of oscillatory neural networks spanning auditory and motor areas in the brain using electrophysiology (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). We will then temporarily disrupt neural function in motor areas of the brain using magnetic stimulation and observe how this affects auditory perception. We then plan to examine how these networks develop in children and the extent to which they are plastic and can change with specific experience. Knowledge of how rhythmic activity functions across the auditory and motor systems is critical for understanding auditory and motor impairments and for designing remediation programs that can take advantage of the inherent plasticity in the system at different ages.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of pretransplant ischemic injury and cardiac allograft vasculopathy
Keywords-MotsClés: DAMAGE ASSOCIATED MOLECULAR PATTERNS; ENDOTHELIAL CELL; HEART; ISCHEMIA-REPERFUSION INJURY; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; RECEPTOR-INTERACTING PROTEIN; VASCULOPATHY
Abstract-Résumé: When a heart is irreversibly damaged and cannot be treated by any other medical or surgical means, heart transplantation is the most beneficial and highly-pursued treatment option for saving the person's life. However, the immune system of the graft recipient usually recognizes the transplant as a 'stranger', leading to organ rejection. Although immunosuppressive drugs are beneficial in the short term, transplants often are chronically rejected over time. In addition, due to the generalized suppression by these drugs, various infections and even cancers are commonly seen in transplant patients. Consequently, searching for new strategies to limit the damage caused by unwanted immune responses and to prolong graft survival has become the key objective in the field of transplantation research. Our proposed research project will focus on the identification of an unknown mechanism of chronic heart graft rejection and the development of novel therapeutic approaches to maintaining long-term heart graft survival. The three novel approaches proposed here include: 1) exploring previously unknown mechanisms that cause heart graft damage before transplantation; 2) discovering the new role of natural killer cells in chronic heart graft injury and why natural killer cells attack the heart graft and; 3) using either genetic manipulation or drug to eliminate early heart graft damage. In this study, we will focus on the interaction between natural killer cells and heart graft cells in the early stages of transplantation as well as long term graft survival. We aim to identify a novel mechanism controlled by a newly identified molecule called RIP3 that controls whether heart cell live or die during transplantation. If controlling this molecule by genetic alternation or by drug inhibition is found to be effective in our animal model of heart transplantation, they may provide new solutions for maintaining heart graft survival in our transplant patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel mechanisms of translation inhibition
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC MECHANISMS; BACTERIAL INFECTIONS; FLUORESCENCE SPECTROSCOPY; IN VITRO TRANSLATION; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; RAPID KINETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Antimicrobial resistances are spreading rapidly, causing a major public health concern. This is particularly dangerous in areas where many different bacterial strains come into contact with each other and antibiotics are frequently used such as hospitals or farms. Multi-drug resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa nosocomial infections are increasingly recognized in the world and are a threat to more than just immune compromised humans. This research program will study the mechanism of antibiotic function in order to develop novel antibiotics, by focusing in particular on antibiotics that target ribosome dependent processes. The ribosome is a large macromolecular complex within the pathogens cell that is part of its machinery to translate genetic information into functional proteins, a process called translation, and critical for its survival. More than 50% of the current antibiotics inhibit bacterial translation by targeting the bacterial ribosome. The detailed understanding of the involved processes is of fundamental importance for the development of new types of antibiotics. In our research program, we will study on the molecular level how antibiotics interfere with these processes, in order to inhibit bacterial translation. The fact that the existing translation inhibiting antibiotics target only a very limited set of the ribosomal functions makes them vulnerable to the development of bacterial resistances. We will identify novel translation inhibition mechanisms and molecular requirements for efficient inhibition of translation in bacteria. On the basis of these results, we will develop novel tests that will allow us to search for chemical compounds that will effectively inhibit bacterial translation. The proposed research will significantly contribute to our understanding of the structural and functional requirements of antibiotic function, providing the framework for rational inhibitor design.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predictive serum biomarkers for response to Interferon-ß(IFN-ß) in relapsing Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNOLOGY; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: At present there is no rational way to instruct an individual with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) , whether or not to use IFN-beta or to try the other first line drug for RRMS, glatiramer. These proposed studies aim at following up on the April 2010 publication in Nature Medicine from the Steinman lab. They could lead to a potential diagnostic test to predict who will benefit from IFN-beta. This would mark the first time that a predictive test would be available for deciding on a therapeutic to MS. If we want to practice economically efficient medicine, such a predictive test would be an important breakthrough. Moreover, it would enable us to start the most efficacious therapy as soon as possible.

Abstract-Résumé: Organisms take up nutrients and break them down to release the energy necessary for cellular maintenance or chemically transform them to make the building blocks necessary for growth.   Mass spectrometry allows close examination of the chemicals within cells. This project will identify previously unknown metabolic pathways within cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of arsenic-enhanced atherosclerosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARSENIC; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; LIVER X RECEPTOR; MACROPHAGES
Abstract-Résumé: Arsenic is a widespread environmental contaminant and listed as the number one health hazard by the EPA. Those individuals exposed to arsenic in the environment are at a greater risk for developing cardiovascular disease.  Therefore, we propose experiments designed to understand how arsenic is linked to the development of atherosclerosis.  Using mouse models, we have shown that low doses of arsenic increase atherosclerosis.  We will utilize the same models to define the lowest effective dose of arsenic with and without a high-fat diet and determine whether these effects can be reversed when we remove exposure to arsenic.  Our previous data from cell culture experiments suggest that arsenic inhibits the function of a master regulator the cholesterol balance.  We will continue these experiments by using mice that lack this protein called the liver X receptor alpha.  Finally, we plan experiments to determine the effects of arsenic exposure on a key cell type in atherosclerosis, the monocyte/macrophage.  We predict that arsenic will increase these cells' adhesion to and migration through the vessel well to form atherosclerotic lesions.  From these experiments, we hope to define safe levels of exposure and identify potential interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Organisation anatomique et fonctionnelle du striatum en conditions normale et pathologiques
Keywords-MotsClés: GANGLIONS DE LA BASE; IMMUNOHISTOCHIMIE; MALADIE DE PARKINSON; MICROSCOPIE ELECTRONIQUE; PRIMATES; RECONSTRUCTION NEURONALE UNITAIRE; SOURIS TRANSGENIQUES; STRIATUM; SEROTONINE; TRANSMISSION NEURONALE
Abstract-Résumé: Les ganglions de la base forment un ensemble de structures hemispheriques profondes impliquees dans le controle du comportement psychomoteur. Le striatum est une composante integratrice cle des ganglions de la base et son fonctionnement harmonieux depend d'un equilibre fragile entre differents systemes neurochimiques de natures opposees. Notre projet de recherche vise a elucider les caracteristiques neuromorphologiques et neurochimiques du striatum en conditions normale et pathologiques. Nous investiguerons plus specifiquement les rearrangements qui s'operent au sein de la microcircuitrie striatale suite a la denervation dopaminergique qui caracterise la maladie de Parkinson. De plus, nous tenterons de demontrer qu'une rupture profonde de ce nouvel equilibre striatal est la cause de l'apparition de mouvements anormaux involontaires (dyskinesies) suite au traitement pharmacologique de la maladie. Les connaissances generees par ce projet de recherche permettront de developper de nouvelles avenues therapeutiques afin d'attenuer les symptomes moteurs de la maladie de Parkinson et les dyskinesies induites par son traitement pharmacologique.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health-related Quality of Life in Children with New-Onset Epilepsy:  A Long-term Follow-up
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD EPILEPSY; CHILDREN'S HEALTH RELATED QUALITY OF LIFE; COHORT STUDY; LONG-TERM FOLLOW-UP
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is one of the most common neurological condition in children, affecting about one in two hundred children. Despite relatively good long-term outcomes for children in terms of seizure control, many children with epilepsy have problems in several areas including behaviour, social interactions, academic achievement, family life and cognition.  As a result, treatment of epilepsy has expanded beyond seizure control such that improving quality of life of children with epilepsy is a major component of optimal management.  In a previous study of about three hundred children aged four to twelve across Canada with new-onset epilepsy, we found that their quality of life was lower than children their same age from the general population but that quality of life improved significantly over the first two years with epilepsy. Quality of life was affected by specific characteristics of the children and their families. Children with the poorest quality of life two years later were those who had poor quality of life right after diagnosis, had cognitive problems, mothers experiencing depression, and high family stress.   We plan to follow these youth, now aged nine to twenty years, as they transition from children with new-onset epilepsy to adolescents and young adults living with epilepsy to continue to assess their quality of life.  We will survey these youth and their parents up to eight years after diagnosis to see whether the same child and family characteristics predict long-term quality of life.  Determining which children experience an improvement in quality of life, a decline, or do not change as they move through adolescence into early adulthood is unknown and is essential to understand which children and families are most at risk for poor quality of life so we develop services and programs to support these families early in their process of adapting to epilepsy to improve long term outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The International Tobacco Control Policy Evaluation Project: Evaluating the impact of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control With an Emphasis on Low and Middle Income Countries
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER PREVENTION; COHORT SURVEY; EVALUATION; FRAMEWORK CONVENTION ON TOBACCO CONTROL; GLOBAL HEALTH; HEALTH POLICY; INTERNATIONAL; POPULATION HEALTH; TOBACCO USE
Abstract-Résumé: Tobacco use has been identified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the world's number one preventable cause of death. In the 21st Century, it is projected that one billion people may die of tobacco use, and the toll will be greatest in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). In 2003, the 192 WHO countries adopted the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), the first-ever health treaty, which specifies a broad set of tobacco control policies that the FCTC Parties (now numbering 172 countries) must implement, e.g., enhanced warning labels, bans/restrictions on advertising/promotion, increased taxation, and smokefree laws. The International Tobacco Control Policy Evaluation Project (ITC Project) is a Canada-led collaboration of leading tobacco control researchers across 22 countries (over 70% of the world's tobacco users) whose mission is to conduct rigorous evaluation of the impact of FCTC policies; it is the only international effort designed to evaluate the FCTC, that is, the only research program that focuses on whether the treaty is having its intended effects. The ITC Project uses state-of-the-art survey methods to answer key questions: Do graphic warnings lead to increased motivation to quit? Are smoke-free laws effective in reducing smoking in public places? Do higher taxes on cigarettes lead to shifts to other tobacco forms (e.g. bidis in Bangladesh) rather than to quitting? We will also examine how policy effects may vary across the 22 countries. The ITC Project has built an extensive research-to-action network in which we disseminate/transfer our findings rapidly in each country to key contacts in government, the research community, and Civil Society, which has led to significant policy changes in several countries, including Canada. The ITC Project has become an effective global system for generating, disseminating, and promoting the utilization of knowledge in the fight against the growing global tobacco epidemic, particularly in LMICs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Maternal Diabetes and Perinatal Programming: Role of Reactive Oxygen Species
Keywords-MotsClés: HYPERTENSION; INTRARENAL ANGIOTENSIN CONVERTING ENZYME-2; KIDNEY INJURY; MATERNAL DIABETES; PERINATAL PROGRAMMING; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES (ROS); RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Striking news recently highlighted that (1) 1 in 16 American women who give birth - and they number more than 250,000 each year - has diabetes (Los Angeles Times, December 17, 2010); and (2) maternal obesity and diabetes are linked to increased risk of childhood chronic kidney disease (CKD) (American Society of Nephrology Kidney News (Vol. 2(12), December 2010)), underscoring that maternal diabetes is a serious medical complication that affects both mother and baby, even in the 21st century. In general,  the prevalence of gestational diabetes is 3-14% of pregnancies world-wide.  In Canada, the incidence of gestational diabetes is 3.7 percent in non-Aboriginal women population and reaches 8-18 percent in Aboriginal women (www.diabetes.ca). During last 5 years, we have found that mice with untreated diabetes during pregnancy give birth to underweight babies whose kidneys display serious malformations. As adults, some of these babies will suffer from hypertension, glucose intolerance and chronic kidney disease. These babies are victims of what is known as perinatal programming, a complex and mysterious condition that affects embryos and adults alike.  In the current grant proposal, we aim to elucidate the mechanisms related to this phenomenon of maternal diabetes induced perinatal programming and develop the prevention strategies in animal model in order to prevent diseases in children whose mothers suffer from gestational diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact de l'ascorbylperoxyde sur le développement pulmonaire du nouveau-né
Keywords-MotsClés: ASCORBYLPEROXYDE; DYSPLASIE BRONCHO-PULMONAIRE; GLUTATHION; NOUVEAU-NE; NUTRITION PARENTERALE; POUMON; PREMATURITE; STRESS OXYDANT
Abstract-Résumé: Les nouveau-nes prematures souffrent de plusieurs complications pathologiques liees a leur immaturite et a leurs traitements. A titre d'exemple, la dysplasie broncho pulmonaire, un mauvais developpement des alveoles du poumon, atteint plus de 50% des enfants nes avant 26 semaines de gestation. Cette maladie chronique du poumon est causee par un stress oxydant pulmonaire. La nutrition intraveineuse que l'enfant recoit a cause de l'immaturite de son systeme gastro-intestinal, est une source importante de molecules oxydantes pouvant cause un stress oxydant au poumon. Notre hypothese est qu'une de ces molecules, l'ascorbylperoxyde, est responsable d'induire une cascade d'evenements tel un stress oxydant, une mort cellulaire anormalement elevee et une perte d'alveoles au poumon. L'ascorbylperoxyde est une forme peroxydee de la vitamine C qui est generee spontanement et specialement dans ces solutions nutritives. Les objectifs du projet de recherche sont 1) de demontrer dans un modele animal que l'ascorbylperoxyde induit un stress oxydant et la perte d'alveoles, 2) tester chez l'animal une alternative nutritionnelle pour corriger le stress oxydant et/ou empecher la formation d'ascorbylperoxyde dans la nutrition intraveineuse et ainsi prevenir la perte d'alveoles et 3) demonter chez les enfants prematures un lien entre les niveau d'ascorbylperoxyde urinaire et la severite de la maladie du poumon. La realisation du projet de recherche permettra une meilleure comprehension des mecanismes en cause et proposera une amelioration des solutions de nutrition intraveineuse afin de prevenir le developpement de cette maladie chronique du poumon.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a web-based program to assist parents in helping the anxious child: A public health approach for prevention and early intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; CHILDREN; EARLY INTERVENTION; INTERNET; PARENTS; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Anxiety is the most common mental health disorder in children with a prevalence of about 8%. Anxiety disorders are accompanied by difficulties in peer relationships, school performance and family functioning, and often persist into adulthood.  Interventions for anxiety in children have been shown effective in clinical populations but these treatments are only available to a small proportion of affected children due to access barriers and the acute shortage of highly qualified personnel. Prevention and early intervention of anxiety in children using cost effective methods are warranted.   Our team of scientists in children's anxiety, internet-based services and distance treatments will develop, and conduct preliminary testing of, a cost effective, web based, parent mediated public health approach to prevention and early intervention of anxiety disorders in young children. We will conduct an open trial of the intervention in preparation for a future randomized trial.

TitreApplicationTitle: Partnering for Change: Understanding the Contribution of Social Entrepreneurship to Primary Health Care Transformation
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT; HEALTH CARE INNOVATION; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTIPLE CASE STUDY RESEARCH; NETWORKING; PARTNERSHIPS; PRIMARY HEALTHCARE; RURAL AND NORTHERN; SOCIAL ENTREPRENEURSHIP; SPARSELY POPULATED HEALTH REGION
Abstract-Résumé: We know that we need strong, effective primary health care services in order to improve the health of the population and create an effective health care system over the long term. We also know that partnerships and networks among communities, health services and health care providers are needed for widespread changes in primary health care to occur. Although we know what is needed, we do not yet have good evidence about how to make these changes over the long term across a health region. The purpose of this research is to understand how networks of partners can be engaged to transform primary health care at community and regional levels. Partners include doctors and other health care providers, community organizations, municipal leaders, the ministry of health, and the regional health authority. The Northern Health Authority in British Columbia is leading a process with its partners to improve primary health care services, beginning in six communities across northern BC. In this research, we will use the lens of social entrepreneurship to examine how primary health care system change actually takes place over a period of four years in these six communities and across the region. We will examine the process of change by interviewing individuals who are involved in the change, examining documents such as minutes of meetings and the results of evaluations, and considering statistics on the use and effectiveness of health services. The research team will describe how the relationships, partnerships and networks within and beyond the communities actually help or hinder changes in services. Through this research we will learn how partnerships and networking contribute to changes in health services and how health care systems can be aligned to better serve the needs of the population, especially in rural and northern Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental course of cognitive and electroretinographic precursors from childhood to adulthood in children and adolescents at risk of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; CHILD MENTAL HEALTH; CHILDREN AT RISK; DETERMINANTS OF RISK; ELECTRORETINOGRAPHY; NEUROCOGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SENSITIVE PERIODS; TRAJECTORIES; VULNERABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: The hundreds of thousands of children at high genetic risk of severe mental health problems carry a load of comorbidity and of developmental and behavioural disorders that represent a challenge for paediatricians and child health care practitioners. Yet, we have little knowledge about the childhood determinants of risk of later appearance of serious mental health problems such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. These devastating diseases affect between 1 and 2% of the Canadian population, and appear in late adolescence and young adulthood. In the majority of cases, they have a chronic course since the exact causes in the brain, the genes and the environment are not well known. For this reason, our treatments are palliative, rarely curative. The human and financial costs are enormous. Understanding the developmental trajectory and the early sensitive periods of vulnerability in the life of children and adolescents at risk is of utmost relevance for developing efficient preventive and curative means.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of mTOR pathway in translational regulation of synaptic plasticity, memory formation and disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: GENERATION OF TISSUE-SPECIFIC KNOCKOUT MICE; IMAGING; LEARNING AND MEMORY; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; TRANSLATION CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Learning, memory and perception rely on an intricate network of proteins that orchestrate higher cognitive functions of the human brain. An important biological process regulating the function of these molecules is protein synthesis, also termed translation. Dysregulation of translation leads to pathological conditions such as Fragile X syndrome, Tuberous Sclerosis and PTEN hamartoma syndrome, all single-gene disorders with high rates of autism.  A key molecule regulating protein synthesis is mTOR (mammalian Target of Rapamycin), which acts as a "sensor" of nutrients, environmental stimuli, growth factors and energy levels helping to regulate cell growth, proliferation and survival. mTOR inhibitors such as the FDA approved drug rapamycin, are widely used in the treatment of transplant rejection and cancer. The role of mTOR in memory formation and in diseases of the nervous system is still elusive. We will use advanced genetic mouse models of mTOR and its associated proteins to study the role of mTOR pathway in memory formation and autism. Knowledge gained from this project has the potential to direct treatment strategies targeting this pathway in patients with memory deficits and also to propose therapies to alleviate the cognitive and neurological symptoms associated with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD). Further understanding of this molecular pathway can have a strong impact on the design of prophylactic and post-diagnosis treatments for patients in Canada and worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting the eukaryotic translation initiation factor eIF4E with ribavirin in breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; BREAST CANCER; CELL LINES; EIF4E; MOUSE MODELS; RIBAVIRIN; TARGETED THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: An important goal in breast cancer research is to develop less toxic and more effective personalized therapies, which can be based on the presence or absence of certain proteins in the tumor. Two proteins (targets) are routinely tested in the assessment of breast cancer: the estrogen receptor (predicting response to endocrine therapies) and Her2 (predicting response to herceptin). We propose to study a new target protein, named eIF4E. eIF4E is present at high levels in about 50% of all breast cancers and these tumors are more aggressive and more resistant to chemotherapy.  Ribavirin, a well-tolerated and widely used anti-viral drug, inhibits the activity of eIF4E and reduces growth of cancer cells in the laboratory. In a recent clinical trial of ribavirin in leukemia we observed dramatic responses. We now suggest that ribavirin may effectively target breast tumors that have high levels of eIF4E. We propose to use breast cancer cells grown in the laboratory to learn how ribavirin blocks growth of these cells and to help us identify possible drug combinations that could improve ribavirin efficacy. We will test the combination of ribavirin with drugs commonly used to treat breast cancer to find new combinations that could be tested in future clinical trials. Additionally, we will use mouse models of breast cancer to confirm any findings from cells grown in the lab. Our research will guide the design of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of a major subgroup of patients with poor-prognosis breast cancer and will hopefully lead to better, personalized therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the PINK1/Parkin mitochondrial quality control pathway in dopaminergic neurons
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOCHEMISTRY; DROSOPHILA; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENETICS; MEMBRANES; MITOCHONDRIA; NEURODEGENERATION; NEURONS; SINGLE CELL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria are organelles with numerous cellular functions, including the production of the majority of cellular energy. Mitochondria contain their own genome, and mutations in this genome are linked to many prevalent diseases, including the neurodegenerative disorder Parkinson's disease (PD). PD is a common age-related movement disorder that is caused by the death of dopamine-secreting neurons in the brain. Mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) accumulate in dopamine-secreting neurons from PD patients, but their role in the disease process, and the cellular factors that eliminate mitochondria that bear these mutations are unknown. I propose to use the fruit fly Drosophila to study the role of the PD-linked genes PINK1 and parkin, as well as other candidate factors in combating the accumulation of mitochondrial mutations. Drosophila is ideal for such studies, because it is the only model system that recapitulates the selective tissue degeneration seen in humans with PINK1 and parkin mutations. We have developed a novel neuronal isolation technique that we will use to understand how PINK1 and Parkin influence mtDNA mutations in dopaminergic neurons. Identification of factors that prevent the accumulation of mtDNA mutations could have direct relevance to the development of treatments for PD and other diseases of aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Posttraumatic Growth and Adjustment in the Spouses of Advanced Cancer Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUSTMENT; ADVANCED CANCER PATIENT; END-OF-LIFE; GROUNDED THEORY; HIERARCHICAL LINEAR MODELING; POSTTRAUMATIC GROWTH; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS; SPOUSE OF ADVANCED CANCER PATIENT; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: The process of dying from advanced cancer often creates intense distress in a marital relationship. These couples are inevitably faced with many uncertainties that require multiple adjustments in their relationship roles and future expectations. Research also reveals that couples frequently report that they have gotten closer and felt stronger after struggling with cancer together. These positive psychological changes have been termed post-traumatic growth (PTG). Currently, a research study titled 'Managing Cancer and Living Meaningfully (CALM)' has been conducted at the Princess Margaret Hospital to assist advanced cancer patients and their spouses. No study has yet examined PTG among only the spouses of advanced cancer patients. As an extension of CALM study, the proposed study will assess: 1) the impact of CALM intervention on adjustment, 2) the prevalence and nature of PTG, and 3) the factors contributing to successful adjustment among the spouses of advanced cancer patients. We hypothesize that greater PTG in the spouses is linked to older age, more attachment security and marital satisfaction, participation in the CALM intervention, and greater PTG of their spouses. Objective 1 and 2 will be fulfilled by in-depth interviews. Interviews will continue until no new information is found. Objective 3 will be fulfilled by two surveys, one before and one after the intervention. These surveys assess PTG and distress, and perceived support from healthcare professionals, attachment security, and marital satisfaction. Based on a previous study, 96 participants will be required for the treatment and control groups to detect a minimal difference. The responses will be compared across a 3-month period and between the spouses in the treatment and those in the control groups using basic and multivariate statistics. The proposed study will gain insight on how CALM improves spousal adjustment near the end-of-life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Age-Related Alterations in Cortical Dynamics: Healthy Aging versus Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; COGNITION; CORTICAL DYNAMICS; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY; FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY; PARIETAL CORTEX; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is associated with cognitive decline and is a major risk factor for mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD). While the world population is aging rapidly, the early diagnosis and treatment of the old-age cognitive disorders have been a great challenge. Development of novel non-invasive neurophysiological techniques is, therefore, essential to understand the neurophysiological underpinnings of healthy versus pathological aging. We propose to employ a novel combination of  non invasive brain stimulation and neuroimaging techniques, namely 'Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)', 'Electroencephalography(EEG)' and 'Diffusion Tensor Imaging(DTI)' that together permit the non-invasive and yet in vivo neurophysiological recordings from various regions of the human cortex with an optimized temporal and structural precision. This combination allows for recording cortical excitability and interhemispheric connectivity in cortical regions that are referentially affected in aging and AD such as prefrontal and parietal cortices. In this proposal, we will use the TMS-EEG and DTI technique to investigate and compare the age-related alterations of cortical excitability and interhemispheric connectivity in motor, prefrontal and parietal cortices in healthy aging population and patients suffering from MCI and AD. We predict that the decline of cognitive function with aging and the severity of cognitive impairment in AD will be related to the alteration of measured cortical processes. This is an important step in identifying the age-related alterations of cortical dynamics in cortical regions implicated in cognitive decline and AD pathogenesis and will aid the development of novel biomarkers for early detection and development of targeted treatment approaches to minimize brain dysfunction and reduce the risk of dementia in the aging population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering the gene-environment interactions underlying the developmental origins of health and disease in response to maternal dietary restriction.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; DEVELOPMENTAL PROGRAMMING; DIETARY RESTRICTION; EMBRYO TRANSFER; FETUS; GENOMICS; HYPOTHALAMIC-PITUITARY-ADRENAL AXIS; METABOLISM; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: The maternal environment can profoundly influence the development and health of offspring. Inappropriate development in utero/the early postnatal period is associated with adverse outcomes including increased incidence of preterm birth, neonatal morbidity and susceptibility to disease in adulthood such as obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Maternal nutritional status before, during and after pregnancy is implicated in driving these outcomes and acts by permanently modifying fetal metabolic, hormonal and homeostatic systems. Yet not all individuals exposed to an adverse environment during critical windows of development will be developmentally compromised or at increased risk for disease. Thus, it is important to understand the contribution of both environmental influences and an individual's genotype to development and health across the life course. Dietary restriction (DR) is common in women of reproductive age in both developed and developing societies. In a mouse model it has been shown that differences in phenotypes exist between offspring of different genetic backgrounds whose mothers were exposed to DR during pregnancy. Using this model, we aim to investigate the role of the maternal and fetal genomes in influencing later health and disease risk in response to maternal DR. We will generate pregnancies containing embryos from two strains of mice. Pregnant females will receive either control diet or be calorically restricted. We will use genetic approaches to examine changes in pathways involved in metabolic and endocrine function in the liver in response to DR and determine if differences in these are driven by the mother and/or fetus. Data resulting from this study will aid in identifying early life biomarkers contributing to disease risk and will inform future studies aiming to develop strategies to make certain babies have a healthy start to life, to prevent and reduce the burden of disease and ensure the long-term health of populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brain amyloid imaging, vascular diseases and Apolipoprotein E4 in aging and dementia.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; AMYLOID DEPOSIT; APOE4; CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASES; MCI; MEMORY; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; PIB-PET IMAGING; STRUCTURAL MRI; WML QUANTIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia, affecting nearly 50% of Canadians over 80 years of age. There is a crucial need to identify individuals who will develop AD, as these individuals would be good candidates for clinical intervention. Although the causes of AD are still debated, many researchers have identified the accumulation of a protein called beta-amyloid as a key characteristic of AD. However, abnormal accumulation of this protein has been observed in 20% of cognitively intact older adults, suggesting that other factors work synergistically with this protein to promote AD onset. The goal of this project is to determine the interaction between beta-amyloid deposition, vascular diseases (i.e., hypertension, diabetes, vascular brain lesions) and genetic factors. We also aim to assess the impact of those factors on cognition (particularly memory). Finally, we aim to determine whether beta-amyloid deposition, alone or combined with vascular and/or genetic factors, can be a useful diagnostic tool for AD. Based on the literature, we hypothesize that the presence of vascular and genetic burdens will modulate the impact of beta-amyloid deposition on cognition. Furthermore, we believe that considering vascular and genetic factors will increase the sensitivity of amyloid imaging to detect individuals who will eventually progress to AD. This project will use data from a longitudinal study of 110 participants. The findings will contribute to our understanding of the impact of beta-amyloid deposition on cognition, as well as the interactions between vascular diseases, genetics and beta-amyloid deposition.

TitreApplicationTitle: High-density lipoprotein genetics and metabolism and aortic valvular stenosis in humans
Keywords-MotsClés: 2-DIMENSION POLYACRYLAMIDE GEL ELECTROPHORESIS; AORTIC VALVULAR STENOSIS; APOLIPOPROTEIN AI; BIOMARKERS; CALCIFICATION; CHOLESTEROL EFFLUX; CHOLESTERYL ESTER TRANSFER PROTEIN; GENETICS; HIGH-DENSITY LIPOPROTEIN; PHOSPHOLIPID TRANSFER PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: Valvular heart diseases are an important and growing public health problem in developed societies. Aortic valvular stenosis (AVS) is the most common valvular disease which is present in more than 3% of patients older than 65 years. We believe that identifying the risk factors as well as the biological mechanisms involved in the pathophysiology of AVS is of critical importance to identify individuals at high risk for AVS, but also to identify the biological mediators that could be targeted to stop the progression of this disease. Although the genetic and molecular mechanisms that influence the progression of this disease have yet to be identified. We have recently tested the hypothesis that high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (often referred to as the good cholesterol) may be involved in the progression of AVS. By treating a group of rabbits predisposed to AVS with a pharmacological compound that raises HDL cholesterol levels while improving its quality, we have recently shown that the clinical indices associated with the progression of AVS were significantly improved compared to rabbits treated with a placebo. This finding has prompted us to launch a series of investigations in humans aiming at studying the relationship between the genes as well as the circulating biomarkers involved in HDL metabolism and the progression of aortic stenosis in humans. At the Montreal Heart Institute, we have a direct access to several hundreds of patients that meet the clinical criteria for AVS and we aim at taking advantage of our expertise in patient care as well as in cardiovascular genomics to unravel the link between HDL and AVS. For that purpose, we will establish the relationship between variants in genes related to HDL metabolism and the risk of AVS and we will perform several assays to test the hypothesis that the HDL of patients with AVS have an impaired ability to reduce the calcification process in human vascular interstitial cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional analysis of protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 22 (PTPN22) and its autoimmune-associated R620W variant in rheumatoid arthritis.
Keywords-MotsClés: FLOW CYTOMETRY; PROTEIN TYROSINE PHOSPHATASE; PTPN22; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS; SKG MOUSE MODEL; T CELL SELECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease affecting approximately 1% of Canadians and ultimately resulting in lowered life expectancy. Enzymes called protein tyrosine phosphatases regulate cellular processes involved in inflammation as well as metabolism and cancer. Several studies have recently linked the gene protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 22 (PTPN22) to autoimmune disease; namely, a variant of this gene, W620, is strongly associated with susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis. This is believed to be through the important regulation of T cells by PTPN22. Mice expressing the W620 variant as well as mice lacking the normal PTPN22 gene will be examined for arthritic disease and its role in disease progression will be determined. Additionally, these mice will be crossed with a well-known rheumatoid arthritis mouse model to monitor the effect of this gene on established disease.The prevalence of W620 in human rheumatoid arthritis underscores the importance of understanding the role of LYP in this disease in order to identify new treatment strategies.

Abstract-Résumé: To understand the role of genes (PGRN, TDP-43, FUS) linked to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). I will investigate the role of the PGRN and its genetic interaction with TDP-43 and FUS which have recently been linked to ALS. Analysis of the role of PGRN, TDP43 and FUS will be performed in vivo in zebrafish where I will knockdown and overexpress PGRN in TDP43 and FUS ALS fish model and evaluate their interactions.Further, I will use these ALS fish model for drug screening to potentially identify molecules that would protect motor neurons in these fish.

TitreApplicationTitle: Initiation of Cooling by Emergency medical services to Promote the Adoption of in-hospital therapeutic hypothermia in Cardiac arrest Survivors: the ICE-PACS Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ARREST; CLINICIAN BEHAVIOUR; EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES; INDUCED HYPOTHERMIA; NEUROLOGICAL OUTCOMES; PARAMEDICS; PRE-HOSPITAL CARE; REMINDER SYSTEMS; RESUSCITATION; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: A cardiac arrest occurs when the heart stops beating, and is a devastating event that often leads to death.  Advances in resuscitation science have dramatically improved the number of patients that survive to be treated in a hospital, but more than half of these survivors still die during their hospitalization. Most patients are in a coma after the cardiac arrest, and many have severe brain damage caused by lack of blood flow during the cardiac arrest. We now know that we can often prevent this brain damage, and save more lives, by cooling a patient's body once they arrive in the hospital. However, our previous research has shown that cooling is often not applied soon enough, or even at all, in the Emergency Department.  This research will test whether we can increase the number of patients that receive this life-saving treatment by having paramedics start the cooling process before the patient arrives at the hospital.  We believe this research will lead to changes in how cardiac arrest survivors are treated in Canada, and improve their chances of surviving without any brain damage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional regulators of the 5-HT1A receptor gene
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; ANTIDEPRESSANT; ANXIETY; CHROMATIN; DEPRESSION; DNA ELEMENTS; MUTAGENESIS; RAPHE; SEROTONIN; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Major depression is the most prevalent mental illness, and 1/6 people are diagnosed as depressed in their lifetime.  Multiple lines of evidence implicate reduced activity of the serotonin system in major depression.  However, current antidepressants produce remission in less than 1/3 of patients. Hence there is a need for a better understanding of the serotonin system in depression, and we have hypothesized that a specific genetic change (polymorphism) in the serotonin system may lead to depression.  This proposal addresses how that change can cause depression using a new animal model.  Our CIHR-funded research has identified a new functional genetic marker for major depression, suicide and reduced response to antidepressants, the C(-1019)G 5-HT1A polymorphism.  This polymorphism prevents the action of genetic regulators and is expected to increase levels of serotonin-1A receptor, which inhibits serotonin activity in the brain, a key hallmark of depression.  We will address the hypothesis that genetic regulators that target the polymorphism will play critical roles in regulation of the serotonin-1A receptor in the brain, with important consequences for serotonin activity and behavior. We will use mouse models lacking key genetic regulators of this receptor and examine the consequences for levels of receptor, serotonin activity and depression behaviours in the mice.  Our initial studies show changes in the levels of serotonin-1A receptors as predicted from our cell models, and we will now examine the mice for depression or anxiety behaviours, and for response to antidepressant treatments.    We will generate important new animal models of depression, which will identify key roles for specific genetic regulators in depression and response to antidepressant treatments.  This new information will provide the basis for new strategies to treat antidepressant-resistant depression by targeting these novel transcriptional regulators.

TitreApplicationTitle: Monitoring of abdominal aortic aneurysm after endovascular repair by ultrasound elastography: feasibility, optimization and validation
Keywords-MotsClés: ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM; ENDOLEAKS; ENDOVASCULAR TREATMENT; NON-INVASIVE VASCULAR ELASTOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is an abnormal dilatation of the aorta in the abdomen secondary to hypertension and atherosclerosis. Surgical treatment of AAA is increasingly being replaced by endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) using stent-grafts (SGs). However, the efficacy of this less invasive approach is often jeopardized by the incidence of persistent flow within the aneurysm, called endoleaks leading to aneurysm rupture if not properly detected and treated. Hence, a life long annual CT-scan surveillance is required increasing the cost of EVAR, exposing the patient to ionizing radiation and nephrotoxic contrast agent. The goal of this project is to adapt and test a new ultrasound technology called ultrasound elastography to improve patient follow-up after EVAR and ultimately avoid the use of CT-scans. This technique measures the deformation of the tissue secondary to blood pressure variation (quasi-static elastography) or to a shear wave generated by the ultrasound probe (dynamic elastography). We will optimize 2 approaches to generate elastic maps of the AAA. One approach will be a quasi-static elastography technique developed by our team giving an estimation of the deformation (strain) of the different components of the AAA by the blood pressure. The second is a dynamic elastography technique that will provide information on the elastic property of the AAA components.  An optimization and validation of the 2 techniques will be first conducted in an animal model of EVAR reproducing successful EVAR and EVAR failure with endoleaks in canine abdominal aorta. Elastographic findings will be correlated to invasive pressure measurement, CT-scan and pathologic examinations. A human feasibility study will be conducted in patients with criteria of success or failure after EVAR based on CT-scan. Finally, a validation will be done in patients having EVAR and  implantation of a pressure sensor to correlate the elastography maps with the pressure within the aneurysm.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examination of the effect of posttranslational modifications of 53BP1 in development and diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: 53BP1; CANCER; CLASS SWITCH RECOMBINATION; DNA DAMAGE SIGNALING AND REPAIR; IMMUNODEFICIENCY; NHEJ; RNF168; RNF8
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how cells repair damage to our genetic information contained in DNA is of outmost importance. This knowledge will lead to preventative measures for numerous human diseases and will have great potential to facilitate development of more effective therapies for cancer.   The protein known as 53bp1 is important for the repair of DNA damage and its absence leads to developmental defects caused by defects in DNA damage repair. Women with inherited mutations of Brca1 have an increased risk for developing breast and ovarian cancers. Remarkably, recent studies of mouse models demonstrated that absence of the 53bp1 gene protects against the development of cancers associated with defective Brca1. We have discovered a novel way to turn off 53bp1 function in mice. We propose to examine the importance of this mechanism in mouse models and human cells. We will investigate if shutting down 53bp1 function will also prevent the development of Brca1-associated cancers. This proposal has strong health relevance and thus is in accordance with the mandate of the Canadian Institutes of Health Research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Auditory processing in typical development and in autism spectrum disorder: insights from the brain and behavior
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULTS; AUDITORY PROCESSING; AUTISM; BRAIN IMAGING; CHILDREN; COGNITION; DEVELOPMENT; MRI
Abstract-Résumé: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex and lifelong brain disorder that affects about 1 in 100 people, but we do not yet know its cause.  The great human and financial struggles that ASD exerts on affected families, makes a strong case for concentrated research efforts on ASD.  People with ASD have problems in social interaction and communication.  They also perceive and feel the world in a different way, particularly in the auditory and visual domains.  For example, while most people pay attention to the global/whole features of a visual scene before the local /detailed features (e.g., seeing the forest before the trees), this trend is reversed in ASD.  In vision, ASD individuals see the local details before the global form (e.g. seeing the tree before the forest).  While this local-based form of perception in ASD has been well documented in vision, less work has been done in audition.  The main goal of this research is thus to study auditory perception in ASD.  For the first time, we will study how auditory perception in ASD is reflected at the level of both brain function and anatomy.  We are particularly interested to study how auditory perception and the ASD brain changes over the course of development.  Studying how people with ASD perceive their auditory world may help to identify a neurobiological marker of ASD.  In turn, this research can help clinicians and educators develop better-targeted therapies and interventions strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: La relation entre l'insomnie, le fonctionnement immunitaire et l'occurrence d'infections chez des patientes atteintes d'un cancer de l'ovaire
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER DE L'OVAIRE; CHIMIOTHERAPIE; FONCTIONNEMENT IMMUNITAIRE; INSOMNIE; PSYCHONEUROIMMUNOLOGIE; RYTHMES CIRCADIENS; SOMMEIL; EPISODE INFECTIEUX
Abstract-Résumé: Pres de la moitie des patients atteints de cancer decederont de la maladie ou des complications des traitements oncologiques. Notamment, la chimiotherapie est associee a un risque accru d'infections, elles-memes associees a des consequences serieuses, comme davantage d'hospitalisations et une qualite de vie et meme une survie reduites. Outre les traitements, des facteurs psychologiques pourraient affecter le systeme immunitaire et predisposeraient les patients a developper des infections, comme le suggerent les nombreuses etudes ayant montre un lien entre le stress et un moins bon fonctionnement immunitaire. Les perturbations du sommeil, frequentes chez les personnes atteintes de cancer, notamment chez celles ayant un cancer gynecologique (50 a 68% des patientes), influenceraient aussi le systeme immunitaire, mais les impacts de ces changements immunitaires sur la sante ont rarement ete evalues. Cette etude evaluera la relation entre la qualite du sommeil, le fonctionnement immunitaire et l'occurrence d'infections chez des femmes traitees en chimiotherapie pour un cancer de l'ovaire. On s'attend a ce que les patientes ayant de l'insomnie aient un moins bon fonctionnement immunitaire et presentent davantage d'episodes d'infections durant et apres la chimiotherapie. Cent patientes traitees pour un premier cancer de l'ovaire seront evaluees avant le debut de la chimiotherapie, a deux reprises durant les deux premiers cycles de chimiotherapie, ainsi qu'a la toute fin de leur chimiotherapie et trois et six mois plus tard. Leur sommeil sera evalue par questionnaire, auto-enregistrement, actigraphe (appareil ressemblant a une montre mesurant les cycles eveil-sommeil) et entrevue telephonique (qui evaluera aussi les episodes d'infection). Differents parametres immunitaires seront mesures par prelevements sanguins. Cette etude permettra de preciser les facteurs psychologiques influencant la condition physique des patientes recevant de la chimiotherapie.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multi-parametric MRI for prostate cancer diagnosis and prognosis
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; DYNAMIC CONTRAST ENHANCED MRI; PROSTATE CANCER; TISSUE CLASSIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer remains one of the most common cancers in North American males and second leading cause of cancer related deaths in men. It is estimated that this year 25,500 men will be diagnosed in Canada alone with upwards of 4,000 deaths. Owing to the widespread use of screening tests, many more less advanced, localized, lower risk prostate cancers are being detected. This prompted increased interest in focal therapy as an alternative to the traditional therapies of surgery and radiation therapy. However, the ultimate success of focal therapy relies on proper patient selection and adequate characterization of the tumour's location, extend and histological grade. We have shown that a combination of different Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) techniques have significantly better accuracy of prostate cancer diagnosis than either technique alone. We propose to further develop this MRI technology. Specifically, we will develop a technique called Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE). This technique allows non-invasive measurements of mechanical properties of tissue, and is often called "remote palpation".  We believe that the combination of MRE and the MRI techniques we have developed so far will significantly improve prostate cancer diagnosis. In addition, we will develop a computer program capable of accurately predicting the tumour's location, volume and pathological grade based on the MRI/MRE measurements. The combination of the proposed MRI/MRE technology with this computer program will facilitate patient selection for focal prostate cancer therapy. We also propose to test the ability of this technology to predict outcome of the combined modality treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interrelationship among physical activity, biomechanical and neuromuscular characteristics in knee osteoarthritis development and progression
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; GAIT; KNEE; MOBILITY; NEUROMUSCULAR FUNCTION; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PATTERN RECOGNITION; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Healthy muscles, joints and bones are needed to maintain mobility and a physically active lifestyle. Evidence is mounting relating inactivity to health problems like heart disease, some cancers, obesity and diabetes. Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is reaching epidemic proportions with 1 in 10 Canadians affected. It results in more difficulty with activities like walking or climbing stairs than any other medical condition for people over 65. OA was typically referred to as a "wear and tear" disease leading to confusion and belief that physical activity makes it worse. While physical activity is recommended for people with OA, this is based on pain relief and improved general health. How diseased cartilage responds to loads is not well understood, and thus we do not know what effect physical activity has on the rate of OA joint changes. Given the benefits of physical activity, we need to understand how to provide people with knee OA appropriate physical activity prescription to reduce symptoms while preventing negative joint changes. OA gets worse quicker in some people than in others, and our previous work shows that joint forces, joint motion and muscle function differ among OA severities. Therefore, our first aim is to confirm these changes in a follow-up study. Then we will see whether these differences in walking and physical activity can predict who will develop knee OA and who will get worse. The results will provide new knowledge that can be used by healthcare professionals and in guiding decisions around physical activity for people with knee OA, as well as in our understanding of different phases of OA. The major driving force is to understand how to prevent degenerative joint changes while achieving benefits that appropriate physical activity can have on improving symptoms (pain and stiffness) and general health of the many Canadians with knee OA.
