TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular dissection of HCV life cycle through the study of virus/host interactome.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLUMINESCENCE RESONANCE ENERGY TRANSFER; CHEMOGENOMICS; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; NS3/4A PROTEASE; NS5A; PARTICLE ASSEMBLY; QUANTITATIVE MASS SPECTROMETRY; RNA REPLICATION; VIRUS HOST-INTERACTIONS; Y-BOX PROTEIN 1
Abstract-Résumé: The infection by the hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a growing public health concern since it affects 170 million people worldwide and is responsible for chronic liver diseases, such as cirrhosis and liver cancer. The standard treatment, involving weekly interferon injection concurrently with the oral administration of ribavirin, is not well tolerated and provides low efficacy. This illustrates the urgent need for the development of new antiviral strategies. The viral proteins interact together and form highly organized and complex cell networks which are used by HCV to control the infection. Additionally, as an obligate parasite, HCV proteins recruit cellular machineries during host infection in order to accomplish critical viral processes. Hence, these virus-virus and virus-host interactions represent potential targets for the development of new classes of antivirals. However, HCV biology and its natural pathogenesis largely remain poorly understood. The aim of this proposal is to understand how virus/virus and virus/host interactions control HCV infection. Especially, we will focus our study on the characterization of NS3/4A and NS5A viral proteins self-interactions and will characterize their respective involvements during the different steps of the HCV life cycle. Moreover, we will address how HCV exploits the interaction between NS3/4A and the cellular protein YB-1 recently identified in our group. Finally, we propose to identify new host machineries that associates with several viral components and to study how they are co-opted by HCV for the benefit of the infection.This study will allow to better understand the pathophysiology and the complexity of HCV infection as well as to identify novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of HCV-infected patients. Indeed, the design of a novel drug class that disrupts the above-mentioned interactions may ultimately represent an efficient therapeutic approach.

TitreApplicationTitle: Homeostatic mechanisms at central synapes
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HOMEOSTATIC PLASTICITY; SYNAPSE; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; TWO-PHOTON MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Our ability to think, learn and remember reflects our brain function. The neurons in our brain are organized in networks through which information flows, is processed and sometimes stored.  The precise functioning of these networks is largely controlled by functional connections between neurons called synapses. The strength of individual synapses is dynamically regulated by experience and activity and can either be depressed or potentiated for brief or prolonged periods of time. These activity-dependent mechanisms, broadly defined as synaptic plasticity, decisively influence how information flows and are widely believed to contribute to the ability of the brain to learn and remember. Both theoretical and experimental work are showing that these activity-dependent mechanisms need to be properly fine-tuned and controlled by what is called homeostatic mechanisms to assure proper network function. Recently, it has been hypothesized that abnormal balance between these opposing mechanisms lead to malfunctioning of neural network function and thus may contribute to several neurological and psychiatric diseases, in particular Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia and addiction. Here, we are proposing novel electrophysiological, optical and molecular approaches to study in details these homeostatic mechanisms at central synapses and determine how they interplay with other forms of synaptic plasticity to control neuronal function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis: the role of G protein upregulation in osteoblasts
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE BIOLOGY; OSTEOBLASTS; OSTEOPOROSIS; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS
Abstract-Résumé: Glucocorticoids are widely used drugs in the treatment of inflammatory diseases as well as some forms of cancer. Long-term use of these agents is limited by profound skeletal growth inhibition in children and osteoporosis in both children and adults. We are investigating the effects of glucocorticoids on bone to help suggest therapeutic interventions in patients receiving glucocorticoid therapy.  Work in my laboratory has shown that glucocorticoids alter the responses of osteoblasts (the cells that make bone) to a number of hormones and neurotransmitters by increasing the amount of G proteins (primarily G11 and to a lesser extent Gs) expressed in the cells. These G proteins transduce the signals from hormone and neurotransmitter receptors to alter cell growth and function. To understand the importance of these changes in G proteins we have created mice in which the G proteins are over-expressed, mimicking the effects of the drugs. In this proposal we are testing the bone density and strength of our transgenic mouse lines that over-express G proteins and observing what happens when we stress their skeletons by feeding them a diet without calcium or removing estrogens in female mice. We will use our transgenic mice to test specific cellular changes and molecular pathways that cause decreased bone density. Finally having identified what the changes in G proteins do to the mouse bones and how they do it we will determine if we can improve their bones with current osteoporosis therapies and try some new drugs that target the specific pathways changed in the bone cells. Together our studies will help us understand how glucocorticoids induce osteoporosis and begin to assess the response of the bones to therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating Dynamic Mechanisms Involved in CNS Regeneration in Parkinson's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CARDIOVASCULAR; DEGENERATION; GENETICS; HEART DISEASE; NEUROSCIENCE; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; STEM CELL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: The recognition that the heart possesses a stem cell compartment that is responsible for the formation of myocytes raises the possibility that alterations in number and/or function of cardiac progenitor cells (CPCs) affect the onset of aging myopathy. As the heart ages, the resident CPCs regenerative capacity decreases, which may lead to the accumulation of old myocytes and the cardiac senescent phenotype. Insulin-like growth factor receptor-1 (IGF-R1) is present in a subset of CSCs which have high proliferative potential. However, it is unclear as to whether the proliferative capacity of these CSC caused by the presence of IGF-R1 or the high level of telomerase. Indeed, the life cycle of CPCs appears to be regulated by an enzyme referred to as telomerase, which is responsible for increasing telomere length. Essentially, shortening of telomeres beyond a critical length triggers cellular senescence and death. Although the role of telomere attrition in cellular aging has been documented in vitro, it remains to be determined whether loss of telomere DNA leads to organ and organism aging in vivo. The aim of the present research proposal is to evaluate the role of IGF-R1 in actively proliferating CSC and determine the role of telomeres in cardiomyocytes and the aging heart.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of moonlighting proteins as novel MMP substrates
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CELL BIOLOGY; ENDOCYTOSIS; GENETICS; GENOMICS; MODEL ORGANISM; PROTEIN COMPLEXES; PROTEIN MODIFICATIONS; VESICLE TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Cells within complex organisms such as humans are comprised of several distinct compartments called organelles, each of which is responsible for distinct cellular functions. Vesicle transport is a process that moves proteins and lipids from one organelle to another to ensure that they have the right components to function properly. For example, when cells receive a signal to grow, vesicle transport ensures that the correct amount of a receptor protein is at the cell surface to receive the signal. This is done either by delivering it from other organelles, or by removing it from the cell surface. Within the vesicle transport system, groups of proteins called endocytic transport complexes regulate where these vesicles are sent. However, while a number of these complexes have been identified and characterized, methods of directing vesicle transport are still largely unknown. Two human proteins called LEPROT and LEPROTL1 have recently been shown to promote growth hormone receptor removal from the cell surface, while LEPROT also affects the obesity receptor to regulate cell weight. A protein very similar to LEPROT and LEPROTL1 exists in yeast called Vps55. This protein forms a complex with Vps68, and together they regulate transport between organelles conferring destruction or recycling of the vesicular components. Thus, Vps55 and 68 likely form a novel endocytic sorting complex in yeast. Two proteins very similar to Vps68 (TMEM50A and TMEM50B) exist in humans, and likely form complexes with LEPROT and LEPROTL1 with similar functions. My research aims to identify all the proteins functioning within these complexes and how they regulate endocytic transport. Given the central role of vesicle transport in cellular activities, and that LEPROT and LEPROTL1 regulate growth and obesity, the outcomes of this research are expected to have a great impact on health and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the host and parasite determinants of Plasmodium vivax infectivity.
Keywords-MotsClés: MALARIA; PARASITOLOGY; PLASMEPSIN V (PM-V); PLASMODIUM EXPORT ELEMENT (PEXEL); PLASMODIUM FALCIPARUM; PLASMODIUM TRANSLOCON OF EXPORTED PROTEINS (PTEX); PROTEIN FOLDING; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; RED BLOOD CELL INVASION; VIRULENCE PROTEIN EXPORT
Abstract-Résumé: This project focuses on understanding a critical process employed by the parasite Plasmodium falciparum, the causative agent of Malaria, during infection of human red blood cells. Malaria is a widespread parasitic disease that infects up to 500 million people and causes  1 million deaths a year. Drug treatments against Malaria are at risk of losing effectiveness due to increasing parasite drug resistance; thus there is an urgent need to obtain a better understanding of the biology of this organism. Malaria parasites are capable of invading and reproducing in human red blood cells (RBCs) and the parasites have developed a sophisticated system that employs hundreds of parasite virulence proteins to alter the surface features of the RBCs. These alterations, mediated by an adhesion protein, cause the infected RBCs to obstruct capillaries in several organs such as the brain, kidney and placenta leading many of the fatal clinical symptoms of the disease.  In recent years a virulence protein export system has been identified that provides the mechanisms to target and transport proteins from within the parasite, across the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM), into the RBC cytoplasm.  Virulence proteins destined for export have a particular amino acid sequence that is recognized and cleaved by a protease named plasmepsin-V (PM-V). Following this, the cleaved protein is ferried by an unknown mechanism to a proposed molecular transporter named PTEX that may allow the protein to cross the PVM and enter the RBC. The focus of my project is to answer crucial questions about the protein export system that include determining the in vivo function of the PTEX transporter and understanding the biochemical function of the components of the transporter complex. These experiments will improve our understanding of this parasite system and may provide new targets for anti-malarial drug development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of developmental exposure to environmental contaminants on brain organization in Inuit youths
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN FUNCTION; CHILDREN AND YOUTH; DEVELOPMENTAL NEUROTOXICITY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ENVIRONMENTAL CONTAMINANTS; NEUROBEHAVIORAL; NEUROIMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: The risks of in utero and early exposure to major environmental contaminants such as heavy metals and legacy persistent organic pollutants on child brain development have been demonstrated using behavioural and global cognitive assessments but our understanding of how these contaminants alter the brain is very little. During the last decade we have been studying prospectively the effects of high exposure to environmental contaminants on child development in a cohort of Inuit children. Important health data were collected in Nunavik but our understanding of the mechanisms underlying the deficits observed in this population is limited because sophisticated tests and equipments cannot be transported in Nunavik. We propose to assess brain integrity using state-of-the-art brain imaging techniques based on Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) in a sub-sample of Inuit youths (n=120) that we have been studying since birth. The whole-brain anatomical structure as well as functional imaging of brain processes will be obtained in relation to prenatal exposure, taking into account current exposure as well as many confounding variables. This research strategy will allow us to establish a global picture of how contaminants alter the development of the brain. Thus this approach will make it possible to identify new potential biomarkers of environmental contaminants neurotoxicity that could guide the development of remedial strategies in the affected children and youths. Furthermore, the identification of action mechanisms will support causal inferences and, therefore, could impact governmental legislations regarding substance regulations and maximum tolerable levels for the Canadian population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Maximizing the effects of self-management interventions on chronic disease outcomes: The development of a Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) web-based patient portal
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMNT; CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE (COPD); HEALTH BEHAVIORS; HEALTH INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; SELF-MANAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: One of the greatest healthcare challenges is the increasing costs and social burden of chronic disease - a challenge which the healthcare system is poorly equipped to address. Self-management refers to learning and practicing skills necessary to carry on an active and emotionally satisfying life in the face of a chronic condition. This requires providing patients with effective tools and strategies to manage their health and to develop the confidence needed to uptake healthy behaviors and stop unhealthy ones. Unfortunately, the support provided by the healthcare system to help individuals manage their health has mainly involved a combination of infrequent brief discussions during physician visits and educational pamphlets, but has not provided the patient with ongoing information and monitoring in response to changes in their health. Self-management support for patients by the care team is recognized as an integral element needed for improving health outcomes by guiding individuals to care for their own health and to make positive health choices. To provide this type of support a direct line of communication is required between the patient and care team, extending the care experience outside of the physician's office or clinic. Health information technology (HIT) offers a unique opportunity to provide regular monitoring by supplying a means for two way communication and exchange of information between the patient and care team. COPD is the 4th leading cause of death in Canada and is one condition where self-management has been shown to be effective for improving health outcomes. This study will evaluate the acceptability and test the effects of using a COPD web-based self-management tool on selected health behaviors and outcomes using focus groups with patients and health professionals and through a randomized controlled trial. If the tool is found to be effective, it will be deployed and further tested on a larger scale and adapted for other chronic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Quantitative CT Myocardial Perfusion Imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: BEAM HARDENING; CT IMAGING; ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE; MYOCARDIAL PERFUSION; QUANTITATIVE IMAGING; TRACER KINETICS MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of disability and death in the United States and Canada, and is associated with substantial and increasing utilization of health care resources. There is increasing concern that routinely used diagnostic methods to identify CAD are not optimal, as only 38% of patients are found to have severe blocked coronary blood vessels that require treatment when these are examined more closely with insertion of catheters (invasive coronary angiography).  Furthermore, evidence from multiple studies now suggests that many patients who had their blocked coronaries reopened (revascularization) may not have benefited from this risky procedure because blood flow downstream to those blocked blood vessels was not limiting. In other words, current diagnostic tests on patients with chest pain who may or may not have CAD are resulting in inappropriate use of scarce health care resources and exposing patients to unnecessary risks. Recently CT scanning with state-of-art multi-row detector scanners has been shown to be a highly promising tool for the identification of heart muscle that is at risk of permanent injury from lack of blood flow but in its current form has artifacts from shading/beam hardening, does not measure actual heart muscle blood flow but measure instead blood flow relative to that in normal heart muscle, and delivers a relatively high radiation dose.  In this application we will develop a low radiation dose CT scanning technique that makes use of the most recent technological advancement of switching rapidly the energy of the x-rays between a high one and a low one during scanning.  This will allow highly accurate measurement of blood flow in heart muscle affected by CAD without reference to that in normal heart muscle.  We will also develop associated methods in image reconstruction and processing that will reduce the radiation dose required in the measurements.

TitreApplicationTitle: OptEC: Optimizing Early Child Development in the Primary Care Practice Setting: Pragmatic Randomized Trial of Iron Treatment for Young Children with Non-anemic Iron Deficiency
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD DEVELOPMENT; NON-ANEMIC IRON DEFICIENCY; PREVENTION AND HEALTH PROMOTION; PRIMARY CARE PEDIATRICS; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: The pre-school years are critical years for children to acquire early learning skills such as language, fine motor and social skills; this is termed early child development. Primary care doctors (family doctors and pediatricians) are in a unique position to identify children with health or developmental problems. Screening is the process of testing healthy people for the earliest signs of health problems, followed by treatment, with the expectation that screening will improve the health of those screened. The focus of this research is screening young children for the earliest signs of iron deficiency (low blood iron levels) followed by treatment with oral iron.  Previous research has shown that children with later stages of iron deficiency have serious delays in their development. Some research has shown that these delays may persist into young adulthood often with a significant reduction in intelligence. Early stages of iron deficiency may be difficult for parents or doctors to detect, and a blood test is usually needed. However, Canadian guidelines do not recommend screening all children for iron deficiency, because there is not enough good quality research to prove that screening is effective.   In this study, we will ask parents to allow their child between the ages of 1 to 3 years to have a blood test for iron levels. If the blood level is low, the child will be randomly assigned to receive either oral iron liquid for 4 months plus diet counseling, or a placebo liquid plus diet counseling. A psychologist will measure each child's early learning ability before and after the treatment.  If this approach to screening children's blood iron levels followed by treatment improves children's development, parents and doctors may consider that routine blood screening tests are justified. Overall, this research is an important step to improving the ways in which primary care doctors can ensure that children have the best start to life-long health and achievement.

TitreApplicationTitle: Routage intracellulaire de TRPC6 et hypertension artérielle pulmonaire.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHIMIE; BIOLOGIE MOLECULAIRE; CALCIUM INTRACELLULAIRE; CHROMATOGRAPHIE; CLONAGE; CULTURE CELLULAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: L'hypertension arterielle pulmonaire (HTAP) est une maladie vasculaire qui est definie par une augmentation de la pression arterielle dans l'artere pulmonaire. Si non traitee, l'HTAP entraine une insuffisance cardiaque droite et eventuellement, la mort. Les maladies pulmonaires responsables d'un defaut d'oxygenation du sang et creant de l'hypoxie, tel que l'emphyseme et la bronchite chronique, sont parmi les causes principales de l'HTAP. L'augmentation de la pression arterielle dans l'artere pulmonaire est causee par un epaississement de la couche de cellules musculaires entourant le vaisseau. Ceci a pour consequence de diminuer l'interieur de l'artere pulmonaire, causant l'augmentation de la pression, la mauvaise circulation sanguine et le refoulement du sang vers le coeur droit. Dans l'HTAP, une expression elevee des canaux calciques TRPCs dans les cellules musculaires de l'artere pulmonaire a ete observee. Nos resultats preliminaires demontrent que les quantites de TRPCs a la surface des cellules sont regulees par des processus dynamiques de transport vers la surface cellulaire (externalisation) ou vers l'interieur de la cellule (internalisation). Par contre, ne connaissant pas les mecanismes precis qui controlent ces processus de transport, l'objectif de ce projet est d'identifier les mecanismes responsables du routage intracellulaire des TRPCs. Ultimement, ce projet permettra d'identifier des strategies pour diminuer l'expression des TRPCs a la surface des cellules musculaires de l'artere pulmonaire, ce qui representerait une nouvelle avenue pour le traitement de l'HTAP.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional studies of membrane transporters
Keywords-MotsClés: MEMBRANE PROTEINS; PROTEIN CRYSTALLIZATION; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; TRANSPORTERS; XRAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Over half of all drugs available today act by interacting with membrane proteins, and there is intense interest in understanding these proteins at the molecular level. Unfortunately, this large class of proteins is only poorly understood at the biochemical and structural level because membrane proteins are notoriously difficult to study. We are using both novel and established methods to study two membrane proteins that are involved in drug resistance. The first is a molecular pump called MsbA, which is able to transport a variety of drugs out of cells. Similar pumps are involved in multi-drug resistance, which is an important problem in cancer chemotherapy. The second is called MacB. This protein pumps antibiotics out from bacteria, contributing to the problem of microbial antibiotic resistance. Our studies on these proteins may lead to ways to counteract resistance mechanisms that reduce the efficacy of drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Viral fusion glycoproteins: Structure-driven analysis and discovery of broad-spectrum antiviral fusion inhibitors
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRAL INHIBITORS; RNA VIRUSES; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; VIRAL ENTRY; VIRAL FUSION; VIRAL GLYCOPROTEINS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: The emergence and re-emergence of new or altered viruses, threat of viral pandemics and widespread antiviral resistance necessitates the urgent development of a broad-spectrum strategy for viral infection. Class I viral glycoproteins are the only virally-encoded protein on the surface of virions, and mediate cellular attachment and fusion. Hence, this class of proteins are a natural target for antiviral therapeutics and vaccines. We will employ a series of proven and innovative techniques ranging from virology, biochemistry, structural biology, biophysics and high-throughput screening, to understand the structural diversity of viral fusion glycoproteins and to identify novel inhibitors that are effective against a diverse set of viruses. Ultimately, we anticipate our work will have the potential to reveal general model principles in the fusion of pH-independent viruses, such as HIV-1. Moreover, this work will provide a blueprint for the development of antiviral inhibitors that are active for a diverse set of viruses.

TitreApplicationTitle: QF2011: The effects of the Queensland Flood on pregnant women, their pregnancies, and their children's early development.
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIORAL ASSESSMENT; BIOLOGICAL MECHANISMS; BIRTH OUTCOMES; DISASTER RESEARCH; EARLY CHILDHOOD DEVELOPMENT; LONGITUDINAL DESIGN; PRENATAL STRESS; PSYCHOMETRIC ASSESSMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Research suggests that maternal exposure to a severe stressor increases her baby's risk for a variety of disorders in adulthood. Animal research has demonstrated that maternal stress hormones pass through the fetus' placenta and affects the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and immune system, which are them associated with later problems. Relatively few studies have been able to study this relationship in humans because it is unethical to stress pregnant women. Project Ice Storm was the first such study to look at how stress arising from a natural disaster affected exposed fetuses and has shown that high levels of maternal stress have lasting effects on cognitive, behavioral, and physical development. However, Project Ice Storm was unable to determine the mechanisms by which maternal stress affects the developing fetus. The aim of The QF2011 Study is to replicate Project Ice Storm while increasing understanding of the biological mechanisms responsible for the effects of maternal stress during pregnancy. We will determine the extent to which the effects of various components of exposure to a disaster on the mother, her pregnancy, and the fetus, are moderated by biological and psychosocial factors, and by two different models of midwifery practice. We are taking advantage of a unique situation: In January, large regions of the state of Queensland experienced the worst floods in 50 years. This happened after researchers at Brisbane's Mater Mothers' Hospital had collected data on maternal depression and psychosocial factors in more than 300 pregnant women for a study comparing midwifery practices. The proposed collection of maternal and fetal blood, placenta, maternal and child cortisol samples, as well as conducting in-depth assessment of the mothers and their children when the children are 1, 2.5, and 4 years of age will enable us to determine the mechanisms by which maternal stress during pregnancy can affect their child's behavior after birth.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Novel, Genetically Modified Mouse Model of Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis and Related Hypermineralization Disorders in the Elderly
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOSINE; AGING; ARTHRITIS; BONE; MINERALIZATION; NUCLEOSIDE TRANSPORT; PURINE METABOLISM; SPINE
Abstract-Résumé: Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH) is a disease of the elderly characterized by mineralization of the spinal ligaments.  It is a relatively common condition, with prevalence around 20% in men and slightly less in women over the age of 65. Symptoms include thoracic spine pain and stiffness and, in severe cases, dysphagia and compression of the spinal cord and nerve roots leading to paralysis. Importantly, the cause of DISH is unknown and there are no specific treatments.  This proposal examines a genetically modified mouse model which develops calcified lesions of the spinal ligaments with remarkable resemblance to DISH in humans.  We will use state-of-the-art imaging and molecular approaches to confirm this potential clinical model, and use it to define the underlying mechanisms related to the development of DISH.   Our proposed studies promise to provide breakthrough insights into the etiology of DISH, and will permit the development and preclinical testing of novel therapeutics to prevent or delay the progression of this debilitating disorder. In addition to providing a model of DISH, these studies may also generate important information on related disorders such as ossification of the posterior spinal longitudinal ligament (OPLL) in the elderly.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing novel treatments for acute kidney injury: Slit2 as a novel therapy for renal ischemia-perfusion injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; CHEMOTAXIS; IMMUNOBLOTTING; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; ISCHEMIA-REPERFUSION INJURY; ROBO1; SLIT2
Abstract-Résumé: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a large and growing problem. Being diagnosed with AKI drastically worsens one's prognosis, increasing the chance of developing end-stage kidney failure and death. The most common cause of AKI occurs when blood flow is reduced to the kidney (ischemia). Injury that occurs after ischemia and subsequent restoration of blood flow (reperfusion), otherwise known as ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), initiates a complex cascade of events involving the release of many different molecules from the injured kidney that recruit cells which can cause inflammation. These inflammatory cells cause damage to the kidney by inducing cell injury, cell death, and scarring. Many current therapies focus on blocking inflammatory cell recruitment to the kidney, but unfortunately usually block only one of the many activated recruitment pathways and thus have had limited clinical success.  Although much attention has been paid to molecules that attract inflammatory cells to the injured kidney, little is known about molecules that repel these cells. Slit2, a molecule known to repel developing nerve cells, has been shown by our group to block the recruitment of inflammatory cells to injured organs. In addition, we have shown that Slit2 levels fall in some cell types that are exposed to IRI-like conditions in the test tube, suggesting that in the setting of IRI, anti-migration cues to the kidney might also be reduced.  This proposal takes a novel approach to the treatment of kidney IRI. Instead of focusing on reducing the many recruitment signals to the injured kidney, we will determine whether levels of a general repellent signal, Slit2, are reduced in the kidney post-IRI. We will further test whether Slit2 administration can block inflammatory cells from reaching the injured kidney, leading to protection of kidney structure and function. The ultimate goal of these studies is to identify a new therapy that will improve patient outcomes post-kidney IRI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dietary control of pathological angiogenesis in diabetic retinopathy model
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CONFOCAL IMAGING; LASER RETINAL MICRO-DISSECTION AND CAPTURE; LIPID DIETS (OMEGA3 VS OMEGA6); LIPID METABOLITE SIGNALING; LIPIDOMICS; NEURO-VASCULAR INTERACTIONS; PROLIFERATIVE RETINOPATHY AND DIABETIC RETINOPATHY; TRANSGENIC MICE; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetic retinopathy is one of the most common complication of diabetes and the leading cause of blindness in working age adults. The lipids we eat play a crucial role in the development of abnormal blood vessels and the protection of neurons in the retina of diabetic patients. We showed previously that a diet rich in omega 3-fatty acids is protective against the development of these abnormal retinal vessels by decreasing inflammation in the retina. However, the enzymes that process essential lipids (such as omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids) and their active products have not been thoroughly investigated. This grant aims to identify specific lipid products of omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids that mediate or prevent the vascular and neuronal damage observed in the diabetic retina. To unravel this important problem, we are using transgenic mice that lack the key enzymes involved in the processing of essential fatty acids and subject them to a model of diabetic retinopathy. Their retinal vessels and neurons are examined, as well as their lipid profile using advanced lipid analysis tools. This research has immediate clinical implications since drugs affecting these lipid enzymes are in use or in clinical trials and may inadvertently influence retinopathy in diabetic patients. Selective drug targets will be identified to induce or enhance the beneficial effects observed with an omega-3 fatty acid replete diet.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chromatin modulation associated with gene regulation: Interplay between histone chaperones and epigenetic marks
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; DNA REPAIR; EPIGENETIC; GENE EXPRESSION; GENETIC SCREEN; GENOME STABILITY; HISTONE; HISTONE CHAPERONE; TRANSCRIPTION; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Cells modulate expression of their genomes in response to different signals. For that, DNA must be transcribed to produce mRNAs that will be subsequently translated into proteins. This gene regulation takes place in the nucleus of cells where the DNA is packaged into a nucleoprotein structure called chromatin. Interestingly, this structure plays a major role in the regulation of genes. To activate or repress genes cells evolved very sophisticated mechanisms that deal with chromatin. Defects in these processes affect gene regulation, interfere with DNA replication, induce hyperrecombination and result in genome instability. Most of these defects are associated with tumorogenesis and cancer. We are specifically studying mechanisms of chromatin modulations associated with gene regulation. We have found factors that are dedicated to unfold chromatin structure, allowing access to DNA and therefore facilitating its transcription. Following transcription, these same factors repair the chromatin structure that has been unfolded, restoring the possibility of gene regulation. In this project we will focus on the role of a specific class of factors called histone chaperones. These proteins have the ability to assemble/disassemble chromatin during transcription.  Interestingly, we discovered that histone chaperone activities modulate specific epigenetic marks. Epigenetic marks are generally modifications of chromatin that are not encoded in the DNA sequence but have a direct impact on gene regulation. We will use biochemical and yeast genetic approaches to understand the relationship between histone chaperones and epigenetic marks and how this interplay regulates genes. Given the importance of the mechanisms to be studied, the advances that we will make should lead to a better understanding of these basic and fundamental mechanisms in other eukaryotes, including humans. This could possibly lead to new innovative therapies to different diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring the impact of cognitive and psychosocial interventions in persons with mild cognitive impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BRAIN HEALTH; COGNITIVE TRAINING; LIFE STYLE; MEMORY; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; PSYCHOSOCIAL INTERVENTION; SELF-EFFICACY
Abstract-Résumé: Mild cognitive impairment refers to a condition in which aged persons exhibit cognitive problems of which the impact and severity is insufficient to meet the criteria for dementia. However, aged persons with mild cognitive impairment are at a high-risk of developing dementia in the subsequent years. Memory interventions are training programs that provide a variety of cognitive and psychological strategies meant to improve memory. These interventions have been shown to yield significant benefits to normal aged persons and small-size studies have shown that they are suitable and beneficial for persons with mild cognitive impairment. The goal of this proposal is to assess with a well-controlled design the efficiency and specificity of cognitive training in persons with mild cognitive impairment. We will also assess the maintenance of the benefits that subjects have from the intervention. Our hypothesis is that cognitive training can improve the cognition of persons with mild cognitive impairment and that this improvement can be enduring. This study is likely to have a significant impact on the well-being of persons with mild cognitive impairment because it will contribute to the development of adapted and scientifically valid cognitive interventions. Accordingly, this type of intervention may greatly contribute to the strengthening of health care services for older Canadians.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding memory changes and brain plasticity in mild cognitive impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BRAIN IMAGING; BRAIN PLASTICITY; DEMENTIA; MEMORY; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Older persons with mild cognitive impairment do not meet the diagnostic criteria for Alzheimer's disease but many of them actually have a very mild phase of the disease. Understanding what happens in the brain of these persons is fundamental for better understanding the brain and cognitive mechanisms that are taking place at a very early stage of the disease development. In our previous studies,we used functional magnetic resonance imaging,a technique that allows visualizing the brain when people memorize words or attend to complex tasks. We found that there is more activation in some parts of these person's brains when compared to older adults with no cognitive deficit. We want to better understand this phenomenon. It may indeed reflect brain attempts to counteract the effect of the disease. We will use brain imaging to assess the brain changes as people progress in the disease. We want to know which brain areas change their level of activation as the disease progresses and the conditions associated with increased brain activation. We will assess if these changes help persons to better perform in memory tasks. Finally, we will offer cognitive training programs to some of these individuals to shed light on the brain mechanisms that support training-related improvement. Overall, this new set of studies will shed light on important phenomena and might provide new and innovative avenues in the characterization and treatment of very early MCI.

NomDuComitéFR: Génomique: Biologie computationnelle et biologie des systèmes
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional characterization of the endogenous retrovirus HERV-H family in human embryonic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CHIP SEQUENCING; ENDOGENOUS RETROVIRUS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE REGULATORY NETWORKS; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; REPETITIVE DNA; STEM CELLS; TRANSCRIPTOME SEQUENCING; TRANSPOSABLE ELEMENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Pluripotent embryonic stem cells hold the promise of being a renewable source of replacement cells and tissues for a number of diseases and conditions including Parkinson's disease, spinal cord injury, heart disease, diabetes, and arthritis. Although clinical trials that use cells derived from human embryonic stem cells (hESC) are already underway, in-depth characterization of all aspects of hESC biology will be paramount to the successful realization of stem cell-derived cures. We recently completed a detailed analysis of the regulatory network of hESCs and identified a family of endogenous retroviruses with a distinctive activity profile that is specific to undifferentiated stem cells. The objectives of the present study are to develop new approaches using next-generation sequencing to accurately map the activity of repetitive regions of the genome and to characterize the function of this family of retrovirus in hESCs. Given that a large fraction of human-specific genomic sequences are derived from endogenous retroviruses, including regions that differ between individuals, their functional characterization in developmental and disease models will be essential.

TitreApplicationTitle: CALIPER: A Canada-Wide Initiative to Close the Critical Gaps in Pediatric Reference Intervals
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; CHILDREN; LABORATORY TESTS; PEDIATRIC DISEASE; REFERENCE INTERVALS
Abstract-Résumé: CALIPER (Canadian Laboratory Initiative in Pediatric Reference Intervals) is a multi-centre study among several children's hospitals across Canada to establish a current and accurate database of pediatric reference intervals (normal values) that represent Canada's children and youth, multiethnic, males and females, from birth to 18 years old. Reference intervals are values that help clinicians interpret their patient's laboratory test results. Availability of accurate pediatric reference intervals is therefore very important when a child with medical concerns is screened for a disease. Unfortunately, there are huge gaps in the information that pediatricians have available to them and this increases the risk of misdiagnosis of children with medical concerns. This is a team application by laboratory scientists in seven pediatric healthcare centres across Canada to address these critical gaps. Healthy children will be recuited in schools, daycare centres, nurseries and other community centres. Small blood samples will be collected and then used to test for a number of important blood parameters. This data will then be analyzed to obtain normal values for children of different age and sex. Data will also be collected and compared among major ethnic groups including aboriginal Canadians. Successful implementation of the CALIPER project will directly contribute to improved pediatric healthcare by ensuring a harmonized approach to laboratory test interpretation across pediatric centres in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translation clinique de la peau bilamellaire reconstruite in vitro par génie tissulaire : application pour le traitement des grands brûlés
Keywords-MotsClés: GRANDS BRULES; GREFFES; GENIE TISSULAIRE; PEAU BILAMELLAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: L'utilisation des greffons d'epiderme cultive autologues a ameliore le traitement ainsi que le pronostic des grands brules. Cependant, l'absence de derme, qui procure les proprietes mecaniques a la peau, est une limitation de cette technique. Nous avons developpe une methode originale qui permet de reconstruire des substituts cutanes comprenant un derme et un epiderme in vitro a partir des cellules du patient, la methode d'autoassemblage. Ces tissus sont autologues et ne renferment pas de materiaux exogenes. Ainsi le risque qu'ils produisent une reaction immunologique est donc ecarte. Le but du projet est d'utiliser ces tissus comme substituts de remplacement pour la greffe pleine epaisseur pour le traitement des grands brules en phase aigue et pour la revision des cicatrices hypertrophiques de diverses origines. La translation vers la clinique de cette technologie novatrice requiert la collaboration de biologistes cellulaires, moleculaires et de cliniciens. Le projet consistera a prelever le tissu, a extraire et cultiver les 2 principaux types cellulaires de la peau, de reconstruire un substitut cutane bilamellaire et de le greffer sur des patients. Nous prevoyons que la prise de greffe ainsi que les proprietes mecaniques de ces peaux bilamellaires seront superieures aux greffons d'epiderme cultive.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assess, Redress, Re-assess: Addressing Disparities in Respiratory Health Among First Nations People. RN
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENT; FIRST NATIONS; INEQUITIES; RESPIRATORY HEALTH; RURAL
Abstract-Résumé: Living and social conditions in some First Nations communities are characterized by personal, social and physical environments that are associated with adverse respiratory outcomes. Characterization of conditions will provide communities with information to assist  in obtaining resources to make change, for example in housing conditions. In partnership with the rural communities of Beardy's and Okemasis First Nation and Montreal Lake Cree Nation, the project will consist of baseline evaluations, intervention activities, and prospective evaluations of respiratory health and intervention activities in children and adults. Based on the 4 phase concept of the First Nations Regional Health Survey, the project aims to evaluate individual factors (air quality, cigarette smoke, chest infections, obesity), and contextual factors (socio-economic, socio-cultural, colonization, access to health services) on the outcomes of asthma (especially in children), chronic bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and obstructive sleep apnea, with the communities undertaking interventions aimed at redressing the issues. This is an opportunity to conduct a project that includes knowledge translation and knowledge exchange by participatory research and intervention where the people are involved in all stages of research and intervention, thereby increasing their ownership and empowerment for change, and is grounded in the community by involving Band Councillors, elders, and youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strategies for gene discovery in schizophrenia:  subphenotypes, deep sequencing, and interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSOCIATION; ENDOPHENOTYPES; EYE TRACKING; FACIAL DYSMORPHOLOGY; GENE SEQUENCING; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; RESPONSE; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a major psychiatric disease that has a life-time prevalence of approximately 1%, and costs up to $4 billion dollars per year to the Canadian health care system. Occurrence of SCZ in family suggests unique vulnerability factors (genes) running in families lead to the development of the disease. Although several studies have been carried out to identify these factors, the results have been mixed. In this study we propose to examine phenotypes (traits) that can be defined more precisely within SCZ patients. We will analyse whether any genetic factors predict response to antipsychotic medication (Pharmacogenetics). This work will guide clinicians in choosing the right medication for an individual patient based on the vulnerability factor(s) they are carrying. Other traits we will study in SCZ patients include age of onset of the illness, and number of affected family members. Furthermore, marijuana use appears to trigger onset of SCZ earlier and create more severe symptoms. We will incorporate marijuana use as a contributing factor in our statistical calculations. All the above analyses will be carried out by precisely analyzing the sequence of nucleotides (DNA sequencing) in individual genes among our SCZ patients. Detailed studies of these SCZ traits will provide the best opportunity to advance our understanding of the complexity and causes of the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examination of Factors that Mediate Effective Treatment of Anxiety in High Functioning Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder using Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY DISORDERS; AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; COGNITIVE BEHAVIORAL THERAPY; GROWTH CURVE ANALYSIS; MEDIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a life-long developmental disorder characterized by severe social-emotional and communicative impairments. Anxiety disorders are the most commonly reported concurrent diagnoses in individuals with ASD, and are more prevalent in ASD than in typical peers, affecting from 11% to 84% of children with ASD. However, little is understood about the factors that might contribute to or underlie anxiety. It is important to understand this co-morbidity because anxiety causes considerable distress and interference with daily functioning and may impact long-term prognosis and outcome. Several well conducted randomized control trials have shown that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based treatment that is effective in alleviating anxiety symptoms in children. Although results are promising, CBT is not effective for all children with ASD. In order to improve treatment effectiveness, the present study will examine mediational processes to understand 'how' and 'why' treatment change is produced versus just whether treatment change occurs. To date, there is no evidence about potential mechanisms of anxiety reduction through CBT in ASD. Thus, the goal of this pilot study is to examine mechanisms by which CBT mediates its therapeutic effects. This will be accomplished by implementing a 14-week group CBT program specifically designed for individuals with ASD, and examining two potential mediators of change: cognitive (i.e., executive function and attentional flexibility) and social (i.e., social skills/awareness). Mediation research is important because it advances theory and also has the potential to lead to improved clinical care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of early overnutrition on beta-cell function
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CELL; DIABETES; LEPTIN; NUTRITION; OBESITY; POSTNATAL DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Ever increasing rates of obesity in the Western world have led to a rising prevalence of type 2 diabetes, affecting over 2 million Canadians. While the association between obesity and diabetes is well-recognized, emerging evidence suggests that overnutrition and rapid growth in early life may also increase diabetes risk. Our research aims to identify hormonal alterations in response to early overnutrition which may affect life-long blood sugar control and may even affect subsequent generations. Furthermore, we will determine whether abnormalities can be improved by a healthier diet. This could potentially lead to screening of at-risk infants and children for hormonal indicators of diabetes risk and lead to early dietary or drug interventions aimed at reducing long-term harm.

TitreApplicationTitle: Randomized Controlled Trials Mentorship in HIV Co-infections and Co-morbidities
Keywords-MotsClés: CO-INFECTIONS; COMORBIDITIES; HIV/AIDS; MENTORSHIP; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this RCT mentoring application is to develop the mentee, Dr. Darrell Tan, into an independent investigator and future leader in clinical trials in the field of HIV/AIDS, particularly in the area of co-infections and complications of aging.  To achieve this goal, the mentee and primary mentor, Dr. Sharon Walmsley, have planned mentorship activities that build on the mentee's research training and benefit from a unique research environment blending the strengths of two large academic hospitals at the University of Toronto, the University Health Network (UHN) and St. Michael's Hospital (SMH), with national and international clinical trial research networks.  Specific mentorship activities correspond to the three objectives of the CIHR mentoring program: developing skills in RCT conception, design and implementation.  The mentee will  participate in the activities of the CIHR Canadian HIV Trials Network (CTN), a partnership of clinical trial sites across Canada with extensive experience in HIV clinical trials; participate in a program of weekly learning sessions with specific objectives covering key issues in clinical trials; lead regular rounds on 'special topics in clinical trials' at the SMH Applied Health Research Centre; continue his role on the CTN scientific review committee; assume increasing responsibility for CTN-240, an ongoing CIHR-funded trial; initiate at least one new clinical trial based on results from the mentee's PhD studies; assist in a new clinical trials capacity-building program of the Kenya AIDS Vaccine Initiative; and build clinical trial capacity at the SMH HIV Clinic by initiating its participation in existing trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preclinical evaluation of polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase as a therapeutic target.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMOTHERAPY; DNA REPAIR; RADIOTHERAPY; SYNTHETIC LETHALITY; TARGETED THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Despite major advances in targeted chemotherapy, the major forms of therapy continue to be surgery, radiotherapy and conventional chemotherapy.  The main target for radiotherapy, and many conventional drugs, is the cell's DNA. Not surprisingly, the levels of DNA damage and the repair of that damage influence cell survival and affects clinical outcome. As a result, DNA repair systems are emerging as therapeutic targets to enhance cell killing by radiation and chemotherapeutic agents. This proposal focuses on an important DNA repair enzyme, namely polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP), which plays a key role in the repair of DNA damage induced by radiation and a broad range of chemical compounds. We have recently identified a chemical (A12B4C3) that inhibits this enzyme and shown that the chemical sensitizes cells to radiation. This proposal is intended to determine the usefulness of targeting PNKP, making use of cells grown in tissue culture and tumour models grown in mice. First, we will examine if treatment with A12B4C3 sensitizes cancer cells to a variety of widely-used chemotherapeutic agents. Second, we will test the ability of A12B4C3 to sensitize cells to radiation under more clinically relevant conditions, taking into account the oxygen status of the cells. Finally, we will examine the potential for A12B4C3 to act as a single agent against cells that lack key proteins shown to be required for cell survival if PNKP is absent. Such preclinical testing of the targeting of PNKP is essential. If the utility of targeting PNKP is confirmed, it will provide a greater impetus to fully develop a drug for clinical use.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
TitreApplicationTitle: Men's Mental Health During the Transition to Parenthood: A Prospective Study to Track Changes, Determinants and Health-Seeking Behaviours
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER-SPECIFIC ASSESSMENT; GENDER-SPECIFIC DETERMINANTS; HELP-SEEKING BEHAVIOUR; PATERNAL DEPRESSION; PROSPECTIVE DESIGN
Abstract-Résumé: Psychological distress and depression in men following childbirth has just recently begun to be recognized and studied. While the rate of postpartum paternal depression in Canadian men following childbirth is unknown, studies conducted in other countries to date suggest that estimates vary from 4-27.5%. Postpartum paternal depression has been associated with engaging in poor health behaviours (i.e. greater use of alcohol and cigarettes), maternal postpartum depression and impaired child development. Despite these negative consequences, very few studies have examined the prevalence, impact and determinants of depression in men during the transition to fatherhood. To address these important knowledge gaps this study will survey men from the time their partner is in the third trimester of pregnancy and track the occurrence and maintenance of depressive symptoms from the first data collection point and at 6-8 weeks, 6- and 12 - months postpartum. We will assess a number of variables (i.e. sociodemographic, medical, lifestyle and psychosocial) in order to identify factors associated with depression for men during the transition to parenthood.  This study will provide a better understanding of the factors which lead to depression in men and will help health care professionals to better identify and treat depression in men.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of contributing heritable and environmental factors to adipokine and glycemic regulation variability during pregnancy and fetal development.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOKINES; EPIDEMIOLOGY; EPIGENETIC; FETAL DEVELOPMENT; GESTATIONAL DIABETES; GLUCOSE REGULATION; HERITABLE RISK FACTORS; INSULIN; PROSPECTIVE COHORT; QUANTITATIVE TRAITS
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes during pregnancy, known as gestational diabetes, is a major health issue. Gestational diabetes increases the risk of complications in both the mother and the offspring, during pregnancy, delivery, and for many years after. Women with gestational diabetes are at increased risk of type 2 diabetes later in their life. Children born from mother who had diabetes during pregnancy are at increased risk for future obesity and diabetes themselves later in life. This could be explained by common genetic and environmental risk factors acting during and/or after pregnancy. Excess weight is a common risk factor for type 2 diabetes and gestational diabetes. Fat tissue produces hormones that might participate in the processes linking obesity and diabetes. Levels of those hormones vary during pregnancy. This project will evaluate genes that influence regulation of glucose, insulin action, and fat-related hormones during pregnancy and their impact on fetus development. We will also assess the influence of diet, physical activity and other characteristics of pregnant women on associations between genes and glucose or hormones levels.  This project will lead to a better understanding of genetic and environmental factors influencing the risk of gestational diabetes and the future risk of obesity and diabetes in offspring. We hope that this knowledge will lead to better ways to prevent and treat obesity and diabetes in future generations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular characterisation of the HIV-2 and SIV Vpx proteins.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESSORY PROTEINS; HIV; MACROPHAGES; MOLECULAR VIROLOGY; RESTRICTION FACTORS; VPX
Abstract-Résumé: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is the causative agent of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).  The virus is estimated to infect 33 million people worldwide, with 2.5 million new infections a year.  In addition, 2 million deaths a year are attributed to AIDS. HIV encodes several accessory proteins that have been found to antagonise host restriction factors that would otherwise affect viral replication and infectivity. This project proposed to undergo the molecular characterisation of Vpx, an accessory protein unique to HIV-2 and SIV (simian immunodeficiency virus).  It has been demonstrated that this viral protein is required for viral infectivity in macrophages, a cell type that has a major role in the dissemination and persistence of HIV, however, many questions remain concerning the functional mechanism of action of Vpx during viral replication. We believe that functional characterisaton of Vpx will lead to further understanding of the requirements for viral infection of macrophages and help to better understand the differences in virus-host interactions between HIV-2 and HIV-1 (which does not encode Vpx).  This may help to understand why HIV-2 is less prevalent and generally less pathogenic than HIV-1 and may allow the development of strategies to reduce the pathogenic potential of HIV-1.

NomDuComitéFR: Formation de recherche en santé A - Post-Ph.D. (HTA)
TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of Arthritis Medications During Pregnancy on Maternal and Neonatal Health Outcomes.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIDEPRESSANTS; GESTATIONAL DIABETES; GESTATIONAL HYPERTENSION; NESTED CASE CONTROL STUDY; PERINATAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; POPULATION HEALTH; POPULATION-BASED RESEARCH; POST-PARTUM DEPRESSION; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: Importance of the research: Antidepressant use is common among pregnant women. However, there is little research on the use of antidepressants in pregnancy and most studies have focused on the health of the baby and not the mother. As the primary caregiver of the child, the mother's health should also be considered when making decisions regarding medication use during pregnancy. Therefore, my goal is to study how taking antidepressants during pregnancy affects the health of mothers during and after pregnancy.   How the research will be done: I will study the whether taking antidepressants increases the risk of developing gestational hypertension and gestational diabetes, two risky conditions for pregnant women. I will also study how use of antidepressants impact post-partum depression, a serious condition that affects women after delivery.  I will analyze the Quebec Pregnancy Registry, a resource containing data on doctor visits, hospital visits, and drug prescriptions for pregnant women in Quebec.    Innovations of the research: This will be the first research to study the overall risks and benefits of antidepressant on mother's health during and after pregnancy.    How the research will impact health of Canadians: Findings from this research will help guide clinical and public health decisions on appropriate use of antidepressants during pregnancy. Overall, this research will help improve the health of women, pregnant women, and mothers.

TitreApplicationTitle: On the development of bone quality parameters for assessing osteoporosis using peripheral quantitative computed tomography
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE QUALITY; DIAGNOSTIC VALUE; DISCRIMINATIVE POWER; FRACTURE PREDICTION; MOTION DETECTION; NORMATIVE VALUES; OSTEOPOROSIS; PQCT & HR-PQCT; SEX-SPECIFIC; STRUCTURAL AND MECHANICAL PROPERTIES
Abstract-Résumé: One in 4 women and at least 1 in 8 men over age 50 has osteoporosis, affecting over two million Canadians. Osteoporotic fractures are caused by poor bone strength, determined by bone density, structure and ability to resist force. Together, these properties constitute bone quality. Osteoporosis is currently diagnosed with two-dimensional bone density scans that predict less than a third of those who fracture. High and low resolution CT scanners each give three-dimensional information on bone quality. However, it is unknown which bone measures are best for diagnosing osteoporosis and which CT scanner provides the most useful information. The goal of this study is to compare high and low resolution CT scanners to identify bone quality measures that best estimate someone's risk for fracture(s). A 5-year multiple centre study will be conducted to measure bone quality using the two technologies at the beginning of the study in over 1000 men and women who are part of the Canadian Multicentre Osteoporosis Study. Detailed fracture information will be collected from participants over the 5 years of follow-up and from the past fifteen years. Bone quality measures from high and low resolution CT scanners will be compared in terms of their ability to predict fractures and to detect someone who had a fracture. The study will also examine how bone quality measures can provide added value to the current standard of care: the use of bone density plus basic risk factors for osteoporosis. To strengthen the results of the study, the analyses will be repeated 200 times using a computer model to see if the same results arise. The information from this study will guide improved diagnosis of osteoporosis by selecting the most informing bone quality measures and seeing how they can complement bone density scans. It will also generate a large nationwide data set available to Canadian researchers who can then examine how exercise, nutrition, drugs and other diseases affect bone quality.

Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Institute of Health Research Randomized Control Trials Mentoring Award will allow Dr. Carolyn Snider, an emergency physician and young scientist, to further develop her clinical research program in intentional injury, specifically focusing on prevention of violent injury among youth. The most common reason for ED visits in Ontario among those aged 15 - 24 is physical assault. However, few clinical trials of ED-based interventions in intentional injury have occurred. Given Dr Snider's credibility in clinical Emergency Medicine, she is uniquely situated to become a leader in clinical trials in her area of research interest. This award will allow Dr. Snider to complement her existing epidemiological training by pursuing advanced education specific to leading pragmatic randomized control trials (RCTs), and thereby contribute to the growth of research in intentional injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prospective investigation of the relationship between food insecurity and health and behavioural outcomes in HIV-HCV co-infection: clues for prevention interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL TREATMENT; FOOD INSECURITY; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HIV-HCV CO-INFECTION; MIXED METHODS RESEARCH; PREVENTION; PROSPECTIVE DESIGN; TREATMENT ADHERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: HIV infection has become a chronic manageable condition in Canada where combined antiretroviral treatments are available. This change has led to an increase in the occurrence of various competing morbidities among HIV-infected populations. This is especially true for hepatitis C virus (HCV) co-infected HIV-positive patients. HIV  positive persons who lack access to food appear more susceptible to having difficulties in managing and treating HIV infection. However few studies have studied the relationship of lack of access to food and HIV-HCV co-infection. The research has two objectives. Objective 1 aims at assessing the level of food insecurity (lack of access to food) among co-infected persons and its effect on HIV and HCV behavours and health. Objective 2 aims at exploring, from the perspective of co-infected persons who are food-insecure, issues of resilience and vulnerability, and to describe their needs for food security and their needs for nutrition and health care. To attain these objectives, the research will collect data every six months on food security as part of an ongoing multisite cohort study conducted in in Canada, and will implement a case study that will involve individual interviews. The longitudinal design of this research and its mixed methods approach will provide for new insights on the relationships between food insecurity and HIV-HCV co-infection related behaviours, treatment and health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Alzheimer Disease Pathobiology and Mechanisms of Neurodegeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; AMYLOID; APH1; GAMMA-SECRETASE; NEURODEGENERATION; PRESENILINS; SUMOYLATION; TRANSGENICS
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a common, progressive and ultimately lethal disease affecting ~5% of adults over 65 years of age and ~30% of adults over the age of 85 years in most Western societies. Both the prevalence and the annual expenditures on AD are expected to increase as the proportion of the population at risk increases over the next 20 years. The currently available treatments are of limited effectiveness as they target the symptoms of the disease but not the root cause. The major features of AD are accumulations of abnormal proteins called amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles within the brain. Amyloid plaques appear as densely packed thread-like fibers that form in the vicinity of nerve cells and blood vessels. Evidence suggests that amyloid is highly toxic and is the primary cause of nerve cell death. Loss of these cells is the underlying event in AD and results in the clinical features of cognitive dysfunction and memory impairments. We have identified the presenilin family of proteins which are the major cause of familial or inherited Alzheimer's disease. Presenilins are unique enzymes and are part of a larger complex (termed gamma-secretase) which directly produces the toxic amyloid in the brain. Presenilins are intimately involved in the disease process as shown by the fact that mutations or changes in their structure accelerates amyloid formation and results in early onset AD (25-40 years of age). However, the exact mechanism by which this is achieved remains unclear. Our research will investigate the molecular organization of the presenilins and their functional partners. This will yield valuable information on how they function and, with this knowledge, it will be possible to control the toxic amyloid species. The ultimate objective of this research is to understand the cellular processes which cause AD and to use that information for the development of safe and effective treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms of Protein Sorting in the Endocytic Pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL BIOLOGY; ENDOCYTOSIS; ENDOSOME; GENOMICS; PROTEIN SORTING; VESICLE TRANSPORT; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Every cell in our body is surrounded by a membrane that protects the inside of the cell from the outside environment. Cells also have compartments inside them that are surrounded by membranes. Nutrients and other molecules that must enter the cell and gain access to the internal compartments are taken up in special containers called vesicles. Vesicles transport these molecules to a central compartment called an endosome where they are sorted for delivery to their ultimate destination. An endosome can be compared to a post office, where letters are sorted according to postal codes. Molecules contain sorting signals that act like postal codes. Special proteins recognize these signals and help direct the molecules to their proper location in the cell. The goal of our research is to discover the proteins that recognize sorting signals at endosomes. Because defects in this sorting process can cause disease, a better understanding of this process is important for human health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Développement, validation et mise à l'essai d'un outil de partenariat aidants-gestionnaires de cas favorisant la réflexion des aidants concernant l'hébergement de leur proche atteint de la maladie d'Alzheimer ou d'un autre type de démences apparentées
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDANTS FAMILIAUX; DEFICITS COGNITIFS; PERSONNES AGEES; RECHERCHE QUALITATIVE; RECHERCHE EVALUATIVE; SOINS ET SERVICES
Abstract-Résumé: Pour les aidants prenant soin d'un proche age atteint de demence, la prise de decision reliee a l'hebergement est jugee stressante car ils doivent adopter le role de « representants ». Au Quebec, les gestionnaires de cas jouent les intermediaires entre l'aidant et le systeme de sante lors de l'hebergement en soins de longue duree. Toutefois, aucun protocole n'est disponible presentement pour soutenir la reflexion des aidants avant qu'une demande d'hebergement formelle ne soit formulee. L'etude proposee vise le developpement et la mise a l'essai d'un outil favorisant la reflexion des aidants en lien avec l'hebergement de leur proche atteint de demence. L'outil sera developpe a partir des ecrits scientifiques portant sur le processus decisionnel des aidants et sera structure sous forme de questions ouvertes que les gestionnaires de cas utiliseront lors de rencontres a domicile pour explorer le sujet avec les aidants. Le developpement de cet outil reposera sur un modele de partenariat qui prone l'inclusion des familles et des intervenants dans l'amelioration des services de sante. Le contenu de l'outil sera valide en organisant des groupes de discussion aupres de 15 aidants ayant heberge un proche atteint de la maladie d'Alzheimer ou de demences connexes et de 15 gestionnaires de cas uvrant aupres de cette population. Par la suite, une mise a l'essai de l'outil sera effectuee aupres de 12 dyades aidants-gestionnaires de cas lors d'une rencontre de soutien a domicile. A partir de l'analyse du contenu enregistre de cette rencontre et d'entrevues avec les gestionnaires de cas et les aidants, la pertinence de l'outil pour favoriser la reflexion des aidants et la faisabilite de l'utilisation de l'outil dans le contexte des soins a domicile seront etudiees. Cette etude permettra la creation d'un outil novateur favorisant l'integration d'une approche de partenariat des le debut du suivi et l'amelioration de l'adequation entre les besoins des aidants et les services offerts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Acute and residual effects of cannabis on young drivers' performance of driving-related skills
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE PSYCHOPHARMACOLOGIC EFFECTS OF CANNABIS; CANNABIS IMPAIRED DRIVING; DRIVING SIMULATION; RESIDUAL EFFECTS OF CANNABIS; YOUNG DRIVERS
Abstract-Résumé: Motor vehicle collisions are the leading cause of death for young people. We have recently found that driving after using cannabis is more common among young Canadian drivers than driving after drinking. While this observation raises concerns, the effects of cannabis on driving-related skills in this age group are not well understood. As well, evidence suggests that residual effects of cannabis on driving-related skills may be observed up to 24 hours later. These residual effects may have important implications for the effects of cannabis use on collisions risk, but little evidence on them is available. This study will examine the effects of a single dose of cannabis on driving-related skills immediately following consumption, 24 hours later, and 48 hours later. To date the residual effect at 48 hours has not been examined. A total of 128 subjects aged 19 and 20 will be randomly assigned to smoke either a placebo or cannabis (12.5% THC potency) cigarette. Participants must be regular users of cannabis, but not heavy/problem users, and must be free of any mental/physical health concerns that would contraindicate an acute dose of cannabis. Following a practice session, participants will attend 3 testing days: drug-administration, 24-hour follow-up, and 48-hour follow-up. The effects of cannabis/placebo on performance of driving-related skills using a high-fidelity driving simulator will be assessed on each testing day. The effects of cannabis on mood, cognition, memory and complex reaction time will also be assessed. Identifying factors that affect the collision risks experienced by young drivers is a public health priority. While many young people believe that cannabis does not impair driving, some recent studies suggest that these may be very dangerous beliefs. This study will provide important information on how cannabis may affect the driving skills of young drivers, to inform efforts to understand and address cannabis-related collisions in this age group.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of PVRL4 (Nectin 4) - A Newly Identified Epithelial Receptor for Measles Virus
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENS JUNCTIONS; CANINE DISTEMPER VIRUS; MEASLES VIRUS; NECTIN 4; ONCOLYTIC VIRUS; PVRL4; RECEPTOR; TIGHT JUNCTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Measles virus infects lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells by attaching to a cell surface receptor called SLAM(CD150). This receptor is upregulated on many lymphoma and leukemia cell surfaces making it a target for measles oncolytic therapy.  Epithelial cells of the trachea and lungs are also infected by measles virus, but the receptor on these cells was not known until very recently. We identified this receptor to be a tumor cell marker called PVRL4 (Nectin 4). This virus receptor is highly upregulated on lung, breast,colon,and ovarian adenocarcinomas, again suggesting that these tumors could be targeted using measles virus therapy. We propose to characterize the molecular interactions of PVRL4 with measles virus. The therapeutic capacity for measles virus in treating adenocarcinomas will be investigated in mouse models bearing lung, breast, and colon tumors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving recovery after peripheral nerve injury
Keywords-MotsClés: GROWTH FACTORS; MUSCLE REINNERVATION; NERVE INJURY; NERVE PHYSIOLOGY; NERVE RECONSTRUCTION; NERVE REGENERATION; NEUREGULIN; NEUROSCIENCE; PERIPHERAL NERVE; SURGICAL NERVE REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with peripheral nerve injury are often left with disabling loss of movement and sensation. Despite prompt surgical repair and extensive rehabilitation, traditional reconstructive surgical techniques involving long nerve grafts rarely provide satisfactory outcomes.  Seeking to improve outcomes for this group of patients, our group has recently demonstrated that side-to-side nerve grafts improve nerve regeneration following chronic injury.  We have shown that side-to-side nerve grafts conduct small numbers of nerve fibers from an uninjured donor nerve to an injured recipient nerve. We hypothesize that the small numbers of added donor fibers 'protect' the denervated distal stump of the injured recipient nerve during axon regeneration by providing trophic support to the Schwann cells of the distal stump. In this proposal we plan to investigate ways to optimize the protective effect and define the molecular pathways responsible for this effect. We will also test whether other modalities known to enhance nerve regeneration after chronic denervation, such as adding neurotrophic factors (growth factors acting on the neuron), synergize with this protective effect.  These projects will help determine the effectiveness of side-to-side nerve grafts in protecting distal nerve stumps from degeneration of their resident Schwann cells, which are necessary to support regenerating nerves, and investigate novel techniques to enhance nerve regeneration. We are hopeful that these findings will have important implications on improving traditional paradigms of surgical nerve repair, resulting in enhanced recovery following severe nerve injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Individual differences in autobiographical memory: cognitive, behavioural, and neural correlates
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; FUNCTIONAL MRI; HUMAN MEMORY; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; STRUCTURAL MRI
Abstract-Résumé: People differ in their ability to remember the details of events and facts from their lives. Although this is self-evident, there is very little research on the nature of these differences and how they relate to other mental and cognitive functions, brain structure and function, psychopathology, or the risk of neurodegenerative disease. The proposed research seeks to determine the underlying psychological structure of autobiographical memory. Individuals scoring high and low on various measures of autobiographical memory will be contrasted on detailed mental, behavioural, neuroimaging, and biomarker data. This research will contribute to knowledge concerning the relationships of memory function to brain health and disease.
