TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms regulating persistent DNA damage signaling and the linked control of cell proliferation and extracellular signals
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE CHECKPOINTS; CYTOKINE SECRETION; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE RECOVERY; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE SIGNALING; ENZYME-MEDIATED DNA BREAKS; HIGH-CONTENT IMAGING; MEDIUM-THROUGHPUT MEASUREMENTS; PERSISTENT DNA DAMAGE SIGNALING; PRIMARY HUMAN CELL CULTURE; TELOMERE DYSFUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Cells of the human body experience and fix DNA damage everyday, a process required to preserve health. This is illustrated in many human diseases, including cancer, which is often caused by errors during DNA repair. Additionally, intentional DNA damage induced by radiation or chemotherapy are often used for cancer therapy, mostly because rapidly dividing cancer cells are very sensitive to high levels of DNA damage. A relatively recent and novel angle of the DNA repair research effort investigates how cells that survive DNA damage can return to normal once the damage is repaired. This is a process called DNA damage response recovery. Our hypothesis is that in some context, the DNA damage response recovery is improperly activated and can interfere with the activity of genes that normally prevent cell growth in the presence of DNA damage. This could explain how some normal cells acquire mutations required for cancer progression, or why some cancer cells can survive DNA damage inflicted during therapy. We also think that the DNA damage response recovery can influence how severely damaged cells communicate with their environment, which has consequences for aging and for therapy-associated side effects. Using normal human cells, we propose to characterize the interactions between the amount of DNA damage, the DNA damage response recovery, the maintenance of proper cell growth arrest, and the ability of the damaged cells to send extracellular damage signals (to communicate). The overall goal of this proposal is to broaden our understanding of how DNA damage signaling is stopped or avoided in humans, with a long-term objective of improving patient care by increasing knowledge about targets that could be used to sensitize cancer cells to therapy-induced DNA damage.

ClasseRechercheFR: DIABETE SUCRE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of autoimmunity in type 1 diabetes by Chromogranin A specific T cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTING CELLS; ANTIGEN PROCESSING AND PRESENTATION; AUTOANTIGENS; IMMUNOMODULATION; IMMUNOREGULATION; REGULATORY T CELLS; TH17 CELLS; TISSUE/CELL REGENERATION; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Juvenile diabetes or Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a chronic health problem that is triggered early in childhood and lasts for a lifetime. T1D is an autoimmune disease in which the body's immune system attacks and destroys the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas. Over 300,000 Canadians from young children to adults are living with T1D and the only treatment available to them is lifelong daily injections of insulin. The complications such as kidney failure, adult blindness, stroke, heart disease, nerve damage and amputation are similar in type 1 (childhood or juvenile) and type 2 (adult onset) diabetes. According to a recent study, the total direct health care costs associated with diabetes in Canada is expected to increase to over $8 billion annually by 2016. Approximately 15% of this cost can be directly attributed to T1D. With the progress made in the past 30 years in the genetics and immunology of T1D it is likely that immunotherapy strategies can be developed to manage and prevent T1D. If immunological approach has to succeed   these have to have specificity so you do not block or destroy other tissues and cells. that can be derived from the specific regulatory T cells. The focus of our research is to explore such strategies by uncovering the underlying basic mechanisms. The studies proposed in this research proposal will allow us to develop new approaches by using regulatory T cells in our laboratory. These cells have the potential to prevent and regulate the disease process. With regulatory T cells we propose to develop antigen-specific immunotherapy to ultimately allow inhibition/regulation of tissue/cell specific immune responses while leaving all other immune responses intact. The results obtained from these studies will have a potential for application in modulating human disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY SEIZURE; DEAFNESS AND COGNATIVE DEFICITS; DEVELOPMENTAL PLASTICITY OF THE MAMMALIAN CENTRAL SYNAPSES; GLUTAMATERGIC EXCITATORY SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; IMAGING TECHNIQUES; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY AND IN SITU HYBRIDIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Information is coded in the form of electric impulses propagating among nerve cells which form complex networks in the brain. Effective communication between these cells depends on the ability of cross-talk among them through release and reception of chemical substance or neurotransmitter. This study uses the hearing system as a model to study the building blocks of establishing effective communication in the early stage of brain development.  Our work may potentially help understand how nerve cells code and transfer information in the mammalian brain, particularly how auditory nerve cells localize the sound source in space, as well as pathological basis underlying hearing loss, audiogenic seizures and other cognitive disorders and diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of nuclear processes and cell fate by MYST-ING tumor suppressor complexes
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLTRANSFERASES; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATIONS; CHROMOSOMAL TRANSLOCATIONS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE REGULATION; GENOME MAINTENANCE AND STABILITY; HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; HISTONE VARIANTS; PROTEIN COMPLEXES; TUMOR SUPPRESSORS
Abstract-Résumé: All cells in a multicellular organism contain the same genetic material.  Despite this fact, different cell types must carry out different functions.  How each cell expresses the required proteins at the correct times and represses unnecessary ones is precisely controlled.  Deregulation of this process can result in malfunctioning cells, cell death or uncontrolled growth (cancer).  The goal of this research plan is to characterize a family of regulators that are fundamental to cell life and known to suppress tumor formation.  Research work including from our laboratory has shown that these regulators (ING's) are at the center of epigenetic (information not contained in the DNA) mechanisms controlling cell growth, stability of the genetic material, stem cell renewal and protection from cancer.  Our research plan is to characterize how these regulators function in fundamental processes that govern cell growth and differentiation as well as in conditions leading to cancer formation.  This in turn will point us to new scientific approaches in applied research to treat the large number of cancers in which ING proteins do not function properly.

TitreApplicationTitle: Direct lymphocyte-mediated antimicrobial mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVATION RECEPTORS; CYTOTOXIC LYMPPHOCYTES; FUNGAL HOST DEFENSE; FUNGI; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNOMYCOLOGY; NK CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Infections, particularly those that affect patients with compromised immunity like AIDS and those resistant to antibiotics, are among the most pressing challenges for mankind. It is not clear how we will defend ourselves against these ever increasing microbial invaders. The answer may lie in studies of the immune system. The information from these studies may provide new and exciting insights for therapies where antibiotics don't exist or where they have become ineffective. With this goal in mind, Dr. Mody's laboratory has been studying a class of cells that was originally identified because of their ability to kill tumor cells and cells infected with virus. Because of their ability to be toxic to, and kill other cells, they are called cytotoxic lymphocytes. Recently, it has been found that these cells can turn their attention to microbes like bacteria and fungi and kill these invading microbes. When they do, they are called microbicidal lymphocytes. Because this finding is so new, the mechanisms of recognition of the microbe, mechanisms of activation of the microbicidal lymphocytes and the killing mechanisms have not been well worked out. Imagine if this potent source of anti-infective cells could be harnessed and applied to therapy. Moreover, recent studies from Dr. Mody's laboratory demonstrate that this lymphocyte-mediated microbicidal response is defective in HIV-infected patients, and his laboratory is working to repair the defect. It is the goal of this proposal to study the normal and defective mechanisms with the purpose of providing new therapies for these challenging infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Best practices: Parent/provider interactions in pediatrics
Keywords-MotsClés: BEST PRACTICES; GROUNDED THEORY/ETHNOGRAPHY; HEALTH CARE PROFESSIONAL/PARENT INTERACTION; INFANTS/CHILDREN WITH COMPLEX; LIFE-THREATENING CONDITIONS
Abstract-Résumé: When a child is seriously ill or dying, family relationships and exchanges with health care professionals (HCPs) - nurses, physicians, and social workers - clearly determine parents' perceptions of care and its outcomes. When relationships are not good or interactions do not go well, parents carry memories of unnecessary additional suffering. When relationships are good and interactions "human", parents carry memories that are healing. Much is written about relationships and interactions gone wrong but little is written about best practices for HCPs despite an emphasis in recent years on communication skills in their professional education. We lack understanding of what makes it possible for some, but not all, HCPs to employ best practices that include not only technical expertise but generous sharing of their full humanity.   The purpose of this study is to analyze best practices of interactions between pediatric HCPs and the parents of children with complex, chronic, and life-threatening conditions (CCCs). Using a qualitative approach, a total of 60-80 parents in 3 settings (Pediatric Oncology, Neonatal Intensive Care, and a free-standing children's hospice) will be observed in interaction with HCPs during their child's hospitalization. Observations will be followed by conversations with HCPs and parents regarding their initial responses to interactions, and then later in-depth interviews about the intent, impact, and meaning of the interactions and the factors that influence them. Findings will delineate best practices, specific factors that facilitate best practices, how interactions change over a hospitalization or hospice stay, and how they compare across clinical settings and among HCPs. Key dimensions of best practices in HCP/parent interactions will be identified for future studies aimed at incorporating best practices into the care of children with CCCs and enhancing the well-being of parents facing one of life's greatest challenges.

TitreApplicationTitle: The potential of new MRI measurements to increase accuracy and cost-effectiveness in osteoarthritis research and management: analysis of longitudinal data from the Osteoarthritis Initiative
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIP; IMAGING; KNEE; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; OSTEOARTHRITIS; OUTCOME MEASUREMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common joint disorder worldwide and disability attributable to knee OA is equal to that of cardiovascular disease and greater than any other medical condition in older adults. The prevalence of knee OA is projected to double by 2020, due in part to increases in obesity and longevity. X-ray diagnosed OA is the most widely used clinical and research measure but it is not strongly associated with knee pain and doesn't show early OA - a critical period for treatment to prevent disability. Conversely MRI is related to knee pain and is able to show early disease and progression but MRI is expensive due to the time to read and interpret images, and is largely subjective. These factors have resulted in small research samples (due to expense) with limited statistical power to show important changes, and a sometimes confusing array of information for physicians.  New MRI software has been developed and pilot-tested that provides readings that are semi-automated and objective (quantitative), leading to faster, cheaper, and more accurate diagnosis. However they have not been validated in large datasets - a necessary step before widespread research and clinical use.  This research will compare the new MRI measures to conventional MRI measures, testing them for the ability to correlate with a patient's pain and function, identify disease progression, and reduce reading times.   Significance: This work will immediately benefit clinical researchers in terms of improved diagnosis at lower costs leading to larger, more powerful studies to assess patient populations with knee OA. This will strengthen disease prevention efforts and lead to earlier clinical interventions to prevent disability. It will benefit treating physicians through development of a single diagnostic score for knee OA (similar to the single bone density score for osteoporosis) leading to earlier and more efficacious treatment.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the physiological roles of host-cell secretory microRNAs in influenza A virus biology
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI HIV/HCV; ANTIVIRAL DRUGS; BIOINFORMATICS; CELL BIOLOGY; DEEP SEQUENCING; INFLUENZA A H1N1; NOVEL BIOMARKERS; RT-PCR; SECRETORY MICRORNA EXOSOMES
Abstract-Résumé: Recently, the breakout of the pandemic infection swine flu (infA/H1N1, 2009), as well as the deadly avian flu (infA/H5-like, 2007), have had serious impacts on the general public. It is crucial to increase our speed and accuracy in identifying these viral infections in order to promote effective public health services, as well as to aid in the discovery of the necessary antiviral drugs needed to stop these infections. Due to the growing viral infection and resistance problems we face globally, it has become an urgent health need to search for an alternative infA virus identification method to combat both concerns.  MicroRNA (miRNA) is a recently discovered, small-sized bio-molecule that appears to be involved in the life cycle/pathogenesis of infA virus and host-virus interactions. Many studies suggest that secretory miRNAs circulate freely in human body fluids. Dr. Jean's team has recently discovered that secretory miRNA profiles are significantly changed upon infA infection (infA/H1N1 and deadly infA/H5-like viruses) in human cells. (Loveday, E.K. et al. 29th Annual Meeting, ASV. 2010.). This research demonstrates for the first time the complex and strain-specific regulation of miRNAs in response to infA infections.  Based on this information, we propose that miRNA profile changes of infA-infected cells can trigger miRNA profile changes of neighbouring cells via exosomes (membrane-like vehicles that transport miRNAs intercellularly) that contain modified miRNA cargo. We propose that this unique intercellular communication event plays a novel and important role in complex infA virus biology and pathogenesis.  This proposed study will help us better understand the fundamental biology of how secretory miRNAs function and are regulated in pandemic H1N1 infA pathogenesis.  This will, in turn, help provide alternative ways to design antiviral programs to combat the problems of increasing infA infections and conventional drug-resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Post-doctoral training in meta-analysis and clinical trials methodology related to fructose, carbohydrate quality, and risk of chronic disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; BLOOD GLUCOSE; CARBOYHDRATES; CHOLESTEROL; CLINICAL TRIALS; DIABETES; FRUCTOSE; META-ANALYSIS; OBESITY; TRIGLYCERIDES
Abstract-Résumé: Fructose is a natural sugar found in fruits and vegetables and added to processed foods and soft drinks mainly as high-fructose corn syrup. The metabolic impact of fructose remains controversial made more so by frequent and often conflicting scientific and media reports. The Canadian Diabetes Association, the American Heart Association, and the World Health Organization discourage high intakes of fructose because high amounts of fructose are thought to increase certain blood fats and cholesterol, which increase the risk of heart disease. However, these concerns are not well-supported by human studies. There are therefore two arms to this project.  The first arm studies the effects of fructose on blood fats, cholesterol, and sugars and body weight by carrying out a systematic review and synthesis of the data taken from all available clinical studies in humans.  This technique, called "meta-analysis", allows all of the available data to be pooled together and re-examined to see if the effect of fructose is the same in all forms and in all people. The findings generated by this proposed will drive the second arm of this project, which will be a series of dietary intervention studies exploring the effects of fruits, vegetables, and whole grain foods (i.e. carbohydrate sources of different quality) on risk factors for heart disease and diabetes. The meta-analyses will help us decide which foods we will test in the clinical trials. This work will help improve the health of Canadians by updating nutrition guidelines for the general public, as well as those with, or at risk of, diabetes and heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translocation and functional specificity of RSK isoforms in cell cycle progression and proliferation
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; CELL PROLIFERATION; CELL SIGNALING AND CANCER; KINASE; PHOSPHORYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cells in the human body can be stimulated by various molecules from the environment, diet, or foreign particles resulting in the activation of proteins which can lead to cell proliferation and survival, resulting in cancer. The requirement for cell growth and proliferation in non-cancerous cells is well understood, however little is known regarding the function of proteins that contribute to cancer cell progression. Current evidence suggest RSK plays a role or is in a pathway that leads to cell cycle progression, proliferation, and transformation, all of which can lead to cancer. In this proposal we have focused our attention to RSK and its family members, which are over expressed in breast and prostate cancer. An important goal of this proposal is to address the functional specificities of RSK and its family members particularly with regards to cell cycle progression. Understanding RSK will allow for the better understanding of caner and discoveries made from this proposal can be used in developing new drug therapies. Therefore, I propose i) to characterize the mechanisms by which RSK moves into the nucleus, ii) to characterize the other RSK family member specificities in response to stimuli, and iii) to determine the role of all RSK family members in cell cycle progression and proliferation

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of BAP1 in Tumorigenesis and Metastasis in Uveal and Cutaneous Melanoma
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER RESEARCH; DEUBIQUITINATING ENZYMES; GENETICALLY ENGINEERED MOUSE MODELS; MELANOMA; METASTASIS; POLYCOMB GROUP PROTEIN; STEM CELL FATE; THERAPEUTIC TARGETS; TUMOR SUPPRESSORS; UVEAL MELANOMA
Abstract-Résumé: The World Health Organization estimates that 2-3 million non-melanoma and 132,000 melanoma skin cancers are diagnosed worldwide each year. Skin cancer is the most common cancer in Canada. In 2009, melanoma constituted only 6% of reported skin cancers cases, but was responsible for 78% of skin cancer-related deaths, according to the Canadian Cancer Society. With early detection, surgical excision is curative for patients diagnosed with cutaneous melanoma. However, patients with metastatic melanoma in which tumor cells spread to distal sites in the skin, lymph nodes and other organs, have a median survival of 6-9 months. Furthermore, uveal melanoma is the most common malignancy of the eye, and accounts for 5% of all melanoma cases. Approximately 50% of these patients succumb to metastasic disease. Recently, a study demonstrated that over 80% of patients with metastatic uveal melanoma have mutations in the BAP1 gene. During my Fellowship, I will work to identify how mutations in BAP1 lead to spreading of uveal tumor cells to distal organs in the body and determine whether this similarly occurs in cutaneous melanoma. I will also develop a preclinical mouse model of uveal and cutaneous melanoma by recapitulating the cancer-associated mutations in the BAP1 gene in the mouse. By understanding how BAP1 mutations lead to melanoma metastasis we will identify novel therapeutic avenues to limit metastasic spread of cancer cells. These therapies will be tested in our pre-clinical mouse model with the goal of translating our discoveries into improved detection and treatment for Canadian patients suffering from this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of oxidative damage by catalytic guanine quadruplexes
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; BIOCHEMISTRY; CONFORMATION; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; GRAM-POSITIVE; MECHANISM; MRNA; REGULATION; RNA; STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Many organisms modulate their response to environmental and metabolic cues with "riboswitches" which are regions of structured RNA that can sense signals from the environment. The signals, and how they bind to the riboswitch affect the folding of the RNA to alter downstream protein synthesis. In turn, altered protein synthesis changes fundamental growth properties of the cell or organism. These controls are essential to growth and adaptation, but are only beginning to be understood. Due to their abundance in bacterial pathogens and their essential and specific nature, riboswitches are prime targets for drug development. This work seeks to characterize structures of RNA in both free and signal-bound forms to determine the mechanism of signal binding, structural change and output. This work will provide important insight into metabolic regulation and sensing in biological systems. Furthermore, understanding these mechanisms will enable targeted development of therapeutics, including specific antimicrobial agents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Compensatory mechanisms of attention and memory in healthy aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BRAIN CONNECTIVITY; COGNITION; EYE MOVEMENT PARADIGMS; FMRI; VISUAL ATTENTION; VISUAL WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is quickly becoming a fundamental healthcare issue in Canada. Even as part of the healthy aging process, there is a general decline in cognitive abilities like attention and memory. What is not well understood, however, is how cognitive decline is related to the changes that occur in the aging brain. Cognition is thought to be the result of the interaction between a large number of different but interconnected regions of the brain - some are responsible for basic sensory processing, while other areas mediate those regions. It has been suggested that age-related cognitive decline might actually be attributed, in part, to changes that occur in sensory processing areas, and previous research has suggested that the other interconnected regions of the brain - those that mediate sensory processing for cognition - actually act to compensate for this loss. It is important, then, to more carefully examine these changes across multiple brain regions and to study how changes in the interactions between different regions of the brain lead to changes in cognitive abilities as part of the aging process. My research will therefore focus on the relationship between changes in different brain regions and cognitive function by comparing the cognitive performance of younger and older adults while simultaneously measuring the interactions between different brain areas. By combining complex behavioural measures with sophisticated neuroimaging techniques, I will be able to investigate the role of attention and memory in compensating for changes in regions of the brain which are responsible for basic sensory processing. With the ever-increasing prevalence of age-related cognitive decline and dementia, this research will have implications for fostering a better understanding of how changes in the aging brain affect cognition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Central Regulation of Autonomic Cardiovascular Function in Human Heart Failure and Obstructive Sleep Apnea
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASULAR FUNCTION; CEREBRAL CORTEX; CONTINUOUS POSITIVE AIRWAY PRESSURE; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; HEART FAILURE; HUMAN; MICRONEUROGRAPHY; MUELLER MANOEUVER; OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA; SYMPATHETIC NERVE ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: More than 5 million North Americans are affected by heart failure (HF). Mortality rates remain high (up to 33% per year) and the prevalence of the disease is increasing. Approximately 33% of HF patients suffer from concurrent obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Both HF and OSA are characterized by high sympathetic nerve activity (SNA), which contributes to mortality. We have shown that HF patients with OSA have higher resting SNA levels than patients without OSA. Furthermore, the treatment of OSA with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) can reduce this elevated SNA outflow. SNA generation occurs in the brainstem but is regulated by higher order cortical regions. Human and animal HF studies have highlighted the potentially important role of the brain in the control of SNA. However, the specific cortical regions involved have yet to be determined; this can be achieved using functional MRI (fMRI). fMRI has already been utilized to identify cortical regions involved in the suppression of SNA in healthy subjects. Specifically, the insula, anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortices have been implicated in SNA regulation. The goals of the current study are to determine whether activity within these cortical structures is altered in HF and OSA, and to ascertain if OSA treatment with CPAP can help to restore healthy cortical regulation of SNA. Our working hypotheses are that: a) resting cortical activity will be higher in healthy subjects versus HF and HF + OSA, and b) following CPAP, resting cortical activity within these specific inhibitory SNA regions will increase in HF + OSA patients. The relationship between changes in SNA, brain and cardiovascular function will be assessed at rest and during tests designed to elicit an acute increase in SNA by mimicking sleep apnea. This project will mark the first attempt to determine the neuroanatomical link between HF, OSA, and altered SNA and may help identify targets within the brain for future therapeutic interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Robotics and Virtual Environments for Hospital and Home-based Rehabilitation Post Stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE; HAPTICS; MOBILITY; REHABILITATION; ROBOTICS; STROKE; TECHNOLOGY ACCEPTANCE; UPPER LIMB; USABILITY; VIRTUAL REALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the leading cause of disability in Canadian adults. The loss of arm movement control, affecting completion of daily activities, is common after stroke. Research shows that intense, repetitive therapy for the affected arm and retraining in everyday activities greatly improve recovery. But rehabilitation with therapists requires a lot of time. Services are not always available in hospitals, and therapy may stop when patients leave the hospital. Ways to improve treatment are being studied. Robot-assisted therapy and virtual reality technology to guide patients through exercise activities have potential to improve outcomes. These devices can also have artificial intelligence, adapting treatment to patient progress. Patients can have more therapy, doing treatment programs planned by therapists without the need for a therapist to be there all the time. Therapists can treat more patients in hospital and at home. Despite benefits, this technology is not often used. Few devices are designed with input from patients and therapists, few are available or they are too expensive, and therapists may not be clear on how to best use these devices in therapy. To address these problems, a prototype intelligent robotic and virtual reality-based system for arm therapy has been developed along with a commercial partner. The design includes the needs of patients and therapists, and is affordable and portable for hospital or home use. In this proposal the usability of the system will be tested with patients and therapists to see if it is acceptable, is easy to use, and improves patient mobility and function. Also, therapists will help to identify training needs and how they can best include the system into current therapy. Findings from this study will be used to improve the system and plan a larger clinical study. If shown to be acceptable, effective and sufficiently low in cost this technology can greatly improve care for those affected by stroke and reduce health care costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Arsenic on DNA Damage and Repair
Keywords-MotsClés: ARSENIC; CANCER; CARCINOGENESIS; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR; ENVIRONMENTAL INFLUENCE ON HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Arsenic is naturally present in the environment. Long known as an acute poison, arsenic has come to be recognized in recent years as one of the most important environmental agents in causing cancers. The primary sites of human cancer associated with arsenic exposure are skin, bladder and lung, but the list may also include kidney and liver. Arsenic in drinking water, for example, currently affects more than 100 million people around the world. However, how arsenic causes various cancers is not understood. The primary objective of this study is to gain a mechanistic understanding of how arsenic causes cancer. Specifically, this study will investigate how arsenic interacts with another cancer-causing chemical and contributes to cancers.   The rationale of this study is that arsenic itself may not react with DNA but it may interfere with cellular repair of DNA damage caused by other agents. Supporting evidence can be found from synergistic interactions between arsenic exposure and cigarette smoking in the induction of lung cancer. One of cancer-causing compounds in cigarette smoking is benzo[a]pyrene (BaP), which is the model we chose. The study consists of three main parts. The first examines whether arsenic affects the formation of DNA damage caused by BaP. The second investigates whether arsenic interferes with the repair of DNA damage that is caused by BaP. The third examines what specific process of the cellular repair is altered by arsenic. An important feature of this study is the use of newly developed ultrasensitive assays for DNA damage and arsenic. It enables the study to be conducted at very low levels of arsenic and BaP relevant to day to day exposure.   The study will provide mechanistic insight for improved understanding of arsenic carcinogenic effects. By understanding causal effect of arsenic, regulatory agencies would be able to develop scientifically sound guidelines and measures to prevent and reduce cancers, particularly induced by arsenic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Collagen VI related myopathies: Defining, exploring and advancing targets for molecular treatments
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CONGENITAL MUSCULAR DYSTROPHIES; GENETICS; MOLECULAR TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Congenital muscular dystrophies (CMDs) are disorders of muscle that present with significant weakness at birth or in early infancy. CMDs as a group are an important yet under-recognized cause of early childhood neuromuscular morbidity. There are currently no causally effective treatments for these disorders. The most common subgroup of CMDs comprise the disorders caused by mutations in the three genes coding for collagen type VI, one of the two major microfibrillar components of the extracellular matrix surrounding the muscle tissue. Dominant mutations (meaning that one affected gene copy is able to cause disease) are the predominant mutation mechanism in collagen VI related muscle disease and the severity of these dominant mutations results from their ability to negatively interfere with any normal collagen VI formed (referred to as a dominant negative effect). This situation poses formidable challenges to the development of molecular treatments, as simple gene replacement approaches will not work because of the continued presence of the offending mutant transcript. With this project we will develop two basic strategies to define treatment options for this difficult situation. One approach is to carefully define why the lack of normal collagen VI is detrimental to the muscle cells in an effort to find molecular targets at which drug therapies could be directed in order to increase the resistance of muscle cells to the collagen VI deficiency. The other more causative approach to the dominant negative mutations in collagen VI that we will pursue is to take down the mutant gene product that is interfering with normal collagen VI production, using a molecular strategy called RNA interference technology. This strategy has the potential of substantially improving the amount of functional collagen VI available. Such targets could eventually also be useful for other muscle disorders in which similar mechanisms play a role.

TitreApplicationTitle: Matricellular Protein Biomimetic Scaffolds to Enhance Skin Regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOENGINEERING; CELL DIFFERENTIATION; CHRONIC SKIN WOUNDS; DERMAL FIBROBLASTS; EPITHELIUM; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX SYNTHESIS; GRANULATION TISSUE; MATRICELLULAR PROTEINS; NANOFIBROUS SCAFFOLDS; TISSUE REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: In normal individuals, most skin wounds close within a few days. However, in patients with lowered immunity, diabetes, vascular problems as well as people who are bed-ridden, skin wounds can stay open leading to development of a "chronic" or non-healing wound. Such wounds commonly cause tremendous psychological and physical suffering for the patient, and often result in limb amputation and even death. Despite extensive research, reproducible treatments for non-healing dermal wounds remain elusive. Chronic wounds are characterized by a failure of cells to move into the damaged area and repair the skin. Skin is composed of many different protein types, which change as skin matures or when it injured. Proteins such as collagen provide skin with structural support, but another type known as matricellular proteins provide cells in the tissue with instructions on how to repair the tissue. These proteins are not normally present, but are upregulated after injury. These proteins are produced in the wound bed and form a scaffold that cells attach to and move on. However, our analysis of chronic wounds has found that many of these matricellular proteins are missing and no scaffold is formed in the wound and it is unable to repair. We hypothesize that by adding matricellular proteins into chronic wounds, cells can be reactivated to enter the wound and close it. We have developed nanofibrous scaffolds that can be thought of as a "highway" on which the cells can crawl into the wound. These fibres are the same size as the ones normally present in the wound and contain the necessary instructional information for wound closure. To test our hypothesis, we will use both cell culture and animal models. This proposal could provide evidence that delivery of matricellular proteins could stimulate repair of chronic wounds.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vaccines that Replicate Neutralization-Competent Structures within the Membrane Proximal External Region of HIV-1 gp41.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL STUDIES; HIV-1 GP41; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNOGENICITY; LIPOSOMES; NEUTRALIZATION-COMPETENT STRUCTURE; NEUTRALIZING ANTIBODIES; PSEUDOVIRAL ASSAYS; VACCINES
Abstract-Résumé: The membrane proximal external region of HIV gp41 (MPER) is a prime target of antibody (Ab)-mediated HIV neutralization; it contains sites where 3 (soon to be 4) broadly neutralizing (bNt) monoclonal (M) Abs bind (2F5, 4E10, Z13, and soon, m66.6), making it an obvious target for an AIDS vaccine. We hypothesize that the failure of previous MPER-based immunogens to elicit bNt MAbs reflects their inability to faithfully mimic the neutralization competent structure (NCS) of the MPER. Our preliminary work has shown that the gp41 transmembrane domain (TM), located adjacent to the MPER, is required for the full exposure of the MPER in the context of the cell surface, since its replacement with the TM from another membrane protein decreased binding by bNt MAb 4E10. Yet repeated immunization of rabbits with a DNA vaccine expressing the gp41 MPER+TM elicited low-titer Abs that cross-reacted weakly with the MPER and did not neutralize virus. Here, we propose to optimize the MPER DNA vaccine and produce protein-boost immunogens that will mimic the NCS.  We will design liposome-based immunogens that present the gp41 MPER+TM in high copy number in lipid bilayers, so as to mimic the NCS of the MPER without added proteins that might distract the Ab response. DNA and liposome immunogens will be produced that have optimized the: (i) MPER, (ii) TM, and (iii) composition of the lipid environment, based on relative binding affinity by bNt MAbs, the absence of binding by non-Nt mutants of the bNt MAbs, and their behavior in a novel membrane leakage assay. Optimized DNA and liposome vaccine candidates will be tested separately in rabbits for their ability to elicit MPER-binding and Nt Abs, then be tested in a combined, DNA-prime protein-boost strategy with the goal of maximizing MPER-specific Ab titers, Nt potency and Nt breadth. These improvements will advance our molecular model of the MPER NCS, and should support further advances in AIDS vaccine design.

TitreApplicationTitle: Efficacy of a web-based seamless discharge communication tool: A randomized controlled trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE EVENTS; COMMUNICATION; COMPUTER-BASED TOOLS; CONTINUITY OF CARE; HOSPITAL DISCHARGE; READMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: When patients are discharged from hospital, there is a crucial need for effective communication of clinical information from physicians and nurses who have cared for the patient in hospital to the health care providers who will assume care in the community. Unfortunately, research has shown that communication at time of patient discharge is typically not adequate and in need of improvement. This study will assess the potential benefits associated with a computer-based discharge communication tool being implemented in Alberta hospitals. The results of this study have potential to inform best practices for discharge communication in all jurisdictions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the Role of PTCHD1 in Autism and Intellectual Disability
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER; COPY NUMBER VARIATION; DISEASE GENE IDENTIFICATION; MENTAL RETARDATION; MOUSE MODEL; MUTATION SCREENING; PROTEIN FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: We recently identified PTCHD1 as a gene involved in autism (Noor et al, 2010). However, to date, little is known about this gene, or its encoded protein. We have already learned through comparison with other proteins that it is similar to receptor proteins that recognize a class of signalling proteins called "Hedgehog", which are very important in neural development. Our preliminary studies show that PTCHD1 can function in a similar way to these "Hedgehog" receptor proteins, however there may be subtle differences between this and the known "Hedgehog" receptor proteins in the way that they function, or there may be other more unique roles for PTCHD1 that have yet to be discovered. We propose here a series of experiments that will further validate PTCHD1's role in autism and intellectual disability, and provide some clues as to how it functions in humans' cells. Understanding the role of this gene may help elucidate a common biological pathway for autism (and intellectual disability), which may allow us to find ways to develop specific therapeutic strategies for autism or intellectual disability.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and Molecular Mechanisms Regulating Synapse Formation and Plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: MOUSE TRANSGENESIS; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; NEURONAL CELL CULTURE; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; SYNAPTOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: The formation of synaptic connections between neurons is a key event during development. Netrins are secreted proteins that function as extracellular cues to direct cell migration. Many types of axons, the processes that connect one neuron to another, require netrin-1 to extend and find their synaptic targets. An important part of the mechanism that allows cells to respond to netrin-1 is a receptor called DCC which is located at the leading edge of a migrating cell. Without netrin-1 or DCC, nervous system development is highly abnormal. We have found that netrin-1 and DCC are made by neurons in the mature brain. While these proteins are absolutely essential for normal development, their significance in the mature brain is not known. In support of the idea that they are important, recent studies have found that mutations in the human genes encoding netrin-1 and DCC are predictive of the age of onset and susceptibility to develop Parkinson's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.  Although this suggests an important role in degenerative diseases in the nervous system, how netrin-1 and DCC might be involved is not known. We have found that these proteins influence synapse formation between neurons in early neural development. Examining the mature brain, we have found that netrin-1 and DCC are located at synapses. Our studies indicate that ongoing expression of DCC regulates synapse structure, and is required for changes in synapse function thought to underlie learning and memory. Consistent with this, we have obtained behavioral evidence that DCC is required for certain forms of learning and memory. Our proposal aims to identify the mechanisms that underlie the contribution of netrin-1 and DCC to synapse formation during development, and their  function at synapses in the mature brain. Investigating this newly discovered role for netrin-1 and DCC will contribute to our understanding of the mechanisms that regulate learning, memory, and neurodegenerative disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development and design of  anti-HIV-1 specific microbicides utilizing the display properties of Caulobacter crescentus
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHARMACEUTICAL; CAULOBACTER; HIV-1; MICE; MICROBICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Transmission of HIV-1, the causative agent of AIDS, is rapidly spreading despite an immense worldwide research effort to counter it. As such, the virus is decimating the populations of children and young adults across Africa and large portions of Asia. In Africa distribution of condoms and ensuring compliance of their use is not a generally viable option.  The cost of pharmaceuticals and issues related to the distribution of any drug or vaccine is prohibitive.  Coupling in the long-standing difficulties in generating an efficacious vaccine, it is obvious that we do not have a solution for this growing pandemic.  Clearly there is a need for disease prevention strategies that are safe, inexpensive to produce and distribute and importantly: are acceptable in the social contexts present in Third World countries. By providing a simple-to-use preventative drug in the control of the female population, we hope to address many of the cultural situations that presently work against preventative strategies. This proposal concerns the development and design of a microbicide; a topically applied blocker of infection that would be used predominantly by women. In this proposal, we plan to take advantage of a harmless water bacterium that efficiently displays molecules on its surface. By displaying molecules that mimic the binding interactions of HIV, we will effectively interfere and block infection. The engineered bacterium can be produced and chemically stabilized at very low cost. An assortment of these bacteria displaying different analogues can easily be prepared that would likely have greater efficacy and broader target range.  A successful outcome of this research would lead to formulation of this reagent into a gel that could be distributed by minimally trained healthcare workers. Although low cost makes it especially appropriate for Third World use, a successful outcome would also result in an useful product for Canada and other first world countries.

TitreApplicationTitle: Energy-Subtraction Cardiac Angiography: A New Approach in X-Ray Imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGRAPHY; CARDIAC IMAGING; DIAGNOSTIC RADIOLOGY; X-RAY DETECTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The vast majority of all patients in Canada diagnosed with vascular disease undergo x-ray angiography to determine the extent of the disease.  Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is currently used to suppress background structures such as ribs and lung fields to provide a clear view of the arterial bed. However, it fails if the patient moves and cannot be used on the heart.  We are developing a method of "energy-subtraction angiography" that will not be affected by patient motion.  As such, it can be used to image the heart and other structures affected by respiratory, cardiac, involuntary swallowing, or other motions.  The method requires the fast acquisition of x-ray images at multiple energies.  It will be the first method capable of bringing the benefits of subtraction imaging to cardiac angiography.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Neonatal induction of cardiac transplant tolerance to T-dependent and independent antigens
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR IMAGING; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; HEART TRANSPLANTATION; IMMUNE REGULATION AND DEVELOPMENT; MHC; MOUSE MODEL; NANOTECHNOLOGY; NEONATE; T-INDEPENDENT ANTIGENS; TOLERANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Severe heart disease in infancy leads to significant disability or death; neonatal heart transplantation is effective treatment. To prevent rejection of a heart transplant, immunosuppressive drugs need to be administered for the patient's lifetime.  We are researching ways in which a heart transplant recipient may accept a transplanted heart without the need for life-long drug treatment. The acceptance of a transplant without the need for drug treatment is called transplantation tolerance. Transplant tolerance is a way that the immune system is taught to accept a transplant as 'self' while at the same time protecting from infection and disease. It was shown more than 50 years ago that the newborn immune system of laboratory mice was especially susceptible to the induction of tolerance to skin transplants. In our laboratory we study neonatal tolerance to heart transplants in mice, a powerful tool to ask questions that would be impossible to study in human infants. Our research group showed that this also occurs in humans.  In this research project we will use our newborn mouse model to study in detail the events leading to heart transplant acceptance. For instance, we will explore the earliest events that occur following neonatal treatment by using special microscopes and fluorescent dyes. We will track the fate and determine the types of cells that are involved in inducing tolerance.  We showed previously that tolerance also occurs in human infants but there is inadequate understanding of the mechanisms involved. Through this project, new knowledge will be generated which may allow expanded applications of tolerance in the clinical setting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Low-Glycemic Index Diet and Other Intervention Trials (RCTs) in Type 2 Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERIAL DAMAGE; DIETARY INTERVENTIONS; ECOPTIC FAT; GLYCEMIC INDEX; INTRAMYOCELLULAR FAT; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI); OBESITY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS; TYPE 2 DIABETES; VISCERAL FAT
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is associated with metabolic complications including insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome, which result in increased risk for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and certain cancers. Emerging evidence suggests that ectopic fat (fat that accumulates around the organs or in muscle) is more harmful than subcutaneous fat (fat that accumulates underneath the skin). Weight-loss trials to date have focused their attention on changing body weight or body mass index, with less attention given to reducing ectopic fat accumulation and chronic disease risk reduction. Low-glycemic index diets, which by design lower blood levels of glucose and insulin by slowing the rate of carbohydrate absorption and digestion, may be one effective strategy to prevent and treat ectopic fat accumulation and its related metabolic complications. The objective of the proposed training grant research is to determine whether lowering the glycemic index of the diet can reduce ectopic fat, and its association with glycemic control and macrovascular disease. Individuals with type 2 diabetes taking oral hypoglycemic medications will be randomized to receive advice to consume a low-glycemic index diet or a conventional high-fibre diet in a long-term randomized controlled trial.  Direct visualization of ectopic fat will be measured by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Other outcomes will include arterial damage measured by carotid ultrasound (CUS) and MRI, glycated hemoglobin and markers of inflammation. The findings generated by this proposed training grant will provide evidence of whether a dietary strategy to lower the glycemic index of the diet is effective at reducing ectopic fat in people with type 2 diabetes and its relation to arterial damage.

TitreApplicationTitle: RCT mentoring program: Physical activity interventions to improve "successful ageing" among vulnerable seniors
Keywords-MotsClés: AGEING; BUILT ENVIRONMENT; MOBILITY; OLDER ADULTS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: The 2006 Canadian Census reported that 1 in 7 Canadians is over the age of 65-a record. In January 2011, the first of the Baby Boomers (born between 1946 -1965) turned 65 years old. This generation, approximately 1/3rd of the population in 2006, will significantly contribute to the expected doubling of seniors over the next 25 years.  The Oxford dictionary defines mobile as "movable; not fixed; free or able to move or flow easily". Poor mobility is a common consequence of aging. It is estimated that among men and women aged 65 years and older, 20% will go on to have poor mobility over the following 4 years. Mobility has been linked to the idea of "successful ageing".  The built environment or "urban form" is broadly defined as all buildings, spaces, and products that are created or changed by people. The relationship between the built environment and health is a relatively new area. However, a few studies have shown that there is a positive relationship between the built environment and health (i.e. "better" built environment, "better" health).  Physical activity is an attractive way to increase the number of people who are ageing successfully, by improving their mobility. It can be relatively inexpensive, for example walking, and it is thought to improve not only mobility but also the health of the heart, muscles, brain and, improve quality of life. But, it is very hard to convince people who are not used to being physically active, for example vulnerable seniors, to do so. In fact, according to a 2011 report from Census Canada, almost 80% of Canadian seniors do not meet physical activity guidelines. Many studies to date have used complicated physical activity programs that may not translate well to the "real world" setting.   The purpose of this Mentoring Program is to develop a simple and sustainable physical activity intervention, while considering the role of the built environment, that will increase the number of people who are "ageing successfully".
