TitreApplicationTitle: Mobile Diabetes Education Teams in Primary Care
Keywords-MotsClés: COORDINATED AND INTEGRATED CARE; DIABETES CARE; DIABETES EDUCATION PROGRAMS; DIABETES SELF-MANAGEMENT EDUCATION; HEALTH SERVICES; IMPLEMENTATION AND EVALUATION; INTERPROFESSIONAL COLLABORATION; PATIENT CARE PROCESSESS; PRIMARY CARE PHYSICIANS; QUALITATIVE; QUANTITATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Due to the under-use of diabetes education programs in Canada, individuals with diabetes are not receiving the comprehensive care that they need in order to manage this chronic illness effectively. Most people with diabetes are receiving care solely from their primary care providers who have expressed a lack of time and knowledge to fully care for and support patients with diabetes. The objective of this research is to evaluate a redesign in how we deliver diabetes care and self-management education using a collaborative approach between primary care providers and diabetes education programs to better manage patients with diabetes. Our project will support primary care providers by offering a diabetes education team (one registered nurse and one registered dietitian) at various primary care sites to assist in the care and management of patients with diabetes. We plan to examine the effects of a Mobile Diabetes Education Team (MDET) on the quality of care patients receive from their primary care providers and patient clinical outcomes. We will analyze the implementation of MDETs, as well as team collaboration and functioning at each primary care site. MDETs will strengthen links between primary care providers and diabetes education programs within the community, increase patient access to diabetes self-management education and support, and potentially improve patient experience and clinical outcomes through enhanced diabetes care. If study results are promising, this model can direct how diabetes prevention, management and care are delivered, and can greatly reduce the burden of diabetes in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Analysis of a Eukaryotic Kinome
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENETIC NETWORKS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN KINASE; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a genetic disease caused by inappropriate, unrestrained cell growth and division.  The regulators of cell division are remarkably conserved, with the same players functioning to promote or inhibit these processes in simple one-celled organisms to human cells.  Dr. Andrews' group will make use of the powerful genetics and experimental accessibility of a simple model organism system - the budding yeast - to systematically explore a family of key cell cycle regulators called kinases.  Advances in genome-scale technologies, genome sequencing projects and astounding technological developments mean that model organism systems remain ensconced at the frontiers of biomedical research and will continue to produce fundamental new insights into cell division and cancer in the coming decade.  The overall goal of Dr. Andrews' research program is to set the stage for the development of new cancer therapies that manipulate the cell division cycle, through the development of a comprehensive 'road-map' describing cell division and cell polarity pathways in normal cells - this roadmap will provide the essential foundation for producing a view of how this map is redrawn in cancer cells.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; GASTRIC CANCER; IL-6; ILK; JWA; MELANOMA; METASTASIS; TISSUE MICROARRAY; TUMOR GROWTH; VEGF
Abstract-Résumé: Melanoma is a type of skin cancer resulting from uncontrolled proliferation of pigmented cells in the skin. The incidence of melanoma is increasing most rapidly in the Caucasian population among all malignancies except for lung cancer in women. Melanoma is associated with one of the highest mortality rates due to its rapid metastasis and patients with metastatic melanoma have a poor prognosis, with a median survival of only 6 to 10 months. Gastric cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. More than one-third of all gastric cancer cases occur in China. Gastric cancer traditionally has a poor prognosis with five year survival less than 5%. We recently found that the novel tumour suppressor JWA plays an important role in the spread of melanoma to other organs. Strikingly, depletion of JWA in both melanoma and gastric cancer cells enhanced the growth of endothelial (blood vessel) cells. In this proposal, we will further investigate how JWA regulates blood vessel formation, cancer progression and metastasis, and test if JWA can be used as a therapeutic target for melanoma and gastric cancer. This project will not only provide insights into the role of JWA in the progression of melanoma and gastric cancer, but may also lead to more effective treatment strategies for cancer patients.

Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory will continue to elucidate the 3-dimensional shapes of important human proteins related to health and disease, especially cancer.  By being able to visualize these proteins we will better explain how they regulate cellular development, growth and death. Knowledge of the shapes will also help to design drug-like molecules that can be used to investigate which of the thousands of human proteins will be most useful for the development of new drugs  a field called chemical biology.  Our research includes a unique partnership with the pharmaceutical companies that are helping to generate new drug-like molecules.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bioethics and Philosophy
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: The new research theme is Impact ethics: Making a difference. The overarching objective is to develop and promote ethical policy in health, science and biotechnology. To this end, the research will critically examine the limits of mainstream bioethics in pursuit of meaningful transformations in how bioethicists perceive, understand and respond to public policy challenges. The research will propose novel strategies for developing just and lasting policy contributions. These strategies will be tested in addressing ethical challenges of the day, such as research involving humans, womens health, public health, pandemic planning, novel technologies, access to health care, and so on.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proteases and Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: My research program is focused on protein-cleaving cathepsin proteases and their role in human diseases. Our laboratory is internationally leading in the characterization of cathepsins as critical contributors to major health problems of our society which includes costly diseases in terms of human suffering and economic burdens such as atherosclerosis, osteoporosis, arthritis, and lung fibrosis.  The proposed research will characterize the functions of these enzymes in these diseases, their mechanisms of action and explore novel approaches inhibit their destructive activities. The ultimate aim of our research is to understand the role of cathepsins in disease and health and to find more effective treatments for Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oncology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: As Canada Research Chair in Oncology, Dr. Chambers is an internationally recognized expert on cancer metastasis.  Metastasis  spread of cancer to new organs  causes most cancer deaths.  Dr. Chambers has developed new ways to image metastasis experimentally. She has identified dormant cancer cells that resist treatment and later form metastases.  She has shown that the protein osteopontin contributes to metastatic ability and is a biomarker for cancer progression in patients.  Since 2003, she has produced over 90 publications, many co-authored by her trainees, and work from her lab is highly cited by other scientists.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Medical Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The Chair investigates the relationships between infectious organisms and its human host. We  use the power of bioinformatics and new technologies to better understand the pathogens in order to develop diagnostic tools and find new drugs to alleviate their impact. The program is unique in that it encompasses the full spectrum of basic research to clinical applications to market products.  It tackles AIDS and Leishmaniasis, diseases with enormous human impact. The Chair also develops sophisticated molecular diagnostic tools for epidemiological studies and focuses on drug discovery for microbial and cancer related targets.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Reproduction, Development and Sexual Function
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: In early pregnancy, specialized maternal immune cells appear where the placenta attaches. One subset enlarges the mothers blood vessels to improve conceptus nutrition and may, with other subsets, effect unique gestational changes in maternal blood pressure. This research project addresses regulation of gestational blood pressure and post-partum immune memory effects through quantification of blood pressure-regulating molecules in circulating white cells from pregnant women and from their babys placental cord. Women with the common, emergency-onset hypertensive disease pre-eclampsia will be compared with matched normotensive controls at diagnosis and follow-up. Mouse models will validate the conclusions and explore potential lymphocyte-based anti-hypertensive approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chromatin Dynamics
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Our genetic material, DNA, is bound to proteins called histones which package DNA. DNA is loosely packed when genes are turned on and tightly packed when genes are kept off. Chemical changes to histones decide which parts of DNA are loosely or tightly packed. Diet, environmental toxins and oncogenes (cancer producing genes) impact on these chemical changes to histones and change the genes being turned on and off. This research will learn how chemical changes of histones are regulated and turn on and off genes in normal and cancer cells. This knowledge will find new ways to kill cancer cells.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Glycobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The molecular networks that shape the structure and function of our cells have evolved incrementally, and are therefore embedded with redundancies and highly interconnected strategies for survival. This provides us with robust responses to changing conditions, but cancer cells also use these design features to enhance their survival. Knowledge of these molecular networks will lead to new drug combinations that take into account redundancies and render tumour cells selectively susceptible. Dr. Dennis' research focuses on molecular interaction and regulatory circuits that control cell proliferation and metabolism to better understand cancer, and the processes of aging.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory Peptides
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Drucker studies the mechanisms of action of gastrointestinal peptides, hormones secreted from the lining of the gastrointestinal tract. These hormones act to facilitate the digestion, absorption, and assimilation of ingested nutrients. Understanding the synthesis, secretion and action of these hormones has enabled Dr. Drucker to develop new therapies for the treatment of gastrointestinal disorders, diabetes and obesity.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Reproductive Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Steroids influence key physiological events in reproduction and throughout the life cycle, and plasma proteins control the access of steroids to tissues.  Geoffrey Hammond has identified and characterized the main steroid-binding proteins and their genes in relation to reproduction and health in humans and other vertebrates.  His group uses crystal structure analysis, molecular biology and computational sciences tools, as well as transgenic mouse models and cell culture techniques, to determine steroid-binding protein function.  The knowledge gained is applied to the diagnosis and treatment of serious clinical conditions, and the emerging field of eco-toxicology.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Cancer Structural Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Cells use molecules and proteins as 'signals' to relay important information regarding cell division, differentiation and growth. When normal processes go awry, cells move towards uncontrolled growth and migrations--often times leading to human diseases such as cancer, neurological and heart disorders and infectious diseases. Dr. Ikuras lab investigates the 3D structures of important proteins involved in signal transmission as it pertains to human diseases. Research into protein structure and protein interactions will help design new therapeutics that enhance or stop biological process. These strategies can be developed to specifically target pathways promoting tumour progression, autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Genomics and Molecular Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Fisheries and aquaculture
Abstract-Résumé: Objectives of my research are to: 1) elucidate the role of mutation, duplications and deletions in regenerating genome stability after a whole genome duplication; 2) understand the role of gene duplication in the generation of increased species specialization and diversification as well as health, and disease; 3) explore new technologies, strategies, and computer analyses in genetic systems and relate them to biochemical and physiological functions.  Research will target salmonid re-diploidization, biodiversity, and functional complexity, with particular emphasis on the immune system and genes associated with temperature tolerance, sex determination, disease and health.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Gap Junctions and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Lairds studies are designed to examine the mechanisms underlying inherited human diseases and cancers in tissue-relevant models, in mutant mice and in patient samples. It is a requirement for normal function that most cells in the human body communicate directly with each other through special cell surface channels called gap junctions. In many diseases these channels are either not produced by the cells (i.e. cancer) or the proteins that make up these channels contain mutations that inhibit their normal function (i.e. skin diseases, development abnormalities).  It is anticipated that Dr. Lairds research will lead to much needed insights into these gap junction related diseases.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Chaire de Recherche du Canada en Génomique Comparative et Evolutive
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Other research on industrial production and technology
Abstract-Résumé: The projected research is at the intersection of genomics, bioinformatics and evolutionary biology, and addresses two fundamental issues: (i) inference of eukaryotic origins, with a focus on the mitochondrial contribution, including a survey of alpha-Proteobacteria that are closest to mitochondria. For this, genome data from primitive eukaryotes (jakobid and malawimonad flagellates) and selected bacteria will be analyzed; and (ii) determine if multicellularity in animals and fungi is based on a common set of functions and genes. This question will be investigated by comparative genomics including protist relatives of animals and fungi, and chytrid and zygomycete fungi that are slowly evolving.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Cellular Signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: The proliferation of cells is regulated by a complex network of biochemical events that ensure that each cell division step is performed correctly and in proper sequence. Accumulating evidence indicates that deregulation of the cell division machinery contributes to uncontrolled cell proliferation and genetic instability typical of tumor cells. The objective of our research program is to understand how key signal transduction mechanisms regulate cell division and explore their requirement for tumor formation and progression. On the long term, this knowledge may prove useful for the identification of novel mechanism-based drugs for the targeted treatment of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The ultimate goal of my research program is to improve human health and life expectancy by enhancing the function of the immune system. Progressive thymus atrophy affects all ageing subjects and can even impinge on younger subjects affected by several serious illnesses (cancer, AIDS etc). Thymic atrophy decreases immune function and increases the incidence of infection, cancer and autoimmune diseases. My first objective is therefore to develop a strategy to prevent or reverse thymic atrophy. Because the immune system has an unmatched ability to eradicate cancer stem cells, my second objective is to engineer vaccines for cancer prevention and treatment. My third objective is to develop new strategies to prevent immune rejection following transplantation.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroplasticity and Pain
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The principal goal of the Canada Research Chair in Neuroplasticity and Pain is to gain new knowledge about normal functioning - as well as dysfunction - of the central nervous system (CNS).  This knowledge will be used for the national development of novel therapeutic agents for CNS disorders.  Research is focused on cell-to-cell signalling, as proper communication between cells is essential for normal growth and development, and for the diversity and richness of the functions of the mature CNS.  Additionally, we have developed research based on our critically important novel discovery in glucose homeostasis and the pathobiology of diabetes.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Genetics of Normal and Cancer Stem Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Inability to induce hematopoietic stem cells self-renewal ex vivo remains a major clinical challenge that excludes thousands of patients each year from transplant therapy. Methods that would permit the expansion of these cells ex vivo would be highly beneficial for these patients, including those suffering from leukemia, one of the five most deadly cancers. Identification of genes involved in the regulation of self-renewal is crucial to develop novel targeted therapies. Using the latest technologies in genomics and bioinformatics, this Chair aimes at making important contributions in the field of functional genomics of normal and leukemic stem cells.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Neuroimmunology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The Canada Research Chair in Neuroimmunology has enabled my laboratory to generate key insights into how the immune system destroys the central nervous system (CNS) on the one hand, and, conversely, how aspects of inflammation are beneficial for regenerative CNS processes.  The Chair has facilitated the translation of basic science findings into clinical trials in multiple sclerosis (MS) and spinal cord injury.  The Chair is unique as it is pioneering the approach to enable repair of the injured CNS by using medications that can enhance immune reactions safely.  The chair has also graduated many trainees now working worldwide.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Proliferative retinopathies at the extremes of life
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The most common eye diseases that seriously affect vision occur at the extremes of life: namely retinopathy of prematurity in very young children, diabetic retinopathy in patients less than 70 years old, and macular degeneration in older subjects. Our laboratory has focused in finding solutions to these disorders of the retina (eye segment which detects light). We have identified mechanisms of disease and developed new drug candidates. We plan to pursue these activities by continuing to build a premier research team in vision science (a priority at Université de Montréal), and link with industrial partners to develop innovative therapeutic modalities.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Recherches physiopathologiques sur la mort cellulaire dans les interactions Hôtes/Pathogènes :Approches fondamentales et thérapeutiques.
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Dans le cadre des maladies infectieuses, la mort cellulaire programmée joue un rôle essentiel dans la persistance ou l'élimination des agents infectieux. Ainsi, des agents pathogènes comme le virus du Sida qui infecte chaque année plus de 4 millions de personnes ou la leishmanie entraînent des dérégulations de ces processus. Nos objectifs sont de préciser ces mécanismes dans le cadre des relations Hôtes/Pathogènes, et d'identifier de nouvelles cibles thérapeutiques. Basé sur mon expérience des modèles de Primate Non Humains, je me propose de développer ces modèles à lUniversité Laval permettant ainsi d'évaluer ces nouvelles approches thérapeutiques indispensables pour lHomme.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Pulmonary Pharmacology
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: Phosphodiesterase (PDE) 4 inhibitors are a new class of drugs being developed for the treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which is more commonly referred to as bronchitis and/or emphysema. Unlike steroids, which are not effective in COPD, the results of several clinical trials of PDE4 inhibitors have demonstrated clinical effectiveness. However, the mechanism of action of this novel class of drugs has not been investigated and, accordingly, is not understood. A primary objective of this research proposal is to understand how PDE4 inhibitors work in COPD such that their clinical effectiveness can be optimized for enhanced therapeutic benefit.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Bio-analytical Technology and Environmental Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Pollution and protection of the environment
Abstract-Résumé: Built on the analytical and environmental chemistry foundation, my research program links to environmental toxicology, public health, and disease diagnosis. Three interdisciplinary research themes include: investigating arsenic compounds and their health effects; monitoring genetic damage caused by environmental contaminants; and developing novel assays for proteins and potential disease markers. The new bioanalytical technology will enable trace-level, environmentally and clinically relevant exposure and outcome research. Studies of arsenic interaction with biological molecules will provide the mechanistic insight necessary to an improved understanding of arsenic health effect. By understanding the causal effect of arsenic, regulatory agencies would be able to develop scientifically sound guidelines and measures to prevent and reduce health problems, particularly those caused by arsenic.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: GeroScience
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: As the baby-boom generation approaches retirement, this demographic phenomenon will intensify the challenges that Canada and most of the developed world faces in supporting the health and social needs of the aging population. The overall aim of this program of research is to understand the dynamic process of normal aging, disease associated aging and adult development by integrating different disciplinary approaches ranging from biological to population sciences. This program of research will provide highly relevant information to help understand the underlying mechanisms of aging and disease and in turn help improve the health of the Canadians and people elsewhere.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Antibiotic Biology and Medicine
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Antibiotic resistance continues to be a critical health problem worldwide with an increasing number of fully resistant bacterial superbugs such as Staphlococcal aureus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A multi-disciplinary structural biology approach including macromolecular x-ray crystallography, NMR, electron microscopy, mass spectroscopy and enzymology will be used to study the structure and function of proteins that are essential to antibiotic resistance by these superbugs and their ability to infect humans. The high resolution molecular information gleaned from these studies will be used as a foundation for the structure-based design and screening of novel antibiotics to fight bacterial infection in the clinic and community.  Many of these bacterial protein targets are membrane associated, a highly challenging frontier of structural biology for which the applicant  has had considerable experience and success.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Interdisciplinary Microbiome Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The surfaces of the human body, including the digestive and upper respiratory tracts are colonized and protected by trillions of bacteria that exist in highly organized ecosystems. Disturbances of these ecosystems are linked to a vulnerability to infections and susceptibility to a variety of diseases. The nominee has developed innovative technologies for identifying and culturing bacteria at these surfaces and has identified mechanisms that underlie their ability to communicate within these complex ecosystems. This knowledge will be used in the prevention and treatment of a variety of diseases including chronic respiratory disorder, obesity and diabetes.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Translational Stroke Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Each year, stroke and traumatic brain injuries affect  about 50,000 and 35,000 Canadians respectively, and about 14,000 stroke and 5,200 trauma victims will die. These and other disorders of major health significance including chronic pain are believed to share similar fundamental processes. Stroke in particular has proven frustrating since new treatments promising in animal models are unsuccessful when translated to clinical trials.  As a neurosurgeon-scientist my translational stroke research program examines the molecular mechanisms underlying these conditions and tests new preclinical models of stroke damage optimized for treatment success in humans.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention d'équipes émergentes en santé maternelle : d'avant la conception jusqu'au nid vide
TitreApplicationTitle: Interdisciplinary HIV Pregnancy Research Group: Care and Research to Optimize HIV-positive Women's Health during Preconception, Pregnancy and Motherhood.
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SYSTEMS; HIV; MATERNAL HEALTH; MOTHERHOOD; POLICY DEVELOPMENT; POSTPARTUM; PRECONCEPTION; PREGNANCY; TEAM BUILDING; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Anti-HIV drug therapy has been very successful at reducing the rate of death for those living with HIV; as well as reducing the rate of vertical HIV transmission from mother to child. These successes, combined with the fact that many HIV-positive people in Canada are of childbearing age, have led many HIV-positive women and HIV-negative female partners of HIV-positive men to become pregnant. This has been confirmed by an increase in the number of HIV-positive women having children. Also the HIV-positive community has said that pregnancy and pregnancy planning are important issues to them. Although prevention of vertical transmission is an important topic, there are several others that are crucial when considering pregnancy and pregnancy planning in the context of HIV. These include the prevention of HIV transmission between sex partners (known as horizontal transmission), healthy pre-conception counselling and managing infertility issues.  This is area that has been under-researched and has tremendous opportunity. Also, because there are an increasing number of pregnancies amongst HIV-positive women, there are now tremendous opportunities for research in all the maternal health stages and HIV including the pregnancy, labour and delivery and the postpartum/motherhood phases. The main goal of this Emerging Team Grant in Maternal Health for women infected with and affected by HIV is to form an Ontario program of research, teaching, mentoring and knowledge translation regarding the care of these women during the three phases of maternal health: 1) before pregnancy, 2) during pregnancy, and 3) postpartum, during motherhood. This program will help to create partnerships among researchers, clinicians, policy makers and community members and help to teach them about how our study findings may impact maternal health in the context of HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Are there Neural Differences of the Self in Eastern and Western Depression? A Cross-Cultural Imaging Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGING; DEPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a global phenomenon and occurs in east and west in increasing frequency. Despite the frequent occurrence there are nevertheless cultural differences in how depressive symptoms are expressed. The present project aims to better understand these cultural differences by conducting an imaging investigation on depressed patients in both Canada and China on western and eastern depressive patients respectively. Thereby the neuronal correlates of resting state activity and during self-relevant stimuli shall be explored and compared between healthy and depressed subjects as well as between chinese and canadian participants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anti-Inflammatory Signaling Pathways of Fish Oil in Cardiovascular Health and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTOR (GPCR); INFLAMMATION; ISCHEMIA; KNOCKOUT/TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS; LOW-DOSE ASPIRIN; POLYUNSATURATED FATTY ACIDS; RESTENOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Fish oils contain special fatty products called omega3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). Studies dating back nearly 40 years demonstrated that Eskimos in Greenland who ate lots of these oils had very low risk for cardiovascular disease (CVD) like heart attacks and stroke. For many years researchers have tried to figure out why these omega3 PUFA are beneficial in our diets. Recently, a protein called GPR120 was discovered to be responsible for some of the actions of these fatty molecules. We are investigating how omega3 PUFA combined with a common drug aspirin will reduce CVD through GPR120 and special anti-inflammatory actions of compounds known as resolvins. Dr. Funk at Queen's University and Dr. Yu at the Institute for Nutritional Sciences, Shanghai Institutes of Biological Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences are combining their expertise and past experience of working together to answer important questions to protect Canadians and Chinese people from the devastating consequences of heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nuclear and cytoplasmic accumulation of Intracellular domain fragment of epithelial cell adhesion molecule (Ep-ICD) is a marker for epithelial cancers and potential target for therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; EPCAM; EPITHELIAL CANCER; HEAD AND NECK CANCER; PROSTATE CANCER; THYROID CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Epithelial cancers constitute a large proportion of human malignancies and are a major global health burden. The term "epithelium" refers to cells that line hollow organs and glands and those that make up the outer surface of the body. Epithelial cancer markers and agents that interact with these markers may be used in clinical practice for disease diagnosis, assessment of cancer progression (prognosis) and monitor effectiveness of treatment. Prognostic markers are clinical measures that reflect the natural history of a disease and can be used to assess the risk of relapse of disease after primary treatment. These markers guide treatment strategies and patient counseling. Currently, there is no established universal molecular marker for diagnosis or prognosis of epithelial cancers. Recently, we have reported a cellular tumor marker called intracellular domain fragment of epithelial cell adhesion molecule (Ep-ICD) in ten epithelial cancers. Here in we aim to investigate the relationship of this marker with response to treatment, disease outcome, and patient survival, to determine its applicability as a marker for disease aggressiveness in prostate, head and neck, breast, and thyroid cancers. Another goal is to develop this marker based tests for identifying these aggressive cancers in the clinics. The industrial partner, Kalgene, is providing the reagents needed to develop these tests. We will also design and test new treatment approaches using this protein for potential cancer treatment. This research will also create intellectual property for Canada and develop trained manpower for translational research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Travail du sexe, marginalisation et santé : approches de recherche visant l'équité en santé en contexte prostitutionnel béninois
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPORTEMENTS DE SANTE; CONTRACEPTION; ISSUES DE GROSSESSE; PREVENTION; SANTE REPRODUCTIVE; TRAVAILLEUSES DU SEXE; VIH; VIOLENCE ET STIGMATISATION; EQUITE EN SANTE; EVALUATION
Abstract-Résumé: Depuis 1992, des chercheurs de l'Universite Laval collaborent avec le Programme national de lutte contre le Sida (PNLS) du Benin a la mise en oeuvre d'interventions de prevention du VIH ciblant les travailleuses du sexe (TS) de ce pays et plus recemment, la composante masculine du milieu prostitutionnel (clients, partenaires reguliers des TS, personnel masculin des sites de travail du sexe). Durant la meme periode, des collaborations ont ete etablies entre des chercheurs de l'Universite Laval et de l'Universite d'Abomey-Calavi, principale universite du Benin, permettant la conduite de plusieurs recherches en matiere de prevention du VIH et des activites de renforcement de capacite de recherche des institutions beninoises. Au-dela du VIH, notre implication aupres des TS nous a permis de constater au fil des ans l'ampleur des problemes sociaux et de sante reproductive vecus par ces femmes. C'est dans ce contexte que nous proposons un programme de recherche dont l'objectif general vise une meilleure comprehension de la situation globale de la sante sexuelle et reproductive des TS du Benin afin de developer, implanter et evaluer des interventions de prevention du VIH et de promotion de la sante sexuelle et reproductive aupres de ces femmes. Nous nous interesserons aussi a l'influence des relations hommes-femmes dans le milieu prostitutionnel sur la violence et la discrimination subies par les TS et sur leur sante reproductive. Le programme de recherche sera mene par une equipe multidisciplinaire de chercheurs en epidemiologie, sante communautaire, sante reproductive, sociologie et prevention de l'Universite Laval, de l'UQAR, de l'Universite du Manitoba et de l'Universite d'Abomey-Calavi. Le PNLS sera partie prenante de nos recherches et utilisera les resultats pour ameliorer les interventions en place. Notre programme s'inscrit dans les domaines de recherche des voies d'equite en sante et des interventions en sante des populations cibles par le present programme.

TitreApplicationTitle: PATHS Equity for Children. A program of research into what works to reduce the gap for Manitoba's children
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; CHILDREN; DISPARITIES; GRADIENT; HEALTH EQUITY; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTI-LEVEL MODELING; POPULATION HEALTH INTERVENTION; PROGRAMMATIC RESEARCH; SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS
Abstract-Résumé: There is much interest in addressing the problem of health inequity. Health inequity is unfair and avoidable or remediable differences in health among social groups. Health equity suggests that all people can reach their full potential and should not be disadvantaged from attaining it due to race, ethnicity, religion, gender, age, social class, socioeconomic status, or other socially determined circumstance. Throughout Canada, policies and programs are developed to reduce health and social inequities. Our program of research will use the unique information-rich population-based Repository of administrative data housed at the Manitoba Centre for Health Policy, to study the impact of multiple programs and policies introduced over the past decade which could potentially impact health and social inequities of Manitoba's children. The Repository's 97 databases are anonymized, but linkable at the person-level and to family units and neighbourhoods, and contain information on health and social services and outcomes, including: births and deaths, use of physicians and hospitals, immunization programs, educational outcomes, early childhood intervention programs, and the use of child welfare, social assistance and public housing. Our focus is on childhood trajectories, including interventions that impact social and health outcomes from birth through to age 18. We will determine which programs, or combinations of programs, improved overall outcomes, but more importantly, which ones narrowed or widened the gap in inequity. Our research team includes partners from nine government ministries, non-governmental organizations, all the regional health authorities and the Healthy Child Manitoba initiative. By working with these decision makers throughout the research process we will ensure that we ask relevant questions, interpret the data in the correct context and can assist in having the research findings translate into action, through evidence-informed policies and programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preventing Severe Maternal Morbidity
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE RENAL FAILURE; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; MATERNAL HEALTH; MATERNAL MORBIDITY; OBSTETRIC SHOCK; POSTPARTUM HEMORRHAGE; PREGNANCY; PREGNANCY COMPLICATIONS; PUERPERAL SEPSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Issues related to severe illnesses among pregnant women and mothers in industrialized countries have received increasing emphasis in recent years for several reasons including the life threatening nature of such illness and the potential for subsequent disability. In addition, changes in maternal characteristics (e.g., increases in maternal age, and pre-pregnancy obesity) and in obstetric practice (e.g., increases in  cesarean delivery) mean that careful monitoring is required if threats to the health of women are to be identified and prevented.   The goal of this application is to create a research team that carries out detailed clinical and epidemiologic investigations of severe maternal illnesses in order to improve maternal health. Specific objectives  1. Bringing together a multi-disciplinary group of researchers who will work collaboratively on specific research projects related to severe maternal illnesses (such as severe maternal bleeding at delivery requiring blood transfusion, kidney failure, heart disease, stoke, puerperal sepsis and obstetric shock).  2. To facilitate the translation of knowledge related to severe maternal illnesses into national guidelines and supporting guideline implementation.  3. To build capacity for research into severe maternal illnesses in Canada by creating a collegial and intellectually stimulating research training environment for students.  The team proposes to carry out these research projects using 3 different methodologies including etiologic studies, studies of best clinical practices and clinical audits using medical records at 15 large perinatal hospitals in Canada.   The knowledge translation acitvities of the team will be carried out along with external partners such as the Public Health Agency of Canada and the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada. These activities are expected to contribute significantly to addressing the burden of illness among pregnant women in Canada and elsewhere.

TitreApplicationTitle: The neurorestorative potential of cholinergic activation in AD.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BASAL FOREBRAIN; NEUROGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: One of the key features of Alzheimer's disease pathology is the loss of brain cells in a group of nuclei called the basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei. The loss of these cells reduces the level of the neurotransmitter, acetylcholine, in the hippocampus resulting in memory impairment. Current drug therapies aim to increase the level of acetylcholine by preventing its natural breakdown. However, these drugs lose their effectiveness as more and more cells are lost. An alternative might be to simply replace the cells that are lost. In previous work, we were able to replace dopamine neurons lost in an animal model of Parkinson's disease by activating a specific dopamine receptor. Using a similar approach, we have been able to generate new cells in the basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei. Here, we propose to further characterize these cells to determine if they are cholinergic neurons. We also wish to determine whether this approach is capable of replacing lost cells in the basal forebrain nuclei and what impact this may have on memory function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting Health Equity by Addressing the Needs of Health Workers:  A Collaborative, International Research Program
Keywords-MotsClés: CAPACITY-BUILDING; CLUSTER RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS OF POP. HEALTH INTERVEN; ECONOMIC TOOLS; EQUITABLE ACCESS TO HIV AND TUBERCULOSIS CARE; GENDER SENSITIVE POLICIES AND PROGRAMS; GLOBAL HEALTH; HEALTH INFORMATION SYSTEMS; HEALTH WORKERS AS VULNERABLE POPULATION; INFECTION CONTROL AND OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH; WORKPLACE AND WORKFORCE HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Working conditions are an important determinant of health equity. Health workers globally  face increasingly difficult working conditions. This is particularly so the case in low and middle income countries, especially Africa, where work overload, inadequate supplies and the challenges of HIV and TB contribute to burnout, stress, and low morale. The World Health Organization, International Labour Organization, and the Joint agency created by the UN to tackle AIDS, have been increasingly concerned about the wellbeing of this (predominantly female) workforce. Gender-sensitive policy recommendations were advanced to strengthen occupational health and infection control programs, prevent discrimination, reduce stigma and improve access of health workers to the prevention, care and support they need. This program was designed to address research gaps identified in the guidelines and to expand knowledge on promoting health equity through improving working conditions generally and for health workers in particular.  With six interlinked studies, this program of research aims to improve understanding of how the various pathways to health stemming from global economic forces impact health equity within, and between, countries regarding working conditions for health workers; to implement and evaluate a complex multi-component public health intervention (based on the WHO-ILO-UNAIDS Guidelines); ascertain the determinants of successful training; evaluate state-of-the-art information technology for knowledge transfer; and produce economic evaluation and budgeting tools. This research program will be conducted by an interdisciplinary international team of experienced experts, with numerous trainees. While focusing on implementation of population health interventions in Africa, the research also draws data worldwide to study the implementation of a much-needed multi-component approach to an important determinant of health equity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Food systems and health equity in an era of globalization: Think, Eat and Grow Green Globally (TEG3)
Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH; FOOD SYSTEMS; HEALTH EQUITY; INDIGENOUS; INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGIES; NUTRITION; OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; PESTICIDE; SUSTAINABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: This program of research addresses the health effects of the global food system through five interconnected projects in Ecuador and Canada. It ranges from the effects of pesticide exposure on banana workers in Ecuador and grape pickers in British Columbia's Okanagan Valley, through healthy eating in schools in Vancouver and Quito, to changing livelihoods among indigenous communities in the Andes and in rural Canada. It is based on enabling people without a voice in how food is produced, marketed and consumed, in making decisions that will allow safer working conditions, healthier eating practices, and preservation of cultural practices based on environmental resources. By combining the results of existing knowledge on food systems and health with new knowledge generated in Ecuador and Canada, this program will move from knowledge to action using information and communication technologies like photography, teleconferencing and web-based meetings to connect the people who grow and eat food with each other, and with decision-makers in government and non-governmental organizations. Ultimately, this will result in policies and programs that will protect health in a coherent way that makes sense in both the North, and the South.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying policy interventions to reduce household food insecurity.
Keywords-MotsClés: BURDEN OF ILLNESS METHODOLOGY; FOOD INSECURITY; INTERNATIONAL COMPARISON; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; POLICY ANALYSIS; SECONDARY DATA ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Household food insecurity refers to the inadequate or insecure access to food due to financial constraints.  This problem, currently affecting about 8 percent of the Canadian population, poses serious threats to individuals' physical, social, and mental health.  Most responses to household food insecurity are community-based, including food banks, soup kitchens, and a variety of gardening, cooking, and food buying programs.  The limitations of these initiatives are widely recognized, but we lack the knowledge base to implement more effective responses.  To address this knowledge gap, we have brought together an international, interdisciplinary team of researchers, working in partnership with key federal departments and several national non-governmental organizations with an expressed commitment to the reduction of household food insecurity. Our program of research is designed to identify viable and effective policy interventions to reduce household food insecurity in Canada. Through analyses of available Canadian and US survey data, we will identify the conditions that give rise to problems of household food insecurity in our country, determine the impact of various policies and programs on this problem, and estimate the health care costs associated with household food insecurity currently. Our research will provide decision-makers working at the federal, provincial, and territorial levels of government with tangible options for action to reduce food insecurity.

Keywords-MotsClés: CO-INFECTIONS; COMORBIDITIES; HIV/AIDS; MENTORSHIP; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this RCT mentoring application is to develop the mentee, Dr. Darrell Tan, into an independent investigator and future leader in clinical trials in the field of HIV/AIDS, particularly in the area of co-infections and complications of aging.  To achieve this goal, the mentee and primary mentor, Dr. Sharon Walmsley, have planned mentorship activities that build on the mentee's research training and benefit from a unique research environment blending the strengths of two large academic hospitals at the University of Toronto, the University Health Network (UHN) and St. Michael's Hospital (SMH), with national and international clinical trial research networks.  Specific mentorship activities correspond to the three objectives of the CIHR mentoring program: developing skills in RCT conception, design and implementation.  The mentee will  participate in the activities of the CIHR Canadian HIV Trials Network (CTN), a partnership of clinical trial sites across Canada with extensive experience in HIV clinical trials; participate in a program of weekly learning sessions with specific objectives covering key issues in clinical trials; lead regular rounds on 'special topics in clinical trials' at the SMH Applied Health Research Centre; continue his role on the CTN scientific review committee; assume increasing responsibility for CTN-240, an ongoing CIHR-funded trial; initiate at least one new clinical trial based on results from the mentee's PhD studies; assist in a new clinical trials capacity-building program of the Kenya AIDS Vaccine Initiative; and build clinical trial capacity at the SMH HIV Clinic by initiating its participation in existing trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Low-Glycemic Index Diet and Other Intervention Trials (RCTs) in Type 2 Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERIAL DAMAGE; DIETARY INTERVENTIONS; ECOPTIC FAT; GLYCEMIC INDEX; INTRAMYOCELLULAR FAT; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI); OBESITY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS; TYPE 2 DIABETES; VISCERAL FAT
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is associated with metabolic complications including insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome, which result in increased risk for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and certain cancers. Emerging evidence suggests that ectopic fat (fat that accumulates around the organs or in muscle) is more harmful than subcutaneous fat (fat that accumulates underneath the skin). Weight-loss trials to date have focused their attention on changing body weight or body mass index, with less attention given to reducing ectopic fat accumulation and chronic disease risk reduction. Low-glycemic index diets, which by design lower blood levels of glucose and insulin by slowing the rate of carbohydrate absorption and digestion, may be one effective strategy to prevent and treat ectopic fat accumulation and its related metabolic complications. The objective of the proposed training grant research is to determine whether lowering the glycemic index of the diet can reduce ectopic fat, and its association with glycemic control and macrovascular disease. Individuals with type 2 diabetes taking oral hypoglycemic medications will be randomized to receive advice to consume a low-glycemic index diet or a conventional high-fibre diet in a long-term randomized controlled trial.  Direct visualization of ectopic fat will be measured by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Other outcomes will include arterial damage measured by carotid ultrasound (CUS) and MRI, glycated hemoglobin and markers of inflammation. The findings generated by this proposed training grant will provide evidence of whether a dietary strategy to lower the glycemic index of the diet is effective at reducing ectopic fat in people with type 2 diabetes and its relation to arterial damage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the Impact of Social Policies on Health Equity: How Policies Designed to Reduce Poverty and Gender Inequality Affect Morbidity and Mortality in Children and Women
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER INEQUALITY; GLOBAL HEALTH; HIV/AIDS AND TUBERCULOSIS; INFANT AND CHILD MORTALITY; MATERNAL MORTALITY; POPULATION AND PUBLIC HEALTH; POVERTY AND ECONOMIC INEQUALITY; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOCIAL POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: For over a century evidence has accumulated that demonstrates the dramatic impact that poverty, economic and gender inequality have on health and health equity. Compared with the magnitude of evidence of the problems created, though, far less is known about what to do about it. This research program will rigorously examine the effects on population health of differing social policy approaches taken around the world to address poverty, economic and gender inequity. In carrying out this work, researchers from North America, Europe, Africa, Latin America and Asia will focus on substantive areas which have been set as priorities by all 192 UN member states through the Millennium Development Goals: infant (under one year old) and child mortality(under 5 years old), maternal mortality, and HIV/AIDS and tuberculosis. Specifically, this research program will:  1) Examine how policies aimed at reducing poverty and gender inequality in high- and low-income countries impact major causes of illness and death in infants and children. 2) Examine how policies aimed at reducing poverty and gender inequality in high- and low-income countries impact major causes of illness and death in women under 50. 3) Examine how policies aimed at reducing poverty and gender inequality in high- and low-income countries impact HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and other major diseases.  Moreover, as a clearer understanding of what works is not enough to improve health and health equity, translating research findings into practical policy change will be a critical element of this program. Leaders from UNICEF, Save the Children, CARE, the World Federation of Public Health Associations and other IGOs and NGOs will join the research program team to ensure effective knowledge mobilization of the evidence.

Keywords-MotsClés: EFFECTIVENESS OF COMPLEX INTERVENTIONS; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH POLICY ETHICS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION AND EXCHANGE; MARGINALIZED POPULATIONS; POPULATION HEALTH INTERVENTIONS; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE INDICATORS; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE INTERVENTIONS; STRUCTURAL VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Health inequities remain a pressing national concern in Canada. One of the most important ways of closing the gap between those who are healthy, and those who are not, is to develop systems of effective, accessible primary health care (PHC)services for people whose lives and health are affected by poverty, social exclusion, and discrimination. However, little is known about how to provide effective services to populations who are most disadvantaged. Through a series of studies, we will develop new evidence about how to improve health equity for this population group. Our team includes researchers in nursing, medicine, social work and community health, and knowledge users who work in public health, government, health authorities, and PHC centres. We are working together to study the impact of a novel PHC intervention that aims to promote the health of people who are living in socially and economically disadvantaged circumstances. The knowledge gained from this research program has the potential to improve how health care can be provided in ways that promote health equity for all.

Keywords-MotsClés: BRITISH COLUMBIA; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; ETHICS AND VALUES; HEALTH EQUITY TOOLS AND FRAMEWORKS; HEALTH INEQUITIES; INTERSECTORAL COLLABORATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION AND EXCHANGE; POPULATION HEALTH INTERVENTIONS; PUBLIC HEALTH POLICY; PUBLIC HEALTH SERVICES
Abstract-Résumé: Canada has long had a commitment to improving the health of all Canadians including those who face social and economic disadvantages. Improvements in the health of the population in the future will be achieved by action on the social determinants of health. For example, where you live or work and how much money you have can determine whether you will be healthy or sick. The way that society is organized means that people have different opportunities and access to resources for health during their lives.  The commitment to improving overall health and addressing differences in health is described in many Canadian documents and has been endorsed by governments and leaders in public health.  Although health is determined by more than health care services, the health sector and particularly public health have an important role to play in strengthening action on the social determinants.  Currently, public health services in British Columbia are being reorganized and this is an important time for learning and enhancing the ability of public health services and practitioners to improve the effectiveness of public health services in responding to unfair differences in health particularly in the promotion of mental health and delivery of substance use services. An important aspect of this work is ensuring a strong public health system with public health providers that have the knowledge, skills, tools and resources to undertake this work.This research will contribute to increasing the effectiveness and contributions of public health for reducing unfair and inequitable differences in health.  This research is a collaborative effort between public health and university researchers and will provide important learnings and improvements about the effectiveness of changes being implemented.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expanding an e-mentoring and leadership program in northern Canadian rural communities for youth interested in exploring careers in the health sciences.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; E-MENTORING; GRADUATION STATISTICS; HEALTH AND SCIENCE PROMOTION; HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS; INUIT; NUNAVUT; YOUTH; YUKON
Abstract-Résumé: DreamCatcher Mentoring (DCM) is an innovative e-mentoring and leadership program that connects high school students in Yukon and Nunavut with Canadian mentors who work in the students' aspired career-of-choice. The DCM program was developed in response to the declining number of students that enter and graduate from high school in northern Canada. DCM staff believes that an empowering, self-directed and high-quality mentorship will give students the confidence, leadership, and skills needed to create attainable goals, complete their education, and work towards their dreams and aspirations. The enhanced opportunities for continued education which flow from this process encourage DCM students to continue their schooling through post-secondary and/or diploma and certificate training.     DCM has developed an innovative form of online mentorship in an effort to provide northern youth with access to a diverse group of enthusiastic and qualified mentors, regardless of their geographical location. Through minimal cost of maintaining a website, DCM has provided a unique opportunity for northern youth to interact with mentors through a secure online environment, connecting them with career professionals they would not have the chance to communicate with otherwise, especially for those students living in rural communities. Mentors are specifically identified so that their occupation matches the 'dream-career' of the students. Once matched, students and their assigned mentors communicate entirely through our secure website, following a tailored curriculum for 4 months each fall and/or spring. DCM staff monitor all postings for the safety of both the student and mentor.   DCM will work in collaboration with our affiliations and networks to promote health-related career mentorships and opportunities to participating students in Yukon and Nunavut schools. With funding from CIHR, we plan to promote this program and actively recruit high-quality mentors.

Our objective is to build on the success of our current partnership, which raises awareness of health research opportunities for Northern youth and inspires them to imagine their futures as potential contributors to vital health research that contributes to the sustainability of Northern rural communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: National and Provincial Science Fairs Program
Keywords-MotsClés: MENTORSHIP; SCIENCE FAIRS; YOUTH OUTREACH
Abstract-Résumé: At Youth Science Canada, we are working hard to ignite an interest for science in our nation's young people. We are deeply convinced of Canada's urgent need for many more youth who not only have science and technology skills, but also a deep passion for using their considerable gifts to make a difference in their world, their country and their future. Established in 1962, our focus is on engaging Canadian youth through science in inquiry and critical thinking. We are Canada's leading organization in the promotion of innovation and the celebration of excellence in science among youth. The National and Provincial Science Fairs Program represents the largest extra-curricular youth activity program in science, technology, and innovation in Canada. Each year, 500,000 Canadian youth do a science project. Of these, 25,000 develop outstanding science projects in order to compete at regional science fairs across the country and qualify for the next level of competition: the Canada-Wide Science Fair (CWSF). Approximately 500 of the top young scientists at regional fairs are selected to participate in the week-long event. Youth Science Canada's partner in the province of Quebec, Conseil du developpement du loisir scientifique, hosts the provincial science fair annually. The top winners form the Quebec delegation at the CWSF. Youth Science Canada has identified seven challenges - the Canada-Wide Youth Science Challenges - that focus on issues important to Canada's youth, the future of our country and our world: Discovery, Energy, Environment, Health, Information, Innovation and Resources. The Challenges are meant to inspire students to exercise their curiosity and creativity by answering a question or solving a problem by doing a science project. The Health Challenge encourages young scientists to do a science project to increase our understanding of the human body, or apply science and technology to improve health, control disease, or support an aging population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Connecting Kids with Scientists
Keywords-MotsClés: HANDS-ON SCIENCE; LIFE SCIENCE OUTREACH; MENTORS; VOLUNTEERISM; YOUTH ENGAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Let's Talk Science (Parlons sciences) is a national, charitable organization dedicated to motivating and empowering children and youth to use science, engineering and technology to develop critical skills, knowledge and attitudes needed to thrive in our world. It creates and delivers programs and services that turn children and youth on to science, keep them engaged in learning and develop their potential to become 21st century citizens and innovators. Let's Talk Science's reach is broad and the core value of increasing access to quality learning opportunities drives all who work and volunteer for the organization.  With this application we are seeking three years of support of $100,000 per year (total $300,000), which will be applied to Let's Talk Science Outreach (LTS outreach), the national volunteer-driven program previously called the Partnership Program. Let's Talk Science Outreach is offered in partnership with thousands of volunteers at 33 universities and colleges across Canada (up in 2010/11 from 30 sites). Approximately one half of all Let's Talk Science Outreach activities are related to life and health sciences and are led by volunteers with expertise in life sciences. With CIHR support, over the next three years, nine new outreach sites will be launched, increased numbers of volunteers (primarily graduate students) will offer hands-on/minds-on science programs for free to an estimated 440,000 youth in hundreds of communities across Canada.  Diverse opportunities will also be offered specifically to Synapse Mentors and other CIHR-funded researchers both through the Let's Talk Science Outreach program and through CurioCity, a new web-based program for teens. Core support is requested for national outreach program staff salaries; volunteer training program; and the delivery of science activities by partnering outreach sites.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular convergence of insulin and muscle contraction signalling at Rab proteins: Implications for type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CO-CULTURE; EXERCISE; GLUT4 GLUCOSE TRANSPORTER; INSULIN RESISTANCE; MUSCLE CONTRACTION; OBESITY; RAB GTPASES (RABS); RAB-GTPASE ACTIVATING PROTEINS (GAPS); TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Our muscles are major regulators of blood sugar (glucose). Meal-time glucose is stored in muscle cells for later use as fuel during muscle contraction (exercise). The gateway for glucose entry is a protein called GLUT4, and this gateway governs glucose storage. Insulin causes the movement of GLUT4 proteins from inside to the surface of muscle cells, and failure of this response is called insulin resistance. It is paramount to understand how insulin regulates GLUT4 and why this fails in people with obesity or diabetes. Interestingly, exercise also increases GLUT4 at the muscle cell surface, although insulin and exercise engage different signals for the same end. Importantly, the exercise response of GLUT4 is not affected by insulin resistance. We therefore hypothesize that learning how exercise controls GLUT4 may be useful to combat insulin resistance, a major cause of diabetes. Our recent work has identified key molecules called Rabs that direct the movement of GLUT4 in response to insulin. Moreover, both insulin and exercise emit signals inside muscle cells that can regulate Rabs. Therefore, we plan to test whether selective Rabs respond to exercise and might be activated directly to overcome insulin resistance. This work will capitalize on the expertise that the Klip and Niu groups have developed in generating cellular models of insulin resistance and in electrically stimulating muscle cell cultures to cause contraction. We will then test whether Rab molecules respond to contraction in muscles isolated from mice, with the view for future development of Rabs as targets for drug development to combat insulin resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Temporal modulation of the proteome and phosphorylome in models of Alzheimer Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; METABOLISMS; NEUROSCIENCE; PATHWAYS/NETWORKS; PHOSPHOPROTEOMICS; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Our understanding of the progression of Alzheimer Disease at the molecular level remains limited.  In recent year, we have realized that specific changes are occurring in lipids that must be reflected at the protein level.  We hypothesize that the study of the global protein changes that occur in very specific regions of the brain will provide a better understanding of the processes involved AD. Ultimately, this would provide new targeting strategies to prevent cognitive decline in vivo. We propose to use global studies of the changes that occur in protein levels(Proteomics) in animal models of Alzheimer Disease in comparison to the corresponding wild-type model.  We also propose to study the global changes in a protein modification associated with signalling (phosphorylation).  The global measurements of protein levels and protein phosphorylation levels in combination with pathway/network models and our expertise in neuroscience will be used to discover specific group of proteins and their phosphorylations that are changing during the disease and might represent novel targets to affect lipid metabolisms.  The potential targets will then be validated using conventional biochemistry and neuroscience methods.  The outcome of this project will be better understanding of the processes involved in AD and novel validated targets for the modulation of metabolic pathways.

TitreApplicationTitle: Function of TMP21 and its role in Alzheimer's Disease Pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; GENETICS; SNP; TMP21; TRANSGENENIC AND KNOCKOUT
Abstract-Résumé: Deposition of amyloid beta protein (Abeta) in the brains is one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's Disease (AD) pathogenesis. Abeta is generated from a larger beta-amyloid precursor protein (APP) by beta-secretase and gamma-secretase cleavages. Gamma-secretase activity was catalyzed by a PS1-containing macromolecular complex. This high molecular weight complex also requires nicastrin, anterior pharynx-defective 1, and presenilin enhancer 2 for its enzymatic activity. Recently, TMP21 was identified as a new member of the presenilin associated complex. Knock down of TMP21 with siRNA caused an increase in Abeta40 and Abeta42 but no change in Notch cleavage. However, the biological function and its role in AD pathogenesis have not been well defined. The ongoing collaboration between Dr. Kun Xia's lab at The State Key Lab of Medical Genetics of China and Dr. Weihong Song's lab at The University of British Columbia discovered that that the TMP21 is ubiquitinated and its degradation is mediated by a proteasome pathway and NFAT plays a pivotal role in regulation of TMP21 expression. Furthermore we discover a novel intron-4 SNP in TMP21 gene associated with AD. Our working hypothesis is that alteration of TMP21 expression plays an important role in AD pathogenesis. This collaborative proposal seeks to continue utilizing the strengths of two complementary labs in Canada and China to define the function of TMP21 and examine the genetic association of TMP21 with AD and its role in AD pathogenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of action of DNA demethylation inhibition as a therapeutic strategy against liver cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENOME; METHYLOME
Abstract-Résumé: Liver cancer is the fifth common cancer in the world and is responsible for 0.5 million yearly deaths in China. There is no cure for liver cancer if detected late but the survival rate is high if it is discovered early.  We have previously shown that liver cancer increases expression of thousand of genes in comparison with normal liver and that this process is driven by a loss of the chemical coating of genes by small chemicals called methyl groups. It is impossible to cure cancer by just silencing several genes. It is critical to devise ways to reverse the entire program. This proposal aims to define the ways to reverse the process of loss of methyl groups (demethylation) and thus provide some new avenues for therapy of liver cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Excellence Research Chair in Neurogenetics and Translational Neuroscience
Abstract-Résumé: Diseases of the brain represent one of the most formidable global medical challenges of the 21st century. Although remarkable discoveries on brain anatomy and function have been made throughout the last century, far less is known about how to effectively intervene when these functions become disordered or diseased. The need to develop effective treatments for neurodegenerative diseases is particularly pressing. Ten million Canadians of all ages, nearly one in three, will be affected by brain disease, disorder, or injury of the brain. The financial burden is enormous, accounting for more than 38% of health care costs when disability is included, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). These societal and financial costs will only increase in the future with an aging population and increasing incidence of brain disorders, such as Alzheimer¿s, Parkinson¿s, and stroke. Dr. Farrer, our proposed CERC recipient, together with the Centre for Molecular Medicine and Therapeutics (CMMT) and the Brain Research Centre (BRC) at UBC, will establish a new research program, the Centre for Applied Neurogenetics (CAN) that will translate neurogenetic discoveries into novel strategies for early detection and new treatments of neurodegenerative diseases to enhance the quality of life for patients. This research program will translate neurogenetic discoveries into novel therapeutics that provide more than symptomatic relief, by identifying and targeting the molecular etiology of disease. In the past twenty years there has been a revolution in genetic and computing technologies that is now being successfully applied to unravel the molecular basis of human disease. The research program¿s objective will be to develop new model systems and novel therapeutics that exploit these fundamental neurogenetic insights. As exemplified by Dr. Farrer¿s work in Parkinson¿s disease ¿ once considered a sporadic disease with little genetic etiology ¿ neurogenetics provides a solid foundation for applied neuroscience research. Parkinson¿s disease affects over 100,000 Canadians and costs $2.5 billion annually, not considering the significant personal cost to patients and their families. Related movement disorders also affect young Canadians, and Dr. Farrer¿s team have also worked on a variety of these childhood syndromes. This paradigm shift has major intellectual significance, providing scientific direction for the field and renewing hope of more than palliative therapies for millions of patients.Dr. Farrer will build upon existing, and establish new national and international networks, develop new collaborative activities that unite high-throughput core facilities with existing resources and infrastructure to foster cross-theme, multidisciplinary research. Studies are to be directly applied to patient diagnosis, etiologic disease models and functional neuroscience, to develop novel therapeutics for the benefit of patients worldwide. This new research program will significantly increase the pool of talented, skilled, creative people available to academia and industry with expertise in clinical neurology, neurogenetics, and neuroscience. This is critical to building and sustaining a highly qualified and globally connected workforce that is urgently needed in these fields.Dr. Farrer¿s research team will advance public policy through improving the understanding, practices and therapies targeted toward neurodegenerative diseases that place an especially large burden upon families, health systems and patients. Dr. Farrer will actively develop and pursue new emerging commercialization opportunities with aggressive technology transfer programs at UBC (UILO), CMMT, and BRC. CAN will establish new spin-off companies and build upon the proven track record of the CMMT and BRC successes to commercialize these discoveries for bench-to-bedside clinical impact. In summary, this CERC Chair will be a catalyst for translational neuroscience research in Canada.

The research program¿s objective will be to develop new model systems and novel therapeutics that exploit these fundamental neurogenetic insights. As exemplified by Dr. Farrer¿s work in Parkinson¿s disease ¿ once considered a sporadic disease with little genetic etiology ¿ neurogenetics provides a solid foundation for applied neuroscience research. Parkinson¿s disease affects over 100,000 Canadians and costs $2.5 billion annually, not considering the significant personal cost to patients and their families. Related movement disorders also affect young Canadians, and Dr. Farrer¿s team have also worked on a variety of these childhood syndromes. This paradigm shift has major intellectual significance, providing scientific direction for the field and renewing hope of more than palliative therapies for millions of patients.Dr. Farrer will build upon existing, and establish new national and international networks, develop new collaborative activities that unite high-throughput core facilities with existing resources and infrastructure to foster cross-theme, multidisciplinary research. Studies are to be directly applied to patient diagnosis, etiologic disease models and functional neuroscience, to develop novel therapeutics for the benefit of patients worldwide. This new research program will significantly increase the pool of talented, skilled, creative people available to academia and industry with expertise in clinical neurology, neurogenetics, and neuroscience.
