TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Excellence Research Chair in Structural Neurobiology
Abstract-Résumé: Communication by nerve cells is controlled by the release of chemical messengers that activate a family of receptors called GPCRs, for G-protein-coupled receptors, on target cells.  In humans there are ~800 different GPCRs that control everything from vision, heart rate and breathing, to even memory and learning.  The objective of this proposal is to understand how these receptors work at the molecular level; how they are involved in neurological and other diseases; and how they serve as drug targets.  In recent years, neuroscience has been transformed by advances in structural biology that allow precise molecular models of component proteins to be built at the atomic scale.  This approach provides in-sights into the inner workings of receptors, channels and transporters ¿ membrane proteins that are the key to the healthy operation of nervous system.  This proposal will continue Dr. Oliver Ernst¿s ground-breaking work with rhodopsin, the light receptor in the eye, and the best characterized GPCR.  This work will be directly translated into studies of other GPCRs of importance in human health and disease.  Furthermore, new experimental strategies will be developed for the production and molecular analysis of these and other membrane proteins of profound clinical importance.  A CERC Unit of collaborating scientists will be created to forge links between the large structural biology and neuroscience communities at the University of Toronto.  Dr. Ernst will be the catalyst for creating a centre of excellence in structural neurobiology ¿ the first in Canada.  Like most industrialized countries, Canada is facing an aging population with a resulting increase in age-related neurological diseases like Parkinson¿s and Alzheimer¿s.  This demographic shift provides an important opportunity for Canada¿s biotechnology industry to translate new knowledge into new therapies that will enhance the well-being of patients and reduce the economic burden on their families and the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Excellence Research Chair in Virology
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) and hepatitis B virus (HBV) remain significant health problems in Canada and worldwide. There are an estimated 200-300 thousand HCV carriers in Canada and 130-170 million worldwide.  There are also an estimated with 220-300 thousand HBV carriers in Canada and 350-400 million carriers worldwide.  On a worldwide basis HBV is one of the commonest environmental causes of fatal cancer, ranking second only to cigarette smoking. The importance of controlling the spread of highly infectious agents was recognized by Justice Krever in his 1994 commission of inquiry into why nearly 30,000 Canadians were infected with HCV by a contaminated blood supply.  Although screening systems (some invented by the candidate) have rendered safe Canada¿s blood system, HBV and HCV continue to spread by other routes and their treatment still requires improvement.  There is no vaccine for HCV and current therapy is effective in less than half of patients. Although there is a good prophylactic vaccine for HBV, for those who do get infected, the therapy with interferon or nucleoside analogues is often inadequate with most patients on nucleoside analogues having to remain on long-term suppressive therapy.This project has six objectives.  Four concern the study of HBV and HCV and two concern the search for novel pathogens.  The first area of research will build upon Dr. Houghton¿s experience studying HBV and HCV vaccine strategies and comprises 4 related objectives.OBJECTIVE 1. To identify a prophylactic vaccine for HCV that can be delivered economically and that will be effective against multiple HCV strains.OBJECTIVE 2. To use a non-human primate model to determine if therapeutic vaccines can also be of benefit in chronic HCV infections.  Since current HCV chemotherapy is only partially effective, can immunotherapeutic vaccination represent a valuable addition to be used in combination with antiviral therapy?OBJECTIVE 3. To study the HCV response in the chimeric mice bearing human donor cells encoding different chromosome 19, rs12979860 polymorphisms. This study is based on the fact that both viral and host factors are known to be responsible for HCV failing to respond to standard therapies.  The UA¿s chimeric mouse model provides a unique tool for investigating these factors.  In these studies, the candidate will investigate whether interferon lambda 3 variants can help predict HCV response to therapyOBJECTIVE 4. To use a woodchuck model to identify candidate vaccines that could be used for treatment of chronic HBV infection.  It is anticipated that these vaccines would be used in combination with current HBV antiviral therapies, with the objective of relieving patients of the need for years of anti-viral therapy.These vaccine studies are aligned with the University of Alberta¿s stated goals to increase research efforts in Virology and Immunology and build on the extensive experience of Dr Houghton. The last two objectives concern pathogen discovery.  Previously, Dr Houghton led a team of researchers who discovered the virus causing non-A and non-B hepatitis (Hepatitis C virus).  He will use this expertise to search for the still-unidentified infectious agents that are thought to be responsible for a number of other inflammatory diseases affecting humans.  This is already an area of significant research effort at the University of Alberta (see collaborators).  This research comprises two objectives:OBJECTIVE 6.  To use the chimeric mouse model to help identify the infectious agent causing cryptogenic hepatitis.OBJECTIVE 5.  To apply genomic, proteomic, immunomic and traditional molecular cloning methods to discover causative agents of inflammatory diseases of man. These studies have the potential to improve the prevention and/or treatment of chronic inflammatory diseases with a particular focus on viral hepatitis, diseases of high relevance worldwide and in Canada, during the term of the CERC.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires d'excellence en recherche du Canada
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Excellence Research Chair in Cognitive Neuroscience and Imaging
Abstract-Résumé: The research program that Dr. Owen and his team will bring to the University of Western Ontario (Western) has three principal goals that build upon a twenty-year career of pioneering neuroscientific studies in Cambridge, U.K., and in Montreal, Canada. His first goal will be to apply the theoretical models and functional neuroimaging approaches that he has developed in Cambridge to one of the most challenging problems in clinical medicine ¿ that of detecting and measuring residual brain function in behaviourally non-responsive patients following severe brain injury. This goal follows from his landmark neuroimaging studies, published in The Lancet, Science and The New England Journal of Medicine, showing that high-level cognitive functions ¿ and even conscious awareness ¿ can be detected in some patients who appear to be entirely vegetative. This work has profound implications for clinical care, diagnosis, medical ethics and medical/legal decision-making (relating to the prolongation, or otherwise, of life after severe brain injury), and also sheds light on more fundamental scientific questions relating to consciousness and the neural representation of our own thoughts and intentions. By establishing a new program of functional neuroimaging research at Western on Canadian brain-injury survivors who are behaviourally vegetative or minimally conscious, Dr. Owen and his team will seek to find new ways to reduce the critically high rate of misdiagnosis in this patient group (currently 43% worldwide), which will have significant implications for the delivery of health care resources across Canada. It is also likely to result in important new predictors of recovery, which may improve therapeutic choices in these patients. Dr. Owen and his team will also work to develop new types of so-called ¿brain computer interfaces¿ to extend his most recent studies showing that some severely brain-injured patients may be able to communicate with the outside world, by simply modulating their brain activity. Dr. Owen¿s second key goal will be to establish a new program of research into the cognitive deficits that characterize neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson¿s disease, Huntington¿s disease, Alzheimer¿s disease and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis. Cognitive impairment is a well-recognized feature of all of these diseases and has been shown to be an important predictor for quality of life for these patients. Expertise that already exists at Western in genetics, cognitive neuroscience, neurology and structural and functional brain imaging will be brought together to reveal new levels of understanding about the nature and causes of cognitive impairment in neurodegenerative diseases which may lead ultimately to early detection and treatment. As the population of Canada ages and neurological and psychiatric disorders place an increasingly heavy burden on the health-care system, prompt identification of ¿high risk¿ individuals will assume great importance. While studies in patients are essential for understanding the underlying causes of disease, they need to be underpinned by a solid grounding in studies of how the healthy brain functions. Dr. Owen¿s third major goal will be to continue to deliver a world-class program of research into memory, attention and other ¿higher¿ functions of the human brain. This work will not only strengthen existing research programs in cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging at Western, but will extend them substantially, creating new research bridges, providing new leadership, training opportunities, commercial possibilities, sustainability and impact. In short, at Western, Dr Owen will be in a unique position to pursue his vision for new directions in cognitive neuroscience ¿ to forge new links amongst basic neuroscientists, biomedical engineers and clinicians ¿ with the goal of promoting translation from cognitive neuroscience to clinical practice.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires d'excellence en recherche du Canada
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Excellence Research Chair in Integrative Biology
Abstract-Résumé: Genome sequencing has revealed gene catalogs of astounding diversity from yeast to man. Researchers face a formidable challenge: how to assign functions to thousands of uncharacterized genes, and how to use this information to understand how genes interact to determine cell function in health and disease. Despite technical advances, mechanisms that relate genetic and environmental variation to human health and disease remain poorly understood. An integrated, systematic approach is needed with careful choice of suitable model organisms. Roth¿s research program integrates experimental and computational technology to discover the function of genes and to determine how they act in concert to specify cellular programs to control development, differentiation, and disease states.Roth is developing technology to measure genetic interaction. Complex human diseases such as cancer are defined by such interactions, i.e., they require multiple mutations. Boone, Andrews (U Toronto) and others are in the process of testing genetic interaction for all yeast gene pairs. However, genetic interactions are strongly influenced by environment.  For example, ~50% of genetic interactions amongst DNA repair genes are not seen until a DNA- damaging agent is added. Global genetic interaction maps are needed under thousands of environmental conditions that challenge diverse functions. Roth is exploiting ¿next-generation¿ DNA sequencing to increase genetic interaction mapping efficiency, using a ¿bar-code fusion genetics¿ (BFG) strategy. Collaboration with Boone, Andrews and Durocher (U Toronto) could allow global genetic interaction maps under multiple environmental conditions (e.g., diverse mutagens). BFG can be adapted to human cells by engineering lentiviruses to carry barcoded reagents (shRNAs) that disrupt human genes.  Collaboration with Moffatt, Wrana and others (U Toronto) would provide the necessary human RNAi expertise.BFG is being adapted to efficiently identify interactions between human proteins and their dependency on specific modifying enzymes. For example, many human oncogenes are kinases that alter interactions of their substrate proteins with other proteins through phosphorylation. No current method can economically allow multiple ¿conditional interaction¿ maps, each generated in the presence of a different oncogenic kinase. Collaboration with Pawson, Wrana and Sicheri (U Toronto) would enable study of oncogenic kinase-dependent protein interactions.Roth is applying machine-learning methods, integrating diverse genome-scale datasets to quantitatively infer gene function and phenotype. Past efforts have focused on yeast and mouse models (the latter with Hughes, U Toronto). These efforts are being extended to predict function and disease involvement. Such predictions can aid genome-wide association (GWA) studies of human disease.Roth is part of a center studying host-virus interactions by mapping protein interactions between viral proteins (EBV, HPV, adenovirus) and human host proteins, and measuring expression in cells after transfection with various viral proteins. Roth is integrating this data to identify human host factors and to identify human variations conferring viral resistance and sensitivity. Collaboration with Frappier and McGilvray (U Toronto) would provide expertise on EBV and Hepatitis C viruses.Ontario and Canada more broadly has significant expertise and accomplishment in systems biology in humans and model organisms. Roth¿s research program would bring synergistic experimental technology and computational expertise to transform both the scope and the level of integration to this research community. His program will keep Canada at the forefront of biomedical research and contribute to the innovation economy by educating highly qualified personnel, generating new intellectual property and commercializing novel products.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of neuroligin/neurrexin trans-synaptic interaction in pre- and post-synaptic coupling during long-lasting synaptic plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS; CELLULAR IMAGING; CULTURED NEURONS; DROSOPHILA; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HIPPOCAMPAL SLICES; MGLUR-DEPENDENT SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; NEUROLIGIN AND NEUREXIN; PRE- AND POST-SYNAPTIC COUPLING; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION AND PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Neuronal communications through chemical synapses, highly organized inter-neuronal structures, are critical for normal brain development and function. Synaptic deficits are associated with many forms of neurodevelopmental and mental disorders. Synaptic transmission and plasticity require coordinated changes in the two connected neurons, but how this coordination is achieved remains unclear. In this joint project, we will investigate the role and underlying mechanisms of the trans-synaptic interacting proteins, neuroligin and neurexin, in the regulation of this synaptic coordination. Both neuroligin and neurexin are known to be linked to human brain disorders, including autism and mental retardation, but the underlying pathogenic process is unknown. We have discovered that neuroligin is dynamically regulated by neuronal activity, suggesting a hypothesis that neuroligin may play a critical role in synaptic plasticity in the adult brain. We will address this hypothesis by employing multiple techniques, including molecular genetic manipulations, functional recording and cellular imaging. The results of this proposal will not only offer new insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying synaptic regulation, but also contribute to understanding the pathogenic process caused by neuroligin and neurexin dysfunction, and therefore may provide potential therapeutic strategies to prevent and treat related brain diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cross-talk between host antiviral and apoptotic signaling pathways in de novo Dengue virus infection
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CYTOKINE; INTERFERON; IRFS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NF-KB; RIG-I?MDA5; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION; VIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Dengue viruses (DENVs) are globally important human pathogens infecting 50-100 million people annually, with ~25-50 thousand deaths, mainly affecting children. DENV is one of the most important public health problems in tropical and subtropical regions of the world, with up to 3 billion people at risk of infection. In Hainan province of China, recent outbreaks resulted in more than 600,000 people being infected and 475 deaths reported. There is no vaccine to prevent DENV infection and no specific antiviral drug to treat infected people; thus development of effective antiviral and vaccine approaches are global priorities. Recent investigations have demonstrated that the replication and pathogenicity of DENV are in part related to evasion of the host antiviral interferon response. Over the past ten years, our research and that of other groups throughout the world, have identified key elements of the immune system that 'sense' and respond to incoming virus infection, specifically viral RNA.  Therefore, the main objectives of the proposed project and collaboration are to: 1) identify the RNA motifs in DENV that trigger the host immune response to defend against infection; 2) investigate how DENV specifically inactivates the interferon antiviral response; 3) understand the cross talk between antiviral signaling and cell death. Understanding these virus-host interactions will provide important insights concerning DENV infection and disease. We also believe this study will contribute to the development of novel strategies for antiviral immune therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Synaptic LTP and fear memory
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIORAL NEUROSCIENCES; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; FEAR MEMORY; HIPPOCAMPUS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Fear memory is the ability to remember fear experience. When fear memory is abnormally strengthened, for example, if you are suffering with post-traumatic stress disorders (PTSD), the trauma you experienced is so overwhelming that you find that you cannot move on and you feel stuck with painful memories that do not fade. Therefore, uncovering the exact mechanisms underlying fear memory will provide essential information for a better understanding of PTSD. The present project designed to explore the mechanism underlying fear memory in rats will be conducted jointed in Dr. Lin Xu's group at Kunming Institute of Zoology in China and Dr. Xia Zhang's group at University of Ottawa Institute of Mental Health Research in Canada. Specifically, Dr. Zhang's group will employ their established protocols to examine the molecular mechanisms, whereas Dr. Xu's group will investigate the cellular and behavioral mechanisms by taking advantage of recording electric activity of brain cells and behavioral changes in freely moving rats. The current project is a natural extension of our previous collaborative research, during the recent several years, on memory and autism, which has been financially supported by a China-Canada joint health research grant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ethics, Social Determinants of Health, and Health Equity: Integrating Theory and Practice
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE PSYCHOLOGY; ETHICS AND POLITICS OF HEALTH; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH INEQUALITIES; MEASUREMENT; PUBLIC POLICY AND PUBLIC HEALTH INTERVENTIONS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOCIAL/DISTRIBUTIVE JUSTICE
Abstract-Résumé: Population health interventions can include policy, programmatic and resource distribution approaches. These interventions raise complex ethical challenges, concerning for example health inequalities, the relations between social efficiency and health equity, the distribution of scare resources and so on. Examining these challenges in order to clarify what types of population health interventions promote health and health equity is an important area of inquiry. This research program therefore aims to investigate the ethical foundations of population health interventions to address the social determinants of health, and to promote health and health equity. It addresses crucial questions like the following: (1) What are the ethical foundations underlying research into the social determinants of health and health inequalities? (2) What are the ethical foundations for determining which measures and research methodologies should be used for assessing health inequalities, and for assessing the efficacy of different interventions in reducing inequality? (3) On what basis should we prioritize different kinds of population health policies and interventions? (4) What populations, sub-populations, and health conditions should we prioritize when addressing health inequalities?

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of progesterone bioavailability at the maternal-fetal interface: relationship to pregnancy outcome
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOCRINOLOGY; GENETIC POLYMORPHISMS; PREGNANCY; PROGESTERONE; STEROID HORMONE ACTION
Abstract-Résumé: Progesterone plays a key role in establishing and maintaining pregnancy, and deficiencies in progesterone's action lead to miscarriage and preterm birth. The reasons for this are not completely understood, but likely involve the immunosuppressive properties of progesterone at the maternal-fetal interface. A plasma protein, known as corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), binds steroids like cortisol and progesterone, and regulates their biological activities. This collaborative research project sets out to: (A) determine whether abnormalities in CBG production and/or function influence pregnancy outcomes in Canadian and Chinese women, and (B) define how CBG controls progesterone action at the maternal-fetal interface. It builds on the discovery of a CBG variant, found in many Chinese women, which is not produced adequately and seems to be beneficial for pregnancy. The project also builds on data obtained in China and Canada which show that CBG is a target for enzymes that destroy its steroid-binding properties. It sets out to define how the production of these types of enzymes by placental cells might control the levels and activity of CBG at the site of placental attachment to the uterus, and how this influences the way progesterone acts to promote and sustain pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms of Hepatic and Intestinal Insulin Resistance: Role of Mesenteric Fat and Ceramides
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE TISSUE; CERAMIDE; DIET; INSULIN RESISTANCE; INTESTINE; LIVER; MESENTERIC FAT; SPHINGOLIPIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Insulin resistance is a very common disorder observed in subjects with conditions such as obesity and type 2 diabetes and is now considered to be an important risk factor in the development of atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease. The incidence of insulin resistant states has been increasing at an alarming rate in not only adults but also adolescent and pediatric populations in most countries worldwide including Canada and China. Despite a high blood level of insulin, these patients actually have resistance to insulin action at the cellular level. Patients with the so called "insulin resistance" syndrome develop high blood levels of fat and cholesterol which puts them at an increased risk of developing heart disease. Our laboratories in Canada and China are proposing a collaborative study to investigate the mechanisms underlying a very important link between comsumption of diets rich in fructose, fat, and cholesterol, and development of inflammation in abdominal fat . Our aim is to determine how generation of certain lipids in abdominal fat (i.e. ceramides) induces liver and intestinal dysfunction, and lead to an insulin resistant state. The long term objective of this research is to increase our understanding of this common disorder in humans, and identify potential drug targets, allowing the development of pharmaceutical measures which can help us control insulin resistance in patients and thus reduce the risk of development of complications such as heart disease.

Abstract-Résumé: Ultrasound-based imaging technologies are the most commonly used due to their price, ease of operation and safety. However, they are not able to accurately detect tumors. In this work, special nanoparticles will be made to increase the sensitivity of ultrasound to the presence and location of tumors. The nanoparticles will accumulate at the location of the tumor and be activated so as to produce the appropriate ultrasound backscatter signals. It is hoped that these agents will help in locating cancerous tissue, but also treating it.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cell Biology of Cardiac Potassium Channel Remodeling in Adult Cardiac Myocytes
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC REMODELING; INTRACELLULAR TRAFFICKING; POTASSIUM CHANNEL; RAB GTPASES
Abstract-Résumé: After heart attacks and in heart failure, changes occur to the heart in its ability to pump blood and underlying this are often changes in the structure of the heart and in the functioning of the cells that compose it. We call these changes in the heart's structure and electrical activity "remodeling." Understanding remodeling is central to predicting the progress and severity of the disease. The aim of this project is to understand how proteins that regulate the electrical activity of the heart are processed by the cells that make up the heart and how those proteins are transported to and from their place of function and sent to be broken down when they are worn out. Very little is known about how these processes occur in heart cells and how it works for proteins called potassium ion channels that are very important in the normal electrical activity of these cells and, thus, the heart. This project aims to learn what "trucks" and "containers" are used to transport these potassium ion channels around the cell and how the cell decides whether to reuse or take apart a potassium ion channel that it has temporarily or permanently removed from its place of function. We have developed new systems that allow, for the first time, the ready introduction of outside genes into muscle cells isolated from real heart. We will use these systems to introduce proteins (defective "trucks," "truck parts," "containers," etc.) to interfere with normal trafficking. We will thereby determine for the first time how the movement of potassium ion channels is carried out in heart cells, and how that movement is changed when a heart becomes diseased. Ultimately, this work may lead to new ways to intervene and perhaps prevent the progression of heart diseases and, perhaps, allow interventions to correct some of the underlying defects that lead to heart disease in the first place.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of CUL4B in the regulation of dopamine transporter function
Keywords-MotsClés: CUL4B; DOPAMINE; DOPAMINE TRANSPORTER; DOPAMINE UPTAKE; NEURONAL APOPTOSIS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease is a brain disorder that impairs ability to move and often progresses to dementia. Degeneration of brain tissue in the midbrain region, specifically neurons which are part of the dopamine neurotransmitter system, is known to be a component of the disease. However, the specific molecular mechanisms causing this degeneration remain largely unknown. Evidence supports the hypothesis that the degeneration seen in Parkinson's is due to susceptibility of dopaminergic neurons to disorganized cell death as a result of increased dopamine oxidation and generation of destructive molecules known as reactive oxygen species. Irregular dopamine concentration plays a role in other brain diseases such as addiction and schizophrenia. Finding ways to modulate dopamine transporter function, the key to regulating dopamine concentration, is a major area of research focus worldwide.  Recent preliminary work by Dr. Fang Liu's lab in Canada and Dr. YaoQin Gong's group in China, demonstrates that a protein known as CUL4B enhances dopamine transporter function uptake and dopamine-induced programmed cell death. CUL4B is a member of the cullin family of proteins and can function as a scaffold in organizing a large family of key enzymes. Investigation of how these enzymes regulate the dopamine mechanisms is greatly needed and will:  -Reveal molecular mechanisms underlying which CUL4B may modulate dopamine transporter-mediated functions -Provide a molecular framework in which to view CUL4B and dopamine transporter interaction -Provide a potential target for developing new therapies to treat dopamine-associated brain diseases  By continuing the Canada-China collaboration, both labs will be able to complete critical work more effectively. Identifying specific targets for therapies to modulate dopamine related diseases is a key step in improving health outcomes for Canadians, Chinese and others around the world who suffer from conditions involving this biological mechanism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Interferon Regulatory Factor 9 (IRF9) in Heart Failure Progression and as a Novel Biomarker of Human Heart Failure through Exosomal Signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR REMODELING; DISEASE BIOMARKER; EXOSOMES; GENE TARGETED MOUSE MODELS; HEART FAILURE; HYPERTROPHY; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTERFERON REGULATORY FACTOR; PROTEOMICS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure, or progressive weakness of heart muscle, is a major public health problem in both China and Canada, affecting 1 in 5 of Canadian population.  Progressive changes in heart structure and function after injury such as heart attack or high blood pressure lead to heart failure.   The challenge is to understand the underpinning process and to detect it early.       This Chinese-Canadian collaborative research team will focus on a new pathway that can lead to heart failure, involving the intrinsic defense system of the body - innate immunity.  One of the key molecule is called IRF9, which is increased in heart failure, and its removal from the heart in mouse models of heart failure can significantly improve the outcome.  We propose to explore the contributions of IRF9 in heart failure progression, and its potential role as an early marker of heart failure.       We will divide up the work between the Chinese and Canadian teams, where the Chinese team will evaluate the contribution of IRF9 in a high blood pressure model of heart failure.  The Canadian team will evaluate the role of IRF9 following a heart attack model.  We will together search for the processes that lead to IRF9 activation that can so effectively change the course of heart failure.  We will evaluate the role of IRF9 as a potential early detector for presence of heart failure in blood samples of patients.  We will also determine if removal of IRF9 can improve the outcome such that it may be a future target for treatment.

Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPPEMENT LOCAL; ENVIRONNEMENT BATI; INTERSECTORIALITE; INTERVENTIONS POPULATIONNELLES; INEGALITES SOCIALES DE SANTE; POLITIQUES PUBLIQUES; SANTE URBAINE; TRANSFERT ET ECHANGES DES CONNAISSANCES; TRANSPORT ACTIF; ETHIQUE EN SANTE PUBLIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: La programmation de recherche proposee vise a realiser un programme de recherche interventionnelle en collaboration avec la Direction de sante publique de Montreal (DSPM) qui a fait de la reduction des inegalites sociales de sante (ISS) un enjeu prioritaire. Plus precisement, heberge a la DSPM, notre equipe produira des donnees probantes et animera un espace de partage et d'utilisation des connaissances sur les effets et processus d'interventions de sante publique visant a reduire les ISS et fondees sur les quatre strategies populationnelles de la Charte d'Ottawa de la promotion de la sante: developper des politiques publiques saines; renforcer l'action communautaire; creer des environnements favorables; et reorienter les services de sante. Le programme de recherche comprend quatre volets inter relies, chacun examinant une intervention de sante publique : la politique etablissant des garderies a contribution reduite; l'intitative montrelaise de soutien au developpement social local; l'intervention d'amenagement urbain pour favoriser les trasnports actifs et securitaires; l'integration des interventions a base communatuaire de la DSPM et d'autres acteurs regionaux. Notre programme de partage et utilisation des connaissances sera en continuite avec l'experience acquise avec le Centre de recherche Lea-Roback sur les inegalites sociales de sante et sera anime par deux personnes dont le role et les pratiques eprouvees sont de creer et maintenir de tels reseaux d'echange. Elles auront pour fonction de favoriser une retroaction en temps reel, a partir de leurs liens avec le terrain, sur les interfaces, ente nos projets et les besoins nouveaux. Enfin, notre programme servira de cadre pour la formation de nouveaux chercheurs en recherche interventionnelle en sante des populations par l'integration d'etudiants aux cycles superieurs, de chercheurs postdoctoraux et de chercheurs en emergence.

Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEMENTARY AND ALTERNATIVE MEDICINE; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; MEDICAL ADHERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease frequently use complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) for treatment of their disease.  Patients often choose these alternative treatment methods because they feel that there less side effects associated with CAM.  Other times, patients start CAM because their disease is not adequately controlled by conventional medical therapy.  It is not known whether the use of CAM affects whether patients continue other medications prescribed by their doctors for IBD.  This study seeks to determine patient and physician attitudes toward CAM and whether the use of CAM affects medication-taking bevavior.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Basis of Interval Colorectal Cancers
Keywords-MotsClés: COLONOSCOPY; COLORECTAL CANCERS
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer is the second most common cause of cancer-related deaths in North America. In Canada, it is estimated that there will be approximately 22,500 new cases and 9,100 deaths attributed to colorectal cancer this year alone. Early and accurate detection of colorectal cancer is essential as it increases the chances of successful cure of the disease. A colonoscopy is a complete examination of the colon and an essential test to diagnose colorectal cancer. However, we recently determined that ~1 in 13 individuals with colorectal cancer in Manitoba had a colonoscopy within 6 to 36 months (termed Interval Colorectal Cancer) prior to their diagnosis. Because these Interval Colorectal Cancers appear soon after a colonoscopy it is essential to understand how they arise. While it is possible that some of the Interval Colorectal Cancers are due to missed lesions during the colonoscopy, it is also possible that these are fast growing tumors or tumors with a difference in tumor biology. In general, colorectal cancers generally arise through one of two mechanisms. Unstable chromosomes or gene pathways is one mechanism (known scientifically as chromosomal instability) known to occur in colorectal cancers that present out of the blue and it is associated with aggressive tumors and poor patient outcomes. Chromosome instability has never been evaluated in Interval Colorectal Cancers and we believe that chromosome instability is highly likely to be associated with Interval Colorectal Cancers and underlies the rapid formation of these tumors. This study will determine the prevalence and extent of chromosome instability within Interval Colorectal Cancers derived from a Manitoban patient population. This study will shed much needed insight into the biology associated with Interval Colorectal Cancers. By understanding how they arise we hope to one day be able to prevent them from occurring.

TitreApplicationTitle: Non Dietary treatment for gliadin-induced enteropathy
Keywords-MotsClés: UPPER GASTROINTESTINAL INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Celiac disease (CD) is a common and complex illness in Gastroenterology. In CD, gluten contained in cereals, causes damage of the lining of the gut wall leading to malabsorption of nutrients.  Patients with celiac disease may develop diarrhea, irritable bowel syndrome symptoms and, particularly in adults, often present with osteoporosis, anemia, infertility or neurological and psychiatric symptoms. Awareness among physicians is growing due to highly accurate blood tests. Recent evidence suggests a rising incidence of CD. Young adults today are four times more likely to develop CD than fifty years ago. Environmental factors such as early life and widespread gluten exposure, intestinal infections and short duration of breast-feeding, have been proposed to have a role in CD.  The cornerstone treatment of CD remains a strict gluten-free diet. This nutritional regime is demanding, and relapses are common because of social isolation, financial issues, or restriction of food diversity.  The main goal of this proposal is to explore and develop novel pharmacological therapies for celiac disease and gluten intolerance. We will test these therapies in animal models of gluten sensitivity established in my lab. The therapies are based on two complementary strategies. First, gluten is incompletely digested in humans, leading to the production of toxic fragments that cause intestinal damage in susceptible persons. We have engineered a bacterium, Lactococcus lactis, a common resident in our gut, to deliver enzymes that degrade the toxic fragments of gluten in the intestine. The second approach will investigate the efficacy of a polymer that binds to gliadin in the gut lumen, to prevent gluten toxicity when administered in a complex food mixture. The development of therapies that allow occasional exposure to low levels of gluten in adults with CD and gluten intolerance is expected to decrease the burden of disease and improve patients' quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Inquiry into the Dynamics of Global Health Governance and its Impact on National Health Systems
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH LAW; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SYSTEMS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MIXED-METHODS CASE STUDY; NETWORK ANALYSIS; POLITICS OF GLOBAL HEALTH; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Research shows that eliminating two-thirds of child mortality and three-quarters of maternal mortality would be possible if only we knew how to better govern global health so that existing solutions were fully implemented. Innovative approaches to governance are clearly necessary, but our understanding of the factors that shape health decision-making at the intersection of national and global levels is currently limited. This study will examine global health governance and its impact on national health systems to inform strategies that maximize available knowledge and resources. Drawing on multiple disciplines, theories and methods, I will: 1) systematically review the research literature to identify the factors that determine actors' influence on global health decisions; 2) conduct a dynamic network model analysis of global health governance; and 3) evaluate global health actors' impact on national health systems over time using both quantitative and qualitative methods. This study will inform better ways to govern global health. Specifically, it will help identify innovative strategies to foster collaboration, leverage competition, and better support international efforts to strengthen health systems in developing countries. Findings will also inform national governments' interactions with global health actors, identify opportunities to catalyze system-wide improvement, and help guide interventions aiming to translate existing knowledge into policy and practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Novel Parent Training Intervention to Support the Language Development of Nonverbal Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
Keywords-MotsClés: AUGMENTATIVE AND ALTERNATIVE COMMUNICATION; AUTISM; INTERVENTION; LANGUAGE; PARENT TRAINING; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Children with autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) experience delays and difficulties in the development of their language and communication skills (Wetherby, 2006) such that researchers have demonstrated that by age nine, approximately a quarter of children with ASD are nonverbal (Anderson et al., 2007). Early communicative skills such as joint attention or the ability to coordinate attention between an object and another person, are predictors of later language development (Mundy & Crowson, 1997). Research has indicated that when parents are educated in methods to appropriately obtain and maintain this state of joint engagement with their child, gains in the child's language and communication skills occur. It is evident that parents possess enormous potential to foster the development of language and communication skills in children with ASD. The inclusion of parents as active participants in intervention is a recommended practice (National Research Council, 2001), however, only a small portion of our research literature addresses parent programming. Thus, we know little about program delivery methods that best support the learning of parents of children with ASD and further, we have yet to fully understand the components of these programs that are related to child language change. Both of these components are essential to inform the clinical delivery of parent training programs in order to ensure that public monies are supporting effective evidence based programming for families of children with ASD. The goals of this project are to: 1) gain an understanding of the level to which parents can learn and then accurately deliver strategies designed to support their child's language development, and 2) examine which strategies best facilitate the child's language development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Food policies to improve diets and reduce chronic disease in India
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE PREVENTION; FOOD POLICY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTISECTORAL POLICY; NUTRITION TRANSITION; QUALITATIVE METHODOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic disease has become a major threat to global health and economic development. It now exceeds infectious disease and malnutrition as the leading cause of death in most low- and middle-income countries, including India. In India, the economic impact of lost productivity due to chronic disease will be severe ($237 billion lost in the next decade), making prevention critical. Prevention can be achieved through diet change, tobacco control and systems of primary care. Among changes to diet, reduction in intakes of trans fatty acids (TFAs) is a high priority and has been identified by the Government of India as a major public health concern. TFA consumption is associated with a higher risk of many chronic diseases including heart attack and stroke. Even relatively low intakes of TFAs can have detrimental effects on overall health. The aim of this project is to identify innovative policies in different sectors (i.e., agriculture, finance, trade and health) with the potential to improve diets and reduce chronic disease in India.  This project will use food supply chain analysis in both national and regional case studies in India to: 1) determine the sources of TFAs in the food supply, 2) identify key points for policy interventions to reduce their consumption and 3) to determine the feasibility of these policies. The project will examine the processes and actors that take food from farm-to-fork, while identifying potential pressure points in the food supply for policy interventions. A feasibility assessment of the proposed policy interventions will be conducted with key stakeholders (including government ministries, public organizations and relevant leaders from the private sector) in India. This project has the potential to improve diets and reduce chronic disease in India by identifying feasible multisectoral policy options. The novel use of food supply chain analysis will provide scope for applying this robust methodology to other key aspects of the food supply.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Longitudinal Examination of Outcomes of Teen Dating Violence Victimization
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE OUTCOMES; PUBLIC HEALTH; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SECONDARY DATA ANALYSIS; TEEN DATING VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Teen dating violence (TDV)-the physical, sexual or psychological violence that occurs within the context of heterosexual or same-sex adolescent dating relationships-is a substantial public health problem in Canada and the US, but little is known about long-term consequences related to victimization. To address this, the present study will investigate outcomes of TDV victimization in a large, nationally representative sample of males and females (the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health)). Add Health participants were selected from across the United States, and data were collected at four time points (spanning a 14-year period) from approximately 10,000 people. Using this sample, we will investigate whether TDV is predictive of negative effects on health and well-being 5 years after victimization; primary outcome measures will include depression, substance use, suicidal behaviors, unhealthy weight control behaviors and sexual risk behaviors. We will also investigate whether negative effects vary by timing or type of victimization, if effects persist 10 years after victimization, and if any 10-year effects are explained by the experience of re-victimization in young adulthood.  To supplement the Add Health analyses, we will also conduct interviews with teens in New York state, in order to determine when (i.e., under what conditions) TDV victimization is considered most harmful. This will be the first study to investigate long-term outcomes of TDV victimization for males and females in a nationally representative sample, and will provide the most comprehensive data to date on adverse outcomes related to victimization. Results from this research can be used to improve secondary TDV prevention programs (i.e., programs that intervene after the problem has occurred), services that can directly impact the health and well-being of teens.

Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE CELL; ASTHMA; BETA2 ADRENERGIC RECEPTOR; BETA2 AGONIST THERAPY; BIOMECHANIC ANALYSIS; BRONCHODILATOR; GENETIC SCREEN; MICRORNA (MIRNA); RECEPTOR DOWN-REGULATION; RNAI (RNA INTERFERENCE)
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is one of the most prevalent chronic conditions affecting Canadians. According to the Public Health Agency of Canada, over 2.2 million Canadians have been diagnosed with asthma by a physician.  Asthma places a heavy burden on the nation's health care expenditures and seriously affects the quality of life not only for individuals with asthma but also for their families. A hallmark symptom of asthma is constriction of the airway, which is triggered by stimuli including allergens, viral infection, exercise, and cold air.  The most common medications for asthma dilate and relax the airway during an asthma attack.  One important class of bronchodilators works by binding to and activating a molecule called the beta2-adrenergic receptor.  Although this class of bronchodilator medications is highly effective, their chronic use often leads to drug tolerance, decreased drug efficacy, and increased hospitalization and emergency room visits. Our project aim is to use a novel genomic research method to study a newly discovered regulator of the drug tolerance mechanism.  In the future, this new regulator could serve as a novel pharmaceutical target for combination therapies, and thereby improve the efficacy of bronchodilator- based therapies for asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of programme retention on the effectiveness of long-term, expanding antiretroviral therapy programme: rates, risk factors, and costs of attrition from an antiretroviral programme in South Africa
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; CASE CONTROL STUDY; CHRONIC CARE; COST-EFFECTIVENESS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIV/AIDS; LOSS TO FOLLOW-UP; PROGRAMME EFFECTIVENESS; RETENTION; SURVIVAL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: South Africa has the largest number of people living with HIV and biggest antiretroviral therapy (ART) programme in the world. ART is life-long, and as programmes mature, the challenge to programme effectiveness is the ability to retain patients in care. At the level of the individual, retention in an ART programme is important as it leads to virological suppression and therefore improved health outcomes. At the population level, those who are retained have a lower risk of death and are less likely to transmit the virus because they are virologically suppressed. Health systems see cost-saving benefits since those who are retained are less likely to develop drug resistance and need the more expensive second line therapy and are less likely to become ill and access health services.  Despite the importance of retention to ART programme effectiveness, most programmes in resource-limited settings can only report the number of people who have ever initiated ART and not the proportion currently in care. The objective of this research is to describe and understand attrition and retention in a public-sector ART service in Cape Town. By analysing the patient database and conducting structured interviews, risk factors for being lost to the programme will be identified by comparing people who are lost to the programme and people who are retained. The costs related to programme attrition will be analysed to assess cost-effectiveness of a retention in care intervention and determine how rates of attrition impact on HIV transmission in the population.  The results of this project will be used to make recommendations about how to improve programme retention. The recommended strategies will impact the individual, population and health system. With the rapid expansion of access to ART and the continued shift of HIV from an acute to chronic disease in low- and middle-income countries, the project will also inform models of care for other chronic disease diseases in similar contexts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Frequency and Mutation Spectrum of Genes Mediating Susceptibility to Obesity in the LABS Cohort
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; DNA MICROARRAY; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENOMICS; HUMAN GENETICS; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; QPCR; RARE GENETIC VARIANTS; SEVERE EARLY-ONSET OBESITY; STATISTICAL GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Background Obesity is a major and increasingly prevalent risk factor for multiple disorders, including type II diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and mortality from all causes. We propose to study extremely obese individuals using cutting-edge genetic techniques in order to better understand the biological basis of this disease.   Hypothesis We hypothesize that extreme obesity is more likely to be caused by a smaller number of highly penetrant genetic factors than less severe forms of obesity.   Methods Our study subjects are extremely obese patients with a BMI > 50 kg/m2 who have had weight loss (bariatric) surgery. We will use Next-generation sequencing and DNA microarray technology to study the genetic basis of obesity in these individuals.  Study Implications Findings from our research could offer unique insight into the molecular genetic basis of obesity and identify new targets and molecular pathways for possible therapeutic intervention. Application of the methods proposed here may also provide insight into the genetic basis of other complex human diseases, in other areas of human biology, and medicine.

TitreApplicationTitle: A community-based approach to developing HIV/AIDS education campaigns for women in Zimbabwe
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIV/AIDS; POPULATION HEALTH; PREVENTION; QUESTIONNAIRE; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: As of 2009, over one million adults in Zimbabwe were infected with HIV, and of those, over 50% were women. Despite the high-profile presence of HIV/AIDS in the media and public-consciousness, few studies have been done to determine the risk factors for HIV infection in the female population of Africa, let alone Zimbabwe. Those studies that have been conducted were focused on high-risk groups (sex trade workers, drug users and pregnant women) and not the general female population. To address this knowledge gap, we propose to investigate behaviours and attitudes that increase the risk of HIV infection in women in Zimbabwe. Participants will be screened to ensure that they are HIV negative at the beginning of the study and at that time will complete a questionnaire concerning their lifestyle and knowledge and attitudes towards HIV and AIDS. The survey will be conducted in person via a one-on-one interview, with a translator present if necessary. The participants will be followed for two years to determine the number of new HIV cases in the study group. Using statistical analyses, we will be able to determine the greatest risk factors for HIV infection in women, comprising not only behaviours, but also attitudes and knowledge gaps. During the two year period we will also investigate the communication methods that participants feel would be most effective for presenting results back to the communities. By combining the two studies, we will be able to develop a community-derived education campaign focusing on reducing HIV infection in women. Currently in Zimbabwe, as in most of Africa, women are increasingly the most at-risk group for contracting HIV. This is in part due to the cultural and educational barriers that prevent women from getting the information they need to protect themselves. It is our hope that by using a culturally appropriate manner to conduct our work and present our findings, we will able to reduce the number of new HIV cases in Zimbabwean women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Children with developmental coordination disorder (DCD): The role of the attentional network in motor learning
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; COHORT DESIGN; DCD; DEVELOPMENTAL COORDINATION DISORDER; INTERVENTION; MOTOR LEARNING; REPEATED MEASURES; SELECTIVE ATTENTION
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, one child in every classroom (5-6%) has significant coordination difficulties. These children struggle to participate in daily life activities and do not reach their academic potential. They withdraw from physical and social activities, and can be at greater risk of obesity, anxiety, and depression. Although we don't know what causes coordination difficulties in children, we do know that these children have difficulty learning motor skills, that their motor skills do not become automatic, and that they are much slower than their peers at completing motor tasks because they rely heavily on visual information. Recent strategies that have been effective in helping children with coordination difficulties learn new motor skills focus on their ability to think through and solve motor problems. We know these strategies work, but we don't know how they work. A recent study examining how children's brains work when they perform a motor task shows that children with coordination difficulties use different areas of their brains than other children doing the same task. The brain areas used predominantly by children with coordination difficulties are those that receive and interpret visual information, as well as areas associated with the control of attention. We know from watching children with coordination difficulties that they concentrate very hard to complete motor tasks. It is possible that for these children, their ability to pay attention to certain parts of the task may influence their learning of that task. This study will look at how changing children's focus of attention to relevant parts of a motor task may help children to complete the task and perform the task under different conditions. Results from this study will help to maximize the effectiveness of interventions and strategies designed to help children with coordination challenges and their families to manage their difficulties and to ensure their successful participation in daily life activities.

TitreApplicationTitle: L'étude des gradients temporels relatifs au rappel des connaissances sémantiques sur les personnes célèbres dans le trouble cognitif léger et la maladie d'Alzheimer débutante
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNAISSANCES DES PERSONNES CELEBRES; IRMF; LOBE TEMPORAL ANTERIEUR; MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; MEMOIRE RETROGRADE; MEMOIRE SEMANTIQUE; NEUROPSYCHOLOGIE; TROUBLE COGNITIF LEGER; VIEILLISSEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Ce projet s'interesse au trouble cognitif leger (TCL) et a la maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) debutante. Les patients TCL se plaignent et presentent des troubles de memoire, sans toutefois repondre aux criteres de demence. Ils forment un groupe beaucoup a risque de developper une demence que les personnes agees saines: 10 a 15 % des TCL convertissent vers une MA chaque annee.  La presence de troubles semantiques chez cette population serait un indicateur precoce du developpement d'une MA. En effet, la memoire semantique est la memoire de nos connaissances generales. Or, ce type de memoire est repute pour ne pas decliner au cours du vieillissement normal. Les deficits des patients TCL seraient d'ailleurs plus importants lorsque leurs connaissances sur des personnes connues (profession, nationalite, etc.) sont evaluees comparativement a leurs connaissances d'objets plus communs (animaux, fruits, etc.).  L'objectif du projet est de mieux caracteriser ces troubles semantiques a l'aide d'une tache experimentale qui evalue les connaissances sur des personnes celebres de diverses epoques et de notoriete variable (personne connue lors d'une periode de temps isolee vs. toujours connue aujourd'hui). La performance de 20 patients TCL et 20 MA (stade debutant) sera comparee a celle de 20 personnes agees en bonne sante.  Cette etude tente aussi d'identifier les mecanismes cerebraux qui sous-tendent de tels deficits semantiques a l'aide de l'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle (IRMf). Ainsi, le patron d'activation cerebrale de 20 patients TCL durant la tache experimentale decrite plus haut sera compare a celui de 20 personnes agees en bonne sante.   Rappelons que la MA touche de nombreux Canadiens chaque annee et entraine d'importants couts sociaux. Ces travaux tentent donc de contribuer a un diagnostic plus precoce des patients, ce qui facilitera le developpement de programmes d'intervention visant a ralentir ou stopper la progression de la MA

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the Impact of Reassurance on Infant Pain: An Examination of Verbal and Non-Verbal Factors
Keywords-MotsClés: FACIAL EXPRESSIONS; INFANT PAIN; PAIN MANAGEMENT; PARENT SOOTHING BEHAVIOURS; PARENT-INFANT INTERACTIONS; REASSURANCE; VERBAL CONTENT
Abstract-Résumé: Untreated pain in early infancy can have long-lasting adverse effects. These effects include poor regulation of negative stress, increased responses to painful events later in life, and psychological consequences such as elevated anxiety, distress, and anger. Healthy infants endure various painful procedures, with needle pain being the most common. Since infants are incapable of soothing themselves, parent behaviours are important during these procedures. Some parent behaviours have been shown to decrease infant distress while others have been associated with increased infant distress. Despite a parent's intention to soothe their infant when using reassuring statements (e.g. "it's okay, you're fine"), several studies have found an association between reassurance and increased infant pain. This study will investigate the underlying mechanisms of reassurance by examining verbal and non-verbal factors expressed by parents, specifically verbal content and facial expressions, when using reassurance. It is hypothesized that verbal content and facial expressions will play a role in helping to explain the link between verbal reassurance and infant pain. The proposed study will involve videotaping parents and their infants during routine immunizations at 2, 6, and 12-months of age. These videotapes will be coded for infant pain behaviours, parental use of reassurance, and parental facial expressions while using reassurance. This study will help us to better understand how verbal content and facial expressions impact infant pain and why reassurance is associated with infant pain and distress. This research has implications for interventions and best practices used by parents during infant immunizations. Findings from this research will help us to implement strategies to relieve infant pain during immunizations and reduce the negative long-term health outcomes associated with infant pain.

Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL PALSY; EXERCISE; FATIGUE; MEASUREMENT; PAIN; PSYCHOMETRICS
Abstract-Résumé: Fatigue can be a limiting factor in daily activities for people living with cerebral palsy. This program of study will first explore the experience of fatigue for those who live with cerebral palsy through interviews. Next, existing measurement instruments that measure fatigue will reviewed and items will be selected if considered relevant to individuals with cerebral palsy. From the review and interviews with participants a new measurement tool specific to measuring fatigue in cerebral palsy will be created, tested and validated. Finally, we will explore and describe any relationships that exist between pain, exercise and fatigue.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neighbourhood characteristics and depressive symptoms among community dwellers with and without diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CO-MORBIDITY; DEPRESSION; DIABETES; LATENT GROWTH CURVE ANALYSIS; LONGITUDINAL DATA ANALYSIS; MULTILEVEL REGRESSION ANALYSIS; NEIGHBOURHOOD ENVIRONMENT; POPULATION HEALTH SURVEYS; PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; SOCIAL EPIDEMIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The neighbourhood in which people live is thought to affect mental well-being. Studies have found a link between neighbourhood characteristics and depression, but the evidence is not well established. Critical gaps still exist in the literature. For instance, little is known about what specific neighbourhood features matter most for depression. How people perceive their environment (e.g. safety, cleanliness and community attachment) and objective characteristics of neighbourhoods (e.g.: green spaces, neighbourhood deprivation and access to recreational facilities) may affect mood differently. It is also unclear for whom this effect is most relevant. Because people with a chronic condition such as diabetes may have less mobility and fewer resources, they might be particularly vulnerable to the quality of their neighbourhood; yet no research has focused on this population. This project proposes to shed light on these questions. The researcher will use data from participants of two large health surveys and will identify the characteristics of neighbourhoods from three sources: national censuses, geographic information systems, and a telephone interview, which will be created to assess the perception that participants have of their neighbourhood. The researcher will use advanced statistical methods to clarify the mechanism by which neighbourhood might affect depressive moods in people with and without diabetes. Findings from this work will provide valuable insight into the mechanism by which the neighbourhood environment may influence mental health, it will help identify vulnerable groups and precarious residential situations that may benefit from interventions, and will guide policy-makers and urban planners in making neighbourhoods happier places to live.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multi-Modal Neuroimaging to Evaluate the Relationship between Cerebrovascular Disease and Alzheimer Disease on Cognitive Decline in vivo
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; ARTERIAL SPIN LABELING MRI; BIOSTATISTICS; CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE; CLINICAL NEUROLOGY; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING/TRACTOGRAPHY; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEURORADIOLOGY; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia. Subjective cognitive testing and a clinical history are still the principal methods for diagnosing AD. Current research suggests that metabolic and functional brain changes occur in AD decades prior to the onset of memory impairment. Alzheimer disease progression measured from brain changes on magnetic resonance images and positron emission tomography may provide more sensitive methods to measure disease progression and status before the presentation of memory impairment.  Moreover, there is growing evidence to suggest that small vessel cerebrovascular disease contributes to cognitive decline in persons with AD. Therefore, an aim of this project is to determine if there is an interaction between small vessel disease and dementia, which may worsen cognition. Advanced magnetic resonance imaging techniques, which are capable of visualizing brain architecture at high spatial resolution, will be used to investigate these relationships. In addition, positron emission tomography will be used to examine AD-specific pathology in persons with cognitive impairment.  A further goal will be to assess whether these brain measures correlate with cognitive performance, in particular, different aspects of executive function and memory. With this integrated approach, these investigations can elucidate brain-behaviour relationships and also better determine which tools may be useful for diagnosis, for monitoring progression and potentially for evaluating therapeutic response.

TitreApplicationTitle: Régulation de la transcription par l'immunoprotéasome
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CMH DE CLASSE I; GENOMIQUE; IMMUNOBUVARDAGE; LYMPHOCYTES T; PROTEASOMES; PROTEOMIQUE; RT-PCR
Abstract-Résumé: Le cancer est la premiere cause de deces au Canada. Chaque jour, environ 475 personnes recevront un diagnostic de cancer et 209 personnes mourront de cette maladie au Canada. Une surveillance immunitaire deficiente est une des principales causes de l'apparition de cancers. Notre equipe de recherche s'interesse a la production de molecules du CMH de classe 1. Ces molecules sont exprimees a la surface de la cellule et sont essentielles dans la surveillance immunitaire des cellules, processus permettant d'eliminer les cellules potentiellement cancereuses. Recemment, notre equipe a demontre par des approches quantitatives globales que l'immunoproteasome (IP) augmente l'abondance et la diversite du repertoire de molecules associees au CMH de classe 1.  L'IP est un complexe proteique retrouve exclusivement chez les vertebres, ce qui suggere qu'il est relie etroitement au systeme immunitaire acquis. Fait particulierement nouveau et interessant, notre equipe a aussi demontre que l'IP module les niveaux d'expression de genes particulierement abondants sur les chromosomes 4 et 8. Le mecanisme precis par lequel l'IP module l'expression de ces genes est inconnu et le role exact de l'IP demeure un grand mystere en immunologie. Neanmoins, l'impact de l'IP sur l'expression genique pourrait expliquer pourquoi l'expression de l'IP est alteree de facon importante dans plusieurs types de cancer. Il est donc d'une importance capitale d'etudier plus en details son mecanisme d'action et son impact sur la transformation tumorale, d'autant plus que des inhibiteurs specifiques de l'IP ont ete recemment crees par chimie medicinale et pourraient etre utilises pour le traitement du cancer. Le projet de recherche que nous proposons est de decouvrir, par des approches globales et non-biaisees, les genes regules par l'IP pouvant influencer la transformation neoplasique. Nous proposons egalement de clarifier le mecanisme d'action moleculaire de la regulation de genes par l'IP.

Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL BIOLOGY; INNATE IMMUNE SYSTEM; MICROSCOPY; MITOCHONDRIA; PHOSPHORYLATION; RNA VIRUS CAPSID PROTEINS; VIROLOGY; VIRUS-HOST INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: RNA viruses cause the vast majority of viral diseases in humans and throughout history, are responsible for many catastrophic events. For instance, more people died as a result of the 1918 influenza pandemic than in World War 1. Even in the vaccine era, RNA virus infections still cause disease in hundreds of millions of people each year resulting in millions of deaths. While vaccination against some RNA viruses has met with great success, with the exception of HIV and some influenza strains, effective therapeutic treatments for most viral diseases are non-existent. The key to developing effective anti-viral treatments is through understanding how RNA viruses manipulate human cells during infection. Using Rubella virus as a model system, my research goal is to elucidate how RNA virus capsid proteins block anti-viral pathways that are meant to limit virus replication. In doing so, I hope to understand the nature of viral diseases as well as identify new targets for anti-viral therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Risk of urinary tract cancer from exposure to arsenic in drinking water.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARSENIC CONTAMINATION IN DRINKING WATER; CANCER RISK; GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SCIENCES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; POPULATION HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH; RISK ASSESSMENT; SPATIAL STATISTICAL MODELLING
Abstract-Résumé: Arsenic is found naturally in the environment and is known to cause cancer. Nova Scotia bedrock contains particularly large amounts of arsenic. Arsenic can enter surface and groundwater supplies and affect the health of people who rely on wells for their drinking water. In Nova Scotia, half of the population draw their drinking water from unregulated wells. In some areas of the province, the amount of arsenic in well water has been reported to be up to 100 times higher than the advisory limit set by Health Canada. However, the health risks associated with arsenic exposure in Canada are not known. Studies from elsewhere (e.g. Taiwan, Argentina, Chile, United States) show that high levels of arsenic in drinking water can cause cancers including those of the bladder and kidney. The occurrence of bladder and kidney cancer in Nova Scotia is amongst the highest in Canada. This research aims to measure the risk of developing bladder and kidney cancers as a result of drinking well water containing arsenic in Nova Scotia, Canada. It will also examine how other factors such as age, sex, body size, socio-economic status and lifestyle may influence the relationship between cancer risk and arsenic. To do this, data from the Provincial Cancer Registry and arsenic information from various government departments will be used. In addition, data on arsenic in the tap water and toenails of 5,000 people in Nova Scotia will be studied. This information will be used to show the relationship between the amount of arsenic in tap water and arsenic body burden, a necessary step to link arsenic exposure to cancer risk. The proposed research aims to improve the health of Nova Scotians and Canadians in general. It will support health and environmental policy; inform the public on the potential risks of well water supplies; and guide the development of a risk reduction strategy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Family Study: Assessment of the risk of family members of victims of out of hospital cardiac arrest for Coronary Artery Disease and Sudden Cardiac Death
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR MODIFICATION; CARDIAC RISK FACTORS; CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE; FAMILIES; GENETICS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH
Abstract-Résumé: The most common cause of unexpected, sudden death is the sudden stoppage of the heart. In the majority of cases, the heart stops pumping when it goes into a dangerous rhythm. The most likely cause of this dangerous rhythm is a blockage in the tubes that carry blood to the heart itself. We want to understand why certain people's hearts suddenly stop functioning, in order to see what can be done to prevent these events from happening in the first place. We know that medical problems like having high blood pressure or high blood sugar can cause blockages in the heart and we also know that these problems tend to run in families. This means, for example, that if your mother or father or brother or sister has high blood pressure, you might too. We also know that your home environment can affect your chances of having heart blockages and dying suddenly.  If, for example, you are overweight or smoke you are also likely to have heart blockages down the road. We think that many family members do not know that they may be in danger of dying suddenly themselves and also why their relative died "out of the blue". We are conducting this research study in order to look at and better understand the medical or environmental causes (risk factors) that are associated with the sudden stopping of the heart (cardiac arrest). In addition, nobody has looked to see if family members of people who die suddenly get any information about why their family member died, or if they know they may be in danger of dying suddenly themselves. This lack of information could make the grieving process very hard for some people and they may suffer for no real reason. We think that by talking to these family members, we will help them to feel better about their loved one's death and will also prevent them from suffering the same fate.

TitreApplicationTitle: Does Resistance Training Reduce Gene-Defect and Symptom Severity In Patients with Mitochondrial Disease?
Keywords-MotsClés: ECCENTRIC TRAINING; EXERCISE; LASER CAPTURE MICRODISSECTION; MITOCHONDRIA; MTDNA; MUSCLE; RESISTANCE TRAINING; SATELLITE CELLS; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Small organelles called mitochondria within our muscle produce energy to power all our movements, from washing our hair to running a marathon. When people are born with genetic defects within their mitochondria, energy production becomes limited, thus leading to debilitating exercise intolerance and loss of functionality. These are the main symptoms of Mitochondrial Myopathy (MM), which worsens with age as numbers of healthy mitochondria decrease. Currently there is no cure or treatment. One proposed therapeutic strategy for MM patients is resistance training. The rationale is based on the normal activation of muscle-specific stem cells called satellite cells, which can be activated by heavy resistance training (e.g. lifting weights) causing them to fuse and transfer their contents into the muscle. Interestingly, patients with MM, despite having damaged mitochondria within their muscle, have completely healthy mitochondria within their satellite cells. Thus, activating satellite cells should trigger them to transfer their healthy mitochondria into the muscle and hence increase energy production and reduce debilitating symptoms.  I hypothesize that resistance training could become a feasible therapy for MM patients. To test this hypothesis I will study ten patients performing four months of heavy resistance training. I will analyze their muscle before and after training for numbers of healthy and damaged mitochondria, activated satellite cells, and cellular capacity for energy production. Changes in muscle strength and endurance will be assessed using exercise tests and quality of life will be monitored with a questionnaire.  My research is expected to show the efficacy of resistance training to improve numbers of healthy mitochondria, functionality, and most importantly quality of life for patients with MM. It will offer, for the first time, a practical, feasible and non-invasive therapy which is so urgently needed.

TitreApplicationTitle: The experiential and cultural dimension of female bisexuality in Canada: What are the clinical implications of being "in-between"?
Keywords-MotsClés: BISEXUALITY; CULTURE; DEPRESSION AND ANXIETY; FEMALE SEXUALITY; HEALTH BEHAVIOUR; LANGUAGE; PRE-DISPOSING FACTORS; QUANTITATIVE; RURAL VS URBAN; SOCIETAL DIMENSIONS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Of all sexual orientations, female bisexuality is the one the least understood due to a lack of research. Although some studies have indicated that women who self-identify as bisexual may have poorer mental health than both heterosexual and lesbian women, little is known about why they appear to be at increased risk. One potential explanation may be that they feel they do not fit into either the mainstream heterosexual culture or the lesbian sub-culture.  This marginalization could be a predisposing factor for mental health problems such as depression, anxiety, self-harm, and suicide.  Further, when understanding female bisexuality it may be important to take into account the cultural setting in which the individual is located. However, no research has investigated whether the lived experience of female bisexuality is related to living in a large urban versus in a small-town setting. In addition, no studies have looked at if French or English cultural affiliation may be associated with the mental health of female bisexuals.  The current epidemiological study will attempt to address these gaps in the literature by recruiting 300 women, equally split into heterosexual, lesbian, and bisexual groups, from Montreal (English and French cultural affiliation, urban setting), Quebec City (French small-town, and Kingston (English small town). Through questionnaires the study will aim to investigate the relation between sexual, emotional, social, and cultural factors to mental health, depression and anxiety in particular. The ultimate goal is to identify the predisposing factors associated with poor prognosis for women who identify as bisexual.  At the moment, there is little support available for bisexual women. It is hoped that the current research, through identifying which factors predispose bisexual woman to psychological problems, may lead to developing effective mental health prevention and intervention strategies to meet the needs of this relatively neglected group.
