TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of O-Island 1 in Enterohemorraghic Escherichia coli
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC; BACTERIOLOGY; ENZYMOLOGY; GRAM-POSITIVE ORGANISMS; INFECTION; MOLECULAR GENETICS; STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS; WALL TEICHOIC ACID
Abstract-Résumé: The emergence of multi-drug resistant bacteria has hindered our treatment of infectious diseases.  For instance, antibiotic resistance has developed rapidly in the Gram-positive pathogen Staphylococcus aureus and now methicillin-resistant strains of S. aureus pose a serious threat to public health.  In order to effectively combat these pathogens, we must develop a new arsenal of antibiotics.  These antibiotics must have entirely novel mechanisms of action so that bacteria have no underlying resistance mechanisms.  However, there is a major hurdle to this approach - bacteria are extremely complex.  Successfully developing new antibacterial drugs thus relies on a deep understanding of bacterial physiology.  Our research group believes that wall teichoic acid synthesis has tremendous potential as a new target for antibacterial drug discovery.  We have therefore undertaken detailed studies so that we can understand the physiology behind wall teichoic acid synthesis.  Teichoic acids constitute a substantial portion of the Gram-positive cell wall, a thick layer that provides structural integrity and protection to bacteria.  My work in particular focuses on the modification of wall teichoic acids by an enzyme that adds sugar residues.  We hypothesize that this modification may promote the pathogenesis of Gram-positive pathogens such as S. aureus.  We are therefore interested in determining if this aspect of the wall teichoic acid pathway is a suitable target for new antibiotics.  Ultimately, we hope that our studies will contribute to the development of new antibacterial drugs so that we can once again take a strong hold on the fight against infectious diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: An ethnographic study of interprofessional collaboration and patient safety in general internal medicine units
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNOGRAPHIC METHODS; GENERAL INTERNAL MEDICINE; INTERPROFESSIONAL COLLABORATION; PATIENT SAFETY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Increasingly, reports are describing the relationship between problems with interprofessional collaboration and patient safety. While governments and health care leaders are consequently investing resources into improving collaboration, there remain concerns that change is slow due to a limited understanding of the complex processes involved. General internal medicine is a clinical area where researchers are beginning to document problems in how physicians, nurses, and other health professionals collaborate. The introduction of various strategies to improve interprofessional collaboration, such as communication tools (for example whiteboards to record information) has been employed, although minimal changes in collaboration have been reported to occur. A link between interprofessional collaboration and improved patient outcomes has been investigated and some support has emerged from research studies, however a firm link between better collaboration and patient safety has yet to be established. The aim of this research study is to conduct an in-depth exploration of interprofessional collaboration and patient safety in general internal medicine units in two hospitals. The study will involve four months of observations in each of the clinical settings and in-depth interviews with 40 health professionals and 20 patients/carers. The findings are expected to uncover the nature of collaborative work patterns and how these may affect patient safety from the perspective of different health professionals, and to gain insight into patients/carers' perceptions whether the presence (or absence) of interprofessional collaboration has affected their care and/or contributed to clinical error. It is anticipated that this research will enable health care leaders to make more informed investments in strategies that will address the complex factors relating to interprofessional collaboration and patient safety.

TitreApplicationTitle: In Vivo Metabolic Consequences of Stem Cell Therapy for the Diabetic Infarcted Heart.
Keywords-MotsClés: FATTY ACIDS; GLUCOSE; INSULIN RESISTANCE; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; STEM CELL THERAPY; SUBSTRATE UTILIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Stem cell research as it relates to regenerating the infarcted heart has exploded as experimental and clinical investigations report exciting therapeutic potential. Cell-based therapies reduce infarct size, promote neovascularization and improve contractile function through the secretion of various factors. Despite these promising results, investigations into the effects of stem cell therapy on cardiac metabolism are limited. Furthermore, no information exists regarding the efficacy of cellular therapy in the presence of obesity and insulin resistance. As these conditions are significant risk factors for cardiovascular disease, they are important considerations in the development of cell-based therapies.  Given the link between cardiac metabolism, vascular density and contractile function, the proposed research will elucidate the effectiveness of MSC therapy to preserve cardiac function and minimize cardiac metabolic aberrations following a myocardial infarction.  Additionally, this research will characterize the biochemical alterations and signalling pathways responsible for improved metabolism and cardiac function following MSC therapy and evaluate the efficacy of MSC therapy in diet-induced insulin resistance (type 2 diabetes).

TitreApplicationTitle: Processing of synaptic inputs within cerebellar circuits
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM CHANNEL; CELLULAR NEUROSCIENCE; CEREBELLUM; COMPUTATIONAL NEUROSCIENCE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNELS; PARALLEL FIBER; POTASSIUM CHANNEL; PURKINJE CELL; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: The cerebellum is an area of the brain responsible for coordination, reflexes, motor learning and even cognitive processes. The output of the cerebellum is determined by the interactions between neurons that form well-defined circuits within the cerebellum. If these interactions or circuitries are disrupted, either through damage or genetic mutations, a variety of neurological symptoms can arise, including the loss of coordination known as cerebellar ataxia. In order to understand how these problems can arise, the underlying mechanisms by which cerebellar neurons control motor output needs to be determined. How each neuron processes inputs and produces output  in the form of nerve impulses (spikes) is determined by the ion channels they express. My research will determine how different ion channels interact in several different types of cerebellar neurons and how that affects their processing. In particular, I am examining how the low-voltage activated "T-type" calcium channels activate a form of inhibitory potassium channel to control neuronal excitability. I have shown that these ion channels interact in Purkinje cells, the main output cell of cerebellar cortex, and affect how the Purkinje cell processes sensory inputs. My research project will continue to examine the role of these ion channels in Purkinje cells as well as neurons in the Deep Cerebellar Nuclei, which provide the only output from the cerebellum to other motor centers. By improving our understanding of how ion channels affect communication between cerebellar neurons, my research will provide a foundation to determine how problems with these ion channels alter cerebellar processing in different disease states, and thus how they might be overcome through medical intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Molecular Control of Actin Remodeling in PI3K-gamma Mediated Regulation of Insulin Secretion
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA CELL; INSULIN; METABOLISM; PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Beta-cells of pancreatic islets of Langerhans release insulin in response to rising blood glucose levels. This release of insulin is essential towards maintaining appropriate blood sugar levels. In disease state, as in type 2 diabetes, insulin release is improperly regulated and decreases dramatically with progression of the disease.   We will investigate the role of a novel regulatory protein PI3K-gamma, as a regulator of insulin secretion. We have previously shown this protein to be a positive regulator of insulin secretion, and have shown that its inhibition leads to a decrease in insulin containing granules at the plasma membrane, which also correlates to an increase in cortical actin structure. We will now determine the molecular mechanism by which PI3K-gamma modulates actin remodeling, and further elucidate the mechanism by which PI3K-gamma controls insulin release.   We will combine state of the art imaging and electrophysiological techniques with molecular biology and whole animal studies. We will investigate electrical function, exocytosis, insulin secretion and signal transduction in beta-cells in which PI3K-gamma has been genetically up- or down- regulated, or inhibited pharmacologically.   Understanding how insulin secretion is regulated will lead to the findings of potential sites of dysfunction and targets for the therapeutic treatment of type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effects of spatial frequency domains on attentional bias and emotional processing in high and low trait anxiety individuals: A brain event-related potential (ERP) study.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; ATTENTION; COGNITION; EVENT-RELATED POTENTIALS; MENTAL HEALTH; NICOTINE; PANIC DISORDER
Abstract-Résumé: Panic disorder is an anxiety disorder that is characterized by recurrent unexpected panic attacks accompanied by persistent anxiety over their recurrence or consequences. This disorder affects many aspects of cognition. One of these is cognitive bias, predominantly hypervigilance for threat cues and danger-laden judgments both characterize and contribute to the maintenance of anxiousness. Research has shown that where as panic disorder patients overly direct attention to threat, nonanxious controls direct attention away from harmless threat stimuli, such as threat words and low-threat pictures, but display an attentional bias towards stimuli with high objective stimulus threat value, such as high-threat scenes and evolutionarily prepared threat stimuli. Rates of smoking among populations with psychiatric disorders, specifically panic disorder, are more than twice as high compared with general population. According to the self-medication theory, individuals use psychoactive drugs, such as nicotine, as a means of coping with stress and regulating, escaping, or avoiding their negative mood states. I will use event-related potentials (ERPs) and performance measures to study with panic disorder patients: 1) the attention bias to threat related pictures and 2) nicotine's affect to reduce attention bias. This study may help elucidate nicotine's affect on anxiety, which in turn may assist in prevention and treatment of nicotine dependence among anxiety patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toward building children's exposome: integrating inhalation exposures for epidemiologic studies of childhood asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTION; ASTHMA; CHILDREN HEALTH; COHORT STUDIES; ENVIRONMENTAL EXPOSURE ASSESSMENT; EXPOSOME
Abstract-Résumé: The prevalence of childhood asthma has increased dramatically over recent decades. Asthma is a complex disease which depends on genetics, lifestyle, and environmental factors. Environmental factors are likely to be important in explaining the increasing trend in asthma prevalence. Air pollution is well-known to exacerbate existing asthma but its role in the development of asthma is less clear. Research has shown that the development of childhood asthma is complex and may be related to both outdoor (e.g. traffic pollution) and indoor (e.g. allergens and endotoxins) air pollution. Combining these known and suspected air pollution sources is a much needed and key step in understanding the role of air pollution in the development of childhood asthma.  The aim of the proposed study is to develop a measure of all exposures coming into contact with the human body via the respiratory route. Incorporating both outdoor and indoor sources will fill the gap for future studies of childhood asthma. We will be using the Canadian Health Infant Longitudinal Development (CHILD) study. CHILD is a population-based birth-cohort national study of 5,000 children that collects information on environmental exposures over a five year period in four cities (Edmonton, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Toronto). We will be linking outdoor air pollution exposure concentrations, measured indoor pollutants, and housing characteristics to define children exposome which is the dynamic mapping of life-course environmental exposures from the prenatal period onwards.   The exposure model will then be used to predict the risk of the development of childhood onset asthma. This risk assessment tool adds important information and has potential policy implications for managing the unrelenting increase of asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Impaired Muscle Health in Exacerbating T1DM Complications.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANIMAL MODELS; CELL CULTURE; EXERCISE; GENE EXPRESSION; MITOCHONDRIAL BIOGENESIS; MRNA STABILITY; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL MODIFICATIONS; SARCOPENIA; SKELETAL MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: The loss of skeletal muscle mass is an inevitable consequence of age, and often results in impaired mobility and a lowered quality of life. Many components of skeletal muscle are thought to foster this progressive degeneration, with mitochondria proving to be one of the most critical contributors. Located within the cell, this organelle generates energy required for movement and metabolism. Studies show that muscle mitochondrial content deteriorates with age, and may be linked to the muscle atrophy observed.  Accordingly, much interest surrounds the search for mechanisms to maintain or enhance skeletal muscle mitochondrial content in an ever-increasing aging population. Recent studies have found exercise to be a stimulant for mitochondrial synthesis in aged skeletal muscle. Specifically, molecular pathways have found that exercise is able to trigger the activity of signalling molecules that activate genes required for organelle synthesis. Not yet known are the alternative pathways following gene activation that may also contribute to mitochondrial synthesis. Thus, the purpose of this project will be to utilize both animal studies and cells in culture to examine the effects of exercise and aging on the alternative pathways regulating skeletal muscle mitochondrial content. We hypothesize that these processes are likely rendered dysfunctional with age, leading to abnormal and reduced mitochondria. We further hypothesize that exercise will prove to be protective against such changes, promoting the maintenance of mitochondria with increasing age. The present research is unique as it aims to provide information regarding the use of exercise as a potential therapy to be used in the prevention of age-induced muscle loss.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ribosomal Biogenesis: Understanding the factor-mediated assembly of the small and large ribosomal subunit in prokaryotes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC ACTION; CRYO-ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; IMAGE PROCESSING; PROTEIN PURIFICATION AND CHARACTERIZATION; RIBOSOME ASSEMBLY; RNA FOLDING; RNA PURIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Due to the increase in bacterial resistance to a wide range of currently used antibiotics, infectious diseases have emerged as a main health problem over the past two decades. Thus, fighting infectious diseases has been highlighted as an area progressively investigated by many research institutions throughout the world. The focus of my project is to find new targets to fight pathogenic bacteria. More specifically, I am targeting the macromolecular machinery responsible for protein biosynthesis in cells. This macromolecular assembly is identified as the ribosome. In bacteria, almost 40% of the energy used by the cell is threaded through the function and the assembly of these intricate nano-machineries. Unfortunately, it is not well understood how the ribosome assembles in bacteria. It is certain however, that the mechanism behind ribosomal assembly differs substantially between humans and bacteria, thus entitling it as a pivotal target, sufficient to impair the capability of these pathogens to cause diseases in humans. In our lab, we are currently employing high-end biochemical techniques to study how the ribosome assembles in bacteria. More specifically, we are using cutting edge electron microscopes in the Canadian Centre for Electron Microscopy at McMaster University to visualize intermediates in the process of the assembly of the ribosome. Not only will my work deepen our understanding of the ribosomal assembly; it will also contribute towards finding novel targets for antimicrobial research to fight various pathogenic bacteria and prevent them from causing diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Computational modeling of the molecular processes underlying the formation of new memories
Keywords-MotsClés: APLYSIA; DESENSITIZATION; LEARNING AND MEMORY; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; PROTEIN KINASE A; PROTEIN KINASE C; PROTEIN TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Among an individual's most personal possessions are their memories. The inability to form new memories or the loss of memories can be some of the most devastating symptoms of aging, disease, or injury, and are critical health issues. A comprehensive understanding of the factors that affect learning and memory during normal physiological conditions will help illuminate the pathological processes underlying the disruption of memory formation and storage. One factor that has been shown to exert a powerful influence on memory formation is the amount and pattern of training. Learning distributed over time has been shown to consistently produce longer lasting memories than trials distributed over short intervals, in every organism that this has been studied. This observation has been investigated particularly well in the marine mollusk Aplysia californica. The nervous system of Aplysia is simple and well characterized, yet capable of forming complex memories, making it an ideal system for the study of learning and memory. Currently, we have a detailed understanding of memory formation in Aplysia at the cellular level. However, there remain many unanswered questions at the molecular level, particularly concerning how the effects of different types of learning are mediated. My research will focus on understanding the molecular processes involved in memory formation using a combination of computational, mathematical, and experimental methods. Mathematical modeling is a powerful tool that can be used to evaluate the dynamic molecular events occurring in neurons during memory formation. Experimental validations of the model will refine the model's representation of the intracellular processes. By gaining a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying memory formation, we can increase our comprehension of the pathologies involving memory deficits and their potential treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of formation of Protein Kinase Mzeta during memory maintenance in Aplysia
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CALPAIN; CELL CULTURE; CELL PHYSIOLOGY; EVOLUTION; LONG-TERM MEMORY STORAGE; MICROSCOPY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN KINASE M ZETA; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: A number of devastating human illnesses involve deficits in learning and memory.   To explain and ultimately treat these conditions, it is important to understand the neurobiological mechanisms underlying formation and maintenance of memory. However, mammalian nervous systems are very complex and, as the mechanisms of memory have changed very little over evolution, a simpler model organism can often be better suited for studying the molecular and cellular processes underlying memory. This project uses the mollusk Aplysia as a simple model to investigate the molecular mechanisms of memory storage.  Recent findings indicate that activity of signaling molecules called Protein Kinase Ms may play a key and fundamental role in maintaining memories after they have been formed. We are using the Aplysia model to understand how PKMs are activated during the storage of a memory. The results of our work are likely to provide new insight into the mechanisms of memory storage that will apply across species, and which may help us understand and ultimately treat memory loss in human conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: An integrated protocol of cognitive-behavioural therapy for co-occurring post-traumatic stress disorder and chronic musculoskeletal pain: A randomized controlled clinical trial.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PAIN; COGNITIVE-BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; EVIDENCE BASED PRACTICE; MENTAL HEALTH; POST-TRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED CLINICAL TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and chronic pain are distressing and often debilitating conditions. Suffering from either condition greatly increases the likelihood of suffering from the other, with approximately 70% of individuals with PTSD facing co-occurring chronic pain. Sadly, individuals with both conditions often face even greater debilitation and distress. Empirically supported manualized applications of psychotherapy have been developed to address the human and economic burden of each condition; however, treatments for PTSD seem to be ineffective in alleviating chronic pain, treatments of chronic pain have minimal effect on symptoms of PTSD, and treatments of chronic pain are less effective when individuals also suffer from PTSD. The first manualized treatment focused on co-occurring PTSD and chronic pain is currently being developed by Dr. Gordon J. G. Asmundson (my supervisor) and myself. Sixty participants diagnosed with both PTSD and chronic pain will take part in a randomized controlled clinical trial to assess the efficacy of this treatment protocol, comparing it to current manualized psychotherapeutic treatments for each of PTSD and chronic pain. It is hypothesized that individuals treated by the newly developed protocol will report greater reductions in PTSD symptoms, perceived pain and disability, fear, avoidance, anxiety, and emotional distress,as well as report greater improvements in objective measures of functional ability and self-efficacy throughout the trial and at the three-month follow-up. The proposed study will strive to set a standard of evidence-based intervention for the prevalent and disabling co-occurrence of PTSD and chronic pain, serving to inform current clinical practices relevant to each condition, reducing the economic burden on society, and providing the incalculable benefit of improving quality of life for those who suffer from PTSD and chronic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of GPNMB-induced breast cancer invasion, tumor formation and metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION TO ECM; ANGIOGENESIS; BASAL BREAST CANCERS; GPNMB; INTEGRINS; INVASION; METASTASIS; NEUROPILIN 1; THERAPEUTIC TARGET; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer affecting Canadian women and is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in women. Once breast cancer cells leave the primary site and spread to distant organs, by a process called metastasis, the disease is largely incurable. We have identified GPNMB as a novel mediator of breast cancer metastasis. We demonstrate that it is enriched within the most aggressive breast cancer subtype, which has a very poor prognosis and limited treatment options. Importantly, we show that high GPNMB levels within the tumor are associated with significantly diminished rates of disease free and overall survival in breast cancer patients, even within the most aggressive subtypes. Thus, GPNMB represents a promising therapeutic target in breast cancer. We will determine the molecular mechanism(s) through which GPNMB mediates its tumorigenic and metastatic effects in breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuropsychological, behavioural, and mental health changes in children with Asperger Syndrome treated with cognitive behaviour therapy for anxiety
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY DISORDERS; AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; EVIDENCE BASED INTERVENTIONS; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONING; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: It is common for children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) to have high rates of concurrent diagnoses, including mood and anxiety disorders. Research suggests that 65%-70% of children with ASD have an additional mental health disorder. It is important to research different interventions as anxiety can greatly interfere in the day-to-day lives of these children. Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) is the primary psychological treatment offered for anxiety disorders in typically developing children, yet only recently has it been used as a treatment for children with ASD and anxiety. This project will examine whether CBT programs designed specifically for addressing anxiety in children with ASD work better and lead to more important changes than programs designed for typically developing children. One such program is Coping Cat, which is widely used by clinicians from community agencies across Canada. I will provide therapy to children with ASD and anxiety, and will compare the treatment outcomes from the program designed for typically developing children, versus a program designed specifically for children with ASD and anxiety. I will also examine different aspects of brain functioning to see whether they predict better treatment outcomes in children with ASD and anxiety. It is of upmost importance for our mental health care system to determine where children are benefiting from these types of therapies, and which interventions lead to better outcomes. This evaluation will contribute to the use of evidence-based therapy in Canada and elsewhere for treating children with ASD and anxiety.

TitreApplicationTitle: Étude des mécanismes cérébraux impliqués dans le traitement multisensoriel des émotions chez les individus autistes et chez les personnes atteintes du syndrome d'Asperger.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITION; AUTISME; IMAGERIE CEREBRALE; INTEGRATION MULTISENSORIELLE; PERCEPTION SENSORIELLE; PSYCHOPHYSIQUE; SYNDROME D'ASPERGER; VISION; EMOTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: La comprehension des emotions d'autrui est une habilete cognitive fondamentale dans la regulation des interactions sociales. Precisement, il est demontre que la perception des emotions est optimisee par le fait que les humains integrent les informations provenant du visage et de la voix de leur interlocuteur. Dans ce cadre, certaines etudes suggerent que les perturbations sociales caracterisant les troubles du spectre autistique sont sous-tendues par un deficit de l'integration audio-visuelle des emotions. Cependant, la majorite de ces travaux ont d'importantes limites. D'abord, ceux-ci utilisent des photographies d'expressions emotionnelles tres peu representatives de la nature dynamique des emotions. Ensuite, les methodes employees ne tiennent pas compte des differences dans le traitement des emotions en contexte unimodal lors de la mesure de l'integration multisensorielle. Finalement, les criteres de selection des participants combinent sans distinction les autistes de haut niveau (AHN) et les individus atteints du syndrome d'Asperger (AS), alors que ces derniers ont des difficultes de socialisation beaucoup plus marquees. Cette etude vise donc a investiguer les capacites d'integration audio-visuelle des emotions chez les AHN et AS a partir d'une nouvelle banque de stimuli dynamiques, et ce en controlant pour les performances individuelles dans le traitement unisensoriel. L'integration audio-visuelle sera d'abord evaluee par une tache de discrimination emotionnelle. Puis, l'activite cerebrale associee a l'integration multisensorielle sera mesuree en Imagerie par Resonance Magnetique fonctionnelle (IRMf). De cette facon, nous souhaitons verifier si les perturbations sociales chez les autistes proviennent de leur difficulte a integrer les differentes composantes emotionnelles chez leur interlocuteur. Ceci permettra d'approfondir les connaissances actuelles sur le fonctionnement perceptif des AHN et AS, et ainsi developper des traitements adaptes a leurs besoins.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examination of the Effectiveness of Dialectical Behaviour Therapy-Skills Training as an Intervention for Borderline Personality Disorder Features Among Adolescent Offenders: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT OFFENDERS; AFFECT DYSREGULATION; BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER; CLINICAL PSYCHOLOGY; DIALECTICAL BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; JUVENILE JUSTICE; LAW; MENTAL HEALTH; PERSONALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Current literature suggests that borderline personality disorder (BPD) may be an underlying factor of adolescent offending, as many adolescents entering the justice system are presenting with mental health issues symptomatic of BPD. To date, the most highly regarded treatment for BPD is dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT). DBT is comprised of aspects of cognitive-behavior therapy techniques, relaxation and soothing skills, and instruction of and improvement of self-awareness skills. The effectiveness of DBT among adults with BPD has been exhausted through various randomized controlled trials (RCTs), demonstrating positive results. Standard DBT has been adapted overtime, one such application includes a focus on the skills training component of DBT (i.e., DBT-skills training; DBT-ST) which has demonstrated similar results to standard DBT. Another application has been using DBT with adolescent populations. Although existing investigations among adolescent populations have had some methodological limitations, positive results have been yielded. The proposed study aims to examine the effectiveness of DBT-ST (18 weeks) as compared to treatment as usual (TAU) among male (n = 50) and female (n = 50) adolescent offenders through a RCT in a Canadian youth custodial facility. Furthermore, gender differences common in the BPD literature (females present with BPD more often than males) will be explored among adolescent offenders in terms of BPD features and treatment outcomes. Lastly, rates of re-offending will be examined by reviewing the Canadian Police Information Centre (CPIC; Canadian national crime database) one year post-treatment. It is anticipated that implementation of an appropriate treatment may improve mental health, behavioural problems, and decrease rates of re-offending among adolescent offenders. The aforementioned program of research has the potential to influence the manner in which the Canadian justice system assesses and rehabilitates youth offenders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Caring Places for Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias:  Examining the Continuum of Rural Care Settings
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE STUDY/QUALITATIVE METHODS; COMMUNITY SUPPORT; HEALTH CARE SETTINGS; HEALTH NEEDS; HEALTH POLICY/PLANNING; HEALTH SERVICES; INFORMAL CARE; MENTAL HEALTH/ADRD; RURAL HEALTH; SUITABLITY OF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: The prevalence of Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) is increasing across the country.  At the same time, older people in Canada are choosing to age in their homes and communities.  Care for the older population in general, and aging people living with ADRD more specifically, is taking place in many diverse settings with medical and social dimensions.  Where people live with, and find care for, ADRD has raised concerns about the uneven availability, accessibility and suitability of services in specific locations, particularly rural areas that generally have fewer formal health services and a higher proportion of seniors than urban areas.  Although most people with ADRD receive care in their homes at the onset of the disease, the majority die in institutionalized settings.  How people living with ADRD experience and use care in rural areas is not yet well understood.  The study examines the continuum of care settings and the suitability of care services for those living with ADRD, including family/support networks, in rural areas.  The research features a case study of service providers, informal carers and seniors in rural Ontario.  It will involve focus groups and interviews to assess the roles, resources, challenges and strategies associated with providing care for those with ADRD in formal and informal settings, as well as oral histories to gather in-depth stories of care from service users.  The research will answer the questions: how do those living with/caring for someone with ADRD experience places of care and what are their specific needs and challenges over the course of the disease?   The research will look at how care needs change in relation to settings of care and the services available in each setting with the goal of developing place-specific and person-centred approaches to care. The research will inform future policy development and contribute in a meaningful way to the lives of those with ADRD, their families and their communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Child pedestrian injury in the City of Toronto: The role of the built environment and active school transportation
Keywords-MotsClés: BUILT ENVIRONMENT; CASE CONTROL; CHILD CYCLIST; CHILD PEDESTRIAN; CROSS SECTIONAL; ROAD TRAFFIC INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Parents indicate traffic injury risk is a leading reason why children are not allowed or encouraged to walk to school. The risk of injury when walking has been highlighted in the media recently with a disturbing spike of twelve pedestrian fatalities in January 2010 in the City of Toronto.  Pedestrian injuries are in fact, one of the leading causes of injury worldwide.      Inactivity in children who don't walk or cycle, however, contributes to the growing problem of obesity and health related diseases.  Increasing walking if planned poorly, can lead to injury.  Unsafe roads or perception of unsafe roads will interfere with any effort to encourage walking to school.  This research will look at how the safety of the physical (built) environment around schools can promote active school transportation (AST) and decrease the risk of child pedestrian injury.  It will also investigate how parents' perceptions of injury influence whether their children walk/bike to school. This research will include analysis including mapping of child pedestrian/cyclist collisions to determining where and when they occur.  Analysis of police collision data will be done to find out how the built environment influences where collisions occur. Observations of how children get to school, the safety of the school built environment including measurement of traffic speed, and surveys of parents regarding how dangerous they think it is for their children to walk/cycle to school will be done. It is important that all these factors be examined together, so that the risk of injury risk and/or the perception of risk will not be a barrier to a healthier more active lifestyle for Toronto's children. Not only does this research address a leading cause of child death, but it also investigates barriers to an active healthy living behavior with lifelong benefits.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relationship between jump landing biomechanics and neuromuscular risk factors for anterior cruciate ligament injury in adolescents.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT; ANTERIOR CRUCIATE LIGAMENT; DYNAMOMETRY; INJURY PREVENTION; LANDING BIOMECHANICS; MUSCLE POWER; MUSCLE STRENGTH; NEUROMUSCULAR TRAINING; VIDEO MOTION ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries of the knee are significantly more common in women as compared to men. The disparity in ACL injury rates between the sexes arises around the time of puberty. Despite this, few studies have involved prepubescent participants.    Landing awkwardly from a jump has been identified as a particularly high risk movement for ACL injury. However there has been limited study on the degree to which the amount of neuromuscular strength and power possessed by an individual contributes to poor movement patterns when landing from a jump. The inclusion of strength and power training in prevention programs have been shown to improve landing technique as well as decrease the incidence of ACL injury in adult and adolescent athletes. Unfortunately, the majority of these studies have combined strength and power training interventions, and so it is difficult to conclude which method of training is more effective in improving jump landing parameters.    The purpose of this project is to first investigate the relationship between the strength and power of the major muscle groups of the hip and knee and the movement patterns demonstrated when landing from a jump in both girls and boys. The secondary purpose is to determine whether high intensity strength or power training involving the legs can change the position of the leg in girls and boys performing a drop jump.    The results of this study will help to identify the key muscle groups that contribute to landing patterns which may put a young person at risk for ACL injury. It will also help to focus on the most effective methods of neuromuscular training to use in order to prevent ACL injury. Considering that ACL injuries are physically, emotionally and financially costly and often lead to long term consequences such as knee osteoarthritis, it is important to identify the most efficient and effective ways of preventing this significant injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the Link between PCP Signalling and Ciliogenesis in Embryonic Development and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELL SIGNALLING; CILIOGENESIS; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; EMBRYOLOGY; GENETICS; IN VIVO IMAGING; PLANAR CELL POLARITY; POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Cilia are hair-like projections that are present on the surface of virtually every vertebrate cell and serve as antenna for environmental signals. They were previously considered evolutionary artefacts, but recent evidence implicating them in diverse human diseases, has revived interest into their formation and function. There is now even a class of human disorders referred to as ciliopathies, which have been shown to have a ciliary basis. These diverse defects include male infertility, obesity, blindness, mental retardation, polycystic kidney disease, and cancer. In addition to sensory cilia, there are also motile cilia that beat and generate directional fluid flow, which among other things, is important during embryonic development. In order to generate continuous flow, the position and tilt of cilia must be coordinated across a field of cells however the processes that control cilia formation are poorly understood. I chose zebrafish as my model organism to investigate the factors that are responsible for cilia formation. Since zebrafish are vertebrates, they share many of the mechanisms that regulate human development and are therefore ideal for modeling many human diseases. In addition, zebrafish develop very rapidly, progressing from egg to larvae stages in less than three days, and their embryos are transparent, enabling the visualization of internal structures. To aid my analysis, I have developed a marker which is a fusion of a protein that normally localizes along the entire length of the cilium to Green Fluorescent Protein. For the first time, cilia can be labelled in living embryos and their structure and motion can be monitored on a fluorescent or laser microscope. Using this tool, I have determined that the protein Vangl2 is required for proper positioning and tilting of motile cilia. I am also studying mutants that do not form cilia to determine the role cilia play in embryonic development and the onset of polycystic kidney disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of microRNA expression by interleukin-10 in activated macrophages
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES; IMMUNOLOGY; IMMUNOREGULATION; INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGES; MICRORNAS; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; REAL-TIME PCR; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammation is a protective response against infection but it must be appropriately controlled and terminated to avoid pathological consequences. A key anti-inflammatory regulator of immune cells is a cytokine (a type of hormone) called interleukin-10 (IL-10). The importance of IL-10 in regulating immune cell function is illustrated by the fact that many tumour cells and intracellular pathogens produce or elicit production of IL-10 to enhance their survival. Thus, understanding the mechanism by which IL-10 regulates the network of intracellular signal transduction pathways will not only provide insight into development of therapeutics mimicking the beneficial, anti-inflammatory effects of IL-10, it will also allow development of strategies to counter the immunosuppressive effects of certain tumours and immune cell pathogens.   Recent research shows that IL-10 may, in part, regulate immune cell function through altering the amount of small RNAs (microRNAs, abbreviated miRNA) found in cells. There are approximately 1000 different miRNAs in the mammalian genome, each of which controls a specific network of genes.  Stimulation of immune cells such as the macrophage with bacteria (or with substances found on the surface of bacteria) leads to changes in the levels of certain miRNAs.  We have found that IL-10 counteracts some of these changes, and may indeed induce some specific changes that are important in IL-10 inhibition of cell activation. One miRNA of particular interest is miR-155.  We now propose i) to continue to investigate how IL-10 regulates miR-155 levels, ii) to systematically identify all the miRNAs whose levels change in cells treated with IL-10, and iii) to determine the contribution of each miRNA to the ability of IL-10 to inhibit inflammation.    These studies will lead to a better understanding of how IL-10 works and the knowledge can be used to develop miRNA-based therapeutic strategies to mimic or inhibit IL-10 action when needed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Signatures of a successful immune response against hepatitis C virus
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALLING; FLOWCYTOMETRY; GENE EXPRESSION; HCV TREATMENT; HEPATITIS C VIRUS (HCV); IMMUNOLOGY; PHOSFLOW; REAL-TIME PCR
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection usually causes a life-long persistent infection in humans that can lead to irreversible liver damage and even cancer.  It is estimated that the number of persons currently infected with HCV in the world is approximately 130 million individuals.  There is no vaccine for hepatitis C and the only available treatment is expensive, has many side effects and is effective only in half of the infected population.  Despite the progress we made in understanding the immune response against hepatitis C, we still lack a great deal of knowledge about what distinguishes a good immune response against HCV that can protect against new infections.  Our previous results demonstrated that a successful immune response is characterized by an increase in the expression of molecules associated with the long-term survival of white blood cells specific for hepatitis C.  In this proposal, we plan to study the early events following infection with hepatitis C.  We will use novel techniques that will measure the activity of genes that are activated in individuals who can successfully clear Hepatitis C infection without the need for therapy.  This will help us develop methods to predict early whether someone will clear the virus or not.  Defining this successful immune response profile will set the ultimate characteristic that should be achieved by new vaccines and should be used as a measure of their efficacy and success.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism through which a novel life-extending compound delays aging by controlling a nutrition sensing signaling network governed by the nutrient-sensory protein kinases PKA and Rim15p
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; BIOLOGICAL NETWORKS; CELL BIOLOGY; CELLULAR AGING; MECHANISMS OF AGING; MICROSCOPY; NUTRIENT SENSING; PROTEIN KINASES; PROTEOMICS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Aging of multicellular eukaryotic organisms, including humans, affects numerous processes within cells. Some of these processes damage cellular macromolecules and organelles, while the others prevent the collapse of cellular homeostasis by repairing the damage. A lifelong accumulation of unrepaired cellular damage causes the progressive decline in the ability of the organism to resist stress, damage and disease, thereby increasing a risk of death. A challenge is to understand how the spatiotemporal organization of damage-producing and damage-repairing processes influences longevity and how cells integrate and control these processes. The baker's yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a unicellular eukaryote, is a valuable model for unveiling the complexity of the aging process in multicellular eukaryotes. Our recent studies have identified several small molecules that significantly delay aging in yeast. We found that these novel anti-aging compounds have several beneficial effects in human cells by delaying processes that promote aging and age-related disorders. Here, I propose a series of experiments that will test how these novel compounds delay aging by influencing the nutritional status of yeast cells, their response to the excess or limitation of nutrients, and their metabolism under various nutritional conditions. Because the anti-aging compounds that I will be using in my study as a research tool for elucidating the mechanisms of aging in yeast also delay the pace of age-related malfunction of human cells, my study is expected to provide the knowledge that is fundamental to understanding the molecular defects underlying numerous disorders of aging, including neurodegenerative diseases, atherosclerosis, chronic inflammation and type 2 diabetes. Therefore, my study is expected to facilitate the development of future therapeutic approaches to the treatment of these disorders and extending human healthspan.

TitreApplicationTitle: Influence of a sex hormone ratio on sympathetic nerve activity
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMANS; MENSTRUAL CYCLE; MICRONEUROGRAPHY; NEURAL RECRUITMENT; SEX DIFFERENCES; SEX HORMONES; SYMPATHETIC NERVE ACTIVITY; SYMPATHOEXCITATION; SYMPATHOINHIBITION; VASCULAR OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: The sympathetic nervous system affects blood pressure, heart rate, and many other important physiological variables. As such, disturbances within the sympathetic nervous system are often associated with diseases such as hypertension and atherosclerosis. The evidence supporting a link between levels of sex hormones (e.g. estrogen, testosterone) and sympathetic nerve activity (SNA) is growing. Most of this evidence comes from clinical populations. For instance, women with polycystic ovarian syndrome often have higher levels of testosterone than controls. These women have increased levels of SNA and are at increased risk for cardiovascular disease. Similarly, postmenopausal women have reduced levels of estrogen relative to premenopausal women, and are at increased risk for cardiovascular disease. Since SNA seems closely related to both hormone levels and the development of disease in clinical populations, it is possible that sex hormones influence nerve activity in healthy young people long before the onset of cardiovascular disease. Therefore, this project will address the question of whether sex hormone levels can predict SNA in healthy young subjects. We will collect data from men and women to determine how gender-based differences in hormone levels affect SNA. We will also test women at two phases of their menstrual cycle to determine how short-term fluctuations in hormone levels affect SNA. In addition, this project will make use of several novel techniques to help clarify the role of sex hormones in cardiovascular control: we will measure a sex hormone ratio which takes both estrogen and testosterone into account in both men and women, a new method of SNA analysis will be used to gain insight into the types of sympathetic neurons that are active at rest and during stress, and finally in addition to stressing the sympathetic system, we will also incorporate relaxation maneuvers designed to inhibit SNA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the role of the microbiota in susceptibility to inflammatory bowel disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL CARE AND HANDLING; CYTOKINE BEAD ARRAY/ELISA; GASTROENTERITIS; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; MICROBIOTA; MICROSCOPY; MULTI-COLOUR FACS; PRIMARY CELL ISOLATION; REAL-TIME QPCR
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including ulcerative colitis (UC), is a debilitating disease characterized by chronic inflammation caused by multiple factors involving the immune system and the intestinal microbiota. It is a disease that is increasing in prevalence worldwide and currently affecting over 200,000 Canadian children, women and men. Recently, the millions of commensal bacteria mammals harbour, termed the microbiota, have been implicated as an initiating factor of this disease. The microbiota is essential for nutrient acquisition, metabolism of indigestible compounds, defense against colonization by pathogens, and the function of the immune system. Patients suffering from UC exhibit significant differences in composition of the intestinal microbiota compared to healthy individuals but it is unknown if this difference precedes and contributes to the onset of UC or if it is a result of UC.   During the disease stage of UC, immune defenses break down, such as the intestinal mucus layer. In my research, I aim to characterize how antibiotic administration changes the composition of the intestinal microbiota and determine if these changes are sufficient to alter immune defenses in the intestine. The intestinal mucus is a critical defense barrier between microbes and host, preventing constant inflammation in response to the microbiota. Our hypothesis is that by changing the composition of the microbiota, using antibiotics, this defense will break down and subsequently increase susceptibility to colitis. The model system I will use involves utilizing the natural mouse pathogen, Citrobacter rodentium, which results in intestinal inflammation with similar features as UC.   This work will increase our understanding of the interplay between the microbiota and immune responses, and how this impacts colitis. Issues central to understanding IBD in general, and may lead to the development of new diagnostic and therapeutic tools.

TitreApplicationTitle: Parental depression and child psychopathology: a comparison of factors that impact child outcome in two longitudinal studies.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD AND ADOLESCENT HEALTH; CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; CLINICAL RESEARCH; DEPRESSION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LONGITUDINAL STUDIES; PHARMACOTHERAPY; POPULATION; PSYCHIATRY; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Children of parents suffering from Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) have an increased risk of developing psychiatric disorders. Nearly one in four people will experience a depressive disorder throughout their lifetime and studies show that more than half of children with a depressed parent will develop a mental health diagnoses such as mood, anxiety, and behavioral disorders. Certain factors can impact a child's vulnerability to developing these disorders and the severity of symptoms present. For instance, when a depressed parent goes into remission from depression (i.e.gets better), their children have significantly fewer mental health symptoms than children of parents who remain depressed. Characteristics such as the parent-child relationship, parental stress, social, and school problems can also impact the child's mental health. In this study, we will characterize and compare mental health symptoms and severity, and overall well-being in two groups of children at-risk for depression.The first group will consist of children of parents undergoing medication treatment for MDD in a clinical study; the second group will include children of parents with depression in a population sample.We will aim to identify specific characteristics (i.e.parental remission)in these samples that can help us explain and predict long-term outcomes for these children.We will also offer education sessions regarding depression to children and parents in the clinical sample and monitor the benefits of these sessions on outcome.This study can offer important insight to better understand factors that influence the health of children of depressed parents. Such knowledge is imperative in implementation and timing of interventions and patient education.For instance, in further understanding the influence of the parent's depression status on child health, we can share the urgency of early and aggressive treatment of parental MDD in the clinic and encourage parents to seek, and stick with treament.

TitreApplicationTitle: Develop Comprehensive Intervention Strategies for TB in Aboriginal Communities Using Mathematical Modeling
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; APPLIED MATHEMATICS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; INTERVENTION STRATEGIES; MATHEMATICAL BIOLOGY; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; PUBLIC HEALTH; TRANSMISSION; TREATMENT DELAY; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: TB incidence in Aboriginal communities is 20 to 50 times higher than that among Canadian-born non-Aboriginal peoples. The high incidence indicates that TB transmission is highly active in these communities. The probability of transmission and chances of new cases is increased if there is a long period between infection and treatment. Social and cultural factors and general lack of access to health care in Aboriginal communities have created a serious treatment delay.  Long treatment delay combined with overcrowded housing and high mobility among reserves creates a real possibility for high transmission. Interventions that reduce treatment delays can have a significant and direct effect on incidence reduction. Mathematical modeling is an effective tool that can qualitatively and quantitatively assess impacts of different intervention strategies and help develop a comprehensive approach to TB control.   The proposed research aims to: 1) develop mathematical models that help describe and understand TB transmission dynamics in Aboriginal communities; 2) use mathematical models integrated with real data to conduct cost-benefit analyses on potential intervention strategies; and 3) provide recommendations based on model outcomes to policy makers.   Using mathematical models to address public health issues is an innovative method of approach. The proposed research is highly interdisciplinary and will be carried out in close collaboration with mathematical modellers and public health researchers. We expect the research will provide insight and recommendations for comprehensive TB control strategies for these communities. The interdisciplinary modeling approach developed from this project can be applied to investigate other infectious diseases and public health issues in Aboriginal communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Relationship Variables on the Outcomes of Quality of Life and Sexual Satisfaction among Multiple Sclerosis Patients with Sexual Dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL MEDICINE; MENTAL HEALTH; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: 55,000 to 75,000 Canadians have Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Sexual dysfunction (SD) is reported in up to 73.1% of MS patients and is associated with significant decreases in quality of life (QOL) and sexual satisfaction. Few studies have examined predictors of sexual satisfaction for MS patients, an outcome that cannot be overlooked given its importance in maintaining strong partnerships and the crucial role of partner support in predicting improved QOL. Relationship variables, such as marital satisfaction, may mediate the relationship between SD and sexual satisfaction/QOL. Uncovering mediators of the relationship between SD and sexual satisfaction/QOL is an important step in identifying targets for a behavioral intervention to enhance such outcomes. Little research has been conducted on psychological interventions for couples living with MS. 110 couples with MS were recruited and participants completed an online survey measuring SD, sexual satisfaction, QOL, relationship satisfaction, and partner support. Year 1: A meditational analysis will be conducted to investigate the meditational role of relationship variables between SD and the outcomes of sexual satisfaction and QOL. Gender differences will also be explored. It is hypothesized that worse scores on relationship variables will be associated with poorer sexual satisfaction and QOL. A dyadic analysis will examine how a couples agreement on relationship variables corresponds to the outcomes of sexual satisfaction and QOL. Interviews will be conducted with 5 of the most and 5 of the least satisfied couples to determine what factors might be important in developing a couples intervention. Year 2: Based on these findings, a couples intervention will be designed and pilot tested to increase QOL and sexual satisfaction among couples.  Research into the development of an intervention for couples with MS is crucial given the dearth of research on interventions for this chronically ill population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Longitudinal study of nightmare frequency in relation to psychosocial adjustment from pre-adolescence to adolescence.
Keywords-MotsClés: CAUCHEMARS; DEVELOPPEMENT; ENFANTS; PSYCHOPATHOLOGIES
Abstract-Résumé: Nightmares are one of the most commonly reported sleep disorders in both children and adults.  Much of the research on nightmares has focused on their assessment and clinical correlates in adult populations but relatively little is known about nightmares in children. Increased nightmare frequency in adults is correlated with important sleep disturbances, including sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance insomnia, increased severity of psychological and psychiatric symptoms, and poor physical health. The few studies having investigated nightmares in children also report important links to measures of psychosocial maladjustment, including stress, anxiety and behavioural problems. Although many adult nightmare sufferers without any history of trauma report that their nightmares started during childhood, the processes by which children's nightmares persist into adulthood remain poorly understood.  The proposed research aims to elucidate developmental processes involved in the emergence and persistence of nightmares in children.  A longitudinal study of 150 children assessed annually from ages 11 to 16 years old will be used to investigate the psychosocial correlates of nightmares in children (e.g., anxiety, emotional difficulties, aggressivity) and to document the evolution of these relationships over time. This research will lead to a better understanding of the development course of nightmares, their correlates, and may also help develop neurocognitive models of nightmare production in children as well as inform treatment strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tissue Engineering Therapies for Bone Regeneration in Cleft Palates
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MORPHOGENETIC PROTEINS; BONE REGENERATION; CLEFT PALATE; GENE THERAPY; GROWTH FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Cleft palate is a congenital defect which develops due to a combination of genetics and environmental factors and occurs in 1.7 per 1000 live born infants worldwide. Infants with cleft palates have an opening in the roof of the upper jaws where the two sides of the hard palate did not fuse together during the infant development. The cleft affects speech, hearing and physical appearance leading to poor long-term health and psychology outcomes of these patients. Children with cleft defects need multidisciplinary health care from birth till adulthood. Treatment of cleft defects typically requires grafting the defect using bone obtained from the same patient to close the cleft defect. But, bone grafting is not always successful. Also for the child, bone grafting needs prolonged healing time together with associated risk of infection and significant pain at both cleft palate site and donor site. Therefore, there is a call for alternative treatments to decrease the severity of the side effects associated with donor site injury and limited supply of donor bone. To overcome current grafting limitations my research focuses on developing tissue engineering approach to provide more effective and minimally invasive treatment options for cleft patients. Naturally occurring proteins that can promote bone growth (bone morphogenetic proteins) will be delivered to bone marrow cells, which are well known for its high regenerative potential. After optimizing the conditions for bone regeneration in cell culture, the bone morphogenetic proteins and cells will be delivered using innovative materials and tested in selected animal model, with cleft palate defect, to insure its biological efficacy and safety. This study will develop an effective bioactive graft and will establish a foundation for tissue engineering solution for cleft palates that have minimal side effects and therefore increasing the quality of life for cleft palate patients.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES
TitreApplicationTitle: The Design and Optimization of 3-OH Anthranilate Analogues as Amyloid-Beta Antiaggregants: A Mechanism of Action Study on a Novel Class of Potential Therapeutics for Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: 3-OH ANTHRANILATE; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE THERAPEUTIC; AMYOLID-BETA PROTEIN; COMPUTATIONAL MODELING; DRUG SYNTHESIS/OPTIMIZATION; DRUG-PROTEIN BINDING; MECHANISM OF ACTION STUDIES; PROTEIN AMYLOIDOSIS; RATIONAL DRUG DESIGN
Abstract-Résumé: Accounting for 100,000 deaths annually, Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the fourth leading cause of deaths in North America, surpassed only by heart disease, cancer and stroke. Existing treatments for AD fail to address the underlying causes of disease progression, and merely provide short-term relief from the symptoms of the disease.  The amyloid hypothesis of AD implicates amyloid-beta (ABeta) protein misfolding as the root of the disease. Small clumps of ABeta have been shown to be toxic to the brain in AD. As such, preventing the formation of these clumps of ABeta may prevent brain damage - addressing the underlying disease cause, thereby preventing AD altogether; not merely masking the disease symptoms.   Using computer modeling we have identified the molecule 3-OH anthranilate (HOA) as a potent antiaggregant - a preventer of ABeta clump formation - and may be a potential AD therapeutic; these results were confirmed using biological testing. Using HOA as a starting point, over 25 similar molecules have been synthesized - 9 of which have are even better antiaggregants. These molecules provide insight into future drug-like molecules that will be synthesized and tested. Over 50 HOA-like molecules have been tested for antiaggregant activity.  To better understand how these drug-like molecules interact with ABeta we are to conduct studies using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Diffusion spectroscopy will be used to investigate molecule-protein interactions. These experiments will provide better insight into the nature of these interactions and will allow us to optimize our computer models; in doing so we will be better able to use our computer models to predict the structure of more potent antiaggregants. With further optimization these new molecules are a starting point for potential drugs to be used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease. Ultimately we wish to develop a new class of molecules to be used as AD therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and evaluation of a knowledge translation strategy to improve influenza immunization rates among pregnant women
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH BEHAVIOURS; INTERVENTION STUDY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Pregnant women are at high risk for influenza-related complications.  Influenza vaccine is a safe and effective way to prevent influenza among pregnant women and their infants.  However, the proportion of pregnant women receiving the vaccine remains low, ranging between 2-14%.  To address this issue, the project goal is to develop and evaluate a strategy to improve influenza vaccine uptake during pregnancy.  The project has the following three objectives: 1) Identify the barriers and facilitators to influenza vaccine uptake during pregnancy; 2) Develop a strategy based on identified barriers and interviews with pregnant women and healthcare professionals; 3) Put the strategy into practice and evaluate the impact of the strategy.  Barriers to influenza vaccine uptake will be identified by reviewing existing literature on vaccine attitudes, beliefs and behaviour of pregnant women and their healthcare providers.  Interviews will be conducted with pregnant women, vaccine providers and healthcare professionals to determine their attitudes and opinions of different strategies to improve vaccine uptake.  A strategy will be developed based on the identified barriers and the results from the interviews. The developed strategy will be put into practice and evaluated.  Influenza vaccine rates during pregnancy will be compared between groups that applied the strategy and groups that did not use the strategy.   The resulting strategy can be used to encourage influenza vaccine uptake among pregnant women in subsequent influenza seasons.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Sustainable Approach to Reducing Worm Infections in School-Aged Children in Developing Countries: A Randomized Controlled Trial of an Educational Intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPING COUNTRIES; EQUITY; GENDER; GLOBAL HEALTH; HEALTH EDUCATION; POPULATION HEALTH INTERVENTION; SCHOOL-AGE CHILDREN; SUSTAINABILITY; TRIAL; WORM INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Intestinal worm infections are a major public health problem in developing countries because they add to malnutrition, increase the risk of acquiring other infections, reduce intellectual capabilities and cause lifelong health deficits.  The World Health Organization estimates that worm infections occur in about 130 countries worldwide and that approximately one billion schoolchildren are at risk of these infections. Infection occurs either by ingesting water, food or other items contaminated with fecal material, or when worm larvae, present in contaminated soil, directly penetrate the skin. Having worms in the gut can impact health in many ways, especially in children. Since worms exist in areas where poverty and malnutrition are highest, children have a double burden. Their growth can be stunted, they are more likely to have anemia, they are absent from school more often and they do not have the opportunity to play like non-infected children. The consequences of worm infections in childhood last a lifetime. There are drugs that can be used to treat worm infections. However, drug programs can be expensive and the effects are only temporary. In order to have a more lasting effect on reducing worm infections, my research proposal aims to study the impact of adding specific information on worm prevention practices in grade schools. In addition, I would like to study if boys and girls use this information in different ways. The study would be conducted in the schools of a poor area of Peru called Belen, where it is known that most schoolchildren are infected with worms. The results of this research would benefit not only Peruvian schoolchildren but all schoolchildren who live in areas where worm infections occur.

TitreApplicationTitle: Confidence, Mobility, and Participation with using a Wheelchair: A study of aging wheelchair users
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CONFIDENCE; ITEM RESPONSE THEORY; MEASUREMENT; OLDER ADULTS; PARTICIPATION; RASCH MODELING; REHABILITATION; SELF-EFFICACY; WHEELCHAIR MOBILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Wheelchairs are an important form of technology for Canadians as over 250,000 Canadians rely on wheelchairs to move around their communities. The use of a wheelchair by those with mobility impairments is expected to facilitate independence, however, 59% of wheelchair users between the ages of 65 and 84, and 76% of users 85 years of age and older are reported to have problems with using their wheelchair. Despite knowledge that such problems lead to compromised mobility and social participation among aging wheelchair users, little else is known about these two important aspects, largely because there is a dearth of research on the determinants of both mobility and participation with using a wheelchair.   Confidence is the belief individuals have in their ability to do things. Because research consistently demonstrates various forms of confidence as important determinants of what people do, confidence with using a wheelchair likewise may have important implications on the mobility and social participation of wheelchair users. These relationships, however, have not yet been investigated, largely because up until now there hasn't been an adequate tool to capture relevant information.  The purpose of this proposed multi-site study is to develop a better understanding of confidence with using a manual wheelchair among aging wheelchair users in Vancouver, BC and Quebec City, QC. This research will use the new Wheelchair Use Confidence Scale (WheelCon) to capture the construct of interest. Because the WheelCon is a recently developed tool, the first study will be to refine the WheelCon using contemporary measurement methods. Next, in a cross-sectional study using regression analyses, we will address the hypotheses that confidence with using a wheelchair is a significant determinant of: 1) wheelchair mobility; 2) self-reported frequency of participation; and 3) satisfaction with participation, among aging wheelchair users after controlling for important covariates.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovering Pathways to Health Equity: Assessing the Impact of Population Health Interventions that Target Behavioural Risk Factors in Reducing Social Inequalities in Coronary Heart Disease in Ontario.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTORS; CORONARY HEART DISEASE; INCIDENCE; MACROSIMULATION MODELS; PATHWAYS TO HEALTH EQUITY; POPULATION HEALTH INTERVENTIONS; PROSEPCTIVE LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS; PUBLIC HEALTH POLICY; SOCIOECONOMIC POSITION
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is a leading cause of illness and mortality in Canada; a condition which disproportionately affects populations who experience the greatest social and economic disadvantage. People of low socioeconomic status, measured as low levels of education, occupation and income, are more likely to develop and die from heart disease compared to people of higher socioeconomic statuses. Studies have shown that risk factors for heart disease, for example obesity, smoking, physical activity and diet, tend to occur more frequently, and often appear together, in individuals with low socioeconomic status. The goal of the study is to help determine which heart disease risk factors are most influential in causing the increase in heart disease among individuals of low socioeconomic status. To answer this important research question, the authors will investigate a series of what if scenarios regarding potential changes to levels of heart disease risk factors in a population of Ontarians. For example, will increasing the number of physically active Ontarians, or decreasing the number of Ontarians who smoke heavily be more effective in closing the gap in heart disease between individuals with low compared to high socioeconomic status? Additionally, the proposed research will explore whether policies and programs to reduce heart disease risk factors should focus on the whole population, or only on individuals with lower socioeconomic status. Answering these questions are essential to identifying which heart disease risk factors, and which groups of individuals, should be targeted by public health programs and policies to reduce the burden of heart disease in individuals with low socioeconomic status. This research will provide policy-makers with the evidence necessary to act, and help reduce heart disease in Ontario.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of PTP1B in prostate cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BIOCHEMISTRY; BIOMARKERS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROSTATE CANCER; PROTEOMICS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SUBSTRATE IDENTIFICATION; TRANSGENICS; TYROSINE PHOSPHATASES
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed malignancy and second leading cause of cancer related death in North American men. An important correlation exists between increased obesity and increased risk of developing prostate cancer. This project will utilize cutting edge research technology to examine the function that a protein named PTP1B plays in prostate cancer. Identified as a target for new anti-diabetic drugs, in collaboration with other members of the laboratory, our preliminary results suggest that increased PTP1B is associated with an increase in initiation and progression of prostate cancer. As these new anti-PTP1B drugs will shortly enter the market for metabolic diseases such as type II diabetes and obesity, it is critical to better understand the consequence of inhibiting PTP1B in prostate cancer. By combining both cellular and animal based approaches, we will identify new cellular markers and targets that can be exploited for both screening and potential treatment options in prostate cancer. My objective is to provide all the validation and crucial information required to rapidly move anti-PTP inhibitors to the prostate cancer clinic. To complete this goal I am also generating a novel prostate cancer mouse model, which will be used to study disease progression and efficacy of PTP1B inhibitors in a preclinical setting. This project is at the forefront of identifying novel prostate cancer markers that can serve as new targets for prostate cancer therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Uterine-derived biological agents for therapeutic application in myocardial infarction
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; UTERINE BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Newts are able to regenerate their tails after losing them to predators. This is one example of tissue regeneration. In adult humans, tissue regeneration is limited. However, the human uterus is a specialized organ with ability for regeneration. The inside lining of the uterus is shed during menstruation but grows back every month. In the case of pregnancy, large amounts of the inside lining of the uterus is lost during labour but is grown back after delivery. This happens in part because the uterus contains specialized cells or cell products that can support tissue regeneration by helping create new blood vessels. In this study, we would like harness the blood vessel producing ability of the uterus to repair the heart in women with heart disease. Hearts in such a condition are in need of new blood vessels. In this project, we seek to identify the signals that support blood vessel generation in the uterus to create a drug that can be injected into damaged areas of the heart after a heart attack to assist the growth of new blood vessels and in this way enhance recovery. The new treatment may be an improved method of enhancing recovery after a heart attack.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of cluster C personality disorders in cognitive-behavioural treatment of generalized anxiety disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER; HIERARCHICAL LINEAR MODELING; PERSONALITY DISORDERS; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL; TREATMENT OUTCOME; TREATMENT RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is a commonly diagnosed mental illness that can have profound effects on professional, personal, and social levels. Its main feature is excessive, uncontrollable worry about a number of events or activities occurring more days than not for at least six months. An empirically-supported cognitive-behavioural treatment (CBT) protocol has been developed based on a cognitive model of GAD that centres around intolerance of uncertainty. However, not all treated individuals achieve full remission of their disorder for reasons that have not been conclusively established.  A potential barrier to effective GAD treatment may be Cluster C personality disorders: obsessive compulsive, avoidant, and dependent personality disorders. These disorders often co-occur with GAD, but there is a lack of consensus as to how this affects treatment response. This study will determine the role of Cluster C personality disorders in the CBT treatment of GAD. The main goals of the study are to determine if: 1) pre-treatment presence of a Cluster C personality disorder predicts poorer response to GAD treatment, and 2) pre-treatment severity of Cluster C personality disorders predicts poorer response to GAD treatment.  The participants are 110 Francophone adults in Montreal between ages 18 and 65 with a primary diagnosis of GAD, recruited from the Anxiety Disorders Clinic of Sacre-Coeur Hospital. Our CBT treatment is administered over 14 weekly sessions with licensed psychologists. The treatment components target specific processes in our model of GAD while building tolerance and acceptance of uncertainty at each stage.  This study will increase our understanding of the impact of Cluster C personality disorders on GAD treatment. If they have a significant impact on treatment outcomes this will inform clinical practice as to the importance of assessing for personality disorders and integrating symptom-specific interventions into the existing treatment.
