TitreApplicationTitle: Predictors of Symptoms Associated with the Menstrual Cycle and Hormonal Contraception
Keywords-MotsClés: FERTILITY; HORMONAL CONTRACEPTION; MENSTRUAL CYCLE; MENTAL HEALTH; PREDICTORS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL AND PHYSICAL SYMPTOMS; PROSPECTIVE AND RETROSPECTIVE DESIGN; PSYCHOENDOCRINOLOGY; REPRODUCTIVE EVENTS; SEXUAL HEALTH; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Recent research suggests that some women week or are prescribed a hormonal contraceptive (HC) due to menstrual  cycle problems such as premenstrual syndrome (PMS). However, HC use can result in physical and emotional side effects. This project will investigate women's experiences of symptoms associated with the menstrual cycle or HC use and whether they relate to past reproductive events or current hormone levels. The main research question is: how do women with such problems differ from relatively healthy women? Participants will be asked to fill out an initial online questionnaire about past and present reproductive events (including puberty, the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, the postpartum period, and HC use) and their associated physical and psychological symptoms. Information pertaining to demographics, personal and familial health, and medication and drug use will also be collected. Physical biomarkers of hormonal effects, the ratio of the length of the second digit to the fourth digit (2D:4D) and middle-phalangeal hair, will be measured by both the participants and a researcher where possible. Finally, women will complete a daily online survey of symptoms across the menstrual cycle (i.e., for approximately 1 month). Ovulation detection strips will be used to estimate the days and phases of the menstrual cycle and thus hormonal changes. Through the proposed research, Canadian may benefit from an increased understanding of the health-related effects of hormonal changes that take place during reproductive events. The results may have implications for women's sexual, mental, and physical health, including the treatment of menstrual cycle problems and the prescription of HCs. For example, it may contribute to the development of screening procedures for the risk of symptoms associated with the menstrual cycle and side effects associated with HC use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Delineate the role of neural stem cells in Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT NEUROGENESIS; AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; ANIMAL MODELS; HISTOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS; NEURAL STEM CELLS; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROSPHERES; SUBGRANULAR ZONE; SUBVENTRICULAR ZONE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive and fatal brain disease. Today, half a million Canadian have AD, with 71,000 of them under age 65. AD destroys brain cells, known as neurons, causing memory, thinking and behavior to become seriously affected. AD patients have less brain tissue compared to normal people and the shrinkage will get worse over time. At present, once a particular ability is lost, it is not known to return. However, it has recently been discovered that some special cells in the brain, called neural stem cells (NSCs), can generate new neurons throughout life, hence a potential therapy to replenish the loss of neurons in AD. Unfortunately, the capacity of these NSCs to generate new neurons declines with age. It is currently unknown whether such decline is, at least partially, causing the death of neurons in AD.  My research will examine whether there are any NSCs and their descendent progenitor cells in AD human patients using post-mortem tissue samples. I will inspect the NSCs and progenitor cells in terms of their distributions, properties and what cell types they give rise to. Likewise, I will also examine NSCs and their descendent progenitor cells in a mouse model of AD and evaluate the ability of NSCs to generate new neurons. Altogether, my research will provide fundamental understanding of neuron-generating mechanisms in humans throughout adult life, the consequence of extensive neuronal loss in AD on NSCs and progenitor cells, as well as the influence of aging on progression of AD. Ultimately, my research will provide valuable information when considering therapeutic application of replacing neurons from NSCs.

La methode appelee Exome, permettra de trouver des mutations rares dans de nouveaux genes qui causent de cette maladie.  Ainsi, en trouvant de nouveaux genes, il sera possible d'avoir une meilleure comprehension des mecanismes pathologiques conduisant a cette maladie et ainsi avoir un plus grand potentiel therapeutique.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Studies and Therapeutic applications of the Neurospora VS ribozyme
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; GENE THERAPY; MOLECULAR ENGINEERING; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE; RADIOCRYSTALLOGRAPHY; RNA; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; VIRAL INFECTION; VS RIBOZYME
Abstract-Résumé: Most of the enzymatic reactions are catalyzed by protein enzymes. There are also some ribonucleic enzymes, known as ribozymes that play essential roles in cells. The Neurospora VS ribozyme is a naturally-occurring ribozyme that has a great therapeutic potential because it recognizes and cleaves RNA substrates that are folded in a stem-loop conformation. By contrast, the other known naturally-occurring ribozymes cleave unfolded single-stranded regions. Given that most RNAs in cells adopt folded complex structures, the VS ribozyme has a unique potential for specific gene inactivation. However, the engineering of the VS ribozyme for cleavage of specific substrates is complicated by the lack of a complete high-resolution structure. My research objective is to determine the complete high-resolution structure of the VS ribozyme by using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy or X-ray crystallography. The proposed study will increase our understanding of substrate recognition and cleavage mechanism by the VS ribozyme. They will also be useful for engineering studies currently underway in the laboratory that aim to design VS-derived ribozymes for gene inactivation. Such ribozymes could be used for biomedical applications, such as in gene therapy treatments against viral infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Suppression of joint inflammation by infection with a helminth parasite: involvement of the nervous system.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVELY ACTIVATED MACROPHAGES; CANNABINOID RECEPTORS; ELISA; H. DIMINUTA; IL-10; IL-4; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INFLAMMATION; LIPOXIN; NEUROIMMUNITY; PCR
Abstract-Résumé: The global burden of musculoskeletal disease is immense, with rheumatoid arthritis being particularly debilitating and painful. All forms of arthritis are associated with major disability and with incidence rates ranging from 0.3-1.5%, hundreds of thousands of Canadians suffer from joint pain and loss of function. The treatments currently available to sufferers of inflammatory joint disease have limited effectiveness chronically and are often accompanied by undesirable side-effects. While the alleviation of patient suffering must be the primary concern, it is important to highlight the societal impact of arthritic disease. For example, in the late 1990s the healthcare costs attributed to arthritis was estimated at 0.8% of the gross domestic product, of which a major portion was due to indirect costs and loss of productivity due to illness. While advances in treating arthritis have been made, the limitations of current therapeutics will only be overcome by a better understanding of the mediators and mechanisms responsible for joint inflammation and pain. Through assessing the host-parasite interaction in mouse models of arthritis, we take a novel approach to unraveling the neuroimmune pathways involved in the pathogenesis and pain mechanisms associated with inflammatory joint disease. We contend that the data gleaned from assessing the biology of the host-parasite relationship between the tapeworm Hymenolepis diminuta in the mouse host will translate into a greater understanding of inflammatory disease and immuno-regulatory reactions, and will serve as the basis for the development of novel approaches to the treatment of joint inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: A role for integrin-linked kinase in oligodendrocyte mediated myelination of the central nervous system.
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOSKELETON; FOCAL ADHESION COMPLEXES; IMAGING; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; MYELIN; OLIGODENDROCYTE; ORGANOTYPIC SLICE CULTURE; REMYELINATION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Our project specific aim is to better understand the role of a small protein, integrin-linked kinase (ILK), in helping the cells of your brain produce the fatty insulating substance myelin.  Previous work in the field has shown a role for ILK in myelin production when cells are grown in a dish.  We have, therefore, generated genetically modified mice lacking the ILK protein specifically in myelin producing cells of the central nervous system.  During early development, these mice display defects in their ability to engulf nerves with myelin.  Interestingly, as the mice age, a compensatory mechanism is activated,allowing nerves to be properly surrounded by a thick layer of myelin.  Future work is aimed at better understanding the biological components involved in the compensatory mechanism; whether by another molecule with similar functions to ILK, or complete replacement of the ILK deficient cells by other normal fully functional myelin producing cells. Elucidating the mechanisms by which myelin is produced is fundamental to our understanding of Multiple Sclerosis, a debilatating disease affecting an estimated 75,000 Canadians.  Our work will allow us to discern important molecular mechanisms involved in communication between the myelin producing cells and their cellular environment.  Through our understanding of the mechanisms governing myelin production we can develop new therapies to aid those suffering from Multiple Sclerosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Age-related pathophysiological changes and targeted therapy in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL).
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA; CYTOKINE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GEFITINIB; HISTONE DEACETYLASE INHIBITORS; SPLEEN TYROSINE KINASE; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH; VALPROIC ACID
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is the most common form of leukemia. CLL is a disease of the elderly, and the survival rate falls with increasing age. We have identified potential factors that may explain this age-related phenomenon, and we are endeavouring to understand their mechanism of action. Another focus of my research project is characterizing new chemotherapy drugs that may be used to treat CLL. We are focusing on two drugs, Valproic Acid and Gefitinib, that are already in the clinics for treating other diseases.  Combining these drugs with the conventional therapy should result in reduced side effects and improved survival. Current experiments are aimed at better understanding the actions of the two drugs on CLL cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transdiagnostic Internet Cognitive-Behaviour Therapy for Cancer Survivors: A Feasibility Trial and Examination of Clinician Perspectives
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER CARE; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; DEPRESSION; INTERNET-COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SELF-REPORT MEASURES; THERAPEUTIC RELATIONSHIP; TREATMENT SATISFACTION
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is the most common mental disorder among cancer patients. Cancer patients with depression experience a poorer quality of life, have a higher risk of death, and incur greater costs to the health care system. Despite these negative implications, over half of cancer patients with mental health problems will not seek treatment for these problems. Research suggests that depression can be effectively treated with therapist guided Internet-cognitive behavioural therapy (I-CBT). I-CBT involves patients viewing therapy materials over the Internet, while receiving support and assistance from a therapist through e-mail. I-CBT may be particularly well-suited for cancer patients, as it could be easily administered and accessed as well as convenient for patients undergoing cancer treatment who may find it difficult to attend in-person appointments with a psychologist. I-CBT would also be cost-effective and relatively easy to incorporate into existing treatment programs for cancer. Despite these practical benefits and the research support for I-CBT, no I-CBT program for treating depression among cancer patients has been developed or tested. As part of the proposed project, cancer patients will receive a 12-week I-CBT program for depression. Prior to, and following the completion of this program, patients will also complete a set of questionnaires assessing depressive symptoms, quality of life, and other relevant outcomes. It is predicted that the I-CBT program will significantly lower depressive symptoms and enhance patients' quality of life.  Given its serious impacts on the individual as well as health care systems, the treatment of cancer-related depression is an urgent research priority.  By exploring this innovative method of providing treatment, the results of the proposed study will assist in reducing the psychosocial and economic burden of depression and cancer among Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Moderating effects of physical exercise and leisure activity on the course of cognitive impairment in prodromal Alzheimer disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; CHANGE POINT MODELLING; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; EARLY DETECTION OF DEMENTIA; HIERARCHICAL LINEAR MODELLING; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; PHYSICAL EXERCISE; POPULATION-BASED RESEARCH; PRECLINICAL DEMENTIA; PROSPECTIVE STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer disease (AD) is a devastating and costly neurological disorder that represents the 6th leading cause of death in North American adults and a serious economic burden on Canadian health care. There is no cure for AD but protective factors such as early life educational attainment and engagement in physical exercise (PE) or leisure activities (LA) later in life may delay the onset of cognitive decline in the years prior to diagnosis. Pending further study, these factors could represent valuable strategies for delaying AD onset and alleviating the burden of AD on Canada's aging population. The proposed program of research will examine the relative effects of LA and PE for ameliorating risk of AD and delaying loss of memory and other cognitive abilities during the dementia prodrome. These analyses will inform a subsequent investigation of the efficacy of PE and LA adjustments for strengthening the association between biomarker and neuropsychological risk profiles of AD. Taken together, these studies will evaluate the efficacy of late-life PE and LE for reducing risk, delaying onset and facilitating early detection of AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the effects of an angiotensin II receptor blocker on aortic valve sclerosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOTENSIN II RECEPTOR BLOCKER; AORTIC VALVE SCLEROSIS; HISTOPATHOLOGY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MICRO-COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; PRE-CLINICAL MODEL; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: The aortic valve is the outlet valve from the left ventricle, the main pumping chamber of the heart. Aortic valve sclerosis, the third most common cardiovascular disease, causes thickening and hardening of the aortic valve, impairing its function. Currently, little is known about how this disease progresses and as such, there are currently no preventative therapies available.  We have developed an animal model that recreates the human condition. Using this model, we have tested the effects of statins (cholesterol lowering therapy) on the progression of aortic valve sclerosis. Consistent with recent clinical trials, statins are unable to prevent progression of valve disease. However, we have recently discovered that an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB), a blood pressure medication, is capable of causing regression of aortic valve sclerosis.  We will build on this recent discovery by examining possible changes at the cellular and molecular levels. We will further examine the cellular changes in the valves obtained from our animal model using various techniques. In addition, we will examine possible molecular mechanisms of action using a cell-based model which mimics disease characteristics at the cellular level.  We anticipate that ARBs will limit inflammation and calcification in diseased aortic valves. Since our animal model closely resembles the human condition, we expect our results will be directly applicable to human patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing neuronal function and axonal integrity after spinal cord injury: an fMRI and DTI study
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL ASSESSMENT; DTI; FMRI; HUMAN; IMAGING; NEUROSCIENCE; SPINAL CORD; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to see the structure and function of the spinal cord immediately following a spinal cord injury would provide essential information for thorough and accurate assessment of a person's condition and to guide therapeutic efforts.  Currently, this information is not available to doctors, and assessments are based largely on what the patient can report about their condition.  Special imaging techniques based on MRI, such as diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have been used to assess the integrity of axons within the spinal cord, and spinal cord neuronal function, respectively.  These methods have the potential to dramatically change how spinal cord injuries are treated in hospitals.  The current study includes the use of multiple MR imaging techniques (DTI and fMRI) and aims to provide novel information regarding spinal cord anatomy and function in both healthy and injured people. Furthermore, we will determine whether the measures obtained from DTI can be used to predict functional outcomes.  Results from this study will be used to create a clinical assessment tool with the aim of providing greater insight to both doctors and patients in order to guide rehabilitation efforts, provide monitoring of treatment progress, and better outcome measures for clinical trials of new treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of H1N1 influenza during pregnancy on infant and early childhood outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: EARLY CHILDHOOD HEALTH; INFANT OUTCOMES; POPULATION-BASED BIRTH COHORT; PRENATAL INFLUENZA EXPOSURE
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza, also known as the flu, is an infectious illness caused by a virus that affects the nose, throat and lungs. Most people who get the flu are mildly affected; but others, for example people with illnesses such as asthma or heart disease, may develop more serious illness leading to hospitalization and/or death. We know that women who are pregnant are also more susceptible to serious illness and complications related to the flu, likely due to complex biological changes that take place during pregnancy. However, our understanding about the impact of the flu in pregnant women on the health of their infants after birth is limited. It is important to know whether babies, whose mothers are infected with the flu while pregnant, have health or developmental problems later in their childhood.   This research project will explore the influence of mothers having had the flu during pregnancy on the health of their infants during the first three years after birth. Furthermore, this research will reflect the specific time period of the recent H1N1 pandemic, about which very little is known concerning the impact on mothers and newborns. An understanding of whether or not those infants whose mothers became ill with the flu while pregnant experience health or developmental problems during early childhood can influence future treatment and preventative measures for pregnant women. It can also help ensure that infants, if they are determined to be susceptible to health or developmental problems due to exposure to the flu before they were born, are identified and receive assessment and care in a timely manner.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the role of Nur77 in lymphocyte development in the thymus
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH; FLOW CYTOMETRY; IMMUNOLOGY; LINEAGE COMMITMENT; LYMPHOCYTE DEVELOPMENT; NK CELLS; T CELLS; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system is responsible for protecting our bodies from infections and cancers. Two types of white blood cells (WBC) in the immune system that have a direct role in the defense against infections and cancers are T cells and natural killer (NK) cells. Both kinds of cells are formed in an organ called the thymus. My research aims to understand the events that take place during the development of T cells and NK cells.   A healthy immune system requires T cells that respond to harmful entities without attacking our own bodies. Autoimmune diseases arise when the immune system attacks self. Autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis, type I diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus afflict the lives of many Canadians. Self-reactive T cells are thought to underlie these and other autoimmune diseases. To prevent autoimmunity, T cells are checked in the thymus for their potential to attack self. Self-reactive T cells are eliminated in the thymus while T cells that react to foreign entities are allowed to leave and circulate throughout the body. My research seeks to understand how certain genes work to induce the elimination of self-reactive T cells. Abnormal NK cells are also implicated in autoimmune disease. My preliminary results suggest that a particular gene promotes the formation of NK cells in the thymus. Defective generation of thymic NK cells could be a factor in susceptibility to autoimmune disease. My future work aims to confirm these results and discover the details of NK cell development in the thymus.   The information gained by my research will greatly increase our knowledge of how autoimmune diseases begin. This has the potential to lead to new strategies to prevent and alleviate autoimmune disease, improving the lives of those who are susceptible to or suffer from these illnesses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Novel CD3+CD4-CD8-Cells in Secondary Anti-Leishmania Immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: DOUBLE NEGATIVE CELLS; LEISMANIASES; REGULATION; SECONDARY IMMUNITY; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Leishmaniases are parasitic diseases that affect both humans and animals. It is caused by species of protozoan parasite belonging to the genus Leishmania, and is transmitted by the bite of female Sand files. The disease is endemic in 88 countries and it is currently estimated by WHO that about 12 million people worldwide are afflicted with the disease with more than1.5 - 2 million new cases occurring every year and 350 million people at risk of infection. Current treatments are very expensive, highly toxic and there are increasing reports of development of drug resistance. Although, the disease occurs mostly in the tropics and subtropics, increased travel, globalization and war, has resulted in the presence of the disease in individuals from non endemic areas. For instance, Canadian and American Soldiers returning from active duty in the endemic areas like Iraq and Afghanistan have been diagnosed with the disease.  Vaccination remains the most cost-effective means of controlling infectious diseases. Unfortunately, there is still no effective vaccine against leishmaniasis. This is in part related to our lack of understanding of the factors that regulate immunologic memory; which is the ability of our defence system to recognize pathogens it has successfully dealt with by the development of cells called memory cells. Any effective vaccine should lead to the development of these memory cells that will protect vaccinated individuals upon subsequent exposure to the infectious agent (immunologic memory). This project will investigate the part a newly described cell population plays in the development and maintenance of immunologic memory in cutaneous leishmaniasis. Results from this study will extend our knowledge and understanding of the factors that regulate memory cell development in leismaniasis as well as other infectious diseases like HIV, malaria and will aid in the development of an effective vaccine against these diseases.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANGIOGENESIS; ARTERIOGENESIS; CAVEOLIN-1; HINDLIMB ISCHEMIA; NITRIC OXIDE
Abstract-Résumé: It is commonly said that the average age of the general population is increasing and will continue to increase in the years to come. One unfortunate outcome is an increase in health problems. Of concern are events such as heart attacks or limb damage due to lack of oxygen (typically associated with diabetes). After such events, there is an attempt by the body to form new blood vessels to areas that have been deprived of oxygen and nutrients. However, both aging and diabetes are associated with a decrease in formation of new blood vessels. The purpose of this research project is to see if we can increase the amount of new blood vessels formed, following events that deprive muscles and body tissue of oxygen and nutrients, by using a novel compound that we have, to promote the release of substances that have been associated with vessel formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Trajectories of obesity in adolescents in BC
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ADOLESCENT HEALTH; BINGE EATING; GENERAL GROWTH MIXTURE MODELING; OBESITY; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is a growing problem in adolescents. Excess weight at this age can lead to significant health problems in adulthood. Currently, a longitudinal study is being conducted in high schools across British Columbia aimed at identifying trajectories of substance use. We plan to add an obesity component to this survey with the goal to model trajectories of obesity in high school students and examine factors associated with each trajectory. This will help in identifying subpopulations at greatest risk of becoming obese at a later age. Interventions can then be targeted to those individuals. We will also explore the association between binge eating and addiction. It is unclear from the literature whether overeating is an addictive behaviour. We will compare behaviours associated with substance use with those associated with binge eating. The results may impact obesity intervention strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Recovery in cultural context: Identifying key processes and domains of recovery in Euro-Canadian and Afro-Canadian persons diagnosed with severe mental illness
Keywords-MotsClés: BAD); CROSS-SECTIONAL SURVEY; CULTURE AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES UTILIZATION; ETHNOCULTURAL DIFFERENCES; IN-DEPTH SEMI-STRUCTURED INTERVIEWS; MAJOR DEPRESSION; MIXED METHODS STUDY DESIGN; RECOVERY IN MENTAL ILLNESS; SEVERE MENTAL ILLNESS (SCHIZOPHRENIA; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF OUTCOMES IN SERIOUS MENTAL ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: The accumulation of daily life struggles might negatively affect the mental health of individuals who do not have appropriate coping resources. In Canada, only one third of individuals in need actually receive mental health services. According to the Mental Health Commission of Canada (MHCC), the agency charged with developing a mental health strategy for Canada, individuals with severe mental illness (SMI) need specialized services and supports in order to recover. Consequently, the MHCC concluded that existing mental health services need to be transformed into 'recovery-oriented services', and that these recovery-oriented services must be 'responsive to the cultural needs of all people living in Canada'. Recovery emphasizes the rights of the person with SMI to a dignified and meaningful life in the community and an active say in their own care. Although the goal of recovery-oriented care is primarily to offer people with SMI effective and culturally responsive interventions, there is at present a lack of knowledge and expertise on cultural competence in this area. Our research aims to fill this knowledge gap. Using quantitative and qualitative methodologies, our study seeks to develop an understanding of the role ethnicity, gender and migration status play in the recovery course of Euro-Canadian and Afro-Canadian patients diagnosed with SMI. Results of our study can inform policy and assist in the development of guidelines which can be operationalized into day-to-day practice, so that mental health services are both recovery-oriented and responsive to Canada's growing diversity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Moving Towards Cultural Safety in Indigenous Contracting: Lessons from British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE STUDY; COMMUNITY-BASED HEALTH SERVICES; CRITICAL ETHNOGRAPHY; CULTURAL SAFETY; HEALTH CONTRACTING; HEALTH POLICY & SERVICES; INDIGENOUS EPISTEMIOLOGIES; INDIGENOUS PEOPLE; MENTAL HEALTH & ADDICTIONS; SELF-DETERMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: In response to the mental health disparities experienced by Aboriginal peoples, and related inequities regarding the accessibility to appropriate mental health care, there has been a shift in health policy to promote culturally safe mental health care delivery models. Practices that are culturally-safe support the principles of Aboriginal self-determination, community capacity building and approaches to health and healing that result in positive health outcomes and reduced health disparities. Yet, recent research indicates that current funding arrangements via proposal-driven contractual agreements are problematic for Aboriginal organizations and in some cases undermine the development of culturally safe mental health and addictions services. The objective of this study is therefore to develop a better understanding of how current policies and funding models of different organizations have shaped the provision of Aboriginal mental health and addictions services in an urban context. A partnership-based approach to study selected Aboriginal agencies in British Columbia will be utilized. In addition, data will be collected through interviews and focus groups with recipients of care, providers, and local and national leaders in Aboriginal mental health. The results from this analysis will inform the development of culturally safe and effective funding arrangements for Aboriginal mental health and addictions care.

TitreApplicationTitle: The health and economic impact of Ontario's Grade 8 HPV vaccination program
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; COST-EFFECTIVENESS; HPV VACCINE; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; POPULATION AND PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Every year, the Ontario government invests about $39 million in a program that offers the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine to all Grade 8 girls in the province. However, almost 50% of eligible girls are refusing to get vaccinated. This poor acceptance has been largely attributed to concerns among parents who feel there is not yet enough information about the real world effects of this vaccine. At the same time, such low uptake threatens public health efforts aimed making the costly initiative worthwhile. The objectives of this thesis are to assess the vaccine's effect on the incidence of genital warts and uptake of Pap screening, and to evaluate the real world cost-effectiveness of Ontario's program.  This study is based on all girls eligible for Ontario's Grade 8 HPV vaccination program between 2007 and 2011. Information on the girls' HPV vaccine use and medical history will be obtained from Ontario administrative health databases. This information will be used to determine if the risk of developing genital warts differs between girls who get the vaccine and girls who do not. In addition, it will be used to determine whether Pap screening, an established mean of preventing cervical cancer, is affected by HPV vaccination. Finally, to determine the economic value of Ontario's HPV vaccination program, a cost-effectiveness analysis will be performed based on the program's first five years of implementation.   In efforts to maximize the health benefits and cost-effectiveness of Ontario's publicly funded HPV vaccination program, it is important that its effects are monitored and evaluated. The results of this study will provide information about the real world effects of the HPV vaccine that could help individuals make more educated decisions about vaccination. In addition, the results can assist public health decision-makers in making informed policy recommendations about ways to improve future HPV vaccine programming.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving the Communication Environment in Haematological Cancer Care
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER COMMUNICATION; HAEMATOLOGICAL CANCERS; INTERPRETIVE DESCRIPTION; KNOWLEDGE DISSEMINATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; LONGITUDNAL STUDY; ONCOLOGY; ONCOLOGY NURSING; PSYCHONCOLOGY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Patients diagnosed with haematological cancers, including leukemia, myeloma, and lymphoma, have highly specialized needs which differ in fundamental ways from those of the general oncology population. The absence of a specific solid tumour site and the typically chronic disease course set the stage for critical interpersonal interactions within a highly complicated and rapidly changing health care environment. Haematological patients may face intense diagnostic and treatment regimens, increased risk for secondary disease, palliation, and end-of-life care decision-making. Although clinical experience and a small body of available research indicate these differences will influence the care communication environment, there is little research into the critical role that health care communication can play in shaping patient care and outcomes.   Beginning with secondary analysis, this study will examine data collected from over 260 mixed oncology patients over the past decade by the UBC Cancer Care Communication Program to explore similarities and differences in communication experience between general oncology and haematology patients. Interview data has been coded in both NVivo and MS Excel and the secondary analysis will be approached using Interpretive Description. This applied qualitative methodology seeks to generate an analytical framework within which emerging themes such as decision making, information interpretation, sense-making, and sustainment of emotional support systems within a shifting world can be explored and interpreted. Rigorous analysis will illuminate the complex challenges associated with effective interactions. Thematic secondary analysis will inform additional data collection through focused interviews with a new haematological patient cohort. The knowledge gained from this study will be used to develop explicit tools for improving practice, as well as publication and presentation within the haematologic health care community.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sox17-Mediated Regulation of Mammalian Endoderm Development
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; DEFINITIVE ENDODERM; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; ENHANCERS; EPIBLAST STEM CELLS; EXTRAEMBRYONIC ENDODERM; GENE REGULATION; GENOMICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The developing embryo contains three types of tissue that go on to form all organs of the body. The definitive endoderm (DE) forms the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts and associated organs such as the liver, lung and pancreas.  Therapeutic application of pluripotent stem cells for the treatment of diseases associated with DE-derived tissues - such as diabetes, cystic fibrosis and hepatitis - is dependent on the ability to efficiently generate and isolate DE from embryonic stem cells.  The generation of pure DE from embryonic stem cells is complicated by the presence of an additional endoderm tissue, the extraembryonic endoderm (ExEn) which acts as supportive tissue for the embryo.  The goal of this research project is to identify molecular interactions that play a role in early endoderm development.  Sox17 is a gene that has been proposed to play an important role in ExEn and DE differentiation.  I will generate Sox17 over-expression models of ExEn and DE using mouse embryonic stem cells and mouse epiblast stem cells.  The generation of ExEn and DE by Sox17 over-expression will provide models for the investigation of the molecular regulation of endoderm development using high throughput genomic approaches.  The combination of over-expression studies and high throughput genomics with bioinformatics will allow me to identify regulatory regions within the genome that control endoderm development.  Regions of the genome that are identified as having a potential role in endoderm development will be validated in mouse embryos.  Understanding the molecular regulation of endoderm development will enhance our ability to generate DE-derived tissues for therapeutic purposes.  Identified endoderm regulatory elements will enable new approaches to isolate DE for the generation of DE-derived tissues.  When translated to human induced pluripotent stem cells, these approaches can generate patient-specific endoderm to study endoderm-related diseases and develop new therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the therapeutic potential of targeting bacterial ribosome biogenesis: a functional characterization of the Escherichia coli GTPase, YjeQ
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC DRUG DISCOVERY; BIOGENESIS; CHROMATOGRAPHY; ENZYME KINETICS; HIGH-THROUGHPUT SCREENING; NUCELIC ACID BIOCHEMISTRY; PROTEOMICS; PULSE-CHASE; RIBOSOME; TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Infectious diseases, caused by pathogenic microorganisms such as bacteria and viruses represent a significant threat to human health. Such diseases can be global in scope, affecting both the developing world and industrialized nations. The media coverage of the recent swine flu outbreaks highlights just how dramatically infectious disease can impact society; devastating human health and crippling economies. In recent years, global health care has been plagued by the emergence and dissemination of multi-drug resistant bacteria, the so-called 'super-bugs' that have rendered many of our most important antibiotics ineffective. Our most promising recourse lies in the development of novel antibiotics that target bacterial infections in new ways. Traditionally, antibiotics have targeted a narrow range of bacterial cell processes. A large proportion of our antibiotic arsenal works by directly interrupting the synthesis of proteins in bacteria by blocking translation, the cellular process by which the genetic code is interpreted to make proteins. Over time, bacteria have come up with multiple ways to circumvent drugs that directly inhibit this process. Translation is carried out by ribosomes, large molecules that mediate the interpretation of the genetic code. These cellular interpreters are absolutely required for protein synthesis in bacteria and thus, are necessary for life and pathogenesis. Like proteins, ribosomes themselves must also be synthesized. Disrupting the synthesis of ribosomes in turn blocks protein translation and ultimately inhibits bacterial growth.  None of the antibiotics that we currently employ for therapeutic purposes work in this way. Thus, in targeting the synthesis of bacterial ribosomes we have an opportunity to develop new drugs that act by a mechanism not yet encountered by bacteria. Such a therapeutic strategy will give an edge to modern health care in the arms race against bacterial resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel mechanism of regulating iron homeostasis in the AIDS-associated pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; CRYPTOCOCCUS NEOFORMANS; GLUTAREDOXINS; GLUTATHIONYLATION; IRON-RELATED PHENOTYPES; MACROPHAGE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; PROTEOMICS; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Cryptococcosis is a disease caused by the fungus Cryptococcus and is common in British Columbia. Cryptococcus primarily infects AIDS patients causing 650,000 deaths yearly. Also, cryptococcosis is an emerging disease in people with a healthy immune system. Mechanisms of survival of the pathogen in humans are not known. The disease commences by inhalation of spores that multiply inside white cells (macrophages) residing in the lungs. These cells are responsible to destroy the invading pathogens. Cryptococcus is able to escape these infected macrophages, and reaches the brain where it establishes a lethal infection (meningitis). In order to establish a successful infection, Cryptococcus must obtain iron from the host. The objective of this study is to understand how the pathogen obtains iron from infected macrophages. We propose to apply state-of-the-art technology to identify mechanisms of iron acquisition in the pathogen upon infection. We expect that elucidating these mechanisms in the pathogen will significantly contribute to the understanding of the host-pathogen interaction. This knowledge will contribute to the design of new drugs against Cryptococcus by blocking its iron uptake pathways.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetic determinants of cardiovascular risk factor
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETIC; FAMILIAL HYPERCHOLESTEROLEMIA; GENOME-WIDE DNA METHYLATION PROFILING; HDL-CHOLESTEROL; PYROSEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in Canada, and it now affects increasingly younger people. Therefore, it is important to better understand risk and protection factors of cardiovascular diseases to improve prevention and care. The most important risk factors for heart disease are obesity, diabetes, blood lipids (cholesterol) and life habits. We also know that heart disease runs in families. However, the specific genetic mechanisms involved have not yet been clearly identified. Some clinical observations suggest that epigenetic factors are an important piece of the puzzle. Epigenetics refers to DNA modification acting as a permissive (gas pedal) or a constraint (break pedal) to gene readings (expression). Since the speed at which gene reading takes place is a major issue in disease development, epigenetics has the real potential to better explain how genes are associated with known risk factors for heart disease and involved in disease development. The aim of my project is to determine how gene reading speed control (epigenetics) is related to heart disease, specially to a specific risk factor for the disease, namely low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentrations (HDL-C; the so-called "good" cholesterol). By the use of high throughput technologies, reading speed of specific human genes will be measured in blood of individuals at high and low risk to develop heart disease, according to HDL-C concentration. A subset of the most promising genes (those showing the most important association) will be selected for deeper analyses in larger groups. The anticipated results of this research program will contribute to a better understanding of how epigenetics influences the long-term risk of obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia and cardiovascular disease. Therefore, this project will yield results that will contribute to build a solid basis for the improvement of cardiovascular disease prevention and eventually to improve the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the functions of a neural-specific splicing regulator in the developing and adult mammalian central nervous system.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; BEHAVIORAL TESTS; CELLULAR DIFFERENTIATION; CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM; CONDITIONAL GENE KNOCKOUT; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IMMUNOSTAINING; MORPHOLINO OLIGONUCLEOTIDE GENE KNOCKDOWN; NEUROGENESIS; NSR100
Abstract-Résumé: Most mammalian genes comprise numerous exons which must be correctly spliced in mRNA to produce a functional protein. Certain exons can be included or skipped to result in different protein products from a single gene. This phenomenon is known as alternative splicing (AS) and it is precisely controlled by splicing regulators. The neural-specific Ser/Arg-repeat protein of 100 kDa (nSR100) is a splicing regulator that is specifically expressed in the nervous system of vertebrates. Although we know that nSR100 is required for the production of mature neurons, its exact function in the mammalian nervous system remains unclear. We think that nSR100 acts as a key factor in driving the differentiation of neurons during embryogenesis and neurogenesis in the mature central nervous system of mammals. We will create mouse lines in which inactivation of nSR100 will be targeted to specific regions in the brain of adults or embryos. We will evaluate the development of the central nervous system and neurogenesis using microscopy on brain sections. We will also assess learning and memory by comparing the performance of mutant and wild type mice in behavioral tests. High-throughput sequencing on brain tissues from these animals will be performed to survey the role of nSR100 in the control of AS in the nervous system. Many nSR100-regulated exons known in mammals are conserved in the zebrafish. In complementary studies, the knockdown of these conserved events combined with live imaging in the zebrafish will unveil the cellular mechanisms underlying the neuronal differentiation program controlled by nSR100. Since nSR100 has also been demonstrated to direct AS in genes involved in neurological illnesses such as the Alzheimer disease, our understanding of its contribution to neurogenesis may help reveal mechanisms leading to these diseases and open new therapeutic approaches for neurodegenerative disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stress, Memory and Hippocampal Volume in Young and Older Adults
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOMARKERS; HIPPOCAMPAL VOLUME; IMAGING MRI; MEMORY; RESILIENCY FACTORS; RISK FACTORS; STRESS HORMONES; TESTING ENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Research studies on memory and aging often show that older adults do not perform as well as young adults. Such lower memory performance has been linked with smaller volume of the hippocampus, a brain region involved in learning and memory. Older adults have also been shown to be more reactive to stress, which is known to impair memory. More recent studies have shown that the impact of stress on memory can be mediated by the characteristics of the testing environment itself. When both older and young adults have had their memory performance tested, this has often taken place at a university setting where participants were tested by young research assistants, and completed tasks that had emphasized memory. Such testing procedures are stressful for older adults, since they enter an unfamiliar setting, with the knowledge that they are being tested for their memory capacities, which may be declining. The novelty and unpredictability of these testing characteristics are known to create a stressful situation. On the contrary, this testing environment is not stressful for university students. In this project, for each age group, we will test each participant under two types of conditions, one that fovours their age group, and is therefore less stressful, and one that does not favour them, and we will test their memory performance under each of these conditions. We will examine the association between hippocampal volume and memory performance in each group, when tested in the different conditions. This study holds very important methodological implications for all future studies on memory loss in aging. This is a crucial field considering the increasing prevalence rates of dementia and Alzheimer's disease

TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing distress and increasing adherence to medical advice among cancer patients through Acceptance and Commitment Therapy.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCEPTANCE AND COMMITMENT THERAPY; CANCER; DEPRESSION; GROUP THERAPY; PSYCHOLOGICAL INTERVENTION; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer patients often experience significant depressive and anxious symptoms commonly referred to as psychological distress. Signs of distress are alarming not only because of their unpleasant nature and contribution to lower quality of life but also because they are major risk factors for non-compliance with medical advice. Distressed patients are also more likely to die from cancer than those who are not distressed. Fortunately, even brief psychological interventions can improve patients' quality of life, physical health and potentially contribute to longer survival. Typically Cognitive-Behavioural Therapies have been used with cancer patients but evidence suggests that Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) may be even more effective. However, past research has limitations: very small number of patients have been tested, only costly individual (as opposed to cheaper group) interventions have been tested and the therapy offered has been sometimes very short (e.g. only 1 session). Consequently, the goal of the current project is to address these limitations by examining the effect of 6-sessions group ACT intervention. It is expected that following the intervention patients will report lower distress, higher quality of life, and greater adherence to medical advice as compared to those who received a Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy. This project involves newly diagnosed patients from the McGill University Health Centre. Patients will be invited to participate in the study by their MD. Research assistant will explain the conditions of participation and ensure the consent to participate is informed. Assessments of distress, quality of life and adherence to medical advice will take place before initial ACT session, after the last ACT session as well as 3 and 6 months later (over the phone). If proven successful over time ACT interventions could be used in public healthcare system as a not expensive way of increasing patients' well-being and adherence to medical advice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Atypical Protein Kinase C Isoforms on Transforming Growth Factor Beta Signalling Pathways in Lung Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALLING PATHWAYS; EPITHELIAL TO MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION; GENE EXPRESSION; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; LUNG CANCER; METASTASIS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN KINASE C; TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR BETA SIGNALLING; TUMOUR SUPPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer related deaths in Canada. Normal cells of healthy lungs grow in a controlled fashion, and only divide and reproduce when new cells are required. In cancer, cells escape the internal regulations that control their growth, and divide uncontrollably into a mass of cells called a tumour. If the tumour is malignant, it grows aggressively and is extremely invasive. Invasive cells from the growing mass can leave their primary site and migrate to other areas of the body in a process known as metastasis. Metastasis is a hallmark of malignant tumours and metastases are responsible for 90% of cancer related deaths in Canada. Thus, designing effective treatment measures to block tumour growth and metastasis is an important area of study. Controlled cell growth is a result of effective cell communication that occurs through specific signalling molecules and proteins produced by our cells. One such signalling molecule is "transforming growth factor beta" (TGFb). TGFb is a small protein that normally acts to control cellular growth, and thus can block tumour cells from expanding. However, in many advanced tumours, the TGFb signal is lost, and its growth suppressive actions are ineffective. Furthermore, increased TGFb levels in advanced tumours can cause cancer cells to metastasize. Abnormal TGFb signalling is a hallmark of almost all solid tumours but the mechanisms leading to TGFb dysfunction are unknown. We have identified an interacting protein called Atypical Protein Kinase C (aPKC) that can alter TGFb signalling. Interestingly, aPKC levels are correlated with advanced lung tumours and thus may contribute to the damaging changes in TGFb seen in lung cancer. Understanding the factors that alter the TGFb signalling pathway leading to increased tumour progression is a main focus of our lab. Our work will foster the development of effective therapeutic strategies for lung cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a predictive index for intraoperative blood transfusions in non-cardiac surgery and its validation as a tool for intraoperative clinical decision making.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT; CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; ELECTRONIC CLINICAL DATA; TRANSFUSION; TRANSFUSION RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: During surgery, blood transfusions help keep patients alive. While blood transfusions keep patients alive, they also present risks of complications for the patients receiving them.    Often, patients going for surgery are seen in a preoperative assessment clinic before their surgery. During this visit, a clinician takes their medical history using an electronic assessment tool.  This tool stores the data in a database, and generates a report for the physicians who will be treating the patient.  The data in the database could be used to help predict which patients are at higher risk of needing a blood transfusion during their surgery.    In addition to the preoperative assessment data, intraoperative data of the patient's current condition during surgery could also provide insight into which risk factors lead to more blood transfusions.  If this data were merged with the preoperative data, a large data set could be used to predict preoperative risk of blood transfusions.  This risk could also be adjusted during surgery for the physicians, based on the intraoperative of the patient's condition.   If we can deterine the risk factors associated with blood transfusions, we should be able to build a tool that alerts clinicians if their patient is at high risk of blood transfusion.  This tool might help physicians avoid giving the patients blood transfusions if they can be alerted early enough, and safely administer some other treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Localisation du langage chez des patients épileptiques en magnétoencéphalographie
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; EPILEPSY; LANGUAGE; LATERALISATION; LOCALIZATION; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: L'epilepsie est le trouble neurologique le plus frequemment rencontre chez l'humain. Un enfant sur 100 est affecte par ce trouble qui a d'importantes consequences tels que des problemes cognitifs (probleme d'apprentissage) et sociaux (troubles de comportement). Le traitement generalement utilise est la pharmacotherapie. Toutefois, chez les patients qui ne repondent pas a la medication, la chirurgie constitue le meilleur traitement alternatif et consiste a retirer le tissu cerebral responsable de l'epilepsie. Avant de proceder a la chirurgie, il faut s'assurer que le geste chirurgical n'aura pas de sequelles sur les fonctions cognitives importantes, telles que le langage, pour eviter que le patient ne souffre de trouble langagier apres la chirurgie. Pour ce faire, il faut etre en mesure de localiser les regions cerebrales responsables du langage. Cette localisation est particulierement importante chez les patients epileptiques parce que la localisation de ces regions semble plus variable chez eux que chez les sujets neurologiquement sains. Presentement, les procedures d'evaluations prechirurgicales utilisees dans les hopitaux impliquent generalement des methodes qui sont tres invasives et qui presentent des risques pour les patients, particulierement pour les enfants. La  magnetoencephalographie (MEG) est un appareil qui est completement non-invasif et qui permet d'enregistrer l'activite du cerveau et de determiner les zones du cerveau responsable du langage. Nous avons selectionne trois taches de langage qui peuvent etre completees dans cet appareil et qui devraient activer les differentes regions du cerveau impliquees dans la production et la comprehension du langage chez des patients epileptiques. Un tel protocole pourrait eventuellement remplacer les methodes invasives qui sont utilisees presentement. De plus, toutes les taches utilisees ici seraient utilisables aupres des enfants epileptiques chez qui il est difficile d'utiliser les methodes couramment employee

TitreApplicationTitle: Marqueurs neuropsychologiques et électroencéphalographiques du développement d'une maladie neurodégénérative dans le trouble comportemental en sommeil paradoxal.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYSE QUANTIFIEE DE L'EEG; DEMENCES; MALADIES NEURODEGENERATIVES; NEUROPSYCHOLOGIE; POLYSOMNOGRAPHIE; TROUBLE COMPORTEMENTAL EN SOMMEIL PARADOXAL; TROUBLES DU SOMMEIL
Abstract-Résumé: La maladie de Parkinson (MP) et la demence a corps de Lewy (DCL) sont deux maladies neurodegeneratives qui partagent de nombreux symptomes comme une atteinte de la motricite, de la cognition, du sommeil et de l'humeur. Les recherches actuelles visent a identifier et a caracteriser les phases precoces des maladies neurodegeneratives dans le but de pouvoir intervenir le plus tot possible dans leur developpement. Le trouble comportemental en sommeil paradoxal (TCSP) se caracterise par l'apparition de comportements indesirables et souvent violents au cours du sommeil. Le TCSP touche environ 1% de la population generale, plus particulierement les hommes ages de plus de 50 ans. Lorsqu'il survient de facon independante a une autre maladie ou syndrome, on parle alors de TCSP idiopathique (TCSPi). Cependant, en raison d'une pathophysiologie commune, le TCSP est aussi etroitement associe a la MP et a la DCL et peut meme preceder leur survenue de plusieurs annees chez certains patients. Le TCSPi est ainsi considere comme un stade precoce du developpement d'une MP ou d'une DCL. Plusieurs anomalies similaires a celles rapportees dans les stades precoces de la MP et de la DCL ont ete detectees dans le TCSPi. On remarque entre autres un ralentissement de l'electroencephalogramme (EEG) a l'eveil ainsi qu'une baisse des performances cognitives au niveau de l'attention, des fonctions executives et de la memoire episodique. Le but de ce projet est de cibler les marqueurs EEG et neuropsychologiques permettant d'identifier les individus avec un TCSPi a risque de developper une MP ou une DCL. Le projet propose nous permettra de mieux definir certains marqueurs impliques dans le TCSPi et dans le developpement de maladies neurodegeneratives. Si nous pouvons preciser le profil evolutif des sujets avec un TCSPi, nous pourrons alors verifier si les traitements de neuroprotection, presentement en developpement, peuvent prevenir ou retarder l'apparition de ces maladies chez ces patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Negative social encounters and changes in metabolic health trajectories: is inflammation a mediator?
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; INFLAMMATION; MECHANISM; METABOLIC SYNDROME; SOCIAL ENCOUNTERS
Abstract-Résumé: Aspects of social environment, such as social support, size of social network, and day-to-day quality of social encounters, strongly influence health and have been implicated in the development of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Metabolic syndrome is considered a CVD precursor, and is characterized as a collection of symptoms: insulin resistance, central adiposity, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia. Although the metabolic syndrome and CVD tend to manifest in mid- to later-life, the processes that produce these diseases begin as early as the first few decades of life. Previous research suggests that adolescent girls who experience more day-to-day negative social encounters have worsening metabolic health (an index of the metabolic syndrome) over a 2 year period, and adolescent girls who experience fewer negative social encounters improved in metabolic health over the same period. This trend persisted even after considering alternative explanations, such as age, ethnicity, oral contraceptive use, socioeconomic status, and health behaviours such as smoking and physical activity. It is possible that negative social interactions have a direct impact on physiological health: poor interpersonal interactions have been associated with increased systemic inflammation. In turn, systemic inflammation has been shown to drive insulin resistance and development of the other metabolic syndrome symptoms. In order to better understand the developmental origins of the metabolic syndrome, and thereby CVD, and to determine a mechanism responsible for the above relationship, our research proposes to assess whether more day-to-day negative encounters are associated with changes in systemic inflammation, and whether these changes in inflammation are further associated with changes in metabolic health. This may be another way that aspects of our psychosocial environment can 'get under the skin' to directly contribute to development of disease in later life.

TitreApplicationTitle: The multi site implementation of online support for young adults with cancer in Canada: Examining interest in online support, psychosocial distress, and professionally facilitated group therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DISTRESS; ONLINE SUPPORT; SUPPORTIVE CARE; YOUNG ADULTHOOD
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the unique impact of cancer on young adults, rising cancer incidence rates in this age frame, and significant levels of emotional distress, there are a clear lack of supportive care resources tailored to young adult cancer patients. However, thanks to increased interest in online services and technological advances, the internet offers a viable method of reaching out to patients across Canada. The multi site implementation of online supportive care services for young adults with cancer is therefore proposed. Six sites across three provinces will be selected, each with urban and rural representation. For research purposes, prior to participating online patients will be asked to complete a questionnaire to assess distress and to consent to review of their medical chart. The online program, care2talk.ca, will offer professionally facilitated weekly therapy sessions, the opportunity to connect with other patients, a chance to share experiences and thoughts, and a comprehensive list of resources tailored to each region. This research will allow for the examination of interest in online support, use of online tools, and will permit us to answer questions such as whether the distress experienced by young adults with cancer can be effectively treated through online group therapy. It is crucial that health care providers become involved in the provision of online support, ensuring continuity of care, improved access to supportive care services, and a secure online environment. Online support through the care2talk program represents a highly innovative method of providing quality, patient centered care. Given the novelty of this field and the doubtless transition to an increasingly online world, the potential exists for Canadian healthcare to become industry leaders in this endeavor.

TitreApplicationTitle: HIV and Aging: Consequences of living conditions and their effects on health outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HIV-RELATED QUALITY OF LIFE; HIV/AIDS; LIVING CONDITIONS; MOS HIV
Abstract-Résumé: Individuals with HIV/AIDS have benefited from the effectiveness of antiretroviral drugs. In 2006, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) estimated that 2.8 million older adults worldwide, aged 50 and over, were living with HIV/AIDS. In Canada, 10% or 6,000 of those with HIV/AIDS are older adults. However, this vulnerable population has been, thus far, neglected in research studies. To date, much is unknown about their living conditions, i.e., gross income, employment status, housing accommodation, drug abuse/addiction or depression, and how these factors affect their long term health status.   This proposed project has two specific aims: 1) to understand whether problematic living conditions, vary with age, and 2) to determine whether differences in their living conditions affect long term health outcomes.   This study will use an existing data set from the Positive Spaces, Healthy Places study. The study is longitudinal, observationally social and clinical cohort in which currently consists of 600 people living with HIV in Ontario. The data were already collected at three time points via face-to-face interviews in 2006, 2007 and 2009. The 5-year follow up data will be collected for the study in 2011.    Results of this study are expected to inform the Public Health Agency of Canada, AIDS Service Organizations in Ontario, researchers, health care providers, and health policy decision-makers in charge of support services and access to care, to help improve the lives of individuals with HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Water Quality and Human Health in a Changing Climate: Gastro-Intestinal Illness in Small Communities in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; GASTROINTESTINAL ILLNESS; GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEM; HEALTH IMPACTS OF CLIMATE CHANGE; HYDROLOGY; POPULATION HEALTH; SPATIO-TEMPORAL PATTERNS OF DISEASE; WATER QUALITY
Abstract-Résumé: High-quality drinking water is fundamental to maintaining and protecting human health and well-being. As water supply and distribution infrastructure ages, land-use and climatic patterns change, and water sources become more vulnerable to contamination, drinking water quality will become an increasingly important public health concern in Canada. Of particular concern is the contamination of drinking water by waterborne pathogens causing gastro-intestinal (GI) illness. Drinking water quality is threatened by contamination with waterborne pathogens that exist in the environment and enter drinking water supplies via various pathways. Once pathogens enter a drinking water supply, waterborne GI illness outbreaks and sporadic cases are likely to occur in the absence of effective water treatment. Our current understanding of risk factors for poor water quality and its relationship to waterborne GI illness is limited. Recent research has indicated that extreme weather events and climatic factors may be linked to poor drinking water quality and disease. Additionally, characteristics of drinking water systems have been shown to influence the incidence of illness in various settings. This project will examine the complex relationship between weather and climatic parameters, water quality and human health in eight small communities across British Columbia. Understanding this relationship will enable an evaluation of the potential impacts of climate change on water quality and human health and therefore can be used to identify possibilities for adaptation in Canada and other settings. Final study results will be disseminated to relevant decision-makers in public health and water management circles. Ultimately, this study will address current research gaps and contribute to improving water quality and protecting human health in a changing climate.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding variations in rural health: connecting service use and outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: RURAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: On average, Canadians living in rural areas tend to be less healthy and experience higher rates of mortality than urban residents. Still, the causes of these differences are not obvious.  Factors not related to the health care system, such as level of income and education, rates and type of employment, and patterns of health shape the health of individuals and communities.  At the same time, residents of rural and remote areas experience more limited access to health care services than their urban and suburban counterparts.  This research will describe variations in mortality among rural and urban areas across British Columbia, with a focus on deaths which may have been prevented by health care.  Then, it will determine whether differences in the use of health services fully explain differences in mortality rates, or if there are other characteristics of individuals and communities which help understand differences in mortality among areas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Différences sexuelles dans les changements du risque cardiométabolique en réponse à l'alimentation méditerranéenne dans un contexte contrôlé
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYSES STATISTIQUES; COMMUNICATION ET EDUCATION; DIFFERENCES SEXUELLES; FONCTION ENDOTHELIALE; HOMEOSTASIE DU GLUCOSE ET DE L'INSULINE; INFLAMMATION; INTERVENTIONS DIETETIQUES; NUTRITION CLINIQUE; PROFIL LIPIDIQUE; SANTE CARDIOVASCULAIRE
Abstract-Résumé: Plusieurs etudes ont demontre des effets benefiques de l'alimentation mediterraneenne sur certains facteurs de risque cardiovasculaires tels qu'une diminution du cholesterol sanguin et de la tension arterielle ainsi qu'une meilleure gestion de la glycemie. D'un autre cote, de recentes etudes suggerent que les hommes repondent differemment des femmes a un changement alimentaire. L'objectif de ce projet de recherche est donc d'etudier les differences entre les hommes et les femmes par rapport aux changements du cholesterol sanguin et d'autres facteurs de risque cardiovasculaires en reponse a une intervention de quatre semaines au cours de laquelle tous les repas sont fournis aux participants selon les principes de l'alimentation mediterraneenne. Pour ce faire, un echantillon de 39 hommes et 39 femmes premenopausees ayant un LDL-cholesterol (mauvais cholesterol) legerement eleve sera utilise. Les participants recoivent pendant quatre semaines tous les repas et breuvages selon un menu respectant les principes de l'alimentation mediterraneenne. Le cholesterol sanguin, la tension arterielle, la glycemie et d'autres facteurs de risque des maladies cardiovasculaires sont mesures avant et apres cette intervention basee sur le mode alimentaire mediterraneen.   Les maladies cardiovasculaires sont encore l'une des causes de mortalite les plus importantes au Canada. Ce projet a donc le potentiel de generer des connaissances qui pourraient aider les professionnels de la sante a effectuer des interventions cliniques davantage personnalisees et efficaces selon le sexe de l'individu dans la prevention des maladies cardiovasculaires et ainsi diminuer la mortalite associee a ces maladies. Ces nouvelles connaissances pourraient ainsi mener a des economies interessantes pour notre systeme de sante en ameliorant la prevention des maladies cardiovasculaires et en diminuant leur cout economique qui est chiffre a plusieurs milliards en frais direct et indirect a chaque annee.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Characterization of the Huntingtin Gene Promoter
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; LUCIFERASE ASSAY; NEUROLOGY; PROMOTER FUNCTION; TISSUE CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington's Disease (HD) is an adult onset brain disorder which is caused by a mutation in the gene that encodes for the protein huntingtin (htt). While there has been considerable research into the role of mutant htt in causing brain cell death, little is known about the normal function of this protein. Understanding the conditions that cause htt to be turned on in the brain is an important step towards discovering the function of both the normal and mutated htt. During its life time a cell will turn on or off certain genes to optimize its survival as its environment changes and the cell ages. Cells use a genetic sequence called a promoter, which lies ahead of a gene, to regulate the expression of genes. Promoters are comprised of sets of genetic sequences that can specify the binding of special proteins called transcription factors (TFs). There are many different types of TFs, some that induce expression and others that prevent it. The combination of TFs at a given promoter regulate how much a gene is expressed, if at all. By regulating the concentrations of different TFs the cell can then control the expression of specific genes. The purpose of the project is to discover and characterize the htt promoter so that we know which TFs are binding to the promoter and how these TFs are affecting htt expression. In order to do this the cellular concentrations of specific TFs will be manipulated and the effect on the htt promoter will be assessed. To assay promoter function the htt promoter will be attached to the same gene that allows fireflies to glow. Thus if the treatment used increases htt promoter activity the cells will glow more than cells without treatment and conversely if the treatment decreases promoter activity the cells will glow less. By knowing which TFs are important for htt expression new drug therapies can be aimed at preventing htt expression which will prevent HD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery of WNT5A functions during embryonic skeletal development in the face
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; CHICKEN EMBRYO; CRANIOFACIAL; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; EMBRYOLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; SKELETAL DEVELOPMENT; WNT
Abstract-Résumé: The face is supported by an intricate arrangement of bones, cartilages and muscles. These structures are set up early in life, during the embryonic period before birth. At this time, all the cells look identical and yet genes are being turned on and off in a precise manner to distinguish the upper and lower jaw. Our work focuses on the early embryonic stages when tiny buds of tissue surrounding the mouth are just forming. We are using the chicken embryo as our model organism because the tissues are accessible during embryonic stages and it is possible to alter the patterns of bone and cartilage formation by changing gene expression. The proteins pursued in this application are called Wingless-related proteins or WNTs. We have already shown that one of the WNTs, WNT5A, is present within the cartilage-forming regions at early stages of development but then is excluded from mature cartilage. In cell cultures of lower jaw tissues, we showed that addition of WNT5A completely eliminates cartilage matrix, even though it is initially formed normally. This is a surprising result and one that we are gong to study further in this proposal. WNT5A activates a less commonly used WNT pathway, the non-canonical pathway, to affect cartilage. In this project, we seek to identify the genes present in the lower jaw whose activity leads to changes in cartilage matrix following WNT5A addition. We are also going to increase and decrease the amount of WNT5A in the embryonic chicken face to see the effects on growth and specification of bone and cartilage in the lower jaw. This will show the role for WNT5A during normal development. One day we hope to use this deep understanding of WNT5A to control skeletal formation in a controlled manner during healing after repair of congenital skeletal abnormalities, traumatic injuries or from bone diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rôle des récepteurs à la neurotensine dans la douleur chronique cancéreuse
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DOULEUR CHRONIQUE; NEUROTENSINE; RECEPTEURS COUPLES AUX PROTEINES G
Abstract-Résumé: Avoir le cancer ne signifie pas forcement vivre dans la douleur. Pourtant, a ce jour, 60 a 90% des patients atteints de cancer avance souffrent d'une douleur moderee ou severe, independamment de leur age ou de leur sexe. Malgre d'importants progres dans la detection precoce et le traitement des tumeurs primaires, les patients atteints de cancers du poumon, du sein ou encore de la prostate, developpent dans 60-85% des cas des metastases au niveau des os. Cet envahissement du squelette par les cellules tumorales se traduit par des douleurs osseuses intenses lesquelles echappent aux therapies medicamenteuses actuelles telles que la morphine et conduisent indeniablement vers une morbidite et une alteration considerable de la qualite de vie. La douleur et le cancer sont donc intimement lies. L'administration centrale de la neurotensine (NT) entraine une reponse analgesique puissante. Cette reponse de type non narcotique est mediee par l'activation des recepteurs NTS1 et NTS2. En utilisant un modele animal refletant de maniere le plus fidele possible les conditions pathologiques observees sur le plan clinique dans les cas de cancer des os, ce projet vise donc a developper une nouvelle classe d'analgesiques non morphiniques ciblant les recepteurs de la neurotensine NTS1 et NTS2. Ces nouveaux composes n'offriront peut-etre pas de solutions de guerison aux personnes atteintes d'un cancer, mais ils pourront tres certainement aider ces patients a rehausser leur qualite de vie a un niveau raisonnable.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diverse Voices: Spirituality and its Relationship with Coping, Adjustment and Mental Health in Children with and without Chronic Illness
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUSTMENT; CHRONIC ILLNESS; CLINICAL PSYCHOLOGY; COPING STRATEGIES; CULTURAL DIVERSITY; MENTAL HEALTH; MULTICULTURALISM AND GENDER; PSYCHOSOCIAL INTERVENTION; SPIRITUALITY; WELL-BEING
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research project will examine the role of children's spirituality in coping, mental health and adjustment in children with and without chronic illness. Previous research has shown that religiosity and/or spirituality has been associated with positive mental health outcomes in children, youth and adults (e.g., Aalsma & Lapsley, 1999; Hill & Pargament, 2003; for a review see Regnerus, 2003). However, systematic research on the connections between spirituality and children's psychological development and well-being has been sparse (Ream & Savin-Williams, 2003). With most research focusing on adults and adolescents (French, et al., 2008), there still remain questions about the role of spirituality in young children's coping, adjustment and mental health. The onset of a chronic illness during childhood can influence physical, psychological and behavioural development, peer acceptance, and family relationship (Suris, Michaud, & Viner, 2004). For some children, spirituality may play a significant positive role in their ability to cope and adjust to their illness. For others, it may play little or no role and for still others it may have a negative impact (e.g., create fears of punishment) on their ability to cope with their illness. This project will contribute to the understanding of children's spirituality and be used to inform psychologists and health care professionals of the role of children's spirituality in coping, mental health and adjustment in children with and without chronic illness. In turn, a main objective of this project is to improve the health of Canadian children by providing more culturally, religiously and spiritually sensitive health services.
