TitreApplicationTitle: Vers une meilleure prise en charge des victimes de violence grave en milieu de travail
Keywords-MotsClés: GENRE; INTERVENTIONS CLINIQUES; MESURES; MILIEU DE TRAVAIL; METHODOLOGIE QUALITATIVE; METHODOLOGIE QUANTITATIVE; PREVENTION; SANTE MENTALE; SEXE; VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Bien que la violence en milieu de travail fasse l'objet de plus en plus d'attention de la part des chercheurs, tres peu de donnees sont disponibles sur les effets des actes de violence grave (AVG) et l'efficacite de la prise en charge des travailleurs selon qu'ils soient des femmes ou des hommes. Le principal objectif de notre programme de recherche est de mener des etudes en milieu de travail orientees sur les besoins specifiques des femmes et des hommes afin d'ameliorer la prise en charge des travailleur-ses expose-es a des AVG ou a risque eleve de l'etre. Notre programme de recherche comprend cinq volets et s'etend sur une periode de cinq ans. Le premier volet consiste a sonder un grand nombre de femmes et d'hommes travaillant dans differents secteurs sur la  frequence des AVG vecus en milieu de travail, leurs consequences et les besoins de soutien chez les individus exposes. Le second volet a pour but d'explorer puis de vulgariser aux milieux de travail des connaissances scientifiques a jour sur differents enjeux et besoins des travailleurs-ses victimes d'AVG. Le troisieme volet a pour but d'evaluer a plus long terme les consequences psychologiques et sociales des AVG en milieu de travail, en tenant compte des differences de sexe et de genre. Le quatrieme volet a comme objectif d'identifier les facteurs contribuant a prevenir la violence en milieu de travail, a attenuer ses consequences et a faciliter la reinsertion au travail. Enfin, a la lumiere des connaissances acquises, le cinquieme volet aura pour objectifs de developper et proposer de nouveaux programmes d'intervention adaptes a la realite des milieux en tenant compte des besoins des femmes et des hommes. Des actions concretes et rapides decouleront du projet et auront un impact positif significatif sur la sante des travailleurs-ses, sur la gestion des incapacites, ainsi que sur les couts sociaux et economiques qui y sont relies.

Abstract-Résumé: The priority that Canadians place on health is reflected in the dramatic decrease in premature mortality and increase in disability-adjusted life expectancy in recent decades. Yet, these benefits are not shared equally by all Canadians. This research program focuses on the sources of differences in health and safety among one of these groups: sex workers, many of whom face elevated risks of violence and premature death. Though research has explored the current legislative context of prostitution in Canada, few studies have systematically investigated the work of police, regulatory agencies and social service providers, as well as the behaviours of customers, managers, and intimate partners as social determinants of sex workers' safety and health. Our research program draws together a multi-sectoral team of knowledge users, collaborators, scholars and trainees, many who have worked for over two decades to raise public awareness about these issues. The team will work collaboratively to: a) identify key factors linked to violence and vulnerabilities in the Canadian sex industry at systems, social, and individual levels; b) estimate the impact of gender on violence-related links between sex workers, clients, romantic partners, supervisors, regulators, and service providers; c) ensure that useful knowledge generated by the research program informs policies and practices aimed at improving the safety and health of sex workers and those they relate to at work and in their personal lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Testing the Effectiveness of an Internet Cognitive Behaviour Therapy Training Program: Impact on Therapist Knowledge and Patient Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY DISORDERS; DEPRESSION; INTERNET COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES; THERAPIST TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: Depression and anxiety are prevalent, disabling, and highly under-treated disorders. The Internet offers a new and exciting medium that can provide efficient and cost effective access to mental health services. Randomized controlled trials have consistently supported a therapist-guided Internet-Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (I-CBT) approach. A therapist-guided I-CBT program is not readily available in Canada. The purpose of this research is to evaluate a therapist-training I-CBT workshop that has been created by our team to treat depression and anxiety disorders. The workshops will be offered to interdisciplinary health care professionals at five health regions in Saskatchewan. Following the workshop, the participants will treat at least two patients while under supervision. Knowledge of I-CBT, online communication skills, and ethical and professional issues will be assessed using a before-after workshop design. Strengths and weaknesses of the workshops expressed by the trainees will also be examined. Patient outcomes will be tracked throughout their treatment. It is predicted that the participants' knowledge of I-CBT will be increased and they will develop competence in the provision of I-CBT. It is also expected that patients treated by the participants will report reduced symptoms of deperssion and/or anxiety. The proposed research has high potential to improve service delivery and the mental health of Canadians. If interdisciplinary professionals can be effectively trained to offer therapy in this modality the potential for change in the health care system is considerable.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Effect of IL-18 on the Activiation of Natural Killer Cell Immunity and Its Relevance in Breast Cancer Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; ELISA; FLOW CYTOMERTY; IL-18 (CYTOKINE); IMMUNOTHERAPY; IN VIVO 4T1 BREAST CANCER MODEL; NK CELLS; NKG2D RECEPTOR; QPCR; TUMOUR METASTASIS
Abstract-Résumé: Natural killer (NK) cells detect and destroy harmful substances within our body that lead to disease, including cancer; however they usually do not invade healthy cells. Unlike NK cells, current therapies utilized by the health delivery system (i.e. chemotherapy) and aimed at eliminating cancer cells, cannot distinguish between healthy and infected cells and a patients condition can deteriorate while undergoing cancer treatments. Based on research to date, if a person has cancer, NK cells decrease their activity and are no longer able to fight off this disease. If there were a way to ensure that NK cells remain active, the body could fight cancers on its own. Additionally, scientists have shown that NK cells may also affect the ability of cancers to metastasize.  This study will look at ways to activate NK cells so that they recognize cancer cells and destroy them. We will culture human NK cells in a lab setting and expose them to specific signals to see if they will attack and destroy cancer cells. We will also use animal models to see if this sort of signaling between NK cells and cancer cells work inside a living system. As breast cancer is the most common cancer in women and shares many similarities with prostate cancer,  I have chosen to do these studies using breast cancer cells and models which represent a variety of breast cancers; thus, the potential to improve the health of male and female populations.  If our studies are successful we can publish research that will provide valuable information to providers of the health delivery system for the potential development of novel breast and prostate cancer treatments, including the use of immunotherapy, alone or in combination with current successful treatments.  We may also be able to predict, based on the behavior of NK cells, whether certain patients with breast cancer will go on to develop cancers in areas other than breast tissue, benefitting the personal health of these patients.

Abstract-Résumé: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is caused by prenatal exposure to alcohol. It is the leading cause of developmental disabilities and birth defects in the Western world.  Individuals with FASD live with lifelong challenges such as learning disabilities, impulsive behaviours, hyperactivity, and poor social skills.  In Canada, people with FASD are over-represented in the foster care system and are often repeat offenders in the correctional system.  There is also an unusually high percentage of children and youth diagnosed with FASD in Aboriginal communities.  This research will address issues of social justice and power distribution, by focusing on peoples' everyday lives in two Aboriginal communities to understand how institutional policy, procedures and programs affect them.  Similarly, this research will analyze how FASD diagnoses and behaviours influence beliefs, opinions, policies and interventions by families, community and support systems.  Interviews will be conducted with family members, community members and leaders, as well as professionals and decision-makers from the health, education, child welfare and corrections systems.  Policies and other written documents that inform how individuals, communities and institutions respond to FASD will also be examined.  Findings will highlight successes and identify gaps in effective support, intervention, and prevention in the field of FASD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Methyl metabolism and methionine requirements in the neonatal piglet
Keywords-MotsClés: 1-CARBON METABOLISM; AMINO ACID REQUIREMENTS; EPIGENETICS; FETAL PROGRAMMING; IN VIVO METABOLISM; INDICATOR AMINO ACID OXIDATION; INDIRECT CALORIMETRY; MASS SPECTROMETRY; METHIONINE CYCLE; UPLC/HPLC
Abstract-Résumé: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins but many also play critical roles in metabolism. For example, methionine is responsible for gene regulation and the synthesis of essential products such as cysteine, taurine, creatine and phosphatidylcholine. The synthesis of these products is critical in infants since breast milk and formula do not provide adequate amounts to a growing neonate. Methionine is an essential amino acid which means that all of the required methionine must come from the diet. Thus, a sufficient dietary intake of methionine is vital for normal metabolism and overall growth. However, the metabolism of methionine also results in the formation of homocysteine which is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Methionine can be regenerated from homocysteine provided the essential nutrients folate and betaine are available. Folate is deficient in most populations and little is known regarding betaine intake. Since methionine can be regenerated by folate and betaine, the dietary intake of these nutrients will impact the methionine requirement. If an infant diet meets the defined methionine requirement, but is deficient in folate and betaine, does the baby need more methionine? What is the total amount of methionine needed for synthesis of these essential products? How do folate and betaine supplements affect this nutrient demand? This proposal seeks answer these questions using isotope tracers and the neonatal pig as a model for the infant. The methionine requirement will be determined when folate and betaine are present as well as when they are removed from the diet. We will also measure the change in methionine regeneration from homocysteine in folate/betaine-deficient animals that are subsequently 'rescued' with either folate, betaine or both.  Since the quality of neonatal nutrition has an impact on the development of obesity and disease into adulthood, we hope that through these experiments we can help explain this phenomenon.

TitreApplicationTitle: Maternal prenatal negative mood & infant stress and immunity: Could increased maternal inflammation during pregnancy be the linking mechanism?
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES); DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHONEUROIMMUNOLOGY; FETAL GROWTH AND BIRTH WEIGHT; INFANT IMMUNITY (SALIVARY IGA); INFANT STRESS REACTIVITY (SALIVARY CORTISOL); MATERNAL INFLAMMATION IN PREGNANCY (CRP; MATERNAL NEGATIVE AFFECT; PRENATAL ANXIOUS MOOD; PRENATAL DEPRESSED MOOD
Abstract-Résumé: Pregnancy is a process of change requiring adaptation. Maternal negative prenatal feelings can interact with this adaptation. Negative feelings, such as depressed and anxious states, may influence the course of a pregnancy. However, there is still very little research on how negative feelings might affect pregnancy and infant health outcomes. Several biological ways through which this might happen have been suggested. A promising new avenue of research is the role that inflammation plays, and the possible link between negative feelings and inflammation. This project aims to examine: 1. whether maternal negative (anxious, depressed) affect is related to increased serum inflammatory markers, which are blood components that signal the presence of inflammation; and 2. whether or not inflammatory markers are related to fetal growth, and to changes in four-month-old babies' salivary stress and immune markers. Our proposed study will clarify how relationships between maternal prenatal negative affect and inflammation can influence the growth of the fetus, and ultimately shape the baby's stress and immune responses (to influence his or her health). The project will involve 200 pregnant women and their babies, recruited during the first prenatal visit from prenatal hospital-based clinics: the French- and English-speaking hospitals in Moncton (NB), and the CRHC hospital in Amherst (NS). We will share the results from our project with participants, their families, and involved communities, as a way to assist them with any future pregnancies. We will also communicate findings to doctors, nurses, hospital workers, and public health officials, to assist them in providing advice and guidance to pregnant women and future mothers-to-be. We will translate the study results into strategies, to manage depression during pregnancy and to improve mothers' and children's health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the molecular etiology of idiopathic generalized epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: CHANNELOPATHIES; EPILEPSY; IDIOPATHIC GENERALIZED EPILEPSY; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Advances in genetic sequencing have taken a tremendous leap forward with the advent of next generation sequencing.  It is now possible to sequence an individual's entire coding sequence, or "exome", quickly and inexpensively.  The technology has been successful in identifying disease genes in rare Mendelian traits.  Idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) is a complex condition with a marked familial aggregation and high concordance in identical twins.  This strongly supports a genetic contribution to this common condition.  A few genes have been identified in individuals with a family history of IGE.  When these genes are tested in cases with no family history, there are individuals with new, or de novo, changes at the epilepsy genes.   We plan to sequence the exome of children with idiopathic generalized epilepsy.  We will also sequence their unaffected parents.  Any changes we observe in the child with IGE but not present in the parents would qualify as an epilepsy gene candidate for a de novo mutation.  We will also explore how well this new technology performs as a potential diagnostic tool for IGE.  If we have a readily available, cheap and quick method of identifying epilepsy mutations, we may halt further investigations for a child and their family. The knowledge may tailor the anti-epileptic medication, provide clarity with regards to long term prognosis, and give information for genetic counseling purposes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Use of genetic tests in practice: role of physicians, guidelines, and health policies and impacts on patients
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES; DECISION-MAKING; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PUBLIC HEALTH GENETICS; USE OF GENETIC TESTS
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of my research program is to improve the use of genetic services in the health care system through a better understanding of the translational process of new genetic advances into genetic tests and services. The main themes of my research are 1) the role of physicians in the use of genetic tests and services in practice; 2) the influence of clinical practice guidelines and other health policies on the use of genetic tests and services by physicians 3) the impact of genetic tests and services on patients and their families. My research program includes 3 projects articulated around these themes. My main project focuses on the use of genetic tests in the evaluation of children with developmental delay. This project evaluates physicians' decision-making process for the use of genetic tests in the evaluation of children with DD, the impact of such testing on patients and families, and actual use of genetic tests in practice. A second project assesses the needs of physicians in anticipation of a future scoliosis susceptibility test, to develop tools to help its introduction in clinical practice. A third project examines the concept of "serious disease" as a criterion for access to pre-implantation genetic diagnosis under Quebec health insurance.  Thanks to my interdisciplinary expertise in genetics and health services research, my research produces evidence that will help inform practice guidelines, educational interventions and health policies to improve the use of genetic tests and services in the Quebec and Canadian health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Concealment to Engagement: Helping Women Overcome Secrecy and Isolation Associated with Eating Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; EATING DISORDERS; MENTAL HEALTH; MIXED METHODS (QUALITATIVE AND QUANTITATIVE); PILOT ANALYSIS; SECRECY; SOCIAL ISOLATION; SOCIAL SUPPORT; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Women with eating disorders (ED) may experience feelings of shame and embarrassment, often choosing to keep their condition secretive, remain socially isolated and avoid treatment. Without support, women may experience negative health outcomes (e.g. cardiovascular, dental, reproductive, and cognitive irregularities), greatly impacting quality in life and exacting further strain on healthcare and community resources. This research aims to understand how women with ED can overcome secrecy and social isolation, and explore how secrecy and disclosure relate to mental health, support seeking and healthcare utilization. This study acts as a pilot in a comprehensive community supported research program aimed at developing a better understanding of, and practical solutions to, the challenges of secrecy and social isolation associated with women's mental health related concerns. Women with a history of ED and related secrecy will be recruited from New Brunswick, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. Empirical methods  will be used to examine relationships among measures for mental health and support seeking (social and healthcare utilization), and length of concealment. Qualitative interviews will be used to determine (1) how women with ED overcome secrecy and social isolation and (2) the needs, resources, preferences and barriers for support intervention. Results will be prepared for publication, media interviews, newspaper articles, and evaluation guidelines. Findings will: (1) contribute new knowledge pertaining to ED, women's health, and social isolation, (2) better societal health by informing service providers and main stakeholders of the support needs, resources, preferences and barriers of women with ED, (3) create public and service provider awareness of women's mental health concerns, and (4) help alleviate strain on the health care system by providing practical solutions  to large-scale mental health concerns so as to improve the wellbeing of women and society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Le contrôle de la distribution des acides gras polyinsaturés dans les glycérophospholipides membranaires.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACIDE ARACHIDONIQUE; ACIDES GRAS; CHROMATOGRAPHIES (TLC; CLONAGE MOLECULAIRE ET TRANSFECTION; DOSAGE ENZYMATIQUES; HPLC ET GC); ISOLATION ET CULTURE CELLULAIRE; PHOSPHOLIPIDES; QPCR; SUREXPRESSION ET ATTENUATION DE L'EXPRESSION; WESTERN
Abstract-Résumé: Les phospholipides sont les constituants lipidiques majeurs des membranes cellulaires et ils contiennent deux molecules d'acides gras. Par contre, il existe une tres grande diversite d'acides gras et de classes de phospholipides. Certains acides gras polyinsatures, comme l'acide arachidonique (AA) et l'acide eicosapentanoique (EPA), sont des precurseurs d'importantes molecules lipidiques bioactives impliquees dans plusieurs processus biologiques importants. Par contre, quelques une de ces molecules sont aussi impliquees dans la progression de plusieurs maladies inflammatoires et de certains types de cancers.  Les acides gras polyinsatures sont generalement entreposes dans les phospholipides membranaires et doivent etre liberes avant d'etre converti en mediateurs bioactifs. Par contre, la distribution des acides gras dans les phospholipides n'est pas symetrique et statique puisque les acides gras sont constamment remodeles (redistribues) par l'activite de plusieurs enzymes. Plusieurs etudes ont demontres que ces mecanismes de remodelage sont importants pour la fluidite membranaire ainsi que pour plusieurs fonctions cellulaires comme l'activation cellulaire, la production de mediateurs d'inflammation et la proliferation cellulaire.  Plusieurs enzymes ayant differentes activites enzymatiques specifiques pour differents acides gras et phospholipides ont ete identifiees, mais leurs roles sur la distribution des acides gras dans les differents phospholipides n'ont pas bien ete caracterises. Certaines de ces enzymes semblent etre impliquees dans le controle de la production de mediateurs lipidiques et de la proliferation cellulaire. Donc, le but de ce projet de recherche sera d'identifier et de caracteriser les enzymes impliquees dans la redistribution des acides gras polyinsatures dans les phospholipides, cette recherche pourrait mener a la decouverte d'importantes cibles therapeutiques contre les maladies inflammatoires et proliferatives

TitreApplicationTitle: L'activité transcriptionnelle des différents variants du promoteur de la 5-lipoxygénase
Keywords-MotsClés: 5-LIPOXYGENASE; ACIDES GRAS POLYINSATUREES; ACTIVITE PROMOTRICE; ATHEROSCLEROSE; FACTEURS DE TRANSCRIPTION; INFLAMMATION; MONOCYTE/MACROPHAGE; NUTRIGENOMIQUE; POLYMORPHISMES; REGULATION ET EXPRESSION DE GENE
Abstract-Résumé: La 5-lipoxygenase (5-LO) est une proteine/enzyme exprimee principalement par les globules blancs. Elle est essentielle pour la production de leucotrienes, des lipides bioactifs associes a plusieurs maladies inflammatoires telles que l'asthme et l'atherosclerose. Cette association entre la 5-LO et les maladies inflammatoires est a la base meme de nos travaux et nous cherchons a comprendre s'il est possible que des petites modifications dans notre ADN soient impliquees dans le lien fonctionnel entre la 5-LO et les maladies inflammatoires. Nous etudions plus precisement une region de l'ADN qui est impliquee dans la production de la 5-LO. Cette region, que nous appelons promoteur, comporte une signature precise de nucleotides (la base du code genetique): nous retrouvons cinq sequences GC en tandem. Chez certains individus, au lieu de retrouver cinq sequences GC, nous en retrouverons trois, quatre ou six (variants). Ces changements sont tres subtils mais sont pourtant associes au developpement de l'atherosclerose. D'ailleurs, le risque entre ces variants du promoteur de la 5-LO et l'atherosclerose est plus important que celui associe au tabagisme et au diabete. Cependant, il serait possible d'eliminer cette predisposition genetique par la consommation de lipides omega-3 provenant d'huiles de poissons, comme l'EPA et le DHA. Mon programme de doctorat consiste a caracteriser les differents variants du promoteur de la 5-LO et de comprendre comment les lipides omega-3 mentionnes ci haut affectent l'activite de la 5-LO (directement et/ou indirectement). La comprehension des mecanismes biologiques existant entre la production de la 5-LO, les omega-3 et l'atherosclerose sera tres importante afin d'etablir des traitements nutritionnels personnalises et menera eventuellement au developpement d'un test rapide afin d'etablir si un individu est plus a risque de developper l'atherosclerose.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring physicians' preferences regarding work and life in rural and remote regions for recruitment and retention policies
Keywords-MotsClés: DISCRETE CHOICE EXPERIMENT; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH WORKFORCE; RURAL AND REMOTE RECRUITMENT AND RETENTION
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of this project is to collect information from physicians in Manitoba on their preferences for working and living in rural and remote regions and the work/life balance they aim to achieve.  All physicians in Manitoba will be asked to fill out a questionnaire that will collect three sets of information.  A discrete choice experiment will measure the trade-offs that physicians are willing to make between salient attributes associated with work and life outside work; a work/life satisfaction questionnaire will provide measures of how physicians rate each of these attributes individually; and socio-demographic information will be collected from each respondent to compare this to respondents' stated preferences (from the DCE and job/life satisfaction questions) and to stratify the data for analysis.  The primary goal is to gather information that is relevant to designing more successful policies to recruit and retain physicians in rural and remote communities.  The DCE and work/life satisfaction questions will be designed with this purpose in mind, and the trade-offs measured by the DCE will elicit the extent to which physicians need to be compensated for specific job characteristics through improvements in other job attributes and in the work-life balance.  This research will also make a significant contribution to the literature by comparing the results of the DCE with the results of the work/life satisfaction questions, and by comparing these stated preferences with respondents' actual choices (their current job).  Currently, most of the literature on job preferences uses job satisfaction questions, which cannot quantify trade-offs that respondents are willing to make to accept some less favourable job attributes in return for attributes that are particularly important to them.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the role played by the Steroid receptor RNA activator bi-faceted system in breast tumor progression.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CO-ACTIVATORS; CO-REPRESSORS; EPITHELIAL-MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION; INVASION; MAMMARY GLAND DEVELOPMENT; STEROID RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: In 2011, 23,000 Canadian women will be diagnosed with breast cancer and 5,300 will die from this disease. Increasing our knowledge of the mechanisms controlling the different steps of the disease is a priority to save these women. When breast cancer appears, cells divide abnormally but do not move. At this stage, when the disease remains localized, targeting is easier, treatment options are better and getting rid of the cancer is likely. Unfortunately, breast cancer cells can evolve and acquire the ability to move out of the breast and colonize other tissues, creating multiple disseminated tumors called metastases. Metastases increase the number of targets to be eliminated and reduce the chances to successfully cure the disease. Metastases, which can appear in tissues such as bone, brain and liver, alter the normal functions of these critical organs. They are therefore ultimately responsible for the death of the patients. As such, understanding events controlling the different steps of tumor progression and invasion will provide preventive and therapeutic targets to eradicate breast cancer.   The present project deals with an intriguing newly discovered molecular system that consists of an RNA (SRA) and its corresponding protein (SRAP). As opposed to most systems, where either RNA, either protein has a function, both molecules are able to control specific event in cells. Accumulated preliminary data point toward SRA/SRAP controlling breast cancer cells invasion, making the study of this system highly relevant to breast cancer research. Using Molecular Biology, archived cancer tissue and mouse models, this project will decipher the mechanisms behind SRA/SRAP action. It will allow us to propose models highlighting the mechanisms by which the bi-faceted SRA RNA/SRAP system controls breast cancer progression. These models will help elaborate novel strategies aimed to specifically block invasion, slow down the progression or prevent the initiation of this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Target identification of novel growth inhibitors for the multiple antibiotic resistant Burkholderia cenocepacia through genome-wide conditional growth expression
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBACTERIAL TARGET; ANTIBIOTIC MECHANISM OF ACTION; BACTERIAL CONDITIONAL GROWTH MUTANT LIBRARY; BACTERIAL TRANSPOSON MUTAGENEIS; BURKHOLDERIA CENOCEPACIA; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; MULTIPLEX PCR; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; NOVEL ANTIBIOTICS; SMALL MOLECULE LIBRARY
Abstract-Résumé: The Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) is a group of multiple antibiotic resistant bacteria that infect cystic fibrosis patients. Once established, the infection is virtually impossible to eradicate. For this reason, new and more effective antibiotics are urgently needed.   Antibiotics work by interfering with functions important for bacterial life (essential functions). Thus, research on new antibiotics involves not only discovering new compounds with antibiotic activity but also finding the essential functions that these molecules target.   To find novel antibiotics we screened a collection of more than 30,000 small molecules and found compounds that inhibit the growth of B. cenocepacia K56-2, a clinical isolate of Bcc. Using molecular genetics tools, we are building a large collection of bacterial mutants in which each clone contains an essential function that can be controlled. We will expose these mutants to the growth inhibitors and by observing the different responses of the clones we will identify the essential functions targeted by the small molecules.   Our research will provide novel antibacterial molecules against Bcc and the understanding of how such molecules kill the bacteria. This knowledge will be very important for further developments of the novel antibacterial molecules into more effective ways to treat Bcc infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding telomerase function: modulation of a stable G-quadruplex structure in human telomerase RNA by the helicase RHAU.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER CELL BIOLOGY; CELLULAR AGING; ENZYME MECHANISM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; RNA QUADRUPLEX STRUCTURE; RNA-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; TELOMERASE
Abstract-Résumé: Human chromosome ends are protected from damage by a stretch of repetitive DNA sequences known as telomeres. In healthy mortal cells, telomere DNA is gradually shortened during successive rounds of replication as a cell ages, and therefore serves as a molecular clock. In cancerous cells the enzyme telomerase ensures maintenance of stable telomere length and therefore enables the indefinite growth and uncontrolled cell division characteristic of tumor formation. Telomerase activation requires both a protein and ribonucleic acid (RNA) component. In particular, proper incorporation of the RNA component is a complex multistep process that is not fully understood. In this proposal, we seek to understand the role that changes in the three dimensional structure of human telomerase RNA play in the process of telomerase activation. We hypothesize that recognition and modulation of an unusually stable structure in telomerase RNA, known as a G-quadruplex, is required for telomerase activation. To test this hypothesis, we will use an integrated experimental approach involving high-resolution structural biology, biophysical analysis, and in vivo functional methodologies to study the biological importance of the G-quadruplex structural element. Given the central role that telomerase plays in maintenance of telomere DNA in cancerous cells, we expect that a detailed investigation of its mechanism of activation will provide significant insight into the biology of several disease states. The results from our investigations will also offer the opportunity for the rational design of therapeutics that can specifically target the assembly of an enzyme essential for cancer cell progression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rabies virus-induced injury to neuronal processes: role of oxidative stress
Keywords-MotsClés: NEUROPATHOLOGY; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; NEUROVIROLOGY; VIRAL PATHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Rabies is a serious problem in Canadian wildlife and it is an important public health problem in developing countries. Human rabies is almost invariably fatal. An understanding of how rabies virus causes disease will be helpful in developing new strategies for the prevention and treatment of rabies and potentially also other viral and neurologic diseases. There is promising recent data from the laboratory of the principal applicant and others that rabies virus causes disease by injuring processes of neurons, including axons and dendrites. This damage is not apparent on routine pathological studies. The applicants have recently demonstrated that the infection likely causes damage by oxidative stress, which involves injury to tissues caused via by-products of the metabolism of oxygen called reactive oxygen species. Oxidative stress is important in a variety of human neurological diseases, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and also in experimental infection of the brain in mice produced by herpes simplex virus. Using studies on cultured sensory nerve cells the mechanisms will be determined by which rabies virus infection produces oxidative damage to neuronal processes. In particular, the role of mitochondria and a variety of key regulatory molecules will be evaluated using techniques that include imaging of live nerve cells and gene silencing technology. This work will give important insights into how rabies virus causes disease of the nervous system. This information will be important in the development of new therapies for patients with rabies and other viral diseases and also be applicable to a variety of other virological and neurological diseases.

Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD PRESSURE TELEMETRY; CALCIUM IMAGING; CELL-CELL COMMUNICATION; DIABETES COMPLICATIONS; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS DYSFUNCTION; HYPERTENSION; IN VIVO PHARMACOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; ISOLATED BLOOD VESSELS; PROTEASE-ACTIVATED RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Doctors know that blood vessels do not work properly in people diagnosed with high blood presure (hypertension) and diabetes. Unfortunately, hypertension is a common health concern for Canadians even those living healthy lifestyles because many people will develop it while ageing. The occurence of type 2 diabetes in children now has set them up for life long problems for their cardiovascular health. The communication signals between two types of cells in blood vessels, endothelial cells and smooth muscle cells, are altered by those diseases and by ageing. This research program is seeking information about a protein (PAR2) that creates communication signals between the endothelial and smooth muscle cells. PAR2 causes rapid effects that may benefit health. These rapid effects are not affected by blood vessel disease. The research program will also look at the slow effects of PAR2. By studying PAR2, we may learn important new things about preserving our cell-to-cell communication in blood vessels. Developing drugs that are resistant to the communication defects in blood vessels would be useful to Doctors for their treatment of patients with heart disease, hypertension and diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Multi-level Model of the Effects of Primary Healthcare Reform on Ambulatory Care Sensitive Hospital Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: AMBULATORY CARE SENSITIVE OUTCOMES; DATA LINKAGE; GEOSPATIAL ACCESS TO CARE; MULTI-LEVEL MODELLING; PHYSICIAN REIMBURSEMENT MODELS; PRIMARY HEALTHCARE REFORM
Abstract-Résumé: A patient's first contact with the healthcare system is usually with a primary healthcare provider, often a family physician. A reform of primary healthcare is proceeding in Canada and other countries under the assumption that changing the delivery of care at this level will translate into improved public health. Although this implied overall benefit to public health is logical, it is important to both research and policy that the reforms are evaluated with regard to their relative strength to improve medical outcomes. The usage of healthcare services and the success of policy reforms are influenced by a complex set of non-medical variables (e.g., socioeconomic and geographic) at various levels of organization (e.g., hospital and bureaucracy). Some reforms will thus be more effective than others and some anticipated health benefits might conceivably not actualize post-implementation. However, very few studies have examined the effects of the proposed reforms on health outcomes.  Changes in health resulting from interventions at the primary healthcare level are generally not observed in a population for many years after implementation. Thus, studies of recent changes to the primary care system have focused on economic feasibility or patient and physician satisfaction rather than their effect on the diagnosis or prevention of disease. However, some changes to primary care have now been in effect for sufficient time to observe whether there have been improvements in related hospital outcomes.  We will gather pre-existing data about physician reimbursement models, geographic accessibility, clinical setting, patient education, wealth, and prior health in Newfoundland and Labrador. We will develop a multilevel statistical model that can be used to determine which primary care reforms help prevent important patient outcomes such as hospitalizations. We will also examine the feasibility of a nation-wide study that will use a similar method.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Cell Survival Genes in Neurogenesis and Neural Regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH AND SURVIVAL GENES; CORTICAL DEVELOPMENT; NEURAL PROGENITORS; NEURAL STEM CELL BIOLOGY; NEUROGENESIS; REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: The discovery of stem cells in the adult brain has generated hope for a future where brain regeneration can occur. Recent studies have enhanced this excitement by showing that stem cells in the brain respond to an injury by producing new cells in an attempt to replace those lost or damaged. This exciting news is tempered by the low numbers of stems cells in the adult brain and these numbers become even smaller with increasing age. Unfortunately, the low numbers of stem cells in the adult brain is compounded by the poor survival rate of newborn cells within the injury site severely limiting the ability of the brain to repair itself.  Transplanting stem cells into the injury site has failed to circumvent these limitations and often results in the death of 80-90% of transplanted cells. Research aimed at promoting the survival of stem cells and newborn cells following a brain injury should therefore greatly enhance neural regeneration in the brain. The goal of my laboratory is to identify the proteins that regulate the survival of stem cells and then manipulate their expression to enhance cell survival in the injured brain. Research from my laboratory has recently shown that Mcl1, a pro-survival protein has dual functions in brain stem cells: to promote stem cell survival and to promote cell differentiation. The goal of this research project is investigate the mechanism by which Mcl1 performs these two distinct functions in brain stem cells. We hope these experiments will identify a novel approach to enhancing cell survival and neural regeneration. Promoting cell survival is the first step in what will need to be a multi-component strategy to promote the generation of new nerve cells to replace those lost due to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson and Alzheimer diseases or following acute injuries such as stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of dietary methyl groups on methionine metabolism and early programming in neonates
Keywords-MotsClés: AMINO ACIDS; EARLY PROGRAMMING OF ADULT DISEASES; ISOTOPE KINETICS; METABOLISM; METHYL GROUPS; PIGLET; REQUIREMENTS
Abstract-Résumé: When infants are exposed to poor nutrition in the womb or shortly after birth, their metabolism is altered to compensate for this situation. It has recently been shown that these infants, who are often born small and then catch-up, actually have a higher risk of developing chronic diseases in adulthood including obesity, heart disease, high blood pressure and diabetes. Some nutrients, such as the amino acid methionine, have dual roles during growth. Methionine is incorporated into protein and is also responsible for methylation reactions which are critical in maintaining health. These methylation reactions also program DNA in infants which can permanently change the person's susceptibility to disease later in life. However, other dietary nutrients such as folate and choline can spare the need for methionine. We intend to measure the methionine requirement in neonates when folate and choline are deficient or in excess. How these dietary situations affect the methylation reactions will also be investigated to monitor the programming pathways for later disease. Overall, this research will help optimize nutrition recommendations for infants and potentially prevent chronic diseases later in life.

Keywords-MotsClés: FOLATE; FORMATE; HOMOCYSTEINE; POLYMORPHISMS; VITAMIN B12; VITAMIN DEFICIENCY
Abstract-Résumé: Impairments in one-carbon metabolism may result either from some vitamin deficiencies (Folate or Vitamin B12) or from genetic causes. These result in increased incidence of neural tube defects and are also associated with cognitive impairment in the elderly, as well as cardiovascular disease. We have found that formate (found in ant stings as formic acid) accumulates in the blood in these situations and may serve as an important indicator of ill health. It may be more than an indicator, it may play a causal role. We will investigate these questions in experimental animals and blood samples from large human populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and functional characterization of SCO-dependent, mitochondrial regulation of cellular copper homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELLULAR COPPER HANDLING; COX ASSEMBLY FACTORS; CYTOCHROME C OXIDASE (COX); GENETICS; HUMAN DISEASES; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; REDOX SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria are small cellular compartments that produce the chemical form of energy (ATP) that supports normal cell function. ATP is produced by the concerted efforts of a number of enzyme complexes. Deficiencies in one of these complexes, cytochrome c oxidase (COX), are associated with a broad spectrum of clinical presentations from isolated myopathies to multisystem disease. SCO1 and SCO2 are two closely related genes involved in delivering copper, an essential co-factor, to COX during its assembly. I recently discovered that SCO proteins also fulfill additional, and unexpected, roles in regulating how the cell handles copper, to minimize the potential toxicity of this essential metal as it is trafficked throughout the cell. Much remains to be learned, however, about how a SCO-dependent mitochondrial signal is generated and subsequently transduced to extra-mitochondrial compartments, to effect changes in cellular copper homeostasis. The overall goal of this research proposal therefore is to identify and characterize the mitochondrial and non-mitochondrial components of this signaling pathway, so as to understand how this pathway ultimately impinges upon the global regulation of cellular copper homeostasis. This may lead to the development of novel therapies with which to treat human diseases that result from an isolated COX deficiency or cellular copper handling defects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging pain fibre activation in the cerebral meninges; Insight into the pathophysiology of migraine headache
Keywords-MotsClés: EXPERIMENTAL METHODS AND INSTRUMENTATION; FLUORESCENCE IMAGING; MIGRAINE; NEUROLOGICAL MODEL; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PAIN; TERMINAL AFFERENT NOCICEPTIVE FIBRE; TWO-PHOTON MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Our research has enabled us to watch for the first time the activation of the nerve fibres that are responsible for the pain experienced during migraine headache.  Migraine is an intensely painful neurological condition that affects up to one fifth of the general population.  Understanding migraine pain is a very challenging problem and thus, despite its widespread occurrence, the cause of migraine remains unknown.  Pain sensitivity within the skull does not arise from the brain itself, but in fact is restricted to the membranous coverings of the brain called meninges.  Pain fibres densely innervate the brain's meninges and abnormal activation of these fibres is considered a central component for the origin of migraine pain.  We have developed a new experimental rodent preparation that maintains the membrane coverings of the brain together with the skull intact and allows the use of microscopy to observe the activation of individual pain fibres during pharmacological, electrical, and light manipulations.  The objective of our research is to gain insight into the mechanisms of pain fibre signaling to better understand the neurological pain processes that occur during migraine.  It is our hope that this will lead to new drug targets and better therapeutic treatments for this devastating illness.

Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; AMYLOID; APOPTOSIS; NEUROBIOLOGY; NEUROTOXICITY; TRANSGENIC MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a common, progressive and ultimately lethal disease affecting ~5% of adults over 65 years of age and ~30% of adults over the age of 85 years in most Western societies. Both the prevalence and the annual expenditures on AD are expected to increase as the proportion of the population at risk increases over the next 20 years.  The currently available treatments are of limited effectiveness as they target the symptoms of the disease but not the root  cause. The major features of AD are accumulations of abnormal proteins called amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles within the brain. Amyloid plaques appear as densely packed thread-like fibers that form in the vicinity of nerve cells and blood vessels. Evidence suggests that amyloid is highly toxic and is the primary cause of nerve cell death. Loss of these cells is the underlying event in AD and results in the clinical features of cognitive dysfunction and memory impairments. The ultimate objective of this research is to understand the cellular processes which cause AD and to use that information for the development of safe and effective treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: From Down Syndrome to Alzheimer's Disease: the molecular mechanism underlying the dementia pathogenesis and the therapeutic potentials
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID; BACE1; DOWN SYNDROME; LTP AND LTD; MOLECULAR GENETICS; TRANSGENIC AND KNOCKOUT; TWO-PHOTON IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disorder leading to dementia. AD affects about 10% of the population over the age of 65. Down syndrome (DS) is the most common genetic cause of mental retardation, affecting approximately one in 700 to 1,000 babies. The majority of DS cases are caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, thus also known as Trisomy 21 syndrome. Individuals with DS inevitably develop characteristic AD neuropathology including neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles after middle age. The underlying mechanism leading to AD pathogenesis is not well defined and there is no effective disease-modified treatment for AD. DS is a valuable human model system for studying AD pathogenesis. Our working hypothesis is that alteration of the gene expression and protein functions plays an important role in AD pathogenesis in DS. This proposal seeks to use unique DS mouse and human model platforms to elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying AD pathogenesis in DS and identify novel biomarkers and drug targets for AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role in Abeta synaptotoxicity of kinases identified through functional and genetic studies in Alzheimer Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ABETA TPXICITY; ALZHEIMER DISEASE; ANIMAL MODELS; DISEASE GENES
Abstract-Résumé: The accumulation of Abeta peptides in the form of neurotoxic soluble aggregates is a key molecular and neuropathological feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Changes in synaptic plasticity mediated by the neurotoxic effects of these soluble oligomeric assemblies of Abeta are thought to underlie at least some of the early cognitive impairments associated with AD. Although hypothesis-driven experiments have produced several leads, the underlying mechanisms remain controversial. Recently, we undertook hypothesis-free genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in search of new genes causally associated with AD. This genetic screen identified two kinase genes (EPHA1 and PTK2B) that are strongly associated with AD (p<10E-10), and that are likely to be involved in the synaptic injury in AD. In addition, we have recently demonstrated that a third kinase, protein kinase D (PKD1) plays a previously unrecognised, but important role in synaptic plasticity. The present proposal will examine how these kinases (and their respective signalling pathways) are involved in Abeta-mediated synaptic toxicity. The proposed programme builds upon: i) substantial preliminary data generated in our labs in China and Canada; and ii) on the unique skills present in each lab. These are critical features which make the program FULLY FEASIBLE. The program will provide KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE AND TRAINING by supporting graduate student, postdoctoral and staff scientist exchanges to labs with different skill sets. This program will provide a BETTER UNDERSTANDING OF THE DISEASE  MECHANISMS. This knowledge will be an essential cornerstone for future TRANSLATIONAL use in the development of BIOMARKERS (that measure activation of these mechanisms and thus disease presence/ activity) and NOVEL THERAPIES (that block these mechanisms). Kinases are highly tractable targets for both SMALL MOLECULE and BIOLOGICAL THERAPIES including those from TRADITIONAL CHINESE MEDICINE.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of the Role of the p7 Protein in the Hepatitis C Virus Life Cycle.
Keywords-MotsClés: HCV ASSEMBLY; HCV CELL CULTURE; HCV LIFE CYCLE; HCV P7 PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is considered a major global health problem. It infects 170 million people worldwide causing liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. The HCV genome encodes a small protein called p7, but until now, limited information is known regarding the role of p7 in the HCV life cycle. Analysis of this role is considered to be a high priority in HCV biology. The aim of this study is to investigate the role of p7 in the HCV life cycle. In order to do this we created multiple changes covering two thirds of the amino acid sequence of p7 in the background of a complete virus sequence. Analysis of these modified viruses showed that p7 is important for infectious virus production. In addition, we have tested the role of this protein at different stages of the viral life cycle and found that the p7 is not involved in release of the virus from the host cell. We also found that these regions of p7 do not affect the recruitment of the major viral structural protein called core to lipid rich areas of the cell where it is believed the virus forms, and did not affect one of the major viral non-structural proteins called NS3 that is important in viral genome replication. Recently, we found that one of our mutations located in a highly conserved region of p7 known as the cytopalsmic loop affects E2 (envelope protein 2) expression levels; an important structural protein that plays a major role in virus entry into host cells. Thus, we will continue to test how p7 affects E2 protein expression at different stages of the viral life cycle. We will test whether p7 interacts with other viral proteins and determine if it acts as an accessory protein to maintain other viral protein functions. In the bigger picture, the observed effect at the highly conserved region of p7 on the E2 glycoprotein makes p7 a great potential target for antiviral agents. We believe that results from our work will provide important contributions regarding HCV nature and treatment discoveries

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular interrogation and a small molecule screen of NUP98-HOXA9 induced AML in the zebrafish
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE MYELOID LEUKEMIA; BETA CATENIN; CHEMICAL SCREEN; MEIS1; MYELOPROLIFERATIVE NEOPLASM; NUP98-HOXA9; TRANSGENESIS; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Despite advances in leukemia therapy, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) continues to pose significant treatment challenges, with cure rates of less than 60% following intensive treatment. Pertinent animal models will be critical to understanding the molecular pathways underlying this disease in order to develop new targeted therapies to improve the outcome. Remarkably, a common tropical fish, the zebrafish, shares the blood cells and genetic programming found in human blood development and additionally, possesses several technical advantages over other animal model systems including small size, and large numbers of offspring that are externally fertilized and transparent. Zebrafish models of human cancers to date have provided new information on cancer development and have been extremely valuable for conducting high-throughput cost-effective chemical screens for new effective agents. We have developed a genetically altered zebrafish model of high risk expressing the NUP98-HOXA9 (NHA9) cancer-causing and found that both the embryos and adult fish demonstrate features in keeping with human disease, suggesting this model can be used to identify new effective treatments as well as better understand how NHA9 causes leukemia. We plan to conduct a drug screen on our NHA9 zebrafish embryos to identify compounds that restore normal blood development and may represent undiscovered therapies in AML. These types of screens are prohibitively expensive in traditional model systems. We will also use genetic manipulations and drug treatments that can be easily visualized in zebrafish embryos to determine how other genes interact with NHA9 and contribute to AML and which cells are specifically involved, providing a better understanding of this disease. The proposed studies have tremendous potential to shed light on the pathways that lead to leukemia in NHA9 AML and improve disease outcome by identifying previously undiscovered chemical agents that may lead to new effective therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Maternal Analgesia for Procedural Pain in Preterm Neonates: Does It Remain Efficacious?
Keywords-MotsClés: KANGAROO MOTHER CARE (SKIN-TO-SKIN-CONTACT); PARALLEL GROUP REPEATED MEASURES DESIGN; PRETERM NEONATES; PROCEDURAL PAIN; SUCROSE ANALGESIA
Abstract-Résumé: When a mother holds her almost naked baby next to her own bare chest, known as Kangaroo Mother Care because it is similar to how kangaroo's carry their young, they both benefit. We know that this caring method decreases the pain response in hospitalized babies who must have painful needle pokes and heel sticks as part of their care. What we do not know is if this works more than once. Does it continue to help the baby's pain across the time of hospitalization?  Current guidelines include the use of sugar water for minor painful procedures, although its continued use has been questioned.This study will follow three groups of babies born prematurely across their hospitalization: one group will be in Kangaroo Mother Care, one group will receive sugar water and one group both for painful procedures. We predict that Kangaroo Mother Care will continue to work across time as well if not better than sugar water.

TitreApplicationTitle: Design, Synthesis and Optimization of New Chemical Entities as Antimicrobial Agents
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC; ANTIMICROBIAL; BACTERIAL INFECTIONS; DRUG DESIGN; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; MOLECULAR MODELLING; ORGANIC CHEMISTRY
Abstract-Résumé: Infectious disease persists as a major medical problem.  Increasingly, bacterial infections are becoming resistant to conventional antibiotics.  Currently, we are facing four "plagues": "re-emerging plague" (as Gram-positive bacteria become less susceptible to conventional antibotics); "new plague" (as Gram-negative bacteria become a more common cause of hospital acquired infections); "white plague" (as tuberculosis re-emerges world wide with resistance to drugs that once worked) and "forgotten plague" (as malaria continues to be a problem and has expanded relevance due to global warming).  This research will use state of the art molecular modelling to design new drugs for the treatment of bacterial infections for one or more of these plagues.  These putative new drugs will be synthesized, purified and tested in a variety of biological and animal models.

TitreApplicationTitle: Practice Pattern Variation in Discontinuing Mechanical Ventilation in Critically Ill Adults: An International Study.
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATION; CRITICAL CARE; INTERNATIONAL STUDY; MECHANICAL VENTILATION; OUTCOMES; PROSPECTIVE OBSERVATIONAL STUDY; WEANING
Abstract-Résumé: Background: The requirement for ventilator support is a defining feature of critical illness. Weaning is the process during which the work of breathing is transferred from the ventilator back to the patient. Approximately 40% of the total time spent on ventilators is dedicated to weaning. The extent of practice variation in how this complex and expensive technology is discontinued from critically ill patients is unknown. Meanwhile, practice variation has been shown to adversely impact upon patient safety and clinical outcomes.   Purpose: To characterize practice pattern variation in weaning and the consequences of weaning variation by implementing an international, prospective observational study in Canada,the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, India and Australia/New Zealand.   Primary Objectives: To describe 1. weaning practice variation among regions in 5 domains (the use of daily screening, preferred methods of support used before initial discontinuation attempts, use of written protocols, preferred methods of evaluating spontaneous breathing, and sedation and mobilization practices).  2. the assocation between selected discontinuation strategies and important clinical outcomes (length of stay, mortality, duration of ventilation).  Methods: We propose to conduct a large scale, observational study involving critically ill adults requiring ventilator support for at least 24 hours to evaluate practices in discontinuing ventilators in 150 centres. We will classify each new admission over the observation period according to the initial strategy that precipitated or facilitated ventilator discontinuation.   Relevance: This novel study will build collaborations with critical care investigators from around the world and industry partners by implementing a large scale, observational study in 6 geographic regions to describe how critically ill adults are liberated from ventilators and the impact of different strategies on important clinical outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gene Delivery of Glucagon-like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) for the Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CHITOSAN; DIABETES; GENE DELIVERY; GLUCAGON-LIKE PEPTIDE-1; NANOMEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: Therapeutic proteins are a new class of drug that has found success in several medical areas. Usually the protein is delivered, however the lifetime of the protein in the body can be very short (minutes), so that large quantities must be taken frequently. An alternative is to deliver the DNA corresponding to the protein and allow the patient's cells to take up the DNA and make the corresponding protein. This gene delivery approach can be difficult since the DNA needs to be packaged in a way that allows cells to take it in, but also to unpackage the DNA once inside the cell and let it be transcribed into the protein. Recent work by our group has developed some very efficient systems to achieve this goal. We use a polymer of glucosamine, called chitosan, to bind to the DNA to form nanosized particles that deliver the DNA to cells. We have applied some of these chitosan-DNA nanoparticles to deliver glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) that is effective against diabetes. We have published data showing that chitosan-DNA vectors expressing GLP-1 can lower circulating glucose in an animal model of diabetes, the ZDF rat. The proposed work aims to build upon this positive data by producing GLP-1 plasmids coding for modified GLP-1 peptides that resist enzymatic degradation and by delivering RNA molecules that inhibit the activity of the main enzyme degrading GLP-1, DPP-IV. These two approaches will increase the effectiveness of the peptide. An additional strategy is to modify the polymer chitosan to limit systemic clearance and produce longer circulating nanoparticles. The nanoparticles will be examined using model cells to assess delivery efficiency. Selected systems will be tested in the diabetic animal model for their efficacy in reducing diabetic signs and symptoms. The result of this project will be some promising new candidates for the treatment of diabetes ready to enter phase 1 clinical testing by the industrial partner of this project, Spencer Pharmaceuticals.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Study of H-Coil Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Late-Life Depression
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN STIMULATION; CLINICAL TRIAL; DEPRESSION; ELDERLY
Abstract-Résumé: Canadians aged 60 and older are the fastest growing segment of the population.  Depression is a very common illness later in life and is a major contributor to high rates of disability, poor quality of life, caregiver burden and poor health outcomes.  Unfortunately, up to 84% of individuals treated for late-life depression (LLD) either do not respond to treatment or respond and then relapse.  Strategies for managing treatment resistance in older adults are problematic due to increased sensitivity to side effects and higher rates of prescription drug use for other medical illnesses. There are very few safe and effective options for treating patients who do not respond to antidepressants.  Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) involves stimulating the brain with a series of magnetic field pulses.  Treatment is administered daily, five days per week, for between 30 and 45 minutes 4 weeks.  In younger adults, rTMS is approved in the United States and by Health Canada for the treatment of resistant depression and has demonstrated an excellent safety profile with good efficacy.  However, few studies have evaluated rTMS for older patients with LLD.  While initial results have shown some evidence of efficacy for rTMS in older adults, several factors have limited its efficacy in older adults.  The major factors responsible for its limited efficacy are changes in the brain that occur with normal aging and the reduced size of the magnetic field generated by conventional coils. Brainsway Limited has developed a patented novel rTMS coil (H-coil) that has a unique ability to overcome the limitations of conventional rTMS coils.  Due to the overwhelming increase in the number of older adults suffering from depression that will occur with the aging of the Canadian population, alternative treatments are desperately needed.  Therefore, in this study we aim evaluate the Brainsway Ltd. H-Coil in older adults with resistant depression.

Keywords-MotsClés: 60 HZ MAGNETIC FIELD; COMPUTATIONAL NEUROSCIENCES; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY; ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; HUMAN STUDIES; MAGNETOPHOSPHENES; NEUROMOTRICITY; PHYSIOLOGICAL TREMOR; POSTURAL SWAY
Abstract-Résumé: Power-lines and electric appliances are the main sources of daily exposure to electric power frequency  magnetic fields (60 Hz MF in North America). International agencies publish safety guidelines recommending MF exposure limits for the public and workers. These guidelines are mainly based on the best estimate available to show what MF strength will induce biological effects in humans. These MF effects still need to be experimentally proven as they are currently only educated guesses. Since 2005 we have been investigating 60 Hz MF exposures up to 3.0 milliTesla (mT) in humans. Our results showed some effects on human movement, psychological tests, and brain activity measured using functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI). Beyond their scientific importance, these results show what happens from an environmental and occupational health point of view. However, they are too subtle to prove a reliable threshold value as defined in the guidelines. This stresses the need for new studies testing higher exposure levels as well. The current proposal is thus focusing on the effect of 60 Hz MF up to 50 milliTesla on: 1) magnetophosphenes (seeing flickering lights) and the related brain electrical activity; 2) the effect on normal brain activity; 3) finger tremor (it is normal to have a little shaking in the fingers); 4) and standing balance. In addition, we will use modeling of brain activity to propose mechanisms of action supporting our experimental results. This complex project will establish, at a typical electrical power frequency, a threshold of exposure that will consistently produce an objective effect, characterize the brain structures involved in that effect, and validate the theoretical mechanisms of action that produce the effect. These results will assist future guideline updates protecting the public and workers' safety, and will produce fundamental implications for future therapeutic applications utilizing any positive effects of exposure to magnetic fields.

Abstract-Résumé: One of the most effective treatments for severe inflammatory and autoimmune diseases is intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg). This treatment is made up of human antibodies derived from the plasma of many donors and is currently the most commonly prescribed plasma product. Although the therapy is effective, we do not understand how it works in many diseases. In addition, understanding the mechanism of its therapeutic action would help us to develop newer therapies that potentially would not have to rely on blood and plasma donations, improving the potential safety and the burden on the plasma supply. Our laboratory has discovered a new mechanism by which IVIG appears to work. We will explore this novel action, which includes increased numbers of cells known as T-regulatory cells. These cells are part of the normal, anti-inflammatory response to disease. By comprehending how immunoglobulin therapy increases T-regulatory cells, we will learn how to harness the power of naturally occurring parts to the immune system (antibodies and T-regulatory cells) to help combat severe inflammatory and autoimmune disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTES; CEREBELLUM; CYTOKINES; GLIA; GLUTAMATE; HYPERACTIVITY; METABOTROPIC GLUTAMATE; MICROGLIA; NEUROINFLAMMATION; SEIZURES
Abstract-Résumé: Some scientists have proposed that several neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders, are associated with an immune reaction in the brain. One group of neurotransmitter receptors, called the metabotropic glutamate receptors, might be involved in this CNS immune response in these disorders.  This study will investigate whether or not manipulating the immune system affects the amounts and activity of the glutamate receptors, and conversely, whether altering the receptors has effects on the immune system.  These experiments will be conducted on mice and cells in culture.  The long-term goal of this work is to ascertain whether pharmacological intervention would be justified in treating the human disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of innovative therapeutic strategies for hemophilia A in a unique hemophilic dog colony.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; BLEEDING DISORDER; CELL THERAPY; GENE THERAPY; GENETICS; HEMOPHILIA; NOVEL THERAPIES
Abstract-Résumé: Hemophilia A is the most common severe inherited bleeding disorder in humans. The severe form of the disease results in spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles, resulting in long-term chronic pain and disability. The current treatment for hemophilia A involves the intravenous infusion of factor VIII protein concentrates, derived from either donated plasma or from recombinant DNA approaches. This treatment is safe and effective but there are limitations to the therapy: the requirement for intravenous infusion is inconvenient and challenging in young children; approximately 25 per cent of patients develop antibodies to the infused factor VIII, and global access to the concentrates is limited by supply and cost.   In this research project, we aim to continue our studies of novel therapeutic approaches to hemophilia A using a well established dog model of the disease. Hemophilia A occurs spontaneously in dogs and the colony of mixed breed miniature schnauzer/beagles has been maintained at Queen's University for the past 30 years. These dogs have severe hemophilia and show a similar pattern of spontaneous bleeding to their human counterparts.   The research proposal has four aims. First, we aim to continue with the long-term maintenance and investigation of the hemophilic dog colony at Queen's. This objective requires the support and coordination of a complex infrastructure involving specialized animal housing, a team of experienced veterinary technologists and veterinarians and the provision of an array of laboratory tests to evaluate blood clotting in the dogs. The next two aims, involve extensions of our previous assessment of gene and cell-based treatments for hemophilia. The rationale for both of these objectives is supported by recent successes in the mouse model of hemophilia. Finally, we will continue to collaborate with industrial partners to determine the safety and efficacy of novel hemophilia treatments in standardized pre-clinical testing protocols.

Abstract-Résumé: There are 37 million patients across the world suffering of Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most widespread form of dementia. In the United States, AD affects over 5.3 million individuals and generates cost estimated to 148 billion dollars. Having a life expectancy potentially reaching up to 12 years following diagnosis, degenerating AD patients require constant care and help, and therefore become a demanding responsibility for their families. In Canada, AD affects half a million individuals and this number will more than double within a generation. These statistics imply that AD will have a significant impact on Canadian economy and society. The production of a novel vaccine is therefore a very attracting and inexpensive alternative to prevent and diminish the impact of AD on the Canadian population. In this research program, we will evaluate and select a lead candidate from a  family of novel synthetic adjuvants with recently discovered AD-modulating properties to develop a new vaccine to treat AD.

Abstract-Résumé: This project involves investigating the role of an autophagy gene, UV radiation resistance associated gene or UVRAG, in T cell biology. Although T cells are known to undergo autophagy, the exact role autophagosomes play in their function remains to be examined. Using the conditional UVRAG deletion in T cells as a model, I plan to examine which T cell functions are affected by the loss of this gene and to dissect the molecular pathways by which UVRAG might be mediating these effects. This research will shed much needed light onto factors regulating T cell homeostasis, a process that, when deregulated, causes immunodeficiencies or leukemias.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multimodal Imaging for Surgical Planning in Epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: DTI; EEG; EPILEPSY; FMRI; IMAGING; MEG; MULTIMODAL IMAGING; NEUROSCIENCE; PSYCHOLOGY; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a disorder of the brain characterized by attacks involving loss of consciousness and changes in behaviour. Epilepsy dramatically impacts the quality of life of those affected, and is often associated with learning difficulties, emotional distress, and psychosocial problems. Although medication is available to control some cases, often epilepsy is resistant to medication. Thus neurosurgery is required to remove diseased tissue that causes attacks. When planning to remove tissue from a patient's brain, the neurosurgeon must avoid damage to areas critical for functions such as language and memory. Traditional tests to localize brain function are often invasive, time consuming, and uncomfortable for the patient. Non-invasive neuroimaging techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), electro- and magneto-encephalography (E/MEG) are available to identify functional and diseased areas of the cerebral cortex prior to surgery. However, these technologies, which look at brain structure and activity, are not yet widely available for clinical application.  This research aims to advance treatment of epilepsy by using multimodal imaging to guide neurosurgical planning in epilepsy.  The proposed study has three parts.  Part one will compare people with epilepsy with healthy people to identify problem areas and deficits.  Part two will use multimodal brain mapping (fMRI, EEG, MEG, and DTI) both before and after surgery to assess the effects of surgical treatment for epilepsy.  Part three will assess the extent to which, if any, multimodal preoperative imaging improves the accuracy of localization of function. This research has the potential to ameliorate the risks and costs of neurosurgery, and provide surgeons with improved navigational tools to advance the efficiency and reliability of neurosurgery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rêves et activation cérébrale chez des sujets souffrant du trouble de comportement en sommeil paradoxal
Keywords-MotsClés: MALADIES NEURODEGENERATIVES; NEURO-IMAGERIE; REVES; SOMMEIL; TROUBLES DU SOMMEIL; VIELLISSEMENT; EMOTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Le trouble comportemental en sommeil paradoxal (TCSP) est une parasomnie caracterisee par des mouvements indesirables et souvent violents pendant les periodes de reves. Ces comportements representent un risque eleve de blessures pour le patient et son partenaire de lit. La prevalence du TCSP dans la population generale est d'environ 0.5% et 85% des patients sont des hommes. Le TCSP est fortement associe au developpement de plusieurs maladies neurodegeneratives, telles que la maladie de Parkinson et il en est dans plusieurs cas le precurseur. Les patients avec un TCSP rapportent plus de reves a caractere agressif, accompagnes d'emotions negatives, que les sujets controles sains.  Les etudes en neuroimagerie effectuees chez des sujets normaux durant le sommeil paradoxal (SP) et les patients atteints d'un TCSP montrent que plusieurs regions du cerveau pourraient etre impliquees dans l'apparition du TCSP. Ces memes regions pourraient etre impliques dans l'apparition de la maladie de Parkinson.  L'objectif global de ce programme de recherche est de mettre en relation les manifestations du TCSP et les mesures du debit sanguin cerebral obtenues en neuro-imagerie. De plus, puisque le TCSP est fortement associe a la Maladie de Parkinson, ces donnees permettront dans un avenir proche de mieux comprendre l'evolution de la maladie, de poser un diagnostique precoce et d'evaluer efficacite d'un traitement. Pour tester ces hypotheses, des sujets normaux et des patients avec un TCSP seront etudies en laboratoire. Pendant la nuit, les patients auront un radiotraceur injecte pour l'etude en neuroimagerie. Les sujets seront ensuite eveilles pour la collecte du contenu des reves. L'acquisition des images du debit sanguin cerebral sera faite en differe le matin au reveil au nouveau laboratoire de medecine nucleaire du Centre d'etude du sommeil de l'Hopital du Sacre-Cur, qui dispose d'un appareil a haute resolution (Neurofocus), unique au Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: DENN domains: regulators of Rab-mediated trafficking pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; DENN DOMAIN; ENDOCYTOSIS; ENZYMATIC ASSAYS; GUANINE-NUCLEOTIDE EXCHANGE FACTORS; INTRACELLULAR TRAFFICKING; MOLECULAR CLONING; PULL-DOWN ASSAYS; RAB GTPASES; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: All living organisms are composed of cells, the smallest functional unit of life. Cells are able to consume nutrients from their surroundings, manufacture molecules within, shuttle those molecules around the cell and subsequently release them back into the extracellular space. The cell accomplishes this by forming bubble-like structures, called vesicles, around the molecules and transporting them from one place to another.  The Rab (Ras-related in brain) family of proteins regulates the movement of vesicles within the cell. There are approximately 70 different Rabs found in humans, each with its own unique role in trafficking. Rabs themselves can be switched on or off by other regulatory proteins. Despite the fact that there have been over 3900 scientific papers published on Rabs, little is known as to how they are regulated.  Our lab recently identified a protein called connecdenn that is able to activate one particular Rab. Connecdenn contains a specific portion called a DENN domain. There are many other proteins that contain a DENN domain, but their function is currently unknown. The goal of my project is to determine whether other DENN domain-containing proteins are able to regulate Rabs as well.  The vesicle trafficking system is crucial for cells to survive. When this transport system fails, the result can be devastating to the entire organism. Not surprisingly, Rab proteins have been linked with many diseases including immunodeficiencies, cancer and neurological disorders. My work will help understand, at a basic science level, how cells work, and may provide clues regarding diseases associated with Rab dysfunction.
