TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the mechanisms of benzene-induced carcinogenicity.
Keywords-MotsClés: BENZENE; CELL SIGNALLING; LEUKEMIA; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; REPRODUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Benzene is a common environmental pollutant found in cigarette smoke and fuel combustion.  Research has indicated that increased exposure of pregnant mothers to benzene is associated with an increased occurrence of childhood leukemia in their offspring.  Unfortunately, the reason for this increased occurrence of blood cancer is not completely understood.  One way by which benzene is thought to be harmful is via its metabolism in the liver leading to the increased production of reactive compounds, termed reactive oxygen species (ROS).  These ROS can react with different molecules within cells, including critical proteins as well as DNA.  Pregnant mice exposed to benzene have been shown to lead to an increased occurrence of tumour formation in the offspring one year post-exposure, providing a valuable animal model to study this process.  To determine whether ROS are involved, I will expose pregnant mice to benzene, or benzene plus an antioxidative enzyme, catalase, which is known to quench certain ROS.  If treatment with catalase decreases the occurrence of tumour formation in offspring, this will suggest that increased ROS plays an important role in benzene carcinogenesis.  To further examine the role of ROS in carcinogenicity of benzene, I will examine the role of benzene in altering cell-signalling pathways.  Some of the proteins that ROS can interact with are proteins involved in explicit cellular signals, important for normal cellular functioning.  Myeloid blood cells will be exposed to either benzene or benzene plus catalase, to determine whether benzene leads to changes in these signalling pathways, and whether this change is attenuated by treatment with catalase.  If the results of both of these studies show that catalase reduces the benzene-induced damage, this would suggest that antioxidants could be an important component of a treatment to prevent the development of childhood leukemia in mothers with increased exposure to benzene.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting recovery in patients receiving wage-replacement benefits
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; DISABILITY BENEFITS; EVIDENCE-BASED MEDICINE; LONG-TERM DISABILITY; PREDICTIVE INSTRUMENT; PREDICTORS OF RECOVERY; REHABILITATION; WAGE-REPLACEMENT BENEFITS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients receiving disability benefits incur a large socioeconomic burden. These patients suffer from a variety of conditions including back pain and other chronic non-cancer pain, and mental illness such as depression and anxiety. Approximately 60-75% of the costs from disability claims are from 10% of claimants, demonstrating the importance of early identification of, and intervention with, this vulnerable group. Currently, no standardized approach exists for identifying high-risk claimants.  We are currently performing a systematic review evaluating studies that explored predictors of recovery among patients in receipt of disability benefits. The results obtained from our review will generate candidate criteria for identifying persons at high risk for prolonged recovery. We will use the candidate criteria to determine the extent to which information in existing databases from private insurers might serve to identify those at risk. We will then determine if the factors identified in the literature predict prolonged recovery among claimants represented in insurance company databases, and if additional factors not yet studied formally appear to have predictive value. The results of these studies will be used to inform the items for an instrument designed to identify claimants at high risk of prolonged recovery following receipt of disability benefits. We will then test the instrument using a cohort of patients in Canada and one in Switzerland.   The results of this study will be of interest to insurance and compensation boards, researchers, clinicians and patients suffering from disabilities. Our study will be the first to develop an evidence-based tool to identify claimants at high risk of prolonged recovery. If successful, our instrument will identify high-risk claimants who can receive intensive rehabilitation efforts early on, which may result in an overall shorter duration of claims and an increased rate of successful claim resolution.

TitreApplicationTitle: Helicobacter pylori Activates Tolerogenic Dendritic Cells and Leads to Regulatory T cell Induction
Keywords-MotsClés: DENDRITIC CELLS; ELISA; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GASTRIC CANCER; GASTRIC INFLAMMATION; HELICOBACTER PYLORI; IMMUNE TOLERANCE; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; REGULATORY T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a bacterium that infects the human stomach and causes several stomach diseases including dyspepsia, ulcers, and even gastric cancer. It resides on the surface of the stomach cells and survives for the life of the host.  Over half of the world's population is infected with this bacterium but less than 20% of infected people get disease.  Close examination of the tissue reveals that the bacteria induce inflammation in the stomach wall, even when the person remains healthy.  Studies in mice and humans have demonstrated that specific immune cells called Treg cells, suppress the inflammatory response and prevent it from getting too severe.  However, this also allows the bacteria to survive better in the stomach.  The purpose of this study is to determine how these Treg cells become activated to suppress the response to H. pylori.  We have shown that another type of immune cells termed dendritic cells are activated by H. pylori and these dendritic cells interact with T cells to induce them to become Treg cells.  This is an unusual activity for bacteria.  We can now grow dendritic cells and T cells from mice in the laboratory and measure the number of Treg cells that become active when H. pylori is added. Our first aim is to divide the H. pylori into different types of components to determine which molecules actually induce the dendritic cells to activate Treg cells.  Or second aim is study the dendritic cells after adding H. pylori to determine the molecular changes that occur including the proteins that get expressed on the surface of the cell, the changes in protein activity that occur inside the cells, and the proteins that get secreted by the dendritic cells after stimulation.  The successful completion of these studies will provide a better understanding of how H. pylori manipulates the infected host and help identify new therapies for stomach diseases and other diseases of the gastrointestinal tract.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the Developmental Origins of the Nucleus Pulposus:  Stem cells within the Intervertebral Disc
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR PHENOTYPE; DEGENERATIVE DISC DISEASE; DEVELOPMENT; INTERVERTEBRAL DISC; NOTOCHORD; SPINE; STEM CELLS; TISSUE ENGINEERING; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS
Abstract-Résumé: Background and Specific Aims: Low back pain is the most common musculoskeletal problem in Canada with a lifetime prevalence of 84%; often associated with osteoarthritis or inflammatory joint diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. Lower back pain is attributed to deterioration of the cartilage-like discs between the vertebrae and more specifically, their inner nucleus pulposus tissue. Currently, there is no effective treatment for the chronic pain associated with disc degeneration; however recent studies suggest that regeneration of the nucleus pulposus tissue can delay the onset and reduce the severity of the disease. The aim of this study is to establish the developmental origins of the cells that form the nucleus pulposus and thus gain a better understanding of how these cells contribute to maintaining tissue health.  Methods and Results: Using novel genetic tools to specifically and exclusively label cells of the notochord, we have used the Cre/LoxP system for conditional mutagenesis.  By targeting the notochord-specific gene Noto for Cre expression, we have developed tools to trace the notochord cells at distinct developmental stages during the formation of the intervertebral disc. We hypothesize that notochord cells give rise to all cells within the mature nucleus pulposus.  Localization of staining on a cellular level demonstrates that both notochord cells and chondrocyte-like are derived from the embryonic notochord. This indicates that notochord cells act as embryonic precursors of all the cells within the nucleus pulposus.  Conclusions:  The goal of this study was to determine the fate and function of notochord cells during spinal skeletogenesis. These experiments show that nucleus pulposus is exclusively derived from the notochord. Therefore, notochord cell have the potential for enabling stem cell therapies that could aid in the treatment of chronic back pain caused by disc degeneration.

Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; INJECTION DRUG USERS; NATURAL HISTORY; PHYLODYNAMICS; PHYLOGENETICS; PUBLIC HEALTH; TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a major public health problem associated with considerable morbidity, mortality and health-related costs. In 2007, 243,000 Canadians were infected. Among infected individuals, one in four will develop cirrhosis and one in eight will die from HCV-related causes. Injection drug users (IDUs) represent the core of the HCV epidemic in Canada, with the majority of new (83%) and existing (58%) infections occurring in this group. In Canada, although research has identified characteristics associated with new cases of infection, little is known about transmission events occurring from pools of infected to uninfected individuals. Further, given ongoing risk behaviours for HCV transmission, it is likely that many IDUs harbour multiple infections. We have assembled a multidisciplinary team of international investigators with expertise across disciplines in the fields of HCV and HIV. The overall goal of this project is to evaluate HCV transmission dynamics among IDUs. First, we are interested in how HCV is transmitted from older to younger IDUs and whether public health initiatives have led to a reduction in transmission. Second, we are interested in understanding how frequently reinfection and mixed infections with HCV occur and what characteristics are associated with reinfection/mixed infections. We plan to conduct this study within well-established cohorts of IDUs in Vancouver, the Vancouver Injecting Drug Users Study (VIDUS) and the At-risk Youth Study (ARYS). Using previously stored blood samples from these studies from 1996 to 2010, we plan to identify participants who developed HCV infection, sequence their virus and investigate HCV transmission networks. We will also use novel technologies to detect mixed HCV infections. Understanding HCV transmission among injection drug users will better guide the development of public health and biomedical strategies for HCV prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Building Community-Based HIV and STI Prevention Programs on the Tundra:  Drawing on Inuit Women's Strengths and Resiliencies
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY PARTNERSHIPS; CROSS-CULTURAL METHODOLOGIES; HIV/AIDS PREVENTION; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOGIES; INDIGENOUS WOMEN; INUIT; NUNAVUT; PARTICIPANT ACTION RESEARCH; SEXUAL HEALTH; STORYTELLING
Abstract-Résumé: There is a dearth of literature about how to develop community-based HIV and Sexually Transmitted Infections prevention programs within Inuit Communities.  The purpose of this study is to examine Inuit Women's Strengths, Resiliencies, and Influences over the Social Determinants of Sexual Health in order to inform future development of HIV and STI prevention programs.  In-depth interviews, combined with storytelling circles, will be used to create a space for Inuit women to share information and experiences that will represent the foundation of future community-based intervention opportunities. Sexual health, relationship dynamics, and family are among the topic that will be discussed.  This research project will use Indigenous methodologies, which include elements of Participation Action Research, to work in partnership with the community to create knowledge.   This strength-based model of inquiry will not only inform future interventions but will provide the community with critical information that can be shared with the hamlet of Kugluktuk as well as other Inuit and/or Indigenous peoples.

TitreApplicationTitle: Psychosocial Factors, Condom Efficacy, and Sexual Risk-Taking Amongst Transgender People in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH BEHAVIOUR; HIV/AIDS; MENTAL HEALTH; PSYCHOSOCIAL FACTORS; RESPONDENT-DRIVEN SAMPLING; SEXUAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Transgender (trans) people are those who identify with a sex and/or gender other than that assigned to them at birth. Trans people are known to have higher HIV prevalence than the general population and high vulnerability to HIV infection because of social marginalization, poverty, and lack of access to healthcare. Qualitative research has documented a number of psychosocial issues that trans people face in the areas of body image, sexual satisfaction, and anxieties about sexual activities. These challenges are often unique to the lives of trans people, who struggle with personal and social perceptions of their gendered bodies. Difficulty with finding respectful intimate partners can compound such challenges, leading to a reduced sense of agency when partners are found. These psychosocial factors may limit the ability of trans people to negotiate condom use and/or make them more likely to take sexual risks, thereby increasing the likelihood of HIV transmission. This proposed research will use quantitative data and epidemiological methods to more accurately understand the impact of body image, sexual satisfaction, and sexual anxiety on condom efficacy and sexual risk-taking amongst trans Ontarians. The research will describe the levels of these psychosocial factors amongst trans people and will then determine how these factors impact HIV vulnerability by increasing or decreasing condom efficacy and sexual risk-taking. This research is part of Trans PULSE, a community-based research (CBR) project that surveyed 433 trans people in Ontario in order to gather quantitative data about the health concerns and HIV vulnerability of this marginalized and under-researched community.  As a CBR project, transgender people have been and will be involved in decision-making through all stages of the research process. Furthermore, the research is focused on producing results of practical use for bettering the health of trans communities through HIV prevention interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the impact of Canada's Sodium Reduction Strategy on dietary intakes of sodium, the overall nutritional quality of the food supply, changes in food labeling, and consumer knowledge and attitudes towards sodium
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN'S HEALTH; CONSUMER AWARENESS; EVALUATING POLICY; FOOD SUPPLY; NUTRITION; NUTRITION LABELLING; NUTRITION POLICY; PUBLIC HEALTH; REAL TIME FOOD SUPPLY MONITORING; SODIUM
Abstract-Résumé: Creating a healthy food environment that is lower in sodium (or salt) is a national priority for improving the health of Canadians by lowering high blood pressure and reducing risk of cardiovascular diseases and stroke.  Current intakes of sodium in Canada are more than double the recommended amount.  The Sodium Working Group (SWG) has recently published a national strategy which aims to lower the current average sodium intake of 3.4 g/day to an average of 2.3 g/day by 2016, with an eventual goal of 1.5 g/day.  The SWG recommendations call for reductions in sodium content of the food supply, public education campaigns, research and independent monitoring.  Our proposed research encompasses two themes, the food supply and consumer awareness and knowledge.  As the SWG recommendations are implemented, we will conduct a detailed analysis of the changing Canadian food supply (sodium levels, nutritional composition, label claims and price) using a database of the nutritional information from ~12,000 Canadian food labels and a database of ~6000 restaurant foods. Using this data from 2010 and updates in 2012 and 2014, the impact of the changing food supply on Canadian intakes of sodium and other nutrients will be studied. We will also use web-based surveys to evaluate the sodium knowledge, attitudes and behaviour of Canadian consumers and their ability to use food label information. Research evaluating the successes and unintended consequences of Canada's Sodium Reduction Strategy will inform policy makers and further support the goal of improving the health of Canadians by reducing sodium intake. Such efforts will help ensure that Canadians receive the maximum health benefits.

TitreApplicationTitle: Population-level prevention and implications for socioeconomic inequities in health:  Dietary sodium as a case example
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH INEQUITIES; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The population strategy of prevention refers to prevention activities that target whole populations (i.e., areas, groups, jurisdictions, institutions, etc) regardless of variation in individual risk status.  Recently, it has been suggested that the population strategy of prevention may inadvertently worsen socioeconomic inequities in health.  We have argued that population prevention will not necessarily worsen socioeconomic inequities in health, and the likelihood of it doing so will depend on whether the intervention is more structural (targets conditions in which behaviours occur) or agentic (targets behaviours directly) in nature.  Despite the enduring existence of and concern about socioeconomic inequities in health in Canada and worldwide, we currently know very little about the implications (equitable or not) of population interventions.  The purpose of the proposed research is thus to examine the implications of population interventions (agentic and structural types) for socioeconomic inequities in health, focusing on dietary sodium as a case example.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nox5 derived reactive oxygen species in vascular and renal injury during hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: HYPERTENSION; OXIDATIVE STRESS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; VASCULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: High blood pressure (hypertension) affects  thirty percent of Sub-Saharan Africans and North Americans. It is the most frequent reason for consultation of family physicians in Canada and is the leading cause of heart disease, kidney failure and stroke worldwide. Despite the fact that this condition is so common and is a major killer, we still do not know exactly what causes high blood pressure. Factors that have been suggested include increased production in the body of free radicals, called reactive oxygen species. High levels of free radicals cause damage to blood vessels, the heart, brain and kidneys and could promote an increase in blood pressure. Processes responsible for increased production of dangerous free radicals are unclear, but special proteins, called Noxs, may be important. The present proposal will focus on understanding how a newly discovered Nox - Nox5 might contribute to free radical production in vessels and the kidney and how it can contribute to blood pressure elevation and kidney damage. The clinical significance of our studies relates to the fact that this Nox may be an important target for new therapies. By learning more about this new Nox5 through research, new and better drugs and strategies for treating, and perhaps even preventing, hypertension and kidney disease may be developed. Considering that hypertension is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in Canada and Sub-Saharan Africa, this would impact significantly on the overall well-being and health of these populations at large.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive symptoms of Schizophrenia: Biological and Clinical correlations
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE SYMPTOMS; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a disabling brain disorder prevalent in both developing and developed countries. Cognitive symptoms like memory impairments are important symptoms of schizophrenia hindering the functional recovery of patients. However, at present available medications have limited efficacy in treatment of cognitive symptoms though are effective in treatment of other symptoms, possibly due to differences in pathogenesis. The proposed study aims to examine biological mechanisms underlying the cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia by using brain imaging modality positron emission tomography (PET). We intend to study the role of dopamine, a neurotransmitter in the cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia. We will also assess the relation between cognitive symptoms and functional outcome in developing country, India to study the cross cultural impact of cognitive symptoms. The study findings will open the road for future studies of the etiology, progression, as well as potential new targets to treat cognitive symptoms in schizophrenia which could have potential theoretical and clinical applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Mcl-1 in regulating placental cell fate
Keywords-MotsClés: BOVINE PLACENTA; CELL CULTURE; CELL CYCLE REGULATION; DECONCONVOLUTION); DIFFERENT MICROSCOPY (CONFOCAL; IMMUNOFLORESCENCE; IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; MCL-1; PLACENTA AND TROPHOBLAST CELLS FATE; PLACENTAL EXPLANT CULTURE; PREECLAMPISA; PREGNANCY; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Preeclampsia (PE) is the unpredictable and devastating disorder of pregnancy that affect about the 5-10% of women with a high ratio of feto-maternal mortality and morbidity.  PE represents important risk factors for long term complications and adult diseases, like hypertension, diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. While the underlying cause of this pathology remains an enigma, it is accepted that the placenta plays a central role in its origin. In particular, we and other groups have demonstrated that placental hypoxia is central to preeclampsia. The objective of my research proposal is to investigate the role of Mcl-1 in regulating trophoblast cell death and proliferation. In particular, I will focus my attention on the role of Mcl-1 and downstream effector caspase 3 in trophoblast cell fate and the phosphorylation mechanisms involved in Mcl-1 stability. Later on, I will investigate if disruption of Mcl-1 stability contributes to the  accelerated trophoblast cell death and proliferation which is seen in preeclampisa This project will significantly increase the understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms that regulate and lead to trophoblast cell death, growth and proliferation. This may also shed light on the events which are altered in preeclampsia and may ultimately be translated into the discovery of novel potential diagnostic markers and therapeutic targets for an early diagnosis and treatment of preeclampsia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hormonal and Mechanistic Evaluation of Increasing risk of diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease in India: from Bench to Bedside.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOKINES; ADIPOSE TISSUE; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; INSULIN RESISTANCE; SUBCUTANEOUS; VISCERAL
Abstract-Résumé: Non-infectious diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular disorders are increasing in incidence in lower and middle income countries such as India. It has also been observed that Asians have higher risk for the development of these diseases as compared to other population groups and the risk is observed to be even higher in immigrants to countries such as Canada. This has been attributed to a number of factors such as changes in diet/lifestyle, genetic factors etc. Although a number of factors are under scrutiny, no reliable associations have been found as yet. Some of the suggested criteria for risk evaluation have been the measurement of body surface area, waist-to-hip ratio, levels of cholesterol in the blood and the distribution of body fat, etc. Along with these, some hormones produced by fat tissue, such as; leptin, adiponectin and ASP, which influence fat metabolism, are also under investigation. The proposed study has been designed so that different attributes, which may be responsible for the above mentioned phenomena, may be studied in both the immigrant (to Canada) and native (to India) populations and compared with the native population (of Canada). It will evaluate a panel of markers which will give us a better insight into cause and effect relationships, assist in identifying better predictive factors as well as targets for intervention.

Abstract-Résumé: Despite ongoing prevention efforts, HIV incidence in South African youth remains remarkably high. Inclusion of high-risk adolescent populations in vaccine trials will be essential to ensure the success of future efforts, but limited data exist on social, ethical, political, and regulatory barriers to recruit minors into large-scale trials in South Africa. Biological changes, particularly at mucosal sites, occurring in adolescents may alter their risk of infection and/or complicate immunologic endpoints of vaccine studies, but there is limited data available to address these issues in any population. We have assembled a multi-disciplinary team of social scientists, ethicists, clinicians, and biomedical researchers to examine these questions using existing cohorts of adolescents recruited in Soweto and Durban, South Africa. Results are anticipated to inform social and biomedical aims of future HIV vaccine studies involving minors.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANTHRACYCLINE TOXICITY; CARDIAC BIOMARKERS; CARDIAC DYSFUNCTION; CHILDHOOD CANCER SURVIVORS; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; GENOMICS; PILOT INTERVENTION STUDY; RISK PREDICTION MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer therapy can place childhood cancer survivors at increased risk for heart disease which can lead to significant illness or early death. Interventions that occur late in the evolution of treatment-related heart disease are usually ineffective at preventing its progression to death or heart transplant. Our team will work in several integrated research cores to test new imaging and biomarker methods that will lead to earlier detection of heart disease before clinical symptoms develop or it becomes apparent on standard imaging tests. We will evaluate the importance of genetic differences between individuals in determining who is at greatest risk of developing heart disease as a result of exposure to cardiotoxic agents. These vulnerable children can then be targeted by modifying their cancer therapy to reduce their exposure to cardiac toxins, or introducing medications that protect the heart from chemotherapy damage. Finally, we will carry out a pilot study investigating a heart failure drug for preventing the progression of heart disease in survivors who show signs of early damage. This team brings together the expertise of clinicians and scientists in pediatric oncology, pediatric and adult cardiology, radiation oncology, genetics, and biostatistics. This is a cross-Canada initiative that will leverage the latest knowledge about cardiac toxicity and create a resource for ongoing research into this important cause of morbidity and mortality in childhood cancer survivors.

Abstract-Résumé: The transmission of HIV from an infected mother to her infant via breastfeeding is remarkably inefficient. Despite repeated exposure to HIV in the breast milk, the majority of infants who are exclusively breastfed (EBF) do not become infected. Interestingly, infants that are EBF are less likely to be infected by their HIV+ mothers compared to infants who receive other sources of liquid or food in addition to breast milk, despite consuming more HIV infected milk. To better understand this unusual finding, our research aims to identify factors in breast milk that protect infants from HIV infection and/or inflammatory responses of the infant gut following different feeding practices that may increase susceptibility to HIV infection.  Our program of work also proposes to examine the effect of previous immune activation in the infant on immune responses to standard childhood vaccinations and to evaluate maternal attitudes and beliefs about breastfeeding and their willingness to enroll their infants in future HIV vaccine trials.  We have assembled a strong, international multi-discipinary team of investigators to carry out these studies in Nigeria and South Africa, countries with the highest number of HIV+ pregnant women. Understanding modes of natural protection as well as immune activation in the HIV exposed but uninfected infant provides critical information to HIV vaccine development and especially testing in developing countries with high HIV prevalence.

Abstract-Résumé: Childhood leukemia treatment affects brain function in about a quarter of the children. The effects, which are mainly seen as attention deficit, remain for long time, and have an impact on children's academic performance and social activity. What factors make some children susceptible to this side effect? Recent reports suggest that mutation of a gene involved in metabolism of one of the vitamins, folate, is responsible. Our study is to find out if not only this gene but also other related genes are associated with this damage. If the responsible genes are found, we may be able to plan a strategy to avoid this side effect.

Abstract-Résumé: We currently have no effect vaccine for the prevention of HIV. Neither do we have a therapy that can completely cure HIV. The current team grant will combine the expertise of a team of cutting edge immunologists, translational biologists and biochemists at the University of Toronto, with clinical epidemiologists at the University of Nairobi Kenya, to uncover new avenues of research that may lead to an HIV vaccine. In addition, new ideas will be explored that can be used to treat HIV infection with the use of immunotherapies. It is hoped that cross-fertilization of expertises between Kenya and Canada will lead to new discoveries that can be applied to rapidly produce an HIV vaccine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genomic determinants of common long-term treatment effects in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia survivors
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; BONE MORBIDITY; CANCER SURVIVORSHIP; CARDIOTOXICITY; CHILDHOOD LEUKEMIA; LONG-TERM DISEASE OUTCOMES/BIOMARKERS; MEDICAL GENOMICS; METABOLIC SYNDROME; NEUROCOGNITION; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING/DNA VARIANTS
Abstract-Résumé: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most frequent cancer in children, accounting for approximately 25% of all pediatric tumors. Advances in our understanding of the pathobiology of this cancer and of its treatment have led to increased survival rates with ~80% of cases being cured with current treatment protocols. However, there is a price to pay for this therapeutic success. Because these patients receive high doses of toxic chemicals during a vulnerable period of their life, they constitute one of the higher risk populations seen by healthcare professionals; more than two-thirds of the survivors experience chronic or late-occurring health problems (including growth problems, learning difficulties, cardiovascular disease, sterility, higher risk of adulthood cancer), often not clinically apparent until decades after treatment. However, the underlying causes of these long-term effects remain unclear. Our multidisciplinary team of basic biomedical researchers, pediatric oncologists and clinicians with diverse backgrounds and expertise aims at investigating a subset of the most common late-occurring adverse effects observed in childhood ALL survivors, including neurocognitive effects, metabolic syndrome, cardiotoxicity and bone morbidity. To better understand the mechanisms through which these adverse long-term effects might arise in childhood ALL survivors we propose a multidisciplinary study to: i) identify genetic variations in childhood ALL patients; ii) identify a set of biologically and clinically relevant biomarkers associated with the selected long-term treatment morbidities; and iii) assess the impact of candidate genetic and biological biomarkers on long-term treatment effects in childhood ALL survivors. Our findings will lead to the development of new strategies and clinical tools that will prevent and/or reduce the occurrence of late-onset treatment related toxicities, and ultimately improve detection, diagnosis and treatment of childhood leukemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Applying Biomarkers to Long-term Effects in Child and Adolescent Cancer Treatment (ABLE Team)
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CHRONIC GRAFT VERSUS HOST DISEASE; CLINICAL INTERVENTIONS; LONG TERM EFFECTS OF CANCER THERAPY; NEPHROTOXICITY; OTO-TOXICITY; THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Fortunately, through the application of modern medical practice, many children are now cured of cancer. Unfortunately many of these survivors experience unwanted side effects that lead to health issues throughout their lives. It would be very helpful if we could predict which children and adolescents have the highest risk of developing these complications. One avenue that offers promise is the development and use of indicators commonly called biomarkers. Biomarkers are substances produced by the body either during the normal course of living or in response to an adverse condition such as an infection or cancer. We have developed a national team called ABLE (Applying Biomarkers to Long-term Effects in Child and Adolescent Cancer Treatment) that will assess biomarkers to identify children at risk and to predict the course of development of their long term complications. Identifying these high risk children means we can pro-actively choose appropriate and timely therapies to minimize or eliminate these effects, thus leading to healthier, happier lives. In this proposal we focus on ascertaining biomarkers associated with hearing loss, kidney failure, clotting problems, and a specific form of tissue rejection called chronic graft-versus host disease which is often seen after the blood and marrow transplantation used to successfully treat blood-based cancers. Ultimately, the ABLE team seeks to provide a national platform for applying biomarkers to other diseases in the future. This initiative is a major step forward to helping children and adolescents treated for cancer lead long and healthy lives after surviving their cancer.

Abstract-Résumé: The CHVI Team in Social and Behavioral Research on HIV Vaccines will launch an expert interdisciplinary social science team in Canada, India and South Africa that will apply rigorous and innovative social research to accelerate the development and dissemination of safe, effective and accessible HIV vaccines. The Team research program addresses key challenges in ensuring fully informed consent among HIV vaccine trial participants; and in engaging the preferences and concerns of vulnerable community end users throughout HIV vaccine development in order to bridge the science-to-practice gap.  Each year of delay in the development and uptake of HIV vaccines results in up to 2 million new HIV infections, 2,500 in Canada alone, which might otherwise have been averted. The CHVI Team will make a significant contribution to training the next generation of HIV vaccine social and behavioral researchers in Canada, and in South-South partnerships and traineeships in India and South Africa, the two countries with the highest numbers of persons living with HIV in the world.

We will use innovative immunologic techniques and cutting edge technologies to search for these rare antibodies in persons infected with HIV.  It is hoped that such antibodies will allow a better understanding of the host's ability to mount and immune response that is capable of halting HIV transmission.  Such antibodies will provide stepping stones towards the design of novel HIV vaccines and allow the development of an effective HIV vaccine for the global community. TitreApplicationTitle: Biomaterials scaffolding for brain reconstruction in stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: NEUROSTIMULATION; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: This project aims to develop innovative technologies using biomaterials applied to brain repair and regeneration for recovery of functions after stroke in animal models.  The specific objectives are:  1. To build bio hybrids made of biocompatible materials, cell and chemical factors able to work as scaffolds for neural precursor cells survival and differentiation at the lesion site.  2. To test in vitro such biohybrids in their ability to promote cell survival, differentiation and axonal growth.  3. To associate to these biohybrids other permissive, neuroprotective or potential neural precursor cells, such as adipose stem cells, olfactory enseathing glial or Schwann cells, or embryonic neural stem cells.  4. To test these biohybrids in animal models of stroke. Specifically, to test the histologic, electrophysiologic and behavioural changes obtained in the models.  5. To determine the effect of brain stimulation on hippocampal neurogenesis in an animal model of stroke.  6. To establish criteria for the possible potential transfer of these results to the clinic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Spreading Depolarization in Small Vessel Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTE; CEREBRAL SMALL VESSEL DISEASE; LACUNAR STROKE; SPREADING DEPOLARIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: There are presently no neuroprotective drugs with efficacy to improve outcomes after lacunar stroke. Fundamental challenges to advancing treatment of lacunar stroke are its heterogeneity in terms of cause, pathology, and the lack of mechanistic endpoints in clinical studies. Mechanistic endpoints, necessary for appropriate targeting of treatment, have been lacking due to our limited ability to validate and monitor relevant pathologic processes in clinical populations. Nonetheless, understanding the mechanisms contributing to neuronal and vascular disruption and developing mechanistic endpoints on the basis of this understanding holds great promise to unravel the heterogeneity of lacunar stroke, assign treatments appropriately, and detect significant treatment effects when they exist. Spreading depolarizations are a pathology of cerebral gray matter that originate spontaneously in injury foci where they seem to facilitate or even mediate irreversible cellular damage. Whether or not they are deleterious to the tissue seems to be intimately linked to the composition of the brain extracellular microenvironment and to the level of brain perfusion and in consequence brain energy supply. Waves of spreading depolarization propagate away from an injury focus. The spreading depolarization waves can be detected electrophysiologically in these uninjured regions where they appear to be relatively harmless In contrast to the deleterious effects in injured areas. These remarkable features suggest that spreading depolarizations could be used as a mechanistic endpoint in clinical studies of SVD to detect lesion progression. Nevertheless, the first step and the purpose of the present grant proposal is to firmly define their role in lesion progression in a relevant animal model for SVD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nuclear signalling by GPCRs and G proteins.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMYOCYTE; CELLULAR SIGNALLING; ENDOMEMBRANE; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; G PROTEINS; IMAGING; NUCLEUS; SIGNALLING COMPLEXES; TRANSCRIPTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: When you think about molecules like adrenaline and how they interact with the cell- you usually think of a cell surface receptor and events controlled from that location. The classical view of cellular signalling through G protein-coupled receptors is that they signal exclusively at the cell surface. However, many recent studies have demonstrated that not all of these receptors are transported to the cell surface and may in fact be targetted to internal cellular structures such as the nucleus, ER and Golgi apparatus. In these sites, they regulate a number of cellular events in a distinct manner from those they regulate at the cell surface. We are interested in determining how these signalling systems are differentially targetted and how they may play novel roles in cellular metabolism in health and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular basis for vascular remodeling in pulmonary arterial hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: MICRORNAS; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary hypertension is a disease of the lung blood vessels characterized by a sustained proliferation of the cells composing the lung blood vessel wall. This proliferation will decrease blood perfusion and thus blood oxygenation. Despite new therapeutic this disease remain lethal with 30% of mortality within 3 years after diagnostic. We propose to study the role of miR-204 in the proliferation of the cell within pulmonary vessels.   Preliminary evidence suggest that the downregulation of miR204 is implicated in the cell proliferation and thus could be of a great therapeutic interest.

TitreApplicationTitle: Can laminin-111 be used to treat Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy alone or in combination with myoblast transplantation?
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL THERAPY; DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; LAMININ; MYOBLAST TRANSPLANTATION; PROTEIN THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of the project is to develop a new treatment for DMD based on the systemic delivery of a protein called laminin 111 alone or in combination with myoblast transplantation. The treatment would be applicable to all DMD patients independently of their mutation. Dystrophin normally links the contracting proteins with the muscle fiber membrane and in turn with the extracellular matrix proteins. These links ensures that the muscle fiber is not damage during contraction. In the absence of dystrophin, these links do not exist and thus the muscle fiber membrane is frequently damage during normal muscle activity. Laminin 111 is a matrix protein, which is normally present during embryogenesis but is absent in adult animals. It has recently been shown that the systemic delivery of this protein can restore the expression of alpha7beta1 integrin and make links between the membrane and the matrix. This protects the dystrophic muscle fiber during contraction. Moreover, laminin 111 has also been shown to increase the migration of myoblasts. Thus in this grant proposal we will investigate whether laminin 111 can by itself slow down the progression of the dystrophy, can improve the transplantation of myoblasts and whether laminin 111 could be delivered permanently by genetically modified myoblasts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of respiratory stimulants on breathing instability in newborn rats
Keywords-MotsClés: CAFFEINE; CAROTID CHEMORECEPTORS; CONTROL OF BREATHING; DEVELOPMENTAL PLASTICITY; NEWBORN ANIMAL MODEL; PLETHYSMOGRAPHY; RECEPTORS FUNCTION AND IDENTIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Extreme premature babies (those born weighting 500 to 1250g) are exposed to respiratory irregularities after birth manifested by apnea (breathing stop), desaturation (decreasing in arterial oxygen content), and bradycardia (decreasing in heart rate). These events are called in medical term "apnea of prematurity" and disappear with development. However, they need to be treated to provide the most adequate conditions for growth and development. The common therapy for these events is the use of caffeine. Because this drug is not completely efficient to reduce apnea, clinicians are still searching for an adequate alternative. It has been suggested recently that progesterone or CO2 may also be used but we lack information on their efficiency, safety and the best postnatal age to use. Using newborn rats as an animal model, we will study and compare the effects on respiration, heart rate and desaturation of caffeine, progesterone and CO2 at different age during postnatal development. Our objective is to determine the best treatment that could reduce respiratory instabilities in newborn. Also, our results should provide valuable knowledge for the development of new specific pharmacological target to relieve apneas in this extremely fragile population of preterm infants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of intestinal epithelial permeability by serine proteases
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; COLON; ELECTROLYTE TRANSPORT; EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; EPITHELIUM; PERMEABILITY; PROTEASE; TIGHT JUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Many chronic, debilitating diseases of the digestive tract (eg inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease and enteric infections) are characterized by increased intestinal permeability or leakiness.  Increased permeability allows bacteria and antigens in the lumen of the intestine to invade the intestinal wall to trigger disease.  Permeability is controlled by the epithelium, a single layer of cells that makes up the inner lining of the intestine. One of the most important components of the epithelial barrier is the tight junction, a cluster of specialized proteins that join epithelial cells together and which limits the passage of material between them.  We are looking at ways to improve the barrier function of the epithelial tight junctions as a way of preventing intestinal diseases. We are particularly interested in the new concept that proteases can regulate tight junctions.  Proteases are enzymes that break down proteins and which have diverse functions throughout the body.  We have observed that certain proteases in the gut can enhance the epithelial barrier by strengthening tight junctions.  The mechanism for this is unclear, but our preliminary studies show that the effect is through a family of cellular receptors called the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) family.  We propose to use epithelial cells grown in cell culture to discover how proteases activate EGFR to bolster the structure of the tight junction and thereby enhance the epithelial barrier.  In addition, we know that the intestine produces protease inhibitors (called serpins) that block the function of many proteases.  We will use a mouse model of inflammatory bowel disease to determine if an imbalance between proteases and serpins contributes to increased intestinal permeability in disease.  It is our hope that these studies will uncover new ways to help patients living with chronic intestinal diseases that are characterized by epithelial barrier dysfunction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac differentiation of embryonic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM; CARDIAC DIFFERENTIATION; CHAPERONES; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality both in developed and developing countries. Understanding cardiac development and physiopathological mechanisms has been become indispensable for development of new and more efficient ways to cure cardiac diseases. Most importantly, congenital heart anomalies represent the most common human birth defect, and are the leading cause of death in the first year of life. Such defects involve structural abnormalities of the heart, primary cardiac muscle disorders, and disturbances of cardiac rhythm. Despite of many pharmacological and surgical treatments they only act on to overload the remaining cardiomyocytes. Generation of cardiac cells from stem cells offer a potential for the future cell replacement therapy.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: Troubles cognitifs légers et dépression gériatrique : comparaison de caractéristiques cliniques et analyse de l'évolution des patients vers la démence
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTEX PERIRHINAL; DEMENCE; DEPRESSION GERIATRIQUE; HIPPOCAMPE; HYPERINTENSITES DE LA SUBSTANCE BLANCHE; MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; MEMOIRE; NEUROIMAGERIE; TROUBLE COGNITIF LEGER; ETUDE LONGITUDINALE
Abstract-Résumé: Un des enjeux de la recherche sur le vieillissement consiste a mieux cerner les differentes facons dont la maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) se developpe. Dans ce domaine, il est reconnu que deux troubles augmentent particulierement le risque de developper la MA chez les personnes agees : (1) le trouble cognitif leger (TCL) et (2) la depression majeure (DEP). Les gens avec TCL presentent un trouble de la memoire dont la severite n'est pas suffisante pour rencontrer les criteres de la MA et dans environ la moitie des cas, des symptomes depressifs legers sont aussi presents. Quant aux personnes avec DEP, elles presentent principalement un trouble de l'humeur et souvent, des problemes de memoire sont aussi presents. Il existe donc plusieurs similitudes entre le TCL et de la DEP. Mais curieusement, tres peu d'etudes ont verifie dans quelle mesure ces deux troubles peuvent aussi differer. La recherche que nous realiserons vise a mieux comprendre les similitudes et les differences entre le TCL et la DEP. Chez les personnes TCL, nous separerons celles qui ont des symptomes depressifs (TCL/D+) et celles qui n'en ont pas (TCL). Tous les groupes seront d'abord compares quant a leur capacite a memoriser de nouvelles informations. Ensuite, la nature des atteintes dans le cerveau sera comparee entre les groupes. Finalement, le risque d'evoluer vers la MA ou une autre demence sera determine et compare entre chaque groupe. Nous formulons l'hypothese que nos mesures reveleront d'importantes differences quant aux caracteristiques du TCL, du TCL/D+ et de la DEP. Ces resultats permettront de mieux comprendre les caracteristiques cliniques pouvant etre observees chez differents groupes de personnes a risque de developper la MA. Par le fait meme, notre etude contribuera a l'amelioration du diagnostic precoce de la MA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Focal adhesion proteins and epidermal integrity
Keywords-MotsClés: BLISTRING DISEASES; CELL ATTACHMENT; EPIDERMIS; FOCAL ADHESIONS; INTEGRIN-LINKED KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: The skin is the largest organ in the body and is very important, because it acts as a barrier against chemicals, physical trauma and infection. The skin is formed by two layers: the outer epidermis, and the inner dermis. The epidermis is normally tightly attached to the dermis, through special structures that could be imagined as Velcro. When these structures are damaged, absent or abnormal, the epidermis separates from the dermis forming blisters. There are people with hereditary disposition to suffer extensive blisterig of the skin, which over time can cause chronic wounds and cancer. We discovered that a protein called Integrin-linked kinase (ILK) is necessary to keep the epidermis linked to the dermis. Our studies will explore how exactly ILK helps the epidermis stay attached to the dermis, preventing formation of blisters.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of sodium-hydrogen exchangers in the development of hereditary cardiomyopathy
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM OVERLOAD; CARDIOMYOPATHY; HEART FAILURE; HYPERTROPHY; HYPOTENSION; NUCLEAR MEMBRANES TRANSPORT; SODIUM OVERLOAD; SODIUM-HYDROGEN EXCHANGER
Abstract-Résumé: Hereditary cardiomyopathy is defined as a genetic disease of the heart that is characterized by an increase in heart size which leads to heart failure and death. Recent work from our laboratory showed in an animal model of hereditary cardiomyopathy, a weakness of blood vessels which is associated with what we call hypotension. Thus, it is possible to postulate that hereditary cardiomyopathy is not only a disease of the heart muscle but it is also a disease of blood vessels. Therefore, it is important to better understand the contribution of the weakness of blood vessels in the development of hereditary cardiomyopathy and sudden death. This will help to develop a new treatment for such a killing disease. Several drugs were reported to slow down the development of heart failure but not the survival of patients suffering from hereditary cardiomyopathy. Recent work in the literature as well as those recently reported by our group showed that the interior of heart cells was more acidic than that of normal cells and treatment to reduce the acidity of the cell completely abolishes the progression of the heart towards heart failure and premature death. The objective of the project is to test the hypothesis that as for the heart, the interior of cells of blood vessels is more acidic than normal and that reduction of the acidity with new generation of drugs will not only prevent the progression of heart disease but also the associated weakness of blood vessels. This work will for sure not only help us to better understand the reason of weakness of heart and blood vessels functioning in hereditary cardiomyopathy but also find a cure of this high killing disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a Therapeutic Oncolytic Poxvirus with Enhanced Systemic Delivery and Potency
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOTHERAPEUTICS; CANCER THERAPY; GENETIC ENGINEERING; IMAGING; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; ONCOLYTIC VIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is the leading disease-associated cause of death in Canada, with the majority of these deaths resulting from recurrent, metastatic or widespread lesions. New therapies are needed, with greater potency yet fewer side effects than conventional treatments. Oncolytic viruses (OV) are a novel therapeutic platform which answers this call; they preferentially infect and lyse cancer cells in a highly selective manner, they have an excellent safety profile, and they attack the cancer in multiple ways. Jennerex Biotherapeutics is a world leader in the development of oncolytic virus therapeutics. We currently have a lead product, JX 594 in late stage clinical trials and have successfully partnered this product with a French Biotherapeutics company, Transgene.  Having a robust pipeline of novel oncolytic virus products is key to the growth and evolution of Jennerex.  The goal of this proposal is to develop of our next generation oncolytic virus (OV) product. Specifically, this proposal builds upon our pre-clinical and clinical findings to date and will direct the rational design of a new OV, by evaluating the inherent anti-tumor activity of different vaccinia virus strains, in order to identify the strain best suited for building a superior therepeutic agent. In addition, we plan to test new strategies for enhancing virus potency against cancer cells, optimizing intravenous delivery of our therapeutic virus, while maintaining safety for the patient.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of autonomic nervous system function, body fat distribution and metabolic profile in children with PWS.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTOKINES; AUTONOMIC NERVOUS SYSTEM; BODY COMPOSITION; CHILDHOOD OBESITY; HORMONES; NUTRITION; PEDIATRICS; PRADER-WILLI SYNDROME; VISCERAL FAT
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of this study is to explore autonomic nervous system (ANS) function in childhood obesity. Canadian childhood obesity rates continue to rise with 8 percent of children (2-17 years) currently obese. Much research has explored factors responsible for the development of obesity, yet few effective treatments exist. This fact highlights the complexity of the pathogenesis of obesity and underscores the need for novel research.   The ANS controls essential functions like breathing, heart rate, digestion, body temperature and hormone levels. Evidence suggests that ANS dysfunction is associated with adult obesity and may play a role in the development of obesity-related complications. The specific characteristics of ANS dysfunction in childhood obesity, however, are not clear. The link between ANS dysfunction and obesity-related metabolic complications is also unknown. We will characterize ANS dysfunction in obese children and examine the relationship between ANS dysfunction, body fat distribution and metabolic profile. To further understand this relationship, we will compare obese children to children with a unique model of obesity and ANS dysfunction called Prader-Willi Syndrome (PWS).   PWS is the most common genetic form of childhood obesity. ANS dysfunction in PWS is suggested by findings of low blood sugar, abnormal sleep, body temperature instability, reduced pain sensitivity, and sudden death. Obese PWS children may also have a lower risk of developing obesity-related diseases (type 2 diabetes), than other obese children. Differences in ANS function might explain these metabolic differences between obese children with and without PWS.   The study will measure ANS function, total and abdominal body fat and hormone levels in obese children. These results will be compared to those of children with PWS. Identification of the specific ANS dysfunction in childhood obesity and PWS could lead to novel therapies for both conditions to improve quality of life

TitreApplicationTitle: Optogenetic investigation of theta and gamma rhythm generation in hippocampus
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; FREELY-MOVING; GABA INTERNEURONS; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; IN VITRO; MEMORY; OPTOGENETICS; PLASTICITY; THETA RHYTHMS
Abstract-Résumé: The hippocampus is a large brain region dedicated for learning and memory. In order to store memory and send memory related information within this structure and with other brain regions, millions of neurons have to synchronize their activity. How do neurons do this and which neurons are important for this? In this grant proposal, we will use a combination of state-of-the-art techniques to determine how neurons synchronize in the hippocampus and we will determine which neurons are key in this process. An understanding of this synchronization pehnomenon will give us a new insight into new treatments for epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetic alterations of the placenta that may be predictive of onset preeclampsia
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; PLACENTA; PREECLAMPSIA; TRISOMY
Abstract-Résumé: Preeclampsia is a serious condition for both mother and fetus in which maternal hypertension arises in pregnancy in combination with significant amounts of protein in the urine. Although preeclampsia may have a variety of underlying causes, there are common changes that occur in the placenta prior to the onset of symptoms. We have found that epigenetic (chemical) changes to the DNA occur in placentas associated with early onset preeclampsia (onset prior to 34 weeks). We intend to measure these changes at 450,000 sites in the DNA simultaneously. We will then compare these to changes observed by growing placental cells at different oxygen concentrations and to changes in placentas that have genetic errors known to be susceptible to preeclampsia. Our goal is to determine which of these epigenetic changes occur early in the disease process. We then plan to use this information to develop tests using placental DNA that is found in the pregnant woman's blood that can help diagnosis of preeclampsia prior to the onset of symptoms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gipr and the control of glucose homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; INTESTINE; OBESITY; PEPTIDE HORMONES
Abstract-Résumé: Incretin hormones are secreted from the gut and aid in the disposal of ingested nutrients by augmenting insulin secretion following meal ingestion. The two pricipal incretin hormones, GLP-1 and GIP, potentiate glucose-dependent insulin secretion by activating their distinct receptors on islet beta cells. Both the GLP-1 and GIP receptors are also widely expressed outside the endocrine pancreas, where they transmit signals to the brain, gut, skeleton, heart, and adipose tissue. The focus of this grant proposal is to elucidate the biological actions of the gut hormone GIP in key tissues through generation and analysis of mutant mice with inactivating mutations in key sites of GIP action.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biochemistry and Molecular Biology of the Lyme Disease Spirochete
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGENIC VARIATION; GENOME DYNAMICS; GLOBAL GENE EXPRESSION; LYME DISEASE; RNA HELICASE; TELOMERE RESOLUTION
Abstract-Résumé: Work in my laboratory focuses on Borrelia burgdorferi, the spiral shaped bacterium (spirochete) that causes Lyme disease. This organism has great clinical importance as Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne disease in North America and Europe. B. burgdorferi was discovered only 30 years ago, has many very unusual characteristics and much of how it functions remains unknown. Our interests are in understanding some of the unusual processes as well as the mechanisms by which it causes disease. We are also interested in being able to apply the knowledge we gain to the development of more effective diagnosis, treatment and disease prevention. Our proposed research program is a continuation of our current work:  1) Telomere resolution - the study of how the unusual hairpin ends (telomeres) on the DNA are formed by the telomere resolvase, ResT. This unique process makes an attractive target for drug development. We will further investigate how ResT interacts with other proteins within the cell and its role in the evolution of the unusual linear DNA molecules found in Borrelia species.  2) Antigenic variation - the process whereby the bacterium can stay one step ahead of the host immune system and establish and maintain a persistent infection. We propose to study how this process is regulated and the details of how the surface antigen is changed.   3) Global gene regulation - we have discovered a new gene involved in turning on and off large numbers of B. burgdorferi genes. This new regulatory gene is required for infection in mice and will help us to gain an understanding of the disease-causing process. 4) Genome dynamics - the very lengthy shape of B. burgdorferi presents an interesting challenge for the movement of over 20 DNA molecules a great distance prior to cell division. To study this process we will use a newly developed method (super resolution microscopy) to analyze the movement of these DNA molecules in time and space.

TitreApplicationTitle: Youth's Voices: Their Lives and Experiences of Living with an Anxiety Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY DISORDERS; ANXIETY DISORDERS INTERVIEW SCHEDULE; ECOMAPS; EXPERIENCES; MENTAL HEALTH; PARENTS; PHENOMENOLOGY; PHOTOVOICE; QUALITATIVE OPEN-ENDED INTERVIEWS; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: Anxiety disorders are one of the most prevalent, distressing, and disabling of psychiatric disorders in youth. If left untreated, anxiety disorders in youth put them at risk in later life for major depression, adult anxiety disorders, substance abuse, and poor physical health. Although research examining anxiety disorders in youth is growing, most of the focus is on addressing prevalence, symptoms, and factors contributing to anxiety disorders, and not on what youth think and feel. Missing is an understanding of what it is like to be a youth living with an anxiety disorder. The purpose of this 3-year study is to arrive at an increased understanding of youth's perspectives and experiences of living with an anxiety disorder. Primary participants are youth (ages 10-18 years) newly referred for one or more anxiety disorders. Youth's parents will also be recruited to provide added insights about how anxiety disorders shape their child's daily life. Data collection methods include interviews combined with photovoice which is a process that involves youth taking photographs to document their experiences. Analysis will involve several steps with the aim of striving for a detailed account of the meanings relevant to youth's experiences of living with anxiety disorders. Overall, this research is very important given the high prevalence of anxiety disorders in youth and the priority given by the Mental Health Commission for the need to advance mental health research in youth. This study will result in foundational knowledge that extends beyond what is presently known about youth living with an anxiety disorder. By obtaining youth's perspective of what it is like to live with an anxiety disorder, our understanding of their experiences will be deepened. The knowledge gleaned from this study may be used to inform existing interventions, and lead to the development of new models of care and treatment services for youth living with anxiety disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of cAMP and training in the recovery of reaching after spinal cord injury
Keywords-MotsClés: CAMP; PLASTICITY; RAT; REHABILITATION TRAINING; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: There are currently no treatments that promote substantial functional recovery following a persons spinal cord injury (SCI). However, findings of adaptive changes, in other words, plasticity, in the adult nervous system are beginning to offer new avenues of potential treatment.  In an animal model of SCI, we have demonstrated that plasticity can be amplified by rehabilitative training, provided that it begins early after an injury. Moreover, we recently found that training success decreases following injury in association with a decline of the level of intracellular messenger molecule, cyclic AMP, in the brain. This intriguing finding forms the basis for the current proposal.  We know that cyclic AMP strongly influences various intracellular processes, including the ability of neurons to grow. Therefore, we will examine whether the post injury decrease in cyclic AMP interferes with the training-induced plasticity, which could explain the progressive decrease in training efficacy. We plan, with this experiment, to determine whether we can establish a causal relationship between the decline in training efficacy on functional recovery over the weeks following injury and the decline in cAMP levels.   We also have a secondary purpose: We want to demonstrate that the decline of cortical cAMP levels is caused by neuronal inactivity and is not a direct consequence of the injury to the nerve cells. We will explore a pharmacological increase of cAMP in combination with training in rats with chronic SCI. These would, we believe, open the door for new treatment approaches.  In summary, we will investigate the reason for the progressive decline of rehabilitation training efficacy following spinal cord injuries and offer new treatment approaches to enhance training effects.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
ClasseRechercheFR: AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE; TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Recovery of locomotion mediated by interneuron regeneration following complete spinal cord injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; AXONAL REGENERATION; COMBINED TREATMENT; INTERNEURONS; LOCOMOTOR RECOVERY; PLASTICITY; REWIRING; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: In contrast to the peripheral nervous system, nerve cells in the central nervous system (CNS: i.e. brain or spinal cord) cannot spontaneously regenerate their connections. Consequently, after a spinal cord injury (SCI) individuals permanently suffer from the loss of sensory, motor, and autonomic function below the level of the injury. Unfortunately there is still no effective treatment to repair the injured spinal cord. A reason for the lack of an efficient treatment despite years of intensive research is that regeneration of nerve cell branches in the CNS is inhibited by multiple factors. Therefore, it is now widely agreed upon that an effective treatment for SCI will have to address various obstacles for nerve cell regeneration at the same time.  A possibility to circumvent the necessity for regeneration of nerve cells originating in the brain following SCI, but still promoting their reconnection to targets that lost their input from the brain below the lesion, is based on findings following incomplete SCI. Our research has shown that injured nerve cells spontaneously sprout new branches above the lesion site and connect to descending nerve cells spared by the lesion. Thereby, these injured cells are reconnecting to their original targets via a relay. A possible relay following complete SCI are nerve cells located in the spinal cord, so called interneurons, that have demonstrated a superior ability to regenerate. Therefore, the goal of this proposal is to extend our previous combined treatment in rats with complete SCI, with the focus to enhance regeneration of interneurons. Then, we will encourage rerouting of injured nerve cells originating in the brain via these interneurons, in order to indirectly reconnect them to spinal networks below the injury.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of nuclear metabotropic glutamate receptors in persistent nociception
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL TESTING; CALCIUM SIGNALING; GLIA; GLUTAMATE; GLUTAMATE BINDING; GLUTAMATE TRANSPORTERS; MGLURS; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; PAIN; SUBCELLULAR MEMBRANE FRACTIONATION
Abstract-Résumé: Neurotransmitter receptors are normally found on the outer cell membrane of nerve cells or neurons. Some receptors have been found as well inside neurons on the membrane of the cell's nucleus. We propose to examine whether increases in newly discovered nuclear membrane receptors for the neurotransmitter glutamate in spinal cord, along with the ones on the cell membrane, contribute to enhanced pain responses in rats with persistent pain. We will assess whether these receptors are increased in rats with hind paw inflammation or nerve injury, and whether there is increased binding and activity of glutamate at cell membrane and nuclear receptors in these rats. Finally, we wish to determine whether drugs which prevent transport of glutamate into cells reduce enhanced pain after inflammation or nerve injury because they prevent glutamate from getting to neuronal nuclear receptors. We will test this hypothesis against previously proposed theories that these drugs block abnormal pumping of glutamate back into the synapse (from the glial cells which normally take glutamate out of synapses), or cause excess glutamate binding at inhibitory receptors on the nerve cells that release glutamate, therefore stopping further glutamate release.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - B: Heart and Circulation
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Dissection of Brain Mechanisms Contributing to HF post MI.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDOSTERONE; BRAIN MECHANISMS; GENETIC CHANGES; HEART FAILURE; K+-ATPASE; MICE; NA+; OUABAIN; SYMPATHETIC NERVOUS SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a progressive disease, slowly, but surely disabling the patient. In recent years, it has become clear that besides the initial abnormality in the heart (now most commonly an heart attack) increased activity of the sympathetic nervous system to the heart plays a major role in the progression of heart failure to terminal disease. Why the sympathetic nervous system shows this increase is not yet understood. In studies in rats we have demonstrated that a myocardial infarction (MI or "heart attack") leads to activation of brain pathways involving a cascade of factors. This cascade causes not only persistent and progressive increase in sympathetic activity but also the progression of the disease. These studies have provided major new insights into the mechanisms leading to the progression of heart failure, which in a later phase, may lead to new approaches to the prevention of progression of heart failure. These conclusions are largely based on chronic infusions of blockers for each of the steps in the cascade directly into the brain of rats. As an alternative, more precise approach, the molecular and genetic determinants of activation of the brain can be pursued in mice by genetic manipulations such as the development of recombinant animal lines from mutant embryonic stem cells. This approach allows the assessment of the effects of in vivo mutations in specific genes on integrative pathophysiology after an MI. In the present studies in mice, we will be evaluating the effects of changes in 2 genes resulting in either enhanced activity in the brain or decreased activity, and expect that the extent of heart failure and mortality will parallel these changes in the brain. Ultimately, this type of studies may contribute to an understanding of the role of genetic variants in the development of heart failure in humans after an MI.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RESPIRATION; EFFETS ENVIRONNEMENTAUX SUR LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Linking gestational stress and respiratory control disorder in the developing newborn
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMOREFLEX; CONTROL OF BREATHING; DEVELOPMENT; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; PLASTICITY; PLETHYSMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Respiratory instabilities and apneas are a major cause of hospitalisation and morbidity in infants born prematurely. Smoking and drug abuse by the mother during pregnancy are significant risk factors for such respiratory disorders. However, respiratory problems related to abnormal function or immaturity of the brain regions that generate and regulate respiratory activity still occur in infants born to mothers that do not use such substances. The factors contributing to respiratory disorders in this population of newborn are still poorly understood. Stress and anxiety during pregnancy is a significant risk factor for the emergence of neurological diseases. While gestational stress is linked to poor birth outcome and increased need for resuscitation in newborn, the potential effect of gestational stress on respiratory activity in newborn is unknown. To address this issue, this proposal will use a clinically relevant rat model to determine whether exposing female rats to a stressful stimulus (fox odour) during pregnancy disturbs the function and development of the neural circuits that regulate breathing in the newborn. Specifically, we will measure apneas and respiratory instabilities along with the breathing responses to changes in blood oxygen and carbon dioxyde, and the presence of liquid in the airways of newborn pups. By studying these effects in different age groups, we will determine whether gestational stress also interferes with normal development of relevant respiratory responses and reflexes. Preliminary data are highly promising and we anticipate that the results from this research will help explain the occurrence of these respiratory disorders in the newborn. This is an important step in the development of prevention and treatment of this highly vulnerable population.

ClasseRechercheFR: AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE; TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting amino acid and biogenic amine neurotransmitters to improve functional outcomes in EAE
Keywords-MotsClés: AMINO ACIDS; BIOGENIC AMINES; CENTRAL SENSITIZATION; D-SERINE; FOS; GABA; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NMDA; PAIN; SEROTONIN
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain has a major effect on the quality of life of patients with MS. "Neuropathic" pain, which arises when there is an injury or disease in the nervous system, is the most prevalent and difficult to treat pain syndrome seen in MS patients. Unfortunately, there are few effective treatments to relieve neuropathic pain in MS because currently very little is known about its underlying causes.  Within the central nervous system (CNS), cells communicate via the release of neurotransmitters. The amino acids glutamate and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) are the two major neurotransmitters required for excitatory and inhibitory signals respectively. Serotonin and noradrenaline, biogenic amines, are also important for communication within the CNS, often suppressing signals between cells. In diseases such as MS, the balance between these different 'excitatory' and 'inhibitory' neurotransmitters can be disturbed. Our research will test the hypothesis that in a mouse model of MS, alterations in the levels of these excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters is the major underlying cause of neuropathic pain and disability that arises in the disease. Using an animal model of MS, we will test how specific drugs, known to significantly alter the levels of these different neurotransmitters, affect pain sensitivity and symptom severity. Because the different drugs that we will be testing affect only certain neurotransmitters systems, we will be able to isolate and identify which of the different affected neurotransmitters is most important for causing pain and disability in the disease. By identifying these underlying causes, we will be in a strong position to develop new treatments for patients with MS that will help to restore function and relieve the pain and discomfort associated with the disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the mechanisms by which resveratrol prevents doxorubicin-induced cardiac dysfunction and heart failure
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC METABOLISM; CHEMOTHERAPY; DOXORUBICIN; HEART FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: While patients who have undergone chemotherapy may be cured of cancer, many suffer from drug-induced damage to other organs, including the heart and blood vessels. Of concern is the fact that patients who show immediate heart injury must be taken off of these drugs and the cancer treatment is halted/delayed. Other patients who may not display obvious and immediate injury to their hearts may show signs of injury to their heart and blood vessels later in life. In both instances, some patients eventually develop heart failure with a poor quality of life and a high probability of death. As this drug-induced damage to the heart can induce heart failure, the experiments proposed in this grant will test a treatment that may protect the heart from damage induced by chemotherapy. If successful, patients may be able to receive higher doses of the anti-cancer agents without concern of drug-induced damage to the heart, ultimately improving cancer treatment and promoting long-term survival of the cancer patient free from risk of heart failure.
