TitreApplicationTitle: Mucosal innate immunity in HIV resistant women
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL PHENOTYPE ANALYSIS BY FLOW CYTOMETRY; CYTOKINE/CHEMOKINE MEASUREMENTS; FEMALE COMMERCIAL SEX WORKERS; GENITAL MUCOSAL IMMUNITY; HIV SUSCEPTIBILITY/RESISTANCE; HIV/AIDS PATHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Most HIV infections are acquired through heterosexual intercourse, and each year the rate of HIV-infected women increases dramatically. Initial exposure to HIV-1 during sexual transmission occurs in the genital tract, however, little is known about HIV-1-specific immune responses at this site. During the previous CIHR mandate (2006-2009), we established an ongoing cohort of heavily HIV-exposed commercial sex workers (CSWs), in Cotonou (Benin), in which we have identified individuals who remain HIV-uninfected (resistant) after more than 3 years of active prostitution. The fact that some individuals remain persistently seronegative despite high exposure to the virus such as the HIV-1-uninfected CSWs presented herein, implies that there are host factors that are highly protective. Interestingly, we have recently demonstrated distinct mucosal inflammatory patterns associated with either susceptibility or resistance to infection. In the current study, we propose to investigate the role of the genital cellular populations and cytokine/chemokine genetic polymorphisms on the modulation of the mucosal inflammatory patterns associated with either susceptibility or resistance to HIV infection. This study will identify key host factors associated with HIV infection and will provide novel insights on their role in modulating the genital mucosal immune response towards HIV.

ResearchClassEN: MENTAL AND BEHAVIOURAL DISEASES; DISEASES AFFECTING SPEECH/VISION/HEARING

TitreApplicationTitle: Physiological, Anatomical and Molecular Organization of the Cerebellum
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBELLUM; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; NEUROANATOMICAL TRACING; OCULOMOTOR PATHOLOGIES; VESTIBULAR; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: The majority of neurons (up to 85%) in the brain are found in the cerebellum. The cerebellum integrates information from various sensory systems and is involved in numerous processes including motor control, learning and cognition. How the cerebellum organizes information from the various senses is still poorly understood. The cerebellum has a unique organization: some neurochemicals are expressed as "stripes" throughout the cerebellum. The most thoroughly studied of these neurochemicals is the enzyme aldolase C, also known as zebrin. Although the exact role of zebrin is not clear, it is expressed in the same way in all vertebrate species studied, indicating that it is essential for cerebellar function. The organization is such that there are stripes of neurons that express zebrin alternating with stripes of cells that do not express zebrin. The goal of the proposed research is to understand how these stripes relate to function and processing of information in the cerebellum. We use a part of the cerebellum known as the vestibulocerebellum as a model. This is an area where visual, vestibular and spinal information is integrated in order to control eye movements, posture and locomotion, and balance.  To understand how information is organized with respect to the zebrin stripes, we will determine how the visual, vestibular, and spinal connections are associated with particular zebrin stripes in the vestibulocerebellum. Moreover, we will record from neurons in particular zebrin stripes to determine the nature of sensory processing within each stripe. These studies will provide basic information about the principles of fundamental sensory organization in the cerebellum. This is critical for understanding diseases of the vestibulocerebellum that cause disturbances of visuo-motor behaviour (e.g., oscillopsia, oculomotor abnormalities, vertigo), and diseases that affect the cerebellum in general such as Wernicke's encephalopathy, Alzheimer's disease and autism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pink Ribbons and Red Dresses: the relationship between disease awareness campaigns, health-related cognitions and perceptions of preventive behaviours.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; DISCOURSE ANALYSISIS; HEALTH PROMOTION; IMPLICIT PARADIGMS; MASS MEDIA; SURVEYS; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: More Canadian women die of heart disease than breast cancer yet most women believe the opposite to be true. Women are also more scared of breast cancer than they are of heart disease, yet feel they have little control over whether they will develop breast cancer or not. The Red Dress campaign was developed to try to raise awareness of heart disease risk in women, but it has not reached as many women as the Pink Ribbon campaign for breast cancer. It is therefore possible that the Pink Ribbon campaign has a more powerful effect on women and results in greater perceived risk of breast cancer than heart disease. This research will investigate how these two campaigns are represented in the media. We will also investigate how the two campaigns influence women from various socioeconomic, education, and cultural groups. We will use surveys and experiments to test the hypotheses that the Pink Ribbon campaign, which has greater exposure and reach through corporate endorsements, influences not only perceptions of breast cancer but indirectly influences risk perception of heart disease. The experiments will test how health messages are processed outside of our conscious awareness. This is important to do because our gut reactions to media can guide behaviour, even if we are not necessarily aware that they are doing so. This research will help inform health promotion efforts. The results will be of interest to both researchers and practitioners who work to prevent heart disease in Canada and who attempt to increase behaviours such as physical activity that have been shown to help prevent both heart disease and breast cancer.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: The endoplasmic reticulum and programmed cell death
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZEHIMER'S; APOPTOSIS; CANCER; CONFORMATIONAL DISEASE; MOLECULAR CHAPERONES; PARKINSON'S; PROTEIN QUALITY CONTROL; STRESS RESPONSE; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Damaged or unneeded cells in living beings have a normal process for elimination, called apoptosis. This normal cell death is programmed into each cell. However, the apoptosis programme can be activated by various cellular stresses thus leading to a wide variety of human ailments, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, liver disease, heat conditions, and diabetes. On the other hand, in certain cases a blockage in apoptosis can lead to cancer.   Calnexin is a crucial protein that is vital for the normal function of the cell. Interestingly however, in recent years we have found that calnexin is also involved in apoptosis. Indeed, our experiments have directly demonstrated that calnexin controls the levels of cell death induced by different stress conditions.  To investigate how calnexin is involved in apoptosis, we are using genetic approaches with a type of yeast that is a simple model to understand the biological functions of human cells. In a first place, the results from our investigation will provide important information to understand how apoptosis is induced by diverse stresses. The knowledge gained in this manner will serve to eventually treat the human diseases in which apoptosis is affected such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and cancer.  Moreover, there is an urgent need to treat hospital-acquired infections, which in general are caused by fungal pathogens. Our studies on apoptosis should also assist in designing drugs to induce death of fungal pathogens and thus combat hospital-acquired infections.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular aging: Mouse molecular models for Werner syndrome.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DNA REPAIR; DNA REPLICATION; GENOMIC INSTABILITY; METABOLISM; MOUSE MODEL OF AGING; OXIDATIVE STRESS; SENESCENCE; TRANSCRIPTION; WERNER SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: One of the most fascinating of human aging syndromes is Werner syndrome (WS). WS is a recessive disorder characterized by genomic instability and the premature onset of several age-related diseases. The precise function of the WS protein (WRN) in genomic stability is not fully understood but data in the literature points toward a role of WRN in DNA recombination/repair pathways during replication or even transcription in cells. Importantly, we have found that loss of WRN protein in human cells affects the expression of genes involved in cellular metabolism and oxidative stress response. Correspondingly, the current theory is that oxidative stress is the culprit of several diseases associated with aging. Thus, the understanding of the mechanism by which WRN prevents oxidative stress will open the route to possible intervention not only in premature aging diseases but also normal aging. Hence, the first aim of this proposal is to determine whether the WRN protein regulates the expression of these genes by interacting directly with their regulatory sequences. Such results will be confirmed in mouse models of WS. Our laboratory has two WS mouse line. One line produces a stable mutant protein with abnormal enzymatic activities. These mice have a reduced health and life span. The other line does not synthesize a WRN protein but has less severe age-related pathologies. The second aim is to understand why mice with a stable mutant WRN protein have more severe pathologies than mice without any WRN protein. Finally, we found that vitamin C supplementation reverses aging in WRN mutant mice. Our third aim will be to cross all our WRN mutant lines with mouse line that lacks the enzyme required for vitamin C synthesis. Such mice will rely entirely on vitamin C provided in the diet like humans. Results obtained from our mice supplemented with vitamin C will be clinically relevant for the prevention or treatment of premature aging syndrome as well as normal human aging.

NomDuComitéFR: Déterminants psychosociaux, socioculturels et comportementaux de la santé
TitreApplicationTitle: A Population-Based Longitudinal Study on Work and Health
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; DEPRESSION; LONGITUDINAL; OUTCOMES; RISK ASSESSMENT TOOL; WORKING POPULATION; WORKPLACE MENTAL HEALTH ACCOMMODATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Mental disorders are prevalent in the labor force. With the fast changes in the world economy and in industrial reorganization in the past years, employees have been facing mounting pressure to be more competitive. Such changes are generating job insecurities for workers and demanding more cerebral skills and mental performance. These work environmental factors may precipitate the onset of mental disorders and lead to significant impacts on productivity. The proposed study will follow a cohort of employees randomly selected across Alberta to investigate how changes in work environment affect the risk of mental disorders, to develop and validate a mental health risk appraisal tool for workplaces and to examine how the use of workplace mental health accommodations affect employees' occupational functioning and mental health outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular changes associated with childhood abuse: An MeDIP-Seq study
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE METHYLATION; MAJOR DEPRESSION; NEUROBIOLOGY; SUICIDE; VULNERABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Children in our society are all too often subjected to physical violence, emotional deprivation and inappropriate sexual behaviours. These negative life experiences are among the strongest predictors of psychiatric illness and suicide in adulthood, with strong and lifelong effects. Recent research has suggested that negative life experiences may increase the risk of psychiatric illness and suicide by changing the chemical structure of DNA. These effects, known as epigenetics were initially observed in animal studies and subsequent research suggested that they also occur in humans. This study will use a combination of techniques to conduct a large study aiming to identify epigenetic changes across the genome that may be associated with early-environmental adversity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Polyamines, depression and suicide
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; EPIGENETICS; POLYAMINES; POSTMORTEM; SEQUENCING; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Resulting from a combination of genetic and environmental risk factors, neurobiological alterations underlie major depression and suicidal behaviors. In recent years, we have found strong evidence to support the involvement of the polyamine stressresponse system in the neurobiology of suicide. Polyamines are small molecules that are released by the body to maintain proper function. In the brain, polyamines act as messengers between cells and are released in stressful situations. The proposed project will further our investigation of the role of polyamines in depression and suicide by examining more closely the biological processes which bring about these effects. In the process, new insight can be gained into novel intervention and potential treatments for suicidal behaviors

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic studies of blood stage malaria: from mouse models to human disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTEMISININ; CYSTEAMINE; ERYTHROCYTE; GENETICS; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; MALARIA; MOUSE MODELS; POSITIONAL CLONING; PYRUVATE KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: Malaria remains a major threat to global health with an estimated 1-2 million associated fatalities per year. The problem of resistance to anti-malarial drugs and the absence of an efficacious vaccine have compounded the malaria problem. Genetic factors play an important role in the initial susceptibility to infection, progression of disease and ultimate outcome of malaria. Our laboratory uses mouse models of malaria to study genes and pathways that influence replication of the malarial parasite in the blood. We have discovered that mutations at PKLR, Pantetheinase, and Char10 loci alter susceptibility to malaria in mice. In this proposal, we will determine if alterations in the same pathways affect susceptibility to malaria in humans, and will explore of novel treatment strategies based on our findings in mouse models.

TitreApplicationTitle: Synthesis and Evaluation of Butyrylcholinesterase Ligands as Brain Molecular Imaging Biomarkers for Alzheimer Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINESTERASE; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AUTORADIOGRAPHY; BUTYRYLCHOLINESTERASE; FLUORINE 18; IODINE 123; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; NUCLEAR MEDICINE; PET SCANNING; SPECT SCANNING
Abstract-Résumé: Cholinesterases are enzymes involved in the breakdown of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter important in brain cell communication, and which is reduced in Alzheimer's disease (AD). AD is marked by loss of memory and deposition of toxic brain proteins, forming abnormal structures called amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. The ability to detect these in the living brain could facilitate early diagnosis of the disease. In AD brains, plaques and tangles contain the enzyme butyrylcholinesterase. The presence of these butyrylcholinesterase "hot spots" in the brain may provide an opportunity for early detection of AD. We received a CIHR grant in 2007 to develop radiolabelled imaging compounds that bind to butyrylcholinesterase for the detection of this enzyme activity in the living brain, using current scanning techniques. Since then, we have synthesized a number of compounds and have incorporated radioactive iodine-123 into such compounds. We have shown their uptake in brain regions known to contain butyrylcholinesterase in the normal living experimental rat.   Our preliminary experiments have also shown that these compounds are indeed taken up in abnormally located butyrylcholinesterase "hot spots" in a transgenic mouse model of AD. Furthermore, we have been able to visualize abnormal deposits, typical of disease, in human AD brain tissue. With this significant advance in our preliminary experiments, we now propose to extend our studies, based on these lead imaging compounds, to identify those molecules with optimum ability to detect butyrylcholinesterase associated with abnormal AD structures. It is anticipated that butyrylcholinesterase imaging agents will permit early detection of AD pathology in the living human brain and will aid accurate diagnosis of this condition during life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engaging First Nations Women in Cervical Cancer Screening: Assessing Factors Related to Screening and Uptake of Self-Sampling
Keywords-MotsClés: CERVICAL CANCER SCREENING; ETHICAL SPACE; FIRST NATIONS WOMEN; HPV TESTING; PAP TESTING; SELF-SAMPLING
Abstract-Résumé: Cervical cancer is the 3rd most common cancer in Canadian women aged between 20 and 49. This malignancy is associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) and is preventable with regular screening. Many First Nations women, however, are not regularly screened. This may contribute to this population having a signficantly higher prevalence of cervical cancer compared to other Canadian women.  We will test the acceptability of a new approach to cervical cancer screening in First Nations women: self-sampling and HPV testing. This approach has been successful in recruiting other under-screened  Canadian women. About one thousand First Nations women between 25 and 70 years old from Northwest Ontario will be invited to particpate. The study will take three years.  We expect that this new practice, in combination with culturally appropriate health information, will increase participation in cervical cancer screening and in due course decrease cervical cancer rates amongst First Nations women.  A key feature of this study is the emphasis on developing trusting and genuine relationships with First Nations communities helping to reduce the burden of cervical cancer within these communities. First Nations community members, and in particular women, will be engaged in all decision making processes.  This work will assist in the implementation of an organized cervical cancer screening program that is culturally safe for the needs of First Nations women. It will further guide to design prophylactic vaccines that are precisely adapted to the truly prevailing HPV types in First Nations women as suggested in other related studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biological variability of the response to protein trafficking correctors of cystic fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL CHALLENGE; CORRECTOR COMPOUNDS; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; HALIDE-SENSITIVE YFP ADENOVIRUS; PRIMARY HUMAN BRONCHIAL EPITHELIAL CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most frequent orphan disease in Canada, and the CFTR gene was discovered by Canadian and US researchers 22 years ago. The CFTR gene codes for a cell surface protein that transports chloride and the most frequent mutant protein is able to transport chloride, but is retained inside the cell. We have identified small molecules that are good correctors of this trafficking defect of the CFTR mutant protein trafficking and these are under intensive development. We have observed that correctors that work well in transformed human lung-derived epithelial cell lines do not necessarily work well in cells obtained from CF patient lung transplants. In addition we have noticed a considerable variation in the functional response to correctors in CF patient lung cells obtained from different individuals. This proposal will address the questions, why do correctors function differently in different cells, and do outside stimuli affect the corrector's ability to function? Our overall hypothesis is that this knowledge will guide us to better targets for drug development for cystic fibrosis.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Studies of Invisible Protein States by NMR Spectroscopy: Application to Protein Folding and Misfolding
Keywords-MotsClés: EXCITED PROTEIN STATES; NMR SPECTROSOCPY; PROTEIN FOLDING; PROTEIN FUNCTION; PROTEIN MISFOLDING AND DISEASE; PROTEIN THERMODYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: The function of a protein derives from its three-dimensional structure and how it changes with time. Although very detailed pictures of protein molecules have been produced it is often the case that they do not completely explain results from functional biological assays, nor do they necessarily illuminate the path for protein engineering or rational drug design. This is, of course, not surprising. A three-dimensional static structure provides a description of the ground state of the molecule. Macromolecular function is, in many cases, highly dependent on excursions to excited molecular states that are only transiently formed and of very low population. Such molecular conformations have traditionally escaped detection using conventional methods for obtaining three-dimensional structural information. The goal of this research is to study how proteins fold into their three-dimensional structures by obtaining atomic level descriptions of the excited state intermediates that are formed along their folding pathways. Studies will also be performed to understand how proteins misfold into fibrilar structures that are implicated in a host of human diseases. Ultimately, an understanding of how such fibers are formed will lead to the rational design of pharmaceuticals that prevent their occurrence.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
TitreApplicationTitle: Typical and atypical development of frontal lobe systems and the maturation of social cognitive function.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASD; CONNECTIVITY; FRONTAL LOBE DEVELOPMENT; MEG; MRI; PREMATURITY
Abstract-Résumé: Social cognitive functions refer generally to the ability to behave in social settings.  Two important underlying skills are emotional perception and the ability to inhibit inappropriate (bad) behaviour.  These abilities are largely controlled by areas of the frontal lobes of the brain which develop until adulthood.  We have limited knowledge of frontal lobe development and its relation to how children acquire social skills, but we know that frontal lobe abnormalities seriously disrupt social cognitive functions.  We will determine the development of these abilities, measuring brain structure, brain function and brain connectivity while children are completing an emotional processing task and an inhibition task.  We will study 7-16yr-olds typically developing children as well as children born very preterm and children with autism.  These clinical groups each affect about 1/100 children.  Both clinical groups have significant difficulties with social behaviour as well as distinct frontal lobe structural abnormalities.  Structural brain imaging (MRI/DTI) will provide measures of grey and white matter, and of structural brain connections.  Functional brain imaging (using magnetoencephalography (MEG) will provide the timing of brain activity, brain dynamics and the strength of functional brain connections.  By studying typical children, we will understand the normal development of these important social skills and the role of frontal lobe maturation; the two clinical groups will allow us to distinguish structural and functional brain abnormalities related to their differing disturbances in social functions.  We know that failure to learn or acquire adequate social skills has a devastating impact on an individual's personal and professional life.  Increasing our knowledge of these problems, the underlying brain processes and their critical periods, will improve our ability to develop and fine-tune appropriate interventions for these two groups of vulnerable children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cell polarity in mammary morphogenesis and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL MOTILITY; DEVELOPMENT; EPITHELIAL; MAMMARY TRANSPLANT; MORPHOGENESIS; POLARITY; STEM CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is a leading cancer in women; it is estimated that over 23,000 Canadian women will be diagnosed, and over 5,000 will die from it this year. Breast cancer is characterized by both over-growth and loss of tissue organization. In normal mammary glands, cells that form ducts have a characteristic top-bottom organization, which is essential for normal function and is disrupted in cancers. The mammary gland is an exceptional model to understand how cells maintain normal organization during development, in which cells grow and invade the surrounding tissue in a controlled manner to generate the mammary gland.  We think similar mechanisms underlay cancer growth and the invasion of tumor cells into surrounding tissue, but that these cells have lost critical regulatory systems. The primary objective of my research program is to understand the mechanisms by which normal mammary glands develop, and how these same systems may be hijacked for cancer progression. In the current proposal, we are investigating an enzyme called atypical protein kinase C (aPKC), which is a crucial organizer of cell organization. The expression of this protein is disrupted in breast cancer, and we previously demonstrated that is essential for normal mammary development. We will examine the mechanism by which aPKC regulates normal invasion and branching of ducts during development by manipulating the expression of aPKC in mice, using techniques we previously established involving stem cell transplants and mammary regeneration. We will examine effects on cell movements and stem cell renewal, and characterized important substrates for the aPKC enzyme.  We will also examine a role for aPKC in breast cancer progression by altering its expression in established mouse model of human HER2/ErbB2+ breast cancer to determine whether it affects tumor growth and metastasis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biogenesis of mucin-containing secretory granules
Keywords-MotsClés: CLATHRIN ADAPTORS; DROSOPHILA; LIVE IMAGING; MEMBRANE TRAFFICKING; MOLECULAR GENETICS; MUCINS; PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL 4-KINASE; PHOSPHOINOSITIDES; PROTEIN SORTING; SECRETORY GRANULE
Abstract-Résumé: The cavities and passages in our bodies that communicate with the outside world are lined with mucous membranes. These membranes are coated with sticky proteins called mucins that protect against infection. Mucins also perform other important functions, for example, aiding with digestion and breathing. In patients with lung diseases such as asthma and cystic fibrosis, excess mucus leads to difficulty in breathing and persistent bacterial infections. Mucins are stored inside cells in special 'secretory granules' until they are ready to be released. Although a lot is known about the signals that cause release of mucins, we know almost nothing about how mucin granules are formed. Understanding this process might help us to identify ways to block excess mucus production and treat respiratory diseases. There is currently no animal model available to study mucus production. To understand mucin granule formation, we have developed the salivary gland of the fruit fly as a model system. This allows us to use powerful genetics and microscopy techniques available in the fly system to learn how mucin containing granules form. So far, we have discovered that several highly conserved proteins found in both flies and humans are important for the initial stages of granule formation, and that when some of these proteins are absent, the mucins are no longer released or wind up in the wrong place inside the cell. The proposed experiments will enable us to understand how these proteins promote mucin granule formation and identify additional proteins that are important for this crucial process. In the future, we will use this information to identify new ways to block excess mucus production that can be used to prevent infections and promote human health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Global regulatory features of mammalian alternative splicing
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; GENE REGULATION; HIGH THROUGHPUT RNA SEQUENCING; IN VITRO AND IN VIVO SPLICING ASSAYS; SIRNA SCREENS; STEM CELLS AND REPROGRAMMING; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Alternative splicing (AS) is an essential step in the regulation of gene expression and allows a single gene to specify multiple genetic messages (mRNAs) and protein products. Almost all human genes produce mRNAs that undergo AS and it is estimated that this process can result in the expression of orders of magnitude more proteins than there are genes. Alternative splicing is therefore a major process underlying the generation of biological complexity associated with the development and functions of complex metazoan organisms. A major current goal is to understand how AS events are regulated and to determine their biological roles. We have recently discovered the first example of an AS "switch" that is required for the maintenance of embryonic stem cell (ESC) pluripotency and the efficient reprogramming of somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). A major goal of the present application is to identify and characterize additional such AS events such that we have a more complete understanding of the regulation and role of the AS regulatory layer in stem cell biology. This research avenue is expected to provide fundamental new insight into gene regulation, stem cell biology, and it may also yield discoveries that have utility in processes directed at producing iPSCs for therapeutic applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessment of Complementary Feeding of Canadian Infants
Keywords-MotsClés: INFANT NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: Infants in Canada are traditionally fed iron fortified rice cereals as their first food. Newly recommended first foods for infants like meat also contain a lot of iron. It may be that the high levels of iron in these foods affect the gut. We will examine 120 infants during early infancy to see if excess iron intake that resides in the gut generates free radicals. This is a concern as many adult disease have a basis in free radical generation that are not manageable. If our hypothesis is correct this will have huge implications for the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cleavage of Serum Response Factor in Viral Cardiomyopathy
Keywords-MotsClés: DILATED CARDIOMYOPATHY; ENTEROVIRAL PROTEASE 2A; ENTEROVIRUS; SERUM RESPONSE FACTOR; VIRAL MYOCARDITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Viral myocarditis is an inflammatory disease of the heart muscle caused by virus infection. It can result in enlargment of the heart and ultimately heart failure, and is one of the most common causes of disease and death worldwide, particularly in children. Many clinical cases of viral myocarditis are attributable to coxsackievirus infection. The treatment for this disease is largely limited. The only definitive treatment for dilated cardiomyopathy available is heart transplantation. Serum response factor (SRF), a  muscle-enriched protein, is known to play a central role in heart development and function. It regulates the gene levels of heart proteins which control the contraction of the heart. Destruction of SRF has been associated with several heart diseases, including dilated (enlarged) heart and heart failure. We have previously demonstrated that coxsackievirus infection led to a cleavage and subsequent dysfunction of SRF in the heart. Here we hypothesize that cleavage of SRF during coxsackievirus infection plays an important role in the progression of the disease to heart failure. To test this hypothesis, we propose to further investigate the cause of virus-induced SRF cleavage and the functional consequence of SRF destruction. We will utilize both isolated heart cells and genetically engineered mouse models where  SRF cleavage products are present in the heart to examine the contribution of SRF cleavage to the damage of the heart. We will also develop a chemical inhibitor to block the cleavage of SRF, to determine whether this will reduce virus-induced heart failure. The successful completion of this project will not only provide valuable insights into the mechanisms of damaged heart function in viral myocarditis, but also facilitate the development of novel therapeutic agents to protect against viral myocarditis and the progression to heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Drug-induced molecular changes in male germ cell chromatin: Consequences to the embryo
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE PROGENY OUTCOME; CANCER CHEMOTHERAPY; DNA PACKAGING; EARLY EMBRYO; EPIGENETICS; MALE-MEDIATED DEVELOPMENTAL TOXICITY; NUCLEAR STRUCTURE; SPERMATOGENESIS; STEM CELLS; ZYGOTE
Abstract-Résumé: The exposure of males to many chemicals may affect their germ cells and result in embryo death, malformations, and behavioural abnormalities in their progeny. We are studying the effects of two treatment paradigms, a single drug,cyclophosphamide, and the drug regimen used to treat men with testicular cancer, bleomycin, etoposide and cis-platin. We have shown that the adverse effects on progeny resulting from paternal exposures to these drugs are associated with altered gene expression in sperm at key stages of sperm production. Our goal is to find out the mechanisms by which paternal exposures affect the structure and organization of the male genome and how these effects may impact on the embryo. These studies will establish a mechanistic understanding of how paternal chemical exposures alter male germ cell quality with the long term goal of preventing adverse effects on subsequent generations. These studies are relevant clinically since an increasing number of young men survive their cancer treatments and seek to be fathers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental Trajectories of Impairments, Associated Health Conditions, and Participation of Children with Cerebral Palsy
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL PALSY; DEVELOPMENTAL SURVEILLANCE; HEALTH CONDITIONS; IMPAIRMENTS; PARTICIPATION; PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of this study is to describe the changes in balance (a primary impairment), range of motion limitations, strength, and endurance (secondary impairments), number and impact of health conditions, and participation in self-care and recreation and leisure activities over a four-year period in young children with cerebral palsy (CP) aged 18 months to 8 years.  We will recruit 120 children in each of the 5 levels of the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS), with the goal of keeping 100 children in each level by the end of four years.  Trained therapist assessors will measure the primary and secondary impairments annually.  Through parental interview, we will track the development of self-care abilities and participation in leisure and recreation activities, as well as the change in health conditions.  Using statistical techniques, we will present the data so that therapists can assist families to determine if other children with CP are developing as expected, better than expected, or more poorly than expected, depending on their GMFCS levels.  Rehabilitation services can be altered to ensure optimal motor development, health, self-care abilities and participation in life activities.

TitreApplicationTitle: An international comparative case study of the health equity impacts of medical tourism in developing nations
Keywords-MotsClés: BARBADOS; CANADA; CASE STUDY; GUATEMALA; HEALTH CARE; HEALTH EQUITY; INDIA; MEDICAL TOURISM; MEXICO
Abstract-Résumé: Canadians take part in medical tourism (MT) when they travel to other countries to intentionally access medical that is typically paid for out-of-pocket. It has been speculated that the travel of international patients from more-developed nations such as Canada to developing nations via MT is exacerbating health inequities in destination countries. Meanwhile, evidence is lacking that clearly demonstrates this is indeed the case. Alternatively, evidence is also lacking to support claims that MT is having a positive impact in developing nations through enhancing health care infrastructure and bringing revenues into the public sector, among other potential benefits. In this international, comparative case study we aim to address this pressing knowledge gap by examining the health equity impacts of MT in six purposefully selected sites: Bridgetown, Barbados; Guatemala City, Guatemala; Monterrey, Mexico; Mexico City, Mexico; Chennai, India; and Delhi, India. The results will be useful to Canadian health service providers and administrators because MT poses particular challenges to this country. While the ethos of our health care system rejects two-tiered care for essential services, the number of Canadian medical tourists paying out-of-pocket to go abroad is already considerable and steadily increasing. Research into MT will allow for valuable insights to be gleaned early on in the global conversation about MT, thus ultimately allowing: Canadian patients to make informed choices regarding engaging in and ethical, safe, and equitable MT; Canadian health care providers and administrators to provide needed guidance to patients; and Canadian health policy makers to ensure that Canada's normative and legal obligations to improve global health equity are being met and that efforts to expand universal health care and sustainable health system financing efforts in developing nations are not being undermined through the MT industry and Canadians' participation in it.

TitreApplicationTitle: Smooth muscle TNF/S1P signalling drives reduced cerebral perfusion in heart failure.
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW; CHRONIC HEART FAILURE; CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT; MYOGENIC TONE; SPHINGOSINE KINASE 1; SPHINGOSINE-1-PHOSPHATE SIGNALLING; TUMOUR NECROSIS FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a devastating cardiovascular disease. Patients with heart failure have an increased risk of stroke and often develop neurological symptoms. Despite its clinical importance, the mechanisms that link heart failure to neurological problems are not understood. We believe that a reduction in blood flow to the brain is responsible for the neurological symptoms that ultimately develop. Our group demonstrates that blood flow within the brain is reduced in mice with heart failure and has identified key signalling mechanisms that cause cerebral arteries to constrict. Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) and sphingosine-1-phosphate are key mediators in this signalling pathway; both are well-studied entities. The core objectives of this proposal are to (i) to integrate these characterized molecular mechanisms into the more complex whole animal setting, in order to directly relate changes in vascular function to altered blood flow and (ii) assess the effectiveness of medications that could potentially be used as clinical therapies in the future. A better understanding of these mechanisms will lead to the establishment of preventative measures that will improve the health of those suffering from heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Social, cognitive and biological regulatory systems: Prospective links to children's psychological symptomatology.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONING; CHILD SLEEP; CHILDREN'S MENTAL HEALTH; DIFFERENTIAL SUSCEPTIBILITY; INTERNALIZING/EXTERNALIZING PROBLEMS; PARENTING
Abstract-Résumé: Do parenting, child sleep and mental abilities interact to predict children's mental health status? Contrary to popular belief, psychological problems such as anxiety, depression, aggression and hyperactivity are common in children and often persist throughout childhood and into adolescence. When searching for the causes of children's psychological difficulties, researchers have often focused on parent-child relationships. We now know that while poor parent-child relations do contribute to the development of psychological problems in children, not all children exposed to non-optimal parenting develop psychological difficulties. This suggests that in addition to parenting, other factors influence children's mental health. In particular, children's biological and mental characteristics could make some children more vulnerable to the effects of low-quality relationships with their parents and at-risk for developing psychological problems, while others might be protected against such problems. This project focuses on two factors that might influence children's mental health in addition to parenting.  First, the quality of children's sleep will be studied as an important aspect of children's biological functioning.  Second, mental abilities that enable children to plan and establish future goals (called "executive functioning") will be studied.  A group of 250 children who have been followed by our research group since birth will be invited to participate in the current project when they are in Grades 1 to 4. We will use tests and questionnaires to examine their relationship with their parents, the quality of their sleep and their executive functioning to determine how these factors interact with each other to determine mental health status. The results of this study will help us to better understand the development of psychological problems in childhood and how we might detect problems early in life so that they can be treated.

TitreApplicationTitle: Conformational changes of the HIV-1 envelope glycoproteins: a structural/functional approach to understand the transition to the CD4-bound conformation and identify new therapeutic targets
Keywords-MotsClés: ENV GPS CONFORMATIONAL CHANGES; GP120; GP120 CD4-BOUND CONFORMATION; GP120-GP41 INTERACTION; GP41; HIV; ISOTERMAL CALORIMETRY; NEW INHIBITORS OF HIV FUSION; SURFACE PLASMON RESONANCE; VIRAL REPLICATION
Abstract-Résumé: In the absence of treatment, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which has already killed more than 33 million people worldwide.  To be able to spread, HIV needs first to enter human cells.  To do so, HIV has developed a unique "key" (envelope glycoproteins, gp120 and gp41) that recognizes a particular "lock" (receptor CD4 and coreceptors CCR5 or CXCR4) in human cells (mainly lymphocytes T CD4 and macrophages).  This "key" needs to "move" into the "lock" (conformational changes of gp120 and gp41) to allow viral entry.  In the absence of no effective vaccines against HIV and with therapies aimed at HIV eradication remaining a far fetched goal, new ways to fight HIV infection are warranted.  Prevention of HIV transmission requires approaches that interrupt the early phase of infection.  The first step of the replication cycle is viral entry into target cells.  If we could block the "key" of the virus with antibodies or small molecules, the virus will not be able to enter the cell and henceforth, it will be unable to replicate.  However, to efficiently block this "key" we must first fully understand how it works.  The goal of this proposal is to advance our understanding of how this "key" works, particularly what are the exact "movements" that are required to allow viral fusion and what parts of the "key"  are responsible for them.  This proposal will advance our understanding of a critical step in the HIV replication cycle and has the potential to develop new inhibitors against the "key" of HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of aminoglycoside antimicrobials with novel or combined modes of action
Keywords-MotsClés: AMINOGLYCOSIDES; ANTIBACTERIALS; DRUG DISCOVERY; RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Aminoglycoside antibiotics have been used clinically for decades as potent antibiotics to fight bacterial infections. Although aminoglycosides exhibit potent bactericidal activity, their widespread use has been compromised by toxicity and resistance. The rapid emergence of aminoglycoside antibiotics-resistant strains has instigated research efforts to develop modified aminoglycoside antibiotics that can delay or avoid acquired resistance by pathogenic bacteria. Previous work in our laboratory has shown that amphiphilic aminoglycoside antibiotics that combine the structural features of aminoglycosides and polycationic amphiphiles form a novel class of hybrid antibiotics that restore activity against clinically relevant aminoglycoside-resistant and multi-drug resistant bacteria. Cell-based assays demonstrate that most amphiphilic aminoglycosides display little to no cytotoxicity at their minimal inhibitory concentrations. In this proposal we plan to extend our preliminary work to other types of amphiphilic aminoglycoside antimicrobials. Structure activity relationships and toxicological evaluation will reveal crucial information for lead optimization. The most active and least toxic compounds will undergo in vivo testing in a mouse model. Another set of experiments will explore the potential modes of action and assess the probability of resistance development. The data obtained in this study will likely lead to the discovery of novel antibacterials with low toxicity and novel or combined modes of action and delayed resistance development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Designing Amphiphilic Polymeric Carriers of DNA for Gene Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; BIOMEDICAL TECHNOLOGY; BONE REGENERATION; CELL BINDING; DRUG DELIVERY SYSTEM; ENDOSOMAL RELEASE; GENE THERAPY; MEMBRANE TRAFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Gene therapy offers the promise of a permanent cure for a wide range of disorders. The ability to permanently replace defective or missing genes is desirable over the current pharmacological interventions, which typically treat the disease symptoms but do little to eradicate the underlying cause. Successful gene reconstitution depends on the use of gene carriers. Naturally-occurring viruses act as effective gene carriers; however, they are not safe since they cause excessive immune reaction and sometimes cause uncontrolled tissue growth. As an alternative to viral carriers, this project will focus on designing gene carriers based on polymers. Polymers are relatively safe, since they are not capable of inserting the DNA molecules haphazardly into the normal genome. However, they are toxic on the cells and they are not very effective in transporting genes into the cells. This project aims to overcome these impediments of the polymeric gene carriers by preparing polymers that (1) can deliver a large amount of genes into cells and (2) do not display toxicity on the cells.  The polymers will be synthesized form positively charged groups that can interact with negatively charged genes, and lipid molecules that can effectively transport genes into the cells. By engineering the right combination of positively charged with lipid groups, we will optimize the effectiveness of carriers for modification of human cells. Successful completion of this project will ultimately accelerate clinical practice of gene therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inégalités sociales, environnement psychosocial au travail, vie active, retraite et santé cardiovasculaire: une étude prospective de 20 ans chez 9000 femmes et hommes
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTRAINTES PSYCHOSOCIALES AU TRAVAIL; GENRE; INFARCTUS; INEGALITES SOCIALES DE SANTE; MALADIE CARDIOVASCULAIRE; RETRAITE; RIGIDITE ARTERIELLE; STATUT SOCIO-ECONOMIQUE; TENSION ARTERIELLE; TRAVAILLEURS ACTIFS
Abstract-Résumé: A l'echelle mondiale et au Canada, les maladies cardiovasculaires (MCV) comptent pour le tiers des deces des femmes et des hommes. Le risque de developper une MCV et le risque d'avoir une pression arterielle elevee augmentent a mesure que le statut socio-economique (c'est-a-dire la scolarite, l'occupation et le revenu) diminue. Des etudes prospectives ont demontre l'importance et l'augmentation d'inegalites sociales de sante cardiovasculaire a toutes les etapes de la vie. Toutefois, peu d'etudes ont investigue les causes de ces inegalites. Des etudes recentes suggerent que les stresseurs psychosociaux au travail expliqueraient jusqu'a 79% du gradient socio-economique des MCV. Par contre, ces etudes souffrent d'importantes limites, dont le recours a un devis transversal et l'utilisation d'instruments de mesure non valides. L'objectif du present projet vise a mesurer la contribution des stresseurs psychosociaux au travail au gradient socio-economique de la pression arterielle, de la rigidite arterielle et de l'incidence des maladies cardiovasculaires. Cet objectif sera poursuivi chez les femmes et les hommes et pour deux etapes de la vie: durant la vie active et apres la retraite. Dans le cadre du present projet, 9000 femmes (48,5%) et hommes seront suivis pendant 20 ans. Ils ont ete recrutes en 1991-93 au sein de 19 entreprises du secteur public quebecois. Ces participants ont ete revus 8 ans plus tard (1999-2001). Le present projet vise a realiser un suivi a 20 ans (2012-15). Comme plus de 20% des travailleurs canadiens sont exposes aux stresseurs psychosociaux au travail, une quantification precise et valide du role de ceux-ci dans le gradient socio-economique de la sante cardiovasculaire contribuera a la lutte contre les inegalites sociales de sante. De plus, mieux comprendre comment s'articulent les inegalites sociales de sante cardiovasculaire selon les etapes de la vie contribuera a l'effort actuel visant a prevenir ces iniquites.

TitreApplicationTitle: Integration of mTOR-p53 pathway crosstalk and miR-34 family in prognostication and prediction of response to bladder cancer therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BLADDER CANCER; DRUG RESISTANCE; MIR-34; MOLECULAR PROFILE; MTOR; OUTCOME; P53; RADIATION THERAPY; RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: In North America, bladder cancer is now the fourth most frequently diagnosed cancer in men and significantly increasing among women. Radiation therapy for localized bladder cancer is particularly attractive as it preserves the bladder and allows for urinary and sexual functions; however, it offers 5-year overall survival rates of only 50%.  Significant toxicity and lack of local control of disease remains problematic.  Furthermore, once distantly metastatic, virtually all bladder cancer patients will succumb to the disease with median survival no better than 18 months even with the best available chemotherapeutic regimens.  Hence, there is a desperate need not only to improve efficacy of organ-preserving therapies for clinically localized disease, but also to improve treatment for metastatic bladder cancer.  We have previously reported that inhibiting a key signaling pathway (mTOR) has a significant impact on tumor shrinkage and increases the success of radiation therapy in bladder cancer.  However, many bladder tumors are aggressive and resistant to radiation despite the addition of mTOR inhibitors.  Our proposal is to investigate the mechanism of cancer resistance to the combination of radiation and mTOR inhibition.  The aim is to identify molecular signals that correlate with aggressive cancer and more importantly, to identify key biomarkers that help predict response to therapy in order to avoid unnecessary toxicity in patients while prolonging survival in others.

TitreApplicationTitle: Completion of the Derivation of a Clinical Decision Rule to Predict Mobility Decline among Independent Seniors with Minor Injuries in the Emergency Department (Phase 1B)
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL DECISION RULE; FUNCTIONAL DECLINE; INJURY; MOBILITY; PREDICTION TOOL/PROGNOSIS; SENIORS
Abstract-Résumé: Community-dwelling seniors frequently sustain unintentional injuries that lead to medical evaluation in the Emergency Department. As the majority of these injuries are minor, most seniors are discharged back into the community. However, these seniors could have a significant risk of mobility and functional decline in the subsequent months. This team of clinicians and scientists aims to develop tools in order to help evaluate and optimize the treatment of injured seniors at high-risk of functional decline or mobility loss.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stop and go: Dissecting fronto-striatal contributions to response inhibition and reprogramming
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; DECISION  MAKING; ERROR PROCESSING; FRONTAL-EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; HUMAN; INHIBITORY CONTROL; LESION METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: "The best-laid schemes o' mice an' men gang aft agley". As Robbie Burns points out, everyone makes mistakes; the trick is to fix them before it is too late! Sometimes, an action is wrong because we have made the wrong choice:  such as hitting the gas pedal, instead of the brakes. Sometimes, the choice is right, but the action needs adjustment: such as when threading a needle. Do these two kinds of adjustment rely on the same brain systems? Errors, whether large or small, are interesting for a second reason:  we automatically try to prevent them. Thus, errors provide a unique window on the general question of how the brain inhibits unwanted actions. We will contrast self-control engaged by internally detected errors to control triggered by an external instruction to stop. We will study both how the wrong response is inhibited, and how the corrective response is generated.  These questions will be tested in patients with focal injury to specific parts of the frontal lobes and basal ganglia. Learning more about the brain circuits involved in these rapid forms of self-control may help us understand what happens in conditions where people get it wrong, such as drug addiction, attention-deficit disorder, or Parkinson disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Motivational and cognitive effects of nicotine in animal models of schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ANTIPSYCHOTICS; COGNITION; DOPAMINE; GLUTAMATE; MOTIVATION; NICOTINE DEPENDENCE; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: The prevalence of smoking and nicotine dependence in schizophrenia is 3 times higher than in the general population.  It has been estimated that high levels of smoking contribute significantly to the 20 % earlier mortality rate in individuals with schizophrenia.  Two major theories of schizophrenia are that it involves overactivity of the neurotransmitter dopamine, or underactivatity of the neurotransmitter glutamate.  Two animal models that reproduce these neurochemical states, as well as the behavioural phenotypes of schizophrenia have been developed.  We will use these models to attempt to understand why people with schizophrenia smoke.  Firstly, we will use these models to assess whether the neurochemical states associated with schizophrenia convey a vulnerability to addiction.  Secondly we will examine whether the cognitive deficits associated with schizophrenia (and reproduced in the animal models) are improved by nicotine. Thus, these experiments will examine whether people with schizophrenia smoke as a form of self-medication to improve attentional capacity, and possibly other cognitive processes. Finally we will determine whether two different antipsychotic drugs (haloperidol and clozapine) influence nicotine self-administration and reinstatement.  Understanding the reasons for the high rate of smoking could help devise better smoking cessation programs for this vulnerable population, and potentially shed light on mechanisms involved in schizophrenia.

TitreApplicationTitle: GPNMB as an emerging therapeutic target in metastatic breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION; BREAST CANCER; GPNMB; INTEGRINS; INVASION; METASTASIS; MOTILITY; PRE-CLINICAL XENOGRAFT MODELS; THERAPEUTIC ANTIBODY-DRUG CONJUGATES; TRANSGENIC MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer affecting Canadian women and is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in these patients. This is a complex disease composed of many forms of breast cancer, each possessing different characteristics with respect to patient prognosis and response to therapy. Once breast cancer cells have spread to other organs, the disease is largely incurable. Breast cancer metastasis currently represents an intensive area of investigation to better understand the mechanisms contributing to the ability of tumor cells to thrive in diverse and foreign microenvironments. We have identified a protein, called GPNMB, which promotes breast cancer growth and helps breast cancer cells become invasive and metastatic. Using mouse models, we have shown that breast cancer cells expressing high levels of GPNMB are better able to spread to the bones and lungs when compared to cells that do not express this protein. We have also found that primary tumors from breast cancer patients express high levels of GPNMB and are associated with a very aggressive type of cancer for which no targeted therapies currently exist. Novel therapeutic agents are being developed to target this protein in cancer, and clinical trials designed to test the efficacy of these agents in patients with breast cancer are now underway. Despite the clinical importance of this protein in breast cancer, little is known about the mechanisms through which it exerts its metastatic effects. The experiments outlined in this research proposal will employ cell culture and animal models to further characterize the ability of GPNMB to promote breast cancer progression and metastasis. We will also identify proteins that associate with and regulate GPNMB-mediated biological functions. Finally, we will investigate strategies to enhance the efficacy of currently available therapeutic agents that are being used to target GPNMB in metastatic breast cancer.

Keywords-MotsClés: FAT; GLP-1; GLP-2; HUMAN; INTESTINE; LIPOPROTEIN METABOLISM; RESVERATROL; STABLE ISOTOPES
Abstract-Résumé: People with obesity, prediabetes and diabetes have elevated blood fats called triglycerides, in part because their intestine and their liver produce large numbers of fat-carrying particles.  We use the technique of stable isotope enrichment to measure intestinal and liver fat particle production in humans. We study many factors that affect the production of fat particles, including various hormones and nutritional factors, in an attempt to understand why the body manufactures too many particles in the above conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: TRPML1 in intracellular Fe2+ and Ca2+ homeostasis/signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CA2+/FE2+ IMAGING; CA2+/FE2+ SIGNALING; CELLULAR BIOLOGY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNEL; LYSOSOMAL PATCH-CLAMPING; LYSOSOME; NEUROBIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The lysosome is viewed as a garbage dump and recycling center inside of the cell. Dysfunction of the lysosome causes accumulation of abnormal materials in the cell, eventually leading to cell death which is manifested by what is known as neurodegeneration. One toxic factor is lipofuscin, a non-degradable yellow-brown pigment granule in the lysosome. Because it is often accumulated with age or seen in aging diseases such as Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease, lipofuscin is also called 'aging pigment'. Lipofuscin production and accumulation is tightly regulated by the level of lysosomal calcium and iron. By using a unique technique that I developed, we recently showed that lysosomal protein TRPML1 regulates lysosomal iron and calcium levels, and that TRPML1 deficient cells display lipofuscin accumulation. Therefore, I propose to study the role of TRPML1 in lysosomal lipofuscin accumulation. I hypothesize that an increase in iron-dependent lipofuscin production and a decrease in calcium-dependent lipofuscin exclusion could be the reasons for the accumulation of lipofuscin in TRPML1 deficient cells and ageing cells. These studies will not only help us understand the pathogenesis of Mucolipidosis type IV disease which is caused by deficient TRPML1 but also have broad implications for the understanding and clinical management of neurodegenerative diseases as a whole.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cortical and subcortical mechanisms contributing to the control of visually-guided locomotion in the cat
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; INTACT CATS; MOTOR CONTROL; NEUROCHEMICAL MODULATION; POSTERIOR PARIETAL CORTEX; SINGLE UNIT RECORDING; VISUALLY-GUIDED LOCOMOTION
Abstract-Résumé: Locomotion is the result of the combined activity of multiple structures at different levels in the nervous system. Neural circuits in the spinal cord produce the basic rhythmical activity of locomotion while structures in the brain with spinal projections modify this activity to the goals of the animal. In most situations, visual information is critical for modifying locomotion and is used to plan anticipatory modifications of gait to avoid an object or to direct the subject towards it. These functions, although performed seamlessly by all sighted, terrestrial mammals, require extensive processing of the visual information in order to plan and execute the appropriate modification of the locomotor pattern. While an emphasis is frequently placed on the cortical circuits involved in visuomotor planning, there is abundant evidence to suggest that subcortical structures, and especially the basal ganglia, are also critically involved in these activities. Patients with Parkinson's disease (a basal ganglia disorder), for example, show characteristic deficits in their walking, including a slow, shuffling gait and, in more advanced stages of the disease, a condition known as freezing of gait, during which they are unable to initiate the next step. This is particularly evident at gait initiation or in more difficult conditions requiring visual control of locomotion, e.g doorways and sharp turns. While the clinical symptoms of these deficits are well described we have almost no information of the neural activity of the basal ganglia during locomotion, especially when obstructed. The current research programme is designed to determine how the basal ganglia contribute to different aspects of walking, such as its speed, force and modification in response to visually-identified obstruction. It is expected that a clear understanding of the neuronal mechanisms underlying the basal ganglia control of locomotion will help to modify treatment strategies and interventions in patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antigen presenting cell membrane lipids as immune sensors
Keywords-MotsClés: DENDRITIC CELLS; MEMBRANE LIPIDS; SIGNALLING
Abstract-Résumé: We propose here to study how lipids in the immune cell membrane can sense solid structures like crystals and beads. This is an important topic related to vaccine development, implant research, drug delivery and inflammatory responses to air pollution. Specifically, we will study what type of signaling events follow lipid binding in response to these solid structures and how they impact immune outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of post-translational modifications of MRE11 in mediating the DNA damage response.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGININE METHYLATION; DNA DAMAGE SIGNALLING; GAR MOTIF; GENETICS; MRE11; SUMOYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: The detection and repair of DNA damage are vital for cell viability. DNA repair defects lead to DNA translocations, deletions and mutations, chromosome breakage leading to genomic instability and cancer. Several human genetic disorders are associated with failure to repair DNA including the rare human recessive diseases include ataxia telangiectasia (AT), Nijmegen breakage syndrome (NBS), ataxia telangiectasia like disease (ATLD), Fanconi anemia, and the Bloom, Werner, and Rothmund-Thompson syndromes.  We discovered that a protein modification called arginine methylation is necessary to repair damaged DNA. It is known that when we expose ourselves to UV light, for example, we introduce DNA damage in our skin cells and this increases the chances of us developing cancer. We showed previously that cells without the enzymes that deposit arginine methylation accumulate DNA damage and are prone to cancer development. We were the first to show this unique role of arginine methylation and herein we propose to continue these studies.   We intend to use a basic science approach to study the role of arginine methylation in the process of repairing DNA damage. Genetic (using mice models) and biochemical approaches will be utilized to define the molecular targets of arginine methylation. What are the targets of the enzymes that deposit the arginine methylation marks required for this role in DNA repair? We also intend to identify molecules that stop the function of arginine methylation and these could be used for cancer treatment.  Our work predicts that if we can inactivate the enzymes that deposit arginine methylation (methylases) this will sensitize cells to radio- and chemotherapeutic agents such that lower doses may be required in the clinic for treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biosynthesis and export of Pseudomonas aeruginosa alginate
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOFILM DEVELOPMENT; BIOPHYSICAL CHARACTERIZATION; EXOPOLYSACCHARIDE BIOSYNTHESIS; MICROBIOLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY AND BIOCHEMISTRY; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA INFECTIONS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Bacterial biofilms are a significant environmental and medical problem. Biofilms begin when free-swimming bacteria attach to a surface, multiply, aggregate into microcolonies and subsequently secrete a slime-like material composed of repeating sugar units. This sugar polymer forms a matrix that acts as a barrier protecting the bacteria from natural host defense mechanisms, and from conventional antibiotics and disinfectants. The Centre for Disease Control estimates that more than 80% of all bacterial infections are biofilm related. A classic example of a biofilm related bacterial infection is the colonization of the lungs of cystic fibrosis (CF) patients by Pseudomonas aeruginosa - an opportunistic pathogen that causes persistent chronic bacterial infections and which if untreated is the primary cause of death in these individuals. In such infections, where antibiotic treatment is currently the only option, novel and innovative methods to treat biofilm related conditions are urgently required. In CF lungs the biofilm is made up predominantly of the sugar polymer or exopolysaccharide - alginate. Recent research has shown that mutation or deletion of proteins involved in alginate biosynthesis significantly affects not only alginate and hence biofilm formation but also increases the bacteria's susceptibility to host defense mechanisms. These observations suggest that proteins involved in alginate biosynthesis are good targets for therapeutic intervention. At present we know very little about the process of alginate polymerization and export, and therefore this grant seeks to determine the structure and function of the proteins involved in this process and in the longer term to construct a three-dimensional model of the secretion complex involved.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural Dysfunction in Human Amblyopia
Keywords-MotsClés: AMBLYOPIA; BRAIN PLASTICITY; CORTICAL FUNCTION; MOTION PERCEPTION; PSYCHOPHYSICS; SPATIAL PERCEPTION; VISUAL DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Amblyopia or lazy eye (incidence 5%) is the greatest single cause of unilateral blindness in the North American adult population.  It results from a disruption to normal visual development in childhood.  The present therapy of patching is not very effective, has severe psycho-social side effects and is ineffective above age 10yrs.   Two recent developments will change the way we think about amblyopia.  First, I have shown that the deficit affects predominately extra-striate cortex.  Second, I have shown that functions, previously thought to be lost from the brains of amblyopic adults, can be restored using transcranial magnetic stimulation, reflecting adult brain plasticity. The present grant directs itself to obtaining a better understanding of 1. the extra-striate cortical deficit and 2. the extent of functional plasticity in this region of the adult brain.  A better understanding of these related issues (i.e. the nature of the loss and its susceptibility to change) is required to develop a new approach to therapy for adults with amblyopia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of pancreatitis elucidated on human pancreas in situ
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOLIC PANCREATITIS; GLUCAGON LIKE PEPTIDE 1; HUMAN PANCREAS; PATHOLOGIC EXOCYTOSIS; SNARE PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Acute pancreatitis (AP) causes a great deal of acute and chronic morbidity and mortality, and at considerable financial costs to health care in Canada. The most common cause of AP is alcohol, affecting 10% of alcoholics. There is still no effective specific treatment directed at the pathogenesis of alcoholic AP because the postulated disease mechanisms could not be directly tested on human pancreatic tissue.  Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)-based therapies, which potentiate glucose-mediated insulin secretion, is the new panacea and most promising treatment for diabetes, and is a multi-billion dollar pharmaceutical market. However, these drug treatments have been shown to exhibit a six-fold increase in AP, the basis of this dangerous side effect is totally unknown.  To effectively address these two conditions, we were first to develop the rodent and human models of preparing fresh pancreatic slices to genuinely examine normal pancreatic exocrine cell biology and disease mechanisms.  Our goals are to: 1) Determine the cellular basis of human alcoholic AP; and 2) Determine the cellular basis of human AP caused by GLP-1 drug treatment for diabetes. This work will elucidate clinically relevant insights underlying human alcoholic and GLP-1-induced AP, which will identify novel treatments for alcoholic AP and impact current diabetes management in patients taking GLP-1 drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular characterization of JMML
Keywords-MotsClés: CBL; E3; JUVENILE MYELOMONOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA; PHARMACOLOGIC INHIBITOR; SRC; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (JMML) is a highly aggressive cancer that affects young children.  There is no cure or effective treatment for JMML, which has an average survival rate of less than 20% past three years of diagnosis.  In an effort to find effective treatment options for children with JMML, we uncovered a new molecular pathway critically involved in the development of JMML.  This research proposal aims to provide insightful mechanistic understanding of why and how JMML develops with the supposition that learned lessons would aid in the development of new and effective therapeutic options for children with JMML.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endothelial Cell Biomechanics: The mechanotransduction of wall shear stress gradients
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; CELL CULTURE MODELS; CELL STIFFNESS; ENDOTHELIAL CELL DYSFUNCTION; F-ACTIN; FLUID SHEAR STRESS; GLYCOCALYX; INFLAMMATION; LEUKOCYTES; MECHANOTRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The cells that line our vascular system, endothelial cells (ECs) are sensitive to changes in blood flow.  There is good clinical and experimental evidence to believe that changes in these cells in regions of disturbed blood flow is an underlying cause of heart attacks and strokes.  This research will identify how ECs sense and change in the presence of disturbed blood flow.  We will use three dimensional EC models to investigate the role of the outer lining of the cells (glycocalyx) in responding to changes in blood flow.  We will also measure structural changes (actin cytoskeleton) in the EC support system to identify if disturbed flow changes the stiffness of the cells.  Using our innovative cell culture models, this research will help define the mechanisms of EC dysfunction and provide new opportunities for the treatment of strokes and heart attacks.

TitreApplicationTitle: The efficacy of Link N as a mediator of repair in Intervertebral Disc Degeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: DEGENERATIVE DISC DISEASE; INTERVERTEBRAL DISC; LINK N; MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS; NUCLEUS PULPOSUS
Abstract-Résumé: Degeneration of intervertabral disc, which lies in between two adjacent vertebrae of spine, is a condition that can be debilitating and painful. Currently, there are two major clinical procedures involving surgery for treating degeneration of disc. However, these procedures only offer a short-term relief of pain and do not address the permanent treatment. It would be ideal if a natural repair process can be induced to treat this disease. We propose that introducing stem cells along with a naturally occurring protein called Link N in to the center of the degenerating disc can induce such natural repair process. In the current grant proposal we will examine this hypothesis by testing various parameters, which indicate the regeneration of the disc. We believe that if successful this approach will replace surgery and can provide long-term benefit to the patients who suffer from this disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: CAPACITY BUILDING; INDIRECT COMPARISONS; INNOVATIVE SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS; KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NETWORK META-ANALYSES; NETWORKING
Abstract-Résumé: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses typically aggregate knowledge about the effects and safety of interventions, such as drugs. They are now used by clinicians, policy analysts and others to help make practice decisions as well and policy/management decisions. A recent estimate suggests that 11 systematic reviews are published daily. As enthusiastic as these developments are there is still much to learn about specific types of meta-analyses, such as multiple treatment comparisons (MTC). Such comparisons may better help understand drug safety and effectiveness. This proposal aims to address several questions about MTC using innovative statistical procedures with freely available software. The answers to these questions will help clinicians and policy makers better understand the usefulness of MTC as part of assessing the safety and effectiveness of drugs. This is important for all Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innovative knowledge synthesis methods collaborative at the Li Ka Shing Knowledge Institute
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG SAFETY; KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS METHODS; NETWORK META-ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Sometimes after a drug has been made available to the public, many people experience harms (i.e., adverse events) from the medication. This may occur because the studies examining the drug weren't large enough to capture all of the harms that can occur in the real world or because the studies did not include all patient populations who would be taking the medication, such as the elderly. In order to examine adverse events that happen after a drug is made available; the Canadian government has asked scientists to come up with novel ways of conducting knowledge synthesis.      Knowledge synthesis allows the combination of many different studies to come up with an answer to a research question. There are many different types of knowledge synthesis and the focus of this proposal is on a technique called Network Meta-analysis. In a network meta-analysis, the effects of a drug are compared with the effects of another drug that have not been directly compared in the same randomized trial. For example, a trial may examine drug A versus drug B and find that drug A is superior to drug B, while another trial may examine drug B versus drug C and find that drug B is equivalent to drug C. The common drug in the two randomized trials is drug B and they have both been compared in the same patient population. Network Meta-analysis provides a statistical method to say that drug A is potentially superior to drug C for this particular patient population.       We have created a strong nation-wide team with expertise across many different areas, such as statistics, knowledge synthesis, drug surveillance researchers, and physicians. By investing in junior researchers, bringing together colleagues nationally and internationally with complementary skill sets and expertise, and leveraging existing networks, we have the opportunity to make substantive gains in the health of Canadians.

Abstract-Résumé: As a vital component of the Data Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN), for addressing safety and effectiveness issues on drugs available on the Canadian market, this team grant proposes the establishment of a pan-Canadian collaborative of health methodologists knowledgeable in applying scientific strategies for accurately and comprehensively assembling the relevant information on a specific safety issue using systematic safety reviews and for developing and employing statistical methods for comparing, combining and summarizing this information across drugs using network meta-analyses.  This collaborative will be a platform for the development and application of sophisticated, cutting edge analytical methods for network meta-analysis and systematic safety reviews, as well as to rapidly respond to emerging concerns and evaluation requests related to real-world safety and effectiveness assessment of products used in routine health practices in Canada.  Linked to national and international experts and health technology assessment partner organizations, the collaborative will build capacity in Canada, thereby enabling high quality drug safety and effectiveness research necessary to inform drug policy and protect the safety of Canadians.  As a demonstration project for using network meta-analysis to assess safety and effectiveness of drugs, the detection of safety signals during the regulatory stage and the assessment of comparative effectiveness and cost-effectiveness for reimbursement will be explored in the case of anticoagulant drug therapies for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation.  In particular, these techniques will be used to examine events such as stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, myocardial infarction, or gastrointestinal bleeding.
