Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVE SURVEILLANCE; ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS; DRUG SAFETY; POST-MARKET SAFETY EVALUATION
Abstract-Résumé: The debilitating and lethal consequences of severe adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are a striking failure of modern medicine. The consequences for patients who experience severe ADRs are catastrophic. In Canada, ADRs claim over 10,000 lives each year and cause many more life-long disabilities. To tackle this complex problem, rapid and efficient identification of potential drug risks is of utmost importance. A very efficient method to identify ADRs and evaluate the risks of a given drug for the Canadian population is active surveillance.  Active surveillance means monitoring the use of drugs in patients by trained clinicians who have specific expertise in the recognition of ADRs. The overall goal is to identify ADRs and then reduce their occurrence in Canadians by better understanding in whom specific ADRs are most likely. This is the vision and prime motivation for the DSEN active Surveillance and Evaluation of Adverse Reactions in Canadian Healthcare (DSEN-SEARCH) Initiative.    Our team will build on its broad experience in surveillance methods and its established network of ADR surveillance clinicians in Canadian health centres. These surveillance clinicians identify and report ADRs, and collect the detailed clinical information that is needed to evaluate potential drug risks. Personal identifiers are not included to protect patient privacy. We have already developed and use a clinical information system that ensures rapid reporting of ADRs from across Canada into a secure database for storage. This will allow DSEN-SEARCH to rapidly begin new surveillance in areas of importance to the CIHR Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network.   The DSEN-SEARCH team of nationally recognized scientists will conduct research, train students and clinicians in best practices for active drug safety surveillance and ensure that research findings are made available to health professionals, patients, regulators and policy makers in order to improve patient drug safety in Canada.

Abstract-Résumé: Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are the 4th leading cause of death and cause an estimated 200,000 severe ADRs each year in Canada. Despite the promise of improved medicines, withdrawals of new drugs (eg. Rezulin, Vioxx) demonstrate the need to identify patients at higher ADR risk. Individual patient variability in drug metabolism genes is a major contributor to the development of severe toxicities, hospitalizations, and deaths from even standard doses of many drugs in clinical use today.   To tackle the complex problem of ADRs requires a multi-faceted team to bring together synergistic expertise from scientists and clinicians in many disciplines in an environment that promotes teamwork. Such an undertaking - with the long-term goal of reducing the incidence of severe ADRs - is the vision for the Drug Safety and Effectiveness (DSEN) Pharmacogenomics of Adverse Reaction EVEnts National Team (PREVENT). PREVENT will conduct pioneering and transformative research to identify genetic factors of priority ADRs identified by the DSEN steering committee. In addition to the discovery of novel pharmacogenomic biomarkers, we will leverage our unique abilities to validate their clinical relevance, from cell-based studies to real world patient populations.  DSEN-PREVENT cores will consist of a detailed patient clinical characterization core, a pharmacogenomics research core with high-throughput genotyping and sequencing platforms, and a translational pharmacokinetics core with state-of-the-art drug level monitoring facilities. Additional cores will provide capacity for ADR economic assessment and ADR ethical/legal issues. PREVENT will support multiple training centres for clinician-scientists, post-doctoral fellows, and graduate students to train the next generation of leaders in this field.  The diverse yet complementary areas of expertise of PREVENT harnesses unique Canadian strengths that will foster innovative research to address the high priority problem of severe ADRs.

Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDIES; COMPARATIVE EFFECTIVENESS; CONFOUNDING BIAS; EXPOSURE MEASUREMENT ERRORS; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; STATISTICAL MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Medication use and health care costs increase steadily with the aging of the Canadian society and the ever increasing number of medications available on the market. Overall, new drugs and treatments contribute to the improvement of population health and increasing life expectancy. However, it is not always clear which of the alternative medications currently in use in practice for a given disease offer the biggest benefits to patients. Thus, the evaluation of comparative effectiveness and safety of treatments is a top priority for both the health research and the society at large. However, accurate comparisons of benefits and risks of different medications require state-of-the-art scientific methods. Our inter-disciplinary team of researchers from 7 Canadian provinces will combine a wide range of scientific expertise. With this highly qualified team we aim to establish Canada as an international leader in comparative effectiveness research. Our new methods will help efficient identification of adverse effects and accurate comparison of therapeutic effectiveness of alternative medications used to treat many diseases. This, in turn, will permit optimizing drug prescribing practice, to minimize the risks and maximize therapeutic benefits.

TitreApplicationTitle: The alphaNAC transcriptional coregulator as a downstream effector of PTH action in bone
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS OF BONE DISEASE; BONE ANABOLIC EFFECT OF PTH; GENE EXPRESSION MONITORING; GENE TRANSCRIPTION; KNOCKIN MOUSE MUTAGENESIS; OSTEOPOROSIS; PARATHYROID HORMONE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis, the most prevalent metabolic bone disease, affects the elderly. Daily subcutaneous injection ('intermittent treatment') with human parathyroid hormone (PTH) (Teriparatide or Forteo®) is the only approved treatment for increasing bone mass in osteoporosis patients. The mechanisms involved in the bone-forming effects of intermittent PTH treatment are not fully understood. Our research is aimed at studying those mechanisms in order to identify new targets for the development of therapeutics for osteoporosis.  We have found that when PTH binds its receptor in bone cells, it activates signals that send the protein alphaNAC to the nucleus of the cells. In turn, the nuclear alphaNAC protein regulates the expression of other genes. We believe that this 'pathway', i.e. the transmission of signals from PTH and its receptor, through alphaNAC, to the nucleus of the cell to affect gene expression is important for the bone-forming action of PTH.  We propose to use several state-of-the-art techniques in cellular biology, molecular biology, and molecular genetics to confirm that the PTH signals that send alphaNAC to the nucleus mediate the bone-forming action of PTH. Once we establish the type and sequence of signals and when the mechanisms are further known, this research will provide the foundation for the development of new drugs for osteoporosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Focal Adhesion Kinase: A Pivotal Factor in the degeneration and regeneration of adult CNS neurons
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; AXON REGENERATION; AXOTOMY; CASPASE; GLAUCOMA; KINASE; OPTIC NERVE CRUSH; OPTIC NERVE TRANSECTION; RETINAL GANGLION CELL; VISION LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), Stroke, and Glaucoma (which causes blindness) are among the most prevalent forms of brain ailment, accounting for an annual burden of more than $20 billion to the Canadian economy. TBI and stroke are also among the leading causes of death in Canada, accounting for over 65,000 deaths annually. The majority of people that survive brain injury are left with permanent paralysis, sensory loss, or cognitive deficits. Despite the great burden that brain injury and disease represent to people, their loved ones, and our healthcare system, there are no clinical therapies for these ailments; the mechanisms by which injured neurons die in the brain remain for the most part unclear.   Injury or disease of brain, spinal cord, or sensory structures like the eyes leads to permanent functional loss. When injured, brain neurons initiate a carefully orchestrated "suicide" program (apoptosis) that leads to cell degeneration. The elements that control this suicide program are conserved throughout different structures of the brain and common to almost all brain ailments. Thus elaborating these mechanisms will be beneficial in the future treatment of many brain diseases or insults. Keeping injured neurons alive is the first step in treating brain disease; the other is promoting regeneration and re-connection of those cells so that normal communication within the brain can be restored.   Our work addresses the fundamental mechanisms that contribute to neuronal death and regenerative failure in the brain. We have recently discovered that events associated with neuron death revolve around a protein call Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK). We will now develop a better understanding of how FAK activity is derailed after brain injury, in order to identify new strategies to keep brain neurons alive and promote their regeneration. The proposed research has the potential to revolutionize the treatment of debilitating CNS insults, for which no therapies currently exist.

TitreApplicationTitle: Potentiels thérapeutiques de la cystamine pour la maladie de Parkinson.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYSES POST-MORTEM; CYSTAMINE; IMAGERIE EN BIOLUMINESCENCE; INFLAMMATION; MPTP; NEUROGENESE; NEUROPROTECTION; NEURORESCAPAGE; NEURORESTAURATION; PARKINSON
Abstract-Résumé: La maladie de Parkinson se caracterise principalement par la perte de cellules au sein de regions specifiques du cerveau. On estime qu'au moment ou le diagnostic est pose, environ 80 % de ces cellules, qui produisent de la dopamine, ont deja cesse de fonctionner. Ce phenomene entraine l'apparition des symptomes principalement moteurs, mais egalement cognitifs, qui caracterisent la maladie. Plusieurs traitements sont aujourd'hui disponibles pour controler ces symptomes. Malheureusement, aucun medicament ne peut encore arreter ou bien meme ralentir la progression de la maladie. Nous avons recemment demontre que la cystamine, un compose chimique, est capable de prevenir la perte neuronale lorsqu'administree avant l'apparition des caracteristiques pathologiques de la maladie. Par l'utilisation de modeles murins de parkinsonisme, nous proposons 1) de determiner si, en plus de ses capacites neuroprotectrices, la cystamine est capable d'arreter, voire meme de renverser le type de mort neuronale retrouvee dans le Parkinson et 2) identifier certains des mecanismes d'action a l'origine des effets benefiques de la cystamine. Les resultats de ces etudes permettront d'orienter l'applicabilite clinique de la cystamine pour des patients atteints de la maladie de Parkinson.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular analysis of Herpes simplex virus type I egress
Keywords-MotsClés: EGRESS; HERPES; HOST PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; HSV-1; IN VITRO ASSAYS; PKD; PROTEIN KINASE D; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Clinical manifestations of the herpes family of viruses vary from cold sores and genital herpes to severe conditions such as blindness, cancer, infections of newborns and potentiating HIV. Although treatments exist, these viruses persist forever in humans once contracted. Moreover, they can be reactivated under certain conditions and even people without symptoms can shed infectious viruses. In an attempt to better understand how herpesviruses propagate, our laboratory examines their intimate interactions with cells, the building blocks of our body. We focus on one member of the family called Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), a virus that is present in nearly 90% of the population. More precisely, we study the mechanism by which the newly replicated virus is transported from its site of assembly in the cell to the cell surface, where it can infect neighbouring cells and individuals. It is hoped that this will lead to novel therapeutic approaches not only against this virus but against the entire herpes family of viruses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advancing the Health Promotion Efforts of Prostate Cancer Support Groups
Keywords-MotsClés: MASCULINITIES AND MEN'S HEALTH; PROSTATE CANCER; PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Psychosocial support and health information are integral to the well-being of men who have prostate cancer, and prostate cancer support groups (PCSGs) have emerged as important community-based resources in Canada and other Western countries. Our previous research reveals PCSGs as an ideal forum for men and their partners to garner support and guidance about prostate cancer and its treatments, and these volunteer, survivor-led resources can reduce the demand on professional psychosocial oncology care services. That said, PCSGs experience challenges in terms of sustainability, and attracting and retaining group members and collaborating with health care providers and services are key issues. The proposed research will extend our previous work with face-to-face PCSGs through three sequential sub-studies underpinned by the overall objective, to advance the health promotion efforts of PCSGs as a means to enhancing the well-being of men who experience prostate cancer and their families. The sub-studies include 1) a survey of health care providers' views of PCSGs, 2) focus group interviews with diverse sub-groups of potential end-users to distil the key components of a web-based PCSG and 3) the design, pre-test and pilot test of a web-based PCSG.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Epstein-Barr Virus Persistence
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; EBNA1; EPSTEIN-BARR VIRUS; LYTIC REACTIVATION; MICRORNA; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a herpesvirus that infects most people and is maintained for life through a combination of latent and lytic modes of infection. EBV latent infection can promote the development of several types of lymphomas and carcinomas due to its ability to promote cell proliferation. EBNA1 is the only viral protein expressed in all forms of EBV latency and EBV-induced tumours and contributes to the induced cell proliferation.  In addition, recent evidence show that small RNA molecules (microRNAs) made by the virus and the cell have important roles in EBV latent infection and EBV-induced cancers.  We are investigating how EBNA1 affects viral and cellular microRNAs and how these microRNAs contribute to the functions of EBNA1. When the virus switches to lytic infection, host cell proteins are manipulated to arrest cell proliferation at one point in the cell cycle while preventing cell death.  We have identified several EBV proteins involved in this manipulation.  We will further investigate how they and other EBV proteins alter normal cellular responses in ways to promote EBV production. Our studies should provide insight into how to inhibit EBV infection and treat EBV-associated cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of ADAM17 in the Pathogenesis of Diabetic Nephropathy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL STUDIES; DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; MESANGIAL CELL; SIGNALING; TRANSFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is the most common cause of kidney failure. In the diabetic kidney, scar proteins (matrix) accumulate in the filtering units (glomeruli) and prevent them from functioning properly. It is not yet known how high glucose levels cause glomerulus (mesangial) cells to produce matrix. Our recent studies have shown that in mesangial cells exposed to high glucose, the protein ADAM17 is activated and involved in matrix production by causing the activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). We have previously shown that EGFR activation by high glucose leads mesangial cells to  produce matrix proteins. I plan to investigate exactly how ADAM17 is activated by high glucose, and whether blocking its activation with drugs can slow or prevent the development of kidney disease in a rat model of diabetes. If effective, this would be a potential new treatment for people whose diabetes has affected their kidneys.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biological Role and Regulation of the Novel Enamel Protein Amelotin
Keywords-MotsClés: DENTAL CARIES; DENTAL ENAMEL; DENTAL EROSION; GENE EXPRESSION; PROMOTER ANALYSIS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Dental enamel is critically important for tooth function, but is compromised by prevalent diseases such as caries. In addition, dental erosion through consumption of acidic soft drinks has become a serious problem in the dental health care field. Enamel, formed in a protein-mediated biomineralization process, cannot be regenerated by a natural mechanism. We have previously identified a novel enamel protein, Amelotin (AMTN), and have found evidence for its role in the formation of the protective, densely mineralized enamel surface layer. In this proposal we try to understand the mechanisms that switch on the expression of AMTN during the formation of the enamel surface, and to find out what the details behind the biological function of AMTN are. This research is geared toward understanding the molecular mechanism of enamel development, particularly at the surface. We expect to apply new findings from this research to develop strategies to prevent enamel demineralization and to regenerate enamel lesions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translational strategies for the clinical transplantation of neonatal porcine islets.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; ISLET TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Advances in transplantation of human islets have established the proof-of-concept for this therapy to emerge as a treatment for patients with Type 1 diabetes. Despite efforts to maximize organ donation the number of human islets available for transplantation continues to limit the number of patients who can be transplanted. One approach to address this rate-limiting problem is to use islets from an animal source such as pigs. This proposal seeks to advance the possibility of pig islet transplantation, since: 1) porcine insulin has been used to treat diabetes for more than 60 years; 2) porcine islets respond to glucose in the same manner as do human islets; 3) pigs breed rapidly and produce large litters, providing a virtually unlimited source of islets; and moreover 4) our group has shown that Neonatal Porcine Islets (NPIs) are able to correct diabetes in the preclinical non-human primate model. We believe that in the near future NPIs will be used for clinical transplantation for patients with Type 1 diabetes and thereby solve the shortage of insulin-producing tissue. Principal challenges that must be met to make transplantation of NPIs a clinical reality include: 1) defining a reproducible strategy for isolating large numbers of clinically grade NPIs; and 2) to develop a means of transplanting NPIs without the need for life-long anti-rejection drugs. Therefore, the objectives of the research proposal are to: 1) To characterize NPIs isolated from wild type and genetically modified pigs obtained from a closed herd. 2) To develop Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) compliant and clinically scale-able protocols for the preparation of clinical grade NPI grafts. 3) To develop a clinically applicable site to implant NPI grafts in a pancreatectomized pre-clinical large animal model. We believe that these studies will facilitate and expedite clinical trials of neonatal porcine islets thereby allowing the treatment of many more patients with Type 1 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Critical Illness in Inflammatory Bowel Disease, Multiple Sclerosis and Rheumatoid Arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; AUTOIMMUNE DISEASE; COHORT STUDY; CRITICAL ILLNESS; HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic immune diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), multiple sclerosis (MS) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), affect more than 5% of Canadians. Critical illness requiring admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) is serious and costly. We do not know much about the inter-relationships between chronic immune diseases and critical illness. The long-term goal of our research program is to identify ways to prevent critical illness in chronic autoimmune diseases including inflammatory bowel disease IBD, MS, and rheumatoid arthritis; mitigate the effects of critical illness on these diseases; or both. In this study we will look at how these chronic illnesses influence the type, severity and outcomes of critical illness. We will also look at how the use of new therapies for IBD, MS and RA affect the risk of critical illness. We will do this by using health claims data, and a database about people who have been admitted to ICUs in Manitoba. The findings from our study will help health care providers to give more accurate information to persons with IBD, MS and RA about their possible outcomes after critical illness. Our findings will also enable us to find out who is most at risk of critical illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transglutaminases and cell-matrix interactions during osteoblast differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; BONE; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CULTURE; COLLAGEN; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis is characterized by bone loss, bone fragility and increased prevalence of fractures. It is a disease hindering the lives of close 2 million Canadians. Osteoporosis and related fractures results in loss of mobility, increased pain and dramatically compromised quality of life. The cost of treating osteoporosis related fractures and immobility is close to 2 billion dollars each year and it is predicted that these numbers will keep increasing as Canadian population ages. The causes for osteoporosis can be linked to genetics, nutrition, medication, and it can occur at any time during life. Achieving high bone mass at younger age protects from bone loss occurring later in life.  Bones are composed of cells and substance between cells called the extracellular matrix which is mostly collagen and mineral. Collagen is produced by resident cells, and in bones it undergoes a stabilization process that is required for proper bone cell function. We have discovered that transglutaminase-enzymes, TG2 and Factor XIIIA, are responsible for this matrix stabilization. Mice lacking these enzymes develop osteporosis and have low bone mass. In this proposal we plan to further explore how these two enzymes jointly promote bone cell activity. Our specific aims are: 1) to complete our analysis of the bones lacking these two enzymes; 2) to study the role of TG2 in bone cell attachment to bone; 3) to study a newly discovered form of FXIIIA on bone cell surface; 4) to study how matrix stabilization occurs in detail and molecular level and how it can lead to better functioning bone cells. From this work we hope to understand how also human bone tissue is made and assembled and how bone cell activity could be given a boost via therapeutics in osteoporosis to maintain optimal bone formation activity thoughout life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dyspareunia: Is it a Women's Problem?
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN SYNDROME; DYSPAREUNIA; HEALTH PSYCHOLOGY; PAIN; SEXOLOGY; SEXUAL PAIN DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Dyspareunia, or genito-pelvic pain associated with sexual intercourse, has traditionally been considered a women's problem.  Although dyspareunia is less prevalent in men, it is not uncommon with current prevalence estimates ranging from 2-9%.  The recurrent and chronic pain associated with male dyspareunia causes much distress and is hypothesized to interfere with sexual functioning, work, and general quality of life. There is currently no known cause or effective treatment for most sufferers; as a result, there is much treatment confusion among health professionals. Based on our previous research on dyspareunia in women, we believe that there are several subtypes or syndromes of male dyspareunia that can be described by their differing pain characteristics (intensity, quality, location, pattern, duration, history). Furthermore, we propose to study the same factors in men that predispose women to experience pain (e.g. elevated levels of anxiety, depression, catastrophizing etc.). Finally, we propose to collect missing sensory (e.g. pain sensitivity), pelvic floor (muscle dysfunction) and psychosocial (e.g. couple/sexual functioning, abuse history) information. In our view, it is only through a multidisciplinary biopsychosocial approach to this recurrent and chronic pain disorder that we will be able to develop effective treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: TAK1: A novel fibrogenic regulator?
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; FIBROSIS; KNOCKOUT AND TRANSGENIC MICE; SCLERODERMA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TISSUE REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Scarring diseases (fibrosis) are one of the largest groups of diseases for which there is no therapy.  We study the fibrotic autoimmune disease scleroderma which affects about 60,000 Canadians. Scarring is caused by a particular form of cell, called the myofibroblast, that is located in connective tissue. If myofibroblasts are too active, scarring disease results.  We think a protein called TAK1 is responsible for the excessive activity of the myofibroblast.  In the long term, we want to see if drugs blocking TAK1 might be used to cure fibrosis. In the first step, the subject of our proposal, we want to test whether blocking TAK1 might affect the development of scar tissue.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining Adaptive Immune Mechanisms of Insulin Resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNE SYSTEM; ANTIBODIES; APOPTOSIS; B CELLS; INNATE IMMUNE SYSTEM; INSULIN RESISTANCE; METABOLIC SYNDROME; OBESITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity and type 2 diabetes are both major global health concerns. When people become obese, they develop a metabolic syndrome which can lead to type 2 diabetes, but its underlying cause is not known. Normal mice that are placed on high fat diets become obese and develop a metabolic disease that is similar to type 2 diabetes in humans. Fatty tissues in these mice contain a high frequency of certain white blood cells, including macrophages, T and B cells that can produce inflammation. By neutralizing or removing this inflammation, the metabolic disease is relieved. Thus, diabetes induced by high fat diet is caused, at least partly, by an abnormal immune response, or inflammation in the body's fat.  Our recent work has shed light onto the role of T cells and B cells in these obese mice and suggests that there are remarkable similarities between the development of type 2 diabetes and the development of autoimmune diseases.  This work has recently been featured in hundreds of news media across the world as one of the pre-eminent new findings in medicine of the past year.   The objective of this research proposal is to build on this work, and investigate the role of T cells and B cells in obesity related diabetes.  We will find out how different types of B cells and the antibodies they produce promote or protect against diabetes.  We will also find out what B cells and T cells are attacking in mice and humans which fuels the process of inflammation in fat leading to diabetes.  Finally we will analyze how an immune regulator molecule called TLR7, which commonly worsens autoimmune diseases like lupus, actually also plays a role in obesity related diabetes.   The results of these experiments promise to lead to new effective ways to prevent, diagnose, and treat diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular regulation of progenitor cell behaviour in the developing retina
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; CELL FATE; DEVELOPMENT; GENE EXPRESSION; GENETICS; NEUROGENESIS; PROGENITOR CELL; RETINA; SIGNALING; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Retinal progenitor cells are immature cells that divide frequently and produce all of the neurons in the retina, such as photoreceptors. The behaviour of progenitor cells represents a fundamental process controlling the growth of the retina before and after birth. Congenital eye malformations occur at a rate of 1 to 2 per 10,000 births in Canada and can lead to severe vision impairment later in life. Furthermore, retinal growth defects after birth are estimated by the World Health Organization to account for ~18% of total blindness worldwide. Abnormal progenitor cells are thought to underlie some of these eye growth malformations. However, the connection between altered gene function and progenitor cell behaviour is not entirely clear, motivating us to pursue this issue in the present grant proposal. We will use genetic tools to understand how progenitor cells "decide" whether to divide to make more cells, or to stop dividing and mature into neurons. Furthermore, we will characterize a new gene that we discovered, which seems to play a role in maintaining the normal structure of DNA inside progenitor cells. This research will make it easier to understand how specific gene mutations alter the rate or extent of progenitor cell division during critical periods of retinal development. It will also provide new insight toward developing techniques to stimulate regeneration in the mature retina.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: Nitrates and Bone Turnover (NABT): trial to select the best nitrate preparation.
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE TURNOVER MARKERS; NITRATES; OSTEOPOROSIS; POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis or "thinning of the bones" affects 1 in 4 Canadian women. While the rates of osteoporosis among Canadians are stabilizing, worldwide the number of people afflicted with osteoporosis continues to rise.  The most serious complication of osteoporosis is a broken bone or fracture.  Fractures due to osteoporosis can result in long hospital stays, dependence on others, and premature death.  While there are several medications that prevent osteoporosis they all have side effects and most cannot rebuild bone. In addition, drugs to prevent osteoporosis are expensive and not available worldwide.  Therefore, it is essential that researchers continue to identify and test new medications for the prevention of osteoporosis.    A previous study by our research group determined that nitrates, common and inexpensive agents used to treat chest pain or angina can increase bone strength by forming new bone.  Nitrates are extremely safe medications and the only side effect, while common, is the development of headaches.  Nitrates are available in a large number of doses and formulations.  It is possible that there is one dose and formulation that results in few headaches and a large improvement in bone formation.  Our current study aims to identify this ideal nitrate by comparing the effects of five different formulations of nitrates on headaches and bone formation.  The nitrate formulation and dose that gives the greatest change in bone formation, together with the least headaches will subsequently be tested in a trial to prevent osteoporotic fractures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tubular dysfunction in diabetes: role of PGE2/EP receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CELL GROWTH; DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY; EP1 KNOCKOUT MOUSE; FIBROSIS; FVB AND DIABETIC (OVE-26) MOUSE MODEL; ISOLATED PERFUSED MOUSE CORTICAL COLLECTING DUCT; ISOLATED PERFUSED MOUSE PROXIMAL TUBULES; SODIUM TRANSPORT; WATER FLOW
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a leading cause of chronic kidney disease, and is recognized as one of the more important causes of morbidity and mortality in Canada. In the kidney, prostaglandins are implicated in the maintenance of glomerular filtration, they regulate cell growth and death responses, affect vascular integrity, and transport of water and electrolytes (sodium, potassium) along the tubules. DN involves disturbances in all these aspects of kidney function, therefore prostaglandins may be targeted to help slow the progression of these changes in the kidney. Though we have long recognized the involvement of prostaglandins in DN, to this day we are unsure of their exact contribution, whether they propagate the renal changes or serve to counteract the harmful effects of other agents. Prostaglandins are mainly produced in the glomeruli and collecting ducts of the kidney, by proteins called cyclooxygenases, which are inhibited by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Diabetes is an epidemic in North America and accounts for 30% of patients with chronic kidney disease. We strongly believe this research can lead to novel targets for the treatment of diabetic kidney disease and improve the lives of those affected.

TitreApplicationTitle: NANOMEDICINES: A Non-Invasive Approach to Neural Sensing, Imaging, and Chaperoning in the Compromised Nervous System
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; GOLD NANOPARTICLES; INFLAMMATION; LIPID DROPLETS; MICROGLIA; MITOCHONDRIA; NANOCARRIERS; NANOPARTICLES; NEURODEGENERATION; SENSORS
Abstract-Résumé: Nanotechnologies have been widely implemented for a variety of applications from cosmetics, apparel, and computers to life sciences and medicine, the latter of which is referred to more specifically as nanomedicines. Nanoparticles (NPs) made of different materials are beginning to fulfill some needs in "nano" and regenerative medicine, i.e. to provide more sensitive means of early detection and measurements of pathological changes in the sick tissues, and to promote tissue repair. However, the effects of these nano-sized biotechnological products on brain cells are unknown. We have been investigating different NPs for the purpose of sensing, imaging and delivering drugs. Gold and some other metallic nanoparticles remarkably affected resident immune cells of the brain, known as microglia. Microglia are the "sensors" of the brain and they can either protect or adversely affect the neurons. The most interesting discovery from our studies is that we can regulate the degree and duration of microglial activation by carefully designing NPs. We also found that nanoparticles can modulate microglial cell functions. This proposal investigates how nanoparticles alter microglial cell activity and how multifunctional systems can be used to repair and restore healthy microglial and neuronal cell functions. In the present studies, we will, (i) develop, test and optimize novel nanostructures as sensors and nano-therapeutics (so called nanomedicines), (ii) use animal models of neuroinflammation to test novel systems with novel properties to normalize excessively activated microglia and help them to restore normal functions, (iii) investigate molecular mechanisms underlying the impairments and therapeutic interventions to enhance their effectiveness. These studies will advance our understanding of the molecular basis of NP action and demonstrate the potential of nano-based systems as safe and effective therapeutics to promote repair and recovery in the compromised nervous system.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DES TUMEURS CEREBRALES; RETARD MENTAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroanatomical late effects in pediatric brain irradiation
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IRRADIATION; LONG-TERM SIDE EFFECTS; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MOUSE MODELS; PEDIATRIC BRAIN TUMOUR TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Recent decades have seen a substantial improvement in the survival of children with brain cancer, the second most common cancer in children. Patients are now living into their adult years. Unfortunately, progressive side effects from brain tumour treatment are very common and represent the most significant long-term complication in childhood cancer survivors. Studies indicate that patients suffer a progressive decline in mental capacity and achieve a lower socioeconomic status, including lower overall levels of education, household income, and full-time employment. These debilitating mental side effects show a strong link with radiation therapy, which, on the other hand, improves survival.   Interventions to eliminate radiation-induced side effects are urgently needed and may take one of two forms: (1) modification of the radiation treatment itself to limit damage to critical brain structures, or (2) post-treatment intervention to preserve brain function. In this proposal, we will determine the potential of both of these methods in an experimental mouse model. The results will, in the first case, provide new guidelines for radiation treatment in children, allowing current treatments to be modified in a fashion that minimizes damage to critical parts of the brain. In the second case, we will identify, in each region of the brain, the cells most important for normal brain development after radiation treatment, allowing strategic selection of therapies to preserve critical cells and stop mental decline after radiation treatment. These results in combination will transform the way clinicians treat brain tumours in children so that future cancer survivors can enjoy the same quality of life as their cancer free peers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Circadian control of immune functions
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN; BIOLOGICAL CLOCK; CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; CLOCK GENES; IMMUNE RESPONSE; IMMUNIZATION; MOUSE MODELS; PATHOGENS; T LYMPHOCYTE
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system is continuously in alert to detect the presence of invaders in an individual.  These invaders can consist of different infectious microbes (virus, bacteria, parasite) and also of our own cells that have become cancer. The recognition of foreign substances by T lymphocytes, via their T cell receptor, induces a variety of responses that permits the elimination of the pathogen or cancer cells.  Numerous aspects of the physiology present 24-hour (or circadian) rhythms: sleep-wake cycles, feeding, hormones, body temperature... These circadian rhythms allow the organism to be adequately adapted to cyclic variations of the environment (day-night cycles, seasons). Circadian rhythms are generated by "biological clocks", which are located in the brain as well as in various other organs. In recent years, many so-called "clock genes" have been discovered; these genes constitute the cogwheels of the biological clocks.  This proposal aims at studying the control by the biological clock of the immune system. We wish to find whether the clocks in cells of the immune system are important for its response to microbes. These studies will eventually give us new tools to develop more efficient immune responses against various infectious microbes and cancer cells, and to treat immunodeficiencies associated with cancer. Our work may also allow the design of more efficient vaccination tools.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - A: Reproduction, Maternal, Child and Youth Health
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Antidepressant use during pregnancy and the risk of metabolic disturbances in the offspring
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIDEPRESSANTS; BETA CELL; FETAL PROGRAMMING OF ADULT DISEASE; OBESITY; PREGNANCY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Women of childbearing age appear to be particularly vulnerable to depression around the time of pregnancy.  As a result it has been estimated that up to 1 in 5 women take antidepressant medications during pregnancy.  Although in adults these drugs can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes, it is unknown whether a woman's antidepressant use during pregnancy increases the risk of diabetes in her children.  Therefore the goal of this project is to determine in an animal model whether maternal exposure to a commonly used antidepressant is related to the development of diabetes in the offspring.  We will also examine the mechanism(s) by which maternal antidepressant use may lead to metabolic disorders in the exposed children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Natural helper cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE; EOSINOPHIL; INFLAMMATION; INNATE LYMPHOCYTE; MUCUS
Abstract-Résumé: Natural helper cells are unique lymphocytes that mainly reside in the gut-associated lymphoid tissues and the lung. When activated, they produce large amounts of specific type of small hormone-like proteins called cytokines. In the gut, natural helper cell-derived cytokines induce mucus production, which mediates expulsion of worms. We have also found natural helper cells in the lung. They are involved in mucus production and recruitment of eosinophils, a type of granulocytes, which are symptoms of asthma. Therefore, natural helper cells seem to be important for the protection against worm infection, but at the same time, they may be harmful as they can cause inflammation of the lung and the gut. Currently, our knowledge of natural helper cells is rather limited as they were discovered only very recently. The goal of this research is to find out how natural helper cells are activated and how they are involved in the inflammation of the lung. This research will likely provide new information on asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and may lead to new therapy targeting natural helper cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of the bioeffects of blood-brain barrier disruption by focused ultrasound: A multifaceted imaging approach
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BLOOD-BRAIN BARRIER; DRUG DELIVERY; FOCUSED ULTRASOUND; TWO-PHOTON MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Drug delivery to the brain is limited by the presence of a specialized structure known as the blood-brain barrier (BBB). A recent technology known as focused ultrasound has been shown to successfully open the BBB and allow access of drugs to the brain from the bloodstream. Focused ultrasound uses sound energy to open a localized region of the BBB which is then able to repair itself after a few hours. Focused ultrasound has successfully been used to increase the entry of various drugs into the brain to treat disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. However, prior to using this technology in clinical setting, it is important to fully understand the implications of focused ultrasound on the brain. We propose using several imaging techniques including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and live-imaging microscopy to observe the brain during BBB opening. Using this approach, we will define the parameters at which BBB opening initially occurs, address the effects of ultrasound on the individual blood vessels and brain cells and gain a better understanding of the overall safety of the procedure. We will also perform experiments in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease to better understand how ultrasound impacts the diseased brain.  Together, the proposed experiments will give insight into the effects of BBB opening by focused ultrasound in the normal brain and in the presence of neuropathology. These experiments are necessary to guide the design of future clinical trials testing this promising technology.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
TitreApplicationTitle: The human growth hormone receptor: regulation of expression during development
Keywords-MotsClés: FETAL AND POSTNATAL GROWTH; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE REGULATION; GROWTH DISORDERS; GROWTH HORMONE RECEPTOR; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALING PATHWAYS; MICRORNAS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; REGULATORY POLYMORPHISMS; TRUNCATED GROWTH HORMONE RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Growth is a complex process, regulated by numerous genes as well as nutritional and environmental factors. Growth hormone (GH) is known to play an essential role in the growing child as well as the adult, through multiple growth-promoting as well as metabolic effects, by binding to its specific receptor (GHR) on target cells. Thus, the ability of GH to exert its actions is intimately linked to the availability of its receptor.  Our objective is to identify and characterise the regions within the GHR gene that are responsible for controlling GHR expression in GH target tissues. This "biological blueprint" will provide the basis for understanding the mechanisms whereby tissue GHR levels change during normal development and differ from one individual to another. In addition, our investigations will pinpoint areas within the GHR gene to examine for the presence of genetic alterations in individuals at all ages who exhibit decreased responsiveness to GH (e.g. abnormal postnatal growth, obesity) or enhanced GH responsiveness (e.g. cancer progression).

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic contribution to food intake and its influence on body mass index in childhood: the Quebec Newborn Twin Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH COHORT; GENE-ENVIRONMENT; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; NUTRITION; OBESITY; POPULATION; SEX AND GENDER DIFFERENCES; TWIN STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: This research aims to assess the influence of genetics on food intake and its contribution to the etiology of human obesity. The general objective is to use a twin-study design to investigate the quantitative genetic, shared, and unique environmental influences on dietary intake, and to estimate its contribution to the development of obesity. Data collected from a birth cohort of 675 twin pairs born between 1996-1998 will allow us to assess the extent to which different food intake and eating behaviours, measured from birth to 9 years of age, and usual dietary intake, measured at 9 years of age, account for the genetic and environmental (shared and unshared) influences on body weight trajectories and the development of obesity to the age of 15 years. This includes an investigation of common, correlated, and interacting genetic and environmental effects on dietary habits and on the development of obesity. This research is important because, in most cases, obesity does not come about as a result of markedly defective biology, but rather by maladaptive behaviours nurtured by an obesogenic environment. A susceptibility to obesity is partly determined by genetic factors, but an "obesity-promoting environment" is typically necessary for its phenotypic expression. Such a genetically mediated susceptibility to environmental exposure may result from gene-environment interactions, mediation, and/or confounders. There is a paucity of literature on gene-diet interactions in childhood obesity, and large twin-birth cohorts are essential for the development of such knowledge.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reconstruction de tissus urologiques par génie tissulaire.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULES PORCINES; CONFOCALE; CULTURE CELLULAIRE; CYSTOGRAPHIE.; GENIE TISSULAIRE; HISTOPATHOLOGIE; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; MICROSCOPIE ELECTRONIQUE; UROTHELIUM; VESSIE
Abstract-Résumé: La vessie est un reservoir elastique responsable de l'emmagasinage de l'urine a basses pressions. Dans certaines conditions pathologiques, la fonction du muscle vesical est alteree et mene a des pressions intravesicales elevees qui, non traitees, resultent en des dommages renaux. Presentement, nous employons les segments intestinaux lors de reconstruction, mais cela amene des complications significatives attribuees aux differences dans les fonctions propres des segments intestinaux et de l'epithelium vesical. Pour sa part, l'uretre, segment tubulaire servant a vidanger la vessie, presente egalement son lot de pathologies qui demande reconstruction, voir son remplacement, en raison de stenoses ou perte de tissus. Pour remedier a ces obstacles, nous proposons de developper de nouveaux modeles de tissus urologiques reconstruits en laboratoire a partir de cellules du patient. Ce projet a pour but de developper un modele animal de vessie reconstruite par genie tissulaire, puis de realiser une transplantation autologue (agrandissement vesical) du tissu chez l'animal. Nous avons egalement mis au point un modele de tube ou uretre reconstruit in vitro pour son implantation autologue chez le lapin.  Impact du projet: L'elaboration d'un modele de vessie et d'uretre reconstruits par genie tissulaire a l'aide de cellules autologues pourrait avoir un impact clinique majeur etant donnees les complications presentement rencontrees dont l'utilisation de segments intestinaux. De plus, demontrer la faisabilite de reconstruire des tissus urologiques ouvrirait la porte a la reconstruction par genie tissulaire des ureteres, et des corps spongieux et caverneux du penis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of NMDA receptors in synaptic transmission and plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GLUTAMATE RECEPTORS; NEUROSCIENCE; PAIN; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; TYROSINE PHOSPHORYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Communication between neurons in the brain and spinal cord is mainly mediated by the excitatory amino acid neurotransmitter glutamate. Glutamate therefore is key to a wide range of normal processes such as sensation, perception, learning and memory, and to many abnormal processes including neurodegeneration, epilepsy, stroke and pain.  Glutamate acts by stimulating receptor proteins, produced by the recipient neuron, which convert the chemical signal provided by glutamate into electrical signals. In recent years we have established that the efficiency of this conversion is highly modifiable and this modifiability is key to controlling neuron-neuron communication. In the present application we will explore  three new types of processes that we have recently discovered which modify the function of glutamate receptors. Our goals are to characterize the biochemical mechanisms underlying these processes and to apply the knowledge we gain to determine how these mechanisms affect neuronal circuits in the brain and spinal cord. We anticipate that our studies will provide a basis for developing new types strategies to improve the treatment of pain, neurodegeneration, epilepsy and stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: The METS (Measurement of Exercise Tolerance before Surgery) Study: An International Multicentre Prospective Cohort Study of Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing For Improving Preoperative Risk Stratification for Major Non-Cardiac Surgery.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOPULMONARY EXERCISE TESTING; FUNCTIONAL CAPACITY; NON-CARDIAC SURGERY; PERIOPERATIVE CARDIAC COMPLICATIONS; PERIOPERATIVE MEDICINE; PREOPERATIVE RISK STRATIFICATION; PROGNOSTIC STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: More than 230 million people undergo major surgery worldwide every year. At least 5 million of them suffer major heart problems after these operations. People with poor physical fitness, or "functional capacity", may be at high risk for having these heart problems. They might also be at high risk for other important problems, such as infections or difficulty breathing after surgery.  At present, doctors estimate fitness for surgery by asking patients about the general types of activities that they can perform. For example, patients will often be asked whether they can climb up 2 flights of stairs. However, this approach (called "subjective assessment") does not perform well at identifying patients at risk for having major heart problems after surgery. We will therefore conduct a large international study to compare the usual approach ("subjective assessment") against 3 other methods to measure fitness for surgery. These methods are an exercise test (called CPET), a questionnaire about physical activities (called DASI), and a simple blood test (called NT pro-BNP).  Our study (called the METS study) will include 1312 patients undergoing major surgery at 8 hospitals in Ontario and the United Kingdom. Before surgery, each participant will undergo a "subjective assessment" of their fitness, complete a CPET exercise test, answer the DASI questionnaire, and undergo a NT pro-BNP blood test. We will then follow the participants for 1 year after surgery to determine which method does best at identifying people who have heart problems after surgery.  By helping to better identify high-risk patients before their operations, our study will help improve their medical care, and therefore reduce their risk of major problems after surgery. It will also help make sure that specialized (and expensive) medical care is used in patients who most need it. Our study will thus significantly help millions of people who have major surgery every year, in Canada and around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and Biological Characterisation of Novel Genetic Markers Associated to the Common of Alzheimer's Disease in a Population Isolate from Eastern Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER; ANIMAL MODELS; BIOMARKERS; GENETICS; PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: This research project seeks to define the function and diagnostic utility of newly discovered genetic risk factors for common Alzheimer's disease. To do so, we plan to use genetic and cell biology tools as well as animal models to carefully examine the function of these genes in the intact and diseased brain. We hope to demonstrate the importance and practical utility of these novel bio-markers for both, the early diagnostic and successful treatment of this terrible form of dementia that affect more than half a million Canadians today.

TitreApplicationTitle: The roles of Hippo pathway in non-small cell lung cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL PROLIFERATION; HIPPO PATHWAY; LUNG CANCER; ONCOGENE; PROTEIN KINASE; RNAI FUNCTIONAL GENOMICE SCREEN; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TISSUE MICROARRAY; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENES; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide, killing 1.2 million people annually (World Health Organization, 2010). Therefore, there is a pressing need to find new therapies for lung cancer. One of the major challenges in lung cancer therapy is to identify the markers or proteins critical for initiation and progression of lung cancer so that they can be targeted to kill cancer cells. Although many markers of lung cancer have been identified so far, only a few can be used as therapeutic target. Therefore, searching for new biomarkers critical for lung cancer development is the key for future diagnosis and therapy. Recently, we have discovered TAZ, a gene in an emerging signaling pathway called Hippo pathway, as a novel protein important for the development of lung cancer. In this research proposal, we will further explore whether other components of this novel pathway also coordinately contribute to lung cancer development and how dysfunction of them cause lung cancer. Our research findings will finally identified a new pathway critical for lung cancer development and will have great implications for the future diagnosis and therapy of lung cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sperm proteins acquired during epididymal transit: functions and usefulness for diagnostic of man infertility.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROLOGY; FERTILITY; MALE REPRODUCTIVE TRACT; SPERMATOZOA
Abstract-Résumé: During the transit along the reproductive tract, spermatozoa acquire new proteins that are involved in the acquisition of fertilizing ability.  The first objective of this proposal is to understand the molecular mechanism underlying fertilization and how these newly acquired proteins are involved in this process.  The second objective is to use these proteins as markers to understand the aetiology of some cases of men infertility and subfertility.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; ANOMALIES CONGENITALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation, downstream targets and functional specificity of the MAP kinases ERK1 and ERK2
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS OF DISEASE; CELL DIFFERENTIATION; CELL PROLIFERATION; EMBRYONIC DEVELOPMENT; MAP KINASES; MOUSE MODELS; PHOSPHOPROTEOMICS; PHOSPHORYLATION; REGULATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The MAP kinases ERK1 and ERK2 are a family of enzymes that play important roles in the control of cell proliferation and differentiation. Accumulating evidence suggests that the ERK1/ERK2 signaling pathway is implicated in the pathogenesis of human diseases including cancer. Inherited mutations in components of this pathway are also associated with a group of developmental disorders causing neurological, cardio-vascular and skeletal anomalies. The objectives of our research program are to understand how the activity of ERK1 and ERK2 MAP kinases is controlled and to define the molecular mechanisms underlying their cellular and physiological actions. We are using a combination of biochemistry, cell biology, proteomics and genetic approaches to address these questions. Specifically, we have generated mouse models in which the genes encoding ERK1 or ERK2 have been inactivated by targeted mutagenesis. These mice are used to study the individual roles of ERK1 and ERK2 and to identify their specific targets. The knowledge gained from our studies should further our understanding of the contribution of ERK1/ERK2 signaling to human diseases and help identify novel and more selective drug targets.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - B: Heart and Circulation
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Ski in myofibroblast regulation in heart failure.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FIBROSIS; CARDIAC MYOFIBROBLAST; CARDIAC REMODELING; CELLULAR AND ANIMAL MODELS; HEART FAILURE; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; MYOCARDIAL PROTECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Congestive heart failure is a major burden to society, in terms of mortality, morbidity and fiscal cost. Our lab carries out research on the heart, with a focus on chronic myocardial ischemia, infarction and cardiac remodeling.  The heart contains numerous cell types including myocytes (muscle cells) and fibroblasts (non-muscle cells). Fibroblasts and activated myofibroblasts contribute to cardiac fibrosis after heart attack due to overproduction of collagen. Myofibroblasts show two key features: -they can contract and rearrange the extracellular matrix between normal heart cells and they make much more collagen then the relatively quiet fibroblast. We study cellular and animal models of human cardiac disease. A key cellular protein called Ski acts as a cellular brake to prevent runaway activation of fibroblasts that leads to fibrosis. Ski has associated with reduced collagen synthesis and even removal of myofibroblasts from damaged heart.  Thus we believe that Ski plays a key role in slowing fibrosis in injured hearts. Our overall premise is that in the healthy heart there is a balance between pro-fibrotic and anti-fibrotic pathways. After a heart attack, we believe this balance tips towards fibrosis and ultimately to overt cardiac fibrosis and heart failure. At a cellular level, Ski inhibits the ability of R-Smads to function in the nucleus. Our objective is to determine the role of Ski in the progression of heart failure and identify the pathways it controls to regulate fibrosis. Our investigation will show that loss of normal Ski function is a crucial event in the development of cardiac fibrosis and cardiac remodeling following heart attacks, and furthermore we will provide answers as to the mechanisms for Ski's effects. Ultimately, this research will translate to the development of novel reagents for the treatment of heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Kinin B1 receptor as a key target in the treatment of hypertension and insulin resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERIAL HYPERTENSION; CARDIOVASCULAR; CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM; INSULIN RESISTANCE; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PHARMACOLOGY; VASCULAR INFLAMMATION; VASOACTIVE PEPTIDES
Abstract-Résumé: We showed that treatments with antioxidants or inhibitors of B1 receptor (B1R) for kinins (local hormone and brain mediator) reversed hypertension and diabetes abnormalities in rat models. The B1R is absent in healthy subjects and its occurrence is the signature of a pathology. We propose that the oxidative stress increases the occurrence of kinin B1R which in turn perpetuates the oxidative stress and its harmful effects on vasculature and other target organs. This project is using an integrative approach to determine the mechanism by which kinin B1R can be induced by the oxidative stress and how this receptor can perpetuate the oxidative stress and causing vascular inflammation which accelerates the development of cardiovascular diseases. Inhibitors of kinin B1R are believed to prevent not only the deleterious effect of these peptides on the vasculature but also to act as potent anti-hypertensive drugs by inhibiting brain neuronal activity. Therefore, the site and mechanism of action of these inhibitors in the brain will be further investigated. This project will be carried out in two rat models of hypertension associated or not with diabetes. Several parameters will be measured in the whole animal (blood pressure, heart rate,plasma levels of insulin and glucose, insulin resistance) and in post-mortem tissues: tissue levels of B1 receptor and of various markers of inflammation and oxidative stress. This work should increase our understanding of the role of kinin B1R in diabetes and hypertension. Inhibitors of this receptor may offer a new therapeutic avenue in the treatment of these diseases. However, to warranty their clinical use, further information regarding the way they operate in our body is mandatory.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transitions Across the Health Care System and the Risk of Rehospitalization in Older Women and Men
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; LINKED DATASETS; OLDER ADULTS; READMISSION; REHOSPITALIZATION; RISK-ADJUSTMENT METHODS; TRANSITIONS
Abstract-Résumé: For older adults, discharge from hospital can be a difficult time. It is often associated with concerns about continuity of care, the patient's readiness for discharge, and the availability of appropriate services outside of hospital. One of the biggest signs that there continue to be problems in the care of patients leaving hospital is the high proportion who are rehospitalized within a short period of time. Several studies have shown that as many as 20% of older patients are rehospitalized within only 30 days of discharge. Due to the frequency and the implications for cost and quality, rehospitalization has been identified as a key area for improving quality and health system efficiency. Policy strategies to reduce rehospitalizations include accountability agreements between health regions and hospitals, public reporting of provider performance, and comprehensive post-hospital care interventions. Central to all of these strategies is the ability to make fair comparisons between providers (usually hospitals) that often care for very different types of patients. However, there are concerns that we still do not know enough about what leads to rehospitalization to appropriately adjust for differences between patients and make fair comparisons. This is particularly the case when it comes to older adults, the group at greatest risk for rehospitalization. The purpose of this proposal is to develop statistical models that would be used to adjust for differences between patients. This work is unique because our models will incorporate information that is most relevant to understanding the needs of older adults; we will explore differences between patients discharged to long-term care and the community, and will include measures of patient complexity that are specific to the geriatric context (such as multi-morbidity, functional impairment, and frailty). This work will result in better evaluation of provider performance and identification of successful interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phase II clinical trial of pantoprazole and docetaxel for men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CHEMOTHERAPY; DOCETAXEL; PANTOPRAZOLE; PHASE II CLINICAL TRIAL; PROSTATE CANCER; PSA RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: Men with metastatic prostate cancer commonly have tumours that have spread to lymph nodes and to their bones, and they frequently experience symptoms of tiredness and pain. Initial treatment is hormonal, with drugs that decrease the level and/or activity of male hormones such as testosterone that stimulate growth of most types of prostate cancer.  Unfortunately men become resistant to hormonal therapy, and the standard treatment for most men is then chemotherapy with docetaxel (also known as Taxotere) given by vein every 3 weeks, together with daily oral prednisone.  This treatment leads to a PSA response (a fall in level of serum PSA by >50%) in about half of the men, and it can also improve pain and quality of life.  The treatment was found in a large randomised clinical trial (chaired by the current PI) to improve the average duration of survival as compared to an older type of chemotherapy.  Several other clinical trials have tried to improve on these results by giving docetaxel and prednisone with other drugs (largely molecular targeted agents), but these trials have been negative.  We have evidence from the laboratory that the commonly used anti-ulcer drug pantoprazole, when given in high doses by vein just before docetaxel, markedly increases the effects of docetaxel delay the re-growth of tumours grown from human tumour cell lines in immune-deficient mice, with minimal increase in toxicity. We have shown also that pantoprazole increases markers of drug activity in such tumours, and that it inhibits the process of autophagy, which is a survival mechanism for stressed cancer cells.  Here we propose to evaluate this combination in a clinical trial for men with metastatic prostate cancer, who would normally receive treatment with docetaxel and prednisone alone.  We will also investigate the correlation of PSA response (the primary outcome measure in our proposed clinical trial) with the levels of autophagy in the tumours of men that are treated.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reversing developmental consequences of NMDA receptor dysfunction in a mouse model of schizophrenia.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIPSYCHOTICS; MEMORY; NMDA RECEPTOR; POSTNATAL DEVELOPMENT; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SOCIAL BEHAVIOUR; STRIATUM; SYNAPSE; TRANSGENIC MOUSE
Abstract-Résumé: The causes of schizophrenia remain unclear, but there is strong evidence to suggest a genetic component to the disease. Even though the susceptibility genes that cause schizophrenia are inherited from birth, the symptoms of the disease are not fully apparent until after adolescence and into early adulthood. We and others hypothesize that improper neural communication and connection during childhood brain development occurs in schizophrenia. Using a genetic mouse model of schizophrenia, we propose to study the emergence of schizophrenia related behaviours through development, and determine whether antipsychotic treatment at early developmental timepoints could improve therapeutic outcomes. Furthermore, we propose to study the ability of the brain to improve function by restoring proper neuronal communication at different developmental stages. In performing these studies, we may gain insight into early diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia, and may determine whether early therapeutic intervention is beneficial for brain function in schizophrenic patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Next generation patient-derived, genetically-defined prostate cancer xenograft models for anti- cancer drug development
Keywords-MotsClés: ACGH; ANTI-CANCER DRUG DEVELOPMENT; CASTRATION-RESISTANT PROSTATE CANCER; COMMERCIALIZATION; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; XENOGRAFTS
Abstract-Résumé: Evaluation of potential anticancer drugs is - at present - commonly carried out with preclinical cancer models that consist of special, immuno-deficient mice carrying grafts of cultured human cancer cells available commercially. While such commercial cancer cell line models have merits for basic cancer research, the cell lines used have evolved biologically during generations of cultures and do not properly represent patients' cancers and consequently do not adequately predict efficacy of anticancer drugs in the clinic. Even when new anticancer drug candidates have successfully passed all stages of efficacy testing performed with commercial cancer cell line models, only about 5% gets approval for clinical usage by the US Food and Drug Administration. The high number of ineffective new drug candidates entering clinical trials indicates an urgent need for better ways of predicting clinical drug efficacy before drugs are tested in humans. Drs. Wang and Collins at the BC Cancer Agency and the Vancouver Prostate Centre propose, in collaboration with BRI Biopharmaceutical Research Inc. (www.bripharm.com), to establish next-generation patient-derived prostate cancer models, which more closely resemble a patient's cancer than the existing standard cancer models. Such next generation models will provide valuable tools for studying the molecular and cellular development and progression of prostate cancer, and for the development of new therapies and their application in personalized prostate cancer therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lipopolysaccharide assembly in Gram-negative bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; BIOPHYSICS; BIOSYNTHESIS; GLYCOSYLTRANSFERASES; LIPID METABOLISM; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; SEPSIS; STRUCTURE-FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: We study how bacteria make a surface molecule termed the O antigen. The O antigen is a component of the endotoxin or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in enteric bacteria. LPS O antigen plays an important role protecting from the immune response those bacteria that cross from the gut barrier and invade the blood and tissues of patients during the process of sepsis. The synthesis of O antigen is a complex process that takes place at the bacterial membrane. Understanding this process is critical to identify novel ways to interfere with the synthesis of O antigen and prevent or ameliorate infections. In our laboratory we use a combination of genetic and biochemical techniques. With genetics, we can determine what genes encode functions for the synthesis of O antigen. We use biochemistry to tease apart what those function are. We have discovered that several protein molecules involved in O antigen synthesis must come together and operate as a protein complex. This grant proposal is focused on elucidating the details about this complex in preparation for our next goal dedicated to devise ways to disrupt the complex and alter the synthesis of the O antigens.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of the C. elegans Intestine
Keywords-MotsClés: CAENORHABDITIS ELEGANS; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; ELT-2; GATA FACTOR; INTESTINE; SUPER-RESOLUTION MICROSCOPY; TRANSCRIPTION; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: The small free-living worm Caenorhabditis elegans has only a thousand cells in its body; its intestine has only twenty cells.  In contrast, human intestines have trillions of cells.  Yet the worm intestine and our own intestine have many similar features and clearly came from some ancient common ancestor.  We have been studying how the worm intestine develops from a single cell to a functioning digestive organ in roughly 12 hours. We have found that the transcription factor that controls most of intestine development (i.e. the particular protein responsible for turning intestine genes on and off) is highly similar to the transcription factor that controls the development of our own intestines.  In this proposal, we first wish to ask questions of mechanism, i.e. how does all this work?  Secondly, we will isolate an entire active gene from the intestine, together with its chromosomal environment, and then identify all the associated proteins (using the technique known as mass spectrometry).  Thirdly, we will being to investigate how intestine genes become active inside the living developing worm embryo, using the newest generation of so-called "super-resolution " microscopes, which can detect single molecules. The hope is that we will begin to understand intestine development at a detail that was thought impossible only a few years ago.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Exercise in Modifying Outcomes for People with Multiple Sclerosis: A Randomized Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: EXERCISE; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; OUTCOMES; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the known benefits of exercise and activity participation, evidence shows that persons with Multiple Sclerosis (MS) are relatively inactive. Physical activity improves the disabling effects of MS and reduces the risk of developing other health problems. Exercise is recommended for all persons with MS, but people with MS do not know what would be best for them to do. Our research team, with input from experts and patients, has developed and pilot tested a MS Tailored Exercise Program (MSTEP). It incorporates exercises of endurance, muscular and core strength, balance, flexibility, muscular power, and speed of movement. As disability does not take a day off, the program is for 6 to 7 days a week using exercises and activities that can fit into a daily routine. The program encourages people to do both steady endurance activities as well as high bursts of exercise to build tolerance to exercise. Participants will be shown how to use different types of exercise equipment such as Nordic walking poles which help people to walk safely, faster and longer. To test MSTEP it is necessary to compare the results of MSTEP to results obtained from standard exercise recommendations. The proof of whether MSTEP is better than usual recommendations will be if a greater proportion of people in the MSTEP program improve their capacity for exercise than in the general approach.  Other benefits to walking capacity, energy, and well-being will also be tested.  As it takes time to change behavior, the duration of the intervention will be one year with follow-up to year two.

TitreApplicationTitle: Validating a new cognitive-behavioural therapy for compulsive checking in OCD
Keywords-MotsClés: CBT; COGNITIVE THERAPY; COMPULSIVE CHECKING; OCD; SINGLE CASE DESIGN; TREATMENT VALIDATION
Abstract-Résumé: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a serious and often severe anxiety disorder affecting over 650,000 Canadians. According to the World Health Organization, it is the 10th leading cause of disability worldwide. Compulsive checking, where an individual repeatedly checks to make sure that something and/or someone is safe, is one of the most common symptoms of OCD, and can lead people to spend hours a day checking and re-checking people and/or objects in their homes, workplaces and beyond. Although there are effective psychological treatments for compulsive checking, they are difficult for people, because patients are asked to face their worst fears repeatedly until their anxiety declines. The challenging nature of this treatment leads many to refuse it outright, or to drop out of the treatment before it has had a chance to be effective. We have designed a new easier treatment for compulsive checking which places emphasis on how people think, rather than on what they do; we believe that this new emphasis should make the treatment more acceptable to those who need it. This new cognitive-behavioural treatment for extreme doubt and compulsive checking follows directly from our previous research on compulsive checking in OCD, and targets people's faulty beliefs about how responsible they think they are, about their memories, and about the dangers that they perceive. This grant will fund a first look at how well this treatment works, and at how acceptable it is. It is our hope that the proposed research will lead to a published treatment manual which therapists across the country and beyond can access and use with their clients and patients.  Also, we hope that the current proposal will lead in three year's time to a future grant application to fund a more thorough examination of the effectiveness and acceptability of the new treatment for compulsive checking and extreme doubt.

TitreApplicationTitle: Validating Nox5 as a target for diabetic renal complications
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; KIDNEY; PODOCYTE; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Background:  It is considered that much of the damage to the filtering ability of the kidney in diabetes occurs as a result of a phenomenon known as oxidative stress.  Objective: This project hopes to identify new targets in order to develop novel treatments to better treat and prevent diabetic kidney disease.  Project description: This proposal postulates that a certain very recently identified form of an enzyme called Nox which promotes oxidative stress known as Nox5, which appear to be preferentially upregulated in the kidney in diabetes, would be an ideal target for generating drugs to reduce the impact of diabetic kidney disease. We will develop a set of mice that possess an abundant level of this stress inducing enzyme in the kidney and test whether their diabetic kidney disease and filtering ability worsens. Kidney disorders remain major causes of morbidity and premature mortality in diabetic individuals. Although currently available treatment strategies addressing, in particular, optimization of glycemic and blood pressure control have been shown to reduce progression of diabetic kidney disease, the effects remain modest.  The studies will employ human kidney cells that will be exposed to high glucose concentrations (to mimic the "diabetic milieu") in order to investigate factors which activate the Nox5 enzyme, thereby promoting oxidative stress.  These studies will thereby strengthen the rationale to consider Nox5 as a potential new target to develop better treatments to reduce a major burden of diabetes - diabetic kidney disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endosomal membrane trafficking in cell physiology and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ARF; CADHERIN; CANCER; CELL ADHESION; CELL MIGRATION; DENN DOMAIN; ENDOSOMES; GEF; INTEGRIN; RAB
Abstract-Résumé: The cell surface is defined by the plasma membrane, which separates the cell interior from the external world. The plasma membrane is studded with proteins that have multiple functions, for example allowing a cell to interact with other cells. These proteins are continuously brought into the cell in a process called endocytosis and are delivered to endosomes. From there they are either targeted for degradation or are recycled back to the plasma membrane. Disruptions in this sorting process have dire consequences, for example, if proteins mediating cell-cell contact fail to return to the surface the cell loses contact with other cells, separates from the tissue and begins to migrate. This is exactly what happens in certain forms of cancer. This project will examine how the recycling process occurs and how it is disrupted in cancer.
