TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Essential Proteases for Bacterial Virulence
Keywords-MotsClés: ACYLDEPSIPEPTIDES; ANTIBIOTICS; BACTERIAL GENETICS; BACTERIAL PROTEASES; BIOCHEMISTRY; CLPP PROTEASES; CRYO-ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ENZYMOLOGY; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The life expectancy of Canadians has almost doubled since the discovery of the first antibiotic (penicillin) in 1928. This increase is the direct result of our ability to control infections with antibiotics. However, these benefits are at risk due to the global spread of antimicrobial resistance that affects all classes of known antibiotics. Therefore, researchers are in a desperate hunt for new lead compounds and new antimicrobial targets. Therapies targeting proteases (proteins that cleave other proteins) have had resound success in the treatment of viral infections, including HIV-1 that causes the acquired immuno deficiency syndrome (AIDS) or parasites such as Trypanosoma cruzi, agent of the Changas disease, that kills 50,000 people in Central and South America every year. In bacterial infections, the use of proteases as antimicrobial targets has been quite limited, mainly because of the fragmented understanding of their complex biology. We study ClpP, a protease that pathogenic bacteria require to exhibit its virulence. ClpP is the target of the new class of antibiotics, acyldepsipeptides (ADEPs). Upon binding, ADEPs unleash the protease activity of ClpP causing the indiscriminate degradation of newly synthesized proteins, which kills the bacterium. We use a multidisciplinary approach ranging from molecular to structural biology to gain a detailed understanding of the mechanism of activation of ClpP by ADEPs. Furthermore, we also investigate the mechanisms by which bacteria control the normal activity of ClpP with the final goal of developing new and more potent drugs against this critical enzyme.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying translational regulons underlying memory formation
Keywords-MotsClés: APLYSIA; LEARNING AND MEMORY; MEMORY TRACE; MGLUR-LTD; MRNA LOCALIZATION; RNA BINDING PROTEINS; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; TOR; TRANSLATION; TRANSLATION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: An experience changes the brain and leaves a trace behind. This trace is what we call memory. The goal of my lab is to understand the trace at the molecular level. Different experiences lead to different molecular traces that last for different periods of time. Our understanding of memory rests on identifying these molecular traces. We take a reductionist approach to studying memory, identifying the simplest system in which we can examine the memory trace. One model is the marine mollusk Aplysia, because in this system the neurons that hold the memory trace have been identified. This is a valuable system as seen by the Nobel Prize awarded to Dr. Eric Kandel in 2000 for his work on memory in this system. We also use cultures of hippocampal neurons from rats. While the changes induced in this system are not as closely linked to memory as in Aplysia, forms of plasticity that are linked to human diseases such as the Fragile X syndrome can be studied in this system. In this application, we study how protein translation is important for forming the memory trace. An experience leads to increased production of proteins from messenger RNAs that already exist. This is a mechanism to make new proteins quickly and the increased levels of these proteins can then change the strength of synapses, leading to a change in the circuitry of the brain and the memory trace. We study this mechanism at the level of the translational machinery, trying to understand how, in neurons, the translational machinery (the machine that converts messenger RNAs into proteins) is regulated by the stimulations that lead to memory formation.  Understanding how memories are formed has important health implications both for pathological conditions such as mental retardation, and physiological conditions such as aging. A better understanding of how memories are formed is important for developing strategies for improving memory in both healthy and diseased populations.

ClasseRechercheFR: SANG; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of the signaling events regulating lymphocyte activation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN RECEPTOR SIGNALING; LYMPHOCYTES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TYROSINE PHOSPHATASES
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal is aimed at defining the cellular and molecular mechanisms that lead to autoimmune disease. In recent years, a variant in a gene known as PTPN22 has been shown to confer risk for many autoimmune diseases. This gene encodes a protein, Lyp/Pep, that is expressed in all immune cells and that belongs to a class of enzymes known as protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs). When active, Lyp/Pep inhibits the activation of T lymphocytes. The disease-associated PTPN22 variant produces a variant protein Lyp620W/Pep619W, but the pathways whereby this variant confers risk for disease are unknown. By deriving mutant mice that express the Lyp/Pep variant, we have shown that the variant leads to reduced levels of Lyp/Pep and, as a result, increases the activation of T, B and dendritic cells. We have also found these same cell defects in human cells expressing the variant form of Lyp/Pep. By capitalizing on the mutant mice as well as our access to human cells expressing the Lyp/Pep variant, we now propose to characterize the precise molecular pathways whereby the variant alters immune cell activation and responses so as to confer susceptibility to autoimmune disease. We will, for example, now study the variants effects on B and dendritic cells as well as T cells, on the development of specialized regulatory T cells and on the capacity of immune cells to migrate to various tissues. We will also mate the mutant mice with other mice genetically predisposed to develop autoimmune disease so as to delineate the extent to which Lyp/Pep interacts with other variant proteins to trigger autoimmunity. Such information will provide a framework for the design of new therapeutic strategies that target the Lyp/Pep variant disease-causing pathway.

TitreApplicationTitle: The neurocognitive basis of suicidal behavior: A neuroimaging study with a model-based approach
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; DEPRESSIVE DISORDERS; EMOTION; FUNCTIONAL NEUROIMAGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; PATHOPHYSIOLOGY; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; SEX DIFFERENCES; SUICIDAL BEHAVIOR; VULNERABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Suicidal behavior (SB) represents a public health issue in most Western countries including Canada. According to the WHO, one million people die by suicide each year worldwide and the rate of attempted suicide is ten times greater. Moreover, suicide completion appears to be more frequent in men whereas suicide attempts are more frequent in women. To date, our ability to predict and prevent SB remains poor. Current research aims to increase our understanding of the processes leading to SB, this in turn, will help to improve our ability to predict and prevent these tragic acts.  There is substantial support in the literature to suggest that SB results from complex interactions between stressors such as divorce or job loss and a particular vulnerability. According to this model, vulnerable individuals are at increased risks of committing a suicidal act when exposed to certain stressful events. It is, therefore, important to understand this vulnerability and how it interacts with stressful environments.  Previously, our group has shown that cognitive factors as well as structural and functional brain alterations act as underlying mediators in the vulnerability to SB. In the present project, we propose to expand the study of these cognitive and neuroanatomical features through functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI), a valuable tool in the current research on the "in vivo" brain. In addition, we will explore the possible role of sex differences in the vulnerability to SB.  We will compare 3 groups of participants: i) 40 patients with a personal history of SB and depression ii) 40 patients with no history of SB but with a history of depression iii) 40 healthy controls. Participants will be between 25 and 55 years old and not depressed at the time of scanning. They will undergo a series of relevant tests during fMRI to assess their sensitivity to social stimuli, their inhibitory abilities, how they perceive themselves and their ability to make decisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Global Ubiquitin-Proteasome System Map
Keywords-MotsClés: MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEOMICS; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Ubiquitin (Ub), an ancient signaling protein, is chemically attached to other proteins in the cell to regulate their function.  The Ub system is critical for normal cellular function, and malfunctions of the Ub system have been linked to many different human maladies, including cancer, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, and mental retardation.    Mass spectrometry (MS) has emerged as an extremely powerful tool to study complex biological samples.  Using a combination of MS and a novel software suite (SUMmOn) that we created, my colleagues and I developed the first automated approach for the identification and characterization of Ub and ubiquitin-like proteins.   Here, using these tools and other advanced molecular biology techniques, we propose to conduct the first complete characterization of the Ub system in the model organism S. cerevisiae (budding yeast).  High density protein-protein interaction mapping will be used to characterize interacting partners for all of the Ub system enzymes, and proteins containing Ub binding motifs.  These data will be used to inform similar studies in the more complex mammalian system.  In this way, we will gain a much better understanding of how the complex and critically important Ub system is regulated, and learn more about the processes that are in turn regulated by this critically important protein.

TitreApplicationTitle: G proteins and membrane signalling in cardiovascular system in health and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENYLYL CYCLASE; ANTISENSE; GI PROTEINS; GQ PROTEINS; HYPERTENSION; MAP KINASE; OXIDATIVE STRESS; VASCULAR HYPERTROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension is a multigenic disease that leads to cardiac hypertrophy (enlargement of the heart) and cardiac failure. We have recently shown that the genes for Gia proteins (Gia-2 and Gialp-3) that decrease the levels of cyclic AMP and increase blood pressure (BP),were overexpressed in genetic (SHR) and experimental models of hypertensive rats (HR). However, the contribution of   Gia-2 or Gia-3 or both in the pathogenesis of hypertension is not clear. Therefore, we will examine the effect of deletion of Gia-2 and Gia-3 proteins by using antisense approach on the development of BP in SHR. To further establish the implication of enhanced expression of Gia proteins in hypertension, we will use SNAP and sodium nitroprusside (SNP), nitric oxide(NO) donors and vasorelaxants , that attenuate  the increased expression of Gia proteins in SHR to examine if these agents could also decrease the BP in HR. We have earlier shown the contribution of enhanced oxidative stress in the augmented expression of Gia proteins in SHR, we will extend our studies to examine the effect of antioxidants on the development of BP and their relationship with Gia protein expression. Since hypertension leads to cardiac hypertrophy and the contribution of vascular Gq protein-coupled signaling in the development of cardiac hypertrophy has been shown, we will investigate if the expression of Gq is augmented in VSMC from different rat models exhibiting hypertension with or without cardiac hypertrophy and cardiac hypertrophy without hypertension and its relationship with vascular hypertrophy. Finally, we will also examine the molecular mechanisms contributing to the enhanced expression of G proteins in hypertension and hypertrophy and by which the antioxidants and NO donors attenuate G protein expression,BP and vascular hypertrophy. It is hoped that the results from this work will eventually form the basis for developing new therapeutic interventions for the management of hypertension and hypertrophy

TitreApplicationTitle: Individualized Risk Prediction in Cardiac Surgery Through Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC SURGERY; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENOMICS; RISK STRATIFICATION; TRANSLATIONAL MEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiac surgery is a common medical procedure, with more than 2,000,000 procedures performed worldwide including 30,000 in Canada.  Despite its life-saving potential, it carries a high risk of complications and approximately 5% of patients (100,000 patients globally) will not survive their hospital stay after cardiac surgery.  Cardio-pulmonary bypass -also known as heart-lung machine- is a technique where a pump takes over the function of the heart and lungs during surgery allowing surgeons to operate on hearts while keeping patients alive.  The inflammatory reaction caused by cardio-pulmonary bypass is thought to be largely responsible for adverse outcomes following cardiac surgery.  However, this inflammatory reaction is poorly understood and can't be predicted.  There is thus an urgent need to develop novel blood tests to identify high-risk individuals, so to redirect them towards other options. Our objective is to improve outcomes in patients undergoing cardio-pulmonary bypass by developing a blood test that will indicate which patients are likely to have an adverse inflammatory reaction, and which patients are likely to respond to anti-inflammatory therapy.  The ongoing publically funded Steroids In caRdiac Surgery trial (SIRS) is evaluating the benefits of an anti-inflammatory agent on major clinical outcomes in cardiac surgery. However, no blood sample is collected as part of the SIRS trial.  We will collect blood samples in patients participating in the SIRS trial.  We will then analyze these blood samples to measure the level of activity of genes of circulating inflammatory cells (white blood cells).   Annually, 30,000 patients undergo cardio-pulmonary bypass in Canada for a variety of cardiac conditions, and 1,500 patients are expected not to survive their hospital stay.  We believe this to be an unacceptable statistic and hope to improve it through better identification of patients not suited for this otherwise beneficial procedure.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; TUMEURS
TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of human RNA polymerase II CTD-interacting proteins in the regulation of gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: CHIP-SEQUENCING; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; CTD; HUMAN TISSUE CULTURE CELLS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PHOSPHORYLATION; RNA POLYMERASE II; RPRD PROTEINS; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: The regulated expression of human genes determines the developmental fates of human cells, and aberrations in this process often lead to cancer.  RNA polymerase II, the enzyme that transcribes most human genes, must initiate transcription in the right places and at the correct frequencies, elongate efficiently through genes, and terminate transcription in the right places, and the RNA molecules produced by RNA polymerase II must be correctly modified.  We have identified three human proteins, RPRD1A, RPRD1B, and RPRD2, about which virtually nothing is known and which interact with particular forms of RNA polymerase II.  We now propose to investigate how these proteins, which are produced in all kinds of human tissues, regulate the various steps in the expression of human genes and, perhaps, how they are related to human disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of Breathing during Sleep: Brainstem Mechanisms of Respiratory Control
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CONTROL OF BREATHING; OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA; RESPIRATORY NEUROBIOLOGY; SLEEP; UPPER AIRWAY MUSCLES
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately one in four Canadians is affected by significant sleep problems that can diminish their health, alertness, safety and quality of life. The most common and serious of the sleep disorders have impairments of breathing as their root cause. One example is sleep apnea, which affects affects up to 20% of adults and is thought to be involved in some cases of sudden unexplained death in infancy. Sleep apnea is defined as cessation of breathing during sleep, and is typically caused by closure of the air passage in the throat in sleep due to relaxation of those breathing muscles (e.g., the tongue) whose activity normally keeps this air passage open. Episodes of breathing cessation in sleep can occur hundreds of times per night, each resulting in temporary suffocation that causes major sleep disruption. Understanding the brain mechanisms causing sleep apnea is important because of the adverse medical, societal and economic costs of this common disorder, such as increased strokes, angina and heart attacks, debilitating daytime sleepiness, increased traffic and work-related accidents, impaired work performance and decreased quality of life. Our research will identify the brain mechanisms that cause changes in breathing across wakefulness and sleep. Research will also identify how commonly used prescription and non-prescription sedating drugs (such as anesthetics, sleeping tablets, painkillers and alcohol) can also depress breathing and the waking-up responses to respiratory distress. This information will identify common mechanisms causing the prevalent problems of sleep and sedation-induced depression of breathing, and will guide pharmacological approaches aimed at preventing or reinstating breathing when it is depressed or fails.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of neutrophil functions by the cytohesin-Arf6 signaling axis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARF6; ARTHRITIS; CD18/CD11B; CELL BIOLOGY; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; CYTOHESIN; INTEGRINS
Abstract-Résumé: Polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) are the most abundant human blood leucocytes, and are considered the first non-specific defence line against infectious agents. Severe recurrent bacterial infections associated with inherited disorders have contributed to our understanding of the essential role of PMNs in bacterial killing and our innate immunity. The inability of PMNs to mount an appropriate immune response is associated with defective adherence, migration from the vascular bed to tissues, or release of various antimicrobial products. PMNs express on their cell surface various markers, of which many are receptors specific for endogenous molecules or components of bacterial cells. These receptors are only activated when they sense bacteria or cellular debris in their environment. In chronic inflammatory diseases inappropriate activation of PMNs causes tissue injuries and destruction. By delineating the processes regulating directed movement and activation of PMNs we may be better positioned to develop new therapeutic approaches to boost our immune system or to control excessive activation of these cells in chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; SCLEROSE EN PLAQUES
TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions of human coronaviruses with the nervous system.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; HUMAN CORONAVIRUSES; MUTATIONS; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROINFLAMMATION; NEURONAL MODEL; NEUROTROPISM; REVERSE GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Neurological diseases are diverse and often not well understood. Some transmissible infectious agents, such as viruses, invade, infect and persist in the central nervous system (CNS: brain and spinal cord). Although a viral origin is suspected, causes of neurological diseases of unknown etiology, such as multiple sclerosis, Parkinson and Alzheimer disease, remain elusive. Therefore, it is essential to understand how viruses interact with the nervous system and cause neuropathology. Coronaviruses are ubiquitous respiratory pathogens that cause a third of common colds, pneumonia, asthma exacerbations and the SARS pandemic. We have shown that human coronaviruses (HCoV) can infect and persist in cells of the human brain, with possible pathological consequences in predisposed individuals. They also cause neurological disease in susceptible mice that can be modified with specific virus mutants. We now propose to continue our characterization of the interaction of HCoV with the CNS, both in human tissue and in an animal model. First, using both reverse genetically engineered and naturally occurring virus mutants, we will study determinants of HCoV biology and adaptation to the CNS environment. Second, we will characterize the consequences of infection of human neurons and different glial cells, as well as primary cultures of CNS cells, on cellular gene expression and characterize the cellular receptor used by the virus to infect neuronal cells.Third, we will continue to characterize our animal model of coronavirus-induced neurological disease by studying the effect of infection on neural function and mechanisms of coronavirus-induced neuroinflammation. Viral persistence in the nervous system and its consequences on neural cell biology may have implications for neurologic diseases. Understanding mechanisms and consequences of virus interactions with the nervous system will be essential to the design of diagnostic and intervention strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of maternal inflammation in the pathophysiology of intrauterine growth restriction and pre-eclampsia
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD FLOW; IMMUNOLOGY; PLACENTA; PREGNANCY; PREGNANCY COMPLICATIONS; RAT MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Intrauterine fetal growth restriction and pre-eclampsia are serious diseases of pregnancy. Babies who are born too small are said to suffer from intrauterine growth restriction. When women get pre-eclampsia they develop high blood pressure during their pregnancy and their kidneys malfunction. Babies who are born too small or of women afflicted with pre-eclampsia can suffer from many immediate health problems. These problems include breathing and feeding difficulties. Women and babies who survive these complications of pregnancy are prone to developing heart disease later in life. Unfortunately, there are no effective treatments for these pregnancy disorders. We propose that an abnormal inflammatory response in the mother causes fetal growth restriction and pre-eclampsia. A hypothesis is that this abnormal maternal inflammation leads to restriction in the flow of maternal blood to the placenta. This restriction in blood flow to the placenta is important for the development of these disorders of pregnancy. Using a rat model, we will test this concept and will explore potential therapies. If we can prevent fetal growth restriction and pre-eclampsia we may also be able to decrease the risk of cardiovascular disease later in life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Receptors controlling natural killer cell functions in anti-tumor immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; IMMUNE SYSTEM; RECEPTORS; SIGNALING; TYROSINE PHOSPHORYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Natural killer (NK) cells are cells of the immune system that play a critical role in the protection of humans against cancers such as leukemias and lymphomas, as well as against viral infections. This activity is especially dependent on the presence of a family of molecules expressed at the surface of NK cells, named the SLAM family of receptors. SLAM family receptors stimulate the ability of NK cells to kill cancer cells, through a molecular mechanism requiring a group of small molecules located inside the NK cells termed the SAP family of adaptors. One of the SAP family adaptors, SAP, is mutated in a human disease named X-linked lymphoproliferative disease, which is characterized by a high frequency of lymphomas. Our recent work uncovered that, in cells lacking SAP, the SLAM family receptors are converted into receptors that suppress the ability of NK cells to respond to cancer cells. This change likely explains in significant part why NK cells from XLP patients fail to protect against lymphomas.    Over the past years, there has been increasing interest towards using NK cell-directed therapies in an adjuvant setting for anti-cancer treatment. However, a better understanding of NK cell regulation is needed to ensure that promising breakthroughs are made in this area. In this proposal, we want to understand better how SLAM family receptors control the ability of NK cells to kill tumor cells. We believe that the studies proposed will not only improve our understanding of the functions of SLAM family receptors, but will also help identify molecules that could be targeted to develop new treatments to control tumor cells and, perhaps, virus-infected cells.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
DomainesScientifiquesFR: REPRODUCTION/GROSSESSE; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Experimental Therapies to prevent pulmonary hypertension and promote lung vascular growth in congenital diaphragmatic hernia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; LUNG; NEWBORN; PERINATAL; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION; REGENERATION; REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH) is a common birth defect affecting 1/2000 live birth. CDH occurs in the baby during pregnancy: there is a hole in the diaphragm (a sheet that separates the belly from the chest). This causes the stomach, liver or gut to move up into the chest. This makes the space in the chest very small and pushes aside the lungs and the heart. Mostly the lungs can't grow making them very small at birth. Babies with CDH have a very hard time breathing at birth and need a mechanical ventilator to stay alive. The breathing problems in these babies are due to two things: (1) Small lungs and (2) high blood pressure in the lung (also called pulmonary hypertension). Today, there is no treatment to make the small lungs grow or lower the blood pressure in the lung in babies with CDH. Because of that up to 40% of babies with CDH die; survivors have long-term health problems, mostly due to ongoing pulmonary hypertension during later childhood. The problem in these babies is that there are not enough blood vessels in their lungs. We will try to make more blood vessels in the lung to prevent or rescue pulmonary hypertension. We will do this by using a cell (the building blocks of our body) that can make new blood vessels. This cell is called an endothelial (the inner layer of the blood vessel) progenitor (a founder) cell, also known as EPC. We found that EPCs exist in the growing lung and that they help the lung grow; in CDH, we want to show that these EPCs don't work as well, and this is why the lungs are small and have high blood pressure. We will use this information to test if giving additional EPCs can make the lung grow and prevent or rescue pulmonary hypertension. Thus, we may discover a new treatment for pulmonary hypertension and improve the outcome of babies with this devastating birth defect. Our findings could also help patients with other diseases in which there is a problem with too few blood vessels such as heart attack, stroke or preeclam

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES
TitreApplicationTitle: Early childhood behavior: Relations to early brain structure/function and maternal mood
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD NEUROBEHAVIOR; FETAL NEUROBEHAVIORAL DEVELOPMENT; INFANT NEUROBEHAVIOR; NEUROIMAGING; PRENATAL ANTIDEPRESSANT EXPOSURE
Abstract-Résumé: Mothers' mood disorders during pregnancy and the antidepressant medicines used to treat them appear to have effects on the developing baby and may contribute to childhood behavioral disturbances. The reasons that some children are affected and others are not remains unclear. In earlier work, we have shown that brain blood flow is altered in the fetus of pregnant women taking antidepressant medications called serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SRI). Owing to recent advances in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) now provides us with the unique opportunity to understand if the changes in brain blood flow are associated with differences in early brain development and child behavior. To answer this question, we will study 3 groups of mothers and their children (depressed/SRI-treated; depressed/non-SRI-treated; and healthy controls) at 4 time points (36 weeks gestation; neonate day 2 and 6; age 24 months). We believe that our work will help us to understand more about very specific areas of early brain develop¬ment that shape child behavior and should lead to improved healthof these children and their mothers.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: New molecular targets in gouty arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CHEMOKINES; GOUT; INFLAMMATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Gout is a form of arthritis, a disease which is one of the most prevalent chronic inflammatory disorders in North America; about 1 in 50 people will develop gout over a lifetime. Gout is characterized by a chronic inflammation of the joints and a progressive destruction of cartilage and bone. It is a painful and incurable process. One of the distinctive features of arthritic joints is their massive infiltration by white blood cells, and in particular neutrophils. The latter have been proposed as a source of several inflammatory mediators (including cytokines) that are present at high levels inside inflamed joints. A recent study, which found that neutrophils are indeed essential to the initiation of arthritis in a murine model, strongly supports this view.  In this proposal, we focus our efforts on cellular signaling intermediates that control the production of cytokines by neutrophils in response to the causative agent of gout, i.e. monosodium urate (MSU) crystals. We have recently identified new cellular intermediates (mainly kinases) that are involved in this important neutrophil response, and we suspect that under conditions that closely mimick the physiological context in which neutrophils interact with MSU crsytals, more such intermediates will be unveiled. From this work, key regulators will emerge, that can be exploited for therapeutic intervention. Accordingly, we believe that molecule-driven strategies, such as the ones we propose herein, have the potential to reap important benefits for the health of Canadians, and in particular ageing citizens, who are most susceptible to suffer from painful acute gout attacks.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of c-Kit and insulin receptor signaling interactions in regulating pancreatic beta-cell function and islet vasculature
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CELL SPECIFIC C-KIT TRANSGENIC MICE; C-KIT WV MUTATION MICE; CROSS-TALK BETWEEN C-KIT AND INSULIN RECEPTORS; HIGH-FAT DIET DIABETES; INSULIN RECEPTOR/INSULIN RECEPTOR SUBSTRATES; ISLET BIOLOGY; ISLET VASCULATURE; PI3K/AKT/GSK3B SIGNALING PATHWAY; STEM CELL FACTOR/C-KIT RECPTOR; VEGF EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is one of the most common metabolic diseases, affecting over 2 million Canadians. It is associated with a multitude of complications (vascular, limb, kidney, eye), leading to considerable morbidity and a major medical as well as financial burden on society. One of the major defects in diabetes is the loss of beta (insulin-producing) cells in the pancreatic islet. The reasons for this beta cell loss are incompletely understood. From studies over several years, we have determined that the c-Kit receptor is critical for the development as well as functioning of beta cells in both the rodent and human pancreas. Recently, we engineered a mouse model that over-expressed c-Kit specifically in the beta cells: we saw an increase in their expression of not only the insulin receptor but also VEGF, a factor that stimulates capillary development, and the pancreatic islets showed an increase in capillary networks. We now propose to determine the mechanisms by which c-Kit has these effects as both insulin production and the degree of vascularity are critical for islet development and function. We believe that these studies will enable us to create more physiologically relevant cell-based approaches for the treatment of diabetes.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences humaines, sciences sociales, droit et éthique appliqués à la santé
AreasOfScienceEN: SOCIETAL & CULTURAL DIMENSIONS OF HEALTH; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH
DomainesScientifiquesFR: DIMENSIONS SOCIALES ET CULTURELLES DE LA SANTÉ; RECHERCHE SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the normativity of health innovation design through the public appraisal of prospective sociotechnical scenarios
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICAL AND SOCIAL ISSUES; HEALTH INNOVATION; PUBLIC UNDERSTANDING OF SCIENCE/TECHNOLOGY; QUALITATIVE METHODS; SOCIOLOGY OF INNOVATION
Abstract-Résumé: The technologies that enter the health care system often generate usability problems (e.g., underuse, overuse or misuse) and questionable social transformations (e.g., pervasive monitoring, dependence upon specialized expertise, being and living "at risk"). Nevertheless, whether their design -the shape they take, the functions they perform and what users may accomplish through their use- has been well thought out is rarely questioned. The goal of our three-year study is to examine the ways in which a prospective method developed in the Netherlands can enrich current understandings of health innovation design.  Our research will focus on three areas where technological opportunities are already emerging and which will alter significantly the moral choices of future generations: enhancement technologies in teenagers, preventive interventions for genetically "at risks" adults, and ageing in a high-tech world. Our team will create plausible scenarios that depict how technical and social changes may affect, within a 20-year timeframe, these three health care areas. We will develop video clips and short stories illustrating each scenario. The three scenarios will then be debated by members of the public in face-to-face focus groups and through an online forum. Our premise is that the use of fiction within deliberative contexts that foster participants' creativity and reflexivity will enable our team to examine a large range of values and usability issues associated to these three thematic areas. As more complex forms of health innovation keep emerging, there is an acute need for user-friendly tools for debating and pondering the direction taken by technological change in health care. Intervening earlier in the development of health technology may not only help reduce undesirable effects, but may also pave the way for the design of more valuable innovations.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - B: Heart and Circulation
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; GÉNOMIQUE, PROTÉOMIQUE ET BIOINFORMATIQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Circadian Control of Cardiac Remodeling
Keywords-MotsClés: CIRCADIAN; DIURNAL RHYTHM; HEART FAILURE; INNATE IMMUNITY; MICROARRAY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; PHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Body processes in mammals cycle with a 24-hour day-night (circadian or diurnal) rhythm, which is controlled by molecular clocks in the brain and other tissues. Cardiovascular disease appears to follow a day-night rhythm as well.  For example, heart attacks (myocardial infarction or MI) are more likely to occur in the morning than at night.  Disturbing rhythms (e.g. shift work or sleep disorders) increases likelihood of heart disease and death.  In preliminary studies we show remarkable variation in gene activity in the heart; 13% of heart genes display rhythmic expression over 24-hour diurnal cycles.  Moreover, we show that disturbing rhythms worsens heart disease; damage subsides only when rhythm disruption ceases.  Rhythm disturbance is a major health risk.  We further demonstrate that timing treatments with body rhythms (chronotherapy) may improve outcome of patients with heart disease.  However circadian control of cardiac remodeling is a major yet relatively unrecognized issue.  We will now determine i) how rhythms and their disturbance contribute to cardiac dysfunction, ii) the molecular circadian mechanisms that affect the structure and function of the heart and how it remodels in disease, and iii) how timing of therapy with ACE inhibitors can improve outcome post-MI.  This represents a fundamental new approach to understanding and treating heart disease. This novel strategy can ultimately benefit patients in clinical settings.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics of Aging in Drosophila
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DROSOPHILA; GENETICS; IMMUNITY; LIFESPAN
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is a universal but poorly understood biological process that involves a complex interplay between environmental and genetic factors.  Model organisms, such as C. elegans and Drosophila, have provided an opportunity to search for and identify specific genes that affect lifespan. To date, these studies have identified several genes that can regulate the lifespan of these organisms. Importantly, several of these genes also appear to correlate with increases in lifespan in both mice and centenarians suggesting that model organisms will provide a valuable tool to identify genes that regulate human aging. We have previously used Drosophila to search for genes that can affect lifespan and found that increased expression of the SOD1 gene or Mgat1 in the neurons of normal flies increases their lifespan by up to 40% and 135%, respectively. These exciting results demonstrate that single genes acting in specific cells such as neurons, can have a profound effect on the lifespan of an organism.  More recently, we have also found that the immune system plays an important role in regulating lifespan although the precise mechanisms involved remain unknown.  The goal of our current research program is to utilize powerful genetic methods available in Drosophila to identify and characterize genes that act within the immune system to increase lifespan. These studies will provide insight into the genetic basis of aging.  More importantly, genes that affect lifespan in an organism could serve as targets for potential therapeutic manipulation of normal aging and could delay the onset and progression of age-related disorders.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: The molecular basis of host cell invasion by Apicomplexan parasites
Keywords-MotsClés: APICOMPLEXAN PARASITES; HOST-PARASITE INTERACTIONS; PLASMODIUM SPECIES; RECEPTOR-LIGAND COMPLEXES; STRUCTURAL BASIS OF VIRULENCE; STRUCTURE GUIDED DRUG DESIGN; THERMODYNAMICS; TOXOPLASMA GONDII; VACCINE ENGINEERING; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Apicomplexan parasites cause significant morbidity and mortality in humans and animals. The two most important genera with respect to human health are Toxoplasma and Plasmodium, the etiological agents of toxoplasmosis and malaria, respectively. Unlike many parasitic diseases, Toxoplasma infections are highly prevalent in developed countries. In fact, one of the largest global water-borne outbreaks of toxoplasmosis occurred in Victoria, British Columbia that affected more than 4000 individuals. Toxoplasma infections produce a wide array of disease states with the most serious derived from congenital transmission, which can result in abortion, neonatal death and fetal abnormalities. Children that survive prenatal infection are likely to suffer a significantly reduced quality of life displaying neurological deficiencies such as mental retardation. Nearly 20% of chronic stage patients develop severe ocular disease and recent investigations suggest that toxoplasmic cysts, originally thought to be asymptomatic, are known to increase risk of brain cancer and neurological impairments such as schizophrenia. Plasmodium spp. are devastating pathogens that place nearly half the human population at risk of malaria, leading to more than 250 million cases yearly with over one million deaths, of which 85% are children under the age of five. Given the clear impact on human health, novel treatments targeting Apicomplexa are desperately needed. A major obstacle, however, is the ability of these parasites to evade the host immune response by taking refuge inside host cells. Determining how these parasites achieve this is central to controlling their pathogenesis. The objective of our research, therefore, is to characterize the strategies used by Apicomplexan parasites initially engage and ultimately invade host cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Fluid Retention and Displacement in the Pathogenesis and Treatment of Sleep Apnea
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOELECTRICAL IMPEDANCE; COMPRESSION STOCKINGS; FLUID RETENTION AND REDISTRIBUTION; SLEEP APNEA PATHOGNESIS AND TREATMENT; ULTRAFILTRATION
Abstract-Résumé: The main treatment for sleep apnea is continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). Although effective in most patients, many cannot tolerate it. It is therefore important to develop new approaches to sleep apnea treatment. We have proposed that fluid retention in the legs during the day and its head ward shift into the neck and/or lungs when lying down to sleep at night contributes to the development of obstructive and central sleep apnea (OSA and CSA, respectively). If so, one new approach to the therapy of sleep apnea might be to prevent this nocturnal headward fluid shift.  To test these possibilities, we aim to  determine whether: 1) intravenous fluid infusion during sleep will cause fluid accumulation in the neck, narrow the throat and induce OSA; 2) the relative degree of fluid shift into the neck and lungs at night is associated with OSA and CSA, respectively; 3) prevention of fluid retention in the legs during the day by compression stockings in otherwise healthy subjects, and removal of excess fluid in patients with kidney failure by ultrafiltration will reduce daytime fluid retention in the legs and head ward fluid shift at night and thereby alleviate OSA. If so, we will have developed an alternate therapeutic approach to sleep apnea.

ResearchClassEN: DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS; CARDIOLOGY
ClasseRechercheFR: DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES; CARDIOLOGIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Injectable Formulations For Growth Factor Delivery
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCOMPATIBILITY; BIODEGRADABLE POLYMERS; CONTROLLED RELEASE; HEPATOCYTE GROWTH FACTOR; POLYMER SYNTHESIS; THERAPEUTIC ANGIOGENESIS; VASCULAR ENDOTHELIAL GROWTH FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Peripheral arterial disease is a condition in which arteries in areas such as the lower leg become blocked. This blockage results in the cells in the tissue fed by the blood in the artery becoming starved, leading to pain, loss of function, and local cell death. The long-term outcome of this disease is amputation of the afflicted limb. One approach to treating this condition is to locally deliver protein drugs that initiate and control the generation of new blood vessels into the area surrounding the blocked artery. These new vessels will feed the tissue that is being starved. To do this, the protein drugs need to be delivered over a period of weeks, and current methods of accomplishing this objective are ineffective. We will examine the possibility of using a low viscosity, biodegradable polymer as an effective delivery vehicle for these protein drugs.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Cell adhesion and migration in the vertebrate gastrula
Keywords-MotsClés: CADHERIN; CELL ADHESION; CELL MIGRATION; EPHRIN; PLANAR CELL POLARITY; TISSUE COHESION; TISSUE SEPARATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cell migration is a fundamental process in the embryo as well as in the adult organism. It contributes to normal development, but it is also a major factor in medically relevant processes such as tumour metastatis, the immune response, or wound healing. In the embryo, cells often have to migrate from their sites of origin to the places where they will eventually be required, and incorrect migration leads to aberrant development and congenital malformations. We study embryonic cell migration in a simple, inexpensive vertebrate model system, the African clawed frog. We ask how cells can migrate as part of a coherent tissue mass, a frequently encountered mode of cell movement. Furthermore, we examine mechanisms which prevent this migrating cell mass from invading adjacent tissues. We found that several genes involved in tumour progression are involved in the control of these migration and tissue separation processes, and we will continue to study their detailed function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of a voltage-gated potassium channel mediated suppression of an axon guidance defect in C. elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE DEFECTS; EVA-1 RECEPTOR; FACILITATION OF UNC-6/NETRIN ATTRACTION; POTASSIUM CHANNEL; SAX-3/ROBO RECEPTOR; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION MECHANISM; SLT-1/SLIT AXON GUIDANCE CUE; SUPPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding the molecular mechanisms that prevent spinal cord regeneration will ultimately identify methods for pharmaceutical interventions that should overcome the hurdles a neuron must overcome to grow and be guided to its normal target cell or tissue type (e.g., another neuron type or muscle). However, identifying these blocking mechanisms and drugs to overcome them will be a painstaking, time-consuming process. On the other hand, changing the electrical excitation/excitability of a neuron is much easier to accomplish, but so far this approach has worked only slightly and only in a few cases to facilitate regeneration in model mammalian systems (e.g., guinea pig). We have recently identified a novel phenomenon in the model developmental animal C. elegans that offers renewed hope that changing the electrical excitability of a neuron will help it to grow to its correct target. We found that the neuron growth and guidance defects caused by mutations in a specific axon guidance cue called slit can be almost entirely suppressed by a mutation known to cause alterations in the electrical excitability of the neuron.  Our proposal is to attempt to understand whether this suppression of an axon guidance defect results from altered electrical excitability of the neuron or from alteration of a molecular signalling cascade affected by the suppressor mutation, and what signalling mechanisms are involved. In either situation these studies should provide unprecedented insights into neuronal mechanisms that can be manipulated to facilitate functional nervous system regeneration.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; LEUCEMIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Mitochondrial delivery of DNA-alkylating anticancer agents
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICANCER AGENTS; DNA ALKYLATING AGENTS; MITOCHONDRIAL DRUG DELIVERY; PEPTIDES
Abstract-Résumé: We are developing compounds that evade the resistance mechanisms that cancer cells use to override the effects of anticancer therapies.  By delivering the drug to a unique site within the cell, therapeutic molecules are hidden from deactivators and made more potent and effective against resistant cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Fungal Drug Resistance and Morphogenesis by Hsf1
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIAL DRUG RESISTANCE; CANDIDA; FUNGAL MORPHOGENESIS; FUNGAL PATHOGENESIS; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTION; HSF1; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MICROBIAL GENOMICS; STRESS RESPONSE; TEMPERATURE SENSING
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer patients and other individuals with reduced immune function, such as those with HIV or undergoing surgery or organ transplantation, are vulnerable to life-threatening fungal infections. Candida species are the most prevalent causes of fungal infection, with mortality rates approaching 50%. Fungal infections are notoriously difficult to treat, in part because fungi are closely related to humans and it is challenging to identify drugs that kill the pathogen but not the host. The efficacy of antifungal drugs is compromised by the emergence of drug resistance.    This research is focused on dissecting the molecular mechanisms by which fungi acquire drug resistance and regulate morphogenesis, which is a trait critical for virulence, or the ability to cause disease. The capacity to thrive at human body temperature is a pre-requisite for a human pathogen, and temperature is a central cue governing fungal drug resistance, morphogenesis, and virulence. This research focuses on the central regulator of the heat shock response, Hsf1, which regulates expression of ~3% of the genome in response to elevated temperature. We recently discovered that Hsf1 regulates drug resistance and morphogenesis of the leading fungal pathogen of humans, Candida albicans. Here, we will investigate the mechanisms through which Hsf1 regulates drug resistance, morphogenesis, and virulence.  Further, we will evaluate the potential of targeting the heat shock response in the treatment of life-threatening fungal infectious disease.  Targeting the human Hsf1 counterpart provides a promising therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases and cancer, and modulation of fungal Hsf1 may also hold great therapeutic potential. Elucidating the circuitry through which Hsf1 regulates drug resistance, morphogenesis, and virulence is poised to both reveal new insights into the fundamental biology underpinning temperature sensing and establish novel and much-needed strategies to save human lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inflammatory markers, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and the longitudinal course of adolescent bipolar disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT; BIOMARKER; BIPOLAR DISORDER; BRAIN-DERIVED NEUROTROPHIC FACTOR; CARDIOVASCULAR RISK; CLASSIFICATION; ENDOTHELIAL FUNCTION; GENOTYPE; INFLAMMATION; LONGITUDINAL STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a severe recurrent mood disorder that affects 2-5% of adolescents and adults. BD involves repeated episodes of mania (elated or irritable mood together with other symptoms) and depression (sadness or lack of interest/pleasure along with other symptoms). Until now, the assessment of adolescents with BD has been highly subjective. BD that occurs during adolescence is considered even more severe than in adults.  This makes the search for biological markers particularly important. Another major problem in BD is early heart disease. Biological markers may also improve our understanding of the link between BD and heart disease. The overall aim of this study is to learn whether specific markers in the blood can help us better understand the course of symptoms, and the increased risk of heart disease, in BD. We are using an advanced technique to examine blood vessel functioning. This gives us an estimate of future heart disease risk. We are comparing symptomatic adolescents with BD to healthy adolescents. We are also looking at changes in biological markers and blood vessel functioning after BD symptoms improve. We predict that the same biological markers are linked both to symptoms and heart disease risk in BD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Work and Health in Later Life: Pathways and Social Patterning in Comparative Context
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COMPARATIVE; EMPLOYMENT; HEALTH; LATENT GROWTH CURVES; LIFE COURSE; LONGITUDINAL DATA; OPTIMAL MATCHING ANALYSIS; RETIREMENT; WELFARE STATE
Abstract-Résumé: In developed countries, people are living longer, healthier lives. As the 'baby boom' generation sits on the precipice of retirement, their better health has policy makers worried about the costs of supporting retirees for longer periods of time. The problem and one of its most widely-touted solutions, extending working life, are talked about mainly in economic terms, and with reference to average improvements in health. As a result, we know very little about the health implications, for individuals, of this policy approach. Is continuing to work at older ages realistic only for those in better health to begin with, or for those with certain privileges? Will the better-off gain, in health terms, from extending working lives, while the less-well-off are harmed? Or, is continuing to work likely to benefit all, and perhaps even reduce health inequalities among older adults? Our study tries to answer these questions by analyzing health and work information collected over many years, on people over the age of 50 in the US, Britain, Germany, Denmark and Italy. We anticipate that our results will help guide Canadian policy makers as they grapple with the issues raised by an ageing and increasingly healthy population.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Canadian HIV quit smoking trial: Tackling the co-morbidities of depression and cardiovascular disease in HIV+ smokers
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; DEPRESSION; HIV; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; MENTAL HEALTH; SMOKING CESSATION
Abstract-Résumé: With newer antiretroviral therapy (ART), people living with HIV/AIDS (PHAs) have greater life expectancies.  However, in aging with HIV, new problems have emerged for PHAs such as increased heart disease. PHAs are much more likely to have a heart attack compared to non-PHAs. While the reasons for this are complex, a leading cause of heart disease is cigarette smoking and nearly half of all PHAs smoke cigarettes. Quitting smoking is very difficult for most people. For smokers who are also experiencing depression, smoking relapse rates are much higher. Since nearly 50% of all PHAs report symptoms of depression, it is not surprising that many PHAs have trouble with quitting smoking. To date, little research has examined methods to help PHAs stop smoking. This exciting research proposal brings together a dynamic multi-disciplinary team of Canadian researchers who will directly evaluate different strategies to determine the most helpful method to assist PHAs quit smoking and to "stay quit". Two hundred and fifty-six PHAs recruited from HIV clinics across Canada will be randomly distributed into one of four groups: (i) varenicline (a medication which helps reduce cravings for nicotine) with counseling designed to address HIV and depression; (ii) varenicline with standard care; (iii) the nicotine patch with counseling designed to address HIV and depression; or (iv) the nicotine patch with standard care. We will then evaluate which of these strategies is most helpful. After antiretroviral therapy, quitting smoking is likely the single most effective way to improve quality of life and to reduce smoking-related illnesses such as heart disease, stroke, lung disease, and cancer among PHAs. We believe that our proposed bilingual "Canadian HIV Quit Smoking study" will provide a significant contribution towards promoting physical and mental well-being and quality of life among PHAs across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural Mechanisms of Motion and Texture Perception
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MOTION/TEXTURE PERCEPTION; NEURAL MODELING; NEUROPHYSOLOGY; NON-FOURIER; OPTICAL IMAGING; SECOND-ORDER; VISION; VISUAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Our rich and effortless perception of the complex mixtures of objects and surfaces comprising the everyday visual world is one of the most remarkable achievements of the human brain. Immediate and accurate parsing of this rich sensory array is crucial in order for us to perform everyday tasks such as object recognition, spatial cognition and visuomotor control. Such high-level visual operations can only be achieved on the basis of meaningful low-level neural representations of gradients and discontinuities of simple visual features such as changes in luminance, contrast, texture, or motion. These neural signals can enable critical basic operations such as detecting figure-ground boundaries, or disambiguating whether contours arise from changes in surface reflectance, illumination, or occlusion boundaries. These low-level processes necessarily precede higher-level visual functions such as object recognition, and are fundamentally important to normal visual perception. The outcomes of this work may enable our understanding of anomalies of the visual system in aging and in clinical pathologies, and the design of tests to assess them. This research will focus on evaluating the idea that gradient or boundary information from luminance and from non-luminance (contrast, texture, motion) cues are initially detected by separate mechanisms, and then combined in different ways to solve different computational problems. The proposed projects will utilize single unit and local population electrophysiology with multi-electrodes, optical imaging, and system identification using natural images, exploiting modern methods of spike waveform classification, time-spectral histograms, and current source density analysis. This research is novel and significant because it attacks the problem of how simple visual features are assembled to provide a basis for perception in complex everyday scenes.

Abstract-Résumé: Sensitization to amphetamine, a drug of abuse commonly referred to as "speed" is a phenomenon resulting in an individual experiencing, after some time, when being again exposed to the drug, a heightened response to the drug, despite the fact that the dose remained unchanged. This process is often long lasting and more likely to develop when the drug is repeatedly administered within the same environment. It works as some form of intrinsic memory, hard wired in brain cells, particularly those using the neurotransmitter dopamine, and recalled at re-exposure with some amplification of effects. This process also occurs upon exposure to repeated stress. It is believed to play a role in why certain individuals develop craving for some of the effects of drugs, hence abuse them or why others become increasingly vulnerable to the consequences of stress, to the point of developing catastrophic reactions to subsequent aversive events, which, in some cases, may trigger the onset or relapse of various forms of mental illness.  The proposed application has two main objectives: the most important is to build on progress, made during the past 5 years,to unravel the mechanisms at play during sensitization. Experiments are designed to study whether sensitization to stimulants involves stable changes of brain chemicals other than dopamine and brain circuits other than the basal ganglia. The second objective of the application, expands the scope of the research towards other forms of brain plasticity, for which long term changes in the hard wiring and functioning of brain chemicals, in response to negative environments, biases emotion regulation and perturbs behavior. Emphasis here will be on the conditioning to fear, experienced in the face of trauma.

Abstract-Résumé: Patients who have suffered peripheral tissue or nerve damage from a trauma, such as an injury or illness, often experience chronic pain.  Chronic pain can happen rapidly after trauma and often persists for months or even years.  Effective clinical prevention and treatment is simply not available due to a poor understanding of the molecular mechanisms involved in chronic pain.   There have been very few studies which have reported possible long-lasting changes during chronic pain, however we believe discovering these changes is essential to our understanding and treatment of chronic pain.  In previous research the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) has been identified as a key area of the brain where changes occur in states of chronic pain. In this renewal proposal, we plan to use integrative experimental approaches to investigate long-lasting, late changes in the ACC neurons during chronic pain.  Using the newly developed 'green' transgenic mice, we will identify those neurons that are responding to pain.  We will then investigate synaptic changes in activated neurons in states of chronic pain.  Understanding of these alterations provide basic mechanisms for how pain is processed in the brain, why chronic pain is resistant to common pain medicines, and will help guide future research into medical treatment for chronic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Outcomes for Adults with Generalized Anxiety Disorder:  Combining Cognitive-Behavioural Treatment and Interpretation Modification Training
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE-BEHAVIOURAL TREATMENT; GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER; INTERPRETATION MODIFICATION TRAINING; INTOLERANCE OF UNCERTAINTY; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; TREATMENT OUTCOME
Abstract-Résumé: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a condition characterized by chronic and excessive worry and anxiety. Our group has developed a cognitive-behavioural treatment (CBT) for GAD that has been tested in four previous clinical trials. The findings show that 60 to 70% of affected individuals attain GAD remission and that 50 to 55% achieve high endstate functioning following the treatment. Although these numbers are encouraging, there remain a considerable proportion of individuals who do not fully benefit from treatment. In our most recent CIHR-funded treatment study, we assessed the impact of information processing on the efficacy of CBT for GAD. Our findings show: a) that the tendency to negatively interpret ambiguous information at pre-treatment was associated with greater GAD symptoms at post-treatment; and b) that patients who were less successful at changing their negative interpretation style were also less responsive to CBT. Given that computerized interpretation modification training has been shown to be effective for decreasing the negative interpretation style of anxious individuals, the goal of the current proposal is to determine whether such training can augment the efficacy of CBT for adults with GAD. A total of 138 individuals with a primary diagnosis of GAD will be randomly allocated to one of two conditions: a) CBT plus interpretation modification training or b) CBT plus non-active training. CBT will consist of 14 weekly sessions, with interpretation modification training (or non-active training) administered prior to each session. Measures of GAD symptoms and vulnerability, psychopathology, generalization, and interpretation style will be administered at pre-, mid-, and post-treatment, as well as at 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-month follow-ups. The proposed study will provide information about the efficacy, clinical usefulness, and mechanisms of interpretation modification training in combination with CBT.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and Preliminary Testing of a Risk-Factor Targeted Intervention to Promote Successful Recovery Following Total Knee Arthroplasty
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ARTHRITIS; DEPRESSION; DISABILITY; JOINT REPLACEMENT; MUSCULOSKELETAL; PAIN; PSYCHOLOGICAL RISK FACTORS; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with severe osteoarthritis of the knee may be considered candidates for knee replacement surgery (Total Knee Arthroplasty; TKA). Although TKA yields significant benefit, it appears that 15-30% of patients will continue to experience pain, mobility restrictions, and disability following surgery. The primary purpose of the proposed research is to develop a 10-week rehabilitation program that will promote successful recovery following TKA. In the first phase of the research, the materials (Information Video, Client Workbook) for the program will be developed. In the second phase of the research, we will ask patients who have already undergone TKA to view the program materials and indicate whether they would have participated in such a program had it been available to them. In the third phase of the research, a sample of 50 patients who are scheduled for TKA will be invited to participate in the intervention program. We will be interested in examining whether the program leads to improvements in pain, mood, and overall participation in day-to-day activities. Pain and distress following TKA have been a neglected topic in health care, ultimately contributing to unnecessary suffering and disability. At present, few if any rehabilitation centres offer services for elderly individuals recovering from TKA. We hope that the intervention we develop will contribute positively to the quality of life of individuals who are recovering from TKA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mapping Neural Function in Individuals with DCC Haplotype
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE MOLECULES; BRAIN DEVELOPMENT; DOPAMINE; GENETIC IMAGING; NEUROANATOMY; NEUROIMAGING; NEUROPSYCHIATRIC DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: In some people the initiation of voluntary movements on one side of the body leads to identical involuntary movements on the other side. Very recently one of the genes ('DCC') was identified. By coincidence the DCC gene has been studied extensively in animal models. The affected animals also show movement disturbances as well as altered brain wiring ('connectivity') and changes in the brain pathways that release dopamine, a chemical transmitter known to affect responses to rewards including drugs of abuse. Based on these observations, we now plan to use modern neuroimaging methods to map (i) brain wiring and function in motor pathways, and (ii) dopamine function in reward pathways in people who carry the DCC mutation. The results are expected to substantially help us understand this specific disorder and more broadly how certain genes guide brain development and the tendency toward various biological and behavioral traits. With this information, new directions could be developed for treating neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of CdGAP (Cdc42 GTPase-activating  protein), a negative regulator of the oncogenic small GTPases  Rac1 and Cdc42
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; LIVE CELL IMAGING; RHO GTPASES; RHOGAPS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TGFBETA SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is the result of deregulated cellular processes such as cell proliferation (increased number of cells, "nodule"), cell morphology (the shape and color of the cell are changed), cell movement and attachment (the cell will move from one site to another site or organ, "metastasis"). My laboratory is studying small molecules, named Rho GTPases, which are implicated in the regulation of these cellular processes. They act as switches that can be turned on or off, and are important both in the functions of a normal cell as well as in the regulation of processes leading to cancer. I have previously identified a novel protein, named CdGAP, which can turn off the Rho GTPases. CdGAP is the member of a large family of proteins and there is now much evidence suggesting that these proteins are affected in human cancers. Moreover, we have recently demonstrated CdGAP as a positive modulator of breast cancer cells. Therefore, we are using molecular and cellular approaches to better understand the role of CdGAP in breast cancer. The goal of this research proposal is to understand at the molecular and cellular level how CdGAP functions in the cell. Understanding how CdGAP is regulated and functions in the cell will provide novel molecular targets for therapeutic agents against breast cancer and will provide invaluable tools to screen human cancers for this protein. This will lead to the reduction of the incidence, morbidity, and mortality from cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Angiogenic factors in identifying placental intrauterine growth restriction.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENIC FACTORS; BIOMARKERS; DIAGNOSTIC TESTS; ENDOGLIN; INTRAUTERINE GROWTH RESTRICTION; PLACENTAL GROWTH FACTOR; SOLUBLE FMS-LIKE TYROSINE KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: During pregnancy, the placenta (afterbirth) carries oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood to the fetus (unborn baby). Sometimes, the placenta does not work properly and the fetus does not receive enough oxygen and nutrients to grow normally. These fetuses are small and sick. They require extra doctor's visits and may need to be delivered early. If the fetus is delivered too early, it may not survive. When the placenta is making the fetus small, it is called placental growth restriction.  On the other hand, some fetuses will be normally small. These fetuses may have small parents and is supposed to be small. These fetuses are healthy and the placenta is giving them enough oxygen and nutrients to properly. These fetuses do not need extra monitoring by the doctor and do not need to be delivered early.  When a fetus is found to be small during an ultrasound, it is difficult for the doctor to tell why the fetus is small. The doctor cannot tell if the fetus is normally small or has placental growth restriction. In most cases, normally small fetuses are treated like placental growth restricted fetuses. They will have unnecessary monitoring which is expensive and may be delivered earlier than needed.  It would be useful for doctors to have a blood test that could identify small fetuses with placental growth restriction. We have found three proteins in the mother's blood that changes when the placenta is not working properly. We will test whether or not the amount of these proteins in the mother's blood can correctly tell us if the fetus is small because of the placenta or because it is normally small. If we find that these proteins can identify placental growth restriction with certainty, it will help doctors focus extra monitoring only on the sick fetus during pregnancy. It would help save healthcare money and resources. It would also help prevent early delivery of the normally small fetus during pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the Signaling Events Modulating Endurance Exercise-mediated PGC-1a Sub-cellular Localization in Skeletal Muscle.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOPURINOL; CO-IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; MITOCHONDRIA; MITOCHONDRIAL DNA; MITOCHONDRIAL-TARGETED ANTIOXIDANT; REAL TIME RT-PCR; ROS SIGNALLING; SKELETAL MUSCLE; TANDEM MASS SPECTROMETRY; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last 50 years, the proportion of the Canadian population over 65 y has nearly tripled, with a concomitant rise in the incidence of aging associated chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, etc. Investigating mechanisms that may prevent chronic diseases and enhance the quality of life has become a public health priority. The foremost risk factor for many debilitating chronic diseases is lack of physical activity leading to obesity, poor fitness, and eventually skeletal muscle atrophy. A key player in the loss of muscle mass associated with inactivity is mitochondrial dysfunction. Mitochondria are cellular "powerhouses" that harness energy to sustain day-to-day activities. Low mitochondrial quality/content is strongly implicated in cancer, obesity, cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes. Epidemiological studies have shown that endurance exercise training extends life expectancy, and reduces morbidity and physical disability; but the exact mechanism(s) are unclear. We have shown that the "conductor" in this process termed PGC-1a responds rapidly to endurance exercise and goes into both the nucleus and mitochondria of the cell, but we do not know what the initiating signals are for this coordinate induction. Animal studies have shown that elevation in PGC-1a content protects from muscle atrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction in old mice. Our proposed study will utilize endurance exercise in healthy mice together with antioxidant supplementation to provide an insight into the cellular signals that dictate PGC-1a mitochondrial localization and promote mitochondrial health. Understanding these mechanism(s) could lead to effective countermeasures for future interventions in diseased populations as targeted means of improving mitochondrial, and therefore muscle health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Household environmental framework pertaining to childhood obesity: Improving our measures of the familial environment
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD OBESITY; FAMILIAL ENVIRONMENT; ITEM BANK; NUTRITION; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PSYCHOMETRIC; QUESTIONNAIRE DESIGN; VALIDATION
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood obesity is rapidly increasing in Canada as well as in all developed countries. Since the family is important in shaping children's behaviours, parents can profoundly influence children's physical activity and dietary habits. Certain parenting practices (e.g., restrictive and controlling practices) have a more negative impact on a child's ability to develop healthy behaviours while other practices have more positive effects. Although parenting practices are widely recognized as an important target for family-based intervention, our ability to understand the influence of the family is hampered by our ability to measure parenting practices. Researchers have developed different ways to measure parenting practices related to physical activity and nutrition; however no agreement has been reached in the scientific community. To remedy this situation this study proposes to first engage the international scientific community in developing a common conceptual framework for assessing parenting practices related to physical activity and nutrition. We will then use this information to standardize our measurement of parenting practices by developing a bank of items. We will assess the validity and reliability of the parenting measures by administering the bank of items to 3150 parents of children 3 to 16 years of age. Lastly, we will conduct a pilot study with 88 families to assess relationships among parenting practices, children's behaviours, and children's weight. Findings from this study will provide the groundwork for future research aimed at understanding the influence of parenting practices. Having better methods to assess how parenting affects a child's weight is relevant to both the research community and health practitioners, and is necessary for designing effective interventions to identify the active component of the familial environment in relation to childhood obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sex, gender and equity in prescription drug access, appropriateness, and affordability
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS; AFFORDABILITY; APPROPRIATENESS; EQUITY; GENDER; PRESCRIPTION DRUGS; SEX
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research will generate important evidence from previously uncorrelated data on how biological and social dimensions of sex and gender influence equity in prescription drug access, appropriateness, and affordability. The research team will employ advanced statistical methods to conduct five interrelated projects that draw on available population-based data: market research data, linked administrative health care data, and national surveys. They will produce an edition of the Canadian Rx Atlas that will focus on sex- and gender-related aspects of medicine use across Canada. They will study how patterns of medicine use are affected by an individual's sex, age, income, ethnicity, and place of residence. They will measure factors contributing to exposure to and outcomes from potentially risky medicine use during pregnancy. They will also quantify how different proposals for a national pharmacare program will affect women and men differently and how these differences change depending on an individual's age, income, and household composition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Seeking the fundamental function of the Timp gene family.
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW NICHE; CELL-CELL COMMUNICATION; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELL; SKELETAL REMODELLING; TIMP GENE FAMILY
Abstract-Résumé: Do Timp genes matter in biology?  Together, the 4 genes of the Timp family control the activity of more than 75 metalloproteinase enzymes that act as molecular scissors outside of the cell as well as on the cell surface. Uncontrolled activity of these enzymes is observed in numerous human diseases, and our past research has shown how individual TIMPs provide a checkpoint for these molecular scissors in cancer, arthritis, heart disease, liver disease and inflammation. However, since TIMPs can substitute for each other, it has not been possible to learn what normal biological processes absolutely depend on this family. To address this question we have successfully generated TIMPless mice that entire Timp gene family. These mice survive embryonic development but die by 10 weeks of age. They display major skeletal abnormalities with disappearance of the growth plate cartilage and loss of bone density. Blood stem cells reside in the bone marrow cavity and give rise to different immune cells. We have evidence these cells are also affected in TIMPless mice.   We postulate that TIMPs play a fundamental role in regulating key signals that affect bone cells and developing immune cells.  The two major goals of our proposal are:   1) To fully identify the timing of bone changes, the cell types responsible for these alterations and the molecular signals that are disturbed due to loss of the Timp gene family;   2) To determine precise changes in blood cell subpopulations and understand if these are caused by loss of Timps in the blood cells or in the surrounding bone cells.  Many pharmaceutical companies have developed drugs to block metalloproteinase activity, but these have met with poor success in the clinic. By understanding the fundamental TIMP-mediated control of these molecular scissors in physiological states, our findings will provide new insights for better application of these drugs.
