Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN UTERINE MYOCYTES; IN-CELL WESTERN ASSAYS; MYOSIN LIGHT CHAIN KINASE; MYOSIN LIGHT CHAIN PHOSPHATASE; PHOSPHORYLATION; PRETERM LABOUR; PROTEIN KINASE C; RHOA-ASSOCIATED KINASE; RT-PCR; WESETRN IMMUNOBLOTS
Abstract-Résumé: Premature birth is the major problem in modern Obstetrics. In Canada, approximately 9 percent of babies are born prematurely. These babies account for 75 percent of all newborn deaths and for the majority of disabilities such as cerebral palsy, mental retardation, blindness, and learning disabilities that persist through childhood and adult life.  There is no evidence that our current treatments to prevent preterm birth result in healthier newborns.  Obstetricians often attempt to stop premature labour by using muscle relaxants to stop premature labour. Unfortunately, these drugs not only affect the uterus but also the muscles of the mother's arteries. This causes low blood pressure that can have very harmful effects for both mother and baby.  We have recently discovered that the muscle cells of the uterus contain a unique mechanism that regulates contractions. Since this mechanism is not present in the muscle cells of arteries, we propose that we can use drugs to selectively prevent premature contractions of the uterus without lowering mother's blood pressure or causing other significant side effects. Several drugs have already been developed to inhibit this unique mechanism in the uterus. We propose to investigate these drugs in uterine muscle and in maternal arteries using tissues from pregnant rats as well as tissues donated by women with normal pregnancies who are having a cesarean section. We also propose to test these drugs in an animal model (rats) to see if they will prevent normal or premature labour. These experiments will ensure that the drugs will effectively stop the uterine muscle from contracting and have no effect on arterial tissues.  Our results could provide the evidence needed to test these drugs in clinical trials with pregnant women who are either at risk of premature labour or in whom premature labour has already started. Finding a successful method to prevent premature birth would be of tremendous benefit not only in Canada but globally.

TitreApplicationTitle: The first characterization of functional CYP450 activities in human cardiac myocytes: Modulation of cardiac potassium channel block due to the local metabolism of QT-prolonging drugs.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; CYTOCHROMES P450; DRUG METABOLISM; HEART; HUMAN; POTASSIUM CHANNELS; QT-PROLONGING DRUGS
Abstract-Résumé: Conventional concepts in pharmacokinetics propose that enzymes (CYP450s) in the liver and intestines are key determinants of the systemic exposure to a drug. As well, it is known that the free drug concentration in tissues is an important factor to consider while predicting drug action and toxicity. In that sense, our laboratories have accumulated data indicating the expression of drug metabolizing enzymes in the heart (human and animal species) and suggesting their role in the control of intracardiac concentrations of drugs. Therefore, we propose to conduct the first study characterizing the functional activities of CYP450s in human heart tissues. Indeed, we were the first laboratory in the world to develop a reliable method for the preparation of human cardiac microsomes that retain metabolic activities. We also have a unique access to 180 human ventricular samples from explanted hearts of patients who underwent cardiac transplant and 7 normal hearts that could not be transplanted. Using these tissues, we have demonstrated the presence of CYP450 mRNAs in the largest cohort of human ventricular samples ever studied. Our next steps are to demonstrate the functional activity of these enzymes, to characterize the specific activity of various isoenzymes using probe drug substrates, to determine the functional activities of theses isozymes towards the metabolism of selected cardiovascular drugs, and finally, to demonstrate that local metabolism of these drugs can effectively change their action. Our study will provide us with very valuable information helping us better understand inter-subject variability in drug action and toxicity. This will also establish the basis for the development of better drug regimen for the treatment of cardiovascular diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Diagnostic Episodes of Care in Patients with Early versus Late Cancers
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO CARE; ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; CANCER; DIAGNOSTIC DELAY; EARLY DETECTION; MULTI-LEVEL ANALYSIS; POPULATION-BASED; RETROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Project Summary: Cancers are more curable when they are diagnosed early. Cancer screening tests can detect a cancer before symptoms are present, but many cancers do not have screening tests. Also, many patients with screenable cancers are actually diagnosed after symptoms start. We are interested in how cancer patients come to be diagnosed and which patients are more likely to be diagnosed early.  Previous research: People who live in poorer neighbourhoods, recent immigrants, and people living in rural areas have a higher chance of being diagnosed late. Our previous work has also shown that the amount of time it takes to get a diagnosis can be longer than it should be, possibly affecting the chance of an early diagnosis. No one has looked carefully at this time period to understand why, for some people, the process is quick and for others it is not. Project description: We will study colorectal, breast, and head and neck cancers. We will use data from the Ontario Cancer Registry and cancer stage data linked to data about all the contacts that patients had with the healthcare system. We will describe and assess predictors of the length of time it takes to get a cancer diagnosis and what aspects of that process are associated with delay. We will look for factors that predict who is a risk of a late diagnosis and we will look for diagnostic paths that are more likely to lead to an early diagnosis. Impact and relevance statement: Our results could be used to better inform programs and guidelines on the cancer diagnostic process which could ultimately increase the number of people who survive. Our results could also help doctors know which of their patients is at risk of a late cancer diagnosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Étude transdisciplinaire du cancer du sein au Mali
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTHROPOLOGIE; CANCER; ETHNOETHIQUE; GENOMIQUE; MALI; SEIN; TELOMERE
Abstract-Résumé: Au Mali, le cancer du sein est un grave probleme de sante publique puisqu'il est plus frequent que dans les pays du Nord et qu'il touche beaucoup de jeunes femmes.  De plus, les patientes ont souvent tendances a se tourner vers les medecines alternatives, ce qui retarde leur prise en charge par le systeme de sante et diminue leurs chances de guerison. Afin d'ameliorer le sort des patientes maliennes nous devons comprendre tous les aspects de leur maladie, ce qui nous permettra d'elaborer des strategies pour ameliorer leur prise en charge medicale.  Je vais tout d'abord etudier les inquietudes et la souffrances des femmes face a leur maladie, les raisons qui les poussent a suivre des traitements traditionnels et l'impact de leur culture et leur famille sur cette decision.  J'evaluerai aussi si les femmes de certains groupes de la population malienne sont plus a risques que d'autres de developper un cancer du sein.  A la lumiere de tous ces resultats, j'essaierai de comprendre les differences biologiques et genetiques qui expliquent la frequence elevee de ce type de cancer chez les jeunes femmes.  Toute les portions de mon etude me permettrons d'acquerir l'expertise necessaire pour mettre en place un systeme de prise en charge mieux adapte en fonction des patientes maliennes en plus de developper un traitement plus efficace contre ce type de cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the Protective Mechanism of Phospho-N17 Huntingtin in Huntington's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CELL BIOLOGY; FLUORESCENT LIFETIME IMAGING MEASUREMENT; FORSTER RESONANT ENERGY TRANSFER; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; LIVE CELL IMAGING; MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES; NEURODEGENERATION; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington's disease (HD) is one of a family of neurodegenerative diseases that occurs in mid-life that affects 1 in 6000. The exact cause of Huntington's disease is a mutation in the gene that codes for the huntingtin protein. From the last 5 years of CIHR funding, we have discovered important new functions for the huntingtin protein mediated by a small region of 17 amino acids (N17). N17 can be chemically modified in brain cells by kinase enzymes. This modification affects two amino acids that are located near the HD mutation. Based on our work, others have shown that if we can keep N17 modified, HD does not develop in the mouse. In 2011, we made two important new discoveries: that this critical modification can be prevented or increased by drugs called kinase inhibitors; and that huntingtin has an important role at the cell cytoskeleton during cell stress.  We have discovered that mutant huntingtin is not properly modified in N17, but that drugs can restore this. These drugs are under development for other diseases by pharma, which has led to new collaborations.  In the next 5 years, we will use sophisticated methods of microscopy that analyse properties of light behaviour in living cells, or Biophotonics. From these methods, we can watch in real time in live cells how the drugs we have identified can restore the mutant protein to a less toxic form. Our goals are to extend this technology to measure the shape of huntingtin protein from cells derived from HD patents, and eventually create an assay that can be used on patient blood samples. This assay can be used as a marker of disease progress, or to tell us if drugs are working in patients. There are tremendous advantages to studying neurodegeneration in Huntington's disease, as there is a single defined cause, and this disease could be used to model drug discovery in more complex neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac Surgery in The Frail and Elderly; Towards optimal decision making in a vulnerable population.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; CARDIAC SURGERY; HEALTH SERVICES DELIVERY; INFORMED CONSENT; PATIENT CENTREDNESS; SHARED DECISION MAKING; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Before providing treatment for a disease doctors must obtain an 'informed consent'. It is important to provide patients with detailed information about the risks, benefits and alternatives to the proposed treatment. While this is a requirement that has been around for a long time, recent studies show that fewer than 30% of patients (30 in 100) understand the risks, benefits, and alternatives to any given treatment. This applies to surgical procedures, like cardiac (heart) surgery. It is even more important in groups where the risks are high. Over the last few years the patients facing potential cardiac surgery have become older, sicker, and are having more complex operations. Thus, their risks have increased. We propose to test an entirely new approach to 'informed consent' where we take patients through a formal teaching process where they learn about their disease, and its potential treatment options. Risks, benefits, and alternatives are emphasized, including not only risk of death, but issues of the likelihood of returning to the same or better quality of life as they currently have. This process will entail high quality educational materials and an informed consent form that details the particular patient's individual (patient specific) risks based on their risk factors. The entire process emphasizes patient choice, and demands that the patients take an active role in choosing the treatment that is best for them. This approach is called shared decision making, and recognizes the patients as the experts in their values and goals for their lives. To show if we are making a difference with this new approach we will assess: Patient Comprehension of the procedures and their disease; Patient Anxiety; Decisional Conflict (the degree to which patients feel confident and comfortable with their choice); and an exit interview where patients provide important information around the informed consent process that is not covered in the formal measures above.

TitreApplicationTitle: CRFR-mediated sensitization of 5HT2A receptor signalling in anxiety and depression
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; CRF RECEPTOR; ENDOCYTOSIS; RECYCLING; RESENSITIZATION; SEROTONIN RECEPTOR; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a widespread and serious disorder that affects the daily lives of 10-15% of Canadians.  There are multiple potential causes of depression, including genetic predisposition, but the majority of cases are influenced by environmental factors.  Nevertheless, treatments currently available for the treatment of depression/anxiety remain less than optimal in terms of onset of action, response, remission rates, and side-effect profiles.  The prevalence and severity of, as well as vulnerability to this disorder is commonly associated with stress.  Corticotropin releasing factor (CRF) is a major stress response regulator and CRF receptor 1 antagonists have demonstrated antidepressant effects for patients with major depression.  We have found that the activation of CRF receptor 1 sensitizes anxiety behaviours mediated by the activation of serotonin (5-HT) 2A receptors in the brain and find that peptides that block the interaction of PDZ domain containing proteins can prevent CRF receptor 1-mediated sensitization of 5-HT2A receptor signaling in cell culture.  Therefore, present grant focuses on three specific aims: 1) To identify the PDZ protein mediating CRF receptor 1-dependent sensitization of 5-HT2A receptor signaling. 2) To understand the consequence of PDZ protein interactions with CRF and 5-HT receptors. 3) To assess effect of peptides designed to block PDZ protein interactions with CRF and 5-HT receptors on CRF receptor1-mediated sensitization of 5-HT2A receptor-mediated anxiety behaviour in mice.  The longterm goal of our experimentation is to design better pharmacological treatments of stress-related anxiety and depression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Metabotropic Glutamate Receptor Scaffolded Signaling Complexes
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; CAMKII; ENDOCYTOSIS; G PROTEIN SIGNALING; METABOTROPIC GLUTAMATE RECEPTOR; NEUROSCIENCE; SPINOPHILIN
Abstract-Résumé: Glutamate is the major excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain. Glutamate acts via two types of glutamate receptors families expressed at connections between neurons and allows for the transmission of information from one neuron to the next and is essential for memory and learning. This proposal focuses on the mechanism(s) by which the activity of metabotropic glutamate receptors is regulated by proteins that interact with these receptors inside of the cell. Alteration in the cellular regulation of metabotropic glutamate receptors has been associated with neuronal cell death in a variety of neurodegenerative diseases including: Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease. The present proposal focuses on proteins that we have identified to interact with glutamate receptors and how these interactions affect the activity of the receptor proteins. Specifically, we have identified two important regulators of neuronal function that have been linked to memory and learning as glutamate receptor binding proteins (calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II and spinophilin). We propose to : 1) identify where these proteins interact the receptors to develop inhibitory peptides, 2) how they contribute to regulating the function of these receptors, and 3) to determine whether a loss of protein expression might effect cellular mechanisms underlying memory and learning. In addition, we propose to assess the contribution of glutamate receptors to the pathology associated with Alzheimer's disease in a Alzheimer mouse model. Specifically, we will assess whether glutamate receptor expression is upregulated in Alzheimer's disease and whether a loss of glutamate receptor expression will slow disease progression in mice. Understanding the role of mGluR signaling in Alzheimer's disease is essential for the development of new therapeutic targets for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Seminolipid homeostasis: its significance in male reproduction
Keywords-MotsClés: ARYLSULFATASE; ELECTROSPRAY IONIZATION MASS SPECTROMETRY; GLYCOLIPID; LYSOSOME STORAGE DISORDER; MALE FERTILITY; SEMINOPLID; SERTOLI CELLS; SPERM; SPERMATOGENESIS; TESTICULAR GERM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Male infertility occurs in 9% of couples, frequently with unknown causes, leading to excessive use of assisted reproductive technology despite the possible negative health consequences on the children born.  Research to find bio-indices of male fertility is greatly needed.  Seminolipid (aka SGG), present at a high level in mammalian male germ cells, is essential for development in the testis, as shown in experimental animals.  SGG on mature sperm is also important for fertilization.  We have recently shown that homeostasis (balanced levels) of SGG in testes, as regulated by Sertoli cells, is relevant for sperm production and sperm fertilizing ability, especially in older males (40 years in men).  Sertoli cells are oblong somatic cells spanning the tubules in the testis, where sperm are produced.  Tight junctions at the basal part of the tubules exist between adjacent Sertoli cells, forming a barrier that excludes blood components from entering the compartment above.  Developing germ cells are in this compartment and nourished by nutrients secreted from Sertoli cells.  Sertoli cells also 'clean up' germ cells that have undergone apoptosis (programmed death), which occurs at a high rate in normal testis.  Certain molecules of apoptotic cells, when existing at high amounts, are toxic to Sertoli cells, and need to be degraded in their lysosomes (organelles with degradation enzymes).  SGG is one such molecule that has to be degraded by arylsulfatase A in Sertoli cell lysosomes.  The failure of this degradation leads to 'lysosomal storage disorder' in Sertoli cells and subsequently a disability to support germ cell development.  Production of good-quality sperm is also compromised in older males.  Our proposed research will provide a better understanding of the significance of SGG homeostasis in male fertility. TitreApplicationTitle: A Randomized Phase III Trial of Preoperative Chemoradiotherapy  vs Preoperative Chemotherapy for Resectable Gastric Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMOTHERAPY; CONTROLLED CLINICAL TRIAL; GASTRIC CANCER; RADIOTHERAPY; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, stomach and esophageal cancer are the 9th and 10th leading causes of cancer death respectively. For patients with stomach cancer, surgery may cure those with localized cancer, but most patients present with more advanced cancer and when treated with surgery, cancer will recur in 70% of patients. Thus, surgery alone is not an adequate treatment. There are currently two 'standard' methods used worldwide to treat patients whose stomach cancer is more advanced - either treatment with chemotherapy before and after surgery, or a combination of radiation plus chemotherapy following surgery. We believe that combining these two approaches will provide even greater benefit, especially if the combination of radiation plus chemotherapy is given prior to surgery. This randomized controlled trial will build on research conducted to date and compare chemotherapy given both before and after surgery with or without adding concurrent chemotherapy + radiation before surgery. The proposed trial is being conducted in Canada by an established network of Canadian cancer investigators known as the NCIC Clinical Trials Group and includes participation by groups in Australia and Europe. The objective of this trial is to determine whether adding chemo-radiotherapy improves patient survival. Important secondary outcomes include evaluation of quality of life, toxicity, cost-effectiveness, cost-utility. The trial will include 750 patients from across the world, including approximately 375 from Canada, and will take 8 years to complete.

TitreApplicationTitle: Randomized Trial Comparing Radical Hysterectomy and Pelvic Node Dissection vs Simple Hysterectomy and Pelvic Node Dissection in Patients with Low Risk Cervical Cancer Defined as Lesions Measuring Less than 2 cm with Less than 50% Stromal Invasion
Keywords-MotsClés: CERVICAL CANCER; COST UTILITY ANALYSIS; INTERNATIONAL MULTICENTRE; PATIENT REPORTED OUTCOMES; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SURGICAL ONCOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Cervix cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in women. Most recent statistics estimate that almost 500,000 women globally will be diagnosed with cervical cancer each year and more than 270,000 annually will die from it. Due to effective screening strategies in developed countries, the incidence of cervical cancer has decreased but the proportion of young women presenting with low-risk early-stage disease has increased. The traditional treatment for these women is radical hysterectomy. This is a very effective procedure and has a high cure rate, but is associated with potentially severe and long-lasting side-effects. These include impairment of bowel, bladder and/or sexual function and infertility, which may lead to poorer quality of life. Some gynecologists who specialize in cancer surgery believe a less extensive surgical procedure (simple hysterectomy) will provide the same cure rate as radical surgery and will reduce the chances of the adverse effects described above. However, no studies have directly compared the effectiveness and the short and long-term side-effects of simple and radical hysterectomy in women with low-risk early stage disease. There is a need to determine which procedure is optimal and to standardize treatments. The proposed trial, CX.5, will be led by an established network of Canadian cancer investigators known as the NCIC Clinical Trials Group and will include participation of other international groups. The objective of CX.5 is to determine whether simple hysterectomy is as good as radical hysterectomy in preventing cancer from recurring and better in preventing the side-effects associated with surgery. Important secondary outcomes include evaluation of quality of life, measures of sexual health, and cost-effectiveness and cost-utility analyses. The trial will include 700 women from across the world, including 135 from Canada and will take 8 years to complete.

TitreApplicationTitle: Image-guided Mitral Valve Repair
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC; IMAGE FUSION; IMAGE-GUIDANCE; MECHATRONICS; SURGERY; VALVE REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Over  the last five decades the success of heart-valve surgery has continued to improve.  Unfortunately however, this type of surgery remains an open heart procedure,  requiring the use of the heart-lung machine and that the heart be stopped in order to be able to perform the repair or replaement. This procedure, even when performed through a small  incision between the ribs without  needing to cut the breast bone, is still relatively invasive, having the possibility of significant side effects and lengthy recovery times. We believe that the progress towards less invasive therapies in valve surgery generally has been hampered by the lack of specialized tools with sufficient maneuverability and the lack of adequate image  guidance for navigation and targeting of these tools. The development  of such tools along with  three dimensional visualization, navigation, and guidance will ultimately result in improvements in delivery of less invasive interventions, better patient care, fewer complications, and reduced operating and post-operative recovery times.   The most frequent cause of a leaky mitral valve of the heart is a tear or elongation of the attachments that anchor    the valve to the heart muscle. The treatment of this disorder involves replacements of this torn tissue with artificial sutures made from gortex material,  generally performed as an open heart procedure on the static heart. For this procedure be performed less invasively in a closed beating heart approach, we propose the development of steerable tools that can be inserted into the heart chambers through an opening in the bottom of the heart. The tools can be tracked and visualized while being controlled remotely. With the guidance of the three dimensional ultrasound navigation and pre-operative models, artificial sutures can be properly placed on the valve and then anchored to the heart muscle. Success of this proposal will also open the door  for other less invasive beating-heart procedures.

Abstract-Résumé: This is a multi-disciplinary, interview based study to follow up on questions revealed by the Ethics Narratives in Humanitarian Aid (ENHA) project. This study will seek to understand ethical issues related to health-oriented humanitarian aid in disaster and disaster recovery in low income countries. We will explore ethical considerations at organizational levels as well as for frontline humanitarian health care providers, to see how these interact and intersect. In order to gain a fuller understanding of ethical issues in humanitarian disaster response, we will also explore the perceptions of local health providers and patients for their views on the ethics of humanitarian health care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms and consequences of atrial ionic remodeling
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIARRHYTHMIC DRUGS; ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; FIBROBLASTS; ION CHANNELS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; REMODELING; WHOLE ANIMAL ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The heart normally beats regularly at a rate that is appropriate for the body's needs. This function is carefully regulated by a highly sophisticated cardiac electrical system that controls the timing and beating rate of cardiac contraction. Sometimes the system goes wrong and the normal rhythmicity of the heart becomes irregular and/or too fast. One condition in which this occurs is called atrial fibrillation, often abbreviated "AF". AF affects about 25% of the population in the course of their lives, and can lead to serious complications including cardiac weakening and strokes from clots formed in the heart. Studies suggest that, at least in some individuals,  AF increases the chances of dying. The purpose of this research program is to discover the causes of AF, in particular by examining highly-specialized channels in cardiac membranes that control electrical functioning. Animal models and isolated cell systems will be used to study the basis, nature and significance of the channel changes occurring with and causing AF. This information will then be used in attempts to develop new safer and more effective treatments for AF.

TitreApplicationTitle: Causal relationship between a LC-omega-3-enriched diet and cognition
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; APOLIPOPROTEIN E EPSILON 4; BLOOD TRANSPORT OF OMEGA-3 FATTY ACIDS; BRAIN UPTAKE; DOCOSAHEXAENOIC ACID; EICOSAPENTAENOIC ACID; FATTY ACID BRAIN COMPOSITION; LIPID METABOLISM; LIPOPROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Nutrition is key to healthy aging for a number of diseases but we have reported imbalances in the distribution of long chain omega-3 fatty acids (LC-omega-3) in the elderly and in the carriers of apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 (APOE4) isoform. Carrying APOE4 isoform is currently recognized as being the most important genetic risk factor of cognitive decline. We believe that dysregulation of LC-omega-3 metabolism is intimately link with higher risk of cognitive decline. The current project will investigate whether there is a causal relationship between LC-omega-3-enriched diet and cognition using, on the one hand, a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled design and on the other hand, transgenic mice carrying human APOE4. In both study, we will focus specifically on the distribution (level) of LC-omega-3 into lipoproteins with age and/or APOE4 isoform to evaluate whether dysfunctional transport of LC-omega-3 is associated with lower cognitive scores on visuospatial capacity, verbal fluency or working memory. In ApoE4 mice, we will evaluate LC-omega-3 brain uptake together with the level of LC-omega-3 in the brain membranes and the level of APOE protein within the brain. The present investigation will provide key basis for understanding how to develop nutritional strategies for healthy aging and the preservation of cognitive functions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and Functional Studies in Very Early Onset IBD
Keywords-MotsClés: CROHN'S DISEASE; FUNCTIONAL STUDIES; GENETICS; IMMUNODEFICIENCY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE (IBD); PEDIATRICS; ULCERATIVE COLITIS; VERY EARLY ONSET IBD (VEO-IBD)
Abstract-Résumé: Lay Abstract: Inflammatory Bowel disease (IBD) causes inflammation in the bowel that can lead to gut bleeding, problems with growth, and other serious consequences. Unfortunately, IBD is common in Canada affecting 1 in 250 people. Surprisingly, IBD has increased 30% over the past decade in Canada with the greatest increase seen in children diagnosed less than 10 years of age. We do not know the exact cause of IBD but understand that patients with IBD have a partial genetic component. This is especially true in very young children who have may have a much stronger genetic component to their disease than adults. These very young children often have a severe form of the disease that does not respond to treatments typically used in older children and adults. Therefore, we have undertaken genetic studies in these young children to determine the cause of IBD in these children and to determine how the genes function to cause IBD. Our recent findings have resulted in life saving treatment options and these findings will help all patients including adults with IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: SIX family transcription factors in adult muscle regeneration.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT MUSCLE PROGENITOR CELLS; DIFFERENTIATION; MUSCLE REPAIR AND REGENERATION; SATELLITE CELLS; SELF-RENEWAL; SIX FAMILY OF TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Skeletal muscle formation, or myogenesis, is a complex process controlled in large part at the transcriptional level, by a network of regulatory interactions where transcription factors (TFs) play a major role. These proteins establish various gene expression programs which enable cell fate determination, commitment to the myogenic lineage, terminal differentiation, muscle cell function, and regeneration. Multiple groups of TFs are known to be at play at each of these steps, but how they work is incompletely understood.  Six1 and Six4, two members of the Six family of TFs, have been shown to play important roles in myogenesis: their function is essential to the formation of skeletal muscle, during embryonic development. However, little is known of their molecular mode of action, and their role in the function of satellite cells, the adult muscle progenitor cells, is poorly characterized.  We have recently identified in a genome-wide manner direct target genes of Six1 and Six4. With this renewal proposal we seek to 1) gain a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms that regulate Six1's and Six4's target gene expression during muscle repair, and 2) apply this new knowledge to enhance the regenerative potential of muscle progenitor cells in view of cellular therapies in muscular dystrophy patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: A randomized trial of ThrOmbectomy vs. PCI Alone for STEMI (TOTAL trial)
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; ANGIOPLASTY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: A heart attack occurs when a blood clot forms and blocks an artery in the heart.  Traditionally, cardiologists have treated heart attack patients by re-opening the blocked artery with a balloon to break up the clot and then place stent.  A new strategy is to use a long tube to extract the clot before placing a stent to avoid the clot from going downstream and blocking smaller vessels.  Small studies suggest that the new strategy is promising and could improve patient outcomes but are too small to be definitive.  The TOTAL trial is a large international randomized trial to determine if thrombus removal (thrombectomy) vs. angioplasty alone improves outcomes in patients with heart attacks.  This trial has the potential to change the way heart attack patients are treated and to save many lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the DNA damage response by SMC complexes
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHECKPOINT; DNA REPAIR; GENOME STABILITY; NIJMEGEN BREAKAGE SYNDROME; PHOSPHORYLATION; RAD50 COMPLEX; SMC COMPLEXES; SMC5-6 COMPLEX; SUMOYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Any mistake in the repair of our genetic material is sufficient to generate genome instability, one of the most potent stimulator of cancer development. The central objective of this proposal is to understand how cells promote effective repair of DNA lesions. To achieve this objective, we focus our work on a family of proteins known as the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) proteins. Our interest in this family of proteins comes from the fact that they are known as central gatekeepers of genome stability, and mutations affecting one of these proteins cause a cancer predisposition disease, the Nijmegen Breakage Syndrome (NBS). The main aim of our work is to uncover how two SMC complexes, the Smc5-6 and Rad50 complexes, interact with damaged DNA in vitro. Then, we aim to uncover how cells regulate the behavior of these SMC complexes when they suffer DNA damage. Ultimately, our work will have a major positive impact on human health by revealing new cellular mechanisms critical for cancer development and by identifying new targets relevant for cancer treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Design of selective heme oxygenase-2 inhibitors and activators-  developing pharmacological tools
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG DESIGN; GASOTRANSMITTER; HEME OXYGENASE INHIBITION; IN SILICO DRUG DESIGN; INHIBITORS/ACTIVATORS; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: The exact role of heme oxygenase-2 is not known although results obtained from genetic models suggest that under or over-activity of this enzyme may be involved in a number of diseases. Potentially, heme oxygenase-2 could be involved in range of human conditions that affect Canadians; these include chronic pain (arguably the costliest disease in developed countries), endometriosis (which affects ~10% of women of child bearing age), blindness due to diabetes and some dementias (Alzheimer Disease).  One reason for our lack of understanding of the function of heme oxygenase-2 is the lack of pharmacological tools (drugs) that can be used to study it; we are poised to fill this void.  Thus, we have identified drug "hits" as inhibitors and activators of heme oxygenase-2.  We propose to exploits these hits as the basis of designing new and better drugs that can be used to study heme oxygenase-2 by using the breadth of expertise possessed by our research team; this includes- medicinal chemistry, x-ray crystallography, computer-assisted drug design, pharmacological testing.  We plan to lay the ground work for the full exploitation of heme oxygenase inhibitor and activator drugs by ensuring that they function in the full range of research models used in drug development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac Manifestation of Laminopathies; elucidation of the functional role of a novel muscle enriched lamin interacting protein (MLIP) in the heart.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC GENE-REGULATION; CELL FATE; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; DILATED CARDIOMYOPATHY; HEART DEVELOPMENT; LAMINOPATHIES; MOUSE MODEL; SUMOYLATION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Heart, skeletal muscle, tendons, neurons, fat, and bone are all subject to disorders called laminopathies that occur when there are mutations in the lamin A/C gene. Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is one of the heart-related laminopathies that lead to an enlargement of the heart that prevents it from beating correctly or efficiently. Very little is known about the process from which mutations in the lamin gene lead to dilated cardiomyopathy. The experiments proposed in this application are focused on revealing the specific genes that are important in the development of both normal healthy and sick hearts such as those with dilated cardiomyopathy. We have recently identified a new gene (MLIP) that is found extensively throughout muscle tissue which directly interacts with lamin, and that may regulate genes. This provides us with a unique opportunity to investigate and understand the groups of genes that are involved in DCM. By manipulating the way MLIP behaves in the heart and then evaluating its effects on the heart through the use of wide variety of established molecular and biochemical experimental methods we will be able to define the role of MLIP in the heart, in health and disease. We will map the activation and inactivation of MLIP through normal and abnormal heart development by staining hearts to visualize MLIP, lamin and other important heart genes using state of the art microscopes. By recognizing the difference between the normal and abnormal heart function, we will better understand the role of MLIP in the heart. The successful execution of this research will substantially expand scientific understanding of dilated cardiomyopathy, particularly in relation to a newly discovered, cardiac gene MLIP and lead to the development of therapeutic treatments that will more effectively treat patients (by minimizing side effects) and ultimately may also prevent some forms of heart disease from occurring in later life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeted Chemotherapy for Inoperable and Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: INOPERABLE AND LOCALLY ADVANCED PANCREATIC CANCER; LIPOSOMES; MAGNETIC RESONANCE-GUIDED FOCUSED ULTRASOUND; TARGETED DRUG DELIVERY; TARGETED HYPERTHERMIA; THERMOSENSITIVE NANOPARTICLES; TRIGGERED DRUG RELEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Pancreatic cancer is an aggressive disease with an extremely high mortality rate, with only 5% of patients surviving past 5-years after diagnosis, ranking it as the fourth leading cause of cancer deaths. Less than 20% of the patients are eligible for surgical removal of the tumors, while the rest only benefit marginally in survival, as the standard-of-care gemcitabine chemotherapy is plagued by poor delivery of the drug to the tumor. This project is focused on developing an improved gemcitabine delivery technology for enhanced treatment of patients with inoperable and locally advanced pancreatic tumors. This group represents ~35% of the total number of pancreatic cancer patients and their prognosis gives them a median survival of just 9-10 months. We have developed an improved nanoparticle formulation (HaT) that reduces gemcitabine clearance by 50-fold from the blood of mice after intravenous injection, compared to the current drug solution given clinically. HaT is stable in the blood, but releases 100% of the drug load rapidly when heated to 40-42°C, leading to a 25-fold increase in delivery of gemcitabine to the locally heated tumor (43°C), compared to the clinical formulation in a mouse model. A single treatment of HaT combined with local heating completely regresses the tumor with manageable side effects. We plan to test the efficacy and toxicity in multiple pancreatic tumor models. The mode of action of this new treatment will also be elucidated. Finally, we will employ an ultrasound system that specifically heats pancreatic tumors, with precise temperature control under MRI guidance, to promote targeted drug delivery with the HaT formulation. The long term goal is to produce an enhanced treatment for patients with locally advanced pancreatic tumors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the Tim-3 pathway in T Cell Exhaustion in HIV Infection: a goal towards developing novel immunotherapies.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANERGY; CELL SIGNALING; CYTOTOXIC T CELL; HIV; IMMUNE SYNAPSE; T CELL; T CELL EXHAUSTION; TIM-3
Abstract-Résumé: One of the greatest mysteries of Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 (HIV) infection has been to understand why the normal immune system is unable to eradicate or control this virus infection as opposed to other virus infections. Our laboratory specializes in understanding how one arm of the immune system, called the T cells, fights viruses, including HIV-1 virus, the virus that causes AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome). It has been found that these T cells that are supposed to fight HIV-1 do a bad job, and have been called dys-functional, or 'exhausted'. Recently a clue to why these T cells are exhausted was demonstrated by numerous publications that have identified some new molecules on these cells that may explain their exhaustion. Our lab has identified one of these new molecules on the surface of these exhausted T cells, called Tim-3 (T cell immunoglobulin mucin molecule type 3). We have found that Tim-3 identifies the most exhausted of these T cells, and is actually in part responsible for their exhausted state. Our current work centers on understanding how this Tim-3 molecule can make a killer T cell weak and also to figure out what signals the Tim-3 molecule sends to the T cell in order it to shut down. Our main aim it to find new ways of stopping the Tim-3 from sending 'weakening' messages to the T cell and by blocking Tim-3 signals so that the T cells can function better with the aim to allow these cells to eradicate HIV in the infected person.

TitreApplicationTitle: Poise-2
Keywords-MotsClés: NATRIURETIC PEPTIDES; NON-CARDIAC SURGERY; NT-PROBNP; OBSERVATIONAL STUDY; PERI-OPERATIVE MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; PERI-OPERATIVE VASCULAR COMPLICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Five hundred thousand adults in Canada, and 2 hundred million worldwide, have major surgery every year.  Several million of these patients will have a major heart problem (example, a heart attack or death) after their surgery.  We recently finished the worlds largest randomized trial testing the usefulness of a commonly used drug (called a beta-blocker) in patients having surgery.  This study showed that the beta-blocker prevented heart attacks but increased the risk of stroke and death after surgery.  These negative effects of beta-blockers after surgery were not known prior to our study.  Our unexpected findings indicate why we need large studies of patients having surgery, to ensure that we are providing helpful and safe drugs.  There is promising evidence that aspirin and clonidine (a drug that lowers a patients heart rate) may help prevent deaths and heart attacks around the time of surgery.  Our proposed study will determine if these drugs can prevent deaths and heart attacks around the time of surgery.  We will randomly assign patients to receive aspirin or placebo, and clonidine or placebo starting 2 to 4 hours before surgery.  Patients will continue to take their study drugs for up to 30 days after surgery.  We will follow all patients for 30 days and 1 year and note any heart attacks, deaths, strokes, or bleeding. This research will improve the treatment of patients having surgery and has the potential to save substantial health care costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolic, cardiovascular and cognitive outcomes and their determinants in young adults born with extremely low birth weights
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; COGNITION; DEVELOPMENTAL ORIGINS OF ADULT DISEASE; DYSGLYCEMIA; GROWTH; INSULIN RESISTANCE; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PREMATURITY
Abstract-Résumé: Although being born with an extremely low birth weight (ELBW; birth weight < 1 kg) is associated with health consequences in adulthood, we have much to learn regarding the contributing factors to a particular health outcome. We are learning about these health outcomes by studying groups of individuals across their lifetime. The McMaster cohort, now 29 to 33 years of age, have been comprehensively studied through childhood and adolescence and remarkably, 90% of the 150 individuals born with ELBW and 140 controls were studied at 23 years of age. We have learned important lessons from them regarding their health and quality of life. Now that they are in their fourth decade, we want to study them again, this time because some studies suggest that infants with low birth weights may have increased risk of having a heart attack related to the development of atherosclerosis or hardening of the arteries.  We plan to measure known risk factors for atherosclerosis including blood pressure, sugar metabolism, cholesterol levels and body fat. We will also measure, using ultrasound, the thickness of the lining of the carotid artery; a good marker for the amount of atherosclerosis one has. Most importantly, because this cohort has been followed since birth, we want to examine possible pathways for the development of these risk factors and atherosclerosis. Factors that might help us include measures of their nervous system, their growth, and their physical activity and fitness.  Evaluating the health of these individuals in this way will help us obtain information important to other individuals born ELBW and in a broader sense will help us learn more about what the causes of heart disease are beginning very early in life.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Children of Multiple Sclerosis: Impact of chronic disease in parents on early childhood development
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD DEVELOPMENT; DATA LINKAGE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH OUTCOMES; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The early years play a crucial role that extend far beyond childhood. Research has shown that challenges facing adult society, including mental health, obesity, criminality competence in reading and writing have their roots in early childhood. Health Canada has stated that having a parent with a chronic illness, such as multiple sclerosis (MS), puts children 'at risk.' However surprisingly little is known about what these risks are or what could be done about them. MS is a chronic illness which often first starts in early adulthood, at a life stage when parenting is an important issue for many. MS affects the brain and spinal cord, leading to disability and coordination problems; its cause is unknown. Both BC and Canada as a whole have some of the highest prevalence rates of MS in the world, with three more Canadians being diagnosed with MS every day. Our study will be one of the first to investigate developmental well-being in children with a parent affected by MS. Our research will link important province-wide data from both the education and health systems to investigate differences in the quality of stimulation, support and nurturing that children receive by the time they reach kindergarten. Our findings could then be used by communities and government to put programs and policies in place to support healthy child development for children in families affected by a parent with a chronic illness such as MS. Insights from this research may also help other patient groups, such as families affected by cancer and other chronic diseases, thereby helping to maximize the potential of all children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engineering Adipogenesis for Soft Tissue Regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOGENESIS; ADIPOSE-DERIVED STEM CELLS; BIOMATERIALS; BIOREACTOR; CELL ENCAPSULATION; CELL-MATERIAL INTERACTIONS; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; IN VITRO/IN VIVO; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research program involves the development of an engineered fat tissue substitute for use in plastic and reconstructive surgery. Injury to the fatty tissues underlying the skin results in scar tissue formation, which causes deformity and can limit patient mobility. The research team will develop new tissue substitutes for soft tissue reconstruction, including breast reconstruction following tumour removal, the correction of birth defects, and soft tissue repair following trauma, to improve patient quality of life. The long-term objective is to minimize scar tissue formation, while promoting the natural regeneration of the patient's own healthy tissues, to fully restore the natural shape and volume of the damaged tissues. One common strategy is to design a scaffold that defines the desired tissue shape, and to seed it with cells that can promote regeneration, such as stem cells. In the proposed research, the team will investigate stem cells isolated from fat, termed adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs), within a variety of naturally-derived scaffolds. Previous research has helped to identify some of the key scaffold properties that impact the ability of the stem cells to grow and differentiate into mature fat cells. While these studies have shown the promise of a cell-seeded scaffold approach, the ideal tissue substitute for safe, predictable, and long-term large volume soft tissue augmentation has not yet been realized. There is a significant need to develop a much deeper understanding of how stem cells respond within different scaffold environments in order to rationally design soft tissue substitutes. The proposed research will make significant progress towards identifying and optimizing the key scaffold properties that regulate fat formation, to engineer optimized tissue substitutes for use in reconstructive surgery.

TitreApplicationTitle: The mechanisms of secondary antibody diversification processes
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVATION-INDUCED CYTIDINE DEAMINASE; ANTIBODIES; B CELLS; CLASS SWITCH RECOMBINATION; DIVERSIFICATION; DNA REPAIR; MISMATCH REPAIR; REARRANGEMENT; SHRNA SCREEN; SOMATIC HYPERMUTATION
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system plays a major role in protecting humans from bacteria, viruses, and toxins (known as antigens). One of the ways that the immune system accomplishes this is by producing antibodies that bind to and neutralize these antigens. Antibodies are small molecules made by B cells. Each B cell makes only one type of antibody which will bind to only one antigen. Unfortunately, these antibodies usually bind weakly to their specific antigen. However, B cells have developed a way to make antibodies bind more tightly to antigens by making small changes (mutations) in antibody genes. This process is called somatic hypermutation. Through this mechanism, those B cells that produce a stronger binding antibody are then stimulated to become antibody producing B cells. B cells also change the stalk of the antibody through a process called class switch recombination. By changing the antibody stalk, the properties of the antibody are changed. For example, IgM antibodies can be changed to IgG antibodies that can be used by macrophages to engulf bacteria that are coated by these antibodies, while IgA antibodies are secreted into mucosal tissue and can neutralize pathogens in the lung or the gut. Recently, some of the enzymes that are involved in somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination have been identified, such as AID. However, much still needs to be investigated about how these two processes are accomplished in B cells and the enzymes that are involved. Our current proposal will focus on class switch recombination. We have recently identified novel genes that function in class switch recombination, and propose to investigate how these genes function in this process. Our proposed work will allow us to determine how an effective antibody response is generated. In addition, because AID and the class switch recombination process are linked to the development of lymphomas, our work will advance our knowledge on the etiology of these types of cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of hypoxia-induced immune escape in cancer and their regulation by nitric oxide
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; HYPOXIA; IMMUNE ESCAPE; IMMUNOLOGY; NITRIC OXIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Our immune system can eliminate cancer as it develops. Cells from our innate immune system destroy tumour cells on first contact without having to be primed, whereas cells from our adaptive immune system recognise and destroy cancer cells after being primed and undergoing expansion. For reasons not well understood, some cancers develop ways to avoid elimination by our immune system. This is referred to as 'immune escape'. As tumours grow, their supply of oxygen can't adequately reach all layers of cancer cells. Consequently, tumours develop poorly oxygenated or 'hypoxic' regions. We have already shown that when tumour cells are exposed to hypoxia they become resistant to destruction by cells of our innate immune system. We now propose that hypoxia also contributes to the ability of cancer cells to avoid destruction by our adaptive immune system and have evidence that it may be possible to interfere with this mechanism of immune escape in cancer. We have preliminary results in support of this hypothesis.  When cancer cells become severely hypoxic they can't produce the molecule nitric oxide (NO). We showed that when NO is not produced, tumour cells are better able to spread, to resist chemotherapy and to evade destruction by our innate immune system. We now propose that a lack of NO production by tumour cells underlies the mechanism of hypoxia-induced resistance to adaptive immunity. Our studies will examine this concept. Furthermore, we should be able to interfere with immune escape by introducing NO activity in the form of drugs that release or mimic NO.  To reach our goals, we will use cell culture and animal models, as well as pharmacological, biochemical, immunological, and molecular tools. The outcomes will increase our knowledge of how cancers evade immune destruction and will have translational value, as re-introduction of NO activity in cancer cells may be used to enhance immunotherapy, or may even be an effective 'stand-alone' therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of F-BAR proteins in lung cancer progression and metastases
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL INVASION; CELL MIGRATION; ENDOCYTOSIS; EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; F-BAR PROTEINS; LUNG CANCER; METASTASES; TUMOUR XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is one of the most frequent types of cancer, but is by far the most deadly with a 5-year survival rate of 14%.  Clearly, there is a real need for improvements in early diagnosis, and development of new therapeutic approaches. Considering that the most frequent cause of lung cancer-related death is due to the spread of lung tumours to other organs, new therapeutics designed to halt the spread of cancer cells could save lives. Our goal is to uncover key proteins involved in the spread of cancer, and thereby identify new therapeutic targets in lung cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional MRI of Brain Physiology
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN PHYSIOLOGY; FUNCTIONAL MRI; ISCHEMIA; MEDICAL IMAGING; MOYAMOYA; MRI METHODS; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) of the human brain is a technique that allows the localization of brain activity with no harmful effects.  Since its development 20 years ago, fMRI has revolutionized neuroscience research on the functional organization of the healthy human brain but its use in the clinical evaluation of patients is limited. The broad goal of our research is to extend fMRI methods beyond detecting where the activity is, to permit quantitative physiological measurements of cerebral blood flow, blood volume, and oxygen consumption.  We believe such methods are essential if fMRI is to have a major impact on the clinical evaluation and treatment of patients.  We will use our new methods to examine the baseline physiology of the brain and its responses to stimulation in both healthy subjects and patients. Specifically, we will study diseases that affect the normal coupling between brain activity and the regulation of blood flow to the brain.  The clinical conditions considered in this study will be moyamoya disease and transient ischemic attacks, also known as mini-strokes.

TitreApplicationTitle: TDP-43-mediated pathogenic pathways in ALS and new experimental therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROINFLAMMATION; SUPEROXIDE DISMUTASE; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: ALS is an adult-onset neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive degeneration of motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord. TDP-43 is a protein detected in pathological aggregates motor neurons of ALS cases and a role for TDP-43 in disease was further supported by the discovery of TDP-43 mutations in familial ALS cases. The physiological role of TDP-43 and the pathogenic pathways of TDP-43 abnormalities are not well understood. Recently, our group generated novel TDP-43 transgenic mice that mimic several features of human ALS. Here we propose to take advantage of these unique ALS mouse models to investigate pathogenic pathways associated with TDP-43 abnormalities and to test new therapeutic approaches. First, we will test whether TDP-43 abnormalities in transgenic mice is associated with misfolding of superoxide dismutase (SOD1). Second, we recently discovered that TDP-43 upregulation can enhance activity of a specific pathway involved in innate immune responses. We propose to clarify what factors trigger this pathway during aging and in what cell types this pathway contributes the most to pathogenesis in TDP-43 transgenic mice. The new TDP-43 mouse models of ALS will also be used to test new therapeutic approaches based on inhibition of this pathogenic pathway.

TitreApplicationTitle: What Shapes Food Practices on School Days? Examining the Role of the School Food Environment.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIETARY PRACTICES; FOCUS GROUPS; FOOD ENVIRONMENT; GIS; MIXED-METHODS; MULTI-LEVEL MODELS; SCHOOLS; SURVEY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Improving the eating habits of children and teenagers is a public health priority in Canada, particularly given increasing rates of obesity and nutrition-related health conditions such as type 2 diabetes. However, nutrition education interventions to date have had little success in improving what adolescents eat. Interventions would be improved with more detailed knowledge about how dietary choices are impacted by the school context where adolescents spend much of their time.  We are therefore seeking funding for a study in Vancouver schools to explore what and where students eat on school days, how and why dietary practices change when students transition to secondary school and how food choices are shaped by the food environment at school (including the policies, programs and types of foods available in and around schools).     This study will build on an ongoing SSHRC-funded community-based research project already underway in Vancouver schools that is initiating changes in school classrooms, cafeterias and gardens to improve the quality of school food and students' knowledge of where food comes from.  CIHR funding will allow us to implement a web-based questionnaire to assess food-related knowledge, attitudes, experiences and practices among students and to conduct focus groups with students. We will combine these novel data with previously collected information about the school food environment.  This study will therefore identify key school-level characteristics that are associated with student-level dietary outcomes and will take advantage of this unique opportunity to inform emerging school policies and interventions to improve the eating habits of Canadian adolescents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gonadal drugs for brain neuroprotection and neuromodulation
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; DOPAMINE; ESTROGEN RECEPTOR; GLUTAMATE; GONADAL STEROIDS; MONKEY; NEUROPROTECTION; PARKINSON; RODENT; SEROTONIN
Abstract-Résumé: Evidence supports the prime importance of steroids in the maintenance of brain function during normal aging. Men/women differences and beneficial effects of estrogens are reported in several mental diseases and neurodegenerative diseases. With the increased life expectancy and the average age of menopause remaining constant, women can expect to live up to one half of their adult lives after menopause. Hormonal replacement therapy in menopausal women was widely used up to recent clinical studies that found more risks than benefits. No better alternative is available. We propose experiments in monkeys and mice to seek compounds with estrogenic activity or that could increase estrogens in the brain to protect, decrease, prevent or delay brain diseases like Parkinson disease. We propose to investigate the mechanism of action of these compounds. Our hypothesis is that we can find novel compounds beneficial for the brain with limited side effects from existing drugs used for endocrine diseases or based on a novel target in the brain, a recently found membrane estrogen receptor. Estrogen-like compounds targeting the brain may be useful for central nervous system symptoms associated with menopause. Raloxifene is an estrogenic drug used to treat osteoporosis in menopausal women; it will be tested for brain activity. Moreover, we seek gonadal drugs useful for central nervous system diseases in men without the feminizing effects of estrogens such as finasteride a gonadal drug used to treat benign prostate hyperplasia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Factors associated with the work integration of people with severe mental disorders in social enterprises located in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: JOB TENURE; PEOPLE WITH SEVERE MENTAL DISORDERS; SOCIAL ENTERPRISES; WORK INTEGRATION
Abstract-Résumé: Close to 80% of people with a severe mental disorder are unemployed, though many are able and available to integrate into the workplace. Furthermore, job tenure is typically brief for this population. Social Enterprises (SEs) seem to offer several advantages over other social professional integration measures. In Canada, SEs are a fairly recent phenomenon with most new SEs being developed in Quebec and in Ontario. For this reason, we want to conduct research to increase our understanding of SEs located in Quebec and in Ontario. The purpose of this study is threefold: 1) Describe the profiles of employees with severe mental disorders working in SEs; 2) Identify the significant factors that predict job tenure for individuals working in SEs and 3) Examine the Return on Investment (ROI) of various SE models and conduct a cost-benefit analysis of SEs. This prospective study consists of three assessment phases for employees with severe mental disorders: Phase 1 (baseline) and Phases 2 and 3 (six month and one year follow-ups). In Phase I: Directors/Human resources managers of SEs located in Canada will be interviewed about their enterprise's structure using organizational indicators of SEs (e.g., percentage of employees with a disability). In parallel, individual and environmental data will be gathered from employees with severe mental disorders working in the SEs. Also, work outcomes (e.g., job tenure) for study participants will be gathered by Human resources every two months for one year following Phase 1. In Phase II and III (6-month and 1-year follow-ups): People with severe mental disorders will also be assessed at 6-month and 1-year follow-ups regarding variables that may change over time (e.g., work accommodation). Finally, the ROI and cost-benefit analyses (Objective 3) will take one year to complete, and will assess the value of the accommodations offered within each SE as well as mental health services used.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation and role of the ERK signalling in colorectal carcinogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT/KNOCKIN MICE; INTESTINAL EPITHELIUM; MAP KINASE PHOSPHATASE; MAP KINASE SIGNALLING; RAS/RAF ONCOGENES; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most common forms of cancer in Canada. One in 14 men is expected to develop colorectal cancer during his lifetime and one in 27 will die of it. Since the entire intestinal tissue is in a constant state of renewal, such turnover involves a countless number of cell divisions, hence a non-negligible risk of genetic alterations. This rapid rate of intestinal tissue renewal as well as exposure to toxic substances, notably through food ingestion, may explain the high prevalence of CRC. Mutations have been identified in K-Ras and B-Raf in patients with colorectal cancer. Ras and Raf proteins are two major players in the MAP kinase pathway. They are crucial downstream regulators of multiple receptor tyrosine kinase-mediated cell growth, transformation, and maintenance of the malignant phenotype in human cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of Brain-Specific ATP-Sensitive Potassium Channels by Physiological Stereoisomers of the Primary Ketone Body Beta-Hydroxybutyrate
Keywords-MotsClés: ATP-SENSITIVE POTASSIUM CHANNELS; DIET; KETONE BODIES; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA
Abstract-Résumé: Dietary and nutritional factors are well known to have profound effects on health and disease. However, only recently have physicians and scientists begun to fully appreciate the impact of metabolism on brain function and neurological illnesses. One prominent example of an effective dietary treatment is the ketogenic diet (KD), so named because ingestion of this high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet leads to the production of important chemicals called ketone bodies by the liver. The KD is a proven treatment for epilepsy, and such diets are increasingly being studied for other disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, and even brain cancer. The broad effectiveness of the KD - and in particular, ketone bodies - suggests that important biochemical pathways and affected within cells. Indeed, recent studies have shown that ketone bodies can protect brain cells from various forms of injury, likely through an action on vital cellular components known as mitochondria, which function to produce energy molecules (such as adenosine triphosphate, or ATP) and without which cells would die. The major goal of the proposed studies is to demonstrate that ketone bodies activate a peculiar channel within mitochondria, referred to as the mitochondrial ATP-sensitive potassium channel or mitoKATP - and in so doing enhances mitochondrial function and viability. Thus far, no one has convincingly demonstrated the existence of these channels, let alone characterized their properties in detail. We hypothesize that not only do these mitoKATP channels exist within brain cells, but also that they can be regulated by ketone bodies. Demonstrating a direct action of ketone bodies on mitoKATP channels will pave the way for the development of novel drugs - based on naturally occurring molecules (i.e., ketone bodies) - which could later be tested and validated in a wide range of clinical neurological disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Infant outcomes in the first year of life associated with maternal H1N1 vaccination
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SYSTEMS RESEARCH; INFLUENZA; POPULATION HEALTH; REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: This study will compare the health outcomes of infants born to mothers who received H1N1 vaccination during their pregnancy with infants whose mothers did not receive the vaccine.  We want to determine if there are differences in illness rates for respiratory infections, visits to doctors or emergency departments and admissions to hospital.  This research is important because: 1) doctors and public health officials need to be able to give accurate information to women about the short and longer term risks and benefits of receiving vaccination in pregnancy, 2) health system planners need to be able to predict how many immediate and longer-term health services will be required during an influenza outbreak or pandemic and, 3) there will no doubt be either another pandemic or emerging infectious disease that requires advance preparation to plan for all outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Contracting with Physicians:  An Alternative to Legislating Against Dual Practice?
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH LAW AND POLICY; PHYSICIAN CONTRACTS
Abstract-Résumé: Canadian provinces legislate to prevent a two-tier health care system in accordance with the Canada Health Act.  These restrictions are increasingly subject to constitutional challenge on the grounds they infringe individual rights to life, liberty and security of the person pursuant to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.  The claim is made that without the option of going private, Canadians are forced to wait long period of times in pubic queues, jeopardizing their health and even on occasion their lives.  There are two major concerns if upcoming litigation is successful in introducing a two-tier system.  First there is departure from the principle that access to care should be allocated on need and not ability to pay.  Second is the concern that wait times for public patients will grow if doctors have an incentive to spend more time treating private-pay patients. In the wake of a successful constitutional challenge, provincial governments will need to respond quickly and must now prepare for the challenges that may arise from a parallel tier and dual practice.  In this research project we explore whether provincial governments through negotiating contracts with doctors could allow a small private-pay sector for medically necessary care and ensure a strong public health care system.  The UK uses contracts in an effort to ensure that its doctors spend a sufficient amount of time treating public patients and we will examine how those contracts function and the feasibility of using a similar policy tool in Canada.

ClasseRechercheFR: GLAUCOME; TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular analysis of FOXC1
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA BINDING; FOXC1; GENE REGULATION; GLAUCOMA; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; VISION LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: For the past 15 years we have used an inherited form of glaucoma, Axenfeld-Rieger Syndrome (ARS), to study the basic mechanisms that cause this blinding condition. Glaucoma is a leading cause of vision loss in Canada, with a prevalence that increases with age. Since the average age of Canadians is increasing, blindness due to glaucoma is of great clinical importance. We have shown that mutation of the forkhead domain C1 (FOXC1) transcription factor causes ARS and glaucoma. We have determined that FOXC1 controls the expression of other genes important in ocular function. Other proteins interact with FOXC1 and in turn regulate FOXC1's function. We thus have first studied FOXC1 to determine how FOXC1 functions, and now plan to use FOXC1 to understand how disruptions in a complex network lead to glaucoma. In this grant proposal we will systematically define the FOXC1 network and then determine its role in glaucoma. We are excited that these proposed experiments might directly lead to improved glaucoma therapies in the short-term.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of microRNAs in Renal Cell Carcinoma Pathogenesis and their Clinical Utility as Tumor Markers
Keywords-MotsClés: DIAGNOSTIC MARKERS; KIDNEY CANCER; KIDNEY CANCER SUBTYPES; MICRORNA; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; RENAL CELL CARCINOMA; SERUM TUMOR MARKERS; TUMOR BIOMARKER; URINE TUMOR MARKERS; VHL
Abstract-Résumé: Kidney cancer is one of the top common cancers in North America. The Canadian Cancer Society reported an estimated 4,800 new cases and 1,650 deaths from kidney cancer in 2010. Early diagnosis of small localized kidney cancer is associated with good prognosis but unfortunately, patients often present with few symptoms and are often diagnosed at the metastatic stage when chances for a cure are dismal. There are different subtypes of kidney cancer and distinguishing between them is done using a microscope, but this can be inaccurate. Accurate identification of the subtype is important because the treatment for kidney cancer subtypes is different. Small molecules called microRNA (miRNAs) have been shown to be involved in the development and progression of cancer and may serve as biomarkers (substances that are increased in cancer and may help with early detection) for kidney cancer. Our preliminary data show that miRNAs have altered expression in kidney cancer when compared to normal kidney. Also, some miRNAs can accurately distinguish between different subtypes of kidney cancer. Our project aims to 1) test the expression of miRNAs in blood and urine of kidney cancer patients to examine their use as diagnostic markers. This non-invasive testing may help diagnosis patients in early stage so they can receive effective treatment; 2) We will confirm the use of miRNAs to help distinguish between kidney cancer subtypes. This will help patients get the most appropriate treatment; 3) In order to understand the role miRNAs play in kidney cancer, we will use kidney cancer cell line models to test miRNA effect on tumor growth and other characteristics that promote cancer. We will focus on miRNAs that we know can play a role in kidney cancer. These experiments will help us understand how kidney cancer develops which will lead to a better understanding of the cancer and the discovery of new miRNA treatments. miRNAs represent attractive new therapies for kidney and other cancers.

Name-Nom: Van Drunen Littel-van den Hurk, Sylvia
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of immune activation by respiratory syncytial virus fusion protein in virus-sized particles
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUVANT; DENDRITIC CELLS; FUSION PROTEIN; IMMUNE MODULATOR; INNATE AND ADAPTIVE IMMUNITY; MUCOSAL IMMUNITY; NEONATE; RESPIRATORY SYNCYTIAL VIRUS; VACCINE; VIRUS-SIZED PARTICLES
Abstract-Résumé: Respiratory infections are a significant cause of illness and death in children and in the elderly. Amongst all viruses involved in respiratory disease, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of brochiolitis and viral pneumonia in infants and young children, resulting in the hospitalization of up to 2% of children in their first year of life. In some children, particularly infants, RSV infections may lead to long-term consequences, such as asthma or increased susceptibility to subsequent respiratory infections. In older children, RSV is likely to be an important contributor to ear infections. RSV can also cause significant disease in the elderly and has been associated with higher mortality than influenza. Unfortunately there is no RSV vaccine. Vaccine development is challenging as newborn infants, who constitute the major target group, are not only prone to infections, they also develop weak immune responses to most conventional vaccines.  Dendritic cells are the immune cells responsible for initiating the immune response to infection and vaccination. The overall objective of this project is to understand the role of dendritic cells in the responses to RSV infection and vaccination and to develop and characterize the RSV fusion protein as a safe and effective subunit vaccine. As subunit vaccines need additional components for full efficacy, we generated a novel vaccine formulation and delivery method, which very effectively stimulate the immune system, not only systemically but also in the respiratory tract. This system will be used for development of a RSV fusion protein-based vaccine that is effective and safe in infants and young children. Such a vaccine will result in lower morbidity and mortality, and reduced long-term problems such as asthma, in all age groups, but particularly in newborn infants.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the physiology of aging by modeling longitudinal changes in networks of biomarkers in humans
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOMARKER; DYSREGULATION; HOMEOSTASIS; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; PHYSIOLOGY; PRINCIPAL COMPONENTS ANALYSIS; REGULATORY NETWORK; STRUCTURAL EQUATIONS MODEL; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Aging researchers still do not know what mechanisms and processes are responsible for aging. Many of the main theories put forward to explain aging have not been well supported by evidence. It now appears that aging is not caused by any single process, but rather by the declining ability of the body to properly regulate many biological processes. This decline arises from the difficulty in maintaining the complex systems necessary for normal functioning, complex systems that involve large numbers of molecules integrated in precisely regulated networks. Although this idea has the potential to explain the aging process, the large number of molecules, the extensive interactions and feedback relationships among them, and the long timescales make experimental approaches unfeasible, and no one has yet tested this "dysregulation" hypothesis of aging. A novel approach is required, one that simultaneously incorporates information about many molecules, their changes over time, and their relationships to each other. This project is the first such approach ever undertaken. It uses hundreds of blood and clinical measures collected in several long-term human datasets. We have access to three of the best such datasets in the world, a unique resource that will allow us to test whether our results can be generalized across different populations. We apply novel statistical methods, including techniques to (a) simplify many measures into fewer, (b) detect a faint signal among noise, and (c) assess causal effects across years. Preliminary analyses have identified multiple new pathways involved in aging and support our hypothesis of dysregulation in aging. The full project will more definitively test this hypothesis, identifying which pathways are involved and how. Understanding biological pathways will in turn allow us to identify social determinants of aging rate, develop clinical tools for measuring patient aging, and further biomedical research on chronic disease pathways.

TitreApplicationTitle: Revision and Validation of the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool in critically ill adults with brain injury
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN INJURY; CLINICAL RESEARCH; CRITICAL-CARE PAIN OBSERVATION TOOL; INTENSIVE CARE UNIT; MEASUREMENT; NEUROLOGY; NEUROSURGERY; PAIN; PSYCHOMETRIC PROPERTIES; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Brain injury such as bleeding in the brain, brain trauma, stroke, or brain tumors often require a stay in the Intensive Care Unit. During this time, patients may be unable to self-report pain. Pain left untreated can lead to poor healing of wounds, heart and breathing difficulties, and might place patients at risk for chronic pain. Being able to assess pain accurately is essential. A few tools have been developed to assess pain in uncommunicative adult patients. However, none of these tools have been specifically developed for patients with brain injury. The goal of the proposed study is to revise a pain assessment tool called the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool to make it more specific and valid for these patients. The tool will then be translated into French and both versions will be tested with a group of patients who have experienced brain injury or undergone a brain surgery procedure. Having a validated tool for brain-injured patients could help to better manage their pain and improve overall health outcomes.
