TitreApplicationTitle: Enzyme Enhancement Therapy for GM1 gangliosidosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ENZYME ENHANCEMENT THERAPY; GM1 GANGLIOSIDOSIS; LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISEASE; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; SMALL MOLECULAR THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: GM1 gangliosidosis (GM1) is 1 of ~50 Lysosomal Storage Diseases (LSDs). Although each LSD is rare as a group they account for ~1/5000 births, making them an important health problem in Canada. LSDs are genetic disorders caused by a deficiency of a single lysosomal enzyme, which for GM1 is beta-galactosidase (b-Gal). The storage material, GM1 ganglioside, is primarily made in the brain, leading to progressive neurodegeneration. No therapy is currently available for GM1. Enzyme replacement therapy has proven effective for ~5 LSDs, but cannot treat LSDs that affect the brain. For these LSDs, like GM1, small molecule based therapies hold the most promise, as they can often reach, and thus treat, the brain. One such approach is Enzyme Enhancement Therapy (EET), which uses small drug-like molecules called pharmacological chaperones (PCs). PCs are able to stabilize a mutant protein preventing its misfolding, allowing it to reach the lysosome and degrade the storage material. However, PCs are not effective for every type of mutation. We have successfully developed EETs for 2 other LSDs (Gaucher and adult Tay-Sachs) and will build on these successes to identify PCs for GM1. Two complementary small molecule libraries will be screened. A direct assay using live cells from a GM1 patient (determined by us to be responsive to EET) has been developed and is currently being used to screen the largest of these two libraries (30,000 compounds). Here we propose to complete this primary screening and further characterize and validate 10 - 20 of the compounds that produced the best enhancement of b-Gal activity in GM1 cells. The structure of the resulting lead compound(s) will then be chemically optimized for maximum efficacy. Ultimately, the optimized PC will be tested in a unique feline model of naturally occurring GM1, whose cells we have confirmed to respond to EET, by measuring levels of b-gal activity and GM1 ganglioside storage in the brain of treated versus untreated felines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translational studies of acquired resistance to antiangiogenic therapies undertaken in new preclinical models of locally advanced or metastatic cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIANGIOGENIC THERAPY; BIOMARKERS; CHEMOTHERAPY; EXPERIMENTAL THERAPEUTICS; LIVER CANCER; METASTASIS; OVARIAN CANCER; TUMOR MODELS; TYROSINE KINASE INHIBITORS; VEGF
Abstract-Résumé: One of the most frustrating aspects of cancer research is the disparity between preclinical therapy results - almost always obtained using tumors transplanted or developed in mice - with those later observed in clinical trials of the same therapy. It is not uncommon to obtain dramatic results in the preclinical models, which then fail completely in patients. One reason postulated for this discrepancy by Dr. Kerbel is the failure of basic researchers to mimic the common clinical situation of advanced metastatic disease. Advanced visceral metastatic disease is extremely challenging to treat successfully and yet has rarely been modeled. Five years ago Dr. Kerbel began developing therapy models of advanced disease in mice beginning with breast cancer. More recently he has extended this strategy to ovarian cancer. Using such models, a remarkably effective treatment was developed consisting of daily low 'metronomic' doses of an oral chemotherapy drug, topotecan, combined with an 'antiangiogenic' drug (pazopanib). Topotecan is approved for 'second line' treatment of ovarian cancer where it is usually given intravenously at toxic maximum tolerated doses. Pazopanib targets new blood vessels in tumors which are necessary for their relentless growth.   This therapy can be given every day for over six months (about 1/4-1/5 a mouse's lifespan) with 100% survival and minimal toxicity. However, resistance eventually develops to the therapy. The purpose of Dr. Kerbel's research is not only to understand the basis for the therapy's remarkable results but if it also works on refractory disease, and why tumors eventually stop responding to it. Of considerable interest in this regard is that this drug combination is showing excellent preclinical efficacy when treating other types of cancer, e.g. breast and kidney cancer, and childhood neuroblastoma. Hence, the proposed studies could have far reaching clinical implications beyond ovarian cancer.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: A novel phosphoinositide signaling pathway contributes to Salmonella pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN POLYMERIZATION; CONFOCAL MICROSOCPY; LIPID BIOCHEMISTRY; MEMBRANE TRAFFICKING; PHOSPHOINOSITIDE SIGNALING; PI3-KINASE; RHO GTPASE; SALMONELLA INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Some bacteria have the remarkable ability to invade our cells and replicate within them during infection.  Such bacteria use special toxins to alter the control systems of our cells.  These toxins cause drastic changes to the membranes of our cells, forcing them to internalize the bacteria and in the process providing them with a specialized compartment that allows the microorganisms to replicate inside our cells.  Salmonella, best known for its ability to cause food poisoning, is one type of bacteria that can parasitize our cells in this manner.  In this study we will examine how a Salmonella toxin, called SopB, can alter cellular membranes to invade our cells.  The membrane alterations caused by SopB are related to those that occur during other human diseases, including cancer, bipolar disorder and Type 2 diabetes.  Therefore these studies will provide a new fundamental understanding not only of bacterial infection but also of other human diseases, possibly allowing the development of new treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Myocardin Activity in Vascular Smooth Muscle by Proteasome Degradation
Keywords-MotsClés: ATROGIN-1; MYOCARDIN; PROLIFERATION; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; TRANSCRIPTION; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Vascular diseases, such as hypertension and atherosclerosis, result from abnormal functions of a major cell type in the blood vessels, called smooth muscle cells. Myocardin is a protein molecule in smooth muscle cells that controls the levels of proteins responsible for muscle contraction. Lower activity of myocardin will result in less contractile proteins in smooth muscle cells, and these cells will lack the ability to contract in response to various factors. They will even grow to form lesions in the blood vessel wall. Therefore, it is very important to study how myocardin activity is regulated. If we understand this, we will be able to develop a way to control vascular disease. What we have discovered in our laboratory is that myocardin must be degraded through a special system, called the ubiquitin-proteasome system, to gain its activity. We called this process "Degradation-Activation", which is novel for myocardin in smooth muscle. In the current application, we propose to investigate the Degradation-Activation mechanism for myocardin. By targeting myocardin, our study will help develop a novel therapeutic approach to vascular disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - C : Systèmes digestif, endocrinien et excrétoire
TitreApplicationTitle: Towards the prevention of type 2 diabetes: improving our understanding of longitudinal changes in glucose homeostatis in youth
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT; CARDIOMETABOLIC RISK FACTORS; COHORT STUDY; IMPAIRED FASTING GLUCOSE; IMPAIRED GLUCOSE HOMEOSTASIS; IMPAIRED GLUCOSE TOLERANCE; OBESITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 2 million Canadians over the age of one (6.2%) had diabetes in 2006-07 and this number will increase by 25% to 2.8 million in 2012. Ninety percent of people with diabetes have type 2 diabetes. Even though type 2 diabetes is still relatively infrequent in Caucasian (White) adolescents, the prevalence of impaired fasting glucose and impaired glucose tolerance both well-established pre-diabetes states, is clearly on the rise. The progression of pre-diabetes to type 2 diabetes is thought to be faster in younger individuals. The consequences of these increasing trends in pre-diabetes in youth are potentially staggering considering the severe health impact of type 2 diabetes. The true "cure" for type 2 diabetes is probably to identify the people at risk and prevent its occurrence. The natural history of type 2 diabetes has been well studied in adults and lifestyle interventions have been shown to delay and possibly prevent the development of diabetes. Such studies are extremely rare in youth, especially in Caucasian youth. Our study will address critical issues related to the natural history of pre-diabetes/diabetes in youth and the transition from normal sugar tolerance to pre-diabetes in adolescence. It will also address the issue of early predictors of abnormal sugar handling by the body and the extent to which these predictors explain why it is not all obese youth that develop type 2 diabetes. From a clinical perspective, our findings will help health professionals identify children most at risk and offer them interventions that are individually tailored. Our study will also inform the choice and timing of effective population-based interventions aimed at reducing the prevalence of pre-diabetes and type 2 diabetes in youth. Our investigation will be conducted within the well-established infrastructure of the QUebec Adipose and Lifestyle InvesTigation in Youth (QUALITY) Cohort, which will allow us to study 630 youth from childhood to late adolescence.

TitreApplicationTitle: The pivital roles of IL1B and IL6 in the timing of birth
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMANS; INTERLEUKINS; LEUKOCYTES; MICE; MYOMETRIUM; PRETERM BIRTH; RECEPTOR ANTAGONISTS
Abstract-Résumé: The most important health problem of pregnancy and birth is premature delivery. Unfortunately, there are no effective means to treat women who will delivery early to delay birth, prolong pregnancy, and improve newborn outcomes. Recent evidence from our established, experienced collaborative team has suggested that two inflammatory mediators, interleukins (IL)-1 beta (IL-1b) and IL-6, affect the timing of birth in animal models of pregnancy. We have developed many new tools to study the roles of these interleukins on the timing of birth. We believe these two mediators stimulate the recruitment of circulating white blood cells (or leukocytes) to the uterus, where they cause more leukocytes to be attracted, and release more inflammatory mediators, to convert the uterus of pregnancy into the uterus of delivery. When IL-1b is administered, animals deliver early; when the gene for IL-6 is absent, delivery is postponed. Two members of our team have developed new pharmacological antagonists to IL-1b and IL-6, and a third member has developed new mouse models where the IL-6 gene is absent. We have also found that depleting circulating white blood cells (or leukocytes), especially macrophages, a rich source of IL-1b and IL-6, leads to delayed delivery. Uterine cells respond to IL-1b and IL-6 by releasing inflammatory mediators, and our team has developed a new test to assess leukocyte activation as preparation for infiltration into the uterus. We will use all these tools to test whether IL-1b and IL-6 are necessary for the process of birth and whether our new antagonists are effective in blocking premature delivery. If they are, these antagonists can be commercialized by our investigators to develop new treatments for prolonging pregnancy in women at risk for premature delivery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing an Internet-based program for anxious youth who visit the emergency department for mental health care: A strategy to increase access to post-crisis care
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS/YOUTH; ANXIETY; INTERNET; POST-CRISIS CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Anxiety is a common mental health problem for Canadian youth. Anxiety that is diagnosed as a disorder and serious enough to require treatment affects up to 10% of all youth by the age of 16. Anxiety disorders can have serious negative effects on a young person's personal relationships, school performance, and family life. These disorders may not be discovered by youth, parents, and health care providers. Even if anxiety disorders are discovered, youth may not get the right therapy. Anxious youth can become sick if their anxiety is not treated properly.   Many youth go to a hospital emergency department when they are sick, for help with their anxiety. This is called a crisis. In Alberta, we studied these crisis visits and found that most anxious youth receive counselling and referral for follow-up care. However, the wait time can be 29 to 40 days before youth see a doctor for follow-up care. During this wait, many youth need to return to the emergency department for more crisis care. We see a need to create a treatment so that anxious youth do not have to wait for care. This treatment would help them after an emergency department visit.  Our team will carry out research to produce and test Wired!, our new Internet-based treatment for youth with anxiety problems. Youth can use this treatment from home after their emergency department visit. Wired! materials will be created and tested by our research team, with frequent input from youth and mental health professionals. Wired! will include information materials and personalized homework assignments to help anxious youth learn ways to manage anxiety. Youth could also talk to a professional therapist through an online discussion board. Our testing of Wired! will start with a pilot study with real patients. In the future, we plan full-scale scientific testing for the safety and usefulness of Wired!.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Hematopoietic transcription factors and their role in leukemogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: AML; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION AND SEQUENCING; EPIGENETICS; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; HEMOGEN; KNOCK DOWN BY RNA INTERFERENCE; LEUKEMIA; QUANTITATIVE PROTEOMICS; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is the most common form of leukemia in adults, yet it has the lowest survival rate with less than 30% of adult patients reaching complete remission. Even patients achieving pathologic complete remission after chemotherapy and bone-marrow transplant will almost invariably relapse if post-remission therapy is not administered. The major cause of the resistance to therapy is thought to be leukemic stem cells, which are present in small amounts compared to other malignant cells but are incredibly resistant to current treatments. Targeted therapies aiming at destroying specifically leukemic stem cells as opposed to current treatments that destroy all dividing cells are required to 1) achieve a better survival rate and 2) to diminish the secondary effects of current AML treatments.  We have recently identified a protein called Hemogen, which regulates the expression of genes in blood cells. Interestingly, this protein is aberrantly expressed in AML patients and its level of expression at diagnosis is inversely correlated to a favorable response to chemotherapy. Preliminary results have indicated that forced expression of Hemogen induces leukemia in mice, while removal of the Hemogen protein from cells of AML patients leads to a decrease in proliferation. All these results strongly suggest that Hemogen has an important role in initiating and maintaining leukemia in patients. In this project, we propose to use cellular and molecular approaches to identify the genes and the proteins that work with Hemogen to induce and maintain leukemia. In addition, we will remove the Hemogen protein from AML blasts and determine the extent to which this could ameliorate the disease.  These experiments are expected to reveal the role of Hemogen in the formation and the maintenance of the leukemic cells. As such, our studies are expected to identify new candidate molecular targets that could be used as a therapy to eradicate leukemic cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mental Health Wellness and Illness Knowledge and Beliefs among Low German speaking Mennonites: Development of Best Practice Guidelines
Keywords-MotsClés: MENNONITES; MENTAL HEALTH ILLNESS BELIEFS; MENTAL HEALTH WELLNESS BELIEFS; MIXED METHODS; RELIGION; RURAL; UNIQUE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: This study will focus on the Low German speaking Mennonite (LGS) families' and communities' perspectives of mental health wellness and illness and their expectations of mental health promotion and mental health care services. Mental health care providers are finding a number of challenges in providing mental health services to this population and recognize that they currently do not have the knowledge or understanding of the unique belief systems to attend to this group's specific needs. In addition, LGS Mennonites mostly reside in rural areas where mental health services are limited placing greater demands on the already stretched resources of health regions and their health and social service staff. Generating information about mental health wellness and illness among this population will demonstrate being proactive in the development of appropriate policies by decision makers and care guidelines and the health care providers that interact with the LGS Mennonite population. Importantly, the LGS Mennonites will experience more quality mental health care provided by the health professionals and social service provides who care for this population.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Genetic and Biochemical Analysis of the Novel Guidance Cue MADD-4
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAMTSL; C. ELEGANS; CELL CULTURE; EVA-1; FORWARD GENETICS; GUIDED CELL MIGRATION; MADD-4; NEUROMUSCULAR DEVELOPMENT; POST-SYNAPTIC MEMBRANE DEVELOPMENT; UNC-40/DCC
Abstract-Résumé: During the embryonic development of humans and other animals, many cells undertake relatively long-range migrations to populate new tissues. Amazingly, the paths taken by the migrating cells are largely the same in different individuals of the same species. This happens because secreted molecular cues interact with receptors on the migrating cells and guide them to their proper destination. Many inherited human diseases result from mutant genes that normally govern cell migration. In addition, the spread of metastatic tumor cells, which are responsible for more than half of cancer-related deaths, is invariably dependent on many of the same proteins that facilitate guided cell migration. A thorough understanding of the genes required for guided cell migration is therefore essential if we are to detect migration-related diseases and develop new therapies to treat them.     In my lab, we use a nematode worm called C. elegans to study the genes required for guided migration. Studies have repeatedly shown that worm genes often have similar functions in other animals, including humans. We recently discovered that motor neurons secrete a previously uncharacterized gene product called MADD-4 to attract muscle cell extensions.  MADD-4 is a member of a protein family that exists in many animals, including humans, but is poorly understood.  We suspect that MADD-4 interacts with a muscle-expressed protein complex called UNC-40-EVA-1 to direct the muscle cell extensions.  Given that very few guidance cues are known, the discovery of a novel cue is exciting.  In this grant application, we propose to: (1) Investigate how MADD-4 interacts with the receptor complex, and (2) Identify and characterize other gene products that work with MADD-4 to guide the migration of cells and cell extensions.  Given our unique reagents and the power of our model system, we are in an excellent position to provide important insight into this well-conserved, but poorly understood protein family.

TitreApplicationTitle: PP2a protein serine/threonine phosphatase mutations in cancer: functional consequences and clinical relevance
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CELL CYCLE REGULATION; ENDOMETRIAL CANCER; MASS SPECTROMETRY; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; OVARIAN CANCER; PP2A COMPLEX; PROTEIN SERINE/THREONINE PHOSPHATASES; SOMATIC GENE MUTATIONS; SYNTHETIC LETHAL GENETIC SCREENS
Abstract-Résumé: DNA sequencing technology has advanced in leaps and bounds during the last few years, and we can now sequence the genomes of tumour cells to identify the gene mutations contained within. Although this is a relatively new field, we are already making discoveries that have the potential to lead to new diagnostic tests and drug treatments for cancer patients. However, new sequencing discoveries will not make an impact on cancer treatment and outcomes without first undergoing extensive investigation and characterisation in the laboratory.   We are now nearing the final stages of a sequencing survey of many hundreds of cancers of the breast, ovary, and uterus. We have discovered that many tumours contain mutations in genes called phosphatases. Phosphatases modify proteins within the cell to change their function and are known to control processes that are disrupted in cancer cells, such as cell growth and division. It is relatively easy to modify the effects of some phosphatases using chemicals, making them an attractive target for drug development.  We propose to investigate the consequences of the phosphatase gene mutations that we have identified in tumours. First, we will check for mutations in these genes in a large number of additional breast, ovarian, and endometrial (uterus) cancers; the aim is to determine how common these genetic alterations are in each type of cancer, and whether they're associated with particular tumour sub-types. We will then determine how mutating the phosphatase genes affects the growth and division of cancer cells. Finally, we will identify genetic weaknesses that are unique to cancer cells that contain phosphatase gene mutations; this is the first step toward developing new anti-cancer drugs that specifically kill these tumour cells.  By the end of this project we will know whether a treatment based on targeting mutated phosphatase genes is likely to be effective, and if so, which cancer patients would benefit the most.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modification of Cystic Fibrosis Phenotypes in the Pancreas and Gut
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSOCIATION; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; DIABETES; GENE MODIFIERS; HERITABILITY; INTESTINAL OBSTRUCTION; MODIFIERS; PANCREATIC FUNCTION; POPULATION-BASED STUDY; STATISTICAL GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a fatal, genetic disease affecting 1 in 3600 Canadians.  Individuals with CF have a variable course of disease severity as evidenced by individual differences in lung disease and rates of common co-morbidities, all of which affect survival.  These include intestinal obstructions, pancreatic damage and CF-related diabetes.  Evidence suggests that variation in disease presentation is caused by other genes, referred to as modifier genes, that modify the course of CF disease.  We propose to identify the genes responsible for these different traits in CF.  Together with the International Consortium for CF Modifiers, we have accumulated the largest CF patient collection for genetic studies in the world.  We have substantial genetic data across the genomes of >7000 CF patients, and we have already made significant progress in mapping modifier genes for lung disease severity and for the intestinal obstruction seen in ~15% of CF patients.  Here we propose to continue our modifier gene study of the intestinal obstruction, identify the specific genes responsible, extend these results to identify modifier genes for CF-related diabetes, and determine whether modifier genes play a role in similar traits in the general population such as Type 2 Diabetes.   Identification of these genes will have a significant impact on CF treatment, therapy and outcomes, as well as provide insight into the causes of other disorders with similar clinical complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing Raman spectroscopic techniques for the prediction and monitoring of cellular and tumour response to radiation therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICALLY ADAPTIVE RADIOTHERAPY; CANCER ONCOLOGY; IONIZING RADIATION; PREDICTIVE MEDICINE; RADIATION THERAPY; RADIOBIOLOGY; RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY; TUMOUR RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: In radiotherapy, radiation doses have been empirically determined and are largely based on previous population outcomes for given treatment sites. Doses are delivered in their entirety without consideration of in vivo disease response. There currently exists no standard method for a) assessing inherent patient radiosensitivity (for the purposes of personalizing pre- treatment dose prescription) and b) assessing disease response during the course of treatment. The global objective of this project is to investigate and implement Raman spectroscopic techniques, in conjunction with established technologies, to a) provide predictive capabilities on tissue radiosensitivity and b) provide technologies capable of monitoring disease response during the course of treatment. While the techniques aim to be, ultimately, site independent, the initial focus of the project will be on prostate cancer, due to local expertise in this area.

TitreApplicationTitle: Paracrine Hedgehog as a Mediator of Castration Resistant Prostate Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: HEDGEHOG INIHIBITORS; HEDGEHOG SIGNALLING; MICRORNA; MOUSE TUMOR XENOGRAFTS; PARACRINE SIGNALLING; PROSTATE CANCER; STEROID BIOSYNTHESIS; STROMAL CELLS; TESTOSTERONE; TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Deaths from prostate cancer (PCa) are the consequence of "castration-resistant" disease (CRPC) that grows and spreads despite the use of hormone therapy.  Research now shows that a factor leading to CRPC is the acquisition of androgen synthetic capability by the tumor as this allows it to replace androgens lost due to hormone therapy.  Our recent work indicates that Paracrine Hedgehog signaling activity, awakened by hormone therapy, can be a factor that enables prostate tumors to make their own androgens.  Hedgehogs are small proteins that activate Hedgehog signaling in target cells and, for a prostate tumor, the preferred targets are the benign stromal cells that surround the tumor.  Previously we showed that hormone therapy drastically increases the synthesis and release of Hedgehogs from PCa cells.  New studies show that Hedgehog action on prostate stromal cells promotes the synthesis and release of testosterone from these cells.  Collectively, our studies then suggest that a complex cross-talk process between PCa cells and surrounding stromal cells (referred to as Paracrine activity) supports the development of CRPC.  The goals of this project will be to explain the reason that hormone therapy increases Hedgehog release from PCa cells and to characterize the process(es) through which Paracrine Hedgehog enables production of androgens from prostate stromal cells as a means of considering ways to block it.  Likewise, we will test new strategies involving combinations of Hedgehog gene knockdown, Hedgehog inhibitors and steroid biosynthesis inhibitors for prevention of CRPC and for treatment of CRPC in our cell models.  Finally, we will establish a practical animal model based on implantation of mixtures of human prostate cells under the outer capsule of the mouse kidney to establish the relevance of Paracrine Hedgehog in PCa development and progression and to test our combination treatment strategies to fight CRPC before they are tested in patients

TitreApplicationTitle: Intervertebral Disc Degeneration and Pain
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE-RELATED DEGENERATION; BIOREACTOR ORGAN CULTURE; HUMAN INTERVERTEBRAL DISC; ISOLATED SENSORY NEURON CULTURE; MICRO-MECHANICAL FORCE; MOLECULAR GENETIC ANALYSES; NERVE GROWTH FACTOR; NERVE INGROWTH
Abstract-Résumé: Introduction:  At present little is known about the molecular mechanisms involved in pain generation associated with intervertebral discs degeneration. At least two different mechanisms or a combination of the two could potentially lead to tissue breakdown and to the release of factors resulting in pain from the intervertebral disc.  The aim of this study is to identify and understand mechanisms that may lead to painful intervertebral discs and to find ways to block the pain mediators. We will use a model system where we subject intact intervertebral discs to varying degree of load to understand the effect of adverse load. Isolated disc and nerve cells will then be used to study and block specific factors or pathways.  Significance to human health:The term discogenic low back pain was coined more than 30 years ago to describe pain associated with disc degeneration, which currently represents an enormous socio-economic cost to the healthcare systems in developed countries. Despite the burden of disease there are no effective diagnostic tools to identify the early degenerative changes in intervertebral discs that result in pain. An improved understanding of the pathophysiology leading to discogenic low back pain will facilitate the development of biomarkers as targets for more specific therapeutic interventions for pain relief, so avoiding invasive and often dangerous surgical procedures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hydrogen sulfide and atherosclerosis development
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION MOLECULE; APOLIPOPROTEIN; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CYSTATHIONINE GAMMA-LYASE; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; HYDROGEN SULFIDE; PROLIFERATION; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is conventionally known as an air pollutant. Recent studies have shown that this molecule of gas in fact is produced in our body.  Cystathionine gamma-lyase (CSE) is the key enzyme for the production of H2S in cardiovascular system.  The importance of H2S in regulating cardiovascular function has been extensively acknowledged as this gas molecule offers protection against hypertension, cardiac infarction, oxidative stress and inflammation. This project will test the hypothesis that reduced vascular production of H2S constitutes a predisposal factor for the occurrence of atherosclerosis, a vascular disease characterized with vascular inflammation, lipid and cholesterol deposition, and narrowing and stiffing of blood vessels. We will firstly examine the development of atherosclerosis in genetically engineered mice that do not possess the CSE gene.  As such, the proposed protective effect of H2S against atherosclerosis development in these animals would have vanished.  We will then investigate the mechanisms by which H2S limits atherosclerosis development.  These hypothesized mechanisms include the interaction of H2S with apolipoprotein E (a polypeptide that limits the onset of hyperlipidaemia and atherosclerosis), prevention of endothelial dysfunction and smooth muscle proliferation, inhibition of the expression of adhesion molecules, and anti-oxidant and anti-inflammation protection. Finally, we will use H2S-based therapeutic approaches to prevent and treat atherosclerosis in different animal models. This project will delineate the importance of CSE/H2S pathway and its interaction with apolipoprotein E in the regulation of atherosclerosis development and the underlying molecular mechanisms. To reveal a causative relationship between vascular H2S production and atherosclerosis development may also provide a new approach for the treatment and prevention of this vascular disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: Internet-based interventions for problem gamblers: Randomized controlled trial of online self-directed cognitive-behavioural motivational therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE-BEHAVIOURAL TREATMENT; INTERNET TREATMENT; PATHOLOGICAL GAMBLING; PROBLEM GAMBLING; SELF-HELP; TREATMENT OUTCOME
Abstract-Résumé: Gambling disorders affect about one in ten Canadian adults. Effective treatments are available but only a small proportion of affected individuals will choose to attend formal treatment.  As a result self-directed treatments have also been developed and found effective. Self-directed treatments provide individuals with information and support to initiate a recovery program without attending formal treatment. In previous research we developed an intervention package that helps people to be motivated to tackle their gambling problem and to use basic behavioral and cognitive change strategies. This intervention is offered in a combined telephone and self-help workbook package.   In two separate evaluations, participants with gambling disorders were followed for one year (N = 314) and two years (N = 101) and showed sustained reduction of gambling involvement. The present study will investigate the efficacy of this self-directed intervention offered as a free online resource. The Internet is an excellent modality in which to offer self-directed treatment for gambling problems. The Internet is increasingly accessible to members of the public and is increasingly used to access health-related information. Online gambling sites are also becoming more popular gambling platforms. A clinical trial  (N=180) will be conducted in which individuals with gambling problems who are not interested in attending formal treatment are randomly assigned to have access to an online self-directed intervention or to a comparison condition.   The comparison condition will be an alternative website that offers a self-assessment of gambling involvement and gambling-related problems.  The participant's use of the resources and their gambling involvement (days of gambling, dollars loss) and their gambling problems will be tracked for a twelve month follow-up period. The results of this research will be important for informing policy-makers who are developing treatment systems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Signal, Safety, and Success: An Analysis of Risk, Benefit, and Translation after Detection of Clinical Activity in Drug Development
Keywords-MotsClés: KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MEDICAL EVIDENCE; PHARMACEUTICAL DEVELOPMENT; PHASE 2 TRIALS; RESEARCH ETHICS; RESEARCH INTEGRITY; RISK; SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH; VALIDITY
Abstract-Résumé: The vast majority of new drugs entered into clinical development never show adequate safety and efficacy. As a result, many patients are harmed and resources spent in failed trials.  This grant is aimed at discovering whether there are ways to better protect patients, learn from failure, and save resources during drug development.  Our preliminary research shows that drug developers often run trials that are based on guesswork or biased evidence; when this occurs, studies can fail and patients are harmed.  We want to determine how frequently drug developers run drug trials based on good clinical evidence, and measure the impact of good evidence in terms of improving patient outcomes in trials and increasing the chances that a drug will later prove effective and safe.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of the genetic and metabolic foundations of intrinsic resistance and phenotypic drug tolerance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG RESISTANCE; DRUG SYNERGY; PERSISTENCE; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is the causative agent of Tuberculosis (TB) which is still a major worldwide problem with current figures showing one third of the world's population infected, 8 to 9 million new cases of active TB and over 2 million deaths due to TB every year. Current vaccines and chemotherapeutic measures are limited in their efficacy and are failing to prevent the spread of disease. Although the present multi-drug schedule of treatment has the potential to cure more than 80% of cases, it lasts at least 6 months and requires that several drugs are taken in the right combinations. Because of this, many patients do not actually receive full and effective treatment. This inappropriate treatment has led to the emergence of multi-drug resistant TB (resistant to two or more of the primary anti-TB drugs) and extensive-drug resistant TB (MDR plus resistance to any fluoroquinolone, and resistance to at least one second-line injectable drug). This is reflected in the fact that up to 2% of patients cannot be cured with today's cocktail of drugs. In addition to acquired resistance to drugs due to genetic mutations, there appears to be an element of intrinsic resistance to antibiotics in Mtb and also non-inherited antibiotic tolerance amongst a sub-population of the bacteria within the host. These latter bacteria are in a distinct physiological state known as persistence or dormancy. It is these persisters that are hard to eradicate leading to the lengthy treatment regimen that in turn leads to poor compliance and the emergence of genetic drug resistance. Our proposal aims to obtain a better understanding of intrinsic resistance and the phenotypic drug tolerance in persister populations of Mtb. Our findings will facilitate the discovery of new therapeutics for the treatment of TB.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF; THERAPIE DU CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: CEACAM1 in colon cancer progression and metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CEACAM1; COLORECTAL CANCER; CYTOKINES; INFLAMMATION; KNOCKOUT MOUSE MODEL; METASTASIS; MYELOID DERIVED SUPPRESSOR CELLS; SHP-1; STAT3
Abstract-Résumé: The protein CEACAM1 is a unique member of a large protein family.  A number of functions have been defined for this protein, based on biochemistry and cell biology techniques.  We have used genetic techniques to completely eliminate the expression of CEACAM1 from the mouse.  The mouse exhibits a number of problems associated with its important functions. One of these is the development of colon cancer once an appropriate triggering event has been initiated. We have recently shown that CEACAM1 plays an important role in the metastatic process; indeed, a specific type of immune progenitor cell that normally expresses CEACAM1 significantly contributes to survival and implantation of the colorectal tumor cells in the liver.  We have also observed that expression of a particular form of CEACAM1, CEACAM1-L, in the tumor cells themselves is sufficient to decrease its metastatic abilities.  To understand how this works, we will first examine which functions are affected by the dissemination of the tumor cells and which motifs within the CEACAM1-L cytoplasmic domain might be conveying these functions.  Then we will examine how CEACAM1-L is involved in the production of an important chemokine mediator responsible for recruitment of immune cells to the site of metastasis.  This will be followed by examination of clinical primary colon cancer samples and metastasis samples from patients for CEACAM1-L expression to gauge whether it is a good indicator of disease progression.  Finally, we will examine in the wild-type mice and the experimental Cc1-/- mice which types of cells normally expressing CEACAM1 are responsible for responses to the invading metastatic cells. We expect that some of our results could lead to a new treatment option or become a biomarker for the prevention of colon cancer progression in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relationship between denervation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and muscle atrophy in sarcopenia
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; MITOCHONDRIAL FUNCTION; MOTOR NEURON; NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION; PERMEABILITY TRANSITION PORE; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; RESPIROMETRY; SARCOPENIA
Abstract-Résumé: The causes of the age-related loss of muscle mass and function known as sarcopenia are unknown. Amongst the most frequently implicated culprits is an intrinsic defect in mitochondrial function, an idea supported by the up-regulation of mitochondrial-driven molecular signals that can cause muscle atrophy in aging muscle. Despite the appeal of this theory, alterations in mitochondrial function could be either a cause or an effect of other processes in aging muscle, and clarifying this will have an important role in dictating the therapeutic approach used in treating sarcopenia. In this respect, our recent data shows that denervation of aging muscle cells is arguably the most important cause of muscle cell atrophy. As such, the experiments proposed in this application will determine the extent to which denervation induces changes in mitochondrial function (wherein the mitochondria do not have a primary defect but are merely responding to upstream signals induced by denervation) versus the extent to which mitochondrial dsyfunction causes denervation in aging muscle (wherein the mitochondria have a specific defect that needs to be corrected to prevent denervation). The answer to this question will ultimately determine whether therapies for sarcopenia should be targeted at correcting defects in mitochondrial function versus being aimed at other processes that could cause denervation of aging muscle cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Informing Fresh versus Old Red Cell Management (INFORM):  A large simple phase III randomized controlled trial
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD SAFETY; MORTALITY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TRANSFUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Hundreds of thousands of Canadians and many million persons worldwide receive a red cell blood transfusion each year. Blood Banks normally issue the oldest available blood, thereby avoiding wastage of stored red cells that exceed the approved shelf-life of 42 days. However, several recent studies have suggested that standard issue (oldest available blood) compared with fresh blood increases the risk of adverse outcomes, including infection, organ dysfunction, length of stay in hospital and death, causing a massive burden of morbidity and mortality and increasing health care costs. If fresh blood is indeed better than standard issue blood, blood banks will be faced with the challenge of maintaining an adequate supply of fresh blood to meet the demands. In a single centre 910-patient pilot study funded by Canadian Institutes for Health Research ("INFORM-Pilot") we have shown that it is feasible to randomize the majority of hospitalized patients to receive fresh compared with old blood and we are now planning a very large, high efficiency and low-cost study ("INFORM"), involving more than 24,000 patients, to properly answer the question. If we find that fresh blood is safer than old blood, methods of blood storage and inventory management might have to be dramatically overhauled whereas a finding of no difference in safety of old blood compared with fresh blood will be reassuring for regulators, blood bankers and patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The use of bone marrow to repair injured salivary glands.
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW TO REPAIR TISSUE; DRY MOUTH; IRRADIATION FOR HEAD AND NECK CANCER; PARACRINE EFFECTS OF BONE MARROW; PROGENITOR AND STEM CELLS; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; REPAIR AND REPLACEMENT; SALIVA; SALIVARY GLAND INJURY; SJOGREN'S SYNDROME; XEROSTOMIA
Abstract-Résumé: Two groups of Canadians have to live with permanently dry mouths (xerostomia) because their salivary gland tissue have been injured or destroyed (about 160,000 who have Sjogren's syndrome, and patients who are receiving radiotherapy as part of their head and neck cancer treatment, which numbers approximate 4,000 new cases annually). These patients experience great discomfort in chewing and swallowing, sore throat, tooth decay, altered taste, and infections. At present there is no adequate treatment for irreversible salivary gland damage and these patients have to constantly sip water to reduce their discomfort a little. The aim of this research program is to offer to these patients effective treatment through the regeneration, replacement, and repair of salivary glands using cells (and their by-products) that are drawn from the patients' own tissues. Specifically, this proposal tests the efficacy of an extract from bone marrow cells (Bone marrow cell extract, BMCE) as a therapy to repair salivary glands damaged by irradiation or Sjogren's syndrome. We will assess the efficacy of BMCE in protecting salivary cells, increasing tissue neovascularization, function, and regeneration. This research is done in human salivary biopsies and in mouse models with irradiated salivary glands or with Sjogren's syndrome. The human salivary organotypic culture allows a longitudinal in situ observation of cellular and molecular events happening during irradiation injury and regeneration. The potential impact of regenerating lost salivary tissues is enormous. A long-term goal of this proposed work is to offer to millions of patients worldwide, having reduced or no saliva output (severe xerostomia), effective treatment options. These include the potential for regeneration and repair of saliva-secreting cells in adult glands.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role Of The Embryonic Morphpogen Nodal In The Regulation Of Breast Cancer Invasion
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; INVASION; METASTASIS; NODAL; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada more than 30% of breast cancer patients will die of their disease, most often because the cancer spreads (metastasizes) to other organs such as the brain and the lung.  In order to metastasize, breast cancer cells must be able to move through the breast tissue.  We understand some of the tools that cancer cells use to move, but we still do not know what causes a breast cancer cell to acquire these tools.  Recent studies have found that highly metastatic, but not poorly metastatic, breast cancers express proteins that are normally restricted to the cells of an embryo.  One of these proteins is called Nodal.  We have discovered that Nodal is common in breast cancers that have spread but is absent in normal breast tissue and rare in very early breast cancers that are not likely to spread.  In this proposal, we aim to understand how and if Nodal promotes breast cancer metastasis.  We will use cells, mouse models and tissue from breast cancer patients to study how Nodal promotes cell movement and if its expression in breast cancer tissues can be used to predict if that cancer is more likely to spread.  Finally, we will examine if blocking Nodal can prevent the movement and escape of breast cancer cells from breast tissue.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Targeting of Critical Domains of AHI-1 Oncoprotein in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia Stem Cells Resistant to Current Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: AHI-1; BCR-ABL; CHRONIC MYELOID LEUKEMIA; DRUG RESISTANCE; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; IMMUNOPRECIPITATION AND MASS SPECTROMETRY; ONCOGENE; PROTEIN BIOCHEMISTRY AND PROTEIN CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SMALL MOLECULE INHIBITORS
Abstract-Résumé: Introduction of Imatinib medication has improved treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), but early relapses and resistant disease prevent many patients from being cured. The frequency of resistance to current Imatinib therapy is 15-20%, increasing to 40% in patients with advanced phase disease. Research has now shown that this is due to the inability of current agents to eradicate the blood cancer stem cells which then maintain the potential for relapse. There is thus an urgent need to develop new therapies that target other critical proteins active in CML blood cancer stem cells so that these critical cells can be eliminated. One candidate target is AHI-1, a newly discovered cancer-causing gene we identified that is involved in murine (mouse) blood cancer (leukemia) development and displays abnormal expression in CML blood cancer stem cells. Interestingly, we have recently found that AHI-1 plays a major role in abnormal blood cancer stem cell activity and resistance to Imatinib therapy in both mouse models and in blood cancer stem cells from CML patients, a strong indicator that AHI-1 is likely to be an important new cancer-causing gene involved in development of leukemia and drug resistance and that developing new drugs that inhibit its abnormal functions in blood cancer stem cells will be a more effective treatment option for CML patients.     The present proposal will explore and solve the protein structure of key parts of the AHI-1 protein and identify the proteins with which it interacts in the development of leukemia and drug resistance in CML blood cancer stem cells. New inhibitors will be identified and discovered based on the structure of the AHI-1 protein using cutting-edge technologies, resulting in the development of molecularly targeted cancer therapies that will be more effective and have fewer side effects than currently used therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting Thrombospondin-1 in medulloblastoma
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOURS; MEDULLOBLASTOMA; METASTASES; PEPTIDE MIMETICS; THERAPEUTICS; XENOGRAFT MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood brain cancers are the leading cause of death and disability in children with cancers. Recently our laboratory discovered that silencing of a potent gene called thrombospondin-1 (Tsp-1) is important for driving tumour growth and metastases in medulloblastoma, the most common type of malignant brain tumour in children. In this grant, we propose to test drugs that mimic the action of Tsp-1 to see if it can be effective in treating and preventing brain tumour metastases in mouse model of medulloblastoma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rare Obesity Disorders Informing Common Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: EXTREME PHENOTYPES; GENOMICS; HEALTH OF VULNERABLE POPULATIONS(CHILDREN WITH DISABILITIES); MECHANISMS SHARED BETWEEN COMMON AND RARE DISEASES; OBESITY AND DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is an increasingly important disease. Many more people are obese now than a generation ago. In 1981, 8.5% of Canadian adults and 2% of Canadian children were obese. Now, 16% of adults and 10% of children are obese. The 5-fold increase in pediatric obesity since 1981 worries doctors, because 75% of obese children will go on to become obese adults, and that means that diseases associated with obesity are on the rise. There has been a 10-to-30 fold increase in type 2 diabetes among North American children with in the past 10 to 15 years. We don't know enough about what goes wrong in an obese person's body that eventually leads to diabetes, heart disease or strokes. Some obese people get these diseases, and some don't. What is different about an obese person who gets sick, compared to a size-matched person that stays healthy? We plan to study people with rare, severe obesity disorders to look for genes that cause them to be very obese. We also plan to study their hormones and fat distribution to find out if some hormones and fat locations are worse than others. We hope that this information will teach us valuable lessons about what hormone pathways go wrong, and in what order, as obese people progress to diabetes and/or heart disease. Equally well, we hope to discover "paradoxically healthy" individuals (e.g. severely obese people with low blood pressure and high good cholesterol levels) who may help us find genes that could be activated to prevent disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Group physiotherapy compared to individual physiotherapy to treat urinary incontinence in aging women: A randomized control trial
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; EXERCISE; GROUP INTERVENTION; PELVIC FLOOR MUSCLE; PHYSIOTHERAPY; URINARY INCONTINENCE; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Urinary incontinence (UI) affects up to 55% of women 65 and over. In Canada, this demographic group is expected to grow from 16% of the population in 2011 to 23% in 2026. The demand for treatment, particularly from assertive baby-boomers, will increase exponentially. Clinical practice guidelines recommend one-on-one pelvic floor muscle (PFM) training as a first-line treatment for stress or mixed UI in women; however, less than a third of older Canadian women currently receive treatment. Inadequate resources, financial and human, are the prime deterrents. The lack of a prediction tool, capable of linking patient's individual characteristics and symptoms to the ideal treatment options, compounds the problem - physiotherapists are unable to predict which women will benefit from PFM training and those that will not. The demand for one-on-one treatment is resource intense and very costly to the Canadian healthcare system and, given the dearth of physiotherapists trained in PFM rehabilitation, impossible to meet. However, initial research suggests group-based treatments may provide the answer, but researchers have yet to evaluate either the long-term impact or cost-effectiveness of group versus one-on-one PFM training for older women. Treatment protocols, which guide Canadian practitioners, cannot be changed without this research. This proposal encompasses a 4-year study to determine if group-based PFM training is as effective as one-on-one training for treating UI in elderly women, and to establish the cost-effectiveness of both. Demonstrating that it is at least as good as one-on-one treatments would warrant including group-based PFM training as a recommended first-line UI treatment; and, should it prove more cost-effective, will reduce both human-resourcing and financial costs per patient. Finally, data will be collected for a sub-study aimed at identifying variables that could, potentially, be used to predict patient responsiveness to group-based PFM training.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anomia in Alzheimer's Disease: Untangling semantic components and delivering therapy with rTMS.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER; IMAGING; LANGUAGE; NAMING; SEMANTIC MEMORY; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with Alzheimer's Disease (AD) not only have memory problems, but they have problems naming objects or pictures termed anomia. Damage to long term memory for concepts in the brain, termed semantic memory impairment, lies at the heart of this anomia,  but the contributions of different brain regions remains to be sorted out.  In this grant we will a) investigate the details of the damage to semantic memory in AD, and how the brains of AD subjects try to compensate for this damage, andf b) try to improve the anomia using transcranial magnetic stimulation. To better understand the nature of semantic memory loss in AD, we will assess the degree of semantic loss in a set of 60 AD individuals, and compare that to the regions of the left brain that are damaged, that show thinning of the outer brain layer (cortex), that show less blood flow response on brain imaging to tasks of picture naming, and that show the presence of amyloid on positron emission tomography  (PET) images. Amyloid is very evident in AD, but may not in fact be causing the naming problems.  At the same time, we will pursue our intriguing data that the semantic impairment causing anomia can be alleviated in AD.  We have found that naming problems can be improved when repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is applied over the skull adjacent to the inferior left parietal lobe  of the brain. This region, we have reason to believe, is able to participate in compensatory circuits that AD individuals can use for naming pictures. In a series of rTMS experiments we will specify the duration and type of stimulation that leads to naming improvement as well as explore the duration of such improvement - all necessary prerequisites to mounting a large randomized controlled trial of the efficacy of rTMS in AD picture naming. Such a large trial is the ultimate goal of this research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms of Malignant Hyperthermia
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM CHANNEL; EXCITATION-CONTRACTION COUPLING; GENETIC DISEASE; MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA; MUSCLE DISEASE; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; RYANODINE RECEPTOR; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: What do calcium ions and deadly fever have in common?  Known mostly for their importance in maintaining bone structure, calcium ions have many other important functions in every cell of our bodies.  One of their tasks includes the contraction of muscle tissue.  At the cellular and molecular level, the contraction of muscle is a very complex event.  One of the key steps involves moving calcium ions from one compartment in the muscle cell (known as the sarcoplasmic reticulum) to another (known as the cytoplasm). When there is a sufficient amount of calcium in the cytoplasm, the muscle cell contracts.  However, the exact amount of calcium is absolutely crucial: too little or too much calcium can cause severe diseases.  This proposal deals with one of these diseases. Malignant Hyperthermia is a disorder that mostly affects patients during surgery. Upon the administration of particular anesthetics, these patients experience a massive rise in body temperature, which is fatal in more than 80% of the cases. The cause for this disease is particular mutations in a protein known as "RYR1". This protein forms a doorway through which calcium ions can move into the cytoplasm. This door can open and close, and when it opens too soon, a deadly fever may be the consequence.  The combination of anesthetics and a mutation in RYR1 can cause exactly this. This is why patients can appear perfectly normal, and problems only arise during surgery. In this proposal, we wish to find out the exact mechanisms by which the disease mutations affect the RYR1 protein.  We study the exact three-dimensional structure of the protein using advanced techniques, and look at the effect of genetic disease mutations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mre11/Rad50/Xrs2 regulates the cohesin complex at sites of replication stress
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER PREDISPOSITION; CHIP-ON-CHIP; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; DNA REPLICIATION; GENOMIC REARRANGEMENTS; YEAST GENOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: One major question in cancer biology is to what extent chromosomal instability is the beginning of tumorigenesis.  Genomic rearrangements are thought to be the means by which cells develop aberrant characteristics that ultimately permit their conversion into cancer cells.  Moreover, cancer development from its earliest stages is associated with oncogene-induced replication stress.  Mrell/Rad50/Nbs1 (MRN) is a complex of proteins important for preventing genomic rearrangements and mutations in the complex predispose individuals to cancer.  This proposal investigates a functional link between MRN and another complex of proteins called cohesin during the process of DNA replication.  The cohesin complex is a central regulator of chromosomal organization and defects in this complex lead to tumor formation as well. Our research will investigate how interaction(s) between these complexes function to maintain genomic information in cells as they replicate their genetic material and divide.  Our goal is to understand why disruptions in either complex lead to similar phenotypic diseases in humans, including related developmental defects and a remarkable overlap is the types of cancer (breast, colorectal,) reported in individuals with NSB1, ATLD and Cohesinopathy disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bipolar disorder in later life:  A mixed-methods, experiential sampling study of health and well-being over time
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; EXPERIENTIAL SAMPLING; GLOBAL POSITIONING SYSTEM; MENTAL HEALTH; MIXED-METHODS; OLDER ADULTS; PSYCHOLOGICAL WELL-BEING; QUALITY OF LIFE; URBAN VS. RURAL COMPARISONS
Abstract-Résumé: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic mental health condition characterized by extreme shifts in mood, behaviour and judgment (onset usually by age 25). More than half with untreated BD abuse alcohol and/or drugs and 60% will have marriages that end in divorce. Suicide by those with BD is greater than unipolar depression. Although (almost) everyone experiences mood variability, people with BD experience profound shifts in mood (e.g., clinical depression, mild elation [hypomania] or extreme elation or irritability). It is estimated that there are today 75,000 Canadians 50+ years of age with BD; moreover, the number of older Canadians with BD will triple over the next 10 years. Despite these growing numbers, psychosocial research focussing on older adults with BD is virtually nonexistent. This proposed 5-year study will include intensive periods of data collection; these 2-week periods will each separated by 8-months. Participants will be prompted at 2-times per day (12 hour window) to report current mood, medication adherence and recent life events. We envision use of a GPS located electronically connected to an iPad or similar tablet-type device. The GPS information (recorded every 20 seconds) will allow us to determine if periods of mania are heralded by expanding geographic range, rapid movement between points or, novelty seeking; conversely, contraction of movements may be a precursor to major depression episodes.  Two-hundred and five participants will be recruited from both urban and rural communities with a 10+ year BD diagnosis; medical information will be obtained during regular psychiatric assessments. We will use a range of contemporary research methods with emphasis on BD in later life (e.g., retirement, bereavement, concurrent physical illness). This study will provide a wealth of information to increase our understanding of BD in older adults where little information currently exists.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oligomeric assembly of GPCR signalling units and functional selectivity
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSENSORS; FUNCTIONAL SELECTIVITY; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTOR; INVERSE AGONISM; LIGAND-BIASED SIGNALLING; OLIGOMERIZATION; RESONANCE ENERGY TRANSFER (BRET-FRET); SIGNALLING EFFECTORS; SIGNALLING EFFICACY
Abstract-Résumé: Chemical transmission is a common mechanism used by cells to communicate. It consists in the liberation, by the transmitting cells (neuronal or endocrine cells), of chemically encoded messages (neurotransmitters or hormones) that are selectively recognized and decoded by receptor devices located on the surface of effector cells. The largest class of such receptors is known as the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) family with several hundred members involved in a wide variety of physiological processes. Dysfunctions of these receptors have been shown to be involved in the development and the complications accompanying various pathological states. They thus represent major pharmacological targets for the development of new drugs candidates with potential applications in all clinical fields. In fact, more than 50% of the drugs prescribed today act by activating or blocking a GPCR. Although significant progress has been made in the last 20 years regarding the structure and mechanisms of action of the GPCRs, our understanding of how drugs promote biological responses through their interaction with these receptors is still rudimentary. Here we propose, using a combination of molecular, biochemical, biophysical and pharmacological approaches, to further investigate the mechanisms underlying drug action through GPCRs. In particular, we will focus on the process controling selectivty , with the objective of developping new therapeutics with better efficacy and selectivity profiles.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impairment of O2 and CO2/H+ Chemosensing in Perinatal Adrenal Chromaffin Cells by Chronic Opioids
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPEROMETRY; CA2+ IMAGING; CATECHOLAMINE SECRETION; CELL CULTURE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HYPOXIA AND CO2/H+ SENSING; HYPOXIA INDUCIBLE FACTOR; MEMBRANE ION CHANNELS; OPIOIDS AND OPIOID RECEPTORS; PATCH CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Drugs of abuse, including nicotine from cigarette smoke and recreational or prescribed opioids for pain management (e.g. heroin or morphine) place a serious toll on the Heath Care System. These drugs directly depress the respiratory system which controls breathing and lead to impaired arousal responses, especially during sleep. One adverse effect in the newborn is failure of special cells in the body to detect a fall in blood oxygen or an increase in carbon dioxide leading to impaired arousal. These cells have sites for detecting naturally-occurring chemicals used for normal communication in the body. However, these same sites are targets for nicotine and opioid drugs. Importantly, the offspring of mothers who take these drugs during pregnancy can experience a high degree of morbidity and death, yet little is known about how these drugs work. We are interested in how these drugs affect special cells in the newborn animal, resulting in their inability to detect and respond appropriately to low oxygen and high carbon dioxide. We have developed an attractive model in the rat where these same cells malfunction when exposed to either nicotine or opioid drugs. Understanding the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms is of central importance for developing effective therapeutic strategies. The goals of the present proposal are to uncover the mechanisms by which opioid exposure causes impaired detection of oxygen and carbon dioxide by these special cells in the newborn.

TitreApplicationTitle: Acute lung injury: from cellular mechanisms to molecular therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY AND REPAIR; CELL BIOLOGY; LUNG TRANSPLANTATION; NANO-DRUG DELIVERY; PATHOPHYSIOLOGY; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Lung transplantation is a lifesaving therapy for patients suffering from end-stage lung disease. However, life-threatening primary graft dysfunction occurs in ~20% of recipients because of ischemia-reperfusion-induced lung injury. My lab has been exploring new therapies for lung injury. We are going to test a new peptide-based drug that may reduce acute lung injury. We will also explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which this new drug may work. More importantly, we will use nano-technology developed in my laboratory, to enhance the delivery of this new drug. The new nano-formula may be used for other ischemia-reperfusion related organ injury, such as acute myocardial infarction and stroke. The new technique may also be useful to deliver other peptide-based drugs. Our future goal is to use this nano-technology to repair damaged donor lung with a Human Ex vivo Lung Perfusion system. We call it Nano-HELP.

TitreApplicationTitle: Randomized controlled trial of anticoagulation vs. placebo for a first symptomatic isolated distal deep-vein thrombosis (IDDVT): The CACTUS-PTS Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICOAGULATION; CALF VEIN THROMBOSIS; COMPRESSION ULTRASOUND; DEEP VENOUS THROMBOSIS; POST-THROMBOTIC SYNDROME; RANDOMIZED PLACEBO CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Blood clots in the deep calf veins (calf vein thrombosis) affect 30,000 Canadians each year. Due to a lack of research on calf vein thrombosis, we are uncertain whether blood thinner treatment (which is used for more serious forms of vein thrombosis, i.e. in the upper leg veins and lung vessels) does more good than harm, hence doctors' practices vary widely--some prescribe blood thinners for calf vein thrombosis, and others do not.   We hypothesize that blood thinner treatment is effective for calf vein thrombosis.  We will do a study of patients with calf vein thrombosis in 10 centers in Canada (as well as 12 centers in France and Switzerland). Patients who provide written consent to participate will be randomly chosen (i.e. like a coin toss) to receive a standard blood thinner by once-daily injection or a placebo injection for 6 weeks. Patients will undergo a repeat ultrasound exam of their legs at day 5 and at 6 weeks to assess for extension of the calf vein thrombosis into more proximal leg veins. Patients will also be assessed for symptomatic lung clots within 6 weeks, bleeding within 6 weeks, and new episodes of venous thrombosis or the post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic leg pain and swelling) within 1 year.   This will be the first randomized, placebo controlled study of blood thinner treatment for calf vein thrombosis. It will provide important information on whether such treatment improves health in the short and long term, as well as on the natural history of calf vein thrombosis. As such, our study will have a direct impact on improving patient care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fostering Adaptive Capacity and Resilience to Climate Change in Sub-Arctic First Nations: Addressing Food Security and Health Issues through Agroforestry Stewardship Practices
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTATION; AGROFORESTRY; CLIMATE CHANGE; FIRST NATIONS; FOOD SECURITY; HOME GARDENS; NUTRITION; OBESITY; SUB-ARCTIC; SUSTAINABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: The Food Security Assembly has defined food security as "the assurance that all people at all times have both the physical and economic access to the food they need for an active, healthy life." Food security has been recognized as a determinant of health. Food insecurity exists when people do not have adequate physical, social or economic access to food as defined above. Position papers on food security in Canada point to the unique food security challenges faced by Aboriginal people living in remote-northern communities. However, the types of interventions in the northern communities have been limited (e.g., conventional gardening). At present, the barriers to the consumption of healthy foods, such as, fruits and vegetables are availability (quality when available) and expense, as identified by First Nation Cree of the Mushkegowuk Territory (western James Bay region of northern Ontario). Our innovative intervention strategy will increase the availability and consumption of vegetables and fruits in sub-arctic First Nations through agroforestry stewardship practices, which can help to improve nutrition and well-being of the people. Agroforestry has been utilized in the tropics, sub-tropics, and temperate climates, as a means to establish or increase food availability in impoverished areas using socio-economic and ecologically sustainable strategies. As the sub-arctic is disproportionately being affected by climate change, there is now an opportunity to employ agroforestry stewardship practices in this region. Agroforestry is a recent term for an ancient practice of combining woody perennials (e.g., trees, shrubs) with crops in spatial and temporal arrangements that optimize beneficial biological interactions and economic outputs. Being more diverse, and thus more resilient to environmental disturbance than conventional agriculture, agroforestry stewardship has the potential to act as a more reliable local-food system, and a refuge for culturally significant plants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translational derepression during ischemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; HYPOXIA; ISCHEMIA; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; RNA BINDING PROTEIN; TRANSGENIC MICE; TRANSLATION DEREPRESSION; VASCULARIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: If the blood supply to a muscle or the heart is blocked, as can happen if a blood clot forms, most proteins stop being made to preserve energy.  However, a select group of proteins are turned on.  These are normally not made even though the message is present but segregated in specialized particles that keep the message silent.  Translation of these messages is normally repressed.  When a muscle becomes ischemic (lacks enough blood supply) and becomes hypoxic (not enough oxygen), these messages undergo translational derepression.  Some of the well known proteins whose message is translationally repressed include the hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF1a) and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA).  We discovered another hypoxia-inducible factor called IRF2BP2 that we have found undergoes translational derepression in ischemic muscle. We also found that IRF2BP2 is required to increase the expression of VEGFA in muscle. A protein called staufen 1 binds to IRF2BP2 messenger RNA and controls its translation.  Another small RNA (miR17) binds to the mRNA of IRF2BP2 (as well as HIF1a and VEGFA)and seems to participate in the control of translation.  We found that some people have a small deletion in the sequence where miR17  binds and that people with documented coronary artery disease have a higher prevalence of this deletion.  Thus, we believe that translational derepression is an important mechanism that controls a cascade that will lead to the formation of new blood vessels and we would like to learn more about it to see if it can be augmented to improve recovery from ischemia.  We propose to determine how the small deletion affects the control of IRF2BP2 translation under normal and hypoxic conditions, to test whether staufen 1 and miR17 control of translation is a general mechanism affecting multiple hypoxia-inducible proteins, and finally using mice that lack IRF2BP2 in muscle and heart, we want to demonstrate its importance in blood vessel formation.

NomDuComitéFR: Déterminants psychosociaux, socioculturels et comportementaux de la santé 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Family Planning to promote regular physical activity:  A randomized controlled trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; GOAL SETTING; PARENTAL PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PERSUASION; THEORY OF PLANNED BEHAVIOUR
Abstract-Résumé: The number Canadian adults and children with cardiovascular disease (CVD) and its risk factors is alarming, and a great burden on the Canadian health care system. Physical inactivity is a modifiable risk factor for CVD and obesity; yet its prevalence is high among children and their parents. Family-based physical activity interventions may arguably be the most important target for CVD prevention, yet parents are burdened by excessive time demands that lower the achievement of physical activity. Our pilot study has shown that teaching parents how to organize and plan family physical activity, using state-of-the-art planning resources, can improve their physical activity. In this study we will expand on the pilot results by randomly assigning families with at least one child between 6 and 12 years old, into either an intervention group, or a standard condition group. The intervention will include planning material on how families can be more active, together. We will measure their level of activity, motivations, and beliefs after six months. Clearly the prevention of CVD through the promotion of physical activity is an important research area. Our intervention represents a low-cost, potentially effective method of physical activity promotion that could result in improved physical activity habits and thus family health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of beta-cell mitochondrial physiology by core anti-apoptosis proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; DIABETES; IN VIVO GLUCOSE HOMEOSTASIS; ISLET BIOLOGY; KNOCKOUT MOUSE MODELS; LIVE CELL MICROSCOPY; METABOLIC STRESS; MITOCHONDRIAL PHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Along with the rise in obese Canadians, there is an alarming increase in the number of Canadians with glucose intolerance and diabetes. In healthy individuals, a rise in blood sugar (glucose) stimulates insulin release from beta-cells in the pancreas. This insulin then helps bring the glucose levels back down again. In some obese individuals and the pre-diabetic state, high levels of fats and glucose damage and kill the beta-cells. A group of proteins, known as the Bcl-2 family, control the survival and death of cells under such stress. Recently it has been proposed that such 'survival/death' proteins may also regulate normal cell function. Bcl-2 and a similar protein Bcl-xL, are well known pro-survival members of this group, but we have not yet determined if these proteins have important roles in the pancreatic beta-cell other than protecting the stressed cell from committing 'cellular suicide'.  Our goal is to identify new connections between beta-cell function and survival. We wish to understand better the mechanisms by which beta-cells normally sense glucose and release insulin and we aim to clarify how these important cells fail under obesity-associated stress.  We will examine if Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL control beta-cell glucose sensing and how these proteins affect the impact of a high fat diet on the risk of developing diabetes. To do so we have generated novel types of genetically-modified mice in which we can use a drug to remove the Bcl-2 or Bcl-xL proteins. We will examine these mice, their beta-cells and their proteins using microscopy and detailed studies of how the genetic defects combined with a high fat diet affects blood glucose levels and diabetes.   Our studies will help reveal important new ways to promote beta-cell survival and function. Such discoveries will help prevent the progression of diabetes in at-risk individuals and ultimately control the growing global diabetes epidemic in Canada and the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural mechanisms of compulsive drug use: a multi-approach study of the Bed nucleus of the Stria Terminalis
Keywords-MotsClés: BED NUCLEUS OF THE STRIA TERMINALIS; BRAIN SLICE ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; COCAINE; COMPULSIVE BEHAVIORS; DRUG SELF-ADMINISTRATION; GABA; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY
Abstract-Résumé: Addiction is a compulsive behavior meaning that addicts spend exaggerated efforts and persist taking drugs despite severe negative consequences for them, their family, and their friends. Accordingly, something in the brains of addicts does not gate properly the urge to take drugs when adverse consequences are obviously inevitable. In fact, drug addicts are well aware of the negative consequences of their habits, but yet, they cannot help returning to spend exaggerated time seeking, taking, and recovering from drugs. It is the objective of the present research proposal to identify the location (s) and mechanism (s) that may underlie the compulsive aspect of drug addiction. Fortunately, there are now reliable behavioral tests in animals that closely mimic compulsive drug use in humans. Here, we will combine rodent models of compulsive drug use with electrophysiological assays. This combination will allow us to understand better where in the brain and by which mechanisms do compulsive drug use stems from and may reveal new therapeutical targets to manage and perhaps cure drug addiction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the methyltransferase G9a in normal hematopoiesis and leukaemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER EPIGENETICS; HEMATOPOIESIS; LEUKAEMIA
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer cells can hijack the machinery normally used to control the gene activity to suppress expression of cancer-fighting genes. While in principle these mechanisms are easily manipulated with drugs, our poor knowledge of which pathways are affected in cancer has prevented us from formulating specific strategies for intervention. We have generated preliminary evidence that one such mechanisms is mediated by an enzyme called G9a. Here, we ask for funding to verify G9a as a gene required in myeloid leukaemia cells but dispensable in normal cells, to better understand its role, and to develop strategies to target it in cancer.
