TitreApplicationTitle: GOING HOME - Recovery and community reintegration of mentally ill men and women discharged from hospital: A prospective, longitudinal study of forensic psychiatric patients
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY; CONTINUITY OF CARE; CRIMINALITY; FORENSIC MENTAL HEALTH; JUSTICE; MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES; RECIDIVISM; RECOVERY; RISK MANAGEMENT; STIGMA
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada and globally, we have seen the closure of psychiatric facilities and changes to mental health and criminal laws which have led to new challenges in caring for people with mental illness.  With this decline in regular mental health service, the criminal justice system has increasingly become the gateway to mental health care and more people now cycle between these systems. This "revolving door" phenomenon comes at a high cost to the mentally ill and to society at large. Our study will examine what happens to the severely mentally ill who are judged not criminally responsible on account of their mental disorder (NCRMD) as they leave hospitals and try to reintegrate into the community. We will interview them and their families at discharge, with follow-ups 6 and 12 months later, as well as review their medical and criminal records. We are particularly interested in the things that support this reintegration ('strengths'), leading to a healthy life, and factors that frustrate the process ('risks'), leading to recidivism and re-arrest.  Examples of strengths are strong family ties, available housing, jobs, and community support services; weaknesses include the absence of these, as well as issues like alcohol/drug abuse, social stigma, and personality disorders.  The study will improve the chances of success for these marginalized people and provide valuable insights into coordination across the health, social services, and criminal justice systems, with prospects of significant cost reductions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic modifiers of caffeine intake and cardiovascular disease risk
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD PRESSURE; CAFFEINE; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTION; GENETIC POLYMORPHISMS; HYPERTENSION; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Caffeine is the most widely consumed stimulant in the world. It is found naturally in coffee, tea and cocoa, and is added to cola beverages and energy drinks. There is increased concern that caffeine may negatively affect our cardiovascular system, however, studies have given conflicting results. Recent research has shown that this effect relates to how caffeine is broken down (metabolized) in the body. People who break it down slowly are at greater risk of heart disease whereas those who break it down quickly seem to be protected. Interestingly, the breakdown of caffeine has little to do with its physical effects on the body, such as alertness and withdrawal, and genes relating to these other effects have yet to be studied. We hypothesize that variation exists in important genes that are involved in both caffeine metabolism and its physical effects on the body, and that these genetic differences also modify the relationship between caffeine intake and the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease. The objective of this research is to determine whether these genetic variations alter the relationship between caffeine intake and disease in large populations of healthy young and older adults living in Canada, adults with high blood pressure in Italy, and those who have had a heart attack in Costa Rica. Given the significant burden of heart disease in Canada and the widespread consumption of caffeine our results will allow us to identify individuals who are more susceptible to disease based on their genes and dietary habits. This information is needed to establish improved guidelines to minimize the risk of cardiovascular disease in vulnerable populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Microfluidic Device to Measure the Deformability of Stored Red Blood Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; DEFORMABILITY; LAB-ON-A-CHIP; MEDICAL DEVICE; MICROFLUIDICS; RED BLOOD CELLS; STORAGE; TRANSFUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Red blood cells circulate in the bloodstream for approximately 120 days, delivering oxygen to all tissues in the body. One of the key characteristics of red blood cells is their ability to squeeze into capillary blood vessels that are many times smaller than their own diameter. Donated red blood cells, collected by the Canadian Blood Service, are stored for up to 42 days before they are used for transfusions. During this time, the deformability of these cells is degraded, impairing their ability to circulate in capillary blood vessels. As a result, the viability of these cells in transfusion recipients is reduced from 120 days to, in some cases, hours or minutes. Currently, there are no simple methods to routinely measure the quality of stored red blood cells, which limit the ability of biomedical researchers to study current storage practices to improve the effectiveness of blood transfusions.  Our research team recently developed a simple method for measuring the deformability of red blood cells from an extremely small volume sample. Our proposal aims to apply this technique to measure the deformability of stored red blood cell to determine their quality when used in transfusions. We further aim to develop improved devices based on this technique that could be used to routinely measure the quality of stored red blood cells. Successful development of these technologies will help to improve blood storage methods and improve the health of infusion recipients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory subversion of host defenses by bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; BACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; GENE EXPRESSION; INNATE IMMUNITY; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; REGULATORY EVOLUTION; TWO-COMPONENT REGULATORY SYSTEMS; VIRULENCE FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Just as humans inherit certain traits from generation to generation, the same is true of bacteria that inherit genetic information from their ancestors. This genetic information specifies not only what type of bacteria it will become, but also how it interacts with it's surroundings, whether it will be pathogenic or not, and whether it is resistant to certain antibiotics for example. We have identified new mechanisms of pathogen evolution whereby bacteria alter the expression of certain genes in response to the host. By altering their regulatory DNA, bacteria can turn genes on or off at certain times or produce more of a certain gene product when it is needed most, allowing them to rapidly respond to their environment and exploit the immediate surroundings, such as in a human or animal host. We found that when bacteria can mutate their regulatory DNA, they are better able to infect animal hosts, however we don't yet know the full extent to which bacteria use this strategy for their virulence or to adapt during human and animal infection. Our work examines how bacterial pathogens sense their host surroundings and the mechanisms that link these host sensors to adaptive gene expression involved in virulence, evasion of our immune system, and ultimately, disease. Using new technologies in genomics and microbial chemical biology, we are creating an unprecedented opportunity for insight into the interface of human and microbial biology by generating new knowledge about infectious disease mechanisms. This knowledge base creates opportunities for innovative drug target discovery with tangible impact into public health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aging, inflammation & white matter damage after ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ENVIRONMENTAL ENRICHMENT; GENE AND PROTEIN EXPRESSION; HEMORRHAGIC STROKE; INFLAMMATION; ISCHEMIC STROKE; MICROGLIA & MACROPHAGES; MICROGLIAL ACTIVATION; WHITE MATTER DAMAGE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the third leading cause of death in Canada, and a major cause of long-term disability. An almost entirely overlooked aspect of stroke research is that it is mainly a disease of the elderly. Given the aging population, the incidence of stroke is expected to increase. There are two main types of stroke. Most are ischemic, resulting from a blood clot that starves brain tissue; the others are hemorrhagic, caused by bleeding into the brain. Many experimental stroke therapies have failed in human trials, and a major issue is that most experimental strategies target events that happen too quickly: before patients reach the hospital. There is also a misconception that both forms of stroke cause similar injury, but hemorrhage more closely resembles brain trauma. Both types of stroke injure the long axons that nerves use to communicate, and this is important in determining the outcome, but not enough is known about how and why this damage occurs. We study the secondary phase of damage that can last for days, and involves inflammation and the brain's own immune cell (microglia). We do not understand how inflammation develops after a stroke, or what the immune cells are doing. Nor do we know how age or stroke type affects the inflammatory response. Another issue involves the common knowledge that a stimulating physical, social and intellectual environment improves the quality of life after stroke, but we do not fully understand why. This proposal addresses three key goals: 1) To understand the similarities and differences in inflammation and axon damage after both types of stroke; 2) To determine the effects of aging on these processes; and 3) To analyze whether an enriched post-stroke environment alters the brain immune response and axon damage. The proposed research will significantly expand our understanding of the inflammatory changes and nerve damage after stroke, and this will help improve the development of more effective treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: An evolutionary proteomics approach to identify short linear motifs in intrinsically disordered regions
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; DISORDER; POST TRANSLATIONAL REGULATION; PROTEOMICS; SHORT LINEAR MOTIFS
Abstract-Résumé: Most biological functions are performed by proteins, and most proteins fold up into regular three dimensional structures that determine their biological function.  However, a large subset of proteins, including many associated with important diseases (such as p53, BRCA1 and CFTR) are not totally folded. They contain so-called "disordered" regions which do not take on a specific structure and do not perform enzymatic functions. The function of most of these disordered regions is not understood, but one model (that has been established in some cases) is that they contain short segments that are important for determining when and where the protein is active.  This project will systematically search for the segments within the disordered regions that are likely to be important based on their patterns of evolution. Then we will confirm that the segments we identify actually control the activity of the proteins in which they are found by doing a series of experiments in yeast (a simple model organism).  If our hypothesis is right, we will be able to better understand the function of the disordered regions. This will be an important step towards predicting how proteins are turned on and off, both in normal cells and when disease-causing mutations occur.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Characterization of Genomic DNA Elements Regulating Epigenetic Silencing
Keywords-MotsClés: BOUNDARY ELEMENTS; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENOMICS; HETEROCHROMATIN; KNOCK-IN; MONO-ALLELIC EXPRESSION; MOUSE EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; TRANSGENES; WAYSTATIONS; X-CHROMOSOME INACTIVATION
Abstract-Résumé: We wish to understand how genes are told that they are to be silent, or that they should be expressed or 'on'.  Most cells in an individual have the same DNA, and therefore the same genes.  Specific tissues express only a subset of their genes, so understanding gene regulation is very important to understanding disease as well as normal human biology.  A dramatic regulation of genes occurs on the X chromosome.  The X chromosome is one of the pair of sex chromosomes, and females have two X chromosomes while males have one X and the Y chromosome.  In order to keep the number of genes that are active the same between male and females one of the X chromosomes is silenced in females.  This silencing spreads along the chromosome and our research is to find the regions of DNA that help or prevent this spread of silencing.  We will do this by comparing the DNA around genes that get silenced with other regions that never get silenced. The DNA that is commonly found in silent or active regions will be tested for its ability to make other genes active or silent in female mouse cells.  Identifying such regions of DNA will further our understanding of gene regulation, and will identify regions of DNA that can protect inserted DNA from silencing which could be useful for future gene therapy attempts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Design, synthesis and evaluation of potential neuraminidase inhibitors for the treatment of many conditions including influenza
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMICAL SYNTHESES; CHOLERA; COMPUTATIONAL DESIGN; INFLUENZA PANDEMICS; MECHANISM-BASED INHIBITORS; NEXT-GENERATION THERAPEUTICS; SIALIDASE/NEURAMINDASE INHIBITION
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza type A and B viral infections continue to be one of the serious health problems facing the human population worldwide.  In addition to the seasonal reappearance of the previously circulated viral strains, the appearance of new viral strains, such as the swine flu virus (H1N1) now circulating worldwide. That is, influenza virus continually changes how it is seen by the immune system by making slight modifications to the proteins that cover its surface.  Small changes such as these mean that every year a slightly different strain of influenza circulates through the Human population and a new vaccine must be developed.  Occasionally, the virus will swap one of its surface proteins with that from a bird-infective influenza strain (in the current example the H5N1 bird flu) and such events have resulted in three major pandemics during the past 100 years.  Fortunately, at the moment the current H5N1 strains are not effectively transmitted between Humans.  However, the worst scenario in the history of influenza outbreaks was the so called "Spanish flu" (1918) which killed nearly 1% of the world's population.  Inhibition of one of the viral surface proteins that is called neuraminidase (the N in H5N1), which catalyzes the release of newly formed virus particles from the infected cells, has proved to be a suitable approach in the design of anti-viral drugs. We propose here to derive knowledge of how the influenza enzyme works.  To do this we tag atoms in our molecules that the virus uses during its replication cycle.  That is, we are planning to use a type of imaging technology that is similar to magnetic resonance imaging or MRI, the machines at hospitals that provide doctors with information used to diagnose problems. We have a similar machine at Simon Fraser University, but instead of scanning the body of a patient, our instrument scans the atoms within molecules.  From these scans we can learn how the molecules are reacting.

TitreApplicationTitle: A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial for the evaluation of a polypill, a low dose aspirin and vitamin D supplementation in primary prevention to reduce cardiovascular disease (CVD) outcomes - The International Polycap Study 3 (TIPS-3)
Keywords-MotsClés: ASPIRIN; CANCER PREVENTION; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE PREVENTION; FIXED DOSE COMBINATION; FRACTURES; POLYCAP; POLYPILL; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Heart attacks, stroke, cancers and osteoporotic fractures are the most common causes of death and disabilities in Canada and in many developing countries. Risk factors such as high blood pressures and high cholesterol, in addition to smoking, obesity, lack of exercise, diabetes and improper diets, are common in our population in Canada and in other countries.  In order to reduce this burden of heart attacks and stroke, different strategies are needed. Simple inexpensive treatments are required to prevent cancers and fractures in our aging populations. In this study we propose to evaluate the effects of a single pill containing 3 blood pressure lowering medications and a cholesterol lowering medication in order to treat the blood pressure and high cholesterol, the two most important risk factors, in people before they suffer from a heart attack or stroke.  In addition, we will also assess the effects of a low dose aspirin which is believed to have effects in reducing heart attacks, stroke and cancer, and vitamin D in its effects in reducing fractures, cancer and other chronic health conditions.  This study, which will be carried out in 7500 people from Canada and several other countries in Asia, South America and Africa, where many recent Canadians come from, is expected to have a big impact on prevention heart attacks, strokes, fractures and cancers, which are the most common chronic health conditions affecting our aging population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Porphysome nanoparticle-enabled minimally invasive transbronchial photothermal ablation of lung cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BRONCHOSCOPE; ENDOBRONCHIAL ULTRASOUND; IMAGE-GUIDED THERAPY; LIGHT DELIVERY; LUNG CANCER; MINIMALLY INVASIVE; MULTIMODAL IMAGING; NANOPARTICLE; PHOTOTHERMAL THERAPY; THERMAL ABLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is responsible for 28% of all cancer deaths, more than breast, prostate and colon combined. Given the substantial mortality benefits with early detection, there will be more patients diagnosed with early-stage disease. Surgery is the standard care for these patients, but approximately 25% are medically inoperable, thus requiring effective alternative treatment. Image-guided laser thermal ablation via optical fiber delivery is one of the most promising non-surgical options. However, its clinical use has two major limitations: 1) the current method of light delivery placing the optical fiber into the tumor through the skin risks serious complications, and 2) very high light doses are needed to completely eradicate tumors due to the low preferential light absorption by the tumor tissue, so that there is risk to adjacent normal tissues. We propose to address both limitations using a novel platform that combines unique technologies developed by our multidisciplinary translational team.   The first element is the use of innovative image-guided transbronchial light delivery, based on clinically-proven methods pioneered by Dr Yasufuku. This allows fiber placement/light irradiation to be done "from the inside" using an ultra-thin bronchoscopic approach, and will resolve the first safety issue. Secondly, Dr Zheng's lab recently discovered all-organic, nontoxic nanoparticles ("porphysomes") that will absorb the light energy with high efficiency, and thereby restrict the thermal damage to the tumor target. These nanoparticles can be actively or passively targeted to the tumor. Finally, photothermal treatment planning, light delivery and dosimetry have been developed by Dr Wilson and applied clinically in localized prostate cancer. Successful integration and validation in preclinical animal models of these world-leading technologies has potential to be rapidly translated into a novel, curative and very safe treatment modality for early-stage lung cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Vascular Dissemination in the Lyme Disease Spirochete
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; BORRELIA BURGDORFERI; ENDOTHELIAL BIOLOGY; FIBRONECTIN; GLYCOSAMINOGLYCANS; HEMATOGENOUS DISSEMINATION; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY; LYME DISEASE; VASCULAR ADHESION
Abstract-Résumé: Blood-borne spread (dissemination) of pathogens is a critical step in the development of serious infectious disease, and is responsible for most of the mortality due to bacterial infection. The dissemination mechanisms of many bacterial pathogens are largely unknown. A key event in dissemination is pathogen adhesion to vascular endothelium, an event which permits circulating microbes to marginate from the bloodstream and decelerate sufficiently to transmigrate through the vasculature into target tissues. My research focuses on the mechanisms used by the Lyme disease bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi (Bb) to disseminate in the bloodstream of its vertebrate host, a process which we can observe in real time and 3D space in living animals by intravital microscopy. Using intravital microscopy, we determined that Bb vascular adhesion is regulated by host fibronectin (Fn), glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) and Fn- and GAG-binding sequences of the Bb adhesion protein BBK32. BBK32 is the only bacterial protein known to mediate vascular adhesion in vivo, and is conserved in other disseminating bacterial pathogens. The aim of my funding proposal is to investigate the biochemical and biophysical properties of the Bb vascular adhesion mechanism, by investigating the contributions of BBK32, host Fn and glycosylated endothelial receptors to shear force-regulated vascular adhesion and dissemination into joints and other target tissues. These studies will provide the first direct insight into the novel vascular adhesion mechanism of a bacterial pathogen in real-time and space, and will identify adhesion mechanisms and molecules with potential for development as novel clinical drug targets.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of fusion oncoprotein stability by the IGF1 receptor axis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CANCER BIOLOGY; CANCER GENETICS; FUSION TYROSINE KINASES; KINASE INHIBITORS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MYELOPROLIFERATIVE DISORDERS; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; SARCOMAS; THERAPEUTIC TARGETS
Abstract-Résumé: Most chemotherapeutic agents used to treat cancers target growing (dividing) cells. Unfortunately, when these agents are used they can affect normal dividing cells, which can have devastating short-term and long-term effects. In this proposal we will attempt to understand how a particular cellular pathway, called the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R) axis, contributes to tumour formation. IGF1R is activated in virtually all childhood malignancies, as well as many adult cancers and IGF1R blocking antibodies have shown impressive anti-tumor activity in childhood sarcomas and breast cancers. However, it remains a puzzle as to how IGF1R actually contributes to malignancy, and the basis for sensitivity versus resistance in different patients is completely unknown. We hope to learn how this signaling axis may be uniquely activated in tumour cells and how it might be more efficiently targeted therapeutically. As a model system, we will study an oncogenic protein called ETV6-NTRK3, which we originally discovered in childhood sarcomas and a form of breast cancer. ETV6-NTRK3-driven cancer cells are dependent on the IGF1R axis for survival. In the previous grant cycle we unexpectedly found that IGF1R stabilizes the ETV6-NTRK3 oncoprotein, and that when IGF1R is chemically blocked the levels of ETV6-NTRK3 protein are rapidly reduced. Therefore an exciting possibility is that IGF1R stabilizes oncogenic proteins in tumour cells. In this proposal we will directly analyze how IGF1R contributes to ETV6-NTRK3 stability. Inhibiting the kinases that control fusion protein stability is a novel way of selectively targeting cancers driven by oncogenic fusion proteins. Since kinase inhibitors for IGF1R are currently in clinical trials, we believe that findings from this proposal may have far-reaching relevance for the many different types of cancers driven by IGF1R-dependent oncogenic fusion proteins.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac Repair by the Epicardium
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC REMODELING; CARDIAC REPAIR; HEART FAILURE; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; NEOVASCULARIZATION; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease is the #1 killer in Canada, and coronary artery disease is a major form of cardiovascular disease. Heart attack or myocardial infarction happens when a coronary artery is completely blocked and blood flow to a region of the heart is cut off. This leads to the loss of heart muscle, heart failure and patient death. Despite many years of research, there is still no cure for myocardial infarction and heart failure.  The epicardium is an outside layer of epithelial cells that cover the heart. Its major function has been traditionally considered to reduce friction between the heart and pericardial membrane during heart contractions. Recent studies suggest that the epicardium is much more than a cover over the outside of the adult heart. During early embryonic heart development, the epicardium contributes to the formation of coronary arteries and growth of heart muscle. In the adult heart, the regenerative potential of the epicardium may be activated following myocardial infarction. The purpose of this proposal is to investigate the regenerative potential of the epicardium to repair the damaged heart following myocardial infarction in mice. In addition, stem cell factor and its receptor c-kit are critical to stem cell survival and function. The effects of stem cell factor and c-kit on the regenerative potential of epicardium to repair the damaged heart will also be investigated. The proposed research will increase our understanding on the role of the epicardium in the repair of the damaged heart following myocardial infarction, and may have therapeutic implications in developing new treatment for myocardial infarction.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of human glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase in maintaining the redox state of the DNA repair enzyme APE1
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; DNA REPAIR; GENOME-WIDE LOCATION ANALYSIS; GENOMIC INSTABILITY; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; OXIDATIVE DNA DAMAGE; OXIDIZED PROTEINS; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATION; PROTEIN STRUCTURE/FUNCTION ANALYSIS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Reactive oxygen species are highly unstable molecules and are produced, e.g., by mitochondrial respiration and activated neutrophils. These reactive oxygen species can attack and destroy various cellular macromolecules such as proteins or enzymes to cause functional inactivation, thereby leading to several human disorders, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Down's syndrome, and Alzheimer's disease.  We discovered that the protein GAPDH can form an association with the DNA repair enzyme APE1, which functions to maintain the integrity of the genome. We show that GAPDH converts the inactive form of APE1, that is, the oxidized APE1 caused by reactive oxygen species, to the active form that is needed to repair damaged DNA.  Reducing the level of GAPDH decreased the activity of APE1 and caused the DNA to accumulate lesions.  Such lesions if not repaired can initiate the formation of cancer cells.  We believe that GAPDH has the ability to maintain the redox state of this key DNA repair enzyme, APE1. We plan to show that decreasing the levels of GAPDH will inactivate APE1 resulting in a range of biological consequences.  We believe that GAPDH plays a crucial role in preventing neurodegenerative diseases by blocking the accumulation of genotoxic lesions that could trigger cell death.  Thus, defects in GAPDH function might serve to predict individuals who are at risk of developing diseases such as cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transitional states of seizures: mechanisms and modulation
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EPILEPSY; GAP JUNCTIONS; NEURODYNAMICS; NEUROTRANSMITTER RELEASE; OPTOGENETICS; POTASSIUM; VOLTAGE CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a common disease affecting over one percent of the world population, with an impact greater than stroke. A terrifying aspect of epilepsy is its unpredictability. When the brain transitions into the seizure state, a big mystery. We will study the cellular and local network mechanisms underlying these spontaneous transitions, and mechanisms for preventing them. We hypothesize that seizure transitions involve large changes in neurotransmitter release from synapses (connections between brain cells). We predict that an increase in the extracellular potassium ion concentration (an ion that is released as the seizure starts) initially activates the epilepsy network, but later, paradoxically stops the seizure. Methods: We will employ electrical recordings from outside and inside brain cells, measure extracellular potassium ion concentrations, and will use microscopy to visualize electrical and ionic activities. We will study brain tissue removed at operation for the treatment of epilepsy in humans (tissue that would be discarded), an enormous advantage since it permits us to develop the key concepts in the most relevant tissue (human) before carrying out more detailed experiments in animal brain tissue. We will use isolated mouse brain tissue and live brain cell recordings from the cerebral cortex of anesthetized mice, some with a focal epileptogenic lesion (similar to humans that we treat and operate upon). Neuronal activities will also be specifically controlled using the new optogenetics, which permits transfection of specific cell types which can then be excited or inhibited by flashes of laser light. Significance: The mystery of the spontaneous transition to seizure needs these fundamental investigations to develop rational therapeutics (pharmacological or electrical) to prevent the brain's transition to the frightening brain state of a seizure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Propriospinal transmission of the locomotor command signal
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAINSTEM STIMULATION; EXTRACELLULAR RECORDING; IN VITRO SPINAL CORD; IN VIVO; LOCOMOTION; PROPRIOSPINAL; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury affects 36,000 Canadians. It is associated with lifetime care costs ranging from $1.25 to 25 million. The brain sends signals to the lower part of the spinal cord that activate neural circuits responsible for walking.  Individuals with spinal cord injury are unable to walk because these connections are interrupted.    Until recently scientists assumed that long continuous nerve pathways were responsible for sending the command signal for walking.   However, our recent experiments showed that another system can be used for this purpose.  It involves relaying nerve signals through a series of short nerve cells, like a water bucket passed from one person to the next until it reaches the fire.  This system should be much easier to repair because relay nerve cells need to re-grow only a short distance, until the next relay neuron below the injury is contacted.  They do not need to re-grow the entire length of the spinal cord, which is the very difficult challenge faced by long continuous pathways.     We now propose to further study this newly discovered relay pathway underlying the activation of walking.  More specifically, we will determine which nerve cells in the brain activate the spinal relay system.  We will examine whether the relay system is present in adult animals (our earlier work used newborn rats).  Finally, we will determine whether artificial excitation of the relay pathway can promote transmission of the signal for walking through the site of spinal cord injury.   If successful, this would allow improved voluntary control of walking despite spinal cord injury.  The long-term goal is to apply drugs to the spinal cord of humans with spinal cord injury to facilitate or enable walking.  Theoretically, this could be done using clinical technology that already exists (drug pumps with small tubes that lead to the spinal cord - for the treatment of other conditions such as pain and spasticity).

TitreApplicationTitle: Chromatin remodeling dynamics during human DNA double strand break repair
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; CHROMATIN DYNAMICS; DNA DOUBLE-STRAND BREAK; GENOME INSTABILITY; HETEROCHROMATIN; HIGH RESOLUTION MICROSCOPY; HUMAN AGEING; MAMMALIAN TISSUE CULTURE; RADIATION EXPOSURE
Abstract-Résumé: The technological age has seen humans increasingly exposed to sources of DNA-damaging radiation. A double-edged sword, radiation has enabled great advances in energy, medical diagnosis and therapy while simultaneously increasing our risk of nuclear accident or attack. The most deleterious lesion caused by radiation is a break in both strands of our DNA, a DNA double-strand break (DSB). Unless accurately repaired by the molecular machinery of our cells, DSBs can lead to genome instability - a fundamental driver of cancer and ageing. We now know that DSBs are much more difficult to repair within certain regions of chromatin, that complex of protein and DNA within which all our genetic information resides. My research endeavors to understand the processes underlying DNA repair in chromatin and, in doing so, improve our knowledge of how radiation exposure influences cancer formation and human ageing, as well as increasing the efficacy of radiation therapy and radiation protection measures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and Cellular Mechanisms of Neural Circuit Formation
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; CELLULAR NEUROBIOLOGY; DROSOPHILA GENETICS; MOLECULAR NEUROBIOLOGY; NEURAL CIRCUIT FORMATION; NEURAL DEVELOPMENT; SYNAPSE FORMATION; SYNAPTIC SPECIFICITY; SYNAPTIC TARGETING
Abstract-Résumé: What guides a nerve cell within a brain to choose a specific partner to connect with during neural circuit formation?  Our research will investigate how the neural receptor Dscam (Down Syndrome Cell Adhesion Molecule) is involved in synaptic targeting decisions.  We will use molecular genetics and imaging in the model organism, Drosophila, to characterize how cell-surface molecules influence synapse targeting decisions and synaptic connectivity.  We make use of a genetically-specified, hard-wired sensory circuit involved in touch perception.  We will analyze how disruption in Dscam's function produces synaptic targeting errors that affect the animal's behavior.  These experiments will help uncover basic molecular and cellular mechanisms used by nervous systems to wire up pre-specified circuits.  Furthermore, the gene for human Dscam lies within Chromosome 21, at a locus called the Down Syndrome Critical Region.  Down syndrome is caused by a triplication of human Chromosome 21, and our experiments will also investigate how triplication of the Down Syndrome Cell Adhesion Molecule gene impairs synaptic targeting.  Our research will help us understand first, how nervous systems develop normally and second, how dysfunction of specific molecules can cause abnormal development.  We hope that by uncovering these molecular underpinnings we will be able to apply these findings to other brain diseases related to neural circuit miswiring.

TitreApplicationTitle: Early phase clinical trials with the small molecule DCA in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: DCA IN PULMONARY ARTERIAL HYPERTENSION
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary hypertension is a deadly disease with unknown cause that kills patients within 3 years from the time of diagnosis if untreated. Available therapies improve the quality of life and alleviate some symptoms but they do not appear to prolong life and they do not reverse the disease. The disease is caused by excessive growth of cells that eventually occlude the lumen of the lung blood vessels, putting strain on the right chambers of the heart that eventually dilate, killing the patients. The lung vessels in this disease behave much like cancer also a disease of excessive cell growth. We have previously shown that an orphan drug called dichloroacetate can reverse the disease in many animal models. More recently we also published evidence that this drug may be effective in humans with one of the deadliest human cancers, brain cancer. This drug does not belong to any pharmaceutical industry and translating this knowledge into humans requires Federal funding. We proposed to conduct the first trials in humans with pulmonary hypertension focusing first on safety and tolerability of this new treatment and second on possible efficacy. If successful, these trials will be critical and the design of larger trials in the future that are required before such therapy is proven to be safe and effective for this condition. In such a case with this therapy might also be a quite cheap therapy since this drug is not owned by any for-profit pharmaceutical industry.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurobehavioural impacts of chronic sleep restriction
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTONOMIC; CHRONIC SLEEP LOSS; CIRCADIAN INFLUENCE; EEG/EMG; GENE EXPRESSION; HOMEOSTASIS AND ALLOSTASIS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; RAT; STRESS; SUSTAINED ATTENTION TASK
Abstract-Résumé: Insomnia and disrupted sleep are increasingly recognized as having important effects on human health and safety, and as having a major economic impact. How much chronic sleep loss affects health and behaviour may depend on how effectively lost sleep can be compensated for by recovery sleep. Yet we know little about how sleep patterns change under chronic sleep loss and how they recover during later sleep opportunities. Animal models allow researchers to study how the body and brain respond to chronic sleep loss and attempt to recover sleep. We recently developed a new rat model of chronic sleep loss that takes into account rats' natural polyphasic sleep tendencies. We now propose to use this model to examine the effects of chronic sleep loss and recovery sleep on behaviour and physiology. Rats will be sleep deprived during repeated cycles over four days and allowed to show recovery sleep between deprivation cycles and after the four days. Sleep patterns and other physiological measures, such as heart rate and body temperature, will be recorded before, during, and after sleep loss. We will study how the biological clock influences the adaptation to, and recovery from, chronic sleep loss, and how chronic sleep loss affects the brain and the body's ability to maintain a biologically adaptive and stable internal environment. We will also examine how sleep restriction affects the rat's ability to maintain attention during task performance, which is the cognitive problem resulting from sleep loss that is most problematic for people. We will also try to identify brain changes that reflect how we adapt to chronic sleep loss. A better understanding of how the brain responds to and attempts to adapt to lost sleep will help us develop new approaches to reducing the impacts of chronic sleep loss on people.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating Quality Improvement Interventions in Colorectal Cancer Surgery in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: COLORECTAL CANCER; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Researchers have called for new ways of improving quality in medicine. This study will evaluate the results of such an approach which has been taking place in LHIN 4, one of 14 LHINs in Ontario. The Quality Improvement in Colorectal Cancer in LHIN4 Project (QICC-L4) is designed to improve the care delivered to patients who have bowel cancer surgery. It was started in the fall of 2006 and is an example of 'integrated knowledge translation'. This means that the LHIN4 surgeons come together and select specific targets for quality improvement and the interventions to improve the selected targets. Over the last seven years, surgical leaders at Cancer Care Ontario have also been starting quality improvement projects in bowel cancer, though these are not 'integrated knowledge translation' projects. A great deal of money and energy has been used to start the QICC-L4 and the Cancer Care Ontario interventions in colorectal cancer. We would like to measure the impact of both sets of efforts.   Objective:To measure if an 'integrated knowledge translation' strategy called the QICC-L4 can improve the quality of care received by patients who have bowel cancer surgery.  Methods: The study will have two parts. In Part I we will interview surgeons and administrators from all of the 14 Ontario LHINs to better understand what sorts of quality improvement activities related to bowel cancer surgery have been taking place across the province. We will group LHINs that have been doing similar things. In Part II we will do a chart review of patients who underwent bowel cancer surgery in years 2006, 2009 or 2011. We will then compare measures in LHIN4 with measures in the other LHINs.  Significance: Better measures in LHIN4 would provide some proof that 'integrated knowledge translation' may be a better way of improving care in bowel cancer surgery, and possibly in many other medical areas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endocannabinoid Signaling as a Regulator of Anxiety
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYGDALA; ANXIETY; CRH; ENDOCANNABINOID; HPA AXIS; INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; STEREOTAXIC SURGERY; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Anxiety disorders are the most prevalent mental illness afflicting Canadians, with the one year prevalence of anxiety disorders at 12% and estimates that approximately one in four Canadians will suffer an anxiety disorder at some point in their life. Anxiety disorders often manifest with common symptoms (hypervigilance, risk assessment and inappropriate fear behaviors), however they can develop either in response to stress (state anxiety) or occur as a biologically inborn tendency (trait anxiety). My body of research to date has illustrated the role of the endocannabinoid system, which is the brains endogenous version of cannabis (akin to how endorphins are the brains self made version of opiates), in regulating emotional behavior and responses to stress. The aim of the current research is to extend our current knowledge of endocannabinoids and anxiety by determining the role this system plays in both state and trait anxiety through a combined research approach incorporating behavioral analysis, biochemistry and drug interventions. Furthermore, this current research avenue will also aim to understand the neural mechanisms that regulate endocannabinoid signaling and thus contribute to the disturbance in this system that can manifest as anxiety. Ultimately, this research will help to elucidate the role of the endocannabinoid system in anxiety and if targeting this system for the development of novel anti-anxiety drugs is a fruitful avenue of research to pursue.

TitreApplicationTitle: The function of hyaluronan binding in the immune system
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL-MATRIX ADHESION; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; IMMUNE CELL MIGRATION; IMMUNE RESPONSE; IMMUNOLOGY; KNOCKOUT MICE; MULTI-COLOR FLOW CYTOMETRY; T CELL ACTIVATION; T CELL MEMORY; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Interactions between white blood cells and their environment in lymphoid organs are critical for their development and function. Blood cells develop from a single stem cell in the bone marrow. In bone marrow transplantation, it is critical that these stem cells home to the bone marrow where the right environment allows them to divide, differentiate and replenish the entire immune system. Likewise, lymph nodes provide an important environment for specific mature white blood cells (T cells) to recognize infectious agents and respond appropriately. We want find out more about these environments and how they facilitate immune cell development and function. In this proposal we will examine the interaction of white blood cells with a specific component of their environment, a sticky, sugary molecule called hyaluronan (HA). HA is an essential component of the cell's environment and its interaction with its receptor, CD44, on immune cells is highly regulated. Our approach is to generate immune cells expressing mutant CD44 receptors that either cannot interact with HA or that bind HA all the time. These cells will be expressed in mice where we can observe both immune cell development and the immune response to infection. Analysis of these mice will test our hypothesis that the interaction with HA supports immune cell development in the bone marrow, enhances the production of fighter T cells and memory T cell responses. This research will provide important new knowledge that can be used to design more effective treatments for immunodeficient patients and bone marrow transplant recipients. It will be a significant step forward if we show that HA enhances fighter and memory T cell responses, as this will have important implications for the development of more effective vaccines. Vaccination is the single most effective way of preventing disease and thus saves millions of lives as well as millions in health care costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the signalling functions of polycomb-mediated ubiquitylation in DNA double-strand break repair
Keywords-MotsClés: BAP1; CANCER STEM CELL; CHROMATIN; DNA DOUBLE-STRAND BREAKS; POLYCOMB; RADIATION THERAPY; UBIQUITYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: The presence of stem cells within human tumours and their increased resistance to therapies are thought to be a major reason why some patients fail therapy.  We have found that a group of proteins that are essential for maintaining stem cells are also involved in the repair of DNA double-strand breaks.  This may provide an important link and expose an "Achilles heel" of tumours.  That is, if we are able to disrupt the function of these proteins, we may be able to sensitize these cancer stem cells such that they are as sensitive to therapy as the remaining tumour.  In order to pursue this goal, we are trying to build a base of knowledge around our original discovery that will help us design strategies to exploit our finding.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of music-supported rehabilitation on behavioural and cortical functions in stroke recovery
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN PLASTICITY; COGNITIVE FUNCTIONS; MOTOR SKILLS; MUSIC TRAINING; NEUROIMAGING; QUALITY OF LIFE; STROKE REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Playing music requires memorizing melodic sequences, planning movements in time, and receiving feedback in sound, touch, and vision. We and other researchers show evidence that training in music- making results in enhanced brain functions related to all of the above activities in healthy children and adults. Thus, a question arises as to how this benefit can be translated to stroke rehabilitation. Indeed, music-supported rehabilitation (MSR) therapy has been recently developed in which stroke patients learn to play music on percussion and keyboard instruments. MSR has been shown to be more effective in improving arm and hand skills than conventional physical therapy for patients at an earlier stage after stroke. MSR also, is an excellent candidate for rehabilitation services to chronic patients who have limited access to expensive therapies because it (MSR) can be easily delivered in community- or home- based settings without a certified therapist. Further, MSR adds an enjoyable context such that patients can easily engage in and focus attention during the training. Therefore, in this project, for the first time we shall systemically examine the impacts of MSR on chronic stroke patients, specifically in terms of patients' outcome on behavioural and brain functions after MSR to those after conventional physical therapy in a randomized intervention assignment. For behavioural outcomes, we will evaluate not only motor skills but also cognitive functions and health-related quality of life. The brain functional recovery will be assessed through a brain-wave recording technique called magnetoencephalography (MEG) which has the sensitivity to detect changes in brain functions in individuals. The knowledge gained from this project will help to examine the efficacy of MSR at chronic stage of stroke recovery and reveal its underlying neural mechanisms which, in turn, will allow us to improve rehabilitation services in the future for stroke patients in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of Vegf receptor activity and angiogenesis by Slit/Robo signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ENDOCYTOSIS; ENDOTHELIAL BIOLOGY; MICRORNA; SLIT/ROBO SIGNALLING; VASCULAR ENDOTHELIAL GROWTH FACTOR; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Blood vessels facilitate the access of cells to oxygen and nutrients, and the growth of new blood vessels (a process known as angiogenesis) is highly regulated. Disease can result from an insufficiency of functional blood vessels. For example, following a heart attack regions of the heart are cut off from a blood supply and massive cell death ensues. On the other hand, excess vasculature can also be the cause or consequence of disease. The growth of solid tumours requires that the tumour can attract new blood vessels to supply the resources required for sustained growth. Also, excess growth of blood vessels in the eyes of diabetic patients can lead to blindness. Understanding how to control blood vessel growth is therefore highly relevant to the treatment of a variety of human diseases. The endothelial cells that line the inside of blood vessels are one of the main targets of angiogenic molecules, including Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (Vegf). Vegf binds to a family of Vegf receptors (Vegfrs), including Vegfr2, and activates signals that instruct endothelial cell to begin to form a new vessel. Signalling in response to Vegf binding to Vegfr2 is highly regulated. We have recently discovered that the Slit/Robo signalling pathway can regulate Vegf signalling. Slit family members bind to Robo receptors to activate a downstream signalling pathway. However, how the Slit/Robo signalling pathway controls Vegf signalling is poorly understood. It has recently been appreciated that Vegfr2 enters the cell following Vegf binding, and that this internalization is required for activation of pathways that lead to new vessel growth. Our preliminary data has suggested that the Slit/Robo pathway may control Vegfr2 internalization. This grant will address how the Slit/Robo pathway controls Vegf signalling. These studies are important for the design of therapeutics that can be used to either promote or inhibit blood vessel growth in the setting of disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modifying Gene Expression with Synthetic Nucleic Acid Therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICANCER; CONTROL OF GENE EXPRESSION; NUCLEOSIDE ANALOGUES; OLIGONUCLEOTIDE THERAPEUTICS; RNAI AND ANTISENSE; STRUCTURAL AND MECHANISTIC STUDIES OF NUCLEIC ACIDS
Abstract-Résumé: The discovery of RNA interference has set the stage for novel drug discovery programs based on the notion that short pieces of DNA or RNA can be made into drugs.  My laboratory at McGill University is interested in generating synthetically modified DNA and RNA structures that are able to "switch off" disease-causing genes, including those related to cancers, inflammation, etc. Interestingly, it turns out that these modified versions of DNA have increased stability to cellular processes that would otherwise degrade them before they could perform their desired functions. Essentially, these molecules are designed to perform a singular function in diseased cells: intercept the messenger RNAs of a disease-related gene, and "switch off" that gene.  More specifically, we intend to design and optimize modified nucleic acids which will allow us to slow down the rate at which malignant brain tumors can spread, potentially laying the foundation for development of attractive drug candidates for cancer treatment. Understanding the processes through which our modified compounds function to intercept the messenger RNA is also an important research endeavor within our group.  In collaboration with biochemists and cellular biologists, we will study the enzymes involved in RNA recognition, because a thorough understanding of this process will aid in the design of more potent nucleic acid derivatives.  These proposed studies expose my graduate and postdoctoral students to a wide range of nucleic acid chemistry and biology research, and to strategies used for identifying candidate molecules and developing them into useful therapeutic drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: DNA unwinding at replication forks
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE; DNA HELICASE; DNA REPLICATION; KINASE; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; PROTEIN-DNA INTERACTIONS; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; REPLICATION INITIATION
Abstract-Résumé: The central question in the proposed research is how are our genes copied? The answers to this question will provide an understanding of a basic cellular process required for life. More importantly, our studies will shed insight into diseased states, such as cancer, where the control of gene copying is often abnormal. Our genes are encoded in DNA, which is like a zipper with the genetic information stored in the teeth of the zipper. In order for the genes to be copied, the DNA must be unzipped by a protein called a DNA helicase. The ability of the DNA helicase to unzip or unwind DNA is very tightly regulated in cells so that it only functions when it is needed. We will examine the different ways in which the DNA helicase is controlled in the cell. We will examine how the DNA helicase is able to unwind DNA. Understanding how the helicase functions will help us understand how it is controlled. We will also examine one way in which the DNA helicase is controlled in response to stress, a time at which copying of the genes is put on hold so that the cell can respond. A third project will examine the function of one of the molecules that controls the helicase, a potential target in the treatment of cancers. Our studies will yield insight into the essential cellular process of copying DNA and will have long term implications for the study and treatment of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization and lineage commitment of progenitor thymocytes
Keywords-MotsClés: DELTA-LIKE; EVA1; IMMUNE RECONSTITUTION; LYMPHOCYTE DEVELOPMENT; LYMPHOCYTE PROGENITORS; NOTCH SIGNALING; STROMAL CELLS; T CELL DEVELOPMENT; THYMUS; THYMUS EPITHELIAL CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The thymus is the principal organ for the generation of T cells, which play a key role in our defense against infectious diseases and cancer. However, alterations in T cell development can lead to the generation of pathogenic T cells that contribute to many autoimmune diseases, including diabetes, arthritis, and multiple sclerosis, or can result in the generation of leukemia. Once T-lymphocyte precursors enter the thymus from the bone marrow, their differentiation occurs in several discrete stages. We have defined early stages in thymocyte development, and also identified the key molecular interactions that are responsible for inducing T cell development. Our analyses revealed that these early thymocytes undergo a set regulated steps that leads them to commit to the T cell lineage. The goals of our studies are to determine the specific nature of signals that are provided by the thymic environment, and identify new molecules responsible for commitment, growth, and differentiation of lymphocyte precursors. These goals are aimed at developing an in vitro system that will support T cell differentiation, which would benefit numerous potential clinical applications towards the treatment of cancer, autoimmune disease, and AIDS.

TitreApplicationTitle: CSF1R as a therapeutic target in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: AML; BIOMARKER; BLOCKING ANTIBODIES; CELL-CELL INTERACTIONS; CSF1; CSF1R/FMS; GROWTH FACTORS; SMALL MOLECULE INHIBITORS; STROMA; TYROSINE KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a highly heterogeneous disease of the bone marrow. The disease originates in the bone marrow, and the cells responsible for persistence of the disease reside there. Within the bone marrow the leukemic cells are surrounded by normal cells that produce a number of protiens that are crucial for maintaining the survival of the leukemic cells. A subset of AML have very high expression of the cell surface receptor CSF1R. This protein interacts with CSF1 produced in the bone marrow cavity. We hypothesize that this interaction is important for the development and persistence of some forms of AML. We have created model systems that will allow us to investigate this, using new drugs that can target CSF1R. The outcome of this research is the potential to improve the outcome of a substantial group of AML patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biochemical, cellular and molecular studies to dissect the contribution of the soluble host carbohydrate binding proteins to HIV-1 pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRUS DRUGS; GALECTIN; GLYCOBIOLOGY; HIV; VIRUS ATTACHEMENT; VIRUS ENTRY
Abstract-Résumé: At the end of 2002, an estimated 56 000 people in Canada were living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection; this is an increase from the estimated 48 900 in 1999. Despite of 8 years of extensive practice of the highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), which can suppress viral load and reduce both morbidity and mortality of AIDS patients, the number of deaths associated with HIV infection in USA was reduced by 64 % (45 765 to16 371). The emergence of resistant  viruses and lack of patient compliance stemming from severe adverse side effects have resulted in many therapeutic failures. Therefore, recent efforts have begun to concentrate on development of antiviral drugs that target other processes in the virus life cycle, such as the entry process. The first HIV entry inhibitor, Fuzeon, was approved last year by FDA and other classes of entry inhibitors are under clinical development. It can be proposed that the overall efficacy of HIV entry inhibitors might be reduced by cellular factors that can promote virus adhesion onto target cells. Our recent data shows that the efficacy of the entry inhibitors is severely compromised in the presence of galectin-1, an endogenous lectin with affinity for beta-galactoside-containing oligosaccharides. Therefore, we propose to test several galectin-1 inhibitor candidates in order to use them as "sensitizers" of HIV entry process for the efficient treatment with the entry inhibitors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Integrative genomic and genetic analyses of consanguineous Pakistani pedigrees aggregated with psychotic/affective disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; CONSANGUINITY; GENE MUTATION; GENETICS; GENOMICS; MENTAL ILLNESS; SCHIZOAFFECTIVE DISORDER; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Pakistan has the highest rate of consanguineous marriage in the world due to historical, religious, cultural and social reasons. A long history of such intracommunity and/or consanguineous marriage has divided the Pakistani population into many rural isolated clans, segregated by geography, language, religion and tribal group, and creating genetic isolates with individual mutation profiles. Consanguineous pedigrees have been successfully used in mapping rare recessive Mendelian disorders in the past. However, the potential influence of such long standing endogamous and consanguineous unions on overall levels of homozygosity genomewide and genetic disease profiles, especially for more common diseases, for such particular genetic isolates remains largely underinvestigated. Schizophrenia (SCZ), schizoaffective (SAF) and bipolar (BP) disorders are common brain diseases in all populations with largely unknown etiology and molecular pathogenesis pathways. Genetic factors have been considered important contributing causes and have been the focus of intensive research efforts in the past decades. To date, the genetic architecture of these three main psychiatric disorders remain largely unknown and very few convincing genetic factors have been identified. We propose to launch a thorough genomewide genetic investigation of 10 collected and clinically well characterized large consanguineous pedigrees from Pakistan to identify causative genetic variants contributing to these major mental disorders. The study of such isolated consanguineous populations with major psychiatric disorders offers a unique opportunity to identify transmitted mutations contributing to SCZ etiology. Thorough genetic and genomic investigations in these pedigrees will also help us better understand the effect of long-term endogamous/consanguineous marriage on the genetic profile and structure of such populations, particularly for complex genetic traits like SCZ.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the Role of Connective Tissue Growth Factor in Intervertebral Disc Development, Health and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNECTIVE TISSUE GROWTH FACTOR; DISC AGING/DEGENERATION; DISC DEVELOPMENT; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; INTERVERTEBRAL DISC; NOTOCHORD CELLS; SPINE; TISSUE SPECIFIC GENE KNOCKOUT
Abstract-Résumé: Low back pain as a result of intervertebral disc (IVD) degeneration is a cause of major disability and constitutes the leading musculoskeletal disorder responsible for days lost from work. Studies show that chronic back pain is increasing at an alarming rate; to the degree that backache has a lifetime prevalence of over 80% in Canada. Our ability to effectively treat disc disease is hampered by an incomplete understanding of IVD development and function. One molecule that has been suggested as a regulator of disc health is connective tissue growth factor (CTGF). Previous studies have shown that CTGF contributes to skeletal development in mice, and has benefical effects on IVD cells in culture. The exact role played by CTGF in IVD development, health and disease has however yet to be established.  To explore the role of CTGF, our lab has begun to investigate when and where it is expressed in the spine. We have established that in early stages of development, CTGF is expressed in the notochord, the embryonic cell type that gives rise to the central tissue of the IVD (nucleus pulposus). Using a novel transgenic mouse, we also show that loss of CTGF specifically in notochord-derived cells deregulates disc formation in the embryo. We therefore propose that CTGF is essential to IVD formation, health and disease and have developed three aims of study to examine this hypothesis using complimentary mouse and cell culture models.  These studies will gain new insight into the role of secreted molecules, specifically CTGF, in maintaining IVD health or accelerating disc disease. In the long term, these studies will identify candidate molecules that could be used as biological treatments to minimize or reverse disc disease and associated back pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intranasal oxytocin for social cognition/function in adults with autism
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULTS; AUTISM; CLINICAL TRIAL; OXYTOCIN
Abstract-Résumé: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) is a group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by deficits in social communication and repetitive behaviors / restricted interests. Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus in the brain and released both into the bloodstream and the central nervous system. It is well known for its role in facilitating delivery and breastfeeding. However, it has also been shown to be involved in social cognition and function as well as in the generation of repetitive behaviors. Given that social deficits and repetitive behaviors are core symptom domains of ASD, and that oxytocin is involved in such behaviors in animal models, healthy volunteers and preliminary studies with adults and adolescents with autism, it is believed that oxytocin may have a role to play in the treatment of autism spectrum disorders. The primary aim of this study is to investigate the therapeutic effects of intranasal oxytocin vs. placebo in adults with autism spectrum disorders. This is a two site, 12 week, randomized controlled trial of intranasal oxytocin (Syntocinon) vs. placebo in adults with ASD.  This study is innovative in that it is translating evidence from basic research (animal model, genetics) into novel therapeutics for ASD.  In addition, given the rarity of clinical trials for adults with ASD, such studies are important and necessary given that the first cohorts of children diagnosed in early childhood are now crossing into adulthood to find no evidence based guidelines for treatment in this age group.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implementation of Evidence-based Psychotherapy for PTSD: Does Technology-Enhanced Consultation Improve Treatment Fidelity and Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE-BEHAVIORAL; DISSEMINATION; IMPLEMENTATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; POSTTRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER; PSYCHOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 9% of Canadians will have Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in their lifetime. In the military veteran population, the lifetime prevalence of PTSD has been estimated to be as high as 20%.  Numerous research studies have demonstrated that short-term, cognitive-behavioral psychotherapies, such as Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT), lead to substantial improvements in PTSD symptoms. However, research suggests that a minority of clinicians provide these therapies in clinical settings. The transfer of this research knowledge into clinical settings remains one of the largest hurdles to improving the health of Canadians with PTSD.  It is well established that attending a 2-day workshop on these therapies alone is insufficient to promote adequate knowledge transfer and sustained skillful use. The current study aims to contrast whether two forms of post-workshop support (6-month duration), with different levels of expert oversight, will result in superior levels of clinician skill and patient outcomes versus no formal post-workshop support. The two forms of post-workshop support are 1) web-enhanced group tele-consultation and 2) standard group tele-consultation. Following a 2-day CPT workshop, 90 mental health clinicians will be randomly assigned to either one of these two support modalities or assigned to no post-workshop support. The primary outcome will be independent expert assessment of the clinicians' adherence and competence in delivering the psychotherapy (via audio-recordings). The secondary outcome will be observed changes in patient symptoms during and following treatment as a function of the clinicians' level of skill. Interviews with clinicians following the consultation period will help identify what helped or hindered their skill acquisition. The study results will help inform how best to implement and and transfer evidence-based psychotherapy (e.g., CPT) to clinical settings to attain comparable outcomes to those observed in research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Propensity scores and marginal structural models in drug safety research
Keywords-MotsClés: MARGINAL STRUCTURAL MODELS; META-ANALYSIS; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; PROPENSITY SCORES; STATISTICAL METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Pharmacoepidemiologic research using administrative data is limited due to confounding by indication and unmeasured confounding.  This research program involves development and evaluation of new methods for causal inference in pharamcoepidemiology, and improvements in implementation of these methods. Methods for causal inference typically require estimates of the propensity score or a variant thereof to account for measured confounding. In this research program we will develop and evaluate approaches to model the propensity score to optimize causal inference. Methods will be evaluated through simulation studies and two substantive pharmacoepidemiologic problems: the effect of high-dose statin treatment on the development of acute kidney injury, and the effect of proton pump inhibitors on pneumonia.  The UK General Practice Research Database will be used as a datas source, and serve as a test-bed for methods work.

TitreApplicationTitle: Renal progenitor cells in kidney development and the response to renal injury.
Keywords-MotsClés: FSGS; KIDNEY DEVELOPMENT; MICROVESICLES; OSR1; RENAL HYPOPLASIA; STEM CELLS; WT1
Abstract-Résumé: There has been great interest in the possibility that stem cells isolated from the bone marrow might useful in regenerating damaged organs such as the kidney. Bone marrow stem cells are easily obtained and migrate to sites of injury when infused into the bloodstream. Unfortunately, it is rare that they actually differentiate into specialized renal cells. On the other hand, the kidney arises from a pool of stem-like renal progenitor cells (RPC) during embryogenesis that are specifically primed to respond to the signals that induce kidney development. In this research program, we propose to study the biology and therapeutic potential of RPC. We will study the biology of isolated RPC in tissue culture and test the theory that some RPC are retained in the adult kidney where they maintain the organ throughout life. Finally, we will pursue our recent discovery that embryonic RPC (unlike bone marrow stem cells) are readily integrated into renal tubules when they are infused into mice with experimental kidney injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chemical Genomic Strategies For New Antifungal Drug Leads
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY PROTEOMICS; DRUGS; GENOMICS; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; NATURAL PRODUCTS
Abstract-Résumé: There is a great need for new antifungal drugs.  Patients who have organ or tissue transplants and many cancer patients have depressed immure systems that make them very susceptible to fungal infections.  However there are very few non-toxic drugs that can be used to kill these pathogens.  To address this clinical need, we have recently developed new methods to combine compounds resulting in highly targeted approaches toward antifungal agents.  These combinations have the potential to act as novel combination therapies.  We propose to systematically explore compound combinations against a number of fungal pathogens and determine the mode of action of the most promising pairs using a genomic platform in yeast, a model fungus for which we have extensive genetic tools and experience.  The results of this study will inform new drug development in clinical area often ignored by the pharmaceutical industry.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Performance in Drivers with Mild Cognitive Impairment: An RCT of Cognitive Training
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; COGNITIVE TRAINING; DEMENTIA; DRIVING; DRIVING SIMULATOR; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONING; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Driving is the primary source of transportation for older adults. Loss of driving privileges is often considered catastrophic by older adults and can result in serious adverse consequences such as social isolation, depression and loss of independence. Clinicians and policy makers are challenged by the conflict presented by growing numbers of older drivers with cognitive impairment who may pose a safety risk to themselves and the public, yet the need to maintain mobility to allow them to continue to function independently in the community. Currently, doctors have little to offer their patients with cognitive impairment that could improve their driving performance and potentially prolong the time that they are able to drive safely, as well as allow them more time to prepare for driving retirement. Diminished sustained attention and speed of information processing, which have been shown to be associated with poor driving performance, are areas of cognition that have been shown to decline in older adults and in persons with mild cognitive impairment. Members of our research team have shown that Goal Management Training can improve sustained attention in healthy older adults. A previous study has shown that speed of processing training can improve driving performance in healthy older adults. The ultimate purpose of our research is to develop interventions to help maintain older adults' mobility and functional independence in order to assist their 'aging at home'. The specific objective of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of a combined program of Goal Management Training and speed of processing training at improving cognitive functioning and driving performance on a driving simulator in mildly cognitively impaired adults 65 years of age and older.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anti-inflammatory effects of docosahexaenoic acid in a mouse model of neuroinflammation: A focus on mechanisms.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARACHIDONIC ACID; DIET; DOCOSAHEXAENOIC ACID; LIPOPOLYSACCHARIDE; MOUSE; NEUROINFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Neurodegenerative diseases are a relatively broad class of neurological disorders, however, recent evidence suggests that dietary n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), commonly found in fish, may be of benefit in preventing or treating these diseases, including Alzheimer's Disease.  One common link between neurodegenerative disorders is that they have a neuroinflammatory component.  It is well established that n-3 PUFA are anti-inflammatory in the periphery, but whether or not they are also anti-inflammatory within the brain is unknown.  The objective of the current proposal is to test if n-3 PUFA are anti-inflammatory within the mouse brain and to evaluate the mechanisms by which they accomplish this.  We have established a mouse model of neuroinflammation to test this hypothesis and our preliminary results strongly suggest that docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is protective against neuroinflammation.  What is not known is  the mechanism by which n-3 PUFA decrease neuroinflammation.  In this application we will test if DHA is directly involved in the downregulation of neuroinflammation or if it works through other fatty acids.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic regulation and molecular mechanisms of TPP riboswitches.  Régulation génétique et mécanismes moléculaires des riborégulateurs TPP.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBACTERIAL COMPOUNDS; BIOCHEMISTRY OF NUCLEIC ACIDS; FOLDING MECHANISMS; GENE EXPRESSION REGULATION; RIBOSWITCHES; RNA FOLDING AND DYNAMICS; RNA-LIGAND INTERACTIONS; SINGLE-MOLECULE TECHNIQUES; THIAMIN PYROPHOSPHATE (TPP)
Abstract-Résumé: Riboswitches are structured RNA elements typically found in the 5' untranslated regions (5'-UTR) of mRNAs, where they regulate gene expression by binding to small metabolites. A major goal of our research is to unravel the molecular mechanisms by which the TPP riboswitches harness the binding of ligands to selectively control gene expression. An understanding of the interactions between riboswitches and their metabolite ligands should provide insights into the ability of RNA to act as a genetic switch. This knowledge might empower future efforts to design novel general antimicrobial drug development approaches for generating analogs of riboswitch ligands, disrupt regulation of key metabolic pathways, and thus be selectively toxic to bacteria that carry these RNAs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biological implications of RNA decapping during vaccinia virus infection.
Keywords-MotsClés: RNA DECAPPING; VACCINIA VIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Poxviruses are large viruses that infect most vertebrates and invertebrates, causing a variety of diseases of veterinary and medical importance that are characterized by local or generalized skin lesions.Vaccinia virus, the prototypic member of the poxvirus family, provides a unique system for combining biochemical and genetic approaches for investigating the replication of viruses.The sequential expression of vaccinia early, intermediate and late genes requires positive viral regulatory factors to switch these geneson at the appropriate times. In addition, the rate at which these stage-specific mRNAs decline requires equally important negative regulation via mRNA decay. Furthermore, the rate of cellular mRNA breakdown also increases after vaccinia infection to help shut down competing host-cell protein synthesis. Until recently, it was unclear how vaccinia achieved this down-regulation of gene expression. However, a newly identified pathway was uncovered which linked the observed decrease in gene expression to the vaccinia virus D10 protein which acts as a decapping protein to remove the 5' RNA cap structure from both viral and cellular mRNAs in vitro. As such, it represents the first RNA decapping enzyme identified from a mammalian virus. More recently, a second decapping enzyme (D9 protein) was identified in vaccinia virus. The aim of this proposal is to elucidate the mechanisms and consequences of RNA decapping during vaccinia virus infection. This research project is relevant to public health different levels. First, it advances our understanding of the basic mechanisms of post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression, which in turn is a central part of the normal framework on which our understanding of cell metabolism and virus-induced disease is built. Moreover, it advances our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of virus replication, which has implications in general for treatment of viral infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Honouring Our Strengths: Indigenous Culture as Intervention in Addictions Treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL AND DRUG ABUSE; COMMUNITY BASED RESEARCH; EVIDENCE BASE DEVELOPMENT; HEALTH AND WELLNESS; HEALTH INTERVENTION; INDIGENOUS TRADITIONAL CULTURE; INSTRUMENT DEVELOPMENT; MEASUREMENT; PROGRAMMING AND POLICY IMPROVEMENT; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Drug addiction among Indigenous peoples is a serious health concern in Canada. Building on our core community-based research team's history of collaborative work, the aim of this project is to evaluate the effectiveness of First Nations culture as a health intervention in alcohol and drug treatment. Health for First Nations is broadly envisioned as wellness and is understood to exist where there is physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual harmony. It is recognized at the National Native Alcohol and Drug Abuse Program (NNADAP) and Youth Solvent Addiction Program (YSAP) treatment centres that Indigenous traditional culture is vital for client healing. However, there is a serious absence of empirical documentation of its impact on client wellness.   This project will gather understanding of how Indigenous traditional culture is understood and practiced at a sample of 12 NNADAP and YSAP treatment centres; from this, a valid instrument to measure the impact of cultural interventions on client wellness will be developed and tested, and the findings applied. The expertise of our diverse team members well-positions us to undertake this project while adhering to the Tri-Council Policy Statement. The outcome will be improved health programming and policy for Indigenous youth and adults in drug and alcohol treatment in Canada.   This project is suitably timed with core processes underway in the NNADAP and YSAP treatment systems. The NNADAP and YSAP renewal process will be finalized in 2011, of which a key recommendation is the establishment of a culturally competent evidence base to document the nature and demonstrate the effectiveness of cultural interventions within treatment programs. Further, a national data management system for NNADAP and YSAP is under development, and the opportunity exists to influence its design so that data specific to evaluation can be collected, and in turn, contribute to the sustainable offering of effective cultural interventions.
