TitreApplicationTitle: HIV Vulnerability and the Work Environment of the Off-Street Sex Industry
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNOGRAPHY; GENDER ANALYSIS; HIV; INTERVIEWS; SEX INDUSTRY; STRUCTURAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS; WORK ENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Men and women who work in Canada's off-street sex industry experience a variety of circumstances that increase their susceptibility to HIV infection. Most research has emphasized individual behaviours of people who work as sex workers and to a lesser extent the economic and social inequities that may increase their risk for HIV. The work environment of the sex industry includes the rules and policies that govern the sex worker and sex buyer relationship, the physical spaces where sex is bought and sold, and the managerial and operational practices that govern the sex worker's activities. Yet, little research in Canada has studied how the work environment may influence  sex workers' vulnerability to HIV infections. And no research has compared the differences in these work environments between men and women who work there, despite the fact that men and women experience vulnerability to HIV infection differently. Our study proposes to examine how the work environment and managerial practices may affect sex workers'  experiences and vulnerability for infection. An analysis of the policies that influence the work environment and the activities of sex workers, sex buyers, managers, and others involved in operating off-street sex venues will provide essential information about how the work environment influences sex worker health. This new knowledge will be used to design targeted interventions to reduce factors in the work environment that affect sex workers' risks for HIV. These interventions will be gender appropriate, thereby increasing their potential for success.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Endothelial, Platelet, Parenchymal and Leukocyte TLRs in Vascular Dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIUM; ENDOTOXIN; INFLAMMATION; LPS; NEUTROPHIL; PLATELETS; SHOCK; TLR2; TLR4
Abstract-Résumé: Shock is a group of cardiovascular diseases that kills 400,000 people a year in North America. All of the patients have activation of white cells which are thought to inappropriately stick in lungs, liver, brain and other organs. Also the white cells that get stuck cause damage leading to ultimately prolonged hospital stays or death. Some of the patients get septic shock which relates to the fact that uncontrolled bacterial infection is the initiating event. Endotoxin is a molecule that is found on certain types of bacteria (gram negative) and our body has learned to recognize this molecule. In small local doses endotoxin is essential for our ability to recognize and clear infections. In septic conditions it is thought that endotoxin is what activates the white cells to get stuck in lungs and liver. Recently, TLR4 has been identified as the  molecule in mammals that can identify endotoxin and activate white cells. A second molecule TLR2 has been identified to detect gram positive bacteria. We will use mice that are deficient in these molecules and using a special microscope to look inside tiny blood vessels we will visualize white cell behaviour. We will determine how important TLR4 is in various tissues. Most scientists are studying TLR4 on white cells, but we believe that in fact TLR4 found on the endothelium (which lines all blood vessels) is important if not essential to get the white cells stuck in the lung, brain and liver. We have made a mouse that has no TLR4 or TLR2.  We also have found that the body makes an inhibitor of TLR4 called Tollip which may dampen the inappropriate cell activation. Finally, almost all work by many labs is being done in test tubes, whereas we are proposing to examine infection response in animals where complexity is increased. We believe that learning more about these molecules in the animal will help us to better understand how white cells can be inappropriately activated to affect the cardiovascular system in disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ultrasound-targeted gene delivery to enhance cell engraftment in the aged heart after ischemic injury
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FUNCTION; CELL TRANSPLANTATION; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; GENE THERAPY; HEART FAILURE; ISCHEMIC CARDIOMYOPATHY; STEM CELLS; ULTRASOUND MICROBUBBLE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a leading cause of death in Canada. After a heart attack, damage and structural changes to the heart can cause it to enlarge. An enlarged heart must work harder to pump blood and will eventually wear out, leading to heart failure. The goal of our project is to combine gene therapy and cell therapy to develop a new and effective treatment to prevent heart failure. A major obstacle of gene therapy is targeting the genes to diseased tissue and not normal tissue. This not only increases the effectiveness of gene therapy, but also reduces side effects.  Microbubbles have been used clinically to enhance imaging of the heart. In our study, we will alter the microbubble to carry genes. We will inject microbubbles into rats with damaged hearts and then direct an ultrasound beam at the heart to burst the microbubbles, releasing the genes into the surrounding heart tissue. These genes will help prevent or repair tissue injury. By varying the study conditions, we will identify the optimal conditions for gene delivery.   Cell therapy involves transplanting stem cells directly into the heart, which can decrease the workload of the heart cells. However, many of the transplanted cells do not survive. Therefore, before injecting the stem cells, we will pre-treat the damaged heart with our targeted microbubbles carrying genes that will improve cell survival.  Our proposed study is innovative since it combines gene and cell therapies and will test a new type of microbubble with greater gene-carrying capacity and the ability to target genes specifically to the heart. Therefore, we predict that our microbubble gene delivery technique will be very effective for pre-treating the injured heart. When combined with cell transplantation, we believe this strategy could be a unique and non-invasive therapy for heart failure. Ultimately, the results of our study will help to prevent heart failure and improve the quality of life for patients who have suffered a heart attack.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improved Delivery of Cardiovascular Care (IDOCC) through Outreach Facilitation
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CONTROLLED BEFORE AND AFTER DESIGN; EVIDENCE BASED MEDICINE; FACILITATION; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PRAGMATIC TRIAL; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases (heart disease, stroke, diseases of the blood vessels) are the leading cause of death and disability in Canada. Research shows that these conditions can be prevented and managed through lifestyle changes such as dieting and exercising, and through controlling potential risk factors such as high blood pressure and cholesterol levels. Family doctor visits provide a unique opportunity to educate patients on lifestyle changes, and to screen and treat potential risk factors. Despite this important role, many family doctors do not follow established guidelines for the treatment of cardiovascular conditions, resulting in care that is less than optimal. We have developed an innovative quality improvement program targeted to family doctors and delivered by a nurse facilitator. They help practices by: a) observing/identifying weaknesses, b) working with practices to develop improvement strategies in areas that the clinic would like to work on, and c) providing doctors with tools to increase their use of established care guidelines.  Project Aim: This project aims to improve care given by family doctors to patients with or at high risk of developing cardiovascular disease.  Project Design: We are working with 83 practices across Eastern Ontario. Each practice will participate in the study for two years, during which time, facilitators will attempt to help doctors improve their overall delivery of care and use of established guidelines. We will look through the medical charts of patients from each practice before and after the study in order to see if there are changes in care delivery and patient health. This evaluation will be used to determine whether this program is an effective means of reducing the number of heart attacks and strokes across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies on the Physiologic and Molecular actions of Parathryoid Hormone (PTH) and of PTH related Peptide in Bone
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE DEVELOPMENT; OSTEOBLASTS; PTH AND PTHRP; VITAMIN D RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: One of the most common causes of disability and death during aging is metabolic bone disease, which includes osteoporosis, bone disease due to cancer, and hyperparathyroidism.  We are studying two major hormones, parathyroid hormone (PTH) and PTH related peptide (PTHrP), which regulate normal bone metabolism, but can also contribute to the development and progression of metabolic bone disease. PTH and PTHrP act via a common receptor, the PTH/PTHrP receptor (PTHR1), on target cells, including bone cells. These hormones also regulate calcium metabolism. Calcium itself can act as a hormone by interacting with a calcium sensing receptor (CaSR). CaSR has been identified in several tissues including parathyroid (which produces PTH), kidney and bone. Although continuously high levels of blood PTH, as occur in hyperparathyroidism, can resorb bone (producing "catabolic" effects), activation of CaSR can lower PTH and CaSR activators, called calcimimetics have been developed to control hyperparathyroidism. In contrast to the catabolic effects of continuous PTH, intermittent PTH administration forms bone (an "anabolic" effect) and is therefore used in osteoporosis therapy. Our goal is to understand how PTH and PTHrP interact with calcium acting via CaSR in producing anabolic and catabolic effects on bone. We have developed genetically modified mice to study the roles of these factors in regulating bone, and will now utilize these models to examine how PTH exerts an anabolic effect on bone in the absence of CaSR, to determine if CaSR activation can influence bone in the absence of PTH, and to examine how CaSR-induced skeletal increases in PTHrP impact on its bone-regulating actions.  These studies should improve our understanding of how to better prevent important and common metabolic bone diseases where bone resorption is a feature, and how to develop improved anabolic therapies for diseases of the skeleton.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel mechanisms of platelet aggregation: Roles of fibronectin and other non-classical beta 3 integrin ligands in thrombosis and hemostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY THROMBOSIS MODEL; FIBRONECTIN; INTEGRINS AND THEIR LIGANDS; MASS SPECTROMETRY AND PROTEOMICS; PLATELET AGGREGATION; THROMBOSIS AND HEMOSTASIS
Abstract-Résumé: Platelets are small cells in the blood that are responsible for clot formation at the site of bleeding. Platelets adhere to an injured site of the blood vessel and clump together in a process called aggregation, forming a platelet plug. However, the same process may lead to thrombosis and blockage of blood flow in the vessel. This is the leading cause of death worldwide, particularly when this blocks blood flow in the vessels of the heart and brain; researchers have tried to make anti-thrombotic therapies to help treat these diseases. Current theory indicates that two proteins in the blood, von Willebrand Factor (VWF) and fibrinogen (Fg), can attach to a molecule on the platelet surface called beta 3 integrin (GPIIbIIIa); this attachment crosslinks different platelets and is required for platelet aggregation. However, using our unique intravital microscopy models, with which we can see in real-time the flow of blood and cells through vessels in live animals, we demonstrated that thrombus formation and vessel blockage occurred in mice lacking these two (VWF and Fg) key molecules. This unexpected finding indicates that other protein(s), besides VWF and Fg, are also capable of making platelets aggregate and blocking blood vessels. We found that this protein(s) binds to the beta 3 integrin and that this requires several other molecules, such as Calcium ions (Ca++), thrombin, and proteins from the blood and from inside platelets. We have begun to identify what other plasma and platelet proteins (e.g. fibronectin, Protocadherin 11X and Occludin) contribute to this process and want to see how these proteins may be useful as new targets for anti-thrombotic therapies. On the other hand, these proteins may be of therapeutic potential to control bleeding in afibrinogemic, hypofibrinogemic and VWF deficient patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathogenesis of fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia and mechanisms of IVIG and anti-FcRn therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS AND FETAL BLEEDING DISORDERS; ANTIBODIES AND CELLULAR IMMUNE RESPONSES; FETAL AND NEONATAL ALLOIMMUNE THROMBOCYTOPENIA; INTRAVENOUS IMMUNOGLOBULIN G (IVIG) AND ANTI-FCRN ANTIBODY; NOVEL ANIMAL MODELS; PLATELET DESTRUCTION AND PHAGOCYTOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Platelets are small blood cells that are responsible for the arrest of bleeding at the site of vessel injury. A low platelet count is called thrombocytopenia. Antibodies to fetal platelets can be induced in the mother by proteins called antigens on platelets, which are inherited from the father but lacking in the mother. These maternal antibodies can cross the placenta and damage fetal platelets leading to a disease called Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia (FNAIT). This disease occurs in 0.5-1.5/1,000 liveborn neonates. It may also cause miscarriage. The major risk associated with FNAIT is severe bleeding, particularly in the brain (intracranial haemorrhage), leading to neurological impairment or death. Currently, the pathogenesis of FNAIT is largely unknown and effective therapy is not available.  We plan to use our newly developed FNAIT mouse models to study: 1) how a mother generates antibodies to different fetal platelet antigens, and how miscarriage can occur in this disease; 2) whether these antibodies also target and injure fetal vessels, which may enhance bleeding and inhibit fetal growth; and 3) whether we can prevent this disease by inducing immune suppression in the mother and how we can treat it more efficiently by using IVIG and anti-FcRn therapies. This study will provide significant information for both the pathogenesis and treatment of FNAIT.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Bone Marrow Derived Progenitor Cells in Brain Tumor Neovascularizatoin
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ANIMAL MODELS; BONE MARROW DERIVED PROGENITOR CELLS; BRAIN CANCER; CANCER THERAPEUTICS; IN-VIVO IMAGING; RADIATION THERAPY; RADIOBIOLOGY; TWO PHOTON LASER MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: It is well established that blood supply to the tumor plays a critical role in supporting tumor growth and malignant recurrence following treatment.  Though in the past two decades through much research we have gained a better understanding of the biology of tumor blood supply there are still mechanisms of blood vessel formation that we do not understand.One such mechanism is how stem cells from the bone marrow can contribute to making new blood vessels in the tumor and help promote their growth.  In this proposal we are focused on better understanding the contribution of bone marrow derived cells to tumor neovascularization and in specific tumor revascularization post-radiation therapy. The results from this study are significant as they explore a new area of tumor angiogenesis and it can provide the basis for novel therapeutic strategies targeting bone marrow derived progenitor cells in cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of Cacna1a in cortical GABAergic interneurons and epilepsy.
Keywords-MotsClés: EEG; EPILEPSY; MICROSCOPY; MOUSE GENETICS; PHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a common disorder affecting 0.5-1% of the general population. Unfortunately, a third of patients remain refractory to current therapies, leading to frequent hospitalizations and decreased quality of life. The mechanisms underlying the more severe forms of inherited epilepsy are still poorly understood. Clarifying these mechanisms is an essential prerequisite to allow for the development of new therapies. For this reason, I am pursuing a series of investigations in mice models of human epilepsies to address the mechanisms that lead to such severe disorders. My recent work has allowed me to generate new mice models of severe congenital epilepsy by causing cell-type specific mutations in calcium channel subunits. With the current proposal, I will investigate which brain inhibitory cell types are primarily responsible for seizure onset in these mutants. Furthermore, I will evaluate the mechanisms by which these calcium channel mutations lead to inhibitory defects in the developing and mature brain. I will achieve this by using a multimodal approach including advanced mouse genetic strategies (to modify specific genes in subsets of neurons thereby affecting their ability to release GABA) as well as immunohistochemical staining and high power microscopy (to assess the impact of these mutations on the shape and development of interneurons), physiological cellular recordings (to demonstrate how these modifications affect cellular functions) and video-EEG recording (to correlate these cellular defects to their consequences at the brain level, namely seizure activity). I believe that this line of study will ultimately result in better diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for patients with severe inherited epilepsies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Canadian UnRuptured aneurysm Endovascular versus Surgery trial - The CURES trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOVASCULAR COILING; INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; RECURRENCE; SURGICAL CLIPPING; UNRUPTURED ANEURYSM
Abstract-Résumé: The treatment of incidentally discovered brain aneurysms that have not yet bled is a vexing problem since the best treatment option remains uncertain. Surgery involves clipping the neck of the aneurysm to prevent blood entry into the aneurysm sac; it requires opening the skull to reach the aneurysm. Endovascular coiling involves introducing metallic coils into the aneurysm sac to occlude it and thus remove it from the brain circulation; the coils are introduced with the help of a catheter to reach the arteries of the brain. There is no scientific proof that one or the other types of treatment, in terms of long term occlusion results or safety profile, is better than the other.  The Canadian UnRuptured Endovascular versus Surgery (CURES) trial is the pilot phase of a randomized trial that aims to compare endovascular coiling to surgical clipping. Randomization ensures that all patients have an equal chance of getting what will turn out to be the best option. It also helps the resolution of the dilemma, by reducing bias in the selection of patients allotted to one or the other treatment.   The CURES pilot trial will recruit 260 patients across Canada, to be followed for one year. The pilot phase of CURES will allow us to:   1) determine whether there is a significant difference in the number of treatment failures between the groups of patients treated with coiling compared to clipping.  Treatment failure is defined as: brain hemorrhage following treatment, failure to totally occlude the aneurysm during treatment, or recurrence of the aneurysm within the first year;  2) provide an estimate of morbidity and mortality values that will provide randomized data to guide the design of the pivotal portion of the study, which will study clinical outcomes.  3) determine feasibility of a larger (estimated 1000 patient) international trial.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functions of Notch Signaling in Hematopoiesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE TRANSFERS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENOMICS; LEUKEMOGENESIS; LINEAGE DECISIONS; LYMPHOCYTE HOMEOSTASIS; MOUSE MODELS; NOTCH SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: The Notch signaling pathway has been highly conserved during evolution and performs critical developmental functions in insects, mice and humans. Defects in Notch activation contribute to many forms of leukemia and cause a wide range of developmental, cardiovascular and neurological defects. Activation of the Notch1 receptor is absolutely required for the development of T-lymphocytes, which have many important functions in the immune system. However, unrestrained Notch1 activation causes T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (T-LL). This aggressive and often fatal disease results from neoplastic transformation of T-cell progenitors as they develop in the thymus. More than 50% of human T-LL cases have activating Notch1 mutations, making Notch1 an attractive target for anti-leukemia therapies.  Importantly, a drug that interferes with Notch1 signaling kills T-LL cells in culture.  However, in a clinical trial, this drug and showed no efficacy against T-LL and caused severe side effects in patients. Therefore, other pathways must be targeted in order to improve survival of patients with T-LL. Using mouse models we have recently discovered that Notch1 must collaborate with pre-T-cell receptor and interleukin-7 signaling to promote normal T-cell development as well as T-cell leukemogenesis. During the course of this work we generated important new resources and a novel conceptual framework to help mechanistically dissect the molecular basis of N1-pre-TCR-IL7 co-operation. Through our proposed studies, we will assemble a molecular understanding of how Notch1 signaling is integrated with pre-TCR and IL7 signaling during normal T-cell development, and elucidate how these pathways become subverted during T-cell leukemogenesis. In the longer term, this knowledge will be used to design new strategies for targeted T-LL therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phase-Specific and Lifetime Medical Costs of Care for Childhood Cancer in British Columbia and Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: "PHASE OF CARE" APPROACH; CHILDHOOD CANCER; COSTS OF CARE; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH SERVICES
Abstract-Résumé: Costing studies can be used to describe the burden of disease and enhance the scientific credibility of economic evaluations. There is currently an ongoing Canadian study looking at cancer costs for adults, yet little is known about cancer costs in childhood. From a public health perspective, childhood cancer survivors are a growing population due to dramatic advances in treatment and supportive care that have improved survival for children diagnosed with cancer. Now, over 80% will survive for five or more years and it is estimated that there are approximately 35,000 childhood cancer survivors living in Canada. This proposal will provide much needed childhood cancer cost estimates that can be used in future economic evaluations. We will estimate long-term and phase-specific childhood cancer costs in British Columbia and Ontario (and thus, accounting for more than half of the childhood cancer survivor population in Canada) with a focus on healthcare costs incurred by provincial governments. The results of this work will be important to understand how much we are spending on cancer care for children and how costs differ among treatments and resources. From a health delivery perspective, these findings will be used to describe where our healthcare dollars (i.e., resources) are being spent. Furthermore, by comparing results from two provinces, we will be able to determine how costs are allocated, highlight any differences in patterns and quality of care, and contrast differences in healthcare access and delivery. Our findings can be used by Ministries of Health and cancer care managers to plan for adequate resources and to maximize value. Cost estimates will also be useful for policy makers to plan for future healthcare budgets, and for researchers to conduct future cost-effectiveness analyses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Severe influenza in infants, children and youths: Role of clinical and epidemiologic risk factors
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; CLINICAL RISK FACTORS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; INFLUENZA; PANDEMIC
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza is a major cause of illness and death worldwide, and exacts a heavy economic burden. Annual influenza epidemics are estimated to affect 5-15% of the global population. Although most cases are mild, these epidemics still cause severe illness in 3-5 million people and 250,000-500,000 deaths worldwide. While relatively mild, the 2009 influenza pandemic demonstrated our limited ability to predict influenza pandemics, to deliver vaccines in a timely manner, and to identify individuals at highest risk. Numerous factors likely contribute to varying severity of illness from influenza infection. These include clinical factors such as age, sex, and socioeconomic status. Individual factors and environmental exposures such as tobacco smoke and imbalances in micronutrient levels (such as vitamin D and selenium) may also explain why some get sicker than others with influenza infection. Our objective is to determine how these factors can be used to identify individuals most likely to get severe influenza. We will do so by studying healthy children with varying degrees of illness severity due to influenza. Over a 4-year period, we will recruit approximately 1,750 children from doctors' offices, a large emergency department, 13 community hospitals within a large metropolitan area, and 9 children's hospitals across Canada. Detailed clinical and epidemiologic data will be recorded. Blood and saliva samples will be obtained to measure some of these factors. To identify potential predictors, we will correlate these variables to an influenza severity scale. Our goal is to increase understanding of who gets severe influenza so that it may help doctors and public health agencies to better target resources towards preventing severe illness in these most vulnerable children.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Basis for Calcium Regulation of Cardiac Sodium Channels
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CALCIUM REGULATION; CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIA; ISOTHERMAL-TITRATION CALOIMETRY; LONG QT TYPE 3 ARRHYTHMIA; PATCH-CLAMP ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; SITE-DIRETED MUTAGENESIS; VOLTAGE-GATED ION CHANNELS; X-RAY CRYSTALOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure impacts the lives of more than 400,000 Canadians, with nearly 50,000 plus new cases diagnosed each year in our aging population.  Nearly the half of these heart failure patients will die unexpectedly from electrical instability in the heart that leads to sudden death.  The exact causes of sudden death are not known but it is generally appreciated that changes in the electrical activity in the heart through a process called 'remodeling' leads to changes in the ability of the heart beat properly.  Our research will contribute to the understanding on the electrical system in the heart and will provide new information of how this electrical system will respond to the changing environment in the failing heart.   Moreover, there are rare inherited diseases that impact the same types of electrical signaling in the heart that occur in failing hearts, and our study will address the basis for these diseases with the goal of developing new drugs for the treatment of all types of cardiac disturbances.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional Networks Regulating Hepatocyte Identity
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFERENTIATION; EMBRYOGENESIS; GENE REGULATION; GENOMICS; HEPATOCYTE; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: There are over 100 types of liver disease and left untreated, these diseases can develop into liver cirrhosis. Thousands of Canadians die each year from liver cirrhosis causing liver failure. Currently the only treatment for liver failure is a transplant. However, treatment is hindered by a shortage of donor tissue. Thus, viable alternatives to donor liver transplant are required. Many researchers are trying to develop methods to make liver cells from other types of cells, including stem cells.  The overarching question guiding our research is "How does the regulation of genes direct development of organs in the embryo?" While all tissues contain the same set of genes, specific subsets of genes are expressed specific cells. Transcription factors are proteins that determine which genes will be turned on or off in each tissue. We are interested in determining how switching genes on and off controls development of the liver in the mouse embryo. In this proposal, we will look will look at critical transcription factors that are involved in liver development and determine which genes these transcription factors control. From this, we will be able to build networks of genes that regulate liver formation. Next, we will test whether the transcription factors identified are able to transform adult cells, such as fibroblasts, into liver cells. Understanding how the liver develops in the embryo could contribute to the development of methods to produce liver cells in the laboratory that can be used for transplantation or gene therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implanting Therapeutic Materials onto Diseased Vessels using Blood Coagulation
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; BLOOD COAGULATION; DISSEMINATED INTRAVASCULAR COAGULATION; FIBRINOGEN TRANSFUSION; LOCAL DRUG DELIVERY; MICROFLUIDICS; SEPSIS; SMALL ANIMAL IMAGING; VASCULAR IMPLANT; VULNERABLE PLAQUE
Abstract-Résumé: The formation of blood clots is an essential biological function for preventing blood loss during bleeding.  Unfortunately, blood clots can form in our blood vessels even when we are not bleeding.  These blood clots can lead to a heart attack, stroke, pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and tissue necrosis.  Current therapies for controlling blood clotting aim at reducing or inhibiting enzymes and molecules that cause blood clotting to occur.  For example, statins reduce cholesterol, a molecule that can inflame blood vessels and lead to atherosclerosis and then blood clotting.  These approaches have improved the quality of life of humans, but one-third of all people will still die due to the formation of a blood clot.  This proposal describes research to develop a complementary approach to the current therapies.  Specifically, we will develop small biopolymers that form synthetic blood clots and replace natural blood clots.  Our hypothesis is that thin layers of these synthetic blood clots could be formed in a controlled manner at regions of inflamed vessels to block large blood clots from forming.  In the future, this technology may also be used to modify blood clots, making them degrade faster, and thereby preventing heart attacks and strokes.  This technology may also lead to a strategy to replace components of blood clotting given during transfusions and reduce our dependence on blood from donors.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent

TitreApplicationTitle: Picturing foster care: A photo voice evaluation of three different fostering models and their implications for perinatal care provision
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; INTERSECTORAL COLLABORATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH; PARENTING IN POVERTY; PERINATAL CARE; QUALITATIVE METHODS; SOCIAL SERVICE PROVISION; VISUAL RESEARCH METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: This study focuses on the health and social service needs of some of the most vulnerable members of Canadian society: young parents living in extreme poverty (either homeless or marginally housed) and their children. The delivery of perinatal care to such young parents is complex, with many families facing an array of health and social concerns. For various reasons, some youth are at risk of losing custody of their babies to child welfare authorities. Using participatory qualitative photo voice methods (including data from participants' interviews and photographs taken by them), this project will examine the impact that experienced child custody loss (or experiences of being 'at risk' of having one's child apprehended) has on families living in poverty, and on the children's aid workers and perinatal healthcare practitioners (HCPs) who care for them. The health and social service delivery implications of such experiences will be explored, and barriers to care identified. The advent of two new programs employing alternative models of foster care provides an important context for this research. The study will explore these new models in comparison with the 'usual standard' of foster care in terms of their relative impact on perinatal care. The study adopts an innovative knowledge translation strategy, culminating in an exhibition of photographs taken by participants. The goal of the exhibit is to promote greater understanding between the three stakeholder groups and to share their experiences with a broader range of stakeholders, including the public and policy makers. This study fosters a unique partnership between health researchers, clinicians, children's aid workers, young parents and other community members, and artists.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sensorimotor control processes underlying object manipulation tasks
Keywords-MotsClés: EYE-HAND COORDINATION; MOTOR LEARNING; OBJECT MANIPULATION; SENSORIMOTOR CONTROL; VIDEO BASED INFRARED EYE TRACKING; VIRTUAL REALITY
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of the proposed research is to better understand how the brain controls tasks involving object manipulation. Understanding object manipulation is important because many daily tasks require manipulation skills and these skills are often severely damaged by stroke and neurological disease and are difficult to recover. A better understanding of the strategies the brain uses to control manipulation tasks will be important both for assessing sensory and motor loss following neurological damage and for devising better therapies for rehabilitation.  The proposed research consists of four interrelated projects. The first project will examine how sequences of actions that make up manipulation tasks (e.g., reaching for, lifting, and moving an object) are linked together to produce dexterous behaviour and how such linking changes with learning. The second project will examine the control of corrective actions that are generated when movement errors occur and that are necessary for successful manipulation. The third project will examine how hand-held tools are integrated into movement control. Finally, the fourth project will examine the ability of people to learn about object properties by observing others manipulating objects.

TitreApplicationTitle: De novo mutations in intellectual disability
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN DEVELOPMENT; DE NOVO MUTATION; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Intellectual disability (ID) is the most frequent severe handicap affecting 2-3% of the population. ID is unexplained in about 50% of cases. Several observations indicate that genetic factors play an important role in these patients by disrupting the cellular mechanisms that underlie learning and memory. We have recently found that novel mutations (not transmitted from the parents) represent a common cause of ID. We have developed a novel strategy to identify these genetic changes in children with ID. We will analyze most of the known genes in affected children and in their parents. We will identify genetic changes that are unique to the children. The identification of these genes will provide several benefits for patients with ID and for their families. Knowledge of these genes will lead to genetic testing, permitting accurate diagnosis and better management. Moreover, our research has the potential of identifying a group of patients who could benefit from the learning-enhancing drugs currently under development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of the transcription factors HEBAlt and HEBCan in T cell development
Keywords-MotsClés: DENDRITIC CELLS; GENE REGULATION; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; RETROVIRAL VECTORS; T CELL DEVELOPMENT; THYMUS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: T cells are critical mediators of the immune response, but they are also prime targets for cancerous transformation.  Therefore, elucidating how T cells are made from stem cells is of paramount importance for understanding both normal immune function and leukemia.  We have discovered that two different proteins, HEBAlt and HEBCan, are important regulators of the developmental pathways that allow stem cells to adopt a T-cell identity.  Our studies suggest that both HEBAlt and HEBCan are needed to make T cells, whereas an imbalance of these factors can lead to a divergence into other immune cell fates.  Specifically, cells with high levels of HEBAlt may become natural killer (NK) cells, whereas high levels of HEBCan may re-direct cells to become dendritic cells (DCs).  Moreover, we have found that HEBAlt promotes cell growth whereas HEBCan inhibits it, suggesting that deregulation of HEBAlt could predispose developing T cells to leukemic transformation. To better understand how HEBAlt and HEBCan work together to direct cells to become T cells, we are using transgenic mice that express either HEBAlt or HEBCan to identify the genes under their control.  These genes encode other proteins that work in conjunction with HEBAlt and/or HEBCan in molecular networks to give the cells their specific functions, and defining these networks will enable us to perturb them towards a desired outcome.  We also aim to understand how the unique portion of HEBAlt, the Alt domain, allows HEBAlt to function differently than HEBCan.  We will change portions of the Alt domain and then see whether the ability of HEBAlt to control gene expression is affected. These studies will provide important insights into the molecular control of immune cell development, and are likely to provide new targets for diagnostic and therapeutic applications for immunodeficiencies, autoimmune diseases, and leukemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Polymer-based Gene Delivery for Rheumatoid Arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; GENE THERAPY; INFLAMMATION; NANOTECHNOLOGY; POLYMER SCIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Recently some new drugs have become available to treat Rheumatoid Arthritis and associated diseases. They are protein molecules called TNF blockers. These drugs are very successful but are very expensive ($20,000-40,000/yr) and need to be injected frequently and can cause side effects since the amount in the body is high after injection and then decreases over time. We have found a safe way to deliver the DNA that makes the protein and to have the body make the protein from the DNA, rather than deliver the protein itself. This approach is called gene therapy. Our technology has been tested in an animal model for Diabetes where it has succeeded. We propose to test this technology for treating Rheumatoid Arthritis in animal models. If successful this new technology will be much less expensive, require less frequent injection and have fewer side effects, therefore representing a major advance in arthritis treatments.

ClasseRechercheFR: STERILITE DE LA FEMME; STERILITE DE L'HOMME
TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and characterization of factors required for meiotic chromosome pairing
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEUPLOIDY; C. ELEGANS; CHROMOSOME PAIRING; MEIOSIS; REPRODUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The germ line of humans and other sexually reproducing species functions to produce the eggs and sperm that fuse to form an individual. To produce viable offspring, the egg and sperm must each contain exactly half of the parental number of chromosomes, an event carried out by meiotic divisions during which identical maternal and paternal chromosomes are paired, and then segregated away from each other. Little is known about how the identical chromosomes recognize each other and pair up, and in this application we propose to identify the proteins that function in the process using a model system that is amenable to genetic analysis and microcopic analysis, the nematode C. elegans. Since these processes are highly conserved, our study will illuminate the mechanisms by which eggs and sperm receive the correct number of chromosomes, an event essential for the survival and development of the next generation.

ClasseRechercheFR: SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL; ÉQUITÉ EN SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing Stigma, Promoting Resilience: Population Health Interventions for LGBTQ Youth
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; BISEXUAL; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY EVALUATIONS; GAY; HEALTH INEQUITIES; LESBIAN; MENTAL HEALTH AND ADDICTIONS; POPULATION HEALTH INTERVENTIONS; POPULATION SURVEYS; QUESTIONING; SEXUAL HEALTH AND RISK BEHAVIOURS; STIGMA; TRANSGENDER; TWO SPIRIT; VIOLENCE AND DISCRIMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Throughout most of the world, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and questioning youth (LGBTQ youth) experience health inequities, including self-harm, suicide and substance misuse, mostly because societal stigma targets them for harassment, discrimination, violence, and rejection. Much of this "enacted stigma" takes place in and around schools, yet research has shown that school connectedness, and safe school environments, are important for all young people's health. What helps create safer, more supportive schools for LGBTQ youth? Although a variety of strategies are being used by schools and school districts across North America, very few of them have actually been evaluated. This multi-site, multi-disciplinary program of research involves researchers and knowledge-users from 7 Canadian provinces and 3 U.S. states, and aims to document the trends in health inequities, risk and protective factors among LGBTQ youth (and those perceived as gay by their peers), to conduct a national Canadian inventory of the strategies used to promote safe and supportive schools, and to identify the strategies that have evidence of effectiveness, both through analysis of population survey data and community participatory evaluations of exemplar schools, school districts, and partnering community agencies. Together, these studies will help document the local contexts for population health interventions that effectively reduce health inequities for LGBTQ youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Our ancestors are in our water, land, and air: A 'Two-Eyed Seeing' approach to researching environmental health concerns with Pictou Landing First Nation
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; AIR QUALITY; COMMUNITY PLANNING; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY HEALTH RESEARCH; ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL JUSTICE; ENVIRONMENTAL CONTAMINANTS; ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH; INDIGENOUS METHODOGIES; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; WATER QUALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Mi'kmaq have inhabited what is now known as Nova Scotia for millennia; it is where their origin stories begin and where they continue to raise their children. For the Mi'kmaq of Pictou Landing First Nation, the estuary known as 'Boat Harbour' and the surrounding landscape have provided them with the foods, medicines, transportation, shelter, and tools they have needed to survive and thrive since time immemorial. In the 1960s, amidst other resource extraction and industrial development initiatives, in an area characterized by economic disparities, a pulp and paper mill began dumping pollutants into Boat Harbour; it continues to do so today albeit with increasingly sophisticated treatment practices. Despite these pollution checks and controls, Boat Harbour has become a dumping ground for toxic waste, a place of fear and unrest, embroiled in political, legal and economic tension, and rife with environmental health concerns for members of the First Nation and for others living throughout Pictou County. Frustrated and anxious about their children's health, the Pictou Landing Native Women's Association has mobilized, wanting to undertake relevant community-based health research in search of a definitive and trustworthy answer to this question: "Are we getting sick from Boat Harbour?". As such, our research goal for this community-based participatory health project is to document and understand the state of health of Boat Harbour's constituents from a Two-Eyed Seeing approach that utilizes a number of Indigenous and western research methods to meet this goal. Given that the Mi'kmaq worldview respects the plurality of knowledge, we expect our Two-Eyed Seeing approach will utilize diverse Mi'kmaq and western knowledge perspectives to confront the socio-political, historical, environmental, legal, and economic imperatives at play in Boat Harbour, all of which play a role in determining the health of the community's residents.

ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; MUSCLES ET OS
TitreApplicationTitle: Supplementation with Eicosapentaenoic Acid (EPA) and Docosahexaenoic Acid (DHA) to Prevent Sarcopenia and Myosteatosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOGENESIS; ESSENTIAL FATTY ACIDS; LIPID METABOLISM; MUSCLE HEALTH; MYOSTEATOSIS; NUTRIENT REQUIREMENTS; SATELLITE CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal stems from our recent observations that muscle wasting is common in people with cancer. Often, muscle loss associates with increased content of fat in muscle.  Each of these features is related to morbidity and survival in people with cancer.  Here, we propose new basic research to understand the biological causes of muscle wasting, as well as propose an intervention to modify muscle loss and fat in muscle. Two questions will be explored. The first of these relates to the reasons for muscle loss and replacement of the muscle tissue by fat tissue.  This may be due to alterations in the muscle cells responsible for regeneration and renewal of muscle, or changes in the signals that govern muscle cell or fat cell growth.  The second question relates to the ability of a nutritional intervention containing fats thought to be important for muscle health to reduce the loss of muscle and fat within the muscle tissue.   Reasons for the benefits will be explored.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preventing Peri-operative Acute Kidney Injury: SIRS & POISE-2 Sub-studies
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; CARDIAC SURGERY; NON CARDIAC SURGERY; RANDOMIZED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: When people have a major operation the kidneys can become injured. We will test medications to prevent this from happening in two large, ongoing randomized placebo controlled trials being done in 30 countries around the world. We can do this by adding extra tests of kidney function to the data collection. In the first trial we will test a type of steroids in patients having cardiac surgery with a bypass pump. In the second trial we will test aspirin in patients having other types of major surgery. In total we will collect new kidney information in 12,500 patients across both trials. These will be the largest trials to test medications to prevent kidney injury ever conducted in a surgical setting. If the treatments prove beneficial they will be used around the world to prevent kidney injury from major operations.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular lipid efflux and HDL formation
Keywords-MotsClés: APOLIPOPROTEIN MIMETICS; APOLIPOPROTEINS; ARTERY WALL; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CELL BIOLOGY; CHOLESTEROL
Abstract-Résumé: Cholesterol is a type of fat that is essential to the function of the cells and organs in the human body.  Accumulation of this excess cholesterol in artery walls, however leads to heart attacks and strokes.  The removal of this excess cholesterol is a major function of the protective fraction of cholesterol-containing particles in blood called high density lipoprotein or HDL.  Currently there are not very effective ways of increasing the amount of HDL in blood to increase this and other protective functions of HDL.  One of the best ways to achieve this is to turn on new HDL formation.  We discovered a modification of HDL proteins that turns on the cell transporter that makes new HDL particles.  The goals of this research are to understand how these modified proteins turn on this transporter, what the structure of these modified proteins is, and whether short fragments of these modified proteins also turn on this HDL-making pathway so that they could be used as new treatments to raise HDL.  The ultimate goal of the research is develop a novel treatment that increased HDL production to reduce the personal and economic burdens of heart disease and stroke.

NomDuComitéFR: Santé publique, santé communautaire et santé des populations
TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing inequalities in the burden of human papillomavirus (HPV) related diseases in Canada through optimal vaccination and screening policies: A multidisciplinary model-based approach
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DYNAMIC MATHEMATICAL MODELLING; ECONOMIC EVALUATION; HEALTH INEQUALITIES/DISPARITIES; HERD IMMUNITY; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS (HPV); POPULATION HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH; SCREENING; VACCINATION
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, human papillomavirus (HPV) is responsible for roughly 3000 new cervical, vaginal, vulvar, penile, anal and head/neck cancers each year. The burden of HPV-related diseases is higher in regions with higher poverty and lower education, and among immigrants and men-who-have-sex-with-men (MSM). Recently, school-based HPV vaccination programs for girls were implemented across Canada at an annual cost of more than $100 million. However, failure to vaccinate girls most at risk of infection and disease (e.g., lower SES, immigrants) could mitigate the anticipated population level benefits of HPV vaccination and accentuate existing health inequalities. Furthermore, other groups such as boys, MSM and older females are not currently included in HPV vaccination programs, producing inequalities. Very few modeling studies have attempted to identify optimal HPV vaccination and screening strategies in terms of cost-effectiveness, and none in terms of reduction in inequalities. To fill this important gap in knowledge, our multidisciplinary team will use state-of-the-art transmission-dynamic modelling techniques combined with high-quality data to answer the following key questions: 1) What is the population-level effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of current HPV vaccination programs? 2) What is the impact of these programs on inequalities? 3) What are the most effective and cost-effective vaccination and screening strategies to reduce HPV-related burden of disease and inequalities? The proposed research will make important methodological contributions as transmission-dynamic models have yet to examine issues related to inequalities following immunization. More importantly, our analysis directly addresses the needs of policy-makers for evidence on equity, in addition to effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. Ultimately, our results will be translated into customized messages to help policymakers optimize HPV vaccination and screening programs, and reduce inequalities.

NomDuComitéFR: Recherche en interventions et en évaluation dans les services de santé 2
DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTÉ; CANCER
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL; POLITIQUE SANITAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Strategic configuration of cancer care services based on clinical, demographic and geographic considerations
Keywords-MotsClés: LOCATION ANALYSIS; MATHEMATICAL PROGRAMMING; ONCOLOGY; RESOURCE ALLOCATION; STRATEGIC PLANNING; SYSTEM CONFIGURATION
Abstract-Résumé: A key component of quality cancer care is timely access to diagnostic and clinical resources. This requires the efficient coordination of services and utilization of resources. Configuring an effective network of cancer care services across a large geographic region presents complex managerial and planning challenges, and has a direct impact on the quality of patient care. This is a very relevant problem for a budget-constrained public healthcare system facing an increasing demand from a growing and aging population. Judicious decisions are required to design a system that meets the needs of the public while maintaining high quality of care. The primary decisions include where to locate facilities, and how to allocate highly specialized resources and staff to each location. The objective of this proposal is to develop and evaluate a methodological framework to determine the strategic configuration of provincial cancer treatment services. This methodology must account for current and future clinical practice, demographic characteristics and geographic considerations. To integrate these considerations requires an evidence-based, data-driven approach supported by analytical methodologies from the operations research field. Failure to incorporate these sophisticated approaches may result in decisions that could result in unnecessary wasteful costs and worse yet, compromise patient care. This proposal is novel in that it is comprehensive, targeted specifically to cancer services, based on advanced analytical methodologies and has an applied focus. This is reflected in the multi-disciplinary research team which includes researchers, clinicians, decision makers and health service leaders from the British Columbia Cancer Agency (BCCA) and researchers (faculty, PhD students and Post Doctoral Fellows) in operations research from the Sauder School of Business at UBC. Results will be tested and implemented at the BCCA.

The main goal of this project is to clarify the mechanisms by which SHP-1 causes these metabolic complications which will help in the design of novel therapeutic strategies.

Abstract-Résumé: La scoliose idiopathique de l'adolescence affecte 3 a 4% de la population canadienne, dont environ 10% auront besoin d'un traitement par corset durant la poussee de croissance pubertaire. La conception des corsets est realisee de maniere relativement empirique, ce qui explique l'efficacite relative de ce traitement. Notre equipe a mis au point des methodes innovatrices de conception, d'optimisation et de fabrication assistee par ordinateur basees sur des modeles de simulation numerique personnalisee a chaque patient, ainsi qu'un systeme d'evaluation et d'ajustement des corsets. Dans ce projet, nous allons evaluer l'efficacite de cette plate-forme de traitement personnalise et demontrer son application clinique.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of personalized immunotherapy to treat lung cancer using gamma-delta-T cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE CELLULAR THERAPY; EX VIVO T CELL EXPANSION; GAMMA-DELTA T-CELLS; HUMAN; LUNG CANCER; TRAIL
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer remains the deadliest of cancers despite notable improvements in its treatment, and hence, there is a clear need for new therapies. Treatment of lung cancer will require multi-pronged approaches to be successful. Recently, the concept of cellular immunotherapy, or using cells from a body's own immune system to treat disease, has matured and generated much interest. This concept is supported by studies that have shown that the immune system has many natural and essential roles in preventing and fighting cancer. Our laboratory has focused on studying a particular type of white blood cell called the gamma-delta double negative T cell (DNT). Gamma-delta-DNTs are the predominant immune cell in mucosal and epithelial tissues such as the lungs. Our recent studies have established that a single injection of gamma-delta-DNTs was able to reduce the growth of a human lung tumor implanted in a mouse. This proposal builds upon this work to further improve the overall effectiveness of using gamma-delta-DNTs as a treatment for lung cancer. We will identify the best source of gamma-delta-DNTs in lung cancer patients and examine several strategies to enhance these cells' anti-tumor abilities. We believe that these results will provide clear insight into the viability of designing a clinical trial to treat lung cancer patients using gamma-delta-DNTs as personalized therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of the DCC Gene in Drug Dependence
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL GENETICS; COCAINE IV SELF-ADMINISTRATION; DCC; DRUG REWARD; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE MAPPING; PROTEIN EXPRESSION; PSYCHOPHARMACOLOGY; QUANTITATIVE TRAIT LOCI; SUBSTANCE DEPENDENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Drug dependence is a significant worldwide public health problem. Drug abusers suffer from physical, psychological, financial and legal problems, and society as a whole is affected by increased health care costs, crime, violence and a toll on children and families. It is now well recognized the public health threats such as infectious diseases (tuberculosis, HCV and HIV) and sexually transmitted diseases are on the rise among drug users in general. Cocaine dependence in particular makes up a significant proportion of clinical case loads; it is a chronic and severe disorder characterized by compulsive drug-seeking and continued drug use despite negative consequences.   Over the past 3 decades, a large body of research has provided strong evidence that drug dependence is heritable. In previous CIHR-funded research, the applicant utilized behavioural genetic techniques to demonstrate that inbred mouse strains such as the A/J and C57BL/6J (B6) show heritable differences in their responses to alcohol, cocaine, morphine and nicotine. The B6 strain shows significantly higher cocaine sensitivity as measured by psychomotor activation as well as higher intravenous cocaine self-administration compared to the A/J. Genetic analyses identified Dcc gene on chromosome 18 as a very strong candidate gene related to the differences between the strains (Boyle & Gill, 2009). The Dcc gene is highly expressed in mesocorticolimbic dopamine neurons, the primary site of cocaine's actions in the brain. The objective of the proposed research is to further examine the role of the Dcc gene in mediating individual differences in cocaine sensitivity and intravenous cocaine self-administration, using a mouse model.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pinpointing Causal Variants for Osteoporosis
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENETICS; OSTEOPOROTIC FRACTURE; RARE VARIANTS; RE-SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately half of women in Canada will suffer an osteoporotic fracture. The financial burden of these fractures is currently large, but is predicted to increase in proportion with the aging of our population, such that by year 2040 just hip fractures alone will incur $2.4 billion in direct costs.  While several environmental exposures have been clearly demonstrated to cause fractures, approximately half of the risk of osteoporotic fractures is due to genetic factors. We have recently employed emerging technologies to identify the common genetic changes which predispose to fracture. These discoveries have improved our understanding of the causes of osteoporosis. However, the risk for any of these common changes is quite low, and it has been difficult to understand if the identified variants actually cause osteoporotic fractures or are merely associated with this disease.  We propose a new research program where we will identify the rare genetic variants (present in ~1-2% of the population) that confer a larger risk of fracture. We will also employ novel methods to understand the function of both rare and common genetic variants in panels of human bone cells. Doing so will allow us to better understand the causes of this debilitating condition and provide novel drug targets for therapy. Our project should have an impact on clinical care and will also help to understand the causes of this common and costly condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fetal programming of hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRENERGIC SYSTEM; ADULT HYPERTENSION; CATECHOLAMINES; FETAL PROGRAMMING; MOLECULAR MECHANISMS; PHENYLETHANOLAMINE N-METHYLTRANSFERASE; SYMPATHO-ADRENAL SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension or high blood pressure afflicts 1 in 4 adults in Canada and is the major contributing factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke and kidney disease. Currently, the underlying cause of 90-95% of all cases of hypertension is not known. Thus, understanding the potential risk factors and mechanisms involved in hypertension is critical to the development of novel treatments for this disease. Recent studies suggest that early-life environmental factors which influence fetal development may cause adult diseases such as hypertension. Although elevated prenatal levels of the stress hormone, glucocorticoids, are involved in programming of adult hypertension, the precise mechanism(s) are poorly understood.  Due to the importance of the sympathetic nervous system, and the role of the adrenergic system in the development and maintenance of hypertension, we hypothesize that fetal programming of adult hypertension by involves permanent changes in adrenergic function involved in cardiovascular regulation.  Thus, the studies proposed are designed to determine how changes in the adrenergic system during prenatal and early postnatal life contribute to the development of hypertension.  Specifically, a focus on the role of the PNMT gene in fetal programming of hypertension will be delineated.  This study will identify the period in postnatal life that is critical in programming of adult hypertension and the potential for preventing the development of hypertension with the use of PNMT inhibitors.  In addition, this study will identify key cellular and molecular mechanisms that are involved in programming of adult hypertension via the PNMT gene.  Ultimately, improving our understanding of fetal programming of adult hypertension can lead to the development of additional molecular targets that may be useful in the primary prevention of adult hypertension and thereby decrease the morbidity and mortality associated with this prevalent disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting the editosome in Trypanosoma brucei - from function to drug discovery
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CHEMICAL SCREEN; DRUG TARGET CHARACTERIZATION; ENZYME KINETICS; RNA PROCESSING
Abstract-Résumé: RNA editing, catalyzed by a multi-protein complex, is an essential process for viability of parasitic pathogens and hence a drug target. These parasitic pathogens are responsible for serious human diseases of African sleeping sickness, Chagas disease, and leishmaniasis. With a mortality rate of 50,000 individuals per year, leishmaniasis is the second most important parasitic infection after malaria, followed by African sleeping sickness with 48,000 deaths per year. Chagas disease also causes 15,000 deaths annually. Transmissions of trypanosomatids are of growing concern as a result of transfusion and organ donation in the industrialized countries such as Canada and US. Canadians, new immigrants to Canada, and soldiers returning from Afghanistan, are also at risk. There are no vaccines for these pathogens, the drugs are toxic with limited effectiveness, and drug resistance is emerging. This project is focused on characterization of essential proteins involved in RNA editing. We will characterize these proteins in detail and identify specific inhibitors against these proteins. The inhibitors will be used to interfere with their functions to determine their exact role in RNA editing. They can also be exploited to develop the means to prevent disease caused by these pathogens.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reverse transmigration of arterial intimal dendritic cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CCL19/21; CCR7 CHEMOKINE RECEPTOR; DENDRITIC CELLS; ENDOTHELIUM; REVERSE TRANSMIGRATION; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Dendritic cells (DCs) are a specialized class of white blood cells that are critical to the body's immune system and are found in the inner artery wall of healthy humans and animals.  We found that DCs are particularly abundant in atherosclerosis-predisposed areas of normal mice, and named these cells resident intimal DCs or RIDCs.  We also found that when blood cholesterol is high, RIDCs take up lipid and transform into lipid-loaded foam cells, which is the first step in the formation of atherosclerosis.  Recently, we discovered that RIDCs exit from the normal artery wall after an inflammatory stimulus was injected into the bloodstream.  However, lipid accumulation in RIDCs as a result of high blood cholesterol blocks their exit.  In this application, our goal is to elucidate the mechanisms underlying RIDC exit from normal arteries, and determine how accumulated lipid inhibits it.  Three experimental aims are proposed in the application based on our preliminary experiments:  Aim 1:  Investigate the functions of a receptor called CCR7 in the exit of RIDCs from the artery wall.  Aim 2:  Investigate the requirement for proteins that stimulate CCR7, called CCL19 and CCL21, and determine if these proteins are produced by cells that line the artery wall.  Aim 3:  Investigate the mechanisms that inhibit the exit of lipid-loaded RIDCs from the artery wall in response to inflammatory stimuli.  We anticipate that information gained from the proposed studies will enable us to overcome the inhibitory mechanisms in lipid-loaded RIDCs in the future, so that lipid can be removed from the artery wall by exiting lipid-loaded RIDCs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards a Better Understanding of Breast Cancer Intratumoural Heterogeneity
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CAM ASSAY; CIRCULATING TUMOUR CELLS; FISH; HETEROGENEITY; METASTASIS; MOLECULAR SUBTYPES; NEOADJUVANT CHEMOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: In recent years we have learnt that breast cancer is not a single disease.  It has several subtypes, each with a distinct molecular profile and different response to treatment. Our understanding of differences between different patients' breast tumours has increased tremendously.  Unfortunately, our understanding of the differences within an individual patient's breast cancer has lagged behind.  Circulating tumour cells (CTCs) are gaining much attention as it has been found that their levels in the blood are related to disease progression.  These may be the cells that leave the breast and set up metastases at distant sites.  We have recently identified several genomic alterations in CTCs that appear to be shared between different breast cancer subtypes.  We would like to see how big a part of the breast cancer is made up of these cells and if the proportion varies with the type of breast cancer.  We also want to find out how they respond to chemotherapy and whether they are preferentially killed.  Finally, we will examine the effect of specific genetic alterations present in CTCs on breast cancer cells to see if they make tumours more aggressive or not.  Through our collaborator, Dr. John Lewis, we have access to an exciting and innovative model which will allow us to test the effect of large numbers of genes from the chromosomal regions we have identified. A better understanding of the different cancer cells that make up a breast tumour, and in particular the cells that enter the bloodstream, will help us understand more about how breast cancers develop and progress and how they develop resistance to therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Midlife Women with MDD: The Effects of Rapid Tryptophan or Phenylalanine/tyrosine Depletions on Mood and Thermoregulation in Depressed Subjects responsive to Estrogen Therapy.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE PHENYLALANINE AND TYROSINE DEPLETION (APTD); ACUTE TRYPTOPHAN DEPLETION (ATD); DEPRESSION; EMOTIONAL REGULATION; ESTROGEN; FMRI; HOT FLASHES; MENOPAUSE; TPH-1; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The transition to menopause is marked by significant hormonal changes and may also be accompanied by depressed mood, hot flashes and night sweats;in addition to other contributing factors such as stressful life events, co-morbid medical conditions and coping skills/ personality traits, these changes might impact quality of life and overall functioning. Estrogen treatment has been widely used to alleviate most of the menopause-associated symptoms. However, the exact mechanisms by which estrogen treatments improve mood and regulate body temperature are still unknown. This study will examine the role of neurotransmitters in estrogen treatment, providing critical information on the biological underpinning of estrogen's effects on symptomatic women during the menopausal transition and early postmenopausal years. Ultimately, the results from these experiments will lead to a better understanding of the ET effects on mood in women and possibly guide the development of novel, safer pharmacological treatments for depression in women across the reproductive life cycle.

TitreApplicationTitle: The gene regulatory network underpinning IL17-mediated innate immunity in the gut.
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPARATIVE GENOMICS; GENE REGULATORY NETWORKS; INNATE IMMUNITY; LEUKEMIA; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS
Abstract-Résumé: The ability to efficiently sequence animal genomes has revolutionized the use of simple invertebrate models for studying problems of human immunity. The sea urchin shares many genes with humans that are absent in more distant invertebrate models. The structural simplicity of its feeding larval stage provides an outstanding and unique model for understanding the regulation of gene expression in the context of gut-associated immunity. The sea urchin larva contain many orders of magnitude fewer cells than any vertebrate model yet uses many of the same genes to regulate immunity. We have identified a core set of regulatory factors that are shared between the sea urchin larval immune system and the gut associated immune system of humans. These genes include developmental gene regulatory factors that are associated with normal blood cell production and leukemia, recognition proteins that are associated with inflammatory disease and cell signaling molecules which are associated with autoimmunity. Here we propose to use the expression of a central immune signaling factor (IL17) as an anchor point for understanding the coordination of immune response across the gut epithelium. We will approach this problem with three strategies: (1) we will investigate initiation of  IL17 expression in the gut epithelium, (2) we will modulate the expression of IL17 to investigate its role in the recruitment and activation of immune cells and (3) we will exploit the simplicity of the larval system to identify new genes that correlate with the expression of the core factors in our gut infection model and function within the same system. Analysis of the sea urchin genome sequence has shown that immunity in this model system is rooted in an ancient control system that is shared with humans. Characterizing this system will lend fresh insight into this fundamental immune function and provide a basis for developing new approaches to controlling disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of broadly cross-protective antibodies against influenza hemagglutinin and the development of better influenza vaccines
Keywords-MotsClés: MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES; PANDEMIC PREPAREDNESS; SEASONAL AND PANDEMIC INFLUENZA; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Each year seasonal influenza kills hundreds of thousands of humans because vaccines need to be constantly updated and do not work well in the young or aged. Moreover there is no approved effective therapy for serious infections with influenza. The next influenza pandemic, which might occur at any time could be much more lethal than that in 2009 and mortality of avian H5N1 influenza is more than 50%. Influenza is such a problem the human immune response is very specific to various mutants of influenza virus, which occur continually. Surprisingly we found that humans can make antibodies (proteins that circulate in the blood and neutralize the influenza virus) that can neutralize a broad range of different influenza viruses.  The planned research will lead to a vaccine that broadly protects against all types of influenza, both seasonal and pandemic influenza.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural excitability in multiple sclerosis: Building the case for functional compensation.
Keywords-MotsClés: EXCITABILITY; FUNCTIONAL DISABILITY; GABA; INHIBITION; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY; MAGNETIZATION TRANSFER RATIO; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NEUROPLASTICITY; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the most common neurological disease affecting young adults in Canada. MS can cause symptoms such as poor thinking and memory, poor use of the arm and hand, and reduced walking ability. Techniques such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provide insight into changes in the brain caused by MS. Yet surprisingly, the severity of these symptoms is hard to predict by looking at images of the effects of MS on the brain. It seems that the brain has mechanisms that allow people to compensate for damage caused by MS.     Our research team is studying a mechanism that could explain why some people have preserved motor and cognitive abilities even though their brain has been affected by MS. We know that activity levels in the brain are determined by a combination of excitatory activity and inhibitory activity in nerve cells. Using TMS, we found less inhibitory activity in the brains of MS patients with good cognitive functioning. We are proposing a series of studies with the goal of understanding this possible mechanism by which people with MS might achieve better functioning. First, we will test whether the inhibitory levels in the brains of people with MS are abnormal compared to people with healthy brains. This may provide clues about what causes changes in brain inhibition. Next we will use MRI to examine whether the beneficial effect of low inhibition depends on the amount and location of MS damage in the brain. Finally, we will use a novel method called magnetic resonance spectroscopy to test for abnormal levels of a chemical called GABA that is an important regulator of inhibition in the brain. We expect the results will help us understand better how the brain responds to disease, not only in MS but also in other neurological disorders. They may also point the way to new therapies to help people with MS achieve their highest possible level of functioning.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advancing the Health and Housing in Transition (HHiT) Study: An extended four-year follow-up of the health of homeless and vulnerably housed adults in three Canadian cities
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEALTH STATUS; HOMELESS PEOPLE; LONGITUDINAL COHORT STUDY; MULTI-SITE RESEARCH; POPULATION HEALTH; QUALITY OF LIFE; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; VULNERABLY HOUSED PEOPLE
Abstract-Résumé: This prospective cohort study builds upon our ambitious ongoing research study entitled The Health and Housing in Transition (HHiT) study, which received a four-year CIHR Operating Grant in 2008. The HHiT study is a prospective cohort study that is tracking the health and housing status of a representative sample of approximately 1,200 homeless and vulnerably housed single adults in Vancouver, Toronto, and Ottawa over a two-year follow-up period. In this renewal grant application, we propose to extend the observation period of our study from two years, as allowed by the funding for our initial grant, to four years. This renewal will achieve the following scientific goals: (i) acquiring new knowledge on the course of homelessness and vulnerable housing over a four-year period; (ii) discovering the connections between housing transitions and health care utilization; and (iii) achieving a deeper understanding of the interactions between housing transitions and health status through qualitative interviews. An extension of the study will take advantage of a unique opportunity to understand the complex longitudinal relationships between housing and health in a well-established cohort of homeless and vulnerably housed single adults. Through detailed analyses of qualitative interviews and our robust longitudinal quantitative data, our study will help determine what types of integrated housing and support services are necessary to achieve housing stability and improved health outcomes for people experiencing homelessness and vulnerable housing. These findings will be invaluable for health and social policy decision makers in developing better evidence-based policies for housing and health.
