TitreApplicationTitle: Avoidance of Radiotherapy in Luminal A Breast Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; COHORT STUDY; INSTRINSIC SUBTYPES; RADIOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Local breast radiotherapy (RT) is standard therapy for all women with lymph node negative (LNN) early stage breast cancer. We have always wondered whether we might be over-treating some of these patients, whose outcomes are so good, even without breast RT. We have previously attempted to ask this question, in the form of a randomized clinical trial, whereby half of the patients did NOT receive breast RT, but were treated only with hormones such as Tamoxifen. Disappointingly, breast RT was still required, in that without RT, >8% of women will experience breast recurrence, which was unacceptably high.      There have been extensive molecular studies conducted on breast cancer, resulting in the identification of different subtypes such as luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, etc.  Many of these molecular platforms are very expensive, so that we have been developing less expensive methods, such as immunohistochemistry, to distinguish the various breast cancer subtypes.  Last year, we successfully determined that women with luminal A breast cancer are the most favourable subgroup, with the highest probability of surviving without local breast recurrence (92%).        Extending this work, using tumours from participants in our randomized trial, we have generated preliminary data which not only corroborated that luminal A patients had the lowest risk of local relapse (~5%), but furthermore, RT had no additional benefit. The current project proposes to complete the evaluation of using six immunomarkers on at least 592 samples, to corroborate our initial observations.  If correct, we will proceed to a future clinical study, where all luminal A LNN breast cancer patients, over the age of 60, will be treated with hormones only, thereby spared from RT, resulting in significant benefit to both patients, and the Canadian health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prevention of Arrhythmia Device Infection Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIA DEVICE; CLINICAL TRIAL; INFECTION; MULTICENTER; PREVENTION; RANDOMIZED
Abstract-Résumé: Infection is a serious complication in patients that have a heart rhythm device (pacemaker or implantable cardioverter defibrillator-ICD). Despite treatment with antibiotics prior to the surgery to implant the device, serious infection leading to hospitalization happens in one out of fifty patients. Most of these patients go on to have a second operation because of the infection, often leading to removal of their device to clear the infection. Additional antibiotic treatment may reduce the risk of infection, but also carries the risk of causing allergic reactions and serious diarrhea. The PADIT study will examine whether additional antibiotics given before, during and after the operation will reduce the risk of serious infection without causing a significant increase in antibiotic related complications. Centers rather than patients will be randomized to the antibiotic therapy plan for a period of 6 months after which the center will cross over to the other antibiotic therapy plan which will be used on all of their patients at that time. Data will be collected on patients at highest risk of infection, including those undergoing a second operation on their device, and those undergoing initial complex heart rhythm device implantation.  This randomized, cluster crossover, unblinded study will be performed in 10,900 patients in 27 hospitals in Canada over approximately 4 years.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular insights into gray platelet syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: BLEEDING AND CLOTTING; BLOOD; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; GFP-FUSION PROTEIN; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; INHERITED BLEEDING DISORDERS; MOUSE MODEL OF GRAY PLATELET SYNDROME; PLATELET ALPHA GRANULES; PLATELET DEVELOPMENT; VESICLE TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Each day cells in your bone marrow called megakaryocytes release vast numbers of tiny platelet cells into your bloodstream. Platelets stop bleeding after injuries by coordinating the formation of blood clots. They are also involved in long-term developments like hardening of the arteries (atherosclerosis) and sudden events like the emergence of clots that block blood vessels to cause heart attacks and strokes. Both normal and dangerous aspects of platelet behavior are linked to their ability to transport and release a wide variety of molecules from cellular storage compartments: alpha granules. Our understanding of how these granules are created and how they function is limited. My objective is to understand alpha granule genesis and function by exploiting our recent discovery of the genetic cause of a condition where alpha granules fail to develop: Gray Platelet Syndrome (GPS). GPS is caused by mutations in the NBEAL2 gene, which is predicted to encode a large protein called neurobeachin-like 2 (NBEAL2). Little is known about the structure, function and expression of this protein, but the gene sequence and studies of related proteins lead us to predict that NBEAL2 interacts extensively with other proteins and membranes inside cells. We will study what NBEAL2 does in experiments using mice that have been specifically made to have the same genetic defect as GPS patients, the Nbeal2-knockout mice. We will watch how their platelets respond to injuries that cause clots to form inside blood vessels, and use them to determine details of NBEAL2 protein function. Our studies will also determine how NBEAL2 is involved in the development of megakaryocytes and platelets. We will locate this protein inside cells and discover how it interacts with other proteins and cell membranes. Knowing how NBEAL2 controls alpha granule development and influences platelet function will help us to design strategies for controlling platelet behaviour in ways that prevent life-threatening clots.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Challenge Module for evaluating advanced motor skills of children with cerebral palsy: From measurement to child-centred goal setting.
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBAL PALSY; GROSS MOTOR; INDIVIDUALIZED GOALS; MEASUREMENT STUDY; OUTCOME MEASURES; PARTICIPATION; PEDIATRIC REHABILTATION; PHYSICAL THERAPY; QUALITATIVE INQUIRY; RASCH ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Meaningful activity participation is an overarching goal of pediatric physical therapy for children with cerebral palsy (CP)and has implications for their mental and physical health, fitness, self-concept and the development of essential skills. For the most functional children with CP, i.e., those in Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS)Level I, the negative impact of apparently 'minor' physical limitations on activity participation in has been seriously under-recognized. Currently, physical rehabilitation for children in Level I, is limited by the lack of available outcome measures to comprehensively assess their advanced gross motor skills; and a lack of knowledge regarding how to engage children in choosing personally meaningful and realistic therapeutic activities. To address these two issues, this study proposes to advance development of the Challenge Module, a measure of advanced gross motor skills developed by our team, and develop guidelines for its use in identifying meaningful physical activities with children and families. Methods: This three-year multi-centre study will use a mixed-methods design. The measurement arm focuses on refining the Challenge using sophisticated measurement techniques (Rasch analysis) with 300 children, followed by a reliability and validity evaluation. The concurrent qualitative arm will involve interviews with 45 children to provide in-depth information on activity preferences to inform development of the goal-setting guideline. Age-appropriate methods developed in our previous research will be used to engage the child participants, including puppet role-playing and use of vignettes. Contribution: The Challenge will for the first time provide the means to comprehensively assess advanced gross motor skills of children in GMFCS Level I. The associated guidelines will address known clinical difficulties in choosing personally meaningful and attainable therapeutic activities with children and families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of metaplasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY-DEPENDENT GROWTH; CALCIUM IMAGING; DENDRITIC ARBOR GROWTH; ELECTROPORATIVE TRANSFECTION; GLUTAMATERGIC TRANSMISSION; IN VIVO IMAGING; METAPLASTICITY; PLASTICITY; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TWO-PHOTON IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: The developing brain undergoes tremendous plasticity involving brain cell growth and formation of interconnections between cells to create functional brain circuits. This exceptionally complex process is highly susceptible to errors that may give rise to common and devastating neurological disorders, including Autism, Schizophrenia and Epilepsy. Therefore, understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms of developmental brain plasticity is essential to determining the origins of these disorders. Here, using direct imaging of brain activity and structural growth at the single-cell level within the intact and awake developing vertebrate brain, along with molecular biological techniques, we have identified a novel molecular pathway mediating developmental brain plasticity. This pathway centers on the protein MEF2, which acts as a molecular switch that sets a brain cell's response to plasticity-inducing environmental stimuli. By investigating this powerful new pathway for regulating brain cell growth we will be able to better understand how sensory stimuli directs formation of complex functional circuits and how these processes can go awry leading to dysfunctional networks underlying developmental brain disorders.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Roles of the BRCT-Domain Protein Rtt107 in the DNA Damage Response
Keywords-MotsClés: BRCT DOMAINS; CELL CYCLE; CHROMATIN; DNA REPAIR; GENOME INTEGRITY
Abstract-Résumé: DNA is the carrier of genetic information that is passed from one generation to the next, and it contains crucial instructions for all cellular function. Cells constantly encounter DNA damage that may be caused by internal or external agents such as oxidative stress or UV light. Repair of DNA damage is crucial to prevent passing on mutated DNA to the next generation. In humans, defects in the DNA damage response may lead to cancer or genetic diseases such as ataxia telangiectasia. Due to the critical importance of the DNA damage response, cells have complex mechanisms to recognize and repair DNA damage, and these pathways are highly conserved in all species. Much of the basic knowledge about DNA repair processes has been discovered in budding yeast, since it is a great model organism for understanding fundamental pathways in the cell. This proposal will study how yeast uses certain genes to enable the proper response to DNA damage. A better understanding of the DNA damage response will provide the basis for studying the defective processes in cancer or genetic diseases, and will ultimately contribute to the development of therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing evidence synthesis for informed decision-making
Keywords-MotsClés: EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS; GRADING EVIDENCE; INDIRECT COMPARISONS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MIXED TREATMENT COMPARISONS; NETWORK ANALYSIS; OVERVIEWS OF REVIEWS; SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients, healthcare providers, and policy-makers rely on high quality evidence to make important decisions about medical treatments. Overviews of reviews are a new method of bringing together high quality health evidence about the effectiveness and safety of different treatments for a health condition or illness. Overviews offer one-stop shopping or a "friendly front-end" for decision-making by bringing together evidence from different, often complex, sources into a single product. Overviews are relatively new in the medical literature, therefore the methods for how they are done are not consistent. Research is needed to refine how they are done to make sure that they include all relevant information and present accurate information about whether or not treatments are safe and effective. Overviews of reviews have the potential to become an important tool for patients, healthcare providers, and policy-makers when making treatment decisions. This research will refine the methods for producing and reporting overviews of reviews to ensure that they provide the highest quality evidence for informed decision-making.

TitreApplicationTitle: Resetting epithelial differentiation as a novel therapeutic approach to treating asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; EPITHELIAL DIFFERENTIATION; EPITHELIUM; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: While allergies are very common, affecting ~40% of the population in most Western countries, only a proportion of allergic people develop asthma. This highlights the importance of tissue and cell specific mechanisms that contribute to the disease. In the current proposal we will address how the structure and function of cells that line the airways, called epithelial cells contribute to asthma. As the interface between the inhaled environment and the internal environment of the lung, the epithelium normally possesses numerous mechanisms to maintain an effective protective barrier. However, the inability of the airway epithelium to effectively defend the lung against normally innocuous inhaled agents in asthma strongly suggests that asthma must involve defects in the epithelial barrier rather than being primarily an allergic disease. We believe that in asthma, certain types of epithelial cells do not go through normal stages of development and differentiation and as a consequence, remain "immature". This in turn leads to a chronic cycle of dysregulated damage and repair which ultimately impacts on the airway's function by increasing inflammation, but also by causing changes to the structure of the airway wall in a process called remodeling, which is similar to a non-healing scar on a skin wound. We have evidence that two key molecules which are specifically involved in epithelial cell development and maturation are not well regulated in asthmatic epithelial cells and this may be what is keeping them in an immature state. We will target these molecules in epithelial cells in culture and mouse models of asthma using a compound that is currently in clinical trials for bowel tumors. This application concentrates on a new pathophysiological mechanism of asthma that places the epithelium at the forefront of disease. Epithelial cells are easily reached by inhaled medications in asthma and as such are therapeutically natural targets.

TitreApplicationTitle: PROMOTE: Preschoolers at Risk - Obesity trajectories & cardioMetabolic factors: Towards Early identification
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMETABOLIC RISK FACTORS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; LIFESTYLE; LONGITUDINAL COHORT; NUTRITION; OBESITY PREVENTION; PRESCHOOL CHILDREN
Abstract-Résumé: The metabolic syndrome is a group of factors including obesity, and abnormalities in blood pressure, insulin, and cholesterol that has been shown to be associated with type 2 diabetes and heart disease in adults. There is emerging evidence that rapid growth in early childhood increases the risk for metabolic syndrome and abnormal blood pressure, insulin and cholesterol in early adulthood. It is unknown how rapid growth in early childhood increases the risk of these important health outcomes, and whether other important factors during early childhood such as diet, physical activity, and sedentary behaviour along with parent health affects growth and cardiometabolic risk. The objectives of this study are to determine how growth trajectories influence cardiometabolic risk in early childhood, and how other important child factors influence this relationship.     We have assembled a group of 2004 1-5 year old children from primary care physician practices. We have completed surveys on diet, physical and sedentary activities, sleep, temperament, and family history of disease, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and family height and weight. We have collected children's height, weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, and blood samples on this group of children. We will repeat these surveys and measurements on a yearly basis at their well child visits for the next 4 years. We will repeat their blood work two additional times; one time at the final year of the study, and one time between enrollment and the final year. We will determine if body mass index and waist circumference influence laboratory tests and blood pressure over time, and whether diet, physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep affects this relationship. The results of this study will help physicians to identify young children who are at risk of heart disease and diabetes, identify critical periods for identification, and allow physicians to provide early advice in order to prevent disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the influence of neighbourhood characteristics and obesity on asthma outcomes in children and adolescents
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSITY; ASTHMA; LONGITUDINAL; NEIGHBOURHOOD; VULNERABLE POPULATION; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma and obesity are important public health priorities that currently affect 15-20% of youth. Both are socially patterned conditions, with the likelihood of being obese or of having asthma differing from one neighbourhood to the next. More recent studies conducted among youth with asthma have observed a great deal of neighbourhood differences in asthma control, considered to be the worldwide standard for monitoring the adequacy of asthma management. In contrast to obesity, however, comparatively few studies have sought to identify specific factors explaining neighbourhood-level differences in asthma control, and little is known about the specific dimensions within built and social environments could be targeted to help improve asthma control. In this study, we examine three dimensions of neighbourhood context believed to affect asthma control: air quality (i.e. traffic related pollutants), built environment (i.e. walkability), and social environment (i.e. area deprivation). We also examine if obesity increases vulnerability to an adverse neighbourhood environment, in a population of asthmatic youth. Our objectives will be pursued using a database comprising a large clinical population of youth diagnosed with asthma, many of which were followed over time. Data from individual patient records and on medication use have already been collected; the current proposal will construct and merge a new database containing indicators of the three neighborhood dimensions of interest. These indicators will be created for several neighbourhood boundaries to allow sensitivity analyses, and over several time points, to capture change over time. We then examine spatial variation in the relationships of interest, and identify which specific neighbourhood characteristics may be involved. This unique infrastructure will also allow us better understand the relationship between asthma, obesity, and neighbourhood context, providing a basis for developing environmental interventions.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; THERAPIE DES CANCERS OSSEUX
TitreApplicationTitle: A small molecule inhibitor of G protein-coupled Receptor Kinase 6 (GRK6) to treat human Multiple Myeloma and related diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; G PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTOR KINASE 6; GENOMICS; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; KINASE INHIBITOR; LYMPHOMA; MULTIPLE MYELOMA; NOVEL THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple Myeloma (MM) is a malignancy of plasma cells that accounts for 2% of all cancer deaths. It is currently incurable. Kinase inhibitors are the fastest growing class of anti-cancer drug, both because of their efficacy and relative feasibility of design. However, a lack of effective kinase targets in MM has delayed successful use of kinase inhibitors for this cancer. We have previously tested all kinases in MM tumor cells to identify Achilles heel vulnerabilities. Fifteen kinases were consistently required for MM cell survival, including many known for roles in cancer. However most kinase vulnerabilities were not tumor-specific as inhibiting these kinases proved equally lethal to many cell types. Importantly, one kinase, GRK6, is selectively vulnerable only in MM cells; inhibiting GRK6 is tolerated in other cells. GRK6 is almost always expressed in MM, but is absent or only weakly expressed in most human tissues. The ability to 'drug' GRK6 without causing excessive toxicity is demonstrated by GRK6-deficient mice, which are healthy. In humans, mutations that cause loss of GRK6 interaction with CXCR4 cause WHIM syndrome, characterized by plasma cell deficiency and hypogammaglobulinemia, confirming that GRK6 is required for plasma cells in vivo. We propose developing GRK6 kinase inhibitors as therapeutics. GRK6 drugs have not previously been described. We have purified GRK6 and developed kinase- and cell-based assays to screen for selective inhibitors. We will use high-throughput screening of large compound libraries, focused biological assays, X-ray analysis of GRK6-drug interaction and directed synthesis of novel compounds to develop drugs that selectively inhibit GRK6, but not other kinases. Their medicinal properties will be examined and the best drugs will be advanced to studies using MM cell lines, tumor samples and animal models of MM. We seek to translate our discovery of an Achilles' heel within plasma cells into a drug to treat MM and related diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inhaled Corticosteroids as risk factors for severe viral infections in asthmatics: lessons from the H1N1 epidemic
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; EPITHELIUM; INJURY; MEDICATION; VIRUS INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: The cells which line the airways, called the epithelium, can be infected with viruses like influenza and rhinovirus causing symptoms of a 'common flu infection'. Sometimes these infections become severe and an individual is hospitalized, sometimes needing help to breathe with the help of a mechanical respirator.  For example, a very high percentage of children admitted to hospital with severe influenza infection during the 2009-2010 pandemic H1N1 influenza season were asthmatic.  Nearly all these patients were on some form of inhaled steroid medication.  Our initial results show that steroids can enhance virus infection in the airway epithelium by activating the cell, like the virus does, during infection. Therefore, with additional cell activation by steroids the virus life cycle is helped-along by steroid assisted activation.  We have begun to examine normal healthy epithelial cells from children and we have already found striking increases in the amount of infection in these cells during steroid treatment. We believe that current asthma medications like glucocorticosteroids (GCS), while excellent anti-inflammatory drugs, and enhance virus infection by pre-activating the cell. We propose two aims. Firstly, we will discover the cellular pathways that are activated in the presence of GCS. Secondly, we will characterize the consequences of GCS treatment on virus infection in epithelial cells obtained from asthmatic children and adults and compare this to the responses of epithelial cells from similarly aged non-asthmatics. Finally we will examine these responses in a mouse model of asthma. In this model, mice have been made allergic to house-dust mites making them relevant to human asthma. If our hypothesis is true, drug treatment strategies that involve GCS will have to be refined or avoided during pandemic or severe influenza seasons.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Genome Function by Histone Variant H2A.Z
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; EPIGENETICS; GENE REGULATION; GENOME FUNCTION; TELOMERES
Abstract-Résumé: DNA, the carrier of genetic information, is packaged into highly organized superstructures inside cells. Genomic DNA wraps around specialized DNA-packaging proteins called histones to form nucleosomes, which assemble into chromatin. Chromatin influences all aspects of chromosome behaviour and genome function. It can be remodelled and modified by large protein complexes to produce a highly dynamic landscape. Such chromatin states can be inherited during cell division, creating an additional complex layer of epigenetic information that is crucial for the identity of a cell. Complex regulatory mechanisms involving chromatin ensure that each cell expresses only the appropriate genes, duplicates its genome with high fidelity, divides only when required and combats constant assaults on its DNA. An ever increasing number of different chromatin modifying proteins are involved not only in cancer but also in severe childhood syndromes and neurodegenerative diseases. The goal of this research is to understand the unique chromosomal neighbourhoods containing a specialized histone variant with interesting functions in health and disease. A combination of genome-wide approaches and more traditional molecular biology techniques will be applied to uncover the unique features and specialized function of the histone variant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the Hedgehog receptor complex and its role in embryonic development
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS; HEDGEHOG; MOUSE; NERVOUS SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT; PATCHED1; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SPINAL CORD
Abstract-Résumé: The Sonic hedgehog (Shh) protein is important for diverse biological processes during embryonic development. For example, Shh functions to pattern the limbs and the nervous system. Despite its importance, the molecular mechanism underlying Shh signaling during embryonic development remains poorly understood.  This proposal focuses on how the Shh signal is received by a cell. The classic view is that Shh initiates signaling by binding the protein Patched1 (Ptch1). While Ptch1 has been thought to act as the main Shh receptor for the past decades, we have recently shown that Shh signaling absolutely requires additional Shh-binding proteins. However, we do not know how these additional Shh-binding proteins function as Shh receptors. It is the goal of this project to characterize this function in detail.  We anticipate that this work will bring insights into the molecular mechanism underlying diseases associated with the Shh signaling pathway and might eventually help developing therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antioxidant effects of n3-polyunsaturated fatty acids in the vasculature.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ANTIOXYDANT; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES; CLINICAL STUDY; MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY; N3-POLYUNSATURATED FATTY ACIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Omega-3 fatty acids from marine origin are recognized for their beneficial effects in the prevention of cardiovascular diseases, the major cause of death in Canada. However, their mechanism of action is not fully understood. With the present application, we plan to determine if omega 3 acids can stimulate the production of a natural antioxidant, named bilirubin. By reducing the oxidation of blood lipids, bilirubin exerts beneficial effects in the vascular system. To reach our objectives, we will combine innovative and state-of-the-art approaches in molecular biology, molecular pharmacology and clinical studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of oxidative stress and TNF-alpha in exercise-induced atrial fibrillation
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIAS; ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; HEART DISEASE; INFLAMMATION; ION CHANNELS
Abstract-Résumé: It is now recognized that, while exercise is invariably beneficial for the ventricular chambers of the heart, intense endurance exercise over many years causes many changes in upper chambers of the heart (i.e. the atria) that lead to conditions predisposing older athletes to an arrhythmia called atrial fibrillation. This conditions is poorly tolerated in these patients and is strongly associated with increased risk of stroke. This grant looks into the possible causes of the atrial changes and tries to identify the source of the atrial fibrillation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Acoustically activated submicron droplets of liquid perfluorocarbon as a new contrast agent for ultrasound imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER DIAGNOSIS; DIFFUSIBLE INTRAVASCULAR IMAGING PROBE; INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST AGENTS; ULTRASOUND IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: This project aims to develop a new contrast agent for ultrasound imaging that will provide diagnostic information not available in current medical ultrasound images. 'Nanodroplets' of a liquid perfluorocarbon, a fraction of a millionth of a metre in size, are injected into a vein and allowed circulate, during which time they diffuse into the body of a cancer because of the tendency of cancer blood vessels to have 'leaky' walls. Ultrasound energy applied through the skin is used to convert the droplet into microbubbles, which are easily detectable using methods developed in the investigator's laboratory and widely used in clinical imaging systems. These images will then be able to show a cancer otherwise undetectable by ultrasound. The project focuses on the optimal composition of the droplets and the sound used to convert them to bubbles; the behaviour of the droplets when injected into animal models of cancer and their detection by ultrasound imaging after acoustic activation. It is anticipated that such a method will provide ultrasound, the most widely used imaging method in medicine, with a new technique for the detection of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular neuroscience of Parkinson's Disease: Retromer (VPS35) dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; HUMAN GENETICS; NEUROGENETICS; NEUROSCIENCE; PARKINSON DISEASE; VPS35
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a debilitating neurodegenerative disease that affects 1 percent of the population over 65 years. PD is already a major health care burden, and will become even more so in our increasingly aging society. Currently there is no cure, and treatments only address PD symptoms. Medications do not slow disease progression and are not without serious side-effects.    To develop more effective treatments for PD requires an understanding of its molecular cause(s) (etiology) and how they influence susceptibility and progression (pathogenesis). The latest susceptibility gene (VPS35) for PD was recently discovered. VPS35 is part of the retromer, the scaffold of an ancient and elaborate cellular recycling system, selective for very specific protein cargos. Our study is to determine which cargo interactions and cellular processes are distressed by VPS35 mutations, and how these disturbances affect brain function and lead to PD.    We believe that by targeting the causes of PD, rather than its consequences, and by creating and characterizing genetic models, more effective therapeutics can be developed.  Our objective is to alleviate motor and non-motor symptoms, by providing neuroprotective benefit, and to lessen the burden of PD to individuals and society.

ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; LIPOPROTEINES, TRANSPORT LIPIDIQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of intestinal lipoprotein overproduction in insulin resistant states by citrus flavonoids.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CHYLOMICRONS; DYSLIPIDEMIA; FLAVONOIDS; INSULIN SIGNALING; MOUSE MODEL OF INSULIN RESISTANCE; OBESITY; VERY LOW DENSITY LIPOPROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: Increased blood levels of lipids (cholesterol and triglyceride), increase the risk of atherosclerosis, the disease underlying most heart attacks and strokes. There is increasing evidence that the overproduction of lipid containing particles (lipoproteins) from the intestine into the blood, in response to dietary fat, occurs in many people at risk for atherosclerosis. This is particularly a problem in people with insulin resistance, a common disorder associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes. One consequence of insulin resistance is that the intestine makes too many lipoproteins in response to dietary fat. Experiments in this proposal are designed to discover the pathways within intestinal cells that cause increased export of lipoproteins in the setting of insulin resistance. Recently, our laboratory discovered that in mice with high blood fats and insulin resistance, diets containing natural compounds known as citrus flavonoids, inhibit lipoprotein formation in the liver. We now believe that these flavonoids also inhibit the formation and secretion of lipoproteins from the intestine, thereby contributing to the prevention of elevated blood fats and atherosclerosis. We want to discover how flavonoids actually work in the intestine at the molecular level and how these powerful biological molecules normalize the formation of intestinal lipoproteins. We will employ an animal model, a genetically modified strain of mice, which develops high blood levels of lipids, glucose and insulin (insulin resistance), when fed a high-fat diet. We will evaluate the ability of the flavonoids naringenin and nobiletin to prevent or reverse overproduction of intestinal lipoproteins and define the mechanisms involved. Our studies will provide new insights into the mechanisms governing intestinal lipoprotein secretion. Furthermore, these experiments could potentially lead to novel therapeutics for the treatment of high blood fats, insulin resistance and atherosclerosis.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; FONCTION RÉNALE, NÉPHROLOGIE, UROLOGIE
TitreApplicationTitle: The Cardiorenal Syndrome in Congestive Heart Failure: Mechanistic Insights
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CONGESTIVE HEART FAILURE; HEMODYNAMICS; RENAL FUNCTION; SYMPATHETIC NERVOUS SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with heart disease often develop symptoms of fatigue and/or shortness of breath. These symptoms are referred to as congestive heart failure. This is a very common condition in Canada and is one of the most common reasons for adults to be admitted to hospital. Many patients with congestive heart failure develop abnormalities in kidney function that often leads to an increase in symptoms and an increase in both the duration and cost of hospitalization. The causes of developing abnormal kidney function in patients with congestive heart failure have been difficult to understand and better prevention and treatment is necessary. The current grant proposal is designed to better understand why kidney function becomes abnormal in patients with congestive heart failure. The hope is that an improved understanding of the causes of abnormal kidney function will improve ability to both prevent and treat this complication.

TitreApplicationTitle: The CORRELATE Study: Canadian Outcomes REgistry Late After TEtralogy of Fallot Repair
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; EXERCISE TESTING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; OUTCOME; PULMONARY VALVE REPLACEMENT; QUALITY OF LIFE; REGISTRY; TETRALOGY OF FALLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common form of cyanotic congenital heart disease that is treated with repair in early childhood. Despite successful TOF repair in early childhood, risk of late mortality, related to pulmonary valve leaking, is cause for concern. Timing of pulmonary valve replacement surgery (PVR) is controversial and impact is not fully understood.  Objective: The objective of our project is to study children and adults with repaired TOF across Canada to describe clinical and imaging characteristics of those receiving PVR, to evaluate practice patterns related to timing of PVR and to determine the impact of these variations on clinical outcome and quality of life.  Study plan: We will create a registry of children and adults with repaired TOF followed in ten major Canadian congenital heart disease centres across the country: in Toronto, Montreal, Halifax, Edmonton and Vancouver. Through this Canadian-wide network we estimate that we will be able to follow close to 2000 patients with repaired TOF. We will review clinical measures, cardiac MRI studies, exercise tests and quality of life surveys. Through this cohort we will characterize who is referred for PVR surgery and for what indications, and in doing so, we aim to better understand the relationships between PVR surgery, cardiac magnetic imaging measurements, exercise testing, quality of life  and overall survival in this population.  Uniqueness of proposal: This study would be the first Canadian-wide collaborative study of children and adults born with congenital heart disease and would provide important information on how to improve the lives of thousands of Canadians with TOF and significant leaking of the pulmonary valve.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; ANOMALIES CONGENITALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental regulation of genomic imprinting in the mouse
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETICS; GENE EXPRESSION; GENOMIC IMPRINTING; GERM LINE; MOUSE DEVELOPMENTAL GENETICS; MOUSE EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; TROPHOBLAST
Abstract-Résumé: Our genetic make-up consists of two equal sets of chromosomes inherited from our mother and father, such that most genes are present as two equivalent copies in our cells. However, some unusual genes in our genome behave differently: for these genes, only one of the two copies is used by our cells, depending on its parental origin. Why or how these particular genes are not active from both copies is not fully understood. This phenomenon, called genomic imprinting, is essential for normal development of the mammalian embryo and is linked to several human diseases, with more than 200 newborns affected each year in Canada, and cancers. Our research program tries to understand how this imprinting works and what might be its function in mammalian biology. To this end, we are studying new models of imprinting defects, using the mouse as a model system. We recently established the first mouse line expressing the green florescent protein under the regulation of imprinting: the fluorescent gene is silenced upon transmission through the paternal germline. We have also developed a new technique allowing us to study maternal and paternal copies of an imprinted domain independently, in the hope of identifying the molecular marks used by our cells to distinguish paternal and maternal copies of these genes in the genome. We are using these unique tools to study the mechanism of imprinting in a mammalian model organism. Through our work we will gain a better understanding of how some of our genome is utilized during development and how we might help patients where imprinting abnormalities have occurred. By contributing to further knowledge on the epigenetic mechanisms regulating our genome, this research also has important implications for area such as reproductive technologies and stem cell research.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: FONCTION RÉNALE, NÉPHROLOGIE, UROLOGIE; APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Sirtuin1 in Diabetic Nephropathy: Experimental and Clinical Studies
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; HUMANS; KIDNEY DISEASE; MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Many of the complications of diabetes, such as kidney and heart disease, are similar to those of ageing, but occurring at a much earlier age.  In other words, diabetes seems to accelerate the ageing process.  Recent research in to the mechanisms that contribute to ageing has identified a pivotal role for a chemical that is present in all cells called Sirtuin-1, or Sirt1.  The more Sirt1 a cell or organism has, the longer it lives.  In our preliminary studies we have shown that Sirt1 levels are dramatically reduced in kidney tissue from individuals with diabetes.  We have further shown that a drug which activates Sirt1, can lessen the extent of kidney damage in a mouse model of diabetic kidney disease.  Given these exciting observations, we now seek to perform more definitive studies in animals with the ultimate goal of providing a new potential treatment for the prevention of kidney disease in diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting long-term success on antiretroviral therapy among individuals failing first-line treatment in Uganda
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SERVICES POLICY; HIV DRUG RESISTANCE; HIV/AIDS; RESOURCE-LIMITED SETTINGS; RESPONSE TO THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Currently most patients receiving HIV treatment in sub-Saharan Africa do not have access to expensive laboratory testing which is commonly available in North America or Europe.  Two recent studies have confirmed that patients generally do quite well in the short term without access to these laboratory tests.  However, the long-term impact of keeping large numbers HIV patients on treatment without laboratory testing which allows early detection of treatment failure is unknown.  This study will look at how frequently HIV individuals fail first-line treatments of HIV positive patients have been receiving treatment through The AIDS Support Organisation for more than 3 years, We will also study factors that affect responses to second-line HIV treatment.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Ovarian Follicular Development: Mechanisms of Dysregulation in PCOS.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CHEMERIN; DIFFERENTIATION; FOLLICULAR CELL FATE; FOLLICULAR DEVELOPMENT AND ATRESIA; FSH; GDF9; GENE AND MIRNA ARRAY; IGF-1; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALLING; MIRNA; OVARY; PCOS; PROLIFERATION; SIRNA
Abstract-Résumé: The ovary serves two prime functions: production of egg needed for specie propagation and hormone biosynthesis important for (i) the auto-regulation of growth and function of the function unit of the ovary (known as the follicle), (ii) expression of female sex characteristics with the onset of puberty, and (iii) preparation of the uterus for implantation of the fertilized egg, pregnancy and birth.   The growth and degeneration (atresia) of an ovarian follicle are complex processes involving the coordinated actions and interactions of brain sex hormones (gonadotropins), intra-ovarian regulators and substances secreted from fat cells (adipokines).  Although recent investigations on regulation of the ovary by gonadotropins have led to their direct application in the treatment of infertility, information concerning how these regulators regulate the growth of the follicle at the cellular is limited.    The overall objective of the proposed research program is to examine how these regulators control of follicular development and atresia as well as how dysregulation of these regulatory mechanisms leads to polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), a multifactoral reproductive and metabolic disorder that accounts of 75% of all anovulatory infertility. These studies will provide a better understanding of the pathophysiology of PCOS as well as new strategies for its treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Microenvironmental strategies for the optimal utilization of anti-angiogenic drugs combinations
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CHEMOTHERAPY; HYPOXIA; RADIATION THERAPY; TUMOUR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Anti-angiogenic therapy involves treatments with drugs that inhibit the growth of blood vessels. In adults angiogenesis only occurs during wound healing, inflammation and a few other instances. Tumour growth necessitates new blood vessel development to feed the enlarging tumour. New generations of anti-angiogenic agents should be much more potent than those used currently. Combination of anti-angiogenic agents with radiation therapy is a tantalizing concept but scheduling needs to be rationally designed to be optimally effective.  Using novel microscopy techniques we propose to characterize the way anti-angiogenic agents affect tumours so that radiation therapy can be incorporated into treatment in the most advantageous manner. MRI methods will be developed to allow the activity of anti-angiogenic agents to be followed and to define the optimal manner to incorporate radiation therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics and Epigenetics of Serotonin System in Suicidal Behaviour: CpG SNP Mapping, Methylation and Allelic Imbalance Analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETICS; GENETICS; METHYLATION; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder affect hundreds of thousands of Canadians and their families. Both disorders are associated with a high risk of suicide. Several studies provide evidence that genetic factors influence suicidal behavior. The major aim of this study is to identify changes in the genetic material that are inheritable but are sensitive to environment and which genes and neurotransmitters are relevant to suicidal behavior. Understanding these factors might enable prediction of suicidal behavior in patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. In this study, we will analyze proteins in the brain that influence transfer of information in different brain circuits. The instructions for creating these proteins are encoded in genes, but how these genes express themselves can be influenced by the environment through epigenetic modifications. We have collected genetic samples as well as detailed clinical information about suicide attempts and suicidal behavior severity scores from 336 bipolar and 497 schizophrenia patients. We will assess whether epigenetic modification is found in the genetic material and has occurred under the influence of external factors such as stress, medications and disease course. Additionally, we will estimate the gene activity of neurotransmitter receptors that are the target of antidepressants and antipsychotics. This analysis will be performed in 165 post-mortem brains donated by the Stanley Foundation including 41 patients who died by suicide. The genetic risk markers for suicide that we hope to identify could, in the future, identify persons at risk and thus facilitate preventive measures such as counseling, family education, and early treatment intervention for these individuals. Furthermore, the identified genes and genetic changes may reveal possible chemical imbalance in the brain of patients who have committed suicide which can be used as targets for development of novel medications for suicide prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: SURVIVCF: Survival and Transplantation in Canadians with Cystic Fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CYSTIC FIBROSIS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICES UTILIZATION; LUNG TRANSPLANTATION; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Canada boasts the highest median survival age for individuals living with cystic fibrosis (CF) in the world. Which factors explain the improvements seen in survival over time in Canada and which groups are at risk for early death has not been established in the current era of CF care. Two pivotal Canadian studies, published over 15 years ago, provided clinically useful information on predictors of survival in CF; however, treatment, complications and prognosis have dramatically changed over the past two decades. Despite advances in care, progressive lung disease continues to be the primary cause of death in CF and ultimately lung transplantation is offered to those with end-stage lung disease. Accurately predicting life expectancy in CF is critical so that healthcare providers can alter modifiable risk factors, intensify medical therapy, consider new therapies, or optimize timing for lung transplantation referral and listing.  We propose a population-based cohort study using linked national CF registry data to systematically identify demographic, clinical, and geographic factors associated with survival in a contemporary CF sample and to identify the best combination of factors which accurately predict survival. Finallly, we will evaluate the impact of lung transplantation on survival in the Canadian CF population and identify the groups most likely to benefit.

TitreApplicationTitle: Creating an information system from a Primary Care Electronic Medical Record Administrative data Linked Database to improve Rheumatoid Arthritis Surveillance and Quality of Care
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE SURVEILLANCE; ELECTRONIC MEDICAL RECORDS; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; QUALITY OF CARE; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a long-term, disabling, inflammatory type of arthritis. Early access to specialists, physiotherapists and treatment are needed to prevent disability. This study will use the Electronic Medical Record Administrative data Linked Database (EMRALD), an electronic medical record (EMR) system which contains anonymous EMR data for over 150,000 patients from over 100 family physicians across Ontario. This database is linked to administrative data (electronic codes for hospital and physician visit records which provide anonymous comprehensive information for health care contacts for all individuals in the province).  We plan to 1)  determine if RA diagnosis codes can accurately identify anonymous subjects with RA from provincial administrative data; 2) identify the number of individuals in the province who have RA; 3) find ways to accurately identify anonymous RA patients within primary care EMR to establish a cohort of patients seen by family physicians; and 4) measure and describe the care that patients receive, to determine if it is optimal or not. By validating the diagnosis of RA in administrative hospital and physician visit data, this study will be the first to provide accurate estimates of the prevalence of RA in Ontario, and identify if these patients receive optimal care. In addition, we will use EMRALD to describe the way patients get referred to rheumatologists  (including delays) and measure care provided to patients with RA by their family physician which can be used to generate knowledge to identify gaps in care and hopefully lead to improved care in the future. The ultimate aim of our study is to improve delivery of care, and outcomes, for Canadians with RA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural analysis of small RNA recognition by Argonaute proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGONAUTE PROTEINS; MID DOMAIN; MIRNA; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; RNA SILENCING; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: In cancer, proper gene regulation is lost. 'RNA silencing' is a fundamental process of gene regulation that affects a wide array of cellular functions including cell growth, conversion to different cell types and cell death. Here, short length RNA molecules called small RNAs combine with members of the Argonaute family of proteins, and together target specific messenger RNAs (encoding for proteins), resulting in a lowering of the amount of that protein present in the cell, hence the term 'silencing'. Research into RNA silencing has exploded in recent years and much has been learned about how this process works at the cellular level. This has led to the development of powerful tools for manipulating cellular protein levels and studying gene regulation by way of laboratory synthesized small RNAs, called small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). siRNAs can also be used in a therapeutic manner to manipulate the levels of proteins associated with cancer and other diseases. However, the mechanisms that underlie RNA silencing at the molecular level in humans are at present poorly understood. This proposal aims to use structural biology to unravel the molecular basis of RNA silencing in humans. These studies will substantially progress our understanding of this fundamental mechanism of gene regulation, improve the use of existing tools for studying gene function (i.e. siRNAs), and potentially lead to the development of new siRNA-based drugs against cancer causing genes, which can have a great impact on human health.

TitreApplicationTitle: ED-directed interventions to improve outcomes after asthma exacerbations
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA EXACERBATIONS; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; GUIDELINES; INTERVENTION; RELAPSE
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma attacks are common causes of Emergency Department (ED) visits, and can result in school and work absenteeism, hospitalization, and significant costs to the health care system. Our previous studies suggested most Canadian emergency physicians follow guideline recommendations; however, follow-up care by primary care providers (PCPs) after ED visits are often delayed (only a third of patients are seen within two weeks). Moreover, preventive interventions (e.g., action plans, immunizations, and education) are rarely implemented in this population. Ineffective management after asthma attacks could increase the risk of undesired events. The objective of this study is to determine if ED-directed guidance on follow-up and self-management provided to PCPs and patients respectively reduces relapse within 90 days. This randomized controlled trial includes asthmatics 17-55 years old who are treated and discharged from EDs in Edmonton and Calgary. Patients must have a PCP with whom to follow-up or one will be found for them. At discharge, 366 patients will be randomized into: a) Usual ED care (PCPs receive a faxed copy of the ED chart); b) Usual ED care + personalized fax to the patients' PCP (e.g., copy of the ED chart and opinion-leader letter encouraging follow-up and management suggestions); or c) Usual ED care + personalized fax to the patients' PCP + involvement of a case manager who will encourage patients to pursue follow-up, provide management review and offer brief education within the next week. In-ED and post-ED medical treatment will be left to the emergency physicians' discretion. Phone calls at 30 and 90 days will document relapses, follow-up visits, and patients' health-related quality of life; health care-related costs will also be measured. This work will present health care providers from the ED and primary care fields with an opportunity to optimize asthma management in a group of asthmatics with the highest risk for poor short and long-term outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of trans- and cis-acting factors in the regulation of mRNA encoding modulators of senescence and the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype
Keywords-MotsClés: HUR; MICRORNA; MRNA; MRNA STABILITY; MRNA TRANSLATION; POSTTRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; POSTTRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS; REPLICATIVE SENESCNECE; SASP
Abstract-Résumé: Aged individuals are characterized by an increase in the number of cells that undergo growth arrest, a phenomenon known as replicative senescence. It is believed that the onset of diseases in the aged population is mediated in part by the increased accumulation of these senescent cells. The conversion of DNA into proteins requires the synthesis of an intermediate template molecule called RNA. Several proteins regulate the export of RNA out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm where it is converted into proteins. The research done in my laboratory focuses on such a protein, named HuR that also regulates the longevity of RNA molecules. Although the identity of genes that mediate scenescene is well defined, very little is know as to how they are regulated during this process. Since HuR has been shown to mediate the induction of scenescene, we hypothesize that it does so by regulating the expression of RNAs involved in this phenotype. The purpose of this study is to assess this possibility and to further verify the role of HuR partners (named microRNA) or the implication of modifications of the HuR protein on replicative scenescene. We therefore aim to establish the pathways and mechanisms by which HuR is involved in replicative scenscence.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hippocampal theta oscillations - generation and synaptic plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVING RATS; COMPARTMENT MODEL; FIELD POTENTIALS; HIPPOCAMPUS; SYNPATIC PLASTICITY; THETA RHYTHM; TIMING
Abstract-Résumé: The hippocampal theta rhythm (4-10 Hz) is prominent during active behaviours such as walking and spatial exploration in rats, and it helps to process neural information including coding and retrieval of memory and integration of sensory and motor signals. Our laboratory has contributed to the concept that theta rhythm is a spatiotemporal wave of membrane potential change that sweeps across the dendrites and cell bodies of the main type of CA1 nerve cells, the pyramidal cells. The present proposal will examine the functional consequence of this dynamic wave of membrane potential change in CA1 pyramidal cells. Changes in the connection between neurons or synaptic strengths have been proposed as the cellular basis of memory. We propose that the sweeping theta wave results in changes in neural connections (synaptic strengths), and the optimal time for change occurs at different phases of the theta rhythm depending on the location of the connection (synapse). In order to provide a detailed understanding of the generation of the theta rhythm, a biophysical model will be fitted to the experimental data obtained by simultaneous recording of the rhythm in the hippocampus. This model will predict how different drugs or lesion may affect the theta rhythm and theta-modulated neural processing. This proposal will help to understand how a brain oscillation provides a means to influence signal processing and memory storage in the hippocampus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Radiolabelled peptides to improve cancer diagnosis by positron emission tomography / Peptides radiomarqués pour améliorer le diagnostic du cancer par tomographie à émission de positron
Keywords-MotsClés: CU-64; F-18 PROSTHETIC GROUP; GA-68 CHELATOR; GASTRIN RELEASING PEPTIDE; NEUROPEPTIDE Y1; PEPTIDE DIMERS; PEPTIDE RADIOPHARMACEUTICAL; PEPTIDE RECEPTORS; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; TUMOR CLASSIFICATION; XENOGRAFTED MICE
Abstract-Résumé: New diagnostic tools can improve the clinical management of patients with breast and prostate cancers, two of the most common types of cancer. Positron emission tomography (PET) is a powerful imaging technique that can follow tracers for the detection of tumors with dedicated scanners.   From previous work, we have identified several tracers that bind proteins involved in breast and prostate cancers. We have also shown that these new imaging tools can be used to detect tumors in some animal models. Although these preliminary results are important, the biological properties of our tracers still have to be improved for their use in humans.   In this proposal, we propose to modify their structures to improve their stability and their efficacy on breast and prostate cancer cells. Once suitable and stable tracers identified, we will perform PET imaging in mice bearing human breast and prostate tumors. The most promising candidate(s) will be injected in rats at 1000x the expected dose for diagnostic use to ensure they will be safe to administer to humans. Finally, we will prepare the submission data for a phase I clinical trial application with the best tracer(s).   Developing new tracers is critical for accurate early detection when breast and prostate cancers can be treated with minimal discomfort, complications and costs. These new tools will also enable assessment of cancer stage and aggressiveness that are critical to identify which patients need to be treated and what treatment should be administered. With the deployment of PET technology in several sites in Canada, the success of this proposal may lead to immediate clinical applications to improve the care of patients suffering from cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure-based analysis and inhibition of protein  secretion pathways in pathogenic bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; DRUG DESIGN; MACROMOLECULAR ASSEMBLIES; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The Type III secretion system (T3SS) is a needle-like apparatus of ~20 highly conserved proteins which provides a mechanism for the direct injection of bacterial virulence proteins through the inner and outer bacterial membranes into the host cell cytosol, a process essential for subsequent pathogenicity. The T3SS apparatus is an attractive target for antibacteial therapies as it is unique to pathogenic bacteria  including those responsible for whooping cough, bubonic plague, typhoid fever and severe food and water borne dysentery. We are using a multi-disciplinary biophysical approach (including x-ray crystallography, Nuclear Magenetic Resonance, labeling/mass spectrometry and single particle Electron Microscopy) complimented by in vivo analysis of designed mutants (including secretion competence, localization and virulence assays) to characterize the overall architecture, key protein-protein interactions, and molecular mechanisms that drive this fascinating system. Many of the components of the T3SS are highly oligomerized and/or membrane associated proteins, which are particularly challenging to study at the molecular level and require the development of new approaches and methods to facilitate their characterization which we have undertaken. In addition we are using a similarly multidisciplinary approach to characterize the structure and mechanism of action of bacterial virulence proteins specifically injected into the host by the T3SS needle apparatus, alone and in complex with their molecular target(s) in the infected human host. Collectively, the high resolution structures of these key protein/protein complexes are being used as templates for the design of antimicrobials and vaccines that are specific for the many notorious pathogens that  encode a T3SS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular Immunotherapy for Septic Shock (CISS): A Phase I Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL TRIAL; DOSE ESCALATORS; MESENCHYMAL STROMAL CELLS; PHASE I; SAFETY; SEPTIC SHOCK; TOLERABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Severe infection with shock (septic shock) in the intensive care unit (ICU) is common accounting for approximately 20% of admissions, of which 40% will die. Septic shock is associated with an immensely uncontrolled inflammatory response from the body that is initiated by the infectious organism. Recent studies done in animals with sepsis suggest that the infusion of stem cells may balance inflammation, help with repair of injured organs, and reduce death. Hence, it represents an exciting and promising potential therapy for septic shock. Cellular therapy has not yet been tested in humans with septic shock and so the safety and optimal dose of these cells is yet to be established.  This is the primary purpose of the CISS Phase I Trial.    The CISS Phase I Trial will enroll 2 groups of patients with septic shock. One group will not receive the cells (control group), but will serve as a comparison group to those who do. The second group will receive increasing doses of cell therapy. Three patients per group will form the low dose, mid dose, and high dose groups. The frequency of adverse events and serious adverse events will be recorded, and blood will be drawn repeatedly over time for inflammation markers in the control and cell therapy groups. Careful monitoring by an independent and expert committee will review the occurrence of adverse events after the completion of each cell dose group. Carefully defined rules for stopping the trial in the case of serious adverse events that are linked the infusion of these cells will be strictly adhered to.   If the CISS Phase I Trial determines that treatment with these cells is safe, then the optimum dose of cells established by this Phase I Trial will be used in a subsequent study to determine whether these cells improve patient outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genomic follow-up of the susceptibility loci for SZ and BP in multi-affected families of Eastern Quebec
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; GENE EXPRESSION; GENETIC LINKAGE AND ASSOCIATION; GENOMICS; PSYCHIATRIC GENETICS; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SNPS; SUSCEPTIBILITY GENES
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic and environmental factors are undoubtedly in cause in the origins of schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BP) diseases. The clinical manifestations of these disorders are varied and complex, which enhances the difficulty to identify the genes involved.  For 20 years, our research team gathered a sample of 1300 members from 48 well-characterized multigenerational families of Eastern Quebec that are densely affected by SZ or BP, in which we were able to identify 10 different chromosome regions where should be located the genes at the origin of the disease. However, our results provided relatively large chromosomal regions including some 1500 genes from which should be identified the true causal genes. The global objective of the current proposal is to identify, among these 1500 genes, those responsibles for our observed linkage signals using a genomic approach. Through the analysis of gene expression and genetic association, we will be able to set apart the causal candidate genes located in the 10 chromosomal regions having shown linkage in our kindred samples. These recent progresses represent the beginning of a new era for psychiatry leading hopefully to three revolutions in our field: i) The development of new treatments based on the understanding of pathophysiology rather than on fortuitous findings. ii) The development of biological diagnostic tests which, in combination with clinical assessments, will support efforts for an earlier identification of cases in order to rapidly initiate treatment and avoid chronicity. iii) The possibility of identifying environmental factors interacting with susceptibility genes that cause psychiatric disorders, paving the way to preventive interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Twin Birth Study: A multicentre randomised controlled trial comparing planned Caesarean section with planned vaginal birth for twins at 32-38 weeks gestation
Keywords-MotsClés: CAESAREAN SECTION; MULTICENTRE; PLANNED DELIVERY; RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TWIN PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: The number of twins being born is increasing because of the use of assisted reproductive techniques. Twins born at term have a higher risk of death or serious morbidity than singleton babies. Retrospective studies have suggested that caesarean section might be a safer method of delivery for twins, compared to attempting a vaginal birth. However, the only way to determine if this is really true is by carrying out a large prospective randomised controlled trial. Our study enrolled 2800 women at 32-38 weeks gestation (from over 120 centres worldwide) with a twin pregnancy in which the first twin is presenting head first. Women in the study are allocated at random to deliver either by caesarean section or to have a vaginal delivery. The outcome will be assessed for all babies and mothers. For babies, the main outcomes are death or serious morbidity in the first 28 days of life and how well they are developing at 2 years of age. For mothers, outcomes include difficulty with urinary or fecal/flatal incontinence at 3 months and 2 years, satisfaction with the method of delivery and quality of life. The results of this study will be used by obstetricians and other health care providers to counsel women with twin pregnancies about the risks and benefits of the different approaches to delivery, so that women can make an informed choice as to their planned method of delivery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms coordinating structural and functional synaptic plasticity: role of GluA2/N-cadherin dependent Rho signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: DENDRITIC SPINE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EXCITATORY SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION AND PLASTICITY; GENETICALLY ALTERED MICE; GLUTAMATE RECEPTORS; IMAGING; LEARNING AND MEMORY; MGLUR-LTD; PHARMACOLOGICAL PERTURBATION; RHO SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Regulated neuronal communications at the synapse, a highly specialized inter-neuronal structure, are critically involved in both brain development and functions. Synaptic deficits are responsible for many neurological and mental disorders, including autism, schizophrenia and drug addiction. Synaptic transmission is not static but instead undergoes experience-dependent modifications, and it is thought through these plastic processes that precise neuronal circuits are made and function properly. Long-lasting synaptic plasticity involves both structural and functional changes and it is imperative that these two processes are coordinated in order to achieve input-specific and persistent modifications. How such coordination is achieved remains a major unresolved and pressing question. The main objective of this application is to identify and dissect the molecular mechanisms required for linking structural and functional plasticity in the central synapse. We have discovered a novel signaling process mediated by glutamate receptor GluA2 and cell adhesion molecule N-cadherin which we propose to coordinate structural and functional remodeling. We will use a combination of genetic manipulations, pharmacological perturbations, functional recordings, biochemical assays, cellular imaging and behavioral analysis to investigate the mechanistic details of this signaling process. The results of this proposal will not only provide new insight into the fundamental mechanisms underlying normal brain function, but may also offer novel therapeutic strategies to alleviate and treat related brain diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Lymphatics as a novel target to treat glaucoma
Keywords-MotsClés: AQUEOUS HUMOUR OUTFLOW; EYE PHYSIOLOGY; GLAUCOMA; LYMPHATIC CIRCULATION; MOLECULAR AND CELLULAR IMAGING; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Glaucoma is a leading cause of blindness worldwide, projected to affect 80 million people by 2020. This devastating disease most often occurs when the eye is unable to clear fluid, leading to a build-up of pressure and, eventually, degeneration of the nerve connecting the eye to the brain. Most patients require multiple types of medications to lower pressure. Unfortunately, there are only a few options, and side effects are common. As a result, many patients require surgery, which itself comes with the risk of complication and blindness.  Thus, there is a real need for new glaucoma drugs - ones with new mechanisms and minimal side effects. Lymphatic vessels, which pump fluid out of tissues, were recently discovered in the eye by our laboratory. We propose to study the effects of lymphatics on fluid drainage from the eye, and to manipulate these vessels to lower pressure in the eye. This work has the potential to stimulate development of new glaucoma medications to prevent blindness.

ClasseRechercheFR: ENDOCRINOLOGIE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of TRPV channels in the thermal and osmotic control of vasopressin neurons
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HYPOTHALAMIC SLICES; OSMOSENSITIVITY; THERMOSENSITIVITY; TRP CHANNELS; VASOPRESSIN
Abstract-Résumé: Changes in blood osmolality (a measure of the body's salt and water content) can lead to severe neurological problems including (in proportion to the anomaly): headache, mental confusion, seizures, coma and death. Changes in osmolality (e.g. during heat stroke, dehydration or hyponatremia), common in the elderly and in hospitalized patients, are caused by asymmetric gains or losses of salt (mainly sodium) and water. The regulation of blood osmolality is achieved in part through changes in antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release from the posterior pituitary gland. The brain regulates this release in response to fluctuations in body temperature and changes in plasma osmolality. Increasing our understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms through which this control is achieved should eventually reveal new and more effective therapeutic  approaches to the treatment of fluid balance disorders. Dr. Bourque's project aims to identify the neurons responsible for the detection of changes in body temperature and osmolality within the hypothalamus using physiological, anatomical and molecular biological approaches. The experiments will define how these neurons and local glial cells interact with each other to control the electrical activity of ADH neurons. Our experiments specifically propose to define the role of a new family of proteins called TRPV channels, that may serve as molecular integrators of temperature and osmolality.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Brain melanocortin-4 receptor and sympathetically-mediated brown adipocyte thermogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; BROWN ADIPOSE TISSUE; CELL CULTURE; ENDOCANNABINOIDS; MELANOCORTIN-4 RECEPTOR; POSITION ELECTRON TOMOGRAPHY; RATS; SYMPATHETIC NERVOUS SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: The unrelenting rise in obesity in most developed countries over the last three decades, together with the rising awareness of the detrimental impact of this condition on health and health costs, have considerably stimulated the research related to the causes and complications of excess fat deposition. Obesity is defined as an excess of adipose tissue that results from an imbalance between energy intake and energy expenditure. The study of the complex brain controls exerted on the intake and expenditure determinants is a prerequisite to understand the pathophysiology of obesity in order to elaborate strategies to prevent and reverse excess fat deposition. Despite its crucial importance, the control of energy expenditure has received much less attention than that of food intake. However, the recent demonstration that brown adipose tissue (BAT) exists in substantial amount in adult humans has rejuvenated interest in the role of energy expenditure, specifically BAT thermogenesis, on energy balance. BAT is an organ with an enormous thermogenic capacity that could dissipate excess body energy (excess body fat). Heat production by BAT is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) through mechanisms and metabolic pathways, which have yet to be fully comprehended. The goal of the proposed research program is to study the brain-SNS-BAT axis in animal (brain circuitries behind SNS-mediated BAT thermogenesis). The proposed program will be conducted by two scientists who have a past history of collaboration and who are world-renowned experts in the neural and cellular adrenergic control of the BAT thermogenesis at various levels. The proposed approaches to achieve the objectives of the research program include functional neurobiological as well as cellular/molecular methodologies and sophisticated metabolic imaging technologies.

ClasseRechercheFR: TUMEURS; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Inner workings of the Ras/MAPK pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: DROSOPHILA GENETICS; MAPK MODULE; PROTEIN KINASE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The Ras protein is a central regulator of cell proliferation and differentiation. Over 30% of all cancers in humans are associated with activating mutations in Ras. Therefore, elucidating the molecular consequences of Ras action will likely provide novel targets for therapeutic intervention against cancer. Ras governs proliferation and differentiation primarily by sending signals through the so-called MAPK pathway, which is composed of several individual proteins. The mechanisms and proteins required for Ras/MAPK function have been remarkably well conserved during evolution. Therefore, we use Drosophila fruit flies as a simpler tool to identify and characterize novel key proteins required for this pathway. Our work has thus far provided key insights with respect to the human Ras/MAPK pathway, some of which are currently being explored for anticancer therapeutic applications. Several basic questions regarding the inner workings of the Ras/MAPK pathway are still left unanswered and we propose here to tackle the most pressing ones using fruit flies as well as mammalian cell culture systems as experimental paradigms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Brain-Based Measures of Alcohol Sensitivity in Early Adulthood
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL DEPENDENCE; ALCOHOL SENSITIVITY; CLINICAL RESEARCH; ENDOPHENOTYPE; FMRI; NEUROIMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Alcohol dependence is a common, costly disorder with a lifetime prevalence of 10-12% in Canada. Characterizing biological risk factors is critical for identifying high-risk groups and tailoring interventions. One promising approach is to identify endophenotypes that index genetic risk for the disorder and provide clues as to neurobiological liability factors.  Sensitivity to alcohol is a promising endophenotype that appears to predict future risk for alcohol dependence. However, prior research is characterized by two notable methodological limitations. First, most studies rely on participants' subjective responses to alcohol as the primary phenotype of interest. Second, most studies use oral alcohol administration, which inevitably yields high variability in blood alcohol profiles. These approaches can increase measurement error, reducing sensitivity to detect biological influences.  Little is known about neural correlates of alcohol sensitivity. The proposed research will integrate fMRI with novel alcohol administration methods to study neural correlates of alcohol sensitivity. In addition to having expertise in fMRI, our research team is the first in Canada to implement a novel intravenous ethanol infusion protocol (the alcohol clamp) for human studies. This project will integrate fMRI and alcohol clamp methods to allow precise control over brain ethanol exposure.  Young heavy drinkers (N=80) with and without a family history of alcohol dependence will complete alcohol and placebo fMRI sessions. Prospective data will be collected to determine whether neural correlates of alcohol sensitivity predict drinking outcomes. This research may inform future genetic studies and facilitate identification of neurobehavioural markers of alcohol dependence risk. Clarifying neural correlates of alcohol sensitivity may help to identify individuals at relatively greater risk for alcohol dependence, ultimately aiding in the refinement of diagnostic and treatment approaches.
