TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenomics of Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; MICROARRAYS; POST-MORTEM BRAIN; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, approximately 250,000 people suffer from schizophrenia. In an attempt to unlock the primary causes of this disease, over the last 30 years, research efforts focused on DNA sequence variation. However, a detailed re-analysis of the scientific literature on major psychiatric disease indicates that another group of factors may be of major importance in the origin of schizophrenia. These factors do not change the structure of DNA, but affect the way genes function, often reducing or enhancing the product a gene normally produces. This study of changes affecting gene expression is an emerging field of research known as "epigenetics", or "epigenomics" when investigation expands beyond the specific area of a gene and across many regions of the whole genome. Using cutting-edge microarray technology that allows millions of measurements to be taken in a single experiment, the DNA modification status of the entire non-repetitive genome in 400 DNA samples will be investigated. The samples are from people with schizophrenia and a comparison group of people without the disease. These experiments will complement traditional genetic research and, hopefully, the work will reveal why certain gene variants appear to increase schizophrenia risk in some people but not others. If this comprehensive epigenomic study substantially changes our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying schizophrenia, it could lead to new diagnostic methods and treatments for major psychiatric illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of M. tuberculosis persistence in the host macrophage
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTATION; APOPTOSIS; MTB ATTENUATION; MTB INTRACELLUAR SURVIVAL; MTB VIRULENCE FACTORS; MTB/HIV COINFECTION; NADPH OXIDASE; PHAGOSOME BIOGENESIS; TB PATHOGENESIS; TB VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: One third of the world's population is infected with tuberculosis (TB). Despite massive immunization campaigns a further 100 million new infections and 2 million deaths occur each year. Moreover, the last decade has seen the rise of drug- resistant TB, which has amplified this public health problem in many countries. Clearly, the current vaccine and drug regimens are inadequate. TB is notoriously difficult to treat because it has evolved to evade the killing mechanisms of the immune system. Typically, invading TB bacteria are engulfed by cells called macrophage, the "scavengers" of the immune system that patrol the body, ingesting and killing invading bacteria. But rather than being killed, TB bacteria takes up residence inside the macrophage. Somehow, it can attenuate multiple steps of our usual anti-bacterial defenses, allowing it to survive within the macrophage. Our goal is to investigate the underlying mechanisms in this process, in order to identify biologically-relevant targets for TB drug design. Our research shows that the TB bacteria produces and secretes key proteins into the host macrophage, which then interfere with intracellular killing mechanisms. In this proposal, we will investigate two such proteins - LpdC and Ndk - to determine how they allow TB bacteria to survive within the macrophage. We will use established cell and molecular biology techniques to address the following questions: 1) How do LpdC and Ndk protect the bacterium from macrophage killing mechanisms? 2) To what extent do LpdC and Ndk help the bacterium to persist in the lung? 3) If the genes that encode the proteins LpdC and/or Ndk are blocked (a "knock out"), does it transform a disease-causing mycobacteria into protective vaccines?

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a Perfusion MRI Technique to Investigate Longitudinal Effects of Chronic Pain on Brain Function
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERIAL SPIN LABELLING; COMPLEX REGIONAL PAIN SYNDROME; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEUROSCIENCE; PAIN; PERFUSION MRI
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain is a major health issue affecting 20% of Canadians. However, current pain treatments are often ineffective, creating enormous emotional and financial burdens on patients, caregivers and the healthcare system. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has had a tremendous impact on the understanding of how pain affects brain function; however, a major limitation with fMRI is that it is incapable of assessing ongoing pain, which is a central component of chronic pain. To address this limitation, our group has been investigating the use of an alternative fMRI method known as arterial spin labelling (ASL) that can be used to study ongoing pain due to its ability to measure cerebral blood flow (CBF) directly. The next, larger challenge, which is the objective of this proposal, is to develop an ASL approach capable of monitoring longitudinal changes in CBF. Such a technique would enable us to investigate the functional changes to the brain caused by chronic pain and, ultimately, could help in the development of more effective treatments that target specific dysfunctional brain networks.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cerebrovascular pathophysiology in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; ANIMAL IMAGING; CEREBROVASCULAR PATHOLOGY; MRI; QUANTITATIVE IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Abnormal function of the blood vessels in the brain has been identified as a potential factor in the development and/or progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD).  Our group has previously identified reduced blood flow in mouse models of AD using specialized magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques.  This technique primarily examined blood flow in the smaller brain vessels, called capillaries.  In this proposed project, we seek to evaluate the function of larger vessels, called arteries and arterioles.  These larger vessels are known to accumulate abnormal amounts of a protein, called beta-amyloid, in AD patients and in mouse models of AD.  This approach may provide an early indicator of the risk for the development and progression of AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inuit Traditional Knowledge for Adapting to the Health Effects of Climate Change (IK-ADAPT)
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTATION; CLIMATE CHANGE; CLIMATE POLICY; COMMUNITY BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; INDIGENOUS PEOPLES & CLIMATE CHANGE; INUIT HEALTH & WELL-BEING; INUIT TRADITIONAL KNOWLEDGE; NEGLECTED TOPICS IN HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Climate change has been identified as the biggest threat to public health this century, and Inuit are one of the most at-risk populations. Communities and northern health systems will have to adapt. The research team assembled here has been working with Inuit communities and policy makers for over a decade, examining what climate change means for health. This has recently included the identification and prioritization of potential adaptation interventions. Here we plan to take the next step and develop, implement, and evaluate pilot interventions in case study communities. Specifically, the project will examine how to document, preserve, and promote Inuit traditional knowledge (IK) for adapting to the health effects of climate change. Previous research has indicated the importance of IK for managing the health effects of climate change, yet there is widespread concern that this knowledge is being lost as elders pass away.  The project will begin by identifying and characterizing how IK can help enhance health in-light of a rapidly changing climate. Working with 6 communities, the research will document IK on health prevention, preparedness, and promotion, with attention directed to maintaining physical, mental, and social well-being in-light of a rapidly changing climate. Secondly, we will explore ways to preserve, promote, and make accessible this knowledge for adaptation to climate change. Potential tools and platforms for doing this will be identified in collaboration with communities and may involve web-based knowledge banks, radio dramas, social media, and digital storytelling. Knowledge promotion interventions will be implemented and promoted and will be evaluated using a number of methods including before and after surveys, and focus groups and interviews to explore the success of messaging. The project will finish by examining the extent to which promotion of traditional approaches could form part of territorial and federal adaptation programming.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a Diabetes Prevention Intervention: Identifying and Targeting Contextually-Relevant Stressors
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; DIABETES ETIOLOGY; DIABETES PREVENTION; DIABETES RISK FACTORS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; FIRST NATIONS PEOPLE; INTERVENTION PLANNING; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: The prevalence of diabetes is higher among Canadian First Nations populations compared to the general population. This disparity began to be noted in the 1980s.  Since that time the problem has worsened; diabetes prevalence has increased, and the condition develops at a younger age and is associated with a higher prevalence of complications compared to the general population. Risk factors for diabetes include family history, unhealthy diet, inactivity, and obesity.  Recent research is pointing to the role of chronic stress in the development of diabetes.   Large diabetes prevention interventions have demonstrated that among those at highest risk the progression to diabetes can be slowed or reduced with lifestyle modifications, specifically diet and exercise. Given that chronic stress is emerging as an independent risk factor for diabetes, stress reduction may help in diabetes prevention.  Therefore, the purpose of this research is to expand our knowledge on the role of stress in the development of diabetes, and to identify new points for intervention aimed at stress reduction. This research will be the first in Canada to explore the relationship between stress and diabetes using community-derived measures of stress and biological markers of chronic stress.  The findings will inform a novel and innovative approach to diabetes prevention and in the future will be transferrable to other Canadian First Nations communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: New directions for the use of genetic information by Aboriginal communities: Lessons learned from Québec First Nations with specific monogenic diseases.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARRIER SCREENING; CULTURAL ISSUES; FIRST NATIONS; GENETIC COUNSELING; GENETIC INFORMATION; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; NEEDS ASSESSMENT; PROGRAM EVALUATION; RECESSIVE DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: We propose to study how First Nations communities in Quebec perceive and use genetic information about 3 lethal childhood autosomal recessive diseases. In the Cree population of Quebec near James Bay, two severe neurodegenerative autosomal recessive diseases are found: cree encephalitis (CE) and cree leukoencephalopathy (CLE). The carrier frequency of Cree leukoencephalopathy was estimated at 1/10 and that of Cree encephalitis at 1/30 in at-risk communities, for an estimated combined disease incidence of 2.8 cases per 1000 live births. Both diseases are usually diagnosed in the first year of life and affected children usually die in infancy. A carrier screening program is in place in at-risk communities thanks to the combined efforts of the Eeyou Awash Foundation, a support group for families of affected children, and the Cree Health Board. North American Indian cirrhosis (NAIC) is a severe liver disease found in First Nations communities of southwest Quebec. Affected children need liver transplant in childhood. For NAIC, the carrier rate is estimated to be 9% in at-risk communities, for a disease incidence of about 2 per 1000 live births. No carrier screening program is in place for this condition.  We propose to evaluate the impacts of the CE/CLE carrier screening program, both in terms of number of carriers identified and in terms of population satisfaction with this program. In parallel, we will study the attitudes of southwest Quebec at-risk communities about a potential carrier screening for NAIC and their needs if such a program was developed. We will use the lessons learned from the CE/CLE experience to inform this needs assessment process in communities at risk for NAIC.  Based on this study, we plan to develop a framework to guide the future development of educational interventions and genetic services for use by First Nations communities, researchers, and health care providers.

Abstract-Résumé: This 3 year research project aims to investigate the impact of the Active Circle initiative- a novel, youth driven approach to the development and delivery of sport, physical activity, and recreation programs in Aboriginal communities across Canada. The main objective of this project is to assess the impact of this community development approach to physical activity, sport, and recreation as a strategy for promoting positive youth development, youth holistic health, and community capacity. We will use mixed methods from indigenous and western research traditions to investigate community-level and individual-level impacts in 12 communities that partner with the Active Circle initiative.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing food choices and practices in the perinatal period for immigrant and new Canadian women.
Keywords-MotsClés: CULTURAL COMPETENCY; ETHNOCULTURAL HEALTH PRACTICES; FOCUSED ETHNOGRAPHY; FOOD CHOICES; HEALTH SERVICES; IMMIGRANT HEALTH; MATERNITY; PERINATAL; POSTCOLONIAL THEORY
Abstract-Résumé: Immigrant women may be regarded as vulnerable in part because they face challenges in accessing and receiving equitable health care  which suits their ethnocultural backgrounds and spoken languages. Moreover, many of their maternal health and birth outcomes are influenced by their ethnic food choices. Research is needed to better understand ethnocultural food choices and practices and to develop and evaluate resources for improving cultural competency of maternity care. In this research study we will ask: How do health beliefs/ practices of immigrant women affect their food choices and practices during the perinatal period? How can current perinatal nutrition recommendations be tailored and delivered as pictorial educational resources to enhance culturally competent perinatal care? Immigrant women in each of three study locations (Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Ottawa), who are pregnant or who have recently delivered their babies, will be invited to participate. They will be asked and trained to take pictures of the foods they consume for a three day period and those that they see as being healthy for maternity. Next, they will be interviewed in relation to these choices and other factors effecting their food choices and practices. With the results from these interviews and subsequent consultations with health care professionals and immigrant support agency workers, we will develop resources which incorporate the women's perspectives into current Canadian nutrition recommendations. A sample of health care professionals and immigrant women will then use the resources and then participate in focus groups to discuss and evaluate them. Wide dissemination of our findings throughout the health professional, public health, and obstetrical communities using multiple formats and media will have great potential to positively affect immigrant maternal and childhood health and well-being.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of adult neurogenesis in learning and memory
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT NEUROGENESIS; AGING; BRAIN PLASTICITY; HIPPOCAMPUS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; LEARNING AND MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Concomitant with aging, the elderly often find they are more easily distracted by multiple stimuli and increasingly unable to memorize events with sufficient context that in their youth would have made up for these distractions. Context is beneficial for memory and interference is detrimental. For example, the reader may experience memory interference when reading about our research and confuse it with another study that deals with memory decline in old age. However, upon re-reading our proposal and relating it to the concept of adult neurogenesis, the reader will realize that our work is distinct. We propose that such decline in memory is due to decreased production of new neurons in the aging brain. New neurons are generated within the hippocampus, the brain region crucial for learning and memory, and within the olfactory bulb, responsible for sense of smell. Evidence suggests a crucial role of neurogenesis in normal function of the adult brain, but the ability to produce new neurons declines drastically with age. Depletion of new neurons by a variety of experimental research techniques causes behavioural deficits consistent with impaired brain function. By identifying functional roles for new neurons, the goal of this research is to explain behavioural symptoms. We will inhibit the formation of new neurons in young animals by application of radiation and measure the resultant loss of function to determine the role of these neurons in certain types of learning and memory. We then will increase generation of new neurons by increasing physical activity and by drug treatment. If the defined types of learning and memory require new neurons, then our treatment should enhance those functions.  Our study will produce results that are important for better understanding of the normal function of the brain and also for its decline with age. Our work will establish a basis for development of therapy by which to improve certain types of learning and memory.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving cardiovascular health for Canadians living with spinal cord injury: effects of exercise and targeted education
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD PRESSURE REGULATION; CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; CLINICAL TRIALS; EXERCISE INTERVENTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; RODENT MODELS; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Annually, over 1000 Canadians sustain a traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) and unwittingly join more than 41,000 Canadians living with this chronic and debilitating injury. The estimated annual costs of care in Canada exceed $1.5 billion. Recent data reveal that people with SCI are developing chronic diseases at younger ages and at greater rates than the able-bodied population. This alarming trend appears to be caused by inactivity-related illnesses, particularly cardiovascular(CV)disease, which is the main cause of death and disease in people with SCI.   Exercise training has the potential to improve strength, performance, and well-being among people with SCI. However, we have little information on the CV effects of training in people with SCI. People with SCI respond differently to exercise. There are also important differences in CV disease between men and women: we do not yet know if this is true for people with SCI, or if men and women with SCI will need to approach exercise differently to improve CV health. This is information that we urgently need to develop exercise programs that will be effective in improving CV health for Canadians living with SCI. The goal of this proposal is to improve CV health for people with chronic SCI through optimized exercise and targeted education. This project gathers a diverse team of 13 prestigious scientists working at 6 Canadian universities. We will use both animal models of SCI and training in people with SCI to examine the effects of exercise on CV risk. We will also determine whether educating health care providers on specific CV problems associated with SCI will help to reduce the financial burden of care, and improve treatment, of people with SCI.   By providing important information on exercise training, and targeted education to clinicians, this project will reduce chronic disease and improve CV health for Canadians living with chronic SCI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring and improving the quality of ambulatory care for people with cardiovascular risk factors and/or chronic cardiovascular diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES; CHRONIC DISEASES; HOSPITAL ADMISSIONS/READMISSIONS; PHYSICIAN NETWORKS; REPORT CARDS; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular risk factors (smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, etc.) and chronic conditions (angina, heart failure, stroke) are an increasing burden to many Canadians and the health care system. Despite advances in prevention and treatment, a wide gap exists between the care people with these risk factors and/or chronic diseases receive and what optimally should be provided. Many care gaps exist including smokers not receiving cessation counselling, people with blood pressure levels and/or cholesterol levels that are too high, resulting in many preventable heart attacks, cases of heart failure and strokes. A major contributor to these care gaps is the fragmented nature of the health care system. Family doctors (providing most of the preventive and chronic care) and specialist physicians, e.g., cardiologists/neurologists (providing most of the acute hospital care) often operate in separate silos with limited care coordination or information sharing.     A new system of chronic disease care is needed where family doctors and specialists work more closely together with patients to provide optimal care. Our team of 22 leading researchers will conduct 3 studies to improve the outpatient care provided to patients with cardiovascular risk factors and/or chronic conditions. We will develop indicators of high-quality outpatient care measurable using 20 large, population-based databases in Ontario. We will study how differences in how care is provided influence differences in the rates of new cardiovascular events in 73 newly identified multispecialty Ontario physician networks (made up of family doctors and specialists). Results will be released in novel public report cards and academic papers, describing how outpatient cardiac and stroke care is delivered across different regions and physician networks in Ontario. This initiative will stimulate health system changes and quality improvement activities resulting in better patient outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Utilizing HIV/AIDS infrastructure as a gateway to chronic care of hypertension in Africa
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; AFRICA; HIV/AIDS; HYPERTENSION; PREVENTION; RETENTION; SUPPLY-CHAIN
Abstract-Résumé: There is insufficient infrastructure in Africa to allow for a rapid of expansion of hypertension awareness, screening and treatment. However, using the infrastructure and lessons learned from the HIV/AIDS epidemic represents an important opportunity to strengthen local health systems by focusing on screening, supply chain management, and treatment and retention in care. Our Team Grant involves country leaders in hypertension from South Africa, Uganda and Rwanda, as well as HIV/AIDS leaders from these countries to create a network of excellence at strengthening the response to both communicable and non-communicable diseases. Our proposed studies involve screening campaigns, modeling the health system requirements of a successful supply-chain, a factorial randomized evaluation of interventions to promote adherence to drugs and retention in care, all in a locally relevant manner that can be scaled up at a sustainable country level. Finally, we aim to build capacity by providing accredited education in supply-chain management.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing an innovative strategy for hypertension detection, treatment and control in two middle income countries (Hypertension Outcomes Prevention and Evaluation: HOPE-4)
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS; CVD PREVENTION; HEALTH SYSTEMS; HYPERTENSION; LOW AND MIDDLE INCOME COUNTRIES
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension affects one billion people and is the commonest cause of death globally. Despite clear evidence of the benefits of BP lowering for over 2 decades, its detection, treatment and control are poor in most countries resulting in a large number of avoidable deaths, heart attacks and strokes. We therefore need a fundamentally new approach to tackling this problem. We therefore propose to develop a model programme to control hypertension in Colombia and Malaysia that involves a contextually relevant multipronged intervention strategy that involves multiple sectors (health, professional societies, governments, regulators, business and legal) that overcomes the barriers, test the effectiveness and costs of an integrated and innovative model pilot programme,and then evaluate it. If successful, the programme can be scaled up and form the basis of national efforts to control hypertension and prevent deaths, heart attacks and strokes in several countries around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: DREAM-GLOBAL: Diagnosing hypeRtension - Engaging Action and Management in Getting LOwer Bp in Aboriginal and LMIC - A Research Proposal
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL COMMUNITIES; CELL PHONES; CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; COMMUNITY INTERVENTION; HEALTH POLICY; HYPERTENSION; INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY; LMIC - TANZANIA; RANDOMIZED TRIAL; SODIUM REDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease and stroke are the number one killers world-wide. When someone has hypertension, the constantly elevated blood pressure damages their blood vessels and the organs that they supply blood to.  This causes stroke, heart attack, heart failure, kidney failure and dementia. Finding and lowering high blood pressure to normal with lifestyle changes and if necessary medications, lowers the risk of these outcomes.  Canada has high rates of blood pressure control compared to other countries in the world, due in large part to the successful dissemination of hypertension guidelines. However remote and disadvantaged communities have not been as successful and need additional measures to help achieve the same level of blood pressure control as the rest of the country. The DREAM-GLOBAL team has extensive experience with project management and cell phone technology as well as working with Canada's Aboriginal Communities and a large community in Tanzania. The DREAM-GLOBAL project will integrate innovations in technology with the implementation of guidelines based blood pressure control and through partnerships with experts in government and industry overcome barriers to lowering blood pressure in Canada's Aboriginal Communities, and in a community in Tanzania. We will develop and test tools that will close the circle of care around people with hypertension by bringing measurement data to the medical record and health care provider and also sending useful medical feedback to the person with hypertension via secure data servers and routine SMS messaging on cell phones. We will test the effectiveness of this system for diagnosing and also for managing hypertension. To begin the process of preventing hypertension we will explore with Aboriginal Communities how to create policies to reduce the sodium content in their food. We have a track record of success in managing hypertension and believe that DREAM-GLOBAL can also become a platform for managing other chronic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Facial Emotion Recognition and Temporal Lobe Abnormalities Associated with the Genetic Vulnerability for Schizophrenia: A Structural and Functional Neuroimaging Family Study
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; COMMUNITY FUNCTIONING; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; EMOTION RECOGNITION; GREY MATTER; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SOCIAL COGNITION; TEMPORAL LOBE; WHITE MATTER
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a severe disorder affecting approximately 340,000 Canadians - about 1% of the population. In 2004, the healthcare and productivity lost cost of schizophrenia in Canada was estimated at $7 billion. Deficits in interacting with the social world are some of the most debilitating aspects of the disorder. Specifically, problems in recognizing emotions on faces contribute to difficulties with many kinds of interpersonal interactions and worsen day-to-day functioning in schizophrenia. Currently, however, there is a lack of information on the biological and genetic underpinnings of these impairments. Therefore, in this project we will use a family study design to investigate deficits in recognizing emotions in people with schizophrenia and their relatives. This study will increase our understanding of brain structure (amount of grey matter), structural connectivity between brain regions (white matter tractography), and functioning (brain activity) associated with temporal lobe regions. Temporal lobe regions are strongly associated with recognition of emotional faces. This study will also investigate the relationship between brain structure and activity and day-to-day functioning in individuals with schizophrenia. We will use magnetic resonance imaging to examine 50 people with schizophrenia, 50 of their siblings, and 50 healthy comparison subjects. Studying healthy family members eliminates the problems of controlling for medication exposure and other illness factors that are often present in studies of schizophrenia. This design makes it likely that deficits that are identified in both affected and unaffected family members are markers of biological changes that are risk factors for schizophrenia. Isolating the biological and genetic basis of problematic social interactions in people with schizophrenia will ultimately aid in developing new treatments to facilitate improved day-to-day functioning.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and characterization of novel substrates of the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1).
Keywords-MotsClés: 4E-BPS; CANCER; EIF4E; METABOLISM; MRNA TRANSLATION; MTOR; S6 KINASES
Abstract-Résumé: The activity of the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) is frequently dysregulated in human diseases characterized by abnormal metabolism and proliferation such as diabetes, cancer and heart disease. Accordingly, compounds modulating the activity of mTORC1 hold great promise for treatments of these diseases. In recent years several of the factors, which mediate the activity of mTORC1 on cellular processes have been uncovered. Notwithstanding these recent advances in the understanding of the mTORC1 pathway, many of the cellular effects of mTORC1 cannot be accounted for by the actions of its known substrates. Thus, to better apprehend the intricate molecular mechanisms underlying the actions of mTORC1, in this proposal we will set out to uncover unknown substrates of mTORC1. To achieve this we will deploy a strategy in which the standard biochemistry and molecular biology techniques will be combined with mass spectrometry. We will further assess how these factors mediate the effects of mTORC1 signaling in normal versus cancer cells using the standard cell and molecular biology and biochemistry techniques. These findings should improve our knowledge of how are mTORC1 signals relayed to cellular processes, which in long-term should open new therapeutic avenues to curb dysregulated mTORC1 signaling in cancer and other human diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Virtual Ward to Reduce Readmissions after Hospital Discharge
Keywords-MotsClés: AVOIDABLE HOSPITALIZATIONS; GENERAL INTERNAL MEDICINE; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; INTERDISCIPLINARY TEAMS; PATIENT-ORIENTED RESEARCH; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS; READMISSIONS
Abstract-Résumé: My colleagues and I have developed and are evaluating a Virtual Ward, a new model of care that attempts to combine the best elements of hospital and community-based care. Although patients being cared for in a Virtual Ward reside at home, they are cared for by a hospital-like interdisciplinary team that collaborates with their primary care provider. Our Virtual Ward cares for patients after they have been discharged from hospital, a time when communication breakdowns and adverse events are especially common. Our team meets daily and provides round-the-clock availability at a single telephone number. Each member of our Virtual Ward team, including the physician, can provide care wherever it is felt to be most appropriate, including the patient's home.   We are conducting a randomized controlled trial comparing our Virtual Ward with usual care. Most researchers would argue that randomized controlled trials are the fairest way to test new health care interventions. We are trying to determine whether patients who are admitted to our Virtual Ward have better health outcomes than patients who are cared for in the usual manner. Over the next 5 years, I will also be leading several additional research projects designed to reduce avoidable hospitalizations.   The MOHLTC and Toronto Central Local Health Integration Network have provided more than $2 million over 3 years to support the operating costs of the Virtual Ward. Both organizations, along with senior administrators from each of the participating hospitals and the Toronto Central Community Care Access Centre are represented on our project's steering committee. These substantial commitments illustrate the relevance of my research program to decision makers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Addressing the 'Knowledge Problem' in Medical Education
Keywords-MotsClés: CURRICULUM; LEGITIMATE KNOWLEDGE; MEDICAL EDUCATION; QUALITATIVE METHODS; SOCIAL SCIENCE METHODS; SOCIAL SCIENCES/HUMANITIES KNOWLEDGE
Abstract-Résumé: The standard education that medical students and residents receive in medical school is focussed almost entirely on biomedical science. While this information is crucial, over the past three decades Canada has led the way in identifying (with the help of patients and their families as well as health professionals) many non-scientific areas  in which physicians need to be competent in order to practice effectively and meet the health needs of Canadians. These non-scientific areas include communicating effectively with patients, working well with other health professionals, and advocating for patients' needs. In addition to biomedical knowledge, physicians need to be taught the kinds of knowledge that will appropriately underpin their abilities to be competent in these non-biomedical domains. Currently much of that appropriate knowledge comes from disciplines outside of biomedical science including those from the social sciences and humanities.  Our study will develop a framework to identify the different kinds of knowledge that need to be taught in medical schools to support the education of physicians who can then be competent in these important non-scientific domains We will compare this framework with the kinds of knowledge currently taught in Canadian medical schools. We will present this information in practical ways that will have a real impact on the education of physicians in the many areas in which Canadians need them to be competent, and thus will ultimately improve the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the functions of the Bub1 and BubR1 kinases during mitosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMOSOME CONGRESSION; HIGH RESOLUTION MICROSCOPY; MITOTIC KINASES; PEPTIDE ARRAYS; PHOSPHOPROTEOMICS; SPINDLE CHECKPOINT; VIDEO-MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Aneuploidy is a genetic state defined by an abnormal number of chromosomes. It is caused by aberant cell division and is the most common genetic affliction in man. It is the primary cause of miscarriage; approximately 30% of spontaneous abortions exhibiting aneuploidy.  Down Syndrome, which is caused by aneuploidy of chromosome 21 (3 instead of 2 copies) is the most common aneuploidy found in newborns affecting a staggering 1/800-1/1000 births. In cancers, aneuploidy is the most common genetic trait. Although the detrimental effects of aneuploidy to human health have been long recognized, the molecular mechanisms that result in aneuploidy remain poorly understood. Aneuploidy is prevented by cell cycle checkpoints that detect errors in, and halt cell division processes until these errors are corrected. One such mechanism, known as the SAC or spindle Assembly Checkpoint functions during cell division to ensure equal segregation of chromosomes, thus preventing aneuploidy. This project aims to understand the regulation of a small but essential group of enzymes that regulate the chromosome division process, and thus play a pivotal role in preventing cancer and other chromosome based diseases. In particular, the catalytic function of these enzymes is poorly understood, and how they are regulated during the different stages of cell division remains unclear. Importantly, misregulation of this activity is a known cause of chromosome segregation errors and thus aneuploidy. Determining how these enzymes regulate targets and are themselves regulated by the fundamental biological process of cell division is critical for understanding the basis of the wide range of chromosome-based genetic diseases. Morover, there has been increasing interest recently in targetting these enzymes as a means of therapeutic intervention, and the work proposed here will facilitate the discovery of novel targets for aneuploidy based diseases, as well as the generation of novel therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Moral Emotions in Children's Externalizing Behaviour: A Mixed-Method Study
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTONOMIC RESPONSE; CHILDREN; EXTERNALIZING BEHAVIOR; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MIXED-METHODS STUDY; MORAL EMOTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Antisocial behaviour problems, such as aggression against people and property or bullying, are widespread among children and adolescents. The long-term outcomes of antisocial behaviour pose major social and health burdens on the individuals, their families, and the Canadian society. Thus, understanding the underlying developmental risk and protective factors for antisocial behaviour is of critical significance. Children's emotional development may serve as crucial protective factor against antisocial behaviour. Previous research has shown that empathy may inhibit antisocial outcomes. However, no research has investigated the differential role of emotions, such as pride or rage, and how these relate to children's antisocial behaviour. The proposed research will investigate the role of guilt, empathy, pride, and rage in children's antisocial behaviour. We hypothesize that these emotions may have divergent effects, with high levels of guilt and empathy preventing antisocial behaviour, while exaggerated levels of pride and rage increasing antisocial behaviour. This research will examine if children with elevated levels of antisocial behaviour differ in their emotional and physiological responses to conflicts about rules and obligations, compared to normally developed children.  Our emphasis on guilt, empathy, pride, and rage is innovative; despite longstanding theorizing that the development of these emotions lies at the core of antisocial symptoms, there is far too little empirical proof. Given the recognition that these emotions play an influential role in how children resolve conflicts with peers, the proposed research will provide timely knowledge on the role of emotional development processes in antisocial behaviour. This knowledge is likely to contribute to the development of new, early intervention strategies (e.g., targeting emotions and awareness of physiological arousal) for reducing antisocial behaviour in children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Teens Taking Charge: An Internet-based Self-management Program for Adolescents with Arthritis: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; E-HEALTH; INTERNET INTERVENTION; JUVENILE IDIOPATHIC ARTHRITIS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SELF-MANAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is a chronic childhood illness that negatively impacts quality of life.  While activities to manage JIA are shared by the child and family, adolescents are expected to assume a greater role in disease management.  Better management early on could help prevent worsening of the disease and symptoms.  Therefore, it is important to develop programs to make it easier for adolescents to manage their disease.  A trial design will be used to determine whether a web-based home management program is effective in reducing symptoms and improving quality of life in adolescents with arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of Microtubule Architecture by Doublecortin
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICS; CORTEX; DOUBLECORTIN; LISSENCEPHALY; MICROTUBULUE; NEURON; NUCLEATION; SINGLE MOLECULE
Abstract-Résumé: The outermost layer of the brain, just below the skull, is the cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex is the seat of our intellect, and in healthy people it has many deep folds. In unfortunate cases, however, a genetic mutation causes a loss of these folds, a disease known as "smooth brain," or lissencephaly. The mutations occur in a protein called doublecortin (DCX). DCX works inside of brain cells, or neurons, to control where neurons are located in the brain and how neurons connect to one another. In humans with DCX mutations, neurons are not located properly in the brain and do not make correct connections, causing mental retardation and epilepsy. We know that DCX works by controlling the shape of the "cytoskeleton," a scaffolding system inside of cells that give them structure, much like the scaffolds used at construction sites. The goal of this grant is to understand precisely how DCX controls the shape of the cytoskeleton and to explain why DCX mutations cause disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional studies of the PIKK family of protein kinases
Keywords-MotsClés: CRYO-EM; GUANINE NUCLEOTIDE EXCHANGE FACTORS; PHOSPHORYLATION AND KINASES; PIKK KINASES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SINGLE-PARTICLE ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; TOR SIGNALING; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; YEAST MODEL SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: TOR is a key signaling protein that regulates cell growth in the body. Abnormal activation of TOR is associated with the uncontrolled cell growth and proliferation observed in many cancerous tumors. TOR is thus increasingly recognized as a compelling target for designing new cancer drugs. In the cell, TOR functions as part of two larger sized protein complexes. However, the molecular mechanisms through which the two TOR complexes coordinate cell growth are poorly defined. I have used a cutting-edge imaging technique called single-particle electron microscopy (EM) to characterize, for the first time, the intricate structural features and internal organization of one of the two TOR complexes. Building on this pioneering study, I propose to apply a multidisciplinary approach, integrating single-particle EM and other biochemical and molecular biology approaches, to determine the differences in overall structure and molecular organization between the two TOR complexes, and to further define their mechanisms of action and regulation. A comprehensive understanding of the molecular function of the two TOR complexes will provide critical insights into the fundamental basis of cell growth regulation and how cancer arises from problems in this process. This work will pave the way for the development of novel cancer treatment that target the TOR complexes, and thereby improve the health outcomes and survival rates of patients inflicted by cancer, a devastating disease that affects over 40% of the Canadian population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring and Modeling Disability, Comorbidities and Rehabilitation among People Living with HIV in Canada: The HIV Health and Rehabilitation Survey
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; DISABILITY; HIV/AIDS; REHABILITATION; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING; SURVEY INSTRUMENT; SURVEY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, HIV is often considered a chronic disease. As people are living longer they may experience a variety of health-related challenges associated with HIV, comorbidities and side effects of treatment. These challenges may be termed disability including symptoms and impairments, difficulties with day-to-day activities, challenges to social inclusion, and uncertainty about health status, that can fluctuate on a daily basis or over the entire life course with HIV. Rehabilitation services, ranging from physical therapy and occupational therapy, to social supports from community-based organizations such as income and food programs and housing support may help to reduce disability for people living with HIV (PHAs). While researchers have explored disability prevalence and rehabilitation service provision in the HIV context, these studies were either conducted at the provincial level, did not incorporate the PHA perspective, or occurred prior to the increasing onset of HIV-related comorbidities.  The purpose of this study is to establish a profile of disability experienced by PHAs in Canada and determine how personal and environmental factors such as comorbidities and related rehabilitation services influence the disability experience. We will conduct the HIV Health and Rehabilitation Survey, a self-administered Internet-based questionnaire with PHAs across Canada. We will use a combination of statistical techniques to document the profile of disability and determine how personal factors (e.g. comorbidities, age, gender) and environmental factors (e.g. rehabilitation, social support, stigma) might exacerbate or alleviate disability experienced by PHAs. This research is critical to building our understanding of the types of disability that PHAs in Canada face, how contextual factors influence the disability experience, and the types of services, strategies and interventions PHAs use to address their health challenges living with HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of invariant Natural Killer T cell development and function
Keywords-MotsClés: CD1D; IMMUNOMODULATION; LIPID ANTIGENS; NATURAL KILLER T CELLS; NKT CELL DEVELOPMENT; OP9-DL1 SYSTEM; TCR RETROGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells are lymphocytes that respond to lipid antigens presented by a molecule named CD1d. Activated iNKT cells rapidly produce large amounts of various soluble mediators that influence ensuing immune responses. Consistent with this, iNKT cells have protective or deleterious functions during the immune responses associated with cancer, inflammation, autoimmunity and infection. Understanding the mechanisms controlling the activation and functional plasticity of these cells is critical and constitutes a major challenge. iNKT cells express particular T cell receptors (TCRs) that are able to recognize a variety of host- (self) as well as microbe-derived lipids presented by CD1d. Self-lipid recognition is important for the development and activation of these cells, although the relevant CD1d-restricted self-lipids remain poorly defined. Recent work, including from our group, demonstrated that iNKT TCRs recognize CD1d-lipid complexes in a "one-size-fits-all" strategy. Within this conserved strategy, the strength of CD1d-lipid-TCR is seemingly modulated the lipid involved, as well as the TCR composition. Whether consequential affinities of CD1d-lipid-TCR interactions ultimately translate into distinct functional responses is unknown.  Here, we propose to address these questions that are a direct extension of our previous findings. Our specific goals are to identify CD1d-restricted self-lipids and define their regulation of expression in health and disease, as well as their role in iNKT cell development and responses. We will also investigate whether the affinity of CD1d-lipid-TCR interactions translates into differential biological responses from these cells. The results from the proposed studies will shed light on crucial aspects of iNKT cell biology, and will ultimately help the rational design of novel immunotherapies that target iNKT cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic dissection of taste circuits and feeding behaviour in Drosophila
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL GENETICS; CHEMOSENSATION; DROSOPHILA; IMAGING; INGESTIVE BEHAVIOUR; MODEL SYSTEM; NEURAL CIRCUITS; NEUROANATOMY; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; TASTE/GUSTATION
Abstract-Résumé: The sense of taste plays a critical role in determining what animals decide to eat. For example, sweet taste guides us towards calorie-rich sources of carbohydrates and bitter taste steers us away from potential toxins. While this drive for calories evolved as an effective survival strategy, it has created an increasing problem for modern human populations - obesity. Understanding the mechanisms by which the brain processes taste information and controls feeding behaviour is an important step in developing strategies to control food intake and prevent obesity and its associated diseases. These mechanisms are not understood in any animal. Our work uses the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a well established and powerful genetic model system, to investigate the neural pathways controlling taste perception and feeding behaviour. We use the fly because the size of its brain is more manageable (about 1 million times fewer neurons than ours), and because decades of research have established unparalleled genetic tools for investigating the neurons and genes that control behaviour. Moreover, flies and humans share remarkable similarities in how they process information from their environment, suggesting that what we learn in flies will help us understand our own brains. The studies proposed here will provide insight into the complex question of how neurons and genes interact in the fly brain to guide their decisions on what - and how much - to eat. In the long-term, we would like to understand whether similar systems operate in mammals, and how they contribute to food consumption and obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the Phosphoinositides and Moesin on the Actin/Microtubule crosstalk during cell division.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN; CELL DIVISION; DROSOPHILA; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; MICROSCOPY; MICROTUBULE
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of this project is to understand the molecular basis underlying how cell division is deregulated in cancer cells. This study will be performed using drosophila fly as a model using modern genetic and cell biology tools to identify and characterize novel genes involved in the control of cell division. In the last past years, Drosophila melanogaster has proven to be an excellent model organism to study such aspects of cell biology. Since most of the molecular functions are conserved throughout evolution, this work will provide new avenues to study the process of cell division across species. Deregulation of cell division being one of the major causes leading to cancer and metastasis, this work will enable a better understanding on the molecular pathways that prevent this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Robotic assisted transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ASSISTIVE DEVICE; BIOROBOTICS; BRAIN INJURY; ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS; REHABILITATION; STROKE; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION; WEARABLE MECHATRONIC SYSTEMS
Abstract-Résumé: During the acute stage after stroke, 80% of individuals suffer from hemiparesis, while in the long-term more than 40% have chronically impaired arm function. Many have attempted to define neural mechanisms for stroke recovery in the hope that understanding these processes will improve rehabilitation interventions and enhance function. Though not insignificant, the main complaint of individuals with stroke is poor hand and wrist function, and integration of movements across all the joints of the upper extremity (UE). Recent efforts have focused on the possibility of promoting recovery from stroke using emerging brain stimulation technologies, which can facilitate cortical excitability, paired with skilled motor practice. On the other hand, the development of robotic devices that can assist with functional movements and direct movement towards more normal patterns is one new approach, which demonstrated to reduce rehabilitation costs while aiding recovery after stroke. Based on this evidence, the applicants propose to develop a novel method that combines cutting edge brain stimulation and rehabilitation robotics to facilitate active UE movements, improve joint range of motion, and promote functional recovery. Recovery will be indexed by changes in muscle contraction and activity, brain plasticity as indexed with TMS paired-pulse mapping, and functional outcome measures of motor recovery. Taken together the proposed research will focus on expanding our understanding of how to optimally stimulate neural plasticity and facilitate UE motor recovery after stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of a brief motivational intervention on adherence behavior in asthmatics: A randomized controlled trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; ASTHMA; MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SELF-EFFICACY
Abstract-Résumé: The high personal and financial costs of asthma appear to be related to poor asthma control. The availability of effective treatments suggests that asthma can be well controlled in most patients, though most (53-58%) Canadians remain poorly controlled. Achieving optimal asthma control relies upon several behavioral factors, particularly daily taking one's medication as prescribed. However, research suggests adherence rates are as low as 32% in patients with asthma. Participation in education programs has increased patient knowledge about the importance of medication adherence, but recent reviews indicate that these programs have not significantly changed medication taking behavior. The purpose of this study is to assess the impact of a brief intervention that uses motivational interviewing (MI) techniques, on asthma medication adherence in a sample of adult asthmatics. A total of 182 patients will be recruited, half of which will receive the intervention, and half of which will not. The primary outcome measure will be adherence to inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), a medication which must be taken daily to be effective. This will be measured at 6 and 12 months post-intervention by verifying how often patients fill their prescriptions. This is done by accessing pharmacy records and drug database files. Secondary outcome measures include: self-reported medication adherence, levels of asthma control, confidence in one's ability to manage asthma, and quality of life. Statistical analyses will compare adherence rates between the intervention and nonintervention groups, and statistical corrections will be made to ensure that other variables that could be associated with medication adherence (e.g., sex, age, asthma severity) cannot account for any post-treatment group differences. This study may provide support for the use of MI techniques to improve medication adherence and asthma outcomes, in order to improve asthma control and quality of life in asthmatics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Magnetic Resonance Frequency Shifts for the Characterization of Multiple Sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL WHITE MATTER; HUMAN BRAIN; IRON; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MR SIGNAL PHASE; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) affects more than 60,000 Canadians and more than 1000 Canadians are diagnosed with MS every year. MS is the most important cause of neurologic disability in young adults and can have a significant negative impact for the health of individuals and for society. Every patient with MS undergoes a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain. Most of the information gathered with MRI is due to subtle variations in signal magnitude which can be translated into images with meaningful information. These images are currently used in MRI of people with MS. The MRI signal, however, has another, promising, yet underexploited property: phase. The phase is best explained by using the analogy of a lighthouse: The MRI signal's magnitude corresponds to the brightness of the lighthouse beam and the MRI signal's phase corresponds to the beam's direction. Just as the lighthouse beam always has a certain direction, the MR signal always has a certain phase. This means that phase information comes for free with almost every MR scan and can be used in addition to the magnitude. Moreover, phase is exquisitely sensitive to changes in tissue occurring due to MS. However, many aspects of MR phase are poorly understood and before we can delve into more sophisticated applications of MR phase imaging, we first need to investigate the sources of phase contrast. Therefore, we propose to investigate the sources of phase contrast in healthy tissue and in brain tissue of people with MS.   In MS, phase information could allow us to investigate the brains of patients in high spatial detail and high sensitivity to tissue changes. Our research will improve the early diagnosis of MS and the monitoring of disease progression and treatment and it will help doctors to make the right intervention at the right time.

TitreApplicationTitle: Individual and Contextual Influences on Mental Health in Immigrant and Non-Immigrant Children
Keywords-MotsClés: DIRECT INTERVIEWS AND ASSESSMENTS; FAMILY; IMMIGRANT YOUTH; MENTAL HEALTH; MULTILEVEL MODELING; NEIGHBORHOOD; SCHOOL
Abstract-Résumé: Children living in immigrant families represent the fastest growing segment of the child population in Canada. Compared to non-immigrant children, immigrant children are far more likely to experience social and economic adversity, and there is growing evidence to suggest that these inequalities are widening. The negative influence of adversity on mental health argues for a close examination of immigrant children. This study will include 1st generation (foreign-born), 2nd generation (Canadian born who have at least one foreign-born parent) and 3rd+ generation (Canadian born whose parents were also Canadian-born) children in grades 4-8 attending schools in Hamilton, Ontario. The objectives of the study are to (1) compare levels of mental health problems between 1st, 2nd and 3rd+ generation children, and (2) to identify individual, family, school and neighbourhood factors that increase risk for mental health problems. Interviewers will collect information from parents and children in their native language. Study objectives will be addressed using statistical analyses referred to as 'multilevel modeling.'       Knowledge coming from this study will serve the following public health objectives. One, it will provide accurate estimates of the mental health needs of immigrant children in Hamilton that will be used for advocacy purposes to increase resource allocations to children's mental health. Two, it will quantify the impact of attending schools and living in neighbourhoods with high immigrant concentrations on child mental health problems that will inform educators and settlement planners for the need to develop targeted integration strategies that promote mental health. Three, it will set priorities for the types of intervention programs needed to improve the mental health outcomes of all children. Understanding the mental health needs of all children is an important first step to creating the necessary conditions for them to achieve to their full potential.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimal timing of elective repeat cesarean delivery
Keywords-MotsClés: CESAREAN DELIVERY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICES DELIVERY; MATERNAL MORBIDITY; NEONATAL MORBIDITY; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: One in 3 women in BC delivers her first child by cesarean birth. Most of these women (80%) have a cesarean delivery in later pregnancies as well ('elective repeat' cesareans). It is currently recommended that elective repeat cesarean deliveries be done when the mother is at least 39 weeks pregnant, because the baby may have breathing complications if it's delivered before this age.   It is therefore concerning that despite the risks to the baby, most elective repeat cesarean deliveries (62%) in BC seem to be happening before 39 weeks. The goal of this research is to better understand current practice in timing of elective repeat cesarean deliveries, and how the age of delivery may affect the health of the mother and baby. Using electronic medical records in the BC Perinatal Database from all women who had an elective repeat cesarean delivery in BC between 2001 and 2010, we will first try to better understand what factors are causing the high rate of early term delivery. For example, is a woman having her cesarean in a smaller hospital more likely to be delivered before 39 weeks than a women having her cesarean at a larger hospital? Finally, there is a concern that planning the surgery for after 39 weeks makes it more likely that the mother will go into spontaneous labour before her scheduled surgery, which may increase the risk of complications for the mother. We will therefore also calculate the week-by-week risks for both mother and baby in order to identify the time in pregnancy at which both risks are lowest.   'Elective repeat cesarean' is currently the most common reason for a cesarean delivery, so the time in pregnancy at which the surgery is done is an issue for a large group of pregnant women. The results of this study will help to make sure that elective repeat cesarean deliveries in Canada are done at the week of pregnancy that leads to the best outcomes possible for both mother and baby.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining function of uncharacterized enzymes by quantitative metabolic profiling using high resolution mass spectrometry
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL NETWORKS; ENZYME FUNCTION; GLYCOLYSIS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; METABOLOMICS; PENTOSE PHOSPHATE PATHWAY; REDOX STRESS; RIBONEOGENESIS; SEDOHEPTULOSE BISPHOSPHATE; YEAST PROTOTROPH
Abstract-Résumé: Organisms take up nutrients and break them down to release the energy necessary for cellular maintenance or chemically transform them to make the building blocks necessary for growth. Mass spectrometry allows close examination of the chemicals within cells. This project will identify previously unknown metabolic pathways within cells. Knowledge of these pathways is necessary to understand how cells use nutrients.  In addition, discovery of new pathways can permit the development of new small molecule drugs to regulate cellular growth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functions of Nod1 and Nod2 in host resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGIC LUNG INFLAMMATION; HOST RESISTANCE TO INFECTION; INTERFERONS; MUCOSAL INFECTION; NOD-LIKE RECEPTORS; NOD1; NOD2; PRIMING OF T AND B CELL IMMUNITY; SKIN INFLAMMATION; TNF-ALPHA
Abstract-Résumé: My research program focuses on deciphering the mechanisms of how the human immune system recognizes pathogens, leading to the subsequent instruction of long-lived immune responses to fend off infectious microbes. Recent advances in our understanding of the human immune system have led to the discovery of several host protein families that specifically detect molecular patterns of pathogens for the instruction of antimicrobial immune responses and the regulation of local and systemic immune-homeostasis. This concept has been further fueled by observations that polymorphisms and mutations in the human genes of the Nod-like receptor (NLR) protein family members encoding host proteins involved in detecting pathogens (e.g. Nod1, Nod2) are linked to both impaired antimicrobial resistance as well as to chronic inflammatory barrier disorders. Thus, the focus of my laboratory is to investigate the cellular and molecular mechanisms induced upon recognition of pathogens by Nod-like receptors, in particular Nod1 and Nod2. The scientific insights gained from the proposed research program will advance our medical and scientific understanding to enable us to tailor preventive vaccination strategies as well as therapies for the intervention of chronic inflammatory disorders to improve the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of TDP-43 in stress granule signaling in ALS
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; BIOCHEMISTRY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; RNA-BINDING PROTEIN; SPINAL CORD; STRESS GRANULES; TDP-43
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by the selective loss of specialized neurons that control voluntary movement. The mechanism and the biological basis of specificity of how these specialized neurons, known as motor neurons, are lost in ALS remains unknown. Environmental and genetics components both play a role in disease etiology. Motor neurons are inherently more susceptible to exposure to stress stimuli. Mammalian cells possess a variety of mechanisms to mediate a cell's recovery from physiological and environmental stresses. I have recently identified TAR DNA binding protein (TDP-43) as a regulator of one cellular stress response: the formation of stress granules. I propose to examine the role of wild type and mutated TDP-43 (a known ALS causing gene) in stress granule signalling and ALS pathogenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Use of laboratory and diary methods to clarify the link between social anxiety and risk for university student problematic drinking
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE PROCESSES; DRINKING MOTIVES; ECOLOGICAL MOMENTARY ASSESSMENT; MEDIATED MODERATION; MOOD MANIPULATION; MULTILEVEL MODELING; MULTIMETHOD; SOCIAL ANXIETY; UNIVERSITY PROBLEMATIC DRINKING
Abstract-Résumé: More than one-third of university students in Canada drink at harmful levels. This behaviour is a major public health concern because of the costs to individuals and society, such as unplanned sex when drinking and drunk driving accidents. The development of effective prevention programs need to be based on an understanding of why students drink so heavily. Despite the typical image of a "party animal", students who are socially anxious and experience extreme discomfort in social situations may also be at risk for heavy drinking. At university, alcohol use often occurs at social events, like parties, which cause great distress for some students. As a way to tolerate these difficult social situations, socially anxious students may be inclined to drink heavily, since alcohol has beneficial tension relief effects. Conversely, social anxiety could protect students against heavy drinking because students may worry that they will embarrass themselves if they are intoxicated. In light of inconsistent findings about the association between social anxiety and alcohol use, the proposed research aims to determine the role of social anxiety as a risk factor for problem drinking in university students. Factors that affect social anxiety and lead to attitudes (alcohol has positive effects) and motives (alcohol helps me cope) that support drinking will be evaluated. Two studies are proposed. First, in a realistic 'bar-lab' setting, students' moods will be modified and real-time effects on alcohol attitudes will be examined. Second, students will use cell phones to report real-time information while drinking, including motives for drinking. This research will help clarify the mixed findings in the literature. The findings will sustain key stakeholders on campus to better develop comprehensive university prevention programs/campaigns. Further, this work may have important clinical implications by identifying specific targets (e.g., attitudes and motives) for clinical intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural properties of glutamatergic neurons in major depression and suicide
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON TERMINALS; BDNF; DENDRITES; DEPRESSION; NEUROANATOMY; PLASTICITY; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: According to the World Health Organization, major depression affects approximately 121 million people worldwide and is ranked as one of the leading causes of disability. Many studies have suggested that the structure of some brain regions, namely those involved in processing emotions, is altered in the depressed brain. Surprisingly, none of these studies have examined the structure of nerve cells (neurons) in these regions. Here, we propose a project that will describe the state of both types of neuronal extensions (dendrites and axons) in cortical and hippocampal tissue samples from depressed suicides and matched control subjects. Postmortem brain tissues will be obtained from the Quebec Brain Bank (Douglas Institute). Studying these microscopic structures which are crucial for neuronal communication should lead to a better understanding of the biological underpinnings of depression and suicide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genome folding and regulation of gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CHROMATIN; CHROMOSOME CONFORMATION CAPTURE; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; EPIGENETICS; FLUORESCENCE IN SITU HYBRIDISATION; NUCLEAR ORGANISATION; REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Every cell in our bodies contains the same genetic material yet cells are functionally very different, expressing distinct genes and, consequently, distinct proteins.  Regulating gene expression at the correct time and in response to the correct signals is critical to the proper function of each cell in our bodies.  Many diseases, including all cancers, occur as the result of dramatic changes in gene expression.  Despite the importance of proper gene regulation, the key DNA sequences that regulate many genes have not been identified.  These sequences are often hidden in large stretches of the genome that are devoid of genes and as a result are difficult to find.  Recent technical advances have allowed identification of these sequences with greater ease but questions remain as to which specific genes are regulated by specific DNA elements.  By using new techniques that identify folds in the genome that bring sequences associated with gene regulation close to the gene, this project will identify the genetic elements that regulate specific genes.  We will also investigate the proteins that are mediating these folding interactions in the genome. Through a better understanding of how specific genes are regulated in each cell type we will be better able to understand diseases that arise as a result of aberrant gene expression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies of the molecular mechanisms by which mutations in the SUR2A NBDs cause cardiovascular diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: ABC TRANSPORTERS; FLUORESCENCE SPECTROSCOPY; KATP CHANNELS; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; NUCLEOTIDE BINDING DOMAINS; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN DYNAMICS; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; SULFONYLUREA RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Potassium ion channels in cells are essential for healthy hearts. These channels are formed from two different types of proteins. One protein, called Kir6.2, forms the channel pore while the other protein, known as SUR2A, regulates opening and closing of the pore. Proper control of the channel is essential as mutations in the gene for SUR2A cause cardiovascular disorders.  We will study the molecular details by which changes in SUR2A cause potassium channels to dysfunction in the heart. SUR2A mutations have many disease-causing defects, including altered ability of SUR2A to sense the cellular concentration of ATP (the energy currency of cells) and the inefficient transport of the channel from where it is made inside the cell to the cell membrane where it functions. These defects result from changes in (1) the 3-D arrangement of atoms in SUR2A, (2) movement of specific regions in SUR2A, and (3) the way that SUR2A interacts with other parts of the channel. Thus, obtaining a 3D picture of SUR2A is critical to understanding cardiovascular diseases. We will focus on the regions of SUR2A that are the sites of disease-causing mutations. These regions, called nucleotide binding domains (NBDs), utilize the energy of ATP to control opening and closing of the pore. Knowledge of the changes in the molecular details of the NBDs caused by the mutations will help develop new treatments for disease.  We will use a technique very similar to medical MRI to get a detailed 3D picture of the SUR2A NBDs alone and bound to other parts of the channel. These experiments will also give information regarding how the 3D shape of the NBDs changes in time, which is important for function. We will compare mutants of SUR2A NBDs that cause disease to the SUR2A NBDs in their normal state. These studies promise to enhance our understanding of how SUR2A mutations cause cardiovascular diseases and this molecular level knowledge will help design new molecules to treat disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Influence of Diabetes on Cancer Screening and Prognosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CANCER SCREENING; DIABETES; HEALTH SERVICES
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer and diabetes are two of the most common diseases in our society, and evidence shows that diabetes is associated with both a higher cancer risk and lower cancer survival. The reasons for these associations are still unclear. Most research has focused on the role of metabolic factors and diabetes drugs. However, few studies have looked at the role of health care factors such as cancer screening. Regular screening for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer has been shown to improve cancer survival. For screening to be effective, abnormal test results need to be followed up in a timely manner. Diabetes may lead to lower cancer screening and delayed follow-up due to competing demands of diabetes care. These health care gaps increase the risk of more advanced cancer stage at diagnosis, which might contribute to the lower cancer survival in persons with diabetes.   The goal of this study is to explore the influence of diabetes on the clinical steps leading to cancer diagnosis, by examining whether they have 1) lower cancer screening, 2) less follow-up of abnormal tests, and 3) a higher cancer incidence and more advanced stage at diagnosis compared to persons without diabetes. This study will use the existing Ontario health care databases between 2000 and 2012 to compare outcomes between persons with and without diabetes eligible for screening. First we will assess for differences in up-to-date screening rates for breast, colorectal, and cervical cancer. Second, we will compare diagnostic follow-up rates after an abnormal screening test. Third, we will assess for differences in cancer incidence and stage of breast and colorectal cancer.   This research is important because the number of people living with diabetes is reaching epidemic proportions, and cancer is a leading cause of disability and death in our society. Addressing potential gaps in cancer screening in persons with diabetes will help to improve cancer care and outcomes for this population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Activity Begins in Childhood (ABC)- a randomized controlled trial to inspire healthy active behaviour in preschoolers
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCELEROMETER; ANTHROPOMETRICS; DAYCARE; EARLY CHILDHOOD EDUCATORS; EARLY INTERVENTION; FAMILY; HEALTH BENEFITS; HEALTHY BEHAVIOUR; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PRESCHOOL CHILDREN
Abstract-Résumé: Physical activity (PA) is an important part of healthy childhood development. Typical Canadian preschoolers spend a great deal of time in daycare, environments which can have a very strong influence on their levels of daily movement. PA levels are low in these settings, with kids spending lots of time sitting.  This project will test the ability of daycare providers to incorporate PA into the daily routine when they are provided with appropriate training and tools to do so.  We will also look at whether engaging the parents and asking them to facilitate PA at home provides additional benefit.  We will use what is called a randomized control design.  This is a type of research study that 'randomly' (like flipping a coin) assigns people, or in this case, daycares, to one group or another.  We are going to have 3 groups to compare.  One group of daycare providers will be trained to increase all types of PA and reduce time spent sitting around. Another group of providers will have the same training but parents of kids in their care will also receive training on how to incorporate PA into their child's daily routine. The last group of daycares will offer their typical curriculum.  Over the course of 6 months we will measure PA using a device called an accelerometer (a 'super' pedometer) and measure height and weight.  We will also evaluate whether the intervention improved motor skills, which includes things like jumping, catching and throwing.  At the end we will compare groups to see if one performed better than the others.  We are intervening in preschoolers, because this is a group that is highly affected by the setting they are in and role models they interact with.  This will be the first study in Canada attempting to modify PA behaviour in licensed daycare centres and looking at parental involvement.   This is important because inactivity is highly predictive of development of chronic diseases like obesity and heart disease and prevention must start early.
