TitreApplicationTitle: Exploration of global control mechanisms of endosomal and phagosomal chemistries and their consequences to macrophage and dendritic cell function in health and disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTATION; CELL BIOLOGY; ENDOSOME; FLUOROMETRY; IMMUNOLOGY; MACROPHAGE; MICROSCOPY; PHAGOSOME; PROTEOLYSIS; REDOX
Abstract-Résumé: Macrophages and dendritic cells are cells of the immune system known as phagocytes (meaning "eating cells").  They are named for their ability to engulf particulate material by a process called phagocytosis.  Following phagocytosis, the engulfed material is broken down within compartments known as phagosomes.  This process has a diverse range of functions in normal growth and development, but also has a critical role in our body's immune defense system.  When macrophages and dendritic cells phagocytose (eat) microorganisms, they break down their proteins (also called antigens) in their phagosomes into small pieces that can be recognized by other cells.  The macrophages and dendritic cells then show these pieces of antigen to T-cells, triggering a powerful immune reaction that our body can remember.  This is important in our defense against foreign organisms, as well as in disease where our immune system mistakes our own cells as invaders (such as in autoimmunity).  Despite their pivotal role, there are fundamental gaps in our understanding of how phagosomes function.   We have evidence that a particular chemistry within the phagosome, known as the redox potential, influences how macrophages and dendritic cells digest protein antigens.  We think that this can control which parts of an antigen are presented and could have consequences to subsequent events in acquired immunity.  In particular, in many autoimmune diseases, which piece of an antigen is presented is critical to how our body reacts.  This proposal aims to further understand how the redox potential affects the way phagosomes process antigen, and in turn, how it influences which parts of the antigen are presented.    This basic scientific research is broad reaching as it has the potential to profoundly impact human health.  In addition to better understanding how our immune system works, this work may lead to different strategies in the management of autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of LXRbeta in Glucocorticoid-Induced Hyperglycemia
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; GLUCOCORTICOIDS; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; KNOCKOUT MICE; LXR; SIGNALLING
Abstract-Résumé: Metabolic diseases, including diabetes and obesity, are reaching epidemic levels in the Western world. Diabetes is characterized by elevated blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia) caused by the body's inability to properly secrete insulin or respond to increasing insulin levels. A known and preventable cause of hyperglycemia is the long-term therapeutic use of glucocorticoid drugs. Glucocorticoid drugs are widely prescribed for diseases in which their potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive actions are desired including rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, certain types of cancers and organ transplants. However, the long-term use of glucocorticoid drugs is limited by undesirable side effects including obesity and type 2 diabetes. These negative side effects are due in part to the glucose production pathway being strongly induced by glucocorticoid drugs. Therefore, there is extensive interest in generating new and improved "dissociated" glucocorticoid drugs that retain anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects without the undesirable side effects. We have identified the liver X receptor beta (LXRbeta), a nuclear hormone receptor that is responsive to cholesterol metabolites, as a novel factor important in selectively modulating the hyperglycemic and not the immunosuppressive effects of glucocorticoid signalling. In this proposal, we will take the unique approach of using the liver X receptor beta knockout mice to uncover the signalling mechanism involved, and in the process identify new determinants of glucocorticoid specificity. This project has high public relevance because it will allow us to identify new drug targets to benefit the diabetic community and to create safer glucocorticoid drugs for the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics and Epigenetics of Serotonin System in Suicidal Behaviour: CpG SNP Mapping, Methylation and Allelic Imbalance Analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; GENETICS; METHYLATION; MONOAMINE; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SEROTONIN; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder affect hundreds of thousands of Canadians and their families. Both disorders are associated with a high risk of suicide. Several studies provide evidence that genetic factors influence suicidal behavior. The major aim of this study is to identify changes in the genetic material that are inheritable but are sensitive to environment and which genes and neurotransmitters are relevant to suicidal behavior. Understanding these factors might enable prediction of suicidal behavior in patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. In this study, we will analyze proteins in the brain that influence transfer of information in different brain circuits. The instructions for creating these proteins are encoded in genes, but how these genes express themselves can be influenced by the environment through epigenetic modifications. We have collected genetic samples as well as detailed clinical information about suicide attempts and suicidal behavior severity scores from 336 bipolar and 497 schizophrenia patients. We will assess whether epigenetic modification is found in the genetic material and has occurred under the influence of external factors such as stress, medications and disease course. Additionally, we will estimate the gene activity of neurotransmitter receptors that are the target of antidepressants and antipsychotics. This analysis will be performed in 165 post-mortem brains donated by the Stanley Foundation including 41 patients who died by suicide. The genetic risk markers for suicide that we hope to identify could, in the future, identify persons at risk and thus facilitate preventive measures such as counseling, family education, and early treatment intervention for these individuals. Furthermore, the identified genes and genetic changes may reveal possible chemical imbalance in the brain of patients who have committed suicide which can be used as targets for development of novel medications for suicide prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal mechanisms underlying the emergence of selective attentional control
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTERIOR CINGULATE CORTEX; ATTENTIONAL CONTROL; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NEURONAL SYNCHRONIZATION; NONHUMAN PRIMATES; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; VENTROMEDIAL FRONTAL CORTEX; VISUAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Our brains contain billions of cells. These cells need to interact to ensure that we successfully achieve our aims in a dynamically changing environment. When aiming to read a newspaper article we narrow our attention to the words and sentences ahead, but we are influenced by the value of alternative actions, like grasping the cup of coffee that promises to be tasteful. Thus, controlling what to attend to at any moment in time is effortful, and it is influenced by the reward promised by alternatives.  This control is achieved by brain cells. Some cells are known to be crucial to control where to attend to, whereas other cells are crucial to evaluate the reward value of the current and alternative goals. Our research program aims to understand how these two gross types of brain cells interact to control successfully attention to achieve our goals. Our research program is particularly innovative in focusing on the dynamic interplay between brain cells in different regions of the brain. This interplay is known to involve rhythmic coordination among many cells from many different regions. And disturbance of rhythmic coordination during attentional control has been implicated in many severe neurological diseases.  Despite clear indications of its importance, it is unknown whether rhythmic coordination of brain activity has causal consequences for failures of attentional control. We aim to uncover this missing knowledge by recording brain activation patterns at the highest spatial resolution in monkeys while they perform a selective attention tasks in a dynamic environment.

TitreApplicationTitle: TRPML1 in intracellular Fe2+ and Ca2+ homeostasis/signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CA2+/FE2+ IMAGING; CA2+/FE2+ SIGNALING; CELL BIOLOGY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNEL; LYSOSOMAL PATCH-CLAMPING; LYSOSOME; NEUROBIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The lysosome is viewed as a garbage dump and recycling center inside of the cell. Dysfunction of the lysosome causes accumulation of abnormal materials in the cell, eventually leading to cell death which is manifested by what is known as neurodegeneration. One toxic factor is lipofuscin, a non-degradable yellow-brown pigment granule in the lysosome. Because it is often accumulated with age or seen in aging diseases such as Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease, lipofuscin is also called 'aging pigment'. Lipofuscin production and accumulation is tightly regulated by the level of lysosomal calcium and iron. By using a unique technique that I developed, we recently showed that lysosomal protein TRPML1 regulates lysosomal iron and calcium levels, and that TRPML1 deficient cells display lipofuscin accumulation. Therefore, I propose to study the role of TRPML1 in lysosomal lipofuscin accumulation. I hypothesize that an increase in iron-dependent lipofuscin production and a decrease in calcium-dependent lipofuscin exclusion could be the reasons for the accumulation of lipofuscin in TRPML1 deficient cells and ageing cells. These studies will not only help us understand the pathogenesis of Mucolipidosis type IV disease which is caused by deficient TRPML1 but also have broad implications for the understanding and clinical management of neurodegenerative diseases as a whole.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing Methodology for Scoring the Five-Level EQ-5D
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH UTILITIES
Abstract-Résumé: Quantifying patients' health-related quality of life is an important component of evaluating the benefits of a new treatment. Health-related quality of life is usually measured through standardised questionnaires. The most popular general-use questionnaire consists of five questions, to each of which respondents must select one of three possible responses. This is felt to be too restrictive and doesn't fully capture the breadth of health states that patients experience.  In response to this, a new questionnaire is being developed, which asks the same questions as the existing questionnaire but allows individuals one of five possible responses to each question. This improves the number of health states that the questionnaire can caputre -- in fact, there are 3125 possible states.   The responses to the questionnaire need to be summarised in a single number, known as the health utility. This proposal evaluates methods for deriving health utilities from the questionnaire responses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving patient-reported outcome measures: Valuation and application of the EQ-5D in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: DISCRETE CHOICE EXPERIMENT; EQ-5D; HEALTH UTILITY MEASUREMENT; HEALTH-RELATED QUALITY OF LIFE; MINIMALLY IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE; POPULATION NORMS; TIME TRADE-OFF
Abstract-Résumé: Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) has become an important piece of information in addition to efficacy and safety when evaluating treatment effects. A common way of gathering HRQoL is to use a questionnaire to obtain the description of a person's health status and assign a value to it. The difference in the values before and after a treatment would be the impact on HRQoL. It has been a consensus among the research community that the values should come from the general public based on the fact that any decision made within a taxpayer-supported health care system (like Canada) will affect all taxpayers. A HRQoL questionnaire, called the EuroQol, developed by an international research group, has been most widely used in the world in the past decades. The first step of the proposed research is to develop a scoring system that can be used to assign values to the health statuses defined by this questionnaire. We will interview a large random sample of the Canadian general population using the EuroQol. The second step is to determine the smallest difference in the values between health statuses that would be meaningful and important to the general public. This will ensure proper interpretation of results from future uses of this questionnaire. The third step will be the application of the questionnaire in 2011 Commonwealth Fund International Health Policy Survey for Sicker Adults in Canada. This application will help describe health status of Canadians with different chronic health conditions. To ensure the voices from the general public being heard when providing health care, the future research direction would be to explore the feasibility of incorporating the EuroQol into routine clinical practice as one of the important indicators of performance of health care and the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: A mechanistic study of G-protein coupled receptor binding and activation by apelin.
Keywords-MotsClés: APELIN-RECEPTOR INTERACTIONS; BIOPHYSICAL CHARACTERIZATION; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; PEPTIDE-GPCR INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The peptide molecule apelin is used as a messenger in the cardiovascular system, brain, and in response to blood glucose. Its involvement has been specifically implicated in cancer progression and atherosclerosis. Apelin functions by interacting with a specific receptor protein. This receptor is located in membranes of many cells in the body. As a whole, proteins found in the membranes of cells such as heart muscle cells and neurons have important roles in controlling proper cellular and body function and are frequently used as drug targets. The activation of the apelin receptor, which occurs upon apelin binding, can cause dramatic physiological effects. These include changes in blood pressure and heart muscle contraction, changes to levels of blood insulin or other circulating hormones, and changes to behavior and neurological function. The HIV virus also makes use of the apelin receptor when it invades human cells, particularly in the brain and nervous system. The molecular-level basis of the interaction between apelin and its receptor is not understood. Using the technique of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR), which allows us to locate and study individual atoms in a molecule, the atomic arrangement and motion in both apelin and its membrane-bound receptor will be studied. These NMR studies will be correlated to information obtained using other biophysical methods. By developing this type of atomic-level understanding, specific drugs can be designed to target either apelin or its receptor, increasing therapeutic treatment options for HIV infection, cancer and a variety of cardiovascular, central nervous system and metabolic disease conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modelling of Radiotherapy Induced Damage in Locally Advanced Lung Cancer by a Novel System Radiobiology Approach
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; MEDICAL PHYSICS; NORMAL TISSUE TOXICITIES; PATIENT-ORIENTED RESEARCH; PROTEOMICS; RADIATION THERAPY; RESPONSE PREDICTION; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TREATMENT PLANNING
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is a leading cause for death among men and women with 5-year survival rate of only 15%. Patients at advanced stages suffer from further poorer prognosis and dire socioeconomic consequences for them, their relatives and the healthcare system. The majority of these patients is diagnosed with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and receives radiation therapy as their main treatment. However, radiation hypersensitivity, which manifests as inflammatory response known as radiation pneumonitis, is a major limiting factor to treatment success and a main obstacle to applying new promising radiation modalities. This is a potentially fatal condition that damages normal lung tissues, therefore, a key goal of modern radiotherapy research is to predict at the time of treatment planning, the risks of pneumonitis for each individual patient. However, because of the inherent complexity and variability of the biological response to radiation therapy, current physical or biological models separately are insufficient to accurately predict this risk. Therefore, in this proposal we plan to investigate a novel system-based approach that would integrate relevant biological information while controlling for physical variations in the same population using artificial intelligence and bioinformatics techniques. We plan to conduct a prospective study in a cohort of locally advanced NSCLC patients who receive radiotherapy at McGill University Health Centre. The data collected in this study and developed methodology would provide new insights into radiation pneumonitis signaling mechanisms and allow for better predictive models of its onset. The findings can be used clinically to personalize patients' treatment plans, reducing the risk of complications or supporting therapy that is more intensive for those patients likely to benefit. This could potentially improve outcomes, provide greater quality care for patients, and reduce associated healthcare costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genomic Disruption in High-Grade Serous Ovarian Carcinomas: Steady State or Continuous Drift?
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMOSOMAL STABILITY; EARLY LESIONS; GENOMICS; HIGH GRADE SEROUS CANCERS; INTRATUMOURAL HETEROGENEITY; NEXT-GENERATION-SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: In North America, ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death due to gynecological malignancies and 75% of women with advanced ovarian cancer are not expected to survive beyond five years. High-grade serous ovarian cancers account for 70% of ovarian cancer cases. These cancers are thought to be chromosomally unstable, which means their genomes are highly susceptible to the introduction of large-scale genetic mutations and rearrangements on a continual basis. This assumption stems from the observation that the chromosomal makeup (karyotype) of ovarian cancers is extremely abnormal. Recent results from our group suggest that this presumption is incorrect. It seems that ovarian cancers undergo a period of chromosomal instability very early on as the cancer is being established which leads to the abnormal karyotype. At the time of disease diagnosis, however, these cancers have already reached a state of chromosomal stability. Thus, with respect to large-scale genomic changes, recurrences and metastases are almost identical to the original tumour. We have found, however, that small-scale changes corresponding to single letter DNA alterations continue to occur as tumours evolve. This finding represents a moment of recognition that 'the emperor has no clothes' with respect to the study of ovarian cancer. For this project, we will conduct an in-depth study of multiple tumour samples from 10 cases of high-grade serous ovarian cancer to determine the extent of genetic variability between tumours and try to discover how these cancers acquire chromosomal stability. We will also compare these results to early precursors of ovarian cancer from the fallopian tubes, to identify when chromosomal instability occurs in cancer evolution. The results of this work could reveal why a large proportion of ovarian cancers do not respond to treatment or develop treatment resistance and has important implications for the development of new treatments for this disease.
