TitreApplicationTitle: My Opioid Manager: A point of care tool for patients with chronic non-cancer pain considering opioids.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC NON-CANCER PAIN; CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE; FOCUS GROUPS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; MIXED METHODS; MONITORING OF KNOWLEDGE USE; ONLINE SURVEYS; OPIOIDS; TOOL DEVELOPMENT; WEBSITE DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: My Opioid Manager will be a tool for patients with chronic non-cancer pain (CNCP) who have been considered for treatment with opioids. Opioids (or narcotics) are potent analgesic medications that can cause various adverse effects (e.g. nausea, constipation, sedation, etc), and complications such as overdose and addiction. In 2010, a group composed of all medical regulatory authorities in Canada released a clinical practice guideline for physicians prescribing opioids for patients with CNCP. The guideline was accompanied by many tools to facilitate its use, dissemination and implementation. One of these tools is the Opioid Manager (OM), which was designed to be used as a point of care tool for physicians. The purpose of this project is to develop a version of the OM for patients, relatives, care givers, and the general public. This will be achieved through consultation with groups of patients with CNCP, using a professional medical writer, and technical services from a graphic designer. In Canada there is a growing problem of misuse and abuse of prescription opioids. It is important that patients are aware of their own risks of opioid abuse, and that they understand the benefits, adverse effects, complications of opioids, and they have realistic goals with opioid therapy. We will examine the efficacy of the My Opioid Manager in improving patient's knowledge and self-efficacy. It is also expected that My Opioid Manager will be used to improve physician's knowledge, attitudes and behaviours related to the management of CNCP with opioids. The ultimate goal is to achieve a balance between chronic pain that goes undertreated and abuse of prescription opioids with serious consequences to the individual and society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Validation of a Screening Strategy for Adverse Drug Reactions in the Emergency Department
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE DRUG RELATED EVENTS; CLINICAL DECISION RULE; EMERGENCY MEDICINE; PATIENT SAFETY
Abstract-Résumé: Adverse drug reactions are unintended and harmful effects caused by medications. They are a common cause of preventable adverse events in medicine. In Canada, adverse drug reactions cause 720,000 Emergency Department (ED) visits each year. Adverse drug reactions are not easy to recognize. In fact, they are misdiagnosed 39-49% of the time in the ED, and the consequences can be serious. If the medication causing the problem is not stopped, the patient's condition can worsen and may even lead to death. Past attempts to develop tools to help community doctors prescribe medications in a safer manner and to help health care professionals identify and treat adverse drug reactions have not been very successful. This is because the resources required to make the diagnosis and readjust the medications are often not available in the outpatient setting. The ED is the ideal setting to address these problems. EDs have all the necessary resources, and patients with the most severe adverse drug reactions frequently go to the ED. In a previous study, we developed a user-friendly screening tool, similar to a checklist, that accurately identifies patients in the ED with adverse drug reactions. Our goal is to evaluate this screening tool on a larger scale to confirm its safety and accuracy. We propose to do this in a study enrolling 3550 patients from seven EDs in three provinces. Nurses will apply the screening tool we will evaluate, and pharmacists will assess all patients to determine who has an adverse drug reaction. We will then determine how many patients diagnosed with adverse drug reactions the screening tool has detected, how easy it is to use, how reliable it is, and what its potential impact is on clinical practice. Once we have evaluated the screening tool, we plan to roll out it out in EDs throughout Canada and internationally. We believe that this will lead to better patient care, less patient suffering and decrease the cost of health care.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE DRUG REACTION; CANCER THERAPY; DRUG SAFETY; GENETIC TESTING; GENOMICS; PEDIATRICS; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; PHARMACOGENOMICS; SIDE EFFECTS; STRATIFIED MEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, severe ADRs claim 10,000 to 21,800 lives each year and cause many more life-long disabilities. In the treatment of pediatric cancer, 40% of patients suffer severe permanently disabling, life-threatening, or lethal ADRs. ADRs alone account for 22% of all pediatric oncology patient admissions into hospital. An individual's susceptibility to an ADR is often determined by their genetic make-up. Building upon a successful track record of identifying novel genetic susceptibility variants to severe ADRs, including cisplatin-induced deafness and anthracycline-induced heart failure, the objective of this research program will be to (1) discover novel genetic and/or clinical factors predictive of severe ADRs, (2) replicate and (3) validate these discoveries, and (4) to implement these tests for the benefit of patients. A pilot program is now underway to establish a genetic testing program to prevent severe ADRs in partnership with the Clinical Molecular Genetics Diagnostic Laboratory at the B.C. Children's Hospital. This program will focus on the translation between clinical genetic results and translation to physicians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Knowledge synthesis methods across multi-disciplinary fields
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG SAFETY AND EFFECTIVENESS; KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS METHODS; META-ETHNOGRAPHY; META-NARRATIVE REVIEW; SCOPING REVIEW; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Sometimes many randomized controlled trials examine the same treatment among similar patients but find different results. When this occurs, researchers may use an approach called a knowledge synthesis. Knowledge synthesis allows the combination of many different studies to come up with an answer to a research question. These methods are also used to find out more information when there is little known about a particular research area.      Within healthcare, researchers have focused on the traditional systematic review method for knowledge synthesis. The traditional systematic review method places a strong emphasis on experimental studies, such as randomized controlled trials. However, sometimes a randomized controlled trial is not possible because the treatment can potentially harm the patient. Less attention has been given to other knowledge synthesis methods that can be used to summarize the results from studies such as interviews and focus groups. These types of studies provide rich details that may not be captured in a randomized controlled trial, including patient values, compliance, and preferences.      Through this scoping review, we will be able to create a chart outlining all the different types of knowledge syntheses across different fields and be able to come up with a map that can be used by researchers to decide which type of knowledge synthesis to use for a particular research question. We will also begin putting together a manual on the methods for the knowledge synthesis methods other than the traditional systematic review. These results will be useful to students, teachers, researchers, companies that do knowledge syntheses, companies that fund knowledge syntheses, and journals that publish knowledge syntheses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hepatitis B Virus Infection (HBV) in Human Immunodeficiency Type -1 (HIV-1) Positive Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRAL DRUG RESISTANCE; ANTIVIRAL IMMUNE RESPONSE; CHRONIC AND OCCULT HEPATITIS B VIRUS; DNA SEQUENCING; HEPATITIS COINFECTION; HIV; LIVER DISEASE; LUMINEX ASSAYS; LYMPHOID CELL CULTURE; MITOGEN STIMULATION; NESTED PCR/NUCLEIC ACID HYBRIDIZATION; QUANTITATIVE PCR; VIRAL LYMPHOTROPISM; VIRUS EVOLUTION AND GENETIC DIVERSITY
Abstract-Résumé: Due to similar blood and body fluid transmission routes, hepatitis B virus (HBV) is an important infection in persons living with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). HBV can cause serious liver disease such as cirrhosis (scarring of the liver) and liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma, HCC). Liver disease is the leading cause of death and hospitalizations in patients living with HIV, and therefore adequate management of hepatitis B is considered a priority in HBV/HIV coinfected patients.  There is increasing evidence suggesting that molecular (genetic) characterization of the HBV, such as development of antiviral drug resistant variants, is an important factor in guiding patient management. Although both HIV and HBV can infect cells of the immune system the role of these immune cell reservoirs in HBV persistence is unknown. Our clinic cares for approximately 2800 persons with HIV and have collected sequential blood samples over 2 decades of follow-up from these patients. Approximately 15% (178/2800) patients were diagnosed with chronic HBV infection. We aim to study these persons to determine how HBV can establish a persistent infection and how this affects clinical outcome such as development of liver disease. We will analyze the genetic sequence of each virus (HIV and HBV) to determine whether coinfection can affect the development of resistance to both HBV and HIV antiviral drug therapy. Finally we will study the effect of coinfection on the host immune response to infection. This comprehensive longitudinal study of HBV and HIV coinfected patients will assess: (1) HBV and HIV genetic evolution, (2) HBV and HIV drug resistance, (3) host immune response and (4) presence of immune (ie., lymphoid) cell viral reservoirs. We aim to determine how viral interactions within dually infected immune cells impact patient clinical outcomes such as acceleration of liver disease, development of liver failure and liver-failure related death.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the 'Functioning, Disability and Health' of Women and Men Living with HIV in Zambia: Shifting Perspectives for a Longer-Term Approach to HIV Care in Southern Africa
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; CRITICAL SOCIAL SCIENCE; DISABILITY; GENDER; HIV; ICF; QUALITATIVE; REHABILITATION; SOUTHERN AFRICA; ZAMBIA
Abstract-Résumé: One-third of all people living with HIV worldwide and 40% of all HIV+ women live in the ten countries in Southern Africa, which includes Zambia. The recent arrival of effective HIV drugs in that region marks a new era in the history of HIV as vast numbers of people living with HIV may expect improved health and far longer lives. HIV in these poor countries is becoming a chronic illness. Thus, research is needed that moves beyond the medical challenges of treatment roll-out and embraces a longer-term approach to HIV as a chronic condition. Rehabilitation is an approach used in Canada with great success ever since treatment turned HIV into a chronic illness here in the 1990's. The leading rehabilitation lens has been the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disablity and Health. But these ideas have not yet been considered for people living with HIV in Southern Africa.  The purpose of our research is to use the WHO framework to explore the experiences of "functioning, disability and health" among women and men living with HIV in Lusaka, Zambia who are on HIV treatment. We plan to have in-depth discussions with 15 men and 15 women at 3 points over the course of 12-18 months to find out about their lives. We want to learn about them as individuals and how context shapes their experiences. In Canada, people living with HIV have described their experience as episodic disability whereby life with HIV is highly unpredictable. We plan to explore how episodic disability might be playing out for people in Lusaka. Along with challenges, we know that people living with HIV can be amazingly resilient, so we plan to explore not just problems but also the successes achieved by our participants in managing their obstacles. Finally, for each of these issues, we will use a gender lens to explore how experiences are the same or different for women vs men. These insights will help inform practice, policy, education and research.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Pyroptosis Induced Intestinal Epithelial Cell Extrusion in the Pathogenesis of Inflammatory Bowel Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIER DYSFUNCTION; BARRIER FUNCTION; CELL EXTRUSION; COMMENSAL BACTERIA; CYTOKINE; INFLAMMASOME; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INTESTINAL EPITHELIAL CELLS; MICROPARTICLE ABSORPTION; PYROPTOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The lining of the intestine is a layer of specialized cells that forms a selective barrier to the contents of the gut. When this layer is healthy, nutrients and water can cross, but toxins and bacteria cannot. When this layer is unhealthy, the result is inflammatory bowel disease, a painful and chronic intestinal disorder that affects an estimated 1% of Canadians. We have shown that greater numbers of gaps in this layer (i.e. missing cells) result in more problems in the gut. We have also discovered that these missing cells die through a special pathway called pyroptosis (fiery death). When the cells lining the intestine die from fiery death, they produce substances that activate the immune system and cause inflammation in the intestine. In addition, fiery cell death results in leaky holes in the intestine, allowing small particles and bacteria to enter into the body. This causes infection and further inflammation. Our objective is to outline the mechanism that leads to the fiery cell death and how all the factors fits together to cause inflammatory bowel disease. This is a new area of research: it was previously believed that the cells lining the intestine were killed as a result of the disease, instead of potentially being the source of the problem. Research into fiery cell death in the development of inflammatory bowel disease may lead to much improved therapies for patients with the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Programme international de recherche action participative pour le rétablissement et la psychiatrie citoyenne : mise au point d'une vision clinique centrée sur la pleine citoyenneté
Keywords-MotsClés: MESURE DE LA CITOEYNNETE; PATIENT-PARTENAIRE; PRATIQUE DE L'APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES INTEGREE; RETBLISSEMENT CIVIQUE; SCIENCE DE L'APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES
Abstract-Résumé: Le Plan d'action en sante mentale du Ministere de la sante et des services sociaux du Quebec souligne "la priorite qu'il faut accorder au retablissement de la personne dans sa globalite et au developpement de moyens qui lui donneront espoir et faciliteront sa participation active a la vie en societe" (p. 11). Le retablissement des personnes utilisatrices de services de sante mentale (personnes en retablissement) ne reste en effet que partiel sans la possibilite pour celles-ci de contribuer a la vie civique en societe et dans la communaute. A cet egard, elles ont besoin de soutien afin que leur retablissement soit complet. Or, a ce jour il n'existe toujours pas d'intervention ciblant specifiquement les dimensions civiques du retablissement.   Mon programme de recherche vise le retablissement civique, et ce par l'atteinte des trois objectifs principaux suivants : 1) conceptualiser et mesurer les dimensions civiques du retablissement de maniere rigoureuse et fiable; 2) mettre au point des interventions individuelles et societales visant les dimensions civiques du retablissement; 3) evaluer l'implantation et l'efficacite de ses interventions quant a leurs effets sur les personnes en retablissement et sur les organisations.  Le cadre conceptuel ce programme est celui de la citoyennete en tant qu'intrication des droits, responsabilites, roles, ressources et relations auxquels les personnes en retablissement peuvent avoir acces a travers les institutions publiques et sociales, de meme qu'a travers la vie associative et communautaire informelle. Pour mesurer les dimensions civiques du retablissement, un nouvel instrument de mesure de la citoyennete a ete mis au point. Il reste encore a tester l'application de cet instrument dans le cadre d'une intervention visant le retablissement civique, en particulier par le biais d'une formation a la citoyennete. Pour developper, implanter et evaluer cette intervention et cette formation, une approche multimethodes sera employee.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Causal Role of Acute Alcohol Consumption in Unprotected Sex among MSM at Risk for Acquiring HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; ALCOHOL; CONDOMS; GAY AND BISEXUAL MEN; HIV; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN (MSM); PREVENTION; RISK; SEX; SUBSTANCE USE
Abstract-Résumé: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a significant public health concern in Canada, and sexual behaviour remains the primary method through which HIV is transmitted among Canadians. Within this context, the consumption of alcohol is frequently seen as a key driver of unprotected sex. However, the evidence for a direct association between alcohol and unprotected sex tends to be mixed, which not only limits our understanding of alcohol's potential causal role in condom use decisions and subsequent HIV acquisition/transmission, but it also adds complexity to the development of effective behavioural interventions aimed at reducing unprotected sex among at-risk populations. The primary stream of the proposed research program will therefore employ a multi-method approach to investigate alcohol's direct causal and/or indirect interactive impact on high-risk sexual behaviour among gay and bisexual men, who continue to be overrepresented in the Canadian HIV epidemic. Study 1 and Study 2 will employ a unique, alcohol-focused experimental paradigm to assess alcohol's causal role in risky sex intentions among HIV-negative and HIV-positive gay and bisexual men, respectively. Study 3 will consist of a field investigation to identify "real-world" linkages between alcohol/substance use and risky sex. Study 4 will build on the findings from these initial studies, and will involve collaborating with clinic- and community-based partners to develop and evaluate an alcohol-focused HIV prevention initiative. A smaller set of complementary initiatives will form the basis of the secondary stream of research, focusing on broader aspects of alcohol, substance use, and HIV prevention. Overall, the proposed program of research could prove to play a key role in future public health initiatives that target the Canadian HIV epidemic on a wide-scale level.

TitreApplicationTitle: REcovery after Hip Fracture in Geriatric Ambulatory Patients Living In Nursing Homes (REGAIN II):  Does an Outreach Program Improve Recovery?
Keywords-MotsClés: HIP FRACTURE; NURSING HOME; RECOVERY; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: BACKGROUND: Hip fracture is the second leading cause of hospitalization in seniors and is associated with loss of function and increased risk of death. Up to 25% of hip fractures occur within long-term care facilities, those providing long-term residential care for dependent individuals. For these residents, current postoperative care involves quickly discharging them from hospital to continue recovery in the long-term care setting. Although these residents are older and may have impaired mental status, at least 70% were walking prior to their hip fracture.  INTERVENTION: Current evidence suggests that patients with impaired mental status can still respond positively to functional exercises. REGAIN I examined how long-term care patients recover after a hip fracture. REGAIN II, the current study, will explore how an exercise intervention {an Outreach Program} that consists of a rehabilitation team who travel to long-term care facilities to deliver exercise treatments to hip fracture patients after hospital discharge affects recovery of function.  Subjects in the intervention arm will receive the Outreach Program  {45 minutes/session; 3 times/week} for 10 weeks following their hip fracture while the control group will receive usual postoperative care. We will also examine if the Outreach Program is a feasible approach to offering treatment after a hip fracture for those who live in a long-term care setting.  All subjects will be assessed at baseline {pre-fracture status}, and 3, 6, and 12 months after fracture. REGAIN II started enrollment in February 2011. EXPECTED OUTCOME: Our simple exercise program may assist recovery after hip fracture and, if effective, may even be applied to other conditions associated with hospitalization and the need for recovery of function {e.g. stroke, pneumonia, heart failure} that are common in nursing home residents.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel pharmacological strategy to boost innate immunity and provide broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity through hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1)
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY; HYPOXIA INDUCIBLE FACTOR-1; IMMUNOLOGY; MICE; MULTI-DRUG RESISTANCE BACTERIA; NEUTROPHIL EXTRACELLULAR TRAPS; PHAGOCYTIC CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The widespread and rapid emergence of multi-drug resistant (MDR) bacterial pathogens pose ever-increasing threats to public health. Persistent infections with these superbugs such as MDR Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are associated with prolonged hospitalizations, as well as increased costs and frequency of poor outcomes or death. Each year, infections from MDR bacteria cause nearly 100,000 deaths in the United States alone. Thus, new and improved strategies to combat infections to prevent the emergence of MDR organisms are needed. This proposal describes a new pharmacological approach to treat microbial infections by boosting the immune system. Recent studies as well as highly promising preliminary data generated from our lab led to the hypothesis that a protein called HIF-1 can significantly enhance host immunity, thus increasing bacterial killing during infections. Using an array of advanced cell biological, genetic and microbiological tools combined with microscopy I will (a) fully characterize how HIF-1 enhances immune cell killing of bacteria (b) extensively explore the role of HIF-1 in bacteria killing using mutant mouse models, and (c) evaluate the efficacy of two HIF-1 drugs recently designed in our lab, at killing MDR bacteria under different infection criteria using a mouse model of MRSA infections. Results from this work will offer new insight into the mechanisms of boosting host immunity and will generate new strategies to eradicate a variety of bacterial infections.

Abstract-Résumé: The basis for the proposed program of research is to significantly extend and enhance, both in terms of scope and methodology, the projects and initiatives in which the applicant has been involved in the recent years. This will be accomplished by conducting original research, building capacity, and translating evidence for uptake into practice and policy around optimal management of chronic disease in primary care settings. Over the next five years I plan on further advancing our knowledge around the optimal transition from clinical efficacy to community effectiveness by focusing on the development of innovative, primary healthcare and community-based strategies and models of chronic disease management that are easily implementable, scalable and cost-effective. These strategies will build on my previous research and work of my partners and collaborators and will include: a) pro-active, family practice/primary health care team based strategies of chronic disease management; b) deployment of volunteer peer health educators to support and enhance these activities; c) integration and enhancement of the role played in the management of chronic disease by community-based pharmacists; d) promotion and support of patient-led testing, monitoring, and management of chronic disease; e) incorporation of successful models, strategies and 'lessons learned' from different jurisdictions in Canada and internationally and, e) mobilization of local partners and organizations with complementary foci on community-based chronic disease management strategies.   I propose to further enhance and foster new links with health-care providers, health-care managers, policy makers and industry partners to accelerate the effective application of research into policies, programs, and practices. I intend to augment mentoring and education opportunities to attract and prepare the next generation of primary care, health services and policy researchers focused on chronic disease management.

TitreApplicationTitle: Generation of a dendritic cell-based vaccine by modulating the expression of protein tyrosine phosphatases.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN PRESENTATION; CO-STIMULATORY MOLECULES; DENDRITIC CELLS; LYMPHOMAS; MATURATION; NK CELL ACTIVATION; PANCREATIC CANCER; PTP PROTEIN KINASE PHOSPHATASES; T CELL ACTIVATION; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Dendritic cells (DCs) are essential immune cells in the initiation and maintenance of anti-tumor immunity. DCs capture tumor-derived proteins (antigens) and process them into tumor-peptides that eventually will be presented on their cell surface (process known as antigen presentation) to other immune cells such as T cells. During this process, DCs differentiate from immature to mature DCs, which is characterized by an increased expression of cell surface proteins and production of stimulatory factors (pro-inflammatory cytokines). These events are required for the activation of T cell and the induction of T cell cytotoxic activity (capacity to kill tumor cells by a cell-cell contact dependent mechanism). The maturation status of DCs is therefore crucial to induce an effective anti-tumor response. Nevertheless, DC-based vaccination protocols have elicited poor clinical responses with no durable tumor rejection and/or prolonged survival.Defects in the DCs number and functions are one of the main factors responsible for the tumour escape from the immune system attack, and these defects contribute in various ways to defects in the T cell cytotoxic activity observed in cancer. The processes of DC maturation, antigen presention and migration to the lymphoid organs (where antigen presentation takes place) are regulated by a variety of enzymes. In particular, a family of protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs) can dramatically alter DCs functions (enhance or reduce) and therefore affect T cell activation and anti-tumor responses. We propose to genetically modify DCs by depleting or over-expressing specific PTPs in order to generate fully mature DCs with potent antigen presentation capacity. Consequently, modified DCs will be resistant to tumor-derived suppression and potent inducers of T cell activation and anti-tumor responses in vivo.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of neuronal Fc-gamma receptor I in the pathogenesis of chronic pain
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN-SPECIFIC IMMUNE RESPONSE; CALCIUM; CALCIUM IMAGING; DORSAL ROOT GANGLION; FC GAMMA RECEPTOR; IMMUNOGLOBULIN G; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; ION CHANNELS; PAIN; WHOLE-CELL RECORDINGS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain is one of the most common symptoms in the immune-related diseases, affecting 100 million people worldwide. Because of economical and social issues associated with chronic pain, there is an urgent need to determine the mechanisms whereby the immunoglobulin G (IgG) immune complex (IC) provokes chronic pain. Studies have shown that Fc-gamma receptor I (FcYRI), the high affinity receptor for IgG or IC, is widely expressed in immune cells and its activation by the IC plays an important role in pain generation by inducing cytokine release from the immune cells. Besides its indirect effects, however, little is known whether the IC directly excites the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons though neuronal FcYRI. This project is proposed to investigate the role of neuronal FcYRI in the pathogenesis of chronic pain at the periphery tissues. Special interest will be firstly given to evaluate pain-related behavior in wild-type and neuronal FcYRI knockout mice in vivo after injection of IC into the hindpaws of mice. Secondly, we will characterize the expression pattern of FcYRI with other nociceptive markers in DRG neurons using immunohistochemistry in vitro. Finally, we will further determine the effects of FcYRI activation on the excitability of DRG neurons and the associated cellular signaling/ionic mechanisms in vitro. This study will reveal a novel immune mechanism of chronic pain driven by the antigen-specific immune responses via the direct effects of IC on neuronal FcYRI. It will provide new therapeutic strategies to prevent and treat chronic pain in immune-related diseases in human using neuronal FcYRI as a target.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of AMPA Receptor Phosphorylation in Homeostatic Scaling of Synaptic Strength
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPA RECEPTOR; LEARNING AND MEMORY; PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: The synapse is the site where neurons in the brain contact one and other and communicate by a process referred to as synaptic transmission. Synapses can change in strength, getting either depressed (weaker) or potentiated (stronger), and it is these changes which are believed to form the basis of learning and memory. A given neuron may have up to 10,000 synapses, each of which may change in strength independently. However, the neuron must maintain the average strength of synapses within a defined range in order to function properly in the brain. If too many synapses become potentiated or depressed the neuron may stray from the normal activity range and cease to function properly. To maintain normal function the neuron uses a process called homeostatic scaling, whereby all or many synapses at once are strengthened or weakened. Importantly, when certain synapses have been potentiated or depressed relative to nearby unaltered synapses the relative differences in the strength of individual synapses must be protected during scaling as these differences form a pattern that forms the basis of memory. The basis for how neurons are able to protect the relative differences in individual strengths of synapses during scaling is not known. If scaling cannot occur properly, synapses may become too strong or too weak, possibly leading to neurological diseases such as epilepsy, where synaptic activity is too high, or schizophrenia, where synaptic activity is too weak. If scaling occurs without protecting individual synapse strength this may eventually lead to memory loss as occurs in some forms of dementia and Alzheimers disease. Therefore, this work will contribute to a basic understanding of brain function and offer new insights into the basis of several neurological diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Proteomic and Degradomic Analysis of the Tumor Microenvironment of Breast Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: (TAILS) TERMINAL AMINE ISOTOPIC LABELING OF SUBSTRATES; BIOINFORMATICS; CALCIUM FLUX ASSAY; CANCER IMAGING; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MACROPHAGE ASSAYS; MASS SPECTOMETRY; PROTEASE BIOCHEMISTRY; PROTEASE INHIBITORS; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is an interactive multi-cell, multi-tissue lesion dynamically linked to the stroma by signaling networks that regulate gene and protein expression, and post-translational modifications within the tumor and microenvironment. By the irreversible processing of bioactive proteins and signaling molecules, proteases modulate angiogenesis, growth, invasion, metastasis, and phenotypic evolution of cancer cells together with micro-environmental and host defense responses. Pioneering work by our lab on the proteomics of Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs) has identified and validated a myriad of new bioactive protein substrates in human breast cancer cells. It also revealed new roles for MMPs other than matrix degradation that may also account for the side effects arising from anticancer MMP inhibitor drugs. However, the protease repertoire-the degradome activity profile, and key substrates in breast cancer metastases remain unknown. Using our protease and inhibitor oligonucleotide microarray, the CLIP-CHIP, the protease transcriptome of the metastatic versus primary breast cancer tumors will be compared. To validate the breast cancer transcriptome, quantitative proteomics will be utilized to compare breast cancer metastases with primary tumors in mouse models. Cell membrane receptors, matrix proteins, signaling molecules, chemokines and proteases that are essential for the establishment and evolution of breast carcinoma metastases in bone, liver and lung will be identified in these proteomes by absolute quantitation isotope-labeled and tandem mass spectrometry. Key mediators will be mechanistically validated for cellular, transcriptome, and proteome responses in cell culture. Elucidating the key proteomic and degradomic features of metastases and primary breast carcinomas will reveal the mechanistic basis for organ trophism, metastases evolution, immune cell evasion and drug resistance, thereby identifying molecular targets to treat breast cancer metastases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting function from taxonomy to reveal insights into the human microbiome
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA; BIOINFORMATICS; CHRON'S DISEASE; DIAGNOSIS; HUMAN MICROBIOME; IRRITABLE BOWEL DISEASE; METABOLIC RECONSTRUCTION; METAGENOMICS; OBESITY; SYMBIOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Bacteria are living all over and within our bodies, and in fact outnumber our own cells 10 to 1. These are mainly "good" bacteria that reside in normal healthy people, but can be killed by the same antibiotics that are used to treat us when we are sick with "bad" bacteria. Until recently, not much was known about the different species of bacteria living on us and how that differed across different sites on our bodies, between individuals, and over our lifetime. Interestingly, recent research has shown that these communities likely have an impact on our nutrition, obesity, immune system, and various conditions such as Crohn's disease and Irritable Bowel Syndrome.  The method used to discover these relationships is to identify the bacterial species and molecular functions that those species encode across various types of people. This is done by sequencing the DNA of each sample as a single jumbled bag of random fragments. Highly sophisticated computer programs are then used to figure out which fragments likely came from a particular species and what bacterial genes are associated with different types of people.   My proposed research is to develop new computational algorithms to better highlight the biological interesting differences between microbiomes from varying sites and people. My methods will utilize the massive amounts of information contained within the more than 2000 bacterial genomes that have already been sequenced by the research community. This information will be used to predict the functions encoded by bacteria that we have not sequenced yet, but are present within our mircobiomes. Once these computer programs are implemented, they will be freely available for all researchers to use and will allow us as well as others to obtain further insight into the human microbiome and its effect on our health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards a Universal Influenza Virus Vaccine
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODIES; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLUENZA; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Seasonal influenza A virus (IAV) outbreaks represent a significant burden to global healthcare systems.  In Canada alone, there were over 39 000 reported cases of IAV during the 2009-2010 season. During the course of a normal season, IAV infections are responsible for 700-2500 deaths. However, rates of infection and mortality can increase greatly during periodic pandemics. The major natural hosts of IAV are aquatic birds, however the virus has been able to adapt well to infection of many mammalian species. Swine, in particular, are susceptible to infection by both avian and human IAVs, making them an important vessel for the generation of reassortant viruses that have the potential to cause serious disease in humans. IAV is also prone to rapid mutation. Together, these factors contribute to the ability of IAV to evade the immune system and cause seasonal disease. The haemagglutinin (HA) protein is the major target of the neutralizing antibody response to IAV. The globular head domain of this protein mutates readily and can then evade pre-existing immunity from prior immunization or infection. Recently, an invariant region has been discovered in the stalk domain of the HA protein. This domain is not normally antigenically predominant on the surface of the virus. However, recent studies by our group and others, have shown that immunization of mice with 'headless' HA protein can elicit a broadly neutralizing antibody response targeted to this conserved region of the HA stalk. Our current work will focus on refining these initial studies by testing multiple iterations of stalk domain-based peptides to determine which provide the greatest and most broadly-active protection. This work will contribute to the development of a vaccine which will have a major impact on the improvement of global health while eliminating the significant economic burder associated with seasonal IAV vaccination programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multi-modal assessment of anti-amyloid intervention in a monkey model of Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING (DTI); DRUG TREATMENTS; FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY; FUNCTIONAL MRI (FMRI); IMAGING; MONKEY MODEL; SPECTROSCOPY; VOXEL-BASED MORPHOLOGY; B-AMYLOID
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disease in adults. Due to our aging population, the number of Canadians with AD is expected to increase dramatically, with more than 1 million affected Canadians by 2038, thereby posing a major challenge to our health care system and society. From a clinical perspective, both improved treatment and an accurate and early diagnosis of AD is required to avert an impending crisis in health care. By the time a diagnosis of AD is established by current methods which include assessment of memory and functional capabilities, substantial damage has already occurred in the brain, limiting the effectiveness of current neuroprotective treatments. It is proposed that the critical factor in the success of AD therapies is the early detection of the disease before patients suffer from clinically detectable dementia. This research aims to establish early biomarkers of AD in a monkey model and assess drug treatments given at different stages of AD progression. Monkeys will be assessed on a battery of behavioral and cognitive tasks as well as monitoring physiological measures commonly altered in patients suffering from AD. High-resolution imaging will be carried out on Canada's only 7 Tesla MR scanner. Monkeys will then receive injections of proteins known to cause AD and then be assessed weekly to track any potential changes. Once the normal progression of the disease model is characterized, new animals will receive drug treatment administered at different post-injection times. The advent of a reliable monkey model for pre-symptomatic AD and symptomatic AD will allow the development of early diagnostic biomarkers as well as a new generation of disease modification and prevention trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiolipin synthesis as a therapy for heart failure in persistent pulmonary hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOLIPIN; GENE DELIVERY; HEART FAILURE; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; PHOSPHOLIPIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) is a rare but life-threatening condition that affects full term babies. When the fetus is in the womb the requirement for oxygen is met by the mother.  Normally at birth, the blood vessels in the lungs widen (dilate) to let blood in and obtain oxygen. However, in PPHN patients the vessels in the lung do not widen. This can be caused by a difficult birth in which the baby does not receive enough oxygen, or an infection. As a result the right side of the heart, responsible for pumping blood to the lungs, needs to work harder causing damage to the heart that reduces the amount of blood it pumps (termed contractile dysfunction).  Contractile dysfunction is the main reason that patients with PPHN do not survive.  Current treatments involve increasing oxygen levels in the blood. While these treatments deliver adequate oxygen to various organs (brain, liver etc.), the heart still becomes damaged and stops contracting properly in many patients.  One reason for contractile dysfunction is that the heart does not produce enough energy. Similar to how a car uses an engine to convert gas to energy, tissues in the body use mitochondria to convert food (sugar, fat) to energy. In the heart, a complex molecule called cardiolipin (CL) is a structural component of mitochondria. When levels of CL are reduced, the mitochondria does not produce enough energy for the heart. Although it is known that CL levels are reduced in PPHN, no one has determined whether  restoring the level of CL in the heart prevents the progression to heart failure.  Using sophisticated and innovative approaches such as an exciting new method for delivering genes to cardiac tissue of live neonatal pigs with PPHN, we will shed light on whether increasing CL levels in the heart is a viable approach to improve the cardiac function in PPHN and thus increase patient survival.

TitreApplicationTitle: Merging existing health and health-related quality of life patient-reported outcomes for children with epilepsy: Development towards national standards
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD; EPILEPSY; FACTOR ANALYSES; HEALTH STATUS; INTERNATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF FUNCTIONING (ICF); MEASUREMENT STANDARDS; PATIENT REPORTED OUTCOME; QUALITY OF LIFE; RASCH ANALYSIS; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: There are many health and quality of life (QOL) issues associated with having epilepsy in childhood. Problems with remembering, concentrating at school, emotional difficulties, making friends and receiving the right supports from teachers and parents are common. These problems are tracked by health care providers using questionnaires so that clinicians and policy makers can figure out which treatments really make a difference in the day to day lives of these children. Unfortunately, most programs use different questionnaires to track these important outcomes. The way these questionnaires are composed makes it difficult to compare their results between epilepsy programs. So how do we know which treatments are making the biggest difference or which kids have the most severe problems? At this time, it is difficult to know for sure, so standards need to be developed to measure health and QOL across programs. Most projects devoted to implementing standards like these, call for clinical programs to adopt new questionnaires. The problem with adopting new ways of collecting this information usually means a program abandons the previously collected data. This project will work to roll out new standards based on the best evidence while figuring out if programs can keep all or parts of the questionnaires that they are already using. According to this way of doing things, programs can continue to use their old questionnaires, keep the data they have on their children, while the project develops ways for the programs to move towards an evidence-based way of doing things that is consistent across the country. Adopting new ways of collecting data when the old ways have some problems is akin to throwing out the baby with the bath water. This project is devoted to finding out what data from the old could and should be kept, while merging that data into new methods for collecting information about health and QOL for children with epilepsy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of dietary changes on long-term weight gain: the role of specific foods and nutritional policies
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE RISK; DIET QUALITY; NUTRITION; NUTRITION POLICY; OBESITY; PUBLIC HEALTH; WEIGHT GAIN
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is a leading cause of death and disability. Diet has an important role in the development of obesity; yet, the role of specific foods is still not fully understood. For example, previous research has shown that processed and unprocessed meats have very different effects on long-term weight gain. Further, it is not known which policies are effective in influencing individuals to make healthier dietary choices. Therefore, I will address these questions through three aims. The first aim is to determine the relationship between specific foods and long-term weight gain. I will investigate the diet of 120 877 people over 20 years to determine if the consumption of poultry, fish, beans, meats and dairy is related to long-term weight gain. The second aim will be an extension of the first and determine how specific foods influence not just long-term weight gain but patterns of weight gain/loss within individuals. We will identify and characterize patterns of weight gain and loss (e.g. weight maintenance, steady weight gain or cycles of weight gain/loss with or without net weight gain) and investigate their relationships to diet. The third aim will investigate the effectiveness of nutritional policies. Several population-level efforts have been developed to influence individuals' food choices with the goal of improving public health; however, no systematic review of the effectiveness of these policies has been done. We will do a comprehensive review of published research on nutrition policy and directly compare the policies to one another to determine which have the strongest evidence for a beneficial effect on preventing/reducing obesity. In the future, we will extend this analysis to investigate the cost-effectiveness of policies and the effect of policies on the risk for diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Overall, results from this fellowship will inform individuals, health professionals and policy developers on healthy dietary choices and effective policies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of epiregulin and epidermal growth factor receptor in mediating variability in chronic and inflammatory pain
Keywords-MotsClés: DORSAL ROOT GANGLION; EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; EPIREGULIN; GENETIC; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INFLAMMATION; INTRATHECAL; NEUROPATHIC; PAIN; TYROSINE KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: The basic scientific understanding of pain processing and modulation has greatly increased over the past few decades. A recently completed 5-year, $20 million multi-gene association study aiming to identify the genetic risk factors for pain in patients developing temporomandibular disorder (TMD) pain has identified several key genetic changes. TMD refers to a set of conditions that affect the jaw muscles and/or joint and is the second leading cause of chronic pain for people who report facial or head pain. Patients that developed TMD pain showed a preponderance of genetic changes in or near the genes coding for epiregulin (EREG) and the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) on chromosomes, 4 and 7, respectively. Typically, mutations that lead to EGFR overexpression (called upregulation) or overactivity have been associated with tumours, including lung cancer and colorectal cancer. There is no existing evidence that these genes affect pain, but the results from the human association study suggests that this system may in fact play a crucial role in pain processing. In the current proposal we will use genetic and pharmacological tools to determine whether activation or inhibition of these genes affects sensitivity to painful stimuli in laboratory mice. Further to determine whether the EREG/EGFR system is upregulated in chronic pain conditions we will use receptor staining techniques to identify the location of these proteins in pain-related regions of the nervous system. This research is important because it will allow us to further understand nociceptive processing and regulation by targeting a receptor system that has not been studied for its role in pain. These experiments could help with the development of new high affinity drugs for the EREG/EGFR system for use in pain management.  Since there are already drugs commercially available for cancer treatment that inhibit EGFR, it is possible that these drugs could have broader therapeutic potential.

TitreApplicationTitle: A randomized controlled trial of bright light therapy on post-treatment fatigue, sleep/wake activity and mood in women with breast cancer.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; BRIGHT LIGHT THERAPY; CANCER-RELATED FATIGUE; MOOD; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SLEEP/WAKE RHYTHM
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer-related fatigue is an often debilitating and persistent condition characterized by an overwhelming sense of exhaustion and is experienced by a significant proportion of breast cancer survivors. The causes of, and contributors to, cancer-related fatigue (CRF) are multi-factorial and include behavioral, psychological and physiological determinants. While current treatments have been demonstrated to alleviate symptoms of CRF, they tend to be highly complex, requiring the concentrated efforts of several healthcare providers and significant and often burdensome behavior change on behalf of the patient.  In contrast, bright light therapy (BLT) is simple to administer and adhere to, reducing patient demand. BLT has demonstrated efficacy in alleviating mood and sleep disorders, both of which are associated with the experience of fatigue. Preliminary research also suggests that the use of BLT during chemotherapy prevents the typical worsening of fatigue commonly experienced while on anti-cancer treatments. However, CRF is known to persist past the completion of treatment in a significant number of breast cancer survivors, leaving a many individuals with a disabling long-term side-effect. This study will be the first to investigate the effect of BLT on post-treatment CRF in women with breast cancer. Further, the study will evaluate the psychological and physiological correlates and consequences of CRF in order to better understand the disorder and the impact of BLT on its underlying mechanisms. The use of light therapy for CRF appears to be particularly important to investigate among cancer survivors in Canada, where the potential exposure to morning light is restricted for a significant portion of the year.

Keywords-MotsClés: CHIP-SEQ; CHROMATIN; DEVELOPMENT; DIFFERENTIATION; ENHANCERS; EPIGENETICS; GENE REGULATION; HUMAN EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; NON-CODING RNA; NUCLEAR ORGANIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Almost every cell in human body contains a complete set of genes, but they are not all expressed in every tissue. A heart cell turns on the genes which make it contract, while a neuron would not express these genes. Thus, a cell must decide which genes to turn on or express and which ones to turn off in a precisely regulated manner. Developmental gene regulation can be accomplished in a variety of ways, but often utilizes specialized DNA sequences called enhancers, which are found far away from the gene itself but have the ability to enhance its expression from a distance. This proposal addresses how enhancer activity and, in turn, gene activity is regulated during differentiation of embryonic stem cells. I will probe the molecular mechanisms by which specific enhancers are bookmarked for activation and then deployed in a proper context during differentiation. This work is important for understanding the process of gene regulation and harnessing regenerative potential of stem cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing novel regulators of erythropoiesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ERYTHROPOIESIS; IRON METABOLISM; MODEL ORGANISMS; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Proper red blood cell development requires the incorporation of iron into a prosthetic group named haem.  This is a multistep chemical process that involves the transport of both iron and haem between various compartments within a cell.  A defect in any steps of this series of chemical reactions has drastic consequences on human health and has been implicated in diseases such as anemias and porphyrias.  Current treatments for these disorders only serve to alleviate acute symptoms and are not long-term solutions.  A major obstacle towards designing better treatment modalities is that many genes that are responsible for the transport of iron or haem have not yet been identified or characterized.  Thus, there is a major impetus to elucidate these genes and to dissect the mechanisms underlying how they may function in haem production.  Our lab has recently identified several genes that become enriched in differentiating red blood cells in a similar fashion as other previously characterized haem-synthesis genes.  These genes all encode proteins that function in the transport of molecules inside the cell, suggesting that they may play a role in regulating the movement of iron or haem.  The goal of this proposal is to examine whether this is the case using an array of molecular tools and a unique combination of genetic approaches in zebrafish, mice, and mammalian cells.  Ultimately, the identification of novel genes involved in haem synthesis and erythropoiesis will shed new light into the cause of several human disorders.  Understanding how these genes function will lead to the development of better long-term therapies for these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term effects of common pregnancy complications on susceptibility to pediatric obesity-metabolic syndrome and response to weight management interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: FETAL PROGRAMMING; METABOLIC SYNDROME; OBESITY; OBESITY PROGRAMMING
Abstract-Résumé: There has been a large increase in overweight and obesity in Canada. One in four adult Canadians and one in ten Canadian children are obese. Moreover, it is estimated that the obesity problem costs Canadians 4.3 billion dollars every year. Traditionally, obesity has been attributed to eating too much and exercising too little. Interestingly, there are some people who develop obesity more easily, despite eating the same and doing similar amounts of exercise. They also have more difficulties losing weight despite using the same treatments and interventions. These differences could be attributed to the genes a person inherits from his/her parents. However, there is emerging scientific evidence that makes us believe that these differences could also result from birth-related influences.  Specifically, people who are born from complicated pregnancies may be more likely to develop complications from obesity and less likely to respond to obesity treatment. The objective of the project proposed for this fellowship, therefore, is to determine whether being born following a complicated pregnancy can affect a person's susceptibility to be obese, have more obesity related complications and have more difficulties losing weight later in life. To test this, we will analyze a series of available databases of children with obesity aiming to identify if obese children born following a complicated pregnancy are more likely to have other health issues (such as diabetes or increase cholesterol levels) when compared to obese children born following a normal pregnancy. We will also examine if children born following a complicated pregnancy are less likely to respond to weight loss treatment.  The results of this study may help describing novel risk factors for obesity and may provide new tools to classify and treat subjects with obesity based on whether or not they were born from complicated pregnancies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Best Clinical Practices Research for Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: BEST CLINICAL PRACTICES; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; INSTRUMENTAL VARIABLES; MATERNAL MORBIDITY
Abstract-Résumé: For most families, pregnancy is a happy time where couples look forward to the birth of a healthy baby.  However, pregnancy can put an additional strain on a woman's body and sometimes women experience adverse events such as heart attacks or strokes while they are pregnant.  We know that women in certain parts of the country are more or less likely to experience these events; however, we do not know why.  This project will use medical information to examine these regional differences and to find out if these differences can be best explained by differences in medical practice or differences in the population of pregnant women.  It will look closely at differences in clinical practice and how these differences impact the amount of time women spend in the hospital after these events occur and what proportion of women survive.  After determining what areas have the highest rate of survival and shortest length of stay, an intervention will be designed based on the best available clinical evidence that aims to reduce the occurrence of these events.

TitreApplicationTitle: Application of an in-vivo bioreactor as a biological platform for skin regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTE-DERIVED STEM CELLS; BIOREACTOR CHAMBER; BURN PATIENTS; SKIN; TISSUE ENGINEERING; TISSUE REGENERATION; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, 10,000 patients are annually admitted due to sever thermal injuries. These patients require early wound coverage to survive. Currently, the treatment of choice is autografts, which has considerable limitations, such as lack of donor sites, especially in extensive burn patients. Therefore, the advancement towards engineered tissue will prove to be a tremendous asset for clinical practices in wound care. However, there are many methods to engineer tissue, one of these is using bioreactors. Bioreactors are able to create an ideal environment for the generation of tissue. Our group has recently developed a bioreactor that allows flow perfusion and sampling of the generated tissue as well as its fluid. Preliminary data has shown that adipocyte-derived stem cells (ASC) are able to improve healing in-vivo. The aim of this study is to use ASC in our in-vivo bioreactor to generate skin in a mouse model. Our hypothesis is that ASC may differentiate into skin in our in-vivo bioreactor. To achieve this, the tissue growth, cellular infiltration, angiogenesis and tissue perfusion in the in-vivo bioreactor will be evaluated. Also, differentiation of ASC to fibroblasts, keratinocytes and endothelial cells will be induced. Conditions of these differentiation processes will be optimized and applied into our in-vivo bioreactor model.  Finally, tissue growth will be accelerated with the incorporation of nutrient-rich perfusates into our in-vivo bioreactor. The knowledge generated through the development of an in-vivo bioreactor plus the generation of skin tissue will set the stage for a new era of tissue engineering resulting in a novel paradigm for how to treat extensive burns and possible chronic wounds, which will translate into better quality of life for patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Resveratrol prevents doxorubicin-induced cardiac dysfunction and heart failure
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; CANCER; CARDIOTOXICITY; DOXORUBICIN; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; HEART FAILURE; HISTOPATHOLOGY; REAL-TIME PCR; RESVERATROL; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Nowadays, many patients can survive cancer thanks to advanced screening and therapy, but the anti-cancer therapy may have serious side effects that affect other parts of the body. For example, doxorubicin which is an effective anti-cancer drug may also cause heart failure. Unfortunately, the exact mechanism of doxorubicin-induced heart failure and the best prevention or treatment for this complication is still not known. Interestingly, resveratrol which is an active ingredient in red grapes and red wine is known to protect the heart from several forms of stress. Resveratrol protects the heart by increasing the activity of an enzyme that improves the energy utilization by the heart. This enzyme is called AMP-activated protein kinase. Therefore, we hypothesize that resveratrol will also protect against doxorubicin-induced heart failure by increasing the activity of this enzyme. In addition, we hypothesize that resveratrol will also enhance the anti-cancer effect of doxorubicin. In order to test these hypotheses, we will perform a series of experiments. First, we will examine the heart function in doxorubicin-treated mice treated with or without resveratrol to confirm the protective effect of resveratrol against doxorubicin-induced heart failure. Second, we will investigate the protective effect of resveratrol in mice that lack the AMP-activated protein kinase to know if the protective effect of resveratrol depends on this enzyme. Third, we will investigate if the administration of resveratrol will increase the anti-cancer effect of doxorubicin in mice with cancer. Together these experiments will help us understand the mechanism of doxorubicin-induced heart failure and to confirm that resveratrol is able to prevent it. This may allow us to use resveratrol in cancer patients to improve the benefit and reduce the risk of doxorubicin-based therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of lactation and oxytocin in depressive-like behaviours during the postpartum period
Keywords-MotsClés: BREASTFEEDING; HIPPOCAMPUS; LACTATION; NEUROGENESIS; OXYTOCIN; POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION; RATS; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Postpartum depression (PPD) affects ~15% of women after giving birth but the causes of PPD are not fully understood. There is significant clinical overlap between women who discontinue breastfeeding and women who are diagnosed with PPD. It is possible that elimination of breastfeeding increases the risk for PPD. The proposed studies are designed to investigate the behavioural and brain consequences of disrupted lactation in a rat model of PPD. First, female rats will undergo surgery to prevent lactation (called a galactophore cut). Control rats will undergo sham surgery. Rats will then be mated and after giving birth, assessed for depressive-like behaviours and brain plasticity, which have been consistently associated with depression.  Oxytocin is a hormone known for its role in milk let down, social bonding, and maternal behaviour. Lactation or nursing behaviours increase brain levels of oxytocin. If disrupted lactation induces depressive-like behaviours and alters hippocampal plasticity, then oxytocin may be involved. The following two studies will determine the role of oxytocin in depressive-like behaviour induced by disrupted lactation. Postpartum females will undergo conditions in which oxytocin levels are reduced (either through surgery or through drug treatment) to determine whether oxytocin levels are important for the development of depressive-like symptoms. Dams will be assessed for depressive-like behaviors and hippocampal plasticity. I hypothesize that disrupted oxytocin will induce depressive-like behaviours and alter hippocampal plasticity consistent with other animal models of depression. Further, oxytocin will reverse these changes. Collectively, this research will identify whether oxytocin levels in the brain play a role in PPD. This research will be important for discovering new treatments for women who develop PPD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Large-scale Analysis of Neuron Type Specificity in the Motion Vision System
Keywords-MotsClés: ALGORITHM; COMPUTATIONAL BIOLOGY; DATA INTEGRATION; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; DROSOPHILA; GENOMICS; NEUROSCIENCE; REGULATORY NETWORK; SEQUENCING; VISUAL SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Motion vision is used to control orientation and movement by perceiving the relative distance to other objects in the three-dimensional structure of the environment. As one of the essential functions of the visual system, motion vision is sensed by a sophisticated coding process culminating in the diverse output of many types of neurons located in different layers of the optic lobe. In the fruit fly, the photoreceptors provide inputs, directly or indirectly, to neurons in the next layer of the optic lobe, the lamina. Lamina neurons then extend their axons into the medulla where they make connections that in turn provide excitatory and inhibitory input onto the motion-sensitive neurons located in the lobula plate, completing the information relay. Although the hierarchy of the neurons involved in motion sensing is extensively studied, the underlying neural mechanisms of their function disparity and their wiring remain largely unclear. In this project, I will attempt to identify the genetic factors that cause the differences between these neurons in terms of their morphology, function and synaptic connections with their proper postsynaptic partners in the visual system by large-scale transcriptomic analysis. I will use fruit fly for these studies due to the fact that the vertebrate and invertebrate motion vision systems are conserved as well as the manageable size of its nervous system, its well-mapped visual circuits and the large number of available genetic techniques. This will be the first large-scale study to investigate the transcriptome of related neurons in the motion visual system. This study will uncover general design principles that outline the precise architecture of neural circuits in the brain and help us understand the molecular etiology of disorders (i.e. synesthesia, epilepsy) associated with abnormal wiring of neural circuits.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the role of miR-181 genes in normal and pathogenic plasma cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: B CELL; MICRORNA; PLASMA CELLS; SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS
Abstract-Résumé: The genetic mechanisms that regulate the development, function and maintenance antibody-producing plasma cells are largely unknown.  Plasma cells are antibody-producing cells that play an important role in the immune response to foreign pathogens. By producing antibodies that are specific to pathogens our immune system is able to effectively control and eliminate the infection.  This study is aimed at determining the role of functional genetic sequences, known as microRNAs, in the regulation of antibody-producing plasma cell development, function and maintenance. MicroRNAs are short non-coding nucleotide sequences that have been shown to play a role in immune cell development and function. Once regarded as "junk" RNAs, microRNAs impact upon the expression of genes in almost half of the human genome. Recently, we discovered that a family of microRNAs is highly expressed in antibody-producing plasma cells.  This was followed by the observation that these microRNAs are predicted to silence genes necessary for the development of antibody-producing plasma cells.  Thus, we hypothesized that these microRNAs play an integral role in antibody-producing plasma cells. We will test this hypothesis using techniques to eliminate this family of microRNAs during antibody-producing plasma cell development.  The findings of this study will provide further insight into the treatment of human diseases caused by the dysregulation of antibody-producing plasma cells, including multiple myeloma (a plasma cell cancer) and systemic lupus erythematosus (commonly known as lupus).  Currently there is no cure for either disease.  Both are widely treated through non-specific immunosuppressive therapy but relapses occur. Discovering a way to specifically eliminate the development and production of antibody-producing plasma cells would provide a specific and potentially more effective treatment for these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of human cytotolytic T lymphocyte polyfunctionality and clonality in vaccinated melanoma patients at the single-cell level.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN-SPECIFIC T CELLS; CD8+ T LYMPHOCYTES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; IMMUNOTHERAPY; MELANOMA; POLYFUNCTIONALITY; SINGLE-CELL SORTING; T LYMPHOCYTE DIFFERENTIATION; TCR CLONOTYPE REPERTOIRE; TUMOR-ANTIGEN SPECIFIC TETRAMERS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer therapy has made tremendous improvements in recent years through the optimization of surgical and non-surgical therapeutic approaches. Novel therapies, such as immunotherapy, are currently being evaluated in clinical trails to specifically target late-stage cancer.  Therapeutic vaccination or immunotherapy consists in the activation of the patient's own specialized cytolytic immune T cells, thereby leading to the specific killing of tumor cells. Contrary to vaccination against viruses, which promotes an immunological attack against a foreign pathogen, in cancer, the immune system must be instructed to recognize the subtle differences between normal and malignant cells. Consequently, an immune response against tumor cells is weaker than against virally-infected cells. To counter this, our team has designed novel vaccination procedures to improve the potency of the immune reaction generated against the tumor. Another aspect currently studied by our group consists in the molecular and functional characterization of the most powerful cytotoxic immune cells among the effectors CD8+ T cells.  Thus, using state-of-the art equipment, the goal of my project is to characterize tumor-specific cytolytic T lymphocytes at the single cell level. With this level of precision, we will be able to follow ex vivo the persistence of the anti-tumor immune response following vaccination of melanoma patients by monitoring the expression of unique T cell receptor sequences at defined time points and in various anatomical compartments. Furthermore, we will be able to further understand why certain CD8+ T cell subsets are more cytotoxic than others, and to pinpoint the mechanisms of T cell recruitment in well-defined clinical situations.  In conclusion, we are convinced that a better understanding of the biology of human immune system and of the intricate interactions between immune and cancer cells will led to significant improvements in the potency of immune-based therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of autophagy and posttranslationally myristoylated huntingtin in Huntington disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; AUTOPHAGY; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; MOUSE BEHAVIOR; MYRISTOYLATION; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROPATHOLGY
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington disease (HD) is an inherited, fatal, neurodegenerative disease characterised by loss of coordinated movement, dementia and psychiatric disturbances. Death usually occurs in 15-20 years after onset of symptoms. It is caused by a mutation of a protein called Huntingtin that causes the protein to build up and inhibit essential cellular functions that leads to neuronal cell death and eventually neurodegeneration. Proper localization of proteins within a cell is essential to their function, activities and for overall cell viability. Improper localization can lead to malfunctioning of proteins and in some cases cell death or cancer. The addition of lipid to specific proteins is one system the cell employs to regulate this process. A form of lipid modification known as myristoylation is essential for some proteins to re-localise in the cell. I recently identified a region of Huntingtin that undergoes this modification. It appears to be essential for maintaining healthy cell balance. I intend to study the role of this modification in the progression of Huntington's disease using a well established mouse model designed in the Hayden laboratory. This modification is a novel site of regulation of Huntingtin protein and may serve as an ideal target for therapeutic treatment of Huntington's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Attribution of Illness to 'Old Age': Addressing an Age-Related Stereotype with Attributional Retraining
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; HEALTH PSYCHOLOGY; PSYCHOSOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Age-related stereotypes can negatively impact older adults' health. One particularly insidious stereotype involves the belief that 'old people are sick' and that chronic illnesses (such as diabetes or heart disease) are a 'normal part of aging.' This stereotype embodies a dangerous logic: If age causes illness - and aging is uncontrollable - then illness is also uncontrollable. When self-directed, this belief can result in a reduced sense of responsibility for health, and can be a barrier to health maintenance behavior (e.g., getting enough exercise). Indeed, research demonstrates that older adults who attribute illness to 'old age' are at an increased risk for detrimental outcomes including hospitalization and earlier death. The objectives of this research are: 1) To examine who is most susceptible to these 'old age' attributions; and 2) To test the effectiveness of a brief attributional retraining intervention designed to address these attributions. Participants (N = 200, ages 45-65) will be assessed in terms of their attributions for illness, socio-demographic factors, psychosocial characteristics, and health behaviors; and will be assigned to either a treatment group (intervention) or a control group (no intervention). It is hypothesized that 1) 'old age' attributions will be associated with greater age, lower education, and poorer health status, as well as several psychosocial variables (e.g., pessimism); thereby allowing for the creation of a 'profile' of individuals who are most at-risk; 2) compared to the control group, participants who receive the attributional retraining intervention will show a decrease in the belief that old age causes illness, and an increase in motivation with regard to health maintenance behaviors. This research represents a first step towards the transfer of research knowledge into action in the area of illness attributions - and has the potential to improve health outcomes among older adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biomaterial factors in methacrylic acid induced wound healing and angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; BIOMATERIALS; DIABETES; GENE EXPRESSION; MEDICAL DEVICES; POLYMERS; SCREENING TOOLS; TISSUE ENGINEERING; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, 15% of diabetics will develop chronic wounds that lower quality of life, increase medical costs and result in numerous amputations.  Advanced wound dressings that enable diabetic wound healing and functional tissue constructs for tissue regeneration are among the many medical needs that depend on therapeutic vascularisation. Implantable glucose sensors are other devices that would also benefit from a vascularised, rather than a fibrotic, foreign body response. This project is directed towards understanding why one particular biomaterial is pro-angiogenic so as to devise strategies for incorporating this material into medical devices that would benefit those who live with diabetes and other diseases.   Previous work in the Sefton lab shows that poly(methacrylic acid-co-methyl methacrylate) beads (PMAAcoMMA beads) promote wound healing and angiogenesis in normal and diabetic animal models compared to  inert controls of poly methylmethacrylate.  The focus here is to understand what it is about the methacrylic acid (MAA) in PMAAcoMMA that causes the changes in gene expression and ultimately angiogenesis.    The aims of this research are to develop new angiogenic materials and to use them as screening tools to identify cells and factors important in wound healing and angiogenesis.  We hypothesize that the MAA is the functional group promoting bead angiogenesis and that coatings and films of varying MAA content and roughness will have modulated biological responses.  In the proposed research, I will help develop a fundamental understanding of the cellular mechanisms of biomaterial-induced wound healing and angiogenesis by exploring cell behaviour and protein adsorption on various MAA-based biomaterials.  The newly synthesize films and coatings may also ultimately lead to the creation of novel devices for diabetic wound treatments and tissue engineering.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: SYSTÈME NERVEUX; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Incentive to Stay Awake? Descending Control over the Ascending Arousal System
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTICAL CONTROL OVER HOMEOSTASIS; FRONTAL CORTEX; HIGH-ENSITY (100 ELECTRODE) ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; INSOMNIA; MEDIAL FOREBRAIN REWARD; NEURAL REPLAY; RATS; SINGLE UNIT AND BRAIN-WAVE RECORDING IN-VIVO; SLEEP HOMOESTASIS; WAKEFULNESS
Abstract-Résumé: It is common to stay awake past our regular sleep time so that particular plans and goals can be achieved. The ascending arousal system of the brainstem and hypothalamus is thought to activate the cerebral cortex and maintain wakefulness. However, this arousal system is insufficient to account for why an individual can stay awake in order to receive a reward. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is the only cortical brain region which can directly influence all of the ascending arousal systems and is also involved in assessing the value of rewards. The series of hypotheses in this proposal seek to answer whether or not the activity the mPFC is necessary for the maintenance of wakefulness under sleep pressure. In the current proposal, a paradigm is used in which animal can predict the future occurrence of a reward only if they maintain wakefulness. This paradigm will allow us to test whether mPFC is helps extend wakefulness under conditions of anticipated reward. Pharmacological (e.g. lidocaine) blockade of the mPFC will be used to directly examine the necessity of the mPFC in this paradigm. Additional experiments will examine whether patterns of neural activity in the mPFC, which reflect the expected reward, are related to the duration of wakefulness maintained. Finally, we will examine whether patterns of neural activity which demonstrates expectancy for the reward are more or less susceptible to sleepiness (i.e. micro-sleeps). This finding would argue that the associative connectivity (e.g. synaptic strength) of the network is involved in maintaining wakefulness. Altogether, this work will attempt to elaborate on the traditional arousal system to include top-down control from the mPFC and will have direct impact on our understanding of insomnia and how we maintain our sleepy life style.
