TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of health service intervention on outcomes for children with ASD in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; DEVELOPMENTAL TRAJECTORIES; INTERVENTION OUTCOMES; SECONDARY ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Every year, many children are diagnosed with autism, currently 1 in 110 children. In Canada, provincial governments have attempted to address the need of this growing population by increasing funding for children with autism to obtain early intervention. Since the challenges in abilities vary widely across the population of children with autism, there are many interventions that could be involved concurrently. These interventions and the intensity of the available health services vary across provinces. Even though research exists on the effects of individual interventions, research has not yet looked at the combination and intensity of interventions that best suit individuals with autism. To examine the factors of health services received and how it relates to his or her developmental outcomes would provide insight on this topic. My research project aims to do this by way of conducting a series of statistical analyses on a large pool of data from a world-renowned study in Canada, the Pathways study in autism. Since 2004, the Pathways study has followed children with autism across Canada from diagnosis into adolescence. The data collected involves tracking their interventions received in addition to being assessed on various measures about their skills and abilities. The Pathways study acts as a natural experiment that studies the progress of these children while receiving various interventions. My research project will identify the interventions, and associated factors, that contribute to various outcomes. This work will generate information that will help parents guide their decisions in health services, and will provide knowledge for provincial policy makers to understand the impact of different intervention clusters on children with autism. This work will improve future autism intervention research by examining how different factors associated with intervention for groups of children with autism, contributes to the measured changes in the abilities of the child.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the Possible Role of Dopamine and Glutamate Gene Networks in Response Inhibition to Understand the Genetics of Childhood Neuropsychiatric Disorders.
Keywords-MotsClés: BASOLATERAL AMYGDALA; COCAINE; CREB; DRUG ADDICTION; RELAPSE; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Long after an addicted individual has become drug-free, simple events or circumstances previously associated with prior drug use (cues; e.g., walking through a particular neighbourhood or hearing a particular song) can reawaken powerful memories that can trigger drug craving and provoke relapse. This type of cue-evoked relapse is a major roadblock to treating addiction. The aim of these proposed studies is to understand the brain mechanisms that mediate the association of cues with the rewarding properties of cocaine and to determine if disrupting expression of this memory can help prevent relapse. We will use a mouse model of drug-taking referred to as cocaine self-administration. Mice learn to press a lever to receive cocaine and a cue (a light). Then after a period of abstinence during which the lever no longer delivers the drug or cue, we measure if exposure to the cue or drug triggers the mouse to respond on the lever again (model of relapse). We will test the hypothesis that the processes that mediate this form of cue-drug learning are similar to those that underlie the formation of other types of memory, such as a fear memory. We will then determine if we can disrupt this 'cue-drug memory' such that mice will no longer seek cocaine even when the cue is presented using the same molecular tools that recently allowed us to block the expression of a previously established fear memory. Given that there are many similarities between a cue-drug memory and a cue-shock memory (a conditioned fear memory), we believe that this may be possible. The results of these studies may have far-reaching implications. Not only will the results of these studies inform us as to the biology underlying the development and expression of cue-cocaine associations, but, these findings could also serve as a foundation for the development of new pharmacotherapies to treat or even prevent drug relapse.

TitreApplicationTitle: An analysis of stakeholder attitudes towards the role and application of informed consent for expanded newborn bloodspot screening
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTITUDES; FOCUS GROUPS; INFORMED CONSENT; INTERVIEWS; NEWBORN SCREENING; QUESTIONNAIRE; STAKEHOLDER
Abstract-Résumé: Newborn screening is the program through which babies are screened for a variety of conditions shortly after birth. Whilst it resembles a traditional public health program - because is aimed at large groups of the parents and offered to people considered healthy - it is done on an individual basis. However, there is a possible conflict between promoting what experts feel is an effective public health program and allowing individuals to make an informed choice, which may include refusals. To date we have little information on the views of different stakeholders (parents, healthcare professionals, policy-makers) about the role of this choice and how best to deal with this possible conflict.  The aim of this research is to explore this role of choice using newborn screening as a case study.   This research is arranged in two parts. The first stage involves interviews and discussion groups with parents, healthcare professionals and policy-makers to explore their views and experiences of choice and informed consent within screening. This will identify key issues to be taken forward.  The second stage involves a survey based on stage one that will be sent to key decision makers, patients, and healthcare professionals. We will analyze responses to look for different sorts of views and see if these are linked to the type of person responding e.g do patients hold different views to healthcare professionals or policy-makers.  We hope that the research will identify where people have similar views and where there are differences, together with how and where they happen. By doing so we hope that we can improve both policy and the informed consent process by making communication clearer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Can Pavlovian Cues Promote Re-emergence of Habits? Dissecting the Interactions between Dorsal and Ventral Striatal Structures using Optogenetics
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; COCAINE; CUES; DOPAMINE; DRUGS; INCENTIVE SALIENCE; INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES; MOTIVATION; NUCLEUS ACCUMBENS; VOLTAMMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: The majority of individuals try potentially addictive drugs (e.g., alcohol, nicotine) at some point in their life. Only a small number of them, however, move from recreational use to compulsive and excessive use that is characteristic of addiction. Furthermore, even following long periods of abstinence, addicted individuals often relapse. In fact, relapse occurs in vast majority of addicted individuals and it represents the greatest challenge in the treatment of addiction. Experimental and clinical evidence suggests that cues or stimuli associated with drug use  (e.g., cigarette smoke, a wine glass, needles, etc.) can themselves acquire motivational properties, and thus spur motivation or craving for the drug and increases the likelihood of relapse. Importantly, there are significant individual differences in the degree to which drug-cues can trigger drug craving.  Human positron emission topography studies, as well as preclinical evidence from rat studies, indirectly suggest that brain neurotransmitter dopamine (DA) levels are correlated with cue-evoked drug craving.  In the current project we propose to assess the relationship between the propensity to attribute motivational value to a drug cue (individual differences in attraction to drug-cues), DA concentrations, and the tendency to relapse to drug seeking. We hypothesize that relapse can be predicted by observing how attracted individuals are to drug-cues and drug-cue evoked DA release.  We will use novel and advanced technology (fast-scan cyclic voltammetry), capable of measuring sub-second changes in DA transmission (real-time DA).  Given that there are great individual differences in susceptibility to addiction and that these differences are poorly understood, the proposed pre-clinical experiments are of great importance. Our results will advance our theoretical understating about addiction as well as interventions and treatments for drug addiction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of small peptide inhibitors to islet amyloid polypeptide formation during type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT; DIABETES; LIPIDS; MICRORNA; PANCREATIC ISLET
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Type 2 diabetes currently affects 2.5 million Canadians. Elevated blood cholesterol is associated with an increased risk of developing diabetes. Interestingly, accumulation of cholesterol in insulin secreting beta cells leads to impaired insulin secretion. ABCA1 is a transporter that removes cholesterol from cells, which in deficiency leads to cholesterol accumulation in beta cells. Objectives: To discover ways to regulate ABCA1 levels in beta cells in order to improve cell function and survival. Research Project: I will use small molecules called microRNA to regulate ABCA1 levels in mouse beta cells and determine effects on beta cell function and survival. Relevance: Since ABCA1 has been shown to have a positive impact on beta cell function, finding ways to increase its levels in these cells may be helpful in ameliorating beta cell defects present in diabetes. Thus these studies are the first to outline a therapeutic strategy to modulate cholesterol in beta cells in order to improve whole body glucose homeostasis.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the transcriptional co-repressor RIP 140 in muscular dystrophy: a therapeutic target?
Keywords-MotsClés: DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; GENE EXPRESSION; MDX MICE; PGC-1 ALPHA; PLASTICITY; PPAR DELTA; RIP 140; SKELETAL MUSCLE; THERAPEUTIC TARGET; UTROPHIN
Abstract-Résumé: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is the most prevalent inherited neuromuscular disorder. This disease is extremely severe as children become wheelchair-bound by early adolescence and death occurs in their second or third decade of life. DMD results from mutations/deletions in the dystrophin gene which prevents production of the dystrophin protein. A therapeutic strategy consists of utilizing a protein normally expressed in dystrophic muscle which, once expressed at appropriate levels and at the correct location, could functionally compensate for the lack of dystrophin. A candidate for such a role is utrophin. It has been demonstrated that increasing the abundance of slow-twitch muscle fibers, which have an abundance of utrophin, can reduce the severity of DMD. The muscle protein RIP 140 has recently been discovered to reduce the expression of slow-twitch muscle fibers in animals. However, the role that this protein plays in DMD is unknown. Thus, the purpose of this proposal is to determine the role of RIP 140 in the pathology of DMD. This study tests the hypothesis that RIP 140 represses the expression of slow-twitch muscle fibers, and consequently utrophin, and thus exacerbates the pathology of DMD. To test this hypothesis, we will employ a measured and systematic approach to determine 1) the expression and localization patterns of RIP 140 in dystrophic muscle, 2) the function that this protein plays in dystrophic muscle, and 3) the direct influence RIP 140 has on regulating utrophin  expression. These pre-clinical studies will be executed with commonly-used and experimentally-validated cell tissue culture and animal models of DMD, as well as a targeted array of physiologic, biochemical and molecular analyses. The results from this proposal will shed new light on the molecular mechanisms of DMD pathology, and may reveal a novel therapeutic target in RIP 140 for future lifestyle and pharmacological interventions designed to contest this unrelenting disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: General Public's Perception of a Quality-adjusted Life Year in Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DISCRETE CHOICE EXPERIMENT; HEALTH ECONOMICS; RESOURCE ALLOCATION
Abstract-Résumé: While the demand for new cancer treatments is rising dramatically, so are their costs. As there is a limited amount of money available for health treatments, decision-makers have to select which treatments to fund. Currently, this decision is based on comparing the benefit provided by the treatment with its cost; this is known as cost-utility analysis. The most common way to measure the treatment's benefit is how much it increases a patient's quantity and quality of life. These two measures are combined into a single number, the quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) gained. Measuring quality of life is very difficult and is highly individual. How the public values the quality of life for a health outcome is vital to maximize the benefits from the health funds available. To do this, decision-makers set upper limits on the cost per QALY for a treatment to be funded. This should be separate from the disease; however, there is evidence that cancer treatments are often approved at higher costs per QALY than for other health conditions.   This project will examine whether the QALY is a good tool to guide decision-makers' assessment of different treatments. Specifically, the project will assess whether QALYs for different diseases are equal and will determine how much it is reasonable to spend to achieve improvements in survival and quality of life in cancer. The project also investigates if other factors (i.e., patient age or disease severity) should be included in healthcare funding decisions.  The proposed project has significant implications for health policy. By determining what the public are willing to pay to gain one QALY in cancer, more informed decisions can be made in terms of what treatments should receive financial support. This will ensure that society is getting the most out of the money allocated to healthcare. Also this will provide information on whether the use of QALYs in decision-making will help to guarantee sustainability in the health system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anti-inflammatory epigenetic mechanisms of liver X nuclear receptors (LXRs) : Interference with chromatin spatial re-organization.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHIP-SEQ; CHROMATIN CONFORMATION; ENHANCED CHIP-4C (E4C); ENHANCERS; EPIGENETICS; GRO-SEQ; INFLAMMATION; INTERLEUKIN 1 BETA; MACROPHAGE; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORIES
Abstract-Résumé: Liver X nuclear receptors (LXRs) are important regulators of macrophage activity, a key cell type of the immune system, and have been implicated in the development of many inflammatory human diseases, including atherosclerosis. One of the most potent properties of LXRs is their ability to inhibit expression of pro-inflammatory genes. However, the inhibitory mechanisms activated by LXRs are not fully understood. Interestingly, a recent study by the Glass lab discovered numerous potential sites in the genome of macrophages lying outside gene sequences that could mediate LXR - DNA interactions. Interestingly, these non-coding regions of DNA, called enhancers, appear to play a critical role in organizing the 3D structure of DNA, which in turn regulates gene expression. As highly precise and coordinated spatial re-organizations of DNA are required to achieve efficient pro-inflammatory gene expression, we hypothesize that activated LXRs bind to DNA in enhancer regions and subsequently interfere with such DNA re-organization, thus resulting in an impairment of gene expression. The investigation of this hypothesis is the primary aim of this project, and will require the use of the latest state-of-the-art technologies in epigenetics and bioinformatics. These will be used to monitor the precise DNA spatial re-organizations that are required for the expression of pro-inflammatory gene interleukin 1 beta, which will be assessed in macrophages in the presence or absence of activated LXRs. The specific enhancers involved in those re-organizations will also be further characterized at the molecular level. This work will provide critical insights into the anti-inflammatory mechanisms activated by LXRs that inhibit pro-inflammatory gene expression. As such, it will contribute key knowledge for the design of better diagnostic and therapeutic protocols for atherosclerosis and other inflammatory diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of pericytes in the development of Alzheimer's disease and the associated cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID-BETA; BLOOD-BRAIN BARRIER; CEREBRAL AMYLOID ANGIOPATHY; NEURODEGENERATION; PERICYTES; SCYLLO-INOSITOL; TRANSGENIC MICE; VASCULATURE
Abstract-Résumé: Pericytes are crucial support cells maintaining a barrier between blood vessels and brain tissue. In Alzheimer's disease, amyloid-beta accumulate in the brain and deposits across this barrier into the surrounding blood vessels, causing abnormal blood flow and worsening the cognitive symptoms associated with the disease. Our research aims to understand 1) whether pericytes die in response to amyloid-beta, and 2) whether the death of pericytes have a major impact in the transport of amyloid-beta between the brain and the surrounding vessels as well as the course of the disease. Our research uses an amyloid-beta-generating mouse exhibiting similar symptoms as Alzheimer's patients as an experimental model for the disease. The role of pericytes in the disease is revealed by two methods, either by 1) changing the amyloid-beta level in the mouse (to determine how pericytes react to amyloid-beta) or by 2) altering pericyte numbers (to determine how loss of pericytes influence disease progression). Identifying pericytes as a major contributor in Alzheimer's disease progression lays the foundation for developing potential therapies that target these cells. Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and quickly becoming more prominent as the population ages. This research provides significant input on developing new methods to combat the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional genomic investigation of the proteome required for inflammasome assembly and of its functional contribution to the control of influenza A virus-induced lung injury
Keywords-MotsClés: CASPASE-1; CIAP; HIGH-THROUGHPUT ASSAYS; IL-1 BETA; INFLAMMASOME; INNATE IMMUNITY; PATHOGEN RECOGNITION RECEPTORS; RIG-I; RNA INTERFERENCE; VIRAL INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: The flu is an illness caused by influenza RNA viruses that infect the respiratory tract of humans. Children, the elderly and people with chronic health problems are at a higher risk of developing serious and potentially life-threatening flu-related medical complications, such as pneumonia. However, these complications can occur at any age, especially in times of severe worldwide outbreaks (pandemics) against which the world population has little or no immunity. Innate immune pathogen sensors are the first line of defense against infection, protecting the host during the development of adaptive immunity and critically affecting the nature of the protective adaptive response. Amongst these receptors, RIG-I, a viral RNA innate sensor, defends the host against viral infections by recruiting inflammatory caspases into macro-molecular complexes termed inflammasomes. However, the molecular interactions that regulate inflammasome assembly in response to viruses remain poorly defined. In this project we use genome-wide RNA interference to identify candidate genes that modulate the caspase-1 inflammatory response to viruses. The obtained knowledge from this research will contribute to a better understanding of the host defense mechanisms against flu and support the development of novel therapeutic agents that could apply to other respiratory infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vectorization of New Anticancer Agents to Target Prostate Cancer Cells via their Conjugation to Testosterone: Design, Synthesis and Biological Evaluation
Keywords-MotsClés: ALKYLATING AGENTS; ANTIANDROGENS; ANTICANCER AGENTS; CANCER CHEMOTHERAPY; CONJUGATION TESTOSTERONE-DRUGS; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; MOLECULAR CELL BIOLOGY; MOLECULAR MODELING; MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY; VECTORIZATION CANCER THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, prostate cancer is ranked first amongst the new cancer cases diagnosed and it is the third most common cancer exhibiting the highest mortality rate and therefore it is of major public health problem. In this context, new treatments are in constant demand to reduce the mortality and morbidity outcomes of that disease. To that end, the research team supervised by Drs. Berube and Asselin is developing a new therapeutical approach based on the use testosterone, a male hormone, to transport anticancer drugs selectively to prostate cancer cells. The antiandrogens (antitestosterone) are members of the anticancer drugs normally used in clinic to slow down the progression of prostate cancer at early stages. However, in advanced stages of the disease the tumours become resistant to the treatments resulting in untimely death. Adjuvant drugs can be added to the chemotherapy of prostate cancer, however, their effects are often of limited efficacy and duration. To date, Drs. Berube and Asselin have conducted studies using molecular models that show how and where to conjugate anticancer drugs to testosterone, which afterward can effectively target and kill hormone-dependent prostate cancer cells. The aim of our research program is to use new chemical methods to prepare new compounds designated as "testosterone-drug" and study their pharmacological properties on prostate cancer cells. Our project will focus on four main objectives involving: i) design of the new molecules using molecular modeling, ii) preparation and characterization of the new compounds, iii) study of their antiproliferative effects on prostate cancer cells versus normal cells, and finally iv) study of the molecular mechanisms involved in prostate cancer cell death. Our endeavour should lead to new medications both more effective and less toxic for patients suffering from prostate cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Parkinson's disease, Parkinsonism and Depression in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging: A population perspective
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIDEPRESSANT; ANXIETY; ANXIOLYTICS; BENZODIAZEPINE; DEPRESSION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PARKINSONISM; SEDATIVE; SLEEP DISTURBANCES
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson is one of the neurodegenerative disease and touch near of 6.3 millions of people in the world. Its prevalence is around 1% for people aged 65 to 69 and reach 5% in people aged 85 and over. Predominant symptoms of the Parkinson disease are motors but some non-motor symptoms like depression and anxiety are also presents. The objective of this study is to assess the impact of depression on the evolution of Parkinson disease. Data from Canadian Longitudinal study on Aging will be used.

TitreApplicationTitle: Atomic level insights into protein folding inside the cell: An in vivo NMR study of protein dynamics
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; BIOPHYSICAL SPECTROSCOPY; BIOPHYSICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE; PROTEIN CHEMISTRY; PROTEIN FOLDING AND MISFOLDING; PROTEIN FOLDING DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Protein molecules are the business end of cellular activity. To be functional, most protein molecules must adopt a correct three dimensional structure (i.e. be properly folded). Misfolding of proteins have been shown to result in many disease processes. Despite our advanced understanding of genetic basis of many misfolding diseases the principles that govern folding are still not well understood. This proposal focuses on a novel method to investigate these principles inside the cell with atomic level insight, and is built directly on recent breakthroughs made at the University of Toronto.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterisation of the recruitment and functions of 53BP1 at DNA damage sites
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER BIOLOGY; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR; DNA-END PROTECTION; METHYLATION; PROTEOMICS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; UBIQUITINYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: DNA double-stranded breaks (DSBs) are induced by exposure to environmental factors such as sunlight and ionizing radiation (IR), the agent used in cancer radiotherapy, but they also occur in a programmed manner in processes such as development and aging. Since DSBs promote genomic instability and cancer progression, cells have evolved a complex response to detect, signal and repair DSBs. Among the cellular events that are triggered by the DNA damage response, the laboratory of Dr Durocher focuses on understanding the mechanisms that promote and regulate the accumulation of a small protein called ubiquitin on the chromatin that surrounds DNA damage sites. While we know that this accumulation is necessary to recruit the DNA repair machinery, we still do not understand how the recruitment of DNA repair proteins occurs and how they regulate repair at the site of DNA damage. The DNA repair protein 53BP1 is known to protect the broken ends of DNA at DSBs from being further degraded, but the molecular mechanisms governing both its recruitment to DSBs and the details of how it protects broken DNA ends remain to be determined. The goal of my post-doctoral training will be to use human cells subjected to ionizing radiation to learn how 53BP1 is recruited to the ubiquitin-labelled chromatin and how it regulates the choice of pathway used to repair the DNA damage. My hypotheses are that 53BP1 is recruited to DNA damage sites by interacting with ubiquitin-labelled chromatin and that it protects DNA ends by recruiting specific proteins to block DNA-end degradation. These studies will highlight the mechanisms that drive DNA repair following DNA damage and will reveal how a defect in these mechanisms can promote loss of genome integrity and cancer progression.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Impact of HIV-1 and Malaria Co-infection on Angiogenesis, Fetal Development and Pregnancy Outcome in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Keywords-MotsClés: CO-INFECTION; FETAL GROWTH RESTRICTION; HIV-1; IMMUNITY; INFLAMMATION; KENYA; MALARIA; MOTHER-TO-CHILD TRANSMISSION OF HIV; PREGNANCY; VASCULAR DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 70% of people infected with HIV reside in sub-Saharan Africa. Women are particularly susceptible to HIV, with HIV rates 3 to 6-times higher in young women than men. Sub-Saharan Africa is also home to 30 million women at risk of contracting malaria during pregnancy each year and HIV increases the severity of malaria in pregnancy. When a mother is HIV positive, her fetus is at increased risk of being born growth restricted and of contracting HIV. Given the overlap between malaria and HIV in sub-Saharan Africa, we believe that malaria in pregnancy may increase the risk of the fetus contracting HIV from its mother. We believe this may occur as malaria initiates an immune response that activates fetal immune cells making them more susceptible to HIV infection. Further, malaria is known to increase the amount of HIV virus in the body, which relates to increased risk of transmission.  During pregnancy, angiogenic factors-proteins that circulate and are directly measureable in the blood- are responsible for coordinating the formation of blood vessels. Altered levels of these angiogenic factors have been associated with impaired fetal growth in preeclampsia and malaria, two major causes of fetal growth restriction globally. HIV is also associated with fetal growth restriction and we hypothesize that altered levels of angiogenic factors may contribute to HIV-related growth restriction.   In the work proposed, we will recruit and follow women throughout pregnancy. At antenatal visits, women will receive standard care including the administration of antiretroviral drugs to limit the risk of the fetus contracting HIV. In addition, a small blood sample will be collected for study purposes. We will measure whether changes in angiogenic proteins in HIV positive women are related to fetal growth restriction and we will determine whether malaria increases the ability of HIV to invade fetal cells.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: The Metabolic Basis of Right Ventricular Failure
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; BIOMARKERS; HYPERTROPHY/FAILURE TRANSITION; METABOLISM; MICORNA SIGNATURE; RIGHT VENTRICLE; TRANSLATIONAL APPROACH
Abstract-Résumé: Failure of the heart muscle to pump blood through the body is a major cause of death throughout the world. Although the heart has two equally important chambers, the right ventricle and the left ventricle, almost all of the efforts of the medical and research communities to treat heart failure focus on the left ventricle. We now recognize critical differences between the two heart chambers and we cannot extrapolate findings from one to the other. The right ventricle of the heart fails more frequently than the left ventricle does, and in several common diseases and conditions associated with high death rates. There are currently no therapies designed specifically to improve the function of the right chambers of the heart. The specific hypothesis pursued is that one of the reasons that the right ventricle fails more easily than the left ventricle is that as it thickens in response to disease process, it cannot keep up with the generation of new blood vessels to supply the growing muscle with more blood. This is called suppressed angiogenesis. We specifically propose that the basis for this suppressed angiogenesis is a unique metabolic environment in the right compared to the left myocardium, in other words that there are key differences in how the fueling of the two chambers is regulated. We believe that this unique metabolic environment is caused by circulating factors that reflect a more generalized disturbance in patients with failing right chambers. Measuring these circulating factors in the blood may allow us to predict failure of the right chambers on time and more importantly show us ways that we could actually prevent it. We propose to study this hypothesis in both animals and patients with standard and novel techniques and cutting edge equipment. Our work may offer for the first time ways to predict right ventricular failure and identify for the first time much needed therapies that are specific to the right ventricle.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL; CLASSIFICATIONS SUPPLEMENTAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Ion channel expression patterns define signal processing across the input layer of the cerebellum
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBELLUM; IMAGING; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; OPTOGENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: The cerebellum is a key brain region controlling the timing and magnitude of both movement and cognitive functions. Although the structure of cerebellum has long been recognized to be divided into ten distinct lobules, the physiological significance of this organization was largely unknown. Evidence from anatomical and imaging studies now demonstrate lobule-specific differences in the processing of motor vs cognitive information over the rostro-caudal (front-to-back) axis of cerebellum. The granule cell layer is the major input layer of cerebellum that shapes initial signal processing in all lobules. We found a differential expression of a calcium and potassium channel complex that we hypothesize will determine the processing of inputs to cerebellar granule cells across the rostro-caudal axis. This work will thus be important to understanding how sensory information that requires different functional outputs is processed across the multiple lobules of cerebellum. By understanding how signals are differentially processed for either motor or cognitive (cerebral) function in different parts of cerebellum we may have the opportunity to develop therapeutic agents to intervene in cerebellar circuitry at specific points to recover function when damage or disease leads to movement or cognitive problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Memory Impairment in Children with Brain Tumors
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOR; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHY; MEMORY; PAEDIATRICS; RADIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumors are the leading cause of death and disability from childhood disease in developed countries. Over the past 25 years, survival rates have improved dramatically. However, survival is often achieved at considerable cost, particularly for children treated with cranial radiation. Cranial radiation is the only curative treatment for most malignant tumors, but it is associated with significant long-term problems in learning and memory. I plan to examine how cranial radiation affects different aspects of brain functioning and how this relates to memory performance. Specifically, I will examine how cranial radiation affects functional neural activity in brain regions important for memory (e.g. the strength and timing of neural responses). I will also examine how cranial radiation affects structural integrity of the brain by assessing white matter, the means by which different brain regions communicate with each other. By understanding how and where cranial radiation affects memory and brain functioning, this will help identify which aspects of memory are most affected which may in turn help to shape future rehabilitative programs (e.g. focus on memory strategies that tap into unaffected brain regions). Further, by identifying the regions of the brain that are most affected by cranial radiation, this may help guide future treatment in order to minimize adverse cognitive outcome (e.g. modify where radiation is administered).

TitreApplicationTitle: Additive Manufacturing of Patient-Specific Implant Augments for Complex Hip Replacement Revision Surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING; COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; HIP; PATIENT-SPECIFIC IMPLANT; REVISION SURGERY; TOTAL HIP REPLACEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Total hip replacement (THR) is the gold standard approach for the treatment of advanced arthritis of the hip. The number of THR surgeries has increased by 59 percent in Canada over the past 10 years, and is expected to continue to increase significantly with the aging population and increase in obesity rates. Unfortunately, while THR is considered to be a very successful surgery, implants do not last indefinitely and may loosen or wear out over time. This can lead to pain and decreased function for patients, necessitating a revision surgery to replace the failing implant. Revision surgery is more complex than the primary surgery, as the bone quality surrounding the implant site is often poor, or may become damaged during the extraction of the original implant. Bone grafts are then required in order to fix a new conventional implant into place, which carries the risk of the graft not being taken up by the host, requiring a second surgery, or even transmitting disease in the case of grafts taken from cadavers. We propose to develop a process for designing and manufacturing new patient-specific implant augments for use in complex revision surgeries. Using anthropomorphic hip phantoms and cadavers, a computed tomography (CT) scan will be taken of the hip. The scan will be used to design a customized implant augment with enhanced fixation properties that can be fixed into place using the patient's existing bone, without requiring a bone graft. The augment will be designed to integrate with a standard THR implant. The implant augment will be fabricated using additive manufacturing technology, in which metal powder is directly fused into the shape of the implant in only a few hours time. After polishing and sterilization the implant augment will be ready for implantation into the hip phantom or cadaver (and, in the future, the patient). After implantation, an x-ray will be taken to ensure proper orientation of the implant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Virtual reality in rehabilitation: Using motor learning theory to develop virtual reality interventions that improve balance and functional mobility in children with motor disabilities
Keywords-MotsClés: BALANCE; INTERACTIVE VIDEO GAMES; MOBILITY; MOTION ANALYSIS; MOTOR LEARNING; MOTOR SKILLS; PEDIATRICS; PHYSIOTHERAPY; REHABILITATION; VIRTUAL REALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Many children and youth with neurological conditions such as cerebral palsy or acquired brain injury have problems with balance and movement that affect how they participate at home and in their communities. Physiotherapists work with these children to reduce this disability by helping them to learn or relearn functional balance and movement skills. Virtual reality (VR) therapy, involving interactive, real-time computer simulations, may enhance this process. VR systems have been embraced for their appeal to children, their demand for movement and balance skills, their rich sensory stimulation, their range of skill levels, and the extra motivation they provide for kids to practice. Despite their popularity, therapists are challenged to use VR effectively. Research is needed to evaluate how therapists can use this technology to improve learning of functional activities like balance and walking skills. These are the goals of this research study. Our approach is informed by contemporary motor learning theory, which outlines strategies for how children best learn when motivated by functional tasks and provided with real-time feedback. Our previous research demonstrates that therapists struggle to use motor learning theory within their VR interventions. Therefore, we will develop and test a VR intervention that teaches therapists how to effectively incorporate motor learning theory. We will first study how different VR systems employ key motor learning principles and then ask therapists about their learning needs related to using VR in clinical practice. We will use this information to create and evaluate a VR intervention protocol. We believe that the role of VR within rehabilitation will continue to grow as new systems are developed and become accessible within mainstream practice. This research is expected to directly impact the effective and efficient use of VR by physiotherapists, reduce disability in this population, and inform further research in this area.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rôle des protéines CNIH4 et TMEM9 dans la maturation et le transport à la membrane plasmique des récepteurs couplés aux protéines G.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSYNTHESE DES RECEPTEURS COUPLES AUX PROTEINES G; BRET; CHAPERONES PHARMACOLOGIQUES; EXPRESSION DES RECEPTEURS; GLYCOSYLATION; GOLGI; MATURATION DES RECEPTEURS; MUTATIONS DES RECEPTEURS; RETICULUM ENDOPLASMIQUE; TRANSPORT DES RECEPTEURS
Abstract-Résumé: Les recepteurs couples aux proteines G (RCPG) sont une classe de proteines exprimees a la surface des cellules et qui ont pour role de transmettre un signal a l'interieur de celles-ci a partir d'un stimulus exterieur appele ligand. Une bonne communication entre l'exterieur et l'interieur de la cellule est primordial pour le maintien d'une physiologie normale. D'ailleurs, plusieurs maladies sont causees par des mutations au niveau des RCPG resultant en des recepteurs qui ne peuvent plus exercer adequatement leur role. Cela se produit lorsque la mutation induit un changement trop drastique dans la forme tridimensionnelle du RCPG le rendant inefficace ou simplement lorsque le recepteur mutant est reconnu comme anormal par le systeme de controle de qualite de la cellule. Eventuellement, ces RCPG ainsi retenus seront degrades et ne pourront donc pas se rendre a la surface de la cellule pour exercer leur role. Dans certains cas, la mutation engendre un recepteur fonctionnel, mais que le systeme de controle de qualite empeche de faire migrer a la surface cellulaire. C'est d'ailleurs la cause de maladies telles que l'hypogonadisme, le diabete insipidus, l'hypothyroidie, le nanisme et l'obesite morbide congenitale. Une meilleure comprehension de ces mecanismes de controle de qualite pourrait donc mener a de nouveaux traitements. C'est dans cette optique que le laboratoire de Dr. Bouvier a recemment decouvert deux proteines appelees CNIH4 et TMEM9 qui interagissent avec plusieurs RCPG en cours de synthese. De maniere surprenante, le laboratoire a demontre que la presence de ces deux proteines est necessaire a la maturation et au transport vers la membrane cellulaire des RCPG. De plus, leur presence libere certains RCPG mutants enfermes a l'interieur par la cellule. Mon projet postdoctoral est donc de comprendre comment ces deux proteines fonctionnent afin d'appliquer ces connaissances au traitement des maladies causees par des mutations resultant en des RCPG emprisonnes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of fibroblast growth factor 2 in hypothalamic-pituitary adrenal axis responsivity and anxiety behavior
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; DEVELOPMENT; EPIGENETICS; FGF2; GLUCOCORTICOID; HIPPOCAMPUS; HYPOTHALAMUS-PITUITARY-ADRENAL AXIS; MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Amongst all categories of mental illness, anxiety disorders have the highest prevalence rate in Canada.  However, despite the alarmingly high incidence of these disorders, little is known about the neurobiological underpinnings of these disorders. Recent work both from our laboratory and others has implicated a role for fibroblast growth factor 2 in anxiety disorders. In my early post-doctoral work, I have shown that removing the function of the fibroblast growth factor gene in mice results in a severe anxiety behavior phenotype, associated with dysregulation of the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis, the major endocrine system which regulates cortisol in humans and corticosterone in rodents: hormones involved in the stress response. The current proposed studies would 1) try to ascertain if this is largely a developmental effect, or whether acute administration of fibroblast growth factor 2 would reverse the anxiety phenotype; and 2) what are the downstream mechanisms through which fibroblast growth factor 2 exerts its effects on the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis by use of gene expression studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Systematic identification and characterization of key molecules in bacterially induced pulmonary hyperinflammation in Cystic Fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-INFLAMMATORY PEPTIDES; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; INNATE IMMUNITY; METABOLOMICS; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; PULMONARY HYPERINFLAMMATION; RESPIRATORY HEALTH; TLR SIGNALLING
Abstract-Résumé: Lung inflammatory diseases, including asthma, bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and bronchitis, are one of the most common and insidious causes of death on the planet. To date we know little about the mechanisms involved or the optimal anti-inflammatory treatments for each of the various lung inflammatory syndromes. In Cystic Fibrosis (CF), pulmonary hyper-inflammation is the single most significant contributor to disease progression and the effective control of inflammation-mediated lung destruction is critical to prolonging the life of those who suffer with this disease. Understanding the inflammatory component of human diseases is difficult due to the dynamic and interconnected nature of the immune system.   My proposed research project is to adopt a top-down systems approach, using a combination of functional genomics and cell biology, to investigate bacterially induced pulmonary hyperinflammation in CF. The project will be carried out in two stages. In the first stage, I will use next-generation transcriptomics and metabolomic profiling technologies to generate detailed information and hypotheses about cellular networks leading to CF pulmonary inflammation. In the second stage, I will further characterize roles of the key intermediates of the networks using a combination of different inhibitory or activating reagents on CF epithelial cells. The mechanisms of a promising immunomodulatory peptide, IDR-1018, will also be studied thoroughly in this context.   Upon the completion of the project, I will have substantially increased our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of hyperinflammation in CF and deciphered the detailed mechanism of how IDR-1018 modulates the inflammatory response in CF epithelial cells. The results will provide knowledge and insight that will be critical in designing new effective anti-inflammatory treatments for CF lung disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional connectivity within the visual cortex: on the interactions between lower and higher visual areas.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZEIMER; FEEDBACK; FMRI; FUNCTIONNAL CONNECTIVITY; MOTION; MULTI-CHANNEL ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NEURONAVIGATION; SCHIZOPHRENIA; V1; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: The brain can be delineated to areas, each of which has a specific function. For example, in the visual system, some areas of the brain process color information while other areas process movement of objects. Brain areas are connected via a network of anatomical connections and cells in different areas communicate by sending messages through these pathways. The messages between areas take the form of electrical pulses, and are an important principle of brain function. It has been suggested that even minor alterations in the communication among brain areas might be the origin of several brain diseases; namely schizophrenia, Alzheimer and autism. Accordingly, the notion of functional connectivity, namely the influence that one area has over another, is now part of our understanding of how the brain works. My research project investigates the nature of communication between regions in the visual part of the brain. To this end I will apply imaging techniques along with neurophysiological ones. To elicit activity in the visual part of the brain, I will use different type visual motion stimuli projected on a screen. I expect that my proposed approach, using a repertoire of recording techniques, will make it possible to investigate interactions between brain areas; i.e. the functional connectivity, which has proven to be difficult in previous studies. Revealing the nature of these interactions is important for understanding the function of the healthy brain. It also sets the foundations for understanding functional disconnection of brain areas in neurological and psychiatric diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Unravelling the Mechanisms of anti-miR-33-mediated VLDL Lowering
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; LIPID METABOLISM; MICRORNAS
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease, a leading cause of death worldwide, is particularly prevalent in Canada and the United States, with abnormal lipid levels in the blood being a common cause of heart attacks and stokes. Lipids are shuttled in the circulation in particles called lipoproteins; high concentrations of low and very low density lipoproteins (LDL, VLDL), as well as low concentrations of high density lipoprotein (HDL), are strong and independent risk factors for the development of cardiovascular disease (CVD). A major therapeutic approach for the treatment of CVD is the modulation of lipoprotein metabolism - this is geared towards lowering LDL and VLDL or raising HDL. Despite a continued interest in HDL-raising therapies, the development of suitable pharmacological agents to increase HDL has been challenging. Recently, an important role for microRNA-33 (miR-33) in lipoprotein metabolism was discovered. microRNAs are powerful regulators of gene expression: by silencing numerous gene targets, a single microRNA can preside over an entire cellular pathway. As such, miR-33 negatively regulates many genes involved in HDL formation, and its inhibition raises circulating HDL by an impressive 25-40% and decreases CVD development in mice. When the effect miR-33 inhibition was tested in higher mammals (monkeys), it markedly raised HDL while also unexpectedly lowering VLDL. However, it is unclear how miR-33 modulates plasma VLDL. A full understanding of the cellular and molecular events that impact on lipoprotein metabolism following miR-33 antagonism is required to ensure that there are no adverse effects resulting from the pharmacological inhibition of miR-33. This project will uncover the mechanism of anti-miR-33-mediated VLDL lowering, and deepen our knowledge as to how endogenous miR-33 that is normally expressed upon cholesterol depletion controls a number of events required to maintain normal lipid homeostasis, shedding insight into the regulation of hepatic lipid metabolism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mental health, cortisol and cytokines among adult offspring of Indian Residential School Survivors
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL MENTAL HEALTH; AFFECTIVE DISORDERS; DEPRESSION; INTERGENERATIONAL TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: Years of colonization and forced assimilation have led to the devastation of Aboriginal communities and cultures. A particularly harmful experience was the government policy of forcing Aboriginal to attend Indian Residential Schools (IRSs; 1800s-1996). Assimilation was the explicit rationale for these schools, and beyond separation from families and culture, many children experienced neglect and abuse. Not surprisingly, the capacity of IRS Survivors to socialize the next generation to cultural norms and practices, including parenting skills, were vastly undermined. Like heightened vulnerabilities observed in Holocaust offspring, IRS offspring reported greater depressive symptoms and distress compared to non-IRS adults. Although several psychosocial factors implicated in the intergenerational transmission of IRS trauma have been identified, the extent to which these effects may be manifested in biological changes is unknown.  Chronic stress and trauma have been associated with dysregulation of the HPA-axis, a major system involved body's response to stress. The HPA-axis responds to threat by regulating cortisol levels to maintain homeostasis, and interacts with immune messenger molecules call cytokines. Altered cortisol secretion and cytokine levels have both been implicated in mental health disorders. The proposed research will assess levels of cortisol and circulating cytokines in 2nd and 3rd generation IRS offspring under normal conditions and in response to stressors. We will also assess how variations in Aboriginal identity might be related to cortisol/cytokine variations in IRS offspring. Though the long history of trauma among Aboriginal peoples may be associated with differences in biological responses to stressors, this possibility has not been explored. Understanding such differences has important implications in the treatment of stress-related disorders in this group, particularly among vulnerable sub-groups of this population, such as in IRS offspring.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of TDP-43 role on SORT1 dysfunction and PGRN altered signal in neurodegenerative diseases.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRAL APPROACH; CELL TRANSFECTION; CO-IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE KNOCKED-DOWN; GENE SPLICING; GST-PULL DOWN; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MOUSE MODEL; PROTEIN BINDING
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is the most common of motor neuron diseases (MND), while frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) is the second most common cause of early-onset dementia. Interestingly, up to 50% of ALS patients do develop some sort of cognitive impairments. In 2006, the TDP-43 protein was found to be an important constituent of aggregates in neurons of MND -FTLD patients, which confirmed the common pathological pathway involved in the two conditions. Mutations in the TARDBP gene encoding the TDP-43 protein have been identified in both ALS and FTLD patients. Neurons of these patients display a nuclear clearing and cytoplasmic sequestration of the normal cellular TDP-43 protein. Lately, it has been found that depletion of TDP-43 in the mouse adult brain modifies the expression of the GRN gene which encodes the progranulin protein. Precisely, mutations in GRN are found in about 5-10% of all FTLD patients and cause TDP-43 cytoplasmic inclusions. It was also demonstrated that depletion of TDP-43 alters the splicing of SORT1 encoding sortilin, a receptor of progranulin. We hypothesize that abnormalities in TDP-43 cause SORT1 dysfunction and consequently alter PGRN signaling. This, in turn, is expected to accelerate TDP-43 pathology and the development of neurodegeneration. Considering this, the aim of the study is to understand the role and interactions of TDP-43, PGRN and SORT1 in the common pathway leading to MND-FTLD. The critical goal is to identify the proper therapeutic targets to eventually develop drugs or treatments that will stop and ultimately prevent neurodegeneration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular regulation of asymmetric satellite stem cell division
Keywords-MotsClés: ASYMMETRIC CELL DIVISION; EPIGENETICS; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; MYOGENESIS; PROTEIN METHYLATION; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; SATELLITE CELLS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SKELETAL MUSCLE; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: A thorough understanding of stem cell biology is key to the success of regenerative medicine, a medical field dedicated to regenerating tissues and organs damaged by disease, injury or aging. The unique power of stem cells lies in their ability to replicate and generate identical copies of themselves, as well as being able to generate specialized cells that contributes to tissue and organ growth throughout the human body. Various types of adult stem cells are found in specific tissues in the body where they serve to repair and maintain the tissues in which they reside. In Dr. Michael Rudnicki's lab, my research focuses on a population of adult stem cells found in skeletal muscle. Our long-term goal is to understand the underlying biology of muscle stem cells in order to exploit their regenerative potential for the treatment of muscle-degeneration diseases such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy. There is currently no cure for these debilitating and life-threatening diseases, which cause progressive weakening and eventual degeneration of skeletal muscle. Muscle stem cells are, therefore, ideal candidates for cell transplantation therapy in order to restore muscle regeneration in patients with muscular dystrophy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Language group differences in the neural underpinnings of language and cognitive control
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BILINGUALISM; COGNITION; COMMUNICATION; EVENT-RELATED BRAIN POTENTIALS; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; LANGUAGE COMPREHENSION; LEXICAL AMBIGUITY; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT
Abstract-Résumé: More than 50% of the world's population is bilingual, yet little research has examined bilingualism in dementia. This research will examine the effect of being bilingual on communication and cognitive function in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD). Communication is critical for quality of life, and difficulties can lead to conflict, isolation or depression, and earlier institutionalization in patients with cognitive impairment. Recent research shows that the experience of being bilingual provides an advantage in cognitive functioning for healthy older adults; however, this has not been examined in MCI and AD, despite reports that being bilingual is associated with a delay in the onset of AD symptoms by over 4 years. We will measure various aspects of cognitive function in monolingual and bilingual healthy young and older adults, and MCI and AD patients, and will examine their ability to resolve ambiguity in language (i.e., when a word has multiple unrelated meanings, e.g., "bank" which can mean "financial institution" or "river's edge"). We predict that bilingualism will be associated with better cognition, communication, and ambiguity resolution.  Measures of electrical brain activity will also be included in the proposed research, which will provide a more complete picture of the subtle changes in language processing associated with MCI and AD, and may provide insights that could aid in the early detection of AD.   The proposed research will increase our understanding of the changes in language and communication associated with MCI and AD. This investigation will be the first to experimentally examine the effect of being bilingual on language processing, cognition, and communication in cognitively impaired patients. The proposed methods will allow us to identify subtle differences in language processing between healthy and cognitively impaired participants, and may thus aid in detecting AD earlier than current methods allow.

TitreApplicationTitle: The safety and efficacy of human induced pluripotent stem cell transplantation after stroke.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL TRANSLATION; FUNCTIONAL OUTCOME; HUMAN INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; ISCHEMIA; PLASTICITY; RECOVERY; STEM CELLS; STROKE; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability. A stroke occurs every 10 minutes in Canada with approximately 50,000 new cases occurring annually. It is necessary to find a treatment that can improve the quality of life for stroke patients. Stem cell therapy is a promising intervention. However, there is controversy surrounding the use of human fetal and embryonic stem cells. Significant optimism exists that induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, which can be created by introducing four transcription factors into fully developed adult cells, could be an effective treatment for brain injury. The appeal of iPS cells is enhanced by several factors, such as reducing the concern for stem cell shortage and the ethical concerns over the need for human embryonic cells. Furthermore, it will be possible to generate iPS cells from a patient's own tissue, negating the need for immunosuppressant drugs. The current project will study the 1) safety, 2) integration, and 3) efficacy and mechanisms of action of human iPS cells in a rodent model of stroke. In these studies human fetal and embryonic stem cells, which improve outcome following rodent models of stroke, will be compared to human iPS cells. We will first assess the risk of tumor formation following cell treatment after stroke in mice. Then we will compare the different cell treatments following rodent stroke, looking for differences in cell survival, migration, and differentiation. In the final study functional outcome and mechanisms of action such as changes in plasticity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of neutrophil evasion by spirochetes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; IMMUNOLOGY; MICROBIOLOGY; MICROSCOPY; NEUTROPHIL; ORAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Periodontal disease is a chronic inflammatory condition that destroys the tissues of tooth support in which tooth loss ensues without proper treatment. Multiple bacteria on the tooth and gum surfaces interact with the host tissue cells to cause tissue damage and evoke an immune response. Periodontal disease is one of the most common chronic conditions affecting greater than 20% of the Canadian population as well as being associated with additional systemic disorders including heart disease and diabetes (Canadian Health Measures Survey, Health Canada 2010). Many cases continue to deteriorate following conventional treatment due to the inability of resolve these infections, and this disease represents a major health concern and health-care burden.   The innate immune system is the first line of defense of the body against invading bacteria. Neutrophils are key cells involved in this response and are able to detect bacteria and travel to the area of infection to capture, kill and remove harmful bacteria from the body. However, many bacteria are able to evade detection and removal by the immune system by perturbing the normal functions of the immune cells. This will allow the bacteria to remain in the host and results in progressive disease development. The goal of this project is to understand in detail the mechanisms of how bacteria are able to perturb normal neutrophil functions to prevent removal of the bacteria. Identification of both bacterial products and the neutrophil pathways involved in evading the normal immune response will allow development of potential therapeutics to improve patient outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of arsenic-induced atherosclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARSENIC; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CELLULAR ADHESION; CHOLESTEROL; MACROPHAGES; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; TOXICOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Arsenic is a widespread environmental contaminant ranked as the number one human health hazard by the American Environmental Protection Agency. This carcinogen enters drinking water supplies both from natural deposits in the earth or from industrial practices. The maximum level of arsenic in municipal drinking water has been set at 10 ppb, but well water in many North American counties averages 9-fold higher this limit. Moreover, high levels of arsenic have been found in the blood of many Canadians. Those individuals exposed to arsenic are at a greater risk for developing cardiovascular disease, such as atherosclerosis. However, the mechanisms by which arsenic enhances atherosclerosis remained largely unknown. Therefore, we propose experiments to understand how arsenic is linked to atherosclerosis formation. Using mouse models, we have shown that even low concentrations of arsenic increase atherosclerosis and altered the plaque composition. We will exploit the same models to define mechanisms by which arsenic induces atherosclerosis. Our previous data from cell culture experiments suggest that arsenic inhibits the function of the liver X receptor alpha protein, an important regulator of the cholesterol balance. We will confirm its involvement in arsenic-enhanced atherosclerosis by using mice that are deficient for this protein. Moreover, we will evaluate the effects of arsenic exposure on monocytes and macrophages, which are key players in formation of the atherosclerotic plaque. These cells bind to the activated endothelium of vessels and migrate in the wall to participate in the formation of the plaques. We hypothesize that arsenic will intensify this process. We also predict that arsenic will skew macrophages polarization toward a more pro-atherogenic phenotype. From these experiments, we hope to characterize mechanisms of arsenic-enhanced atherosclerosis, define safe levels of exposure and identify potential interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impaired Early Visual Processing in Schizophrenia: Paths to Social Cognition
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EVENT RELATED POTENTIALS; NEUROCOGNITION; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SOCIAL COGNITION; VISUAL PROCESSING
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a severe and persistent mental illness that is marked by impairment across a variety of domains including neurocognition (e.g., memory, attention, planning and organization), social cognition (i.e., information processing of social stimuli such as emotion recognition, social cue perception, and inferring the intentions of others), and social functioning (e.g., quality of relationships, work functioning). There is evidence that social cognition contributes to social functioning above-and-beyond the contributions of neurocognition. However, the nature of the relationship between neurocognition and social cognition is unclear. Understanding the underpinnings of social cognitive impairment is paramount for development of effective interventions to improve social functioning in schizophrenia. A robust finding in the literature is the association between early visual processing and performance on social cognitive tasks. Impaired early visual processing may impact social cognition directly via insufficient activation of "social brain" regions, and indirectly via disruption of "downstream" social and non-social cognitive processes. The purpose of the proposed study is to study the effects of impaired early visual processing on higher-order neurocognition and social cognition in two large samples of patients with schizophrenia (first episode and chronic schizophrenia). Early visual processing will be tested both electrophysiologically and behaviourally. Participants will complete a comprehensive neurocognitive and social cognitive test battery, and measures of functional outcome. To our knowledge, the proposed study will be the first to examine the impact of early visual processing on social cognition while simultaneously considering the contribution of higher-order neurocognition. The findings of the proposed study are expected to inform treatment research by identifying cognitive targets for psychosocial intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Early life gene-environment interactions and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis function
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE PREVENTION; DEVEOPMENTAL ORIGINS OF HEALTH AND DISEASE; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; HYPOTHALAMIC-PITUITARY-ADRENAL AXIS; WOMEN'S AND INFANTS' HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: It is well established that exposures during pregnancy influence maternal and infant health outcomes. Furthermore, an expanding field of research suggests that early life exposures have a profound impact on the risk of chronic diseases in adulthood. My research will examine interactions between early life exposures and genetic variants in relation to determinants of chronic disease risk. Despite the overwhelming importance of early life exposures, most studies of chronic disease focus on adult exposures only. I will analyze data from the established Western Australia (Raine) Pregnancy Study. The Raine study recruited 2900 pregnant women between 1989 and 1991, and detailed data are now available from over 21 years of follow-up. One of my specific research projects will evaluate the interactions between genetic variants and early life stressors (e.g., preterm birth, age at puberty) on the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal (HPA) axis function. The HPA axis regulates stress response and HPA axis dysfunction has been associated with several chronic diseases (e.g., hypertension, obesity, depression). The identification of early life determinants of adult disease risk has important implications for health policy initiatives and the development of targeted interventions aimed at reducing the burden of chronic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Self-Reactive, Epitope-Specific B Cells in the Pathogenesis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOANTIBODIES; AUTOANTIGEN SPECIFIC B CELLS; AUTOIMMUNE; CYTOF; INFLAMMATION; MCTD; PROTEIN MICROARRAY; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS; TETRAMER ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by the destruction of multiple organ systems by autoantibodies, which are antibodies that bind to the cells and tissues of patients with SLE. The specific "self" molecules targeted by autoantibodies are called autoantigens. To date, most research has focused on analyzing bulk populations of B cells in SLE and the autoantibodies they produce, yet little is known about rare autoreactive B cells that are specific for a single epitope, or region within an autoantigen.  For my CIHR funded research, I will take advantage of a bank of blood samples from >400 SLE patients that is available to the Utz lab. I propose to 1) Employ state of the art technology developed in the Utz lab in collaboration with Intel, called silicon peptide microarray, to determine the precise epitopes within two known autoantigens, called U1-70K and histone H2B, that are targeted by the SLE patients' autoantibodies; 2) Generate molecular "tags" that will allow me to identify and purify B cells that make autoantibodies against these epitopes from the patients' blood samples; and 3) Utilize a new technology, called CyTOF, to analyze thousands of single epitope-specific B cells from the patients' blood samples, as well as the inflammatory molecules each cell expresses.  The proposed studies will add to our understanding of how B cells contribute to the symptoms of SLE, and will identify the precise epitopes that SLE patients' autoantibodies recognize. If the epitopes were chemically joined to toxin molecules, they could serve as therapeutics to destroy autoreactive B cells. These studies will provide insights into ongoing clinical trials. This is particularly important given that one B cell targeted therapy was approved for treatment of SLE this year, and others recently entered human clinical trials. Further, epitope-specific B cells have the potential to serve as much needed diagnostics for SLE.

TitreApplicationTitle: Macromolecular crowding in protein misfolding and aggregation studied by single-molecule force spectroscopy
Keywords-MotsClés: MACROMOLECULAR CROWDING; PARKINSIN'S DISEASE; PRION DISEASE; PROTEIN (MIS-)FOLDING DISEASES; PROTEIN AGGREGATION; SINGLE-MOLECULE FORCE SPECTROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: In order to fulfill their essential roles in the cell, proteins have to fold into specific three-dimensional structures. Understanding how this takes place is a key scientific challenge, especially because proteins can also fold into the wrong structures and form insoluble aggregates, causing numerous diseases and problems in biotechnological applications. Most protein folding studies are carried out with isolated proteins in simple aqueous solutions, but in fact the cell is a very crowded and diverse environment. This project will investigate how the "crowding" of the protein by other molecules affects the folding, misfolding, and aggregation of proteins, focusing on proteins that are related to protein misfolding diseases like Parkinson's disease and mad cow disease. We will use a technique called optical tweezers to grab onto the ends of individual protein molecules and gently apply force to the molecules, pulling the protein structures apart and then watching them refold in the absence and presence of crowding molecules. Precision measurements of the motions of the molecules during unfolding and refolding will give us a detailed picture of the folding process and how it changes under crowded conditions. This information will give us a better understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms of protein misfolding diseases, and should help to find methods for preventing and treating them.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of the Dopamine Transporter function: The effects of drugs of abuse
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE TRANSPORTER; DRUG BINDING; DRUG DESIGN; DRUG OF ABUSE; LIGAND-RECEPTOR INTERACTIONS; MOLECULAR DYNAMICS SIMULATIONS; MOLECULAR MODELLING; MUTAGENESIS AND CHEMICAL CROSS-LINKING; NEUROTRANSMISSION AND NEUROLOGICAL DISORDERS; NMR AND CD
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide, the UN estimates that there are more than 50 million regular users of abused psychostimulants such as cocaine and amphetamine (AMPH), placing a burden on the individual and society due to its profound medical and psychological complications including dependence, overdose, and death. The addictive properties of such drugs are mediated through elevation of extracellular dopamine (DA) by inducing DA efflux via the dopamine transporter (DAT) and inhibition of DA reuptake. Neurotransmission mediated by DA in the brain is regulated through DAT function, and plays a major role in cognitive, emotional and behavioral functions. Abnormalities in the DA system have been implicated in not only drug addiction but also in other psychiatric and neurological disorders, such as schizophrenia, and Parkinson's disease. It is no wonder that DAT, the protein that carries out the DA reuptake process at the plasma membrane and also the major molecular target of AMPH and cocaine, constitutes the major focus of much research and is of major interest in developing new therapeutic strategies for drug addiction. The main objective of this project is to contribute to this field by investigating the molecular details of binding specificity and mechanistic interactions of drugs of abuse with novel 3D structural models of DAT. The binding and effects of transport of these drugs are complex and hence require a detailed understanding of both the binding modes and the dynamic consequences of the ligand-DAT interactions. To achieve our objectives, we will use technologies such as sophisticated molecular modelling methods and the use of supercomputers. The results will then guide collaborative applications of experimental techniques such as mutagenesis and chemical cross-linking to validate and incorporate our findings in the physiological and pharmacological understanding of the systems. Our study should thus prove instrumental in the design of new therapeutic approaches for drug addiction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparative Effectiveness of Drugs Using Electronic Health Records from Canada, US and the UK.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS; COMPARATIVE EFFECTIVENESS; COMPOUTERIZED DECISION SUPPORT; COMPUTERIZED PRESCRIBING; ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORD; EVIDENCE-BASED PRESCRIBING; INDICATION-BASED PRESCRIBING; PATIENT SAFETY; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; PHARMACOSURVEILLANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Prescription drugs play a rapidly expanding and important role in the prevention and treatment of common health problems. Over 60% of adult Canadians have used at least one prescription drug in the past 6 months, and six or more drugs are taken by 18% of the older population. While there are considerable benefits from modern drug therapy, the frequent occurrence of adverse drug-related events and the uncertainty about effects of drugs after they enter the market have highlighted fundamental shortcomings in the ability to actively monitor drugs after their approval.  Electronic health records, computerized prescribing and automated patient follow-up systems are health information technologies that are being increasingly used to improve the quality of care around the world. These new health information technologies provide an unprecedented opportunity to develop an active surveillance system that will monitor and provide patients and physicians with real-time feedback on the comparative safety and effectiveness of new drugs.  Conducting active surveillance on a collaborative international scale will provide more rapid information about drug safety and effectiveness from users around the world as well as permit more personalized risk/benefit analysis for subgroups where drugs may have a different risk/benefit profile. The purpose of this project is to develop state-of-the-art methods of i) monitoring, and  ii) analyzing the comparative risk and benefit of new drug therapies, in real-time, through an international prospective surveillance system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanism of cysteine catalysis by mammalian enzyme cysteine dioxygenase implicated in Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and other neurodegenerative diseases.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMISTRY OF NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES; CYSTEINE DIOXYGENASE; ENZYME KINETICS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MOSSBAUER SPECTROSCOPY; NON-HEME MONO-IRON(II) PROTEIN; RAPID STOP FLOW; REACTION INTERMEDIATES; RESONANCE RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY; ULTRA RAPID FREEZE-QUENCH
Abstract-Résumé: Elevated levels of iron and cysteine have been long implicated in a number of neurodegenerative diseases (NDD), including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, the latter affecting 2% of all people over the age of 65. A reduced activity of cysteine dioxygenase (CDO) has been reported in patients suffering NDD. CDO is an iron-dependent enzyme conducting the prime step within cysteine metabolism. The fact that intracellular CDO concentration is tightly linked to cysteine levels through the ubiquitination pathway and that a genetic basis for CDO deficiency has yet to be reported illustrate the current lack of an explanation of the etiology of this disease, which warrants biochemical and biophysical investigation of CDO catalysis. This strategy could possibly provide a mechanistic basis for reduced CDO activity in the context of NDD. Our experiments will generate the kinetic and spectroscopic evidence to explain the role of iron in catalysis by CDO. Understanding the mechanisms by which the build-up of iron and cysteine occurs is essential for effective treatment of Parkinson's and other neurodegenerative diseases. This knowledge is fundamental to advances in understanding CDO's activity and role in health and disease.
