TitreApplicationTitle: Hitting the target: the estimated prevention of foreign-born tuberculosis through evidence-based screening in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIGH RISK POPULATIONS; IMMIGRATION; PUBLIC HEALTH; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Immigration is the largest determinant of tuberculosis (TB) epidemiology in low incidence immigrant-receiving countries.  Without the successful prevention of TB in the foreign-born, it is nearly impossible for these countries to make progress towards TB elimination.  However, screening for latent TB infection (LTBI) has not been systematically implemented among immigrants due to concerns about its cost-effectiveness.  This is due to the limited identification of high-yield target groups and uncertainty about the number of secondary TB cases that can be prevented.  Although immigrants referred by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC) for medical surveillance may comprise a high-yield target group, this also has never been confirmed.  This study will analyze foreign-born TB cases in Canada from 2003 to 2010, with a focus on case characteristics (including gender,age, country of birth, time since arrival, and CIC medical surveillance referral status) in order to identify high-yield groups for targeted screening for LTBI.  The number of high-yield cases that could be prevented with evidenced-based screening will be determined.  By extrapolating provincial molecular epidemiological data, the number of secondary cases attributed to transmission from high-yield case targets will also be estimated. The study will also determine if previously recommended high-yield target groups remain valid and if CIC medical surveillance referrals have a higher incidence of TB than demographically similar immigrants.  Consistently identified high-yield targets for screening for LTBI among the foreign-born provides a strong rationale to support the implementation of routine targeted screening. If consistent targets are not identified, the feasibility of cost-effective screening is significantly reduced and alternative strategies will need to be identified. Findings related to CIC medical surveillance referrals are also anticipated to have significant policy implications for CIC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reservoirs of antibiotic resistance: a functional metagenomic study of environmental resistance using several model systems
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; FUNCTIONAL METAGENOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: In the past 50 years, antibiotics have been critical in the fight against many diseases and infections. Their discovery was one of the leading causes for the dramatic rise of average life expectancy in the 20th century and their significance to public health would be impossible to overstate.  Upon the introduction of penicillin into general clinical practice in 1944, formerly deadly illnesses such as strep throat and tuberculosis became instantly curable.  Today, our dependence on antibiotics is absolute. Bacterial resistance development to antibiotics is inevitable.  Outbreaks of antibiotic resistance strains such as MRSA (methicillin resistance Staphylococcus aureus) or VRE (vancomycin resistant enterocci) can be deadly.  Some believe that society may revert back to a pre-antibiotic era in which no antibiotics will be effective against bacterial infections if no drastic changes are made in the trends of antibiotic resistance development.  Clearly, new insights into antibiotic resistance are required.  Recently, the environment has been recognized as a source of antibiotic resistance genes.  Most antibiotics are produced by soil bacteria.  Resistance genes and their ancestral genes are present in environmental antibiotic producer bacteria, non-producer bacteria and in disease causing bacteria.  The transition of resistance genes from their less efficient relatives in the environmental to disease causing bacteria and the factors contributing to this transition are not well understood.  This proposal aims to explore the development of antibiotic resistance by 1) studying ancestral environmental antibiotic resistance genes using several innovative systems and by 2) examining the evolutionary relationship between antibiotic resistance genes associated with disease causing bacteria and their related environmental antibiotic resistance genes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure and function of polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase, a potential target in cancer therapy.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER RESEARCH; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR PROTEIN; INHIBITORS; POLYNUCLEOTIDE KINASE/PHOSPHATASE (PNKP); STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Our DNA is constantly damaged by external sources, and unrepaired lesions result in genetic mutations that can initiate cancer. Under such selective pressure to maintain our genetic material, complex mechanisms have evolved to sense and repair the DNA damage. The laboratory studies the structural details of proteins involved in these DNA repair mechanisms. In particular, the polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP), which acts on broken DNA ends, has been shown to be essential in many DNA repair processes. This research project proposes to understand how PNKP recognizes and repairs broken DNA ends. Moreover, our collaborator recently identified a small molecule that inhibits phosphate activity of PNKP, but its mode of action remains unknown. The understanding of the mechanism of action of this inhibitor combined to the characterization of the interactions between PNKP and broken DNA ends will help to develop new cancer therapies with the design of more potent PNKP inhibitors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ex Vivo IL-10 Gene Therapy in a Pre-Clinical Lung Transplantation Survival Model
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE THERAPY; INFLAMMATION; INTERLEUKIN-10/GENETICS; LUNG TRANSPLANTATION; LUNG/PHYSIOPATHOLOGY; TISSUE AND ORGAN PROCUREMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last two decades, lung transplantation has become the mainstay of therapy for selected patients suffering from many types of end-stage lung diseases (e.g. emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension and cystic fibrosis) refractory to medical management. Lung transplantation has enjoyed increasing success with better early and late survival rates. However, the number of patients requiring lung transplantation has been increasing and largely exceeds the number of donors available. As a result, the death rate on the waiting list is 20% to 30% in most lung transplant centers.   The best alternative will be to expand the number of donors. Indeed, we currently are able to use only 15% to 25% of the lungs that are offered to us from brain dead donors; 75% to 85% of donors are rejected due to various forms of lung injury. Hence, any strategy that would increase our utilization rate of lung donors from 15% to even 40 -50% could potentially double and even triple the number of lung transplants performed every year.   Our project, using a large animal model will study a very novel concept: ex-vivo (outside the body) repair of damaged lungs for transplantation. After organ retrieval and ischemic storage we will treat the donor lungs ex-vivo for 12 hours in a special pump perfusion system while repairing the organ with interleukin-10 gene therapy. This is a potent anti-inflammatory gene that can potentially refurbish injured lungs and also pre-prepare the organ to decrease incidence of rejection after transplantation. We will be able to evaluate the lung function in the perfusion system to document improved lung function and confirm that after transplantation in a survival pig lung transplant model. The consequent improvement in the quality of donor lungs with ex-vivo gene repair will have a significant impact on the number of transplants performed each year and on the outcome after lung transplantation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phase II trial of Azacitidine plus Deferasirox in higher risk Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS)
Keywords-MotsClés: AZACITIDINE; DEFERASIROX; EFFICACY; MYELODYSPLASTIC SYNDROMES; PHASE 2 TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Myelodysplastic syndromes are common blood disorders that can affect as many as one in 1000 Canadians over the age of 65. They are characterized by low blood counts that require frequent blood transfusions.  The development of iron overload in these patients is inevitable. The iron deposits in vital organs such as the heart and the liver and can lead to organ dysfunction.  Deferasirox is a well-studied drug that helps remove iron from the body. Most people with this disorder die due to progression of their disease to acute leukemia through multiple mechanisms. Iron overload in patients with myelodysplastic syndromes has been shown to be associated with shorter survival, and potentially a higher chance of leukemia. In a certain subgroup of higher risk patients, the drug azacitidine has been shown to decrease the chance of progression to leukemia and death from it. Thus, it is presently the standard of care for these patients. However, 50% of higher risk patients are still unresponsive to this medication, leaving a large group of patients for which other treatment options are emergently needed. Given that a large proportion of higher risk MDS patients fail to respond to azacitidine, and the evidence that iron deposition may lead to increased leukemic transformation, we would like to study whether iron removal from the body with deferasirox potentiates azacitadine in its effects on overall survival, as well as the chance of leukemia transformation. This question needs to be addressed in a randomized controlled trial, and the first step is a preliminary study to determine if the combination of azacitidine and deferasirox has any biologic effect. This study will determine whether this combination leads to blood count improvement over azacitiditine alone. If this drug combination ultimately proves more useful than azacitidine alone with respect to survival, this has the potential to impact the care of a large proportion of patients with myelodysplastic syndromes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the role of human isomiR-181a in myelodysplastic syndromes
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGONAUTE PROTEIN; BONE MARROW FAILURE; CROSSLINKING IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; ISOMIR-181A; LUCIFERASE ASSAY; MYELODYSPLASTIC SYNDROMES
Abstract-Résumé: Recent studies have established the critical role of microRNA (miRs) in the development of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). By analyzing deep sequencing data from The Cancer Genome Atlas project, we revealed that a distinctive miR-181a variant (isomiR) with a single 5-nucleotide (nt) addition is the dominant isoform expressed in patients. Given this addition is predicted to alter the target spectrum of isomiR-181a compared to wild-type miR-181a, we hypothesize that the effect of miR-181a is secondary to its isomiR, and the overexpression of isomiR-181a alters signaling pathways in hematopoietic stem cells associated with marrow failure syndromes. We will overexpress miR-181a and its isomiR with vector control in CD34+ cells, and perform HITS-CLIP combined with bioinformatics to decode mRNA binding sequences, with validation by luciferase assays in a high-throughput system. Immunoblotting will be used for further validation on protein expression. Predicted mRNA targets will be analyzed by IPA and DAVID programs, and the impact of critical biological pathways will be identified by enforced expression of miR-181a, isomiR-181a or vector control in CD34+ cells, followed by quantification of apoptosis, proliferation and CFC assays. A LNA oligonucleotide may be used to knock down miR181 and the isomiR. To functionally validate their role in MDS in vivo, NOG mice will be transplanted with CD34+ cells lentivirally transduced with miR-181a and isomiR-181a, and hematopoietic effect will be examined by blood counts, smear morphology of blood and marrow and progenitor assays. We expected that the expression of target protein will be inversely correlated with miR-181a and its isomiR, but only overexpression of isomiR-181a will induce MDS-like findings. We believe that appreciating the mechanisms by which miR participate in the biology of marrow failure will lead to the identification of predictive biomarkers and potentially novel therapeutic approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Animal Models of Depression as a Comorbidity in Epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANHEDONIA; BRAIN STIMULATION REWARD; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; DEPRESSION; INTRACRANIAL SELF STIMULATION; MOOD DISORDERS; PLEASURE; REWARD; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has shown promising results in treatment-resistant depression. DBS involves the electrical stimulation of brain sites through chronically implanted electrodes. The mechanism of the effectiveness of DBS remains unknown. This proposed study will examine the effects of DBS in a rodent model of anhedonia - the diminished ability to experience pleasure - a core symptom of depression.  Rats trained to give themselves electrical stimulation to their brain's pleasure/reward areas will be challenged with chemical, environmental and social stressors to induce anhedonia. They will then be treated with DBS and the effectiveness of DBS to relieve the anhedonia symptoms will be assessed.  This study will determine if DBS is effective in this model of anhedonia and provide a basis for more intensive studies of the mechanisms of DBS.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel brain stimulation intervention to investigate the pathophysiology and modulate plasticity in dystonia
Keywords-MotsClés: DYSTONIA; INTERVENTION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PATHOPHYSIOLOGY; PLASTICITY; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is a technique for non-invasive stimulation of the human brain, and has been in use for approximately 20 years in clinical and research environments. It is safe and painless. Different areas of the body are mapped out in a stereotyped manner in the brain, such that different muscles can be targeted. TMS was initially used to investigate brain function, in particular in neurological disorders. The most exciting recent development in this field was the finding that targeted protocols (TMS interventions) could modulate plasticity (increase or decrease brain activity) for minutes to hours beyond the period of stimulation. This offers the potential for targeted, non-invasive treatment in neurological disorders, which could be used as an alternative to or in combination with conventional pharmaceutical and physical therapies.   We have recently developed a novel TMS intervention which is able to increase or decrease brain activity, according to stimulation parameters. Such modulation of brain excitability would be desirable and is likely to be therapeutically beneficial in neurological disorders in which brain excitability is abnormal. One such condition is focal hand dystonia which is characterised by debilitating muscle contractions during repeated specific tasks such as writing. This is thought to arise from excessive excitability and plasticity in motor areas of the brain in genetically susceptible individuals. We therefore wish to apply this non-invasive intervention to the hand area of the motor cortex in dystonia patients in order to downregulate hyperexcitability. We hypothesise that this will lead to a reduction in brain excitability and dystonic symptoms. We will also apply this intervention in combination with another TMS intervention and expect that this will further improve the efficacy and therapeutic benefit of the intervention. These studies will also further our understanding of the mechanisms underlying dystonia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pallidal deep brain stimulation for dystonia: neuronal activity, stimulus parameters, and motor output
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; DYSTONIA; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MOVEMENT DISORDER
Abstract-Résumé: The most exciting new treatment for movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease (PD), tremor, and dystonia is deep brain stimulation (DBS), which refers to high-frequency electrical stimulation delivered through surgically implanted fine electrodes into specific brain regions. DBS can markedly reduce patients' tremors, stiffness, slowness, and abnormal muscle contractions. Whereas the benefits of DBS in patients are well recognized, the way it achieves these benefits is unknown. My research AIM is to understand how DBS works at the level of brain cells and the brain circuits where DBS electrodes are implanted. I am specifically concentrating on how it works for dystonia, a debilitating movement disorder. Dystonia produces involuntary muscle contractions and writhing movements that limit mobility, often with pain and can make sufferers completely unable to function. While DBS for dystonia is very effective in most cases, it requires more variable parameters of electrical stimulation to yield clinical benefits and it takes from weeks to months to become effective after surgery, unlike DBS for other movement disorders such as PD and tremor. Furthermore, it requires more battery power to maintain stimulation, causing discomfort and potential complications due to battery replacement surgery. Therefore, we need toclarify how such variable electrical stimulation affects activities of brain cells and dystonic muscles. During DBS electrode implantation surgery for dystonia patients, we are able to access brain cells by lowering a microelectrode into target brain area. Using this technique, we will examine the electrical activity of brain cells in the DBS target site and abnormal muscle activity in dystonia patients in response to a variety of DBSparameters. This will allow us to determine how DBS affects target brain cells as well as muscle output. These studies will help us develop the optimial stimulation paradigms to maximize the clinical benefit of DBS for dystonia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chemical biology approaches to understanding glycosylation mediated gene silencing
Keywords-MotsClés: CARBOHYDRATE CHEMISTRY; CELL BIOLOGY; ENZYME INHIBITORS; ENZYMOLOGY; EPIGENETICS; GLYCOBIOLOGY; MASS SPECTROMETRY; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: How genes are regulated within cells defines how they become different during development of an organism and, in turn, give rise to different tissues. These differences between cells occur despite all cells encoding the same genome and the differences that develop can be passed on from cells to their progeny. This ability to inherit traits that do not arise from changes in the genome is known as epigenetic inheritance, and constitutes a field of research activity known as epigenetics. The ability to understand how external stimuli alter the regulation of gene expression is of considerable general interest and has implications in many diseases as well as, downstream, in potentially defining postive social policies that will encourage a healthier population.      The molecular mechanisms within cells that govern how external stimuli give rise to epigentic differences are not well understood.  Consistent with their being a wide range of external types of stimuli, there appears to be multiple mechanisms contributing to the epigentic regulation of gene expression. I am to investigate one surprising new mechanism that has been recently uncovered but which little is known about.    Recently it has been shown that an enzyme that acts in cells to install sugars onto other cellular proteins is a key player in silencing the expression of genes. This enzyme is essential for appropriate silencing of genes and the proper body development of a commonly used model organism; the fruit fly. However, though we know this enzyme is involved we do not understand the molecular mechanisms by which it acts to silence genes. This enzyme responds to available nutrients and so it seems possible that it might act to sense nutrient supply and tune gene expression. Using a variety of approaches I aim to carry out studies that will enable an understanding of how this enzyme acts as an epigenetic regulator of gene expression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Providing Quality Care Safely: Accounting for the Knowledge of Frontline Careworkers in Residential Care for Older Persons
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; AIDES; GENDER; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; INJURY; LONG-TERM CARE; NURSING HOMES; PROMISING PRACTICES; QUALITY CARE; WORK ORGANIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: While frontline careworkers comprise the majority of the residential care workforce and are responsible for the bulk of hands-on elder care, they are often excluded from decision-making processes. Recent studies are drawing links between this marginalization and the perpetuation of injury, violence and poor quality care. This study investigates a promising practice that integrates the knowledge and experience of frontline careworkers within the institutional processes of residential facilities, resulting in fewer injuries and better quality care. This practice involves regular meetings between frontline careworkers and managers. These meetings are facilitated and follow an agenda set by the careworkers themselves. By observing these meetings, conducting focus groups with frontline careworkers and interviewing managers, this study seeks to: 1) explain why this program has been so successful, 2) better understand what is required to provide quality care safely, and 3) make recommendations that can benefit other facilities and jurisdictions. Results of this study will be distributed through presentations and publications tailored to a wide range of audiences, including academics, administrators, policymakers, careworkers and the general public.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cost-Effectiveness of Using BRCA1/2 Genetic Testing to Guide Breast Cancer Treatment: An Observational Study of Women in the United Sates.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; COST- EFFECTIVENESS; GENETIC TESTING; HEALTH DISPARITIES
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic testing can be used to detect patients with higher risk of recurrence or spread of breast cancer. Current clinical guidelines suggest that patients with higher risk of breast cancer recurrence or metastasis should be referred for genetic testing to determine whether they may need more aggressive treatment in order to reduce risk of recurrence. Considering the hereditary nature of some subtypes of breast cancer, a positive test result may also be used to recommend monitoring of at-risk relatives of affected patients. This study aims to use large, nation-wide observational databases to: 1) assess clinical benefits and economic costs of using genetic testing to guide treatment of breast cancer among women, and   2) investigate health disparities in access to genetic tests and appropriate follow-up care among minorities and lower income patients across the US. This study will investigate both clinical benefits and costs that are associated with genetic testing and therefore will inform policy makers and practitioners about the overall cost benefit trade-off of using genetic testing to guide treatment of breast cancer. Furthermore, this study will investigate the existing gaps in terms of equal access to health care resources (using the example of genetic tests for breast cancer) among minorities and low income patients. This is the first study about the clinical and economic value of genetic testing for breast cancer based on a large observational data. My research will generate useful empirical and methodological results for health policy makers and may potentially be used to improve clinical guidelines for using genetic testing for breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the space-time distribution of 'offload delays' and ambulance accessibility in Nova Scotia
Keywords-MotsClés: AMBULANCE SERVICE COVERAGE; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT CROWDING; GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEMS; GEOGRAPHIC POSITIONING SYSTEMS; HEALTH SERVICE ACCESSIBILITY; HEALTH SYSTEMS RESEARCH; PATIENT OFFLOAD TIME; SERVICE ACCESS INEQUALITY; SPATIO-TEMPORAL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Ambulance services are an integral part of healthcare systems.  In Nova Scotia, as well as other parts of Canada and other countries, ambulances are increasingly tied up for a longer period of time at some urban hospitals due to emergency department  crowding.  This has become a serious health service system issue.  The longer ambulances stay in hospitals to transfer the patients, the longer they are unable to respond to other calls.  Escalation of the patient offload delay problem results in many areas not having adequate ambulance access.  However, we do not know exactly what the relationships between the offload delay problem and ambulance service access are, or what areas in the province are at risk of losing ambulance access if the offload delay problem escalates.  This research applies a novel approach of using a global positioning system (GPS) which tracks minute-by-minute locations of all ambulances in Nova Scotia.  I estimate the area (sq km) that all available ambulances can cover over time, assess the correlations between the events of offload time and increase in areas without ambulance access, and examine the population most affected.  The proposed research is one of the first in the province or anywhere to use GPS data to analyze spatial and temporal patterns of ambulance access.  Findings of this research can inform policy about target offload times in order to avoid ambulance capacity-loss and the population and areas vulnerable to the risk of losing access to ambulances.  This research presents an innovative tool which can help ensure the cost-effectiveness of decision-making on ambulance service allocation, and supports the effort to reduce health inequalities.  The tool can be used to help the sustainability of many other health services anywhere in Canada and beyond.

ProgramNameEN: Fellowship Award - Priority Announcement: Fragile X (SHOPP)
NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités : fragilité du chromosome X (PPPOS)
TitreApplicationTitle: FMRP expression in DG mediates NMDAr function
Keywords-MotsClés: BDNF SIGNALING; DENTATE GYRUS; FMR KNOCK-OUT MICE; FRAGILE-X SYNDROME; HIPPOCAMPAL NEUROGENESIS; LEARNING AND MEMORY; LONG-TERM POTENTIATION AND LONG-TERM DEPRESSION; NMDA RECEPTOR; SYNAPTIC PLASITICTY
Abstract-Résumé: Fragile-X syndrome (FXS) is the most common form of inherited intellectual disability and can be considered as the best characterized form of autism spectrum disorder. The disorder is caused by repressed transcription of the gene Fmr1 which codes for the Fragile-X Mental Retardation Protein (FXMR). Our preliminary results have shown that FMRP have interaction at the synapse in the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus (brain region for learning and memory). An alteration in the ratio of AMPA receptor to NMDA receptor in the DG was found in the Fmr1 knock-out mice. We have shown clear and robust impairments in NMDA receptor-dependent long-term potentiation and long-term depression (a form of learning and memory formation) in the DG of adult male Fmr knock-out mice. We also found that Fmr KO mice showed a learning impairment on context discrimination, a learning task that is also impaired in animals that lack functional NMDA receptors in the DG. Others also report that FMRP is regulated by brain-derived neurotrophin factor that influences neuronal survival and maturation and regulates synaptic plasticity. Since DG is a site of specific impairment in FXS, we aim to evaluate the role of DG in the pathophysiology of FXS and how FXS regulate synaptic plasticity in DG. Using well established Fmr KO mice, we will examine if there are physiological or morphological deficits in DG and alterations in behaviours that are DG dependent. We also examine the relative importance of the DG to cognitive impairment using DG-specific Fmr KO and DG-specific Fmr knock-in mice. In addition, we aim to determine how FMRP alters the BDNF signaling pathway in the DG, which may in turn affect the functions of NMDA receptor in synaptic plasticity. This work will be critical for determining the linkage between Fmr1 expression and specific form of learning and memory and will unmask how Fmr1 gene products are involved in structural and functional processes in the mammalian brain

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités : recherche biomédical/clinique sur le VIH/SIDA
TitreApplicationTitle: Generation of HIV resistant T cell progenitors from human induced pluripotent stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: ACQUIRED IMMUNE DEFICIENCY DISEASE (AIDS); HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELL (HSC); HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS (HIV); INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELL (IPSC)
Abstract-Résumé: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infects immune system cells and either kills them or impairs their function, and can lead to acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS). An impaired immune system is unable to surmount a proper immune response against infections and diseases. HIV-inflicted people that receive uninfected bone marrow progenitor cells are very likely to have these cells infected with HIV as well. Furthermore, availability of compatible progenitor cells is very limited. To address these problems we propose to use in vitro sources of stem cells, as well as a special type of stem cell that can be obtained by reprogramming adult cells such as skin cells. We have already been successful in generating immune system cells from these sources, providing a potentially unlimited supply of cells. These cells can be readily modified in order to acquire resistance to HIV infections, and their efficacy can be assessed in the laboratory. Our work would provide a novel, patient specific approach for developing patient-specific prevention and treatment to HIV infection.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités : recherche biomédical/clinique sur le VIH/SIDA
TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the role of T cell metabolism in HIV-induced chronic immune activation and immune dysfunction.
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; CHRONIC IMMUNE ACTIVATION; HIV; IMMUNE DYSREGULATION; METABOLIC PHENOTYPE; MTOR SIGNALING PATHWAY; POLYCHROMATIC FACS ANALYSIS; POLYCHROMATIC IMAGING FACS ANALYSIS; T CELL METABOLISM
Abstract-Résumé: The molecular and cellular pathways that lead from HIV infection to AIDS are complex, multifactorial and not understood. However, a number of recent studies have identified several key immune features in HIV infected individuals that characterize the progression to AIDS. One such feature is the state of general chronic immune activation in HIV individuals, which is a better predictor of AIDS progression than viral load. We have yet to understand the underlying causes and maintenance of chronic immune activation that is often exasperated by immune dysfunction in HIV individuals. The depletion of CD4+ T cells and the expansion of non-functional CD8+ T cells confound the search for underlying factors. Since chronic immune activation is a key player in the pathogenesis of AIDS, therapeutic interventions to reduce it may positively impact the overall immune function in HIV individuals. Altered metabolism in T cells in HIV individuals could be an underlying factor of chronic immune activation. Mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), a protein molecule, is a key regulator of metabolism that once activated directs T cell activation, differentiation and function. mTOR controls not only the positive signals to direct functions of T cells but also the negative signals to turn itself off when not required. Dysregulated mTOR has been implicated in cancer where normal growth is sacrificed for uncontrolled growth to the detriment of the organism and likewise loss of mTOR retards growth. The hypothesis of my project is that in HIV infection T cells fail to either turn off or tone down mTOR activities leading to chronic immune activation and immune dysfunction. To date, mTOR functions with metabolism have not been investigated in T cells from HIV. The goal of my project is to define the interplay between mTOR, metabolism and chronic immune activation, and with this knowledge therapeutic interventions could be developed to reduce chronic immune activation and immune dysfunction.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités : recherche biomédical/clinique sur le VIH/SIDA
TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptomic and proteomic screening of host genes modulated by HIV-1 in human macrophages : a highly sensitive strategy for the identification of new susceptibility/restriction factors.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; HIV; MACROPHAGES; MICROARRAY; PROTEOMICS; RESTRICTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Macrophages are immune cells that play one of the most crucial roles in HIV-1 progression. They are among the first cells to be infected after primary contact with the virus and display a strong resistance to HIV-induced cell death. Thus, these long-lived cells constitute a persisting and highly mobile reservoir able to transfer the virus and spread the disease to the entire immune system. Nevertheless, very little is known about cellular events accompanying HIV-1 life cycle and productive infection in macrophages. This lack of data is largely due to the low rate of HIV infection efficiency obtained with these cells in lab experiments (1 to 15% of infected cells). Since the small number of infected cells is "diluted" by the elevated number of non-infected ones, it is very hard to detect and analyse phenomena leading to a complete HIV-1 infection. In this project, I propose to use a modified virus that allows the discrimination and the isolation of infected cells from the resistant population. A detailed analysis of these separated cells will lead for the first time to a highly sensitive detection of early modulated genes and proteins controlling HIV-1 successful replication in macrophages. As a complement to this approach, video-microscopy on living cells will provide a better comprehension of dynamic cellular processes involved in the infection. Therefore, the overall objective of the proposed project is to identify several new factors favouring susceptibility or resistance to HIV-1 infection. The acquired data will deepen our understanding of the mechanisms used by the virus to spread the infection throughout the immune system. By this approach, we aim to facilitate the development of new specific therapeutic strategies against AIDS progression.

TitreApplicationTitle: HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Clinic: Risk factors for Failing to Attend, and Facilitating Care for High-Risk Patients.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; DRUG ADHERENCE; HIV; HIV PREVENTION; POST EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS
Abstract-Résumé: There are an estimated 1 million people living in the USA with HIV, 21 percent of whom are unaware of their diagnosis. A major issue today relates to decreasing transmission of HIV infection to uninfected individuals, particularly amongst those who are infected but unaware of their diagnosis that are unwittingly transmitting the virus to others.  Several populations are disproportionately affected by HIV, including African Americans, Hispanics, injection drug users, and men who have sex with men.    Many patients are exposed to HIV and seek care in local Emergency Departments.  These HIV-exposures are primarily sexual or from needles. HIV transmission can be prevented in close to 100% of these patients if they seek care early (within 72 hours), and if patients adhere to a 28-day medication regimen. Unfortunately, up to 20% of those who seek care in the Emergency Department after an HIV exposure do not follow up for subsequent care in specialized clinics. This is of major concern as these patients are known to the healthcare system and are at high risk of HIV acquisition. HIV acquisition can be easily prevented in these individuals with appropriate care and follow up.  The purpose of this study is to determine who these individuals are in terms of age, sex, race, socioeconomic status, language, and type of exposure. In addition, we aim to seek the utility of an age, sex, language, and culturally appropriate telephone call intervention to enable access to care.   A better understanding of who fails to show up to HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis clinic will guide medical providers to create more accessible health care. The ultimate goal is to reduce HIV transmission in individuals with high-risk exposure and ultimately prevent further HIV transmission in the community.

TitreApplicationTitle: Women's Health Rights and Realities: The Policy and Practice of Integrating HIV and Sexual and Reproductive Health Services in Latin America
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNOGRAPHY; GENDER AND HEALTH; GOVERNANCE; HEALTH EQUITY; HIV AND AIDS; INTERNATIONAL HEALTH POLICY; MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH; MEXICO; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SEXUAL AND REPRODUCTIVE RIGHTS
Abstract-Résumé: Since 2003, Mexico has advanced towards universal access to health care. In theory, access to HIV and Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) services is guaranteed. Integrating HIV and SRH, especially preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission and unwanted pregnancies among women with HIV, promotes the health of women and children, and is cost-effective. Unfortunately, my previous research shows that despite federal funds to provide contraceptives for all women, HIV testing during prenatal care, and anti-HIV medications during pregnancy and labour and delivery, these services are not consistently available in public clinics and hospitals.  My post-doctoral research will generate proposals to improve accountability in the delivery of HIV and SRH services in Mexico. Working with policy-makers and affected women, I will identify culturally appropriate, politically feasible mechanisms to empower low-income women, including those living with HIV, to demand their health rights. Increased access to HIV and SRH services will improve individual and population health and contribute to achieving the health-related Millennium Development Goals by reducing child and maternal mortality and tackling the expansion of the HIV pandemic.  HIV does not respect national boundaries and threatens social and economic development globally. Reversing the HIV pandemic is a public good in our interdependent world. My research is especially relevant for Canadians given increasing social and economic exchange with Mexico through migration and trade. Canada is an important leader in international maternal-child health, and my research will contribute to achieving the goals of the Partnership for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health. My research is consistent with CIHR's mandate to develop research capacity which addresses global health challenges in a priority country (Mexico) by preventing and controlling pandemics, strengthening health policy and health systems, and advancing gender equality.

TitreApplicationTitle: The drug use- and HIV-related health impacts of increasing labour market participation for marginalized, HIV-positive people who use illicit drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: EMPLOYMENT; HIV/AIDS; INJECTION DRUG USE; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Employment has long been identified as intrinsically linked to individual health. Among HIV-infected people who use illicit drugs, employment may be a key influence on addiction recovery and other health outcomes. Previous research with HIV-positive and at-risk drug using populations identified a range of individual, contextual and structural barriers to employment over and above drug use, including HIV-infection. It also identified employment attributes that encourage labour market participation. Given the potential health benefits and high barriers to labour market participation for HIV-positive and at-risk people who use illicit drugs, alternative labour market participation models appropriate to individuals who face episodic interruptions in their ability to work are badly needed. Under the supervision of Drs. Thomas Kerr at the University of British Columbia and Tom Patterson at the University of California at San Diego, the proposed post-doctoral project seeks to develop and pilot an adaptive employment intervention for HIV-infected illicit drug users. The proposed intervention design will be based on feasibility assessments and will draw on innovative work models such as Amazon.com's Mechanical Turk, where individuals voluntarily undertake tasks suited to their ability and availability and are paid on a task-by-task basis. Participants will have access to a community generated job bank where they can undertake paid activities compatible with their drug use, health status and health and social services access. Prospective participants will be randomized for participation from an existing CIHR/NIH-funded cohort study of injection drug users (n=750) that collects socio-demographic, behavioural and clinical HIV-related measures. This will facilitate evaluation strategies that match existing longitudinal data with intervention participation outcomes. Evaluation will focus primarily on impact of intervention participation on HIV viral suppression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chemical Biology Screen to Identify Drugs for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; HIGH CONTENT SCREEN; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington's Disease (HD) is a genetic neurodegenerative disorder that affects families worldwide. HD is caused by a mutation in a single gene encoding the huntingtin protein. Affected individuals have a 50% chance of passing this gene on to each child. The symptoms of the disease include involuntary movement, loss of motor coordination, cognitive impairment and psychiatric disturbances, caused by degeneration of brain cells and leading to death, ten to twenty years after onset. Currently, no treatment or cure exists for HD. Studies in the Truant research group focus on the normal function of the huntingtin protein, in hopes of finding novel drug targets for HD. One of the discoveries recently made in our laboratory is that the huntingtin protein is involved in a cell stress response. We found that this stress response is altered in cells with mutant huntingtin. Cell stress is an important factor in many neurological diseases, in fact, a similar stress response is dysfunctional in Alzheimer's disease. We have developed biological tools that can be used to compare the stress response in normal cells versus mutant huntingtin cells in response to a range of potential drugs. The goal is to identify potential drugs that cure the stress response in mutant huntingtin cells and to pursue these compounds to be further developed in collaboration with pharmaceutical companies such as CHDI Inc. The proposed experiments will advance our understanding of normal and mutant huntingtin function, and provide leads for the therapeutic intervention of HD. These advances may have implications in other neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's Disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genotype and Phenotype Correlations in Very Early Onset Inflammatory Bowel Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CROHN'S DISEASE; EARLY ONSET INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; GENETICS; GENOTYPIC CORRELATIONS; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; PHENOTYPIC CORRELATIONS; ULCERATIVE COLITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a group of chronic conditions that affect up to 1 in 250 people in Canada. It causes growth hindrance, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding and may require surgical intervention. Estimates of the economic impact of IBD are placed at $1.75 billion per year. IBD includes Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis, and is thought to be due to a combination of a number of factors resulting in a disordered immune response. The current thinking is that there are a number of factors involved, including genetic, environmental and abnormal responses to normal bacteria found in all humans. Over the past decade, studies have shown that IBD has increased in frequency by 30%, increasing most in the younger age groups. Very early onset IBD or VEO-IBD (10 years of age and younger) presents differently than in older pediatric and adult IBD patients, showing a different disease location and behavior. As well, we realize that these patients have a different clinical course and outcome. This has implications on surgical and therapeutic choices, as they do not respond to common treatments used with other pediatric IBD patients. Our current understanding is that patients with VEO-IBD have more of a genetic predisposition to the underlying cause of their condition, as they have not had enough time for environmental and bacterial exposure to be a significant player. We plan to characterize the type, behavior and clinical outcomes of our VEO-IBD population at SickKids. As well, we plan to look for genetic differences in these patients and attempt to find specific disease patterns with which they correlate. This method has in the past resulted in discoveries of disease-altering treatment options in some patients which, in some cases, were considered life saving. As many of these patients are thought to share genetic patterns with adults, the implications of our research may be far-reaching and helpful to potentially all patients with IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the microbiome in determining disease phenotype and driving carcinogenesis in IBD patients with and without PSC
Keywords-MotsClés: CARCINOGENESIS; GENETICS; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INTESTINAL MICROBIOME; NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory Bowel Disease(IBD),namely Ulcerative Colitis(UC) and Crohns Disease(CD) affects about 0.5 percent of Canadians. UC involves only the large bowel while CD may involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract. Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis(PSC) is a liver disease which affects 2 percent of patients with IBD. Patients with IBD affecting their colon(colonic IBD) are at increased risk of developing colon cancer(CRC), a risk which is even further elevated in patients with colonic IBD and PSC. Why patients with IBD involving the colon are at increased risk of colorectal cancer and why this risk is even further elevated in patients with concurrent PSC is not known. Because of the increased risk of CRC in patients with colonic IBD it is current practice to assess these patients intermittently by performing colonoscopy where tissue samples called biopsies can be taken to assess for abnormalities of the cells which line the colon called dysplasia, which may precede the development of CRC. The human intestine contains huge numbers of bacteria and it has been shown that these bacteria may trigger UC and CD. Emerging evidence has also suggested that bacteria may play a role in determining disease behaviour and cancer development. New techniques now allow the characterisation of intestinal bacteria using tissue and stool samples. The aim of this study is to assess the amount and type of intestinal bacteria in colonic IBD patients with and without PSC, PSC patients without IBD and healthy patients to evaluate whether there are differences between these groups which may explain their contrasting disease behaviour and cancer risk. We will also assess whether the composition of intestinal bacteria within these groups is influenced by genetic factors and immune system responses.  Our findings may provide insights into the processes underlying disease behavior, cancer development and PSC evolution in IBD and potentially lead to new diagnostic and treatment strategies.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités - maladies inflammatoires de l'instestin
TitreApplicationTitle: Autophagy and bacterial sensing in intestinal homeostasis and Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD).
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; INFLAMMATION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INNATE IMMUNITY; NOD SIGNALING; TRANSGENIC/KO MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory Bowel Diseases are a group of inflammatory conditions of the colon and the small intestine. IBD related pathologies are painful and significantly limit the quality of life. It is estimated that 1 out 180 Canadians suffer from IBD and incidence rates across the country are among the highest in the world. As the molecular mechanisms responsible for IBD are poorly understood, current therapies mainly aim at managing the symptoms. Thus, a better understanding of the mechanisms regulating IBD is needed in order to develop new therapeutic approaches. Recent studies have revealed that three pathways are highly involved in IBD, namely the NOD pathway that is responsible for gut microflora sensing, autophagy, a cell recycling process also implicated in bacterial handling, and Th17 lymphocytes, immune cells particularly involved in anti-microbial immunity. The relationship among these pathways remain however poorly understood. We have recently conducted a functional screen to unravel new regulators of the NOD pathway. Among the identified regulators, ULK2, a key initiator of autophagy was identified. The central place of this protein in autophagy and bacterial sensing renders ULK2 an interesting target to understand the relationship between bacterial sensing, autophagy and induction of the inflammatory response in the gut.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the Hippo pathway by the methyltransferase Set7 in the gut during homeostasis and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETICS; EPITHELIAL CELL BIOLOGY; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; LARGE AND SMALL INTESTINE; PARASITE IMMUNOLOGY; STEM CELL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The intestine is one of the most important barriers in the body as it is responsible for absorbing nutrients and vitamins from food in addition to blocking out infectious germs. The goal of this project is to determine the role of a specific group of molecules in the function of the cells that line the intestine (called intestinal epithelial cells or IECs). The molecules we study are part of a pathway called the Hippo pathway, so named because if this pathway is perturbed, organs grow to a very large size. It is also known that the Hippo pathway is very important in the development of inflammatory bowel diseases and colon cancer. So understanding how this pathway is controlled will provide new drug targets to treat these diseases. Our results will hopefully lead to new drugs that will have a positive effect on the well-being of millions of Canadians and people around the world.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités - maladies inflammatoires de l'instestin
ClasseRechercheFR: COLITE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of signalling pathways in maintaining T regulatory cell function
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR BIOLOGY; IN VIVO MOUSE MODELS; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; T CELL IMMUNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Autoimmune diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis, arise from an overactive immune response against substances and tissues normally present in the body. If this over reactivity against self persists for a long time it results in chronic inflammation. There are no known cures for autoimmune diseases; currently at best there are mildly alleviating treatments. For instance, patients with autoimmune diseases are typically given drugs to suppress the immune system to diminish immune responses in general. This type of treatment means that the individual becomes susceptible to infection and cancer as their immune system is effectively turned off. My project focuses on an immune cell called a T regulatory cell (Treg), these cells have the ability to suppress immune responses and normally prevent autoimmune diseases. The way that Tregs turn immune responses off is not clearly understood, and the goal of my project is to discover how Treg cells work. In parallel, I will also study how they interact with other types of immune cells. Gaining a greater understanding of how the actions of Tregs are controlled will help to develop new therapies for diseases caused by an over active immune response thus reducing the dependency on non-specific immunosuppressive drugs. Each year there are over 800,000 new cases of Inflammatory bowel disease diagnosed, in Canada alone there are over 200,000 people suffer from this debilitating disease. Thus, this research aims to improve the quality of life for a significant part of the Canadian population.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités - maladies inflammatoires de l'instestin
TitreApplicationTitle: Relative roles of Nod1 and Nod2 in specific cell types during intestinal inflammation.
Keywords-MotsClés: HOST DEFENSE; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INNATE IMMUNITY; NOD1/NOD2
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a lifelong, chronic condition marked by debilitating flare-ups of inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract of which the causes are unknown and there is no cure.  Recently, however, research has made significant strides towards understanding the mechanisms behind this disease, particularly through the use of studies that scan and compare the entire genomes of patients with IBD versus healthy patients to identify variations of genes that can lead to greater susceptibility to the disease.   A vast majority of these genes seem to be involved in the recognition and response to bacterial infection, which supports the hypothesis that IBD arises as the result of a dysfunctional immune response to the vast numbers of harmless bacteria that line the surface of the gastrointestinal tract.  Two of the first genes identified were Nod1 and Nod2, which are both responsible for detecting peptidoglycan, a component of the coating that surrounds individual bacteria cells.  It is known that mutations in Nod1 and Nod2 that make an individual more likely to develop IBD result in these genes functioning at a sub-optimal level, but how this ultimately leads to IBD remains unknown.   This goal of this project is therefore to identify the specific cell types in which Nod1 and Nod2 are active in order to better understand their role in intestinal inflammation.  We will use state of the art techniques to selectively block the expression of either Nod1 or Nod2 in a mouse for each cell type.  These mice will then be subjected to either experimental intestinal inflammation or infection with an intestinal pathogen such as Salmonella typhimurium.  By doing this, we will be able to better understand exactly what the functions Nod1 and Nod2 have in the intestine, how the loss of these functions can lead to IBD, and ultimately what we can do to target Nod1 and Nod2 function therapeutically to treat or cure patients with IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Human Visceral Pain Mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HUMAN VISCERAL PAIN; HYPERSENSITIVITY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME; PHARMACOLOGY; VISCERAL AFFERENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic visceral pain (CVP) (e.g. pain arising from the gastrointestinal tract) is one of the most frequent reasons for seeking health care. Pain can arise from organic disease, e.g. inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but in fact 50% of all patients presenting with visceral pain have no detectable structural or biochemical abnormalities. These patients are categorized as having a functional gastrointestinal disorder such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). The mechanisms of CVP are poorly understood.  There is increasing evidence that CVP increases sensitivity, or hypersensitivity, of nerve fibres that sense stimuli within the gut.  However, drug development has lacked direction due to a rush to extrapolate from the normal condition or from animals to humans.  Therefore there is a need to for a translational program that can identify targets within the human gut to treat CVP.  This project will involve electrical recordings as well as chemical coding to identify differnt subtypes of sensory nerves within the human gastrointestinal tract.  We will then use different drugs to identify potential targets within these sensory nerves.  Finally, we will use tissues from resections of IBD patients and patients with acute appendicitis to determine how these targets change during inflammation.  Furthermore, we will use tissue resections from hypersensitive appendix patients to determine how previously identified targets are changed in CVP.  As a result, this project will identify targets involved in pain that can be modulated during inflammatory and functional bowel disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Helminth parasites, regulatory macrophages and the control of enteric inflammation.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGINASE; COLITIS; CYTOKINES; HELMINTHIC PARASITES; IMMUNE REGULATION; INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGES; RNA EXPRESSION; T CELLS; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: The onset of inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) is a complex interaction amongst genetic and environmental factors. However these diseases share common mechanisms such as cytokine (TNF alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-12) and chemokine (CCL5) secretion patterns and recruitment of immune cell populations (neutrophils, macrophages, T cells) which can cause tissue damage. Hence, therapies are aimed either at dampening inflammatory cell influx or blocking pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion. An assessment of the immune response to parasitic helminths (worms) has revealed the presence of macrophages with both anti-inflammatory and tissue repairing abilities, termed alternatively activated macrophages (AAMs). The the use of this cell population arises as a novel therapeutic approach. However, mechanisms underlying AAM induction, efficacy and possible side-effects are poorly understood.  Extending from our earlier observation that AAMs can block chemically-induced colitis in mice, this project will add novel data on the induction and phenotype of helminth-induced AAMs, cytokine- induced AAMs and a regulatory macrophage (elicited by the consumption of cell debris).  The ability and mechanism of action of these cells in the modulation of colitis in laboratory models will be compared.  Ultimately we seek to better understand the AAM/regulatory macrophage as a cell with the potential to be used as an anti-inflammatory treatment for IBD.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités - maladies inflammatoires de l'instestin
TitreApplicationTitle: Commensal microbiota and innate immune interactions during colitis
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMENSAL MICROBIOTA; EPITHELIAL BARRIER; FISH-IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; MICROBIAL COMMUNITY ANALYSIS; QUANTITATIVE REAL TIME PCR; RIP2; T CELL TRANSFER COLITIS MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, are thought to result from dysregulation of normal interactions between intestinal microbes and the immune system. However, little is known of the role of resident gut bacteria in stimulating immune responses that ultimately lead to colitis. In this study, we will first compare bacterial community composition in immune-deficient (Rag-/-) mice that are transplanted with either naive T cells (develop colitis), or naive and regulatory T cells (do not develop colitis). The relative abundance of bacterial groups from different intestinal locations will be analyzed using DNA fingerprinting techniques. We will then explore these bacterial relationships in immune-deficient mice that also lack the ability to activate a signaling pathway for production of pro-inflammatory and antimicrobial compounds that function in limiting bacterial entry into intestinal cells. This pathway is normally stimulated after bacterial cell wall components are recognized by intracellular receptors (Nod1 and Nod2) and mutations in genes coding for these receptors have been associated with Crohn's disease. We will analyze mouse intestinal tissues for production of pro-inflammatory and antimicrobial compounds and, using microscopy and fluorescent labels, view the spatial relationships between bacteria and the intestinal lining. Finally, we will test how changing the composition of bacterial communities impacts on the development of colitis. This study should shed light on the mechanisms by which resident microbes contribute to chronic inflammation associated with IBD.

ProgramNameEN: Fellowship - Priority Announcement - Inflammatory Bowel Disease
NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités - maladies inflammatoires de l'instestin
TitreApplicationTitle: Bacteria and Mucus: A dysfunctional relationship leading to IBD
Keywords-MotsClés: DSS COLITIS; IBD; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTESTINAL EPITHELIUM; INTESTINAL MICROFLORA; MOUSE MODELS; MUC2; MUCUS; TOLL-LIKE-RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a group of illnesses, all characterized by persistent inflammation of the colon and small intestine.  We still have only limited knowledge as to what triggers IBD, but recent research suggests the breakdown of mucus integrity may be a cause. Additionally, it is known that the intestinal microbiota has a significant ability to modulate the intestinal mucus layer, impacting both its composition and thickness.  We hypothesize that defects in mucus function leads to exaggerated bacterial contact with the immune system, thereby worsening colitis.   In both IBD and the commonly used DSS colitis model, shifts in mucus thickness, composition, or glycosylation may render the mucus layer increasingly permeable to the resident bacteria of the gut.  This allows them to associate too closely with the intestinal epithelium, stimulating MyD88 mediated toll-like receptors (TLRs) and other elements of the innate immune system, resulting in inflammation along the intestinal epithelium and impacting the ability of the host to control the mucus layer, and the intestinal microflora.   We propose to test this hypothesis with Muc2 KO and C3GnT KO mice deficient in Muc2, and mucin glycosylation.  We will examine how these two models react when treated with 3% DSS to induce colitis, and how the mucus barrier is maintained under these circumstances.  During these treatments, we will monitor the severity of the induced inflammation, and how the microflora begins to infiltrate the mucus layer over time.  We expect that the loss of the outer mucus layer in the muc2 KO or mucin glycosylation in the C3GnT KO, we expect to see the mucus layer become more permeable to the intestinal microflora.  We believe this mechanism to be similar to what occurs in IBD, where the mucus layer becomes more permeable, allowing the bacteria to become more closely associated with the intestinal epithelium, trigger inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring implementation of evidence-based services for children with DCD in Québec
Keywords-MotsClés: BEST PRACTICES; CHILDREN WITH PHYSICAL DISABILITY; DEVELOPMENTAL COORDINATION DISORDER; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; ORGANIZATION OF SERVICES; PEDIATRIC; QUALITY OF SERVICES; REHABILITATION; SERVICE DELIVERY MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Joshua is in Grade 1. Although he reads well printing, getting ready for recess, eating his lunch and activities in gym class all seem to be challenging. Joshua's teacher refers him to rehabilitation services for 'fine motor problems'. Due to long waitlists, it is sixteen months before the referral is passed along to an occupational therapist (OT). Joshua is now a frustrated child who frequently acts out in order to avoid motor-based activity. The OT notices significant motor impairment. She gives the teacher some recommendations but no self-care issues are addressed and Joshua's parents have no idea how to manage the issues he is having at home and in the community.   Children like Joshua with Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) are in every classroom in Canada. We now know that interventions can help Joshua function better and improve his quality of life. However, the poor organization of services makes it difficult for children like him to access appropriate help. Moreover, services are often based on traditional thinking, which focuses on evaluating and treating 'impairments'. Rehabilitation services need to be timely, grounded in real-life needs, and aimed at building capacity for all the partners involve in the care of these children. A new model of service delivery, based on sound evidence, has been developed and piloted in a region in Ontario, with exciting results. The goals of this research project are to compare the organization of services in Ontario and Quebec; to explore the possibility to use the new model of services for physiotherapy (PT); to develop French training to support modification of OT and PT practice; and to explore the possibility to adapt this model in the Quebec service organization. Results from this research will provide us with a better understanding of how to improve practice and how to organize services to foster children's quality of life and system efficiency.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of B cell lymphoproliferative disease associated with hepatitis C infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODIES; B CELLS AND LYMPHOMA; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 170 million people worldwide are chronically infected with the hepatitis C virus (HCV), with thousands dying yearly from this disease. A subset of HCV patients develop serious complications ranging from skin rashes to joint pain to even kidney failure due to a specific autoimmune response by B cells, the white blood cells in our bodies that produce antibodies. These patients are also at much higher risk for developing B cell cancers. How HCV, and not other viruses, causes B cells to produce abnormal proteins called cryoglobulins is poorly understood. Cryoglobulins are the proteins causing inflammation and damage of tissues that over time can lead to the complications mentioned above. In this study we will first investigate how B cells are changed in HCV patients compared to hepatitis B virus (HBV) infected patients and uninfected, healthy controls. Next, we will determine how HCV affects B cell activation as we hypothesize that HCV directly stimulates B cells to produce cryoglobulins. Understanding how this process occurs can lead to novel drug treatments to prevent future complications for many patients with chronic HCV infection. In addition, our work could have broader implications in the understanding of B cell responses in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and lupus where cryoglobulins are also produced.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prospective Cohort Study to Determine the Etiology of Undifferentiated Febrile Illnesses in Cebu City, Philippines
Keywords-MotsClés: DENGUE VIRUS; FEBRILE ILLNESS; INFLUENZA VIRUS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MASSTAG-PCR; RESPIRATORY VIRUSES; TROPICAL MEDICINE; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Efficient laboratory diagnosis of infectious diseases is increasingly important in clinical management and public health. Clinical syndromes such as febrile illnesses are infrequently specific for a single pathogen. In order to decrease the cost of and time to diagnosis, there is a need for assays that allow multiple agents to be tested simultaneously. MassTag technology is a new system, which tests for between 30 - 40 infectious agents in a single experiment and has been shown to reliably determine the cause of respiratory infections and encephalitic or hemorrhagic fevers.  Acute, febrile illnesses in Asian countries may be due to a variety of infectious agents. Studies in Thailand and the Philippines have found the proportion of undiagnosed febrile illnesses to be close to 55% and 30% respectively. In metro Manila, researchers were unable to determine a cause of fever in greater than three-quarters of cases. Without a diagnosis, physicians are limited in the treatment they can provide. The aims of this study are to monitor subjects for fever and use the newly developed MassTag technology to rapidly determine the cause of their fever. It is hypothesized most fevers will be due to influenza and other respiratory viruses and dengue virus infections. However, the remaining febrile illnesses will likely be due to a variety of infectious agents including Rickettsiosis, leptospirosis, infectious gastrointestinal agents, bacterial respiratory tract infections and other viruses.  MassTag technology can be used to screen multiple infectious agents in a single experiment to determine an infectious cause of the illness. This limits the number of samples required, cost for and time to diagnosis and can help direct treatment improving patient care. The system can also be used for diagnostics in other situations including the intentional release of an unknown bioterrorism agent or in outbreak investigation and management.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical Trial in Vascular Atherosclerosis and Biology Imaging:  Prospective Evaluation of the Ability of Magnetic Resonance Imaging Detected Carotid Intraplaque Hemorrhage to Predict Individuals with High Cardiovascular Risk Phenotype
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARDIOVASCULAR RISK; CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MORTALITY; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; OUTCOMES; PERIPHERAL VASCULAR DISEASE; POPULATION HEALTH; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke and heart attack are a leading cause of death in Canada.  Identifying patients who are most at risk for stroke and heart attack is a challenge for physicians. Physicians often rely on the degree of narrowing of arteries due to plaque to identify patients that might go on to have a stroke, heart attack or related death. Identification of these patients provides an opportunity for early intervention. For example, in the right clinical setting, a patient with high grade narrowing of their carotid artery (a major vessel providing blood to the brain) might have an operation to remove the plaque to decrease their risk of stroke.  However, the use of narrowing of arteries to identify patients that will have a stroke and heart attack is limited. For instance, some patients with low grade narrowing of arteries also have stroke. Also, some patients with high grade narrowing of arteries may never have a stroke. Consequently, ways other than degree of artery narrowing are necessary to identify patients at increased risk.   Early studies suggest that instability of artery plaque rather than artery narrowing might better identify patients at risk of heart attack and stroke. Advances in imaging technology allow physicians to identify unstable plaque features like the presence of bleeding within the plaque or intraplaque hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is able to detect intraplaque hemorrhage.  Carotid artery intraplaque hemorrhage detected with MRI may better identify patients at risk of stroke and heart attack. Our study aims to answer which method is better at identifying patients at risk of heart artery and stroke: artery narrowing or unstable plaque? In other words, we aim to assess the ability of MRI detected intraplaque hemorrhage to predict stroke, heart attack and related death.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vitamin D vs placebo in the prevention of viral-induced exacerbations in preschool aged children with asthma  a pilot RCT
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY INFLAMMATION; ASTHMA; MEDICATION EFFICACY; NUTRITIONAL REQUIREMENTS; PAEDIATRICS; RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SERUM BIOMARKERS; SUPPLEMENTATION; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is the most common chronic condition affecting Canadian children. More than one in ten children in Canada suffer with asthma. Insufficient Vitamin D levels are also becoming more prevalent in Canada due to the low level of sun exposure. Interestingly, Vitamin D levels are even lower in children with asthma compared to the general population. Previous research has indicated that low levels of Vitamin D has negative effects on the control of asthma in children. This includes poorer lung function, and more severe asthma attacks. In addition, it appears that steroid medications, commonly used to treat and control childhood asthma, are not as effective in children with low levels of Vitamin D. Infact, children require higher doses of inhaled steroids if they have insufficient levels of Vitamin D. This study proposes to provide a Vitamin D supplement to children with asthma over a 3 month period. The study will measure whether increasing Vitamin D levels in asthmatic children improves their asthma control and lung function. It will also assess whether inhaled steroid medications are more effective when combined with Vitamin D. This is important as inhaled steroids are the most common medication used to treat childhood asthma. Vitamin D is also an easily accessible and safe supplement for population use.   Given the burden of asthma, the high prevalence of Vitamin D insufficiency and the ease of correction, and the predominant use of inhaled steroids to control childhood asthma, the potential outcomes of this study have wide-spread importance to the delivery of health care and population health.

TitreApplicationTitle: cAMP-Dependent gene transactivation: a novel mechanism underlying the anti-inflammatory activity of PDE4 inhibitors in COPD.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; EPITHELIAL CELLS; GENE TRANSACTIVATION; PHOSPHODIESTERASE 4; ROFLUMILAST
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic disease of the lungs that includes bronchitis (excessive mucus production) & emphysema (lung destruction). COPD takes a long time to develop, affects middle aged and elderly people and is caused, usually, by chronic cigarette smoking. Worryingly, it is the only cause of death that is increasing worldwide and it is predicted that it will be the third leading cause of death by 2020. Currently, COPD is a huge health issue that is under-recognized, under-diagnosed and under-reported. Until very recently, COPD could not be well treated. However, in November 2010 Health Canada approved a new medicine, called roflumilast, which is a phosphodiesterase (PDE) 4 inhibitor, for people with severe COPD. Clinical trials have shown roflumilast to be clinically effective although side effects have also been reported. However, what currently is unknown is how PDE4 inhibitors work in COPD. Accordingly, understanding the mechanism of action of these new medicines is the primary aim of this project. We will adopt a multidisciplinary approach-using lung taken from normal human subjects and patients with COPD. In COPD, one of the typical findings is the presence of inflammation in the lungs, which is related to disease severity. The primary aims of this project are to determine the effects of PDE4 inhibitors on the expression of genes that can inhibit the inflammation found in COPD and to dissect out the biological machinery inside cells that are used by these new medicines to activate these genes. These studies should provide a clear picture of how PDE4 inhibitors work in COPD. We believe that roflumilast "switches on" a variety of genes in the human lung that inhibits the processes that produce COPD. By understanding how roflumilast and other PDE4 inhibitors work in COPD will allow "better roflumilasts" to be made. Such an advance could provide an effective means of managing a lung disease that has reached pandemic proportions.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: T Cell Immunity in HIV-1/HCV Coinfection
Keywords-MotsClés: CD4+ T CELLS; CYTOKINES; HCV; HIV-1; HIV/HCV COINFECTION; IMMUNOLOGY; LIVER DISEASE; LIVER FIBROSIS; T CELL EXHAUSTION; T CELL RESPONSES
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infects close to 300 million persons worldwide, is a major cause of end-stage liver disease and is the primary reason for liver transplantation in North America. Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infects close to 40 million individuals worldwide. In those coinfected with HIV-1 and HCV, despite the availability of antiretroviral treatment for HIV-1 infection, end-stage liver disease due to HCV is an important cause of morbidity and mortality. Defining the causes of HCV disease progression in the setting of HIV-1 coinfection are necessary to improve therapeutic options and slow the development of liver disease, given that the current therapy for HCV disease in HIV-1 infected individuals is often ineffective. This proposal will examine why HIV-1 worsens HCV disease. Firstly, we will study whether HIV-1 infection can influence the immune response of co-infected persons such that it is less effective at containing HCV. We will then investigate whether coinfection with HIV-1 leads immune cells to secrete factors which may inhibit the antiviral activities of particular immune cells that are vital to the anti-HCV immune response. We will further study whether HIV-1/HCV coinfection leads to an accumulation or poor regulation of immune cells that secrete inflammatory factors, in the liver, thereby leading to liver inflammation and damage. The proposed research could uncover the causes of immune dysfunction observed in HIV-1/HCV infected persons may lead and improvement in the health of these individuals through the development of immune-based therapies to lessen the HCV burden and slow the development of serious liver disease and related mortality.
