ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF; MALADIES DU FOIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a Therapeutic Antigen-Specific Nanovaccine for the Treatment of Primary Biliary Cirrhosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE TRANSFER; GENE-KNOCK OUT MICE; IMMUNE CELLS (NK; IMMUNOMODULATORS; LIVER METASTASIS; LIVER MULTICHANNEL FLUORE SPINNING DISK INTRAVITAL MICROSCOP; NEUTROPHIL EXTRACELLULAR TRAPS; NEUTROPHILS); NKT; OPSONIZING ANTIBODIES (IGA AND IGG); T AND DENDRITIC CELLS; TUMOR AND IMMUNE CELL INTERACTION VISUALIZATION; TUMOR CHALLENGE STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: Many different tumors metastasize to the liver. For example, following colon cancer surgery, it is thought that cells either already in the circulation or those that mobilize from the tumor into the circulation lodge in the liver. The immune system does not recognize these cells as foreign. However, if we could put a bulls-eye on these tumor cells so that the immune system would recognize them, then we would have a way of getting rid of them. We propose to make antibodies that will work as bulls eyes and have immune cells destroy the tumor cells. As one example, the best killing machine of bacteria in the body is the neutrophil, a type of white blood cell. We propose to convince the neutrophils that tumor cells are just like bacteria and need to be killed. We will help tissue-specific immune cells in the liver called Kupffer cells recognize tumors as foreign and kill them. We will also study whether interaction between specific and non-specific immune cell types lead to effective tumor eradication.   Understanding how the body works is critical to designing effective drugs. Being able to image and see how tumor cells are killed gives us insight into which cells are important for the killing. Once we know which cells are important we can then help them by activating them to help kill the tumors. Being able to identify which cells are important may impact not just on metastases to the liver, but to primary tumors as well as to metastases in other organs. Drugs are available so what we want to do is determine which are the most effective. Although I have been an immunologist studying infections using imaging expertise, recently we generated sufficient data to get funded by the Alberta Cancer Board to start studying tumor cells. As many as one million colorectal cancer patients will develop metastatic tumors. Preventing this will benefit Albertans, Canadians and beyond.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessment of health care patterns for elderly lung cancer patients in southern Ontario.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMOTHERAPY; ELDERLY; GERIATRIC ONCOLOGY; LUNG CANCER; PRACTICE PATTERN; PROGNOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The elderly population, defined as those older than 65 years of age, is growing in Canada, with the number of seniors in Canada expected to more than double between 2005 and 2036. Recent Canadian statistics show that 43% of new cancers in 2010 were diagnosed in those older than 70 years. With no change in this distribution we can expect a rapidly increasing number of cancer cases in the elderly as "baby boomers" age. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death and half of lung cancers are diagnosed in patients over 70 years old.   Unfortunately, elderly cancer patients have not been well represented in clinical trials, so there is less guidance for how to treat them, although, the few available trials have shown that chemotherapy helps elderly lung cancer patients. How many physicians are applying these findings to their daily practice is unclear. Decision-making about chemotherapy is also complicated by age-related changes in organ function, which leads to an increased risk of dangerous side effects from treatment and makes it harder to predict the degree of benefit in an individual. With the expected increase in numbers, we need to better understand how we are currently treating elderly lung cancer patients to both improve their outcomes and plan resources in the future.  We propose a project that will improve our understanding of care for elderly cancer patients and what influences their survival. By examining data the Ontario Cancer Registry, Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES), and patient charts from three periods over the last 20 years, we can determine the factors that influence referral to receive treatment, whether or not a patient receives chemotherapy, and how long they survive.  Changes in proportion of elderly lung cancer patients receiving chemotherapy will show if trial data are applied in daily practice. We will also create a tool to help predict survival, valuable information in discussions about treatment every day.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physical, Emotional and Social Stressors and their Impact on Quality of Life of Caregivers of Elderly Patients with Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREGIVER BURDEN; CAREGIVER CHARACTERISTICS; ELDERLY CANCER PATIENTS; EMOTIONAL; FUNCTIONAL IMPAIRMENTS; PHYSICAL; PSYCHOSOCIAL
Abstract-Résumé: The population is aging. By 2030, 70% of all cancers are expected to be diagnosed in persons age 65 and over. Older adults with cancer often have difficulties with every day tasks such as walking, bathing, making meals, and doing chores. As a result many patients rely on help from family and friends to help them continue to live in the community. This can place significant burden on caregivers.  We believe that people who care for older adults with cancer are likely to be elderly themselves and have more health problems than those who care for younger cancer patients. As a result, we believe caregiver strain is common in this group, especially in those caregivers who have difficulties with their own every day activities.  We will interview patients age 65 and older, with cancer, admitted to City of Hope Comprehensive Cancer Center, and their main caregiver. Caregivers will complete a questionnaire gathering information about the amount of time spent and type of help they provide. Information about their personal health, any difficulties they may have with their own every day activities, and any help they receive will also be recorded. The degree of caregiver stress that is present, physically, emotionally and mentally, will be determined. This will be related to information about the patient, including cancer characteristics, treatment course, nutrition, non-cancer health problems, and emotional health.  Understanding how common caregiver stress is in those who care for older adults with cancer, as well as identifying factors that place them at higher risk, is important. It allows doctors to better identify patients and families who may need extra supports to manage at home. It also the allows the health care system to develop and institute the resources that are needed to support caregivers, who care for the growing population older patients with cancer and who are integral to helping our older adults remain well enough to stay at home and out of hospitals.

TitreApplicationTitle: A phase 2 clinical trial exploring the clinical and correlative effects of combining doxycycline with standard bisphosphonate therapy in patients with metastatic breast cancer. (The Achilles study).
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE METASTASES; BREAST CANCER; CLINICAL TRIALS
Abstract-Résumé: Bone is the most common site of metastatic spread of breast cancer. The consequences of bone metastases include pain, poor mobility, a reduced quality of life and worsening survival. Patients are also at a considerable risk of skeletal related events (SREs) such as needing surgery and/or radiotherapy to bone, pathological fractures, spinal cord compression, and hypercalcemia. Avoiding such complications is therefore essential.  Bisphosphonates are a class of drugs that are highly effective in reducing bone breakdown. They are widely used in patients with bone metastases to try and minimize skeletal complications and are considered the standard of care in such patients. However, despite their extensive use, about a third of patients with bony metastatic disease will still go on to experience a SRE, and there is no evidence they prolong survival. Innovative strategies to enhance their effectiveness are therefore needed.  We have previously performed studies that would suggest that the cheap and widely available antibiotic, doxycycline, might well increase the anti-cancer effects of bisphosphonates in patients. A previous clinical study looked at the effects of doxycycline as a single agent in women with breast cancer that has spread to the bones and showed some modest efficacy.  Based on our work, we hypothesize that adding doxycycline to the bisphosphonate treatment of patients will increase the anti-cancer activity of bisphosphonates. The results of this study could help us individualize the care of patients and also reduce the mortality and morbidity associated with bone metastases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prospective audit of parenteral nutrition in high-risk hospitalized surgical patients in Canada.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDIT; HOSPITALIZED PATIENTS; LINE INFECTIONS; MALNUTRITION; NUTRITION SUPPORT TEAMS; REFEEDING SYNDROME; SURGICAL PATIENTS; TOTAL PARENTERAL NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: General surgeons are increasingly performing more invasive surgeries on elderly patients who are malnourished or at high risk for malnutrition. These patients are often unable to be fed adequately using in the gut when hospitalized and require intravenous nutrition (or parenteral nutrition) to meet their caloric demands. Feeding patients adequately improves recovery and mortality.  Evidence suggests we are under-utilizing parenteral nutrition in these patients, and the use of parenteral nutrition practice varies widely. We are likely under-utilizing parenteral nutrition because of a lack of specialized physicians, cost, and fear of complications which includes the risk of blood infections. We therefore propose the creation of an audit or evaluation of parenteral nutrition utilization including appropriate use, costs, different forms of administration, and complications.  This will provide valuable information for us to improve education of surgeons and nutrition support teams and other hospital support systems to make sure we are utilizing parenteral nutrition in situations where it will provide benefit to patients and we are doing it in a safe and cost-efficient manner.

TitreApplicationTitle: The METS (Measurement of Exercise Tolerance before Surgery) Study: An International Multicentre Prospective Cohort Study of Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing For Improving Preoperative Risk Stratification for Major Non-Cardiac Surgery.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOPULMONARY EXERCISE TESTING; FUNCTIONAL CAPACITY; PERIOPERATIVE CARDIAC COMPLICATIONS; PERIOPERATIVE MEDICINE; PREOPERATIVE ASSESSMENT; PREOPERATIVE RISK STRATIFICATION; PROGNOSTIC STUDIES; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: More than 230 million people undergo major surgery worldwide every year. At least 5 million of them suffer major heart problems after these operations. People with poor physical fitness, or "functional capacity", may be at high risk for having these heart problems. They might also be at high risk for other important problems, such as infections or difficulty breathing after surgery.  At present, doctors estimate fitness for surgery by asking patients about the general types of activities that they can perform. For example, patients will often be asked whether they can climb up 2 flights of stairs. However, this approach (called "subjective assessment") does not perform well at identifying patients at risk for having major heart problems after surgery. We will therefore conduct a large international study to compare the usual approach ("subjective assessment") against 3 other methods to measure fitness for surgery. These methods are an exercise test (called CPET), a questionnaire about physical activities (called DASI), and a simple blood test (called NT pro-BNP).  Our study (called the METS study) will include 1312 patients undergoing major surgery at 8 hospitals in Ontario and the United Kingdom. Before surgery, each participant will undergo a "subjective assessment" of their fitness, complete a CPET exercise test, answer the DASI questionnaire, and undergo a NT pro-BNP blood test. We will then follow the participants for 1 year after surgery to determine which method does best at identifying people who have heart problems after surgery.  By helping to better identify high-risk patients before their operations, our study will help improve their medical care, and therefore reduce their risk of major problems after surgery. It will also help make sure that specialized (and expensive) medical care is used in patients who most need it. Our study will thus significantly help millions of people who have major surgery every year, in Canada and around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing the Duration of Antibiotic Therapy for Bloodstream Infections
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC STEWARDSHIP; ANTIBIOTIC TREATMENT; BACTEREMIA; COHORT STUDY; CRITICAL CARE / INTENSIVE CARE; DURATION OF THERAPY; MULTICENTRE; OBSERVATIONAL; PROSPECTIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Bloodstream infections are a common and serious problem, affecting 15% of critically ill patients, increasing their length of hospital stay by 3 weeks, adding $40,000 in excess hospital costs, and tripling the risk of death. At the same time, antibiotic overuse is also a common and serious problem, in that 30-50% of antibiotic use is unnecessary or inappropriate, and results in avoidable drug side effects such as kidney failure, Clostridium difficile colitis, increased costs, and spiraling antibiotic resistance rates.  The greatest contributor to antibiotic overuse is excessive durations of treatment.  Extensive research has demonstrated that shorter duration antibiotic therapy (± 1 week) is as effective as longer duration therapy for a variety of infectious diseases, but this question has never been directly studied in the setting of bloodstream infection. Our systematic review of the medical literature and national survey of Canadian infectious diseases and critical care physicians support the need for a trial comparing shorter (7 days) versus longer (14 days) antibiotic therapy for bloodstream infections. Prior to performing this trial, through the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group, we propose this Canada-wide prospective observational study in order to: 1) confirm that there is variability in current treatment practices; 2) identify which patients and pathogens are appropriate to include in a future trial; and 3) confirm that the benefits of antibiotics are achieved within the first week. By defining the optimal duration of treatment for bloodstream infections, our research program will help maximize the clinical cure of individual patients, while minimizing their risk of drug side effects, C.difficile, and antibiotic resistance. Since this intervention would require no new technology, and would reduce (rather than increase) health care costs, it would offer immediate benefits to patients and the healthcare system.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the stringent response and 4-hydroxy-2-alkylquinolines in the antibiotic tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC TOLERANCE; BIOFILMS; MICROBIOLOGY; PSEUDOMONAS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic bacterial infections are difficult to treat and often cannot be cleared by antibiotics. A devastating example of such infection is the Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infection in patients with the genetic disease cystic fibrosis. Most patients acquire the infection early in life and remain chronically infected for the rest of their lives despite aggressive antibiotic therapies. These chronic infections cause severe respiratory symptoms, decline in lung function and ultimately death from respiratory failure.   One important reason why antibiotics fail to eradicate the chronic infections is because they are caused by biofilms. Biofilms are a form of growth where bacteria live in structured clusters, embedded in a polymer matrix. Bacteria growing in biofilms are very resistant to antibiotics and the host's immune system and the mechanisns of this resistance are still largely unknown.   Our preliminary studies showed that a stress response called the stringent response is important to the bacteria's ability to grow and stay alive in biofilms, and to be resistant to antibiotics. The stringent response is a mechanism that allows bacteria to adapt to starvation and many stressful conditions. We also found that the stringent response regulate a family of molecules called 4-hydroxy-2-alkylquinolines and these may be involved in the antibiotic resistance of biofilms.   We are interested in understanding how the stringent response are involved in antibiotic resistance. Our studies are focused on understanding how the stringent response regulates these quinoline molecules, on defining the exact role of these molecules in biofilm antibiotic resistance, and examining whether these findings could be useful for development of future therapies against biofilm infections. With the lack of new antibiotics in development and the severe health burden of biofilm infections, new treatment strategies that target biofilms are much needed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating Urban-Rural Disparities In Oral Health And Oral Health Services: A Quebec Profile
Keywords-MotsClés: DETERMINANTS OF ORAL HEALTH; MIXED METHOD; ORAL HEALTH INDICATORS; ORAL HEALTH SERVICES; RURAL/URBAN ORAL HEALTH CARE DISPARITY; SATISFACTION WITH ACCESS TO DENTAL CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Those who live in rural communities may be prone to oral health problems because of geographic remoteness, socioeconomic deprivation, and inadequate access to dental services. In fact, oral health care disparities and underutilization of dental care have been reported in rural Canada. Rural Canadians have a lower level of population to dentist ratio, lower dental insurance coverage and decreased dental services compared to their urban counterparts. Furthermore, there has been limited attention given to rural oral health research in Canada. Therefore, we need to provide information and to design programs aimed at improving community based services. In collaboration with the Quebec National Institute of Public Health, we will collect data on the clinical oral health status of 2670 primary schoolchildren living in 10 regions of Quebec. We will also send questionnaires to 3500 parents or caregivers of these children and we will collect additional data on the parent's oral health, predisposing factors (socio-demographic, psychological characteristics), enabling resources (income, mode of transportation, dental insurance, etc.), dental needs, and satisfaction with dental care. This data will allow us to compare rural/urban differences in oral health and level of satisfaction with dental care, as well as their underlying contributing factors. This study will provide information that policy makers and clinicians can use in planning for the provision of appropriate rural oral health care. Furthermore, these results will help in the development of effective policies based on what the communities perceive as their needs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of cardiac metabolism and growth by DJ-1
Keywords-MotsClés: HEART FAILURE; KNOCKOUT ANIMALS; METABOLIC TRANSFORMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Canada and has been identified as the second leading cause of extended hospital stays. In the adult, the heart is incapalbe of regenerating itself. This renders the heart particularly vulnerable to injury. Our existing medical therapy can only slow the progression of the disease. Alternatives to medical therapy are limited to transplantation or mechanical devices. The quality of life and the prognosis for this group of patients remains poor. In addition, more than $1 billion of Canada's annual health budget is being spent for the care of patients with HF, rendering this disease an ever increasing socioeconomic burden. Therefore, it is exceedingly important to consider alternative and/or complementary approaches that allow discovery of alternate treatment strategies that will effectively restrict cardiomyocyte loss and hypertrophy (see below). Providing a new and effective therapy for HF will not only improve the quality of life for patients but also reduce the costs associated with patient care. DJ-1, a protein implicated in early-onset familial forms of Parkinson's disease, is highly expressed in the heart. Its biological function in these cells, however, remains elusive. We have data to support a protective role for DJ-1 in preventing the development of heart failure. Another important finding is that DJ-1 is involved in maintaining a balance of metabolism within heart muscle cells. This proposal describes detailed studies that would be instrumental in helping us defining the role of DJ-1 in the heart. As such, DJ-1 may represent an unique target for the development of novel therapies for the treatment of heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecules & Mechanisms Mediating Proximal Tubular Calcium Flux
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HYPERCALCIURIA; KIDNEY STONES; OSTEOPOROSIS; PROXIMAL TUBULE
Abstract-Résumé: We aim to understand how the kidney prevents urinary calcium loss. A failure to do this can result in kidney stones and/or thin bones (osteoporosis) The inappropriate loss of calcium in the urine is called hypercalciuria. We seek to determine the mechanism by which hypercalciuria occurs, so as to be able to develop specific treatments for kidney stones and osteoporosis. Calcium in our blood is filtered by the glomerulus. In order for it not to be wasted in the urine it must be reabsorbed back into the blood by the renal tubule. The majority of this takes place in the first part of the renal tubule or proximal tubule. This is also the part of the tubule which fails to completely reabsorb calcium in people with hypercalciuria. We therefore seek to understand how calcium is reabsorbed from the proximal tubule. Calcium, in this part of the tubule, moves between the tubular cells. However, what allows calcium to move between these cells but prevents the movement of other molecules is not known. What has been recently appreciated is that a group of proteins form very specific pores between cells throughout tubular organs of the body. These proteins are called claudins.  Specific pore forming claudins control the movement of molecules between cells. Unfortunately we do not know which claudins are in the proximal tubule. We will therefore first identify what claudins are in the proximal tubule. Next we will infer a role for these claudins in calcium homeostasis by feeding mice a low calcium diet and examining how much of these claudins are in the proximal tubule. We will also examine claudin expression after perturbing calcium homeostasis by administering hormones that alter tubular calcium handling. This will provide us with candidates whose calcium permeability will be tested in a cell culture model. These studies will provide insight into, and novel therapeutic targets for, the treatment of hypercalciuria, kidney stones and osteoporosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strategies to enhance cardiac repair by resident cardiac stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGESTIVE HEART FAILURE; GENE THERAPY; REGENERATION; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a growing epidemic. While medical advances help people live longer, the number of patients with heart failure is increasing at a staggering rate. Currently over 400,000 Canadians are living with heart failure- but many will not survive for long. Heart failure is also the most serious killer in cardiovascular diseases.  Currently, heart failure claims more lives than lung cancer, stroke, AIDs and breast cancer combined.  This study is designed to explore new ways to repair these broken hearts.  Currently, doctors are exploring techniques to re-implant a patients own blood and heart stem cells into these damaged areas.  Our early work has shown that while these cells strengthen the heart, improvements have limits.  Irregardless, doctors are starting preliminary studies exploring even these modest gains in small numbers of very ill patients.          This proposal will build upon our earlier work by exploring how these stem cells repair hearts.  We expect that understanding these mechanisms will help us to engineer new therapies that will allow a patients own heart to heal itself.  We will grow stem cells directly from blood samples and small pieces of heart tissue.  Both samples will be donated by volunteer patients whose treating doctor has recommended they undergo cardiac surgery.  We will first study these cells in dishes to study increase our understanding about the specific cells and hormones that repair hearts.  Then, we will inject these cells into mice with weakened heart muscles to prove that findings in the dish are relevant to the whole heart.   This work will provide us the knowledge and opportunity to enhance the cell genes that increase cell survival and regeneration.  These enhanced stem cells will be the next step in tailoring new stem cell sources for our patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and characterization of intestinal and colonic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: COLITIS; COLON CANCER; GASTRIC CANCER; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last decade, the notion that tissue regeneration or healing is maintained by organ specific stem cells, the so-called "tissue stem cells", has created great excitement in the medical community. Tissue stem cells are characterized by the ability to give rise to multiple cell types and have self-renewing ability.  In the intestinal tract, the stem cell pool is thought to comprise of both rapidly dividing "active" stem cells, as well as more "quiescent", slow-dividing master stem cells that are available in times of stress or injury.   Despite the importance of tissue stem cells in homeostasis and disease, identification of these cells has proven challenging as these cells are not readily distinguishable from other cells. Recent work has demonstrated that the protein Lgr-5 marks a group of actively dividing stem cells known as the crypt base columnar cells. Nevertheless, it remains unknown whether there is more than one stem cell pool or long-lived quiescent stem cells within the intestinal crypt.  Our group has focused on the protein cytokeratin-19 (K19) that is an intermediate filament critical to the cell cytoskeleton.  We recently showed that K19 labels cells near the crypt base, and we hypothesize that K19 labels intestinal and colonic stem cells. Thus, we will use K19-BAC-CRE and K19-BAC-CreERT2 transgenic mice to genetically label K19+ intestinal and colonic stem cells following tamoxifen administration. We will also assess the contribution of K19+ cells to cancer upon targeted introduction of genetic mutations in K19 expressing cells. Finally, we will compare K19+ and Lgr-5+ cells with respect to stem cell properties and RNA expression profiles to better characterize these two populations.   We aim to show that K19 labels a unique population of intestinal and colonic stem cells and examine their role in injury and cancer. These studies will help shed light on the cellular origin of colon cancer, and identify novel therapeutic targets for treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and Characterization of Human Liver Cancer Stem Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CANCER STEM CELL; CELLULAR BIOLOGY; HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA; LIVER; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PRIMARY CELLS; TISSUE CULTURE; TUMOR INITIATION; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Primary liver cancer is the fifth most common cancer worldwide and the most rapidly increasing cause of death from cancer in North America.  Patients with early stages of disease can be effectively treated with surgery, but treatments for patients with more advanced disease are ineffective and the prognosis is poor.  The ways in which liver cancers develop and progress are not well understood; a better understanding should lead to opportunities for the development of more effective treatments.  Recent studies in other types of cancer have shown that only a few cells in a tumor, called cancer stem cells, are responsible for starting the tumor and determining how it grows, spreads, and responds to treatment.  The role that such cells may play in liver cancer is not well understood.  The goals of this study are to determine whether liver cancers originate from cancer stem cells, and if so, to determine unique characteristics of these cells that will allow them to be isolated.  To achieve these goals, we will obtain samples of liver cancers from patients having surgery for this condition and grow the human liver cancers in laboratory mice and in flasks.  This approach will provide us the most realistic model for studying human liver cancer.  We will determine what fraction of the liver cancer cells can actually start new tumors in these models, and we will decipher the unique signatures these cancer stem cells have.  The ability to specifically identify the cells responsible for liver cancer development will allow further research to better understand how these cells work and may reveal unique properties of these cells against which new treatments for liver cancer can be developed in order to help the many people who suffer from this common and often lethal disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating Mechanical Ventilation Discontinuation Practices and Research Recruitment Processes in Critically Ill Adults: A Research Program
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOMATED WEANING SYSTEMS; CONSENT; INTERNATIONAL; MECHANICAL VENTILATION; PROSPECTIVE OBSERVATIONAL STUDY; RANDOMIZED TRIAL; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Nearly 40% of the time spent on ventilators is directed at weaning or transferring the work of breathing from the ventilator back to the patient. While evidence exists to support use of selected techniques, many factors limit their use in practice resulting in weaning practice variation. Automated weaning systems aim to limit practice variation and reduce the time spent on ventilators. The influence of different weaning practices on outcomes is unknown. Meanwhile, implementing research in the intensive care unit (ICU)is challenging as it requires consent from surrogates, investigates conditions with high death rates and is undertaken during emergencies. Difficulties in conducting ICU research prolongs study periods, limits broad application of study findings and delays awareness of important study findings.  Goals: This research program has focused on (i)characterizing the extent of weaning practice variability nationally and internationally, (ii)evaluating new technology that automates weaning in a multicentre study and (iii) identifying the challenges of conducting clinical research in the ICU setting.  Methods: In renewing my Phase 2 Award, I will build and expand my research program by: 1. conducting an international study (in Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, India and Australia/New Zealand) of how clinicians wean patients from ventilators and how different approaches influence outcomes. 2. combining results of several small trials comparing automated weaning to other strategies to see if a large trial is warranted. 3. evaluating whether a physician introduction of the research team to surrogate decision makers can be implemented  Relevance: The first two studies will inform the design of future weaning studies to reduce weaning practice variation and improve outcomes. The last study will enable conduct of a larger trial comparing how different approaches for introducing ICU research influence participation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of pancreatitis elucidated on human pancreas in situ.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOLIC ACUTE PANCREATITIS; AUTOPHAGIC VACUOLES; BASOLATERAL EXOCYTOSIS; GLUCAGON-LIKE PEPTIDE 1 & EXENDIN-4; HUMAN PANCREAS SLICES; INTRACELLULAR PROTEASE ACTIVATION; PANCREATIC ACINAR CELL; SEC/MUNC 18 (SM) PROTEIN; SNARE PROTEINS; SPINNING DISC CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Acute pancreatitis (AP) causes a great deal of acute and chronic morbidity and mortality, and at considerable financial costs to health care in Canada. The most common cause of AP is alcohol, affecting 10% of alcoholics. There is still no effective specific treatment directed at the pathogenesis of alcoholic AP because the postulated disease mechanisms could not be directly tested on human pancreatic tissue.  Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)-based therapies, which potentiate glucose-mediated insulin secretion, is the new panacea and most promising treatment for diabetes, and is a multi-billion dollar pharmaceutical market. However, these drug treatments have been shown to exhibit a six-fold increase in AP, the basis of this dangerous side effect is totally unknown.  To effectively address these two conditions, we were first to develop the rodent and human models of preparing fresh pancreatic slices to genuinely examine normal pancreatic exocrine cell biology and disease mechanisms.  Our goals are to: 1) Determine the cellular basis of human alcoholic AP; and 2) Determine the cellular basis of human AP caused by GLP-1 drug treatment for diabetes. This work will elucidate clinically relevant insights underlying human alcoholic and GLP-1-induced AP, which will identify novel treatments for alcoholic AP and impact current diabetes management in patients taking GLP-1 drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of E3 Ubiquitin Ligase Mule in Colon Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: COLON CANCER; HOMEOSTASIS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR; UBIQUITIN LIGASE
Abstract-Résumé: Colon cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths in North America. The majority of which have no family history of the disease. At the core of every cancer are key genetic events that contribute to cell growth and thus, tumor formation. Colon cancer is a multistep process with a preferred sequence of events. However, new proteins that are deregulated in colon cancer are constantly being discovered. We propose to focus our studies on Mule, which is overexpressed in half of all colon cancers. Functionally, Mule tags a specific set of proteins to be recognized by a 'cellular garbage can'. This role is important for maintaining a balance between proteins that regulate cell growth and those that regulate cell death. The loss of this equilibrium usually results in cancer. In this proposal, I will investigate if Mule is essential in maintaining the balance between cell growth and death in the intestine. These studies will allow us to understand the effects of Mule overexpression in cancer, and if this results in tipping the scale away from cell death, and towards cell growth. Establishing the role of Mule in the normal and diseased intestine will elucidate whether Mule is a good candidate for cancer therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Factors associated with mucosal recovery in patients with celiac disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELIAC DISEASE; COPING; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GLUTEN-FREE DIET; MICROPARTICLES; PATIENT ADHERENCE; PROTEOMICS; QUALITY OF LIFE; SERUM BIOMARKERS
Abstract-Résumé: Celiac disease is a common disease associated with symptoms such as bloating, diarrhea, weight loss and fatigue and laboratory abnormalities such as iron deficiency. It is defined by small intestinal villous atrophy and inflammation. The only treatment is a gluten free diet, which can be challenging because gluten is present in many common foods.  Celiac disease and the requirements of a gluten free diet can affect how individuals manage day to day. There has been research looking at some of the effects, but there is still much to learn about ways to support those with celiac disease in managing their disease effectively.  Persons with celiac disease must be assessed regularly to ensure they are following a gluten free diet and to check for nutrition and health complications that may develop. Repeat intestinal biopsy is the only accurate test of whether the intestine is healing and there is a need for less invasive tests. Two possibilities that have not been well explored are proteins and microparticles. Microparticles are small fragments of cell membranes from stimulated cells.  In this study of 125 adults with celiac disease, physical outcomes, psychological functioning, and behavioral adjustments to the disease will be measured at diagnosis and 6, 12 and 24 months after diagnosis. This will help to determine how quality of life is affected by having celiac disease, as well as what helps people to be successful in managing the disease. Blood samples will also be analysed to identify proteins and microparticles which are sensitive and specific markers of changes seen on intestinal biopsies.  This study will map the processes whereby individuals adjust to celiac disease and determine new medical tests and better methods to support individuals with celiac disease. Identification of these factors will lead to better clinical management tools and education strategies that would improve the quality of life and health of individuals with celiac disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anxiety & depression in survivors of peadiatric brain tumours; a neurobiological perspective
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD CANCER; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; RADIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumors are the leading cause of death and disability from childhood disease in developed countries. Advances in treatment over the last 25 years have yielded dramatic improvements in survival rates, but have come at a cost to survivors. Cranial radiation is often required following surgery for cancerous tumors, yet this harsh treatment causes considerable damage to the developing brain and results in a variety of learning, memory, behavioral and emotional problems. I plan to focus on anxiety and depression experienced by survivors of brain tumors, and will relate these symptoms to structural changes in brain regions important for emotions. By using brain imaging, I will examine how cranial radiation damages white matter. White matter is the 'highway' by which brain regions communicate with one another, and it is particularly vulnerable to damage during childhood because it continues to grow until early adulthood. Unlike learning and memory problems, which have been shown to result from radiation induced structural damage to white matter, the symptoms of anxiety and depression in childhood brain tumor survivors have yet to be examined in relation to brain functioning. If cranial radiation damages white matter in structures important for controlling emotions, these children could be more vulnerable to problems in anxiety and depression. Understanding how damage to key parts of the brain important for emotional functioning may cause anxiety and depression is important for reducing emotional problems in children treated with cranial radiation for brain tumors. This understanding could result in the modification of current treatments to include increased emotional monitoring, support, and promote the development of protective strategies during the administration of cranial radiation to preserve key brain structures that control emotion.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of macrophage activity by interleukin-6
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVELY ACTIVATED MACROPHAGES; COLITIS; GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INTERLEUKIN-6
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) describes two chronically occurring conditions of the gut: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis - permanent conditions that dramatically reduce the quality of life of those afflicted. Canada currently has one of the highest rates of IBD in the world.  The exact cause of IBD has not been determined, but it is thought to be associated with an uncontrolled immune response to the normal bacterial flora of the intestine. In this regard, macrophages are an interesting focus of study, as they are a cell that can respond to bacteria and exert either pro- or anti-inflammatory effects. In the McKay laboratory, a particular subtype of macrophages known as alternatively activated macrophages (AAMs) have been shown to reduce the severity of chemically-induced colitis in murine models.  The mechanism(s) by which these cells exert there effect has not yet been determined. Therefore, the focus of this project is to study how the in vivo environment influences the induction and function of AAMs, focusing in particular on the cytokine interleukin(IL)-6. IL-6 is an important molecule, constitutively produced by many tissues of the body and up-regulated in a number of inflammatory diseases, including IBD. Preliminary data has indicated that IL-6 is able to enhance the phenotype and anti-inflammatory properties of AAMs by a yet undetermined mechanism.  Determining the role of IL-6 (if any) in the in vivo differentiation of AAMs will provide useful information which could potentially be used to translate data derived from murine studies into an individually targeted therapy for patients with IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Impact of Major Depressive Disorder and Psychotropic Medications on Driving Performance
Keywords-MotsClés: DRIVING; INJURY PREVENTION; MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER; PSYCHOTROPIC MEDICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Vehicular crashes are common in Canada and frequently lead to injury and/or death. Understanding the factors that may contribute to vehicular crashes is important to prevent injury and/or death that may result from vehicular crashes. Both Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and the psychotropic medications used to treat MDD can induce cognitive and psychomotor disturbances. Consequently, both MDD and psychotropic medications may be detrimental to the task of driving. Presently, there is a paucity of research examining the impact of these variables, specifically in teasing apart the effect of MDD from that of medications. Therefore, the present study seeks to elucidate the influence of MDD and psychotropic medications, such as antidepressants, on driving performance in a clinical population and using a driving simulator.  This study will recruit participates who have MDD and are treated successfully with antidepressant medications,  MDD participants who are taking antidepressants but are not successfully treated, MDD participants who are untreated, and healthy controls. All participants will complete a battery of questionnaires assessing driving habits, depression, and cognitive and psychomotor functioning. Lastly, all participants will complete a 30 min simulated drive in the laboratory. Participants will complete all measures again at a 6-month follow-up. We expect that individuals with MDD who are treated unsuccessfully or not treated at all with antidepressant medications will display poor performance compared to controls, and participants whose MDD has been treated successfully with antidepressant medications will not display impairments in driving performance compared to controls. The findings of this study could lead to advances in the health of populations; namely, this study could be a starting point in raising awareness of the impact of psychotropic medications and mental illnesses on driving performance as to prevent future injury and disability.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examination of the effects of interprofessional collaboration on nurse productivity: An important consideration in health human resources planning.
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPETENCY ASSESSMENT; FOCUS GROUP; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; INTERPROFESSIONAL COLLABORATION; INTERPROFESSIONAL COMPETENCIES; MIXED METHODS; NEEDS-BASED HEALTH HUMAN RESOURCES PLANNING; NURSING; TEAM DELIVERED CARE; WORKFORCE PRODUCTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Our health care system has been faced with a number of challenges with its health workforce. Leading the list are shortages of various health providers, difficulties attracting health providers to available jobs, and once hired, difficulty keeping them in those positions. These demands affect how well the health care system functions to meet the needs of its citizens. Health human resources planning is a strategy used to address these types of challenges by determining whether the right number and skill mix of providers are in the right place at the right time to meet the health needs of people. However, equally important and rarely examined, is the need to consider how these providers work together and what impact this has on the quality and safety of the care they provide, for the sustainability of our health care system lies in the ability of providers to work together, with patients and families, in teams. Traditionally, providers have been taught in isolation from one another. Seldom do they have the opportunity to learn with, from and about one another, and this will impact how well they work together once in the health care system. If they learn in isolation, they are more apt to work in isolation and will rarely call upon one another to share their knowledge and skills because they are not fully aware of what the other can offer. Consequently, if providers do not work together as a team and share their knowledge and expertise, inefficient duplication of care occurs. Nurses, the largest professional group in health care, have been reluctant to collaborate with others, possibly because they have not been taught how to or because they are not sure how working together effects their workload. This research study will examine the relationship between the knowledge and skill required to work collaboratively, nurses' abiility to do so, and the impact working collaboratively has on nurses' ability to work effectively and efficiently.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the impact of patient-oriented financial incentives on exercise self-efficacy, motivation and adherence in a cardiac population.
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR MODIFICATION; CARDIAC REHABILITATION; HEALTH INCENTIVES; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: There is increasing interest in alternative approaches to promote exercise in the general population as well as in high risk, high cost groups (e.g., cardiac patients, a rapidly growing demographic in Canada). Indeed, participation in cardiac rehabilitation, a comprehensive outpatient program which includes structured exercise, prevents costly hospitalizations and reduces cardiac deaths by 25 percent. Despite the unquestionable health benefits and the existence of post-program supports, exercise adherence after cardiac rehab is suboptimal, dropping precipitously by up to 75 percent one year following program completion. Provisions, therefore, for the long-term continuation of exercise after cardiac rehab are necessary. Constructs from behavioral economic and self-determination theory, along with evidence from randomized clinical trials, suggest that financial incentives, such as paying people to exercise, may promote healthy behaviors. Incentives are gaining popularity as governments and private companies increasingly implement incentive programs to curtail rising health care costs and boost productivity. Very little is known, however, about the structure of efficacious incentive programs (e.g., type, magnitude of incentive), especially of those provided in a Canadian context (the majority of incentive research has been conducted in the U.S.) and to targeted groups like cardiac patients. Realizing the potential of incentive programs in Canada, and among high-risk, high-cost subpopulations, therefore, will be contingent on research that improves the understanding of factors (e.g., the shared features and individual characteristics of cardiac patients) that may influence incentive program uptake and efficacy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the Moral Distress of Mental Health Care Providers: Experiences and Consequences
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICS; GROUNDED THEORY; HEALTH CARE PROFESSIONALS; HEALTH HUMAN RESOURCES; HEALTHCARE; MENTAL HEALTH; MORAL DISTRESS; PATIENT SAFETY; QUALITATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: One of the biggest health care challenges in Canada is the sustainability of health human resources. There is growing research evidence that ethical challenges in the work environment and the subsequent moral distress (MD) of nurses and other health care providers (HCPs) affect job satisfaction, attrition of HCPs, and likely also patient safety. Improving the work environment of all HCPs is key to sustainable health human resources.  Most of the research in MD has been done in acute care, with little attention paid to other areas, including mental health (MH).  Moral distress for MH HCPs is an understudied area, and research to develop interventions to address MD is only just beginning across all areas of practice. Further research in MH is necessary to better understand the experiences and consequences of moral distress of HCPs A qualitative (grounded theory) methodology will be used to uncover institutional and individual processes involved in the experience of moral distress in mental health. The theoretical framework that results from this research will be used to inform future work in the development of interventions to address MD, decrease HCP attrition, and increase safe patient care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Taking control of Chronic Disease in Canada: The Role for Metabolic Syndrome in Public Health
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; DECISION ANALYSIS; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; ECONOMIC BURDEN OF DISEASE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH PROMOTION; METABOLIC SYNDROME; PREVENTION STRATEGY; PREVENTIVE MEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: "Taking control of Chronic Disease in Canada: The Role for Metabolic Syndrome in Public Health" will take a comprehensive look at metabolic syndrome (MetS) in Canada. Previous studies have demonstrated the association of MetS with the future development of leading causes of death, such as cardiovascular disease (CVD) and diabetes. This study will lay the evidence base for MetS in public health by first demonstrating the prevalence of MetS, it's association with subclinical disease, and the heightened projected rates of future disease among individuals with MetS. An analysis of the proportion of cases of CVD and diabetes that can be attributed to MetS, and the cost of illness incurred by MetS, will inform an examination of the burden of this pre-disease risk condition on Canadians. These two papers lay the foundation for a health promotion and knowledge translation analysis of chronic disease prevention and management. This final paper will review current efforts and suggest the use of MetS as a pluripotent risk indicator that can be targeted so as to prevent a broad range of chronic conditions.   There are continued health disparities between vulnerable populations in Canada. Public health efforts should aim to prevent such disparities and achieve the best health for all. Given that the distribution of MetS between population subgroups is proportionate with the distribution of chronic diseases, we suggest that MetS is a potential equitable chronic disease prevention target. Furthermore, based on its association with a wide array of chronic diseases (CVD, diabetes, rheumatic diseases, schizophrenia, polycystic ovarian syndrome and chronic kidney disease), we suggest that MetS has the added potential to be a broad reaching prevention target. Consequently, this thesis aims to contribute to our knowledge about the potential role for MetS in public health prevention and policy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The examination of a novel viral vector and immunogens for HIV/SIV vaccine development in a non-human primate model
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CELL CULTURE; GENOME SEQUENCING; HERPESVIRUS; HIV; IMMUNOLOGY; MOLECULAR CLONING; NON-HUMAN PRIMATES; VACCINE DEVELOPMENT; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the major advances in HIV therapy, the AIDS epidemic continues to spread. Researchers are striving to prevent HIV infection through vaccination. This proposal describes a new approach for the development of an HIV vaccine, using human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) as the delivery system. HCMV infections occur during early childhood and most of these infections are subclinical with no apparent symptoms. HCMV establishes a life-long infection in people where it stays hidden with periodic appearances to boost immunity. This ability of HCMV to "self-boost" represents a significant benefit over other HIV vaccine delivery methods and may help address the key issue of temporary and fading vaccine protection.  We are testing whether this vaccine will work in monkeys using the monkey version of HIV termed Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV) and the monkey version of HCMV termed cynomolgus macaque CMV (CyCMV). We have now determined the DNA sequence of CyCMV which will allow us to genetically manipulate CyCMV to introduce SIV proteins (molecules that will be recognized and provoke an immune response). Subsequently, we will determine if the CyCMV vaccine delivers the SIV proteins and if they stimulate an immune response. We will measure the strength of the immune responses and determine if vaccinated monkeys who are exposed to SIV resist infection. If we see evidence of protection from SIV infection, we will optimize the vaccine and test the equivalent HCMV/HIV vaccine in humans.   This research directly relates to the goals and mandates of the CIHR with respect to the advancement of HIV prevention technologies and interventions research. It is hoped that the proposed project will provide a fresh field of exploration and lead to new understandings of the protective efficacy and immune correlates associated with HIV vaccination. An effective vaccine is our best hope for stopping the spread of HIV in Canada and the new infections acquired daily around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and characterization of immunologically relevant T Cell epitopes of HIV-1 Nef
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY MICROARRAY; BIOINFORMATICS; ELISPOT; EXON ARRAY; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENE EXPRESSION; GENETICS; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 (HIV-1) is a deadly pathogen that affects many people globally. According to the World Health Organization, 33.3 million people around the world were living with HIV, with 2.6 million new infections and 1.8 million deaths in 2009 alone. An effective vaccine for HIV is one of the most important needs for global health today. Despite two decades of intense study and research, there is still no such vaccine. To develop an effective vaccine against HIV-1 it is important to understand the natural protective immunity against the virus. Since HIV-1 depends on the host for survival and not everyone infected by HIV-1 will develop AIDS, understanding of the immune response that can control viral infection could help in developing a vaccine. One way to characterize the protective immune response is to study host and virus interactions. These host-viral interactions are indicated by the positive selection mutations in the virus which allow it to escape host immune responses. By characterizing these mutations we can identify the vulnerable regions of HIV-1 that are targeted by the host immune system. My PhD research project focuses on identifying and characterizing the positive selection mutations in Nef, one of the accessory proteins of HIV-1. It is part of a large comprehensive study to characterize protective immune response against HIV and it will help advance our understanding of protection against it. Further, my research project will promote the development of a novel vaccine to combat HIV-1 infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the impact of cervical HPV infection and clearance on mucosal HIV susceptibility.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL SCIENCE; COINFECTIONS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIV; HPV; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: HIV transmission after sexual exposure is the exception rather than the norm. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) including gonorrhea, chlamydia, and herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) have been associated with an increase in susceptibility to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), likely due to the recruitment of HIV target cells. Studies have shown that human papillomavirus (HPV) is one of the most prevalent STIs worldwide and is associated with various types of cancer, especially of the cervix. Recent studies have demonstrated an association between HPV status and HIV acquisition, but the underlying immune mechanism is unclear. The purpose of my study is to determine if HPV infection results in an increase of HIV target cells in the female genital tract of HIV uninfected women. HPV vaccines have been slow to roll out in lower income countries where the HIV burden is the highest; defining how HPV increase HIV transmission will be a powerful public health tool to promote effective HPV prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Medication Adherence in HIV+ Women: The Impact of Cognitive Deficits and Substance Use
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; DEPENDENCE; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONING; HIV; MEMORY; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; POLYSUBSTANCE; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: Optimal management of HIV involves adherence to complex medication regimens that are apt to be reliant on the patient's cognitive capacities. Noncompliance causes viral replication, leading to accelerated disease progression and associated cognitive impairments in memory and executive functioning (EF). Cognitive capacities are further compromised by polysubstance use (PSU), a common co-morbidity of HIV. This project aims to expand our understanding of how memory and EF are affected in HIV+ women who are co-morbid for PSU and the impact of these specific cognitive deficits on medication adherence. Hierarchical regression analysis will be used to evaluate, in a female cohort, the hypothesis that HIV and PSU will produce memory and EF impairments. Memory and EF will be examined using the Hopkins Verbal Learning Test- Revised and the computerized Intra-/Extra-Dimensional task, respectively. PSU will be quantified by frequency, duration, and amount. Logistic regression will be used to determine the extent that cognitive deficits compromise adherence, which will be quantified using prescription refill records. Female participants will be recruited from two CIHR-funded studies: 1) HIV+ women and a matched control group, with varied drug use history and 2) downtown eastside of Vancouver, where high percentages of HIV and current substance use exist in the female cohort. Women are underrepresented in neuropsychological research pertaining to HIV, despite increasing rates of infection in Canadian women. The current work will identify women at risk for poor adherence and associated disease progression based upon their substance use patterns and neurocognitive abilities. Study findings will inform future treatment planning by identifying the importance of providing necessary supports to facilitate adherence. Further health implications include highlighting the relevance of appropriate interventions, such as drug counselling, in HIV+ women with co-morbid PSU.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the social context of injection drug use and HIV risk amongst young, Aboriginal women in an urban Canadian setting
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; CRITICAL ETHNOGRAPHY; GENDER AND HEALTH; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH PROMOTION; SOCIAL ECOLOGY; SUBSTANCE USE
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, Aboriginal women have higher rates of HIV when compared to other populations of women. Injection drug use (IDU) increases susceptibility to HIV infection, and data illustrates that young, Aboriginal women who use injection drugs are particularly susceptible to HIV infection. However, the complexity of the relationship between IDU and vulnerability for HIV infection among young, Aboriginal women is poorly understood. Specifically, there is lack of understanding regarding the larger social, economic, historical, and personal factors that influence IDU practices. Thus, the proposed project will explore the social context of young Aboriginal women's drug use in an urban context. The project will investigate how women use injection drugs, who they use with, where they use, and how and where they obtain the equipment to use to highlight the social, economic, historical, and personal factors that influence IDU practices. Data collection will involve interviews with 40 Aboriginal women aged 19-30 who are presently using injection drugs. Recruitment of participants for the study will occur with the support of an advisory committee of Aboriginal women in collaboration with sites in a neighbourhood where I and the research team have established relationships. The study will also include participant observation in the neighbourhood where women use drugs, and will focus on individual, interpersonal and structural factors that influence IDU practices. Examining the social context of Aboriginal women's injection drug use is essential to develop meaningful and effective HIV prevention efforts. If a clearer understanding is gained with regards to how young Aboriginal women are using injection drugs, meaningful health service programming can be developed. Ultimately, these health services will be designed specifically for the needs of this highly vulnerable population to minimize the transmission of HIV and improve health outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advancing Peer-Delivered HIV Prevention Programs: Elucidating the Complex Role of Peer Workers
Keywords-MotsClés: BEST PRACTICES; HARM REDUCTION; HIV PREVENTION PROGRAMS; PEER WORK; PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT; SERVICE DELIVERY
Abstract-Résumé: Peer workers are members from a specific community who provide health information and support to others of the same community. Peer outreach has been a crucial component in HIV prevention programs because peers are able to reach members of their community who do not typically access these services, and act as a bridge between the community and formal health care services. Because peer workers tend to be seen as trustworthy, the services they offer gain legitimacy in the eyes of their community. However, little is known about the nature of peer work and the effect of the work itself on peer workers. This community-based qualitative research project asks novels questions about peer work, including how role challenges affect peers and their ability to provide services.  Peers wear different hats - they are clients and patients, they are service providers, and they are friends of the people to whom they provide services. It can be unclear for peer workers in which capacity they should respond in a given situation. The boundaries between these different roles are often blurry and can create tensions for the peer workers who are on their own journeys of recovery and development. The project involves interviewing 20 peer workers and 10 program supervisors from community health centres in different areas of Toronto and then teasing out their stories to create a narrative of peer workers' experiences. This research will provide a more nuanced and complete picture of peer work, and will contribute to the theoretical and practical literature upon which peer program best practices may be developed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of PTEN nuclear translocation in NMDAR-mediated exciotoxic neuronal death in Huntington's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; CELL SIGNALING; EXCITOTOXICITY; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; NEURODEGENERATION; NEURONAL DEATH; NEUROSCIENCE; NMDA RECEPTORS; PHARMACOLOGY AND THERAPEUTICS; PTEN
Abstract-Résumé: The NMDA receptor (NMDAR) is a key receptor in the brain for excitatory neurotransmission.  Over-excitation of NMDARs leads to excitotoxicity, which has shown to have a role in the pathogenesis of several neurological diseases such as stroke, ALS and Huntington's Disease.  Directly blocking NMDARs with antagonists has shown to be an ineffective clinical therapeutic for NMDAR-mediated excitotoxic diseases, likely due to the critical role of NMDARs in normal brain function. Instead, it may be possible to target signaling pathways downstream of NMDAR activation by modulating cellular activity related to cell death specifically, while leaving cell survival  NMDAR function intact.   Recent studies in our lab have indicated that nuclear translocation of Phosphatase and Tensin Homolog deleted on chromosome ten (PTEN), a tumor suppressor, has a key role in NMDAR-mediated excitotoxic neuronal death.   To target this, we have designed the Tat-K13  interference peptide and have shown that Tat-K13 can block PTEN nuclear translocation and prevent neuron damage after NMDA excitotoxicity.   Preliminary studies in our lab have supported the hypothesis that PTEN nuclear translocation may have a role in NMDAR-mediated excitotoxic neuron death in Huntington's Disease (HD).  Using biochemistry, I have shown that PTEN nuclear translocation is significantly increased in neurons from HD transgenic mice after NMDA treatment.  Similarly, blocking PTEN nuclear translocation using Tat-K13 significantly reduces NMDAR-mediated excitotoxic death in cultured striatal, cortical and hippocampal neurons from HD transgenic mice. These results strongly support my hypothesis. My current study will address my hypothesis by 1) determining the neuroprotective effects of Tat-K13 in HD, both in cultured cells and live HD transgenic mice and 2) characterizing the mechanism of PTEN nuclear translocation leading to neuron death.  This study may be an important step towards developing new therapeutics for HD.

TitreApplicationTitle: An evaluation of the management of hypertension by pharmacists with prescribing authorization, and the clinical effectiveness and feasibility of remunerating pharmacists for providing clinical hypertension care to improve cardiovascular outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; HEALTH PROFESSIONAL REMUNERATION; HYPERTENSION; INTERPROFESSIONAL COLLABORATION; PATIENT-CENTERED CARE; PHARMACIST PRESCRIBING; PHARMACY PRACTICE; PRACTICE-BASED RESEARCH; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
Abstract-Résumé: High blood pressure (BP) can contribute to heart attack, stroke, and heart failure, and is often easily controlled with lifestyle and drug therapy, making pharmacists capable of caring for patients with high BP due to their drug therapy expertise. Previous research has shown that community pharmacy BP programs can lower BP more effectively than usual physician-based care, even when the pharmacist is limited to making drug therapy recommendations to the patient's physician who must prescribe drug changes.  The province of Alberta allows pharmacists to prescribe medications. Here, we are conducting a study where patients are randomized to pharmacist-based care (monthly pharmacist BP assessment with medication adjustment) or usual care for 6 months. Since the sustainability of this type of program requires pharmacists to be paid for their time, we are also studying two different pay methods: (1) fee-for-service (a flat fee paid per visit regardless of BP outcomes) and (2) payment-for-performance (a flat fee per visit with bonuses for lowering BP to certain levels). We will be studying whether pharmacists with prescribing authorization are able to lower patients' BP moreso than usual care, and also studying whether BP lowering achieved depends on how pharmacists are paid.  We will also review the literature to determine if payment-for-performance for health professionals has an impact on the quality or cost-effectiveness of care provided to patients, and also to see how pharmacists are paid worldwide for providing care through similar programs and the outcomes achieved by those programs.  Our goal is to study the effectiveness of pharmacist care including prescribing in lowering BP, and how we should be paying pharmacists for their time. Pharmacist management of high BP can potentially lower a patient's risk of heart attack, stroke, or heart failure, and also potentially improve patients' access to care reducing the burden of chronic disease in the population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical application of novel chip-based technology for determination of sphingosine-1-phosphate-dependence of microvessel dysfunction in patients with heart failure
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERY-ON-A-CHIP PLATFORM; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; HEART FAILURE; HUMAN TISSUE; MICROFLUIDICS; MYOGENIC RESPONSE; RESISTANCE ARTERIES; SPHINGOSINE-1-PHOSPHATE SIGNALING; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH; TUMOUR NECROSIS FACTOR-ALPHA
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease is the current leading cause of illness and death worldwide, and poses a significant burden on healthcare resources. Small, microscopic blood vessels called resistance arteries critically control blood flow to various organs and overall blood pressure. Animal experiments show that abnormal changes in resistance artery structure and function occur in common cardiovascular diseases such as heart failure. Therefore, it is important to determine how resistance arteries are affected and controlled in order to develop new treatments for cardiovascular disease.  Our lab has discovered that a small molecule called Sphingosine-1-Phosphate (S1P) controls normal resistance artery function in healthy mice. Moreover, S1P activity is abnormally increased in mice with heart failure, causing disease-related changes in resistance artery function.  Given these findings, we expect that: 1) increased S1P is also responsible for resistance artery dysfunction in heart failure patients, and 2) blocking increased S1P activity should normalize resistance artery function and produce beneficial effects.  We have also developed a new platform for studying resistance artery function called the Artery-on-a-Chip (AoC) that is more efficient and user-friendly than current standard techniques. We plan to use new AoC technology to test patient blood vessel samples from gut and muscle tissue collected during surgery.  This cutting-edge research represents the first investigation of human gut and muscle resistance artery function in cardiovascular disease patients, and will uncover valuable information that will add to our understanding of what causes heart failure. Correlating human resistance artery function to an individual patient's medical status and history will reveal new diagnostic and therapeutic insights.  This work will lead to the development of innovative technology that may improve and personalize how we treat heart failure.

Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION; CARDIAC MUSCLE; HYPERTENSION; INTIMAL HYPERPLASIA; MOUSE MODELS OF CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; VASCULAR DISEASE; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC) are essential for the proper functioning of the cardiovascular system, and alterations in VSMC function play crucial roles in the development and progression of multiple vascular diseases.  Our lab has previously shown that the c-Myb protein (encoded by the c-myb gene) is required for proper VSMC multiplication and maturation.  However, the role of c-Myb in vascular diseases in adult mice has been difficult to examine as c-myb-deficient mice do not survive past embryos.  We have obtained a mouse that has 90% reduced function of the c-myb gene, but is non-lethal so we can study adult mice with a defect in c-Myb protein function.  We will be using two models of vascular disease to examine what role the gene c-myb has in vascular disease.  The outcomes of the study will enhance our understanding of c-Myb-dependent processes in vascular diseases in mouse models and contribute to the overall understanding of mechanisms of cardiovascular diseases.

Abstract-Résumé: My research objective is to combine quantitative methodology with Indigenous theory to research Indigenous population health by identifying key priorities and strategies through the understanding of Indigenous women's maternal health definitions, status, access to, and interactions with the health care system. I will explore the  relationship between Indigenous women's maternal health (pregnancy, birth & postpartum) and key complex and interrelated health determinants through the creation of a public health pilot survey of Indigenous women's maternity experiences in the Okanagan, British Columbia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using quantitative and qualitative methods to investigate the sexual health of First Nations Peoples living with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD)
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; FETAL ALCOHOL SPECTRUM DISORDERS; MIXED METHODS; PUBLIC HEALTH; SEXUAL HEALTH; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is a diagnosis given to people who experience physical, mental and/or behavioural problems because their mothers drank heavily during pregnancy. Even though scientists and doctors are aware that people with FASD tend to make risky decisions, and therefore could be much more likely to make risky sexual choices (like having sex without protection) there is almost no information on what the sexual health of people with FASD looks like. FASD affects nearly 1% of Canadians and the rate is even higher in many Aboriginal communities in Canada. This proposed research project aims to improve the personal health of people with FASD who live in First Nations communities and to improve the health of the entire FASD population living in Canada.  This project will take place in a First Nations community that is working to lower their extremely high rates of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Our previous work with this community has shown that FASD is contributing to their high STI rates, and that the community wants to help those community members with FASD.  We need to find out what the sexual health of people with FASD looks like, and how we can improve the sexual health of Aboriginal people with FASD though research and intervention. This study will administer a survey to collect information about sexual health, like condom use and risky sexual behaviours, from people with FASD living in our collaborating First Nations community. Then we will do interviews with people with FASD, their health care workers and family to find out how we can create a sexual health intervention for people with FASD living in the community. This project will help the collaborating community begin to heal the STI problems they face. Also this project is important for people with FASD across Canada and the world, because it will bring attention and resources to studying and improving the sexual health of people with FASD.

TitreApplicationTitle: A study of the risk and protective factors for suicidal behaviour in Aboriginal communities in Labrador.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; CASE-CONTROL DESIGN; COMMUNITY RESEARCH METHODS; CROSS-SECTIONAL DESIGN; EPIDEMIOLOGY; PREVENTION; RURAL AND REMOTE PRIMARY CARE; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Suicide in Aboriginal communities is a global health concern. In Labrador, Innu and Inuit communities struggle with high suicide rates, especially among young people. Although many studies have been done in this area, it is not known what interventions are most effective in preventing suicide in rural Aboriginal communities. Researchers and the health care system have identified important areas for future research, such as basic statistical information, community healing programs, and prevention services. Communities in Labrador need information to help identify at-risk groups, develop effective prevention programs, and improve access to health care services. As part of my doctoral research, I am working with Aboriginal governments, the Goose Bay hospital, and other community groups to gather information about suicide. The goal is to better understand the factors that increase the risk for suicide attempts and suicide deaths and to identify other factors that protect against these risks. To achieve this, I will be collecting and analyzing information on suicide attempts and suicide deaths from a community survey, medical records, and interviews with people who have attempted suicide and their caregivers. Community groups will use the results of my research to develop health services and policies to improve mental health in Labrador.

Abstract-Résumé: Maternal and infant health is a main indicator of a country's overall quality of life and health. In Canada, Aboriginal populations experience lower levels of maternal and infant health as compared with the general population. However, there is currently a lack of accurate data describing this difference. The aims of the study are 1. to describe the rates of tobacco and alcohol use during pregnancy by young Aboriginal girls and 2. to understand this behaviour from the perspectives of Aboriginal girls to help design effective programs to reduce alcohol and tobacco use during pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cancer survival of First Nations and Métis adults in Canada: follow-up of the 1991 census cohort
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; CANCER SURVIVAL; HEALTH INEQUALITIES; POPULATION-BASED RESEARCH; RECORD LINKAGE
Abstract-Résumé: Past studies have found that aboriginal peoples were at decreased risk of being diagnosed with cancer compared to the general population. These studies and others have also shown, however, that their risk of cancer is increasing over time and some findings suggest that once diagnosed with cancer, aboriginal people are less likely to survive than non-aboriginal people. Overall, the patterns of cancer in aboriginal peoples appear to be different from those in the general Canadian population. These population-level patterns are challenging to study, mainly because it is difficult to identify aboriginal people in administrative health databases. As a result of this challenge and others, there exists little research about the burden of cancer in these groups, despite the fact that it is among the top three causes of death in First Nations and Metis. A recent merging of three national databases has provided an opportunity to, for the first time, examine cancer survival in Canadian First Nations and Metis nationwide. Using linked data from the 1991 Canadian long-form Census, the Canadian Mortality Database and the Canadian Cancer Database, we intend to fulfill three objectives: 1) to describe cancer survival among First Nations and Metis adults in Canada; 2) to identify trends in survival (A) over time and (B) by broad geographical region; and 3) to compare the above to patterns and trends in non-aboriginal people. The proposed study will provide First Nations and Metis groups and their cancer control partners with a description of their cancer survival patterns and a metric by which to determine how they compare to each other and to the general population. In so doing, the proposed research aims to generate the information necessary to plan and provide effective, culturally-appropriate cancer control programs.
