TitreApplicationTitle: Developing and evaluating an STI/HIV risk assessment intervention tool: implications for scaling up
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PREDICTION MODELS; ONLINE HEALTH SERVICES; PREDICTIVE ALGORITHM; RISK ASSESSMENT; RISK SCORING; SELECTIVE SCREENING CRITERIA; SEXUAL BEHAVIOR; STI/HIV
Abstract-Résumé: In British Columbia, sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are distributed unequally across the population, with youth (15- 24 years of age) bearing a significant burden of infection. Undiagnosed and untreated infections often lead to serious reproductive sequelae and/or opportunistic co-infections (e.g., HIV). Interventions involving active case finding and early treatment of infections are priorities for public health efforts. One population-level intervention provided by the BC Centers for Disease Control (BCCDC) is Internet-based testing or iTest, which aims to improve STI/HIV testing amongst youth and other groups that experience high rates of STI/HIV. When users access iTest, the website recommends tests based on a risk score for STI/HIV risk and then provides appropriate laboratory requisitions. The purpose of the proposed research is to develop, refine, test and validate a practical risk-scoring (or prediction) tool to support the continuum of potential uptake or scale-up of iTest. This risk-scoring tool will be comprised of a set of selective screening criteria which will be valuable for minimizing costs, targeting testing to higher risk individuals, increasing the probability of detecting infection among asymptomatic men and women, and reducing the unnecessary testing of those without infection. The proposed study aims to: (1) Develop the STI risk-scoring tool that will be used in iTest; (2) Assess the capacity of the risk- scoring tool to adequately discriminate between those who are infected and those who are not; and (3) Determine the utility of the risk-scoring tool and iTest's 'fit' for province-wide scaling up. Using multivariable analysis, the risk-scoring tool will be developed from data collected at the largest publicly funded sexual health clinic in Vancouver between 2001 and 2010 (n=76,000). The validity or usefulness of the risk-scoring tool will be evaluated in two additional clinical settings in Vancouver.

TitreApplicationTitle: A risk stratification model for adult patients with obstructive sleep apnea: development and evaluation.
Keywords-MotsClés: OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA; PREDICTIVE MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is the most common sleep-related breathing disorder, affecting 3.4% of Canadian adults in 2009. OSA has been found to be associated with increased risk of death, heart attack, stroke, diabetes and depression. There are a variety of factors, such as hypoxia (low oxygen levels), sleep deprivation, and daytime sleepiness that put people with OSA at higher risk of these outcomes. However there is no consensus on how to predict if and when these outcomes will occur. The primary purpose of our study is to determine what physiological and clinical factors most accurately predict the development of any cardiovascular outcomes. We will obtain OSA-related data from a large comprehensive database from a sleep clinic at a hospital; outcomes occurring over the next 5 years will be extracted from administrative databases. In secondary analyses we will investigate predictors of individual cardiovascular diseases (heart attack, stroke), diabetes and depression. Using the results of our analyses, we will classify patients as being at low, intermediate, or high risk of poor outcomes. Knowledge of a patient's risk will allow targeting of more effective, appropriate, and efficient treatment and follow-up strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Perinatal outcomes in multiple sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NEUROEPIDEMIOLOGY; PERINATAL OUTCOMES; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic degenerative, autoimmune disease of the brain and the spinal cord. It is the most common cause of neurological disability in young adults in the Western World, affecting approximately 75,000 Canadians. The onset of MS typically occurs when men and women are of childbearing age, making pregnancy-related issues in MS of real importance. It remains unknown whether mothers with MS and their newborns have a greater risk of prolonged hospitalization after childbirth compared to mothers in the general population. This research is important because a prolonged hospital stay is associated with a greater risk of hospital-acquired infections, a more difficult transition from hospital to home and increased healthcare costs. Furthermore, aside from the issues of genetic inheritance, it is unclear how chronic illnesses such as MS in fathers could affect the health of their offspring. Previous research has found that men with MS were more likely to have abnormal sperm and sex hormone levels; hence, it is important to investigate the birth outcomes to fathers with MS. In addition, since men with MS are commonly treated with disease-modifying drugs (DMD) and are not routinely advised to stop DMD treatment prior to fathering offspring, it is essential to explore the potential harm of DMD use in fathers with MS who conceive children. Concerns related to pregnancy in patients with MS are a crucial area of research as the disease affects many Canadians in their childbearing years. The results of these studies will help MS patients and their clinicians make better-informed decisions regarding the appropriate management of pregnancy, with the ultimate goal of improving pregnancy and birth outcomes for MS patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Real-Time Measurement of Physical Activity Patterns in Type 2 Diabetes and Hypertension through GPS Monitoring and Accelerometry
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCELEROMETRY; DISEASE PREVENTION; ENVIRONMENTAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; GENDER-SPECIFIC DIFFERENCES; GIS-MAPPING; GLOBAL POSITIONING SYSTEM (GPS) MONITORING; HYPERTENSION; PATIENT-ORIENTED RESEARCH; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Many people with diabetes and high blood pressure die from heart attack or stroke. Being active can prevent this from happening. Unfortunately, people with diabetes and high blood pressure tend to be inactive. In order to help people increase activity levels, we need information on what factors affect activity. Researchers believe that how 'walkable' a person's neighbourhood is determines how active a person is. Although this makes sense, we do not know where people spend most of their time. This is a problem because if people spend all of their time at friends' houses or at work then how active they are will likely not depend on characteristics of their neighbourhoods. In order to help people with diabetes and high blood pressure become more active, we first need to figure out where these people spend most of their time. This is the primary aim of my study. After the amount of time spent in home neighbourhoods is quantified, my secondary aim is to determine if neighbourhood 'walkability' is associated with activity level, regardless of how much time people spend in their neighbourhoods. Data will be collected on patients attending clinics in Montreal. Activity level and location will be assessed for one week using accelerometers and Geographic Positioning System units, small machines that are easily worn on the wrist or clipped onto a backpack. Neighbourhood 'walkability' will be assessed by having participants answer some questions on what they think about their neighbourhoods and by a special computer program that will tell us exactly how 'walkable' each neighbourhood is based on the patients' home postal codes. Mathematical models will then be used to figure out, for people who spend a lot of time in their neighbourhoods and for people who do not, if there is a link between neighbourhood features and activity level. Doing so will inform the development of interventions designed to increase activity levels and help reduce the risk of heart attack or stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving design and analysis of longitudinal studies of prognosis in uncommon diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; EPIDEMIOLOGY; LATENT CLASS METHODS; LONGITUDINAL MODELING; LUPUS; OUTCOMES; PROGNOSIS; RARE DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Many chronic diseases with onset in childhood are uncommon or rare compared to adult diseases. As pediatric expertise in these conditions advances, more children with chronic diseases survive into adulthood. Families, physicians and healthcare policymakers are interested in the prognosis-the course and outcome-of patients over time. Understanding prognosis will help physicians optimize patient management. Small patient numbers and suboptimal study designs have hindered the study of prognosis in uncommon diseases; our ability to draw strong conclusions has been limited. Though the number of patients afflicted by an uncommon disease is low, effective treatments can mean the difference between a productive life and chronic disability. Childhood-onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (cSLE), an uncommon inflammatory disease, afflicts many organs. Children with cSLE have more aggressive disease than adults. It is known that adult SLE patients develop early heart attacks and die early. The course of cSLE patients is unclear. This doctoral program will use new statistical methods (rarely used before to study rare diseases), to visualize disease activity and damage trends for cSLE patients into adulthood and identify predictors of disease course. We will combine information collected from cSLE patients in our center, with their information in adulthood from our collaborators. This is the largest (>500 patients) cSLE cohort in the world. We will gain new understanding of cSLE and predictors of disease course. Our methods are efficient and effective-fewer patients will be needed and we can draw stronger conclusions about the effects of identified predictors than previously. The knowledge gained from these studies will be generalizable, not only to cSLE but to all chronic uncommon diseases. Clinical researchers may use these methods to improve understanding of prognosis. Patients, physicians and policymakers may use the information to make informed decisions for the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Subtypes of Depression in Multiple Sclerosis: The Impact of Best Evidence Knowledge Acquisition and Educational Knowledge Interaction on the Assessment, Diagnosis and Management of Depression in Multiple Sclerosis amongst Patients, Caregivers and Health Care Providers
Keywords-MotsClés: COPING; DEPRESSION; EDUCATION; INTERVENTION; MIXED METHODS; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED PILOT TRIAL; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is commonly thought of as an inability to walk, with confinement to a wheelchair or nursing home bed inevitable.  While disease progression is expected in MS, disability is not the main concern for persons with MS and their families; it is depression and disconnection.    Depression is found in 25-50% of the MS population, compared to only 10-15% in the general population.  Depression impacts quality of life and the day to day functioning of MS patients.  Depression in MS is further complicated by the fact that depression, like MS, can be related to neurological damage.  Thus, patients, caregivers and health care providers often have difficulty differentiating depression symptoms from MS symptoms.  The aim of the study is to improve the understanding and management of depression in MS by characterizing, clarifying and educating MS patients, caregivers and health care providers about the physical, psychological and social aspects of depression, as well as the optimal coping and treatment strategies.  There will be four phases to this research: a systematic review of the literature on depression in MS; a mixed methods study to gather information about MS patients', caregivers' and care providers'  perceptions and experiences with depression in MS; development of a depression management educational program for MS patients and their families; and a randomized controlled pilot trial of the effectiveness of the education program for managing depression.  MS is the most common neurological disease among young Canadians, as unfortunately, Canada has one of the highest rates of MS in the world.  This research will add to the current body of knowledge regarding depression in MS, provide a springboard for better understanding and managing depression among the MS population, and address one of the most significant quality of life concerns for MS patients and their families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Les interactions pharmacologiques impliquant les benzodiazépines chez les personnes âgées dans le système de soins primaire : analyse des conséquences cliniques et économiques.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTIQUE; INTERACTIONS MEDICAMENTEUSES; PHARMACOLOGIE; PHARMACOECONOMIE; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGIE; UTILISATION DES SERVICES DE SANTE; VEILLISSEMENT; ECONOMIE DE LA SANTE
Abstract-Résumé: Les personnes agees sont considerees comme etant de grands consommateurs de benzodiazepines, un medicament indique pour l'anxiete et l'insomnie. Toutefois, les consommateurs de benzodiazepines sont a risque d'interactions medicamenteuses avec plusieurs autres classes de medicaments. Parmi les consequences possibles se trouve une augmentation de l'effet sedatif qui provoque un risque accru de blessures et de fractures. L'objectif de ce projet de recherche est d'evaluer la gravite de cette problematique en evaluant les consequences cliniques et economiques des interactions medicamenteuses impliquant les benzodiazepines et leur impact sur la qualite de vie des personnes agees au Quebec. De plus, ce projet a pour objectif d'etudier les traitements alternatifs aux benzodiazepines dans l'optique de reduire le fardeau associe a la prescription non optimale de benzodiazepines dans la population agee. Ainsi, ce projet de recherche pourra informer les decideurs du systeme de sante de la gravite de cette problematique en vue d'optimiser la prescription de medicaments psychotropes chez la population agee et afin d'augmenter l'efficience des systemes de sante canadiens.

TitreApplicationTitle: Low back pain in Quebec's Multidisciplinary pain Treatment Clinics: how good and how much?
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PAIN; DIRECT COSTS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENDER; GEOGRAPHICAL SYSTEM; HEALTH COSTS; LOW BACK PAIN; PHARMACOECONOMY; POPULATION HEALTH; RURAL AND URBAN
Abstract-Résumé: Health economics and pharmacoeconomics are emerging approaches for the valuation of chronic conditions.  With the aging population, chronic conditions are more frequent and health expenses are exploding.  Studies also show that working-age males meet with greater work absenteeism due to chronic pain, resulting in important socioeconomical loss for the industrialized economies.  Meanwhile, we need to take action to improve the health system as the capacity to support medical care could be affected in a close future by limited federal/provincial budgets reaching a ceiling for health expenses.  In this research program, we propose to develop this crenel within the Quebec Pain Research Network by the joint efforts of research teams from UdeS, UdeM and UMcGill.  We will determine the direct costs in Multidisiplinary Pain Treatment Facilities (MPTFs).  Those data will allow, in the long-term, to perform a cost-effectiveness study based on the level of recovery achieved in the MPTFs.  Overall, this will detail where the costs for LPB management are the greatest and provide insights for explaining potential inequalities.  Accordingly, decision-makers will be able to propose adapted programs either to physicians or the population to balance the health costs while providing improved management and benefits for LBP coping patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Paying for primary care: The impact of reform in Ontario on costs and access
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO CARE; ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEALTH SYSTEM COSTS; PAYMENT MODELS; PRIMARY CARE; SELECTION EFFECTS
Abstract-Résumé: Primary healthcare is widely viewed as a crucial part of a high performing healthcare system, and Canada, like many other countries, has seen a series of efforts to reform how it is financed and delivered. In the early 2000s, the Ontario government began experimenting with a number of new primary care reform models. These models were designed to change the way family physicians are compensated and the environments in which they practice. The purpose of the proposed research is to evaluate the impact of the implementation of these primary care reform models on health system costs and access to care. Using the individual primary care physician as the unit of analysis, the proposed research will answer three research questions. First, what are the incentives imbedded in the Ontario primary care models, and what impact would theory predict they have on physician behaviour?  The second question asks: What is the impact of physician self-selection, and are there systematic differences in physician characteristics that increase their likelihood of joining particular models? The final question asks: What patient characteristics are associated with enrolment in different primary care reform models, and did the distribution of patients within and across models change over the time horizon of primary care reform? The results of this research should help inform better matches between payment models, practice models and the types of patients being served, particularly high cost patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring the sixth vital sign: A prospective, longitudinal analysis of distress in head and neck cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIER ASSESSMENT; CANCER; CLINICAL RESEARCH; DISTRESS; HEAD AND NECK CANCER; MENTAL HEALTH; MIXED METHODS RESEARCH; PATIENT-ORIENTED RESEARCH; PSYCHOSOCIAL ONCOLOGY; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Everyone diagnosed with cancer experiences some level of distress related to their diagnosis and treatment. This problem is amplified in those with head and neck cancer (HNCa), a population who report the highest rates of anxiety, depression, and suicide compared with other cancer sites. Distress has become so problematic that the Canadian Strategy for Cancer Control has recommended it be formally recognized as the "sixth vital sign", implying that distress monitoring should occur as routinely as the monitoring of heart rate or blood pressure. Despite this recognition, less than 10% of distressed individuals are identified. Failure to acknowledge and treat distress in HNCa jeopardizes treatment outcomes, decreases quality of life (QOL), and increases healthcare costs. This study will determine how the experience of living with HNCa affects specific areas of one's life (e.g., physical impact, emotional strain, social isolation) and also what barriers prevent identification and management of distress. With this data, clinicians can tailor psychosocial interventions to the needs of those with HNCa. Initially, 200 individuals with HNCa will be invited to complete surveys of their QOL and distress level during the first year following diagnosis. A subset of these individuals will be invited to participate in interviews to describe the experience of distress following diagnosis, providing valuable information including factors contributing to the exacerbation of distress and its consequences. Following this, a sample of individuals with HNCa, their caregivers, hospital administrators and clinicians will be invited to attend focus groups to discuss barriers to effective distress management at the personal, professional, and administrative levels. Thus, this study will: (1) offer insights into the consequences of distress for those with HNCa and (2) explore barriers at the personal, professional, and administrative levels that prevent effective distress management in HNCa.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of flaxseed and flax oil on blood pressure and vascular health in hypertensive patients in a randomized double blinded placebo controlled clinical trial.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FUNCTIONING; CARDIOLOGY; FLAXSEED; HYPERTENSION; NUTRITION; VASCULAR HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Background:High blood pressure is a prevalent condition worldwide that is important to treat because it is a major risk factor for heart disease.  In 2008, 13.4 million people died of heart disease, stroke, or other cerebrovascular diseases which accounted for one quarter of all deaths globally in 2008. Approximately 19% of Canadians aged 20-79 years are living with hypertension (20% with pre-hypertension) & the prevalence increases with age to 53.2% in those aged 60-79. Additionally, in 1998, 13.2 million visits were made to physicians in Canada for hypertension management. Functional foods have been attributed with health promoting characteristics that can improve disease states & quality of life. My study will be investigating the functional food flaxseed & natural health product flax oil. Flaxseed is a Canadian grown crop that has many nutritional components: omega 3 fatty acid alpha-linolenic acid, lignans, protein, antioxidants, & fibre. These components may all contribute to heart health & lower blood pressure. Flax oil will also be investigated (containing alpha-linolenic acid) to understand if the beneficial components are the fatty acids or a synergistic effect of all the components of flaxseed.  Hypothesis:The patient group administered flaxseed will experience the greatest decrease in blood pressure & the greatest improvement in vascular health.  Experimental Details:The proposed project will investigate the effects of flaxseed & flax oil on blood pressure, vascular health, exercise performance, cardiac functioning, & incidence of stroke/heart attack in patients will newly diagnosed high blood pressure. The clinical trial will be randomized, double blinded, & placebo controlled. Significance:This study will elucidate the potential cardiovascular benefits of flaxseed & flax oil. Our hope it to find a way to help reduce the prevalence of heart disease, promote health & the quality of life of Canadians while reducing the burden on our healthcare system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Emotion Regulation Deficits and Social Impairments in Children with High-Functioning Autism and Asperger's Syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; EMOTION REGULATION; FAMILY; HIGH-FUNCTIONING AUTISM/ASPERGER'S SYNDROME; PSYCHOEDUCATION; PSYCHOTHERAPY; SEX DIFFERENCES; SOCIAL WELL-BEING
Abstract-Résumé: The social and emotional problems experienced by children with high-functioning autism (HFA) or Asperger's syndrome (AS) can be immense. Frequently observed difficulties such as emotion dysregulation problems (e.g., irritability and temper outbursts) can also greatly interfere with these children's functioning. However, the ways by which emotional dysregulation processes contribute to the social difficulties of HFA/AS are yet unclear, and there is a need for the development of interventions to improve emotion regulation abilities in these children, potentially enhancing their overall well-being. The proposed research examines whether a family-based intervention (Multi-Family Psychoeducational Psychotherapy; MF-PEP) will improve the social and emotion regulation deficits among children with HFA/AS. Given the current lack of empirically-supported treatments for children with HFA/AS and the paucity of research on emotion regulation among these children, this proposed study will be one of the firsts in expanding our understanding of ways by which emotion regulation difficulties influence the social difficulties experienced by children with HFA/AS. Moreover, this study will evaluate a promising treatment for children with HFA/AS, potentially providing significant insights into strategies that researchers and clinicians can use to alleviate the tremendous burden these children and their families must carry day after day.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using Technology to Improve the Management & Prevention of Chronic Disease Within the Practice of Physical Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH SERVICE DELIVERY; MIXED METHODS; MOBILITY; PATIENT-ORIENTED RESEARCH; PHYSICAL THERAPY; REHABILITATION; SELF-DIRECTED TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: One of the most dramatic demographic trends worldwide is the aging population and the demographic and economic forces associated with this trend will challenge health service leaders and policy makers in the coming decades. High blood pressure, cholesterol, overweight, and physical inactivity are all common risk factors for many chronic diseases and conditions, including age-related diseases. In an effort to help maintain functional independence and quality of life, especially in the face of an aging population, novel and innovative approaches to health promotion and health service delivery are needed. This will require a shift from our current models of care towards a model that relies more upon the use of technologies (e.g. telemedicine, self-directed technology such as smartphones) as well as allied health professionals (e.g. physical therapists). These types of technologies may be effective tools for brief and frequent communication between health professionals and patients and to monitor clinical outcomes (e.g. hypertension) as well as health outcomes (e.g. mobility, quality of life). Additionally, self-directed technology may act as an effective method for consistent data collection, which can facilitate patient-oriented research. To achieve measurable changes in the health of Canadians -and lessen the corresponding burden on our healthcare system associated with our aging population- it is not only necessary to conduct high quality research, but to also translate the knowledge gleaned to facilitate practical strategies that will keep our aging population moving, healthy and functionally independent. My proposed research plan will contribute to the knowledge base for both a) the use and application of self-directed technology as a potential agent to improve access to healthcare for Canadians, as well as b) the best practice guidelines in physical therapy for the use of self-directed technology in the management and prevention of chronic disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physiotherapy practice and third party payers: issues in professional ethics
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS; CONFLICTS OF INTEREST; EQUITY; HEALTH POLICY; MUSCULOSKELETAL PROBLEMS; PHYSIOTHERAPY; PROFESSIONAL ETHICS; REHABILITATION; THIRD PARTY PAYERS; WORK RELATED INJURIES
Abstract-Résumé: Physiotherapists are specialists in the musculoskeletal system. Many therapists' caseloads include patients who are on workers' compensation. The frequency of physiotherapy sessions has recently been questioned by health insurers, other third party payers, by the media and the Order of physiotherapists in Quebec. Of concern is that the workers' compensation system - and the expectations and pressures by third party payers - may create powerful incentives that can unduly influence decision-making by health professionals regarding service provision. Delays in receiving services as well as frequency of treatments may be related to the source of payment, raising concerns about equity and appropriate access to health services in both public and private settings. Yet, professional codes of ethics for physiotherapists in Quebec include only minimal guidelines on the subject. In this project, we will explore the ethics challenges raised by this situation in Canada and propose some ways forward. It is imperative for health professionals to be conscious of ethical issues in their clinical practice. This project has three components. We will analyze policies of different provincial and national agencies (orders, association, worker compensation board) across Canada. We will conduct a survey with physiotherapists across Canada using clinical vignettes to examine differences in delays and treatment frequency between patients who are or are not covered by workers compensation insurance. We will then explore physiotherapists' perspectives on this subject through individual in-depth interviews. We aim to develop ethics guidelines and policies for physiotherapists concerning conflicts of interest and equity in the distribution of health services. This work is extremely important in view of the limited number of physiotherapists in Canada and the increased need for rehabilitation services that is forecasted due to the aging of the population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Supportive Decision Making for Diverse Populations: A Needs Assessment Tool and Relational Guidelines
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTONOMY; CLINICAL ETHICS; FEMINIST ETHICS; GROUNDED THEORY; HEALTHCARE DECISION MAKING; PATIENT-CENTRED CARE; RELATIONAL APPROACH; SURROGATE DECISION MAKING
Abstract-Résumé: In recent decades, the primacy of respect for autonomy in Western bioethics has led to various legal requirements and formalized attempts to promote patients' self-determination and to protect them from potential exploitation. Nonetheless, our preliminary research shows that healthcare providers (HCPs) continue to face challenges in working with patients, long-term care residents, and families in making healthcare decisions that respect people's autonomy.  This project will explore problems in the current practices of decision making and strategies to support patients/families of culturally diverse backgrounds as they determine appropriate care plans.  Interviews and focus groups in Vancouver and Toronto with diverse patients and surrogates (Chinese-speaking, Punjabi-speaking, English-speaking, and Aboriginal communities) as well as HCPs will be conducted. This project will: 1. Achieve better understanding of decision making processes for patients of diverse backgrounds in complex healthcare situations; 2. Identify patients', families', and HCPs' attitudes towards individual and system barriers and successes in promoting supportive decision making; 3. Develop a needs assessment tool as well as supportive decision making guidelines that will facilitate complex decision making with/for diverse and vulnerable populations.  As our healthcare system is presumably founded on equity and fair distribution of resources, this project will help to promote our system's ability to live up to the promises of universality and accessibility, two of the principles emphasized in the Canada Health Act of 1984.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroimaging for Disorders of Consciousness: Charting the Canadian Ethics Landscape
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADA; CLINICAL TRANSLATION; DISORDERS OF CONSCIOUSNESS; EMPIRICAL ETHICS; ETHICS; GUIDELINES; INTERVIEWS; MINIMALLY CONSCIOUS STATE; NEUROIMAGING; SURVEYS
Abstract-Résumé: Each year approximately 50,000 Canadians suffer a brain injury, and many of these individuals lose consciousness, some for days, some for months, and some for years. New technologies, such as magnetic resonance imaging, are currently being developed to improve the diagnosis, prognosis, and care of these historically neglected patients. This growing field of research raises a number of ethical concerns including high rates of misdiagnosis, end-of-life decision-making, and difficult resource allocation issues. To date, however, these issues have received limited attention. The bulk of the work that has been done, furthermore, has not focused on the Canadian context, a context that is characterized by unique system, resource, and attitudinal qualities. As a consequence, key practice communities (Canadian neuroimagers, clinicians, and ethicists) lack guidance that is adequately grounded in the lived reality of working with brain-injured patients. The purpose of this study is to identify and explore the ethical challenges associated with these developments in neuroimaging for Canada, and to produce guidelines vital to the development of best practices in research and health care for Canadians with brain disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of parental sodium intake on offspring
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; BLOOD PRESSURE; GENE EXPRESSION; RODENT; SODIUM; TELEMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: The adverse health effects of a high sodium intake have been well studied in adults. However, there are now indications in the scientific literature that sodium may begin to have important health effects during early development. Animals studies suggest that a high sodium intake by mothers during pregnancy and lactation may promote altered blood pressure and kidney function in her offspring when they later grow up to be adults. Recent animal studies suggest that, potentially, the diet of the father could also be relevant. In our research, we will use sensitive methods in rats to determine what effects a mother and father's sodium intake may have on their offspring, the mechanisms by which this may happen, and whether such effects on offspring may be passed on to subsequent generations as has been demonstrated in the case of several other nutritional factors. Collectively, our results will allow us to better understand the effects a parent's sodium intake may have in our population, and what to look for when searching for a similar effect of sodium in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of Specific Inhibitors of Alternative Splicing Events Crucial to HIV Replication: A New Anti-HIV/AIDS Strategy
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; ALTERNATIVE SPLICING INHIBITORS; ANTI HIV/AIDS DRUGS; DHA ANALOGUES; DRUG DISCOVERY; HIV; SCREENING; SPLICEOSOME
Abstract-Résumé: An estimated 33 million people live with HIV/AIDS. Although access to Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy (HAART) has dramatically changed the prognosis of HIV infection, issues of drug compliance, resistance and side effects necessitiates the constant need for new drugs. This project defines the objectives and milestones of our continuing research to develop small molecule inhibitors of alternative splicing as a new therapy for HIV/AIDS. Key regulators of alternative splicing are a family of SR proteins, which include SRSF1. This SR protein plays a generally redundant role in human RNA splicing. However,  in HIV-1 infected cells it specifically regulates alternative splicing events that are vital to the production of critical HIV proteins that are regulators for the expression of HIV-1 viral genes, for the synthesis of full-length genomic RNA and, ultimately, for the production of progeny virions. An important advantage to blocking SRSF1 as an anti HIV/AIDS strategy is that targeting a human protein decreases the chances of mutations and subsequent resistance to drug therapy. Our research has focused on the design of ring-opened non cytotoxic mimics of the SRSF1 inhibitor IDC16. This has led to the identification of 4 novel di(hetero)arylamide (DHA) type compounds that display activity comparable to AZT. This result forms the basis for the research outlined in our proposal, whose ultimate objective is to develop a new anti-HIV/AIDS drug.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of Myeloid Dendritic Cell Subsets Contributing to HIV-1 Immunity versus Cell-to-Cell Dissemination: A Translational Study in Subjects with Slow and Rapid Disease Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CD16+ MONOCYTES; CDNA MICROARRAYS; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HIV-1; MYELOID DENDRITIC CELLS; REAL-TIME PCR; RNA INTERFERENCE; VIROLOGICAL SYNAPSE
Abstract-Résumé: The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV) establishes a lethal infection by mechanisms that are not clearly understood and viral eradication is not achieved under the current antiretroviral therapies (ART). Potent antiviral responses depend on the ability of antigen presenting cells (APC) to induce antiviral  adaptive immunity. Myeloid dendritic cells (DC) are one major type of APC. HIV hijacks the function of DC in adaptive immunity for its own survival advantage. HIV alters the ability to DC to process and present HIV antigens and thus DC fail to induce potent anti-HIV T-cell responses. In addition, DC transmit efficiently virions to CD4+ T-cells and therefore contribute to viral dissemination and persistence. Circulating monocytes are precursors for DC and are used in cell-based immune therapies against cancer and HIV infection. Monocytes are heterogeneous in their stage of differentiation and immunological function. HIV disease progression is associated with the dramatic expansion of a subset of monocytes expressing the molecule CD16 (up to 50% in AIDS patients). Our previous reports demonstrated that CD16+ monocytes, as opposed to CD16- monocytes, are a source of pro-inflammatory molecules and selectively contribute to HIV dissemination in CD4+ T-cells. This project is based on the hypothesis that DC derived from CD16+ monocytes play a deleterious role in HIV pathogenesis, while those derived from CD16- monocytes are able to degrade HIV and prime efficient HIV-specific T-cell responses. Our objective is to identify the molecular basis of these differences by using a systems biology approach. This knowledge will suggest new therapeutic strategies against HIV aimed at interfering with CD16+ monocyte deleterious function. The expected results will recommend the use of CD16- monocytes in DC-based therapies to promote potent anti-HIV immunity, while avoiding viral dissemination.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exosomes acts as an intercellular communicator in HIV-1 pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: DCIR; DENDRITIC CELLS; EXOSOMES; HIV-1; HIV-1 PATHOGENESIS; IMMUNE RESPONSES; INFLAMMATION; LYMPHOCYTES T CD4; NANOPARTICLE PURIFICATION; NEUTROPHILS; TH17
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of the research is to characterize the role of exosomes in acute HIV-1 infection. Exosomes are nanovesicles released from many cell types and bear certain similarities to HIV-1 particles. Serving generally as garbage cans, they carry proteins or microRNA, which means they could also regulate complex functions including immune response by acting as intercellular communicators. Since they are released from HIV-1-stimulated dendritic cells (DCs) or CD4 T lymphocytes (CD4TL), we think they are active participants in the early events of HIV-1 pathogenesis. Initial interaction between HIV-1 and DCs occurs through virus-associated lectin attachment factors, for which we have identified the dendritic cell immunoreceptor (DCIR). This allows the virus to escape from the immune response and be transported to the lymphoid organs, where it gains entry into CD4TL by cell-to-cell transmission from DCs. Subsequent replication leads to severe and irreversible depletion of CD4TL (TH17), which appears to be a major factor in the ineffectiveness of the immune response to HIV-1. The chronic inflammation due to increased microbial translocation and possibly associated with defective neutrophil function, another early sign of AIDS progression, also appears to result from TH17 depletion. The so-called early events involve complex interactions between HIV-1, DC, CD4TL and neutrophils, and exosomes might serve as intercellular communicators between them and hence as biomarkers of different disease stages. We therefore propose to investigate the following hypotheses: 1) that exosomes are involved in communication between TH17 and neutrophils; (2) that binding of HIV-1 to DCIR leads to the release of exosomes from DCs and CD4TL and (3) that proteins and microRNA contained in these exosomes are useful biomarkers for the development of AIDS.

TitreApplicationTitle: The HIV Tat Protein Removes the Interleukin-7 Receptor from the Surface of CD8 T-Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CD8 T-CELLS; HIV/AIDS; INTERLEUKIN-7; RECEPTOR ENDOCYTOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: HIV infection leads to profound immune dysfunction. A number of immune cells are affected by HIV including both CD4 and CD8 T-cells. CD8 T-cells are essential to fighting viral infections and by limiting their activity HIV predisposes individuals to a number of opportunistic infections. Inactivating CD8 T-cells is also a likely means by which HIV itself evades the immune system.  How HIV inactivates CD8 T-cells is not yet understood. IL-7 is a small protein carried in the blood that the immune system uses to activate CD8 T-cells. We have shown that the majority of CD8 T-cells in HIV+ patients do not express the receptor for IL-7 and thus cannot receive the activation signal. We have also shown that a protein produced by HIV known as Tat specifically down regulates the IL-7 receptor on healthy CD8 T-cells in culture.   This research project seeks to determine exactly how the HIV Tat protein removes this essential IL-7 receptor from the surface of CD8 T-cells. Determining how this occurs is important to our understanding of how HIV causes immune dysfunction. This work is also expected to lead to new therapeutic strategies designed to increase immune function and potentially establish immunologic control of HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ras-responsive elements in HIV-1 replication and AIDS pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; GENE SILENCING; HIV-1; SIGNALING; T CELL; TFII-I; TRANSCRIPTION; USF; YY1
Abstract-Résumé: During the course of infection with HIV a population of T helper cells, critical for immune response, are produced which have the viral genome inserted into the cell chromosome, but where the virus is completely shut off. These are known as latently infected cells, sometimes referred to as latency, and this latent virus cannot be eliminated from the body because the immune system doesn't know that it is there. These latently infected cells contribute to disease because replication of the virus becomes turned back on when these cells try and help mount a response to an infection. The continual development of latency and reactivation of the virus ultimately reduces this critical T helper cell population to a level where individuals can no longer fight off common infections. We have identified a factor, called RBF-2 that is critical for controlling the ability of the virus to shut itself off to produce latency, but is also required for turning the virus back on in T helper cells that try to help fight infection. Our results indicate that it does this by organizing the virus DNA, inserted into the chromosome, into specific conformations that allow it to shut itself off and then turn back on again. Our goals are to identify interactions with other proteins that confer these properties, and to evaluate whether drugs that inhibit RBF-2 function might be useful for treating HIV infections. We suggest that RBF-2 inhibitors will be useful in the early stages of infection to prevent the appearance of these latently infected T helper cell populations, or in combination with other drugs to force latent virus out of hiding so that they can be eliminated.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Small Group Intervention to Reduce HIV Sexual Transmission Risk Behaviour Among HIV Positive Men Who Have Sex With Men: Gay Positive Sex (GPS)
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL INTERVENTIONS; HIV PREVENTION; HIV-POSITIVE POPULATIONS; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: The objectives of this project are to compare a peer-delivered HIV prevention intervention for HIV-positive gay men against being on a 6-month waitlist with appropriate referrals that already exist in the community.  Specifically, the intervention should result in a decreased likelihood of having risky sex versus being on a waitlist.  This project builds on findings from a previously CIHR funded project that focused on developing, implementing, and evaluating the current intervention which is called Gay Positive Sex (GPS). GPS consists of a series of 7 counselling sessions during which Motivational Interviewing counselling techniques are used in order to facilitate changes in participants' behaviours (e.g., reduction of risk behaviours, increase in healthy behaviours). GPS comes at a time when HIV rates have begun to rise among men who have sex with men, and when rates of unprotected sex have been rising among men who have sex with men.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring and Modeling Disability, Comorbidities and Rehabilitation among People Living with HIV in Canada: The HIV Health and Rehabilitation Survey
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; DISABILITY; HIV/AIDS; REHABILITATION; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING; SURVEY INSTRUMENT; SURVEY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, HIV is often considered a chronic disease. As people are living longer they may experience a variety of health-related challenges associated with HIV, comorbidities and side effects of treatment. These challenges may be termed disability including symptoms and impairments, difficulties with day-to-day activities, challenges to social inclusion, and uncertainty about health status, that can fluctuate on a daily basis or over the entire life course with HIV. Rehabilitation services, ranging from physical therapy and occupational therapy, to social supports from community-based organizations such as income and food programs and housing support may help to reduce disability for people living with HIV (PHAs). While researchers have explored disability prevalence and rehabilitation service provision in the HIV context, these studies were either conducted at the provincial level, did not incorporate the PHA perspective, or occurred prior to the increasing onset of HIV-related comorbidities.  The purpose of this study is to establish a profile of disability experienced by PHAs in Canada and determine how personal and environmental factors such as comorbidities and related rehabilitation services influence the disability experience. We will conduct the HIV Health and Rehabilitation Survey, a self-administered Internet-based questionnaire with PHAs across Canada. We will use a combination of statistical techniques to document the profile of disability and determine how personal factors (e.g. comorbidities, age, gender) and environmental factors (e.g. rehabilitation, social support, stigma) might exacerbate or alleviate disability experienced by PHAs. This research is critical to building our understanding of the types of disability that PHAs in Canada face, how contextual factors influence the disability experience, and the types of services, strategies and interventions PHAs use to address their health challenges living with HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Emphysema and inflamm-aging in HIV-seropositive patients
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; EMPHYSEMA; HIV; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive lung disease affects ~10% of adult Canadians and is the 4th leading cause of death, and the 3rd leading cost of health care expenses. In susceptible individuals, premature aging of the lung can be triggered by exposure of noxious materials, such as cigarette smoking, environmental pollution, and infection. Surprisingly, this condition will continue to progress even after the noxious exposure has ceased years ago. The widespread use of highly effective treatment for HIV infection has improved the survival of these patients from 10-2 to 1-3 per 100 person years.  These individuals are dying frequently of coronary artery disease, malignancies, and emphysema, but two decades earlier than in the general population.  A disease such as emphysema that takes decades to evolve gives physicians time to intervene, but it also makes it difficult to decide what we do has made a difference until years/decades later. For a variety of reasons, HIV infection has put emphysema on a fast track, allowing the disease and its complications to develop in years instead of decades. There are several benefits of the proposed study to Canadians. By finding out the reason why emphysema is so common and why it occurs at a younger in HIV patients will enable the health care professionals and officials come up with a better strategy to manage the problem with public health measures, pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatment. Because of the aggressive nature of the condition, we will be able find out if the treatment would work over a shorter time course (months or years instead of decades). We will also gain important insight into the aging process, such as how a viral infection and emphysema may contribute to premature aging, and vice versa. Finally, this study may identify individuals who are at risk of developing emphysema with simple blood tests and lung function, so that a concerted effort can be directed to those who will be most likely in need of help.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring interactions between HIV and the RNA interference pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: AGO2; DICER; HIV; LYMPHOCYTES; P-BODIES; RNA INTERFERENCE; TRBP
Abstract-Résumé: The Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is the causative agent of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS). When HIV enters a cell, the cell tries to defend itself using an array of different mechanisms. One mechanism that has been studied for several decades is the interferon pathway. This pathway is important in the cell defence against many different viruses, but ultimately fails against HIV infection. Another mechanism is called RNA interference. RNA interference uses a protein complex to target chemical messengers in the cell called RNA. HIV uses RNA instead of DNA to encode its genome, and is thought to be targeted by RNA interference during infection. The success of HIV infection indicates that the virus has managed to manipulate the RNA interference pathway. We will study the interactions between HIV and the proteins involved in RNA interference to determine how it influences the cell response and the outcome of disease. Our goal is to identify targets to enhance cellular responses to the virus.

Abstract-Résumé: Studies have demonstrated that despite the fact that healthcare is fully subsidized and access to anti-HIV medications are  free to patients - gross inequities in access and retention persist to these drugs.  Certain groups, such as Aboriginal and IDU, have shown to have limited access to anti-HIV drugs. Among individuals receiving these drugs, specific groups have increased likelihood of treatment interruptions, including younger individuals, those from poor socio-economic strata, Aboriginals, women, IDU, hepatitis C co-infected. The aim of this study is therefore to understand how socio-demographic, economic, behavioural and structural factors differentially impact uptake of and retention on anti-HIV drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strategies and Actions for Independent Living (SAIL) Evaluation Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTROLLED; ECONOMIC EVALUATION; EFFECTIVENESS; FALL PREVENTION; HOME CARE SERVICES; INTERVENTION STUDY; NON-RANDOMIZED; QUALITATIVE COMPONENT
Abstract-Résumé: Home care clients are at particularly high risk for falls and related injuries by virtue of their degree of frailty, lack of independent mobility and presence of multiple chronic conditions. The objective of this study is to determine the impact, cost effectiveness and sustainability of the Strategies and Actions for Independent Living (SAIL) program, and the sub component of the SAIL program - the Home Activity Program (HAP), as strategies for reducing falls and their consequences among home care clients. The SAIL interventions include staff training, fall and injury surveillance, individualized client prevention plans and a Home Activity Program.  The study design is a three-arm, non-randomized intervention conducted over 12 months, with over 1,200 clients. One arm will receive the full SAIL program, another arm will receive the SAIL Home Activity Program (HAP) alone, and a third arm will serve as the control with routine home support service delivery. The impact of the full SAIL program and the HAP component alone will be determined through the use of a fall surveillance system linked to the Inter-RAI Home Case (RAI-HC) Assessment toot and through analysis of data from validated mobility assessment tools commonly used among older adults (the Time-up-and-Go, Life-space assessment, Sit-to-Stand and the Tandem Stance). An economic evaluation will determine the incremental improvement of the HAP program alone compared to the full SAIL program, and both compared to routine home support delivery. Economic measures include a quality of life measures (EQ-5D), relevant RAI-HC data on health service utilization and key informant interviews. The sustainability of implementing the SAIL will be determined through a qualitative analysis of semi-structured key informant interviews with Home Care management, staff, clients and family members.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transitions and Trajectories in Late Life Care: Patterns and Predictors
Keywords-MotsClés: CARE TRANSITIONS; COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH; LATER LIFE; LIFE COURSE PERSPECTIVE; LONG-TERM CARE; LONGITUDINAL ANALYSES; MIXED MODELS; RAI-MDS DATA; TRAJECTORIES
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed study examines the main transitions that older adults experience as clients of home care, assisted living and long-term residential care.  In collaboration with health care decision-makers from the Fraser Health Authority and the province of British Columbia, two research questions will be addressed: (1) What are the most common pathways by which older adults transition through the long-term care system (e.g., home care, assisted living, residential care)?; and (2) How do individual factors (social, psychosocial, health) influence these transitions?  A better understanding of the patterns that emerge and the factors that influence care transitions is critical for enhancing the quality of life of older adults and their families and for developing policy and program recommendations for health system improvements.

TitreApplicationTitle: Respiratory function at birth
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR FUNCTION; HEMODYNAMICS; LUNG INJURY; NEONATAL RESUSCITATION; NEONATAL TRANSITION; POSITIVE PRESSURE VENTILATION; RESPIRATORY FUNCTION TESTS
Abstract-Résumé: Establishing breathing immediately after birth is vital for the survival and long-term health of newborn babies. Most premature babies have difficulty in breathing at birth and need help (resuscitation). The treatment for this is to gently inflate their lungs with a resuscitation device and a facemask. The device commonly used is the T-piece Resuscitator which is used all round the world. During resuscitation the clinician predicts the volume she/he wants to apply for any inflation (tidal volume). She/he also has to recognize leaks around the facemask and adjust the mask position if a leak appears. A Respiratory Function Monitor can measure both the tidal volume and the amount of exhaled carbon dioxide (CO2). CO2 is produced in the body tissues, transported in blood to the lung and eliminated from the lung during exhalation. Thus, CO2 can be detected in exhaled gas. During breathing assistance a Respiratory Function Monitor can identify if there is a leak around the facemask, the volume delivered with each inflation and the amount of CO2 exhaled. A Respiratory Function Monitor is routinely used in the hospital intensive care nursery to guide ventilation. We believe that in the Delivery Room measuring the tidal volume and the exhaled CO2 in infants needing breathing assistance immediately after birth will provide clinicians with important information about the infant's breathing and how much the clinician needs to help the breathing of these infants. Aims: 1) describe how much CO2 babies exhale immediately after birth; 2) identify correlations between exhaled CO2 and tidal volume during breathing assistance; and 3) identify associations between exhaled CO2, tidal volume and cardiac output immediately after birth. Expected outcomes: Information about correlations between exhaled CO2, tidal volume and cardiac output, which may offer a potential non-invasive delivery room measurement of lung-heart function to improve breathing assistance in the immediate newborn period.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating Self-Management and Educational Support in Extremely Obese Patients Awaiting Multidisciplinary Bariatric Care (EVOLUTION)
Keywords-MotsClés: COST-EFFECTIVENESS; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; LIFESTYLE MODIFICATION; OBESITY; PATIENT SELF MANAGEMENT; QUALITY OF LIFE; SELF-EFFICACY; WAIT LIST; WEIGHT MANAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Extreme obesity is present in 9% of the Canadian population.  Extremely obese people have a high chance of developing health problems and dying early.  Our national guidelines recommend that extremely obese individuals receive multidisciplinary treatment, meaning that a number of specialized care providers should be available to help administer obesity treatments to these patients.  However, this type of treatment is scarce in Canada and wait times average 5 years.  We oversee a large regional obesity program called the Edmonton Weight Wise Obesity Program.   Our team is composed of clinicians and decision makers that have worked together to grow and improve Weight Wise over the last 8 years.  In fact, we are now in charge of expanding Weight Wise to the the rest of Alberta.  Weight Wise now has a wait list of 2 years and 2000 people are waiting for treatment.  We performed a survey of the patients on the wait list and discovered that they self-report extremely poor health and feel that the long wait times are partly responsible for this poor health.  To try to support these patients as they wait for multidisciplinary care, we designed a group based self-management intervention, consisting of Weight Wise Community Modules.  Patients attend this program over six months to receive weight management education (diet, exercise, stress management, coping strategies).  We propose to determine if these modules actually help to reduce weight and improve quality of life in the wait listed patients.  We also wish to examine whether or not these modules are cost effective.  The community modules are useful, we will expand their use to the rest of Alberta and we suspect that other provinces will wish to implement a similar program.  If these modules are not useful, we will need to find a more effective way to support wait listed patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Impact of Assistive Technology on Users and their Informal Caregivers: A Mixed-Methods Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY; COMMUNITY CARE; IN-DEPTH INTERVIEWS; INFORMAL CAREGIVERS; MIXED METHODS; OLDER ADULTS; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Many people with mobility limitations use assistive technology, such as wheelchairs and bathroom grab bars, to help them perform daily activities. However, little attention has been paid to the impact of these devices on their caregivers. This neglect produces an incomplete portrayal of the outcomes of assistive technology provision, which has significant implications for policy and practice. In order to address this deficiency an assistive technology intervention has been developed that is inclusive of assistance users and their caregivers.   This intervention involves a detailed in-home assessment of the person's current assistive technology, the negotiation of a personal assistive technology plan with the person and his/her caregiver, and the timely provision of devices and training.   To test the effectiveness of this intervention we will perform an experiment. We will enrol 120 individuals with mobility limitations and 120 of their caregivers in the study. Participants will be assigned to either the experimental or the standard care group. Outcomes for individuals with mobility limitations and their caregivers will be measured before and after intervention using a variety of standardized instruments.   We expect this experimental intervention will 1) increase the daily activity and social participation of assistance users; 2) reduce the amount of caregiver assistance required; and 3) decrease the physical and psychological demands on caregivers.   The evidence produced by this study will enable service providers to offer assistive technology interventions that are more attuned to the needs of both individuals with mobility limitations and their caregivers and enable providers to lobby for better funding for equipment and follow-up intervention services.

TitreApplicationTitle: A mixed method evaluation of the impact of the Dr. Peter Centre on health care access and outcomes for persons living with HIV/AIDS who use illicit drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: HARM REDUCTION; HIV/AIDS; INTEGRATED HEALTHCARE; SAFE INJECTION SITE; SUPERVISED INJECTION SERVICES; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Persons living with HIV/AIDS (PHA) who use illicit drugs often experience poorer health outcomes than those who do not. The Dr. Peter Centre (DPC) is a community-based HIV/AIDS health care centre located in Vancouver, British Columbia (BC) that is run by the Dr. Peter AIDS Foundation. As a strategy to address this problem, the DPC offers a combination of services to vulnerable PHA, many of whom use drugs. These services include harm reduction services (including supervised injection services), social programs, counselling services, meals, housing referrals, and referrals to mental health resources. The reasoning behind this approach is that ameliorating barriers such as drug use, poverty, homelessness, food insecurity, unemployment and mental health issues will help PHA access appropriate health care. Both the Office of the Provincial Health Officer of BC and the Provincial Health Officers Council have endorsed client-focused health care as a health care delivery model that should be expanded in BC, and health authorities in other provinces are also interested in learning more about this. To help guide the future development of client-focused health care, we propose to evaluate the effectiveness of exposure to the DPC on treatment outcomes for HIV infection and well-being of DPC clients. The project team is a collaborative partnership between the DPC, the BC Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS and decision-makers from BC and Saskatchewan. Affected community members will participate in the research process and on the Community Advisory Group, which will provide input throughout the study period. The results of the study will be used to develop recommendations for action by policy makers and health service providers, as well as educate and sensitize them about the concerns of PHA who use drugs, thus helping them to better support patients who have traditionally been disengaged with the health and medical system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sexual Health Services and Sexual Health Promotion Among Undergraduate Students in the Maritimes
Keywords-MotsClés: ATLANTIC CANADA; HEALTH CARE DELIVERY; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; ONLINE SURVEY; PROCESS EVALUATION; SEXUAL HEALTH; STUDENT WELLNESS; UNIVERSITY STUDENT HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Sexually transmitted infections, unwanted pregnancies and other negative sexual health outcomes are well known threats to undergraduate university students' health and wellbeing.  In addition, concerns about such issues as sexual assault and sexual identity, are common on university campuses. University students must be well served by student health services in order to reduce negative sexual health outcomes. In some cases student sexual health services are not delivered effectively to students nor do they meet the unique needs of students in Atlantic Canada.    Objectives: This project, which involves researchers and university health program planners, in Maritime Canada, will implement a three year, action oriented, health policy research program as follows. Year one: Collect, analyze and summarize data on student sexual health care needs, priorities and health care delivery and promotion gathered through an online, anonymous and tested sexual health services questionnaire at eight  universities in Maritime Canada.  Year two: Through an integrative, knowledge translation process with knowledge users, students and sexual health researchers, identify and implement priority health care initiatives at all participating universities. Year three: Assessment of the knowledge translation and utilization process and health care changes.    Impacts: We anticipate that our partners in this Maritime university project will be able to address their students' sexual health concerns and needs with meaningful data from the survey and collectively work toward developing  solutions that will improve the reach, applicability and acceptability of sexual health care services and health promotion programs to undergraduate students. This project will help us improve sexual health services among undergraduate students and ultimately reduce associated the health and social burden associated with negative sexual health outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study the interactions between Hepatitis C virus proteins and nucleoporins
Keywords-MotsClés: BIMOLECULAR FLUORESCENCE COMPLEMENTATION; CELL BIOLOGY; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; MICROSCOPY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PEPTIDE; PROTEIN EXPRESSION AND PURIFICATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; SITE DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Although there has been considerable work in the hepatitis C virus (HCV) field, there are still many unanswered questions regarding the HCV life cycle. HCV infects over 300,000 Canadians and 170 million individuals worldwide and it is the major cause of liver disease including liver cancer. About 5,000 to 10,000 Canadians are newly infected each year and approximately 1,000 deaths due to HCV occur annually in Canada. Until recently the only licensed treatment was a combination of pegylated interferon alpha (IFN-alpha) and ribavirin which was successful in only 45 to 50% of the patients infected by genotype 1, the genotype which is most commonly found in infected patients. A new oral anti-viral drug targeted to the HCV protease has increased the success rate for treatment to 75%, but this therapy is associated with significant side effects and is very expensive. There is a need for additional new anti-viral drugs. The high rate of mutations in the virus during its life cycle leads to rapid growth of resistance to most new drugs targeting viral proteins. Therefore, the study of interactions between viral proteins and host proteins, which are required for the viral life cycle, may result in a better understanding of the infection cycle. This research may also discover new targets for improved anti-HCV drugs that may be less affected by virus mutations. In this work we are going to study the novel interactions of HCV proteins that are responsible for the recruitment of the host nucleoporins proteins to the replication sites in the infected cell. In this research, we will try to develop peptides to specifically interrupt interactions of particular viral and host proteins (nucleoporins) which may be used as a lead compound for novel anti-HCV drug development. This work will give us a better understanding of HCV life cycle and will provide us with more possibilities for improved drugs to defeat the virus.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effectiveness of a brief intervention on improving health outcomes for homeless people with unmet health needs.
Keywords-MotsClés: BRIEF INTENSIVE CASE MANAGEMENT; COORDINATED ACCESS; HOMELESSNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Homelessness rates in Canada have increased dramatically over the last 20 years. Homeless people have high rates of mental and physical illness, substance use and a higher mortality rate than those who have housing. In the absence of appropriate community-based services, homeless people rely on hospital emergency department visits or inpatient hospitalizations for health care, associated with longer hospital stays and higher costs. To address health disparities and improve health system effectiveness, the Toronto Central Local Health Integration Network funded a brief intervention, Coordinated Access to Care for the Homeless (CATCH), for homeless people with unmet health needs.  The proposed prospective mixed methods study aims to evaluate the impact of this intervention on health outcomes and health service use among CATCH participants. The study also aims to examine the continuity of care experienced though this intervention, from both participant and health system perspectives, to better understand the critical ingredients of this intervention, targeting frequent users of hospital services.    For the purpose of the study, 225 homeless people will be recruited over an 18 month period among consecutive referrals to the CATCH program and followed for 6 months. Furthermore, we propose to complete individual interviews and focus groups with 54-60 stakeholders, including program participants.  The study will add to the knowledge base in important ways, as service coordination, and its association with health outcomes, has seldom been examined in the context of homelessness.  Given competing demands for limited healthcare resources, it is of great interest to policy makers, service providers, homeless individuals and their families, to determine which service delivery models are effective and for whom. The present study will reduce knowledge gaps in an important area and provide essential information to help guide program planning and resource allocation in Ontario.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modeling the Influence of Chronic Illness and Family Environment on Self-concept and Mental Health Outcomes in Adolescents
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT; CHRONIC ILLNESS; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; FAMILY ENVIRONMENT; GROWTH CURVE MODELING; MENTAL HEALTH; PARENTAL DEPRESSION; POPULATION HEALTH; SECONDARY ANALYSIS; SELF-CONCEPT
Abstract-Résumé: About 50% of adults with mental disorders experienced their onset during adolescence. Among those at elevated risk for mental disorder are adolescents with chronic illnesses (AWCI), representing about 1 in 5 adolescents in Canada. In this vulnerable group, self-concept, our internal depiction of social acceptance, capabilities, worth, and physical appearance, may be an important mechanism linking the experience of a chronic illness with elevated risk for mental disorder. In healthy people, poor self-concept in adolescence is linked to depression, substance abuse, criminal behaviour, and lower education, while positive self-concept protects against declines in health. However, no studies have used national databases to study self-concept in AWCI and there is a lack of research demonstrating the influence of self-concept on future mental disorders in AWCI. My research program is designed to show that self-concept can be altered to reduce the risk of psychiatric disorder among AWCI. To achieve this, I will conduct a number of studies using the Canadian National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth (1996-2009). The research questions include: 1) Are questionnaires developed to measure self-concept in healthy adolescents appropriate for AWCI? 2) Do AWCI have poorer self-concept compared to healthy adolescents? 3) What individual and family factors predict self-concept in adolescents with and without chronic illness and do predictors differ across gender? 4) How does the family environment impact self-concept and does self-concept predict mental health problems in adolescents with and without chronic illness? Given the number of AWCI in Canada, the burden on individuals, families, and society, and the lack of existing research, it is important to establish the leverage that self-concept might provide in protecting against mental disorders. I envision the results being used to develop interventions to improve self-concept and prevent onset of mental disorders in AWCI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nutaqqavut (Our Children) Health Information System: A partnership approach to informing the prevention of infant mortality and childhood respiratory illness in Nunavut.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; CPT1A GENETIC VARIANT; INFANT MORTALITY; MATERNAL CHILD HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Nunavut leads the country for adverse early child health outcomes, in particular, rates of infant hospitalisations (>300/1000) for respiratory infections and infant mortality rates three times greater than the rest of the country. In our 1999-2008 review of IM cases the leading causes were sudden unexpected death and respiratory infection. We also showed in preliminary studies that Nunavut infants with a gene variant important in the way fat is used for energy (CPT1A P479L) had a fivefold greater risk of sudden death or death due to infection. Paradoxically, we also showed this gene variant is common in Nunavut infants (>60%) suggesting protection historically, perhaps with a diet high in fat but low in sugars. In the context of other contributors to infant mortality, we will explore the effect of the CPT1A variant and whether there are broader effects on early Inuit health. In addition to respiratory infection being a leading cause of IM, many more infants are hospitalized for this reason. As with IM, assessing the broad underlying determinants is crucial to provide insights into prevention strategies. We aim to develop a profile of infants most likely to present with lung infection and determine which infants are at greatest risk for severe decompensation. Based on evidence we will optimize the vaccination protocols locally for a sometimes detrimental virus, RSV, and assess effectiveness of the program. Our partnership with Health and Social Services, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc, Qaujigiartiit Health Research Centre, in conjunction with the newly implemented Nutaqqavut "Our Children" Health Information System (NHIS), provides unique tools and local input to address these priorities. The over-arching goal is to obtain evidence to determine which modifiable risk factors affect infant health in the most detrimental way. Policy decisions on RSV vaccine, newborn screening and public health prevention strategies are urgently needed and will be informed with these results.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving health system efficiency in latent tuberculosis treatment through text messaging.
Keywords-MotsClés: LATENT TB INFECTION; MHEALTH; TB SERVICE DELIVERY; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Treatment for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) is important for the control of disease progression and prevention of disease transmission. However, a large proportion of people who are prescribed pills for LTBI do not finish treatment. Advances in cellular phone communications and the increase in the use of text messaging present new opportunities for health systems to conveniently reach increasing numbers of people and strengthen client-centered care. We have developed a support program for patients with LTBI to encourage them to take the required amount of medications. This program, called WelTel-LTBI, consists of a weekly text message asking "How are you?" Participants will be asked to reply indicating that they do not have any problems (e.g."OK."), or alternatively, that they have an issue to discuss (e.g. "Not well."). Participants who have indicated there is a problem will be referred to the Tuberculosis (TB) Clinic nurses for follow-up and will be triaged as needed. In a previous clinical trial, we demonstrated that weekly text messages sent to HIV positive patients on antiretroviral treatment helped increase medication adherence and decreased their viral load counts. The objective of this study is to determine what impact this program has on the health of LTBI patients and on the Canadian health care system, including the cost-effectiveness of WelTel-LTBI compared with standard care for LTBI. This study will focus on the initial roll-out of WelTel-LTBI, which will include two provincial TB Control Clinics. The results of this study will be used to expand this program throughout British Columbia. This research is an important step forwards in advancing the science of using wireless communications technology in health care to improve health outcomes in LTBI patients both in Canada and abroad.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intervention models for preschoolers with autistic spectrum disorder (ASD): A population-based comparative effectiveness study
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; COST EFFECTIVENESS; EARLY INTERVENTION; HEALTH POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: More and more Canadian children are being diagnosed with autistic spectrum disorders (ASD). These disorders lead to significant differences in children's ability to interact, communicate, and play like other children, and can have a devastating impact on families. Canadian provinces have invested substantial financial resources in early intensive behavioural intervention (EIBI) programs for children with ASD. However, there are gaps in our knowledge of the impact of these programs. Currently, we do not know whether some EIBI programs are more effective than others. Moreover, we do not know the costs of different programs in relation to how much they improve outcomes for children and their families. Our team of researchers and decision makers will compare the effectiveness of two provincial EIBI programs, one available in New Brunswick and the other in Nova Scotia. The programs differ in several ways, including the intervention methods, how many hours of intervention are provided, and how long intervention is available to families. The progress of the children will be assessed when they begin intervention, after 12 months of treatment, and finally, before they start school. We will obtain information about interventions and their costs from families, service providers and administrators. This study may show us that some aspects of each of the programs are important for helping children to make the most progress before they enter school. Although the costs of these different components may differ, we will examine whether some benefits might justify greater investments. This information is greatly needed to guide policy and more effective delivery of services to the large and diverse population of children with ASD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Parent training for challenging behaviour in children with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD): Strongest Families for FASD
Keywords-MotsClés: DISTANCE TREATMENT; FETAL ALCOHOL SYNDROME DISORDERS; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; PARENT TRAINING; PARENTAL STRESS; STRONGEST FAMILIES
Abstract-Résumé: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is  a significant cause of neurobehavioural deficits in children. Parents/guardians, who care for children with FASD, are often confronted with significant behavioural issues without support or detailed advice on how to manage these symptoms. To compound the problem, these issues interfere with typical social, cognitive and personal development.   Strongest Families, a distance parent-training intervention program, has recently been effective in supporting children with profound behavioural problems. The aim of this project is to engage parents/guardians, decision makers and experts in FASD, as well as the parent training specialists, to develop and evaluate a new version of the Strongest Families program using a rigorous Randomized Controlled Trial.
