TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a Canadian framework for evaluation and decision-making for expensive drugs for rare diseases through innovation, value, and priority setting.
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH POLICY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; ORPHAN DRUGS; POLICY MAKING; PRIORITY SETTING; PUBLIC FORUMS; RARE DISEASES; SOCIETAL VALUE; WILLINGNESS TO PAY
Abstract-Résumé: As our understanding of diseases and how to treat them evolves, so too must our decision making procedures for providing fair and cost effective treatments for those living with an illness. Today, one area of policy and decision making in particular lags behind, that for treating rare diseases. There are approximately 7,000 known rare diseases worldwide, with 250 new ones discovered annually. An estimated 1 in 12 Canadians and 55 million people in Europe and the US have a rare disease. Available treatments for these rare diseases can cost more than $500,000 a year per patient, and treatment can be lifelong. Given the high cost of treatments, and the number of patients being diagnosed with a rare disease, the financial burden of treating these patients is rapidly increasing. However, there is a strong moral justification not to deny treatment because of cost, and government payers therefore face difficult choices about whether or not to provide coverage. Approving funding for a drug may mean that some other treatments or socially desirable programs (e.g. education) may not be funded. And while approval for funding may be encourage innovation and development of more new treatments; it may also be setting a benchmark against which other companies, who seek primarily to increase profits rather than help people, price their products. At present there is no policy framework to help decision makers navigate the complex factors involved when making decisions about paying for orphan drugs. This project brings together a multidisciplinary team of experts in matters relating to treatment for rare diseases, and will incorporate input from the public and key stakeholders to develop such a framework. It will facilitate priority setting for orphan treatment decisions constrained by a limited budget, that considers the relevant developmental, clinical and economic factors and ethical principles, as well as being consistent with the values of society at large.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing Effective Policies for Managing Technologies for Rare Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: COVERAGE DECISION MAKING; HEALTH POLICY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; RARE DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: The number of promising technologies for rare diseases has grown recently, bringing new hope to patients.  Simultaneously, they have challenged public policy makers who have to decide which technologies to fund.  As the number of patients is small, most of these technologies are too expensive for any individual patient to afford and evidence on how well they work is often limited.  Thus, the 'risk' of making a wrong funding decision is often higher than for technologies that treat common conditions.  The consequences of a wrong decision can be significant - poorer patient outcomes and waste of scarce resources.  Therefore, policies enabling access to technologies that optimize both the health of patients and the use of healthcare resources are needed.  We describe plans for an Emerging Team on Effective Policies for Managing Rare Diseases.  It will bring together members from all stakeholder communities (including patients & families, physicians, policy makers, industry, and the public) in order to generate the knowledge base needed to develop innovative policies.  Its activities encompass 5 inter-related themes:  coverage decision-making; values & preferences; clinical effectiveness measures; social, legal & ethical issues; innovation policy. These themes represent areas that must be incorporated in such options.  Guided by an integrated inter-disciplinary group of researchers, policy-makers, physicians, patients, and industry representatives called the Knowledge Integration Hub, activities will build upon lessons learned from national and international experiences with technologies for rare diseases and those for common conditions.  They will examine the methods  proposed for addressing issues related to each theme.  The anticipated outputs are policy options that span research & development, regulatory approval, and coverage decision-making for new health technologies for rare diseases, and approaches to implementing them that reflect emerging best practice.

Abstract-Résumé: Our team proposes a program of research to position Canada as a world leader in evidence-informed health care for children with rare diseases, beginning with inborn errors of metabolism (IEM). We have a strong team with expertise in many areas of academic research and in providing clinical care for children with IEM. We are supported by a multidisciplinary advisory board that includes patient and family representatives. Our proposed research program builds on existing partnerships and on a new research framework. This framework highlights the importance of measuring outcomes from a range of perspectives and emphasizes key challenges in developing effective health care for children with rare diseases. To support our research, we will develop a unique information system for Canadian children with IEM. With families' permission, this information system will enable us to study children's health outcomes and their use of health services, including associations with the treatments they receive. Importantly, we will also incorporate patients' and parents' self-reported well-being and their experiences with health care. We will use our findings to make recommendations for improving care for children with IEM and other rare diseases. We will also train new researchers and providers and develop a sustainable research network in this field.

Abstract-Résumé: Hereditary spastic paraplegias (HSPs) are rare neurological disorders with onset anywhere from early childhood to later adulthood, which are caused by the transmission of specific mutated genes. HSPs represent the second most important group of the motor neuron diseases. There are no treatments to prevent, stop, or reverse HSP. Identifying novel HSP genes and characterizing these, as well as the previously identified HSP genes, is needed to provide insights into pathogenesis, a bit like adding pieces to a puzzle allows us to progressively get a clearer understanding of the overall picture. We will create an HSP clinical registry/genomic DNA bank and standardize diagnostic procedures. We will validate a molecular diagnostic test and work to identify novel HSPs causative genes. The impact of mutations in these novel genes will be measured in simple model organism (worm, flies and zebrafish) and cellular models. HSPs represent the second most important group of the motor neuron diseases. There are no treatments to prevent, stop, or reverse HSP. Identifying novel HSP genes and characterizing these, as well as the previously identified HSP genes, is needed to provide insights into pathogenesis, a bit like adding pieces to a puzzle allows us to progressively get a clearer understanding of the overall picture. Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BEHAVIORAL ANALYSES; BIOLUMINESCENCE IMAGING; CYSTAMINE; NEUROPROTECTION; NEURORESTORATION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; POST-MORTEM ANALYSES
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease is mainly characterized by the loss of cells in specific regions of the brain. It is estimated that at the time where the diagnosis is made, approximately 80 percent of the cells that produce dopamine, have already ceased to operate. This leads mainly to movement disorder, but also cognitive symptoms that characterize the disease. Several treatments are available today to control these symptoms. Unfortunately, no drug can halt nor slow down the progression of the disease. Dr. Cicchetti's group has recently demonstrated that cystamine, a chemical compound, is able to prevent the loss of neurons when administered before the onset of the pathological characteristics of the disease. Using mouse models of parkinsonism, we now propose to test, in addition to its neuroprotective capacity, 1) whether cystamine is able to stop, or even reverse neuronal death in Parkinson's disease and 2) identify and understand some of the mechanisms of action for the beneficial effects of cystamine. The results of these studies will be critical to determine the clinical applicability of cystamine for patients suffering from Parkinson's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting Mitochondrial and Oxidative Vulnerabilities as a Novel Strategy for Cancer Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CANCER; CELL CULTURE; COMBINATION THERAPY; FLOW CYTOMETRY; MICROSCOPY; MITOCHONDRIA; MOUSE MODELS; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PROTEIN CHEMISTRY
Abstract-Résumé: Many current cancer drugs are non-specific and produce many harsh side effects. The natural compound pancratistatin (PST) has been shown to have selective anti-cancer activity with minimal effect on noncancerous cells. However, its availability for clinical work is limited due to its low yield in nature. I have found novel synthetic analogues that selectively kill cancer cells with better efficiency than natural PST. My preliminary work has shown these drugs to be very effective in killing blood, brain, colon, prostate, ovarian, and bone cancer at very low doses. Notably, these drugs are more effective against pancreatic cancer than gemcitabine, the only moderately effective drug available for this notoriously drug-resistant cancer. Furthermore, this derivative was able to reduce tumour growth in animal studies. Interestingly, combining these analogues with the natural compound piperlongumine (PL), another anti-cancer agent, produced an enhanced effect against an array of cancers. No adverse effects were exhibited by various noncancerous cells with these PST analogues alone and in combination with PL. Side effects produced by non-specific targeting and drug-resistance remain as large obstacles with present cancer drugs. I present an approach targeting multiple vulnerabilities of cancer cells with 2 low toxic cancer drugs, which may decrease the likelihood of drug resistance; thus, lower doses of each drug are needed for the same desired effect, minimizing minor side effects, if any, these drugs may have at higher doses. Discovering targets of these PST analogues may give rise to a novel outlook in the field of cancer research and provide a scaffold for design of new therapeutic approaches. Given the unprecedented selective anti-cancer activity that I have uncovered, I propose a promising strategy that may serve as a safer and more effective alternative to the cancer therapies currently available.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Genetics in Chronic Pain
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PAIN; GENOMIC ANALYSIS; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; NICOTINIC ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain ranks as one of the most debilitating and common health conditions, more prevalent than cancer, heart disease and diabetes combined. Associated with increased mortality rates (including suicide) and decreased lifespans, chronic pain exacts an enormous economic toll on society. Chronic pain displays immense individual variability, whereby some people recover fully from injuries and infections, while others suffer persistent pain for years. Since much of this variability is known to be genetic, the identification of those genes affecting chronic pain severity is imperative to promote early intervention and drug development. To identify genes related to chronic pain, we used an advanced genetic technique called expression genomics in mice with experimental nerve injury and isolated the Chrna6 gene. Specifically, we found that in strains of mice that experience greater symptoms of nerve (neuropathic) pain, the Chrna6 gene is less active,  producing less of its protein product, the alpha6 subunit of the so-called nicotinic receptor. This finding suggests that drugs acting on this receptor might be effective analgesics against chronic pain. To further evaluate this hypothesis, we intend to test transgenic mutant mice with non-functional or abnormally high-functioning Chrna6 genes. We predict that the loss-of-function mice will exhibit higher levels of pain and the gain-of-function mice will experience lower levels. By subjecting these mice to a variety of chronic and acute pain conditions, followed by a series of electrophysiological, behavioural and pharmacological experiments, we intend to elucidate the Chrna6 mechanism of action. By specifically targeting those genes responsible for pain variability, we hope to gain a better understanding of gene involvement in pain perception, ultimately leading to novel therapeutic approaches and individualized treatments that target the symptoms of chronic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: eIF4E phosphorylation and the tumour microenvironment: implications in signalling, invasion and metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; EIF4E PHOSPHORYLATION; METASTASIS; MIGRATION; TRANSLATION INITIATION; TUMOUR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is the leading cause of mortality in Canada, and metastases are responsible for most of these cancer-related deaths. Unfortunately, we still don't fully understand the processes by which cancer cells eventually metastasize. Worse, we still have few tools which would allow us to prevent metastases and stop the cancer in its tracks.   However, we do know that cancer cells need to rapidly produce proteins that will favour their rapid growth and allow them to move through the body and cause metastases. We also know that a master regulator of protein synthesis, called eIF4E, favours the production of these proteins and the progression of cancer. We have also recently demonstrated that for eIF4E to promote the growth of tumours, it must be slightly modified by a process called phosphorylation. However, it remains to be determined whether this modification is important for the cancer cells to metastasize.   This project aims to determine whether eIF4E phosphorylation allows tumour cells to metastasize. Initial experiments are very promising and indicate that modifying eIF4E is actually critical for cancer cells to metastasize. Importantly, we aim to determine whether we can use a drug to block this event and therefore prevent cancers from metastasizing, hopefully leading to life-saving treatments for Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional connectivity of resting state activity as a neuroimaging biomarker for Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BIOMARKERS; BRAIN NETWORKS; FMRI; FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEUROIMAGING; RESTING STATE
Abstract-Résumé: With an aging population, Canada faces a pervasive increase in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although known to cause intellectual decline and dysfunction, AD is poorly understood. Biomarkers currently used to diagnose AD capture limited aspects of the disease at particular timepoints, usually well after brain tissue has significantly deteriorated. Prior to the detection of AD, healthy brain regions appear to initially compensate for dysfunction and gradual deterioration in diseased regions. By using brain imaging technology to identify these initial adaptations, we may develop a valuable biomarker for AD.  Neuroimaging methods non-invasively measure brain activity. From these measures we can quantify relationships between different brain areas. Regions that interact in synchrony are defined as networks. In past AD research, this method relied on identifying a priori regions for analysis. Using a novel data-driven approach, I will investigate as yet unexplored brain regions to determine the connection between changes in brain networks and different stages of AD development. Comparing healthy controls with AD patients, I will also measure the functional, structural and vascular changes associated with these variations.  From this method I anticipate developing a successful classification system for different phases of AD pathogenesis. Since this analysis is data driven and not directed by a priori assumptions, I also anticipate that related neurophysiological changes will be discovered in unexpected brain regions.   My goal is to identify an effective brain imaging biomarker for Alzheimer's disease. The benefit is early diagnosis of AD and the identification of associated neurophysiological changes. This will facilitate the development and effectiveness of treatment interventions. This method may also lay the groundwork for future research on other poorly understood illnesses. Most importantly, however, my research addresses a critical health issue facing Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using real-time electronic health information from a multi-national pharmacosurveillance system to assess the safety and effectiveness of oral hypoglycemic drugs among patients with type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: MEDICAL INFORMATICS; META-ANALYSIS METHODS; NON-PARAMETRIC MODELS; PHARMACOSURVEILLANCE; RISK PREDICTION MODELS; SURVIVAL ANALYSIS; TIME-DEPENDENT COVARIATES
Abstract-Résumé: Many new drugs are appearing on the market to treat common chronic diseases such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes.  In the pre-market stage, new drugs are often tested on small, unrepresentative samples of patients.  As a result, the effects of these drugs on people of different ethnicities and gender, as well as people with different clinical conditions are often unknown.  Post-market surveillance of new drugs is therefore important in order to monitor their safety and effectiveness after they enter the market.  Voluntary reporting is one of the most common methods of post-market surveillance, but this method is insufficient as it only captures 2%-10% of adverse drug events (ADE).  This indicates the need for improved methods of post-market surveillance.  In recent years, there has been a call to explore ways in which electronic health records (EHR) could be used for post-market surveillance of new drugs.  EHRs are valuable resources because they contain rich, clinical information on prescribed therapies, medical diagnoses, and lifestyle factors that is updated in real-time.  EHRs could therefore be used to create a real-time surveillance system that identifies large cohorts of people taking different drugs and monitors them for important clinical outcomes.  This would allow researchers to assess the safety and effectiveness of new drugs in a timely fashion and compare available drug therapies on the market.  In this study, I will be using EHRs from a real-time multi-national pharmacosurveillance system to assess the safety and effectiveness of different types of oral hypoglycemic drugs in patients with type 2 diabetes.  This surveillance system will monitor millions of people in Canada, the USA, and England, and allow for a robust analysis of the benefits and risks of different drug types.  The results from this study will hopefully help physicians and patients improve the selection and use of oral hypoglycemic drugs and reduce the occurrence of ADEs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Balance and mobility re-education using virtual reality in children with development delay.
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL PALSY; DYNAMIC BALANCE; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY; TREATMENT; VIRTUAL REALITY
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this study is to determine the effectiveness of a balance and mobility retraining program using virtual reality in children with developmental delay such as cerebral palsy (CP) and developmental coordination disorder (DCD).  Ten children between 12 and 18 yrs will take part in a 4 week intensive training program using virtual reality game applications. Children will return several times to measure their clinical abilities and brain function before and after the intervention (repeated measure multiple baseline single subject research design). We will measure changes in their level of mobility impairment as well as changes in brain function using specialized brain imaging techniques that allow us to identify how the brain is reorganized after training. Results of the study will provide evidence for the level of effectiveness of virtual reality treatment applications in children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards Equity in Population Health: Comparing Evolving Policy in World Health Care Systems
Keywords-MotsClés: DEMOGRAPHIC TRANSITIONS; HEALTH INEQUALITY; HEALTH POLICY; INTERNATIONAL COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS; LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS; MULTI-LEVEL MODELLING; POPULATION HEALTH; PUBLIC/PRIVATE HEALTH CARE; QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Health expenditures as a proportion of GDP in developed countries have skyrocketed in the past 50 years.  The rise in spending has correlated with better population health, by most measures, but the health gains are almost exclusively in the highest socioeconomic classes, exacerbating already wide health inequalities.  In 2008, a report by the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health stated that such inequalities are "killing people on a grand scale". The report recommended the development of universal public health coverage/care as a main avenue of improving health equality.  Some countries have implemented full universal healthcare policies, and unexpectedly, they still see the health inequality gap increasing.  Moreover, other countries that have a mix of public and private systems, if regulated properly, can end up responding better to the needs of the lowest classes.  Faced with the costs implied by the coming demographic transformation to an ageing population, governments of the world must prepare themselves with the evidence-based policy instruments that will allow them to achieve the dual goals of health policy: both improving overall public health, while closing the health inequality gap.  This research begins with the questions: Why has universal health care alone failed to equalize public health outcomes and access among all socioeconomic classes?  How can governments faced with the expensive prospect of an ageing population control costs, increase public health, and decrease health inequalities?  What is the optimum public/private health care policy mix that achieves these goals?  To answer these questions, I employ the Health Insurance Access Database at McGill University's International Research Infrastructure on Social Inequalities in Health.  A longitudinal analysis of evolving health policy is compared with micro-level public health data in 18 OECD countries from 1990-2010.

TitreApplicationTitle: Model-based prediction of mastication and swallowing outcomes for head and neck surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVANCED FINITE ELEMENT METHODS; ADVANCED IMAGE PROCESSING; BIOCHEMICAL MODELING; BIOMEDICAL APPLICATIONS; COMPUTATIONAL FLUID DYNAMICS; DEFORMABLE TISSUE MODELING; DYSPHAGIA; ORAL HEALTH; PATIENT SPECIFIC MODELING; SWALLOWING MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Three-dimensional computer modeling of anatomical structures is an indispensable tool for surgical planning. An outstanding example is reconstruction of the jaws that is a complex geometric surgery. The microvascular fibular free flap is the workhorse for jaw reconstruction and is internationally pervasive for management of head/neck cancer, trauma and certain congenital defects. Geometric modeling methods have greatly improved the geometric (anatomical) predictability of these complex microvascular reconstructive procedures. They have also enabled the introduction of surgical innovations that reduce treatment time remarkably, from 2-4 years down to 12 weeks. The endpoint of these procedures is to improve functional outcomes of care. However, geometric modeling is static, and cannot predict functional outcomes such as how effectively a patient will chew or swallow. These outcomes enormously impact patient's quality of life, with swallowing deficits producing significant risk of morbidity and mortality due to aspiration. Thus, we propose creating dynamic, 3D, patient-specific computer models of oral and upper airway anatomy to predict functional mastication and swallowing outcomes for head and neck surgery. Our predictions will optimize functional outcomes through simulation and design of surgery, surgical guides, prostheses and implant installation. Our project will also provide the science and tools to enable dynamic biomechanical modeling used for other surgical procedures besides jaw reconstruction. We have assembled a world-class interdisciplinary team of investigators, collaborators and knowledge transfer users, with proven technical expertise, track record and ability to work together for this project.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of nutritional labelling on menus: a quasi-experimental study.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALORIE LABELLING; LABELLING POLICY; MENU LABELLING; NUTRITION LABELLING; NUTRITIONAL INFORMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is a growing public health problem. Recent estimates indicate that one-quarter (25%) of adult Canadians are obese and an additional 37% are overweight, while more than one quarter of Canadian children and youth are either obese or overweight. Food consumed at restaurants and fast-food outlets accounts for a growing proportion of dietary intake among Canadians, and is believed to be an important contributing factor in the obesity problem. Currently, Canadians receive little or no information regarding nutritional content of restaurant food. The Ottawa Hospital has recently implemented a novel nutrition labelling program, which includes calorie and nutrient amounts, as well as a healthy eating symbol directly on menu boards. The Hospital has implemented this program at one site and will be implementing the program at a second site in 2012. The current study will examine the impact of these nutritional labelling interventions using a quasi-experimental design, collecting data at both sites before and after implementation.  Exit surveys will be conducted with 500 cafeteria patrons at each site at baseline and at follow-up, for a total of 2,000 participants. Sales data, provided by The Ottawa Hospital, will also be collected over a 6-month baseline and follow-up period at both sites. The study will examine the effect of nutritional information on awareness of calorie and nutrient content, consumption of calorie and nutrients and the extent to which the influence of nutritional labelling varies by socio-economic status and among sub-groups in the population. This study is among the first to examine nutritional labelling of menus in Canada and has the potential to inform provincial and federal level policies on nutritional labelling. Overall, the study will help to evaluate the impact of point-of-sale nutrition labelling using a rigorous research design in a naturalistic setting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Études des réseaux neuronaux responsables de la respiration chez la lamproie
Keywords-MotsClés: CENTRE DE GENESE RESPIRATOIRE; LAMPROIE; LOCOMOTION; MODULATION; NEUROANATOMIE; RESPIRATION; RYTHME RESPIRATOIRE; SYNCHRONISATION; TRONC CEREBRAL; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGIE
Abstract-Résumé: La respiration est une activite motrice rythmique essentielle maintenue tout au long de la vie. L'activite respiratoire augmente egalement en fonction du mouvement afin de s'adapter a la demande energetique. Des reseaux de neurones appeles « generateurs de rythme » sont responsables de produire les contractions musculaires rythmiques necessaires a la respiration. Ces reseaux de neurones sont localises dans le tronc cerebral et presentent une organisation similaire chez tous les Vertebres. Meme si la respiration est une activite rythmique soutenue, la frequence et l'intensite des mouvements respiratoires sont modulees entre autres selon les besoins energetiques. Des mecanismes neuronaux centraux jouent un role important dans cette modulation. Les etudes anterieures au laboratoire de Rejean Dubuc ont demontre que l'activation des centres locomoteurs du tronc cerebral serait responsable d'augmenter le rythme respiratoire avant et durant l'activite locomotrice. Cependant, le substrat neuronal qui sous-tend la modulation de la respiration en lien avec le mouvement demeure peu connu. Nous tirerons profit d'une preparation de Vertebre basal, la lamproie, afin etudier le role des proprietes de reseau et les proprietes intrinseques des neurones dans la genese du rythme respiratoire, en plus d'etudier les mecanismes cellulaires impliques dans la modulation de l'activite respiratoire en lien avec le mouvement. Dans leur ensemble, les resultats de ces etudes contribueront a une meilleure comprehension des mecanismes synaptiques et intrinseques des neurones responsables de la genese du rythme respiratoire et de sa modulation. Ces connaissances sont essentielles a la comprehension des maladies pouvant impliquer les centres respiratoires, telles que le syndrome de la mort subite du nourrisson et l'apnee du sommeil centrale.

TitreApplicationTitle: Women in Pain: Exploring the Neuropathic Components of Vulvodynia to Improve Diagnosis and Treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC GENITAL PAIN (VULVODYNIA); HEALTH-RELATED QUALITY OF LIFE; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; PAIN ASSESSMENT; PAIN CLASSIFICATION; POSTHERPETIC NEURALGIA; PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL TESTING; PSYCHOSOCIAL CORRELATES; VULVODYNIA SUBTYPES
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain is an unpleasant experience that is difficult to treat. Accurate classification of pain conditions drives treatment, as similar conditions respond similarly to treatment. The first step of pain classification is assessment, which begins with an extensive pain history. Pain can have elements of nociception and neuropathy, each requiring considerably different treatment approaches. If neuropathic pain is suspected, confirmatory tests are conducted. Standardized techniques and measures should be used to investigate the nature of pain conditions and justify use of certain treatments.  Despite the availability of quality assessment tools, many conditions have not been fully explored. One such condition is vulvodynia (i.e., female genital pain). Although research suggests that it is best classified as a chronic pain condition, no systematic study has determined what type of pain it is. The next step is to determine if this condition is neuropathic (resulting from dysfunction of the nervous system) or nociceptive (resulting from factors outside the nervous system). To address this, I am conducting multiple studies examining various subtypes of vulvodynia, and comparing results to women suffering from an established neuropathic pain condition, postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). First, I am conducting an online survey using a series of validated questionnaires to assess neuropathic and nociceptive pain characteristics and functional disturbances. Next, women with PVD and PHN will take part in an in-person sensory testing study including a gynecological assessment by a genital pain specialist. Finally, this information will be combined and presented to a neuropathic pain specialist for formal diagnosis. The results of this study will change how vulvodynia is understood, researched, and treated. It may also lead to the development of a diagnostic tool for physicians that will improve diagnosis and treatment outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Removing obstacles to treating Parkinson's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; DOPAMINE; NEURAL DRUG MICROINJECTION; NON-HUMAN PRIMATE; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; SACCADIC EYE MOVEMENT; SINGLE-UNIT NEURONAL RECORDING (IN VIVO); SUBSTANTIA NIGRA; SUBTHALAMIC NUCLEUS
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a fatal and incurable degenerative disorder of the central nervous system that affects more than 6.3 million people worldwide.  PD is initially associated with movement-related symptoms such as rigidity, slowness of movement, and difficulty with walking and gait.  As the disease progresses, cognitive and behavioral deficits can also occur.  Despite increased interest, PD treatment options remain limited, and are associated with severe side effects and decreased efficacy over time.  Three obstacles hinder development of more effective treatment options: 1) our lack of knowledge of the cortical circuits in a healthy brain which can be involved in PD; 2) incomplete understanding of the pathological changes in neural circuitry during PD; and 3) limited understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying current PD treatments (symptom-based treatment).  This study aims to address these obstacles using the saccadic eye movement system in monkeys as a behavioral readout.  A saccade is the fast movement of an eye, head, or other animal body part.  The saccadic eye movement system is an excellent model for examining changes in the brain, because it is easy to measure, and there is considerable knowledge of the underlying neural circuitry which participates in controlling gaze.  Deficits in saccadic eye movements in PD in many ways mirror observed PD motor deficits, and are also improved by current PD treatment options.  Since recording eye movements is fast and inexpensive, the saccadic eye movement system is also practical to use in a clinical setting. By training monkeys to perform saccadic eye movements, this study aims to address current obstacles to new PD treatment options by 1) continuing to record interactions between specific areas of the healthy brain which can be involved in PD; 2) recording changes in key brain regions in a PD monkey model; and 3) determining neural activity underlying some current PD treatment options.

TitreApplicationTitle: SUrgical and Pharmacological novel intERventions to Improve Overall Results of Saphenous Vein Graft patency in coronary artery bypass grafting surgery. The "SUPERIOR SVG" Study: An International Multi-centred Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CORONARY ARTERY BYPASS GRAFTING; DOUBLE BLINDED; FISH OIL; GRAFT PATENCY; INTERNATIONAL MULTI-CENTERED; NO-TOUCH VEIN HARVESTING; PLACEBO; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; SAPHENOUS VEIN GRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Ischemic heart disease (IHD) due to coronary artery blockages is the leading cause of death in the world. Coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG) improves survival and symptoms in patients with extensive coronary obstructions; in 2008, almost 15,000 Canadians underwent CABG. The saphenous vein (SVG) harvested from the leg is the most frequently used graft to bypass blockages on the heart. Unfortunately, 15-25% of all bypassed SVGs become diseased and fail within first year after surgery, increasing the risk of another heart attack or death. Injury to a layer of the SVG called the endothelium during surgery is a sentinel event for future vein graft disease after surgery. This trial investigates whether a novel surgical technique of vein harvesting, called the 'No-Touch' technique, which minimizes endothelium injury along with a daily fish oil supplement, can improve 1 year failure rates of the SVG, compared to conventional harvesting techniques and no fish oil supplement (placebo). Method: This trial involves multiple surgical centers. Eligible CABG patients will undergo conventional(C) or no-touch technique(NT) and receive placebo(P) or a 2-gram fish-oil supplement per day(FO) for 1-year following surgery. The trial's design randomly puts each patient into one of four categories: NT+FO(Group A); NT+P(Group B); C+FO(Group C); C+P(Group D). At end of 1-year, each patient will undergo a CAT scan and clinical follow-up to determine graft failure rates and incidence of any major adverse cardiac events (MACE). Hypothesis: We believe that vein graft failure and MACE rates will be lowest in Group A, intermediate in Groups B, C, and highest in D.  Clinical Impact: If our hypotheses are true, then patients undergoing CABG may have a better quality of life, require less cardiac procedures, and live longer. This has the potential to change current surgical practice, post-operative care, and improve lives of many patients undergoing CABG in Canada and world-wide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the pro-cardiac activity conferred by Gata5 and Smarcd3b in the zebrafish embryo: an approach to identify novel regulators of cardiac progenitor development.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC PROGENITORS; CARDIAC REGENERATION AND REPAIR; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; GENETICS; HEART DEVELOPMENT; HEART DISEASE; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is the second leading cause of death in Canada, killing over 50,000 people every year. Given the prevalence and severity of this condition, it is crucial that we understand the molecular mechanisms that underlie the proper formation of the heart. This understanding will allow us to predict, prevent and alleviate this disease.  Our current understanding of heart development remains incomplete, with a significant gap in knowledge with regards to the early steps of this process. We know very little about how cells are first instructed that they will become heart cells, how these cells get to the right spot in the embryo for proper development and how they are maintained during this process.  We have identified two molecules which in the early embryo are able to turn cells which would not normally form part of the heart into a cardiac progenitor: the building block of the organ. This is a type of cell which can then be instructed to form all of the major cell types in the heart. By studying how these two molecules are able to perform this function, we will be able to identify how the early steps in the development of the heart are regulated. These steps are crucial to understand because 1) defects in cardiac progenitor development can result in heart defects at birth which affect 1% of all newborns 2) it may allow us to form heart cells from other types of cells in order to repair the heart following disease and 3) we may be able to mobilize the heart to regenerate itself following injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the role of the mammalian target of rapamycin in the renal glomerular filtration barrier and tubular epithelium.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; MAMMALIAN TARGET OF RAPAMYCIN; PROTEINURIA; RENAL INJURY; TRANSGENIC MICE; TRANSPLANT
Abstract-Résumé: The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a protein that is found in every mammalian cell and is central to the control of many cellular functions including metabolism, growth, and division and is essential to life. Given its multitude of functions, mTOR is tightly regulated and loss of this regulation leads to disease. Drugs that block the function of mTOR are important in the management of patients with solid organ transplants, cancer, diabetes, polycystic kidney disease and atherosclerosis among many other conditions. However, the therapeutic usefulness of these drugs is hampered by their toxicity to the kidney. In light of the rapidly expanding indications for mTOR inhibitors, it is important that we better understand the mechanism underlying this toxicity. We have developed a novel genetic mouse model that will allow us to remove mTOR completely from select cell populations in the kidney. Our aim is to use this mouse model to study the mechanism underlying the kidney injury associated with mTOR inhibition and investigate possible therapies.  In addition, this work will contribute significantly to the existing knowledge of the complex molecular pathways involved in mTOR regulation. Finally, the success of our study and novelty of our mouse model will foster collaboration with other research groups to establish a link between mTOR and disease mechanisms in other organ systems. This will allow clinicians to better harness the potential of mTOR inhibitors for the management of patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term effects of increased wheat fiber intakes on oral glucose tolerance in hyperinsulinemic adults
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREAL FIBER; CLINICAL TRIAL; COLONIC FERMENTATION; GLUCAGON-LIKE PEPTIDE-1; HUMAN STUDIES; INSULIN RESISTANCE; ORAL GLUCOSE TOLERANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Insulin resistance (IR), a decreased responsiveness of tissues to insulin, is the earliest defect associated with development of type 2 diabetes (T2D). In patients with normal blood glucose, IR results in a compensatory increase in plasma insulin (hyperinsulinemia) which could in turn exacerbate IR.  Currently, 11.2 million Canadians are affected with hyperinsulinemia and over 8 million have pre-diabetes or diabetes. Evidence from prospective studies suggests that cereal fiber intake reduces the T2D risk; although short-term clinical trials have failed to show a significant association. This discrepancy suggests that beneficial effects of cereal fiber intake might take a long time to develop. It is also likely that adaptation in colonic fermentation of cereal fiber and increased secretion of fermentation products, such as short chain fatty acids (SCFAs), influence the results. SCFAs could improve glucose response by stimulating intestinal glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) secretion which can improve insulin sensitivity. However, the effect of long-term increased cereal fiber intakes on glucose tolerance is not yet clear. This research is aimed to investigate whether 1-year increased wheat fiber intake improves oral glucose tolerance in hyperinsulinemic adults; and if so whether adaptation in colonic SCFA production and a resulting increase in GLP-1 secretion, or insulin sensitivity are responsible for this effect. Hyperinsulinemic patients (n=70) will be randomly assigned to receive either a high-wheat (24g/d) or a low-wheat (0.5g/d) fiber cereal for 1-year. Every 3 months, a standard oral glucose tolerance test will be performed, SCFAs, GLP-1 and insulin sensitivity will be determined and data from high and low-fiber groups will be compared. We aim to identify the mechanisms for the epidemiological association between diabetes risk and cereal fiber intake and provide a safe non-pharmaceutical treatment for management of IR among patients at risk of developing T2D.

TitreApplicationTitle: Socioeconomic status, child developmental health and within-family relationships: Examining the differential effects of families, persons and dyads using the Social Relations Model
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; DEVELOPMENTAL HEALTH; FAMILY; MULTILEVEL MODELING; RISK; SOCIAL RELATIONS MODEL; SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Socioeconomic status is associated with better relationships amongst family members. Moreover, family relationship quality is an important determinant of child health. However, this pattern is complicated by the fact that two people influence the content and quality of interactions. It has been difficult to isolate what certain individuals "contribute" to a relationship, versus what is common to the family, and what is specific to a particular partnership. Similar difficulties arise when trying to determine which aspects of family life contribute to developmental health. These limitations can be addressed by taking a unique approach to family research and observing individuals interact in multiple one-on-one contexts (e.g. mother-oldest child, mother-father, mother-youngest child, father-oldest child, and so on). The proposed study of 501 families will adopt this research paradigm and, subsequently,  determine (a) what aspects of family life are impacted by socioeconomic status and (b) what aspects of family life are driving child health outcomes. These findings will have implications for social policy and program design.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying driver mutations in childhood medulloblastoma by novel functional genomic approaches
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOUR; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; HUMAN CANCER GENETICS; MEDULLOBLASTOMA; MOUSE MODELS; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; PEDIATRICS
Abstract-Résumé: The most common cause of non-accidental death in children is from cancer, and the most common cause of cancer death is from medulloblastoma, a type of paediatric brain cancer. Current treatment involves surgery in conjunction with radiation and chemotherapy resulting in a 70% 5-year survival rate, however this aggressive treatment often leaves survivors with a severely decreased quality of life. We know that medulloblastoma is caused by mutations in genes. Some of these mutations are important at the start of a cancer's life cycle, but are no longer necessary as a cancer grows and spreads. Other mutations occur by chance alone, and are not required to either the early cancer, or the late cancer. Most crucially, some mutations are important for the ongoing survival of the cancer, providing a critical opportunity for drug development. This proposal outlines a novel technique using functional genomics to find the mutations that are still required by both the primary cancer, and the cancer cells that have spread, while ignoring non-contributing mutations. We propose that by targeting these particular genes with novel therapeutics, we will be able to not only cure the cancer, but also reduce toxic side effects to improve the quality of life for survivors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the genomic complexities of choroid plexus tumor development to improve diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of young brain tumor patients
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; BRAIN TUMORS; CANCER PREDISPOSITION; INTEGRATIVE GENOMIC ANALYSES; MEDICAL GENOMICS; MICROARRAY ANALYSES; MOLECULAR DIAGNOSTICS; PEDIATRIC ONCOLOGY; PERSONALIZED THERAPIES; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Choroid plexus carcinomas (CPC) are malignant pediatric brain tumors arising most frequently in infants under 1 year of age. Long-term survival of CPC patients remains close to 30% due to incomplete tumor resection, and high metastatic potential through the spinal canal. On the other hand, most survivors display neurocognitive and/or sensory deficits. Molecular diagnostic and prognostic markers are necessary to classify tumor subtypes accurately and modulate therapeutic dosage according to predictions of drug response. Alternative therapeutic methods are necessary to reduce cerebral hemorrhage risk associated with surgical resection and improve clinical outcome. The comprehensive genome-wide analysis we propose aims at identifying markers for tumor diagnosis and patient prognosis, as well as genes implicated in the development and progression of CPC. Candidate markers will be validated in an independent cohort of human brain tumors, and candidate gene targets will be validated against a mouse model of CPC for the creation of novel targeted treatments. This personalized approach will improve patient survival and reduce long-term side effects commonly associated with current treatment protocols.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cohibin-driven turnover of non-coding RNA regulates rDNA repeats and cellular lifespan
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; GENOME STABILITY; NON-CODING RNA; NUCLEAR ENVELOPE; REPLICATIVE LIFESPAN; RIBOSOMAL DNA REPEATS; SIRTUIN GENES
Abstract-Résumé: There are many parallels between factors that affect yeast cellular lifespan and those that affect aging and age-related diseases in humans.  One example is a family of enzymes called sirtuins, which are involved in the formation of silent DNA structures.  In budding yeast, a sirtuin protein called Sir2 is required for the silencing of transcription at intergenic regions located between ribosomal DNA genes (rDNA).  This function of Sir2 represses hyper-recombination within this highly repetitive chromosomal domain.  As cells age, Sir2 levels decrease leading to loss of silencing at these intergenic regions and aberrant recombination events.  This chromosomal instability shortens the lifespan of cells.  A recent discovery revealed that rDNA is anchored to the nuclear envelope by relying on nuclear membrane proteins.  Disruption of these anchors releases rDNA from the envelope and changes the number of rDNA genes present on the chromosome and we have demonstrated that this disruption also shortens lifespan.  These nuclear membrane proteins have been shown to associate with enzymes thought to have some role in non-coding RNA (ncRNA) processing and the accumulation of ncRNA transcripts has previously been linked with decreased rDNA stability.  What we intend to investigate is whether the nuclear membrane proteins are in fact recruiting RNA regulatory proteins to help limit the accumulation of ncRNA molecules and preventing them from disrupting rDNA homeostasis or shortening lifespan.  The proteins anchoring rDNA to the nuclear envelope in yeast are conserved in humans.  In fact, mutations in these proteins lead to premature aging and developmental diseases such as Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy.  By studying the impact of these anchoring proteins as well as their associated RNA regulatory proteins on yeast lifespan, we expect to uncover key features of the mechanisms behind normal aging, premature aging, and age-related diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Governance and accountability of health care professions in Ontario:  A policy analysis of recent amendments to the Regulated Health Professions Act
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCOUNTABILITY; CASE STUDY; GOVERNANCE; HEALTH POLICY; LEGISLATION; NURSING; POLICY ANALYSIS; REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: The governance and accountability of health profession regulators are undergoing significant transition. In 1991, Ontario passed the Regulated Health Professions Act, establishing an entirely new regulatory framework for 23 regulated health professions.  This framework underwent amendments in 2009 through the enactment of Bill 179.  The changes were dramatic, particularly for their effect on the relationship between the regulators and the state through increased oversight and accountability mechanisms.  The amendments have significantly increased the ability of the government to "regulate the regulators."  The health profession regulatory bodies vigourously opposed these new measures and their enactment shows a marked change in government policy. Because the primary purpose of regulation is to protect the public, regulatory policy changes such as this can have a direct impact on the safety and quality of health care for Canadians. This research will provide much needed analysis and insight into the key factors and forces behind these changes in the governance and accountability of the regulated health professions, which will assist regulators and policy makers in other jurisdictions as regulation evolves across the country.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chlamydia-induced Reactive Arthritis: Does Macrophage Polarization Play a Defining Role?
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CELL CULTURE; CHLAMYDIA; ELISA; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTION; IMMUNOLOGY; MACROPHAGE; QPCR; REACTIVE ARTHRITIS; RHEUMATOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Chlamydia is a bacterial pathogen which can cause debilitating arthritis, especially in sexually active young populations, for which there is no definitive or curative treatment. Reports from Health Canada show that every year around 50,000 Canadians are diagnosed with Chlamydia infection. Research suggests up to 5% of those infected by Chlamydia will develop arthritis. In most individuals Chlamydia is controlled at the point of entry, the genital tract, by our immune system. Chlamydia can escape the initial point of infection and travel around the body such as to the joints. In a few people the immune response is inefficient at controlling Chlamydia resulting in Chlamydia-associated arthritis. As yet it is not known how the joint immune cells fail to control Chlamydia resulting in chronic inflammation and arthritis. We have established a mouse model of Chlamydia-induced arthritis in which high levels of a factor secreted by immune cells, interferon gamma, protects against arthritis. In human Chlamydia-associated arthritis interferon gamma levels are also abnormal, making this a good animal model of disease. Macrophages are a type of immune cell that are plentiful in healthy and arthritic joints. These cells are activated by interferon gamma to an inflammatory state which effectively control bacteria. It is not yet known whether resistance to Chlamydia is mediated by interferon gamma-activated macrophages. In this project we will use mouse models of Chlamydia infection to investigate whether interferon gamma activated macrophages can control Chlamydia and whether alteration of interferon gamma levels prior to infection may provide resistance to arthritis. This area of research may provide a new approach for therapy based on reversing the aberrant immune response which underlies Chlamydia-associated arthritis. Knowledge gained will be directly transferable to general Chlamydia infections, thereby leading to an improvement in the health and well being of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Potential Legal and Policy Implications of Medical Tourism on International Migrants' Access to Health Care in Receiving Countries
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH LAW AND POLICY; MEDICAL TOURISM; MIGRANT HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Medical tourists -- namely, consumers travelling to another country for private health services while enjoying tourist activities during the pre- and post-treatment periods -- are increasingly courted by countries worldwide. In contrast, studies have shown that other international migrants tend to have poorer health outcomes because of limited health care entitlements in receiving countries. There is insufficient literature that examines medical tourism in relation to international migration more generally. Specifically, what is the potential impact of medical tourism on laws and policies concerning international migrants' access to health resources across borders? I will conduct a systematic review and analysis of laws, court decisions and policy documents from five countries -- Canada, U.S., U.K., India and Taiwan -- to compare and contrast how health care entitlements have differed between medical tourists and international migrants. This comparative approach will allow me to uncover the extent to which the disparity in health care entitlements between the two groups is a global trend. I will then identify the underlying reasons for such a disparity and review literature for evidence regarding whether these reasons may be adapted to similarly improve other international migrants' health care access. My study will help government officials in Canada and abroad to develop more coherent and equitable policies when considering extending health benefits to various types of international migrants. For judges who have to decide the rights of medical tourists and other international migrants, my study urges them to consider the broader impact of their rulings and to adhere their reasoning to the principle of equality under the internationally recognised right to health. As such, my study will have a positive impact on millions of international migrants, many of whom in Canada, whose access to health resources in receiving societies is often severely curtailed.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Promise of Law for Public Health
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH LAW; LAW; LEGAL THEORY; OBESITY; PRIVATE LAW THEORY; PUBLIC HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH LAW; PUBLIC HEALTH THEORY
Abstract-Résumé: Almost one in four Canadian adults are obese; another 35% are overweight. Overweight and obesity are concerning in terms of associated increased morbidity and mortality, decreased quality of life, and cost to society, with $4.3 billion spent on direct and indirect costs associated with obesity in 2001. This important public health problem is being examined by many disciplines, including law. Many public health law scholars, however, consider legal solutions to the obesity epidemic solely under the paradigm of government intervention through legislation or regulation, and ignore potentially important private law interventions (for example, those falling within the scope of contract law, property law, and tort law, which considers private wrongs and negligence).  This legal study will identify private law remedies that can be used as public health interventions (e.g., limiting use of restrictive covenants on commercial leases for grocery stores; personal injury lawsuits for obesity-related health problems; litigation around misrepresentations and fraudulent claims). The study will further identify opportunities for public health researchers to conduct natural experiments (e.g., examining outcomes of interest before and after a policy change, ideally using a suitable comparison group) which are an important method for understanding and improving public health, since randomized controlled trials of policy implementation or legislation are often impossible. Therefore, this project serves as a legal foundation for future, rigorous explorations into the effects of policy or legislative changes on population obesity. In addition to the practical applications, public health law scholarship will benefit from an articulated vision of the relationship between private law and public health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional connectivity of neuronal networks in childhood epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNECTIVITY; EPILEPSY; FUNCTIONAL IMAGING; SYNCHRONY
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood epilepsy is one of the most common neurological conditions, affecting approximately 1% of children.  Up to one-third of those affected have poor seizure control despite best medical management. Prolonged uncontrolled epilepsy is associated with poor cognitive outcomes as seizures are thought to adversely affect the developing brain.  For a subset of patients, surgical intervention may be beneficial.  The success of surgical treatment is however directly dependent on the accurate localization and resection of epileptogenic cortex.  The current research aims to study epileptogenic networks in children undergoing evaluation for surgical resection and their effect on functional brain processes.  Data from subdural electroencephalographic recordings and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) will be studied using functional connectivity tools and graph theoretical analysis.  The goals of this research are to: (1) develop safer and more effective surgical strategies based on an understanding of aberrant connectivity of epileptogenic cortex; (2) study the effects of seizures on resting-state brain networks, and correlate findings with neuropsychological assessments to establish a surrogate marker of functional impairment; and (3) assess network remodeling following resection of epileptogenic cortex through a longitudinal resting-state fMRI study of children following epilepsy surgery.  The findings of this study are expected to inform the medical community, identify biomarkers of disease-related impairment and lead to more innovative and effective treatments for this common and morbid childhood disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and application of analytical methods for network meta-analysis to assess the safety of drugs and improve the health of Canadians
Keywords-MotsClés: BAYESIAN METHODS; DRUG SAFETY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS; HEALTH RESEARCH METHODOLOGY; INDIRECT COMPARISONS; META-ANALYSIS; NETWORK META-ANALYSIS; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Novel methods are needed to assess the safety of drugs. Current approaches are limited because drug safety information is often considered in isolation and valuable information is not integrated together. The proposed area of research is related to the development and application of a methodology, known as network meta analysis, for assessing drug safety. The differences between current approaches for assessing drug safety and the proposed network meta analysis approach can be summarized using a sportsbook analogy. Current approaches are analogous to a sportsbook only considering past games between two teams of interest when establishing odds for a game. A network meta analysis approach is analogous to a sportsbook establishing odds based on all information from all previous games played by all teams. To explore the application of network meta analysis for assessing drug safety, we will consider two demonstration projects using real world safety data: (1.) risk of serious infection using biologics; (2) retrospective analysis which re-investigates past drug safety issues (e.g., adverse events with use of thiazolidinediones or selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors). By advancing the development, application, and methodologies of network meta-analysis, we should obtain a more accurate picture of a drug safety profile earlier in the product lifecycle and hence decrease the risks associated by drugs used by Canadians. Our research will also contribute to advancement of knowledge in this field. We will conduct theoretical research to adapt the methods and procedures that are currently applied for assessing efficacy to evaluate uncommon or rare safety events.

TitreApplicationTitle: Occupational Performance Coaching, a novel patient-centered intervention to improve participation in personally valued activities following stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY REINTEGRATION; OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY; PARTICIPATION; STROKE REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a disabling condition that can cause problems with movement, speech, thinking and emotions.  Approximately 300,000 Canadians live with the effects of stroke.   Stroke survivors define recovery as return to a life that includes personally valued activities carried out within their various roles (e.g., spouse, grandparent, worker, volunteer). The variety and degree of problems experienced by individuals following stroke make this recovery challenging. Effective treatments are needed to enhance the knowledge, skills and confidence stroke survivors need to return to their important and valued activities. In this research project, I will adapt Occupational Performance Coaching, an innovative intervention designed for families of children with challenges in their everyday activities, for use with stroke survivors.  Occupational Performance Coaching (OPC) shares similarities with proven approaches for self-management of chronic diseases including Chronic Disease Self-Management and health coaching. I will develop an OPC approach for stroke rehabilitation based on input from stroke survivors and health professionals who treat clients with stroke.  I will then try this approach with 12 stroke survivors.  I will compare the ability of this group to return to their personally valued activities 2 weeks, 3 months and 9 months after discharge with that of a similar group of 12 stroke survivors who do not receive OPC. As well, I will also do in-depth interviews with those who received the treatment to get their feedback on the helpful and less helpful aspects of OPC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Développement de lignes directrices pour la recherche évaluative en réadaptation à base communautaire
Keywords-MotsClés: LIGNES DIRECTRICES; METHODES MIXTES; READAPTATION COMMUNAUTAIRE; SANTE MONDIALE; EVALUATION DE PROGRAMMES
Abstract-Résumé: Il est grand temps que le domaine de la sante mondiale porte une plus grande attention aux personnes handicapees, puisqu'elles sont fortement desavantagees aux plans de la pauvrete, de la sante et de la participation dans la communaute. L'etude de doctorat porte sur la readaptation communautaire, une strategie de developpement qui s'assure que les personnes handicapees soient integrees dans leur communaute et puissent etre en bonne sante. Ce type de readaptation est implante dans plus de 90 pays, principalement dans les milieux fortement defavorises des pays en developpement, mais aussi dans certaines regions du Canada. Meme si cette approche est promue par l'Organisation mondiale de la sante, le nombre insuffisant d'etudes et d'evaluations de programmes rigoureuses limite grandement sa reconnaissance et son implantation a plus grande echelle. Le projet de doctorat consiste en la conception d'un guide pour faciliter l'evaluation des programmes de readaptation communautaire. Une recension des ecrits et une consultation d'experts par l'entremise d'un questionnaire en ligne sont prevues, afin de determiner les principales recommandations qui devraient etre mises de l'avant pour ces etudes. Puis, les recommandations identifiees seront validees quant a leur faisabilite et utilite par la conduite d'une evaluation  d'un programme de readaptation communautaire d'une communaute rurale d'Afrique du Sud. Cette organisation offre des services aux enfants vivant en situation de pauvrete et ayant des problematiques de malnutrition, VIH-SIDA, et alcoolisation ftale. Les retombees de ce projet incluent : 1) faciliter l'evaluation des programmes de readaptation communautaire et les ameliorer, et 2) documenter les conditions dans lesquelles ils contribuent le plus a la sante et la participation sociale des personnes handicapees. L'etudiante espere egalement sensibiliser les acteurs en sante mondiale quant a la necessite d'inclure les personnes handicapees dans leurs interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ambulatory care sensitive conditions identified in hospital data: Which admissions are deemed avoidable?
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; AMBULATORY CARE SENSITIVE CONDITIONS; DIABETES; HEALTH CARE SYSTEM INDICATOR; HEALTH INFORMATION; HYPERTENSION; MEDICAL CHART REVIEW; METHODOLOGY; SYSTEM PERFORMANCE; VALIDITY
Abstract-Résumé: Many chronic conditions, including diabetes and high blood pressure, can be effectively managed in the community (primary care) with appropriate medical screening, monitoring and follow-up. These chronic conditions are also referred to as ambulatory care sensitive conditions (ACSC).  Since 1993, ACSC hospitalizations have provided the basis for measuring the quality and performance of primary health care in many regions and countries.  In Canada, the Canadian Institute for Health Information uses national hospital admission data to report the number of ACSC hospitalizations. This information is important because it can be used as a tool to measure the performance of the health care system which in turn is used to inform health policy, manage the primary health care system, improve our understanding of the factors that influence health, and identify gaps in health care for the Canadian population.   While hospitalizations for ACSCs are not always preventable, it is important to determine the amount of admissions which are preventable. Thus, the purpose of this research is to develop new ways to identify and measure the number of hospital admissions in Canada that are truly avoidable by examining two highly common conditions,  high blood pressure and diabetes.  Determining the number of ACSC hospitalizations that are avoidable will inform health policy decision-makers on the appropriateness of using ACSC hospitalizations as a measure of the quality and performance of primary health care.  This important information may signal an opportunity to improve the planning or delivery of primary health care services to better meet the needs of the Canadian population.  It is essential that health care planners are provided this information so they can explore the reasons for poor primary care performance and develop interventions appropriately.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting health equity: A comparative study between Canada and Finland
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADA; COMPARATIVE RESEARCH; EXPERT INTERVIEWS; FINLAND; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH POLICY; POLICY ANALYSIS; POLICY DOCUMENTS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; WHO
Abstract-Résumé: My PhD research project will be a comparative analysis of Canadian and Finnish public policies that promote health equality and tackle health inequalities. I will focus on governmental strategies, policy formation processes, and barriers against policy implementation. The theoretical background for this study will be based on existing research literature on policy analysis, social determinants of health, and health inequalities. This study can help to identify best practices to improve individual and population health in Canada.   My study is divided into three stages. First, I will identify how health equity and various strategies to tackle health inequalities are represented in Canadian and Finnish policy papers. I will carry out systematic analysis of official and public documents produced by governments, ministries, and national research institutes in Canada and Finland over the past decades. Second, I will look at how the World Health Organization's recommendations on health equity have disseminated in national policies and research priorities in Canada and in Finland. Third, I will interview Canadian and Finnish government officials, researchers, and policy advocates (N=20, total 10 informants each nation) to find out what barriers they see in the implementation of policies that promote higher levels of health equity among population groups.   My research data will consist of both 1) policy documents, and 2) supporting interviews with Canadian and Finnish government officials, researchers, and policy advocates (N=20). The policy documents of this study will consist of papers produced by the Canadian and Finnish governments and research institutions. In my analysis, I will utilize frameworks and methods derived from the literature on policy processes and the qualitative content analysis of textual materials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clarifying how Alcohol Facilitates Recovery from Stress in Coping-Motivated Drinkers
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL CUE EXPOSURE; ALCOHOL MISUSE; COPING-MOTIVATED DRINKING; CRAVING; MODERATE TO HEAVY DRINKERS; NEGATIVE REINFORCEMENT; PHYSIOLOGICAL MEASUREMENTS; STRESS; TRIER SOCIAL STRESS TEST; UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Alcohol misuse is common among university students in Canada. Approximately one-third of students drink at harmful levels. This behaviour costs individuals and society, as heavy drinking leads to many negative health outcomes, such as death and/or injury from drunk driving accidents. Research has identified two primary motives for drinking. Students either drink to increase positive feelings or to decrease feelings of stress (so-called coping-motivated drinking). Evidence suggests that the relationship between stress and alcohol use is complex. It remains unclear as to how alcohol reduces stress in coping-motivated drinkers. Some studies have found that people who drink to cope show higher bodily and emotional responses to stressful events. This led researchers to believe that alcohol dampens these elevated stress responses, eventually leading to strong alcohol cravings in times of stress. However, this prediction has not been supported because of methodological limitations in existing studies. The proposed study will improve on these limitations and clarify how alcohol reduces stress in coping-motivated drinkers. In a realistic bar lab, participants will complete two public-speaking stress tasks. Immediately following each task, participants will either be exposed to an alcohol or neutral (water) cue. Coping-motivated drinkers are expected to show higher bodily and emotional responses to stress, along with stronger alcohol cravings, compared to controls. Also, coping-motivated drinkers are hypothesized to show the largest reductions in stress when alcohol is administered following the stress tasks. This research will help clarify the link between stress and alcohol use in university students. Further, this work has the potential to inform clinical treatment and prevention programs targeting alcohol misuse in young Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Disarming the enemy: reversing antibiotic resistance with inhibitors of Vat enzymes.
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; DRUG DESIGN; ENZYMATICS; MICROBIAL DRUG RESISTANCE; MICROBIAL PHYSIOLOGY; PROTEIN DYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: In 2011, it was estimated that at least 20 new antibiotic classes must reach the market within the next 50 years if modern healthcare is to keep pace with microbial drug resistance (1).  In particular, the alarming rise of multidrug resistant, Gram-positive pathogens has called into action streptogramin antibiotics.  Streptogramin antibiotics are composed of two chemically-distinct groups (A and B), both of which are produced simultaneously by soil bacteria.  Individually, both groups halt cell growth, but together, they actually kill pathogens.  Streptogramins bind a unique site within the protein synthesizing machinery of pathogens, thereby blocking protein synthesis.  Currently, streptogramins are used as drugs of last resort against serious infections.  However, widespread resistance against streptogramins threatens their clinical use, as well as the outcomes of patients infected with resistant Gram-positive pathogens.  Resistance against group A streptogramins is sufficient to impair streptogramin antibiotics entirely; of particular concern are Vat enzymes which inactivate group A streptogramins only.  Therefore, we wish to identify novel inhibitors of Vat enzymes in order to reverse and characterize this resistance.  A pilot screen has identified candidate potent inhibitors that will be tested for pharmaceutical relevance and cytotoxicity.  Further, the genetic and evolutionary controls of streptogramin production will be investigated.   Given the desperate need for novel antibiotics, this project will provide important insight into microbial drug resistance, and aid in translational research where drug design is tailored specifically towards certain pathogens and the patients they infect. (1) Coates et al. 2011. British J. Pharm. 163:184-194.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing hypothermic neuroprotection to recover fine synaptic structure and sensorimotor function in vivo following cerebral ischemia and reperfusion
Keywords-MotsClés: CHANNELRHODOPSIN-2; DENDRITIC SPINE; EXCITABILITY; HYPOTHERMIA; INTRINSIC OPTICAL SIGNAL IMAGING; STROKE; STRUCTURAL PLASTICITY; TWO PHOTON IMAGING; VOLTAGE SENSOR DYE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: The only widely validated treatment for both global and focal stroke that does not involve induction of reperfusion is hypothermia. However, there is a risk of central nervous system side effects (e.g., impaired plasticity). Moreover, the mechanism of neuroprotectant effects of hypothermia in stroke is unclear. Using two-photon microscopy (TPM), our group found that application of local cooling of the cortex using cold water perfusion does not prevent but delay the onset of ischemia-induced dendritic damage in living mice. In the following years, I will initially study whether hypothermia and re-warming processes cause side effects on dendritic circuitry, spine mobility using TPM, as well as unexpected effects on neuronal excitability and motor-sensory circuitry using optogenetic method in living mice. This might help to optimize application of hypothermic therapy in human. Furthermore, the functional outcome of treatment with hypothermia following stroke will be assessed by testing motor-sensory mapping and neuronal excitability using intrinsic optical signal (IOS) imaging as well as channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) optogenetic motor mapping. By completing this project, I would be able to optimize the application of local hypothermia on brain, as well as assess functional recovery treated with hypothermia following stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and Application of Nanofibers Releasing Anti-Fibrogenic Factors for Treatment of Dermal Fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-FIBROGENIC FACTORS; CELL-CELL INTRACTIONS AND CELL SIGNALING PATHWAYS; DRUG ENCAPSULATION; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX REMODELING; FIBROTIC RABBIT EAR MODEL; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; NOVEL WOUND CARE PRODUCTS; POST-BURN HYPERTROPHIC SCARRING; PROTEIN PURIFICATION AND IDENTIFICATION; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: Skin fibrosis, such as hypertrophic scarring and keloid, is frequently seen fallowing trauma, thermal injuries and surgical incisions. These conditions, caused by excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) production or abnormalities in ECM remodeling, are clinically raised, firm, itchy, bulky, and inelastic and limit the mobility of joints. Current treatment modalities for this devastating condition still remain unsatisfactory, raised a great need for innovation within wound care industry. Our goal is to develop a new generation of anti-scaring wound care products including wound dressing for open wounds and strips for closed wounds. In this regard a safe recently found anti-scaring small molecule will be encapsulated in nanofibers to produce slow releasing drug delivery systems. The effect of these drug delivery systems on functionality, ECM production and viability of skin cells will be evaluated. Biofunctional wound dressing and strips will be developed by using these nanofibers and efficacy of these novel wound care products in improving and/or preventing scaring will be evaluated in animal models.  These novel wound care products that will facilitate controlled release of the anti-scaring drug, will improve healing outcome and the quality of life in millions of patients who are prone to develop scaring after burn injuries or surgeries. The benefits of our novel anti-scaring system for both the health care providers and Canadian patients is four-fold:1)to ease the pain and many difficulties associated with wound contractures that affect physical activity;2) to improve and/or prevent skin disfiguring conditions in these patients who likely to have long-term psychological implications;3)to reduce the cost of long term treatment, rehabilitation and many post-reconstructive surgeries and finally,4)to provide valuable knowledge for the fields of both drug delivery and wound healing, while producing results and information that can be easily translated to the clinic.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of MEF2B in Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; CHROMATIN STRUCTURE; DIFFUSE LARGE B-CELL LYMPHOMA; FOLLICULAR LYMPHOMA; HISTONE MODIFICATION; LYMPHOMAGENESIS; MICROARRAY; MOUSE MODEL; MYOCYTE ENHANCER FACTOR 2; NON HODGKIN LYMPHOMA
Abstract-Résumé: Lymphomas, which are cancers of the immune system, are the fifth most common cancer in Canada. Lymphomas can arise when cells acquire changes in their DNA (called mutations) that affect regions (called genes) that encode regulators of cell growth. Identifying mutations present in lymphoma DNA but not normal DNA from the same person can suggest ways to target therapies to affect the tumor but not normal cells. Intriguingly, several of the most frequently mutated genes are involved in packaging the DNA so that it fits into the nucleus of the cell. The manner in which the DNA is packaged is very important, because it affects the manner in which genes are interpreted by the cell. One gene, MEF2B, is frequently mutated in lymphomas, and is thought to be involved in DNA packaging. My objective is to determine if and how mutations in MEF2B can contribute to causing lymphoma. I will investigate how MEF2B mutations affect DNA packaging, cell growth, and the frequency of lymphoma in mice.  I hope to improve our understanding how abnormal DNA packaging may contribute to the development of lymphoma. If certain DNA packaging changes are specific to cancerous cells, we may be able to selectively kill cancer cells by designing drugs that target DNA packaging changes.
