TitreApplicationTitle: In vivo clonal evolution of medulloblastoma brain tumour-initiating cells in response to therapy: Discovering the refractory brain tumour-initiating cell population
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOUR INITIATING CELLS; CANCER STEM CELLS; CHEMOTHERAPY; CT-PET IMAGING; FLUORESCENT-ACTIVATED CELL SORTING; HUMAN-MOUSE XENOGRAFT MODEL; LENTIVIRUSES; MEDULLOBLASTOMA; MICROARRAY GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; RADIOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: The Cancer Stem Cell (CSC) hypothesis suggests that tumours are organized into a hierarchy with a rare population of cells, termed CSCs, having the ability to initiate, proliferate, and maintain tumour growth. This is in sharp contrast to all other cells of the bulk tumour, characterized by a limited proliferative capacity and specified lineage potential. Brain tumours represent the leading cause of childhood cancer mortality, of which medulloblastoma is the most frequent malignant pediatric brain tumour. The recent identification of brain cancer stem cells, termed brain tumour-initiating cells (BTICs) has confirmed a stem cell origin for medulloblastoma pathogenesis. The most clinically compelling component of the CSC hypothesis holds that the CSC evades current therapy and is responsible for disease recurrence and metastasis post-therapy. Although there is strong evidence that CSCs are chemo- and radio-resistant, no studies prospectively demonstrate these treatment-resistant CSCs to be exclusively causative in cancer relapse and recurrence. The objective of this study is to generate a global profile of medulloblastoma BTICs as they evolve in response to therapy through gene expression and stem cell biology analyses conducted on our medulloblastoma BTIC mouse model. We hypothesize that comparative BTIC analyses of mice surviving all treatments to those mice that fail therapy will generate a differential profile of the refractory BTIC, and thereby permit the identification of BTICs that respond to or evade specific interventions. For the first time, we will be able to offer a comprehensive molecular profile of the treatment-resistant BTIC population that is responsible for cancer relapse or progression. Novel therapies directed at these specific medulloblastoma stem cells may improve the overall survivorship of medulloblastoma patients, especially in those who remain refractory to current treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Out and About: the association between the neighborhood built environment and older adults' mobility and health
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BUILT ENVIRONMENT; HEALTH; MOBILITY; OLDER ADULTS; WALKABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: The mobility of older adults (their ability to move around their neighborhood) can be greatly limited by a poorly designed built environment (BE). Broadly speaking, the BE refers to how neighborhoods and communities are designed, accounting for land use and transportation systems. Limited mobility is a risk factor for disability, cognitive impairment, and social isolation and is associated with an increased risk of admission to residential care and mortality. Thus, maintaining mobility in older age is an important part of healthy aging. Therefore, the objectives of my study are; 1. to determine the association between the BE and older adults' mobility and, 2. to determine the association between BEs that are either well or poorly designed and the health and social participation of older adults who reside in those neighbourhoods. Participants will be randomly selected from diverse (high and low walkable) neighborhoods. I will evaluate participants' mobility using accelerometers, global positioning systems, and travel diaries. I will use self-report questionnaires to assess participants' self-rated health and social participation. I will compare participant profiles across high and low walkable neighbourhoods. My ultimate goal is to enable older adults to maintain their functional independence by better understanding those elements of the BE that enhance or inhibit their mobility.

TitreApplicationTitle: Addictions and Mental Health Planning in 21st Century Canada - Examining Cultural Safety Through an Indigenous Planning Paradigm
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATIVE PLANNING; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; CULTURAL SAFETY; DECOLONIZATION STRATEGIES; INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE; NARRATIVE INQUIRY; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; STORYTELLING METHODOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Conditions in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside neighbourhood, where many Indigenous peoples live with poverty, addictions and mental health issues, are well documented. A model of addictions planning for Indigenous peoples is urgently needed that takes into account multiple streams such as mental health, poverty, homelessness, and histories of trauma and abuse, especially the Indian residential school experience. There is a need for a continuum of care that is community-driven and includes multiple agencies and service providers. My doctoral research will analyze existing systems of health care planning as they relate to addictions and mental health and identify possible goals and objectives for future planning. I will interview administrators, front-line workers and clients to explore "ideal models" while grounding the research in what it would take to actually implement them in Metro Vancouver. Addictions and mental health issues have wide-ranging impacts beyond the health and justice systems. This project will bring together those who have an interest in improving and harmonizing health services in addictions and mental health and are willing to imagine a new direction forward.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of external control of hematopoietic stem cell fate decisions
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW TRANSPLANT; CELL CYCLE REGULATION; CELL FATE DECISIONS; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELL; IN VITRO STEM CELL EXPANSION; LEUKEMIA; MASS CYTOMETRY; MICROFLUIDICS; SIGNALLING; TRANSCRIPTOME ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding the complex molecular machinery that allows blood stem cells to increase their numbers is important for many reasons. These include a need to develop better methods to treat patients with defective, injured or diseased blood cell outputs. In addition, there is a critical need to develop more effective and less toxic methods of treating leukemia, which depend on similar mechanisms for their growth as do normal blood stem cells. Because blood stem cells are extremely rare and change in subtle ways during development, progress in understanding how to expand them has been slow. This project will exploit recent technical advances that make it possible to identify new pathways that control normal human blood stem cell responses to external factors.   I will use established methods to isolate highly purified living blood stem cells from normal tissues. I will then monitor their survival, rate of division, and retention of stem cell properties in single-cell cultures established in a microchip system that allows each cell to be exposed to different factors. In parallel, I will determine which genes the cells have been stimulated to express and, from that information, make inferences about the molecular components of the cell's response machinery which can then be subjected to more rigorous biological tests.  The information gained will lead to new methods for growing blood stem cells outside of the body with retention of their full regenerative ability. Based on promising preliminary results already obtained and my proposed use of even more powerful analytical tools, I expect this project will advance the longstanding and significant goal of improving the clinical utility of blood stem cells for transplantation and other applications in regenerative medicine. Further, this research should also provide a better basis for understanding how blood stem cells become leukemic and hence identify new targets for therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of B Cells in the Pathophysiology of Chronic Graft-Versus-Host Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNITY; B CELLS; BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION; CANCER; CHRONIC GRAFT-VERSUS-HOST DISEASE (CGVHD); PRIMARY IMMUNODEFICIENCIES
Abstract-Résumé: For many Canadians with cancer and immune disorders the only cure is a bone marrow transplant. One of the biggest obstacles to a successful transplant is the occurrence of chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD). Chronic GVHD occurs when the newly transplanted immune system turns against its host's body and attacks organs. The biological mechanisms responsible for chronic GVHD are not well understood. Chronic GVHD has many features in common with autoimmune diseases and inherited immune deficiencies. The dysfunction of B cells, a type of immune cell that produces antibodies, are known to play a prominent pathological role in these diseases. We believe that there is a similar B cell dysfunction that occurs in cGVHD. By better understanding this dysfunction, we will be able to develop better treatments and preventative strategies for cGVHD, improving the success of bone marrow transplant in curing many devastating diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Neurotrophins in the Pathophysiology of Endometriosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE/RECRUITMENT; DIAGNOSTIC BIOMARKERS; ENDOMETRIOSIS; ENDOMETRIOSIS-ASSOCIATED PAIN; FEMALE INFERTILITY; LASER CAPTURE MICRODISSECTION; NEUROTROPHINS/NEUROTROPHIN RECEPTORS; REAL-TIME PCR; REPRODUCTIVE IMMUNOLOGY; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Endometriosis is a chronic disease of unknown cause characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterus. It affects over 10% of women of reproductive age, from all ethnic and social groups. It is a major cause of infertility, pain, and suffering at the physical, emotional and social level. Treatment options are sub-optimal. Endometriosis is a condition that we believe is under-diagnosed as its symptoms are identical to other gynecological and gastrointestinal disorders, and clinical biomarkers do not exist. In 2002 the annual cost of endometriosis in the US was estimated to be $22 billion, assuming only 10% prevalence. In 2009 in Canada, it was estimated to be $1.8 billion. This is a lot more than comparable chronic conditions.  Neurotrophins are a family of secreted growth factors which promote the survival and growth of neurons. One of them, Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) has been shown to be increased in the uterus of women with endometriosis. This study looks at the role of BDNF and its receptor tyrosine receptor kinase B (Trk B) in endometriosis-related pain, and survival of tissue outside of the uterus.  Methods: Using samples collected during laparoscopic surgery these factors will be measured and compared between women with and women without endometriosis. Cell culture work will be used to examine the relationship between BDNF and its receptor, to understand why BDNF and Trk B are increased in women with endometriosis, and to further understand how BDNF and Trk B are involved in cell proliferation and death. Finally, blood samples will be collected to measure BDNF and determine if it can be used as a marker for endometriosis.  Importance: Results of this study will help understand how endometriosis progresses and how tissue survives outside of the uterus. This will lead to new therapies and diagnostic tests for endometriosis. This research will have a significant impact on the lives of many women.

TitreApplicationTitle: A series of studies on using social networks to inform and support evidence-informed public health practice in Canada: investigating public health organizational networks, and online sources of public health evidence
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATIVE FILTERING; EVIDENCE-INFORMED DECISION MAKING; HEALTH EVIDENCE DATABASES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PUBLIC HEALTH SYSTEM; QUALITATIVE STUDY; SOCIAL NETWORK ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: My PhD thesis will involve a series of sequential studies to explore the role of social networks to improve public health decision-making in Canada. I am investigating the pattern by which the staff in public health departments in Canada turn to each other to get advice in making public health decisions. I will assess how an empowering organizational intervention will affect their interaction patterns and their choices for advice-seeking. The findings will be used to inform policy-makers to utilize and engineer informal staff networks to improve the quality of health decisions and facilitate organizational reforms in public health system. In a relevant qualitative study, I will bring the network maps, depicting the interaction patterns, to the staff, and will explore how they interpret the networks, and what real-life stories they tell about social interactions. This will be a unique model to deepen our understanding about work-related social networks in the public health context, and to translate the network analysis findings into health policy-makers? language. In parallel, I will do a methodological investigation on how dependable the open-ended network questions are, and how the minds of respondents are framed by the way the questions are asked. The findings will help the researchers utilize valid tools to capture informal social networks. I will also assess the role of social network methodology in promoting public health decision making in the context of online health evidence resources. I will investigate if guiding the users of a Canadian public health evidence database (http://health-evidence.ca) by showing them the list of relevant articles, defined by the behavior of other users (the users who visited article A, also visited article B), will facilitate finding useful and relevant research evidence. This will assist in the development of a framework for applying social network theories to online evidence resources to optimize knowledge translation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessment of the relationship between innate immune system ontogeny, infant feeding mode and susceptibility to infection in HIV-exposed but uninfected infants
Keywords-MotsClés: BREASTFEEDING; CHILDHOOD INFECTION; HIV-EXPOSED UNINFECTED INFANTS; INNATE IMMUNE SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Although HIV-positive women are at risk of passing the HIV infection to their infants during birth and during breastfeeding, the majority of infants born to HIV-positive women never become infected with HIV. However, it has been discovered that even these HIV-exposed but uninfected (HEU) infants are more likely to be hospitalized or die of childhood infections than infants born to HIV-negative mothers. We currently do not understand what makes these HEU infants more vulnerable to infections. Our research group is studying the development of the immune system during the first years of life in a group of South African HEU infants. We are attempting to determine whether their exposure to HIV from their mothers has caused a change in their immune systems that leaves them more at risk of infections. Another factor that may be important in the risk of HEU infants is whether or not they are fed breast milk. This is because breastfeeding is known to protect infants from common childhood infectious diseases. Because of the potential importance of breastfeeding amongst HEU infants, our research group is working to develop a reliable method of collecting information on the feeding behaviors of South African HEU infants. Our plan is to then relate their consumption of breast milk to how their immune systems develop in order to understand whether this contributes to their risk of contracting infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Locomotor networks in the lumbosacral spinal cord of the human
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTRICAL STIMULATION; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING(FMRI); LOCOMOTOR NETWORK; NEUROPROSTHESIS; PARALYSIS; REHABILITATION; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: A study by the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation in the US reported that 1 in 50 people live with paralysis in North America (~ 6 million people), with spinal cord injury (SCI) being the leading cause for paralysis. Restoring standing and walking after paralyzing injuries or diseases has been a central research and clinical goal. A novel approach developed in our lab, called intraspinal microstimulation (ISMS), has been shown to produce robust standing and functional walking of the paralyzed hind limbs in animal experiments. This method involves the implantation of very fine, hair-like wires, in a small region of the spinal cord. Minute levels of electrical current are passed through these wires to activate existing networks in the spinal cord that produce standing and walking movements. As part of my PhD work, I will use non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques to determine the distribution of the networks involved in standing and walking in the spinal cord of humans. My work will lead, for the first time, to the understanding of the organization of locomotor networks in the spinal cord of humans. I will use this knowledge to advance ISMS towards clinical implementation.  My experiments will involve able-bodied volunteers and volunteers with spinal cord injury. Contractions in individual muscles in the legs will be elicited through non-invasive electrical stimulation during MRI scanning. The distribution of the locomotor networks in the lumbosacral spinal cord that coordinate the activity of the muscles in the legs will be identified. The study will then be extended to investigate more complex muscle activation patterns such as synergistic activation of multiple muscles and rhythmic activation of muscles as seen during natural walking.  My work will have a substantial impact on the fields of neuroscience and rehabilitation. It will also facilitate the implementation of promising interventions, such as ISMS, for restoring standing and walking.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and evaluation of knowledge translation methods as a part of community-driven research on Helicobacter pylori in northern Aboriginal communities
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES; CIRCUMPOLAR HEALTH; COMMUNITY-DRIVEN PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; EPIDEMIOLOGICAL METHODS; HEALTH LITERACY; HELICOBACTER PYLORI; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NORTHERN CANADA
Abstract-Résumé: Community-driven research is currently underway in northern Aboriginal communities to address concerns about Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that has been identified as a major cause of peptic ulcer disease and stomach cancer. While the transmission of H. pylori has decreased in developed countries, evidence suggests that northern Aboriginal populations have a disproportionately high prevalence of H. pylori infection, and relatively low success from treatment aimed at eliminating the bacteria. Although identified by northern public health providers and communities as a health care concern, limited data are available about H. pylori occurrence in northern Canada. A collaborative initiative is in progress that aims to describe the burden of disease and risk factors associated with H. pylori infection, and seeks to identify effective public health strategies for control of this infection; this research links community representatives, faculty from various disciplines at the University of Alberta, as well as Northwest Territories and Yukon health care practitioners and health authorities. An important component of this research is the movement of knowledge created through research into implementation by users such as community members and healthcare providers, a process known as knowledge translation. Because of differences in knowledge structures and world views between Aboriginal communities, researchers and health officials, the development of tools to strengthen this process is essential. The current research seeks to identify appropriate knowledge translation strategies and to evaluate their effectiveness; this work will aid the research program currently underway and will also broaden our understanding of best practices in knowledge translation within participatory research in northern Aboriginal communities and across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Old Bones: The Effects of Osteoarthritis on Skeletal Age Markers
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING AND SENESCENCE; BIOARCHAEOLOGY; BIOCULTURAL APPROACH; BONE BIOMECHANICS; DEMOGRAPHY; LIFE HISTORY; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PALEOPATHOLOGY; SKELETAL AGE-AT-DEATH ESTIMATION; SKELETAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: We use archaeology to study the ancient and recent human past, to seek patterns and explanations, and to discover ourselves. Many people study the human experience; I want to tell the stories of our collective past through the bones of our ancestors. Much information can be gleaned from the skeleton (sex, age, ancestry, diet, body size etc). Human osteologists study bones because they preserve when all other soft tissues decay. I am interested in examining the relationship between age, health, and disease from skeletal evidence to better understand how the human body changes over the lifetime of an individual.     The aging process is inevitable. Everybody grows old. Over the life course we engage in a variety of tasks, activities, and behavior, all of which shape the body both inside and out.  But we are also living longer. As a result osteoarthritis (OA) has become the most common joint disease in contemporary populations worldwide, occurring most often in the spine, knee, hip, and hands. OA in bones and joints affects 1 in 10 Canadian adults, as well as 85% of the population over the age of 75. By 2031, the number of Canadians with OA is predicted to increase by 124%. Globally, OA represents a major health crisis in aging. Since life expectancy has doubled in the last century, it is not surprising that the archaeological record also reflects an extremely high prevalence of OA. The onset, presence, and severity of OA poses a major mobility limitation in future generations.       My research will demonstrate how adult bone matures in order to understand the fundamental processes (and progression) of aging in humans. If we understand how bone ages, we can develop strategies to improve health in modern societies. This is an important study that will help to explain human histories. Understanding the process of skeletal aging helps to describe demography, population health, longevity, individual lived experiences, and the relationship between biology and culture.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a culturally sensitive community-based health program to improve the health status of people living with osteoarthritis in an underserved rural community of Mexico.
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; COMMUNITY-BASED REHABILITATION PROGRAMS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; ETHNOGRAPHY; HEALTH FORUMS; INTERNATIONAL HEALTH; OSTEOARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis is a chronic disease that affects the joints of the body producing pain and limitations of physical activities. Osteoarthritis is the most common of the chronic musculoskeletal diseases in Mexico. There is evidence that osteoarthritis affects the health of people living in communities in poor rural regions of Yucatan, Mexico. Therefore, it is important to develop a health program directed at improving the health of people living with osteoarthritis in underserved rural communities of Yucatan. The main objective of this project is to develop a community based program to improve the health of individuals living with osteoarthritis in Chikindzonot, a community located in the countryside of Yucatan, Mexico. To accomplish this, we will conduct the following steps in which we will: 1) determine which evidence based interventions are available to improve the health of people with osteoarthritis; 2) investigate the extent to which osteoarthritis affects the health of Chikindzonot's habitants and will examine reasons why people are getting this disease; 3) explore the community's beliefs and perceptions about osteoarthritis; 4) form a discussion group with various people from the community; 5) present the information that has been  assembled in the previous steps of this project to community members; and 6) ask community members to make a judgment about the components of the health program that should be adopted to improve the health of individuals living with osteoarthritis in Chikindzonot. The results of this project will help us to understand the process of developing and creating community based programs, and will help the community of Chikindzonot to define what is needed to improve the health status of its members living with osteoarthritis and to determine how they can cover these needs.

TitreApplicationTitle: The incidence, functional consequences and clinical significance of secreted frizzled-related protein 2 promoter hypermethylation in melanoma.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; EPIGENETICS; MELANOMA; MICROENVIRONMENT; STEM CELLS; WNT PATHWAY
Abstract-Résumé: Melanoma is a cancer that arises from melanocytes, pigment-producing cells that are found predominately in the skin.  The incidence of melanoma has increased dramatically in Western populations and worldwide the number of cases has doubled within the past twenty years.  In the early stages, melanoma can be cured with surgery, however, there are currently few effective treatment options once it has progressed to a metastatic stage -- where additional tumours start growing in organs apart from the primary tumour.  This is why it is the deadliest form of skin cancer; although melanoma accounts for only 4% of skin cancers, it is responsible for over 80% of skin cancer deaths.  Clinically, biological markers that play a role in this invasive and metastatic phenotype would be useful for determining patient prognosis as well as for properly designing new therapeutic regimes.  Recently, epigenetic silencing of stem cell-associated secreted frizzled-related proteins (sFRPs), antagonists of the Wnt pathway, has been shown to play an instrumental role in the development and aggressiveness of multiple cancers (eg. breast and colorectal cancer).  This epigenetic silencing involves the use of heritable changes to DNA that does not alter the primary DNA sequence itself.  The goal of this project is to delineate the role of sFRP-2 in melanoma tumourigenicity and to determine the method of epigenetic silencing involved in this process.  We will investigate the presence and functional significance of this epigenetic silencing in vitro.  Following this, we will correlate sFRP-2 expression to clinical prognosis.  The findings of our research will help define the melanoma phenotype and have the potential to provide a previously unknown molecular target for directed therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Testing the Impact of Resource Availability on Patterns of Referral to Inpatient Stroke Rehabilitation in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESSIBILITY; HIERARCHICAL REGRESSION; MULTIVARIABLE MODELING; REHABILITATION; RESOURCE AVAILABILITY; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a serious and debilitating condition.  Every year, approximately 20,000 people experience a stroke in Ontario, many of whom are left with serious disability.  Research from around the world suggests that rehabilitation after stroke can play an important role in helping patients to recover physical and mental function and to improve their overall quality of life.  However, previous research in Ontario suggests that there may be differences in how easily patients are able to access rehabilitation depending on where in the province they live.   Generally speaking, three forms of rehabilitation are available to patients after stroke: inpatient (in-hospital), outpatient, and community-based.  The purpose of this study is to use information from people who have experienced a stroke in Ontario to confirm that differences really do exist in their opportunity to access rehabilitation.  If differences are confirmed, the study will then test to see if there is a relationship between the amount of money spent on rehabilitation in regions across Ontario and the ease with which patients living in these regions are able to access rehabilitation.  Two general theories will be tested.  The first is that patients who live in regions where less money is spent on inpatient rehabilitation will have poorer access to these services.  The second is that mild patients who live in regions where less money is spent on outpatient or community-based rehabilitation will be more likely to be admitted to hospital for rehabilitation; even though they would be better served in the community.  Testing these theories will help government officials to better understand the role that their spending plays in the availability of rehabilitation, and to begin to identify regions where more rehabilitation resources are needed.

TitreApplicationTitle: A New Marker for Dialysis Adequacy
Keywords-MotsClés: DIALYSIS ADEQUACY
Abstract-Résumé: Dialysis is a supportive therapy in patients with minimal kidney function. It helps by removing toxins and extra fluid. The overall health of dialysis patients needs to be assessed regularly. This includes, but is not limited to, determining the dialysis dose patients receive and their kidney function. To determine the dose of dialysis, blood levels of specific proteins are measured before and after dialysis. Because patients with some kidney function, despite being on dialysis therapy, live longer than patients with no kidney function, it is important to preserve and to monitor kidney function. Traditionally, routine monitoring of kidney function requires patients to collect a 24-48 hour urine sample, which is cumbersome for patients.   Cystatin C is a protein that has shown to be better at estimating kidney function in patients who are not on dialysis. However, there are very few published studies in dialysis population. Our recent study suggests that cystatin C is removed by dialysis. This means cystatin C may not provide a reliable estimate of kidney function in dialysis patients without taking into account the dialysis dose. We will conduct four novel studies to determine the relationships between dialysis treatments, kidney function and cystatin C levels.   Our first and second projects have been completed. We confirmed that cystatin C is removed by dialysis and its level after dialysis is affected by the amount of fluid removal. We also demonstrated a single cystatin C value can be used to calculate the remaining kidney function with a knowledge of dialysis dose. The third study will assess the effects of changing dialysis dose on cystatin C levels. Finally, the findings of these studies will be externally validated using the Frequent Hemodialysis Network Trials stored blood samples. All these projects will be completed during my PhD training and serve as the basis for my thesis and larger studies in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining genome-wide binding changes of epigenetic regulators CTCF and cohesin-complex in ATRX-knockout mouse brain
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRX; EPIGENETICS; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITIES; NEURODEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Intellectual disabilities like autism, Rett syndrome and ATRX syndrome affect 2-3% of children, which is approximately 140,000 children in Canada. Epigenetics is the study of heritable changes to gene regulation by mechanisms other than DNA sequence, such as DNA packaging and organization. Recent research shows that genes mutated in intellectual disabilities are often epigenetic regulators that impact gene expression in the brain. However, the role of these genes in brain function is poorly understood.   This study will investigate the role of the epigenetic regulators CTCF and cohesin in the developing brain using a mouse model for an intellectual disability called ATRX. Specifically, changes in DNA-binding of CTCF and cohesin will be determined between the genetically-modified mice with no ATRX, and normal mice, across all genes using DNA sequencing of the CTCF-bound DNA. Then I will identify the genes that are deregulated due to altered DNA-binding of CTCF or cohesin, and determine their role in the development of cognitive impairment.  This project hopes to improve the life of Canadians by increasing the understanding of i) epigenetics in brain function and ii) epigenetics in intellectual disabilities, in order to improve treatment and diagnosis of children with these disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: CP Cycle to Fun
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL PALSY; EXCERCISE VIDEO GAMES; EXERTION INTERFACE; FITNESS; GAME DESIGN; GAME EVALUATION; GAMES FOR CHILDREN; GAMES FOR HEALTH; NETWORKED GAMES; PARTICIPATORY DESIGN
Abstract-Résumé: "As children with cerebral palsy (CP) become teenagers, they experience a cycle of deconditioning resulting in a deterioration in physical function. Children who have CP and are walking with a mobility aid often need to transition to using a wheelchair as they become adolescents. There are many reasons for this loss of function, but poor physical fitness and muscle weakness are significant contributors. In addition, youth with CP become increasingly socially isolated, which, as well as declining physical abilities, negatively impacts their quality of life. Virtual world ""exergames"", games that require physical activity to play, hold great promise in engaging youth with CP in physical exercise, and because they can be played over a network from home, can increase social interaction with peers.   In this project, we will investigate the design, development and efficacy of multiplayer exergames as a tool for improving the physical fitness of youth with CP while reducing their social isolation. Using the EQUIS Lab's exergame development tools, we will construct a persistent world game in which players use a recumbent bicycle to control an avatar. Each player requires a Windows PC attached to a high-speed network to facilitate collaborative play and social interaction. The design of the exergame will be participatory, directly including the youth with CP in the process. In addition to the collaborative design and testing sessions, two in-home experiments will be conducted, each over a two month period. 20 youth (10 with CP and 10 peers) will evaluate the exergame's impact on physical fitness and gross motor function in youth with CP.   In this project, six interdisciplinary researchers from Queen's University and Holland Bloorview Hospital will collaborate on health-related research to train 15 highly qualifed personnel in developing and evaluating exergames for youth with cerebral palsy."

TitreApplicationTitle: Microfluidic platforms coupled to mass spectrometry for the quantitative analysis of circulating convertases and substrates
Keywords-MotsClés: CONVERTASES; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MICROFLUIDIC; MRM ASSAYS; PROTEOMIC REACTOR; SUBSTRATES
Abstract-Résumé: "Proprotein convertases (PCs) and their substrates are important players in many human diseases including cardiovascular diseases, neurodegenerative diseases, mental health, cancer/metastasis and viral infections. Some convertases (PCSK9) and PC-substrates are secreted in circulation and have local or distal effects that impact human health. Changes in their circulating isoforms and levels can have drastic effects on health. Difference in isoforms due to single cleavage can lead to gain or loss of function. Therefore, the accurate measurement of the level of the different circulating isoforms is key to drug development and the treatment of diseases. Unfortunately, they are often present in minute amounts in circulation and have different bioactive and/or inactive isoforms that need to be distinguished. Conventional antibody based detection approach have provided mitigated results. We propose instead to develop microfluidic technologies combined with mass spectrometry 1) for the identification of PC substrates and 2) for the quantitative monitoring of some PCs and substrates in circulation. We will put in place a platform based on the microfluidic proteomic reactor coupled to mass spectrometry for the discovery of novel PC substrates, with an initial focus on the substrates of PC7. As well, we will develop another platform based on larger-capacity proteomic reactor coupled to multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) mass spectrometry for the rapid and absolute quantitation of circulating PCs (PCSK9) and circulating PC substrates. The outcome of this project will be: Novel platforms for the identification substrates and for rapid and quantitative monitoring of circulating PCs and substrates, as well as a set of proprietary mass spectrometry- based assays."

TitreApplicationTitle: Second generation liver tumour radioembolization with biodegradable monosized Re-188 micrspheres
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA EMITTER; BIODEGRADABLE POLYMERS; BREMSSTRAHLUNG MICORSPHERES; DOSIMETRY; IMAGING; INTERNAL RADIOTHERAPY; NANOTECHNOLOGY; NUCLEAR MEDICINE'; RADIOPHARMACEUTICAL
Abstract-Résumé: "The Canadian Cancer Society reports that the incidence of primary liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) is on the rise, with 1,700 cases, and 700 associated deaths in 2010. In addition, secondary liver cancer, with the most common form being metastatic colorectal carcinoma, is also on the rise in Canada, with 22,000 new cases and 9,100 associated deaths in 2010. For patients with liver cancer or metastases that are unsuitable for surgery, radioembolization becomes a viable, effective and safe treatment. In this treatment, radioactive microspheres are directly administered into the hepatic artery which provides the hepatic tumours with 80-100% of their blood supply. The microspheres become trapped in the small blood vessels of the tumour vasculature where they irradiate the tumour. Radioembolization is currently performed with two different types of microspheres loaded with Y-90 (SIRspheres from Sirtex, Australia; and Theraspheres from Nordion, Canada). This approach demonstrates significant response, but possesses inherent limitations.   Our project addresses them all. We propose (1) to use a new type of microspheres which are biodegradable, monosized and cheap, and (2) to replace Y-90 by Re-188 which has beta emissions almost identical to Y-90 and also emits 155 keV gammas allowing for quantitative imaging and accurate patient-specific dosimetry. Additionally,Re-188 can be conveniently obtained from a W-188/Re-188 generator. Our microspheres loaded with Tc-99m will be used for shunt assessment and therapy planning, then loaded with Re-188 in patient-specific activity concentrations. Accordingly, the number and size of microspheres will be adjusted for each patient. In the scope of this project we will develop the necessary therapy platform that includes automated Re-188 radiolabelling, dosing, quantification and imaging. To reach the aim of providing Canadian liver tumour patients with this improved second generation radioembolization therapy."

TitreApplicationTitle: Practical implementation of real-time low-dose x-ray imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC CATHETERIZATION PROCEDURES; DOSE REDUCTION; FLAT PANEL DETECTORS; FLUOROSCOPY; LEAD OXIDE; NOVEL PHOTOCONDUCTIVE MATERIALS; REGION OF INTEREST IMAGING; X-RAY IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: "The role of real-time x-ray fluoroscopic imaging is expanding and important for diagnostic, evaluation and image guided interventional applications. In 2010, it is estimated that there were over 3 million cardiac catheterization procedures performed in North America using x-ray fluoroscopy. One of the main reasons for this frequency is the increased prevalence of catheter based therapies. Angioplasty, particularly balloon inflation with the addition of a stent, has markedly improved the success of the procedure by reducing the rate of re-stenosis, allowing for a less invasive treatment of complex lesions that were previously exclusively treated with coronary bypass surgery. Cardiac intervention procedures are quite long and require multiple x-ray exposures to a patient. As a result, the radiation dose from a single interventional fluoroscopic procedure can be 1-10 times that in CT. It has been recognized that this is unacceptable and must be reduced.   The x-ray fovea or the region of interest method (ROI) has been identified as a means of reducing this dose but it has not yet been clinically implemented by the major manufacturers. The ROI method is based on the realization that the eye of an interventional physician can only see a small region of the image with high resolution, because it is limited by the human eye's fovea size. Peripheral vision is needed to maintain context. However, it is not necessary to provide a high quality image in the peripheral region for the eye-brain system to process the image. Thus, there is a huge potential for reduction of exposure to a patient if only the ROI actively being viewed by the physician is of high quality (i.e., refreshed at the real-time rate and full exposure level). The exposure to the peripheral area can be minimized by reducing dose rates without the observer being aware of this loss."

TitreApplicationTitle: The development of single cell microfluidic technologies for analysis of microRNA expression and epigenetic state with application to hematopoietic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; HEMATOPOIESIS; MICROFLUIDICS; MOLECULAR BARCODING; MRNA EXPRESSION; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; SINGLE CELL ANALYSIS; STEM CELL; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: "This project will create new and robust technology to assess the transcriptional heterogeneity of single cells at a genomic level. The prototype example to be used as a test case is the stem cell of the hematopoietic system where compelling evidence now indicates that different fate decisions are determined in part by mechanisms that are self-propagating through many self-renewal divisions. Understanding the molecular basis of these mechanisms is fundamental to current intense efforts to expand hematopoietic stem cells ex vivo, to develop safer and more effective gene therapy protocols, and to elucidate mechanisms of leukemogenesis in individual patients. The technology to be developed, validated and tested in proof-of-principle experiments on highly purified populations of normal mouse and human hematopoietic stem cells will enable microRNA (miRNA) expression and epigenomic marks to be examined on hundreds of individual cells from small samples with high fidelity and at low cost. MiRNA analyses will utilize on-chip extraction, barcoding and PCR amplification of sequences in nanolitre volumes to generate sufficient material for standard sample indexing and automated library construction. Following sequencing to sufficient coverage, single cell miRNA expression levels will be determined by counting the number of unique barcodes for each gene, thereby allowing their absolute quantification independent of amplification biases. Epigenomic analyses of single cells will use on chip processing of histone DNA complexes and detection of H3K27me3 and H3K4me3 modifications at specific regulatory sites pre-identified by CHIP-SEQ. This will represent a truly interdisciplinary team effort offering a unique discovery-to-application experience for trainees at all levels as well as members of the biotech and clinical sectors who already recognize the commercialization and potential of the IP and products to be generated"

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of small molecule viral sensitizers to boost vaccine manufacturing
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICS MANUFACTURING; ENHANCERS OF VIRAL PRODUCTION; INFUENZA VACCINE; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOGY; PROTEOMICS; SMALL MOLECULES; STRUCTURE ACTIVITY RELATIONSHIPS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL PROFILING; VACCINE MANUFACTURING
Abstract-Résumé: "Virus-based vaccines are society's most successful pharmaceuticals for the prevention of deadly human diseases. Diseases like smallpox, polio, measles, mumps and rubella have been essentially eliminated from human populations where widespread vaccination programs have been implemented. One characteristic common to all vaccines is that they must be engineered or selected to have attenuated growth characteristics in order to ensure an acceptable safety profile in humans. While attenuation of the ability of a viral vaccine to block cellular innate immune responses creates an extremely safe product, it also impairs the growth of the virus in cell lines used for industrial manufacturing, decreasing the timely delivery of vaccines. The acute vaccine supply shortages experienced during the 2009 H1N1 vaccination program underscore the need fortimely manufacturing of large amounts of vaccine. Our Solution: We have discovered that it is possible to use small molecules to target and inhibit the same cellular pathways that virus virulence genes target. Our lead compounds, coined virus sensitizers or VSes, can significantly enhance the growth of viral therapeutics, in some cases by over 1000 fold. A key advantage of using small molecules to boost vaccine production is that neither the virus-based vaccine nor the manufacturing cell line need be genetically modified. This minimizes the regulatory hurdles for implementing our technology to improving vaccine manufacturing, enabling faster translation to improved health outcomes for Canadians. To translate our technology to an industrial setting, several key issues need to be addressed. These include (1) Optimization of VSe activity and physiocochemical properties (2) Assessment of VSe toxicology and end-product bioequivalence (3) Validation of VSe impact in small scale manufacturing applications, which will be done in collaboration with our technology end user Jennerex Biotherapeutics, and (4) Identification of VSe molecular targets. This proposal describes our multi-disciplinary approach to address these key questions."

TitreApplicationTitle: Biointerface science:  proteoglycan 4 (PRG4) with and without hyaluronic acid as a novel ocular surface boundary lubricant & contact lens coating
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; BIOMATERIALS; BIOMECHANICS; BIOTRIBOLOGY; CONTACT LENS; HYALURONAN; OCULAR SURFACE; PROTEOGLYCAN 4 (PRG4)
Abstract-Résumé: "Dry eye disease is a major health-care issue and drain on health-care resources worldwide, with symptoms of discomfort, damage to the ocular surface, and a significant reduction in quality of life, with no current therapeutically effective treatments. Cells at the ocular surface, which forms a biointerface when sliding against an opposing tissue or contact lens, are subject to significant friction forces generated with eyelid blinking. These forces can be exacerbated by contact lens wear particularly in the presence of a compromised tear film, another symptom of dry eye. Proteoglycan 4 (PRG4), also known as lubricin, is a protein originally discovered in synovial fluid and on the surface of articular cartilage that has recently been discovered at the ocular surface. PRG4 has been shown to function in a dose-dependent manner, both alone and in combination with hyaluronic acid (HA; also present in synovial fluid and tears), to reduce friction at a cartilage-cartilage, and recently, an ocular surface biointerface, in a boundary mode of lubrication (surface-to-surface contact). Given the presence of PRG4 at the ocular surface where it presumably acts as a boundary lubricant, it is hypothesized that delivery of this protein, either alone or in combination with HA, will lead to decreased symptoms of dry eye, particularly in contact lens wearers. The planned experiments will be completed using novel and sophisticated biophysical, biochemical and biomechanical methods to first generate, purify, and characterize native and recombinant PRG4. Then assess their ability to both function as an effective friction-lowering boundary lubricant at contact lens - cornea/eyelid biointerfaces, and, with and without additional chemical modifications, interact with and improve properties of novel silicone hydrogel contact lens materials +/- HA incorporation. This work will result in the development of more comfortable contact lens materials and bandage contact lenses, and could lead to the development of the first real treatment for dry eye. The potential social and economic impact of this work to Canada is extensive. A novel, more lubricious contact lens and/or artificial tear solution would significantly improve the quality of life of millions of Canadians suffering from dry eye. "

TitreApplicationTitle: Anti-microbial scaffold materials for cutaneous wound healing
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-MICROBIAL MATERIALS; BIOMATERIALS; HYDROGELS; NANOPARTICLES; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; TISSUE ENGINEERING; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: "This proposed research is focused on the development of new functional biomaterials for the repair of chronic degradation and infection of skin. Loss of nerves and sensitivity occur in the skin of extremities in chronic type II diabetes, often resulting in epithelial erosion and ulceration. In addition to the loss of sensitivity, the chronic ulceration renders the skin prone to bacterial infection that can lead to gangrene and amputations. In addition, although skin and skin substitutes have been around for a long time for use in burn patients, there are still issues with scarring, especially for deeper skin wounds that involve the dermis and sub-cutaneous fat tissue. Successful strategies for such reconstruction of skin depend crucially on the availability of scaffold materials that (1) recapitulate the native extracellular matrix (ECM) environment (a largely collagenous matrix with proteoglycans and cell interactive proteins such as laminin and fibronectin) and (2) incorporate anti-microbial or anti-septic constituents for preventing or managing infections. The assembled team has complimentary expertise in the development of hydrogel scaffold materials (based on natural and synthetic macromolecules) for regenerative medicine, engineered peptides with anti-microbial activity, microbiology of biofilms, and particle-based nanomaterials for drug delivery and diagnostic applications. In this project, we will apply our expertise to create novel nanocomposite biomaterials for skin regeneration based on engineered collagen scaffolds that incorporate modular designer proteins with cell binding, antibacterial activity, and signally abilities and metallic nanoparticles with innate and patient-safe antimicrobial activity."

TitreApplicationTitle: Non-linear multimodal mircoendoscopy for lung cancer pathology
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER DIAGNOSTICS; COHERENT ANTI-STOKES RAMAN SCATTERIN; LUNG CANCER; MICROSCOPIC ENDOSCOPY; NONLINEAR MICROSCOPY; OPTICAL IMAGING; PATHOLOGY; SECOND AND THIRD HARMONIC GENERATION; TWO-PHOTON FLUORESCENCE; ULTRAFAST LASERS
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the leading cause (~28%) of cancer-related deaths. This proposal addresses two major challenges in the management of individuals at high-risk for lung cancer: A) differential diagnosis of peripheral lung lesions, and B) detection of dysplastic lesions in the central bronchus. Current technologies, such as low-dose CT and standard white-light bronchoscopy, can image dysplastic lesions but their specificity for detecting malignant tissue is very poor. Hence, there is an urgent need to classify detected lesions in situ accurately and in a minimally-invasive way. We propose to optimize, validate and integrate complementary non-linear optical techniques, including two or more of second harmonic generation (SHG), third harmonic generation (THG), coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) and 2-photon autofluorescence (TPF), for label-free in situ microimaging. We hypothesize that non-linear endoscopic microimaging, integrated into ultrathin scanning-fiber bronchoscopy (an emerging disruptive medical technology), will significantly increase the accuracy, and particularly the specificity, of differential diagnosis of suspicious lung lesions, including peripheral nodules, and thereby enable targeted local destruction of malignant tissue.

TitreApplicationTitle: A high-efficiency ultrasonic power link for implantable medical devices
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; COCHLEAR IMPLANTS; HEARING DEVICES; IMPLANTABLE DEVICES; POWER DELIVERY; ULTRASONIC TRANSDUCERS; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: "We propose to develop a high-efficiency transcutaneous ultrasound link to provide power to implanted hearing devices. This requires a cohesive combination of engineering expertise to develop new technology, and clinical/physiological expertise to realise its potential in terms of new surgical options and to test its ability to deliver functionally. At present, implanted hearing devices are powered with a set of radiofrequency induction coils that transfer power through the magnetic field. Such systems have some serious and fundamental limitations: Induction coils trade off size and efficiency, with smaller devices being less efficient, and are quite sensitive to alignment and positioning errors. The high sensitivity to alignment error forces the use of alignment magnets which make it impossible to perform MRI scans on the implanted patient without either removing the magnet, or accepting large shadow areas in the images. MRI scanning is the definitive test for many disorders, and many implantees are children, 40% of whom will require an MRI at some point in their lifetime, so addressing this issue is of great concern. The other major limitation of RF coils is the size/efficiency tradeoff. In order to achieve acceptable coupling efficiencies (typically 25% to 30% in commercially-available implants) coils must be 50 mm or more in diameter. This limits the range of possible implantation sites and requires a large and uncosmetic external unit. The stigma attached to the large and visible external unit is a serious concern, particularly in young patients. The present proposal aims to address these shortcomings in present technology by moving to a different power delivery modality: acoustic ultrasound energy. In our system an external ultrasound transducer is driven from a high-efficiency RF oscillator. This creates an ultrasound wave that propagates through the tissue. A second, implanted transducer converts the ultrasound energy into electrical energy and a high-efficiency rectifier converts the RF to DC to recharge an implanted battery or capacitor. Recent advances in piezoelectric materials and processing techniques make it possible to achieve very high electromechanical coupling efficiencies in ultrasonic transducers. Unlike induction coils, however, there is no inherent size/efficiency tradeoff with an ultrasound link and so it is possible to deliver power to an implant with comparable efficiency in a device one tenth the diameter of an inductive link. Three specific technologies that we are working on will be key to creating a competitive ultrasonic link. First, we will be using the ultra-high-efficiency piezoelectric PMN-PT composite, a material which we have developed an extensive expertise in manufacturing and working with. Second, we will be manufacturing focused transducers to reduce the alignment sensitivity of the device. Third, we will be constructing high-efficiency impedance matching layers to reduce the amount of power reflected at the transducer-tissue interface. As a proof-of-concept of the idea of ultrasonic power delivery we have constructed and tested two 5 mm-diameter air-backed PMN-PT uncurved and unmatched transducers. We were able to demonstrate transfer of up to 200 mW of power with an efficiency of 32% through 6 mm of water and 15% through 5 mm of tissue. We have developed mathematical models to understand the loss sources and find that with improved matching layers, a composite transducer and focusing, efficiencies of up to 50% through 5 mm of tissue are theoretically achievable. The device development will be complemented by clinical research into how best to take advantage of the new   surgical possibilities available with a much smaller device and how to secure the device without the use of an implanted magnet. In particular, the feasibility of implanting the device in a mastoid recess and in the pinna will be examined. "

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of novel plasma biomarkers to predict treatment response in acute exacerbations of cystic fibrosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE PULMONARY EXACERBATIONS; ANTIBIOTIC THERAPY; BLOOD BIOMARKERS; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; LUNG FUNCTION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; SYMPTOMS
Abstract-Résumé: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common fatal genetic disease and 1 out of every 3600 infants in Canada is born with the disease. Due to a genetic abnormality, CF individuals develop thick and sticky mucus in their lungs, which makes them vulnerable to repeated lung infections. Flare-ups of lung infection adversely impact on the quality of life of CF individuals and are responsible for most of the morbidity and costs related to CF care. Based on 2009 Canadian CF patient registry statistics, CF individuals spent over 20,000 days in hospitals mainly due to flare-ups of lung infection. Treatment of lung infection flare-ups in hospital involves the administration of intravenous antibiotics and chest physiotherapy. Most individuals are hospitalized for 10 to 21 days and decisions about treatment response are often guided by a global assessment of improvement in patient symptoms and/or lung function. Unfortunately, this assessment can be insensitive and unreliable, providing the motivation to search for better markers of treatment response. We believe one way to overcome these limitations is to develop a companion blood test that can assist clinicians in treatment decisions by separating out those patients that are not responding to therapy so that treatment can be modified earlier, and by separating out those that are responding to therapy so treatment can be stopped earlier. This will enable more rational and timely use of scarce resources and avoid unnecessary risk of side effects from drugs. The important information gathered in this preliminary study will help in the design of future studies using blood tests to monitor and/or predict treatment response, with the ultimate goal of improving the overall health and quality of life of people with CF in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phenylbutyrate use to target phosphorylation pathways in human disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; DIABETES; ENERGY METABOLISM; HISTONE DEACETYLASES; OSTEOPOROSIS; PHOSPHOPROTEOMICS; UNFOLDED PROTEIN RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: We aim at deciphering the ways by which the drug phenylbutyrate (PB) acts on the body. PB is used in the rare genetic diseases known as Urea Cycle Diseases, in which a block in the transformation of ammonia from proteins to urea leads to significant disease. PB allows the body to get rid of ammonia in the urine while bypassing the liver's urea cycle. We have also demonstrated that PB can be useful in another rare disease known as Maple Syrup Urine Disease, by activating the defective enzyme. PB also has been shown to be effective in common disorders such as diabetes, cancer and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease.  Yet, we don't fully understand why it is beneficial in such conditions. We have been studying this drug for several years and we believe we have finally understood how it mainly acts on the body. Indeed, with the novel powerful technology known as phosphoproteomics, we can understand how drugs affect cellular signaling pathways. Proteins are not only the building blocks of our body; they also transmit signals within a cell, often by phosphorylation, which is the chemical change studied by phosphoproteomics. Using this technology, we found that PB activates the main regulator of energy in the body, the protein called AMPK. AMPK senses when the energy is low, then other proteins to conserve energy and generate more energy. This pathway could explain the beneficial effects of PB in common disorders. Indeed, metformin, the most widely used anti-diabetic drug, also exerts its effects by activating AMPK. The experiments we propose would aim at proving our hypothesis, and then harness this new knowledge to use PB more wisely. For example, since we know that the AMPK pathway is important to prevent osteoporosis, we propose to test whether PB can prevent osteoporosis in mice. Our preliminary results and published experience with PB make us very confident that we have now understood the key mechanism of action of this promising drug.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis: Understanding Canadian Genetic Counsellors' preferences related to indications, patient family structure and costs.
Keywords-MotsClés: DISCRETE CHOICE METHODOLOGY; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PREIMPLANTATION GENETIC DIAGNOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is a medical technique that allows for a couple who is at high risk for having a child with a genetic condition to have testing done while avoiding pregnancy termination if the child is affected. It takes advantage of a process known as in-vitro fertilization (IVF), which allows for an egg and a sperm to be combined outside of the uterus and then transferred back to achieve pregnancy. This technique is costly with some associated clinical risks for the mother as well as the infant. Quebec is currently the only province that covers the costs of PGD/IVF. In all other provinces, access to PGD is out-of-pocket for the couple and provided through private clinics. Limited policy guidelines as well as varying clinicians' practices regarding criteria such as: 1) conditions that would benefit from PGD, 2) the type of family structures suitable for PGD recommendation and 3) equity regarding costs, are all issues that need to be addressed. Genetic counsellors (GC) are the first-line health professionals who explain the benefits and limitations of PGD to the patient population. However, Canadian studies that look at standardization and preferences of this group are limited or lacking. This research explores the preferences of Canadian genetic counsellors by using focus groups to finalize the study design, as well as a questionnaire to GC that 1) determines the demographics, knowledge and comfort level of the genetic counsellors and 2) uses specific experimental PGD scenarios involving costs, family structure and types of genetic diseases, in order to identify the criteria for access and to inform health policy. Besides informing policy using experimental data, the study will not only provide awareness about the PGD preferences of GC to the public across the country, but hopefully optimize its increased incorporation, accessibility and delivery to individuals within the Canadian health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and Feasibility Testing of a Home-Based Physical Activity Intervention for Family Caregivers of People with Advanced Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFECT; FAMILY CAREGIVER; FATIGUE; PALLIATIVE/END-OF-LIFE CARE; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PILOT STUDY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SUBJECTIVE SLEEP QUALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Families play an important role in the care of people with advanced cancer at home. However, facing the loss of a loved one and undertaking new and demanding responsibilities contribute to caregivers experiencing major sleep disturbances, high levels of fatigue, significant impacts on their physical health, and extreme psychological difficulties. Caregivers need to be able to care for themselves in order to protect their own health and continue to provide care. However, our knowledge about ways to help caregivers practice self-care is limited. The benefits of physical activity in healthy individuals, including helping them feel better, sleep better, and experience less fatigue, are well known. A home-based physical activity program is a logical way to address the self-care needs of family caregivers while respecting their desire to stay near the patient. A simple home-based physical activity intervention will be designed together with a physiotherapist. The intervention will consist of active lifestyle coaching with the aim of increasing caregivers' physical activity each week. How caregivers feel, their level of fatigue, and their self-perceived sleep quality will be measured at the start of the intervention and then every two weeks in order to evaluate the effects of the physical activity intervention. This initial study will be conducted to assess, revise, and finalize the details of the home-based physical activity intervention and determine the possibility of conducting a larger study. This intervention study is new and will provide guidance to health care providers that, if effective, will enable them to support family caregivers in addressing their self-care needs. The intervention will be designed to have minimal cost, which is expected to be outweighed by the economic benefit to our health care system as caregivers are kept healthier, potentially enabling them to provide care at home for a longer period and preventing them from becoming patients themselves.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endoscopic Ultrasonography in Ontario: Healthcare Utilization and Outcomes from 2003 to 2011
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADIAN POPULATION-BASED STUDY; COMPLICATIONS; DEMOGRAPHICS; DIAGNOSIS; ENDOSCOPIC ULTRASOUND; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HOSPITALIZATION; OBSERVATIONAL STUDY; PROCEDURE; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is a relatively new technique that provides high-resolution ultrasound imaging to examine the walls of the digestive tract as well organs near the gastrointestinal tract such as the lungs.  EUS can be used to diagnose and treat diseases of the esophagus, stomach, lung, bile duct, pancreas and colon.  The high resolution imaging offered by EUS allows for safe sampling of lumps and lesions and has been shown to be more accurate at determining the extent to and spread of certain cancers (for instance cancers of the esophagus and pancreas) compared to other imaging techniques such as computed tomography scan (CT scan) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).  On the other hand, it is costly and requires highly trained specialists.    Very little is known about how EUS is currently being used, how this may have changed over time or potential inequalities in patient access to EUS.  Furthermore, no studies have evaluated health events following EUS at the community-level in Canada.  Therefore, the present study aims to describe 1) who receives EUS (including patient factors and underlying diagnosis), 2) how EUS is being delivered (physician characteristics and types of procedures) and 3) important health events that occur after EUS is provided (such as complications and admissions to hospital) in a real world setting using Ontario health administrative databases.  The overall goals of this study are to raise awareness among physicians and health care managers about how EUS is delivered and important clinical events related to EUS in Ontario, and thereby encourage informed decision-making regarding patient care and resource allocation for patients who may benefit from EUS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anorectal Dysmotility and Sensory Threshold Volumes in Inflammatory Bowel Disease Patients with Overlapping Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: BAROSTAT BALLOON; CROHN'S DISEASE; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME; MANOMETRY; NATURAL HISTORY OF DISEASE; POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION; TRANSIENT RECEPTOR POTENTIAL VANILLOID TYPE 1; ULCERATIVE COLITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), known as inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), are chronic inflammatory conditions of the digestive tract. Canada has one of the highest incidence and prevalence rates of IBD in the world. Based on our group's validated administrative definition, it is estimated that approximately 19,000 IBD patients reside in the province of Alberta. Quality of life of IBD patients is negatively affected and is driven primarily by the clinical symptoms. Currently the goal of medical therapy is to control the symptoms by reducing the intestinal inflammation. However, many patients continue to suffer from debilitating irritable bowel syndrome-like (IBS) symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating and diarrhea despite healing of their bowel lining. As per our meta-analysis, 57% and 37% of treated UC and CD patients fall into this category, respectively. These patients have poor quality of life and undergo unnecessary and potentially harmful investigations. Despite the clinical importance, little is known about the course, pathogenesis and associated digestive disorders in these patients (IBD-IBS). In our proposed study, we will closely follow 80 adult IBD patients for 3-6 months after they are started on medical therapy in Calgary Health zone. We will identify IBD patients who develop IBS-like symptoms and compare the presence of multiple inflammatory markers in the blood, stool and colon biopsy samples with IBS patients and healthy controls.  This will be the first study in IBD-IBS patients to prospectively examine the proposed inflammatory markers  in response to treatment and associate these findings with abdominal pain. It will characterize the natural history of IBD-IBS, associated digestive conditions and risk factors which will enhance physician awareness in management of this disease. Moreover, knowledge about the risk factors and pathogenesis of IBD-IBS will lead to identification of potential prophylactic or therapeutic targets.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of blood pressure variability on severity of cerebral small vessel disease and cognition in the SPS3 Study
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION/DEMENTIA; EPIDEMIOLOGY; NEUROIMAGING; STROKE/CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Cerebral small vessel disease encompasses ischemic strokes, hemorrhages, silent strokes, vascular cognitive impairment and dementia. It is the lead cause of vascular cognitive impairment and dementia, affecting approximately 250000 Canadians. Hypertension is a powerful risk factor for stroke, small vessel disease and cognitive impairment and affects nearly 7 million Canadians. Though there is a clear relationship between blood pressure and risk of small vessel disease, there is also emerging evidence that variability of blood pressure (unprovoked, irregular fluctuations) may also play an important role in risk of stroke and cognitive impairment.  Our aims are to define variability of blood pressure and examine its relationship with small vessel events including stroke, brain abnormalities on MRI and cognitive impairment using data from the Secondary Prevention of Small Subcortical Strokes (SPS3) study, which is a randomized controlled trial with 3000 participants with more than 58000 blood pressure measurements. We also wish to examine other factors that may affect blood pressure variability, including age, race, gender and class of blood-pressure lowering medication.

TitreApplicationTitle: Radiometals produced by liquid targets for molecular imaging of cancer

Abstract-Résumé: New breast cancer drugs are increasingly targeted to specific proteins involved in cancer progression, such as the epidermal growth factor receptor (HER2). These new drugs typically benefit only a small proportion of patients, at very high cost to the health care system (over $40,000 per patient per year for Herceptin, which targets HER2). Physicians need information about whether a drug target is present in patients' tumours before selecting these expensive treatments. The presence of a predictive protein, also called a biomarker, can be determined by taking a tumour biopsy using special laboratory techniques. However, it is often impossible to biopsy tumours that have spread, and biomarker content may vary from one tumour site to another. Molecular imaging technologies such as positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography (PET/CT) can be a powerful, non invasive tool to detect biomarkers, using extremely low concentrations of radioactive probes. The purpose of this project is to develop novel radioisotope production technologies used for PET/CT imaging. With these radioisotopes, the project will develop new imaging agents that will allow physicians to find out if patients express a variant of HER2 that is associated with resistance to the current drug used to treat HER2 positive breast cancers. The radioisotopes of interest are called zirconium-89, gallium-68, yttrium-86 and scandium-44. Many of these radioisotopes are currently unavailable in Canada. The traditional production methods to make them involve the use of solid targets, which are irradiated by a cyclotron, but this approach requires specific equipment and expertise unavailable in most facilities. TitreApplicationTitle: Optimization of novel dual action prodrugs for treatment of osteoporosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ALENDRONATE; BISPHOSPHONATE; BONE TARGETING; EP4 RECEPTOR AGONIST; MICRO-COMPUTER ASSISTED TOMOGRAPHY; PRODRUG; PROSTAGLANDIN E2; SLOW RELEASE
Abstract-Résumé: "While bone loss in osteoporosis is well treated today, therapy is usually initiated only after considerable bone loss has occurred. Therefore, there is an important medical need for agents that are effective at restoring lost bone to normal levels. Bisphosphonate compounds, for example, alendronate, are regarded as standards of care for treating osteoporosis and related bone diseases; these agents target and bind to bone, and halt and partially reverse osteoporotic bone loss by inhibiting osteoclasts, specialized cells that remove bone tissue.   Unfortunately, bone loss reversal is small and unsustained, even after prolonged treatment. The natural hormone PGE2 stimulates bone growth via agonism at the EP4 receptor subtype in animals and in humans, but is associated with unacceptable side effects (generally gastrointestinal disturbance). To avoid these side effects and to derive an additive or synergistic effect for stopping bone loss in osteoporosis and restoring bone mass to normal levels, we have designed and synthesized several novel dual-action bone-targeting pro-drugs wherein alendronic acid is conjugated through an enzymatically-cleavable linker to one of two potent and selective EP4 receptor agonists. We have shown that when these conjugates are dosed intravenously, they are well tolerated acutely, and they are taken up by bone, where they bind to the bone tissue and liberate the two active drugs over an extended period of time. This project seeks to further optimize and characterize the best conjugates, to select the optimal compound, to define its minimum effective dose and optimal route of administration and then to develop an extensive preclinical data package, in collaboration with CDRD Ventures Inc. (CVI), that is suitable to support full clinical development of the drug. This approach offers the promise of a once-a-week or once-a-month treatment that will dramatically impact the health of millions of people in Canada and around the world."

TitreApplicationTitle: Patient-specific cartilage implants: development and surgical implantation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BIOREACTORS; CARTILAGE REPAIR; CHONDROCYTES; COMPUTER-ASSISTED SURGERY; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Damage to articular cartilage by arthritis or injury causes significant morbidity as the tissue has little potential for repair. One approach to resurface the damaged area with engineered cartilage. However, as only a limited number of cells can be extracted from a patient, the approach is restricted to the repair of small, localized defects. To extend potential treatment to a larger, more clinically relevant patient population, large-size  constructs need to be developed. However, the confounding problem with large-sized implants is that the patient's anatomy at the lesion site needs to be taken into account as inadequate graft matching and imperfect restoration of the joint surface can lead to premature implant failure. The objective of this proposed study is to develop patient-specific engineered cartilage implants suitable for the repair of large, clinically-sized defects. Recently, we have developed an approach to create large-sized cartilage constructs (> 3 sq. cm) from a small population of cells (< 20,000) without a separate cell expansion phase or scaffold. The cells are cultivated in a bioreactor which elicits the extensive growth of cartilaginous tissue that can be matched to the shape, curvature and thickness of the defect site. To deliver the patient-specific implants at the desired location and orientation, we will use our computer-assisted surgical strategies developed for cartilage repair. This project translates the results from our previous work to develop and surgically implant, patient-specific engineered cartilage constructs to offer the prospect of treating large defects associated with osteoarthritis (OA) or trauma that cannot be addressed with currently available techniques. Ultimately, with these new technologies, patients will benefit from better clinical outcomes through proper implant matching resulting in a lower risk of implant failure. We expect that our methods will repair degenerative changes due to OA, and potentially delay or eliminate the need for joint replacement surgery

TitreApplicationTitle: Stem cell counting: Development and application
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL DIFFERENTIATION; CELLULAR BIOLOGY; HEMATOPOIESIS; LEUKEMIA; MICROFLUIDS; PCR; STEM CELL; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: "The stem cells of the blood-forming system (hematopoietic stem cells, HSCs) are rare, comprising only 1 in every 20,000 bone marrow cells. Because they are the only cell in marrow with the capacity to sustain blood cell production throughout adult life, they play a central role in many blood cell disorders and most leukemias. They are also the principal therapeutic entity responsible for the regenerative effectiveness of marrow or cord blood transplants. There is accordingly a need to be able to enumerate them in many circumstances of practical clinical importance. Outcomes of clinical HSC transplants, for example to treat blood diseases such as leukemia, depend critically on the number of HSCs in the donor sample. Unfortunately, there presently exists no practical means of counting HSCs directly. Instead, researchers that need to enumerate them must resort to extremely cumbersome and expensive assays that involve injecting the cells into mice and then waiting a minimum of 5 months before obtaining a result. The enormous effort, time and cost it takes to enumerate HSCs are major limiting factors in blood stem cell research and clinical practice.We propose here the development of a technology for direct and rapid marker-based enumeration of HSCs within half a day, in any cellular sample regardless of biological state and without requirement for prior enrichment. Our proposal brings together a multidisciplinary team of world experts in the fields of stem cell bioengineering (Zandstra), materials and microfluidics (Kumacheva), stem cell biology (Iscove) and single-cell cytometry (Audet). The anticipated outcome will be a high-throughput microfluidics automatable system (Stem Cell Counting Chip - SCCC) which will be translated, with the help of Centre for the Commercialization of Regenerative Medicine and STEMCELL Technologies, into a device usable in any hospital for the robust enumeration of rare cell types such as HSCs. We expect the SCCC to revolutionize stem cell research and regenerative medicine by providing the tools to enumerate HSCs in donor samples or in patients, in real time."
