TitreApplicationTitle: Reconciling the promotion of active transportation and personal exposure to traffic-related air pollution in Canadian urban areas
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVE TRANSPORTATION; AIR POLLUTION; BIKE SENSING; EXPOSURE; HEALTH EFFECTS; LAND-USE; URBAN POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: "Traffic-related air pollution has a large impact on the health of urban populations. There is sufficient data to conclude that chronic exposure to ambient air pollution is associated with the incidence and mortality from cardiovascular disease, especially ischemic heart disease, and from lung cancer. As well, there is overwhelming data implicating acute exposures to air pollution causing a variety of immediate health effects. There is no escape from air pollution, especially in large urban areas, although there are small-scale variations that depend on traffic and land use. Recent research suggests a strong association between the built environment and physical activity suggesting that compact urban areas contribute to decreased automobile dependency and increased walking and cycling. Indeed, Canadian cities are investing into cycling infrastructure, bike sharing programs, and large campaigns to promote bicycling as an affordable, environmentally friendly alternative transportation mode. Yet, while compact urban areas promote active transportation, they also trap pollutants instreet canyons thus magnifying concentrations of traffic-related air pollution. Due to their proximity to traffic, high respiration rates, and longer journeys, cyclists are at risk of being exposed to higher concentrations of air pollution as compared to other road users"

TitreApplicationTitle: High-throughput screening of cell contraction for applications in regenerative medicine and drug testing
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; CARDIOMYOCYTES; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES; CELL CONTRACTION; FIBROSIS; HIGH THROUGHPUT DRUG SCREENING; MYOFIBROLASTS; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; TECHNOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: "We will develop and test a novel method to quantify the contractile activity of cultured cells that will be established as a high throughput screening (HTS) format for industrial applications. HTS quantification of cell contraction is a pivotal yet not available functional test with important fields of application: 1) Functional contraction tests for mesenchymal stem cells to be used to enhance tissue repair, e.g., chronic wound healing associated with diabetes (>3 Mio Canadians, ~13 Bio $) or to regenerate diseased cardiovascular tissues (>10 Mio Canadians, ~18 Bio $). 2) HTS of drugs to tune cell contractility in the cardiovascular system, in fibrosis and in cancer research. We have recently developed a novel rubber polymer that allows optical analysis of cell contraction. Essential improvements over existing deformable culture substrates can turn the new material into a widely-used assay: a) it can be provided in any cell culture format; b) it can be tuned to respond to the specific requirements and force levels of different cell types; c) it is compatible with all standard biochemical and genetic tests; d) it has superb optical properties, and e) it has ideal storing and shipping properties. We will pursue two main objectives: 1) To upgrade our technology for ready-to-use applications, we will apply novel protocols to promote cell adhesion, enable automated analysis, and tune substrates to specific cell types of industrial interest. 2) To translate the technology to a HTS format for industrial use, we will establish multi-well HTS wrinkling plates. With support from our company partners and profiting from our own expertise, we will apply our HTS system to industrially relevant fields: mesenchymal stem cell therapy, anti-fibrosis and anti-cancer drug testing. Together, contraction-associated diseases represent a hundreds of Bio $ burden for the Canadian healthcare system. Providing for the first time an HTS in vitro contraction test will result in dramatically reduced costs for Canadian health care and drug development."

TitreApplicationTitle: Surface-oriented antibody capture of endothelial progenitor cells for the reduction of post-stent restenosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY IMMOBILIZATION; BIOCOMPATIBILITY; ENDOTHELIAL CELL CAPTURE; SELF ASSEMBLED MONOLAYER; STENT DEVICES; SURFACE CHEMISTRY
Abstract-Résumé: "Atherosclerosis involves the deposition of plaque on the interior walls of arterial vessels and results in the narrowing or stenosis of arteries. Although successful, often-used angioplasty suffers from non-uniform arterial widening and restenosis due to post-surgical recoil of the artery. To mitigate these shortcomings, stenting has been used as an alternative in suitable candidates. Stents are expandable cylindrical scaffolds that are implanted within narrowed arteries. They are typically constructed from medical grade stainless steel and can be implanted as bare metal stents (BMS), or as drug eluting stents (DES) depending on patient candidacy.   Despite the advantages of BMS/DES over angioplasty, their effectiveness remains limited by complications associated with biocompatibility. For instance, post-stent restenosis due to neointimal hyperplasia (cellular hypertrophy, proliferation and deposition of extracellular matrix on the stent and around the site of implantation) remains a significant problem. In light of the challenges that both BMS and DES face, further research into alternative strategies for the reduction of both NH and physiological attack of the stent surface is warranted. A promising alternative to BMS and DES is an antibody-based coating that is capable of capturing endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs). EPCs are attractive targets for the reduction of NH since they are present in the bloodstream and have been found to participate in the re-endothelialization of damaged arterial vessels and the inhibition of neointima formation. An early version of this involves a polymer layer on the device and indiscriminate binding of protein.   This proposal concerns a new approach for stent surface modification that incorporates control of both the interfacial population of antibodies, and their correct orientation for optimal binding of EPCs. The Thompson group has examined the surface chemistry of medical grade stainless steel using atomic force microscopy   (AFM) and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) with a focus on the formation of surface hydroxyl (-OH)"

TitreApplicationTitle: Fully implantable wireless multi-electrode ECoG monitoring system
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN-COMPUTER INTERFACES; EPILEPSY; WIRELESS INTEGRATED CIRCUITS
Abstract-Résumé: "Approximately 50 million people worldwide are epileptic. Epilepsy is the third most common neurological disorder, and ranks second in terms of costs to society. Approximately 15% of epilepsy patients undergo surgical resection of the source of the seizures in the brain. Preoperative assessments are done to localize the focus, and to ensure that the resection can be accomplished without producing neurological deficits. These conventional procedures involve implanting an electrocorticography (ECoG) electrode array over the cortex for several weeks. During this time wires from the ECoG electrodes have to be connected to bench-top electrophysiological equipment. As a result, patients have to be tethered making this approach cumbersome and unsafe. Also, the patient's skull has to be opened during the entire time of the procedure which increases the risk of infection. The proposed fully implantable wireless ECoG system will allow patients to move freely and eliminate the risk of infection or reimplantation while under observation for epilepsy focus localization and brain function assessment. Motor disabilities such as paralysis due to chronic stroke, spinal cord injury, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are also prevalent and costly to society. Patients with sensory-motor disabilities can be treated or significantly improve quality of their life by using a fully implanted wireless ECoG brain-computer interface (BCI). We propose to develop a 256-electrode fully integrated wireless ECoG monitoring system which will revolutionize clinical neuromonitoring. We will develop an implantable microchip that performs programmable neural signal recording and neural stimulation and sends recorded neural data wirelessly through skin to a computer. Power and control commands are also sent to the chip wirelessly. We will integrate the chip with surface and depth electrode arrays to deliver a novel capability to remotely record and stimulate at 256 sites in the brain. We will perform in vivo testing of the system in guinea pigs and monkeys. We will translate the results to Canadian neurologists and neurosurgeons, neuromodulation companies, epilepsy and BCI communities, and to the many patients who may benefit from this technology."

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidation of the regulatory role of scleraxis in cardiac fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FIBROBLAST; CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; COLLAGEN; CONDITIONAL GENE DELETION; DOMINANT NEGATIVE MUTANT; FIBROSIS; GENE REPORTER ASSAYS; PRESSURE OVERLOAD; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATORS; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: When the heart becomes damaged (e.g. heart attack) or must overcome increased resistance to pumping (high blood pressure), it must work harder to maintain its normal output of blood. In response to increased workload, heart cells enlarge in an attempt to compensate. For reasons not fully understood, there is also elevated deposition of strong fibres, made primarily of the protein collagen, within the heart wall ("cardiac fibrosis"). This process stiffens the heart and impairs contraction and relaxation, resulting in heart failure. We recently demonstrated that a regulatory protein called scleraxis, normally found in collagen-rich tissues like tendons and heart valves, is also made by the heart cells responsible for fibrosis- cardiac fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. Furthermore, scleraxis directly controls the synthesis of collagen proteins. We hypothesize that not only is scleraxis sufficient to control this synthesis, it is also necessary- if scleraxis is not present, there will be less fibrosis. We will test this hypothesis by surgically causing fibrosis in mice lacking the gene encoding scleraxis. If our hypothesis is correct, these mice will exhibit less fibrosis than those with an intact scleraxis gene. There are no publicly- available therapies specifically targeting cardiac fibrosis as yet despite its drastic impact on patient outcomes. This is due to an incomplete understanding of the regulatory pathways involved in fibrosis. This work will identify scleraxis as a required regulator of collagen synthesis in the heart, and thus as a potential target for drug therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Skeletal Safety of Chronic Proton Pump Inhibitor Use: Evaluating Bone Density, Structure and Strength
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVANCED RADIOGRAPHY; FINITE ELEMENT ANALYSIS; FRACTURE; OSTEOPOROSIS; PROTON PUMP INHIBITORS
Abstract-Résumé: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are widely used for the treatment and prevention of gastroesophageal reflux disease and ulcer disease, and are among the most commonly prescribed drugs in all of medicine. Recent studies have suggested that the chronic use of PPIs may significantly increase the risk of developing hip fracture, though the relationship is far from proven. To date, there is not yet a proven mechanism through which PPIs increase the risk of fracture, and there is great uncertainly as to whether PPIs truly lead to an increase in fracture risk. Because of this uncertainly, there is considerable confusion among patients and clinicians as to whether they chould be concerned about the risk of fracture in patients who are chronically using this mechanism.  Currently, there are no studies which have demonstrated whether PPIs truly have an effect on bone structure and strength. With this proposed study, we will compare bone structure and strength between  patients who have been exposed to PPIs for 5 or more years to those who have never received PPIs. This will be performed by using volumetric quantitative CT scanning (vQCT) and the use of finite element analysis (FEA), which is a computer created model to determine whether PPI use is associated with changes in bone structure that could make them more susceptible to fracture.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of neuroinflammatory mediators in energy homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE; ENERGY HOMEOSTASIS; FOOD INTAKE; GENE EXPRESSION; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; NEUROIMMUNOLOGY; NEUROINFLAMMATION; QUANTITATIVE PCR
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is a rising health problem worldwide and is considered an important risk factor associated to chronic diseases including type II diabetes, stroke, cancer and cardiovascular disorders, among others. It is believed to be largely due to western-style diet suppressing the mechanisms that control food intake in the brain. In addition, a diet rich in fat induces inflammation of brain and other tissues. However, it remains unclear how the inflammatory events modulates the appetite control centers. Therefore, I will test the hypothesis that high fat diet induces an inflammatory response in the brain that lead to overfeeding behavior and consequent weight gain. Mice will be fed with high fat diet for different length of time to investigate the inflammatory response in different brain areas and how the inflammation influences body weight and food intake control mechanisms. Understanding the mechanisms by which high fat diet modulates food intake would allow development of strategies that could be applied for obesity treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using the zebrafish as a pre-clinical animal tumour model for drug discovery and the evaluation of anti-leukemia agents
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE T-LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA; AKT AND P13 KINASE INHIBITORS; ANIMAL TUMOUR MODELS; IN VIVO IMAGING; LIGHT MICROSCOPY; MICE; PERSONALIZED THERAPY; PRE-CLINICAL DRUG TESTING; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: "T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is a high risk subtype of the most common leukemia affecting children. Although intensive chemotherapy treatments have improved survival in this disease, a significant number of patients do not respond to therapy or relapse. For these patients, a better understanding of the molecular pathways underlying the development of this disease holds the promise of personalized therapy with improved outcomes and fewer side effects. Two common pathways affected in T-ALL are NOTCH and PTEN/PI3K. Drugs targeting NOTCH signalling, called gamma secretase inhibitors (GSIs), have been effective against subtypes of T-ALL with NOTCH mutations. However, GSIs have had limited success in clinical trials due to side-effects including gut toxicity, and a significant proportion of leukemias are insensitive to GSIs. Recently drugs targeting the PTEN/PI3K pathway have shown promise for the treatment of T-ALL in both cell culture and mouse models of T-ALL. T-ALL cell lines are typically used for drug screening but they do not accurately represent the complexity of interactions between the leukemia cells and the human body. Transplanting human leukemia cells into mice may better represent human disease but is a costly and slow method of screening new anti-cancer compounds or to evaluate the drug sensitivity of an individual patient's cancer to a particular therapy. We have developed an innovative approach to transplant human cancer cells into zebrafish embryos, which can then be used for rapid pre-clinical drug testing for anti-leukemia agents. We propose a two-pronged approach testing new drugs developed by GlaxoSmithKline that block PI3K signaling   in human T-ALL cell lines and primary patient samples, using both zebrafish and mice. The results of this study will provide validation of the zebrafish model as a cost-effective and rapid means of identifying new agents for the treatment of T-ALL, as well as demonstrating the potential of this model system to personalize cancer therapy."

TitreApplicationTitle: "Laser-adjustable" sutures for glaucoma trabeculectomy surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: GLAUCOMA; INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE; MICRO TECHNOLOGY; MICROMACHINING; SUTURE; TRABECULECTOMY
Abstract-Résumé: "MEDICAL PROBLEM: Glaucoma, a degenerative disease of the optic nerve, is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the world. In Canada alone, over 11,000 glaucoma operations are performed each year.  A major limitation of current glaucoma surgery is the inablility to precisely adjust the amount of intraocular pressure (IOP) post-operatively. IOP must be lowered as precisely as possible because an IOP that is lowered excessively can lead to blinding complications. Traditional 'trabeculectomy' surgery involves the creation of a scleral flap (a guarding trap door of tissue) and a small opening (fistula) to permit fluid egress from the eye's rigid corneo-scleral layers. This fluid is then captured under the mucus membrane layer of the eye called the conjunctiva, and reabsorbed by the body. The scleral flap is secured with standard sutures; however, precisely gauging the suture tension to attain the desired pressure lowering is difficult. Hence, in an attempt to avoid overly low IOP, most glaucoma surgeons suture the scleral flap tightly and perform 'laser suture lysis' as needed to break the sutures and allow the scleral flap to loosen. Unfortunately, completely severing sutures in this manner is frequently associated with a precipitous drop in IOP and hence this approach fails to adequately address the need for precisely-controlled IOP lowering.   OBJECTIVES: In response to the need for precise incremental IOP lowering, we have designed a new ""laser-adjustable"" device for implantation during glaucoma surgery. The new device integrates a miniature mechanical structure capable of redistributing the mechanical tension of the suture when the device interacts with laser light. This leads to a conformational change, which decreases the tightness of the suture without completely severing it. This allows for incremental and controlled IOP lowering. The laser required to alter the device is a safe and has been used for decades in eye care and is widely available in all ophthalmology departments. Our proposed project builds upon our initial work and will involve prototype optimization and testing."

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery of biomarkers of alzheimer's disease using comprehensive and quantitative metabolomics
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; ANALYTICAL CHEMISTRY; DISEASE BIOMARKERS; ISOTOPE LABELING; MASS SPECTROMETRY; METABOLITE IDENTIFICATION; METABOLOME PROFILING; METABOLOMICS; QUANTITIVE ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: "Currently 1 out of 11 Canadians suffers from some form of dementia. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading form of dementia. An AD diagnosis can only be made through a lengthy and expensive process involving in the systematic elimination of other possible causes of cognitive impairment. While diagnostic accuracy of AD can be 90%, it is often made in the later disease stages where irreversible brain damage has already occurred. There is no cure for AD. Developing drugs for treating the disease is hindered by the lack of definitive chemical biomarkers that can be used for monitoring the disease progression, particularly in the earlier stages of AD. Thus, finding sensitive biomarkers for the early diagnosis or detection of AD is critical for managing and treating this devastating disease.   While several proteins have been proposed as potential AD biomarkers, none has shown good specificity or sensitivity in clinical applications. The objective of this project is to apply newly developed mass spectrometry-based quantitative metabolomic techniques to search for small molecule biomarkers of AD. Our hypothesis is that in the early stages of AD, certain metabolic changes must be occurring in the brain and that by monitoring one or more key metabolites involved in these metabolic processes it may be possible to diagnose early-stage AD. To increase the likelihood of discovering specific AD biomarkers, we propose to apply state-of-the-art tools to comprehensively profile the metabolomes of urine, blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from AD patients. We will work with DynaLIFE Inc., a clinical diagnosis laboratory in Edmonton, to extent this study to validate the sensitivity and specificity of these biomarkers for diagnosis of AD. The anticipated results from this research include (1) verified (and validated in a small scale study) biomarkers for the early diagnosis of AD and (2) robust and inexpensive analytical methods for detecting these biomarkers. We believe that, if successful, this work could transform the management and treatment of AD and produce significant benefits to Canadians and the Canadian health care system."

TitreApplicationTitle: Toward a rational and novel therapy for clostridium difficile infection
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL DETECTION; BIOINFORMATICS; BIOSENSOR; CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE; FLUORESCENE; FUNCTIONAL NUCLEIC ACIDS; IN VITRO SELECTION; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MICROBIOTA; SPARSITY
Abstract-Résumé: "Clostridium difficile (C. difficile) infection (CDI) is one of the most frequent causes of health care-associated infectious diseases in Canada and other industrialized countries, with a mortality rate of approximately 6%. A Canadian study has reported that CDI for in-hospital adult patients is 65 per 100,000 patient-days in Canada. In addition, recurrence rates following standard antibiotics therapy are high, particularly for the elderly (greater than 40% for those over the age 65). Healthy bacteria in the colon are the key defense against CDI; the primary risk factor for developing CDI is the use of antibiotics because they kill these healthy bacteria allowing C. difficile to proliferate. Current treatment for CDI relies on other antibiotics (metronidazole or vancomycin), which lends itself to treatment failure as CDI is caused by exposure to antibiotic(s) to begin with. Fecal transplantation, where a bacteria mixture extracted from a stool sample from a healthy, screened individual is rectally administered to an affected patient, is developing into a highly effective therapy as it leads to restoration of healthy bacterial population in the infected patient and eradicating C. difficile. However, this therapy also comes with challenges: the need to identify a suitable donor for each patient; the lengthy time and cost required to screen for transmissible pathogens in the donors; as well as negative psychological factors. Given the unacceptable failure and recurrence rates using standard therapy, an alternative treatment is of paramount importance. Our team sets out to better understand CDI and to develop a rational and novel, microbiota based therapy to combat CDI. We expect to generate valuable information about innate bacterial community assembly patterns in both CDI patients and healthy individuals, establish effective microbiota to combat proliferation of C. difficile, develop novel probes for C. difficile surveillance, and most importantly set up the stage to pursue microbiota transplantation therapy as a new approach to combating CDI."

TitreApplicationTitle: "Interpenetrating network of a well-defined PEG hydrogel and two biocides as advanced solutions for burn wound care"
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIAL; HYDROGEL; INTERPENETRATING POLYMER NETWORK; NANOTECHNOLOGY; NOVEL DRESSINGS FOR BURN WOUNDS; RADICAL POLYMERIZATION; SURFACE MODIFICATION; WOUND HEALING; WOUND INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: "A burn is a type of injury to the skin caused by fire, heat, electricity, chemicals, radiation or friction. It occurs in all age groups. Burn wound infection remains the leading cause of skin graft failure and one of the leading causes of burn injury related mortality. Dressings impregnated with silver compounds are the mainstay of treatment for burn wounds. However, many commercially available silver based wound dressings cause trauma upon removal because of adhesion to the wound bed. A recent study has shown that burn dressing related pain is related to more severe depressive and posttraumatic stress symptoms. Furthermore, emerging resistance associated with silver based wound dressings is a growing concern.   The overall objective of this project is to develop a new method to deposit both a well-defined poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) hydrogel and a biocide (Ag nanoparticles or N-chloramines) onto wound dressings imparting both antimicrobial and atraumatic properties. This project aims to solve two problems: 1. Exploration of an alternative antibacterial agent to silver in view of the emerging resistance associated with silver based wound dressings. 2. Improvement of the adherence profile of burn dressings. It is hypothesized that 1.the well-defined PEG hydrogel, while repelling cell adherence, can promote cell migration and proliferation underneath it on wounds; 2. The diffuse rate of biocides can be controlled by the network structure of the PEG hydrogel to achieve minimal cytotoxicty and satisfying antibacterial efficacy. The proposal is truly interdisciplinary in nature, informed by the end users' needs and will create invaluable opportunities to train interdisciplinary HQP who can gain research knowledge and expertise spanning from biomedical engineering to clinical wound care practice. It also potentiates a greater opportunity for the commercialization of the basic research to clinical application with support from our partner Smith & Nephew. The availability of a practical and convenient burn wound management system for burn wound victims would definitely contribute to improving the quality of life for these patients and reducing overall healthcare cost in long term."

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the effect and mechanism of action of a Chinese herbal formulation as a potential anti-obesity therapeutic.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; HERBAL FORMULATION; IN VIVO OBESITY MODEL; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NUTRITION; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity represents a global disease affecting approximately one third of the greater than 1.7 billion overweight population. The rapidly increasing prevalence of obesity increases the risk of developing several serious related complications, imposes an enormous burden on the health care system, and continues to negatively influence the quality of human life. Thus, control of body weight is a top priority in nutritional and medical research. The global obesity trend also happens to be occurring in the face of a weight-loss product market largely characterized by mediocre long-term results and safety concerns, and an increasing global trend towards the development of safe and effective alternative products from natural sources. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and the use of herbal formulations is becoming an increasingly attractive form of alternative medicine, and is considered to have huge potential as a starting point for the development of natural products for the management of body weight. This study will aim to determine the effectiveness and safety of a Chinese herbal formulation as a potential weight loss product. The product will be fed to obese rats, on a schedule similar to human use of currently approved weight loss products. In a strictly controlled animal facility, the ability of our product to prevent weight gain will be assessed. Afterwards, in a laboratory setting, relevant tissues collected from the animals will be used for investigation into how the product affects a number of factors related to body weight control. Studies using related cell lines will then help uncover how the product works to produce the observed safe and effective weight loss results. The success of these studies will allow for the publication of valuable scientific information and unveil the potential for the development of our product into a novel weight loss product for human use, from a safe, natural source.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel antimircrobial and biofilm resistant coatings for urological and blood storage devices
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBACTERIAL SURFACES; ANTIBIOTICS RESISTENCE; ANTIMICROBIAL PEPTIDES; BACTERIAL CONTAMINATION; BIOCOMPATIBLE POLYMER COATINGS; BIOFILM RESISTENCE; BLOOD STORAGE DEVICES; IMPLANT ASSOCIATED INFECTION; POLYMERIC BIOMATERIALS; UROLOGICAL CATHETERS
Abstract-Résumé: "This research addresses serious challenge in hospital acquired infections: the prevention of bacterial infections associated with urological devices and bacterial growth in blood products for transfusion. Urinary catheters is one of most frequently used medical device in hospitals in North America and catheter associated infections account for a major share of hospital acquired infectious. In addition to increased mortality, these complications add millions of extra health care costs. Currently, antibiotics are our only method of attempting to deal with these infections, but do not work well due to intrinsic multidrug resistance of biofilms on catheter surface. The transfusion of bacterial contaminated blood products is another longstanding serious complication. In North America, approximately 15 million units of packed red blood cells and 4.5 million units of platelets are transfused every year. The incidence of bacterial contamination associated with the storage is as high as 1 per every 2000 units. This represents a huge cost to the health care system. Our collaborative project seeks novel solutions to these issues by developing new generation antibacterial surface coating on urinary catheters and blood bags without employing classical antibiotics. Since catheters, and blood bags are made of common plastic materials, similar technology can be applied to each devices. The project is based on the latest breakthroughs at UBC on screening and optimization of short broad spectrum cationic antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and their application to implant surfaces. The objectives of the project will be achieved by i  development of hydrophilic polymer brush based AMP coating for catheters, and blood bags and the optimization of their antimicrobial/anti-biofilm activity and biocompatibility, ii) elucidation of the mechanism of action of surface immobilized AMPs, iii) in vitro and in vivo evaluations of AMP coated blood bags and catheters in an animal infection model. The project will establish a strong collaboration among, science, engineering and medicine, and provide unique HQP training opportunities. The novel anti-infection coatings will also provide a general method for preventing bacterial infections associated with other medical devices."

TitreApplicationTitle: Real time guidance surgical navigation system for scaphoid fracture fixation
Keywords-MotsClés: CALIBRATION; FRACTURE REDUCTION; IMAGE GUIDED SURGERY; IMAGE REGISTRATION; ORTHOPAEDIC SURGERY; REAL TIME IMAGING; SCAPHOID; STATISTICAL ATLASES; ULTRASOUND; WRIST FRACTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Of the more than 300,000 wrist fractures that occur in North America each year, 90% include fracture of the scaphoid, a cashew-shaped small bone. The conventional treatment comprises immobilizing the wrist in a cast for several weeks, until union is detectable on X-ray images. Complications, including malunion or nonunion (that if untreated cause progressive wrist arthritis) are common, and lead to surgical treatment involving placing a screw in the central one-third of the bone. Since the scaphoid is locally as narrow as 6 mm, the surgical intervention is challenging, may result in damage to cartilage or the surrounding small bones, and demands strict accuracy with error tolerance of less than 2 mm. There is currently no efficient intra-operative means for accurate screw placement, short of surgical exposure that inevitably causes scarring and devascularization, and may dislodge previously non-displaced bone fragments. Less invasive techniques involve liberal usage of X-ray fluoroscopy, which often provides suboptimal images whilst exposing patient and surgical team to significant doses of ionizing radiation. Hence, there is an acute need for a minimally invasive, nonionizing navigation technique for visualizing the relative location of wrist anatomy and the screw for accurate fracture reduction. Ultrasound guidance is highly promising for this problem, as it is non-ionizing and real-time.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preventing postural hypotension, syncope and falls with smart materials and monitoring
Keywords-MotsClés: AGEING; DIELECTRIC ELASTOMER ACTUATORS; OEDEMA; ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION; PREGNANCY; SPINAL CORD INJURY; SYNCOPE; VARICOSE VEINS
Abstract-Résumé: "Disorders associated with excessive swelling of the legs are common. This swelling can be associated with pain, the production of varicose veins, reduced blood pressure (hypotension) when standing and cause light-headedness, fainting and falls. These events can significantly affect quality of life and, in severe cases, lead to death. It is well documented that up to 30% of the elderly have standing hypotension. Approximately 1 in 62 Canadians suffer with swelling (about 7 million people in North America. Swelling is common during pregnancy ranks highly as one of the causes of varicose veins. Control blood flow and volume in the lower limbs of spinal cord injury patients is also a health risk for the 86,000 Canadians living with spinal cord injury. Current physical remedies to these disorders include air compression leg massagers, which do not allow for ambulatory use, and compression stockings, which attempt to limit blood pooling and fluid build-up in the legs during walking. However, neither of these devices is able to adapt to the changing physiological conditions of the patient while compression stockings can provide only passive assistance to oedema. The main goal of this interdisciplinary project is therefore to develop a novel smart-technology-assisted therapy to effectively assist with fluid volume control in the legs of humans with excessive swelling or standing hypotension. Our objectives are to develop the technology and therapeutic application protocols required to provide effective blood pressure and volume control in three initial groups: spinal cord injury, pregnant women and the elderly. We will develop smart stockings whose compressive pressure can be modulated through external stimuli. These stockings will be embedded with Dielectric Elastomer Actuators (DEA), which are inexpensive smart materials that can deform through electrical activation. We propose an innovative solution that can potentially drastically alleviate cardiovascular disorders caused by swelling and chronic or temporary standing hypotension which can be used both in medical and domestic settings. The proposed technology is potentially inexpensive and portable."

TitreApplicationTitle: A MEMS-based ocular drug delivery device
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTROLLED DRUG DELIVERY; MAGNETIC DIAPHRAGM; MEMS; OCULAR RETINOPATHY
Abstract-Résumé: "Vision impairment often results from diabetes (proliferative diabetic retinopathy), affecting 500,000 Canadians (National Coalition for Vision Health). The annual Canadian health care costs of proliferative diabetic retinopathy are around one hundred million dollars (Statistic Canada). Current treatment options include laser ablation and vitrectomy, both use physical forces to remove overgrown blood vessels/blood clots in the eye. However, while up to 30% of patients received vitrectomy suffer from vision loss after 2 years of treatment, the long-term damages from the laser treatment have not been well understood. More recently, anti-angiogenic agents such as steroids and anti-growth factors, are proposed to treat advanced retinopathy. However, these agents need to be continually administered via regular intraocular injection using a needle and associated side-effects are retinal detachment, hemorrhage, and patient morbidity. Recently, docetaxel (an anticancer agent, DTX), has been identified as a powerful anti-angiogenic agent that inhibits capillary cell growth with minimal toxicity at the concentrations tested. We propose a magnetically controlled MEMS (Microelectromechanical Systems) device to administer DTX such that both side effects and health care costs will be minimized as our continual, on-demand drug delivery device needs only to be administered once over a period of 6 months."

TitreApplicationTitle: Optical guidance during neurosurgery for deep brain stimulation electrode implantation in the treatment of Parkinson's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR IMAGING; COHERENT RAMAN; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION SURGERY; MYELIN; NEUROSURGICAL SURGICAL GUIDANCE; OPTICAL SENSING; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; SPECTROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: "Deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery is a therapeutic avenue for late-stage Parkinson's disease patients who do not respond anymore to standard medication (L-Dopa). The surgery consists in the insertion of an electrode in the subthalamic nucleus (STN), a millimeter-sized region of the brain known to be the major driving force of the basal ganglia. The electrodes act to saturate the electrical activity of the STNs and alleviate the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease. This surgery does not cure the diseases, but instead manages its symptoms for approximately a decade, an extremely significant improvement on the quality of life of patients. The clinical outcome depends critically on the good positioning of the stimulating electrode in the dorsal region of the STN. Its accurate surgical placement is performed by measuring the local electrical neuronal activity with a smaller, less invasive measuring electrode prior to insertion of the final, larger stimulating electrode. Most importantly, the measuring electrode is first removed before the final stimulating electrode is inserted with only a coarse real-time X-ray for guidance.    Our team (neurosurgeon, specialists in imaging, fibers and lasers) proposes to design, develop, test, and deliver a small optical fiber-based device compatible with commercial electrodes to provide context and cellular information to unambiguously identify the STN and its neighbouring structures during the placement of the final stimulating electrode in DBS. This will provide real-time feedback to the surgery team for better electrode placement and more benefits to the patient with less secondary side-effects."

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing neonatal brain fuction with fMRI
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTER SCIENCES; ENGINEERING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEONATES; NEUROSCIENCE; PREMATURE BIRTH
Abstract-Résumé: Brain injury before or during birth can lead to cognitive and behavioural deficits that have long-term implications. If care is to be provided when it is most effective, these deficits must be detected early. Neonates, however, have a limited range of neurobehavioural responses and current tests are inadequate. Although a substantial literature now exists on using neuroimaging to measure brain function in adults, this work has not been translated effectively to assessing function and dysfunction in the neonatal brain. A first key challenge is that neonates are different from adults, both behaviourally and physiologically; they cannot be asked to remain still during the imaging process and the chemical structure of their brain differs significantly from that of the adult brain. We will apply new acquisition and analysis methods to solve these problems, thereby establishing reliable neuroimaging protocols for the neonatal brain. A second challenge is to sensitively and reliably assess cognitive function in neonates. We will identify suitable stimulation protocols, drawing on a hierarchical design that has been previously applied by our team to the problem of assessing cognitive function in adult patients who are diagnosed as vegetative. In the first weeks of life, we will use functional neuroimaging to characterize basic sensory processing, recognition and memory, and acquire state-of-the-art neuroanatomical measures. A third challenge is to evaluate how to combine these measures to best predict later developmental outcome. In collaboration with the Children's Hospital and London Health Sciences Centre, we will develop a tool for clinical practice that combines anatomical, functional and neurobehavioural assessments to improve diagnostic accuracy and facilitate early intervention

TitreApplicationTitle: Simultaneous optical imaging of oxygenation and blood flow for chronic monitoring of stroke and seizure activity
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHOTONICS; BLOOD FLOW; EPILEPSY; FLUORESCENCE; IN VIVO RODENT IMAGING; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; OPTICAL BRAIN IMAGING; STROKE; VCSEL LASER DIODES
Abstract-Résumé: "Patients surviving ischemic stroke often express delayed epileptic syndromes. Late poststroke seizures occur after a latency period lasting from several months to years after the insult. These seizures might result from ischemia-induced neuronal death and associated morphological and physiological changes that are only partly elucidated. There is a need for low-cost imaging technique that will observe these changes and assist in treatment evaluation. We have recently shown that wide field optical imaging can be used for fast simultaneous imaging of blood flow and oxygenation in a rodent brain, a surrogate to neural activity. Building on ongoing collaboration for the past two years with researchers and clinicians in Toronto's hospitals and with QImaging, a worldwide leading biomedical imaging camera maker from Surrey, BC, we will translate these results to pre-clinical studies in the hospitals and to commercialization of the imaging system by QImaging. Our objectives are: (1) to demonstrate an optical system to image and quantitatively map brain oxygenation and blood flow in vivo in rodents; (2) to develop a low cost, lightweight portable camera for longitudinal epilepsy and stroke studies in freely behaving rodents (critical for the study of disease processes and evolution), and (3) to evaluate the effects of specific treatments in the same animal (thereby greatly increasing sensitivity); Our project will provide an important imaging tool for better insight on the relation between seizures and underlying brain disorders such as hypoxic-ischemic injury, stroke, or hypoglycemia over long time periods and to translate these findings for future improvement of existing NIRS systems for patient care and evaluation in neonates and children."

TitreApplicationTitle: Thérapie tissulaire de la cornée: utilisation d'un élastomère thermoplastique pour la bioingénierie du stroma cornéen
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCOMPATIBILITE; CONCEPTION ET FABRICATION 3D; CULTURE CELLULAIRE; GREFFES; GENIE TISSULAIRE; POLYMERES; POTENTIEL THERAPEUTIQUE; THERMOPLASTIQUES; TOPOGRAPHIE DE LA CORNEE; ELASTOMERES
Abstract-Résumé: "La cornee est le tissu transparent qui forme le devant de l'oeil. Son architecture particuliere fait en sorte que tout changement dans sa structure resulte en une perte de vision. Plus de 50 000 greffes de cornees sont effectuees chaque annee en Amerique du Nord pour traiter la cecite. La reconstruction en laboratoire de cornees humaines est une alternative fort prometteuse pour le remplacement des tissus corneens malades. Cette reconstruction requiert: 1) une expertise en nanomateriaux, 2) une expertise en genie tissulaire, 3) une expertise en etude des formes tridimensionnelles et 4) une expertise medicale pour comprendre le besoin clinique et assurer le transfert des connaissances du laboratoire au patient. Or, cette combinaison d'expertises est ici regroupee pour la premiere fois pour ce projet de recherche. Nous elaborerons un polymere 3D nanostructure sur lequel nous cultiverons les cellules de la cornee. Le but ultime etant de recreer une cornee ayant une forme, une epaisseur et une transparence similaires a celles des cornees humaines. Ces nouveaux tissus pourraient servir d'alternatives pour guerir differentes maladies de la cornee."

TitreApplicationTitle: Positron emission tomography imaging methods to investigate host cell resistance to antibodies against the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; HER-2; HERCEPTIN RESISTANCE; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; TUMOUR XENOGRAFT TRANSPLANT
Abstract-Résumé: An important goal in cancer research for personalized medicines is to develop techniques that can evaluate therapeutic strategy early on to assist oncologists in making improved therapeutic decisions. Recently, significant investment has been made in Canada by all levels of government to establish new facilities focusing on Positron emission tomography (PET) research and expected to play important role in Canadian healthcare. This unique medical imaging technique can extract biochemical information about an individual's disease at any location in the entire body without any surgical procedures and can provide pictures representative of overall tumour biochemistry, as opposed to a biopsy for tumour diagnosis. This project aims to develop PET imaging methods to eventually replace biopsy procedures to better predict which breast cancer patients are most likely to benefit from receiving Herceptin, a drug for Her2 positive metastatic breast cancer (Her2 is expressed on tumour cells while healthy cells do not show this molecule) and we will also investigate why women who have Her2 positive breast cancer that initially respond to Herceptin almost always become resistant within one year, a common and serious problem in cancer therapy. For this project, we will use a unique breast cancer cell line as a tool to study Herceptin therapy and resistance because these cells closely mimic the behavior of breast cancer in human patients. We will identify biochemical differences in Herceptin sensitive and Herceptin resistant tumours as well as metastatic disease to further understand why patients develop resistance and can this resistance be accurately predicted using PET. Also, less than half of all women who are prescribed Herceptin therapy receive therapeutic benefit. So, an accurate method to screen breast cancer patients for Herceptin therapy can avoid the unnecessary side effects of Herceptin, eliminate the time wasted to determine the therapy and decrease the health care cost.

TitreApplicationTitle: Subject-specific Electromyography-Driven Musculoskeletal Model of the Hip Joint Applied to Femoroacetabular Impigement Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: FEMOROACETABULAR IMPINGEMENT,; HIP , ELECTROMYOGRAPHY , SUBJECT-SPECIFICITY; MOTION ANALYSIS, MRI, CT SCAN,; MUSCULOSKELETAL MODELING; NONLINEAR RELATIONSHIPS, JOINT LOADING
Abstract-Résumé: Femoroacetabular impingement is a hip bone deformity that affects up to 25% of young active male adults. If not treated, it can degenerate into hip osteoarthritis, a cause of long-term disability. In 2000, 10% of Canadians were suffering from osteoarthritis, imposing an economic burden of $4.4 billion. This warrants an increased awareness of the development mechanisms of femoroacetabular impingement to contribute to the osteoarthritis prevention. An early diagnosis of femoroacetabular impingement is not always possible because the aetiology is still unclear. High mechanical stresses at the site of the bone deformity are postulated to be one of the causes. Since in vivo measurements are invasive, musculoskeletal models are the most ethically acceptable approach to estimate the joint loadings and mechanical stress. To our knowledge, no subject-specific musculoskeletal models exist for this joint. However, studies demonstrated that the specificity of a musculoskeletal model is crucial to obtain reliable results. Therefore, the purpose of this research is the development of a subject-specific musculoskeletal model of the hip, to estimate the joint loading, with the ultimate goal of understanding the development of femoroacetabular impingement. The musculoskeletal model will require the anatomical description of the hip joint and the biomechanical simulation of the principal muscles wrapping this articulation. Once validated, the model will estimate the hip contact forces of patients at different progression levels of femoroacetabular impingement (normal, asymptomatic and symptomatic), greatly contributing to our knowledge of the preventative joint degeneration strategies and femoroacetabular impingement to osteoarthritis development mechanisms. Moreover, the integration of the subject-specific anatomy and muscles activity makes this thesis an original contribution to the field of biomechanics.

TitreApplicationTitle: An interdisciplinary approach towards the development of a disease-stabilizing treatment for Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BUCHWALD-HARTWIG AMINATION; CATALYSIS; CROSS- COUPLING; DRUG DESIGN; INORGANIC CHEMISTRY; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; NEURODEGENERATION; ORGANIC SYNTHESIS; PALLADIUM
Abstract-Résumé: "The aim of this research is to develop small drug-like molecules that concomitantly prevent the aberrant misfolding and aggregation of amyloid beta, tau and alpha-synuclein - three amyloid peptides implicated in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). With a Canadian-based biotechnology company (Treventis Corporation) identified as a potential industrial partner, the technology will be transferred with the aim of developing a disease-modifying drug to treat AD. Through a multi-disciplinary collaboration, the following objectives will be achieved: 1) A series of recently identified New Chemical Entities (NCEs) will be screened in vitro through a battery of anti-aggregation and cell toxicity assays (Weaver group - biochemistry/microbiology); 2) 120 NCEs will be synthesized in total by the medicinal chemistry group (Reed group - medicinal chemistry) and optimized for drug-like properties and anti-aggregant potency; and 3) New palladium-catalyzed technology will be developed and utilized to allow access to the core structure of the targeted NCEs, thereby allowing access to structural variation within the NCE family that would otherwise not be feasible by use of conventional synthetic organic methods (Stradiotto group - inorganic chemistry and catalysis). This novel, multi-component collaboration will be crucial for the success of this project, and will provide an ideal platform for interdisciplinary training in the translational chemistry of drug design with emphasis on addressing AD - one of the most pressing health-care challenges facing modern society."

TitreApplicationTitle: Is better man belly bus' than good food waste: The sociocultural dimensions of managing the chronic disease type 2 diabetes mellitus
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE, TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS,; COMPLIANCE, PATIENT AGENCY, ETHNOHISTORY; CULTURAL COMPATIBILITY, DIET IN CHRONIC DISEASE; LIFESTYLE TRANSFORMATION, QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; MEDICAL ANTHROPOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic diseases are some of the major causes of illness and death internationally and their prevalence continues to rise. Dietary habits are among the most important and modifiable causes of chronic diseases, with changes producing significantly improved outcomes in such diseases as type 2 diabetes (or diabetes). Diabetes is very prevalent amongst persons of Indian descent in Trinidad, with similar prevalence rates found amongst the First Nations peoples in Canada and Native Americans in the United States. For Indian Trinidadians, as for First Nations peoples and Native Americans, complex relationships between cultural identity, history, memory, religion and power are instantiated through symbolic features of their dietary practices. Though these populations differ greatly and have been affected by different historical forces, they all display considerable resistance to dietary change. They are described similarly in the literature as noncompliant, a term with moral overtones that may negatively impact the medical care they receive. Given the complex significance of diet, transformations require not the compliance of an individual patient, but of complex interconnected systems of patient agency: regular family routines, established networks of friends and community relations. I will perform qualitative research to explore the interaction of medical notions of compliance and patient notions of agency in the context of family, social networks and ethnic community. Integrating epidemiological and ethnographic methods, I will explore the perceptions and perspectives of both doctors and patients to re-frame the management of diabetes. The outcome I intend is a series of recommendations to assist medical practitioners that are culturally compatible with the Trinidad cultural space. I intend for these results to provide a general framework that can be extrapolated for the lifestyle management of other chronic diseases in diverse cultural contexts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Diagnostic Methods for Imaging Amyloid Beta in the eye in association with alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE OPTICS; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID BETA; BIOMARKERS; EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; HUMAN AND ANIMAL STUDIES; OPTICAL AND FLUORESCENCE IMAGING; RETINA; SCANNING LASER OPHTHALMOSCOPY; UHR OPTICAL CHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: "There is no cure and no early detection method broadly available for Alzheimer's disease (AD). Definite diagnosis is only after death. AD has a large negative impact on individual health and an enormous cost to society. Early diagnosis and improved disease tracking lead to earlier and better treatment. Amyloid beta forms deposits in the brain early in AD. We will develop a simpler method to image amyloid beta deposits in the living neural tissue at the back of the eye. Campbell's group has shown that these deposits should be large enough to be detected in images of the eye. They could then be used to diagnose and monitor the worsening stages of AD. We will explore the association between amyloid beta in the retina and the severity of AD. Amyloid beta deposits in retinas will be assessed after death. We will characterize the location, density, size and shape of retinal deposits. In a separate UBC study, the stage of AD will be measured in the clinic before death. Their  brains are being imaged using PET and MRI scans. In addition, markers of AD in their blood and spinal fluid are measured. Characteristics of the retinal deposits will be compared with the stage of AD assessed by all the other measures. The living brains and retinas of a mouse model of AD will be imaged as they develop AD and after death. The time of appearance and characteristics of the amyloid beta deposits in the retinas and brains will be compared. Raman spectroscopy will be investigated as a noninvasive detection method of amyloid beta deposits in the retina. From these studies, we will understand the relationship between amyloid beta deposits in the retina and the severity of AD. We will then optimize the design of a novel system which will aid the diagnosis of Alzheimer disease by imaging the living retina. From the mouse model of AD, we will collect preliminary data on the performance of the system. The eye provides a clear view of neural tissue. Diagnosis of AD via this new imaging technology will be less expensive and more accessible to patients than current brain imaging methods."

TitreApplicationTitle: Realistic lung deposition models and measurements (REALiSM^2)
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRBORNE NANOPARTICLES; ATMOSPHERIC AEROSOL; ENVIRONMENTAL AEROSOL; INHALATION AEROSOL; PHARMACEUTICAL AEROSOL; REGIONAL LUNG DEPOSITION
Abstract-Résumé: "Aerosol particles may have either positive or negative effects on human health. On the positive side, pharmaceutical aerosols are specifically designed to deliver drugs to the lung, while on the negative side, some particles in the atmosphere or the workplace have been shown to have a toxic effects on human health. In both these applications it is important to know the regional particle dosage i.e. the amount of particles that deposit in each area of the lung. However, existing models to predict regional dosages have not been validated in children, and do not apply to low density and nonspherical particles (such as diesel agglomerate particles). To overcome these limitations, we will construct replicas of portions of the human lungs of children and adults from which particle deposition can be measured and validated models developed. The replicas will be made using CT scans of child and adult subjects and a rapid-prototyping machine. Using a variety of experimental techniques that we have used previously to study extrathoracic deposition, the particle deposition in the replicas will be measured without human exposure. Furthermore, experiments will be done with a variety of particle morphologies and densities, including ultra-low density particles and soot nanoagglomerates. In parallel to this research, and in order to facilitate rapid, on-site field measurements of aerosol exposure, we propose to adapt our airway replicas into an electronic lung. The electronic lung will detect the particles by electrically pre-charging the particles and detecting their deposition by the use electrometers in each region of an artificial lung. This will allow rapid characterization of aerosol exposure directly in terms of how much aerosol deposits in the different lung regions. The results of this research will allow improved measurement and assessment of the risks associated with exposure of airborne particulate matter as well as improved respiratory drug delivery, particularly in children, but also in adults. Given the considerable morbidity and mortality associated with both respiratory disease and inhalation of airborne particulates, the proposed research will provide important improvements to the health of Canadians."

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of the genetic regulation of fetal hemoglobin production in humans
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-THALASSEMIA; CD34+; DNA GENOTYPING; DNA METHYLATION; FETAL HEMOGLOBIN; GENETIC ASSOCIATION STUDY; NEXT-GENERATION DNA RE-SEQUENCING; RNA-SEQ; SICKLE CELL ANEMIA
Abstract-Résumé: Sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia are blood diseases caused by inherited mutations in the gene that encodes a subunit of hemoglobin, the oxygen carrier in the blood. Studies of the natural history of these diseases have identified fetal hemoglobin as a strong modifier of disease severity: sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia patients with high fetal hemoglobin levels have less severe complications and a longer life expectation. Re-activating fetal hemoglobin production in these patients represents to date the single most promising therapeutic strategy. We and others have identified genes that regulate fetal hemoglobin production in humans. As a proof-of-principle of the value of these gene discoveries, one of our collaborators on this project recently showed that inactivation of a gene that we had identified using a genetic strategy (BCL11A) can rescue the blood phenotypes observed in a mouse model of sickle cell disease (Xu et al., Science, 2011).   We recently showed that genetic variation at the known fetal hemoglobin genes explains 50% of the heritable variation in fetal hemoglobin levels. The central objective of this proposal is to generate comprehensive genetic, transcriptomic and epigenomic datasets that will help identifying the remaining genes that modulate fetal hemoglobin production in humans. Identification of new genes involved in fetal hemoglobin regulation might guide the development of new drugs to treat patients with sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rapid in vitro screening of nanomaterial distributions and toxicity
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DISTRIBUTION; DRUG DELIVERY; EMBRYONIC ORGANISMS; IMAGING; MATURE ORGANISMS; NANOMATERIALS; NANOTECHNOLOGY; SCREENING PROTOCOLS; TOXICITY
Abstract-Résumé: "Develop screening tools for rapid toxicity and biodistribution assessment of nanomaterials. Using our biological models and findings (from first CHRP grant), we will develop devices and protocols to rapidly screen for the toxicity of nanomaterials. Our   current CHRP grant has shown the following: 1) uptake of nanoparticles (NPs) from the blood stream depends primarily on charge and then on size; 2) endocytosis of NPs into vascular endothelial cells also depends critically on the charge and size of the NP and on the conditions of blood flow; 3) the aggregation state of the NPs in the blood stream affects uptake.   NOVELTY: The screening of nanoparticle toxicity is laborious and expensive. Given the large number of different NP compositions, surface chemistries, shapes, and aggregation states, it is not realistic to evaluate each of these conditions using standard toxicological strategies. Here we propose to develop devices and protocols that would accelerate the analysis of NP toxicity and enable researchers to establish the properties of a nanomaterial responsible for certain toxic responses. The approach to rapid screening will be a two-stage assessment. The first stage will screen the nanomaterials' propensity to form aggregates, to associate with serum proteins, and to partition into a model cell membrane environment. The second stage will assess the distribution of NPs in a blood vessel mimetic flow chamber."

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1) Signaling on Chronic Phase and Blast Crisis Phase of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC MYELOID LEUKEMIA STEM CELLS; CYTOKINES; INNATE IMATINIB RESISTANCE MECHANISMS; INSULIN-LIKE GROWTH FACTOR AND DRUG RESISTANCE IN LEUKEMIA
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML) results when bone marrow cells acquire an abnormal enzyme called BCR-ABL. Newly developed drugs that inhibit the BCR-ABL enzyme show promise as agents to control CML. However, some patients do not to respond to these drugs or their disease eventually becomes resistant to their beneficial effects. Thus, it is important to more completely understand the mechanisms that regulate the growth properties of CML in order to develop new therapies to replace or complement current treatments. We have discovered that abnormal IGF-1 gene activity contributes to the aggressive growth properties and drug resistance of CML. The objective of this proposal is to determine the mechanisms by which IGF-1 confers these properties on CML cells. This information will be invaluable for improving CML diagnosis and identifying new therapies designed to eradicate the CML cells responsible for drug resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: A muscle density, bone microarchitecture, falls, and physical activity analysis of the Saskatoon Canadian Multicentre Osteoporosis Study Cohort
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCELEROMETRY; AGING; BONE; FALLS; FRACTURE RISK; FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY; HIGH RESOLUTION PQCT; HUMANS; PERIPHERAL QUANTITATIVE COMPUTED TOMOGRAPY (PQCT); SKELETAL MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Falls account for more than half of emergency room visits and most osteoporotic fractures in the elderly. Research suggests that high amounts of fat within muscle tissues (low muscle density) can increase the risk of hip fracture and hospitalization. Muscle density decreases in tandem with muscle function. On the other hand, bone structure and strength adapt to the forces created when muscles contract to move the body. The role of muscle size, strength, and density on bone structure is not fully understood. We have previously demonstrated that females who report falls exhibit lower muscle densities within their legs. There is also evidence from younger adults that low muscle density is linked to low levels of physical activity. However, similar studies in the elderly rely solely on unreliable physical activity questionnaires, warranting more conclusive research. To investigate these knowledge gaps I will invite 153 community-dwelling elderly men & women for baseline and 12-month follow-up measurements. We will measure their muscle and bone properties using state-of-the-art computed tomography imaging technologies, clinical test used by physical therapists, and objective measures of physical activity by using small activity monitoring devices (accelerometers). This will allow me to define the ability of  leg muscle size and density to predict fall risk. My study will also define the ability of physical activity to predict muscle density; and the ability of muscle density, size, and physical activity to predict bone structure in the upper and lower body. This work seeks to address important knowledge gaps in our understanding of muscle and bone health and physical activity in the elderly. More importantly, the results will help to devise new prevention and rehabilitation targets in older individuals who are at risk for falls and fractures.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Efficacy Trial of Therapist Assisted Internet Cognitive Behaviour Therapy Program for Individuals with a Chronic Health Condition
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC CARE MODEL; CHRONIC HEALTH CONDITIONS; MENTAL HEALTH ISSUES; PRIMARY HEALTHCARE; QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE METHODS; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL; SELF- MANAGMENT OF HEALTH; THERAPIST ASSISTED INTERNET COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic health conditions, such as diabetes and chronic pain, are pressing public health issues facing Canadians, as they account for significant disability and loss of health-related quality of life. Traditional face-to-face Cognitive Behaviour Therapy is effective in assisting individuals with the resulting emotional impact of having a chronic health condition (i.e. depression, anxiety, anger, frustration). Internet-based interventions can overcome service access barriers such as time, mobility, and geography. One such program is Therapist Assisted Internet Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (TACBT). TAICBT involves patients reviewing several sessions of psychoeducation over the internet, followed by contact with a therapist who provides support and directs therapeutic activities via e-mail. Preliminary research supports the efficacy of TAICBT for anxiety, depression, and panic. This study seeks to develop a TAICBT program to support adults with the self-management of chronic health conditions, living in rural and urban communities in Southern Saskatchewan. The study will involve conducting an efficacy trial of this TAICBT program. This TAICBT program will focus on assisting individuals with self-management of their condition, which is consistent with the Chronic Care Model. Topics to be covered include: Supporting management of the condition (e.g., exercise, diet, sleep), maintaining important life roles, relaxation training, and managing depression and anxiety, which are commonly associated with a chronic health condition diagnosis. This TAICBT program is intended to benefit a broad spectrum of the Canadian population with chronic health conditions, especially those populations of individuals that may not be large enough to justify more disease specific, targeted programs. With the large impact chronic disease has on the Canadian population, it is vital to learn to treat chronic diseases effectively, using the latest available knowledge and technology in practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Managing arthritis using physical activity: Identifying disease- and activity-specific psychosocial beliefs to improve adherence.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY-SPECIFIC PSYCHOSOCIAL BEIEFS; ADHERENCE; ARTHRITIS; DISEASE MANAGEMENT; DISEASE-SPECIFIC PSYCHOSOCIAL BELIEFS; HEALTH PROMOTION; LAB-BASED RESEARCH; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SURVEY RESEARCH; THEORY DRIVEN
Abstract-Résumé: Three out of every five Canadians have some form arthritis by age 65. Arthritis causes personal health challenges, such as lower quality of life and disability, and comes with a national cost. In Canada, an imposing $6.4 billion a year is linked to arthritis-related increases in health care use (e.g., hospital stays, medications) and decreases in work productivity. Although there is no cure for arthritis, it can be managed. Regular physical activity for 150+ minutes each week is key for people to effectively manage their arthritis, reduces their health care use, and is cheaper than other treatment options (e.g., prescription drugs). Unfortunately, 60% of Canadians with arthritis are not active enough to reach the recommended level. Motivating these people to be more active and stick with activity in the long term remains a major problem. Our research will identify the key beliefs necessary to motivate people to do regular activity. Our approach is novel because we use two theories to study two different types of changeable beliefs. We will study beliefs that people have about their disease (e.g., how arthritis affects their health) as well as beliefs that people have about trying to remain active when faced with the demands of everyday life (e.g., fitting physical activity into a busy schedule). Our studies are important because they will identify beliefs that are central to motivating activity and that must change in some people to help them better manage their arthritis. Using our findings, our future goals are to develop and offer an effective physical activity and belief change program to help people stick with doing regular activity at the recommended level so they can better manage their arthritis. This, in turn, will contribute to less health care demands and costs. Helping people with arthritis to be more active will produce both individual and societal level impacts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and functional characterization of SCO-dependent, mitochondrial regulation of cellular copper homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELLULAR COPPER HANDLING; COX ASSEMBLY FACTORS; CYTOCHROME C OXIDASE (COX); GENETICS; HUMAN DISEASES; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; REDOX SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria are small compartments within the cell that make ATP, the chemical form of energy that supports normal cell function. ATP is produced by the concerted effort of a number of enzyme complexes. One of these enzyme complexes, called cytochrome c oxidase (COX), requires copper for its activity, and an inability to deliver copper to the enzyme during its assembly results in a severe COX deficiency, and causes muscle, heart, liver and brain disease in children. I recently discovered that Synthesis of Cytochrome c Oxidase 1 (SCO1) and SCO2, two of the many proteins that deliver copper to COX, also fulfill novel and unexpected roles in regulating how copper is handled elsewhere in the cell. This additional function likely serves to minimize the potential toxicity of copper as it is transported, and ensure that it is appropriately distributed throughout the cell; however, much remains to be learned about how this process is coordinated and, in particular, how SCO proteins communicate with other proteins found elsewhere in the cell to ultimately control how copper is handled. Therefore, the overall goal of my research proposal is to use cultured patient cells and transgenic mouse models as tools to identify and characterize the various components of this pathway. By doing so, we will understand much more about how mitochondria make fundamental contributions to the safe handling and appropriate distribution of copper throughout the cell and, indeed, the entire body. This in turn may lead to the development of novel therapies with which to treat human diseases that result from an isolated COX deficiency or cellular copper handling defects, which are currently lacking.

TitreApplicationTitle: The physiological impact of postmenopausal oophorectomy on hormone levels in women with BRCA1 mutation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGENS; AROMATASE; BRCA1/BRCA2; BREAST BIOPSY; BREAST CANCER; DIAGNOSTICS; ESTROGENS; MICROFLUIDICS; OOPHORECTOMY; POSTMENOPAUSAL
Abstract-Résumé: "Hormonal factors are critical in determining a woman's risk of developing breast cancer. This is true both for women in the general population and for women with an inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation. Much of the evidence for hormonal breast carcinogenesis comes from clinical and epidemiologic studies of circulating estrogen and other hormones; however, it is believed that local breast tissue levels of hormones are much more relevant than blood levels. Traditionally, scientists and clinicians have not been able to measure breast tissue levels with accuracy because of inadequate technology and access to samples. This problem could be solved if an assay were developed to reliably measure representative hormone levels in a very small amount of breast tissue obtained through a needle biopsy.   Surgical removal of the ovaries (i.e., oophorectomy) among women with a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation is associated with significant reductions in breast and ovarian cancer risks. We have recently shown that the reduction in risk associated with surgical menopause is much stronger than that associated with natural menopause. This suggests that the postmenopausal ovary is producing hormones that contribute to the risk of breast cancer. Studies directly quantifying levels of androgens, estrogens and aromatase activity in the both the pre- and postmenopausal breast tissue will help elucidate a role of endogenous hormones. We will evaluate a new technology that uses a miniaturized, integrated method for hormone analysis that relies on digital microfluidics and only requires one-microliter in a group of high-risk women by quantifying breast hormone levels before and after oophorectomy. We can then measure the impact of oophorectomy on the tissue levels of these hormones. We propose to develop the technology for this series of experiments. We will collect blood and breast tissue samples using fine-needle microaspiration, a relatively non-invasive "

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure and Mechanism of the Plasma Membrane Chloride/Bicarbonate Exchanger, AE1
Keywords-MotsClés: AE1; BICARBONATE TRANSPORT; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; FLUORESCENCE; GAS EXCHANGE; MEMBRANE TRANSPORT; PH REGULATION; RED BLOOD CELL; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: The outside of each of our cells is made of a membrane, whose role is to hold in the cell contents and to regulate the normal composition of our cells by moving waste out of the cell and required raw materials into the cell. Membrane proteins carry out the tasks of moving substances in and out of the cell to regulate life. In our red blood cells, half of the cell's surface is occupied by a membrane protein called AE1. The abundance of the protein reflects the key roles of the protein, aiding in the cell's ability to carry carbon dioxide waste, and controlling the cell's skeleton, to maintain the cell's rigidity as the red cell moves throughout our blood system. Our goal is to understand how AE1 caries out its critical functions. This will provide information relevant to 1. stability of red blood cells in blood banks, 2. the infection of red cells by malarial parasites and 3.The basis for some blood group antigens.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implication of DEPTOR in the regulation of glucose/lipid homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOGENESIS; GLUCOCORTICOIDS; GLUCOSE AND LIPID HOMEOSTASIS; INSULIN RESISTANCE; INSULIN SIGNALING; LIVER METABOLISM; METABOLIC DISEASES; MTOR SIGNALING; OBESITY; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity, which is caused by an imbalance between energy intake and expenditure, increases the risk of developing multiple disorders including insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemias, cardiovascular diseases, and cancers. The excessive accumulation of adipose tissue in the obese is associated with elevated circulating fatty acids and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Together with nutrient excess, these molecules impair systemic glucose and lipid homeostasis by reducing the ability of the liver and the muscle to normally respond to insulin. Treating obesity through diet and exercise proves to be very difficult in the long term. Therefore, safe molecular strategies aimed at improving metabolism in peripheral tissues represent interesting approaches to treat obesity-related diseases. The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a protein that senses nutrients and growth factors and regulate anabolic processes in various organs. Over the last decade, several groups have observed that mTOR activity is elevated in the tissues of obese humans/mice and contributes the promotion of insulin resistance and to the deterioration of glucose/lipid homeostasis. Recently, we have identified DEP domain containing mTOR-interacting protein (DEPTOR) as a protein that binds and inhibits mTOR. The role of DEPTOR in regulating tissue function and systemic glucose/lipid metabolism in the normal state or in obesity is unknown. Whether DEPTOR could affect the metabolic profile of the obese by modulating mTOR activity has never been tested. This research proposal aims to determine the implication of DEPTOR in controlling metabolism and to understand its role in the development of obesity-related metabolic disorders.
