TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the system level costs and benefits of improving equity in access to psychological services for depression in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: INCREASING EQUITY IN ACCESS TO VULNERABLE POPULATIONS; THE COSTS AND BENEFITS OF PSYCHOTHERAPY FOR DEPRESSION; THE SYSTEM LEVEL COSTS OF PUBLICLY FUNDED PSYCHOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: The cost-effectiveness of psychological therapies for the treatment of many common mental disorders such as depression has been shown in many studies worldwide: there is a significant improvement in recovery and remission rates.  In Canada, the Standing Senate's committee 'Out of the Shadows at Last' reports an underuse of evidence based psychological therapies as part of a complete treatment package of mental health care. A recent report of the Alberta Ministry of Health and the newly created Mental Health Commission of Canada on the treatment of depression supported psychological therapies as effective and access as a key issue to be explored in our health system. A recent Canadian study showed that income and education barriers exist for people with mental health needs when it comes to the use of specialty providers of psychotherapy such as psychologists offering evidence based treatments as part of adequate and quality mental health care treatment options.  The purpose of this project is to inform policy makers by determining the costs and benefits to society of rendering psychological services available for people not already covered or have insurance for such services thus decreasing disparities in equity to access mental health services in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Correction of the dystrophin gene with Zinc Finger Proteins and TAL effector nuclease.
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG DEVELOPMENT; DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; GENE CORRECTION; GENE THERAPY; TALEN; ZFN
Abstract-Résumé: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy is due to mutations in a gene coding for a protein called dystrophin, a protein normally located under the plasma membrane of the muscle fibers. In 70% of the patients, the mutation is a deletion of one or several exons. These deletions are such that the total number of nucleotides, which are deleted is not a multiple of 3 nucleotides.  To translate the genetic code into proteins, a group of 3 nucleotides called a codon permits to identify the right amino acid to include in the protein. When there is a deletion, which is not a multiple of 3 nucleotides, the codons are changed and thus the amino acids that are included in the protein are changed. Moreover, a stop codon is eventually met and the synthesis of the protein is terminated prematurely. This incomplete dystrophin protein cannot attach to a group of proteins that are in the membrane. The present application aims to modify the dystrophin gene using Zinc Finger Nucleases and Tal effector nucleases to restore the expression of a dystrophin protein, which will be missing some parts but which will be nevertheless functional.

Keywords-MotsClés: CORNEA; CORNEAL DYSTROPHY; GENETIC DISEASE; HIGH THROUGHPUT ASSAY; ION TRANSPORT; MOUSE MODEL; PROTEIN MISFOLDING; SMALL MOLECULE CORRECTORS; VISION; WATER
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this application is to find ways to cure and prevent three forms of genetic blindness (Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy, Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy and Harboyan syndrome). The cornea is the outmost layer of the eye. In corneal dystrophy diseases, the cornea fills with fluid that makes vision hazy and significantly impairs vision. At present the only treatment for this condition is corneal transplant. The three conditions have in common that they are caused by mutations of a poorly understood gene called SLC4a11. The goal of our studies is to develop treatments for these corneal dystrophies, by testing the way to "fix" the diseased SLC4a11 protein in appropriate mice and cell culture models.

Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; CALCIUM IMAGING; CONFOCAL IMAGING; DORSAL ROOT GANGLIA; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; ION CHANNELS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PAIN
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory investigates the role of pore proteins in the membrane of nerve cells that detect pain signals. These proteins detect noxious stimuli when a person, for example, burns their hands or hits their finger nail with a hammer. In disease conditions, these proteins become highly sensitive to the stimulus and will activate the nervous system to produce pain sensation for non noxious stimulation (moderate temperature or light touch). Such chronic pain conditions can last for years and affect over 25% of the Canadian population with a strong impact on patient's quality of life. My research program will use unique approaches from molecular studies and behavioral studies in the whole animal to understand how aberrant function of these proteins is regulated in disease conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Régulation des récepteurs de la neurotensine: Implication dans le contrôle de la douleur
Keywords-MotsClés: DOULEUR; INTERACTIONS MOLECULAIRES; INTERNALISATION ET TRAFIC DES RECEPTEURS; NEUROPEPTIDES; RECEPTEURS COUPLES AUX PROTEINES G
Abstract-Résumé: Le but de ce projet est d'elucider les mecanismes d'action et les roles des neuropeptides et de leurs recepteurs dans le cerveau. Un de ces neuropeptides, la neurotensine (NT), joue un role important dans les mecanismes de controle de la douleur. Des donnees recentes suggerent que les recepteurs NTS1 et NTS2 joueraient un role majeur dans les effets analgesiques de ce neuropeptide. Nous proposons donc de caracteriser les interactions entre la NT et ses recepteur au niveau moleculaire, cellulaire et physiologique. Notre hypothese est que la reconnaissance de ces recepteurs par la NT, au niveau de la surface des neurones, va entrainer des changements des proprietes de cette cellule receptrice au niveau membranaire mais aussi intracellulaire. En effet, la transmission de l'information ne s'arrete pas a la membrane, mais se poursuit par penetration du complexe NT-recepteur a l'interieur de la cellule. Ces rearrangements moleculaires vont alors avoir des repercussions sur le fonctionnement de la cellule cible et a plus grand echelle sur le corps humain tout entier. Analyser et comprendre les mecanismes sous-jacents a l'activation de ces recepteurs est une etape d'autant plus importante que l'on estime que 60% des medicaments prescrits actuellement ont pour cible ces familles de recepteurs. De ce fait, la perspective de developper de nouveaux outils pharmacologiques qui, en perturbant l'activite de ces recepteurs, modifieront la receptivite des neurones vis-a-vis des neuropeptides endogenes, mais egalement vis-a-vis de molecules exogenes lors de traitements medicamenteux est donc particulierement importante. Ce projet devrait donc aider a caracteriser l'implication des recepteurs de la NT dans l'inhibition de la transmission de la douleur chronique et pourrait etre utile au developpement d'analgesiques nouveaux, l'objectif ultime etant de faire progresser les connaissances sur le cerveau pour soulager les souffrances humaines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Returning to Work after Depression: Implications for Women's Health
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; GROUNDED THEORY; MENTAL HEALTH; QUALITATIVE; RETURN TO WORK; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, 62%of women are employed and women make up almost half of the workforce. For women who wish to work,being unable to has a negative impact on their health and well-being. A chronic illness, such as depression, can interrupt or prevent women from working. Depression is increasing world wide and it is more common in women than in men. In fact,depression is responsible for an ever increasing number of people of working age who are off sick or on disability benefits and pensions. When women do return to work they may experience difficulties such as discrimination. In this research project we are going to interview women who have experienced a depression to determine what would help them return to work.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dopamine modulation of prefrontal cortex network activity
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MULTIPLE-UNIT; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; SCHIZOPHRENIA; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: The prefrontal cortex is located in the front of the brain above the eyes. This brain region has a number of functions but is thought to be critically involved in our ability to work with internal representations (i.e. thoughts) to generate appropriate actions. The ability to work with internal representations is called 'working memory' and is disrupted in a number of psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia and addiction. A chemical is present in the prefrontal cortex, called dopamine that changes the way the cells in this part of the brain communicate. We proposed that imbalances in dopamine associated with these diseases causes cells in the prefrontal cortex to allow too much or too little information to access the patient's thoughts or 'working memories'. In this grant application we propose to examine how cells in the prefrontal cortex represent information on a task that taps working memory. In addition we propose to use new technologies that allow us to precisely change dopamine levels in the prefrontal cortex. We will explore how changes in dopamine affect the way cells in the prefrontal cortex communicate with each other and whether it is consistent with our theory. In order to understand the pathology of schizophrenia and addition one must first understanding the basic biology of the brain systems involved. This proposal is a  step forward in this direction.

TitreApplicationTitle: New Mechanisms, Therapeutic Targets and Technologies for Bone Health
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE REGENERATION; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; LIPID NANOPARTICLES; MESENCHYMAL STEM/PROGENITOR CELLS; PROSTAGLANDIN RECEPTOR AGONIST; RETINOIC ACID RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST; SIRNA; SMALL MOLECULE THERAPEUTICS; TARGET VALIDATION
Abstract-Résumé: Bone health is critical to the health and quality of life of Canadians. Strong bones provide a frame for mobility and protection against injury, whereas fragile bones (e.g. osteoporosis) are susceptible to debilitating fractures resulting in extended hospitalization, long-term disability and mortality, especially in the elderly. The cost in health care is enormous (fractures alone cost the system an estimated $1.9 billion in 2010). This project will focus on the development of small molecule compounds and nanomedicines that stimulate bone regeneration, and it will identify new therapeutic approaches by improved understanding of the biology of bone renewal. The project is led by a multidisciplinary team of internationally recognized experts in bone disease and drug development. The team will develop novel bone-seeking pro-drugs that combine bone resorption suppressing activities with bone formation stimulating activities, in a drug design that slowly releases active components to stimulate high quality bone formation. The team will develop new lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations of drugs to target bone marrow and safely promote bone regeneration. In model systems, these LNPs will provide proof-of-concept for new drug targets and potentially new therapeutics for development. By studying stem and progenitors cells in the bone and the natural controls that guide their maturation toward either bone forming or bone resorbing cells, the team together with key collaborators will discover and validate new targets and initiate the development of the next generation of bone regenerative therapies. This project can deliver new and effective agents to the clinic and set the stage for the next generation of drug targeting and bone formation treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evidence-based fracture management supports to optimize fracture recovery, future bone health and optimal physical activity after distal radius fracture.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PAIN; DISTAL RADIUS FRACTURE; FEAR OF FALLING; JOINT BIOMECHANICS; KNOWLEDGETRANSLATION; OSTEOPOROSIS; OUTCOME MEASURES; PREVENTION; SCREENING; TRAUMATIC ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: A broken wrist is the most common broken bone. Younger people, particularly men, are likely to break their wrists through traumatic sports or work accidents with substantial force. Most broken wrists occur in older individuals. Women over 50 have a 15% chance of getting a broken wrist. In 90% of cases, it is caused by a fall from level ground. Some of these people are at risk of future bone health problems, including arthritis and osteoporosis. Some people become very afraid of falling again and stop many of their normal physical activities which can lead to poor health. Some people develop permanent pain. All of these problems can be managed with more intensive investigation and treatment. It can be difficult to get the broken bones back in their normal position during the healing process and it is unknown which surgical techniques work best. A team is needed to develop a pathway to ensure that every individual gets the right type of investigations and treatment. In the lab, bone specimens and computerized models will be used to determine to what extent bones must be realigned to prevent future joint problems such as arthritis. Studies on patients will determine which factors place people at risk of having bad outcomes. We will develop a screening tool to allow doctors and therapists to determine which people are at risk so they get the right investigations and treatments. The team will also investigate methods to ensure that doctors and therapists use these screening tools. The team's scientists have expertise in modeling fractures in the laboratory, and conducting studies on patients to identify risk. The team also includes experts in moving new research into clinical practice. This will ensure that patients with wrist fractures received the new approach to evaluating and fixing their fracture, as well as the methods to ensure that their future bone health and overall physical activity are protected.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the behavioral and cerebral changes associated with pain empathy and its modulation in caregivers
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; COGNITION; EMPATHY; FMRI; HEALTHCARE; PAIN; PSYCHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Pain plays an important part in signaling and preventing tissue damage and warns us about underlying illness. However, pain often reaches proportions beyond its initial function and, once chronic, can be very incapacitating, leading to loss of productivity and quality of life. Accurate evaluation of patients' pain by care providers is crucial for effective pain management. Building on previous research on pain communication, this project merges the expertise of scientists from different disciplines including health care, health psychology and cognitive neuroscience. The objective of the innovative series of studies proposed is to investigate how prolonged exposure to the pain of others changes behavior and the organization of brain functions, and whether such changes affect pain assessment and pain management. Finally, an intervention to improve empathy for pain in care providers and ultimately improve pain management for patients will also be tested. The proposed studies will lead to clinically relevant results that will provide a deeper understanding of the potential underlying causes of pain under-management, and help develop strategies to improve both the patients' and the care providers' well-being.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pseudomonas aeruginosa complex adaptations
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; BIOFILMS; BIOINFORMATICS; GENOMICS; MICROBIOLOGY; OUTER MEMBRANE; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA; SWARMING MOTILITY; SWIMMING MOTILITY; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how the major hospital pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa adapts to host conditions, and development of new treatment approaches. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is a bacterium that continues to be a major cause of hospital-acquired infections (180,000/year in North America). PA is naturally resistant to certain antibiotics, and it is able to further adapt to the presence of antibiotics, and other situations it encounters in infections, to become even more resistant (termed adaptive resistance). Therefore, PA infections are very difficult to treat. We were involved in sequencing the first PA genome in 2000, providing a genetic blueprint for this organism. This blueprint has shown us that PA is tremendously complex and has revealed clues as to the basis for this organism being a feared pathogen. The genetic complexity of PA is mirrored by its ability to adopt specific 'lifestyles' under particular circumstances (e.g., association with the lung surface or antibiotic exposure). Many of these lifestyle changes are relevant to human infections because they increase the ability of PA to infect and persist in patients, and facilitate the development of adaptive antibiotic resistance. Our studies will continue to investigate the underlying basis for these lifestyles, and how certain genes impact on the ability of this bacterium to cause infections and antibiotic resistance. Our work will contribute to understanding lifestyles that are relevant to human infections, and will provide an improved comprehension of a very important and deadly pathogen. These studies will continue to yield information that will impact future treatments. In this regard we have identified small proteins, termed peptides, capable of specifically inhibiting PA undergoing these lifestyle changes, for example swarming, which is one of several ways bacteria can move. We will thus investigate whether these peptides assist in resolving extremely antibiotic resistant infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the immunological basis for early-life infections in preterm infants
Keywords-MotsClés: INNATE IMMUNITY; LONGITUDINAL HUMAN STUDY; MOLECULAR MECHANISMS; PREMATURE INFANTS; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTOR; VULNERABILITY TO INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, about 40,000 children are born prematurely each year and one in six will develop an invasive infection in their first weeks of life. Unfortunately, many of the life-saving interventions premature babies are exposed to during their first weeks of life put them at very high risk of infection. An infection at this age can be very serious and result in life-long health problems or may even lead to death. One of the body's most vital functions is its ability to fight off infections. Immune cells recognize infectious invaders and protect against them, while keeping us healthy. The reasons why adults, or even babies born at term, are able to fend off infections much better than these vulnerable preterm infants remains poorly understood. Our goal is to examine the way human immune cells work early in life to understand why premature babies are particularly susceptible to infection. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of when and why babies are most susceptible to infection will help doctors avoid exposing babies to risky procedures during their highest vulnerability periods and will provide us with the information we need to develop better diagnostic tests and treatments to prevent the serious consequences of infections in these infants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modeling the public health impact of TB and HIV diagnostics
Keywords-MotsClés: COST-EFFECTIVENESS; DIAGNOSIS; HIV/AIDS; MODELING; PUBLIC HEALTH IMPACT; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The combined epidemics of HIV and tuberculosis (TB) have had a huge negative impact in both the developing and developed world. Early diagnosis and rapid initiation of treatment are essential to control both infections. Although there are many accurate rapid tests to diagnose HIV, an unacceptably large proportion of HIV infections are still undiagnosed, and therefore untreated, which fuels the epidemic. For TB, less than perfect tools and diagnostic delays are to blame for the ongoing transmission in at risk regions. Unlike HIV, a simple handheld test for TB is currently not available, but the landscape is looking more promising for affordable easy to use molecular tests, which can be used at the point-of-care to reduce diagnostic delays. Such tests, including the widely-publicized Xpert MTB/RIF test, have the potential to transform TB control, but they must be scaled up and adapted to local conditions. In the rapidly changing world of diagnostics, we need to know: Which technologies, implemented at which level of the health system, with which performance characteristics, will have greatest impact on the TB and HIV epidemics? Combined epidemic-economic models are important tools for answering these questions, as they have the unique ability to project the costs, cost-effectiveness and public health impact of alternative diagnostic strategies in a single unified platform.  We propose to construct a dynamic model of a TB and HIV epidemic, and to compare our results for India, where HIV and TB are important health problems, and Canada, a low risk region. We will use the model to estimate the public health impact, cost and cost-effectiveness of using the Xpert test routinely for TB diagnosis, and the impacts of using a rapid handheld test for HIV screening. Our model and the data we generate will help inform and guide policymakers on TB and HIV diagnostic issues.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of RNase III-dependent regulation of gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: DSRNA BINDING PROTEIN; GENE REPRESSION; MESSENGER RNA; POSTRANSCRIPTIONAL GENE REGULATION; PROTEIN MODIFICATION; RIBONUCLEASES; RNA DEGRADATION; RNASE III; SINGLE CELL ANALYSIS; STRESS RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: The sequencing of the human genome and the discovery of RNA interference revealed that both mRNA maturation (e.g. Splicing) and stability play much more important roles in the regulation of gene expression than previously predicted. It is now clear that gene expression during development is largely controlled through changes in the splicing and degradation pattern of mRNAs. More interestingly, it has recently been shown that RNAi might be linked to cancer, cardiovascular diseases and DiGeorge syndrome thus linking a possible defect in mRNA decay to human disease. Indeed, we have shown recently that alternative splicing pattern could serve as markers for ovarian and breast cancer. However, despite these exciting findings, there is no systematic effort to demonstrate the overall contribution of RNA metabolism to cell function and link it to human disease. By studying the factors that regulate mRNA response in yeast we will provide the first integrated view of the mechanism controlling conditional mRNA decay in any organism, and will provide a model to test in mammals. On the long term, the result of the proposed studies will help us produce a portrait of how cellular RNA drive cellular phenotypes and lead to human disease. This global understanding of RNA metabolism is expected to generate more precise markers and drug targets for complex human disease like cancer. Meanwhile, the goal of this proposal is to understand the biological function of basic components of the eukaryotic cell.

TitreApplicationTitle: Use of TGFbi to improve the efficacy of islet transplantation and promote islet regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE KNOCKOUT MICE; ISLET SURVIVAL; ISLET TRANSPLANTATION; TGFBI; TRANSGENIC MICE; TYPE I DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Islet transplantation is an effective treatment for type I diabetes. However, islets when isolated from the pancreas for transplantation will lose the support from their usual surroundings and tend to die. TGFbi is a molecule that is normally found in the surroundings of islets. We showed that it is helpful to the health and growth of islets. We intend to use this molecule to promote the health and growth of the transplanted islets. We will also dissect TGFbi molecularly to see which part in this molecule is critical for its function on islets and which part is harmful, in order to create a most effective molecule. We will study how TGFbi exerts its effects on islets. The results of our study can be used in patients to improve the effectiveness of islet transplantation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cancer incidence and survival in First Nations and Métis adults in Canada: follow-up of the 1991 census cohort
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; CANCER INCIDENCE; CANCER SURVIVAL; HEALTH INEQUALITIES
Abstract-Résumé: First Nations, Inuit and Metis have historically had a lower risk of getting cancer than the general population.  This is changing however, as their risk of cancer increases over time.  Once diagnosed with cancer, First Nations, Inuit and Metis people are suspected to be less likely to survive their cancer than their non-indigenous peers.  The patterns of cancer in First Nations, Inuit and Metis are challenging to study, mainly because it is difficult (if not impossible) to identify the records of First Nations, Inuit and Metis people in administrative health databases.  This challenge, among others, has led to a lack of research about the burden of cancer in these groups, despite the fact that cancer is among the top three causes of death in First Nations and Metis.  A recent merge of three national databases has provided an important opportunity to examine cancer risk and survival in Canadian First Nations and Metis.  Using linked data from the 1991 Canadian long-form Census, the Canadian Mortality Database and the Canadian Cancer Registry, we intend to fulfill four objectives: 1) to describe the incidence of cancer among First Nations and Metis adults in Canada; 2) to describe cancer survival among First Nations and Metis adults in Canada; 3) to identify trends in incidence and survival, (A) over time and (B) by province/territories; and 4) to compare all the above to non-First Nations, Inuit and Metis.  The proposed study, involving collaboration between Cancer Care Ontario, Statistics Canada, the Assembly of First Nations and the Metis National Council will provide First Nations and Metis groups and their cancer control partners with a description of their cancer burden and a metric by which to determine how they compare to each other and to the general population.  Using rigorous methods, the proposed research aims to generate the information necessary to plan and provide effective, culturally-appropriate cancer prevention and control programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of intestinal microbiota in host responses to dietary gluten and to gluten binders.
Keywords-MotsClés: GLUTEN BINDING POLYMERS; GLUTEN-INTOLERANCE MOUSE MODELS; INTESTINAL MICROBIOTA
Abstract-Résumé: Celiac Disease (CD) is a common digestive disorder affecting children and adults. When people that have the genes for CD (HLA-DQ2 or DQ8) eat cereals that contain gluten, it creates an inflammatory reaction that causes damage to the intestine and does not allow food to be properly absorbed. People with CD also suffer from osteporosis, depression, infertility, and have increased risk to develop Type 1 diabetes and some cancers. In Canada, 1:100 persons are affected and gluten intolerance is more frequent today than 40 years ago. There is no treatment for CD except for the gluten-free diet. This is a life-long committment and is very expensive for families as gluten-free foods are costly and not covered by the health care system. Moreover, it is not recommended in milder forms of gluten intolerance that cause symptoms but do not damage the intestinal lining. This increases the possibility to progress from milder gluten intolerance to the severe condition of CD. The growing number of CD cases and gluten intolerance is alarming and we do understand the reasons behind this increase, but may relate to changes in our environment. Thus, we propose to investigate the role of good (probiotics) and bad gut bacteria in CD and gluten intolerance. We will use mice with no gut bacteria (germ-free) that express the human genes present in people with CD that can be colonized with gut bacteria from patients with CD and healthy people. Our results will contribute to a better understanding of the environmental factors that can promote food intolerances. With this knowledge, preventative therapies for CD and gluten-related disorders could be possible in the future. These will improve the quality of life of gluten intolerant patients as well as reduce the risks and health care costs associated with complications of CD and associated diseases such as Type 1 diabetes and cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enteroendocrine control of nutrient assimilation
Keywords-MotsClés: GUT ENDOCRINE SYSTEM; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INTESTINE; PEPTIDE HORMONES
Abstract-Résumé: Glucagon-like peptides, principally GLP-1 and GLP-2,control gut motility, nutrient absorption, islet function, and nutrient disposal and assimilation. The mechanisms through which these peptides exert their actions are mediated through two structurally-related receptors. Our proposal seeks to examine how both GLP-1 and GLP-02 exert both unique and shared actions that regulate the intake, absoption and regulated disposal of digested nutrients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of MRPs and GSTs in Arsenic Detoxification
Keywords-MotsClés: ARSENIC; CANCER PREVENTION; GLUTATHIONE TRANSFERASES; MEMBRANE TRANSPORT; MULTIDRUG RESISTANT PROTEINS; SANDWICH-CULTURED HEPATOCYTES; SELENIUM
Abstract-Résumé: To protect our bodies from daily exposure to cancer causing chemicals, cells have protective pathways in place. These include surface (or membrane) protein pumps that can prevent harmful chemicals getting into cells. If chemicals by-pass the pumps and enter the cell, metabolic enzymes (or proteins that speed up change within the cell) can modify them to a less harmful more water soluble form, that must be pumped out across the cell membrane. We are investigating how protein pumps and metabolic enzymes protect cells from the cancer causing environmental poison arsenic. We will investigate how these proteins function and how slight variations in their genetic code can influence their ability to protect cells from arsenic. Characterization of metabolic pathways and protein pumps involved in preventing the accumulation of cancer causing chemicals, such as arsenic, lays the foundation for identifying interindividual gene differences that could predispose people to chemically-induced cancers. This is critical for the development of strategies to prevent arsenic-induced cancers and toxicities. Furthermore, although these protein pumps and metabolic pathways are protective in healthy tissue they can also protect cancer cells and make tumours unresponsive to cancer drug treatment. Thus, understanding how these proteins function is important not only for effective cancer prevention, but also cancer treatment strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of T cell priming within Lymphoid Microenvironments by members of the TNF Superfamily
Keywords-MotsClés: CROSS-PRIMING; DENDRITIC CELL; MUCOSAL IMMUNITY; T CELL; TNF SUPERFAMILY; TYPE I IFN
Abstract-Résumé: Cells of the immune system must communicate with each other in order to initiate an immune response to pathogens. These seemingly chance encounters become possible within the context of highly organized organs called lymph nodes. In the context of lymph nodes, multiple molecular pathways orchestrate how immune cells are drawn together in order to initiate an exchange of signals between those cells that carry the pathogen into the lymph node (dendritic cells), and those cells that respond to the pathogen (lymphocytes). The makeup of these signals is what ultimately dictates whether an immune response will proceed or if it is aborted. Understanding such signals will inform vaccine design, provide strategies for eradicating cancers and give clues as to how we may quiet autoimmune responses.

TitreApplicationTitle: The control of whisker motion in rodents
Keywords-MotsClés: CENTRAL PATTERN GENERATOR; EXPLORATORY BEHAVIOR; OPTOGENETICS; RESPIRATION; RODENTS; SNIFFING; WHISKING
Abstract-Résumé: Many senses require self-generated movement to extract information from the world: eye movement for vision, limb movement for touch, sniffing for olfaction, etc. The correct interpretation of sensory messages depends, however, on understanding how sensor movements are regulated because motor strategies determine the features of sensory messages processed by the brain. We use the vibrissa system of rodents as a model for addressing the role of movement in sensory processing. Our specific aims are to identify and characterize the brainstem circuitry that controls rhythmic whisker movements in rodents (whisking) in order to understand how motor cortical areas act on this circuitry for controlling voluntary movement parameters (speed, direction intensity, etc). The control of sensor motion (hand and eye for example) is severely affected in several neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders, which may lead to perceptive errors and hallucinatory sensations.  Beyond sensory coding, whisking constitutes an overt expression of the emotional and motivational state of rodents. A detailed knowledge of this behavior could provide simple metrics for assessing the animal's subjective valuation of objects and experiences. Such metrics would be of particular interest, for instance, to assess motor and motivational deficits in mouse models of neuropsychiatric disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms Regulating Apoptotic Body Phagocytosis and its Impact on the Development of Atherosclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; BIOPHYSICS; CELL BIOLOGY; EFFEROCYTOSIS; INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGE; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PHAGOCYTOSIS; SUPER-RESOLUTION MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal aims to identify new strategies for preventing stroke and heart disease, conditions which cause nearly one-third of all deaths in Canada. These diseases are caused by atherosclerosis - the formation of plaques in the heart filled with dead macrophages.  Heart attacks and strokes occur when these plaques burst and the fragments block arteries in the heart or brain. Therefore, preventing the formation of these plaques is a key strategy for preventing these diseases. Atherosclerotic plaques form when macrophages in the heart consume large quantities of cholesterol; a process which leads to the death of these cells.  Dead cells would normally be removed through a process termed efferocytosis, but for unknown reasons efferocytosis is defective in atherosclerosis patients. Left uncleared, these dead cells burst, which in turn attracts additional macrophages to the heart.  These new macrophages also become cholesterol-laden and die, creating a circular process which drives the formation of an atherosclerotic plaque. We hypothesize that the uptake of cholesterol leads to alterations in the signal transmission pathways used to identify and remove dead cells, thereby causing atherosclerosis by preventing the normal removal of dead cells within the heart. We will test this hypothesis through experiments aiming to 1) understand the normal functioning of the efferocytic process, 2) identify which component of efferocytosis fail during atherosclerosis, and 3) test methods to counteract any atherosclerosis-induced defects we identify. Current therapies target cholesterol through diet and drugs, a practice which is clearly insufficient given the ever increasing number Canadians impacted by these diseases. By targeting a different aspect of atherosclerosis we aim to identify new therapeutic approaches which will complement current treatment regimens, thereby breaking the circular process which drives the formation of atherosclerotic plaques.

TitreApplicationTitle: Next generation anti-androgens for the treatment of castration-resistant prostate cancers
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN RECEPTOR; CHEMICAL GENOMICS; COMPUTER-AIDED DRUG DESIGN; DRUG RESISTANCE; HORMONE RESISTANCE; PROSTATE CANCER; SMALL MOLECULE DRUGS
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed non-skin cancer in Canadian men and one of the leading causes of cancer-related death. If diagnosed early, when still confined to the prostate, it is frequently curable by surgery or radiotherapy. Treatment for locally advanced, recurrent or metastatic prostate cancer is primarily some form of androgen withdrawal therapy, which is generally designed to block either the production of androgens or their binding to the androgen receptor (AR). Unfortunately, the effectiveness of this type of treatment is usually temporary due to progression of surviving tumor cells to a castration-resistant state. With no curative treatment options for castration-resistant prostate cancer, the median life expectancy is approximately 18 months.   Part of the problem is that all anti-AR agents currently used to treat patients act by direct binding to the AR hormone binding site and hence are vulnerable to mutations which frequently arise in this region of the molecule. The proposed research aims to address this problem by using computer modeling, biological screening, structural biology and massive parallel sequencing technology to develop an entirely new class of anti-AR drugs which will target three other distinct regions of the AR (called BF3-, AF2- and AR dimerization sites) to inhibit its activity. We anticipate that these new anti-AR drugs will replace or supplement existing anti-AR therapeutics and will provide new options for treating patients with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of GnRH action
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CATENIN; CELLULAR SIGNALING; CRE/LOX; HORMONAL REGULATION; MOUSE MODEL; NEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; NUCLEAR RECEPTOR; PITUITARY; REPRODUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Fertility is dependent upon the coordinated activities of the brain, the pituitary gland (which sits at the base of the brain), and the gonads (ovaries and testicles). These organs communicate with one another via chemical messengers called hormones, which are produced in one organ and then travel to another via the bloodstream. For successful reproduction, the brain sends a signal called gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) to the pituitary. In response, the pituitary produces and secretes the gonadotropin hormones, which travel to the gonads to: 1) instruct them to make steroid hormones, such as estrogen and testosterone, and 2) stimulate the growth of eggs and sperm. Estrogen and testosterone travel back through the circulation to the brain and pituitary to inhibit further release of GnRH and gonadotropins. In this way, an equilibrium in the system is established. This balance is critical for fertility; perturbations at the brain, pituitary, or gonadal level cause infertility. For example, people with deficiencies in GnRH production or action fail to go through puberty and/or are infertile. Drugs that act like GnRH and others that block its actions are used clinically to treat diverse conditions, including delayed puberty, infertility, and hormone-dependent diseases (for example, breast and prostate cancers). Nevertheless, our understanding of how GnRH produces its actions is incomplete and roughly 70% of GnRH-deficiencies remain unexplained. The goals of this proposal are therefore to understand how GnRH stimulates gonadotropin hormone production and secretion. We will use powerful genetic mouse models to understand these processes in living animals. The results of these studies may provide an understanding of currently unexplained causes of GnRH-deficiency and, in so doing, identify novel therapeutic targets in the treatment of human infertility and hormone-dependent disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analysis of of Soma-Germline interactions in the fly testes.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION; CYTOSKELETON; DIFFERENTIATION; DROSOPHILA; GAP JUNCTIONS; GENETICS; GERMLINE; SPERMATOGENESIS; STEM CELLS; TUMOR
Abstract-Résumé: Stem cells are essential for animal development and allow the maintenance and regeneration of tissues. Stem cells have the ability to divide and to develop into many types of adult cells throughout the lifetime of an organism. A key feature of stem cells is that they can divide to generate either new stem cells or new differentiated cells. In the testes and ovaries interactions between germline stem cells (GSCs) and their surrounding somatic cells play an essential role in regulating GSC function. Abnormal regulation of stem cells in the testes and ovaries give rise to tumor formation. Our long-term interest is in studying the mechanisms that underlie germline-soma communication and how these mechanisms act to regulate GSC differentiation and proliferation. The proposal focuses on the role of the two types of proteins in some-germline communication: those that regulate cell shape ('cytoskeletal regulators') and those that mediate the passage of biological signals between cells ('gap junction proteins').   We have two hypotheses: (i)Direct contact between soma and GSC is essential for their communication and consequently for GSC function. We propose that cytoskeletal regulators have an essential role in the formation of direct contacts between the soma and GSCs.  (ii)We propose that biological signals that pass through gap junctions between soma and germline have an essential role in regulating GSC function.  Using genetic screens in the fruit fly we will identify and characterize cytoskeletal regulator and gap-junction proteins that are required for soma-GSC communication and stem cell function. We will use flies carrying mutations in the genes that encode cytoskeletal regulators and gap junction proteins to deplete these proteins in the testes and study the resulting effects on GSC function. By investigating soma-GSC communication our work provides insight into the biology of germline tumours and the mechanisms of sperm production.

TitreApplicationTitle: Memory and stress related to medical examination among sexually abused children
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; CHILDREN'S MEMORY; INTELLECTUAL FUNCTIONNING; MEDICAL EXAMINATION; PAIN; SEXUALLY ABUSED CHILDREN
Abstract-Résumé: Child sexual abuse is prevalent in the general population and can lead to serious health outcomes. Research on the capacity of children to recall events experienced has shown convincingly that they can provide accurate accounts of these events. However, the testimony of children tends to be incomplete and fragmentary. Children omit to report key information about touches on their body, the perpetrator and the location where the abuse occurred. In addition, these children are also more likely to have some delays in cognitive and language abilities that may impact their testimony. The proposed research concerns the evaluation of child capacity to recall touches on their body, persons and location after an ano-genital medical examination. Participants will include children with a wide range of cognitive functioning, the latter in terms of intelligence, memory, and verbal skills. Anxiety and pain experienced during the medical examination and its impact on children's memory will also be assessed. A total of 135 sexually abused children from 6 to 12 years old will be recruited. These children will be interviewed according to a structured protocol used in investigative interviews, one week after their medical examination. In addition, use of the interview protocol alone will be compared against two other retrieval strategies: interview protocol plus drawing and interview protocol plus mental context reinstatement. Results will help better understand children's memory and their capacity to recall physical touches in a context similar to the one for current investigative interviews. Results will also help medical staff better prepare children and parents for the medical exam so as to reduce its potential negative impact.

TitreApplicationTitle: Amyloid-beta regulation of hippocampal synaptic plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID BETA; BEHAVIORAL NEUROSCIENCE; ELETROPHYSIOLOGY; ENDOCANNABIOID; HIPPOCAMPUS; LONG-TERM DEPRESSION; MEMORY IMPAIRMENT; MOLECUALR BIOLOGY; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Deposition of a protein called amyloid beta (Abeta) in the brain has long been believed to be a central pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, a large number of recent studies have clearly shown a link between early changes of AD-related memory impairment and soluble Abeta-elicited impairment of long-term neural transmission.  There are two major types of brain cells: neurons and glial cells. All the scientific evidence accumulated during the past century has shown key roles of neurons in brain functioning with glial cells providing nutrition, support, etc. Our recent article accepted for publication in 2012 March 3rd issue of the top-elite journal Cell provides the first evidence that astrocyte type of glial cells regulates neuronal transmission and subsequently working memory - a supporting actor becomes the leading actor! As a natural extension of this pioneer research, we have conducted a series of pilot experiments, which, together with other indirect lines of evidence, lead us to hypothesize that soluble Abeta stimulates brain cells to produce endocannabinoids (chemicals existing in our brain that act as cannabis or marijuana), which activate astroglial cells to regulate neuronal transmission, resulting in impairment of working memory. We will employ a variety of cutting-edge technology to critically examine this hypothesis in rats and mice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidation of protein interaction networks for the human transcription factors
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CHIP-SEQUENCING; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEOMICS; RNA INTERFERENCE; TRANSCRIPTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The regulated expression of human genes determines the developmental fates of human cells, and aberrations in this process can lead to cancer and many other diseases.  As well, the use of transcription factors to change the developmental fates of human cells underpins important recent progress in regenerative medicine.  The transcription of human genes is controlled by about 1600 distinct transcription factors, which are proteins that recognize specific DNA sequences in the vicinities of the genes whose expression they control.  A great deal of effort has been devoted to deciphering the DNA sequences recognized by transcription factors and identifying the DNA sites that they bind to in human cells.  However, the complexity of human gene regulation is achieved by groups of these transcription factors working together to recruit components of the transcription machinery to particular genes.  We propose to identify which of the human transcription factors interact with each other and which of the many components of the human transcriptional machinery are targeted by each of these transcription factors.  Understanding how human transcription factors collaborate with each other to regulate human gene expression promises to facilitate the future development of regenerative medicine and the future development of drugs that target gene expression to treat human disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Self-Conscious Emotions and Alcoholism
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ALCOHOLISM; CAUSAL ATTRIBUTIONS; EMOTIONS; GUILT; LONGITUDINAL METHODS; PRIDE; SHAME; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Alcoholism poses major financial, social, and health burdens on Canada, so understanding why some alcoholics recover and maintain sobriety, whereas others do not, is a critical national priority. The proposed research will test whether "self-conscious" emotions (i.e., emotions that require self-evaluations, such as shame, guilt, and pride), and the cognitive processes that elicit them, influence alcoholics' recovery and long-term health. Studies have shown that while shame promotes maladaptive social and mental-health outcomes (e.g., aggression, depression), guilt has generally beneficial effects (e.g., increased empathy, high self-esteem). Correspondingly, two distinct kinds of pride ("hubristic" and "authentic") have similarly divergent effects, with hubristic pride promoting anti-social behavior and psychopathology, and authentic pride promoting pro-social behavior and mental health. The proposed research will test whether recovering alcoholics who experience guilt and authentic pride, rather than shame and hubristic pride, in response to major life events, demonstrate greater health and recovery benefits over time. We will also test whether distinct cognitions underlying these emotions contribute to health outcomes, and, if so, whether self-conscious emotions account for the effects of cognitions on health. We will address these aims by studying emotions, cognitions, and health and recovery outcomes over time in newly sober alcoholics, and comparing these individuals with long-term sober, recovered alcoholics. Our emphasis on self-conscious emotions is quite novel; despite longstanding assumptions that shame lies at the core of addiction, previous studies have not examined whether regulating shame, and experiencing guilt instead, promotes recovery. Furthermore, no previous research has examined the role of pride in addiction. The proposed research is likely to pinpoint new treatment methods (e.g., targeting emotions) for those seeking recovery from addiction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endocannabinoid pharmacology and hippocampal synaptic plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIORAL SCIENCES; CANNABINOID TYPE 1 RECEPTOR; ELETROPHYSIOLOGY; ENDOCANNABIOID PHAMACOLOGY; G PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTOR; HIPPOCAMPUS; LONG-TERM DEPRESSION; LONG-TERM POTENTIATION; MOLECUALR BIOLOGY; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: This project follows directly from our earlier research and investigates the possibility that naturally occurring cannabinoid compounds in the human brain of the kind found in marijuana can impair and enhance neuronal transmission.  The potential medical benefits of the work lie in the fact that the medicine use of exogenous cannabinoids (or exCB, the compounds found in marijuana) is limited by side-effects. Since our brain already contains such exCB-like compounds, our research into their neuropharmacology (how they work in the brain) could point to potential therapeutic strategies for treating various brain disorders without the side-effects of cannabis.  The compelling scientific aspect of the work centers on our earlier finding that marijuana cannabinoids do impair working memory through the agency of glial cells, considered as mere providers of support and nutrition for neurons, the crucial 'nerve' cells in brain function. We have already carried out pilot studies, which along with other indirect evidence, lead us to believe that varying levels of brain eCB can regulate astroglial cells (a type of glial cells) and thus neuronal transmission to impair or enhance working memory. We will employ a variety of cutting-edge technology to critically examine this hypothesis in rats and mice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure, biosynthesis, and function of bile acids in C. elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: BILE ACIDS; C. ELEGANS; CHOLESTEROL; GENETIC ANALYSIS; LIPOPROTEINS; MITOCHONDRIAL OXIDATIVE STRESS; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: In the present grant application I propose to use an animal model to understand why some of the risk factors that lead to cardiovascular diseases develop preferentially in aged individuals. These risk factors, which often occur together, are obesity, diabetes, elevated blood cholesterol, and hypertension. One characteristic that several of these risk factors have in common is an association with elevated levels of toxic free radicals produced by mitochondria. Mitochondria are the part of the cell in which energy is generated from nutrients. This is why it has often been suggested that these pathological conditions could be treated with antioxidants, which neutralize free radicals. This may also be why these risk factors develop in an age-dependent manner, because aging is accompanied by a continuous increase in the production of free radicals. We are using the nematode roundworm C. elegans to study the effects of elevated free radical production on bile acids. These are hormone-like substances that regulate the storage and consumption of fats, cholesterol and sugars in the body. In this model animal we have found that mitochondrial free radicals deregulate the normal mechanisms of synthesis of bile acids in such a way that the animals are taking up more cholesterol than is normal. This was fully unexpected and provides a new hypothesis of how and why free radical generation is linked to the risk factors for cardio-vascular diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tailored cognitive-behaviour therapy for individuals with severe mental illness in supported employment programs - effects on work outcomes and related variables.
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; EMPLOYMENT; EVIDENCE BASED INTERVENTIONS; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SEVERE MENTAL ILLNESS; WORK
Abstract-Résumé: More than 80% of individuals with a severe mental illness such as schizophrenia wish to work in regular competitive jobs. To date, the best vocational programs offered follow the supported employment model in helping people quickly obtain work. Even though their success rates are higher than other vocational programs, only approximately 50% of participants obtain employment with many losing their jobs after a few months. Of the reasons found to explain these results, inappropriate expectancies, poor coping strategies as well as erroneous beliefs about the workplace or their own work abilities are often mentioned. The current proposal takes a first step towards determining the effects of a tailored group intervention aiming at modifying expectancies, beliefs and coping strategies using cognitive behavioural strategies, and offered within a supported employment program. Such an intervention could potentially improve work integration of individuals with severe mental illness at a fairly low cost. This study will also help us better understand the contribution of beliefs, expectancies, and coping strategies on work behaviours and work outcome, while controlling for other competing concepts. This study is currently underway - this renewal will help complete the study and increase our sample size, and include a measure of employment specialists' competencies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Aspergillus induced chronic airway disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ASPERGILLUS FUMIGATUS; CHRONIC LUNG DISEASE; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; INFLAMMATION; MAST CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The mold Aspergillus fumigatus colonizes the lungs of up to half of patients with cystic fibrosis, whose lung function then worsens. Antifungal therapy is rarely successful in eradicating the fungus, suggesting a need for new therapies for this condition. We have found that galactosaminogalactan (or GAG), a molecule on the surface of Aspergillus, can induce the activation of mast cells, a type of white blood cell found in the lung. This activation results in the release of inflammatory substances which actually promote fungal growth and increase inflammation in the lung. In this proposal, we will determine how mast cells worsen Aspergillus airways disease, and test the ability of new therapies that target mast cell-fungal interactions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sex differences in spinal immune system involvement in chronic pain
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; CYTOKINES; IMMUNE SYSTEM; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MICROGLIA; PAIN; PHARMACOLOGY; SEX DIFFERENCES; T CELLS; TRANGENICS
Abstract-Résumé: One of the biggest advances in our understanding of basic mechanisms underlying chronic pain is that neurons are not the only cells involved, but rather that cells of the immune system, even within the nervous system, play an important role as well. As is typical in pain research, the vast majority of existing studies documenting the role of immune cells in pain have been conducted on male subjects. We have preliminary data suggesting that the relative importance of certain immune cells in pain is strikingly sex-specific, with microglia appearing to play an exclusive role in male mice and T-helper cells perhaps being more important in female mice. The proposed studies will verify and extend this hypothesis. These studies have important implications for analgesic drug development, since microglial inhibitors are currently undergoing clinical trials; our data suggest they will be ineffective in women, who comprise the clear majority of chronic pain patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Differential requirements of the transcription factor IRF5 in the generation and maintenance of T-cell responses during visceral leishmaniasis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE TRANSFER; CELL-SPECIFIC KNOCK-OUTS; INFLAMMATION; MICE; PARASITIC INFECTION; SIGNALLING; T-CELL RESPONSES
Abstract-Résumé: Upon encounter with a pathogen, the organism reacts by generating an inflammatory response. This response is aimed at killing the pathogen, but can also damage the tissue. Hence, the organism must maintain a balance between inflammation and tissue protection. Some pathogens, however, manage to escape the attack by the inflammatory response by strongly inducing tissue protective pathways. These pathways typically suppress the protective immune response in order to reduce inflammation and consequently tissue damage. However, they also facilitate the establishment of persistent infections. The proposed research aims at investigating the mechanisms by which the parasite Leishmania donovani can deregulate this balance and establish persistent infection. Understanding the mechanism by which Leishmania induces immune suppressive tissue protective pathways will help us design novel therapeutic interventions to prevent the establishment of chronic infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Obstructive sleep apnea and mild cognitive impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: DEMENTIA; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; NEUROIMAGING; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA; POLYSOMNOGRAPHY; QUANTITATIVE ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) is a major health problem, particularly in the aging population. OSAS is a sleep-related breathing disorder that causes sleep disruption and intermittent nocturnal hypoxemia, which can lead to daytime sleepiness, cognitive deficits, neuronal degeneration, and cerebral dysfunctions. OSAS in the aging population can cause enough cognitive deficits to warrant a diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a risk factor for dementia. From 5 to 20% of MCI individuals will develop Alzheimer disease (AD) or other dementia each year and therefore, up to 50% of subjects with MCI will develop dementia after 3 years. The prevalence of MCI in patients with OSAS is unknown but it is expected to be high since OSAS shares several risk factors with MCI (apolipoprotein epsilon 4 (APOE4) allele, hypertension and, obesity, and metabolic syndrome). No study has looked at the contribution of OSAS to the evolutionary profile of MCI. Treatment of OSAS with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) at least partially improves cognitive functioning. However, no study has performed a longitudinal investigation of cognitive dysfunctions in OSAS patients treated with CPAP and no one has assessed the predictive value of biological markers of cognitive decline measured at baseline (pre-treatment) in the development of dementia during long-term follow-up. In this research program, subjects with co-morbid OSAS and MCI conditions will be studied at baseline using polysomnography, neuropsychological testing, electroencephalography, and neuroimaging. After baseline, they will be continuously treated with CPAP and followed annually with neuropsychological testing during 3 years. They will be compared to a group of OSAS subjects without MCI, to a group of subjects with MCI alone and to a group of healthy control subjects, also followed for 3 years.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toll-like receptor anti-inflammatory response in cardiac inflammatory states
Keywords-MotsClés: INNATE IMMUNITY; NFKB; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS; VENTRICULAR FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The main function of heart cells is to contract in order to provide blood pressure and blood flow to all parts of our bodies. However, we and many other investigators have found that heart cells also demonstrate evidence for a second function. Specifically, when heart cells are challenged by lack of blood or oxygen, by toxic molecules, and by molecules that are part of the response to infections, heart cells respond with an "inflammatory response". Importantly, this cardiac inflammatory response is associated with decreased contraction function of the heart. An anti-inflammatory response is also triggered which limits the effects of the inflammatory response.  The goal of the research proposed in this application is to determine which molecules in the heart are responsible for initiating the anti-inflammatory response and how these molecules accomplish their effects. Understanding these steps and the mechanism of decreased heart function may lead to improved strategies to prevent and treat decreased heart function that occurs following heart attacks, following open-heart surgery, during heart failure, during heart transplant rejection, and during severe infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: CD103 in the control of pulmonary inflammation.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE TRANSFERS; AIRWAY EPITHELIAL CELLS; CD103; DENDRITIC CELLS; E-CADHERIN; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENETICALLY MODIFIED MICE; INTEGRINS; PULMONARY INFLAMMATION; T REGULATORY CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The inflammatory response is essential for survival. Indeed, the accuracy and effectiveness of the immune system is key in multiple protective reactions such as clearing of infections and repairing of injuries, particularly in areas which are in direct contact with possible pathogens such as the lung. However, the control of the intensity and duration of the inflammatory response is equally important in maintaining homeostasis. A loss of control of this defence mechanism can lead to irreparable wounding and alterations in lung function. In the case of many inflammatory lung diseases such as asthma, the intensity and chronicity of the inflammation is responsible for most symptoms. The mechanisms regulating the inflammatory response as well as the steps leading to chronic lung inflammation have been the subject of the majority of basic research in the field of inflammation. Although these studies opened many therapeutic avenues, most current therapies aim at blocking the inflammatory response which can cause a variety of undesirable side effects and resistance, strengthening the need for new therapeutic strategies. We believe that therapies targeting molecules participating in the control of the lung inflammatory response, in the attempt to restore homeostasis would possess a considerable advantage over traditional and current therapies. However, the exact mechanisms under which the control of the pulmonary inflammatory response is regulated are poorly understood.  Recently, our laboratory has made the striking observation that mice lacking the alpha-E integrin CD103 develop worse asthma. Therefore, using mouse models of asthma, genetically modified mice and in vitro studies, we focus on better understanding the role of this specific moelcule in the developement of airway inflammation, in the hope of shedding a light on this mechanism as a possible interesting new therapeutic avenue.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mucopolysaccharidosis I Disease:  Tools for Discovery and Design of Chaperone Therapeutics Based on Unique Enzyme Production Systems and the Elucidation of the Structure of alpha-L-Iduronidase
Keywords-MotsClés: ENZYME ENCHANCEMENT THERAPY; LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISEASE; MUCOPOLYSACCHARIDOSIS TYPE I; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS) are a group of devastating genetic diseases affecting about 1 in 25,000 individuals; in their most severe forms, they lead to death sometime during the first ten years of life. Mutations in the gene encoding the lysosomal enzyme alpha- L-iduronidase (IDUA) are the primary cause of one of the MPSs known as mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I). In order to correlate the greater than 100 disease-causing mutations with disease severity amongst MPS I patients, it is of paramount importance to understand the effect that they have on IDUA. This would shed some light as to why certain single-change ('point') mutations produce a severely abnormal IDUA enzyme and thus lead to severe MPS I disease, while other point mutations produce an IDUA enzyme with only minor structural perturbations, and are manifested by attenuated forms of the disease. As the 3-D structure of IDUA is not known this correlation cannot be made accurately. Therefore, the primary objective of this proposal is to determine the 3-D structure of IDUA so that the known genetic changes can be pinpointed on the structure of IDUA and their consequences can be understood. In order to produce enough enzyme for this structure determination we are proposing to make human IDUA in plants. The 3-D structure of IDUA will be determined by the method of X-ray Crystallography. Once the structure of IDUA is known it will be possible to elucidate the enzymatic mechanism and therefore to understand in detail the effects that the various mutations have on the enzymatic activity. In addition, the structure of IDUA will be used to design small molecules that will help the mutant enzymes to fold into a functional conformation that will ultimately allow the mutant IDUA molecules to have enhanced enzymatic activity. For some patients suffering from intermediate or attenuated forms of MPS I disease, these so-called 'pharmacological chaperones' could be used as effective therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the earliest events of cardiovascular progenitor development using the zebrafish embryo.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC PROGENITORS; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; EMBRYOLOGY; GENETICS; HEART DEVELOPMENT; ORGANOGENESIS; STEM CELL DIFFERENTIATION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease remains the major cause of death in North American adults. Further, congenital heart defects (CHDs) occur in roughly 1% of live births, and have a severe impact on the health and mortality of children. Despite many years of research into heart development, little is known about how the cells that build the heart arise. These cells are termed "cardiovascular progenitor cells", or CPCs. In the embryo, CPCs must be formed and move to the correct location in order to allow heart development to occur. Subtle errors in this process can lead to CHDs. Recent studies have further shown that cells resembling CPCs in the adult can aid in repair of damage caused by heart attack.   The objective of this work is to understand the earliest events that guide CPC development. To carry out these studies, we will use the zebrafish embryo model, a recently developed system that has revolutionized studies on early heart development. Unlike mice and other models where genetic studies can be carried out, the zebrafish embryo develops outside the mother, allowing CPCs to be observed directly. We have identified genes that can cause cells to migrate and contribute to all cell types of the developing heart, much like CPCs. We will use the zebrafish to analyze how the identified genes drive and regulate development of CPCs. We will also test for the ability of these genes to repair zebrafish models of CHDs and heart damage.   The genes that regulate heart development are highly conserved across animal species. Discovering how zebrafish CPCs are made and develop will drive future efforts to repair what is, at present, irreparable heart damage in human patients. Understanding the signals that lead to CPC recruitment will allow for the enhancement of natural heart repair. Knowing how CPCs are made and function will allow for the production of cells or factors that can be added to the damaged heart, leading to non-surgical interventions for CHDs and cardiac regeneration/repair.

ClasseRechercheFR: MUSCLES ET OS; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Structure and function of the mammalian TRAPP multisubunit tethering complex
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; GOLGI; MEMBRANE TRAFFIC; SEDLIN; SEDT; TETHERING FACTORS; TRAPP
Abstract-Résumé: In order for the cell to function properly, each intracellular compartment must receive the appropriate complement of proteins and lipids. Mislocalization of even a single component results in any number of human disorders. It is, therefore, not surprising that many different factors work in concert at many different steps to ensure that correct transport of the proteins and lipids is achieved. Virtually every transport event is mediated by small vesicle carriers. Contained within these vesicles is part of the information needed for delivery to the correct compartment. Likewise, the target compartment also contains proteins that recognize the vesicle. Finally, soluble components that cycle on and off of the vesicle and the target membrane are also required. It remains unclear how the actions of each component are coordinated to ensure the overall transport process. We have been focusing on understanding the role of a large multisubunit protein complex called TRAPP in transport between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and the Golgi. Mutations in TRAPP subunits have been linked to a specific skeletal defect as well as to a form of mental retardation and microcephaly. This complex activates a protein called a GTPase and can bind to ER-derived transport vesicles. Although the complex was originally thought to tether vesicles to Golgi membranes, there are numerous subunits, implying other functions and interactions. Indeed, we have found that the complex interacts with several proteins that are themselves involved in vesicle transport. Using a combination of biochemistry, cell biology and structural biology techniques we will address the function and interactions of this complex. We will also develop assays to measure the trafficking of large molecules such as collagen that are not properly transported in the skeletal defect mentioned above. A detailed understanding of the organization and interactions of TRAPP will shed light on its function in health and disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE; TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Local Delivery of Therapeutic Biomolecules to the Injured Spinal Cord
Keywords-MotsClés: BIODEGRADABLE; DRUG DELIVERY; INJECTABLE HYDROGELS; POLYMERIC PARTICLES; SPINAL CORD INJURY; TISSUE REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Traumatic spinal cord injury is devastating.  It comes without warning to our most physically active youth.  There is no cure for spinal cord injury, and only limited surgical interventions are available.  There are some biomolecules that have generated significant excitement in the community, but their delivery to the injured spinal cord has become a limitation to their ultimate clinical use. The blood-spinal cord barrier limits most molecules from entry into spinal cord tissue.  Those molecules that enter into the spinal cord tissue have to be delivered in such high doses that they have undesirable side effects. We have designed an innovative delivery strategy where biomolecules are incorporated into a biodegradable biomaterial that can be easily injected in the fluid-filled cavity that surrounds the spinal cord. This minimally-invasive delivery strategy ensures that the biomolecules are delivered locally - that is directly to the injured tissue - without any deleterious effects on the tissue itself.  In fact the biomaterial has a net positive effect on the tissue.  Here we propose to advance this innovative strategy to deliver a combination of clinically-relevant biomolecules that require local release for efficacy.  We will study the tissue and functional benefit in both medically-relevant subacute and chronic spinal cord injury models.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transforming Care at the Bedside with Involvement of Patient's Representatives: Improving Quality of Care.
Keywords-MotsClés: MISUSE; MORBIDITY; MORTALITY; NON-MEDICAL OPIOIDS USE; PER CANADIAN PROVINCE TRENDS; PUBLIC POLICIES; QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH; TRENDS OF OPIOIDS USE
Abstract-Résumé: The use of prescription opioid analgesics (i.e., POs) in North America has risen substantially in recent years and the amount of POs dispensed has more than doubled from 2000-2010 in Canada. POs are essential medications for effective pain care; however, their non-medical use is associated with major negative health consequences such as accidental overdose deaths. The issue of PO misuse, harms and interventions has become a major public health and policy challenge in Canada.  Fischer and colleagues have recently examined quantitative and qualitative medical PO dispensing patterns in the 10 Canadian provinces for the period 2005-2010. They found an overall increase in POs dispensed during this period in all provinces, primarily driven by use increases in strong POs. However, significant inter-provincial differences (amounting to almost factor 4) were found regarding the population-based quantities of POs used, as well as in the types of POs used.  Based on the current literature and Fischer et al.'s data, the proposed research project aims at clarifying a number of essential issues. The project will extend Fischer et al., analysis of quantitative and qualitative PO dispensing patterns across the Canadian provinces for the period 2011-2013, will identify the determinant of the inter-provincial differences (e.g., electronic Prescription Monitoring Programs) and finally will assess to which extent the qualitative and quantitative differences in provincial PO dispensing patterns are associated with differences in morbidity mortality outcomes.
