TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of lipid metabolism by xenin
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL RHYTHM; GUT HORMONE; HYPOTHALAMUS; LEPTIN; LIPID METABOLISM; LIPOLYSIS; OBESITY; SYMPATHETIC NERVOUS SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is a significant risk factor for several medical problems including diabetes and heart diseases, and therefore mortality.  Lifestyle modification (caloric restriction and exercise) is the only therapy readily available to most obese patients.  Unfortunately, the amount of weight loss is limited after lifestyle modification.  Only one drug is currently approved for the long-term treatment of obesity in Canada.  Therefore, there is a huge demand for a treatment protocol which can overcome the limitation of lifestyle modifications.  Recent intensive studies suggest that a number of hormones produced by the gut play a critical role in the regulation of the metabolism and body weight.  Xenin is one of the gut-produced hormones.  Injection of xenin reduces food intake, body weight, fat mass, and increases levels of genes which stimulate a fat breakdown process called lipolysis.  These findings led us to hypothesize that xenin stimulates lipolysis and xenin treatment reverses obesity and obesity-associated abnormal fat metabolism.  To address this hypothesis, we propose to determine (1) the role of xenin in fat metabolism (more specifically, lipolysis), (2) the mechanism underlying the lipolysis-stimulating effect of xenin and (3) the beneficial effect of xenin treatment with or without caloric restriction in reversing obesity and obesity-associated abnormal fat metabolism. It is expected that the outcome of the proposed study will provide powerful information in establishing improved therapeutic protocol for the treatment of obesity and will have significant impact on the health of Canadians as well as residents in many other countries where obesity and obesity-associated impairments are serious health problems.

ClasseRechercheFR: SANG; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Leukocyte Ig-Like Receptor-B1 Regulation and Function
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE REGULATION; INHIBITORY MOTIFS; INNATE IMMUNITY; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; POLYMORPHISM; RECEPTOR SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this study is to fully understand how cells of the immune system integrate signals to respond only when appropriate. Failure to tightly regulate this process results in needless damage to tissues and can lead to full-blown autoimmunity where the immune system mounts a sustained attack aimed at organs in the body. Our current focus is to study this process in human natural killer cells. These cells are part of the innate immune system and they are important in the body's defense against viruses and tumor development. Natural killer cells must distinguish normal healthy cells from a cell that has been infected by a virus or one that is malignant. Natural killer cells make this fateful decision using a collection of cell surface proteins that are called receptors, some of which send a positive signal that a cell is infected and some of which send inhibitory signals to indicate the cell is healthy.  These receptors are called natural cytotoxicity receptors and killer cell inhibitory receptors respectively. We are using a combination of approaches to understand how the biochemical signals emanating from the receptors after engagement are integrated within the natural killer cell using a combination of cellular, biochemical and molecular techniques. We are also studying how genes encoding these receptors vary between people and how this variation impacts the immune response. The knowledge gained through these studies will help understand how these molecules contribute to the immune response and may be applied to the design of more effective vaccines for viral diseases and treatments for autoimmunity and cancer.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancing the anabolic effect of perioperative nutrition by insulin and maintenance of normoglycemia
Keywords-MotsClés: COLORECTAL CANCER SURGERY; INSULIN THERAPY; MUSCLE PHYSIOLOGY; NORMOGLYCEMIA; PERIOPERATIVE NUTRITION; PROTEIN METABOLISM; STABLE ISOTOPE TRACER STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: Loss of muscle protein and mass are the main causes of fatigue after bowel surgery which may result in a longer hospital stay and a higher rate of complications. This problem is especially relevant for patients after surgery for bowel cancer because cancer itself causes a waste of muscle protein. Anesthesiologists can decrease the muscle wasting after surgery by choosing the type of pain treatment (analgesia) and by giving nutrition (sugar and protein). Our group recently observed that optimal pain relief with epidural catheters (these are placed in the so called epidural space, which lies between the spine and the skin of the back) in combination with a low calorie protein diet intravenously (through the vein) maintains the body's protein stores after bowel cancer surgery. The goal of our new research program is to find out whether this protein saving effect of excellent pain control and nutrition can be further improved by adding the hormone insulin to our therapy. We recently have developed a safe way to give insulin to patients who have cancer surgery and expect that insulin together with a high protein diet will lead to the optimal preservation of protein in muscle and other vital organs.  Optimizing nutritional therapy will help patients to better overcome the stress of surgery and, eventually, improve their recovery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Plane-wave quantitative ultrasound imaging of blood mechanical properties
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE AND CHRONIC INFLAMMATION; BLOOD CHARACTERIZATION; BLOOD CLOTTING; CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS SURGERY; DEEP VEIN THROMBOSIS; DYNAMIC ULTRASOUND ELASTOGRAPHY; PULMONARY EMBOLISM; QUANTITATIVE ULTRASOUND IMAGING; RED BLOOD CELL AGGREGATION; ULTRASOUND BIOMICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: This grant application is proposing the development of quantitative ultrasound imaging methods to quantify in vivo mechanical properties of blood under flowing and clotting conditions. Plane-wave image processing is proposed to optimize image accuracy and to allow implementing an innovative dynamic elastography method with in situ radiation pressure generation. Proposed plane-wave implementations of quantitative ultrasound imaging methods will constitute a new era in non-invasive imaging of blood.       The dynamic reversible structural changes in red blood cell aggregation properties under flowing conditions will be monitored with cellular imaging methods based on the spectral properties of backscattered echoes, whereas dynamic ultrasound elastography methods are proposed to quantify the viscoelasticity of clotted blood. Validated methods will be applied to monitor hyper-aggregation of red blood cells promoted by acute inflammation during cardiopulmonary bypass surgeries in humans, and to follow the structural maturation of deep vein thromboses and the impact of thrombolytic therapies in a rabbit model.      The implementation of proposed quantitative ultrasound imaging methods on a plane-wave scanner is highly innovative. Indeed, plane-wave imaging constitutes a new framework in ultrasound; it allows producing images at a high frame rate of a few kHz, thus permitting sufficient processing time for image quality optimization. Plane waves are also used to produce supersonic shear waves in dynamic elastography imaging; in this project plane-wave processing will allow implementing the original shear wave induced resonance elastography method developed by our group.

TitreApplicationTitle: Plasticity in airway smooth muscle
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE; ASTHMA; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; MUSCLE BIOCHEMISTRY; MUSCLE MECHANICS; MUSCLE STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Asthmatics experience wheezing and difficulty breathing because their airways become narrowed. Abnormal contraction of the muscle in the airways is one of the major causes of the airway narrowing seen during an asthma attack. Although we know that airway muscle is involved in acute life-threatening asthma attacks, the exact mechanism of how this occurs is not clear. Some recent studies suggest that the muscle is abnormal in asthmatics. However, how the muscle abnormality results in excessive narrowing of the airway is yet to be determined. A major obstacle to our understanding of the abnormal behavior of asthmatic airway muscle is the lack of knowledge of the basic biochemical mechanism of contraction in normal airway muscle. It is clear that if we do not know how normal muscle works, we will not be able to determine what is abnormal in the asthmatic airway muscle and fix the defect. In this application we propose to study both the normal behavior and biochemical composition of airway muscle and the changes that occur in asthma. We will use the high-resolution imaging technique of electron microscopy to examine the protein structure inside the muscle cells and relate the changes in the structure to the changes in the mechanical and biochemical properties of the cells. The results of our research will advance our understanding of the fundamental process of muscle contraction and how this process could be altered in asthma. The research will also lead to identification of targets inside the muscle cells that could be useful for better drug treatments for asthma.   Over 3 million Canadians suffer from asthma and the disease kills 20 children and 500 adults every year in Canada. The incidence of asthma is increasing in Canada. Every year in Canada there are 146,000 emergency room visits due to asthma attacks and over $12 billion is spent on asthma in Canada. A better treatment for asthma will go a long way in reducing the cost to society in the long run.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adjunctive nutritional strategies to overcome sarcopenic muscle loss in aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BRANCHED-CHAIN AMINO ACIDS; CASEIN; CITRULLINE; HUMAN; MILK PROTEINS; PROTEIN METABOLISM; SARCOPENIA; STABLE ISOTOPE; WHEY
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins are present in almost every tissue in our body. When we eat protein our body responds by making new proteins in almost every tissue; however, we now know that certain proteins tend to allow certain tissues to make new proteins better than others. When we are young children our bodies make new proteins, in response to consumption of dietary protein, at a very rapid rate to allow tissues to grow. As adults, however, while our body still responds to protein ingestion by making new proteins the response is not one of growth but of tissue protein renewal. This protein renewal, referred to as protein turnover, is a necessary process for all tissues to replace damaged older proteins. As we age we lose some of skeletal muscle mass at a rate of approximately 1% per year. This process, known as sarcopenia, results in declines in muscle mass to a point where certain older people can become weak and may experience metabolic abnormalities associated with low muscle mass such as type 2 diabetes. It is unknown why we lose skeletal muscle mass with age but the hypothesis we will test here is whether in older persons there is an inability , or what we are calling a 'resistance', of skeletal muscle to making new proteins with ingestion of food. We will use a protein from cows' milk (whey) in addition to other protein ingredients and sugars to determine how a younger and an older persons body and muscle uses the protein to make new muscle and other body proteins. We will also use weightlifting exercise as a stimulus for promoting even greater new muscle protein synthesis with ingestion of protein and a potential potent countermeasure to aged-related sarcopenia. Our novel experiments will shed new insight into how aging affects our use of dietary protein and how hat use contributes to age-related muscle loss.

TitreApplicationTitle: MicroRNA-15 dysregulation in sporadic Alzheimer's disease: testing the "multiple hit" hypothesis in neurodegenerative disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; LENTIVIRUS; MICRORNA; MOUSE MODELS; NEURODEGENERATION; NONCODING RNA; POSTTRANSCRIPTIONAL GENE EXPRESSION REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: While we know what causes rare genetic forms of Alzheimer's disease (AD), it remains unclear how aging, and the gradual loss of function associated with it, can cause the frequent sporadic AD. Over the last years, a complete new way of regulating gene expression has been discovered: microRNAs are very small RNA molecules that are expressed in the brain and fine-tune many biological functions. We speculate that loss of such microRNA regulation can be involved in sporadic AD development. We have already tested to a certain degree this hypothesis by measuring microRNA levels in brain of AD patients, and we have found that there are indeed significant alterations when compared to healthy controls. We now want to test whether when we make similar changes experimentally in the brain of mice, we will obtain signs of AD. In this project, we will focus of a particular family of microRNAs, that is, the miR-15 family, previously shown to modulate some aspects of AD pathology in cultured cells. We anticipate providing new mouse models for sporadic AD. Furthermore, we will explore to what extent we can use microRNA molecules to treat AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Postpartum Progression to Type 2 Diabetes in Women with Recent Glucose Intolerance in Pregnancy: Pathophysiology, Biomarkers, and Clinical Implications
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CELL FUNCTION; GESTATIONAL DIABETES MELLITUS; GLUCOSE INTOLERANCE IN PREGNANCY; TYPE 2 DIABETES; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is defined as high blood sugar that is first recognized during pregnancy. It is a common condition affecting up to 14% of pregnant women. Importantly, women who have had GDM are at increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2DM), particularly within the first 6 years after their pregnancy. Indeed, we have previously shown that women with recent GDM have subtle abnormalities shortly after their pregnancy including a reduced ability of the pancreas to secrete insulin. It is not known, however, if further decline in this ability to secrete insulin ultimately leads to T2DM in affected women or if this process can be tracked by following certain factors in the blood (called biomarkers). The aim of our research is to determine whether deterioration of insulin secretion is the key factor that leads to the development of T2DM in young women following GDM. Towards this goal, we have recruited a cohort of women with and without GDM who are undergoing evaluation in pregnancy and at regular intervals for the first 6 years thereafter. At each study visit, we are assessing their ability to secrete insulin, the levels of certain biomarkers in the blood, and whether or not they have T2DM. This study will help to shed light on the early changes in the body that lead to the development of diabetes in young women of childbearing age (who represent the segment of the Canadian population that has had the largest increase in diabetes in the past decade). This research may lead to improved ways to treat these early changes and thus possibly prevent the development of T2DM in women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Repeat Emergency Department Visits Among Long-Term Care Residents in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT VISITS; LINKED ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; LONG-TERM CARE; OLDER ADULTS; REPEAT EVENTS MODELS; TRANSITIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Long-term care (LTC) residents are a vulnerable segment of the older population. They have a high burden of dementia and other illnesses as well as significant limitations in their independent functioning. Because of this, they are at high risk for emergent health problems, such as a serious fall or an acute complication of an existing chronic condition (like diabetes), that results in a visit to the emergency department (ED). While these ED visits are often necessary, they also represent the health system's inability to respond to residents' needs before they become a serious health crisis. Equally as problematic are findings that suggest that many residents make multiple ED visits because their underlying needs were not addressed during the first visit resulting in additional ED visits. To date, there is little research that describes such repeat ED visits by LTC residents, the consequences of these visits, or how to target interventions to reduce their occurrence. In our research, we will use data from Ontario to identify all LTC residents and follow them for up to one year. All ED visits during this time will be counted so that we can estimate the frequency of repeat ED visits. Advanced statistical methods will allow us to comprehensively describe patterns of repeat ED visits, identify resident risk factors, and estimate the contribution of each the LTC and hospital sectors to repeat ED visits. Our results will help to focus quality improvement efforts aimed at safely minimizing ED use by identifying opportunities for intervention in both LTC homes and hospitals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of mechanical forces on lung development
Keywords-MotsClés: ALVEOLARIZATION; BRONCHOPULMONARY DYSPLASIA; CELL DEATH; CELL GROWTH; DEVELOPMENT; STRETCH; VENTILATION
Abstract-Résumé: Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation is a common clinical scenario, which can lead to lung injury. When assisted ventilation is required in very premature infants, the lungs are at risk for altered growth and development which can lead to a disease called bronchopulmonary dysplasia. About one fourth of infants who weigh less than 1250 g are diagnosed with the disease which has major consequences for respiratory health later in life. In this proposal, we will investigate the effects of adverse ventilation (over-stretch) on lung development. We will use a cell culture system of fetal rat lung cells that can be subjected to stretch and investigate proteins involved in cell growth and death. Newborn rats (model for premature infants) will be hyperventilated to overstretch the lung cells in the whole body and again proteins important for cell growth and death will be studied. Finally, we will ventilate newborn animals with a similar ventilatory strategy as currently used in the clinic and investigate whether the identified proteins are altered under these conditions. The findings should provide alternative ventilatory and therapeutic strategies to counter adverse lung development associated with preterm delivery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Polymer-Grafted Allogeneic Leukocytes and Systemic Immune Modulation
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOENGINEERING; LYMPHOCYTE; POLYMER
Abstract-Résumé: Experimental and clinical use of biomaterials is of increasing importance in medicine.  Among these biomaterials are polymers (long molecules made up of repeating simple subunits) that can be used to protect donor proteins, cells and tissues from the recipients immune system.  Previously, most research has been focused on the local interface of the polymer-modified donor product with the recipients blood plasma and immune cells.  However, recent studies from our laboratory have demonstrated the polymer modification of white blood cells from blood donors can be used to modulate the entire (systemic) immune system of the recipient.  This immunomodulation results in a significant decrease in inflammatory immune cells and a significant increase in immune (regulatory) cells important in reducing inflammatory responses.  It is our hypothesis that polymer-modified white blood cells may be clinically useful in the preventing inflammatory reactions to donor proteins, cells and tissues and, of equal or greater value, in inhibiting autoimmune diseases (i.e., where the individual's own immune system attacks the persons own tissues).  To test and further develop this potentially important clinical tool, the polymer chemistry (type of polymer, how much polymer and size of polymer) will be optimized in vitro (in the test tube) and in vivo (inside the mouse).  We will also determine if the donor white blood cells can be biologically inactivated to reduce any potential risk to a recipient.  Finally, to test the clinical value of this polymer-mediated immunomodulation approach an animal model of autoimmune diabetes will be used.  Should this polymer-mediated immunomodulation prove effective in these studies, this approach may be clinically useful in both tissue transplantation (e.g., kidneys) and for the treatment of autoimmune diseases (e.g., diabetes and arthritis).

TitreApplicationTitle: Energy metabolism in the newborn heart.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; HEART; ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE; ISOLATED HEART TISSUE; MYOCARDIUM; NEWBORN
Abstract-Résumé: In some babies the heart does not properly form during fetal development, resulting in abnormalities in the anatomy of the heart. These defects, called, "Congenital Heart Defects" (CHD's), can be life-threatening, and heart surgery may be necessary to repair the CHD's. This necessitates that the heart be stopped during the operation, resulting in a period of time where the heart does not receive any oxygen, a condition called "cardiac ischemia". If cardiac ischemia persists for extended periods of time, damage to the heart muscle can occur. It is therefore important to develop strategies to protect the heart during surgery to correct CHD's. Following birth, the heart of the newborn switches from using sugars to using fatty acids as it's main source of fuel. This switch in energy metabolism can increase the likelihood of damage to the heart muscle during ischemia. What is responsible for the dramatic switch in fuel use by the heart in the hearts of newborns is not completely understood. We will also use an experimental rabbit heart model to determine what is responsible for the dramatic increase in fatty acid use in the newborn period. We will also determine how this switch in energy metabolism contributes to damage to the heart muscle during cardiac ischemia. Our studies should help the development of new therapeutic strategies to protect the newborn heart during cardiac surgery to correct congenital heart defects, thereby improving the health of infants who are born with CHD's.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dignity Talk: a novel palliative care intervention for patients and their families
Keywords-MotsClés: BEREAVEMENT; DIGNITY IN CARE; END-OF-LIFE; FAMILY; GRIEF; HELPLESSNESS; PALLIATIVE CARE; PSYCHO-SOCIAL INTERVENTION; PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Dying patients and their families face many challenges near the end-of-life. Not only do patients often experience physical distress, but they also have feelings of loss of dignity, isolation, and uncertainty. Family members also face many challenges. They bear witness to the suffering of loved ones, and they face uncertainty, loss, and at times a mounting sense of helplessness.   The purpose of this study is to introduce and evaluate a new intervention called Dignity Talk, meant to enhance end-of-life experience for both patients and their families. Dignity Talk is based on a set of questions by which terminally ill patients and their family members can engage in meaningful conversations with each other. It is intended to lessen feelings of loss and helplessness and enhance feelings of connectedness by facilitating conversations that tap into a sense of meaning and purpose, sharing of memories, wishes, hopes, and giving guidance to those who will soon be left behind.  In Phase 1, 20 patients and family members will help finalize the method and Dignity Talk question framework (is it easy to understand, do we have the right questions, and is the wording sensitive). In Phase 2 of the study we will ask 100 patient-family pairs for feedback about Dignity Talk: what influence it had on their palliative care experience, whether it works well, and whether this intervention should become a regular part of palliative care. We will also ask for feedback from health-care providers in both phases. Four to six months after the death of their loved one, we will contact the family member to ask their thoughts about Dignity Talk, how it shaped their experience of their grief and bereavement.  We expect that the study will show that Dignity Talk can be an effective, highly accessible palliative care intervention, which will enhance the end-of-life experience for palliative patients and the families who support them.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Tumor necrosis factor receptor family members in control of chronic viral infection
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC VIRAL INFECTION; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HIV; LYMPHOCYTIC CHORIOMENINGITIS VIRUS; MOUSE MODELS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SPLENOMEGALY; T LYMPHOCYTES; THERAPY OF CHRONIC VIRAL DISEASE; TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR BETA
Abstract-Résumé: Upon infection our body's immune system must ramp up to control the infection; then, once the infection is eliminated, the immune system goes back to its resting state and our symptoms disappear. But what happens when the immune system cannot get rid of the infection?   This leads to chronic infection, such as occurs with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Hepatitis B and C viruses. If the immune system stayed fully active during chronic infection we would damage our body through excess inflammation. Thus, the immune system has evolved ways of reducing the immune response during chronic infection. This has the advantage of preventing death from inflammation, but the disadvantage that one ends up with a life-long infection that can have long-term negative consequences.  My laboratory is studying a family of molecules that are induced on white blood cells during viral infections. These molecules help the white blood cells clear the infection.  We recently asked what happens to these molecules during a chronic infection when the immune system can't get rid of the virus.  We found that during prolonged infection one such immune stimulatory molecule was still there but no longer worked. We further investigated and found that the immune stimulatory molecule on the surface of the white blood cell no longer worked because one of the molecules its uses to send signals inside the white blood cell had been degraded. Our proposal is aimed at asking how other members of this family of molecules behave during chronic infection and in understanding the processes that allow enlarged spleens to shrink back to normal and reorganize after a long infection. The results of these studies will inform new therapeutic approaches aimed at the chronic stage of HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving access to community-based primary health care (CBPHC) for African immigrant and refugee families
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO COMMUNITY-BASED PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; AFRICAN IMMIGRANTS; AFRICAN REFUGEES; ENVIRONMENTAL SCAN; FAMILIES; HEALTH AND SOCIAL SERVICE PROVIDERS AND ADMINISTRATORS; HEALTH EQUITY; OPEN-ENDED INTERVIEWS; PHENOMENOLOGY; QUALITATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Immigration numbers in recent years have increased dramatically in Manitoba. Not only has the number of migrants from African source countries increased, but an increasing proportion of them are refugees. This is a concern considering the health of refugees is generally poorer in comparison to those who voluntarily chose to migrate to Canada. However, African immigrants can also experience health inequities due to a number of factors (e.g., socioeconomic status, poverty). Ensuring timely and appropriate access to community-based primary health care (CBPHC) for immigrant and refugee families and their children is critical to improving their health. The primary purpose of this 3-year qualitative study is understand recent African immigrant and refugee families' experiences of accessing CBPHC in Winnipeg and to engage them in identifying ways to improve access and quality of care. Recognizing that immigrant and refugee families with children experience increased needs, childrearing families from African source countries will be recruited. Health and social service providers and administrators will also be recruited to help ensure a more detailed understanding of families' experiences in accessing CBPHC. Multiple data collection methods will be used including an environmental scan of existing CBPHC services and programs and open-ended interviews. Analysis will shed light on immigrants' and refugees' experiences of accessing CBPHC with attention to how various factors shape their experiences. Recommendations for improving access and quality of CBPHC will be identified. Findings from this study will help to inform how best to reduce health inequities and improve access to CBPHC for African immigrant and refugee families. African immigrant and refugee families will have meaningful involvement and play an active role in defining issues, considering solutions, and identifying priorities specific to their access of CBPHC which supports CIHR's model of citizen engagement.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studying the involvement of the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRAF6 in vascular remodeling events
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOTENSIN II; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CONDITIONAL KO MICE; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; INDUCIBLE TET SYSTEM IN VIVO; POLYUBIQUITINATION; PROTEIN KINASES; TRAF6; UBIQUITIN E3 LIGASES; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease (CVD), including heart disease, stroke and peripheral vascular disease, is the leading cause of death in Canada and in Western society. When death is not the end point, CVD jeopardized the quality of life. CVD is also the leading cause of hospital admissions and despite progress in its prevention, detection, and treatment, which exact an enormous toll in Canada, it will still kill thousand of Canadian this year. Several risk factors for coronary artery disease (CAD) have been well documented including gender, age, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking, diabetes, family history, physical inactivity, overweight and excessive alcohol. However these factors explain only part of attributable CVD, and other factors must be involved. Indeed, a growing body of evidence supports the concept that local and systemic chronic inflammation may play a role in the initiation and progression of atherosclerosis and its complication (angina crisis, stroke and sudden death). In the arteries, atherosclerosis is characterized by a recruitment of cells of the immune system into the vessel wall, an accumulation of circulating cholesterol followed by an increase in the number of vascular muscle cells, the major component of the vascular system. These processes lead ultimately to plaque formation, which diminish blood flow and ultimately leads to myocardial infarction or stroke. The underlying cause of this chronic inflammation and how its specifically relates to CAD is at the moment unknown. Evidence generated by our group of research now suggests that a class of enzymes know as E3 ubiquitin ligases might be involved in chronic inflammation reaction present in the vasculature. This research proposal will therefore address the role of a master regulator of inflammatory reactions, the E3 ligases TRAF6, in vascular growth and inflammation as well as atherosclerosis development by the generation of a novel transgenic mice model.

TitreApplicationTitle: The nickel-regulated transcription factor NikR from H. pylori and E. coli
Keywords-MotsClés: ACID ADAPTATION; DNA-BINDING PROTEINS; METALLOREGULATORS; MUTANT PROTEINS; NICKEL HOMEOSTASIS; PATHOGENIC BACTERIA; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of this research is to determine how nickel use is regulated in bacteria. Nickel is an essential nutrient for many forms of life, including pathogenic bacteria such as Helicobacter pylori, which causes ulcers, gastritis and gastric cancers, and Escherichia coli, which can cause gastrointestinal illnesses.  However, although these bacteria need nickel, they have to use it carefully because this metal can also be toxic if it is not handled carefully, so bacteria expend a lot of resources to control the distribution and accumulation of nickel.  If these resources fail, the bacteria get sick and fail to grow.  The focus of this grant is to understand how nickel use is regulated in several types of bacteria, and in the case of the H. pylori system, how the regulation of nickel is connected to the environmental niche of the organism:  the human stomach.  We will determine the chemical and biological details of the major proteins involved in these systems, and in doing so we will learn how we can disrupt their activities.    This study will contribute to our knowledge of how heavy metals are used in biology, a fundamental aspect of life.  Furthermore, the toxicity of transition metals, even essential nutrients like nickel, is a problem that must be dealt with by all organisms, and the nickel proteins serve as an excellent model system to study metal-dependent regulation.  Finally, it is thought that humans do not have a dietary requirement for nickel, so the systems that control nickel in bacteria might provide unique targets for very selective antibiotics. Despite the huge advances in antibiotic development, bacterial infections remain a serious health problem, and new types of treatment are needed. In order to realize the potential of a new strategy for antibacterial agents an understanding of the details of these multi-faceted nickel systems is essential.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of triacylglycerol hydrolase in lipid metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; LIPOLYSIS; LIPOPROTEINS; NAFLD; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is strongly associated with excessive fat storage in multiple tissues including the liver, where this fat deposition leads to abnormal liver functions and risk for cardiovascular disease and diabetes. Increased liver fat deposition stimulates the export of particles that carry bad cholesterol (LDL). We have shown that a protein called Ces3/TGH plays an important role in regulating the cholesterol export from the liver into blood. We have developed mice that are deficient in this protein and have shown that these animals have less harmful blood lipid levels and are protected from high-fat diet-induced cardiovascular disease, fat accumulation in the liver and have improved sugar metabolism. Therefore, decreasing the function of this protein would seem beneficial in treatment of obesity-related metabolic complications. In the proposed research we plan to investigate the mechanisms by which Ces3/TGH regulates fat absorption, fat storage, address mutations in this protein in humans, and research a novel animal model in effort to develop therapeutics for the treatment of obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms and the manipulation of the fetal neuroimmune response to inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; FETAL HEALTH; HEART RATE VARIABILITY; INFLAMMATION; NEUROIMMUNOLOGY; VAGUS
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system can cause inflammation that damages organs. The normal brain and the normal immune system "talk" to each other and influence each other. By emitting "cholinergic" signals, the brain limits the ability of the immune system to cause damaging inflammation. When a fetus suffers from infection, the immune system's inflammatory response can damage his or her brain and make it more likely to develop chronic inflammatory diseases after birth. Lifelong disabilities can result. When doctors suspect such condition, they deliver the baby urgently, usually by Cesarian section. However, doctors cannot accurately predict which fetuses need urgent delivery and which pregnancies can be safely allowed to continue. My research team develops monitors that better detect which fetuses are truly distressed by measuring certain mathematical properties of the fetal heart beat directly controlled by "cholinergic" brain signals. Now, we are learning how to improve cholinergic anti-inflammatory brain signaling using electric nerve stimulation as the first step to develop drug treatments. By harnessing the brain's innate power to reduce dangerous inflammation, we think we can protect the fetal brain, reduce unnecessary Cesarean sections, and decrease the number of babies born with increased risk to develop newborn or adult neurological diseases due to inflammatory brain damage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rhamnose biosynthesis: alternative antibiotic targets
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICS; CARBOHYDRATES; CHEMISTRY; ENZYMES
Abstract-Résumé: Bacterial resistance is increasing, so there is a pressing need to discover new medicines to treat infectious diseases. We will perform drug innovation and prepare molecules with new antibacterial activity. These molecules are new and have not been prepared previously. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was responsible for more deaths in North America in 2007 than HIV / AIDS and is one of many emerging new bacterial infections arising from drug resistance. There is a limited choice of drugs available to manage infections from drug resistant bacteria. This indicates that there is a strong need to develop new antibacterial drugs, yet pharmaceutical companies are exiting the infectious diseases area. In this research project, we will use chemical and enzymatic methods to discover new potential drug leads for bacterial infections. These new molecules are designed to specifically target a biosynthetic pathway that is found in bacteria but not in mammalian cells. This pathway is found in all gram positive, gram negative and mycobacteria thereby making it an attractive target for the development of a broad-spectrum anti-infective. This pathway has not previously been targeted by any currently approved drugs, nor by any known natural products, nor is there any significant work in the literature regarding the inhibition of this pathway. Our inhibitors are designed using knowledge of the enzyme(s) mechanism and structure. We have already demonstrated our expertise in the evaluation of the enzymes from different bacterial pathogens in in vitro studies, and we have demonstrated our expertise in the chemical synthesis of potential enzyme inhibitors. We have developed NMR methods to evaluate binding. We will make molecules that are structurally different to many known antibiotics, thereby exploring new chemical space. Compounds will be evaluated as specific enzyme inhibitors (IC50 and Ki), against bacterial cells (MICs), and for toxicity using human kidney cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: MicroRNAs and gene regulation on vascular remodeling in hypertension from mice to humans
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOTENSIN/ALDOSTERONE; EXPERIMENTAL AND HUMAN ESSENTIAL HYPERTENSION; GENE EXPRESSION; MESSENGER RNA; METABOLIC SYNDROME; MICRORNA; VASCULAR REMODELING
Abstract-Résumé: High blood pressure is one of the most important causes of disease and death in humans. It leads to heart attacks, strokes and failure of the kidneys. In large measure this is because it causes injury to blood vessels. Genes regulate the degree to which elevated blood pressure injures blood vessels, thus playing an important role in the magnitude of disease of blood vessels associated with and consequently the severity of complications of high blood pressure. MicroRNAs are newly discovered small nucleic acids that regulate expression of genes, and mRNAs direct the production of proteins that will both form the blood vessels and exert beneficial or nefarious effects on their structure and function, thus modulating injury induced by elevated blood pressure. By identifying microRNAs and mRNAs that are increased or decreased in blood vessels of mice and humans with high blood pressure, and determining how they interact, we hope to identify new targets to improve diagnosis and treatment of high blood pressure, and thus improve health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibitory Synaptic Plasticity and Chloride Regulation
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY AND CALCIUM IMAGING; GABA; HIPPOCAMPUS; INHIBITORY SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; INHIBITORY SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; KCC2 AND CHLORIDE
Abstract-Résumé: The ability of animals to adapt to their ever-changing environments depends in large part on their ability to learn and remember.  Our research is centered on the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying learning and memory.  Using state-of-the-art recordings we are able to measure the electrical activity simultaneously from two neurons which are being modified in response to electrical signals that simulate learning.  This neuronal modification in response to electrical activity is called synaptic plasticity.   This grant is focused on understanding how synapses that use the brain chemical GABA are modified during synaptic plasticity.  In particular we are trying to understand the role of a key neuronal protein in this process.  The protein we are interested in is called KCC2; the function of this protein is to maintain electrical gradients across the neuronal membrane. KCC2 is essential for survival, as the absence of this protein at birth results in death due to respiratory failure.  Currently there are no known treatments for restoring KCC2 expression. Our goal is to discover the mechanisms that regulate KCC2 so that we can develop prevention strategies and therapeutic treatments for those disorders associated with KCC2 dysfunction. These discoveries will transform the treatments available for neurological disorders associate with the loss of this protein including neuropathic pain, stroke, and epileptic seizures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Les hommes et la santé: à la recherche de modèles masculins sains
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPORTEMENTS DE SANTE; GENRE
Abstract-Résumé: Au Canada, les hommes ont une esperance de vie de cinq annees inferieures a celle des femmes. Cette difference pourrait s'expliquer en partie par le fait que les hommes sont moins nombreux que les femmes a adopter les comportements promoteurs de sante (comme une saine alimentation, une consommation moderee d'alcool, l'abstention tabagique, une saine gestion du stress, un recours preventif aux soins medicaux). Afin d'ameliorer l'efficacite des messages de promotion de la sante destines aux hommes, il est necessaire de mieux connaitre les facteurs associes a l'adoption des comportements promoteurs de sante chez differents sous-groupes d'hommes. L'etude proposee examinera l'influence de l'identite masculine, de l'age, du statut socioeconomique, du groupe de pairs, de la situation conjugale, de la valeur accordee a la sante, du lieu de controle et du sentiment d'auto efficacite sur les comportements promoteurs de sante des hommes. Une etude quantitative par questionnaire sera realisee aupres d'hommes adultes, dont la moitie travaille dans des milieux typiquement masculins et l'autre moitie dans des emplois mixtes (occupes a part egale par des hommes et des femmes). Les repondants seront recrutes grace a la collaboration de syndicats partenaires.  A partir des participants a cette enquete, un echantillon a variation maximale sera selectionne afin de participer a des entretiens en profondeur dans le cadre du volet qualitatif de l'etude. Au total, 64 hommes seront choisis en fonction de leur utilisation des comportements promoteurs de sante (eleve ou faible), de leur statut socioeconomique (faible ou eleve), et de leur groupe de pairs au travail (typiquement masculin ou mixte). Cette etude permettra d'adapter les interventions en promotion de la sante aux besoins particuliers des hommes appartenant a differents sous-groupes et d'augmenter ainsi leur efficacite.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term usage and efficacy of a neural prosthesis for the hemiplegic hand
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL ELECTRICAL STIMULATION; STROKE; TELE-REHABILITATION; UPPER EXTREMITY
Abstract-Résumé: Electrical stimulators are sometimes used in clinics to improve hand function for a short time after stroke, but they are too cumbersome to be used in daily life. We have developed a device that can be used on a permanent basis, called the HandStim. It consists of a wristlet with an in-built stimulator that is controlled by tooth-clicks detected by a sensor similar to a blue-tooth earpiece.  Participants will be randomized into three groups. The control group will be provided with conventional exercise equipment with which they will be trained to do exercises at home for 1 hour/day for the first 6 weeks.  They will be encouraged to use their more affected hand in daily life during this time and for the remaining 20 weeks. The second group will receive HandStims and the same exercise regime for the first 6 weeks, followed by 20 weeks of self-directed HandStim usage in daily life. The third group will receive HandStims and a ReJoyce system, on which they will perform exercises 1 hour/day for 6 weeks, two sessions per week being tele-supervised. They will also be encouraged to use their HandStims in daily life for the remaining 20 weeks. The exercises in all three groups will involve shoulder, elbow and wrist movements as well as grasp-release and dexterous manipulation. The first two groups will be contacted by phone twice a week for 6 weeks and all three groups fortnightly for the remaining 20 weeks, to monitor compliance and compile motor activity logs. In the FES groups, usage (number and duration of grasp-release cycles) will be captured by counters in the stimulators and downloaded when the participants return to the laboratory for assessments. This will provide data for health-care providers on the likely usage of the HandStim by stroke survivors.   The premise of this study is that the HandStim/ReJoyce combination will become a model for the future of upper extremity rehabilitation after stroke and spinal cord injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of long non-coding RNAs in glioblastoma progression and angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; GLIOBLASTOMA; LONG NON-CODING RNAS; MOUSE MODELS; TUMOUR INITIATING CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Glioblastoma is the most common adult brain tumour and one of the most difficult cancers to treat.  Tumours, like normal human tissue, require a blood supply to deliver nutrients in order to survive.  For this reason, there is an effort to develop drugs which prevent blood vessels from forming in a tumour as a means to treat cancer.  Unfortunately, this approach has thus far had little effect on prolonging the survival of glioblastoma patients.  To improve treatments for glioblastoma patients, it is essential to understand why these therapies fail.  It was recently found that glioblastoma cancer cells can change into blood vessels within the tumour, which then contribute to supplying the necessary nutrients for tumour growth.  However, blood vessels made from glioblastoma cells are not sensitive to drugs which prevent growth of normal blood vessels.  This might help explain why current treatments which block vessel growth do not improve patient survival.   Most current cancer treatments are inadequate and provide only temporary improvement, followed by relapse with the patient becoming sicker.  Our aim is to understand how glioblastoma cancer cells can turn into blood vessels to feed the tumor and ultimately to develop new drugs to block this process.  Although we will focus on glioblastoma, our findings will be relevant to all brains tumours, and cancer in general given that tumors require a blood supply to survive.  The ultimate goal of this work is to develop more effective treatments for brain tumours and improve the lives of afflicted patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Cedar Project: Exploring vulnerabilities to HIV, HCV, and STIs among young Aboriginal people who use drugs in urban and rural settings
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HCV; HIV/AIDS; MHEALTH; MULTI-DISCIPLINARY; RESILIENCY; RURAL AND REMOTE HEALTH; STIS; SUBSTANCE USE
Abstract-Résumé: Reasons for increased vulnerability to HIV and hepatitis C (HCV) among young Aboriginal people who use illicit drugs are not understood well and most information is limited to urban centres such as Vancouver's downtown eastside. First Nations leadership and Aboriginal HIV/AIDS service organizations in BC are deeply concerned about increasing rates of HIV and HCV infections among their youth and the lack of understanding about why this is occurring in rural and remote locations, including on reserves.  The Cedar Project is a community-based and Aboriginal-governed research program located in Prince George, a forestry and mining town in the northern interior of British Columbia; in Chase, a forestry and tourism municipality in south-central BC; and in Vancouver's downtown eastside. The aim of Cedar is to study HIV and HCV related vulnerabilities of Aboriginal young people, aged 14 to 30 years who use injection or non-injection drugs.  Since the study's beginning, Aboriginal collaborators and investigators, collectively known as the Cedar Project Partnership, have governed the entire research and knowledge translation process.  Together with the Cedar Project partnership, we now propose to: 1) broaden the study to include Aboriginal youth in Chase; 2) implement a surveillance initiative for sexually transmitted infections; 3) explore what helps and what hinders these youth entering into successful addiction treatment; and 4) test whether using mobile phone technology can help prevent HIV and HCV and improve health outcomes in these vulnerable young people.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of apoE in mild traumatic brain injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ABC TRANSPORTERS; APOLIPOPROTEIN E; CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT; MOUSE MODELS; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: In North America, traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability for people under 40 years of age. We are only now beginning to understand that concussion is indeed a mild TBI that can have long-term consequences, including an increased risk for Alzheimer's Disease (AD). AD and TBI have similarities and differences that are important to understand. For example, amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are always found in AD brains, but TBI brains mostly contain tangles with only about 30% also containing plaques. Understanding how TBI triggers amyloid and tangle formation is very important, because treatments originally designed to block amyloid or tangle formation in AD may also be useful for TBI. Additionally, apoE is by far the most important genetic risk factor for AD and has also been suggested to affect TBI outcome. A major role for apoE in AD is getting rid of amyloid plaques. However, it is not known whether apoE also functions in this way after TBI. Finally, a key question is whether the consequences of TBI are different if the injury is experienced in youth compared to mid-life. The Wellington laboratory will use their unique animal model of concussion to begin to answer these questions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of hyaluronan in the growth and function of the skeletal system.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; BONE; CARTILAGE; CHONDRODYSPLASIA; DEVELOPMENT; GROWTH; HYALURONAN; KNOCKOUT MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Hyaluronan is a polysaccharide present throughout the body, but is particularly abundant in the skeletal system, where it is essential for the normal structure and function of the cartilage models that form the long bones and vertebrae, and for regulating the metabolic activity of their constituent cells, the chondrocytes. Prevention of hyaluronan synthesis in cartilage during fetal development results in a neonatal lethal dwarfism, in which the formation and growth of all bones derived from cartilage are abnormal.  This implies that depletion of hyaluronan not only impairs chondrocyte metabolism and cartilage function, but also prevents the normal formation and subsequent modeling of the resulting bone by its constituent cells, the osteoblasts and osteoclasts.  The current proposal is designed to extend these observations from the fetus to post-natal life, and to evaluate how hyaluronan influences the formation of bones such as the skull that are not derived from cartilage.  This will allow us to understand whether hyaluronan deficiency in the growth plates of juvenile bones will impair growth, whether hyaluronan deficiency in the articular cartilage of the joints will promote the onset of degenerative arthritis, and whether hyaluronan deficiency in skull will prevent its normal formation.  It will also determine the mechanism by which hyaluronan depletion exerts its effect on the different cell types.  Understanding how hyaluronan deficiency leads to the formation of abnormal cartilage and bone is a prerequisite for determining whether hyaluronan administration can be used as a therapeutic strategy in conditions where cartilage and bone formation and function are impaired, such as in aberrant fracture healing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure function analysis of the dual protein kinase-RNase signaling proteins and the eIF2a protein kinases
Keywords-MotsClés: CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; PHOSPHOREGULATION; PROTEIN KINASE; RNASE; SIGNALING; SUBSTRATE RECOGNITION; X-RAY
Abstract-Résumé: Ire1 and RNaseL are protein kinases with the unique ability to cleave RNA. The two proteins function in very different cellular processes owing in large part to difference in their ability to recognize and cleave messenger RNA targets. RNaseL plays a key role in inhibiting the ability of viruses to replicate in human cells while Ire1 plays a key role in allowing cells to adapt to the accumulation of toxic levels of unfolded proteins. The two protein kinases act in conjunction with a second pair of kinases, namely PERK and PKR, which provide backup to their essential cellular functions.  RNaseL cleaves RNA non-specifically, which allows it to degrade all cellular and viral RNAs in response to the detection of viral infection. In contrast, Ire1 recognizes one messenger RNAs amongst thousands of genes expressed in the cell, to initiate a non-conventional splicing reaction. RNaseL and Ire1 play important roles in many human diseases. RNaseL is critical for the interferon-mediated antiviral responses during West Nile virus, hepatitis C virus, and herpes simplex virus type 1 infections by limiting the accumulation of viral RNAs. In addition, mutation of the RNASEL gene correlates with an increased incidence of prostrate and pancreatic cancers. The function of RNaseL is also perturbed in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome. Defective Ire1 function has been implicated in human diseases such as familial Alzheimer's disease, diabettes, bipolar disorder, colitis, and neural death following trauma. Ire1 function is also essential for the growth of certain tumours.  In this proposal we aim to achieve a detailed understanding of the atomic structure of Ire1, RNaseL, PERK and PKR using x-ray crystallographic methods. Our underlying hope is that our studies will open new avenues for clinical intervention to treat human disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Subcellular Redistribution of Proteins Following DNA Damage: A Role for the MCM Complex in DNA Repair.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR; DNA REPLICATION; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; HOMOLOGOUS RECOMBINATION; IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEOMICS; SUBCELLULAR LOCALIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Radiation therapy and many of the commonly used cancer chemotherapeutic drugs target DNA for cytotoxicity. The subsequent cellular response to these cancer treatments in both malignant and normal cells/tissues determines the efficiency of the treatment. This response is a complex cellular process involving multiple DNA repair pathways that are specifically activated depending on the type of DNA damage. These pathways have been shown to have great potential as targets for cancer therapy and our understanding of how the cells respond to DNA damage will play a crucial role in the development of new anticancer strategies. We have developed a unique set of techniques that combines cellular fractionation protocols allowing purification of different cellular compartments, as well as mass spectrometry techniques that allows identification and quantification of thousands of proteins at the same time. We used these techniques to characterize the changes in cellular localization of proteins following treatment of human cancer cells with etoposide, a chemotherapeutic drug that causes DNA damage. Initial preliminary experiments provided unexpected new evidence showing that DNA damage alters the properties of a protein complex normally involved in DNA replication during cell division, the MCM complex.  In this application, we propose to apply this novel approach combining quantitative proteomics and protein biochemistry to identify and characterize other members of the complex and elucidate the mechanism in which they play a role in the cellular response to DNA damage. It is hoped that this information will lead to a better understanding of how different classes of chemotherapy drugs can cause specific DNA damage in normal and malignant cells and identify more direct therapeutic intervention by identifying specific molecules/interactions that can serve as targets for drugs designed to selectively inhibit proliferation of cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Allosteric Regulation and Biased Signaling of Prostaglandin F2alpha receptors.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOSTERIC AND BIASED SIGNALING; CANCER; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; MOLECULAR PHARMACOLOY; PRE-TERM DELIVERY; PROSTAGLANDIN
Abstract-Résumé: Our research focuses on a class of membrane receptor, for molecules called prostaglandins involved in premature birth and some forms of cancer (e.g. colorectal, endometrial). Pharmacological therapies targeting these receptors would greatly reduce the personal and socio-economical burden associated with these problems.  Our research has unveiled the properties of a new class of drugs that act in an unconventional way on these receptors to selectively affect the response of the natural hormone.  We propose to characterize the functional domains of these receptors, known as "allosteric" sites, targeted by our newly discovered compounds, to iteratively generate more selective and efficacious drugs.  Our research should have great impact on managing pre-term labour, which is associated with more than 75% of neonate mortality, as well as in the treatment of endometrial and colon cancers which have a 20% rate in mortality among women, and represent the second leading cause of cancer-related death among Canadians, respectively.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies in Molecular Parasitology
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIAL PEPTIDES; GENOMICS; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; LEISHMANIA; MACROPHAGES; MITOCHONDRIA; MOLECULAR PARASITOLOGY; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Leishmania is a parasite of humans that causes a disease called leishmaniasis that can be fatal if not treated. There are three forms of leishmaniasis: cutaneous, mucocutaneous and visceral, that are elicited by various species of Leishmania. This disease is found in 98 countries with the estimated number of cases currently at 500,000 for visceral and 1.5 million for cutaneous leishmaniasis. There is no vaccine and the drugs used to treat leishmaniasis are very toxic to humans. As with many other parasites, Leishmania has a two stage life cycle involving an insect vector, the sandfly, and humans. Leishmania is transferred to humans when an infected sandfly takes a blood meal. Leishmania then infect and multiply inside white blood cells. Research is proposed to identify the genes and molecules in both Leishmania and human white blood cells that are involved in promoting the infection, growth and persistence of Leishmania. These studies are aimed to identify new drug targets and new drug therapies for the treatment of leishmaniasis.  Current treatments for leishmaniasis are becoming increasingly ineffective due to the emergence of drug-resistant strains. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop new classes of drugs that are active against Leishmania. Antimicrobial peptides are naturally occurring peptides used in organisms ranging from bacteria to mammals as part of a defense mechanism. Some of these have been shown to have anti-leishmanial activity. Our research will study the effectiveness of these peptides to treat different forms of leishmaniasis. This will involve re-designing the peptides for use in humans.  Due to the similarities between Leishmania and other intracellular pathogens, understanding the mechanisms involved in causing leishmaniasis and the development of new therapies, will also help in the treatment and prevention of similar diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Communication and Crosstalk Between Fibroblasts and Heart Cells in the Mammalian Myocardium
Keywords-MotsClés: ATP; ATRIAL RHYTHM DISTURBANCES; CELLULAR ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; CONNEXINS; FIBROBLAST; ION CHANNELS; MATHEMATICAL MODELLING; MYOCYTE; PATCH CLAMP; PURINERGIC RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed experimental and modelling studies will result in an improved understanding of the principles and cellular mechanisms which govern the physiological, pharmacological and pathophysiological responses of non-muscle cells (fibroblasts) isolated from the hearts of adult mammals. Fibroblasts are thought to function only as mechanical and metabolic 'support cells' for cardiac cells (myocytes). Myocytes are the heart cells which contract; collectively they produce the heart beat. Our approach will be multidisciplinary, that is it will employ techniques from a number of different scientific disciplines. Cellular electrophysiological methods (patch clamp) will be complemented by simultaneous records of membrane potential using voltage sensitive dyes, and spectrophotometric measurements of changes in intracellular calcium. The planned studies will address a number of fundamental questions: i) What is the electrophysiological or ionic basis of the fibroblast resting potential? (ii) Do myocytes and fibroblasts interact by cell-to-cell current flow (electrotonically) or through chemical messenger systems or both? iii) Do fibroblasts synthesize and secrete biological substances which alter heart contractility? Most of these experiments will be carried out using acutely isolated fibroblasts from the ventricles of adult mouse and rat hearts. However, fibroblasts from human atrium will also be utilized. We will take advantage of genetic information and some aspects of molecular medicine so that, where possible, our data can be related to Clinical Physiology and Pathophysiology. Where appropriate, our findings and data from the literature will be integrated by developing a mathematical model of cardiac fibroblast/myocyte interactions. This model will aid in the design of new experiments and provide a valuable teaching tool for trainees, graduate students and clinical fellows.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physical Activity and Breast Cancer Etiology: the Underlying Biological Mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL MECHANISMS; BODY WEIGHT; BREAST CANCER; EXERCISE; IMMUNITY; INFLAMMATION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; OXIDATIVE STRESS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Physical activity reduces breast cancer risk and, thereby, is an excellent means for primary prevention. An improved understanding of how physical activity reduces breast cancer development is needed in designing optimal lifestyle interventions. To date, research has focused on individual biologic pathways, such as changes in body fat, hormone levels, insulin resistance or inflammation. The aim of this project is to evaluate a biologic model relating multiple inter-related pathways for breast cancer using data from the Alberta Physical Activity and Breast Cancer Prevention (ALPHA) Trial. The ALPHA Trial was a randomized controlled trial of 320 inactive postmenopausal women that examined the effects of a year-long moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise intervention on biomarkers for breast cancer. As part of the present project, a supplementary study will collect data on biologic endpoints not previously examined in the ALPHA Trial. The project will simultaneously estimate the exercise-induced change on sex hormones, body fat, insulin resistance, inflammation, immunity and oxidative stress. Analyses will be performed using advanced statistical modeling methods to quantify the direct and indirect effects of the exercise intervention on different pathways and, therefore, identify the predominant pathways affected by the exercise intervention. This project is one of the first to examine the simultaneous effects of an exercise intervention on multiple inter-related endpoints within a randomized controlled design. The findings from this project will contribute to an understanding of the beneficial biological effects for a given dose of exercise and help guide future healthy lifestyle recommendations to obtain the desired preventive effects for reducing breast cancer risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of the Mechanisms of Idiosyncratic Drug Reactions
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; DRUG METABOLISM; IDIOSYNCRATIC DRUG REACTIONS; IMMUNOTOXICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Drugs can be a great benefit for the treatment of diseases, but they can also cause serious side effects or adverse reactions. One type of adverse reaction that is particularly difficult to prevent is the idiosyncratic drug reaction (idiosyncratic means particular to an individual).  These are adverse effects that do not involve the therapeutic effect of the drug and do not occur in most patients, but when they do occur they can be quite serious and it is usually impossible to predict who will have such and adverse reaction.  It appears that most of these adverse reactions are allergic in nature, that is they are mediated by the immune system, but they are hard to study.  It would be quite useful to reproduce such adverse reactions in animals so they could be more easily studied, but they are also unpredictable in animals.  We have developed animal models of two types of idiosyncratic drug reactions involving the skin (skin rash) and the liver.  These models are being used to understand and ultimately prevent such adverse reactions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Organizational change to protect worker health
Keywords-MotsClés: DISABILITY; HEALTH CARE; ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGE; WORK INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: The protection and improvement of the health of employees in health care institutions is a substantial challenge. This project proposes to measure the impact of three year organization change plan in Ontario's largest multi-site acute care community hospital system employing more than 4,300 staff. The objectives of the organizational change plan are to reduce the incidence of work-related musculoskeletal disorders, improve workplace practices in the area of return-to-work and disability prevention and strengthen the culture of safety in the organization in the Niagara Health System. Over the three year period 2011-2013, the objectives of the organizational change plan are to reduce the incidence of total compensation claims registered with the Ontario Workplace Safety and Insurance Board by 25% and to reduce the total days of disability provided wage replacement benefits by WSIB by 25%. This proposed research project will document the process and measure the outcomes of the organizational change plan. The research plan has three components: 1) a comparison of workers' compensation claim incidence and duration in the Niagara Health System to a comparable Ontario health care system for a three year period prior to and following January 2011, 2) a repeated survey of a sample of approximately 350 NHS staff for each of three years (2011, 2012 and 2013) and 3) two detailed case studies of the organizational change process, using both qualitative and quantitative research methods.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing and Validating the BUSS (Bladder Utility Symptom Scale)-  A Disease-Specific Utility Instrument for Bladder Cancer Health-Related Quality of Life
Keywords-MotsClés: BLADDER CANCER; PREFERENCES; QUALITY OF LIFE; UTILITY
Abstract-Résumé: The quality of life of patients with bladder cancer is important. Most treatments for bladder cancer cause some side effects that can affect quality of life. The choice of treatment depends on the type and stage of bladder cancer but also on patients' personal perceptions/opinions of different side effects. It would be useful to know more about the quality of life of patients with bladder cancer before and after different treatments. We propose to develop a questionnaire, the BUSS (Bladder Utility Symptom Scale), that patients with bladder cancer can complete to measure their quality of life. This questionnaire will be similar to one that we developed several years ago for patients with prostate cancer (the PORPUS  or Patient Oriented Prostate Utility Scale). There are several steps required to develop a questionnaire. These include : 1) Review published articles to find the items that should be included on the questionnaire; 2) Ask patients and experts to meet in focus groups to determine how important each item is to patients with bladder cancer; 3) Choose the items for the final questionnaire, based on their responses; 4) Decide upon the types of answers for each item; 5) Test the questionnaire in a group of patients to make sure that the wording is clear and appropriate; 6) Develop a method to score the questionnaire; 7) Test the revised questionnaire in a second group of patients with bladder cancer. In this study, we plan to do all 7 of these steps. The BUSS will provide a way to measure quality of life in bladder cancer patients before and after different treatments. It will measure the effect of bladder cancer and its treatment on quality of life. This information can be used to help make decisions about bladder cancer treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: GPR120-dependent activation of hypothalamic anti-diabetic mechanisms by omega-3 fatty acids
Keywords-MotsClés: G PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTORS; HYPOTHALAMIC NEURONS; INFLAMMATION; INSULIN; INSULIN RESISTANCE; OMEGA-3 FATTY ACIDS; OREXOGENIC NEUROPEPTIDES; REAT-TIME POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS
Abstract-Résumé: Diets rich in fish oils lower the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) by supporting insulin signalling and effective energy utilization by our bodies.  In part, these benefits are mediated by the fatty acid (FA) receptor, GPR120, which strengthens the insulin response and decreases overall inflammation in our fat, liver, and immune cells.  Despite a critical function of GPR120 in these tissues, the role of GPR120 in the brain, an essential organ in the regulation of overall insulin responsiveness, appetite control and energy homeostasis, awaits elucidation. The abundant expression of GPR120 together with the ability of dietary FAs to assess the brain promotes us to study the ability of this FA receptor to modulate the insulin response, inflammatory tone, and production of feeding signals by the brain. GPR120 activation in the brain will be tested by exposing our rat cell line isolated from the brain with the FAs found in fish oils and analyzing their insulin sensitivity, inflammatory response, and expression of appetite signals using well established techniques. Impaired insulin response, widespread inflammation and obesity are major predisposing and precipitating factors in the onset and progression of T2DM.  As such, furthering our understanding of the anti-diabetic effects of fish oils in preventing or repairing these conditions is essential in the development of targeted therapies for the treatment of this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Candidate Neuronal Circuits in Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; FUNCTIONAL MRI; MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER; PROTON MAGNETIC RESONANCE SPECTROSCOPY; SCHIZOPHRENIA; VOXEL-BASED MORPHOMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a brain disorder caused by a number of genetic, hypoxic and/or viral factors.  Promising genetic correlates of schizophrenia have emerged in recent years but none explain more than a tiny fraction of cases. The challenge of our time is to characterize the final common pathway of schizophrenia and other major psychiatric illnesses. The goal of the present application is characterize these neuronal circuits with advanced magnetic resonance imaging techniques which open a window on brain chemistry, structure, and function. First episode schizophrenic and mood disordered patients will be studied before treatment, after stabilization on medication and at three years after onset of illness and compared to healthy volunteers studied at baseline and at the end of three years. A better understanding of the chemical, structural, functional anomalies in brain circuits associated with schizophrenia and mood disorders could lead to the first brain imaging test to aid diagnosis. It may also demonstrate which changes are progressive in different networks in each condition, potentially opening new avenues for treatment of these disabling disorders if a degenerative component can be demonstrated

TitreApplicationTitle: The Influence of Diabetes on Cancer Screening and Prognosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CANCER SCREENING; DIABETES; HEALTH SERVICES
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer and diabetes are two of the most common diseases in our society, and evidence shows that diabetes is associated with both a higher cancer risk and lower cancer survival. The reasons for these associations are still unclear. Most research has focused on the role of metabolic factors and diabetes drugs. However, few studies have looked at the role of health care factors such as cancer screening. Regular screening for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer has been shown to improve cancer survival. Diabetes may lead to lower cancer screening due to competing demands of diabetes care or other risk factors. These health care gaps increase the risk of more advanced cancer stage at diagnosis and higher cancer mortality in persons with diabetes.  The goal of this study is to explore the influence of diabetes on the clinical steps leading to cancer diagnosis, by examining 1) whether they have lower cancer screening, 2) the risk factors for lack of cancer screening, and 3) a higher cancer mortality and more advanced stage at diagnosis compared to persons without diabetes. This study will use the existing Ontario health care databases between 1994 and 2012 to compare outcomes between persons with and without diabetes eligible for screening. First we will assess for differences in up-to-date screening rates for breast, colorectal, and cervical cancer. Second, we will examine how provider, health system and patient factors may lower cancer screening rates in patients with diabetes. Third, we will assess for differences in cancer mortality and stage of breast and colorectal cancer.   This research is important because the number of people living with diabetes is reaching epidemic proportions, and cancer is a leading cause of disability and death in our society. Addressing potential gaps in cancer screening in persons with diabetes will help to improve cancer care and outcomes for this population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Basis of cyclic AMP-Signal Translation in Eukaryotes by Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOSTERY; CAMP; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES; DYNAMICS; EPILEPSY; HCN; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE (NMR); PKA; SIGNALING; STRUCTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiac myxomas are tumors that can cause stroke and/or heart failure.  These cardiovascular disorders, and others including acute ischemic stress, are associated with a defective reading of the signal transmitted in the cell by a second messenger called cyclic adenosine monophosphate or cAMP.  The translation of the cAMP signal plays a critical role also in the development of bradycardia (i.e. life-threatening low heart rates) and epilepsy.  The long-term goal of this project is to elucidate the structural and dynamical changes that translate the cAMP signal into a specific biological response necessary for the survival of the cell.  We will use Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy to investigate how, under physiological solution conditions, the cAMP second messenger interacts with and modifies two of its most important target proteins, the cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) and the hyperpolarization-activated and cyclic nucleotide-gated channels (HCN).  The effect of the cAMP second messenger on the PKA and HCN proteins is currently poorly understood at a structural level and NMR has only very recently been used to investigate this at atomic resolution.  NMR will reveal not only the structural changes in PKA and HCN caused by cAMP, but will also characterize how the dynamics of PKA and HCN is affected by cAMP.  Knowledge of both structure and dynamics on both proteins is required in order to fully understand at a molecular level how cAMP works in the human heart and brain.  The elucidation of the structural and dynamical changes associated with cAMP-binding is expected to help define general rules applicable to the design of drugs for cardiovascular and neurological disorders.
