TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical and biological implications of monoallelic gene expression in pediatric malignant brain tumors.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD CNS TUMORS; EXOME SEQUENCING; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE MUTATIONS; SEQUENOM
Abstract-Résumé: Malignant brain tumors are the leading cause of death in childhood cancer. There is an urgent need for new therapies to improve survival for these children.  In the human genome, each gene has two copies, one from the mother and one from the father. In normal tissues, genes from both parents are active. When only one copy is used, it is called monoallelic expression or MAE.  The extent and significance of MAE in cancer is unknown.  We recently discovered by using genetic tools that in brain tumors, there is abnormal high level of MAE.  MAE increases with tumor aggressiveness and it is specific for some important cancer genes. Furthermore we have shown that for these genes MAE may be used by cancers to achieve a more aggressive disease. Based on these findings we think that MAE is crucial for childhood malignant brain tumors and can be utilized by us as a tool to uncover new therapies and predict survival for children with brain tumors. In this proposal, we will build on our initial exciting observations and will discover genes affected by MAE in pediatric brain tumors. In addition, we will manipulate these genes using current technologies in the following steps: 1.We will uncover genes which have MAE in pediatric malignant brain tumors using whole genome sequencing tools. We will then find the genes from this list which we can use to predict survival and tailor different therapies to these children. 2.We will then investigate the mechanisms which cause MAE. We will look specifically for mechanisms that we can inhibit and use to treat these children. 3. Finally, we will compile the genes uncovered in our initial steps and choose the best targets. We will then inhibit MAE in patient derived cell lines and find new medications that can be brought forward for clinical use soon. When we complete these studies, we will be able to design novel treatments for these devastating diseases. Moreover, our findings will open a window to the unknown role of MAE in cancer

TitreApplicationTitle: A prospective study of the role of genes and folates in postpartum psychopathology in women at increased risk.
Keywords-MotsClés: FOLATE; GENETICS; POSTPARTUM PSYCHOPATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Women who have a history of mental health problems have higher chances than other women to have mental health problems after delivering a baby. Mental health problems after delivering a baby, like depression and psychosis (loss of contact with reality) are very difficult for new mothers and their families. It is important to better understand what causes these problems so that we can develop new ways to help. In this study, we will recruit women who have previously had mental health problems and look at genetic differences and measure how much of a particular kind of B vitamin women have in their blood. We want to see if these things can contribute to the risk for developing mental health problems after delivering a baby. If we find that they do contribute to a woman's risk, we might be able to develop and test new strategies to help these women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactional dynamics in health care organizations: A network analysis of services for the elderly
Keywords-MotsClés: FORMAL/INFORMAL CARE SYSTEM; MIXED METHOD; ORGANIZATION; SOCIAL NETWORK ANALYSIS; SOCIAL PROCESS
Abstract-Résumé: The health systems of many countries are being forced to adapt to aging populations, at the same time as they are grappling with rapidly escalating costs and considerable organizational challenges. In this context, Quebec, like other jurisdictions, has been experimenting with different care practices such as integrated care programs and local service networks. The specificity of these approaches is that they aim to coordinate complex interactions amongst a large number of different types of professionals and organisations. These issues have normally been studied as organisational problems or at best, problems of "continuity of care", but these approaches are inadequate to the new, complex context of care. In this study, we analyse the new organisational context of elder care focusing on front-line practitioners and family members caring for older people with chronic health problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: microRNA regulation of ABCA1 and its impact on beta cell function
Keywords-MotsClés: ABCA1; BETA CELLS; CHOLESTEROL; DIABETES; MICRORNA; MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes is a major cause of disease and death, currently affecting 2.5 million Canadians. ABCA1 is crucial for removing cholesterol from cells thereby preventing its accumulation within cells. Lack of ABCA1 in beta cells leads to cholesterol accumulation in these cells, reduces insulin secretion and leads to impaired glucose tolerance in mice. In addition, ABCA1 may affect glucose tolerance via its essential role in HDL production by the liver. Low plasma HDL in humans is a risk factor for development of diabetes. The objectives of our proposed studies are to: 1) Assess novel approaches to up-regulate ABCA1 in beta cells and its impact on insulin secretion. 2) Determine how alterations in plasma HDL induced by changes in liver ABCA1 levels affect beta cell function in mice.  3) Evaluate how genetic variations in ABCA1 change glucose metabolism in humans We will examine whether small molecules called microRNA can be used to increase ABCA1 levels in beta cells and thereby reduce beta cell cholesterol accumulation, improve insulin secretion and glucose tolerance in disease mouse models. Secondly, we will use these microRNAs to change ABCA1 levels in the liver and assess its impact on glucose tolerance and beta cell function in mice. Lastly, we will evaluate beta cell function and glucose metabolism in family members with genetic alterations in ABCA1 activity. These studies will provide crucial information about liver effects on beta cell function and the role of ABCA1 in cholesterol regulation and insulin secretion in beta cells, and may contribute to the development of therapeutic strategies to modulate cholesterol in beta cells and reverse or prevent diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of a hybrid and injectible Nanoparticle BMP Delivery System on Bone Regeneration during Distraction Osteogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE CONSOLIDATION; BONE MORPHOGENETIC PROTEINS; DISTRACTION OSTEOGENESIS; EXTERNAL FIXATOR; GENE SILENCING; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MICROCT; MOUSE MODEL; NANOPARTICLE DELIVERY SYSTEM; QUANTUM DOTS
Abstract-Résumé: Distraction osteogenesis (DO) is a surgical technique used to treat limb length discrepancies, deformities and bone loss secondary to trauma, infection and tumours. DO involves performing an osteotomy and gradually distracting the two bone segments with an external fixator, which generates new bone within the distracted gap. One of the problems associated with DO is the long period of time the fixator has to be kept on until the bone has consolidated, which may cause numerous social and medical problems for the patient. Different methods have been studied to accelerate the consolidation phase, including the use of Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs). However, the use of large doses of exogenous BMPs is costly and may trigger the onset of unknown side effects. Thus, the first aim of this study is to evaluate the in vivo efficacy of a BMP nanoparticle delivery system (a system we have developed and tested in vitro and in vivo) during DO to provide a sustained release of low doses of BMPs over a prolong period of time. The second aim is to investigate if the bioavailability and efficiency of endogenous BMPs can be increased by reducing the expression of BMP antagonists using targeted gene silencing at the distracted site. Results from this study will help decrease the time required for the fixator to be kept on and improve the functional outcome of patients undergoing DO.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protein folding and quality control within the endoplasmic reticulum
Keywords-MotsClés: CALNEXIN; CALRETICULIN; CIS-TRANS PROLINE ISOMERIZATION; DISULFIDE BOND; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; ER ASSOCIATED DEGRADATION; GENOME-WIDE SHRNA SCREEN; HUMAN DISEASE; MOLECULAR CHAPERONE; PEPTIDYL PROLYL ISOMERASES; PRION PROTEIN; PROTEIN AGGREGATION; PROTEIN DISULFIDE ISOMERASES; PROTEIN FOLDING; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; QUALITY CONTROL; RNA INTERFERENCE; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; STRUCTURE-FUNCTION ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins that reside on the surface of cells or that are secreted from cells are initially made in a compartment called the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The ER provides an environment that helps proteins fold into their correct three-dimensional shape and it is also responsible for "quality control", a process in which proteins that do not fold correctly are retained and ultimately destroyed. Many human diseases, such as cystic fibrosis and juvenile emphysema, are caused by mutant proteins that do not fold correctly, leading to their retention and destruction in the ER. This is unfortunate because some of these mutant proteins could still function if the quality control system of the ER would release them and allow their movement to their correct cellular location.  We are studying several groups of molecules of the human ER, including the molecular chaperones calnexin and calreticulin, more than 25 enzymes of the thiol oxidoreductase and peptidyl prolyl isomerase families, as well as "ERAD" molecules that are dedicated to the recognition and disposal of improperly folded proteins. Our current experiments are designed to modify or eliminate each of these molecules to determine their functions in protein folding and in quality control, and the extent of cooperation between them. We and others are finding that some of these molecules promote proper protein folding, others participate in quality control, and some are involved in both processes. Our goal is to obtain a thorough understanding of their functions and how their actions are coordinated so that we can design therapeutic strategies to improve the folding of disease-associated mutant proteins and to promote their exit from the ER.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Pharmacogenetics of Bevacizumab: A Companion Correlative Study of the Ovarian Cancer Clinical Trial, ICON7
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-ANGIOGENESIS; OVARIAN CANCER; PHARMACOGENETICS; PREDICTIVE BIOMARKERS
Abstract-Résumé: Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death from gynecologic malignancy in North America. Several international clinical trials have shown improved survival for women receiving bevacizumab (Avastin), a new molecular-targeting drug that blocks blood vessel formation. This drug is given in combination with standard chemotherapy consisting of two drugs, carboplatin and paclitaxel. Many Canadian women participated in ICON7, one of these trials that set a new standard. However, not all women benefit from this treatment and many suffer from side effects such as severe high blood pressure, especially important as prolonged treatment with bevacizumab (> 1 year) is required to see a benefit.  Whereas some inherited variations in our genetic code (DNA) affect hair and eye colour, others may affect how well we respond to certain drugs. Previous investigators suggest that it might be possible to predict whether someone will benefit from bevacizumab therapy and, importantly for quality of life, who will develop intolerable side effects, by examining specific variations in a person's genes. The standard carboplatin and paclitaxel chemotherapy drugs in this trial are also used, daily across Canada, to treat ovarian and many other different cancers; these drugs are also associated with side effects. Thus, we will also examine whether we can predict either the benefit or side effects associated with these chemotherapy drugs. Predictive genetic information can be obtained from a simple blood test at the time of diagnosis, which can then be used in the clinic to guide patients and their doctors in making treatment choices. In this proposal, to identify and confirm genetic variations as predictors of survival and side effects, we will study them in patients participating in the ICON7 trial, confirming our findings in a set of other clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Androgen Receptor Activation by Glucocorticoid Metabolite: a Novel Player in the Physiopathology of Respiratory Distress Syndrome in Neonates
Keywords-MotsClés: BPD; DISEASE: PROBLEM LINK TO PREMATURE BIRTH AND; EXPERTISE: LUNG BIOLOGY AND PHYSIOLOGY; GENERAL ENDOCRINOLOGY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; LUNG DEVELOPMENT (IMPAIRED ALVEOLAR AND CAPILLARY GROWTH); MICROARNS; PLACENTAL PHYSIOLOGY; PRIMARY CULTURES OF ENDOTHELIALS-FIBROBLASTS ENRICHED CELLS; RDS; SIRNAS; STEROID SYNTHESIS/METABOLISM/ACTION; TECHNIQUES: GENESHIP MICROARRAYS
Abstract-Résumé: Androgens are considered as male sex hormones and they are normally produced by testis. On the other hand, we have demonstrated that they are produced in the developing lung of both sexes where they should play a physiological role. Consequently, how can the lung use androgens to regulate its normal lung maturation while higher levels of testosterone exist in male fetuses? This remains an open question. On the other hand, we have shown that the fetal lung expresses many of the adrenal gland genes in such a way that a hormone named 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) is produced. While DOC has glucocorticoid (GC) properties, we have shown that it is further transformed in the lung into 5alpha-DH-DOC, a molecule that has rather androgen properties. Based on our previous data showing that some cells of the lung can inactivate testosterone (but not 5alpha-DH-DOC) by an enzyme named 17beta-HSD2, we now start to understand the complex situation making of androgens efficient regulatory molecules in the lung. We hypothesize that 5alpha-DH-DOC plays a normal androgenic role in both sexes and that this is possible because 17beta-HSD2 keeps testosterone away from lung cells where 5alpha-DH-DOC plays a role of regulator. It is well documented that GCs can accelerate lung maturation while androgens "break" the action of GCs. In cases of high risks of premature birth, GCs are administered to mother about to deliver prematurely. This treatment accelerates lung maturation, but the problem is that many fetuses do not respond to antenatal GC. The present application aims to study DOC and 5alpha-DH-DOC synthesis and to accelerate lung maturation by administering an enzyme inhibitor that will block 5alpha-DH-DOC synthesis. This will decrease the amount of androgen-like molecules naturally produced by the lung itself and this is true for both sexes. We expect that this inhibitor will stimulate the action of glucocorticoids and, consequently, accelerate lung maturation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reactive Oxygen Species, Bcl-2-Modifying Factor and Tubular Atrophy in Diabetic Kidneys
Keywords-MotsClés: BCL-2-MODIFYING FACTOR; DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY; GLUCOSE SIGNALING; INSULIN SIGNALING; KIDNEY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PHYSIOLOGY; RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN SYSTEM; TRANSGENIC AND KNOCKOUT MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with diabetes.  It is estimated that approximately 30-50% of the diabetic patients in Canada and in the USA will eventually develop DN leading to chronic renal failure (or end stage renal disease). Kidney fibrosis and tubular atrophy are closely associated with progression of DN though underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This proposal, which concerns the molecular mechanism(s) of high glucose, oxidative stress and Bcl-2-modifying factor (a cell death gene) action on the development of programmed cell death in diabetic kidneys, will increase our knowledge and understanding of their role(s) in the pathogenesis of DN, thereby contributing directly to improved clinical treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of Type 1 Diabetes Risk by Immune Response to the Intestinal Microbiome
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNE DISEASES; GENOMIC ANALYSIS; INTESTINAL MICROBIOME; METAGENOMICS; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; RODENT MODELS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) results from autoimmune destruction of beta cells in the pancreas, the only cells that make the vital hormone insulin. Despite daily insulin injections, individuals with T1D have an increased likelihood of heart disease, stroke, kidney disease, and blindness. T1D is caused by multiple genetic risk factors and poorly defined environmental factors.  The incidence in Canada and other developed countries has been rising at the rate of 3-5% per year over the past 50 years. There is strong evidence that variations at many genes confer T1D risk; however, our genes do not change as quickly as the increases in disease incidence suggesting a role for changing environmental factors. Our intestines carry a complex bacterial community (the gut microbiome) that is essential for normal metabolism and, for the normal development and function of the immune system. Using special laboratory rodent strains carrying genetic variations causing T1D, we have shown that their gut microbiomes differ from those of closely related disease-resistant rodents, and that transfer of normal gut bacteria from low-risk into high-risk animals protects them from T1D. Our project will use state of the art genomic and immunological approaches to determine how benign intestinal bacteria can be used to protect from T1D, to understand "diabetes-protective" bacterial products and the changes they induce in the immune system that confer protection.  In addition to our work in rodent models we will determine how variations in the gut microbiome during early childhood affect the development of T1D in a large, multi-national study of children with high genetic risk for the disease.  Our goal is a safe, biotic intervention that delays progression of beta cell destruction or prevents diabetes. A therapy that produced these outcomes in even a fraction of high-risk children would confer a highly significant health impact in Canada and around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Which Direction to Go? An Optogenetic Interrogation of the C. elegans Motor Circuit
Keywords-MotsClés: C. ELEGANS; CALCIUM IMAGING; MOLECULAR GENETICS; MOTOR CIRCUIT; OPTOGENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Interneuronal communications determine all animal behaviors. It has long been difficult to detect neural circuit activity in live animals, and to study how they generate behaviors. Using the C. elegans nervous system as a model, we will develop a cutting-edge imaging system to visualize and manipulate the activities of neural networks, and to correlate them with different modes of locomotion. We will apply this system to identify the circuit defects in genetic mutants with defective motor outputs, and to elucidate the fundamental principles and mechanisms on how nervous systems ensemble to enable motor and cognitive functions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Feasibility Study of the Adult Congenital Heart Disease - Coping And Resilience (ACHD-CARE) Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; ANXIETY; DEPRESSION; PSYCHOSOCIAL INTERVENTION; QUALITY OF LIFE; RESILIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, there are more than 50,000 adults with congenital heart disease (CHD) who need regular cardiac care. Although their lives were saved as children, they are not 'cured.' They have a chronic illness that starts before birth, can require multiple surgeries and hospital stays, and often leads to early death. It can also impact their mental health and social lives. One in three will have problems with depression or anxiety and most will not be treated for this. There have been no studies of programs to improve the mental health or quality of life of adults with CHD. We will do a 'pilot study' to help decide whether to later do a larger trial of a group program to improve the mental health, social lives, and quality of life of adults with CHD. The program is called the Adult Congenital Heart Disease-Coping and REsilience (ACHD-CARE) Program. We plan to enroll 40 patients. They will have a 50-50 chance of being assigned to the ACHD-CARE Program or receive usual care. All patients will answer survey questions 3 times (before the program, right after the program, and again 6 months later). Patients in the ACHD-CARE Program will attend 8 weekly group sessions. They will learn ways to cope and also be able to talk with other patients about what they have gone through. In this pilot study, we will learn if patients are willing and able to take part in the trial and complete study tasks. We will also figure out a timeline and cost of the study. We will study how patients respond to the ACHD-CARE program. All of this information will help us decide if we should go ahead with a larger trial. If we have positive results, we would next do a multi-site trial with other Adult CHD programs across Canada. We hope that, in the future, the ACHD-CARE Program could be offered to and help many adults with CHD in clinics across Canada. We think this goal is consistent with CIHR's aim of creating new knowledge that leads to better health for Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of beta-amyloid peptides in kainic acid-induced toxicity and its implications in temporal lobe epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTES; BETA AMYLOID PEPTIDES; EXCITOTOXICITY; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROPROTECTION; TEMPORAL LOBE EPILEPSY
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by the occurrence of spontaneous recurrent seizures. It affects  about 50 million people worldwide and its prevalence increases with age especially in population with dementia. Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is the most common form of human epilepsy with recurrent seizures originating from mesial structure such as hippocampus and then propagates to other brain structures. One of the major pathological features associated with TLE is the "hippocampal sclerosis" which is characterized by atrophy, glial proliferation and loss of neurons in selected regions of the hippocampus. There is evidence that increased level of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate plays a critical role in the generation of seizures as well as loss of neurons in TLE patients, but the underlying cellular mechanisms remain unclear. Evidence assimilated over the last decade indicate that increased levels of glutamate is involved not only in TLE but also in the degeneration of neurons trigger by amyloid beta (Ab) peptides, which are critical in the development of Alzheimer's disease pathology, the most common type of dementia affecting the elderly population. These results, together with the evidence of Ab deposition in the brain of some TLE patients, raise the possibility that Ab peptides may have a role in the loss of neurons in TLE. To address this issue our laboratory is currently investigating the implications of Ab peptides in the development of seizures and loss of neurons observed in animal model of TLE as well as in mice that have been genetically modified to produce excess Ab peptides. Additionally, we will measure the levels of Ab peptide in the brain samples obtained from patients with TLE. This study will determine the underlying basis of a role for Ab peptides in TLE and will define whether inhibition of Ab production can attenuate the degeneration of neurons and/or progression disease pathology in epilepsy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Analysis of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures: Statistical Methods for Response Shift (PROM-RS)
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFERENTIAL ITEM FUNCTIONING; ITEM RESPONSE THEORY; LONGITUDINAL DATA; MEASUREMENT ERROR; QUALITY OF LIFE; SELF-REPORT MEASURES; STATISTICAL METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Self-reported measures of health outcomes like quality of life, satisfaction with treatment, functional ability, and disease symptoms, can contribute to improved decision making in a patient-centred healthcare system. Insights into patients' own experiences with their health can be obtained by using these measures. However, there are a number of challenges associated with the development and analysis of patient-reported outcome measures. In longitudinal studies in which the outcomes are repeatedly measured over time, response shift, a form of measurement bias, can result in incorrect conclusions about change. Previous research has shown that when response shift is present in a set of data, it will often lead to the conclusion that no change exists, when in fact there is a real change within the patient population. Our research will develop statistical methods to detect the presence of response shift in longitudinal patient-reported outcome measures. These methods will be evaluated and compared using computer simulation techniques, to better understand how they perform under different data-analytic conditions. Then, we will apply them to existing datasets to test for response shift in patient populations with stroke and osteoporosis-related fractures, two health conditions that can result in substantial change in quality of life and patient functioning. This research will benefit clinicians and measurement scientists as they develop new patient-reported outcome measures. It will also contribute to improving the validity of studies about the effects of new treatments and healthcare interventions on patient outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preservation of Gingival Health and Adhesion Signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL ADHESION; CELL SIGNALING; COLLAGEN; FIBROBLASTS; GINGIVAL HEALTH; NORMAL PERIODONTIUM
Abstract-Résumé: Gum tissue around the teeth provides an important protective and sealing function. This tissue prevents germs from getting into the deeper tissues that hold the tooth to the jaw bone. Currently we don't understand how gum health and function are preserved, particularly when the gum is inflamed in various types of gum diseases. The purpose of this study is to define the cell and molecular systems that maintain the attachment of the gums to the teeth and what factors can lead to the breakdown of healthy gums.

TitreApplicationTitle: Design of Lipid Nanoparticle Systems for the Systemic Delivery of siRNA
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CATIONIC LIPID; DRUG DELIVERY; ENDOSOMAL RELEASE; GENE SILENCING; INTRACELLULAR DELIVERY; LIPID NANOPARTICLE; LIPOSOME; SIRNA; TARGETING
Abstract-Résumé: Small interfering RNA (siRNA) oligonucleotides can efficiently and specifically "silence" the production of particular "target" proteins in cells by binding to the mRNA that codes for that protein. This results in a catalytic destruction of the targeted mRNA and thus the target protein is not made. The siRNA molecules against particular proteins have major potential as therapeutics. For example, targeting and silencing oncogenes that promote the growth of tumours should inhibit tumour growth. Alternatively, silencing proteins such as Apo- B, which is essential for formation of the low density lipoproteins, should inhibit the plaque formation associated with heart disease. However, siRNA molecules cannot currently be used as in vivo therapeutics because they are rapidly broken down in the circulation, do not accumulate at disease sites and cannot get into cells. Lipid nanoparticles (LNP) have been demonstrated to have potential as delivery systems to overcome these problems. However, the cationic (positively charged) lipids used in these systems can be toxic, the efficiency of accumulation at disease sites is low and intracellular delivery properties have not been optimized. The studies to be performed in this work are aimed at developing cationic lipids that have reduced toxicity and improved intracellular delivery properties and can be used to deliver siRNA to a variety of tissue types in the body.

TitreApplicationTitle: Malaria and HIV Disease Interactions In Pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOBAL HEALTH; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; INNATE IMMUNITY; MALARIA
Abstract-Résumé: Mounting evidence has established that two of the most important infectious diseases, malaria and HIV-1, adversely interact particularly during pregnancy. However, relatively little is known about the mechanisms underlying these interactions and how we might most effectively intervene. This proposal will investigate the basis for the effect HIV on malaria and will address critical knowledge gaps in our understanding, suggest new ways to recognize women at risk, and identify novel interventions for these immensely important global health priorities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sepsis-induced skeletal muscle dysfunction: Role of autophagy
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; IMMUNOBLOTTING; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MUSCLE CONTRACTILITY; REAL-TIME PCR; SEPSIS; SKELETAL MUSCLE; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Sepsis is a systemic disease very common in intensive care units with high mortality. Patients with sepsis frequently develop muscle weakness that involves the diaphragm and limb muscles. Muscle weakness particularly that of the diaphragm leads to prolonged mechanical ventilation and high mortality. The mechanisms behind this muscle dysfunction are unclear. In this project, we will explore whether a newly described mechanism of protein recycling, autophagy, is excessively induced in skeletal muscles in sepsis. We will also investigate whether inhibition of autophagy can restore muscle function in sepsis and will identify the mechanisms responsible for induction of autophagy in septic skeletal muscles. Murine models of sepsis will be used throughout the proposal. In addition, we will compare the diaphragm to limb muscles to identify whether the diaphragm is selectively affected by autophagy in sepsis. Our first objective is to document the extent and timing of autophagy in skeletal muscles during the course of sepsis. Our second objective is to evaluate the importance of autophagy in sepsis-induced muscle dysfunction. This will be done by inducing sepsis in mice that are incapable of inducing autophagy in skeletal muscles. Our third objective is to investigate the roles of oxidants derived from the mitochondria in inducing autophagy in septic skeletal muscles. This will be achieved by using mice overexpressing a gene that scavenges mitochondrial oxidants and by using a peptide that can selectively reduce mitochondrial oxidants.  Our fourth and five objectives are to identify the contribution of selective triggering mechanisms located in the mitochondria and the nucleus of skeletal muscles in inducing autophagy and causing muscle dysfunction in sepsis. For this purpose, we will use compare sepsis-induced muscle dysfunction in normal mice and transgenic mice that are deficient in cyclophilin D, PARKIN and FoxO transcription factors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Study of the factor VIII life cycle and its implications for factor VIII immunogenicity.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; IMMUNOLOGY; INHERITED BLEEDING DISORDER; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MOLECULAR GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Hemophilia A is the most common severe inherited bleeding disorder. The disease is caused by inherited mutations of the clotting factor VIII (FVIII) gene that result in absent or low levels of FVIII or a FVIII protein that lacks function. Current treatment for hemophilia A involves frequent transfusions with FVIII protein. This treatment is safe and effective, but 25% of treated patients develop an immune response to the protein. The overall aim of this research program is to investigate details relating to how and where FVIII is produced and cleared from the blood. For each of these objectives, the impact on FVIII immunogenicity will be determined.  The project's first aim will be to determine where and under what conditions FVIII is made by various cell types in the body. These studies will focus on the production of FVIII by the liver, by the lining cells of blood vessels, the endothelium, and by cells within the thymus where the immunologic education of lymphocytes takes place.  These studies will involve the study of FVIII in cultured cells maintained under different environmental conditions and will also involve the study of mice in which the production of FVIII has been genetically disrupted in specific cell types. These experiments will tell us about cell type-specific and environmental influences on FVIII production and the impact of the site of FVIII production on immunogenicity.    The second series of studies will focus on mechanisms involved in the removal of FVIII from blood. These studies will determine the role of two recently identified scavenger receptors that have been linked through genetic association studies to the regulation of FVIII levels. These studies will determine the cell types that possess these receptors, will assess the ability of FVIII to bind to the receptors with and without its partner protein, von Willebrand factor, and will investigate FVIII clearance and immunogenicity in mice in which these receptors have been deleted.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the mechanisms that regulate DNA replication
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA REPLICATION; DNA-BINDING PROTEINS; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; PROTEIN CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; REPLICATION CHECKPOINT
Abstract-Résumé: Every few hours highly compacted chromosomes in our cells have to be unwrapped, copied, repacked and divided equally between two daughter cells. These steps have to be completed and timed exquisitely to preserve life. Indeed, mistakes during DNA replication (the process of copying the genome) lead to major chromosomal rearrangements and cell death.  Our group studies the molecular mechanisms that govern DNA replication. As in life, so too in science, a picture is worth a thousand words.  Using structural biology, we take pictures of the proteins that control DNA replication at work.  We combine the information from these images with additional in vitro and in vivo data to understand why DNA replication occurs at a specific time of the cell cycle. In particular, we are interested on understanding how two master regulators of DNA replication, SeqA in bacteria and Dbf4 in eukaryotic cells, initiate DNA replication only when the cell is ready, pause it when replication blockages are encountered and ensure that each daughter cell ends up with the correct genetic content. Importantly, several replication protein kinases, whose activity is regulated by Dbf4, have been identified as promising anticancer drug targets. Therefore, the outcome of this research will help develop alternative approaches to target these critical kinases and will lay the foundation to understand universal regulatory mechanisms that balance the treacherous line between health and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vascular Endothelial Cell Activators and Shear Stresses in Health and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CAMP; CGMP; ENDOTHELIUM; PHOSPHODIESTERASE
Abstract-Résumé: Numerous hormones and drugs have effects which are beneficial to the optimal functioning of the cardiovascular system. However, when used in combination, or at less than optimal concentrations, these agents can have negative effects on cells of the cardiovascular system. While there are many sites at which drugs and hormones can interact to bring about these unwanted effects, one factor which is likely important involves our limited knowledge concerning the mechanisms by which hormones and drugs influence cell functioning. Our studies are aimed at testing the hypothesis that the actions of hormones, or drugs, in cells are regulated by a system that allows local cellular effects and that unwanted effects arise, at least in part, due to unwanted effects in other parts of the cells. It is our belief that by increasing our understanding of the mechanisms through which cells organize their signaling systems, that more selective drug effects can be ensured.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of errors on memory performance and brain activity in healthy younger and older adults
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; FUNCTIONAL NEUROIMAGING; MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: An encouraging and growing finding in memory and aging research is that one can indeed teach the older brain 'new tricks'. Uncovering ways to optimize this new learning now becomes an important next step for researchers. Making errors is an inherent part of learning but whether it is harmful or beneficial for older adults' memory performance is unclear. One research branch shows that errors hinder memory for target information, especially among older adults, while another research branch finds evidence that the process of making errors is instrumental to subsequent learning. No attempt has been made to meaningfully relate these research branches and inform the conditions in which errors may boost or harm memory among young and older adults. We propose a framework of error processing in episodic learning, inspired from theories of cognitive control, in which we argue that error processing can rely on either self-initiated or reactive control processes. Inspired by this framework, our central hypothesis is that younger and older adults differ in how they control errors during learning, with older adults relying more on reactive control, in contrast to younger adults who can flexibly engage both modes of control, and that these age differences in error control are evident in different patterns of brain activity. We propose two neuroimaging studies that manipulate the extent to which self-initiated or reactive control is invoked to test the behavioural and neural effects of these different types of errors on memory. Understanding how younger and aging brains deal with error processing in learning situations is critical for informing educational and workplace training practices as well as the further development of memory rehabilitation protocols for individuals with brain injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the Sarcoma Tumor Initiating Cell: Implications for the Development of Novel Treatments for Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS; MOUSE MODELS; SARCOMA; STEM CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Sarcomas are cancers that derive from tissues of the musculoskeletal system. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (previously called malignant fibrous histiocytoma or MFH) is the most common sarcoma of the soft tissues, and has a very poor prognosis compared to other cancer types, with only 40% of patients surviving five years. Sarcomas are composed of a diverse population of cells. We are studying how the different subpopulations of cells within sarcomas behave differently, and found that they contain a small population of cells that act like stem cells. Like in normal tissues, this small population of stem cells maintains the tumour over time, giving rise to the various diverse cell types within a sarcoma. Our previous work showed that targeting the stem cell population in this tumour, using drugs that act on genes turned on in these cells, causes degeneration of the sarcoma, and as such could be an effective treatment approach. In this work, we will identify unique genetic characteristics of the stem cells in human and mouse  sarcomas. This information will be used to develop genetic tests to subclassify these tumor types and predict prognosis. Many of the unique genetic changes in the stem cell population can be targeted using new drug approaches. Such approaches will be tested using our mouse model of sarcoma. Those that are successful can be rapidly translated to patient care. Thus, this work will result in improvements in survival for patients with this sarcoma.  Such treatments are particularly needed due to the poor prognosis and lack of successful treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: It Takes Two To Tango- On the Role of Collaborative Problem-Solving for Spousal Health Dynamics in Old Age
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATIVE PROBLEM-SOLVING; COUPLES; HEALTH; LONGITUDINAL RESEARCH; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; STRESS; TIME-SAMPLING
Abstract-Résumé: Canada has an increasingly aging society with the number of Canadians above the age of 65 years doubling within the next ten years. It is well known that marriage impacts health, but the underlying mechanisms are not well understood. Importantly, most research investigating the impact of marriage on health with aging looks at married individuals rather than both members of the couple. This limits our ability to understand the spousal dynamics and mutual influences that characterize the daily lives of older couples. Therefore, we will conduct an in-depth investigation of the way in which spouses collaboratively solve the problems they encounter as part of their daily life routines, and how this translates to their stress and health behaviors. We will also follow participating couples for two years to better understand how daily life processes accumulate and impact their long-term health. Combining expertise from psychology and geriatrics will allow us to generate new knowledge on spousal resources (e.g. collaborative problem solving) and bio-behavioral processes (e.g. stress hormones, physical activity) with the potential for significant implications for future research and practice. Ultimately, we believe this study will help develop daily life interventions to capitalize on the potential of couples to promote healthy aging in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and cloning of the biological receptors for B7-H3 and B7-H4
Keywords-MotsClés: B7 FAMILY MEMBERS; B7-H3; B7-H4; CLONING; CO-INHIBITORY MOLECULES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; SIRNA SCREEN; T CELL COSTIMULATION; TUMOR IMMUNOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: T cells are a type of white blood cell that protect against infections and kill cancer cells. To escape T cell-mediated destruction, tumor cells often express inhibitory ligands on their surfaces that suppress host T cell responses against the cancer. B7-H3 and B7-H4 are two examples of such inhibitory ligands and are highly expressed on a broad range of cancer cell types. When B7-H3 or B7-H4 binds to its unknown receptor on an attacking T cell, the immune response targeted against the tumor is blocked, allowing the malignancy to grow. In this project, I propose to identify the receptors that bind to B7-H3 and B7-H4, and to investigate how these receptor-ligand pairs suppress anti-tumor T cells. The results of my work may point towards the development of therapeutic agents that promote anti-tumor responses and thus shrink cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hemozoin and Malaria Biomarkers: Role in the modulation of inflammatory responses  and development of Malaria-related Pathologies
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL MALARIA; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTION; INORGANIC CRYSTAL; MACROPHAGE; MALARIA; MICROBIOLOGY; PRO-INFLAMMATORY MEDIATORS; SIGNALING MECHANISMS
Abstract-Résumé: In the past, we have been able to clearly demonstrate that the protozoan parasite Leishmania can affect the MO signaling leading to its dysfunctions, thus providing a secure niche where the parasite can divide and progress within its infected host. These functional inhibitions have been correlated to the activation of the host phosphotyrosine phosphatase SHP-1 conducting to signaling pathways alteration (Jak2-STAT1, NF-kB). Now, in order to have a global view on how protozoan parasites have evolved to directly or indirectly affect MO functions that favor their installment and propagation within the mammalian host, we are very keen to dissect the signaling mechanisms by which the parasite Plasmodium manipulates its host at the cellular and molecular levels.  In this regard, we consider that HZ could play a pivotal role as an immunomodulator during malaria infection.  On the one hand, it could contribute to inflammatory responses potentially involved in fever and anemia and, on the other hand, inhibit important MO functions (Antigen presentation) involved in the development of protective immunity. Until now, very few studies have scrutinized the signaling mechanisms involved in HZ-mediated MO modulation in vitro and in vivo.  Consequently, the proposed study should permit to further reinforce the importance of HZ in the development of malaria-related pathology, and to better understand how this metabolic waste can modulate host inflammatory response conducting to specific pathologies.  Results obtained from this study could provide insight into the development of new treatments to reduce fever and anemia occurring during the course of malaria infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biomarkers for the detection of aggressive prostate cancers: Application of targeted proteomics to clinically stratified expressed prostatic secretions and urines
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; PROSTATE CANCER; PROSTATIC SECRETIONS; PROTEOMICS; URINE
Abstract-Résumé: A biomarker is a biological substance that is used to evaluate the presence, progression, or treatment-response of a disease. To be clinically useful, a biomarker should be readily accessible (i.e. body fluids) and provide sufficient sensitivity and specificity by minimizing false negatives and false positives. There is currently no clinically useful biomarker for the accurate prognosis of the disease course of prostate cancer. In this application we will build on data collected over the last three years using shotgun proteomics of expressed prostatic secretions. We will leverage our expertise in targeted proteomics and our excellent collaborations with clinicians in Virginia and here in Toronto to systematically develop high-throughput assays for candidate quantification in expressed prostatic secretions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Large-scale development of inhibitors to intracellular cancer targets using an integrated computational and combinatorial approach
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR PERTURBATION; DRUG DISCOVERY; PROTEIN INHIBITOR; PROTEIN INTERACTION; SIGNALING PATHWAY
Abstract-Résumé: We have seen great advances in the understanding of cancer. Likewise, our knowledge about how to manipulate proteins, the body's machinery, has greatly increased. However, the discovery of new drugs remains at a slow and, surprisingly, decreasing pace. This is partly due to the fact that the number of target proteins for drugs has stagnated. This in turn is caused by the pharmaceutical industry focusing on a few select protein types due to the high risk and cost of drug development. In this project, we will create a new list of potential target proteins that will serve as new candidate drug targets and develop inhibitors based on peptides to them. We will accomplish by combining a unique combination of techniques from computational biology, combinatorial biochemistry and cancer biology. Briefly, we can make use of knowledge from genomic and network sciences to prioritize proteins that are more likely to have greater effects in cancer. Such a method will be fed by the rich amounts of data on cancer cell lines that have been generated in the past few years as well as other sources of genomic data. Secondly, we will utilize sophisticated models from structural biology to select proteins that are optimally suited for peptide binders and predict their sequence. In a second step, we will make use of state-of-the-art combinatorial chemistry that will yield potent inhibitors against these proteins. Lastly, with our collaborators from cancer biology, we can screen selected inhibitors for biological efficacy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional genomics of cilium formation and maintenance
Keywords-MotsClés: BARDET-BIEDL SYNDROME; C. ELEGANS; CELL BIOLOGY; CILIA; CILIOGENESIS; CILIOPATHY; GENETICS; GENOMICS; HUMAN DISEASE; IFT
Abstract-Résumé: Cilia are antenna-like cellular structures used for numerous physiological and developmental processes. In humans, motile cilia perform critical functions, such as clearing debris from respiratory systems or allowing sperm movement. Non-motile (sensory) cilia protrude from the cells of most organs and carry out essential roles in sensing the external environment. For example, sensory cilia are needed for photoreception (vision), as well as olfaction (smell). Defects in sensory cilia, as is the case with Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) patients, result in ailments that collectively affect nearly all organs. Clinical manifestations of such 'ciliopathies' include blindness, cystic kidney disease, brain malformations, obesity, smelling and hearing deficiencies, and skeletal anomalies.  We propose to shed new insights into how cilia are formed and maintained. Using the small nematode C. elegans as a powerful, genetically-manipulable model organism, our group first identified (through genomics approaches)  and analysed many cellular factors (proteins) that participate in the formation of cilia-including some implicated in BBS. Our goals are to uncover additional constituents of the 'machinery' needed for cilia formation and maintenance, and characterise at the molecular level their mechanisms. The studies will make use of various complementary approaches, including genomics, genetics, and cellular biology. Importantly, we will take advantage of innovative resources and experimental tools that are either not available for, or not easily applicable to, other researchers using mammalian (e.g., human cells) or vertebrate (e.g., zebrafish) model systems. Lastly, we will collaborate with human geneticists to uncover new genes implicated in ciliopathies. Together, our findings will help us make significant strides towards understanding basic fundamental mechanisms of cilia formation and maintenance-which are seen as increasingly relevent to human health and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biophysical principles of intra- and inter-molecular recognition in protein folding and interactions involving disordered proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICS OF SOLVATION AND ITS ROLE IN PROTEIN BEHAVIOUR; COMPUTATIONAL MODELING; COOPERATIVITY AND INTRINSIC DISORDER; MANY-BODY INTERACTIONS; PROTEIN DYNAMICS; PROTEIN FOLDING AND PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Advances in modern biomedical research depend on a knowledge of the molecular basis of life. Proteins are a diverse class of biomolecules performing various vital functions in all living things. The three dimensional shape --- or shapes --- of a protein is encoded by its specific sequence of amino acids, and this sequence is in turn encoded by a gene. For some proteins, folding into a highly ordered globular shape is essential for function, whereas misfolding can lead to diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. In this context, switch-like folding is important for avoiding undesirable, disease-causing aggregation. For other proteins, however, a disordered form is necessary for them to function.  Therefore, developing a fundamental understanding of how proteins fold and unfold is of great intellectual and technological significance, and will benefit all areas of biomedical research. Ultimately, this knowledge should be deducible from chemistry and physics. Currently, however, it is not yet feasible in most cases to predict a protein's folding and dynamic behaviours from its amino acid sequence because no one understands well enough the intricate forces that guide some proteins to fold while the same set of basic forces can lead other proteins to adopt a fuzzy collection of disordered shapes. Current knowledge is also limited as to the forces that lead proteins to recognize their specific partners, a process that is crucial for biological function. Taking clues from available data and working closely with experimentalists, we will develop computational models toward systematically unraveling the workings of these forces.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure-based design and discovery of improved anti-amyloidogenic compounds
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYLOID; AMYLOID BETA; CD SPECTROSCOPY; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; NMR; PRION; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; SYNUCLEIN
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins are the "machines" of the cell. Each protein has a distinct 3-dimensional shape, defined by its amino acid sequence. This amino acid sequence tells proteins how to fold into their correct shape so they can function. Sometimes proteins don't follow their amino acid instructions and they accidently misfold into the wrong shape. These misfolded proteins tend to clump together with other misfolded proteins, much like the way milk curdles when heated. These protein clumps are called plaques and if plaques appear in the brain, they can cause serious problems. Alzheimer's (AD), Parkinson's (PD) and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) are all examples of progressive neurodegenerative diseases characterized by protein misfolding and protein plaque formation. Each condition involves the misfolding of one or more disease-specific proteins. In Alzheimer's disease it is the amyloid-beta protein, in Parkinson's disease it is alpha-synuclein and in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease it is the prion protein. Currently, no effective treatment is available to stop these diseases or prevent protein plaque formation. Recently several chemicals have been discovered that appear to prevent the misfolding of these disease-causing proteins. Some of them are naturally occurring compounds such as tetracycline (an antibiotic), EGCG (found in green tea) and curcumin (found in turmeric).  Others are synthetic compounds such as ibuprofen and rifampicin. The question is: What is unique about these compounds that allows them to stop protein misfolding? Using structural biology techniques that allow us to see the atomic structures of proteins, we have started to determine where and how these chemicals bind to the properly folded and misfolded forms of these disease-causing proteins. If we can better understand their mechanism of action it may open the door to discovering even better anti-clumping compounds and eventually to the development improved therapies for AD, PD and CJD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Risk factors and Risk Perception for Diabetes Among South Asian Women with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus Living in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS; DIABETES; ETHNICITY; GESTATIONAL DIABETES MELLITUS; LIFESTYLE MODIFICATION; MIXED METHODS: QUALITATIVE & QUANTITATIVE; PROSPECTIVE COHORT; RISK FACTORS; SOUTH ASIAN WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: South Asians (SA) are one of the largest ethnic populations in Canada and more likely to develop type 2 diabetes.  Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a temporary condition of pregnancy and could represent a growing population of young SA women at higher risk for diabetes.  It is unclear to what extent SA women have risk factors for diabetes and could differ from Caucasian women. Further, there is a clear need to understand the risk perception of diabetes and the ethno-cultural barriers to lifestyle modification.  The study objectives are: 1) To quantitatively assess differences in the risk factors, diabetes risk perception, self-efficacy and social support between SA women and Caucasian during pregnancy and post-partum. 2) To qualitatively explore the ethno-cultural barriers to lifestyle modification among SA women with GDM during pregnancy and post-partum.  This study will use data from a multi-centre observational study of Ontario women with GDM. Data on clinical, demographic, and psychosocial variables collected from questionnaires and medical charts during pregnancy and postpartum will be compared between SA and Caucasian women. Qualitative interviews will be conducted in a subset of SA women to identify less recognized themes and issues.   This study will allow for the identification of risk factors and ethno-cultural barriers unique to SA women diagnosed with GDM that might further exacerbate their diabetes. This study will also allow for a greater understanding of diabetes risk factors in SA women, which will inform strategies to increase their knowledge and skill for risk reduction behaviors to prevent future diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the Sam68 RNA binding protein in normal and diseased cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; BREAST CANCER; CELL ADHESION; CELL PROLIFERATION; COLON CANCER; LUNG CANCER; P53; RAS; RNA BINDING PROTEINS; SAM68
Abstract-Résumé: The growth of normal cells is tightly regulated during the cell cycle. Cancer cells, on the other hand, have lost this tight regulation and as such grow and proliferate without much control from the external surroundings. The RNA binding protein Sam68 is a sensor of  growth factor-induced proliferation and regulates key pathways termed RNA metabolism. We identified the protein Sam68 as a marker for certain primary human breast tumors. We generated mice that lack Sam68 and examined breast tumor formation. To our delight removal of the Sam68 gene delayed onset of mammary tumorigenesis in mice suggesting that Sam68 may be a therapeutic target for treatment or prevention. We noticed that cells without Sam68 have lost their potential to move around in the body, a property that cancer cells take advantage of to metastasize. We will study how the absence of Sam68 prevents cell migration and cell division and this will provide new information about ways to stop cancer cells from moving around in the body. Our results suggest that neutralizing Sam68 function with a small drug should be useful for cancer therapeutics: either to cure/treat or to prevent tumorigenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Amino acid starvation pathways in the host response to bacterial infection
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; BACTERIAL INFECTION; CELL SIGNALING; CELLULAR STRESS; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTION; MTOR
Abstract-Résumé: We study how our cells respond to infection by bacteria. In preliminary work, we have identified a critical new aspect of this response to the infection: we have observed that the entry of these micro-organisms into our cells induces a very rapid metabolic starvation. Indeed, approximately 1 hour after invasion, our cells respond as if they were missing amino acids, which are key building blocks of our molecules. Not only did we observe that the infected cells are starved, but we also showed that this has critical consequences for the way we respond to these intruders: by mounting a starvation response, our cells promote a "self-eating" (also known as autophagy) process, which replenishes amino acids, but also favors the destruction of the bacteria. The discovery of this cellular process triggered after infection might prove to be important for the development of new therapeutic strategies against bacteria that cause diseases in humans, such as listeriosis, salmonellosis or tuberculosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of cytoskeletal organization in controlling B cell activation
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN DYNAMICS; B CELL RECEPTOR; B-CELL LYMPHOMA; B-LYMPHOCYTES; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; CYTOSKELETON; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS; TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION (TIRF) MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: B-lymphocytes protect us from infection by making antibody proteins that eliminate pathogens. To differentiate into an antibody-producing cell, a B cell must first become activated. This involves binding of the B cell receptor (BCR) on the surface of the B cell to parts of the pathogen (antigens) that are captured by other cells and displayed on their surface. When a B cell contacts an antigen-presenting cell (APC) bearing the antigen it recognizes, it changes its shape and spreads across the surface of the APC so that its BCRs can detect additional antigens. This is followed by contraction of the B cell and formation of BCR clusters that initiate intracellular signaling pathways that lead to B cell activation. These changes in cell shape and BCR clustering require reorganization of the B cell's cytoskeleton, the structural elements that control cell shape as well as the ability of proteins such as the BCR to move within the cell membrane. We have elucidated a pathway by which antigen binding by the BCR causes cytoskeletal changes. The key step is activation of cofilin, a protein that severs actin filaments, a major structural element of the cytoskeleton. This allows BCRs to move more freely and form clusters, and promotes the formation of new cytoskeletal structures that cause the cell to spread. We have recently shown that B cells that have been exposed to danger signals that are indicative of microbial infection exhibit enhanced spreading when they contact APCs. We will now test whether B cells that have received danger signals can detect very small amounts of antigen such that they are activated more rapidly during an infection. This may suggest new ways to enhance B cell responses to infection. We will also test whether some types of B-cell lymphomas have altered cytoskeletal regulation that allows them to receive continual survival and growth signals from the BCR in the absence of antigen. This could lead to new approaches for treating such cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing Preclinical Optical Imaging Tools for Studying Vasculature, Microenvironment, and Radiation Response of Solid Tumours In Vivo.
Keywords-MotsClés: GENOMIC AND PROTEOMIC PROFILING; HYPOXIA AND OXYGENATION; INTRAVITAL OPTICAL MOLECULAR IMAGING; PHOSPHORESCENCE LIFETIME IMAGING; PHOTOACOUSTIC MICROSCOPIC IMAGING; RADIATION RESPONSE; SPATIO-TEMPORAL DYNAMICS; TUMOR CELL DEATH AND VASCULAR DAMAGE; XENOGRAFT AND ORTHOTOPIC TUMOR MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Tumor vasculature and hypoxia (a lack of oxygen, O2) greatly influence tumor response to RT and both are attractive targets for improving response to therapy (e.g. new hypoxia-activated drugs are in clinical testing with RT to improve treatment outcome). However, studying the complex co-dependent relationships between the response of tumor cells, their vasculature and hypoxia (incl. with therapeutic agents) in animal models of cancer has been a major challenge. To address this, new imaging technologies are needed that are nondestructive and have micron-scale resolution capable of visualizing radiobiological changes in solid tumors in real-time, non-invasively and over time at the cellular level in vivo. These changes are mediated by cell-signaling molecules exchanged between tumor components, driven by genetic & protein changes and influenced by hypoxia - all contributing to overall treatment response. Understanding them better could help us exploit them to benefit outcome. Thus, this project will develop next-generation imaging tools combing new small animal x-ray microirradiator technology with an "all-optical" intravital microscopy imaging platform in transparent window chamber mouse models to enable unprecedented study of the tumor vasculature, hypoxia, and radiation response in solid tumors in vivo. New photoacoustic (light + ultrasound) microscopy and phosphorescence imaging methods will measure tumor vascular O2 in situ, and quantitative genomic & proteomic techniques will measure genetic-protein changes either driving or influenced by RT and hypoxia in vivo. We will steer these studies towards more clinically-relevant primary human orthotopic tumor models - something never done before. These innovations will overcome a substantial barrier in radiobiology research and may provide new clinically-applicable insights about complex interactions and potential mechanisms of RT, hypoxia and emerging anti-cancer drugs underlying radiation response in solid tumors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of miRNAs and their Specific Gene Targets that are Critical for Prostate Cancer Metastases
Keywords-MotsClés: METASTASIS; MIRNA; ONCOLYTIC VIRUS; PROSTATE CANCER; THERAPY; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: It is likely that specific miRNAs, a class of non-protein-encoding, small RNAs may be potential therapeutic targets for controlling metastases. Accordingly, the hypotheses to be tested in this proposal are that: (i) metastasis-associated miRNAs can be identified via a comparison of metastatic and non-metastatic human prostate cancer models; and (ii) some of the metastasis-associated miRNAs and/or their target genes will provide potential therapeutic targets for metastatic prostate cancer. To test this hypothesis, we will combine and synergize the unique expertise and extensive resources of the four independent PIs. A highly novel approach will be used to compare the miRNA profiles of paired metastatic and non-metastatic models derived from the same patient by applying a new generation of sequencing technology to initially identify and then functionally validate miRNAs linked to metastases. While the metastasis-linked miRNAs may themselves serve as therapeutic targets in that regard, identification of the specific genes that they directly regulate may reveal more specific gene markers and targets, particularly since most miRNAs regulate a wide variety of genes. For this purpose, a very new and innovative experimental strategy for screening for these miRNA-regulated genes is proposed which takes advantage of our experience with viral-based systems and complementary synergies.  If we are to have any major impact on current survival rates, then new alternative treatment strategies need to be developed to target molecular events responsible for the development of prostate cancer metastases. The outcomes from this research should provide new therapeutic targets for controlling prostate cancer metastases in patients with advanced or recurrent disease. It is likely that clinical candidates for these purposes will be available after the 5-year term of this application.

TitreApplicationTitle: Placental Response to Heparin: Implications for the Prevention of Pre-eclampsia
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC REGULATION; GLIAL CELL MISSING; HEPARIN; PLACENTAL DEVELOPMENT; PLACENTAL EXPLANTS; PLACENTAL INSUFFICIENCY; PREECLAMPSIA; VILLOUS CYTOTROPHOBLAST
Abstract-Résumé: Pre-eclampsia describes a potentially-serious type of high blood pressure occurring in mid-pregnancy that may make the mother very unwell and lead to either premature delivery or death of the developing baby. The placenta, or afterbirth, that connects the developing baby to its mother, is mostly responsible for this disease. To date no drug has been shown capable of reversing the disease, the only cure being delivery of the baby (and thus removal of the placenta. The blood-thinner drug heparin, used for the past 40 years to keep blood from clotting during, for example, heart bypass surgery, is today's most exciting prospect to fight this disease. Women considered high-risk for developing pre-eclampsia are unlikely to get it if they are treated with heparin. However, blood-thinner drugs can be dangerous in pregnancy. Our research in the past 3 years suggests that the protective effect of heparin is not due to its blood-thinner properties. Instead heparin seems to make the placenta work more normally and relax the mother's blood vessels - thus lowering her blood pressure. In this proposal, we aim to discover how heparin works to prevent this disease. We will study the effects of heparin on normal and pre-eclamptic placental tissues at delivery. In addition we will treat different types of pregnant mice at risk for high blood pressure with heparin to see how heparin works in a living animal. We will see if the helpful effects are retained in modified heparin that will not thin out the blood. If this is the case, our research will lead to much safer drugs to prevent pre-eclampsia so that women do not have to fear the side effects that can result from taking heparin to improve their pregnancy outcome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the Role of Cortical Inhibition in Late-Life Depression
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; LATE-LIFE DEPRESSION; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; TREATMENT OUTCOME
Abstract-Résumé: At least 50% of older adults with depression fail to improve with first-line antidepressant treatment and there are limited clinical trial data to guide management of patients who develop treatment resistance. Our centre is involved in a large academic clinical trial.  All patients coming to this study receive a 3 month course of an antidepressant. This study creates an opportunity to advance our understanding of the biological mechanisms underlying treatment-resistance and how to predict treatment response in late-life depression (LLD).  Cortical inhibition (CI) is an important brain function that shows a specific pattern of disturbance in younger patients with treatment-resistant depression.  As the aging process leads to a decrease in CI, this may be of particular importance in treatment-resistant late-life depression. Yet, this has not been studied. Using a non-invasive neurophysiological technique called  transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), CI can be measured in a reliable and accurate manner. Therefore, the proposed study will take advantage of the clinical trial platform to evaluate CI in a sample of older depressed adults.  We aim to determine if CI deficits at baseline predict treatment resistance to venlafaxine XR.  In addition, we will compare CI in depressed older adults to a group of age- and sex- matched, non-depressed older adults. Insights generated by this research will add to the understanding of treatment resistance in LLD in several important ways.  First, these findings will help to clarify the biological mechanisms of depression in older adults.  Second, these findings may serve to provide early identification of patients who will not respond to medications, ultimately leading to more personalized treatment decisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Masculinities and migration: Analyzing the impact of gender discourses on Latino gay men's safe sexual practices in Canada.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO SERVICES; BODY MAPPING; GENDER AND SEXUAL ANALYSIS; HIV STUDIES; INTERSECTIONALITY; LATINO GAY MEN; QUEER THEORY; SEXUAL MIGRATION; SEXUAL STORIES; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Similar to Latino gay men immigrants in the United States, Latino gay men immigrants in Canada are at higher risk of becoming infected with HIV when compared to white gay men and other ethno-racial groups. Research in the U.S. has shown that Latino gay men are affected by social vulnerabilities (including social determinants of health), homophobia, gender expectations (masculinities), race and class intersections. Evidence suggests that Latino gay men immigrate to the United States or Canada as a strategy to deal with the highly gendered, homophobic and heteronormative social pressures prevalent in Latin American societies. In fact, hundreds of Latin American men claim Canadian protection, applying as sexual orientation refugees every year.  Studies have found that members of this cohort can find that sexual freedom in this new environment carries challenges such as marginalization, individual's anonymity, as well as isolation, language and cultural barriers. In conjunction with the social determinants of health, these affect the safe sex practices of Latino gay men immigrants. There is a great need for qualitative research to comprehend the 'sexual experiences' which comprise the metaphoric and material 'journey' of Latino gay men immigrants. Using Queer theory, sexual stories and body maps as theoretical frameworks, I will interview 12 to 18 Latino gay men immigrants who have been in Canada for no less than 1 year and no more than 5 years. In addition, in order to make sure the narratives of Latino HIV positive are heard, at least 4 to 6 of the recruited participants will be HIV positive. The interview will employ a semi-structured format. Narratives will be transcribed, coded and analyzed. Body maps will be drawn based on participants' narratives. Research results and body maps will be presented as  knowledge transfer/dissemination activities to communicate the results to the community, academia, social services providers and key stakeholders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Taking Action 2: Aboriginal Youth and Alliance Building in HIV Prevention.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL YOUTH; COMMUNITIES; HIV PREVENTION; PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH; RACE; SOCIAL MOVEMENTS; SOLIDARITY/ALLIANCE BUILDING; YOUTH LEADERSHIP
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal youth are over-represented in the HIV epidemic due to legacies of colonization, as well as social, political and economic isolation. Alternative strategies are needed to address sexual health promotion and HIV prevention with Aboriginal youth, which is imperative to priorities 1, 2 and 3 of CIHR's HIV/AIDS Research Initiative Strategic Plan 2008 - 2013. A number of policies and programs have been created to encourage youth leadership in preventing HIV. One such program is the Taking Action project, which is the result of a partnership between the Canadian Aboriginal AIDS Network (CAAN), the Native Youth Sexual Health Network (NYSHN), Gendering Adolescent AIDS Prevention (GAAP), CIHR and several academic institutions. This doctoral research will take data from the digital stories (3-5 minute visual narratives that fuse images, video, audio recordings of voice, music and text to create compelling accounts of experience) produced by and the individual interviews conducted with the 20 youth participants in phase 2 of the larger Taking Action project. This research will examine how Aboriginal youth leaders understand their identities, and perceive the potential for solidarity building approaches within HIV prevention. Research questions include: 'How does a sense of identity (race, gender, sexuality, community affiliation, colonial history etc.) impact the work these young HIV leaders do and why they do it? 'How do Aboriginal youth leaders view alliance building between different aboriginal communities and across other ethnic/racial lines within the HIV prevention movement? What barriers and facilitators to such community alliances are identified by the youth? 'In what ways do these youth understand the comparisons and contrasts of different communities' vulnerability to HIV?  This research will provide a greater understanding of the potential for Aboriginal youth leadership in the resource sharing and solidarity building approaches of HIV prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Restoring Health in Our Community
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; HIV PREVENTION; INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE SYSTEMS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MIXED METHODS; PUBLIC HEALTH INTERVENTION; SEXUAL HEALTH; SOCIAL AND CULTURAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: First Nations and other indigenous people of Canada are over-represented in Canada's human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) epidemic. We think HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are physical symptoms of physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual abuse experienced through misuse of power in relationships (e.g. residential schools, family violence).  This trauma has resulted in loss of traditional knowledge and practice on how to live the good life, a healthy life.    The medicine wheel is a symbol of health that reminds us that we are physical, mental, emotional and spiritual beings. Clockwise movement around the wheel shows: 1) flow through the various stages of life from child to elder, 2) flow of relationships, responsibility, and knowledge between people for each stage of life (e.g. adults are opposite children because adults are responsible for children), and 3) the aspect (physical, mental, emotional, spiritual) being actively developed at a given stage of life. We believe that past, present, and inter-generational trauma has put the medicine wheel out of order, leading to disease.  We will develop a community-led HIV intervention to restore the medicine wheel.  We will test this intervention with a small group of people before bringing it to the whole community.  We need this test run so we can make sure the intervention is working properly and so we can fix any problems with its delivery.  It is vitally important to figure out how to restore the medicine wheel, and if restoring this balance will prevent HIV transmission, both for the lead community, and for other First Nations communities that share this common cause of disease.  Our project will support the creation of new knowledge that will inform the Federal Initiatives to prevent the acquisition and transmission of new infections, reduce the social and economic impact of HIV/AIDS, and contribute to the global effort to reduce the spread of HIV and mitigate the impact of the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stable Homes, Strong Families: Housing and Health for Aboriginal Peoples Living with HIV and AIDS
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; DIGITAL STORYTELLING; HIV AND AIDS; HOUSING; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOGIES; POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: Thirty years into the HIV and AIDS epidemic, Aboriginal peoples continue to be disproportionately affected in increasing rates of infection(1). A factor driving this situation is housing instability(2). Aboriginal peoples are over-represented among Canada's homeless populations(3) or are living in single-room occupancy hotels and other transitional living arrangements(4). Unstable housing contributes to health disparities, can prevent access to appropriate health service, and is associated with poor physical health, mental illness and HIV-related risk behaviour, such as drug use and exchanging sex. Although various housing and health initiatives have attempted to structurally address these complex issues, unfortunately social housing designs are often based on Western constructs and force Aboriginal peoples to live in homes in ways not originally intended or that inadvertently suppress cultural identity(7). This study aims to identify and work towards addressing gaps in appropriate housing options that support cultural identity and concepts of home for Aboriginal peoples living with and affected by HIV and AIDS. A multiple method approach involving a programmatic and policy scan and digital story-telling will be used by our academic and community-based research collaborative to work with Aboriginal people living with and affected by HIV and AIDS to explore cultural meanings of housing and home and how this links with health status and HIV transmission. This will be used within an integrated approach to knowledge translation and exchange to support a culturally appropriate response to Aboriginal housing needs in the context of HIV. Our community-based research design is consistent with Indigenous scholarship, the principles of Ownership, Control, Access and Possession, and the Federal Initiative to Address HIV/AIDS in Canada.
