TitreApplicationTitle: Family Matters: Informing a family-based model of care with Aboriginal families affected by HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; CULTURAL STRENGTHS; DECOLONIZING RESEARCH; HIV/AIDS; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOGIES; STORYSHARING
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal peoples in Canada are disproportionately affected by HIV and AIDS - more women and young people are affected within the Aboriginal population than Canadians overall (PHAC, 2010). Mother-to-child transmission accounts for very few infections in Canada, however Aboriginal children are over-represented among these cases (PHAC, 2010). The dynamics of the epidemic among Aboriginal communities suggest implications beyond individuals living with HIV, however very little is known about what this means in the context of the broader family. This study seeks to address this gap by engaging with Aboriginal families affected by HIV to identify Aboriginal-specific recommended solutions toward the development of programmatic intervention models that address and support all members of a family affected by HIV. Grounded in a community-based approach and indigenous research framework, we will engage Aboriginal families affected by HIV throughout a multi-method study undertaken in 3 phases, respecting the principles of OCAP and integrating knowledge translation and exchange (KTE). Phase 1 will involve a programmatic scan of formal and informal services, supports, policies and programs designed for Aboriginal people living with HIV and their families. Phase 2 will involve storytelling circles in 4 sites across Canada to explore the impact of HIV on families, based upon the perspectives of different members of Aboriginal families affected by HIV. In Phase 3 we will host a family gathering of affected Aboriginal families to share our findings, strategize meaningful KTE approaches and identify priority intervention options. Each phase builds on the previous one with careful attention to KTE throughout to build engagement in the research and increase the uptake, reach and impact of the findings to ensure that this important research contributes to new knowledge, awareness and action related to the needs of Aboriginal families living with HIV and AIDS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health in Middlesex Men Matters (HiMMM): A Community-Based Study of Social Exclusion, Homophobia, Communication, Health Care and HIV in Middlesex County, Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: BISEXUALITY; EXTERNAL HOMOPHOBIA; HEALTH COMMUNICATION; HEALTH SERVICES ACCESS; HIV; HOMOSEXUALITY; INTERNALIZED HOMONEGATIVITY; RESPONDENT-DRIVEN SAMPLING; SOCIAL EXCLUSION; SURVEY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Health in Middlesex Men Matters (HiMMM) is a mixed-methods community-based study of three factors identified by London-Middlesex LGBT2SQ communities as impacting their health most profoundly: communication, homophobia, and social exclusion. HiMMM is researching the impact of these issues specifically on gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GB-MSM), with a focus on HIV-related impact. Data to be used for analysis include existing transcripts from 20 stakeholder interviews conducted during HiMMM's capacity-building phase, and survey data (expected n=400) from GB-MSM participants currently being recruited using respondent-driven sampling. Taken together, the qualitative and quantitative analyses produced by HiMMM will 1) provide information on current levels of sexual risk-taking; 2) allow us to compare these levels in a mid-size Canadian city with those in major cities; 3) describe processes through which communication, internalized homonegativity and external homophobia, and social exclusion impact the health of GB-MSM, and; 4) quantify the effects of these factors on sexual risk, HIV testing, and access to GB-MSM-supportive physical and mental health services. Findings will be made available through local town hall meetings, open-access peer-reviewed publications, fact sheets, and videos. Paper and electronic documents and video will be distributed through networking, conferences, our website, and knowledge exchange organizations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting and Owning Empowerment and Resilience among African, Caribbean and Black Youth in Windsor (POWER)
Keywords-MotsClés: AFRICAN; BLACK; CARIBBEAN; HIV/AIDS; RACIAL-ETHNIC MINORITY; RISK; VULNERABILITY; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: POWER (Promoting and Owning Empowerment and Resilience among African, Caribbean and Black Youth in Windsor) is a community-based research project that seeks to establish a profile of the risks and vulnerabilities of African, Caribbean and Black (ACB) youth (aged 16-25 years) in Windsor, Ontario. This is a collaboration between researchers and community partners that seeks not only to identify and explain a problem, but also to develop a strategy for addressing it. The POWER team brings together researchers who have studied the HIV epidemic since its inception, an emerging generation of new researchers, organizations at the forefront of youth service delivery and HIV prevention in Windsor, and community workers with decades-long records of advocacy for ACB and newcomer communities. POWER has four immediate objectives: 1) Implement a community mobilization strategy to engage various sectors of the Windsor-based ACB community; 2) Describe individual-level HIV risks and their correlates among ACB youth in Windsor; 3) Identify and examine macro-level contributors to HIV vulnerability among ACB youth in Windsor, and 4) Enhance the capacity of community (including community youth) and academic partners to undertake collaborative, policy-oriented work. The research component of this project uses surveys with a projected sample of 650 ACB youth, youth-led community mapping, and individual and group interviews with youth and adult key informants. Activities related to community mobilization and enhanced capacity for future work are ongoing throughout the project and centre on active in project leadership and knowledge translation and exchange with youth and adult community leaders through meetings, community fora and jointly prepared materials to support programming and advocacy. The long-term objective of this study is to synthesize all research findings to create the foundation for a successful community-based HIV risk reduction strategy for ACB youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Trans MSM Sexual Health Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BISEXUAL MEN; GAY MEN; HIV; SEXUAL HEALTH; SOCIAL DETEMINANTS OF TRANS HEALTH; TRANS HEALTH; TRANS MEN AND SEXUAL DECISION MAKING; TRANS MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; TRANSGENDER
Abstract-Résumé: To date, studies of both transgender people and gay men have paid little, if any, attention to the HIV prevention and sexual health needs of gay, bisexual or queer trans men who have sex with men (TMSM). The little research that does exist has identified individual and interpersonal HIV-related risk factors (eg. navigating disclosure of trans status) but has not evaluated their impact on sexual decision-making or behaviour through in-depth qualitative interviewing.  This research aims to better understand the nature of HIV risk amongst TMSM.  Its goal is to enhance the well-being of TMSM by collecting in-depth information about their sexual health issues, concerns, sexual decision-making processes, and the social context of their lives.  This study will create a base for effective and culturally-relevant knowledge exchange by providing a detailed and rich understanding of how social exclusion works to produce unique HIV prevention and sexual health challenges for TMSM in Ontario.    In this project, we will undertake a qualitative exploration of the experiences of TMSM in Ontario. Forty in-depth interviews will be conducted with TMSM, providing opportunities to discuss more complex issues related to identity, sexuality, sexual health and service needs.    In the Canadian context, there is a dearth of knowledge about the health- and HIV-related issues facing TMSM.  This project will contribute significantly to the limited pool of information available about TMSM by providing in-depth information focussed specifically on their unique needs.  Moreover, it will provide a theoretical understanding of what TMSM  experience thus enabling us to create a rich and comprehensive understanding about the extent and scope of social exclusion in these communities and the impact on sexual health as well as HIV risk.  This qualitative study will also provide a rich understanding of the ways that social exclusion may impact access to HIV prevention services for TMSM.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of 3D nuclear chromosome and gene positions on cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: 3D POSITIONS OF CHROMOSOMES; 3D POSITIONS OF GENES; C-MYC; CHROMOSOME PAINTING; GENOMIC INSTABILITY; INTERPHASE NUCLEUS; MBANDING; NUCLEAR ARCHITECTURE; THREE-DIMENSIONAL IMAGING; TUMOR ACCELERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Overall research interest. Dr. Mai studies the three-dimensional (3D) organization of the nucleus and how alterations of the nuclear organization impact on cancer development. The study subject and previous work by the applicant. This application focuses on an ideal model for human cancers: mouse chromosome 11 and blood cancers called plasmacytomas. The applicant has shown that a specific region of chromosome 11 (called 11E2) is often abnormal in aggressive plasmacytomas, while it remains normal in slow growing plasmacytomas.  Goals of this study. This grant is centered around the hypothesis that the nuclear position of chromosome 11 and/or of the genes on this part of chromosome 11 can affect the aggressive behavior of this model blood cancer. To this end, the applicant proposes to 1) determine the nuclear positions and orientation of chromosome 11 in normal white blood cells as well as in slow developing vs. fast developing plasmacytomas; 2) examine for fast-developing plasmacytomas, whether chromosome 11 and/or the genes within 11E2 are found in 'activity centers' (transcription factories) that promote the level of gene activity seen only in fast developing plasmacytomas; 3) define one pathway that may lead to the nuclear repositioning of chromosome 11 and involves a protein called c-Myc. Significance of the project. The region on mouse chromosome 11 that is associated with fast-onset plasmacytoma development is conserved between mouse, rat and human. It is affected in tumors of lymphoid and non-lymphoid origin including ovarian, breast, brain and lymphoid cancers. This work will likely uncover how this conserved region allows for accelerated tumor development and may allow for the development of a test that will allow one to differentiate between slow growing vs. aggressively growing tumor cells. In the future, therapeutic strategies could be designed based on these findings.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuron-glial mechanisms in neural circuitry plasticity and homeostasis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTE; GLIA; NEURAL CIRCUITRY; PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Neural circuits have a remarkable challenge within the brain. They need to be stable in order to preserve important information while at the same time have enough flexibility to accommodate new information. An imbalance of these processes leads to inefficient brain function and likely plays a significant role in diseases such schizophrenia and depression. In recent years, much has been learned about mechanisms that contribute to brain plasticity, especially at the level of synapses, the specialized sites of connection between two neurons within a brain circuit. Changes in the ability of neurons to release or detect neurotransmitter are known to change the efficiency and strength of synaptic transmission. Homeostatic mechanisms are also enlisted to adjust the properties of synaptic connections to ensure that the activity of neurons remains within a useful working range (not too high or too low). Thus, an important balance of plasticity and homeostasis is needed to support proper brain activity. Despite our knowledge of these diverse plasticity mechanisms, the cellular and molecular events that underlie these processes are not fully understood and remain an important focus of neuroscience research.    New discoveries have found that astrocytes, a type of glial cell in the brain, play an important role in synaptic transmission and plasticity. However, we are only beginning to understand how astrocytes regulate the function of neurons and neural circuits to modify and preserve brain function. In this grant renewal, we will combine in vivo and in vitro analysis using a range of genetic, molecular, biochemical, imaging, behavioral, electrophysiological and optogenetic approaches to uncover how neurons and astrocytes intercommunicate. This grant will provide fundamental information about how the brain encodes information and reveal important clues and potential therapeutic avenues for treating conditions where disregulation of neural circuits and brain function occurs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Avoiding the Backlash: Identifying Features of Bullying Prevention Programs that Increase or Decrease Unintended Negative Responses (Reactance) in Grade 5, 6, 7, and 8 Students and Educators.
Keywords-MotsClés: BULLYING PREVENTION; DISCRETE-CHOICE CONJOINT EXPERIMENTS; EDUCATORS; FOCUS GROUPS; MIXED METHODS; REACTANCE; STUDENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Although great effort has been devoted to the prevention of bullying, bullying remains a serious Canadian public health problem.  Involvement as a bully or victim is associated with poor school attendance, underachievement, dropout, health complaints, sleep difficulties, anxiety, depression, and suicide.  The difficulties associated with bullying persist into adulthood as poorer health and mental health outcomes. Unfortunately, reviews of prevention trials suggest that programs designed to prevent or reduce bullying often yield very modest benefits. Our studies suggest that certain features of bullying prevention programs may limit their effectiveness by eliciting an unintended negative response, reactance.  Reactance has been reported when prevention programs are perceived as an effort to change attitudes, restrict access to important activities, or limit decision control.  Importantly, our studies suggest some features of bullying prevention programs may also reduce reactance.  We have also found evidence that some features of these programs may elicit reactance among educators, and a subsequent reduction in support for the implementation of these programs.    We propose to conduct focus groups with 60 students and 60 educators to explore the features of bullying prevention programs that elicit reactance, ways reactance is expressed, how reactance undermines outcome, and features that reduce reactance.  Next, we will use survey methods from marketing research to model the influence of different features of bullying prevention programs on reactance by 1200 educators and 2000 students in grades 5, 6, 7, and 8, a period when bullying increases, students become more independent, and there is a greater likelihood of reactance.  We will identify features of bullying prevention programs that are most likely to increase or decrease reactance, identify the demographic and behavioral predictors of reactance, and simulate a program that minimizes reactance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nascent chromatin structure and the response to DNA damage during replication
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; DNA REPAIR; DNA REPLICATION; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; GENETIC INTERACTIONS; HISTONE MODIFICATION; HOMOLOGOUS RECOMBINATION; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: DNA damage can lead to the inactivation or misregulation of important genes and cause cancer. Fortunately, cells possess DNA repair mechanisms that allow them to survive in the presence of DNA lesions such as breaks in the DNA. However, these repair mechanisms also allow cancer cells to resist to chemotherapy treatments that kill cells by causing DNA damage. Investigating the responses to DNA damage is thus crucial to our understanding of cancer biology and to the development of new treatments. In order to fit in the tiny confines of the cell, DNA is packaged into a structure called chromatin. We are investigating how chromatin structure participates in the response to DNA damaging drugs that are used in cancer chemotherapy. We anticipate that a better understanding of these fundamental processes will permit the discovery of novel factors involved in DNA repair which could be targeted to sensitize cancer cells to chemotherapy treatments. This research may also identify new ways to categorize tumors and to better define the appropriate treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and synaptic mechanisms of TDP-43 proteinopathy using zebrafish.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELLULAR IMAGING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NEUROPHARMACOLOGY; PATCH-CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), or as it is commonly known Lou Gehrig's disease, is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the death of a large proportion of motoneurons in the cerebral cortex and spinal cord. The disease onset is in midlife but can occur earlier and progresses from muscle weakness to paralysis and eventual death within 2-5 years. There is one pharmacological treatment for ALS, riluzole, and it is believed to extend the life of individuals with this disease by 2-3 months. Part of the poor success of riluzole can be attributed to our incomplete understanding of the cellular and functional abnormalities resulting from causative mutations in genes such as TARDBP (encoding TDP-43). Mutations in TDP-43 have been found in ALS. Few animal models of TDP-43 mutations have been described and none have characterized the physiological deficits that occur in ALS which result in paralysis. To advance our understanding of this disease I propose to use a zebrafish model previously described by our laboratory in which mutant human TDP-43 or normal TDP-43 is expressed in zebrafish. There are two goals of this research proposal. Firstly, I will investigate the underlying pathophysiology of TDP-43 mutations occurring at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), which result in poor synaptic transmission. I will use cutting edge electrophysiological and cellular imaging techniques to examine synaptic transmission across the NMJ to ascertain what the dysfunction is and which pharmacological tools will be most useful in restoring synaptic transmission. Secondly, I will investigate the cause of increased excitability of motoneurons in the spinal cord. In particular, I will examine glutamatergic synaptic transmission which is hypothesized to be augmented and be deleterious to motoneurons in ALS patients. This research proposal lays the groundwork needed for a thorough understanding of basic physiological mechanisms of ALS-related motoneuron dysfunction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering the bases of sex differences in the brain and their role in psychiatric disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN DEVELOPMENT; BRAIN IMAGING; ENDOCRINOLOGY; MOUSE MODELS; NEUROANATOMY; PSYCHIATRY; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood mental health disorders tend to affect boys and girls differently. Autism, for example, is much more likely to be found in boys than in girls, whereas girls are more likely to suffer depression in their teenage years. Understanding why these diseases differ according to the sex of the child is thus an important part of understanding the diseases themselves. In this project we want to study how sex differences develop in the brain. To do this we will employ advanced brain imaging methods in mice along with using mouse models to understand which of these sex based brain differences are due to sex chromosomes (since boys have an X and Y chromosome and girls have two X chromosomes) versus differences in sex steroids (testosterone and estrogen). Lastly, we will use mouse models to examine which of these sex differences in the brain account for sex differences in anxiety disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: PEOPLE'S PETS AND POPULATION HEALTH PROMOTION: A province-wide qualitative study of animal bylaws
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTHROPOLOGY; ANTHROZOOLOGY; HEALTH PROMOTION; HUMAN-ANIMAL STUDIES; IMPLEMENTATION SYSTEMS; POPULATION HEALTH; SOCIO-LEGAL STUDIES; URBAN STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: Members of the public are used to thinking about pets as aids in healthcare, but the importance of people's pets for the public's health is not limited to sick people. Pets bring joy to people's lives and can help people feel a sense of belonging. Feeling responsible for a pet can lead people to assimilate health information (e.g., how feline diabetes compares with type 2 diabetes in people) and to adopt healthy routines (e.g., dog-walking). Half of all Canadian households include pets, and many more would have a pet, if only their circumstances would allow. These pets are usually treated like family members. As an example, the Calgary Food Bank routinely screens for the presence of pets in the home, because people will sometimes feed a pet before themselves, and surrendering or abandoning a pet is unthinkable, even when income is low.  This study will be the first -- in any field -- to investigate how municipalities are balancing people's attachments to their pets, on the one hand, with complaints and concerns about other people's pets, on the other hand. Our starting place is that the presence of pets in cities and towns shouldn't be taken for granted, so we will look carefully at municipal bylaws that allow people to keep pets, as long as they follow rules. We know from research on smoking bans that the wording of bylaws is important, so we will pay close attention to what pet bylaws say -- and what they leave out. Research on smoking bans has also taught us that the implementation systems surrounding bylaws are critical, so we will not stop at "the letter of the law." By conducting 44 in-person interviews in cities and towns across Alberta, we will learn first-hand about what it is like to draft, amend and implement bylaws on pets. Through these interviews, we will engage potential end-users of this research, and we will collaborate with these organizations in sharing our findings with the general public via the mass media.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of TDRD3 and arginine methylation in stress granules dynamics: implications for breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGININE METHYLATION; BREAST CANCER; CANCER HALMARKS; CHEMORESISTANCE; MOLECULAR AND CELLULAR BIOLOGY APPROACHES; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION; RNA BINDING PROTEINS; STRESS GRANULES; STRESS RESPONSE; TUDOR DOMAIN
Abstract-Résumé: The function of many proteins can be modulated by specific temporary modifications to their building blocks (amino acids). These reversible modifications are the basis for how cells can relay signals from outside the cell all the way to regulating gene expression. In these signaling cascades, modified amino acids are usually recognized by specific interaction domains, that serve to either relay and/or integrate the signals. The modular nature of these domains, and the flexibility of their binding properties, have likely facilitated the evolution of cellular regulatory pathways. My laboraroty is interested in understanding the physiological role of methylation, a protein modification that is slowly emerging as a novel regulator of many cellular processes. Consistent with a role in regulatory cascades, methylation can affect the way protein interact with other proteins, is reversible, and a module that specifically recognizes methylated amino acids, the Tudor domain, has recently been uncovered. Intringuingly, Tudor domains are often found in proteins implicated in processes related to ribonucleic acid (RNA). From these considerations and results obtained in our recent studies, we propose that Tudor domains will serve as molecular adaptors to integrate methylation regulatory signals, and relay this information to influence RNA-related events. In order to explore this model, we will focus on a recently discovered Tudor domain-containing protein, named TDRD3 and study how this proteins participates in the cellular responses that help to promote cell survival in the face of various stress conditions relevant to cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of septins in ciliogenesis and primary cilia function
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS COLI; CILIOPATHY; CYTOSKELETON; HEDGEHOG SIGNALING; MEMBRANE MOBILITY; MICROTUBULE; POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE; PRIMARY CILIUM; SEPTINS
Abstract-Résumé: The primary cilium is an antenna for cells, sensing the environment and receiving important signals. Almost all cells have a cilium and defects in cilia growth cause a wide range of diseases and cancer. Septins are a family of proteins that are required for cilia growth, but it is not known why. We have found that septins activate an important series of proteins that had not previously been implicated in cilia growth. In this proposal we will determine how septins do this, and what other roles they may have in controlling the function of the cilium. These studies will shed new light on these important structures and may provide new avenues for therapeutic approaches to ciliopathies.

Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the fourth most common type of cancer and second most common cause of cancer-related deaths for both men and women (Canadian Cancer Society, 2011). Due to increased screening, earlier diagnosis of CRC, and treatment improvements, mortality rates have declined for both men and women. Therefore, people with CRC are living longer life-spans. However, treatments which improve survival can also cause lasting side effects and symptom management problems that endure for years. Data are surprisingly lacking on the long-term physical and psychological symptoms, symptom management problems, and their effect on quality of life (QOL) after treatment for and recovery from CRC. The proposed research will address these gaps in our knowledge by identifying the long-term physical symptoms (e.g., fatigue, bowel dysfunction), psychological symptoms (e.g., depression, fear of cancer recurrence), symptom management problems, and their effect on quality of life in a population-based cohort of CRC survivors at least 10 years post-diagnosis and their age and gender-matched unaffected controls. Consented participants will complete validated self-report questionnaires assessing physical symptoms, psychological symptoms, symptom management, and QOL. TitreApplicationTitle: How to reform the health care system: Stakeholders' views about problems and solutions to increase performance and ensure sustainability
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH POLICY ANALYSIS; PERFORMING HEALTH CARE SYSTEMS; REFORMS IMPLEMENTATION; STAKEHOLDERS' EXPECTATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: There is a broad consensus that the Canadian health care system needs to implement significant reforms to increase its performance and, ultimately, to ensure its sustainability. There is strong scientific evidence that high performing health care systems present several desirable characteristics. In Quebec, all publicly appointed Commissions identified characteristics and recommended policy options consistent with scientific evidence. However, even if the various reforms that were conducted in the last 20 years led to important structural changes in the administrative and delivery system, many critical elements were systematically ignored with the consequence that only partial reforms were implemented and the desired results were not achieved. The unimplemented elements were always those that entailed significant transformations for powerful interest groups. The objective of the project is to analyze and compare the perceptions of various stakeholders within the health care system (physicians, nurses, administrators) and to put them in relation with the current scientific evidence on interventions aimed at increasing performance. Firstly, interviews with spokespersons representing main stakeholders groups will document each group's position on a given set of propositions related to key characteristics of high performing healthcare systems. Secondly, a survey will be distributed to a sample of each group of stakeholders in order to test whether the discourses of organized group representing stakeholders do correspond to the views of their members. Better understanding the social positions and believes of major stakeholders will help identify their expectations. It is an essential step for analyzing if there is a way to reconcile their views, for identifying topics on which stakeholders perceptions should be influenced and levers that could be used in order to implement critical measures for developing a performing health care system and ensure its sustainability.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of lifestyle and genetics on the progression of type 2 diabetes among women and children exposed to gestational diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD OBESITY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENETICS; GESTATIONAL DIABETES; LIFESTYLE; POSTPARTUM; PREGNANCY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Gestational diabetes, marked by high blood sugar levels during pregnancy, is a common problem. Women and their children exposed to gestational diabetes are at higher risk for developing diabetes later in life. We know that healthy diet and exercise improve sugar metabolism, but we do not know whether lifestyle and/or genetics have a role in the progression of diabetes among those affected by gestational diabetes. We also do not know whether affected women's lifestyle choices after the childbirth have an impact on risk of obesity and diabetes in their children.  We aim to study whether lifestyle and/or genetics are related to the progression from gestational diabetes to diabetes later in life. We will also study whether affected women's lifestyle choices after the childbirth have an impact on risk of obesity in their children.  We will test our objectives within longitudinal research studies following women for over 20 years. The Nurses' Health Study II is an ongoing study following 116,430 female nurses. Women are asked to report their medical and lifestyle information every other year. They also donate blood and urine samples to test genetic and biomarkers. We assembled women with a history of gestational diabetes to test our research questions. We are also following their children through Growing-Up Today Study (GUTS) and GUTS-II and collecting children's growth information.  In current practices, women are only advised to monitor blood sugar levels during the first year after the pregnancy affected by gestational diabetes and are offered no lifestyle advice beyond the pregnancy. Our proposed study will assist in finding risk factors for diabetes and in developing diabetes prevention strategies specific to these high risk young women and their children.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICOAGULATION; BLOOD; CANCER; COAGULATION FACTORS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; VENOUS THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer may cause the blood to clot easier, and as a result, new clots in the veins of arms, legs and lungs are very frequent in patients with cancer. The consequences of these new clots are related to reduced quality of life, delay in treatment against cancer and death. The best way to avoid clots is by using blood thinners before clots are formed in the veins of these patients.  A major problem is that not all cancers would equally expose patients to these complications. So, it is important to identify who are the patients with an increased probability for developing clots. This is valuable information for doctors as these patients are the ones who may benefit the most with blood thinners.  Recently, new medication is available for preventing clots in patients at risk for clotting. The new medication offers improvements over existing blood thinners, but they have not been evaluated for the prevention of clots in patients with cancer. If they are shown to be useful for preventing new clots in cancer patients, then, this treatment could be used for as long as the cancer is active.  In this study, we propose to select cancer patients at high risk for developing vein clots with the goal to determine if administration of new blood thinners decreases the formation of new clots. Today, the number of new cancer patients is increasing, so, developing an effective and safe way to prevent vein clots in these patients will improve their care and optimize the use of medical resources.

TitreApplicationTitle: Refining Genotype-Phenotype Correlation of ADPKD
Keywords-MotsClés: GENOTYPE-PHENOTYPE CORRELATION; KIDNEY VOLUME IMAGING; POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common inherited kidney disorder that accounts for 5% of all cases of end stage renal disease (ESRD) in Canada. Previous studies of patients recruited from dialysis centre suggest that mutations of PKD1 and PKD2 account for ~85% and 15% of cases, respectively. More recent studies of less selected patients suggest a higher frequency of PKD2. In general, patients with PKD1 tend to have more severe disease with larger kidneys and earlier progression to ESRD than patients with PKD2. However, significant disease variability within each gene type is well documented and the factors responsible for this variaiblity have not been well defined.   We will study a large cohort of unselected families to re-estimate the relative frequencies of the two disease gene types for ADPKD. Using magnetic resonance imaging, we will generate total kidney volume (TKV) to provide a sensitive measure of disease severity, to be correlated with the putative disease-causing gene variants identified in our study patients. From this study, we expect to generate new knowledge to improve the clinical prognostication of  ADPKD. Such knowledge will provide the essential first step towards developing Personalized Medicine for the optimal management of patients with this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing novel wound healing strategy by inducing cutaneous adipose tissue regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: FLOW CYTOMETRY; HAIR FOLLICLES; IMMUNE PRIVILEGE; ISLET TRANSPLANTATION; REAL-TIME PCR
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with type I diabetes have to inject insulin every day to live due to the loss of insulin producing islet cells. Insulin injection saves life, but often results in poor control of blood sugar levels. Transplantation of the insulin-producing islets of the pancreas is a therapeutic treatment option for re-establishing sugar responsive insulin secretion. However, success of islet transplantation requires lifelong use of highly toxic anti-rejection medications. The objective of this proposal is to develop a new strategy to locally protect transplanted islets from rejection using naturally immune privileged cells. Our aim is to use hair follicle cells to coat the islet cells and to provide a protective shield. It has been demonstrated that specific tissues in hair follicles protect themselves from rejection when transplanted from one person to another; a feature called immune-privilege. This project aims to first address whether hair follicle derived cells protect against immune responses in cell culture conditions. We will coat islets with hair follicle derived cells and make sure the islets can still make insulin. Finally, we will transplant coated islets into a laboratory model of diabetes and confirm that the islets still work and are hidden from the immune system. Our proposal will contribute new knowledge for protecting transplanted islets using naturally immune privileged hair follicle derived cells. If this novel therapy proves effective, it will provide a simple way to treat type 1 diabetes more efficiently with fewer complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions between astrocytoma cells and blood vessels
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROGLIOMA CELLS; CELL CULTURE; FIBRONECTIN; IMMUNOHISTOLOGY; INTEGRINS; LENTIVIRAL VECTORS; PERIVASCULAR MIGRATION; RNA INTERFERENCE; VESSEL CO-OPTION; VESSEL DESTABILIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumors are a major cause of cancer-related deaths among children and young adults. These tumors grow by transforming the existing vasculature, leading to edema and other complications. They invade adjacent nervous tissue, often by picking their way along blood vessels, making a complete removal of the tumor by surgery almost impossible. The overall objective of our research program is to elucidate the mechanisms by which brain tumor cells induce vascular changes and migrate in a perivascular manner. The specific objective of the current project is to determine whether these mechanisms involve cell adhesion molecules, such as fibronectin and its receptors. We intend to meet this challenge by using cutting-edge techniques of cell biology in order to inhibit or overexpress the molecules of interest. The expected results should not only help to understand the development of brain tumors, but also to identify new therapeutic targets. We hope thereby to contribute to improving the lives of thousands of patients.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of beta-amyloid burden on cognition in normal aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID DEPOSITION; COGNITION; NEUROIMAGING; PIB-PET
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in Canada. Because the Canadian population is growing older and because age represents the greatest risk factor of developing the disease, it is important to better understand the differences between normal aging and the earliest signs of AD. The recent development of techniques for in vivo imaging of brain amyloid protein aggregations, one of the main pathological features of AD, offers new research perspectives in terms of understanding the nature and evolution of brain pathology in AD. Pittsburgh Compound B (PIB), which binds to betaamyloid (AB) deposits in the brain, may prove very useful in studying the relationship between these abnormal aggregations in the brain and cognitive function in aging. Recent PIB studies indicate that 10-30% of normal older persons show a pattern of binding similar to AD. Therefore, it is important to determine if these individuals may be at greater risk of later developing AD. Our objective is to use PIB scanning to investigate the relationship between AB deposition and cognitive performance in normal aging. We will study the relation between PIB retention in the brain and neuropsychological performance in healthy older adults. Our main hypothesis is that cognitively normal older individuals who show greater PIB uptake in the brain will show mild deficits on neuropsychological tests when compared to older individuals with low PIB uptake. The contributions of this study will be to improve our comprehension of the relation between the amount of AB deposition in the brain and cognition in normal aging. It will help understand if cognitively normal persons with AB deposition are on a trajectory toward AD. PIB imaging may help detect AB pathology in asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic individuals, and anti-amyloid therapies and non pharmacological interventions may be most helpful at this stage, before the onset of other pathological processes in the brain.

ResearchClassEN: DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS; VIRAL
ClasseRechercheFR: DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES; MALADIES A VIRUS
TitreApplicationTitle: Studies on new antiviral (hepatitis B virus) agents
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-HEPATITIS AGENTS; ANTIVIRAL AGENTS; CHEMOTHERAPEUTICS; DNA VIRUS; DRUG DESIGN DISCOVERY; DRUG SYNTHESIS; DRUG THERAPY; MECHANISM OF ACTION
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a serious global health problem, with more than 400 million chronically infected individuals in the world.  Estimates indicate that at least 2 billion people worldwide have been infected with HBV. Chronic HBV infection leads to liver damage, cirrhosis and liver cancer with high mortality, and 1.2 million deaths/year are attributed to HBV. In North America, ~300,000 new cases occur each year, resulting in ~43,000 chronic infections and 3,000 deaths. HBV infections (400 million) outnumber the HIV/AIDS cases (~33 million), and are a major medical problem worldwide. Alarmingly, HBV is far more infectious than HIV, especially following mucosal contact.  Current antiviral therapy remains inadequate due to limited efficacy, severe side effects, rapid development of resistance and most importantly viral recurrence with exacerbation of liver pathology after cessation of therapy. Therefore, there is a real unmet need to discover new classes of efficacious and non-toxic anti-HBV drugs that can bring more complete virus suppression, reduce toxicity and avoid drug resistance problems. We have recently discovered new families of potent inhibitors of HBV that are also effective against drug-resistant HBV, a significant issue in HBV therapy. In the proposed work, we will investigate detailed antiviral properties in animal models, and understand mechanism of action of these promising agents. The proposed studies will delineate new approaches for the treatment of chronic HBV infections. Novel agents may emerge from these studies, which could then be developed as a new generation of efficacious antiviral drugs to combat drug resistance, and improve the life expectancy and quality of life of the HBV infected people in Canada and worldwide.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the Amygdala-Prefrontal Cortical Circuit in Opiate Motivation, Learning and Memory
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; AMYGDALA; DOPAMINE; IN VIVO ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MEMORY; MESOLIMBIC SYSTEM; NEURONAL RECORDING; OPIATES; PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Opiate-class narcotics such as heroin and morphine represent highly addictive drugs of abuse, capable of inducing rapid dependence and withdrawal. Indeed, addiction to opiates, either illicit or prescription based, represents a rapidly growing public health crisis in many parts of Canada. A primary reason for the intractability of opiate addiction stems from their highly rewarding properties. Thus, opiates can produce powerful associative memories in opiate users that are linked to the drug taking experience. Once these memories are triggered, previously addicted individuals may relapse to opiate taking, even years after successful abstinence. Our research team is targeting regions of the brain that process these powerful opiate-related associative memories. Specifically, we focus on the amygdala and prefrontal cortical brain pathway and how signaling through specific neurotransmitters called dopamine and glutamate may modulate the processing of opiate-related addiction memories within this neural circuitry. We use an integrative combination of in vivo electrophysiological recordings of single neurons, behavioural pharmacology and neuronal population recordings during opiate-related associative memory procedures to understand the precise neuronal and neurochemical mechanisms underlying the rewarding and dependence producing properties of opiates. Our ultimate goal is to identify pharmacotherapeutic targets aimed at reversing or preventing the ability of these drug-related memories to induce compulsive drug-seeking behaviours, dependence and withdrawal.

TitreApplicationTitle: The "viral toxin": understanding binding, internalization and signaling of double-stranded RNA.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRAL IMMUNITY; CLASS A SCAVENGER RECEPTORS; DSRNA; INNATE IMMUNITY; PATHOGEN INFECTION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Double stranded RNA (dsRNA) is a common form of nucleic acid found in virus-infected cells, but not in healthy cells. Virus infection often causes cells to die, releasing dsRNA into the extracellular space. It has been known for many years that extracellular dsRNA acts as a "viral toxin", causing many of the symptoms associated with "the flu". Of no surprise, dsRNA is a potent activator of the innate immune response and causes the rapid induction of the cytokine interferon. Although cells have many proteins that recognize and bind dsRNA once it is within cells, for many years it was unknown how cells recognize dsRNA outside of cells. We recently found that class A scavenger receptors (SR-As) are critical for the production of interferon in response to extracellular dsRNA. However, it is unknown how SR-As function in this role. Furthermore, it is unclear how dsRNA brought in by SR-As reaches the cytoplasm, where many dsRNA-binding proteins are found, as SR-As bring dsRNA into cellular vesicles via  endocytosis. Once in the cytoplasm, a protein called IRF3 is critical for making interferon. Since it plays such an important role, most viruses have evolved ways to degrade or inactivate IRF3. We recently found that IRF9 can make interferon in response to dsRNA in the absence of IRF3. This is a new role for IRF9, thus nothing is known how IRF9 is working. In this grant, we propose experiments to understand in detail the events that allow extracellular dsRNA to make interferon. Extracellular dsRNA not only causes clinical symptoms of virus infection, it also plays an important role in autoimmunity. In addition, synthetic dsRNA is being tested in clinical trials as an adjuvant. Thus, understanding how host cells recognize and respond to dsRNA is of wide clinical importance, particularly for the development of effective therapies against severe virus complications and autoimmune diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissemination of an Efficacy-Proven Intervention for Promoting Pap Test among Chinese Immigrants using Information Technology
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER SCREENING; DISSEMINATION; HEALTH INEQUALITIES; IMMIGRANTS HEALTH; INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY; INTERVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Cervical cancer screening is free in Canada and is a highly effective in preventing the cancer. Chinese immigrants, a large, fast growing ethnic minority group in Canada (about 4% of the nation's population in 2006 Census), however, have an appreciably lower usage rate of cervical cancer screening and at a higher risk of cervical cancer, compared to the general population of Canada.   To make the nation's cervical cancer screening program effective overall, we must address this health disparity in high-risk populations such as female Chinese immigrants.  In the proposed project, we attempt to disseminate, using Internet, an education package that has been proven to be highly effective in previous research studies for promoting the screening among Chinese immigrants. The package contains culturally-tailored and linguistically-appropriate education materials (video, pamphlet, motivational brochure, and local clinic information) and this will be combined with navigation assistance provided by a local Chinese community service center, ASSIST. We will evaluate the public health impact of the dissemination using an evaluation framework called RE-AIM that considers practicality and feasibility in assessing impacts.  Our team has extensive relevant experiences and expertise to conduct this research. With strengths rendered by Internet, the 3-team collaboration (our research team, ASSIST community organization, and Alberta Health Services provincial healthcare agency) aims to reach a large number of local Chinese immigrants and increase their uptake of cervical cancer screening. With results from the RE-AIM evaluation, it also aims to inform other provinces and cities for future implementations of similar dissemination for their potential impact, resource requirements, feasibility, and sustainability.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of DGAT2 in triacylglycerol synthesis and lipid droplet formation
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTE; LIPID BIOCHEMISTRY; LIPID DROPLET; OBESITY; PROTEASOME; PROTEIN INTERACTION; STRUCTURE/FUNCTION; SUBCELLULAR LOCALIZATION; TRIACYLGLYCEROL; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Triacylglycerol (TG) is the major source of stored energy in humans. However, excessive accumulation of TG in tissues can lead to obesity, diabetes and heart disease. Obesity has now reached epidemic proportions in Canada with 25% of the Canadian population now considered obese, while 60% are considered overweight. In the last 20 years, deaths attributable to complications from obesity have doubled and billions of dollars per year are spent on health care costs that are attributable to obesity. Clearly mechanisms to prevent the excess accumulation of TG would be extremely important for controlling obesity and related diseases.  Our laboratory is focused on studying the mechanisms of TG synthesis in fat cells (adipocytes). Two proteins, diacylglycerol acyltransferase-1 (DGAT1) and diacylglycerol acyltransferase-2 (DGAT2) are responsible for producing TG in mammals. Numerous studies have shown that these two enzymes have important but distinct roles in TG metabolism and that DGAT2 is responsible for producing the majority of TG.  The main objective of this study is to investigate the cellular and molecular processes in adipocytes that are required for DGAT2 to synthesize TG. Specific areas that we intend to focus on include determining if the efficient synthesis of TG is dependent on the interaction of DGAT2 with other proteins or on its specific location within a cell. We also will determine if TG levels can be controlled by modulating the degradation rate of DGAT2 to increase or decrease TG synthesis.    DGAT2 represents an ideal potential drug target for developing inhibitors to treat obesity and related metabolic disorders. By understanding how this enzyme works in cells to produce TG, we can generate information that may be useful for developing effective treatment strategies for human diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive inhibition, and its modulation by emotions, in depressed patients at-risk for suicide: a functional MRI study.
Keywords-MotsClés: MENTAL HEALTH; NEUROIMAGING; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Some people are more negatively affected than others when facing difficult and stressful situations. This difference may notably lead some individuals to more easily become depressed, have suicidal thoughts and even attempt or commit suicide. The current research project will examine why people are differently vulnerable to stressful situations and why some individuals, when depressed, may choose to commit a suicidal act while others will not. Examining the functioning of the brain in these individuals may enable us to improve our understanding of suicidal behaviour. More specifically, we will aim at investigating the brain regions involved in regulating cognitive function in an emotional context. To this goal, we will measure and compare brain activity during the execution of a test using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) between 40 depressed subjects with a history of suicide attempts, 40 depressed subjects without any history of suicidal behaviour and 40 healthy controls. Findings from this study will shed light on the pathological mechanisms underlying the vulnerability to suicidal acts, and ultimately, will enable to improve detection of depressed patients at-risk for suicide and prevention of suicidal behaviour.

TitreApplicationTitle: The epigenetic impact of deregulated poly(ADP)ribosylation in breast cancer.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; EPIGENETICS; GENE REGULATION; MOUSE MODELS OF CANCER; NOVEL THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is characterized by abnormal, uncontrolled division of cells. Recent evidence has shown that one of the initiating steps leading to this type of malignant growth in breast cancer is the silencing (switching off) of tumor suppressor genes. These genes typically control cell growth to ensure that proliferation does not exceed normal limitations, but once these genes are turned off, cancer can arise. Turning these genes back on is a relevant therapeutic goal and several drugs that reactivate tumor suppressor genes have been tested in clinical trials. However, the rational development of these types of drugs has been hampered by our lack of understanding as to why these tumor suppressor genes become silenced in the first place. My previous work uncovered a mechanism whereby tumor suppressors become silenced in breast cancer cells due to the dysfunction of an important regulatory protein. Recently I discovered that this dysfunction is due to elevated levels and heightened activity of a protein called PARG in breast cancer cells. My current work suggests that inhibitors of PARG may be useful new therapeutic agents for breast cancer. Therefore, my current research efforts focus on understanding in more detail how PARG regulates tumor formation and exploring the potential of PARG inhibitors as novel therapeutic agents to fight breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying New approaches to optimize Thrombus characterization for predicting Early Recanalization and Reperfusion with iv tPA using Serial CT angiography (INTERRSeCT)
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGRAPHY; COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; ISCHEMIC STROKE; PERFUSION IMAGING; RECANALIZATION; THROMBOLYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The treatment of strokes has greatly improved over the last few decades with the development of drugs, which limit the damage produced by stroke.  In addition, physicians are able to use imaging technology to see the brain and its vessels in new ways using CT scans.  These scans can reveal an existing blood clot lodged in the blood vessel resulting in the stroke within the brain.  These scans, if repeated can also determine if the blood cot dissolved away so blood flow is restored to the brain.  Currently, there is an urgency to clear the blood vessels of clots as early as possible from the occurrence of the stroke to improve the patient's chances for recovery.  Yet we do not know if a given treatment will be successful in achieving clot dissolving.  In this grant, we plan to take CT scan pictures of the blood clot in the blood vessel and repeat the CT scan of the blood vessels four hours later to determine if the clot has dissolved.  This approach will be performed after the drug treatment has been given to each patient.  We will then know how often the blood clot dissolves using the drug treatment.  We will also be able to identify features about the patient and features on the first CT scan of the brain and blood vessels which predict that the clkot will dissolve within four hours when a specific drug treatment is given.  This research design, will for the time, help to create a "score card" based on the patient history and CAT Scan that will assist the physician to determine the best course of action to take.  The research will be conducted at multiple sites and will enroll 350 patients over three years.  Information about how much recovery each patient achieves will also be collected and compared to whether the blook clot dissolved.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Lsr2 in Mtb persistence and drug tolerance
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE REGULATION; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; LATENT INFECTION; LSR2; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), continues to be one of the leading causes of death due to an infectious disease globally, with an estimated 8.8 million new cases and 1.45 million deaths in 2010. In the majority of individuals infected with Mtb, the bacteria establish a latent, asymptomatic infection that can persist for decades. About 5-10% of latently infected individuals will develop active disease in their lifetime and host immunosuppression (HIV coinfection) markedly increases the risk of reactivation. As much as one-third of the world's population is latently infected, representing a large reservoir for potential reactivation and subsequent spread. Latent TB infection presents major challenges to effective control of TB since currently available drugs cannot kill latent organisms. Mtb persisters, which are characterized by reduced or altered metabolic activity and enhanced drug tolerance, are a major contributor of latent infection. However, the origin of Mtb persisters and the mechanism of drug tolerance remain poorly understood. The goal of my project is to elucidate molecular mechanisms underlying Mtb persistence and drug tolerance. My laboratory has recently identified Lsr2 as a global regulator of Mtb. Our preliminary data suggest Mtb employs Lsr2 as a key molecular switch in the formation of persisters. In this application, I designed a number of experiments to address the central role of Lsr2 in Mtb persistence and drug tolerance. Our studies will help to elucidate the genetic and metabolic pathways involved in Mtb persistence and identify potentially new therapeutic and diagnosis targets of latent TB infection.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - C : Systèmes digestif, endocrinien et excrétoire
TitreApplicationTitle: Are circulating fibrocytes associated with a worse renal outcome in patients with glomerulonephritis?
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW DERIVED PROGENITOR CELLS; CIRCULATING FIBROCYTES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GLOMERULONEPHRITIS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; TUBULOINTERSTITIAL FIBROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Glomerulonephritis is a form of kidney injury that involves inflammation of the small filters of the kidneys (glomeruli) with associated loss of kidney function. The majority of patients can recover when treated with potent drugs that suppress the immune system. Despite treatment, some patients will continue to have a decline in kidney function which does not appear to be caused by the initial inflammation, but by a progressive scarring of the kidney tissue.  The cause of this scarring or fibrosis is not clear. One possibility is that special cells are recruited from the bone marrow (in a similar manner to the way inflammatory cells are recruited to injured tissue). These cells are called 'fibrocytes' as they appear to be similar in some respects to 'fibroblasts' that are known to cause scarring in tissues.  It is not clear whether these fibrocyte cells are good are bad. They may cause scarring in tissue, or they may be involved in healing and repair. Glomerulonephritis provides a unique opportunity to understand the role of these fibrocytes in disease.  Most patients get a kidney biopsy to diagnose the disease so we can look for the presence of these cells in the tissue and in the blood at the same time. We can see whether the number of fibrocytes predict whether the patient will recover renal function or not. By studying the role of fibrocytes in this disease, we will gain further insights into the causes of loss of kidney function and hints that may lead us to new potential treatments.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de fonctionnement : programme de recherche en collaboration avec l'industrie
TitreApplicationTitle: New strategies for overcoming bacterial resistance to antibiotics
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICCS; BETA LACTAMASES; BETA LACTAMS; CARBAPENEMS; CHECKERBOARD SYNERGY; ENZYMOLOGY; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; MICROBIOOGY; MOLECULAR MODELING; ORGANIC SYNTHESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Increasingly, bacterial infections, particularly those acquired in hospitals, are being caused by bacteria that are resistant to current antibiotics. In order to ensure that a last line of defense is available in such cases, antibiotics, such as the carbapenems, to which resistance was very rare, are restricted to use in hospitals. This prudent practice has delayed the onset of resistance to these essential antibiotics. Unfortunately, certain bacteria now produce enzymes called carbapenemases that destroy these last line of defense antibiotics. Thus bacterial infections that were once readily managed through the judicious use of carbapenems are now becoming life-threatening, especially for patients whose immune systems are compromised such as cystic fibrosis patients, burn victims, the elderly, AIDS patients, cancer patients and organ transplant patients. The goal of this project is to discover pharmaceuticals that inactivate the bacterial carbapenemases. Such drugs would be co-administered along with the carbapenems in order to block the bacterial resistance mechanism thus making the carbapenems effective against bacteria that are currently resistant. The proposed research involves a partnership between a research group at the University of Waterloo that has much expertise in relation to carbapenemases and a new pharmaceutical discovery company that is dedicated to finding practical solutions to antibiotic resistance. If the project succeeds, the health of Canadians will benefit from reduction in suffering and mortality. Also, substantial savings in health care costs would be expected from a reduction in the length of hospitalization that would result form the discovery of effective antibiotics. Additionally, there is potential for substantial growth of the company in the event of commercialization of a carabapenemase inhibitor and, since the collaborating company is incorporated in Ontario, there is potential for significant job creation in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Increasing the Effectiveness of the Diabetes Prevention Program Through If-then Plans and Mental Practice: A Parallel Randomized Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES PREVENTION; HABIT FORMATION; IMPLEMENTATION INTENTIONS; LIFESTYLE MODIFICATION PROGRAM; MENTAL PRACTICE; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PROGRAM EFFECTIVENESS; WEIGHT LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: Currently, five million Canadians meet the criteria for pre-diabetes. Lifestyle modification programs like the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) have been shown to be very effective in preventing the progression from pre-diabetes to diabetes. However, such programs are expensive because they are delivered in one-on-one sessions by highly trained professionals. Group-delivered versions of the DPP are cheaper, but are considerably less effective. We propose that the effectiveness of the Group-DPP can be increased by integrating tools into the program that help people creating new eating and physical activity habits and maintaining these habits in the long-term. Specifically, we propose to integrate if-then plans (concrete action plans that specify when, where, and how one will carry out a new behaviour) and their mental practice into the Group-DPP curriculum. To test the hypothesis that habit-creating tools render the Group-DPP more effective, we will conduct a randomized controlled trial in which participants with pre-diabetes will be assigned to either the standard Group-DPP or its enriched version. In the enriched version, if-then plans and their mental practice will be integrated into each session of the program based on methods we have developed and tested in our past research. We expect that (1) the enriched Group-DPP will lead to greater weight loss and a greater reduction in other pre-diabetes-relevant risk outcomes than the standard Group-DPP, (2) the habit formation in the enriched Group-DPP will occur faster and newly formed habits will be sustained for a longer period of time than in the standard Group-DPP, and (3) the greater effectiveness of the enriched Group-DPP will be due to stronger habit formation. Significance: This research can,  without adding costs, make future diabetes prevention programs more effective, thereby reducing diabetes rates.

TitreApplicationTitle: Iron metabolism and immune system interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEMIA; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; IRON ABSORPTION; IRON METABOLISM; IRON TRANSPORTERS
Abstract-Résumé: Macrophages and lymphocytes are uniquely situated and suited for a modifier role in iron metabolism, either directly or through mediating molecules, which they produce. We will study the influence of immune system components, such as receptors, cell types and immune mediators, and identify the contribution of signaling pathways to the maintenance of iron homeostasis. These studies could potentially have important therapeutic applications not only in the management of iron overload, but also in treating conditions such as anemia and other iron-related diseases. Moreover, they will provide a better understanding of some basic aspects of the immune system and their relationship to the fundamental process of iron metabolism.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; SCIENCES DENTAIRES/BIOLOGIE ORALE
TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Novel Markers of Alveolar Bone loss: Developing New Diagnostic Approaches for the Most Prevalent Forms of Bone Loss
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE; DIAGNOSIS; MONOCYTE MACROPHAGE; OSTEOIMMUNOLOGY; PERIODONTAL DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Periodontal diseases also known as "Gum Disease" are the most common inflammatory/destructive conditions of bone and affects up to 80 percent of the North American population during their lifetime. In addition to the financial burden (4 billion dollars per year in Canada alone), new evidence indicates that periodontal diseases also impact systemic health. While current therapies provide improved outcomes, our ability to diagnose these osteoimmunologic diseases prior to the onset of bone destruction is very limited. Accordingly, there is an urgent need to accurately define the various periodontal diseases, their risk/outcome determinants and to translate this knowledge into diagnostic tools and therapeutics that can control bone loss and reduce the socioeconomic burden. To address these challenges, we have assembled a health research team with specific expertise in macrophage and bone biology and with cutting-edge technologies including high-throughput mass spectrometry and biomarkers of oral disease. We will synergize our activities to characterize the circulating and tissue monocyte/macrophage phenotypes, and the cytokine, chemokine and terminally-modified cytokine profiles of human subjects with periodontal diseases. We will use these data to develop diagnostic and prognostic signatures for these high prevalence, bone-destructive diseases. We will determine whether modified cytokines/chemokines are key elements that regulate bone loss in these high prevalence bone diseases. An improved understanding of these processes will enable early diagnoses and prevent bone loss. The data emerging from these studies will elucidate diagnostic/prognostic markers and new therapeutic targets that are required to maintain bone health in patients with periodontal diseases and possibly other less prevalent and therefore more difficult to study osteoimmunologic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Behavioural and neurophysiological effects of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in the primate oculomotor system
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; FRONTAL EYE FIELDS; MOTOR CONTROL; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; OCULOMOTOR SYSTEM; PARIETAL CORTEX; SACCADES; SUPERIOR COLLICULUS; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has emerged as an important tool for investigating human brain function, and a potential treatment mode for a variety of neurological and psychiatric disorders. TMS provides a safe and effective noninvasive means of stimulating the human brain by inducing weak electrical currents in a brain region underneath a magnetic coil. However, despite the growing use of TMS, there lacks an in-depth understanding of its precise neurophysiological effects, and the mechanisms by which such effects influence behaviour.   We seek to bridge this gap by combining TMS with neurophysiological recordings within the oculomotor system of behaving non-human primates (NHPs). The oculomotor system moves the line of sight via saccadic eye movements, and the oculomotor system in NHPs provides the dual advantages of being both well understood and highly homologous to that of humans. We propose to leverage these advantages by applying TMS to the frontal eye fields (FEF) of NHPs. The first objective is to develop a methodology for TMS-FEF in NHPs, with a particular emphasis on replicating the effects of TMSFEF observed in humans. Once developed, this animal model will permit the pairing of TMS-FEF with neurophysiological recordings from neural areas either downstream, upstream, or on the other side of the brain from the stimulated FEF. Such recordings will yield fundamental information about the neurobiological effects of TMS in the primate brain, ultimately leading to a better appreciation of its effects in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Establishing a New Research Agenda Regarding Population Health Ethics and Young People's Health
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV/STIS; ONLINE STI/HIV TESTING; POPULATION HEALTH ETHICS; SOCIAL SCIENCE METHODS AND THEORIES; YOUTH SEXUAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The Internet is a medium that offers unprecedented reach to populations at risk for STIs/HIV. Youth (ages 15-24) bear a significant burden of STI/HIV infection, particularly in some communities (e.g. rural, with large youth populations), and have been shown to be particularly receptive to internet-based services. The STI/HIV Division at BC Centre for Disease Control (BCCDC) has recently developed GetCheckedBC (GCBC), a new online STI/HIV testing intervention. Youth are important target clients for the GCBC. Targeting interventions towards population sub-groups (e.g., young people) is not a new strategy. However, the population health ethical implications of targeting population subgroups are only beginning to be examined. Little is known about how this approach to intervention may operate differentially within and across targeted groups and there is concern that these approaches may exacerbate health inequity (particularly among the most vulnerable population subgroups). Furthermore, targeted approaches tend to be heavily focused on agentic practices (that is, on changing the individual behaviour), rather than structural interventions (on changing the conditions in which the behaviour occurs).   This proposal brings together an interdisciplinary team of researchers and trainees who are new to the field of ethics. The proposed pilot study nested within the current application will examine how the GCBC experience attempts to ameliorate individual risk, as well as the ways in which it deploys an institutionalized discourse that attempts to deconstruct social structures that (re)produce social injustices (e.g., heteronormativity; misogyny) that have important implications for young people's sexual health. The pilot study also will form the basis of two PhD dissertations. Overall, this provides a first step towards strengthening new proposals related to population health ethics to be submitted in other CIHR funding opportunities

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Switches and Membrane Dynamics: Uncovering the principles and mechanisms of mitochondrial fusion.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL FRACTIONATION; CELL-FREE ASSAY; FUSION; GENOME-WIDE SCREEN; MITOCHONDRIA; NEURON; OLIGODENDROCYTE; REDOX
Abstract-Résumé: There are hundreds of mitochondria inside each cell who work as combustion engines. They use the oxygen that we breath to burn fat and sugar, and the energy derived from this is used as fuel for our bodies. We have long assumed that these cellular furnaces sit idly within the cell, without much attention to the general state of the cell. Recent data has changed this view, since we have realized that they are extremely dynamic structures, fusing together, branching and splitting into pieces. This proposal describes our approach to try and understand why the mitochondria behave as an interconnected group, and what this means to the cell, the tissue, and the body. Indeed, mutations in mitochondrial fusion proteins leads to serious degenerative diseases. We hope that by characterizing the details of mitochondrial shape-shifting, that we will identify new therapeutic approaches to treating degenerative disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rôles, régulation, mécanismes d'action du récepteur opioïde delta dans la douleur
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRESSAGE DES RECEPTEURS; AFFERENCES PRIMAIRES; ANALGESIE; DOULEUR; INFLAMMATION; LIGANDS D'AFFINITE; MICROSCOPIE CONFOCALE; MICROSCOPIE ELECTRONIQUE; OPIOIDES
Abstract-Résumé: Malgre l'existence d'une multitude de medicaments ayant des proprietes analgesiques, le traitement de la douleur demeure souvent problematique. Nonobstant des effets secondaires importants (constipation, nausee, sedation), les composes alcaloides demeurent les drogues les plus efficaces pour soulager la douleur chronique. Le mieux connu de tous les alcaloides demeure sans contredit la morphine, appartenant a la famille des opiaces. La morphine et ses derives se lient et activent au moins 3 types de recepteurs couples aux proteines G, soit les recepteurs opioidergiques mu (MOPR), delta (DOPR) et kappa (KOPR). Bien que ces trois sous-types de recepteurs possedent des proprietes analgesiques, les actions de la majorite des narcotiques utilises en clinique ont pour cible le recepteur MOP. A l'oppose de ce dernier, l'activation des recepteurs DOP n'entraine que peu d'effets secondaires. En conditions normales (i.e. chez des animaux sains), le pouvoir analgesique des agonistes selectifs delta est plus faible que celui de la morphine. Au cours des dernieres annees, il a cependant ete montre que sous certaines conditions, l'activation de DOPR peut contrer les sensations douloureuses avec une efficacite voisine a la morphine. Dans mon laboratoire, nous nous interessons a l'etude des mecanismes de regulation de l'adressage a la membrane des recepteurs DOP dans des conditions de douleur chronique d'origine inflammatoire ainsi qu'aux effets d'un traitement prolonge avec des agonistes selectifs delta. Une meilleure comprehension de ces mecanismes pourrait aider au developpement de strategies pour augmenter l'efficacite des therapies contre la douleur et ainsi augmenter la qualite de vie des patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Roles of the Histone H2A Deubiquitinase MYSM1 in Hematopoiesis and Immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; HEMATOPOIESIS; HISTONE MODIFICATION; IMMUNE RESPONSE; LYMPHOCYTE DIFFERENTIATION; OXIDATIVE STRESS; REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION; TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: The cells of our blood and immune system are produced in the bone marrow, from a small population of hematopoietic stem cells, in the process of cell division and differentiation known as hematopoiesis. Hematopoiesis requires precise regulation of gene expression and efficient repair of DNA damage, and its disruptions result in many life-threatening disorders. In recent work we and others demonstrated the essential role of protein MYSM1 in the process of hematopoiesis (Nijnik et.al., Blood 2011; Jiang. et.al., Immunity 2011). MYSM1 binds DNA and catalyzes the removal of ubiquitin from a DNA-packaging protein Histone H2A. MYSM1 therefore functions to organize the DNA in our cells, controlling gene expression and potentially also DNA repair. The proposed research program will characterize the functions of MYSM1 at different stages of hematopoietic process and the molecular mechanisms of its activity. This will enhance our knowledge of the fundamental biology of hematopoiesis, blood, and immune systems, and in the long-term may contribute to better understanding and treatment of hematological disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Regulation of Myogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION SEQUENCING (CHIP-SEQ); DIFFERENTIATION; EPIGENETICS; MASSIVELY PARALLEL DNA SEQUENCING; MRF4; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; MYF5; MYOD; MYOGENESIS; MYOGENIN; PAX3; PAX7; PROGENITORS; STEM CELLS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL NETWORKS
Abstract-Résumé: In adult skeletal muscle, satellite cells are specialized cells whose job is to replenish muscle tissue lost through damage or disease.  At the molecular level, the behavior of the satellite cells and their descendants in carrying out this role is regulated by a variety of factors.  These include Pax3, Pax7 and the MyoD family of transcription factors, which act to switch on or off target genes, and factors such as HATs, HDACs and CTCF, which alter the conformation of the DNA itself, thereby affecting target genes.  In Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), the activity levels and targets of these factors become altered, resulting in a dysregulation of satellite cell function that exacerbates the disease.  However, the extent and nature of these alterations in the regulatory network are not well understood.  In this proposal, we outline an experimental program designed to clarify the normal and DMD-altered roles of the major regulators of myogenesis.  Our study will be based primarily on high-throughput genome-scale measurements of the DNA-binding sites of the various regulatory factors, of DNA packaging and conformation, and of target gene expression under various conditions.  These experiments will provide important new insights into the regulation of myogenesis, and will facilitate the development of new therapeutic strategies for many muscle diseases, including muscular dystrophy.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE DE PARKINSON; MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of PINK1 Processing in Mitochondrial Function and Parkinson's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: KINASE; MITOCHONDRIA; NEURON; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PROTEASE; SIGNALING; TRAFFICKING; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects over 100,000 people in Canada and the numbers will only grow as the population ages. PD involves the death of dopamine neurons in the midbrain, which leads to devastating motor and functional impairment. Although treatment is available, its effectiveness diminishes over the long term. Hope for a more definitive treatment lies in basic biomedical research. Already, important advances have been made using molecular and genetic approaches. Not very long ago, genetics was not thought to be important in PD. However, in the past 15 years, several genes have been identified which cause familial forms of PD. My laboratory has a longstanding interest in understanding the normal function of these PD genes and how defects in the genes lead to PD. A convergence of work over the past few years has led to the discovery that mitochondria, the cell's energy power plant, are a focal point of the degenerative process in PD. The aim of this application is to decipher how one of these PD genes, PINK1 impacts mitochondrial function normally and what goes wrong in disease.
