TitreApplicationTitle: Stemness and cellular hierarchy in the human intestinal crypt
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT STEM CELLS; CELL-MATRIX INTERACTION; DIFFERENTIATION; GENE REGULATION; INTESTINE; LINEAGE SPECIFICATION; SIGNALIZATION; STEM CELL NICHE
Abstract-Résumé: The intestine is lined with a single layer of epithelial cells that ensure nutrient uptake. Because of the hostile environment in which they are found these cells are replenished rapidly and continuously throughout our lifetime. A stem cell population, located in the lower regions of the glands, divides constantly producing the required cells.    The use of genetic mouse models has identified a host of signals mediating changes that these cells must undergo in order to go from immature cells to fully functional cells. When these signals or processes go awry cells no longer receive the correct instructions leading to different pathological conditions, such as cancer.  In comparison, little is known about how these functions in man.  In the current grant we propose to study the cellular and molecular mechanisms than regulate stem cells and cell organization in the glands. We have developed a special normal intestinal cell line that behaves as a stem cell allowing us to manipulate their environment and directly study how these cells react. Better understanding of the cellular organization in the human intestinal crypt would significantly impact many fields related to gastroenterology namely intestinal stem cell biology, tissue repair and carcinogenesis, in addition to the potential therapeutic use that these cells may offer in the near future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular pharmacology and functions of the atypical chemokine receptor CXCR7
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHEMOKINE; G-PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTOR; LEUKEMIA; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Chemokines are small secreted proteins that permit cells to orient in the body. Cells detect the chemokines by expressing chemokine receptors on their surface. They move in the direction of the source of the chemokine. For example, the chemokine SDF-1 is produced in the bone marrow. Hematopoietic stem cells, that is the precursors of all blood cells, lodge in the bone marrow because they respond to SDF-1 via the chemokine receptor CXCR4. Unfortunately, also cancer and leukemia cells respond to SDF-1. As a consequence, they also move towards the bone marrow, where the special environment protects them from chemotherapy.  Our project analyses a newly discovered chemokine receptor, CXCR7, which also recognizes SDF-1. However, its function is poorly understood, and it does not permit cell migration. We find that CXCR7 dampens the activity of CXCR4, for example in leukemia cells. As a consequence, cells that express CXCR7 migrate less. Potentially, CXCR7 expression on individual patient leukemias may predict the success of chemotherapy. Thus, dosage of chemotherapy could be individually adapted and toxic overtreatment be avoided.  Our project aims at better understanding on HOW CXCR7 is doing this. We also want to understand how it works on the molecular level, and what kind of drugs could be used to better take advantage of the potential of CXCR7 as a drug target in leukemia and cancer.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU POUMON; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: A Systems Genetic approach using primary cultures and genetically engineered mouse models of glioblastoma to elucidate novel pathways and therapeutic treatments
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER RESEARCH; EPIGENETICS; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; LYMPHANGIOLEIOMYOMATOSIS (LAM); MOUSE MODELS; SMALL MOLECULE INHIBITOR SCREEN; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; SYSTEMS GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare devastating lung disease that predominantly affects young women and results in proliferation of lung smooth muscle, growth throughout the lungs leading to obstruction and respiratory failure. There are two forms of LAM: Sporadic LAM for which the genetic basis is unknown and TSC-LAM in women who have the familial disease tuberous sclerosis complex (mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes). TSC1/2 are well-characterized tumour suppressor genes that contain a GTPase activating protein (GAP) and that loss of TSC1/2 leads to hyper-activation of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), a multi-subunit kinase that regulates cell growth, invasion, metabolism and resistance to apoptosis. Lung transplants are often the only treatment option for late stage LAM patients with a 5 year survival rate of only 65%. The lack primary cell lines or appropriate disease specific model organisms often limits LAM research. Recent advances in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS) in which human fibroblasts are reprogrammed to pluripotent stem cells using a genetic defined set of factors (KLF4, SOX2 and OCT4) show promise in allowing for the generations of patient specific disease models such as LAM. Our Hypothesis is that generation of iPS cells from fibroblast patients of TSC-LAM and normal control wildtype iPS cells can be differentiated to smooth muscle lung cells and serve as a model to identify novel drug targets and epigenetic alterations. In this proposal we aim to generate and validate human primary cell culture models and mouse xenograft models that can recapitulate LAM. Using these validated models we will explore LAM for epigenetic alterations and use these models as pre-clinical models to identify new therapeutic agents that are effective against LAM and not normal control tissue. Deciphering the methylome and using drug discovery will allow for novel insights and treatment options in to LAM.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of intracellular calcium pulsars in native endothelium
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ENDOTHELIUM; INTRACELLULAR CALCIUM; MITOCHONDRIA; OXIDATIVE STRESS; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES
Abstract-Résumé: Endothelial cells are cells lining the blood vessels and they play a crucial in the control of blood pressure and vascular tone. Mechanisms involved in the regulation of blood flow by the endothelium require intracellular Ca2+ ions as key signalling molecules. Our lab focuses on the investigation of the fundamental mechanisms controlling intracellular Ca2+ in endothelium. We have recently identified a unique and spontaneous Ca2+ signalling pathway in endothelium termed "Ca2+ pulsars". This novel Ca2+ signal has been shown to activate proteins at the cell membrane called ion channels and other proteins called kinases.  Ca2+ pulsars are suggested to be involved in regulation of vascular function. However, the mechanisms underlying the regulation of this intracellular calcium signalling in the endothelium remain to be established. We seek to determine the relationship between Ca2+ pulsars and an important intracellular organelle, the mitochondria, which have been shown to regulate intracellular calcium. State-of-the-art confocal microscopy on living tissue and fluorescent probes will be used in conjunction with pharmacological approaches to assess the impact of mitochondria on Ca2+ pulsars and membrane potential of vascular cells, therefore on vascular function. Our work will provide novel insights on key mechanisms underlying the regulation of intracellular calcium signalling and its involvement in endothelial function and dysfunction. This research may provide crucial information regarding therapeutic targets for vascular disease such hypertension.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of epithelium-derived IL-33 in driving lung inflammation in Cystic Fibrosis patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ALARMINS; CELL DEATH; EPITHELIUM; INFLAMMATION; LUNG DISEASES; MOUSE MODEL OF INFECTION; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA; PULMONARY EXACERBATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SPUTUM
Abstract-Résumé: More than 3 million Canadians cope with a serious pulmonary disease related to inflammation. Recent reports suggest that with global warming and aging of the population, these numbers are bound to increase further. Inflammation is a complex biological response to injurious stimuli to protect and repair affected tissues. This response directs inflammatory mediators to the site of injury via increase permeability of blood vessels. Hallmarks of inflammation have been recognized since antiquity but the molecular mechanisms underlying this complex process are just becoming apparent. Chronic inflammation is the result of prolonged inflammation, which cannot fully resolve itself and leads to progressive tissue destruction. The mainstay treatment for many inflammatory diseases is steroids. These are highly effective in the treatment of most cases of asthma, but a small number are steroid-resistant. Other chronic inflammatory diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cystic fibrosis are largely resistant to the therapeutic effect of steroids, while patients are still susceptible to their side effects. Therefore alternative treatments are required for these diseases. The main objective of this research program is to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying pulmonary chronic inflammation and identify novel strategy to re-establish the balance of inflammation. We propose to achieve this by obtaining a clearer understanding of key signals emanating from cells lining the airways in response to bacterial infection. It is becoming apparent that when cells are infected and die they release factors that can further augment inflammation. This research proposal will investigate such a factor, called IL-33, to understand its role when released from epithelial cells that have died because of bacterial infections. This proposal aims to determine whether or not targeting IL-33 would be beneficial in decreasing the burden of inflammation of Cystic Fibrosis patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Behavioural and neurophysiological responses to tonic cutaneous stimulation in the spinal cord-injured cat
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; CLONUS; CUTANEOUS; ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; LOCOMOTION; PHARMACOLOGY; REFLEX; SPASTICITY; SPINAL CORD; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Networks of neurons within the spinal cord that are involved in producing movements of the limbs normally receive descending commands from the brain as well as signals from receptors located in joints, muscles, and skin.  Spinal neurons must integrate and process this information on a continuous basis to smoothly control movement.  After spinal cord injury, inputs from the brain are lost or disrupted and networks of neurons within the spinal cord must learn to work without them and with greater reliance on signals from the periphery.  The loss of descending control often dramatically impairs the ability to walk and produces undesirable changes in function that can lead to abnormal motor behaviours, such as spasticity.  This is because the processing of sensory inputs from the periphery by spinal neurons is modified.  A major obstacle in repairing spinal cord injuries is our poor understanding of the regulation of spinal neurons that generate motor behaviours, both before and after damage.  My research aims to understand how sensory inputs from the skin regulate networks of neurons within the spinal cord that generate simple (e.g. reflexes) and more complex (e.g. locomotion) motor behaviours.  Encouraging recent results indicate that mechanically stimulating the skin overlying the back can reduce spasticity by interacting with spinal networks that produce rhythmic bursting.  This is of obvious clinical interest because it is a non-invasive and non-pharmacological approach that could alleviate symptoms of spasticity while promoting functional recovery.  My research will provide a better understanding of the control of spinal networks in a freely behaving animal model of spinal cord injury.  I expect that results will translate into clinical solutions that improve the lives of spinal cord-injured humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: The critical role of human metapneumovirus fusion protein in the pathogenesis, treatment and prevention of childhood viral infections
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUVANTS; ANIMAL MODELS; FUSION INHIBITORS; FUSION PROTEIN; HUMAN METAPNEUMOVIRUS; IMMUNIZATION; PATHOGENESIS; REVERSE GENETICS; TREATMENT; VACCINES
Abstract-Résumé: Human metapneumovirus is a newly-described respiratory virus that has been associated with bronchiolitis, pneumonia and asthma exacerbations especially in young children. It is an important pathogen that has been consistently reported as the second or third cause of hospitalization for respiratory tract infections in children less than 3 years of age.  In the next 5 years, we plan to study in more details the pathogenesis (mechanism of disease) of this new viral pathogen in cell culture systems and in a relevant mouse model of pneumonia by focusing mainly on the role of the fusion protein in viral entry into the cells. In particular, we seek to determine whether more fusogenic viruses producing syncytia (large mutinucleated cells) obtained from patients' samples or generated in the laboratory will be more virulent and thus will result in increased mortality in mice. We finally propose to develop and evaluate new antiviral agents (mainly fusion inhibitors) and vaccine candidates (intra muscular and intra-nasal subunit and live-attenuated vaccines) in two animal models (mice and cotton rats).   These studies are particularly relevant since there are no approved therapeutic or prophylactic modalities against such viral infection at the present time. At term, our work should lead to a better understanding of human metapneumovirus mutations associated with severe infections and to the development of innovative strategies to treat or prevent respiratory diseases caused by this important pediatric pathogen.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phase II: Clinical Decision Rule for High Risk TIA Patients in the ED
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL DECISION RULE; EMERGENCY MEDICINE; STROKE; TRANSIENT ISCHEMIC ATTACK
Abstract-Résumé: This study will validate a decision rule (or guideline) for physicians to use to determine which patients with transient ischemic attack, (TIA or mini-stroke) seen in emergency departments (ED), are at high risk of a stroke within the next 7 days. During a TIA, an individual experiences a sudden loss of neurological function with complete resolution over minutes to hours. TIAs are common; 20,000 patients are diagnosed with TIA in Canadian EDs annually. Most patients do well following a TIA; however, TIAs precede up to 20% of strokes. With a stroke, patients also suffer from a sudden loss of neurological function; however the neurological deficit lasts for more than 24 hours and may be permanent. Stroke is the leading cause of adult disability and the 3rd leading cause of death in Canada. Many strokes can be prevented if the cause of the TIA is identified. Defining the cause requires evaluation by a stroke specialist and a series of investigations. Unfortunately, with limited resources available, most centres do not have specialists assess all patients, nor do they perform all tests while patients are in the ED (i.e. CT scan, ultrasound of heart and neck arteries, electrocardiogram (ECG)). Knowing who is likely to have a stroke is critical in deciding the priority of testing. Our research team has developed the Canadian TIA Score, to determine the risk of an impending stroke. This score identifies patients at minimal, low, high and critical risk of a stroke within 7 days. This study will test the Canadian TIA Score in a new set of TIA patients to ensure it is safe and reliable. It is anticipated that minimal risk patients will follow-up with their family physician, low risk patients will see a specialist within one week, high risk patients will undergo testing in the ED with prompt follow-up and critical risk patients will see a specialist in the ED. We believe that the Canadian TIA Score will improve patient outcomes through the efficient use of existing resources.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of motor neuron identity and circuit development
Keywords-MotsClés: HINDBRAIN; MOTOR NEURON CIRCUIT; MOTOR NEURON DEVELOPMENT; MOTOR NEURON DISEASE; MUSCLE CONTROL; REGENERATION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that 2 out of 100,000 people will be diagnosed each year with the degenerative motor neuron disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Patients suffering from ALS face a severely impaired quality of life and a rapid degeneration causing death. An important part of ALS research involves investigations into why motor neurons are selectively lost in this disease, and how they might be replaced in order to restore the functions of sufferers. In this regard, understanding how motor neurons are generated and become part of neural circuits controlling motor functions is of utmost importance for the development of successful strategies of neuron replacement therapy for ALS and other motor neuron diseases. The present application seeks to characterize the mechanisms that govern the development and connectivity of selected motor neurons known to be vulnerable to degeneration in ALS. More specifically, it is proposed to investigate how motor neurons that control respiration, swallowing and mastication acquire their specific cellular properties and become connected to their target muscles. The results of the proposed investigations will provide new insight into how to promote the regeneration of particular types of motor neurons with defined characteristics. Restoring muscle functions through the production of new motor neurons from either endogenous or transplanted stem/progenitor cells represents one of the highest priorities in the treatment of many neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Post-transcriptional Regulation of Utrophin in Skeletal Muscle: Implications for New Therapeutic Strategies for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; DYSTROPHIN; MRNA STABILITY; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; SKELETAL MUSCLE; THERAPY; TRANSLATION; UTROPHIN
Abstract-Résumé: One possible approach to counteract the effects of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) consists in up-regulating the levels of a protein normally expressed in dystrophic muscle which could then functionally compensate for the lack of dystrophin. An ideal candidate for such a role is utrophin. Therefore, it becomes essential to understand the mechanisms regulating expression of utrophin in skeletal muscle to identify cellular targets that could ultimately be manipulated pharmacologically in order to increase expression of utrophin in muscle of DMD patients.

ClasseRechercheFR: TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION; AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE
TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation and treatment of traumatic axonal dysfunction after spinal cord injury
Keywords-MotsClés: CERVICAL SPINAL CORD INJURY; IMAGING; NEURAL PRECURSOR CELLS; REMYELINATION; SELF-ASSEMBLING NANOFIBRILS; STEM CELLS; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is debilitating and despite great efforts, there are currently few treatment options to improve recovery. Following SCI, recovery is limited due to scarring, inflammation and loss of myelin (surrounds and insulates nerve cells). Previous research conducted by our team has shown that transplanting stem cells can help recovery after SCI; however, how these cells work is not fully understood. We propose to build on this work by investigating strategies to increase the effectiveness of stem cell transplantation and examine how stem cells improve recovery.  Our first project will examine the effectiveness of stem cells in cervical (neck) SCI. We will utilize stem cells taken from the brain, or made by modifying ordinary skin cells into what are known as induced pluripotent stem cells. We will assess the outcome of implanting these cells by measuring behavioural improvement and how well the nerve tissue can send and receive signals from the limbs. Our second project will look at whether stem cells can produce improvements when they are made incapable, by genetic modification, of reproducing the myelin. This will directly address how important remyelination is when repairing SCI. Our third project will focus on determining if growth and regeneration of the electrical connections in the spinal cord has also been induced by the implantation of stem cells. This aim will determine which type of neurons are connected, and which contribute to recovery after SCI. Our final project will examine two methods to create a more supportive environment for the integration and efficacy of implanted stem cells. The first method will be injection of self-assembling peptides and the second a scar-buster called chondroitinase ABC.  The goal of this proposal is to help uncover the mechanisms underlying stem cell therapy. This could lead to improvements that can be translated to the clinic, bringing stem cell therapies closer to being used in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel regulatory features of eukaryotic ribosomal proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: CULTURE HUMAN CELLS; EXTRA-RIBOSOMAL FUNCTIONS; FISSION YEAST; GENE REGULATION; GENOMICS; NUCLEAR RNA SURVEILLANCE; PROTEOMICS; RIBOSOMAL PROTEINS; SPLICING; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Ribosomal proteins (RPs) are abundant RNA-binding proteins that normally function in the folding of ribosomal RNA molecules to allow the formation of the ribosome, the molecular machine responsible for protein synthesis. Surprisingly, however, mutations in RP genes can perturb specific cellular processes, which is not expected if RPs function exclusively in the universal process of making ribosomes. Consistent with the view that RP may have specialized cellular roles, mutations in RP genes are the underlying genetic defects of a collection of human disorders known as ribosomopathies, which have distinct clinical phenotypes. The molecular basis whereby mutations in RP genes cause specific clinical syndromes remains unclear, however. We have recently discovered new auxiliary functions of RPs in yeast and human cells. A major goal of the present application is to the characterize mechanisms by which RPs play such regulatory roles as well as identify additional RP specialization events. Elucidation of molecular mechanisms whereby selective abnormalities in RPs cause specific biological defects and/or phenotypes will hopefully lead to novel therapeutic strategies for these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions between glucagon-like peptide-2 and intestinal insulin-like growth factor-1 signalling in the regulation of intestinal growth and function
Keywords-MotsClés: ERBB; GLUCAGON-LIKE PEPTIDE-2; GROWTH; INSULIN-LIKE GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; INSULIN-LIKE GROWTH FACTOR-1; INTESTINAL BARRIER FUNCTION; INTESTINAL STEM CELLS; INTESTINE; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Disorders of the intestinal tract, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and, to a lesser extent, short bowel syndrome (SBS), are a significant cause of morbidity in Canada, with Canadians having the highest incidence of IBD in the world. Current treatment options for these patients are limited. However, the exciting recent development of the hormone glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2), which both increases the size of the intestine and improves the ability of the intestine to prevent bacteria from reaching the blood stream, has resulted in successful phase 3 clinical trials for SBS and phase 2 trials for IBD. Furthermore, a long-acting GLP-2 analogue (Gattex) is pending FDA approval for use in patients with SBS.  Despite the likelihood that GLP-2 will soon be in use as a novel therapeutic approach, its mechanism of action is not well understood. We have recently shown that GLP-2 action on the intestine requires a mediator, specifically another growth factor named insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), as well as the protein/receptor that carries out the actions of IGF-1 in the intestinal cells. We will continue these studies to examine the intracellular signals that link GLP-2 to intestinal growth and barrier function, as well as to identify the specific stem cells in the intestine that multiply in response to GLP-2, thereby increasing intestinal growth. The results of these studies will enhance our understanding of the pathways by which GLP-2 exerts beneficial effects on the intestine, and may lead to better therapeutic approaches to treat patients with intestinal disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cell Linage & Brain Development
Keywords-MotsClés: ASYMMETRIC DIVISION; DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS OF THE NERVOUS SYSTEM; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; NEURAL STEM CELLS; REGIONALIZATION OF THE NERVOUS SYSTEM; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: In many neurological and psychiatric disorder it is not clear which cell type is primarily affected. The present proposal attempts to define the neural stem cell lineage - the cellular lineage steps between the pluripotent cell of the blastocyst and mature neurons and glial cells. More specifically, we will investigate the mechanisms leading from the first embryonic neural cell (the primitive neural stem cell) to the definitive neural stem cells that are found later in embryogenesis and in the adult brain, thus making the identification of cell types affected in neurological and psychiatric disorders easier. Furthermore, we propose to study a rare population of quiescent primitive neural stem cells that persist into the adult brain, and appear to have the ability to reconstitute the definitive neural stem cell pool after the definitive pool has been removed. In addition, new signalling mechanisms enriched on the cell surfaces of primitive versus definitive neural stem cells will be tested for their abilities to specifically activate one of these two neural stem cell types, with potential clinical therapeutic implications. Finally, we will ask if damaged proteins and chromosomes containing older chromatids are selectively sorted to one of the two progeny of asymmetrically dividing stem cells. Moreover, in live video imaging and lineage reconstruction of single primitive or definitive neural stem cell clones will reveal if asymmetric segregation of these determinants affects the fates of the cells in these lineages.

TitreApplicationTitle: Build Better Bones with Exercise (B3E)
Keywords-MotsClés: EXERCISE; FALLS; FRACTURE; OSTEOPOROSIS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Exercise is often advised for individuals with osteoporosis. Research suggests that exercise can prevent falls, and may prevent bone loss. However, it is possible that exercise might increase the risk of fractures, particularly in high-risk individuals. Fractures and injuries directly attributable to exercise in hip and vertebral fracture patients have been reported in several studies. There is limited research available from which to develop guidelines for safe and effective exercise prescription among individuals with hip or vertebral fractures. When someone has a heart attack they receive exercise rehabilitation funded by the health care system, but if they break a bone in their spine due to osteoporosis they are sent home with pain medication that may increase their risk for falls. To be able to advocate for individualized exercise-related services for individuals with vertebral fractures we need research demonstrating that it is effective and feasible to implement in existing health care systems. The long-term goal of our research team is to conduct a large multicentre study to evaluate whether tailored home exercise can prevent fractures in high-risk individuals. The current proposal will address the feasibility of such a trial, but will also evaluate the effect of exercise on quality of life, posture and many other outcomes important to individuals with vertebral fractures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Concurrent gene silencing of multiple TLR signaling patheays using targeted nanoparticles for DC-mediated immune tolerance in heart transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: DENDRITIC CELLS; GRAFT REJECTION; HEART TRANSPLANTAION; IMMUNE TOLERANCE; RNAI/SIRNA; TLR
Abstract-Résumé: Heart transplantation is currently the only possible procedure that is performed for the prevention of an end-stage heart failure. Implanted grafts, however, are identified as foreign invaders and are exclusively attacked by our  immune systems, resulting in transplant heart rejection .  While rejection as can be prevented by the use of immunosuppressive drugs, these drugs possess many potential adverse effects and also reduce one's ability to fight against various infections and cancer, putting transplant patients at increased risk for both of these.  Moreover, these anti-rejection drug are toxic, expensive and need to be taken life time for the heart transplant patients. Thus, it is crucial to develop a new anti-rejection treatment without need of continuous use of immunosuppressive drugs. The objective of this proposed research is to develop a new method to stop an immune response so that the transplanted heart graft will not be rejected. In this proposed study, we will use an advanced blocking method called siRNA  to block the detector molecules. siRNA is 1000 times more powerful than any other methods that are being used in clinics and  laboratories. First, we will create different siRNA that can specifically inhibit TLR genes. Next, we will test the efficacy of preventing graft rejection after blocking the detector TLR molecules. The recipients will be treated with siRNA following a heart transplantation. Finally, we will investigate the mechanism underlining siRNA-based anti-rejection in heart transplantation. The success of this study will lead to a new anti-rejection treatment, which does not require adhering to toxic and expensive immunosuppressive drugs on a daily basis. The patients will no long suffer adverse effects of the drugs and will not live under possible occurrences of infections and cancers. Therefore, this new anti-rejection treatment will significantly improve the patient's quality of life after heart transplantation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular regulation of cigarette smoke-induced pulmonary disease by the aryl hydrocarbon receptor
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; ARYL HYDROCARBON RECEPTOR; CELL CULTURE; CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; CIGARETTE SMOKE; FIBROBLAST; INFLAMMATION; MICRORNA (MIRNA); OXIDATIVE STRESS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) refers to two diseases- emphysema and chronic bronchitis- that restricts normal breathing. COPD is the forth leading cause of death in the Canada, and although current therapies can slow disease progression, COPD is incurable. Cigarette smoking is the most important risk factor for COPD, a disease associated with chronic inflammation and irreversible loss of the air sacs where oxygen is exchanged. Lung cells such as fibroblasts and epithelial cells contribute to inflammation, and their death may account for loss of air sacs in emphysema. Our studies are aimed at understanding how lung cells stop inflammation and survive repeated exposure to cigarette smoke. Using our cell-based (lung fibroblasts, epithelial cells) and preclinical mouse model of cigarette smoke exposure, we will assess the therapeutic potential of a cellular protein called the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) in reducing inflammation (cytokine, chemokines, lipid mediators) and a cell death process called apoptosis. Using techniques like western blot, histological staining and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), we will also determine in lung samples obtained from Canadians with COPD, the expression of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor. Even though quitting smoking reduces the likelihood of developing COPD, it does not warrant that chronic inflammation and damage associated with long-term tobacco use will not progress to lung disease. The research conducted here has the potential to lead to new approaches that would block some of the untoward health consequences of tobacco smoke. These might include increasing AhR expression or activity in an individual with COPD to prevent additional lung destruction and improve airflow by attenuating inflammation. Given that nearly half of the Canadian population is composed of current and former smokers, the inherent benefits in terms of new and more selective therapies to treat tobacco smoke-associated lung disease is enormous.

TitreApplicationTitle: Augmin-mediated regulation of mitotic spindle assembly and architecture.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL CYCLE; CENTROSOME; CYTOSKELETON; GENOME STABILITY; MICROSCOPY; MICROTUBULES; MITOSIS; MITOTIC SPINDLE; RNA INTERFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: The mitotic spindle is an essential cellular structure that physically carries out the task of accurately transmitting your genetic material (chromosomes) to progeny cells as they grow and divide. Without a properly functioning mitotic spindle, chromosomes would not segregate accurately to each daughter cells leading to a condition called aneuploidy that can causes devastating diseases like cancer and Down syndrome. We recently identified a new complex composed of eight proteins that plays a very important role in specifying robust assembly of the mitotic spindle. This protein complex called Augmin is conserved in a plethora of different organisms (from flies to humans) suggesting that its function has been largely maintained during evolution. The main objective of this proposal is to better understand the biochemical composition and spatiotemporal regulation of Augmin as well as to precisely understand its specific role in mitotic spindle assembly. An important aspect of the work proposed here is to understand how the Augmin complex is regulated during the cell cycle and how it functionally interacts with other proteins required for mitotic spindle assembly.  Overall this work will lead to a better understanding of mitotic spindle assembly in general and a better comprehension of how defects in its activity can lead to cancer formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of ischemia-induced postnatal neovascularization by clinical phenotype and oxidative stress: Role of micro RNAs
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; ENDOTHELIAL PROGENITOR CELLS; MICRO RNA; NEOVASCULARIZATION; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Classical cardiovascular risk factors such as hypercholesterolemia and cigarette smoking are associated with an impairment of neovascularization, the protective growth of new vessels in response to ischemia. However, the precise mechanisms that are involved in that physiopathology remain to be determined. Micro RNAs (miRs) are small noncoding RNAs that are emerging as key regulators of several physiological and pathophysiological processes, including neovascularization. We propose that cardiovascular risk factors involving excessive oxidative stress levels lead to dysregulation in the pattern of expression of miRs. Using a combination of in vitro and in vivo models, our study will identify important novel mechanisms that are involved in the modulation of ischemia-induced neovascularization in pathological conditions. Micro RNAs could eventually represent novel therapeutic targets to improve neovascularisation and restore tissue function in ischemic cardiovascular diseases.

Keywords-MotsClés: AWARENESS; BELIEFS; CAPACITY; INTERVIEW; KNOWLEDGE; ORGANIZATION; PARTICIPACTION; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SURVEY
Abstract-Résumé: In 2007, ParticipACTION was relaunched in Canada with the goal of inspiring and supporting active living and sport participation for Canadians.  At this time, baseline data was collected at a) the individual level (in terms of awareness of ParticipACTION, attitudes toward physical activity, and physical activity behaviour) and b)  the organizational level (in terms of organizational capacity, readiness and advocacy regarding physical activity). The purpose of the proposed research programme is to collect follow-up data five years after the relaunch to provide evidence of the short-term impact of ParticipACTION at these individual and organizational levels.  This research will be invaluable in assessing the impact of ParticipACTION on the Canadian physical activity landscape. Most importantly, results from this research programme are essential for informing future planning and promotion for a healthy, active Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: MRI characterization of neurovascular function in carotid artery disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; BRAIN PHYSIOLOGY; CAROTID ARTERY DISEASE; COGNITIVE FUNCTION; FUNCTIONAL MRI; HYPERCAPNIA; HYPEROXIA; OXIDATIVE METABOLISM; OXIDATIVE STRESS; RESTING STATE CONNECTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Atherosclerosis, commonly known as "hardening of the arteries", can lead to a narrowing and partial blockage of the carotid arteries, which are the main blood vessels carrying oxygenated blood to the brain.  Such a blockage may reduce blood flow in the brain (affecting its supply of oxygen), and the underlying atherosclerosis may also impair the function of smaller blood vessels within the brain.  Even if the individual does not suffer a stroke, both of these effects may interfere with the ability of brain cells to function properly, resulting in subtle reductions in an individual's performance on certain mental tasks.  The aim of this study is to use new magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) methods to perform detailed measurements of how oxygen is delivered and consumed in the brains of people  with narrowing of the carotid arteries caused by atherosclerosis.  The information gathered will include measures of the brain's ability to increase blood flow and oxygen utilization when needed, and tests of a patient's speed and accuracy when carrying out tasks that are believed to be sensitive to reductions in oxygen availability.  The knowledge gained from this study will aid in the preservation and recovery of brain function in individuals suffering from diseases of the heart and blood vessels.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physiology and Biochemistry of small regulatory RNAs
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC REGULATION; MRNA DEGRADATION; RIBONUCLEASE; RIBOSWITCH; RNA CHAPERONE; SMALL REGULATORY RNA; TRANSCRIPTION; TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Bacteria are organisms that can survive almost everywhere, from below 0'C in cold polar seas, to boiling hot springs. Not only bacteria can survive at excessive temperatures but also in extreme acidity, salt concentration, and starvation. Unfortunately, this enormous adaptation capacity also makes them able to resist to antibiotic treatments. To live in such extreme conditions, Bacteria use many strategies that help them adapt and continue to growth. Among the different strategies developed by bacteria to adapt to severe conditions is the use of small molecules called small regulatory RNAs. One of these small molecules, called RyhB, is found in the bacterium Escherichia coli that live in the gut of mammals, including human. The small regulatory RNA RyhB has been demonstrated to modify the composition of the bacterial cell during iron starvation. By doing this, we think the small molecule RyhB assists the cell to adapt against the lack of Iron. This metal is an essential nutrient for most organisms because it is central in the energy metabolism. Unfortunately, iron is often scarce in environment. This scarcity of iron can lead to diseases and stimulate bacterial infection. Our goal is to understand the mechanism of small regulatory RNAs by studying RyhB and various other small RNAs. We think that the study of the small RNAs will eventually help us understand the development of microbial disease and improve antibacterial therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging brain connectivity in temporal lobe epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN CONNECTIVITY; BRAIN NETWORKS; EPILEPSY; EPILEPSY SURGERY; GRAPH-THEORETICAL MODELING; HIPPOCAMPUS; LIMBIC SYSTEM; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; QUANTITATIVE MRI; TEMPORAL LOBE EPILEPSY
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy affects about 1% of the general population. In up to 30% of patients, seizures cannot be controlled despite the best possible medication. The most common form of drug-resistant seizures is a focal type of epilepsy with seizures originating from a region of the brain called the temporal lobe. A lesion in the temporal lobe is often responsible for the seizures; its surgical removal can greatly attenuate or completely stop epileptic attacks. However, the post-surgical outcome remains poor in about 40% of patients.   Although in temporal lobe epilepsy, seizures originate within a confined region of the brain, increasing evidence indicates that the brain is abnormally organized in several interconnected regions distant from the temporal lobes.   The aim of this project is to understand how various brain regions interact with each other in epilepsy. We will use new state-of-the-art MRI analysis techniques that provide measures of structural and functional brain connectivity. These biomarkers will help clinicians to identify more accurately patients who will benefit from surgery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biochemical and genetic studies of the mechanism of poxvirus replication and recombination
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA REPAIR; EPIFLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; GENOME SEQUENCING; RECOMBINATION; REPLICATION; VACCINIA VIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: Poxviruses are large viruses that cause infections in many organisms. These viruses still cause some disease in humans, although the most famous poxvirus, variola virus, was eradicated 40 years ago using a worldwide campaign of vaccination using the related vaccinia virus. Although epidemic smallpox is gone, and the variola virus stocks are now stored under armed guard, it would be possible to remake ("reactivate") live variola virus using a combination of old genetic methods and new DNA synthesis technologies. The vaccinia virus that was in the smallpox vaccine also appears to have gone wild again, back into buffalo and cattle in India and South America, and may be evolving into a new human pathogen. Thus while smallpox has been eradicated, poxviruses continue to be a threat to human health. In fact, vaccines and drugs continue to be developed and stockpiled, to guard against the reappearance of smallpox or a related disease.  My research concerns itself with trying to understand how poxvirus DNA is copied, what virus and cell proteins catalyze these reactions, and how this can lead to the production of recombinant viruses. These replication reactions are of great interest because the majority of antiviral drugs inhibit the virus replication machinery, and our past work with some of these compounds has helped others develop new smallpox drugs. Recombinant viruses are produced when two different viruses infect the same cell, and they are of interest because the resulting progeny contain a mix of both parent virus DNAs and can sometimes exhibit new and dangerous properties. A lot of recombination is also seen in poxvirus reactivation reactions of the kind that could be used to revive smallpox. By studying vaccinia virus recombination, our work will provide insights into what role recombination might play in the evolution of existing and new poxviruses and what biosecurity risks might be posed by poxvirus reactivation technologies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the Relationship between White Matter Integrity and the Speed of Neuronal Processing in Children with Brain Tumours
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOUR; COGNITION; DEVELOPMENT; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHY; PAEDIATRICS; RADIATION; SYNTHETIC APERTURE MAGNETOMETRY; VISUMOTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumours are the leading cause of death and disability from childhood disease in developed countries. With treatment advances over the last 25 years, survival rates have improved dramatically. However, survival is often achieved at considerable cost, particularly for children treated with cranial radiation. Cranial radiation is the only curative treatment for most malignant tumours and is highly correlated with cognitive morbidity, including lowered intelligence and poor school achievement. In this proposal we will target the biological origins of the cognitive morbidity following cranial radiation for paediatric brain tumours. Cranial radiation damages the fatty tissues (white matter) that surround brain cells. This white matter damage is likely a major cause of long-term learning problems in children who survive brain tumours. It is not yet known how damage to white matter has an impact on the brain function that underlies thinking. To answer this question, we will investigate the relationship between white matter and the characteristics of brain activation in children treated for brain tumours. Using neuroimaging we will measure white matter and brain activation to a visual cue and during a motor response in patients treated with cranial radiation for brain tumours. Pilot work in our lab has shown that children treated with cranial radiation for brain tumours exhibit slower responses in the visual and motor regions of their brain and brain patterns that are characteristic of increased effort.  In our proposed research we will further this work as well as test whether white matter damage influences this disorganized brain functioning in patients treated for brain tumours. Through this work we may be able to identify brain tumour patients who are most at-risk for long-term learning problems and develop interventions to help reduce the lifelong impairments they experience.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel approaches to modulate key targets in the pathogenesis of Huntington Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; EXCITOTOXICITY; GENE SILENCING; HUNTINGTON DISEASE; PROTEOLYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington disease (HD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with no way to alter the course of the illness. The underlying genetic defect is a trinucleotide expansion in the huntingtin (htt) gene. A promising therapeutic approach for HD is to selectively prevent the expression of mutant htt. We will use antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) to test this approach in mouse models, targeting single nucleotide polymorphisms that are only present on the mutant and not the wild-type htt gene. Additionally, cleavage of mutant htt by caspase-6, phosphorylation and excitotoxicity are implicated as crucial factors in the pathogenesis of HD. In order to further validate caspase-6 as a therapeutic target, we will ablate caspase-6 expression and test the impact on the phenotype in an HD mouse model. Methods to increase phosphorylation will also be assessed as to their impact on phenotypic features of HD. We will furthermore investigate factors that lead to the activation of caspase-6 and thus represent additional targets for therapy development. In the excitotoxic pathway, we have identified the aberrant localization of NR2B receptors as a pathogenic mechanism, and we will modulate this mislocalization through genetic and therapeutic trials in an HD mouse model. Additionally, we will test compounds that modulate the signalling pathway downstream of NR2B receptors to ameliorate excitotoxicity. The basis of this proposal is to validate novel therapeutic approaches for the treatment of HD in vivo. The end result is to provide essential information for therapeutic strategies and evaluate compounds which prevent and/or ameliorate the disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease: Role of Intestinal Microbiota and n-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid Supplementation
Keywords-MotsClés: BIFIDOBACTERIA; ENDOTOXIN; FISH-OIL; INFLAMMATION; INTESTINAL MICROBIOTA; NON-ALCOHOLIC FATTY LIVER DISEASE; NUTRITION; POLYUNSATURATED FATTY ACIDS; SHORT-CHAIN FATTY ACIDS
Abstract-Résumé: About 20-30% of Canadians have non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which is a fat buildup in the liver with or without inflammation. The disease can damage the liver and sometimes requires liver transplantation.  Our team has received a grant from the Canadian Institute of Health Reseaearch (CIHR) to examine the role of diet, especially antioxidant vitamins and fat, in fatty liver disease. We also give fish oil to patients with fatty liver to see if this is beneficial for their liver. This project is almost completed. In addition, we have collected stool from our patients, as the latest research shows that the kind of bacteria in the gut could also influence the course of fatty liver disease. We are now seeking funding to characterize the bacteria in the stool and to measure bacterial products in stool and blood of patients with fatty liver compared to healthy controls. This study is new and important, as it could lead to new treatments for patients with fatty liver disease. If the gut bacteria are different in patients with fatty liver, we might in the future try to treat fatty liver with beneficial bacteria (probiotics) or carbohydrates that promote the growth of these "good" bacteria (prebiotics). Nobody has ever tested, whether fish oil could change human gut bacteria. Therefore we would also like to measure gut bacteria before and after 1 year treatment with fish oil in patients with fatty liver.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of damage and potential treatments for antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA-SYNUCLEIN; ANIMAL MODELS; ANTIPSYCHOTIC DRUGS; DOPAMINE; GSK; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; NEUROINFLAMMATION; PARKINSONISM; TAU; WESTERN BLOTTING
Abstract-Résumé: Antipsychotic drugs are commonly used to treat schizophrenia and other psychotic illnesses. While these drugs are effective therapeutically, they have detrimental side effects as well. One of the more common and debilitating side effects is parkinsonism, which is comprised of a number of movement and muscle control problems reminiscent of those experienced in Parkinson's disease. Our lab has demonstrated that antipsychotic drugs have an unintended effect in which pre-synaptic dopamine-producing neurons are damaged over time. It is likely that this damage is responsible for the parkinsonian symptoms observed in clinical populations. Our lab has further demonstrated that antipsychotic-induced damage to dopaminergic neurons is dependent upon dopamine reuptake into the cells, suggesting that increased dopamine concentrations within the neurons may be responsible. We propose a model whereby antipsychotic drugs damage dopaminergic neurons by increasing dopamine synthesis, thereby increasing cytoplasmic dopamine concentrations. This in turn would lead to oxidative stress, the aggregation of damaging alpha-synuclein and tau proteins, and an inflammatory immune response raised against dopamine-producing neurons. Rats will be treated with antipsychotic drugs and brain slices will be stained for various proteins of interest. This will enable us to determine how various antipsychotics affect the aggregation of proteins in dopaminergic neurons and promote the activation of inflammatory cells. Furthermore, it will allow us to assess the ability of potential treatments to reverse these effects. For example, alpha lipoic acid will be used to reduce oxidative stress, and lithium will be used to reduce inflammation and tau phosphorylation. Through the proposed research, we hope to shed light on the mechanisms underlying antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism and take initial steps towards finding effective treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Single cell analysis of telomerase activity and regulation
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; LIVE CELL IMAGING; RNA TRAFFICKING; TELOMERASE; TELOMERES; TERRA; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: In order to properly grow and divide, normal cells must maintain the integrity of their genome. Telomeres cap the ends of chromosomes and are essential to maintain their stability. Telomere shortening leads to genomic instability and favors the rise of cancers.  Our laboratory is using the budding yeast as a model organism to further understand how cells regulate their telomerase in order to maintain the telomeres at the extremities of their chromosomes. Most of our knowledge on telomerase relies on the detection of telomerase activity in large populations of cells. However, little is known about the behavior of telomerase in single cells, as it acts on a single telomere. For this purpose, we recently developed an assay to study telomerase molecules in single living cells. Using this approach, the factors involved in the accumulation of telomerase in the nucleus will be identified.  The events leading to the recruitment of telomerase at a single short telomere will be studied in real time, in single cells. Finally, we will explore how telomerase is regulated in a telomere-specific manner by focusing especially on telomeric repeat-containing RNA (TERRA). For now, due to its powerful genetics and cell biology tools, such study can only be performed in yeast. However, as in humans, disruption of telomerase trafficking in yeast is known to result in abnormal telomeres and in an increased instability of the genome. Identifying the pathways involved in the regulation of telomerase and telomeres will help to understand how tumors arise and develop into cancer, and also reveal new potential targets for cancer therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurosciences and the Afterlife of Death: Re-imagining Notions of Suicidal Risk
Keywords-MotsClés: KIN; MEDICAL ANTHROPOLOGY; MENTAL HEALTH; NARRATIVE ANALYSIS; NEUROSCIENCES; PSYCHIATRY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; RISK; SCIENCE STUDIES; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: Suicide has often been associated with particular subpopulations such as those people who are socially marginalized or, alternatively, who suffer from mental illness. Together, these explanations have created a perception of suicide as linked to both individual negative experiences as well as collective factors - often these levels of explanation are seen to interact, for instance, when collective stressful circumstances lead to individual emotional problems. New research emerging from the neurosciences is suggesting new ways in which these factors might interact while at the same time trying to identify who might ultimately attempt suicide either in response to adverse life experiences or psychiatric disorders. The neuroscience explanations suggest that adverse early childhood experiences and inherited traits might lead to higher suicide rates among a neurologically-specific portion of the population. In order to test this hypothesis, scientists are enrolling the family members of people who have committed suicide, referred to as "suicide completers", in studies to either assist in after-death psychological assessments of suicide completers or to participate in fMRI studies to determine whether living family members exhibits suicide risk factors presumed to be shared with their dead kin. This study will explore the ways in which participation in neuroscience research is changing perceptions of the dead (e.g. their reasons for committing suicide), perceptions of the suicidal risk among their living kin, the relatedness (interpersonal and biological) of kin to suicide completers and suicide risk in general. Further, we are interested in the ways in which new scientific explanations of suicide are being integrated into people's previous beliefs about suicidal behaviour and interacting with the means by which people make sense of suicide.

Keywords-MotsClés: GROWTH FACTOR; METASTASIS; PLANAR CELL POLARITY; PROTEOMICS; SYNTHETIC ANTIBODIES; WNT SIGNALLING
Abstract-Résumé: During development, Wnt proteins control cell fate determination, cell proliferation as well as directed cell movement. We have identified new proteins important for these processes during development and in cancer cells.  Using different animal models and cell biological assays we propose to characterize the function of these proteins.  This proposal will help continue understand the intracellular signalling pathways controlled by Wnt proteins and intend to test the efficiency of synthetic antibodies as potential treatment for metastatic breast cancer.

Abstract-Résumé: The Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES) is an independent, non-profit organization, whose core business is to conduct research that contributes to the effectiveness, quality, equity and efficiency of health care and health services in Ontario. January 2012 was the official launch of ICES's 6th program: ICES Kidney, Dialysis and Transplantation (ICES-KDT). There are 12 principal investigators and 40 additional researchers across five Universities in Ontario. New research in this theme is timely. Kidney disease is common (affecting an estimated two million Canadians), frequently co-existent with other important chronic diseases, and associated with adverse health and economic consequences (~$2 billion/yr spent on renal disease care). Many patients fail to receive optimal care. There is a shortage of organs for transplantation and in 2008, 215 Canadians died waiting for an organ transplant. ICES-KDT will focus its activities in four research themes: acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, kidney donation and renal replacement therapy. Over the next five years, 2012 - 2016, we will complete 15 new analyses, add to the ICES holdings, and train 40 new individuals in the analysis of Ontario healthcare databases (> 30 trainees and > 10 colleagues and junior Faculty).

TitreApplicationTitle: The mechanism of neurovascular remodelling after focal ischemia
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICAL MODELLING; BRAIN MICROCIRCULATION; FOCAL ISCHEMIA; FUNCTIONAL HYPERAEMIA; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; RODENT MODELS OF FOCAL ISCHEMIA
Abstract-Résumé: In the healthy brain, neurons and blood vessels work in concert so that blood flow increases when neurons become active. This neurovascular coupling is compromised in stroke, whereby a blockage of a major artery results in a sharp decline in blood flow, causing damage to the neurons, and inducing sudden paralysis, impaired speech, and/or loss of vision. If the blood clot is dissolved rapidly, the likelihood of a complete recovery is very good. However, due to the very narrow window (3-4.5 hours) for safe and effective treatment, only ~2% of patients receive these drugs; most suffer significant disabilities, and up to a third are institutionalized. Uncertainty surrounding the cellular changes that are needed for full recovery of brain function is a major factor preventing the development of more effective therapies to rehabilitate patients following stroke. It has become clear that recovery is strongly affected by changes that occur in the neurons and blood vessels in the peri-infarct zone, the impaired, but potentially salvageable brain region peripheral to the area directly affected by the loss of blood supply. The goal of the present proposal is to understand the changes in the neurovascular coupling in the peri-infarct zone in the weeks following stroke. This work will be conducted using advanced 3D imaging in live rats that have received stroke. The responses of neurons and blood vessels to sensory stimulation will be contrasted between untreated animals and those treated with specific drugs to restore healthy levels of neuronal activity and vessel tone, in the hope of reestablishing healthy neurovascular coupling. These experiments will interrogate the mechanisms by which changes in the neurons and blood vessels support rehabilitation and thereby guide the development of new treatments that may be applied in the chronic stage following stroke and that thus stand to benefit a vast majority of patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Efficacy of careful medication and tailored case management follow up treatment for children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHD; FOLLOW UP; OUTCOME; PSYCHOSOCIAL; PSYCHOSTIMULANTS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is one of the most prevalent psychiatric conditions affecting 5-10% of children and 4.4% of adults with a poor long term outcome.  In adolescence and adulthood, people with ADHD continue to suffer from disabling symptoms of the disorder.  Compared to people who do not have ADHD, they fail at school and drop out more often, have more employment problems, have more sexually transmitted diseases and unwanted pregnancies, more frequent and severe traffic violations and car accidents, more arrests, convictions and incarcerations, and suffer from more other co-occurring psychiatric disorders.  Such poor long term outcome is not due to lack of effective treatments, since research has reliably shown that medications are effective in relieving symptoms of ADHD and a combination of medications and psychosocial treatments produces improvements in various areas of functioning, including academic, social, and emotional.  However, once treatment is completed, and the patients are sent out to the community for follow up, the treatment gains gradually diminish and are completely lost after two years of follow up.   Community follow up has been documented to be poor by a number of studies.  Our guiding hypothesis is that the poor long term outcome in ADHD is, at least in part, due to the inadequacy of community follow up in maintaining treatment gains.  We aim to show that after 3 months of tailored medication and psychosocial treatment, 2 years of a medication monitoring and tailored case management follow up will be superior to standard community follow up in maintaining treatment gains.  Hopefully, such a finding will inform practice guidelines and thus improve long term outcome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating Accountability, Transparency and Governance in Brazil's Pharmaceutical System
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAZIL; GLOBAL HEALTH; GOVERNANCE; HEALTH EQUITY; PHARMACEUTICAL POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: Corruption in the pharmaceutical sector is an increasing problem because it prevents many patients from accessing medicines that they need.  When pharmaceutical drugs are of good quality and used properly by the patients, they offer an affordable solution to many health problems. For example, if essential drugs are provided to poor populations at reasonable prices, many of their diseases can be cured or prevented. This is particularly true in Latin America, which has a collection of very poor populations that suffer from a variety of diseases.  Good governance, accountability and transparency (GAT) are critical for the proper functioning of the pharmaceutical system. To study GAT, we will undertake a case study of Brazil. This project aims to identify laws, regulations and policies that are present in Brazil to improve access to essential medicines, to study how they have been implemented and to determine if they have helped promote good governance, accountability and transparency. The results from this study have the potential to lead to better health outcomes, particularly for the poor populations in Brazil, and more generally to contribute to improving access to medicines in other countries in Latin America.

TitreApplicationTitle: Coupling domains of the 5-HT1A receptor
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; CALCIUM; CAMP; DEPRESSION; G-PROTEIN; IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; PEPTIDOMIMETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Major depression is the second most debilitating disease in Western countries after heart disease.  Drugs used to treat depression target the serotonin system, but require weeks to be effective and are not always successful, often leading to suicide attempts.  The serotonin-1A (5-HT1A) receptor mediates antidepressant actions, but also inhibits serotonin activity.  Drugs that inhibit the 5-HT1A receptor on serotonin neurons potentiate antidepressant actions; however these compounds completely inhibit the receptor, leading to adverse events. We propose to elucidate 5-HT1A receptor structure in order to generate an entirely new type of blocker that is specific for the relevant receptor signal.  We have identified two key structural portions of the 5-HT1A receptor (the i2 and i3 loops) and mutated them.  Single mutations of these loops block selective signals of the receptor, rather than blocking all of its actions as with current drugs.  We will expand this characterization to determine which 5-HT1A mutants affect specific brain signals of the receptor. We will examine the ability of the wild-type or the 5-HT1A mutant receptors to "rescue" the abnormal anxiety behavior of mice lacking 5-HT1A receptors.  These studies will be the first to clarify which 5-HT1A receptor signals are important for behavior and should be targeted for antidepressant development.  If a 5-HT1A mutant is found that prevents inhibition of serotonin neurons but preserves the beneficial actions of the receptor, we will design compounds based on the structure of the 5-HT1A i2 and i3 loops of that mutant to enhance antidepressant activity.  Thus by targeting the 5-HT1A i2 and i3 loops, we hope to generate inhibitors that are specific for key inhibitory brain signals of the receptor.  If successful, selective compounds to inhibit discrete signals could serve as a prototype a wide variety of therapeutic drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functionalized nanoparticles applied to photoacoustic molecular imaging of atherosclerotic plaque.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARBON NANOTUBES; MOLECULAR PROBES; PHOTO-ACOUSTIC IMAGING; TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases are a major cause of death in industrialized nations. New methods to help diagnose, monitor and potentially find a cure are required to reduce their impact on society. Imaging science has a major role to play in all of these aspects as it can provide quantifiable data that can be used to diagnose and monitor disease but also contribute to the evaluation of new drugs. In recent years, a new biomedical imaging technique combining light pulses and ultrasound has emerged under the name of photoacoustic tomography. When compared to other imaging techniques, it can provide high resolution images combined with high sensitivity to contrast agents. This project will develop both contrast agents and this new imaging technique and evaluate its accuracy, sensitivity and quantification capabilities in the context of atherosclerosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of non-classical protein secretion pathways of importance in renal fibrosis triggered by the paracrine apoptotic program
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; AUTOPHAGY; CASPASES; CONNECTIVE TISSUE GROWTH FACTOR; FIBROSIS; NANOVESICLES; P53; RENAL FAILURE; TRANSPLANTATION; VASCULAR RAREFACTION
Abstract-Résumé: Injury to the vessels providing blood supply to the kidneys leads to abnormal renal healing, a leading cause of renal failure. We found that dying vascular cells release Connective Tissue Growth Factor (CTGF), a mediator implicated in abnormal healing. Fibroblasts, cells present within the kidney, also produce increased amounts of CTGF when stressed. Here we plan to characterize the genes and molecular pathways controlling the release of CTGF by dying vascular cells and stressed fibroblasts using cell and molecular biology strategies in association with evaluation of human kidney biopsy samples.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic signatures and functional phenotypes implicated in HIV-1 transmission and drug resistance
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV DRUG RESISTANCE; HIV PRIMARY INFECTION; HIV TRANSMISSION; PHYLOGENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Montreal provides a unique environment for a comprehensive study on HIV transmission dynamics.  The Male-Sex-Male (MSM) epidemic, including transmitted drug-resistant sub-epidemics, has continued to rise in the era of antiretroviral therapy. Ongoing funding by this CIHR has assisted in the creation of integrated viral sequence datasets from all genotyped persons in Quebec. A severe bottleneck in HIV transmission has created a selection pressure wherein forty viral variants account for half of new infections (n=530) in the province over the last decade. Characterization of the genetic signatures and biological features of these strains will be investigated. Genetic drift of these primary strains will be deduced under selective immune, host, and antiretroviral drug pressure. The information generated by this study can be applied towards the development of vaccine and antiretroviral strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a decision support tool in post-mastectomy breast reconstruction surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; BREAST RECONSTRUCTION SURGERY; DECISION MAKING; DECISION SUPPORT; DECISIONAL CONFLICT; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PATIENT SATISFACTION; PLASTIC AND RECONSTRUCTIVE SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Post mastectomy breast reconstruction surgery is known to be oncologically safe in addition to having a positive effect on the psychological well-being of women with breast cancer. Yet, many breast surgery patients do not elect to have post mastectomy breast reconstruction, and those that do attend a plastic surgery consultation often find that they are faced with difficult and complex decisions regarding surgical options and complications that they are not prepared to make. Currently, there is no clear framework to help women faced with mastectomy to understand the risks and benefits of available breast reconstruction treatment options in Canada. Previous research has demonstrated that decision aids are effective for individuals facing difficult health treatment and screening decisions. Effective care for post mastectomy breast reconstruction patients in Canada is critically underdeveloped; it is important that healthcare professionals and mastectomy patients understand the treatment options and their implications. We propose to develop a decision support tool in order to help post mastectomy breast cancer patients make well-informed decisions about their breast reconstruction options and reduce their uncertainty about treatment options. This project will be conducted in three phases: a) development of the support tool with input from clinical experts and women living with mastectomy, b) pilot testing of the usability of the tool, and c) formal preliminary evaluation of the effectiveness of the support tool to help women with mastectomy make informed decisions about breast reconstruction surgery treatment options.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurocognitive Intermediate Phenotypes in Borderline Personality Disorder: A Family Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER; FUNCTIONAL NEAR-INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY; INTERMEDIATE PHENOTYPES; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a serious form of mental illness associated with chronic suicidality, severe mood fluctuations, and dangerous impulsive behaviours. Efforts to understand the neurobiological causes of BPD have met with limited success. This is because BPD represents a heterogeneous clinical disorder comprised of multiple complex symptoms and traits which may be supported by distinct neurobiological systems. Identification of intermediate phenotypes, or biological liability markers, of BPD may help unravel the diverse causes of this illness. The goal of this research is to isolate the most promising intermediate phenotypes for BPD in patients and their first-degree relatives who are at increased genetic risk for the illness, and comparing them with individuals with no personal or family history of mental illness. Participants will complete cognitive tests (e.g., memory, concentration) and brain imaging procedures using functional near-infrared spectroscopy to probe areas of the frontal cortex responsible for impulse control. We anticipate that patients and their relatives will show deficits on cognitive testing and decreased activation of the frontal cortex on brain imaging, lending support to these measures as putative intermediate phenotypes for BPD. The results of this study have the potential to improve the future care of these patients in a number of ways. First, this work will help characterize neurobiological abnormalities in BPD patients and their relatives, paving the way for biological tests to identify individuals at risk for BPD and focus efforts at early intervention and prevention. Second, these results will aid in parsing the heterogeneous presentation of BPD, helping to direct treatments that target subsets of patients with specific biological vulnerabilities. Finally, the discovery of intermediate phenotypes for BPD will help construct the road-map for isolating which genes confer susceptibility to this devastating illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: You can't always get what you want: A self-determination based examination of the difference between implicit and explicit outcome expectations and their influence on exercise adherence.
Keywords-MotsClés: EXERCISE ADHERENCE; OUTCOME EXPECTATIONS; SELF-DETERMINATION; SELF-EFFICACY; SOCIAL-COGNITIVE THEORY
Abstract-Résumé: When people begin exercise they do so for a variety of reasons.  Some of the reasons they are willing to make public, some they are not.  We are interested in finding out if the motivational characteristics of the 'public' or 'explicit' expectations of exercise are different from the 'private' or 'implicit' expectations of exercise.  In fact, we specifically posit that the 'explicit' reasons will display more desireable motivational characteristics whereas the 'implicit' expectations will display more controlling characteristics that are likely to undermine exercise adherence. We further believe that the non-acheivement of the implicit outcomes will have a negative influence on exercise persistence. Finally, we plan to develop imagery based interventions that will enhance the motivational characteristics of all the outcome expectations and so improve exercise adherence by reducing the negative effects of not getting what we want.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying signalling pathways that regulate memory maintenance.
Keywords-MotsClés: MEMORY MAINTENANCE; PLASTICITY; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Many common neurological diseases are associated with memory loss. The characterization and identification of normal mechanisms that allow memories to persist has been a major goal of neuroscientists in order to target these therapeutically. Memories are believed to be stored by stable modifications in the connections between nerve cells. There are many drugs that can interfere with the formation of new memories. However, none of those drugs can modify memories once they have been created unless they are applied immediately after memory retrieval. A recent discovery has shown that a molecule called PKMzeta is crucial for maintaining long-term memories in several invertebrate and vertebrate species. If the activity of this molecule is blocked in specific brain regions, after the memory has been formed, these are erased, even when the inhibitor is given months after the initial learning. This finding indicates that memories persist because of ongoing processes in the brain. We have focus then in identifying these processes that allow memories to persist after they have been created. We demonstrated that PKMzeta is required to prevent the removal of a pool of molecules (receptors) at specific locations of the cell membrane where the neurons make contact. These receptors are responsible for the strength of the connections between neurons and without them memory cannot be expressed. The focus of this research proposal is first to identify the precise molecular pathways that control the stability of these receptors at the neuronal connections sites and therefore control the memory persistence. Secondly, we will attempt to find if these processes are modified in response to memory restore. We believe that the identification of the mechanisms that maintain memory and their dynamics will have very important implications for the treatments of memory related diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hyperpolarized Xenon-129 Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Radiation-Induced Lung Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION; GAS EXCHANGE; LUNG CANCER; LUNG INJURY; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; PERFUSION; RADIATION THERAPY; VENTILATION; XENON GAS
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is currently one of the largest contributors to long-term morbidity in Canada and will likely continue to be for the foreseeable future. Treatment of lung cancer by radiation is significantly limited by injury to normal lung tissue which can have long-term adverse effects manifesting throughout the subject's life, even well after remission. In this proposal, hyperpolarized xenon-129 anatomical and functional MR imaging techniques will be developed, optimized and tested in human populations undergoing thoracic irradiation. These approaches are expected to reveal regional markers of the time-course of lung injury associated with radiotherapy providing: (i) earlier detection of injury, (ii) fundamental insight into mechanisms of injury and (iii) improved therapies to reduce health-care burden. Furthermore, it is expected that this research will also have relevance to other lung diseases including lung inflammation, chronic obstructive lung disease, asthma and acute lung injury.
