TitreApplicationTitle: Sampling methods for health surveys in difficult settings: a simulation study
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOBAL HEALTH; STATISTICAL SIMULATIONS; SURVEY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: There is often a need for health surveys in Low Income Countries, war zones or areas suffering from disasters. The surveys may measure the health status of the population, such as the proportion of children who have been immunized for infectious diseases. Yet it can be difficult to conduct the surveys because often there is very limited information to allow a proper sample to be selected. Researchers have developed several ways around this problem, but none of these methods is ideal; they all have some flaws, so the final results may be at least somewhat incorrect or have a large margin of error. This project aims to find out which sampling method produces the best results in different situations.  It will do so by using a computer to create virtual populations. The criteria programmed into the computer will try to make the populations as realistic as possible, while varying characteristics such as the proportion of children immunized. The computer will take samples from the virtual populations using the different sampling methods. Many thousands of samples will be taken for each method, so that we can understand how well each method performs depending on the population characteristics.  The results will help governments and NGOs to get the best information possible when they direct resources to improving the health of particular populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of NOD-like receptors in lung immune response against respiratory virus infection
Keywords-MotsClés: BRONCHIOLITIS/PNEUMONIA; INFLUENZA VIRUS; LUNG INFECTION; LUNG INNATE IMMUNITY; NLRP3; NOD-LIKE RECEPTORS; NOD2
Abstract-Résumé: Lung infection by influenza virus is responsible for annual seasonal infection that affects several million people in the world, especially among the elderly and children. To date, vaccines and drugs are still insufficient to control respiratory infection caused by influenza virus. New approaches are thus urgently needed to treat and even to prevent such infections. In this regard, the recent discovery of natural detectors which recognize viral components and expressed in several cell types, including lung epithelial cells and lung infiltrating cells, may provide alternative strategy to develop new therapeutic approaches. We thus propose to evaluate the mechanism of action of muramyl dipeptide which was found to control influenza virus infection by activating the innate viral detector named NOD2. NOD2 is expressed by cells of lungs and by circulating blood cells which are also involved in viral clearance. Administration of such molecules alone or in combination with antiviral agents may be beneficial to rapidly suppress influenza virus infection and to restore normal lung functions.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; ETATS MORBIDES MAL DEFINIS
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional and molecular characterization of tubular lysosome biogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: DENDRITIC CELLS; GTPASES; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALING; LYSOSOMES; MACROPHAGES; MEMBRANE TRAFFICKING; MICROSCOPY; MOTOR PROTEINS; PHAGOSOMES; TUBULATION
Abstract-Résumé: We aim to better understand the regulation of the immune system, which may aid in the development of novel strategies to mitigate infectious and/or autoimmune conditions.  Macrophages and dendritic cells are white blood cells that search and engulf pathogens by a process called phagocytosis.  After phagocytosis, pathogens are sequestered in a new organelle called the phagosome.  While phagosomes are initially innocuous, they eventually fuse with lysosomes to become a phagolysosome, a highly acidic and degradative organelle.  As a result, pathogens are killed and digested.  Phagosome maturation also generates protein fragments (peptides) that are loaded onto the major histocompatibility complex-II (MHC-II).  The peptide-MHCII complex is then transported to the surface of macrophages and dendritic cells for antigen presentation, which helps activate the immune system to generate antibodies.   In resting macrophages and dendritic cells, lysosomes and the MHC-II compartment (MIIC), a lysosome-related organelle, are small and globular - however, upon exposure to bacterial compounds, lysosomes and the MIIC are converted into a tubular network, on which stunningly little is known.  Importantly, MIIC and lysosome tubules are implicated in antigen presentation, phagosome maturation and retention of pinocytic uptake.  This proposal describes pioneering research aimed at better understanding the function and biogenesis of tubular lysosomes and MIIC by: 1. Examining the molecular mechanisms responsible for lysosome tubulation in macrophages.   2. Dissecting the effect of tubulation on lysosome physiology. 3. Studying the molecular mechanisms of tubular MIIC formation and their role in MHC-II secretion and trafficking from phagosomes in dendritic cells. We expect this research to represent a major leap forward in the understanding of these poorly characterized organelles and that it may guide in the development of therapies against infectious and autoimmune conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intrapleural DNase and Tissue Plasminogen Activator in Pediatric Empyema (DTPA trial)
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD; DORNASE ALPHA; EMPYEMA; INFANT; LENGTH OF STAY; PLEURAL; PRESCHOOL; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TISSUE PLASMINOGEN ACTIVATOR
Abstract-Résumé: Bacterial pneumonia can be complicated by the development of excess fluid and pus (pleural empyema) around the lungs in children. The incidence of pleural empyema in children has increased significantly in the last 10 years.    Short term morbidity for this condition is substantial, but unlike in adults, the long term outcome of this condition for children in developed countries is favourable. Inserting a chest drain and then adding a medicine (tissue plasminogen activator -  tPA) to break down organized pus has been shown to be an effective therapy for reducing the duration of illness. However, this treatment is still suboptimal and prolonged hospitalization is common. Recent data from adults suggests that adding an additional medicine (DNase) to decrease the viscosity (thickness) of the fluid improves drainage and leads to better patient outcomes; however, there are no published studies on children.   This proposal is a multi-centre randomized controlled trial comparing the time to discharge from hospital after chest drain insertion in previously well children who present with pleural empyema, treated with intrapleural DNase and tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) by chest drain for three doses over 48 hours compared with three doses over 48 hours of tPA alone. Other outcomes related to effectiveness, safety and cost will be assessed as well.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathophyisological mechanisms of dystonia: insights from deep brain stimulation and brain plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; BRAIN PLASTICITY; DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION; DYSTONIA; HUMAN SUBJECTS; MOVEMENT DISORDERS; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISM; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Dystonia is a brain disorder associated with excessive contraction of muscles, leading to twisted positions of the arms and legs.  It causes severe disability in the affected patients. How abnormalities in the brain causes dystonia is not known.  A treatment that involve insertion of electrodes into the brain for electrical stimulation, know as deep brain stimulation (DBS), is an established treatment for patients with advanced dystonia. However, it has not been known how DBS works.  Brain plasticity refers to how the brain changes and adapts in situations such as learning and memory, and in response to injury.  Dystonia may be due to abnormal and excessive plasticity. The proposed research will study whether brain plasticity is abnormal in dystonia and whether DBS can correct the abnormal brain plasticity.  We will also investigate whether differences among individuals in a gene that encodes a protein in the brain known as "glial-derived neurotrophic factor" influences brain plasticity and the response to DBS in dystonia patients.  The results will improve our knowledge of how brain abnormalities lead to dystonia and provide better ways to predict the patients' response to DBS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protection and Regulation of Oral and Gastrointestinal Mucosal Epithelial Barriers by MAO B Inhibitors and Their Novel Polar Derivatives
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPHIREGULIN SHEDDING; ANIMAL MODELS; BARRIER; CELL CULTURE; DRUG REDEVELOPMENT; ELISA; GASTROINTESTINAL DISEASE; INFLAMMATION; MONOAMINE OXIDASE AND THEIR INHIBITORS; PERIODONTAL DISEASE PATHOGENESIS; TIGHT JUNCTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Oral and stomach lining cells provide an important function by protecting hosts from infection caused by bacteria or their toxic products.  Cells must join together to form a barrier that protects underlying tissues from this bacterial challenge.  Periodontal disease and gastrointestinal (GI) tract infections are associated in part with disruption of this natural barrier.  Previously we identified a class of enzymes that are increased in periodontal disease and, when inhibited by a family of existing drugs, the disease was diminished.  This grant provides preliminary evidence that these drugs improve the barrier and has identified a possible mechanism by which this occurs.  Specifically, we identified a cell surface-associated molecule that is released when cells are challenged by bacterial cellular factors and release of this molecule is associated with reduction of the barrier.  The class of drugs that reduces these effects is commercially available and is clinically used to treat patients with Parkinson's disease.  In our potential clinical application, we do not want drugs to be crossing to the brain if this is not required.  We will therefore redevelop the drug so that it is no longer able to do this but will still protect oral and gut barrier function.  Development of these modified drugs may prove to be a new and innovative approach to manage common oral and GI tract diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cdk5: Its Regulation and Function
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOSKELETON; DEVELOPMENT; DIFFERENTIATION; PHOSPHORYLATION/DEPHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN KINASES
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disorder, with over 18 million people worldwide afflicted by this disease.  Cognitive symptoms in AD correlate with loss of synapses that results from impaired synaptogenesis.  Cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5), which is abundant in the synapse and modulates synaptogenesis, is aberrantly upregulated in AD.  The notion is that Cdk5 deregulation results in synaptic and cognitive impairment in AD.  Cdk5 activation requires interaction with p35 or p39, but recently, we made the discovery that phospholipase D2 (PLD2) binds and activates Cdk5, and Cdk5-PLD2 interaction promotes synaptogenesis.  Interestingly, we observed increased Cdk5-PLD2 interaction in the 5XFAD AD mouse model, which exhibits increased Cdk5 activity, neuronal loss, and synaptic and cognitive failures. Thus, although Cdk5 activity is required for normal synapse dynamics, overactivation is detrimental and may contribute to neurodegeneration.  Our HYPOTHESIS is that a subset of Cdk5-mediated synaptogenesis is modulated by Cdk5-PLD2 through specific targets.  Two Cdk5 substrates that promote synaptogenesis are the calcium-calmodulin-dependent serine protein kinase (CASK) and PLD2.  We also found that beta-adducin, a protein kinase C delta substrate, is a Cdk5 downstream target.  These led us to a model in which Cdk5-PLD2 targets proteins that promote synaptogenesis. Our overall OBJECTIVE is to understand how Cdk5-PLD2 mediates synaptogenesis. Our SPECIFIC AIMS are to examine whether: (a) CASK and PLD2 are preferred Cdk5-PLD2 substrates, (b) Cdk5-PLD2 activity mediates changes in synaptic currents, and (c) Cdk5-PLD2 modulates synaptogenesis through CASK, PLD2 and the PKC delta-beta-adducin pathway, and investigate whether Cdk5-PLD2 contributes to neuronal loss in 5XFAD mice.  Understanding the mechanism by which Cdk5-PLD2 regulates synaptogenesis could provide new clues in the design of new therapies for impaired cognitive symptoms in AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of NK cells in innate defense against mucosal viral infections
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ANTIVIRAL IMMUNITY; HSV-2; INNATE IMMUNITY; NK CELLS; TYPE I INFS; VIRAL INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) is a virus and causes the most common sexually transmitted infection (STI) worldwide with over 1 billion infected individuals. In Canada and the US, nearly 55 million people carry HSV-2 and up to 4 million of them suffer from frequent recurrent outbreaks of genital herpes. In addition, genital herpes is a risk factor for other STIs, such as HIV-1. Currently there is no effective vaccine or treatment against HSV-2. A better understanding of the host defense against HSV-2 is required for an efficient control of this ubiquitous pathogen. Here we propose experiments to understand our innate defense against herpes at the genital tract.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of T cell immunity by the Inducible Costimulator (ICOS)
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY; CALCIUM SIGNALING; COLLAGEN INDUCED ARTHRITIS; COSTIMULATION; GRAFT VERSUS HOST DISEASE; HELPER T CELLS; IMMUNOLOGY; KNOCKOUT MICE; PHOSPHOINOSITIDE 3-KINASE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Our immune system is supposed to fight off dangerous pathogens such as viruses but save our body's own cells.  Also, it should tolerate harmless environmental antigens such as pollens.  Many diseases are caused not only by failing immunity against pathogens but also by immune cells erroneously attacking body's own cells (autoimmunity) or over-reacting to innocuous antigens (allergy).  A group of white blood cells, termed T cells, play central roles in guiding the immune system to keep the fine balance between immunity and tolerance.  To do so, T cells utilize two types of cell surface sensors, namely, T cell antigen receptor (TCR) and T cell costimulators.  Using TCR, T cells distinguish whether the antigen is self or non-self; through the costimulators, T cells can tell the level of danger the antigen conveys.  Upon antigenic challenges, T cells integrate the "signals" generated by TCR and costimulators and mount full immune responses to only those that are both "non-self" and "dangerous".  Obviously, manipulation of T cell costimulators has proven to be an effective way to potentiate the immunity (e.g., during vaccination) or suppress undesirable immune reactions such as autoimmune diseases, allergy, inflammation, and graft rejection.  The "inducible costimulator (ICOS)" is one of the most potent T cell costimulators in multiple aspects of T cell immunity.  Using genetically modified mouse models we generated, our research group is elucidating how ICOS works at the molecular and cellular level.  Based on the knowledge we gain from our studies, we test the role of ICOS and its signaling components in mouse models of human diseases: parasite infection, rheumatoid arthritis, and complications in bone marrow transplantation (graft vs. host disease).  Our research aims to link basic T cell biology to improvement of human health.

Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW; ERK; GAB2; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; MAPK; MOUSE MODELS; NEGATIVE FEEDBACK; PHOSPHORYLATION; RSK; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Blood cells are made in the bone marrow and originate from stem cells. Bone marrow stem cells are present in very low numbers, but yet, are responsible for the generation of all types of blood cells. These cells are normally inactive but will proliferate in response to stress, growth factors or after transplantation. However, how this is regulated is poorly understood. Our lab studies a protein called Gab2, which is essential for stem cell growth. We identified new means by which Gab2 is regulated by growth factors, and the goal of this proposal is to study these mechanisms in detail. Our results will help characterize Gab2 function and the molecular mechanisms that control stem cell proliferation.

Keywords-MotsClés: 16 WKS OMEGA-3 FATTY ACIDS SUPPLEMENTATION; CLINICAL STUDY IN OBESE SUBJECTS; IN VIVO AND AND EX VIVO MODELS; INNATE IMMUNITY AND NLRP3 INFLAMMASOME; INSULIN SENSITIVITY AND SECRETION; LIPOPROTEIN METABOLISM; POSTPRANDIAL DIETARY FAT CLEARANCE; STABLE AND RADIOACTIVE ISOTOPE TRACING; WHITE ADIPOSE TISSUE FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: While obesity increases the risk for cardiometabolic diseases like cardiovascular disease and diabetes, not all obese are at equal risk for these diseases. Unravelling the mechanisms that predict and promote diabetes is vital to identify and treat the highest-risk obese subjects and prevent their progression into diabetes.   In this project we will investigate the role of the particles that carry cholesterol and fat in the blood in the activation of certain immune pathways in human fat tissue and how this may promote metabolic diseases. We will also investigate whether omega-3 fatty acids, which are the type of fat found in fish oils, can provide a natural way for the reduction of these risks in humans, irrespective of weight-loss in obese subjects. To do so, we will enroll about 80 overweight and obese subjects in a 16-weeks dietary intervention using omega-3 fatty acids supplementation and examine their cardiometabolic risks before and after the intervention in the whole body and specifically in fat tissue biopsies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Hace1 tumour suppressor--a novel regulator of the oxidative stress response
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; HACE1; HYPOXIA; METABOLISM; NADPH OXIDASE; OXIDATIVE STRESS RESPONSE; RAC1; RHO-FAMILY GTPASE; TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR; WILMS' TUMOUR
Abstract-Résumé: Tumour suppressors are genes that prevent cells from becoming cancerous by controlling their growth and division. We have identified a novel tumour suppressor called Hace1 in a type of childhood kidney cancer, but have since found that loss of Hace1 function (e.g. through mutation or deletion of the Hace1 gene) can cause many different kinds of cancer. We believe that Hace1 mediates its protective effects via regulation of the cell's response to oxidative stress; when oxidants (which can damage the exposed, vulnerable DNA that is present in dividing cells) are detected, Hace1 kickstarts a process that prevents the cell from dividing. Loss of Hace1 therefore sensitizes cells to DNA damage, which in turn can create cancer-causing mutations in other genes. In this project, we propose to find out exactly how Hace1 responds to oxidative stress, by identifying which proteins it binds to and regulates. We will also determine whether information about the presence or absence of Hace1 in tumour cells can be used in the clinic - for example, cells that lack Hace1 may be more sensitive to chemotherapy drugs that act by damaging the DNA of cancer cells while leaving normal cells unharmed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of CFTR and sphingolipids in hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
Keywords-MotsClés: CA2+ SIGNALING; CFTR; HYPOXIC PULMONARY VASOCONSTRICTION; LIPID RAFTS; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION; PULMONARY VASCULATURE; SPHINGOLIPIDS; TRP CHANNELS; VASOREGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is the mechanism by which the lung redistributes blood flow from poorly ventilated to better aerated areas. This effect is important to improve gas exchange and oxygen uptake. However, the signaling pathways underlying this response are far from clear. Here, we hypothesize that sphingolipids play an important role as signaling molecules in hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Sphingolipids are an important lipid component of the cell membrane, and determine the formation of so called lipid rafts. These lipid rafts are small microdomains which serve as integrative clusters for many signaling molecules. Some sphingolipids can traffic through the cell membrane via a transporter protein called cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR). Mutations in the CFTR gene cause the fatal disease cystic fibrosis. Importantly, patients with cystic fibrosis have problems to optimize their pulmonary gas exchange, suggesting their hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction response may be impaired. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is also blocked in patients infected with the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which secretes a factor that inhibits CFTR. Therefore, we propose sphingolipid signaling through CFTR as an important mechanism to optimize gas exchange in the lung. Using a combination of state-of-the-art analytical techniques in cultured cells, isolated organs and experimental animal models, we will put this hypothesis to the test. The results of this project are expected to profoundly expand our understanding of one of the basic regulatory mechanisms of lung function and gas exchange. The identification of a critical role for CFTR in hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is expected to open new therapeutic strategies to improve gas exchange in patients with cystic fibrosis or Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections. In this way, the proposed research will improve public health, and decrease future health care costs and disabiliti

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating Therapeutic Decision-Making, Outcomes and Resource Utilization in Chronic Stable Angina: an interprovincial population-based study
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOPLASTY; BYPASS SURGERY; HEALTH CARE COST; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PRACTICE VARIATION; QUALITY OF LIFE MEASURES; REGRESSION MODELLING; STABLE ANGINA
Abstract-Résumé: This project will examine why patients with stable heart disease (referred to as stable angina) are sometimes treated with only medications, and in other situations undergo procedures such as angioplasty or open-heart surgery.  We will try to understand the causes of this variation and the consequences in terms of health care costs, quality of life, and survival, using provincial-wide registries in Ontario and Alberta.  We hope to determine if the variation is due to differences in the types of patients, or if it is mostly physician behaviour or hospital culture that dictates the choice of treatment.  To understand if this variation is important, we will determine if patients treated in a particular way, or at a particular type of hospital do better or use fewer health care resources. We believe untangling the root causes of this variation in practice is the first step in improving how care is delivered to this large group of patients.  The results of this project will lay the foundation for a larger research program in which tools to help physicians make the best decision for their particular patient can be developed and evaluated.  We believe this in turn will help make the best use of scarce health care dollars and improve the outcomes for patients with heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of Gliotactin, the tricellular junction and permeability barrier formation
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD-BRAIN BARRIER; EPITHELIA; GLIA; PERMEABILITY BARRIERS; SEPTATE JUNCTION; SINGALING; TRICELLULAR JUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Epithelial cells such as those found in intestine or skin are divided into distinct domains. One of these domains contains cell adhesion proteins necessary to ensure a tight seal between cells. This tight seal forms a permeability barrier that stops the flow of liquid and pathogens between cells and ensures that the two sides of the cell are isolated. This is an essential part of the formation of intestine, skin, stomach, kidney etc. It is clear how the permeability barrier forms at the boundary between two cells but less is known about how the corners of cells create the permeability barrier. At the corners, three cells come together and the pore between them is blocked by a unique structure called the tricellular junction. To study how this important junction forms, we study the Gliotactin protein, which is uniquely located at the contact point between three neighbouring cells in Drosophila (fruit fly). In fruit flies, like in humans, the tricellular junction is essential to create a permeability barrier at the corners of cells. Gliotactin is a membrane protein that localizes to the tricellular junction and is necessary for its formation. If we understand how Gliotactin is controlled we can then understand how the tricellular junction is created and how it functions. Gliotactin is highly conserved with a family of protein in humans called Neuroligins. The function of these proteins in the formation of cell junctions/barriers outside the nervous system has never been studied. Therefore we can take advantage of the ease of the genetics and cell biology capable in Drosophila to understand the function of this family of proteins in epithelial cells in all animals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulating endocannabinoid transmission as a novel treatment strategy for nicotine addiction
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; CRAVING; ENDOCANNABINOID; NICOTINE; REINSTATEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Leading addiction researchers from Canada and the United States are embarking on a multi-year, collaborative project to develop a new therapy for nicotine addiction. The research team includes six scientists led by Dr. Bernard Le Foll, Clinician-Scientist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and Associate Professor in the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Toronto. More than 3 million deaths per year worldwide are attributable to smoking, and the use of tobacco is on the rise in developing countries. Consequently, tobacco use is one of the few causes of mortality that is increasing, with deaths projected to reach 10 million annually in 30-40 years. Nicotine, a component of tobacco smoke, is the cause of tobacco dependence. Unfortunately, medications currently available help only a minority of patients stop smoking. Previous research has implicated the cannabinoid CB1 receptors located in the brain in nicotine addiction. Drugs acting on the cannabinoid CB1 receptors have been shown to be effective to help smokers quit smoking, but had some psychiatric side effects. Here, a novel class of cannabinoid CB1 drugs that appear to not create those psychiatric side effects will be evaluated for their ability to block motivation for nicotine and nicotine reward using various animal models. This project with direct relevance for health may allow for the development of new therapies for smokers, which is a major cause of preventable deaths in Canada and in the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Heme uptake and metabolism by pathogenic Staphylococcus aureus.
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; HEME; METALLOPROTEINS; SPECTROSCOPY; STAPHYLOCOCCUS
Abstract-Résumé: Iron is growth essential for almost all human pathogens and thus bacterial iron acquisition systems are recognized generally as virulence factors. Many of the protein components used to bind and transport iron and iron complexes such as heme, are external and thus are readily accessible for therapeutic purposes. This proposal focuses on investigation of the mechanisms employed by iron transport systems in a clinically important human pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus. S. aureus causes debilitating and life threatening infections and the rapid spread of methicillin resistant S. aureus (MRSA, a so-called superbug) in both community and hospital settings, has accelerated the need for understanding this pathogen's virulence repertoire for the development of new therapeutic approaches. The iron transport system selected for study has components shown to be required for optimal growth under iron limitation and for colonization or pathogenesis in model animal systems. One protein, IsdB, is a component of a vaccine in clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeted MicroRNA-126 Therapy For Chronic Ischemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; GENE THERAPY; MICRORNA; TARGETED MICROBUBBLES; ULTRASOUND; VASCULAR ENDOTHELIUM
Abstract-Résumé: Despite advances in medical and surgical therapies, patients with hardening of the blood vessels (atherosclerosis) in the heart and legs continue to suffer and die. For patients who fail to improve with usual treatments, novel treatments involving genes have been developed with the goal of improving blood flow to tissue that is suffering from reduced vessels and flow. More recently, studies have unveiled a new class of gene regulators called microRNAs (tiny gene fragments) that have powerful effects on many aspects of heart and vascular disease, including the formation of new vessels. We have developed novel techniques using ultrasound and tiny bubbles that can be used to deliver genes to blood vessels, without the use of direct injections. We have now taken this technique to deliver microRNAs that can promote vessel growth, and work with other gene therapies to grow new blood vessels to tissue. This present research, if successful, will lead to a non-invasive method of delivering novel gene treatments to promote new vessel formation and improve symptoms and function in patients with severe blockages in the blood vessels supplying the heart and legs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of cerebral cavernous malformations
Keywords-MotsClés: C. ELEGANS GENETICS; CEREBRAL CAVERNOUS MALFORMATIONS; CYTOSKELETAL REARRANGEMENTS; FUNCTIONAL PROTEOMICS; GOLGI POLARIZATION; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALLING; MASS SPECTROMETRY; TUBULE FORMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cerebral Cavernous Malformations (CCMs) are defects of the brain capillaries that can arise by inheritance of mutations in one of three 'familial' genes (CCM1, CCM2 or CCM3) or sporadically by unknown mechanisms/genes.  In many ways this disease is like a ticking time bomb.  Patients can live a normal life without knowing they have CCMs but, without notice, experience a range of symptoms as mild as headaches or as severe as seizures and even stroke.  There are currently no therapeutic options for patients except removal of these raspberry-like lesions by invasive neurosurgery.  While surgery is generally a final option it can lead to long lasting effects on balance, behaviour and memory.  Because there is very little known about the molecular events that lead up to CCM disease we propose to study the basic function of these proteins using two very powerful but complementary approaches.  Drs. Gingras and Derry are experts in the study of proteins and genes, respectively, and have integrated their research expertise to understand the most fundamental aspects of CCM biology.  In this grant application, they propose to study how the CCM proteins communicate signals within and between cells to prevent the vascular defects that cause this disease in patients.  The Gingras laboratory has discovered new components of the CCM signaling network using biochemical approaches while the Derry lab has developed a model of this disease in the tiny roundworm C. elegans.  Together, their combined efforts will provide a much clearer picture of how the CCM1, CCM2 and CCM3 proteins work, which should uncover new non-surgical methods for the clinical management of this devastating disease in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prevention of Pressure Ulcer Formation using Intermittent Electrical Stimulation
Keywords-MotsClés: DEEP TISSUE INJURY; ELECTRICAL STIMULATION; FINITE ELEMENT MODELING; NEUROPROSTHETIC DEVICE; PRESSURE ULCERS; TISSUE MECHANICS; TISSUE OXYGENATION
Abstract-Résumé: Pressure ulcers, also known as bed or pressure sores, are serious lesions of the skin, fat and muscle that are common in people who are unable to move on their own. They often develop in people with spinal cord injury, in the elderly, people in coma or even people who undergo long surgeries. About 60,000 people die each year in the US from complications related to pressure ulcers. Superman (Christopher Reeve) died from blood poisoning resulting from an infected pressure ulcer. None of the interventions currently available have been able to prevent the formation of these ulcers. We developed a novel electrical stimulation approach that periodically produces contractions in muscles compressed between a bone and an external surface (e.g., the muscles we sit on). The contractions produce "fidgeting movements" similar to the subconscious adjustments in posture frequently performed by people who have full mobility and sensation. The goal of this project is to test whether this approach is effective in preventing the formation of pressure ulcers.  If successful, this intervention could play a very important role in improving the lives of people with reduced mobility and sensation. It will also save the Canadian health care system approximately $3.5 billion a year.

Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; POST MORTEM; PROTEOMICS; PSYCHOSIS; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SYNAPSES
Abstract-Résumé: Connections between nerve cells are altered in schizophrenia. Our proposal focusses on proteins found in the specialized points of connection between nerve cells. Specifically, we are studying the way these proteins interact to allow communication to occur, and to understand how nerve cell-to-cell communication is altered in schizophrenia. The interactions between proteins will also be studied as targets for developing new medications for schizophrenia.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of XIST in Human X-Chromosome Inactivation
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETICS; FISH; HETEROCHROMATIN; NON-CODING RNA; REPORTER GENE SILENCING; RNA BINDING PROTEINS; SIRNA; X-CHROMOSOME INACTIVATION; XIST
Abstract-Résumé: Human females have two X chromosomes, while males have a single X chromosome and the sex-determining Y chromosome. The X chromosome contains over a thousand genes, so in order to avoid a dosage difference between males and females, one of the two X chromosomes in females is inactivated. We study this inactivation process in order to understand how genes can be silenced during mammalian development. We have identified that the critical initiating factor in this inactivation is expression of a gene, called XIST.  Unlike most genes XIST does not encode a protein, but rather functions in the nucleus of the cell as a functional RNA. This RNA is the only RNA that is only expressed from the X chromosome that is silenced, and it 'coats' the silenced X chromosome, causing the other genes on that chromosome to become inactive. Our experiments will show how the RNA can silence genes, coat the chromosome, and alter the structure of the coated chromosome. To address these questions we will use cell lines that make the RNA when treated with antibiotic and use smaller parts of the RNA to identify which regions are critical for functionality.  We can then identify the proteins that interact with the RNA to understand how RNAs can cause silencing.  There are many other potentially functional RNAs in humans, and our work will lead to new understanding of the function of these RNAs.

TitreApplicationTitle: INTERSTROKE: Importance of Conventional and Emerging Risk Factors for Stroke in Different Regions and Ethnic Groups of the World
Keywords-MotsClés: PREVENTION; RISK FACTORS; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is a major public health problem that contributes significantly to the global burden of disease. Stroke is the third leading cause of death worldwide (after coronary heart disease and cancer), and accounted for 9.5% of all deaths in 1999, two-thirds of which occurred in the developing world. Phase 1 of the INTERSTROKE study was completed in April 2010, included 6,000 participants from 22 countries (published in Lancet 2010). Phase 1 provided preliminary findings and suggested that ten risk factors accounted for 90% of the population-attributable risk for stroke, namely hypertension, smoking, physical inactivity, diet, abdominal obesity, psychosocial factors, apolipoproteins, diabetes mellitus and atrial fibrillation. However, the importance of these risk factors within individual regions remains unclear, but is essential information for regional and national health authorities to develop Stroke Prevention Programs. Moreover, the importance of novel risk factors (particularly genetics) is not known, but presents an important research question that may lend important insights into mechanism of disease and potential therapeutic targets. In Phase 2 of INTERSTROKE, we will include 30,000 people (15,000 with stroke and 15,000 without stroke) and determine the importance of risk factors within regions and different stroke subtypes. In addition, we will determine whether genetics (and other suspected factors) are associated with an increased risk of stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sex hormone-binding globulin: beyond the plasma transport of sex steroids.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN; ESTROGEN; GENETIC POLYMORPHISMS; MOLECULAR AND CELL BIOLOGY; REPRODUCTION; SEX HORMONE-BINDING GLOBULIN; TRANSCRIPTION; TRANSGENIC MOUSE; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) transports sex steroids (androgens and estrogens) in the blood and regulates their access to tissues.  In humans, the liver produces the SHBG that circulates in the blood.  However, SHBG is also produced by sex steroid-sensitive cells of the kidney and small intestine and remains inside these cells, and a truncated SHBG is produced in developing sperm.  This proposal sets out to determine how the human SHBG gene is regulated in these specialized cell types, how it accumulates within some cells, and what impact this has on controlling the local actions of sex steroids.  We have also identified new genetic variants in the human SHBG gene and will define how these alter the production and function of SHBG in the blood and in sperm. Understanding how SHBG expression is controlled in different cells, and how SHBG acts locally within tissues and specific cell types will provide insight into SHBG's broader physiological roles. Importantly, this will be help establish how SHBG polymorphisms can be used to predict disease risk, and how abnormalities in SHBG production and/or function may contribute to the etiology of specific diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translational control of gene expression in Foxp3+ regulatory T cell function.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNITY; DIABETES; FOXP3; IMMUNE TOLERANCE; INFLAMMATORY CONDITIONS; REGULATORY T CELLS; T CELLS; TRANSLATION CONTROL  OF GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Treg cells) are a subset of immunosuppressive lymphocytes that play central roles in the control of immune tolerance to self and non-self antigens. CD4+Foxp3+ Treg cells must integrate a spectrum of inflammatory, and other environmental stimuli to coordinate their action and orchestrate immune responses in vivo.  Foxp3, a forkhead-winged helix transcriptional factor, is a master regulator of Treg cell genetic programming and lineage specification of Treg cells. Transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms of gene regulation enable T cells to respond to inflammatory events, by altering the nature, amounts and activities of specific proteins required for their controlled and coordinated modulation of immunity.  We found substantial changes in mRNA translation of specific mRNAs between CD4+ Treg and Teff cell subsets upon activation, and translationally regulated mRNAs are enriched for mRNAs encoding proteins involved in distinct biological processes. Specifically, we show that the mRNA encoding a pivotal translation initiation factor, eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E), is translationally suppressed, accompanied by down-regulation of eIF4E protein levels, in activated Treg cells as compared to Teff cells. Strikingly, differential eIF4E induction between T-cell subsets correlate with translation of eIF4E-sensitive cell cycle related mRNAs, and modulate proliferation and Foxp3 expression. Thus, our preliminary data shows that distinct, translational programs differentially orchestrate fundamental cellular processes in CD4+ T cell subsets: the eIF4E mRNA, is translationally suppressed in activated Foxp3+ Treg cells, and imprints these cells with a Treg-specific translational gene signature involved in lineage indentity and stability of function. We will investigate the molecular pathways that regulate eIF4E-dependent, translational control of gene expression in Foxp3+ Treg cells in mouse models of inflammation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Importance of cyclin D1-USP11 interaction for the homologous repair pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER BIOLOGY; CELL CYCLE; DEGRADATION; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR; UBIQUITINATION/DEUBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Exposure to environmental factors, including sunlight, ionizing radiation and chemical reagents, constantly challenges the integrity of our genetic information (i.e DNA). To ensure that our DNA is faithfully transmitted and to prevent the development of cancer, cells have evolved a complex network to detect, signal and ultimately repair DNA damage, which is coupled to an arrest in cell proliferation.  It is still poorly understood how DNA damage signaling/repair and cell cycle arrest are coordinated but recent evidence suggests the implication of the cell cycle protein cyclin D1 (D1). Tight regulation of D1 protein level is critical as overexpression of D1 can predispose to the development of cancer. The major goal of my project is to characterize the mechanisms regulating D1 levels and its biological functions in cell cycle progression and DNA repair. In particular, I will define the interaction of D1 with the deubiquitinating enzyme USP11, which could protect D1 from degradation and be a potential target for the development of anti-cancer drugs. We will verify whether modulation of USP11 levels impacts the stability and the endogenous level of D1 as well as cell cycle progression and DNA repair. We will also investigate the clinical importance of D1-USP11 interaction and screen for drugs that could affect D1 level and cancer progression. This study will give insight into the mechanisms coordinating DNA signaling/repair and cell cycle progression and could reveal how a defect in these mechanisms can promote cancer progression. Ultimately, our study could provide with potential drug target to treat patients affected by D1-overexpressing cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of synaptic processing by a Cav3-Kv4 ion channel complex
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTION POTENTIAL DISCHARGE; CALCIUM CHANNELS; CEREBELLUM; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNELS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PATCH CLAMP; POTASSIUM CHANNELS; SIGNAL PROCESSING; SYNAPTIC PHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The brain is able to process information because ion channels that drive electrical activity provide the means for cells to communicate. All communication takes place at synaptic junctions, where ion channels can modulate incoming signals. This research project will examine signal processing in the cerebellum, a brain region critical to both motor control and cognitive (mental) functions. The cerebellum has an input layer of granule cells that receive mossy fiber input, a molecular layer for processing signals, and an output layer of Purkinje cells, all of which are folded into 10 different lobules over the rostro-caudal axis. Despite work performed to date, the functional roles of different lobules has remained an enigma. However, fMRI studies now show that cerebellar function is divided into motor control in rostral lobules and cognitive function in caudal lobules.      In the past grant period we uncovered a novel complex between ion channels that generate calcium influx and potassium efflux (termed the Cav3-Kv4 complex). We found that these channels work in tandem, such that Cav3 calcium influx enhances Kv4 potassium efflux, allowing control over the excitability and timing of electrical impulses in neurons. We now find that the Cav3-Kv4 complex is expressed in granule cells, providing the means to shape signal processing at the first stage of cerebellar circuitry. Moreover, the expression pattern of Cav3 and Kv4 channels changes across lobules, leading to: Hypothesis - Cerebellar granule cell excitability and response to mossy fiber input is differentially regulated across cerebellar lobules by the expression pattern of the Cav3-Kv4 channel complex.  This work will be important to understanding how sensory inputs carrying different forms of information are differentially processed across the multiple lobules of cerebellum, potentially identifying synaptic mechanisms that can be targeted for intervention in disorders of cerebellar function.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Macrophage function changes with age and contributes to susceptibility to infectious disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ELDERLY; HOST DEFENCE; IMMUNOSENESCENCE; INFECTION; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; MACROPHAGE/MONOCYTE; NASOPHARYNGEAL CARRIAGE; PNEUMONIA; STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately a third of deaths in the elderly (65 yrs and older) occur due to infectious disease and of these infection, respiratory infections such as pneumonia and influenza are the most common. Indeed approximately 90% of pneumonia deaths in Canada occur in the elderly. Infections like pneumonia often occur after a period of immobility or a hospital stay (e.g. a hip fracture) and are mark the start of a decline in health and independence. Keeping the elderly healthy and infection free would provide them more years of independence and reduce the cost of care. Conventional wisdom states that the elderly are more susceptible to infectious disease because their immune system just "doesn't work" but the data supporting this belief is thin. Indeed, our recent data demonstrate that age-associated immune decline is a very complicated story. For example, when challenged with the bacterium that causes pneumonia specialized white blood cells called macrophages from the elderly mount a very strong pro-inflammatory response but for reasons we don't understand this response does not protect them from infection. Despite having such a strong pro-inflammatory response their macrophages are defective in recognizing, eating (phagocytosing) and killing bacteria. We believe that it is these defects are what predispose them to acquiring infections, especially pneumonia, and that once they acquire an infection these and other immune defects make it very hard for them to clear the bacteria.  The aim of this study is to discover how aging alters macrophage responses to bacteria with the long-term goal of discovering how we can improve macrophage function and prevent infections in the elderly.

ProgramNameEN: CEEHRC Epigenomics Platform - Epigenomic Mapping Centres (EMC)
NomDuProgrammeFR: CCREES Plateforme en épigénomique - Centres de séquençage épigénomique (CSE)
TitreApplicationTitle: Multidimensional Epigenomics Mapping Centre (EMC) at McGill
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Ten years after completion of the Human Genome Project providing us the first full sequence of bases in our genome the research community is now joining forces for its next challenge: epigenome mapping. This global effort is necessary to answer how does the genome deploy hundreds of different programs leading to different fates in cell development, altered cell function and sometimes in disease even when the genome sequence remains unchanged. By systematic mapping of variable modifications in DNA-bases such as methylation, differential packing of DNA around proteins (histones) and resulting changes in gene expression one can gain insight how epigenetic modifications in genome govern its function. To join global efforts (The International Human Epigenome Consortium) we will establish an Epigenome Mapping Centre (EMC) at McGill University that builds upon a high-throughput sequencing infrastructure with a critical mass of expertise and technology available to contribute significantly in deciphering the functional code of the human genome. Our work is internationally coordinated and will support research initiatives across the Canadian research community. We draw upon our previous experience in studying human genome function and molecular mechanisms involved in disease coupled with our expertise in advanced technologies applicable for epigenomics. We apply epigenome mapping to understand interactions between environment and genome in human blood cells, to interpret diseases impacting metabolism using tissue samples and to study how epigenetic changes can alter function of the brain. EMC McGill is a national hub housing a critical mass of epigenomics expertise supported by state-of-the-art genomics infrastructure. The integrated operation contributes to Canadian leadership in epigenome research, the next frontier in biomedicine.

NomDuProgrammeFR: CCREES Plateforme en épigénomique - Centres de séquençage épigénomique (CSE)
AreasOfScienceEN: GENOMICS, PROTEOMICS, AND BIOINFORMATICS; HEALTH RESEARCH
DomainesScientifiquesFR: GÉNOMIQUE, PROTÉOMIQUE ET BIOINFORMATIQUE; RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ
TitreApplicationTitle: Centre for Epigenome Mapping Technologies
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOINFORMATICS; CANCER; CHROMATIN MARKS; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENOMICS; GENE REGULATION; HUMAN HEALTH; MULTIDISCIPLINARY; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: The term epigenome refers to chemical modifications of DNA and proteins that control genome (a term referring to all the DNA within our cells) structure and activity.  In contrast to the genome, which remains mostly the same throughout an individuals life, the epigenome changes during development and aging, in response to various external stimuli and as diseases emerge.  Epigenome changes can result in profound changes in which genes are turned on and hence how cells behave.  Thus, an understanding of what epigenome states exist in different cell types and how these states are specified are critically important to many aspects of human health and disease.  We propose to build on our internationally leading experience in epigenome mapping to establish a major Canadian centre of epigenome analysis that will demonstrate an ability to deliver complete reference epigenome information on a full spectrum of normal and diseased human cell types; to improve the technology for broader applications in the future; and to make this technology rapidly available to Canadian scientists.  To accomplish this goal we have developed an integrated program with internationally recognized biologists and clinicians with specialized access to, and knowledge of, the normal and diseased cell types we will analyze.  This collaborative team effort will transform our understanding of the relationship between epigenome modifications and how genes are turned on or turned off, and lay the foundation for larger studies to revolutionize our understanding of how diseases develop and how to anticipate and treat them more effectively.

ProgramNameEN: CEEHRC Epigenomics Platform - Epigenomic Data Coordination Centre (EDCC)
NomDuProgrammeFR: CCREES Plateforme en épigénomique - Centre de coord des données épigénomiques (CCDE)
TitreApplicationTitle: Integrative Epigenomic Data Coordination Centre (EDCC) at McGill
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; DATA COORDINATION; DATABASES; DISTRIBUTED PROCESSING; EPIGENETICS; GENOMICS; INTEGRATIVE ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Epigenetic processes play a key role in organizing genomic information to modulate gene expression and control cellular functions. To gain insights into the molecular mechanisms of the cell, there is a fundamental need to generate reference maps and integrate across multiple levels of genetic and epigenetic information for various human tissues and animal models. The International Human Epigenome Consortium (IHEC) and the Canadian Epigenetics, Environment, and Health Research Consortium (CEEHRC) have recognized this need and are supporting the generation of reference epigenomic maps for a wide range of cell types. The sheer volume of data associated with these initiatives requires significant informatics support and the development of quantitative analysis and tools to explore and study these genome-wide maps. We propose an integrative Epigenomic Data Coordination Centre (EDCC) at McGill, which will be a national hub to support data collection, processing, storage and dissemination for projects funded under the CEEHRC initiative and facilitate integration with the IHEC. The outcome will include data pipelines and tools using standardized formats and vocabularies for verification, validation, and analyses across the CEEHRC network. The EDCC McGill will also develop a framework that leverages Compute Canada national resources to support large-scale processing, sharing and visualization of epigenomics data. The platform will enable epigenetic researchers on a national level to query and exploit this valuable resource.

Abstract-Résumé: In addition to the genetic information that is stored in the order of the four bases that make up our DNA, modifications to the DNA itself and also the proteins that encapsulate it also influence the function and behavior of our genetic material .  Recent DNA sequencing techniques make it possible to identify and record such modifications. As these modifications will be different between cells types and within tissues at varying stages of development a large "atlas" of these epigenetic modifications needs to be established. For these data to be most effective we need a mechanism to store the results of these experiments and to disseminate this information to the scientific community. The proposal will provide such an repository allowing easy data deposition and access as well as analytical tools to further enhance the utility of the data.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development of radiolabelled ghrelin analogues for the molecular imaging of prostate cancer through targeting the growth hormone secretagogue receptor.
Keywords-MotsClés: GHRELIN; GROWTH HORMONE SECRETAGOGUE RECEPTOR; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; MOLECULAR IMAGING; PEPTIDE CHEMISTRY; PET; RADIOPHARMACEUTICALS
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in Canadian men with over 20,000 cases expected in 2010. Early and accurate diagnosis of the disease is critical for effective treatment planning and especially important is the ability to correctly identify prostate cancer versus benign hyperplasia (BPH) of the prostate, which can have similar symptoms. Current non-invasive imaging techniques are unable to accurately evaluate the normal/BPH prostate versus cancerous prostate. Recent work in our lab demonstrated that analogues of a peptide called ghrelin were able to target prostate cancer by means of targeting a specific biomarker, the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHSR).  In this proposal, imaging agents will be developed that target this biomarker, the GHSR. These imaging agents will be radiolabelled with a medical isotope, allowing for the non-invasive imaging of this receptor using positron emission tomography (PET), which is an imaging technique routinely used in hospitals worldwide. The outcome of the proposed research will be the ability to differentiate normal or BPH prostate from that of prostate cancer, through the use of imaging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of Hemostasis by Enveloped Viruses
Keywords-MotsClés: COAGULATION; DENGUE VIRUS; HERPES SIMPLEX; INFECTION; PROTEASE ACTIVATED RECEPTORS; TISSUE FACTOR; VASCULAR DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: We have been studying the molecules that link common viruses to heart disease, including herpes simplex type 1 (HSV1), type 2 (HSV2) and cytomegalovirus (CMV). We have discovered that each can activate crucial blood clotting enzymes directly on their surface because of constituents within a struc-ture called an envelope. The significance of our findings is that these viruses can bypass our body's usual check-points for making too much clot. However, many other enveloped virus types can alter blood clotting and like HSV1, HSV2 and CMV, may influence vascular disease. Ever since we started our studies with HSV1, HSV2 and CMV, which are "sibling" members of the Herpesvirus family, we considered these as a model for enveloped viruses. In the current proposal we will extend our expertise to the Flavivirus family, which has a serious impact on the world's health as some of the members are dengue virus (DEN), West Nile virus and hepatitis C virus. Of these, we will focus our efforts on the four types of DEN for several reasons: it is known to affect both clot forming and clot breaking by poorly understood mechanisms; it is responsible for one of the most prevalent viral causes of epidemics globally; it is transfusion transmitted and is therefore a risk to blood systems; it exists at relatively high number in blood during infection where it can influence blood clotting; and it requires lower level bio-containment facilities compared to other members of the Flavivirus family. Like the Herpesviruses, we have already propagated and purified DEN for supporting preliminary biochemical clotting studies. As a safety measure, we will also evaluate the viability of DEN in blood products. Greater attention to en-veloped virus infection may reduce the incidence and severity of heart disease. Furthermore, by under-standing the direct link between the virus surface and clotting, new targets for the development of treatments for vascular diseases and virus infection is anticipated.

TitreApplicationTitle: Maternal And Perinatal Placental Ethnicity Development ("MAPPED") programme: a policy-directed clinical research programme to attain healthy mothers and healthy newborns in Canada.
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNICITY; FETAL; HEALTH POLICY; IMMIGRATION; MATERNAL HEALTH; NEONATAL; NEWBORN WEIGHT; OBESITY; PLACENTA; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: I propose to evaluate how several maternal characteristics -- her immigrant & ethnic status, social and marital stability, obesity, hypertension & diabetes -- affect a) her well-being in pregnancy, b) the risk to her fetus of stillbirth, birth defects, prematurity & abnormal birthweight and infant growth, and c) how these pregnancy & post-delivery factors affect the health of the mother & her newborn short-term (e.g., infant growth) & long-term (e.g., maternal heart disease and stroke).   In the specific Research Proposal included in my Chair application, I focus on how newborn weight and infant growth differ according to maternal ethnicity and immigration status. I aim to evaluate the accuracy of the World Health Organization charts (currently used to plot infant growth) within the major ethnic groups in Canada. I have already shown that birthweight may be lower for newborns of South Asian and East Asian mothers.      The results of the Research Proposal, and my overall body of work, will be patient-centered, policy-oriented & pragmatic. I have developed a working team of local and Canada-wide scientists, decision-makers and trainees to ensure that I achieve all objectives of the Chair, within proper timelines, for the betterment of mothers and infants across Canada, including new immigrants and ethnic minority groups. I have fantastic support from my university, a great environment to grow, and the time and space to bring forward another generation of maternal-child health researchers and health policy brokers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards an Understanding of the Effective Change Processes in Drama Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: DRAMA THERAPY; EMOTIONAL EXPRESSION; EXPERIENCING; PSYCHOTHERAPY PROCESS
Abstract-Résumé: Drama therapy is a form of mental healthcare that uses drama and theatre tools (e.g. role-play, puppets, masks, improvisation) to help clients. Drama therapy is an essential treatment as it provides clients an alternative form of expression and communication. Drama therapy has demonstrated to be effective with a number of clinical populations, including victims of trauma, individuals with Selective Mutism, and adults with developmental disabilities. Despite these successes, research has yet to demonstrate why drama therapy is effective. Two parts of drama therapy thought to be responsible for client change are dramatic projection and embodiment. Dramatic projection involves the movement of the client's inner conflicts onto dramatic material (e.g. characters, puppets, etc.), and embodiment is the client's physical expression of roles and emotions. In more common forms of psychotherapy, emotional arousal and experiencing (how involved the client is in therapy) have been found to play a significant role in the client change process. It has been hypothesized that clients have higher levels of emotional arousal and experiencing in drama therapy than in other forms of therapy. The proposed study will determine if there is a relationship between the psychotherapy processes of experiencing and emotional arousal, and the drama therapy processes of dramatic projection and embodiment. Video of drama therapy exercises and interventions will be examined. Segments involving dramatic projection and embodiment will be identified, and the experiencing level and emotional arousal level of the drama therapy participants will be rated.  The experiencing and emotional arousal level in segments with and without dramatic projection and with and without embodiment will then be compared. The proposed study will improve clinical practice by giving clinicians a better understanding of effective drama therapy processes and how to use them to bring about client change.

Abstract-Résumé: Une pratique reguliere de l'activite physique est associee a une bonne sante physique et psychologique. En ce sens, l'objectif de ce projet de recherche est d'evaluer l'efficacite de differentes interventions visant l'augmentation du niveau d'activite physique de la population. Plus specifiquement, ces interventions, basees sur une approche ecologique, visent la modification de l'environnement bati afin de faciliter le transport actif (ex: marcher ou prendre le velo pour se deplacer vers l'ecole ou le travail). Des donnees obtenues aupres de plus de 10000 participants et leurs milieux de vie seront analysees afin d'evaluer l'impact des interventions sur la sante des individus (ex: distribution du poids dans la population, qualite de vie, blessures/deces par traumatisme routier, etc).

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging important steps in the formation of brain metastases
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; IMAGING AGENTS; INFLAMMATION; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; OPTICAL IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: The incidence of secondary brain cancer (brain cancer metastasis) is rising worldwide, including in Canada. This is because advances in cancer treatment are more effective at curing primary cancers, that is cancers that develop in any organ such as the brain, breast, prostate and others. Unfortunately, cancer that has already migrated to a distant organ (called a secondary cancer) will have more time to develop and grow. There is mounting evidence that inflammation to blood vessels can facilitate the development of secondary cancer. We propose to use medical imaging to visualize inflammation in animals and establish a link with the formation of brain cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Growth arrest and osteoporosis in Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients treated with glucocorticoids
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE BIOLOGY; BONE HEALTH STUDY; BONE HISTOMORPHOMETRY; BONE QUALITY STUDIES; CELL SIGNALLING; CHRONIC DISEASE; DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; GLUCOCORTICOID INDUCED OSTEOPOROSIS IN CHILDREN
Abstract-Résumé: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy is a debilitating disease resulting in progressive muscle weakness and early death for which there is no cure. Over the past decades, the use of high dose steroids (glucocorticoids) for long periods of time, has resulted in a substantial improvement in their muscle strength, a decrease in complications associated with the disorder, and survival. As part of this treatment, the effected boys develop severe osteoporosis (resulting in bone fractures) which is thought to be due to a combination of the underlying disease and the steroids. There is little information on predicting, preventing, or treating this complication. We plan in this proposal to use animal models to learn how osteoporosis develops and then develop new ways of preventing and treating this complication. At the same time, we will examine tests in children who are starting high doses of steroids to help us predict which of the children might develop osteoporosis. At the conclusion of all these studies, we will be in a position using the animal studies and the studies in children to propose more effective ways in managing this common and severe complication.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regeneration of motor neurons controlling movement and respiration from embryonic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; CELL REPLACEMENT THERAPIES; MOTOR NEURON DEVELOPMENT; MOTOR NEURON DISEASE; MOTOR NEURON REGENERATION; MOUSE EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that 2 out of 100,000 people will be diagnosed each year with the degenerative motor neuron disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Patients suffering from ALS face a severely impaired quality of life and a rapid degeneration causing death. An important part of ALS research involves investigations into why motor neurons are selectively lost in this disease, and how they might be replaced in order to restore the functions of sufferers. In this regard, understanding how motor neurons are generated and become part of neural circuits controlling motor functions is of utmost importance for the development of successful strategies of neuron replacement therapy for ALS and other motor neuron diseases. The present application seeks to characterize the mechanisms that govern the development and connectivity of selected motor neurons known to be vulnerable to degeneration in ALS in order to use this information to develop motor neuron replacement therapies. More specifically, it is proposed to investigate how motor neurons that control muscles involved in voluntary movement and breathing acquire their specific cellular properties and become connected to their target muscles. It is then proposed to use this information to develop strategies to promote the regeneration of these particular classes of motor neurons from pluripotent embryonic stem cells. The results of the planned investigations will provide new insight into how to promote the regeneration of particular types of motor neurons with defined characteristics. Restoring muscle functions through the production of new motor neurons from either endogenous or transplanted stem/progenitor cells represents one of the highest priorities in the treatment of many neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS.

NomDuComitéFR: Déterminants psychosociaux, socioculturels et comportementaux de la santé 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Integrated Mindfulness-based Cognitive Behaviour Therapy versus Cognitive Behaviour Therapy for Provoked Vestibulodynia
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; DYSPAREUNIA; GENITAL EXAMINATION; MINDFULNESS; PROVOKED VESTIBULODYNIA; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Provoked vestibulodynia (PVD), or pain at the opening of the vagina with any kind of touch, affects approximately 16% of otherwise healthy women. The most common treatment involves medical management with less than half of women improving. Most women seek help from a variety of different providers for years before experiencing any improvement in their pain. Women with PVD commonly experience a decline in their sexual health, relationship satisfaction, and emotional well-being as a result of frequent painful intercourse or attempts at gynaecologic exams. Thus, psychological approaches that address the genital pain, in addition to these other domains of the woman's life, are very much needed. One previous study found that cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) administered in groups over 10 sessions significantly reduces genital pain and improves different domains of quality of life. Over the past 10 years, the PI has developed a psychological treatment that integrates skills in mindfulness meditation, cognitive therapy (challenging unhelpful or maladaptive thoughts), and behavioural skills (e.g., muscle relaxation) for women with sexual desire and arousal disorders and found significant improvements on most measures of sexual response and quality of life. We have recently adapted this treatment for women with PVD and have pilot tested it in a small group of 33 women with PVD. In our pilot work, we found that four 90 minute sessions significantly decreased pain and improved measures of sexual health and mood. The goal of this study is to expand the program to 8 sessions, and to compare it to the previously tested CBT (which does not include mindfulness meditation). If found effective, the findings from this study will be used to assist ob/gyns and family doctors who are usually the first point of contact for women seeking treatment for distressing genital pain. We also have future plans to make our treatment available online to reach geographically remote women.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
TitreApplicationTitle: Early and preclinical diagnosis of Parkinson's disease using olfactory testing and Diffusion Tensor Imaging of olfactory bulb and substantia nigra.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIAGNOSIS; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; MRI; OLFACTION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Clinical Parkinson's disease (PD) can only be diagnosed when most dopamine neurons are damaged or have already died. It is important that better ways be found to detect early PD.  Years before PD motor symptoms are present, changes occur in olfaction and sleep. By themselves, these changes are not enough to reveal that PD is developing. We suggest that the combination of smell testing with tests of sleep behavior and with a sensitive magnetic resonance imaging technique called diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) will together allow us to detect PD years before motor symptoms appear. There are new treatments that might be able to stop PD at this very early stage, before lasting damage is done or motor changes are seen. Our study is divided into 2 phases.  In Phase I (partly supported by Parkinson Society Canada) we studied 14 newly diagnosed PD patients and compared them to 14 healthy control subjects. In agreement with many studies, the sense of smell was impaired in the PD patients.  Diffusion tensor imaging revealed a significant decrease in a measure of water diffusion in olfactory tract and bulb, extending earlier findings. Changes were also found in the substantia nigra of PD patients.  Phase Ib of our proposed study is to look at cognition first in our PD patients then in a population of patients with cognitive impairment.  Finally, the large part of our proposed study (Phase II) is to see if we can detect PD in people at risk for PD but who do not yet have PD.  We will scan using a smell identification test a large population (1,200 subjects) of neurologically normal subjects (age-matched siblings of PD patients).  Subjects with the lowest 10% and highest 10% in smell testing will be assessed for sleep disorders and scanned using DTI.  Subjects with sleep disorders will have a high risk for PD.  Our study will determine whether the combination of tests for olfaction, sleep disorders and DTI will allow effective detection of early stage PD.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the physiological function of the plasminogen receptor, S100A10 (p11).
Keywords-MotsClés: METASTASIS; P11; PLASMIN; PLASMINOGEN; PROTEASES; S100A10; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: It is now accepted that inflammation is necessary to maintain and promote the growth of the benign breast cancer cells within the tumor and also to teach these benign cancer cells how spread and become metastatic and therefore lethal. One of the key players in the inflammatory response, blood cells called macrophages, must chew their way through the tissue material that surrounds the tumor in order to reach the cancer cells in the tumor. My laboratory has shown, in a mouse model of lung cancer, that macrophages use a protein on their cell surface called S100A10 to allow them to chew through the tissue barriers and reach the tumor. If macrophages are prevented from expressing S100A10, they cannot chew through tissue barriers and and do not reach the tumor site and as a result tumor growth is reduced by as much as 90%. We plan to use the PyMT mouse model of breast cancer to determine if macrophages use S100A10 to regulate their chewing activity in order to allow them to reach the breast tumor site and promote tumor and metastatic growth. Similarly, we will also test the possibility that the cancer cells themselves may also use S100A10 to chew through the tissue barriers and metastasize to the lungs. The PyMT mouse is an exceptional model system because these mice develop breast tumors and lethal metastases in a similar way to human breast cancer. Thus by crossing the PyMT mouse with our S100A10-null mouse, we will produce mice that develop breast cancer but whose macrophages and cancer cells cannot express S100A10. By comparing the rate of growth of the breast tumors and the development of metastatic foci between PyMT mice that express and others that cannot express S100A10, we will determine if S100A10 plays an important role in breast cancer. If S100A10 does play a role in tumor growth and/or metastasis it could represent an important target for development of a new class of drugs that block the function of this protein.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Cx26 and Cx30 in skin aging
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNEXINS; EPIDERMIS; GAP JUNCTIONS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MUTATION; SKIN DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: It is a general requirement for normal function that adjacent cells within human tissues communicate directly with each other through special channels called gap junctions. In over 10 distinct human diseases these channels are either not produced by the cells (e.g. many cancers), or the proteins (connexins) that make up these channels contain mutations that inhibit their normal function (e.g. skin diseases, deafness, neuropathies).  There are 21 connexin genes in the human genome and multiple connexins can be expressed and intermix in the same cells, leading to a complex array of gap junction channel types within tissues and organs. This is most evident in the epidermis of the skin where up to 10 different connexins are expressed and mutations in anyone of 5 of these connexins result in a variety of human skin diseases. Importantly, mutations in some of these same connexins cause additional disease burden which includes hearing loss and the disease symptoms tend to become evident during aging. In this study we will investigate how connexin mutations cause human diseases of the skin and why these disease manifest as a patient ages. Once it is better understood how connexin mutations cause diseases of the skin in aged patients it is anticipated that these findings could be translated to pre-clinical studies and possible treatments of gap junction-linked diseases.

Keywords-MotsClés: ARTICULAR CARTILAGE; GPCR RECEPTORS; INFLAMMATION; JOINT; PAIN; PRECLINICAL STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain is an important medical issue that affects the society in several ways. Osteoarthritis is one of the pathology which causes severe, long-term pain and physical disability that is without an effective treatment. Patients afflicted with this disease consult because of pain; however, the pain is a late manifestation that appears only when the degenerative changes (damages) are advanced and the disease severe. Here we propose to test the ability of two specific and selective antagonists commercially available in order to prove their putative effectiveness on joint pain and damage. This new proposed strategy has the potential to develop new drugs to be proposed in early diseases development and that contributes to the exacerbate inflammation and pain existing during the in late stages of osteoarthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Season, Light Exposure and Serotonin Transporter Binding
Keywords-MotsClés: LIGHT THERAPY; SEASONAL AFFECTIVE DISORDER(SAD); SEROTONINTRANSPORTER
Abstract-Résumé: Rates of seasonal affective disorder (SAD) range from 1 to 6 percent (highest at Northern latitudes). 40 percent of people with SAD switch to clinical depression and 25 percent of healthy people have seasonal changes in mood, energy, appetite and sleep affecting function. In 2008, we discovered that the mood supporting chemical serotonin is removed more in people brain scanned during winter than people brain scanned during the summer. This was published in the top psychiatry journal (Archives of General Psychiatry).  This earlier study scanned different people in summer and winter. In the proposed study, we would like to brain scan the same people in summer and winter. Also, we would like to see if seasonal changes in serotonin removal are greater in people with SAD.   Finally we would like to understand whether light exposure will decrease the serotonin removal.If the season change in serotonin removal is greater in SAD, then we should develop ways to prevent it. If light prevents the serotonin removal, we can then test out different ways of doing light exposure (timing, color etc.) so as to best prevent the serotonin removal in small groups of people, using the brain scan as a calibration. This would hasten development of better light treatment for preventing seasonal sadness in winter.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE EVENTS; ARGON LASER TRABECULOPLASTY (ALT); INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE (IOP); OPEN ANGLE GLAUCOMA (OAG); RCT; SELECTIVE LASER TRABECULOPLASTY (SLT); VISUAL ACUITY
Abstract-Résumé: Lasers are important therapy in glaucoma. They are a pivotal point in treatment between medical and surgical care. Over the last 10 years a new laser has emerged as the usual laser treatment: Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT). SLT works as well as the older laser used: argon laser trabeculoplasty (ALT). However SLT has many theoretical benefits over ALT including causing less damage to the tissue it affects. One of the potential patient centered benefits of this laser is that it may be repeatable. It is even possible that the old laser ALT may be useable after an SLT treatment. This study aims to uncover whether repeat laser is possible after SLT and if so which laser is more effective (ALT vs SLT). The potential of repeating laser therapies may delay surgical treatment and its complications. Also understanding which laser to use will help eye doctors know how to treat their patients at this point of the disease.
