TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating Pathways of Child Health Inequalities: An International Perspective
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; ASTHMA; CHILD DEVELOPMENT; CHILD HEALTH; CHILDREN; HEALTH EQUITY; OBESITY; SOCIOECONOMIC GRADIENT; SOCIOECONOMIC INEQUALITIES; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: Early child development lays the foundation for later health. Being poor during childhood is a known predictor of poorer adult health. Scientists do not have a clear understanding of when or for how long being poor during childhood can affect later health. They also do not know how being poor "gets under the skin" to affect health. Our team plans to study the pathways that link early poverty with child health. We will work with scientists across five different countries: Canada, United States, Netherlands, Sweden, and United Kingdom. In each country, a longitudinal birth cohort will be studied. Each birth cohort includes a group of children followed from birth to age 10 years. These children had their health measured many times over the 10 years. There are three parts to our project. First, we will define measures of being poor so we can make equal comparisons across countries. Second, we will study possible pathways linking family poverty and child health. Child health outcomes include asthma, blood pressure, obesity, and learning problems, among others. Third, we will consider country income inequality. Income inequality refers to the difference between the people who make the most money and the people who make the least. We will study how country income inequality affects child health. Our team includes leading scientists who have been already studying poverty and child health in their countries. We hope that the results of our study will lead to changes in public policy to improve child health. Our results will allow us to see if being poor has the same impact on child health in different countries with different social policies. We will share our results with government leaders who can change public policy that can improve child health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of cGMP signaling in diabetic cardiomyopathy.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC FUNCTION; CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CELL SIGNALLING; DIABETES; HEART METABOLISM; LIPOTOXICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Background: There is an alarming worldwide increase of patients suffering of diabetes of which 80 percent will die of a heart attack. Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is characterized by important alterations in the capacity of the heart to handle blood nutrients, particularly lipids, for energy production that is essential to its good function. These alterations are characterized by damages at the level of the mitochondria, which are the cell energy factories. In order to find new therapeutic strategies counteracting these abnormalities, a better understanding of the cellular mechanisms underlying them is mandatory. In this regard, our recent work using genetically modified mouse displaying enhanced activity of a specific cell signaling pathway in the heart, namely cGMP signaling, suggested that this pathway could be a target for therapy. In fact, hearts from these mice were found to be protected from lipid alterations induced by fasting and to mitochondrial damage induced by the absence of a structural protein (dystrophin). We thus hypothesized that enhanced activation of cGMP signaling may be cardioprotective in context of diabetes by preventing cardiac lipid metabolic alterations and mitochondrial injuries. Description and objective of the project: We will document the metabolic and functional cardiac effects of enhancing cGMP signaling in an animal model of type 2 diabetes induced via low doses injections of streptozotocin (to partially destroy the pancreas). To do so, both a genetic and a pharmacological approach will be used. We will induce diabetes in 1) genetically modified mice that are over activating or reducing the cGMP signaling pathway and to 2) mice treated or not with sildenafil (a drug increasing blood cGMP level).  Relevance to population health: Since there are pharmacologic agents already in use in the clinics to increase cellular cGMP levels, such as sildenafil, this project could provide a new therapeutic approach for the treatment of DCM.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the quality of rehabilitation for total joint arthroplasty along the continuum of care.
Keywords-MotsClés: JOINT ARTHROPLASTY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; QUALITY INDICATORS; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: More than 77,000 Canadians undergo hip or knee replacement surgery each year. Most patients need rehabilitation to help their recovery after surgery, but there is large variation in how and when rehabilitation is provided across Canada. Further, no agreed upon standard of rehabilitation care exists. The use of quality indicators is one method to assess the variations and gaps in rehabilitation care. Building on the applicant's PhD research, the proposed postdoctoral study aims to develop a set of indicators to measure and improve the quality and consistency of rehabilitation for patients undergoing joint replacement surgery. Quality indicators should be based on the best available evidence, often in the form of systematic reviews or clinical practice guidelines. Such a synthesis of the evidence is available from the candidate's doctoral research. Using internationally accepted methods, a set of indicators will be developed for hip replacement and knee replacement rehabilitation separately. Using a Delphi survey approach, an expert panel made up of clinicians, researchers and consumers will rate the proposed indicators and decide on the final sets. These new quality indicators will then be tested in one health zone in Alberta to assess their ease of use by clinicians and health care planners for monitoring quality of care after joint replacement surgery. Future research will build on this pilot data to ensure the quality indicators are acceptable and can be implemented in other Alberta health regions and across Canada. This project offers a viable, evidence-based, stakeholder-informed solution toward improving the quality of rehabilitation care after hip and knee replacement. In addition, it contributes knowledge on the development and use of quality indicators in the rehabilitation sector.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the Rb-E2F pathway in adult neurogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT CELL CYCLE; NEUROGENESIS; PROGENITOR CELLS; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: In the past it was always believed that the adult brain cannot regenerate damaged brain tissue and that brain cells (neurons) must last throughout life. More recently, it was found that the adult brain contains stem cells and progenitor cells which have the capacity to regenerate new neurons to improve brain function.  A major challenge is that most neural stem cells lie dormant in the adult brain and their numbers decline with age. It is therefore essential to identify new strategies to activate and expand the adult stem cell population. We have shown that the Rb/E2F pathway plays a key role in expanding and maintaining adult neural precursor cells by activating genes that expand the stem cell population in the brain. In the studies described in this proposal, we will identify exactly how Rb/E2F pathway functions to control the stem cell population and devise strategies to modify the activity of this pathway in the adult. The overall goal is develop new strategies by which to regenerate damaged brain tissue.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of poly(A) binding protein in gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: EIF4G; GW182; MIRNA; MRNA TURNOVER; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE; PAIP; PAM2; POLY(A) BINDING PROTEIN; TRANSLATION; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: The vast majority of physiological events that take place in living organisms occur through the actions of proteins. Every protein produced in our body results from the process of translation, by which genetic material in the form of mRNA transcripts is converted to these protein mediators of cellular function. A large number of cellular factors influence translation, one of which is PABP, or Poly(A) binding protein. PABP is a key regulator of the production of proteins, as it binds mRNA transcripts and enables effective translation. Importantly, PABP has been found to also influence the degradation of mRNA, which ultimately influences the amount of protein each mRNA copy can yield. Thus, PABP is a complex and crucial component of proper cellular regulation. To advance our understanding of the fundamental molecular biology processes that enable normal cell function, we aim to determine how PABP functions by studying its structure as it binds to different factors. We also seek to understand how associating with different binding partners can alter the role PABP plays on protein production.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Biological actions of GnRH in human trophoblast and endometrial stromal cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; HORMONE RECEPTORS; INFERTILITY; PLACENTA; PREGNANCY; UTERUS
Abstract-Résumé: The human placenta is a highly invasive organ that invades into the underlying maternal tissues and vasculature, thereby ensuring a continuous blood supply to the developing fetus throughout pregnancy. Hence, the establishment of a successful pregnancy depends on the coordinated development of the embryo and the maternal endometrium. The goal of these studies is to define the roles of gonadotropin-releasing hormones (GnRHs) in human trophoblast and decidual cells. We will continue define the molecular mechanisms that mediate the biological actions of GnRH-I and GnRH-II on established cell culture models. A better understanding of the hormonal, cellular and molecular determinants of implantation and placentation will allow us to delineate the events involved in the establishment of pregnancy under normal and pathological conditions, and reduce the incidence of unfavourable maternal and fetal outcomes.

ClasseRechercheFR: MUSCLES ET OS; AFFECTIONS DE LA MOELLE EPINIERE
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Netrin in motor neuron axon guidance
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; DEVELOPMENT; EMBRYO; GENETICS; LIMB; MOTOR NEURON; NERVOUS SYSTEM; NETRIN; NEURAL CIRCUIT; SPINAL CORD
Abstract-Résumé: The basic units of nervous systems are circuits formed by precisely interconnected neurons. Neurons connect by extending processes called "axons" that are guided to their targets over long distances. Loss of accuracy in this guidance can have disastrous effects on the wiring of our nervous system, such as mental retardation, autism and schizophrenia. Knowing how our nervous system is wired is therefore extremely important if we want to understand how such diseases develop and what could be done to cure them.   In this proposal I outline experiments that address the role of a protein called Netrin, in connecting "motor neurons" in the spinal cord to their muscle targets in the limb. We have preliminary data that show that Netrin is important for this process and here, I propose experiments that will make us understand how Netrin binding to growing axons is translated into a signal that tells the axon which way to turn, grow out more, or stop growing. We know that such signals are also playing important roles in preventing broken axons from re-connecting, for example following spinal cord injury. Our findings will have important implications for our understanding of nervous system assembly in the embryo and the processes that prevent its re-assembly following injury.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Specification of the human cardiovascular lineages from pluripotent stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC DEVELOPMENT; ENDOCARDIAL CELLS; ENGINEERED HEART TISSUE; EPICARDIAL CELLS; VENTRICULAR & ATRIAL CARDIOMYOCYTES
Abstract-Résumé: The focus of this research proposal is to develop methods to produce the major cell types of the human heart from stem cells and then study how these cells interact with each other to generate functional heart tissue.   The long-term goal is to generate specific types of heart cells as well as heart tissue that can be used for transplantation, to study heart disease in a Petri dish and to study how drugs affect heart function.  The studies in this grant proposal are based on recent findings in our lab that have identified methods to make all the major cell types in the heart, including myocardium, the heart muscle cells, epicardium, the cells that provide structure to the heart and endocardium, the cells that line the inside of the heart and contribute to the development of valves.  The studies proposed in this application will investigate how each of these different cell types functions and how they interact with each other to make functional human heart tissue.  The outcome of these studies has a number of important implications for improving public health.  With access to these different human heart cell populations, it will be possible to create engineered heart tissue in a Petri dish that most closely resembles human heart tissue.  This tissue can be used to identify new drugs that may affect heart cell growth and function as well as for testing to identify the unexpected toxic effects of newly produced drugs.  Elimination of such drugs early in production will ultimately lead to the development of safer and cheaper drugs.  If produced from stem cells from patients with specific disease, the engineered tissue will provide a new method for studying human heart disease in a Petri dish.  Finally, engineered human cardiac tissue provides an ideal graft for transplantation for the repair of hearts damaged by a disease.  This type of cell replacement therapy provides a new approach for the future treatment of patients with progressive heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Long chain omega-3 fatty acid supplementation and inflammation in metabolic syndrome: clinical and mechanistic studies
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL STUDY; HEART DISEASE; INFLAMMATION; LONG CHAIN FATTY ACIDS; MOLECULAR STUDIES; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is currently a major public health hazard in most industrialized countries, including Canada. Inflammation appears to be a key component of the obesity-related risk of heart attacks, being perhaps even more important than blood cholesterol. Although research suggests that the numerous health problems associated with obesity including heart attacks have a nutrition basis, there is still an urgent need for further research in this area. Indeed, studies suggest that change in various aspects of lifestyle has been shown to have a significant impact on health outcomes. Fish oils are generally known to reduce the risk of heart attacks but it is unknown if this occurs through anti-inflammatory effects. It is also not known if the inflammation status of obese men and women at risk of heart attacks is differentially modified by different fish oil supplementations. The primary objective of this 4-year research project is to investigate the impact of different fish oils on inflammation in individuals at risk of heart attacks and to examine whether men and women respond differently to various fish oils. This novel research will provide insightful information on how and which fish oils work best to reduce the risk of heart attack associated with obesity and its underlying inflammation state. Results from this study may help tailor more specific recommendations regarding the use of fish oils as part of a heart healthy diet.

TitreApplicationTitle: Leptin Regulation of Glucose Homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; GLUCOSE; INSULIN; ISLET; LEPTIN; TRANSGENIC
Abstract-Résumé: We have found a link between leptin, the so-called obesity hormone and tissues that regulate blood sugar levels.  Mice with a genetic defect in the leptin gene eventually develop obesity and a syndrome resembling type 2 diabetes.  This condition disappears when the mutant mice are treated with leptin.  Remarkably, leptin can also effectively treat diabetes that is not associated with obesity (type 1 diabetes).  The goal of our research is to determine how leptin lowers blood sugar levels.  We will explore the contributions of leptin actions on multiple tissues in the body as well as the brain, which could reveal novel strategies to treat diabetes.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; STERILITE DE LA FEMME
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Dissection of Small RNA Pathways that Impact Chromatin
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGONAUTE; C. ELEGANS; CENTROMERE; CHROMATIN; CHROMOSOME ARCHITECTURE; EPIGENETICS; GENE SILENCING PATHWAYS; REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION; RNAI; SMALL RNA
Abstract-Résumé: Centromeres are structures on chromosomes that are essential for the proper separation of the DNA during cell division, acting as a molecular handle for the cell to latch onto and pull chromosomes apart. Defects in centromeres lead to inequities in the division of chromosomes, and result in the inheritance of too few or too many genes in daughter cells. Having too much or too little DNA underlies diseases such as cancer, leads to genetic disorders such as Down syndrome, and impacts overall fertility. Thus, understanding how centromeres are built and controlled is critical for devising treatments or preventative measures for such conditions.   One newly discovered cellular mechanism for regulating centromeres is executed by tiny RNA molecules, known as small RNAs. Small RNAs normally play key roles in regulating gene expression during development, and in combating cellular invaders such as viruses. The notion that small RNAs influence the construction of centromeres in animals opens a new and exciting field of study, and leads to a more complete understanding of how centromeres are regulated.    We will use the soil nematode, C. elegans, to uncover the functions of particular small RNA pathways in organizing centromeres and properly separating chromosomes. C. elegans is a well-established research model, possessing many of the same key tissue types and cellular functions as humans. Many important advances in understanding other small RNA mechanisms initially were made using C. elegans, and subsequently were found to extend to humans. Thus, the worm provides an ideal context in which to study small RNA pathways.    Because properly building and separating chromosomes ensures the appropriate transmission of DNA to new cells and prevents mutations, understanding how small RNA pathways regulate such processes provides key insights into fertility, normal human development, cancer emergence, and ideally could lead to new therapeutic agents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Pediatric Weight Management Registry (CANPWR): Identifying the characteristics of successful change in Canadian pediatric weight management programs.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD OBESITY; DETERMINANTS; HEALTH OUTCOMES; INSULIN RESISTANCE; INTERVENTION; LONGITUDINAL
Abstract-Résumé: Rates of obesity in Canadian children have increased 3 fold over the last 3 decades; 27% of Canadian children are now overweight or obese. We now understand that these children have health problems relating to their obesity as children and into adulthood. These health risks have resulted in urgent calls to prevent obesity AND to improve the care of children who are overweight. While we have a few studies that tell us that weight management programs can work over the short term, we know that not all children respond the same to these programs - and many do not respond at all. We also do not know if these programs can induce changes beyond 6 months to 1 year. The Canadian Pediatric Weight management Registry (CANPWR) is a study designed to address these questions in weight management programs across Canada, and a small,pilot study has begun. We plan to enroll 1600 children over 2 years across 8 leading Canadian weight management programs. The participants will begin the study as they enter one of the weight management programs and will be followed for at least 3 years. We will collect information about the child's health status (body measurements and metabolic health including sugar metabolism and cholesterol levels) and we will seek to understand what causes variation in health status by examining potential causes or determinants. These determinants may be individual, family or program type determinants. Most importantly, we will measure changes in health status over time and potential reasons why some experience change and some do not. This information is expected to help us design programs best suited to improving the health of individuals and families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Ryanodine Receptor in Cardiac Alternans and Ventricular Fibrillation
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM IMAGING; CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIAS; CARDIOMYOPATHIES; DISEASE MUTATIONS; EXCITATION-CONTRACTION COUPLING; RYANODINE RECEPTOR; SINGLE CHANNEL RECORDINGS; SR CALCIUM RELEASE; STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: In the heart, muscle contraction is triggered by the release of calcium from the internal calcium stores called the sarcoplasmic reticulum, whereas muscel relaxation is achieved by moving the released calcium back to the the stores. To ensure stable muscle contraction and relaxation, i.e. heart beats, calcium release and reuptake must be precisely controlled. However, in some pathological settings, this calcium cycling is disturbed, leading to alternating changes in calcium release and musche contraction in a beat-to-beat basis, a phenomenon known as calcium alternans that can cause electrical alternans in the heart, resulting in irregular heart beats and sudden death. At the moment, the mechanism underlying these beat-to-beat variations is unclear. The objective of this research proposal is to investigate how alternating changes in calcium release occurs and how defects in the calcium release channel lead to calcium release alternations and irregular heart beats. Recent studies from Dr. Chen's laboratory have provided some important clues to these fundamental questions. A variety of cutting-edge technologies will be employed to study the role of the channel in controlling calcium release and how this process is affected by disease-causing mutations in the channel.  These proposed studies will shed novel and exciting insights into the molecular basis and regulation of Ca2+ release, and have profound implications for the prevention and treatment of various heart diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding VANG-1/Van Gogh and PRKL-1/Prickle function during neurite growth inhibition in C. elegans
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; AXON REGENERATION; C. ELEGANS; GENETIC SCREENS; NEURONAL POLARITY; PLANAR CELL POLARITY
Abstract-Résumé: Animal behaviour is ultimately determined by the coordinated assembly of neurons into a complex and precise network of connections involving each other and their peripheral targets. Failure to assemble normal neural circuits during embryonic or childhood development can result in severe movement, behavioural, and/or learning deficits. Mechanisms that inhibit neurite growth play an essential role in sculpting neuronal connections by blocking inappropriate neurite formation, repelling growth cones during axon pathfinding, and terminating axon growth at target sites. We are interested in understanding these mechanisms using the anatomically simple nervous system of C. elegans as a model system. We have shown that VANG-1 and PRKL-1, core components of planar polarity signalling, specifically inhibit inappropriate neurite growth along directional vectors that are otherwise permissive for growth. To gain further insight into this process we propose to use genetic and biochemical approaches to understand how VANG-1 and PRKL-1 interact and to identify new pathway components. In the long term, we believe that factors that inhibit neurite growth may act as targets in new strategies to promote regeneration of axons damaged by neurodegenerative diseases, stroke or brain and spinal cord injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engineering biosensors for fluorescence imaging of neuronal signalling in whole animals
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIORHODOPSIN; CALCIUM ION INDICATORS; DANIO RERIO (ZEBRAFISH); FLUORESCENCE; GREEN FLUORESCENT PROTEIN; NEURONAL IMAGING; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; SIGNALLING; VOLTAGE INDICATORS; XENOPUS TADPOLES
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins are the tools that orchestrate and perform the countless biochemical reactions required for thought, growth, and proliferation. Proteins are also one of the most important classes of tools used for the study of these very same biochemical processes. For example, fluorescent proteins from marine organisms enable researchers to genetically target fluorescent probes to the nerve cells of a model organism and thus visualize neuronal dynamics in whole animals. However, while structure is important, neuroscientists are much more interested in visualizing neuronal function. We propose to use protein engineering to create the next generation of imaging tools which will make the visualization of neuronal function a widely accessible experimental reality.      Protein engineering is an endeavour that is focused on improving the properties of proteins and rendering them more useful for practical applications. To achieve the goals of this grant we propose to focus our protein engineering efforts on specific classes of proteins: fluorescent protein-based biosensors of intracellular messengers, and rhodopsin-based biosensors of membrane potential. Using powerful protein engineering and directed protein evolution strategies, we will modify and optimize these biosensors for improved performance in functional neural imaging. The resulting biosensors will be validated in model systems and initially applied to studies of central nervous system development and synaptic transmission. Ultimately, these new probe molecules will provide the neuroscience community with new windows into the transmission of signals through neural networks, and will lead to an improved understanding of the fundamental processes underlying brain function and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of health insurance vs. unconditional cash transfer on socio-economic and neurobiological welfare measures of the poor: evidence from randomized experiments in the slums of Nairobi, undertaken by an international collaboration between a "Jua kali" community, Kenyan health insurance providers, economists, neuroscientists, and Kenyan policy decision makers
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; HEALTH INSURANCE; NEUROBIOLOGICAL WELL-BEING MEASURES; POVERTY REDUCTION; STRESS; UNCONDITIONAL CASH TRANSFER
Abstract-Résumé: The lack of health insurance and the persistence of poverty are intricately related. According to the 2001 World Development Report, "reducing vulnerability to economic shocks, ill health, disability, and personal violence, is an intrinsic part of enhancing well-being of the poor and encourages investment in human capital and in higher-risk, higher-return activities". In this way, health insurance may mitigate the risks faced by poor individuals.  Health insurance schemes generally improve health care access, but not always for the very poor, if, for example, transport costs to the hospital are in fact the largest expenses. An unconditional cash transfer of the same amount may actually be more beneficial as the poor are better placed to know their needs and if they do not squander their money on unnecessary non-durables.  The relative merit of health insurance over UCT is thus an open empirical question, and has never been studied before. This project will address this gap in the literature by providing the first randomized experiment on the relative merits of health insurance vs UCT, by comparing a group of poor households offered free health insurance to a control group offered the cash equivalent. The survey will include questions regarding the economic situation of the member and his/her family. Moreover, to assess health and psychological well-being, saliva and blood samples will be collected to measure biomarkers of stress, in particular cortisol and cytokine levels. An important question concerns the willingness to pay for insurance. The partnership will thus implement six different interventions aimed at increasing take-up of health insurance.   These randomized experiments will thus directly inform insurance providers and policy makers about the scale-up of health insurance vs UCT provision, not only in Kenya but also elsewhere in the world, and have the potential to benefit the lives of millions of people currently out of reach of these products.

TitreApplicationTitle: Magnetic resonance imaging biomarkers in ALS
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; BRAIN; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEURODEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disabling, rapidly progressive, and fatal neurodegenerative disorder. There is no treatment that significantly slows progression. Increasing age is an important risk factor for developing ALS; thus, the societal impact of this devastating disease will become more profound as the population ages. A significant hurdle to finding effective treatment has been an inability to accurately measure brain degeneration in humans. Advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques hold promise in this respect, and may assist in aiding diagnosis, prognostication, and the efficient testing of new drugs.   In this multicentre study, different MRI features of brain degeneration will be measured in a large sample of patients with ALS. The ability of these MRI features to track disease progression will be tested.

ClasseRechercheFR: GLAUCOME; TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Ocular Biomechanics and Glaucoma:  Finite Element Modeling of the Optic Nerve's Response to Biomechanical Insult and it's Role in Astrocyte Activation
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; FINITE ELEMENT MODELLING; GLAUCOMA; GLIAL CELL ACTIVATION; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; OPTIC NERVE; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Glaucoma is the world's most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting more people than all other neurodegenerative diseases combined. It is also the second leading cause of blindness worldwide, but is both difficult to detect and those with the disease do not notice symptoms until late in disease development. High pressure in the eye is known to be a major risk factor for glaucoma. However the mechanisms by which raised pressure damages the nerves at the back of the eye are poorly understood.   Previously we used computer modeling to determine which characteristics of an eye determine its sensitivity to the effects of high pressure. We propose to continue this approach with new high resolution, engineering analysis of the optic nerve to predict how high pressure damages the neural tissue.  We will combine the computer models with experimental models of glaucoma. In these experimental models cells are grown then stressed in various ways, including stretch and compressive strain, designed to mimic the biomechanical environment experienced within the optic nerve. The resulting proteins are harvested and analyzed to determine the mechanisms responsible for the development of glaucoma. We propose to refine and further develop these cell-based models to take advantage of our new bioengineering findings. In this way we hope to better understand the insult generated by increased pressure in the eye; apply the estimated insult to cells of the optic nerve and in so doing identify markers for the early, objective diagnosis of glaucoma, along with potential pathways for the development of new therapies. The combination of the experiments and the modeling approaches will help us explore in much more detail than is possible with only one approach. The proposed research can improve personal and population health by finding new ways to diagnose glaucoma along with defining new potential therapies for this insidious, blinding disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ultraviolet light mediated induction and acceleration of SLE
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOANTIBODIES; AUTOIMMUNITY; DENDRITIC CELL; FLOW CYTOMETRY; TRANSGENIC MICE; ULTRAVIOLET LIGHT
Abstract-Résumé: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a systemic disease in which the immune system is overactive ad damages normal tissue. Excessive sunlight exposure is known to induce a lupus skin rash in predisposed people and can also worsen systemic lupus erythematosus. Why people with lupus develop these untoward reactions to sunlight is not yet clear. We have developed an animal model of sun induced worsening of systemic lupus erythematosus using a strain of mice known to be prone to diabetes. As we can study these mice after intense sun exposure and before disease onset, we will use these mice to learn about the abnormal reactions that occur in the skin and that lead to systemic illness. We will also examine patients with SLE and determine the role the skin and sun exposure may have in affecting disease. These studies will allow us to better council patients with regards to sun exposure and may lead to new, skin-directed treatments for disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving vision-targeted health-related quality of life in Parkinson's disease: A feasibility study for orthoptic treatment of convergence insufficiency.
Keywords-MotsClés: CONVERGENCE INSUFFICIENCY; ORTHOPTIC/VISION TRAINING; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; VISION-TARGETED HEALTH-RELATED QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) suffer from many motor symptoms such as resting tremor, rigidity and postural instability. However, they also suffer from many non-motor symptoms, including eye and vision symptoms.  Of particular interest is the fact that many patients with PD suffer from reading difficulty, eyestrain when reading and sometimes double vision. These symptoms are often linked with a condition called "convergence insufficiency" (CI), which is characterized by difficulty of the two eyes to converge on close objects or to maintain convergence on close objects for a prolonged period of time. The consequence of this for a person with PD is that they may not be able to enjoy reading because of symptoms such as eyestrain, headaches, blurred vision, fatigue or double vision. The prevalence of CI in the general population is about 5% and can be treated very successfully with eye exercises, a therapy called orthoptic treatment (OT). Very little is known regarding CI in a population of patients with PD and OT has never been attempted to help these patients. In this study, we will verify the effectiveness of OT to decrease the signs and symptoms of CI in patients with PD, and determine if successful OT improves vision-targeted health-related quality of life in those patients. If beneficial effects can be demonstrated, this study has the real potential of improving reading ability and comfort in PD patients, as well as their quality of life, through a benign intervention.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
ClasseRechercheFR: VIEILLISSEMENT; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of circulating insulin on metabolism and mammalian longevity
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY AND PROTEIN HOMEOSTASIS; EXTRA-PANCREATIC INSULIN IN THE BRAIN; HEALTHY AGING; HORMONAL AND NEURONAL CONTROL OF LONGEVITY; INSULIN AS A TISSUE GROWTH FACTOR; INSULIN RESISTANCE AND GLUCOSE HOMEOSTASIS; KNOCKOUT MOUSE MODELS; MECHANISMS OF AGING AND LONGEVITY; REGULATION OF ADIPOGENESIS BY INSULIN; REGULATION OF LIFESPAN BY DIET AND CALORIC RESTRICTION
Abstract-Résumé: Both genetic and environmental factors are thought to contribute to growth, healthy aging and longevity. Studies in worms and flies have clearly demonstrated that the insulin signaling has a negative effect on longevity. Seemingly counterintuitive evidence has also been presented that mice lacking the insulin receptor in fat also have improved lifespan. However, there has been no direct demonstration that insulin itself modulates tissue growth or longevity in mammals. An ideal way to test this hypothesis would be to vary the amount of insulin in genetically engineered mice. The total lack of Insulin genes leads to diabetes at birth, but mice live normally with only one copy of the Insulin gene. Mice have two insulin genes: Insulin 2, which has a broad tissue distribution like human insulin and Insulin, which is restricted to the pancreas. The Insulin 1 gene is therefore an ideal tool to examine the specific effects of circulating insulin on metabolism and longevity. We have taken advantage of this and begun to characterize mice with two of the four copies of the insulin gene, as well as mice with only one insulin gene copy. Our preliminary data suggest that mice lacking all but 1 insulin gene allele are smaller but healthier than controls with reduced fat and lower blood sugar levels. Since these are all features of mice with extended lifespan, we have good reason to properly examine longevity in a controlled study. Our data also provide novel evidence that insulin negatively controls energy expenditure in fat tissue. Our findings have the potential to change multiple paradigms in the fields of aging and metabolism, but directly implicating insulin in this integrated system. The findings are likely to translate to humans, where high circulating insulin is a prominent feature of the emerging worldwide epidemics of obesity and type 2 diabetes and human lifespan is predicted to fall for the first time in recorded history.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - C : Systèmes digestif, endocrinien et excrétoire

ClasseRechercheFR: SYSTEME GENITO-URINAIRE; AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES
TitreApplicationTitle: Non-invasive monitoring of pediatric kidney allograft injury to improve diagnosis and patient outcome.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; CHEMOKINES; KIDNEY; METABOLOMICS; PEDIATRIC; PROTEOMICS; REJECTION; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Kidney transplantation is a life-saving treatment for children with end-stage kidney failure. A major threat to success is rejection, where the body's immune system attacks and destroys the transplanted kidney. If rejection isn't treated early, it results in permanent injury that can lead to loss of the transplant and a return to dialysis.  Currently, tests that monitor kidney function will miss early or mild rejection. Instead, we screen with repeated kidney biopsies, which are risky and unpleasant.  This research program will use proven techniques to identify signs of kidney injury and rejection in the urine of children who have had a kidney transplant. It will focus on the first year after transplant, since this is the highest risk for rejection. We will look for metabolites and chemokines that we have tested before to identify when injury or rejection is present. Metabolites are small molecules produced by our cells as part of their function or as waste products. Chemokines are a different type of molecule that is produced by our immune system to signal inflammation. We already know some of the changes that occur with rejection. We now plan to validate that the same changes are present in other Canadian children with kidney transplants.  We will ask children with a new kidney transplant and their families to participate in this study. They will provide a urine sample for analysis whenever they have a kidney biopsy and also at regular intervals after transplant. We will verify the metabolite and chemokine levels that are linked to rejection, and could predict rejection in other children. Once it has been refined, we will determine whether it improves outcome by using it as a test for real-time monitoring and limit our use of regular kidney biopsies. We hope to demonstrate that this will improve the accuracy to detect rejection early, reduce the number of biopsies and improve the health and long-term kidney function of children with a transplant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Virtual Reality based Spatial Memory Intervention for patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: ANATOMY; FMRI; HIPPOCAMPUS; SPATIAL MEMORY; VBM; VIRTUAL NAVIGATION
Abstract-Résumé: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is an intermediate stage between normal aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD). AD causes degeneration in the hippocampus (HPC) and this has been linked to memory loss. We propose to test patients with MCI and healthy controls on a computer training program specifically aimed at stimulating the hippocampus, in order to help alleviate the memory loss caused by AD.  We previously developed a virtual task to test the ability to find objects in the environment. The caudate nucleus (CN) and hippocampus are brain regions involved in this ability. We found that the participants who used environmental landmarks (such as trees and buildings) a strategy we call "spatial learning", involved activity in the hippocampus. The other participants used a strategy called "response learning" which relies on the CN. This strategy involves learning a route by performing a sequence of movements repeatedly (turn right at the end of the road). We found that people using spatial learning have more grey matter in the HPC than people using response learning. Since the HPC is affected by AD, we developed a spatial memory training program for MCI patients in order to try and stimulate this region.  Participants will undergo a 2 month program of two 60-minute sessions per week totaling 16 hours of spatial memory training over 8 weeks. We will test 143 MCI patients and healthy elderly over four years. Only half of them will go through the training program. The other half will act as controls and will be engaged in other stimulating activities that do not involve spatial memory in order to discriminate changes due to the spatial memory intervention program from non-specific changes associated with training at our research laboratory. If successful, this program will lead to better navigational skills, greater functional autonomy and better quality of life in patients and healthy participants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Potentiation of cancer immunotherapy by HDAC inhibition
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER IMMUNOTHERAPY; HISTONE DEACETYLASE INHIBITORS; ONCOLYTIC VIROTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Viruses that selectively kill tumor cells as a result of natural tropism or genetic engineering are termed oncolytic viruses. Some of these viruses are currently enrolled in clinical trials and show promising results. However, despite their destructive potency against tumor masses, consistent long-term regression has yet to be achieved. We have recently developed an approach to potentiate the killing capacity of oncolytic viruses and sustain tumor regression through the stimulation of robust antitumor responses. Furthermore, we have identified an anticancer drug that can simultaneously enhance oncolytic activity and antitumor immunity. This has led to dramatically improved therapeutic outcomes. Our proposed studies are designed to understand the mechanisms underlying this synergy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Visual Motion Compensation in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: BAYESIAN OPTIMAL OBSERVER; BRAIN; CAUSAL INFERENCE; COMMON CAUSE; DISORDERS OF MISATTRIBUTION; HEALTHY POPULATIONS; PERCEPTION OF MOTION; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SENSORY-MOTOR
Abstract-Résumé: When we move, our senses tell us we are moving. With our eyes we see motion, with receptors in our skin, muscles and joints we feel motion and in concert with our balance organs (our vestibular system) we perceive motion. Together, the action of our muscles and sensation of motion are all bound to provide a single experience of self initiated motion. It is the nervous systems job to create this experience. When information arrives coincidentally from two or more senses the nervous system is tasked with identifying whether or not this information has come from a common source, such as our own movement, in a process called causal inference. Causal inference is important because without it we would not know whether or not we actually moved. In schizophrenia, causal inference breaks down and in some cases these peoples' ability to identify their own movements is reduced. The purpose of this research is a) to examine how sensory information, specifically visual and vestibular (sense of balance) information, must be matched in order to attribute it to a common source, b) to examine how visual and vestibular information must be matched with body movement in order to feel like body movement caused the sensations and c) to determine if causal inference based on visual and vestibular cues is impaired in patients with schizophrenia exhibiting delusions of control. This study will identify how visual and vestibular information is combined in the brain to provide a unified sensation of motion and identify the conditions necessary for us to attribute our actions to causing motion. In addition, this study will determine if these processes are impaired by schizophrenia providing a foundation from which to better understand how the disease process influences causal inference based on visual and vestibular cues.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the Underlying Mechanisms and Treatment of Repeated Concussions
Keywords-MotsClés: ANATOMICAL MRI; CHRONIC TRAUMATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY; DIFFUSION MRI; FLUID PERCUSSION INJURY; NEURODEGENERATION; NEUROINFLAMMATION; RAT MODEL; REPEATED CONCUSSIONS; TAUOPATHY; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Concussions account for 80% of all traumatic brain injuries (TBI). Despite the high incidence of concussion, there is currently a poor understanding of what occurs in the brain following this injury and, as a result, there is much debate surrounding the medical treatment of concussion. Medical concern is further increased for individuals who are at risk of suffering multiple concussions, such as athletes and military personnel, as growing evidence indicates that repeated concussion can result in neurodegenerative disease. Given the lack of understanding, high incidence rates, and growing costs associated with TBI, it is imperative that research is carried out that addresses this issue.  Animal models provide a means to examine the factors involved in concussion, as well as potential treatments, in experiments that cannot be conducted using human patients. My previous research has utilized repeated mild lateral fluid percussion injuries (mLFP) in the rat to investigate the effects of repeated concussions. These studies found that repeated mLFPs cause cumulative and chronic  changes consistent with those observed in athletes who have experienced repeated concussions. Specifically, these studies have implicated neuroinflammation and hyperphosphorylated tau in the cumulative, chronic, and neurodegenerative effects of repeated concussion.  The proposed project will use this animal model of repeated concussion, and apply advanced imaging, immunohistochemical, molecular, and behavioral techniques, to further examine the underlying mechanisms of repeated concussions, as well as their potential treatment. Specifically, through the use of genetically modified mice and novel concussion therapies, these studies will examine the roles of hyperphosphorylated tau and neuroinflammation in repeated concussions. Together these studies will greatly contribute to our understanding of repeated concussion  and hold important implications for their management in the clinical setting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Massively Parallel Whole Genome Sequencing for the Clinical Identification of Mutations That Cause Intellectual Disability
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; GENE MUTATION; GENOTYPE-PHENOTYPE CORRELATION; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; WHOLE GENOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Intellectual disability (ID) is a life-long and debilitating condition with deficits in cognitive functioning and social skills, often with behavioural issues such as autism, epilepsy and other disabilities. ID affects 2-3% of children globally making it one of the most common disorders. As a disease category, its health care cost is massive-almost equal to the combined economic impact of stroke, heart disease and cancer. Moreover ID places a profound psychological burden on a family with an affected child. In about half of children with ID, no cause is recognized, exacerbating the emotional trauma for the family and hindering patient care. The highest yielding current diagnostic test for ID is microarray, which detects gains or losses of genetic material called copy number variants (CNVs) in 15% of patients. In addition to CNVs, DNA sequence changes or mutations are known in about 300 genes that cause ID. Testing for these mutations must be done one-by-one in a time-consuming and expensive process.Medical management is immediately improved once a diagnosis is established, often leading to educational and social support for the family. A new technology, 'next generation sequencing' or NGS is able to read the child's entire DNA sequence in a single test. NGS can also detect CNVs, making it a powerful and comprehensive screen for a causative genetic change. We will use NGS to look for causative mutations in 10 affected children in whom no recognizable cause has been found by standard assessment, and both their normal parents. Testing both parents, will enable us to  distinguish inherited normal genetic change events from mutations that have newly arisen in the child and are likely disease causing. We will then test the genes identified in 50 unrelated children with ID, to establish their frequency. This project will potentially diagnose patients with ID, discover new genes for the disease and help establish NGS as a tool in routine clinical testing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Use of Calcium Channel Blockers to Prevent Prostate Cancer Metastases: Impact on Survival
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKERS; METASTASIS; MORTALITY; PROSTATE CANCER; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, prostate cancer is the most common form of cancer diagnosed in men, accounting for over one quarter of all cancers and more than ten percent of all cancer deaths. Men with prostate cancer metastasis have the poorest outcomes.  A number of previous studies, as well as some recent results from laboratory experiments in animals, have shown a protective association between certain medications, known as calcium channel blockers, and the development of cancer.  The goal of this study is to determine if calcium channel blocking medications can potentially prevent prostate cancer metastases. British Columbia is the ideal place to conduct this research, as all necessary data on patient disease history and drug use are available through the B.C. Cancer Registry and B.C. Ministry of Health. All data provided are anonymized to protect the privacy of patients.  Men diagnosed with prostate cancer in B.C. between 1986 and 2011 will be identified using data from the B.C. Cancer Registry. Linked data from B.C. PharmaNet will provide information on the dispensing of calcium channel blocking medications. Information on cancer metastases and survival rate will also be collected. We will conduct analyses to determine if specific calcium channel blocking medications improve patient outcomes. Results of our study will be published in medical journals and presented to national and international researchers and clinicians interested in prostate cancer.  If an association is found between calcium channel blocker use and survival or metastases appearance in prostate cancer patients, then calcium channel blockers could potentially be prescribed to either prevent metastases or prolong survival in prostate cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of high density lipoproteins (HDL) on valvular calcification.
Keywords-MotsClés: AORTIC VALVES; APOA-I; CALCIFICATION; HDL; OSTEOBLASTS; OSTEOCLASTS
Abstract-Résumé: Aortic stenosis (AS) is a pathology afflicting aortic valves and having many similarities with atherosclerosis. Histological features of AS suggest a chronic inflammation that culminate with a proeminent calcification of aortic valves. At this time, aortic valve replacement is the only available solution for patients suffering from AS. However, our group has recently obtained results suggesting the possibility to develop medication for patients suffering from AS.Indeed, we have demonstrated that administration of ApoA-I mimetic peptide can induce the regression of valvular calcification. However, the mechanism by which this peptide induces this effect remains unknown. Given that ApoA-I is a main component of HDL, these results suggest that lipoproteins could be implicated in the regression of calcification. However, to our knowledge, there are actually no studies on this topic. Thus, our hypothesis is that HDL have the ability to prevent and regress valvular calcification by influencing anti-calcifying proteins and osteoclast-like cells. We are confident that the understanding of events leading to activation or inhibition of osteoclast activity in this illness will be helpful for the elaboration of therapeutic strategies. Moreover, since AS has many similarities with atherosclerosis, the understanding of AS could also serve benefit the treatment of atherosclerosis. Given the social importance of this research and the high therapeutic potential, we are confident that results will lead to high quality publications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing multi-modal neuroimaging methods and re-training interventions to examine and improve cognitive control functioning in addiction
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ANTERIOR CINGULATE CORTEX; COGNITIVE CONTROL; CRAVING; DOPAMINE SYSTEM; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MULTI-MODAL NEUROIMAGING; NICOTINE DEPENDENCE; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Addiction is a very complex and heterogeneous disorder. It is increasingly evident that addiction is fundamentally a disorder of neural and cognitive mechanisms that implement reward-related learning, but individual differences in the transition to addiction remain largely unexplored. Understanding such differences is critical for the development of therapies that are tailored appropriately for different subpopulations of substance abusers. To address this issue, many experts encourage the development of multimodal neuroimaging approaches for understanding individual variations in cognitive function and dysfunction in addiction. The proposed project accords with this 'up and coming' approach and will investigate how complex reward representations (effort, saliency, motivation) are functionally connected and organized in the brain, how these contribute to individual differences in cognitive function and dysfunction, and whether such dysfunction can be rehabilitated. Specifically, combined functional and diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging will be used to identify the functional and structural connectivity underlying complex neural representations related to effort and salience in both healthy and nicotine dependent individuals. Then, these methods will be utilized to evaluate the effectiveness of a craving-control behavioral intervention (aimed to restore the balance between the relative impulsive processes and reflective/control processes), in combination with transcranial magnetic current stimulation (aimed at stimulating the cognitive systems mediating complex reward processing). Success in these efforts will accelerate our understanding of individual differences in cognitive vulnerabilities related to addiction and facilitate the development of science-based treatment interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Communicating with unresponsive patients in critical care: using event-related potentials to enable interaction with family and health care professionals
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY; AUGMENTATIVE AND ALTERNATIVE COMMUNICATION; CRITICAL CARE; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY; EVENT-RELATED POTENTIALS; FAMILY AND CAREGIVERS; UNRESPONSIVE PATIENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Communication in critical care settings is impossible for many patients as a result of either severe injury or life-sustaining measures used in intensive care.  These conditions not only impede traditional methods of communication such as speech and gesture, they often result in fatigue, pain, and confusion which prevent patients from using assistive technologies for communication.  This inability to communicate (1) is responsible for a greater than 40% misdiagnosis rate in levels of consciousness; (2) is a source of profound distress for patients, their family and health-care professionals; and (3) has grave consequences with respect to end-of-life decision-making.  Recent research has demonstrated that event-related brain potentials (ERPs) can show a patient's responsiveness, even if the patient is only passively paying attention to their environment.  The objective of this research is to develop and test a system that enables interaction with patients in critical care by giving family and health care professionals the ability to perceive a patient's ERPs.  Our central hypothesis is that the ability to perceive a patient's responses will reduce feelings of stress and helplessness in both the patient and family, aid in the continuous monitoring of a patient's state of consciousness, and ultimately improve patient outcome.  The successful completion of this research will provide a surrogate form of communication with patients in critical care, enabling family and caregivers to make more informed choices of treatments and interventions, and to retain a sense of connection and control within the volatile environment of critical care.  This research will have a major impact on how we interact with individuals who are both temporarily and permanently unable to communicate; thus, it has the potential to positively impact the overall quality of the Canadian healthcare system and the quality of life of Canadians living with a severe communication disability.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health Service Use and Outcomes Following the First-Episode of Psychosis: A Comparison of Users and Non-Users of Early Intervention Services
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS & YOUNG ADULTS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICES; PSYCHOSIS; STIGMA
Abstract-Résumé: An episode of a psychotic disorder, the most serious form of mental illness, is a very confusing, frightening, and difficult time for patients and their family. Clinicians and researchers working in the field of psychotic disorders are attempting to intervene early in the course of illness by identifying individuals at high-risk for psychosis (HRP). Intervening in this high-risk group may prevent or delay the onset of psychosis and reduce morbidity and disability from this debilitating disorder. However, there are legitimate concerns regarding the risks associated with intervening in individuals who have not yet developed a diagnosable disorder, especially given that many individuals will not go on to develop the full symptoms of psychosis. One such concern is the high risk of stigma, both from external sources and self-stigma. No studies to date have examined the consequences of identifying individuals at risk on the stigma experiences of young people at a high risk of psychosis. This study will investigate the effects of stigma in this high-risk population, and look at the impact of stigma on the use of mental health services. Specifically, this study will examine the extent to which baseline measures of stigma are associated with patterns of health services use preceding identification as HRP, and the impact of stigma on subsequent engagement with health services. The results will further our understanding of some of the barriers patients face when seeking help for the early symptoms of a psychotic disorder. This information could help health care administrators and policy makers to provide less stigmatizing services, and can help inform interventions aimed at countering the pervasive stigma faced by individuals suffering from mental illness. This is a crucial component of the discourse on HRP to determine whether the benefits gleaned from preventing potential cases of psychotic disorder outweigh the risks of identifying and labelling those at highest risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving cholesterol efflux by targeted disruption of hepatic lipase interactions with the cell surface
Keywords-MotsClés: CHOLESTEROL; CHOLESTEROL EFFLUX; HEPATIC LIPASE; HIGH DENSITY LIPOPROTEIN; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE (NMR); PEPTIDE DRUGS; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; RECOMBINANT PROTEIN; REVERSE CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the Western world. The blockage of blood vessels is one of the major causes of this disease. The blockage is initiated by the uptake of blood fats carried by "bad cholesterol" (or LDL) into blood vessel walls. Existing medications are designed to reduce the levels of "bad cholesterol" and other bad fats in the blood. However, medications are also needed to promote both the removal of the cholesterol and bad fats from the vessel walls by "good cholesterol" (or HDL) and the removal of these fats from the body. The removal of the fats from blood vessels could slow disease progress or even reverse the blockage process. We will study an enzyme that might create more HDL in the blood from already existing HDL molecules. This enzyme, called hepatic lipase, breaks down fats on HDL. When this occurs, proteins fall off of HDL that can go on to make new smaller HDL molecules. Hepatic lipase is not normally free in the blood to carry out this process. Instead, hepatic lipase is normally bound to tissues such as the liver. We will design and test molecules that may specifically release hepatic lipase into the blood. Interruption of hepatic lipase binding should lead to the production of new smaller HDL. We will also test if the breakdown of fats from HDL by released hepatic lipase will result in the removal of the cholesterol and bad fats from cells that are typically found in blood vessel walls. Our engineered molecules may be used as a beneficial treatment against the initiation of blockages in blood vessels.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tubedown signaling pathway as a therapeutic target for age-related retinopathies
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLTRANSFERASE; AGE-RELATED RETHINOPATHIES; AGING; ANIMAL MODEL; ENDOTHELIUM; NEOVASCULARIZATION; PERMEABILITY; SIGNALING PATHWAY; TRANSGENIC; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: During aging, vision loss is a devastating problem that greatly impacts upon the quality of life and the maintenance of functional autonomy. Both proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are the leading causes of blindness in aging populations. Both diseases involve the overgrowth of blood vessels in the retinal tissue of the eye. New therapies are needed to prevent and improve treatment of these age-related retinal diseases. We discovered Tubedown, a factor present in healthy retinal blood vessels but reduced during retinal aging and during overgrowth of retinal blood vessels. Using laboratory mice, we have found that loss of Tubedown from retinal blood vessels is an important predisposing factor for the progression of experimental retinopathy which mimics several of the hallmarks of human AMD and PDR. This project will examine the involvement and importance of potential effectors of Tubedown in retinal blood vessels during aging and during overgrowth of retinal blood vessels in existing mouse models and human specimens. We will also examine how Tubedown effectors can be targeted for the treatment of age-related retinal disease in mouse models. Manipulation of Tubedown effectors in retinal blood vessels may provide a new and specific therapeutic approach for preventing and treating age-related retinal diseases such as AMD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural Basis of Visual Behavior
Keywords-MotsClés: EYE MOVEMENTS; NEURONAL ACTIVITY; POSTERIOR PARIETAL CORTEX; RHESUS MONKEY; SUPERIOR COLLICULUS; VISUAL ATTENTION; VISUAL COGNITION; VISUAL PERCEPTION; VISUAL PROCESSING; VISUAL WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: What we see in the world around us depends on our ability to regulate the incessant, voluntary movements of our eyes that direct our gaze to salient visual details. Grasping the full content of a visual situation, however, requires not only the perception of visual information but also the efficient deployment of visual attention and working memory capacity. These cognitive processes are indispensable to direct our gaze to details that are both novel and relevant to the task at hand. How we judiciously control our gaze to take snapshots of the visual world is Dr. Pare's primary research focus. In this project, his team will study brain regions that process visual information and provide guidance signals for the programming of eye movements. The goal is to develop accurate descriptions of the brain mechanisms that not only make us perceive the world the way we do but also select any of our actions. The results will help answer key questions, such as how does our visual system represent simultaneously the many visual details available during each gaze fixation and decide which one to look at next? How do we retaining the information about which details in a visual scene we have already been examined so that we do not look at them repeatedly? How do we gather visual information seamlessly, even from complex visual situations? Answers to these questions are essential to build a comprehensive understanding of the important cognitive processes taking place in our brains. The results of this research are also expected to advance our understanding of neurological diseases, such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's Diseases, as well as psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Cognitive processing is impaired in these conditions, and they also deteriorate with age. This basic research thus promises potential benefits in health care by providing important insights that could lead to better drugs and therapies for many Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Nod proteins in mucosal defense against bacterial pathogens
Keywords-MotsClés: CROHN'S DISEASE; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; MICROBIOTA; NOD-LIKE RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Nod proteins are host factors that detect bacterial invasion at the level of the gastrointestinal tract. In certain cases of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), especially in Crohn's disease, Nod proteins are dysfunctional. In normal conditions, Nods trigger an immune response in the mucosal lining of the intestine following bacterial detection in order to protect the host from severe infection. Our interest in this grant proposal is to understand the mechanisms that orchestrate this immune reaction driven by Nod proteins and how inefficient responses might impact on the development of IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evading and subverting host cell machineries to ensure HIV-1 genomic RNA fate
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOSOMES; HIV-1/AIDS; INTRACELLULAR TRAFFICKING; NUCLEAR PORE PROTEINS; NUP62; PROTEOMICS AND MASS SPECTROMETRY; RILP; UPF PROTEINS; VIRAL EVASION STRATEGIES; VIRUS-HOST INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: HIV-1 is the causative agent that causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome or AIDS. Since 1981, more than 25 million people have died of AIDS. It is estimated that close to 44 million people worldwide are infected (United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS) and in Canada, recent data released by the Public Health Agency of Canada show that there are about 4000 new HIV-1 infections per year. Without effective treatments or a cure, the socio-economic impact will continue to be disastrous. Several drugs have been developed to target specific processes of the virus replication cycle and have been instrumental in maintaining and enhancing the quality of life and life expectancy of infected individuals. However, HIV-1's ability to adapt leads to sequence variation in the viral genetic material and the inevitable development of resistance to most current drug therapies. This is an all-too-common occurrence that leads to treatment failure and juggling of alternative drug regimens. Without a cure, there is an urgent need to identify new therapeutic targets for drug design to block HIV-1 infection and replication. The proposed projects described in this application represent our efforts to further our understanding on how HIV-1 co-opts some of the cell's major machineries to ensure an environment that allows for efficient viral gene expression. With this knowledge, we can envisage the development effective and new drugs with potent anti-viral activities.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of G-protein and beta-arrestin signaling in the action of the dopamine D2 receptor
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; DOPAMINE RECEPTOR; G-COUPLED PROTEIN RECEPTOR; IN VITRO; IN VIVO; MOLECULAR NEUROBIOLOGY; MOUSE MODELS; REGULATING MECHANISMS; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION PATHWAYS
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a chronic debilitating mental disorder afflicting 1% of the population worldwide. The symptoms of schizophrenia fall into three general categories including positive symptoms (hallucinations and delusions), negative symptoms (social withdrawal, blunted emotional affect) and cognitive deficits.  Although the etiology is unknown, there is evidence to suggest that deregulation of a neurotransmitter called dopamine is involved. More specifically, one of the dopamine receptors, D2R has been suggested to be more functionally relevant given that all antipsychotic drugs are D2R antagonists and that intracellular signalling cascades that the D2R regulates have been implicated in schizophrenia. Recent developments have shown that intracellular signalling of the D2R is complex and that there are distinct signalling mechanisms (G-protein or beta-arrestin). What is unclear is the contribution these two signaling branches have in normal physiological and pathological manifestations of dopamine action. Thus, the current study addresses the role of the two distinct signalling mechanisms of the D2R.  To accomplish this goal an in vivo (mice) approach will be used, where the D2R in the brain can only signal through one of the two signalling branches (G-protein or beta-arrestin). These mice will undergo a series of tests to investigate behavioural, cellular and morphological changes.  Comparing these mice models will demonstrate the role of the individual D2R signalling branches and help to understand the potential contribution these D2R branches have in schizophrenia.  By understanding the mechanism of how the dopamine system contributes to normal physiology and how its dysfunction contributes to schizophrenia will help to identify potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

OrgNm: Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM)
TitreApplicationTitle: Scientifically sound and ethically justifiable: towards a new understanding of evidence in psychiatry
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS; DIAGNOSIS; EPISTEMOLOGY; EVIDENCE; EVIDENCE-BASED MEDICINE; PSYCHIATRY; QUALIATATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Although the contemporary era has been seen tremendous advances in medical technology, psychiatrists do not have sophisticated blood tests and scans to diagnosis problems as do doctors in other areas of medicine. As a consequence, there has been a longstanding debate about whether psychiatric diagnoses are really objective, or whether they just reflect the opinions of the time. Over the last twenty years, psychiatrists have been taught to base their practice on research studies, rather than on what they learn from their clinical experience or from patients during individual appointments. Basing practice on research studies seems more scientific, and psychiatrists have come to regard this new approach as reassurance that psychiatry is just as objective as any other area of medicine.    Research studies do contribute one kind of knowledge to practice, but they do not tell us everything we need to know in order to practice psychiatry well.  As a result, practitioners are left with many unanswered questions about what to do with knowledge they obtain from sources other than research studies. For example, complicated interactions might occur between patient and doctor in a session that give insights into the diagnosis. Is it ethical to take into consideration these insights? If so, under what circumstances?  Is it ethical to practice only on the basis of research studies?  Our research project addresses exactly these questions. We will investigate what kinds of knowledge should be used as the basis of psychiatric practice and, in particular, the determination of psychiatric diagnosis. Our project is vitally important to ensure that both practitioners and patients are aware of the strengths and weaknesses in the knowledge that lies behind psychiatric diagnoses.  The results of this project will help to establish what kind of knowledge is needed for scientific and ethical psychiatric diagnoses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engineering niches to support the development of definitive blood progenitors from human pluripotent stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD DEVELOPMENT; CELL AND TISSUE ENGINEERING; PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; STEM CELL NICHE; T-CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Human pluripotent stem cells (stem cells) have the potential to generate cells and tissues capable of treating many degenerative diseases. The clinical evaluation of stem cell-derived cells is limited by challenges in guiding their differentiation and maturation into relevant target cell types (such as blood cells), and by our inability to produce sufficient quantities of these target cells to enable clinical trials. As we have demonstrated over the last 5 years, novel technologies to engineer the environment around stem cells (so called "niches") represent powerful tools to understand fundamental mechanisms in stem cell fate control and to enable the robust generation of early stem cell derivatives.  This project will take advantage of our ability to generate mesoderm (a primary developmental cell layer that gives rise to tissues such as blood and endothelial cells) to engineer artificial niches to guide the generation of adult-like blood cell progenitors from stem cells. Furthermore, we will specifically demonstrate the developmental capacity of these adult-like blood cell progenitors by guiding their differentiation into functional immune cells (T-cells) using a novel 3-D assay. This project will provide new fundamental insight into the origin of definitive human blood progenitor cells, enable the generation of these cells from a renewable source of stem cells, and lay the foundation for the use of these cells to model immune diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hormonal, genetic, and psychosocial factors in the developing parent-child relationship: A follow up study of parents and their toddlers
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTACHMENT; FOLLOW-UP; MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH; OXYTOCIN; PARENT-CHILD INTERACTION; PSYCHOSOCIAL RISK
Abstract-Résumé: New information from the fields of psychology, genetics, and neurobiology has given us a better understanding of the developing parent-child relationship. Many factors affect the way in which parents interact with their infants and young children, including their own history of adversity, their genetic predisposition to respond in certain ways to stressful situations, psychological symptoms, and hormones like oxytocin (OT) which promote good caregiving behaviour. Our team has been studying the role of OT in mood and anxiety symptoms during pregnancy and the early postpartum period, as well as its association with maternal social cognition and early mother-infant interaction at 8 weeks after birth. The proposed study will follow mothers and their children who are now 2 years of age, to investigate the biological, genetic and psychological factors that affect parent-child attachment. This research will contribute not only to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying parent-child attachment, but also to the identification of factors that might make parents and children more vulnerable to disturbances in the parent-infant relationship, and who may benefit from early intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: The use of highly prolactin-elevating antipsychotics and the risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: DATABASE; ENDOMETRIAL CANCER; GPRD; OVARIAN CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: While antipsychotics have been used successfully for a number of psychiatric disorders, there is some evidence which suggests that they may possibly, via their sustained elevation of prolactin levels, increase the risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer. To date, only two studies have been conducted on the subject, with findings suggesting a strong increased risk. However, these studies had important methodological shortcomings limiting the interpretation of their results. Given the increasing use of antipsychotics, particularly for off-label indications and the risk of these potential adverse events, additional studies are need to investigate this association. Therefore, the objective of this study is to determine whether highly prolactin-elevating antipsychotics, when compared to mildly-elevating or prolactin-sparing antipsychotics, are associated with an increased risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer. This will be achieved by conducting a cohort study using the General Practice Research Database, a large primary care database from the United Kingdom. This database contains medical information on over 110,000 female patients who used antipsychotic agents between 1989 and 2009, followed until the end of 2011. Given the important public health impact of these gynecological cancers, this large population-based cohort study will provide the medical community, patients, and regulatory agencies with strong evidence on the long-term safety of antipsychotics.
