TitreApplicationTitle: Best Strategies for Implementation of Clinical Pathways in Emergency Department Settings
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE ASTHMA; BEHAVIOUR CHANGE TECHNIQUES; CHANGE BARRIERS; CLINICAL PATHWAYS; IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGY; INTERVENTION MAPPING; ORGANIZATIONAL CONTEXT; PEDIATRIC; PROCESS EVALUATION; THEORETICAL DOMAINS FRAMEWORK (TDF); VOMITING AND DIARRHEA
Abstract-Résumé: A clinical pathway (CP) is a tool used by healthcare teams to organize and document care for specific medical conditions. Based on the best available research, and organized into specific treatment recommendations to be tailored for each patient, CPs have many potential benefits such as improved patient care and safety, decreased healthcare costs and efficiency through standardized care plans anticipated by the entire health team. While most hospitals create their own CPs with local experts, high-quality CPs are created by teams of clinical and research experts from all relevant health professions. Local implementation of expert-developed CPs can be a challenge and effective implementation approaches are unknown. In this three year study, we will design and evaluate best strategies for effective implementation of two expert-developed CPs.  This study will use provincial CPs related to pediatric emergency care: a Pediatric Asthma CP and a Pediatric Vomiting & Diarrhea CP (developed in Ontario and Alberta, respectively). Both are high quality CPs designed for use in any emergency department (ED) and have not been implemented in Ontario. In addition to adaptations at the hospital system level, full implementation requires a number of behaviour changes among health professionals. We will use an established theory framework to develop an organized, complete approach to promote the changes required for implementation in 16 community EDs. Once the CP has been prepared for use in each hospital and the health professionals have been taught how to use it, we will review patient outcomes to observe important differences and evaluate the costs to achieve any benefits gained. We will use a process log to track progress and learn from the experience with each hospital. This work will enhance our understanding of key requirements for practical, feasible, effective implementation of CPs at the local level, and may lead to better use of research findings in clinical practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: A randomized trial comparing "Push" versus "Pull" technology for mobilizing pain evidence into practice across different health professions
Keywords-MotsClés: INTERDISCIPLINARY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; KNOWLEDGE UPTAKE; NURSING; PAIN; PHYSICIAN; PUSH-OUT EVIDENCE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS; REHABILITATION; TECHNOLOGY BASED KT
Abstract-Résumé: Pain is a problem for many Canadians. Unfortunately, many doctors, nurses,therapists and psychologists have trouble keeping up to date and applying the latest research that might help patients suffering with pain. This study will determine whether sending alerts about new pain research directly to these health professionals, and providing them with access to accumulated alerts, will help. The study will compare information access and use of evidence in practice in different health professionals who treat pain. We will compare physicians, nurses, therapists and psychologists at the beginning of the study and after having access to different ways to find out about new pain research. One group will receive alerts about new pain studies that have been found to be high quality and relevant to patient care, and will be able to search the alerts database.  The other group will be able to find the same studies, but must search for them on a website database. We will include 670 doctors, nurses, therapists and psychologists in this study. A process like tossing a coin will determine which group volunteers get put into first. After 6 months of getting pain research information one way; study volunteers will switch to the other approach. We will measure how much pain research health providers access and how they use it to make choices about managing pain problems. We expect that reminding health care providers about new research findings directly will help them, since difficulty finding studies and lack of time prevent them from using the latest research. We expect that reminders will help them make better decisions about caring for patient's pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: South Asian HeArt Risk Assessment (SAHARA) Project
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR; CULTURE; ETHNICITY; INTERNET; INTERVENTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTI MEDIA; PREVENTION; RANDOMIZATION; SOUTH ASIAN
Abstract-Résumé: People who originate from the Indian subcontinent known as South Asians are the fastest growing group of non-white Canadians. They suffer an excess prevalence of abdominal obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease. They also develop these risk factors at significantly lower body weight and at younger ages compared to people of European origin.  The purpose of SAHARA (South Asian HeArt Risk Assessment) is to recruit 320 South Asians from Ontario and British Columbia, who use the internet, email and other multimedia devices. Among these participants we will compare the effectiveness of a one year interactive multi-media health behaviour intervention to usual care in reducing cardiac risk factors.  This intervention enables participants to set their health goals and provides health messaging and feedback designed to improve their dietary habits and physical activity.  In addition, we will test if knowledge of genetic risk for heart attack influences behaviour change and their heart health risk factor profile. The information generated from SAHARA will enable individuals, physicians, health professionals, and policy makers to develop risk factor modification programs to prevent cardiovascular disease in this high-risk group.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring trans-acting potential of a magnesium riboswitch in Salmonella typhimurium
Keywords-MotsClés: RIBOSWITCHES; SALMONELLA PATHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Salmonellosis, a foodborne disease mainly caused by Salmonella typhimurium, is a major public health burden with 1.3 billions cases reported worldwide annually, from which thousands of people die. One major virulence factor of Salmonella is the PhoPQ system responding to magnesium (Mg2+) starvation and controlling many genes involved in Mg2+ transport and in resistance to the host immune system. One of these genes, mgtA, encodes a Mg2+ transporter. The mgtA mRNA harbors a riboregulatory element called riboswitch responding to Mg2+ to control MgtA protein synthesis. In Mg2+-rich conditions, mgtA mRNA binds Mg2+ and adopts a structure preventing MgtA production. In Mg2+-poor conditions, mgtA mRNA switches to a conformation allowing MgtA synthesis. Our preliminary data suggest that the mgtA riboswitch could also act as a trans-acting RNA regulating, through direct basepairing, the expression of pagC mRNA, encoding an outer membrane protein important for Salmonella survival in macrophages. My project will aim to confirm the trans-acting potential of mgtA riboswitch and to determine the role of this regulation in the control of Salmonella virulence. Considering the possibility that additional virulence genes may be potential targets of mgtA riboswitch, this novel regulatory function for the mgtA mRNA would represent an efficient strategy for fine-tuning gene expression in response to different Mg2+ concentrations experienced by Salmonella during the course of infection. My work will then provide a better understanding of how Salmonella uses RNA to sense its environment and regulate virulence gene expression upon host infection. Because riboswitches and other RNA-based regulations are now considered as novel interesting targets for new generations of antibiotics since the emergence of many potentially deadly drug resistant forms of Salmonella, my researches will eventually help to improve the development of promising antimicrobial therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cherubism:  A Rare Human Bone Disease Reveals New Pathways Regulating Bone Homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: 3BP2 ADAPTOR PROTEIN; MACROPHAGE PHAGOCYTOSIS; OSTEOBLAST DIFFERENTIATION; OSTEOCLAST DIFFERENTIATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The PH and SH2 domain containing adapter protein 3BP2 is mutated in Cherubism, an autosomal dominant disorder that leads to abnormal cranial facial development due to the inappropriate activation of osteoclasts. We have deciphered the molecular mechnanism underlying the cause of Cherubism and as a result have discovered a new set of proteins that control bone synthesis and bone resorption. We have identified two proteins which work together to put the brakes on 3BP2.  One protein is called Tankyrase is a member of a family of proteins called PARPs which have become implicated in new anti-cancer therapies. The other protein is called RNF146 and is part of a large family of enzymes that add ubiquitin onto proteins.  We show that both proteins have unanticipated effects on bone cells grown in tissue culture conditions. We will make mice that no longer express Tankyrase or RNF146 and test whether they demonstrate abnormalities in bone synthesis and resorption. We have shown that PARP inhibitors that have been developed to target other PARP family members and are currently being used in the clinic also inhibit the activity of Tankyrase.  We will test whether these inhibitors affect bone mass and integrity.  Lastly, we have identified new proteins, which interact with Tankyrase in addition to 3BP2 suggesting that the biologic function of Tankyrase is complex.  We will study two possible candidate Tankyrase substrates and their role in inflammation and bone metabolism.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of V-ATPase subunit isoforms as therapeutic targets for diverse diseases including bone loss in inflammatory arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ACIDIFICATION; ARTHRITIS; BONE LOSS; ION TRANSPORT; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; OSTEOCLASTS; PROTON PUMPS; V-ATPASES
Abstract-Résumé: Many essential 'housekeeping' functions in the body require acid to be pumped across the membranes of cells and tissues. Acid is pumped into lysosomes, cellular recycling bins that break down old cell components into reusable building blocks, and it is pumped into urine to rid the body of the excess produced during physical activity. Bone repair requires that specialized cells (osteoclasts) secrete acid to dissolve the bone surface prior to its being replaced by new bone. In all these cases, variants of one ubiquitous acid pump, known as V-ATPase, perform the job. Genetic mutations that impair V-ATPase activity are known to cause diseases, such as cutis laxa (wrinkly skin disease), renal tubular acidosis (too much acid in the body), and osteopetrosis (heavy, brittle bones). In contrast, abnormal increases in V-ATPase activity can also lead to diseases, such as osteoporosis (thin, fragile bones) and inflammatory arthritis (eroded joints). In tumours, V-ATPases can acidify and degrade the surrounding tissue, helping cancer cells to detach and spread to other parts of the body. Our goal is to investigate aspects of V-ATPase structure and function that are still poorly understood: the structures and organization of its protein constituents, the variations that cause it to be sent to different locations within cells of the body, factors that control its activity to match its location, and how genetic mutations in V-ATPase genes cause disease. Understanding these factors will reveal new strategies to manipulate the V-ATPase acid pump activity in a manner that is required to alleviate disease. These strategies will enable specific targeting of bone cell or cancer cell V-ATPases without affecting the acid pumps that are engaged in vital housekeeping functions. Specific targeting is a crucial requirement for developing new drugs for the prevention of bone loss in osteoporosis and inflammatory arthritis, or the spread of cancer, without causing serious side effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Seeing the forests and the trees - Innovative approaches to exploring heterogeneity in systematic reviews of complex knowledge translation interventions to enhance policy decision making
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEX INTERVENTIONS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; META-SUBSETS ANALYSIS; PATIENT CARE AND OUTCOMES; POLICY DECISION MAKING; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT INTERVENTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Policy makers and mangers need to identify effective knowledge translation programs to improve the quality and outcomes of care for people with diabetes.  There are a substantial number of studies testing different programs to improve quality and outcomes of care for people with diabetes. Systematic reviews summarise all the available evidence to support decisions by policy makers and managers. We have completed a systematic review of knowledge translation programs to improve the quality and outcomes of care for people with diabetes. We identified 142 randomised controlled trials. Unfortunately using current methods and published data, we were only able to make general recommendations for policy makers and managers about which knowledge translation programs to use. In the proposed study we will use new analytical methods (only now feasible due to increases in computing power) and approach authors of randomized trials for additional information to identify what programs and parts of programs are most likely effective in different settings. The resulting information should be of direct relevance to policy makers and managers developing knowledge translation programs to improve the quality and outcomes of care for people with diabetes. In addition, we will generate further knowledge about the value of these new methods.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the ZNF217 oncoprotein in genome stability and cell cycle control
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CHROMATIN; DNA; DNA METHYLATION; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; ONCOGENE; TRANSCRIPTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Breast Cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in women with an estimated 250,000 newly diagnosed cases per year in North America alone. Despite the success in defining genetic pathways in some familial forms of breast cancer, over 90% of breast cancers are not of familial origin. The identification and characterization of these nonfamilial genes would allow for earlier and more specific diagnostic and prognostic tests and the development of new treatment strategies. ZNF217 is a protein which is believed to play a causal role in breast and ovarian cancers. Under normal conditions, cells require relatively small amounts of ZNF217. In many patients with breast cancer, ZNF217 is highly overproduced. We have determined that the overproduction of ZNF217 changes the chemical structure of DNA within important genes that normally protect us from cancer. Consequently these genes no longer function properly. Our goal is to understand the nature of this chemical modification and its implication to tumour progression so that we may try and develop treatments to correct this problem.

TitreApplicationTitle: Drospirenone-containing combined oral contraceptives and the risk of arterial thrombosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; DATABASES; DROSPIRENONE; DRUG SAFETY; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; ORAL CONTRACEPTIVES; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; SIDE EFFECTS; STROKE; THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Combined oral contraceptives, or birth control pills, are used to prevent unwanted pregnancies.  Worldwide, over 100 million women use birth control pills.  One known side effect of taking birth control pills is an increased chance of having blood clots compared with not taking these pills.  Recent safety reviews conducted by Health Canada and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have found that the newest type of birth control pills, which contains the hormone drosperinone, has been linked to the increased formation of potentially life-threatening blood clots (called venous thrombosis) compared with other types of birth control pills.  However, these reviews primarily focused on the venous side of the circulatory system.  While the FDA did look at the arterial side of the circulatory system, which includes both the heart and the brain, the results of their analysis conflict with those of other studies.  With only conflicting data available and millions of women taking these pills worldwide, additional studies are urgently needed to determine if these pills are safe.  If they increase the risk of arterial blood clots such as heart attacks or strokes, we may be greatly underestimating the harmful effects of these pills.  For this reason, we will use data from a United Kingdom database called the General Practice Research Database to study this important drug safety question.  Using this database, we will identify all women who took birth control pills between 2000 and 2012.  Once these women are identified, we will compare the number of women who had heart attacks and strokes while taking each of the different types of birth control pills.  This two-year study will provide a complete picture of the safety profile of these birth control pills.  In doing so, it will provide regulatory agencies such as Health Canada, doctors, and patients with the information required to make informed decisions regarding the risks and benefits of these pills.

TitreApplicationTitle: Color vision and image analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: COLOR VISION; FORM PERCEPTION; HUMAN VISUAL PSYCHOPHYSICS; IMAGE SEGMENTATION; NATURAL SCENE STATISTICS; TEXTURE PERCEPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Color vision is not only important for identifying the colors of objects -  it is also useful for determining the spatial layout, shapes, depths and motions of objects, a process I term  image analysis. This application is for funds to continue my research into the role that color vision plays in image analysis.  This research builds on my previous work that has established that color vision is capable of mediating a variety of processes such as stereoscopic depth perception, and is particularly useful for distinguishing material changes (such as surface paint) from illumination changes (such as shadows and shading).   The current trajectory of my research is underpinned by the conviction that in order to understand how color vision contributes to image analysis it is essential that color be studied in conjunction with other dimensions such as luminance and texture, rather than just on its own.  In fact the failure to study color in conjunction with luminance and texture has led researchers on the one hand to overestimate some contributions of color vision, for example to the perception of image blur (an important cue for determining depth), while on the other hand to underestimate other contributions (such as for determining the shape of an object from the pattern of its shading).   My research aims to redress the shortcomings in previous research by conducting behavioural (psychophysical) studies using normal human test subjects as well as color-blind persons, using specially designed stimuli that probe how color vision combines with luminance and texture vision for image analysis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Mechanisms Governing Hypothalamic Development and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL FATE DECISIONS; DIFFERENTIATION/MIGRATION; GENE DISCOVERY; GENE EXPRESSION; HYPOTHALAMUS; IN UTERO ELECTROPORATION; LINEAGE STUDIES; NEURODEVELOPMENT; NEUROGENESIS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The human brain is comprised on 100 billion neurons that are organized into either distinct layers or defined clusters ("nuclei"). Over the past decade, the developmental neuroscience community has been focused on dissecting how neurons become organized into layers. Comparatively, little is known about how neurons become organized into nuclei. One reason for this disparity is the assumption that nuclei lack a precise organization. This is mistaken - on the contrary, most brain nuclei exhibit an impressive suborganization. One brain region that organizes its neurons into nuclei is the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus processes cues from our surrounding and internal environments to control physiologies that ensure our survival, such as eating when we are hungry.   The hypothalamus also is an advantageous brain region to begin to understand how neurons become organized into nuclei because its nuclei express unique markers that label distinct subdomains. Thus, we can track the birth and migration of these markers as a way to understand how nuclei are formed. Here, we will use our unique collection of molecular markers to study how neurons that reside in one nucleus - the ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus - are born and move to their final position.  It is important that we start to understand how the brain gets its nuclei. Not only because, broadly speaking, 66 billion of the brain's 100 billion neurons are organized into clusters, but also because neuroendocrine disorders are becoming more common in the general population and these diseases are probably caused on some level by a disruption of nuclei organization. Before we can adequately design therapies to treat these disorders, we first need to understand how nuclear brain structures develop.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Proof of Principal Randomized Controlled Trial of Chronic Remote Ischemic Conditioning to Modify Post-Myocardial Infarction Remodeling
Keywords-MotsClés: MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; REMOTE ISCHEMIC PRECONDITIONING; VENTRICULAR REMODELING
Abstract-Résumé: During a heart attack, an artery carrying blood and oxygen to the heart becomes blocked, which causes damage to the heart muscle. When possible, a clot-busting drug is given or a procedure called angioplasty is performed soon after a heart attack starts, to open up the blocked artery and restore blood flow to the heart. While this can be an effective treatment to reduce permanent damage to the heart, patients can still experience heart failure afterwards. Consequently many patients require medications to support their heart after a heart attack. Recent research has shown a new technique called Remote Ischemic conditioning or RIC, is effective at protecting the heart muscle in a heart attack. RIC is produced simply by repeated inflation and deflation of a blood pressure cuff on an arm or leg to temporarily cut off and then restore blood flow to that limb. We believe this triggers the release of molecular factors that protect heart muscle. In a recent study in humans, it reduced the amount of permanent damage to the heart muscle when applied before the angioplasty procedure. Our recent animal studies have shown that RIC may also help the heart muscle recover after a heart attack if applied everyday during the month after a heart attack, by preventing heart failure. This is important for two reasons: first, currently we can only treat heart failure with medications, and second, some people have heart attacks but are not suitable to have angioplasty and so are at greater risk of heart failure. Daily RIC may provide an easy and effective new treatment to prevent heart failure after a heart attack. This application proposes a preliminary study in humans to see if daily RIC can help heart muscle recovery after a heart attack.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: MiTy Kids (Metformin in Women with Type 2 Diabetes in Pregnancy Kids Trial)
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD OBESITY; PREGNANCY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Background & Rationale: There is increasing evidence that, during pregnancy, exposure to maternal diabetes is associated with increased risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes in children & adults. Metformin, a drug commonly used in people with diabetes outside of pregnancy, improves insulin action. The Metformin in Women with Type 2 Diabetes Trial (MiTy) is a randomized trial, where pregnant women with type 2 diabetes are randomised to receive metformin or a placebo added to their usual treatment of insulin. We are currently testing the hypothesis that metformin treatment during pregnancy may lead to improvements in pregnancy outcomes. We hypothesize that an improvement in insulin action at a critical time of development (during pregnancy) may also translate into metabolic improvements and reduction in risk for obesity in the offspring. Primary Research Question: In offspring of women with type 2 diabetes, does treatment with metformin during pregnancy reduce adiposity & improve insulin action in infants at 2 years of age compared to women who didn't receive metformin? Methods: This is a prospective observational study of offspring of mothers who participated in the MiTy trial. The primary outcome is childhood adiposity at 2 years as measured by BMI (body mass index) z-score and skin fold thickness. Sample Size: The MiTy trial is enrolling 500 mothers. Accounting for loss to follow-up and perinatal loss, we will have 450 offspring giving 80% power to show a difference in BMI z-score (a measure of obesity) and skin fold thickness. Value of Study: Rates of diabetes and obesity are increasing exponentially, and there is evidence that diabetes in pregnancy may play a role in increasing the rate of obesity and diabetes in offspring. By examining the long-term benefit of receiving metformin during pregnancy in women with diabetes, if a benefit was found, this would be a valuable addition to the fight against increasing rates of obesity and diabetes in future generations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of specific ubiquitin-based inhibitors targeting oncogenic deubiquitinating enzyme USP1
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPY; COMBINATORIAL LIBRARIES; DEUBIQUITINATION; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; OSTEOSARCOMA; PHAGE DISPLAY; PROTEIN ENGINEERING; UBIQUITIN; USP1
Abstract-Résumé: Effective strategies to treat cancer rely on our ability to interfere with cellular processes that are deregulated in tumors. One such biological process is the regulation of protein stability by a small protein called ubiquitin, which attaches to other proteins and acts as a signal for their destruction. This process is regulated by various enzymes, which add or remove the ubiquitin label. In recent years, deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs), which catalyze the removal of ubiquitin, have attracted increasing attention as novel targets for drug development because they are crucial mediators of key intracellular processes. In humans, there are nearly 100 DUBs, including a subgroup called ubiquitin-specific proteases (USPs). One of these USPs, USP1, has recently emerged as a promising target for pharmacological intervention in the most common bone cancer, osteosarcoma. Preventing USP1's activity in osteosarcoma is predicted to reduce cell growth and decrease spreading of cancer cells to other organs, and to render cells more sensitive to chemotherapeutic agents. Unfortunately, the lack of selective molecules to prevent USP1 functions, called inhibitors, has severely hampered attempts to manipulate it for therapeutic benefits. The goal of my post-doctoral training is to develop highly specific and potent inhibitors for USP1. Using state-of-the-art protein engineering technology, I propose to make ubiquitin-like molecules that will associate tightly with USP1 in a manner that will block its catalytic function, and thus, act as inhibitors. I will also create a system to inhibit USP1 in human cells in a controllable way. Finally, I will characterize these inhibitors in osteosarcoma cells to confirm their ability to interfere with USP1's biological functions. In conclusion, this work will generate invaluable tools to understand and modulate USP1 activity in human cells and will shed light on effective cancer therapy of aggressive malignant osteosarcoma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Are Primary Care Teams effective? Evidence from Quebec's Family Medicine Groups on preventive care and from patients with multiple chronic conditions
Keywords-MotsClés: CAUSAL INFERENCE WITH OBSERVATIONAL DATA; CO-MORBIDITY; EFFICIENCY OF HEALTH CARE SERVICES; HEALTH CARE COSTS; HEALTH CARE SERVICES UTILIZATION; POPULATION HEALTH; PREVENTION; PRIMARY CARE; PRIMARY CARE REFORM
Abstract-Résumé: Reforms to Canadian primary health care have advanced at a rapid pace over the last decade, with the consistent goal of improving the efficiency of the health care system: that is, improving the health of individuals and populations at similar or lower costs. Only limited evidence on the impacts of these reforms currently exists, particularly with respect to utilization patterns, system costs, and health outcomes. In a previously CIHR-funded project, we are evaluating the impacts of the centerpiece of Quebec's primary care reforms - Family Medicine Groups (FMGs). A typical FMG consists of 6 to 10 physicians working with 2 nurses to provide services for 10,000 to 20,000 registered patients. Our initial results suggest that FMGs have little to no impact on emergency department use, hospitalizations, or costs over a 3-year period among elderly or chronically ill patients. These results raise questions about the impacts of FMGs at a more micro level. Specifically, do the aggregate impacts mask important differences among sub-populations or sub-types of health care services? Given FMGs focus on enhanced access and better coordination of care, impacts may be concentrated among certain types of patients and of services, in particular: 1. patients with multiple chronic diseases, who require more coordination across providers and settings to ensure high quality care and better health outcomes 2. preventive services including mammography, colonoscopy, and bone density screening tests, as well as annual major complete exams We propose evaluating the impacts of FMGs on utilization and costs among these patients and services, as well as investigating the effects on disease management and adherence to relevant clinical guidelines. A rigorous evaluation of the effects of FMGs on these particularly vulnerable patient groups and important preventive services will inform both whether and how interdisciplinary, team-based delivery models work in achieving their goals.

TitreApplicationTitle: New lipid and protein factors regulating hepatic TAG homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: APOCIII; ER STRESS; HEPATOSTEATOSIS; LUMENAL LIPID DROPLETS; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TRIACYLGLYCEROL; VLDL OVERPRODUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity, type-II diabetes, and other lipid-metabolism related diseases (such as high blood concentrations of cholesterol, triglycerides, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease) have become epidemic worldwide, including in Canada. Most of the symptoms associated with these metabolic disorders are caused by imbalanced triglyceride metabolism (termed triglyceride homeostasis) in the liver. In this research proposal we address four aspects of triglyceride homeostasis in the liver, namely triglyceride synthesis, triglyceride storage, triglyceride turnover (i.e. degradation), and triglyceride secretion as protein-lipid complexes called lipoproteins (such as LDL, commonly known as the "bad cholesterol"). In our laboratories, we have generated several mouse models that are genetically modified to suit for the studies of hypertriglyceridemia (i.e. too much triglycerides in the blood), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and other abnormalities in triglyceride metabolism. The ultimate goal of our research is to identify new protein markers for diagnosis and prevention of lipid-metabolism related diseases, as well as to identify targets for therapeutic interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of a conserved yeast Forkhead Box longevity pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: ANAPHASE PROMOTING COMPLEX (APC); BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CYCLE PROGRESSION; FORKHEAD BOX TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MOLECULAR MECHANISMS OF LONGEVITY AND STRESS RESPONSE; MOLECULAR MECNAISMS OF CANCER; NUTRIENT RESPONSE PATHWAYS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; UBIQUITIN TARGETING; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Throughout human evolution, one question has remained constant: can we live forever? We are continuously bombarded with products, diets and exercise regimens that supposedly add years to our life. Can this be? Is there an alterable program, whether genetic or environmental, that can be tweaked to allow longer life? Advances in modern medicine have certainly led to a dramatic increase in average lifespan over the last century. However, the maximum human lifespan has curiously remained constant. Research out of many laboratories indicates that in a variety of organisms a genetic program exists to control lifespan. The conservation of this genetic lifespan program extends into the brewing yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, where numerous longevity genes have been isolated and characterized. Interestingly, mutations that increase genomic stability, glucose utilization or oxidative stress resistance have been demonstrated to extend lifespan in yeast, as well as in flies and worms. Our research examines genes in yeast that affect longevity by altering DNA/chromatin structure, cell cycle progression or the protein degradation pathway. When these genes are mutated, yeast cells suffer a reduced lifespan. These genes are also found in multicellular organisms. Our goal is to better understand the molecular mechanisms in yeast, so we can apply our findings to higher organisms, including humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Changes in Opioid Reward in Neuropathic pain
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL PAIN ASSESSMENT; DOPAMINE RECEPTORS; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; NEURO-GLIA INTERACTIONS; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; OPIOID RECEPTORS; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS
Abstract-Résumé: One category of chronic pain that is particularly challenging to treat is neuropathic pain; pain caused by damage or dysfunction to the nervous system. In addition to the obvious sensory disturbances that accompany neuropathic pain, this condition is associated with an important affective or emotional component. The negative affect, or how much the pain is bothersome significantly impacts quality of life, and leads to the common co-morbidities of psychiatric disorders such as depression; patients with NP pain are twice as likely to suffer from depression and anxiety. Our preliminary data suggest that the brain circuitry recruited for opioid-induced reward is different in neuropathic compared to pain-naive animals. This difference appears to involve non-neuronal glia cells in brain regions important for emotion. Our proposed research will test the hypothesis that neuropathic pain causes activation of non-neuronal cells, microglia, in brain regions important for pleasure and reward. We will use a multidisciplinary approach consisting of behavioral, biochemical, pharmacological, and morphological techniques in a rodent model of neuropathic pain to investigate how opioid reward circuitry is changed in such chronic pain states.  The specific aims will determine the contribution of microglia cell involvement and the circuitry in opioid reward in neuropathic animals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Extended Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis Comparing Rivaroxaban to Aspirin Following Total Hip and Knee Arthroplasty (EPCAT II)
Keywords-MotsClés: DOUBLE-DUMMY; EXTENDED VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM PROPHYLAXIS; OUT OF HOSPITAL; RANDOMIZED; TOTAL HIP ARTHROPLASTY; TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY
Abstract-Résumé: Blood clots in the legs and lungs are common complications following hip and knee replacement surgery. Guidelines state to give anticoagulants (blood thinners) for up to 14 days after knee replacement and 35 days after hip replacement. In this study we intend to prove whether aspirin works as well as blood thinners to prevent blood clots after hip and knee replacement surgery. Patients will be randomized (like a flip of a coin) to receive either aspirin or the blood thinner rivaroxaban after all patients receive a short course of anticoagulants following surgery. The rates of blood clot complications will then be compared in the two groups over a 90 day post-operative period. This study has the potential to show a cheap, safe medication is an effective alternative to anticoagulation therapy following THR or TKR which would result in considerable cost savings to the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Systems Approach towards the Therapeutic Modulation of Human Bromodomains
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; BROMODOMAIN; CHROMATIN; DNA-PROTEIN INTERACTION; EPIGENETICS; INTERACTION DOMAIN; LYSINE ACETYLATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: To function, cells must integrate numerous signals into coordinated outputs. Many of these signals are generated by proteins, biomolecules involved in virtually every process of living cells. As such, to understand living organisms, it is critical to scrutinize proteins. Following the completion of my graduate studies, I began my post-doctoral research focusing on a poorly understood cellular signal present on protein, namely lysine acetylation. Lysine acetylation is known to influence many processes affecting proteins associated with DNA and to mediate physical interaction between proteins. Bromodomain, a protein domain (or portion) found in over 40 human proteins, forms a deep cavity in proteins (as per a lock) which is essential for binding to other proteins with acetyl lysines (which would act as a key in this analogy). The overarching goal of my post-doctoral work is to define the specificity of bromodomains for acetylated proteins in the same manner that a locksmith would want to catalogue key-lock pairs. To achieve this goal, I have begun leveraging the expertise that I acquired during my graduate studies to study all proteins impacting lysine acetylation in human cells with an emphasis on protein containing bromodomains. After my first year of post-doctoral training, I already have made great progress toward this goal and I am currently further characterizing some initial findings. In particular, I am studying one protein which is mutated and is the root cause of a rare cancer, NUT midline carcinoma. To complement my research, I have also established collaborations with national and international groups interested in lysine acetylation and in better understanding the function of bromodomains. As a result, I am well positioned to achieve an in-depth characterization of lysine acetylation and bromodomain in a timely fashion which is key to the rational design of novel therapeutic agents with broad implication to the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Influence of Pubertal Timing and Events on Asthma in Singletons and Twins
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; BIRTH WEIGHT; ENVIRONMENT; GENETICS; PUBERTY; RESPIRATORY DISEASES; TWINS; WEIGHT STATUS
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is the most common disease in children, affecting nearly one in every 8 children worldwide.  This creates a huge burden on healthcare.  Yet, asthma does not affect boys and girls in the same way.  Before puberty, more boys have asthma.  After puberty, more girls have asthma.  This sex shift in asthma rates in believed to result, at least in part, from puberty-related events such as menarche, weight gain and hormone changes.  Drugs used to treat asthma may also affect puberty, as they slow growth.  As such, better understanding asthma in older children and young adolescents may reduce the risk of this disease.  This study has two hypotheses: 1.Pubertal staging is linked with asthma diagnosis, and  2.Drugs used in the treatment of asthma affect pubertal staging and growth.  This study will use data collected from two groups of children: singletons and twins.  By including data from twins, we can consider exposures such as puberty, weight and asthma drugs, while controlling for genetics.  Fraternal twins share 50% of their genes and identical twins share 100% of their genes.  Data from singletons will increase the generalizability of our study.   We will use data from Sweden, which has national registries of births and all prescription drugs, including asthma drugs.  Combined with data from these two groups of children (singletons and twins), this study will glean insight into puberty and asthma treatment on asthma itself.  To date, there are 2950 twins in this study, including 157 (7.5%) who have asthma, and 4089 singletons in this study, including 221 (6.6%) who have asthma.  The majority of girls in both studies are in mid/late puberty, while most boys are in early puberty.  The aims of this study are to  1. Better understand how puberty influences asthma,  2. Better understand how asthma drugs influence puberty and growth, and  3. Make these findings known to healthcare professionals and policy makers to help reduce the burden of asthma in child

TitreApplicationTitle: Personality, Recurrence of Depression, and Differential Treatment Response: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy and Antidepressant Medication for Major Depressive Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE-BEHAVIOURAL TREATMENT; GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER; PSYCHOMETRICS; PSYCHOTHERAPY; THERAPIST CHARACTERISTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Clients of therapists who exhibit certain characteristics (such as empathy, warmth, and support) show greater improvement during psychological treatment (Dowd, 2005). Therapist variables, however, are rarely examined in the context of cognitive-behavioural treatment (CBT; Lambert, 1992). This remains true despite the fact that effective administration of CBT requires therapists who are appropriately empathetic and challenging, as clients are often encouraged to enter into anxiety-provoking situations during treatment (Woody & Ollendick, 2006). In order to examine the impact of therapist characteristics on symptom change, a client-rated measure of therapist characteristics will be constructed. This Therapist Behaviour Assessment (TBA) will comprise of two distinct subscales: 1) empathetic and caring, and 2) challenging and direct. A sample of 110 individuals with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD; as assessed by two diagnostic interviews) will receive CBT for the disorder, and will complete the TBA during the third treatment session. The factor structure of the measure, as well as the reliability and validity of each subscale will be examined. It is hypothesized that a higher overall rating of therapist characteristics will predict greater self-reported GAD symptom change over time. It is also hypothesized that a higher overall rating of therapist characteristics will predict lower clinician-rated GAD severity at post treatment. This study has the potential to provide therapists and researchers with a valid client-rated measure of therapist characteristics in CBT. It may also inform therapists how to behave at different stages of the treatment process in order to maximize treatment efficacy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Completeness of Physician Billing Claims Administrative Health Databases in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTH DATABASES; CHRONIC DISEASE; COMPLETENESS; DATA QUALITY; PAN-CANADIAN STUDY; PREVALENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Canada is internationally renowned for its large administrative databases and their value for describing the health of the nation's population. Databases that contain anonymized records of physician services are particularly important for studying chronic diseases, like diabetes, because they contain diagnostic information. However, the number of physicians being paid using the conventional fee-for-service method is decreasing, which reduces the amount of physician service information captured in administrative databases. This results in gaps in the completeness of information about the health of Canada's population and downward bias in estimates of the number of persons with chronic diseases. Our research will develop and compare different methods to estimate the completeness of physician databases in Canadian provinces and territories and apply them to study under-estimation for three chronic diseases (diabetes, hypertension, and bowel diseases) in four provinces, including Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Nova Scotia. Computer simulations will also be used to compare the efficiency and performance of these methods. Recommendations will be developed about choosing a method for measuring the quality of physician databases. This research will help data managers and users across Canada focus on opportunities improve data quality. Ultimately, this research will lead to better information about the health of Canada's population.

TitreApplicationTitle: From phenotypes to pathways: global exploration of cellular networks using yeast phenomics
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOMATED MICROSCOPY; CELL BIOLOGY; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENETIC NETWORKS; IMAGE ANALYSIS; PHENOMICS; SYNTHETIC GENETIC ARRAY; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Genome sequencing projects have revealed the massive catalogue of genes in a variety of organisms, from yeast to man. Biologists are faced with a major challenge as they confront this embarrassment of riches; how to assign functions to thousands of uncharacterized genes, and how to use this information to identify the proteins that function together to regulate fundamental cellular processes. Functional genomics technologies enable researchers to study all genes simultaneously and systematically in a specific assay and their development and application is providing unprecedented global views of gene function in healthy and diseased cells. We are developing novel genomics technologies and applying them in large-scale studies using a yeast model system. Yeast are single celled microorganisms that are related to humans evolutionarily, with thousands of genes homologous to those in humans. Our systematic approaches will accelerate the pace of yeast research and provide proof-of-principle analyses for analogous approaches in more complex cells and organisms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Do the causes of infertility play a role in the health of children born to couples with low fertility?
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD HEALTH; INFERTILITY; INFERTILITY TREATMENT; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: In vitro fertilization and other medical technologies allow many couples with fertility problems to have a child. Children born as a result of assisted conception have a higher risk of preterm birth and other adverse outcomes, and we have limited knowledge about whether their later health may be affected by having been conceived through infertility treatment. To date, research has focused primarily on assisted reproductive technologies as the main cause of adverse outcomes. However, several underlying conditions can affect fertility, and it is thus important to also study the various causes of infertility for their potential to affect perinatal and child health. Although several experts have identified this as a priority, research in this area is very limited. As, in August 2010, Quebec has implemented a publicly funded program to provide infertility treatment to eligible couples, and other Canadian provinces may soon follow in its footsteps, we need a timely answer to these questions. We will use clinical data from women who attended a large infertility centre over a period of 15 years and a sample of women who gave birth in the same hospital during the same time period. By linking these with data from the Regie de l'Assurance Maladie du Quebec (RAMQ), we will be able to follow children over time for a number of endpoints and assess their health as a function of both infertility treatment and the underlying causes of infertility in their parents. This study has the potential to not only improve our understanding of the risks associated with infertility and its treatment, but also to help provide more informed care to couples experiencing fertility problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetics of gene expression in the lung to elucidate the molecular causes of asthma and smoking-related lung diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; COPD; GENE EXPRESSION; GENOME-WIDE ASSOCIATION STUDY; GENOMICS; GENOTYPING; LUNG CANCER; LUNG TISSUES; REGULATORY SNPS; SMOKING
Abstract-Résumé: Over 3 million Canadians suffer from lung diseases, which pose a significant challenge for the health care system. Asthma runs in families and is in part attributable to genetic factors. Similarly, a genetic predisposition is persuasive in chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD) and lung cancer since only a fraction of smokers develops these diseases. Recent genetic studies were particularly successful to identify the genetic factors of asthma, COPD and lung cancer. Despite these successes, these new genetic factors are merely statistical in nature and the biological mechanisms by which they alter individual risk for disease are still largely unknown. The aim of the current study is to validate and refine discoveries derived from the latest genetic studies on lung diseases. To achieve this goal, a large collection of human lung tissues available in our institution will be studied. These tissues have been taken from patients undergoing lung cancer surgery. Extensive clinical data are available for all patients, including lung function, smoking history, medication, and comorbidities. With modern genomic technologies, we can study these lung specimens and identify genetic markers that influence the abundance of genes in the lung. We can then overlap these genetic variants with those previously associated with asthma, COPD, and lung cancer. This fundamental molecular understanding will provide unprecedented biological information to reveal why some individuals are more susceptible than others to develop these lung diseases. We foresee high-impact outcomes to decrease the burden of these diseases including the identification of new drug targets and more cost-effective management of afflicted patients through personalized medicine. This project will take advantage of the best genomic approaches, the large volume of lung tissues available in our institution, and the renowned clinical expertise that we possess to manage, characterize and treat patients with lung diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cost-effectiveness of a population-based active TB control program for tuberculosis, Lima, Peru
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVE CASE FINDING; COST-EFFECTIVENESS ANALYSIS; EVALUATING HOUSEHOLD CONTACTS; HIGH RISK POPULATIONS; IMPLEMENTATION SCIENCE; PUBLIC HEALTH; STEPPED WEDGE IMPLEMENTAITON; TARGETED INTERVENTIONS; TB TRANSMISSION; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: An estimated nine million Tuberculosis (TB) cases and two million TB deaths occur every year, with the most severely affected among the poorest and most vulnerable populations.  Until recently, the focus of TB programs worldwide has simply been on treating TB cases who present to clinics, however this strategy of awaiting cases has done little to accelerate the goals of one day eliminating TB.  TB cases who are coughing and do not start treatment can continue to spread the disease, and quickly finding and engaging those with TB disease in the community is considered a top public health priority. Peru has one of the most well-established TB programs, yet continues to see new cases of TB every year and has one of the highest TB rates in the Americas.  The local Direccion de Salud in San Juan de Lurigancho, the district with the highest TB incidence in Lima, Peru, have decided to proactively introduce a program for evaluating families of TB cases in order to more rapidly engage families and detect secondary cases within households. This Home Visitation Program proposes to visit homes in order to better engage with families, describe and explain TB risk factors and evaluate household members for TB disease.  We are proposing to take advantage of the roll out of this Home Visitation Program in order to have the extremely rare opportunity to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of introducing such a program.  Detecting family members with TB sooner, could mean they are enrolled sooner in their TB disease, could improve their positive health outcomes by curing their TB disease and could mean interrupting the continued spread. Demonstrating that active case-finding among adult household contacts is cost-effective in a low-resource, TB endemic setting has the potential to revolutionize how these programs approach TB control, and hopefully, to finally realize the goal of a world where TB is no longer one of the captains of the men of death.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protection against cardiac damage in the living heart by mitochondrial protein S-nitrosation: fundamental and therapeutic implications
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOPROTECTION; MITOCHONDRIA; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION THERAPY; NITRIC OXIDE; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Ischemia-reperfusion (IR) injury comprises the tissue damage and dysfunction caused by the removal and subsequent reintroduction of oxygenated blood supply.  These pathologies are by far the leading cause of death in the world, including most prevalently the injuries from myocardial infarction (heart attack).  Additionally, in the clinical context of surgery and organ transplantation, IR damage is unavoidable and detrimental to patient outcomes.  Nitric oxide (NO) is cardioprotective during IR, encouraging the development of NO donors as drugs, however none has proven clinically useful and the protective mechanism remains elusive.    This project will build on the findings from my PhD work from which I discovered a central mechanism of damage during heart attacks that could be targeted and protected against using a novel NO-derived therapeutic drug.  Uniquely, this drug protects when given intravenously at a time corresponding to when those suffering from heart attack typically receive medical attention.  This project will build on this very exciting initial finding to understand how to protect against heart attack damage in the clinic, as well as through lifestyle and dietary interventions that encourage the same mechanism of protection.  This will set the stage for clinical trials for tissue protection from heart attack, for which no drug currently exists.  Also, it will greatly inform strategies for preventative lifestyle interventions against heart-attack damage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and characterization of host proteins required for Coxiella burnetii survival and replication in host cells using siRNA screening
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL INFECTION; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CULTURE; COXIELLA BURNETII; EFFECTOR PROTEINS; IMAGING; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; RESPIRATORY PATHOGEN; SIRNA TECHNOLOGY; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: The causative agent of Q fever, Coxiella burnetii, is a bacterial pathogen that causes disease worldwide. Q fever manifests as an acute flu-like illness that is often self-limiting; however, chronic infection can be life threatening to humans and infection of pregnant women often results in premature birth and spontaneous abortion. This disease is especially prevalent in farm workers, veterinarians, and those who come in contact with infected animals.  In addition to farm animals, domesticated cats and dogs can also carry this pathogen.  Infection has been diagnosed throughout Canada with a large prevalence in Nova Scotia. Coxiella burnetii infects humans primarily by inhalation of aerosolized bacteria, which then can be internalized by specialized cells in the lung called alveolar macrophages.  Once the bacteria have entered these cells the bacteria are able to replicate to high numbers, which is required for disease manifestations.  The bacteria possess very specialized factors, which they use to manipulate normal processes in mammalian cells.  The goal of this project is to identify specific components of the targeted processes and how they contribute to survival and growth of the bacteria within the macrophages.  We will do this by depletion of specific cellular components using small interfering RNAs.  This technology has provided insight into infection processes of other pathogens such as Listeria and Chlamydia.  Depletion of crucial mammalian cell components will be followed by analysis of bacterial replication and we will identify components that increase or decrease bacterial growth inside mammalian cells.  Systematic depletion of mammalian cell components important for bacterial growth will enable identification of these components and their importance in growth of C. burnetii in mammalian cells.  Understanding the role of these mammalian components will assist in development of therapeutics to control growth of C. burnetii and limit the spread of Q fever.

TitreApplicationTitle: A zebrafish-based screening strategy for the identification of tissue-selective PPARgamma agonists.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; DRUG SCREENING; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; PROTEOMICS; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that nearly 3 million Canadians suffer from the complications of diabetes. Among these, the majority suffer from type 2 diabetes mellitus, which is characterized by the failure of cells to take up glucose in response to insulin. These patients are generally treated with a combination of lifestyle modifications and various oral anti-diabetic medications.  Drugs in the thiazolidinedione family for example, increase the ability of cells to take up glucose in response to insulin and are an effective means of lowering blood sugar. Unfortunately, recent evidence has linked this class of drugs to some serious side effects including cardiovascular complications and an increased risk of bone fractures, thereby limiting their long-term clinical utility. It has been known for some time that thiazolidinediones increase insulin sensitivity by activating a molecular switch known as PPARgamma inside of cells. However, the mechanism underlying many of the side effects remains elusive. I hypothesize that the inappropriate activation of PPARgamma in a subset of tissues is a major contributor to the side effects of thiazolidinedione treatment and that the development of drugs capable of selectively activating PPARgamma only in tissues where it is required will generate a safer class of insulin sensitizing medications. In order to accomplish this I will utilize a genetically modified zebrafish model in which all cells have been engineered to produce a fluorescent marker upon activation of PPARgamma. This model will allow me to treat large numbers of zebrafish with a large number of prospective medications and easily identify drugs that promote tissue selective activation of PPARgamma. All drugs exhibiting a high degree of tissue selectivity will subsequently be tested for insulin sensitizing effects in a mouse model of diabetes. Ultimately, this research will advance our understanding of the role of PPARgamma in diabetes, paving the way for improved anti-diabetic drugs.

Keywords-MotsClés: CAUSAL MODELLING; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; NATURAL EXPERIMENTS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Health researchers believe that transportation and poverty reduction programs influence health. These and other big programs like cancer screening and anti-smoking laws are very hard to evaluate. This is because there are an incredible number of things, like your age or income, that could bias the results of the evaluation. To solve the problem of bias researchers use a method called the randomized controlled trial. Randomized controlled trials are the best way to understand how medications or surgeries work and if they should be allowed on the market. But randomized controlled trials have weaknesses when it comes to understanding big programs like transportation or poverty reduction. There are some new research methods that keep all of the good parts of randomized controlled trials and help improve some of their weaknesses for understanding big programs. Unfortunately, these new methods have not been used very much in health research.  During my project I will learn and use these new methods to understand how big programs like transportation and poverty reduction influence health. This is important because if our understanding of these big programs is biased we can never be sure if they are good or bad for health. If we can never be sure if they are good or bad for health we will not be able to change these programs and make them the most beneficial for everyone's health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparison of autonomic and vascular function late following repair of coarctation of the aorta by surgical and endovascular methods
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULTS; ARTERIAL STIFFNESS; BAROREFLEX CONTROL; COARCTATION OF THE AORTA; CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE; FLOW MEDIATED DILATATION; HYPERTENSION; MUSCLE SYMPATHETIC NERVE ACTIVITY; PLASMA CATECHOLAMINES; RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN-ALDOSTERONE SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, 1 in 100 or 1% of all babies are born with a heart defect. Coarctation of the aorta (CoA) is one defect causing narrowing of an important large blood vessel which supplies blood to your body, the aorta. CoA often causes high blood pressure (hypertension) in the arms, low blood flow in the legs, and significantly increases the risk of premature death.  Correction of CoA is recommended and different types of repair, such as surgical (very invasive) or catheter based (less invasive) are available. Unfortunately, successful repair does not cure patients, and many still develop hypertension and die early. After repair, children and young adults demonstrate changes in their blood vessels, causing them to be less elastic, and in their pressure sensors (baroreceptors), that help regulate blood pressure. One important factor in controlling blood pressure is the activity of the sympathetic nervous system, although no studies have examined direct sympathetic activity and its modulation by the arterial baroreflex.  We propose to examine muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA), arterial baroreflex modulation of MSNA, vascular function, and neurohumoral factors in your blood which can influence blood pressure in adults with repaired CoA, compared to healthy adults. We also want to examine if it makes a difference in our measures if patients have CoA repair by surgery (invasive) or catheter based (less invasive).  We believe that patients with repaired CoA have high sympathetic activity, which if found may provide clinicians a better understanding of the causes of their hypertension and help in its treatment. It may also help identify which type of repair method is better for Canadians with CoA. The ultimate goal of this research is to improve the survival of Canadians living with repaired CoA by understanding how the condition affects the body after repair.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation and function of NFE2L3: linking transcription factor activity to carcinogenesis.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARCINOGEN; CNC PROTEINS; DETOXIFICATION; DNA DAMAGE; GENE REGULATION; HEMATOPOIESIS; LYMPHOMA; MOUSE MODELS; THYMUS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Transcription factors are important molecules that control whether genes are active or not in a specific cell within an organism. Our research focuses on the functions of the CNC transcription factor family. Abnormal regulation of members of this group of proteins has been shown to cause cancer. Here, we propose to determine the role of the CNC protein NFE2L3 in cancer using human cell culture and animal models. We found that the activity of NFE2L3 is heavily regulated within cells. We also have generated a novel mouse model deficient in NFE2L3. Interestingly, the absence of this protein makes the animals more sensitive to exposure to carcinogen, as the NFE2L3 deficient mice develop a higher number of lymphomas, a type of blood cancer. Our studies are aimed at uncovering novel regulatory pathways implicated in the control of NFE2L3 activity in cells, in mice and in humans. Furthermore, we will investigate the response of our animal models to carcinogen in the presence of a chemotherapeutic agent. Our studies will contribute to the design of novel treatment options for cancer patients suffering from blood cell cancer.

Abstract-Résumé: The commitment to democratization entails securing both the "right to health" (WHO, 2007) and the related "right to knowledge" (UNESCO, 2010). Sexual orientation and gender minority status are frequently overlooked in the identification of "unique populations" vis-a-vis cancer health disparities and related knowledge and treatment divides. This project addresses the escalating need in Canadian public health for evidence that will assist sexual/gender minority health programs, community cancer health organizations, and healthcare professionals in the design of culturally competent healthcare systems. The purpose of this three-year study is to articulate how, in practice, sexual orientation and gender, in diverse locations, shape access to cancer health knowledge, and critically, its actual mobilization in treatment and survivor health decision-making. Cancer health and care professionals, in Canada (and elsewhere) would benefit, we hold, from a better understanding of how groups that are historically marginalized in health care settings and discourses negotiate an invariably complex choreography of knowledge in health and care decision-making.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stress-reducing effects of palatable foods: brain mechanisms and implications for obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; BOMBESIN-LIKE PEPTIDES; CORTICOTROPIN-RELEASING FACTOR; GHRELIN; INGESTIVE BEHAVIOR; MICRODIALYSIS; NEUROPEPTIDES; OBESITY; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: The current obesity "epidemic" in the developed world is a major health concern; over half of adult Canadians are now classified as overweight or clinically obese. A particularly worrisome trend is the increased prevalence of obesity in young people. Although the reason(s) for increasing obesity rates remain unclear, one important factor is the role that stress plays in overeating and weight gain. Stress changes the way we eat resulting in a shift in food choices away from healthy foods to more fatty, energy dense foods (comfort foods). Youth are particularly vulnerable to the effects of stress making this an ideal time window to examine the relationship between stress and eating. We recently showed that adolescent rats exposed to stress displayed increased anxiety later in life. Interestingly, these effects were reduced or absent if rats were allowed to eat comfort food during and after the stress exposure. Although this suggests that eating comfort food is beneficial, this high fat/carbohydrate diet, combined with stress also resulted in signs of metabolic syndrome and obesity. The current proposal aims to explore the potential chemical processes that are altered in the brain (during adolescence) that might contribute to the increased comfort food consumption, and how these comfort foods may reduce signs of stress. In particular, the experiments will focus on the role that a chemical messenger (bombesin-like peptides) plays in this process. Bombesin-like peptides, which are located in feeding and reward centers of the brain, are released when comfort foods are eaten and also during stress and therefore might be important in the proces(es) by which comfort foods reduce levels of stress. It is hoped that these studies will help us understand why we might choose to eat comfort food during times of stress and how it makes us feel better. Ultimately this research may point to new interventions for the prevention and treatment of obesity.

Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERIOVENOUS MALFORMATION; BLOOD VESSELS; BONE MINERALIZATION; ECTOPIC CALCIFICATION; ELASTIN; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; GENETICS; MATRIX DEGRADING ENZYMES; MATRIX GLA PROTEIN; TRANSGENIC AND KNOCKOUT MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Lay Summary: Abnormal mineral deposition in the soft tissues (calcification) can be seen in some life-threatening diseases. Mineral accumulation in the blood vessels is a common example of soft tissue calcification. Vascular calcification can be seen in diseases, such as atherosclerosis, chronic kidney diseases and type II diabetes. Soft tissue calcification can further complicate the prognosis and management of these diseases, which may in turn lead to increased morbidity. Although vascular calcification is prevalent in aging population and considered as a risk factor for many vascular diseases, the underlying mechanisms that regulate vascular calcification is poorly understood. A better understanding of the determinants of this complex process will identify novel therapeutic targets to prevent and manage vascular calcification in humans. The long-term objective of our study is to understand the process of vascular calcification and to identify its genetic determinants. Our objective for this project is to analyze the vascular calcification trait in a mouse model that lacks a potent anti-mineralization protein in the vascular tissues. In this model, absence of the anti-mineralization protein leads to massive deposition of minerals in the arterial walls. We plan to investigate the cell behaviour in the calcified arteries of this model and also investigate how alterations of protein synthesis and breakdown in the vascular walls may affect the calcification process. Finally, we will treat this model with a pharmacologic agent to inhibit protein breakdown with a goal to prevent vascular calcification.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diesel Exhaust and Mechanisms of Asthma
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; DIESEL; HUMAN; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma has major health consequences and economic consequences the world over. The airways of people with asthma are inflamed and react to irritants by narrowing and making it more difficult to breathe. This typically results in an "asthma exacerbation" whereby the asthmatic experiences shortness of breath, at minimum, and may need urgent medical attention.   Diesel exhaust (DE) is associated with asthma exacerbations, but how and why this occurs is unclear. One proposition is that DE causes "oxidative stress", which is damage to cells and body tissues due to certain chemical characteristics of DE particles. Recently, we have shown that oxidative stress is responsible for airway narrowing in asthmatics. We now want to know if this is made worse by the addition of a common allergen (such as that from grass or the birch tree).   In our lab, we create DE and finely control its concentration while volunteers inhale it for 2 hours. The concentration of DE is typical of that in a mining operation or on the streets of several developing cites in Asia. Such a short exposure time has no permanent effects but can reveal mild changes in the airways and blood (these return completely back to normal within hours) to help us decide if our hypothesis is correct. Each volunteer subject is exposed, on different days, to DE and to clean air. We after the DE (or clean air) exposure, we add allergen (grass or birch) to the lung, to see if that worsens the effect of DE, and to create the "real world" situation (where multiple asthma triggers are present at one time).   This research will allow a better understanding of DE-related airways disease, help workers' advocates and compensation boards better understand the harms of occupational exposure to diesel exhaust, and inform evolving measures to protect all Canadians exposed to traffic-related pollution (such as recommendations regarding exhaust filters or fuel composition, or personal anti-oxidant supplements).

TitreApplicationTitle: Activity Begins in Childhood (ABC)- a randomized controlled trial to inspire healthy active behaviour in preschoolers
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCELEROMETER; DAYCARE; EARLY CHILDHOOD EDUCATORS; EARLY INTERVENTION; FAMILY; HEALTH BENEFITS; HEALTHY DEVELOPMENT; MOTOR SKILL DEVELOPMENT; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PRESCHOOL CHILDREN
Abstract-Résumé: Physical activity (PA) is an important part of healthy childhood development. Typical Canadian preschoolers spend a great deal of time in daycare, environments which can have a very strong influence on their levels of daily movement. PA levels are low in these settings, with kids spending lots of time sitting.  This project will test the ability of daycare providers to incorporate PA into the daily routine when they are provided with appropriate training and tools to do so.  We will also look at whether engaging the parents and asking them to facilitate PA at home provides additional benefit.  We will use what is called a randomized control design.  This is a type of research study that 'randomly' (like flipping a coin) assigns people, or in this case, daycares, to one group or another.  We are going to have 3 groups to compare.  One group of daycare providers will be trained to increase all types of PA and reduce time spent sitting around. Another group of providers will have the same training but parents of kids in their care will also receive training on how to incorporate PA into their child's daily routine. The last group of daycares will offer their typical curriculum.  Over the course of 6 months we will measure PA using a device called an accelerometer (a 'super' pedometer) and measure height & weight.  We will also evaluate whether the intervention improved motor skills, which includes things like jumping, catching and throwing.  At the end we will compare groups to see if one performed better than the others.  We are intervening in preschoolers, because this is a group that is highly affected by the setting they are in and role models they interact with.  This will be the first study in Canada attempting to modify PA behaviour in licensed daycare centres and looking at parental involvement.   This is important because inactivity is highly predictive of development of chronic diseases like obesity and heart disease and prevention must start early.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Multicenter Prospective Cohort Study of Adverse Events Among Patients Discharged with Sentinel Cardiovascular Emergency Department Diagnoses
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE EVENT; ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; CARDIOVASCULAR DIAGNOSES; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; FOLLOW-UP; HEART FAILURE; PATIENT SAFETY; SYNCOPE
Abstract-Résumé: What is the problem? Almost a million Canadians visit emergency departments every year seeking healthcare due to heart-related problems. When complications are related to healthcare, the consequences can be serious and devastating. Common heart-related reasons for patients coming to the emergency department include those who have fluid on the lungs (heart failure), heart rhythm problems (atrial fibrillation) and fainting (syncope). Why is it important? Researchers have discovered that a high proportion of these healthcare related complications (called adverse events) are preventable. Understanding the cause of these healthcare related complications will better enable solutions to prevent future unintended harm to Canadians. What will this study achieve? The goal of this study is to determine what systemic and patient factors increase the risk of preventable healthcare related complications among emergency department patients with heart-related problems. We are focusing on a high risk group of people who are sent home from the emergency department: people over the age of 50 who have heart failure, atrial fibrillation and syncope. We will follow over 6500 patients across 10 Canadian emergency departments using health record review and telephone interviews. We will then ask teams of emergency doctors to review the records of patients who subsequently died, were admitted to hospital, visited an emergency department, saw their own doctor or felt worse 14 days after their first visit to the emergency department. This team of experts will identify complications related to healthcare received on the initial emergency department visit. What will be the impact of this study? Patient safety has been identified as a pressing national and provincial priority in healthcare. The results of this study will help prevent healthcare associated complications for people with these heart-related problems by producing the data needed to create patient safety enhancing solutions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The investigation of LRRK2 G2019S transgenic rats and their relationship to Parksinson's disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL TESTING; DOPAMINERGIC SYSTEM; MICRODIALYSIS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PET IMAGING; TRANSGENIC RODENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease can be debilitating to affected individuals. The disease places a substantial burden on care-givers and society. It affects approximately 0.3 % of the population. To develop effective new treatments requires a greater understanding of the underlying disease-causing mechanisms. The use of appropriate animal models that have been shown to capture the salient aspects of the disease will also be required.  LRRK2 G2019S transgenic rats carry a mutated form of the LRRK2 gene. This mutation substantially increases the risk of Parkinson's disease in humans. The study of these rats will help us understand the disease-causing mechanisms in Parkinson's, which will facilitate the design of new treatments to slow the disease progression of to prevent it. To achieve these ambitions requires the detailed study of these rats. We need to directly compare, at the molecular level, the disease in humans with the deficits produced in the transgenic animals. This direct comparison can be achieved using positron emission tomography (PET), an imaging technique that is commonly used in both species and which provides a key link between the animal model and the human disease. This project will study the transgenic rats using a variety of methods, including: i) Non-invasive PET imaging, with various radiotracers that measure the function of the dopaminergic system (a system known to be affected in Parkinson's). ii) microdialysis, which directly measures neurotransmitter levels in the brain. iii) behavioural tests to assess Parkinsonian-like movement deficits in the rodents. iv) a variety of post-mortem tissue assays. The findings will be directly compared to the results from human PET imaging; several such studies are currently in progress at our research centre. The proposed project will further our understanding of the disease and will determine the extent to which the LRRK2 G2019S rat is a good model for future research and treatment development.
