Abstract-Résumé: Every cell in our bodies receives signals which tell it whether to grow and divide, to differentiate into a specific cell type (e.g. a muscle cell or a neuron) or even to commit suicide.  These signals are transmitted by classes of proteins, known as enzymes, which modify other proteins.  These modified proteins are in turn recognized by specialized proteins to dictate the proper cellular response.  A key regulatory system in the cell utilizes a chemical group called "acetyl" for the modifications and the response to signals.  In many cancers, the enzymes responsible for the addition of the acetyl modification and the proteins that recognize this modification are mutated.  Drugs that target the process of acetyl modification and recognition are being developed and are showing great promise in the clinic to treat diverse cancers.  Yet, despite this fact, there is very little known regarding how specificity is acquired in this acetyl modification pathway.  For example, there are 42 distinct proteins that are able to recognize the acetyl modification.  Similar to a lock and key mechanism, these proteins need to recognize the acetyl modification only in the context of specific proteins, but what these proteins are is unclear at the moment.  The co-applicants have established a strong expertise in the use of an approach called mass spectrometry, which essentially identifies proteins using a unique "fingerprint" that each protein produces, and structural biology, which allows them to "see" how the lock and key mechanism functions.  By combining these techniques with molecular and cell biology approaches, the applicants will determine how the acetyl modification system is organized.  They will also test newly designed drugs that target the acetyl modification system to assess in a timely fashion which of the new drugs hold potential as therapeutic agents.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Amyloid-induced islet inflammation and beta cell dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYLIN; BETA CELL; DIABETES; IAPP; INFLAMMASOME; INNATE IMMUNITY; ISLET; ISLET AMYLOID; ISLET INFLAMMATION; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with type 2 diabetes are unable to produce sufficient insulin to meet demand and blood sugars rise as a result. The disease worsens as insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas lose their function and die. Loss of beta cells is thought to be due to several causes, one being the formation of toxic protein aggregates called islet amyloid, formed by accumulations of another small protein made along with insulin, called islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP). In type 2 diabetes the islets in the pancreas, where the insulin-producing beta cells reside, also show signs of inflammation. We recently found that aggregates of IAPP - the toxic amyloid deposits - may play an important role in inducing this inflammation within the islet. In this proposal we try to understand the mechanism by which IAPP aggregates induce islet inflammation in diabetes, and evaluate therapeutic approaches to block amyloid-induced inflammation. Findings from these studies may aid in the development of strategies to preserve beta cells in persons with type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessment of sterol metabolism in heterozygous and homozygous sitosterolemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ABCG8/G5; CHOLESTEROL; PLANT STEROLS; SITOSTEROLEMIA; STABLE ISOTOPE
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in Canada. High blood cholesterol is a risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. Studies have shown that daily intake of plant sterols or ezetimibe can lower blood cholesterol concentrations. It is unknown whether plant sterols and ezetimibe have different mechanisms of action on cholesterol metabolism. Studying individuals with a rare disease such as sitosterolemia provides important insight into the mechanisms underlying cardiovascular disease risks.  Sitosterolemia is a genetic disease caused by a defect in the genes that code for proteins that normally carry plant sterols out of the body. Homozygous sitosterolemia is characterized by high accumulation of blood cholesterol and plant sterol levels which can lead to atherosclerosis at an early age and high risk for heart attack. The current treatment of choice for homozygous sitosterolemia is the drug ezetimibe. Compared to individuals with homozygous sitosterolemia, people with heterozygous sitosterolemia are not clinically sick but may have increased blood cholesterol concentration. Studies in people with homozygous and heterozygous sitosterolemia will help us to better understand how plant sterols affect cholesterol function in the body to reduce cardiovascular disease risk. The main goals of this research are, therefore, to (a) study the effects of plant sterol intake on blood plant sterol, and cholesterol concentration and metabolism in individuals with heterozygous sitosterolemia compared to non-carriers; and (b)study the effects of ezetimibe treatment on plant sterols and cholesterol metabolism in patients with homozygous sitosterolemia. This study will have important relevance to the health and wellness of Canadians by contributing to an improved understanding of the underlying mechanisms regulating cardiovascular disease development, as well as in the identification of some genetic traits that correlate with various aspects of cholesterol metabolism.

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
TitreApplicationTitle: Hedgehog signaling and medulloblastoma tumorigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBELLUM; GENETICS; HEDGEHOG; MEDULLOBLASTOMA; MOUSE; PATCHED1; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Medulloblastoma is a very aggressive childhood cerebellum cancer and the most common brain tumor in children. One of the important causes of medulloblastoma is aberrant activation of the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway. Our lab recently identified a novel receptor for the secreted protein Shh. Using molecular and genetic approaches, we propose to identify the role of this receptor in medulloblastoma tumorigenesis. Defining the role of this novel Shh receptor in medulloblastoma will improve our knowledge on the molecular events involved in this cancer. Hopefully, this research will facilitate the discovery of more effective therapeutic agents that will help treat or prevent medulloblastoma and possibly other cancers that result from aberrant Shh signaling.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implicating Novel Genes in Familial Parkinsonism
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE DISCOVERY; GENETICS; GENOME SEQUENCING; NEUROGENETICS; PARKINSON DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson disease (PD) is the most common neurodegenerative movement disorder affecting ~1% of the population at 65 years, and increasing to 4-5% in 85-year-olds. PD affects over 100,000 Canadians and costs $2.5 billion annually, not considering the significant personal cost to patients and their families. The current treatments for PD do not address the causes of disease, but simply manage the symptoms. The development of preventative measures is hampered by our understanding of its molecular causes.  New sequencing technologies facilitate the identification of pathogenic mutations in novel genes in familial PD. The latest susceptibility gene (VPS35) for PD was discovered by applying these methods to a Swiss family in which multiple people were affected. The finding immediately improves an early and accurate diagnosis. Moreover, each gene/mutation helps implicate biological networks in disease, provides the targets and tools to model its pathogenesis, and enables therapeutic advance. This application is to apply similar genetic screening, sequencing and genotype approaches to implicate novel genes/mutations in the pathogenesis of PD. Gene mutation discovery will initially focus on 30 families that appear to have inherited PD down the family line. During the duration of the award, additional families and population resources will be referred by an extensive network of international clinical collaborators.   We hypothesize further gene discoveries will illuminate a limited number of biological pathways in disease. The proteins encoded and network perturbed provide the rational and targets for novel treatments. More efficacious drugs, which provide symptomatic benefit by halting disease progression, may cure this common disease. We intend to improve the quality of life for Canadians living with PD, and reduce the future burden of this disease on society by providing an unequivocal genetic foundation upon which translational neuroscience may focus.

OrgNm: CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Jewish General/CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Hôpital juif
TitreApplicationTitle: Measurement of Frailty to Identify High-Risk Elderly Patients Referred for Surgical and Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; AORTIC STENOSIS; AORTIC VALVE REPLACEMENT; FRAILTY; GERIATRIC CARDIOLOGY; MULTICENTER STUDY; MULTIDISCIPLINARY; OUTCOMES; PROSPECTIVE COHORT; TRANSCATHETER AORTIC VALVE IMPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: 1 in 22 adults will be diagnosed with significant narrowing of the aortic valve, known as aortic stenosis (AS), by the time they reach their 8th decade.  Considering that this segment of the population is expected to double by 2036, forecasts indicate that the number of older adults with AS will rise exponentially.  When patients with AS develop symptoms, aortic valve replacement (AVR) is the only proven treatment.  Before deciding to send a patient for AVR, the doctor calculates and is guided by the predicted risk that the patient will be able to survive surgery.  However, the process of risk prediction using existing risk scores is inaccurate in many complex elderly patients, in large part because these scores do not reflect the patient's physiologic reserves which will be called upon at the time of surgery.  Frailty is a state of decreased physiologic reserves and vulnerability to stressors.  Several tools exist to assess frailty, some based on physical tests and others on questionnaires, yet there is no agreement on which tool to recommend.  We will compare 5 frailty tools to determine which best predicts death or major complications after AVR when added to existing risk scores.  Additionally, in a subset of patients, we will explore muscle mass measured by computed tomorgraphy as an up-and-coming tool to assess frailty.  The overall objective of these projects is to improve our ability to predict risk by measuring frailty in elderly patients undergoing AVR.  By doing so, we hope to assist doctors in guiding patients suffering from AS to the appropriate therapy. Moreover, by integrating frailty into risk scores, we will provide policymakers and researchers with more accurate predictions of risk to analyze performance and conduct trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effectiveness of an internet-based decision aid in enhancing safety behaviors, reducing exposure to violence and improving mental health among women experiencing intimate partner violence
Keywords-MotsClés: DECISION AIDS; HELP-SEEKING; INTERNET-BASED INTERVENTIONS; INTIMATE PARTNER VIOLENCE; MENTAL HEALTH; TAILORED INTERVENTIONS; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: One out of four Canadian women experience Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) in their lifetimes, and most are negatively affected in terms of their mental and physical health. Our goal is to develop accessible, culturally appropriate interventions for women that limit IPV and its negative consequences. One of the most widely recommended interventions for women who experience partner abuse is safety planning. A safety decision aid helps women weigh the dangers of leaving or staying in a relationship, and provides an opportunity to plan safety for themselves and their children based on their own priorities and living situation. Using an experimental design, we will test whether a personalized, interactive internet-based safety decision aid helps women make decisions about safety, increases their use of safety strategies, improves support, prevents re-abuse, and improves mental health among women who are currently in an abusive relationship. A sample of 500 abused women will be assigned, by chance, to either complete the safety decision aid (SDA) intervention or to a control website. Women will be asked to self-report online their decision making related to an abusive relationship, their safety-seeking behaviours, perceived social support, mental health and exposure to repeat violence when they start the trial and 3, 6, and 12-months later. We will also interview 60 women about their use of the SDA in order to understand the strengths and limitations for different groups of women, including those living in rural settings, Aboriginal women and women with same-sex partners.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards a Cervical Spine Injury Tolerance Criterion that incorporates Lateral Bending Loading
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE; CADAVER MODEL; FRACTURE; INJURY BIOMECHANICS; INJURY PREVENTION; SPINAL CORD INJURY; SPINAL INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a significant health concern with an annual incidence of 13,000 in North America. These injuries have considerable financial and social implications, both for the injured individual and for society, as they lead to permanent disabilities.  The neck can suffer such catastrophic injuries when a person suffers a head impact while travelling head-first as can happen when a person is checked from behind in hockey or goes over the handlebars while mountain biking. In this research we will study these types of injuries using cadaver experiments to determine if impacts with the head leaning laterally result in worse bony and spinal cord injuries than occur with the neck straight. We can use this information to improve training techniques, protective equipment and helmets and also to help surgeons to develop improved treatments for people who suffer these injuries.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm : Enhanced guidance by elastic registration between CT-Scanner and fluoroscopy
Keywords-MotsClés: ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM; C-ARM CT; CT-SCANNER; DIGITAL SUBSTRACTION ANGIOGRAPHY; ENDOVASCULAR REPAIR BY STENT-GRAFT; IMAGE FUSION AND REGISTRATION
Abstract-Résumé: An increasing incidence of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) is observed in our ageing  population. Since it is less invasive, endovascular repair (EVAR) by stent-graft (SG) insertion is frequently indicated in patients with intermediate and high-operative risk. Patient selection and stent planning for EVAR is done on CT-scans based on specific anatomic criteria. SG are inserted in the catheterization laboratory under digital substraction angiography (DSA) and fluoroscopic guidance. With this technology, no soft-tissue differentiation is available during the intervention and important information are lacking such as thrombus and aneurysm extension close to proximal and distal landing zones. Our team has recently patented a software allowing the extraction of the AAA (lumen and thrombus) from pre-operative CT-scanner. In collaboration with Siemens medical, we have integrated this technology to the Siemens workstation in the catheterization laboratory. We can now import the aortic lumen and thrombus meshes segmented from pre-operative CT-scans and perform a rigid registration with fluoroscopy and DSA data to enhance visualization of soft tissue during EVAR.  Our preliminary results are encouraging in terms of feasibility and visualization. However, the delivery device of the SG and the guidewire used during the intervention are stiff and induce a deformation of aortic lumen and thrombus. This deformation impairs the accuracy of rigid registration. We propose to improve registration accuracy by implementing an elastic deformation of aortic lumen and wall based on the segmentation of endovascular devices (delivery device, guidewires and catheters) inserted during the procedure and by biomechanical modeling.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinically meaningful change in function and disability in older adults over 2 years: who is at risk for decline?
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DISABILITY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; FUNCTION; MEASUREMENT; MOBILITY; PHYSICAL THERAPY; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: One in three Canadians over the age of 65 have some form of restriction in physical functioning that interferes with their ability to move around within their environment. Problems in physical functioning are predictive of risk for future disability, institutionalization and mortality.  Consequently, there is increasing focus on identifying the best physical function screening tools to identify at-risk patients who need early treatment. However, before we can implement appropriate treatment and prevention programs, there is a need to improve our understanding of existing measures of physical function. There is also a need to determine which types of physical problems contribute most to risk of future disability; this information is essential for designing the most effective treatment strategies. The purpose of this study is to estimate the increments of change in measures of function and disability that are likely to be most meaningful to patients and clinicians, and to identify which physical problems influence decline in function and disability over time.  This information will allow us to develop a risk stratification tool to identify older adults who are at the greatest risk for developing restrictions in physical functioning and who need early preventative treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural mechanisms of compulsive cocaine intake
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; COCAINE SELF-ADMINISTRATION; COMPULSIVITY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NEURAL MECHANISMS
Abstract-Résumé: Addiction is a compulsive behavior meaning that addicts spend exaggerated efforts and persist taking drugs despite severe negative consequences for them, their family, and their friends. Accordingly, something in the brains of addicts does not gate properly the urge to take drugs when adverse consequences are obviously inevitable. In fact, drug addicts are well aware of the negative consequences of their habits, but yet, they cannot help returning to spend exaggerated time seeking, taking, and recovering from drugs. It is the objective of the present research proposal to identify the location (s) and mechanism (s) that may underlie the compulsive aspect of drug addiction. Fortunately, there are now reliable behavioral tests in animals that closely mimic compulsive drug use in humans. Here, we will combine a rodent model of compulsive drug use with neurochemical and electrophysiological assays. This combination will allow us to understand better where in the brain and by which mechanisms do compulsive drug use stems from and may reveal new therapeutical targets to manage and perhaps cure drug addiction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural mechanisms underlying working memory in the primate visual dorsal pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EYE MOVEMENTS; MICROELECTRODE ARRAYS; MONKEYS; NEURONAL NETWORKS; SINGLE CELL RECORDINGS; VISUAL; VISUAL CORTEX; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Working memory is known as the ability to retain information for short time periods in the absence of visual inputs. It has been demonstrated that some neurons in parietal, frontal and temporal cortical areas of primates are able to sustain their firing rate during tasks that require maintaining the features or locations of visual stimuli in working memory. This has led to the suggestion that neuronal networks within these areas are directly responsible for visual working memory maintenance. More recently imaging studies have suggested that some areas of the visual cortex show BOLD signal activation during working memory tasks. This controversial result, however, has not been well replicated by electrophysiological studies in non-human primates. Our first goal is to determine in which areas of the visual dorsal pathway the coding of working memory by single neurons emerges. Furthermore we will conduct experimental manipulations to determine the exact mechanisms by which neuron maintain memory information through their firing rate in the absence of visual inputs. These results will considerably advance our knowledge of how working memory is encoded in the primate brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hypolipidemic Effects of Dietary Trans-11 Vaccenic Acid Supplementation in Naïve Hyper-Lipidemic Subjects
Keywords-MotsClés: APOB48; DYSLIPIDEMIA; FATTY ACIDS; TRANS-11 VACCENIC ACID
Abstract-Résumé: Trans fats can be formed industrially under extreme heat when making semi-solid fats. However, it is less well known that certain trans fat can also be formed naturally in ruminant animals such as cows. Vaccenic acid (VA) is the major ruminant trans fat found in foods such as dairy and beef products. While it is widely accepted that industrial trans fat increases heart disease risk, animal data from our laboratory and other scientists have shown that VA may actually lower several types of fat and cholesterol in the blood. High blood fat or cholesterol is a feature of metabolic syndrome associated with increased heart disease risk. Understanding the action of VA in humans is essential to further distinguish the effects of natural from industrial trans fat on heart disease. The objective of this study is to assess for the first time the effect of VA on blood fat, cholesterol and other heart disease risk factors in men. The proposed study will be a carefully controlled dietary intervention where the participants receive 2 weight-maintaining diets consecutively for 4 weeks each: 1) a control diet and 2) a diet rich in VA (represent 6.7% of total fat). All foods will be provided to participants to ensure adequate and equal nutrient intake and that intake of VA is maintained at targeted level throughout the study. We expect that increasing VA in the diet will significantly decrease blood fat and cholesterol levels. We also hope to assess changes in genes and pathways in important organs that control fat production (including the intestine), which will help us understand the reasons behind the proposed health effects. Collectively, these novel findings will help support the hypothesis that consumption of VA not only has different (potentially beneficial) effects in humans relative to industrial trans fat, but could be considered an effective nutritional intervention for individuals with high blood fat who are therefore at high risk for heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oxygen and brain injury in the newborn: unprecedented role for fatty acid receptors and characterization of potential therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; DRUG CHARACTERIZATION; NEURODEVELOPMENT; REACTIVE SPECIES; RECEPTOR; VASCULAR DEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Premature newborns are particularly vulnerable to neurologic insults which lead to severe neurological sequelae as well as frequent neurodevelopmental disorders. Widespread anomalies of brain circulation underlie the insults incurred by preterm infants. The exposure to the high postnatal oxygen concentrations relative to those in utero has been amply shown to exert adverse effects on lung and retina of the immature newborn. We recently showed that was also the case for the brain, wherein diffuse loss of microvessels (critical to maintain oxygen and nutrient delivery to tissues) was observed throughout the brain of immature animal subjects, consistent with broad diminished circulation detected in premature newborn human infants.  A major role for reactive species of oxygen and nitrogen has been proposed. However, scavenging these reactive species is often difficult, and moreover certain stable products generated by these toxic substances are themselves toxic to the brain, notably trans-arachidonic acids (TAAs). To date, there is no means of interfering with the actions of these abnormal substances that linger in tissues (including brain) long after the oxidation took place. We identified for the first time a receptor that may be a principal target of TAAs, and have generated novel molecules that interfere with the actions of TAAs. Pilot data reveal that these molecules could protect newborn brain from widespread loss of vessels. The objective of this project is to confirm the identification of TAA target and characterize molecules that interfere with deleterious effects of TAA on newborn brain.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Control of Inflammatory Responses
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES; EPITHELIAL CELLS; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY
Abstract-Résumé: One of our bodies' first lines of defence against invading pathogens is a process called inflammation, which is mediated by cells of the innate immune system. However, when these innate immune cells carry out their beneficial functions to remove pathogens, they inflict some unavoidable damage on surrounding healthy tissues. If this inflammation becomes excessive, it can contribute to a host of ills like chronic inflammatory diseases, autoimmune disorders, neurodegenerative disorders like Parkinson's, cardiovascular diseases, and cancer. All these medical conditions have debilitating and sometimes life-threatening complications and are expensive to treat. Current therapies are inadequate because they do not address the fundamental cause of these conditions: a failure in the body's mechanisms needed to control inflammation and direct immune responses to fight tumor development. Consequently, it is essential to identify the key steps immune cells use to mount and resolve inflammatory responses, and to learn how we can regulate these processes to prevent disease.  Our laboratory has shown that certain members of a family of proteins known as rhomboids are important for the production of an inflammatory signaling molecule called TNF. When these rhomboid proteins are missing, a mouse cannot control its inflammatory response properly. We have also shown that another signaling molecule called TSLP is required for the normal healing of tissues damaged by excessive inflammation. However, TSLP has other effects that can promote cancer development. Our proposal seeks to use genetically engineered mice to understand how the rhomboids and TSLP carry out their physiological roles. Our objective is to find ways to manipulate the rhomboids and TSLP or their target molecules in order to control excessive inflammation. We will also investigate whether loss of TSLP function slows tumor development. Our ultimate goal is to devise new drugs to combat harmful inflammation and cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Subversion of autophagy by the Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CYTOKINE; DNA DAMAGE; HERPESVIRUS; HIV; KSHV; ONCOGENE; SENESCENCE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TUMOUR
Abstract-Résumé: Our laboratory is dedicated to revealing the strategies that viruses employ to infect host tissues and establish chronic disease. In people suffering from AIDS, co-infection with the Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV, human herpesvirus-8) causes a tumour known as Kaposi's sarcoma (KS). It is not known precisely how KSHV causes tumour formation, but the emerging model is that different viral gene products collaborate to reprogram host cells and undermine host anti-viral and anti-cancer defences.   Through our CIHR-funded research program, we seek to better understand how KSHV undermines a host defence known as autophagy. Autophagy is a recycling mechanism that engulfs and degrades cellular structures to liberate raw materials and energy. Virus structures can also be targeted by the autophagy machinery, thereby preventing virus replication and alerting the immune system. Thus, autophagy can be thought of as a form of anti-viral defence. Autophagy also plays an essential role in a host anti-cancer defence known as oncogene-induced senescence. Our recent studies have demonstrated that KSHV encodes a viral protein, v-FLIP, that facilitates bypass of oncogene-induced senescence, thereby allowing KSHV infected cells to proliferate and initiate cancer.   We seek to better understand precisely how KSHV undermines autophagy at different stages of the viral replicative cycle, and determine the consequences for viral fitness and the fate of the infected host cells. The ultimate objective is to use this knowledge to develop new anti-viral therapies that prevent KS tumour formation.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Critial Control Points of Oncogenic Myc
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-CANCER THERAPEUTIC; MYC ONCOGENE; PHOSPHORYLATION; POSTTRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SUMOYLATION; UBIQUITYLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer arises when a single cell acquires several mutations, which in turn cause that cell to escape normal control mechanisms and divide uncontrollably to form a tumour.  A potent cell growth molecule, called Myc, is commonly found unleashed in the majority of human cancers.  Clearly developing a drug to block Myc would mark a key therapeutic advance, but such a drug has not yet been possible to develop using traditional approaches.    We believe that by understanding how Myc drives cells to form cancers, we will unveil novel strategies to develop anti-cancer agents that inhibit Myc.  Surprisingly, the modifications on the Myc molecule and cellular interacting molecules that are essential for Myc to drive cancer have not yet been discovered.  To fill this gap, we have combined the unique expertise of two labs (Penn and Raught).  Using newly developed biological probes in combination with state-of-the-art instrumentation we have been able to visualize Myc in tumour cells.  With this major advance we now aim to: 1.Exploit our new research advance and fully delineate the modifications on the Myc molecule associated with cellular growth and tumorigenesis.  We will then determine which of these is functionally critical to cancer development. 2.Identify Myc interacting molecules that enable Myc to be such a potent driver of so many cancers across a variety of cell types (e.g. breast and lung cancer).  This knowledge will allow drugs to be developed to block Myc from interacting with its important partner proteins. 3. Determine the machinery responsible for the key modifications essential for Myc to drive normal cells to become cancer cells.  With this information we will be able to develop drugs to block the machinery and therefore inhibit Myc function.  Thus, by identifying Myc modifications and interactors, we anticipate the development of two different yet complimentary strategies to develop drugs to block Myc and stop cancer cell growth.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention de fonctionnement : programme de recherche en collaboration avec l'industrie
TitreApplicationTitle: Prevalence of Sub-Clinical Atrial Fibrillation in Patients with Cardiovascular Risk Factors Detected Using an Implantable Loop Recorder (ASSERT-2)
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTORS; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; ELDERLY; IMPLANTABLE ARRHYTHMIA MONITOR; PREVENTION; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation is an irregular beating of the heart which can lead to stroke in individuals who have high blood pressure, diabetes, a weak heart muscle or other risk factors for stroke. If atrial fibrillation is identified, effective treatment is available to prevent stroke. However, in many individuals, atrial fibrillation causes absolutely no symptoms and standard heart monitors have a limited ability to detect this silent atrial fibrillation. There are now small heart monitors (the size of a USB drive) which can be easily implanted under the skin of the chest and can continuously monitor the heart's activity for many months; greatly increasing the chance of detecting silent atrial fibrillation. With this technology, it may now be possible to diagnose silent atrial fibrillation before an individual suffers a stroke and provide that individual with appropriate treatment to prevent stroke. As a first step in this line of research we plan to follow 250 individuals with risk stroke factors for approximately 2 years, to determine how many have silent atrial fibrillation; in whom we may be able to prevent stroke.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Solution NMR Study of the Functional Dynamics of a Primitive Proteasome
Keywords-MotsClés: PROTEASOME; SOLUTION NMR; STRUCTURE AND DYNAMICS; SUPRAMOLECULES
Abstract-Résumé: Many critically important processes in the cell are regulated by very large molecular complexes acting essentially as microscopic machines. Like their macroscopic counterparts, these tiny machines are not static. They contain movable 'parts' and the changes in conformation are very often crucial for proper function. Not surprisingly, an understanding of the way that these systems work has been a longstanding goal of biochemists and structural biologists alike. We will use novel Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy methods to understand the way in which a class of molecular machines, called proteases, that targets proteins inside the cell for degradation once they are no longer needed for function or when they age - approximately 5% of our proteins are degraded each day! This tightly controlled process is carried out primarily by the proteasome in higher organisms and the HslUV protease in bacteria. The HslUV protease has many of the features of the eukaryotic proteasome, yet it is comprised of only two polypeptide chains that form hexameric ring structures, HslU and HslV. Thus, HslUV can serve as a "simple" model biochemical system. I propose to use a suite of solution NMR experiments and isotope labeling techniques optimized for studies of supra-molecules to probe the interactions between HslU and HslV and between HslUV and substrates. The overall goal of the proposed research is to provide a molecular picture of the important changes in structure and dynamics along the path by which substrate is degraded. The knowledge obtained from the model HslUV system will improve our understanding of the eukaryotic proteasome complex, which is implicated in cancer, autoimmune diseases and neurodegeneration and is a target for rational drug design.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy on markers of health in women who carry a BRCA mutation
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE HEALTH; CANCER PREVENTION; CARDIAC HEALTH; COHORT STUDY; NATURAL HISTORY; PROPHYLACTIC SALPINGO-OOPHORECTOMY; QUALITY OF LIFE; SEXUAL HEALTH; SURGICAL MENOPAUSE
Abstract-Résumé: Women who inherit a change in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene have significantly elevated risks for breast, ovarian and fallopian tube cancer. Preventive removal of the ovaries and fallopian tubes is recommended for these women to reduce the risk of cancer. This surgery is recommended at age 35 or after childbearing is complete, resulting in premature menopause. Many of these women are unable to take hormone replacement therapy due to a previous diagnosis of breast cancer. The impact on health and quality of life for women who have preventive surgery is not well studied. Critical questions remain, including the impact of preventive ovarian surgery on cardiac health, bone health, and overall quality of life. The purpose of our study is to evaluate the impact of preventive ovarian surgery on the health of 150 women who undergo the procedure over the next two years. Markers of cardiac and bone health will be measured before and after surgery. Questionnaires measuring sexual function, menopausal symptoms and overall quality of life, before and after surgery, will be compared. We will compare these women with women of the same age who have not undergone preventive removal of the ovaries and fallopian tubes. These women will be followed for ten years for relevant clinical events. This information will be useful for women who must make a decision about preventive ovarian surgery. It will also help physicians care for their patients who have a high risk for breast, ovarian and fallopian tube cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of translational control in higher eukaryotes
Keywords-MotsClés: PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins are the fundamental building blocks of all organisms. They act as machines that perform a wide variety of functions in the cell including the breakdown of nutrients, formation of antibodies for protection against viruses, mediating cell growth and division, and importantly, control the activity of our genes. The process of protein synthesis in higher organisms, such as mammals, consists of copying a gene from DNA located inside the nucleus of a cell, moving this copy (called mRNA) out of the nucleus, and translating that message by producing a protein molecule. Our research focuses on the last step of this process, called mRNA translation. A cell can control mRNA translation by adjusting the levels of specific proteins in response to a particular need or stress. Our laboratory has identified multiple factors involved in regulating translation and we work towards understanding how the cell controls this function.  We have shown that controlling mRNA translation plays a vital role in cell viability, learning and memory, adipose tissue metabolism, viral infection, and tumour formation. Our research will contribute towards a broader perspective on how cells perform these fundamental processes and ultimately help us to design innovative treatments against diseases such as mental disorders, obesity, AIDS, and cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gender, Sex and Work Injury, Illness and Disability
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; COHORT STUDY; DATABASE LINKAGE; GENDER HEALTH; OCCUPATIONAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; OCCUPATIONAL INJURIES; WORKER'S COMPENSATION
Abstract-Résumé: Disparities exist in health outcomes and health-care access/utilization for women and men, yet little is known about differences in work injury and illness, workers' compensation, or disability outcomes within the Canada context.  Using a population of Canadian workers with a workers' compensation claim, the purpose of this study is to investigate differences in workers' compensation experiences by gender/sex for a) rates of work injury and illness for workers in the same occupation and industry, b) disability outcomes such as duration of claim for the same type of work injury or illness, and c) the amount and type of health care utilization and benefits for the same work injury or illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Be Healthy in Pregnancy (BHIP) with Nutrition & Exercise
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION; CLINICAL TRIAL; EXERCISE INTERVENTION; FETAL DETERMINANTS OF INFANT OUTCOMES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH; NUTRITIONAL INTERVENTION; OBESITY; PREGNANCY OUTCOMES; PRIMARY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Excess weight gain in pregnancy is a major health problem affecting 55-75% of Canadian women who enter pregnancy overweight or obese and about 40% of women who are normal weight. Such excess weight gain puts mothers at risk for health problems such as diabetes, high blood pressure and developing or sustaining obesity after pregnancy and puts their babies at risk of being born too large or developing related health problems. While guidelines for healthy pregnancy are currently provided through clinical and public health programs, they do not appear to be effective since excess pregnancy weight gain and adverse pregnancy outcomes are still widely observed. Our research questions is: Will a safe and practical structured nutrition and exercise program introduced in early pregnancy compared to standard prenatal care increase  the chance that mothers will achieve a pregnancy weight gain within the current recommendations; and secondly, improve health measures in the mother and infant at six months post-partum?   The combined nutrition and exercise program is based on our recent research along with new information about the needs and preferences identified by pregnant women and their care providers. Mothers will be randomized in their first trimester of pregnancy to structured high dairy protein nutrition plan and walking exercise program or the usual (standard) care by their care provider including advice on the current web-based guidance for healthy pregnancy weight gain recommended by Health Canada. Mothers will be assessed for weight, physical activity and adherence to the nutrition plan until birth and at follow-up with their infants at 6 months after birth.  The research team will work with partners in community, public health and professional associations to ensure that new information from the research will be quickly transferred to programs to assist women to have healthier pregnancies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gamma-secretase inhibition for treatment of spinal cord injury
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD VESSEL SPROUTING; CONDITIONAL KNOCK-OUT; LASER-CAPTURE MICRO-DISSECTION; ORTHOTOPIC TUMOURS; QUANTITATIVE PCR; RETINAL ANGIOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Growth of new blood vessels (angiogenesis) supplies oxygen and nutrients to normal cells and tissues as our bodies develop, grow and change throughout life. In some diseases, including cancer, angiogenesis becomes abnormal, and contributes to disease progression. In cancer, abnormal angiogenesis occurs within tumours, and allows tumours to grow and spread. Like other cells, tumour cells require a blood supply to survive. Therefore, eliminating the blood supply to tumours is one strategy for fighting cancer.  There are many signals that trigger angiogenesis in tumours. Some current cancer treatments block these signals, in an effort to prevent the growth of new blood vessels and to starve the tumour. The problem with this approach is the multitude of signals: if we block one signal from the tumour, another signal may still promote blood vessel growth. The goal of this work is to target the cells that make new blood vessels (endothelial cells or ECs) directly: rather than attempt to block signals to these cells, we will stop the cellular processes that allow ECs to grow and divide.  ECs undergo a significant change when they shift from a resting state to an active state. In their active state, they begin to grow, migrate, and multiply, and to form new blood vessels. In order to change from resting to active, ECs must change the way they produce energy. Evidence indicates that glutamine, an amino acid that is abundant in the blood, is required for ECs to undergo this switch. In these experiments, we will 1) study the role of glutamine in ECs, and 2) use animal models to determine how glutamine contributes to the formation of new blood vessels in normal embryonic development and in cancer. We will use mice implanted with various types of tumours to determine whether interfering with glutamine is an effective cancer therapy. Targeting EC metabolism directly is a completely new approach to cancer treatment, and may prove effective against many different types of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: HPV Vaccination Discourses, Practices and Spaces: Affects and Effects on Youth's Bodies and Subjectivities
Keywords-MotsClés: DISCOURSES; ETHNOGRAPHY; FEMINIST; GENDER; HPV; POSTSTRUCTURALISM; QUALITATIVE; SEXUAL HEALTH; SPACES; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: PROBLEM. Recently, we have seen an explosion of research on the human papillomavirus (HPV) as well as on HPV vaccination (HPVV) in various countries. HPVV campaigns have stirred debates on the link between HPV and cervical cancer as well as on HPVV safety, effectiveness, cost, and ethics. Despite serious concerns, little is known about HPVV in Canada. It may be that youth are insufficiently informed about HPVV and the need for preventative sexual health practices (e.g., regular Pap smears, condom use) to prevent sexually transmitted infections, in which case, the expected HPVV health gains would turn to health losses. At the moment, however, there is no research on how Canadian youth experience HPVV.  OBJECTIVES. Our project aims to document the deployment of HPVV discourses in Canada and its impact on Canadian youth. With regards to HPVV discourses, our objective is to examine how they are deployed, disseminated, understood, taken up and/or resisted across home, school, media and health spaces. With regard to youth, we aim to investigate their experiences of HPVV and to deepen our understanding of how they make sense, negotiate or resist HPVV discourses.  METHOD. In Facet I of the project, we will draw on ethnographies to interrogate how HPVV discourses are deployed in home, school, and health-related spaces in 4 provinces (QC, ON, MB, BC). We will also content-analyse various electronic media, paying attention to Canadian messaging about HPVV. In Facet II, we will use photo-voice, drawing, and focus group methods with 12-16 years old male and female students. We will also interview parents, teachers, and health professionals. The total sample (N=170 participants) will be diverse in terms of sex/gender, sexuality, race/ethnicity, dis/ability, class, and rural/urban status. We will favour poststructuralist methods for our ethnographies and for the analysis of the "texts" (photographs, drawings, interview transcripts, policy materials) we collect.

TitreApplicationTitle: Synergistic microRNA-binding sites, and 3' untranslated regions: a dialogue of silence
Keywords-MotsClés: 3' UNTRANSLATED REGIONS; C. ELEGANS; CELL FREE ASSAYS; FUNCTIONAL SCREEN; MICRORNAS; MRNA DEADENYLATION; TRANSGENIC REPORTERS; TRANSLATION REPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past few years, an important new class of molecules influencing cell behavior was discovered: the microRNAs. About one thousand of these little regulators are at work in human cells, and they have been implicated in almost every biological process, but also in numerous diseases including cancer. MicroRNAs mostly act as repressors of genes by directly binding to a portion of the messengers of genes (mRNAs) termed the 3 prime untranslated region (3'UTR). Understanding exactly how microRNA function in controlling gene expression represents an important new frontier in biomedical research. With this grant proposal, we put forward experiments aimed at understanding how microRNA interact with sites on mRNAs, and more precisely how they interact with one another. Using molecular biology and genomic tools, we will determine how sites interact synergistically, a configuration of microRNA sites coined synmiRS. We will define the parameters that govern such interactions, and probe the mechanism underlying the cooperative potentiation of gene silencing directed by the miRNA silencing machinery. Finally, we will examine how the remolding of the 3'UTR portions of mRNAs affect the interactions of microRNA-binding sites, and their capacity to modulate gene activity. Better understanding of how microRNA interact with mRNAs will allow to discern the biologically important microRNA-binding sites in the genome from weak or non-functional ones. Hence, this project offers much promise in grasping the impact of microRNAs in important biological processes, and their roles in diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multicenter pilot study on assessment and prevention of platinum-induced ototoxicity
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER SURVIVORSHIP; CLINICAL TRIAL; DEXAMETHASONE; EPIDEMIOLOGICAL NETWORK; GENETIC TESTING; HEARING LOSS; ONCOLOGY; OTOTOXICITY; PLATINUM CHEMOTHERAPY; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Recent advances in cancer treatment are leading to rapidly increasing survival rates. The current five-year survival rate for children with cancer is 80%. Cisplatin and carboplatin are two of the most successful and widely-used anticancer drugs; however, they lead to ototoxicity in the majority of the children. Ototoxicity manifests as a permanent severe hearing loss and ringing in the ears. This can have devastating consequences on communication, school performance, social interaction, and overall quality of life. There is currently no treatment or prevention for ototoxicity, but the steroid Dexamethasone is a promising candidate. In a previously funded CIHR grant, our group has discovered intratympanic dexamethasone injection to prevent hearing loss from ototoxicity in the guinea pig. This finding has been confirmed by other groups in 5 other animal studies. Intratympanic dexamethasone is also widely used clinically to treat sudden hearing loss, and other auto-immune ear disorders. The safety and efficacy of this treatment has been well-established in numerous clinical studies for the above-mentioned disorders.  While our group has started the first hearing protection clinical trial in Canada using the anti-oxidant Ringer's lactate in adult patients, there are currently no pediatric trials and no publications on intratympanic (IT) dexamethasone for platinum-induced ototoxicity.  The purpose of this pilot study is to estimate the protective effect of IT dexamethasone that may be worth confirming in a subsequent larger study and to evaluate the safety and feasibility of methods for later use in a large-scale study across Canada.  This pilot study will be conducted at 4 major paediatric oncology sites in 2 provinces, and will lay the ground for a larger, pan-Canadian trial involving our established network of 13 paediatric oncology centers, all of whom see the urgency and necessity for such a trial.

TitreApplicationTitle: Statistical methods of estimating genetic associations of low detectability
Keywords-MotsClés: BAYESIAN INFERENCE; BIOSTATISTICS; EMPIRICAL BAYES; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENOME-WIDE ASSOCIATION STUDY; IMPRECISE PROBABILITY; LARGE-SCALE INFERENCE; LOCAL FALSE DISCOVERY RATE; ROBUST BAYESIAN; STATISTICAL GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: In large-scale genetic association studies, thousands of letters of DNA code are measured for hundreds of people with a widespread disease and for hundreds of people without the disease. The goal of this research is to create mathematical methods of accurately determining which DNA letters are associated with the disease in the sense that people with a variation in a certain DNA letter are at higher or lower risk of contracting the disease.   We will use the new methods to aid in the discovery of DNA letters associated with three widespread health problems: coronary artery disease, severe obesity, and colorectal cancer. That will be accomplished on the basis of data from several large-scale genetic association studies. We will determine what such discoveries reveal about the causes of the health problems, which can lead to prevention and treatment interventions. In addition, the methods we develop will be provided to other research groups to help them discover the causes of other widespread diseases.  The methods currently used to interpret large-scale genetic association data were designed to avoid all false discoveries of association, but only at the expense of missing many detectable associations. Advances in methods of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) increase the number of detected true associations by allowing false discoveries as long as the overall average proportion of discoveries that are false is below set rate such as 5%. Likewise, the local FDR (LFDR), as a probability that a given DNA letter is not associated with the health problem, would be highly informative for inferring causes of disease. We will develop reliable methods of estimating the LFDR and the strengths of association for new prevention and treatment interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Analytic Methods for the Next Generation of Complex Trait Studies
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPLEX TRAITS; GENE BY ENVIRONMENT; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENOME-WIDE STUDIES; LONGITUDINAL STUDY DESIGN; STATISTICAL GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Investigators of common diseases and traits in human populations can now measure genomic variation at an unprecedented level of detail and assess molecular mechanisms with advanced technologies, but analytic capacity to understand and interpret the large volume of information is still limited.   Our aim in the proposed research is to apply statistical theory and methods to answer two main questions:  1)  Under a study design in which people are measured repeatedly through time, can advanced modeling techniques help to distinguish between two possibilities? One possibility is that genetic differences between people are associated with differences in levels of a known risk factor but are not directly associated with differences in disease outcome. The other is that genetic differences between people are associated with differences in disease outcome through another unidentified genetic or environmental pathway.  2)  Given that we have measurements of risk factors and disease status in a large number of people together with readily available genome-wide information on common genetic markers, how can we choose an informative subset of people in which it is efficient to collect expensive information on uncommon genetic variation and molecular function to assess hypotheses about biological mechanism?  We anticipate that the extent to which information about association can be translated into understanding of biological mechanism will largely determine the extent to which promising new avenues for disease preventive or treatment can be developed for population groups and individuals.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Genetics of Hereditary Upper Gastrointestinal Cancers:  Beyond CDH1 Germline Mutations
Keywords-MotsClés: BRCA2; CANCER SUSCEPTIBILITY; CDH1; ESOPHAGEAL CANCER; GASTRIC CANCER; HEREDITARY CANCER; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; PANCREATIC CANCER; PRECURSOR LESIONS; PROPHYLACTIC GASTRECTOMY
Abstract-Résumé: Although less than 5% of cancers are obviously hereditary, that is they are predominantly caused by inherited and not environmental factors, these cancer cases can often be prevented if the causative mutations (genetic changes) are known.  Our team has shown that cancers can be prevented in the 45% of families with hereditary gastric cancer where we can find a mutation in the CDH1 gene. We are also developing screening and unique management plans for familial pancreatic cancer families with known mutations. In this study, we propose to find the mutations causing cancer in other unexplained upper GI cancers (esophageal, gastric, pancreatic and others). We will apply full genome sequencing (a state-of-the-art technique for deciphering an entire human DNA sequence) to make these discoveries. We will also examine the tumours to determine if mutations found are really causative of the cancers. We will test additional families for all mutations discovered and rapidly disseminate our discoveries internationally so that testing for new genes can become routine in clinical laboratories as soon as possible. We will also study the tumors from these families to see if they are distinct in terms of treatment opportunities compared to sporadic cancers.  Through this research we will develop and disseminate tools to prevent cancers in families at high risk for upper GI cancer. The research team includes senior researchers, new and incoming recruits and trainees; we believe the project will provide great opportunities for mentorship of the junior members as they to build careers as clinician scientists and for the trainees who will work with us on this project.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring global health
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICS; HEALTH MEASUREMENT
Abstract-Résumé: The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) project quantifies the burden of both morbidity and premature mortality across the world. It has become an important, if controversial, indicator of the state of global health as well as an instrument to inform and guide health policy at global and national levels. Originally developed in the 1990s, the methodology underlying the GBD is currently undergoing its first significant revision, with updated results to be published later this year. This project seeks to evaluate, from an inter-disciplinary perspective, the suitability of the revised methodology on which the GBD health measure is based for its intended and actual use in policy decisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the Ethics of the Dominant Business Model in the Canadian Pharmaceutical Sector; Tackling Institutional Corruption through Regulatory Reforms
Keywords-MotsClés: BUSINESS MODEL; COST AND PRICES OF MEDICINES; GHOSTMANAGEMENT OF MEDICAL LITERATURE; INNOVATION POLICIES; INVESTMENT AND PROFITABILITY; OFF-LABEL USE; PHARMACEUTICAL PROMOTION; PHARMACEUTICAL SECTOR; RESEARCH ETHICS; THERAPEUTIC INNOVATION
Abstract-Résumé: Is the dominant business model of core pharmaceutical companies built on ethical foundations? Is the earning capacity of drug companies in line with the improvement of public health? In the last 15 years, fewer new drugs have arrived on the market, and the vast majority of them do not represent any therapeutic advancement as compared to what already exist. Nevertheless, dominant pharmaceutical companies are gaining record profits in spite of the lack of therapeutic innovation. This paradox can be explained if we consider the hypothesis that the main on-going business model is the aggressive promotion of me-too drugs in a way that institutionally corrode evidence-based medicine.  If this hypothesis is correct, it means that the profit-motive is not encouraging the development of new drugs.  Promotional expenditures surged during that period and medical research is ever more organized as a promotional campaign creating bias in medical practices. A growing amount of evidence shows the emergence of unethical practices in medical research for marketing purposes. For example, drug companies are systematically multiplying ghostwritten studies showing benefits for products, disclosure of adverse data in clinical trials is still incomplete and a growing amount of researchers have reported intimidation when they published adverse research results.   The question before us is thus to understand if the profit-motive is embedded in a market structure encouraging unethical practices instead of innovative therapeutics. And if it is the case, what could be done to reconcile pharmaceutical profits and public health, especially when current innovation policies put in place by the Canadian government aim at increasing revenues instead of therapeutic innovation? What could be done in terms of regulatory reforms to re-organize the market structure in order to have a profit-motive serving the interests of patients as well? How can we reconcile business imperatives and health ethic

TitreApplicationTitle: Screening for HIV-Associated Neurocognitive Disorders: Evaluation and Clinical Application
Keywords-MotsClés: EVALUATION; HIV-ASSOCIATED NEUROCOGNITIVE DISORDERS; HIV/AIDS; NEUROCOGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; SCREENING TOOLS
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 50% of adults with HIV will experience an HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND). Even in their mildest forms, HIV-associated cognitive impairments can seriously affect people's ability to work, adhere to their medication and function in their daily lives. However, the health care system lacks information and tools that could help reduce the impact of HAND and improve quality of life. There is an urgent demand for effective practical brief screening tools that can be administered by primary care providers.  The research project will: 1. Study/characterize 500 adults with HIV with HAND and associated comorbidities 2. Establish the test performance characteristics and clinical utility of five cognitive screening tools in detecting HAND in an urban sample of Canadians living with HIV 3. Identify differences in test performance characteristics according to: the presence or absence of comorbid conditions; and the severity of neurocognitive impairment 4. Develop and disseminate screening guidelines to HIV-treating clinicians to enhance assessment and treatment of patients with HAND. Participants will be administered a complete "gold standard" neuropsychological battery as well as five brief screening tools: HIV Dementia Scale, Hopkins Verbal Learning Scale/WAIS III Digit Symbol, Montreal Cognitive Assessment, Computer Assessment of Mild Cognitive Impairment and the CogState. The research team will evaluate the sensitivity, specificity, positive/negative predictive power of the brief screening tools by comparing their results with those of the complete battery. Findings will be used to develop screening guidelines for practitioners. This study is a foundational piece of a comprehensive, national, multi-centre, transdisciplinary program of research--the proposed CIHR Centre for Neuro-AIDS Research--to conduct clinically relevant, patient-centred research to address the neurocognitive and associated mental health consequences of HIV/AIDS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurodevelopment of preschoolers exposed perinatally to bisphenol A and phthalates; interactions with diet and neurotoxicant co-exposures
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; BISPHENOL A; CHILD NEURODEVELOPMENT; COGNITION; DIETARY-TOXICANT INTERACTION; ENVIRONMENTAL NEUROTOXICANTS; MATERNAL NUTRITION; MERCURY; MICRONUTRIENT INTAKE; PHTHALATES
Abstract-Résumé: Evidence has recently emerged that increasing maternal exposure to the widespread environmental contaminants, bisphenol A (BPA) and phthalates, is negatively associated with a broad range of neurodevelopmental and behavioural outcomes in young children. The effects in children beyond the age of 3 have not been well studied, but animal models suggest that these deficits may be permanent. Maternal and infant nutrient status is also an important determinant of neurodevelopment, but this data has not been available in any previous human study of BPA or phthalate exposure. We will make use of an established prospective pregnancy cohort (the Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition study; APrON) to advance the current state-of-knowledge by examining the associations between perinatal BPA and phthalate exposure on neurodevelopment while considering the likely interaction with key nutrients in mothers and their infants. Specifically, we will analyze the concentrations of BPA and phthalate metabolites in spot maternal urine samples, measure the status of nutrients in perinatal blood samples from the mother and infant, and evaluate child performance at age 3, and again at age 5, on measures of intelligence, motor function, executive function, memory and behaviour. We hypothesize that perinatal exposure to BPA or phthalates will be associated with lower performance, but we will further examine if the effects are attenuated by sufficient nutrient status, or made worse by low nutrient status, methylmercury co-exposure, or lead co-exposure. We will also test if children who were exposed to higher levels of BPA and phthalates in the perinatal period have slower rates of development between ages 3 and 5. We anticipate that the results of this study will contribute to public health protection in Canada and abroad. By identifying nutrients in the perinatal period that can attenuate the subsequent adverse effects in children, risk mitigation strategies may be quickly communicated.

TitreApplicationTitle: PAWP, a candidate sperm-borne oocyte-activating factor
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSISTED REPRODUCTIVE TECHNOLOGIES; CALCIUM RELEASE OR OSCILLATIONS; EGG ACTIVATION; FERTILIZATION; INFERTILITY/FERTILITY; INTRACYTOPLASMIC SPERM INJECTION; PAWP; PERINUCLEAR THECA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SPERM-BORNE OOCYTE ACTIVATING FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Infertility is now estimated to effect 70 million couples worldwide, about 40% of who suffer from male infertility.  A key treatment technique for infertile couples is intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), whereby a sperm is microinjected directly into the oocyte.  However, ICSI is only 40% successful.  Treatment failure could be due to the sperm's inability to induce fertilization because of the absence of a sperm-borne oocyte activating factor (SOAF) that has not yet been identified. We have recently identified and partially characterized a strong SOAF candidate protein known as PAWP. In this project we advance our findings by understanding the mechanism of action of PAWP during fertilization in the mouse and confirming it in human fertilization. Infertile patients will also be screened for the expression level of PAWP as a potential diagnostic biomarker. Identification of this factor as a non-redundant SOAF and understanding the mechanism of its action will help translate our basic knowledge into developing a new diagnostic tool for male infertility.  For assurance we will also eliminate the PAWP gene in the mouse and use this infertile knockout model to investigate new methods for the treatment of infertility. We can then validate recombinant PAWP as a biological supplement to increase the success rate of ICSI.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Randomized Air Filter Intervention Study of Air Pollution and Fetal Growth in a Highly Polluted Community
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTION; BIRTH WEIGHT; EXPOSURE ASSESSMENT; FETAL GROWTH; INTERVENTION; PARTICULATE MATTER; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: A growing body of evidence links exposure to air pollution during pregnancy with adverse birth outcomes such as low birth weight and pre-term birth.  Unfortunately, studies to date have had major limitations - including poor air pollution exposure assessment, insufficient statistical power, and bias introduced by other risk factors (confounding) - that make interpretation very difficult.  Intervention studies provide the opportunity to overcome many of the limitations of previous studies and can provide compelling evidence of a causal relationship.  Portable indoor air filters represent a promising intervention for reducing exposure to particulate matter air pollution because they are relatively inexpensive and reduce concentrations indoors, where individuals spend the vast majority of time.  This study will use portable indoor air filters in a randomized intervention study to investigate the relationship between particulate matter air pollution and indicators of fetal growth in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, one of the world's most polluted cities.  The large changes in air pollution exposure introduced by this intervention in this highly polluted setting provide a unique opportunity to efficiently and cost-effectively study this potentially important relationship among a relatively small sample of women, while addressing the limitations of previous studies.  In addition,  the outcomes of this study will inform recommendations given to women, both in developing countries and in polluted settings in developed countries, for minimizing air pollution-related risks during pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of translational mechanisms in the retrograde regulation of Synaptic homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CAP-DEPENDENT TRANSLATION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GENETICS; RETROGRADE SIGNALING; SYNAPTIC HOMEOSTASIS; SYNAPTIC SIGNALING; TARGET OF RAPAMYCIN; TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: It has been recognized for some time that the stability of neuronal activity in the nervous system hinges on a coordinated action of different molecular mechanisms that respond to changes in synaptic activity. We provide evidence that de novo protein synthesis in response to changes in synaptic activity leads to generation of a signal that feeds back to the nerve terminals to regulate the level of neurotransmitter release. We propose to use the powerful genetic tools available in Drosophila to unravel the molecular mechanisms that participate in the regulation of this process. Our preliminary findings suggests that genes that have been associated with human disease, namely Parkinson's disease, may play an important role in this process. Therefore, our findings may provide important steps towards our understanding of how neuronal activity is regulated and how it could be affected during disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adult vs. Fetal Programs in Leukemia Pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA; CELLULAR TRANSFORMATION; DEVELOPMENT; GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTORS; NOTCH; ONCOGENES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Blood cancers come in both acute and chronic forms, and are generally composed of either lymphoid or myeloid cells. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is typically regarded as a childhood disease and although most children are cured with standard chemotherapy, 10-20% suffer relapse and eventually succumb to their disease. ALL also affects adults and despite the fact that the leukemia cells themselves appear essentially identical to those in pediatric ALL, the majority of adults succumb to their disease. Recent studies of normal blood cells have revealed there are significant differences in how these cells are programmed in children and adults, and it is possible these differences underlie the disparity in clinical outcome in pediatric vs. adult ALL. We propose to identify what the differences are between leukemic blood cells in children and adults, and to determine whether these differences can be exploited to design new therapies to improve clinical outcomes for adults and the subset of children who suffer relapse.

TitreApplicationTitle: Alcohol, energy drinks and other stimulants: an emergency room study assessing the effects of gender, context and substance use on injury risk
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL USE; CASE-CONTROL; CASE-CROSSOVER; DRINKING CONTEXT; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; ENERGY DRINKS; GENDER; INJURY; SIMULTANEOUS POLYSUBSTANCE USE; STIMULANT USE
Abstract-Résumé: Alcohol use increases the risk of injury according to the quantity consumed. This relationship varies according to where drinking takes place (e.g. a bar, public place, private home) and type of activity engaged in (e.g. driving, eating a meal). The present study will explore how injury risk changes when a person is also using some kind of stimulant, such as an "energy drink", cocaine or amphetamine-type drugs. Increasingly, risky substance use involves a pattern of combined alcohol and other drug use and there is evidence that this further increases the risk of injury. Canada has regulations to limit the caffeine content of alcoholic beverages. Unfortunately, most combined alcohol and energy drinks consumed in Canada are not pre-mixed and, instead, drinkers combine separate alcoholic and energy drinks. There may be a need for further regulation of energy drink in places where alcohol is sold. We propose the first controlled study of how combined alcohol and energy drink consumption increases injury risk. The team has considerable experience with emergency room studies investigating substance use and other activities immediately before their injury. One member of the team invented the "case-crossover" study design, which has been increasingly used in epidemiological research worldwide. We will apply this method so that individuals presenting to the ER will provide information not only on their substance use and other activities immediately before their injury or acute illness, but also, (i) at the same time the previous week, (ii) the last time they were in the particular setting in which they experienced their injury or illness. We will then estimate how risk of injury increases with increasing doses of alcohol, energy drinks and other illegal stimulants separately and in combination. We will also investigate how these estimates vary by gender, age and context of substance use. The results will be shared with policymakers and other researchers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of HK2 in Regulating Brain Tumor Metabolism and Angiogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG DISCOVERY; HEXOKINASE 2; HYPOXIA; MALIGNANT BRAIN TUMORS; NEO-VASCULARIZATION; SIGNALING PATHWAY REGULATION; TUMOR ANGIOGENESIS; TUMOR METABOLISM; WARBURG EFFECT
Abstract-Résumé: Annually 10,000 new Canadians are diagnosed with brain tumors and majority of them will not survive beyond a year. Unfortunately, malignant astrocytomas result in a disproportionate loss of patient years and significant deterioration in quality of life. Given their poor outcome, brain tumor patients can not advocate for themselves and unlike other cancers in the past 2 decades level of prevention, early detection, and therapeutic outcomes for brain tumors has not improved. It is therefore critical to focus our efforts on improving outcome for patients with malignant brain tumors, raise awareness and recognition of this fatal tumor and advocate for funding support of innovative research and social programs that improve patient care. Our proposal is focused on a new and as yet relatively unexplored area of tumor biology, which is highly relevant to GBMs: altered tumor cell metabolism. Altered metabolism plays a critical role in survival of GBM tumor cells, as we and others have shown through previous work. We will use innovative strategies to explore the impact of altered tumor metbolism on tumor growth and resistance to chemo- and radiation therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prognostic markers and biology of relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; GENOMICS; HODGKIN LYMPHOMA; MICROENVIROMENT; RELAPSED DISEASE; TUMOR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is the most common form of lymphoma affecting young people under the age of 30 in the Western world. Despite remarkable therapeutic advances over the past half century, 25% of people with this disease relapse after treatment. The majority of these individuals receive further treatment, consisting of both chemotherapy and bone marrow transplantation ("second-line treatment"). The survival rate of such relapse treatments is about 50%. The tumors in HL contain rare malignant cancer cells (Hodgkin Reed Sternberg cells) and the so-called "tumor microenvironment" is mainly made up of immune cells which are attracted and manipulated by the malignant cells. We have recently shown that features of the tumor, mainly related to the makeup of the microenvironment, can be used to predict whether the first treatment of the HL will cure the patient. However, our knowledge about the biology of relapsed HL is rudimentary at best and currently there are no tumor markers that allow us to predict whether second-line treatment will cure a patient who has relapsed. We have access to tumor samples from both the time of diagnosis and lymphoma relapse from 147 HL patients who received treatment. We will examine these pairs of biopsies to determine differences in both the cancer cells and the microenvironment using microscopy, special stains and expression of genes. We will use this information to build a tool to predict whether second-line treatment will cure a patient after they have relapsed. Our work will inform these patients and their doctors about likely outcomes of treatment and will also identify patients who might respond better to other treatment options. These studies will provide a greater understanding of why patients with HL relapse to potentially develop new treatments to cure HL relapse patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mcl-1 as a regulator of ovarian reserve.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH; MATERNAL AGING; OOGENESIS/FOLLICULOGENESIS; PREMATURE OVARIAN FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: Finite number of female reproductive cells (eggs) at birth and their accelerated loss during fourth decade of life are two physiological factors regulating ovarian lifespan. As a result of premature exhaustion caused by excessive death, dwindling numbers of eggs lead to premature loss of ovarian function. Ovarian failure, whether natural or induced, is due to the loss of ovarian follicles and the factors that they provide, resulting in dramatic changes in women's health. This period in women's life coincides with increased risk for development of cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, neurological dysfunction and muscle atrophy.  We do not fully understand what drives premature loss eggs and what can be done to prevent it. Goal of this proposal is to study what molecular pathways are activated during commitment of eggs to demise in animal model and determine if these pathways may be altered in a genetic condition leading to premature ovarian failure or other forms of female infertility in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aboriginal Men's Narratives: Reclaiming Our Lives
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL MEN; MIXED METHODS; NARRATIVES; PARTICIPATORY; PHOTOVOICE; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: The purpose of the proposed study is to explore Aboriginal men's experiences and perceptions of the positive steps to health and wellbeing to inform an understanding of what constitutes appropriate, culturally safe health and social services and support for men whose lives have been influenced by multiple forms of trauma and violence and are shaped by substance use, poverty, chronic illness etc. This is a participatory study employing a mixed methods approach which includes:  in-depth individual and focus group interviews, photovoice, observations, analysis of clinic utilization data and an analysis of the health organization. The research objectives are: 1. to explore the men's perspectives of  health and well-being  and their experiences of those factors that have shaped positive health and well-being; 2. to explore provider's perspectives on health and well-being  and  their experiences of what constitutes positive health and social supports for  men; 3. to explore the perceptions of the wider lived community, e.g., elders, women etc. regarding the health promotion needs of men; 4. to examine the organization of men's groups, financial issues, contracts, professionalized or community services, philosophical underpinnings of groups and their approach etc. within the recruitment site;  5. to document men's utilization of health care, i.e., frequency of clinic visits, nature of visits, linkages to other resources etc., and men's groups; and 6. to engage with partners and participants in the dissemination of knowledge. Men, particularly those living with histories of mental health and addictions issues and trauma, access care less frequently and often only seek treatment late in the illness process when medical conditions and symptoms are severe. Despite this, men's health issues have been largely glossed over by decision making bodies and little is known about men's distinct health experiences and their health and social support needs.
