TitreApplicationTitle: PrP N-terminal sequences and biological endpoints in Prion and Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S; CELL-TO-CELL SPREAD; DEMENTIA; INFECITIVITY; ION CHANNELS; METALLOPROTEINS; PRIONS; PROTEIN FOLDING; TRANSGENICS; TRANSITION METALS
Abstract-Résumé: Prion diseases such as mad cow are caused by a normal component of brain cells, the cellular prion protein, "PrPC", folding into the wrong 3D shape. Interestingly we and others have described that PrPC participates in early chemical events in a different disease, Alzheimer's, that also features cell-to-cell spread of a misfolded protein. In this work we have found that PrPC exists in three forms and that one form is especially relevant to how prion diseases occur and may also play a special role in the early events of Alzheimer's.  We will explore these concepts using petri dish and animal model experiments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fabry Disease: Mechanisms and Next-Generation Therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: FABRY DISEASE; GENE THERAPY; KIDNEY; LENTIVIRUS; LYSOSOMAL STORAGE DISORDERS; MICROARRAY; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Fabry disease is the second-most prevalent lysosomal storage disorder. It is X chromosome-linked but manifests in both males and females. Enzyme replacement therapy is the current treatment of choice but this approach does not address the genetic defect and is very expensive and cumbersome to administer. Our previous funding on this topic led to a number of publications and a recent grant award from the CIHR to perform the 'first-in-man' gene therapy trial for this disorder. Here we seek to build on that success and employ some new models we have generated previously to better understand how this disorder develops and to begin to facilitate implementation of next-generation therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diagnosing Ovarian Cancer Early (DOvE)by targeting symptomatic women
Keywords-MotsClés: EARLY DETECTION OF OVARIAN CANCER; REDUCING FALSE POSITIVE RESULTS; TRIAGE OF SYMPTOMATIC PATIENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Ovarian cancer is the 5th most common cause of death from cancer in Canadian women. The high death rate is largely due to late diagnosis. Studies have shown that the majority of women with ovarian cancer experience symptoms before diagnosis, but these symptoms are vague. Several influential organizations have recommend testing of women experiencing these symptoms, in the hope of increasing the proportion of women diagnosed in Stage I, when the tumor is still confined to the ovary. However, there was no evidence that testing symptomatic women would achieve early stage diagnosis. The DOvE (Diagnosing Ovarian Cancer Early) project was started with the primary aim of evaluating whether providing fast-track evaluation to symptomatic women 50 years or older would result in a higher proportion diagnosed in Stage I. In the pilot phase, we evaluated 1455 symptomatic Montreal women with a blood test and transvaginal ultrasound. We found 10 times more invasive cancers in symptomatic women than expected. The tumor-volume was smaller and more amenable to complete removal, which substantially improves survival. Our results also showed that high-grade serous cancer (HGSC), the type responsible for 90% of deaths from ovarian cancer, often does not start in the ovary, but in the fallopian tube and spreads to the pelvis and abdomen even before it gets on the ovary. So, it would appear that until now we have been concentrating on the wrong place - the ovary. In the next phase of the study we intend to offer the DOvE service in 12 satellite clinics in Montreal sited in areas with a dense proportion of older women, who are more at risk of HGSC. This strategy will allow us to evaluate about 14000 symptomatic women in the highest risk-group and diagnose approximately 100 cancers early enough for the women to benefit from complete surgery. We will also develop predictive models to identify the women at the highest risk so that such a service can be offered all over Canada and the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biological mechanisms contributing to increased risk of facial clefting
Keywords-MotsClés: AVIAN EMBRYO; CELL MIGRATION; CLEFT LIP; CONVERGENT EXTENSION; CRANIOFACIAL DEVELOPMENT; GENE EXPRESSION; GROWTH FACTOR SIGNALING; MORPHOGENESIS; PATTERN FORMATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION IN DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: One of the most common birth defects in Canada is cleft lip with or without cleft palate.  Clefts arise during the embryonic period and lead to significant social and physical burdens for affected individuals.  There are thought to be multiple genes that together contribute to increased risk of clefting. In addition environment also plays a role. We are using the avian embryo because it is one of the few animals in which it is possible to directly work on the face while it is developing. Furthermore, it is possible to induce cleft lip reliably. Our goal in this grant is to increase or decrease the levels of growth factors specifically in the areas of the face that form the lip and study their effect on lip fusion. Using cells extracted from the face we will be exploring the effects of one type of signal, WNT proteins, on gene expression. DNA from these facial cells will be laid over highly sensitive microarrays containing all of the chicken genes. We will interrogate the arrays and through this analysis we will make surprising and significant discoveries about genes that contribute to clefting. In addition we are going to transfer human mutations in one of the WNT genes that cause a craniofacial syndrome into the chicken. The goal is to explain the effect of the mutations on the way the protein works within the face. We use novel techniques that we developed in our own lab to tag facial cells with fluorescent markers so that we can map their movements within the growing face. To visualize the results several cutting edge imaging techniques will be used including a unique 3D scanner developed specifically for embryos and a white light, laser confocal microscope.  Using these tools we will understand much more precisely how changes in gene function can increase susceptibility to clefting. These results will lead to better understanding of the causes of clefting as well as other facial birth defects.

TitreApplicationTitle: New mothers' thoughts of harm: Prevalence and relation to OCD and child harm
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; INTRUSIVE THOUGHTS; MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH; OBSESSIVE COMPULSIVE DISORDER; PARENTING BEHAVIOURS; POSTPARTUM MENTAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Many new mothers experience unwanted thoughts of harm related to their infant. In our own work, all of the mothers we interviewed reported unwanted thoughts of harm coming to their infant, and half reported unwanted thoughts of harming their infant.  Thoughts of harming one's infant can be very upsetting, and occur even among women who have no history of violence, and who hold a deep desire to protect and care for their infant. As very little research on postpartum thoughts of harm has been conducted, professionals are unsure about how to respond to them. Inappropriate responses can have serious consequences. If the thoughts mean that a woman is at risk of harming her infant, then acting to protect the infant is necessary. However, if the thoughts are a common and normal part of early parenting, taking dramatic steps to protect the child may make the mother feel unnecessarily afraid that she is a threat to her infant.  Among vulnerable women, this may make it more likely that she develop emotional difficulties such as anxiety or depression. The purpose of this research is to learn more about new mothers' unwanted thoughts of infant-related harm: how common these thoughts are, how mothers experience and respond to them, how they relate to maternal mental health, and whether they predict child harm. To find this out, we are recruiting a large, representative sample of pregnant women in British Columbia.  Women will be assessed from late in pregnancy through to 3-months postpartum.  We will assess the occurrence, content, and experience of thoughts of harm as well as how women respond to them.  We will assess their relation to postpartum maternal anxiety and depression, and the possible connection to child harm.  We hope that our research will help new mothers who experience unwanted thoughts of harm related to their infant, and make it easier for care providers to respond appropriately to them.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sphingosine 1 phosphate: A double-edged sword regulating vascular tone in pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTHELIAL PERMEABILITY; INTRAUTERINE GROWTH RESTRICTION; NITRIC OXIDE; PREECLAMPSIA; PRESSURE MYOGRAPH; SPHINGOSINE 1-PHOSPHATE (S1P); TUMOUR NECROSIS FACTOR ALPHA; UTERINE AND PLACENTAL ARTERIES; VASODILATION; WHOLE TISSUE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Blood in a pregnant woman contains the oxygen and nutrients that allows her unborn baby to grow well. Blood from the mother flows to the uterus and placenta to nourish the unborn baby. If this blood flow is decreased, the growth of the baby is reduced leading to many complications just after birth. Their risk of heart disease when they become adults is also increased. When arteries are widened or relaxed, blood flow is increased. When narrowed or constricted, blood flow is reduced. The vessel lining normally acts as a partial barrier and controls the access of factors in the blood to the smooth muscle cells that cause constriction. In unhealthy pregnancies, the barrier becomes leaky. One factor that can affect the barrier is sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P). This factor relaxes the blood vessel if it remains inside. However, it constricts the vessel if it leaks through the barrier to reach the muscle layer. This study looks at a novel role for S1P in controlling leakiness of blood vessels in the mother that control her blood pressure and also the ones that feed her baby. We will also look at the role of S1P in controlling relaxation compared to constriction in these vessels. We will study how inflammation can change these normal responses and cause high blood pressure in the mother and reduce blood flow to the baby. We propose that S1P will reduce leakiness and increase relaxation of arteries in normal pregnancies. On the other hand, in mothers with inflammation, we predict that S1P will leak through the vessel lining and cause the muscle layer to constrict. This will increase blood pressure in the mother and reduce blood flow to the baby. Our work will be done using a mouse model and we will also study human placental arteries from normal and abnormal pregnancies. Knowing what happens in normal pregnancy and during inflammation will help to develop methods to improve growth of the unborn baby and prevent high blood pressure in the mother.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mapping structural and functional connectivity of epileptic and eloquent brain networks using ultra-high-field MRI
Keywords-MotsClés: CONNECTIVITY; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; EPILEPSY; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; HIGH FIELD MRI; IMAGING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; SURGICAL PLANNING
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder that affects up to 1% of Canadians, resulting in repeated spontaneous seizures.  Close to one third of all epilepsy patients do not have control of seizures with drugs, thus for many of these patients surgery is the only treatment option.  In this procedure, the surgeon attempts to remove all the brain tissue causing the seizures without damaging pathways between vital areas of the brain, such as those involved in vision, language, and movement.  Planning for these surgeries can be extremely challenging because of these constraints. In fact, only 60% of patients become seizure-free after surgery, and nearly all patients develop vision problems due to removal of important brain pathways. The objective of this research is to use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to examine the internal network of pathways and activity in the brain, and use these connections to determine precisely which brain regions to remove and to avoid.  Using the most powerful human MRI in Canada allows for investigation of brain with a level of detail not possible before.  By scanning patients before and after they undergo surgery, we can investigate the how integrity of the brain networks and the amount of tissue removed affects surgical outcomes. The proposed work will be the first to study connectivity in epilepsy patients using ultra-high-field MRI, potentially leading to a greater understanding of the way the epileptic brain is connected and which brain networks are involved in epileptic seizures.  Furthermore this work can ultimately lead to the promise of minimally-invasive epilepsy surgery, where the smallest possible region of brain is resected to achieve the best result.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolic and Epigenetic Reprogramming in Liver Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL METABOLISM; EPIGENETICS; GENETICALLY ENGINEERED MOUSE MODELS; LIVER CANCER; METABOLIC ENZYMES; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; RNAI SCREEN; TISSUE/CELL CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: There is an immediate and critical need for improved strategies to treat biliary cancer, a tumor type for which most patients die within one year of diagnosis. In recent years a new era of targeted molecular therapeutics has emerged for treating cancer. This new generation of targeted therapies is more effective, less toxic and can produce dramatic clinical responses in a subset of treated patients. The clinical response to a particular targeted agent is dependent on specific genetic abnormalities within an individual's tumor. New targeted therapies can block these specific cancer-driving pathways and thereby exploit the tumor's vulnerability. In this regard, mutations have recently been detected in enzymes called IDH1 and IDH2 that regulate pathways by which the cell produces energy and the building blocks for multiple cellular processes. Thus the identification of these mutations provides a completely new model of how basic metabolic processes gone awry can lead to cancer development. Understanding in depth how mutations in these genes cause biliary cancer and identifying ways to specifically kill cancer cells harboring these mutations are key challenges in developing improved approaches to managing these cancers. My project will involve the study of novel genetically engineered mouse models to determine how these mutations function in driving cancer development, and to test whether these mutations are critical in sustaining the growth of advanced cancers. I will also use new genetic technologies that will allow me to identify additional biochemical pathways that are abnormal in IDH mutant cancer cells and that therefore are potential new drug targets. Overall, these studies will define distinct subgroups of biliary cancer, provide new insights into cancer therapeutics, and directly inform the design of refined clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sensitivity to pain-related physical activity: underlying physiological mechanisms and clinical importance for chronic knee osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOBEHAVIORAL RISK FACTORS; CLINICAL MANAGEMENT; MUSCULOSKELETAL PAIN; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PAIN-RELATED DISABILITY; PHYSICAL FUNCTION; PROGNOSIS; PSYCHOSOCIAL RISK FACTORS; SENSITIVITY TO PAIN-RELATED PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint condition that afflicts 24 million North Americans. Advanced knee OA is associated with increased pain and reduced function, symptoms that persist for approximately 20% of patients even after receiving the best available treatment (i.e. Total Knee Replacement, TKR, followed by strengthening exercises).  Recent research suggests that certain patients are more prone to experience increasing levels of pain as they perform physical activities. An increased understanding of the mechanisms and clinical importance of this sensitivity to physical activity may help more patients recover from TKR surgery. The proposed study aims to explore the processes underlying sensitivity to physical activity, and its value in predicting recovery. 100 people awaiting TKR and 50 healthy individuals will be tested. Testing consists of completing measures of emotional distress and disability, as well as a 20-minute physical performance task. Measures of pain intensity and different physiological processes (e.g. hormone and inflammation regulation) will be tested before and after the physical task. For participants receiving surgery, testing will be repeated at 3 and 6-months following TKR. Data analysis will focus on determining whether chronic knee arthritis is associated with increased sensitivity to physical activity, and whether this is related to individual differences in emotional distress and/or physiological function. Further analysis will determine whether levels of sensitivity predict recovery following TKR surgery. This study seeks to advance clinical practice and theory by exploring the multi-modal aspects of pain and disability. This research is expected to improve the predictive accuracy of whether patients recover following TKR, a clinical group projected to rise by more than 600% over the next 20 years. This study also stands to pave the way for innovative treatments that alleviate personal suffering associated with chronic pain

TitreApplicationTitle: Communicating with patients who appear to be in the vegetative state.
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN INJURY; BRAIN-COMPUTER INTERFACE; CONSCIOUSNESS; MINIMALLY CONSCIOUS STATE; VEGETATIVE STATE
Abstract-Résumé: How can we unequivocally know that another person is consciously aware? Recently, my own research has called into question several core principles that underpin the diagnoses of the vegetative (VS) and minimally conscious states (MCS), in particular, the extent to which we can truly consider that a brain injured patient is unaware simply because they exhibit no overt behavioural responses to stimulation. One of my research aims is to develop a battery of tests that can measure the brain responses of these patients, and the extent to which they are aware, at the bedside using the non-invasive technique of electroencephalography (EEG). I will then use these brain responses to develop EEG-based brain-computer interfaces that will allow them to communicate by means of their thoughts alone. As a CIHR Postdoctoral Fellow, I will seek to refine and extend this technique in larger groups of patients, for example, to enable 'real time' communication. If successful, this will have a profound impact on the lives of the patients (as well as their families and care-givers) by allowing them to express their needs and wishes for the first time since their injuries. A further aim of my research is to investigate the clinical utility of these methods, for example, can some EEG markers of awareness be used to predict a patient's chances of recovery? To determine this, I will follow a cohort of patients with regular EEG and behavioural assessments in the first few days after their injury, and over the months and years that follow. Currently, accurate prognostication for this patient group is extremely challenging, but the types of information that these longitudinal assessments return will provide clinicians with vital information to guide their decisions in that critical period following severe brain injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of FGF23 in Chondrocyte Regulation and Longitudinal Bone Growth
Keywords-MotsClés: CHONDROCYTE REGULATION; FGF23 AND ESTRADIOL SIGNALLING; LONGITUDINAL BONE GROWTH; MOUSE MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Longitudinal bone growth is a complex process. It occurs at the growth plate when resting chondrocytes proliferate and differentiate into hypertrophic chondrocytes that mineralize and give rise to bone. Disruptions in chondrocyte regulation and/or mineralization during development can lead to fractures and rickets. It is well document that estrogen promotes chondrocyte differentiation in animal but not cell models, which suggests that estrogen needs to interact with some co-factor, not present in cell cultures, to modulate longitudinal bone growth.  To date, the co-factor has not been identified. Studies have shown that estrogen can stimulate bone forming cells to produce fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF-23). Moreover, FGF-23 can stimulate differentiation of growth plate chondrocytes in animal models. Building on this research, the proposed study will investigate whether estrogen and FGF-23 work in combination to promote chondrocyte differentiation and longitudinal bone growth. I hypothesize that there is a positive feedback loop that bone uses to regulate its own production. Growth plate chondrocytes produce estrogen that stimulates bone forming cells to synthesize FGF-23 that then works in combination with estrogen to promote longitudinal bone growth.  The proposed study will test the effects of estrogen and FGF-23 in mice that have these hormones versus those that do not. The skeletal growth will be monitored by micro-computed tomography and dynamic histomorphometry, while growth plates will be analyzed by quantitative histology. Positive finding from this study will determine whether FGF-23 and estrogen work in combination to modulate longitudinal bone growth and may help to support better clinical approaches for treating fractures and rickets.

TitreApplicationTitle: Automated Parallel Synthesis of Cyclic Peptide Libraries for Drug Discovery in the Ubiquitin-Proteasome System
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL PROBES; DEGRONS; E2 AND E3 ENZYME INHIBITORS; ORGANIC METHODOLOGY; PARALLEL SYNTHESIS; PEPTIDE MIMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins are the workhorses and building blocks of life. A tremendous range of tasks at this microscopic cellular level must proceed in concert to maintain health. This is facilitated by a complex communication and control system that depends on a constant flux of associations and dissociations at the molecular level. Included in this system are a class of proteins called ubiquitins. Abnormal functioning of the ubiquitin system has been implicated in cancer among other diseases. Research at the Tyers group has helped reveal some of the intricacies of the ubiquitin system, providing an opportunity to correct disease-causing states. To achieve the latter, suitable chemical tools will have to be developed. A target class of molecules has been chosen based on precedence established in the Tyers group, the feasibility of the chemistry, and the ability to rapidly evolve their structure through the milestones of sufficient activity and drug-like properties. In particular, molecules inspired by nature called cyclic peptides will be used. Part of what facilitates access to these molecules is the potential to use robotics to accelerate the rate at which the necessary changes can be made to these cyclic peptide chemical tools.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bridging the divide between Abeta and tau molecular etiologies in Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ABETA PEPTIDE; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MOLECULAR ETIOLOGY; NETWORK ANALYSIS; TAU PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: The concomitant accumulation of extracellular aggregates of Abeta peptides and intracellular deposits of the tau protein are a neuropathological feature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD) from other neurodegenerative diseases. Despite considerable interest in the aberrant cellular biology that drive the formation of these deposits the molecular player(s) that tie Abeta-mediated neurotoxicity to aberrant tau biology have not been identified. We hypothesize that the molecular chain of events connecting Abeta and tau perturbations in AD is short and can be revealed through a careful investigation of the molecular environments of Abeta and tau that capitalizes on improvements to mass spectrometry workflows and technology made over the past few years. Thus, we will for the first time carry out a large-scale unbiased biochemical search for molecular interactors of Abeta using human brain extract as the biological source material. A similar analysis will be employed to comprehensively map molecular interactions of the tau protein. Candidate mediators of Abeta toxicity which will emerge from this work will be subject to thorough validation, that include methods for monitoring the effect of altering the expression levels of these candidates on the in vivo detachment of fluorescently labeled tau from microtubules.  These efforts will further capitalize on computational network analyses and a multiplex western blot assay that can capture cell status information beyond monitoring perturbations to Abeta and tau biology.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel IDR peptide therapeutics for Pulmonary Hyperinflammation in Cystic Fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY SCREENING; BACTERIAL LUNG INFECTION; CYCTIC FIBROSIS; LIPOSOMAL FORMULATION FOR ENHANCED STABILITY; LUNG INFLAMMATION; PEPTIDE DRUG DESIGN; TRANSCRIPTOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common life-shortening inherited disease in our society. CF is caused by a mutation in the CF transmembrane regulator gene (CFTR), which leads to the accumulation of a thick and sticky mucus in the lungs.  CF patients usually have chronic lung inflammation often associated with bacterial infection and continual colonization. Recently, a novel innate defence regulator peptide was identified that suppressed bacterially induced hyperinflammation in CF airway cells and protected mice against bacterially induced lung inflammation.  This project will focus on understanding the molecular mechanisms of action of this peptide regulator as an inhibitor of bacterially induced hyperinflammation in CF.  Optimization of this peptide sequence will also provide important information for progression to the clinic and a potential treatment for lung inflammation which would significantly improve the quality of life of CF patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of host genes that directly impact susceptibility to infection by Herpes Simplex Virus type 1: from mouse model to human.
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE MAPPING; HERPES SIMPLEX ENCEPHALITIS; HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS TYPE 1; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; IMMUNOGENETICS; INNATE/ADAPTIVE IMMUNITY; MOUSE CHEMICAL MUTAGENESIS; SUSCEPTIBILITY TO VIRAL INFECTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Due to emerging or re-emerging pathogens (HIV, Influenza, Plasmodium...), infectious diseases have been a major concern for healthcare organizations all over the world. To understand the complex systems that represent host-pathogen interactions, Dr S.Vidal's group with others groups from Mc Gill University have decided to join their efforts to created an innovative discovery platform integrating mouse chemical mutagenesis and large-scale phenotyping to identify host genes that directly impact susceptibility to pathogens of global significance. As a part of this unique research program, the goal of my project is to identify and characterize novel genetic host determinants of susceptibility to infection by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). In order to achieve this goal, (1) I already produced mutant mice using chemical mutagenesis and screened them for susceptibility to infection with HSV-1; (2) I will identify the causative host genes that impact susceptibility to its infection; (3) I will determine by which mechanism(s) these genes interfere with cellular and biochemical pathways and determine their role at molecular level (protein function); (4) I will characterize the role of these genes in humans. Hence, my project will elucidate host genes involved in host-pathogen interactions and will also permit a more holistic knowledge of cellular dysfunctions leading to the severe inflammation of the central nervous system associated with HSV-1 infection. Combining fundamental approaches such as model organism together with clinical studies in humans will provide deeper insight into defective or dysregulated mechanisms of immunity and will be instrumental to develop pertinent drug targets.

TitreApplicationTitle: Kinetic gene-expression analysis of differentially regulated insulin signaling pathways in insulin resistance associated with aging and T2D
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DIABETES; GENE EXPRESSION; INDUCIBLE TRANSGENIC MOUSE MODELS; INSULIN RESISTANCE; INSULIN SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Insulin resistance is generally considered a metabolic syndrome leading to the development of type 2 diabetes. Interestingly, partial insulin resistance promotes longevity in worms, flies, and mouse models. This presents a paradox with differential consequences of insulin resistance. It has been postulated that different insulin-activated pathways are turned on in partial and severe insulin resistance. However, the exact mechanisms involved in this paradox are largely unknown. To identify and compare the different insulin-modulated pathways, we will analyze the gene expression of important molecules implicated. Using the inducible mouse models with doxycycline regulation, we will be able to adjust insulin signaling with the amount of two important mediators, insulin receptor (IR) and its substrate IRS-1. We will gradually decrease the expression of IR and IRS-1 by 20%, 40%, 60%, 80% and near-complete disruption by varying the dosage of doxycycline given to these mice. We will then collect their liver, muscle, fat and brain at 2, 4, 8, 26 and 52 weeks after doxycycline administration to perform gene-expression analyses and to generate a comprehensive profile with differential degrees of insulin resistance throughout the aging period of one year.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effects of adult aging on the underlying mechanisms of sensorimotor control
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ELECTROMYOGRAPHY; HUMAN; MICRONEUROGRAPHY; MOTOR UNIT; MOTOR UNIT REMODELING; MUSCLE FUNCTION; MUSCLE WEAKNESS; SARCOPENIA; SENSORIMOTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The fastest growing age group in Canada is comprised of those 65 years of age and this population is expected to double within the next 25 years.  With natural adult aging, muscles and nerves of the human body undergo degenerative changes which are characterized by reductions in strength due to the loss of muscle mass.  The results of this ongoing process lead to muscle weakness and an overall decline in function, which is highly linked to physical disabilities, risk of falls, quality of life, and ultimately, mortality.  However, to date, much focus has been placed on age-related diseases (e.g., cancer, heart disease) and little is known about the biological mechanisms of natural aging.  Therefore, I will study how natural aging alters the functioning of muscles and the nerves that supply them.  I will use a unique technique, known as microneurography, a research tool in which recordings are made in awake humans using small needle electrodes (i.e., similar to acupuncture needles) inserted through the skin and into a nerve branch. This technique will allow me to record from single cells activating the muscles as well as individual sensory receptors that feed information back from the muscles to the spinal cord and brain.  Because this technique permits a level of investigation currently unparalleled by other methodologies, I will determine how factors associated with adult aging may impair muscle function, and hence, performance during activities such as lifting objects or standing balance.  The findings of my proposed experiments will relate to the known difficulties and limitations elderly individuals have with performing tasks involved with activities of daily living. Through understanding the mechanisms underlying these limitations, future studies will focus on the design and evaluation of functional training programs for improved muscle function and quality of life in older adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studying The Effects of The RNA-RNA Interactions on The Expression of Protein Factors Involved in Leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE REGULATION; LEUKEMIA; MICRORNA; RNA QUANTIFICATION; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: Project Summary. The phenotype of a cell can be linked to the quantity and the nature of proteins present in the cell (proteome). Different regulatory mechanisms take place and modify the proteome. Aberrant modifications of this population lead to pathological phenotype such as cancer. These modifications take place in transcription factors regulatory mechanism then impact the transcription of the genome (transcriptome) and by consequence the proteome. Another recently identified regulatory mechanism that impacts the proteome compete with the translation and involves microRNAs (miRNAs). These down-regulates specific mRNAs by binding to the mRNA. In order to have a better understanding of the leukemia phenotype (proteome) we propose to investigate the role of microRNA regulatory mechanism in leukemia cells and to modify them. By modifying this regulatory mechanism instead of the transcription factors regulatory mechanism we will act much closer to the protein expression. Project Description. The project can be decomposed in two parts. First, we propose to understand and to predict the role of modifications in the miRNA regulatory mechanism in leukemia cells. Using computer science and absolute quantification of miRNA and mRNA, we propose to create a model that explains and predict the phenotype of leukemia cells. The second part of the project is to investigate the impact of Single Nucleotide Polymorphism in the miRNA regulatory mechanism in the context of leukemia. Impact and Relevance Statement. The miRNA regulatory mechanism is very complex and cascade of regulatory events can take place. The only way to anticipate the impact of a modification in this mechanism is to draw the complete picture of regulatory events. Using this model we will be able to understand and to provide targets to act specifically on leukemia phenotype and provide better treatments.

Abstract-Résumé: Cell function is controlled by a vast network of gene and protein interactions. The Research Chair will exploit new genome-scale technologies - in the fields of systems biology, chemical biology and synthetic biology - to understand biological networks in human health and disease. These approaches will be focused on the processes that control cell growth and division, which are universally perturbed in cancer and other disorders. Synthetic biology will be used to develop sophisticated assays to understand the multiple genetic interactions that underlie human network function and to develop novel therapeutic modulators.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a microsimulation tool to inform finance decision-making in healthcare
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH CARE COSTS; HEALTH FINANCING; HEALTH SURVEY DATA; MICROSIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Policy-makers face increasing pressure to address funding issues related to the financing of healthcare services including those both in and out of the Medicare basket.  There are several financing options being considered including new revenue sources (i.e. tax revenues, payroll taxes and user fees) and insurance models (i.e. social health insurance).  There is currently a lack of empirical, population based evidence regarding the potential effect of these funding options in Canada at the population and individual level (i.e. equity). Microsimulation models such as the Social Policy Simulation Database and Model (SPSD/M) developed by Statistics Canada has been used for decades by policy makers and finance departments to evaluate "what-if" scenarios regarding potential new financing and taxation policies.  The model currently lacks the necessary health and healthcare utilization information required to allow its application to issues related to health system financing. As such, there are two primary objectives of the proposed project: 1) To enhance and further develop the SPSD/M model using existing health survey and administrative data; and 2) To apply the enhanced SPSD/M model to evaluate financing options for selected healthcare services through various "what-if" scenarios.   Once developed this micro-simulation tool can be used by policy makers and academics to inform a broad range of financing issues and options in healthcare.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; CANADIAN LONGITUDINAL STUDY ON AGING; LONGITUDINAL STUDY OF AGING; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Longitudinal studies of aging are designed to enable researchers to study the complexity of aging over time.  Often the goal is to capture outcomes such as the development of disease, the onset of disabililty, institutionalization, and death.  These studies are expensive to conduct and many require lengthy follow up for the collection of adequate data (e.g. sufficient number of endpoints) needed for analysis.  In this research we propose to investigate, both from a theoretical and empirical perspective, statistical methodology to accelerate the generation of results from longitudinal studies of aging, particularly those that pertain to outcomes that occur over time.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel approaches to aging physiology: Using statistics and data mining to understand dysregulation of biomarker networks in human populations
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOMARKER; CLUSTER ANALYSIS; DATA MINING; DYSREGULATION; HOMEOSTASIS; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; PHYSIOLOGY; REGULATORY NETWORK; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Aging researchers still do not know what mechanisms are responsible for aging. The main theories put forward have not been well supported by evidence. It now appears that aging is not caused by any single process, but rather by the declining ability of the body to properly regulate many biological processes. This decline arises from the difficulty in maintaining the complex systems necessary for normal functioning, systems that involve large numbers of molecules integrated in precisely regulated networks. Although this idea has the potential to explain the aging process, the large number of molecules, the extensive interactions and feedback relationships among them, and the long timescales make experimental approaches unfeasible, and no one has yet tested this "dysregulation" hypothesis of aging. A novel approach is required to simultaneously incorporate information about many molecules, their changes over time, and their relationships to each other. This project, the first such study, uses hundreds of blood and clinical measures collected in several long-term human datasets. We have access to three of the best such datasets in the world, a unique resource that allowing us to test whether results can be generalized across different populations. We apply novel statistical and informatics methods designed for high-dimensional data, including techniques to (a) find clusters of similar individuals and identify their shared biological patterns, (b) detect a faint signal among noise, and (c) assess causal effects among pathways across years. Preliminary analyses have identified multiple new pathways involved in aging and support our hypothesis of dysregulation. Our project will further test this hypothesis, identifying which pathways are involved and how. Understanding biological pathways will in turn allow us to identify social determinants of aging rate, develop clinical tools for measuring patient aging, and further biomedical research on chronic disease pathways.

TitreApplicationTitle: Accuracy of using automated methods of adverse events detection
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CARE HOSPITALS; ADVERSE EVENTS; AUTOMATED DETECTION; HEALTH INFORMATICS; MACHINE LEARNING; NATURAL LANGUAGE PROCESSING; SURVEILLANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Each year, adverse events (AEs) are responsible of 44,000 to 98,000 deaths in acute care hospitals, and it is estimated that 30% to 40% of all AEs are preventable. Recent research suggests that understaffing and the use of less qualified nursing staff are important contributors to the incidence of AEs in these settings. With a shortage of nurses that is expected to worsen in the coming years, there is a need to identify the optimal nurse staffing levels (i.e., the number of nurses and mixes of skills, education, and experience) that are needed to minimize AEs. To this end, the association between nurse staffing levels and the incidence of AEs, and the thresholds for safe staffing levels, need to be determined by conducting longitudinal studies. An important prerequisite to examining these central questions in the management of nursing staff in acute care hospitals is to identify accurate, timely and effective methods for measuring AEs. However, most acute care hospitals do not have such methods for monitoring AEs. With the advent of electronic medical records and the digital capture of clinical data - which were paralleled with the development of automated methods for encoding and classifying narrative clinical data -, an exciting opportunity has emerged to identify potentially more accurate and timely methods of AE detection. Taking advantage of this new opportunity, the objective of this study is to assess the accuracy of using automated methods for detecting AEs from electronic clinical data. Specifically, the accuracy of using automated methods of AEs detection will be assessed in comparison with the information contained in patients' medical charts (gold standard). The results of this study will likely produce more accurate and timely measures of AEs detection, a critical requirement to advance existing approaches to nursing staff allocation in acute care hospitals. Moreover, these measures could be used to assess and improve acute care hospitals' performance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Redesigning governance mechanisms in intergovernmental health care relations
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCOUNTABILITY; CITIZEN ENGAGEMENT; COLLABORATION; COMPARATIVE HEALTH POLICY; FEDERALISM; MULTI-LEVEL GOVERNANCE; MULTIDISCIPLINARY APPROACHES; SOFT LAW; SUSTAINABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: This project is a multidisciplinary examination of recently-established and newly-emerging approaches to governance as possible means of overcoming what has often been the intransigent relations of health care federalism in Canada. Discussions regarding the sustainability of the Canadian health care system focus almost exclusively on financial considerations (cost containment, value for money, productivity, efficiency, etc). Less discussed, but equally important, are issues of political sustainability: can the Canadian health care system be governed consistently over time in a well-ordered, predictable, and synergetic manner, or will dysfunctional federal-provincial relations severely impair the capacity of governments to provide cost-efficient and innovative health care to Canadians?Health care in Canada is irreducibly intertwined with the politics of federalism. While discussions over health care federalism have become increasingly polarized, there is good comparative international evidence to indicate that the complexity of modern health care requires more, rather than less, coordination and collaboration between jurisdictions. There may be ways of re-thinking the manner in which federal-provincial  relations  are conducted in the field of health care that can improve the capacity of both orders of government to provide effective, sustainable, and accountable health care across Canada in a less antagonistic and turbulent way.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a generic health-related quality of life (HRQL) preference-based measure for preschoolers: Mapping the Health Status Classification System Preschool (HSCS-PS) to the HUI2/3 scoring algorithm.
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH RELATED QUALITY OF LIFE; HEALTH STATUS; MEASUREMENT; PEDIATRIC; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Health related quality of life (HRQL) is a measure of a person's well-being. Measuring a person's well-being is important to provide information to help make decisions about policy, programs, and treatments. There are many types of HRQL measures that can be used in adults but there are few for children, especially those under five years of age. It is important to measure HRQL in early childhood since these years have an important effect on adult life. If we are able to measure HRQL, factors that affect a child's well-being can be described, and steps can be taken to help improve HRQL through programs and policies. This study will take an existing system that describes HRQL in children 2.5 to 5 years of age (preschoolers), and match these health descriptions to a similar system that is used in children (over 5yrs of age) and adults to measure HRQL. The adult system not only describes HRQL but gives us a score that is based upon community health values. By linking the two systems, researchers will be able to provide a HRQL score for preschoolers which can be compared to scores for older children and adults. A score for HRQL is important since it allows researchers and decision-makers to determine whether differences or relationships are present. This study will also test how well this scoring system measures HRQL in preschoolers by using the system in both healthy children and children who have health problems. Creating this system to measure HRQL in preschoolers is important because it will allow for more research into issues that affect well being in this group, as well as help to develop and evaluate programs and policies to improve the lives of children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating health trajectories over the life course and across generations: A longitudinal analysis of the transmission of health and socioeconomic inequality from parents to their adult children
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD ADVERSITY; HEALTH BEHAVIOURS; HEALTH DISPARITIES; HEALTH RISK AND RESILIENCE; INTERGENERATIONAL TRANSMISSION OF HEALTH RISK; LATENT CLASS ANALYSIS; LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS; STRUCTURAL DISADVATAGE AND HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: It is well understood that socioeconomic status is positively associated with health, and that disadvantaged social circumstances in childhood can set individuals on pathways that result in the accumulation of further disadvantages that lead to poorer health over time. However, this body of work treats health inequality as a process that operates within the span of the individual life course, overlooking the transmission of health inequality across generations within families.  We understand little about the process through which health inequality is passed along through families beyond that childhood social contexts, such as poverty, are important. In part, this oversight is related to the methodological challenges associated with assessing the intergenerational transmission of inequality, as well as the lack of longitudinal data that follow both children and their parents across a significant portion of their lives. In this study, we will use a unique and relatively unexplored intergenerational component of the U.S. Panel Study of Income Dynamics, which began in 1968 and continues to follow original sample members and their adult children as they form their own households. Using quantitative methods, such as latent class analysis, we will examine (1) the long term consequences of disadvantaged childhood circumstances; (2) the relationship between adult social and economic resources and health; and (3) the intergenerational transmission of health risk and health behaviours. We anticipate the findings from this work will further our understanding of the mechanisms through which inequalities in health are perpetuated or alleviated across the life course and across generations. Moreover our findings relate directly to health and social policies targeted at reducing health disparities by investing in early life inputs.  Understanding why health trajectories within and between families differ is important for mapping how inequalities are perpetuated and can be reduced.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a conceptual framework for understanding and measuring occupational health and safety vulnerability
Keywords-MotsClés: LABOUR MARKET EXPERIENCES; OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY; PRIMARY PREVENTION; WORK INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Vulnerability is defined as the potential openness to attack, or physical or emotional wounding. In the area of occupational health and safety (OH&S) vulnerability can be defined as an increased risk of experiencing a work-related injury or illness compared to some reference standard. Often subgroups of labour market participants, for example younger workers, new workers, immigrants or visible minorities are labelled as vulnerable. Yet, this categorization of workers does not identify the specific characteristics that place these workers at higher risk of experiencing a work-related injury. Using feedback from various OH&S stakeholder groups, this project will develop a measure of OH&S vulnerability among labour market participants that moves beyond demographic worker characteristics towards factors that are more proximal to risk of injury or illness at the level of the worker.  We will then develop a refine a measure of OH&S vulnerability that can be used for public health surveillance purposes.  The development and implementation of this measure will allow new knowledge to be generated about factors relevant to the occupational health and safety primary prevention, as well as the reduction in inequalities, of work injuries and illnesses in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: From Association to Causation: Using Natural Experiments to Evaluate the Impact of Population Health Interventions on Health Inequalities
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH BEHAVIOURS; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH INEQUALITIES; METHODS FOR CAUSAL INFERENCE WITH OBSERVATIONAL DATA; POLICY EVALUATION; POPULATION HEALTH INTERVENTIONS; PREVENTION; PUBLIC HEALTH POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: A wide range of public health policies and population health interventions have been implemented with the goal of improving population health.  The extent to which the causal effects of these policies have been measured is uneven, and little to no attention has been paid to their effects on vulnerable population groups.  These interventions and policies are likely to affect individuals of different socioeconomic status differently, thereby reducing or magnifying existing differences in health behaviours and health outcomes.  We propose using innovative analytic methods to measure the causal impacts of several population health interventions on health inequalities.  In the context of cancer prevention and screening, several policies aim to change individual behaviour but may do so differently across socioeconomic groups.  Tobacco control policy, including taxation and restrictions on where smoking is permitted, have been successful in reducing overall tobacco consumption but their effects on socioeconomic inequalities in smoking are largely unknown.  We will use variation in the timing of these policies across Canadian provinces to evaluate their impacts on smoking behaviour and health inequalities across socioeconomic groups.  Clinical guidelines that recommend cancer screening at certain ages among the general population and organized cancer screening programs also have the potential to improve population health and to affect inequalities in cancer outcomes.  We will evaluate whether these two policy tools impact inequalities in cancer screening behaviour and in rates of cancer detection.  An improved understanding of the effects of population health interventions on health inequalities will enhance policymakers' abilities to tailor such interventions to address both aggregate population health outcomes and variations across vulnerable subgroups.

TitreApplicationTitle: Les conditions de mise à profit des connaissances par les acteurs de santé publique lors de la formulation des politiques publiques
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTEURS DE SANTE PUBLIQUE; CONTEXTES D'INTERVENTION; FORMULATION DE POLITIQUES PUBLIQUES; MISE A PROFIT DES CONNAISSANCES; PROCESSUS DELIBERATIFS
Abstract-Résumé: L'importance des determinants sur la sante des populations, tels que l'environnement, le revenu, l'education, est reconnue depuis plusieurs decennies. On dispose d'ailleurs de nombreuses connaissances scientifiques a cet egard. Leur utilisation lors de la formulation des politiques publiques represente toutefois un veritable defi. L'experience des acteurs de sante publique au Quebec montre que le recours a des avis scientifiques ou revues de connaissances varie beaucoup lors de la formulation des politiques. Par exemple, les connaissances sur les risques pour la sante de l'utilisation de l'amiante ont eu un impact limite sur les decideurs gouvernementaux tandis que les connaissances sur l'utilisation du cellulaire au volant ont mene a des modifications de la reglementation. Cela a conduit notre equipe a s'interesser aux conditions favorisant l'utilisation des connaissances lors de la formulation des politiques publiques. Nos travaux anterieurs ont montre la pertinence d'etudier de plus pres la dynamique entre les groupes d'acteurs lies a un domaine de politiques publiques, comme la securite routiere, la pauvrete ou la qualite de l'eau potable. Recemment, des chercheurs ont distingue differentes configurations pour qualifier la dynamique entre ces groupes. Ils suggerent que l'utilisation des connaissances produites par les experts varie selon l'une ou l'autre de ces configurations. Par l'examen de differents cas, ce projet contribuera a renforcer les connaissances existantes en etudiant de plus pres les conditions de mise a profit des connaissances. Les resultats obtenus seront ensuite transposes dans un format permettant aux acteurs de sante publique d'apprecier ces conditions et d'anticiper les strategies a mettre de l'avant dans un domaine particulier d'intervention. Ce projet vise donc a maximiser les retombees des connaissances scientifiques sur la sante de la population en ameliorant la prise en compte des impacts sur la sante dans les politiques publiques.
