ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Experimental Cardiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: We study the phenomenon of cardiac hypertrophy which is basically an abnormal excessive growth of the heart that eventually, if left unchecked, contributes to heart failure.  My laboratory uses an integrated multifaceted approach which applies information learned using isolated heart cells to an animal model of heart failure.  Importantly, we study not only the mechanisms by which the heart grows abnormally but also the adaptive mechanisms which keep this process in check.  Our vision is that this work will unravel the complex nature of heart failure, a disease which is rapidly increasing in frequency, and lead to novel therapeutic approaches.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Virology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Despite impressive advances, most virus infections remain untreatable and new approaches to antiviral therapy are urgently required. My research seeks to determine how viruses reprogram the molecular machinery within our cells to produce more virus particles and evade our immune defenses, leading to tissue damage, virus spread, and disease. We are focusing on several herpes simplex virus proteins that subvert key cellular functions. One of these destroys cellular mRNAs and enhances the decoding of viral mRNAs, thereby hijacking the cellular protein synthetic machinery.  Another destroys the genome of mitochondria, the power plants within our cells, inflicting massive and irreversible genetic damage on infected cells. A third viral protein reprograms key cellular signaling pathways to increase virus replication and block our immune responses. We hope that by determining exactly how these and other viral proteins work we will learn how prevent their activity, thereby blocking virus replication and shoring up our immune defense mechanisms.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurobiology of Huntington's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Huntingtons disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor symptoms, psychiatric and cognitive decline. There is no cure for the disease. Our goal is to understand the mechanisms that lead to the death of brain cells in HD and to develop effective therapies. We focus on lipids that are affected in HD and that may contribute to disease progression. We have discovered that one particular lipid, GM1, has therapeutic effects in models of HD. Our studies will elucidate the role of this and other lipids in HD and their potential use for the treatment of HD

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Biology of Membrane Active Proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: The assembly of peptides and proteins into macromolecular complexes is integral to normal biological processes and the pathogenesis of many diseases. As a Chairholder, Dr. Sharpe will employ diverse biochemical and biophysical tools to determine the molecular basis for protein assembly, and the link with functional roles in health and disease.  Specifically, his work will have three main foci: (i) Understanding how amyloid and prion proteins lead to neurodegenerative disease; (ii) Developing anti-HIV-1 therapeutic strategies that target viral membrane proteins; (iii) Determining the basis for the physical properties of elastin, the protein responsible for elasticity of arteries and lung tissue.

ProgramNameEN: Synapse  CIHR National Youth Outreach Program
NomDuProgrammeFR: Programme Synapse  Sensibilisation nationale des jeunes des IRSC
ResearchClassEN: NONE OF THE ABOVE; SUPPLEMENTARY CLASSIFICATIONS
ClasseRechercheFR: AUCUNE DES CATEGORIES PRECEDENTES; CLASSIFICATIONS SUPPLEMENTAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Gene Researcher for a Week Program
Keywords-MotsClés: INSPIRE YOUNG CANADIANS TO PURSUE A CAREER IN GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Since its inception in 2003, the Canadian Gene Cure Foundation's (CGCF) Gene Researcher for a week (GRFAW) program has educated, mentored and inspired over 200 of Canada's brightest high school students. The program; conceived by a group of Canadian scientists including Dr Michael Hayden and Dr Thomas Hudson; engages students in grades 11 and 12 to work with a host scientist and their research team during their Spring Break week.  GRFAW inspires high school students in grades 11 and 12 who have an innate curiosity for science.  It aims to broaden the scope and knowledge of science for these students by showing them how the theoretical concepts taught in the classroom can be applied practically in a real laboratory.     Gene Researcher for a Week is differentiated from other youth science programs because it pairs students with a scientist and their research team who mentors the student for one week. GRFAW participants are given the opportunity to use the very latest lab equipment to conduct real ground-breaking research. Between 2003 - 2011, 233 students from across Canada experienced hands-on research under the guidance of senior scientists in universities, hospitals and clinics across the country.  More than three quarters of the alumni have gone on to purse an education in the sciences. Every year, the Foundation receives over 300 applications from eager students all across Canada competing for one of the coveted placements.  In 2011 a record 44 Canadian students were awarded placements at 28 host labs. Applications were received from every province with the exception of PEI and the Territories. The Foundation's goal is to increase the number of students participating to 50 in 2012. There is a distinct need for this unique one-on-one mentorship in Canada. By enabling Canada's brightest young scientists to taste the impact they could have in this exciting field, we will be securing the future for our global presence in this important area of science.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health Sector Management program at the Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto
Keywords-MotsClés: BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION; HEALTHCARE MANAGEMENT; VENTURE CAPITAL
Abstract-Résumé: This program is a two-year full time Master of Business Administration program aimed at training scientists to be actively involved in the health sector management, including enhancing the knowledge-translation of biomedical discoveries, establishing biopharmaceutical companies, and improving the effectiveness of the healthcare system of Canada.  Trainees will be equipped with skills and knowledge of management in health care delivery systems, pharmaceutical and biotechnology sales and marketing, life sciences product commercialization, and related consulting and financial industries.  This training is important for educating future senior managers who obtained health-related Ph.D. degree previously to contribute to a better healthcare system and take more responsibilities of leading healthcare industry ahead.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: X-Ray Imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Light Source synchrotron presents an incredible opportunity for developing new applications and methods of x-ray imaging applied to improving the health of all Canadians. The characteristics of the synchrotron x-rays allow a number of advanced imaging techniques that are not possible in standard laboratories or clinics. The Chair leads the technical development and operation of the globally unique BioMedical Imaging and Therapy facility (BMIT).  His research is dedicated to developing novel methods of x-ray imaging and applying them to critical problems in pre-clinical human and veterinary medicine in the areas of stroke, cardio-vascular, bone and joint, and tumor imaging.  The vision is to integrate the pre-clinical applications of BMIT into the modern standard suite of medical imaging technologies in Saskatoon.  Such a cluster of imaging tools will be unique world-wide.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Integrative Cardiovascular Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Floras performs inter-disciplinary patient-oriented research to discover mechanisms responsible for the initiation and progression of cardiovascular disease and to propose and test new treatments.  He has introduced to the University methods to study the regulation of the heart and circulation by the nervous system, by blood vessel cells, and by naturally occuring regulatory molecules. He works collaboratively within and outside Canada with colleagues who share this research vision. The result is an internationally recognized integrative cardiovascular biology research program that addresses causes and therapies of common debilitating conditions such as heart failiure, hypertension, kidney failure, diabetes and sleep apnea that has attracted post-doctoral trainees from around the globe.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Proteomics and Systems Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The study of human diseases is often limited by the amounts of sample available.    We propose to develop proteomic and lipidomic technologies for the study of minute amount of samples and to pursue their applications in systems biology of human diseases.  We will develop proteomic and lipidomic technologies to probe the global changes and the sub-cellular changes that occurs in proteins and lipids during disease,s and we will apply these systems biology approaches for the study of neurodegeneration with an initial focus on Alzheimer`s Disease.  This will lead to new technologies, drug targets, and biomarkers.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Mitochondrial Dynamics
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this research program is to develop new therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of neuronal degeneration.  Mitochondria are the cellular furnace, combusting the oxygen we breathe to break down sugar and fat to generate heat and energy.  However, as with all furnaces, the mitochondria also emit dangerous reactive intermediates that damage the cell. In degenerative disease, it has become apparent that repair mechanisms are often faulty and, over time, the mitochondria lose functionality and kill the cell.  This research will both identify drug targets and perform screens to rescue mitochondrial behavior, metabolism and repair in neurodegeneration.

OrgNm: Montreal Heart Institute/Institut de cardiologie de Montréal
ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in translational and personalized medicine
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The research program focuses on the development of innovative diagnostic tools and therapies for vascular diseases, the first cause of mortality worldwide. Therapies centered on HDL-cholesterol (good cholesterol), inflammation and heart rate are the three targets that we focus on and consider most promising against atherosclerosis (fatty build-up in artery walls) and related diseases. We also aim to discover markers in blood (for example, composition of HDL particles) or on imaging to predict future cardiovascular diseases and responses to treatments. We will translate this research into rigorous clinical testing to ultimately contribute to the health of Canadians and patients worldwide.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Health Policy and Citizen Engagement
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: This Chair in Health Policy and Citizen Engagement focuses on increasing citizens understanding of science and health policy. A website called healthydebate.ca, which attempts to educate and engage citizens about health care issues, will be developed and evaluated. A new film-based technique called Brokered Dialogue will be used to understand the different perspectives of patients, scientists, physicians, politicians, and the media about the controversy regarding whether chronic cerebrospinal venous insufficiency (CCSVI) causes multiple sclerosis. Dr. Laupacis will also conduct health services research, such as a randomized trial evaluating a new multi-disciplinary team on patients chances of being readmitted to hospital.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Medicine Using Synchrotron Light
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Biochemical processes determining normal cell growth involve a complex network of protein-protein interactions. The Chair will conduct research in the area of host-pathogen interactions and will characterize structurally and functionally the mechanisms used by pathogens to subvert the host cell toward pathogen survival and replication. His research team will produce quantities of target proteins, determine their structures and examine their roles in human health and disease. The determination of protein structures relies on the synchrotron radiation provided by the Canadian Light Source facility and the innovative new technologies developed there. This research will lay foundations for next-generation disease prevention and treatments.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurocognitive Aging
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: This research program aims to understand age-related changes in cognition.  Using brain imaging, we can measure brain activity as individuals are engaged in tasks, and assess how this activity differs in older adults compared to young persons. We also can assess how variable brain activity is (as an index of how flexibly brains can adapt to different task demands), how this is reduced with age, and how it impacts behavioural performance.  This research will add to our understanding of the fundamental changes occurring in the brains of older adults and inform our interventions for improving quality of life.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Statistical Methods for Health Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Statistical methods provide a foundation and framework for rigorous scientific inquiry and hence form the basis for sound medical research. New and emerging challenges in the health sciences have arisen in recent years due to greater appreciation of the complex multifactorial nature of chronic disease processes, increasing ability to capture massive amounts of data, and a growing interest in making use of existing health data bases to answer medically important questions. Cook's research involves the development of innovative, rigorous and efficient statistical methodology which addresses these new challenges, thereby advancing the understanding of disease prevention, progression, and treatment.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Innovate SARD:  Development, Validation and Testing of New Strategies to Improve the Outcome of Persons Living with Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases (SARD)
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Innovate SARD is a research program with the aim to improve the quality of life of persons with a systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease (SARD).   Lupus is one SARD that I have studied well and that I will use as a model for SARD.  The specific objectives of Innovate SARD are: 1) to improve the health of persons with SARD; 2) to rapidly find what are the most promising findings and use them to help those living with SARD get better faster; and 3) to train a new generation of people that will be better equipped to help persons with SARD.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: DIDRA Tier I CRC in Viral Vaccinology and Therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory has played a major role in discovering the cellular attachment proteins for measles virus and studying gene therapy options against hepatitis C. Human receptors for measles virus have been expressed in mice to create animal models for studying the pathogenesis of measles virus or assessing the effectiveness of new combination vaccines against hepatitis C, human AIDS, and influenza viruses.  We recently discovered that measles virus binds to a tumor marker called PVRL4 (Nectin 4) expressed on the surface of breast, colon, lung, and ovarian cancer cells. This discovery could lead to therapeutic measles virus vaccines against these cancers.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Protein-enhanced Biomaterials
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: The chair program aims to apply the molecular strategies that were developed during the first term of the chair, to tether bioactive proteins in an oriented and optimal fashion for the development of bioactive materials. This approach offers a great potential for the control and optimization of cell - materials interactions to be applied to the fields of gene therapy and regenerative medicine. The Chairholder will validate his approach with specific growth factors that will be tethered onto a) chitosan/DNA nanoparticles and b) polysaccharidic coatings or scaffolds. Ligand tethering will result in a synergistic enhancement of the polymer properties, thereby augmenting their potential applications. These combinations of ligands and materials will be optimized in order to maximize their potential to be applied to the field of gene therapy and to the treatment of vascular diseases.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Stem Cell Neurobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The discovery of stem cells within the adult brain has revealed exciting new possibilities for promoting brain health and repair. The Chair in Stem Cell Neurobiology is helping advance our understanding of neural stem cells in the contexts of learning and memory, aging, Alzheimers disease, and spinal cord disorders, such as spinal cord injury and Multiple Sclerosis. Moreover, the rich and unique training environment created around the Chairs research program, involving innovative projects, cutting-edge technological platforms, and a network of specialized collaborators, is helping train a next generation of stem cell scientists. This research and training will benefit Canada.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cell Signalling and Proteomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Cell growth and proliferation are regulated by a network of proteins that act in concert to prevent normal cells of the body from becoming cancerous. When mutations occur within these networks, several cellular signalling pathways that promote cancer development and growth become activated. This research program combines molecular and cell biology, genetics, and novel cutting-edge proteomics technologies to study signalling pathways important for cancer cell growth and proliferation. Importantly, the identification of critical components within these signalling pathways may lead to the development of improved anti-cancer treatment.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: gynéco-oncologie moléculaire
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Asselin seeks to understand the cellular and molecular signalling mechanisms that control the fate of cells in the endometrium (ie survival  vs. cell death). Backed by a team of 13 people, his group will study normal physiology (pregnancy, embryo implantation) and pathologies of the reproductive tract (gyneacological endometrial and ovarian cancers). Very few studies concerning the regulation of apoptosis in the uterus have been published to date. Dr. Asselin and his team also developed patented molecules for targeting specific hormone-dependent cancers. The proposed program will elucidate new pathways and will propose innovative strategies for gene therapy of chemoresistant and metastatic cancers and treatment of female infertility.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Parkinson's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The Canada Research Chair in Parkinson's Disease aims to develop new diagnostic and treatment options for patients with Parkinson disease through an internationally collaborative program in translational neuroscience.  Recruited from Harvard Medical School and Brigham & Women's Hospital in late 2006, Dr. Michael Schlossmacher has launched a new research laboratory in Ottawa dedicated to understanding the basic pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease, development of biomarkers for improved diagnosis and treatment of patients, as well drug screening to identify novel therapeutics.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurobiology of Motor Learning
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, NA
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of my work is to understand how the brain recovers from stroke.  I discovered that after stroke the pattern of brain activity associated with learning a new movement differs from normal. Further, it is clear that both the stroke-damaged and opposite side of the brain are affected by stroke.  Importantly, both sides of the brain play a role in the recovery process and are key for brain reorganization after damage.  My CRC has enabled better understanding of both how the brain changes after it is damaged and what therapies positively impact these processes to optimize functional recovery.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Cardiovascular Tissue Engineering
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Every seven minutes one Canadian will experience myocardial infarction (MI), and over 16,000 will die each year from it. Upon MI, the patient may lose over one billion beating heart cells, cardiomyocytes,  that cannot be replaced by the body. The goal of the proposed CRC program is to engineer a  replacement heart tissue starting from human pluripotent stem cells. To achieve this goal, Dr. Radisic will develop new biomaterials that will keep the cells alive and functional during tissue engineering process and enable vascularization upon implantation. She will also develop new microfluidic methods to separate cardiomyocytes from heterogeneous cell populations.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuro-oncology and Human Stem Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Werbowetski-Ogilvies research focuses on using human stem cells to study the most common and highly invasive malignant brain tumours: glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) and medulloblastoma. Even after treatment, these tumours typically recur leading to poor clinical outcome. Researchers are also faced with the challenge of identifying brain tumours in their early stages. Dr. Werbowetski-Ogilvies laboratory is addressing these issues using human embryonic stem cells and their cancer-like derivatives to identify proteins that mark the early events during brain tumorigenesis. Dr. Werbowetski-Ogilvie is also further characterizing invasive brain tumour cells to identify new biomarkers that can better predict clinical outcome.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Proteomics in Cancer Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Proteomics is the study of the protein complement of an organism, organ, cell or organelle at a given time, often in response to internal (e.g., disease) or environmental cues (e.g., drug treatment). The promise of clinical proteomics lies in its ability to compare proteomes of patients, pinpointing individual proteins involved in disease cause/progression. The goal of Dr. Kislingers CRC Tier 2 renewal application is the development of a multifaceted proteomics platform for cancer biology involving biochemical and IT tools using a combination of patient tissues/fluids and model systems, to identify clinically useful biomarkers of disease and ultimately improve patient outcome.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Intestinal inflammation, microbiota and nutrition.
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Nutrition and food hygiene
Abstract-Résumé: Celiac disease is a prevalent, chronic inflammatory disease of the small intestine, caused by the ingestion of gluten-containing cereals. The role of gluten in disease expression is not restricted to classic celiac disease, but is also a factor in functional gut disorders, such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). The underlying mechanisms by which gluten intolerance leads to such diverse clinical presentations ranging from autoimmune disease (celiac disease) to functional disease (IBS) are unknown. I will explore the mechanisms underlying gluten intolerance; investigate the interactions between gluten and intestinal microbiota; and develop non-dietary approaches to prevent gluten intolerance and IBS.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive Neuroscience of Memory
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: This Tier II Canada Research Chair in Cognitive Neuroscience of Memory will use a converging-methodologies approach to understand the organization of memory and to remediate deficits when they are observed. This work will use eye movement monitoring to provide an index of memory, and magnetoencephalography to reveal the underlying neural systems that support memory in younger adults, older adults, neuropsychological and neuropsychiatric patients. This approach will result in novel and cost-efficient assessments of cognition and brain function. This research program will also characterize two methods to remediate memory deficits, thereby establishing the basic research needed to develop cognitive rehabilitation protocols.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular Mechanisms of Cerebral Blood Flow Control
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: Brain blood flow is exquisitely controlled by local changes in brain activity in order to deliver appropriate amounts of oxygen and glucose to desired regions.  A spectrum of neurological problems are closely linked to abnormalities in brain blood flow, yet surprisingly we know very little about how brain cells signal to blood vessels to regulate this process.  My laboratory will use new fluorescence microscope technologies to image within the brain at the cellular level to study how brain cells communicate with local blood vessels.  By understanding the molecular mechanisms of this process, my research will discover new targets for disease intervention.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Microbial Genomics and Infectious Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Research in Dr. Cowens laboratory explores the mechanisms by which fungal pathogens evolve drug resistance and cause infectious disease, a primary cause of human mortality worldwide.  They focus on the leading fungal pathogen of humans, Candida albicans, and use cutting-edge technologies and scientific approaches to identify key determinants of its ability to cause disease and evolve resistance to drugs used in the clinic.  Their innovative and interdisciplinary approach incorporates experimental evolution, whole-genome sequencing, functional genomics, proteomics, high-throughput drug screening, imaging, molecular genetics, and infection models to discover critical new therapeutic strategies to combat infectious disease and save human lives.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Our research is devoted to obtaining atomic descriptions of protein-drug interactions, and to relating the structure and dynamics of proteins to their biological functions. In the first area, our focus is on actin-targeting natural products. These exist in many different forms but all share a remarkable ability to kill cancer cells by inhibiting actin-based cell division and movement. Our research in the second area involves a recently discovered class of cytoskeletal motor protein that may be unique to pathogenic fungi. Knowing the key structural design features underlying the functions of these molecules could guide more effective anticancer and antifungal drug development.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Multiple Sclerosis Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS), a terribly disabling demyelinating disease without curative therapy, exerts a heavy toll on Canadians, being unusually widespread here. Early MS exists in different subtypes, maybe explaining why it has not been amenable to a single treatment.  Metals are important for myelination and metal dysregulation may be implicated in some subtypes. CRC candidate, Dr. Popescu will use innovative, powerful synchrotron, molecular and neuropathological approaches to characterize these subtypes in humans, identify relevant models and develop novel therapies. This unique Canadian Light Source-based research program will provide critical new insight into demyelinating disease and improve the health of Canadians.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Neurodegenerative Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Activation of caspases and cleavage of specific proteins are a critical event in the pathogenesis of several neurodegenerative diseases. Caspase-6, a type of molecular scissors, functions as an initiator caspase through its ability to cleave and activate other caspases and activation of caspase-6 is observed in preclinical Alzheimers and Huntington disease brain. The overwhelming evidence on the role of caspase-6 in neurodegenerative diseases supports caspase-6 as a key drug target. The CRC in Neurodegenerative Diseases will aim at increasing the understanding of the biology of caspase-6 and other initiator caspases in order to develop successful therapeutic approaches to inhibit caspase activation pathways. Such knowledge will provide valuable new insights into the fundamental mechanisms underlying neurodegenerative diseases and provide a much-needed understanding of the crucial factors that determine regulation of caspases. The overall goal of this work is to identify therapeutic approaches to delay or prevent neurodegeneration.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Early Intervention in Psychiatry
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Severe mental illness, such as depression, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, usually starts early in life and children of parents with severe mental illness are at high risk to develop severe mental illness themselves. This is a proposal to test early interventions that may reduce the risk of developing mental illness among adolescents and young adults at high risk. I propose to select at-risk adolescents among children of parents with severe mental illness and randomly offer them one of several interventions that may reduce the risk of developing severe mental illness and prevent life-long disability.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Psychiatry
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Pharmacological approaches modulating the molecular response to neurotransmitters are the method of choice in psychiatry. However, the molecular mechanisms contributing to the etiology or treatment of mental disorders have remained unexplained. The research program undertaken by this chair is based on the use of animal models to understand the roles of fundamental biochemical processes in mental disorders. It exploits a combination of approaches based on behavioral studies, pharmacology, imaging and biochemistry and have allowed to uncover new mechanisms of action for the regulation of behavior by psychiatric drugs. Such discoveries are expected to have a major impact on the development of therapeutic approaches for mental disorders.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Molecular Neurogenetics
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Cell migrations occur along basement membranes  comprising secreted glycoproteins (proteins modified by sugars) assembled into sheets that lay over the surface of non-migrating cells. We have discovered a protein that allows only fully modified glycoproteins into basement membranes where they can guide cell migrations. This study is revealing mechanisms of basement membrane assembly and glycoprotein function used in normal and metastatic cell migrations.  We have also discovered that neuron activity can suppress a mutation that normally causes axon guidance defects. Knowledge of the molecular mechanism of this suppression could enhance efforts to regenerate spinal cords in humans.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of our research is to understand how nerve cells form connections, how they modify those connections with experience, and how such connections are perturbed in psychiatric disorders. Connections between nerve cells, called synapses, are the basic units of communication in the brain. We study molecules that trigger formation of synapses, and how genetic variants associated with increased risk of autism and schizophrenia alter synaptic function. This research bringing together fundamental molecular mechanisms of brain development with genetics of neurodevelopmental disorders will lead to a better understanding of how such disorders occur and eventually, I hope, to improved therapies.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental Neurobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: My research program focuses on determining how cells in the mammalian nervous system differentiate, survive, and  establish connections during development, and using this information to try and develop therapeutic strategies for treating the damaged or degenerating nervous system.  Within this broad context, our specific objectives are to define the way the environment controls neural stem cells, to understand how neurons and their connections are maintained over the mammalian lifespan, and to determine the therapeutic potential of a novel population of skin stem cells that we have defined with regard to repair and regeneration.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Biotechnology and Genomics - Neurobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: Calcium channels play essential roles in the nervous system and are important targets for therapeutic treatment including migraine, epilepsy, chronic pain, addiction and blindness. In order to better understand how calcium channels contribute to these diseases and to develop effective treatments, the work will combine the latest high-throughput gene sequencing, gene cloning and brain cell electrophysiology techniques to identify the exact nature of the calcium channel variants relevant to disease pathophysiology. This multidisciplinary approach will advance our understanding of calcium channel functional complexity in the normal and diseased states and further translate newly designed drugs to the pharmaceutical industry.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Chaire de recherche du Canada en signalisation du cancer colorectal et de l'inflammation intestinale
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Au Canada, le cancer colorectal est la deuxième cause de décès par cancer. Comme les autres cancers, le cancer colorectal est dû à des mutations de gènes qui ajustent la prolifération et la survie, résultant en une multiplication anarchique des cellules touchées. Plusieurs des gènes mutés encodent pour des protéines impliquées dans la transmission de signaux émis par les facteurs de croissance ou inflammatoires. Dailleurs, linflammation de lintestin est associée à une augmentation du risque de développer un cancer colorectal. Le programme de recherche du Dr Rivard vise à identifier les sentiers de signalisation impliqués dans la progression du cancer colorectal et dans la réponse inflammatoire intestinale.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The Canada Research Chair in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging will develop MRI techniques that allow the diagnosis and monitoring of neurological disease in patients at some of the highest magnetic fields available for human MRI use. In addition to an enhanced ability to image human brain function, use of these sophisticated MRI systems has potential for earlier diagnosis of diseases such as multiple sclerosis and could allow treatment approaches to be tailored to the specific biology of patients in illnesses such as brain tumours. Early diagnosis and informed therapies are important, as most available treatments work best when applied early.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental Immunology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Zúñiga-Pflückers research program aims to understand the molecular and cellular controls that initiate and regulate the development of T-cells, the master regulators of the immune system.  Dr. Zúñiga-Pflücker created a simple tissue culture system in which stem cells can be efficiently instructed to become T-cells. This approach enables the three main research areas that address T-lineage commitment and differentiation, role of Notch signaling, and generation of human progenitor T-cells for immune-reconstitution. The aim is to eventually be able to restore immune function in a variety of conditions, including in the treatment of HIV/AIDS and leukemia.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular & Developmental Neurobiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Bouliannes research program aims to uncover the mechanisms underlying the development and function of the nervous system and to establish models of human aging, neurodegenerative diseases and obesity using fruit flies.  Her work has uncovered how cells are specified within the brain and how they communicate with each other to regulate various behaviors as well as learning and memory. Dr. Boulianne has also identified novel genes and mechanisms that are implicated in both aging and Alzheimers disease, which may shed light on the early events leading to disease pathogenesis and provide novel targets for therapeutic intervention.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Angiogenic and Lymphangiogenic Signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: In cardiovascular pathologies, inflammation promotes angiogenesis and in turn angiogenesis can enhance the inflammatory process suggesting that these processes are mutually dependent.  The interdependency between the inflammatory and vascular components in asthma is poorly understood; however with the identification of the Angiopoietin family of ligands, whose biological targets include both endothelial and inflammatory cells. Dr. Dumont's research is currently investigating a novel Angiopoietin-ligand drug that recapitulates the activity of this growth factor.  His research team is investigating the biology of this signalling axis and the utility of this new drug compound in diseases such as diabetes, cancer, artherosclerosis and lung injury.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Mathematical Modeling and Health Economics of Infectious Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: Preventive medicine, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Decisions regarding infectious disease control are increasingly made with significant input from mathematical and economic models. The aim of the research program is to use modeling to study the natural history and transmission dynamics of infectious diseases, predict the effectiveness/cost-effectiveness of control strategies, and identify optimal strategies to reduce health inequalities. Research will mainly focus on the study and control of human papillomavirus related diseases, varicella and herpes zoster at the population-level and within vulnerable subgroups. The work will be used to address methodological challenges related to infectious disease modeling and economic evaluation to provide better tools for policy decision-making.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in the Cognitive Neuroscience of  Attention and Expectation
Keywords-MotsClés: Other research, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Generously supported by several federal/provincial/philanthropic contributions, including from the Canada Research Chairs Program, our programmatic research agenda focuses on clarifying how factors such as expectation, suggestion, and attention influence higher brain functions.  We seek to unravel such phenomena using converging multiple techniques, including sophisticated variations of neuroimaging of the living human brain.  Over the past years, we have shed considerable light on the psychological, physiological, and neurobiological substrates involved in such novel processes.  Our findings pave the road toward a more scientific understanding of these effects alongside the development of applied and practical prospects for both healthy and pathological populations.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Human Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Since the establishment of my research group at McGill University in September 2006, my laboratory has pioneered novel approaches for the sensitive detection of regulatory variants altering gene expression in human cells. In addition to novel methods, we have spearheaded the exploration of different human cell types at the population level, allowing us to show frequent links between human disease and regulatory variation. We have also demonstrated how disease-associated regulatory variants work at the molecular level. These advances and our on-going work pave the way for understanding common disease-associated genetic variation and provide global insight into human gene regulation.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurodegeneration and Repair
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinsons disease, Alzheimers disease, and ALS affect a substantial and growing number of Canadians. Unfortunately, there has been little advancement in the development of effective strategies for the treatment of these devastating neurological conditions. One common aspect of all of these disorders is that loss of brain function is associated with nerve cell death. The goals of Dr Cregansresearch program are to understand the mechanisms that (1) control nerve cell death and (2) alter the reparative/ regenerative activity of stem cells in the affected nervous system. This information will then be used to develop novel pharmacological agents to minimize the loss of brain function in neurodegenerative conditions.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in synthesis of novel radiopharmaceuticals for Positron Emission Tomography (PET) in neurology and oncology
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, NA
Abstract-Résumé: PET is an imaging modality in nuclear medicine detecting tumors or giving a direct look at biochemistry in the brain. The compounds used are radiopharmaceuticals, visualizing a disease such as Alzheimers and Parkinson's and various types of cancer. It is an important tool which requires expertise from nuclear medicine and also from chemists synthesizing these compounds. The syntheses are very complex and restricted to research groups with specially equipped personnel. We introduced a procedure based on a silicon-fluorine-18 bond providing an easy introduction of fluorine-18 into complex biomolecules. This chemistry needs further work to help spread its availability to patients.

Abstract-Résumé: My PhD was in Global Health and Epidemiology. I co-founded the research project, entitled South African Virologic Evaluation (SAVE) study, as a collaboration between Karolinska Institute, Stockholm, Stanford University, California and the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD) in Johannesburg. I was the line manager of 4 research assistants and played the role of liaison between the hospital, pharmacy and the research laboratory. In addition I was managing the research project budget.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Globalization and Health Equity
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Social medicine
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research builds on earlier studies and seeks to understand better how contemporary globalization can be directed to improve population health equity. Several globalization-related pathways that affect population health will be studied. These include: the effect of the migration of health workers on health systems and population health; and the effect of the increased commercialization of cross-border patient flows (medical tourism) on health system access and population health. It also examines the role of globalizing comprehensive primary health care reforms in improving population health; as well as how national governments take into account health goals in their foreign policy.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurodegeneration and Protein Misfolding Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The prion diseases, such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans and bovine spongiform encephalopathy in cattle, are caused by the propagated misfolding of the prion protein. The functions of most proteins, including the prion protein, depend upon the precise three-dimensional structures of their mature, folded forms; when misfolding occurs, problems arise. Propagated protein misfolding plays a role in other neurodegenerative syndromes, including Alzheimer's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Parkinson's disease. Dr. Cashmans work is aimed at understanding the biochemical governance and consequences of protein misfolding, and the development of novel and effective diagnostics and therapeutics for neurodegenerative diseases and other diseases in which protein misfolding participates.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Human Genome Epidemiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Preventive medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Huge investment in genetic research is expected to result in the proportion of the population for which genetic testing is applicable growing from 2% to >60%. The research program addresses steps needed to enable such translation of genetic discoveries into human health application. The objectives are to (1) evaluate and further develop guidelines on methodology and reporting of studies investigating genetic and related variation on human health; (2) integrate evidence on genetic predisposition to neurological disorders, colorectal neoplasia, and orofacial clefts, and conduct new studies to address gaps; and (3) develop and evaluate disease prevention approaches that incorporate genetic information.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Adipose Tissue
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: The recognition of obesity as a disease, and its implication in cardiovascular disease and diabetes have brought adipose (fat) tissue research to the forefront in the last decade.  Notwithstanding public awareness, obesity is increasing. Changes in fat metabolism alter adipose hormones, affecting local tissues and the whole body.           The Canada Research Chair in Adipose Tissue (Katherine Cianflone) at the CRIUCPQ, Laval University is a focal point for the interaction of investigators and health science professionals in Obesity/Metabolism, Cardiology, and Respirology involving normal and pathological conditions. This provides interactions of researchers, their students, bariatric surgeons, cardiologists, respirologists and their patients.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Knowledge Translation
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Knowledge translation is the synthesis, dissemination, exchange and application of knowledge to improve health outcomes, provide more effective health services and strengthen the health care system. The research conducted in the CRC in Knowledge Translation advances our understanding of the forces that foster or impede using knowledge for improvements in health services. The research program aims to develop a better  understanding of how to increase the use of best practices, and in so doing aims to improve quality of care, quality of life and quality of end of life for the frail, vulnerable elderly in residential long term care (nursing home) settings and quality of work life for their care providers. The end goal is system change that ensures these improvements in quality are sustainable.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Influenza Neuraminidase Inhibitors - Development of Orally Bioavailable Agents
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-VIRAL; DIFLUOROSIALIC ACID; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; INFLUENZA; MECHANISM-BASED INHIBITION; NEURAMINIDASE INHIBITOR; ORAL BIOAVAILABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Influenza neuraminidase (also known as a sialidase) is a clinically validated enzyme target for control of influenza infections. Of the four approved drugs that inhibit this enzyme, only Tamiflu (oseltamivir) is orally available, and thus dominates the neuraminidase inhibitor (NAI) market. Tamiflu, and to a lesser extent Relenza (zanamivir), are stockpiled by many countries as first line defence against pandemic influenza in conjunction with vaccination programs.  Emerging resistance against Tamiflu, and requirement for delivery of Relenza by inhalation, creates a need for new drugs that evade current and emerging NAI resistance mechanisms and yet can be dosed orally. The Withers laboratory has created the "difluorosialic acids" (DFSAs), a novel class of NAI that is completely inactive against the human enzyme and demonstrates superior in vitro binding kinetics on the viral neuraminidase. DFSAs exhibit a uniquely slow "off-rate" once bound to the target, resulting in a bound residence time that is two orders of magnitude higher than that of Relenza. DFSAs have structural similarity to the natural substrate sialic acid in order to reduce development of resistance. Initial leads have shown activity in vitro, and in cell-based assays against several seasonal influenza A and B strains including a Tamiflu-resistant mutant, resulting in our first patent application (2009). Additional chemistry has yielded new compounds with a greater than ten-fold potency improvement over early leads.  We have demonstrated in vitro activity against a broad array of wild type and Tamiflu/Relenza resistant mutants of influenza A and B, and a dose response relationship of efficacy in a mouse model.  These compounds are the subject of a second patent application. Funding is sought for further development of this promising class of compounds, to optimize the chemistry to produce an orally available form of DFSA which retains this activity profile in vitro and in vivo.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; SYSTEME GENITO-URINAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Applications of Lactic Acid Bacteria in Infection Prevention and Treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA-GALACTOOLIGOSACCHARIDES; ANTIMICROBIAL PEPTIDES; CLONING; DNA SEQUENCING; EXOPOLYSACCHARIDES; HAEMAGGLUTINATION ASSAYS; HIGH PRESSURE LIQUID CHROMATOGRAPHY; LACTIC ACID BACTERIA; MICROBIOTA CHARACTERIZATION; PROBIOTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Bacteria are becoming resistant to a vast array of different antibiotics and the discovery of new drugs for combating infections is lagging behind. Therefore, alternative prevention and treatment options are urgently needed to address this serious issue. The primary aim of my doctoral research is to use so called "friendly" Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB), and some of the compounds that they produce to aid the development of new probiotic applications that can promote health through studies in farm animals and respective models. One part of my research was focused on the use of potentially beneficial LAB in treating uterine infections in dairy cows. My research results showed that the selected LAB were able to lower the occurrence and the severity of the disease, indirectly increase milk production and prevent dairy cows from being culled. With promising results obtained, I began conducting a different study on using LAB produced sugar polymers or glycans for preventing gastrointestinal infections. Since certain components of the cell surface of intestinal cells that harmful bacteria bind to cause infection are identical to those found on the surface of red blood cells, I chose to use red blood cells from pigs as my test system. I found that only glycans isolated from a bacterium called Lactobacillus reuteri but not currently available commercial glycans were able to prevent the binding. Wanting to generate more different types of glycans and prevent a wider range of harmful bacteria from causing infection, I subsequently cloned an enzyme which produced more specific types of glycans. Overall, I believe my studies are tremendously relevant to the area of biomedicine as they will help with the development of new therapeutic applications as functional foods and nutraceuticals for preventing and treating urogenital and gastrointestinal infections in farm animals and people alike.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of an anti-proliferative therapeutic that disrupts CaM-cyclin E interactions in vivo.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-PROLIFERATIVE THERAPY; DRUG-ELUTING STENT; PEPTIDE THERAPY; POST-ANGIOPLASTY RESTENOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Mesh like metal tubes called stents, designed to slowly release drugs that prevent heart blood vessel re-narrowing, are called Drug Eluting Stents or DES.  While they have been very effective at reducing re-narrowing, they have been complicated by poor repair of the inner lining, known as the endothelium, which can result in sudden clot formation in the artery, heart attack and even death.  We have developed a new protein-based therapy called the CBS peptide, which we propose to test in pre-clinical rabbit models of artery re-narrowing that resemble the human condition.  Our proposed studies also include a careful analysis of the dose, duration of action and safety of this new therapy delivered on a DES.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel point-of-care method of handling human waste in healthcare institutions: technical improvements and evaluation.
Keywords-MotsClés: BEDPANS; COMMERCIALIZATION; EVALUATION; HEALTHCARE INSTITUTION; HUMAN WASTE; INFECTION CONTROL; POINT-OF-CARE TECHNOLOGY; TECHNOLOGY; TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER
Abstract-Résumé: Rising infection rates are causing unnecessary suffering and death and are taxing the healthcare system as well as patients and families. Disposal of human waste in hospitals is associated with a significant risk for the spread of infection. For example, it is often necessary for patients in hospitals to use a bedpan because they cannot be transferred into a bathroom. The bedpan must then be transported to a central location for disposal of the contents, washing and disinfection. This task is associated with a significant risk for the spread of infection. Recently, small macerating disposal devices that can be installed within individual bathrooms have been distributed principally by our commercial partner but acceptance has been limited because of cost and maintenance issues. We have produced a working concept prototype that addresses both of these issues. We propose to develop a more sophisticated second generation prototype and evaluate it in CareLab, Toronto Rehab's simulated patient room laboratory. Care, maintenance and housekeeping staff from acute, rehabilitation and complex continuing care facilities will evaluate the function of the new prototype. This proposal is designed to add value to the intellectual property and confirm specific design criteria. Our commercial partner has committed funds for this POP stage and will participate in this phase of development and testing. The recommendations from the testing will strengthen our commercial partner's interest in the product and allow us to design and build a third generation prototype suitable for clinical testing. The intended eventual outcome of this project is a new product and operating procedure that will reduce infection hazards, particularly Clostridium difficile, associated with current methods of toileting patients in bed. Collaboration throughout this process from the commercial partner will hasten the technology transfer process and, if successful, result in manufacture in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery of Novel Biomarker Panels for Psoriatic Arthritis Susceptibility and Severity Using High-Throughput Transcriptional Profiling Technologies
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; BIOMARKERS; GENOMICS; INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIS; MICROARRAYS; PSORIASIS; PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS; SEVERITY; SUSCEPTIBILITY; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Psoriasis is a common inflammatory skin disease that affects 2-3% of the population in North America. Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) is a specific form of arthritis that affects 30% of patients with psoriasis. Earlier studies suggested that PsA was a mild disease, but more recent experience has shown that it is more severe than previously recognized. Diagnosing PsA is difficult, as it requires examination by a specialist as well as imaging. There are currently no reliable blood tests to predict which psoriasis patients will develop PsA. In most cases, psoriasis precedes the onset of PsA. This temporal association offers a unique opportunity to identify the biological changes that occur in psoriasis patients that lead to the development of mild or severe arthritis. The proposed study aims to discover and characterize these biological changes, and develop a technology that can identify and diagnose the early stages of arthritis in psoriasis patients. Such a technology would help clinicians to individualize treatment for psoriasis patients and possibly prevent joint damage and disability associated with PsA. Since the biological basis of the relationship between psoriasis and PsA is unknown, the proposed study is also poised to generate breakthroughs in the human biology of psoriasis generally, and PsA specifically.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phase I/II Interventional Clinical Trial of Balloon Venoplasty for Chronic Cerebrospinal Venous Insufficiency in Multiple Sclerosis Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOPLASTY; CCSSVI; CHRONIC CEREBROSPINAL VENOUS INSUFFICIENCY; CLINICAL TRIAL; DOUBLE BLIND; EXTRACRANIAL VEINS; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; PATIENT REPORTED OUTCOMES; PHASE I/II; SHAM CONTROLLED
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple Sclerosis is an autoimmune disease of the brain, optic nerves and spinal cord. Over 60,000 Canadians are affected by this life long, disabling condition. The cause and cure remains unknown. Approximately 50% of MS patients have signs of narrowed or blocked veins in the neck known as Chronic Cerebrospinal Venous Insufficiency (CCSVI). The Canadian Study Group on CCSVI in MS includes neurologists with expertise in MS working with surgeons and radiologists. This group will conduct a phase I/II safety and efficacy study on a controversial new treatment for CCSVI that involves balloon dilation (angioplasty) of blocked veins. 100 MS patients with evidence of CCSVI will participate in a controlled study of balloon dilation compared to placebo. All patients will receive the treatment (cross over study) and be followed for 2 years and measures to determine the effect of treatment will include quality of life scales, disability scales, and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain. An independent data safety committee will periodically review the conduct of the study. Recruitment will commence in 2012.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetic regulation of myogenic stem cell function
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR QUIESCENCE; DIFFERENTIATION; EPIGENETICS; LINEAGE COMMITMENT; MUSCLE PROGENITORS; MYOGENESIS; REGENERATION; SELF-RENEWAL; STEM CELLS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Following muscle injury or strength training exercise, satellite cells residing in the muscle proliferate and fuse, renewing or increasing the size and strength of the muscle. The number of satellite cells and the regenerative capacity of muscle decrease during aging and in diseases such as muscular dystrophy. During development and in the adult, the transcription factor Pax7 regulates genes necessary for the maintenance and proliferation of satellite cells and is required for the survival of these cells. This project aims to build a better understanding of the requirement for Pax7 and how it functions. We have found that to activate genes, Pax7 recruits MLL, a histone methyltransferase, which relaxes DNA packing, facilitating access for transcription. Previous studies have found that MLL is required for expression of developmental regulators that are necessary to maintain other types of adult stem cells. We are developing a genetically modified mouse in which MLL is removed from muscle satellite cells. In cultured muscle progenitor cells lacking MLL (MLL KO), expression of Pax7 is weakly reduced, but expression of Pax7 targets is lost, as is proliferation. Over-expression of Pax7 overcomes the MLL KO defect and Pax7 target gene expression and proliferation are recovered. In this study, we aim to determine; 1) the effect of the loss of MLL on the accessibility and expression of Pax7 target genes, 2) the effect of the loss of MLL on muscle regeneration in-vivo, 3) the mechanism by which Pax7 can activate genes without MLL, and 4) whether MLL is required for expression of other myogenic developmental regulators. Determining how over-expressed Pax7 is able to overcome DNA packing based gene expression restrictions, and identification of new developmental regulators important for muscle will be informative for devising new strategies to save satellite cells in diseased muscle and for generation of satellite cells from non-muscle tissue for cell replacement therapy.

Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY HEALTH SYSTEMS; GLOBAL CHILD HEALTH; HEALTH POLICY; IMPLEMENTATION SCIENCE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MONITORING AND EVALUATION; MULTILEVEL MODELLING; NUTRITIONAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; PROGRAM SCALE-UP; SPACIAL EPIDEMIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Iron deficiency anemia is one of the most common forms of malnutrition in the world, particularly among infants and children in developing countries. Anemia can be treated with iron pills, but there is some concern that giving iron pills to children living in areas where malaria is common, such as sub-Saharan Africa, will increase their chances of becoming infected with malaria. This research will assess whether a different form of iron (a powdered form that is mixed with food) can be safely given to children 6-35 months of age living in rural Ghana to treat and prevent anemia without making them sicker from malaria and other infections. This research will also involve looking at certain characteristics of the households and villages where the children live, as well as the surrounding environment, and evaluating whether these characteristics are related to better or worse health outcomes. The information gained from this research will tell us, not only whether a powdered form of iron can be safely given to children in high malaria areas, but also how this nutrition intervention could be effectively used in community health programs throughout Ghana and in other African countries.

TitreApplicationTitle: Évaluation systématique d'interventions ergonomiques visant la prévention durable des troubles musculosquelettiques en milieu de travail: identification des stratégies d'intervention performantes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYSE THEMATIQUE; CONTEXTE D'ENTREPRISE; EFFICACITE DES INTERVENTIONS; INTERVENTION ERGONOMIQUE; MODELE CAUSAL; PRATIQUES PROFESSIONNELLES; PREVENTION DES TROUBLES MUSCULOSQUELETTIQUES; RECHERCHE EVALUATIVE; SANTE ET SECURITE DU TRAVAIL; ETUDE DE CAS MULTIPLES
Abstract-Résumé: Les troubles musculosquelettiques (TMS), telles les entorses et les lesions en "-ite", se classent au premier rang des maladies et lesions indemnisees chez les travailleurs quebecois. Les TMS entrainent de lourdes consequences, tant au niveau de la personne, par la presence de douleur et d'incapacite, qu'au niveau de l'entreprise, par les couts relies a l'indemnisation et a l'absenteisme. Or, les ergonomes sont des intervenants-cles dans la prevention durable des TMS en milieu de travail. Cependant, bien que la recherche reconnaisse l'apport des interventions ergonomiques en entreprise, la facon de realiser ces interventions en les adaptant au contexte du milieu de travail est tres peu connue. Autrement dit, les strategies adoptees par les intervenants pour reussir a mobiliser les acteurs de l'entreprise et favoriser des actions menant a des transformations du travail demeurent tres peu decrites, ce qui compromet la comprehension des mecanismes qui en assurent l'efficacite. Ce projet propose donc de mieux comprendre le processus de l'intervention ergonomique menee en milieu de travail en documentant en profondeur chacune de ses composantes et son contexte aupres d'un groupe d'intervenants en ergonomie. Un modele decrivant les relations entre les actions de l'intervenant et les resultats au niveau de l'entreprise sera produit pour chaque intervention etudiee. La mise en commun des modeles permettra de faire ressortir les strategies les plus effcaces, soit celles qui ont permis aux intervenants d'influencer l'implantation des transformations du travail. Ce projet facilitera le tranfert des connaissances liees a la pratique en constituant une reference pour les ergonomes afin de choisir les strategies d'intervention les plus efficaces en fonction du contexte de l'entreprise.

TitreApplicationTitle: Repair mechanisms of human skin-derived precursors differentiated into Schwann cells (SKP-SCs) transplanted into the injured rodent spinal cord.
Keywords-MotsClés: AXONAL REGENERATION; CELL TRANSPLANTATION; CONTUSION INJURY; ENDOGENOUS SCHWANN CELL RESPONSE; GLIAL SCAR; MOTOR/SENSORY TESTING; REMYELINATION; SCHWANN CELLS; SKIN-DERIVED PRECURSORS; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury (SCI) affects an estimated 42,000 Canadians and represents a substantial financial burden for the Canadian health care system. The motor, sensory and autonomic dysfunctions associated with SCI result primarily from the loss of projecting axons (which carry electrical signals) and the loss of glial cells (that insulate axons with myelin to maintain the speed of those electrical signals). Replacing those lost cells is one potential strategy to treat SCI. My research aims to determine the potential benefits of treating chronic SCI by transplanting myelinating (i.e., insulating) glial cells known as Schwann cells into the injured rat spinal cord. These particular Schwann cells (known as SKP-SCs) are of great interest because they can be generated from cells found in human skin (SKPs) rather than being harvested from peripheral nerve - the traditional source of Schwann cells. SKP-SCs have been shown to myelinate and enhance the growth of axons in acute and sub-acute SCI. SKP-SCs would be advantageous for use in clinical settings because they can be made from adult human skin, and can thus be transplanted into the same person who donated the skin to produce the cells; eliminating the need for harmful immunosuppressive drugs normally required to prevent cell rejection. The adult source of these cells also eliminates ethical concerns that plague cells from fetal/embryonic sources, and unlike the harvest of Schwann cells from peripheral nerve, isolating SKPs from skin carries little risk of permanent nerve damage. Given that the largest proportion of the SCI population consists of individuals with chronic injuries, we propose to examine the outcome of transplanting human SKP-SCs in a rodent model of chronic SCI to further establish their potential for clinical translation. In addition, we will conduct a detailed analysis of the response of the host spinal cord to SKP-SC transplantation, to determine how SKP-SCs influence natural repair mechanisms post-SCI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the role of innate-like lymphocytes in the suppression of fatal autoimmunity in lupus-prone congenic mice.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNITY; B REGULATORY CELLS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENETICS; IMMUNOLOGY; MOUSE CONGENICS; MOUSE TRANSGENICS; NKT CELLS; SUPPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Systemic lupus erythematosus (lupus) is a lifelong disorder that affects an estimated 1 in 2,000 North Americans. In lupus petients, the body's immune response which normally protects against viral and bacterial infections incorrectly attacks the cells of the body; this initiates an autoimmune response resulting in inflammation of the joints and vital organs. Despite years of research, the mechanisms of lupus are largely unknown and consequently treatments are limited. Our lab investigates the complex factors that contribute to lupus by using mouse models. The immune systems of mice and humans are incredibly similar and our studies can provide insights into human disease. We work with a strain of mice called New Zealand Black (NZB) which develop lupus-like symptoms. Using rigorous breeding techniques, our lab has developed more defined strains that have inherited genetic information from the parental NZB mice. This technique allows us to better understand how specific genetic information directly impacts on lupus. Using this approach, it was noticed that not all genetic information from New Zealand Black mice contributed to disease. Unexpectedly, some portions of genetic information seemed to have a suppressive effect on lupus progression. From our previous studies, we believe that some unique cells of the immune system are responsible for this protection. My project focuses on understanding this suppression and discovering the underlying genetic factors that protect against lupus. The distinct mice bred in our lab allow for a new perspective on this complex genetic disorder and could potentially reveal new targets for therapy.
