TitreApplicationTitle: Developing and piloting quality indicators for children in primary care
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; CONSENSUS STUDY; EVIDENCE-BASED MEDICINE; FAMILY MEDICINE; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PATIENT-ORIENTED RESEARCH; PEDIATRICS; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; QUALITY INDICATORS
Abstract-Résumé: The care of children plays an important role in family medicine as children under 15 years represent 12-18% of all consultations. However, there are concerns about the quality of pediatric primary care in several countries and a number of international figures agree that there is a lack of evidence-based quality indicators for children in Canada and the UK. Taking advantage of the primary care delivery system currently in place in the UK and its potential use as a model for Canada, I aim to develop indicators of quality care for children in family practice. Due to the lack of clinical research in this area, I will complete three studies in parallel to comprehend and evaluate the scale of the problem prior to developing indicators: (1) identify the high quality evidence-base for interventions delivered to children in primary care; (2) outline the number of emergency hospital admissions for primary care preventable admissions in children; and (3) explore family physicians viewpoints on the quality of care of children. To focus on developing a small number of high quality and appropriate indicators, I will create an expert panel of UK family physicians to generate professional agreement on the quality indicators using consensus methods. Lastly, using a large database of primary care records in the UK, I will evaluate the quality of care for children using the proposed indicators. To translate the findings to Canada, I will evaluate the applicability and relevance of the indicators amongst a panel of Canadian family physicians. The results of this study will fill an existing knowledge gap by providing quality of care measures for primary care in Canada and the UK. The establishment of relevant, high impact quality of care indicators will enable researchers, funding agencies, policy makers and administrators to measure performance, establish benchmarks, and identify care gaps where improvement is most needed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antimicrobial Induced Tolerance Mechanisms in Staphylococcus saprophyticus and their Role in Recurrent and Device Associated Urinary Tract Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; ANTIBIOTICS; CELLULAR INTERNALIZATION; HORMESIS; PERSISTER CELL; RECURRENT URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS; STAPHYLOCOCCUS SAPROPHYTICUS
Abstract-Résumé: Management of patients with urological devices and recurrent urinary tract infections (rUTI) is a chronic problem for physicians as re-emergent infections are common even after years of therapy. Unfortunately, these recurrent or persistent infections have a profoundly negative impact on the quality of life of individuals suffering with them. Currently, there are no methods to treat rUTI, however, management strategies do exist, and often involve providing patients with long-term, low-dose antimicrobials to keep infections at bay and decrease symptoms. Interestingly, our research is beginning to reveal that these low-doses of antimicrobials may actually have a negative impact on infection, even if they successfully treat the symptoms. Specifically, at low levels antibiotics can alter bacteria in novel ways which may actually promote persistence within the urinary tract. Preliminary data suggests that low-dose antimicrobial pre-treatment induces an adaptive response, reducing the effectiveness of subsequent challenge with higher concentrations, essentially making the organisms more difficult to destroy. These adaptive responses occur rapidly, and may be dependent on the organisms transitioning from active or 'awake' to dormant or 'hibernating' state. The purpose of this study is to investigate how sub-inhibitory antibiotics make these changes, and how they might contribute to rUTI in Staphylococcus saprophyticus, a prominent human bacterial uropathogen. Importantly, simply altering the timing of antibiotic delivery may serve to eradicate infections over therapy duration. It is expected that this work will aid in the development of new antibiotic strategies to ultimately treat tolerant infections and improve therapy outcome and management of device associated and rUTI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Factors influencing the effectiveness and appeal of Traffic Light labelling among Canadians.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADIAN; FRONT-OF-PACKAGE; LABELLING; NUTRITION; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Diet-related health problems place a great burden on the Canadian economy as levels of obesity and chronic diseases continue to rise. Nutritional labelling on food products has emerged as an important population-level intervention for promoting healthy eating habits. International evidence suggests that front-of-package (FOP) labels may be more effective at helping consumers choose healthier products compared to back-of-package nutrition information alone. Traffic Light (TL) labels are located on the FOP and highlight amounts of key nutrients in red, amber and green Traffic Lights that signify high, medium and low amounts of a nutrient, respectively. Although these labels have been implemented voluntarily in the UK, few studies have examined their effectiveness in Canada. The current study aims to examine the effectiveness and appeal of TL labels among Canadian consumers. Study results have the potential to inform key policy decisions regarding the implementation of TL labels in Canada. Mandatory TL labelling could help consumers choose healthier options when grocery shopping, which would ultimately help to decrease rates of obesity and diet-related health conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Print and Online Educational Materials for Primary Care Physicians
Keywords-MotsClés: EVIDENCE-BASED CARE; GUIDELINES; HUMAN FACTORS ENGINEERING; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION TOOLS; MIXED METHODS; PREVENTIVE HEALTH; PRIMARY CARE; USABILITY TESTING
Abstract-Résumé: Evidence-based medicine can improve the lives of Canadians by increasing the quality of care and reducing variance in the care provided. However, it has been shown that published evidence is not being used by health professionals in the provision of care. This study aims to increase the use of evidence-based medicine, primarily in the form of clinical practice guidelines, through the optimization of educational materials for primary care physicians. Studies have shown that print educational materials have small to moderate effects on physician behaviour, however, little is known about their development process and how different design features impact physician behaviour. This study will review both health services and multidisciplinary literature to inform the proposal of a process for the development of educational materials. Focus groups will be conducted with primary care physicians to ensure that this process incorporates their content and design needs. Lastly, the study will use the proposed process to create a prototype of an educational tool that will be tested by primary care physicians in the hopes of determining which design features optimize its usability. This prototype will be based on a clinical practice guideline produced by the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care, which will be distributed to select primary care clinics in Ontario.

TitreApplicationTitle: Évaluation et validation du score de propension à hautes dimensions dans le cadre d'études observationnelles
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATABASES; DISCRETE EVENT SIMULATION; DRUG RESEARCH; METHODOLOGY; PHARMACO-EPIDEMIOLOGY; UNMEASURED CONFOUNDER
Abstract-Résumé: Les etudes observationnelles se basent principalement sur les donnees presentent dans les banques de donnees medico-administratives. Les etudes observationnelles sont utilisees pour repondre a des questions de recherche portant sur l'avenement d'evenements rares, lorsque les evenements arrivent apres de longues periodes d'exposition ou lorsque la randomisation n'est pas ethique. Cependant, plusieurs facteurs confondants ne sont pas enregistres dans ces banques de donnees (le poids, bio-marqueurs, etc.). L'impact de ces facteurs confondants non-enregistres pourrait aussi dependre du devis d'analyse utilise.  Plus specifiquement, j'examinerai la problematique entourant l'association entre l'utilisation de contraceptifs oraux (CO) et les thromboses veineuses. Plusieurs groupes ont examine cette problematique grace a des etudes observationnelles mais ont obtenus des resultats divergents. L'utilisation de differents devis d'analyses epidemiologiques et le fait que plusieurs facteurs confondants ne sont pas enregistres dans les banques de donnees medico-administratives utilisees pourraient expliquer cette divergence dans les resultats obtenus.  Mon projet de recherche visera a simuler une cohorte de patientes exposees a differents niveaux d'expositions de CO et d'enregistrer les donnees obtenues dans un format similaire a celui disponible dans les banques de donnees medico-administratives. Par la suite, les donnees seront analysees selon differents devis d'analyses epidemiologiques utilises dans le cadre d'etudes observationnelles. Les resultats seront compares entre eux afin de comprendre et quantifier l'impact du devis d'analyse et des facteurs confondants sur les resultats des etudes observationnelles.  Mon projet ameliorera les connaissances dans ce domaine frequemment utilise en Sante Publique et par les decideurs gouvernementaux ou les agences regulatrices en Sante et permettra une utilisation plus appropriee des etudes observationnelles dans le futur.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTOR PROTEINS; ADP-RIBOSYLATION FACTOR 1; EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; GROWTH RECEPTOR BINDING PROTEIN 2; INVASIVE BREAST CANCER; RAS ACTIVATION; RECEPTOR SIGNALLING CASCADES; SMALL GTPASES; SRC HOMOLOGY 2 DOMAIN-CONTAINING PROTEIN; SRC KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer in North American women, with 1 in 9 women being diagnosed with invasive breast cancer some time during her lifetime. The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) has been shown to play an important role in the initiation and progression of breast cancer. While current therapies targeting the EGFR are successfully being used in the treatment of breast cancer, many patients are resistant to its actions. Therefore, it is essential to develop other means of targeting the EGFR. We propose that the protein ARF1 may represent a novel target to diminish the activities of EGFR. We have shown that ARF1 plays an important role in the growth of cancer cells and in metastasis and that these actions are dependent on the EGFR. The current work will focus on further characterizing the role of ARF1 in breast cancer and lead to the discovery of novel diagnostic and therapeutic tools that may be used in the treatment of breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Contribution of Cognitive Bias and Memory Processes to the Positive Symptoms of Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: EARLY INTERVENTION; PERSONALITY; PSYCHOSIS; RISK FACTORS; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SCHIZOTYPY
Abstract-Résumé: Despite its low prevalence of 1%, schizophrenia accounts for upwards of $6 billion in lost productivity and health care costs. The longer the illness goes untreated, the poorer the prognosis becomes. Thus, it is important to identify individuals at high risk early on so that they may benefit from preventative interventions. Schizotypy refers to non-clinical traits which are present in the general population but signify an increased genetic vulnerability to schizophrenia. Schizotypy and schizophrenia are characterized by shared characteristics and can be conceptualized as being on the same continuum. Thus, schizotypy is valuable for probing the mechanisms involved in the progression of personality traits to the pathology of schizophrenia. We aim to see whether people with schizotypal personality traits show impairments on tasks that engage mechanisms impaired in individuals with schizophrenia. These impairments are linked to the formation and maintenance of delusions. We plan to test their memory and judgment and to track performance on all tasks every 6 months over 4 years. We expect to find a relationship between performance on memory and judgment tasks and performance on the cognitive tasks that tap into delusional thinking. We plan to compare the performance of those schizotypal individuals who go on to develop psychosis against those who do not, to better understand the ways in which deficits can combine to subtly erode cognition and gradually form pathological thought. Another important feature of this study is the ethnic composition of our sample. Our sample will be drawn from a multiethnic university campus with a high proportion of immigrants who are particularly vulnerable to developing psychosis. Our findings will be applicable to a particularly vulnerable group and hold great promise for early identification of high-risk individuals. Our findings can also be used to develop more effective cognitive behavioral interventions for treatment of delusions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of metabolic stress on pancreatic islet death and dysfunction, and their role in islet transplantation failure.
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CELL DEATH; CELL IMAGING; CELL SIGNALING; DIABETES; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IL-1BETA; ISLET TRANSPLANTATION; METABOLISM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 Diabetes mellitus is a serious disorder that results from the destruction of the insulin secreting cells of the body. The current treatment for this disease consists of the administration of insulin injections. Insulin injections, however, cannot accurately control blood glucose levels in all patients, and may still result in the development of high blood glucose-induced complications. The results of current treatment, therefore, are both painful and costly. In recent years, transplantation of the tissues that contain insulin-secreting cells, known as islet transplantation, has emerged as a long-term treatment for type 1 diabetes. Islet transplantation is able to provide insulin-independence to most recipients, and more importantly, islet transplantation has been shown to improve blood glucose levels when compared to conventional therapies. Despite these advancements, less than 10% of islet transplant recipients remain insulin independent after 5 years, indicating a failure of the transplant. This failure of islet transplants was traditionally attributed to immune-mediated destruction of the transplant, yet the ability of the transplants to fail in the absence of an immune-mediated has been demonstrated. These findings have lead to the suggestion that other factors may be responsible for the failure of the islet transplants. Recently, high blood sugars and fats have been shown to induce islet death and reduce insulin secretion. These factors can increase inflammation, and may be able to induce immune-mediated destruction of the transplant. We plan to determine whether high blood sugars and fats, known as metabolic stress, are required for, or complicit in, the long-term loss of islet transplants. In particular, we will examine which part of the islets are affected by metabolic stress, and identify potential drug targets which could be used pre-, post-, or co-transplantation to delay, or possibly prevent, future islet transplant failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of insulin in regulating immune responses in type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE TISSUE; CYTOKINE; FLOW CYTOMETRY; IMMUNO-METABOLISM; INFLAMMATION; INSULIN; MOUSE MODEL; REGULATORY T CELL; SIGNALING; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: The obesity linked type 2 diabetes (T2D) accounts for 90% of the 346 million cases of diabetes worldwide, a staggering number that will continue to rise. The long-term consequences of T2D include an increased risk of heart attacks, strokes, amputation, kidney failure and blindness. This disease is a major burden to the health care system and the well-being of Canadians, and a better treatment is needed. T2D happens when the body loses the ability to respond to insulin, a hormone that is needed for the body to absorb sugars as source of energy. As a result, the body cannot maintain normal blood sugar levels. Interestingly, there is also increased inflammation in T2D, especially in the fat. T2D patients are continually exposed to high levels of insulin, from diet or from the over-production of insulin. We think that the exposure to high levels of insulin in T2D inhibits the anti-inflammatory function of regulatory T cells (Tregs), a type of immune cells that can suppress unwanted inflammation. The inhibition of Treg function then leads to excessive inflammation, which makes insulin resistance worse. If this idea is true, this research will lead to a deeper understanding of the close link between T2D and the immune system. Next, we will also explore whether we can use the immune system to fight T2D. We will study if Tregs would make an effective therapy for T2D since they have the ability to both suppress inflammation and reduce insulin resistance. Overall, the research results obtained here may lead to a new treatment for T2D and have a significant impact on the quality of life and well-being of many Canadians that suffer from T2D.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Examination of the Variability of Sleep and Fatigue in those With and Without Insomnia
Keywords-MotsClés: FATIGUE; INSOMNIA; SLEEP; STABILITY; VARIABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Insomnia is a devastating disorder which is associated with significant nighttime as well as daytime impairments. In particular, fatigue is the most prominent daytime complaint among people with insomnia. While studies have found a positive association between sleep and fatigue in poor sleepers, it remains unclear how the sleep disturbance and daytime fatigue are interrelated. One possibility to further understand this relationship would be to examine the variability, or the day-to-day fluctuations, of poor sleep and fatigue. For example, we can determine whether daytime fatigue reliably follows a poor night of sleep, or whether levels of fatigue are not dependent on the previous night's sleep. By exploring the temporal fluctuations among these two constructs, we can understand whether poor sleep and daytime fatigue occur in accordance with one another over time, or whether they are relatively independent phenomena. The objective of my doctoral research is to examine the variability of the relationship between sleep and fatigue among people with insomnia and a good sleeper comparison group. To this end, I will collect two weeks worth of sleep and fatigue data, as well as data on relevant cognitive constructs. Collecting data from both those with and without insomnia will allow for between-group comparisons. The findings from this study can help to improve and inform fatigue-related adjuncts to insomnia treatments. For example, if it is found that reports of daytime fatigue are relatively independent of poor sleep among those with insomnia, this finding can help to invalidate the myth that poor sleep causes fatigue. By understanding that other factors, aside from poor sleep, may have a stronger impact on daytime fatigue, insomnia sufferers may alleviate some of the burden they put on their sleep, which would thus reduce sleep-related anxiety and help improve their overall functioning.

TitreApplicationTitle: Economic impact of spondyloarthropathies: estimates from the DESIR cohort of patients with early, undifferentiated spondyloarthropathy
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; COST-EFFECTIVENESS; DIRECT COSTS; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; OPTIMAL MANAGEMENT; QUALITY OF LIFE; RHEUMATOLOGY; SPONDYLOARTHROPATHIES; WORK PRODUCTIVITY LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: Spondyloarthropathies (SpAs) are a group of chronic, inflammatory diseases that cause significant disability and diminished quality of life. Studies show that SpAs such as ankylosing spondylitis (AS) and psoriatic arthritis (PsA) come with high costs to society, stemming from intensive health care use (direct costs) and work productivity loss (indirect costs). However, there are few data on long term costs among patients with early SpA symptoms, which can evolve to various forms of the disease. To improve patient care and minimize health care costs, there is a need to identify predictors of elevated costs among patients with different forms of SpAs, and to know how different treatment practices affect costs over time, as treatments may be cost effective if they reduce long term health care use and work disability. The DESIR cohort is a group of 708 patients in France who have early SpA symptoms, such that doctors are unsure which SpA will develop. This study will analyze data from the DESIR study as patients are followed over time to 1) estimate the cost of SpAs in the first two years of symptoms, 2) identify predictors of increased costs, and 3) determine the cost-effectiveness of optimal SpA management, i.e., the best available treatment defined by the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR).  Costs will be calculated from the societal perspective, describing costs by category (direct versus indirect costs), by payer type (public health insurance versus private), and the distribution of costs over time. The associations between costs and patient, disease, and treatment characteristics will be explored using multivariate regression analyses. The cost effectiveness of optimal SpA management will be estimated using EULAR guidelines and quality of life data from DESIR. The total costs and quality adjusted life years of both groups will be calculated and adjusted for confounders, and incremental cost effectiveness ratios will be calculated and defined.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the Risk of Adverse Events following Recommended Pediatric Vaccinations in the General Population and Vulnerable Subgroups of Children in Ontario, Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE EVENTS FOLLOWING IMMUNIZATION; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; METABOLIC PROFILING; NEWBORN SCREENING; PEDIATRIC VACCINE SAFETY; POPULATION HEALTH; SELF-CONTROLLED CASE SERIES MODEL; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research will focus on the analysis of adverse events following immunization (AEFI) for Ontario children during the first two years of life.  Adverse events of interest will include overall measures of health services utilization (e.g. emergency room (ER) visits, hospital admissions,visits to a family doctor) and specific types of adverse events, such as fever, seizures brought on by high fever, swelling and inflammation.  Ontario health administrative data and newborn screening data will be used to identify vulnerable subgroups of children, such as those with diseases affecting metabolism, children with birth defects, or children from low income families, and explore whether these children are at increased risk of experiencing AEFIs.  We will also use the newborn screening results for each child, which include the concentrations of  numerous important metabolic factors, to develop statistical models to see if we can predict which children are most likely to experience AEFIs.  The proposed research could lead to a better understanding of which children are most likely to experience AEFIs, potentially leading to changes to recommended immunization schedule in subgroups of children identified as being at higher risk.  This could lead to the avoidance of  many AEFIs in vulnerable children. Our work could also lead to a better system of AEFI surveillance in general for Ontario allowing timely detection of problems with new vaccines after they are introduced, and a better understanding of the timing and nature of AEFIs experienced by Ontario children, and their impact on health services utilization.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the role of DJ-1 in Parkinson's disease: Role of VDAC1
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; DJ-1; MITOCHONDRIA; NEURODEGENERATION; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; TRANSGENIC MODELS; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disease, is characterized by resting tremors, slowness in execution of movement, and rigidity of limbs. This disease is defined by the loss of a specific set of neurons in the brain.  The connection between oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and PD was made over 20 years ago and continues to grow stronger with recent findings.  Although the majority of PD cases are sporadic, there is a small percentage of cases that are inherited genetically.  DJ-1 is one of several genes that, when mutated, cause PD.  Previous reports indicate that DJ-1 goes to mitochondria to help handle oxidative stress however how DJ-1 does this is unknown.  Our preliminary data suggests that a mitochondrial protein involved in regulated cell death called voltage dependent anion channel (VDAC) as well as two other PD-linked genes - Parkin and Pink1 - are involved in the signalling pathway that causes DJ-1 to go to mitochondria.  We believe that during times of increased oxidative stress DJ-1 goes to the mitochondria in response to a signal possibly from VDAC.  This movement to mitochondria also seems to be dependent upon the presence of both Parkin and Pink1, both of which have been demonstrated to maintain mitochondrial health during stress.  Determining how DJ-1 helps protect cells against cell death, specifically at the mitochondria, will help understand why cells die in PD.  Understanding why neurons in PD die will help improve treatment options and will lead to a cure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Disentangling the neural circuitry and neurochemistry of cognitive effort in rodent models of cost/benefit decision-making
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CHEMICAL LESIONS; COGNITIVE EFFORT; COST/BENEFIT DECISION MAKING; DECISION MAKING; DOPAMINE; EFFORT; INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES; NEUROANATOMICAL INACTIVATIONS; PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: We are constantly confronted with decisions involving both benefits and associated costs.  One such type of decision involves whether we should exert effort in order to obtain a reward.  We may choose to be lazy, expending minimal energy or resources for a minimal reward, or we may choose to work for a greater reward.  Understanding the neural basis of mental effort may provide new therapeutic targets for illnesses such as depression and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, where lack of motivation and poor effort strategies can hinder decision-making.  A substantial body of research has revealed a circuit of brain structures involved in effort decision-making; when these structures are damaged, some patients have reported losing their sense of mental strain altogether.  Rats with similar brain damage no longer exert a greater physical effort (such as climbing a barrier or pressing a lever multiple times) for a greater reward, though their ability to perform such effortful tasks is unaffected.  To date, animal models of effort decision-making have only involved tasks that differed in the level of physical investment required, whereas most human studies utilize tasks where cognitive effort is varied.  A novel animal model has been designed by Dr. Catharine Winstanley's laboratory to probe decision-making involving cognitive effort.  Rats can choose either an easy task where the potential reward (sugar) is small or a hard task where the potential reward is large.  Using this task, we will examine three aspects of decision-making: the brain structures and neurochemistry that underlie mental effort, the relationship between cognitive and physical effort (i.e. if are they the same, in terms of the brain), and finally some of the biological differences between hard-working and "lazy" animals. This research may provide insight into treating the compromised decision-making that a significant number of patients live with daily.

TitreApplicationTitle: L'importance de la chymase dans l'activité du système des endothélines, en présence ou en absence d'athérosclérose, chez la souris
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSE; CHYMASE; ENDOTHELINE; PRESSION ARTERIELLE; RECEPTEURS DE L'ENDOTHELINE; SOURIS GENETIQUEMENT MODIFIEE
Abstract-Résumé: L'endotheline-1 (ET-1) est le plus puissant vasoconstricteur connu chez les mammiferes. Sa voie de synthese la plus connue implique le clivage d'un precurseur, la Big-Endotheline-1 (38 acides amines) par l'enzyme de conversion de l'endotheline (ECE), ce qui donne l'ET-1 (21 acides amines). Plus recemment, il a ete demontre qu'une autre enzyme, la chymase, clive la Big-ET-1 en un autre peptide, l'ET-1 (1-31) (31 acides amines). Celui-ci n'a aucune activite demontree in vivo. Il doit subir un autre clivage, par l'endopeptidase neutre (NEP), pour donner l'ET-1 biologiquement actif. L'importance physiologique de cette voie n'a cependant pas ete etudiee en detail. Notre laboratoire a rapporte recemment que le blocage pharmacologique de la chymase diminue de facon importante l'activite du precurseur, la Big ET-1, chez la souris (Simard et al, 2009). Notre laboratoire s'est penche sur la protease mastocytaire 4 (mMCP-4). Des similarites entre la chymase humaine et la mMCP-4 sont deja connues, entre autres dans la synthese d'un autre vasoconstricteur, l'angiotensine-II (Ang-II). La mMCP-4 joue aussi un role dans l'atherosclerose (Bot et al, 2011). Notre but est de determiner le role de la mMCP-4 dans la biologie de l'ET-1 chez la souris saine ou souffrant d'atherosclerose. Notre hypothese est que la mMCP-4 joue un role important dans la synthese de l'ET-1 chez la souris en sante, et encore plus chez la souris souffrant d'atherosclerose, une situation inflammatoire ou la mMCP-4 est augmentee. Nous pensons que la mMCP-4 contribue au role atherosclerotique de l'ET-1. Nous croyons que ce projet permettra de mieux comprendre une nouvelle cible medicamenteuse potentielle, la chymase, dans le traitement de plusieurs maladies cardiovasculaires, comme l'atherosclerose. L'inhibition de la chymase permettrait de bloquer a la fois la production d'Ang-II et d'ET-1, et ce de maniere plus ciblee au lieu d'inflammation pathologique.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiovascular autonomic control in acute spinal cord injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ARRHYTHMIA; AUTONOMIC DYSREFLEXIA; AUTONOMIC NERVOUS SYTEM; BLOOD PRESSURE; BLOOD PRESSURE REGULATION; CARDIOVASCULAR; HEART RATE; HEART RATE VARIABILITY; ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Around 86,000 Canadians are living with the devastating consequences of spinal cord injury (SCI). In addition to loss of movement and sensation, many individuals with SCI have abnormal control of blood pressure and heart rate. This can lead to alternating periods of extremely high and low blood pressure, as well as irregular heartbeats, which can lead to unpleasant heart palpitations. Many people with SCI will experience these potentially life-threatening problems on a daily basis.   Damage to cardiovascular nerves in the spinal cord is the likely cause of these problems. However, it is difficult to assess how severely these nerves have been affected. Another concern is that cardiovascular problems after SCI change with time, making their treatment and management difficult.   I will measure the severity of injury to cardiovascular nerves in the spinal cord from non-invasive measurements of the normal variations in blood pressure and heart rate. These variations are due to changes in the nervous control of the heart and blood pressure; therefore, they provide information about how well the nerves are working. Risk factors for irregular heartbeats as well as episodes of high and low blood pressure will also be determined. I will take cardiovascular measurements five times in the first year after SCI and will also administer a questionnaire at each visit. This will enable us to track how the cardiovascular system is changing with time after injury, and how this impacts cardiovascular symptoms that individuals with SCI experience.  This project will help build a complete picture of the cardiovascular problems that occur after SCI, and how they change with time after injury. This will be important for future development of treatments to improve cardiovascular problems in people living with SCI. Ultimately, this study will help improve quality of life for individuals with SCI.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Value of HPV Genotyping in Cervical Cancer Screening
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER SCREENING; CERVICAL CANCER; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: It is now well established that human papillomavirus (HPV) is a necessary cause of cervical cancer and the most common sexually transmitted infection (STI) worldwide. Additionally, most sexually active women will acquire HPV infection in their lifetime. While the vast majority of these infections will be transient, a fraction of them will become persistent and may lead to pre-cancerous lesions. Detection of these lesions through screening is critical to the prevention of cervical cancer. While screening approaches have largely relied on Papanicolaou cytology (i.e., the Pap test), molecular techniques detecting HPV DNA have shown greater sensitivity in identifying cervical cancer and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). However, the value of qualitatively defining HPV genotypes in cervical specimens, in addition to determining HPV positivity, remains unclear. In an attempt to better prioritize case management and inform risk stratification procedures, we plan to examine whether determining the HPV genotype (via a PCR assay) in cervical specimens helps predict current and future risk of high-grade CIN in primary screening more accurately than simply testing for HPV infection with oncogenic types (via the Hybrid Capture 2 test). This study will use data and samples gathered from the Canadian Cervical Cancer Screening Trial (CCCaST), a CIHR-funded randomized controlled trial that compared the relative efficacy of HPV and Pap testing in primary screening for cervical cancer precursors in Montreal and St. John's, Canada. The proposed study will generate new knowledge regarding the value of HPV DNA testing in primary care screening, and assist the formulation of evidence-based practice guidelines for cervical cancer screening in Canada and elsewhere.

TitreApplicationTitle: The social-structural production of drug use-related health risk among street-involved non-injection illicit drug users
Keywords-MotsClés: NON-INJECTION DRUG USE; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH METHODS; QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH METHODS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SUBSTANCE USE; VULNERABLE/MARGINALIZED POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Numerous studies have identified injection drug use as a risk factor for the transmission of blood-borne viruses such as HIV and hepatitis C (HCV). Recently, however, research has shown that street-involved non-injection drug users also have high prevalence rates of HIV and HCV infection. Non-injection drug use (particularly crack smoking) appears to be a risk factor for blood-borne virus infection, suggesting a direct association between non-injection drug use and HIV and HCV. Despite this, research on, and public health interventions aimed at, non-injection drug use are lacking. This study will examine social and structural factors that influence and shape the drug use and related health risk behaviours of non-injection drug users.  This will be a mixed methods study, using quantitative and in-depth qualitative interviews to collect data from three types of street-involved drug users: 1) those who have never injected, 2) those who formerly injected but no longer do so, 3) those who use drugs by both injection and non-injection methods. Comparison of these 3 forms of drug use will allow for a better understanding of factors and behaviours specifically associated with non-injection drug use.  This research has direct and important implications for both public health and health policy. By better understanding how social and structural factors shape the drug use and subsequent health of non-injection drug users, this research will help guide the development of targeted prevention and treatment interventions for non-injection drug users. Further, this research will crucially draw attention to the health inequalities faced by the most vulnerable and marginalized people in our society. The proposed research will also provide evidenced-based input for a public health approach to substance use and addiction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innovative Knowledge Translation Methodologies and Interventions to Enhance Youth Mental Health
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY HEALTH; EFFECTIVENESS STUDIES; FOCUS GROUPS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTAL HEALTH PROMOTION; MIXED METHODS; PUBLIC HEALTH; QUALITATIVE INTERVIEWS; SOCIAL NETWORK ANALYSIS; SURVEY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: In recent years, the importance of effectively sharing research findings with knowledge users (e.g. practitioners, general public, policy makers), a process termed knowledge translation, has been identified as a priority and viewed as critical to improving health outcomes. However, most of the research in this area has focused on developing strategies to share clinically relevant knowledge, with inadequate attention given to the needs of those seeking to improve population-level health outcomes through work in community settings. This study will address this knowledge gap through the development and assessment of an innovative strategy aimed at sharing research findings to target what the World Health Organization has recently identified as the most significant health problem facing young people today, mental health issues. This study will utilize Dialogue Workshops, an intervention in which youth and adults are brought together in community settings to discuss contemporary health and social issues. In these Dialogue Workshops, research evidence about youths' experiences of emotional distress (e.g., stress, anxiety, depression) will be shared. It is believed that creating a venue for youth and adults to come together to discuss youth's experiences with emotional distress will help to foster connectedness and empathy towards adolescents' experiences; two factors shown to promote mental health outcomes in youth. The effectiveness of this intervention will be assessed using novel research techniques to track the spread of knowledge gained through participation in the Dialogue Workshops within the community. Additionally, factors that foster mental health will be measured. This study will contribute new understandings and guidance for those involved in community-based knowledge translation and will provide evidence for a strategy aimed at promoting the mental health of Canadian youth.

Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL INFECTION; CROHN'S DISEASE; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; MONONUCLEAR PHAGOCYTES; MUCOSAL IMMUNITY; NOD-LIKE RECEPTORS; NOD1 AND NOD2; SALMONELLA TYPHIMURIUM
Abstract-Résumé: Nod-like receptors (NLRs) belong to a family of intracellular receptors that recognize specific patterns on pathogens and restrict bacterial infection in the gut. Nod1 and Nod2, two NLR family members, have been implicated in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD); in particular Nod2's association with Crohn's disease, yet a clear understanding of how dysfunctional Nod activation leads to aberrant inflammation is still lacking.  The lamina propria (LP) of the gut is the tissue just underneath the epithelial cell layer. Mononuclear phagocytes (MPs) within the LP are key orchestrators of tolerance and inflammation, but the role of Nod proteins in these pathways is undefined. I am studying a particular class of MPs that present CX3CR1 molecules on their cell surface. Compared to mice that have CX3CR1, mice that lack CX3CR1 are more susceptible to colitis caused by bacterial infection. Also mice which lack the Nod proteins have fewer MPs expressing CX3CR1 in the infected cecum. This supports the idea that CX3CR1 MPs play a role in defense of the gut barrier by a mechanism that is dependent on Nod proteins. My goal is to understand how Nod proteins control the development of inflammation by regulating the function of these MPs within the LP. I want to determine whether signals from the epithelial cells to recruit MPs to the LP are dependent on Nods. I also want to determine using microscopy where the MPs are recruited in relation to the bacteria, and whether they engulf the bacteria after infection. All together, I hope to get a clear picture of how Nods might regulate the MP cell population, which is thought to be the first line of defense against microorganisms that have broken the epithelial barrier. I hope that my research reveals how modulation of Nod function might provide a means for controlling intestinal inflammation, like in IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Ethnographic Approach to Examining the Health Equity Impacts of Medical Tourism
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADA; GLOBAL HEALTH; HEALTH EQUITY; INDIA; MEDICAL TOURISM; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Medical tourism (MT) involves patients' privately purchased and arranged travel across national borders in order to access medical care. It is consistently speculated that patients' travel from more-developed nations such as Canada to developing nations is creating and/or exacerbating health inequities in destination countries. Evidence that clearly demonstrates this is, however, lacking. Meanwhile, supporters of the highly privatized MT industry claim that it can lessen health inequities through enhancing medical resources and bringing in revenues. Evidence that this indeed happens is also lacking. My PhD research will address this pressing knowledge gap through examining the on-the-ground health equity impacts, both positive and negative, of the MT industry in Delhi, India.  To accomplish this I will undertake extensive field research in Delhi, which will involve conducting observations at key MT sites and interviewing stakeholders. India is a global leader in the MT industry and Canadian patients are known to privately purchase medical care there, including in Delhi's numerous large MT hospitals. The findings of my research will offer important evidence that can be used to support or refute key aspects of the health equity debates that surround the global health services practice of MT. As Canada and many other nations that are home to medical tourists are signatories to international declarations aiming to instill health and health equity globally, the findings of this study will also help health policy makers in patients' home countries to ensure that these normative and legal obligations are being met, rather than undermined, by enforcing an equitable, ethical, and safe MT industry and practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Notch ligands in intravenous immunoglobulin-mediated induction of regulatory events
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; ASTHMA; IMMUNE MODULATION; IMMUNOGLOBULINS; NOTCH LIGANDS; REGULATORY T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), a blood product made from human antibodies derived from donor plasma, is an effective treatment for many severe inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. We do not understand exactly why or how it works in many conditions. Understanding the precise "whys" of how the treatment works will allow for better treatment options, because it will be able to be prescribed for those conditions that most warrant it. Furthermore, synthetic drugs that do the same things as IVIg may be developed with this knowledge. We have discovered a potential explanation for how IVIg works, by acting on immune system cells called dendritic cells to change how they activate other parts of the immune system. By examining how IVIg affects specific molecules on the dendritic cells known as Notch ligands, we will be able to comprehend how to tailor the anti-inflammatory response obtained by treatment, allowing for better therapies for inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of Sphingomyelin Phosphodiesterase 3-Mediated Regulation of Bone Mineralization
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BONE MINERALIZATION; DEVELOPMENT OF SKELETAL TISSUE; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Bones and teeth are hard tissues, the usual sites for physiologic mineral accumulation. These mineralized tissues protect the internal soft organs, help in locomotion, facilitate food processing and more importantly serve as a reservoir for essential mineral ions required for proper body functions. A poor hard tissue mineralization, as seen in rickets, might cause a serious health concern, while soft tissue mineralization in diseases like osteoarthritis is an undesirable event. The long-term goal of this proposal is to identify novel mechanisms regulating tissue mineralization. Towards this goal, I plan to characterize a mouse model, which shows severely under-mineralized bones and teeth. Recently, a genetic mutation in this model has been identified. This mutation in the sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 gene (Smpd3) results in a nonfunctional enzyme involved in the metabolism of several fat-soluble functional molecules. Small fat soluble molecules through complex mechanisms can regulate many cell functions. One such molecule is phosphocholine, which is generated by SMPD3, the enzyme mutated in our mouse model. In this study, I will use diet-based and genetic approaches to investigate the role of phosphocholine in bone mineralization. I believe this work might provide clues to a novel mechanism regulating the mineralization process in our body. Unveiling such mechanisms should eventually identify new therapeutic targets and improve the management of human pathologic conditions related to abnormal tissue mineralization.

TitreApplicationTitle: Social Networks and Health: From Concepts to Intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; GLOBAL HEALTH; HEALTH POLICY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MEDICAL SOCIOLOGY; NETWORK ANALYSIS; PUBLIC HEALTH; STATISTICAL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Individuals are connected, and so too is their health. But despite robust evidence of a relationship between social structure and health, the mechanisms whereby each influences the other remain poorly understood. Chronic stress has been proposed as a process through which unfavorable social positions produce poor health outcomes, but interventions to reduce such disparities will demand a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms. Meanwhile, mathematical models predict that the efficacy and adoption of many public health interventions could be radically enhanced by harnessing the distributive powers of social networks, but the idea has yet to be tested in the real world. In two parallel projects, I aim first to develop new methods to uncover the causal pathways between social structure and disease, then to translate these concepts into novel interventions to improve population health.  A first project investigates the relationship between social network position and biochemical markers of chronic stress. By tracking the evolution of both biomarkers and network position for thousands of individuals, we aim to test the hypothesis that the effects of social structure on individual health are mediated through cumulative stress, and that these effects can be tracked in dynamic populations with network-theoretic and biochemical methods. My research is ultimately motivated by a desire to translate novel theory and evidence into more effective policy and interventions, and in a second project I am leading an interdisciplinary team in designing the first controlled trial of network-optimized public health interventions. By introducing interventions to individuals occupying network positions theorized to accelerate the dissemination of information and behaviour change, we will test the hypothesis that tailoring public health interventions to local network structure can enhance the spread and adoption of those interventions and thereby improve population health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation and Function of Periostin in the Development of Gingival Fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA AND PROTEIN ARRAYS; DRUG SIDE-EFFECT; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; FIBROBLAST; FIBROSIS; GINGIVAL OVERGROWTH; GUM; HISTOLOGY; MATRICELLULAR PROTEIN; PERIOSTIN
Abstract-Résumé: All connective tissues are composed of cells and extracellular matrix (ECM), the basic building blocks of the tissues. The cells regulate the amount of extracellular matrix by only adding new matrix when old is destroyed. However, in some diseases, the balance of matrix production and destruction is skewed leading to an overall increase of matrix. This is known as fibrosis, which is described as an uncontrollable growth of a tissue that results in functional impairment. Our research is focused on drug-induced gingival fibrosis (DIGF), which is an overgrowth of gum tissue that is common in patients taking nifedipine and phenytoin, which are drugs for cardiovascular disease and epilepsy treatments, respectively. DIGF causes tooth displacement, speech impairment, breathing difficulties, and in severe cases, results in the teeth loss. The only treatment is surgical removal, but DIGF often recurs. Therefore, new treatments need to be discovered. However, the drugs' effect on the cells and growth of the tissue are not understood. It is currently suggested that the overgrowth in gingival ECM results from inducing gingival fibroblasts to differentiate into contractile myofibroblasts which subsequently results in greater matrix production. Our preliminary findings showed greater myofibroblasts in DIGF patient samples compared to healthy patients. Evidences suggest that periostin, a recently classified matricellular protein, controls myofibroblast differentiation. We have already shown that periostin is upregulated in DIGF tissues compared to healthy tissues. However, the role of periostin in the development and progression of DIGF has not yet been established. Our hypothesis is that periostin is upregulated by nifedipine and phenytoin in gingival tissues where it mediates fibroblast-myofibroblast differentiation. The aim of this project is to investigate whether periostin could be a novel therapeutic target to prevent DIGF.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural, mechanistic and inhibitory analysis of the NDM-1 metallo-beta-lactamase from newly arisen superbug bacteria
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; BETA LACTAM ANTIBIOTICS; BETA-LACTAMASE; ENZYME KINETICS; ENZYME MECHANISMS; INHIBITOR DISCOVERY / DESIGN; SITE DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; SUPERBUG BACTERIA; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Beta-lactam antibiotics such as the penicillins and cephalosporin's are the largest class of clinically used antibiotics and have had a major impact on human health.  However, so-called superbug bacteria have arisen that display complete resistance to all antibiotics. For beta-lactam antibiotics, the most important resistance mechanism is the expression of beta-lactamase enzymes capable of hydrolyzing the lactam ring.  This activity renders the antibiotic useless against its usual target (the cell-wall cross linking enzymes known as transpeptidases). Recently, a novel metallo-beta lactamase called NDM-1 has been discovered in enteric bacteria that displays broad spectrum antibiotic resistance.  This enzyme poses a serious threat, as there are currently no antibiotics available that can inhibit it. Therefore, the goal of this proposal is to characterize novel NDM-1 inhibitory compounds. Inhibitors discovered using a high throughput screening as well as a recently characterized class of potentially "universal" beta-lactamase inhibitors will be analyzed in complex with the NDM-1 protein. Crystallographic and kinetic analysis will facilitate the characterization of these inhibited enzyme complexes. Taken together, the proposed research will provide structural, mechanistic and kinetic insight into an enzyme that poses a serious threat to human health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autobiographical memory in schizophrenia: A virtual reality investigation
Keywords-MotsClés: DELUSIONS; MEMORY; PSYCHOSIS; RECOGNITION; SCHIZOPHRENIA; VIRTUAL REALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychiatric illness that typically emerges in late adolescence/early adulthood and costs an estimated $7 billion Canadian dollars each year. Although major improvements have been made towards the treatment of certain symptoms associated with schizophrenia (e.g., hallucinations), other areas including cognition remain negatively impacted. Of particular importance in schizophrenia are memory impairments for every day, real life events. The study of real life, every day memory, however, has posed a major obstacle to researchers in that they have been unable to determine the veracity of patients' personal memories. Consequently, it is possible that researchers to date have been studying accounts of events that are only loosely based on reality. In the proposed study, we will assess memory for real life events in a virtual reality environment, in which we are able to control each aspect of the participants' experiences. Virtual reality has proven its usefulness in the treatment of anxiety disorders as well as in the investigation of spatial memory, and is well suited to studying memory for real life events. By furthering our understanding of how patients with schizophrenia remember the events they experience, I plan to inform the design of new treatment strategies or early intervention programs to ensure that patients feel a consistent sense of self, improving their functioning in the real world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of 20-HETE in pathological vasoconstriction following cortical spreading depression
Keywords-MotsClés: 20-HETE; CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW; SPREADING DEPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Cortical spreading depression (CSD) is a slowly propagating wave of brain cell depolarization that occurs in neurological disorders such as migraine, stroke, and traumatic brain injury.  Experimental and clinical evidence suggest that blood flow in the brain is decreased following CSD, and may contribute to the pathologies associated with CSD.  However, the mechanisms underlying blood flow changes after CSD are unclear.  Preliminary data show that the level of 20-HETE, a molecule that causes blood vessels to constrict, increases after CSD.  Therefore we hypothesize that changes in 20-HETE levels may contribute to changes in blood flow following CSD.  The aim of this study is to further characterize 20-HETE production and its pathophysiological role in CSD, using a combination of pharmacological, biochemical, and imaging techniques in both brain slices and intact preparations.  We will chemically induce CSD in the brain, and monitor changes in blood vessel diameter and blood flow as 20-HETE levels are manipulated.  The proposed study is anticipated to improve our understanding of the mechanisms involved in pathological changes in brain blood flow after CSD, facilitating the development of therapeutic approaches for various neurological conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the Anaphase Promoting Complex in regulating the DNA repair proteins Ataxia Telangiectasia Mutated and 53BP1
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; ATAXIA TELANGIECTASIA MUTATED; CANCER; CELL CYCLE; DNA REPAIR; KINASE; MITOTIC CHECKPOINT; PROTEASOME; RADIOTHERAPY; UBIQUITIN LIGASE
Abstract-Résumé: The Proteins Ataxia Telangiectasia Mutated (ATM) and 53BP1 are essential for repairing damaged DNA, especially in response to ionizing radiation, one of the most common forms of cancer therapy. Ionizing radiation is known to be most effective in killing cells during the division phase of the the cell cycle. However, the reasons are poorly understood. We hypothesize that ATM and 53BP1 are degraded during cell division, thus preventing DNA repair. We believe ATM and 53BP1 are targets of the Anaphase Promoting Complex (APC/C), which is a protein complex whose role is to degrade inhibitors of cell division. The objective of this research is to establish that these proteins are targets of the APC/C and then determine how this relates to the killing of cancer cells. We believe the results will have extensive implications for the treatment of cancer with radiotherapy and chemotherapy with DNA damaging drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Brain mechanisms underlying temporal fluctuations in spontaneous pain investigated with functional and structural MRI
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; FMRI; PAIN; TEMPOROMANDIBULAR DISORDER
Abstract-Résumé: Pain affects millions of Canadians on a daily basis, and associated treatment costs present a significant financial burden to our society. Chronic pain is difficult to control with available treatments, partly due to a lack of knowledge about underlying brain mechanisms. Many sufferers of chronic pain experience ongoing pain which can shift from high to low intensity and vice versa several times within a period of seconds or minutes. The goals of this research projectare to identify the brain mechanisms that explain why chronic pain is variable over time and why different chronic pain patients experience different patterns of fluctuations in pain intensity. Healthy volunteers as well as chronic pain patients with fibromyalgia and posttraumatic temporomandibular disorder will undergo functional MRI scans that measure blood flow and activation in the brain while their pain experience changes over time. The studyparticipants will also receive diffusion-weighted MRI and resting state functional MRI scans which, respectively, allow analyses of anatomical connections and functional relationships between brain areas. The studies will allow us to identify brain regions where activity changes before, during and after increases and decreases in pain. Furthermore, we will identify individual differences in brain connectivity that account for different patterns of pain experienced by different chronic pain patients. This research can provide brain region targets for chronic pain treatments, such as drugs, cognitive therapies or brain stimulation. Our studies of brain connectivity can inform the assessment of potential side effects of treatments (based on how targeting one brain region would impact other regions/functions) and can guide personalized medicine (based on individual differences in brain structure and function). Overall, the research can lead to reduced daily suffering of Canadians affected by chronic pain and reduced public health-related costs of pain.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse au doctorat - Bourse d'études supérieures du Canada Frederick Banting et Charles Best (BESC-D)

TitreApplicationTitle: Contribution of reperfusion therapy to ischemia/ reperfusion injury in acute myocardial infarction
Keywords-MotsClés: HEMORRHAGE; ISCHEMIA/ REPERFUSION INJURY; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MICROVASCULAR OBSTRUCTION; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Heart attacks are caused by blockages of arteries of the heart and are one of the most common causes of death in Canada. Powerful therapies aim at restoring blood flow and save tissue that it as risk but has not yet died, helping the patient to survive.  In up to two thirds of the patients, however, blood flow cannot be restored completely, although the re-opening of the blocked blood vessel is successful. This has a very strong negative impact on the patient's health and survival.   The reasons for this lack of blood flow are not yet fully understood. Animal studies have found bleeding within the heart as a contributor. Importantly, animal experiments also have shown that bleeding could increase the total damage that happens in a heart attack.  Until now, not much is known about the impact of bleeding into the heart. In my previous work, I developed a new imaging method. This allows us to see, for the first time, if there is a bleeding in the patient's heart, and if so, where exactly it is located and how much bleeding has occurred. To image the bleeding, we use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Other MRI methods were developed in the recent years. Together, they allow us to get a complete assessment of the injury that has occurred, including injury to the muscle cells of the heart, damage to the small blood vessels and inflammation.   In the proposed project I will use MRI to understand how and and when these different types of tissue injury occur, and how they influence each other. I will investigate tissue injury before and after heart attack therapy. We will learn, if and when bleeding occurred and how it changed the patients heart function, and possibly survival.   Knowledge obtained from this study will allow us to define tissue targets for new therapies and it will allow us to improve the therapies that we already have. Overall, this project may significantly improve the therapy and outcome of our patients with heart attacks.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pratiques parentales coercitives et fonctionnement du circuit neuronal de la peur chez des jeunes anxieux et en bonne santé
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYGDALA; ANXIETY; CHILDREN; CINGULATE GYRUS; FEAR CIRCUITRY; FMRI; HARSH PARENTING; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: Ce projet de recherche vise a mieux comprendre le fonctionnement cerebral des jeunes de 12 a 17 ans, en lien avec leurs niveaux d'anxiete et les pratiques parentales exercees par leurs meres.   Les troubles anxieux pediatriques peuvent etre grandement handicapants pour les jeunes qui en sont atteints et ont de fortes chances de perdurer a l'age adulte. Des resultats d'etudes precedentes montrent des liens entre l'adversite vecue tot dans l'enfance (par exemple, les pratiques parentales coercitives), le developpement de troubles anxieux, et des alterations du fonctionnement cerebral, plus particulierement au niveau de deux structures: l'amygdale et le gyrus cingulaire anterieur.  Bien que ces liens aient ete demontres chez l'adulte, tres peu d'etudes ont investigue cette problematique chez les jeunes. Pourtant, nous savons que puisque le cerveau n'est pas completement developpe a l'adolescence, son fonctionnement n'est pas necessairement le meme que chez l'adulte. Comprendre ce fontionnement et ses liens avec l'anxiete et l'adversite alors que les individus sont encore jeunes est crucial, afin d'identifier les jeunes a risque et de rapidement developper et implanter des interventions ciblees, avant que l'anxiete ne devienne chronique.  Afin de mieux comprendre ces liens, nous soumettons des jeunes anxieux ou non, dont les parents exercent ou non des pratiques parentales coercitives, a des taches validees de conditionnement et d'extinction de la peur, qui solicitent les structures cerebrales d'interet. Les jeunes effectuent les taches dans un scanner d'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle. Les activations cerebrales des quatre groupes de jeunes (anxiete elevee/mere coercitive, anxiete faible/mere coercitive, anxiete elevee/mere non coercitive, anxiete faible/ mere non coercitive)seront ensuite comparees.

TitreApplicationTitle: COPD exacerbations: Understanding the course of change and recovery in extra-pulmonary outcomes.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTERIAL STIFFNESS; BIOMARKERS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE; CYTOKINES; EXACERBATIONS; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) severely limits breathing and is the 5th cause of death worldwide. Inflammation drives COPD progression. Although inflammation is a protective response against harmful stimuli in the body, it becomes detrimental when present in high amounts. As COPD worsens, patients suffer from many other conditions especially heart disease. The health of COPD patients considerably deteriorates when they experience exacerbations. These events of significantly worsened respiratory symptoms enhance inflammation, and increase patient hospitalization and mortality.  It is thought that inflammation contributes to increased arterial stiffness, a measure of vascular health and indicator of heart disease, and increases patient risk of heart disease. Yet, little is known about the relationship between these two processes in COPD and there are no data on changes in arterial stiffness during COPD exacerbations. Therefore, it is not known whether vascular health decreases as a result of COPD exacerbations and contributes to a greater risk of cardiovascular events. This study will assess the extent to which inflammatory markers found in blood and measures of arterial stiffness change over time during COPD exacerbations. We will be evaluating 40 patients while they are stable, experiencing an exacerbation and as they recover from an exacerbation. Arterial stiffness will be measured using a specialized electrocardiogram and blood pressure sensor with the assistance of a cardiologist. To measure the amount of inflammatory markers, blood will be collected and inflammatory markers quantified using commercially available kits. This study will contribute novel knowledge about the link between heart disease and COPD. It will identify inflammatory and cardiovascular targets that could objectively characterize the progression of COPD exacerbations and that could be modified to slow the course of COPD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effets de la consommation d'acide alpha-linolénique sur l'inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: ACIDE ALPHA-LINOLENIQUE (ALA); CELLULES MONONUCLEAIRES PERIPHERIQUES SANGUINES (PBMC); CINETIQUE DE PROTEINES; CYTOKINES PROINFLAMMATOIRES; INFLAMMATION; METABOLISME; NUTRIGENOMIQUE; PROTEINE C-REACTIVE (CRP)
Abstract-Résumé: L'inflammation des arteres, tout comme le cholesterol, est maintenant reconnue comme un element cle dans la progression de la plupart des maladies du coeur. Il est bien connu que les matieres grasses, dont les acides gras omega-3, influencent de differentes facons les facteurs de risque des maladies du coeur comme l'inflammation. Les omega-3 peuvent etre de sources vegetales (ex : canola, lin) ou de sources marines (ex : poissons, crustaces). Differentes etudes suggerent que les omega-3 d'origine marine  pourraient attenuer l'inflammation et ainsi reduire le risque de maladies du coeur. Toutefois, l'impact des omega-3 d'origine vegetale sur l'inflammation est beaucoup moins connu. Il s'agit d'un point important dans le contexte ou les apports en poisson et en omega-3 qui en decoulent sont tres faibles dans la population. La consommation d'huiles vegetales riches en omega-3 pourrait alors s'averer des plus utiles en prevention des maladies du coeur. Le present projet vise donc a etudier les effets de la consommation d'omega-3 d'origine vegetale sur les marqueurs sanguins et les mecanismes de l'inflammation chez des sujets a risque de maladies du coeur. L'etude proposee permettra de mieux comprendre les processus par lesquels la consommation d'huiles riches en omega-3 d'origine vegetale exerce ses effets benefiques potentiels comparativement aux dietes nord-americaines traditionnelles.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the Airway Epithelial Inflammatory Response to Pseudomonas aeruginosa in Cystic Fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTATION; AIRWAY EPITHELIUM; BACTERIOLOGY; CHRONIC INFECTION; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; IMMUNOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA; RESPIRATORY FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: Pseudomonas aeruginosa lung infection is the leading cause of death in individuals with the genetic disease cystic fibrosis(CF). CF leads to excessive mucus secretion from airway epithelial cells (AECs) and inflammation in the lungs. Early in life, CF patients suffer with transient acute P. aeruginosa infections that can be cured by antibiotic treatment coupled with the patient's own innate immune system. By late adolescence, however, the lungs of most (~80%) CF patients are chronically infected with P. aeruginosa and this cannot be eradicated by any known therapy. Chronic infections aggravate inflammation in the CF lung, leading to progressive and irreversible damage of tissues. The phenotypic properties of P. aeruginosa associated with acute infections are very different from those that chronically colonize CF airways. This study aims to determine whether the different phenotypic properties adopted by P. aeruginosa during acute and chronic infections elicit different inflammatory responses from CF AECs. I will characterize the inflammatory response of CF AECs to P.aeruginosa clinical isolates that are collected "early" from patients (during acute infections) versus those isolates that are collected "late" (during chronic infections). I expect that P. aeruginosa "early" and "late" isolates will elicit different patterns of inflammation from CF AECs. I also expect that the pattern of inflammation elicited by "late" isolates will preclude bacterial clearance by the innate immune system and facilitate bacterial persistence in CF airways. Determining how Pa alters the inflammatory response of AECs during chronic infection is crucial for understanding how Pa causes respiratory failure in the CF lung. By understanding the mechanism(s) by which Pa stimulates an aberrant inflammatory response in CF AECs, this research is poised to reveal new biological targets for the rational design of drugs against chronic Pa infections in the CF lung.

TitreApplicationTitle: MicroRNA induction of survival increases cell transplantation efficacy in spinal cord injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENESIS; CERVICAL CLIP COMPRESSION INJURY; MICRORNA; SPINAL CORD INJURY; STEM CELL TRANSPLANTATION; SURVIVAL AND APOPTOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Despite decades of medical research, damage to the spinal cord remains largely irreversible. Stem cell transplantation therapies have shown some promise in restoring spinal cord function. However, one of the major problems limiting the effectiveness of stem cell transplantation in spinal cord injury is that very few of the transplanted cells survive in the nutrient-poor and inflammatory environment of the injury site. One way of increasing transplanted cell survival is to prepare them for these toxic conditions prior to injection, reducing the shock to the cells. In this project I will use microRNAs (a tool for temporarily turning off the expression of specific genes) to indirectly increase cellular levels of hypoxia-inducible factor 1a (HIF1A). HIF1A regulates the cell's ability to cope with oxygen and nutrient deprivation and reduces levels of cell death resulting from these conditions. By increasing cellular levels of HIF1A prior to stem cell injection into a spinal cord injury site, it is predicted that cells will show a more robust survival rate inside of the lesion. Increasing stem cell survival the injured spinal cord will in turn result in better regenerative outcomes following transplantation.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Antigen Presentation by Colonic Epithelial Cells in IBD
Keywords-MotsClés: ABLATION OF MHC CLASS I AND II GENES; AUTOIMMUNE RESPONSE; CROHN'S DISEASE; HISTOPATHOLOGY OF IBD; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASES; ULCERATIVE COLITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are the two most common forms of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), affecting more than 200,000 people in Canada. IBD is characterized by a chronic inflammation of sections of the gastrointestinal tract causing abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea and weight loss.  A growing field of evidence suggests that an abnormal response of the body's immune system plays a role these two main forms of IBD. However, the question of the precise mechanism of IBD development remains unanswered. The popular theory is that the development of IBD is caused by an abnormal immunological response against the natural bacterial microflora of the gut causing the subsequent breakdown of cells in the intestinal wall as part of an indirect cytotoxic effect. The proposed study aims to investigate the possibility of an alternative/additional site of damage where the inappropriate immune response is mounted directly against the cells of the intestinal lining causing bowel injury and acute inflammation, which later develops into a chronic condition. By blocking the autoimmune receptors on the colonic epithelial cells, we aim to determine the relative contribution of the direct bowel damage to the development of IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: A New Approach for Acute Myeloid Leukemia Treatment: siRNA Nanoparticles to Turn-Off Infinite Proliferation and Evasion of Apoptosis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; CANCER; DRUG DELIVERY; LEUKEMIA; NANOMEDICINE; NON-VIRAL GENE THERAPY; SMALL INTERFERING RNA (SIRNA)
Abstract-Résumé: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is caused by uncontrolled growth of abnormal white blood cells that accumulate in the bone marrow and interfere with the production of normal blood cells. AML is initially treated with chemotherapy but the drug therapy is not curative at the advanced stage of the disease and its effectiveness is limited by intolerable toxicities emerging after intensive therapy as a result of non-specific actions of drugs on healthy tissues. The ideal intervention will employ anticancer drugs that target the aberrant pathways specifically in the transformed cells, rather than displaying broad activities that affect normal cells. Towards this goal, this project will take a systematic approach to develop small interfering RNA (siRNA) based therapeutics for treatment of AML. We will formulate the siRNA into nanoparticles and evaluate its ability to curb uncontrolled cell growth and induce apoptosis in leukemic cells. Successful completion of this project will facilitate our efforts to bring a novel therapeutic platform to the clinical realm in the treatment of AML.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimisation du traitement immunosuppresseur en transplantation de cellules souches hématopoïétiques chez les patients cancéreux.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCERS HEMATOLOGIQUES; CELLULES SOUCHES HEMATOPOIETIQUES; IMMUNOSUPPRESSEURS; MALADIE DU GREFFON CONTRE L'HOTE; MARQUEURS MOLECULAIRES; MONITORING THERAPEUTIQUE; PHARMACOCINETIQUE; PHARMACODYNAMIE; PHARMACOGENOMIQUE; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: La transplantation de cellules souches hematopoietiques (du sang) est une therapie potentiellement curative pour plusieurs cancers comme la leucemie. Malgre l'utilisation de medicaments immunosuppresseurs pour prevenir les complications frequentes et souvent mortelles liees a la greffe, celles-ci surviennent chez 25 a 50% des transplantes. L'optimisation de la therapie immunosuppressive est l'un des plus importants facteurs modifiables qui pourrait ameliorer le pronostic des patients greffes. Les resultats insuffisants obtenus actuellement avec les therapies immunosuppressives s'expliquent en partie par le manque de connaissances des liens unissant l'exposition a la medication (concentration du medicament dans le sang, le degre d'inhibition atteint a la cible therapeutique (effet du medicament a son site d'action) et le risque de complications. Cette etude vise a etudier cette relation afin de determiner les facteurs specifiques les plus prometteurs pour optimiser, au niveau individuel, la therapie immunosuppressive et ameliorer le pronostic des patients. De plus, a titre exploratoire, certains facteurs genomiques pouvant modifier ces liens seront evalues.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Influence of Custodial Environments on Non-Suicidal Self-Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTECEDANTS; COMMUNITY; CONSEQUENCES; CUSTODY; FORENSIC; FUNCTIONS; GENDER; NON-SUICIDAL SELF-INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) involves the acute, intentional destruction of body tissue without the intent to die. In custody settings in particular, NSSI often results in significant costs in terms of health care resources, as those who engage in NSSI are often transferred to psychiatric facilities and are at risk of death by suicide. To inform areas for treatment intervention, many researchers have focused on the function of, or reasons for, engaging in NSSI. However, existing studies of NSSI in custody have tended to focus on psychiatric populations or individuals with specific mental disorders, or rely on extremely small sample sizes. Moreover, previous studies examining NSSI in custody populations have focused on primarily female or male samples, preventing direct gender comparisons of the functions of NSSI. For my doctoral project, I intend to examine the prevalence, method (e.g., cutting, burning, etc.), frequency and function of NSSI among both male and female inmates recruited from adult custody centres in the Lower Mainland (B.C.). Participants will be asked to retroactively report their NSSI behaviours prior to custody, their current NSSI behaviours in custody, and will be followed up in the community after incarceration to assess any changes in their NSSI behaviour. By focusing on the function of NSSI, this research has important implications in terms of developing treatment interventions and custody protocols that specifically address factors that maintain NSSI in these settings. Ultimately, this research will help reduce the occurrence of potentially life-threatening self-injurious behaviours and decrease the use of health care resources in custody settings. As a result, this research may help to improve health outcomes for individuals who are released and monitored in the community. Finally, my examination of gender differences may provide information on whether and how to tailor specific programming for women versus men in correctional settings.

TitreApplicationTitle: Linking psychological factors with clinical disease: The role of glucocorticoid sensitivity
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS AND GENOMICS; HYPOTHALAMIC-PITUITARY-ADRENAL AXIS; INFLAMMATION; PSYCHOBIOLOGY OF HEALTH; PSYCHOSOCIAL STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Mounting evidence has suggested psychological factors, including chronic life stress and low social status, increase the risk of mortality to several clinical diseases including heart disease, stroke, and certain forms of cancer. These findings have raised an interesting question on how stressful life experiences "get under the skin" to influence physical health. Currently, there is speculation that sensitivity to cortisol--a hormone released during stressful experiences that suppresses immune activity--may influence physical disease. My previous research in this area found that individuals reared in disadvantaged households possess hyper-vigilant immune systems that no longer respond to cortisol. This elevated state of immune activity is strong risk-factor for heart disease, age-related declines in mental functioning, and diabetes. To further advance knowledge in this area, I have proposed two projects that will examine the biological determinants of cortisol sensitivity. In one project, I will examine how a certain gene in the cortisol receptor may predispose individuals to developing resistance to cortisol, which may in turn increase their risk for clinical disease. In the other project, I will examine how chronic life stressors influence the intracellular mechanisms involved in conveying cortisol's immunosuppressive actions. Together, these projects will enable me to investigate how biological changes that accompany psychological stress may increase risk for clinical disease.
