TitreApplicationTitle: Novel calorimeter detector systems for accurate clinical dosimetry of light ion radiation therapy beams
Keywords-MotsClés: FINITE ELEMENT METHOD; GRAPHITE CALORIMETRY; HEAT TRANSPORT MODELING; LIGHT ION BEAMS; MEDIUM AND HIGH LET RADIATION DOSIMETRY; MONTE CARLO SIMULATIONS; NOVEL DOSIMETRY INSTRUMENTATION; RADIATION DOSIMETRY; RADIATION PHYSICS; WATER CALORIMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of radiation therapy in cancer treatment is to cure and/or palliate symptoms of cancer by delivering a prescribed radiation dose to a well-defined target volume while minimizing the dose to healthy tissue. To this end, there is a gradual move towards new techniques of therapy such as intensity modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) or new modalities of therapy such as light ion beam therapy (proton, carbon ion), all of which allow the dose to be conformed to the target volume to an unprecedented extent with the goal of improving patient outcome in terms of better tumour control and lower complication rates. In order to achieve this, however, it is essential to accurately determine the absorbed dose (energy deposited in tissue per unit mass) that will be delivered by these complicated treatments. This research focuses on developing novel instruments and data analysis techniques for the determination of absorbed dose in photon, electron, and light ion beams. The objective is to conduct an experimental study to validate the use of a graphite probe calorimeter, which is currently under development, as a clinical photon and electron dosimeter. Addition objectives of this project are (i) to investigate the application of the aforementioned graphite probe calorimeter as a clinical dosimeter of carbon ion radiation therapy beams, and (ii) to design and validate a cutting edge sealed water calorimeter for the same purpose. Up until now, no work has been performed in the area of carbon ion water calorimetry, and as such, no primary standard for determining absorbed dose to water in this type of beam exists. Once developed and characterized, our devices will significantly improve the accuracy of radiation dose measurements in clinical photon, electron, and light ion beams, which in turn will result in improved outcomes for cancer patients treated with these modalities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Older adults' mental health information needs and preferences: Bridging the gap in knowledge translation to increase mental health service utilization
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CLINICAL SAMPLE; COMMUNITY SAMPLE; DECISION-MAKING; HELPSEEKING/SERVICE UTILIZATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTAL HEALTH; MIXED-METHODS RESEARCH; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: The number of adults 65 years and older is increasing dramatically, characterizing Canada as an aging society. Unfortunately, a large and growing number of older adults is experiencing mental health problems, leading researchers to warn of an impending crisis in geriatric mental health. Despite a high prevalence of mental health problems, older adults are particularly unlikely to seek professional help. A probable barrier to helpseeking is a lack of accessible information about cost, duration, and effectiveness of treatments for mental health problems (i.e., a deficit in knowledge translation (KT)), which hinders effective treatment decision-making. The first (qualitative) objective of the proposed study is to examine, for the first time, the mental health information needs and preferences of older adults. Themes identified in the first phase of this study will be used to accomplish my second (quantitative) objective - to ensure generalizability and expand on findings generated in phase 1. A clinical sample of 15 older adults (65+) and a community sample of 15 older adults (65+) will complete the first phase of this study, consisting of in-depth interviews exploring reasons for and barriers to seeking help, mental health information preferences (content, format, source, and amount), and preferred services for the treatment of mental health problems. Results of this phase, in addition to questions pertaining to participants' experience of stress, anxiety, and depression, sociodemographic characteristics, mental health literacy, and preference for involvement in treatment decision-making will inform the development of a quantitative survey, to be completed by a community sample of 200 older adults. Findings of this study will lead to the next phase of my KT research program - the creation and quantitative evaluation of a mental health treatment decision aid for older adults - which will be beneficial in enhancing treatment decision-making of older adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: Insect Cell Carriers for Systemic Delivery of Oncolytic Viruses
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL CULTURE; DELIVERY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; ONCOLYTIC VIRUSES; TARGETING
Abstract-Résumé: Oncolytic viruses preferentially infect and kill cancer cells while leaving normal healthy cells intact. These viruses have proven to be a viable form of cancer therapy; however, there are barriers that exist which limit their efficacy as a method of treatment. A major barrier to cancer therapy with oncolytic viruses is the immune system, which is well-trained to eliminate foreign pathogens from the circulation. One strategy to circumvent this problem is to use cells as a delivery vehicle for the oncolytic viruses. These so called carrier cells not only deliver the virus to the tumor site but they also protect the virus from neutralization in the blood-they essentially act as Trojan horses. Recently, our group has begun to explore insect cells as carrier cells for viruses. Preliminary studies have shown that these insect cells can deliver virus to the site of the tumor. My research focuses on identifying ways to target the carrier cells to the tumor more effectively to increase the delivery of the virus. Since oncolytic viruses are currently being evaluated in clinical trials, the findings of the proposed research can have a significant impact on how these cancer fighting viruses will be administered to patients and how well they work. Currently there exists no real solution to the problem of virus neutralization during systemic delivery and insect cells may offer a solution to this problem.

TitreApplicationTitle: Emotion coaching in mothers of daughters with eating disorders - what predicts it and how is it related to daughter's symptoms?
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTION PROJECT METHOD; ANOREXIA NERVOSA; COUPLES; EATING DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Reports of patients who have recovered from anorexia nervosa show that they can perceive a supportive partner as "the driving force" behind their recovery. However, very little is known about the experiences of these couples and the challenges they face. Such knowledge is necessary to develop empirically-informed interventions for couples living with anorexia. The few existing studies have shown that such couples struggle with communication, openness, and intimacy. These studies, however, focused mostly on the perspective on the partner with anorexia. Studies also show women with anorexia and their partners differ in their perceptions of their relationships, suggesting that in order to fully understand these experiences, both partners need to be given a voice. The purpose of this study is to examine, from the perspective of the couple, the experience of a relationship in which one partner has anorexia. This will be achieved by asking the following research questions: 1. What is the role of a romantic relationship in coping with anorexia? 2. What is the experience of anorexia in the relationship? 3. What is the style of communicating about anorexia among partners? This study will use the Action-Project Method, which was created to explore behaviour, internal experiences and their meaning in dyads. Partners will engage in a conversation about research topics both with the researcher and among each other. These conversations will be videotaped and analyzed to find overarching themes and communication patterns. The results of this study can be used to inform the development of interventions that target the specific needs of couples living with anorexia.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Effect of Slit2 on Retinal Ganglion Cell Survival After Optic Nerve Crush Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MICROSURGERY; NEURONAL REGENERATION; NEURONAL SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Blindness in glaucoma is a result of the death of retinal ganglion cells over time in the eye. Retinal ganglion cells transmit the signals received by the retina, through the optic nerve, to the brain. The cause of death of retinal ganglion cells in glaucoma is unknown. One theory involves the immune system as a main player in the progression of disease in glaucoma. Slit2 is a protein that has been shown to inhibit immune cell migration and chemotaxis in vitro. It has also shown to have an anti-inflammatory effect in vivo in an animal model of kidney disease. The use of other anti-inflammatory drugs such as minocycline has shown to significantly improve retinal ganglion cell survival after optic nerve injury in animal models. The effect of Slit2 on retinal ganglion cell survival will be determined by injecting Slit2 following optic nerve crush injury. Retinal ganglion cells die over a four week period following optic nerve crush injury. Surviving retinal ganglion cells will be counted and compared to animals that did not receive treatment. It is anticipated that Slit2 will improve the survival of retinal ganglion cells after injury. Understanding the mechanisms of retinal ganglion cell death and the role of Slit2 can increase our knowledge about glaucoma and identify novel therapies to slow or fully stop the progression of this and other ocular diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tails that Kill: Characterization of the bactericidal activity of Pseudomonas aeruginosa F-type pyocins
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISATNCE; BACTERIAL BIOFILMS; BACTERIAL INFECTION; BACTERIOPHAGE; BACTERIOPHAGE-RELATED THERAPEUTICS; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; GENETIC ENGINEERING OF BACTERIOPHAGE; LUNG INFECTIONS; PHAGE-TAIL-LIKE BACTERIOCIN (PTLB); PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA
Abstract-Résumé: In the last few decades there has been a rapid emergence of untreatable, bacterial infections that are resistant to multiple drugs. Multi-drug-resistant-Pseudomonas aeruginosa is of specific concern because it is a common cause of infections in immunocompromised and Cystic Fibrosis patients. Following infection, it is very difficult to eliminate this pathogen because it is naturally resistant to most antibiotics and can form aggregates, which allow it to escape the host immune response. Further, multi-drug-resistant strains are emerging rapidly. Since antibiotics are not effective in many Pseudomonas infections, alternative therapies are being explored. A promising alternative is the use of F-type pyocins, which are molecules produced by P. aeruginosa to kill other strains of P. aeruginosa. These particles have been shown to be extremely lethal and are thought to specifically bind to molecules on the surface of P. aeruginosa cells in order to kill them. However, our knowledge about these molecules is very limited, and therefore, in my studies I aim to characterize F-type pyocins. Specifically, I will characterize the killing activities of different F-type pyocins that I have already isolated and investigate all the protein subunits of these molecules that are required for these activities. I will also study what they interact with on the P. aeruginosa cell surface to kill them, and what determines this specificity within the F-type pyocins. In the long run, the knowledge gained from this study will be used to engineer F-type pyocins that are optimized for high purification yields, bactericidal activity and specificity. This work with Pseudomonas will be of high importance to the health of Canadians who live with Cystic Fibrosis, and the knowledge gained will have general applicability for all bacterial infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Longitudinal modeling of cognitive decline in a non-demented elderly population
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BIOMARKERS; BIOSTATISTICS; COGNITIVE DECLINE; COHORT; DEMENTIA; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GROWTH MIXTURE MODELLING; LONGITUDINAL; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer disease (AD) and other dementias represent one of the most important public health challenges facing modern society. Presently, 36 million people worldwide live with dementia and this number is projected to reach 66 million by 2030, and 115 million by 2050.   Cognitive decline is the primary symptom of clinical AD. However, the magnitude and rate of cognitive decline varies significantly between individuals. Little is known about what makes an individual follow a particular path of decline, or indeed the specific trajectories of these different paths. Statistical modeling of cognitive data obtained over time from groups of at-risk individuals is needed to identify these different paths. We propose using a new statistical methodology called growth mixture modeling, which can identify subgroups of individuals who follow similar paths, and are exploring several available longitudinal cohorts of at risk individuals that might serve as the discovery and replication datasets for this work. While cognitive decline is the defining feature of AD, researchers are increasingly using disease biomarkers and imaging data to study disease progression. There is similar variability in change over time in these measures, so this methodology will have application to those outcomes as well.   We expect that identifying these paths will be useful in a number of important ways. It will help us to better characterize exactly who follows a particular path, and to identify risk factors associated with following a particular course of decline. Such knowledge could be of particular public health importance, given the failure of treatments at later stages of the disease. Additionally, we may be able to refine predictions of prognosis for individuals at earlier stages of the disease. Finally, it may also provide insights into the underlying causes of disease progression in AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mapping Social Networks for Translating Knowledge from Community-Based Participatory Research into Policy and Practice Change: The Impact of the Kahnawake Schools Diabetes Prevention Project
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NETWORK MAPPING; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SOCIAL NETWORK ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Participatory research (PR) is an approach to research where academic researchers work in equitable partnership with those effected by the issue being studied, or with those who must eventually use or act on the knowledge created. PR thus integrates the translation of research knowledge into action for change by engaging these end-users at the beginning of the knowledge-creation process.  The action and change sought through PR is specifically intended to benefit its local stakeholders, yet findings must be able to be translated to other settings.  The success of PR efforts in creating action for change relies heavily on the formal and informal interpersonal and inter-organisational relationships that develop among its stakeholders. These relationships form a social network, defined as the pattern of ties existing among a set of individuals, organisations or other social actors.  An examination of this social network will thus give us insight into the process by which PR knowledge is translated into action for practice and policy change beyond the local context in which it was originally created and for which it was intended. Using the Kahnawake Schools Diabetes Prevention Project, a long-standing community-based health promotion PR project, as a case study, this proposed study will use social network analysis techniques to describe the network of relationships among the various stakeholders (individual and organizational), and the importance of these relationships in the dissemination or uptake of research findings into policy and practice locally, to the wider Aboriginal community, and throughout Canada more generally. This will lead to a better understanding of how research results move into practice, and of how to best use stakeholder-engaged research such as PR, to bridge the often large gap between what we learn from research and what we do in practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of genotype and epigenotype in serotonin transporter effects on depression and anxiety-related behaviours
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; BEHAVIOR; DEPRESSION; EPIGENETICS; GENE ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; GENOTYPE; MENTAL HEALTH; MICRODIALYSIS; RODENT; SEROTONIN
Abstract-Résumé: My proposed doctoral research project focuses on identifying mechanisms in the brain that influence vulnerability and resilience to anxiety and depression. Individual differences in the response to stress have profound effects on the risk for anxiety and depressive disorders. In Canada, one in 4 individuals suffers from anxiety or depression, disorders with large social and economic costs. Two potential mechanisms for individual differences in disease risk include gene by environment interactions and epigenetics. Epigenetic mechanisms can change in gene function in a long term manner without altering DNA sequence (i.e. genotype). A recent study done by the Fleming lab (where I plan to do my doctoral work) demonstrated that a naturally occurring genetic variation in the serotonin transporter gene (5HTT) in a rodent model, analogous to variation in 5HTT gene observed in humans, is associated with individual differences in the neuroendocrine response to stress, stress sensitive glucocorticoid receptor distribution in the brain's hippocampus and anxiety behaviour. Serotonin or drugs that enhance serotonin activity in brain cells grown in cellular culture significantly induce glucocorticoid gene expression and alter the gene in an epigenetic manner. Yet no study has examined the interaction between genotype and epigenotype in the regulation of gene expression and behaviour. I hypothesize that genetic differences in 5HTT confer differential stress responses at least in part via epigenetic modification of glucocorticoid receptor expression. I propose to study this phenomenon using pharmacological, molecular, and behavioural techniques. I will use rats that differ in 5HTT genotype to investigate evidence for (1) altered serotonin levels in the brain in basal and stress challenged conditions, (2) altered epigenetic status of the glucocorticoid receptor gene and (3) differential effects of drugs that alter serotonin activity in depression and anxiety-related behaviour

Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; HYPERTENSION; MYOGENIC TONE; PERFUSION MYOGRAPHY; RESISTANCE LEVEL ARTERIES; SPHINGOSINE KINASE 1; SPHINGOSINE-1-PHOSPHATE; TUMOR NECROSIS FACTOR ALPHA; TYPE 1 AND TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS; VASCULAR COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES MELLITUS
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes increases the risk of diseases if the heart and blood vessels (cardiovascular disease). Disease of the blood vessels can increase the risk of high blood pressure, heart attack, and other life-threatening conditions. Blood vessels are important for controlling blood pressure. Blood vessels enlarge or constrict, making it easier or harder for blood to flow through them. Diabetes is known to cause changes to the structure and function of blood vessels. Diabetes tends to enhance constriction of blood vessels, and this can lead to high blood pressure. My research has identified new molecules in the wall of the blood vessel that drive these changes to structure and function, and the enhancement of constriction. The molecular targets identified by this research project may likely help treat the cardiovascular complications of diabetes.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANEURYSM; ANGIOTENSIN II; ANGIOTENSIN RECEPTOR TYPE I; AORTA; AORTIC DISSECTION; HYPERTENSION; MARFAN SYNDROME; VASCULAR DYSFUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Marfan Syndrome (MFS) is a genetic based disease that occurs in approximately one in every five thousand individuals. Individuals with MFS are at risk for life-threatening cardiovascular problems, the most severe being when the large blood vessel that supplies blood from the heart to the rest of the body (the aorta) tears, which often leads to sudden death. Before the aorta tears, the aorta becomes weakened and enlarged. Although surgical treatment and drugs are available for MFS, the vast majority of patients with higher-risk forms of MFS have changes in their aortas and die at a relatively young age. This speaks to the need for new and improved methods of treatment for MFS patients. As such, this project aims to expand our knowledge about MFS and provide new information upon which to design new drugs. To do this, focus will be placed on completely blocking a particular cause of MFS using animal models and looking at the impact on MFS. This will allow for greater understanding of the pathogenesis of MFS and identification of targets for new drugs that will help improve the length and quality of individuals with MFS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measurement of outcomes of interventions aimed at reducing substance abuse and/or mental health problems: a study to develop a standardized outcome measure
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; DISABILITY; DISTRESS; FUNCTIONING IN DAILY LIFE; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HEALTH SERVICES EVALUATION; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MENTAL HEALTH; PATIENT-ORIENTED RESEARCH; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: In 2004, neuropsychiatric conditions accounted for 31.6% of the total burden of disease in Canada (as measured by disability adjusted years of life lost). Despite being responsible for a large proportion of the burden of disease, currently no provincial or national framework exists in Canada to measure the burden of substance abuse and/or mental health problems, and international quantification of this burden is also limited. As such, there exists the need for a system to characterize the population with substance abuse and/or mental health problems, and to evaluate sensitivity to change in that population after interventions. We propose to focus on three dimensions, namely disability, functioning in daily life, and distress in the affected individuals. To determine the viability of developing such a system, we will undertake a longitudinal cohort study to characterize individuals with substance abuse and/or mental health problems who present at either the Emergency or Ambulatory departments or the Crisis Clinic at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) in terms of these aforementioned dimensions. We will then correlate changes over time in these variables with health services and support utilization by using CAMH records and databases from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences. For this study we will recruit approximately 1,400 people aged 17 years or older with substance abuse and/or mental health problems who present as indicated above at CAMH. This is the first project of this kind and will help establish the feasibility of evaluating outcomes of health services and support within the studied population. If successful, the results of this study will be disseminated both nationally and, with help of the World Health Organization (a formal partner in this project), globally.

TitreApplicationTitle: Applied clinical informatics for genome analysis of patients with treatable intellectual disabilities
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; COMPUTATIONAL BIOLOGY; GENE REGULATION; GENETICS; GENOMICS; IDENTIFICATION OF CAUSAL MUTATIONS; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITIES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; METABOLIC DISORDERS; METABOLIC NETWORKS
Abstract-Résumé: Human DNA is over 3 billion units long and composed of four types of chemical building blocks: A, C, G, and T. A DNA mutation represents a change in one or more of the building blocks at specific place(s). Most of these changes are benign and commonly shared among the human population. However, there are also mutations that are rare, only present in a specific individual, family, or sub-group of people. Such mutations can sometimes cause a disease to manifest, such as cancer, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anemia, or intellectual disabilities. Due to high financial costs, past technologies restricted scientists to the study of only small portions of the human DNA. Newer technological advancements have brought this cost down to an affordable level (from over 2 billion to under 5000), allowing researchers to obtain the complete DNA sequence for an individual. Nevertheless, we are still limited by the ability to understand and interpret this data. By figuring out a way to compare a patient's DNA to "normal" DNA, we can decipher which mutations are most likely to cause a disease.  For my doctoral research in bioinformatics -a multidisciplinary field uniting computational, statistical and biological sciences- I am developing software that can analyze DNA sequences to find mutations responsible for a disease.  As mentioned above, most mutations are benign, and it is crucial for investigators to pinpoint which ones are responsible for causing the actual disease. I will accomplish this by implementing a ranking method that sorts the mutations in the order of relevance to the disease. If successful, the mutations at the top of this ranked list will be the mutations that are likely candidate causes for the disease. Although throughout my project my data focus will be on patients with treatable intellectual disabilities, the final product of my research is applicable to a wide range of diseases, and will advance the use of DNA sequences in health care services.

Abstract-Résumé: One-third of the elderly Canadian population will eventually be diagnosed with dementia at some point in their lifetime. The most effective research in this area will provide policymakers with information on management strategies that result in keeping people with dementia stable and healthy. My research will focus specifically on variations in clinical and non-clinical (home & community care service) use and the relationship of those varying levels of care to three major outcomes: 1) length of stay at home 2) number of transitions prior to permanent move to a long-term care (LTC) facility 3) number of visits to the Emergency Room (ER). The implications of the study will be discussed with various stakeholders.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Nod-like receptor pathways in obesity and Type 2 Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: INFLAMMATION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; MICROBIOTA; OBESITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is rapidly becoming a major health concern worldwide and can lead to the onset of associated diseases such as Type 2 Diabetes (T2D). T2D is caused by the body's development of resistance to insulin, eventually resulting in inability to control one's blood sugar levels. Recent evidence has demonstrated that obesity produces a chronic state of inflammation within the body, which is one of the primary factors resulting in insulin resistance. We are investigating the role of two different inflammatory pathways in the onset of T2D and have identified the proteins Caspase-12 and Rip2 as playing important roles in the development of this disease. Our research will attempt to determine the mechanism responsible through the use of various mouse models of obesity and T2D. This information will be important in unraveling how the immune system and inflammation can lead to insulin resistance and provide insight into potential therapies for treating T2D.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Public Health Emergency Response in Light of Traditional Public Health Values
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS; DISASTER RESPONSE; EQUITY; HEALTH BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE; POPULATION HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH ETHICS; QUALITATIVE METHODOLOGY; SOCIAL JUSTICE; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Significant interest has recently emerged in the area of public health emergency preparedness and response, largely as a result of events like SARS, the Japanese and Haitian earthquakes, and the persistent threat of future infectious disease pandemics. Scholars have developed ethical frameworks to guide policy and practice in preparing for and responding to such emergencies, often espousing the values of utility, efficiency, and maximization. However, these emerging frameworks do not accommodate or apply traditional ethical values of public health, such as social justice, equity, and concern for vulnerable populations and the social determinants of health, which, if not applied, can have the effect of exacerbating existing health inequities. My research will use a mixed-methods design consisting of (1) qualitative key informant interviews with public health policy-makers, practitioners, and ethicists, and (2) a content analysis of relevant public health emergency preparedness guides and ethical frameworks. The objective of my research is to systematically identify where gaps exist between traditional ethical values in public health and the ethical frameworks that guide our public health emergency response, and prescribe how traditional public health values can be incorporated and applied in public health emergency preparedness and response. This study has significant implications for public health as well as disaster and emergency preparedness and response. Public health emergencies will continue to pose significant ethical challenges, which will only be exacerbated if traditional public health values are neglected.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Influence of Telomere Dynamics and Genomic Instability on Disease Progression in Myelodysplastic Syndromes
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENETICS; FLUORESCENT IN SITU HYBRIDIZATION; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; HEMATOLOGY; IN VITRO STUDIES; IN VIVO STUDIES; MICROARRAY; MICRORNA; MULTIPLE MYELOMA; QRT-PCR
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple Myeloma (MM), an incurable disease, is the second most common haematological malignancy with a prevalence of 65,000 patients in North America and an estimated 3000 deaths per year. The addition of the proteasome inhibitor Bortezomib to the treatment protocol in MM has led to a significant improvement in patient survival. However, MM cells eventually acquire resistance to Bortezomib resulting in disease progression and eventually patient death. A small class of genes called microRNA (miRNA), were recently shown to be important in the regulation of cancer cell behaviour. Nearly all transformed cells, including malignant plasma cells, have an altered miRNA expression, although the effect of miRNA on resistance to therapeutics in myeloma is not yet known. Based on our preliminary work, we have postulated that miRNAs are implicated in the acquired drug resistance of MM cells. We have shown that by manipulating miRNA expression in MM cells we are able to increase the cell's sensitivity to Bortezomib. Uncovering the mechanisms of drug resistance will add to our understanding of the biology of this fatal disease and ultimately improve MM patient survival. Upon completion of this project, there will be a greater understanding of the influence of miRNA on the biology of myeloma cells. Subsequently, it may be possible to identify novel therapeutic targets for this incurable disease. The results of this project may have implications to cancer therapy beyond the disease investigated in this project.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying novel players in the DNA damage and repair pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENETIC NETWORKS; HIGH-THROUGHPUT; SACCHAROMYCES CEREVISIAE; SENSITIZED BACKGROUNDS; SUB-CELLULAR MORPHOLOGY; SYNTHETIC GENETIC ARRAY ANALYSIS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Since the completion of the Human Genome Project, which identified that there are approximately 20 000 - 25 000 genes in human DNA, research has been working to identify the function of each of these genes. Baker's yeast is a good model for this task, since it is easier to work with than human cells and many genes are similar. Deleting specific genes in yeast and establishing the effect of that deletion on the cell allows for the identification of the function of the gene. The use of screening technologies like Synthetic Genetic Array (SGA) allows thousands of these deletion mutants to be created quickly and easily. However, these mutants may appear to grow normally but have serious defects within their cells. To counter this I am using a new and exciting technology that combines SGA with high-throughput microscopy, allowing for the visualization of these defects. DNA damage is a hallmark of human cancers, and I hypothesize that this strategy will reveal new similarities between the DNA damage response pathways of yeast and humans. To identify these similarities, I will screen the entire yeast genome looking for mutants that have an increased number of the small, bright foci that indicate DNA damage. I will screen cells that have a single gene deletion, cells that have two or more genes deleted, and cells that have been exposed to chemicals that damage DNA. These sensitizing factors worsen cellular defects, allowing for the identification of genes that are involved with the cell's response to DNA damage in novel ways that have not yet been revealed. By uncovering new genes that affect how the cell responds to DNA damage in yeast, I will be able to identify new genes that play a role in the regulation - and more importantly the deregulation - of this pathway in humans. Such knowledge could have great health benefits, specifically in the development of therapeutic intervention and cancer treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparison of methods to synthesize clinical and economic information for the health technology assessment of novel drugs used in small patient populations with methods used in larger clinical populations and communication of this information to decision makers.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOSTATISTICS; CRITICAL APPRAISAL; ECONOMIC EVALUATION; HEALTH POLICY DECISION MAKING; HEALTH TECHNOLOGY ASSESSMENT; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NETWORK META-ANALYSIS; ONCOLOGY; PLAIN LANGUAGE COMMUNICATION; RARE DISEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Evaluating the benefits, safety and costs of new drugs can be challenging when there are only a small group of patients in whom to test a new drug.  This occurs often with new cancer drugs that are targeted at a small group of patients with a specific genetic background. It is always important that the safety and effectiveness of a new drug is compared with treatments that are currently being used.  When high-quality information from large randomized studies comparing a new drug with current treatments is not available, as is sometimes the case for rare diseases, other relevant data could be considered.  Comprehensively assembling all relevant data from other sources such observational studies or adaptive design trials should be explored in the case of a rare disease. Statistical and economic methods to incorporate these types of evidence into assessments of new drugs have not been fully developed yet. Political decision makers, doctors and the public may not have a clear understanding of some of the technical methods used in a drug assessment, e.g. economic modeling, value of information analysis, network meta-analyses, Bayesian procedures.  It is hypothesized that: (a) statistical and economic methods can be further developed in the context of rare diseases that would allow additional relevant information to be considered; (b)  poor understanding by non-scientists of new statistical and economic techniques for drug assessment may prevent these new methods from being used. Therefore, developing user-friendly language and ways to share this technical information could improve health policy decision-making.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural Correlates of Threat and Emotion Processing in Panic Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFECTIVE NEUROSCIENCE; ANXIETY; ATTENTIONAL BIAS; EMOTION; EVENT-RELATED POTENTIALS; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; EXPERIMENTAL PSYCHOLOGY; PANIC DISORDER; PREDICTORS OF RELAPSE; STROOP TASK
Abstract-Résumé: Panic disorder (PD) is a psychiatric disorder characterized by unpredictable attacks of intense fear accompanied by severe physical anxiety symptoms (e.g. palpitations), often followed by a persistent fear of having another attack in the future. It affects about 2% of the general population. PD is a serious, chronic condition with a high degree of impairment on the patient's life. Since many of the symptoms of PD resemble those of clinical diseases, PD patients frequently use medical services and undergo costly diagnostic procedures to rule out conditions such as heart disease. This places not only a financial burden on the medical system, but also comprises social and functional impairment of the affected patient. Hence, it is important to identify the origin of the anxiety symptoms of PD patients. It has been proposed that PD patients have faster processing of threatening information (e.g. a spider) in our environment compared to healthy persons. This is called an attentional bias. My previous research has focused on which brain areas might be involved in persons at risk for anxiety disorders when these attentional biases occur, and in which way they function differently compared to in healthy persons. For this study, we used a technique called EEG, which makes it possible to measure the electrical activity generated in the brain. We found that people who are affected by anxiety have a different pattern of brain signals than people who are not. In my proposed project, I now would like to study attentional biases to threat in PD patients and compare them to our results obtained before. We expect that PD patients will show evidence of greater arousal to threat words displayed as differential activity in the brain. 6 months after the study, the PD patients' relapse status will be assessed, and the original data set will be divided into subgroups, and reanalyzed in order to test whether the behavioral and ERP markers previously identified can also predict relapse.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the molecular mechanisms that control the development of tumor dendritic cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CANCER IMMUNOLOGY; DENDRITIC CELL; GR-1+  TOLEROGENIC DENDRITIC CELL; INNATE IMMUNITY; TOLERANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Current common therapies for cancer include surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy. These therapies often have undesired side effects due to their toxicity and lack of specificity. The idea of stimulating the immune system to kill cancer cells is promising. Cancer patients generally have a poor immune system to defend against tumors and cancerous cells, including the initiation of an immune response.  A specialized immune cell in the body, dendritic cell, is responsible for the initiation of the specific adaptive immune response. Cancer cells have the ability to escape the immune system, this poses a challenge in novel therapies that target cancer using immune cells. The overall goal of the project is to understand the communication between cancerous cells and dendritic cells. We hypothesize that molecules secreted by tumors are able to signal with dendritic cell precursors, triggering transformational changes. These changes prevent dendritic cells to initiate immune responses towards tumors. To address this hypothesis, we will isolate dendritic cells from mice and incubate the cells in a tumrr-like environment. We will observe the development of the dendritic cells and attempt to understand factors that influence their transformation. The results obtained from the project will advance our understanding of the mechanisms involved in the development of impaired immune responses to cancer, and lead to new strategies to treat cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Cancer Survivorship Through Health Promotion Strategies
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER SURVIVORSHIP; COMPLEMENTARY MEDICINE; DECISION MAKING; HEALTH CARE RESOURCE UTILIZATION; HEALTH PROMOTION; PRIMARY CARE; QUALITATIVE METHODS; QUALITY OF LIFE; SECONDARY DATA ANALYSIS; SELF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: A significant gap exists in the Canadian cancer care system to address the needs of growing numbers of patients surviving cancer. Despite being cured, many survivors experience life-long physical, psychological, sexual, social, and financial challenges after treatment is complete. Survivors are increasingly seeking out self care health promotion strategies such as diet, exercise, and complementary medicine (e.g. natural health products, acupuncture) to address these challenges and maximize health outcomes. Emerging research shows significant value of many health promotion behaviors (e.g. exercise, diet, weight maintenance, Vitamin D) in reducing cancer recurrence risk, managing symptoms, and promoting optimal coping and wellbeing. Safe and informed practice of self care health promotion strategies could therefore improve survivors' morbidity outcomes and quality of life, reducing unnecessary health care resource utilization and costs. However, in Canada there is a paucity of comprehensive programs, tools or established models of care to offer survivors decision-making and ongoing support regarding the practice of self care health promotion strategies beyond the immediate post treatment period. To inform development of these resources, this study seeks to explicate survivors' current and desired health promotion knowledge, practices, unmet needs and impacts (including economic); and health care providers' recommendations on optimal deployment of resources in support of survivors' self care health promotion behaviors. Study findings will inform development of explicit tools, resources and models of care offering survivors consistent and effective support for practice of potentially life prolonging and enhancing health promotion strategies. Study findings also will inform tool development to guide future analysis of the economic impact of survivors' self care health promotion practices, providing important new knowledge for survivorship model of care design.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relational Moral Experience of Parental Decision-Making in the NICU
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS; NEONATAL-PERINATAL MEDICINE; NEONATOLOGY; PHENOMENOLOGY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Newborn medical care is full of decision-making events. In the newborn intensive care unit (NICU), death of the child is often the result of withholding or withdrawing of medical support - a deliberative medical-moral decision. While end-of-life decisions are certainly grave choices, they are but one of the many decisions confronting practitioners and families. Decisions may involve a new direction-of-care such as pursuing particular medical therapies or surgeries, or simply may be part of day-to-day happenings such as leaving the bedside or raising a concern. While disputes between the practitioners and families can often be easily resolved, sometimes communication breaks down, leaving them at an impasse. Involvement of legal authorities and the public media may be the costly result. It is clear that practitioners need a nuanced understanding of this parental experience as decision-making constitutes a core part of their professional practice.  This project responds to this need by taking a qualitative look into parents' experiences of decision-making. In particular, it focuses on the parents of premature or sick infants requiring hospitalization in a NICU. Here, decisions may be made in the context of a parent-child relationship that is still new, fragile, and emotionally overwhelming, yet often compromised by the interaction of infant illness, medical technology, and multiple professional caregivers.  The outcome of this research proposal is the completion of texts that portray the moral experiences of NICU parents. The texts are both academic studies to build on existing relational ethics research, as well as a practical source for knowledge translation to professionals and the general public, to culminate in insightful care practices.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of neonatal pain, brain microstructure, stress and maternal factors on internalizing behavior at age 18 months in children born very preterm
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD BEHAVIOR; CHILD CORTISOL; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; MOTHER-CHILD INTERACTION; NEONATAL PAIN; NEURODEVELOPMENT; PREMATURE BIRTH
Abstract-Résumé: Every year, approximately 8% of infants in Canada are born very preterm (<32 weeks gestation). Advances in medical technologies have allowed the majority of these infants to survive, however their long-term developmental outcomes, including problems with behavior, have not improved. As part of their life-saving care preterm infants undergo repeated painful procedures that that induce stress during a period of rapid brain and stress system development. Brain injuries and abnormal stress levels are common in these vulnerable infants. Subsequently, as early as 18 months of age, children born very preterm have been described as having more stress behaviors (anxiety) compared to their term-born peers, which can lead to a substantial burden of suffering for the individual, family, and social systems. However, very little is known about the relationships between neonatal pain-related stress, brain development, stress hormone levels and behavioral outcomes in these children. Therefore, using state-of-the-art interdisciplinary methods we aim to determine how neonatal pain, stress and abnormal brain development affect the development of anxiety behaviors in young children born very preterm. The results of this research will provide a foundation for understanding mechanisms of altered behavior in children born preterm. Relationships among stress, outcomes and coping are complex in preterm infants, who appear to be more sensitive to their environment than term-born peers. A positive social environment is viewed as a key factor for optimizing long-term outcomes in children born very preterm, who are known to have more difficulty appropriately responding to stress. Therefore, we will also assess mother-infant interactive behaviors and examine the extent that they are protective against adverse effects on later behavior at 18 months. Characterization of optimal caregiver behaviors can be used to lead evidence-based interventions to improve the lives of children born preterm.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovering optimal targets for adoptive T-cell immunotherapy of leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN REGOGNITION; CANCER; CELLULAR BIOLOGY; IMMUNOTHERAPY; MHC I; PEPTIDE; T LYMPHOCYTE FUNCTION; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: More than 100,000 individuals treated for hematological malignancies owe their life to allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (AHCT). Cure of leukemias by AHCT is due mainly to the graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) effect, in which tumor cells are eradicated by the donor T-cells. In this form of cancer immunotherapy, donor lymphocytes are neither selected nor activated prior to transfer. Unfortunately, this creates two major problems. First, 60% of graft recipients suffer from graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), a disease often lethal but always incapacitating. Second, donor T-cells that have not been activated can be tolerized by tumor cells, resulting in an attenuated form of GVL. These two caveats can be circumvented by the injection of activated antigen-specific CD8 T-cells. Antigens that are recognized by T cells are generated by the interplay of protein synthesis and protein degradation. The peptides generated within the cells are exported at the cell surface for immune recognition.   Two types of antigens can be targeted for antigen-specific immunotherapy: 1) Antigens that are present only on cancer cells compared to their normal counterpart (TAAs) and 2) Antigens that arise from inter-individual variations in the genome that translate to differential peptide expression at the cell surface (MiHAs). Several studies in humans have demonstrated independently the value of TAA- and MiHA-specific T-cells for eradication of solid tumors and leukemia, respectively. Importantly, the value of TAAs and MiHAs as target for antigen-specific cancer immunotherapy has never been assessed against the same tumor. In this study, our main goal is to directly compare the therapeutic efficacy of T-cells targeted to these two types of antigens. We believe that the crucial insights gained from our studies will serve a guide for selecting the best antigens for antigen-specific leukemia immunotherapy in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Glyoxalase-1 and Cell Therapy in Defective Ischemia-induced Neovascularization in Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CIRCULATING PROGENITOR CELLS; DIABETES; ISCHEMIA; NEOVASCULARIZATION; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is a chronic disease that affects an estimated 285 million people worldwide. Currently in Canada, more than 9 million people are living with diabetes or prediabetes. Hyperglycaemia, a common consequence of uncontrolled diabetes, typically leads to a reduction in blood vessels and impaired wound healing.  An important process in wound healing is the formation of new blood vessels from pre-existing vessels. This process is called angiogenesis.  In diabetics, angiogenesis is impaired, which has been attributed, in part, to a dysfunction in circulating angiogenic cells (CAC).  A better understanding of the mechanism(s) that control CACs and blood vessel formation in diabetes is needed. Methylglyoxal is a highly toxic product of glucose metabolism. Normally, in healthy individuals, methylglyoxal is removed by the enzyme Glyoxalase-1 (GLO1). In diabetes, the body's defense against methylglyoxal becomes overwhelmed, allowing it to accumulate. Based on current evidence, it appears that CAC dysfunction in diabetes is affected, at least in part, by methylglyoxal accumulation. This represents a potential target for reversing the defective formation of blood vessels found in diabetes. Essentially, restoring the function of the GLO1 enzyme may reduce methylglyoxal levels and help CAC function and new blood vessel growth in diabetes. The exploitation of this pathway for therapy constitutes the focus of the present proposal.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Gene-Environment Interaction Model of Theory of Mind Development
Keywords-MotsClés: AVPR1A GENE; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTION; MATERNAL SENSITIVITY; MEDIATION; MODERATION; OXTR GENE; PSYCHOPATHOLOGY; SOCIAL COGNITION; THEORY OF MIND
Abstract-Résumé: Theory of mind is the ability to know that other people act according to mental states (beliefs, desires, emotions, etc.). Children typically show this ability around 4-years-old. However, children with poor theory of mind often experience many problems, including behavioural and social difficulties. Deficits in theory of mind are also a core feature of autism. Thus, it is important to understand what factors contribute to theory of mind so that we can support children's healthy development. In this project, we look at how both genes and children's experiences with their environment influence their theory of mind. Two candidate genes are examined, one from the vasopressin system and one from the oxytocin system. These genes are examined since they have been shown to be important for social interactions that theory of mind is needed for. We also look at how the child's environment affects theory of mind. Specifically, we look at how parenting behaviour early in life impacts theory of mind ability. This environmental factor was chosen since parenting has widely been shown to influence many childhood outcomes, including social, emotional, and academic competencies. In fact, some of my previous research has shown that a mother's level of sensitivity toward her child affects numerous early skills that can be considered precursors to theory of mind, such as cooperation and empathy. Finally, we look at how genes and environments work together to shape theory of mind development. There is now an abundance of research showing that development occurs due to each child's unique combination of genes and experiences. To accomplish this, we investigate gene-environment interaction models, which tell us about the combinations of factors that promote healthy development, and those that may produce poor outcomes. By knowing this, we can develop effective interventions and policies that aim to support children's functioning in everyday life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular regulation of skeletal muscle stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG SCREENING; MOLECULAR SIGNALLING; MUSCLE REGENERATION; MUSCLE STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Muscle regeneration in injury and disease requires the activation, proliferation and differentiation of muscle satellite cells. Recent research have demonstrated that satellite cells are self-renewing and Muscle regeneration in injury and disease requires the activation, proliferation and differentiation of muscle satellite cells. Recent research has demonstrated that satellite cells are self-renewing and compose of a heterogeneous population of stem cells and progenitors. Our lab has identified the satellite stem cell population (Kuang et al., 2007; Cell) and demonstrated that increasing the tissue content of these cells results in a direct enhancement on regeneration kinetics (Le Grand et al., 2009; Cell stem cell). However, the maintenance and regulation of satellite stem cells is not well understood.  To study the cell signalling network controlling the homeostatic levels of satellite stem cells and their response in regeneration, we have developed a novel drug screen platform to examine the proliferation kinetics of satellite stem cells on ex-vivo cultured muscle fibers. Screening against a library of compounds targeting developmental pathways (~380 compounds) will allows us to identify cellular pathways that modulate the proliferation of satellite stem cells. Characterization of these target pathways will unveil new insight into the molecular regulation of these stem cells during regeneration. In addition, compounds with a positive effect have the potential to be directly translated into therapeutic options for degenerative muscle disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Relationship Between PTSD and Comorbid Post-trauma Mental Health Conditions Among Canadians
Keywords-MotsClés: COMORBIDITY; CROSS-LAGGED PANEL DESIGN; DEPRESSION; LONGITUDINAL DESIGN; POSTTRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER; RESILIENCE FACTORS; RISK FACTORS; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING; SUBSTANCE USE; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: Over 75% of Canadians experience a traumatic event during their lives, and 9% of these individuals develop posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD is a chronic and debilitating mental health condition associated with substantial personal and societal costs, including overuse of healthcare resources and reduced workplace productivity. The estimated annual cost of PTSD is $40 billion. Many people with PTSD also develop major depressive disorder and substance use disorders, which are associated with additional economic costs. Yet, PTSD is generally investigated without considering these commonly co-occurring disorders. As a result, it is unclear if PTSD leads to depression and substance use. In addition, few attempts have been made to identify the factors that predict PTSD, depression, and substance use. This study will extend the literature by examining the relationships among PTSD, substance use, and depression symptoms over a one-year period in individuals who have experiencing a traumatic event. This study will also examine the risk and resilience factors that predict PTSD symptoms, and PTSD symptoms with co-occurring substance use or depression symptoms. Several of theses factors include sex, social support, and life stressors. A better understanding of the relationships between PTSD, substance use, and depression is necessary to identify Canadians at the greatest risk to develop these conditions after experiencing a trauma, and to improve treatments for individuals living with these conditions. The results of this study will guide treatment and prevention efforts, ultimately improving the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Variation in nicotine/nitrosamine pharmacology alters smoking behaviours and lung cancer risk: A genetic association and biomarker study
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC ASSOCIATION STUDY; GENETIC VARIATION IN CHRNA5-CHRNA3-CHRNB4; GENETIC VARIATION IN CYP2A6; GENETIC VARIATION IN CYP2B6; GENETICS OF LUNG CANCER RISK; GENETICS OF SMOKING BEHAVIOUR; NICOTINE AND NITROSAMINE PHARMACOLOGY; SMOKING BIOMARKER STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Smoking is the leading risk factor for lung cancer, but we cannot easily predict which smokers will develop cancer. The risk of lung cancer is influenced by how the body reacts to chemicals in cigarette smoke part of which is driven by our genetics. The metabolic enzyme, CYP2A6, and the nicotinic receptor gene cluster, CHRNA5-CHRNA3-CHRNB4, interact with the addictive chemical in cigarette smoke, nicotine, and interact with nitrosamines, which are potent lung carcinogens. Variation in the CYP2A6 and CHRNA5-CHRNA3-CHRNB4 genes affects the number of cigarettes smoked per day and lung cancer risk, but the combined impact of having variation in both genes is unknown. We found that variation in both CYP2A6 and CHRNA5-CHRNA3-CHRNB4 combined to further increase the number of cigarettes smoked per day and the risk of lung cancer. We also found that the association of CYP2A6 and CHRNA5-CHRNA3-CHRNB4 with lung cancer risk was especially strong in individuals smoking less than 20 cigarettes per day. Our study was in European American smokers. We plan to extend our findings to African American smokers, who are at a higher risk of lung cancer despite smoking fewer cigarettes per day. We will also investigate another nicotine and nitrosamine metabolizing gene, CYP2B6, to increase our ability to predict whether a smoker will develop lung cancer. To gain insight into how variation in these genes affects smoking behaviours and lung cancer risk, we will quantify the amount of nicotine and nitrosamines in smokers. By identifying smokers at increased risk of lung cancer, our findings can be used to target at-risk smokers for smoking cessation programs and other disease prevention strategies. By understanding the genetic influences on smoking behaviours and lung cancer risk, our findings will also guide new treatment strategies for smoking cessation and for lung cancer. This genetic approach can be applied to characterize the risk for other diseases attributable to smoking.

TitreApplicationTitle: Family-centred care in childhood diabetes: Parents' and health providers' experiences.
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREGIVING; CHILDHOOD DIABETES; FAMILY-CENTRED CARE; GROUNDED THEORY; HEALTHCARE DELIVERY; HEALTHCARE PROVIDERS; PARENT CAREGIVERS; QUALITATIVE STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Parents are increasingly involved in their children's medical care. Parents participate in care routines, coordinate services, and make treatment decisions. This participation is consistent with the idea of family-centred care. Research recognizes that family-centred care is associated with higher satisfaction with care, and better parental and child emotional and social well-being. Family-centred care is also linked with increased responsibility and burden on parents. As much as parents often want to be involved, managing complex care routines in light of multiple other responsibilities is no easy task. To develop true collaboration and partnership, a better understanding of family-centred care that carefully captures the experiences of both parent caregivers and healthcare providers is crucial. In this study, I plan to conduct interviews with parents and healthcare providers caring for children with diabetes. More specifically, I will explore how the current emphasis on parental involvement and partnership in healthcare is understood and experienced by parent caregivers and healthcare providers, and how it impacts their care work and relations with one another. Childhood diabetes is of interest because it is one of the most common childhood chronic illnesses, and requires an adoption of intensive nursing routine and frequent interactions between parents and healthcare providers. Given the increasing number of children with a chronic health condition and the growing number of parents involved in home-based healthcare work, knowledge and understanding of healthcare delivered in a family-centred manner has important implications for developing best practices in healthcare and social services, and in turn improving the health and quality of life of parent caregivers and their children.

TitreApplicationTitle: L'influence sur l'alliance thérapeutique d'une intervention cognitive-comportementale administrée par vidéoconférence dans le traitement du trouble d'anxiété généralisée
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLIANCE THERAPEUTIQUE; THERAPIE COGNITIVE-COMPORTEMENTALE; TRAITEMENTS EFFICACES; TROUBLE D'ANXIETE GENERALISEE; TELEPSYCHOTHERAPIE
Abstract-Résumé: S'inquieter represente une experience universelle, l'etre humain etant sans cesse confronte a de multiples situations ambigues et incertaines. Neanmoins, pour les individus souffrant du trouble d'anxiete generalisee (TAG), les inquietudes representent un reel cauchemar. Le TAG est un trouble caracterise par des inquietudes excessives et incontrolables, affectant considerablement la qualite de vie de ceux qui en souffrent. S'ajoutent aussi d'importantes repercussions socioeconomiques, le TAG etant associe a une utilisation demesuree et inadequate des services de sante. Le traitement de choix pour le TAG consiste en une therapie cognitif et comportementale (TCC). Toutefois, la TCC est peu accessible en regions eloignees etant donne un manque de specialistes possedant l'expertise necessaire pour l'administrer. La videoconference pourrait regler ce probleme en permettant aux individus souffrant de TAG de recevoir une TCC par un expert et ce, peu importe la distance les separant. Toutefois, il est important de se demander s'il est possible d'etablir une relation therapeutique de qualite malgre la distance physique. Comme la qualite de la relation entre le therapeute et son patient joue un role majeur dans l'efficacite d'une psychotherapie, il est necessaire de se questionner sur l'influence de cette technologie sur le developpement d'une relation therapeutique de qualite et, consequemment, sur l'efficacite du traitement. Dans cette etude, 60 individus souffrant de TAG recevront une TCC. Suite a une repartition aleatoire, la moitie d'entre eux recevra une TCC en face a face alors que l'autre moitie la recevra par videoconference. La presente etude evaluera ainsi l'impact de la videoconference dans une TCC pour le TAG sur le developpement de la relation therapeutique. Les resultats permettront d'amelioration des conditions de vie des individus TAG n'ayant pas acces aux ressources leur etant dues aux moyens d'une implantation eclairee de services de videoconference.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genome wide analysis of de novo copy number variation in families with autism spectrum disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; BIOINFORMATICS; COPY NUMBER VARIATION; DE NOVO; FAMILIES; GENOME WIDE; MICROARRAY; MUTATION; RECURRENT; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISM
Abstract-Résumé: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are known to have a strong genetic component; however, very few of the genes causing this risk have been identified. It is known that some of the genetic risk of ASD is caused by deletions or duplications of large sections of DNA called copy number variations (CNVs). The evidence for CNVs causing ASD is especially strong for large CNVs and de novo CNVs (new mutations seen in the child but not present in either parent). To date the largest study of CNVs in ASD was undertaken by our laboratory and totaled 4,457 samples from the Simons Simplex Collection (SSC). This study estimated that over 250 specific CNVs contribute to the genetics risk of ASD, however across all the literature only six of these specific CNVs have been identified with confidence. There is tremendous potential for more of these specific regions to be identified by larger CNV studies. The current project proposes to add an additional 7,000 samples from the SSC to the 4,457 already analyzed; this will be combined with data from 5,500 samples in the Autism Genetic Resource Exchange (AGRE) collection. The complete analysis will total about 17,000 samples, including parents, unaffected sibling controls and over 5,000 affected individuals. Comprehensive analysis of a dataset on this unprecedented scale will identify many more of the specific CNVs contributing to the genetic risk of ASD. These specific CNVs can be used inform ASD clinical diagnosis, allow future studies to investigate how these regions cause ASD, and potentially provide targets for the treatment of ASD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancing human pluripotent stem cell differentiation to pancreatic progenitors by control of endogenous cell signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: CO-CULTURE; DIABETES; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; ENDODERM; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; INSULIN-SECRETING CELL; PANCREAS; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; TISSUE ENGINEERING; TRANSPLANT
Abstract-Résumé: Type 1 diabetes mellitus, formerly juvenile diabetes, is a health condition caused by a lack of insulin, a hormone that lowers blood glucose. Patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus cannot produce insulin because their immune system has destroyed insulin-secreting beta cells in the pancreas. In the absence of insulin, their blood glucose rises, causing dysfunction in the eye, kidney, nervous system, heart, and circulatory system. These health problems represent a significant burden on both patients and the Canadian health care system. There is currently no cure for type 1 diabetes mellitus, and patients have an average 15 year reduction in life expectancy.  Insulin injections are currently used to replace insulin the body normally synthesizes, but even the most diligent patient will eventually experience complications related to higher than normal blood glucose. Transplantation of insulin-secreting beta cells from cadaver donors can restore normal insulin and blood glucose regulation, but there are too few donors to meet demand for cells. A possible solution to the limited numbers of insulin-secreting beta cells for transplantation is the creation of large amounts of these cells from human pluripotent stem cells. Human pluripotent stem cells can be converted, under the right conditions, to any type of cell in the body. My project will generate insulin-secreting beta cells from human pluripotent stem cells capable of treating type 1 diabetes mellitus. This approach has the potential to increase the quality of life for patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus and reduce the demand on the Canadian health care system.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; CLONE/SUBCLONE; GENETICS; IMMUNOLOGY; METABOLISM AND DESEASE; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; OBESITY; PROTEIN MANIPULATION AND EXPRESSION; RNAI/SHRNA; TUMOR SUPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is characterized by the excessive accumulation of white fat and is one of the most serious public health problems worldwide. Obesity is initiated from an imbalance between energy intake and expenditure and is a major risk factor for metabolic disorders such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Data from our lab showed that removal of folliculin gene (FLCN) in a simple organism (C. elegans) results in lean worms.  I observed that deletion of FLCN results in decrease in lipid production during 3T3L1 pre-adipocytes differentiation suggesting loss of FLCN could prevent fat store. I  plan to investigate the potential role of FLCN on fat metabolism and its molecular details using mouse model. This study will lead to an advance in understanding precisely of obesity and its molecular mechanism, and  could open new avenues for clinic therapeutic intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Wnt pathway activation in the maintenance of telomere integrity in intestinal crypt cells of telomerase-deficient mice.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; GASTROINTESTINAL PHYSIOLOGY; GENOMIC INSTABILITY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MOUSE GENETICS; STEM CELLS; TARGETED THERAPIES; TELOMERES; TRANSGENIC APPROACHES
Abstract-Résumé: The process of aging involves cell division and a subsequent shortening of telomeres - protein-DNA complexes that "cap" ends of chromosomes. Telomeres contribute to chromosome stability, and critically shortened telomeres are "uncapped," setting off a DNA damage response and results in programmed cell death (apoptosis) or cell cycle arrest (senescence).  Telomerase, present in many stem cells, is a protein-RNA complex that elongates telomeres. We study a mouse model lacking the RNA component of telomerase (TR), which exhibits telomere shortening across all tissues. One of the main pathologies that emerges is within the gastrointestinal (GI) epithelium. Physiologically, these mutant mice waste away compared to their wild-type littermates. Histologically, the mutant intestines exhibit morphologic distortion, inflammation, and increased telomere uncapping and apoptosis in intestinal crypts, where intestinal stem cells (ISCs) are located. The observed pathology is similar to human inflammatory bowel disease and some aging-related GI disorders.  We found that the expression of stem cell-specific genes under the control of the Wnt pathway are diminished in the TR mutants. Remarkably, pathology and stem cell gene expression in mutant mice are rescued by bone marrow transplant from wild-type donors, despite the fact that donor-derived cells do not contribute directly to the epithelia of the recipients. We hypothesized that the rescue was mediated by the Wnt pathway, and we have indeed recapitulated the rescue using short-term pharmacologic treatment with Wnt pathway agonists. Stimulating the Wnt pathway resulted in decreased apoptosis and improved telomere capping in the ISCs, improving overall GI health. We will explore the hypothesis that Wnt signaling improves telomere capping by upregulating key capping proteins. Understanding how Wnt signaling promotes telomere function in ISC biology holds promise for developing therapies for GI and aging-related diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Define the role of regulatory T cells in modulating inflammasome activity
Keywords-MotsClés: FLOW CYTOMETRY; INFLAMMATION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INTESTINAL EPITHELIUM; NALP3 INFLAMMASOME; RT-PCR; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is an incurable inflammatory disorder that constitutes a significant public health burden in Canada. What causes IBD is unknown, but it is believed to be an abnormal inflammatory response that attacks the tissue in the intestinal tract. Normally, a type of white blood cells called regulatory T cells (Tregs) helps to suppress unnecessary inflammation, and boosting the activity of Tregs could prevent or treat IBD. A protein called NLRP3 is required for the production of certain potent inflammatory proteins. Therefore, NLRP3 has been thought to play a pathogenic role in inflammatory disorders, such as IBD. Recently, it was identified that functional NLRP3 was crucial for maintaining a healthy gut. Supporting this idea, several studies found mice that did not make any NLRP3 got IBD more easily compared to mice that did make NLRP3.  My research is focused on evaluating how Tregs affect NLRP3 function. While Tregs generally shut off inflammatory responses, we found that they were able to enhance NLRP3 function and the production of inflammatory proteins. In order to understand this process, I will study how Tregs regulate NLRP3 function and the biological consequences of this regulation.  This research will help our current understanding of the protective role of NLRP3 and Tregs and help to provide a better view of how Tregs function in IBD and also evaluate their potential as a therapy to prevent or treat IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Symbiont-encoded proteins as modulators of the host innate immune response in a model sponge-archaeal symbiosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARCHAEA; EVOLUTION; GENOMICS; IMMUNOLOGY; MICROBIOME; PHYLOGENETICS; SERPINS; SYMBIOSIS; TRANSCRIPTOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: The proper development and healthy functioning of the gastrointestinal tract and immune system in humans and other organisms depends on their association with symbiotic microorganisms. However, the molecular recognition mechanisms used to establish such relationships and differentiate symbiotic microbes from disease-causing pathogens are not well understood. Sponges are the most ancient group of extant animals that host vast and complex microbial communites. Therefore, sponge-microbial symbioses represent some of the oldest associations between animals and microorganisms, thus serving as useful model systems to explore symbiotic interactions. The first sponge-archaeal association described is the symbiosis between the sponge Axinella mexicana and its symbiont, Cenarchaeum symbiosum. The symbiont genome encodes for proteins potentially involved in mediating symbiosis, including five serpins, a protein family present in viruses and all domains of life implicated in a variety of functions including cell signaling and hormone transport. C. symbiosum serpins may be important in mediating this symbiosis by modulating the sponge immune response. The goal of this study is to identify the mechanisms underlying the A.mexicana-C. symbiosum relationship for cell signaling such that the symbiont does not elicit a host innate immune response without impairing the ability of the host to respond to pathogens and infections. Cultivation-independent approaches will be used to identify serpin targets and the host molecules involved in innate immune signaling. The results of this research will provide insight into evolutionarily-conserved pathways used in immune recognition with the possibility to discover novel, as yet-unknown mechanisms of cellular communication. Comparative analysis between sponge, insect and mammalian signaling pathways will shed light on how organisms, including humans, interact with and benefit from their microbial symbionts.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIOXIDANTS; OBESITY; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: A majority of North Americans are overweight or obese. Obesity is a well known risk factor for various heart diseases. One underlying feature of cardiovascular diseases is the presence of oxidative stress, which can damage the mitochondria, cellular structures that are crucial for energy production. Oxidative stress is a condition that occurs when free radicals cannot be neutralized adequately by cellular antioxidants. In the heart, glutathione is a major antioxidant, which is known to be decreased in obese humans and animals.  I believe that glutathione is reduced in obese hearts due to faulty biosynthesis. Thus I will investigate the enzymatic mechanisms responsible for creating and maintaining the levels of glutathione in the heart of obese mice by comparing samples from the hearts of mice fed a low fat diet versus high-fat diet (obese). This research will provide a better understanding of the regulation and expression of glutathione in the obese heart and may lead to strategies to better manage and prevent cardiovascular disease in individuals by improving the levels of this antioxidant.

Keywords-MotsClés: CHIP; CHONDROGENESIS; CHROMATIN; EPIGENETICS; GENOMIC LOOPING; HISTONE MODIFICATION; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; NON-CODING RNA; SKELETAL DEVELOPMENT; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: The human genome contains vast amounts of DNA that does not code for genes.  Previously thought of as 'junk' DNA, new evidence suggests that these sequences help determine when and where genes are active, through processes referred to as 'epigenetic regulation'.  DNA defects in these non-coding regions can lead to human disease, as is the case in Campomelic Dysplasia (CPMD), a disease characterized by severe short stature, facial deformities, and defective bone development.  My research aims to understand how epigenetic factors, like the protein CTCF, and non-coding genomic sequences regulate gene expression using cartilage development and the CPMD genomic region as a model.  These discoveries will help us understand how defects in non-coding regions normally contribute to genetic skeletal diseases and have potential impact for personalized medicine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving the health of artisanal and small-scale gold miners: Development, implementation, and assessment of an innovative knowledge transfer program.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTISANAL AND SMALL-SCALE GOLD MINERS; CANADA; CAPACITY BUILDING; GENDER; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MERCURY; MINING TECHNOLOGY; MONGOLIA; OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY; POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: With the high price of gold and the status of the global economy, artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM), is a rapidly expanding industry that involves men, women and children. ASGM does not require any specialized equipment or training, and represents an important mechanism for poverty alleviation. However, ASGM often uses mercury to purify the gold, a dangerous heavy metal that then contaminates the local environment and the atmosphere. Mercury can then travel long distances and deposit all across the globe. In Canada, mercury deposits from the atmosphere have contaminated the traditional food of Inuit populations and led to serious health concerns. The use of mercury in ASGM is a global transboundary issue and priority area for organizations such as the World Health Organization and United Nations.   This project will drastically reduce the usage of mercury and improve the health of ASGM communities in Mongolia, which will have positive implications for the health of Canadians. Firstly, we will introduce a world-class knowledge translation educational program on safer mercury-free mining practices. Secondly, we will assess the health of an ASGM community in Mongolia and health improvements introduced resulting from this project. This will be an important contribution towards understanding the health and safety issues of mercury use in ASGM. Lastly, we will share the developed educational program and knowledge with other ASGM sites and international policy development in order to further reduce mercury usage and emissions.
