Keywords-MotsClés: ENVIRONMENTAL SCAN; GENDER; HEALTH SERVICES AND POLICY; INTERNATIONALLY EDUCATED PROFESSIONALS; KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS; PANCANADIAN; SCOPING REVIEW; SEX AND HEALTH; SURVEY DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Nearly 10% of Canadian nurses were educated in another country. Unfortunately, a larger percentage of internationally educated nurses never become licensed or work as nurses in Canada. Thus the healthcare system is not able to benefit from the knowledge, skills and experience these nurses bring with them when they come to Canada. This research project will examine the reasons why some internationally educated nurses are successful in becoming nurses in Canada, and identify the programs available to help them pass a licensing examination and find work in their profession. Information from this research can be used to develop and modify educational programs and social program to assist internationally educated nurses become eligible to practice their profession and find work in Canada. The knowledge gained can also be used to develop training programs to help internationally educated nurses develop the competencies required to work in clinical settings that need more manpower, such as long-term care facilities. Employers and regulatory agencies can use the information to develop strategies to retain internationally educated nurses in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gender-based determinants of psychological adaptation and work reintegration following physical workplace violence
Keywords-MotsClés: MENTAL HEALTH; POSTTRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDERS; RETURN TO WORK; SEX AND GENDER DIFFERENCES; WORKPLACE VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Work plays an important role in our society where employment is considered to be the norm. Moreover, work has several benefits on health. However, when the workplace becomes a "toxic environment", keeping your job becomes tricky, such as when a worker is victim of physical workplace violence (PWV) (e.g. assault). According to Statistics Canada, certain occupational groups are more at risk of exposure to PWV (e.g. workers in the healthcare). PWV can have multiple consequences on physical and psychological health. Moreover, PWV can also have numerous repercussions for the victim, the organization, and society. It has been shown that people experiencing PWV are more at risk to develop posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and have more trouble going back to work. Also, the relation to the perpetrator (supervisor/colleague/patient/outsider) may impact work-related outcomes in specific ways. Furthermore, there are gender differences/similarities regarding the causes and consequences of PWV, the risk of developing PTSD as well as health-seeking behaviours and work reintegration process. Despite the importance of the issue, little is known regarding the aftermath of PWV, particularly on returning to work after a sick leave. Therefore, the general objective of this project is to better understand the determinants of psychological adaptation and work reintegration following PWV, considering gender differences. Specific objectives are to: 1) assess the consequences of PWV on mental health and work-related outcomes; 2) establish the profiles of workers who go on sick leave after experiencing PWV and to study the trajectory of their work reintegration process and their quality of work life; and 3) evaluate facilitators (e.g. social support) and barriers (e.g. fear) for work reintegration after PWV having caused or not PTSD. For these objectives, gender differences will be taken into account. This project will contribute to the development of original knowledge on PWV.

Abstract-Résumé: Canadian men are more likely to suffer from the leading causes of death than women, partly due to men's poor engagement in health promotion programs and activities. There is a lack of research evidence to guide the development of men-centred health promotion services and programs. That said, workplace health promotion programs are known to assist workers to reduce risk behaviours (e.g., smoking) and improve healthy practices (healthy eating and exercise habits); however, women are more likely to participate and benefit from such programs than men. This suggests that we are missing opportunities for engaging men in health promotion activities in the workplace. The proposed project will explore men's needs and recommendations in order to create a workplace health promotion program that will help men improve their health.   A needs analysis will assure that the program is grounded in the men's experiences and preferences as a means to engaging men with their health and health promotion activities. The first phase will include conducting one-on-one interviews with managers and focus groups with men working at Vancouver General Hospital (VGH). Findings from these interviews and focus groups will inform the second phase, to design a health promotion program for men that will be piloted at VGH. The final phase will involve pilot testing the program and applying for funding to launch a full scale project that will include evaluating the program at a range of venues, including several large employers which have expressed interest in hosting a program. The proposed 3 year project is supported by the Men's Health Initiative and affiliated researchers from UBC, and hosted by VGH and Vancouver Coastal Health Authority.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Prospective Investigation of the Relationship between Division of Household Labour and Women's Sexual Pleasure and Desire
Keywords-MotsClés: DAILY DIARIES; GENDER ROLES; HOUSEHOLD LABOR; PROSPECTIVE DESIGN; QUESTIONNAIRES; SEXUAL DESIRE; SEXUAL DESIRE/INTEREST DISORDER; SEXUAL PLEASURE; UNPAID WORK
Abstract-Résumé: Many women worry that they have too little sexual desire, and this affects their relationships and mood. Research has not found any physical differences between women with high and low levels of sexual desire. Since women's desire often decreases in long-term relationships, it is possible that relationship issues cause or maintain low desire.  For instance, doing an unfair amount of household work (e.g., chores, childcare) may cause women to resent their spouses, feel more depressed, or remember experiencing less pleasure the last time they had sex, all of which can reduce desire. This study aims to investigate how the division of household work affects sexual desire, mood, and the pleasure women experience during sex. We will need to exclude women who have current depression. In conclusion, we want to understand the effect of couples' division of household work so that we can better focus our treatment of women who have low desire.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the influence of motor and cognitive symptoms on the well-being of male and female spouse-caregivers of persons with Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BURDEN; GENDER DIFFERENCES; INTERVIEWS; LIFE SATISFACTION; MEDIATING FACTORS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PARKINSON'S DISEASE DEMENTIA; SPOUSE CAREGIVERS; SYMPTOM-SPECIFIC PREDICTORS OF WELL-BEING
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) are chronic, progressive and result in constant care. AD presents as cognitive decline, PD is identified by motor impairment and PD associated dementia (PDD) results in combined motor-cognitive dysfunction. Dementia caregivers suffer from higher stress than other groups. Despite this, unique challenges associated with different caregiver groups have yet to be compared. Objective: understand unique contribution of cognitive decline (AD), motor impairment (PD) and combined motor-cognitive dysfunction (PDD) on caregiver well-being. Evaluation of life-satisfaction and depression will determine well-being in 3 spouse-caregiver groups. Burden, coping and gender differences will be examined. Caregiving stress is associated with worse well-being. We expect this study will show how combined cognitive-motor dysfunction influences worse caregiver well-being than declining cognition or motor impairment alone. Dementia affects 4% of older adults, with 5-million new cases/year. The growing burden of dementia care presents unique challenges for healthcare. The bulk of this burden falls on spouse-caregivers, emphasizing research needs to focus on how to best support this group. Care-for-caregivers has increased in recent years, yet how unique symptoms impact their well-being still needs to be addressed. Current research shows stress, burden and poor health in dementia caregivers. This study will contribute novel research by comparing well-being related to specific cognitive and/or motor symptoms in 3 caregiver groups. These findings will advance knowledge by identifying symptom-specific predictors of caregiver burden, health and well-being. Understanding symptom-specific predictors of well-being will inform resources that improve caregiver support and quality of life, even as dementia progresses. By sustaining dementia caregivers and ensuring their burden is reduced we improve quality of life of both caregivers and receivers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Etude de l'impact du polymorphisme naturel du VIH1 groupe O sur la résistance aux antirétroviraux et sur la cinétique d'apparition des mutations de résistance
Keywords-MotsClés: CAPACITE REPLICATIVE; MUTAGENESE DIRIGEE; MUTATIONS DE RESISTANCE; RESISTANCE GENOTYPIQUE; RESISTANCE PHENOTYPIQUE; VIH-1 GROUPE O
Abstract-Résumé: Le VIH est un virus doue d'une forte variabilite genetique evolutive ce qui a pour consequence directe la difficulte, depuis sa decouverte, d'evaluer et d'adapter sans cesse les techniques de diagnostic, de suivi, de traitement comme par exemple la mise au point du vaccin. Le VIH se divise en deux types, VIH1 et VIH2, eux-memes comprenant plusieurs groupes et sous-types. Le VIH1 de groupe M (VIHM) est le virus le plus repandu et responsable de la pandemie actuelle. Cependant, l'infection par des variants plus rares comme le VIH-1 groupe O (VIHO) est une preoccupation constante car ces variants sont tres differents du VIHM et peuvent donc etre mal detectes par les techniques actuelles qui sont developpees a partir du VIHM. De plus, la variabilite plus importante de ces variants peut avoir un impact sur la reponse aux traitements et le developpement de la resistance. Ainsi, ce travail de recherche se propose de faire avancer les connaissances sur ce virus dans le domaine du developpement de la resistance en analysant la sensibilite du virus aux antiretroviraux et les mecanismes de l'emergence de la resistance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Telomere Length as a Putative Biomarker of Human Immunodeficiency Virus-Associated Cognitive Impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANTIRETROVIRAL TREATMENT; COGNITION; DEMENTIA; HIV/AIDS; NEUROLOGY; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; NEUROSCIENCE; TELOMERE; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: More than 33 million people are infected with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) worldwide, including 30.8 million adults.  Up to 50 percent of adults with chronic HIV infection have some form of cognitive impairment, including dementia. This study aims to look at a marker of cellular aging - telomeres - in people with HIV, comparing those with and without HIV-related cognitive impairment for telomere length. Telomeres are sequences of DNA found at the ends of chromosomes.  Telomeres shorten with the life of a dividing cell. Disorders of telomeres, also known as the "telomeropathies," are associated with premature organ failure and aging. To date, there is limited information on telomeres in HIV-associated cognitive decline.  We will take a well-studied cohort of volunteers with HIV who have donated blood every 6 months for approximately 7 years.  This study is called the CNS HIV Anti-retroviral Therapy Effects Research (CHARTER) cohort and involves participants at 6 universities.  We hope to discover whether loss of telomere length is an important marker of cognitive impairment in people with treated HIV.  This information will be useful in understanding the mechanisms of HIV in the nervous system in aging individuals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Appraising the Social and Ethical Dimensions of HIV Treatment-As-Prevention
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS; CRITICAL SOCIAL SCIENCE; ETHICS; HIV/AIDS; PUBLIC HEALTH; QUALITATIVE; TREATMENT TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: This project explores recent advancements in HIV that promote the use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) as a way to not only slow the progression of HIV in individuals, but also reduce HIV infection in at risk communities. A number of research studies, many conducted in Canada, have shown the benefits of a treatment-as-prevention approach where people living with HIV are put on treatment early to improve their health and reduce their infectiousness. However, some scholars have raised concerns about the possible consequences for people living with HIV and health care providers tasked with monitoring treatment adherence. In particular, concerns have been raised about the implications for people who refuse treatment or are unable to adhere to their drug regimen. Currently, those most affected have not been included in these debates. This project will interview people living with HIV and healthcare providers working in the HIV sector to explore the ethical and social dimensions of these new prevention approaches. The goal is to find ways of addressing practitioner and community level concerns in a way that attends to the complexity of  HIV. This research has implications for the management of other chronic illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Redesigning care models for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV among indigenous women in Papua, Indonesia
Keywords-MotsClés: CULTURE; GENDER; HIV; INDIGENOUS; INTERVENTION; MATERNAL-CHILD HEALTH; PREGNANCY; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Indigenous women's access to HIV services is shaped by gendered cultural norms surrounding pregnancy, childbirth, and newborn care.  Increased scrutiny from kin to a pregnant woman's diet, medications and mobility, and approaches to childbirth and newborn care that depend on the advice and practices of female kin constrain women's ability to keep their HIV status a secret. Complicated familial relationships are only one set of challenges; a second area of difficulty is relationships built with outreach and support providers who are typically nurses, doctors, or non-governmental organization staff. It is unclear how different models of care within the normative model of PMTCT may affect women's ability and willingness to use HIV services. In a highly stigmatized environment, this intervention study seeks to improve pregnant women's health and HIV outcomes through an understanding of the relationship between PMTCT service providers, their models of outreach and care, and the needs and experiences of indigenous HIV positive pregnant women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Respondent Driven Sampling as a Tool for Community-Based Health Assessment and Health Service Evaluation within the Context of Addiction and Mental Health among Aboriginal people in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; COMMUNITY-BASED METHODS; HEALTH INEQUALITIES; MENTAL HEALTH; SUBSTANCE USE; SURVEY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: First Nations, Metis and Inuit populations experience poorer mental and physical health compared to other Canadians. One reason for this is that there is very little health information available on these issues. There is also a lack of culturally appropriate tools and methods for identifying and measuring health and social characteritics from an Indigenous perspective.  More mental health and addictions information that is based in local culture and is representative of these communities is needed.  This research project will build on a proven community-based method called Respondent Driven Sampling (RDS) to get Aboriginal families to participate in a cohort study.  RDS is a unique tool because it relies on people to recruit their own peers into the study and generates unbiased population health information.  In particular, data on mental health conditions and the use of illicit drugs will provide much needed knowledge on how frequent and serious these issues are, particularly in off-reserve Aboriginal communities.  The information gathered through this research will help ongoing Aboriginal community services and program evaluations and will contribute to the overall deficiency in available public health information on Aboriginal people in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Perspectives on Revitalizing and Supporting Sustainable Food Systems and Improving Food Security from Three Remote First Nations Communities in Northern Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: FIRST NATIONS; FOOD SECURITY; FOOD SYSTEMS; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH AND ANALYSIS; REMOTE AND NORTHERN HEALTH; VISUAL UNDERSTANDING ENVIRONMENT (VUE) MAPPING
Abstract-Résumé: Food insecurity has been described in the research literature as an urgent and pervasive public health issue for Aboriginal people (First Nations, Metis, and Inuit) in Canada. Historically, the entire way of life for Aboriginal people revolved around their food source, self-sustenance, and a subsistence livelihood. However, in recent decades, Aboriginal populations living in northern communities have been increasingly vulnerable to the transformation of local culture and society, including a significant shift from a primarily subsistence way of life. Local food production in remote and northern communities is a potential avenue for improving food security, yet little information is known about how to support sustainable local food systems.   The main purpose of this project is to gain a better understanding of the factors that help a community collectively move towards greater food security by their improvement of local food systems from the perspectives of community members in three remote First Nations communities in northern Ontario. The study uses a survey questionnaire  and interviews that have been approved by community advisory committees in each community. Findings from the questionnaires and interviews will be used to create a conceptual model for each community that depicts key demographic, social and personal (belief and values) variables at the individual level as well as barriers to and supports for food security and local food systems at the community level.  This proposed research can improve the health of First Nations populations living in northerly locations by identifying factors that can support local northern food systems and policies to strengthen community food security initiatives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sharing Women's Knowledge: Understanding Mobility, Relationality, and Identity as Pathways to Improving Urban Aboriginal Maternal and Family Health and Birthing Services
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGIANL MATERNAL AND FAMILY HEALTH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; POPULATION MIGRATION/MOBILITY; RESPONDENT DRIVEN SAMPLING; URBAN ABORIGINAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: In recent decades, Aboriginal peoples in Canada have become increasingly urbanized. Due to a history of social, economic, and political inequalities, urban population growth has been accompanied by high rates of movement between reserve/rural areas and urban areas, as well as within urban areas. Aboriginal women make up a large proportion of this mobile population, and the majority are lone parents. Frequent moving can impact health, and frequent movers and urban newcomers may experience unique difficulties in accessing health services. Further to this, Aboriginal women face poorer health when compared to non-Aboriginal Canadian women and many do not access timely prenatal care, which may contribute to poor health outcomes for mothers, children, and families. Despite these circumstances, urban Aboriginal women remain under-represented in Canadian Aboriginal health research. To address these knowledge gaps, this research addresses the distinctive health needs of mobile urban Aboriginal women of reproductive age. This project seeks to understand how factors such as moving from place to place, being part of social networks, and accessing culturally relevant health services impact holistic health. We also examine how frequent movement to or within the city of Toronto impacts access to prenatal and childbirth services for young Aboriginal families. This project is undertaken in partnership with an Aboriginal-led community health service program that provides maternity care to Aboriginal mothers. We will conduct a survey that focuses on the health and health care service experiences of 500 Aboriginal women of reproductive age and 500 of their children. Their knowledge will be used to inform responsive, culturally relevant health care interventions that will serve to improve the health of Aboriginal women and families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inter-Organizational Collaboration for Patient Transitions: Exploring the Relationship between Policy and Practice in England and Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: CRITICAL SOCIAL THEORY; GERIATRICS; GERONTOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HOME CARE; HOSPITAL DISCHARGE; OLDER ADULTS; PATIENT TRANSITIONS; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Older adult patients often have complex needs associated with multiple chronic conditions, which complicates the process of discharging older adults from hospital to return home to independent living. The process of being discharged from hospital to home is referred to as patient transitions, and health service providers from hospitals and home care agencies must communicate and collaborate effectively to ensure transitions are as efficient and manageable as possible for older adults and their families. Collaboration amongst health service providers from hospitals and home care agencies is known to be influenced by certain factors that facilitate or inhibit how well they work together, including formal 'policy' issues such as required documentation and performance reporting as well as informal 'practice' issues such as professional expectations and relationships. How these factors affecting collaboration influence the way health care organizations work together to ensure efficient and manageable transitions for elderly patients with complex needs has not been the focus of research in health care. This research project seeks to describe how service providers and administrators of health care organizations and government policy makers perceive 'policy' and 'practice' factors to facilitate or inhibit efforts of health care organizations to work together when helping older adult patients with complex needs transition from care in a hospital to living independently at home. By comparing the findings from research interviews in London, England and Toronto, Ontario, this study will provide a more thorough description of the facilitating and inhibiting factors than would be possible if focused on a single site. The findings of this study will be integrated into efforts to improve communication and collaboration between service providers at hospital and home care agencies, improving the transition process from hospital to home for older adult patients with complex needs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional characterization of HIV-1 viral infectivity factor (Vif): A novel axis for the design of anti-HIV drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS (ACQUIRED IMMUNODEFICIENCY SYNDROME); HIV (HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS); NMR SPECTROSCOPY; PROTEIN BIOCHEMISTRY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; SURFACE PLASMON RESONANCE; VIRAL INFECTIVITY FACTOR; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Once HIV enters its target cells in the human immune system, it releases its genetic material. In order for the virus to fully replicate in those immune cells, it needs to make a DNA copy of its genetic material. To prevent the generation of this DNA copy, the infected cells activate potent immune system enzymes termed the apolipoprotein B mRNA-editing catalytic polypeptide3 (APOBEC3) family of restriction factors. These enzymes cause aberrations in the viral genetic material, thereby inactivating the viral infection. However, fully-replicating HIV encodes for a protein termed viral infectivity factor (Vif). Vif binds to APOBEC3, targets it for degradation, and neutralizes the antiviral effect of APOBEC3.  In our research, we propose to study the structure of HIV's viral infectivity factor (Vif); a protein discovered 20 years ago and currently believed by many researchers to be the most attractive target for the development of new anti-HIV drugs. The structural studies on this very difficult viral protein had been practically impossible, before I worked out the optimal conditions to prepare exceptionally high levels of soluble protein. Given my preliminary results, our lab is now in a strong position to study and fully describe the atomic-resolution structure of Vif. Vis's structure will give us, and the HIV research community worldwide, clues to the mechanistic action of Vif in general, and on APOBEC3 in particular. In addition, Vif's structure will provide a 'blueprint' for future design of new classes of HIV-1 therapeutics that can inactivate highly mutagenic HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of childhood bullying on high-risk sexual behaviour among gay and bisexual men.
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV PREVENTION; HIV TRANSMISSION; MSM; PSYCHOLOGICAL PREDICTORS; SEXUAL FUNCTIONING; SEXUAL HEALTH; SEXUAL RISK BEHAVIOURS
Abstract-Résumé: Despite education and prevention efforts aimed at reducing high-risk sexual behaviour among men who have sex with men (MSM), MSM continue to have disproportionately higher rates of HIV infection than any other group in Canada. MSM also suffer from mental health problems such as mood, anxiety, and substance abuse disorders at a higher rate than their heterosexual counterparts, and research has shown a positive correlation between psychological problems and sexual risk-taking among adult MSM. One possible cause of mental health problems and HIV risk behaviour is the severity of bullying during childhood.  Evidence suggests that being the recipient of childhood bullying is associated with poor mental health outcomes among MSM. The present study will examine the association between childhood bullying severity and high-risk sexual behaviour among MSM such as number of high-risk sexual partners and number of instances of unprotected anal intercourse.  It will also examine the role that social anxiety, internalized homophobia, and self-esteem play in the association between childhood bullying and high-risk sexual behaviour among MSM. The present study will help researchers to better understand some of the factors that influence risky sexual behaviour in order to design more effective HIV prevention and mental health programs for this vulnerable population with the goal of reducing both mental health problems and HIV sexual risk behaviour in this high-risk population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular telomere and mitochondrial aging in HIV infection and associated factors
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; GENETICS; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNOLOGICAL CELL SEPARATION; QUANTITATIVE PCR; TELOMERE ATTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: HIV is a virus that causes immune dysfunction and can be passed from mother to child. People living with HIV age faster but it is unclear whether this is related to HIV infection or to antiretroviral therapy (ART). ART is used to treat HIV+ children and adults. It is also used in HIV+ pregnant women to decrease mother-to-child transmission of the virus, but is known to cross the placenta and expose the foetus to drugs. ART can also inhibit the replication of telomeres that protect the ends of our DNA molecules from damage. Inhibition of telomere replication results in telomere shortening each time a stem cell divides. Short telomeres are linked to shorter life, accelerated aging, and the earlier appearance of age-related illnesses such as cardiovascular and neurodegenerative diseases. HIV itself can also damage telomeres and potentially accelerate aging.  The objective of my project is to investigate the rate of telomere decline over the lifetimes of HIV+ and HIV uninfected (HIV-) children born to HIV+ mothers who were treated with ART during their pregnancy, and compare these to HIV- control children. I will measure telomere length in blood samples that were collected throughout the life of HIV+ children who have never taken ART and compare to HIV+ children who have been on ART almost their whole life and also to HIV- children, born to HIV+ or HIV- mothers. I will try to determine what effect on telomere length is related to the virus or ART, or both. The results from this project will help us understand aging in people living with HIV and may help HIV caregivers to decide when to start or stop ART in HIV+ children or HIV+ pregnant women.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effects of run sprint interval training on dietary intake
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION; DIETARY INTAKE; INTERVAL TRAINING; METABOLIC ADAPTATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: In 2010, Statistics Canada reported that over 50% of Canadians are overweight or obese. As we know, nutrition and physical activity play major roles in the prevention and treatment of obesity and are a required element of a healthy lifestyle.  Finding ways to make these two easily incorporable into people's lifestyles is still a challenge for dietitians and exercise physiologists, and different strategies are being investigated.  One strategy, a running regimen that is up to 50% less time consuming than regular continuous running, is sprint interval training (SIT).  SIT is characterized by repeated small bouts of "all-out" sprints followed by longer rest intervals. Previous studies conducted on SIT have found significant fat loss and metabolic adaptations in participants in the SIT group similar to the endurance-training group, but in much less intervention time.  Results demonstrated considerable increased energy expenditure in the recovery phase after the exercise but the total expenditure could not account for the chronic fat loss, suggesting that food intake is affected or substrate oxidation, such as fat utilization, changes over weeks of training.  This research project will combine the areas of nutrition and kinesiology in measuring the effects of SIT on the acute and chronic dietary intake of participants over the course of a 6-week training program.  Through food diaries and recorded buffet meals, food intake of participants will be measured and evaluated before and throughout the exercise program.  Results from this study will help understand the effects of this exercise regimen on food intake, metabolism and could lead to further research on the fat loss capacity of SIT.  Ultimately, dietary and physical activity recommendations could be generated to the general adult population as part of a weight loss program.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Subvention d'équipe : appel à projets conjoint en recherche sur le vieillissement - ERA-AGE2
TitreApplicationTitle: AAL-WELL:  Ambient Assistive Living Technologies for Wellness, Engagement, and Long Life
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; MULTI-CULTURAL; OLDER ADULTS; SMART HOMES; TECHNOLOGY; TRANSDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH; USER DRIVEN RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: With people across the world living longer, we need to find new ways to support them to live and age as well as possible. This involves helping people to maintain their independence and keep physically and mentally active for as long as they can. The AAL-WELL project aims to explore how a new type of technology called ambient assistive living (AAL) technology can be used to promote active and healthy aging, particularly amongst people with mild cognitive impairment, who may need additional help and support in their everyday lives. The project comprises four parts in which we will work with older adults in three different countries to identify their priorities for active and healthy aging, develop novel AAL technologies to support these priorities and test the technologies in the real-world by putting them into the older adult's homes. Our focus will be on identifying the priorities of older adults in two key areas - independent completion of self-care activities and keeping mentally active. In part one we will learn about the needs and preferences of older adults, particularly to find out how they vary in different countries and cultures, to help us work out what  types of technologies we should build and what features we need to include. Next, we will take this information and use it to develop specific examples of innovative and novel AAL technologies, which we will show to older adults to get their feedback at each stage of the development process. Once we have made these new technologies we will ask older adults in each of the three countries to test them out in their own homes. As the project team is spread across three countries we will also carry out various activities to ensure that the information collected in AAL-WELL is relevant to people with different national and cultural backgrounds and that it reaches the appropriate organisations and services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hearing, Remembering, and Living Well: Paying Attention to Challenges that Older Adults Face in Noisy Environments
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ATTENTION; COGNITION; EFFORT; HEARING; MEMORY; MOBILITY; NOISE; SECOND LANGUAGE; SPEECH UNDERSTANDING
Abstract-Résumé: It has become increasingly clear that the difficulties that older adults have in understanding what people are saying limit their access to public spaces and interfere with their ability to socialize. Clearly, the inability of older adults to understand what is being said in the noisy situations of everyday life limits their activities, and often results in loss of standing in the family and community.  As a result of the "greying" of the population, governments, non-government organizations, and seniors themselves are becoming increasingly aware of the issue, and, as a result, there is a buildup of pressure to take steps to make public spaces "hearing accessible" to older adults, and to help them overcome or compensate for their hearing difficulties.  The purpose of this grant is to conduct the research that will permit these interested groups to take steps to remedy this situation based on scientifically collected evidence.  Specifically, the goals of this research are to: 1) identify the situations in which older adults experience communication difficulties; 2) develop means of determining, on an individual basis, the nature of any hearing or attentional problems contributing to these difficulties; 3) develop assistive hearing devices and training strategies that will help older adults cope with  these communication problems; and 4) develop a set of recommendations as to how public gathering spaces can be made more "hearing accessible" to older adults.

TitreApplicationTitle: Healthy Ageing in Residential Places
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCOUNTABILITY; AGEING; GENDER; HEALTH POLICY; LONG-TERM CARE; OWNERSHIP; QUALITY OF CARE; THEORIES OF CARE; WORK ORGANIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Active ageing allows "people to realize their potential for physical, social, and mental well-being throughout the life course and to participate in society, while providing them with adequate protection, security and care when they need"(World Health Organization). Most policy focuses on keeping people out of long-term residential care, even though many people live in these places now and will in the future. Little attention has been paid to the ageing labour force in these places or to the fact that residential care is mainly care for women by women. With a view of health that includes mental, physical, emotional, social and spiritual aspects, we seek to identify healthy ageing strategies for long-term residential care that allow both staff and residents to live better, and perhaps longer, more fulfilling lives, potentially saving money by reducing the medical and other care required for residents and staff. Our international project is based on comparative, collaborative, case studies lead by experienced teams. It will offer detailed information on physical, economic, environmental, social, and behavioral conditions that shape and define healthy ageing for residents and staff in specific facilities. It begins by collecting and analyzing existing information and research reports on Canada, the UK, Sweden and Norway to set the context for understanding specific residences. Our main technique involves a new method in this field - rapid site-switching ethnography, designed to capture the rich detail necessary to identify strategies for active, healthy ageing by bringing local and foreign researchers together to study two facilities in each country. They will observe staff and residents, provide the residents with cameras as a way of expressing their views, and interview staff and residents about their experiences, bringing fresh eyes to these sites while ensuring a local perspective.

TitreApplicationTitle: International Network for Evaluation of Outcomes (iNeo)  of Neonates: A Quality Improvement Project via Collaborative Comparison of International Health Services for Neonatal Care
Keywords-MotsClés: BENCHMARKING; DEVELOPING POLICY/PRACTICE CHANGE; HEALTH SERVICES EVALUATION; INFANT; INTERNATIONAL COMPARISON; OUTCOMES; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT; VERY PREMATURE
Abstract-Résumé: Various national neonatal networks have been established which collect data from their network sites. These networks have performed remarkably well in analyzing data on a periodic basis to compare outcomes within their constituents. Despite practically similar technological advances and understanding of pathological processes, marked variations in outcomes have been reported internationally. In our preliminary analyses, we identified differences in outcomes of very preterm and very low birth weight infants from Canada, Japan and Australia-New Zealand. It is perceived that these variations could be due to differences in population characteristics, severity of illness when infants are born, methods of health care delivery, and other factors related to the units/countries where babies are cared for. It is important to characterize the reasons for such differences and then identify areas of improvement for all networks. Our objectives in this multicentre, multinational study are to: (1) Compare neonatal outcomes, processes of care and health care services for very low birth weight neonates among various international neonatal networks; (2) Identify areas of improvement in neonatal outcomes relevant to individual neonatal networks; (3) Implement changes that are needed to improve outcomes; and (4) Continually evaluate the impact of data-informed and evidence-linked practice changes relevant to different heath care systems. This project will lead to improved outcomes of neonates and ultimately lead to overall improvement in global health. At this stage population-based networks from Australia and New Zealand, Canada, Israel, Japan, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and the UK have agreed to participate in this endeavour. We will develop a uniform platform for data collection, transfer, analyses, reporting, and feedback and then identify areas of improvement, implement improvement strategies and re-evaluate outcomes to complete a continuous cycle of improvement of care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physician Recommendations for Cancer Screening: Examining the role of physician perceptions of health literacy, language proficiency and culture
Keywords-MotsClés: CHART STIMULATED RECALL; CHINESE AMERICANS; DOCTOR-PATIENT COMMUNICATION; HEALTH DISPARITIES; INTERVIEW; MINORITY WOMEN; PREVENTIVE CANCER SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: Breast and colorectal cancer are two of the leading causes of cancer death among Chinese American women.  In fact, incidence of invasive breast cancer has declined among all US women from 2000-2007 except Asian American women; incidence for this group increased. Early detection through regular screening increases survival rates. Compared to non-Hispanic whites, older Chinese American women have lower rates of breast and colorectal cancer screening participation and received fewer FOBT screening recommendations. Physician recommendation is the primary factor for participation in cancer screening. Yet, older women who speak English-as-a-second language are more likely to experience language and literacy barriers to patient-physician communication. Physicians who perceive communication barriers (e.g., health literacy, English language proficiency (ELP), cultural or gender based barriers) to engaging in productive conversations about the risks and benefits of preventive cancer screening may be less likely to initiate these conversations in order to focus on more pressing medical issues.    While much is known about cancer screening and treatment disparities among minorities in Canada and the USA, little research has focused specifically on disparities experienced among Asian populations. Using physician interviews, this research will explore physician self-reported approaches and perceived barriers to communicating with patients about cancer screening and seek to understand whether perceptions of patient characteristics such as health literacy, ELP, culture or gender influence the initiation of cancer screening conversations or recommendations. Understanding the barriers obstructing physician recommendation for cancer screening is the first step to ensuring equitable and timely access to important preventive cancer screening for all women.

Abstract-Résumé: This Tier 1 CRC renewal will enable Dr. Scott to focus on her research centered on the antibody response against HIV-1 infection and novel AIDS vaccines. The proposed research program encompasses five projects: 1) a novel prime-boost vaccine that elicits antibodies against highly conserved neutralization sites on HIV-1; 2) filamentous bacteriophage as a vaccine carrier; 3) features of antibodies elicited during chronic HIV-1 infection, and by bacteriophage as a mimic of chronic infection; 4) nanobiosensors for analyzing the antigen-specificity of antibodies secreted by single cells; and 5) gradients of genetic relatedness within viral networks and their implications for HIV vaccines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional connectivity of neuronal networks in childhood epilepsy
Keywords-MotsClés: EPILEPSY; FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY; FUNCTIONAL IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood epilepsy is one of the most common neurological conditions, affecting approximately 1% of children. Up to one third of those affected have poor seizure control despite the best available medical management. Prolonged uncontrolled epilepsy is associated with problems with mental ability as seizures are thought to adversely affect the developing brain. For a subset of patients, brain surgery may be beneficial. The success of surgical treatment is however directly dependent on the accurate identification  of brain areas responsible for causing seizures. The current research aims to study epileptic brain networks in children undergoing evaluation for brain surgery, and the effect of altered brain networks on brain function. Data from electrodes surgically placed onto the surface of the brain and brain scans will be used to study brain networks in epilepsy. The goals of this research are to: (1) develop safer and more effective surgical strategies based on an understanding of aberrant connectivity of epileptogenic cortex; (2) study the effects of seizures on brain function, and correlate these findings with mental function; and (3) examine how surgical removal of brain areas affects the development of brain networks. The findings of this study are expected to inform the medical community and lead to more innovative and effective treatments for children with epilepsy.

Background: Research has shown that key factors of healthy aging such as level of physical activity, social participation or mobility can vary depending on where older adults live. Yet we still fail to understand how environments influence healthy aging. In a context of aging populations and growing urbanization, calls have been issued for more sustainable urban (re-)development and implementation of local solutions to address global environmental and health issues. To date, few studies have accounted for daily mobility of older adults in order to understand how individual social, cultural or financial resources and the characteristics of life environment interact to produce healthy aging profiles. However, novel sensors such as GPS devices or accelerometers - which measure the level of energy we spend - now make it possible to gather precise information on people's daily mobility, levels of physical activity, or to assess perceptions or feelings at given times. TitreApplicationTitle: The pathogenic role of tumor-associated macrophages in Hodgkin lymphoma
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE-EXPRESSION PROFILING; HODGKIN; IMMUNE BIOLOGY; LYMPHOMA; MACROPHAGES; OUTCOME CORRELATION
Abstract-Résumé: Lymphomas are malignant tumors of a subset of white blood cells, so-called lymphocytes. Among lymphomas, Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common subtype in young people in the Western world. Fortunately, most of the patients suffering from this disease are cured by current treatments. Nonetheless, about 20% of all patients die from treatment failures or late complications related to treatment. Our goal is to better understand the biological underpinnings behind treatment failure.  Tumor biopsies from patients with Hodgkin lymphoma contain numerous cells that are part of an inflammatory reaction of the immune system that is unsuccessful at eradicating the lymphoma. In particular, we are interested in macrophages, a cell type that takes part in this reaction. The main function of macrophages is to protect our body by engulfing foreign organisms such as bacteria. But they are also present in the biopsies of many tumors and there is increasing knowledge documenting that these tumor-associated macrophages are beneficial for tumor survival and hence detrimental for patients. By our own work, we know that those Hodgkin lymphoma patients whose biopsies contain increased numbers of macrophages often present with recurrence after treatment and die.  This project aims at describing the exact function of tumor-associated macrophages in Hodgkin lymphoma. We want to find out what signals macrophages send to tumor cells and vice versa, entertaining a potentially devastating crosstalk of these cell types for affected patients. The ultimate goal will be to target these signals and prevent macrophages from supporting the tumor. Our findings could lead to a completely novel treatment approach by targeting not only the tumor cells themselves, but also the environing immune cells that nurture lymphoma cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and validation of clinical prediction rules of quality of life in head and neck cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CLINICAL PREDICTION RULE; DEPRESSION; HEAD AND NECK CANCER; HPV; PATIENT-REPORTED OUTCOMES; PREDICTION SCORE; PREDICTIVE FACTORS; PROGNOSTIC FACTORS; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Head and neck cancers severely impair quality of life (QOL) as they affect breathing, eating, speaking, and physical appearance. Up to 50% of patients with these cancers suffer from depression, which is the highest rate among oncology patients. Regular evaluations of QOL and depression are essential to correctly identify and treat these issues, as well as to optimize treatments. However, routine assessment is not common due to the time and resources required. In head and neck cancer, there is no clinical prediction score for QOL and depression, although predictions scores can simplify and increase diagnostic and prognostic assessments. Moreover, HPV infection is recognized as a favourable prognostic factor in head and neck cancer, and its role in QOL and depression has never been evaluated   Our objectives are to identify predictors of QOL and depression in head and neck cancer, to evaluate the role of HPV as a prognostic factor, and to develop and validate a clinical prediction score of QOL and depression.  This study will take place at Notre-Dame Hospital, where the largest number of head and neck cancer patients are treated in Quebec. The first step will identify the most significant predictive factors of QOL and depression, including HPV.  The second step is the creation of prediction scores using the most significant prognostic factors of QOL. The third step is the prospective validation of these scores over 24 months.  This is the first study to develop clinical scores to predict QOL and depression in head and neck cancer. This is also the first study to evaluate the role of HPV in QOL and depression. Current research and clinical practice does not routinely evaluate QOL and depression in head and neck cancer. This issue will be addressed by creating a simple rule that can eventually be implemented in clinical practice after proper validation. We hope that this will increase routine evaluation of QOL and depression in research and in clinical practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Non-motor Communication Impairments in Parkinson Disease and the Impact on HRQoL for Individuals with Parkinson disease and Family Care Partners
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL; COGNITION; COMMUNICATION; DISCOURSE; FAMILY CARE PARTNERS; LANGUAGE; PARKINSON DISEASE; QUALITY OF LIFE; STANDARDIZED ASSESSMENT; VERBAL FLUENCY
Abstract-Résumé: To date, the focus of speech language pathologists working in Parkinson disease (PD) has been on the motor-based symptoms of speech quality and swallowing. However, there is growing evidence that cognitive changes (thinking, memory, concentrating) may begin early in the disease and affect as many as 80 percent of individuals with PD.  These cognitive deficits may have a negative effect on the ability to use rule based language systems to communicate (reading, writing, speaking, understanding) resulting in issues such as slow processing of information, difficulty finding words, and difficulty planning thoughts and ideas. While assessment and management approaches have been developed for cognitive-communication deficits in other conditions, such as dementia Alzheimer's type there is a paucity of specific assessment or management options for language related cognitive-communication changes in PD.  The current study proposes to use both standardized and non-standardized language measures along with quality of life measures to: 1) Quantify the language and communication deficits in PD (e.g., word finding, discourse production, discourse comprehension) and 2) study the relationship among communication impairments, perception of communication change, cognitive status (impaired vs. unimpaired), and quality of life reported by individuals with PD and their family members.  We propose to study 60 individuals with PD (30 with mild cognitive impairment and 30 without) along with 30 healthy controls.  We anticipate that the results will improve understanding of the variable clinical presentations of PD, improve clinical care of individuals with PD and will assist clinicians in navigating the complexity of communication and cognition impairment in PD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing the spinal cord neurovascular response to sensory stimuli using functional optical coherence tomography.
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL IMAGING; MRI; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; NEUROPLASTICITY; NEUROSURGERY; NEUROVASCULAR COUPLING; OPTICAL IMAGING; SPINAL CORD INJURY; SPINE; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury is a devastating condition that prevents individuals from being able to sense the environment (touch, heat, etc.) or being able to walk or use their arms. Current assessments of sensory and motor function are subjective and are conducted by asking individuals if they are able to perceive touch or can move their arms or legs. These subjective assessments provide valuable information but are limited in their ability to fully understand spinal cord circuits and how these circuits become damaged after injury. Our research team is involved in projects that aim to objectify these measurements using non-invasive techniques such as spinal functional MRI (fMRI). A current limitation of spinal fMRI is a lack of understanding of how the spinal cord changes when it processes specific sensory or motor information. For example, if one is to heat the skin of an individual, we know from past studies of animal spinal cords that certain neurons transmit information to the brain - but we do not know how the spinal cord blood vessels and supporting cells respond to this neural activity. It is this change in blood flow and supporting cell swelling that make up the signal that can be measured with non-invasive techniques. For example, non-invasive spinal fMRI, a technique that we have successfully adapted for use in humans, is currently of limited use because we do not understand what it is measuring. The work presented here will use an animal model to characterize the relationship between neural activity and the supporting cell response, a phenomenon referred to as neurovascular coupling. By characterizing the neurovascular response for specific sensory activation paradigms we will elucidate a response function that can then be used to model non-invasive fMRI studies. Furthermore, this animal model will be used to validate the signal across different forms of measurement: optical coherence tomography (the focus of this work), animal high-field MRI and human MRI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deformable Dose Reconstruction to Optimize the Planning and Delivery of Liver Cancer Radiation Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICAL MODELS; COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; CONE-BEAM CT; DEFORMABLE IMAGE REGISTRATION; LIVER CANCER; ORGAN MOTION; RADIATION INDUCED TOXICITY; RADIOBIOLOGY; STEREOTACTIC RADIOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Radiation therapy is being investigated for liver cancer patients unsuitable for other local therapies. High precision techniques are required because the healthy liver and surrounding organs may be damaged by the dose required to kill liver tumours. The majority of patients are receiving suboptimal doses because of this risk of damage to normal tissues. Advances in imaging have allowed the internal patient anatomy to be seen in 3D, guiding the treatment each day. However, breathing motion, soft tissue deformation, and patient positioning errors, cause discrepancies between the intended and delivered dose. A novel deformable image registration algorithm allows images, such as the ones used for image guidance, to be spatially registered with higher degree of accuracy than previously available. It enables the radiation dose in the abdomen to be reconstructed over the entire treatment course, substantially improving our estimates of the true delivered dose. This technique will be applied to previous patients treated with online image-guided radiotherapy. Improved liver radiotherapy will be designed and evaluated at planning, by maximizing tumour dose without normal tissue over irradiation, and at treatment delivery, through more precise tumour targeting. Characterizing uncertainties in the delivered dose under current treatment techniques may allow clinicians to treat future liver cancer patients with a higher degree of accuracy and personalized treatment. Improving the therapeutic ratio in liver radiotherapy could result in improved tumour control. Additionally, a better understanding of the delivered dose can help evaluate clinical outcomes in terms of tumour dose-response relationships, and radiation-induced toxicity of healthy tissue.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hemispheric interaction and ventral prefrontal contributions to cognitive reserve in the aging brain
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BEHAVIORAL NEUROLOGY; COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE; COGNITIVE RESERVE; COGNITIVE TRAINING; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; FRONTAL LOBES; FUNCTIONAL IMAGING; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; NON-INVASIVE BRAIN STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: While some seniors have significant thinking difficulties, others can perform cognitive tasks as well as young adults. In order to prevent cognitive decline in elders, it is critical to understand which brain structures promote successful aging. The frontal lobes are a prime candidate based on the fact that they undergo the most dramatic change of any brain region across the life span and the fact that this region has been linked to cognitive function. Patients with frontal lobe damage face frustrating thinking problems including difficulty multitasking and vulnerability to distraction, two problems that are also encountered older adults. Brain imaging studies show that young adults rely only on one side of the frontal lobe whereas older adults engage both right and left frontal lobes during difficult cognitive tasks. This pattern of brain recruitment points to the capacity for reorganization (plasticity) of the brain in adulthood. This research will investigate the balance between frontal lobe degeneration and plasticity during healthy brain aging using two neuroscience techniques: functional brain imaging and noninvasive brain stimulation. These techniques will be used to examine changes in brain activity between younger and older adults as they perform an attention-demanding task and to probe the mechanism underlying these changes. The ultimate goal of this research is to use these findings to develop training strategies to improve thinking in older adults and in patients suffering from brain illnesses such as Alzheimer's disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CLINICAL OUTCOME; FETUS; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; INTENSIVE CARE UNIT; NEONATE; POSTPARTUM; PREGNANCY; PROGNOSTIC MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Although the maternal mortality rate has decreased significantly in Canada over the past three decades, 6 of 100,000 mothers suffer fatal outcomes of pregnancy. Recently there is a trend towards increasing maternal age and potential attendant morbidity and mortality. Additionally, since healthcare in Canada is administered provincially and territorially, geographical diversity can lead to different healthcare service densities in Canada.  This diversity may also result in different access to care and clinical outcomes for severely ill pregnant patients and their babies. We aim to evaluate geographic and temporal differences which may allow identification of areas for improvement in services and therefore reduction in maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of Language on Health-Care Utilization, Morbidity and Mortality among Diabetics in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; IMMIGRANTS; LANGUAGE BARRIERS; PROSPECTIVE COHORT
Abstract-Résumé: An estimated 2.7 million Canadians (7.6% of the population) are diabetic and given present trends, this figure is projected to rise to 4.2 million by 2020. The prevalence of diabetes type II is 2-6 times greater among immigrants compared to Canadian or US born populations. Diabetes is a chronic disease where effective communication is critical for patient education and self-management of disease. Canada is a multicultural society where 20% of the population is foreign born and 70% have a mother tongue other than English or French. This is important because, language barriers are associated with decreased access to health care, lower adherence to treatment and follow-up and increased length of hospital stay. Although poorer glycemic control has been documented among immigrants, little is known about the impact of language barriers on glycemic control. In Canada, the use of professional medical interpreters is quite variable across centers, as there are no laws requiring that interpreters be provided and most centers do not have funding for professional interpreters. This study would be the first to address the impact of language barriers and use of professional interpreters in a diverse multicultural population on a chronic disease with important public health importance. Providing translation for all persons who need it has the potential to improve the quality of health care delivered in Canada and improve health outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring How Advanced Cancer Patients Experience High or Low Existential Well-being: A Mixed-Methods Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CUTANEOUS MELANOMA; DOCTOR-PATIENT RELATIONSHIP; PHYSICIAN SUPPORT; SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; SKIN SELF-EXAMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Early cutaneous melanoma (CM) detection and removal has been established as the most effective way of reducing CM-related mortality. A method called skin self-examinations (SSE) has been shown to improve early CM detection and thus reduce CM mortality by 63%. However, 85% of CM survivors do not engage in SSE. Research has demonstrated that treatment adherence and medical outcomes are improved when patients' perceive greater support from medical staff4. Additionally, self-determination theory proposes that patients' motivation to maintain healthy habits depends on feeling they can make autonomous decisions, confidence to perform the health behaviour competently, and relating to others regarding their illness. However, no research has examined how doctor-patient interactions influence SSE adherence. The goal of this research project is to examine the impact of doctor's support of such factors through their interactions with patients on long-term SSE adherence. I hypothesize that CM patients who feel their physician supports SSE will demonstrate better SSE adherence 3 and 12 months following SSE education. I also hypothesize that patients whose physician fosters their self-determination will enhance the effect of perceived physician SSE support on SSE adherence. Given that CM patients' prioritize building a relationship with their physician and following their physician's advice, this study will generate greatly needed data about the impact of physician support of SSE the doctor-patient relationship and on short- and long-term SSE adherence. Results will inform follow-up care practices and SSE education to increase SSE behaviour. This will improve early detection of CM in high-risk patients and lower CM-related mortality.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nutrition and physical activity measurement tool development for First Nation youth in remote sub-arctic communities
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL NUTRITION; COLLABORATIVE APPROACH; COMMUNITY INITIATIVES; EDUCATION; FOCUS GROUPS; HEALTH PROMOTION; MIXED METHODS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; TOOL DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal Canadians face a disproportionately high burden of obesity and chronic disease, where diet and physical activity are modifiable risk factors. Many barriers exist to healthy eating and adequate physical activity in remote First Nations (FN). However, there exists little information about the eating habits of on-reserve Canadians, leaving individual communities lacking in the knowledge and expertise needed to address the problem. Given the diversity of challenges faced by each FN community, research into locally acceptable, effective, and sustainable public health initiatives to improve diets and physical activity levels is of value. This, however, is challenging when there exists few (or no) validated tools to measure physical activity and eating habits in FN youth living in the remote north.  The goal of this research is to validate tools that will inform improved public health interventions to decrease the burden of chronic disease in FN populations. It is hypothesized that the availability of such tools will provide an improved understanding of diet and physical activity patterns, and support sustainable public health interventions for improved nutrition and physical activity habits. A mix of quantitative and qualitative methods will be used to obtain a measure of physical activity in a large sample of FN youth in northern Ontario and to identify the appropriateness of the International Physical Activity Questionnaire in this population; to validate a measure of physical activity among on-reserve FN youth living in remote, northern locations; and to evaluate the appropriateness of the Healthy Eating Index for on-reserve FN youth. Community members will be collaborators at all phases of the project. The tools generated by this research will help to inform interventions to reduce current health inequities and, in turn, draw the attention of key decision-makers to take further action to adequately support successful interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Imaging Functional Recovery in Stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE AFFECTS; BEHAVIOUR TESTING; DIET AFFECTS; FOCAL ISCHEMIC STROKE; MAGETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; PRECLINICAL ANIMAL MODELING; STROKE RECOVERY; TWO PHOTON FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Over 50,000 strokes occur in Canada each year: 15% are lethal, making stroke the 3rd leading cause of death. Out of the 300,000 Canadians living with the effects of stroke, half suffer from moderate to severe impairments. That the rehabilitation of this patient population is not more effective largely reflects the uncertainty surrounding the structural and functional changes which govern recovery. Uncertainty surrounding the cellular changes that are needed for full recovery of brain function is a major factor preventing the development of more effective therapies to rehabilitate patients following stroke. It has become clear that recovery is strongly affected by changes that occur in the neurons and blood vessels in the peri-infarct zone, the impaired, but potentially salvageable brain region peripheral to the area directly affected by the loss of blood supply. The goal of the present proposal is to understand the changes in the neurovascular coupling in the peri-infarct zone in the weeks following stroke. This work will be conducted using advanced 3D imaging techniques that allow visualization of individual neurons and blood vessels in brains of live rats that have received stroke. The responses of neurons and blood vessels to sensory stimulation will be contrasted between untreated animals and those treated with specific drugs to restore healthy levels of neurovascular activity. These experiments will interrogate the mechanisms by which changes in the neurons and blood vessels support rehabilitation and thus guide the development of new treatments applicable over long therapeutic time windows, thereby benefitting a large population of patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of childhood dysregulated diurnal cortisol patterns in predicting trajectories of adolescent internalizing disorders: A multi-wave longitudinal study.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; DEPRESSION/ANXIETY; DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOPATHOLOGY; DIURNAL CORTISOL; GROWTH TRAJECTORIES; INTERNALIZING DISORDERS; MENTAL HEALTH; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Mid to late adolescence is the peak onset period for internalizing disorders, including anxiety and depression. To date, we do not know whether childhood dysregulated diurnal cortisol can predict clinical diagnoses of internalizing disorders across the transition to adolescence. The proposed study will examine the questions: 1) Does dysregulated diurnal cortisol in pre-adolescence (ages 10-12), predict development of depressive and anxiety disorders in early and mid adolescence (ages 13-15 and 16-18, respectively)? 2) Will patterns of dysregulation at pre-adolescence be differentially linked to types of internalizing disorder (i.e. anxiety disorder or depression), or to age of onset? 3) Are there differential predictors of internalizing disorders for girls and boys, in terms of dysregulated diurnal cortisol patterns and other predictors at pre-adolescence? Participants will be ~120 children recruited from the Concordia Longitudinal Risk Research Project, a large intergenerational study of families from disadvantaged backgrounds. Children have been followed across 5 time points every 3 years since early childhood. Salivary cortisol samples will be taken at 2-hour intervals over two consecutive days during between ages 10-12, and again at ages 13-15, to assess diurnal cortisol. Children's depression and anxiety will be assessed using clinical diagnostic interviews K-SADS and ADIS, respectively. Hypotheses to be tested using growth mixture modeling (M+) include: 1) Atypical diurnal cortisol patterns at pre-adolescence will predict new internalizing disorders at early-adolescence and mid-adolescence, controlling for baseline internalizing disorders and on-going behavioural problems; and 2) The relations between dysregulated diurnal cortisol patterns and other predictors will differ for girls and boys. Dysregulated diurnal cortisol at pre-adolescence might serve as a bio-marker indicating elevated risk for internalizing disorders during adolescence.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional characterization of Pseudomonas aeruginosa minor pilins
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL DIVERSITY; MINOR PILINS; PILUS ASSEMBLY; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA; STRUCTURE; THERAPEUTIC TARGETS; TYPE IV PILI; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is among the most common causes of hospital-acquired infections. This bacterium can take advantage of a weakened immune system and cause infections in people with severe burns, HIV and cancer. It is also a cause of chronic lung infections in those with cystic fibrosis, leading to the death of many of these patients. The first step of infection involves bacterial attachment to host cells by long sticky fibres called type IV pili (T4P). Each type IV pilus is made up of thousands of protein subunits called the major pilin and without these proteins, the bacteria can't attach and cause infection. The importance of these major pilin proteins in infection makes them excellent vaccine candidates. Unfortunately, there is considerable diversity among these proteins from different strains of P. aeruginosa, making the development of a broadly-protective vaccine difficult. Interestingly, there is a group of pilin-like proteins, called the minor pilins, which show more similarity between different strains of P. aeruginosa than the major pilin. These minor pilins are incorporated into the pilus and are very important for T4P assembly and function. The minor pilins, therefore, may make better vaccine candidates than the major subunits. However, the exact role of the minor pilins in pilus function is poorly understood. We hypothesize that the minor pilins group together at the tip of the pilus to allow the pilus to extend from the cell. To test this idea, we are studying the interactions between these minor pilins and key regions within the proteins that are required for pilus assembly and function. We are also working on determining the molecular structure of these proteins, which will help us figure out how these proteins physically come together and help identify possible areas of the proteins to use in a vaccine. This work will help us understand the functions of minor pilins and aid in the design of vaccines to prevent P. aeruginosa infections.

Abstract-Résumé: Background: Numerous surveys have shown that lesbian, gay and bisexual (LBG) people report poorer mental health, including greater victimization, depression, stress, anxiety, substance use, and suicide, compared to non-LGB people. Suggested explanations for these inequities include exposure to discriminatory behaviour and stigmatization, isolation, low social supports, disclosure reactions, stressful life events, heterosexism, homophobia, and service utilization. Few Canadian studies examine the role of sexual orientation (SO) in mental health and service utilization in Canada. Research objectives & Methods: (1) To critically review and examine existing concepts, theories and measures underlying SO in the context of youth mental health. This work will be guided by (a) comprehensive literature review, informed by the Cochrane methods, and (b) secondary analysis of existing qualitative interviews (N=452, ages 15-29 years) to identify key constructs related to SO and gender identity as described from youth's perspectives. (2) To identify the effect of SO on self-perceived mental health in a nationally representative sample of Canadians. LGB Canadians are hypothesized to have lower perceived mental health compared to their heterosexual counterparts. (3) To examine mental health service utilization patterns in a nationally representative sample of Canadians, and conduct subgroup analyses that compare patterns across SO and gender identity categories. SO is hypothesized to be a significant predictor of mental health service utilization, with LGB youth reporting lower service utilization levels than non-LGB youth. For objectives 2-3, a series of logistic regressions will be performed using 2007-2008 Canadian Community Health Survey data, with additional subgroup analyses for youth aged 18-25. Keywords-MotsClés: 13C NMR; CELL METABOLISM; DOPAMINERGIC NEURONS; INDUCIBLE PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; KINASE SUBSTRATES; METABOLOMICS; MICROSCOPY; MITOCHONDRIA; OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease, PD, is a debilitating and incurable neurodegenerative disease that is particularly prevalent amongst the elderly here, in North America. In PD, a specific set of brain cells die. This causes severely impaired movement control in patients. Although the mechanism through which cells die is not fully understood, cellular metabolism has been widely implicated. A particular form of PD, called familial or early-onset PD, is a hereditary form of the disease that can be attributed to mutations in specific genes. Studying these mutants is essential to improve our understanding of PD as a whole. The loss of one protein, called PTEN-induced putative kinase 1, PINK1, is well known to cause early-onset forms of PD. Furthermore, this protein has been implicated in cellular metabolism, though how PINK1 contributes to this remains unknown. The reason that this question still remains unanswered can probably be attributed to the lack of good PD models. Neither animal models nor cells from other organs than the brain can fully recapitulate what occurs in human brain cells. However, recent advances in cell engineering now allow us to make human brain cells from skin cells harvested from PD patients. This provides us with a model in which to study PD that is much more relevant to what occurs in the human brain. Therefore, we will use this exciting new model to study defects in energy production and cellular metabolism in cells from patients lacking PINK1. By studying engineered human brain cells that lack PINK1, we expect to better our understanding of the metabolic defects that occur in PD and, ultimately, contribute to the development of better treatments for PD patients.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; BULLYING; HEALTHY RELATIONSHIPS; MENTAL HEALTH; POSITIVE DEVELOPMENT; VIOLENCE PREVENTION; YOUTH HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Healthy development in children and youth depends on the quality of their relationships with family, peers and community members.  Positive relationships have been found to be predictive of healthy adult functioning and unhealthy and traumatic relationships were found to be predictive of later hostile relationship patterns including the perpetration of bullying, harassment, and dating violence.  These findings suggest that healthy relationships are a critical mechanism in the development of healthy functioning in multiple domains.  Currently, there is a lack of healthy relationships programs based on scientific evidence that are also systematically evaluated for efficacy.  The proposed research involves the creation (with input from adolescents) of an electronic healthy relationships curriculum that focuses on youth competencies and capacities in the areas of healthy peer, parent, and partner relationships.  Approximately one hundred and fifty adolescents (aged 14-16) will be recruited online and from youth-serving organizations to complete the training.  Pre, post, and six month follow up assessments will be conducted to determine the efficacy of the program. The following areas will be assessed in adolescent participants: knowledge of healthy relationships and conflict resolution; quality of relationships (including positive and negative aspects) with peers, romantic partners, and family; interpersonal aggression and victimization; and emotional and psychological functioning. The intended outcomes are to develop an evidence-based program that effectively engages, equips and inspires youth to peacefully resolve conflicts, to develop healthy relationships, and to prevent the adverse effects of adolescent interpersonal violence and social isolation.

Abstract-Résumé: Leukemia is a type of cancer that originates from the bone marrow and results in an abnormal proliferation of white blood cells, leading to immune system break down and affecting both children and adults. In fact, between 2003 and 2007, the most frequently diagnosed childhood cancer was leukemia (Canadian Cancer Statistics 2011). Our laboratory studies a protein called Mixed Lineage Leukemia (MLL), a key etiologic factor linked to several forms of leukemia. Unfortunately, patients harboring mutations within the MLL1 gene have a poor survival prognosis. It has been recently shown that in order for MLL to have oncogenic activity, it must form multi-protein complexes with several other proteins.  My projects aim at determining, using X-ray crystallography, the crystal structure of MLL1 in complex with its regulatory proteins. Based on the molecular information of the mechanistic basis controlling complex assembly, we will be able to design novel therapeutic platform for leukemia drug research.
