TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of dating relationships on youth health: A qualitative gender relations approach
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNOGRAPHY; GENDER; INTERSECTIONALITY; PLACE; QUALITATIVE INTERVIEWS; RURAL HEALTH; SOCIAL CONTEXT; YOUTH HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Canadian young people are struggling with health issues: 15% or 1.2 million youth suffer from mental illnesses, rates of sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhea and chlamydia have increased among young people over the past decade, and dating violence and problematic substance use continue to compromise the health of young Canadians. As some sub-populations of youth are more susceptible to ill-health, researchers are increasingly looking to the social context of health (i.e. social determinants rather than biological factors) to address health inequities. Adolescent dating relationships, defined as early romantic encounters and relationships during the teenage years, have generally been overlooked by public health as part of the social context in which teens' health behaviours and coping strategies develop. To address this gap in the literature, I will conduct in-depth qualitative interviews with youth ages 13-19 in two distinct communities (Vancouver, a large metropolitan community and Fort. St. James, a rural, resource-based town) to better understand the role of dating relationships in the everyday lives of youth. The interviews will be analyzed using intersectional gender relations theory to determine how gender, diversity and place impact teens' dating relationships. The study findings will be used to develop intervention strategies to address dating issues in both communities. Ultimately, my doctoral research will contribute to our understanding of how social and structural factors impact dating relationships in adolescence and will offer public health intervention strategies to promote positive relationships and the health of Canadian youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Effect of Altered Proteolysis on Autophagy: Impact on Mutant Huntingtin Clearance
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; MEDICAL GENETICS; MUTANT HUNTINGTIN CLEARANCE; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASE; POLYGLUTAMINE AGGREGATES; PROTEOLYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington disease (HD) is an adult-onset, neurological disease that affects muscle coordination and eventually results in cognitive decline and dementia. There are presently no effective treatments or cures and death occurs approximately 15-20 years after disease onset. HD is caused by an inherited mutation in the huntingtin gene, leading to the production of an altered version of the huntingtin protein that accumulates as aggregates. These aggregates can be cleared from the cell through autophagy, a mechanism that degrades unwanted proteins. During the development of this disorder, we know that autophagy becomes defective over time. We also know that certain proteases (proteins which cut other proteins) including caspase-6 (C6) have increased activity and it has been shown that these proteases in fact cleave key proteins involved in carrying out autophagy. The hypothesis is that cleavage of autophagy proteins by C6 leads to their loss of function and subsequent impairment of the autophagy process. This then results in reduced clearance of aggregates and further progression of the disease. I will determine what the functional impact is on autophagy-mediated clearance of protein aggregates following cleavage of autophagy proteins by C6. I will then reduce the activity of these proteases and render these autophagy proteins resistant to cleavage in order to increase autophagy and promote aggregate clearance. Thus, the goal of this project is to investigate the relationship between altered protease activity and impaired autophagy, and how this contributes to the pathogenesis in Huntington disease. We can then use this information to develop specific therapies aimed at inhibiting C6 and promoting the clearance of aggregates, ultimately resulting in the amelioration of HD symptoms. This research is significant as it will reveal important mechanisms involved in the progression of Huntington disease and will lead to the development of new therapeutic approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: The moral economy of mental health care in the Yukon Territory: Negotiating 'sovereignty' and 'community'
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; ANTHROPOLOGY OF POLICY; COMMUNITY-LED CARE; DEVOLUTION; ETHNOGRAPHY; HEALTH CARE POLICY; HEALTH REFORM; INTERGOVERNMENTAL RELATIONS; MENTAL HEALTH; MORAL ECONOMY
Abstract-Résumé: This research investigates the negotiations that take place around the organization, funding, and delivery of mental health care in the Yukon Territory, focusing on the development of services relevant to First Nations clients. It will examine how the mental-health-related needs of different (but frequently overlapping) communities are constructed, what visions of the "common good" are being advocated in the arena of mental health, and by whom, and in what ways these visions are contested and transformed through the practices of negotiation and cooperation that First Nations governments, the Yukon Territorial Government, and other governmental and non-governmental stakeholders engage in. It also investigates linkages between the devolution of First Nations health services and broader transformations in health policy in Canada, particularly with respect to ongoing tensions between desires for universality and local control in the health care system. The research will take a mixed-methods approach incorporating participant observation in mental health facilities and governmental offices in Whitehorse, interviews with policy-makers and administrators, and textual analysis of relevant policy documents and public discussion forums.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing nosocomial transmission of tuberculosis in South Africa: A population-based molecular epidemiologic study
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; GLOBAL HEALTH; HUMAN RESOURCES FOR HEALTH; INFECTION PREVENTION AND CONTROL; MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS; NOSOCOMIAL TRANSMISSION; OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH; POPULATION AND PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Recent increases in rates of TB among HCWs, as well as hospital-based outbreaks of multidrug-resistant TB among HIV-infected patients, have led to greater concern about the risk of Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission in healthcare settings, particularly in Africa. A recent study estimated that the risk of exposure to TB for hospital workers may be 40 times greater than that for the general population. This study therefore aims to decrease the nosocomial transmission of TB among HCWs and patients by mapping the routes of transmission using molecular epidemiological methods and to quantify risk in order to develop comprehensive prevention measures. Genotyping will be used to examine the polymorphic marker congruence between patient and HCW TB cases.  This study will be conducted at six regional hospitals in South Africa; two in the Free State Province, two in the Western Cape and two in KwaZulu-Natal. Research tools will include a knowledge, attitudes and behaviour questionnaire to assess individual and organizational barriers to compliance with infection control practices for TB, a comprehensive facility-level infection control assessment, investigations of case-to-contact transmission among HCWs and patients, where active TB disease is the outcome of interest, and molecular epidemiological methods for all positive cases involving a HCW to document nosocomial transmission links.  Findings will inform the implementation of TB infection control measures as well as an education and training program. Consistent application of infection control principles across the healthcare spectrum is important not only in resource-strained settings such as South Africa, but in Canada as well with the emergence of pandemic influenza, SARS, and other infectious diseases. This research is necessary to ensure that we adequately promote and protect the health of our valued HCWs and all patients in the era of emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bridging the gaps between evidence, policy, and injury prevention
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD INJURY PREVENTION; HEALTH POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: Injuries are the leading cause of death among children between 1 and 19 years old.  The number of children who die of injuries in Canada has decreased over the past several decades.  There are some policies that have been shown to help keep children safe, including bicycle helmet laws, booster seat laws, graduated driver's licensing, and health care systems that organize the way children get care if they are injured.  However, in Canada, these policies are different across the country.  This research aims to answer three questions: 1. Do decision-makers understand what is a strong policy, i.e., one that is based on scientific evidence? 2. How are decisions to adopt these policies made? 3. Can we use the information we have to make Canadian injury prevention policies better? We will present decision-makers with the results of previous research on these policies and help them understand where their policy fits with the evidence.  Examples of case studies of successful and not successful policies will be examined to try to understand factors that influence decision-making. Finally, we will see whether presenting this evidence will guide future decisions around injury prevention policies across Canada.

Abstract-Résumé: Fundamental to fostering the health and well-being of Canadian children and youth are investments in best practice services and targeted policies to improve their lives. To ensure meaningful health services and policies, the Canadian Pediatric Society stresses the need to develop and sustain innovative research programs. Effective initiatives that are meant to improve children's and youth's health and health care services must be grounded within and be responsive to their life-situations. The main goal of my research program is to conduct applied child and youth health services and policy research that involves and is germane to health system managers, policy makers and healthcare providers as well as children and youth who are directly impacted by the research. To achieve this, I focus on three areas: 1) children and youth living with chronic physical and mental illness; 2) children and youth living with disabilities and complex health needs; and 3) promoting health and access to health care for children and youth. Training the next generation of child and youth health researchers is a key priority of my research and includes mentoring them in applied health research and in facilitating knowledge translation and exchange (KTE) and linkage with decision-makers. My research program is important as of ten years ago the voices of children and youth in health research were virtually absent. I have led the field by providing them the opportunity to articulate a broader vision of their health needs. I have used an integrated KTE approach in my studies by engaging children, youth, clinicians, key decision-makers, and policy makers in the entire research process. My research has significant potential to improve existing health services and supports as well as inform the development of new services and policies that promote health equity and reduce disparities in Canadian children and youth.

Abstract-Résumé: Up to 18% of children have chronic health conditions including developmental disorders, and 14-18% of Canadian youth have mental health needs.  We know that there are significant gaps in the quality of care and access to services for these children and youth in Canada.  Primary care reform, the development of multi-speciality healthcare networks and current strategies to   address the developmental and mental health needs of children and youth in Ontario show promise in improving their care and outcomes.   This chair award will build on the development of an exciting new data repository that I am leading to merge education, health care, mental health and developmental service data at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences in collaboration with senior policymakers across three relevant Ministries.   I will create a comprehensive program of research to enable ongoing evaluation of these policy strategies aimed at providing improved coordination of care for children and youth with chronic health and mental health conditions.  The overarching objectives of this chair application are to:   1. conduct policy-relevant research to evaluate current health system reform strategies in Ontario that aim to improve access to and coordination of services for children and youth with chronic health and mental health conditions to improve their health outcomes 2.  lead in the continued development of a child and youth  cross-sectoral data repository in Ontario (ChYLD) for the purposes of research, training and policymaking to improve child health  3. build on existing links with senior decision-makers and use effective knowledge exchange strategies to ensure the research is relevant and informs policy development  4. continue to train and mentor applied child and youth health services and policy researchers and build a national network of maternal/child and youth researchers

Abstract-Résumé: Improved knowledge translation in the field of chemistry is in demand by the public and health researchers since it can not only inform public health decisions but also lead to fruitful interdisciplinary collaborations between scientists. Mobile technologies represent an ideal platform for the development of scientific outreach tools for both health practitioners and scientists because they permit facile access to information at the bedside and lab bench, respectively. Multi-media representations are also known to significantly improve learning and retention, while molecular-level illustrations and animations can reduce misconceptions in chemistry. Accordingly, an interactive e-book prototype featuring 2D and 3D interactive visualizations of processes at the molecular level will be developed. This project is intended to improve science literacy in the field of chemistry for both the lay public and biology and health researchers.

TitreApplicationTitle: What They did for Art: How the Industrial Revolution Advanced Art and Destroyed the Artist's Health
Keywords-MotsClés: ART; CHEMISTRY; DISEASE; HEALTH; INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION; SCIENCE HISTORY
Abstract-Résumé: During the industrial revolution, there was a rush to capitalize on the new elements being discovered, and the new forms of chemical manipulations that were being introduced. Chemists and artists alike changed the way we look and interact with the world. For example, William Henry Perkin's accidental development of the aniline dye, mauveine, allowed clothes to be permanently dyed mauve for the very first time and changed the fashion industry forever. Another example, is the use of the glow-in-the-dark element, radium, to paint the dials on wristwatches which made clocks decipherable in the dark and in turn fatally poisoned the women painters who moistened the tips of their brushes to increase painting precision.   This research project will study the inventions and innovations that stimulated artists to create new forms of art from the middle of the nineteenth century to middle of the twentieth century, as well as the health consequences they suffered as a result. Health topics such as lead poisoning experienced by printers, the mercury poisoning affecting Canadian beaver hat-makers, the skin diseases faced by photographers, and the lung diseases contracted by printmakers will be covered. Examples such as these will highlight the sacrifices made in the name of art in Canada at a time when there were no safety guidelines for manipulating toxic chemicals, and no way of identifying or treating the subsequent diseases.   The resulting feature article will inform the public about the important issues that plagued the artistic community in Canada during the Industrial Revolution, and will help mediate a conversation between health policy-makers and the public about the importance of following guidelines when handling hazardous materials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of PTEN
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; PI3K/PTEN PATHWAY; PROTEIN CRYSTALLIZATION & STRUCTURE DETERMINATION; PROTEIN:PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; SURFACE PLASMON RESONANCE; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: The function of the PTEN protein in normal cells is to turn off cellular pathways that cause cell growth and cell survival. So PTEN blocks tumor formation. In many different kinds of human cancers (e.g. breast, prostate and endometrium), the PTEN protein is present at reduced levels, or contains mutations that make it less effective. When the PTEN protein is missing, or even reduced, cells grow in an uncontrolled way and form a tumor.  PTEN is also important in controlling cellular responses to insulin and may be a suitable target for treatment of patients with type II diabetes.   PTEN activity modifies an important component of the cell membrane. We have previously discovered that the p85 protein can bind to and increase the activity of PTEN, making it more effective at suppressing tumor formation. In this proposal, we will characterize PTEN and p85 mutations found in human tumor samples, and some that we have engineered to prevent p85 from binding to PTEN. We will determine how these mutations impact PTEN regulation by p85, and PTEN biological functions. We will also use the Canadian Light Source to determine several protein structures: for PTEN in its inactive form, for the part of p85 that binds PTEN, and for a complex containing both p85 and PTEN. This will help us better understand the importance of different parts of each protein and the impact of cancer-associated mutations. A better understanding of p85 and PTEN regulation will enable the identification of patients with critical p85 and/or PTEN mutations. As we move to more personalized medicine, it is important to identify the molecular changes present in each patients tumor to identify those most able to benefit from the newly emerging precise targeted treatments directed at components in this pathway.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanism of the human copper transporting ATPases
Keywords-MotsClés: ATPASE; CISPLATIN; COPPER TRANSPORT; DRUG RESISTANCE; MENKES DISEASE; NMR; PROTEIN STUCTURE; WILSON DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Copper is required for the activity of many enzymes involved in respiration, neuron function, formation of connective tissue, endocrine processes, and radical detoxification in the human body. Wilson disease protein (ATP7B) and Menkes disease protein (ATP7A) regulate copper concentration in the cell and deliver copper to biosynthetic pathways. These enzymes are targets of many mutations that cause severe metabolic disorders. Importantly, ATP7B and ATP7A are involved in cancer resistance to platinum-based chemotherapeutic drugs. To understand the critical steps in the activity cycle of the copper transporters, we will investigate the structure, molecular motions and interactions of the isolated domains, or functional modules, of the Wilson disease protein using multidimensional Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR), a technique uniquely suited for studying protein structure and dynamics in solution. We will trace the sequence of molecular events involved in substrate binding by copper-transporters and analyze the structural basis of several frequent disease causing mutations. Using synchrotron radiation, NMR, and biochemical techniques, we will investigate mechanism of cancer resistance to platinum-based anticancer drugs associated with ATP7B and ATP7A. This work is expected to improve the understanding of an important class of transport proteins and provide a new insight into the molecular basis of the disorders of copper metabolism. Structural information on Wilson disease protein will facilitate design of the new inhibitors and modulators of copper transporters, which will help to overcome certain types of drug resistance in cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Internationally Educated Nurses' Professional, Cultural, and Social Integration in Canadian Nursing Workplaces: Designing Culturally Competent and Evidence-Based Retention Programs.
Keywords-MotsClés: CULTURE; HEALTH CARE ADMINISTRATION; HEALTH CARE SERVICES; HEALTH CARE SYSTEM; IMMIGRATION; INTERNATIONALLY EDUCATED NURSES; NURSING WORKFORCE; PROFESSIONAL PRACTICE; SOCIAL INTEGRATION; WORKPLACE INTEGRATION
Abstract-Résumé: Like other Western countries, Canada has a growing need to 'import' internationally trained nurses to address an acute nurse shortage. The current registered nurses (RNs) shortage mainly relates to an aging nursing workforce with a mean age of 53 years old which means that a large cohort of nurses will retire at the same time. This will exacerbate the current nursing shortage. The Canadian Nurses Association (2011) indicates Canada will be short almost 60,000 full-time positions by 2022. Canada is not alone; according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (2009), more than 581,500 full time nursing positions need to be filled by 2018 to address a shortfall of at least 760,000 nurses. The solution to the shortage, however, presents its own issues and challenges. Canadian studies have shown that cultural, social and professional differences can affect the integration of the internationally trained nurses and thus have an impact on our healthcare services. However, more work needs to be done to fully understand the cultural factors, particularly religious beliefs and values related to gender equity. Social customs and communications skills also play a significant part in workplace relations. The ability to work in an interprofessional health team, for example, could pose a challenge for internationally trained nurses. How can we equip them for this mode of practice? This study will explore the everyday experiences of internationally educated and Canadian educated nurses in their working environment. We will explore the challenges both they and health organizations face, Once we have identified the individual, social and institutional factors that can affect working relations we will then be in a position to create a viable solution: culturally conscious and culturally sensitive mentor programs for nurses. Centered in Saskatchewan, this study and its outcomes will extend beyond SK.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of dendritic cells in hepatitis C patients and applications to dendritic cell-based therapy.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNITY; DENDRITIC CELLS; GENE EXPRESSION; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; IMMUNE MODULATION; IMMUNOTHERAPY; INNATE IMMUNITY; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus is one of the viruses that cause liver disease. An estimated 170 million people are infected with hepatitis C virus, which amounts to approximately 3% of the world population. Although acute infection is often insidious, about 80% of infected people remain chronic carriers. The persistent infection eventually results in either mild chronic hepatitis or extensive liver damage. Treatment with interferon-alpha and ribavirin is effective in some chronic hepatitis C patients, but 40-50% of patients do not respond and the drugs are expensive and associated with severe side effects, so the development of alternative treatments and vaccines is critical. Amongst al the immune cells involved, dendritic cells are critical for the development of immune responses to infectious agents and to vaccination. However, there is evidence that the dendritic cells of chronic hepatitis C patients are functionally impaired. Since this may make it difficult to induce an immune response to the virus or a vaccine in the patients in vivo, we plan to isolate the dendritic cells from the blood of healthy and hepatitis C virus-infected individuals, and compare their functional properties. This will then allow us to select stimuli to effectively activate the hepatitis C patients' dendritic cells. These activated dendritic cells can then be loaded with hepatitis C antigens and used as delivery vehicle for a therapeutic vaccine against chronic hepatitis C. Such therapy would circumvent the impaired dendritic cell function of chronic hepatitis C patients in vivo by giving necessary maturation stimuli ex vivo. Even if, as others suggest, hepatitis C virus does not affect dendritic cell function, dendritic cell-based vaccines induce very strong cell-mediated immune responses and thus are expected to be promising as a therapeutic in chronic hepatitis C patients, and also as a prophylactic for high-risk populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Emerging health researchers and the commercialization of academic science
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATIVE ETHNOGRAPHY; COMMERCIALIZATION POLICY; INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LAW; LIFE SCIENCES; SEMI-STRUCTURED INTERVIEWS; SURVEYS; UNIVERSITY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this project is to understand the two-way relationship between emerging health researchers and commercialization practices at Canadian universities. This project will measure in several ways how commercialization practices such as patenting influence the work, interactions, and values of these health researchers, and how their participation in such practices, in turn, shapes the commercialization process. In health research, commercialization is about capturing scientific discoveries in order to make products like drugs and medical devices. Canadian governments, research funding agencies, and universities have put into place many policies to encourage commercialization. But research shows that individual health researchers - their insights and involvement - are usually the key to commercialization. Although we have a sense of why and to what degree established university health researchers participate in commercialization, we have no idea about how often emerging health researchers (graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, junior clinician-investigators and assistant professors) are exposed to it, or what effects those experiences have on their research, career paths, and goals. We also do not know how emerging health researchers affect commercialization practices and outcomes. Therefore, with commercialization becoming a common component of university health research and policy-makers emphasizing the importance of mining "young talent" for commercialization, it is critical that we develop an evidence-based understanding of the dynamic relationship between emerging health researchers and commercialization. This project will use several research techniques to build such an evidence base. The results will help government agencies and universities to develop commercialization policies that are better tailored to future generations of health researchers and, in so doing, help Canadians, the would-be beneficiaries of their health research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of the ethics of disaster research in low resource settings
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS; HUMANITARIAN AID; NATURAL DISASTERS; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; RESEARCH ETHICS
Abstract-Résumé: Research in disasters can lead to improvements in disaster relief and better understanding of how disasters impact populations. Recent increased emphasis on disaster research has spurred expanded discussion regarding the ethical implications of this field of inquiry. Low-resource disaster research is associated with a range of distinctive ethical features including heightened vulnerability, insecurity and instability, need for rapid response, challenges to distinguish practice from research, amongst others. However, there remains uncertainty regarding what ethical guidance can best orient research in low-resource disaster settings.  The proposed project will address this gap and respond to the following question: What are the processes and ethical principles that can reliably guide ethics review for research in low-resource disaster settings?  The research study includes two primary lines of inquiry:  (1)A systematic assessment of the disaster research literature with the goal of identifying characteristics of disaster research in low-resource settings and their ethical implications; and  (2)A qualitative, interview-based study to examine the experiences of members of Research Ethics Boards that are highly experienced in reviewing disaster research protocols in order to better understand ethical issues arising in disaster research and its review, opportunities and obstacles to address these issues, and implications for ethics review of disaster research. We will draw on this analysis, as well as examination of existing research ethics guidance, to develop a tailored normative framework. The framework will identify how relevant characteristics ought to be factored into the design of disaster research protocols and orient the process of ethics review. The final phase of the project will include knowledge transfer and exchange activities focused on two groups: disaster researchers and Research Ethics Boards that review disaster research.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Cultural Context of Modern Neuroscientific Research: Exploring the Impact of Institutional Research Settings and Professional Migration Patterns
Keywords-MotsClés: CULTURAL CONTEXT OF NEUROSCIENCE; CULTURAL CONTEXT OF PSYCHIATRY; HISTORY OF BIOETHICS; HISTORY OF MEDICINE; HISTORY OF NEUROETHICS; HISTORY OF NEUROSCIENCE; INTERNATIONAL CONTEXT OF NEUROSCIENCE; ORGANIZATION OF RESEARCH INSTITUTIONS; PHYSICIAN MIGRATION; PUBLIC MENTAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: This history of medicine research project investigates some important cultural influences on modern neuroscience with a focus on institutional, organizational and researcher migration issues.  The research follows an integrated group biographical, institution and network historiographical approach, while investigating biographical, conceptual and organizational information on emigre neuroscientists, who were forced to leave their home countries in the 1930s and 1940s and came to North America due to the political changes in Central Europe.  The historical project also analyzes the role of international networks that facilitated the forced migration of this group of approximately 600 neurologists, psychiatrists and other medical researchers and clinicians, as well as their integration into North American neuroscience centers, the reciprocal changes of these research settings and the ways, how they were locally modified.  By applying a cultural view to neuroscience history, the project gives new insights into the nature of progressive and regressive factors of individual forms of research organization, the development of institutional models and their impact on modern neuroscience, thus contributing to the advancement of ELSI knowledge in medicine and providing historical information for use among respective stakeholders (researchers, administrators, organizational leaders) in the Canadian and International Neurosciences.  This project investigates some major institutional settings and patterns of migration and adaptation in North American neuroscience between 1910 (when the first interdisciplinary neuroscience centres emerged in Europe) and 1970 (when the Society of Neuroscience had its first US meeting), in order to determine its receptiveness to external impulses and its permeability for foreign researchers and physicians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cell biological mechanisms of TDP-43 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; ASTROCYTE; CELL BIOLOGY; MOTOR NEURON; OXIDATIVE STRESS; STRESS GRANULES; STRESS RESPONSE; TDP-43
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by the selective loss of specialized neurons that control voluntary movement. The basis of how these specialized neurons, known as motor neurons, are lost in ALS remains unknown. Environmental influences have long been linked to ALS and motor neurons are known to be very sensitive to chemicals and environmental stress. Mammalian cells possess a variety of mechanisms to mount a stress response and thus mediate a cell's recovery from physiological and environmental stresses. We have recently identified TDP-43 (TAR DNA binding protein) as a regulator of one cellular stress response: the formation of stress granules. TDP-43 mutations are causative for ALS. Thus, this project is aimed at exploring the cell biology of stress granule dynamics mediated by TDP-43 and understanding how disease-causing mutations may disrupt these processes.

Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC DEVELOPMENT; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL SURFACE; HUMAN DISEASE; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEIN INTERACTION; PROTEOMICS; SKELETAL MUSCLE; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Muscle contraction is triggered by the release of calcium into muscle cells from a storage compartment inside the cells, referred to as the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Muscle relaxation is initiated by return of calcium to the storage compartment. Thus, all movement and every heartbeat is dependent on calcium fluxes. Calcium release channels are the major protein responsible for releasing calcium from the storage compartment to bring about muscle contraction. Malignant hyperthermia, a toxic response to anesthetics, and central core disease, causing muscle weakness, are skeletal muscle diseases that are caused by mutations in the skeletal muscle form of the calcium release channel. Mutations in the cardiac form of the calcium release channel cause cardiac arrhythmias that result in sudden death. Our group is studying the mechanisms regulating proper calcium release and uptake in muscle to understand how altered function can lead to disease. Knowledge of the mechanism of action of these proteins could lead to new ways to treat or prevent inherited, and even acquired, muscle defects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rank/Rankl/OPG: a new pathway that regulates skeletal muscle disuse, aging and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM MOBILIZATION; CELL SIGNALING; DYSTROPHIES; EXCITATION CONTRACTION COUPLING; MUSCLE ATROPHY/DYSFUNCTION; MUSCLE FORCE; MYOPATHIES; PROTEASES; RANK/RANKL/OPG; SARCOPLASMIC RETICULUM
Abstract-Résumé: Bones and skeletal muscles constitute approximately 65% of human body weight. Bones and skeletal muscles undergo atrophy (loss of muscle and bone mass) following aging, prolonged bed rest, stroke, spinal cord injury, burns, neurodegenerative diseases, space flight, immobilization, denervation and several other debilitating conditions. It becomes obvious that skeletal muscles and bones share many biological characteristics in response to mechanical, hormonal, metabolic and pharmacologic environments. Although the biological signaling pathway called Rank/Rankl/OPG pathway is well-known to control bone mass and osteoporosis, its role in skeletal muscle has yet to be investigated. In this proposal, we use different in vivo and in vitro approaches to understand how this pathway influences muscle function under various disuses or pathological conditions. We found with the use of genetic deletion that this biological pathway plays key roles in muscle function and muscle degenerescence and also controls, to some extent, the expression of slow and fast twitch muscle fibers. This proposal is of special significance in that it may provide through the blockage of Rank/Rankl function the basic and clinical foundations for the design of novel therapeutic strategies for a wide variety of musculoskeletal and neuromusculoskeletal diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying novel roles of calcineurin signaling in the control of multiple complementary pathways affecting the dystrophic phenotype
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCINEURIN MODULATORS; CELL BIOLOGY; INTRACELLULAR CALCIUM MODULATORS; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALING; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; PLASMID TRANSFECTIONS; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL; QRT-PCR; TRANSGENIC MICE; UTROPHIN EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: One of the most promising therapeutic strategies for countering muscular dystrophy is to replace the missing muscle dystrophin protein that is a signature of this disease with its protein "twin sister" utrophin, which is present in small amounts in the muscles of people that have muscular dystrophy. We were the first to provide exciting new evidence showing that utrophin is under the control of another muscle protein, calciceurin, which we had previously shown to be an orchestrator of muscle growth.  Indeed, we showed that when calcineurin is turned on within a muscle, utrophin is also forced to appear in abundance all over the muscle in areas usually reserved for dystrophin, and by virtue of this replacement is thus capable of rescuing fibers that are damaged by muscular dystrophy.  Within the time frame of this proposal, we plan to further define the role of calcineurin in this rescuing of damaged dystrophic muscles and plan to identify novel other players in this symphony to help us better understand this disease and develop strategies and interventions to reverse its damaging effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Misfolding of Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase by pathological FUS and TDP43: relevance to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; NEURODEGENERATION; PRION-LIKE; PROTEIN MISFOLDING; RNA PROCESSING; TEMPLATE DIRECTED MISFOLDING
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is an incurable neuromuscular disease characterized by progressive paralysis of the muscles of the limbs, speech, swallowing, and respiration due to the progressive degeneration of motor neurons. Multiple laboratories, including our own, have recently shown that protein misfolding of Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD1) can be propagated in cell culture in a prion-like manner. However, genetic mutations of FUS and TDP43, in addition to SOD1 and some others can all result in clinicopathologically indistinguishable ALS. In this research, we test the hypothesis that misfolded and/or mislocalized FUS and TDP43 can trigger the misfolding of SOD1, which is subsequently propagated throughout the motor nervous system in ALS. Understanding the final common molecular pathway of ALS will aid in the identification of novel diagnostics and treatment targets for this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Population health ethics: Investigating the implications of 'targeting' socially-defined population subgroups to promote health
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHICS AND HEALTH EQUITY; GLOBAL HEALTH; HEALTH AND PLACE; HIV/STIS; POPULATION HEALTH ETHICS; QUALITATIVE METHODS AND POLICY ANALYSIS; SOCIAL SCIENCE METHODS; STI/HIV TESTING; YOUNG MEN; YOUTH SEXUAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Targeting interventions towards population sub-groups (as defined according to their shared social characteristics) is not a new strategy; this approach has inspired the bulk of population health interventions in Canada and abroad. However, the ethical implications of targeting population subgroups is only beginning to be examined. Using STI/HIV testing interventions targeted at young men (across low-, middle-, and high-income settings) as examples, the proposed study offers an opportunity to address knowledge gaps within the field of population health ethics. The proposed study examines the ethical implications of targeting socially defined population subgroups to promote population health. The proposed study raises questions about ethical ways to intervene to address a serious population (and personal) health problem - STI/HIV rates among young men. The proposed longitudinal 5-year study will capture and track the ethical implications of STI/HIV testing interventions that target young men and the study objectives include:  1.To identify and track the dominant narratives appearing in policy and programming documents pertaining to STI/HIV testing of young men in three types of places (e.g., low-, middle-, and high-income settings) and to examine whether particular values and ethical principles are privileged in the discourse presented across these documents and over time; 2.To analyze interview accounts from men, service providers and policy makers regarding their experiences with STI/HIV testing interventions in order to assess the ways in which equity issues (e.g., population-level benefits as compared to individually-oriented benefits; more immediate impacts juxtaposed to longer term effects) are perceived and experienced in a variety of settings;  3.To assess the ways in which dominant institutional discourses regarding STI/HIV testing for young men are taken up (or rejected) and how that might vary across settings over time.

TitreApplicationTitle: An HIV Prevention Intervention for HIV-Negative Men Who Have Sex With Men Via Reduction of Social Anxiety and Substance Use in Sexual Situations
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV/AIDS; INTERVENTION EVALUATION; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; SEXUAL RISK BEHAVIOUR; SOCIAL ANXIETY; SUBSTANCE USE
Abstract-Résumé: The Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) epidemic among men who have sex with other men (MSM) in Canada is on the rise. Nearly half (44.1%) of new cases of HIV are among MSM due to unprotected anal intercourse between HIV-positive and HIV-negative MSM. There is therefore a critical need for HIV prevention interventions in Canada. Social anxiety, or anxiety about being evaluated in interpersonal situations, is a reliable risk factor for HIV acquisition among MSM. Fortunately, social anxiety is also highly modifiable via behavioral counseling. The present study will provide pilot data for a novel and innovative HIV prevention intervention for MSM using empirically supported cognitive-behavioral therapy to reduce social anxiety and occurrence of unprotected anal intercourse. The intervention will be administered to 20 HIV-negative MSM who experience social anxiety and have had unprotected anal intercourse within the past 3 months. The intervention will consist of 10 sessions of cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) for treatment of social anxiety and related substance use in sexual situations. Participants will complete assessments at baseline, post-intervention and at 3-months follow-up to monitor frequency of unprotected intercourse and levels of social anxiety.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and Validation of an Algorithm to Impute Missing Stop Dates of Antiretroviral Therapy Regimens
Keywords-MotsClés: ALGORITHM; ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; HIV/AIDS; IMPUTATION
Abstract-Résumé: The development of medications to treat HIV infection has significantly improved both survival rates and quality of life among HIV infected individuals.  As these individuals are now living longer, there is interest in studying whether HIV infected individuals are at higher risk for other diseases such as diabetes, cancer and kidney disease and whether these diseases are more severe in this population.      The best way to study the interaction of HIV with other diseases is to use data collected through longitudinal studies and through databases maintained by clinics, hospitals and provincial registries. However, this data may not always be documented with sufficient detail since the dates on which new medications were started are usually recorded quite well in medical charts but the dates on which medications were stopped are not recorded as well.  Accurate ARV regimen history information is essential for longitudinal clinical HIV research projects examining effectiveness of regimens or side effects of regimens, such as lipid abnormalities or cardiovascular outcomes.         In this research project, we will develop an algorithm to impute missing stop dates for antiretroviral therapies.  The algorithm will consider the class of drug, other drugs in the regimen, calendar year in which the drug was started, and other factors.  This algorithm will be developed using data from the Ontario HIV Treatment Network Cohort Study (OCS) and will be validated using data from other settings where more complete information is available on medication histories through pharmacy records. This algorithm will be useful for many Canadian and international HIV cohort studies and will be important for a large number of research projects examining associations of cumulative medication use with the development of comorbidities and adverse events and associations of particular regimens with response to treatment or the development of toxicities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Close encounters of a Natural Killer kind: Understanding how NK cells protect against HIV infection.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY DEPENDENT CELL MEDIATED VIRAL INHIBITION; ANTIBODY DEPENDENT CELLULAR CYTOTOXICITY; CORRELATES OF PROTECTION FROM INFECTION; HIV/AIDS; HLA; IMMUNE FUNCTION; KILLER IMMUNOGLOBULIN-LIKE RECEPTORS; NK CELLS; NK RECEPTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The term HIV exposed seronegative (HESN) is used to describe individuals who remain uninfected despite multiple exposures to HIV. Our research program aims to understand why HESN are resistant to HIV infection, which is information that is potentially important for the design of preventive vaccines for HIV. Previously, we showed that Natural Killer (NK) cells are an important component of protective immunity to HIV in HESN. NK cells become activated rapidly upon encountering HIV infected cells and secrete anti-viral factors that can suppress HIV replication or kill HIV infected cells. They can do this directly or indirectly by antibody dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). In ADCC, NK cells are brought into close contact with the cells they kill via an antibody (Ab) bridge that links NK cells with HIV infected cells. In a group of subjects who were mostly injection drug user (IDU) HESN we found that genes for certain NK receptors (NKR) and NKR paired with the HLA ligands they recognize, were associated with protection from infection. NK cells from subject with protective gene combinations had higher anti-viral activity than those from individuals with control genotypes. We propose here to verify these results in sexually exposed HESN. We will study the mechanism used by NK cells to mediate their anti-viral effect. In the only modestly successful HIV vaccine trial conducted to date, induction of non neutralizing Abs, which may function through ADCC were found to correlate with protection from infection. We will investigate whether gene combinations that influence direct NK activity also influence the potency of NK activity mediated by ADCC. This research has relevance to the design of preventive vaccines for HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Measuring mitochondrial aging, application to HIV infection and therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; DEEP SEQUENCING; HIV; MITOCHONDRIAL AGING; MITOCHONDRIAL DNA MUTATIONS; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: We all accumulate mutations within our mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)genome which encodes proteins necessary for our cellular energy production. The more mutations we accumulate, the less we can produce energy, the less we can maintain the health of our tissues.  This damagingof the mitochondrial  is believed to be one of the main reasons behind aging and age-related diseases. mtDNA mutations  can be inherited or caused by inflammation and oxidative stress. However, certain drugs such as the ones used to treat HIV are believed to also induce mtDNA mutations.   Evidence is accumulating that HIV-infected people age faster than non-infected people. They have diseases normally seen in older people earlier in life. It is unclear whether this is because of their HIV infection(which can cause chronic inflammation) or because of the side effects of the antiretroviral drugs they take to treat their disease. It is technically challenging to study mtDNA mutations because there are hundreds of copies of mtDNA in each cell. We have developed a deep sequencing-based methodology to detect low frequency mtDNA mutations and distinguish them from background PCR and sequencing errors. We will use a cell culture model to determine whether commonly used HIV drugs can indeed induce mtDNA mutations.  We will also test samples collected from HIV+ and HIV- individuals, young and old, treated with antiretroviral or not, to investigate the relationship between mitochondrial aging, biological aging, HIV infection and exposure to HIV therapy. It is important to figure out what may accelerate aging in HIV+ individuals: the virus or the medications? It may affect how we treat HIV+ people. This research will provide tools that can be used to study mitochondrial aging in any setting or disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the role of rectal and oral innate mucosal immune factors in HIV-exposed, but uninfected men who have sex with men
Keywords-MotsClés: BINDING INHIBITORS; HIV REPLICATION; HIV-RESISTANCE; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNE ACTIVATION; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; MICROBICIDES; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Since the beginning of the pandemic, HIV/AIDS has affected over 60 million individuals worldwide and currently infects over 33 million people.  In Canada and around the world, men who have sex with men (MSM) are one of the highest risk groups for HIV acquisition, and the development of preventative technologies (such as microbicide gels) for this group remain a priority for combating the spread of HIV/AIDS.  Unprotected anal sex between men continues to dominate patterns of HIV transmission but our lack of understanding of the immunity of this compartment is a major barrier in the development of preventative therapeutics.  New biomedical tools may be developed by studying HIV-exposed uninfected individuals (HESN), who are exposed to the virus but remain infection-free for many years.  We have been studying a group of HESN MSM who represent a model of protection and understanding their immune systems may help us design novel therapeutics.  We have determined that HESN MSM have a unique immune response that is defined by an increased amount of antimicrobial protein factors in both their rectal and oral mucosa, which we believe are protecting from infection from HIV.  These protein factors have shown the ability to inhibit HIV and since they reside at the portal of entry for HIV and we believe they are playing a role in protecting against infection.   This proposal will examine the role of these factors in HIV protection and help us to develop them into a novel therapeutic.  The hope is that this information could be used to design a novel microbicide formulation against HIV which could be used by groups at high risk of HIV infection, such as men who have sex with men.

TitreApplicationTitle: Culturally grounded suicide intervention in Cree Nation communities
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY; CULTURE; FIRST NATIONS; INTERVENTION; PUBLIC HEALTH; RISK FACTORS; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: This grant requests support to continue the work of the CIHR-funded Swampy Cree Suicide Prevention Team (2007-2012). The Team includes members of the Swampy Cree Tribal Council communities (eight Northwestern Manitoba communities), university-based investigators and international consultants. The Team's two main research focuses are: 1) understanding who is at risk for suicide among Swampy Cree communities, and 2) developing culturally-appropriate suicide prevention strategies. Over the last five years, the Team has been successful in finding out from the communities about why they believe suicide is a problem in their communities and how to fix it. We have also done studies with large Aboriginal populations to further support these ideas. Over the next five years, the Team will focus on sharing new First Nations specific suicide prevention programs for families and adolescents in the Swampy Cree communities. An important focus of our work will be to train First Nations community members to be able to run these programs on their own in their remote reserve communities. By working with government and Chiefs in the communities, the knowledge we gain fromour work can have a direct impact on people in these community.

TitreApplicationTitle: GetCheckedBC: Developing new knowledge to inform the province-wide implementation of an online STI/HIV testing service for youth
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER; HEALTH AND PLACE; HEALTH INEQUALITIES; ONLINE STI TESTING; PARTICIPATORY METHODS; SOCIAL CONTEXT; YOUTH SEXUAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The Internet is a medium that offers unprecedented reach to populations at risk for STIs and HIV. Youth (ages 15-24) bear a significant burden of STI/HIV infection in BC, particularly in some communities (e.g. rural, with large youth populations), and have been shown to be particularly receptive to internet-based services. The STI/HIV Division at BC Centre for Disease Control (BCCDC) has recently been funded to develop GetCheckedBC (GCBC), a new online STI/HIV testing intervention. Building on a previous study that informed the planning and development of the GCBC content and approach, with a specific focus on understanding the saliency and credibility of online approaches for youth, the current study will focus on efforts related to scaling-up the GCBC across BC's five Health Authorities over the next five years. We acknowledge that many aspects of a young person's social position interact to determine their use of testing (furthermore, service providers also are influenced by social context). In BC, at least three sub-groups of youth may be considered priority populations (youth who identify as LGBT; racialized youth; street-involved youth). The current proposal will actively engage young people who are clients (or prospective clients) of GCBC, as well as service providers, to understand youth's experiences with GCBC and to examine the effects and diffusion of the use of GCBC in the youth population. The proposed five-year study will use qualitative and quantitative methods to develop new knowledge to inform effective, province-wide scaling up of GCBC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cervical Cancer Screening in Urban Areas: Contributions of Traditional and Spatial Analyses of a Population Health Database to Inform the Improved Provision of Health Services on the Island of Montreal
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO HEALTH SERVICES; CERVICAL CANCER; SCREENING; SPACE-TIME GEOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Invasive cervical cancer can be prevented if women receive regular screening tests.  One of the most efficient ways to ensure that women receive these tests at adequate intervals is to establish organized screening programs.  Quebec is one of only two provinces that have not begun to establish an organized cervical cancer screening program and, in fact, very little is known about screening practices among women who live in this province.  Because it will likely take some time for a province-wide program to be established, there is a role for local public health agencies to develop targeted programs to improve the demand and availability of screening within their jurisdiction. This project aims to describe the socio-demographic characteristics (such as age, educational attainment, income, and country of birth) of women residing on the island of Montreal who have not recently received cervical cancer screening.  Additionally, we aim to describe in which neighborhoods women who have not recently been screened reside and to assess the characteristics of these neighborhoods (such as the density of physicians or the percentage of people who live in poverty) that explain the observed patterns.  We will achieve these aims by analyzing data from several waves of the Canadian Community Health Survey that have been linked to a dataset that contains information on the characteristics of Montreal neighborhoods called MEGAPHONE (Montreal Epidemiologic and Geographic Analysis of Population Health Outcomes and Neighbourhood Effects).  Understanding factors that predispose and enable women to be screened will permit public health decision makers to assess the need to develop programs that increase women's understanding of the importance of screening and aid women in obtaining a screening test.

TitreApplicationTitle: LUNCHES - Let's Understand Nutrition and Children's Health in Elementary Schools: Direct observation of packed lunch contents and intake in grades 3 and 4 students (aged 7-10 years) in the balanced school day vs. the traditional schedule.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD OBESITY; DIRECT OBSERVATION OF FOOD INTAKE; PACKED LUNCH INTAKE; POPULATION AND PUBLIC HEALTH; SCHOOL POLICY
Abstract-Résumé: The Balanced School Day (BSD) schedule is an alternative to the traditional elementary school schedule (TS), whereby recess and lunch breaks are reorganized into two nutrition/physical activity breaks. The BSD originated at one Ontario school in 2000, and the concept has since been implemented in well over a 1000 schools in Ontario and other provinces. The implementation of the BSD is well-intentioned, as it is thought to improve the school learning environment by providing 100-minute blocks of instructional time. However, the total amount of eating time in the BSD is double that of the TS and there is a lack of research studying the impact of this change on children's food intake during school. While it is thought that these two nutrition breaks are beneficial, it is also possible that the provision of two "mini-meals" could have a negative impact on food intake and obesity. This is a major public health concern given that 25% of Canadian children are identified as overweight or obese. Children spend a significant amount of time at school and foods eaten there are important contributors to their total daily intake. Thus, research studying the nutritional impact of the BSD is needed. This study aims to investigate the nutritional value of packed lunch contents and intake of students in the BSD vs. the TS. In addition, a parental survey, to capture factors which may impact student intake, and a comparison of the prevalence of overweight and obesity will be assessed in the two schedules. Not only will this data determine whether there are differences in children's packed lunch contents and intake in the two schedules, it will also help to address ongoing concerns that parents and teachers have with children's packed lunch contents and intake. This research will be useful for school boards and public health units to understand the nutritional value of packed lunches and may facilitate future work on interventions to improve nutritional quality of packed lunches.

TitreApplicationTitle: PAR2-calcium signalling in vascular endothelium.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; ENDOTHELIUM; PHARMACOLOGY; PROTEINASE ACTIVATED RECEPTOR; RECEPTORS; SHARP MICROELECTRODE; SMOOTH MUSCLE; VASCULAR; WESTERN BLOT
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease is an increasing health concern in Canada. High blood pressure, a common component of many cardiovascular diseases, is associated with dysfunctional blood vessels. Some drugs which would normally be used to treat patients with cardiovascular diseases are less effective because of blood vessel dysfunction in people with high blood pressure. However, our research has discovered novel molecules which target a protein called PAR2; these molecules are still effective in blood vessels during high blood pressure. It is known that PAR2 communicates messages between cells in blood vessels using calcium. How these calcium signals are communicated under conditions of high blood pressure is not understood. We intend to measure PAR2 communication signals at a cell level with state of the art microscope techniques in an experimental model of high blood pressure. By expanding our knowledge in this area of cell signalling during high blood pressure, we anticipate to uncover new strategies to counter blood vessel dysfunction in patients suffering from cardiovascular diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovering the neuroendocrine features of obesity with food addiction
Keywords-MotsClés: APPETITE REGULATION; DIABETES; DUAL-ENERGY X-RAY ABSORPTIOMETRY; FOOD INTAKE; GUT HORMONES; NEUROPEPTIDES; OBESITY; YALE FOOD ADDICTION SCALE
Abstract-Résumé: The present-day obesity epidemic is an immediate health concern for nations globally as the increased prevalence of obesity is associated with conditions including type two diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. This is of importance to the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador, as it has one of the greatest obesity rates in the country. The new concept of "food addiction" suggests that food can induce an addictive process, similar to drugs of abuse, and therefore lead to food overconsumption. Food addiction in humans can be assessed by the Yale Food Addiction Scale. We hypothesis that obesity with food addiction is a specific subgroup of human obesity and this subgroup has unique hormonal features which influence appetite (in the gut and brain). Therefore, our research objective was to: 1) observe the percentage of Newfoundlanders who are classified as food addicted in the obese and general populations; and 2) compare blood concentrations of appetite-regulating hormones between obese food addicted subjects and obese non-food addicted subjects (as well with healthy controls). The ongoing CIHR-funded Complex Diseases in the Newfoundland Population: Environment and Genetics (CODING) Study will be used for the proposed project (500 current and 500 newly recruited participants). All participants will be administered the YFAS. Additionally, body fat will be measured using dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Blood samples will be taken to determine levels of various hormones involved with appetite and metabolism, and these hormones will be measured using technology provided in the lab. We feel our study is highly novel and very feasible. We hope to define a new subgroup of obese patients (obesity with food addiction) by the group's unique appetite-regulating hormonal characteristics. By isolating this distinct subgroup of common obesity, it will help to better elucidate treatment and prevention plans to improve overall health status.

TitreApplicationTitle: NMR Structural Studies of Surfactant Protein B (SP-B)
Keywords-MotsClés: LUNG SURFACTANT; MEMBRANE PROTEIN; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; SOLID STATE NMR; SOLUTION NMR
Abstract-Résumé: Lung surfactant is a complex mixture of biological molecules that lines the air-sacs in the lungs. In order for us to breathe, it is essential the lung surfactant is present and functioning properly. Premature infants often have difficulty breathing because they are born before their bodies have produced enough lung surfactant, a condition called Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS). In order to survive, these infants need to be treated with lung surfactant from another source (e.g. from animals), until their bodies start making enough of their own lung surfactant. People of any age with severe illness or injury often develop a condition called Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) which is frequently fatal. Unfortunately, surfactant replacement treatment has not been shown to save the lives of those with ARDS.   To produce an effective treatment for ARDS and other diseases that result from lung surfactant deficiencies and improve the treatment for infants, we need to better understand how lung surfactant works. One of the most important components of lung surfactant, a protein called Surfactant Protein-B (SP-B), is also one of its least well understood components. For a long time, we and others have sought to understand SP-B better by trying to determine its structure, i.e. the special shape it folds into that allows it to function properly. However, this has been very difficult since no one has been able to produce a sample of SP-B that would allow the structure of this protein, as it is found in the lung, to be observed in the laboratory. In collaboration with colleagues in Spain, we have recently succeeded in establishing methods to produce SP-B for structural studies. Now we are using this method to find the shape of SP-B. This will tell us which of its structural features are essential in order for it to carry out its function and enable the design of improved treatments for respiratory distress disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and epigenetic determinants for juvenile-onset ovarian tumourigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGENS; ENDOCRINOLOGY; EPIGENETICS; FOLLICULAR DEVELOPMENT; GENETICS; GRANULOSA CELL TUMOUR; JUVENILE-ONSET; PARENT-OF-ORIGIN EFFECT; SEX CHROMOSOMES; SUSCEPTIBILITY GENES
Abstract-Résumé: Major contributions to our understanding of cancer susceptibility genes have come from investigations of families that show genetic heritability for specific cancers. Genes that confer cancer susceptibility play a particularly important role in the etiology of pediatric cancers, as they appear at a time of life when cancer risk due to environmental exposure is very low. Our ability to identify genetic determinants for cancer susceptibility may be limited if the cancer is rare in the human population. Several subtypes of ovarian cancer are more rare than the typical epithelial ovarian cancers that appear in post-menopausal women. Our research has focused on genes that contribute to spontaneous ovarian granulosa cell (GC) tumour susceptibility in female mice of a particular laboratory strain, as a model genetic system for the development of pediatric ovarian tumours that appear in infants and young girls. A genetic region on mouse Chromosome 4 and two regions on Chromosome X have been identified that confer pediatric ovarian GC tumour susceptibility in mice; furthermore, these regions are evolutionarily similar to segments of human Chromosome 1 and X. If the tumour-susceptibility genes can be identified in mice, the same genes and pathways can be further investigated in pediatric GC tumours, with the goal of successful health interventions to prolong life, preserve fertility, and ensure the long term endocrine health of infants, young girls and women who develop this subtype of ovarian cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Cross-sectional and Case-control Analysis of Physically Independent and Physically Dependent Cohorts of Octogenarians: Part One of the Life after 80 Study
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COMMUNITY SERVICES; HEALTH CARE DELIVERY; INTERFACE NURSE; OLD-ELDERLY; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE
Abstract-Résumé: The old elderly, those people aged 80 and over, are the fastest growing group of the population. This group is often thought to be in poor health. However, the physical and mental health, living situations, and activity levels of this group are quite wide-ranging. Some do indeed reach the age of 80 having accumulated many medical problems. However, at the other end of the spectrum, many of those aged 80 and over are healthy, active, and alert with very few chronic medical problems,few or no ongoing medications, and living independently without assistance. What is different between these two groups now? What was different about their life's circumstances and  experiences that might have contributed to their current situation? What is likely to happen to them in the coming years? These are questions we hope to answer with the current study, a comparison of old elderly individuals who are physically independent and those who are not. We plan to recruit 200 study participants through family physician offices, personal care homes, and nursing homes; 100 in each group (physically independent versus physically dependent). After each person is recruited we will begin collecting information about him or her This information will include basic demographics (age, sex, education level, marital status, etc.), as well as assessments of activities of daily living, lifestyle, current medical conditions and medications, self assessed health status, depression, general happiness, and life expectancy (both in terms of number of years and quality of life). This study will improve our understanding of the health outcomes and needs of the aged.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Ras-dependent oncolysis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPY; CELL SIGNALING; INTERFERON (IFN); IRF1; ONCOLYTIC VIRUS; RAS/MEK; TRANSCRIPTION; VIRUS INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Oncolytic viruses are engineered or naturally occurring viruses that replicate in cancer cells, but not in normal cells. They have become a focus of attention for cancer therapy in recent years as clinical studies have shown them to be quite promising. However, the biochemical mechanisms of their tumor selectivity still remain to be studied. In this proposal, we will investigate how one of the oncogenic cell signaling pathways, Ras/MEK, promotes the replication of certain oncolytic viruses in cancer cells. We believe that the Ras/MEK pathway inhibits function of a cellular protein known as interferon regulatory factor (IRF)-1, which is known to block viral replication, resulting in efficient replication of oncolytic viruses in cancer cells. Our study will provide a novel insight into the molecular mechanisms of viral oncolysis as well as the future development of new oncolytic viruses with improved efficacy and safety.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of FGF23 in fetal phosphorus metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: FETAL MINERAL METABOLISM; FETAL-PLACENTAL MINERAL TRANSPORT; FGF23; PHEX; PHOSPHORUS METABOLISM; SODIUM-PHOSPHATE COTRANSPORTER; VITAMIN D/CALCITRIOL; X-LINKED HYPOPHOSPHATEMIC RICKETS
Abstract-Résumé: Phosphorus initiates critical steps in the formation of the skeleton and in its subsequent mineralization; without phosphorus, calcium cannot bind, and the skeleton is deformed and weak (rickets or osteomalacia). Recently fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF23) has been shown to be a key regulator of phosphorus balance in the adult. Osteocytes secrete FGF23 to cause the kidneys to excrete phosphorus. Certain hereditary and acquired conditions are now known to be due to excess or deficiency of FGF23 which causes specific disturbances in serum phosphorus levels, skeletal morphology and strength, and muscle strength and function.  Despite the explosion of knowledge pertaining to the role of FGF23 in adult skeletal and mineral metabolism, essentially nothing is known about its role during fetal development. Phosphorus plays essential roles in the formation and mineralization of the fetal skeleton, it is actively pumped across the placenta from the maternal circulation, and it circulates at higher blood levels than in adult. Does FGF23 play a role in regulating these processes?  The hypothesis is that FGF23 acts during fetal development to regulate placental phosphorus transport, stimulate renal phosphorus excretion, prevent excessive hyperphosphatemia, and facilitate skeletal mineralization. The clinical relevance is that not only will the normal physiological role of FGF23 in fetal life have been clarified, but the data will inform whether the human conditions of tumor calcinosis and X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) alter phosphorus and skeletal metabolism before birth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of  Novel Copy Number Variants using a  Custom Genome Wide Microarray Chip for Diagnosis of Familial Spondyloarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS; COPY NUMBER VARIATIONS; MISSING HERITABILITY; PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS; STRUCTURAL VARIATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Spondyloarthritis (SpA) represents a collection of chronic inflammatory conditions that primarily affect the spine, peripheral joints and exhibits several extra-articular features particularly psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and uveitis. The most common forms of SpA are ankylosing spondylitis (AS) and psoriatic arthritis (PsA). SpA constitutes a major health challenge because of its prevalence in Canada (affecting 400,00 Canadians), its propensity to affect young adults, and the necessity for lifelong medical management. Despite a high heritability for SpA, including identification of multiple genes via genome-wide association scans , only a fraction of the entire disease heritability is explained.     Copy number variants, (CNVs) are  a prominent source of variation in the human genome and are increasingly being associated with known genomic disorders, suggesting that they may underpin the pathogenesis of complex diseases.      CNVs have not been comprehensively assessed in SpA. We hypothesize that CNVs represent highly penetrant genetic variation accounting for part of the missing heritability in SpA families that have multiple affected individuals.      With the use of our custom two million probe microarray chip that we have developed, we will analyze 20 large informative SpA families with multiple affected members.  CNVs identified from these families will then be tested in 900 individuals with SpA. By elucidating  the entire genetic contribution of  SpA ,including CNVs, this will hopefully lead to a better diagnostic tool and increased understanding of these disease so that the present challenges in managing SpA (substantial delay in diagnosis, inability to predict disease course and marked heterogeneity in treatment response) may be overcome.

Abstract-Résumé: The PHAC/CIHR Influenza Research Network (PCIRN) is a national network of influenza researchers, created in 2009 with funding from a CIHR grant under the Pandemic Preparedness Strategic Research Initiative (PPSRI). In 2012 PCIRN represents 90 investigators from more than 30 institutions across Canada, comprising leading experts in the fields of vaccine safety, vaccine effectiveness, and program evaluation. PCIRN's objectives are to develop, test, and implement methodologies related to the evaluation of influenza vaccines as they pertain to safety, immunogenicity, effectiveness, and program implementation and evaluation. PCIRN is also designed to support Canadian pandemic preparedness on an ongoing basis. For the 3-year renewal, PCIRN will comprise 6 infrastructures: the Clinical Trials Network of 8 sites, conducting rapid clinical trials and planning a 3-year study comparing Fluad and TIV; the Serious Outcomes Surveillance Network of 40 adult sites will strengthen ongoing assessments of vaccine effectiveness in its test-negative case control study, better define influenza burden of disease, and enhance its capacity to respond rapidly to emerging vaccine safety signals; the National Ambulatory Network will expand to provide the most valid data on the safety of the seasonal influenza vaccine in various age groups to Public Health prior to the mass campaign; a Clinical Investigations Network of 10 hospital sites will be established to conduct clinical investigations of  reported allergic symptoms following immunization; the Program Delivery and Evaluation Network will connect to public health units and vaccine delivery units to evaluate applied public health strategies related to influenza immunization programs; and the Reference Laboratory Network of 5 sites will maintain the PCIRN biobank and conduct novel influenza assay development. Training the next generation of pandemic researchers will continue to be a high priority for PCIRN.

TitreApplicationTitle: Influence of motor behaviour on sensory feedback to primary motor cortex
Keywords-MotsClés: NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PRIMARY MOTOR CORTEX; STRETCH REFLEXES; UPPER LIMB; VOLUNTARY MOTOR CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Humans are able to perform a broad range of motor skills, from the rapid spinning of an elite diver to the precise staccato of a violinist. Recent theories suggest that sensory feedback from the limb (and vision) are essential for performing these voluntary motor skills. In particular, the theory suggests feedback is always present and that the properties of the arm and the movement goal influence the use of this feedback for controlling the limb. Our recent studies on humans show how feedback from the limb is used to modify and correct perturbations (unexpected bumps applied to the limb) during reaching or other motor tasks. The timing of these corrections suggest that they are generated from signals transmitted down to the spinal cord from primary motor cortex. Primary motor cortex is known to be important for voluntary control, but its use of feedback for control is not well recognized nor understood. The present proposal will highlight how feedback to this brain region scales with perturbation magnitude, interacts with spinal activity and importantly is modified based on the behavioural goal. This research will change our view on how primary motor cortex controls movement by emphasizing the importance of sensory feedback. This knowledge provides a foundation for understanding how various neurological disorders such as stroke impact brain function and motor performance. The behavioural tasks used in this proposal will also be used in parallel studies to quantify motor deficits in various patient groups.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of action of DNMT1 inhibitors; a pharmacoepigenomic analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Our genes that are inherited from our parents are marked by a chemical coating during gestation and are packaged in a highly organized manner in the nucleus of all cells. The chemical coating called "DNA methylation" and the packaging termed "chromatin modification" programs our genes so that they perform their dedicated tasks in the different organs and tissues of our body. We now know that this marking of the genome termed "epigenome" is altered in response to environmental signals. Disruption of the normal pattern of the epigenome results in human disease. One of the hallmarks of cancer is aberrant DNA methylation, which consists of increased methylation of tumor suppressor genes and global hypomethylation. We therefore proposed 16 years ago that DNMT inhibitors are candidate anticancer drugs. The working hypothesis is that inhibition of DNMTs causes DNA demethylation and activation of tumor suppressor genes.   It is becoming apparent that changes in DNA methylation play a role not only in cancer but other diseases as well. The proper therapeutic utilization of the vast potential of DNMT inhibitors in cancer as well as other conditions requires that we understand the molecular mechanism of action of DNMT inhibitors. The advances in whole-genome methylation mapping and the progress in our lab in methylome bioinformatics allow us to delineate, at the genomic level, the molecular mechanism of action of DNMT inhibition and unravel their therapeutic potential.   In this project, we will define the epigenomic targets that are affected by inhibition of the different DNMT isotypes and their combination in a panel of primary untransformed and cancer cells. Second, we will define the role of active demethylation in the mechanism of action of DNMT inhibitors. Third, we will delineate the mechanisms through which DNMT inhibitors induce the DNA damage response and the therapeutic implications of these mechanisms for developing clinically active DNMT inhibitors.
