TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Anti-Leishmania Immunity by CD3+CD4-CD8- (Double Negative) T Cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMONOLOGIC MEMORY; IMMUNOLOGY; INFECTION AND IMMUNITY; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; PARASITIC DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Leishmaniases are parasitic diseases that affect both humans and animals. It is caused by protozoan parasite belonging to the genus Leishmania. The disease is endemic in 88 countries and it is currently estimated by WHO that about 12 million people worldwide are afflicted with the disease with more than1.5 - 2 million new cases occurring every year and 350 million at risk of infection. There is no effective vaccine against leishmaniasis and the current treatments are very expensive, highly toxic and there are increasing reports of development of drug resistance. Although, the disease occurs mostly in the tropics and subtropics, increased travel, globalization and war, has resulted in the presence of the disease in individuals from endemic areas. For instance, Canadian and American Soldiers returning from active duty in the endemic areas like Iraq and Afghanistan have been diagnosed with the disease.  Vaccination remains the most cost-effective means of controlling infectious diseases. Unfortunately, there is still no effective vaccine against leishmaniasis. This is in part related to our lack of understanding of the factors that regulate immunologic memory; which is the ability of our defense system to recognize pathogens it has successfully dealt with and to make those protective molecules faster during a subsequent exposure. Any effective vaccine should lead to the development of cells called memory cells that will protect vaccinated individuals upon subsequent exposure to the infectious agent (immunologic memory). This project will investigate the part a newly described cell population plays in the development and maintenance of immunologic memory in cutaneous leishmaniasis. Results from this study will extend our knowledge and understanding of the factors that regulate memory cell development in leishmaniasis and could aid understanding of other infectious diseases like HIV, malaria and tuberculosis

TitreApplicationTitle: The epidemiology of resilience following child maltreatment: An examination of protective factors across the lifespan.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD MALTREATMENT; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENDER; INTERVENTION; LIFESPAN; MENTAL HEALTH PROMOTION; POPULATION HEALTH; PROTECTIVE FACTORS; RESILIENCE; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: To date, child maltreatment research has focused mainly on risk factors and poor outcomes with fewer studies examining resilience following child maltreatment and protective factors associated with mental health (e.g., absence of mental disorders and high quality of life). Resilience is generally described as the ability to maintain or regain mental health after adverse exposure. A protective factor is an indicator that is associated with an increased likelihood of a positive outcome. A review of the literature indicated that supportive relationships show a consistent association with healthy outcomes. What is still largely unknown is the prevalence of mental health in the general population following child maltreatment exposure in comparison to non-maltreated individuals. What other protective factors are associated with mental health and how can resilience be enhanced? Fostering resilience after child maltreatment has the potential to improve mental health for individuals and populations. The current proposal is unique because it will lead to new knowledge that will guide the development of intervention strategies to promote protective factors in facilitating resilience among individuals with a history of child maltreatment exposure across the lifespan-from adolescence to later adulthood. An epidemiological perspective will be applied to understand the prevalence of child maltreatment and mental health, the relationship between protective factors and mental health cross-sectionally and over a 3-year period. Noted strengths of this research include accessing large nationally representative Canadian and US data, examining sex and gender differences, using a lifespan approach, accessing longitudinal data, using high quality measures of child maltreatment and mental health, and inclusion of several protective factors in one study.

TitreApplicationTitle: Obesity and Development of a Diabetes Mellitus-Like State in Pregnancy: Investigating a Role for Regulation of the Human Placental Growth Hormone Genes
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETIC EVENTS/NON-CODING RNAS; HIGH FAT DIET-INDUCED GESTATIONAL DIABETES; HUMAN PLACENTA; HUMAN PLACENTAL HORMONE GENES; PREGNANCY; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: THE PROBLEM is that 1 in 25 women will develop glucose intolerance, or diabetes mellitus (DM)-like state during pregnancy. This increases the risk to the baby, as well as for obesity and type 2 DM (needing insulin) in later life. WHAT'S GOING ON? There is certainly a genetic component as some ethnic groups are at increased risk, but it is unclear why some pregnant women who develop DM release less insulin than is needed. Human (h) placental hormones, including placental lactogen (CS) and placental growth hormone (GH-V), help to increase the number of insulin-producing pancreatic cells, but CS/GH-V production is also affected by glucose and insulin levels. Thus, changes in CS/GH-V production may contribute to DM. WE BELIEVE that the food we eat can both affect the placental environment, and use of our genetic material, DNA, and therefore the genes that code for proteins, including CS and GH-V. This happens in part by (epigenetic) changes in levels of small nucleic acids (non-coding RNAs) used to switch genes "on" or "off" during pregnancy. These modifications may contribute to, or worsen DM in pregnancy. They may also reflect "tracks" left by changes to the environment that can be "followed" for monitoring and deciding on any treatment. The study of the human CS/GH-V genes is problematic, however, because it is difficult to take placenta samples during pregnancy, and the GH-V gene is only found in humans and other primates. AS A SOLUTION we made mice containing the human CS/GH-V genes, which will be fed a high fat diet in pregnancy to create a DM-like state. The effect on changes to the "on/off" status of the CS/GH-V genes will be studied. The equivalent "changes" will also be tested in human blood and placental samples from overweight women diagnosed with DM to help prioritize the "changes" to be studied further. WE HOPE to learn more about how this disease progresses, identify markers and develop a "humanized" mouse model to begin to assess possible treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of AKAP121 in cardiac hypertrophy and metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CELL METABOLISM; EXERCISE; KNOCKOUT MICE; PRESSURE OVERLOAD; SEX; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Stress like high blood pressure makes the heart work harder. Like other muscles, the heart gets bigger to meet the additional demand. At the same time, the heart switches its fuel dependence from fats towards sugars. These changes may be an attempt to reduce the stress and improve heart performance, but over time they contribute to dysfunction of the heart and lead to heart failure.  Our CIHR-funded projects explore two proteins that may link abnormal heart growth to altered fuel selection. We have shown that the protein AKAP121 blocks the growth program in isolated heart cells. Our data also indicates that this antigrowth protein may be lost in response to stress on the heart. Here we will track the loss of this protein, which may show subtle but important differences in women and men. We will also use genetically altered mice to see if the complete AKAP121 loss predisposes the heart to abnormal growth, or whether additional AKAP121 is protective.  The second protein, PGC-1a, is a powerful controller of pathways that regulate how fuel (sugar, fat) is consumed by the heart and turned into work. Both PGC-1a and AKAP121 appear to be reduced when the heart is stressed. Furthermore, AKAP121 regulates signaling by another protein, PKA, which in turn controls how much PGC-1a is made. In this project, we will study whether AKAP121 loss both increases heart cell size and causes loss of PGC-1a. If this is the case, the heart would be facing a situation where growth signals have been switched on (due to loss of AKAP121), while at the same time signals controlling normal fuel use (via PGC-1a) to produce energy would be lost. Our work will for the first time determine the role of AKAP121 in regulating both growth and fuel use signals in the heart, and will determine whether strategies to maintain AKAP121 levels may be protective.

TitreApplicationTitle: Living well with celiac disease: Improving medical monitoring and self-management of celiac disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CELIAC DISEASE; CHRONIC DISEASE; CLINICAL MONITORING; INTESTINAL PERMEABILITY; MUCOSAL RECOVERY; PATIENT SELF-MANAGEMENT; PROSPECTIVE LONGITUDINAL; TREATMENT ADHERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Celiac disease is a common health problem associated with symptoms such as bloating, diarrhea, weight loss and fatigue. People with celiac disease may also develop anemia and have a greater risk for osteoporosis and some types of cancer. The only treatment is self-management with a lifelong gluten-free diet. Maintaining a gluten-free diet is difficult and can be particularly challenging in social situations. Gluten is present in many foods and is often not labeled, so it can be difficult for an individual to know whether gluten has been consumed. This difficulty is compounded by the lack of useful tools for routine medical monitoring of patients with celiac disease. Diet review with a dietitian is time consuming, duodenal biopsy is invasive and available tests for antibodies in blood may miss a patient who eats small amounts of gluten. Tests using different antibodies or using sugars to measure how the intestine is working have the potential to be useful, but have not been fully tested. The requirements of a gluten-free diet are demanding and can negatively affect how persons with celiac disease manage day to day. There has been research looking at some of the effects, such as depression, but there is still much to learn about ways to support those with celiac disease to cope effectively. In this study we will follow adults newly diagnosed with celiac disease for two years. Health outcomes, psychological functioning, and behavioral adjustments to the disease will be assessed at diagnosis and 6, 12 and 24 months after diagnosis. This tracking over time approach will help to determine the ways in which individuals are affected by celiac disease, as well as what helps people to be successful in managing the disease. This study will also help determine the best medical tests and methods to support persons with celiac disease. This knowledge may lead to medical and self-management strategies which would improve the health of those living with celiac disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Muscarinic receptor antagonism as a novel mechanism for sensory nerve repair.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CHEMOTHERAPY-INDUCED NEUROPATHY; CONFOCAL IMAGING; IN VIVO ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MITOCHONDRIA; MUSCARINIC RECEPTORS; NERVE REGENERATION; PAIN SENSITIVITY; PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY; SENSORY NEURON
Abstract-Résumé: Objective Diabetic sensory neuropathy and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) are neurodegenerative diseases characterized by loss of nerve fibers in the skin. Both diseases cause significant pain and eventually lead to sensory loss. The impact of these diseases on human health is enormously damaging and there are no therapies. Our recent work has uncovered an endogenous signaling pathway in neurons that negatively modulates nerve fiber growth of sensory neurons. The neurotransmitter, acetylcholine, is produced by sensory neurons and skin cells and activates the muscarinic receptor.  Inhibiting the function of the receptor in sensory neurons using selective drugs or by genetically removing the gene significantly increases nerve fiber growth.   We propose a "cholinergic constraint hypothesis" describing a role for acetylcholine in restricting growth of nerves within the skin. The general objectives are: a)To suppress the muscarinic receptor pathway to repair nerve endings damaged by diabetes or anti-cancer agents. b)To determine the mechanism whereby receptor blockade enhances nerve growth with a focus on a role in control of calcium signaling and mitochondrial function.  Impact statement The proposed studies have a strong translational potential if successful. Our work with topical delivery of muscarinic blocking drugs (already FDA-approved for another indication) has progressed to a point where phase II clinical trials are envisaged for late 2012 for treatment of diabetic neuropathy. A company, WinSanTor, Inc., has recently been set up and will oversee delivery of this plan. This proposal, if funded, will enable the work to broaden in scope and permit this therapeutic approach to be performed in a wide range of distal dying-back neurodegenerative diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oligodendrocyte dysfunction in schizophrenia: mechanism and target of treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIPSYCHOTICS; MYELIN; NEUROPROTECTION; OLIGODENDROCYTE DYSFUNCTION; SCHIZOPHRENIA; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a complex and severe brain disorder that results in symptoms such as hallucinations, inappropriate emotion, difficultly socializing, inattention, and difficulty with learning and memory. The brain has millions of neurons that communicate with each other and are responsible for all aspects of our behaviour and thought processes. The neurons are surrounded by myelin sheaths that allow neurons to communicate with each other effectively. A breakdown in myelin results in abnormal thoughts and behaviour. Current studies suggest that schizophrenia may involve abnormalities in myelin. Studies from our laboratories have shown that the break-down of myelin in mice can cause symptoms that are similar to the symptoms found in patients with schizophrenia. When myelin was allowed to repair, the abnormal behaviour gradually disappeared. The current proposal will investigate the role of myelin, antipsychotic treatment, and stress in a mouse model of schizophrenia. We will examine how myelin damage results in schizophrenia-like behaviour. We will also examine if antipsychotic drug treatment can prevent myelin breakdown and/or aid in myelin repair and behavioural recovery. Finally, we will investigate the role of stress in recovery from myelin damage and schizophrenia-like behaviour. This research will increase our understanding of schizophrenia and the role of stress in the disease. In addition, it may open up new ways to treat schizophrenia by using existing drug treatments differently or developing new treatments that will work on myelin more directly.

TitreApplicationTitle: Culturally grounded suicide intervention in Cree Nation communities
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY; CULTURE; FIRST NATIONS; INTERVENTION; PUBLIC HEALTH; RISK FACTORS; SUICIDE
Abstract-Résumé: This grant requests support to continue the work of the CIHR-funded Swampy Cree Suicide Prevention Team (2007-2012). The Team includes members of the Swampy Cree Tribal Council communities (eight Northwestern Manitoba communities), university-based investigators and international consultants. The Team's two main research focuses are: 1) understanding who is at risk for suicide among Swampy Cree communities, and 2) developing culturally-appropriate suicide prevention strategies. Over the last five years, the Team has been successful in finding out from the communities about why they believe suicide is a problem in their communities and how to fix it. We have also done studies with large Aboriginal populations to further support these ideas. Over the next five years, the Team will focus on sharing new First Nations specific suicide prevention programs for families and adolescents in the Swampy Cree communities. An important focus of our work will be to train First Nations community members to be able to run these programs on their own in their remote reserve communities. By working with government and Chiefs in the communities, the knowledge we gain fromour work can have a direct impact on people in these community.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bringing of innate and adaptive immunity in chlamydial Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: HOST DEFENSE; IMMUNE RESPONSES; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; MEDICAL MICROBIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Chlamydiae are globally important human bacterial pathogens that cause infectious diseases with serious sequelae. The lack of a clear understanding of the mechanisms of protective/ pathological reactions has been a major obstacle for the rational development of a vaccine. We recently demonstrated that the interaction between the innate and adaptive reponses  are important for the proper development protective immunity against chlamydial infection. Specifically, we found that many types of leukocyte cells including dendritic cell (DCs), NKT cells and T cells play a role in this process. Our objective for the proposed study is to examine the interaction between NKT cells, DCs and T cells during Cpn infection with a focus on the effect of NKT on DC subsets and its impact on T cell responses and disease outcomes.  We will use mouse model of lung infection with Chlamydia to examine the interaction of NKT and DCs. Different types of mice including those with deficiency in particular cells and molecules. We will examine the immune responses, disease process and the outcome of infection in the special and normal control mice. We will also examine the changes in how cells look like and changes in cell functions especially those aspects related host dense against chlamydial infections and diseases.  This study will provide insight into the linkage between innate and adaptive immunity which are the two arms of immune responses. The study may lead to identification of new mechanisms related to chlamydial immunity and pathogenesis. Such knowledge will be very useful for the rational design of a chlamydial vaccine in particular and be helpful in understanding immune regulation, host defense and vaccine develop

Abstract-Résumé: Moderate to vigorous physical activity (MVPA) has been shown to have numerous benefits in patients living with type 2 diabetes. However, in order to achieve these benefits, it is recommended that people living with type 2 diabetes accumulate at least 150 minutes of MVPA per week.  Unfortunately, studies are inconsistent regarding whether a gender difference exists in MVPA levels for these patients using self-reported PA measures. Further, regardless of the potential gender MVPA disparity, research in type 2 diabetes patients has also neglected the importance of identifying common and gender-specific MVPA correlates that are needed to inform PA intervention development.  Thefore, the present project has 5 objectives: (1) to determine the total number of minutes of MVPA in 141 male and 141 female patients living diabetes for a 1-week period using an objective PA measure, (2) to map "where" patients are expending the total number of minutes of MVPA by linking accelerometry measures with a global positioning system (GPS) overall and by gender, (3) to examine the association between the time spent in MVPA and the MVPA location characteristics (i.e., the socioeconomic status, urban vs. rural, and access to MVPA opportunities associated with each MVPA location) overall and by gender, (4) to determine if the MVPA location characteristics (i.e., environmental) interact with the (a) intrapersonal (e.g., self-efficacy), (b) interpersonal (e.g., social support from family), and (c) institutional (e.g., perceived quality of care) levels of the social ecological model in the same way for male and female patients, and (5) to build capacity across Nova Scotia pertaining to MVPA issues via hosting a forum in each site's community that involves the research team as well as patients, family / friends, healthcare practitioners, and community stakeholders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Birthing Relationships and Rural Health Practices: The Experiences of Queer Women and Their Perinatal Care Providers.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIVERSE POPULATIONS; GENDER/SEXUALITY; HEALTH EQUITY; INTER-PROFESSIONAL RESEARCH; LGBTTQQ RESEARCH; PHENOMENOLOGICAL/QUALITATIVE METHODS; PROVIDER-CONSUMER RELATIONSHIPS; QUEER BIRTHING WOMEN; RURAL HEALTH CARE; SOCIAL EXCLUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Queer birthing women experience social exclusion in the Canadian health system based on gender and sexual orientation. Yet little research has been conducted on the experiences of these women, even less in rural care.  Homophobia, heterosexism and intolerance continue to be embedded in health care structures that are invisible and not well understood by perinatal providers. Heterosexist language and resources are especially pervasive outside of urban centers creating social and institutional conditions of exclusion. Likewise, providers often lack the necessary education to work productively with queer women during birth. Although providers often approach birthing with the intent of doing good, taking up a position of neutrality or attempting to treat everyone the same leaves providers ill equipped to account for the ways in which social conditions impact the birth experiences of queer women in rural life.   Providers working with birthing women may unknowingly reinstate normative patterns resulting in homophobia and gender binaries. This is particularly salient in birthing contexts, where the standards of care have been heteronormatively constructed. There is an urgency to understand how perinatal practices contribute to health inequities in the lives of birthing women who are queer, in addition to the ways certain providers may challenge those patterns to maximize rural birthing care.  This phenomenological study will examine how queer women experience birth across six rural sites in Nova Scotia, and how rural providers experience their work with queer birthing women.  A total of 25-30 queer women, 15-20 nurses, 15-20 physicians, and 4-5 midwives will participate in interviews and focus groups. Findings from the study will articulate strategies for optimizing perinatal care in the context of social exclusion. The results will be useful for best practice guidelines and continuing education for providers working with queer birthing women in rural care

TitreApplicationTitle: Emerging health researchers and the commercialization of academic science
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATIVE ETHNOGRAPHY; COMMERCIALIZATION POLICY; INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LAW; LIFE SCIENCES; SEMI-STRUCTURED INTERVIEWS; SURVEYS; UNIVERSITY RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this project is to understand the two-way relationship between emerging health researchers and commercialization practices at Canadian universities. This project will measure in several ways how commercialization practices such as patenting influence the work, interactions, and values of these health researchers, and how their participation in such practices, in turn, shapes the commercialization process. In health research, commercialization is about capturing scientific discoveries in order to make products like drugs and medical devices. Canadian governments, research funding agencies, and universities have put into place many policies to encourage commercialization. But research shows that individual health researchers - their insights and involvement - are usually the key to commercialization. Although we have a sense of why and to what degree established university health researchers participate in commercialization, we have no idea about how often emerging health researchers (graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, junior clinician-investigators and assistant professors) are exposed to it, or what effects those experiences have on their research, career paths, and goals. We also do not know how emerging health researchers affect commercialization practices and outcomes. Therefore, with commercialization becoming a common component of university health research and policy-makers emphasizing the importance of mining "young talent" for commercialization, it is critical that we develop an evidence-based understanding of the dynamic relationship between emerging health researchers and commercialization. This project will use several research techniques to build such an evidence base. The results will help government agencies and universities to develop commercialization policies that are better tailored to future generations of health researchers and, in so doing, help Canadians, the would-be beneficiaries of their health research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Beta-catenin as a regulator of cancer cell survival
Keywords-MotsClés: ANOIKIS; APOPTOSIS; BETA-CATENIN; CANCER; CELL SIGNALING; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX
Abstract-Résumé: The cells lining many human organs (epithelial cells) form a single layer. Cells that detach from this layer die. Cancer cells are often derived from epithelial cells. To be able to form three-dimensional tumors and spread throughout the body cancer cells have to be able to survive outside of the epithelial layer. Understanding the mechanisms that control their survival is necessary for designing cancer treatment based on killing tumor cells outside of their original location. Many proteins that drive cancer progression trigger not only survival but also death signals in tumor cells. The survival signals prevail in these cells. It is now thought that treatments blocking the survival signals but preserving the death signals can be particularly effective in killing tumor cells. Whether or not tumor cells that are detached from the original epithelial layer carry any death signals that can be used for enhancing the efficiency of approaches aimed at killing them has never been explored. To this end, we are studying a protein called beta-catenin, which contributes to the progression of many cancers. Genetic alterations in tumor cells activate beta-catenin and allow it to trigger signals that rescue detached cells from dying. A protein called Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor 1 (TNFR1) is known to block cell death. We have found recently that in addition to survival signals, beta-catenin induces a death signal in tumor cells. This signal is mediated by beta-catenin-dependent loss of TNFR1. We will test in the proposed study whether colon cancer cells are killed outside of their original location if beta-catenin is removed from these cells and whether they are killed even more efficiently if beta-catenin-induced death signal mediated by TNFR1 loss is preserved in these cells after beta-catenin is removed. If successful, our work could provide mechanistic basis for the design of novel therapies aimed at blocking the survival of cancer cells outside of their original location.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Carboxypeptidase-D in Prostate Cancer Growth and Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROGEN; CARBOXYPEPTIDASE-D; CHIP ASSAYS; GENE EXPRESSION; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; NITRIC OXIDE; PROLACTIN; PROSTATE CANCER; REPORTER ASSAYS; SCID MICE XENOGRAFTS
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most frequently diagnosed cancer among men, afflicting one in seven Canadian men in his lifetime. PCa is typically treated by surgery and radiation, and may be combined with androgen ablation therapy. The latter aims to reduce serum androgens and to inhibit the androgen receptor in PCa cells. Although PCa often responds well initially to androgen ablation therapy, there is a high risk of recurrence since most patients become refractory to androgen withdrawal. The prognosis for recurrent PCa is poor as treatment options are limited, and may be ineffective. Our proposed research is on the enzyme carboxypeptidase-D (CPD) as a potential therapeutic target for PCa. We have recently reported that CPD acts to promote survival of human PCa cells in culture. In screening excised prostate tissues from men diagnosed with PCa, we have observed that CPD levels are highly elevated in primary, high-grade PCa and in recurrent PCa, as compared to low levels in normal or benign prostate tissues. Therefore, our studies implicate a role for CPD in the growth and survival of PCa cells, and in the progression of PCa tumours. We have also reported that CPD levels are increased in PCa cells by androgens and prolactin, suggesting that androgen ablation alone is insufficient to block CPD action. Our proposed study will fully elucidate regulation of the CPD gene, and how the CPD protein acts to promote growth/survival of PCa cells in culture, and in PCa tumours implanted in a mouse model. Our study will give a greater understanding as to how CPD contributes to the pathological progression of PCa, and is an essential step towards the discovery of new and more effective hormone ablation therapies for the treatment and/or management of this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Opportunities for very early intervention in youth at high risk for severe mental illness
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY DISORDERS; BIPOLAR DISORDER; COGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT; DEPRESSION; EARLY INTERVENTION; HIGH RISK STUDIES; PSYCHOTIC LIKE EXPERIENCES; RECURRENT DEPRESSIVE DISORDER; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SEVERE MENTAL ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depression, tends to develop in adolescence and cause life-long disability. These diseases share many risk factors, the strongest of which is having one or both parents with mental illness. Recent accrual of knowledge on antecedents to mental illness may enable us to predict mental illness and develop interventions to forestall its onset. However several key questions remain to be answered regarding the target group specific interventions. The proposed study will map antecedents across childhood and adolescence among individuals at familial risk for severe mental illness. Children and young people aged 3 to 15 will be recruited if at least one of their birth parents suffers from schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or recurrent severe depression. Four known antecedents will be assessed at recruitment and three annual follow ups: delay in cognitive development, anxiety, psychotic-like experiences and affective lability. These antecedents are potential targets for preventive interventions. We will map the development of antecedents across ages to demarcate the age group that is most likely to benefit from interventions. We will establish the presence of developmental antecedents against a comparison group of offspring without family history of severe mental illness. We will test specificity of each antecedent to parents' diagnosis to decide whether diagnosis-specific or transdiagnostic interventions are more likely to be efficient. Rate of consent for being contacted with offers of interventions among offspring with antecedents will help estimate the numbers available for testing specific interventions. This project will advance knowledge on the development of severe mental illness among young people at familial risk and prepare grounds for testing of interventions aimed at reducing the risk of illness and avoiding life-long disability.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of AIIt in homocysteine-mediated vascular dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: ANNEXIN A2; FIBRINOLYSIS; HOMOCYSTEINE; PLASMIN; PLASMINOGEN; S100A10; THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: A diet low in folic acid (found in leafy greens) and high in the amino acid methionine (found in many meat products), can lead to high blood levels of homocysteine (Hcy), which in turn is a risk factor for heart attack and stroke.  Damage to the blood vessels that results in heart attack and stroke occurs because Hcy blocks the busting up of tiny clots that form in the blood which then accumulate in the tissues and may also grow into larger clots. My laboratory has shown that a protein, AIIt, that is present on the surface of the cells that form the blood vessels, controls the production of an enzyme, plasmin, which is responsible for busting up blood clots. Mice that have no AIIt produce much less plasmin and have a dramatic accumulation of blood clots in their tissues. We intend to show that Hcy prevents the blood vessel cells from breaking down these blood clots by binding to AIIt and blocking its ability to produce plasmin. We will test this hypothesis by feeding mice a diet that is high in methionine and low in folic acid, which will give the mice high blood levels of Hcy. We will then compare the blood clot busting ability of these mice with control mice fed a diet with normal levels of folic acid and methionine and having normal levels of Hcy. We will then see if these changes in the ability of the mouse to destroy blood clots correlate with changes in the structure of AIIt caused by Hcy. We will isolate the cells that line the blood vessels in two forms, one which has AIIt and another which does not and directly compare the effect of Hcy on the clot busting ability of these cells. We will also determine why the modification of AIIt by Hcy blocks the ability of AIIt to generate plasmin and bust up blood clots by incubating purified AIIt with Hcy in test-tubes and documenting where in AIIt Hcy binds and how this binding blocks the ability of AIIt to generate plasmin.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pregnancy characteristics and maternal long term weight-related outcomes: a cohort study.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOKINES; BIOLOGICAL MEDIATORS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CHRONIC DISEASE RISK; DIABETES; EPIDEMIOLOGY; LIFE COURSE HEALTH; OBESITY; PREGNANCY; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Nova Scotia is at the forefront of the obesity epidemic in Canada. Weight gain and obesity-related health conditions in women may be related to pregnancy characteristics like how much weight a woman gains during her pregnancy, conditions like pre-eclampsia or gestational diabetes, and the birth weight of the children. Current knowledge, however, is sparse and the data on which it is based can be flawed. For example, it often relies on potentially biased self-reports about pregnancy and body weight and rarely takes into account diet and physical activity. Information about the biological factors that may lead to adverse outcomes is virtually nonexistent. The objective of this study is to quantify the association between pregnancy characteristics and many long term maternal health outcomes including: weight gain and body composition; chronic health conditions (e.g., diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease); and biological factors in the blood. The participants will be Nova Scotian women enrolled in the Atlantic Partnership for Tomorrow's Health (A.PATH) cohort between 2009 and 2010. Each A.PATH participant had measurements of body composition taken by a nurse, provided a blood sample, and completed a questionnaire about health conditions and lifestyle characteristics. Health service utilization data will provide complementary data about obesity-related health conditions. Past pregnancy information for each participant will be derived from the Atlee Perinatal Database, a provincial database in existence since 1980 that has detailed clinical information for all deliveries.  The depth of the information collected will ensure that this project will be an important contribution to this underdeveloped research agenda. The knowledge gained will enhance the understanding of the development of chronic health conditions that affect so many women in Canada and could improve the identification of high risk women so that they may take preventive precautions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Network for Canadian Oral Health Research
Keywords-MotsClés: CAPACITY BUILDING; COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH; CRANIOFACIAL PAIN; DENTAL CARIES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; ORAL HEALTH; ORAL HEALTH DISPARITIES; PATIENT ORIENTED OUTCOMES; RESEARCH NETWORK; SALIVARY BIOMARKERS
Abstract-Résumé: The oral health of Canadians has improved dramatically over the past 30 years; children are much less likely to have tooth decay than in the past and older Canadians are keeping more of their natural teeth than their parents and grandparents did. This is good news - good oral health is essential for overall health and wellbeing. While a lot of progress has been made, many challenges remain: we now know that oral disease is linked to other conditions such as diabetes, pneumonia and cardiovascular disease; we know there is a growing issue around oral disease among the frail elderly; and we know that there are groups of Canadians who still have high rates of oral disease and little access to oral care.  We can attribute much of the improvement in oral health to research into the causes, treatment and prevention of oral disease. Canada is home to a number of internationally known oral health researchers. Until now, however, most have worked individually or in small groups.  This Network for Canadian Oral Health Research will link oral health researchers from ten universities across Canada. The network will: create a registry of researchers, their interests and resources; gather researchers from varied backgrounds but with shared research interests at workshops to plan new research; and work to share the outcomes of research with policy makers, dental professionals and the public. This network will create ways for oral health researchers to share ideas and resources so they can work together to continue to improve the oral health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Maternal-Infant Microbiome and Immunity (MIMI) Network
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOBAL HEALTH; IMMUNOLOGY; MATERNAL HEALTH; MICROBIOME; PEDIATRICS
Abstract-Résumé: There are ten times as many bacterial cells in our body than human cells. This community of microorganisms (called the microbiome) plays an important role in influencing human health. For example, in our gut, bacteria aid in the digestion and absorption of nutrients, keeping dangerous microbes in check and directing our defense system's response. Thus, the understanding of how the microbiome contributes to human health is of great importance.  Understanding the human microbiome is a daunting task because of its complexity. First, there are very different communities of bacteria present in different parts of the body. Second, these bacterial communities arise from different initial sources and interact with the human defense system in different ways. Third, the human microbiome is affected by a variety of genetic and environmental factors. Finally, people living in different areas of the world have different bacteria living in and on them. These and other factors require that the study of the microbiome should be approached from a global health perspective.  We propose the establishment of MIMI, the Maternal-Infant Microbiome and Immunity Network. This network is centered on how the microbiome and immune system interact in the mother and child, as the mother is the initial source of the child's microbiome.  MIMI will formalize the collaboration of three groups with expertise in paediatrics and immunology, maternal health and probiotics, and DNA sequencing and data analysis. By bringing these groups with complementary expertise together, MIMI will amplify each group's strength, build research capacity in the field of microbiome analysis, and to transfer knowledge and thus inform maternal and child health policy. MIMI will contribute towards self-sustainability by making Network Members competitive for national and international funding.

TitreApplicationTitle: Kidney Cancer Research Network of Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOBANKING; CENTRES OF EXCELLENCE; CLINICAL TRIALS; GENETICS; KIDNEY CANCER; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; SURVIVORSHIP
Abstract-Résumé: Each year, 5100 Canadians are diagnosed with kidney cancer and 1650 people will die from the disease. While there has been an improvement in treatment strategies with the development of targeted drug therapies, more research is required to help improve outcomes for kidney cancer patients. To address this, clinicians of many specialties, scientists and cancer survivors propose to form the Kidney Cancer Research Network of Canada (KCRNC). In close collaboration with the kidney cancer patient advocacy group, Kidney Cancer Canada (KCC), the network will develop guidelines around important issues associated with kidney cancer and to establish these protocols as standards of practice. Specific goals include: (1) Establish a Canadian patient information system linked to a biobank containing specimens collected from these patients. Standards will be established regarding data and tissue collection so that information obtained across sites could be used in research studies (an option not currently available).(2)Support the development of clinical trials aimed at uncovering novel,improved,or more targeted therapeutics and treatment regimens for kidney cancer patients.(3) Develop quality indicators to optimize outcomes, improve accountability and develop initiatives to improve the quality of health care delivered to kidney cancer patients. (4) Establish standards for the use of genetic testing and counseling for kidney cancer.(5) Develop a Survivorship Care Plan for kidney cancer survivors and their families for the specific needs of this population.(6) Perform research on the various sub-types of kidney cancer to help develop personalized medicine strategies. In contrast to many other cancer types, kidney cancer affects a modest number of Canadians who are managed by a small number of expert and committed clinicians. Therefore, the results from these efforts will provide an excellent opportunity to generate models that can be applied to other types of more prevalent cancer

TitreApplicationTitle: The GREAT (Guideline-driven, Research priorities, Evidence synthesis, Application of evidence, and Transfer of knowledge) Network
Keywords-MotsClés: GUIDELINE IMPLEMENTATION; INFANT HEALTH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MATERNAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Enhanced quality of care for mothers and infants are priorities identified by the UN and the international health community. Together, interested stakeholders have come together to develop a potential strategy for meeting these goals.        We propose to link a WHO-initiated group with knowledge translation researchers in Canada to create a multidisciplinary Network of individuals and organizations interested in advancing the quality of care in low and middle income countries, initially focused on maternal and infant health. This Network is focused on bringing together the researchers with the relevant knowledge users.  It represents a unique opportunity to leverage research that is being led in Canada and to apply it to an international challenge.  Specifically our objectives are to: 1.Develop an interdisciplinary collaborative network of partners and stakeholders (including clinicians, health care managers, researchers, members of the public) interested in improving maternal and infant health in low and middle income countries (LMIC) through effective knowledge translation (KT) 2.Develop a research agenda relevant to the needs of partners in LMIC and advance the science and practice of KT through understanding how to adapt, implement and evaluate guidelines that span community-level and hospital-based care, improvements in access to care and in the referral process in LMIC 3.Build capacity in the science and practice of KT across stakeholder groups in LMIC

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Critical Care Knowledge Translation Nework
Keywords-MotsClés: CRITICAL CARE; KNOWLEDGE SYNTHESIS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION NETWORK; PRACTICE AUDITS
Abstract-Résumé: The care of critically ill patients is a core function of hospitals. Critically ill patients are typically treated in Intensive Care Units (ICUs) and have high rates of mortality and prolonged disability. In addition, ICU care is a limited and expensive resource. The implementation of research findings into practice may improve the outcomes of critically ill patients. However, there are excessive delays between the conduct of research and the implementation of its results into bedside care. This is particularly problematic in critical care where practice is changing rapidly and where large amounts of practice changing research are being constantly generated. It is has been estimated that the best way to improve the outcome of the critically ill is not through the conduct of new research but rather by the implementation of currently known research evidence. The Critical Care Knowledge Translation Network seeks to address this by bringing together researchers, health care administrators and experts in implementing new knowledge into bedside practice in a Canada wide network. The aim of the network will be to increase the adoption of research evidence in order to improve the outcomes and reduce the health care costs of treating critically ill patients. It will do this by collating all relevant research into accessible formats and then using known strategies to increase the adoption of this research into practice. The network will conduct periodic audits of practice to determine where the largest evidence to practice gaps occur and to determine the impact of its implementation efforts. The areas of practice with the largest gaps will be targeted for network efforts. The network will run for three years with the initial funding received but further funding will be sought such that it can be continued thereafter.

TitreApplicationTitle: Congenital Heart Block International Research Network (CIRN)
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-RO ANTIBODY; AUTOIMMUNITY; BIOBANK; CONGENITAL; HEART BLOCK; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; NETWORK
Abstract-Résumé: Congenital Heart Block (CHB) occurs from damage to the fetal heart's conduction system from specific antibodies coming from the mother. This causes either fetal death or the need for a pacemaker for life. These antibodies (anti-Ro) are present in 1-2% of all pregnancies, but only 1-2% of pregnancies with these antibodies are affected by CHB (1/10,000 pregnancies). Anti-Ro antibodies are sensitive for CHB, but not very specific in predicting it. Once a mother has one child affected by CHB, she then has a 20% chance for her next child to be affected. The risk is increased, but not 100%, which suggests that a more specific antibody exists, or that other factors are important. In twin pregnancies where one fetus or child has CHB, the other has a 50% chance of CHB. Thus, hereditary (genetic) factors also have some influence on the development of this disorder. Several laboratories in both Europe and North America have an intense interest in CHB, have developed 'banks' of serum from affected and unaffected pregnancies, have theories as to the target of the antibodies, and are beginning to develop more sensitive tests and more effective treatments based on their understanding of the disease. These groups have now met together on two occasions (for 1 day in 2004 and 3 days in 2010) and recognize the value in working together (sharing ideas and samples), with some collaborative work already started (Sweden-Finland-U.S.; Canada-Sweden). With the new understanding of CHB, we now recognize that we need to better characterize the samples already collected and improve and expand sample collection for further studies (collect at specific times in pregnancy, split samples for potential sharing, collect genetic material (DNA) from family). We therefore propose a formal network of investigators meeting on a regular and frequent basis, with a steering committee, sharing of ideas and samples, and regular yearly scientific sessions for further planning and sharing of knowledge.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of fatty liver and hypercholesterolemia regulated by miR-17
Keywords-MotsClés: FATTY LIVER; HYPERCHOLESTEROLEMIA; MIRNA; MOLECULAR SIGNALING; NUTRITION
Abstract-Résumé: Fatty liver disease is a reversible condition where large vacuoles of triglyceride lipids accumulate in liver cells via the process called steatosis. Fatty liver occurs worldwide in those with excessive alcohol intake and those who are obese.  Hypercholesterolemia is a form of hyperlipidemia, which is the presence of high levels of cholesterol in the blood. Cholesterol is one type of fat. It is one of three major classes of lipids and can be manufactured by all animal cells. Since low density lipoprotein (LDL) is the major carrier of cholesterol, increased levels of LDL in the blood may be a consequence of diet and can cause fatty liver and vascular diseases. MicroRNA is a short ribonucleic acid molecule that can regulate gene expression and play important biological functions. Our previous study demonstrated that transgenic mice expressing a microRNA named miR-17 developed fatty liver and hypercholesterolemia spontaneously. This work was initiated by the China-Canada Joint Health Research Initiative Program starting in 2007. We plan to investigate how miR-17 induces fatty liver and hypercholesterolemia. The genes associated with these effects will be the major subject of our research. We will also investigate the clinical significance of this founding and potential of developing agents for gene therapy for the treatment of fatty liver and hypercholesterolemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translational Genetics Research in Dementia
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; CLINICAL SYMPTOMS; FRONTOTEMPORAL DEMENTIA; GENETIC EPIDEMIOLOGY; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: In 2008, it is reported that nearly half a million Canadians suffered from dementia. This number is expected to double to over a million by 2038, costing our society over $150 billion per year in health care expenditure.  Recent advances and understanding of Alzheimer Disease (AD) and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD), two major types of dementia resulting in loss of brain function, holds promise for early detection, prevention, and treatments of these devastating conditions. While these discoveries provide important insights into the mechanisms of these diseases, genetic variations in the currently known genes account for less than half of the risk attributed to the development of dementia.  On the other hand, a number of environmental risk factors such as head injuries, lower educational level, smoking, and other vascular health factors such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia, all contribute to increase the risk of developing dementia over an individual's lifetime. We will conduct a program of studies using the detailed data collected from our clinical patient groups to the earliest symptoms that develop in patients with genetic forms of FTD. We will also analyze the relationships between various genetic and environmental risk factors and how they interact in the mechanisms that lead to AD and related dementias. In addition, we will use the newest genetic technology to effectively analyze families with a strong history of dementia to look for new genetic mutations responsible for these diseases. This will help us understand how the genetic and environmental factors interact together to cause dementia and will help us identify new treatment strategies. Our goal is to identify patients at the earliest stage of cognitive impairment in order to deliver effective therapies, which will ultimately improve the daily functioning and quality of life in our growing elderly population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pharmacogenetics of juvenile idiopathic arthritis: A genome wide association study on the efficacy and toxicity of methotrexate and etanercept therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; ETANERCEPT; JUVENILE IDIOPATHIC ARTHRITIS; METHOTREXATE; OUTCOME; PHARMACOGENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) (joint disease) is a chronic rheumatic disease of childhood characterized by joint pains and destruction that can lead to a lifelong battle with this crippling disease. Although the outcomes of JIA have improved over the last decades, the disease is still associated with significant effects on the child's normal development and quality of life. The majority of children continue to require treatments that suppress the immune system many years after diagnosis. While suppression of the immune system can lead to favourable responses, it can also be attended by very serious complications such as overwhelming infections. This research focuses on identifying key genetic variations that predict treatment response and also the serious side effects. An international partnership of expert physicians and researchers in childhood arthritis was established. Children's disease course and treatment outcome will be carefully characterized. The child's genetic make-up will be determined from saliva samples and correlated with treatment response and side effects. The results of the study will enable physicians to optimise the treatment of childhood arthritis and avoid side effects by tailoring medications towards the individual's genetic make-up.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying causes of autism spectrum disorder through next-generation sequencing in combination with genetic linkage
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER; GENETIC LINKAGE; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; RARE VARIANT GENETIC ASSOCIATION
Abstract-Résumé: The principal aim of this proposed research project is to identify susceptibility genes for autism spectrum disorder (ASD). ASD is a relatively common disorder of childhood development that impairs communication and interaction, and thereby impacts significantly on quality of life and the ability to live independently, such that the burden on healthcare is very large. The genetic basis of this disorder is well established, but only a handful of genes that cause ASD have so far been identified. This proposed study, however, will take advantage of a new technology that allows the genetic code on each chromosome to be elucidated at the most basic structural level (termed sequencing) to identify genetic abnormalities in genes that are associated with ASD. Instead of examining the sequence across all chromosomes, however, efforts will be focussed on those regions that are  genetically 'linked' ('genetic linkage') with ASD.  The idea of genetic linkage refers to the identification of regions where affected members of families share more genetic material.  Within these regions, the genetic sequence of individuals with ASD will be compared with a control sample to look for variation in the sequence ('variants') that are seen more often in the ASD cases. Research such as this offers to hope of understanding the cause of autism such that more effective treatments can be introduced, caregiver burden can be reduced and the quality of life for those affected can be improved.

Keywords-MotsClés: CHANNELOPATHIES; EPILEPSY; IDIOPATHIC GENERALIZED EPILEPSY; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a common condition that affects nearly 1% of Canadians. Genetics is known to contribute significantly to the overall susceptibility for epilepsy.  The majority of individuals are thought to have epilepsy due to many factors including the environment and genetics.  However, there are some families who have epilepsy due to a single genetic change.  These genes can be difficult to identify given the uniqueness of any given family and the techniques previously available (eg Sanger sequencing).  Next-generation sequencing is a new method capable of reading all of the genes throughout our genome (>22,000). We plan to use this new technology to identify novel epilepsy genes as well as search for changes at the known epilepsy genes.  By providing a molecular diagnosis, we can give accurate genetic counseling, we can provide information about the natural history, also halt or limit further testing, and potentially optimize the available anti-epileptic therapies.

Abstract-Résumé: Introduction: In recent years, an entry-to-practice competencies and standards document was developed which outlines the foundation of knowledge, skills and attitudes all dental hygiene students must achieve upon graduation in order to become practicing professionals.  The national dental hygiene education community is diverse, consisting of 2-year and 3-year diploma programs, several baccalaureate degree-completion programs and one 4-year entry-to-practice baccalaureate program.  Educators with a variety of backgrounds and training are to utilize these competencies in the development of their school's curriculum for programs of varied lengths.  However, most have played no role in the development of the national competencies. This qualitative study will explore the process for implementation and evaluation of the national competencies by dental hygiene educators across Canada.  Transparency and collaboration among educators nationally will promote consistency in course objectives so dental hygiene students may graduate with the required standards of skills and knowledge for delivering optimal oral health care.   Methodology:  A questionnaire consisting of open-ended questions regarding implementation and evaluation of the national competencies will be distributed to the members of the Canadian Dental Hygienists Association Educators group.  The questionnaire will also request specific information from participants to identify their education, training and details of their school of employment to provide context to our findings.  Responses will be categorized into key themes and will be anonymized.

Abstract-Résumé: The Aboriginal HIV & AIDS Community-Based Research Collaborative Centre (AHA Centre) unites the diverse Aboriginal health and HIV research communities in Canada. The impact of HIV & AIDS in the Aboriginal community demands a sustained response, well informed by culturally relevant research. In 2008, census data indicated Aboriginal people accounted for 3.8% of the population in Canada and the Public Health Agency estimated 8.0% of all prevalent HIV infections. Often times within the Aboriginal community, the overlap of 'vulnerabilities' exacerbates the complexity of an effective response to HIV.  The AHA Centre is co-led by Ms. Renee Masching, Canadian Aboriginal AIDS Network with Dr. Charlotte Reading, University of Victoria and consists of a 17 member leadership team, of which 12 members are of Aboriginal descent and 2 are respected Elders. Summarizing the vision and mission; the Centre will strategically contribute to an effective response to HIV & AIDS-related issues relevant to Aboriginal Peoples in Canada and international Indigenous populations. The team will foster an innovative environment striving for scientific excellence and trust where investigators with a wide range of experience, Aboriginal community members and Aboriginal People Living with HIV & AIDS share responsibility for direction setting and decision making.  Our community-based research team privileges Indigenous knowledges, engage in two-eyed seeing and a decolonizing approach to research. This approach emphasizes the strengths of communities and meaningfully integrates western methodological approaches. The AHA Centre's focus includes partnership and capacity building, research promotion and support, and action oriented knowledge translation. The structure of the AHA Centre entrenches community leadership linked with expanded resources from which to draw policy, practice, research and cultural expertise to stop the spread of HIV and establish excellence in care, treatment and support.

Building on the successful foundation of the CIHR Centre for Research Evidence in Action for Community Health in HIV/AIDS (REACH) -- a national collaborative research network, we will establish a vibrant, sustainable national collaborative among HIV/AIDS researchers, people living with HIV, community-based organizations, clinicians and policy makers that will foster rigorous, relevant CBR that will improve the health and well-being of people with or at risk of HIV. The Centre will provide direct financial and infrastructure support to seven Core Regional Teams that will guide and drive regional initiatives that respond to local needs. The Centre will support the regional teams by: 1) Building Readiness for CBR through the development of an online CBR readiness tool and comprehensive database of CBR on HIV/AIDS in Canada; 2) Building and sustaining relationships and partnerships across the sector by strengthening relationships with priority populations and communities, establishing partnership development resources and directly connecting people and building teams; and 3) Building CBR Capacity by providing direct support and training for research and KTE to seed new projects, help teams get funded, improving practices for engaging peer research associates, and moving knowledge into action.

Keywords-MotsClés: ADVANCED GLYCATION END PRODUCTS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CELL THERAPY; DRUG DELIVERY; HYDROGELS; MICELLES; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; POLYMERS; REGENERATION; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease is one of most important killers of people worldwide. Therapies to regenerate the heart and blood vessels by using the patient's own adult stem cells have so far been modest in humans. Work from the applicants suggests that this may be due to the diseased tissue being inhospitable to transplanted cells. The presence of "toxic" products in the tissue is one reason why transplanted cells have trouble surviving and/or participating in effective repair. In this research, we will design a drug delivery system that will reduce the toxicity of the diseased tissue. We will also investigate the use of tissue engineered materials to deliver and enhance the retention of transplanted cells in the damaged tissue. We anticipate that by improving the regenerating environment and the number and function of transplanted cells, our novel tissue engineering strategies will eventually make humans more responsive to stem cell therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of protein acetylation in Mtb metabolism and virulence
Keywords-MotsClés: METABOLISM; MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS; PROTEIN ACETYLATION; VIRULENCE
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of this project is to identify acetylated proteins of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) and elucidate the role of protein acetylation in Mtb metabolism and virulence. Mtb, the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), infects one-third of the world's population and causes approximately 2 million deaths annually. The success of Mtb as a pathogen is partly due to its ability to adapt to and persist in diverse host microenvironments. During persistent infection in the host, Mtb is thought to exhibit reduced or altered metabolism and how Mtb coordinates its metabolism during different phase of infection remains incompletely understood. Protein lysine acetylation has been studied in the context of histone modification in eukaryotes. Recent studies show that acetylation of non-histone proteins occurs prevalently in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. An emerging theme from these studies is that metabolic enzymes involved in central metabolic pathways and intermediary metabolisms are subjected to acetylation. Protein acetylation in Mtb has not been well studied. Given the intimate link of Mtb metabolism and infection, we hypothesize that protein lysine acetylation may play a critical role in Mtb metabolism and its adaptation to host microenvironments. The goal of our studies is to systematically identify these acetylated proteins and elucidate the role of protein acetylation in Mtb metabolism and virulence. Our studies may uncover novel targets for chemotherapeutic intervention. Screening of inhibitors of protein acetylation or deacetylation may be an attractive strategy for new drug development against TB.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interaction between REGgamma and p53 in heart infectious disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; COXSACKIEVIRUS; P53; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; REGGAMMA; VIRAL MYOCARDITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Virus infection can cause inflammation of the heart muscle, termed viral myocarditis, ultimately leading to enlarged heart and heart failure. Viral myocarditis and its long-term consequences are among the most common causes of disease and death in China and North America, particularly in children. Enteroviruses, such as coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3), are the most prevalent viruses associated with this disease. There is currently no specific treatment available for viral myocarditis. The tumor-suppressor protein p53 plays a pivotal role in the induction of cell death and the repression of virus replication. Our previous studies have shown that CVB3 infection leads to a loss of the p53 protein, suggesting that the virus may maximize its own replication by regulating p53 levels. Indeed, as a joint effort, we have recently demonstrated that REGgamma, a protein degradation activator, is modified during CVB3 infection to support efficient viral replication through facilitating p53 degradation. In this joint proposal, we aim to further explore the interplay between REGgamma and p53 in the progression of viral myocarditis. Three specific aims are proposed: 1) To study the interaction between REGgamma and p53 and the role of such interplay in CVB3 replication in isolated heart cells; 2) To investigate the mechanisms of how p53 regulates CVB3 replication in isolated heart cells; and 3) To determine the severity and progression of CVB3-induced myocarditis in genetically engineered moue models to examine the significance of REGgamma or p53 loss in virus-induced infection and damage of the heart. These studies will provide novel insights into the mechanisms of CVB3 infection and will assist in the development of new therapeutic approaches against viral myocarditis, greatly impacting on health care in both China and Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Amblyopia: extent of cortical loss and restoration of cortical function
Keywords-MotsClés: AMBLYOPIA; ANIMAL BEHAVIOUR; EXTRA-STRAITE FUNCTION; HUMANS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; NON-HUMAN PRIMATES; PERCEPTUAL LEARNING; PSYCHOPHYSICS
Abstract-Résumé: This application represents a unique interdisciplinary collaboration between two laboratories, one in Canada specialized in human cortical function and in particular a developmental disorder called amblyopia (incidence 3%), and one in China specialized in animal studies and in a training paradigm called perceptual learning. The first phase of the project will reveal the extent of the cortical deficit in human amblyopes and, in particular, whether it involves both dorsal and ventral extra-striate pathways. This will be done using detailed psychophysical testing of humans with amblyopia using paradigms developed in-house.  Once this is completed we will validate the animal model and then allow us to delineate the cellular basis of this behavioral deficit using multi-electrode recording in the same amblyopic animals.  The second phase of the project involves developing and refining methods to recover lost cortical function. First, in humans with amblyopia (Canada) we will measure the extent to which brain function can be recovered using perceptual learning, a method whereby training in the detection of a particular stimulus confers general and lasting visual sensitivity benefits as a consequence of cortical plasticity. The final step, using the non-human primate model in China, is to better understand the cellular basis of this recovery using multi-electrode recording to ascertain whether the improved function is a result of an increase in response gain or a decrease in response variance of cortical cells in the affected area.  Using the complementary neuroscience expertise of two labs we will be able to delineate the extent of the cortical loss both perceptually and at the cellular level. We will also be able to assess if the current success of perceptual learning to restore V1 function can be extended to the extra-striate cortex where it is suspected that most loss occurs.  Finally, a better understanding of the cellular basis of this recovery will be obtained.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating food security interventions across geographically and culturally distinct Aboriginal communities
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL NUTRITION; COLLECTIVE CASE STUDY; FOOD SECURITY; INTERVENTION EVALUATION; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal persons (including children) are more likely to endure food insecurity than non-Aboriginal persons. Food insecurity exists whenever the availability of nutritionally adequate and safe foods or the ability to acquire acceptable foods in socially acceptable ways is limited or uncertain.  It includes the fear of not being able to provide or obtain food, and, in severe cases, hunger due to food shortages. Our aim is to support community-researcher partnerships in evaluating interventions to reduce food insecurity in multiple Aboriginal communities with the aim of enhancing and expanding the evidence base concerning effective food security interventions across a diversity of contexts. The research will not be limited to studying impacts or effects (i.e., change of prevalence of food insecurity); rather it will also document the reach of interventions, their differential uptake, suitability to local contexts, effectiveness, sustainability, the side effects or multiplier effects (co-benefits and risks), and the benefit Aboriginal people ascribe to having the intervention. Traditional evaluation research implies that the University researchers are the sole bearer of authority, decide what intervention is needed and then choose the criteria for evaluation. In contrast, we will use participatory evaluation, a partnership approach in which local stakeholders actively engage in the evaluation, ensuring that the evaluation focuses on locally relevant questions that meet the needs of program beneficiaries. In addition to providing knowledge about how to create sustainable food security programs in Aboriginal communities, the outcomes of the research will be an improved conceptualization of food security for Aboriginal peoples, and the development of appropriate tools for the measurement of food security in Aboriginal communities.

Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is an epidemic.  Patients with diabetes develop problems with their eyes, kidneys, and heart.  These problems arise because of abnormalities in the cells that make up the blood vessels.  The objective of this study is to test the hypothesis that curcumin (curry extract) will prevent the damage to the blood vessels.  Our Chinese collaborators have produced modified curcumin that stays in the body for a long time and is not toxic.  Using cells in culture and animal models of diabetes, we will test these modified curcumin products to determine whether we can prevent all blood vessel problems in diabetes.

Abstract-Résumé: The common underlying cause for type 1 and type 2 diabetes is the deficiency of pancreatic beta-cell. Beta-cells were once thought to be non-proliferative cells; however it is now well appreciated that these cells indeed maintain the proliferative potential in response to increased insulin demand resulting from metabolic disorders. Therefore, evaluation of cell cycle regulation in Beta-cells is essential for better understanding of pathogenesis and prevention of diabetes.  b) Objective of the research proposal Our objective is to define the essential role of the tumour suppressor retinoblastoma (Rb) protein and its family member, p107 that govern cell cycle and cell death in pancreatic beta-cells.   We have investigated the role of Rb and p107 in pancreatic beta-cells through mouse model experiments. Mice without the expression of Rb in beta-cells lead to enhanced cell number and improved the insulin secretory response when confronting blood glucose change, which indicates loss of Rb in beta-cells can have a beneficial role in promoting beta-cell growth and cell function. Interestingly, mice with combined loss of Rb and p107 in beta-cells exhibit an unexpected decline in cell number. We wish to further explore the role of Rb proteins in the regulation of beta-cell proliferation and function.    This project will lead to a better understanding of the biology of pancreatic beta-cell that plays an important role in the development of diabetes, leading to new strategies for prevention and treatment of diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metabolic deceleration as a mechanism for the anti-diabetic effects of metformin and berberine
Keywords-MotsClés: BERBERINE; DETOXIFICATION; FATTY ACIDS; GLUCOLIPOTOXICITY; LIPOLYSIS; METABOLIC DECELERATION; METFORMIN; MITOCHONDRIAL COMPLEX-I; PANCREATIC BETA CELL; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Excess supply of nutrient fuels, viz., carbohydrates, proteins and fats, can lead to toxicity by disturbing the normal cellular functions in the body, resulting in obesity and diabetes. Thus, continuous exposure of pancreatic beta cells to high fat and glucose causes their failure to produce insulin in response to changes in blood glucose concentrations. In the whole body other tissues also do not respond normally to insulin and cannot effectively use blood glucose under conditions of excess fuel supply. These toxic effects of excessive fuels can be due to reduced useable energy production, production of mis-folded proteins and elevated production of harmful free radicals. It is particularly important to understand about the way the cells escape from the toxicity of excess fuels in conditions like obesity and diabetes, which are often associated with fuel oversupply. In the present proposal, we are proposing that the well-known anti diabetic drugs metformin and berberine act by reducing the toxic effects of nutrient fuels. We plan to investigate how these drugs help beta cells of pancreas to handle excess fuels. We also plan to examine if these two anti-diabetic drugs reduce the fuel toxicity in the body tissues and make these tissues to become more sensitive to insulin. We will investigate the details of the fuel detoxification that is brought about by metformin and berberine in the beta cells and in other body tissues like liver, muscle and adipose tissue. The information obtained from these studies will help in understanding the importance of fuel detoxification as a way of treating diabetes and obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ketogenic Diet for Spinal Cord Injury - Preclinical Studies
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOR; BLADDER FUNTION; CERVICAL SPINAL CORD CONTUSION; HISTOPATHOLOGY; INDEPENDENT REPLICATION; KETOGENIC DIET; PAIN; PRECLINICAL DATA FOR TRIAL; RATS; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: About 4 million people worldwide live with paralysis from traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) and an estimated 200,000 SCI occur every year. Yet there is no cure and treatment is limited to surgery to stabilize the spine, and physical rehabilitation. We found that rats recover better from spinal cord injury (SCI) at the neck when eating a diet low in carbohydrates and rich in fats beginning after the injury. Known as a ketogenic diet (KD), this diet is used medically for the treatment of seizures which do not respond to medication. In past experiments, when rats experienced neck SCI, those eating the KD used the paralyzed front limb three times more frequently and were twice as successful to grasp. We are not aware of any treatment for the injured neck spinal cord that is more effective in promoting recovery of basic functions like grasping, nor easier to administer. We must address important questions in our animals before we can test this treatment on humans: (i) how long must the diet be maintained, (ii) how long can we delay the start of KD treatment after injury and still see a benefit? We will also determine whether (iii) common high calorie, carbohydrate-rich diets are damaging for the recovery of the injured spinal cord and (iv) how KD and rehabilitation treatments affect each other. The last goal is important, as rehabilitation is currently the most widely-accepted treatment after human SCI. We focus on the front limb function because hand and arm use is the highest priority for people living with neck SCI. In addition, bladder problems are very important to people living with SCI. The Canadian and Chinese groups have complementary skills, including methods for studying arm function and bladder problems.  This research partnership between Canada and China will also enable multiple researchers to confirm each others results before starting human trials of this therapy and to transfer skills to Chinese researchers most able to conduct human trials of KD.

Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIC STRAIN; INFLAMMATION; MENINGITIS; SEPTIC SHOCK; STREPTOCOCCAL TOXIC SHOCK-LIKE SYNDROME; STREPTOCOCCUS SUIS; TOLL LIKE RECEPTORS; ZOONOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Infections caused by Streptococcus suis (S. suis) are considered a global and an economical problem in the swine industry. Moreover, it is also an emerging disease that is transmitted from pigs to humans. In fact, it is one of the most important causes of adult meningitis in Asia.  During the last years, different epidemic episodes took place in China with serious cases of not only meningitis but also general infection that ended with death of the affected persons in a few hours: a shock syndrome called streptococcal toxic shock-like syndrome. When infected, the human body reacts with inflammation (such as fever) to combat and kill the pathogen. However, some bacterial pathogens will not die and will, indeed, induce such a strong inflammation that it does not serve anymore to the individual and becomes detrimental to the patient. In fact, it can be responsible for the clinical signs and death. The pathogen uses the host (patient) to induce the severity of the disease. We will study (using a mouse model) how animals respond to the infection and why some strains (Chinese) seems to kill animals by shock very fast by inducing exaggerated inflammation. We will also study what exactly happens in the brain of animals infected by S. suis. Since it is not easy to clearly differentiate strains with high virulent potential, we will develop a wide genome analysis system to be able to clearly differentiate one strain from another. This is extremely important since from outside all strains are very similar. We have a highly complemented team: worldwide recognized experts on S. suis infection, international recognized specialist in brain inflammation and a Chinese team with a great expertise on genetic studies on the evolution of bacterial pathogens. The combination of Canadian expertise and the fluid communication with our colleagues in China are unique and place our team at the front line on this research.
