TitreApplicationTitle: Eremophilenolides compounds reduce allergic inflammation by inhibiting mast cell activation
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGIC INFLAMMATION; ALTERNATIVE MEDICINE; ASSAY GUIDED FRACTIONATION; HUMAN MAST CELLS; IMMUNOLOGY; NMR; RODENT MODELS OF ALLERGIC DISEASE; TH2 MEDIATED DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) is widely used to treat allergic disease such as asthma and allergic rhinitis in Asian societies and is used by many in the United States and Canada. The scientific basis for its use however, is relatively sparse.  Allergic disease is caused by an abnormal immune response that causes many different symptoms including inflammation, smooth muscle hypersensitivity, mucus production, vascular leak and tissue remodeling. Traditional pharmaceuticals treat most or some of these symptoms but have been associated with unpleasant side effects and are not effective in all patients.  Chinese medicine has traditionally employed mixtures of herbs in composite formulas for the treatment of various ailments.  Petasites or giant butterbur is an ancient herb that has been used for more than 400 years in the treatment of allergic disease in China. We have found that at least 2 pure compounds derived from Petasites have significant anti-inflammatory effects in animal models and in vitro cell cultures. In this proposal, we will confirm our preliminary results in more rigorous animal model studies, examining the mechanism by which these compounds inhibit several aspects of allergic inflammation and explore the possible use of these compounds (individually or in combination) for the treatment of allergic disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: MicroRNA regulation of normal and malignant hematopoietic stem cell biology
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; HEMATOPOIESIS AND HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; LEUKEMIA; MICRORNA; MIRNA; MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Hematopoiesis is a developmental process during which a few hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) develop and differentiate into multiple lineages of blood cells. Interestingly, recent experiments show that blood tumors such as leukemia also have a similar developmental hierarchy, in which a few leukemia stem cells (LSC) function as self-renewable "seeds" that continuously populate the entire tumors. Since both HSC and LSC are slowly proliferating cells and are more difficult to eliminate by routine chemotherapy, it is fundamentally important to understand how these stem cell functions (including differentiation and self-renewal) are controlled intracellularly by various mechanisms.       MicroRNA (miRNA) of ~22-nucleotides is a class of newly discovered regulators of gene expression and plays an important role in a variety of biological processes. However, the physiological and pathological roles of these molecules in stem cell biology and leukemogenesis remain to be explored. The goal of this proposal is to investigate the role of miRNAs, miR-29a, in hematopoiesis and leukemogenesis. This subject is based on our recent findings showing that: 1) miR-29a is highly expressed in hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) and downregulated in hematopoietic lineage progenitors. 2) miR-29a overexpression in HSCs blocks B-cell development. It also leads to myeloid proliferative disorders and eventually development of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). 3) miR-29a is upregulated in about 50% of human AML. In this proposal, we will test the hypothesize that miR-29a regulates the expression of genes that control HSC and LSC function and dysregulation of miR-29a expression may lead to myeloproliferative disorder and AML, using various animal models co-developed by Dr. Fei's and Dr. Gu's laboratories. Completion of this work will help to elucidate the role and mechanisms by which miR-29a regulates hematopoiesis and leukemia genesis. It may also provide a useful target to treat leukemia such as AML.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neutraceuticals and diabetes:  Nrf-2 activation is a critical mechanism underlying the effect of certain plant-derived compounds in preventing insulin resistance.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; INSULIN RESISTANCE; NEUTRACEUTICALS; NRF-2; OBESITY; OXIDATIVE STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: The rates of diabetes are increasing worldwide and along with this, the associated complications consisting of kidney, eye and cardiovascular diseases. While the cause of diabetes is not completely understood, a major factor is overnutrition (poor diet) and obesity which results in resistance to the blood sugar regulating hormone, insulin. Insulin resistance is a key precursor to diabetes and contributes to high blood pressure and hyperlipidemia, leading to cardiovascular complications. The cellular and molecular mechanisms causing insulin resistance are complex but one contributing component is oxidative stress, that exists when the cell cannot neutralize the excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) produced.  It has been found that a number of plant-derived compounds, some from traditional foods used historically for the treatment of diabetes, improve insulin resistance. This research will investigate the scientific mechanisms by which some of these compounds act.  A number appear to activate the cell's own antioxidant defense mechanism to counteract the excess ROS. This occurs by modulating the action of a gene regulating protein called, Nrf2. Other compounds activate an enzyme, AMP-kinase, normally activated by exercise and fasting. This work will explore these mechanisms in important metabolic targets of insulin, fat, muscle and liver, as well as in mice that develop diabetes, e.g. by feeding a high fat diet.  The molecular actions of these compounds, e.g. berberine (from a Chinese herb), curcumin (from the spice turmeric), will be determined, singly and in combination, along with their effects on insulin action in various cells and tissues, as well as total body metabolism. This research will promote the development of new ways to prevent and treat type 2 diabetes and its complications, major global health care burdens and bring traditional medicine into the modern scientific era to provide therapy to large populations at reduced cost.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identify new causative genes for recurrent moles in China
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE; GENETICS; HUMAN MOLECULAR GENETICS; PREGNANCY; REPRODUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Hydatidiform mole is an aberrant human pregnancy with no embryo. The paradoxical nature of this condition has fascinated and puzzled scientists in all civilisations since the time Hippocrates. There are several forms of this condition. The common form is sporadic, not recurrent, and affects 1 in every 1000 pregnancies in Western societies. This incidence is higher in some geographical regions mainly in South Eastern Asia. By studying a rare familial form of this condition, our group identified the first and major gene, NLRP7, for this condition. The current proposal aims at identifying additional genes responsible for recurrent moles and fetal loss in Chinese patients. Reproductive wastage is a common condition that affects 15 to 20% of clinically recognized pregnancies. However, little is known about their underlying molecular mechanisms. Studying these pathologies and identifying their underlying causes provide hope for patients with these conditions for future genetic testing and prevention and at the same time will save our health system the high cost of unnecessary and redundant tests performed for patients with recurrent reproductive wastage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids as regulators of metabolic pathways: A mechanistic study
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; FISH OIL; OMEGA-3 FATTY ACIDS; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: There are two types of fats essential for normal growth and development: the omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids.  These are essential fatty acids and must be supplied by diet as the body can not make them. People living in industrialized Western countries eat up to 30 times more omega-6 than omega-3 fatty acids, resulting in a relative deficiency of omega-3 fats. Omega-6 metabolic products are inflammatory in nature and make the body more prone to heart diseases, strokes, and cancer. Eating diets rich in omega-3 fatty acids or taking fish oil supplements can restore the balance between the two fatty acids and can possibly reverse these disease processes. The omega-3 fatty acids increase the concentrations of good cholesterol (high density lipoprotein) while decreasing the concentrations of bad cholesterol (low density lipoprotein).  We are proposing to report the beneficial effects resulting from optimizing the dose of omega-3 fatty acids in correlation with omega-6 fatty acids present in the diets. This will be done using C57BL/6 mouse model. The gender specific effects will also be investigated. We will further establish the mechanisms by which these fatty acids regulate metabolic pathways.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expanding treatment and care research to address mental health problems in Canadians with ASD across the lifespan
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; COMMUNITY SERVICES; FAMILY; HEALTH SERVICES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTAL HEALTH; TREATMENT AND CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Mental health and behaviour problems are the most common set of associated conditions for individuals with ASD across the lifespan, placing tremendous burden on the individual and family, as well as on the educational, community, vocational, and healthcare systems. Up to 70% of individuals with ASD are estimated to have mental health problems. We need to provide better treatment and care to people with ASD who are at risk for, or develop, mental health problems. Over the next five years, I aim to implement a Canada-wide, strategic research program to improve the mental health of people with ASD. I will focus on the individual with ASD, their family, and the service system. I will identify risk factors for mental health problems in individuals with ASD by following children, adolescents, and adults with ASD over a three-year period, measuring mental health at 6-month time points. I will conduct treatment research by providing a novel therapy to help youth with ASD who have been traumatized by chronic bullying and have mental health problems, evaluating and refining the treatment, and teaching trainees and clinicians how to provide therapy to people with ASD. I will also study how family caregivers access services for people with ASD across the country, and identify the gaps in care. The Chair support will allow me to conduct specific foundational studies, engage with a broad range of stakeholders on an ongoing basis, translate the knowledge gained to inform policy and practice, and train and mentor the next generation of researchers and practitioners in state-of-the-art methods to improve treatment and care for individuals with ASD in Canada. In the end, this Chair will have a substantial impact on the health and well-being of Canadians with ASD and their families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding and Improving Brain Health in HIV Now
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITION; EXERCISE; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HIV; MEASUREMENT; MENTAL HEALTH; NEUROPLASTICITY; QUALITY OF LIFE; SELF-MANAGEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: People living with HIV are worrying about their memory, and with good reason. Even with good control of the infection, up to 50% may have cognitive or depressive symptoms. These changes in thinking and mood are usually mild, but they seem to matter in everyday life:  they can affect functioning at work, the ability to stick to treatments, and the quality of life of both patients and their family and friends. The causes of these changes in brain health are not clear:  Do they result from HIV-induced brain injury? Accelerated aging? Toxic effects of medication? Or the stress of living with a serious chronic illness? The answer may be "all of the above". We propose that poor brain health in HIV is due to multiple factors, and aim to characterize these in a representative sample of people with HIV drawn from 3 clinics in Montreal and Vancouver. Those showing signs of poor brain health will be assessed in detail, and all will be followed regularly over time to understand the biological, psychological and social factors that affect brain health, the impact of these symptoms on function and quality of life, and their evolution over time. Sub-groups will participate in specific studies using brain imaging and special blood tests to better understand the mechanisms that underlie this problem. We don't have to wait for these results to act, though:  Everyone with symptoms will be helped to take steps to improve their brain health, and will have the chance to try one of three interventions that have shown promise in other neurological illnesses:  physical activity, brain health self-management, or cognitive training. We will identify the elements of these programs that are most effective in improving brain health in people with HIV, and work to make them widely available.  This project brings experts in neuroscience, epidemiology, and HIV together in a new team, to carry out innovative, action-oriented research aiming to make a real difference in brain health in HIV in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards a transformative understanding of HAND
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; COMORBIDITY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNOLOGY; MICRORNAS; NEUROLOGICAL DISEASE; NEUROLOGY; PROPROTEIN CONVERTASE
Abstract-Résumé: Despite universal access in Canada to therapies for HIV infection, people living with HIV/AIDS still suffer immensely from AIDS-related impairment of thinking processes. These HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) impose burdens to health, to daily personal function at home and at work, to society and to the economy. Our new multi-disciplinary team will investigate several interlinked elements of HAND: the frequency and distribution of HAND in the population, risk factors and diagnosis, molecular and cellular causes, and potential therapies for HAND. Our team includes established HIV researchers (Power, Gill, Cohen) as well as internationally recognized researchers new to this area but with expertise in virus research, cell biology, inflammation, nerve system degeneration and bioinformatics (Seidah, Hobman, Broadhurst). The team also includes knowledge users directly engaged with people living with HIV/AIDS and related community organizations. Over the past 25 years, team members have built a patient information database and collection of patient blood specimens that is the cornerstone of our proposed research. Our research will combine these patient data and biospecimen archives with our animal models of HAND, and with our expertise in genomics and statistical data interpretation of molecular information. Research goals are to investigate new mechanisms of disease, to develop novel disease markers for HAND diagnosis, and to find interventions to treat and/or prevent HAND. In addition to addressing the complex issues of HAND in people living with HIV/AIDS, our team will train new researchers in brain disorders that accompany HIV/AIDS. The overarching goal of this proposal is to create knowledge about the disease and the mechanisms underlying HAND. Such knowledge will guide our development of new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies that together can eradicate HAND.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular Aging and HIV Comorbidities in Women and Children
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE HEALTH; COHORT STUDY; HIV COMORBIDITIES; IMMUNOSENESCENCE; MARKERS OF AGING; MITOCHONDRIAL TOXICITY; TELOMERE SHORTENING
Abstract-Résumé: Now that HIV+ people are treated with combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) and live longer, it is becoming clear that they seem to experience diseases and conditions associated with aging at an earlier age, and at greater frequency. Similarly, treatment of HIV-infected pregnant women with these same medications is very successful at preventing infection of the infants with HIV. However, it is becoming apparent that the children who were exposed to fairly toxic drugs in the womb are not as healthy as children born to uninfected mothers. In both cases, it is not totally clear if it is exposure to the virus itself or to the inflammatory state created by viral infections, or to adverse effects of the drugs themselves, or a combination of these factors. Our research will work toward identifying the risk factors associated with various health problems in HIV+ women, from hormonal and reproductive abnormalities to increased bone fractures. We will study preterm births, developmental deficiencies and autism in HIV-exposed uninfected children who were exposed to cART during their fetal development. Finally, we will investigate body fat redistribution and lipid abnormalities in HIV+ children treated with cART. In all these study populations, we will also investigated how markers of aging and markers of inflammation are affected, how they change over time and relate these measures to the diseases and conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determinants of increased risk of cardio-vascular diseases in HIV-infected individuals
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CELLULAR POPULATIONS; CMV; HIV; HOST GENETICS; IMMUNOPATHOGENESIS; INNATE IMMUNITY; SNP
Abstract-Résumé: Antiretroviral therapy has considerably changed the HIV epidemic, transforming this infection into a chronic manageable disease.  However, HIV persists in latent reservoirs and strategies aimed at viral eradication have been elusive, so far.  This persistence is thought to result in a chronic state of immune activation leading to various states of inflammation, which have been associated with non-AIDS defining illnesses such as :  increased risk of cardio-vascular diseases (CVD); bone metabolism disorder; dyslipidemia; diabetes; neuro-cognitive disorders; early aging, etc..  These disorders affect HIV-infected individuals at various degrees.  We wish to further characterize the pathways leading to these disorders, more specifically to the increased risk of CVD and also identify predictors in order to better prevent negative outcomes and target our primary care interventions.  We have assembled a team of world renowned leaders in the fields of CVD and HIV research, who will provide the insights and dynamics required to tackle what has become the perfect storm from the collision of two major chronic illnesses:  the premature aging associated with HIV-1 and the endemic CVD burden of our society.  Our team is composed of biomedical and clinical scientists from cardiology, immunology, host genetics and virology, as well as epidemiologists and population health experts, who join in an integrated approach to take into account the complex interactions between host, virus and environment. Objectives:  The primary objective of our study is to better understand the pathogenesis leading to premature CVD in HIV-infected individuals and identify predictors that could be used for early diagnosis and prevention strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating associations between socio-cultural gender perspectives and vulnerability to violence and HIV among women in sex work in Karnataka, South India
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER ROLES; HIV VULNERABILITY; STRUCTURAL INTERVENTIONS; VIOLENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Women in sex work are among the most vulnerable to HIV in India, and particularly in the southern state of Karnataka where the HIV prevalence is one of the highest in the country. This research project will be conducted in collaboration with the peer-run community-based organization Chaitanya Mahila Sangha in the Bagalkot district of Karnataka that works with female sex workers and their community to understand more about the social factors leading to their high vulnerability to HIV. Most research to inform HIV prevention has focussed on influencing behaviour change in terms of increasing condom use with clients. However, HIV programs in Karnataka are recognizing that women are now using condoms a lot more with clients, but not so much with their intimate partners. This will undermine efforts to prevent the spread of HIV among this vulnerable population, and by extension the general population. Research has been done in Karnataka to show that women's vulnerability to the spread of HIV is related to many social factors leading to higher rates of violence and a reduced ability to use condoms in the intimate relationships of female sex workers. The goal of this research project is to better understand the ways that perpectives on gender norms and roles held by female sex workers and their non-paying intimate partners might be leading to decreased use of condoms or increased experience of violence in these relationships. The goal of this research is to inform Chaitanya's programs and others working with female sex workers to prevent HIV by creating a framework for improving self-esteem, trust, respect, and awareness of HIV risk among women in sex work, their intimate partners, and the wider society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intersecting Stigmas: Understanding the experiences of trans people living with HIV
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH; HIV STIGMA; HIV/AIDS; MENTAL HEALTH; QUALITATIVE; SOCIAL EXCLUSION; TRANSGENDER; TRANSPHOBIA
Abstract-Résumé: Transgender/transsexual (herein referred to as trans) communities face serious challenges in accessing health and social services, and experience unparalleled levels of discrimination, stigma, and violence. To date, there has been little exploration of how service barriers, systemic erasure, pervasive experiences of transphobia and other forms of discrimination affect trans people living with HIV. As such, the aim of this project is to contribute to a gap in the literature by providing an understanding of how multiple layers of social exclusion interact to create complex mental health and well-being concerns for trans people living with HIV. Implications for healthcare provision, mental health policies, funding, service delivery and programming will be offered. This project will use semi-structured interviews with 20 trans people living with HIV and 10 service providers to address the following research objectives: (1) Contribute to an understanding of the ways in which social exclusion, transphobia and erasure work in combination to produce unique health-related needs for trans people living with HIV. (2) Contribute much needed knowledge about the current health-related issues and concerns facing trans people living with HIV in Ontario. (3) Contribute much needed knowledge about the current mental health-related issues and concerns facing trans people living with HIV in Ontario. (4) Contribute much needed information about the impact of living with dual stigmas; identifying as trans and living with HIV. (5) Contribute important information about barriers to effective HIV-related care for trans people living with HIV in Ontario. (6) Ensure that the work results in effective and community- and policy-relevant knowledge transfer and exchange in such a way that it can contribute programming and policy solutions toward the development of trans-relevant and sensitive HIV services for trans people living with HIV in Ontario.

Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; COMMUNITY HEALTH; HIV/AIDS; HIV/AIDS TESTING; QUALITATIVE METHODS; RISK TAKING BEHAVIOUR
Abstract-Résumé: This project will explore barriers to HIV testing on the Fort McKay First Nation reserve. Fort McKay is a reserve that is 60 km from the nearest town and over 500 km from HIV specialists or services. During my time doing health outreach with street entrenched people of nearby Fort McMurray I found that many of them were from Fort McKay. Though these individuals knew they were at risk for HIV due to high risk behaviors they still chose not the get tested. Now that I am working in Fort McKay I would like to explore the topic of HIV testing on the reserve.  Throughout Canadian HIV epidemiological data, researchers are quick to point out that Canadian aboriginals are over represented in the infected population. Testing is an essential component of HIV prevention. Awareness of status substantially affects sexual behavior by decreasing risk-taking and can therefore prevent new infections. Regardless, the information health professionals have on HIV testing within First Nations communities is limited.  This project will focus on the experiences of Fort McKay First Nation surrounding HIV testing; I would like to create a narrative of barriers to testing within the community. The target population will be community members who have, are at risk for, or have been affected by HIV. This study will be carried out using qualitative interviews and two discussion groups.   This project will provide the Fort McKay First Nation health center with a clearer picture of barriers to HIV testing within the community. The findings will also be shared with Chief and Council and can be integrated into community wide health initiatives.

Abstract-Résumé: Some persons get Alzheimer's disease (AD) in young age (before age 65) because of genes inherited from one of their parents. This is called Early Onset Familial Alzheimer Disease (EOFAD). Some of these autosomal dominant genes have been identified, but in half of the families they are still unknown. Persons carrying such genes show changes in their brain chemistry long before they develop symptoms. This study aims at finding as many families as possible in Canada and in China with EOFAD, study which genes are involved in those families, and study the brain chemistry using brain scans, spinal fluid examination, neuropsychological tests over 18 months. TitreApplicationTitle: Role of ACE2 in Heart Disease: Pathophysiology, Molecular Mechanisms and Therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES MELLITUS; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; HEART FAILURE; KNOCKOUT MOUSE MODEL; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease remains a significant health problem and a major cause of morbidity and mortality. The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) is a central regulator of cardiovascular function and plays a key role in the pathophysiology of hypertension, heart failure and coronary artery disease. The peptidase action of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) converts Ang I to the octapeptide Ang II, which is the central mediator of the RAS. In human heart failure and diabetes, activation of the RAS has been linked to the initiation and progression of heart disease. Ang II acting via AT1 receptors impairs mechanical and electrical aspects of the heart function. Angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) degrades Ang I and Ang II to Ang 1-7 and Ang 1-9, respectively, hence functioning effectively as a negative regulator of the RAS. In human heart failure, expression of ACE2 is upregulated thereby counterbalancing an activated RAS while several key pharmacotherapeutic agents including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor and aldosterone receptor blockers, enhance ACE2 activity.Our goal is to determine the role of ACE2 in heart disease and diabetes-induced cardiovascular complications. We will be using experimental models of heart disease and diabetes similar to the disease processes affecting our patients. we will examine the effect of high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and obesity in mice lacking ACE2 and we will used rescue strategies including recombinant ACE2 and viral-mediated overexpression of ACE2 to rescue these murine models of cardiovascular disease. Our findings will provide novel insights for therapy, in particular the possibility of using human recombinant ACE2 as potential therapy in patients with heart disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER; RECHERCHES PSYCHOSOCIALES ET COMPORTEMENTALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Episodic memory training for persons with Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; COGNITION; COMMUNICATION; EPISODIC RECENT MEMORY; INTERVENTION; MEMORY TRAINING; REHABILITATION; SPACED RETRIEVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Memory impairments are the behavioural hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), and they can place severe restrictions on the person's ability to function in many activities of daily living. As a result, a family's capacity to care for the individual in the home becomes threatened and the likelihood of needing to get outside support or even place the person in a care facility increases. Because AD is a degenerative condition, there is a common perception that nothing can be done to help improve the person's memory in daily life. However, recent research findings have shown that people with dementia can benefit from memory rehabilitation. One method of enhancing information retention and retrieval in AD is through the use of a mnemonic technique called Spaced Retrieval (SR). In SR training, a client is asked to recall a piece of information (e.g., what time lunch is) over successively longer intervals by associating that information with an action (e.g., looking at a calendar). The proposed phase 2 study will build upon findings from a recent CIHR-funded phase 1 pilot study in which we demonstrated the potential benefits of SR training in helping eight individuals with AD or related disorder recall information from recent events (e.g., an activity with a grandchild; a holiday party). In the proposed study, we will measure the effectiveness of SR training with a larger sample of persons with AD who have different degrees of cognitive impairment, and we will provide longer periods of training and follow-up assessment of training outcomes. The results are expected to provide new understandings of how SR memory training can be used effectively with persons who have AD to increase their recall of recently occurring events, and with the potential of enhancing their ability to communicate and function in everyday activities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Retinopathy in a Cone-Rich Rodent Model of Spontaneous Type 2 Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; DIABETIC RETINOPATHY; EARLY SCREENING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MECHANISMS OF RETINA DEGENERATION AND DHA THERAPEUTIC ACTION; NUTRITION; VISION LOSS; VISUAL FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Over 3 million Canadians have been diagnosed with diabetes, and this number is rapidly rising: at the current rate, 3.7 million Canadians will be living with diabetes in 2020. One of the complications of diabetes that contributes heavily to the medical and social burden is vision loss due to diabetic retinopathy. The escalating rate of early onset diabetes in Canada further increases the risk, allowing more time for the development of diabetic retinopathy. According to the Public Health Agency of Canada (2011), more than half a million Canadians are afflicted with diabetic retinopathy today; this figure, too, will rise dramatically in the coming years. There is currently no animal model that can combine the advantages of cone-dominant vision, as in the human retina with chronic diet-induced development of diabetic retinopathy resembling that seen in humans; especially after sustained hyperglycemia over 75% the lifespan. We propose to develop a novel animal model that optimally mimics the visual losses caused by type 2 diabetes in humans. Our lab has shown that vision in the Nile rat closely mimics day vision in humans, unlike vision in common lab rodents such rats and mice, which have a very poor daylight vision. Contrary to most rodents, this novel animal model spontaneously develops diabetes in captivity, when fed standard rodent chow, modeling the medical history of human patients. Our preliminary results show that the Nile rat exhibit hallmarks associated with human diabetic retinopathy. Most importantly, the development of the Nile rat, as a novel animal model, will enable researchers to study clinical interventions aimed a preventing and treating this disease that causes blindness in a large proportion of our populations.

ClasseRechercheFR: ANOMALIES CONGENITALES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: TashT: a new mouse model for Hirschsprung disease (aganglionic megacolon)
Keywords-MotsClés: AGANGLIONIC MEGACOLON; ENTERIC NERVOUS SYSTEM; HIRSCHSPRUNG DISEASE; INSERTIONAL MUTANTS; NEURAL CREST CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Hirschsprung disease (aganglionic megacolon) is a common birth defect of the gastrointestinal system, affecting 1 in 5000 newborn infants. Clinical signs include severe constipation and distended bowel due to a non-motile colon. Untreated, aganglionic megacolon is lethal. Developmentally, there is a failure of peripheral nerve cells to colonize the intestinal system during early gestation, resulting in a lack of enteric neural ganglia and thus defective neuromuscular function and normal peristalsis (motility). Aganglionic megacolon is a complex genetic disease that can involve mutations in multiple genes as well as environmental factors. It is estimated that mutations in known genes account for less than half of the cases of megacolon observed clinically. Therefore, further research must be conducted to improve diagnosis, treatment and genetic counseling. To this end, we have developed a novel mouse model for aganglionic megacolon which we have named TashT. TashT animals develop megacolon by two weeks after birth and succumb by three weeks. We have generated these mice via a random mutation approach and have identified the mutation site in a region of Chromosome 10 that has not been previously associated with Hirschsprung disease. We propose studies to determine which gene of this region is affected by the TashT mutation and which cellular mechanisms are disrupted in the TashT megacolon mice. We will also determine if the gene affected by the TashT mutation interacts with other known megacolon-associated genes as well as with environmental insults such as stress. Altogether, these studies will significantly further our understanding of the genetics and pathophysiology of this extremely severe enteric neuromuscular disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Insomnie idiopathique: mesure de l'activité corticale par potentiels évoqués cognitifs
Keywords-MotsClés: FONCTIONNEMENT DIURNE; INSOMNIE IDIOPATHIQUE; POTENTIELS EVOQUES; SOMMEIL
Abstract-Résumé: L'insomnie touche plus de 15% de la population generale. Trois principaux types d'insomnie existent dont celui qui debute dans l'enfance, nomme insomnie idiopathique. Ce type d'insomnie est habituellement severe et peut handicaper les personnes atteintes. Curieusement, malgre des rapports importants de difficultes de sommeil, les personnes souffrant d'insomnie idiopathique rapportent rarement des consequences diurnes qui interferent avec leur fonctionnement quotidien. Deux hypotheses ont ete emises pour expliquer l'origine de ce type d'insomnie: 1) le systeme de regulation du rythme veille/sommeil est deficient et 2)les systemes d'alerte/vigilance sont hyperactifs. Ce que nous connaissons de l'insomnie idiopathique nous est principalement transmis par des observations cliniques. A cet egard, peu d'etudes empiriques se sont penchees sur les consequences diurnes de l'insomnie idiopathique ainsi que sur le profil nocturne de ces individus. Les mecanismes de protection du sommeil et l'activite cerebrale chez les personnes atteintes de ce type d'insomnie sont donc encore meconnus. Nous entendons verifier la seconde hypothese, soit celle de la presence d'hyperactivite des systemes de vigilance en utilisant des mesures fines d'analyses de l'electroencephalographie. Les potentiels evoques seront utilises afin de mesurer le traitement de l'information nocturne et diurne chez les personnes souffrant d'insomnie idiopathique. Les informations obtenues grace a ce projet pourront ensuite etre utilisees afin d'offrir de meilleurs traitements a ces individus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Gut Pathophysiology: epithelial metabolic stress and barrier function
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIER FUNCTION; COMMENSAL FLORA; EPITHELIUM; ER STRESS; METABOLIC STRESS; MITOCHONDRIA; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: The layer of epithelial cells that line the intestine have an important barrier function: regulating the absorption of nutrients and, at the same time, restricting the entry of potentially harmful and disease causing bacteria or other foreign matter into the body.  Many disease conditions, including the inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD: incurable conditions affecting 1 in 160 Canadians) are accompanied by increased leakiness of the epithelial barrier.  Indeed, descriptions of increased permeability of the gut preceding the onset of intestinal inflammation have led to the postulate that loss of epithelial barrier function can provoke intestinal disease, including IBD.  We have shown that reduced energy (i.e. metabolic stress) in the epithelial cell reduces the barrier function of the epithelial cell layer.  Focusing on the role that this may play in intestinal inflammation, I will use a variety of model systems to assess the mechanism(s) by which metabolic stress affects epithelial integrity and allows bacteria to cross from the lumen of the intestine into the body.  The outcome of these studies will be a better understanding of the nature and regulation of intestinal permeability, and the identification of ways to control epithelial barrier function to enhance human digestive health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of diabetes on brain function and recovery from ischemic stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: 2-PHOTON MICROSCOPY; ANGIOGENESIS; BEHAVIOUR; BLOOD FLOW; DIABETES; IMAGING; NEURAL PLASTICITY; RECOVERY OF FUNCTION; SOMATOSENSORY CORTEX; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: It is now estimated that a North American child stands a 1 in 3 chance of becoming diabetic. This staggering figure has an enormous cost, both for the general population that must cover diabetes related health care costs (15.6 billion per year in Canada) and for the individual that will likely suffer disabling complications. For example, people with diabetes are 2-4 times more likely to suffer a stroke and their prognosis for recovery is very poor relative to the general population. In our previous 3 year CIHR grant, we showed that recovery of paw function after stroke was impaired in diabetic mice, which could not be rescued by insulin therapy. Furthermore, poor stroke recovery was not associated with a larger stroke, but rather, profound impairments in how surviving brain regions re-organized their function after stroke. At the present time, very little is known about how diabetes affects the circulation of blood in the brain. Proper circulation is crucial for normal brain function as well as recovery from stroke. The primary goal of the current research proposal will be to use live animal imaging technologies that will allow us to visualize blood flow, blood vessel leakage and remodeling in the diabetic mouse brain before and after a stroke. We will then try to link changes in the circulatory system with the re-wiring of neuronal circuits in parts of the brain important for stroke recovery. Given our preliminary data showing that diabetes leads to more leaky blood vessels and altered blood flow after stroke, we will explore the possibility that too much of a blood vessel related growth factor (called VEGF) may be responsible for poor stroke recovery in diabetics. Ultimately, the proposed project will generate new information regarding the effects of diabetes on the brain, which will stimulate new treatment options for those Canadians suffering from diabetes related sequeleae.

ClasseRechercheFR: GLAUCOME; TROUBLES DE LA PAROLE, DE LA VISION ET DE L'OUIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of retinal ganglion cell dendrite degeneration.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; APOPTOSIS; DENDRITE; GLAUCOMA; MAMMALIAN TARGET OF RAPAMYCIN (MTOR); NEURODEGENERATION; RETINAL GANGLION CELL; SYNAPSE; TUMOR NECROSIS FACTOR-ALPHA (TNFALPHA); VISUAL FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. At present, there is no cure for glaucoma and current therapies are inadequate. Loss of vision in glaucoma results from the irreversible death of retinal ganglion cells, the neurons that send visual information from the retina to the brain. The current proposal will focus on novel observations made by our team to provide an in-depth characterization of key pathways leading to retinal ganglion cell degeneration. Specifically, we will test the hypothesis that early deficits in retinal ganglion cell dendrites initiate a cascade of cellular damage that ultimately results in dysfunction and death. The scientific foundation of this project lies on our recent observation that substantial dendritic abnormalities occur early in an experimental mouse glaucoma model, and that this response is caused by a loss of the 'mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR)' activity, a key intracellular regulator of cell growth and protein synthesis. This research program will create knowledge concerning the molecular and cellular mechanisms of RGC dendritic damage, and it will validate novel targets for the development of therapeutic strategies to protect vision in glaucoma.

TitreApplicationTitle: In vivo analysis of integrin function in tissue maintenance and morphogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION; BLOOD CELL; DROSOPHILA; EPITHELIAL CELL; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; IMAGING; INTEGRIN; MORPHOGENESIS; PROTEIN TURNOVER; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: Integrins are the main molecules in the human body that link cells to the extracellular matrix (ECM), a mixture of complex sugars and proteins that forms the base upon which tissues are built. Integrins are very important for many biological processes in the human body and disruptions in integrin function are associated with a large number of diseases. We are interested in understanding the mechanisms by which integrin carry out their diverse functions. Our proposal deals with analyzing three processes that are play important roles in human health: muscle attachment to tendons, wound healing in epithelial tissues such as skin, and blood cell migration such as that used by white blood cells during infection. The powerful genetic and imaging tools and the relative simplicity of the fly genome means that fly is a terrific model in which to analyze integrin function. We have spent the last few years building a large array of reagents and tools that allow us to systematically analyze integrin function in these three processes in the context of the intact living organism; often in real time. Results of this study will shed important light on how integrins are controlled during tissue formation and tissue maintenance, and also provide insight into how dysregulation of integrin function leads to disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Nuclear Receptor Regulation of Early Gestation
Keywords-MotsClés: DECIDUALIZATION; ENDOMETRIUM; GESTATION; MECHANISM OF TRANSCRIPTION; NUCLEAR RECEPTOR; TRANSGENIC MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Successful establishment of gestation in humans and other mammals requires complex interactions between the embryo and the uterus.  An important change in the uterine lining or endometrium is the differention of a cell population to become the decidual tissue.  Functional placentation requires that this differentiation occur, and its absence correlates with gestational pathology and embryo mortality.  We have new evidence demonstrating that an intercellular signaling molecule in the nuclear receptor family known as liver receptor homolog-1 (Lrh-1) is essential for successful decidualization of the endometrium.  We propose to further investigate this phenomenon using endometrium specific ablation of the gene in question in a transgenic mouse model and by exploring Lrh-1 signaling in human endometrial cells in vitro.  We will analyze global gene expression patterns in both whole animal and cell models and explore the effects of Lrh-1 ligands in inducing endometrial differentiation.  We will further investigate the molecular methods of transcriptional regulation of marker genes for decidualization.  These studies are expected to provide new insight into important problems of human gestational health.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Ontario Child Health Study Sequel
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD MENTAL HEALTH; CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Mental health, the ability to regulate our emotions and behaviour and to cope with stress, is essential to development and life quality for all children. Yet very little is known today about the mental health of Canadian children. Since the last major study of childhood mental health, the Ontario Child Health Study (OCHS) carried out by our group in 1983, there have been changes in Canada which may put children at risk. These changes include increases in income inequality, in family dissolution, in the growth of visible minorities, perceptions of discrimination and in neighbourhood poverty.  We therefore propose to study the mental health of a representative sample of Ontario children and adolescents aged 4-18 years (n=10,530) living in 7,020 families and 180 neighbourhoods and attending 240 schools throughout the province. The study is a sequel to OCHS and will be done in collaboration with Statistics Canada. The study has five objectives: (1) to estimate the prevalence of childhood mental disorders such as depression, anxiety and ADHD; (2) to assess how these disorders may be linked with other chronic health conditions and with social and academic difficulties; (3) to examine the extent to which families with children exhibiting mental health needs are receiving mental health programs and services; (4) to determine if the prevalence of childhood mental disorders has increased between 1983 and 2013, in association with increases in socio-economic inequalities; and (5) to investigate the larger contextual (family, neighbourhood, school) influences on risk for childhood mental disorder. Information will be collected from parents, teachers and older children, and from administrative records available from Ontario service providers. Results will be shared with policymakers, who are collaborating on the study, and with the public for purposes of informing the development of new programs and policies to benefit children in Ontario and beyond.

ResearchClassEN: ATTENTION DEFICIT HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER (ADHD); PSYCHO-SOCIAL AND BEHAVIOURAL RESEARCH
ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLE D'HYPERACTIVITÉ AVEC DÉFICIT DE L'ATTENTION (THADA); RECHERCHES PSYCHOSOCIALES ET COMPORTEMENTALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Parents as Friendship Coaches for Children with ADHD
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTION-DEFICIT/HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER; PEER RELATIONSHIPS
Abstract-Résumé: About 1 and 20 Canadian children have Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Often times, children with ADHD have trouble getting along with peers, which can cause them to feel sad or lonely, and also make it more difficult for them to finish school, avoid drug problems, and have productive family lives and careers as adults. For some children with ADHD, even though they are receiving other treatments such as medication or therapy, they still have difficulty with their peer relationships.  We have found, however, that parents may be able to help their children with ADHD to make better friendships. This study tests a new treatment to train parents to be "friendship coaches" for their children with ADHD when their children are in elementary school. We are examining the ways in which parents can help their children with ADHD to learn better social skills, to choose the right friends, and to develop good bonds with peers.  Our hope is that this treatment will help children with ADHD to get along better with their peers, which will lead to these children having happier and healthier lives as teenagers and adults. If the treatment is successful, then we will be able to offer this service to families of children with ADHD in the future.

ClasseRechercheFR: SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Secondary electron collision cross sections for use in radiotherapy and radioprotection/Sections efficaces de diffusion des électrons secondaires pour utilisation en radiothérapie et radioprotection.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMOLECULAR DAMAGE; BIOMOLECULES; CANCER TREATMENT; CELLULAR MOLECULES; CHEMORADIATION THERAPY; DNA DAMAGE; ELECTRON SCATTERING CROSS SECTIONS; ELECTRON SPECTROSCOPY; ELECTRON STIMULATED DESORPTION; ELECTRON TRAPPING; LOW ENERGY ELECTRONS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MICRODOSIMETRY; MODELLING OF RADIATION DAMAGE; NANODOSIMETRY; RADIATION DAMAGE; RADIOSENSITIZERS; RADIOTHERAPY; SECONDARY ELECTRONS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer imposes a massive burden of suffering on Canadians each year. Radiotherapy, the therapeutic use of radiation, is one of the major and most effective cancer treatment modalities. Specifically, 50 to 60% of patients will receive radiotherapy during the course of their illness, either with a curative intent or as a palliative treatment. Radiotherapy is rarely used alone, and is involved in a complex strategy including other therapeutic modalities to decrease repopulation, metastases and thus improve survival. For each treatment in radiotherapy, hospital physicists calculate as precisely as possible the amount of radiation (i.e., dose) to be delivered to the patient and its distribution, rate and fractionation (i.e., the number of irradiation periods to deliver a given dose). These calculations, which depend on many parameters, including the type of cancer cells, their location, the other therapeutic drugs being administrated and previous surgery, must be performed from data related to the interaction of the radiation with molecules in the cells. More particularly in targeted radionuclide therapy, in order to increase considerably the benefits of this type of therapy and consequently the survival rate of patients, radiation physicists must now obtain information on the effect of the low-energy electrons generated by radionuclides at the nanoscopic scale in the cancer cells during the treatment. The main goal of our research is to provide this information by studying more specifically the probabilities of low-energy electrons to produce specific energy deposits and/or damages in biological materials. Such information can also serve in the development of new drugs that can enhance the radiosensitivity of cancer cells. The proposed research has implications not only in radiotherapy, but also on the long term effects of low dose radiation from radionuclides used for diagnostic purposes and more generally from those naturally occurring in the environment.

ClasseRechercheFR: LEUCEMIES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibiting oncogenic kinases to target metabolism in AML
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; KINASES; LEUKEMIA; METABOLISM; RNAI
Abstract-Résumé: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive blood cancer.  The majority of patients with AML still die from their disease and therapy for this condition is essentially unchanged in the last 20 years.  Even though we have learned more about the genetic abnormalities of AML, it has proven difficult to directly target these genetic mutations.  Here, we propose to target a downstream effect of these genetic mutations - cell metabolism.   Recently, we demonstrated that AML cells are unique in the metabolic requirements and their dependence on a form of energy production called oxidative metabolism.  We also recently demonstrated that AML but not normal cells can be killed by inhibiting protein synthesis in the mitochondria and blocking oxidative metabolism.  In this proposal, we will investigate the regulation of metabolism in AML.  Specifically, we will address the role of kinases and their inhibitors in affecting metabolism in AML.  The results from this work will highlight a unique strategy to shift the metabolic profile of a cancer cell.  By shifting the metabolic profile, we can make the AML cells vulnerable to inhibitors of oxidative metabolism and inhibitors of mitochondrial protein synthesis.  Thus, our work will highlight a new therapeutic strategy for AML that could be tested rapidly in the clinic.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL; DISTRIBUTION DES SOINS DE LA SANTE
TitreApplicationTitle: Incentive payments to British Columbia primary care physicians for chronic disease management: What is the effect on patient care?
Keywords-MotsClés: INCENTIVE PAYMENTS; PATIENT OUTCOMES; PHYSICIAN SERVICES; PRIMARY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Primary care is considered to be the foundation of the healthcare system. The province of BC offers incentive payments to encourage physicians to offer comprehensive primary care to their patients. There is now almost $100 million per year spent on these payments.   Despite this large investment, there has not yet been a rigorous evaluation of their effect on either how physicians practice or whether patients benefit. This project will conduct such an evaluation.   Our main question of interest is "what effect have Chronic Care Annual Bonus and Complex Care Initiative payments had on: continuity of care; hospitalization rates; total cost per patient (GP, specialist, diagnostic, hospital and pharmacy); and disease-specific quality indicators (for chronic disease incentives) among patients with qualifying chronic conditions"?   In addition, we will look at the characteristics of physicians who did and did not bill incentives, the patients for whom incentives were billed and the how many people are now diagnosed with the qualifying chronic conditions.  This study will use existing data for the whole population of British Columbia. Data will include information on physician payments, hospitalizations and prescription drug use. All data will be anonymous so it will not be possible to identify individual physicians or individual patients.   The existing research literature does not tell us for certain what effect incentive payments have on patient care. BC is in a unique position to add to this literature because the province started incentive payments without at the same time changing the service delivery model, for example by encouraging the formation of group or multi-specialty practices. This research will provide much needed evidence to policy-makers about the intended and unintended consequences of these programs relative to their cost.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: IgA Plasma Cells: Where, How and What
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVATION INDUCED CYTIDINE DEAMINASE; ANTIBODY; B LYMPHOCYTE; GERMINAL CENTRE; IGA; INNATE B CELLS; MUCOSAL TISSUES
Abstract-Résumé: B lymphocytes are an important component of the immune system due to their ability to produce antibodies, molecules that can neutralize pathogens. Such antibody responses occur when B lymphocytes that are specific for the pathogen obtain help from pathogen-specific T lymphocytes. These cellular interactions take place within a complex microenvironment called the Germinal Centre which is located within lymph nodes or the spleen. However, it takes approximately one week to initiate a Germinal Centre response, and this puts the host at risk of succumbing to infection in the early days post-exposure. As a stop-gap, humans have an innate immune system that responds rapidly to microbial exposure. Interestingly, even though B and T lymphocytes are considered part of the adaptive immune system, some B and T lymphocytes have innate properties. This is particularly true in the mucosal tissues (gut, lung, reproductive tract) and in the skin, all of which are locations where pathogens first invade our bodies. We know much less about innate lymphocytes and how they participate in immune response compared to their adaptive counterparts. We are studying innate B cell responses, with particular focus on those innate responses that occur in the gut. In particular, we are interested in how innate B cells produce the mucosal antibody IgA, and whether IgA-secreting B cells may have special properties that allow them to fight off infections.

OrgNm: Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM)
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of aberrant hormone receptors in the pathophysiology of primary aldosteronism
Keywords-MotsClés: ABERRANT G-PROTEIN COUPLED  RECEPTORS (GPCR); ACTH RECEPTOR; ADRENAL CORTEX; CLINICAL INVESTIGATION; FAMILIAL PRIMARY ALDOSTERONISM; GENE EXPRESSION; GIP RECEPTOR; POTASSIUM CHANNEL MUTATIONS; PRIMARY ALDOSTERONISM; WNT-B CATENIN ACTIVATION
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension (high blood pressure) affects more than 1 billion people worldwide (~25-30% of population) and contributes to approximately 7million cardiovascular deaths/year (such as heart attack, stroke with paralysis). Excess production by the adrenal glands of a hormone called aldosterone causes salt retention by the kidneys, increased blood volume and high blood pressure; this is called primary aldosteronism. It is responsible for 6-12% of hypertension in humans and would thus affect almost 3% of the population. Primary aldosteronism carries for affected patients 5-10 times higher risks of stroke, heart attack and other cardiovascular risks than the most common form of high blood pressure called essential hypertension. The mechanisms causing the development or unilateral or bilateral tumors or increased size (hyperplasia) of the adrenal glands responsible for primary aldosteronism are poorly understood. Our group and other researchers have recently found that the abnormal presence and function of several hormone receptors (like a lock in a door that the hormone opens if it is the good key) in affected adrenal tissues are responsible for the increased secretion of aldosterone in this disease independently from its normal control mechanisms. Our proposed studies will clarify the role of this abnormal regulation of aldosterone by various hormone receptors. They will be conducted in patients affected by this disease and compared to normal individuals. In addition we will study adrenal tumors after removal by surgery and the adjacent adrenal tissue  We expect to improve the diagnosis of this important cause of hypertension. Identification of aberrant hormone receptors should allow new treatments by drugs capable of blocking those receptors. This should result in normalisation of blood pressure but also in the reversal of the increased risk of cardiovascular events in individuals affected by primary aldosteronism.

ClasseRechercheFR: SCLÉROSE LATÉRALE AMYOTROPHIQUE (SLA); RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Synaptic targets for therapeutic protection of motor function in a genetic model of ALS
Keywords-MotsClés: ALS/FTLD; FUS/TLS; GENETIC NETWORK; MOLECULAR MECHANISMS; MOTOR FUNCTION AND MOVEMENT; NEURODEGENERATIVE GENES; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION; TARDBP TDP-43; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Motoneuron diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) start by impairing movement and ultimately can cause death due motoneuron loss.  While suppression of cell death has been the major but so far largely unsuccessful target for therapeutic discovery, prevention of pre-clinical loss of motor function is a potentially more effective approach.  Recently, the proteins TDP-43 and FUS have been discovered as the major constituents of cellular inclusions from the spinal cord of ALS patients.  Normally these proteins regulate transcription in particular of synaptic genes, whereas their mutations cause ALS and other disorders.  We hypothesize that these mutated RNA processing enzymes lead to pre-clinical synaptic dysfunction, making the synapse a prime target for therapeutic development for these as yet untreatable diseases.  However, synaptic defects have not been characterized for these new disease genes.  We have therefore developed simple zebrafish models that are amenable to powerful synaptic and genetic analyses, including chemical genetic drug screening that has identified potential synaptic therapeutics with one of our compounds being tested on patients.  A recent explosion in the genetics of motoneuron diseases has indicated that many of the genes causing the same familial disorder are also implicated in other disorders as well.  Rather than acting individually, we will test the hypothesis that these genes may interact in a genetic network and that defining the network will reveal novel targets for therapeutic development.  Characterizing these genetic and synaptic interactions requires multigenic analyses with in vivo models of motor function such as are possible in the zebrafish.  This project will explore genetic interactions between mutated human genes expressed in zebrafish and will develop new pharmacological approaches by studying the role of calcium channels and their drugs of action on spinal cord neurons.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of pain on the motor system: Neural mechanisms and implications for rehabilitation
Keywords-MotsClés: FORCE FIELD ADAPTATION; GAIT; MOTOR CORTEX; MOTOR LEARNING; MOVEMENT; PAIN; PLASTICITY; REACHING; REHABILITATION; TRANCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Pain is one of the most common and disabling symptoms following injury. In motor rehabilitation programs, a large proportion of patients receiving intensive training to improve their motor function are experiencing pain. Compared to patients with similar injuries but without associated pain, patients experiencing pain exhibit poorer recovery. Basic research using experimental pain in humans and animals have shown that pain interfere with the functioning of the regions of the brain and the spinal cord that are involved in the control of movements, and that these influences can interfere with motor learning capacities. The general aim of this research program is to answer a very simple, but highly clinically relevant, question: How well can patients learn new motor tasks (and even more importantly retain what they have learned) if they are in pain while receiving rehabilitation? Specifically, we will determine whether the presence of pain interferes with motor learning associated with training in a new motor task, as well as investigate underlying mechanisms in the brain and the spinal cord. To attain this objective, two studies will be conducted to investigate both the effect of experimental pain (e.g. induced in healthy participants) and of clinical pain resulting of different types of injury on motor learning capacities. These capacities will be assessed using robotic devices that can perturb movement (either gait or upper limb movement) and measure how well and how quickly people can compensate for that perturbation to retrieve their natural movement pattern. If our hypothesis that pain interfere with motor learning is confirmed, it would suggest that the same motor rehabilitation intervention would be less effective if administered in the presence of pain, or if it induces post-intervention pain. The next step would be to assess potential intervention approaches that might decrease this negative impact of pain on motor learning.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: The amyloid and beyond; A molecular answer to forget me not.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER DISEASE; CELL BIOLOGY; CELL SIGNALING; COGNITIVE MECHANISM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PRESENILIN; PROTEIN INTERACTION; SECRETASE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer disease (AD) is associated with aging and is described as a degenerative disorder of the human central nervous system that destroys the brain and leaves its victims unable to function on their own. Mutations in the presenilin-1 (PS1)gene are associated with the most aggressive subtype of Familial Alzheimer Disease (between 25 and 60 years of age). Although PS1 is a key element in the AD puzzle, the cellular role and regulation of both normal and mutant forms remains to be unambiguously identified. Presenilin is required for amyloid formation, cell differentiation and developmental signaling. The overall goal of my research project is to identify the biological function of PS1 and to elucidate the biochemical pathways in which the mutated form of this protein leads to the  neurodegeneration observed in AD. Results derived from this proposal will help elucidate PS1 biological functions both in amyloid formation and cell signaling. We also propose to develop a new therapeutic tool to decrease the accumulation of amyloid in the brain of Alzheimer disease patient. Altogether, our results will assist in the development of novel treatments for Alzheimer disease. Therefore, this project has a significant chance of improving the quality of life of aging people.

TitreApplicationTitle: Age- and sex-specific contribution of nuclear or membrane progesterone receptors on respiratory control in mice.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREATHING RECORDINGS; CONTROL OF BREATHING; EEG-EMG RECORDINGS; ICV SIRNA INFUSION; KO MICE; MEMBRANE RECEPTORS; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; PROGESTERONE; SEX-SPECIFIC EFFECTS; SLEEP-DISORDERED BREATHING
Abstract-Résumé: Periodic cessation of breathing during sleep - or sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) occurs in moderate or severe form in 1 of every 15 adult subjects, and in a large proportion of babies born before term. So far, there is no easy treatment options for SDB, and a drug-based therapy for SDB would be a remarkable breakthrough. The occurrence of this disorder is much lower in adult women because they have high circulating levels of progesterone, a sex hormone which acts on the brain to stimulate breathing. How precisely progesterone exerts this effect remains unknown. Broadly speaking, progesterone exerts its biological functions through different sets of specific receptors, the nuclear progesterone receptor (nPR) lies inside the nucleus of the cells and mediate some effects of progesterone by altering genes expression, while the membrane progesterone receptor (mPR) is inserted into the cellular membrane and mediate other effects of progesterone through intracellular biochemical pathways. My team have shown that these progesterone receptors are present in brain areas that are involved in the control of respiration, and the main objective of this proposal is to question the relative contribution of nPR and mPR on respiratory control and  SDB during sleep in mice. We are using several strategies based on genetic disruption of expression of nPR and/or mPR to asses their relative contribution to respiratory control during sleep. So far or results tend to indicate that nPR and mPR exerts distinctive, and powerful effects on respiratory control during sleep, and reduces the occurrence of SDB in mice. These effects appear to be age, and sex-dependent. On the long-term, we hope that newly developed drugs targeting these receptors might become an available option for the development of a drug-based strategy for SDB.

OrgNm: Ottawa Hospital Research Institute/Institut de recherche de l'Hôpital d'Ottawa
TitreApplicationTitle: Signaling mechanisms of D1-class dopaminergic receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: DESENSITIZATION; DOPAMINE; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTOR KINASE; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; INTERNALIZATION; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROMYELOCYTIC LEUKEMIA ZINC FINGER; PROTEIN KINASE C; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; SENSITIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Dopamine is an important chemical that controls numerous functions in the brain. Dopamine transmits its information via the attachment to proteins called receptors, which are located at the outside of the nerve cells. Humans have five genes coding for dopamine receptors. A faulty activity in dopamine receptors is linked to numerous disorders such as schizophrenia and Parkinson's. Administration of drugs attaching to dopamine receptors that control their activity is currently used to treat schizophrenic and Parkinson's patients. However, these drugs produce unwanted side-effects. Our research focuses on how cells control the dopamine D1 and D5 receptor activity. We will explore the role of a biochemical process called phosphorylation. Phosphorylation is controlled by enzymes termed kinases, which promote the attachment of phosphate to specific spots on proteins. In cells, phosphorylation controls protein activity, transport, recycling and degradation. Specifically, our studies will map the spots on D1 and D5 receptors that are subjected to phosphorylation by different kinases. These studies will uncover the phosphorylation bar codes (also known as "phosphoproteomics") of D1 and D5 receptors. In addition, our work will identify brain proteins that bind to dopamine D1 and D5 receptors to form specific dopamine receptor networks or interactomes. Our research will be conducted using a wide range of techniques such as DNA transfection, immunoprecipitation, whole-cell phosphorylation assay, mass spectrometry and microscopy. A better knowledge of the phosphoproteomics and interactomes of D1 and D5 receptors will help us to better understand how these two receptors work in normal and diseased brains. Most importantly, information gained from our research will be useful in the development of novel drugs and therapeutic approaches for various diseases associated with impairment in dopamine function such as schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the Efficacy of an Attention Modification Program for Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain Patients with Fibromyalgia
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTENTIONAL BIASES; ATTENTIONAL MODIFICATION; CHRONIC MUSCULOSKELETAL PAIN; FIBROMYALGIA; INTERNET; PAIN; RCT; TELEHEALTH; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: There is growing consensus among researchers and therapists that chronic pain changes how people think and changing how people think appears to change how people cope with chronic pain.  Using computer software administered in laboratories, researchers have been increasingly able to demonstrate automatic (i.e., unconscious) differences in the thoughts of people with pain; specifically, people with pain automatically react to pain-related words.  Researchers have now demonstrated that we can use similar computer software to change those automatic reactions, resulting in less pain.  The results have been very encouraging, with people reporting far fewer symptoms - including reduced pain - after using the software for only a few minutes a day, twice a week, for four weeks.  Perhaps most exciting, we can now administer this treatment protocol through the internet, making the potential benefits available to most Canadians from the comfort of their homes; however, the research is still preliminary and several avenues remain to be explored.  First, the protocol has only been successful in three studies, one with patients who had acute back pain, one with patients who had chronic back pain, and one with patients who had fibromyalgia.  Although participants in the studies said the protocol reduced their pain, rigorous extension and replication are required. Second, in all three studies the protocol was administered in laboratory settings and we need to test if it will work if we administer it in patient's homes.  Third, we need to know whether the protocol can also reduce physical disability. Fourth, we need to assess how long the changes last.  The proposed project will explore these research avenues and the results will provide critical insights into this potentially revolutionary contribution to managing chronic pain.  If successful, the protocol will provide a highly accessible and extremely cost-effective method for reducing chronic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adiponectin Signaling Pathways and Kidney Disease Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPONECTIN; AMPK; ANGIOTENSIN; CAMP; DIABETES; KIDNEY; NADPH OXIDASE
Abstract-Résumé: Statement of the health problem: Obesity and diabetes mellitus are growing health care problems, and both are risk factors for heart disease and stroke. Diabetic nephropathy further increases cardiovascular risk, and recent studies show that diabetic nephropathy is rising along with the number of new cases of diabetes.   Objective: Diabetic nephropathy is a consequence of the effects of high glucose concentrations on kidney cells including activation of the renin angiotensin system (RAS). The objective of the current proposal is to better understand how obesity contributes to the onset and progression of diabetic nephropathy. Studies will test the hypothesis that changes in proteins produced by fat cells influence the susceptibility of the kidney to high glucose-induced and RAS-induced kidney injury. We expect to establish that the kidney is an unexpected but important target tissue for the fat-derived protein, adiponectin. Blood levels of adiponectin decline with obesity, and we believe that adiponectin protects the kidney from injury. Our preliminary data shows that adiponectin can lessen the response of kidney cells to high glucose and activation of the RAS, and that loss of the gene for adiponectin is associated with increased diabetic kidney injury in mice.   Experimental Plan: In order to test our hypothesis that adiponectin protects the kidney from the harmful effects of glucose and activation of the RAS, we will study cultured kidney cells from the kidney, and determine if adiponectin can reduce the response of these cells to glucose and the RAS. The cellular studies will provide the basis for examining the effect of deletion of the genes for adiponectin on the onset and progression of diabetic nephropathy and kidney injury due to activation of the RAS in mice. We will then determine if treatment with adiponectin will lessen diabetic nephropathy and kidney injury due to activation of the RAS in mice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and functional neuro-anatomical correlates of memory for context across the adult lifespan.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT LIFESPAN; CONTEXT MEMORY; EPISODIC MEMORY; HEALTHY AGING; HIPPOCAMPUS; MIDDLE AGE; NEUROIMAGING; PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Healthy aging is associated with increased difficulties in remembering spatial and temporal contextual details about past personal experience.  Interestingly, not all healthy older adults exhibit context memory deficits. In our previous study 30% of older adults aged 60 -75 yrs performed as well as young adults on context memory tasks (high performers). Also, since these memory and brain changes are already present by the age of 60, this suggests that these changes must emerge during middle age (40 -55 yrs). However little is known about the brain correlates of context memory in middle age.  The proposed research program will use neuroimaging to measure task-related brain activity in healthy young, middle aged and older adults as they perform context memory tasks. We will also measure brain volumes and cortical thickness in these subjects. The middle aged adult sample will consist of equal numbers of adults with or without a family history of AD. The goal of this research program is to examine how age-associated changes in brain structure (volume/thickness) and function impact context memory performance across the adult lifespan.  Specifically we will compare the structural and functional correlates of context memory in high versus low performing older and middle aged adults to understand the compensatory neural mechanisms that help maintain context memory as we age. By comparing middle aged adults to young adults we will determine: (1) when these deficits emerge, (2) what neural changes are associated with their emergence and (3) how having a family history of AD influences these observations.  Results from the proposed study will help us identify neural changes associated with the initial emergence of memory deficits in middle age.  Our results will also indicate if the emergence of these deficits, and their neural sequelae, are influenced by a family history of AD.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Flavivirus host cell interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; CAPSID PROTEIN; DENGUE VIRUS; HELICASES; HOST INTERACTIONS; NUCLEUS; PATHOGENESIS; PEROXISOMES; TIGHT JUNCTIONS; WEST NILE VIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: RNA viruses cause the vast majority of viral infections in humans.  Despite their medical importance, there are very few therapeutic options to treat infections caused by these viruses. Conventional antiviral therapies that target viral enzymes have met with limited success because RNA viruses exhibit a high mutation rate, which leads to drug resistance. Our laboratory is focused on identifying antiviral targets for West Nile virus and Dengue virus. Globally, these viruses infect over 100 million people each year. Because they are "gene poor", RNA viruses encode very few proteins, often less than 10. Research from our laboratory and others, indicates that RNA virus proteins are multifunctional and interact with a surprisingly large number of host cell proteins. From a health perspective, these host proteins may be targets for antiviral therapy. In theory, viruses should not develop resistance as quickly to drugs that target host cell proteins. To serve as anti-viral targets though, it must be possible to inhibit the activities of these host proteins through pharmaceutical intervention without major toxicity. This is of course the basis for most drugs in use today. The exciting part is that in theory at least, the simpler the virus, the more host proteins that are required for replication and dissemination, each of which represents a potential target for therapeutic intervention.
