TitreApplicationTitle: Information systems-enabled outreach program for Adverse Drug Events
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY; PATIENT SAFETY; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: One of the most common health care interventions in any healthcare setting is a medication prescription. Unfortunately, up to 25% of outpatient prescriptions are associated with adverse drug events (ADEs). ADEs decrease patient health directly and can lead to non-adherence, which in turn have negative consequences.  We have recently conducted a pilot project in which we tested the feasibility and potential utility of an information technology enabled outreach program for monitoring patients receiving and outpatient prescription. This intervention involved the use of an interactive voice response system programmed to automatically call ambulatory care patients following a prescription. If the system identified a potential medication problem, then a pharmacist was notified who subsequently contacted the patient, modified the therapy accordingly, and informed a physician when necessary. Our pilot project included 568 patients with diverse illnesses in two Canadian cities. On 21-day interviews we determinedhigh levels of patient and provider acceptability of the system. The program identified 56 of 125 (45%) ADEs and 10 of 26 30%) of primary non-compliance events. We observed very few episodes of ameliorable ADEs. These events were more common in a previous study of outpatient ADEs.  We feel these results justify a randomized control trial to assess the effectiveness of our intervention for improving patient -centered outcomes. We plan to randomize ambulatory care patients receiving incident prescriptions for one of four conditions (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, depression, and anxiety) to our intervention versus routine care to determine whether the system reduces the severity and duration of outpatient ADEs and improves adherence to medication care atthree and 12 months.  This study will provide important information to guide future applications of our approach beyond the specific question asked in this protocol.

TitreApplicationTitle: L'efficacité d'une intervention psychologique administrée par vidéoconférence pour traiter le trouble d'anxiété généralisée (TAG)
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCES AUX SOINS DE SANTE MENTALE; ANALYSE DE NON-INFERIORITE; ANXIETE GENERALISEE; ESSAI CLINIQUE; THERAPIE COGNITIVE-COMPORTEMENTALE; TELEMEDECINE/TELESANTE; TELEPSYCHOTHERAPIE
Abstract-Résumé: Le Trouble d'anxiete generalisee (TAG) altere considerablement le fonctionnement et la qualite de vie de ceux qui en sont atteints. La therapie cognitive et comportementale (TCC) a prouve a maintes reprises son efficacite. Par contre, le nombre restreint de therapeutes formes a la TCC et le fait qu'ils se retrouvent majoritairement dans les centres urbains pose un probleme d'accessibilite pour les patients qui vivent dans des lieux ou il n'y a pas de specialistes. La telepsychotherapie (psychotherapie appliquee en videoconference) se presente alors comme solution interessante. Les premieres etudes d'efficacite portant sur la telepsychotherapie pour certains troubles d'anxiete revelent des resultats prometteurs et des replications sont en cours ailleurs avec de plus grands echantillons. Comme aucune etude controlee et rigoureuse n'a ete realisee aupres d'individus ayant un TAG, il est essentiel de verifier l'efficacite de la TCC en videoconference comparativement en face a face. Deja, nos etudes pilotes nous permettent d'anticiper des resultats favorables.  L'etude examine l'efficacite d'un traitement applique par videoconference avec des participants ayant un TAG, recrutes dans 5 cliniques universitaires specialisees associees a des centres ruraux, et affectes aleatoirement a l'une ou l'autre des 2 conditions soit:(a) un traitement psychologique standard applique en face a face (condition temoin de reference); (b) le meme traitement psychologique applique uniquement videoconference (condition experimentale). Divers strategies sont deployees pour maximiser les controles methodologiques.  Cette etude permettra de preciser si un traitement offert a distance par videoconference peut etre "aussi" efficace qu'un traitement applique de facon traditionnelle en face a face, et plus pratique en termes d'accessibilite que le traitement en face a face. La telepsychotherapie deviendrait alors une solution valide permettant d'augmenter l'acces aux soins de sante mentale.

TitreApplicationTitle: Longitudinal Trajectories of Depressive Symptoms through the Transition from Post-secondary Education into the Workforce: The Influence of Social Supports and Employment Characteristics
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; EMPLOYMENT AND MENTAL HEALTH; SOCIAL SUPPORTS AND MENTAL HEALTH; TRANSITION TO WORK; YOUNG ADULTS
Abstract-Résumé: CONTEXT We will examine changes in depressive symptoms as young adults transition into the workforce, and assess how this is influenced by employment quality and access to social support. As young adults attempt to transition into the workforce, the failure to obtain full-time, long-term employment in their field can have negative consequences on mental health. In Canada, this link between depression and the transition to work is complicated by provincial differences in unemployment rates. As a result, many young adults must choose between leaving their communities and supports to pursue their career goals, or remaining connected to their support system and facing the prospect of unemployment or taking any kind of work that is available. This study will not only elucidate the links between mental health, employment and social supports during this developmental period, but will also examine whether these relationships vary by sex and geographic region.  METHOD Data will be drawn from several cycles of the National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth, a comprehensive, population-based survey of youth across Canada, jointly maintained by Statistics Canada and Human Resources and Social Development Canada. Data will be analyzed using advanced statistical modelling techniques.  IMPORTANCE In the current economic climate, it is important to study links between depression and the transition to work. This will provide information to help shape future social policies and intervention strategies. For example, if low quality work leads to worse mental health outcomes, this would highlight the need to assist unemployed youth to launch their long-term career goals, instead of only helping them to find any available work. Our study also extends existing knowledge to a Canadian social context and lays the groundwork for future research on intervention strategies to alleviate possible negative mental health consequences of failing to make an optimal transition to work.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory logic of the cortical-to-subcortical lineage switch
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL LINEAGE; GLIOMA; MURINE VERSUS PRIMATE; NEOCORTEX; NEUROG2/ASCL1 GENETIC SWITCH; NEURONS; OLIGODENDROCYTES; PRIMED MULTIPOTENT PROGENITORS; PRONEURAL GENES; RAS/ERK SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: The neocortex is the region of the brain where higher cognitive functioning occurs, allowing us to perceive stimuli in the environment and have conscious thought. We study how the different cells that make up the neocortex are generated in the developing embryo. In particular, we focus on two genes (Neurog2/Ascl1) that together are responsible for generating the cellular diversity that characterizes this region of the brain. We have found that Neurog2/Ascl1 function like a switch - with the activation of one of these genes leading to the deactivation of the other. If the Neurog2/Ascl1 switch is disrupted, tipping the balance in favor of one gene versus the other, we observe a change in the ratios of the different cell types that make up the neocortex. This can have devastating consequences. For instance, we have found that a disruption of the Neurog2/Ascl1 switch occurs in some brain tumors. Our goal is to determine how Neurog2 and Ascl1 remain in their proper balance so that normal brain development can occur, and brain tumors do not arise.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Stepped Care Model for the Wider Dissemination of Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia among Cancer Patients: Efficacy and Cost-Effectiveness
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; COGNITIVE-BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; COST-EFFECTIVENESS; INSOMNIA; INTERNET; NON-INFERIORITY DESIGN; SELF-HELP TREATMENT; STEPPED CARE MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Insomnia is very common in cancer patients. When left untreated, insomnia can lead to numerous serious consequences (e.g., psychological disorders) for the individual and significant costs for society (e.g., increased medical consultations). Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), a form of psychotherapy, is now considered the treatment of choice for insomnia and its efficacy has been demonstrated in clinical studies conducted in cancer patients (Savard et al., 2005; Espie et al., 2008). Unfortunately, CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is not widely accessible as only a few cancer clinics have mental health professionals formally trained in the administration of this treatment. Innovative models of treatment delivery are therefore needed to make sure that every cancer patient with insomnia receives the care he/she needs. A stepped care approach in which patients only receive the level of treatment that they need, often beginning with a minimal, less costly, intervention followed by more intensive treatment if required, has shown some promises for other psychological disorders (e.g., depression). Although its relevance has been emphasized to make CBT-I more accessible (Espie, 2010), its utility has never been investigated. The main goal of this randomized non-inferiority study is to assess the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of a stepped care CBT-I as compared with standard care. Our hypothesis is that a stepped care approach will not be statistically inferior in terms of efficacy as compared to usual care, while being much less costly (better cost-effectiveness ratio). Three hundred cancer patients (mixed cancer sites) with insomnia symptoms will be assigned to: (1) stepped care CBT-I (n = 200) or (2) standard care (n = 100), consisting of 6 weekly sessions administered individually by a professional.

TitreApplicationTitle: Loss of VAPB Function in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis-8 (ALS8)
Keywords-MotsClés: ALS8; AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; NUCLEAR ENVELOPE; NUCLEAR PORES; VAPB; VESICLE TRAFFICKING
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is commonly referred to as Lou Gehrig disease. It is caused by premature death of motor neurones that control skeletal muscles. Their death results in in loss of voluntary muscle control and paralysis. Approximately 90% of ALS is sporadic with the remaining 10% classified as familial caused by inheritance of the mutated gene in affected families. A familial form of ALS, designated ALS8, is caused by a mutation in a gene known as VAPB. This mutation resulted in production of a defective mutant VAPB protein. The function of this protein is currently unknown. We found that cells expressing mutant VAPB have a defective nuclear envelope. The nuclear envelope serves as a physical barrier separating genes in the nucleus from the rest of the cell or cytoplasm. Each cell contains ~3,000 nuclear pores in the nuclear envelope that act as gatekeepers regulating movement of molecules in and out of the nucleus (e.g. messenger RNA made in the nucleus are transported out to the cytoplasm to be translated into proteins). Nuclear pores are made up to ~50 different proteins. Most pores are made shortly after a cell divides. Once assembled, pores are extremely long-lived lasting the entire lifespan of a cell. This means that when damaged, pores are not easily replaceable in cells that no longer divide, such as neurones. We found that pore components are pre-assembled in the cytoplasm and these pre-assembled units are guided by VAPB to the nuclear envelope for final assembly into functional pores. Mutant VAPB cuts off this supply route to the nuclear envelope. This leads to progressive deterioration of the pores, a process that is normally associated with ageing but accelerated in ALS8 patients. One of the goals of this study is to understand how damages caused by mutant VAPB can lead to motor neurone death.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Biological and Clinical Significance of Platelet Derived Growth Factor Receptor in Papillary Thyroid Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; METASTASES; PLATELET DERIVED GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; THYROID CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Thyroid nodules are very common in Canada and papillary thyroid cancer is the most common thyroid malignancy. Surgical treatment of papillary thyroid cancer in many cases will not provide a cure and the tumor will give rise to metastases within the lymph nodes of the neck. In order to provide better surgical treatment and to guide oncologists when selecting adjuvant therapy, we will use molecular techniques to identify pathways that lead to metastatic disease. Platelet derived growth factor (PDGF) is a well known signaling pathway that is up regulated in a number of malignancies including thyroid cancer. Markers specific to PDGF may be used to determine if certain patients are at risk of lymph node metastases. We have also shown that PDGF may be a target for new therapies. Though our work we believe patients will benefit from earlier diagnosis in thyroid cancer as well as have more options for therapy if they have metastatic disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enzymatic Modification of Endotoxins
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOTOXIN; INFLAMMATION; LIPID A; MEMBRANES; PROTEIN STRUCTURE; SEPTIC SHOCK; VACCINE ADJUVANT
Abstract-Résumé: Our research on the structure and function of membrane proteins attacks one of the most important and challenging problems in contemporary biochemistry. Our most recent work has been focused on an outer membrane enzyme PagP from pathogenic Gram-negative bacteria. PagP transfers a palmitoyl group from a phospholipid molecule to the lipid A or endotoxin component of lipopolysaccharide. This simple modification provides bacterial resistance to host antimicrobial peptides and attenuates the inflammatory response signaled through the toll-like receptor 4 pathway. By understanding how the structural and dynamic properties of PagP relate to its biological function, we hope to design inhibitors that might be useful for the treatment of infections and to synthesize novel endotoxin analogs that function as antagonists for the treatment of septic shock or as vaccine adjuvants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ketamine-induced NMDA receptor hypofunction in nonhuman primates as a model for cognitive deficits in schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: FRONTAL LOBE; KETAMINE; NMDA; NONHUMAN PRIMATES; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Almost every patient who suffers from schizophrenia has cognitive problems. These problems can be seen in a reduced attention span, difficulties to memorize things, poor judgment skills, and in difficulties to plan and prioritize everyday life. The cognitive deficits are most likely the most important factor for poor outcome in people with schizophrenia. Although drugs are quite successful in treating hallucinations and delusions, they often fail in treating these cognitive deficits.  Cognitive deficits can easily be tested with simple eye movement tasks. Brain researchers have long known that people who suffer from schizophrenia show telltale eye movements under certain conditions. Told to fix their gaze on a visual target, for example, they are unable to resist the reflexive urge to glance away at a peripheral stimulus, like a flash of light. Subjects without the disorder can override the impulse. It has been known for a long time that a certain type of drug which blocks the action of the neurochemical glutamate can mimic the symptoms of schizophrenia to a degree where even psychiatrists cannot tell the difference. In our research program, we will utilize this fact and try to mimic this eye movement deficit in monkeys. We will then study how the blockade of this glutamate receptor changes the activity of brain cells and their communication with each other.  We aim to understand how neurochemicals influence cognitive functions in the primate brain. By better understanding how certain neurochemicals impair cognition, we hope to identify drugs that will improve the cognitive core deficit in schizophrenia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Behavioral and eye movement indices of cognitive and neural integrity in aging.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; EYE MOVEMENT MONITORING; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHY; MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Memory typically declines with age.  Our research has shown that monitoring eye movements provides a valuable tool by which we can observe the integrity of memory without requiring verbal reports.  However, these eye movement markers of memory have not been linked definitively to neural activity at the moment at which they are occurring.   By directly linking eye movement indices of memory to neural activity, eye movements may ultimately be used as a marker by which we may discern neural integrity.    We will monitor eye movements to understand the influence of aging on the encoding (formation) and retrieval (access) of information regarding items and their spatial and temporal relations - the 'what', 'where' and 'when', respectively, of memory that describe the personal events in our lives. We will simultaneously record neural activity using magnetoencephalography(MEG), which will reveal how aging influences the activity of neural regions underlying encoding and retrieval. Our research team will be the first to use eye movement monitoring in conjunction with MEG recordings to precisely document the influence of aging on memory.   To establish the direct link between eye movements, neural activity and memory, we will instruct participants to alter their eye movements, and examine the resultant changes on neural activity and memory. Additionally, research has shown that prior knowledge can be used to facilitate the formation of new memories; we will examine how this occurs, with respect to eye movement behavior and neural activity.  This will provide converging evidence that changes in memory performance can be linked decisively to changes in eye movement behavior and neural activity.  All together, this work will provide the foundational research that eye movement monitoring may be an accessible and cost-effective means to infer cognitive and neural integrity in clinical and/or community settings.

TitreApplicationTitle: Quality of cancer care in remote-dwelling Canadians
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; QUALITY OF CARE; RURAL OR REMOTE RESIDENCE LOCATION; SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: We will use a large database of >3 million community-dwelling adults residing in Alberta between 2000 and 2011. We will identify their residence location, link to demographic, clinical, claims and laboratory data, and use specialized techniques to characterize where they live in relation to medical services and physician practices. We will use this unique dataset to determine the risk of breast cancer in each region, examine how likely residents of each region are to receive cancer screening, and determine the quality of cancer care for residents of each location. Results will identify areas where cancer care and access to screening are good quality and where there is room for improvement.

TitreApplicationTitle: PET tracers for imaging bradykinin B1 receptor expression in cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTAGONISTS; BRADYKININ B1 RECEPTOR; CANCER IMAGING; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTOR; PET; RADIOTRACERS; TARGETED THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is the leading cause of death in the developed countries including Canada. To reduce mortality rate, new tools for early diagnosis and characterization of cancer, and new specific and effective treatment options are urgently needed. Bradykinin B1 receptor (B1R) is a protein often overexpressed on membranes of cancer cells but not on normal cells. This makes B1R an excellent diagnostic marker and therapeutic target for cancer. Since the binding of endogenous ligands to B1R induces tumor growth and facilitates metastasis, potent drugs to block the activation of B1R by endogenous ligands have been developed, and their abilities to inhibit the growth of B1R-positive human cancer cells and their xenografts in mice have been demonstrated. In spite of potential application of B1R-targeting drugs for cancer therapy, there is no technology currently available for identifying B1R-positive cancer patients who can benefit from emerging B1R-targeted therapies. To solve this problem, we propose here to develop radiolabeled B1R-targeting probes for non-invasive imaging of B1R expression in cancer. We will design and synthesize potential B1R-targeting probes amenable for radiolabeling. We will measure their binding affinity to B1R expressed in human cancer cells, select high affinity B1R-targeting probes for radiolabeling, and determine their biodistribution profiles in normal mice. For promising radiotracers that have high binding affinity to B1R and preferred pharmacokinetic patterns, we will evaluate their suitability as cancer imaging agents in mice bearing B1R-positive human cancer xenografts. The success of this proposed research will generate radiotracers suitable for early diagnosis and characterization of prostate, lung and breast cancers that often overexpress B1R. These radiotracers will facilitate the development of B1R-targeting drugs and optimize their therapeutic dosage based on the blockade of B1R in the tumours.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Determinants of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; CANCER IMMUNOTHERAPY; CANCER PREVENTION; CARCINOGENESIS; CHLDHOOD LEUKEMIA; HOST-TUMOUR INTERACTION; PRE-LEUKEMIA
Abstract-Résumé: Acute leukemia is the most common cancer in children and new treatments are urgently needed. Previous work has suggested that a child's environment may influence whether leukemia develops or not. In this study we will look at the how an immune system fighting infections can tip the balance away from leukemia and towards a healthy life. This work may provide new ideas about how to treat and prevent this devastating childhood disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of NPM mutation and NPM-MLF1 translocation on gene regulation
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETIC REGULATION; GENE EXPRESSION; GENOMIC MUTATION; HEMATOPOIESIS; HUMAN BONE MARROW; LEUKEMIA; MOUSE MODELS; NUCLEOPHOSMIN; PROTEIN COMPLEX
Abstract-Résumé: The NPM gene is one of the most frequently mutated gene in hematological malignancies including acute myeloid leukemia. It is implicated in multiple cellular processes and thus, it remains unclear how the NPM mutation can favour leukemia. Since NPM can regulate gene expression, we began a study to define which genes are influenced by NPM and if/how the mutation of NPM affects regulation of NPM target genes. Our preliminary results suggest that NPM regulates the expression of specific tumour suppressor genes and oncogenes. We will extend this investigation and question the influence of NPM on other genes. To gain information on mechanisms deregulated by the mutation of NPM or by the translocation NPM-MLF1, we are looking at proteins interacting with NPM and with the mutated forms of NPM. Our results suggest that NPM is indeed involved in transcriptional regulation and it can act as a transcriptional activator or repressor. This study will bring new information on the role of NPM and how the mutation or translocation of NPM can affect gene expression and hence, promote hematological malignancies including acute myeloid leukemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies on the plasticity of CNS cholinergic neurons
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; BASAL FOREBRAIN; CHOLINERGIC NEURONS; COGNITION; DOWN'S SYNDROME; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MUSCARINIC RECEPTOR; NERVE GROWTH FACTOR; NEUROCHEMISTRY; PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Our recent pharmacological studies revealed the existence of a group of enzymes in the brain responsible for the production and degradation of the protein Nerve Growth Factor (NGF). NGF is crucial for the "healthy" status of a group of neurons known as basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (BFCNs). These brain cells have key roles in learning and memory and are damaged in individuals with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Previous investigations from our group showed that the NGF pathway is affected in AD brains, so that NGF fails to mature and breaks down more quickly. These changes mean that there are reduced levels of NGF to BFCNs and explains how their degeneration occurs in AD. The present grant renewal aims to investigate whether this pathway is responsible for the "well-being" of BFCNs that contact NGF releasing areas. We propose that alterations in the NGF metabolic pathway exist in any situation where amyloid-beta (Abeta) peptides build up, as they do in AD. To test this, we will explore the NGF metabolic pathway in our rat model of AD and in the brains of Down's syndrome (DS) sufferers. These people have an extra chromosome containing the gene expressing the precursor protein for the formation of Abeta (the peptide fragment central to AD development). Most DS individuals accumulate Abeta and develop AD by mid-life. We also want to investigate if the inhibition of molecules which break down NGF can reverse the deficits seen in AD. In these studies we will use our rats which mimic AD memory deficits. We will conduct a pharmacological investigation to test if cholinergic degeneration worsens AD pathology and if the use of drugs which protect the brain can delay onset of AD. Our investigations are important as it is estimated that a delay of 5 years in disease onset could reduce the incidence of AD by half.

TitreApplicationTitle: Randomized controlled trial of a minimal versus extended Internet-based intervention for problem drinkers
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL ABUSE; BRIEF INTERVENTION; INTERNET-BASED INTERVENTION; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Alcohol is one of the leading contributors to premature mortality and disability. Most people with alcohol problems will never seek treatment. There is a need to develop alternate ways to help problem drinkers outside of formal treatment settings.  One promising strategy is Internet-based interventions for problem drinkers. Our first randomized controlled trial found that we could reduce alcohol consumption by about six drinks per week at a six-month follow-up using a minimal, personalized feedback Internet-based intervention. Our second randomized trial demonstrated that an extended Internet-based intervention that contained a range of cognitive-behavioural and relapse prevention tools could produce greater reductions in problem drinking compared to that provided by the same minimal intervention at a six-month follow-up. Building upon this research, the current project will assess whether this extended Internet-based intervention can have a sustained impact on problem drinking. Specifically, the major objective of this project is to conduct a randomized controlled trial comparing the impact of an extended Internet-based self-help intervention for problem drinkers to a minimal Internet-based intervention in the general population of problem drinkers over a two year period.   Problem drinking participants will be recruited through media advertisements across Canada and will be randomly assigned to the minimal or extended Internet-based interventions.  Six-month, twelve-month and two-year drinking outcomes will be compared between experimental conditions. It is predicted that participants receiving the extended Internet intervention will display sustained improved drinking outcomes compared to participants in the minimal Internet intervention condition. This programmatic line of research will advance the science of Internet-mediated intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: eIF4E-mediated translational control of synaptic function in memory formation and autism
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER; CRE-LOX CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT; HIPPOCAMPAL SLICE CULTURES; LEARNING AND MEMORY; LONG-TERM SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; SYNAPTIC PHYSIOLOGY; TRANSGENIC MICE; TRANSLATION INITIATION; WHOLE CELL RECORDING
Abstract-Résumé: Synthesis of new proteins, a process called translation, is necessary for persistent changes in synaptic strength that underlie learning and memory. Learning and memory impairments are important aspects of some of the most common and debilitating neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease and related dementia, as well as in genetic brain disorders such as mental retardation and intellectual deficiency. Moreover, dysregulation of translation in neurons has been linked to synaptic dysfunction and autism spectrum disorders. Translation of mRNA into protein is also regulated at the level of synapses. A major site of regulation of translation initiation is by eIF4E control of the eIF4F complex which brings together the mRNA and ribosome. We found that this regulatory site controls long-term synaptic changes underlying learning and memory, and more recently that its dysregulation in mice leads to synaptic aberrations and autistic-like behavioral phenotypes. However, the activity-dependent mechanisms by which eIF4E controls translation and synaptic function in the different types of neurons in the hippocampal network remain poorly understood. We propose to build on our previous work and identify the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which eIF4E controls translation and synaptic function in specific hippocampal cell types leading to memory formation in normal conditions, and how dysregulation leads to autism.  Identifying and elucidating these cellular and molecular mechanisms are the first step in developing new approaches to tackle the important health problems associated with autism spectrum disorders and neurological disorders with memory impairments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relationship between serotonergic innervation, dopaminergic deficit and levodopa induced dopamine release patterns in PD treatment-related complications: a longitudinal imaging study
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINERGIC SYSTERM; NEUROIMAGING; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; SEROTONERGIC SYSTEM; TREATMENT-RELATED COMPLICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and is estimated to affect on average 300/100,000 of the general population. The main clinical symptoms are slowness of movement, tremor and rigidity, attributed to the loss of the neurons responsible for the synthesis of dopamine, a neurotransmitter involved in motor control. There is at present no cure for PD and treatment is based on pharmacological therapies aimed at replicating the action of dopamine in the brain. Unfortunately for most PD patients the benefits of dopaminergic treatment are short lived; they start experiencing treatment-related side effect either of motor nature (aggravating involuntary movements) or psychiatric (often compulsive behavior) within 4 to 6 years after initiation of treatment. Although there is convincing evidence that such complications might be related to abnormal signaling of the dopaminergic system, the mechanisms underlying such complications are not completely understood. Recent studies suggest that in addition to the dopaminergic system, the serotonergic system (related to mood, sleep, appetite regulation) is also affected in PD and that it might play an important role in the origin of treatment- related complications as well as in some non-motor deficits associated with PD. We hypothesize that there are specific patterns associated with the deterioration of the dopaminergic neurons and PD- induced alteration of the serotonergic nerve terminals that, while improving response to levodopa therapy early in the disease, predispose to the occurrence of treatment-related complications. We will use longitudinal in-vivo imaging to investigate the existence of such patterns and their evolution as a function of disease progression. Identification of such patterns will lead to new avenues of treatment that will minimize deleterious side effects and will help design optimal patient specific treatment strategies.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of macrophage functions during infections
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; INTRACELLULAR TRAFFICKING; LEISHMANIA; MACROPHAGE; PHAGOCYTOSIS; VIRULENCE
Abstract-Résumé: The macrophage plays an essential role in host defense against infections. One aspect of the proposed research is aimed at better understanding the mechanisms by which macrophages engulf and destroy unwanted microorganisms. This process, known as phagocytosis, involves numerous membrane fusion events, to allow for the formation of a microbicidal compartment, the phagolysosome. Another aspect of the proposed research is to understand how pathogens can interfere with the formation of a microbicidal phagolysosome, to avoid destruction by macrophages. Ultimately, the knowledge obtained may lead to the development of novel ways to treat infections.

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms and function of AID-dependent antibody diversification
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVATION INDUCED DEAMINASE; ANTIBODY GENE DIVERSIFICATION; ANTIBODY ISOTYPE SWITCHING; ANTIBODY MEDIATED IMMUNE RESPONSE; GENETICALLY MODIFIED MICE; LYMPHOCYTE B; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN STABILITY; SUBCELLULAR LOCALIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Antibodies are fundamental components of the immune system because they can recognize and neutralize almost any pathogen or toxin. We need to be able to produce a sufficiently large repertoire of antibodies to match a virtually infinite number of antigens. To do this, the antibody genes are changed (mutated) in each B lymphocyte after it first comes in contact with the antigen. These changes produce antibodies that better bind the antigen and that have acquired new functions to appropriately dispose of the antigen. These modifications of the antibody genes are essential for the immune response but have associated risks. They can predispose to cancer or produce antibodies that recognize our own tissues and cause autoimmune diseases. We study the mechanism modifying the antibody genes, focusing on the initiating enzyme that is named AID. Both, deficiency in, and exacerbation of, AID activity are pathogenic. This can be due to malfunction of AID itself or of factors that modify AID. We are studying the mechanisms that determine the amount and localization of AID in B lymphocytes. The amount of AID is determined in large part by modulating its stability (i.e. how long does it last). The right levels of AID are critical for adequate immune responses. The localization of AID is important because AID changes the genetic information. AID localization is regulated by restricting its access to the cellular compartment, which contains the genome, so as to minimize the possibility that it mutates off target. Understanding these processes is understanding fundamental biological processes important for the immune system. Our research also provides insight into the etiology of certain cancers and autoimmune diseases caused by AID as side effects. Our findings could suggest targets for diagnostic, prognostic and therapy for common human diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: Preclinical Development Of Inhibitors Of Podocalyxin-Driven Tumor Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; INVASION; METASTASIS; OVARIAN CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Podocalyxin is a cell surface molecule that contributes to the poor outcome and the metastasis of  breast, ovarian, prostate, liver, pancreatic, kidney and colon cancers. We have developed experimental models to investigate how podocalyxin contributes to breast cancer metastasis specifically. We will now use these models to determine which members of a set of  podocalyxin function-blocking compounds that we are developing are able to inhibit this metastasis. Therefore, the overarching goal of this project is to identify novel anti-metastatic compounds with the potential to be broadly applicable as therapeutic agents in a wide variety of tumour types.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Skeletal Muscle Energy Sensing and Insulin Sensitivity in Obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: AMP-ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASE; FATTY ACID OXIDATION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; METFORMIN; MOUSE MODELS; OBESITY; PROTEIN ACETYLATION; PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION; SALICYLATE; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Nearly 50% of Canadian are overweight or obese. The most common side effect of obesity is insulin resistance or pre-diabetes. Muscle is the main user of energy in the body and is important for controlling blood sugar levels. In obesity muscle accumulates fat and does not respond to the hormone insulin, which contributes to the development of pre-diabetes. In the current proposal, we will examine the role for a metabolic sensing molecule, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), in regulating fat metabolism and insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle. These results will identify new ways to improve insulin sensitivity which will lead to new therapies for type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 4 in Endocrine Homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL GROWTH; ENDOCRINE TUMORS; ENDOCRINOLOGY; HORMONE REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: This project examines the impact of a cancer related gene on hormone regulation and the associated risk of diabetes. The primary observations are made in humans. Modeling of this information is in cell and mouse sytems allowing studies which cannot be performed in humans. Importantly, however, the data derived from experimental systems will again be validated in human populations.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
ResearchClassEN: DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS; ENDOCRINOLOGY
ClasseRechercheFR: DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES; ENDOCRINOLOGIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Structure, function and pharmacological regulation of the mitochondrial Translocator protein (TSPO; peripheral benzodiazepine receptor) in cholesterol transport and steroid formation
Keywords-MotsClés: BENZODIAZEPINES; CHOLESTEROL; MITOCHONDRIA; NEUROSTEROIDS; PHARMACOLOGY; STEROIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Eukaryotic steroid hormones are responsible for the maintenance of the organism's homeostasis, adaptability to the environment, and developmental and reproductive functions. Many tissues of the body have the ability to metabolize steroids. However, few tissues are able to synthesize steroid hormones from the substrate cholesterol. These tissues are the gonads, adrenals, placenta and brain. Steroid synthesis begins with the transport of the substrate cholesterol from intracellular stores into mitochondria to be converted to pregnenolone. Translocator protein (TSPO), formerly known as peripheral-type benzodiazepine receptor, is a ubiquitous drug- and cholesterol-binding protein found primarily in the outer mitochondrial membrane. Although TSPO is found in many tissues, it is expressed at the highest levels in steroid synthesizing cells.  Using a combination of biochemical, pharmacological and molecular approaches, as well as animal models, we will test the hypotheses that (i) changes in TSPO organization and levels in the mitochondria determine the amount of cholesterol available for testosterone synthesis in Leydig cells, the testosterone-producing cells of the testis, ultimately affecting testicular function, and (ii) pharmacological activation of TSPO can lead to a direct induction of androgen formation. The proposed studies aim to unveil the structure and regulation of expression of the Tspo gene as well as to develop novel pharmacological means to induce androgen formation in vivo. Elucidation of  the mechanisms underlying steroid synthesis is critical to understanding the origin of diseases associated with reduced androgen formation, including infertility and metabolic syndrome, and developing novel therapies for their treatment. These studies will also pave the way for the development of novel pharmacological strategies for manipulation of the adrenal and brain function, tissues where TSPO plays a regulatory role in corticosteroid and neurosteroid formation.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - A: Neurobiological Basis of Behavioural Processes
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Long-term consequences of maternal immune activation on behaviour and brain: Role of chemokine signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; BEHAVIOURAL TESTING; BRAIN; DEVELOPMENT; IMMUNE SYSTEM; IN VIVO ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; PROTEIN ANALYSIS; PSYCHIATRIC ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: According to the Canadian Mental Health Association 20% of Canadians will experience mental illness at some points during their lives. Although there is strong evidence showing the genetic causes of some psychiatric disorders, recent studies have indicated that the environment also plays a major role in the causes of psychiatric disorders, in particular schizophrenia. One such factor contributing to psychiatric disorders in adulthood is prenatal infection, or exposure to an infection while in utero. My research explores this connection by using rat models. I will first simulate an infection in pregnant rats and then monitor the offspring by measuring brain activity during various behavioural tasks. The offspring are later treated with novel antipsychotic medications to help reduce the abnormal symptoms associated with psychiatric disorder. The second phase of the project involves attempting to block the effects of the infection in the pregnant rats before it triggers the cascade of events leading to psychiatric symptoms. Using a pharmacological compound that has been proven to reduce the symptoms of severe respiratory infections in animals, I will administer it to pregnant rats to block the effects of infection that disrupt the brain development of their offspring. By combining immunological research related to infection with that focused on psychiatric disorders, I propose an approach to treating psychiatric disorders that focuses on prevention rather than the treatment of symptoms.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ; SYSTÈME NERVEUX
TitreApplicationTitle: An international, multi-center, prospective, inception cohort study of neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE)
Keywords-MotsClés: LUPUS; NERVOUS SYSTEM DISEASE; OBSERVATIONAL COHORT; OUTCOMES; SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS
Abstract-Résumé: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease which can cause inflammation and damage to any part of the body. It occurs in 1 in 1000 people and affects 9 times more women than men. As the disease occurs most frequently in young and middle aged women, there is a significant social and economic impact associated with it.  One of the most serious manifestations of SLE is involvement of the nervous system which can result in a variety of neurologic and psychiatric manifestations. Despite its importance, it remains one of the least understood features of the illness. Dr. Hanly and his colleagues, who have already conducted a number of research projects in this area, proposes to lead an international study to learn more about the types, consequences and causes of nervous system disease in lupus patients and eventually to develop better treatments.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of motor unit protection by exercise training in aging muscle
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DENERVATION; ENDURANCE EXERCISE TRAINING; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; MITOCHONDRIAL FUNCTION; MOTOR UNIT; NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION; SARCOPENIA; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: Regular endurance exercise training slows the age-related loss of muscle mass and function known as sarcopenia. Despite ample evidence this is the case, the cellular mechanisms by which this occurs are largely unknown. The proposed experiments focus upon a previously identified molecule in muscle that increases with regular endurance exercise training and decreases with normal aging. This molecule, known as PGC-1, is typically thought of in terms of its ability to regulate the creation of the intracellular powerhouses known as mitochondria. However, recent evidence shows that PGC-1 can also regulate key proteins necessary for activation of muscle cells by nerve cells, proteins which decline in aging muscle and lead to loss of the ability to activate muscle cells. As such, this grant will examine the impact of regular endurance exercise training on PGC-1 and how this relates to the maintenance of the proteins necessary for activation of muscle cells by nerve cells. The ultimate end-point of this research is to better understand the mechanisms by which exercise training benefits aging muscle so that novel therapeutics can be developed for those who are less able to exercise.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: CNS nutrient sensing and the regulation of lipid, glucose and energy homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN/LIVER; DIABETES; DORSAL VAGAL COMPLEX; FOOD INTAKE; GLUCOSE AND LIPID METABOLISM; HIGH-FAT FEEDING; HYPOTHALAMUS; NUTRIENT SENSING; OBESITY; PANCREATIC INSULIN/GLUCOSE CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity affects more than 25% of Canadians and is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, which affects more than 5% of Canadians. The prevalence of obesity associated type 2 diabetes has been increasing world-wide due largely to increased availability and consumption of high calorie nutrients and sedentary life style. In this renewal proposal, we will continue dissecting CNS nutrient sensing mechanisms that regulate glucose, lipid and energy homeostasis in normal, obese and diabetic rodents. These studies will identify novel nutrient sensing mechanisms in the brain that inhibit hepatic glucose and lipid production as well as food intake, and thereby revealing novel therapeutic candidates to restore glucose, lipid and energy homeostasis in diabetes and obesity.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTÉ
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Innovations to enhance the capacity of practice guidelines to improve health and healthcare systems: AGREE-REX (Recommendation EXcellence)
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE; EVALUATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION/IMPLEMENTATION SCIENCE; QUALITY APPRAISAL
Abstract-Résumé: Practice guidelines (PGs) are systematically developed statements to help in decisions made by patients, clinicians and policy makers. In a previous grant, our team created the AGREE II, the revised international standard for PG development, reporting, and evaluation. While necessary it is not sufficient; the AGREE II does not specifically address the clinical credibility of the recommendations, which is important for their implementation. Our current AGREE A3 project focused specifically on PG recommendations. To date, we have designed the Recommendation EXcellence Framework (REX-F). It reflects five domains, 18 sub-domains and several attributes related to PG recommendation implementability. The five domains are Format, Feasibility, Language, Rigour of Development and Considered Judgment. Using established methods and the REX-F as a foundation, our objective is to create AGREE-REX, a resource to direct the development, reporting, and evaluation of clinically credible recommendations. The AGREE-REX will be comprised of an Assessment Tool, a User's Guide, and a toolkit of practical strategies called Resource-REX. An iterative three-stage process will be used to create the Assessment Tool and User's Guide so that reliability, validity and usability are established. A fourth stage will be used to create the toolkit of existing tools designed to facilitate the development of clinically credible recommendations. The deliverable of this project will be a scientifically sound and practical tool, AGREE-REX, that will direct the development, reporting and evaluation of clinical recommendations so that their credibility is optimized.

AreasOfScienceEN: CELL BIOLOGY; RENAL FUNCTION, NEPHROLOGY, UROLOGY
DomainesScientifiquesFR: BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE; FONCTION RÉNALE, NÉPHROLOGIE, UROLOGIE
ClasseRechercheFR: SYSTEME GENITO-URINAIRE; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Protein kinases in the kidney
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; APOPTOSIS; BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL PHYSIOLOGY; CYTOSKELETON; GLOMERULAR INJURY; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEIN KINASES; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; STRESS PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: The health of an organism largely depends on the accuracy of signals sent among constituent cells. Much of this information is transmitted inside cells through specific proteins, called protein kinases. Activity of protein kinases contributes to the maintenance of normal cell structure and function, while disorders in protein kinase activation or function can contribute to disease. Nearly 20% of childhood diseases that lead to end stage kidney failure are due to primary disorders of kidney development. In adults, acute kidney failure (e.g. post-operatively or due to infections) and kidney inflammation are common medical problems with substantial morbidity and mortality. In this proposal, we will study abnormalities in cellular pathways in the kidney involving protein kinases, and how disordered regulation of protein kinases leads to kidney disease. The results of these studies will eventually lead to improved strategies for therapies of developmental kidney disorders and kidney injury.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DE LA PROSTATE ET DE LA VESSIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Integrated Approach to Discover Prostate Cancer Biomarkers in Seminal Plasma
Keywords-MotsClés: INDOLENT AND AGGRESSIVE PROSTATE CANCER; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROSTATE CANCER BIOMARKERS; PROTEOMICS; SEMINAL PLASMA
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, prostate cancer is the most frequently diagnosed neoplasm and the third leading cause of cancer mortality in men. The current main strategy to diagnose asymptomatic prostate cancer is based on analysis of serum Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA). The well-known low specificity of serum PSA leads to a large number of unnecessary biopsies due to its high false-positive rate. Additionally, PSA could not discriminate between low-grade and high-grade prostate cancer, leading to over-diagnosis and over-treatment. Here, we will address the current PSA limitations through (i) identification of seminal plasma protein biomarkers that complement the serum PSA test and increase its specificity for detecting cancer; (ii) identification of seminal plasma biomarkers that discriminate between less aggressive (low-grade) and more aggressive (high-grade) prostate cancers. The benefits of identifying such markers are clear: improved detection and prognosis of this cancer should lead to reduction of unnecessary prostate cancer biopsies, to better treatment decisions and likely to decreased morbidity.

CommitteeNameEN: Psychosocial, Sociocultural & Behavioural Determinants of Health 2
NomDuComitéFR: Déterminants psychosociaux, socioculturels et comportementaux de la santé 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Self-regulation of common age-related challenges: Examining psychobiological pathways to healthy aging.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL FUNCTIONING; HEALTHY AGING; PHYSICAL HEALTH; PSYCHOLOGICAL WELL-BEING; SELF-REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: This research program will examine how older adults can manage common problems (e.g., health threats, stressful events, life regrets) and protect their emotional well-being, biological functioning (e.g., cortisol and immune function) and physical health. It is expected that older adults can maintain their psychological and physical health if they are able to engage in overcoming problems that can be resolved, and if they are able to disengage from goals that are unattainable due to a problem. Such an adaptive adjustment to the opportunities for overcoming a problem is expected to results in long-term pathways of emotional well-being, biological functioning, and physical health.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
ClasseRechercheFR: METABOLISME ET NUTRITION; INFACTUS DU MYOCARDE
TitreApplicationTitle: The Involvement of CD36 in the Regulation of Myocardial Metabolism and Function
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; CARDIAC ENERGY METABOLISM; CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CD36; DIABETES; EX VIVO HEART PERFUSIONS; HEART FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: The heart uses fat as a source of energy to help maintain its ability to pump blood efficiently. The contractile cells of the heart have a protein called CD36 that plays a major role in taking up fat into the cell. Notwithstanding the importance of the use of fat for energy, pre-clinical evidence has suggested that partial inhibition of the use of fat for energy in the heart can prevent injury to the heart.  In addition, people with heart disease can also be prescribed drugs that partially inhibit the use of fat for energy and these treatments show benefit to the function of the heart. That said, there is controversy as to whether these drugs actually partially inhibit the use of fat for energy or whether they have benefits via altering other unrelated pathways.  As a result, it is unclear as to whether partially inhibiting the use of fat for energy is truly beneficial to the injured or diseased heart.  In addition to the uncertainty about the benefits of the use of fat for energy, there is also a growing body of evidence suggesting that this approach may actually contribute to poor function of the heart (in all instances but especially in diabetic patients).  Based on this, we will test whether inhibition of CD36 function (which will decrease fat uptake into the heart as well as limit the use of fat for energy) is beneficial or detrimental to the heart in a variety of diseased states. These studies will ultimately lead to a better understanding of the importance of CD36 in the heart as well as allow us to ascertain whether drugs designed to inhibit CD36 in the heart (or related pathways that partially inhibit the use of fat for energy) may contribute to improving the performance of the heart in patients with heart disease and/or diabetes.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Biomarkers in ankylosing spondylitis: Implications for pathogenesis and therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS; DIAGNOSTIC/PROGNOSTIC MARKERS; PATHOGENESIS; THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a disease with joint inflammation and mainly spinal joint outgrowth leading to spinal fusion (ankylosis)and deformity. The prevalence of AS is between 0.1 - 1.8%. The disease affects predominantly men between the age of 20 and 40 years. Currently, there are at least two outstanding issues with the diagnosis and management of AS: (1) The diagnosis of AS is delayed in most cases, due to the required radiographic evidence of sacroiliitis which might take 5-10 years to develop after the initial onset of symptoms such as chronic low back-pain. (2) Anti-TNF (Tumor Necrosis Factor) therapy for AS patients is the most effective treatment for reducing joint inflammation and improving the quality of life. However, this treatment does not lead to significant slow down of joint deformity in the patients. For improvement of joint functions, anti-ankylosis agents are required. Thus, the availability of biomarkers would not only facilitate rapid diagnosis, but would also provide earlier/better assessment, prognosis and management of the disease.  Over the years, we use a mouse mutant which develops progressive ankylosis to understand the process of joint fusion. These mutant mice show many important common features with AS patients. Recently, we showed that AS patients and the mutant mice share important similarities in their immune responses. This research proposal is based on our recent conceptual breakthroughs in the understanding of AS. We expect that our research in this area will provide better diagnostic/prognostic markers to differentiate clinical subsets of the heterogeneous AS disease. More importantly, this research avenue could lead to novel approaches to potential anti-ankylosis therapy not only for AS, but also for other spinal-related diseases.

CommitteeNameEN: Social & Developmental Aspects of Children's & Youth's Health
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of Developmental Coordination Disorder on the physical health of young children: A five-year study of motor coordination, physical activity, physical fitness and obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; DEVELOPMENTAL COORDINATION DISORDER; OBESITY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is the term used to describe children who we used to call "clumsy". In Canada, about 1 to 2 children in every classroom has DCD. Parents and teachers tell us these kids have problems learning to do everyday motor activities like tying shoelaces, playing ball and climbing stairs. Some research has shown that these kids are more likely to be overweight and unfit by the time they are teenagers. We believe this is because they struggle with sports and play and, since they know they are not good at it, they choose not to do it. The problem is that the right research study has not been done yet so we do not know if this is the case or if there are reasons why they have these problems. Other research studies have looked at older children who already had trouble doing motor activities or who were already overweight and unfit. To understand how to help kids with DCD, we need to begin when they are young and still learning how to be active and play with their friends. In our study, we will test the motor skills of 2100 children ages 4 and 5 because we are not sure that we can identify kids with DCD until age 4. We expect to identify 300 children who have DCD according to medical criteria and we will randomly pick another 300 who are developing typically and who do not have motor problems. These children will then be seen every 9 months for a total of 5 visits. During these visits, we will examine their motor coordination, how much physical activity they do, how fit they are, their diet and how much they weigh. What makes our study new and exciting is that we will study how all these things relate to each other and how they change over time. Understanding these relationships, and working with knowledge users who can put the implications of these into practice, will help us make sure that kids with DCD are able to get the right type of support, at the right time, so they don't become unfit or obese.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Mechanisms of Leishmania Pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL REGULATION; EXOSOMES; HIGH THROUGHPUT SEQUENCING; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; LEISHMANIASIS; MACROPHAGE; PATHOGENESIS; PI3K; RNA
Abstract-Résumé: The Leishmaniases are a group of infectious diseases caused by parasites belonging to the genus Leishmania.  According to the World Health Organization there are 12 million current infections worldwide and two million new cases occur every year (Leishmaniasis Control, www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis).  Leishmaniasis is mainly found in tropical and sub-tropical regions around the globe.  Like many neglected diseases, it is primarily endemic to developing nations and thus presents additional socio-economic burdens to already impoverished people.    Leishmania parasites invade human macrophages, cells that normally resist infection. A Leishmania infection will prevent a macrophage cell from generating its normal arsenal of microbicidal compounds, allowing the parasites to survive, replicate, and subsequently infect neighboring cells.  As of yet, few mechanistic explanations for this phenomena have been reported.  However, our recent studies have shown that leishmania parasites release proteins by packaging specific proteins within small vesicles inside the cell.  These vesicles and their cargo are then released from the cell as microvesicles.  This research proposal includes aims to identify the  proteins that are contained in these vesicles, what lipids make up these vesicles, and finally, what appearance these vesicles take on.  In addition, we are proposing research to investigate if these vesicles can deliver their cargo to infected macrophages.  Lastly, we plan to determine if any of the proteins secreted by leishmania parasites, both those packaged in microvesicles and those potentially released by some other mechanism, help the leishmania parasite in preventing the macrophage from producing its arsenal of microbicidal compounds.  This research will greatly improve the current understanding of leishmania biology and pathogenesis, and has the potential to aid in the discovery and development of novel drugs and therapeutics.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: RECHERCHE DANS LE DOMAINE DE LA SANTÉ; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: The mechanical causes of osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: JOINT INJURY; JOINT KINEMATICS; JOINT LOADS; MOTION ANALYSIS; OSTEOARTHRITIS; ROBOT; SPATIAL LINKAGE
Abstract-Résumé: Not all individuals who sustain severe knee joint injuries go on to develop osteoarthritis. Our previous work has shown that  changes in gait patterns and inflammation are known to occur immediately after a ligament or meniscal injury for all individuals. We propose that such individuals who do develop OA have on-going biomechanical changes in their gait patterns following injury. Furthermore,  these changes may inhibit  repair or replacement of key damaged knee structures. It is essential to detect these biomechanical changes early to prevent the initiation and progression of OA in these individuals. We have been able to develop a sensitive and innovative technology for identifying minute changes in gait. We are now well positioned to use this technology on our well established animal model of OA development to study the early detection of osteoarthritis.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: The ERR pathway: control of energy metabolism and its implication in metabolic disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE EXPRESSION; LIPID DISORDERS; METABOLISM; METABOLOMICS; MICRO RNA; MOUSE MODELS; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Energy homeostasis is the balanced regulation of fuel intake, storage and expenditure by a person. While a constant supply of energy is required to maintain the basal metabolic rate of the whole individual, energy is also differentially generated and utilized by individual cell types and organs in response to endogenous or exogenous signals specified by various developmental and physiological needs and stimuli. Regulated control of energy production and utilization thus allows the organism to function effectively in a broad range of environmental conditions. On the other hand, disturbance of energy homeostasis over a long period of time can contribute to the etiology of many diseases such as diabetes, obesity, heart failure and even cancer. Imbalance in metabolic homeostasis may originate from nutritional deprivation or overabundance, genetic variations and disorders as well as from gradual loss of efficiency in control systems during the aging process. Consequently, improving our knowledge of how metabolic homeostasis can be maintained through the life of the organism and defining, at the molecular level, control mechanisms that can be manipulated to prevent and treat metabolic-related diseases are of indisputable medical significance. Nuclear hormone receptors play a major role in controlling energy homeostasis, and this grant application is directed at increasing our knowledge of how one sub-family of nuclear receptors, referred to as the estrogen related receptors (ERRs), influences this process in normal physiology and diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES DU FOIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Hepatitis C Virus Lymphotropism and Persistence
Keywords-MotsClés: HCV LYMPHOTROPISM; HCV PATHOGENESIS; HCV PATHOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES; HCV RECEPTORS; HCV VARIANTS; HEPATITIS C; HEPATITIS C VIRUS; OCCULT HCV PERSISTENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is one of the most common blood-born human  pathogens which causes chronic liver inflammation, called hepatitis C. Complications of this infection, such as liver cirrhosis and cancer, are currently the main indications for liver transplantation. In Canada, estimated 250,000 people are chronically infected HCV, but many others are unaware that they are infected. The virus infects not only the liver, but also the host's immune (lymphatic) system. We were among those who first discovered that HCV also infects human immune cells and have established the system in which the patient-derived virus can infect these cells in culture. We also identified molecules essential for HCV infection of human T lymphocytes. In addition, we uncovered that HCV replication persists for a very long time in both liver and immune system after termination of a symptomatic disease. Our findings are entirely original and they are of significant clinical and epidemiological importance. In further studies, we want to determine the molecular and biophysical properties of HCV that infects and replicates in the human immune cells, uncover mechanisms underlying virus ability to infect different subsets of these cells, and recognize the virus potential contribution to the development of proliferative (cancerous) diseases of the lymphatic system, such as lymphomas. Our research should generate new information on the nature of HCV lymphotropism and the mechanisms of HCV life-long persistence. It also should create base for the development of new antivirals targeting HCV at the extrahepatic sites of replication.

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Gfi1 as a modulator of the ATM/DNA-PK DNA damage response pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE RESPONSE; LEUKEMIA; PROGRAMMED CELL DEATH; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS; TRANSGENIC AND KNOCKOUT MICE
Abstract-Résumé: When cells are subjected to gamma irradiation or certain chemotherapeutic drugs, the chromosomes and in particular the DNA within the chromosomes are damaged. As a consequence, the cells respond by stopping cell division to repair the damage. If the repair is not possible because the damage is too extensive, the cells initiate a self-destruction process called programmed cell death. We have discovered that a particular protein, called Gfi1, which normally regulates gene activity and the packaging of chromosomes in a cell, can modulate the cellular response to DNA damage. Cells that lack Gfi1 overreact to the DNA damage signal and accelerate the initiation of programmed cell death. Of interest, DNA damage is also the underlying cause for the anti-cancer efficacy of ionizing radiation and many chemotherapeutic drugs. Thus, a better understanding of the pathways and regulatory mechanisms of the cellular response to DNA damage is important for making further advances in cancer treatment. In particular, one way to improve cancer therapy would be to selectively sensitize tumor cells to DNA damage inducing drugs or gamma radiation, thus allowing the use of lower doses to effectively cure or control the disease while obviating unwanted side effects. In this project, we intend to clarify the role of the Gfi1 regulatory protein in this process and in the DNA damage response. We propose that in particular blood cells need Gfi1 to counteract a destructive DNA damage response pathway. Our work will clarify which effect the ablation of the Gfi1 protein has in blood cells and whether or how Gfi1 deficiency can sensitize them to an accelerated death. This knowledge can be used for a future therapeutic strategy, in which blood cancer cells (leukemia cells) are sensitized to accelerate their self-destruction during a therapy with chemotherapeutic drugs that cause DNA damage.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of indiscriminate cytokine signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR IMMUNOLOGY; CHRONIC INFLAMMATION; CO-INFECTION; CYTOKINE SIGNALLING; CYTOKINES; DENDRITIC CELLS; PARASITE INFECTION; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: An effective immune response requires the cooperation of many different cell types, and clear communication between them is essential. I study a family of signalling molecules known as cytokines, soluble proteins that act as intercellular messengers, relaying instructions from one immune cell to another. This role gives cytokines a strategic importance in influencing the type and quality of the immune response. Misguided or persistent cytokine signals are hallmarks of damaging inflammatory diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease and asthma. Surprisingly little is known about how far or for how long cytokines signal. It has often been thought that the sender and recipient have to be in very close proximity, if not directly touching. In contrast, my data suggests that cytokine signals can spread widely, act indiscriminately, and affect very many cells. It is as if, instead of being whispered into the ear of a neighbour, cytokine instructions are delivered by megaphone and are heard by the whole crowd. The aim of this project is to find out how cytokines affect bystander cells, those not intended to be the primary target of the signal. Our hypothesis is that indiscriminate cytokine signalling changes the subsequent behaviour of bystander cells in multiple ways. We will test our hypothesis using a series of transgenic mice that allow us to analyse cytokine signalling and cytokine production as they happen, in a physiological immune system. Our goals are to determine the extent of indiscriminate cytokine signalling during an immune response, to test its impact on other immune responses, and to identify the mechanisms by which it operates. This is important because we believe that indiscriminate cytokine signalling contributes to the severity and spread of chronic inflammatory conditions, and an appreciation of the underlying mechanisms is an essential step in effective intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Validation of the human farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (hFPPS) as a therapeutic target and design of pre-clinical candidates for the treatment of multiple myeloma and neurodegenerative diseases.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S; DRUG DISCOVERY; FARNESYL PYROPHOSPHATE SYNTHASE; MULTIPLE MYELOMA
Abstract-Résumé: The enzyme farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (hFPPS) is responsible for the biosynthesis of farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP), a key metabolite in the biochemistry and physiology of the human body.  Abnormally high activity of hFPPS has been implicated in numerous cellular processes that are associated with cancer and the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's. Recent clinical trials in prostate cancer have shown that zoledronic acid (ZOL, an hFPPS inhibitor) can decrease levels of tumor marker (PSA) while an increased disease-free survival was seen in breast cancer patients treated with ZOL.  A landmark trial in Multiple Myeloma (MM) showed improved overall survival in patients treated with ZOL.  Autopsy reports have shown high levels of hFPPS activity in the brain tissues of Alzheimer's patients.  High levels of FPP in the brain have been shown to increase production of the protein phospo-Tau, which is strongly implicated in the death of neuronal cells in the brain. However, it is not known whether metabolic dysregulation of hFPPS is the cause of the Alzheimer's disease progression or whether it is a consequence of some, yet unknown factor.       The goal of our research is to develop inhibitors of hFPPS that have good biopharmaceutical properties, so that we can properly investigate the role of the hFPPS blockade in cancer and the progression of the Alzheimer's disease.  We have already designed "prototype" molecules that are potent and selective inhibitors of hFPPS, are able to block proliferation of MM cancer cells and decrease phospho-Tau levels in human immortalized neurons.  These compounds exhibit superior pharmaceutical properties to those of the currently available drugs that target hFPPS (such as ZOL) and are less toxic

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of Treatment Consultation Recordings on Oncology Patient Outcomes: A Prospective, Parallel Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CONSULTATION RECORDINGS; INFORMATION PREFERENCES; PATIENT SATISFACTION; PSYCHOLOGICAL WELL-BEING; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TREATMENT DECISION-MAKING
Abstract-Résumé: The time period from diagnosis through to the end of treatment is challenging for patients. Patients need information, assistance with decision making, and emotional and social support to help cope with their diagnosis and treatment. The first meeting with the cancer doctor is especially anxiety-provoking for patients who will learn, for the first time, their treatment options and likelihood of being cured.  This anxiety causes many patients to have difficulty remembering the important pieces of information that their cancer doctor tells them during this consultation.  The main goal of this study is to demonstrate the benefits of giving cancer patients an audio-recording of their first consultation with their cancer doctor.  We will include newly diagnosed patients from cancer centres in Winnipeg and Calgary.  The types of cancer that will be included in this study are brain and neuroendocrine.  Patients with these types of cancer are more likely to have confused thinking, and therefore may have the most to gain from receiving their consultation recordings.  The study will include 262 patients, and those who sign consent forms to participate will be assigned by chance to either receive their treatment consultation recording or not.  Patients will receive their recording immediately after their consultation, and will be able to listen to the recording at any time either alone, or with family and friends.  To figure out whether the consultation recording provides patients with benefits, we will administer some questionnaires to patients at 1 week after the consultation, and again at 3 and 6 months after the consultation.  These questionnaires will assess the following patient outcomes: i) anxiety and depression, ii) perception of being informed about the disease and treatment, iii) satisfaction with cancer care, iv) satisfaction with the doctor, and v) the extent to which patients are satisfied with their degree of involvement in treatment decision making.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of HO-1 in Aging & Parkinsonian Neural Tissues III
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTES; BRAIN IRON; DOPAMINE; HEME OXYGENASE-1; MITOCHONDRIA; NEUROPATHOLOGY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; PARKINSON DISEASE; TRANSGENIC MOUSE
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder in the developed world. Although several drugs are available to alleviate some of the symptoms of PD (such as tremor or stiffness), we sorely lack medications which slow the destruction of nerve cells in the affected brain regions. Two abnormalities observed in the PD brain which are thought to contribute to nerve cell damage in this disease are 1) the excessive accumulation of iron and 2) injury to mitochondria, the cells' power generators.  Our laboratory has collected evidence that both of these abnormalities may be caused by an enzyme called heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) which is overactive in the brains of PD patients. We recently created a mouse model that mimics the increased brain HO-1 seen in individuals with PD. In the current proposal, we will document the deleterious effects of this excessive HO-1 on the structure and chemistry of the brain and the behaviour of the animals. We will then try to cure these mice and other experimental models of PD with medications that purge the brain of excess iron and a new drug we are developing that blocks the action of HO-1. If successful, this study may herald a novel and rational approach to the prevention of brain cell loss in PD and provide fresh hope to sufferers of this debilitating condition.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; VIEILLISSEMENT
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Analysis of Proteins Involved in Telomere Maintenance and Genome Integrity
Keywords-MotsClés: GENOME INTEGRITY; PHOSPHORYLATION; TELOMERE MAINTENANCE; TRF1
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is the leading cause of premature death in Canada and the Canadian Cancer Society has estimated that one out of every four Canadians is expected to die from cancer. Understanding molecular events leading to cancer will provide crucial knowledge for the design of anti-cancer therapeutics. A hallmark of cancer is genome instability, which can arise from disruption in telomere maintenance and genomic integrity. Telomeres are heterochromatic structures found at the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes, which function to protect the natural chromosome ends from being recognized as damaged DNA, thereby helping maintain genomic integrity. Telomere repeat binding factor 1 (TRF1), a component of the shelterin complex composed of five other protein subunits, plays an important role in the maintenance of telomere length and structure. TRF1 is a negative mediator of telomerase-dependent telomere length maintenance, which is activated in over 80% of human cancers. A telomerase inhibitor is currently in clinical trials. TRF1 is subjected to extensive post-translational modification including phosphorylation. In this proposal, we aim to investigate the mechanism by which phosphorylation regulates the function of TRF1. Knowledge gained from the proposed studies on TRF1 is expected to aid in the design of anti-cancer therapeutics and treatment of cancer patients.
