TitreApplicationTitle: The Role Of Histone Deacetylase 6 Complexes In Rett Syndrome Pathophysiology
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIORAL OUTCOMES; CELL BIOLOGY; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; EPIGENETICS; EPILEPSY; HISTONE DEACETYLASES; MOUSE MODELS; PROTEIN ACETYLATION; RETT SYNDROME; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Rett syndrome is a devastating genetic condition that affects mostly girls at a young age. It is one of the worst types of conditions, as the affected girls are born without any obvious problems, and develop in a seemingly normal manner for the first year of so of life. Then, and often abruptly and without warning, girls with Rett syndrome lose most of their acquired abilities - they stop speaking, lose purposeful hand movements, begin showing autism-like behaviours, frequently develop epilepsy, and often have difficulty eating and digesting food. Repetitive hand-wringing is a common symptom of Rett syndrome - you have probably seen children doing this; they likely have Rett syndrome. At present there are no effective treatments or cures, despite its prevalence being more common than the rate of paralytic spinal cord injury in the general population.  To facilitate developing treatments, mouse models of Rett syndrome have been developed.  We have been using these models to identify functional deficits that we hypothesize are responsible for causing the behavioral and physiological impairments seen in the patients.  Our work has identified a novel system as a strong candidate.  We have found that this system, called histone deacetylase type 6, or HDAC6, is massively over-represented in the Rett syndrome mouse brain, and as such, that its activity is also greatly above normal levels. Intriguingly, we have also found that treating Rett syndrome mice with a drug that blocks HDAC6 activity decreases epilepsy rates in the mice, and improves their balance. While encouraging, we have yet to identify whether other behavioural deficits in these mice are similarly improved by the drug, or whether the cellular pathways affected by the over-activity of HDAC6 are normalized by drug treatment.  Addressing each of these questions is required before this drug can move forward in the pipeline towards clinical trials.  The current grant application is geared to answer these question

TitreApplicationTitle: Design and Function of Antimicrobial and IDR Peptides
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIAL PEPTIDES; BIOINFORMATICS; DRUG RESISTANCE; DRUG TARGET; HOST DEFENCE PEPTIDES; INNATE IMMUNITY; NOVEL THERAPEUTICS; PEPTIDE ANTIBIOTICS; QSAR; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The therapy of infectious diseases is under threat because antibiotic resistance is rising rapidly, while very few new drugs are under development or entering the clinic. One promising group of compounds are called host defence or antimicrobial peptides. These are small proteins that are produced by virtually all organisms, including plants, insects, and humans. Host defence peptides are a major component of the immune defences against infections because they lead to the death of microbial pathogens and modify immune responses. Our lab has been developing modified versions of these molecules as a new treatment for infections, and took first generation antimicrobial peptides into clinical trials. Here we propose to develop even more effective peptides to enable their successful clinical development as therapeutics for infections. We will investigate strategies to modify these peptides to prevent their usual destruction by enzymes called proteases that abound in the body. By making large numbers of these peptides and testing their activities, we will develop improved peptides for testing in the clinic. Specifically, we will determine whether these peptides work in combination with and improve the activity of conventional antibiotics. We will also continue to develop peptides that favourably boost the immune response of the host. In particular, we will try to understand what the peptides do to the cells of the immune system that make them effective in modifying our immune response. These peptides have enormous potential and we propose that by the end of the current grant funding period, they will enter into clinical trials to determine their potential for treating human infectious and inflammatory diseases.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Motor Recovery and Rehabilitation
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Following damage to the brain, a large number of individuals worldwide experience arm and hand movement problems that impact their ability to perform daily life activities and their quality of life. Rehabilitation is aimed at maximizing an individuals potential to recover or retrain lost motor function using adaptive capacities of the brain. This research program aims at elucidating the mechanisms underlying the disordered control of movement in children and adults with brain damage using detailed movement and clinical analyses. The program also focuses on the development of new and more effective training programs for arm and hand rehabilitation using cutting-edge technology.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Immune Mediated Gastrointestinal Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Despite improved health and longevity, immune mediated bowel disorders are increasingly diagnosed, at ever younger ages. Crohn's disease is an incurable inflammatory bowel disease for which Canada has the world's highest reported incidence. My research project applies an innovative translational research plan devoted towards understanding the causes of immune mediated gastrointestinal disorders, earlier diagnosis, improved treatments and ultimately their prevention. Our multidisciplinary team applies diverse methodologies to study interactions between the hosts genes, immune response and environmental risk factors, particularly microbes and diet. Other projects examine nutriceutical modulation of the host immune response and prevention of complications, such as colon cancer.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: During the term of the Tier 2 chair Dr. Song has established a world class Alzheimer research program at University of British Columbia and made significant discoveries on how BACE1 gene expression is regulated and its role in Alzheumer's Disease pathogenesis, key mechanisms underlying Alzheimer's Disease pathogesis in Down Syndrome, and Alzheimer's Disease drug development. The application from Tier 2 to Tier 1 will enable Dr. Song to continue elucidating the underlying mechanism  of Alzheimer's Disease pathogenesis and identifying novel biomarkers and drug targets for Alzheimer's Disease. Dr. Songs team will also work with an international group to establish a Canada-China translational medical research program for Down Syndrome and Alzheimer's Disease.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Inner City Medicine
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: In many cities around the world, there are low-income neighbourhoods in which poverty, mental illness and drug addiction come together to bring about substantial health and community concerns.  Particularly vulnerable populations include ethnic minorities (e.g., Aboriginal persons), homeless and drug-addicted individuals, and street-involved youth. Among these populations, hepatitis C, HIV and other costly chronic diseases, as well as related disorders such as soft tissue infections, pneumonias and other poverty-associated conditions, commonly contribute to substantial morbidity and mortality, in addition to excessive healthcare expenditures. This innovative research program proposes unique approaches to address these concerns, for the betterment of all of society.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Development Studies
Keywords-MotsClés: Social structures and relationships, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Professor Rosenbergs program of research mainly focuses on a joint project in Canada and China to be carried out with colleagues from around Canada and in the Chinese Academy of Sciences Institute of Geographic Science and Natural Resources Research, Beijing University, and the Chinese Centre for Disease Control.  They will develop social deprivation indices for both countries that are sensitive to their respective older populations, and analyse the relationships among social deprivation of older persons, their health, and health care.  The results have implications for the future of older populations in both countries and globally.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: The Social Contexts of Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed program of research examines the health effects of demands and resources in social contexts. There are three main objectives: (1) A longitudinal study of stress in work and family roles; (2) knowledge dissemination; and (3) leadership in the Sociology of Health. Schieman is directing a national longitudinal study that expands existing knowledge about stress and health among Canadians. His research pursues novel questions about the ways that stressors in work and family contexts influence changes in health. The research will yield theoretical innovations and practical implications for processes in the work-family interface and its implications for population health.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Human Immunology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: This Chair will support Dr. Madrenas' leadership as Chairman of the Department of Microbiology and Immunology at McGill University.  His recruitment spearheads the development of a cutting-edge program in Human Immunology that extends the world-class profile of research in Infection and Immunity at McGill.  Dr. Madrenas brings his leadership in multidisciplinary research in Immunology and Microbiology, especially in those aspects related to the mechanisms that regulate the activation of the cells of the immune system during infections and inflammatory diseases.  Research led by Dr. Madrenas and his group at McGill will not only accelerate the pace of discovery in Basic and Clinical Immunology and Immunotherapeutics but also translate these discoveries into clinically feasible treatments for infections and inflammatory diseases and organ transplantation. In addition, the Chair will play a key role in the design and implementation of an internationally-renown Human Immunology training program in Montreal and provide community outreach with public education programs.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Molecular Therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: The objective of Cancer Proteomics is to achieve better outcomes for cancer patients. By developing and applying advanced methods in mass spectrometry, the proteins in normal and cancer tissue will be comprehensively compared. The purpose is to discover the abnormal cancer-causing proteins in tumours, and to monitor the effectiveness of innovative new drugs designed to target them. Clinically similar cancers often have distinctly different sets of abnormal proteins. This is why many new anti-cancer drugs fail. We envision a revolution in cancer diagnosis and treatment wherein cancers are effectively diagnosed and treated individually, according to their distinctive proteomes.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental Nephrology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: The excretory capacity of the kidney depends on branched tubes, the collecting ducts, and the urinary pelvis and ureter, generated during fetal development through the branching morphogenesis process. Disruption of this results in renal malformation, the major cause of childhood renal failure. Dr. Rosenblums research examines mechanisms around this process in normal and malformed kidneys and aims to: determine how Bone Morphogenetic Proteins (BMP) and their effectors control collecting duct formation by studying mice deficient in genes that transmit BMP signals; how signaling by Hedgehog proteins controls branching morphogenesis and develop therapeutic targets; and finally, identify genes mutated in kidney malformation and their functions.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Diabetes and Metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The overall long term goal of the Canadian Research Chair in Diabetes and Metabolism is prevention and treatment of diabetes, a major pandemic in Canada, affecting 2.6M people (8%) and costing $16B annually. Biochemical, genomics, proteomics, metabolomics and molecular biological approaches are being used to identify the mechanisms implicated in glucose regulated insulin secretion and that are responsible for the ß-cell failure in type 2 diabetes.  The applications of this work include modification of our diet to help prevent diabetes, the identification of novel drug targets and biomarkers of ß-cell mass and function, and diabetes treatment efficacy monitoring.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Gastrointestinal Inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite that infects 10% of the world's population and causes up to 100,000 deaths/year.  It is the third leading cause of death by parasitic infections. At present, there are no vaccines to prevent or control the parasite. Drug treatment is expensive with adverse side effects. In this research program Dr. Chadee has identified and expressed two essential molecules released by E. histolytica that are involved in tissue invasion. His research is focused on studying the intricate mechanisms by which these molecules destroy or suppress the body's defenses allowing the parasite to penetrate and to invade the intestine. Using this knowledge, it is hoped to develop a vaccine against the parasite and to develop newer and smarter drugs to eliminate infections.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurologic infection and immunity
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Immune activation is a chief cause of the disease process in neurological diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND). Dr. Powers group has delineated several disease mechanisms involved in MS and HAD, which involve both viral and host genes. His laboratory has also discovered molecules which efficiently modulate the brains innate immune system leading to protective effects on brain cells. Dr. Power will investigate the role of the brains inflammatory machinery by adopting a combined approach in which he will analyze brain tissues, models of neurological disease and the actions of several neurotherapeutic molecules developed in his laboratory. These studies will lead to new disease mechanism insights together with novel preventative and/or therapeutic options for inflammatory neurodegenerative diseases.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Bioethics
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other research relating to social structures and relationships
Abstract-Résumé: Ethical issues pervade human subjects research, and continued research on its ethical foundations is required to respond to challenges faced by scientists and to preserve public trust in science. The proposed research program will strengthen the moral foundations of research. It will provide for the first time a rigorous account of the ethics of trust and trace implications of this view for scientists and mechanisms to bolster public trust in science. It will extend the application of clinical equipoise to new types of research, and it will continue work on the ethics of cluster randomized trials through an international collaboration.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms regulating immunologic disease
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Autoimmune diseases are among the most common and debilitating chronic diseases and there is an urgent need for improved strategies to manage these conditions. This research is aimed at defining molecular pathways which regulate normal immune responses and which, when perturbed, lead to immunologic diseases. Through definition of gene variants conferring risk for such diseases and development/characterization of mouse models of immune dysfunction, this research will identify the gene variants and molecular pathways engendering common immunologic diseases. By providing new insights into the causes of immune diseases, these data will illuminate new strategies enabling more effective treatment and better outcomes.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Cell Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Cells are bound by a thin membrane that must dynamically change, allowing them to move, divide or communicate with neighboring cells.  Dr. Trimble's research explores how cells modify their membranes which has led to important discoveries, including insight into the fundamental machineries necessary for adding new membrane to the surface, and identification of a novel class of proteins that form scaffolds to regulate membrane properties.  He has also discovered that proteins in the membrane move in unexpected ways.  Since the same machineries are involved in all cells, these insights may lead to important treatment of diseases ranging from cancer to schizophrenia.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Spinal Cord Networks
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: A consequence of injuries or diseases affecting the brain or spinal cord is a deficit in movement. Neural circuits of the spinal cord responsible for movement are not understood. To identify mechanisms by which the spinal cord produces motor behaviours, I focus on three distinct spinal microcircuits: circuits directly responsible for controlling muscles, circuits within the spinal cord that produce the patterns of activation of motor systems, and circuits that the brain uses to control spinal circuits. Such knowledge will form the foundation of new strategies to improve movement in people with injuries or diseases affecting the nervous system.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Parasite Biotechnology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Neglected tropical diseases caused by helminth parasites exact an enormous toll on humans and their animals. We know little about the molecular negotiations between host and parasite that lead to a successful or resolved infection. Our research aims to illuminate the molecules used by parasites to influence the ability of the host to prevent infection, and to understand how drugs used to control infections may intervene in these processes in favor of the host. This research will identify new strategies for vaccination or drug discovery to provide better control of these widespread infections, improving animal health and helping to block the cycle of poverty they maintain.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 1
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 1
TitreApplicationTitle: Hypertension and Vascular Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension is the number one cause of disease and death worldwide, and prevalence of diabetes is increasing dramatically, both conditions leading to heart attacks, stroke and kidney disease. The present project will examine rodent and human vessels to demonstrate mechanisms of injury in these conditions. Studies will focus on potent constrictors of blood vessels, and the role played by defense mechanisms, particularly the immune system. Genes altered in blood vessels of rodents and subjects with hypertension and kidney disease or diabetes will be investigated. These studies will provide novel targets for therapy that will lead to improved outcomes for Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Imaging Systems and Image-Guided Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Focused ultrasound provides highly localized energy deposition deep into tissue for diagnostic or treatment purposes. The focal energy delivery can induce tissue coagulation without damage to the overlying or surrounding tissue and it has been clinically tested for noninvasive tumor ablation. In addition modifying the pressure waves can induce various other biological effects, including occlusion of blood vessels, disintegration of thrombi, and increase in blood vessel wall and cell membrane permeability. This ongoing research aims at harnessing the power of ultrasound for non-invasive interventions and to develop image-guided devices for patient treatments

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel protective roles for ATP-sensitive potassium channels in the heart
Keywords-MotsClés: AMP ACTIVATED KINASE; ATP-SENSITIVE POTASSIUM CHANNEL; CARDIOPROTECTION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNELS; IONIC HOMEOSTASIS; ISCHEMIA REPERFUSION INJURY; PATCH-CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Heart attacks are a major cause of death and disability in Canada. The proposed research will  help determine how cellular pathways in the heart may be harnessed in the clinic to reduce the damage sustained to the heart during a heart attack. Furthermore, we will investigate whether commonly used anti-diabetic drugs may actually contribute to heart damage in people with diabetes taking these medications. It is the overall aim of this research to increase the quality of life of Canadians after a heart attack and reduce the economic burden of caring for patients who develop chronic heart disease after a heart attack.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of bacterial silencing proteins in virulence gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIOLOGY; GENE REGULATION; HORIZONTAL GENE TRANSFER; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MICROBIAL EVOLUTION; PATHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Bacteria frequently exchange genetic material (DNA) with other bacterial species.  By doing so they are able to rapidly evolve in response to their ever-changing environment.  For example, bacterial genes responsible for antibiotic resistance are often obtained by genetic exchange; a major factor that accounts for the rapid spread of drug resistant bacteria in hospitals and communities.  Bacterial genes involved in disease (virulence genes) are also typically transferred between bacterial species and this also has played a major role in the emergence of new pathogens.   Genetic exchange can harm the bacterial cell, however, if the new genes they acquire are incompatible with the genes they already have.  My laboratory has found that E. coli and Salmonella have a protein, called H-NS, that can distinguish self genes from those genes acquired from other bacteria and subsequently turn the foreign genes off.  By shutting these genes off the bacteria can acquire foreign genes without compromising their own fitness by doing so.  Over a longer period of time the bacteria can develop ways of turning the foreign genes on under the right conditions.  Our lab and others have now determined that H-NS regulates the vast majority of virulence genes in bacteria that cause dysentery, plague, cholera and salmonellosis.  In close collaboration with Dr. Jun Liu (U. Toronto) we also found a molecule that shuts down foreign DNA in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the cause of tuberculosis, suggesting that shutting down foreign genes is a strategy commonly employed by many bacterial pathogens.  Our future studies will determine exactly how H-NS and related proteins shut down newly acquired bacterial virulence genes and, subsequently, how such genes are turned on under the right conditions.  By understanding these processes we hope to develop new therapeutic strategies for the control of bacterial infections.

OrgNm: Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM)
CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
AreasOfScienceEN: MUSCLE, BONE, OR JOINT; CELL BIOLOGY
DomainesScientifiquesFR: MUSCLES, OS OU ARTICULATIONS; BIOLOGIE CELLULAIRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Role and mechanisms of action of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) in cartilage development and osteoarthritis in vivo
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CARTILAGE; CHONDROCYTES; ENDOCHONDRAL OSSIFICATION; MTOR; OSTEOARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Despite extensive research, the mechanisms by which osteoarthritis (OA) can be prevented or treated still remain to be determined. Cartilage is the most critical tissue in our body which is destroyed during OA. Cartilage consists of only one type of specialized cells called chondrocytes and during ageing these cells have tendency to die faster resulting in accelerated destruction of the cartilage and surrounding tissues. Using animal models and human OA cartilage samples we have identified a biological process of cell survival called autophagy. During ageing and OA, this process of autophagy does not function very well i.e. this process is weaker resulting in decreased cell protection and increased cell death. Our preliminary studies suggest that one of the central biological factors which results in the downregulation of autophagy is mTOR. Our hypothesis is that during OA, mTOR function increases and as the result autophagy decreases resulting in greater cell death and cartilage destruction. To prove this hypothesis and generate new treatment to prevent or stop OA, this study will investigate the specific role of mTOR in cartilage development and OA using genetically modified mice and then we will compare mice data to specimens collected from normal human and OA patients. This study will be able to specifically answer the following questions: (1) Does mTOR control growth and development of cartilage? (2) Does mTOR control autophagy and chondrocyte survival in the cartilage? (3) Does mTOR inhibition can stop or prevent cartilage damage?  (4) Does mTOR inhibition stop the production of harmful mediators which destroy the cartilage and bone during OA? I anticipate that this study will show that mTOR is the key biological factor which initiates excessive cell death and cartilage degradation associated with OA. Thus targeting mTOR could generate new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of OA and related diseases.

CommitteeNameEN: Behavioural Sciences - C: Behavioural Studies, Neuroscience and Cognition
NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - C: Études du comportement, neuroscience et cognition
TitreApplicationTitle: Comparing the nature and evolution of Mild Cognitive Impairment in individuals with and without Parkinson's disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANATOMICAL MRI; COGNITIVE DEFICITS; DEMENTIA; EXECUTIVE PROCESSES; FUNCTIONAL MRI; MEMORY; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; NEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL EVALUATION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is primarily recognized for its motor symptoms. However, deficits in cognition such as learning, memory and problem solving are noted at the early stages of PD. In some patients, these can evolve rapidly, strongly affecting daily life, eventually resulting in dementia. Indeed the rate of dementia in PD is six-fold that of the general population.   Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) refers to a syndrome where significant cognitive deficits are present, but that minimally affects daily life. It is used in general aging to predict various forms of dementia, especially in Alzheimer's disease. The concept of MCI, may also useful in PD for the early prediction of dementia. Finally, the variety of cognitive deficits found in PD suggests that they might not all be specific to the disease, but also might share some common origins with the cognitive impairments found in elderly individuals without PD.   The aim this research is to compare the nature and evolution of MCI in both PD and non-PD individuals. We will follow large groups of PD and non-PD individuals longitudinally, using neuropsychological measures of their cognitive functions as well as imaging of brain anatomy and function, to find out which cognitive deficits and associated brain changes are specific to PD. Furthermore, it will allow us to predict the speed of cognitive decline in PD in function of the nature and early presence of MCI. Finally, it will permit for the detection of anatomical and functional brain patterns that can determine the occurrence of dementia in both PD and non-PD individuals.  This project promises to enhance our understanding of the nature and evolution of cognitive dysfunction in PD and in the aging population in general. The intent is to identify those measures that best predict early and later cognitive dysfunction in PD with the hope that prompt recognition will allow early intervention, leading to more favorable long-term cognitive outcomes.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of frailty on cardiac function in health and disease in aging mice: a model for therapeutic interventions to treat frailty
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ANIMAL MODEL; CARDIAC FUNCTION; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; FRAILTY; SENESCENCE
Abstract-Résumé: As anyone who has ever attended their high school reunion knows, people age at different rates.  Because a person's actual age is not always the same as their biological age, some older adults are fit and others are frail.   Frailty is a major health care problem, because frail people are often harmed by traditional medical care.  For example, even though fit people in their nineties can benefit greatly from cardiovascular surgery, more than half of frail older adults either die or end up in long-term care after such surgeries.  Even so, we know very little about frailty and its effects on organs like the heart, in part because we have not had an animal model to investigate frailty and its potential treatment.  Our research group has just discovered how to measure frailty in aging mice.  We measured many different health problems in individual mice and used this information to estimate a frailty index score.  We found that individual heart cells become very large in frail animals.  However, the ability of these large cells to contract declines, which would reduce the force of the heartbeat.  This suggests that frailty is associated with harmful changes in heart cells that may make the heart more susceptible to heart diseases.  The goal of the current research project is to understand how frailty affects the heart's ability to function under normal conditions and during times when blood flow to the heart is reduced.  As part of this study, we will look at how frailty develops over time in mice and we will compare our results to what is known about frailty in people.  We will also give older mice a drug that may help treat frailty and we will explore how this treatment works.  This research project is important because it will help us understand the links between frailty and heart disease.  This study will also develop a new way to test treatments for frailty in older people.

OrgNm: Montreal Heart Institute/Institut de cardiologie de Montréal
TitreApplicationTitle: Intracrine endothelin signalling in the cardiac ventricular myocyte
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTOR; MYOCYTE; NUCLEAR ENVELOPE; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Enlargement of the heart occurs when the heart is continuously exposed to conditions such as elevated blood pressure and/or increases in the amount of certain molecules, such as hormones, in the blood. Certain factors, including endothelin, also stimulate the heart to enlarge, or hypertrophy. We are investigating how endothelin, a naturally occurring regulatory protein, produces this enlargement of the heart. If the underlying cause for hypertrophy (e.g., increased endothelin release, high blood pressure) continue to be present and hypertrophy continues, a point is reached where the heart can no longer function properly. In this proposal, the means by which endothelin stimulates the muscle cells of the heart to enlarge are being studied. There are many steps in the chain of events initiated by endothelin acting upon a cardiac muscle cell. The first step is the interaction of endothelin with specialized proteins, dedicated to binding endothelin, called receptors. The final results include changes in the growth and function of the heart. The muscle cells of the heart contain two types of endothelin receptor. These receptors activate a network of signalling systems, similar to a telephone network, within the cell. In this project, the function of endothelin receptors that are located on the cell nucleus will be studied to determine their role in regulating the growth and function of muscle cells in the heart.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent

TitreApplicationTitle: Integrated molecular approaches to the diagnosis and epidemiology of pregnancy-associated malaria in Latin America
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CONGENITAL MALARIA; DELIVERY OUTCOMES; DIAGNOSIS; MALARIA; PLACENTAL MALARIA; PLASMODIUM FALCIPARUM; PLASMODIUM VIVAX; PREGNANCY; REAL-TIME PCR
Abstract-Résumé: Pregnant women are especially vulnerable to malaria which can cause serious harm to the mother and baby. We found that in Colombia, the scope of pregnancy-associated malaria is grossly under-estimated due to poor diagnostic tests. In this study, we propose to use sensitive molecular tests to assess the timing, frequency and biological response to infection during pregnancy and at delivery. We will determine the risks of malaria to the health of the mother and fetus, and identify new diagnostic tools to improve the detection and ensure prompt treatment of these infections in pregnancy.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Inflammatory pain
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory investigates the role of pore proteins in the membrane of nerve cells that detect pain signals.  These proteins detect noxious stimuli when a person, for example, burns their hands or hits their finger nail with a hammer.   In disease conditions, these proteins become highly sensitive to the stimulus and will activate the nervous system to produce pain sensation for non noxious stimulation (moderate temperature or light touch). Such chronic pain conditions can last for years and affect over 25% of the Canadian population with a strong impact on patient's quality of life.  My research program will use unique approaches from molecular studies  and behavioral studies in the whole animal to understand how aberrant function of these proteins is regulated in disease conditions.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Developmental Genetics and Cell Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: During embryonic development, dramatic changes in cell shape and movement (called cell polarity) transform a uniform ball of cells into complex organs like the kidney and brain. Zebrafish is an ideal model organism for understanding these changes  they develop remarkably similar to humans, yet zebrafish embryos are transparent and easily grown under a microscope. Dr. Ciruna has also established powerful experimental techniques to genetically manipulate zebrafish embryos, and to actually image microscopic changes in cell polarity that occur during organ formation. The proposed research exploits these advantages to determine how abnormal cell polarity ultimately causes birth defects, cancer and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Genomics of Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The central goal of the Moffat lab is to identify novel cancer cell vulnerabilities and through functional genetic screens and develop new tools and technologies to develop a deeper biological insight into oncogenesis.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Small RNA Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, NA
Abstract-Résumé: RNA interference (RNAi) is a cellular process whereby theexpression of a specific gene is silenced. Because of itsspecificity and the conservation of RNAi mechanisms fromplants to humans, RNAi possesses great therapeutic potentialand has revolutionized research. Closely related to RNAi areendogenous gene silencing pathways that are criticalregulators of proper gene expression during development,differentiation and gamete formation. Misregulation of thesepathways can lead to oncogenesis or infertility.  We use avariety of technologies in the model nematode, C. elegans,to dissect the molecular mechanisms and functions of thesevital and incredibly useful gene silencing pathways.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Architecture of Signal Transduction
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: During embryonic development cells communicate with each other and respond to environmental signals in order to evolve and organize into highly specialized structures such as tissues or organs. These cues are integrated by the cells and influence processes such as fate determination, migration or proliferation. In several human diseases such as cancer these same signals are defective.  Using cutting-edge proteomic, cell biological and biochemical tools we are investigating how the Wnt family of proteins, which constitute one of the most important of these signals, are integrated by signalling pathways inside the cells and how they are defective in cancer.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Physical Activity, Mobility, Cognitive Neuroscience
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: The worlds population is aging  at a rate that is unprecedented in human history. Maintaining both neurocognitive function and physical function is essential for healthy aging. My research program is focused on understanding how exercise can prevent both neurocognitive and physical decline in older adults.  To date, I have discovered that exercise improves both cognitive performance and brain function in older adults. Further, these benefits are evident even in older adults with some degree of cognitive impairment. My research program will highlight exercise as an effective strategy for promoting healthy aging at a population level.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Biology of Membrane Proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Research in the Moraes lab examines protein and ion translocation across bacterial membranes.  In particular, Dr. Moraes dissects the components of these pathways examining their interactions in molecular detail.   Biochemical tools such as X-ray crystallography provide atomic resolution 3D-models of the proteins, while surface plasmon resonance, isothermal calorimetry or bio-layer interferometry are used to determine kinetic parameters and validate models that describe the mechanism of action. These membrane proteins function together as a complexes to facilitate efficient transport that is essential for pathogenic bacteria to survive within the host, thus this research provides the basis for developing novel antimicrobial therapeutics.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Lipid science and technology
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: Antibiotic peptides and biosurfactants are part of the self-defense system of many organisms, including humans. They act by inducing holes or pores in the cell membrane of, for example, certain bacteria. This renders them promising candidates for killing bacteria that have become resistant against classic antibiotics. Biosurfactants are also powerful biopesticides to protect our crops against fungal and other pathogens without compromising our health and environment. Dr. Heerklotz's research is part of an interdisciplinary effort involving medical sciences, microbiology, and biotechnology, which seeks to help in understanding and optimizing the activity of these compounds and their selectivity to a certain target organism.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Stem Cell Signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Doble studies the signalling circuitry within stem cells that controls their unique ability to either make more stem cells or to transform into specialized cells such as nerve, blood or muscle cells. Understanding the signals thatregulate stem cell properties will help us develop specialized cell growth conditions that will turn on the signals promoting stem cell self-renewal or alternatively, turn on the signals  that cause efficient stem cell conversion into specific cell types.This research is an important step towards bringing safe stem cell therapiesto the clinic for regenerative medicine applications.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Vesicle Transport and Cell Signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Other research
Abstract-Résumé: Our cells need to communicate in between each-others in a process called cell signalling. Misregulation of this process can lead to various diseases, including cancers. Vesicular trafficking controls the level of signalling receptors that are present at the cell surface and consequently is a major regulator of cell signalling. Dr Emerys research program aims at elucidating how vesicular trafficking regulates signalling molecules involved in various processes linked to stem cell maintenance, cancer development and metastasis formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aging, incontinence and pelvic floor dysfunctions in women
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The first of its kind in Canada, a Canadian Research Chair on Aging, incontinence and pelvic floor dysfunctions in women, under the leadership of Dr. Chantal Dumoulin, will positively impact millions of women. The Tier-2 Chair will be located in the research centre of the Institut Universitaire de Gériatrie de Montréal (CRIUGM), a Université de Montréal affiliated research centre. The ultimate goal is to improve continence care for elderly Canadian women, including increased accessibility to treatment, by ensuring that rehabilitation interventions (first line treatments) are better targeted and can be scale up by government healthcare services in a cost-effective manner.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Perinatal Programming
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: A clear relationship exists between maternal health and disease risk in offspring. Poor maternal nutrition leads to an increased risk of diabetes, obesity and reproductive dysfunction in her offspring. My research investigates how poor perinatal nutrition impacts reproductive, metabolic and ageing outcomes. It aims to uncover molecular pathways regulating the inter-relationships between the mother, the placenta and the fetus and how changes in these pathways result in increased offspring disease risk. The major impact of my work is in the life sciences but also has influence in obstetrics; uncovering important molecular details of how maternal nutrition impacts on offspring health.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Social Psychophysiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Social structures and relationships
Abstract-Résumé: An increasing number of Canadians are providing care for relatives with chronic illnesses. Prolonged caregiving stress can increase risk for poor health. This research program aims at identifying the bio-psycho-social factors influencing caregiving burden. Caregiving stress can lead to negative emotions (depression or anxiety), interfere with health behaviors, (regular exercise, healthy diet), and impact social relationships (increased family conflict or limited social activity). These factors may contribute to detrimental changes in immunity. Fortunately, supportive interpersonal relationships can attenuate caregiving burden. The role of the hormone oxytocin in producing the protective effect of social relationships on health will also be investigated.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental Cortical Physiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Pharmaceutical products
Abstract-Résumé: The Lambe Lab research team focuses on the prefrontal cortex, a brain region critical for attention as well as the regulation of anxiety. We study the development of prefrontal cortical neurons and circuitry using the tools of electrophysiological recording and multiphoton imaging. These techniques allow us to assess functional receptors and local circuitry at different points in development and determine how these are changed by molecular, pharmacological, and behavioural manipulations. Such information is important to identify vulnerabilities in the development of brain circuitry and to design novel therapeutic interventions for attention and anxiety disorders.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Virology and Oncotherapy
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Health
Abstract-Résumé: My research program at the Li Ka Shing Institute of Virology at the University of Alberta explores viruses that selectively kill cancer cells, called oncolytic viruses. Our studies focus on human reovirus, a non-pathogenic RNA virus that inherently targets transformed cells and is currently in phase III clinical trial as a cancer therapeutic. My laboratory seeks to understand why some cells are more permissive to reovirus than others, and to identify viral gene modifications that improve reovirus oncolysis. We have discovered reovirus variants (i.e. mutants) that exhibit superior oncolytic potency relative to wild-type reovirus. Using reovirus variants, we are now exploring how specific viral genes can promote reovirus replication in cancer cells. We are also using various molecular techniques to identify reovirus genes that induce cellular anti- and pro- reoviral responses in normal and cancer cells, respectively. Ultimately, our goal is to optimize reovirus oncotherapy using reovirus variants with enhanced potency towards specific cancers.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Neurobiology of Stress
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Stress is a major contributing factor to the rise in prevalence of mood and anxiety disorders. The neural mechanisms through which stress influences vulnerability to mental illness are not well understood, but involve structural and functional reorganization of neural circuits in the brain. The endocannabinoid system is the brains version of cannabis, and its physiological role involves regulating emotional behaviour and responses to stress. The proposed research program aims to understand how the endocannabinoid system regulates vulnerability and resilience to mood and anxiety disorders.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Nutritional Lipidomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Nutrition and food hygiene, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Nutritional lipidomics examines the effect of diet on cellular lipids.  Dr. Stark examines the relationship between omega-3 fatty acid intake, tissue levels and health.  He will also determine cellular mechanisms by which women accumulate higher levels of omega-3 fatty acids.  Dr. Stark uses rapid analytical techniques that he has developed, and molecular biology techniques in cell culture, animal and human studies.  This research will lead to specific recommendations for the intake of omega-3 fatty acids by women and men, and novel and commercializable technologies that will allow for routine screening of fatty acid profiles to determine heart disease risk.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroscience and Brain Imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, Biomedical engineering and medicines
Abstract-Résumé: Recent studies have demonstrated changes in brain activity not only when stimuli are presented to human subjects, but also at rest. It has been suggested that spontaneous brain activity, which is synchronous over large regions of the brain, is an important principle of brain function. This proposal is aimed at investigating the relationship between spontaneous changes in neuronal activity and the concomitant changes in blood flow. The results may authenticate MRI as a method for investigating spontaneous activity in healthy human subjects, and as a means for diagnosing changes in synchronous brain activity in both neurological and psychiatric diseases.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Translational Magnetic Resonance Imaging Research
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) offers tremendous opportunities for advancing medical imaging research. New methods for molecular and metabolic MRI show extraordinary promise for improving the detection, staging and management of critically important diseases like cancer, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). The goal of this program is to translate these new MRI techniques to clinical use by developing: 1) enhanced methods for the clinical imaging evaluation of metabolic liver disease; 2) novel hardware to enhance clinical MRI; and 3) metabolic imaging techniques that use novel hyperpolarisable contrast agents to gain new insights in diseases like cancer and NAFLD.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Cardiovascular Proteomics and Molecular Therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiomyopathies represent a significant cause of morbidity and death in Canada andworldwide. Because of the poor prognostic outcome of late stage disease, innovativepreventive and therapeutic measures are needed urgently. These developments willrequire a more complete understanding of the molecular events involved in thisdisease, which is currently poorly understood. Several signaling pathways involved incardiomyopathies are linked to intracellular cardiac calcium. Therefore, the potentialrole of calcium and calcium regulatory proteins has been of particular interest infinding a mechanistic solution to the degeneration observed. The goal of this projectis to investigate the role of several critical calcium regulatory proteins to developa greater understanding of the events that lead to cardiac disease, and ultimately toprovide novel therapeutic targets for the prevention and treatment of these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mécanismes de Régulation de l'Expression des Gènes
Keywords-MotsClés: Biomedical engineering and medicines, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Le fonctionnement harmonieux des cellules dépend de leurs aptitudes à répondre et à sadapter aux changements extracellulaires. Pour sadapter, les cellules activent ou répriment leurs gènes en  modulant leurs transcriptions. Pour comprendre la régulation de la transcription, on ne peut faire abstraction du rôle dynamique de la chromatine. Celle-ci permet la condensation des génomes eucaryotes dans le noyau, et joue un rôle capital au niveau de la transcription génique.  Les travaux du titulaire vont contribuer, de manière significative, à une meilleure compréhension des modulations de la structure de la chromatine associées à la transcription des gènes.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Human Cancer Stem Cell Biology
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Dr. Singh's research program applies a developmental neurobiology framework to the study of brain tumours. Her Canada Research Chair has capitalized on her previous discovery of an abnormal stem cell that drives brain tumour formation (the brain tumour initiating cell, or BTIC). The Chair has fostered innovative, highly specialized projects that have permitted a functional characterization of stem cell signaling pathways that are disrupted in BTICs. Dr. Singh is currently studying the regulation of BTIC signaling pathways in glioblastoma, brain metastases and childhood medulloblastoma, with an ultimate goal of selectively targeting the BTIC with appropriately tailored drug and molecular therapies.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Life course oral epidemiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Social medicine
Abstract-Résumé: My research program studies chronic oral disease (COD) aetiology including oral cancer and inflammation, using epidemiological and life course approaches. The goal of this program is to better understand the causes of COD and their links with major chronic diseases and includes two major projects: 1) HeNCe Life, an international study, examines the role of life-course socioeconomic environments, infection (viral), behavioural and genetic factors in the development of cancer in the mouth, throat and larynx among Indians, Brazilians and Canadians; 2) QUALITY Cohort study investigates the associations between obesity and COD (gum diseases and dental caries) throughout childhood, adolescence and early adulthood.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Atherosclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Atherosclerosis is the number one cause of death and disability worldwide.  Inappropriate changes in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC), the cells that form a major part of arteries, can trigger and hasten the progression of atherosclerosis. MicroRNA-145 is a small molecule that is found in VSMCs and is believed to play a crucial role in regulating genes that control overall cellular and tissue health and development. We will investigate whether microRNA-145 protects blood vessels by slowing down and/or inhibiting inappropriate structural changes in VSMCs.  Our findings will identify new methods by which atherosclerosis may be retarded or prevented.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Rehabilitation for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: My research focusses on rehabilitation for individuals with ChronicObstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). COPD is a leading cause of morbidity andmortality worldwide and results in significant economic and social burdens. In Canada,COPD is the fourth leading cause of death in men and the seventh leading cause ofdeath in women. Goals for managing COPD include prevention of disease progression andrelief of symptoms. Cardiopulmonary rehabilitation improves the ability to exerciseand carry out activities of daily living which enhances life satisfaction forindividuals with COPD. This program of research will examine ways to maximize theeffects of rehabilitation through the use of various exercise training and testingmodalities. In addition, we will establish novel and innovative ways tomeasure and enhance physical activty in individuals with COPD with the ultimate goalof enhancing quality of life.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Social Inequalities in Child Health
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Social medicine
Abstract-Résumé: Growing up poor constitutes one of the greatest threats to human health, and societies that have more social and economic inequality tend to have worse health outcomes. It is unclear when during the lifespan socioeconomic factors have the most impact on health, and which protective factors in the social environment matter most during these sensitive stages of development. My research a involves multilevel, developmental analysis of social and economic inequalities in children's health and links between income inequality and health. The policy relevance of this work lies in optimally timing and targeting interventions that will reduce social inequalities in health.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Epidemiology
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: My research focuses on integrating genetic, clinical and biological data, by developing innovative study designs and using new analytic tools, to understand better the causes of chronic diseases. My current research involves genetic and environmental factors associated with thrombophilia  a coagulation anomaly that elevates the risk of clots in peoples blood vessels  and its relationship to Metabolic Syndrome  a group of disorders that increase peoples risks for cardiovascular disease and diabetes.  The ultimate goal of my work is to prevent and manage these potentially devastating illnesses through an enhanced understanding of their genetic architecture and underlying biological mechanisms.

ProgramNameEN: Canada Research Chairs - CIHR Funded - Tier 2
NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Integrative Physiology of Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Recent data suggests there are 350-million diabetics worldwide. Three million of these cases are Canadians who in 2010 incurred costs of $12.2 billion. Novel strategies to reduce diabetes prevalence are urgently needed. My research aims to understand the biological processes linking obesity with diabetes. Specifically we are interested in identifying: (a) molecules involved in regulating body weight, (b) the reason obesity causes insulin-producing cells of the pancreas to malfunction, and (c) novel risk factors for diabetes. Our goal is to identify therapeutic targets to reverse/prevent diabetes and provide empirical evidence to support lifestyle interventions.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Cell Division and Chromosomal Organization
Keywords-MotsClés: Other medical research, NA
Abstract-Résumé: Cell division occurs continuously in our bodies from conception to death, on the one hand generating all our tissues and organs, while on the other directly responsible for cancer mortality. Surprisingly, the fundamental rules governing cell division are still unknown. In the Maddox lab, we aim to understand the first principle concepts of cell division. We use various approaches including cutting edge light microscopes and computer analysis tools and multiple cell model systems. By innovating new methods, we are able to propose and test new hypotheses for cell division.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying the role of Fragile-X Mental Retardation Protein (FMRP) in hippocampal learning and memory processes.
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; FRAGILE-X SYNDROME; HIPPOCAMPUS; NEUROANATOMY; NMDA; SEX DIFFERENCES; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Fragile-X Mental Retardation Protein (FMRP)is a protein that is expressed in neurons throughout the brain. When this protein is absent, humans will develop the most common form of mental retardation, Fragile-X Syndrome. FMRP itself is interesting because it interacts with over 800 different proteins in the brain. Our work seeks to determine if disruptions in it's interactions with other synaptic proteins, particularly the n-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor, play a role in causing the learning and memory deficits chracteristic of Fragile X Syndrome. We also seek to determine if reversing deficits in FMRP expression can rescue learning and memory performance.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Spinal Cord Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: Each year, over 1000 Canadians sustain an acute spinal cord injury (SCI), and join close to 40,000 across our nation living with one of the most physically and psychologically devastating of injuries that one can survive.    Unfortunately, we currently have no treatments to regenerate the injured spinal cord.   My research program focuses on translation  that is, moving discoveries from the laboratory into the clinical setting for individuals with SCI, and also, taking what we learn from human patients and using this to direct and focus scientific research in the laboratory.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Biofilm Microbiology and Genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Health
Abstract-Résumé: The pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes chronic lung infections that claim the lives of most patients with the genetic disease cystic fibrosis (CF).  In the CF airways, these bacteria stick together in slimy aggregates termed biofilms.  It is not understood why biofilms cause chronic lung disease; however, recent findings hint that the biofilm environment selects for mutant bacteria that are adept at persisting in the lung.  My research uses genome sequencing technology, biochemistry and genetics to characterize these mutants and to figure out how this changes virulence.  This research is important because it is uncovering long sought links between biofilms and chronic infectious disease.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Chaires de recherche du Canada - financées par les IRSC - Niveau 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Psychiatric genetics
Keywords-MotsClés: Medical research, hospital treatment, surgery, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding and treating neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders is a major public health priority. Dr Ernst aims to use new sequencing technology to identify genetic mutations in people with these disorders.  Investigating genes implicated in brain diseases allows for the better understanding of disease progression and brain function.  Dr Ernst uses patient donated skin cells to derive brain-like cells to understand how specific mutations lead to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders.  These studies provide a means to identify underlying brain dysfunction of affected individuals and offer a patient-specific route to new therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canada Research Chair in Health Informatics
Keywords-MotsClés: Health, Other medical research
Abstract-Résumé: Critical care has traditionally been one of the most resource intensive and costly areas of healthcare. Even though patients are surrounded by state of the art medical devices, the information they create are poorly utilized. Great opportunities exist for more advanced patient care if new computing approaches process this high frequency patient information and watch for subtle changes indicating changes in patients conditions much earlier than these events are detected now. This research will extend the innovative and emerging research completed during the first term. It has the potential to revolutionize healthcare by saving lives and reducing costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: An enhanced method to measure chronic disease burdens using health administrative data
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORKS; CHRONIC DISEASE SURVEILLIANCE; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; METHODOLOGY FOR SURVEILLIANCE; PREVALENCE ESTIMATION; VALIDATE CASES
Abstract-Résumé: Accuracy of the estimating the chronic disease burden is crucial for budgeting and evaluating the performance of strategies. Due to the reliability and validity for surveillance of chronic disease using administrative data, the errors, such as false positive cases exist. The purpose of this study is to develop a method to adjust the biased prevalence of chronic disease for surveillance using health administrative data. Specifically, the objectives are; 1) to develop and validate the methods to adjust the biased prevalence using chart review data; 2) apply the methods to estimate hypertension prevalence overtime using health administrative data. We will use chart review data as a reference standard and link it with administrative data to develop and validate the methods to adjust the biased prevalence of hypertension overtime. We will use optimizing data period and classification modeling method to minimize the error for identifying cases more accurately. Classification modeling is a process, not only using ICD9/10 diagnosis codes but also multiple data features to develop the algorithms to discriminate the individuals as cases and non-cases. We will estimate parameters associated with "true" hypertension cases of chart review data in classification model, and use these parameters to discriminate the individuals in administrative data as case and non-case. The discriminative performance and prediction error of the classification algorithms will be evaluated using the area under receiver operative curve (ROC). We will use the condition of hypertension as an example to illustrate the method. The method will be externally validated using British Columbia data. The performance for the method to identify chronic conditions will also be tested using Alberta EMR data from Canadian Primary Care Sentinel Surveillance Network (CPCSSN). We will then apply the newly developed methods to Alberta health administrative data and estimate the prevalence of hypertension over time.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phase 2: Investigations into Usability and Safety of Scooters in Challenging Winter Environments
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESSIBILITY; AGING; ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY DESIGN; MOTION SIMULATOR; SAFETY; SCOOTER; SIMULATED ENVIRONMENT; TESTING STANDARDS; WHEELED MOBILITY; WINTER ENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: For many older people, powered mobility devices are the only option for achieving independent mobility. Mobility scooters are the most popular form of powered mobility device and are used by nearly 100,000 Canadians, primarily older adults. Scooters are powered wheeled assistive mobility devices designed for people who have good upper body control but difficulty walking (Russell et al. 1997; LaPlante 2003). In 2006, scooter sales exceeded powered wheelchair sales by a ratio of 2:1 in Canada and 4:1 in the U.K. (Statistics Canada 2006). Scooter users face significant challenges maneuvering both indoors and outdoors. There is a particularly limited understanding of scooter performance outdoors in winter environments. Ice, snow, and slush pose serious challenges to safe independent mobility for these users. These conditions can cause slipping making it difficult to stop safely and maintain desired direction. They can also increase the potential for sliding and tipping accidents, especially when turning or traveling over sloped surfaces adjacent to curbs.  There are currently no standard tests for evaluating scooter performance in winter. Standard tests are necessary as they allow consumers and clinicians to make informed decisions on the selection of scooters. Standard tests are also necessary to provide manufacturers with minimum performance criteria and a test method to substantiate outdoor performance claims. We propose 4 studies which will result in the development of standard tests of winter performance for mobility scooters, an evaluation of a range of currently available scooters, and target areas for overcoming the mobility problems faced by the large and growing population of elderly scooter users in winter. Toronto Rehab's new laboratories make it possible to safely study scooter performance in a variety of controlled and reproducible challenging winter environments, as proposed in this study. Pilot testing has shown the feasibility of this approach.

TitreApplicationTitle: Methods to overcome the prothrombotic activity of thrombi
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROMES; ANTICOAGULANTS; FIBRIN; FIBRINOGEN; PLATELETS; THROMBIN; THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Most heart attacks and strokes are caused by blood clots that block arteries supplying blood to the heart or brain.  These blood clots are comprised of small cells, known as platelets, together with fibrin, a strand-like substance that provides the clot with a net-like structure.  Patients with heart attacks or strokes are often given aspirin and/or Plavix (platelet inhibiting drugs) and blood thinners (anticoagulants).  Although this treatment helps, currently available anticoagulants still have problems.  Thus, some patients will have ongoing clotting despite the use of anticoagulants, whereas others will respond to treatment, but have recurrent clotting when the anticoagulants are stopped.  Ongoing and recurrent clotting are undesirable because the longer and more completely that heart or brain arteries are blocked, the more damage that occurs.  This application focuses on (a) defining the reasons why blood clots in arteries are so resistant to inhibition by currently available anticoagulants, and (b) developing new blood thinners that can overcome the limitations of currently available agents.  Already we have identified two new anticoagulants that appear to be better than existing drugs.  We now plan to extend these findings using a combination of test tube-based experiments and rabbit studies that are aimed at comparing the efficacy and bleeding potential of our new blood thinners with those of currently available anticoagulants.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multifrequency Ultrasound: Technology and Applications
Keywords-MotsClés: ACOUSTIC MATERIALS; CANCER MODELS; ELASTOGRAPHY; IMAGE GUIDED THERAPY; LINEAR ARRAY; MOUSE IMAGING; POTENTIATED THERAPEUTICS; THERAPY; TRANSDUCERS; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: A new ultrasound transducer array technology is proposed that will enable the use of multiple frequencies emanating from a single device.  In essence this will permit simultaneous tissue manipulation and imaging from the same device.  Multi-frequency transducer arrays will enable a variety of new imaging and therapeutic options including improved micro-vessel imaging, tumour mechanical properties (elasticity)imaging, treatment acceleration, molecular imaging and improved contrast imaging.  Finally methods for three dimensional analysis of ultrasound microbubble contrast using multi-frequency approaches will be developed.  The new approaches will be based on models developed in our laboratories and implemented on state of the art commercial instrumentation.  Multifrequency ultrasound will be evaluated in mouse models of renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma to develop novel imaging biomarkers associated with key aspects of tumour response to therapy. In particular quantitative predictors of tumour resistance (failure of therapy) will be sought.  By more fully characterizing the actions of targeted drugs alone and in combination in high quality animal models, it is hypothesized that more informed choices can be made before proceeding to expensive phase II and III clinical trials of new targeted therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: IRES-dependent translation of heat shock proteins in the pathogenesis of coxsackievirus myocarditis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR CHAPERONE; COXSACKIEVIRAL PATHOGENESIS; HEAT SHOCK PROTEIN 70; INTERNAL RIBOSOME ENTRY SITE (IRES) - DEPENDENT TRANSLATION; VIRAL MYOCARDITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Viral myocarditis (heart muscle cell damage by infection) is an infectious heart disease. Coxsackie virus, a virus discovered in Coxsackie Village near New York City, is a very common causal agent of myocarditis, particularly in children, adolescents and pregnant women. In the late phase of this disease, it often leads to heart failure and death. To date, there is no effective treatment and vaccine. To improve the therapy, it is essential to understand the roadmap of virus-host interactions in the causing of heart disease and find the strategy to design drugs to block the road leading to viral injury of the heart. Heat shock protein 70 (Hsp70) is a key gene involved in response to various biological stresses caused by heat, high pressures, toxic compounds, viral infection, etc. We and others have found that Coxsackievirus infection induces dramatically increase in Hsp70 protein production in the heart. We hypothesize that Coxsackievirus-induced over-production of Hsp70 protein in the heart is responsible for this heart disease. In this project we will study why this virus can increase Hsp70 protein production in the heart, how produced Hsp70 protein can assist virus to cause heart damage and which gene(s) in the roadmap can serve as the potential target for drug development to block the disease occurrence. We will conduct the study first by using isolated heart muscle cells growing in culture dishes and then using the whole heart of mice to mimic human disease. By using mice lacking of Hsp70 gene and comparing with mice having this Hsp70 gene, we will provide better understanding of the roles of Hsp70 in Coxsackievirus-caused heart disease and possibly identify the novel targets in the roadmap for the drug development to treat the viral infection.

Leishmaniasis is a fatal infection if not treated. The proposed research will identify key genes that make Leishmania a deadly disease and this will provide a foundation for the development of novel treatments.
