TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of Feeding Type and Nutrient Fortification on the Gut Microbiome of Very Low Birth Weight Infants
Keywords-MotsClés: DONOR MILK; FEEDING TOLERANCE; HUMAN MILK; INFANT NUTRITION; MICROBIOME; VERY LOW BIRTH WEIGHT INFANTS
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, the leading cause of infant death and disability is preterm birth. Provision of the best care is critical, and key to this is nutrition. In term babies, mothers' own milk is the best nutrition, as it contains live cells and indigestible sugars that promote colonization of the infant gut with protective rather than pathogenic bacteria. Beneficial colonization is the first line of protection against overwhelming infection and inflammation, both common and potentially devastating in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants. VLBW infants have altered bacterial colonization as a result of several factors including antibiotic use and living in a crowded neonatal intensive care unit. Most mothers of VLBW infants are unable to express enough milk to entirely feed their babies and need to supplement with either formula or pasteurized human donor milk (PDM). Gut colonization may be more favourable in VLBW babies fed mothers' own milk, however this is not known, as most research has focused on term babies using culture techniques missing 80% of all organisms. It is also unclear what effects pasteurization of PDM, which kills all live cells, and adding cow's milk-based nutrient fortifiers to milk, necessary to meet the high nutrition demands of these infants, may have on gut colonization. The goal is to characterize bacteria colonizing the gut in VLBW infants fed mothers' milk, PDM or formula, using sophisticated molecular techniques and extracted bacterial DNA from stool. Stools will be collected for 7 weeks from 135 VLBW babies. A subset of 30 samples will be used to study metabolic activities carried out by gut bacteria, which will further define the potential physiological roles that the microbiome plays in the gut and how these may change with different feeding regimes. These findings will provide a key reference for optimal gut colonization in VLBW infants and guide policy development for nutritional strategies to best promote the health of fragile babies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bacterial chromosome replication control by novel proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICS; CAULOBACTER CRESCENTUS; CELL-CYCLE; CHROMOSOME REPLICATION; DEVELOPMENT; DNA BINDING; GENTIC SCREENING; PHOSPHO-RELAY; PROTEOLYSIS; REPLICATION ORIGIN
Abstract-Résumé: By studying how bacteria grow, and specifically how they choose to replicate their chromosomes, we can better understand how to control them with novel antibiotics that must be found to fight emerging resistant strains.  Bacteria choose to replicate their chromosomes by starting at one place termed the replication origin, and they dedicate special proteins to act there to begin replicating.  We isolated the replication origin and special proteins (called DnaA, CtrA and CC3319) from a common aquatic bacterium called Caulobacter crescentus.  This bacterium is especially easy to study and therefore serves as a model for more difficult bacteria.  Caulobacter's growth and chromosome replication can be followed in stages that display the steps required for chromosome replication.  We eventually hope to understand how bacteria "decide" to replicate, and to a biochemist this means asking how proteins bind and influence each other during changing circumstances.  When bacteria are tricked into making the wrong replicating decisions, they become much more vulnerable and less pathogenic.  In the future, we might augment our dwindling arsenal of antibiotics if we find chemicals that bind special replication proteins and trick bacteria into making wrong (and often lethal) replication decisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel mechanisms regulating functional recovery in stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; ALPHA 7 NICOTINIC ACETYLCHOLINE; ASTROCYTES; HSP90; ISCHEMIA; NEURONAL DYSFUNCTION; NEURONS; PRION PROTEIN; STI1; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the third leading cause of death in Canada. The risk factors for stroke increase with age; after age 55 the risk of stroke doubles every 10 years. Age is a non-modifiable risk factor for stroke and the elderly have worse outcomes. Age has also been suggested to be the cause of poorer outcomes for stroke in women, which normally live longer and present with stroke at a greater age compared to men. The societal costs of stroke are tremendous and it is estimated that stroke may cost our health system $3 to 5 billion/year. Unfortunately, the approved treatment for stroke remains limited. The prion protein plays important functions against neuronal insults, including stroke. This protein has a critical role in prion diseases, such as mad cow disease in bovines and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans.  In prion diseases neurons die, and neurotoxicity depends at least in part on the corruption of functions of the prion protein. Understanding how the prion protein protects against neuronal dysfunction that causes cell death in stroke and normal aging is the major goal of our research. We have found that a protein named STI1, which interacts and activates the prion protein, plays an important role in stroke. Decreased levels of STI1 or the prion protein in the brain decrease the ability of mice to recover after experimental stroke. We will use a combination of genetic manipulation, to change levels of key genes, as well as drugs that activate these pathways, to determine improved outcomes in experimental stroke. This research will reveal novel therapeutic targets and potentially novel drugs that could be used to improve survival and/or functional recovery in humans who suffered stroke-induced brain injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms for differentiation of pituitary POMC cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DIFFERENTIATION; CHROMATIN; PAX; PIONEER FACTOR; PITUITARY; POMC; REPRESSION; TBOX; TRANSCRIPTIONAL COACTIVATORS
Abstract-Résumé: Transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms for differentiation of pituitary POMC cells  Toutes les cellules des organismes complexes tel l'Homme contiennent le meme genome et donc les memes genes. Toutefois, l'assemblage de ces organismes complexes est possible parce qu'au cours du developpement embryonnaire, differentes cellules se differencient pour acquerir des fonctions propres. C'est ainsi que certaines cellules deviennent des neurones du cerveau alors que d'autres prennent l'identite et la fonction des cellules musculaires. C'est un probleme fondamental en biologie que de comprendre les mecanismes sous jacents a l'acquisition de telles identites et par consequent comprendre comment des sous ensembles de genes sont utilisees dans l'une ou l'autre des cellules. Ce probleme est d'autant plus d'actualite que nous avons maintenant la possibilite d'utiliser des cellules souches pour re-programmer ces cellules multipotentes en cellules utiles en therapie, telles que les cellules beta pour traiter le diabete ou les neurones dopaminergiques pour traiter la maladie de Parkinson. Nos travaux de recherche utilisent des cellules de la glande hypophysaire pour etudier ces mecanismes et entre autres pour comprendre l'effet 'pionnier' de certains regulateurs cle de l'identite cellulaire. Ces effets pionniers agissent en partie par le remodelage de la chromatine, ce materiel qui sert a empaqueter notre genome. En expliquant comment se reprogramment la chromatine et l'expression des genes, nos travaux visent a faciliter la reprogrammation des cellules elles-memes et ainsi contribuer au developpement de therapies cellulaires basees sur l'utilisation des cellules souches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibitors of deiminases targeting demyelination
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMICAL PROBES; DEIMINATION; DEMYELINATION; MOLECULAR INTERACTIONS; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a devastating disease that affects people of all ages. Currently, there are over 2.2 million people worldwide diagnosed with MS.  To date, there is no cure and the available drugs merely provide indirect relief to symptoms. At the root of this disease, patients lose control of their body over time as the proper functioning of the central nervous system (ie. primarily brain) slowly degrades. This occurs when the nerves in the brain are attacked by the immune system, damaging the important insulating membrane called myelin. There are a number of theories that attempt to understand the causes and progression of this condition, although none completely explain and provide solutions to find a cure for MS.  In patients who have MS, the myelin protein is modified more extensively than in normal by enzymes called deiminases. It is known clinically that these enzymes modify myelin proteins 40-90% more in the brains of MS patients than in normal brains. Thus, it was hypothesized that if one inhibits these proteins, one can stop the abnormal modification of myelin protein. Using a test drug called 2-chloroacetamidine (2CA), it was shown that treatment with 2CA improved the clinical scores, stopped the deterioration of the myelin membrane and also promoted the myelin formation on the nerves, in four different animal models of MS. Based on this encouraging data, we rationally designed drug-like molecules and tested one compound on the enzymes and a small study in mice.  Both studies showed promising results. We propose to investigate the enzymes called deiminases, and evaluate potent drug-like compounds in mouse models of multiple sclerosis. We will investigate the ability of these compounds to prevent damage to the nerves and potentially promote normal myelin formation. Results and observations from this research project will have direct relevance for the development of novel drugs for diseases such as multiple sclerosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Laryngeal and esophageal consequences of nasal respiratory support in newborns
Keywords-MotsClés: GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX; HIGH-FREQUENCY OSCILLATORY VENTILATION; LARYNX; NEURALLY-ADJUSTED VENTILATORY ASSIST; NEWBORN; NON-INVASIVE RESPIRATORY SUPPORT; OVINE MODEL; SWALLOWING
Abstract-Résumé: Neonatalogists increasingly use non-invasive modes of respiratory support for treating respiratory insufficiency in newborns. Thus, a ventilator blows air/oxygen through the nose (via a mask or small nasal cannulae) instead of into a tube inserted into the windpipe. That however can lead to unwanted consequences, such as blowing the gas into the digestive system instead of the lungs, due to closure of the larynx, acting as a small valve at the entrance of the windpipe. In the forthcoming 5 years, we propose to study and compare different modes of non-invasive, positive pressure respiratory support with regards to those unwanted effects. For that purpose, we will use our well-established full-term and preterm lamb models of nasal respiratory support. New knowledge drawn from those experiments will then be transfered to neonatal intensive care units for helping clinicians to make better choice between the various respiratory support modalities.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Intervertebral Disc as A Source of Low Back Pain In Humans and in Animal Models
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; DISCOGENIC PAIN; INTERVERTEBRAL DISC DEGENERATION; LOW BACK PAIN
Abstract-Résumé: Low back pain is the most common chronic pain condition in working age adults, effecting 10-15% of the population. One cause of low back pain is degeneration or herniation of the intervertebral discs in the spine. Pain that originates from the discs is referred to as discogenic. Very little is known about how discogenic pain develops and how it can be effectively treated. We propose to use both human subjects and animal models to improve our understanding of discogenic pain. Ultimately this improved understanding could lead to improvements in the treatment of chronic low back pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reversal of neuronal and cerebrovascular pathology in Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; ANGIOTENSIN TYPE 1 RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST; ANIMAL MODELS; CEREBRAL CIRCULATION; MEMORY; STATIN
Abstract-Résumé: Despite very active research on Alzheimer's disease (AD) over the past years, there is still very little to offer to patients as a choice of new therapy. It has been argued that this disappointing outcome is due to our poor understanding of the initial culprit of the disease. Several studies in patients indicate that a chronic reduction in blood supply to the brain occurs before the cognitive decline, and actually contributes to the neuronal failure. Dysfunctional blood vessels would impact on basic needs of the brain for fuel, and lead to neuronal injury, accumulation or faulty clearance of deleterious molecules and, ultimately, to neuronal degeneration. Studying the relationships between cerebrovascular pathology and memory deficit in AD using a classic mouse model of the disease, we found that it is possible to totally rescue both memory and brain perfusion. We also developed a new mouse model that recapitulates the full spectrum of neuronal, cognitive and cerebrovascular landmarks of the human disease. We will use these two models to better identify the relationships between cerebrovascular dysfunction and memory loss, and understand how drugs currently used for the treatment of cardiovascular diseases can rescue both deficits. We hypothesize that preserving a healthy cerebral circulation together with intact neuronal function will offer more effective treatments for AD. Further, we suggest that it is possible to rescue memory independently from reducing the levels of amyloid-beta, a highly toxic protein that accumulates in the brain of AD patients. Our goals are to identify the altered molecular pathways in brain and blood vessels that can be targeted therapeutically to concurrently rescue memory and brain perfusion.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparative effectiveness research for the drug treatment of atrial fibrillation.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR; DRUG SAFETY; NETWORK META-ANALYSIS; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Prescription drugs are a cornerstone of modern medicine, and have made significant contributions in reducing morbidity and mortality. Despite these benefits, there remain unresolved issues in drug evaluation which can result in negative consequences on clinical care. Current limitations in the evaluation of drug effectiveness include a lack of direct comparative studies and a lack of systematic inclusion of all pertinent evidence, particularly from real world settings. This can result in studies lacking the power  to detect rare but meaningful side effects. To address these shortcomings we propose to employ new research techniques ( network meta-analysis and cross design synthesis) which both aim to broaden the evidence base that may be included in drug evaluation thereby providing a more complete and comprehensive view. Specifically we will employ these techniques to evaluate the effectiveness of new and old anti-arrhythmic drugs for atrial fibrillation, the most common cardiac rhythm disturbance.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Synapsin II in Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIPSYCHOTIC DRUGS; BRAIN IMAGING; COGNITIVE AND EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; DEVELOPMENTAL NEUROBIOLOGY; GENETICS; PRE-SYNAPTIC PROTEINS; PRECLINICAL ANIMAL MODELS; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SCHIZOPHRENIA-LIKE PHENOTYPES; SYNAPSIN II
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a debilitating human mental disorder affecting about 1% of the population (approximately 400,000 people in Canada). This disease can manifest in various ways, and is characterized by positive symptoms (hallucinations,delusions, disorganized behaviour), negative symptoms (poverty of speech, lack of emotional experience, inability to experience pleasure, lack of social interaction, attention impairment), and cognitive dysfunction. While symptom types are independent from each other, they can co-exist in the same patient. Unfortunately, the cause of schizophrenia is unclear and currently available drug treatments for this illness are not without severe side effects. This project deals with a protein called synapsin II found in the presynaptic site, the site from which chemicals called neurotransmitters are released. Recent works from various laboratories, including our own, have demonstrated the role of synapsin II in the neurobiological mechanisms involved in schizophrenia. The preclinical animal model developed in our laboratory mirrors the behavioural abnormalities displayed by subjects with schizophrenia. Further studies proposed in this application will greatly advance our understanding of this mental illness. This project will investigate the role of synapsin II at pre-pubertal and post-pubertal stages (adulthood), and its effect on the development and progression of schizophrenia. A combination of several technologies (brain imaging, gene expression, estimation of behavioural abnormalities by computerized systems, immunohistological techniques) will be used to answer fundamental questions. By understanding the potential mechanistic role of decreased synapsin II in the brain region called the medial prefrontal cortex in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, progress can be made towards a better understanding of this devastating mental illness and the development of novel therapeutic approaches with higher specificity and fewer adverse effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunizing Infants against Pain: A hospital-based postnatal parent education program about reducing infant immunization pain
Keywords-MotsClés: EVIDENCE-BASED MEDICINE; HEALTH EDUCATION; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; IMMUNIZATION; INFANT/CHILD; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PAIN MANAGEMENT; POPULATION HEALTH; PRIMARY CARE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Children are routinely subjected to numerous painful immunization injections in the first years of life. Although safe, effective and convenient methods exist to reduce pain from these procedures, very few infants benefit. This has negative implications for the health outcomes of children as how parents manage pain over the first years of life lays the foundation for how children will express and regulate pain over their lifetime. Poor management of pain can lead to abnormal pain responses and future chronic mental health and physical discorders. Parents consistently report that they are not educated about how to manage pain and express concerns about pain experienced by their children. Ten percent of parents are nonadherent with immunization schedules in an effort to reduce infant suffering. This study will address this knowledge to care gap by evaluating hospital-based educational interventions directed to new parents about how to reduce pain during infant immunizations. Targeting parents for education about pain management is fundamentally necessary for any improvements that can be achieved. The research questions have been developed in consultation with parents, clinicians, researchers and policy makers as part of a broader research and knowledge translation strategy aimed at not only improving immunization pain management and vaccine uptake, but also improving the health outcomes for children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Simulating cost-effectiveness of screening strategies for preeclampsia risk in pregnant women
Keywords-MotsClés: COST-EFFECTIVENESS; PREECLAMPSIA; SCREENING STRATEGIES; SIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Preeclampsia (PE) is a threatening disease that affects nearly 5% of Canadian pregnant women and represents a major cause of maternal and fetal morbidity such as prematurity. Identifying women at risk allows a better monitoring of the pregnancy and has the potential to decrease adverse consequences. Several screening modalities are proposed to identify women at risk and clinical laboratories are pressured to implement them. Yet, the sensitivity, the specificity and the costs of the tests vary widely. Recently, different multivariate models have been proposed but a better rational is needed before implementing a screening strategy to identify women at risk for PE. We propose to undertake a simulation study to provide information on the cost/effectiveness of various relevant prediction models. Simulations are proposed because they are a suitable methodological approach to compare under similar conditions a large number of possible screening scenarios to be evaluated, as are the options for screening for women at risk for PE. This study will compare the actual preeclampsia management to various potential or existing screening options for the risk of developing the disease. These results should be particularly relevant and timely for decision makers who currently face pressures to introduce new tests aiming to identify the risk of the disease in pregnant women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Abdominal visceral fat measured in early pregnancy as a novel and practical early predictor of gestational diabetes mellitus
Keywords-MotsClés: GESTATIONAL DIABETES MELLITUS; GLUCOSE DYSREGULATION; INSULIN RESISTANCE; MATERNAL HEALTH; METABOLIC SYNDROME; METABOLISM; PRE-DIABETES; TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS; VISCERAL ADIPOSITY
Abstract-Résumé: Women with gestational diabetes (GDM) are at higher risk of having large babies, delivery problems & type 2 DM in the 4th-7th decades of life. The central cause may be deep abdominal fat and perhaps liver fat, reflective of a process called "insulin resistance" (IR). Current screening for GDM at 24-28 weeks of pregnancy uses a blood sugar test, which may be too little, too late, since IR may contribute to large baby growth starting in early pregnancy. We need a better method to identify women at risk of developing GDM who may have IR in early pregnancy. In a pilot study, we showed that ultrasound assessment of maternal deep abdominal fat at 12 weeks of pregnancy predicted sugar problems in later pregnancy. We will expand & improve on that study among a multicultutral cohort of 500 pregnant women. We will measure deep abdominal fat using ultrasound at 12 weeks of pregnancy, & assess how each predicts both blood sugar levels at 24-28 weeks & mother & baby health outcomes. In a sub-study, 1 in 4 of the 500 participants will have another ultrasound of their deep abdominal fat 6 weeks after delivery, alongside blood & insulin levels, to see how they each change from early pregnancy. GDM affetcs 3-10% of all pregnancies, and is a common health concern. Our research will generate an early GDM screening tool easily integretated into clinical practise, to enable earlier dietary therapy than is possible now. This should improve pregnancy outcomes, and may also help idendify women with GDM who are at highest risk of type 2 DM following their pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the effects of social, behavioural and metabolic factors on early childhood growth trajectories among Aboriginal Canadians
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; BREAST FEEDING; DIABETES MELLITUS (TYPE 2); EPIDEMIOLOGY; INFANT AND CHILD GROWTH; NUTRITION; OVERWEIGHT; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Adult onset (type 2) diabetes is a major public health challenge for First Nations communities in Canada. This condition often leads to long term complications, reduced quality of life and early death.  For almost 20 years, Sandy Lake First Nation and health researchers at the Universities of Toronto and Western Ontario have worked closely together to address the challenges of diabetes in this community.  Our successes to date have included the identification of risk and protective factors for new onset diabetes as well as diabetes complications, and the emergence of an independent, community-run diabetes prevention program.  The objective of the current grant is to improve our knowledge of diabetes in the community and to understand the importance of newly discovered diabetes risk factors.  Specifically, we plan to study the impact of social and behavioral factors of both mother and baby (including nutrition, social support and food security) on the growth of babies and young children over time.  These are factors that are potentially very important in the evolution of diabetes, yet they have received very little formal study among First Nations communities. This research will provide valuable information to enhance ongoing community intervention programs (www.sandylakediabetes.com).

TitreApplicationTitle: Diagnosis, prognosis and classification of retinopathies: Comparing time-amplitude domain (TAD) with time-frequency domain (TFD) analyses of the electroretinogram.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ELECTRORETINOGRAM; ERG MODEL; HUMAN; MATHEMATICAL MODELS; RESIDUAL VISION; RETINOPATHY; TIME-SCALE ANALYSIS; VISIUAL FUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The electroretinogram (ERG) identifies the electrical response evoked by the retina in response to a light stimulus of adequate energy. The ERG is to the retina what the electrocardiogram is to the heart. The ERG is essential not only for the diagnosis but also for the proper management of patients affected with a variety of retinal distrophies. Clinical ERG protocols usually require that photopic and scotopic ERGs be obtained from patients in order to assess rod and cone functions separately, as there are some retinopathies that can hinder one of the two retinal pathways preferentially, at least in the initial phase of the disease.  However, with progression usually one of the two retinal pathways is lost to the pathology, leaving the complementary one solely responsible for visually guided behaviors. Significantly reduced ERGs, with ill-defined morphologies, are often the only retinal signal remaining from patients affected with severe degenerative retinopathies. These residual retinal responses are often challenging to analyze. The aim of this research proposal is to demonstrate that use of newly developed mathematical tools can help in extracting, from residual ERGs, valuable clinical information. The possibility of using residual ERGs to stage the progression of severe debilitating retinopathies will allow us to construct a disease-symptoms classification system that will enable us to offer more accurate diagnoses and prognoses for the affected patients. This classification system will undoubtedly have a significant impact on the management of these patients, especially if cures become available.

TitreApplicationTitle: International Population-Based Evaluation of Drug Therapies Used to Manage Type 2 Diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR SYSTEM; DIABETES; HEALTH OUTCOMES; MORTALITY; PHARMACOTHERAPY; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Treatment of type 2 diabetes often requires the use of several oral drugs. Overall, these drugs help to lower blood sugar levels and reduce the risk of kidney, eye, and nerve damage. Differences appear to exist, however, with respect to the effect of each drug on the risk of cardiovascular disease (i.e., heart attack and stroke disease). For example, previous research has suggested that metformin, a common medication to lower blood sugars in diabetes, may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, while newer agents may in fact increase the risk. Given the wide spread use of newer drugs in the treatment of diabetes, better evaluation of the cardiovascular effects of these agents is required.   The range of drugs available to treat diabetes in Canada has recently expanded with the approval of a new oral drug to lower blood sugars - sitagliptin.  Sitagliptin is part of a new class of diabetes drugs that are quickly becoming a common choice to control blood sugars, yet their effects on heart disease and stroke are not known.   This study will measure the risk of heart disease and stroke in people using sitagliptin relative to other drugs, like metformin. Information from this study will help clinicians better determine which combination of drugs is safe and effective for the treatment of type 2 diabetes patients in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of T cell Activation by Stomatin-Like Protein 2
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNOLOGY; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; SLIPINS; STOMATIN-LIKE PROTEIN 2; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The defense of the body against infections relies on the function of a group of cells and organs known collectively as the immune system. One of the key cells in the initiation and regulation of specific immune responses against microbes is the T lymphocyte. T lymphocytes are also critical players in allergies, some autoimmune diseases such as diabetes or multiple sclerosis, and in the rejection of transplanted organs. Therefore, knowing how T cells are turned on and off is important not only to understand the working of the immune system in health and disease, but also as a way to develop novel treatments for those human diseases mediated by T cells. The aim of my laboratory is to identify the signals involved in the activation of T cells as well as how these signals are regulated.  We have recently found out that a novel molecule known as SLP-2 plays an important role in the activation of T cells by bringing the different components needed for their activation to the proper place inside the cell. We have discovered that changing the amount of SLP-2 expressed by the T cell changes the capacity of T cells to respond. More importantly, we have preliminary evidence that the amount of SLP-2 is increased in diseases with activation of the lymphocytes such as inflammatory responses, as well as in cancers of blood cells such as lymphomas and leukemias. The aim of this proposal is to understand how SLP-2 works and apply this knowledge to develop novel treatments to suppress undesirable T cell responses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effectiveness of Sitagliptin in Patients with Diabetes and Heart Failure: Population Based Cohort Study
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; DRUG THERAPY; HEALTH SERVICES; HEART FAILURE; MORTALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is present in 25-40% of all patients with heart failure and 20-30% of patients die within 1 year.  Significant controversy exists on how best to control blood sugars in patients with diabetes and heart failure. Currently, doctors are limited to only a few oral drugs to control blood sugars. Recently, a new oral diabetes medication, sitagliptin, has been marketed in Canada. Initial information strongly suggests sitagliptin has favorable effects on the heart.  However, whether these initial benefits result in improved health in real-world patients with diabetes and heart failure is unknown.    The goal of our study is to improve the management of people living with heart failure and diabetes. In particular, we want to see whether the newly available drug, sitagliptin, can reduce the need to be hospitalized and increase the number of patients who survive relative to other commonly used medications to control blood sugars in patients with heart failure and diabetes.  We have purchased data on approximately fifteen thousand patients living with diabetes and heart failure. Within this data, we have information on the types of drugs they used, other disease conditions, and any tests that their providers may have performed (e.g., kidney tests, cholesterol). We also have all of their complete health care utilization including admissions to hospital and information on patients whom died. Using this information, we will observe differences in the need for hospitalization and the risk of dying for people who used sitagliptin compared to people who did not use sitagliptin over time after accounting for differences in their age, sex, and disease characteristics.  Our study will be the first to evaluate sitagliptin in heart failure patients and will help clinicians and patients weigh the risks and benefits of this therapy relative to other oral drugs to lower blood sugars in patients with heart failure and diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intensive motor training after perinatal stroke to enhance walking
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL PALSY; CHILDREN; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; LOCOMOTION; PERINATAL STROKE; PLASTICITY; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Perinatal (around birth) stroke is devastating, because it permanantly affects a child for life. Almost all such children are diagnosed with cerebral palsy (CP), the most common cause of physical disability in children, of which approximately 70% have walking problems.  Symptomatic treatment involving bracing, Botox injections, and/or surgery is the current norm, executed after the problems emerge, and is of limited efficacy. Recent studies in kittens have shown that weakened brain pathways, similar to those in perinatal stroke, can be strengthened through intensive training at an early, CRITICAL PERIOD when the developing nervous system is most plastic, thereby restoring lost motor function. Surprisingly, intensive motor training during a critical period of nervous system development (estimated to be < 2 yr of age) is not a part of current therapy. Most CP children in Alberta receive leg therapy only ~1x/mo, starting around 2 yr of age. Thus, we ask if intensive leg therapy to improve walking produces better short- and long-term effects when applied DURING (< 2 yr old) vs AFTER (> 2 yr old) the critical period, and compared to when there is no intensive training at all.  A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is needed to answer this question; this study establishes the ground work for such an RCT.  Children with perinatal stroke from the two age groups will be trained to step on a motorized treadmill and to initiate movements with the impaired leg (kicking, climbing stairs, etc.) for 1 hr/day, 4 day/wk for 3 mo. We will compare their change in walking and leg function over the 3-mo training period to that of same-age children who receive standard treatment, and we'll track them at 4 yr of age. We will also use electrophysiological measures of the children to understand how the training affects neural pathways. This study will set the stage for an RCT to establish the neural mechanisms, efficacy and optimal timing of intensive leg training after perinatal stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular analysis of synapse development
Keywords-MotsClés: GABAERGIC SYNAPSE; HIPPOCAMPUS; IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE; KNOCKOUT MOUSE; MOLECULAR NEUROBIOLOGY; NEURON CULTURE; SYNAPSE DEVELOPMENT; SYNAPTIC ADHESION PROTEIN; SYNAPTIC PATHWAYS IN AUTISM
Abstract-Résumé: Brain development requires orchestrated formation of connections between nerve cells. These synaptic connections are the main units of communication in the brain, where chemical neurotransmitter signaling occurs. This research is about molecules that drive formation and organize the properties of nerve cell connections. The best-known triggers of nerve cell connections are proteins called neuroligin and neurexin. Binding of neuroligin on one nerve cell to neurexin on another nerve cell induces localized synaptic connection and neurotransmission. We recently identified novel signals that regulate the function of neuroligin, suppressing its ability to drive nerve cell connections. We will use a combination of molecular genetics, cell culture, fluorescence imaging, and electrophysiology to assess mechanisms of action of these novel regulators of neuroligin and to determine their role in brain development and function. Genetic variants in neurexin, neuroligin and their regulators increase risk of developing autism and schizophrenia. Thus, a goal of this research is to understand how these genetic alterations change brain chemistry and connectivity, and to develop more effective directed therapies for improving mental health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Classification and control of the electrical activities in the brain's neural networks under epileptic seizure conditions
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORKS; COMPUTER MODELS; EMPIRICAL MODE DECOMPOSITION; EPILEPSY; INTRACELLULAR AND EXTRACELLULAR RECORDINGS; NEURAL ENGINEERING; NEUROMODULATORS; RODENT HIPPOCAMPAL PREPARATIONS; SPATIOTEMPORAL SIGNAL PROCESSING; WAVELET TRANSFORM
Abstract-Résumé: Epilepsy is a disorder manifested by recurrent seizures. It affects ~1% of the population and is intractable in ~25% of patients. The currrent treatments include: anticonvulsive drugs, ketogenic diet, surgery and electrical (vagal and deepbrain) stimulation. The drug therapy may have significant side effects, and the existing electrical stimulation therapies have limited demonstrated efficacy for treating intractable epilepsies. The aim of this research is to provide the foundation for an alternative therapy which involves a "smart" device that learns a patient's seizure signature, and then delivers an appropriate electrical stimulus to supress the seizures.  We are proposing the development of software and hardware for an electronic device for classification of the various states of the brain's electrical epileptiform activities and then delivering appropriate "responsive" electrical stimuli to the brain tissue, at the right time and location, to suppress full-blown seizure events.   In the long term, this might significantly improve the quality of life for epileptic patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Synaptic signaling and remodeling by CaM kinase II
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM SIGNALING; CALPAIN; DENDRITIC PROCESSING; DENDRITIC SPINE; GLUTAMATE RECEPTORS; NMDA RECEPTOR; OPTICAL IMAGING; SINGLE MOLECULE IMAGING; SUPER RESOLUTION MICROSCOPY; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: During development the billions of cells that constitute our brain establish circuits through the formation of trillions connections, termed synapses. The circuits allow our brain to think, function, sense -and react to- our external stimuli. To improve our brain functions, these circuits remodel themselves by modifying their synapses. These processes can occur not only in development, but also in adult life. On the other hand, synaptic remodeling can also lead to the destructive changes in circuit connectivity that underlie brain disorders, including degenerative diseases, epilepsy and mental disorders. We have learned a great deal about the molecular processes that underlie constructive (learning) or destructive (disease) changes in brain circuitry, but much about these complex processes remains to be discovered. To learn more about synaptic remodeling, we are studying these processes at the cellular and molecular levels using a neuronal tissue culture model and biophotonics. We use advanced optical imaging approaches to probe molecular interactions inside nerve cells down to their individual synapses. We combine these approaches with monitoring synaptic transmission between neurons in these circuits, in order to link our live optical imaging observations with changes in synaptic transmission. Our research may have a significant impact on our understanding of the fundamental processes of brain function and may help elucidate the mechanisms that lead to alterations in brain circuitry in cognitive diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adolescent Socialization via the Internet:  An Exploration of the Social Cognitive and Contextual Correlates of Online Risk Behaviour
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ADOLESCENT HEALTH; AGGRESSION; DEVELOPMENTAL WELLBEING; INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY; PARENTS; PEERS
Abstract-Résumé: Adolescents spend a large amount of time online socializing with friends and acquaintances.  Indeed, communication technologies allow teenagers to be in near constant connection with their peers.  However, with this connectedness comes an increased risk of being exposed to cyberbullying, as well as privacy concerns related to disclosure of personal information online. This longitudinal research intends to explore how parents and peers relationships may be influencing these more adverse aspects of online socializing. Ideally this research will help ensure that the Internet, which is now a ubiquitous aspect of daily life, is a safe space for all children and youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: A randomized clinical trial of Oral analgesics Utilization for CHildhood musculoskeletal injuries (The OUCH Trial)
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALGESIC; CHILDREN; CLINICAL TRIAL; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; MUSCULOSKELETAL INJURIES; PAIN; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: Pain management of children presenting to the Emergency Department (ED) with a trauma to a limb is poorly treated even though musculoskeletal traumas (e.g. fractures, severe sprains) are considered to generate moderate to severe pain intensity. In spite of the fact that pain is considered one of the main symptoms for which children present to the ED, pain treatment remains suboptimal. In fact, children are less likely to receive an analgesic, and especially a strong analgesic, when compared to adults with similar traumas. This study aimed to improve pain treatment of children presenting to the ED with a musculoskeletal trauma to an arm or a leg. We will compare two different analgesic treatments (experimental) to a standard treatment (control) to find out if one of the experimental treatments controls the pain better than the standard treatment. Our secondary aim is to demonstrate that both treatments are safe to be administered to children and that they cause minimal side effects while providing adequate pain relief. We strongly believe that children should receive a better treatment for their pain. Adequately relieving acute pain in children is critical. Inadequate pain treatment can have detrimental effects; it can result in extended length of hospitalization, slower healing, emotional trauma, suffering, and altered pain processing in adulthood by decreasing the pain stimulus threshold of children. It also generates unnecessary stress in both the children and parents, and increases the risk of developing chronic pain on the long term. Given this knowledge, we feel that our study will provide evidence that will translate to an improvement of clinical practices regarding pain treatment of children with musculoskeletal traumas in the ED.

TitreApplicationTitle: Motor control: Brainstem control of locomotion
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN CONTROL; IMAGING; LOCOMOTION; MODULATION; SPINAL CORD INJURY; TRANSGENIC MICE; WHOLE CELL PATCH CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury is devastating due to the physical, societal, and economical harms incurred on individuals as well as on our society. Although the spinal cord contains all the circuitry necessary to locomotion, in the absence of commands from the brain, people with spinal cord injuries are unable to walk. Motor recovery can be partially achieved by strategies or therapies intended to regenerate axons from the brain to the spinal cord. Some of these approaches have reported such promising results in animal models that clinical trials are currently underway. However a major obstacle to achieving this goal is the lack of identification and characterization of appropriate targets at the brain and spinal cord levels, as well as the lack of knowledge of the mechanisms of plasticity of these targets. The current program aims to investigate the pathways between the brain and the spinal cord that are important to initiation and modulation of locomotion. This will enable us to identify and characterize the nervous circuits that need to be repaired in order to improve functional recovery following spinal cord injury or neurotrauma affecting the gait.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developmental dysgenesis of the mammalian brain: underlying mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETIC DISORDER; GROWTH FACTORS; NERVOUS SYSTEM; NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic or environmental alterations that lead to abnormal development of the human brain have been implicated in disorders ranging from intellectual disability to autism. While a significant amount of work is now focused in this area, we still have little understanding of the causes of these disorders. In this regard, over the past five years, we have provided evidence that some of these disorders might be caused by abnormal development of the neural stem cells that build the brain. Here we propose to ask whether genes that have been implicated in complex cognitive disorders like autism spectrum disorder function, at least in part, by perturbing neural stem cells and, if they do, to determine how this happens. We also propose to ask whether and how environmental perturbations like maternal infection can exacerbate the deleterious effects of mutations in these important genes, with a specific focus on growth factors.  It is our hope that by understanding the causes of these devastating disorders, we will ultimately be able to derive new therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: NOninvasve Repeated THerapeutic STimulation for Aphasia Recovery - NORTHSTAR
Keywords-MotsClés: APHASIA; BRAIN STIMULATION; RECOVERY; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: The current standard of care for rehabilitation of patients with aphasia after stroke is conventional speech and language therapy (SLT). Due to economic realities on most stroke units, SLT can often not be given with optimal intensity in the first weeks after the stroke. Developing new adjuvant therapies which may render SLT sessions more effective is thus one approach to improve rehabilitation outcome. Recent functional imaging studies in post-stroke aphasia, of our own group and others have shown that the recruitment of brain regions in the unaffected hemisphere seems to be an inferior strategy for recovery of language function as compared to re-activation of brain regions in the vicinity of the infarct. Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques, such as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) or transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) are new methods to modulate brain activity (e.g inhibiting contralateral over-activation). Evidence from our own feasibility study in sub-acute stroke suggests that these new techniques, when applied in conjunction with conventional SLT, may help to normalize brain activation patterns and might yield better rehabilitation outcome than SLT alone. With NORTHSTAR, we propose a multicenter proof-of-concept study to investigate the safety, feasibility and efficacy of these new non-invasive brain stimulation methods as adjuvant therapies for subacute post-stroke aphasia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cerebral blood flow in obstructive sleep apnea
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW; ENDOTHELIAL DYSFUNCTION; HYPOXIA AND HYPERCAPNIA; MECHANISMS; OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA; VENTILATORY STABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: In healthy humans, brain blood flow is influenced by changes in the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the circulating blood. However, the brain's important ability to regulate its blood flow is impaired in disease processes such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). People who have OSA stop breathing intermittently throughout the night, resulting in repeated episodes of low oxygen and high carbon dioxide in the blood. Because of these repeated episodes, the ability of the brain vessels to regulate blood flow becomes impaired. This impairment can lead to hypertension and stroke. The mechanisms that regulate brain blood flow in health, and how these mechanisms become impaired with disease, is poorly understood. It is thought that nitric oxide (NO) plays a major role in regulating blood flow in several vascular beds, including the brain. In a first study, we will determine, in an experimental human model of intermittent hypoxia during sleep, the effects of intermittent hypoxia on the regulation of brain blood flow and the role of changes in brain blood flow on the stability of breathing. In a second study, we will determine the extent to which the brain blood flow response to low oxygen is altered in a broad range of patients with moderate to severe OSA. We will compare the responses in the brain with those in the forearm. Finally, our research will determine if the brain blood flow impairments observed in untreated OSA patients can be corrected after treatment with night-time continuous positive airway pressure. This work may help us better understand conditions such as hypertension, OSA, stroke and aging, in which endothelium-dependent relaxation (i.e., relaxation of cells that line brain blood vessels) by NO is impaired. Our research will provide useful information about how well treatment for OSA reverses brain blood flow impairments that may lead to stroke. Ultimately, this will translate into improved health and disease prevention for Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Glycosyltransferases and their role in protein folding and quality control
Keywords-MotsClés: GLYCOSYLTRANSFERASES; POFUT1; POFUT2; PROTEIN FOLDING; PROTEIN-O-FUCOSYLTRANSFERASE; UDP-GLC:GLYCOPROTEIN GLUCOSYLTRANSFERASE; UGGT
Abstract-Résumé: Glycosyltransferases are enzymes that add monosaccharides to either proteins or carbohydrates.  In the ER of eukaryotic cells there are glycosyltransferases that are involved in ensuring that proteins destined for the cell surface or for secretion are properly folded.  Although this role is of fundamental importance in the proper functioning of the cell, little is know about how these enzymes mediate their functions.  By determining the structures of these enzymes we seek to understand how they recognize and glycosylate misfolded proteins. In the long term this work would be expected to have value in the development of therapeutics against viruses such as influenza and HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Unraveling the immune mechanisms of delayed onset of T cell immunity against pulmonary tuberculosis
Keywords-MotsClés: DESTRUCTIVE LUNG DISEASE; IMMUNE REGULATION; LUNG INFLAMMATION; LUNG MUCOSAL IMMUNITY; PULMONARY TUBERCULOSIS; T CELL RESPONSES
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic lung infectious disease which has been haunting humankind for thousands of years. One third of world population is latently infected. Every year 9 million people develop TB disease and about 2 million people die. Young children are particularly prone to TB. BCG is the only TB vaccine which has been used for 90 years but it has failed to effectively control TB in the lung. One unique phenomenon that scientists have noticed is that anti-TB immunity develops in a much slower pace after infection in the lung than the immunity against other types of lung infection. It is believed that this represents one important reason for the failure of BCG to protect the lung. Our current project sets out to decipher the mechanisms behind the mysterious sluggish immune responses to TB infection. Enhanced knowledge will help us design the new immune strategies to enhance lung protection in BCG-vaccinated young children.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of FOXP3 and IL-1-family cytokines in regulating CD4+ T cell subsets in healthy humans, and in patients with chronic skin inflammation.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNITY; FIBROBLASTS; GRAFT VERSUS HOST DISEASE; INFLAMMASOME; INTERLEUKIN 1; SKIN INFLAMMATION; SYSTEMIC SCLEROSIS; T HELPER CELLS; T REGULATORY CELLS; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system is designed to recognize the difference between harmful and non-harmful foreign proteins, and to not react against proteins that normally exist in an individual. Unfortunately, when the processes controlling these functions breakdown diseases such as autoimmunity and allergy can result. Although many different types of white blood cells work together to regulate immune responses, one of the major players is the CD4+ T cell. Via their ability to make proteins that send messages between cells, known as cytokines, CD4+ T cells have a central role in directing immunity in health and disease. We are interested in studying how the development and function of different types of CD4+ T cells is controlled since when they can cause much of the tissue destruction and injury in patients with autoimmune diseases. Our past research has revealed possible new pathways of regulation and in this proposal we will conduct research that is aimed at discovering how these new pathways work. The result will be a better understanding of how CD4+ T cells can cause disease and how their inappropriate function can be turned off in patients with chronic inflammatory diseases. .

TitreApplicationTitle: Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: etiology involving troponin mutations
Keywords-MotsClés: CA HANDLING; CARDIOMYOCYTE; CRYSTAL STRUCTURE OF TROPONIN COMPLEX; ISOTHERMAL CALORIMETRY (ITC); MOLECULAR DYNAMIC SIMULATION; MOLECULAR DYNAMIC SIMULATIONS; MYOFILAMENT CALCIUM SENSITIVITY; NMR STRUCTURE OF TROPONIN C; TROPONIN C
Abstract-Résumé: Familial hypertrophy cardiomyopathy (FHC) is a congenital heart disease which causes the walls of the heart to thicken (hypertrophy) and disrupts the organization of the heart's contractile machinery.  Even though numerous genetic defects (mutations) have been associated with FHC, the underlying cause is not understood.  As a result of this disease the heart restructures itself not just on a gross level that can be seen by echocardiography but also on a microscopic level, often resulting in irregularities in contraction and electrical disturbances (arrhythmias).  As a consequence of these events premature sudden cardiac deaths (SCD) are a common outcome of FHC.  The first objective is to address a possible mechanism for FHC.  We will explore one of the major hypotheses as to the cause of FHC by making mutations in the molecules (troponin C) which sense the signal (calcium concentration inside the heart cells) that serves as the coupling between cardiac excitation (as seen on an ECG) and contraction. We believe that mutations in the troponin complex which is made up of three protein including troponin C which are associated FHC alter the manner in which molecule interacts with calcium and we will test this hypothesis.  We will address the idea that sudden cardiac death in patients with FHC is due altered calcium handling at the cellular level and that the risk for SCD precedes the development of hypertrophy.  The work will be undertaken at many different levels of organization from a detailed structural analysis of the troponin C molecule, all the way to comprehensive studies on possible changes in the structure and function of the heart that occur as a result of the mutations engineered into this molecule.   This project focuses on events that occur very early on in the development of the disease.  We believe that because sudden cardiac death is often the first symptom of abnormality for these individuals, it is critical to understanding the underlying cause.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endocannabinoids in the regulation of gastrointestinal motility disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOCANNABINOIDS; ENTERIC NERVOUS SYSTEM; GI MOTILITY; INTESTINAL INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Precise patterns of gastrointestinal (GI) motility are required for the optimal digestion of food, absorption of nutrients and expulsion of waste.  There are serious health consequences when GI motility is disturbed in diseases such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).  Disordered motility causes impaired swallowing, heartburn, vomiting, early fullness, bloating, constipation, or diarrhea.  Both slowed and accelerated GI motility are frequently accompanied by abdominal pain and discomfort.  GI motility disorders affect millions of Canadians by negatively impact their quality of life and limiting daily activities.    Cannabis and its extracts (cannabinoids) have been used for centuries to alleviate the symptoms of GI motility disease by improving appetite, and reducing diarrhea, cramping and pain. The body makes molecules whose actions resemble cannabinoids which were discovered relatively recently and are called endocannabinoids.  Endocannabinoids are found in the GI tract and regulate gut motility in health.  Their role in GI motility disorders is not well understood.  We propose to explore the idea that by manipulating the levels of endocannabinoids can be used to treat disordered gut motility.  We will examine how endocannabinoids are involved in motility control in mouse models of GI disease.  Then using newly developed chemicals that increase or reduce the levels of endocannabinoids we will develop approaches to normalize disordered gut motility.         Cannabinoids represent powerful potential therapeutics for disorders of gut motility.  We will be able to make advances that could be translated to clinical applications for the treatment of motor disorders of the gut, including IBS and IBD, for which currently there are few effective therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The isolation and characterization of a novel population of neural stem cells in the adult brain.
Keywords-MotsClés: IN VIVO MOUSE MODELS; LINEAGE TRACING; NEURAL STEM CELLS; PLURIPOTENCY; PROLIFERATION; REGENERATION; STROKE; TRANSGENIC ANIMALS
Abstract-Résumé: Neurogenesis, the process of generating functional neurons from precursor cells, was traditionally thought only to occur during embryonic development. It is now well established that active neurogenesis occurs into adulthood. The neurogenic cells are derived from neural stem cells (NSCs) that reside in the adult brain in a well defined region lining the lateral ventricles. Our recent work has identified a novel population of adult stem cells within this same region, that display characteristics of pluripotency - an indication that they have the ability to differentiate not only into neural cell types, but into all cells that comprise the tissues of the body. The identification of this novel population of NSCs in the adult brain challenges our current understanding of the neural stem cell lineage and neurogenesis in the adult brain. In this proposal we will further characterize this rare population of cells and examine the lineage relationship between embryonic and adult derived neural stem cells and rigorously examine their pluripotentiality.  Together, these findings will advance our understanding of the neural stem cell lineage and neurogenesis in the adult brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding glucocorticoid action in the airways: Unravelling complexity
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; COPD; GENE EXPRESSION; GENE REGULATION; GLUCOCORTICOIDS; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: In asthma there is inflammation of the lung and which, if left uncontrolled, leads to worsening of symptoms, increasing discomfort and disability.  If unchecked this results in irreversible airway damage (airways remodelling) and ultimately, in the context of a severe asthma attack, possibly death.  Clinically, the most effective drugs to combat lung inflammation are inhaled synthetic glucocorticoids (corticosteroids).  By reducing the production of inflammatory mediators that are released by cells in the lung, these drugs resolve lung inflammation to improve asthma symptoms.  In this proposal, the molecular mechanisms by which glucocorticoids act to reduce inflammation are examined.  Glucocorticoids bind to a specific protein, the glucocorticoid receptor, which represses the synthesis (expression) of multiple inflammatory proteins.  While glucocorticoids work in the majority of asthmatics, many individuals could benefit considerably from an improved effectiveness. In this proposal, I critically examine mechanisms by which glucocorticoids may dampen inflammation in the lung. By understanding these processes, we will be better placed to improve the clinical effectiveness of these drugs. Finally, it is possible that not all the effects of glucocorticoids, in respect of modulating inflammation, are anti-inflammatory. By identifying potentially unhelpful aspects of glucocorticoid action, we can again take steps to improve therapies for those asthmatics who do not respond well to existing glucocorticoids.

TitreApplicationTitle: TiPARP is a mono-ADP-ribose transferase and a repressor of aryl hydrocarbon receptor activity
Keywords-MotsClés: ARYL HYDROCARBON RECEPTOR; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; GENE REGULATION; GENOMICS; PARP INHIBITORS; TCDD INDUCIBLE POLY(ADP) RIBOSE POLYMERASE (TIPARP); TRANSCRIPTIONAL REPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Poly(ADP-ribosylation) is a modification to a protein that is important for cell growth, DNA damage and changes in the expression of other proteins. Proteins that cause this modification are called poly-ADP-ribose polymerases or PARPs.  Blocking the action of PARPs is a potentially promising anti-cancer therapy. TiPARP is a member of the PARP protein family that is regulated by another protein called the aryl hydrocarbon receptor or AHR. AHR mediates most, if not all, of the toxic effects of environmental contaminants called dioxins. However, the biological function of TiPARP and its role in human disease, as well as its potential role in AHR action remain elusive. The overall objectives of this study are to elucidate the mechanism of action of TiPARP, determine how TiPARP protein expression is regulated and determine its role in the AHR signalling. To attain these objectives, we will use molecular and cellular biology techniques in conjunction with biochemical approaches and animal models. By determining the function of TiPARP and its role in AHR action, this research has the potential to lead to the development of new strategies for human disease and enable better estimates of the health risks associated with exposure to chemicals that activate AHR.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metallo-beta-lactamases; mechanistic and evolutionary studies for broad specificity and inhibitor binding.
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-LACATAMASE INHIBITOR; BETA-LACTAM ANTIBIOTICS; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; EXPERIMENTAL EVOLUTION; FUNCTION-STRUCTURE RELATIONSHIP; METALLO-BETA-LACTAMASE; MUTATIONS; NMR; SUBSTRATE SPECIFICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Pathogenic bacteria, such as P. aeruginosa. E. coli and K. pneumonia, can cause serious infectious diseases such as pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and diarrhea. These bacteria are becoming resistant to many commonly used antibiotics. In addition, the spreading of such pathogenic bacteria that are resistant to multiple antibiotics has become more rapid during the past decade. The resistant bacteria area serious threat to Canadian and global health, and new strategies are needed to combat them. The underlying cause for bacterial resistance is the action of a group of enzymes called beta-lactamases, which destroy beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin. Moreover, on-going changes in bacterial beta-lactamase genes in nature are producing more potent enzymes to destroy even our newest antibiotics.  This proposal describes research to study the ways that beta-lactamase enzymes change and adapt to antibiotics. We will combine experiments to identify mechanisms of change with detailed studies of enzyme function so that we can develop ways to block their activity. Ultimately, the information obtained in this research program will be used to develop novel, persistent and sustainable antibiotics and inhibitors against pathogenic bacteria.

TitreApplicationTitle: Subversion of host epithelial cell processes by Chlamydia infection.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEUPLOIDY; CHLAMYDIA INFECTION; CYTOKINESIS; EPITHELIAL CELLS; GOLGI; HOST PATHOGEN
Abstract-Résumé: Our lab studies how cells are affected by bacteria infection. We are interested in the bacterium, Chlamydia, which is the most common cause of sexually transmitted infections worldwide. Chlamydia usually infects the cells that line the human body, termed epithelial cells. We are interested in how this bacterium manipulates epithelial cells once it gets inside the cell. In order for Chlamydia to survive inside epithelial cells, it must obtain nutrients from the cell. We will study how Chlamydia manipulates cellular processes to acquire such nutrients, namely host cell amino acids and lipids. We believe that part of this pathogenic strategy involves blocking the process of cell division, resulting in host cells with more than one nucleus (multinucleated cells). Multinucleated cells are well linked to tumor formation and other studies have identified Chlamydia as a risk factor for human cervical cancer. In this proposal, we will determine the cellular targets of Chlamydia in epithelial cells and directly examine whether the Chlamydia-induced multinucleated cells can indeed lead to tumor formation. Chlamydia infections cause significant morbidity throughout the world and our studies may identify novel therapeutic targets for more effective intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Establishment of a role for docosahexanoic acid in the treatment of breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTINEOPLASTIC DRUGS; BREAST CANCER; DHA; DIET; FATTY ACIDS; MEMBRANES
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among Canadian women as 1 in 9 women over their lifetime will be diagnosed with this form of cancer.  In 2010, approximately 445 Canadian women per week were diagnosed with breast cancer and 5,300 died from this disease.  The vast majority of these women would have been offered some form of chemotherapy treatment.  Long chain polyunsaturated omega-3 fatty acids, found in fatty fish from cold water, have been shown to decrease breast cancer growth in laboratory animals and human cancer cells in culture (e.g. in petri dishes).  Recently, studies from our group have suggested that one of these omega-3 fatty acids, docosahexanoic acid or DHA, can improve the ability of a common chemotherapy drugs to kill breast cancer cells.  Our studies indicate that DHA can kill cancer cells using some of the same death signals that chemotherapy drugs use.  We are proposing that treating breast cancer cells with DHA will improve the effectiveness of current breast cancer chemotherapy drugs.  We will test this idea by growing human breast cancer cells grown in dishes in the lab and determining if the signals used by DHA to kill cancer are the same as the signals used by chemotherapy drugs. We anticipate that feeding the cells DHA will increase these signals after chemotherapy treatment.  Then, we will use a rodent model, commonly used to test cancer treatments, to demonstrate that feeding DHA before and during chemotherapy treatment improves the action of the drugs and the side effects experienced by patients. Our studies will provide evidence that an inexpensive dietary treatment will improve drug effectiveness without additional toxic side effects to the patient.  Our work has the potential to significantly benefit women diagnosed with breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translational and post-translational control of the mammalian circadian clock
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL ASSAYS; CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; GENE REGULATION; GENE TARGETING; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MICRORNA; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; UBIQUITIN LIGASE
Abstract-Résumé: Circadian (24-hr) rhythms of behaviour and physiology, including sleep-wake cycles and fluctuations in hormones and body temperature, are present in virtually all organisms, and allow them to keep track of, and adapt their needs according to, the time of day. In mammals, these rhythms are driven and maintained by biological clocks throughout the body, including the master circadian pacemaker in the brain, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which responds directly to changes in environmental light-dark (day-night) cycles. A set of core "clock genes" expressed in biological clocks represents the machinery that maintains time. The long-term goal of my research is to understand how biological clocks, in particular the SCN clock, are controlled, and how loss of proper control affects the physiology and behaviour of the organism. Recently, we found two novel genes in the mouse SCN that control circadian rhythms: microRNA-132 and UBR4. Both genes are activated by light. While we have data showing that miR-132 affects the ability of the SCN to react to light, virtually nothing is known about the role of UBR4 in biological timing. Thus, our goal here is to understand the functions of miR-132 and UBR4 in the control of circadian rhythms and how they interact with core clock genes to influence the timing process. We would also like to identify specific pathways that link miR-132 and UBR4 to the clock machinery. Since biological clocks affect many aspects of human health and disease (e.g. cancer, mental health disorders, obesity, and cardiovascular diseases), this work will provide new insights into mechanisms that maintain proper functioning of the biological clock and potential causes of circadian dysfunction during disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Real world Comparative Effectiveness and Safety of Dabigatran versus Warfarin
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICOAGULANTS; COMMUNITY LABORATORY DATA; COMPARATIVE EFFECTIVENESS; DABIGATRAN; HEALTH INFORMATION PRIVACY; LINKED HEALTHCARE DATABASES; PROPENSITY SCORE; RETROSPECTIVE COHORT DESIGN; WARFARIN
Abstract-Résumé: Dabigatran is the first in a series of new anticoagulants approved for atrial fibrillation (AF), which is the most common chronic heart rhythm problem in Canada and a common cause of stroke. Warfarin has been the standard anticoagulant for more than 50 years, with more than 5 million prescriptions written in 2010 in Canada. It is one of the most effective medications in chronic use. Dabigatran was approved for AF in 2010, and its use has increased rapidly amidst huge controversy over its relative effectiveness (stroke reduction) and safety (bleeding, heart attacks, lack of antidote, stopping) compared to warfarin. Dabigatran was the most common drug cause of severe or fatal injury reported to the United States FDA in 2011. Public drug plans in Canada, which provide for more than 95% of Canadian seniors, have indicated a strong interest in further evidence as to whether dabigatran is really as good or better than warfarin in usual clinical practice, and which patients will do better on which drug. We plan to compare the safety and effectiveness of these drugs using British Columbia health databases on prescription drugs, hospitalizations, medical services, and deaths with a novel linkage to laboratory test results. In a study group of over 40,000 new users of dabigatran or warfarin, followed for at least 12 months, we will compare the frequency of strokes, dangerous blood clots, heart attacks, hospitalization for bleeding, and deaths. Our unique, secure access to patient-specific laboratory results, allows us unprecedented ability to explain which patients will do better on dabigatran and who will do better on warfarin, using key tests of kidney, liver and blood function. Our team includes experts on anticoagulant drugs and their use by patients, plus experts on the British Columbia databases and on statistical methods for studies of drug effectiveness and safety.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physiology Basis of Resting-State Functional MRI
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICAL MODELING; BLOOD-OXYGEN LEVEL DEPENDENT (BOLD); CEREBRAL BLOOD FLOW (CBF); CEREBROVASCULAR REACTIVITY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY; HIGH TEMPORAL-RESOLUTION BOLD IMAGING; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHY (MEG); NEURONAL ACTIVITY; RESTING-STATE FMRI
Abstract-Résumé: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a powerful technology offering unprecedented opportunities for studying the healthy and diseased brain. In particular, functional MRI (fMRI), one of the most momentous developments in medical imaging, measures signals related to brain activity, and the methodology has since found applications in the treatment of diseases such as stroke, Parkinson's and epilepsy. The past decade has witnessed an exponential growth in the application of resting-state fMRI in scientific and medical research. Resting-state fMRI has been used to derive functional connectivity, with the participants completely at rest. Functional connectivity is a main focus of the Human Connectome Project, which has received tremendous attention in the scientific community. However, the physiological mechanisms of the resting-state fMRI signal are not fully understood, raising questions and concerns regarding its interpretation.  The overall objective of the proposed research is to advance the understanding of resting-state fMRI. In light of the urgency in understanding resting-state connectivity, we propose to decipher the physiological mechanisms underlying the resting-state fMRI signal in the healthy adult population through novel acquisition and modeling approaches. The proposed research will provide improved methods for measuring the resting-state fMRI signal underlying functional connectivity. This signal is critical for the appropriate characterization of neuronal health in the healthy brain, and particularly valuable for the early detection of functional degeneration. The methodology described here are technically innovative, being at the cutting edge of MRI development. The ultimate goal of this work is to achieve a more complete physiological understanding of functional connectivity, which is essential for establishing it as a powerful tool for studying human brain connectomics, and more importantly, as an early biomarker for disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuronal mechanisms of stress-induced overeating
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOR; BINGE EATING; FEEDING; IN SITU HYBRIDIZATION; LATERAL SEPTUM; MULTICHANNEL RECORDING; NEURONAL TRACING; NUCLEUS ACCUMBENS; PREFRONTAL CORTEX; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Binge eating is a serious health problem that affects about 3% of the population. Affected people describe daily exhausting struggles with this disorder, which is disastrous from the psychological and metabolic points of view. Accumulating evidence suggests that bingeing episodes usually represent attempts to cope with chronic stress by overeating palatable food. This fact by itself is quite surprising given that evolutionarily the role of stress was to decrease appetite and inhibit digestion. The anorectic effect of stress generally provides the possibility of redirecting blood flow to the muscles and focusing the sensory systems on immediately managing the stressful situation. The present project will seek out how chronic stress may alter the neuronal mechanisms which instead of an anorectic reaction would trigger overeating.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the role of Nodal signaling in the establishment and maintenance of pregnancy
Keywords-MotsClés: EMBRYO IMPLANTATION; MOUSE; PLACENTA; TGF-B SIGNALING; TRANSGENIC; UTERUS
Abstract-Résumé: It has been estimated that over 10% of all pregnancies exhibit some form of complication. One of the most common and dangerous is preterm delivery. A child that is born prematurely may suffer severe consequences which may lead to death of the child. Furthermore, mothers that give birth to a child prematurely often have high blood pressure and kidney problems, a condition known as preeclampsia. Severe preeclampsia can potentially lead to death if not detected at an early stage. Why certain women are at high risk of preterm birth and preeclampsia is poorly understood and multiple causes have been associated with these complications. Our lab has been looking at the function of a protein called Nodal that is expressed in the uterus during pregnancy. We have eliminated this protein in mice and found that in the absence of Nodal, the mothers have preterm birth and preeclampsia. Our studies have also shown that Nodal is affected in families that suffer from early onset of preeclampsia demonstrating a role for this protein in humans. In this proposal, we will study the effect of removing Nodal in the uterus of mice to understand its role in preterm birth. Understanding the function of Nodal will allow us to further understand the causes of preterm birth and preeclampsia and eventually give us tools to detect and potentially improve treatments in women experiencing preeclampsia and at high risk of preterm birth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Function of SMAD7 in growth and differentiation of skeletal muscle
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; GROWTH; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: A variety of muscle diseases and ageing related muscle wasting result from a loss of muscle mass. We have discovered a gene called Smad7 which regulates skeletal muscle growth. So far these observations have been made in cultured muscle cells. In the proposed work we would like to develop this work further to understand how Smad7 has this effect on muscle cells and also to determine whether it fulfills the same function in living animals.

TitreApplicationTitle: An autologous cell therapy approach to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy using engineered muscle tissue derived from induced pluripotent stem cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL THERAPY; GENE THERAPY; IMMUNOGENECITY; IPSC; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; MYOBLASTES; ZINC FINGER NUCLEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is due to a mutation of the dystrophin gene, which leads to the absence of this protein in the myofibers and as a consequence to muscle fiber damage and muscle weakness. There is currently no cure for this deadly disease. We believe it should be possible to restore, at least partially, muscle functions by injecting muscle cells (myoblasts) derived from a donor not affected by the disease.  Unfortunately this strategy is greatly limited by the fact that the donor myoblasts would not be immunologically compatible and thus would be rejected by the patient immune system. The use of immunosuppressive drugs is thus required, leading to severe side effects that compromise the success of the graft. Here, we have collected preliminary results showing that it is possible to modify DMD patient own myoblasts so that they express a non-mutated copy of the dystrophin gene and to generate a large number of these gene-corrected myoblasts through the use of a new technology involving the generation of stem cells called induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). This novel strategy should allow treating DMD patients using a cell therapy strategy without the need to use immunosuppressive drugs.
