TitreApplicationTitle: The burden of depression on mortality over six decades
Keywords-MotsClés: DEPRESSION; EPIDEMIOLOGY; MORTALITY; RISK FACTORS; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Major depression afflicts about 5% of the Canadian population in any year, and costs the Canadian economy more than $14 billion each year. It degrades social functioning and physical health significantly, and its most severe consequences include early death. Because prior studies on depression and mortality were based on fairly short follow-up times, the existing evidence derives from depression's short-term effects. The current application proposes to investigate the association between depression and death with a long focus: six decades. We will do so in one of the longest running studies of psychiatric disorders - the Stirling County Study - that dates back to the early 1950s and consists of three successive samples (1952, 1970, and 1992) involving 4,140 subjects. We propose to link these survey responses to Statistics Canada data up to 2011, thereby providing 59 years of follow-up data on mortality for the 1952 sample, 41 years of follow-up data on the 1970 sample, and 19 years of follow-up data on the 1992 sample. The proposed research has three specific aims. The first aim is to investigate premature death associated with depression in the three Stirling County Study Samples, and to determine whether mortality rates differ by gender and socioeconomic status. The second aim is to determine which types of depression are most strongly associated with mortality, by investigating clinically identified sub-types of depression thought to be most severe, and scientifically identified sub-types based on results of statistical analyses of depressive symptoms recorded among participants in 1992. The third aim is to investigate the role of other risk factors for disease in the association between depression and mortality, focusing on alcoholism, obesity, cigarette smoking, and heart problems. The successful completion of these aims will yield new insights into the consequences of depressive illness and will contribute to reducing the public health burden of depression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeted nanomedicines for gene therapy applications.
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG DELIVERY; GENE TARGETING; GENE THERAPY; GLAUCOMA; IN VIVO TESTING; NANOPARTICLES; NEUROPROTECTION; NON-INVASIVE DELIVERY SYSTEMS; NON-VIRAL GENE DELIVERY; PHARMACEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: The objective in gene therapy is the introduction of a missing or defective gene into the cell nucleus where the encoded protein can be expressed. During the transfection process the DNA crosses several barriers such as the cellular, lysosomal, and nuclear membranes prior to expression.This research program will develop efficient non-viral gene delivery systems for application through the cornea and cellular barriers to achieve local expression of therapeutic proteins for in the retina after topical needle-free application as eye-drops. Clinical application of this new technology will be in patients with glaucoma, where it is expected to protect the optic nerve and preserve vision.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Rescuing the insulin exocytotic defects in type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOSKELETON; DIABETES; EVANESCENT MICROSCOPY; INSULIN EXOCYTOSIS; LENTIVIRUS; MULTIPHOTON MICROSCOPY; PATCH CLAMP ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; SNARE PROTEINS
Abstract-Résumé: In pancreatic islet beta-cells, only a small number of insulin secretory granules (SGs) are docked onto the plasma membrane (PM) and only a fraction of these docked SGs are competent or 'primed' for immediate release. Each of these sequential steps leading to secretion - release from a reserve pool within the cytoskeleton mesh just beneath the PM, insulin SG mobilization and docking onto the PM, where they undergo some time to get  primed in order to become competent to undergo membrane fusion (exocytosis), are mediated by distinct sets of molecules. We recently found that majority of insulin SGs undergoing exocytosis actually arise from 'newcomer SGs' that undergo only minimal to no docking time on the PM before exocytosis; and that SGs could fuse with each other (SG-SG fusion) without having to all get to the PM to undergo exocytosis. These two novel modes of exocytosis are very efficient and could compensate for the secretory deficiency in diabetes believe to be due to the loss of fusion-competence of the pool of docked SGs. In the previous granting period, we found several of the molecules mediating the recruitment of newcomer SGs and SG-SG fusion, which we now would like to express in the pancreatic islets of diabetic rats by viral infection to see if this will improve glucose control and insulin secretion in diabetes. We also discovered and will further explore a novel protein (Septin 5) that is part of the cytoskeleton, which when disrupted could release more insulin SGs to undergo exocytosis.  Insights gained from this work may reveal novel sites within these alternate pathways of exocytosis which could be targeted for drug design to optimize insulin secretion to achieve normal glycemic control in diabetes, and avert the ensuing acute and chronic diabetic complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulating Rab-mediated membrane trafficking in cell physiology and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: DENN DOMAIN; ENDOSOMES; GEF; GUANINE-NUCLEOTIDE EXCHANGE FACTOR; MENTAL RETARDATION; NEURITE OUTGROWTH; RAB; SYNAPSE DEVELOPMENT; TGN; TRANS-GOLGI NETWORK
Abstract-Résumé: Cells are highly compartmentalized and proteins move between the compartments in small membrane bound transport carriers. This process, called membrane trafficking allows proteins to function at their proper cellular location.  Membrane trafficking is highly regulated and alterations in the proteins that mediate and regulate membrane trafficking is a feature of many human diseases. One key class of proteins functioning in this process are Rabs, small proteins that act as switches by changing their chemical state. Rabs also regulate cell shape by controlling the actin cytoskeleton. We have identified a new class of proteins that regulate these regulators. This grant application will characterize these proteins in order to learn more about membrane trafficking and actin cytoskeleton dynamics and what goes wrong with these processes in disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; METABOLISME ET NUTRITION
TitreApplicationTitle: Sex-specific regulation of food intake: the role of relaxin-3
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY WEIGHT; CRF; FEEDING; FEMALES; GENE SILENCING; IN SITU HYBRIDIZATION; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALING; RELAXIN-3; SEX; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: The rate of incidence of stress-induced binge eating and prevalence of obesity associated with this disorder is approximately10 times higher for women compared to men. The underlying neuronal basis of this sexual dimorphism is not yet known. However, the causes triggering and precipitating eating disorders have become more evident. Thus, chronic stress and repeated food restriction have been identified as strong antecedents and relapse factors of binge eating. Repeated episodes of overeating increase the prevalence of obesity. To study the neuronal and molecular mechanisms of eating disorders in females, we have developed a rat model in which chronic stress and repeated food restriction trigger overeating and increase body weight in female but not male rats. Our results suggest that sex-specific regulation of brain expression of orexigenic neuropeptide relaxin-3 may be a cause of overeating and increased body weight in chronically stressed females. This research proposal is focused on the role of relaxin-3 in sex-specific regulation of food intake and body weight in female rats. The results of this project will help to understand why approximately 90% of individuals hospitalized for eating disorders are women, and will suggest pharmacological and neurogenetic therapeutic strategies.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: The Contribution of Leptin to Myocardial Hypertrophy, Remodelling and Failure:  Mechanisms and Studies Into Leptin-Adiponectin Interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPONECTIN; CELL SIGNALLING; HEART FAILURE; HYPERTROPHY; LEPTIN; MITOCHONDRIA; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Leptin (derived from the Greek word Leptos which means thin) is a small protein synthesized primarily from fat cells called adipocytes.  Leptin levels in the blood are generally quite low but are greatly increased in obesity.  Although the major function of leptin is to supress appetite by acting on specific regions in the brain, it also acts directly on the heart to produce an abnormal increase in heart growth called hypertrophy (which contributes to heart failure) and also, interestingly, leptin is produced by the heart itself.  The present study aims to understand the complex mechanisms by which leptin exerts its deleterious effect.  Adipocytes can actually produce a variety of these proteins which are collectively called adipokines.  Among these adipokines is one called adiponectin which exerts effects opposite to those of leptin and which is generally considered as a beneficial factor. As for leptin, adiponectin is also produced by the heart.  Our theory is that a balance between leptin and adiponectin production will determine the overall effect of leptin, in other words maintaining high adiponectin levels will attenuate the effects of leptin.  Thus, using a large number of experimental approaches we will study the nature of this interaction and its underlying mechanisms.  We hope and anticipate that this study will reveal the importance of key adipokines to the development of heart failure.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation and Function of MEF2 in cardiac and skeletal muscle
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC DISEASE; GENE EXPRESSION; HYPERTROPHY; MYOGENESIS; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: MEF2 is a protein molecule in the heart and skeletal muscle that serves to orchestrate the control of many genes. In this regard, MEF2 serves as a communication hub between signals from outside the cell and the control of gene expression within the cell nucleus. Thus, MEF2 sits at a pivotal point in regulating key aspects of heart and skeletal muscle cell function. We are trying to understand the nature of these processes and also learn how to modulate them pharmacologically so that some control over cardiac gene expression can be exerted in pathological circumstances such as heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Heat stress in older adults and individuals with type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BODY HEAT STORAGE; DIABETES; EXERCISE; HEAT STRESS; METABOLISM; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SKIN BLOOD FLOW; SWEATING; THERMOREGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Prolonged exposure to hot environments or performing strenuous physical activity can heat the body.  This heat is lost by contact with cool air and by sweat production, which cools the body as the sweat evaporates.  However, when the body is unable to cool itself by sweating, several heat-induced illnesses such as heat stress or heat exhaustion and the more severe heat stroke can occur, and can result in death.  Aging and chronic medical conditions such as Type 2 diabetes may cause changes in the body's normal response to heat.  This means that older adults and individuals with Type 2 diabetes may be at a greater risk of suffering from a heat-related injury or death.  This project will assess the extent to which aging and Type 2 diabetes affect the body's ability to dissipate heat.  We will use the world's only whole-body direct calorimeter (a device for making very accurate measurements of the amount of heat emitted by the human body) to assess how older adults and individuals with Type 2 diabetes respond to increasing levels of heat stress at rest and during physical activity.  By understanding how heat stress may develop in these individuals, we can develop appropriate heat planning and management strategies to protect our aging population and workforce and those with chronic disease from the detrimental health effects associated with heat exposure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Presynaptic NMDA receptors in neocortical plasticity
Keywords-MotsClés: LTD; LTP; MICROCIRCUIT; NEOCORTEX; NMDA RECEPTOR; STDP
Abstract-Résumé: We study learning and memory in the brain, because this is important for essentially everything that the brain does. Decades of research have highlighted the importance of N-Methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors in learning in the healthy brain, as well as in pathologies due to epilepsy, schizophrenia, or illicit drug use. Much of this work focused on receptors that were on the receiving end at connections between neurons, but more recent research has revealed that there are NMDA receptors located on the transmitting side. This raises the possibility that some interpretations published in the prior literature are flawed or even erroneous, since some researchers may have focused on the wrong location. Because NMDA receptors are at the heart of memory processing in the healthy brain, and because they are implicated in a multitude of disease states, a much improved understanding of these novel NMDA receptors is therefore desperately needed.  Our proposed research aims to elucidate the precise location of these novel receptors as well as their function in short-term information transmission and in long-term information storage in the brain. Our proposed project will clarify this field of research, which is presently rife with controversy. It will shed light on so-called synaptic diseases that are due to e.g. illicit drugs or epilepsy, where NMDA receptors have long been implicated.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional and Symptom Trajectories in Elderly Chronic Kidney Disease Patients and their Association with Dialysis Initiation
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DIALYSIS; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; ELDERLY; FUNCTIONAL STATUS; QUALITY OF LIFE; SURVIVAL; SYMPTOM BURDEN; TRAJECTORY OF ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: More than 50% of people starting dialysis in Canada are > 64 years old.  Older patients have extremely high rates of death, hospitalization and functional decline after starting dialysis. Dialysis may provide little or no benefit for some older patients. Certain older patients managed without dialysis may live almost or as long as patients who start dialysis, with better preservation of function and quality of life.  Unfortunately, we are unable to identify patients for whom dialysis is unlikely to result in a benefit, thus limiting the ability to align treatment with patients' goals. This study would be the first to evaluate clinically meaningful outcomes of patients > 64 years with stage 5 CKD; and to relate these findings to healthcare use.  We will a) characterize survival, function, quality of life, symptom burden, and transition to institutionalized care in patients after development of stage 5 CKD and b) in the last year of life, taking into account the presence or absence of dialysis.  We will also identify characteristics associated with poor and good outcomes.  Predicting these trajectories will aid timely and effective planning of supportive services. Identifying patients likely to do poorly with dialysis and well without dialysis, will influence patient decision-making, help effective planning of dialysis services, and help determine care plans aligned with patients' goals; c) characterize health care resource use for this population and determine factors associated with resource use.  Defining healthcare use will identify unmet needs and help develop health service policies that allow more efficient resource use. Study results will inform the development of decision aids for clinicians and older patients around dialysis starts that could be tested in randomized trials.  They will also inform the development of care pathways for older patients unlikely to benefit from dialysis, which could then be evaluated for their impact on patient outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Upscaling data to develop knowledge translation theory for child healthcare contexts
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE STUDY; CHILD HEALTH/PEDIATRICS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MIXED METHODS; THEORY BUILDING
Abstract-Résumé: Healthcare for children is not immune to the significant challenges of ensuring that clinical research is informed by the best available research evidence. Clinical practice guidelines and clinical pathways are strategies used within healthcare to ensure clinical practice is based on the best available research, however, little is known about the factors that affect how these strategies are used in child healthcare settings. Understanding the unique patterns and nuances of child healthcare settings is critical to ensuring that the best available health research is consistently implemented in child healthcare practice. This innovative study will explore the mechanisms and factors that shape the use of clinical practice guidelines and clinical pathways that have been implemented in child health care settings, in Canada. By employing ground breaking techniques, data from five previously funded and completed studies will be combined and reanalyzed to develop this needed nursing science. Without the added costs of new data collection, time consumption and significant human resources, this project will be accomplished in the most effective way. This project has the potential to yield large dividends in terms of improved child health outcomes and more efficient care utilization. The resulting knowledge will be important to senior health administrators and decision makers, health care professionals and health service researchers to ensure that child health care is based on the best available research, knowledge and science.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of Emergency Department Probiotic Treatment of Pediatric Gastroenteritis: Randomized Controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: DISEASE SEVERITY; ECONOMIC ANALYSIS; EMERGENCY MEDICINE; GASTROENTERITIS; PROBIOTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Background: In Canada, gastroenteritis results in nearly 240,000 emergency department visits by children each year. Children seen in emergency departments often develop moderate to severe disease following their evaluation. This may include having prolonged symptoms resulting in an inability to attend daycare and for their caregivers to return to work. Because the vast majority of cases are caused by organisms against which antibiotics are ineffective, medications are not routinely recommended; however, a new option has emerged. Probiotics, which are live bacteria that have a beneficial effect on the health of the host, have demonstrated promise in recent trials in hospitalized children. Positive findings include the ability to reduce the durations of diarrhea and hospitalization. Because of a paucity of strong evidence, particularly from developed countries and outpatient settings, at present, probiotics are rarely used in clinical practice.  Study Design: We propose to conduct the first multicentre, North American, emergency department clinical trial of probiotic therapy in children with gastroenteritis. Employing Canada's largest pediatric emergency medicine research network, Pediatric Emergency Research Canada, and five geographically diverse pediatric emergency departments, 886 children will be randomly assigned to receive a probiotic powder or placebo twice daily for five days.  Objectives: We will answer four questions: 1-does providing a probiotic agent to children reduce the severity of disease; 2-what side effects occur when a short course of probiotics are provided; 3-how do probiotics work in children with gastroenteritis; 4-is probiotic use cost-effective.  Significance: Together, these outcomes will address all the important questions regarding probiotic use in this population - clinical effectiveness, safety, mechanism of action, and economic benefit.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: The reversibility of vasectomy used for contraception in men
Keywords-MotsClés: ANDROLOGY; CONTRACEPTION; INFERTILITY; MALE FERTILITY; REPRODUCTIVE TRACT; SPERMATOZOA
Abstract-Résumé: Vasectomy is now the male contraceptive choice for more than 100 millions men worldwide. Due to changes in their personal life, an increasing number of men undergo surgical vasectomy reversal. The surgical success of this procedure reaches 70-85% while prognancy occurs in only 15% of these surgical successful cases. While female contraception safety and reversibility have been exhaustively documented over the last decades, male contraception reversibility remains questionable. This research proposes to investigate the sequelae occurring to the male reproductive tract in vasectomised men and how this can affect fertility following surgical vasectomy reversal.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating behavioural, electrophysiological, and neurochemical facets of dorsal auditory stream impairment in persons with schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY PROCESSING; DORSAL-VENTRAL PROCESSING STREAM; EEG; ERP; EVOLUTION; GABA; MRS; NEURODEVELOPMENT; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: The brain can be subdivided into circuits that occupy its top (dorsal) and bottom (ventral) parts. This dorsal-ventral organization is manifest in the expansion of the brain's surface (cortex) across species and the maturation of the brain from infancy to adulthood. Research suggests that neurodevelopmental disorders, including Schizophrenia (SCZ), may be caused by the improper development of dorsal circuits. For example, vision is controlled by separate dorsal and ventral pathways that work closely together and SCZ has been linked to abnormalities in the dorsal visual pathway. The auditory system is organized in a similar fashion. However, whether SCZ also results in dorsal auditory pathway dysfunction is untested. This is an important step because auditory hallucinations, a prominent SCZ symptom, may arise explicitly from irregularities in this pathway. This proposal also examines the neurophysiology and neurochemistry of these problems. Specifically, activation of the dorsal auditory pathway results in prototypical brainwaves, known as gamma oscillations. In turn, gamma oscillations are controlled by a brain chemical known as GABA. Compromised gamma oscillations and GABA neurotransmission are believed to underlie many of the symptoms of SCZ. However, it is not clear whether these anomalies are related to disturbances in dorsal versus ventral circuitry. Therefore, this study will ascertain if (a) people with SCZ have dorsal auditory pathway impairment and (b) this impairment is due to deficient GABA neurotransmission and consequent disruption in gamma oscillations. Auditory performance will be measured using computerized hearing tests, while brainwaves and GABA will be measured using noninvasive, specialized neuroimaging techniques - electroencephalography and magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Defining which brain systems underlie the development of SCZ may lead to new treatments specifically targeting those brain circuits that are critical to symptom production.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Development and Evaluation of State of the Art Prognostication in a Novel Palliative Care Program for Patients with Advanced Chronic Kidney Disease in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DIALYSIS; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; FUNCTIONAL STATUS; PALLIATIVE CARE; PROGNOSIS; SURVIVAL; TRAJECTORY OF ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Palliative care has historically focused on advanced cancer.  However, people with advanced non-cancer conditions also need excellent end of life care.  We have shown that patients dying with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) have extensive end-of-life care considerations. They have exceedingly high mortality rates of 20% - 25%/ year and typically experience substantial physical, emotional and spiritual suffering and high levels of disability for many months or years before death.  These patients rarely access palliative care services and the quality of their dying experience is poor.   This study aims to characterize the functional decline of patients dying with stage 5 CKD and evaluate and refine prognostic strategies to identify those with shortened survival within a novel palliative care program implemented recently within the Northern Alberta Renal Program (NARP). Specifically, we will 1) characterize the functional decline in the last year of life.  This will aid timely and effective planning of palliative and supportive care services for patients with advanced CKD and help better determine the optimal time to shift to a palliative approach to care; 2) validate the prognostic model that has been integrated programmatically as part of the renal palliative care program within NARP and further develop this model with the overall aim of establishing a clinical and research standard to identify patients with the shortest survival.  The ability to prognosticate survival is critical to provide effective and timely palliative care and will permit appropriate alignment of palliative care resources to the needs of CKD patients.  The results from this study will help improve referral, clinical practice, and overall access to palliative care services for patients with advanced CKD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innate lymphocyte development
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW STEM CELLS; COMMON LYMPHOID PROGENITOR; INNATE LYMPHOCYTE; LYMPHOCYTE DEVELOPMENT; NATURAL HELPER CELL; NATURAL KILLER CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Recently, new types of lymphocytes called innate lymphocytes have been discovered.  Unlike conventional lymphocytes, which respond to specific antigens and generate antibodies and cell-mediated immunity, innate lymphocytes do not respond to specific antigens. Instead they are activated by small hormone-like proteins called cytokines produced by other cells and they produce their own cytokines, which act on surrounding cells. Innate lymphocytes can be divided into multiple families based on the cytokines they produce. They are mostly found in the gut and lung and serve as a first line of defense against worms, some bacteria and fungi. The production of too much cytokines by innate lymphocytes also causes tissue inflammation, which leads to diseases such as asthma and inflammatory bowel disease.  The goal of this study is to find out how innate lymphocytes are generated from stem cells in the bone marrow. Currently, how conventional lymphocytes are generated from bone marrow stem cells is well studied. In contrast, very little is known about how innate lymphocytes are generated. Recently we and others have found the proteins that are critical for the generation of different families of innate lymphocytes. We have also found immature innate lymphocytes in the bone marrow. Based on those previous studies, we now plan to find out how individual families of innate lymphocytes are generated from immature lymphocytes in the bone marrow and how these processes are controlled.  Innate lymphocytes have to be continuously produced from immature lymphocytes in the bone marrow. We hope to find a way to control the number of specific family of innate lymphocytes without affecting other lymphocytes. This study may lead to new ways of treating asthma and inflammatory bowel disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Neurosciences cliniques et des systèmes - A
TitreApplicationTitle: Activation of Metalloproteinases in AMD - A Novel Strategy for Treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION; AMYLOID BETA; DRUSEN; FRACTALKINE; GEOGRAPHIC ATROPHY; INFLAMMATION; PHOTORECEPTORS; PROTEASES; RPE; TNF-A
Abstract-Résumé: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the elderly. Unfortunately, current treatments only exist for the advanced form of AMD and begin after significant eye damage has already occurred. Chronic inflammation and abnormal formation of new blood vessels play a significant role in this complex multifactorial disease. Our proposal will focus on special enzymes, called proteases that shape the cellular environment in the retina. Abnormal activation of these proteases can cause inflammation by releasing harmful molecules such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF) in the eye. Our group has developed a way to use the proteases so that instead of harmful factors, they release therapeutic factors. It is important that the therapeutic factor is only released when it is needed to minimize any potential side effects in the retina The long term goal of this novel and first-in-class strategy is to have the retinal cells release the engineered therapeutic factors only at the site of inflammation and injury, in timely manner, and only when the injurious processes have reached a certain critical threshold. Our proposed "smart" therapeutic strategy will be positioned in retinal cells in advance of disease, and work as needed to reduce the negative systemic and off-target effects frequently associated with current therapies for eye disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cortical connectivity in neurodevelopment and neurodegeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN NETWORKS; BRAIN-BEHAVIOUR; CONNECTIVITY; MRI; NEURODEGENERATION; NEURODEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Different brain regions grow and degenerate in a coordinated pattern. We will map the differences in this pattern across individuals, across normal development, abnormal development and in neurodegenerative disease. Using large brain databases already in existence, we will relate these structural connectivity differences across individuals to differences in normal performance in memory, language and motor skills as they change over time and as they are degraded in Alzheimer's Disease. Finally, we will use animal models of brain plasticity during learning to investigate the microstructural basis of structural connectivity observed with MR imaging in human brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implications of pathologic changes to bone material properties on the skeletal stability of the metastatic spine
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICAL TESTING; COLLAGEN; DAMAGE; FINITE ELEMENT ANALYSIS; MICROIMAGING; MINERAL; RODENT MODEL; SKELETAL METASTASES; SPINE
Abstract-Résumé: Many malignant cancers (for example breast, lung, and prostate cancer) can spread (metastasize) from their site of origin. A very common site of this spread is to the bone. The spine is the most common bone tissue affected. Metastatic disease in the bony spine (vertebrae) can present as bone destroying (osteolytic), bone forming (osteoblastic) or as a mixture of the two (mixed). Diseased vertebrae can cause pain and have an increased risk of breaking (fracture), impacting physical mobility. We aim to understand the differences that exist in the quality of bone affected by metastatic cancer (including tissue level material changes) in order to develop better computer based / imaging methods that can accurately identify the initiation of damage in bone and its progression to fracture. This research will determine the complex behaviour of cancer spread in the bony spine using state-of-the-art medical imaging, experimental and computational methods. The ability to accurately determine the structural integrity of the metatstatic spine will provide an important foundation on which improve diagnosis. As well this information will provide focus to the development and evaluation of targeted local (i.e. minimally invasive therapies) and systemic treatments with respect to their effects on bone tissue. This research will ultimately help Canadians through better understanding of the essential changes in bone due to cancer that have the greatest effect on spinal stability and the risk of vertebral fracture and direct us in developing and better assessing the potential of new and existing therapies for bone metastases.

TitreApplicationTitle: SNCAIP: A novel oncogene restricted to Group 4 medulloblastoma
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BRAIN TUMORS; ONCOGENES; PEDIATRICS
Abstract-Résumé: The most common type of pediatric brain cancer is called medulloblastoma.  Medulloblastoma is made up of four different types of cancer, with the most common being called Group 4 medulloblastoma.  Unfortunately we know the least about the genes that drive Group 4 medulloblastoma.  We have now discovered a new gene that appears to drive Group 4 medulloblastoma and therefore propose to study how it causes cancer, and if it can be used as a target to fight cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation into molecular mechanisms and physiological roles of activity-dependent AMPAR trafficking
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPA RECEPTOR; ANIMAL PHYSIOLOGY; BRAIN SLICES; CELL BIOLOGY; CULTURED NEURONS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EXOCYTOSIS; RECEPTOR TRAFFICKING; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: Communication between neurons occurs at specialized junctions known as synapses via a process known as synaptic transmission: neurotransmitter molecules are released from presynaptic neurons, bind to membrane receptors on the surface of postsynaptic neurons, and initiate various processes within the neuron. The strength of the synaptic transmission may then, theoretically, be regulated by changing either the presynaptic neurotransmitter release or the responsiveness of postsynaptic receptors. Research in our laboratory has focused on the mechanisms by which postsynaptic receptors are regulated. We have recently provided the first evidence suggesting that the numbers of receptors expressed on postsynaptic domains can be rapidly regulated, and that these rapid changes in postsynaptic receptor numbers may be a novel and efficient means by which the strength of synaptic transmission can be altered. In this application, we propose experiments to investigate how such rapid changes in the number of postsynaptic receptors, and hence synaptic transmission strength, are initiated and carried out. Interneuronal communication is fundamental for all aspects of brain function and alteration of this process underlies many brain disorders including epilepsy, stroke, and mental disorders. As such, our proposed studies can be expected to lead to better treatments for these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: RNA Binding Protein Regulation of Cellular Migration and Adhesion During Cancer Cell Dissemination and Metastases Formation
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER PREVENTION; CARCINOGENESIS; CELL SIGNALING; CELLULAR ADHESION; CELLULAR MIGRATION; FOCAL ADHESION; LIVE CELL IMAGING; METASTASIS; RNA-BINDING PROTEINS; TUMOR DISSEMINATION
Abstract-Résumé: The RNA-based control of biological processes has always been overlooked in cancer progression and metastases formation. With this proposal, we will uncover how RNA-binding protein can modulate protein expression in order to influence metastatic cancer cells homing toward specific tissues. Growing evidence reveals that tissue microenvironments secreting specific growth factors greatly influence the implantation of migrating cancer cells at specific sites. Our preliminary work on Sam68 showed that this RNA-binding protein involvement in the regulation of mRNA metabolism is highly modulated by posttranslational modifications resulting from complex signaling pathways whose activation originates from external stimulation, such as the microenvironment. These changes in Sam68 mRNA processing activity can directly affect cell morphology, adhesion and migration. In depth analysis suggest that this was not restricted to Sam68, since altering general mRNA translation can also affect cellular adhesion and migration. These observations clearly indicate that mRNA translation modulation, through the regulation of RNA-binding protein, is an essential process for cancer progression and metastatic cell adhesion and migration.   This program examines how RNA-binding proteins activities are modulated by the microenvironment and how this affects cellular adhesion, focal adhesion maturation, changes in cellular morphology and migration. Elucidating how RNA-binding proteins regulates these cellular events is essential since they are mandatory steps for early events in tumor cell dissemination from the primary site to secondary sites to form metastases, the leading cause of cancer-related deaths. Our research will offer novel strategies that could lead to new therapeutic possibilities in order to decrease cancer related mortality due to metastases formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting successful return to work in worker on disability due to low back pain
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATE STATE MODELS; COX REGRESSION; LOW BACK PAIN; PHASES OF DISABILITY; PHYSIOTHERAPY; PREDICTION; PREDICTIVE ACCURACY; PRIMARY CARE RESEARCH; PROGNOSIS; WORK DISABILITY PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Low back pain costs in Canada are estimated at 11 to 23 billion dollars. Most costs are caused by productivity losses and compensation. Some of the costs and suffering can be diminished by identifying those at high risk. Workers that are at low risk will most likely return to function and work with limited assistance. Those at high risk might benefit from early or more intensive intervention. If a worker hurts his/her back at work, many people want to know how long it will take before return to work. The worker wants to know because a prolonged recovery period may lead to insecurity and anxiety and have financial consequences. The workplace wants to know whether it should make alternate work arrangements. The workers' compensation organisation and health care provider want to know, to guide intervention decisions for early and safe return to work. In this study we will examine which combination of factors best predicts important outcomes for injured workers that enter a rehabilitation program aimed at improving function and return to work. We will review information routinely collected at the workers' compensation organisation (WSIB). Next, we will add data collected by the healthcare provider (CBI Health) and data on outcomes like function and successful return to work specifically collected for this study. We will use well established (but currently underused) statistical approaches to built predictive rules. The final product will be an easy to use prediction tool. The tool will provide projections of different injured worker outcomes such as return to productivity, function, job satisfaction, successful return to work and recurrences. The tool will be of interest to injured workers, workers' compensation board professionals, rehabilitation professionals, employers and researchers. We will reach these communities through specific audience briefings, presentations and by the publication of papers in trade and scientific journals

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional ability assessment in early dementia and mild brain injury using cognitive-motor integration.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; COGNITION; CONCUSSION; EYE-HAND COORDINATION; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; MOTOR CONTROL; MOTOR DISABILITY; MOTOR LEARNING; SENSORY MOTOR INTEGRATION
Abstract-Résumé: Two prominent health issues facing Canadians are 1)the impact of dementing illness on the elderly and 2)the impact of concussion (mild traumatic brain injury) on young athletes and workers. Whether caused by trauma or degenerative disease, the effect of mild brain insult on one's functional abilities is not well understood. Our research to date has documented that "cognitive-motor integration", or tasks which rely on rules to plan a movement (such as "push the computer mouse forward to move the cursor up"), is impaired both in the early stages of dementia, and following mild traumatic brain injury. The goals of the present research are twofold. First, we will apply our previous research into a validated, clinically feasible cognitive-motor assessment tool to detect dementia in its early-stages. We will also examine the utility of this assessment tool to predict which individuals will progress from mild cognitive impairment to dementia. Second, we will expand our preliminary research demonstrating that young adults show impaired cognitive-motor integration following concussion. The ability to think and act simultaneously is something that is crucial for safe performance at work and in the sport arena. Diagnosing its impairment would be an important component of functional ability assessment. Such abilities are not captured by current tests in adults, and is not at all explored in youth. Overall, our research will provide a basic understanding of how our brains process rule-based information to make accurate movements in our everyday lives, and will provide tools to assess how these brain processes can degrade with neurological disease and brain injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Microbial influence on respiratory allergen responsiveness from birth to adulthood
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGIC ASTHMA; COMMENSAL BACTERIA; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GERM FREE MICE; IMMUNOLOGY; IMMUNOSUPPRESSION; INFANCY; INFLAMMATION; MICROBES; MOUSE MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma affects over 300 million people worldwide and is the most prevalent chronic disease in children. The prevalence of asthma in Canada currently stands at ~12% in children and over 6% in adults; it is the leading cause of absenteeism from school and the third leading cause of work loss. Allergic Asthma (AA) represents over 2/3 of all cases of asthma.The last 30 years have delivered astounding progress of many facets of the pathogenesis (how it works) of this disease. In stark contrast, elucidation of its origins, i.e. its etiology (why it occurs), remains elusive. This is a central issue because deciphering the conditions underlying the onset of AA may be fundamental for the design of primary prevention strategies. Programming of allergen responsiveness, i.e. sensitization versus tolerance, largely occurs within the first 2 years of life. We propose that environmental exposure to commensal bacteria (good microbes) within this interval is essential to develop components of the immune system of the lung that facilitate allergen tolerance. Conversely, exposure to pathogenic bacteria (bad microbes) will subvert the naturally pro-tolerant lung environment in early life, permit sensitization and imprint long-lasting features of asthma. We will use a murine experimental system to study the precise evolution of immune responses in the normal lung as well as responsiveness to house dust mite, the most prevalent aeroallergen worldwide, from birth to adulthood (8 weeks). We will, then, determine the impact that distinct microbial exposures have on these responses. Lastly, we will investigate specific cellular and molecular mechanisms that we think are important to program tolerance to aeroallergens in early life, i.e. the first 2-3 weeks of life in mice. A number of studies will take advantage of mice bred in a fully sterile facility (germ free mice), the only one in Canada and one the very few in the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeted delivery into brain capillary endothelial cells for the treatment of Alzheimer disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER; BRAIN; BRAIN CAPILLARY ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM; DRUG DELIVERY; DRUG TARGETING; GENE THERAPY; IN SITU CEREBRAL PERFUSION; LIPOSOME; MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: One third of Canadians will be affected by a brain disease during his or her lifetime. While the population is getting older, the risk of suffering from Alzheimer, stroke, Parkinson, etc. increases exponentially after age 65. Most people do not realize that the socioeconomic burden of brain diseases dwarf those of cancer and cardiovascular disease combined.  Unfortunately, the research and development of new drugs for brain diseases lag behind. The main problem resides in the fact that the blood-brain barrier (BBB) severely restricts the passage of drugs from the blood to the brain. The vast majority of advanced drugs are too large to pass through the BBB and virtually all strategies developed so far to cross the BBB without damaging it have failed in humans. Indeed, the brain is like a walled city, in which the BBB represents the walls. The total length of the BBB of a normal human brain spans approximately 600 km. We think that instead of forcing our way through the wall, we could use it as a target. Since the BBB plays a role in most brain diseases, targeting the BBB may exert a therapeutic effect deep into every corner of the brain. Moreover, the BBB itself can be used as a launching base from which drugs can be secreted into the rest of the brain.  More specifically, we are proposing to use fatty nanocontainers (called liposomes) that use natural transport systems located in the BBB, the equivalent of the guarded gates in the walled city analogy. Drugs or gene medicine will be encapsulated into these liposomes, which will then be ferried inside cells of the BBB using specific vectors after a simple intravenous injection. This tactic is reminiscent of the Trojan horse strategy because the liposomes are built to trick the brain's screening system (or city guards). Therefore, the present study could lead to the development of a universal brain drug delivery system for clinical applications for brain diseases such as Alzheimer's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Compassion: An empirical approach to cancer patients perspectives and experiences of compassion at the end of life.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CLINICAL CARE; COMMUNICATION; COMPASSION; END OF LIFE; GROUNDED THEORY; PALLIATIVE CARE; QUALITATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Compassionate care has long been identified by patients, clinicians, professional bodies, and leading health care organizations as an essential component of quality health care, especially in the context of suffering at the end of life. Features of compassionate care have been shown to be strong predictors of patient satisfaction; clinician-patient communication; patient distress, patient complaints, and malpractice suits. While the importance and provision of compassionate care seems fairly self-evident, an expanding gap has developed between what is intuitively known and what is clinically practiced. While compassionate care is recognized as a cardinal virtue and standard of care by clinicians, health care organizations and government, evidence suggests that clinicians and future health care professionals are increasingly challenged to integrate compassionate care within their clinical purview. A remarkable deficiency in the literature is the absence of patients' perspectives and experiences of compassion--the advocates and potential benefactors of compassionate care.  This study will determine how advanced cancer patients facing the end of life define and experience compassion as received from health care professionals. The components of compassion identified in this study will provide the foundation for an empirical  model that can be readily incorporated into clinical practice, resulting in reduced burden and enhanced quality of life for advanced cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Iron regulatory proteins: pathophysiological functions in metabolism and cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; ERYTHROPOIESIS; HIF2A; HYPOXIA; IRON METABOLISM; IRON RESPONSIVE ELEMENTS; IRP1; IRP2; MOUSE MODELS OF DISEASE; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL GENE REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Iron regulatory proteins, IRP1 and IRP2, are master switches that regulate the expression of several iron metabolism genes in the cytoplasm of cells. Their expression is critical for life as mice lacking both iron regulatory proteins die early during embryonal development. By contrast, animals bearing targeted inactivation of either IRP1 or IRP2, respectively, are viable. While IRP1 deficient mice were reported to lack any discernible pathology, we found that they exhibit defects in erythropoiesis and glucose metabolism. Here, we propose experiments to uncover the underlying mechanisms. We also established first links between iron regulatory proteins and cancer biology. We provided evidence that IRP1 suppresses and IRP2 enhances carcinogenesis. We plan further experiments to uncover the mechanisms by which IRP1 and IRP2 modulate tumor growth.

TitreApplicationTitle: HCV Treatment as Prevention among HIV Co-Infected Individuals: Great Promise and Big Challenges
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL INTERVENTION; BURDEN OF DISEASE; HCV; HEPATITIS C; HIV/AIDS; INCIDENCE; MATHEMATICAL MODELING; MORTALITY; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: The burden of the hepatitis C (HCV) and the human immunodeficiency (HIV) viruses among individuals who inject drugs (IDU) remains a major public health challenge. Note that these diseases do not only affect IDUs. For example, the US launched a campaign in 2012 to test "baby boomers" given they have been exposed to HCV in the past; they calculated that 1 in 30 "baby boomers" are unaware of being infected with HCV. Also in the US, it was calculated that 21% of individuals infected with HIV are unaware of their infection. In Canada, especially in British Columbia (BC), the situation is very similar. Unfortunately, there is neither a preventive HCV vaccine nor a preventive vaccine or a cure for HIV. Currently, the treatment for HCV is very complicated, associated with a high occurrence of side-effects and a low cure rate. Among individuals infected with both HCV and HIV, the management of their diseases is further complicated, and they are at a higher risk of mortality. Based on the success of using the "HIV Treatment as Prevention" strategy to decrease the burden and transmission of HIV, we propose to evaluate a parallel "HCV Treatment as Prevention" strategy to decrease the combined burden of HIV and HCV and, secondarily, to decrease the spread of both HIV and HCV. This proposal will develop a methodology to forecast the future of both HCV and HIV epidemics in BC, considering different scenarios of testing, treatment coverage and retention into treatment for both diseases. There is no time to wait for the "perfect regimen" or a vaccine that will prevent HCV and HIV. Many lives will be saved if we act expeditiously taking advantage of the currently used and newly approved drugs. Failure to do so will lead to avoidable healthcare costs and further stress to healthcare systems already struggling to cope with the existing demand.

ClasseRechercheFR: AUTRES MALADIES VENERIENNES; SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Transmission Reduction and Prevention with HPV Vaccination (TRAP-HPV) Study:  A Randomized Controlled Trial of the Efficacy of HPV Vaccination in Preventing Transmission of HPV Infection in Heterosexual Couples
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS; IMMUNE RESPONSE; INFECTION; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection can cause cancers of the cervix, vulva, vagina, anus, and oropharynx in women or cancers of the anus, penis, and oropharynx in men. Two prophylactic vaccines have been proven to be highly effective in preventing HPV infection and the genital precancerous lesions caused by it. However, we do not know yet if a previously infected individual, once vaccinated, would be less infective to her or his sexual partner. We plan to conduct a study, called Transmission Reduction And Prevention with HPV vaccination (TRAP-HPV) study. It will include 500 sexually active couples (total of 1000 individuals) in university student health clinics in Montreal (age 18-26 years). It will be a randomized placebo-controlled, double-blinded intervention trial. Study participants will be followed up to 12 months. Behavioural and biological data will be collected at the time of study enrolment, then at months 2, 4, 6, 9 and 12 post-enrolment. The results of this trial will be invaluable in informing federal and provincial policies regarding vaccination of women and men.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of excitation-contraction coupling by interaction between sodium-calcium exchangers and transient outward potassium currents
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTION POTENTIAL; ARRHYTHMIAS; CALCIUM; CONTRACTION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HEART DISEASE; ION CHANNELS; SODIUM
Abstract-Résumé: We have recently uncovered a unique way that changes in electricity in the heart through potassium currents (which occur invariably in heart failure, cardiac hypertrophy and cardiomyopathy) influence the process involved in controlling calcium levels in myocytes. This mechanism involves complex interactions between four major ion transporters in the heart: L-type calcium channels, sodium-calcium exchangers, sodium channels and (transient outward) potassium channels. After further characterizing these interactions, we will investigate how these transporters change their interactions in hearts disease. These interactions are important to understand because it is well known that the levels of transient outward potassium channels and sodium-calcium exchanger activity change dramatically in heart disease. These changes are linked to dysruptions in the level of calcium needed to drive the heart's contraction.

TitreApplicationTitle: D-dimer testing, tailored to clinical pretest probability, to minimize initial and follow-up ultrasound testing in suspected deep vein thrombosis: A management study
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL MANAGEMENT; COHORT STUDY; COST; D-DIMER; DEEP VEIN THROMBOSIS; DIAGNOSIS; VENOUS THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: A D-dimer test is a blood test that measures proteins that are formed when the body breaks down leg blood clots (e.g., deep vein thrombosis; DVT). If a D-dimer test is normal, it is very unlikely that a patient has a DVT. However, because other illnesses also increase D-dimer levels, an abnormal D-dimer level has been considered unhelpful.  We recently completed a study that showed that, rather than labelling D-dimer results as "positive" and "negative" in the same way in all patients, it is better to use a higher D-dimer cut-off value (i.e., level that separates a negative from a positive result) if,  after examining the patient, the doctor thinks that there is "Low DVT probability". This allowed DVT to be ruled-out, without performing an ultrasound, in 50% more patients. Analysis of that study's findings also suggested a number of other ways to improve how D-dimer testing is used to diagnose DVT.  We will now use this new information to further improve DVT diagnosis in 1,500 patients from 10 hospitals. Patients will be assessed as Low, Moderate or High DVT probability, and have D-dimer measured. DVT will be ruled-out if D-dimer is <1,000 with Low or Moderate DVT probability, or <500 with High DVT probability. Those who do not have DVT ruled-out will have an ultrasound. If the ultrasound does not show DVT, instead of repeating the ultrasound a week later in all patients, it will only be repeated if D-dimer is >3,000 with Low or Moderate probability, or >1,500 with High probability. We will then follow patients for 3 months, expecting that very few will have thrombosis (<1%), thereby confirming the safety of this diagnostic approach. We will also calculate cost savings.  This diagnostic approach will reduce ultrasound testing by 50% and the need to return to hospital by over 75%. As 2.5 million North Americans are investigated for DVT each year, this reduction in ultrasound testing is important to patients, health care providers and to society.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; OBESITE
TitreApplicationTitle: tRNA synthesis and the control of mRNA translation and growth by the Target-of-Rapamycin (TOR) pathway
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELL GROWTH; DROSOPHILA; INSULIN; MRNA TRANSLATION; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; TOR KINASE; TRNA SYNTHESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how cells grow and divide is a fundamental question in biology. During animal development the proper regulation of cell growth is essential for controlling organ and organism size. While in cancer, deregulated cell growth is often an early event in tumor formation. The processes that control growth are remarkably similar across different species. For example, in both humans and fruit flies similar genes regulate growth and mutations in these genes often lead to cancer. These similarities allow us to use the fruit fly as a simple, yet powerful genetic system to study what genes and molecules controls growth. We made the striking discovery that overproduction of a single molecule, called transfer RNA, can accelerate growth and increase body size in fruit flies. Transfer RNA plays a critical role in the synthesis all of the proteins and enzymes in a cell, including those essential for growth. Our goal in this grant is to understand how the production of tRNA is controlled and how increase in the production of transfer RNA can drive growth. Abnormal production of transfer RNA is often seen in cancer cells, therefore our work in fruit flies may provide clues to help us understand the runaway growth that makes this disease so devastating.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development of cooperation in relationships: Protective processes for children vulnerable to mental health problems
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD DEVELOPMENT; CONFLICT; COOPERATION; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; DEVELOPMENTAL TRAJECTORIES; FAMILY RELATIONSHIPS; MENTAL HEALTH; SOCIAL RELATIONS MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: Family relationships are the strongest 'environmental' correlate of children's mental health problems. Yet because of methodological problems in the study of relationships we do not yet know whether the strength of this relationship comes from the individuals involved (a trait aspect to behavior, e.g. negativity, that a person carries with them into different relationships), the unique combination of two people in a dyad (a child is easy for one parent but difficult for the other) or the family as a whole (an emotional climate pervades the family).  This project proposes a follow-up of a birth cohort of children, their older siblings and their parents (501 families enlisted in 2005-2006) who have taken part in four waves of data collection as part of the Kids, Families and Places (KFP) study. The inclusion of up to four children per family, with data from both parents, has allowed us to track the relationship between individual characteristics of family members, relationship dynamics and children's mental health across early life.  In the present study we propose visiting our families two more times. We use two novel methods to investigate the development of cooperation in family relationships. One method involves every member of the family interacting with every other member and fitting a complex statistical model that allows us to isolate effects of individuals, from effects of dyads, from effects of the whole family. We use data from the first 4 waves to explain variation between individuals (both genetic and early developmental data), dyads (the interaction of the personalities of each member of the dyad) and families (cumulative social disadvantage). In our second study by coding 10 minutes of interaction for each dyad during conflict and cooperation tasks, we examine the moment-to-moment interactional processes that encourage or discourage cooperation and how these interactional patterns predict children's mental health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural Studies of Parkinson's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; MITOCHONDRIA; MITOPHAGY; NEURODEGENERATION; NUCLEAR MAGNETIC RESONANCE; ORGANELLAR QUALITY CONTROL; PROTEIN; SMALL-ANGLE X-RAY SCATTERING; UBIQUITINATION; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease (PD) is caused by the loss of dopamine producing neurons in region of the brain known as the substantia nigra. Recently, the study of genetic forms of PD has revealed the central role of damaged mitochondria in the death of neurons. These studies shown that the protein parkin, which is absent or mutated in many familial cases of PD, is required for the identification and recycling of damaged mitochondria. Parkin is a member of a large, diverse family of proteins called ubiquitin ligases.  These proteins catalyze the attachment of a small protein, ubiquitin, to targeted proteins as a signal for the degradation of the target protein.  We hypothesize that in a similar manner, parkin targets damaged mitochondria for degradation. In the absence of parkin, damaged mitochondria accumulate in neurons, which leads to neuronal dysfunction and ultimately cell death.   Using structural biology, we propose to determine the three dimensional structure of parkin in order to determine how it functions to specifically target damaged mitochondria.  Studies by ourselves and others have shown that parkin is recruited to cell membranes through a process that involves protein phosphorylation. We will determine the site of phosphorylation and the mechanism of activation of parkin's ubiquitin-ligase activity. These studies will deepen our understanding of the quality control system that is responsible for maintaining health mitochondria and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for slowing the progression of PD or even preventing its occurrence in susceptible populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of oscillatory brain networks in understanding age-related decline in speech perception
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; AUDITORY MEMORY; AUDITORY NEUROSCIENCE; FAMILIARIZATION; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHY; NEURONAL NETWORKS; OSCILLATORY BRAIN ACTIVITY; PERCEPTION; SIGNAL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: For elderly people, understanding speech is difficult when others are talking at the same time because the surrounding noise interferes with the speech sound. This obstructs the brain process of interpreting and understanding what has been heard. Moreover, noise gets in the way of memorizing and becoming familiar with the sound, which otherwise makes comprehension easier.  With our research we want to understand the functional brain changes that make speech understanding difficult in older adults. Knowing the underlying brain mechanism is important for providing effective support through training or technical devices.  Our research builds on established models of auditory processing in the brain. The hypothesis is that sound is analyzed in the brain in a sequence of steps to enhance the relevant speech sound and to separate it from irrelevant noise. Our aim is to identify the brain network, in which sound becomes meaningful and to study how this network is affected by noise. We will be using magnetoencephalography for recording brain activity. From our previous studies we know that brain waves with a certain rhythm are characteristic for communication within the auditory system. We developed auditory stimuli, which specifically elicit such brain oscillations, and we plan to study how they are affected by age and background noise.  The research outcomes will provide new knowledge about how the brain processes speech. The results will help to develop and improve assistive technologies and intervention approaches for hearing impaired adults. Moreover, the results will inform us about brain function in general, specifically how brain regions communicate with each other. It will thus inform us about how to help the aging population maintain successful communication and to protect them from social isolation and early cognitive decline.

TitreApplicationTitle: Function and Regulation of T-type Ca2+ Channels in the Cerebral Circulation
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM CHANNELS; CEREBRAL ARTERIES; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SMOOTH MUSCLE CONTRACTILITY; STROKE; T-TYPE CHANNELS
Abstract-Résumé: Brain blood flow is controlled by vessels that respond to changes in tissue metabolism, nerve activity and blood pressure. To modify vessel size, these stimuli must alter the level of calcium in smooth muscle cells. The calcium level in smooth muscle is set by the electrical state of the cell and steady state calcium influx through pores called calcium channels. Scientists have typically assumed that there is only one type of calcium channel present in smooth muscle. We, however, have found a second type called T-type calcium channels. In this proposal, we will use electrical, molecular and physiology techniques to probe the function of T-type calcium channels in single cells and whole vessels. This research will further our knowledge of how biological stimuli and calcium channels regulate vessel diameter and brain blood flow. This knowledge is important as these calcium channels are often targeted by the drug industry to reverse the harmful effects of high blood pressure and stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of Skeletal Muscle Stem Cell Activity by microRNA and Cytoplasmic mRNP Granules
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS; MICRORNA; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; REGENERATION; SATELLITE CELL; SKELETAL MUSCLE; STEM CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Muscular dystrophies are a group of neuromuscular disorders that are characterized by progressive weakness and wasting of muscles, impeding the ability to walk, speak and ultimately breathe. There is currently no cure.   Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most severe and prevalent of the muscular dystrophies, affecting 1 in 3500 newborn males. The condition results from the absence of the structural protein dystrophin, causing weakened muscle fibres and persistent muscle damage. This results in chronic cycles of muscle fibre degeneration and regeneration, leading to the exhaustion of the pool of muscle stem cells that are responsible for skeletal muscle regeneration.  In order to restore muscle function, stem cell-based therapies for muscular dystrophies should be pursued because they represent the only broad strategy that has the potential to introduce a normal version of the diseased protein into dystrophic muscle. It is also the only strategy that aims to replace the pool of skeletal muscle stem cells required for muscle regeneration. For stem cell based therapy to be effective, it is important for the transplanted stem cell to replace the function of the muscle specific stem cells of the host. Namely, they must contribute to regeneration and return to a quiescent state, primed and ready-to-go, such that they can rapidly activate in response to future rounds of muscle injury.   This research proposal will investigate the mechanism by which a quiescent muscle stem cell locks down the expression of muscle tissue specific determination factors by sequestration of their corresponding messages. When the stem cell is activated, this lock is opened and rapid production of the protein now permits tissue repair.  Applications of the current proposal include development of stem cell based treatments and discovery of modifiers of muscle stem cell activity within the body as novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of muscular dystrophy.

Abstract-Résumé: Exposure to a severe stressful event can result in long-lasting psychopathological consequences with the result that patients become hyper-sensitive to stressors not directly related to the traumatic situation (i.e. post traumatic stress disorder). Specifically, exposure to a single stress can sensitize our system to future stressors through actions on the the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. My laboratory investigates synapses that regulate the activity of central stress command neurons neurons in the hypothalamus. Here we seek funding to better understand the cellular mechanisms that allow stress to prime brain pathways and contribute to the development of hypersensitivity to stress. This process may underlie clinically relevant disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder in which the entire stress system, is sensitized to future experiences by an intense stressor so understanding the neurobiological consequences of stress exposure will provide potential treatment targets for this and other stress disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prescription opioid misuse among at-risk youth: Investigating drug use trajectories and associated risk behaviours to inform policy responses
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION TREATMENT; AT-RISK YOUTH; DRUG OVERDOSE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; ILLICIT DRUG USE; INJECTION INITIATION; PRESCRIPTION OPIOIDS; PROSPECTIVE COHORT; SEXUAL RISK
Abstract-Résumé: Increasing misuse of prescription opioids among North American youth is a disturbing trend. After marijuana, prescription opioids are the most commonly misused drugs among youth. In 2007, 20.6% of Ontario high school students reported misusing prescription opioids in the past year. The negative impacts of the rising trend in prescription opioid misuse are becoming increasingly apparent. Drug poisoning is now the leading cause of death from injuries in the US, and this increase has been largely attributed to prescription opioids. There are signals that prescription opioid use among at-risk youth may promote transitions into heroin use and initiation into drug injection, drastically increasing the severity of opioid dependence and elevating the risks of experiencing other drug-related harms. Despite these concerning findings, no longitudinal evaluations of this phenomenon have taken place, and our knowledge of prescription opioid use among youth is limited to retrospective and cross-sectional studies. To address this gap, we propose to build on an existing cohort of more than 700 poly-substance using street-involved youth in Vancouver -the At-Risk Youth Study (ARYS)- and recruit 200 youth who misuse prescription opioids that will be nested within the larger ARYS cohort. Our objectives are to: longitudinally monitor and evaluate trends in the availability, acquisition and use of POs among at-risk youth; evaluate the influence of PO misuse on the natural history of illicit drug use, including initiation into and cessation of injection drug use; identify and monitor risks and health impacts of PO misuse; and examine reach, coverage and impacts of policies and interventions on PO availability, use and health impacts. Our aim is to generate a body of evidence that will inform policy responses to address the crisis of prescription opioid misuse among at-risk youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Human studies on the neuropsychology and cognitive/behavioural neuroscience of memory and its disorders.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BRAIN-DAMAGE; EPISODIC AND SEMANTIC MEMORY; FRONTAL LOBE; FUNCTIONAL (AND STRUCTURAL) NEUROIMAGING; MEDIAL TEMPORAL LOBE (HIPPOCAMPUS); MEMORY AND COGNITION; RECENT AND REMOTE MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: How do memories change with time and what are the neural mechanisms that are associated with these changes? It is well known that as time passes, memories of some experiences retain the same vivid qualities that they had shortly after the experience occurred. Other memories, however, fade with time and become schematic, in that the perceptual details that make the memory vivid are lost, but the gist remains. Still other memories are lost entirely. These processes, which vary across individuals, are affected by normal aging, and by neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer's Disease, that damage brain regions associated with memory. The Trace Transformation Theory (TTT) we developed characterizes the relation between the type of changes a memory undergoes with time and experience, and the neural mechanisms that support them. Specifically, TTT posits that memories that retain their vivid qualities remain dependent on the hippocampus, a region in the temporal lobe, whereas those that are transformed to more schematic memories become independent of the hippocampus and are mediated by structures in neocortex, particularly a region on the underside of the frontal lobes. By using behavioural and brain imaging techniques, we plan to test these ideas in neurologically-intact young and older adults, and in patients with memory disorders caused by brain damage or dysfunction. Together, these studies will illuminate the neuropsychological processes and mechanisms that are involved in forming, retaining and retrieving recent and remote memories. In addition, we have shown that this research has direct application, not only for creating diagnostic tools to identify memory disorders, but also for increasing our understanding of how detailed and schematic memories contribute to a variety of non-memory domains, such as fluency, creativity and problem solving, that are essential components of activities of daily living.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Type IV pilus as a dynamic transport apparatus
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL SECRETION; ENTEROPATHOGENIC E. COLI; FILAMENTOUS PHAGE; MACROMOLECULAR COMPLEXES; MEMBRANE PROTEINS; MEMBRANE TRANSLOCATION; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; TYPE IV PILI; VIBRIO CHOLERAE; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Many antibiotics in use today are victims of their own success: they effectively kill harmful bacteria but in the process, they allow new antibiotic-resistant bacteria to thrive. Antibiotics that disarm rather than kill bacteria may reduce the likelihood of resistant strains emerging. The Type IV pili are important arsenal form many bacterial pathogens, including those that cause the diarrheal disease cholera, the sexually transmitted disease gonorrhoeae, bacterial meningitis, and fatal lung infections in cystic fibrosis patients. These hairlike filaments on the bacterial surface are required for adherence, motility and many other functions. A complex machinery assembles the pili from pilin building blocks. In some bacteria pilus assembly is reversible, with pilus retraction allowing the bacteria to move along slimy surfaces and to import nutrients into the cell. We plan to exploit pilus retraction as a vehicle to deliver antibiotics into bacterial cells to inactivate pilus assembly or act on some other critical bacterial function to render it harmless. The assembly/retraction process is poorly understood and thought to require an energy source provided by a "retraction ATPase". We have obtained evidence suggesting that retraction occurs in Vibrio cholerae, the causative agent of cholera disease, but does not require a retraction ATPase. This primitive Type IV pilus system instead uses a pilin mimic that jams pilus assembly, causing the pili to retract spontaneously. We propose that retraction is in fact necessary for all pilus functions in V. cholerae. For this research proposal we will definitively demonstrate that V. cholerae pili are retractile and that retraction is required for pilus functions, and will design proteins that can act as carriers for new antibiotics that target Type IV pilus assembly or other key bacterial functions. Our results will have important implications for other bacterial pathogens that rely on Type IV pili to establish infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of receptor signaling within clathrin-coated membrane microdomains.
Keywords-MotsClés: AKT; EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR RECEPTOR; METABOLISM; PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL PHOSPHATES; PROLIFERATION; QUANTITATIVE LIVE CELL FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; RECEPTOR TRANSACTIVATION; SIGNALLING SCAFFOLD; SRC; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Tumors are made up of cells that can be recognized by doctors and scientists as a result of several changes they exhibit compared to the normal cells that surround them. One of the changes found in many cancer cells is an increase in the uncontrolled function of certain hormone receptors, in particular one named Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). EGFR signals to cells and tells them to proliferate, survive and to migrate and when uncontrolled, these traits can lead to cancer and metastasis. EGFR is expressed on the outside surface of cells, and when it binds to a hormone called Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF), it begins to move to a cell's interior, a process termed 'internalization'. Scientists have found that EGFR functions differently when it is at the cell surface compared to after it has been internalized. How does EGFR function differently when it is in different parts of the cell? The proposed research will seek to understand how the hormone receptor EGFR works differently depending on where in a cell the receptor is found.  EGFR is very important for cancer progression, as when researchers working in a laboratory artificially induce an otherwise normal cell to contain high amounts of EGFR, it causes the cells to become cancerous. These results have led scientists to develop drugs that reduce the action of EGFR to try to treat cancer patients. Although some initial success had been achieved by this strategy, the tumour cells in patients unfortunately become resistant to these drugs, and the cancers returned. So, while drugs that seek to block EGFR show particular promise, new strategies to achieve this goal are required. Understanding how EGFR functions differently at distinct locations within a cell, and how this process is disrupted in tumours may provide novel targets and approaches to treat cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the Mechanism of Action of Small Molecule Modulators of CFTR
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CYSTIC FIBROSIS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MOLECULAR TARGET; PRIMARY RESPIRATORY EPITHELIAL CULTURES; PROTEIN BIOCHEMISTRY; PROTEIN BIOPHYSICS; RESPIRATORY HEALTH; SMALL MOLECULE THERAPIES; SYNTHETIC CHEMISTRY
Abstract-Résumé: The new drug ivacaftor (or VX-770),targets the basic defect caused by a relatively rare Cystic Fibrosis mutation: G551D-CFTR (present in 4-5% of CF patients) and significantly improves lung function in these patients. VX-770 was approved for use in the USA in February and is being reviewed for approval for Canadian patients with this mutation. Such fast-tracking reflects the urgency felt by the CF patient population for medications which will increase their lifespan past the mid-forties. VX-809 is known as a corrector compound and it entered clinical trials for treatment of patients bearing the major CF causing mutation: F508del-CFTR (present in 90% of patients). However, VX-809 treatment failed to translate to a significant improvement in lung function. VX-809 entered clinical trials without any knowledge regarding its molecular targets and this blind spot is limiting to progress in developing the next generation of clinically effective and safe small molecule corrector compounds.  The goal of our research programme is to understand how such partially effective corrector compounds act to rescue F508del-CFTR  in order to drive the development of more effective treatments for patients with the major CF causing mutation.
