TitreApplicationTitle: Novel mediators of beta-cell lipotoxicity
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA CELL; DIABETES; FREE FATTY ACIDS; HYPERGLYCEMIC CLAMP; IN VIVO; INFLAMMATION; LIPOTOXICITY; OBESITY; OXIDATIVE STRESS; SIRTUINS
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity affects more than 25% of Canadians and is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, which affects more than 6% of Canadians. Both obesity and diabetes are major and increasing causes of morbidity and mortality. Recently, inflammation of the pancreatic islets has been found in type 2 diabetic patients. Elevated levels of fatty acids in the circulation (fatty acids are released from the adipose tissue) are often present in obesity, and may lead to type 2 diabetes in predisposed individuals by causing inflammation  of the pancreatic beta cell which secretes insulin.  The objective of this proposal is to investigate how elevated fatty acids lead to inflammation of the pancreatic islets that causes beta cell malfunction. More specifically,  we will identify the receptors and signaling molecules involved and whether fat also reduces the antinflammatory defenses. These studies are important to identify targets to prevent and treat malfunction of beta cells during the development of diabetes and during the progression of beta cell failure in type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structure-Function Analysis of Cardiac Ryanodine Receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: CALORIMETRY; CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIAS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOY; GENETIC DISEASE; HEART MUSCLE; STRESS; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Every beat of our heart requires cardiac muscle tissue to contract. This contraction is a finely orchestrated process, whereby many molecular events take place in each cardiac muscle cell.  One crucial signal consists of calcium ions.  Calcium ions are small molecules that play important roles in many different cells in our bodies. They are known primarily for their role in maintining bone structure, but they also play a key role in the contraction of muscle:  just prior to each contraction, calcium ions flow from the outside of the cell to the inside, and from one compartment of the cell to another. This simple 'flux' of calcium is what then triggers the cell to contract.   The basic principle of using calcium is simple and elegant. Every cell and cellular compartment is surrounded by a membrane, and calcium ions cannot pass through these. However, particular proteins, named 'calcium channels' can form pores through the membrane. These pores can open and close, and thus decide when calcium can pass through or stay on one side.  It is of the utmost importance that these pores function properly: anything that goes wrong with opening or closing of the pore, will lead to either too much or too little calcium inside the proper compartment. This will directly influence the contraction of the heart, and lead to cardiac arrhythmias and even sudden cardiac death.  In this grant proposal, we study such particular calcium channels. We particularly focus on how genetic mutations, known to result in cardiac arrhythmias, can cause faulty channels, and we study molecules that can alter the behavior of the pores. As such, we gain fundamental insights into disease mechanisms, and also try to devise new small molecules (drugs) to treat cardiac arrhythmias.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of protein arginylation in skeletal muscles
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGINYLATION; MYOFIBRIL; MYOFILAMENT; MYOSIN-ACTIN INTERACTION; PROTEIN REGULATION; SARCOMERE; TITIN MOLECULES
Abstract-Résumé: Muscle contraction is a basic function of life. Muscles allow us to move and to breathe, and provide the heart with the strength for pumping blood to the different parts of our body. Muscle contraction is a complex process that has several regulatory mechanisms. Some of these mechanisms are well known, and have allowed us to understand how muscles work in conditions of health and disease. However, there are still several forms of regulation that are not well understood. The reasons for such limitation are likely technological. Among these forms of force regulation that are not well understood, there is one process called protein arginylation: a cellular process catalyzed by a specific enzyme (arginyl-tRNA-protein transferase), responsible for transferring arginine (Arg) from tRNA into proteins. We have collected evidence that arginylation is a global protein regulator in skeletal muscles with multiples functions, including cell development, contractility, aging and muscle health. The goal of this proposal is to investigate further the specific role of arginylation on muscle proteins, contractility and muscle health. Novel and accurate methods of measurement that include sub-cellular structures and single molecules isolated from muscles will be used in our laboratories. These experiments will provide information on how this newly discovered form of force regulation dictates muscle functioning. Therefore, the outcome of this research has implications for everyday life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation and role of P2Y6 nucleotide receptor in colorectal cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL AND CELL MODELS; CELL INVASION; CELL SURVIVAL; COLORECTAL CANCER; EPIGENETIC REGULATION; EPITHELIAL CELLS; EXTRACELLULAR NUCLEOTIDES; GPCR; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second cause of cancer-related dead in Canada.  Nonetheless, the lack of appropriate diagnostic and prognostic markers and resistance to treatments are still hallmarks of CRC.  We know from previous studies that the P2Y6 receptor is located in the proliferative compartment of colon.  This particular localization suggests that P2Y6 might be involved in the proliferation of intestinal epithelial cells.  Hence, recent results are supporting the pro-proliferative role of P2Y6 on a subtype of cancerous colon epithelial cells.  In fact, cells harboring mutation in tumor suppressor genes APC and TP53 display enhanced expression of P2Y6 when compared to cells not having these mutations. The HYPOTHESIS supporting this project is that the up-regulation of P2Y6 expression and activity promotes carcinogenesis by conferring a growth advantage to cancerous intestinal cells.  We will prove the hypothesis through two aims.  AIM 1: To determine the molecular modifications regulating P2Y6 expression and activity in epithelial colorectal cancer cells.  AIM 2: To characterize P2Y6 receptor functions in the promotion of colorectal carcinogenesis.  The plan experiments will use cellular and molecular biology techniques applied to cell and CRC-related animal models.  We will than translate our results to patient by using human biopsies of CRC tumors.  The expected outcomes will show that: 1) P2Y6 expression increases in cancer cells with mutation in tumor suppressor genes APC and TP53.  2) That cells expressing high levels of P2Y6 are less sensitive to cancer treatments as this receptor favor tumor growth.  From a clinical point-of-view, we expect: 1) that P2Y6 expression levels might be use as biochemical indicator to modulate CRC treatments.  2) To target P2Y6 with blocking molecules to sensitize intestinal cancer cells to chemotherapeutic agents in order to block colorectal carcinogenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery and Characterization of UROD Inhibitors for Cancer Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPY; CHEMICAL BIOLOGY; CHEMO-SENSITIZATION; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREEN; IRON HOMEOSTASIS; RADIATION SENSITIZER; ROS
Abstract-Résumé: Our research group recently discovered that stopping the uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) protein in cancer cells sensitizes them to radiation therapy, one of the most common cancer treatments.  Further work found that genetically stopping UROD eliminates cancer cells, prevents resistance to radiation therapy, and sensitizes cancer cells to chemotherapies.  Correspondingly, many human cancers have abnormally high UROD amounts, and patients respond worse to radiation therapy if they have more UROD in their cancer cells.  We therefore propose to create and evaluate chemicals that stop (i.e., inhibit) UROD.  These chemicals will be used as tools to study the effects of inhibiting UROD in a wide variety of different cancer cells and in animal models of human cancer, while allowing an exploration into how UROD works.  Furthermore, these chemicals will provide information as to how new UROD-inhibiting drugs may work in cancer and may themselves be developed into new cancer drug treatments.   Specific Aims: 1. Identify chemical inhibitors of UROD:  We have already used previous scientific knowledge to develop computer-based methods for identifying potential UROD-inhibiting chemicals.  In parallel, we will use automated robots to rapidly assess 100,000 compounds for their ability to stop UROD.  The knowledge provided from the computer-based and robot-based methods will help us design even better UROD-inhibiting chemicals.  2. Characterize UROD inhibitors and mechanisms of action: The properties of the UROD-inhibiting chemicals will be examined using various types of human cancer cells.  These compounds will also be tested with many standard cancer therapies, teasing out interactive effects.  3. Evaluate UROD inhibitor activity in human-animal cancer models: The strongest UROD-inhibiting chemicals will be tested in mouse models of human cancer.  This will allow us to evaluate the safety and efficacy of such compounds.

TitreApplicationTitle: Family Physicians' Identity Formation: Exploring Impression Management Processes in Institutional Academic Contexts
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE STUDY; DISCOURSE ANALYSIS; FAMILY MEDICINE/GENERAL PRACTICE; IMPRESSION MANAGEMENT; INSTITUTIONAL THEORY; PROFESSIONAL IDENTITY; PROFESSIONAL IMAGE CONSTRUCTION; QUALITATIVE INTERVIEWING; RHETORICS
Abstract-Résumé: Medical students' interest in family medicine as a career choice has been declining persistently in Canada and other developed countries, particularly since the second half of the 1990s. Several factors that help explain this decreasing trend have been identified, e.g. the income gap between specialists and family doctors. However, the influence of processes of professional identity formation in medical schools has been largely unexplored. Building on a prior CIHR-funded investigation in which we studied family medicine 'reputation' and medical students' 'identification' (or de-identification) with family medicine in four international academic centers, our research team is now interested in examining how family physicians contruct their professional 'image' in the same contexts. In organizational literature, the strategies adopted to do so are called 'impression management'. We are convinced that this study, which makes up part of our international research portfolio on family physicians' professional identity, will significantly contribute to enhance family medicine in academic centers. Involving researchers from France, the United Kingdom, Spain, and Canada, this research will ultimately support upstream interventions aiming to fulfill individual professional aspirations while helping research societal expectations concerning medical care.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorders: From Bench to Bedside
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CLINICAL RESEARCH; DRUG SCREENING; HUMAN GENETICS; MODEL ORGANISMS OF DISEASE; PEROXISOME DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: The PBD are inherited childhood conditions that are only moderately rare, but have been neglected in terms of clinical investigations and therapeutic interventions. They are caused by defects in any one of 14 peroxisome biogenesis genes and result in faulty assembly of peroxisomes. Peroxisomes are cellular organelles that contain enzymes involved in lipid metabolism. In the PBD, peroxisome numbers are reduced and peroxisome enzymes are deficient. For most patients, peroxisome malfunction affects development after birth, and causes destruction of brain white matter, vision and hearing losses, liver disease and bone problems. Treatment options are urgently needed; at present there is only supportive care, which does not address the underlying genetic and enzyme defects. Since the disease course is one of progressive deterioration, it should be correctable by therapies that improve peroxisome function.      Our goal is to substantially accelerate the discovery and clinical application of novel drug treatments for the PBD. To streamline therapies we will partner expert peroxisome researchers in basic biology, translational research and clinical trials. We will tackle this task by (1) studying mouse and insect models to better understand the disease (2) screening drug libraries in patient cells to find drugs that can improve peroxisome functions, and screening gene pathways in insect cells to find pathways that affect peroxisome function and can be modified by drugs and, (3) improve patient diagnosis by developing a novel gene sequencing platform and longitudinal patient natural history studies, in which we can gather the data required for initiating future therapeutic trials.       Finally, the impact of this research goes beyond the PBD, as peroxisome malfunction is reported in Alzheimer's disease, premature newborn lung disease and type II diabetes. Thus, improved understanding of peroxisome functions is predicted to impact on treatment of more common conditions

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and cellular mechanisms of chemoresistance in ovarian cancer.
Keywords-MotsClés: AKT; GELSOLIN; HUMAN OVARIAN TUMOUR; MITOCHONDRIAL FISSION AND FUSION; MITOCHONDRIAL P53 IMPORT; P53 PHOSPHORYLATION AND ACTIVATION; PPM1D; XENOGRAFT
Abstract-Résumé: Despite recent advances in cancer research, ovarian cancer remains one of the most lethal forms of cancer, due primarily to late diagnosis and to loss in responsiveness to chemotherapy (chemoresistance).  Ovarian cancer is commonly treated with the drug cisplatin, and while many patients initially respond, chemoresistant tumours frequently recur.  However, the precise mechanisms by which chemoresistance develops are not well understood. Most chemotherapeutic drugs function by inducing programmed cell death (apoptosis) of the cancer cells, thereby eradicating the tumour, and recent evidence suggests that dysregulation of apoptosis may be an important factor for chemoresistance.  The overall objective of the proposed research program is to improve our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of chemoresistance. We hypothesize that chemosensitivity of ovarian cancer cells is determined by the ability of the tumor suppressor p53 to be activated and to target the cellular organelles and induce apoptosis. Gelsolin, a intracellular protein associated with the cellular structural network (cytoskeleton) is believed to be important in the regulation of apoptosis, if and how it play an important role in the control of chemosensitivity in ovarian cancer is not well understood.  These processes are modulated by the enzyme Akt in chemoresistant ovarian cancer cells. The proposed program will provide new insight into how chemoresistance occurs, and valuable information for the development of new chemotherapeutic agents and gene targeting strategies to combat this deadly disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of human memory B cells by Fc receptor-like (FCRL) molecules
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODIES; ANTIBODY REPERTOIRE; FC RECEPTOR-LIKE MOLECULES; IMMUNOREGUATION; MEMORY B CELLS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Antibodies are important proteins in the defense from disease causing pathogens. Memory B cells and plasma cells are the two principal cell populations that establish and maintain antibody levels. This is significant in light of the fact that most, if not all successful vaccines induce antibodies that neutralize the invading pathogen. Consequently, it is of critical importance to identify the mechanisms that regulate the activation of memory B cells. We identified a family of proteins termed Fc Receptor-Like (FCRL) that is predominantly expressed on memory B cells. These proteins have a strong regulatory potential on the activation of B cells. Of interest, the FCRL4 family member is expressed only by a subpopulation of human memory B cells that is impaired in the infectious diseases HIV and malaria and encodes the majority of the antibodies that are specific for HIV. The FCRL proteins represent a level of regulation of memory B cells that so far is not understood. Specifically, FCRL4 subjects a defined subpopulation of memory B cells to an additional level of regulation, the reason of which is unknown. In this research proposal we address several aspects of FCRL-mediated regulation of memory B cells. Key to the understanding of FCRL molecules is the elucidation of the mechanism by which FCRL4 regulates the activation of memory B cells. In a second approach we will examine the characteristics of the antibodies that are produced by FCRL4-bearing memory B cells. In a third approach we will investigate the origins and developmental fate of FCRL4-bearing memory B cells. The results from these studies will give us a better understanding of the mechanisms that regulate human memory B cells. This in turn will aid in the development of new vaccine designs to diseases to which current vaccination strategies are not successful and will help to understand how failure of proper FCRL-mediated regulation contributes to B cell disorders.

NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: iPS cells to model vascular disease in patients with Williams Beuren syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL ENGINEERING; DIRECTED DIFFERENTIATION; DRUG SCREENS; ELASTIN; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; PROGENITOR CELLS; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; VASCULAR DISEASE; WILLIAMS BEUREN SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Williams-Beuren (WBS) syndrome is a genetic disorder that causes narrowing of major arteries including the aorta as well as blood vessels to the lungs, brain, kidneys, gut and the coronaries. This is due to deficiency of a protein, elastin, causing smooth muscle cells in the vessel wall to start multiplying leading to thickening and narrowing of the vessel walls. The narrowing often recurs despite surgery and is a cause of early mortality and complications like hypertension, stroke and organ dysfunction in later life. Although a relatively rare disorder, the cardiovascular consequences can be severe. There are no therapies to treat this progressive vascular disease. We have established one of the largest collections of samples from WBS patients for this project. We are employing cutting edge reprogramming techniques to study cells directly from the patient and to model the disease in a dish. This has advantages compared to animal models and will allow rapid drug screening to occur.  The objective is to generate smooth muscle cells from the skin cells of WBS patients, study the pathways that cause these cells to proliferate and test the effect of drugs that can restore elastin synthesis and/or reduce cell proliferation. These drugs will be promising candidates for clinical trials in these patients using a unique translational pipeline that we have established at our centre. The project will help find new therapies for WBS patients that have the potential to reduce the burden of vascular disease, reduce complications and improve survival in patients with WBS. Importantly, vascular disease found in WBS patients resembles that seen in patients with atherosclerosis, stent restenosis and coronary disease after heart transplant. Therefore, the drugs identified in this project may prove useful in treatment of these other conditions in the future to improve the health and quality of life of people with heart disease and stroke.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: Hypoxic control of tumor cell invasion and metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; FURIN; HYPOXIA; INVADOPODIA; LYSOSOME TRAFFICKING; METASTASIS; NHE-1
Abstract-Résumé: For cancer cells to grow and make metastasis they have to degrade the surrounding tissues, a process that is influence by a particular microenvironment of the tumor that is the lack of oxygen which triggers acidosis.  Growing evidence connects newly identified cancer cell structures, invadopodia, to metastasis. Invadopodia concentrates the enzymes involved in tissue breakdown and cell invasion. Despite the crucial importance of invadopodia in tumor spread, few are known about the mechanisms involved in their formation.  We have demonstrated that hypoxia is a strong inducer of invadopodia formation and cell invasion in cancer cells.  In this project, we are searching for the specific mechanisms involved in invadopodia formation and cell invasion trigger by the tumor microenvironment (lack of oxygen and acidosis). We will test the possibility that hypoxia influences the pH of tumor cells and its microenvironment through molecular modifications of an exchanger involved in cellular pH homeostasis.  As a consequence, we will test the hypothesis that enhanced functions of pH-sensitive proteins involved in tumorigenesis is one of the mechanism by which hypoxia promotes invadopodia formation and tumor invasion.  This will be assessed using different molecular biology tools as well as unique methods to investigate invadopodia formation and functions in live cancer cells. We also propose to use in vivo metastasis assays in mice and tissue samples from normal patients and highly invasive breast cancer patients to relate our basic studies to metastatic disease.  The spread of cancer cells to distal sites of the body is the major cause of cancer patient death.  The identification of new mechanisms involved in invadopodia formation and function will be important for developing new markers of disease progression as well as new strategies to interfere with this life-threatening disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hip Fracture Evaluation with ALternatives of Total Hip Arthroplasty versus Hemi-Arthroplasty (HEALTH):  A Multi-Centre Randomized Trial Comparing Total Hip Arthroplasty and Hemi-Arthroplasty on Revision Surgery and Quality of Life in Patients with Displaced Femoral Neck Fractures
Keywords-MotsClés: EXPERTISE-BASED; HEMI-ARTHROPLASTY; HIP FRACTURE; MULTI CENTRE; ORTHOPAEDICS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; TOTAL HIP ARTHROPLASTY
Abstract-Résumé: Hip fractures occur in 280,000 Americans and 36,000 Canadians annually. The number of hip fractures is likely to exceed 500,000 a year in the United States and 88,000 a year in Canada. Hip fractures are associated with serious temporary and sometimes permanent impairment of independence and quality of life. Hip fractures can be fixed with partial (hemi) or total hip replacement (arthroplasty). Some surgeons support hemi-hip arthroplasty (HA) because it can reduce dislocation, deep vein thrombosis, lessen blood loss, shorten operating times, and is a technically less demanding procedure. Others support total hip arthroplasty (THA) because they believe it improves patient function and quality of life. Previous hip fracture trials have had study design limitations, specifically small sample sizes and surgeon expertise, leading to less certainty in the study results. This has left the best surgical approach for displaced femoral neck fractures unresolved. Therefore we propose a large multi-centre, concealed expertise-based randomized trial design that includes 1,434 patients assigned to treatments performed by surgeons considered to have expertise in the surgery to which the patient has been randomized, or who has expertise in both procedures. Surgeons across North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia will participate. Study personnel will monitor critical aspects of peri-operative care and rehabilitation. The primary outcome is revision surgery within 2 years of the arthroplasty. The secondary outcomes include health-related quality of life, functional outcomes and mobility, and health-related quality of life. We will assess patients at hospital admission, 1 week, 10 weeks, 6 months, 9 months, 12 months, 18 months, and 24 months after surgery. This trial will not only change current orthopaedic practice, but will set a benchmark for the conduct of future orthopaedic trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Caffeine as a Therapeutic Agent in Parkinson's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CAFFEINE; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Parkinson's disease is a common neurodegenerative disorder in which patients experience progressive motor disability and many disabling non-motor symptoms. Recent studies have consistently found that people who do not use caffeine are at higher risk of developing Parkinson's disease.  This suggests that caffeine may have potential as a treatment for PD.    To investigate this, we recently completed a trial where we gave PD patients caffeine.  Although it was mainly focused on daytime sleepiness, we found a very interesting benefit on the motor manifestations of disease.  There have been other lines of evidence that have suggested caffeine could be useful in PD.  The question now is how useful can caffeine can be, and also whether it could even have long term benefits in PD.   To test this, we are proposing a three-stage trial to assess caffeine.  We will randomly give patients either caffeine 200 mg twice per day (about three cups of coffee per day) or a matching placebo.  In the first six-month stage, we will hold medications constant, to see whether caffeine does have motor benefits.  Then we will perform a four-year extension stage to define if the effects of caffeine persist (or even magnify), and to see if caffeine helps reduce dose of other PD meds and/or prevents their side effects.  Finally, we will finish with a six-month stage in which we will place all patients on caffeine - this will allow us to assess caffeine's use in later disease, but more importantly, will assess whether early use of caffeine produces long term changes beyond its immediate effects.    If caffeine can be found useful for PD, it may have extremely important advantages, including low cost, established safety, and perhaps even long term neuroprotective benefits.  Such an opportunity should not be missed.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; THERAPIE DU CANCER DU SEIN
TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of MR Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer Imaging as a marker of tumour environment and pH
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; APOPTOSIS; CANCER; CEST; DIAGNOSIS; MRI; PH; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: We propose to use a newly-developed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast mechanism, 'chemical exchange saturation transfer' (CEST), to study tumour progression and response to therapy.  The contrast in CEST images reflects the exchange of protons attached to biologically-relevant molecules such as proteins, peptides, sugars, and lipids with freely moving water molecules.   Consequently, CEST is sensitive to the changing environment of the tumour cells, such as increases in mobile proteins with tumour proliferation or changes in pH which could occur if the cells are not adequately close to a blood supply or upon cell death.   We will explore this versatile imaging method in an animal study, in which animals will be implanted with tumours and then monitored by CEST MRI before and after treatment with chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy.  Once the animal protocol has been optimized, we will make a transition into a clinical study of cancer treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovery and Development of Small Molecule Toxin Antagonists to Treat C. difficile-Associated Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL TOXINS; CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE; DRUG DISCOVERY; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; IN VIVO EFFICACY; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; MICROBIOLOGY; PATHOGENESIS; PHENOTYPIC SCREENING; VIRULENCE
Abstract-Résumé: In the past decade, there have been several outbreaks of Clostridium difficile ("C.diff") in hospitals across Canada and around the world due to the emergence of more infectious strains of this microbe. These "superbug" strains are troubling because they are resistant to many antibiotics, and have been shown to produce higher levels of the gut-damaging toxins that are responsible for the symptoms of the disease, which can range from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colon disease.  Despite the increasing need for new drugs to treat these resistant infections, the pipeline of novel therapeutics to treat C.diff and many other drug-resistant infections has not kept pace.  The changing economics of antimicrobial drug discovery has forced many pharmaceutical companies to reduce their research and discovery efforts in this area - at the worst possible time.  The CIHR has responded to this new reality with the creation of the Industry-Partnered Collaborative Research (IPCR) grant program, which provides funding to "encourage and facilitate mutually beneficial university-industry collaborations in health research".  Through this program, Dr. Melnyk and researchers from the pharmaceutical company Merck seek to develop a new class of innovative drugs that control C.diff by blocking the effects of the toxins. This "anti-toxin" strategy is expected to reduce the symptoms of disease without harming the natural bacteria in the gut, which will decrease the pain and suffering of the disease and reduce recovery times after infection. A strong argument could be made that C. diff is the most important uncontrolled bacterial pathogen in Canadian hospitals today, and so there has never been a greater need for new drugs to manage this deadly bug. The approaches that Dr. Melnyk and his colleagues at Merck are undertaking are focused directly on improving the health of Canadians and decreasing the burden on health care systems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidation of the roles of Wnt signaling in the mammalian ovary
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOCRINOLOGY; FERTILITY; OVARY; REPRODUCTIVE BIOLOGY; TRANGENESIS; WNT SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) by the pituitary gland increases dramatically at the end of the follicular growth cycle, causing three key events to occur.  The first is ovulation, the release of the oocyte from the follicle.  The second is cumulus expansion, wherein a layer of cells surrounding the oocyte disperses and becomes entrapped in a viscous matrix that is required for later fertilization.  Third, LH causes the reorganization of the ovulated follicle into a new glandular tissue termed the corpus luteum, which secretes the large amounts of progesterone necessary for the establishment and maintenance of pregnancy.  Whereas the role of LH in these three events is well known, how exactly it exerts these effects remains incompletely understood.  Here, we propose that a newly discovered family of signaling molecules known as the WNTs may be key effectors of LH action.  Our published and preliminary results have shown that WNT4, WNT5a and WNT11 as well as the WNT receptors FZD1 and FZD4 are induced in follicular cells by LH, and may then serve to mediate ovulation, cumulus expansion and progesterone biosynthesis.  This proposal will seek to confirm these preliminary results, in part by studying mice that lack these WNT and FZD genes, in which we expect LH-regulated effects to be compromised or blocked altogether.  We will also study the mechanisms whereby WNTs and FZDs transmit their biological signals, and identify the genes that they regulate.  Finally, we will study the biological roles of SFRP2 and SFRP4, which may serve to limit or modulate WNT signaling activity.  Together, our studies will uncover new information regarding how LH acts, and about the biological roles and mechanisms of action of WNTs.  This research should also provide new insight into fertility disorders such as ovulatory failure and luteal insufficiency.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role or the autonomic nervous system and renin angiotensin system in chronic aortic valve regurgitation.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADRENEGIC SYSTEM; AORTIC VALVE REGURGITATION; CARDIAC MYOCYTES CULTURE; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; HEART HYPERTROPHY; HEART VALVE DISEASES; METABOLISM; MICRO-PET IMAGING; RENIN ANGIOTENSIN SYSTEM; TRANSGENIC MICE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: When the heart is subjected to pressure (hypertension) or volume overload (heart valve regurgitation), adaptive remodelling of cardiac tissue occurs. Sustained overloading of the heart over the years induces heart enlargment, an independent risk factor of heart disease. Eventually, hypertrophy and cavity dilatation will reach maximal capacity and heart failure will develop as those compensatory mechanisms reach their ultimate limit. We intend to concentrate our efforts on aortic valve regurgitation, a form of chronic volume overload of the heart left ventricle. To date, no medical therapy has been proven effective to delay the need of valve replacement through surgery. In addition, the surgical alternative is often not available to the populations most affected by this disease(developing world) We propose here to study in an new animal model (mouse) of this disease the impact of a new pharmacological approach. We will investigate at the cellular and molecular levels the nature and the range of the benefits on the heart this new way of treating this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dopaminergic Neuronal Survival During Aging and Neurodegenerative Stress
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DCC; DEGENERATIVE STRESS; DOPAMINERGIC NEURONAL SURVIVAL; MOUSE TRANSGENESIS; NETRIN-1
Abstract-Résumé: Dopamine is an important mediator of a wide variety of physiological processes and is implicated in diseases of aging, including the premature loss of midbrain dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease. Although some factors that regulate dopaminergic neuronal survival have been found, effective therapies to treat age related degeneration have not been identified.  The cause of neuronal loss in most patients with Parkinson's disease is considered "idiopathic" or unknown. Recent evidence suggests that some patients with Parkinson's disease have deficiencies in the gene for a secreted protein named netrin-1 or in the genes encoding its receptors. The midbrain dopaminergic nerve cells are particularly rich in receptors for netrin-1, and both the midbrain dopaminergic nerve cells and their targets normally express high concentrations of netrin-1. Our group and others have discovered that netrin-1 promotes the survival of nerve cells. We have recently obtained evidence that reduced expression of a netrin-1 receptor results in progressive loss of midbrain dopaminergic neurons with aging. We propose to investigate the idea that a deficiency in netrin-1 function can lead to dopamine neurons becoming more vulnerable to age related neurodegenerative stresses.  Our proposed study aims to identify the function of a novel factor, which appears to be defective in some patients with age related neurodegenerative disease that we hypothesize is required to maintain the health of dopaminergic neurons.

OrgNm: Institut de recherches cliniques de Montréal
TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of Hox genes' function in limb morphogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMOSOME ENGINEERING; CONGENITAL MALFORMATIONS; GENE REGULATION; HOX GENES; MOUSE GENETICS; ORGANOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Between 3 to 5% of births are affected by congenital malformations and 20 to 30% of infant deaths are due to genetic disorders. A large number of genetic disorders have been linked to dysfunction of genes from the Hox family but the molecular mechanisms by which these genes act remains poorly understood. The objective of this proposal is to improve our understanding of how this gene family controls organ growth and development. To achieve this goal, we will primarily focus our work on studying the function of Hox genes in mice developing limbs, which has proven a valuable model to study vertebrate development for its accessibility to genetic manipulations. Improving our knowledge of the molecular network linked to Hox function will help in unraveling the molecular causes of Hox associated disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the Molecular Chaperone Hsp90 in Fungal Development, Drug Resistance, and Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIFUNGAL DRUG RESISTANCE; CANDIDA; FUNGAL MORPHOGENESIS; FUNGAL PATHOGENESIS; GENETIC NETWORKS; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTION; HSP90; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MICROBIAL GENOMICS; STRESS RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer patients and other individuals with reduced immune function, such as those with HIV or undergoing surgery or organ transplantation, are vulnerable to life-threatening fungal infections. Candida species are the most prevalent cause of fungal infection, with mortality rates approaching 50%. Fungal infections are notoriously difficult to treat, in part because fungi are closely related to humans and it is challenging to identify drugs that kill the pathogen but not the host. The efficacy of antifungal drugs is compromised by the emergence of drug resistance.    This research is focused on dissecting the molecular mechanisms by which fungi acquire drug resistance and regulate morphogenesis, a trait critical for virulence, or the ability to cause disease. We discovered that the molecular chaperone Hsp90 is a key regulator of fungal drug resistance, morphogenesis and virulence. Hsp90 helps hundreds of proteins in the cell fold and function. When Hsp90 function is compromised, proteins misfold and cellular signaling goes awry. Here, we will provide the first global analysis of all the proteins that Hsp90 interacts with in the leading human fungal pathogen, Candida albicans. We will discover novel regulators of Hsp90 function and new targets through which Hsp90 governs drug resistance, morphogenesis, and virulence. We will also evaluate the potential of targeting the Hsp90 chaperone network in the treatment of life-threatening fungal infections.  Targeting the human Hsp90 counterpart provides a promising therapeutic strategy for cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and inflammatory diseases, and modulating fungal Hsp90 holds great potential for treating infectious disease. Elucidating the circuitry through which Hsp90 regulates drug resistance, morphogenesis, and virulence is poised to both reveal new insights into the fundamental biology underpinning protein homeostasis and cellular signaling, and establish novel and much-needed strategies to save human lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathways to weight: The influence of neighbourhood environments on the weight status of adults
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULTS; BUILT ENVIRONMENT; DIETARY BEHAVIOUR; NEIGHBOURHOOD; OBESITY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; POPULATION HEALTH; SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS; SURVEY; WEIGHT STATUS
Abstract-Résumé: More than one-half of Canadian adults are currently overweight or obese and this proportion is likely to increase in the future due to our increasingly unhealthy lifestyles. There has been recent focus on the built environment's role in determining behaviours related to overweight and obesity, including physical inactivity and poor diet. Opportunities for regular physical activity or healthy diet are not always available, particularly in less affluent neighbourhoods. Socioeconomically disadvantaged groups are at higher risk of obesity, are less physically active, and have poorer diets yet our understanding of how contextual (built characteristics) and compositional (socioeconomic status) neighbourhood characteristics influence physical activity, diet, and weight status are still rudimentary, particularly in the Canadian context. This project will involve a random cross-section of 2497 adult study participants from Calgary (Alberta). Participants will complete a postal survey that will capture their physical activity-related energy expenditure, caloric intake, height and weight, and socio-demographic characteristics. Participants will also receive a body measuring tape to capture waist and hip circumference. Indices reflecting the neighbourhood environment's supportiveness for physical activity and a healthy diet within 1-km of participant's homes will be estimated from existing municipal databases and field audits of streetscapes. The relationships between neighbourhood environment indices and socioeconomic status, energy expenditure and caloric intake, and multiple indicators of weight status (BMI and measures of central adiposity including waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio) will be estimated. Findings will be useful for informing urban planning and policy decisions that may support healthy weight status and socioeconomic health-related disparities among Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rapid Genetic Testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 in Newly Diagnosed Breast Cancer Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: BRCA1; BRCA2; BREAST CANCER; GENETIC TESTING; SERVICE DELIVERY
Abstract-Résumé: In 2011, it was expected that there would be 23,400 new cases of breast cancer diagnosed in Canada, of which approximately five percent are due to mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes.  There is recent evidence that these BRCA-associated breast cancers should receive different, more targeted treatments compared to women with sporadic breast cancer to decrease risks of new cancers and increase the chance of survival. However, due to the current genetic testing criteria and the length of time that genetic testing takes within Canada, testing at the time of breast cancer diagnosis is not generally offered, and if it is, test results are not available prior to breast cancer surgery.  This may be leading to women electing for less personalized and targeted treatments, which has the potential to affect cancer-related mortality. With new genetic technology, rapid genetic testing for BRCA mutations is an option and genetic test results can be available within one week.  However, it is unclear if provision of BRCA genetic test results at time of diagnosis would result in uptake of targeted surgical and medical treatments. The overall objective of the study is to evaluate the impact of rapid genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 in newly-diagnosed breast cancer patients on surgical and medical treatment choices, compared to women who receive standard genetic testing.  Exploratory aims will include the evaluation of psychosocial functioning and satisfaction in women who receive rapid genetic testing at the time of breast cancer diagnosis.  In this project we will compare the uptake of surgical and medical treatments two years after breast cancer diagnosis between BRCA mutation carriers who receive rapid genetic testing and those who receive standard genetic testing.  Exploratory aims (psychosocial functioning and satisfaction) will be assessed in all women who participate in the rapid genetic testing (including BRCA1/2 positive and BRCA1/2 negative).

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulatory roles of hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 and 4 in gastrointestinal metabolic disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; DIFFERENTIATION; FAT METABOLISM; GASTROINTESTINAL PHYSIOLOGY; GENE EXPRESSION ASSAYS; GENE SILENCING; GENE TRANSCRIPTION; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; MOUSE CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT; PROTEIN-DNA INTERACTION
Abstract-Résumé: The overall organization of the adult intestinal epithelium is the result of several steps during development that will instruct this epithelium to express specific genes. The adequate regulation of these genes is crucial to ensure correct functions of intestinal epithelial cells for production of intestinal hormones as well as processing and transport of luminal nutrients. A defect in these features is associated with intestinal and metabolic diseases. My laboratory has identified specific proteins that can regulate intestinal genes. Published observations from my laboratory derived from animal models and cultured epithelial cell lines support the idea that these proteins are important to ensure intestinal epithelial functions. I propose to further document the mechanistic effect of genetically altering these gene regulators in mice and cultured human cellular models in relation to intestinal epithelial metabolism functions. This approach will ultimately lead to the discovery of novel targets and therapeutic strategies to limit metabolic disorders that are closely linked to intestinal pathologies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural representations underlying the planning and control of object manipulation tasks
Keywords-MotsClés: FMRI; HUMAN; MOVEMENT PLANNING; MULTI-VOXEL PATTERN ANALYSIS; NEURAL MECHANISMS; OBJECT MANIPULATION; SENSORY-MOTOR CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of the proposed research is to better understand how skilled object manipulation tasks are planned and controlled in the human brain. Planning to manipulate an object (e.g., a cup) is highly complex, and involves, among other things, predicting the weight of the object as well as sequencing together a series of distinct motor acts (e.g., reaching towards, grasping, lifting and transporting the cup) in order to attain some overarching goal (e.g., drinking). We will use behavioural methods and brain imaging techniques (functional magnetic resonance imaging, fMRI) to examine the neural representations that underlie two fundamental components of object manipulation: the prediction of object weight and the sequencing of distinct action phases in order to obtain a goal. The first project will examine how and where in the brain knowledge about object weight, used when lifting, is represented. We will also examine how and where in the brain predictions about weight based on object material are generated. The second project will explore how object manipulation tasks that involve the linking of multiple action phases are coded in the brain. Characterizing and mapping human neural activity associated with the planning of object manipulation will provide critical insights into both normal and impaired cognitive brain function as well as aid the development of brain-machine interfaces, which aim to restore complex motor functions to movement-impaired patient populations (individuals with neurologic disease, injury, or limb loss).

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Pseudomonas aeruginosa type IV pilins
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; MICROBIOLOGY; PROTEIN GLYCOSYLATION; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; TWITCHING MOTILITY; TYPE IV PILI
Abstract-Résumé: Many bacteria hold onto surfaces using long hair-like filaments called pili.  Without these filaments, they can't initiate infections very easily because they are readily swept away.  Some bacteria use their pili as minature grappling hooks, to move along surfaces.  The bacteria extend the pili, hook them onto a surface, and retract them into the cell, pulling themselves forward.  This movement is important during infection because it allows the bacteria to spread rapidly away from the initial point of contact.  Mutations that paralyze the pili so they can't retract make the bacteria unable to cause disease.  In this grant application, we propose to study the components that make up the filaments.  We want to know exactly what the filaments are composed of, how the components are assembled and disassembled during extension and retraction, and how expression of the components is controlled, so we can block these processes.  Some bacteria decorate their pili with sugars, and we recently found out that they do this because it protects them from predators called bacteriophages.  Bacteriophages can infect bacteria by hitching a ride on the pili while they're retracted, so the bacteriophages are pulled inside the bacteria and kill them.  The sugars prevent many bacteriophages from sticking to pili, but some have figured out how to get around this protective shield.  Those types of bacteriophages will be used as tools, to show us where the vulnerable parts of the pili are.  Together, these studies will help us to find new ways to interfere with the production or the function of pili, which in turn have potential to reduce bacterial infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nef: an HIV-1 protein at the forefront of pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOSOMES; HIV-1; MEMBRANE TRAFFICKING; MICROSCOPY; PATHOGENESIS; THERAPEUTICS; VIRAL REPLICATION
Abstract-Résumé: My laboratory studies how the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) evades killing by the immune system and leads to the development of acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS). Specifically, we are interested in studying the HIV-1 protein Nef, which is required for the virus to thrive and is necessary for the progression to AIDS. Nef exerts this pathogenic effect by interacting with host cellular proteins and overtaking their normal functions to the advantage of the virus. One such example is the removal of specific receptors from the surface of virally infected cells. These receptors, called major histocompatibility complex (MHC-I), alert neighboring immune cells that they are virally infected so they can be destroyed. Nef can remove MHC-I from the cell surface, thereby preventing virally infected cells from being detected and destroyed by the immune cells. The interaction between Nef and the host cell protein Src Family Kinase (SFK) is essential for the ability of Nef to keep MHC-I molecules hidden inside the cell. This grant proposal is focused on the discovery and testing of novel drug like compounds that can inhibit the interaction between Nef and SFK, and thereby block the ability of Nef to keep virally infected cells hidden from the immune system. To do this, we will use both cell culture models as well as a mouse model of AIDS. This grant will also more precisely elucidate the mechanisms used by Nef to remove MHC-I from the cell surface, leading to a greater understanding of how Nef allows HIV-1 to evade the immune system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms and potential of mesenchymal stromal cell-to-myofibroblast activation in skin dermis regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; MESENCHYMAL STROMAL/STEM CELLS (MSCS); MYOFIBROBLAST; REGENERATION; TISSUE FIBROSIS; TISSUE REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: After severe skin injury such as burns, our body rapidly but imperfectly repairs the damage, leaving behind a stiff scar. Scarring is a clinical burden because skin is losing vital functions. During normal repair, local fibroblasts are activated into myofibroblasts (MFs) to secrete and organize large amounts of fibrous collagen by exerting strong pulling forces. This action is beneficial since it prevents our tissues from breaking but it leads to scarring when the repair demands of our body exceed its regenerative potential. To support healing and to regenerate damaged organs, adult mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) have entered clinical trials. MSCs retain the capability to differentiate into different specialized cells (e.g., skin, cartilage, bone) and truly regenerate organs. MSCs can be obtained from bone marrow biopsies, expanded in cell culture and re-transplanted to the same patient. Pivotal cell culture expansion activates MSCs into MFs. It is unclear whether MF-MSCs are beneficial or detrimental for skin repair and regeneration.   We hypothesize that becoming MF will influence the capacity of MSCs to regenerate the dermis of injured skin. We will induce and suppress MF activation to test the effect on MSC pluripotency and to assess whether the MF is a terminal or transient state of the MSC. We will use innovative soft culture substrates to suppress MF activation of MSCs. We will analyze genetic changes (epigenetics) resulting from soft substrate culture to decipher the mechanism of this mechanical memory. In mouse experimental models, mechanically primed MSCs will be transplanted into normally healing and fibrotic wounds to test their impact on the repair process. In co-cultures with fibroblasts, we will reveal the mechanistic cross-talk between primed and fibrotic MSCs and the local repair cells of the body. Understanding and controlling the mechanisms of MSC fibrogenesis will augment the success rate of tissue regeneration therapies using MSCs.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of IDO1 vs IDO2 on tumour immune evasion  and immune therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: 3 DEOXYGENASE (IDO); CANCER IMMUNOLOGY; DENDRITIC CELLS; GENE SILENCING; IMMUNE THERAPY; INDOLEAMINE 2; MELANOMA; SIRNA
Abstract-Résumé: Dr Min is working on the mechanism of cancer immune evasion that is a major hurdle impeding cancer immune-based therapies.  Our immune system is naturally equipped with ways to recognize and destroy cancerous cells. In order to survive and grow, tumors must therefore be able to avoid and weaken the immune system. Dr Min and his research team will develop a new cancer treatment through destroying suppressive molecules in immune cells, using a newly developed gene silencing strategy called siRNA. This new treatment will be safer and more robust with great potential in clinic anti-cancer therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Miyonohk âyâwin kiskinwahamâtowin (a many sided thing): Outdoor education, injury prevention and Edmonton's First Nation, Metis and Inuit youth
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL UNINTENTIONAL INJURY PREVENTION; ABORIGINAL YOUTH; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; CULTURAL SAFETY; INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGES AND PEDAGOGIES; OUTDOOR EDUCATION; SAFETY EDUCATION; SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF RISK AND RISK TAKING
Abstract-Résumé: Injuries are a major contributor to premature mortality for Indigenous youth in Canada, occurring at a rate four times that associated with non-Indigenous youth. Turning this situation around will require significant research, capacity-building, and knowledge dissemination as this pertains specifically to First Nation, Metis and Inuit contexts. This study, involving a team of academic researchers, community leaders, Indigenous Elders, school heads, injury prevention specialists, and others, is centered on the efficacy of culturally focused, land-based outdoor education for fostering urban Indigenous youth leadership in the area of unintentional injury prevention. Of particular interest is the manner in which cultural safety, a critical understanding of Indigenous injuries, and peer teaching opportunities influence the ways in which Indigenous youth leaders in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada understand and act in relation to unintentional injury prevention. A related focus is an examination of the impact of cultural learning modalities, such as those associated with hunting and fishing, for inspiring the creative development of an injury prevention resource, to be used by youth leaders to teach safety skills and knowledge to their rural and urban peers. The study employs communitybased participatory research methodology, an approach to research that seeks to put communities in the lead on inquiry and action on urgent Indigenous health issues. Access to the research outcomes, and to the injury prevention resource itself will be promoted through social media technologies. Given a fast growing, young Indigenous population with increasing access to the Internet, the impact of this study has significant potential to extend nationally and beyond. The research will also be disseminated in traditional academic contexts, and to key policy makers e.g. school boards, municipalities, and government departments, providing a strong incentive for changes to policy that reflect Indigenous-focused injury prevention strategies that work.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pharmaco-behavioural study of genetic & environmental risk factors in children with ADHD:using brain imaging phenotypes to further dissect etiological pathways
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHD; BEHAVIOUR; BRAIN IMAGING; CHILDREN; GENE ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; GENETICS; MATERNAL SMOKING; METHYLPHENIDATE; PREGNANCY; PSYCHIATRY
Abstract-Résumé: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is the most common psychiatric disorder in children, occurring in 8-12% of the population. Symptoms tend to persist through adolescence to adulthood in the majority of cases causing academic, occupational and social impairment. The disorder has a complex etiology - both genetic and environmental factors (particularly maternal smoking during pregnancy) have been associated with ADHD. During the last 10 years we have collected the largest sample of children with ADHD with very comprehensive information on their clinical, neuropsychological and response to medication profiles. Our results have strongly implicated maternal smoking during pregnancy as an important factor that possibly increase the risk for a more severe form of the disorder. We have also been able to show that a gene very important in brain physiology, is strongly implicated in ADHD in the children whose mothers smoked during pregnancy. In the present study, we propose to show that this gene may also have an impact on brain development. We also propose to expand our collection of the same high quality data. This will allow us to identify other genetic factors that interact with maternal smoking (and other environmental factors) to increase the risk for ADHD. This work will lead to a better understanding of ADHD and ultimately to more effective and safer treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inherited bone marrow failure syndromes: from genomic discoveries to biology
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER PREDISPOSITION; EXOME SEQUENCING; GENETIC; HEMATOPOIESIS; INHERITED BONE MARROW FAILURE SYNDROMES; LEUKEMIA; RNA PROCESSING; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFSs) comprise over 20 rare genetic diseases; e.g. Fanconi anemia and severe congenital neutropenia. The blood producing organ (bone marrow) in the patients does not work from early childhood, leading to low blood counts. Patients suffer from infections, fatigue and bleeding, which often require life-long transfusions or bone marrow transplantation, and also have a high risk of cancer. Since the medical needs and response to treatment vary among the diseases, accurate diagnosis is crucial. We found that many patients with inherited types of bone marrow failure have new diseases that had not been previously defined. These new IBMFSs are likely caused by mutations in new bone marrow failure genes. In 2001 we established a nationwide registry of IBMFSs (database and sample repository) with more than 300 patients. We propose to identify new genes for bone marrow failure by using a new technology (called exome sequencing) and characterize a subgroup of 42 patients who are suspected to have new diseases. Then, we propose to study one new IBMFS with a new bone marrow failure gene that we successfully discovered using the above approach, to understand how the disease ensues. Specifically, we will focus on a breakthrough discovery from our lab that a perturbation of chemical machinery in the cells, called RNA degradation, causes a human disease with severe bone marrow failure. We will study how mutations in the new bone marrow failure gene change the delicate balance of gene products (RNA) and impair blood cell formation in two complementary disease models: patient blood cells and zebrafish blood cells. The results of our study will have a major impact on the care of patients with IBMFSs by providing new genetic tests to establish diagnoses, counsel the families, and tailor treatment and cancer surveillance plans. Our findings will help understand how marrow failure develops, and prompt research for new therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Integration of clinical, biomarker, and genetic data for prediction of adverse outcomes in diabetes.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; DIABETES; GENETICS; KIDNEY DISEASE; RISK PREDICTION
Abstract-Résumé: Over 9 million Canadians currently have diabetes or prediabetes.  In people with diabetes, heart disease is the leading cause of death and accounts for over half of all mortality.  In fact, individuals with diabetes have double the risk of heart disease as compared to individuals without it.  Furthermore, diabetes is the leading cause of kidney disease in Canada and also the first cause of kidney replacement therapy, also called dialysis.  Despite all of this, there is currently no tool to help physicians determine which individuals with diabetes are at high risk of developing heart or kidney complications.  Our project seeks to develop such tools by combining blood analysis with genetic analysis.  To do so, we will use blood and genetic samples from a large clinical study of insulin (the ORIGIN trial).  Our hope is that development of such tool will help provide early and maximal preventive therapy to individuals with diabetes at high risk of complications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Roles of chromatin architecture in germline genome stability
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEUPLOIDY; C. ELEGANS; CHROMATIN; CHROMOSOME STRUCTURE; DNA REPAIR; MEIOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: The germ line cells of sexually-reproducing animals are destined to give rise to the eggs and sperm necessary for the propagation of the species. Consequently, germline DNA must be protected from acquiring mutations that will be transmitted to the next generation and can result in susceptibility to diseases like breast cancer. The DNA of all eukaryotic cells is organized into chromatin through association with a complex of histone proteins and other DNA-associated proteins. The modification of histones is known to result in changes that make the chromatin more or less accessible to proteins required for transcription of genes during development. Here, we address the role of histone modifications in facilitating the repair of unexpected DNA damage in the germ cell lineage of the nematode C.elegans. We have identified a protein, HTP-3, that is localized to the germ cells throughout development and is required to both establish a germline-specific chromatin architecture and to accurately repair DNA damage. In this proposal, we will first investigate how germline chromatin is established and the role of HTP-3 in this process. We will then examine how germline chromatin is modified in response to the presence of DNA breaks, and the role of these DNA-damage responsive chromatin changes on germ line and DNA repair processes. These experiments will reveal how the germline genome is configured and how this architecture can ensure that unexpected mutations are accurately repaired to restore an intact genome for the next generation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of chromatin remodeling in the genesis of pediatric and young adult astrocytomas
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; DNA METHYLATION; EXOME SEQUENCING; HISTONE MARKS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; RNA SEQUENCING; SH-RNA SCREEN
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumours including astrocytomas are the most frequent solid cancers and the leading cause of cancer-related mortality and morbidity in children. The focus of my research program is to improve our understanding of these deadly brain tumours and identify relevant therapeutic targets, as little is known about what make them grow and develop. We collected a sizeable number of samples from all grade and age astrocytomas, a unique collection from across the world and established an international collaborative network. Using state of the art tools we explored the genome (DNA), epigenome (what protects and regulates our DNA) and transcriptome (messengers from our DNA) of high- and low-grade tumors. Our results demonstrated that adult and pediatric tumours are distinct and need to be studied separately. Importantly, we identified targets that are driving pediatric high grade astrocytomas and aim herein to further investigat their function. The proposed work aims to identify factors rapidly amenable to targeted intervention tailored to the tumor biology. Our ultimate goal is to provide in the near future novel therapeutic avenues to children that currently have limited options for clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of emotional mimicry and oxytocin on frontotemporal dementia
Keywords-MotsClés: EMOTION; EMOTIONAL EXPRESSION PROCESSING; EMPATHY; FMRI; FRONTOTEMPORAL DEMENTIA; MIMICRY AND MIRROR NEURON SYSTEM; OXYTOCIN; SOCIAL COGNITION
Abstract-Résumé: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, typically striking adults in mid-life (age 50-60). Pathologic protein accumulations and neuronal loss in FTD slowly destroy brain regions of frontal and/or temporal cortex, causing previously high functioning individuals to develop striking behavioural and cognitive problems. Hallmark to the disease is a progressive loss of the capacity for empathy, even for one's own family members, which is magnified by a complete lack of insight into their personality and behavioural changes. At present there are no treatments which can ameliorate the emotional blunting, lack of empathy or decline in social behaviour.  Our long-term goal is to characterize the neural pathways by which empathy and basic emotional capacities break down in FTD in order to develop novel treatment approaches for these symptoms. The present investigation will use functional brain imaging to determine the key brain abnormalities behind the emotional impairments in FTD. This study will examine brain function while patients and healthy controls view and attempt to mimic emotions in others. Recent work has shown that these methods reliably increase emotional states in healthy adults, and when used with brain imaging, provide a window into the function of brain regions critical for experiencing emotions and empathy. In addition, the effects of oxytocin, a drug recently shown to improve empathy in healthy individuals and some patient groups, will be examined in patients with FTD. Specifically, the impact of the drug on empathy-related behaviours and emotion-related brain function in patients with FTD will be determined for the first time. At the successful completion of the study, we will have delineated the mechanisms of emotion deficits in FTD, developed novel techniques by which the effects of treatments for these symptoms may be tested, and determined whether oxytocin can improve empathy in patients with this disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Quality care for all: A system-level evaluation of performance and equity in addiction treatment
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION TREATMENT; EVALUATION; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS; MULTILEVEL MODELING; SERVICE EQUITY; SYSTEMS RESEARCH; TREATMENT PROCESS
Abstract-Résumé: Addiction treatment providers everywhere share the common goals of delivering services to treat and prevent problems related to substance use, and support their clients in achieving long-term recovery. The contexts of services vary considerably, however, in terms of local levels and types of need, programming, and resources. To ensure that services are delivered in an effective and equitable manner, population-based research is needed to monitor treatment processes and outcomes, and to identify potential gaps in the system. Remarkably few studies have addressed these issues in Canada, hampering efforts to improve the quality and delivery of services for addiction. Using data from an information system that monitors clients and their use of services for drug and alcohol problems in Ontario, we will measure and characterise clients' patterns of service use over time. Looking at people's encounters with the addiction treatment system over an 8-year period (2005-2012), we will consider a number of important aspects of care quality, such as whether clients in detoxification received additional counseling or treatment, whether clients in outpatient treatment received at least 4 outpatient visits in the first 6 weeks after admission, and whether clients in residential treatment received additional outpatient services to assist them with transitioning back to the community. We will also look at whether and how client characteristics, such as ethnicity, mandates to attend treatment, and homelessness, affect the treatment process and quality of care. An important contribution of this work will be the findings pertaining to how such client characteristics interact to influence encounters with the treatment system over time. This work will help to improve our understanding of addiction treatment system equity and effectiveness, and our ability to identify and address any gaps in the system.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Connecting the Cell-Type Specific Chromosome Architecture to Gene Regulation, Development and Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCERS; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; CHROMOSOME ARCHITECTURE; DEVELOPMENTAL SYNDROMES; EMBRYONIC STEM CELL; EPIGENETIC; GENE REGULATION; GENOMIC; PLURIPOTENCY; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Like computers, our cells depend on operating systems to drive normal functions. The gene expression programs are the source code our cells rely on to play their biological functions. Corrupted programs can trigger disease. Embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are under scrutiny for their potential in regenerative medicine and represent a great model system to study rules controlling the gene expression program. Factors regulating gene expression programs are often mutated in human diseases and ESCs are a unique model-system to study these transcription-related disease mechanisms. Cellular operating systems require a web of connections to deliver an accurate gene expression program. Each individual gene can be access following a precise number of commands that need to be executed in an orderly fashion. From the last 30 years of research, multiple regulators emerged to control the cell-type specific gene expression program including transcription factors, chromatin regulators and other co-factors. These factors influence the immediate environment surrounding a gene. Using ESCs, we recently discovered a secondary architecture across the genome established by SMC complexes, a protein family conserved through evolution. SMC complexes connect the regulation of the gene expression program with the chromosome architecture opening a new folder of possibilities to regulate genes.   Subunits of SMC complexes are often mutated in cancer and developmental syndrome including the Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS). CdLS is an autosomal dominant syndrome affecting 1 per 10,000 live births and typically characterized by a wide array of developmental defects. Defining how the cellular operating system is regulated is crucial to get one step closer to understanding defective gene expression programs in diseases such as CdLS. Furthermore, this research could open new treatment avenues for other diseases caused by transcription-related events.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prescription medications and the risk of motor vehicle crashes.
Keywords-MotsClés: MOTOR VEHICLE CRASHES; PRESCRIPTION MEDICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Each year in Canada, 125,000 motor vehicle crashes (MVCs) result in over 12,000 serious injuries, and 2,400 fatalities at a cost of $63 billion. Many drivers use medications that slow reaction time, cloud judgment and impair the skills required for safe driving. This problem may be increasing because of an aging population and increased use of impairing medications. Young drivers are also at high risk of crashing and may be particularly susceptible to the effects of impairing medications. Unfortunately, despite international efforts, the risk to road safety associated with most medications is poorly understood. This lack of knowledge prevents authorities from developing effective policy, public education campaigns, and medication warning labels designed to prevent people from driving while using impairing medications.   Numerous studies have investigated the crash risk associated with prescription medications and some progress has already been made. European experts developed a consensus document that classifies medications according to suspected crash risk. Unfortunately, for most medications, there is little real world evidence to show whether or not they really increase the chance of crashing. Therefore this classification is based mostly on expert opinion and may be inaccurate.  In this project, we will study the association of all major classes of prescription medications with crashes. We will do this by linking driver records and police crash reports with prescription records. This rich data will allow us to overcome many of the limitations of previous research. We will use sophisticated methods to find out if drivers who take medications are more likely to crash than other drivers and if they are more likely to crash when using medications than at other times.   Our long term goal is to make our roads more safe. We plan to do this by providing evidence that will be used to develop road safety policy, public education campaigns, and medication warnings.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: IL-7 in Lymphocyte Development and Immunity.
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINE RECEPTORS; IMMUNOTHERAPY; INFLUENZA/A VIRUS; LYMPHOCYTES; MODULATING INNATE AND ADAPTIVE IMMUNITY; VIRAL INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system plays a multi-faceted role in determining how the body reacts appropriately to pathogens (immunity), environmental triggers (allergens) and normal versus foreign tissues (such as a fetus in pregnancy versus transplant rejection). An intricate network of triggers including immune hormones called cytokines, regulate these outcomes. Loss of control of these cytokines or the biochemical pathways they activate can lead to diseases, such as autoimmunity, immune deficiencies and inadequate response to infection. Treating diseases with few side effects requires knowing the molecular processes involved in disease development. The cytokine IL-7 is a major immunotherapeutic undergoing clinical trials for cancer, immune restoration after transplantation or HIV and hepatitis C viral infection. We use gene-targeted mouse models to identify the steps that that are controlled by IL-7 that are necessary for normal lymphocyte development and immune responses to microbes. By interrupting specific signals in a biochemical pathway, we examined whether the disruption affected normal cells and found some important effects on immune response to pathogens. A better knowledge of cytokine signaling in vivo will further our understanding of lymphocyte regulation to help identify potential therapeutic strategies to cancer and to enhance immunity against infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of CYP26B1-mediated retinoic acid metabolism in regulating osteoblast differentiation in normal bone and heterotopic calcification of cardiovascular tissue
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE REMODELLING; BONE REPAIR; CYP26; GENETIC MOUSE MODEL; OSTEOBLAST DIFFERENTIATION; OSTEOGENESIS; RETINOIC ACID METABOLISM; VASCULAR CALCIFICATION; VITAMIN A
Abstract-Résumé: Retinoic acid (RA), the active form of vitamin A, plays an essential role in the formation and maintenance of many tissues both during embryonic development and in the adult. The activity of RA needs to be controlled by mechanisms ensuring that certain cells at specific times are exposed to RA, while others are not. We have discovered a family of proteins (the CYP26 enzymes -A1,-B1 and -C1) which are expressed in different tissues at different times during development and are critical for the correct formation of structures as prominent as the trunk and limbs and as intricate as the bones of the inner ear and hair follicles. We have created mouse knock out models for each of the CYP26 family members, as well as a set of CYP26-specific chemical inhibitors, which we will use to examine the role that these enzymes play in the formation and maintenance of bone. Furthermore, evidence suggests that RA can have a protective effect against the pathological formation of bone in other tissues such as blood vessels, which can arise as a result of injury, or in patients suffering from diabetes or chronic kidney disease. We will therefore examine whether genetic removal or chemical inhibition of CYP26 members can prevent or reverse formation of bone in soft tissues which can lead to cardiovascular disease and death. Currently, there is very little in the way of treatment for ectopic bone formation; our studies will serve as an important step towards developing novel therapeutic strategies for addressing this unmet medical need.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; ATHEROSCLEROSE
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular characterization of lipid transport by the scavenger receptor SCARB1
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CHOLESTEROL; ENDOCYTOSIS; HDL; HYPERCHOLESTEROLEMIA; SCARB1; SCAVENGER RECEPTOR; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Cholesterol is a critical component of cells, but too much cholesterol in the body can lead to heart attacks, stroke and a host of other diseases.  One critical way that the body controls the levels of cholesterol in the blood is to shuttle some of it to the liver in HDL particles to be released into feces.  HDL particles in the blood, (the so-called good cholesterol) deliver cholesterol to the SCARB1 protein on the surface of liver cells, but how this protein extracts the cholesterol from HDL particle has been a mystery.  We recently determined the molecular structure of a related protein, SCARB2, and this has allowed us to show that SCARB1 contains a tunnel through the middle of the protein that serves as a passageway for the cholesterol to transit from the HDL particle directly to the liver cell surface.  In this proposal we will examine this structure to fully define how SCARB1 does this, and to determine other properties of the protein that contribute to the transport of other fats.  Through these studies we hope to identify new targets that we can use for therapeutic control of cholesterol levels in the blood.
