TitreApplicationTitle: Genomic analysis of Cannabis sativa
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; DNA SEQUENCING; GENE EXPRESSION; GENOMICS; METABOLISM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Cannabis sativa (marijuana) is used to treat a range of diseases and conditions such as spasticity and neuropathic pain in multiple sclerosis, nausea/vomiting from chemotherapy, and severe cancer pain. More than 19,000 Canadians (May 2012) suffering from terminal or debilitating diseases have authorization from Health Canada to use medicinal cannabis. Its unique effects are due to the presence of a group of chemicals called cannabinoids, which include delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and more than 70 related chemicals found only in the cannabis plant. THC is responsible for the mood-altering and pain-relieving effects of cannabis. Despite its widespread, legal use by patients in Canada, there is a paucity of research on the cannabis plant and its medicinal effects. We propose to sequence and map the genome of Cannabis sativa and analyze this information to determine how cannabinoids are made. The underlying goal of this work is to better understand how cannabis produces medicinal compounds so that its potential to treat disease and alleviate suffering can be exploited. There are three main objectives of our proposed research: 1) to produce a genetic map of the cannabis genome, which will allow the fragmented pieces to be assembled into a more complete reference for use by researchers worldwide; 2) to use this genomic information to identify the proteins (transcription factors) that control the expression of the cannabinoid pathway; and 3) to identify the genes that encode the enzymes of the cannabinoid biochemical pathway. In addition to the knowledge useful for biotechnological modification of cannabis, this research will shed light on the evolutionary history and domestication of this important medicinal plant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of TDAG51 in apoptotic cell death associated with cardiovascular disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANOIKIS; APOE-DEFICIENT MICE; APOPTOSIS; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM STRESS; T-CELL DEATH-ASSOCIATED GENE 51 (TDAG51)
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease accounts for the majority of deaths in North America. Acute clinical manifestations of heart disease result from the rupture of atherosclerotic lesions, resulting in blood clots and vessel blockage. Programmed cell death has been well documented in animal and human atherosclerotic lesions, and contributes to lesion rupture and clot formation. Although cell death influences lesion growth, stability and clot formation, the cellular mechanisms and/or factors responsible for this effect are incompletely understood. We have reported that a specific cellular factor, termed T-cell death associated gene 51 (TDAG51), causes cell death and contributes to atherosclerotic lesion development. Our findings demonstrate increased expression of TDAG51 within lesion resident endothelial cells and macrophages. Furthermore, deficiency in TDAG51 causes a significant reduction in atherosclerotic lesion development in established mouse models of atherogenesis. The overall objective of this research proposal is to better understand how TDAG51 contributes to the development and progression of heart disease. The findings from this research project will allow us to better understand the role of TDAG51 and to develop novel therapeutic stategies for the treatment/prevention of heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Impact of a Physician Detailing and Sampling Program for Generic Atorvastatin
Keywords-MotsClés: GENERIC DRUGS; HEALTH CARE COSTS; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PHARMACEUTICAL MARKETING; PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
Abstract-Résumé: Generic drugs provide a savings opportunity that is underutilized in Canada. While generics represent over 80% of prescriptions dispensed in the United States, Canadian rates are much lower at around 60%. In 2010, Manitoba Health implemented an innovative program aimed at increasing the use of generic atorvastatin. Our study will investigate the effects of this physician detailing and sampling program on statin utilization and costs, market share of generic statins, and the choice of starting statin.

TitreApplicationTitle: Évaluation des effets et bilan de l'implantation du programme d'intervention en toxicomanie offert par le Centre de réadaptation en dépendance de Québec à l'Établissement de détention de Québec
Keywords-MotsClés: POPULATION CARCERALE; REINSERTION SOCIALE; TOXICOMANIE; EVALUATION DE PROGRAMME
Abstract-Résumé: Bien que prives de leur liberte, les detenus maintiennent leur droit a des services de sante adequats. Ainsi, les delinquants toxicomanes incarceres doivent avoir acces a des soins en lien avec leur consommation abusive de substances psychoactives (Brochu et Schneeberger, 2000). Au Quebec, un protocole d'entente liant le Ministere de la Securite publique au Ministere de la Sante et des Services sociaux specifie que la responsabilite de l'offre de traitement en toxicomanie aux personnes detenues incombe aux centres publics de readaptation pour personnes dependantes de la region (Brochu et Plourde, 2012). Depuis septembre 2009, le Centre de readaptation en dependance de Quebec, en collaboration avec le Centre d'education des adultes Conrad-Barbeau et l'etablissement de detention de Quebec, offre un programme d'intervention en toxicomanie en milieu de detention. Ce programme tout a fait unique et novateur offre a la clientele carcerale aux prises avec une problematique de consommation une occasion d'approfondir sa reflexion sur ses habitudes de consommation pendant sa periode d'incarceration tout en contribuant a orienter les usagers vers les ressources appropriees une fois leur liberation obtenue. Or, tout prometteur qu'il semble etre, ce programme n'a, a ce jour, ete soumis a aucune forme d'evaluation. La presente demande entend combler cette lacune et generera des retombees tres concretes pour l'intervention en toxicomanie en milieu carceral. Ce projet s'inscrit dans l'esprit de la necessite de conduire des recherches pour ameliorer notre comprehension des pratiques efficaces et leur impact sur la sante et la reinsertion sociale des detenus. Son caractere novateur se situe dans le fait qu'au Quebec, peu de programmes et d'initiatives font l'objet d'evaluation, d'autant plus lorsqu'elles sont sous la responsabilite de plusieurs entites gouvernementales.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the optimum treatment cutoffs for high-sensitivity troponin assays in patients presenting to the emergency department with suspected cardiac ischemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC TROPONIN ASSAYS; CARDIOVASCULAR EVENTS; EMERGENCY MEDICINE; PROGNOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiac troponin is a protein released from heart cells into the blood just prior to and during a heart attack. Hence, increased troponin levels in the blood are used to make or confirm the diagnosis of a heart attack in patients who go to the emergency department (ED) with chest pain. Within the next year, Canadian hospitals will begin to use newer troponin blood tests that can detect lower levels than the current ones. The problem is that no one knows what levels of the new tests best diagnose a heart attack. Also, there is evidence that the troponin levels can even predict which patients are at greatest or least risk of a heart attack or other serious heart problem within the next week, month or 6 months but, again, we don't know what these levels are.  We propose to recruit 1887 patients who come to the ED with chest pain or other symptoms of a heart attack and perform the newer blood test when they arrive and 3 hours later. Without interfering in their care, we will then follow these patients to determine if any of them had a heart attack or other serious heart problem within the first week, first month and six months after their ED visit. This information will allow us to determine what troponin levels best identify patients at the highest risk for a heart problem early (within the first week) and which patients would benefit from hospital admission and treatment for their disease. We will also be able to determine what levels are the best for identifying patients at the highest risk for a heart problem at 30 days and 6 months.  In short, the results of this study will enable physicians to identify patients who are not currently recognized as being at high risk for a serious heart problem and treat them appropriately while also avoiding hospital admission and treatment of patients who could be managed equally well as outpatients. Thus, this study has the potential to improve patient health and safety while also reducing hospital costs and ED overcrowding.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dystonin - a cytoskeletal linker protein critical for neuronal function
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CYTOSKELETAL LINKER PROTEINS; ESTABLISHED AND PRIMARY CELL CULTURE MODELS; INTRACELLULAR TRAFFICKING; MICROTUBULE DYNAMICS; MOUSE MODELS; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES; NEURONAL INTEGRITY; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: Defects in cytoskeletal proteins have a primary role in many neurodegenerative diseases. In working towards therapies for these diseases, it is important to understand the basic context in which the conditions occur. Implicit in this is an understanding of the basic architectural makeup of cells and the molecular determinants that are required in establishing a normal framework. Our work on dystonin cytoskeletal proteins show that they are fundamental in facilitating communication from the nucleus to the plasma membrane by ensuring the stability of the cellular scaffold. The work proposed will shed light on the role of this protein in intracellular trafficking and organelle organization. Since cytoskeletal defects are central features of many neurodegenerative disorders, elucidation of the exact role of dystonin in neurons should not only enhance our understanding of the versatile nature of these large modular proteins, but should help provide fundamental insight into the aetiology of these disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impairment and work disability of workers' compensation claimants in Ontario, a cohort study of new claimants from 1998-2006
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; IMPAIRMENT; WORK DISABILITY; WORK ILLNESS; WORK INJURY; WORKERS' COMPENSATION
Abstract-Résumé: We plan to examine work disability and benefits adequacy of long- and short-term disability claimants who experienced a work injury during the period 1998 to 2006 and received benefits from the Ontario Workplace Safety and Insurance Board. As in the case of earlier analysis by Tompa et al. (2010a), claims information from the WSIB administrative files will be linked to the Longitudinal Administrative Databank (LAD), which is a 20% simple random sample of Canadian tax filers. Based on our previous work, we expect to identify approximately 19% of this frame in the LAD. For each claimant we will identify a sample of uninjured counterparts that have similar socio-demographic characteristics and earnings profiles prior to the injury year using rigorous control matching techniques. We will then evaluate the impact of temporary and permanent impairment on work disability for various strata, namely age bracket, sex, region of residence, occupation, pre-injury earnings, level of impairment rating, and nature of injury. Comparison of claimants to controls will ensure that factors other than the work injury and ensuing health deficit are adequately addressed in the analysis of work disability. The analysis will evaluate work disability and the adequacy of supports received under the current and previous workers' compensation programs in Ontario using various statistical techniques. Previous analyses we have undertaken considered injured workers receiving benefits under a program that was in place in the 1980s and another in place through most of the 1990s in Ontario. The proposed study will allow us to evaluate how impairment, work disability and benefits adequacy in the current program compares to the earlier programs. This information will be invaluable to better design supports that minimize the impact of injury and the ensuing health deficit on work disability. Sub-group analysis will also provide insight into how to better target supports.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advancing theory, improving prevention: A multi-level longitudinal investigation of addiction risk
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; AETIOLOGY; CONCEPTUAL MODELS; LIFE COURSE; LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS; RISK; SUBSTANCE USE; THEORY
Abstract-Résumé: Tobacco, alcohol and illicit drug use pose major threats to public health. Many different individual and social factors are known to both place people at risk and protect them from substance related harms and addiction, yet remarkably few studies have tested these factors over time or considered how they interact with one another. As a result, it is not well-understood why some people use substances excessively and become addicted, while others do not. This gap in knowledge has hampered our ability to design and implement effective programs for prevention and treatment. The goal of this work is to improve our understanding of the development and progression of substance involvement. Using data from a population health survey of adolescents and young adults, we seek to describe how risk and protective factors interact with one another and test hypotheses about how these factors and their interactions predict substance use and related problems. By improving our understanding of how substance use and addiction develop, these findings will have potentially high impact by informing the design of more effective prevention and treatment interventions.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of articular cartilage homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHONDROCYTE BIOLOGY; OSTEOARTHRITIS; POLYPHOSPHATE; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is characterized by cartilage degradation and ectopic mineralization. It manifests clinically as joint pain, stiffness and loss of range of motion. This disease disables approximately 1 in 6 Canadians over the age of 15, causing pain and limiting the quality of life. OA has a major impact on health care costs ($4.4 billion/yr in Canada). In the absence of cure, current therapeutic modalities are aimed at reducing pain and increasing joint function. Non-invasive interventions such as exercise and weight loss are the first line of treatment, followed by anti-inflammatory medications. These latter treatments alleviate symptoms but do not inhibit the processes that result in the changes characteristic of this disease and may actually accelerate joint destruction. Failure of these treatments usually culminates in surgical intervention. Thus there is a pressing need for novel biological treatments that are well tolerated, with few or no side effects and are able to prevent the development of end-stage OA. Naturally occurring compounds seem an ideal treatment. We have evidence that indicates that polyphosphate (PP), a naturally occurring macromolecule composed of long polymers of phosphates present in most cells, and tissues such as bone and cartilage is involved in the maintenance of cartilage and thus is suitable to treat OA. This proposal is directed towards determining the regulation of polyphosphate levels in normal cartilage and how these change with osteoarthritis. Developing an effective treatment for arthritis will reduce the burden of the disease and improve quality of life. Understanding the mechanisms regulating endogenous PP levels should identify an entirely new approach to preventing cartilage degeneration and lead to the development of novel therapeutics for the treatment of OA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Linking clonal genomes to tumour evolution and therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: CLONAL EVOLUTION; CLONAL FREQUENCY; CLONAL HIERARCHIES; DIGITAL PCR; DRUG SELECTION; MICROFLUIDICS; SINGLE CELL GENOMICS; TRIPLE NEGATIVE BREAST CANCER; TUMOUR CLONALITY; TUMOUR XENOGRAFTS
Abstract-Résumé: Recent technological advances have allowed us to identify a plethora of gene mutations present in tumours from breast cancer patients. Certain mutations are thought to be responsible for disease progression, and are the targets of anti-cancer drugs. We have recently observed that, as aggressive cancer tumours evolve over time, many additional mutations develop, making the cancer drug-resistant and impossible to treat. New methodologies are desperately required that will allow researchers to better understand, diagnose and treat this deadly disease. Tumours are not mutationally uniform or static. They are, in fact, mosaic -- constantly evolving, much like an ecosystem. The goal of the proposed project is to extend current analyses of genetic mutations in aggressive breast cancer tumours to characterize this mosaicism at the single cell level. We will identify tumour mutations as they arise by grafting human cancer cells into mice, a technique previously performed by our group. We will also determine the effect(s) of anti-cancer drugs on the introduction of specific mutations within this system. Next, we will undertake single cell analysis to determine the identities and hierarchies of genetic mutations within individual tumour cells. The results of these studies will also allow us to refine current computational methods for characterizing tumour mutations as they develop. Finally, in collaboration with other research groups, we will address these questions using samples from a variety of human tumour specimens. As it stands, the details of how genetic mutations in tumours from breast cancer patients develop/evolve are poorly understood. Our proposed studies have the potential to answer specific questions about how breast cancer arises, progresses and becomes resistant to treatment. These findings will have a global impact within the cancer research community, both in terms of our understanding of this deadly disease, as well as in the diagnosis/treatment thereof.

TitreApplicationTitle: Active consolidation of neuronal morphology in the mature nervous system.
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON; GUIDANCE; MIGRATION; OUTGROWTH; SEMAPHORINS; SYNAPSE
Abstract-Résumé: Directed cell motility is an essential biological function for a variety of cells and tissues.  This is particularly important in the development of the nervous system and the formation of neural circuits.  During development neurons must extend long cellular processes and establish precise connections with other neurons in order to wire up the brain correctly.  This process relies on the precise distribution of guidance cues to direct neuronal growth to the appropriate target followed by the establishment of the appropriate synapses.  From this stage on throughout the life of the organism the axon must maintain its morphology so that persistent communication can occur between groups of neurons.  How this morphology is maintained in the mature nervous system and how it may be regenerated or modified after traumatic injury or disease related degeneration is not understood.    The aim of this research proposal is to identify the intracellular signalling mechanisms that are important for regulating neuronal morphology in the mature nervous system.  We have previously shown that a specific protein called calpain negatively regulates neuronal growth in developing neurons.  That is, the activity of this protein prevents the formation of neuronal branches and additional axons as neurons grow.  We will extend these observations by examining whether calpain inhibits neuronal branching and growth in an intact developing nervous system.  In addition, we will test the novel hypothesis that this protein activity is also necessary to prevent branch formation and growth in the mature nervous system.  This would be the first series of experiments that would directly test whether active signaling is necessary to maintain the normal morphology of the mature nervous system.

TitreApplicationTitle: T-box selector genes in Dorsal-Ventral leg development
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL-SIGNALING; EMBRYONIC DEVELOPMENT; LIMB DEVELOPMENT; MOLECULAR GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Limbs in all animals, from fruit flies to humans, begin as small clusters of embryonic cells. The cells in these clusters divide and become distinct from each other (a process called differentiation) during development resulting in an enormous increase in cell number, and size. My lab wants to understand limb development. Ultimately, we would like to know every step that shapes a clusters of cells in the embryo to the fully-formed of adult limb. We employ the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, as a model organism. The fly has the advantage of great genetic methods that allow for to find important genes and to turned them on and off in development. One of the key events that happens in cells is that they express special genes called "selector genes". Selector genes encode proteins that turn other genes on or off and are the key to deciding what sort of structure a cell will "choose" to make. We are studying a selector gene called midline, which controls the development of the entire ventral surface of the fly leg. When midline is not functioning all ventral structures develop as dorsal instead (if you imagine that the palm of your hand developed instead as a second version of the back of your hand then you would have a pretty good idea about the effect of midline mutants). The opposite happens too: when we turn on midline in dorsal cells, they turn into ventral (now imagine the back of your hand instead looking like a second palm!). We are trying to understand how midline is able to do this to cells. We think that midline can turn one set of genes on - the genes that make cells be 'ventral' and turn other genes off - the genes that make cells be 'dorsal'. What is most amazing, is that same sorts of genes also act in human development and cause all sorts of human congenital anomalies (birth defects) and so by understanding midline we will not only learn something new and fundamental about biology, but it may also help us to understand why congenital anomalies happen.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the Role of Type VIII Collagen in Atherosclerotic Plaque Stabilization
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; HUMAN TISSUE SCREENING; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALING; MACROPHAGES; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS; TRANSGENIC MICE; TYPE VIII COLLAGEN; VULNERABLE PLAQUE
Abstract-Résumé: Atherosclerosis is one of the most significant causes of morbidity and mortality in Canada today.  It is a multifactorial and complex disease, therefore understanding the pathogenesis and treatment involves study in many different areas.  The main objective of my research is to study interactions between cells in the artery wall and the proteins in the matrix that surround them.  The matrix proteins can stimulate growth and migration of the cells which contribute to thickening of the artery wall, and excessive accumulation of these proteins can also contribute to thickening.  Ultimately, this could lead to occlusion of the arteries. We are currently studying the expression and function of one of these proteins, type VIII collagen, which is produced in abundance in atherosclerosis, but very little in the healthy artery.  Our work involves screening atherosclerotic plaques from patients with atherosclerosis, mouse models and cell culture models of artery disease.  We use genetic manipulations, imaging and molecular and biochemical techniques to study the behaviour of cells.  Our methods allow us to move back and forth easily between the human disease, cells and animals.  We are one of few labs in the world studying cell-matrix interactions in atherosclerosis, and the functions of the type VIII collagen protein, therefore our work is very novel and important to shed light on critical mechanisms involved in the development and complications of atherosclerosis, and will facilitate the development of new drugs to target the disease process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining SIGIRR's role in epithelial homeostasis and host defense during infectious colitis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELING; ATTACHING/EFFACING BACTERIA; COLITIS; EPITHELIUM; GASTROENTEROLOGY; IBD; INNATE IMMUNITY; NEGATIVE REGULATOR
Abstract-Résumé: The health of our digestive system depends on the cells that line our intestines. These cells form a tight barrier that prevents the bacteria that live in our intestinal tract from leaking into our body and causing an immune response. These 'resident gut bacteria' do many good things, including competing with potentially dangerous 'invading' bacteria to prevent intestinal infections. The cells of our intestinal lining can sense bacteria, but they generally do not attack them. Instead, studies show that if our intestine becomes damaged, or in people who have Inflammatory Bowel Disease, our intestinal lining can undergo a slow healing process that occurs in response to bacteria. We wanted to find out why, and so asked (1) why don't our intestinal cells respond more strongly to bacteria, and (2) would higher responsiveness to bacteria improve healing of the intestine?   We found that the cells lining the intestine make a protein called SIGIRR that suppresses the ability of cells to respond to bacteria. We obtained mice that were missing SIGIRR and then tested their response to a bacterium called Citrobacter that infects and damages the intestine. Without SIGIRR, the intestinal cells had a much stronger response and much better healing. At the same time, the intestinal cells also caused more inflammation and released many proteins that kill bacteria. Surprisingly, these proteins killed only the "good" resident bacteria, so that there was less competition with the invading Citrobacter bacteria, which left the intestine open to infection. Now we propose to test whether SIGIRR's actions are solely due its expression by intestinal cells, and define what immune signals are stronger when SIGIRR is absent. We also want to understand why only resident bacteria are killed in mice missing SIGIRR. These studies will clarify how SIGIRR promotes intestinal host defense, apparently sacrificing intestinal healing to enhance harmonious/protective interactions with resident bacteria.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multicenter Prospective Study of Low-Flow, Low-Gradient Aortic Stenosis - TOPAS Study - Phase III
Keywords-MotsClés: AORTIC STENOSIS; CARDIOVASCULAR IMAGING; COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; DOPPLER-ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; HEART VALVE SURGERY; LEFT VENTRICULAR DYSFUNTION; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; TRANSCATHETER VALVE THERAPY; VALVULAR HEART DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with narrowing of the aortic cardiac valve (i.e. aortic stenosis, AS) and concomitantly a reduced cardiac output (i.e. low blood flow across the valve) represent the most challenging subset among patients with valvular heart disease. In the setting of a low cardiac output, it is often difficult to separate patients with true severe AS (TS AS) from those with pseudosevere AS (PS AS). The distinction between these 2 subgroups is essential because the patients with TSAS will generally benefit of aortic valve replacement surgery (AVR), whereas the patients with PS AS will not. Beyond the distinction between TS AS and PS AS, it is also important to assess the extent of impairment of the cardiac muscular function because patients with more severe impairment of muscular function undergoing AVR have a very high risk of operative mortality regardless of the degree of valve stenosis. Unfortunately, the diagnostic tools (echocardiography) currently used to assess the severity of valvular obstruction and the cardiac function in patients with low-output AS are far from being optimal, and as a consequence, several patients are misdiagnosed and thus do not receive the appropriate therapies. The objective of this prospective multicenter study is to develop and validate new indices and criteria based on echocardiography, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT) imaging, and blood cardiac hormones (BNP) that will contribute: (1) to better separate TS AS from PS AS, (2) to accurately assess the extent of cardiac function impairment, and (3) to better predict the operative risk for AVR and the evolution of cardiac function and symptoms after AVR. We believe that a strategy based on echo, MRI, CT, and BNP will contribute to improve the risk stratification and the clinical decision making in these high-risk patients with AS and low cardiac output.

TitreApplicationTitle: Astrogliosis in Angiotensin II-induced neurovascular uncoupling.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOTENSIN II; ASTROCYTES; CEREBRAL CIRCULATION; HYPERTENSION; INFLAMMATION; LASER DOPPLER FLOWMETRY; MICROGLIA; NEUROVASCULAR COUPLING; TOLL-LIKE RECEPTORS; TWO-PHOTON MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Angiotensin II exerts detrimental effects on cerebral circulation, but the underlying mechanisms remains to be elucidated. In particular, Angiotensin II impairs the increase in cerebral blood flow produced by neural activity (neurovascular coupling), a critical mechanism that matches substrate delivery with energy demands in brain. Because impaired neurovascular coupling increases the vulnerability of the brain, it is important to understand how changes in vascular tone in response to neural activity may be altered. Our preliminary data showed that Angiotensin II exerts powerful proinflammatory effects in brain cells including astrocytes. Astrocytes play a pivotal role in neurovascular coupling by transducing neural activity into a Ca2+ increase that modulates cerebrovascular tone. However, in some brain pathologies, astrocytes may become reactive, a process also called astrogliosis and characterized by inflammatory responses and alterations of Ca2+ signalling. Accordingly, the major objective of this research program is to study the role of inflammation in the effect of Angiotensine II on neurovascular coupling. In particular, we will investigate the effect of different components of the immune system on neurovascular coupling and astrocyte molecular signaling. These studies will be conducted in brain slices as well as in living mice coupled to state-of-the-art microscopy techniques. Thus these studies will improve our understanding of Angiotensin II induced neurovascular coupling impairment, and may provide further therapeutic target to reduce premature disability and death from dysfunctional cerebral blood flow.

TitreApplicationTitle: D-dimer to select patients with a first unprovoked venous thromboembolism who can have anticoagulants stopped at 3 months: Extension of follow-up.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICOAGULANT THERAPY; CLINICAL MANAGEMENT; CLINICAL OUTCOMES; COHORT STUDY; D-DIMER; VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM
Abstract-Résumé: Patients who have a venous thrombosis ("blood clot") in their legs or lungs without apparent cause (e.g. no recent surgery or cancer) have about a 50% risk of another thrombosis in 10 years if they stop anticoagulant therapy ("blood thinners"). A new episode of thrombosis is very unlikely if patients remain on treatment but anticoagulant therapy increases bleeding and is a burden.  If we could identify the patients with a low risk of another thrombosis they could stop treatment, whereas those with a high risk could stay on treatment.  There is evidence that normal D-dimer blood tests indicate a low risk of another thrombosis.    We are doing a study to determine if it is correct to stop treatment after 3 months in patients with unprovoked thrombosis who have normal D-dimer results; those with normal results stop therapy and those with abnormal results continue therapy. We then follow patients to make sure they remain well. By March 2013 we will have followed the 410 patients in this study for an average of 2.5 years, which is the length of time for which we were funded. We are now asking for funds to follow these patients for an additional 3 years. This would more than double follow-up (to an average of 5.5 years), would be relatively inexpensive to do (less than half the original study cost), and would greatly increase the knowledge gained from this study. In particular, it would enable us to: 1) obtain a much better measurement of the rate of having another thrombosis, and to compare this rate between males and females; and 2) determine the long-term, as well as just the short-term, risk of another thrombosis. Both are very important. First, the results may have different meaning in males and females, because the risk of another thrombosis is much higher in males. Second, it would be wrong to stop treatment if normal D-dimer results did not mean a low long-term, as well as short-term, risk of another thrombosis.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - A: Cells and Tissues
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - A: Cellules et tissus
TitreApplicationTitle: Stress regulation of heart fibrosis through integrin-mediated activation of TGF-beta
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; CARDIAC FIBROSIS; INTEGRINS; MYOFIBROBLAST; REGENERATION; TGF-BETA; TISSUE FIBROSIS; TISSUE REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Fibrosis is a major cause for heart failure and death with no effective therapies available to date. When an infarct destroys parts of the heart muscle, connective tissue fibroblasts are activated into myofibroblasts (MFs) to repair the damage. They start secreting large amounts of fibrous collagen to glue the intact parts of the heart muscle together. Frequently, heart repair does not end and fibrous collagen accumulates to a stiff fibrotic scar. The scar hinders electrical transmission between heart muscle cells, mechanically obstructs the pumping function of the heart, and reduces its distensibility. Worse, the stiffness of the scar itself turns healthy cells into cells that will foster the stiffening process, ultimately leading to heart failure.   It is our objective to stop MF activation by blocking mechanical activation of TGF-beta1, the most potent pro-fibrotic growth factor known. We have discovered that MFs pull TGF-beta1 out from stores in the extracellular matrix, literally like candy out of a wrapper. Liberated TGF-beta1 stimulates more MFs. To prevent vicious cycle, we will interfere with unique proteins, called integrins that MFs use as a handle to pull. We have already identified the integrins possibly activating TGF-beta1 in cardiac MFs. We will now test how cell force and matrix stiffness control their efficacy to activating TGF-beta1 using a variety of biomechanical assays. Using an animal model of heart fibrosis, we will test the importance of our integrin candidates by turning them on and off with molecular biology and specific drugs. Generally inhibiting TGF-beta1 in clinical strategies is impossible, because TGF-beta has many beneficial actions, such as reducing inflammation, regulating blood vessel growth and preventing tumour formation Our approach specifically addresses MF integrins to prevent TGF-beta activation. Other cells, using other mechanisms to activate the factor will not be affected.

TitreApplicationTitle: Safety and Outcomes of Accepting Hypertensive Individuals as Living Kidney Donors
Keywords-MotsClés: HYPERTENSION; KIDNEY; LIVING KIDNEY DONATION; ORGAN DONATION; PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY; SAFETY
Abstract-Résumé: Kidney failure is a serious health condition that affects more than 40,000 Canadians. The best treatment for kidney failure is a new kidney by transplantation. Unfortunately, patients with kidney failure often wait for many years to receive a new kidney. Many patients die while they are waiting. Family and friends of patients who need a kidney often wish to donate one of their kidneys. It is safe for a living person to donate one of their kidneys if they are healthy. In the past, only healthy people were allowed to donate a kidney. However, because so many people are waiting for a new kidney, doctors now allow some people with high blood pressure to become a kidney donor. However, this is being done with little information on the long-term safety. We will study the long-term outcomes of people with high blood pressure who donate a kidney. We will compare living kidney donors who have high blood pressure to two comparison groups: living kidney donors with normal blood pressure and healthy, non-donors. We will determine if kidney function is worse in donors with high blood pressure four years after donation. As well, we will study the outcomes of people who receive a kidney from a donor with high blood pressure. This information will help doctors, potential kidney donors and kidney transplant recipients make informed decisions about accepting a kidney from a person with high blood pressure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Validation du Panic Screening Score, un instrument de dépistage des attaques de panique associées aux douleurs thoraciques inexpliquées lors d'une consultation dans une unité d'urgence
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; EMERGENCY MEDICINE; MULTIDISCIPLINARY; PANIC ATTACK; PANIC DISORDER; PREDICTION; SCREENING; UNEXPLAINED CHEST PAIN; VALIDATION
Abstract-Résumé: Chaque annee, environ 400 000 Canadiens consultent a l'urgence en raison de douleurs thoraciques qui demeurent inexpliquees au moment du conge. Pres de 80 % des douleurs thoraciques inexpliquees evoluent de facon chronique, et ce, en depit de leur origine medicale benigne. Ces douleurs limitent la capacite des patients a travailler, a s'occuper de leur famille et a faire de l'activite physique. Consequemment, elles sont a l'origine de multiples consultations medicales souvent infructueuses. La recherche montre que pres de 45 % des douleurs thoraciques pourraient etre expliquees par un probleme d'anxiete, soit les attaques de panique. La recherche montre egalement que moins de 8 % des patients presentant des attaques de panique sont identifies lors du sejour a l'urgence. Le Panic Screening Score pourrait pallier la sous-identification des attaques de panique associees aux douleurs thoraciques inexpliquees lors du sejour a l'urgence en permettant aux medecins de les depister efficacement. Cette etude vise donc a ameliorer et evaluer (valider) le Panic Screening Score aupres de 3000 Canadiens dans deux unites d'urgence. La realisation de ce projet de recherche est essentielle a l'eventuelle utilisation du Panic Screening Score par les medecins d'urgence canadiens. Son implantation dans les unites d'urgence a le potentiel d'ameliorer la sante de pres de 180 000 Canadiens chaque annee puisque les traitements des attaques paniques sont efficaces dans plus de 80 % des cas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the molecular mechanisms of autophagy regulation
Keywords-MotsClés: ATG PROTEINS; AUTOPHAGY; MACROMOLECULAR ASSEMBLY; MOLECULAR GENETICS; PROTEIN KINASE; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; SINGLE-PARTICLE ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; YEAST MODEL SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Neurodegenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease, are the leading causes of disability in Canada. These devastating conditions are caused by the progressive loss of function of brain cells called neurons. As this pathological phenomenon is strongly linked to the buildup of damaging protein masses in neurons, one potential treatment is to activate the neuronal cells' internal machineries to remove these toxic protein masses. Autophagy is a pathway used by all cells in our bodies to break down large objects such as organelles and protein aggregates and to recycle their components for other processes. The overall goal of our research is to determine how the machinery involved in mediating autophagy is regulated and from the knowledge gained identify molecular strategies to increase the level of autophagy in cells. Our proposed studies focus on a protein complex called the Atg17-Atg29-Atg31 complex. The Atg17-Atg29-Atg31 complex plays a crucial role in initiating autophagy and in regulating the level of activity of this pathway. Using an advanced imaging method called single-particle electron microscopy (EM), we will capture the overall shape or detailed molecular structure of this complex. This structural information, together with results from complementary biochemical experiments, will enable us to determine how the different modules of the Atg17-Atg29-Atg31 complex are organized and how this complex performs its biological function. Upon completion, these studies will advance our molecular understanding of the Atg17-Atg29-Atg31 complex and will provide mechanistic insights into its role in autophagy regulation. In the long term, knowledge gained from our research will pave the way for the development of autophagy-targeted therapeutics for treating neurodegenerative diseases, and improve the quality of life of the large number of Canadians suffering from these disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promotion of breast cancer metastasis by tumour hypoxia and myeloid cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CHEMOTHERAPY; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HYPOXIA; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MACROPHAGES; METASTASIS; MYELOID-DERIVED SUPPRESSOR CELLS; PRE-METASTATIC NICHE; TUMOUR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Nine out of ten Canadians killed by cancer, die because their tumour has spread to other parts of their body. The spread of cancer (metastasis) occurs when tumour cells escape the original primary tumour and colonize other organs to form life-threatening tumour metastases. We are beginning to realize that normal cells can help metastatic tumour cells to survive and grow into tumour metastases. If we can understand how normal cells encourage the development of tumour metastases, we will be able to design more effective therapies to treat metastatic cancer.  We have discovered that poorly oxygenated (hypoxic) cells in breast tumours produce proteins that cause normal cells to be released from the bone marrow, enter the bloodstream, and build-up in tissues such as the lung and liver. These bone marrow cells create nests for metastasizing tumour cells to inhabit, providing fertile regions of tissue that allow tumour cells to grow into large tumour metastases. We predict that preventing bone marrow cells from building up in tissues will disrupt the growth of tumour metastases.  My research team will use animal models of breast cancer to study the proteins produced by hypoxic tumour cells that cause bone marrow cells to build-up in the lungs and liver. We will also study how surgical primary tumour removal, chemotherapy treatment, and the use of new drugs that target hypoxic tumour cells affect the number and function of bone marrow cells in tissues. We predict that bone marrow cells remain in tissues after therapy and can promote the later development of metastatic tumour recurrences.  To improve the health of Canadians we need to better understand metastasis, the leading cause of cancer-related deaths. This proposal will provide important insights into how hypoxic breast tumour cells corrupt normal cells to increase the spread of breast cancer, and will provide a strong basis for the design of new and effective treatments for patients with metastatic cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of intestinal microbiota in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease pre and post bariatric surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: BARIATRIC SURGERY; DIET; INFLAMMATION; LIPOPOLYSACCHARIDE; MICROBIOTA; NON-ALCOHOLIC FATTY LIVER DISEASE; STEATOHEPATITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Fatty liver disease is a fat buildup in the liver with or without inflammation. The disease can damage the liver and sometimes requires liver transplantation. Almost all people who are morbidly obese and require weight-loss surgery have fatty liver.  New research shows that the kind of bacteria in the gut might contribute to the development of obesity, fatty liver and inflammation. Weight-loss surgery clearly changes the gut bacteria, probably because of the surgical changes to the gut, the weight loss and the food intake, which is very different after surgery. We think that differences in the gut bacteria could influence fatty liver in morbidly obese patients before and after weight-loss surgery.  Therefore, we would like to measure the bacteria in the stool of patients with fatty liver undergoing weight-loss surgery A) at the time of the surgery, to see, if there is a difference between those who have fatty liver without inflammation and those who have the more severe form of fatty liver with inflammation. We are also planning to measure bacterial products in the stool and in the blood of our patients.  B) We then want to follow the same patients for one year after their weight loss surgery to find out, whether changes in the gut bacteria are connected to improvement or worsening of their fatty liver disease.  This study is new and important, as it could lead to new treatments for patients with fatty liver disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: (Co) Producing Narratives on Access to Mental Health Services in Rural Communities: A Participatory Project with Young People Experiencing Psychosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTS-BASED HEALTH RESEARCH; DIGITAL STORYTELLING; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; INTERPRETIVE INQUIRY; KNOWLEDGE CREATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION STRATEGIES; PARTICIPATORY METHODS; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; RURAL HEALTH; YOUTH EXPERIENCING PSYCHOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Youth experiencing psychosis who live in rural communities face increased risks. Rural youth are often disadvantaged by virtue of their age and the geographical context in which they live. They face significant barriers to equitable and appropriate primary health care, and particularly specialized mental health care. This research will address issues of access to (mental) health care by generating new knowledge about help-seeking by youth who have experienced a first episode of psychosis in a rural community.  The project uses digital storytelling, an innovative arts-based research methodology.   We examine rural youth help-seeking behaviours and seek to understand how we might best support youth at home, school, and community, and inform practices in youth (mental) health, education and welfare service settings. The project uses a unique participatory qualitative arts-based method - digital storytelling - to address barriers to accessing services and to explore how participatory arts-based health research contributes to youth engagement and social competencies. Because lack of engagement and social isolation are a central issue for youth seeking help in the context of first episode psychosis, the innovative methods used in this study have the potential to increase youth involvement in research and contribute to the evidence base that will influence their care.

TitreApplicationTitle: The RAS-hVPS34-PTPRD pathway in lung tumorigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; HVPS34; LUNG CANCER; PTPRD; RAS
Abstract-Résumé: Unfortunately, the 5-year survival rate for lung cancer patients is still less than 15%, often because patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage and respond poorly to current treatments. Therefore, a better understanding of lung cancer development is needed to effectively cure lung cancer patients. High-throughput DNA sequencing of lung cancers identified several novel mutations. Some of these were located in the gene, PIK3C3, which encodes a protein called hVPS34 (human Vacuolar Protein Sorting 34). However, it is unclear whether these mutations are promoting lung cancer development. We also noticed that most, if not all, PIK3C3 mutations always co-occurred with mutations in RAS and PTPRD, two genes mutated commonly in cancer. This finding suggests that PIK3C3, RAS, and PTPRD mutants might cooperate in a novel pathway to support lung cancer development.  Based on preliminary experiments, we hypothesize that lung cancer-associated PIK3C3 mutations impair normal hVPS34 function and cooperate sequentially with RAS and PTPRD mutations to promote lung cancer development. We will test this hypothesis using a combined biochemical, biological, and mouse genetic approach. By elucidating the pathway which allows PIK3C3, RAS, and PTPRD mutations to cooperate in detail, we will gain insight into lung cancer pathogenesis and potentially establish a new paradigm in cancer development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidation of intracellular signaling networks involved in tumorigenesis and cancer metastasis using high-throughput screening methods in vivo.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; IN VIVO; KINASE; METASTASIS; TRANSMEMBRANE PROTEINS; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Metastasis of a primary tumour is the main cause of more than 90 percent of all cancer patient deaths, but surprisingly little is known about the mechanisms driving metastasis. Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells detach from the primary tumour and move to other body parts (secondary sites) via the blood or lymphatic system. If the cancer cells settle and survive in important secondary sites such as the lungs, liver, bones, or brain, they can form secondary tumours (metastases) that disrupt the normal functions of these tissues, often killing the patient. Treatment options for metastatic disease are currently very limited. Our laboratory has discovered that tumour cells lacking the expression of a gene called RhoC show a significantly reduced ability to survive in the lungs. Furthermore, mice transplanted with these RhoC-deficient cells develop markedly fewer lung metastases. We propose to engineer the expression of about 4000 different transmembrane proteins (cell surface molecules) in our RhoC-deficient tumour cells and then inject these manipulated cells into mice and monitor metastasis. Our goal is to find cell surface molecules whose expression enhances the metastatic abilities of tumour cells. Such molecules may be major drivers of metastasis and thus represent potential targets for new anti-cancer therapies. We believe that our proposal will both shed light on how the process of metastasis operates and create new options for the treatment of metastatic disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transgenerational Effects of Antenatal Glucocorticoid Treatment: Mechanisms of Programming
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTENATAL GLUCOCORTICOIDS; DEVELOPMENT; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; HYPOTHALAMO-PITUITARY-ADRENAL AXIS; PREGNANCY; PRETERM LABOUR; TRANSGENERATIONAL
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately 10% of pregnant women are treated with glucocorticoid (GC) in late gestation, to promote lung maturation in babies at risk of preterm delivery. While GC therapy improves the ability of the baby to breathe, we have shown that such treatment can permanently alter the ability of offspring to mount a hormonal response to stress. Studies are also emerging indicating long-term effects in humans. Animal studies have shown that changes in the regulation of hormones associated with the stress response results in altered susceptibility to disease in later life, including hypertension and psychological illness. We have shown that the effects of antenatal GC therapy can pass to the second generation where endocrine effects are even more pronounced than in the first generation. Recently, we have also shown that antenatal GC therapy can lead to profound changes in the structure of genes, altering the way that they are switched on or off. The guinea pig will be used, since extensive brain and neuroendocrine development occurs during fetal life, and this is similar to humans. These studies will establish novel mechanisms (including glucocorticoid-induced changes in gene structure) by which adult endocrine function is 'programmed' by excess glucocorticoid exposure during fetal life. We will also determine the processes involved in transgenerational transmission. This knowledge will allow us to refine therapies, maximizing beneficial actions at the lung, while preventing any detrimental effects in the brain and developing endocrine system, which we have now shown to persist for multiple generations.

TitreApplicationTitle: SMN and Post-transcriptional Regulation in Motor Neurons: Implications for Spinal Muscular Atrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGININE METHYLATION; CELLULAR AND ANIMAL MODELS; MOTOR NEURONS; NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION; PROTEIN ARGININE METHYLTRANSFERASES; RNA BINDING PROTEINS; RNA GRANULES; SPINAL MUSCULAR ATROPHY; TUDOR DOMAIN
Abstract-Résumé: Loss of a protein named SMN (for 'Survival of Motor Neurons') is responsible for spinal muscular atrophy, a disease that affects 1 in every 10000 newborns and is the leading genetic cause of infant mortality. It is characterized by a degeneration of the motor neurons in the spinal cord, resulting ultimately in muscle weakness, paralysis and death during early childhood. SMN has recently been dubbed 'the master assembler', because it acts as a molecular scaffold to promote the assembly of large macromolecular complexes involved in various cellular processes, related to the biology of RNA. However, this function of SMN should be equally important for all cells and it remains unclear why only spinal cord motor neurons are affected by loss of SMN. It is thought that the many protein-protein interactions in which SMN is involved might be regulated by a protein modification, namely arginine methylation. My research strategy has made use of antibodies that recognize this modification to identify new interacting partners of SMN in motor neurons. This has led to the identification of novel functions for SMN and should help rationalize how deficiencies in functions essential to all cells can cause specific degeneration of the motor neurons of the spinal cord and facilitate the development of new strategies for therapeutic intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Increasing vitamin K intake to improve long-term anticoagulation stability in patients treated with warfarin.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICOAGULATION; CLINICAL OUTCOME; DIETARY INTERVENTION; GENETIC POLYMORPHISM; INR; PROSPECTIVE DESIGN; QUALITY OF LIFE; STABILITY; VITAMIN K; WARFARIN
Abstract-Résumé: Warfarin is the most widely prescribed oral anticoagulant for the treatment and prevention of thromboembolic diseases. The high inter-individual variability in warfarin dosing is an ongoing problem that is worsening as the population ages and eligible patients increase in numbers. Despite efficient monitoring programs, up to 30% of warfarin users suffer serious bleeding and thromboembolic events. Numerous genetic and clinical factors are known to affect anticoagulation treatment. According to recent reports, differences in certain genes (VKORC1, CYP2C9), age, race, weight, height and concomitant medication account for up to 60% of the interindividual variation, the other 40% being explained by unspecified factors. In recent years, dietary vitamin K (VK) has emerged as an important factor of long-term anticoagulation stability. Small studies point to more stable anticoagulation in patients with high VK intakes, and prospective trials have shown that patients receiving small doses of supplemental VK spend significantly more time in therapeutic range, require fewer warfarin dose changes, and suffer less bleeding and thrombotic complications over time. Whether similar beneficial effects can be achieved through diet remains unknown at this time. In light of this, we propose to conduct a randomized, placebo-controlled, prospective study that will assess, over a 6-month period, the anticoagulant stability of warfarin-treated patients consuming high versus standard amounts of VK daily. The proposed VK dietary intervention could have significant public health and financial impacts as patients with stable anticoagulation have lower complications and require less medical monitoring, both of which have serious financial implications. Furthermore, such intervention has the potential to greatly improve the quality of life of this group of patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tumour-Initiating Cells in Oral Cancer Patients: Predictors of Outcome and Identification of Candidate Therapeutic Targets
Keywords-MotsClés: HEAD AND NECK SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA; NOVEL THERAPEUTIC TARGETS; PROGNOSTIC MARKERS; TUMOUR INITIATING CELLS; TUMOUR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with oral cavity cancers are treated with surgery, chemo and radiation therapy. Even with this aggressive treatment, only 40 to 50 percent of patients survive beyond 5 years, indicating a dire need for improved therapies. We also need ways to predict which patients will do well, so they can be spared toxicities, versus those who have a poor prognosis and should be treated more aggressively.  Recent work suggests that there is a distinct population of cells within tumours that initiate and sustain tumour growth. Such tumour initiating cells (TICs) may be responsible for therapy-resistance. In addition to cancer cells, tumours contain normal cells from the body called stromal cells. We believe that the TICs use stromal cells the way a seed uses the soil. It is possible that by blocking the nutrients the stromal cells provide to the TICs, we may be able to interfere with cancer growth. This new avenue of research has yet to be translated into improved outcomes for patients. It is a major objective to demonstrate that knowledge of TICs and stromal cells will lead to improved diagnosis, prediction of responses, and superior treatments. This application has two major goals: 1) to understand the biology of TICs and stromal cells so we can develop ways to kill them; and 2) to determine whether the presence of TIC-related attributes is predictive of prognosis. We will separate out the TICs, stromal cells and other cell types in the tumour and determine what genes each is expressing. This will help us to understand how the TICs give rise to tumours and survive therapy, as well as how stromal cells support TICs, allowing us to develop new strategies to eliminate TICs, stromal cells, or both. We will also interrogate a number of TIC-related attributes to determine if any of them can provide a clinically useful test to determine which patients may benefit from more aggressive therapy, and which may be spared the toxicities of the current treatment protocols.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; RECHERCHE SUR LES MÉDICAMENTS
TitreApplicationTitle: Engineering Microenvironments for Cardiac Regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMYOCYTE; DRUG SCREENING; HEART; MICROFABRICATION; MYOCARDIUM; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Beating heart cells, cardiomyocytes, cannot regenerate on their own. Thus, hearts affected by heart attack or other heart diseases have limited ability to regenerate. Beating heart cells can only be reliably obtained in large numbers from pluripotent stem cells. The problem with this approach is that these cardiomyocytes are immature, they resemble cells found in the hearts before birth. The goal is to make cells similar to those found in adult human hearts, so that we can help patients with heart disease. This process is called maturation.  In this proposal we will apply engineering methods, through use of electrical stimulation and mechanical control of the environment in which cells are growing to mature cardiomyocytes derived from human pluripotent stem cells. We will also make small human tissues using the same approach and test its utility in drug screening. We can discover new cardiac drugs or drug side effects using these engineered human heart tissues.  Finally, we will use animal experiments to determine the level of cardiomyocyte maturation required to best heal a heart affected by a heart attack.

TitreApplicationTitle: Better education for better teamwork: Understanding the discourses to improve the practices of interprofessional education
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATIVE PRACTICE; CRITICAL SOCIAL THEORY; DISCOURSE ANALYSIS; FOUCAULT; HISTORY OF HEALTH PROFESSIONS EDUCATION; INTERPROFESSIONAL EDUCATION
Abstract-Résumé: Poor teamwork in health care systems is estimated by the Canadian Patient Safety Institute to cost over 300 million dollars in acute care alone, and lead to thousands of patient deaths per year. Health care professionals must find ways to collaborate more effectively with each other to meet patient and societal health care needs in the complex health systems of the twenty-first century. Better interprofessional collaboration can improve professional relationships, enhance patient safety, increase efficiency and coordination, reduce medical errors, reduce health care costs, greater provider and patient satisfaction and improve health care outcomes. Interprofessional education (IPE) is considered a key means to enable this transformative change. Surprisingly, despite significant investment in IPE worldwide, many issues remain, and evidence to support the efficacy of IPE is inconclusive at best. Understanding the interplay of educational practices and power can open the field to new possibilities for better health professions education. This research addresses this important issue by identifying and analysing the taken-for-granted assumptions that underlie IPE though an examination of IPE discourses. Discourse analysis is based on the importance of language in shaping how we think, what is valued, and what individuals and institutions are accepted as important and powerful.  In this research, key IPE documents are assembled and analysed to identify the effects of various discourses. This will allow for better understanding of how different professions, disciplines and stakeholders understand and use these IPE discourses. High quality healthcare practitioner education is fundamental to the delivery of high quality healthcare. By identifying areas of strength as well as gaps and limitations in current approaches to IPE, this work will enable more effective ways of training health care practitioners to provide the collaborative, systems-based care our society requires.

TitreApplicationTitle: Short bowel syndrome and glucagon-like peptide-2 therapy: actions and mechanisms studied in neonatal piglets
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; GLUCAGON LIKE PEPTIDE 2; GROWTH HORMONE; GUT ADAPTATION; ILEUM; INTESTINAL FAILURE; NEONATAL PIGLET; NEONATE; PREMATURE; SHORT BOWEL SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Short bowel syndrome (SBS) occurs after loss of a large part of the small intestine, which absorbs food. This occurs often in premature babies, due to diseases that start during pregnancy or after birth, and require surgery. The remaining intestine is not able to absorb nutrition for the babies to survive and grow. More than one third of the babies die from complications, mainly of the intravenous nutrition they must have to live and grow. SBS is the most common cause for small intestine transplantation in Canada, although half of these young children die waiting for a transplant, due to a lack of donors. We need better solutions for babies with SBS, who are unable to improve their intestinal absorption over time (called adaptation), to avoid their early death or need for transplantation. Otherwise, 1% of all children aged less than four years may die from this condition. Based on our research to date, we believe a hormone called glucagon like peptide-2 (GLP-2) is a potential solution. This hormone helps the intestine to grow in newborn babies and is produced in a part of the intestine called the ileum, which is the part most often surgically removed in babies with SBS. We want to study GLP-2 treatment and adaptation in piglets, a recognized animal model for small babies with SBS. We believe that GLP-2 treatment will increase adaptation in SBS piglets; especially if it is given early after surgery and if they don't have ileum. By studying piglets we can learn more about how GLP-2 works to help the intestine grow and adapt then could be learnt from studies in babies, without multiple invasive procedures to collect intestinal tissue. We will study SBS piglets, measuring growth and adaptation, with and without GLP-2 treatment. At the same time we will also study a new way to measure adaptation (measuring arginine, an amino acid made in the intestine of babies and piglets) so that we can do better studies in babies in the future, without needing to collect tissues.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of RhoGDIalpha in the pathogenesis of congenital and childhood nephrotic syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGENITAL NEPHROTIC SYNDROME; IDIOPATHIC FOCAL SEGMENTAL GLOMERULOSCLEROSIS; MINIMAL CHANGE DISEASE; PODOCYTE; RHO-GTPASE; RHOGDI
Abstract-Résumé: The kidneys filter plasma at the level of the glomerulus,where the first step of urine formation occurs. Normally the glomerular filtration barrier prevents the loss of plasma proteins into the urine. In nephrotic syndrome, there is a defect in the glomerular filtration barrier and this leads to protein leakage across the barrier with subsequent edema (swelling of body with water). Congenital nephrotic syndrome has an early onset within the first 3 months of life and is treated by removing the kidneys to stop the protein loss: this then leads to a need for dialysis and future transplantation. We have identified a new gene (called RhoGDIalpha) to cause hereditary nephrotic syndrome. We propose to perform studies to understand how this mutation in RhoGDIalpha leads to a specific defect in the glomerular filtration barrier. We will further extend our findings into non-hereditary forms of nephrotic syndrome and will study the role of this protein in common causes of nephrotic syndrome in childhood.

TitreApplicationTitle: Family Atherosclerosis Monitoring In Early Life
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTORS; CAROTID INTIMAL MEDIA THICKNESS; CHILDHOOD OBESITY; LONGITUDINAL BIRTH COHORT
Abstract-Résumé: Heart attacks and strokes are the leading cause of disability and death worldwide. The causes including high cholesterol, smoking, obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes, psychological stress, improper diets and physical inactivity are well known. But, we do not know how early in life and why the metabolic risk factors: high cholesterol, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure develop in individuals and how early in life these will lead to hardening of the arteries in young people. Our objectives are - 1. To determine if children who have high levels of these risk factors are at higher risk of developing hardening of the arteries, measured by ultrasound by age 10 years. 2. To determine how these metabolic risk factors develop and lead to the artery hardening in children who are 10 years old. 3. To study the influence of maternal determinants during pregnancy (diet, physical activity, tobacco use, weight gain) and after birth, household determinants (parents health and behaviours including diet, physical activity, tobacco use, socioeconomic status and psychosocial stress), childhood determinants (diet, weight gain, physical activity) and selected genes, on the development of the metabolic risk factors during childhood and early teens. This information is critical to our understanding of the development of these risk factors and to helping in the design of comprehensive and effective preventive strategies to prevent heart disease and stokes in future generations of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Determinants of Corticosteroid Actions in Glucose Metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; COACTIVATOR; FGF21; GLUCOCORTICOID RECEPTOR; GLUCONEOGENESIS; HEPATOSTEATOSIS; LIVER X RECEPTOR BETA; LXR ANTAGONIST; STRESS HORMONE
Abstract-Résumé: Metabolic diseases, including diabetes and obesity, are reaching epidemic levels in the Western world. Chronic activation of the glucocorticoid receptor signaling pathway by stress hormones can contribute to diabetes and metabolic dysfunction. Diabetes is characterized by elevated blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia) caused by the body's inability to properly secrete insulin and/or respond to increasing insulin levels. A known and preventable cause of hyperglycemia is the long-term therapeutic use of glucocorticoid drugs. Glucocorticoid drugs are widely prescribed for diseases in which their potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive actions are desired including rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, certain types of cancers and organ transplants.  However, the long-term use of glucocorticoid drugs is limited by undesirable side effects including obesity and type 2 diabetes. These negative side effects are due in part to the glucose production pathway being strongly induced by glucocorticoid drugs in the liver.  We have a strong interest in understanding the molecular connections between stress hormones (glucocorticoids) and the ultimate response obtained in tissues such as the liver. We have identified new proteins that are important in selectively modulating the glucose metabolism pathway without affecting the anti-inflammatory effects of glucocorticoid signalling.  In this proposal, we will use in vivo mouse models and in vitro primary cultures to uncover the different signalling mechanisms involved, and in the process identify new determinants of glucocorticoid specificity. This project has high public relevance because it will allow us to identify new drug targets to benefit the diabetic community and to create safer glucocorticoid drugs for the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Infodemiology and Infoveillance: Exploring the use of social media and web-metrics to monitor and measure knowledge use
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH INFORMATICS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The broad aim of this project is to explore whether we can measure the impact of new scientific knowledge through metrics based on social media such as Twitter. Analyzing Internet and social media content on a large scale may be a useful and highly innovative approach to provide additional real-time metrics for knowledge translation researchers and practitioners (e.g. in the field of public health). The research will provide new methods for knowledge translation, health, and health services research; for the evaluation of health promotion campaigns; and for public engagement. The research program will also evaluate to what degree social media-based metrics can complement and predict traditional measures of research "impact" such as citations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Histone Deacetylation and the DNA Damage Response
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; DEACETYLATION; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR; HISTONE; NUCLEOSOME; SIRTUIN
Abstract-Résumé: Cells are frequently exposed to chemicals that damage DNA molecules. DNA breaks are an extremely harmful form of DNA damage that needs to be repaired both efficiently and accurately to maintain cell viability and restore the integrity of genetic information. Fortunately, cells contain a number of dedicated DNA repair machineries. Because DNA is tightly packaged into chromosomes, cells first need to modify the proteins that package DNA in order to repair the damage. Our laboratory discovered a natural modification of DNA packaging proteins. We showed that blocking the removal of this modification using vitamin B3 is a novel and potentially effective way to fight human fungal infections. This is important because systemic fungal infections that occur following cancer chemotherapy are associated with high mortality rates. Our strategy is based on killing fungal pathogens by causing massive DNA damage without inflicting damage to human cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Knee Meniscus Reconstruction Using Mesenchymal Stem Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: JOINT REPAIR AND REGENERATION; MENISCUS; OSTEOARTHRITIS PREVENTION; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; STEM CELLS; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Meniscus injury is a major risk factor for the development of osteoarthritis, a disease characterized by erosion of knee joint cartilage. Injury to the meniscus is one of the most common knee joint problems and as long as hockey, basketball, soccer and skiing remain popular pastimes in Canada, meniscus injuries will be on the rise. Osteoarthritis currently affects 1 in 10 adult Canadians. As the population ages, it is expected that the number of Canadians with the disease will increase. The annual healthcare cost associated with osteoarthritis is in excess of $4.4 billion in Canada. The meniscus serves as the major load distributor of the knee joint and protects the surface of knee cartilage. Unfortunately, when injured it cannot heal itself because it has a very limited blood supply. Current treatments involve surgical removal of damaged meniscus. However, the absence of meniscus in knee joints accelerates the development of osteoarthritis of the knee. Therefore, it is paramount that new treatment methods are developed. This proposal will investigate the possibility of using patient's own stem cells to make a living meniscus substitute for transplantation. Our work to date has provided strong evidence that the combination of patients' own meniscus cells and stem cells form tissue with meniscus-like properties. The proposed work will be a crucial first step in developing a living tissue replacement for knee meniscus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mitochondrial suppression  in pulmonary hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: HYPOXIA; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; POLYMORPHISMS; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION; VASCULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Disturbance of the way that energy is produced in the cell usually results in disease. There is evidence that disturbance in the energy production in the cells forming the blood vessels of the lungs results in a deadly disease called pulmonary hypertension.  In this disease high blood pressure in the lungs results in too much straining of the right chambers of the heart which eventually fail, causing early death. Effective therapies in this disease are urgently needed. Here we plan to investigate how two important components of mitochondria (the energy producers on the cell) can contribute to pulmonary hypertension. We will use animals and human tissues to prove this idea and attempt to develop new therapies for this disease. If successful, we can then try to test them in humans. This is a new approach to this disease that holds promise for novel and effective therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterizing structural changes that retarget enteric reovirus towards tumours.
Keywords-MotsClés: HOST SUSCEPTIBILITY; INFECTIVITY; ONCOLYTIC VIRUSES; REOVIRUS; VIRUS DISASSEMBLY; VIRUS REPLICATION; VIRUS STABILITY; VIRUS STRUCTURE; VIRUS TROPISM; VIRUS-HOST INTERACTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: While some viruses are harmful, other viruses provide safe and innovative tools to deliver therapeutic genes or selectively kill cancer cells. Mammalian orthoreovirus (reovirus) infects most individuals through the intestine but is non-pathogenic. Reovirus replicates preferentially in cancer cells relative to healthy cells, thus offering a promising oncotherapy. For reasons poorly understood, over 99 percent of reovirus particles fail to establish infection, even in cancer cells. Our program explores factors that impact reovirus infectivity and can be fine-tuned to improve reovirus oncotherapy. We recently isolated two reovirus mutants with higher infectivity towards many cancer cells. These 'next-generation' reovirus mutants prolong survival in a mouse model of melanoma, indicating that tumour clearance can be improved by increasing reovirus infectivity towards cancer cells. We also discovered that specific mutations in two reovirus proteins, sigma 1 and lambda 2, account for improved oncolysis by the reovirus mutants. Our project will discover precisely how these mutations promote infectivity of reovirus particles. We hypothesize that these mutations help reovirus disassemble when it enters a cells. We will therefore explore the effects of sigma 1 and lambda 2 mutations on reovirus disassembly and identify critical protein domains that promote successful reovirus disassembly in cancer cells. We also hypothesize that mutations in sigma 1 and lambda 2 that promote infection of cancer cells concurrently make reovirus less stable in the intestine, which is the natural route for reovirus infection. Our project will therefore evaluate if next-generation reovirus mutants are weakened towards the intestine, and therefore present a safer alternative to wild-type reovirus. Overall, our studies will reveal new mechanisms that impact infectivity of reovirus particles towards tumor cells and will help us understand how to improve reovirus cancer therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the Social Determinants of Children's Developmental Health with a Population-Level, Pan-Canadian Database
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD HEALTH; EARLY CHILD DEVELOPMENT; POPULATION DATABASE
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed research project presents unprecedented opportunities to examine social determinants of children's developmental health at a Pan-Canadian population-level. We will examine neighborhood-level associations between children's developmental health and associated socioeconomic and demographic characteristics across Canada. The analyses will draw on a database that is worldwide unique, containing geo-coded data on developmental health and socioeconomic variables from common tools: Data on children's developmental health have come from the Early Development Instrument (EDI), a tool that assesses five core domains of children's developmental health. Data on neighborhood-level socio-economic status and demographic characteristics have been obtained from Canadian Census and Taxfiler data, including variables on income, education, employment, occupation, poverty, wealth, immigration, and residential transiency. We will examine the following key research questions: First, we will analyze and compare social gradients of developmental health for virtually all jurisdictions in Canada. Second, we will analyze social determinants of developmental health across different subpopulations. Third, we will analyze neighborhood-level trends of developmental health and their associations with socioeconomic and demographic changes over time. Our analyses will allow us to answer critical research questions about children's health from a population health perspective. Given the internationally unique database and our research team's interdisciplinary expertise, the proposed project has the potential to make significant contributions to research on children's developmental health, and will have critical implications for early childhood development practice, programs, and policies.
