TitreApplicationTitle: Influenza virulence and host defense
Keywords-MotsClés: AVIAN IMMUNOLOGY; AVIAN INFLUENZA; HOST IMMUNE RESPONSE TO VIRAL INFECTION; INNATE IMMUNITY; NON-STRUCTURAL PROTEIN 1 (NS1); PATTERN RECOGNITION RECEPTORS; POLYUBIQUITINYLATION; RIG-I CYTOSOLIC RNA HELICASE; TRANSCRIPTOME ANALYSIS; VIRULENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Bird flu continues to circulate in Asia, and there is very real concern that it could recombine with human strains and create a new pandemic. Bird flu is extremely deadly and has killed over 60% of the 600 people it has infected in the last 10 years. We are interested in learning from the natural host how to combat and survive avian influenza. Ducks, but not chickens or humans, can survive many strains of bird flu. With our last grant, we showed that ducks, but not chickens, have a functional flu detector called RIG-I. Humans also have this flu detector gene, but the virus has mastered several ways of shutting it down. In this project we want to learn how this detector is activated by flu in ducks, and how ducks avoid the numerous ways that flu shuts it down in humans. By learning this, we hope that we can devise ways to stop the virus from shutting down our protective responses when we are critically ill with flu. Also, we can understand what changes can happen in the flu virus under strong immune selective pressure. Finally, we will identify the proteins in ducks that work to prevent harm from flu. Some of these may open new avenues for medical intervention in critically ill patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Health Outcomes, Utilization, and Safety in the Elderly with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (HOUSE-IBD) Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CROHN'S DISEASE; ELDERLY; HEALTHCARE UTILIZATION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; MEDICATION-RELATED ADVERSE EVENTS; SURGERY; ULCERATIVE COLITIS
Abstract-Résumé: The inflammatory bowel diseases are a group of related disorders including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis that occur more frequently in Canada than most other countries.  The symptoms of IBD, which mostly affect the gut, often start in the second and third decade of life, but can recur off and on for a lifetime.  They can lead to complications that require hospitalization and bowel-related surgeries. With the aging population, we expect that more and more people over the age of 65 years will be affected by IBD.  Treating IBD in elderly patients can present a unique challenge to healthcare providers.  Older patients may have coexisting conditions that require increased use of health services or may not tolerate medical and surgical treatments as well as younger IBD patients.  Through this study we will assess whether IBD patients diagnosed at an older age suffer more complications from their disease.  The study will also identify the specific healthcare needs of the elderly related to their IBD.  Finally, it will evaluate whether medical and surgical treatments typically used for IBD are safe in older patients.  The information from this research will provide guidance for physicians and health policy makers on how to best deliver care and treat elderly IBD patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms in Fracture and Wound healing.
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CATENIN; FRACTURE REPAIR; HEMATOPOIETIC CELLS; TRANSPLANTATION; WOUND REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: About one third of all individuals will sustain a fracture, with 5% having difficulty healing their fracture. Bone that does not heal goes on to a non-union resulting in short and long-term disability.  Bone healing problems occur in patients with disease such as cancer, and increase in frequency with aging.  Fractures that do not heal require multiple surgeries, impair mobility, and are associated with an increased morbidity and even mortality, especially in patients with other underlying medical problems.    We discovered a crucial role for a protein called beta-catenin during fracture healing, and identified a drug that could be used to inhibit this protein. Another drug, already used in patients, can be used to activate beta-catenin.  Beta-catenin controls how the healing cells in fractures become bone, and when the protein level is too high or too low, fractures will not heal normally. In this proposal, we will study two common conditions in which fracture healing is poor:  that seen in the elderly, and that seen in patients with leukemia.  We found that in both these situations, abnormal beta-catenin plays a role in the poor fracture healing.  In this proposal, we will use mouse models to see if altering beta-catenin could be used to improve fracture repair in these situations.  Based on this information, we will test a pharmacologic approach to improve fracture repair, using drugs that either activate or inhibit beta-catenin.  This work will identify a new therapeutic approach to improve the outcome in patients with leukemia or in elderly patients who are prone to poor bone healing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translating genetic discoveries into therapeutic strategies for inherited diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: CYSTIC FIBROSIS; GENE REGULATION; GENE THERAPY; GENETIC DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Knowledge gained in genetics over the past few decades has revolutionized our ways to identify changes in human genes responsible for diseases. It speeded up the development of methods for disease diagnosis and helped to understand disease mechanisms/patho-physiology. However, the current major challenge to realize the full potential of therapeutic benefits from advancements in genetics is the slow progress in translating our knowledge into clinical therapeutic applications. Conceptually, correction of a genetic mutation that causes a disease should allow us to cure the disease at its cause, not its symptoms, thereby, revolutionizing the human medicine. But, technically, it is difficult to deliver genetic materials, efficiently and safely despite the hype generated in early 1990s. The first major challenge is the lack of novel delivery vectors with a high efficiency and easy production in high quality. The second major challenge is host immune responses that eliminate the cells with delivered genes. The main objective of the proposed research is to overcome these challenges by designing and testing novel strategies for achieving efficient delivery of therapeutic genes to diseased cells using animal models relevant to human genetic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prenatal maternal stress and brain maturation during adolescence: Project Ice Storm
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN DEVELOPMENT; MATERNAL STRESS; NATURAL DISASTER; PSYCHOPATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: To determine the influence of prenatal events on brain development, we will investigate the possible effects of maternal stress during pregnancy, resulting from the 1998 Quebec Ice Storm, on brain maturation during adolescence. In June 1998, our team identified mothers who were pregnant during the January 1998 ice storm, obtained maternal reports about the levels of stress experienced during the storm, and established a cohort of children born from these pregnancies (n=120). These children were assessed (cognitive abilities, mental health, physical growth) at several time points before the age of 14 years and will be assessed again at 15 and 16.5 years. We also acquired images of the brain structures with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) from these children (Time 1: age 11.5 years; Ice Storm cohort, n=69) as well as in a group of children born in the year before the ice storm (Time 1: age 11.5 years; PreStorm cohort, n=60).  Here, we propose to collect additional MRIs of these children's brains in the IceStorm and PreStorm cohorts during middle (age 16.5 yr) and late (age 18 years) adolescence. Using these data, we will evaluate age-related changes in the connections in the brain (i.e., white matter) during adolescence, from 11.5 to 18 years of age, and examine whether or not prenatal maternal stress affects normal development of these connections and, in turn, risk of mental health problems. Altogether, the proposed research will increase our understanding of prenatal factors on brain development and, in turn, individuals' risk and resilience to psychological problems later in life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endoplasmic reticulum stress, Ca2+ permeation pathways and neuronal death.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S; AMYLOID; ER STRESS; HIPPOCAMPUS; NMDA RECEPTORS; PANNEXIN; PATCH CLAMP; STORE-OPERATED CALCIUM ENTRY
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that attacks parts of the brain involved with learning and memory.  The overarching goal of the research proposed in this application is to uncover mechanisms that could be targeted for the development of therapeutic agents capable of preventing neuronal death in Alzheimer's disease.  The associated neurodegeneration is known to correlate with the accumulation of cellular stressors.  How this contributes to disease is not understood.  Recent evidence suggests that cell stress may progressively interfere with the function of the endoplasmic reticulum, an intracellular organelle that plays a vital role in a variety of cellular functions.  Our preliminary findings suggest that as endoplasmic reticulum function deteriorates it provokes increased activation of a family of plasma membrane channels called pannexins, previously shown to be involved in cell death.  Understanding how the endoplasmic reticulum regulates pannexin channel activity will provide novel insight leading to the rational design of innovative drugs of benefit in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease, and potentially other neurodegenerative disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Follow-up Care After a Visit to the Emergency Department: Assessing the Frequency and Timeliness in Patients with Chronic Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; CARDIAC DISEASE; CONGESTIVE HEART FAILURE; CONTINUITY OF CARE; EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; HYPERTENSION; MORTALITY; OUTCOMES; PRIMARY CARE; TRANSITION OF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: CONTEXT: Each year 12 million people visit an emergency department (ED) in Canada, with the highest rates among older persons. Some will be admitted to hospital, but many are discharged home. Between the extremes of admitted and discharged patients there are patients for whom both options are possible. Discharge from the ED avoids the high cost of a hospitalization, risk of a hospital-acquired infection, and of delirium and permanent decline in the elderly. However, in order to safely discharge these patients a system of care must be in place to ensure a prompt follow-up appointment with the family physician (FP) or specialist. Because this system is often unreliable, many patients are simply admitted to hospital.  THE PROBLEM: With the aging of the population, ED visits are expected to accelerate. Using patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) as an example, it is estimated that AF in the population will increase by 250% by the year 2050. ED visits for AF increased by 88% from 1994 to 2006, and are expected to increase similarly for other chronic diseases as well.  METHODS: Using databases that include all Ontario ED visits, we will identify older patients seen in an Ontario ED with 1 of 3 common cardiovascular diseases: AF, high blood pressure, and heart failure. We will identify a group of patients for whom emergency doctors would standardly recommend early follow-up care with either the FP or specialist. We will see how many of those patients actually saw a doctor within 3, 7, and 30 days of the ED visit. Next we will determine whether lack of follow-up was associated with a higher death rate, return ED visits, and taking recommended medications.  IMPACT: The study results will provide the first scientific evidence as to whether the current system of care between the ED and FP is adequate. It will allow us to make informed decisions as we proceed to a future study to evaluate interventions that aim to improve the transition of care between the ED and the FP.

TitreApplicationTitle: A self-categorization theory approach to fostering physical activity adherence among older adults: A randomized controlled feasibility trial.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; COHESION; GROUP DYNAMICS; HEALTH PSYCHOLOGY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTOLLED FEASIBILITY TRIAL; SELF-CATEGORIZATION THEORY; SOCIAL IDENTITY THEORY
Abstract-Résumé: Regular physical activity is associated with a diverse range of physical and mental health outcomes, with the effects being particularly pronounced among older adults. Despite these health benefits, involvement in physical activity has been found to decline over the course of adulthood with older adults in particular risk of inactivity. A growing body of evidence, however, suggests that group-based settings that are sensitive to both the age-composition and gender-composition of their constituent members may represent an opportune means of supporting the improved adoption and maintenance of older adults in physical activity programs. The overall purpose of this research is to test the effectiveness of a group-based physical activity program for older adults that is sensitive to both age-congruent and gender-congruent contextual factors, in supporting their sustained involvement in physical activity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interventions for dyslexia: Effectiveness and neurological correlates
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDREN; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; DYSLEXIA; FUNCTIONAL MRI; PSYCHOEDUCATIONAL ASSESSMENT; READING REMEDIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Developmental dyslexia is a common reading disability. In addition to poor school performance, children with dyslexia may show mental health problems such as attention deficit disorder, depression and anxiety, and social problems such as antisocial behaviour and homelessness. These academic and mental health issues may persist into adulthood, and negatively affect a person's job prospects and quality of life. Therefore, increasing reading skills in childhood is very important to their overall health as adults. There are few treatment programs, however, that have any research evidence supporting their effectiveness. A new reading intervention program called ABRACADABRA is being used in some Canadian elementary schools. This free web-based program has been shown to strengthen reading skills in children in primary grades, and it may be particularly successful in children with dyslexia. The goal of our research is to understand the brain regions and connections that are related to reading ability, while providing a rigorous scientific evaluation of the ABRACADABRA program. The results of our research will provide new evidence on the effectiveness of ABRACADABRA for treating reading disability. It will also reveal the brain changes that are correlated with improved reading skills.

TitreApplicationTitle: A virus-based strategy for measurement of circulating tumour cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CASTRATION-RESISTANT; CIRCULATING TUMOUR CELLS; METASTASES; ONCOLYTIC VIRUS; PROSTATE CANCER; TARGETING
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer ranks as third biggest cancer-killer of men, with over 4,000 Canadian men expected to die of this disease this year. Primary tumours rarely kill patients directly, but often shed malignant cells that are able to seed new tumours at distant sites within the body such as in the bone marrow. These new tumours, called "metastases", are responsible for 90% of cancer deaths. In most cases, the cancer cells must enter and circulate in the bloodstream before seeding a secondary tumour, with the circulating tumour cells, or "CTCs" as they are usually referred to, generally considered a necessary pre-condition and predictor for the occurrence of distant metastases. Finding new sensitive methods for very early detection of cancer dissemination before full blown, clinical metastases are evident should allow quicker intervention and hence save lives.    The Veridex CellSearch system is the only FDA-approved method for clinical monitoring of CTCs, but it requires very expensive equipment and a dedicated operator which many hospitals and cancer centers cannot easily afford. Also this system relies on a cell surface marker, which may not be universally expressed on all tumour cells. Accordingly, the primary objective of our proposed project is to develop new, highly sensitive, inexpensive and readily accessible methods for accurately measuring the presence of CTCs at the earliest possible time.  To achieve this, we will test three very novel, virus-based methods to detect and quantify CTCs in small blood samples taken from the patient: a direct measure of a virus-induced fluorescent protein marker in CTCs and two super-sensitive indirect methods using a secretable enzyme and immune response markers to gauge the number of CTCs. These new assays should provide an opportunity for earlier detection and treatment of metastases which should translate into increased survival for patients with advanced, metastatic prostate cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac Troponins and Sex Differences in Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE; DIAGNOSIS AND PROGNOSIS; OUTCOMES; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Currently, to confirm a heart attack, a blood test is used to measure the level of a specific protein, called cardiac troponin.  Cardiac troponin is present in heart muscle.  When the heart muscle is damaged as a result of a heart attack, troponin is released into the bloodstream and therefore can b measured using a troponin test.  The blood level of cardiac troponin must exceed a specified limit, called the diagnostic cut-point, in order to confirm the diagnosis of a heart attack.  Based on current guidelines, the same diagnostic cut-points are being used for both men and women even though we know in both healthy and sick populations women have lower levels of troponin at all ages.  This difference may be a reflection of sex differences in how heart disease manifests in women compared to men.  Our research will determine whether the cut-points for both the detection of a heart attack and for the assessment of risk for future unfavorable events, such as rehospitalization and death, should be different in women compared to men.  This knowledge will help improve the clinical management of women with heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of ET-1 and Ang II induced cytosolic and nuclear ROS generation in nuclear T-tubules formation in hypertrophy and ageing of human vascular smooth muscle cells.
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM HOMEOSTASIS; NUCLEAR MEMBRANES RECEPTORS; NUCLEAR T-TUBULES; NUCLEAR TRANSPORT; PHARMACOLOGY OF NUCLEAR MEMBRANES RECEPTORS; VASCULAR AGING; VASCULAR HYPERTROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Un taux anormalement eleve de calcium est un signal universel que l'on retrouve dans differentes pathologies, telles l'atherosclerose et l'hypertension. Il est a noter que ces deux pathologies peuvent etre associees au processus de vieillissement et peuvent dependre du sexe (homme versus femme). Plusieurs facteurs de risques majeurs pour cette maladie, tels l'hypertension et l'atherosclerose, se caracterisent par des fonctions anormales des cellules qui constituent les vaisseaux comme les cellules du muscle lisse vasculaire. Cette anomalie est associee a une augmentation anormale du calcium intracellulaire, causant une augmentation de la pression arterielle. Fait interessant a noter est que cette augmentation du calcium intracellulaire semble aussi avoir lieu au niveau du noyau de la cellule du muscle lisse vasculaire. De plus, des evidences grandissantes supportent l'hypothese que cette augmentation anormale du calcium du noyau de la cellule est regulee par des proteines recepteurs presentes dans les membranes du noyau ainsi que par des invaginations des membranes du noyau de la cellule. L'objectif principal de ce projet est de tester l'hypothese que certaines hormones liberees des cellules immunitaires, comme l'endotheline-1, peuvent etre consideres comme les premiers messagers pathologiques de l'atherosclerose et l'hypertension. De plus, ces facteurs peuvent avoir une propriete en commun, induisant une augmentation du calcium intracellulaire et en particulier au niveau du noyau. Si cela s'avere vrai, cela supporte l'hypothese que l'augmentation anormale du calcium du noyau est un messager pathologique majeur dans les maladies des vaisseaux sanguins. L'activation des proteines recepteurs de l'endotheline-1 et de l'angiotensine II des membranes du noyau cellulaire contribue a cette anomalie. Le developpement d'un medicament touchant ces proteines des membranes du noyau constitue une cible efficace pour traiter l'hypertension et l'atherosclerose.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Vascular Dendritic Cells in Atherosclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGEN-PRESENTING CELLS; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CHRONIC INFLAMMATION; DENDRITIC CELLS (DCS); GENETICALLY MODIFIED MICE; HEMATOPOIETIN FLT3 LIGAND; INNATE IMMUNITY; MONOCYTES/MACROPHAGES; REGULATORY T CELLS; SUBSET OF DENDRITIC CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The second leading cause of death in Canada is heart disease, most of it caused by atherosclerosis. In this disease process, there is build-up of cholesterol and other materials that alter the inner lining of arteries supplying blood to the heart, leading to blood clots, chronic inflammatory responses and heart attack. The inflammatory responses in atherosclerosis involve many types of immune cells such as monocytes, macrophages, T cells and dendritic cells (DCs). In contrast to numerous studies regarding the disease-promoting roles of macrophages and T cells, the roles of DCs in atherosclerosis are unclear. Our groups and others have uncovered DCs in the healthy and atherosclerotic blood vessels.  Here, we hypothesize that vascular DC subsets will have differential effects on the course of atherosclerosis. In the present proposal, we will first characterize subsets of DCs in healthy and atherosclerotic blood vessels. Then, using genetically modified mice to selectively manipulate DC subsets, we will investigate their function in the context of atherosclerosis. DCs are now believed to orchestrate the interactions of more than a dozen type of immune system cells, and they also play a role in preventing the immune system from attacking the body's own tissues. Therefore, understanding the basic biology of dendritic cells and their subsets will lead to ways to harness them therapeutically in treating or preventing atherosclerosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Genetic Determinants of Human Sleep and Circadian Rhythms
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIGRAPHY; CEREBRAL CORTEX; CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; POLYMORPHISM; SLEEP; STATISTICAL GENETICS; STROKE; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: Sleep and circadian rhythms (24h biological rhythms regulated by an internal biological clock) have a huge impact on human performance, and affect many common diseases.  However, despite their importance to human biology and performance, our knowledge of the genes important for human sleep and circadian rhythms is incomplete. The overall goal of this study is to identify genes associated with sleep and circadian behavior, to explore the mechanisms whereby they act, and to apply these findings to the prediction of sleep and circadian rhythms in the real world.  To do this, we will take advantage of the observation that sleep and circadian behavior varies between individuals and some of these differences appear to be inherited.  We will use actigraphs - wristwatch-like accelerometers - to non-intrusively measure sleep and circadian behavior in several preexisting large groups of volunteers in Ontario and elsewhere.  Using already-available genetic data form these same individuals, we will examine for natural gene variants associated with variation in sleep and circadian behavior, and examine the effects of these variants on gene expression.   Finally, we will apply our findings to the prediction of sleep and circadian behavior in a community-based population, and to the prediction of stroke timing in individuals who have suffered a stroke.     This study has the potential to identify new genes regulating human sleep and circadian behavior, thereby deepening our understanding of human sleep and circadian rhythms.  In so doing, it may eventually lead to new treatments and management strategies for shift-work, jet lag, and sleep disruption that have enormous social and medical consequences for millions of Canadians, and may facilitate genetically-guided personalization of school, work, travel and other schedules to optimize human performance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ultrasound Guidance for Epidural Analgesia and Anesthesia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANESTHESIA; EPIDURAL; IMAGE PROCESSING; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: The majority of pregnant Canadian women have epidural anesthesia (an "epidural") to ease the pain of labour and delivery. Currently, this is a challenging procedure for the anesthesiologist and it takes approximately one hundred patients for a resident to train and achieve competency. This is a long training curve because the insertion of an epidural needle into the spine requires a delicate sense of touch to pick the puncture site above the target epidural site and then push the needle until it enters the epidural space, without overshooting and entering the spinal cord. Even for experienced anesthesiologists, the presence of obesity and spinal deformities can still make this a challenging procedure. Complications include accidental puncture of the membrane around the spinal cord, headaches, nerve damage and very rarely paralysis. The rate of these complications plus the failure to achieve sufficient anesthesia is estimated to be 6-25%. This is due in large part to incorrect needle placement. We propose to use a new 3D ultrasound technique to make epidural needle placement more accurate. In particular, we will develop smart rendering methods of the 3D ultrasound data to clearly show the target epidural space and the needle. We will also make it easy to operate by automatically showing the ideal ultrasound image of the target. This will be implemented on standard ultrasound machines are the now available in most anesthesiology departments. The outcome of this research will be a working 3D ultrasound system that works reliably on a wide range of patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the Physical and Functional Interactome of Mitochondria in Yeast
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY PURIFICATION; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MITOCHONDRIAL BIOLOGY; MITOCHONDRIAL GENETIC INTERACTIONS; MITOCHONDRIAL PROTEIN COMPLEX; NETWORK BIOLOGY; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria generate the majority of a cell's energy supply and are required for a large number of diverse cellular functions, including ion homeostasis, respiration, and cell death. Mitochondrial biochemical processes are highly integrated both within and outside the mitochondria (i.e. extramitochondrial pathways). Due to their importance in basic cellular processes, defects in mitochondrial function cause or contribute to a diverse set of human diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. Yet, despite their known importance, the role of mitochondrial dysfunction in human diseases is often difficult to pinpoint due to incomplete information about mitochondrial proteins, interactions, and pathways. This proposal seeks to address this deficit by creating detailed mitochondrial physical (protein-protein) and functional (gene-gene, or genetic) interaction maps. Large-scale proteomic and genetic screening procedures, optimized by the proposed research, will be used to comprehensively identify the physical interactions, multiprotein complexes, and pathway relationships among mitochondrial genes in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Physical interaction data will be combined with complementary information on epistatic relationships among these same genes to guide identification of functional pathways and essential mitochondrial complexes. This integrative approach will uncover novel functional mechanisms in mitochondrial biology, facilitating discovery of new therapeutic targets for the treatment of mitochondrial diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Wheelchair Self-efficacy Enhanced training program to improve wheelchair Use in older adults: The WheelSeeU feasibility study
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; MANUAL WHEELCHAIR; PEER TRAINING; REHABILITATION; SELF EFFICACY; SKILLS TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: Mobility impairments are the most common barrier to independent living for aging Canadians, which can lead to loss of social connections, isolation, and reduced quality of life.  The wheelchair is arguably the most important mobility device. However, more than half of Canadians over the age of 65 years who receive a wheelchair require assistance getting around. One of the reasons for the high prevalence of mobility dependence may be because older adults receive little to no training for wheelchair use. Therefore, many stop participating in activities because the physical and cognitive demands associated with wheelchair use are too much for them or their caregiver. This is a costly problem, both socially and financially. Although some training programs exist, clinicians do not have the time or resources to provide optimal training for older adults. The Wheelchair Self-Efficacy Enhanced Use (WheelSeeU) program is a peer-lead community-based training program specifically designed for older adults. A peer-trainer facilitates 6, 2-hour sessions in the community using self-efficacy enhancing strategies to improve wheelchair use through individualized goal setting and customized task-specific practice. WheelSeeU creates positive reinforcement through the inclusion of family, who are encouraged to take part in the training sessions. This study investigates the potential for using WheelSeeU with older adults in Vancouver and Quebec City, shortly after they obtain a wheelchair. Once we confirm that WheelSeeU is feasible and effectively improves older adults' wheelchair skill, broader studies can be conducted including a national randomized clinical trial with older adults. WheelSeeU offers promise for improving wheelchair use, self-efficacy, mobility and satisfaction with participation in important activities for older adults, while reducing caregiver burden and providing rehabilitation services without undue cost on the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Immune Dysfunction: The Role of Damaged Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CYTOKINES; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM AND PROGENITOR CELLS; MESENCHYMAL STROMAL CELLS; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is the most frequent form of chronic inflammatory polyarthritis with a prevalence of 1-2% and an incidence of 50 in 100.000 cases. Patients with RA not only have a reduced quality of life but they have an increased premature mortality risk.  Defects in the function of immune cells, which ultimately make the immune system less efficient and more likely to react against self-tissues, characterize RA. The abnormalities of the immune system involve not only mature cells, but also their precursors known as hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC). HSPC are the cells that give rise to all the immune and blood cells of our body. In order to do so, HSPC must actively divide (proliferate). In RA patients, the proliferative capacity of HSPC is impaired and thus, their ability to generate the entire immune system is hampered. The mechanism(s) accounting for the proliferative defects of stem cells in RA are largely unknown.  RA-HSPC accumulate genomic damage, which is depicted by their early telomere shortening and high number of DNA breaks. We postulate that DNA damage in RA-HSPC triggers the production of inflammatory cytokines, which in turn provide a "stop proliferating signal" to other HSPC and their environment. This proposal will test this hypothesis, define the molecular mechanisms underlying this process and evaluate how modulating the production of HSPC cytokines impacts the efficiency of mature immune cell generation in RA.  Understanding the role of HSPC in RA pathogenesis by defining the factors that account for their central functional defect (proliferative arrest), will provide new information concerning the etiology and potentially novel therapeutic targets for this debilitating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Taimailiriallariaqangngituk Kangiqsualujjuaq-mit* Understanding a Tuberculosis outbreak in Kangiqsualujjuaq to prevent more
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; BACTERIAL GENOMICS; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; OUTBREAK; POPULATION HEALTH; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) rates vary within Canada, with the highest incidence observed in the Inuit. On this backdrop of already high rates of TB, an unprecedented outbreak developed in 2011/2012 at Kangiqsualujjuaq (George River), a village in Nunavik, where 89 persons (9% of the total population) have been diagnosed with active TB disease. We plan to conduct two inter-related investigations to determine the cause(s) of this outbreak.    To investigate whether the outbreak is due to epidemiologic factors, such as inadequate housing, poor nutrition and/or lifestyle-associated risk factors, we will conduct two case-control studies.  To investigate whether the outbreak is the result of a more virulent strain of M. tuberculosis, we will sequence the DNA of the outbreak strain and test its virulence in experimental models of disease.  If we find that housing, nutritional or life style factors are strongly associated with the outbreak then public health interventions can be directed toward correcting these problems.  If the bacteria prove to be more virulent than before the outbreak, this will necessitate a very different public health response, potentially including community-wide antibiotic treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Functional Nuclear Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex is Important for a Mitochondria-Independent Generation of Acetyl-CoA and Histone Acetylation in the Nucleus
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; EPIGENETICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The regulation of genetic information in the cell depends on the function of the energy factories of the cell, the mitochondria. This way energy availability can be coordinated with the growth of the cell, which is regulated by the nucleus. However, there are conditions that the cells show increased growth but the mitochondria are inhibited, like cancer or low oxygen levels. In this work we propose to characterize a completely new mechanism by which the cell can regulate the genetic information independent of the mitochondria. We will use several sophisticated techniques to prove this new idea, which is supported by our early preliminary experiments. If we are correct, this new information will shed light in many unexplored areas of medicine and biology, where energy merges with genetic regulation and may result in the discovery of new therapies for devastating diseases like cancer, but also neurodegenerative diseases of heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing Potentially Inappropriate Prescribing (PIP) and predicting patient outcomes in Ontario's elderly population using the modified STOPP criteria in large administrative health databases (the PIP-STOPP study)
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE DRUG EVENTS; ELDERLY PATIENTS; EMERGENCY ROOM VISITS; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH CARE RESOURCE USE; HOSPITALIZATIONS; INAPPROPRIATE PRESCRIBING; MEDICATION COST; MORTALITY; SCREENING TOOL
Abstract-Résumé: The elderly are at a higher risk than the rest of the population for adverse drug reactions. This is due to high numbers of medications prescribed per person, increasing numbers of prescribers as well as the elderly's greater sensitivity to medication effects due to natural age-related changes in the way the body deals with medication. Emergency room visits and unplanned hospital readmissions amongst the elderly are commonly due to adverse drug reactions. Many of these are avoidable and a number of tools have been developed to identify potentially inappropriate medications, with varying degrees of success. This study will apply a novel and promising tool to health data kept by the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long Term Care.  It is hoped this tool will identify instances where patients were prescribed inappropriate medications and will show links between inappropriate prescriptions and patient outcomes, such as ER visits and hospitalizations. This tool is usually used by looking at individual patient charts in family physician clinics, so it is hoped that by applying it to provincial data, the rates and costs of inappropriate prescribing can be estimated for the whole elderly population of Ontario.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel strategy to selectively target tumor cell growth and chemosensitivity
Keywords-MotsClés: KEAP1; P13KINASE; SELECTIVE CHEMOSENSITIZATION; THERAPEUTIC RESISTANCE; TRANSCRIPTIONAL PROTEIN NRFF2
Abstract-Résumé: The greatest threat to cancer patients is resistance of tumors to treatment. Overcoming resistance will have a major impact on survival. We are studying a system that cells use to protect themselves from damage. Tumors use this system to become resistant, so if we can block this defense, we might be able to delay or even overcome resistance. We have a number of strategies, and we have already identified new chemicals that can do this. We will move this forward to animal studies to confirm this activity, and also test our prediction that this will have very little toxicity.   We have recently discovered that this cell defense system not only makes tumors resistant to chemotherapy, but also to some of the most recent and advanced treatments that 'target' specific mechanisms that tumors cells use to stimulate their growth and survival. We therefore believe that our strategy can dramatically enhance the anti-tumor effect of a wide range of treatments, while at the same time protect normal tissues from toxicity.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; MALADIES INFECTIEUSES ET PARASITAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Host factors involved in polyomavirus genome replication
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA REPLICATION; HELICASE; INHIBITORS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PEPTIDE; POLYOMAVIRUS; PROTEOMICS; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Polyomaviruses (PVs) are the cause of several diseases in humans, especially in individuals that are immunocompromised, such as AIDS patients, or those taking immunosuppressive drugs, such as organ transplant patients. The JC virus (JCV) causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a disease of the brain commonly seen in AIDS patients. BKV on the other hand is the cause of BK-induced nephropathy, a major source of kidney transplant failures. Two recently discovered PVs, MCV and TSV, have been associated, respectively, with Merkel cell carcinoma, a rare but aggressive form of skin cancer, and trichodysplasia spinulosa, a rare skin disease seen exclusively in immune-deficient patients. Few therapeutic options are available to treat PV-associated diseases as no specific antiviral drug targeting these viruses currently exists.  We propose to study how polyomaviruses usurp the cells that they infect in order to replicate (i.e. make copies of) their viral DNA genome, with the ultimate goal of discovering specific aspects of the infection process that could be targeted for antiviral drug discovery. A single viral protein, termed the "large T antigen", is required from the virus to replicate its genome, the rest of the proteins participating in the replication process being from the infected cell. We will identify which proteins from infected cells are required for viral DNA replication, in particular those that can bind to the viral large T antigen or that can alter its activity. We will also try to identify peptides that interfere with the functions of large T antigen, as such peptides are ideal tools to validate these functions as candidate antiviral targets.  The proposed studies will greatly enhance our understanding of polyomavirus DNA replication and provide a basis for the discovery of inhibitors of this viral process, an essential first step in the development of antiviral drugs to treat polyomavirus induced-diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vesico-Ureteric Reflux and Reflux Nephropathy: from Mouse Models to Childhood Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN GENETICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MOUSE GENETICS; MOUSE MODELS; REFLUX NEPHROPATHY; URINARY TRACT DEVELOPMENT; URINARY TRACT INFECTION; VESICO-URETERIC REFLUX
Abstract-Résumé: Urine infections in children are one of the most common causes of admission to hospital in North America.  Many of these children have a defect in the formation of the urinary tract known as vesico-ureteric reflux that predisposes them to urine infection and in some to kidney failure.  In this grant, we will explore mouse models with vesico-ureteric reflux to discover the genetic changes that lead to this urinary tract malformation.  We will also introduce urine infection in these mice to understand how infection can cause damage to the kidneys.  Our work in the mouse will be applied to a clinical study in which we are collecting DNA from children with vesico-ureteric reflux. This work will have important implications for understanding which children with vesico-ureteric reflux are at risk for kidney failure and it will provide new insight into how urine infections cause kidney damage.

ClasseRechercheFR: SANG; DISTRIBUTION DES SOINS DE LA SANTE
TitreApplicationTitle: Age of Blood in Children in Pediatric Intensive Care Units (ABC-PICU): a multicenter international pragmatic double blind randomized clinical trial on the efficacy of "short storage" red blood cell units to decrease the incidence of new or progressive multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) in critically ill children
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD BANK; CHILDREN; MULTIPLE ORGAN DYSFUNCTION SYNDROME; PEDIATRIC CRITICAL CARE; POLICY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; RED BLOOD CELL; STORAGE LESION; STORAGE TIME; TRANSFUSION
Abstract-Résumé: Presently, when red blood cell transfusion is required, blood banks transfuse the oldest unit available. In North America that means red cells stored up to 42 days may be transfused to critically ill children despite some concern that older blood may have negative effects. There is also a widely held belief that the freshest red cells possible may benefit more vulnerable patients. Therefore, some critically ill children are routinely transfused fresh red cells without evidence that this is best practice. If fresh red cell units are better, then fresh blood should be provided to all critically ill children. On the other hand, if fresh blood is shown to be no different or harmful, then those who offer fresh red cells to certain critically ill children should stop doing so given extra costs and potential ethical concerns associated with inequitable use of a scarce resource. Critically ill patients often develop a disorder called multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) which can affect all their organs (heart, lungs, brain, etc); as more organs are affected the likelihood of death increases. Based on the premise that transfusion of older blood might worsen organ failure, this study plans to assess the effect of transfusion on the gravity of organ failure in 1538 critically ill children admitted to pediatric intensive care units. We will compare a group receiving standard issue red cell units (which are older) to a group receiving fresher red cells (stored for 7 days or less). Negative findings (no difference) will reassure clinicians and blood bankers as well as patients regarding the safety of the present delivery systems. Positive findings (fresher red cells decrease MODS) will confirm that prolonged storage has clinical consequences, would modify transfusion policies so that fresher red cells are transfused in critically ill children and would challenge the transfusion community to develop methods to mitigate the negative effects of prolonged red cell storage.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; TUMEURS
TitreApplicationTitle: Bortezomib mediated BRCAness in Myeloma cells: novel therapeutic approach combining PARP1-2 and 26S proteasome inhibitors.
Keywords-MotsClés: MULTIPLE MYELOMA; PARP AND DNA REPAIR; PHASE I CLINICAL TRIAL; PROTEASOME INHIBITORS
Abstract-Résumé: Multiple myeloma is the second most common form of blood cancers and it remains incurable despite the addition of novel therapeutic strategies for this disease. Cancer cells invariably escape the therapeutic effect of drugs by rearranging their genetic make up overtime, an event known as genomic instability. We have identified a novel approach that takes advantage of these modifications in myeloma cells. Combining drugs that block the machinery responsible for DNA damage repair with agents that block the recycling factories, we have successfully induced catastrophic and irreversible damages that are lethal to myeloma cells. In the current research proposal we first intend to study in depth the mechanisms through the combination of these drugs induce myeloma cell death and also uncover potential mechanisms of resistance and ways to overcome them. In addition we will conduct a clinical trial to define the safety and feasibility of combining these classes of drugs in myeloma patients. We strongly believe that such approach has uncovered the Achilles heel of myeloma cells.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Post-Stroke Brain Deterioration: Role of Abeta and Neuroinflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYLOID; BEHAVIOUR; BRAIN AT RISK; CO-MORBIDITIES; IMAGING; MASS SPECTROMETRY; NEUROINFLAMMATION; RODENT MODELS OF DISEASE; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Unless prevented, one in three over the age of 60 will suffer a stroke, Alzheimer's disease (AD) or both.    Some patients who have a stroke develop characteristics seen in an AD brain.  If patients have pre-existing AD related pathology, the consequences of stroke are worse. Currently there are few options available to stroke patients that would protect them from developing AD pathology and secondary cognitive decline.  To address this, we have created new rat and mouse models of AD and stroke.  This proposal will: 1) Carefully reveal the relationship and timing of AD pathology and inflammation following a stroke and how this relates to cognitive impairment;  2) Examine where and how AD pathology occurs following a stroke; and 3) Target specific inflammatory and AD related molecules to reduce AD pathology and cognitive decline following a stroke.  We will use powerful real-time imaging techniques to detect the timing of the developing AD pathology and inflammation following stroke in the live rat.  We will look at how AD and stroke together accelerate the deterioration of the brain. By understanding the timing and mechanisms by which AD and stroke interact, we will identify a therapeutic window for treatment.  With a window of opportunity identified, we will look at new treatment options that simultaneously block AD pathology and inflammation from occurring.   We are only just experiencing the beginning phase of an aging generation.  Some patients develop brain changes associated with AD following a stroke.  Aging patients with pre-existing signs of AD pathology in the brain may not demonstrate cognitive impairment until after they've had a stroke. This proposal will address both these situations. Results from these proposed projects will provide new treatment options for patients who have suffered a stroke.  More importantly, we may provide an explanation as to why some patients suffer from dementia following a stroke, while others do not.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rac1 in skeletal development and homeostasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CARTILAGE; CHONDROCYTE; GROWTH PLATE; OSTEOARTHRITIS; OSTEOPOROSIS; RAC1; SKELETAL DEVELOPMENT; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: The growth and function of most of our skeleton is controlled by the activity of cartilage cells (chondrocytes). Thus, abnormal behavior of chondrocytes does not only result in skeletal growth disorders, but can also contribute to adult skeletal diseases such as osteoarthritis and possibly osteoporosis.  However, the molecular mechanisms controlling chondrocyte behavior are not completely understood. We have previously generated mutant mice where we specifically deleted the gene for the signaling protein Rac1 in chondrocytes. These mice show severe skeletal deformities and reduced growth, demonstrating an essential role for Rac1 in cartilage development. We will now expand on these studies by a) testing the molecular mechanisms mediating Rac1 effects in chondrocytes, b) examining how Rac1 signaling in chondrocytes controls bone formation through other skeletal cells such as osteoblasts and osteoclasts, and c) determining the role of Rac1 in osteoarthritis. These studies will provide important insights into the basic mechanisms controlling skeletal development, function and disease, and will ultimately contribute to improved prevention and management of skeletal diseases such as osteoarthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hippocampal neurogenesis and regulation of memory
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; CORTEX; FORGETTING; GENETICALLY-ENGINEERED MICE; MEMORY; MEMORY DISORDERS; NEUROGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: We can remember in detail what we were doing 5 minutes ago, yesterday and even the day before yesterday.  But unless something momentous happened a month or a year ago, we are unlikely to remember our day-to-day activities from that period with anything like the same clarity. What this means is that much of what is initially remembered must, over time, be forgotten. It is thought that this forgetting of unimportant things is beneficial as it unclutters the mind, allowing new information to be more efficiently encoded. Yet, despite this, very little is known about how forgetting works. Recently our group has discovered that the ongoing generation of new nerve cells (or neurogenesis) regulates forgetting. As these new nerve cells integrate into brain circuits, they change those circuits leading to a loss of information (or memories) stored in those circuits. In this grant we will explore this new discovery. Our experiments will address how neurogenesis promotes forgetting, how forgetting the 'old' may improve learning the 'new' and whether excessive forgetting during infancy is caused by high levels of neurogenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Experimental and theoretical approaches applied to population coding
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL BEHAVIOR; COMPUTATIONAL NEUROSCIENCE; CORRELATIONS; NEURAL CIRCUITS; NEURAL CODING; NEUROSCIENCE
Abstract-Résumé: As you are reading this text, hundreds of billions of neurons in your brain are firing action potentials, thereby enabling you to understand what is written. As in any good democracy, the activity of the individual neuron counts for little and it is instead the activities of large neural populations that determine most behaviors (e.g. understanding what is written). Now, there is accumulating evidence that the activities of neurons are not independent but are instead correlated (i.e. the fact that one neuron fires an action potential influences whether a neighboring neuron will also fire an action potential or not). Moreover, a growing body of evidence suggests that these correlations are not static but are instead dynamic and depend on context (e.g. whether you are paying attention to this text or not). This research aims at understanding how correlations vary and what functions they serve in the brain. Our results are expected to help doctors be more effective in their diagnosis and treatment of people suffering from impaired sensory function and/or mental disorders.

NomDuComitéFR: Aspects sociaux et développementaux de la santé de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Persistent Postconcussive Symptoms in Children: A Clinical Prediction Rule Derivation Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PREDICTION RULE; CONCUSSION; EMERGENCY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; PEDIATRIC; PERSISTENT POSTCONCUSSIVE SYMPTOMS; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Concussion, a mild traumatic injury common in children and adolescents, is a complex pathophysiological process affecting the brain. The lay press is inundated with reports of tragic consequences of concussion, and children are not immune. Persistent postconcussive symptoms (PCS) is defined as the persistence of somatic, cognitive, physical, psychological or behavioural changes lasting more than one month following injury. PCS significantly impacts children and their family's quality of life through school absenteeism, depressed mood and loss of activities.  Validated, easy-to-use prognosticators do not exist for clinicians to identify children at highest risk for PCS. As a result, physicians cannot accurately inform children and parents whether they should expect longer symptoms, nor initiate pharmacotherapy or other management to reduce the occurrence or severity of PCS.  Our objective is to derive and validate a clinical prediction rule for the development of PCS in children and adolescents presenting to the emergency department (ED) following acute head injury. We have three aims: (1) determine PCS incidence at one-month follow-up in children aged 5-17 who sustain a concussion; (2) derive a rule to predict PCS from variables present in the history and physical examination; and, (3) assess the accuracy, reliability and acceptability of the prediction rule in a subsequent cohort. Using a prospective, multicentre study at eight large Canadian pediatric EDs, we will recruit the largest prospective epidemiological cohort of children with concussions in the literature.  This work will provide rigorous evidence to determine PCS incidence in children and its impact on quality of life. Our results will enable clinicians to identify children at highest risk for PCS, optimize treatment and provide families with realistic anticipatory guidance. This study will also establish a strong and vital evidence base to advance concussion research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms of islet amyloid mediated beta cell death
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRAL TRANSDUCTION; ANIMAL STUDIES; BETA CELL APOPTOSIS; BETA CELL FUNCTION; CELL CULTURE; HISTOLOGY; INSULIN; ISLET AMYLOID; ISLET TRANSPLANTATION; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is characterized by progressive dysfunction and death of insulin producing beta cells in the pancreas which results in elevated blood glucose levels. Patients with T2D require life-long oral treatment to control their blood glucose and eventually most of them will require insulin therapy. Islet amyloid deposits are protein aggregates formed by a small protein named islet amyloid polypeptide that is produced in the pancreatic beta cells. Amyloid deposits are toxic to beta cells and contribute to progressive beta cell death in patients with T2D.   In patients with type 1 diabetes (T1D), beta cells are destroyed by the immune system leading to insulin deficiency and increased blood glucose levels. Patients with T1D require life-long insulin therapy or replacement of beta cells with human islet transplantation. Importantly, toxic amyloid deposits also form in islets transplanted into patients with T1D which is associated with beta-cell death and may eventually lead to islet graft failure.   In these studies, we will use pancreatic islets (cluster of cells containing beta cells) from mice and cadaveric human pancreatic donors as well as mouse models of islet amyloid formation, to investigate the molecular mechanisms by which amyloid formation destroys beta cells. We will use various molecular techniques to identify the cellular proteins that contribute to amyloid-induced beta-cell death and the cellular regulators of these cell death pathways. Through these studies we hope to find new therapeutic approaches to preserve insulin producing beta cells in patients with T2D and prolong survival of islet grafts in patients with T1D and thereby improve the lives of diabetic patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hypoxia in micrometastases as a cause of treatment failure in the adjuvant setting
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUVANT CHEMOTHERAPY; HYPOXIA; METASTASIS; PANCREATIC CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Chemotherapy has its greatest impact on cancer survival statistics when it is given immediately post-operatively, rather than when used to treat advanced disease. It does this because many patients undergoing curative-intent surgery harbour microscopic regions of cancer spread that eventually become manifest as disease recurrence, but can be eliminated by postoperative chemotherapy.  With advanced cancer, even when chemotherapy is initially successful it is not capable of eliminating every cancer cell.  Even though adjuvant chemotherapy saves thousands of Canadian lives per year, very little research has been done into the reasons for treatment failure.  Recently we found that small liver metastases developing in mice carrying tumours derived from pancreatic cancer patients contain regions of low oxygen content (hypoxia). Hypoxia is known to cause resistance to standard chemotherapy drugs, used to treat pancreas cancer patients postoperatively, but it also sensitizes cells to a new class of drug designed to become active under low oxygen conditions.  The purpose of this research is to test if the combination of standard and hypoxia-activated drugs can prevent the growth of small liver metastases derived from pancreatic cancers. If successful, this approach can be readily applied in the clinic.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting outcome in Parkinson's disease cognitive impairment
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; PARKINSON'S DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Impairment in thinking and memory frequently accompanies Parkinson's disease (PD) and becomes more severe as the disease progresses.  The impairment can be mild, not interfering significantly with social or occupational functioning (PD-Mild Cognitive Impairment) or can be more severe - PD-dementia.  Little is known about the frequency of worsening to dementia, what determines whether or not mild cognitive impairment worsens to dementia or if we can predict when and if this will occur.  In a group of 139 patients with PD without dementia at baseline we propose to follow them for the development of dementia and to identify clinical, demographic and genetic factors that are associated with worsening cognitive abilities and progression to dementia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of delaying age of onset of binge drinking on adolescent brain development: A proposal to add neuroimaing measures to the CO-Venture Trial.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; ADOLESCENTS; ALCOHOL AND DRUG MISUSE; NEURODEVELOPMENT; NEUROTOXICITY; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: The CoVenture Trial is a CIHR-funded cluster-randomised trial that will investigate the effects of a selective youth alcohol prevention programme on long-term substance use, mental health and cognitive outcomes, which in turn, might be implicated in longer-term risk for addiction. The current proposal aims to add neuroimaging measures to this on-going trial to investigate the brain mechanisms underlying the cognitive and behavioural effects of adolescent alcohol exposure and its prevention. A subset of trial participants at highest (N=120) and lowest (N=30) risk of taking up binge drinking will be recruited to undergo three neuroimaging assessments before, two years and four years after random assignment to intervention or control conditions. The intervention condition will consist of an evidence-based alcohol prevention programme, which has been shown to delay onset of binge drinking and reduce quantity of alcohol consumption by 50% in three previous randomised trials. Sensitive, non-invasive structural and functional magnetic resonance neuroimaging (MRI) strategies will be used in an integrated fashion to examine the impact of harmful alcohol intake on measures of brain structure and function during adolescence. In particular, functional MRI paradigms will be employed which specifically target reinforcement-related and inhibitory control processes, as well as addressing more general cognitive functioning.The present study exploits a rare opportunity to investigate, prospectively, the effects of alcohol exposure and early prevention on adolescent brain development. The expected results could identify biological risk markers for addictions, provide a better understanding of the complex pathway from early drinking to problem drinking, and guide public policy on one of the costliest health problems in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: La and La-related protein function in RNA metabolism and human disease
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE EXPRESSION; HOST-VIRAL INTERACTIONS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; MRNA TRANSLATION; RNA CHAPERONES; RNA PROCESSING; RNA PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; RNA STRUCTURE AND FOLDING; YEAST GENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: The normal function of human proteins is to support the healthy growth of cells. Importantly, certain proteins can also play important roles in the infectious cycles of human pathogens and the development of cancer through abnormal participation in other processes. One such family of proteins includes the La protein and La-related proteins. La proteins normally play critical roles in the processing of cellular RNAs that are required for normal gene expression, in part by ensuring that these RNAs fold into the correct form required for their function. However, a large body of evidence also indicates that many human viruses, including hepatitis C, hepatitis B and HIV, depend on La function for productive viral infections. Notably, abnormal La activity has been observed in the livers of human patients infected with hepatitis C. Furthermore, abnormal La function has also been implicated in the irregular expression of important genes in leukemia and cervical cancer. While we have an increasingly strong understanding of the role La proteins plays in RNA processing in normal cells, knowledge of the mechanisms by which La proteins abnormally contribute to human disease states is severely lacking. This proposal aims to target this knowledge gap. Major research questions that we hope to address include: how do La proteins bind and recognize different types of RNA targets (i.e. its normal, cellular RNAs vs. viral RNAs)? What specific function of La proteins is required in their abnormal associations with disease related RNAs? Finally, how do the more recently discovered La-related proteins, which have also been implicated in viral pathogenesis and cancer, fit into this picture? By enhancing our understanding of the contribution of this family to these disease states, the work outlined in this proposal aims to identify new targets for therapeutic intervention for a number of challenges to human health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gifting Life: Exploring Donor Family Members' Embodied Responses to Anonymous Organ Donation in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ANONYMITY; DONOR FAMILIES; GIFT OF LIFE; HEART TRANSPLANT; INTERDISCIPLINARY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; VISUAL METHODOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada every three days someone dies waiting for a transplant. Our previous research found that many heart transplant recipients have feelings of distress. They find writing an anonymous thank you letter to the donor family very difficult and distressing. It is hard for them to write without talking about details about themselves. Patients want to know about the person whose gift they have received. They want to connect in some way with the donor family. However, the law in Canada does not allow donor families and transplant patients to know each others' identity.   The purpose of this study is to explore how heart donor family members feel and think about organ donation, the gift of life and not knowing the organ recipient. We believe this information will help us understand why families donate and may improve organ donation. It may impact current clinical practice and the policy of anonymity. The philosopher Merleau Ponty teaches us about how we experience life. He says that human experience is always under construction and in a state of becoming. Mauss helps us to understand what it is to give and receive a gift. This will help us understand how organ donor family members understand the gift of life and the need for anonymity. Using audiovisual taped interviews allows us to capture both body and verbal expressions. Participants will be members of the organ donor's family, over 18 years of age and able to speak English. They will give informed consent. Trained researchers will do interviews that will be audio videotaped and analyzed by the research team.  This type of research offers insights that typical questionnaires do not address. Our research with heart transplant patients using these methods has been extremely productive. It is changing clinical practice. The current question is critically important to allow us to better understand how donor family members feel about anonymous organ donation and the gift of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of disrupted-in-schizophrenia-1 in the regulation of dopamine D2 receptor signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; D2 RECEPTOR SIGNALLING; DISRUPTED-IN-SCHIZOPHRENIA-1; DOPAMINE RECEPTOR; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; RECEPTOR INTERNALIZATION; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a severe, chronic, and debilitating mental disorder. It affects 1 of every 100 Canadians.  The disease impacts a vast array of brain systems, seriously affecting a person's thoughts, feelings, and ability to function. Researchers have worked for decades to understand the biological pathways involved in schizophrenia and identify the root causes of the disorder. Over time, research provided evidence supporting the "dopamine D2 receptor hypothesis." This theory contends that there is an association between an impaired striatal dopaminergic neurotransmission and schizophrenia. In support of this theory, many studies found a positive correlation between the D2 binding affinity and effectiveness of anti-psychotic drugs. Additionally, mutation in a gene, called Disrupted-in-schizophrenia-1 (DISC1), recently emerged as a potential key. This genetic mutation appears to increase risk of schizophrenia. However, the specific biological mechanisms that increase risk are not understood. Detailed investigation of these biological mechanisms is an important priority.  By investigating the role of DISC1 in the regulation of D2 receptor signaling, the project will:  1. Reveal molecular mechanisms underlying which DISC1 may modulate D2 receptor-mediated functions.  2. Provide a molecular framework in which to view DISC1 and D2 receptor interaction. 3. Provide a potential therapeutic target for the development of novel antipsychotics. Abnormalities in the communication between these two proteins may underlie psychiatric diseases such as schizophrenia. This project aims to provide a new avenue to identify specific targets for therapeutics to modulate dopamine deficit diseases and thereby improve health outcomes for Canadians suffering from schizophrenia as well as other conditions which involve this biological mechanism.

TitreApplicationTitle: The ectodermal basis of early limb bud morphogenesis and malformation
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL INTERCALATION; CONGENITAL LIMB DEFICIENCY; ECTODERM; FGF; LIMB INITIATION; MORPHOGENESIS; MULTICELLULAR ROSETTE; P63; PLANAR CELL POLARITY; WNT
Abstract-Résumé: Limb deficiencies are among the most common and disabling of all birth defects.  Several known mutations that cause human limb birth defects exert their harmful affects upon the development of the outer (ectodermal) layer of cells that wrap around the early embryonic limb bud.  While the identity of some of the genes that cause these birth defects is known, their mechanisms of action are not known.  In our laboratory, we pioneered methods that permit us to visualise the live development of cells within the embryonic mouse limb.  Our experiments show that dynamic cell rearrangements in the outer ectodermal layer helps to shape the early limb bud and allows it grow outward from the body wall.  We propose that mutations which cause limb birth defects do so by disrupting the coordination of dynamic cell behaviours in the ectodermal layer.  To test this idea, we will generate mutations in mice in the same genes that cause human limb birth defects.  We will then specifically study the outer ectodermal layer of cells in living mouse embryos to assess their behaviour.  We expect to find that cells in the ectoderm will not be coordinated to grow outward properly, and this lack of coordination will cause limbs to be misshapen, short or absent altogether.  Understanding how the limb develops properly is an important step to designing further experiments intended to regenerate new limb tissues for therapeutic purposes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing an innovative, evidence-based decision support tool to improve osteoarthritis care planning and health service management for diverse patient population Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINALS; ARTHROPLASTY; GEOGRAPHY; HEALTH SERVICE DELIVERY; HIP AND KNEE; MODELLING; OSTEOARTHRITIS; RURAL; SYSTEM DYNAMICS MODELLING; WAIT TIMES
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic condition affecting more than 10% of Canadian adults and costing a total of $27.5 billion annually in terms of medical bills, missed work, and lost wages. The burden of this condition is anticipated to escalate in the future as more people are expected to develop OA. Hence, Canadian health policy makers need to make appropriate decisions about how to align costly health care resources to improve population health and manage this condition. However, such decision making is difficult as we lack knowledge of how these decisions translate into intended and unintended consequences, yet long-term planning is required to effectively address the needs of future patients. To assist with this, we propose to develop a decision support tool designed to equip policy makers with the information needed to make evidence-based decisions relating to the OA care system. Our overall objective is to develop a quantitative system tool that policy makers can use to inform strategic OA resource management and planning decisions among diverse populations as they seek to improve system performance and patient outcomes while controlling costs. The tool, based on a simulation technique called system dynamics, will reveal the effects alternative policies may have on the performance of the health system, resource requirements, costs, and patient outcomes in both the short- and long-terms. Based on our expert team knowledge, experience, and preliminary research, we propose to develop a tool that will be flexible and comprehensive, taking into account patient demographics, geographical variations, comorbidities, and patient health outcomes. Currently there is a dearth of such tools that enable system-wide analysis, resulting in resources often being used inefficiently. Hence, a key benefit of this tool is that it will allow health services planners to test the effects of new policies prior to their implementation and before major investments of time and resources.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering the Role of UBR1 E3 Ubiquitin Ligase using a C. elegans Model
Keywords-MotsClés: C. ELEGANS; CONGENITAL DISORDER; E3 UBIQUITN LIGASE; GABAERGIC SYNAPSE; MENTAL RETARDATION; NERVOUS SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT; SELECTIVE PROTEIN DEGRADATION; UBR-1
Abstract-Résumé: In humans, mutations in a gene UBR1 lead to the Johanson-Blizzard Syndrome, a congenital disorder with hallmark features in mental retardation and pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. UBR1 encodes an enzyme that targets other proteins for degradation. In the absense of UBR1 these substrates become hyperactivated and cause the clinical features in those patients. However, substrates of UBR1 remain completely unknown. Using the C. elgans model we recently found a critical requirement of UBR1 at synaptic transmission, and putative UBR1 targets that can augment the nervous system defect associated with UBR1. Our proposed study will shed light on the pathological cause of, as well as help define targets for treatments for the Johanson-Blizzard syndrome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Asthma medications during pregnancy and the mother's health
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATABASES; ASTHMA; ASTHMA MEDICATIONS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; MATERNAL OUTCOMES; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; PREGNANCY
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is an increasingly common serious medical condition during pregnancy.  According to current practice, it is safer for pregnant women with asthma to be treated with asthma medications than it is for them to have asthma symptoms and exacerbations, which is uncontrolled asthma. However, we do not know with certainty whether or not asthma medications used during pregnancy to prevent asthma manifestations, namely inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) and long-acting beta-agonists (LABA), can have negative effects on the mother, such as hypertension and diabetes during pregnancy. We will undertake a large study within the province of Quebec to address these issues. Our study will determine: i) the risk of developing diabetes during pregnancy among asthmatic women using ICS compared to those not using them; ii) the risk of developing diabetes during pregnancy and hypertension during pregnancy among asthmatic women using LABA in addition to ICS compared to those using ICS but no LABA. Knowing whether or not specific medications used to treat asthma increase the risk of pregnancy related diseases is absolutely necessary to help women and clinicians to accurately estimate the benefit/risk ratio of treatment alternatives, choose the best treatment for each woman, and do their best to avoid adverse maternal outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preventing memory loss after general anesthesia by inhibiting alpha 5 GABAA receptors
Keywords-MotsClés: ANESTHESIA; BEHAVIORAL ASSAYS; COGNITIVE DYSFUNCTION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GABA; HIPPOCAMPUS; LEARNING; LONG-TERM POTENTIATION; MEMORY; NEUROTOXICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Over 234 million patients undergo general anesthesia each year. A major adverse effect of most general anesthetics is memory loss, which may persist for days to months. Such memory loss is associated with prolonged hospitalization, increased costs, loss of independence and even increased mortality, yet no treatments are available. Our exciting preliminary results suggest the first safe, plausible and effective strategy to prevent post-anesthetic memory loss. We have also identified a potential underlying molecular mechanism. Specifically, we previously identified a receptor in the brain that, when activated, causes memory deficits. We have now discovered that when anesthetics activate these receptors, they unexpectedly trigger a long-lasting increase in the number of these receptors, which persists long after the drugs are eliminated. Pretreatment with a drug that interferes with the initial anesthetic activation of the receptors prevents long-term memory loss. We anticipate that our results will be rapidly translated into new therapies to prevent memory loss after general anesthesia and possibly other related memory disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of cellular Inhibitors of Apoptosis (cIAPs) in muscle biology and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: INHIBITORS OF APOPTOSIS (IAPS); MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; NUCLEAR FACTOR-KAPPA B (NF-KB); SKELETAL MUSCLE ATROPHY; SKELETAL MUSCLE REGENERATION; TUMOR NECROSIS FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The Nuclear Factor kappaB (NF-kappaB) signaling pathway is a complex signaling module that is critical for normal skeletal muscle function, such as promoting recovery in response to muscle injury.  However, there is strong evidence that NF-kappaB signaling is also involved in the pathology associated with various muscle diseases, such as Duchenne's muscular dystrophy (DMD), inflammatory myopathies, and skeletal muscle atrophy.  As such, NF-kappaB has become an attractive drug target for the treatment of muscle disease.  We have recently found that the cellular inhibitors of apoptosis, cIAP1 and cIAP2 (genes cloned in our laboratory and shown to be involved in the regulation of cell death) are required for various aspects of NF-kappaB signaling in skeletal muscle.  This discovery has raised the exciting possibility that cIAP1/2 may be a potential therapeutic targets for various muscle diseases that rely on NF-kappaB signaling.  We propose to elucidate the role and mechanism of action cIAP1/2 in NF-kappaB signaling in skeletal muscle, and evaluate its contribution to the pathology of muscular dystrophy and skeletal muscle atrophy.  Moreover, as we have in hand several drugs and reagents that potently and specifically target both cIAP1 and cIAP2 for destruction, we will evaluate the therapeutic potential of these reagents in the treatment of muscle disease.

ClasseRechercheFR: STERILITE DE L'HOMME; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Tudor domain proteins in normal development and cancer.
Keywords-MotsClés: GERM LINE DEVELOPMENT; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MOUSE MUTAGENESIS; PIWI-PIRNA PATHWAY; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATIONS; PROTEIN KINASE; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; TUDOR DOMAINS
Abstract-Résumé: Disruptions in genome integrity during gametogenesis are leading causes of infertility and birth defects in humans. One major factor that causes germline genome instability is a family of transposable elements (TE), parasitic DNA elements that move around the genome by insertion mutations. To tame TE activity, germ cells use an evolutionarily conserved small RNA based cellular machinery, the Piwi-piRNA pathway, to suppress transposon invasion. Tudor proteins, a group of proteins that contain a protein-binding module termed the Tudor domain, have recently emerged as essential regulators of the Piwi-piRNA pathway. They organize and stabilize the Piwi-piRNA silencing complex by directly interacting with Piwi proteins. Tudor-Piwi interactions are crucial for the organization of the Piwi-piRNA pathway, as mutations of Tudor genes in mice cause TE activation, disruption of spermatogenesis and male infertility.  Given the importance of Tudor proteins as fertility factors, in this proposal, we seek to systematically investigate the biochemical basis and functional significance of Tudor domain directed protein-protein interactions in Piwi-piRNA pathway, providing a potential for targeting Tudor domains as therapeutics. Our work will particularly focus on a Tudor domain-containing protein kinase, STK31, a potential drug target for male contraception and cancer. Completion of this project will shed light on the functional significance of protein-protein interactions in organizing cellular machineries and the genetic causes of male infertility in humans.
