TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of response and resistance to epigenetic therapy in hematological malignancy
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; DIFFUSE LARGE B CELL LYMPHOMA; EPIGENETIC DRUGS; ER STRESS; EZH2; GENE REPRESSION; HEMATOLOGICAL MALIGNANCY; HISTONE DEACETYLASE INHIBTORS; UNFOLDED PROTEIN RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: In addition to the many differences in the genetic code that may determine health and disease, cells may modify the action of our genes by what are called epigenetic mechanisms.  Epigenetic markers on our genetic material are important in normal heredity and development, but have also been shown to be critical factors in the growth of many cancers.  An important new strategy for anti-cancer therapy uses drugs that target epigenetic changes, with drugs called histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) and DNA methyltransferase inhibitors (DNMTi), leading the way in the clinic.   To date, HDACi have been approved for treatment of a rare skin lymphoma and have shown clinical activity in some patients with a range of different hematologic (blood) cancers, although even responsive malignancies almost inevitably develop resistance to these new drugs. The overall goal of our research is to understand why a small percentage of patients with various hematological malignancies show dramatic clinical response to therapy with epigenetic drugs, while most do not respond.  To address this question, we propose to study cells derived from patients with hematologic cancer that respond to HDACi and derive resistant cells.  By comparing the molecular features of these sensitive and resistant cells, we hope to understand both how patients who initially respond become resistant to therapy with HDACi, as well as why some patients are resistant initially.  Based on our preliminary data, we will study specific intracellular pathways associated with the development of resistance, and the possibility that other new drugs, such as DNMTi, that block these pathways could prevent or reverse the development of resistance to HDACi.  We will confirm results in cell lines by studying malignant cells taken directly from patients with lymphoma or leukemia, with the long term goal to develop improved epigenetic therapy in the clinic.

OrgNm: CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Jewish General/CIUSSS de Centre-Ouest-de-l'Ile-de-Montréal-Hôpital juif
TitreApplicationTitle: Chelation, Mobilization and Metabolism of Storage Iron
Keywords-MotsClés: ANEMIA OF CHRONIC DISEASE; CHELATION; HEMOGLOBIN RECYCLING; IRON METABOLISM; MACROPHAGES
Abstract-Résumé: Iron is a precious metal for the organism because of its unsurpassed versatility as a biological catalyst. However, when in excess, iron can damage the body. Because of the limited ability of the body to excrete this metal, iron overload can develop as a result of continuously elevated absorption of dietary iron or administration of excess iron via blood transfusion. Patients with iron-loading refractory anemias (i.e., thalassemias), who require regular transfusions, will die unless they are treated with drugs that can eliminate iron from the body by iron chelating agents (chelators). One of the goals of our research is to develop effective iron chelators and new strategies to treat patients with iron overload. We have developed the pyridoxalisonicotinoyl hydrazine (PIH) and showed thet PIH and its analogs highly efficiently remove iron from the body. We designed structures of novel PIH analogs that should be much more effective than PIH in eliminating iron in excess. We shall continue in these studies and characterize the novel chelators both chemically and biologically. Importantly, we shall also investigate how iron is released from iron-storing cells, since understanding of this is crucial for design of new and efficient strategies for management of iron overload.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of oxidized phospholipids in the pathogenicity of lipoprotein(a)
Keywords-MotsClés: APOLIPOPROTEIN(A); ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CELL SIGNALING; GENE EXPRESSION; INFLAMMATION; LIPOPROTEIN(A); MACROPHAGES; MONOCYTES; OXIDIZED PHOSPHOLIPIDS; VASCULAR ENDOTHELIAL CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) is a fat/protein complex that circulates in blood. High concentrations of Lp(a) in the blood place individuals at a higher risk of having a heart attack or stroke. Lp(a) consists of a lipoprotein particle identical to low density lipoprotein (LDL) as well as an additional protein called apolipoprotein(a) (apo(a)). It is apo(a) that is thought to be responsible for the unique effects of Lp(a) in the body. Lp(a) can promote a process called atherosclerosis, which involves deposition of fatty material and overactive inflammation in the artery wall and which is ultimately the cause of the blood clots that form in arteries to cause heart attacks and strokes. We believe that a particular modification of apo(a), with compounds called oxidized phospholipids, underlies many of the harmful effects on apo(a), especially on cells of the arterial wall. We propose to identify the location of this modification, and make mutant forms of apo(a) to which this modification cannot be attached. We can then compare the effects of the normal (modified) and mutant (unmodified) forms of apo(a) on atherosclerosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: New insights into mast cell development and contribution to malignant progression - further exploitation of the zebrafish model
Keywords-MotsClés: ENU SCREEN; MAST CELLS; MTOR; SYSTEMIC MASTOCYTOSIS; TRANSGENESIS; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Mast cells are blood cells involved in allergic reactions, inflammation and contribute to causing some cancers. Normal mast cell development remains unclear. We took advantage of the transparent zebrafish to study normal mast cell development and model a human mast cell disease called systemic mastocytosis. This disease can be a mild skin rash or evolve into an aggressive leukemia that is currently uncurable. We will use this zebrafish model to find molecular pathways that are activated in this disease and test new treatments. Mast cells may also cause the spread of other cancers due to their involvement in the inflammatory response to cancers.  We will make a zebrafish that has fluorescently labeled mast cells and use these fish to study the interaction of mast cells with human tumour cells that we can transplant into the fish. Finally, using our model of systemic mastocytosis, we will complete a genetic screen, which can be done efficiently in zebrafish, to find genes that contribute to causing the more aggressive types of systemic mastocytosis. These experiments will be aided by using the fish with fluorescent mast cells. This work will provide important new information about how abnormal mast cells evolve into leukemia and participate in the progression of other cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardioprotection through a reduction in cardiac CapZ
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN CAPPING PROTEIN (CAPZ); HEART FAILURE; ISCHEMIA-REPERFUSION; MYOCARDIUM; MYOFILAMENTS; PROTEIN KINASE C (PKC); Z-DISCS
Abstract-Résumé: In heart failure, cardiac muscle contraction is negatively altered by a family of molecules called "Protein Kinase C" (PKC). We found that reducing CapZ protein blocks PKC-dependent inhibition of contraction. We hypothesized that reducing CapZ protects hearts against heart failure.    Myocardial infarctions or "heart attacks" increase PKC activity in heart muscle cells. Increased PKC activity decreases heart function and damages tissue. We hypothesized that transgenic mice deficient in cardiac CapZ protein are protected against infarctions. Normal mouse hearts exhibited significant damage and dysfunction following infarction, while CapZ transgenic mice had minor tissue damage and significantly better function than mice with normal CapZ levels. We will determine if a peptide that decreases CapZ protects hearts against infarctions. We will also examine how CapZ is controlled during heart attacks, information that may be used to develop new therapies.    Coronary artery disease increases PKC activity in the heart. Chronic PKC activation drives hearts into failure by reducing contractility. We hypothesized that reduced CapZ protects against heart failure. A preliminary study found that occluding a coronary artery caused significant dysfunction in normal mice, but by comparison CapZ deficient transgenic mice performed significantly better. We propose to complete this study and examine the potentially protective ability of decreased CapZ throughout heart failure.    Reducing CapZ blocks PKC depression of heart contraction through an unknown mechanism. We have created a PKC activation model to identify how CapZ controls PKC. Preliminary studies support the feasibility of our model. We propose experiments to test our hypothesis that decreased CapZ works by blocking the ability of G-proteins to initiate PKC activation.    This proposal investigates a novel therapeutic target for heart failure and will determine how CapZ works in heart.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Therapeutic Evaluation of STeroids in IgA Nephropathy Global (TESTING) Study - Canadian Network
Keywords-MotsClés: IGA NEPHROPATHY; METHYLPREDNISOLONE; RANDOMIZED PLACEBO CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is a common cause of renal disease in Canada, especially amongst younger and otherwise healthy Canadians.  The risk of progression to dialysis or transplantation in IgAN is significant, approximately 35% after 10 years, highlighting the need to identify treatments capable of reducing this risk.  Several small, inconclusive studies have suggested that treatment of IgAN with a short course of steroids (such as methylprednisolone) may reduce the risk of renal function decline.  A large randomized controlled trial is therefore needed to more definitively describe the benefits of steroids in IgAN.  We propose to create a Canadian network to recruit patients with IgAN to study the effect of steroid vs. placebo on progression of kidney disease. This study will utilize the infrastructure of a larger multi-centre study to develop a Canadian network for clinical trials and translational research in glomerular disease. All patients will receive the currently established standard of care for patients with IgAN, namely aggressive blood pressure control with medications that also reduce protein in the urine.  We will follow patients for 6 years for the risk of progression to dialysis, kidney transplantation, a 50% reduction in renal function, or death due to kidney disease.  We anticipate that patients treated with methylprednisolone will experience these renal outcomes 30% less often than those given placebo.  This will be a large international trial recruiting 1300 patients from Canada, China, India, Australia and the United Kingdom and will be the largest ever conducted in patients with IgAN.  This funding application is to support the recruitment of patients from Canadian centres.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regional and temporal variations in incidence, prevalence and outcomes of critical illness among pregnant and post-partum women and newborns in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; CLINICAL OUTCOME; FETUS; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; INTENSIVE CARE UNIT; NEONATE; POSTPARTUM; PREGNANCY; PROGNOSTIC MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: There are no national studies of pregnancy-related critical illness and death in Canada. Although the maternal mortality rate has decreased in Canada over the past three decades, it remains at 6-7 per 100,000 live births. Maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality is a critically important health outcome for individuals and the population. Continued improvement of pregnancy-related outcomes for mothers and babies is identified by the World Health Organization as a key marker of success of any healthcare system.   Over the past two decades, there has been a recent trend towards increasing maternal age in many developed countries. Maternal age is associated with increased pregnancy-related morbidity and may lead to greater morbidity and mortality for Canadian mothers and their babies.   Further, since healthcare in Canada is administered provincially and territorially, geographical diversity can lead to different healthcare service densities in Canada. This diversity may also result in different access to care and clinical outcomes for severely ill pregnant patients and their babies. We will perform the first national study aiming to evaluate geographic and temporal differences in maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality, which may allow identification of areas for improvement in services and therefore reduction in maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of the Cdc34 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme in cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DIVISION; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; E2 CONJUGATING ENZYME; E3 UBIQUITIN LIGASE; HUMAN CELL LINE; MOUSE GENETIC MODEL; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; PROTEIN INTERACTION; SMALL MOLECULE; UBIQUITIN PROTEASOME SYSTEM
Abstract-Résumé: Ubiquitin is a small protein that is used to tag many important regulatory factors in the cell for destruction or other regulatory fates. Ubiquitin is attached to many thousands of target proteins through the precisely controlled action of a complex enzymatic cascade. These attachment processes are essential for all aspects of normal cellular function. Recently, it has become apparent that the ubiquitin system is misregulated in most if not all human cancers. First generation drugs directed against the ubiquitin system have demonstrated enormous potential in cancer therapy. In this proposal, we will investigate the role of specific enzymes that catalyze ubiquitin attachment in important cellular processes implicated in cancer formation, and develop new potential therapeutic lead compounds that specifically rectify aberrations of the ubiquitin system in cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical, molecular and pathophysiological characterization of Pol III-related leukodystrophies
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL CHARACTERIZATION; EXOME SEQUENCING; HYPOMYELINATION; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MOUSE MODEL; PATHOPHYSIOLOGICAL MECHANISMS; POL III-RELATED LEUKODYSTROPHIES; POLYMERASE III; RNA EXPRESSION ARRAY
Abstract-Résumé: Leukodystrophies are a group of degenerative diseases characterized by involvement of the white matter (myelin) of the brain. They are divided into demyelinating (i.e. myelin destruction) and hypomyelinating (i.e. lack of myelin formation) based on their magnetic resonance imaging features. Our group identified recessive mutations in POLR3A and POLR3B as the cause for three different hypomyelinating leukodystrophies. Two other groups identified mutations in these genes in two other leukodystrophies. These new diseases are now known as Pol III-related leukodystrophies. Since these five disorders have only been recently described, there is still much to learn about them. Some patients with a compatible clinical presentation do not have mutation in either gene, suggesting that other gene(s) are mutated. POLR3A and POLR3B encode for two of the 17-subunits of the polymerase III, which is responsible for transcription of DNA into RNA. In particular, Pol III is responsible for the transcription of a very specific subset of small RNAs. Previous experiments suggest that mutations in POLR3A and POLR3B lead to misassembly of Pol III and to a reduced production of specific small RNAs. This research proposal aims at: (1) Completing the clinical, radiological and genetic characterization of these diseases, (2) Studying the impacts of POLR3A and POLR3B mutations on Pol III structure and its major interactors, (3) Characterizing the impact of mutations on Pol III RNA transcription and, (4) Characterizing a Polr3a transgenic mouse. The proposed project will lead to a better understanding of the neurodegenerative Pol III-related leukodystrophies clinically, genetically and pathophysiologically. It will lead to earlier diagnostic, better genetic counselling and medical care for these patients, but also to better understanding of the process of normal myelination, the pathophysiology of hypomyelination which will allow the identification of potential treatments.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - C : Systèmes digestif, endocrinien et excrétoire
TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of novel proteins as diagnostic or mechanistic targets for renal allograft inflammation.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY-BASED PROTEIN PROFILING; ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; CATABOLOMICS; INTERSTITIAL FIBROSIS/TUBULAR ATROPHY & INFLAMMATION; ISCHEMIA REPERFUSION INJURY; PROTEOMICS; RENAL TRANSPLANTATION; SELECTED REACTION MONITORING MASS SPECTROMETRY; SUBCLINICAL AND CLINICAL REJECTION; URINE BIOMARKER
Abstract-Résumé: Kidney transplant rejection can only be diagnosed by transplant biopsy, which is costly, inconvenient, and carries a small risk of complications. Therefore, biopsies cannot be obtained frequently to monitor the health of the transplant. This monitoring is important since rejection (or inflammation) of the transplant can happen and is not always detectable with standard blood tests. New urine tests may benefit transplant patients by detecting complications in their kidney, such as different types of inflammation, early enough to intervene and could avoid invasive biopsies.  The study of proteins and how they interact is referred to as "proteomics". Recent developments in proteomic methods make it possible to rapidly screen for proteins in the urine that may be diagnostic of transplant rejection. This proposal will use proteomics to study how transplant rejection happens and test different proteins for their ability to detect rejection. Ultimately the goal is to develop a point-of-care non-invasive monitoring test for the rapid diagnosis of rejection. This may lead to the prevention or early treatment of kidney rejection/inflammation and improve patient care and kidney transplant survival.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sucrose Practices for Pain in Neonates (SPiN); A Program of Research
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTEXT; DEVELOPMENT; EFFECTIVENESS; NEONATES; OUTCOMES; PAIN; SUCROSE
Abstract-Résumé: Recent studies show that babies in hospital undergo an average of 4 to 5 painful procedures, such as heel lances, every day. Sucrose (sugar water) has been shown to be effective for reducing babies' pain during painful procedures. Unfortunately, sucrose is not used as often as it could be to reduce babies' pain. This may be due to lack of certainty about the least effective amount of sucrose to use and concerns about the long-term effects of repeated use of sucrose on infant development. Factors within the hospital units where babies receive care may also influence caregivers' decisions to use sucrose. In this research we will conduct two main studies. In the first study we will determine the lowest amount of sucrose needed to manage babies' pain effectively. In the second study we will explore (a) if this amount of sucrose can manage pain when it is used repeatedly for all painful procedures while the baby is hospitalized and (b) whether consistent use of sucrose influences the development of babies when they are 18 months old. During the second study, we will also examine the hospital units where the babies receive care. We will look at staff support for research, time and resources and other factors that promote and prevent sucrose use. The results of these studies will be used to determine the best management of babies' pain during painful procedures in hospitals to achieve the best outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting the need for community care for chronic kidney disease following hospitalization with acute kidney injury
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; END-STAGE RENAL DISEASE; RISK INDEX; RISK PREDICTION MODELS; RISK SCORE
Abstract-Résumé: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common problem characterized by a sudden reduction in kidney function typically due to medical or surgical complications that occur in hospital. AKI has important long-term consequences since people with AKI are at high risk of chronic kidney problems including kidney failure requiring dialysis. New guidelines recognize the importance of follow-up for these conditions after hospital discharge; however little is currently known about how to separate people who will have stable kidney function following AKI from others who will develop progressive kidney diseases. This highlights the need for a practical tool to identify survivors of AKI at risk for progressive chronic kidney disease after hospital discharge. We propose a new study using data from Alberta and Ontario to develop and evaluate such a tool.  This new tool will identify high risk individuals that will require more intensive follow-up in the community, and low risk people who can safely receive routine follow-up. Given the high morbidity and costs associated with kidney failure, and existing care gaps for chronic kidney disease management in survivors of AKI, this approach is needed to identify high risk patients for intense follow-up and to improve outcomes.  This work will promote efficient use of resources and will facilitate future studies that assess the impact of new interventions designed to improve the health of people after AKI.

TitreApplicationTitle: MR-Guided Revascularization of Occlusive Peripheral Arterial Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC TOTAL OCCLUSIONS; ENDOVASCULAR TREATMENT; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; PERIPHERAL VASCULAR DISEASE
Abstract-Résumé: Occlusive peripheral arterial disease occurs when blockages in blood vessels limit the blood supply to the leg.  This disease is widespread and represents a major societal burden.  Approximately 20% of those over the age of 59 years suffer from this disease, which results in over 160,000 limb amputations being performed per year in the US alone.  Our goal over the next 5 years is to extend the role of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to increase the number of patients who can have this disease treated using minimally invasive percutaneous techniques using catheters and wires advanced through blood vessels.   X-ray fluoroscopy, the imaging modality that is currently used to guide percutaneous procedures, has relatively poor soft-tissue contrast.  This makes it difficult to visualize blockages and to ensure that a revascularization device stays within the vessel during the procedure.  This limits success rates and restricts minimally invasive treatment to short blockages in large arteries (which occur much less frequently than long occlusions further down the leg).  Other treatment options include bypass surgery, which has substantial associated risk, and medical therapy, which has been shown to have limited effectiveness.  MRI, unlike x-ray, has excellent soft-tissue contrast and with MRI it is possible to develop a detailed picture of blocked vessels that can greatly aid in guiding revascularization procedures.  Through a program of technical developments we plan to advance methods and devices which will enable the MR-guided revascularization of blocked blood vessels.  We anticipate this will facilitate less invasive treatment in a significant population that would ordinarily be subjected to more invasive surgery or to less effective treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of tumourigenesis and tumour cell metabolism by the energy sensor AMPK
Keywords-MotsClés: AMP-ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASE (AMPK); APOPTOSIS; CANCER BIOLOGY; CELLULAR METABOLISM; LYMPHOMA; METFORMIN; PEUTZ-JEGHERS SYNDROME; TUMOUR METABOLISM; TUMOUR SUPPRESSORS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is essentially a disease in which cells lose their normal restraints on cell division. However, the ability of a cell to successfully grow and divide depends significantly on the cell having enough energy and building blocks to complete the task. Fundamentally all cells need energy to survive. Interestingly, cancer cells commonly display changes in how they generate energy, and often use metabolic pathways that are distinct from normal cells. Understanding how cancer cells generate energy may provide new ways to specifically target cancer cells while leaving normal cells untouched. We have found a key regulator of energy metabolism in cancer cells known as the AMP-activated protein kinase, or AMPK.  We have found that AMPK acts as an energy sensor in cells, and stops cell growth when it senses changes in energy levels.  AMPK does so in part by interacting with several well-known tumour suppressors, suggesting to us that AMPK plays a key role in cancer.  This proposal aims to study the role of AMPK in cancer progression and to understand how AMPK regulates energy use in cancer cells. Ultimately we would like to determine whether AMPK is a suitable therapeutic target for the treatment of cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular Regulation of Dendritic Cell Function
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; DENDRITIC CELLS; IMFLAMMATION; IMMUNIZATION; IMMUNOLOGY; INTER-CELLULAR COMMUNICATION; METABOLISM; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system possesses the unique capacity to protect us from a broad range harmful threats including microbes, parasites and cancer. Dysfunctional immunity makes us susceptible to these threats and misdirected immune responses can cause disease and suffering through detrimental immunopathological reactions, seen in diseases such as inflammatory and autoimmune conditions. All immune responses are not created equal, and for the maintenance of health, the immune system must strike a balance between effective responses to serious threats and pathological responses. In order to achieve this balance each immune response must be tailored to the type of threat or invasion the body faces. At the heart of the immune response are dendritic cells, which possess powerful capabilities to determine the type of immune response that will develop. Dendritic cells integrate information from the environment, such as pathogen type and inflammatory mediators, and become differentially activated depending on the type of stimuli they receive. Through this differential activation, dendritic cells are able to transmit pathogen/threat-specific information to other components of the immune system.   Work described in this proposal will study novel mechanisms which regulate dendritic cell function and therefore regulate the development of specific types of immune responses. Specifically, we will study a transcriptional repressor which keeps dendritic cells in a resting state; we will study how cellular metabolism affects dendritic cell function; and we will examine the ability of Notch ligands, previously thought to instruct T cell responses, to regulate dendritic cell activation. This work will provide new insights into the creation and control of specific inflammatory microenvironments in both health and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predictors of Family Caregiver Labour Force Participation and Quality of Life Across the Home-Based Palliative Care Trajectory
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; HEALTH SERVICES; INFORMAL CAREGIVING; LABOUR ECONOMICS; PALLIATIVE CARE; PUBLICLY AND PRIVATELY FINANCED RESOURCES; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: The home palliative care environment is labour intensive and characterized by physical and emotional strain, where the caregiving demands can be enormous. With an aging population and increased emphasis on home-based care, the dependence on family members to provide care will continue to propagate. Many caregivers miss time from the labour force because of their intense caregiving responsibilities. While family caregivers assume most of the responsibility, there is a paucity of research that has comprehensively assessed this responsibility and how it affects economic and health outcomes. Understanding the predictors of labour force participation (LFP) may inform the targeting of services to those families for whom interventions to support their status may be more effective. A greater appreciation of the differences in caregiving intensity for those who participate in the labour force and those who do not as well as the factors which predict participation are necessary for practitioners, health managers, and policy decision makers to ensure that families receive efficient care. There are three main purposes to this study: 1) to identify the effect of unpaid caregiving on caregivers' LFP, across the palliative care trajectory; 2) to assess demographic, health, and caregiving factors that influence caregivers' LFP; and 3) to assess demographic and caregiving factors that influence caregivers' quality of life, over the palliative care trajectory. Caregivers will be recruited from two palliative care programs: Toronto and Niagara.  Participants will be asked to provide information on their LFP, health status, and quality of life, in biweekly interviews from admission until death. All other required data will be obtained from regional databases maintained by the palliative programs.  This study will be relevant to policy makers, interested in reconfiguring the health and labour systems to address the needs of palliative care patients and their families.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - A: Fondements neurobiologiques des processus comportementaux
TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting cognitive recovery using endogenous neural stem cell activation and rehabilitation following stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; COGNITION; DRUG DELIVERY SYSTEM; ENDOGENOUS ACTIVATION; NEURAL STEM CELLS; REHABILITATION; STROKE; TISSUE REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Stroke is the leading cause of permanent neurological disability in Canada with over 50,000 new cases annually. There are no current medical therapies for alleviating the chronic functional impairments following stroke. The identification of multipotent neural stem cells in the adult mammalian brain has spurred significant interest regarding the potential for stem cell therapy to treat neurological injury or disease.  However, activating resident stem cells in the brain has proven to be insufficient to promote repair and combinatorial strategies such as using drugs and small molecules to enhance the repair process, are required.  Similarly, rehabilitation has tremendous impact on recovery, but not enough to achieve complete repair.  In this proposal we will explore the ability of stem cell activation, rehabilitation and the combination of both strategies, to repair the injured brain following stroke.  Most important we will apply our strategies to treat cognitive impairment, which is one of the most frequent and devastating outcomes for victims of stroke.  Despite the prevalence and importance, little work has been done towards developing tools to enhance cognitive repair.  Further, nearly all stroke studies are performed in young animals in spite of the fact that the incidence of human stroke rises appreciably in middle age and neuroplasticty declines across the life span.  Herein we will explore the efficacy of our combined strategies in young, and then older animals.  We will significantly increase the clinical relevance of our studies by further engineering a novel system to deliver drugs directly to the brain to achieve stem cell activation.  Hence, in combination with rehabilitation strategies, we will achieve interventions for the treatment of stroke that can be translated to the clinic.

ClasseRechercheFR: INFACTUS DU MYOCARDE; APOPLEXIE, INSUFFISANCE CARDIAQUE
TitreApplicationTitle: Microsomal prostaglandin E2 synthase-1 in Ly6Clo monocytes regulates left ventricular remodeling after myocardial infarction.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOACTIVE LIPID MEDIATORS; CARDIAC REMODELING; COMPETITIVE ADOPTIVE TRANSFER; FLUORESCENCE MOLECULAR TOMOGRAPHY - COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; LY6CLO MONOCYTES; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MICROSOMAL PROSTAGLANDIN E2 SYNTHASE -1; MYOCARDIAC INFARCTION; SPLENIC MONOCYTE PROGENITOR CELLS; TRANSGENIC KNOCKOUT MICE
Abstract-Résumé: The most common cause of death in Canada due to heart disease is congestive heart failure (CHF), which happens when the heart is damaged (e.g. by a heart attack) and the ability of the heart to pump blood is impaired. The key to saving lives and preventing premature death and disability due to CHF lies in basic research into the causes of CHF.   Alterations in the production of prostaglandin, chemicals we all make, occur in the heart of patients who sustain a heart attack and develop CHF. Prostaglandins impact how the heart pumps and how heart cells grow. Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) is the most important prostaglandins, and is produced by an enzyme called microsomal prostaglandin E2 synthase (mPGES).   In our previous CIHR funded studies, we showed mice that lack mPGES develop worse CHF than mice with this enzyme after a heart attack, and that mice that we genetically engineered to lack mPGES in white blood cells also get worse CHF after a heart attack. In preliminary studies, we identified the white blood cell (Ly6Clo monocytes) that makes mPGES in the heart. This research proposal will focus on determining how mPGES in Ly6Clo monocytes regulates heart function after a heart attack.

NomDuComitéFR: Santé publique, santé communautaire et santé des populations
TitreApplicationTitle: Development and integration of alerting algorithms and response protocols for public health surveillance of respiratory infections
Keywords-MotsClés: ALGORITHM; OUTBREAK DETECTION; POPULATION HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH SURVEILLANCE; RESPIRATORY INFECTION; SYNDROMIC SURVEILLANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Syndromic surveillance uses data from events that occur before a clinical diagnosis of an illness, such as absences from school or visits to emergency departments (ED), for public health surveillance. Its use has been growing in popularity because of the potential to detect outbreaks and other unusual events earlier than traditional surveillance (e.g. laboratory confirmed diagnosis) and due to the increasing availability of such data electronically.  Our 2010 survey of Ontario local public health agencies (OLPHAs) showed that 50% used syndromic surveillance systems, with the 2009 influenza pandemic accelerating its growth. In Alberta, the Alberta Real Time Syndromic Surveillance Net (ARTSSN) in use since 2003, has also recently expanded throughout the province. Despite such growth, we found that syndromic data had limited influence on local decision-making during the pandemic in Ontario.  This finding raises questions of the value of syndromic surveillance systems if the data are not linked to a public health response.  The absence of protocols guiding users on how to respond to unusual events detected in syndromic data has been identified as a barrier to using these data.  As a result, we plan to test whether the development and application of tools designed to detect unusual events and guide response will improve the usefulness of syndromic surveillance systems.   The study has two phases.  First, thresholds for detecting unusual events will be developed using existing ED and school absenteeism data. Concurrently, protocols for interpreting and responding to these alerts will be created.  Second, OLPHAs and Alberta health zones with access to syndromic surveillance will be randomly assigned to use these new protocols or to use standard-practice approaches.  The effectiveness of these new protocols will be assessed by comparing the number of generated alerts and public health responses, and by user perceptions of their value.

NomDuComitéFR: Santé publique, santé communautaire et santé des populations 2
TitreApplicationTitle: Do pregnancy characteristics help to predict the future risk of maternal cardiovascular outcomes? A population-based longitudinal cohort study.
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; COHORT; DIABETES; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HYPERTENSION; PREGNANCY; RISK PREDICTION; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The Heart and Stroke Foundation's 2010 Report warned of "a perfect storm of heart disease looming on our horizon." It explained that unhealthy behaviours, obesity, high blood pressure, and diabetes are becoming so much more common in young Canadian women that heart disease will explode in the next generation. Health care providers use "risk assessment tools" to predict their patients' chances of having a heart attack or stroke - patients whose chances are high can then be offered help to improve their lifestyle or given medications, for example to control their blood pressure. Common risk assessment tools, however, need measurements such as cholesterol levels that are recommended only for older women and do not include pregnancy characteristics although previous studies have suggested they could be useful. Our aim in this study is to develop risk assessment tools that can be used in young women for cardiovascular disease (heart disease and stroke), and for two conditions that often precede its development, diabetes and hypertension (high blood pressure). The tools will be based on pregnancy information and other risk factors like body weight and smoking. We propose to use two databases in Nova Scotia for this study. The first is the Atlee Perinatal Database that contains detailed information on over 90,000 mothers and their pregnancies since 1988. The second is health care records that will be used to identify occurrences of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and hypertension in these women. The mathematical equations, which combine lifestyle and pregnancy information, that best forecast a woman's chances of developing these conditions will be determined. Our approach to achieving our aim could not be done elsewhere as time efficiently and with as high quality data. Our team includes researchers and health care providers with expertise in epidemiology, statistics, and obstetrics to ensure that our results are valid and useful for health care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the role of mucosal epithelial barrier function in HIV pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC IMMUNE ACTIVATION; HIV PATHOGENESIS; MOUSE MODEL; MUCOSAL BARRIER; MUCOSAL IMMUNITY; PRIMARY EPITHELIAL CELL CULTURE; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Clinical studies show that women are more susceptible to HIV-1 infection compared to men; but the reason for this difference is not well understood. HIV is transmitted in women primarily through sexual transmission, therefore it seems logical that in order to understand why women are more susceptible to this infection, we should try to understand the exact events that take place in the female genital tract leading up to establishment of HIV infection. Our recent studies have shown that when HIV causes inflammatory changes in the female genital tract leading to disruption of the mucosal barrier that is the body's primary defense against entry of HIV . We found that this breach in the mucosal leads to leaking of both HIV as well as other bacteria across the epithelium. This could allow HIV to establish infection as well as cause chronic inflammation that is seen in HIV-infected individuals. With this knowledge, we recently tried to determine if treatment with immune factors, such as IL-22 cytokine that is known for its anti-inflammatory function in the intestine tract, could prevent disruption of mucosal barrier by HIV-1 in the female genital tract. Indeed, we found that if genital epithelial cells were treated with IL-22, they became resistant to inflammatory changes caused by HIV. In the current proposal, we propose to understand the underlying mechanism of how the mucosal barrier is disrupted by inflammatory factors and protected by IL-22 and to test in a humanized mouse whether this can be used as a prophylactic treatment to prevent HIV infection. This research will inform strategies to prevent HIV infection in women, in particular those who are at higher risk for HIV infection, such as women who have unprotected sex, immigrant African-Caribbean and Aboriginal women who have higher biological risk

ClasseRechercheFR: SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL; DIABETE SUCRE
TitreApplicationTitle: Comparative Safety and Effectiveness of the Incretins
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; COMPARATIVE EFFECTIVENESS RESEARCH; DATABASE ANALYSIS; DIABETES; DRUG SAFETY AND EFFECTIVENESS; HEALTH OUTCOMES; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Incretins are intestinal hormones that help regulate blood glucose levels.  The newest medications approved in Canada to treat type 2 diabetes, called 'incretin-based therapies', work by either enhancing or directly mimicking the regulatory effects of the body's natural incretins. Antidiabetic medications are studied thoroughly before they are approved for use. However, a drug's potential to cause unintended side effects - and even any beneficial effects it might have on reducing the complications of diabetes long-term (such as cardiovascular disease) - are unknown when the drug is first marketed.  Given the increasing popularity of incretin-based medications for type 2 diabetes, an evaluation of the postmarketing safety and effectiveness of these agents is essential.   We propose to study the real world safety and effectiveness of incretin-based medications using a database of detailed healthcare records for individuals with type 2 diabetes including information on: prescription medication use, diagnoses made by general practitioners and specialists, laboratory tests performed by health care providers (e.g., cholesterol levels, kidney function), and hospitalizations and death. We will use the information in the database to assess the risks and benefits of using incretin-based therapies compared to other commonly used antidiabetic therapies. Our study will contribute to an understanding of the real world effects of the newest medications to treat type 2 diabetes and will help patients, clinicians, and policymakers assess the overall risks and benefits of these medications.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; THYROIDE
TitreApplicationTitle: Membrane domain regulation of receptor signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CAVEOLAE/RAFTS; CAVEOLIN; GALECTINS; GLYCOSYLATION; MEMBRANE DOMAINS; METABOLISM; PSEUDOPODIA; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; THYROID CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer cells metabolize glucose differently than healthy tissue, a process called the Warburg effect. However, while cancer researchers have made tremendous progress understanding how genetic mutations drive tumor progression, our understanding of the interplay between tumor metabolism and signaling remains poorly defined.   At the cell surface, receptor distribution to "membrane domains" regulates receptor signaling. Our labs have worked together to reveal how how two membrane domain regulators, caveolin-1 and galectin-3, function synergistically to promote cancer cell signaling, migration and invasion. We have now found that caveolin-1 promotes the distribution of multiple metabolic enzymes, including pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), a key regulator of the Warburg effect, to protrusive cell surface domains called pseudopodia (false feet), that are critical to cancer cell signaling and migration, and thereby metastasis.   We will explore the role of caveolin-1 and galectin-3 on the pseudopodial distribution of PKM2 and other metabolic enzymes and how that impacts cellular metabolism. We will then identify the sugar-carrying proteins in pseudopodia that mediate the synergistic activity of galectin-3 and caveolin-1 and determine whether changes in metabolism affect their association with membrane domains. Finally, we will extend these studies to thyroid cancers and determine whether these metabolic changes are also observed in tumors in mice and in human cancers as well as validate whether caveolin-1, galectin-3 and/or PKM2 represent serum markers for improved thyroid cancer diagnosis.  The proposed studies, linking membrane domain regulation of pseudopodial signaling to tumor cell metabolism will define novel paradigms for our understanding of cancer progression. It will also lead to the development of serum-based diagnostic assays for clinical assessment of thyroid cancer, impacting directly on management of the treatment of thyroid cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the role of Msi2 in the regulation of hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal
Keywords-MotsClés: HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; RNA BINDING PROTEIN; SELF-RENEWAL; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: A feature unique to stem cells is their ability to copy themselves through a process known as self-renewal, which enables them to regenerate tissue. Self-renewal is essential for treatments aimed at expanding normal stem cell populations for life-saving procedures such as bone marrow transplants. Despite its importance, this process is not well understood, especially in hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) of the blood. Using viruses that stifle the production from a given gene, I have recently identified the cell fate determinant Msi2 as an essential regulator of mouse HSC. Though these results point to a possible application for Msi2 in achieving HSC expansion, such a strategy is dependent on the demonstration that it's function is similar in the more clinically relevant human setting. In the proposed research I will elucidate the role of Msi2 in human HSC through strategies that modulate its levels in human hematopoietic cells. By specifically elevating Msi2 levels in discrete cell types, I will explore how this protein functions in promoting stem cell self-renewal and/or imparting HSC characteristics to non-stem cells. I will also apply gene knockdown techniques to detail the effects of Msi2 loss on HSC self-renewal, proliferation and cell death. Lastly, a tagging approach will be implemented to allow the isolation of cells that normally have high levels of Msi2. We will explore whether using this strategy the elevated presence of Msi2 under different growth conditions can be used to purify HSCs. Such a demonstration would not only provide an important proof of principle for future drug screens to identify potent Msi2 activating compounds for use in HSC expansion protocols but could also begin to identify some of the regulators of Msi2 itself. Together, these studies will provide an in-depth understanding of the function of Msi2 in human HSCs, knowledge that could be used to harness the self-renewal process in regenerative therapies.

NomDuComitéFR: Diabète, obésité, troubles lipidiques et lipoprotéiques
TitreApplicationTitle: Inhibition of foam cell formation and the inflammatory response: Relationship to atherosclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: APOLIPOPROTEINS; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; FOAM CELLS; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LIPOPROTEINS; MACROPHAGES; MOUSE MODELS; NUCLEAR HORMONE RECEPTORS; SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Cells in the lining of arteries accumulate fat, including cholesterol, resulting in the development of atherosclerotic plaques, the disorder underlying most heart attacks and strokes. These cells, known as foam cells, increase the size of the plaque and secrete inflammatory molecules that destabilize the plaque, substantially increasing the risk of a heart attack. Two cell types end up becoming foam cells. Macrophages that enter the lining of the artery wall from the blood stream and a specific smooth muscle cell, which enters the lining from deeper in the vessel wall. We recently discovered that when these cells are grown in tissue culture and exposed to human fat particles similar to those found in the artery wall, two detrimental outcomes result. These cells accumulate fat, becoming foam cells, and produce inflammatory molecules. We also discovered that if these cells were treated with a synthetic molecule that activates a specific receptor within the cell, known as PPAR delta, both fat accumulation and inflammatory molecule secretion were inhibited. The objectives of this proposal are to find out if this also occurs within the artery wall. We will use a genetically modified strain of mice, which develops high blood levels fats, glucose, insulin (insulin resistance) and atherosclerosis, when fed a high-fat diet. We will determine if treatment with a specific PPAR delta activator, decreases both foam cells and inflammatory molecules within the plaque, and if this leads to the regression of plaques. It is anticipated that we will discover novel methods for preventing foam cell formation, which in turn may reveal new ways to prevent and treat atherosclerosis.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical, Pathological, Genetic and Biomarker Studies of Frontotemporal Dementia
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; BIOMARKERS; C9ORF72; FRONTOTEMPORAL DEMENTIA; FRONTOTEMPORAL LOBAR DEGENERATION; NATURAL HISTORY; PRODROME; PROGRANULIN; TDP-43
Abstract-Résumé: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a devastating disease that is characterized by profound changes in behavior, personality, language and movement. It is the second most common cause of dementia under the age of 70 years, most frequently having its onset between the ages of 40 and 65. Almost half of FTD patients have a positive family history, often with a very strong inheritance pattern. Unfortunately, there are still significant gaps in our understanding of how the disease begins and progresses which have hampered attempts to develop accurate diagnostic tests and effective treatments. In 2006, we discovered that mutations in the progranulin gene cause 5-10% of all FTD and 20-25% of its familial forms. This spurred our efforts to better characterize the presymptomatic, prodromal and full-blown stages of FTD. Initial studies of subjects from our FTD families with progranulin mutations have demonstrated distinctive changes on neuropsychological testing and neuroimaging that precede the development of dementia by many years. This past year (2011), we discovered another gene (C9ORF72), in which mutations are an even more common cause of FTD and which are also the most common genetic cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), linking these two neurodegenerative diseases. As a result of this research, we now have one of the largest and best-characterized collections of clinical, genetic, and neuropathological FTD materials of any center in the world. Continuing to investigate and follow our FTD and ALS subjects will allow us to define the earliest stages of these disorders. Combining this knowledge with our genetic and pathological data will assist us in developing new diagnostic markers and will set the stage for the development of novel and rational therapeutic approaches for these currently untreatable diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: RETARD MENTAL; TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and Epigenetic Determinants of Syndromic Intellectual Disability
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; EXOME SEQUENCING; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Intellectual disability (ID) is a term used when there are limits to a person's ability to learn at an expected level and function in daily life. About 1% of people are affected by ID, an important medical and socioeconomic problem. ID can be caused by genetic and/or environmental factors. Some patients with ID can be categorized into subgroups, known as syndromes when there are additional clinical features present. At this time for ~60% of ID patients there is no known cause. Identification of the cause is important in order to understand the basis of the disorder which could lead to the development of targeted treatments. In this proposal we will explore the role of epigenetics in ID. Epigenetics is a science studying modifications of DNA and associated proteins. These modifications are involved in packaging DNA. In human cells there are ~500 proteins (epiproteins), which are involved in writing and erasing epigenetic marks. Normally, some of these marks vary across tissues. Mutations in more than 20 different genes encoding epiproteins i.e. epigenes are involved in ID syndromes, suggesting that faulty epigenetic marks could play an important role in ID. We have identified aberrations in epigenetic marks in patients with four ID syndromes. These marks can distinguish such ID patients from healthy controls, and from each other. We want to explore the role of aberrant marks in these syndromes, and define the frequency of aberrant marks in patients with ID. We will also use a new technology called exome sequencing, which examines the DNA sequence of all genes in an individual, to check if patients with ID carry mutations (changes) in epigenes.   This research will help to elucidate the molecular causes of ID, and lead to the development of diagnostic tests for ID syndromes. Also, as epigenetic marks are potentially modifiable by medications, targeting such epigenetic marks could present novel opportunities for developing therapies for individuals with ID.

TitreApplicationTitle: Real-time microscopy during high-frequency mechanostimulation of living cells
Keywords-MotsClés: LIVE-CELL IMAGING; MECHANOTRANSDUCTION; MICROSCOPY; OSTEOARTHRITIS; OSTEOPOROSIS; SKELETAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Human cells respond to mechanical forces, allowing our tissues to change and adapt to different loads and forces. For example, during prolonged bedrest, an individual's skeleton will actually lose mass, because there is reduced load on each bone.  While this effect is easily observed, it is not clearly understood.  Part of the problem is that there are several ways in which mechanical forces might influence cells, including direct mechanical pressure, strain (i.e. stretching), shear stress (similar to the effect produced by water flowing over an object), and acceleration (which is associated with mechanical vibration).  When we manipulate cells during experiments, we often apply multiple mechanical effects simultaneously, making it difficult to understand which one dominates.  It is also difficult to observe the cells under a microscope while we are manipulating them, which means that we cannot see what happens immediately after the mechanical stimulus is applied.  This lack of understanding of how cells respond to mechanical loads hinders the development of effective new therapies for diseases such as osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, hardening of the arteries, emphysema and cancer.  We propose to develop a set of new devices and software that will allow researchers to study cells and tissue cultures under a microscope while they are being manipulated.  The mechanical forces that must be applied are very small (with displacements that are smaller than the diameter of a human hair!), and they must be applied at frequencies between 1 and 90 Hz.  We believe that recent technical developments will make it possible to perform these studies reliably and cost-effectively, providing a new capability to study the way that cells respond to external forces and loads.  The improved understanding that will result will be beneficial in the development of new treatments (e.g. mechanical therapies, biologic compounds or drugs) for diseases such as arthritis and osteoporosis.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Cellular and molecular regulation of T cell tolerance
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOIMMUNITY; T CELL; THYMUS; TOLERANCE
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system is vital for protecting individuals against pathogen infections and cancers. Paradoxically, the immune system is also responsible for initiating autoimmunity by attacking healthy self-tissues. T cells are white blood cells that play a critical role in both immunity and autoimmunity. Normally, T cells that are able to recognize and destroy healthy self-tissues are eliminated during their development in the thymus while useful T cells that can combat infections are released into the circulation. Humans and mice that have mutations in genes that impair the elimination of self-reactive T cells develop autoimmunity due to a lack of self-tolerance. Therefore, in order to develop treatments for autoimmunity, it is essential to understand all the mechanisms utilized during development to enforce self-tolerance within the T cell pool. Using mouse model systems, we previously determined that there are multiple ways the immune system enforces self-tolerance. These include the removal of self-reactive T cells as well as the inactivation of self-reactive T cells. We now seek to uncover the cellular and molecular mechanisms that regulate both methods of inducing T cell tolerance. This information will be valuable in devising strategies to treat autoimmunity in genetically susceptible individuals, but also has implications in organ transplantation and cancer immunotherapy.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; RECHERCHE SUR LES MÉDICAMENTS
TitreApplicationTitle: Optimal VAsopressor TItratiON (OVATION) Pilot Randomized controlled Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: PILOT STUDY; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SHOCK; TITRATION; VASOPRESSORS
Abstract-Résumé: Patients who are admitted to intensive care units commonly suffer from illnesses that cause life-threatening low blood pressure. In this context, intensivists (physicians who care for patients in intensive care units) administer potent medications that increase blood pressure. Unfortunately, these medications cause adverse effects and it is not clear that they are better than the condition they are meant to treat. In this study, we intend to demonstrate the feasibility of a larger study that will investigate if administering medications to achieve higher blood pressures (that are near normal) is preferable to restricting the use of these medications by tolerating lower blood pressures. Patients will randomly receive blood pressure increasing medications for a higher or lower blood pressure target. In the definitive study, we will compare 90-day survival between groups but in this pilot study, we will validate that it is feasible to adhere to the protocol and achieve a different average blood pressure in each group while on study medication. This study is an important part of a research program that has the potential to change how we administer dangerous medications to the sickest of the sick in our hospitals - ultimately leading to safer, better patient care.

ResearchClassEN: VIRAL; DRUGS- PHARMACEUTICAL SCIENCE/CHEMISTRY & NON MEDICAL USE OF DRUGS
ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; DROGUES - SCIENCES PHARMACEUTIQUES/CHIMIE ET UTILISATION NON MÉDICALE DES DROGUES
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanisms involved in resistance to different classes of HIV RT inhibitors
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRALS; BIOCHEMISTRY; DRUG RESISTANCE; HIV; REVERSE TRANSCRIPTASE
Abstract-Résumé: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) pandemic remains an important global problem. Despite the remarkable success in the development of anti-retroviral drugs (ARVs), by far not everyone benefits from available treatments and new infections are inadequately prevented. In the absence of a cure, infected individuals have to take ARVs for the rest of their lives. The enormous variability of the virus is also tightly associated with the emergence of drug resistance that can cause treatment failure if patients do not adhere to their drug regimen. Resistance conferring mutations can reduce susceptibility to each of the available classes of drugs, although the more recently approved combinations of ARVs appear to better control this problem. However, we are currently witnessing a paradigm-shift in ways antiretrovirals are used. Ongoing difficulties in the development of vaccines triggered the use of ARVs also in prophylaxis to reduce the risk of transmission and to prevent new infections. For these reasons, it will be important to continue to develop novel drugs with limited cross-resistance to the approved ARVs. The major objective of the proposed studies is to form a concrete basis for the development of novel inhibitors of HIV reverse transcriptase (RT) using mechanism-driven approaches.

TitreApplicationTitle: Altered Angiotensin II AT1 Receptor in Cardiac and Renal Disease: Translational Development of Novel F-18 Labeled Ligands for PET Imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: CANDESARTAN; DIABETES; ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY; FLUORO-18 ANALOGS; HEART FAILURE; HYPERTENSION; LOSARTAN; PET IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: The renin angiotensin system plays a key role in the regulation of sodium and water balance and in the development of heart failure. Hyperactivity of the renin angiotensin system contributes through a variety of mechanisms to cardiac, vascular and renal diseases. The rate of sickness, hospitalization, and mortality for patients remain high despite recent therapy advances.  In addition, large proportions of the health care expenses in Canada relate to patients with heart failure. The primary rationale for this project is that animal models of human cardiovascular diseases including myocardial infarction and hypertension have altered cardiac and/or kidney angiotensin AT1 receptor (protein) expression. Our long-term goals are to develop an imaging compound, capable of detecting changes in the AT1 receptor binding in living human heart and brain using positron emission tomography (PET) imaging. We are developing products with a longer lasting isotope, F-18. This allows us to ship to other sites and scan multiple subjects in one day.  To develop these compounds, we need to produce them and evaluate their characteristics in a living animal (rat & pig). We will then evaluate how they measure changes in animal models of both heart and kidney diseases. We will also measure changes in response to therapy.  From there we will study the products in healthy human volunteers. Successful development of these novel products will establish a new non-invasive imaging probe for quantifying AT1 receptors (proteins) in humans. Such an approach would present a unique opportunity to advance understanding of the pathophysiology of cardiovascular diseases including heart failure, infarction, hypertension, vascular disease and diabetes; and a means to direct and measure therapy responses. The experiments in this proposal are innovative because of the novel products development for cardiovascular imaging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Statin use and the prevention of recurrent venous thromboembolism in the elderly: The STAVENO study
Keywords-MotsClés: NESTED CASE-CONTROL DESIGN; OUTCOMES; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; RECURRENCE; STATINS; VENOUS THROMBOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), which is a term used to describe blood clots in the legs and lungs, is the third most common cardiovascular disorder after stroke and heart attack, and predominately affects older men and women. It is estimated that 1 in 100 Canadians over 70 years of age will be diagnosed with a VTE and that 3-20% will develop a second VTE episode (or recurrence) within 12 months of completing treatment with anticoagulants (i.e. blood thinners). As a result, clinical practice guidelines recommend that indefinite anticoagulation be considered in certain patients with first-time VTE in order to prevent long-term recurrence and associated complications such as chronic venous insufficiency of the leg, and even death from a fatal blood clot in the lungs. However, because anticoagulants are associated with an elevated risk of major bleeding in the elderly, indefinite anticoagulation is not always an option for older patients with VTE. Recent evidence suggests that statin medications which are commonly prescribed for the treatment of elevated levels of cholesterol may protect against the development of a first-time VTE. We hypothesize that statins may also protect against recurrence of VTE. As a result, we propose to investigate whether statin medications in older patients diagnosed with first-time VTE can reduce their risk of another VTE by means of a population-based study that will use anonymously linked data from the Quebec administrative healthcare database. This will allow us to follow a large number of patients with VTE over a 10-year period to determine the effect of statin use on risk of recurrence. The results of our study will improve our understanding of recurrent VTE in the elderly, and if a protective effect is seen then our evidence justifies carrying out clinical trials of statins for the prevention of recurrent VTE in older patients.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; RECHERCHES PSYCHOSOCIALES ET COMPORTEMENTALES
TitreApplicationTitle: Determinants of Individual Differences in Maternal Care
Keywords-MotsClés: ATTACHMENT; ATTENTION; GENETICS; INFANT TEMPERAMENT; MATERNAL BEHAVIOUR; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Parenting is an important influence on child health and development. Yet we know very little about the range of factors that directly influence parental care. The behaviour of parent towards their offspring is the result of cognitive and emotional processes that are regulated by brain function, which can reflect a variety of influences. Variations in genes that regulate specific aspects of brain function are one obvious candidate influence. Included among these are variations within the oxytocin, dopamine, and serotonin systems. Likewise, the quality of the environment within which parent child interactions occurs influences parental behaviours. Thus, environmental present stressors and past experiences affect the quality of parent child interactions, as does the behaviour of the child. We suggest that these influences interact to determine parental care.  In these studies we will analyze mother-child interactions in a cohort of 400 mother-child dyads recruited into the Maternal Adversity, Vulnerability and Neurodevelopment Project (MAVAN). We code for specific mother child interactions and child attachment at ages ranging from 6 to 60 months of age. The primary focus of the present study is maternal behaviors exhibited between 48 and 60 months. We predict that the three gene families will relate differently to mothering, with dopamine associated with attention, serotonin with affect, and oxytcin with early nursing and attachment. These gene variants are also predicted to interact in their effects with mothers' early experiences, stressors, and the age and characteristics (e.g., temperament) of the child.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of definitive hematopoietic development from human pluripotent stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFERENTIATION; HEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELLS; MESODERM; NODAL; PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; PRIMITIVE STREAK; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: This research proposal focuses on understanding how to direct human pluripotent stem cells [embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and reprogrammed pluripotential stem cells (iPSCs)] to generate different types of blood cells in a Petri dish.  In these studies, we propose to manipulate a critical regulatory pathway that controls the development of specific cell types from these stem cells.  These experiments are based on recent findings from our laboratory that indicate it is possible to control blood cell development by controlling this pathway with factors that either activate or inhibit its activity. The studies proposed in this application will study in detail the regulation of blood cell development, with the goal of defining the precise conditions for generating the desired cell populations.  The outcome of these studies has important implications for improving public health in Canada.  By understanding the precise control of blood cell development from human stem cells, it will be possible to generate different blood cell populations for therapeutic applications.  For instance, the efficient differentiation of red blood cells or megakaryocytes from stem cells would provide a novel disease free source of cells for blood cell and platelet transfusions.  Access to human T lymphocytes would provide a transplantable source of cells to treat patient with specific immunodeficiencies.  Finally, the generation of blood forming stem cells from the human pluripotent stem cells would provide a new source of cells for bone marrow transplantation.  In addition to providing novel sources of cells for transplantation, the ability to generate a broad spectrum of blood cells from patient specific induced pluripotent stem cells provides a unique opportunity to study the causes of different blood cells disease in a Petri dish.  This approach will provide new insights into the earliest stages of these diseases and in doing so, identify novel targets for developing new treatments for them.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian e-Platform to Promote Behavioral Self-Management in Chronic Heart Failure: CHF-CePPORT
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC HEART FAILURE; E-HEALTH; LIFESTYLE COUNSELLING; PANCANADIAN NETWORK; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic Heart Failure (CHF) is a growing public health issue in Canada. Hospital re-admission within 1-year after diagnosis is 25-40%, and the 5-year rate of CHF death is 50%. Counseling by multidisciplinary health care teams helps CHF patients to improve self-care behaviors (for medications, diet, exercise, smoking cessation and symptom monitoring), and this reduces the rate of death and CHF hospitalization. In the absence of intervention, patient adherence to these behaviors is below recommended standards and quality of life among CHF patients becomes progressively compromised. A major challenge is to make self-care counseling available without overtaxing health care resources.  This 3.5 year proposal will establish and evaluate a Canadian e-based program of multidisciplinary counseling to help CHF patients initiate and maintain recommended self-care behaviors. We will recruit 278 CHF patients in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver. We hypothesize that a 12-month program of e-Counseling + Usual Care vs. general eInfo + Usual Care will improve quality of life, self-care behaviors and heart health. This proposal is based upon previous clinical trials in CHF, e-health and preventive lifestyle counseling by our team. It builds upon our established collaboration with the consumer eHealth program of the Heart and Stroke Foundation of Ontario. The novel contribution of this research is that it will establish an infrastructure for a pan-Canadian e-platform in preventive e-counseling for CHF. A key feature of this proposal is that our multidisciplinary team will work with the Heart and Stroke Foundation to share our findings and e-health resources with the public and other health care professionals in Canada, which will help to galvanize research and clinical work in eCounseling. Our clinical trial will strengthen eCounseling services in order to improve the quality of life of patients with CHF.

TitreApplicationTitle: Complex Mental and Social Activities to Promote Cognitive Function in Older Adults with Chronic Stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE FUNCTION; DEMENTIA; EXERCISE; MENTAL ACTIVITY; QUALITY OF LIFE; SOCILIZATION; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Worldwide, one in six older adults suffers a stroke and doubles one's risk of dementia. In fact, cerebrovascular disease - such as stroke - is the second most common cause of dementia. However, current stroke rehabilitation does not adequately deal with the cognitive consequences of stroke (e.g., memory disorders, impaired reasoning) - especially for those who are in the chronic phase (i.e., at least 12 months has passed since their stroke).   Exercise training is a promising strategy to promote cognitive function. However, there is insufficient quality evidence for stroke survivors. Furthermore, stroke survivors often have physical impairments that significantly limit their ability to exercise. We propose that participating in intellectual and social activities, such as playing bridge, is an alternative and effective treatment to exercise training for promoting cognitive function in stroke survivors. It is an attractive alternative as its participation is less physically demanding.  The proposed study aims to determine the effect of two distinct treatments - 1) an exercise training program and 2) a cognitive and social enrichment program - on cognitive function in adults who have had a stroke at least 12 months ago. Whether the cognitive benefits of the exercise training program or the cognitive and social enrichment program are retained six months following the cessation of the programs will also be evaluated.  The proposed research is timely as there is an urgent need to reduce the burden of cognitive impairment and dementia in our aging population. Critically, if the onset and progression of dementia could be delayed by a modest one year, there will be nearly 9.2 million fewer cases of dementia in 2050. For the individual affected by stroke, reducing the severity of their cognitive deficits could promote functional independence and quality of life. This, in turn, could lead to reduced health care.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Studies on Histone Acetyltransferase Targeting, Activity and Specificity
Keywords-MotsClés: BIACORE; CHROMODOMAINS; CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; DOSAGE COMPENSATION; HISTONE ACETYLTRANSFERASE; MULTISUBUNIT COMPLEX; MYST FAMILY
Abstract-Résumé: We will study members of a family of proteins that are required for the maintenance of normal structure and function of our chromosomes. Chromosomes are the packaged forms of our genetic material, and must be maintained properly for the proper storage and repair of damaged DNA, and transmission of genetic information to future generations. We will study a group of enzymes called histone acetyl transferases that are essential for the maintenance of our DNA in chromosomes and also for the regulated decoding of our genetic information into proteins.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vitamin K in brain function: studies of mechanisms of action.
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; ASTROCYTES; CELL SIGNALING; COGNITION; INFLAMMATION; MENAQUINONE-4; MICROGLIA; NEURONS; OXIDATIVE STRESS; VITAMIN K
Abstract-Résumé: Nutrition plays a central role in brain function and cognition at all stages of life. Historically discovered for its role in blood coagulation, vitamin K (VK) has recently emerged as an important nutrient for brain function. In recent years, our team has contributed significant knowledge to this emerging function showing that low VK status results in cognitive impairment, an outcome associated with alterations in sphingolipid metabolism and signaling pathways in specific brain structures. This negative effect of VK on cognition was observed in aged rats who had been fed low amounts of VK throughout their lives, and in animals treated with warfarin (Coumadin), a potent anti-VK agent used in a variety of clinical entities (e.g. atrial fibrillation, thrombosis, etc). In this application, we propose to elucidate the action of VK in cogntition by determining what cell types (neurons, astrocytes, etc) are most affected by VK deficiency and whether processes such as inflammation and oxidative stress are part of the action of VK. We also plan to determine whether the VK-induced cognitive impairment can be reversed through restoration of VK status in brain. Through an integrated approach that includes nutrition, cellular biology, biochemistry and behavioural sciences, this proposal addresses an important emerging function of VK which could have significant public health impact. Surveys conducted in North America including Canada have been reporting high prevalence of sub-optimal VK intakes. Furthermore, in light of the pharmacological action of warfarin, individuals treated with this drug could be at greater risk of cognitive problems. A comprehensive understanding of the actions of VK in brain and behavioural functions will contribute essential knowledge that could influence future nutritional recommendations for this vitamin outside its primary role in blood coagulation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development, Application and Evaluation of Multistate Models for Risk Estimation and Screening Interventions in Lynch Syndrome Families and Familial Colorectal Cancer Type X Families
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINIC- AND POPULATION-BASED STUDIES; GENETIC RISK; LYNCH SYNDROME; MMR GENES; MULTISTATE MODEL; OPTIMAL SCREENING MANAGEMENT; SCREENING EFFICIENCY
Abstract-Résumé: The overall impact of screening in Lynch Syndrome (LS) and Familial Colorectal Cancer type X families (FCCTX) (i.e. LS families with no mutation identified) remains uncertain.  This uncertainty remains because methods are not yet available to study this problem and because a large number of families are needed to thoroughly understand it. In this project, we propose to evaluate the impact of screening on cancer occurrences and deaths in LS and FCCTX families and to identify the major factors affecting screening effectiveness. This research will address many important clinical issues affecting LS and FCCTX families: a) Estimate the risks of developing successive cancers among individuals who had and did not have screening given their mutation status; b) Identify and describe the poor responders to screening (e.g. individuals screened but who developed cancer); c) Provide realistic expectations about intervention responses over time; d) Characterize disease risk in the FCCTX families. e) Determine genetic risk in LS and FCCTX families using screening history and other known risk factors. This research project will provide appropriate guidelines for screening protocols in LS families and families who carry other disease genes in the US, Canada and around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the role of Cav 1.4 calcium channel in B lymphocyte biology
Keywords-MotsClés: B LYMPHOCYTE; CACNA1F; CAV1.4; KNOCKOUT MOUSE MODEL; L-TYPE CALCIUM CHANNEL; LYMPHOCYTE ACTIVATION; T LYMPHOCYTE
Abstract-Résumé: The immune system is a complex network that consists of many cell types. Lymphocytes are one particular cell type of the immune system that become activated when the body is infected, to kill off the invading pathogen. However, sometimes lymphocytes can become inappropriately activated when the body is not infected and this can result in an autoimmune disorder. The way that lymphocytes become activated is not completely known. The element calcium is one component in these cells that is required for their activation. However, the means by which calcium gains entry into lymphocytes remains unknown.  We have recently identified two variations of a protein that form a channel that is found on the surface of lymphocytes and may allow calcium to enter. We predict that these calcium channels play a role in lymphocyte activation and may be responsible for the inappropriate immune responses that lead to autoimmune diseases such as arthritis. In this CIHR renewal, we will test this idea by comparing a normal mouse to one that has had the calcium channel deleted. We will look for any reduction in immune strength in the absence of the calcium channel and this will help us further understand the channel's role. Identifying calcium channels responsible for calcium movement into lymphocytes may lead to the generation of novel drug targets that would allow investigators to block the immune activation that causes diseases such as arthritis and diabetes.
