TitreApplicationTitle: Cost-related Nonadherence to Prescription Drugs in Canada: a multi-method study
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO CARE; HEALTH CARE COSTS; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; PHARMACEUTICAL POLICY; PRESCRIPTION DRUGS
Abstract-Résumé: Many Canadians do not fill prescriptions, skip doses, or split pills in order to reduce their drug costs-a phenomenon known as cost-related nonadherence (CRNA). Prior research conducted by members of our team has shown that 1 in 10 Canadians are unable to afford their prescription medications. However, we have a very limited understanding about the characteristics of individuals who cannot afford their prescription drugs, what medications they are foregoing, what trade-offs they are making and how their decision making about drugs takes place. Our study will use surveys and patient interviews to investigate: (1) who currently experiences CRNA (province, age, gender, chronic conditions); (2) which prescription drugs are forgone (how often and how many); and (3) the trade-offs Canadians are making between prescription drugs and other important necessities such as food.

TitreApplicationTitle: Control of vascular smooth muscle cell aging
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL AGING; SIRTUIN; VASCULAR REMODELING; VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Aging of cells within blood vessels can have an adverse effect of the health of arteries and can lead to heart attacks, aneurysms, and strokes.  One important cell type in arteries is the smooth muscle cell.  The goals of this project are to determine the extent to which accelerated aging of smooth muscle cells can be found in vascular disease and to identify molecular pathways that control how quickly or slowly smooth muscle cells age.  These goals will be accomplished with several strategies.  First, we will examine segments of aortas retrieved from individuals in whom the aortic walls have become stretched to an unsafe level.  Second, we will use cell culture and mouse systems to determine if aging of smooth muscle cells can be slowed by a vitamin-like molecule that affects molecular cascades involved in aging.  Finally, we will create a mouse in which smooth muscle cells are genetically modified to be missing a gene that appears to be critical to slowing the aging process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interactions between components of the HCV replication complex
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; FRET; HCV; REPLICATION COMPLEX; SINGLE MOLECULE STUDIES; VIRAL REPLICATION
Abstract-Résumé: According to the WHO, approximately 150 - 200 million people worldwide are infected with the hepatitis C virus (HCV), with close to 300000 infected individuals living in Canada. Chronic infection with the virus is strongly associated with severe liver disease, including hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis. HCV infection is also a major cause of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in developed countries, including the US and Canada. While HIV/AIDS can be treated with more than 30 available antiviral agents that comprise six different classes of drugs, specifically targeted anti-HCV drugs are just being approved for clinical use. Here we propose to characterize the interactions between the various viral and cellular components of the HCV replication complex to pave the way for novel approaches to effectively interfere with propagation of the virus.

TitreApplicationTitle: Manipulation of asthmatic response by protein tyrosine phosphatases
Keywords-MotsClés: ANGIOGENIC GROWTH FACTORS; ASTHMA; CHILDREN; CYTOKINES; ENDOTHELIAL CELLS; GRANULOCYTES; INFLAMMATION; MONOCYTES/MACROPHAGES; PROTEIN TYROSINE PHOSPHATASE
Abstract-Résumé: Introduction: Asthma is a chronic disease characterized by inflammation and permanent changes in the airways and alveoli of the lungs, a process called remodeling. Many treatments have been tried to decrease inflammation with the goal of ameliorating asthma, but these have had limited benefit. Presumably, new treatments that could affect both immune cells and lung cells might be more successful. A family of enzymes called protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTP) regulates the production of soluble factors and other signals that affect inflammation. Because of this, an approach targeting PTP might be better than the current therapeutic strategies for asthma, which only affect only one cell type at a time. Hypothesis: The activity of PTP can be manipulated to control the inflammatory responses driven by immune cells and lung cells, and to prevent remodeling of the airways in chronic asthma. Objectives: My laboratory has found one PTP, called PTPRB, that can affect the way cells of the immune system and lung cells secrete soluble factors in an acute model of allergic airway inflammation that can be used to study asthma. Specific Aims: 1.To study the effect of decreasing the activity of PTPRB in a model of chronic allergic airway inflammation that resembles asthma. With these experiments, we want to understand the molecular mechanisms that are responsible for the altered production of soluble factors by cells of the immune system and lung cells.   2.To study the role of PTPRB in the relationship between inflammation and the development of lung remodeling. For these experiments, we will perform bone marrow transplantation between mice, to create combinations of immune cells and lung cells having different levels of PTPRB activity.  Potential Impact: The discovery that PTPRB can ameliorate asthma could establish a new therapeutic approach, where a pharmacological PTP inhibitor drug could be used to decrease inflammation and lung damage at a young age.

TitreApplicationTitle: The use of beta-blockers and the prevention of cancer-specific mortality
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIHYPERTENSIVE DRUGS; BETA-BLOCKERS; BREAST CANCER; CANCER-SPECIFIC MORTALITY; DATABASES; PROSTATE CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate and breast cancer are the most frequently diagnosed malignant tumors among men and women in developed countries. As a result, the clinical and economic burden of these cancers is likely to increase in the foreseeable future. Recently, several laboratory studies have shown that beta-blockers, drugs used to treat hypertension and heart failure, may have strong anti-cancer properties. To date, the few studies that have investigated the association between the use of these drugs and cancer outcomes in patients with prostate and breast cancer have reported conflicting results. Such discrepancies are likely due to important methodological shortcomings. Nonetheless, there is a strong biological rationale to investigate the potential anti-tumour effect of these agents. Thus, the objective of this study will be to determine whether the use of beta-blockers is associated with a decreased risk of cancer-specific mortality in patients with prostate and breast cancer. This will be achieved by conducting two cohort studies (one for prostate and the other for breast cancer) by linking four large electronic databases from the United Kingdom (UK); the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, the Hospital Episode Statistics database, the UK Cancer Registry, and the UK Office of National Statistics. The study cohorts will consist of 5,500 men diagnosed with prostate cancer and 6,000 women diagnosed with breast cancer between January 1, 1997 and December 31, 2009 with follow-up until December 31, 2012. While beta-blockers appear to hold promise as novel treatments in patients with prostate and breast cancer, it is too premature at this stage to launch expensive and lengthy randomized controlled trials. Thus, using appropriate pharmacoepidemiologic methods, this study will provide the medical strong evidence on the long-term effects of these agents in patients with these cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: In Vitro, In Vivo, and Bioinformatic Studies on the Function of SH3 Domains
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; BIOPHYSICAL ASSAYS; EVOLUTION; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTION; SH3 DOMAIN; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; SITE-DIRECTED MUTAGENESIS; TRP FLUORESCENCE; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: All cellular functions are governed by a complex network of signaling pathways involving interactions between hundreds of proteins. When these networks are perturbed by mutations or environmental disturbances, diseases, such as cancer, can result. For each of these proteins to function properly, their interactions with other proteins must be precisely regulated in a manner that is responsive to the environment both inside and outside the cell. Therefore a detailed knowledge of how proteins recognize and bind to the correct protein targets is required to elucidate the processes that go awry in disease states. In this proposal, we study a particularly common protein-protein interaction domain, called the SH3 domain, and use yeast as a model system to study the function of these domains. Our work utilizes an innovative combination of in vitro characterization of mutant proteins, computational studies, and biological assays in yeast. The goals of this work are to understand how proteins specifically recognize other proteins and how this recognition impacts the functioning of the cell.

TitreApplicationTitle: Are Cesarean Deliveries Associated with a Long-Term Increased Risk of Small Bowel Obstruction?
Keywords-MotsClés: CESAREAN DELIVERIES; DATABASE RESEARCH; LOG TERM COMPLICATIONS; SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Cesarean deliveries are becoming one of the most commonly performed surgeries in Westernized countries today with an estimated 1 in 4 births today being performed by cesarean delivery. While most research suggests that cesarean deliveries are considered both safe for the mother and baby, the long term consequences of cesarean deliveries has not well been established. We have long known that most abdominal surgeries results in internal scar formation which can lead to the development of small bowel obstruction, a clinical condition requiring recurrent hospital admissions and sometimes multiple operations. Whether cesarean deliveries can increase the risk of developing small bowel obstruction remains unknown.  The purpose of our study is to evaluate the association between cesarean deliveries and the development of small bowel obstruction. The importance of this study is to gain enough information to properly inform women who chose to undergo a cesarean delivery not only of the short term risks but also of the long term risks associated with this common surgery. Women and physicians alike should be well informed of the long term risks of cesarean delivery so that an informed decision can be made that will take into consideration not only the potential benefits of the procedure but as well the potential long term risks that may result from the cesarean delivery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sex differences in radiation-induced direct and indirect effects in brain: from sex-specific molecular mechanisms to organismal repercussions
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIORAL DEFICITS; BRAIN; DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; GENE EXPRESSION; HORMONES; RADIATION THERAPY; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Radiation therapy is an important diagnostic and treatment modality in cancer. Yet, it causes numerous deleterious side effects. Amongst those, radiation exposure leads to significant neuro-cognitive deficits in patients. Post-irradiation neurological effects include deficits in attention, concentration, memory and executive and visuospatial functions. These side-effects are very bothersome for patients, and the mechanisms of their occurrence are not understood.   It is currently becoming more and more apparent that radiation effects are sex- and tissue specific. Yet, virtually nothing is known about radiation effects in male and female brain. Furthermore,  the mechanisms of sex-specificity have yet to be precisely delineated. It is well-known that radiation effects are seen in the distal unirradiated naive tissues and organs, these are known as the bystander effects.   We have led the way in the analysis of sex-specificity of bystander and radiation effects in brain. Here we will build on our expertise and analyze the sex-specificity, the sex-specific mechanisms and biological repercussions of radiation effects in brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigations of Genetic Pathways Underlying Superior Retinal Colobomata, Defects in Closure of a Novel Ocular Fissure
Keywords-MotsClés: COLOBOMATA; CONGENITAL DISEASE; EXOME SEQUENCING; FISSURE CLOSURE; FORKHEAD GENES; RETINOIC ACID SIGNALING; SUPERIOR FISSURE; TALEN-MEDIATED MUTANTS; VISION SCIENCE; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: The eyes form from extrusions of the brain. These complex tissues must subsequently fold and reorganize into a multilayered tissue that includes blood vessels. To do this, it forms a hole (fissure) located in the bottom-most retina at the 6 o'clock position. During embryo development, if the fissure fails to close, a portion of the lower retina dies, with such severe birth defects causing blindness. Collaborative research between Lehmann and Waskiewicz laboratories has identified evidence for a novel opening in the top-most region of the forming eye, which challenges the current model that the eye forms with a single fissure in the bottom of the retina. Patients with 'superior colobomata' display an opening in their upper retina and iris, with such defects leading to profound blindness. Using a vertebrate model organism, Zebrafish, we have identified a structure that forms in the top-most retina and has the properties of a temporary divider between cells. This research will investigate the function of this structure, first using microscopes and living zebrafish embryos to see if cells use this structure as a type of 'gatekeeper' to divide the forming eye into two equal halves (Aim 1). We will then investigate the genetic pathways that specify where this structure will form and when it will close (Aim 2). Finally, we will attempt to determine which mutations cause superior colobomata in humans. We have determined the DNA sequence of four patients with this disorder, thereby identifying candidate genes in causing superior colobomata. We will determine which mutations are likely to be disease-causing by creating animal models that lack the function of each of these mutated genes (Aim 3). These three aims will elucidate the genes that cause this newly discovered blinding disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Visualizing Hebbian Structural Plasticity in the Developing Brain
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY-DEPENDENT; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ELECTROPORATION; IN VIVO IMAGING; MORPHOMETRY; NMDA RECEPTOR; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS; RETINOTECTAL; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; VISUAL SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Proper development of the brain is the result of a collaboration between the expression of genetically encoded molecular guidance cues and the influence of sensory experience which refines the final connectivity.  Neurodevelopmental disorders including autism and schizophrenia have been attributed to the failure of neuronal connectivity to refine correctly.  We use the Xenopus tadpole as a simple vertebrate nervous system for studying developmental brain refinement.  Because this animal is amenable to live imaging and electrical recordings in the intact animal, we have been able to directly observe (and perturb) the dynamic remodeling of brain circuits in response to specific sensory inputs during development.  This proposal will use novel technological innovations to develop a better understanding of the process of experience-dependent refinement of neural circuits and the mechanisms that underlie these key developmental events.

TitreApplicationTitle: Déhospitalisation psychiatrique et accès aux services de santé mentale. Regards croisés Ontario-Québec, 1950-1912
Keywords-MotsClés: 1950-2012; ANGLO-MONTREALAIS; DEINSTITUTIONNALISATION; FRANCO-ONTARIENS; HISTOIRE DE LA SANTE MENTALE; NORMES MEDICALES ET PARAMEDICALES; SERVICES COMMUNAUTAIRES; SOCIOLOGIE DE LA SANTE; SOINS PSYCHIATRIQUES; STIGMATISATION
Abstract-Résumé: Considerant qu'un Canadien sur neuf hospitalise pour maladie mentale retournera a l'urgence moins d'un mois apres sa sortie d'hopital, il nous interesse de documenter les itineraires "transinstitutionnels" des personnes souffrant de troubles psychiques. Cette programmation de recherche entend mener une enquete socio-historique sur l'evolution des services de soins de sante mentale des communautes de langue officielle en situation minoritaire, en particulier les communautes francophones de l'Est et du Nord ontariens ainsi que celle de la region du Montreal anglophone. Ces regards croises entre deux regions francophones de l'Ontario et l'Ouest du Quebec visent une meilleure comprehension de l'impact des facteurs de "langue de service" et de "culture" dans l'offre de services en sante mentale. Cette recherche sur plus d'un demi-siecle evaluera la prise en charge et l'acces aux traitements psychiatriques (sociaux et chimiques) des personnes ayant des troubles de sante mentale. Elle se penchera sur les enjeux professionnels de ce secteur de sante, sur l'evolution des ressources humaines disponibles, sur l'accessibilite selon la region (nombre de psychiatres, infirmieres, travailleurs sociaux, educateurs) et sur la congruence (ou l'incongruence) des programmes annonces avec les decisions prises. Cette programmation de recherche permettra d'etablir une vue d'ensemble des changements de politiques publiques en matiere de sante mentale en Ontario et au Quebec, des determinants sociaux de sante mentale et, enfin, des indicateurs developpes en sante publique dans les deux provinces de notre enquete : l'Est et le Nord ontariens ainsi que l'Ouest du Quebec.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies on Hepatitis C - Host Pathogen Interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: HEPATITIS C VIRUS; MEMBRANOUS WEB; NUCLEAR PORE COMPLEX; PATHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a bloodborne pathogen that is a major cause of liver disease worldwide with approximately 170-200 million chronic carriers of HCV worldwide.  In Canada, approximately 250,000-300,000 people are infected with an estimated 30 per cent eventually developing worsening liver diseases including cirrhosis or liver cancer.  HCV is one of the leading causes of end-stage liver disease leading to liver transplantation in North America and western Europe.  The interaction of HCV with the host cell causes some unique changes in the membranes of the cell.  This includes the formation of a unique "membranous web" that serves as the site of virus production as a separate compartment within the cell cytoplasm.  The precise structure and function of the membranous web remains unclear.  Studies in this grant will provide new insight into the formation and function of the membranous web and possibly lead to new approaches to disrupt viral production in the infected liver cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel mechanisms of CFTR regulation
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY DISEASE; BACTERIAL INFECTION; CELL SIGNALLING; CHLORIDE CHANNEL; EPITHELIAL SECRETION; INNATE IMMUNITY
Abstract-Résumé: Our airways and other organs are lined by sheets of epithelial cells that secrete ions and fluid and defend against pathogens. Appropriate regulation of anion secretion is essential for health, as evidenced by the lethal disease cystic fibrosis (CF) in which there is too little chloride secretion, and cholera, in which there is too much. The control of secretion by hormones and neurotransmitters has been extensively studied, however the regulation during infection and inflammation is less well understood. CFTR (CF Transmembrane conductance Regulator) is the apical anion channel that malfunctions in CF and cholera. It mediates chloride and bicarbonate secretion when phosphorylated, and also modulates calcium signaling and the release of inflammatory mediators. This proposal is to study mechanisms that control apical CFTR channels during host defense against bacteria, using novel electrophysiological and fluorescence assays to examine transfected cell lines and highly differentiated airway epithelial cells from human lung transplant recipients. Studying novel mechanisms that control apical CFTR will provide new insight into secretion, calcium signaling and inflammatory mediators, and may identify potential therapeutic targets for the treatment of cystic fibrosis and other secretory diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ultrasound Imaging Investigation of Resistance and Adaptation to Targeted Anti-cancer Therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIANGIOGENIC THERAPY; BLOOD FLOW IMAGING; CONTRAST ULTRASOUND IMAGING; DRUG RESISTANCE; DYNAMIC CONTRAST ENHANCED IMAGING; IMAGING CANCER BIOMARKERS; TUMOUR ANGIOGENSIS; ULTRASOUND IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: A new class of therapies target the developing (or 'angiogenic') blood vessels of a cancer, which both deliver oxygen and nutrients essential for tumour growth and provide a pathway for its metastatic spread. Antiangiogenic drugs inhibit the signals that tumours send to the host to stimulate growth of such new vessels. However, many patients develop resistance to these treatments: the proposed research develops and applies imaging methods designed to monitor response of cancer blood vessels to such treatments so as to aid in their improvement. We will image blood flow in both animal models of cancer and patients with renal cell carcinomas under therapy to investigate how this response changes as resistance develops and whether imaging can successfully predict its onset. Imaging measures of blood flow will use contrast-enhanced ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging, aligned to register the same tissue and extended to cover the three-dimensional volume of a tumour. Measurements will be compared to biological markers of tumour activity, helping elucidate how resistant tumours evade antiangiogenic treatment and enabling assessment of new therapeutic approaches. The aim is to help develop strategies to delay the onset of resistance in patients undergoing antiangiogenic therapy and provide new clinical instruments for serial noninvasive assessment of their efficacy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus and the Risk of Incident Cardiovascular Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; DATABASE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GESTATIONAL DIABETES; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; PREGNANCY; RISK STRATIFICATION; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: Gestational diabetes is a type of diabetes that occurs during pregnancy.  It often disappears after the baby is born.  However, gestational diabetes increases the chances of later developing type 2 diabetes, an important risk factor for heart disease.  Despite this knowledge, few studies have examined the effect of gestational diabetes on the chances of developing heart disease.    We will address this question using information from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, or CPRD.  The CPRD is a United Kingdom-based database.  It contains medical records for over 12 million patients seen at over 425 general practitioner practices.  We will include all pregnant women in the CPRD between 1990 and 2012.  We will compare the number of women who develop heart disease among those with gestational diabetes to that among pregnant women without gestational diabetes.  In addition, we will determine how much of the increased risk of heart disease can be explained by the development of type 2 diabetes.  Finally, we will examine if considering gestational diabetes in addition to traditional heart disease risk factors such cholesterol, blood pressure, and obesity improves our ability to predict which women will get heart disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optical coherence tomography for assessment of early radiobiological response in-vivo
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL TUMOUR MODELS; BIOMEDICAL OPTICS; CANCER; MEDICAL IMAGING; OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY; RADIATION BIOPHYSICS; RADIATION THERAPY; RADIOBIOLOGY; SPECTROSCOPY AND SPECKLE ANALYSIS; WINDOW CHAMBER
Abstract-Résumé: Novel optical technologies can provide detailed microscopic information about tissue structure and physiology in a noninvasive manner, without patient discomfort. This otherwise unobtainable information can help the physician in selecting the best treatment, thus greatly benefiting the patient.  For example, it can be used for early disease detection, resulting in more effective treatments and higher cure rates.  It can also provide detailed understanding of the progress of various therapies to ensure that they are working, and to enable their improvements for increased effectiveness. We will concentrate on the latter direction in this research, by using state-of-the-art optical methods to monitor tissue changes caused by X-ray cancer treatments.  Specifically, a new imaging technology based on spectroscopic and textural optical coherence tomography (s/tOCT) will be developed and applied to examine X-ray irradiated normal and cancerous tissues. The goal of this project is to develop and quantify reliable and robust s/tOCT signal 'features' that result from radiation treatments.  Such analysis in both tumour and in surrounding normal tissues should provide early indications of radiation therapy response, and yield valuable insights into the mechanisms of radiation damage ('what happens, where, and when').  These changes, once quantified and validated, can help optimize and personalize radiation treatments, with ultimate clinical implementation made possible by the compact, practical and robust nature of OCT 'photonic' technology.  Patient-specific individualized irradiations can then become feasible. This may improve the effectiveness of radiation therapy (a widely used cancer therapy technique) and may help in use/choice of other treatments (e.g., adjuvant chemotherapy), with potential to yield more cancer cures and reduce patient suffering.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; MALADIES DU FOIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular dissection of TIMP3-dependent hepatocellular carcinoma
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOGENOUS PROTEASE INHIBITOR; HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA; MOUSE GENETICS; MOUSE MODELS; P53; SENESCENCE; TIMP3; TUMOR PROGRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Most human cancers develop excess metalloproteinase activity as they advance to more aggressive stages. These enzymes degrade the connective tissue and shed critical inflammatory signals from the cell surface. A small family of inhibitory proteins called Timps keeps these proteases under control. Our ongoing work on liver disease and liver cancer has discovered that mice lacking the Timp3 gene are highly resistant to developing liver cancer. This is a surprising observation because Timp3 mutant mice are generally prone to inflammation, which is a well known promoter of liver cancer. Our recent data show that Timp3 mutant liver cells undergo permanent growth arrest when exposed to DNA damaging agent, likely due to increased p53 activity. We propose that TIMP3 regulates the powerful tumor suppressor gene p53 by triggering a new chain of events; particularly, molecules that underlie TIMP-dependent inflammation become co-opted to control the earliest stages of liver cancer. Our studies will generate new knowledge for the treatment of liver cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion Study III (LAAOS III)
Keywords-MotsClés: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; CARDIAC SURGERY; LEFT ATRIAL APPENDAGE; STROKE; SYSTEMIC ARTERIAL EMBOLISM
Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common heart rhythm disorder that leads to one-sixth of all strokes. Prevention of strokes in AF is achieved through the use of blood thinners such as coumadin. Although these blood thinners are effective, they are limited by the risk of serious bleeding, by physician and patient reluctance to use, and by noncompliance and discontinuation. The left atrial appendage is a structure on the upper chamber of the heart that is the most common source of stroke in patients with AF. This structure is easily accessible during open heart surgery for removal, and has been an area of interest for stroke prevention. However, there is currently no strong evidence that removing it works.  The LAAOS III trial proposes to randomly (like the flip of a coin) assign patients with AF undergoing heart surgery for other reasons to have the left atrial appendage removed or not. These patients, other than this small procedure which has been shown to be quite safe, will be treated in the usual manner. The current proposal is for the first 300 patients of approximately 4700 to test assumptions that have been made in planning the full study. The full study of 4700 patients, followed for an average of 4 years, will determine if removing the left atrial appendage can reduce stroke and other complications on top of usual therapy.  A positive study will change the way heart surgery is performed on AF patients and result in a large reduction in the number of strokes in a large population. Further, it will promote further research into this approach that could be applied beyond AF patients undergoing heart surgery.

DomainesScientifiquesFR: APPAREIL CARDIO-VASCULAIRE; FONCTION RÉNALE, NÉPHROLOGIE, UROLOGIE
TitreApplicationTitle: Pilot trial of Hemodialysis patients undergoing Aldosterone antagoniSm with Eplerenone (PHASE)
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDOSTERONE; END-STAGE RENAL DISEASE; EPLERENONE; HEMODIALYSIS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Forty percent of patients that require dialysis for kidney failure die within three years mostly due to heart disease. High blood pressure and heart failure are common problems in patients that require dialysis and are key causes of death due to heart disease. Eplerenone is a drug that is very effective in reducing blood pressure and improving heart failure in patients that do not require dialysis. There is currently no evidence to tell physicians whether eplerenone would have similar benefits in patients that require dialysis. This evidence can only be reliably generated by performing a large scale study. Before such a study is undertaken, we must determine whether eplerenone will be well tolerated and safe in patients that require dialysis. We will perform a pilot trial called the Pilot trial of Hemodialysis patients undergoing Aldosterone antagoniSm with Eplerenone (PHASE) to determine if eplerenone is a well tolerated, safe medication to study in a very large, global study that will show whether or not eplerenone reduces important outcomes for patients like death from heart causes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel roles for cysteinyl leukotrienes in oxidant induced airway injury from chlorine
Keywords-MotsClés: 5-LIPOXYGENASE PATHWAY; ANTIOXIDANTS; ASTHMA MODEL; EPITHELIAL REPAIR
Abstract-Résumé: Inhalation of chlorine from acccidental spills or from acts of terrorism causes severe airway damage that is caused by the reactive nature of chlorine. Oxidation of many cellular proteins occurs and inflammation is triggered. The damage is almost certainly largely attributable to hypochlorous acid which is also a major product of neutrophils, a common cell involved in acute inflammation.  We have demonstrated that cysteinyl-leukotrienes, compounds usually associated with allergic reactions, are released following chlorine. Although usually associated with pathology it appears that leukotrienes exert protective effects through actions on the principal receptor for their actions  in the airways CysLTr1. We propose to elucidate the novel protective role of leukotrienes against the oxidative injury caused by chlorine and to explore the possibility that defective anti-oxidant mechanisms underly the susceptibility related to CysLTr1 deficiency.

TitreApplicationTitle: Depression 2 to 4 years after traumatic brain injury: a longitudinal study of psychosocial predictors, impacts, and barriers to access mental health resources.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO TREATMENT; DEPRESSION; HELP-SEEKING BEHAVIORS; LONGITUDINAL; PREDICTORS; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Brain injury caused by head trauma can have many consequences for the injured person, as well as for family members and the person's social and professional environment. Quite abruptly, persons with traumatic brain injury need to adapt to new limitations ranging from having problems with walking to having trouble to think efficiently and with maintaining healthy relationships. These adaptations can be very challenging for many individuals, and feelings of discouragement, anxiety and depression may arise. Unfortunately, depression becomes a significant problem for a large proportion of these patients, and this condition can complicate the rehabilitation and social reintegration processes by diminishing the person's level of energy, motivation, and hope for the future. This research project aims at understanding how depression develops during the first few years after a brain injury, paying close attention to factors such as stressful life events, coping strategies, anxiety levels, sleep and fatigue problems, use of alcohol or drugs to cope with life challenges, and how people are supported by their spouses, families and friends. We also seek to obtain a portrait of the impact of depression after TBI and to verify whether people who suffer from clinically significant depression are receiving adequate treatment for it, and what kind of help is available to them (e.g. medication, psychotherapy, self-initiated strategies). By understanding the factors leading to depression after brain injury, we hope to be able to devise not only effective treatments, but also prevention strategies that we can put into place at the appropriate time after the injury. Indeed, because these people are faced with many challenges, helping them to keep a positive outlook on life, to better accept their limitations, to use their strengths to solve their problems and to better manage their stress and energy should help them reintegrate their community and improve their quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ethnicity-based differences in emergency department care of patients with symptoms of acute coronary syndrome.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME; EMERGENCY CARE; ETHNICITY; HEALTH CARE EQUITY; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; QUANTITATIVE
Abstract-Résumé: When doctors and nurses use accepted guidelines for quickly treating patients who come to the emergency department (ED) with a possible heart attack, patients do better. Research shows that there are ethnicity-based differences in the symptoms these patients have, when and why they seek care, the treatments they receive, and how well they fare afterwards. There is also Canadian evidence that there may be ethnicity-based disparities in the care some patients receive, and it has been suggested that health professionals may unconsciously treat patients of different ethnic backgrounds differently. But it is not known if there is ethnic variation in the care given to Canadian patients with heart attack symptoms in the critical first hours after coming to an ED, or in their experiences of this care. We will collect information from the health records of patients who come to EDs with symptoms of heart attack. We will record events and times such as what provisional diagnosis is assigned to the patient, how often they receive pain medication, how long until certain tests are performed and what treatments are offered. We will also collect information about things that might affect delivery of care, e.g., the number of doctors and nurses who are on duty. Patients will also complete a short questionnaire about their reasons for coming to the hospital, how long they waited before coming and why, and what their experience in the ED was like. We will review this information to see if there are ethnicity-based differences in the care received by patients with heart attack symptoms. Our findings could identify important disparities, which could in turn inform future projects to correct these disparities, for example, education of health professionals about ethnic differences in ideas of health and illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ethnic disparities in healthcare use for infectious diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; ETHNICITY; HEALTHCARE USE; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; LINKED DATA SETS; MEDIATION
Abstract-Résumé: Infectious diseases are still a major cause of illness and death in Canada. As an example, the Ontario Burden of Infectious Diseases Study found that in a population of 12.2 million people, infectious diseases cause over 7 million healthcare episodes and nearly 5,400 deaths each year. Canada is home to many different ethnic groups, with 16% of the population belonging to a visible minority (i.e., non-White) group as of 2006, and this is expected to double to 29-32% by 2031. Certain ethnic groups are more likely to have chronic medical conditions such as heart disease and diabetes. Previous studies suggest that there may also be differences between ethnic groups in terms of infectious diseases. The goals of this research are to see if there are differences between ethnic groups in terms of healthcare use for several types of infections, and to understand the mechanisms that might explain these differences. In particular, we want to know if socio-economic status (e.g., income, education), lifestyle behaviours (e.g., diet, exercise, smoking), and medical conditions (e.g., diabetes, asthma) explain any differences that exist. We will use information from telephone surveys and healthcare records for hospitalizations, emergency department visits, and doctors' office visits from Ontario to do this research. We will also account for many other factors that might affect the relationship between ethnicity and infections. This research will improve our understanding of how ethnicity relates to health, so that better ways to prevent infectious diseases can be developed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Microfinance opportunities to improve quality of life and clinical outcomes among HIV+ patients in Africa: A randomized trial
Keywords-MotsClés: ECONOMICS; GRANTS; HIV/AIDS; LIVELIHOOD; MICROFINANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Many people in Africa who have HIV-AIDS are affected by poverty. For many, this is as a result of their sickness, and they may have lost members of their family or be unable to provide for their children. We will evaluate whether providing small grants to groups of patients can have important effects on their own physical health as well as the health of their families. Using a cluster randomized trial design in Uganda, we aim to determine if 100 dollars per person in a patient-support group will lead to a successful group business venture that will affect the patient's health and the livelihood of their families. Control groups will not receive a grant. This study will take two years to complete and assess a patient's quality of life, clinical indicators, household livelihood security, and whether their children are able to attend school by providing school fees.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the influences of social context and structure on young people's parenting experiences
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNOGRAPHIC RESEARCH; IN-DEPTH INTERVIEWS; INTEGRATED KTE; MIXED METHODS; PARENTING; POLICY ANALYSIS; SOCIAL INEQUALITIES; TEEN PREGNANCY; YOUNG PEOPLE; YOUTH HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: In 2009, approximately one out of six children born in British Columbia (BC) was born to an early-age mother (<25 years of age), with a total of 1,430 live births recorded among mothers younger than 20 years old (an additional 6,201 births occurred in 20-24 year olds). Unarguably, early-age parenthood poses serious challenges for young people and their children. However, we also need to account for the influence of social context (e.g., power relations) and structural factors (e.g., levels of unemployment and poverty). The proposed study offers an opportunity to better understand how relevant policy and programming efforts can be improved to promote health and well being amongst young parents and their families.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Pilot Randomized-Controlled Trial of Lipoprotein(a) Lowering for the Prevention of Aortic Valve Disease - Translating genomic knowledge for cardiovascular prevention.
Keywords-MotsClés: AORTIC STENOSIS; CALCIFICATION; GENOMICS; LIPOPROTEIN (A); PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; PREVENTION; RANDOMIZED-CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Aortic valve disease is the most common form of heart valve disease and is a major burden to society. Aortic valve disease is also expected to become more prevalent with the aging of the Canadian population. Currently, over 1 million individuals in North America have aortic stenosis, which is a narrowing of the aortic valve, and leads to symptoms of heart failure and sometimes death. Valve replacement with its potential costs and complications remains the only avenue for treatment.  Despite the major importance of this disease, there are currently no medical treatments to prevent the development of aortic stenosis.  The lack of preventative treatments stems in large part to a poor understanding of the causes of this disease. Using cutting edge genetic technologies, we have recently identified that individuals with a genetic predisposition to elevations in a type of cholesterol not normally screened, called lipoprotein (a), have a much higher risk of developping aortic valve disease. We have also shown that lipoprotein(a) causes hardening of the valve, a very early sign of valve narrowing. We plan to evaluate in a randomized controlled trial whether lowering this unusual form of cholesterol at an early stage of this disease could slow or stop the development of aortic valve narrowing. We are currently proposing a pilot project to evaluate the feasibility of this type of study.  If succesful, our proposed treatment would be notable in two ways. First, it would represent the first medical treatment to prevent valve disease, which could lead to major reductions in the societal burden of this important disease. And second, it would herald a major success for genomic medicine as it would represent one of the first treatments borne from recent genetic studies. In these ways, our proposal could significantly impact the health of many Canadians while also highlighting the innovative research performed in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Non Invasive Prediction of Scoliosis Progression
Keywords-MotsClés: 3D TRUNK SHAPE ANALYSIS; PROGRESSION; SCOLIOSIS; SIMULATION; SURFACE TOPOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a 3D deformation of the human trunk that affects between 1% and 3% of the general population. Among patients with AIS, 8% to 9% will be treated by brace and about one in 1 000 will need surgery. While 1 in 25 people have mild scoliosis deformities, 1 in 200 adolescents have deformities that progress to the point of requiring treatment. Since there is still no reliable way to predict which cases will progress, AIS patients are monitored with a series of X-rays acquired every six months during rapid adolescent growth. However, cumulative exposure to X-rays radiation significantly increases the risk for certain cancers. Although orthopaedists mainly look at the shape of the spine in the patient's X-ray images, during clinical examination other symptoms can be observed by the clinician, such as tilted shoulders and waist when the patient is standing, or a hump on the back when the patient is bending forward. Furthermore, external body appearance is what AIS patients are most concerned about, as opposed to the shape of their spine. Therefore, the aim of this project is to assess the risk of progression for AIS patients and to predict how the whole 3D shape of the trunk will change over time. To do that, we will capture the external trunk shape at regular intervals (using optical 3D cameras) and combine that with the internal spine shape as seen in the X-rays. We will analyse how the whole trunk evolves over the course of a patient's visits using a set of shape measurements and mathematical tools. This will allow us to identify the changes in trunk shape that can be used as reliable early predictors of scoliosis progression. In the longer term, we wish to develop a non invasive predictive tool to monitor scoliosis progression. In addition to reducing the frequency of X-ray exposures, this tool will assist orthopaedists in making timely treatment decisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting Antidepressant Treatment Response in Major Depressive Disorder: An Integrated Clinical and Neuroimaging Approach
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; MAJOR DEPRESSION; NEUROIMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Major Depression is a widespread and debilitating illness. Although a variety of treatments for depression are available, there is currently no way to predict ahead of time which treatment will work best for which individual. Researchers have discovered that there are differences in brain structure and function in people with depression compared to those without depression that can be measured with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This study is divided into two phases. In the first phase, we will scan the brains of people with depression before treatment, and after 2 and 8 weeks of treatment with an antidepressant to look for indicators (biomarkers) that may help us identify predictors of treatment response. In the second phase of this study, people will be followed clinically for an additional 8 weeks during which those who respond to treatment will continue being treated with the antidepressant and those who do not respond will receive add-on therapy with a second medication. The second phase of the study will help us to identity factors that predict sustained response, as well as those that can help differentiate potential subgroups of people with depression. Ultimately, this information will help us to understand fundamental brain changes in depression, and to use this information to provide the best treatment possible for an individual. In addition, findings from this study may provide us with information about new ways to treat depression in the future, including new medications as well as non-medication treatments that work on these fundamental brain changes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Systematic Investigations into psychological, physiological and endocrinological effects of stress in the brain
Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA-AMYLASE; ATTENTIONAL BIAS; CORTISOL; GENDER; PSYCHONEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; SEX; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Stress has the potential to cause illness, although the exact mechanisms are unknown. We have recently developed a new set of stress tests that allow us to separate the psychological effects of stress from the physiological and endocrinological effects of stress, for the first time in human stress research. Applying these tests in a series of human studies in combination with neuroimaging will allow us to find out whether the adverse effects of stress on health depend on the psychological, endocrinological, or physiological effects of stress, and how these effects are mediated in the brain. This will allow identification of potential targets for treatment and the development of new stress intervention paradigms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Design and in vivo delivery of novel anti-inflammatory agents
Keywords-MotsClés: APTAMERS; CD200; CD200R1; IMMUNE MONITORING; INFLAMMATION; MOUSE MODELS; PEPTIDES; TNF ALPHA
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammation is a term that describes how our body's immune system reacts to damaged tissues, infections or the presence of agents that cause irritations such as allergens.  If the tissue or organ involved is progressively damaged or if an infection or irritant persist, the resulting  inflammatory responses become chronic leading to a range of immune response-related diseases, exemplified by medical conditions such as hay fever, atherosclerosis, Crohn's disease and rheumatoid arthritis.  In this proposal, we plan to generate synthetic, targeted biomolecules that will specifically block or dampen uncontrolled immune responses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toward epigenetic therapy for colon cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMICAL PROBES; COLON CANCER; COLORECTAL CANCER XENOGRAFTS; EPIGENETICS; EPIGENOMIC MAPPING; PATIENT-DERIVED CELL LINES; TUMOUR-INITIATING CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: The Structural Genomics Consortium (SGC) is a charitable organization operating out of the Universities of Toronto and Oxford to support drug discovery through pre-competitive, open access research. A significant component of SGC research is in the area of epigenetics, a relatively new field of biology that is thought to hold great promise for the discovery of new medicines. Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression caused by mechanisms other than changes in the underlying DNA sequence.   In this proposal, the SGC at the University of Toronto will partner with Abbott, a pharmaceutical company, to create small drug-like molecules, or "chemical probes", that are potent, selective and active in cells. The compounds will be used to investigate the role of epigenetic mechanisms in Colon Cancer and potentially identify new drug targets using patient-derived cell lines.  The research output from this project will be published jointly with Abbott, and related structural and epigenomic data will be placed in public databases. The chemical probes, antibodies and other reagents will also be made publicly available without restriction on use.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of individualized fortification of breast milk on somatic growth and neurodevelopmental outcome in preterm infants - The IFO Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION; BREAST MILK COMPOSITION; BREAST MILK FORTIFICATION; GROWTH; MILK ANALYSIS; NEURODEVELOPMENTAL OUTCOME; PRETERM INFANTS
Abstract-Résumé: Survival of preterm infants <32weeks of gestation has improved dramatically, however many grow poorly after birth. Inadequate nutrition in early life is a major factor in the restricted growth of these infants, which can lead to problems in brain development and increase the risk of chronic diseases in later life. Breast milk (BM) is recommended as the best source of nutrition for preterm infants, to which powdered fortifiers containing protein, minerals and energy are added to provide additional nutrients. The nutrient content of BM varies between mothers as well as between lactations of the same mother. Currently powdered fortifiers are added to BM in standard amounts and even with the addition of fortifier, the BM feeding may have a nutrient content below the recommended minimum amount for optimal growth. In a recent pilot study we demonstrated that the addition of fat, carbohydrate and protein can be individually adjusted to optimal levels with positive benefits for growth. The proposed research will investigate individualized fortification (IFO) of BM based on daily analysis of the BM's fat, protein and carbohydrate content in a randomized double blind controlled trial. IFO as well as a commercial fortifier will ensure that BM contains the target amounts of nutrient. Growth and development of infants receiving IFO will be compared with that of infants fed mother's BM that has been supplemented only with the standard amount of current routine fortifier. Postnatal growth of the infants will be assessed by measuring weight, length and head circumference as well as fat and lean mass using highly accurate, non-invasive methods throughout the intervention period and at the first follow-up visit at 3 months corrected age. Neurological development and fat and lean mass will be analyzed at age 18 months. We expect that IFO will improve the nutritional intake of preterm infants, optimize growth, and thus positively impact neurodevelopment and health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Towards an understanding of structural drivers of HIV/STI and protective factors among sexual and gender minority youth in Kingston, Jamaica
Keywords-MotsClés: BISEXUAL; GAY; HIV AND AIDS; JAMAICA; LESBIAN; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; MIXED METHODS RESEARCH; RESILIENCE; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS; SOCIAL CAPITAL; TRANSGENDER; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: Stigma and discrimination negatively impact the wellbeing of sexual and gender minority youth (SGMY). For example, SGMY are more likely to be homeless, enhancing vulnerability to sexual and physical violence, sex work and drug use. These factors elevate risk for HIV and sexually transmitted infections (STI). Yet little is known about the linkages between stigma, discrimination and HIV/STI risk among SGMY in the Caribbean region, with the highest HIV prevalence in the world after Sub-Saharan Africa. Young (under 25 years old) men who have sex with men (MSM) in Jamaica have HIV infection rates of 28% - the highest in the region. Stigma and discrimination reduce access to HIV prevention. SGMY in Jamaica reported hate crimes, sexual and physical violence and homelessness. Intersectionality theory highlights the challenges (e.g. stigma) and opportunities (e.g. resilience, social capital) that emerge from having stigmatized identities. Resilience and social capital have been understudied among SGMY.   This 3-year study aims to understand HIV/STI risk and protective factors among SGMY in Kingston, Jamaica. Phase 1 (qualitative): 60 cognitive interviews with young SGMY, including MSM (n=20), women who have sex with women (WSW) (n=20), transgender people (n=20) and key informants (n=12) to explore conceptualizations of HIV/STI risk and protective factors. Phase 2 (quantitative): survey among MSM (n=150), WSW (n=150) and transgender people (n=150) to assess associations between structural factors (e.g. stigma), protective factors (e.g. resilience) and HIV/STI risk. Phase 3: participatory action research using arts-based approaches (e.g. theatre) to share research findings with SGMY and diverse community stakeholders in roundtables, forums, and street theatre. Project goals are to understand associations between structural factors,  protective factors and HIV/STI risks among SGMY to inform HIV/STI prevention.

Keywords-MotsClés: ALPHA-AMYLASE; ATTENTIONAL BIAS; CORTISOL; GENDER; PSYCHONEUROENDOCRINOLOGY; SEX; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Stress is one of the great health burdens of our society. According to the World Health Organization, the direct and indirect adverse health effects of stress will become the second leading cause of disease in industrialized countries by 2020. The exact mechanisms by which stress is causing disease continue to be under investigation. We have recently developed a new set of stress tests that will allow us to better understand how stress can lead to disease. We here plan to apply these tests in a series of human studies to systematically investigate, the mechanisms of stress. The findings of these studies can ultimately lead to the identification of potential targets for treatment and the development of new stress intervention paradigms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Probiotics: Prevention of Severe Pneumonia and Endotracheal Colonization Trial (PROSPECT): A Feasibility and Proof of Concept Pilot Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CRITICALLY ILL; FEASIBIITY; INFECTION; INTENSIVE CARE UNIT; PILOT STUDY; PNEUMONIA; PROBIOTICS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Probiotics are commercially available live bacteria thought to have health benefits when ingested. Our literature review of probiotic studies in the intensive care unit (ICU) found that in patients who receive probiotics, there is a 25% reduction in lung infection, known as ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). There is also an 18% reduction in the chance of developing any infection in the ICU.  However, the studies reviewed were small and not well done. Therefore, whether probiotics are really helpful or not is unclear.  Before a large carefully performed study is done to evaluate the effects of probiotics in critically ill patients, a pilot trial is needed.  We plan to study the feasibility of such a trial in mechanically ventilated ICU patients in 4 ICUs in Ontario, investigating whether orally ingested L. rhamnosus GG (a common probiotic) prevents VAP and other infections.  The 4 goals of the pilot study will be to ensure that we can successfully enrol patients; follow the protocol faithfully; make sure patients don't receive additional probiotics, and estimate how much pneumonia exists in these patients.  In a separate substudy, we will evaluate the effects of probiotics on lower lung infiltration with potential harmful bacteria, stool bacteria, markers of immunity called cytokines, and markers of infection called endotoxin levels.  We plan to enroll 100 adults admitted to ICU and receiving mechanical ventilation. Following informed consent, patients will be randomized to either L. rhamnosus GG group or an identical placebo.  Twice daily, patients will receive probiotics or placebo in a feeding tube. We will record all infections and other important outcomes in the ICU. This study is very important in the ongoing search for more effective strategies to prevent serious infection during critical illness.  Probiotics may be an easy-to-use, readily available, inexpensive approach to help future critically ill patients around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of action of full antiestrogens
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIESTROGENS; BIOLUMINESCENCE RESONANCE ENERGY TRANSFER; BREAST CANCER; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; PROTEIN COMPLEMENTATION; PROTEIN TURN-OVER; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; SHRNA; SUMOYLATION; UBIQUITINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer affects one woman out of nine in North America. Therapeutic progress has led to a regression in death rate from breast cancer, but drug efficacy remains limited as relapse and progression of the disease taking place eventuallly in a significant fraction of cases. To design more efficient drugs, it is important to fully understand the mechanisms of action of current molecules, a process that paradoxically often takes longer than their implementation in the clinic. In this application, we focus on a class of molecules used for the treatment of a specific type of breast cancer that expresses receptors for the sex hormone estrogen. These so-called full antiestrogens have a higher degree of activity in repressing estrogenic action than molecules currently used in standard treatment, but need improvements to maximize action on tumor cells. While there is currently active research in developing new molecules, their mechanisms of action remain imperfectly understood. Following up on our previous research that has led to the identification of novel mechanisms of action of these molecules involving modifications of the estrogen receptor and modulation of its interaction with regulatory proteins, we will now identify the specific features of these molecules that are responsible for these properties, and recapitulate the chain of events that underlies their therapeutic activity.

CommitteeNameEN: Clinical Investigation - B: Arthritis, Bone, Skin and Cartilage
NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique - B : Arthrite, os, peau et cartilage
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism of osteoclastic bone resorption: collagenase activity of cathepsin K
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CATHEPSINS; COLLAGEN; INHIBITORS; OSTEOPOROSIS; PROTEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis affects the lives of millions of Canadians and is a major burden to health care systems worldwide due to an increasing elderly population. Typical treatment regimes such as hormone replacement therapy or bisphosphonates have either various side effects or patent expiration issues. We and others have identified cathepsin K, a cysteine protease predominantly expressed in osteoclasts and responsible for the degradation of bone collagen, as a novel pharmaceutical target for the treatment of osteoporosis and various forms of arthritis. Active site directed inhibitors which block the total proteolytic activity of this protease are presently in several advanced clinical trials and proved highly effective in improving the quality of bone. However, major problems of this approach are off-target and off-site effects which caused the termination of at least two clinical trials. A highly effective cathepsin K inhibitor should only inhibit the osteoclast mediated collagen degradation in bone without affecting the protease's activities in other cell types and avoid the inhibition of related proteases with other functions. This clearly indicates the need for a better understanding of the biology and mechanism of action of cathepsin K. Our laboratory is interested in the elucidation of mechanisms of specific and disease-related matrix protein degradation by cathepsins, their biological functions and the development of novel inhibitors based on their specific mechanism and function in health and disease. Our objective is to understand the cathepsin K specific mechanism of collagen degradation, how to exploit this knowledge in developing novel and highly selective inhibitors, as well as the elucidation of potential off target and off-site inhibition effects and how to avoid them. This understanding will help to develop very needed novel and more specific types of treatment methods for various erosive skeletal diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: PEAU ET TISSUS SOUS-CUTANES; RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES
TitreApplicationTitle: Using the skin to control inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGY; CONTACT HYPERSENSITIVITY; CORTICOSTEROID; DENDRITIC CELLS; REGULATORY T CELLS; SKIN INFLAMMATION; TOPICAL MEDICATION; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: We have shown that the application of creams onto the skin prior to vaccination can improve the response to the vaccine. Interestingly, the application of vitamin D-like creams or steroid-containing creams alters the skin so that cells that prevent inflammation in response to injected or skin-applied substances are generated. This is of potential value not only in the treatment but prevention of overactive inflammatory responses as occur in skin irritation (nickel allergy), in the treatment and prevention of allergies (including nasal stuffiness, asthma and eczema) and in the treatment and prevention of systemic inflammatory diseases. We will use established mouse models to optimize this treatment method. We will also explore the effect of skin-applied medications on the effectiveness and irritation induced by the standard treatment of hay fever. This general method of altering systemic inflammation may be of benefit for the prevention or treatment of diverse systemic inflammatory diseases such as type 1 diabetes or multiple sclerosis.

NomDuComitéFR: Biologie cellulaire et moléculaire du cancer
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Isocitrate Dehydrogenase 1 mutations in tumorigenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ASYMETRIC CELL DIVISION; CANCER; EPIGENETICS; GENETICALLY ENGINEERED MICE; GLIOMA; ISOCITRATE DEHYDROGENASE; LEUKEMIA; METABOLOMICS; ONCOGENES
Abstract-Résumé: Cancers are defined by their tissue of origin and arise as the result of a series of mutations that lead to tumor progression. Specific mutations in the isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1) enzyme, an enzyme that normally functions as a part of a cell's central metabolic system, are commonly found in brain tumors and leukemias. When mutated, IDH1 acquires a new function and begins producing a new biochemical product called 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG). 2-HG is normally found at very low levels in cells and tissues, but in tumors with IDH1 mutations, it builds up to very high levels. Previous studies performed by ourselves and others suggest that these high levels of 2-HG interfere with several basic cellular processes which leads to loss of cellular self-regulation, inappropriate cell division, and ultimately, tumor development. We have developed genetically engineered mice that carry the specific IDH1 mutation found in tumors as model systems for studying the effects of this mutation on animal physiology and the development of IDH1-associated cancers. Using these mice, we will express the mutation in specific and relevant mouse tissues including the brain and bone marrow in order to examine the effects on normal tissue development and function as well as tumorigenesis. We will probe the molecular mechanisms thought to underlie the ability of these mutations to cause cancer in order to understand fully these IDH1-associated diseases. A better understanding of how IDH1 mutations act to promote tumor development and tumor progression may lead to strategies to diagnose, monitor and treat patients with these types of tumors.

NomDuComitéFR: Génomique: Biologie computationnelle et biologie des systèmes
TitreApplicationTitle: The eukaryotic RNA-protein recognition code
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTATIONAL MODELLING; MICROARRAYS; MOTIF FINDING; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION; PROTEIN HOMOLOGY; RNA-BINDING PROTEINS; STATISTICAL LEARNING
Abstract-Résumé: There are hundreds of different types of cells in our body but almost all of them have an identical set of genes. The reason that heart cells are different from liver cells is differences in gene activity. A better understanding of the regulation of gene activity would not only improve our ability to predict why certain mutations cause cancer but also improve our ability to fight disease-causing human parasites.  The general principle of gene regulation is that regulatory proteins recognize codes encoded in the gene, or nearby the gene, in the genome.  By knowing what these regulatory codes are, and which proteins recognize these codes, we can more easily study gene regulation.  Recently it has become clear that most gene regulation activity occurs post-transcriptionally, i.e., after the gene has been copied from DNA (where it is stored in our genome) to messenger RNA.  This means that many important regulatory codes are encoded in RNA sequence and are being recognized by RNA-binding proteins.  Although it is often possible recognize whether or not a protein will bind an RNA code based on its amino acid sequence, it has proven difficult to tell exactly what that RNA code is.  So, although sequencing an organism's genome will reveal what RNA-binding proteins it has, it won't tell us what codes these proteins recognize.  Our specific aim is solve this problem.  We propose to use high volume biochemical methods to determine the RNA binding preferences of hundreds of carefully selected RNA-binding proteins from a diverse set of organisms.  Based on these measured binding preferences, we then propose to use advanced computational methods to design an algorithm that will predict the binding preferences for arbitrary protein sequences.  We will validate this algorithm by testing some of its predictions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Blood-based protein test for early detection of breast cancer using antibody colocalization microarrays
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY MICROARRAYS; BIOMARKERS; BREAST CANCER SUBTYPE; EARLY DIAGNOSIS; MULTIPLEXED SANDWICH IMMUNOASSAYS; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: One in eight women will be diagnosed with cancer during her lifetime, and the earlier the cancer is detected the better the chances of survival.  We propose to develop a new technology that can detect many different proteins associated with cancer in the blood of patients. The technology will be exquisitely sensitive, and will be capable of identifying and quantifying over one hundred different proteins in the blood within a background of unrelated proteins that are up to a trillion times more concentrated. By measuring many proteins simultaneously, we will establish a molecular portrait (or fingerprint) of a person's blood. We will capture protein portraits for a large number of healthy women and cancer patients, and using computational data analysis, compare the portraits between the two groups to identify the molecular signature of breast cancer. This molecular signature will then be tested in a second group of patients and healthy women to confirm its accuracy.  A successful outcome will result in a simple-to-use test to diagnose cancer using a droplet of blood. Such test could be used in combination with mammography, notably for women with dense breasts where it is difficult to detect breast cancer, and where a molecular signature may help confirm or infirm a preliminary diagnosis. In the long term, we envision that this test could be used by family doctors for early diagnosis of breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: rTMS for Working Memory Deficits in Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: MRI; NEUROIMAGING; SCHIZOPHRENIA; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a debilitating disorder that exacts enormous personal, social and economic costs. Currently, 300,000 Canadians suffer from this illness, which is characterized by a constellation of clinical symptoms (e.g., hallucinations, delusions, impaired cognition) and life-long functional disability. Memory impairments are one of the most difficult to treat problems in SCZ that underlie the poor day-to-day functioning of these patients. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been shown to be an effective and safe in the treatment of schizophrenia. We have recently evaluated rTMS for the treatment of these memory impairments in schizophrenia in a small sample. Our data shows that by stimulating frontal regions of the brain there is an improvement in memory. Additionally, we will complete advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) before and after the study for each participant to help better understand the effects of treatment on the brain. In the proposed study we intend to investigate if rTMS can improve memory performance in a larger sample of patients with schizophrenia and determine if the treatment might help change the structure of parts of the brain that are important for certain types of memory. If our findings hold, these data will provide promising new treatments for memory impairments in schizophrenia. Having additional treatment options available is vital to improve our patients' quality of life and functioning that may provide hope for those who would otherwise suffer from persistent illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of cathepsins in vascular calcification
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CATHEPSINS; COLLAGEN; ELASTIN; ENZYME ASSAYS; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; OSTEOPOROSIS; PROTEASES
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases (infarct and stroke) remain the main causes of death in Canada.  A typical feature of vascular diseases is the calcification of blood vessels, i.e. the formation of bony material in the circulation system. Calcification makes blood vessels brittle and affects blood flow. Interestingly, there is a strong correlation between osteoporosis, the loss of bone, and the formation of mineral deposits in arteries.  Arterial calcification is predictive of cardiovascular mortality and is tightly associated with aging and arterial remodeling. Calcification happens in particular in the extracellular matrix of blood vessels.   The main extracellular matrix components, elastin and collagen, are both heavily degraded by cathepsins during the hardening of arteries (atherosclerosis) but also during the balooning of blood vessels (aneurisms).  However little is known about the mechanism of calcification and whether the degradation of the matrix leads to mineralization or vice versa and whether the calcification is a kind of protective but out of control response to the vessel destruction. One protease, cathepsin K, is of particular interest as we and others have demonstrated that this enzyme is critically involved in the weakening of arteries and at the same time responsible for bone degradation.  Efforts are underway to introduce a cathepsin K inhibitor for the treatment of osteoporosis to the market.  We predict that this inhibitor will be highly beneficial to prevent arterial degradation and calcification as well.  Thus, our objectives are to understand the role of cathepsins in arterial calcification and to device strategies to treat cardiovascular diseases.

CommitteeNameEN: Cardiovascular System - B: Heart and Circulation
NomDuComitéFR: Système cardiovasculaire - B: Coeur et Circulation
TitreApplicationTitle: TLR4 signaling in acute and chronic responses to remote ischemic conditioning
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOPROTECTION; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; REMOTE ISCHEMIC CONDITIONING
Abstract-Résumé: Our research has shown a new technique called Remote Ischemic Preconditioning or RIPC, is effective at protecting the heart and other organs when their blood supply is cut off. RIPC is produced simply by repeated inflation and deflation of a blood pressure cuff on an arm or leg to temporarily cut off and then restore blood flow to that limb. Because of its simplicity, and the effectiveness in animal experiments, RIPC has moved rapidly to studies in patients with cardiovascular disease, including those undergoing heart surgery, and those being treated for heart attack and stroke. The way these benefits occur with RIPC are not fully understood but at least in part are related to reducing the amount of inflammation in the body as a whole and, in particular, within the affected area. Furthermore, we have recently shown that in addition to its immediate effects, RIPC reduces heart damage and inflammation leading to heart failure, when animals are treated daily for 28 days after heart attack. Our preliminary evidence suggests that RIPC reduces inflammation by modifying a specific immune receptor on the white cells in the blood that are responsible for inflammation. This proposal will examine in detail how RIPC modifies inflammation within the heart and prevents immediate and long-term damage.

ClasseRechercheFR: ARTHRITE/ARTHROSE; RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: The Risk of Pulmonary Embolism and Deep Vein Thrombosis in Major Rheumatic Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTH DATA; ARTHRITIS; CARDIOVASCULAR; CO-MORBIDITY; MORTALITY; POPULATION-BASED; PREVENTION INTERVENTIONS; PUBLIC HEALTH; RHEUMATIC DISEASES; RISK
Abstract-Résumé: Due to persistent inflammation, people with arthritis are at risk of developing cardiovascular complications, which are the primary cause of premature death in this population. VTE is a form of cardiovascular condition that causes blood clots in deep veins (deep venous thrombosis) of the legs that sometimes travel to the lungs (pulmonary embolism) and prove life-threatening. Despite this, up to now, research has focused on determining the link between rheumatic disorders and more common types of cardiovascular disease that cause clots in the vessels of the brain (stroke) and the heart (heart attack). To address this important gap, the primary objective of this study is to evaluate the risk of VTE in patients with key rheumatic conditions, defined as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (including lupus, scleroderma, dermato-polymyositis, Sjogren's disease, and systemic vasculitides) for our study purposes. This will be achieved by using a unique health database from British Columbia to identify the number of cases who developed VTE events for the first time after the disease. This number will be compared with the number of new cases from the general population without these diseases. Given the current research, we hypothesize that rheumatic diseases will have an increased risk of VTE. In addition, we will test if some of the anti-rheumatic treatments protect against VTE. Our results have the potential to impact the care, decrease the disease burden and improve survival of patients with arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing the burden of tuberculosis in the foreign-born through an expanded program of post-landing Immigration Medical Surveillance: a nation-wide study in Canada, 2003-2010.
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; IMMIGRATION; PUBLIC HEALTH; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada and other high-income immigrant-receiving countries, a growing proportion of tuberculosis (TB) cases are foreign-born. This trend has led to a general consensus that TB control strategies in these countries must prioritize the screening and treatment for latent TB infection in foreign-born persons. In Canada, this strategy primarily occurs within the context of the Medical Surveillance Program and is restricted to persons identified as having inactive pulmonary TB or a history of TB during an immigration medical examination. Persons referred to Medical Surveillance account for approximately 15% of foreign-born TB cases and represent a high-risk group for active TB, the likelihood of TB being four to five times that of non-referred immigrants. Nevertheless, it is probable that some immigrants not eligible for Medical Surveillance have a risk of TB that is at least as high as some referrals. The purpose of this study is to determine if the inclusion criteria for the Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC) Medical Surveillance Program should be expanded to include other immigrant groups on the basis of an equal or greater risk for active TB as current referrals. Through ongoing partnerships with Health Canada and CIC, this aim will be achieved by linking and analyzing two national datasets. The first dataset consists of foreign-born TB cases diagnosed in Canada in 2003-2010 as per the Canadian TB Reporting System. The second dataset of all foreign-born persons (referrals and non-referrals) who arrived in Canada in 2003-2010 will be provided by CIC. As the first nation-wide study that defines and compares the risk of developing active TB among Medical Surveillance referrals and non-referrals, it is anticipated that the study results will inform an evidence-based redesign of the Medical Surveillance Program that optimizes the inclusion of immigrants at high risk for active TB and leads to fewer missed opportunities for preventing TB in the foreign-born.
