TitreApplicationTitle: Parents, Sons and the HPV Vaccine: What Factors Influence Decision-Making Over Time?
Keywords-MotsClés: FOLLOW-UP SURVEY; HPV VACCINE; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS (HPV); PARENT DECISION-MAKING; PARENTS; PSYCHOSOCIAL FACTORS; RANDOM NATIONAL SURVEY; SONS; STAGES OF DECISION-MAKING; UPTAKE RATES IN MALES
Abstract-Résumé: The human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection. HPV accounts for 5.2% of the worldwide cancer burden and 90% of genital warts. An effective vaccine has been approved and recommended for both young males and females (aged 9-26 years). In Canada, publicly-funded immunization programs for the HPV vaccine are currently only available to girls aged 9-13 years. Some provinces offer catch-up programs for girls up to 18 years-old. Across Canada, vaccination rates among females are variable and insufficient to protect the entire population. Additionally, uptake rates in males are extremely low (estimated at 1-10%). Parents of boys who wish to obtain the vaccine must often assume the cost (approximately $400-$500 for 3 doses). Therefore, parents must evaluate many factors (e.g., benefits vs. cost, social influences) before deciding whether or not to vaccinate their sons. We are interested in what parents know about HPV and the HPV vaccine, their attitudes towards the vaccine and which factors influence their decision-making process. First, we will conduct a random Canada-wide on-line survey of 3000 parents of boys (aged 9-16) to assess knowledge, attitudes and beliefs about the HPV vaccine. Parents will be grouped according to their stage of adoption in the decision-making process. Second, we will conduct a follow-up study 1 year later to assess whether parents' vaccination decision status has changed and which factors influenced these changes. Furthermore, the survey data will provide us with an estimate of the most recent uptake rates in young Canadian males. This is one of the first longitudinal studies of which we are aware that aims to identify the key factors that influence changes in parents' HPV vaccine decisions over time. This innovative approach will better inform public health strategies and educational interventions towards this important population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prediction of Extubation Readiness in Extreme Preterm Infants by the  Automated Analysis of CardioRespiratory Behavior
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIO-RESPIRATOPY; EXTUBATION; MACHINE LEARNING; PATIENT MANAGEMENT; PREMATURE INFANTS; RESPIRATION
Abstract-Résumé: More than half of pre-term infants, born at 28 weeks or less, have breathing problems severe enough to require mechanical ventilation for them to survive. In deciding when to remove them from the ventilator, the physician must balance conflicting issues. On one hand, it is desirable to discontinue ventilation as early as possible to avoid the adverse side effects of ventilation. On the other hand, an infant who is removed from the ventilator too early may need to be reconnected. This is not straightforward and is associated with additional adverse side effects. At present, the physician has few tools to assist in this decision and consequently more than 25% of the attempts to disconnect preterm infants from ventilation fail. Previous results have shown that infants who can be removed from ventilation successfully have different patterns of heart rate and breathing than those who fail. We will build on these results by combining non-invasive cardio-respiratory measurements, novel advanced signal processing algorithms, and machine learning methods. These will be used to create a tool that will predict the probability that mechanical ventilation can be successfully discontinued for a particular infant. This tool will provide physicians with the quantitative information needed for the informed management of ventilation of pre-term infants and hence improve patient care

TitreApplicationTitle: Mortality risks in later life from exposure to pandemic influenza in early life:  the 1890 and 1918 influenza pandemics in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIGENIC IMPRINTING; FETAL ORIGIN HYPOTHESIS; HISTORICAL DEMOGRAPHY; IMMUNITY; INFLUENZA PANDEMIC; LIFECOURSE; MORTALITY; RECORD LINKAGE
Abstract-Résumé: The worldwide spread of a novel influenza A (H1N1) virus in 2009 reminds us that influenza still represents a significant threat to public health. As was the case during its famous predecessor in 1918, the H1N1 strain that circulated in 2009 primarily targeted age-groups that are usually spared by influenza: adolescents and young adults. This project attempts to solve the mystery of high young adult mortality during the Spanish flu pandemic of 1918. We hypothesize that exposure to a virulent strain of influenza during critical periods of development results in physiological impairments that increase the risk of death from pandemic influenza in later life. We also posit that developing specific antibodies to a given influenza strain in early life may actually subvert the immune system, thereby increasing the risk of death when the individual is infected by a novel strain in later life. We will test whether early life exposure to pandemic influenza in 1890 increased the risk of dying from influenza during the next pandemic of 1918.  To do this, we will link exact ages at death from publicly available historical records for Ontario and Quebec to information contained in census and other records that describe each individual's socioeconomic and environmental conditions during exposure to influenza and in later life. Drawing on historical demographic data and taking advantage of the most recent advances in developmental biology and immunology, this project brings a novel and exciting alternative to commonly held views about the unusual age pattern of mortality in 1918. Such knowledge could substantially improve crisis management were a new virulent and similarly age-patterned outbreak of influenza to emerge again on the world stage.

TitreApplicationTitle: Vascular inflammation in the diabetic retina: involvement of kinin B1 Receptor
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETIC RETINOPATHY; ENDOTHELIAL DYSFUNCTION; KININ; MICROANGIOPATHY; MICROCIRCULATION; OCULAR BLOOD FLOW; RETINA; TYPE 1 DIABETES; TYPE 2 DIABETES; VASCULAR INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Vision loss results from the death of neurons from the diabetic retina consecutive to edema and blood supply failure. These pathological events are due to inflammation and oxidative stress in response to increased blood sugar. We reported that the receptor B1 (B1R) for kinins, associated to inflammation, is markedly expressed in the diabetic retina. B1R is a key player in retinal vascular lesions, i.e. abnormalities in vessel morphology and function. Blockade of this receptor could prevent diabetic retinopathy. Importantly, the B1R is a valuable therapeutic target as it is expressed only in damaged tissues thereby reducing considerably adverse and side effects of drugs. The contribution of B1R in increasing the inflammation, alteration of the vascular bed of the retina, deficit of blood supply and other pathological features of the diabetic retina will be studied in rat models of type 1 diabetes. These factors will be measured in the post-mortem retina. Also, ocular treatments with a selective inhibitor of B1R will be given to prevent or reverse the development of the disease. The precise localization of B1R on retinal microvessels and other cells will be examined. Over 300 million people in the world will be diagnosed with acquired Mellitus diabetes by the year 2025. Most of them will develop a retinopathy. The present proposal may help to better understand the aetiology of diabetic retinopathy leading to vision loss. It could result in use of very potent drugs designed for retinopathy treatment and administered by eye drops.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of the transcription factor CREB in mammalian memory
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; KNOCK OUT MOUSE; LEARNING; MEMORY; MOLECULAR AND CELLULAR NEUROSCIENCE; NEUORNAL EXCITABILITY; SPINOGENESIS; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR; TRANSGENIC MOUSE; VIRAL VECTOR
Abstract-Résumé: Memory disorders, from inherited forms of mental retardation to the gradual weakening of memory with age to the ravages of Alzheimers disease, exact an increasing economic toll and dramatically affect the health and quality of life of millions. Indeed, over 30 million North Americans suffer some type of clinically recognized learning or memory disorder. As yet, there are no cures and few effective treatments for these disorders. Novel approaches to the treatment of memory impairments will benefit greatly from building on basic research studying the molecular and cellular basis of normal memory formation. Previous data from a wide variety of species from sea slugs and fruit flies to rodents and humans implicate a protein named CREB (short for cyclic adenosine 3,5-monophosphate responsive element binding protein)in the formation of long-term memory. My colleagues and I showed that increasing CREB function in a relatively small portion of brain nerve cells (neurons) enhances long-term memory formation in rodents. Our findings raise the possibility that increasing CREB function in a small portion of neurons may reverse memory deficits associated with a variety of disorders. This proposal will examine the mechanisms underlying this memory enhancement produced by increasing CREB function in a small portion of neurons and examine the potential therapeutic effects of increasing CREB function in the treatment learning and memory disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Resting-state network analysis of sensorimotor processing during the formation of memory in the human brain
Keywords-MotsClés: ARM MOVEMENT; BRAIN; FMRI; FUNCTIONAL CONNECTIVITY; MOTOR LEARNING; RESTING STATE NETWORKS
Abstract-Résumé: One of the severe limitations of using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to study control of movement is the need to prevent head movement during the MRI scan. Since all segments of the body are connected, movement of limb segments tend to perturb head position. The supine posture and restricted space within the bore of the magnet also prevents subjects from performing many of the most interesting activities. We have developed a new technique to study changes how different areas of the brain communicate that does not require any movement during brain scanning. This technique is called resting-state network analysis. As the name suggests the subject simply relaxes while the brain scan is being performed. We propose to use this technique to investigate how functional connections in the brain change while learning and recalling a new skill. The methods which we are developing have potential applications for improving therapeutic techniques for rehabilitation of impaired movement after damage to the brain.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Peroxisome Assembly
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; ESCRT COMPLEX; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; MODEL ORGANISMS OF HUMAN DISEASE; ORGANELLE BIOGENESIS; PEROXISOME; PEROXISOME BIOGENESIS DISORDERS; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Peroxisomes are one kind of intracellular membrane-enclosed compartments called organelles. Peroxisomes perform a number of different important biochemical functions, most notably in fat metabolism and the detoxification of reactive oxygen species like hydrogen peroxide. The necessity of peroxisomes for normal human development and physiology is underscored by the lethality of the human peroxisome biogenesis disorders, genetic diseases in which peroxisomes fail to be assembled correctly in the cell. As the pathway that leads to the formation of peroxisomes has been highly conserved during evolution, we exploit yeast as a model system to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the peroxisome biogenesis disorders. Of the thirteen genes which when mutated give rise to the peroxisome biogenesis disorders, twelve were first identified in yeast. Therefore, yeast is a valid and valuable system with which to investigate the molecular bases of the peroxisome biogenesis disorders. Our research aims for a comprehensive molecular understanding of how peroxisomes are made in the cell and how this assembly pathway goes awry in cells of peroxisome biogenesis disorder patients, with the ultimate goal of developing a rational therapeutic intervention for treating these patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mining the ADNI database - what can we learn about Alzheimer's?
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTATIONAL ANATOMY; MR IMAGE ANALYSIS; SIGNAL PROCESSING
Abstract-Résumé: The ADNI project provides publicly-available, standardized MR imaging database with a focus on Alzheimer's disease. This initiative is a unique and invaluable research resource allowing researchers to develop and validate computational brain MR image analysis tools applicable for extracting signatures of Alzheimer's disease seen in brain MR images. These signatures can be used for early detection of disease. The brain MR image measurement algorithms developed on this database can also potentially be used in the clinic for assisting in assessing the location and extent of brain damage caused by the disease and whether ongoing treatments have had an effect in slowing the progression of the disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; CEREBRO-VASCULAR PATHOLOGY; DISEASE TRAJECTORY; HIGH-DIMENSIONAL NEUROMORPHOMETRY; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; VASCULAR DENSITY MAPS; VASCULATURE TREE SEGMENTATION; WHITE MATTER HYPERINTENSITIES SEGMENTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Our group intends to use our two novel automated methodologies to assess cerebro-vascular disease (CVD) as a co-morbidity with Alzheimer's in the large-scale ADNI database. The first technique estimates CVD burden from standard T2- and PD-weighted scans, while the second provides a neuromorphometric measure related to disease state. Together, they provide a comprehensive estimate of concurrent disease burden in individual subjects. We will characterize this relationship throughout the natural history of mild cognitive impaired individuals, at high risk of progression to Alzheimer's, in the ADNI dataset. To our knowledge no other group has analyzed ADNI data retrospectively to test this important neuropathological interaction.

Abstract-Résumé: The CTSN was launched in 2007 to develop and conduct studies, mostly controlled randomized trials, to evaluated surgical interventions and related management approaches, for the treatment of cardiovascular diseases. The network was established to provide the rigorous evidence upon which key clinical treatment strategies could ultimately be based. However, the clinical research enterprise is generally challenging and frequent difficulties with patient recruitment, as well as retention into trials are experienced. It is well known that surgical trials are especially challenging for a variety of reasons. The CTSN has not been immune to such difficulties and although current trials are anticipated to complete enrolment within the initial grant budget, there remains a strong need for better approaches to identify, recruit, randomize, and retain patients and logistically manage cardiothoracic surgical trials. Thus, the object of this funding opportunity announcement is to solicit for experienced Core Clinical Centers that propose innovative strategies to successfully operate trials within the preview ofthe CTSN.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and epigenetic hierarchies distinguishing pluripotent and trophoblast stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIGENETICS; EXPRESSION PROFILING; PLURIPOTENCY; PREGNANCY DISORDERS; REGULATORY NETWORKS; STEM CELLS; TROPHOBLAST
Abstract-Résumé: The human placenta is a critical organ for the development of the baby and for the ongoing health of the mother. It is made up of different cell types but the most important is the trophoblast, which acts as the interface between mother and baby. Any problem in the development or function of the trophoblast from the very earliest stages can lead to early pregnancy loss, preeclampsia and small birthweight babies.  Trophoblast forms very early in development at the same time as the cells that can make all the tissues of the baby itself are set aside. Embryonic stem cells arise from these so-called pluripotent cells and are powerful tools for modeling development and treating degenerative diseases. Trophoblast stem cells can also be generated from the early mouse embryo and they can be used to study placental development and pregnancy disorders. Much is known about the genes and epigenetic (non-DNA heritable changes) profiles that make embryonic stem cells pluripotent. Much less is known about how they decide not to make trophoblast and how the trophoblast cell identity is established.  We will use different methods from the six different labs in Canada and Japan to develop a complete understanding of the molecular epigenetic networks that distinguish pluripotency and trophoblast development. We will then use this information to generate human trophoblast stem cells by transforming human pluripotent cells or placental cells with appropriate combinations of trophoblast-specific regulators. These cell lines will be great tools to explore human placental development and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a treatment for Friedreich ataxia based on the administration of TALE proteins targeting the frataxin promoter.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL PENETRATIN PEPTIDE; FRATAXIN; FRIEDREICH ATAXIA; GENE EXPRESSION; TALE PROTEIN
Abstract-Résumé: Friedreich's ataxia is caused by a reduced expression of frataxin due to a longer GAA trinucleotide repetition in intron 1 of this gene. A potential treatment for Friedreich's ataxia is thus to increase frataxin gene expression. The gene coding for TALE proteins can be modified to produce proteins that attach specifically to a desired DNA sequence. We have already produced 12 genes encoding proteins TALEFrat specifically targeting different sequences of 12 nucleotides, located in the DNA region that controls the human gene frataxin expression. The TALEFrat genes were fused with an amino acid sequence, called VP64, and we showed that it induced the expression of a gene located after the targeted sequence. The first objective of our research project is to determine whether the TALEFrat/VP64 plasmids also increase frataxin in normal and Friedreich patient fibroblasts. YG8 mouse is a model of Friedreich's ataxia in which the two murine frataxin genes have been rendered nonfunctional. However, this mouse contains an additional gene containing the frataxin gene of a Friedreich patient. We will therefore verify whether the TALEFrat/VP64 increase the expression of frataxin in fibroblasts from these YG8 mice. The experiences of this first objective will enable us to select the TALEFrat/VP64 most effective in culture cells. The TALEFrat/VP64 does not normally penetrate in cells. However, these proteins can be fused with a sequence of amino acids that allows it to enter cells. The second objective is to verify that the most effective protein TALEFrat/VP64 coupled with such a peptide can enter in human and YG8 cells in culture and in YG8 cells following injection in the mouse blood. The third objective is to verify whether the TALEFrat/VP64 administrated to YG8 mice induce the expression of frataxin and prevents the development of symptoms of Friedreich ataxia in this animal model.

TitreApplicationTitle: Automated dementia diagnosis based on texture analysis of neurologic images
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AUTOMATED DIAGNOSIS; BRAIN IMAGING; COMPUTERIZED IMAGE ANALYSIS; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: When a patient first shows signs of possibly having a form of dementia, even experienced physicians using the best diagnostic tools currently available have difficulty in accurately determining what type of dementia that patient might have or even if the signs are simply those of normal aging. This is unfortunate, as treatments for one type of dementia may not be effective for another type and treatments may be of most benefit if given to patients early in their disease progression. The intent of this proposal is to develop methods, based on computerized image analysis of medical images, to diagnose different types of dementia earlier and more accurately than could otherwise be done. The methods will synthesize information from several types of images, including types that show details of brain anatomy (such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging, MRI) and types that show variations in brain physiology (such as Positron Emission Tomography, PET, or Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography, SPECT). To derive the methods, we will make use of data collected during the large, multi-centre, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) study. This and similar large databases contain patient images and information about the patients' dementias that we can use to train an automated diagnostic system. This system should aid physicians in determining the most appropriate course of treatment for patients with dementia and should also help in the development of new treatments by helping in the selection of patients for clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modelling the heterogeneity of brain aging and dementia risk - integrating brain structural and functional changes
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE BIOMAKERS; BRAIN; DATABASES; DEMENTIA; DYNAMICS; HETEROGENEITY; MODELING; NEUROIMAGING; VASCULAR RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) becomes more common as the brain ages, but not everyone is affected equally. Understanding why brain aging is slower in some people than in others, and why some people can even improve, would offer a major advance for successful risk factor control and dementia prevention. Even seemingly small changes in bio-markers and vascular risk factors can accumulate to affect memory and thinking. Current methods require such changes to being fairly big, and to go mostly in one direction, i.e. getting worse. Our method allows many small changes to be combined. Likewise, we developed a measure that combines Brain Atrophy and Lesions in a single Index (BALI). We also developed a new analytical method, which takes into account that small improvements are also often seen. Together, the new methods allow us to precisely model the dynamics of brain aging: not just decline, but also stability and improvement, and link it with risk and protective factors. This CIHR grant provides a perfect opportunity to develop this important research. We will extend these novel studies to validate and generalize the methods using different neuroimaging databases, including both large multi-site consortia databases and existing local datasets. We will link brain MRI data with data on biomarkers, brain function, and with clinical and lifestyle assessments. In this way, we will look at the relative contributions of brain structural changes on brain function in both men and women. The research will allow us to study how the heterogeneity in brain structure and function evolve. Results of these analyses will benefit a better understanding of brain aging that can potentially lead to the slowing of it and the prevention of dementia. This research will be conducted collaboratively in two established neuroimaging centers in Halifax and in Toronto and will involve first line knowledge users, to promote knowledge translation and clinical application.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetics and stemness in human hematopoiesis and leukemia: a new generation of stem cell targeted regenerative and leukemia therapeutics
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CHROMATIN OPENNESS; EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; HEMATOPOIESIS; HISTONE MODIFICATION; HUMAN HEMATOPOEITIC STEM CELLS; HUMAN PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; HUMAN PROGENITOR CELLS; LEUKEMIA; RNA SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Human blood cells are created in a highly organized process dependent on hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), which are at the beginning of a line of cell divisions that create families of cells. These cell families, or lineages, mature into blood cells e.g. red and white blood cells. There is evidence that leukemia cells are organized similarly with leukemic stem cells (LSC) at the top of this lineage system. Recently, there have been technical advances in the study of epigenetics; a mechanism that describes how genes are turned on or off without changing the sequence of the DNA. In the mouse, we know epigenetics are important in generating mature cells from HSCs, but we do not know what happens in human blood cell changes or in human leukemia. About 40,000 transplants occur annually worldwide; the majority of these are a part of cancer therapy or for other blood diseases including aplastic anemia and immune deficiency. Despite this success, many hurdles remain. Most transplant recipients are genetically different from their donor and only one third of patients who require a transplant have access to a related donor. Making human HSCs from another source of stem cells could be a potential solution. There are current methods of engineering blood stem cells but they lack the ability to generate HSCs. In parallel, there has been little progress in the cure rates for elderly patients with leukemia.  Some evidence points to epigenetics as a new target for leukemia. To answer these questions, we plan to compare epigenetic data from HSCs and other mature blood cells with HSCs and mature cells made from engineered stem cells. We will also compare normal epigenetic data to epigenetic data from human bulk and LSC enriched fractions. We hope to improve methods for engineering stem cells made from HSC, better understand leukemia and potentially identify new therapeutic targets. We will also provide a new major resource with our epigenetic road map of the blood system and leukemia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Diagnostics and Prognostics for Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias: Machine Learning Analysis of Existing Neuroimaging Datasets
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S; BIOMARKERS; DEMENTIA; DIAGNOSIS; MACHINE LEARNING; MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; METABOLOMICS; NEUROIMAGING; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; PROGNOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease affects about 1 in 5 people age 75-84 and 2 in 5 people over 85. The treatments that are currently available for Alzheimer's are more effective when they are started early. Our goal in this study is to develop new diagnostic and prognostic tools that can help clinicians to treat Alzheimer's disease more quickly and more effectively.  The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), the Australian Imaging Biomarkers & Lifestyle Flagship Study of Ageing (AIBL), and the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS) are three research projects on Alzheimer's disease.  These projects assembled large databases of brain imaging scans as well as genetic and metabolomic data from hundreds of patients with Alzheimer's and healthy individuals. ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS have generously made these very valuable, expensive datasets available to the research community. We will use advanced machine learning algorithms, also known as artificial intelligence, to analyze these datasets. Specifically, we will look for biomarkers that could allow for earlier, more accurate diagnosis and prognosis of Alzheimer's disease thereby allowing for earlier, more effective treatment for the condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Directing Cellular Identity to Move Towards Progenitor Cell Therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BASED THERAPY; CELL THERAPY SAFETY; DISEASE MODELS; DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; EPIGENETICS; GENE CORRECTION; IN VITRO DIFFERENTIATION; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; REPROGRAMMING; RETT SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Stem cells have sparked huge hopes for the prospect of curing a range of devastating diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, diabetes, spinal cord injury and several forms of blindness. The recent discovery that stem cells can be made from biopsies from patient's own skin has further increased the hopes of finding real cures for these conditions without the need for transplantation from donors, and so avoiding the risk of tissue rejection. The process that takes place when a skin cell becomes a stem cell (the so-called "reprogramming") is, however, not yet fully understood. Many aspects of this process still need to be carefully investigated before we can claim them suitable for medical application. To bring these tremendously promising prospects to the bedside of patients so desperately waiting for a cure, we will have to find ways to efficiently produce large numbers of cells for transplantation while at the same time safeguard against the formation of cancer-producing cells. A large international effort has recently been launched by one of the team laboratories to determine exactly how reprogramming happens inside the cells. Building on the results of this endeavor, six world-class laboratories have joined forces to make future stem cell-based therapies both efficient and safe: the Canadian Nagy, Ellis and Tremblay and the Japanese Yamada, Woltjen and Shinkai laboratories.  The aim of this proposal is to carefully scrutinize the data we have at hand about the reprogramming processes to find cells that will be the most suitable for regenerative medicine therapies: efficient and safe from a tumorigenic perspective.  We will first evaluate our initial findings using a mouse model, and later follow up our leads in a human system. Finally, we will produce cells for preclinical studies that are both efficient to treat Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy as well as safe from the perspective of not producing tumors in the recipient.

TitreApplicationTitle: Delineating pathways causing vulnerability to neuropsychiatric symptoms in Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; GENETICS; MRI; NEUROPSYCHIATRIC SYMPTOMS
Abstract-Résumé: Neuropsychiatric symptoms in Alzheimer's disease and the related dementias are among the most disabling and difficult aspects for caregivers and treating health professionals to manage. Despite the high prevalence of these behaviours, little is known about the factors which lead some patients to develop florid behavioural symptoms while others may progress to severe dementia without experiencing such phenomenon. The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) offers a rare opportunity to study a large number of well characterized patients in different stages of Alzheimer's disease, to address these critical gaps in our knowledge about why and how some patients with Alzheimer's disease develop delusions, hallucinations or extreme disinhibition.  In this project, we will analyze the detailed information collected on Alzheimer patients with and without these behavioural symptoms, to evaluate which brain regions and functions seem to be affected when neuropsychiatric symptoms are present. We will also link this analysis to an evaluation of patients' genotypes- specifically a comparison of the versions of genes related to neurotransmitters and Alzheimer's disease that may differ between patients with and without specific neuropsychiatric symptoms.  The project is significant because it will begin to determine the factors which influence the development of neuropsychiatric symptoms in Alzheimer's disease. This knowledge is critical because these symptoms and behaviours are some of the most difficult, devastating, and costly aspects of the disease for families and caregivers. The knowledge gained in this study will aid in the development of new treatment approaches for neuropsychiatric symptoms in Alzheimer's disease as well as other dementias and neuropsychiatric disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Riboswitch ligand inhibitors for MRSA and staphylococci / Ligands de riborégulateurs agissant comme antibiotiques contre le SARM et les staphylocoques
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; INFECTION MODELS; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; MICROBIOLOGY; MRSA; RIBOSWITCH; RNA; STAPHYLOCOCCI; STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS
Abstract-Résumé: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is causing dramatic increases in the incidence of antibiotic resistant infections in Canadian hospitals and across the globe. Disturbingly, resistant pathogens such as MRSA are now also emerging in the community, infecting persons of all ages often with no apparent risk factor. MRSA strains are usually resistant to multiple drug classes (beta-lactams, macrolides, aminoglycosides, tetracyclines) and resistance to vancomycin, the last efficient drug against this pathogen, is already reported since 2002. The three major problems caused by MRSA are mortality, wasted time and cost for the healthcare system.  The development of a novel class of antibiotics that tackles MRSA infections would be most welcome.  Recently, our research led to the discovery of a new antibacterial target that is shared among some bacterial pathogens and that is absent from the mammalian host.  Of special interest, this new target is an RNA molecule with a regulatory function (a guanine riboswitch) that is essential to certain bacteria. Our work also led to the identification of a small-molecule ligand with drug-like properties able to bind the guanine riboswitch and prevent expression of essential genes with subsequent bactericidal action.  We further demonstrated the antibacterial activity of one of such antibiotic compounds in experimental therapies for Staphylococcus aureus intra-mammary infections (mastitis) in mice and cows.    The general objective of this research proposal is to provide the necessary proof of principle to further develop novel and potent antibiotics to control infections in humans caused by the antibiotic multi-resistant superbug MRSA. The demonstration of compound efficacy in animal models that are relevant to MRSA infection in humans (CIHR-POP, Phase I) will reduce the risks associated with the commercialization of these molecules and attract a partner for Phase II.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aging and large-scale brain networks: Using functional connectivity and structural covariance modeling to predict conversion from normal to pathological aging.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMERS DISEASE; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; MEMORY; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; MRI; NEURAL NETWORKS
Abstract-Résumé: The social, economic and personal burden of Alzheimer's Disease or Related Dementias (ADRD) is steadily increasing in Canada. It is anticipated that in the coming 30 years over 1 million Canadians will be affected by ADRD with an economic burden of over 150 billion dollars. At the same time our understanding of the brain changes that lead to ADRD is increasing rapidly and interventions to slow the disease course continue to emerge. In this context, early detection of AD onset is becoming critically important.  This research project will use brain imaging data to study how connections between brain regions change into older adulthood and in those individuals who progress to ADRD. The primary aim of the research is to develop measures of brain connectivity that could be used to predict the onset of ADRD at the earliest stages, potentially even before behavioural symptoms arise.  By developing reliable and robust brain-based measures that portend the onset of ADRD, we aim to expand the window of intervention for persons at risk for ADRD. Early intervention can alter the progression of the disease, increase quality of life and extend functional independence for individuals, thereby reducing burdens on family, care-givers and the Canadian Health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuroimaging Profiles of Neuropsychiatric Subgroups in Mild Cognitive Impairment and Early Alzheimer's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; CLUSTER ANALYSIS; DELUSIONS; MILD COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; MRI; NEUROIMAGING; NEUROPSYCHIATRIC SYMPTOMS; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; PET
Abstract-Résumé: Delusions, rigidly-held false beliefs, occur in up to 50% of people with Alzheimer's disease (AD), as well as in some people with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) who do not yet have dementia. People with delusions are at risk of early institutionalization, and their caregivers experience increased stress and burnout. More research is needed to understand why some people develop delusions while others do not. Our study will use data from the Alzheimer Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), a large multicentre study involving brain imaging, genetic tests, and measures of psychological functioning in people with MCI and AD assessed several times over up to 4 years. We will examine MRI and PET images to identify specific changes in brain structure and function associated with the development of delusions in people with MCI and AD. We will also look at factors, such as visual-spatial ability and genetic markers, which may provide clues to the causes of delusions. Increased understanding of how brain changes lead to delusions will enable better treatment strategies. Information about risk factors will make it easier to predict which people with MCI or dementia will develop delusions. Early identification will promote timely intervention to support these individuals and their caregivers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Advanced post-processing of diffusion tensor imaging data for early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; COMPRESSED SENSING; DIAGNOSTIC AND PROGNOSTIC BIOMARKERS; DIFFUSION TENSOR IMAGING; EARLY DIAGNOSIS; FIBRE TRACTOGRAPHY; HIGH ANGULAR RESOLUTION DIFFUSION IMAGING; STATISTICAL INFERENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia associated with loss of synaptic integrity and neurodegeneration, which lead to memory impairment and other cognitive problems. Although there is currently no known treatment that slows the progression of AD, strong evidence supports that early detection and intervention may play a critical role in delaying the onset or progression of the disease. Accordingly, the main objective of this research project is to develop new biomarkers for early diagnosis of AD. The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) provides an exclusive opportunity for the research community to investigate various AD-specific neuroimaging biomarkers. Among diverse clinical data available through ADNI is the data acquired by means of Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI). As opposed to other imaging modalities, DTI is unique in its ability to provide information on the connectivity and micro-structural integrity of white matter, both of which are known to be affected at the early stages of neuropathological AD. Despite its successful application to early diagnosis of the disease, however, the potential of DTI is far from being fully exploited. The main reason for this is insufficient descriptive power of DTI modelling, which limits its applicability for analyzing the complex organization of neural fiber tracts. To alleviate this problem, we will reanalyze the DTI data using a two-stage strategy. At the first stage, we will exploit some recent advances in modern information processing to extrapolate the DTI data into High Angular Resolution Diffusion Imaging (HARDI) measurements, which are known to provide much more accurate assessment of the diffusivity of white matter as compared to DTI. At the second stage, the resulting HARDI data will be used to elucidate advanced diffusion metrics, which can serve as predictive and/or early diagnostic biomarkers, and could be used as covariates in future treatment or prevention trials.

Abstract-Résumé: High levels of blood cholesterol are associated with serious cardiovascular complications including stiffening of the arteries and atherosclerosis, ultimately leading to heart attacks. Reduction of circulating levels of the bad cholesterol carrier, known as low density lipoprotein (LDL), is the best treatment to prevent long term cardiovascular disease and its associated complications. Since the early 1990s prescriptions of the oral drugs known as `statins` saved many lives and improved the health of millions of people. However, as much as 20% of the patients either do not respond to statins or are intolerant to this drug due to side effects. Accordingly, alternative drugs are needed for these patients and to further reduce LDL in many hypercholesterolemic individuals. The present invention describes a single domain antibody approach to block the function of the LDL regulating protein PCSK9 that we discovered in 2003.  The project aims to validate the identified antibodies in model mice, as a prelude to pre-clinical studies.

ProgramNameEN: Proof of Principle Program - Phase I
NomDuProgrammeFR: Programme de démonstration des principes - phase I
TitreApplicationTitle: PrOTYPE: An Enabling Technology to Improve Ovarian Cancer Care
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER TYPE PREDICTION; DIAGNOSTICS; GENE EXPRESSION; GENOMICS; HISTOLOGICAL SUBTYPE; OVARIAN CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Ovarian cancer is the most lethal gynecological cancer and survival rates have not significantly improved for over 30 years. Recently, researchers have recognized that ovarian cancer is a series of different subtypes that have distinct genetic changes, responses to treatment, and outcomes. It follows that these subtypes should be regarded as different diseases and researched and managed accordingly. Treatment of ovarian cancer that considers subtype will rely on accurate subtype classification. To address this, we have developed a novel test called PrOTYPE (Predictor of Ovarian cancer Types) that predicts ovarian cancer subtype. PrOTYPE is able to classify ovarian cancer subtypes with >94% accuracy compared to an expert gynecological pathologist. It is important to note that not every hospital has an expert gynecological pathologist. PrOTYPE analysis, however, would be able to provide expert-quality review to all clinical centres, either through direct testing or sending samples to a centralized clinic with PrOTYPE. PrOTYPE also provides accurate classification on pre-surgical biopsies. This is revolutionary as these samples are too small to be reliably classified by pathologists using current methods. Pre-surgical biopsies are collected when ovarian cancer patients have disease that is so extensive that the choice is made to treat first with chemotherapy, to reduce the burden of tumour before surgery. This is in contrast to typical treatment, which begins with surgery before administration of chemotherapy. PrOTYPE classification will allow for the first time, subtype-specific treatment decisions to be made from pre-surgical biopsies. We believe that PrOTYPE classification of ovarian cancer types will result in more personalized management of ovarian cancers which will lead to better outcomes and increased survival for women with this disease.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Programme de démonstration des principes - phase I
ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; ARTHRITE/ARTHROSE
TitreApplicationTitle: Development and Testing of Small Molecule Allosteric Modulators for the Treatment of Pain.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOSTERIC; CANNABINOID; DRUG DISCOVERY; PAIN
Abstract-Résumé: The body contains receptors which are activated by compounds called 'cannabinoids'.  These are called cannabinoid CB1 and CB2 receptors. Cannabinoids called 'endocannabinoids' are produced in the tissues where they interact with cannabinoid receptors to modulate physiological responses. Endocannabinoids are involved in leaning and memory, appetite stimulation, pain processing and mood. The levels of these compounds in the body increase in certain diseases where they act to relieve symptoms.  Compounds which inhibit the enzymatic breakdown of the endocannabinoids are being tested in clinical trials for the treatment of pain, depression and anxiety. Activators or 'agonists' of the CB1 receptor are not ideal as drugs because they produced unwanted psychoactive side-effects.  We have discovered compounds which act in such a way that they do not activate the CB1 receptor, but rather enhance the effects of the endocannabinoids. In this application we will modify the chemical nature of this compound to make it a better drug and we will investigate the effectiveness of the compound as a new therapeutic treatment for various types of pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of the Mammalian Membrane Two-Hybrid (MaMTH) technology, a novel protein interaction and drug discovery tool
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER RESEARCH; DRUG ASSAY PLATFORM; HIGH-THROUGHPUT PROTEIN INTERACTION ASSAY; MAMMALIAN MEMBRANE TWO HYBRID; PROTEIN PROTEIN INTERACTION; SIGNALLING PATHWAYS
Abstract-Résumé: Every cell in the human body contains proteins. They are major part of the skin, muscles, organs, glands and also body fluids. While carrying out the essential functions of our body, proteins don't work in isolation, they form living machines, complexes of dozens of proteins that fit together like a jigsaw puzzle. To see the whole picture and to understand how biochemical process work in our cells, scientists need to identify which pieces, or proteins, fit next to or interact directly with each other.  Among all proteins in human cells, a special role can be assigned to those associated with cellular membranes (so called membrane proteins) because their malfunctioning contributes to many human diseases including cancer, cardiovascular, neurodegenerative diseases and developmental disorders. However, due to their complex chemical features the study of membrane proteins has historically been extremely problematic making the study of their interacting proteins even more challenging.  The purpose of this proposal is to develop and implement a novel assay that can detect and monitor protein-protein interactions in human cells for this most difficult class of proteins. Such a method may have great applications for the field of molecular medicine since it may be used to identify novel proteins as components of many essential cellular processes. Furthermore, this assay will be of importance for the field of drug discovery since it may be used to identify drugs that disrupt a defined set of membrane protein interactions that occur only in a certain human disease.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Programme de démonstration des principes - phase I

TitreApplicationTitle: Phase 1 Trial of a novel transvenous phrenic nerve pacer for diaphragm activation in mechanically ventilated critically ill patients.
Keywords-MotsClés: DIAPHRAGM PACING; PHRENIC NERVE STIMULATION; PROOF OF PRINCIPLE
Abstract-Résumé: Mechanical ventilation is a life-saving technology upon which the intensive care unit (ICU) is based; yet, it is a double-edged sword which induces direct and indirect lung damage and can rapidly lead to diaphragmatic weakness and dysfunction. Caring for patients in the ICU is exceedingly expensive; $2.5 billion or 0.5% of the GDP in Canada alone. To address these challenges we are developing the Lungpacer® Breathing System for use in the critically ill which is a novel, temporary, easily placed phrenic nerve pacing system which consistently and safely activates the diaphragm and whose format and insertion are similar to catheters commonly used in the ICU. It is anticipated to have a major impact by reducing the direct and indirect harms associated with mechanical ventilation, maintaining diaphragmatic thickness, strength and endurance, and finally, by facilitating strengthening of the diaphragm in those patients already on a ventilator who have already undergone diaphragmatic atrophy. The diaphragm is the primary muscle responsible for breathing and by preventing it from weakening by disuse on a mechanical ventilator we will reduce the time it takes for a patient to wean from a mechanical ventilator, where about 40% spent on a mechanical ventilator is during weaning. The Lungpacer® Breathing System is a novel way to treat patients on mechanical ventilation and will significantly reduce healthcare costs through improved patient outcomes, where an anticipated 10% reduction in days on the ventilator will yield a healthcare payer return on investment of over 10:1 and facilitate more efficient use of ICU resources. This grant will support the critical transition step from testing in animals to the initial testing in consenting adults in both short term (90 minutes) and longer term (7 day) trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Anti-Biofilm Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; ANTIBIOTICS; ANTIMICROBIAL PEPTIDES; BIOFILMS; DRUG FORMULATION; INNATE DEFENCE REGULATOR PEPTIDES; MEDICAL IMPLANTS; PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA; STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS
Abstract-Résumé: The current therapy for infectious diseases is facing twin threats. On the one hand antibiotic and antiviral resistance is rising rapidly; on the other there are relatively few novel compounds or strategies under development or entering the clinic. The frequent growth of bacteria as biofilms, which are surface-associated bacterial communities that grow in a protective matrix, is of great concern. Biofilm infections are especially difficult to treat with conventional antibiotics, and are a major problem in trauma patients with major injuries and individuals with an implanted medical device, causing 60% or more of all clinical infections. Based on our breakthrough observation that a human peptide LL-37 is able to inhibit biofilm formation and dissolve existing biofilms, we screened for and obtained small, protease-resistant peptides that have potent broad-spectrum anti-biofilm properties. Here we propose to perform pre-clinical investigations on these peptides as a novel treatment for biofilm infections, preparatory to commercialization.

TitreApplicationTitle: Real-time Ultrasound Quantitative Elastography of the Prostate
Keywords-MotsClés: 3D ULTRASOUND; IMAGE GUIDANCE; PROSTATE BIOPSY; QUANTITATIVE ELASTOGRAPHY; ULTRASOUND ELASTOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is diagnosed when the biopsy results confirm the presence of cancerous cells. Prostate cancer biopsy involves collecting tissue cores from the prostate using a needle under trans-rectal ultrasound guidance. The goal of the radiologist who performs the biopsy is to provide a random sampling of the prostate, as cancer can appear anywhere in the prostate.  The goal of this project is to develop an ultrasound transducer that, in addition to conventional ultrasound images, provides a quantitative map of the prostate stiffness. Such a quantitative map of the tissue stiffness is called an elastography image, and can be thought of as being an objective form of palpation. With ultrasound elastography images, a radiologist can target biopsies to cover more of the stiffer tissue or tissue with variable stiffness, instead of trying to find cancer in a random manner. As cancer has been shown to be stiffer than normal tissue, it is hoped that such an approach will be more effective at finding cancer, thus reducing the number of biopsies required.

TitreApplicationTitle: Injectable dense collagen-silk fibroin derived polypeptide hydrogels for bone regenerative therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE REGENERATION; DENSE HYDROGELS; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; INJECTABLES; REGENRATIVE MEDICNE; SILK FIBROIN; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: The need to augment or replace bone defects may be caused by age related disease, trauma, or degenerative conditions. Current bone repair techniques possess inherent limitations. Therefore there is an ever-increasing demand for new biomaterials for the repair, replacement, construction or augmentation of bone. We have developed a dense collagen gel hybridized with anionic silk fibroin derived polypeptides, which can potentially be used to induce osteogenesis in bone regenerative medicine. The overall objective of this project is to determine its potential as a medical device and its utility in cell delivery for the repair of bone defects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of new class of antiviral drugs for influenza A virus infections
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRAL; CHEMOTHERAPEUTIC AGENTS; INFLUENZA A VIRUS; NUCLEOSIDES; RNA POLYMERASE
Abstract-Résumé: An estimated one billion people get infected annually with seasonal influenza around the world, with 3-5 million severe cases and 500,000 deaths, especially in vulnerable populations such as children, the elderly, and immunocompromised people.  Besides seasonal influenza, intermittent pandemic influenza poses real threats with increased mortality and morbidity.  In the last century, the world has been severely hit by influenza pandemics three times (1918, 1957 and 1968).  We have witnessed the emergence of two highly pathogenic influenza strains with pandemic-potential H5N1 (2003) and H1N1 (2009), which infected millions in the last decade alone.  An outbreak of pandemic influenza similar to the 1918 Spanish flu could claim lives of more than 100 million young healthy people worldwide within a short period of time.  Vaccines are available for preventing influenza infections; however, they have several limitations such as efficacy and availability, which is dependent on timely production and supply. Further, influenza vaccines must be updated every year since viral surface protein changes easily.  Emerging resistance to currently available anti-influenza drugs undermines the desperate unmet medical need for discovery of novel anti-influenza drugs.  Therefore, new classes of effective agents, working through different mechanisms, are urgently required.  Recent research in our laboratory has led to the identification of a new family of compounds that are potent and selective inhibitors of various influenza virus strains.  These molecules also possess activity against drug-resistant strains.  The overall goals of the proposed research project are the investigation of the antiviral effectiveness of these promising agents in animal models that will advance our technology and develop commercializable candidate drugs for the treatment of influenza infections.  These studies will provide a major impact on the health of Canadians and people worldwide.

Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most common cause of adult-onset dementia, is a major threat to the autonomy, mobility, and overall functionality of persons in the developed world. UBC scientists have identified and characterized a defined specific target for Abeta oligomers, known to be toxic in Alzheimer's disease. Cangene Corporation, a Canadian biotechnology company, has licensed the technology to develop antibody treatments for Alzheimer's. UBC and Cangene will now establish efficacy in mouse models of the disease by testing active vaccination and passive injection with oligomer-specific epitope and antibodies, respectively.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Novel Regenerative Drug Therapy to Restore Natural Insulin Secretion in Diabetes Mellitus
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES MELITUS; DRUG DISCOVERY; INGAP ANALOGUES; INGAP-ISLET NEOGENESIS ASSOCIATED PROTEIN; ISLET NEOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: INGAP Peptide (Exsulin) is a first-in-class pancreatic islet regeneration agent that regrows insulin-producing cells in the diabetic pancreas. The lead peptide candidate is currently in Phase 2 development for treatment of insulin-dependent diabetes. Regeneration of pancreatic islets restores the metabolic hormones responsible for normal physiologic glycemic control and promotes a return of natural insulin production, can lower HbA1c with fewer hypoglycemic events, and decrease the chronic and life-threatening complications of diabetes, thus representing a significant breakthrough in diabetes management. In the proposed study, new and more potent analogues of INGAP peptide will be developed to enhance its activity in patients with diabetes.

However, most of the additives used in the  drug industry have important limitations that prevents their use in specific conditions. We have recently discovered a new type of gel that combines a unique set properties that cannot be found in any other drug additive. Accordingly we are applying for funds in order to proof that this new gel can be used as  drug additive at an industrial level, and surpass currently available products.

TitreApplicationTitle: Treatment Planning and Guidance Software Platform for Minimally Invasive Ablation Therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPY; MINIMALLY INVASIVE THERAPIES; OPTIMIZATION; RADIOFREQUENCY ABLATION; SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT; TREATMENT PLANNING AND GUIDANCE
Abstract-Résumé: A new, minimally invasive approach to treating cancer tumours has been gaining momentum over the past few years. These treatments deliver a needle-like device to the tumour through a small puncture hole in the skin under the guidance of imaging technology such as ultrasound or computed tomography (CT). Once in place, either heat (thermal ablation) or cold (cryotherapy) is generated in a controlled fashion to destroy the tumour but spare the surrounding tissue. This approach has shown promise in its ability to treat cancer with fewer side effects and shorter recovery times than surgery, yet surgery remains the option of choice. There are several barriers to widespread adoption of minimally invasive therapies. They can effectively treat only small tumours, their success rates, in terms of complete tumour ablation, are lower than surgery, and they have long learning curves.  We believe that software can address many of the issues that are limiting the growth of minimally invasive therapies. Treatment planning software can help physicians define approaches and treatment protocols that are personalized to each patient. Optimization software can ensure the most effective treatment with the least invasiveness. Guidance tools can ensure that the treatment is delivered according to plan. We propose to build a software platform for minimally invasive ablation treatment planning and guidance by combining tools that have already been developed at University Health Network. We will model our software and approach after radiation treatment planning, which has been a standard in radiation therapies for many years.  We believe treatment planning and guidance software will increase the effectiveness and safety of minimally invasive procedures, leading to wider use. Patients will benefit from treatments that offer the same benefit as surgery with fewer complications and shorter hospital stays. The Canadian people will benefit from lower health care costs for cancer treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Influence of motor behaviour on sensory feedback to primary motor cortex
Keywords-MotsClés: NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PRIMARY MOTOR CORTEX; STRETCH REFLEXES; UPPER LIMB; VOLUNTARY MOTOR CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Humans are able to perform a broad range of motor skills, from the rapid spinning of an elite diver to the precise staccato of a violinist. Recent theories suggest that sensory feedback from the limb (and vision) are essential for performing these voluntary motor skills. In particular, the theory suggests feedback is always present and that the properties of the arm and the movement goal influence the use of this feedback for controlling the limb. Our recent studies on humans show how feedback from the limb is used to modify and correct perturbations (unexpected bumps applied to the limb) during reaching or other motor tasks. The timing of these corrections suggest that they are generated from signals transmitted down to the spinal cord from primary motor cortex. Primary motor cortex is known to be important for voluntary control, but its use of feedback for control is not well recognized nor understood. The present proposal will highlight how feedback to this brain region scales with perturbation magnitude, interacts with spinal activity and importantly is modified based on the behavioural goal. This research will change our view on how primary motor cortex controls movement by emphasizing the importance of sensory feedback. This knowledge provides a foundation for understanding how various neurological disorders such as stroke impact brain function and motor performance. The behavioural tasks used in this proposal will also be used in parallel studies to quantify motor deficits in various patient groups.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Programme de démonstration des principes - phase I
TitreApplicationTitle: Buccal Lamin A as a Novel Biomarker for Frailty
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BIOMARKER; CARDIAC SURGERY; FRAILTY; LAMIN
Abstract-Résumé: Given the aging patient population and rising healthcare costs, physicians have become acutely aware of the need to prevent patients from receiving costly but un-useful procedures.  Age alone is a flawed way to predict which patients will suffer poor outcomes when exposed to invasive procedures.  Frailty is a geriatric condition that reflects biological age ("true age") and presents a better way to characterize elderly patients and their risks.  Several tools exist to measure frailty (questionnaires, physical tests) but their adoption has been limited because they are felt to be subjective and time-consuming.  A biomarker for frailty would be highly desirable but has yet to be developed.  We discovered a novel association between frailty and lamin A - the nuclear protein commonly known for its role in the accelerated aging syndrome Progeria.  We found that lamin A levels declined with age, and furthermore, declined in parallel with frailty status.  Since we and others noted that lamin A was not expressed in blood, we derived a test to measure lamin A levels in buccal cells harvested from a simple cheek swab.  Using a quantitative flow cytometry platform, we quantified lamin A levels in an accurate and reproducible manner.  This grant involves developing our own monoclonal antibodies against lamin A and its precursors and further optimizing and validating our diagnostic test to meet the rigorous standards needed for commercialization.  The application of our test will be evaluated in clinical studies where we will use our lamin A test as a biomarker for frailty to predict which patients are likely to suffer poor outcomes after cardiac surgery.  This is central to the contemporary practice of personalized medicine, where we can now consider offering less invasive therapies to our vulnerable patients.  Beyond exploring lamin A as a predictor of outcomes, we will measure lamin A in healthy volunteers of various ages to determine age-adjusted normative values.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the relationship between climate change and food-borne diseases: Leveraging technology and scientific evidence to predict global food-borne disease outbreaks
Keywords-MotsClés: CLIMATE CHANGE; FOOD SAFETY; FOOD-BORNE DISEASES; GEOSPATIAL MAPPING; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; SURVEILLANCE
Abstract-Résumé: No study has systematically examined the impact of climate patterns on global food safety, and specifically on the emergence of food-borne diseases. This topic has been identified as a key research priority by the Public Health Agency of Canada, the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization (WHO). Drawing on United Nations climate data and novel technologies for automated disease outbreak detection (HealthMap), this study will explore the potential relationship between climate change and the global incidence of food-borne diseases, via three Aims: Aim 1: Validate the use of infectious disease surveillance data sources for tracking spatiotemporal trends in global food-borne disease risk and burden. This study will assess the validity of the HealthMap outbreak detection system for accurately detecting the global burden of food-borne diseases; clarify biases inherent in the automated surveillance system; and enhance validity of subsequent model-building processes. Aim 2: Build spatiotemporal models to estimate the effects of climate change on food-borne disease burden globally. Drawing on validated data from Aim 1, the study will identify food-borne diseases most sensitive to climate change, and build disease-specific predictive spatiotemporal models of the effects of climate on food-borne disease risk and burden. Aim 3: Forecast potential effects of global climate change on select food-borne diseases. Using models developed in Aim 2 and climate change data, this study will evaluate the predicted change in the spatiotemporal dynamics of select food-borne diseases under different climate change scenarios. Findings from this study will inform Health Canada's public health strategies aimed at preventing and mitigating the impacts of food-borne diseases. Globally, they will inform WHO food safety monitoring and evaluation strategies, enhancing global health security measures under the International Health Regulations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inflammatory markers, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and the longitudinal course of adolescent bipolar disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENT; BIOMARKER; BIPOLAR DISORDER; BRAIN-DERIVED NEUROTROPHIC FACTOR; CARDIOVASCULAR RISK; CLASSIFICATION; ENDOTHELIAL FUNCTION; GENOTYPE; INFLAMMATION; LONGITUDINAL STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a severe recurrent mood disorder that affects 2-5% of adolescents and adults. BD involves repeated episodes of mania (elated or irritable mood together with other symptoms) and depression (sadness or lack of interest/pleasure along with other symptoms). Until now, the assessment of adolescents with BD has been highly subjective. BD that occurs during adolescence is considered even more severe than in adults.  This makes the search for biological markers particularly important. Another major problem in BD is early heart disease. Biological markers may also improve our understanding of the link between BD and heart disease. The overall aim of this study is to learn whether specific markers in the blood can help us better understand the course of symptoms, and the increased risk of heart disease, in BD. We are using an advanced technique to examine blood vessel functioning. This gives us an estimate of future heart disease risk. We are comparing symptomatic adolescents with BD to healthy adolescents. We are also looking at changes in biological markers and blood vessel functioning after BD symptoms improve. We predict that the same biological markers are linked both to symptoms and heart disease risk in BD.

Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CHEMOTHERAPY; DRUG DELIVERY; NANOPARTICLE
Abstract-Résumé: Chemotherapy is often the standard of care for advanced cancer. However, non-specific delivery of the chemotherapeutics results in significant side effects, reducing the therapeutic outcome and patients' quality of life. Dr. Li's research is focused on developing innovative drug delivery technologies to improve the specificity of drug delivery to tumors to increase cancer therapy and patients' quality of life. He will focus on further development of two proprietary technologies invented in his lab for the next five years: First, a polymeric conjugate platform, named Cellax, designed to target water insoluble drugs to tumors. Second, a temperature sensitive formulation developed to burst-release drugs within locally heated tumors. The ultimate goal is to translate these technologies into clinical use to enhance cancer therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathways to weight: The influence of neighbourhood environments on the weight status of adults
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSITY; DIET; INEQUALITIES; NEIGHBOURHOOD ENVIRONMENT; OBESITY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; URBAN PLANNING
Abstract-Résumé: More than one-half of Canadian adults are currently overweight or obese and this proportion is likely to increase in the future due to our increasingly unhealthy lifestyles. There has been recent focus on the built environment's role in determining behaviours related to overweight and obesity, including physical inactivity and poor diet. Opportunities for regular physical activity or healthy diet are not always available, particularly in less affluent neighbourhoods. Socioeconomically disadvantaged groups are at higher risk of obesity, are less physically active, and have poorer diets yet our understanding of how contextual (built characteristics) and compositional (socioeconomic status) neighbourhood characteristics influence physical activity, diet, and weight status are still rudimentary, particularly in the Canadian context. This project will involve a random cross-section of 2497 adult study participants from Calgary (Alberta). Participants will complete a postal survey that will capture their physical activity-related energy expenditure, caloric intake, height and weight, and socio-demographic characteristics. Participants will also receive a body measuring tape to capture waist and hip circumference. Indices reflecting the neighbourhood environment's supportiveness for physical activity and a healthy diet within 1-km of participant's homes will be estimated from existing municipal databases and field audits of streetscapes. The relationships between neighbourhood environment indices and socioeconomic status, energy expenditure and caloric intake, and multiple indicators of weight status (BMI and measures of central adiposity including waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio) will be estimated. Findings will be useful for informing urban planning and policy decisions that may support healthy weight status and socioeconomic health-related disparities among Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 and pancreatic beta-cell neogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA-CELL; DIABETES; DIFFERENTIATION; GROWTH FACTOR; INSULIN; LINEAGE TRACING; PANCREAS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes mellitus, a metabolic disorder often associated with obesity, affects more than 2 million Canadians and 190 million people worldwide. The increased prevalence of diabetes constitutes a significant socio-economic problem. Thus, there is great need for new treatments.  Insulin is produced in the pancreas by specialized cells, the beta-cells. Beta-cells play a central role in the development of diabetes. Type 1 diabetes results from selective destruction of beta-cells, whereas type 2 diabetes arises from a progressive deterioration of beta-cell mass and function. Thus, the reduction in the number of beta-cells is a common feature of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The ability to stimulate beta-cell regeneration could be a novel approach in the treatment of diabetes.  Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) is a promising drug in the treatment of diabetes. It's long-acting analog is commercialized under the name Byetta. A growing body of evidence suggests that GLP-1 could promote the formation of new beta-cells in the pancreas. The formation of new beta-cells is termed "beta-cell neogenesis". In this proposal, we seek to demonstrate that GLP-1 promotes beta-cell neogenesis and to identify the molecular mechanisms involved in the process.

TitreApplicationTitle: Isolating Neurocognitive Intermediate Phenotypes in Borderline Personality Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER; COGITIVE NEUROSCIENCE; ENDOPHENOTYPE; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a serious form of mental illness affecting 2% of adults and upwards of 20% of psychiatric inpatients. These patients place an enormous financial burden on the Canadian healthcare system because they typically require frequent hospitalizations and intensive outpatient psychiatric services to treat suicidality and other dangerous behaviours. Efforts to understand the neurobiological causes of BPD have met with limited success. This is because BPD represents a heterogeneous clinical disorder comprised of multiple complex symptoms and traits which may be supported by distinct neurobiological systems. Identification of intermediate phenotypes, or biological liability markers, for BPD may help to unravel the diverse causes of this illness and optimize treatments for subsets of patients with distinct forms of this illness. The goal of this research is to isolate the most promising neurocognitive intermediate phenotypes for BPD as part of a family study to determine whether the first-degree relatives of these patients show abnormalities on cognitive testing and functional brain imaging procedures. Using information derived from these measures, a second study will determine whether specific patterns of brain activation can predict which BPD patients will achieve the greatest benefit from the most effective psychological treatment for reducing self-harming behaviours in this illness. The results of this research program have the potential to improve the future care of these patients by helping to construct the road-map for isolating which genes confer susceptibility to BPD, thereby focusing efforts on early intervention and prevention. Importantly, this research will also assist in directing appropriate treatments to target subsets of BPD patients with specific genetic and neurobiological vulnerabilities, helping to improve the effectiveness of interventions and increasing access to treatment services for patients with this illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Metallo-beta-lactamases; mechanistic and evolutionary studies.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; BETA-LACTAMASE; EXPERIMENTAL EVOLUTION; INHIBITOR BINDING; MOLECULAR EVOLUTION; MUTATIONAL EFFECTS
Abstract-Résumé: Pathogenic bacteria, such as P. aeruginosa. E. coli and K. pneumonia, can cause serious infectious diseases such as pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and diarrhea. These bacteria are becoming resistant to many commonly used antibiotics. In addition, the spreading of such pathogenic bacteria that are resistant to multiple antibiotics has become more rapid during the past decade. The resistant bacteria area serious threat to Canadian and global health, and new strategies are needed to combat them. The underlying cause for bacterial resistance is the action of a group of enzymes called beta- lactamases, which destroy beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin. Moreover, on-going changes in bacterial beta-lactamase genes in nature are producing more potent enzymes to destroy even our newest antibiotics. This proposal describes research to study the ways that beta-lactamase enzymes change and adapt to antibiotics. We will combine experiments to identify mechanisms of change with detailed studies of enzyme function so that we can develop ways to block their activity. Ultimately, the information obtained in this research program will be used to develop novel, persistent and sustainable antibiotics and inhibitors against pathogenic bacteria.

Abstract-Résumé: The muscles from the lower limbs are commonly affected in persons suffering from a chronic respiratory disease. This is important because this may cause exercise intolerance, quality of life and even life expectancy. This is also important because muscles can be treated.  The purpose of this research program is to try to understand why do persons with chronic respiratory disease such as emphysema have problems with their muscles. We hope that our research will lead to better treatment of this condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of mTORC1 downstream pathway in regulation of breast cancer tumorigenesis.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; GENETICS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is a malignant disease with high prevalence in Canadian population. Across the country there will be an estimated 23000 new cases of breast cancer and 5100 cases of breast cancer-related death in 2012. This disease is characterized by uncontrolled growth and proliferation of the previously normal cells which eventually may invade the surrounding tissues and progress to metastasis. Unfortunately, we still do not fully understand how the normal mechanisms which control the processes of cell growth and proliferation go awry in cancer cells. The mTORC1 complex is known to be one of the major suspects and we have some promising new data that suppression of this complex may help in treatment of breast cancer. Also by using cell culture methods we have recently discovered that two master regulator of protein synthesis, called 4E-BPs and S6Ks are mainly responsible for the effect of mTORC1 on cell growth and proliferation. However, it is not clear whether the role of 4E-BPs and S6Ks in regulation of cell growth and proliferation also has any actual significance in development of breast cancer in the tissue. In addition, the molecular mediators downstream of 4E-BPs and S6Ks and their significance in breast cancer biology are not fully understood either. This project therefore aims to use a comprehensive approach to fully delineate the role of 4E-BPs and S6Ks in breast cancer development and determine their downstream mediators and effectors. By understanding this pathway, we will be able to design novel therapeutic approaches for treatment of breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Brain-Based Measures of Alcohol Sensitivity in Early Adulthood
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL DEPENDENCE; ALCOHOL SENSITIVITY; ENDOPHENOTYPE; FMRI
Abstract-Résumé: Alcohol dependence is a common, costly disorder with a lifetime prevalence of 10-12% in Canada. Characterizing biological risk factors is critical for identifying high-risk groups and tailoring interventions. One promising approach is to identify endophenotypes that index genetic risk for the disorder and that may provide clues as to neurobiological liability factors.  Sensitivity to alcohol is a promising endophenotype that appears to predict future risk for alcohol dependence. However, prior research is characterized by two notable methodological limitations. First, most studies rely on participants' subjective responses to alcohol as the primary phenotype of interest. Second, most studies use oral alcohol administration, which inevitably yields high variability in blood alcohol profiles. These approaches can increase measurement error, reducing sensitivity to detect biological influences.  Little is known about neural correlates of alcohol sensitivity. The proposed research will integrate fMRI with novel alcohol administration methods to study neural correlates of alcohol sensitivity. In addition to having expertise in fMRI, our research team is the first in Canada to implement a novel intravenous ethanol infusion protocol (the alcohol clamp) for human studies. This project will integrate fMRI and alcohol clamp methods to allow precise control over brain ethanol exposure.  Young social drinkers (N=80) with and without a family history of alcohol dependence will complete alcohol and placebo fMRI sessions. Prospective data will be collected to determine whether neural correlates of alcohol sensitivity predict drinking outcomes. This research may inform future genetic studies and facilitate identification of neurobehavioural markers of alcohol dependence risk. Clarifying neural correlates of alcohol sensitivity may help to identify individuals at relatively greater risk for alcohol dependence, thus informing refinement of diagnostic and treatment approaches.
