TitreApplicationTitle: Medical Annotation of the Human Genome Sequence
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOGENOMICS; DISEASE PREDISOPOSITION; DNA & CHROMOSOME VARIATION; GENOMIC MICROARRAY; QUANTITATIVE & COPY NUMBER ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Rapid progress in nanotechnology and information science is bringing whole genome sequencing into the affordable realm to millions of persons and useful for many purposes in health research. Building from the experiences and infrastructure of the first five years of this GSK-CIHR Pathfinder Program Endowed Chair, I will enhance our contributions in using whole genome sequencing to study the mechanisms and genes involved in disease. I will continue to study the genetic factors involved in autism spectrum disorder using the new genome sequencing approaches, and the lessons learned from this project will also inform on other disease study designs. To maximize the translational impact, I will partner with clinical geneticists, counsellors, molecular diagnostic experts and others. The funding will enable me to consolidate my overall research program, and to initiate "blue-sky" ideas holding the potential to re-define methodologies and dogma in the field.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innovation in Addiction Treatment (IAT) Research Program
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIORAL METHODOLOGY; INNOVATIVE TREATMENT; OPIOID DEPENDENCE; OPIOID SUBSTITUTION TREATMENT; PUBLIC HEALTH; RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Injection-drug users are extremely susceptible to drug-related health risks, including HIV, hepatitis C, and overdose. Although treatments for drug addiction are available, they are not always effective for those with the most severe cases of addiction. A key issue is that many members of this vulnerable population exist outside of the health care system and, as a result, injection-drug users continue to place themselves, and those in their immediate community, at risk of drug-related health risks.  The Innovation in Addiction Treatment (IAT) research program focuses on studying alternative drug addiction treatments that can be used to reach vulnerable populations existing outside of the health care system. For example, previous research studies in Europe and Canada have shown that medically prescribed heroin can effectively attract and retain injection-drug users into the health care system and can ultimately improve the health of this vulnerable population. Unfortunately, the negative stigma attached to the medical use of heroin is a barrier to its implementation in many settings. Based on a previous study, the IAT research program is testing whether licensed pain medications can successfully treat the most severe cases of heroin dependency and study how this approach compares to medically prescribed heroin. After patients are effectively stabilized with injection treatment, it will determine if pain medication administered as an oral liquid can be used instead of injections. The program pays special attention to sub-populations of women and Aboriginal people that have experienced high rates of victimization, including physical and sexual abuse, or violent or traumatic experiences which dramatically impact their health.  These treatments might directly benefit the people with the most severe cases of heroin addiction and will also measure the beneficial impacts in their communities as well.

TitreApplicationTitle: Psychobiological sequelae of victimization in adolescents and emerging adults: An investigation into the early roots of mental health and behavioral problems
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; DNA METHYLATION; EARLY ADVERSITY AND VICTIMIZATION; HAIR CORTISOL; HPA AXIS; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MENTAL HEALTH PROBLEMS; PHYSIOLOGICAL MEDIATORS; SENSITIVITY AND CUMMULATIVE EFFECTS OF ADVERSITY; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Youths growing up in adverse environments such as neglectful or abusive families are more susceptible to develop mental health problems, to experience difficulties with their peers and to encounter problems with the law throughout their lives. While these associations are widely known, from the general public to policy makers, it has proven difficult to translate knowledge into actions that effectively prevent these outcomes that pose a danger to the person and society as a whole. One explanation might be that we know very little about the processes whereby early victimization gets "under the skull, skin and cells" to instigate long-term risk towards mental health (e.g., depression, conduct disorder, substance use disorders). Animal research has taught us that early adversity jeopardizes brain development and disrupts our biological systems designed to help us cope with stress. These changes are believed to affect long-term vulnerabilities to mental health. The objective of this 5 year research plan is to further understand how early victimization influences adolescents' and young adults' biological functioning and how these relate to increased vulnerability to mental health problems and behavioral difficulties. Three research initiatives will be pursued to tackle this question, each using distinct but complementary strategies to generate a more comprehensive portray of the long-term impact of victimization that can be implemented into more effective strategies for adolescents and young adults who experiences childhood victimization to help them reverse their susceptibilities by fostering their potential.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Epidemiology of Resilience Following Child Maltreatment Exposure: An Examination of Protective Factors Across the Lifespan
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD MALTREATMENT; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENDER; INTERVENTION; LIFESPAN APPROACH; MENTAL HEALTH PROMOTION; POPULATION HEALTH; PROTECTIVE FACTORS; RESILIENCE; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: To date, child maltreatment research has focused mainly on risk factors and poor outcomes with fewer studies examining resilience following child maltreatment and protective factors associated with mental health (e.g., absence of mental disorders and high quality of life). Resilience is generally described as the ability to maintain or regain mental health after adverse exposure. A protective factor is an indicator that is associated with an increased likelihood of a positive outcome. A review of the literature indicated that supportive relationships show a consistent association with healthy outcomes. What is still largely unknown is the prevalence of mental health in the general population following child maltreatment exposure in comparison to non-maltreated individuals. What other protective factors are associated with mental health and how can resilience be enhanced? Fostering resilience after child maltreatment has the potential to improve mental health for individuals and populations. The current proposal is unique because it will lead to new knowledge that will guide the development of intervention strategies to promote protective factors in facilitating resilience among individuals with a history of child maltreatment exposure across the lifespan-from adolescence to later adulthood. An epidemiological perspective will be applied to understand the prevalence of child maltreatment and mental health, the relationship between protective factors and mental health cross-sectionally and over a 3-year period. Noted strengths of this research include accessing large nationally representative Canadian and US data, examining sex and gender differences, using a lifespan approach, accessing longitudinal data, using high quality measures of child maltreatment and mental health, and inclusion of several protective factors in one study.

TitreApplicationTitle: Synaptic Plasticity in Neocortical Microcircuits
Keywords-MotsClés: LTD; LTP; MICROCIRCUIT; NEOCORTEX; NMDA RECEPTOR; STDP
Abstract-Résumé: We study learning and memory in the brain, because this is important for essentially everything that the brain does. Neuroscientists believe that learning and memory as well as the refinement of neuronal circuits during development are due to changes in synaptic connections among interconnected neurons, known as synaptic plasticity. How the young brain is wired up as it grows and develops is still not fully understood. For example, the visual brain regions must actually learn how to see -- this is not innate but acquired via synaptic plasticity. This complicated process can go wrong in so-called synaptic diseases. We study synaptic plasticity in cells of the the visual brain region, how it works, and what it does to brain function.  Synaptic plasticity is complex. It varies with cell type and brain region, because different cell types have different functions in the brain. To understand these functions, we investigate the different forms of plasticity that different brain cells are equipped with.  The properties of different forms of synaptic plasticity are determined by their mechanisms, so to understand learning in brain we investigate these different mechanisms. For example, it should be possible to turn learning on and off so that only useful information is learned in the brain. We have discovered one such switch in the brain, which are now exploring.  We also study the consequences of synaptic plasticity. Synaptic plasticity is for example needed to wire up the visual brain regions correctly so that we can see. But synaptic plasticity is also often involved when things go wrong. For example, sudden damage to the brain may produce too much activity in brain cells, which may via plasticity generate epilepsy in an otherwise healthy brain. Understanding synaptic plasticity is thus important for understanding the brain in health as well as in disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Executive Functioning in Children and Adolescents with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD)
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE OUTCOMES; BEHAVIOUR; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONING; FETAL ALCOHOL SPECTRUM DISORDER; INTERVENTION; PRENATAL ALCOHOL EXPOSURE; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) leads to physical, mental, behavioral, and learning disabilities as a result of prenatal alcohol exposure. Children with FASD have difficulties with executive functions (EF) including planning, thinking flexibly, problem solving, and working memory (cool  EF) as well as tasks involving emotion and decision making (hot EF). Individuals with FASD also display adverse outcomes including behavior problems, mental health issues, delinquency, and substance abuse, as well as problems adaptive to society. The goals of the proposed project are to examine: 1) the pattern of hot and cool EF difficulties in children and adolescents with FASD compared to control children 2) how both hot and cool EF contribute to adverse outcomes; 3) whether EF can be improved with targeted cognitive interventions. Participants will include children and adolescents (aged 11 to 17 years) with FASD and non-exposed controls. They will complete tests of cool and hot EF and their parents/caregivers will complete various rating scales regarding the participants behavior. Next, two groups of children with FASD will receive a targeted intervention: one focused on working memory and one focused on self-regulation, the third group will serve as a waitlist control. We hypothesize that children with FASD will have deficits in both hot and cool EF, but that they will have greater impairment on hot EF measures. We also expect that EF (and particularly hot EF) will be associated with adverse outcomes in FASD. Finally, we expect that the EF interventions will lead to improvements in EF. The research will inform our understanding of EF in FASD and thus has implications of the health and development of children and adolescents with FASD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating the Physical and Functional Interactome of Mitochondria in Yeast
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY PURIFICATION; INTERACTOME; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MITOCHONDRIAL BIOLOGY; MITOCHONDRIAL GENETIC INTERACTIONS; MITOCHONDRIAL PROTEIN COMPLEX; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria generate the majority of a cell's energy supply and are required for a large number of diverse cellular functions, including ion homeostasis, respiration, and cell death. Mitochondrial biochemical processes are highly integrated both within and outside the mitochondria (i.e. extramitochondrial pathways). Due to their importance in basic cellular processes, defects in mitochondrial function cause or contribute to a diverse set of human diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. Yet, despite their known importance, the role of mitochondrial dysfunction in human diseases is often difficult to pinpoint due to incomplete information about mitochondrial proteins, interactions, and pathways. This proposal seeks to address this deficit by creating detailed mitochondrial physical (protein-protein) and functional (gene-gene, or genetic) interaction maps. Large-scale proteomic and genetic screening procedures, optimized by the proposed research, will be used to comprehensively identify the physical interactions, multiprotein complexes, and pathway relationships among mitochondrial genes in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Physical interaction data will be combined with complementary information on epistatic relationships among these same genes to guide identification of functional pathways and essential mitochondrial complexes. This integrative approach will uncover novel functional mechanisms in mitochondrial biology, facilitating discovery of new therapeutic targets for the treatment of mitochondrial diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES DE SOMMEIL; MALADIES ORGANIQUES DU SYSTEME NERVEUX CENTRAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Pathophysiology of Sleep Disorders: a Multimodal Neuroimaging Approach
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN IMAGING; EEG; FMRI; HYPERSOMNIA; NARCOLEPSY; SLEEP; SPECT
Abstract-Résumé: The causes of sleep disorders are still not clearly understood. Disorders of sleep are however very frequent, cause threatening risks of accidents, and impair productivity and quality of life. I propose to use sophisticated neuroimaging techniques to identify the brain regions responsible for disorders of sleep. This approach will particularly be applied to the study of specific sleep disorders responsible for sleepiness during the day: narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia.  Patients with narcolepsy inappropriately fall asleep during the day for short periods of time without being able to resist the urge to sleep. Narcolepsy is often accompanied by sudden episodes of muscle weakness triggered by emotions and termed cataplexy. Sleepiness in narcoleptic patients with cataplexy is related to a lack of a substance in the brain called hypocretin. However, some patients with narcolepsy never experience episodes of cataplexy. Idiopathic hypersomnia closely resembles narcolepsy, and also involves daytime sleepiness but no cataplexy. There is no lack of hypocretin in patients with narcolepsy without cataplexy and idiopathic hypersomnia, and their causes are thus poorly understood. Finally, all these patients with daytime sleepiness also have a poor quality of sleep at night with frequent awakenings. The reasons for such sleep disruption remain unclear.  My objective is to use brain imaging during wakefulness and sleep in narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia: 1. to elucidate the causes of daytime sleepiness, 2. to understand the causes of sleep disruption in these patients. This modality of investigation will be further applied to other sleep disorders, such as sleepwalking, and to sleep disturbances in neurological disorders. Identifiying the brain regions responsible for sleep disorders will not only improve our understanding of the causes, but will also allow to better diagnose, better predict the evolution, and ultimately better treat these disabling disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: A comparative and cross-jurisdictional research program on work and health
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPARATIVE HEALTH RESEARCH; ECONOMIC SECURITY; HEALTH INEQUALITIES; LABOUR MARKET EXPERIENCES; LONGITUDINAL SURVEY ANALYSES; MULTI-COUNTRY COMPARISONS; OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH; SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC POLICY; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS; WORKERS COMPENSATION
Abstract-Résumé: My proposed program of research concerns how we can develop social, economic, and workplace policies to reduce health inequities over the working life course. The program is organized around two research areas.First, building on existing and emerging national and international research collaborations a series of comparative and cross-jurisdictional studies on occupational health and safety and workers' compensation will be conducted that have the focus of identifying differences in policies and practices that could lead to safer workplaces, reduced work-related injury and diseases and promote effective and timely return to work for workers who are injured or become ill due to work. Second, a series of comparative and cross-national studies on the health effects of availability of, and the nature of, work will be conducted. This research builds on previous scholarship that found that the negative association between unemployment and health was smaller in societies with greater economic and social supports for unemployed workers. It will examine a broader range of work experiences and health outcomes across a set of high-income countries that have different ways of organizing and structuring their labour market. This research program will advance our understanding of work-related health inequalities in Canada and internationally. It innovates by developing and extending comparative methods and by building and extending data and research partnerships that will have long-standing and practical impact. Its focus in investigating contextual effects across jurisdictions - whether they are institutional or structural aspects or specific policies - will provide evidence on the mechanisms through which we can effectively intervene in improving health in the workplace and in reducing work-related health inequalities.

Abstract-Résumé: Infectious diseases are the most common cause of death in children worldwide, and also contribute to death, disability and decreased quality of life in people of all ages. The advent of routine vaccine programs has been hailed as one of the most important interventions, other than clean water, in public health.  This research program will take place at the Canadian Center for Vaccinology (CCfV), in Halifax, Nova Scotia, which is a collaboration of Dalhousie University, the IWK Health Centre, and Capital Health. This integrated, interdisciplinary research program brings together investigators from diverse disciplines (basic biomedical, clinical, and social sciences and the humanities) to focus on vaccine discovery, evaluation, and implementation through knowledge translation. The funding from the Chair will allow the applicant to focus on immunization strategies that protect children, from the fetal period through to adulthood. In particular, development and improvement of vaccines, vaccine presentation (how the vaccine is given to the recipient), and vaccine programs that prevent influenza and Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) and other clinically significant respiratory pathogens in both healthy and high-risk children, their families and communities will be the target of the applicant and the CCfV team.

TitreApplicationTitle: Computational deconstruction of pain processing
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTATIONAL NEUROSCIENCE; DYNAMICAL SYSTEMS THEORY; NEURAL CODING; NEURONAL EXCITABILITY; NEUROPATHIC PAIN
Abstract-Résumé: Recall a bad sunburn. Imagine the searing pain caused by your shirt collar touching your neck, or by the shower water on your back. Stimuli that normally attract no attention, or that should be soothing, now make you recoil in pain. If the sunburn was instead a nerve injury, the same hypersensitivity and spontaneous burning pain might develop, but never relent.      Pain caused by damage to or dysfunction of the nervous system is known as neuropathic pain. This type of pain affects a staggering one in 15 people and remains notoriously difficult to control with available treatments - morphine may actually make it worse. Unlike "normal" pain, neuropathic pain exists in the absence of noxious input to the nervous system, which points to neural processing within the pain pathway itself as having somehow gone awry. But how? And how do we fix it?      Sensory information is encoded in the brain by the rate and patterning of action potentials. Action potentials, or spikes, are short pulses of electricity generated by individual nerve cells. Accurate perception of sensory input thus depends on neurons generating spike trains correctly. If spike generation were to become abnormal, information could be lost or corrupted, producing negative (loss-of-function) or positive (gain-of-function) neurological symptoms. Spike generation and neural encoding of sensory information are thus inextricably linked and are crucial issues for basic neuroscience and for clinical neurology.       The overarching goals of my research are to understand the neural coding of pain signals and how aberrations in that neural coding give rise to neuropathic pain. We do this using computer simulations, mathematical analysis, and an array of experimental techniques. By unraveling precisely how pain information is encoded by the nervous system and how that encoding is disrupted after nerve injury, we hope to develop new therapies to eliminate neuropathic pain.

TitreApplicationTitle: KATP Channel: Electrical Transduction of Cellular Metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICS; CHANNELOPATHY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; GENETIC MUTATION; ION CHANNEL; KATP CHANNEL; METABOLISM-EXCITATION COUPLING; PATCH CLAMP; POTASSIUM CHANNEL
Abstract-Résumé: Many diseases are caused by a disruption of mechanisms that regulate voltage across cell membranes. The most frequent culprits in these 'membrane excitability disorders' are proteins with 'transporter' or 'channel' functions. Our research is focused on ion channel proteins, which form pores in cell membranes that allow charged ions to pass through, generating electrical currents and influencing the membrane voltage. Much like household lights, these ion channel proteins can be switched on or off, by opening or closing 'gates' in the ion-conducting pore, and the mechanisms that control this process are collectively referred to as 'gating'.  We are currently studying a family of ion channels known as inwardly-rectifying potassium (Kir) channels, which regulate diverse processes, from beating of the heart, to hormone release. Recent studies have linked genetic mutations in Kir channels to cardiac arrhythmias, vascular defects, and severe disorders including Andersen's syndrome, Bartter's syndrome, and DEND (Diabetes with Epilepsy and Neuromuscular Defects), demonstrating a broad spectrum of physiological roles of these channels. Our focus is the KATP channel - a remarkable Kir channel type that is regulated by the 'fuel' (ATP) that drives all cells, and is therefore a sensor for the metabolic state. These channels generate an electrical signal correlated with cellular metabolism, and this serves as a critical trigger for insulin release from pancreatic beta-cells. KATP channel mutations are recognized as an important cause of (and therapeutic target for) genetically inherited insulin disorders, ranging from diabetes (too little insulin released) to hyperinsulinism (too much insulin). Additionally, KATP channels are the most densely expressed potassium channel in the heart, but their cardiovascular function remains enigmatic and controversial, underscoring the need for further investigation of regulatory mechanisms of this ion channel type.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of early adversity on the developing serotonin system in humans: A monozygotic twin study of epigenetic mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH WEIGHT; EMOTION REGULATION; EPIGENETICS; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; NEURODEVELOPMENT; SEROTONIN
Abstract-Résumé: A number of studies have shown that individuals born to mothers who were exposed to severe stressors during pregnancy are at increased risk of developing psychological problems later in life. The brain chemical serotonin may be important in this process. Animal studies have shown that adversity during pregnancy can alter the activity of serotonin and the function and structure of brain regions playing a role in the regulation of emotions in the newborn. These alterations can persist until adulthood. In the proposed project, we will investigate whether these long-lasting alterations also occur in humans. To study this, adolescents will undergo a brain scan (called fMRI) while viewing faces with emotional expressions. This is a standard procedure to measure, in the laboratory, how the brain reacts to situations that elicit emotions. Adversity will be indexed by birth weight since lower birth weight is indicative of greater adversity during pregnancy. We expect that birth weight will predict the function of those parts of the brain that are important in emotion regulation. We will also investigate one of the mechanisms by which adversity during pregnancy may affect the brain: via changes in gene expression. One of the genes that we will look at is the serotonin transporter, a gene that determines how much serotonin is used in the brain. These questions will be examined in twin pairs that have been followed almost yearly since they were born. We hope that this project will increase our understanding of the specific role of early environmental influences on brain development, gene expression and mental health. Results should eventually lead to a better understanding of possible early ways to foster optimal brain development and prevent mental health problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Viral and Human Predictors of Reponses to HIV Therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; DRUG RESISTANCE; GENOTYPING; HIV; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; PHARMACOGENETICS THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: HIV is a virus that destroys the immune system. If untreated, it typically leads to the fatal disease called AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome) within 10 years. Over 70,000 Canadians have HIV. HIV infection can be treated with a life-long drug cocktail known as highly active retroviral therapy or HAART. This therapy has transformed HIV into a more manageable chronic condition. HIV treatment works by greatly reducing the amount of virus in the bloodstream. This not only prevents AIDS, but also reduces the chances of transmitting HIV to others. Treating HIV therefore yields both individual and public health benefits. Our group has spearheaded the "Treatment as Prevention" strategy in British Columbia, with the goal of virtually eliminating AIDS and HIV transmission.  President Obama has embraced it as a cornerstone of the US approach in Africa, seeking an AIDS-Free Generation. However, resistance to these drugs can occur and be the major cause of treatment failure, threatening the success of these initiatives. Using cutting-edge DNA sequencing technologies, we will develop new methods for personalized delivery of HIV therapies:  1) We will introduce an improved HIV drug resistance test based on the latest DNA sequencing technology and share our methods and computer software with laboratories worldwide. The benefits of this improved test will be increased numbers of patients receiving effective HIV treatments.  2) We will implement new systems for real-time HIV drug resistance surveillance in Canada. This active monitoring approach will detect geographic or population "hotspots" with high rates of drug resistance, reducing the risk of transmission of HIV and drug resistant HIV in the population.   3) We plan to develop and validate improved methods for individualised treatment of HIV based on human genetics. The benefit of this testing would be reduced rates of unwanted drug side-effects and a lower risk of needless medication exposure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Estimating Health Service Utilization Associated with Multimorbidity: A Comparison of Self-Reported Health Service Utilization and Chronic Disease Status Data with Routinely Collected Administrative Health Care Utilization Data in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATABASE DATA; AGING; CHRONIC DISEASE; HEALTHCARE UTILIZATION; SELF-REPORTED QUESTIONNAIRE DATA
Abstract-Résumé: While much is known about the health care utilization associated with individual chronic conditions, less is known about health care utilization associated with multiple chronic conditions. At best, treating diseases in isolation is inefficient and can lead to duplication of care, however there is evidence that resulting fragmented and poorly coordinated treatment can be harmful for patients with multimorbidity. The problem is that Canadian health services research to date has used an overly simplistic approach to describing multimorbidity; little data is available on specific factors associated with, or modifying the relationship between, multimorbidity and health care utilization.  Attempts to study the impact of multimorbidity are complicated by the lack of consensus on how to define and measure the construct. As well, one must consolidate and interpret evidence from different data sources. Large health care utilization databases are also frequently used to study health service use and disease status. Prior methodologic studies have compared the agreement between health care utilization data from self-report and administrative sources but none have incorporated the concept of multimorbidity. We propose to link individual-level data from Ontario residents 45 years and older participating in the Canadian Community Health Survey 2007/2008 with administrative databases to address the following objectives:   1)To compare the agreement between different sources of multimorbidity and health utilization data; and  2)To examine the impact of using different definitions of multimorbidity, including specific constellations of chronic conditions, on estimates of health care utilization. 3)To provide population-based evidence on how multimorbidity is associated with healthcare utilization and how this association is modified by other factors such as age, sex, and working status.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of indiscriminate cytokine signalling
Keywords-MotsClés: CO-INFECTION; CYTOKINE REPORTER MICE; CYTOKINE SIGNALLING; CYTOKINES; DENDRITIC CELLS; IMMUNOLOGY; PARASITE INFECTION; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Our immune system is our chief defence against infection, but it is a double-edged sword. Inappropriate or over-exuberant immune responses can be harmful or even fatal. The optimal response is one that is strong enough to clear the pathogen but not so strong that it also kills the host, and I am working to understand how that balance is achieved. I study a family of signalling molecules known as cytokines, soluble messengers used by cells of the immune system to communicate with one another. It has been thought that cytokine signalling is tightly controlled in time and space, so that cytokines very precisely relay their message from one cell to another. The aim of this proposal is to find out whether cytokine signals also affect cells that are not the intended target. My hypothesis is that cytokine signalling can be indiscriminate, and that many cells not intending to participate in the immune response are nonetheless affected by the cytokine signals taking place around them. My prediction is that such indiscriminate cytokine signalling can alter the subsequent behaviour of these bystander cells. I will test my hypothesis using a series of transgenic mice that allow me to follow cytokine production and cytokine signalling as they happen, in a physiological immune system. My work will clarify a critical aspect of how cytokines control immune responses, and I anticipate that this knowledge will facilitate the development of new strategies for therapeutically manipulating immune responses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Action of the CCR4-NOT complex is mammalian gene silencing networks
Keywords-MotsClés: ARGONAUTE; CCR4-NOT COMPLEX; GENE EXPRESSION; GW182; MICRORNAS; MRNA STABILITY; MRNA TRANSLATION; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL CONTROL; TTP
Abstract-Résumé: The CCR4-NOT complex is a type of cellular machinery that controls the activity of genetic material (messenger RNA), which in turn serves as the template for the synthesis of proteins in mammals.  The CCR4-NOT complex helps regulate such biological processes as fat metabolism, germ cell development and many others.  Moreover, its ability to regulate messenger RNAs is often disregulated in cancers and other diseases.  We are studying how the CCR4-NOT complex is recruited to specific messenger RNAs, and how, once recruited, it shuts down protein synthesis and brings about messenger RNA degradation.  Understanding these fundamental mechanisms of how the CCR4-NOT complex functions will allow us to design new molecular diagnostics for screening diseases and potentially target these diseases through novel therapeutic avenues.

TitreApplicationTitle: The epigenetics of genetics in cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CANCER; EPIGENETICS; GENOMICS; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the second leading cause of death in North American women. Ten different breast cancer subtypes are known. The estrogen receptor alpha (ESR1) drives the expression characterizing the luminal A and B subtypes, which account for two-thirds of all cases. Accordingly, drugs antagonizing ESR1 activity provide the first-line therapy, known as endocrine therapy. However, over 40% of patients fail to respond and tumors have commonly metastasized by the time resistance is diagnosed leading to death. While ESR1 usually remains abundant in resistant cells, its role is ill defined and efforts to identify alternative mechanisms driving resistance have failed to find a cure. Previous work has shown that endocrine therapy treatment increases NOTCH activity in endocrine therapy responsive breast cancer cells. Our preliminary observations suggest that NOTCH signaling is over-activated in endocrine therapy resistant breast cancer cells. This suggests that NOTCH signaling may play a role in endocrine therapy resistance. Genome-wide epigenetics mapping has revealed that regulatory elements are marked by an epigenetic signature based on the methylation of lysine 4 on histone 3 (H3K4me). Recently, we showed that this epigenetic signature is reprogramed in cancer compared to normal cells imposing a unique oncogenic expression profile. Whether epigenetic reprogramming contributes to resistance to endocrine therapy in breast cancer and how this relates to ESR1 and NOTCH signaling is unknown. We will address this by comparing the genomic map of this epigenetic signature from endocrine therapy-resistant and responsive breast cancer cells. Furthermore, because this epigenetic signature marks active regulatory elements, analysis of regions uniquely reprogrammed in responsive or resistant breast cancer cells will address the contribution of ESR1 and NOTCH signaling in endocrine therapy-resistant breast cancer cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: TARGeting Child Health:  Creating a preventive child health research program
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA EXACERBATIONS; CHILD HEALTH; PEDIATRICS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SUPPLEMENTATION; UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTIONS; VIRAL INFECTIONS; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: There is little doubt that the foundation of adult health begins in childhood. Opportunities to enhance child health through preventive interventions hold the promise of improving the health of Canada's children and the adults they become. Common nutritional problems including vitamin D deficiency, iron deficiency, and obesity could present such an opportunity. Over the past three years at the Applied Health Research Centre of the Li Ka Shing Knowledge Institute at St. Michael's Hospital, I have laid the foundation of a program of research aimed at meeting the challenge of preventing these common nutritional problems in the early years. To accomplish this, I have with my colleagues, developed the only Canadian primary healthcare research platform for children called TARGet Kids! (The Applied Research Group for Kids). Through TARGet Kids!, new strategies to involve young children in health research have been developed and have been combined with state of the art research methods and the engagement of the doctors who care for these children.  Over the next five years, I will scale up TARGet Kids! by following participating children through time, by linking their data to other powerful databases and by expanding TARGet Kids! across Canada.  Further, I will use this  cutting edge platform to develop and test preventive interventions targeting vitamin D deficiency, iron deficiency and childhood obesity. Ultimately, through the development and testing of preventive interventions that doctors can use for common nutritional problems in the early years, this program will redefine preventive child health in Canada and improve the health of Canadian children and the adults that they become.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intravascular Biomaterials for Coagulation and Cardiovascular Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; BLOOD COAGULATION; DISSEMINATED INTRAVASCULAR COAGULATION; FIBRINOGEN TRANSFUSION; LOCAL DRUG DELIVERY; MICROFLUIDICS; SEPSIS; SMALL ANIMAL IMAGING; VASCULAR IMPLANT; VULNERABLE PLAQUE
Abstract-Résumé: The formation of blood clots is an essential biological function for preventing blood loss during bleeding. Unfortunately, blood clots can form in our blood vessels even when we are not bleeding. These blood clots can lead to a heart attack, stroke, pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and tissue necrosis. Current therapies for controlling blood clotting aim at reducing or inhibiting enzymes and molecules that cause blood clotting to occur. For example, statins reduce cholesterol, a molecule that can inflame blood vessels and lead to atherosclerosis and then blood clotting. These approaches have improved the quality of life of humans, but one-third of all people will still die due to the formation of a blood clot. This proposal describes research to develop a complementary approach to the current therapies. Specifically, we will develop small biopolymers that form synthetic blood clots and replace natural blood clots. Our hypothesis is that thin layers of these synthetic blood clots could be formed in a controlled manner at regions of inflamed vessels to block large blood clots from forming. In the future, this technology may also be used to modify blood clots, making them degrade faster, and thereby preventing heart attacks and strokes. This technology may also lead to a strategy to replace components of blood clotting given during transfusions and reduce our dependence on blood from donors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Atomic-Resolution Dynamics of GTP-Bound Ras Proteins Probed by NMR Spectroscopy
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER RESEARCH; CONFORMATIONAL DYNAMICS; NMR SPECTROSCOPY; ONCOGENIC RAS
Abstract-Résumé: Proteins are large, essential biological molecules that regulate and participate in all cellular processes. Their roles in human health and disease are the subject of intense research worldwide. One protein called Ras functions as a molecular switch whereby signals received from receptors on the surface of cells are transmitted to intracellular pathways that ultimately affect gene expression crucial for cell growth, differentiation and survival. Ras cycles between active and inactive states in cells through binding of small molecules called GTP and GDP, respectively. Mutations in Ras can lead to a prolonged active state causing unintended signaling inside cells. It is known that such aberrant Ras signaling leads to approximately 30% of all human cancers. Previous studies have suggested that the active state of Ras exists in at least three different conformations, however, the nature of these conformations is not clearly established. In this work, we will elucidate the three-dimensional structures of these different states and how they interconvert. A comparative analysis between 'normal' Ras and oncogenic mutants is expected to provide important insights into the oncogenesis mechanism and the atomic-resolution structural information that will be forthcoming will ultimately support rational drug design for cancer treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Translational Approach to Targeting the Perioperative Period With Innovative Cancer Therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: HEPARIN; IMMUNOMODULATION; KILLER CELLS; LOW MOLECULAR-WEIGHT; NATURAL; NEOPLASM METASTASIS/THERAPY; NEOPLASM SEEDING; ONCOLYTIC VIROTHERAPY; PERIOPERATIVE PERIOD; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH; VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM/SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Most solid tumours are treated with surgery before they spread to other organs. Dr. Auer and others have shown that surgery itself can increase the spread of cancer to distant sites. Despite this, very few treatments are given around the time of surgery because they are too toxic for a recovering patient. A number of changes happen following surgery including increased blood clotting and preventing an overwhelming reaction from the immune system. While these changes are important for patients to heal, they can be exploited by cancer cells, helping them to spread.  In this proposal Dr. Auer will find out why surgery helps cancer cells to spread and study how to reverse these effect using novel cancer treatments that can be safely given to patients around the time of surgery. Dr. Auer has developed an animal model where a mouse undergoes surgery followed by an injection of cells to simulate cancer cell spread. Dr Auer will use this model to study the reasons for the spread of cancer after surgery and to find the best combinations of treatments to prevent this from happening. Dr. Auer also has two clinical trials that involve giving treatments around the time of surgery in order to prevent the cancer from coming back. In these studies she will analyze blood from cancer patients, taken before and after their operation and before and after new non-toxic treatments, to study what happens in human cancer patients.  Most patients with solid tumours, like breast or colon cancer, have an operation to remove the tumour, but for a number of patients the cancer will come back, often spreading to distant organs. Many patients get toxic treatments, like chemotherapy, many weeks after surgery to try and prevent this. Dr. Auer's research is focused on trying to understand what is involved in the spread of tumour cells after surgery so that more effective, less toxic treatments can be given to patients around the time of their operation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Infectious Diseases Epidemiologic Advances using Linked Data (IDEAL-Data)
Keywords-MotsClés: BURDEN OF DISEASE; EPIDEMIOLOGY; ETHNIC DISPARITIES; HEALTHCARE USE; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; LINKED DATABASES; OBSERVATIONAL STUDIES; VACCINE EFFECTIVENESS; VACCINE PROGRAM DELIVERY; VACCINES
Abstract-Résumé: Infectious diseases are still a major cause of illness and death in Canada. The Ontario Burden of Infectious Diseases Study found that in a population of 12.2 million, infectious diseases cause over 7 million healthcare episodes and nearly 5,400 deaths each year. Vaccines are among the greatest achievements in public health, preventing many infectious diseases. My research involves studying patterns of infectious diseases and the impact that vaccines have, both at the level of individuals and in populations, so that we can better prevent these diseases. Linking records about individuals across multiple databases (while maintaining the privacy of the individuals) is very useful for research studies. These linkable databases have been used in many studies about heart disease, cancer, and drug safety, but they have not been used as much for infectious diseases. My research will use many different databases, including healthcare records (e.g., hospitalizations, visits to doctors), information from telephone surveys, and laboratory results to answer important questions about infectious diseases. I will do research in four main areas: 1) understanding patterns of influenza (the "flu") and influenza vaccines ("flu shots"), in particular whether there are differences in the frequency of influenza and other types of infections between various ethnic groups, and measuring how well influenza vaccines work in seniors; 2) ranking various infectious diseases in terms of their impact on the health of the population and estimating how much infectious diseases cost to the healthcare system; 3) understanding patterns of healthcare use for some other infectious diseases such as HIV (the virus that causes AIDS) and hepatitis B and C; and 4) improving the way influenza vaccination programs are delivered in Canada. This research will improve care for patients as well as the delivery of public health programs, so that the impact of infectious diseases can be reduced for all Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and Evaluation of iWalk: A Web-based Guide to Facilitate Evidence-informed Assessment of Walking after Stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE ADHERENCE; COMMUNITY-BASED EXERCISE; HIV/AIDS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OUTCOMES MEASUREMENT; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS; REHABILITATION; STROKE; WALKING
Abstract-Résumé: More than 50% of people who suffer a stroke are unable to walk on their own and require intensive rehabilitation with a physical therapist to relearn how to walk again. It is important for physical therapists to assess walking using standardized tests at the beginning of therapy and over time to see how people with stroke are responding to treatment. High quality tests that can be used to see how fast and how far a person can walk are excellent tests to use in people who have trouble walking after a stroke. Although information about walk tests is available in research reports, physical therapists are not using this information or these walk tests in clinical practice. Educational guides are needed to pull all the research information together in one place so therapists can access the information more easily. Posting guides on the Internet means the guide will be available to physical therapists across the world. If we also post videos to show therapists how to give these walk tests to patients, and describe examples of how to use test scores with patients, then physical therapists may be more likely to use these tests. We would like to develop a guide for the Internet, and use videos and patient examples to show therapists how to use walk tests with patients. Then we will invite about 30 physical therapists who work in Ontario and Nova Scotia to review the guide and use the information in their clinical practice. After they use the guide, we will interview them to hear about their experiences using the guide, and to learn what specific features of the guide helped them to begin using walk tests, or to use walk tests more consistently than before to evaluate walking problems in people who have had a stroke. Our results will help others to develop guides that will make it easier for healthcare professionals to adopt new and better ways of delivering healthcare.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting the Molecular Mechanisms of the Alternative Nuclear Export and Endoplasmic Reticulum Targeting of Secretory mRNAs.
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM; MRNA LOCALIZATION; NUCLEAR TRANSPORT; POST-TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION OF GENE EXPRESSION; SECRETION
Abstract-Résumé: During gene activation, segments of DNA are transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA) in the nucleus. These RNA transcripts are processed, exported into the cytoplasm and then delivered to particular regions, depending on elements that are found within each mRNA. After arriving at their proper subcellular destination, the mRNAs are then translated into proteins. In order to be exported from the nucleus and then localized to particular regions, each mRNA must acquire particular protein factors that assist them at each of these steps. It however remains unclear how different mRNAs acquire these protein factors. The majority of mRNAs code for "cytosolic" proteins, which remain within the cell. However, a substantial fraction of mRNAs, originating from 15-20% of all human genes, are targeted to the surface of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where they are translated into proteins that must cross a membrane. These "secretory proteins" are either delivered to the interior of an organelle, or exported to the extra-cellular environment. My lab has been studying how cells regulate the transport and distribution of mRNAs encoding secretory proteins. We have discovered that mRNAs encoding secretory proteins contain a number of RNA elements that confer special properties to the transcript. One of these elements promotes the nuclear export of these secretory mRNAs. A second mechanism helps to target and then anchor these mRNAs to the surface of the ER. We have uncovered proteins that are required for the nuclear export and the ER-anchoring of these mRNAs. In this proposal I will outline my plans to dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying these two processes. Since the pathways we discovered regulate the expression of secretory proteins, our work will provide deeper insight into mechanisms involved in inflammation, diabetes, cancer and other pathologies arising from the misregulation of cellular secretion.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Long-Term Mechanical Ventilation in Canada: A Programmatic Approach
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH REALTED QUALITY OF LIFE; HEALTH SERVICE TRANSITION; LONG TERM MECHANICAL VENTILATION; PROLONGED MECHANICAL VENTILATION
Abstract-Résumé: The number of individuals that require prolonged and long term mechanical ventilation (PMV/LTMV) (breathing support) as a result of acute illness or progression of chronic disease continues to rise. Currently in the Canadian health care system there is insufficient capacity to deliver care to ventilator-assisted individuals in both the acute and chronic care sectors. As well, significant barriers exist to the negotiation of transition point in the health care system e.g., transitioning from acute to chronic care needs. This results in suboptimal care, decreased quality of life for individuals and their families, and inappropriate use of expensive and limited acute care resources. This project, developed through consultation with multi-professional experts in mechanical ventilation, will enable and inform seamless integrated care, development of clinical best practices, identification of health information needs of patients and families and description of health care use and costs. We propose to explore these issues for individuals (a) at-risk for LTMV in the community, (b) requiring LTMV in the community, (c) requiring PMV/LTMV in an institution; and (d) transitioning from paediatric to adult care requirements. We will conduct our project in four stages. We will meet our study objectives through the conduct of expert surveys to define key transition points, the development of a national inventory of providers of services to individuals at risk, or requiring PMV/LTMV, national surveys, and interviews of patients and families. Through the conduct of this project we will establish a national network focused on improving care delivery for our target population thus promoting collaboration and partnerships across health sectors, professions, and jurisdictions, as well as sharing of best practices to improve health outcomes, patient safety, and quality of life for our target population across the continuum of care.

TitreApplicationTitle: microRNA-33 Regulation of PGC-1?: Role in Atherosclerosis and Obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; DIABETES; FATTY ACID METABOLISM; INFLAMMATION; MICRORNA; MITOCHONDRIA; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease affects over one million Canadians, and costs the Canadian healthcare system over 20 billion dollars annually.  Atherosclerosis, a leading cause of heart disease, is a buildup of cholesterol, immnune cells, and calcium in the arteries that feed your heart muscle with blood.  Diabetes is also an important risk factor for heart disease, and can develop in a similar way to atherosclerosis.   We propose to study how a small RNA molecule, called microRNA-33, affects the risk factors for heart disease.  Specifically, we want to know if miR-33 turns on/off a gene called PGC-1alpha, which is an important factor involved in how our bodies use energy.  PGC-1alpha can increase "good" fat, reduce diabetes, and improve heart disease.  We believe that miR-33 controls PGC-1alpha, so therapies to inhibit miR-33 would increase PGC-1alpha and would improve diabetes and atherosclerosis.  We also believe that PGC-1alpha is controlled by other small RNA molecules, so we aim to identify all of the ways PGC-1alpha is controlled.  These studies will help identify ways to increase PGC-1alpha and improve cardiometabolic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurobehavioral controls of food reward and metabolic sensing in the midbrain
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR; DOPAMINE; ELECTROCHEMISTRY; EMOTIONS; FOOD REWARD; INTRA-CERBEBRAL INFUSIONS; LEPTIN; LOCOMOTOR ACTIVITY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: One last morsel of food remains on your dinner plate. You hesitate but in spite of feeling full you manage to eat the last bite. Your plate is clean and your hunger is satisfied. Without a conscious thought of eating anything more your eyes glance over the dessert menu. The anticipation of the novel sensory experience presented by the tasty treats makes you perk-up, and before you know it you are devouring another mouthful. The rewarding effects of palatable foods can drive us to eat not only when we are hungry and need to replenish energy stores but also in states of satiety when energy is replete. Which mechanisms in the brain are responsible for motivating us to consume foods rich in fat and sugar? Our work explores the neural pathways that underlie motivation for food and other behaviours that regulate body weight. Circulating hormones like leptin target mesolimbic neural circuitry to influence feeding in part by affecting dopamine, a neurotransmitter playing a fundamental role in motivation and reward. On the one hand, our goal is to discover how hormonal and nutrient signals influence dopamine signalling and food-motivated behavior. On the other hand, our work aims to determine how eating a palatable, high-fat diet over time causes adaptations in brain reward circuitry that promote over-eating and negative mood states. As we are confronted with the health, social and economic consequences of obesity and nutritionally-related illnesses, elucidating the mechanisms that regulate motivation for high-fat and -sugar food remains an important goal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Maternal and infant health associated with maternal country of birth
Keywords-MotsClés: GENDER INEQUALITIES; HEALTH SERVICES; IMMIGRATION; INFANT HEALTH; INFANT MORTALITY; MATERNAL HEALTH; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Despite substantial progress in reducing maternal and infant deaths, serious illnesses in the perinatal period are still a big concern for both the mother and her child. Infants who survive serious morbidity around birth may still experience disabilities and other health disorders later in life. Compared to industrialized nations, maternal mortality may be 100 times higher in some developing countries. Female disadvantage is another global problem.   Compared to men, women are at disadvantage in terms of survival and overall health and quality of life in many nations. For example, almost 4 million excess female deaths occur every year, the majority of them in Asia and Africa. About 35% are never born or die at birth, 15% die in early childhood and 33% in their reproductive age. Poor infant, child and maternal health are intimately related as female disadvantage impairs the ability of mothers to take care of themselves and their children.  Canada increasingly receives immigrants from world regions where maternal mortality and female disadvantage is quite common, such as Asia and Africa. However, little, if any, is known about how female immigrants and their newborns fare, or if the female disadvantage that is known to exist in some countries persist after immigration to Canada. On the other hand, some immigrants may be healthier than the Canadian-born. Learning what make them healthier might be beneficial for the whole population. To examine these issues, this research program will study 2.6 million births (and their mothers) in the last two decades in Ontario, 500,000 of which were born to immigrant women. I have built a strong research team that will work in collaboration with immigrant community organizations to ensure that our findings translate into more equitable and improved care of mothers and their children.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Context in Facilitating or Hindering Knowledge Translation Targeting Healthcare Professionals
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOUR CHANGE; CONTEXT; INTERVENTIONS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; RESEARCH USE
Abstract-Résumé: Healthcare professionals' use of research is suboptimal despite increased awareness of and accessibility to research findings. Context is increasingly recognized as a central influence on research use and an important factor to be considered in knowledge translation interventions targeting healthcare professionals. However, there is little empirical evidence to support this claim. The purpose of my research program is to improve healthcare professionals use of research and research-based behaviours by designing, implementing, and evaluating context-optimized interventions (i.e., that are tailored to and/or act on context). In the attached proposal, I will conduct an analysis of context to construct a definition of context and identify its key features important to research use by healthcare professionals. Three separate inquiries will be conducted. First, I will conduct a concept analysis of context as it is described in the literature. Second, I will complete a secondary analysis of qualitative data from 10 studies of healthcare professionals on the perceived contextual barriers and facilitators to their use of different research-based behaviours. Third, I will conduct semi-structured interviews with knowledge users to elicit their perceptions of a definition of context and its key features. A working definition(s) of context and a list of its key features important to healthcare professionals' use of research will be derived from this analysis. This will form the basis for discussion in an international consensus process. This project will enhance our understanding of context and identify a set of contextual key features important for knowledge translation targeting healthcare professionals. Subsequent projects in my program will include: a systematic review of existing measures of key features of context; assessment of the reporting of context; and testing of a contextually optimized intervention to improve healthcare professionals' use of research.

Abstract-Résumé: The distribution and organization of these fats are regulated by a variety of proteins, referred to as scramblases and flippases.  Not surprisingly, mutations in these proteins are proposed to influence a myriad of disorders including male infertility, bile acid accumulation in the liver, diabetes, obesity and neurological defects. TitreApplicationTitle: Biology and clinical significance of the tumour microenvironment in lymphoid cancers
Keywords-MotsClés: GENOMICS; LYMPOID CANCER; OUTCOME PREDICTION; PATHOGENESIS; TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Malignant lymphomas are the fifth most frequent cancer in humans, affect patients of all ages, and despite generally effective treatments, a significant number of patients still die of their disease. In certain subgroups of lymphoma, the malignant cells are surrounded by normal immune cells, yet these cells are unable to muster an effective immune attack against the tumor. In recent years, researchers have made significant progress in understanding how the malignant cells are evading the immune system. However, this improved knowledge has not yet been successfully translated into better treatments for patients. The herein proposed research focuses on two related subtypes of lymphoma - called Hodgkin lymphoma and Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma - that often affect adolescents and young adults.  We will study the exact mechanisms of immune system escape investigating certain genes that we have found altered in earlier studies. We will focus on the effect of these alterations on tumor surrounding immune cells and on macrophages (a type of white blood cells that ingests foreign material) in particular, in order to characterize novel drug targets and to pave the way for innovative clinical trials. Using state-of-the art genome-wide sequencing methods we will also define the complete landscape of genetic alterations in Hodgkin lymphoma and primary mediastinal B cell lymphoma. Furthermore, we will focus on the development of genetic tests that predict therapy resistance in childhood and adult Hodgkin lymphoma and identify patients at high risk of relapse.  Our studies will be very important for physicians and patients as our research will develop clinical tests that provide information about the individual prognosis of lymphoma patient and will help developing new drugs and personalized treatments. Ultimately, these treatment improvements will lead to higher cure rates and fewer side effects for patients suffering from malignant lymphomas.

TitreApplicationTitle: Knowledge Transfer in Genetics: Evaluation of the Use of Genetic Tests in Clinical and Community Settings
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL UTILITY; ETHICAL; GENETIC SCREENING; GENETIC SERVICES; GENETIC TESTS; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEALTH TECHNOLOGY ASSESSMENT; INTERDISCIPLINARY; LEGAL AND SOCIAL ISSUES; PROGRAM EVALUATION; QUALITATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: My research program examines the translation of new genetic knowledge in clinical practice and their impacts on patients and their families. The main themes of my research are 1) population screening for genetic diseases; 2) evaluation of genetic tests in clinical practice 3) impact of health policies on the use of genetic tests and services. Under those themes, I have three currently ongoing projects. My main project studies how First Nations communities in Quebec perceive and use genetic information about 3 lethal childhood autosomal recessive diseases. The second project is to develop tools for successful integration of an eventual predictive test for scoliosis in clinical practice. The third project examines the meaning of "serious disease" in the context of the recent modifications to the Quebec health insurance mandate to cover pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) for "serious monogenic diseases".  Through this work, we will acquire knowledge that will help develop educational interventions adapted to the needs of physicians to improve the use of genetic tests. We will also produce knowledge that can inform the development of future clinical practice guidelines in Quebec and Canada. The high costs associated with most forms of genetic testing in the context of a single payer system and the desire to provide equal access to tests across provinces make it even more important to provide Canadian professionals with guidance based on local evidence.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cerebral and psychomotor development in babies with infantile spasms
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBRAL OXYGENATION; INFANTILE SPASMS; LONGITUDINAL AND PROSPECTIVE STUDY; NEAR INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY; NEUROCOGNITIVE OUTCOME; NEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL ASSESSMENT; PEDIATRIC EPILEPSY; TREATMENT MONITORING; TUBEROUS SCLEROSIS COMPLEXE
Abstract-Résumé: Infantile spasms (IS) is one of the most devastating and treatment-resistant epileptic syndromes in infancy. It affects one in every 2,000 babies. IS is characterized by three main symptoms: halt or decline in psychomotor development (crawling, walking, talking, social interaction, etc.), epileptic spasms, and abnormal electrical brain activity seen in the electroencephalogram (EEG). The first spasms usually appear between age 3 and 7 months. Most cases are treated successfully with hormones or anticonvulsive drugs. However, the developmental outcome remains poor in most of these infants. Mental retardation is a serious consequence of IS, and has been reported in 71% to 88% of patients. Of the children who have normal overall intelligence and are able to attend regular school, most have specific deficits such as motor, memory, or language problems, as well as learning difficulties. Previous studies have shown that early diagnosis and treatment of IS may improve the developmental outcome. The main aim of this research program is to prevent and minimize developmental and psychomotor deficits in infants with IS by conducting three sets of studies: 1) identification of predictive markers for IS to allow for earlier diagnosis, 2) development of a new, noninvasive technique for IS treatment monitoring to better understand the effects of anticonvulsive drugs on the developing brain, and ultimately, to enable earlier adjustments in treatment, and 3) investigation of specific developmental profiles and psychomotor outcomes in children with IS in relation to age at onset, causes of IS, and IS treatment. Early detection and treatment of IS should help prevent cognitive and developmental deficits, thus improving the quality of life of these patients and their families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development and bioimaging of blood-brain barrier vectorized nanoparticles
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOENGINEERING; BLOOD-BRAIN BARRIER; MONOCLONAL ANTIBODY; NANOPARTICLES; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES; NEUROIMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: One third of Canadians of all ages will be affected by a brain disease during his or her lifetime. While the population is getting older, the risk of suffering from Alzheimer, stroke, Parkinson, etc. increases exponentially after age 65. Most people do not realize that the socioeconomic burden of brain diseases dwarf those of cancer and cardiovascular disease combined.  Unfortunately, the research and development of new drugs for brain diseases lags behind. The main problem resides in the fact that the blood-brain barrier (BBB) severely restricts the passage of drugs from the blood to the brain. The vast majority of advanced drugs are too large to pass through the BBB and virtually all strategies developed so far to cross the BBB without damaging it have failed in humans. Indeed, the brain is like a walled city, in which the BBB represents the wall surrounding the city. The total length of the BBB of a normal human brain spans approximately 600 km.  Here, we are proposing to generate new vectors and determine which one is the best to target the natural transport systems located in the BBB. These transport systems are the equivalent of the guarded gates in the walled city analogy, as they allow the entry of their friends. Then, these vectors will be conjugated to nanoparticles to ferry drugs inside cells of the BBB. We will then verify with advances techniques whether our vectorized nanoparticles stay in the BBB or penetrate deeper in the brain. Such a tactic is reminiscent of the Trojan horse strategy because the nanoparticles are built to trick the brain's screening system (or city guards). Therefore, the present study could lead to the development of new brain drug delivery systems for clinical applications in Alzheimer's disease and many other brain disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: ARMS UP/Assisted Robotic Movement after Stroke using Brain Power: Controlling robotics with EEG
Keywords-MotsClés: 1101 HUMAN HEALTH; 1211 MEDICAL AND HEALTH SCIENCES; 6308 BEHAVIOURAL NEUROSCIENCE; 6311 MOTOR SYSTEMS AND PERFORMANCE; AGING; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY; MOTOR LEARNING; REHABILITATION; ROBOTICS; STROKE
Abstract-Résumé: A major limitation after stroke is poor arm function.  This severely hampers both recovery from stroke and also is a major contributor to reduced quality of life. Despite increased understanding of how the brain recovers from stroke effective therapies that stimulate return of stroke affected arm function remain elusive.  This problem is particularly acute for people with more severe stroke who suffer the worst outcomes and are most disabled.  Thus, there is a critical need for new technologies that will facilitate recovery and functional capability after stroke.  Research has been performed showing that different intentions may be recorded through the use of non-invasive recording from the brain using electroencephalography (EEG). This enables the detection of when someone is trying to move the arm. Our research team has already demonstrated and built an exoskeleton robotic system that can assist in moving the arm.  In this proposal we aim to marry these two technologies to enable an integrated system that allows control of the robotic exoskeleton using thinking as captured by EEG.    We have assembled an ideal team to carry out this proposal including experts from neuroscience, adaptive technology engineering and clinicians who will serve as our users.  In addition this project is well positioned to lead to further technological developments, be transferable to industry and stimulate job growth for Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: The transition from acute to chronic pediatric pain: An examination of the pediatric fear-avoidance model and pain memories among children undergoing major surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE PAIN; ANXIETY; CHILDREN; CHRONIC PAIN; FEAR-AVOIDANCE; GENDER; MEMORY; PAIN MECHANISMS; PEDIATRIC PAIN; TRANSITION TO CHRONICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Unfortunately, chronic pain is surprisingly common in childhood and adolescence, particularly among adolescent girls. Children who develop chronic pain are likely to grow up to become adults with chronic pain and this has enormous economic, psychological, and social costs to individuals and society. Our recent research shows that short-term pain turns into persistent pain for up to 50% of children following surgery and children's memories for pain may be important in determining why pain problems become chronic over time. However, we are only beginning to understand why some children are at risk for developing chronic pain whereas other children cope better with the pain or heal completely and go on to have healthy, productive lives without pain. It is critical to identify the childhood risk and protective factors that predict who develops chronic pain and who does not so that we can design interventions to stop pain from extending into adulthood. Based on strong research, we recently developed the "pediatric fear-avoidance model of chronic pain" to explain why pain becomes chronic for some children and not others. The objective of our study is to test this model and examine memories for pain among children undergoing major surgery so that we can identify risk and protective factors for the development of chronic pain. The results of this research will not only indicate the best ways to help children undergoing painful medical procedures and surgery but will also help protect children from developing chronic pain problems throughout their lives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Non-Invasive Tracking of Endogenous Progenitor Cell Recruitment and Inflammation Following Myocardial Infarction
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL THERAPY; CYTOKINE SIGNALING; INFLAMMATION; MOLECULAR IMAGING; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; PROGENITOR CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: In a heart attack, lack of oxygen to some heart cells causes damage. This damage includes inflammation a response to injury causing swelling a pain. Chemical signals direct stem cells from the bone marrow to the damaged area. The role of inflammation in stem cells getting to and staying in the injured area is not well known. Genetic changes to stem cells can make them more effective to target the injured area and prolong their stay. Addition of chemical signals to the cell's genes could also increase healing. A "switch" can be encoded to turn on and off these signals.  We will build a stem cell that includes an on/off switch and a protein (NIS) that we can detect using an imaging technology to show: a)Whether genetic changes affect stem cells in the body b)Whether the on/off switch works in the living animal c)How many stem cells home to the injured tissue after a heart attack d)How long the stem cells stay in the injured area  We will measure inflammation to show how it affects the stem cells after heart attack. Stem cells are made from mouse bone marrow to include NIS on their surface. These cells are implanted into a set of mice that have their natural stem cells (bone marrow) removed. The NIS stem cells can be tracked by giving a radioactive probe that sticks to NIS. The signal can be detected using a SPECT camera. This provides a map of NIS cells in the body. We will test the on/off switch by giving or withdrawing a drug to operate the switch and measuring NIS cells. We will then measure the movement of stem cells. Mice with NIS bone marrow will be given a heart attack by tying off a blood vessel in the heart. We will measure the radioactive signal in the heart over time to determine how many cells move to the injury and how long they remain. Other radioactive probes that measure inflammation will also be given. We will compare inflammation to NIS cell levels to determine the effect of inflamed tissue on stem cell survival.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the role of in-school food advertising and adolescent dietary outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: DIETARY PRACTICES; FOOD AND BEVERAGE ADVERTISING; MULTILEVEL REGRESSION; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: The prevalence of obesity and related chronic diseases among Canadian youth has risen significantly over the past several decades, in part because of poor dietary patterns. While many factors influence diet, food and beverage advertising is thought to be important because of its significant association with the food preferences and choices of youth. These associations are not surprising given that many youth lack the necessary cognitive abilities to understand and/or resist the persuasive intent of advertising. To date, minimal research has explored whether associations between food advertising and dietary outcomes extend to settings outside the home, and none have looked at these relations within the context of Canadian schools where youth spend much of their day. Without this information, employing a multi-sectoral approach to reduce the negative impact of advertising on youth is unlikely. The purpose of this proposal is two-fold. First, all in-school food advertising will be documented and described within a sample of Vancouver schools. Second, connections between school-level food advertising and student-level dietary outcomes will be examined. These objectives will be met by developing and piloting a measurement tool and coding protocol to capture all in-school food advertising and by using multilevel statistical methods to analyze existing data from the CIHR-funded Food Practices on School Days Study, a cross-sectional study (n~1,000) that builds on a larger 5-year SSHRC Community University Research Alliance program that was funded to initiate a variety of food system and curricular initiatives in Vancouver Schools (K-12). Research findings will: provide insight into the prevalence of food and beverage advertising within Vancouver schools; help to determine associations between food and beverage advertising and the dietary outcomes of youth; and guide future school-based interventions and/or policy decisions for improving dietary outcomes among youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expanding treatment and care research to address mental health problems in Canadians with ASD across the lifespan
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; COMMUNITY SERVICES; FAMILY; HEALTH SERVICES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTAL HEALTH; TREATMENT AND CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Mental health and behaviour problems are the most common set of associated conditions for individuals with ASD across the lifespan, placing tremendous burden on the individual and family, as well as on the educational, community, vocational, and healthcare systems. Up to 70% of individuals with ASD are estimated to have mental health problems. We need to provide better treatment and care to people with ASD who are at risk for, or develop, mental health problems. Over the next five years, I aim to implement a Canada-wide, strategic research program to improve the mental health of people with ASD. I will focus on the individual with ASD, their family, and the service system. I will identify risk factors for mental health problems in individuals with ASD by following children, adolescents, and adults with ASD over a three-year period, measuring mental health at 6-month time points. I will conduct treatment research by providing a novel therapy to help youth with ASD who have been traumatized by chronic bullying and have mental health problems, evaluating and refining the treatment, and teaching trainees and clinicians how to provide therapy to people with ASD. I will also study how family caregivers access services for people with ASD across the country, and identify the gaps in care. The Chair support will allow me to conduct specific foundational studies, engage with a broad range of stakeholders on an ongoing basis, translate the knowledge gained to inform policy and practice, and train and mentor the next generation of researchers and practitioners in state-of-the-art methods to improve treatment and care for individuals with ASD in Canada. In the end, this Chair will have a substantial impact on the health and well-being of Canadians with ASD and their families.
