TitreApplicationTitle: Bone microarchitecture and estimated bone strength in patients after kidney transplantation
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MICROARCHITECTURE; BONE STRENGTH; CORTICAL POROSITY; FINITE ELEMENT ANALYSIS; HR-PQCT; KIDNEY DISEASE; MEDICAL IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Kidney disease is a serious disease that affects around 2 million Canadians. In addition to the loss of kidney function, patients with kidney disease have an increased risk of bone fracture. This risk is even higher after kidney transplant. The resulting fractures are extremely debilitating, reduce an individual's quality of life, and cost the health care system a significant amount of money to treat. This research project uses a new medical imaging technology (high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography; HR-pQCT) that provides detailed images of bone structure in patients. This tool is a significant improvement over the tools currently used (dual x-ray absorptiometry; DXA) because it measures bone density and three-dimensional structure. Using this new technology and computer models, we can analyze a patient's bones and provide individualized estimates of his/her bone strength. Because of the limitations of the current tools, there have been conflicting reports regarding the effects that kidney disease has on the skeleton. Using this exciting new 3D technology, we will be able to gain a better understanding of what is actually happening in the bones of kidney transplant patients and put health care professionals in a better position to identify and manage those at risk of fracture. We will be working with groups of patients who have undergone a kidney transplant and given varying regimens of corticosteroids to prevent transplant rejection. We will apply this new technology to analyze changes in bone density and structure. Finally, we will use computer models to estimate the bone strength. This research will provide important insight into the bone quality of patients with kidney disease and their fracture risk. Even a small reduction in the number of bone fractures due to kidney disease and kidney transplant will have a major impact on both the quality of life of those Canadians suffering from the disease and the associated health care costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining gender/sex differences in the relationships between work stress and disease, work injury risk, and the consequences of work injury
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; EPIDEMIOLOGY; GENDER/SEX; HEALTH BEHAVIOURS; HYPERTENSION; WORK INJURY AND ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Women make up nearly half of labour force participants, yet much of what we know about the relationship between working conditions and health is based on measures developed on men and frameworks tested in male-dominated workplaces. Little is known about why work-related risk factors for disease or injury may differ for men and women. In addition, gender differences in the return-to-work process and outcomes after injury are not well-understood. This research program will generate new research across three areas where there are significant gaps in knowledge concerning the work and health experiences of men and women. These are: (1) The psycho-social work environment, including job control, psychological demands and social support, and the development of hypertension and diabetes among men and women; (2) Gender and sex differences in work-related risk factors for occupational injury and disease; (3) Individual, workplace and health-care provider factors leading to differences in the return-to-work outcomes after work-related injury among men and women. This research program will lead to a more nuanced understanding of how sex/gender shape injury risk, the relationship between the work environment and chronic illnesses, and time off work after a work-related injury. By involving an independent advisory committee consisting of leading occupational health and safety stakeholders throughout the research process, this new research knowledge will in turn help shape the development of gender- and sex-sensitive policies and practices to improve the health of all working Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting DNA repair in cancer therapy: the promising role of synthetic lethality
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; DNA REPAIR; SYNTHETIC LETHALITY; TARGETED CANCER THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: This research projects deals with cancer therapy and how to introduce a new targeted therapy for some types of cancer by making use of their biological characteristics. It is known that tumors often fail to make particular proteins. This is not fatal for the tumor cells and in fact is sometimes the reason that they grow better than normal cells. However if the loss of this protein is combined with the loss or inhibition of another protein, the combination either kills the cancer cells or makes them very sensitive to chemotherapy or radiotherapy. This phenomenon is called synthetic lethality. Because the normal cells produce the first protein, the loss of the second protein is not particularly harmful to them and so if we can find a way to inhibit the second protein only the cancer cells will be killed or weakened. The trick is to identify the synthetic lethal partnerships, especcially those where an inhibitor of the second protein is already available or being developed.   Recently, our group identified a chemical that inhibits an important enzyme inside the cell called polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP), which is required to mend DNA damaged by radiotherapy and chemotherapy. When we screened to see if PNKP has any possible synthetic lethal partners we identified an important protein called PTEN that is frequently missing or inactive in breast cancer cells. We intend to confirm that the combined loss of PNKP and PTEN does indeed kill or weaken breast cancer cells grown. We will use breast cancer cells grown in dishes and as tumours in mice. We also intend to learn more about the underlying mechanism for synthetic lethality by looking for synthetic lethal partners of another DNA repair protein related to PNKP called DNA polymerase beta.    This research is expected to have potential therapeutic value because it targets cancer cells and should leave normal tissue relatively unaffected, which would translate into decreased side effects in the patient.

TitreApplicationTitle: The contribution of common and rare exonic functional variants on adiposity and their interactions with dietary fatty acid consumption.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSITY PHENOTYPES; BIOINFORMATICS; DIETARY FATTY ACIDS; EXOME CHIP; GENE-DIET INTERACTION; GENETIC ASSOCIATION ANALYSIS; HUMAN ADULTS; META-ANALYSIS; OBESITY; RARE AND COMMON VARIANTS
Abstract-Résumé: The social and economic burden of obesity and its complications will probably increase in the upcoming years due to the expected rise of obese individuals. This situation urges the need to understand why some individuals are predisposed to develop obesity. The control of body weight is complex where environment and genetic factors are implicated. It has been estimated that the susceptibility of individuals to develop obesity is 40 to 70% explained by variations in their DNA (genetic variations). Previous large studies in different populations have tried to identify which genetic variations may influence obesity risk. Several genetic variations which are frequently observed in the population (common), have been linked with obesity risk, but with a small contribution to this risk. Other genetic variations less frequent in the population (rare), but with greater contribution on obesity risk, are poorly identified to date, but may reveal further genetic susceptibility to develop obesity. The proposed project aimed at identifying these rare genetic variations and to evaluate the contribution of common and rare genetic variations on obesity risk in a large sample of 10,000 patients from the Montreal Heart Institute Hospital Cohort. This project will also verify whether the effect of common and rare genetic variations on obesity risk may vary depending of the patient's diet. Indeed, patients with genetic susceptibilities to develop obesity may have a greater risk in the context where their dietary habits also favor the development of obesity, such as the type of fat consumed. The proposed project will improve our understanding on how genetics and nutrition contribute to the susceptibility of individuals to be obese. This will then help to establish efficient prevention strategies, and helping physicians and health professionals to choose the appropriate intervention for each patient, such as personalized modifications of lifestyle habits or effective drug treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and functional characterization of leukemia initiating cells in acquired aplastic anemia
Keywords-MotsClés: APLASTIC ANEMIA; CANCER STEM CELL; LEUKEMIA; PRE-LEUKEMIC CELL; STEM CELL AGING
Abstract-Résumé: Aplastic anemia is a relatively rare but devastating blood disease in which the bone marrow fails to produce new blood cells. Despite advances in therapy, approximately 10% of patients will evolve to severe myelodisplastic syndrome (MDS) or acute myelocytic leukemia (AML). A major unresolved question is the nature of the initiating cell that eventually expands during the aplastic phase and gives rise to secondary disease. AA is a difficult disease but is an extraordinary opportunity to study the early events that eventually lead to leukemia formation. In this study we intend to explore the primitive cell compartment in the bone marrow using state of the art phenotypical profiling to identify the pre-leukemic cell. We then subject the identified population of cells to a battery of assays to prove that they are clonally expanded. In sight of new high throughput sequencing advancement that allows us to study the whole genome in very low number of cells, we are now able to determine the early genetic aberrations at the time of diagnosis and  monitor the genetic alterations after treatment and after development of MDS/AML. This study will provide a comprehensive map of mutational evolution and new insight into AML pathogenesis.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of tumour-associated stroma in human pancreatic cancer pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER ASSOCIATED FIBROBLASTS; GENOMICS; TUMOUR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is one of the five most fatal forms of cancer. Despite decades of advances in cancer therapy for many other types of cancer, there has been minimal impact on the overall survival of PC patients. Two reasons may explain this clinical roadblock.  First, symptoms often present late when the disease has spread to many organs, when surgical interventions aiming to cure patients do not work. Second, PC is highly resistant to cancer drugs. The ability of drugs to reach and kill PC cells is very poor compared to other types of cancer. This is due to the intense inflammation that surrounds the cancer and causes blood vessels within the tumour to collapse. As a consequence of the scarce blood supply within the tumour, cancer drugs cannot penetrate in sufficient quantities to shrink tumours in patients. This inflammation is provoked by the build-up of fibroblasts, a non-cancerous cell type that borders the cancer. Many laboratories worldwide have shown that the accumulation of fibroblasts can block drug delivery to the cancer. This has led to a new vision for cancer therapy in the future whereby drugs that attack fibroblasts as well as cancer cells are given to patients in parallel. The idea behind this theory is that one drug would attack fibroblasts to increase blood supply, and provide the second cancer-killing drug access to the tumour cells. To accomplish this goal, we need to be able to isolate, study and learn how cancer fibroblasts cause inflammation within the tumour. I have now developed cell-based studies to separate cancer cells and fibroblasts. This will allow me to monitor the true role of fibroblasts, and how they cause the menacing inflammation that limits the drug delivery to neighbouring cancer cells. In this application, I will study the biology of how fibroblasts mediate inflammation in pancreatic cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of Airway Wall Structure in Asthmatics Following Bronchial Thermoplasty using Optical Coherence Tomography
Keywords-MotsClés: AIRWAY SMOOTH MUSCLE; ASTHMA; BRONCHIAL THERMOPLASTY; OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Despite advances in drug therapy and establishment of treatment guidelines, a significant proportion of health care expenditure, morbidity and excess mortality are related to a small but significant number of patients with severe and persistent asthma symptoms.  Furthermore, even in patients with chronic asthma that are controlled by current therapy, there is a preference to try to minimize the amount of pharmaceuticals that patients require.  We propose to use a new high resolution imaging technique, optical coherence tomography (OCT), to study the mechanism of chronic persistent asthma. Twenty subjects with chronic persistent asthma will undergo a new procedure known as bronchial thermoplasty to destroy the airway smooth muscle (ASM).  Bronchial thermoplasty is a non-pharmaceutical clinically approved method for the treatment of uncontrolled asthma that ablates ASM and has been shown to reduce asthma symptoms.  However, it is unclear exactly what structural changes occur within the airway wall following treatment and it is unclear why some subjects benefit from bronchial thermoplasy while others do not.  The objective of this study will be to evaluate asthma subjects immediately prior to and immediately following bronchial thermoplasty as well as at week 18 and 52 post-thermoplasty.  Airway wall measurements will be obtained using OCT which has been shown to be able to allow investigators to see epithelial and sub-epithelial structures such as ASM in-vivo with near microscopic resolution.  By examining the changes in the airway wall that are caused by bronchial thermoplasty and comparing these changes before and after treatment with other clinical measurements we can describe the important airway wall structures responsible for the asthmatic response.  We believe that these findings will allow us to discover novel pathways and candidate molecules that are targets for therapy and improve therapeutic options for patients with chronic persistent asthma.

TitreApplicationTitle: Electrocortical correlates of persistent pain
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER; BRAIN; CHRONIC PAIN; EEG; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; LASER-EVOKED POTENTIALS; MULTI-VARIATE PATTERN ANALYSIS; NOCICEPTION; PAIN
Abstract-Résumé: Pain is the most common clinical symptom, and over 18-20% of Canadian adults report chronic pain. It is a massive burden for the health system: chronic pain alone costs the  Canadians more than $30 billion/year. Techniques to see the brain areas active during sensation and feelings have been used to understand what generates pain, with the aim of reducing it in patients. However, a clear "pain region" has not been found. Furthermore, these studies usually use short-lasting painful stimuli, which are very different from the pain felt by patients, which lasts for much longer periods of time. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to identify brain activity related to persistent pain (i.e. pain that lasts longer than a few seconds). To sample the brain activity I will use a technique called electroencephalography (EEG) that allow precisely measuring the electrical currents of nerve cells (called neurons), even when they "fire" at very short time. This is important to understand how the neurons talk to each other in an almost real-time fashion. If successful, this project will help clarifying the activity of nerve cells specifically related to pain, and provide us with an objective measure of pain, which is a much needed and still unavailable tool in clinical practice and scientific research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physician Reference Guide for the Treatment of Depression in Pregnancy with Antidepressant Medication: A Knowledge to Action Guide
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIDEPRESSANT MEDICATION; EVALUATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PERINATAL DEPRESSION; PHYSICIAN TREATMENT REFERENCE GUIDE; SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW AND METAANALYSES
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a serious disorder but it is under-treated during pregnancy.  There are challenges to Knowledge Translation (KT) in the area of antidepressant exposure during pregnancy including conflicting research results and physicians' lack of synthesized evidence-based resources.  In a previous phase of our program of research, we created a Physician Reference Guide (KT tool) to bridge the knowledge to action gap, identified by both knowledge-users and our previous synthesis of research literature regarding antidepressant medication use during pregnancy.  Our aim is to facilitate consistent and evidence-based discussions with patients in the treatment planning process with the use of the KT tool.  In the proposed project, we plan to implement the KT tool with knowledge-users of three different medical specialties to evaluate its impact.  The implementation process with physicians of various specialties will also further our understanding of how the knowledge to action gap may be successfully bridged in this area of complex and mixed scientific evidence in order to improve patient care.  Our proposed research plan includes both short and long term dissemination strategies.  These objectives are aligned with accelerating the application of scientific evidence and enhancing our understanding of knowledge application to improve the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Combining cognitive training with aerobic training to maximize physical and cognitive recovery after stroke
Keywords-MotsClés: AEROBIC TRAINING; COGNITIVE IMPROVEMENT; REHABILITATION; STROKE PATIENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Every year nearly 50, 000 people in Canada suffer a stroke, which affects their movement and walking skills as well as their cognitive abilities. Exercise training after stroke can improve muscle strength and endurance, allowing patients to participate better in daily functional activities. Aerobic exercise may also improve cognitive function, however, there is little research focusing on this improvement in stroke survivors. Instead, stroke rehabilitation  programs tend to only include simple physical tasks that do not challenge the participant's cognitive processes.  We propose that rehabilitation programs that combine cognitive training within aerobic exercise can best improve the physical and cognitive recovery of post-stroke patients.  Before testing the impact of this type of training program we must first make sure that our rehabilitation program is applicable to patients with different levels of cognitive and physical impairment. To do this we will analyse previously acquired data to determine how cognitive tasks affect walking in patients with varying levels of impairment. Next, we will develop the new tools and technology required to capture the behavioural and cognitive changes that occur during this type of novel training program. Finally, we will test the developed software and technology with 30 post-stroke patients to determine how well the cognitive tasks can be incorporated into the exercise sessions, and how difficult the cognitive task is on its own. These data will allow us to design a rehabilitation program that maximizes the cognitive and physical improvement in post-stroke patients. The long-term goal of this research plan is to implement this low-cost, accessible training program, designed to improve cognitive and physical health, in in-patient, community and in-home rehabilitation settings.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting Androgen Receptor dimerization as a potential therapy for Prostate Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: PROSTATE CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is a leading cause of cancer related death in men.  Although often curable when diagnosed early, tumours that become recurrent or metastatic are difficult to manage. Prostate tumour growth is driven by androgens, hormones that are produced by the body such as di-hydro-testosterone (DHT).  Accordingly, treatment for patients involves reducing DHT production or blocking the specific interaction of this hormone with a protein residing within prostate cells called the androgen receptor (AR).  These treatments are temporary, however, and the tumour cells invariably change at the genetic level into a "castration resistant" form, allowing growth even in the absence of DHT.  Substantial progress has been made in understanding how androgens act at the molecular level.  Within prostate cancer cells, the DHT molecule binds to the AR protein, "activating" the AR then causing the production of other cellular factors that promote tumour growth.  For the activated receptor to exert its function, two AR proteins must form an assembly, a molecular process known as "dimerization".  Thus, a treatment that specifically interferes with AR dimerization could prevent AR activation and possibly work in castration resistant cancer cells that are androgen independent. The research group at the Prostate Centre has successfully screened for compounds (i.e. drugs) that can block the interaction between the AR and DHT in living cells. This progress will be extended to screen for drugs that interfere with AR dimerization.  Initially, biochemistry methods will be used to detect AR assemblies and gauge the effect of drugs on purified AR in solution (in vitro). Promising compounds will be tested in cultured prostate cancer cells and eventually in mice (in vivo).  Targeting AR dimerization, rather than DHT binding, could potentially suppress tumour growth in even castration resistant patients, and would be a significant breakthrough in treatment of prostate cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring B cells as key cellular players in controlling HIV propagation within mucosal tissues
Keywords-MotsClés: B LYMPHOCYTES; HIV; IGA; MUCOSAL TISSUES; TNF-INOS-PRODUCING PLASMA CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: HIV infection is a major health problem worldwide and development of novel vaccines strategies is imperative to halt transmission. Since the virus invades mucosal tissues, vaccines that specifically prime white blood cells within mucosal tissues is a reasonable approach. The mucosal immune system, that is the white blood cells that reside in the gastro-intestinal tract, the airways and the reproductive tracts, have special properties to balance immune readiness against pathogens with tolerance to normally harmless food and commensal bacteria. In order to harness this large population of immune cells for protection against HIV, we need to understand how these cell function and how they are regulated. The post-doctoral work that is proposed is centered around a population of immune cells called "B lymphocytes" in the gut mucosa. We will take advantage of some newly discovered properties of these cells to rationalize vaccine design for protection against HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Cardiac Genes Responsible for Cardiomyocyte Maturation and Regeneration
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMYOCYTES; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EPIGENETICS; GENE THEREPY; HEART FAILURE; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT  STEM CELLS; MATURATION; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; PROLIFERATION; RNA-SEQ
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. In Canada alone, diseases of the heart represent 20.6% of all total causes of death (Statistics Canada, 2009). During a heart attack, heart cells die and the surviving heart cells do not possess the ability to expand (proliferate) to replace the lost cells. However, during development, heart cells do possess the ability to proliferate and only after birth do the heart cells change to a more mature non-proliferative cell state. To understand which genes are responsible for heart cell proliferation and maturation, we will identify differentially expressed genes (by RNA-seq) during development. Once these genes are identified, we will introduce genes that are differentially expressed during development into cardiomyocytes grown in culture. These cardiomyocytes are made from adult cells which can be differentiated into multiple cell types (human induced pluripotent stem cells). Finally, we will verify if introduction of these differentially expressed genes can promote cardiomyocyte proliferation and maturation. Insights from this project have wide reaching benefits within cardiovascular medicine since identification of which genes promote cardiac proliferation can be applied to cardiac regeneration therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Supporting diabetes population health risk tools in practice: Partnerships to guide adaption, implementation and evaluation
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE STUDY; DIABETES; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; KNOWLEDGE TO ACTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MIXED METHODS; POPULATION RISK TOOLS; RISK ALGORITHMS
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is rising at an alarming rate in Canada. Without urgent preventative action, diabetes will continue to deteriorate the health status of the Canadian population and overwhelmingly burden the health care system. Health policy makers at all levels have authoritatively stated diabetes prevention as a key priority through policy announcements and strategic system investments; however, there is uncertainty on the type, intensity, and target of health interventions that will achieve the most effective and efficient impact overall and in priority populations. Risk algorithms are tools that predict the future risk of a disease for an individual, which have widespread use in clinical practice. To date, risk algorithms have rarely been applied to the population level to inform prevention strategies or public health practice.  We have developed and validated the Diabetes Population Risk Tool (DPoRT), which estimates future diabetes risk based on routinely collected population data.  This practical tool was specifically designed to be applied to the population level and has resulted in an innovative way to make routinely collected health data useful for informing diabetes prevention strategies and support local decision making and planning. To date work to understand how best to integrate this tool into practice is lacking thereby limiting the uptake. The goal of this study is to implement and evaluate an integrated knowledge translation strategy with local and provincial public health decision-makers in two provinces to facilitate the application of this innovation. Overall, this research will identify strategies on how to best to apply risk tools in practice in order to inform diabetes prevention across Canada. The results of this work will be useful to policymakers and public health officials interested in diabetes prevention as well as lead to improvements in the integration of data into policy decisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Single-cell Alternative mRNA Splicing Patterns in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE MYELOID LEUKEMIA; ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; BONE MARROW; CYTOF MASS CYTOMETER; HEMATOPOIETIC CELL DIFFERENTIATION; PRINCIPAL COMPONENT ANALYSIS; RNA-SEQ; SINGLE CELL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: One of the reasons blood cancers originate is because of mutated genes. However, we know other processes related to genes are also involved in the development of blood cancer. Genes frequently recombine their sequences to change their function, this is a normal process known as 'alternative splicing'. Previous research tells us that 'alternative splicing' might be defective in blood cancer cells, and may be part of the reason why they are so dangerous. We will use a new technology to analyze the status of the 'alternative splicing' process, comparing healthy blood cells with blood cancer cells in mice. We expect that blood cancer cells will have different 'alternative splicing' than healthy cells. If we understand what the differences are in 'alternative splicing' between healthy cells and blood cancer cells, we might be able to design drugs to correct the differences in blood cancer cells in order to fight cancer. We will examine our hypothesis in a model of the blood cancer known as acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but believe our study will ultimately be relevant to other blood and non-blood cancers as well.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engineering of Interferon pathway agonists
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLORECOGNITION; BACTERIAL SWARMING; BACTERIAL TERRITORIALITY; MICROBIOLOGY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN BIOCHEMISTRY; PROTEIN-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEUS MIRABILIS; SELF RECOGNITION IN BACTERIA; SUBCELLULAR LOCALIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: Central to the immune system of animals is the ability to distinguish between self (own) and non-self (foreign or cancerous) cells in order to attack or isolate the non-self cells. For example, the main cause of organ transplant rejection is the incompatibility of cell surface markers between donor and recipient, even between closely related individuals and the current treatment of immune suppression helps only so far. Little is known of how the complex human immune system developed over time, but the ability to separate from non-self likely developed early on as bacteria also have a primitive immune system. When two different clinical isolates of the opportunistic pathogen Proteus mirabilis meet on a surface, a visible boundary forms at the interface of the two populations, indicating that the bacteria can distinguish between self and non-self. In this bacterium, self-recognition is minimally regulated by two separate gene clusters, including one that defines strain-specific identity. This simple immune-like system, found in a diverse array of bacterial pathogens, does not parallel the complexity of the human immune system, but unlike animal models, P. mirabilis is simple and genetically tractable, containing only a single chromosome with a division cycle of 40 minutes. Utilizing P. mirabilis, I will dissect the molecular mechanisms that underpin interactions between self and non-self cells. Specifically, my research will focus on the binding interaction between two molecules, each of which encodes the definition of self-identity; each protein, like an antigen, says precisely which population was its forbearer. Moreover, I will examine how this protein-protein interaction communicates a population-wide signal to dictate whether an opposing population is self or not. The knowledge gained from this bacterial immune-like system will propel a greater understanding of not only the human immune system and potentially related diseases, but also of a pathogen's behaviour.

TitreApplicationTitle: The histone deacetylase SIRT6 as a novel tumor suppressor that controls pancreatic cancer metabolism
Keywords-MotsClés: AEROBIC GLYCOLYSIS; CHROMATIN DYNAMICS; EPIGENETICS; PANCREATIC CANCER; SIRTUINS; TUMOR METABOLISM; TUMOR SUPPRESSOR
Abstract-Résumé: Pancreatic cancer is the fourth leading cause of cancer death in Canada and one of the most aggressive and deadly malignancies. Late diagnosis and limited therapeutic options make pancreatic cancer a pressing clinical problem. In the 1920s Otto Warburg observed that cancer cells take up and use large amounts of sugar in order to support uncontrolled tumor growth. Despite being described close to a century ago, very little is known about how this change in metabolism occurs. A better understanding of this process especially in pancreatic cancer will help us to design new drugs that target the tumor cell addiction to glucose without harming normal cells. Sirtuin 6 (SIRT6) is a protein that modulates compaction of DNA (chromatin), and it has been found to be a critical regulator of genes that control glucose uptake and utilization in cells. Importantly, SIRT6 is deleted in many human pancreatic cancer cell lines and tumors. This application for a fellowship award proposes to investigate whether genetic loss of SIRT6 contributes to the development of pancreatic cancer formation. By studying gene expression and DNA compaction in pancreatic cancer cells, proposed studies will determine how SIRT6 increases glucose uptake and use. Then we will test whether restoring SIRT6 or blocking the glucose addiction will inhibit pancreatic tumor growth. Modulation of SIRT6 activity may lead to new therapies to tackle aberrant metabolism and provide new treatment options for patients with this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Régulation du métabolisme énergétique des cellules de cancer du sein par la voie AMPK/PGC/ERR
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; CANCER DU SEIN; EFFET WARBURG; GENOMIQUE FONCTIONNELLE; METABOLISME CELLULAIRE; METABOLISME ENERGETIQUE; RECEPTEURS NUCLEAIRES; REGULATION TRANSCRIPTIONNELLE
Abstract-Résumé: Les cellules tumorales ont la plupart du temps un metabolisme energetique qui est different des cellules saines, ce qui est probablement implique dans l'apparition et l'agressivite du cancer. Mes travaux portent sur une des voies majeures de regulation du metabolisme energetique: la voie AMPK-PGC-ERR. Une meilleure comprehension des mecanismes moleculaires de cette voie, mais aussi des alterations qui surviennent en presence de cancer, permettrait de mieux comprendre le cancer du sein et, eventuellement, de permettre la decouverte de nouvelles voies therapeutiques. Par exemple, cela pourrait se faire en modifiant le metabolisme energetique des cellules tumorales, qui est different des cellules saines.

TitreApplicationTitle: "Like a ship that's always righting itself:"Self-management of bipolar disorder, from evidence to action.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIPOLAR DISORDER; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; QUALITY OF LIFE; SELF-MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES; WELLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: Bipolar disorder (BD), a condition characterized by repeated episodes of depression and over-elated mood, affects over half a million Canadians and results in substantial costs to the healthcare system. While many people with BD take medications to stay well, medications alone are always enough to ensure optimal quality of life. One growing area of research relates to the role of 'self-management strategies' (the decisions and actions a person can take to better cope with their health condition) for BD. This project will be conducted by the Collaborative RESearch Team to study psychosocial issues in BD (CREST.BD; www.crestbd.ca), a unique CIHR-funded network that brings together researchers, clinicians, people with BD and their supports to research and exchange knowledge on BD. We have conducted two key studies in this area. First, we examined the strategies used by people living successfully with BD. Second, we collected more generalizable evidence on effective strategies in an international sample. Our studies used a broad definition of 'evidence', important because people with BD can have significant knowledge about how best to manage BD in real life.  In this study, we will share this knowledge with two user groups, people with BD and BD healthcare providers. We will: 1. Build and test the effectiveness of an online Wellness Centre containing evidence on self-management strategies for BD; 2. Design and test methods to help the user groups use the evidence in the Wellness Centre (e.g. workshops or a 'Living Library' where users access a CREST.BD member for self-management support).  Our participatory research approach will ensure that both user groups will be involved in each step of the research. Study findings will help improve the health and quality of life of Canadians with BD by giving them knowledge and empowering them to manage their condition more effectively and help healthcare providers better support and care for people with BD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the Role of TDP-43 in Polyglutamine Toxicity

Abstract-Résumé: Mutations in TDP-43 (TAR DNA-binding Protein) and FUS (Fused in Sarcoma) have been identified in patients with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Frontotemporal dementia, while TDP-43 and FUS protein accumulations are observed in a growing number of neurodegenerative including Huntington's Disease (HD). My preliminary data shows that reducing TDP-43 and FUS activity rescues toxicity in worm and mammalian polyglutamine (polyQ) models. Based on my genetic analyses with worms the mechanism may rest with (1) Increased proteotoxic stress within the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) and/or (2) Inappropriate regulation of TDP-43/FUS target RNAs. I request support to investigate the molecular basis of TDP-43, FUS and huntingtin toxicity in primary neuronal culture from CAG140 knock-in mice.

TitreApplicationTitle: Collagen Specific Dyes for Breast Tumour Imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; BREAST CANCER; CANCER BIOLOGY; COLLAGEN; DIAGNOSTICS; IMAGING; MODULAR DELIVERY; MORPHOLOGY; NONCOVALENT IMMOBILIZATION; STROMA
Abstract-Résumé: Mammographically dense breast tissue, the result of elevated collagen deposition, is one of the greatest risk factors for breast cancer. While these densities alone do not indicate cancer, a causal link between the collagen arrangement and metastasis has been recently established. It has been shown that organization of collagen fibers aligned perpendicular to the tumour boundary corresponded to sites of tumour invasion and poor patient outcomes. Unfortunately, current mammography techniques lack the resolution to image collagen at this level, and alternative imaging capabilities are only applicable for excised tissue samples. I propose a strategy to target and image collagens undergoing this rearrangement using collagen specific dyes, allowing the detection of new biomarkers for tumour invasion.

TitreApplicationTitle: Change in proteinuria and risk of adverse outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY AND BIOSTATISTICS; DIABETES; DISEASE PREVENTION; DISEASE SURVEILLANCE; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; NEPHROLOGY; PROTEINURIA; QUANTITATIVE ANALYSES
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is the progressive loss of kidney function which can occur over a short or longer period of time. CKD is a common condition, affecting around 16% of the population worldwide. People with CKD have poor outcomes with high mortality rates and these rates increase as kidney function gets worse. Recent studies have shown that even in people with normal kidney function, proteinuria (the presence of protein in the urine) is associated with an increased risk of death, kidney failure, and cardiovascular disease. It is therefore important to develop guidelines to provide recommendations about the detection and management of proteinuria. However, our knowledge of the changes in this important marker of CKD is still currently limited. We therefore propose this program of research to determine a clinically important change in proteinuria which reflects CKD progression and predicts poor outcomes.  We will perform this work using 3 complimentary data sources: observational data from the Alberta Kidney Disease Network (AKDN), randomized controlled data from the RENAAL trial and the IDNT, and pooled individual participant data from the CKD-Prognosis Consortium. The AKDN maintains and extensive database incorporating laboratory and administrative data on all patients in Alberta and this data will be used as the primary source.  Utilizing a range of data sources, this project will provide valuable information on the effect of the change in proteinuria on adverse outcomes, and the magnitude of the change in proteinuria associated with increased risk of kidney failure. This work will be critically important as it will help identify those with "rapid" CKD progression in need of relevant care. The results from this project will contribute to current clinical practice guidelines which will help inform clinicians on the management of risk factors in people with CKD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting DNA repair mechanisms in cancer - developing inhibitors of Nudix proteins: NUDT1, NUDT5 and NUDT15 as cancer therapeutic agents
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-CANCER DRUGS; BLOOD CANCER; BREAST CANCER; COMBINATION THERAPIES; DNA REPAIR; DRUG DESIGN; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; DRUG DISCOVERY; MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; STRUCTURE ACTIVITY RELATIONSHIP
Abstract-Résumé: Despite advances in cancer treatment, cancer is a leading cause of death in Canada and will kill more than 75 000 Canadians this year.  The search for new cancer treatments is a key for limiting the impact of this disease and saving lives.  A newly established avenue for the development of cancer therapeutics is targeting DNA repair mechanisms.   Due to changes in how they generate energy, cancer cells produce large amounts of damaged nucleoside bases, which are the main building block of DNA.  If damaged nucleosides are incorporated into DNA, the cell  recognizes that the DNA is damaged and it will self destruct. To overcome this, cancer cells have robust DNA repair mechanisms that prevent damaged nucleoside bases from being used in DNA synthesis. We have recently discovered that members of the Nudix family of proteins are involved in DNA repair and are critically important for cancer cell survival.  Conversely, healthy cells have very low levels of damaged nucleosides and thus, inhibiting Nudix proteins in healthy cells will have minimal effect.   The proposed research aims to develop inhibitors of Nudix proteins as cancer therapeutic agents.  This will be done by screening large libraries of potential inhibitors against purified Nudix proteins, then using medicinal chemistry techniques to develop these inhibitors into better drug candidates.  These potential drugs will be examined in a panel of different cancers with a particular focus on breast and hematological cancers.  It is hoped that these novel inhibitors will provide a new and valuable weapon to be used in the fight against cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of genetic risk factors in severe pediatric tuberculosis
Keywords-MotsClés: HUMAN GENETICS; IMMUNE RESPONSE; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; MYCOBACTERIAL PATHOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Most humans, particularly those living in developing countries, are exposed to virulent, air-borne human-tropic mycobacteria at some point in their lives. These include M. tuberculosis, which causes clinical disease among a minority of exposed individuals. Despite widespread use of antibiotics, 8 million new cases of tuberculosis (TB) are reported annually worldwide, resulting in almost 2 million deaths. Distinct forms of clinical disease in children vs. adults have been observed in M. tuberculosis endemic areas. Pediatric and adult TB differ markedly in epidemiological features, clinical appearance, and pathogenesis. Severe, disseminated and often-fatal TB in children results from hematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis during primary infection of genetically vulnerable individuals. The inter-individual variability in response to M. tuberculosis is thought to result in part from polymorphism in host immune response genes, however the causal mutations have not yet been identified. Therefore TB, particularly severe life-threatening infections among children, is not only an infectious disease but also a genetic disorder. We propose a multi-disciplinary project, integrating basic and clinical immunology and genetics, to discover TB susceptibility genes in children and develop rational therapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Disruption of serial order learning in Parkinson's disease:  Input specificity and restoration of function by optogenetics.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL OF PARKINSON'S DISEASE; BASAL GANGLIA; CHANNEL-RHODOPSIN2; DOPAMINE; DORSAL STRIATUM; MOTOR CORTEX; OPTOGENETICS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PATCH-CLAMP ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; SERIAL ORDER LEARNING
Abstract-Résumé: Over the course of a day, we are frequently required to perform a long sequence of simple actions in the service of a larger objective. Getting dressed, climbing into your car, or brewing a pot of coffee, all require a series of smaller steps (i.e., put fresh filter in basket, add grounds, fill reservoir with water) to reach the desired outcome. This cognitive process, termed serial order (SO) learning, allows us to place complicated steps into their proper order to accomplish a larger objective. One part of the brain, the striatum, is critical for SO learning.  It manages the order of actions, seemingly on autopilot, but we don't know how it does this.   In Parkinson's disease (PD), SO learning breaks down and patients are unable to coordinate their actions and are often unable to finish sequences (such as leaving a shirt half-buttoned). Sadly, this disruption in SO learning can be resistant to the stimulant medications often used to treat symptoms of PD. To study SO learning, I teach mice a simple SO task: They must poke their noses into two holes in the correct order (i.e., poke hole A then poke hole B) to obtain a food pellet.  We can use these animals to find out more about how this behaviour works, and what has gone wrong with it in patients with PD.  I hypothesize that some of connections between brain cells (synapses) of the striatum are responsible for SO learning. Therefore, when a patient has PD, these connections may be disrupted. Recently, neuroscientists have discovered a way to make brain cells activate in response to light (Optogenetics). We will use this technique to re-activate the synapses in the striatum and, hopefully, restore the function of mice that have been given an artificial form of PD.  Nearly 100,000 Canadians suffer from PD, with more cases being diagnosed daily.  This proposal aims to examine how the disease disrupts SO learning and studies a novel technique to treat its symptoms.

Keywords-MotsClés: ABCA1; ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; AMYLOID BETA; ANTI-SENSE OLIGONUCLEOTIDES; MICRORNAS; NEUROINFLAMMATION; NEUROPATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a growing healthcare and social concern worldwide which affects 500,000 Canadians and, in the absence of effective therapies, is projected to affect 4 million by the year 2050. Recent evidence suggests that a protein called ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), which acts as a membrane transporter for cholesterol in cells and is present in many cells in the body including the nerve and glial cells in brain, plays a beneficial role in AD by facilitating the clearance of the toxic amyloid beta peptides from the brain. We have recently found that ABCA1 in the brain, in addition to regulating cholesterol metabolism, also plays important role in neuroinflammation, which is an important factor in AD. Hence, we are interested in studying the specific role of brain ABCA1, specifically the distinct contribution of neuronal and astrocytic ABCA1, on the progression and severity of AD-like neuropathology in a transgenic mouse model of AD. In parallel, we will also explore the therapeutic potential of enhancing the expression of ABCA1 in brain as a means of reducing neuroinflammation and amyloid deposition in a mouse of AD. The findings from these studies will help us better understand the interplay of brain cholesterol and inflammation in AD pathogenesis, as well as provide further support for ABCA1 as a therapeutic target in AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of genetic variants associated with renal function in type 1 diabetes.
Keywords-MotsClés: BURDEN TEST; DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY; EXOME CHIP; GENOME WIDE ASSOCIATION; LONGITUDINAL ANLAYSIS; MIXED MODELS; REPEATED MEASURES; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of kidney failure in North America. Once diabetic kidney disease develops, a person is at much higher risk of heart disease and death. Twin and family studies have provided evidence that genes play a major role in the development of diabetic kidney disease. Yet, genetic studies have not been successful in identifying those genes associated with diabetic kidney disease. This may be due to the fact that prior genetic studies of diabetic kidney disease have used only a single measurement of kidney function at one point in time, and have not been able to use rich clinical data collected over years of diabetes disease. It may also be that prior studies have been limited to common (present in 5% or more of the population) genetic variants, and have not been able to examine less common forms of genes (low-frequency variants), thought to have the greatest impact on gene function.  We are proposing a genetic study examining the rate of change of kidney function over time, using both common genetic variants and low-frequency variants, in over 2,800 individuals with T1D from four long-term studies of diabetes complications. These include landmark clinical trials and cohort studies in T1D, each with measures of diabetes, kidney function and related risk factors including blood sugar and blood pressure, collected over decades of diabetes disease. These studies represent some of the best studies of T1D populations to date, with participants contributing the vast majority of their lifetime diabetic experiences to these studies. Using this information we will be equipped to make genetic discoveries and insights into diabetic kidney function. This will improve our understanding of the causes of kidney disease in people with T1D, a well as improve prevention and care of diabetic kidney disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Driving in Dementia Decision Tool
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOMOBILE DRIVING; DECISION TOOL; DEMENTIA; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Background. The goal of this study is to adapt and evaluate a tool to help physicians decide when a patient with mild dementia should be reported to transportation authorities because their dementia has made them unsafe to drive. This is a growing concern given the increasing senior population in which both car accidents and dementia are seen in greater numbers.  Physicians often do not comply with legislation that requires them to report patients with medical conditions affecting driving to transportation authorities. This is often because of a reluctance to interfere with the patient's independence and concerns about negative impact on the doctor-patient relationship.   Research Plan. This study aims to test and evaluate a new Driving in Mild Dementia Decision Tool (DMD-DT). This tool will include a computer program to help physicians make decisions about reporting to transportation authorities as well as an individualized educational package for patients and their families.  Doctors will be assigned to one of two groups - the DMD-DT group or a control group. Physicians in the DMD-DT group will receive guidance from the computer program on the decision-making process as well as a personalized educational package for patients and caregivers. In contrast, physicians in the control group will only be given a reminder of the mandatory reporting legislation. The main outcomes of the study include whether the physician reports the higher-risk patients to transportation authorities, and the impact on the doctor-patient relationship.   Public Health Impact. The DMD-DT will streamline physician decision-making about driving in dementia and increase the reporting of unsafe drivers.  This will lead to more appropriate decision-making, not punishing safe drivers, and improved public safety through fewer crashes by unfit drivers with dementia. The study will take place in Ontario but the DMD-DT will be adapted to other provinces with mandatory reporting legislation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the mechanism of eIF3e-mediated epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition during breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CELL BIOLOGY; EPITHELIAL-TO-MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION; INTERNAL RIBOSOMES ENTRY SITES; METASTASIS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among Canadian women. This year, an estimated 22,700 Canadian women will find out that they have this disease. Sadly, about 5,100 will also die of it. Breast cancer becomes more aggressive when normal breast cells transform to adopt invasive properties by a process termed EMT. Following EMT, cancer cells can move throughout the body and spread the tumor.  Recently, our research team has identified an important protein in the regulation of EMT, termed eIF3e. In healthy breast cancer cells, eIF3e is essential for the expression of most proteins. However, 37% of breast cancers are associated with decreased expression of eIF3e. Until recently, the mechanism by which decreased eIF3e expression lead to breast cancer was unknown. Interestingly, we have just shown that a depletion of eIF3e leads to metastasis through EMT. This role for eIF3e in EMT and cancer progression was totally unexpected. However, work still needs to be done as the mechanism by which eIF3e regulates EMT is still unknown. Accordingly, the goal of my research project is to characterize the mechanism by which a decrease in eIF3e level leads to EMT. Our results indicate that following eIF3e depletion, the selective expression of a set of proteins is responsible for EMT. Interestingly, invasive properties of breast cancer cells are dependent on this set of proteins. When we will understand how eIF3e depletion leads to the selective expression of this set of protein, we will be able to understand EMT.  As stated above, EMT is a crucial process during cancer progression. Gaining a better understanding of this process may lead to the identification of novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multi-modal object representations human orbitofrontal cortex
Keywords-MotsClés: EMOTION; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MULTIVARIATE PATTERN ANALYSIS; OLFACTION; SOCIAL COGNITION
Abstract-Résumé: How does the brain represent the pleasure from both the scent and appearance of a rose?  Or the sights, sounds, and scents of a newborn infant?  The aim of this research is to examine how the brain implements complex processing from all of the senses by using repurposed, smell systems.  We will apply methods where we can read the information contained in the patterns of activity of neurons to examine how the brain process information from different senses. The link to public health in Canada is direct; a defective sense of smell is linked to brain diseases and mental disorders including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, autism, schizophrenia, depression, and many more.  Loss of the sense of smell also accompanies the mental decline of normal aging, half of adults 65 to 80 years old have a poor sense of smell.  Changes to the sense of smell can be used to diagnose disease, however we propose that the connection between smell and disease is deeper.  A deficit in smell may be a cause of mental disorder not a consequence of it since brain regions involved with smell have been repurposed to evaluate all sorts of information.  This research could highlight new avenues for treatment and prevention of many neurological and psychiatric disorders including mental decline of aging. We predict that smell regions of the brain have been repurposed to process information from the other senses, including vision and hearing.  Since pleasantness is the primary axis of odour evaluation and pleasantness is not limited to just smells, we predict that the brain will use the same algorithms to extract pleasantness information from smells, sights, and sounds. We will use sophisticated 'mind-reading' techniques where we can directly examine the information contained in patterns of neuronal activity in response to odours, faces, and vocalizations.  This can reveal whether smells, sights, and sounds activate the same neurons and whether they share a neuronal code.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intraoperative surgical margin assessment in breast cancer surgery using spectroscopic imaging
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; MOLECULAR IMAGING; ONCOLOGY; PATHOLOGY; SPECTROSCOPIC IMAGING; SURGICAL MARGIN ASSESSMENT
Abstract-Résumé: In breast cancer surgery, the concept of surgical margin assessment is important to successful treatment. The goal of the surgeon is to remove all the cancer in the breast, while conserving as much healthy tissue as possible. However, the exact boundary between cancerous and healthy tissue is often difficult to determine during surgery. For this reason, up to 40% of breast cancer patients have tumor involvement at the margins of specimens taken during their primary resection surgery which is not diagnosed by pathology until up to 24 hours later; these patients must be recalled for a second resection surgery at a later date. The purpose of the proposed research is to build and train an optical imaging system capable of providing a fast and accurate evaluation of the presence of cancer cells in the margins of breast resection specimens. This technology could prevent many of these second surgeries by providing enough information, directly in the operating room, to allow the surgeon to remove more tissue during the first surgery. The project will involve designing and building a clinical-compatible system, training the system with tissue samples, and the system will be used subsequently in clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determinants of Unplanned Acute Care Utilization among Home Care Clients: A System-level Study of Community-based Health Care Utilization and Geographic Factors
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE AND COMMUNITY CARE INTERFACE; CENSUS-LEVEL ANALYSES; FRAIL COMMUNITY-DWELLING OLDER ADULTS; HEALTH CARE SERVICE ORGANIZATION; MUTI-LEVEL MODELING; PROPENSITY ANALYSES; RETROSPECTIVE COHORT DESIGN; RISK ASSESSMENT; SYSTEM-LEVEL DETERMINANTS; UNPLANNED ACUTE HOSPITAL USE
Abstract-Résumé: Hospital care is the largest category of Canadian health care expenditure. The main users of hospital acute care are older adults over the age of 65, particularly those that are frail. Home care clients are amongst the most frail and at risk seniors living in the community. Provinces are attempting to align community health care services in order to meet the needs and preferences of frail older adults as well as avoid costly acute hospital use. The effect of system-level factors on unplanned acute care use by frail older adults, such as the use of community-based health services, is largely unknown. An expansion of census-level research is required in this area in order to effectively organize health services in the community.  The objective of this Postdoctoral research program will be to determine the influence of system-level factors on the patterns of acute care service utilization among home care clients age 65 and older (accounting for 17% of all seniors in Ontario). This retrospective cohort study will be conducted with the extensive use of population-level clinical and administrative data as well as advanced multilevel modeling. As such, this research project leverages information systems that are the product of substantial public investment.    This research will produce publications as well as useful policy support tools. In particular, the policy support tools will help health care administrators at the local and provincial level to improve the effectiveness of community-based primary health care and supportive care. Knowledge produced by this study will provide concrete directions for improving service provision and program planning for provincial aging at home and primary care initiatives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of TNF alpha in inflammation-induced impairments in glucagon-like peptide-1 release
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; GLUCAGON-LIKE PEPTIDE 1; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: The rate of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is increasing worldwide. T2DM is associated with obesity, which reduces the ability of the body to respond to insulin, leading to high blood sugar levels. Recently, obesity has also been shown to result in increased levels of inflammatory molecules, like tumour necrosis alpha (TNFa), in the blood - these factors are known to impair the normal actions of insulin. In contrast to TNFa, glucagon-like peptide 1(GLP-1) is a hormone that promotes both insulin secretion and insulin action, and is vital to maintaining normal blood glucose levels; however, the blood levels of GLP-1 are reduced in obesity. Therefore, we propose that TNFa has a direct role in this reduction in GLP-1 secretion. To address this, we will determine the effect of TNFa treatment on GLP-1 secretion from GLP-1-producing cells. Next, as we have already established that GLP-1-producing cells have receptors that respond to TNFa, the precise receptor and how it works inside the GLP-1-producing cell to reduce GLP-1 secretion will be investigated. Finally, how obesity affects GLP-1 secretion will be examined using mouse models that lack the TNFa receptor or that are treated with a TNFa inhibitor. TNFa is emerging as an important link between obesity and the development of diabetes. The results of these studies will enhance our understanding of how TNFa is able to alter the secretion of GLP-1, a hormone that is essential for normal blood glucose levels. Our findings will have direct relevance to the mechanisms underlying obesity-associated development of T2DM.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mortality of people incarcerated in provincial facilities in Ontario: A 15 year retrospective cohort study
Keywords-MotsClés: COHORT STUDY; MORTALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Internationally, people who are incarcerated tend to have poorer health than the general population, however, little is known about the health status of this population in Canada. Knowledge of the burden of disease of this population would make it possible to prioritize areas for intervention including public health interventions and health system changes.  In this study, I will determine the mortality rate and causes of death for people who were incarcerated in provincial correctional facilities between 1995 and 1996, by linking with death certificate data from 1995 to 2011. I hypothesize that the age- and sex-specific mortality rates of people who have been incarcerated in provincial facilities in Ontario will be high relative to the general population in Ontario, and that in particular, the mortality rates due to preventable diseases such as hepatitis C, HIV, and unintentional injuries will be relatively high.  This study will be used to inform where research and program development should be focused for incarcerated populations in Ontario and elsewhere in Canada. If the hypotheses are correct that the mortality rate is higher than for the general population and that a substantial proportion of deaths are from preventable causes, I will go on to develop interventions to prevent premature death and I will advocate for greater attention to the health of people who are incarcerated in Canada including more accessible and higher quality health services during and subsequent to incarceration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tumour-stroma interactions during breast-to-brain metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW-DERIVED CELLS; BRAIN METASTASIS; BREAST CANCER; CYSTATINS; CYSTEINE CATHEPSINS; EPITHELIAL CELLS; MICROENVIRONMENT; PROTEOLYTIC NETWORKS; STROMAL CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer affects 1 in 9 Canadian women. The leading cause of death from breast cancer is when it spreads to a distant organ site (called "metastasis"). Metastasis of breast cancer to the brain is a detrimental event during disease progression, as there are currently no effective therapeutic options for treating this stage of disease at this particular secondary location.   Two important components of cancer are: (1) the tumour, and (2) the tumour's environment. A therapy that kills the tumour, and locally disrupts the environment so that it is unfavourable for tumour growth will likely optimize efficacy of treatment.  Recently, we have identified 3 factors that are important for breast cancer to spread to the brain. These factors are called Cathepsin C, Cathepsin L, and Cystatin 3. Two of these factors are specific to the tumour, and the third is specific to the tumour's environment. In patients, we have found that each of these factors correlates with increased brain metastasis and poor overall survival.  Experimental Plan and Hypotheses: By interfering with Cathepsin C, Cathepsin L, and/or Cystatin 3, we hope to block the ability of breast tumours to spread to the brain. Targeting these three factors will not only harm the tumour cells directly, but will also alter the environment in the brain so that it cannot support tumour growth.   One of the most valuable aspects of this project is that we have access to patient tissue sets that include a sample of (1) normal breast, (2) breast tumours, and (3) brain metastasis. Importantly, each set (1-3) is matched to a single patient, and we have sets from 60 patients in total (these are called "patient-matched" samples). This is extremely valuable for research, since it is extremely rare to have a large number of patient-matched tissue. Within each individual patient, we can determine how the normal breast tissue changed to become cancerous, and how the breast tumour changed to support brain metastasis

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering the role of CD40/CD40 ligand interaction in germinal center development using multiphoton intravital microscopy
Keywords-MotsClés: CD40; CD40 LIGAND; CELL MIGRATION PATTERN; GERMINAL CENTER; IN VIVO IMAGING; MOLECULAR INTERACTION; MULTIPHOTON INTRAVITAL MICROSCOPY; T AND B COLLABORATION; T FOLLICULAR HELPER CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: B lymphocytes are known to combat against invading pathogens or to neutralize toxins by producing antibodies. B cell responses are tightly regulated within germinal centers (GCs), where B cells meet and collaborate with other types of cells, especially T cells. My proposed study focuses on CD40/CD40 ligand (CD40L) contacts between B and T cells. Early studies indicate that CD40/CD40L interactions play a pivotal role in the generation of GCs. However, recent findings challenge this dogma by showing that CD40 signaling, rarely seen in GC B cells, antagonizes GC B cell programming instead. In addition, there are several points at which CD40/CD40L interactions might occur, leading to further confusion about where and when this molecular interaction exerts its key influence on GC development.   The aim of this study is to better understand the role of CD40/CD40L interaction between B and T cells at different locations and stages of GCs. For this purpose, I will incorporate dynamic inhibition of CD40/CD40L interactions with real-time in vivo imaging to visualize GC B cell movement.  First, at selected time points after inhibition of CD40/CD40L interaction, potential mechanisms mediating the abrogation of GCs will be assessed. Then, I will track GC B cell movement in vivo using the cutting-edge in vivo imaging technology to determine if established migration patterns are altered before and after blockage of interaction. In some experiments, CD40/CD40L signaling will be elevated and the GC B cell migratory behavior in vivo will be correspondingly examined for potential deviations or exaggeration of pre-existing moving patterns.    Together, I am addressing critical questions about the GC with both new technologies and a fresh conceptual perspective. Answers to these fundamental questions have not only basic value in terms of our understanding the immune response, but also implication for vaccines design.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optical silencing of neocortical inhibitory circuits during sleep
Keywords-MotsClés: 2-PHOTON; CALCIUM IMAGING; CIRCUIT MAPPING; CORTEX; GABA; NEURAL SYNCHRONY; PLASTICITY; SLEEP; UNCAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Sleep is an essential function for life. Impairments in sleep accompany or underlie nearly all brain disorders. Mammalian sleep alternates between rapid eye movement (REM) and nREM (or slow wave) sleep. During nREM sleep the cortex exhibits transient periods (<2 s) of widespread increases in activity known as UP states. These UP states reactivate groups of neurons and are hypothesized to solidify the connections between neurons and aid in sleep dependent memory consolidation. As UP states are modulated by learning, they are thought to serve as the link between sleep and memory. Despite decades of research, we still lack sufficient knowledge regarding how these UP states organize the timing of neurons and how UP states contribute to learning. In the following proposal, a series of experiments are outlined which aim to reveal the types of cells responsible for UP states and how UP states are involved in sleep dependent memory processes. Using cutting edge technologies including two photon microscopy, glutamate and GABA photo-uncaging, Ca2+ imaging, electrophysiology, and circuit activity mapping, we will be able to obtain neural activation and silencing with single cell precision during spontaneous UP states in vivo. These experiments will provide a mechanistic outline of how UP states are generated and test the causal relation between UP states, sleep, and memory. Together, this combinatorial optical approach will test the causal relation between these network events and sleep dependent memory in the neocortex. These experiments will provide a framework for understanding the function of different sleep states and aid in understanding why sleep disturbances negatively influence learning and memory.

TitreApplicationTitle: Closed-Loop Control of Anesthesia
Keywords-MotsClés: 1102 - BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; 1901 - BIOMED TECHNOLOGY; 2509 - CONTROL SYSTEMS; 518 - MEDICAL EQUIPMENT AND APPARATUS; ANALGESIA; ANESTHESIA; AUTOMATED DRUG DELIVERY; CONTROL SYSTEMS; INTRAVENOUS ANESTHESIA; PATIENT SAFETY
Abstract-Résumé: We are all dependant on computers to perform complex and high risk tasks that make us safer, such as flying on commercial airplanes. Computers that automatically control such tasks are safer than humans as they are much better at performing repetitive tasks with accuracy and precision. They do not necessarily act alone but can augment what we do (such as antilocking brakes in our cars). Despite the potential to improve safety in healthcare; computer controlled automation has not been widely adopted. Errors causing significant harm are still a major problem in healthcare. For patients undergoing surgery, calculation of the correct drug dose is the most common error. These errors mostly occur due to human limitations e.g. fatigue, short attention span and patience while doing quick and accurate calculations repeatedly. Computer controlled drug delivery is the process of giving drugs to patients, where the computer calculates the dose and delivery timetable. This is especially important in the operating room, as the anesthetist has to safely keep a patient unconscious while also performing a range of other tasks. Our goal is to develop iControl, an automatic control system for administering two key types of anesthesia drugs during surgery: one to keep the patient unconscious and another to suppress pain. As each patient responds differently to these drugs, the key to automated drug delivery is the ability to measure its effect; a problem our team has been working on for 10 years. A device for measuring unconsciousness is commercialized and now we have invented a new way to measure pain suppression. Our goal is to combine these in a single device to optimize the delivery of anesthesia. iControl will use constant feedback of drug effects to make frequent adjustments to the drug delivery rates. iControl will not replace the anesthesiologist, but instead act as an autopilot, thereby enhancing his abilities and improving the safety and quality of care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular mechanism of HIV blockade by a novel antiviral chemokine, XCL1.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMOKINES; ELISA; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HIV ATTACHMENT; HIV DRUG THERAPY; HIV INFECTION; HIV SUPPRESSION; NEUTRALIZING ANTIBODIES; REAL TIME PCR; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Although many milestones have been reached in understanding interactions between HIV and host immune cells, major gaps remain in our knowledge of how immune cells can control HIV. Key players in the immune response to HIV infection are CD8+ T cells. Although these cells are commonly known to be antiviral by inducing death of infected immune cells, they can also secrete soluble factors known as chemokines, which can suppress HIV directly. Previous research described the production of chemokines by CD8+ T cells as the main drivers of CD8-derived anti-HIV activity. This discovery created a long-lasting impact on the understanding of AIDS pathogenesis, and led to the development of a novel drug therapy for HIV infection, based on the HIV suppressive activity of the newly discovered chemokines. Interestingly, recent evidence indicates the presence of additional, undefined, chemokines produced by CD8+ T cells that can significantly suppress HIV infection. Thus, the purpose of my study is to define the anti-HIV activity of a new CD8+ T cell-derived chemokine, namely XCL1.  My research will describe how XCL1 can block HIV infection. More specifically, experiments will show at what stage of the HIV life cycle it is that XCL1 exerts its inhibitory effects. Therefore, this study could be a critical first step in the development of new drugs and therapeutic strategies aimed at controlling HIV infection.  Furthermore, strategies to induce production of XCL1 in human hosts could be considered in future HIV vaccine designs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the beneficial effects of resveratrol in the treatment of heart failure
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM SENSITIZERS; DRUG DESIGN; FLUORESCENCE SPECTROSCOPY; HEART FAILURE; IN SITU PROTEIN STRUCTURE; MUSCLE PHYSIOLOGY; THIN FILAMENT; TROPONIN
Abstract-Résumé: The heart is the cornerstone of life; for most of our lives it relentlessly drives blood throughout our bodies, keeping us alive by supplying our cells with oxygen and nutrients. Considering its life-sustaining role, it is not surprising that the heart's failure carries grim consequences. Heart failure is defined as the inability of the heart to sufficiently supply the body with blood. Although there are a number of drugs that have proven to be effective for heart failure's short-term treatment, no lasting solution has been identified: approximately half of all people with heart failure will die within 5 years of diagnosis. A unique treatment that carries promise is the pharmacological improvement of heart function by enhancing the muscle directly. Heart muscle contracts when calcium binds to the protein troponin, and drugs that strengthen contraction by increasing troponin's sensitivity to calcium are termed "calcium sensitizers". Despite their obvious therapeutic potential, surprisingly little is understood about how these drugs function. In the proposed research we will examine the molecular mechanism of these compounds. We have synthesized a panel of small molecules that will be tested for their influence on muscle contraction. We will also monitor how these and other calcium sensitizers affect the structure of troponin in cardiac muscle. The results will help us formulate a chemical and structural basis for how these molecules increase the calcium sensitivity of troponin; insights that will provide a firm basis for the development of new, more effective, calcium sensitizers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunometabolism: linking nutrients and pathogens to diabetes during obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; IMMUNOMETABOLISM; INFLAMMATION; INNATE IMMUNITY; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LIPID METABOLISM; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Canadian society is experiencing an epidemic of obesity, brought on by diets with a surplus of calorie dense foods and inactivity. Obesity can cause insulin resistance, which is the biggest factor for causing type 2 diabetes. It is now known that obesity is accompanied by a low levels of chronic inflammation, and this has been shown to directly cause insulin resistance, which precedes type 2 diabetes. At the front line of the fight against these disorders are immune cells such as macrophages. These specialized cells play a critical role in keeping us healthy by defending against foreign invaders (such as bacteria). Importantly, it has been shown that during obesity, various components of a Western diet (nutrients and their byproducts) may directly activate immune cells, contributing to the state of 'chronic inflammation', which leads to metabolic disease. To make matters worse, obesity is also associated with an increase in bacterial components in the circulation, which also contribute to chronic inflammation. The objective of this proposal is to determine how dietary factors and the increased immune stimuli found in obesity team up to worsen metabolic disease. We will investigate this in macrophages and test how this interaction affects metabolic targets such as liver and adipose tissue, which are the key tissues that are susceptible to obesity-induced inflammation and defective in diabetes. Given the combined expertise of the Supervisor and candidate in immunometabolism and insulin action, and the infrastructure and resources available at McMaster, it is our goal to shed light on the connection between obesity, inflammation and metabolism to identify new ways to prevent type 2 diabetes.

Abstract-Résumé: Detecting the presence of an infectious disease like tuberculosis is important to stop the infection from spreading to family members or others that are in close contact with the patient. The test used in a doctor's office is very simple and inexpensive but will only detect the incidence of TB when the patient is infectious. Proposed is the creation of a simple blood glucose type test for TB that can be accomplished at a clinic with little cost and training - ideal for the developing world and areas in Canada that are resource poor. This method relies upon an electrochemical detection of specific sequences of DNA that are characteristic of the TB pathogen. In addition, this method will enable the identification of drug resistant strains of TB  (MDR-TB), and critically important area in regions of Canada with a large influx of immigrant from regions where MDR-TB is known to be prevalent.
