TitreApplicationTitle: Elucidating Master Regulators of Colon Cancer Metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL LINES; CHIP-SEQ; COLON CANCER; EPIGENOMICS; GENOMICS; METASTASIS; MICROARRAY; MOUSE MODELS; SHRNA; TRANSCRIPTOME
Abstract-Résumé: Colon cancer remains one of the most common types of cancer and is a leading cause of cancer related deaths worldwide. The vast majority of colon cancer related deaths are due to the spread of colon cancer to other organs (metastasis).  Thus, preventing the spread of colon cancer and successfully treating it once it has spread are among the most important aims in colon cancer research. Although we have made some progress in chemotherapy, evidence suggests that the majority of patients undergoing drug therapy experience severe, debilitating, and even lethal adverse side effects that considerably outweigh the benefits. Accordingly, determining specifically what controls the spread of colon cancer is essential and should allow clinicians to deliver the most appropriate therapy and spare patients from ineffective and expensive treatments. To help eradicate colon cancer, it is of paramount significance and the objective of this research proposal to achieve accurate detection of risk of colon cancer spreading and to develop a better understanding of why this happens. I plan to comprehensively characterize regulators of colon cancer metastasis and to subsequently develop novel strategies for colon cancer therapy.  This research proposal is primed for success because it is based on a strong foundation of highly innovative preliminary data from analyzing over 240 unique human colon cancer tumors and because my lab and I have the breadth of experience, history of achievement in cancer genomics, and highly original approaches to yield definitive results.

TitreApplicationTitle: The origin, polarization state and function of macrophages in central nervous system injury
Keywords-MotsClés: INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGES; MICROGLIA/MONOCYTES; SPINAL CORD INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury can be a devastating and life changing event. After a traumatic event in the spinal cord, the body's immune system becomes mobilised, and specialised cells begin clear up dead and scared tissue. This inflammatory immune response is essential to this healing process; however, if it is too aggressive, or not switched off at the right time, immune cells can end up damaging, and sometimes removing, healthy tissue. The process is primarily performed by one of the immune system's front line cells, the macrophage (which means 'big eater'). Macrophages phagocytose (devour) unwanted tissue and can either come from the blood or a central nervous system resident immune cell called microglia. The specific roles of blood borne and resident microglia after spinal cord injury, up to now, have been difficult to study, as these types of cell, when clearing damaged tissue, are indistinguishable from one another other.However, we now have an exciting new tool that causes macrophages from the blood (and not resident microglia) to glow green, allowing us to investigate their precise role in spinal cord injury. Once we learn more about the macrophage and microglial contribution after injury, we may be able to help activate or deactivate them where necessary, helping to reduce damage after spinal cord trauma.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Wnt7a in skeletal muscle
Keywords-MotsClés: GENETICS; METABOLISM; MUSCLE; SATELLITE STEM CELLS; TRANSGENIC MOUSE; WNT7A
Abstract-Résumé: Satellite stem cells are a specialized group of muscle cells that are capable of regenerating muscle tissue following injury. Understanding the biology regulating this regenerative capacity is therefore critical for the development of stem-cell based therapies for degenerative muscular disorders such as Muscular Dystrophy.  The Rudnicki lab previously utilized a genetic approach to identify an important protein known as Wnt7a that can stimulate muscle growth when applied to cultured muscle cells. The goal of my research project is to create a genetic mouse model that has elevated levels of Wnt7a in muscle tissues to determine the effect of this protein in a living organism. These mice will then be bred to another mouse model for muscular dystrophy.  I will investigate the effect of Wnt7a on muscle stem cell function, muscle fiber growth, and motor function and behavior in these mice. The expected outcome of this research is that Wnt7a will improve muscle regeneration and motor function in mice modeling muscular dystrophy, making this protein a potential regenerative therapy for muscular dystrophy and other disorders marked by muscle wasting and degeneration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Resilience and chronic spinal pain
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC PAIN; RESILIENCE; SPINAL DISORDERS; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELLING
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic spinal pain is a common problem causing significant disability. Its impact on an individual's quality of life can be considerable, affecting physical and mental health. Research has focused on identifying factors that predict a poor recovery.  Alternatively, the concept of resilience focuses on identifying people who respond well to treatment. Resilience, defined here as 'the ability to bounce back' when faced with challenging health conditions is emerging in the field of chronic pain with particular attention to its role in pain management.  Currently there has been no study of the ability of people to bounce back from chronic spinal pain.  Physiotherapy treatment addresses the problems of physical pain and disability, which are often affected by other risk factors, such as fear of movement, that may increase the likelihood of having chronic pain.  Treatment approaches to deal with fear of movement such as gradual return to activity, have had limited success. The study of resilience will increase our understanding of why some people adjust better than others.   By identifying the role of resilience to recovery from chronic spinal pain, programs to prevent chronic pain and build resilience can be put into place thereby decreasing the burden of this population on our healthcare system.  This study will recruit patients with spinal pain attending physiotherapy from a multidisciplinary rehabilitation clinic in Toronto Ontario.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Intelligent Needle Adjustment Assistant for Prostate Brachytherapy
Keywords-MotsClés: 1101 HUMAN HEALTH; 1102 BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; 1901 BIOMEDICAL TECHNOLOGY; 2601 ROBOTIC CONTROL AND AUTOMATION; DEVICE DEVELOPMENT; NEEDLE STEERING; PROSTATE BRACHYTHERAPY; SEED MISPLACEMENT; SURGEON ASSISTANT
Abstract-Résumé: Brachytherapy is a popular treatment for men with early prostate cancer due to its high success rate, minimal side effects, and patient convenience. It involves the insertion of needles loaded with tiny radioactive seeds into the prostate. Once the needles are fully inserted, they are pulled back to permanently leave the seeds in locations inside and around the prostate, where high doses of radiation released from them kill the cancer cells.  For successful brachytherapy, the radioactive seeds should be implanted in their planned locations (targets) inside or around the prostate with high accuracy. However, current techniques only enable surgeons to place a seed to within 5 mm of an intended target, which is a relatively large inaccuracy as the average prostate is only about 50 mm in total diameter.   We intend to develop a hand-held instrument for surgeons that will help them place seeds closer to their intended targets. More accurate seed placement will considerably improve the treatment of prostate cancer. Delivering radiation with pinpoint accuracy will lead to better prostate cancer control and fewer side effects (e.g., difficulty urinating or experiencing rectal discomfort) for patients. Our research results can also allow for using seed implantation for treatment of prostate cancer situations not possible with the current imprecise technique; one example is treating only a part of the prostate (as opposed to the current practice of placing seeds throughout the whole prostate) for very early prostate cancers.  Our research will create an intelligent needle adjustment assistant consisting of a hand-held device for the surgeon and an associated computer program that together will ensure seeds reach their intended targets in an accurate, repeatable and controlled manner as the surgeon manually inserts a needle. The assistant does so by automatically correcting the needle tip's bevel location and heading as it is inserted into the prostate by the surgeon.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcutaneous microsphere vaccine technology
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUVANT; BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING 1900; DRUG DELIVERY; HUMAN PHARMACEUTICALS 504; LIFE SCIENCES 1200; LIFE SCIENCES RESEARCH 6400; MICRONEEDLES; MICROSPHERES; NANOPARTICLES; SKIN
Abstract-Résumé: Common "killed" microbe vaccines such as hepatitis vaccine, must be given repeatedly to be effective. Influenza vaccine must be given yearly. This is costly and inconvenient. In recent work we have shown that vaccines can be incorporated into dissolving spheres that release bursts of vaccine in the skin at timed intervals. We will use this system to obtain the same effect as repeated administration, but with a single administration. The spheres will be delivered into the skin painlessly using new microscopic hollow needles that allow painless administration. We plan to optimize this new method of vaccination by combining the skills of an immunologist, a pharmacy scientist, a mechanical engineer and a clinical vaccinologist. The projected advantages of this new vaccine system are lowered cost, pain free administration, and increased efficacy

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating The Interaction Between Prefrontal And Striatal Dopamine In A Novel Model Of Schizophrenia Pathology On Tasks Related To The Positive, Negative, And Cognitive Symptoms Of Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; DOPAMINE; PREFRONTAL; SCHIZOPHRENIA; VENTRAL STRIATUM
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is an incurable chronic and disabling mental disorder. Symptoms are classified into three domains: positive or psychotic symptoms (eg hallucinations, delusions), negative symptoms (eg anhedonia, a decreased response to rewarding stimuli), and cognitive deficits (including attentional deficits and poor decision-making). Current treatments are only effective at controlling psychosis; negative symptoms and cognitive impairments continue to affect these patients. Schizophrenia research should therefore address the entire range of symptoms to improve treatments and animal models can provide valuable information in this regard. An ideal schizophrenia model should mimic known neurochemical dysfunction present in affected patients. Schizophrenia is hypothesized to be a developmental disorder. During development, an incident may occur that permanently reduces dopamine (DA) in the prefrontal cortex. Then in late adolescence, in response to environmental stressors, DA in the striatum abnormally increases and neurons within this region become hyper-sensitive to DA. The combination of reduced DA in the prefrontal cortex and increased DA in the striatum results in the presentation of schizophrenia.  The proposed experiments involve an animal model of schizophrenia based on these hypotheses. DA pathways in the prefrontal cortex will be disrupted in rats early in development, reducing DA in this region. Rats will then develop an amphetamine-induced sensitized state in late adolescence, which is dependent upon increased striatal DA. The combination of these two manipulations is analogous to the proposed pathology of schizophrenia. This two-hit model, as well as rats receiving only one treatment, will be tested on translational tasks relevant to each symptom domain. Validating the model in relation to schizophrenia-like behaviours and neurochemical abnormalities will aid in the development of ideal pharmaceutical agents by providing the ability to screen novel drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phospho-regulation of Disordered Proteins and their Complexes in Synaptic Plasticity.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLOSTERY; FLUORESCENCE; INTRINSICALLY DISORDERED PROTEINS; MACROMOLECULAR INTERACTION; NUCLEAR MAGNETCI RESONANCE; PROTEIN DYNAMICS; PROTEIN POST TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATION; SMALL ANGLE X-RAY SCATTERING; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; THERMODYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Until recently, there has been a long-held view that, for proteins to perform their biological functions, they must fold into well-defined structures. However, it is becoming increasingly evident that a broad category of proteins does not fold into stable structures, yet they carry out critical functions in many biological processes. More importantly, dysfunctions of these intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are implicated in numerous diseases such as cancer, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and chronic pain. Detailed structural characterizations of IDPs and their complexes are very limited. As a result, there is currently a poor understanding of the molecular basis of function and malfunction of IDPs. A major goal of this project is to expand our understanding of the structural and dynamic properties of IDPs and their mechanism of regulation by posttranslational modification. Combination of NMR, fluorescence and small angle X-ray scattering techniques will be used to provide detailed kinetics, thermodynamics and structural information on these disordered protein ensembles and their complexes. To achieve this goal, two intrinsically neural disordered complexes and their phosphorylation dependences will be investigated. The first is the interaction of N-methyl-D-aspartate class of glutamate receptors (NMDARs) with the non-receptor tyrosine kinase, Src, which is involved in chronic inflammatory and neuropathic pain. The second is the eIF4E:4E-BP2 complex which inhibits protein synthesis, a process critical for synaptic plasticity, learning and memory formation in the central nervous system. Detailed structural models of these dynamic complexes and their regulation by phosphorylation will give us specific insights into the underlying biophysical mechanisms of their biological functions. Our results will also facilitate development of novel therapeutics that target NMDAR:Src and eIF4E:4E-BP2 interactions for the treatment of chronic pain and other neurological diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the impact of drug policy reform on HIV-related risk behaviours and access to methadone maintenance treatment among injection drug users in Mexico
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG POLICY; HIV/AIDS; INJECTION DRUG USE; METHADONE MAINTENANCE TREATMENT; MEXICO; MIXED-METHODS RESEARCH; MULTILEVEL MODELING; NORTH AMERICA
Abstract-Résumé: The illicit drug trade in North America continues to proliferate, with the three countries of the continent - Canada, the United States, and Mexico - responding to the risk for HIV and other drug-related harms among injection drug users in a variety of ways. Perhaps the most acutely affected is Mexico, marked by high levels of drug-related violence since the 2006 launch of a national "War on Drugs". In light of ongoing violence and HIV transmission, in August 2010 Mexican policymakers passed a law decriminalizing the possession of small amounts of illicit drugs, and stipulating that repeat drug offenders be sent to addiction treatment or, barring that, to jail. However, concerns exist regarding implementation of the law, given that addiction treatment has yet to be adequately scaled up. As such, the law has been met with both praise and criticism regarding its potential for unintended consequences. The proposed project would therefore investigate the impact of this drug policy reform on risk of HIV transmission and addiction treatment access among injection drug users in Tijuana, a town on the Mexico-United States border disproportionately affected by injection drug use and HIV. Observational data from cohort participants will be employed to determine to what extent policy reforms have been implemented, and to assess their impact on indicators of HIV risk and other negative health and social outcomes. This data will be supplemented by population-level census data on variables such as mortality, health, and median neighbourhood income, in order to conduct multilevel analyses that will provide further context for the health and social outcomes observed. Further, in-depth interviews with a subset of cohort participants who report being arrested will be analyzed qualitatively to provide a comprehensive mixed-methods approach to determining the impact of drug policy reform on the health of injection drug users in Mexico.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the impact of beta-subunit interactions on voltage gated potassium channel regulation using unnatural amino acid mutagenesis and mass spectrometry.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOPHYSICS; CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIA; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ION CHANNELS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; PHARMACOLOGY; UNNATUAL AMINO ACIDS
Abstract-Résumé: A cardiac arrhythmia is an electrical disturbance in the heart, which can cause a wide variety of potentially life threatening conditions. The root of these disturbances is a malfunction in the protein channels that open and close to transmit the bioelectric currents signaling each heartbeat. Different types of channels are responsible for triggering, sustaining or terminating these electric signals; an arrhythmia occurs when the opening or closing of one or more of these channels becomes mistimed. One of the key channels responsible for terminating the electrical signal is the voltage gated potassium channel, KCNQ1. This channel is regulated by a family of five much smaller accessory proteins, which physically associate with the channel's exterior. Each family member interacts with the channel differently to effect its movements and change its conducting properties, depending on the needs of the heart. These accessory proteins are necessary for healthy function; however, several inherited mutations in their genes can result in early or late termination of the heart's signaling, causing an arrhythmia to develop. In our project we aim to better understand the mechanism for how each of the different accessory proteins regulates KCNQ1. To achieve this we will combine a new crosslinking technique, electrophysiology and mass spectrometry to find and characterize the key sites of interaction between the channel and its different accessory proteins. This analysis will give us insights into the atomic level movements of the channel and how the different accessory subunits encourage or impede those movements to control the channel's properties. Our proposed experiments will fill crucial gaps in the knowledge of how these accessory subunits regulate KCNQ1 and ultimately cardiac function. This information will aid in designing better pharmaceuticals to help restore and maintain healthy electrical activity in the heart.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel approach towards understanding the functional biology of the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) protein CLN3
Keywords-MotsClés: BATTEN DISEASE; CELL BIOLOGY; CLN3; DICTYOSTELIUM DISCOIDEUM; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; KNOCKOUT MUTANT; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NEURODEGENERATION; NEURONAL CEROID LIPOFUSCINOSIS; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Batten disease is the most common neurodegenerative disorder to affect children. The central nervous system is the most dramatically affected organ where neuronal dysfunction leads to vision loss, epilepsy, progressive mental retardation, and a reduced lifespan. Batten disease results from mutations in the CLN3 gene, which encodes a transmembrane protein of unknown function. The high conservation of CLN3 from yeast to human has allowed for studies of the protein in simple model organisms, yet the precise function of CLN3 remains incompletely understood. The purpose of my research is to determine the normal function of CLN3. I will create genetic models of mutations and knock-out the gene in the model organism Dictyostelium and then study how the loss-of-function causes defects at the cell and multicellular level. In this organism there is a single CLN3 gene that is highly similar to human. Dictyostelium cells display remarkably similar biological behaviors to mammalian cells and this model organism has been used with great success to study other proteins that cause neurodegeneration (e.g. Huntington's, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's disease). By creating a new biomedical model system deficient for CLN3, I will be able to characterize the resulting defects with unparalleled cellular clarity, given the well defined cell biology and unique life cycle of Dictyostelium. I can then introduce the human CLN3 protein into these cells to assess rescue of defects and can also introduce human CLN3 proteins that contain different mutations to study how these mutations specifically affect its function. Understanding the functionality of CLN3 and the effect of CLN3 mutations will significantly advance our knowledge of the biological pathways that are affected in Batten disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Polymers for Proteomic Enrichment of Early Cancer Biomarkers
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CANCER; MULTIFUNCTIONAL POLYMERS; PATIENT DIAGNOSIS; PEPTIDE ENRICHMENT; PEPTIDES; POLYMERS
Abstract-Résumé: . Despite the global research effort aimed at cancer prevention and treatment, cancer is still a major killer of Canadians. The cost of diagnosis and treatment to our health care system is staggering. We need better, early and accurate diagnostic tests of cancer to provide the best early treatments to improve treatment outcomes and reduce loss of life.  Cancer can be detected early in patients by finding tumor molecules that leak into the bloodstream. These scarce proteins and their breakdown products are known as tumor biomarkers. However, collecting sufficient amounts of such biomarkers to make an early and accurate cancer diagnosis is a challenge. Blood is a very complex sample to analyze, containing many different proteins where the high amounts of some normal proteins mask the cancer biomarkers. Compounding this challenge is that some biomarkers are also present in healthy people, although at lower levels, but sometimes even with the modifications or mutations that are found in greater amounts in the cancer biomarkers. Together this makes cancer biomarkers very difficult to detect using current techniques and clinical tests.  We aim to develop new techniques that will improve the detection of such biomarkers. We have designed and produced a specialized polymer material that displays many "molecular hooks" to pull out small protein pieces (called peptides) from complex patient samples such as blood. The peptides are then identified by a technique called mass spectrometry. We propose to develop five new polymers to enrich for five specific types of modified peptides that are found in malignant breast and oral cancers, but not normal tissue or benign tumors. By analyzing the unique fingerprint of these peptides we will establish a set of biomarker proteins that will be developed as a new clinical test for breast, oral and other types of cancer and to assess treatment options. Moreover, select biomarkers will point to new drug targets to treat cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Photoacoustic Imaging for Image Guided Prostate Cancer Interventions
Keywords-MotsClés: 1101 HUMAN HEALTH; 1102 BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; 1900 BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; 2505 PHOTONIC DEVICES AND NETWORKS; CATHETER; IMAGE REGISTRATION; NANOSECOND PULSED LASER; PHOTOACOUSTIC IMAGING; PROSTATE CANCER; ULTRASOUND
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy and second leading cancer-related cause of death in North American men. Despite advances in ultrasound (US) and magnetic resonance imaging, there is still a need for imaging techniques which can perform real-time, intra-operative imaging of PCa during diagnostic and treatment procedures. The applicants propose to develop a photoacoustic (PA) imaging system that can be used for in vivo PCa imaging and validate its effectiveness on detecting PCa through patient study. PA imaging utilizes a laser to excite US signal in tissue and a US machine to detect the signal. It has been demonstrated in human breast and small animal imaging where excellent views of blood vessels and tumors have been achieved. PA imaging has never been applied to in vivo PCa imaging on patients due to some technical challenges. The applicants propose a method to overcome those challenges and develop the first in-vivo PA imaging system for clinical study of PCa. The applicants will further use the developed PA imaging system to acquire clinical data on blood vessels and oxygenation from PCa and find their correlation with tumor malignancy and metastasis. This work can have an impact on the treatment of PCa and derive significant health benefits for Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predicting readmission to hospital for adults with chronic medical conditions
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; CHRONIC MEDICAL CONDITIONS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; OUTCOMES RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: The impact of chronic medical conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, and stroke are a major concern for health systems in Canada and abroad. These conditions often occur together and are associated with poor health outcomes including hospitalization and death. Readmission to hospital is also common and results in adverse outcomes and high costs in patients with chronic disease. The ability to accurately predict readmission after hospital discharge is important, as it would enable health care workers to focus post-discharge interventions on patients at highest risk of readmission.  Unfortunately, validated prediction tools are either not currently available or are limited by the use of a single clinical data source. Linking population-based survey data with national administrative data will provide a detailed and rich data source that will enable exploration of patient characteristics, clinical factors, and environmental factors that place patients at risk for hospital readmission. It will also be used to develop a tool to predict the risk of readmission amongst Canadians with chronic disease.  This novel methodology has important implications for patient care and health policy. The development of a prediction tool will not only assist clinicians and hospital administrators in identifying patients at risk of readmission, it will also enable discharge instructions and interventions to be targeted to reduce this risk and ultimately improve patient care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Non-Invasive Probe to Assess the Quality and Suitability for Transfusion of Stored Red Blood Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: 1201 LIFE SCIENCES (INCLUDING BIOTECHNOLOGY); 1901 BIOMEDICAL TECHNOLOGY; 3505 ANALYTICAL SPECTROSCOPY; 518 MEDICAL EQUIPMENT AND APPARATUS; AGEING OF STORED RED BLOOD CELLS; BIOANALYTICAL CHEMISTRY; BIOMEDICAL OPTICS; NONDESTRUCTIVE ANALYSIS OF CELLS; RAMAN SPECTROSCOPY; RED BLOOD CELL STORAGE LESION
Abstract-Résumé: Managing the supplies of donated blood products (i.e. plasma, red cells, platelets) is an increasing challenge faced by blood service agencies the world over in part because, even under the best known storage conditions, these products steadily degrade and different products age at different rates. Units of red blood cells (RBCs), for example, can only be stored for 42 days before they are considered unusable. The accumulated degradation that begins immediately upon collection is called "storage lesion" which refers to the effects of an ensemble of chemical, physiological and morphological changes in stored RBC that can be harmful to some patients upon transfusion. Importantly, blood from different donors ages differently, and different patients exhibit different sensitivities to storage lesion present in transfused blood. Hence, for some units and/or some patients, the 42-day window is actually too long. Yet significantly reducing the storage age limit raises the risk of RBC shortages as the number of discarded units due to outdate would rise considerably. What is badly needed is a way to separate those units that are still suitable for transfusion from those units that should not be used. We propose to address this important need by developing an optical method based on Raman spectroscopy (RS) that would be able to assess the state of stored blood rapidly and accurately, without needing to remove samples from the bag. The goals of the proposed research are: 1) to characterize RBC ageing in stored human blood using Raman spectroscopy; 2) to identify specific spectral markers for RBC storage lesion and correlate these markers with conventional biochemical assays; 3) to develop a turn-key, hand-held RS-based probe for nondestructively assessing the condition of stored RBC in situ within conventional storage bags. This project will yield new non-invasive sensing technology that will help ensure better and more uniform quality of transfused RBCs for Canadian patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implementing highly specialized and evidence-based pediatric eating disorder treatment in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: EATING DISORDERS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PSYCHOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Eating disorders, which include anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, are common in adolescent females and can have serious emotional and physical consequences, including death.  Despite our knowledge about the severity of these illnesses, our previous research indicates that adolescent patients are not receiving the best available treatment. The goal of the proposed project is to reduce the gap between what research tells us is the best known treatment and what treatment is actually delivered. We will work with four pediatric eating disorder treatment programs in Ontario to increase the use of Family-Based Treatment, a proven effective therapy to treat eating disorders among children and adolescents that places parents in charge of the refeeding process. We will train therapists in this treatment model, as well as provide support to these therapists on a monthly basis so that they can use the model appropriately in practice. We will study research-informed methods that have previously been used successfully in other areas of health care to increase the use of evidence-based treatments.  This study will ultimately help to ensure that young people with eating disorders receive the treatment known to have the best outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The sex-specific epigenetic impact of early versus adult life stress in animal models of stress-induced depression
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; CHROMATIN MODIFICATIONS; DEPRESSION; DNA METHYLATION; DNA METHYLATION IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; EPIGENETICS; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTION; HIGH-THROUGPUT SEQUENCING; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Environmental stressors (both early (ELS) and adult-life (ALS) stressors) increase the risk for depressive-like disorders. ELS and ALS occur at distinct periods of neuroplasticity, implying the involvement of different molecular pathways. In addition, as females have been shown to be more susceptible to the effects of stress, these mechanisms likely differ in a sex-specific fashion. While most of the research using animal models of depression has focused mainly on male mice, recent advances have made it possible to extend this research to females as well. The consequences of stress on mood disorders has been suggested to be mediated via alterations in the epigenetic control of gene expression in various brain regions, and similar mechanisms have also been attributed to the therapeutic effects of antidepressant drugs. However, the general and sex-specific epigenetic alterations induced by ELS and ALS, as well as the molecular mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of antidepressants in the brain are still poorly understood. Thus, we propose to develop a series of experiments to identify the general and sex-specific molecular alterations induced by ELS and ALS, as well as the molecular targets of antidepressant drugs, in animal models of stress-induced depression using genome wide DNA methylation and gene expression high-throughput next-gen sequencing. These experiments will be followed by functional characterization of top candidate gene networks using genetic mutant mice, optogenetics experiments and viral mediated gene transfer. These experiments have the promises to pinpoint sex-specific gene networks differentially involved in the effects of early versus adult life stress and to define molecular pathways by which antidepressants may induce their effect on mood regulation.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of viral quantity and diversity on neurovirulence in HIV/AIDS
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; DEMENTIA; HIV; NEUROVIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the success of antiretroviral therapies, approximately 25% of persons with HIV/AIDS inevitably exhibit one or more nervous system disorders, which also predict reduced survival. The abundance and type of virus (HIV-1) in the blood are important indicators of HIV-associated immunodeficiency and response to treatment. Conversely, the amount and kind of HIV-1 in the brain and the response to treatment of virus in the brain remain unknown. The objective of this proposal is to investigate what properties of HIV-1 are responsible for the processes causing HIV-associated brain disease and how these processes are affected by antiretroviral therapy. We will investigate how virus quantity and genetic variation cause brain disease in different models, as well as the effects of specific antiretroviral drugs that penetrate the brain. Our findings will lead to new preventative and/or therapeutic options for HIV infection of the nervous system and will contribute to the understanding of how HIV-1 might be eradicated from the body.

TitreApplicationTitle: Does Metronomic Chemotherapy Preferentially Target Ovarian Cancer Stem Cells?
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIANGIOGENIC THERAPY; CANCER STEM CELLS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; METRONOMIC CHEMOTHERAPY; OVARIAN CANCER; PRECLINICAL IN VIVO TUMOUR MODELS; THERAPY RESPONSE; TUMOUR IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: My project attempts to change what is one of the most frustrating aspects of cancer chemotherapy, especially for patients with advanced metastatic disease, namely the all-too-often limited benefits in prolonging survival or achieving cure.  These limited benefits are still the norm even when tumours are induced to significantly shrink by exposing patients every few weeks to the highest doses of chemotherapy they can tolerate i.e. 'maximum tolerated doses' (MTDs), which can cause very toxic side effects.  One reason to account for this is that there resides within tumours low numbers of what are known as 'cancer stem cells' (CSCs).  These cells tend to be highly resistant to MTD chemotherapy in contrast to the 'bulk' population of non-CSCs.  So conventional chemotherapy spares CSCs during tumour shrinkage allowing them to repopulate the tumour mass after therapy. Our group has been working on an investigational therapeutic concept known as low-dose 'metronomic' chemotherapy (MC) where the chemotherapy is given frequently with no prolonged breaks (e.g. daily oral drugs).  Despite less toxicity, and hence no need for breaks, it can be remarkably effective in preclinical studies even when treating advanced metastatic disease in mice.  Based on several observations there is reason to think that this counterintuitive therapeutic outcome is based on the possibility that MC targets the CSC subpopulation.  My project is designed to confirm this hypothesis by comparing the effects of several MTD vs potent MC regimens in mice models of advanced metastatic ovarian cancer, using three independent assays to detect CSCs.  Some experiments will also involve assessing the impact of adding an 'antiangiogenic' drug that targets the tumour's growing vasculature to MC since such combinations can cause remarkable anti-tumour effects.  The results of these experiments could change the perception about chemotherapy and CSCs, and foster more aggressive clinical trial development of MC.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development of an eosinophil-specific bioactive paper detection system
Keywords-MotsClés: 1101; 1211; 2006; 3504; ASTHMA; BIOACTIVE PAPER; BIOMARKER; DIAGNOSTICS; EOSINOPHIL PROTEIN; SPUTUM
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma and COPD are common airway diseases, Flare-ups (exacerbations) cause significant morbidity. The majority of these are associated with an allergic type of bronchitis that is characterized by the presence of a white blood cell, eosinophil, that can be detected in sputum. However, this is not assessed currently by physicians. Exacerbations can be significantly reduced when treatment using anti-inflammatory drugs are adjusted by measuring this cell in sputum and it also leads to much better control of the disease and prevention of future exacerbations. However, this process requires a specialist laboratory and is not practical on a large scale. The objective of this project is to develop a paper-based dip stick technology that can accurately identify an eosinophil specific protein that can used as a point-of-care diagnostic test for the management of airway diseases.

Keywords-MotsClés: AMINOGLYCOSIDE PHOSPHOTRANSFERASES; ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE; ENZYMES (5404); HUMAN HEALTH (1101); MEDICAL AND HEALTH SCIENCES (1211); MEDICINAL CHEMISTRY; ORGANIC SYNTHESES (3703); RATIONAL BASED DRUG DESIGN; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Multidrug resistant microbes have become one of the top global health challenges and place a massive burden on the Canadian health care system. One approach to overcome this problem involves inhibiting the enzymes responsible for conferring resistance to the antibiotic. We have recently discovered a family of compounds that blocks the action of a series of aminoglycoside phosphotransferases (APH) and wish to develop the compounds to ultimately provide an optimized, on- target, on-mechanism lead suitable for development into a therapeutic agent.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of an Antimicrobial Resistance Diversity Index (ARDI) to guide initiatives and investment in public health, antimicrobial stewardship and infection control
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE; HUMAN HEALTH 1101; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MATHEMATICAL BIOLOGY AND PHYSIOLOGY 2957; MATHEMATICAL MODELLING 2960; MEDICAL AND HEALTH SCIENCES 1211
Abstract-Résumé: Antimicrobial-resistant germs do not respond to one or more antibiotics. Patients who acquire infections from these germs have longer hospital stays, an increased risk of death, and their care is more expensive. In Canada, the number of antimicrobial-resistant germs appears to be increasing, but we do not have a good way of measuring "resistance", and so it is difficult for researchers and healthcare experts to be certain what is happening with antimicrobial resistance. The goal of our project is to invent a summary statistic that measures total resistance by combining information of different types - for example, information on resistance to different types of drugs; resistance to different numbers of drugs; and resistance in different species of microbes. We will analyze data from Canadian hospitals and use our statistic to understand how quickly total resistance is increasing year-to-year and to compare between hospitals and geographic regions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a pumpless lung assist device which acts like an artificial placenta for neonates with respiratory failure.
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTIFICIAL PLACENTA
Abstract-Résumé: Respiratory failure is the major cause of morbidity among neonates with birth weights less than 1,500 g. Mechanical ventilation has dramatically improved neonatal outcome during the last decade. However, this approach is not effective enough in neonates with severe respiratory failure to prevent fatality or side-effects that lead to long-term impairment. Constructing a lung assist device (LAD) which imitates the placental gas exchange would be a milestone in innovation for neonatal medicine. Such a device would allow for additional gas exchange under end-stage lung failure when mechanical ventilation becomes inadequate. To create such a LAD we will combine and develop the following features: oxygenator with low priming volume, the extracorporeal circulation only driven by the heart (pumpless), flow control and monitor, large bore vascular access via umbilical vein and artery, hemocompatible inner surfaces (no activation of blood clotting) and effectiveness for a body weight range of 0.5-5 kg. During the last 18 months we have formed an interdisciplinary research group of physicians, engineers and students who have assisted in developing a LAD prototype as a stack of microfluidic oxygenators. Using a newborn hypoxic piglet model (n=6) we demonstrated the proof of principle. To develop inner surfaces of the LAD which do not activate blood clotting, we studied coating properties of the material using radiolabelling. To achieve a large bore access we developed the design of an expandable catheter in collaboration with a medical technology company. This artificial placenta concept has been protected by filing a provisional US Patent, No. 61526288. The proposed LAD acting as an artificial placenta will be easy to install, cost effective and can be safely operated by standard neonatal intensive care personnel. The proposed LAD could become the next leading tool to aid infants with end-stage lung failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Attention from the top down: prefrontal control of the basal forebrain cholinergic system
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; ALZHEIMER'S; ATTENTION; AWAKE BEHAVIOR; BASAL FOREBRAIN; CHOLINERGIC; CIRCUIT TRACING; HISTOLOGY; OPTOGENETICS; PREFRONTAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Our ability to willfully direct our attention to a particular feature of the environment is a hallmark of conscious experience. The flexible control of attention requires the prefrontal cortex (PFC), which can influence sensory processing in distant brain regions. The PFC is believed to do this through direct connections to sensory cortex and an indirect pathway that involves the basal forebrain (BF). The basal forebrain (BF) provides acetylcholine to the cortex and is critically involved in the regulation of sleep, alertness and attention. New evidence suggests that the BF sends bursts of acetylcholine to brain areas involved in sensory processing to boost their sensitivity to incoming information. We hypothesize that the PFC integrates information about the task at hand and uses that information to control the BF, which modulates cortical function to help the brain selectively attend to important incoming stimuli while ignoring distractions. Evidence for this hypothesis includes the observation that sensory stimulation causes release of acetylcholine primarily within those areas processing the stimulus. The specific release of acetylcholine requires the intact function of the PFC, which is also the only part of cortex that sends information to the BF. The circuit linking PFC, BF and sensory cortex is thought to be a fundamental part of conscious attention, but an inability to selectively control has prevented a detailed understanding of its function until now. To test this hypothesis, we will use genetically engineered viruses to trace connections between the PFC and BF and then activate that circuit selectively using novel optical techniques. Acetylcholine levels, neuronal activity, and behavior will be assessed in mice to determine the function of this circuit and its role in attention. Ultimately, this work may facilitate new therapies for disorders of attention and cognition such as Alzheimer's disease, whose burden will only increase as our population ages.

TitreApplicationTitle: Muscle Strength and Myokines: Novel Factors for Metabolic Disease in Overweight Youth?
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMETABOLIC RISK FACTORS; CHILDHOOD OBESITY; CYTOKINES; EXERCISE; INFLAMMATION; METABOLIC SYNDROME; MUSCLE MASS; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Regular physical activity reduces the risk for obesity-related chronic diseases, in particular type 2 diabetes. We have found that a person's muscle strength is a physical activity-related variable that reduces the risk for type 2 diabetes risks in overweight individuals. The association between muscle strength and health outcomes has not been extensively studied in overweight youth and the mechanisms for this link remain poorly understood. Some scientists have recently discovered that muscles release protective factors (called myokines) that may explain the reduced risk for chronic diseases in people who exercise regularly.  At least three major research questions remain unanswered and will be explored within the next few years in our lab:   1) Is cardiometabolic risk lower among overweight youth with higher muscle strength?  2) Are youth with type 2 diabetes characterized by low muscle strength and an adverse myokine profile?  3) Does resistance training improve cardiometabolic risk and myokines profile of youth with type 2 diabetes?   We will use national data to test for an association between muscle strength and type 2 diabetes in children. We will also test for determine if muscle strength and myokines are lower in children with type 2 diabetes. Finally, we will see if improving muscle strength will improve the myokine and type 2 diabetes risk profile in children. The results will broaden our understanding of why some children are at a particular risk for type 2 diabetes and potentially how we can reduce that risk

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the gendered dimensions of place, HIV risk, and violence among street-involved youth who do sex work in Vancouver, Canada: a longitudinal ethnographic investigation
Keywords-MotsClés: ETHNOGRAPHY; GENDER; HIV/AIDS; INNER CITY DRUG SCENE; PLACE AND SPACE THEORY; SEX WORK; URBAN HEALTH; VIOLENCE; VISUAL ANTHROPOLOGY; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: In Canadian urban settings, drug-using youth who are street involved and exchange sex for money, shelter and/or drugs are particularly vulnerable to HIV, sexually transmitted infections and high levels of violence. In greater Vancouver, rapid urban development, recent policy initiatives such as the creation of supportive housing for at-risk youth, and legislative changes in criminal policies around sex work and drug use (e.g., the possible decriminalization of sex work in Canada, mandatory minimums for drug sentences), have the potential to transform young people's experiences of safety, risk and harm in the places in which they live and work. The proposed ethnographic study will explore how these various changes impact young people's health over time. A key focus will be the effect of these changes on where and how young people conduct sex work (e.g., online, indoors, outdoors), and the relationship between these places and HIV and drug-related risks. I will also explore how young people's gender (their ascribed roles and relative power as men and women and sexual minorities) shapes experiences of different kinds of violence in the places where they live and work. Over a three-year study period, I will conduct participant-observation in the places frequented by young people, as well as formal and informal in-depth interviews with both young men and young women who use drugs and do sex work. In addition, I will use visual methods (e.g., the creation of photo essays, maps) to better understand young people's perspectives on risk, harm and safety in relation to different places. The results from this research will be important in informing the development of health policy and interventions that address the complex environments that shape HIV and drug-related risks, harm and safety among young people who use drugs and do sex work.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the relationships between residential stability, physical and mental health, and quality of life in homeless and vulnerably housed individuals: A longitudinal multi-site cohort study in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH AND QUALITY OF LIFE OF HOMELESS; HOUSING AND HOMELESSNESS; LATENT CLASS GROWTH MODELING; LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS; POPULATION HEALTH; PSYCHOMETRICS; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Housing is a basic human need and a significant socio-economic determinant of population health. In Canada, an increasingly large number of individuals are facing homelessness and inadequate housing, with tens of thousands of people being homeless on any given night. Homelessness and inadequate housing have considerable negative impact on individuals' physical and mental health as well as their quality of life. In order to elucidate factors that affect residential (in)stability, and the interactions between inadequate housing, health, and quality of life, longitudinal research is needed. This project draws upon Canada's first longitudinal multi-site cohort study of homeless and vulnerably housed individuals (HVHIs). In this study, 1,200 HVHIs are interviewed annually over a 5-year period in Ottawa, Toronto, and Vancouver. The interview surveys assess demographic characteristics, residential trajectory, physical and mental health diagnoses, quality of life, psychological distress, family history, social support, risk behaviours, service utilization, contact with the legal system, and life events. These data are being linked to participants' health insurance databases providing information on their health care utilization. Complex statistical methods will be employed to examine the relationships between housing, health, and quality of life among the HVHIs over time; the combination of individual, contextual, and health factors that predict residential (in)stability; and how the health status, psychological distress, social support, risk behaviours, quality of life, and use of health care services change during or after periods of residential stability.  This research is critical for understanding the relationships between inadequate housing, health and quality of life, and for creating research knowledge that can be used to inform programs and policy decisions for improving the health and quality of life of Canadians who are homeless or vulnerably housed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Influence of Glucose Metabolism on the Neural Regulation of Food Reward in Adolescents
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; FLAVOUR; FLAVOUR LEARNING PREFERENCES; FMRI; FOOD INTAKE; FOOD REWARD; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; NEURAL RESPONSE; OBESITY; PRE-DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: The obesity epidemic has unfolded in a matter of decades, not millennia, and cannot therefore be attributed to a drift in the genome. Rather, the temporal characteristics of the epidemic more closely track environmental and lifestyle changes, such as increased availability of palatable and caloric foods and drinks (among others). Obesity is a serious problem in children and adolescents, as obesity at this period of growth predicts obesity and chronic diseases such as diabetes in adulthood. However, one important observation is that not everyone is becoming overweight or obese. This has led to the suggestion that individual factors, such as differences in reward regions in the brain, may interact with environmental cues and metabolic changes, to predispose some to overeat. Importantly, preliminary work from the Small laboratory indicates that brain reward circuit response to flavour is regulated by glucose metabolism in healthy weight adults. More specifically, change in blood glucose levels following ingestion of a flavoured caloric beverage closely regulates neural responses to the flavour of that beverage when later consumed in the absence of calories. We hypothesize that adolescents with pre-diabetes will have increased blood glucose response after a caloric drink, which will be reflected by greater activation in brain reward circuits. Therefore, the objective is to examine whether changes in glucose metabolism in adolescents (12-16 y) with pre-diabetes enhances the ability of caloric drinks to regulate reward circuits in the brain and control food intake. Neural responses (measured using fMRI) to non-caloric novel flavours will be assessed before and after one of the flavours was associated with calories by means of the addition of maltodextrin. The findings of the proposed research will provide a clearer understanding of how glucose homeostasis influences the neural regulation of food reward in adolescents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a mobile multimodal assistive technology for the navigation of persons with disabilities in urban area
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESSIBILITY MAPPING; ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY; COGNITIVE DESIGN; DISABILITY CREATION PROCESS; MOBILITY; MULTIMODAL INTERFACE; PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES; REHABILITATION; SPATIO-TEMPORAL DATABASES; WEB MAPPING
Abstract-Résumé: Social participation of persons with disabilities represents a challenging problem for Canadian and international societies. According to Health Canada, Over 3,300,000 Canadians report some level of disability that poses a unique problem to their health. Recent data published by Statistics Canada shows that the proportion of persons with a disability, aged 15 and more, has increased from 14.6% in 2001 to 16.6% in 2006. For a large majority of these persons, the ability to move independently is essential for their daily activities and for their efficient engagement in their social roles (e.g. work, go to school, go to the market, participate in community life, etc.). However, the mobility of these persons is significantly constrained by their disabilities as well as the environment in which they perform their daily activities (obstacles such as stairs, sidewalk, doors, architectural barriers, etc.). To address these challenging issues, experts from both the engineering and health/rehabilitation sciences communities are involved in this exciting interdisciplinary project. While the experts in geomatics will address issues related to mapping of accessibility information in urban area and its real-time communication to mobile devices of the persons with disabilities, experts from health/rehabilitation field will consider important issues related to definition of the accessibility criteria with respect to specific characteristics of persons with disabilities as well as the testing protocols. The research will be conducted with close implication of the municipality of Quebec as well as the «Institut de Readaptation en Deficience Physique de Quebec» (IRDPQ).

TitreApplicationTitle: Perk Tutor: Ultrasound-guided Needle Placement Training Platform
Keywords-MotsClés: IMAGE GUIDANCE; PERCUTANEOUS INTERVENTION; SKILL ASSESSMENT; TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: Needle placement interventions have become the standard of care in many diagnostic and therapeutic procedures, such as biopsies, aspiration or tissue ablations. Needle-based surgery has numerous advantages over open surgery but it is a delicate process where precise translation, rotation motions, bending and insertion forces all effect the outcome. The means for desired maneuvering of the surgical device are extremely limited. Unlike conventional surgery, the surgeon does not have direct visual feedback inside the body.    There are challenges to overcome in learning needle placement interventions and in performing them on patients. Trainees have traditionally learned needle interventions in an apprenticeship model. In addition to exposing patients to risk during the learning curve, this model tends to be slow and inherently subjective. It lacks objective, quantitative assessment of surgical skill and performance.     We propose to develop Perk Tutor, a computer-assisted training system in a simulated clinical environment with anthropomorphic models and real instruments. Trainee performance will be quantified and optimal learning scenarios provided for skill acquisition and retention. We will prove that Perk Tutor can effectively prepare novice learners for clinical encounters with patients.     This approach to teaching and learning is consistent with competency-based medical education (CBME) which emphasizes learner-centred abilities rather than time spent learning. The Perk Tutor will generate knowledge for the first known implementation of a competency-based curriculum in needle placement interventions. The investigators, knowledge users and collaborators will provide interdisciplinary training for two graduate students and two postdoctoral fellows. Medical residents?

TitreApplicationTitle: Nanoplasmonics Enhanced Laser Gene Delivery for Retinal Degenerative Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: 1101 HUMAN HEALTH; 1102 BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; 1901 BIOMEDICAL TECHNOLOGY; AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION; CELL TRANSFECTION; GLAUCOMA; LASER THERAPY; PLASMONIC NANOPARTICLES; RETINITIS PIGMENTOSA; RETINOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Retinal degenerative diseases are the leading causes of vision loss and affect millions of individuals in Canada. These diseases are either incurable or can be only moderately ameliorated with current therapies. As an emerging solution, delivering therapeutic genes into impaired cells shows promising results in proof of concept studies, and several clinical trials are undergoing. However, in most cases, gene delivery is based on viral vectors, whose safety is controversial. Viral vectors present disadvantages, such as size limitation, high immunogenicity and potential mutations of transduced cells. Hence, the lack of efficient, non-toxic and persistent gene delivery strategies undermine the full potential of gene transfer therapies against retinal degenerative diseases. The proposed research program aims to develop a non-viral ocular gene delivery technique using ultrafast lasers amplified by plasmonic gold nanoparticles. Our method has been proven able to deliver naked genes into cells with high efficiency and very low cytotoxicity. The proposed project includes optimising the technology for retinal neurons, refining tissue selectivity with biofunctionalized nanoparticles specifically targeting diseased cells, and determining the effectiveness of laser gene delivery in vivo by using mouse models of retinal neurodegeneration. Given the extensive use of lasers in current ophthalmic practice, our technology may be seamlessly inserted to existing clinical setups for treatment of retinal degenerative diseases. This project will be performed by a multidisciplinary team of researchers with highly complementary expertise in femtosecond lasers, biophotonics, ocular optics and retinal cell biology in close collaboration with two user organisations: Optina Diagnostics and the Foundation for Fighting Blindness.

Abstract-Résumé: In this proposal we aim to investigate the use of optical imaging and electroencephalography (EEG) to monitor brain function in the intensive care unit. While each technique independently only partially informs on brain status, we will investigate here the benefits of combining the monitoring of brain activity with EEG with the ability of near-infrared spectroscopy to measure blood volume and oxygenation. This work will develop both an apparatus adapted for the intensive care unit and algorithms to generate alarms to inform clinicians of pathological events. A pilot study in a group of patients will be undertaken to validate the system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bioengineered chimpanzee adenovirus-based vaccines against tuberculosis: Optimization of immunologic property, formulation and delivery for bench-to-human applications
Keywords-MotsClés: AEROSOL DELIVERY; BIO-FORMULATION; BIOENGIEERED TUBERCULOSIS VACCINES; CHIMPANZEE ADENOVIRUS VECTOR; GENETIC VIRUS-BASED VECTORS; HUMAN ADENOVIRUS VECTOR; HUMAN HEALTH; LUNG TUBERCULOSIS; MUCOSAL IMMUNITY; MUCOSAL VACCINATION
Abstract-Résumé: Lung tuberculosis (TB) is one of the leading global infectious causes of death. TB still remains a serious health concern in Canada due to ever-increasing immigrant populations (latent TB), high incidence rates of TB in First Nations communities, and much increased susceptibility to TB by HIV co-infection. The drug-resistant cases have been seen in most Canadian provinces.  BCG, the only TB vaccine, has been used globally for 90 years but it has failed to effectively control global TB epidemic. It is now believed that BCG will continue to be administered to humans and novel effective immunization strategies are urgently needed for boosting the protective immunity in the lung. In this regard, the work carried out by us and others over the last 10 years indicates the bioengineered recombinant virus-based, such as human type 5 adenovirus-based (AdHu5), TB vaccines to be of promise. However, AdHu5-based vaccines have met with the challenge that the majority of humans have the preexisting immunity against AdHu5 which may compromise both the safety and efficacy of AdHu5-based immunization.  To address this quest, we have formed a strong interdisciplinary Team consisting 2 biomedical vaccinologists, 1 chemical and 1 medical engineers, and 1 health/infectious disease specialist. Together, we will develop bioengineered chimpanzee adenovirus-based TB vaccines which are expected to be safe and effective in humans as humans do not have pre-existing immunity towards them. Various formulations will be developed for enhanced stability. A new way of vaccine delivery to the lung will also be developed. Their safety and efficacy will be evaluated in animal models of TB. The selected candidate will then be evaluated in humans. The success of our project will be facilitated by participation from two Canadian-based vaccine corporate partners. Our project is expected to lead to the commercialization of a most promising TB vaccine for improving the health of Canadians and beyond.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impliquer les patient dans l'identification, la priorisation et l'élaboration du plan d'évaluation des sujets en ETMIS
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; IMPLICATION DES PATIENTS; PRIORISATION; SELECTION DES SUJETS D'EVALUATION; EVALUATION DES TECHNOLOGIES DE SANTE
Abstract-Résumé: En tant que beneficiaires directs des services de sante, les patients ont une connaissance concrete de l'impact d'un traitement, d'une technologie ou d'un mode de dispensation des soins. La prise en compte de leur perspective est donc consideree comme une priorite croissante en evaluation des technologies et des modes d'intervention en sante(ETMIS). La selection des sujets d'evaluation represente un defi constant pour toutes les agences d'ETMIS car le nombre de technologies ou de modes d'intervention necessitant une evaluation depasse de facon importante les ressources disponibles. Plusieurs auteurs insistent sur l'importance d'impliquer les patients lors de la selection des sujets d'ETMIS afin de mieux tenir compte de leurs valeurs et de leurs besoins. Le but de ce projet est de mettre en oeuvre et d'evaluer des interventions visant a impliquer les patients dans la selection des sujets d'ETMIS dans le domaine du cancer et dans le developpement du plan d'evaluation des sujets selectionnes. Le theme du cancer a ete choisi parce qu'en plus d'etre la premiere cause de mortalite au Canada, il est associe a des questions et enjeux tres vastes qui englobent toute la gamme des services de sante. Ce projet comprend trois principaux volets: 1) une consultation menee aupres de gestionnaires, professionnels de la sante et groupes de patients sur tout le territoire de l'Est du Quebec afin d'identifier les sujets d'ETMIS d'interet dans le domaine du cancer; 2) la priorisation des sujets par des groupes de travail qui seront mis sur pied dans chaque region, puis la production d'une liste finale des priorites par un comite central; 3) le developpement du plan d'evaluation du sujet selectionne par un groupe de travail forme specifiquement pour realiser cette evaluation. Les patients seront impliques a toutes ces etapes et l'equipe de recherche evaluera le processus et les resultats de cette implication.

TitreApplicationTitle: Chair:  Gender, Work and Health
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA FOR HEALTH RESEARCH; COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS/INTER-JURSISDICTIONAL RESEARCH; GENDER/SEX DIFFERENCES; WORK DISABILITY; WORKERS' COMPENSATION
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed Chair in Gender, Work and Health will establish a research, training/mentorship and integrated knowledge translation program with a focus on gender and sex differences in workers' compensation and work disability outcomes, including inter-organizational, inter-jurisdictional and inter-sector comparisons. The Chair's research program will include projects on gender/sex differences in work injury and illness rates in British Columbia.   In collaboration with provincial, national and international partners, the program of research will also investigate gender and sex differences in work disability outcomes across work disability insurance systems in British Columbia, and across workers compensation systems in Canada (BC, Manitoba, Ontario) and in other countries (BC, Canada; Victoria, Australia, New Zealand).  The Chair includes knowledge translation and exchange activities as an integral component of on-going and emerging partnerships with workers' compensation and work disability organizations, to implement best practices and reduce inequities based on evidence of gender/sex differences (this is abased on an existing partnership model between the University of British Columbia and WorkSafeBC).  Finally, the Chair includes capacity building activities through graduate student trainee and faculty mentorship opportunities in occupational and environmental health at the University of British Columbia (established for over 20 years); and a leadership role on accounting for gender/sex differences in work and health research via research partnerships in British Columbia, Canada and Australia/New Zealand.

TitreApplicationTitle: From paper to practice: managing musculoskeletal conditions with decision support systems
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE; CLINICAL DESCISION SUPPORT SYSTEMS; CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES; EVIDENCE BASED MEDICINE; HEALTH LITERACY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; KNOWLEDGE UPTAKE; MUSCULOSKELETAL DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions are a major burden on individuals, health systems and social care systems.  Although ' the cure' has yet to be identified,  extensive research conducted in the last decade provides high quality evidence regarding the best available treatment options to guide treatment planning. Although, Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPG), have been developed to specifically support knowledge translation by providing a succinct summary of the evidence and recommended treatments, clinical care for MSK conditions often does not follow CPGs. The aim of the proposed project is to advance the knowledge translation (KT) for managing chronic MSK diseases by improving dissemination, access and uptake of evidence-based recommendations. The project will integrate best evidence-supported technology with input from patients, clinicians and stake-holders to develop a novel computer-based clinical decision support system (CDSS) that assists clinicians to diagnose and manage MSK patients. The CDSS will be supplemented by an evidence-supported training package that guides clinicians on how to integrate the tool into practice. The CDSS will be evaluated in clinical practice using the gold-standard approach - a randomised controlled trial. Clinical outcomes will be adherence to CPGs in practice, provision of patient resources, and referrals to appropriate services. It is hypothesized that integration of the CDSS into clinical practice will result in improved clinical outcomes compared to normal practice. This research could transform how we manage chronic MSK conditions to vastly improve efficient provision of the best-available treatment options for patients, allowing them to return to a meaningful and productive life. This research will have direct implications for the 1 in 3 Canadians who have a chornic MSK problem that limits their activities of daily life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mesenchymal Stem Cells in Chronic Lung Disease of Prematurity: Culprit or Savior?
Keywords-MotsClés: BRONCHOPULMONARY DYSPLASIA; DIFFERENTIATION ASSAYS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; LUNG DEVELOPMENT; MESENCHYMAL STEM CELLS; OXYGEN INJURY; PRIMARY CELL CULTURE; RAT/ BABOON MODEL FOR BPD; STRETCH INJURY; TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR BETA
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada 8% of all babies are born preterm, between 24 and 37 weeks of gestational age. One of the most common complications seen in these children is bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Most preterm infants need mechanical ventilation and supplemental oxygen to stay alive; unfortunately, this also damages the developing lung leading to an arrest in lung growth. Currently no treatment is available for BPD. Babies with BPD are often sent home with oxygen (O2) and continue to have respiratory diseases such as asthma or emphysema later in life. Our body contains stem cells, a pool of cells that direct growth by developing into different cell types. Stem cells may play an important role in BPD. Ventilated babies are more likely to develop BPD, if mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are present in lung fluid. Conversely, we showed that treatment with (liquid produced by) bone marrow or human cord-derived MSCs can prevent an O2 induced arrest in lung growth in a newborn rat model of BPD. Thus, the role of MSCs during lung injury and repair remains unclear. We will investigate whether MSCs in the newborn lung are perturbed by high O2 exposure, leading to BPD, and if they can be restored by factors secreted by healthy cord-derived MSCs. Once isolated, MSCs will be evaluated for differences in appearance, cell surface protein expression and secreted factors. We anticipate that O2 exposed lung MSCs will become pro-fibrotic (scarring) producing more of the pro-fibrotic transforming growth factor (TGF)-beta1 and TGF-beta2 molecules compared to TGF-beta3 (scarless wound healing) whereas human cord-derived MSCs will not. Furthermore, liquid from healthy human cord-derived MSCs will be added to evaluate if its therapeutic effect is mediated by normalizing the lung MSCs. A better understanding of the role and effect of stem cells will allow the development of regenerative therapies to prevent BPD in preterm children, and will also benefit adults with lung diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Intra-operative Optical Coherence Tomography for corneal transplant surgery in Keratoconus
Keywords-MotsClés: 1102; 1211; 1901; 3110; BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; BIOMEDICAL IMAGING; BIOMEDICAL OPTICS; BIOMEDICAL TECHNOLOGY; CORNEA; IMAGE PROCESSING; KERATOCONUS; MEDICAL AND HEALTH SCIENCES; OPTICAL COHERENCE TOMOGRAPHY; OPTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Keratoconus (KC) is a degenerative eye disease that causes structural changes in the cornea resulting in opaqueness, thinning and shape alterations. The changes cause significant vision distortions, such as multiple images, streaking and sensitivity to light. KC affects approximately 0.1% of the general population, with vision deterioration significantly reducing the patient's ability to drive a car or read a normal print. Up to 25% of all KC cases progress to the point when thinning of the cornea is excessive, and corneal transplant surgery is necessary. Currently, corneal surgeons are aided only by optical microscopes that allow for a magnified view of the surgical field, but fail to provide precise evaluation of the depth and smoothness of the surgical cut, the thickness of the remaining tissue (lamellar keratoplasty), and the shape, thickness and centration of the donor cornea. Furthermore, the process of suturing causes extreme shape changes in the donor cornea, which can lead to high degree of astigmatism that may require post-surgical wear of specially designed corrective contact lenses.   We have developed a high resolution optical imaging system that can generate in real-time, cross-sectional and 3D images of the human cornea. Here we propose to integrate the imaging system with a surgical microscope, which will allow for 3D, cellular resolution view of the donor cornea during corneal replacement surgery. The novel intra-operative imaging system will provide real-time feedback to corneal surgeons about: the depth and smoothness of the surgical cut, the optical transparency and shape of the donor cornea, and the corneal shape changes during suturing. This feedback will lead to improved surgical procedures with reduced post-surgery complications. When used outside of the surgical room, the system can improve the screening and diagnosis of KC patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Design of a high content personalized medicine screening tool for the treatment of cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMOLECULE PATTERNING; BREAST CANCER; CANCER CELL INVASION; ENGINEERED 3-DIMENSIONAL CELL CULTURE; HIGH CONTENT SCREENING; HYDROGELS; PANCREATIC CANCER; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; REGENERATIVE MEDICINE; TUMOUR ORGANOIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Drug treatments for cancer patients are largely based on the part of the body where the cancer originated and its appearance under the microscope. New personalized treatment approaches are needed to improve survival and reduce the side effects of ineffective treatments.  Our goal is to design a drug screening tool against which all available treatment strategies can be tested prior to their use clinically.  To this end, we propose to: (1) design a 3D culture system in which to better understand cellular organization; (2) engineer a 3D biopatterned hydrogel; and (3) grow human-derived cancer cells in the 3D matrix against which drug treatments will be tested.  By creating a platform to test treatments against an individual patient's cancel cells, we aim to advance the development of personalized cancer medicine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancement of nerve regeneration with controlled release of neurotrophic factors
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; CONTROLLED RELEASE; DRUG DELIVERY; NERVE INJURY; NERVE REGENERATION; NEUROSCIENCE; NEUROTROPHIC FACTORS; POLYMERS
Abstract-Résumé: Nerve injury produces lifelong disability in many patients. Despite the best current surgical methods, clinical results remain suboptimal. We have previously demonstrated, delivery of growth factors improves functional outcomes in rats with severe peripheral nerve injuries. We now propose using a more clinically-applicable polymer-based drug delivery system to enhance peripheral nerve regeneration. We have developed a prototype of a microsphere-based delivery system which enhances nerve regeneration by delivering glial cell line derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), a potent growth factor, to injured nerves. In Aim 1 we will determine the extent to which the delivery system provides GDNF to nerve tissues. We will then place the GDNF delivery system around either chronically injured rat nerves (in Aim 2) or into a rat model of clinically available decellularized nerve grafts (in Aim 3) to provide sustained GDNF delivery. Both experimental paradigms model closely the actual clinical realities of human nerve injuries. We will determine the extent to which sustained delivery of GDNF augments current surgical treatments for peripheral nerve injury using a variety of advanced metrics. Our industrial partners are eager to incorporate our findings into their existing commercially available processed nerve allograft product.

TitreApplicationTitle: Milieu d'hébergement intelligent pour la clientèle ayant une déficience physique avec prédominance cognitive : de l'implantation à l'évaluation
Keywords-MotsClés: 1101 SANTE PUBLIQUE; 1207 TECHNOLOGIE DE L'INFORMATION; 2604 APPLICATIONS DE SYSTEMES INTELLIGENTS; 2704 TRAITEMENT REPARTI ET SIMULTANE; DES ORDINATEURS ET DES R; HABITATS INTELLIGENTS; INTELLIGENCE AMBIANTE ET INTERFACES TANGIBLES; MAINTIEN A DOMICILE ET REMEDIATION COGNITIVE; READAPTATION ET PARTICIPATION SOCIALE; SENSIBILITE AU CONTEXTE ET RESEAU DE CAPTEURS; TRAUMATISMES CRANIO-CEREBRAL
Abstract-Résumé: Au Canada, environ 100 000 personnes sont victimes d'un traumatisme craniocerebral (TCC) annuellement. Environ 10 % d'entre eux devront resider dans un centre d'hebergement de longue duree non adapte a leur situation de vie. Afin de repondre a leurs besoins, le Centre de readaptation de l'Estrie a construit en 2011 une Residence, qui heberge actuellement 10 personnes. La Residence offre un encadrement constant pour favoriser la participation dans les activites de la vie quotidienne des residents malgre leurs troubles cognitifs et de comportement. Bientot cette Residence sera equipee d'aides technologiques a la cognition pour favoriser la responsabilisation et l'autonomisation des residents. La preparation des repas est une des cles de leur autonomie. C'est une activite complexe qui presente des risques necessitant une supervision constante.  Ce projet comporte deux volets dans lequel tous les chercheurs et collaborateurs, incluant residents et intervenants de la Residence, interagiront. Le volet « technologie » developpera un assistant culinaire destine aux personnes TCC pour les aider a preparer leur repas. Son implementation s'appuiera sur la reingenierie de Archipel, un cadriciel pour developper des ortheses cognitives. Archipel sera aussi ameliore par de nouvelles capacites plus evoluees pour le diagnostic et pour l'assistance. Le volet « recherche evaluative » documentera l'implantation et l'efficacite des technologies. Pour evaluer l'integration des technologies dans la Residence (implantation), des donnees seront recueillies a l'aide d'entrevues, d'observations lors de la realisation des repas par les residents, ainsi que d'analyses de documents emis par le CRE. Enfin l'efficacite de l'assistant cognitif sera evaluee pour chaque resident individuellement, en observant leurs capacites a se preparer des repas avant, pendant et apres l'introduction des aides technologiques (jusqu'a 12 mois apres). Leur satisfaction envers les technologies sera aussi mesuree.
