TitreApplicationTitle: The Association between Insomnia and Autonomic Dysfunction
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTONOMIC DYSFUNCTION; CARDIOVASCULAR; HEART RATE VARIABILITY; INSOMNIA; LONGITUDINAL; POLYSOMNOGRAPHY; PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGY; SLEEP; SLEEP DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Sleep problems are common in the general population, characterized by complaints on difficulties falling and staying asleep, frequent nocturnal and early awakenings, and overall non-restorative sleep coupled with daytime impairments. Insomnia is the most prevalent sleep disorder that produces detrimental effects on personal health (increasing one's risk of developing psychological and physical problems) and society at large; contributing a large portion of economic burden in direct (greater health care costs) and indirect (work-related injuries) costs. The specific objective is to examine heart rate variability as a potential pathophysiological underlying mechanism in one's and familial susceptibility to insomnia and related comordities (cardiovascular disease). While there is substantial data on psychological and cognitive risk factors, physiological markers have been less studied. Given the paucity of information in this area, this program has critical implications for population health status and health care utilization, such as the identification of risk factors in the etiology, pathogenesis and treatment of insomnia. This is crucial for the improvements in health and health care (successful preventive and intervention strategies) and is instrumental in generating new knowledge to identify additional biomarkers of the hyperarousal state of insomnia. Using a multidimensional approach, this project is scientifically, clinically, and socially relevant for health outcomes among Canadians with insomnia, as it will promote implementation of new clinical policy (via knowledge translation) and improve optimal health (quality of life) and therapeutic benefits. Further, the research is innovative, timely and will be carried out in one of the largest insomnia research programs in Canada that focuses on non-pharmacological interventions; and thus, will have direct economic implications by reducing the costs and morbidity associated with this debilitating sleep disorder.

TitreApplicationTitle: Host genetic control of latent tuberculosis infection
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; EQTL; EXOME SEQUENCING; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; POPULATION GENETICS; RNA-SEQ; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious human disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis which results in more than two million deaths each year. Transmission of TB occurs by aerosol from infectious patients to unaffected persons. However, only a proportion of those exposed to M. tuberculosis will become infected with the tubercle bacillus. Of those who are infected, less than 10% will go on and develop clinical TB disease over their life time. People who are infected with M. tuberculosis and who show no symptoms are said to have latent TB infection. One hundred years of studies have assembled strong evidence that progression from exposure to infection and from infection to clinical TB disease are under strong host genetic control. In my project, I will study the genetic control of the transition from exposure to infection. My main hypothesis is that human resistance to latent TB infection is due (i) to a collection of rare mutations (<5% frequency) with strong biological effects, and (ii) to subtle, genetically controlled fluctuations of biological activity in the pathways used by the human host to fight off the invading tubercle bacillus. To test my hypothesis, I will have access to a unique resource of biological samples from Cape Town, an area with one of the globally highest rates of TB. In addition, I will have access to the latest genome technologies via the Genome Quebec and McGill University Innovation Centre and to the high performance computing clusters of Compute Canada. My project is, however, fundamentally distinct from previous studies of host genetics of infectious disease. My major goal is to integrate the findings that I will make into a higher level of systems genetics. I expect that genetic variation associated with very modest effect size when considered alone will reveal its true importance for maintaining cellular homeostasis and fighting off invading pathogens once analysed in the context of higher order cellular pathways.

TitreApplicationTitle: Global analysis of the role of alternative splicing in the regulation of protein stability
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; BIOINFORMATICS; DEGRONS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; GENE EXPRESSION; PROTEIN MODULAR ARCHITECTURE; PROTEIN STABILITY; RNA SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Each tissue in our bodies is made up of cells that undertake radically different functions from the neurons in our brains to the skins cells that encapsulate us. However, all our cells are programmed from the same basic sequence of As, Gs, Cs and Ts that make up our genetic code. How does this diversity arise from the same basic ingredients? An important mechanism to create this diversity is known as alternative splicing, which generates different protein products from a single gene. In this study, we investigate whether this process of alternative splicing can create different protein products, produced by the same gene, with different lifetimes or half-lives? And if so, how do these differences propagate onto the diversity of signalling pathways? These question have yet to be asked in a systematic way but could help us unravel why cells in different tissues communicate and signal in distinct ways. These finding could be vital in helping to understand why, for example, there is tissue-specific cancer? It could also help medical researchers in the future to design more contextual, tissue-specific drugs.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; ATXN1; ATXN1L; BEHAVIORAL TESTS; NEUROANATOMY/HISTOPATHOLOGY; NEURODEGENERATION; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; POLYGLUTAMINE DISEASE; SPINOCEREBELLAR ATAXIA; TAMOXIFEN-INDUCIBLE CRE
Abstract-Résumé: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) - one of nine familial disorders that are caused by expansion of a tract of glutamines - is a devastating neurodegenerative disease affecting individuals in their second to fourth decade of life. The expanded amino acid tract in the protein ATAXIN-1 (ATXN1) alters its shape (misfold) and interactions with other proteins, which causes it to accumulate and become toxic to cells. Understanding the role of ATXN1 in cells and what it interacts with is critical to understanding the disease. Another ATXN1 family member, named ATAXIN1-Like (ATXN1L), can interact with ATXN1 and can compete with the mutant form to prevent its toxicity in mice. A principal goal in the field of polyglutamine diseases is to grasp the mechanisms governing the misfolding of proteins so as to develop effective therapies. Therefore, uncovering the normal function(s) of ATXN1 and ATXN1L within neurons, particularly in the adult brain, is critical to understanding how glutamine expansion induces neurotoxicity. This study proposes to uncover the physiological role of ATXN1 and ATXN1L in adult mice. To do so, we will characterize the functions of ATXN1 and ATXN1L in the mature mouse nervous system first by deleting them in adult animals and then looking at what happens to brain cells as a result. We will evaluate which proteins and RNAs change in brain cells when ATAXN1 and ATXN1L are deleted and pinpoint which of these changes can mediate neurotoxicity. These experiments will identify molecular pathways involved in the physiological functions of these proteins and might reveal changes that are amenable for targeted treatment. Collectively, these findings are expected to uncover the roles of ATXN1 family members within the brain and expose plausible mechanisms whose deregulation results in SCA1. Likewise, discoveries made from this research stand to inform about other polyglutamine diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Thermogenèse des adipocytes bruns induite par le système nerveux sympathique (SNS) et la voie du récepteur cérébrale à la mélanocortine de type 4 (MC4R)
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETE DE TYPE 2; METABOLISME ENERGETIQUE; OBESITE; RECEPTEUR MC4R; SYSTEME NERVEUX SYMPATHIQUE; THERMOGENESE; TISSU ADIPEUX BRUN
Abstract-Résumé: The unrelenting rise in obesity in most developed countries over the last three decades, together with the rising awareness of the detrimental impact of this condition on health and health costs, have considerably stimulated the research related to the causes and complications of excess fat deposition. Obesity is defined as an excess of adipose tissue that results from an imbalance between energy intake and energy expenditure. The study of the complex brain controls exerted on the intake and expenditure determinants is a prerequisite to understand the pathophysiology of obesity in order to elaborate strategies to prevent and reverse excess fat deposition. Despite its crucial importance, the control of energy expenditure has received much less attention than that of food intake. However, the recent demonstration that brown adipose tissue (BAT) exists in substantial amount in adult humans has rejuvenated interest in the role of energy expenditure, specifically BAT thermogenesis, on energy balance. BAT is an organ with an enormous thermogenic capacity that could dissipate excess body energy (excess body fat). Heat production by BAT is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) through mechanisms and metabolic pathways, which have yet to be fully comprehended. The goal of the proposed research program is to study the brain-SNS-BAT axis in animal (brain circuitries behind SNS-mediated BAT thermogenesis). The proposed approaches to achieve the objectives of the research program include functional neurobiological as well as cellular/molecular methodologies and sophisticated metabolic imaging technologies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Irradiation-Sterilized Skeletal Allografts with Superior Biomechanical Performance through Collaborative Multidisciplinary Translational Research
Keywords-MotsClés: 1102 BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; 2001 MATERIALS STRUCTURE; 2006 BIOMATERIALS; 519 OTHER MANUFACTURED PRODUCTS AND PROCESSES; ALLOGRAFT; BONE; IRRADIATION EMBRITTLEMENT; MECHANICAL PROPERTIES; OSTEOCONDUCTION; PROPERTIES AND TESTING; TOUGHENING
Abstract-Résumé: Musculoskeletal allografts are pieces of tissue, such as bone or tendon, from an individual who has donated their body to medicine and this tissue is used in surgeries to repair injuries and problems in orthopaedic patients. In order to reduce disease transmission from the donor to the patient, radiation is used to kill bacteria and viruses which may exist in/on the donated allograft tissue. Unfortunately, the radiation also damages the tissue making it weak and less able to perform in mechanically demanding roles. Recently, we have developed a method to produce irradiation sterilized bone allografts with much better mechanical performance. The proposed project will allow us to further optimize and verify our results in human bone, conduct critical trial experiments in an animal model, and to scale up our invention to full-scale production processes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Temperature measurement in cortical bone and bone marrow during magnetic resonance guided focused ultrasound thermo-therapy in a porcine model
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING (1102); BIOPHYSICS (3113); BONE TUMOUR THERAPY; HIGH-INTENSITY FOCUSED ULTRASOUND; MAGNETIC RESONANCE THERMOMETRY; MATHEMATICAL MODELLING (2960); MEDICAL AND HEALTH SCIENCES (1211); RELAXATION TIME MAPPING; TEMPERATURE MODELING; THERMAL ABLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Current localized treatments of benign bone tumours in children suffer from significant side effects including the invasiveness of surgical removal with bone reconstruction, and the associated risk of developing secondary malignancy from high-dose radiation therapy. Magnetic resonance guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) is a noninvasive thermo-therapy that has recently been clinically approved in Canada for uterine fibroid ablation and is currently in clinical trials in Canada for palliative management of bone metastasis pain. It is also showing promise as an effective local treatment, when combined with chemotherapy, for malignancies throughout the body. The principle therapeutic technique underlying MRgFUS is the noninvasive focusing of high intensity ultrasound energy to induce thermal necrosis in a target volume as small as a rice kernel. Localized temperature elevations in the target tissue can be monitored noninvasively and in real time inside a clinical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner. However, conventional MRI thermometry is limited to water-based soft tissues, such as muscle, and temperature is not measured in cortical bone and fat-based tissues such as bone marrow, preventing its use as a primary local treatment for bone tumours. Since many bone tumours grow within both the cortical bone and bone marrow, accurate assessment of temperature in both of these tissues during treatment is required to ensure adequate thermal necrosis. We hypothesize that bone marrow temperature can be measured accurately by quantifying the change in magnetic relaxation time of the fat-rich bone marrow during heating, and that the temperature distribution across the cortical bone can be calculated from the surrounding measured temperatures in the muscle and bone marrow. This method will enable the safe application of MRgFUS for local treatments of benign bone neoplasms and will improve treatment and quality of life for paediatric bone tumour patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Experimental and numerical investigation of the prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation of fractures to the distal radius with distal radial ulnar joint involvement.
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE; FINITE ELEMENT MODEL; FORWARD FALL; FRACTURE; IMPACT; MUSCULOSKELETAL MODEL; RADIUS; REHABILATATION; ULNA; WRIST
Abstract-Résumé: Distal radius fractures that occur as a result of a forward fall are an increasingly widespread problem that can result in a number of long-term disabilities and currently cost the healthcare system approximately $500 million annually.  Therefore, the overall purpose of my proposed research is to advance the understanding of the prevention, treatment and rehabilitation of distal radius fractures with a focus on improving patient outcomes and quality of life. The response of the distal upper extremity to impact loading, indicative of a forward fall, will be quantified using a custom designed impact device.  Cadaveric specimens will be taken to failure and a surgeon will repair the resulting fracture. The kinematics of the distal radial ulnar joint (DRUJ) will be measured before and after fracture.  This impact methodology will also be used to assess a variety of fracture prevention interventions and a classification system of these interventions will be developed.  The second aspect of this research will focus on incorporating modeling methods into clinical applications.  A finite element modeling assisted surgery method will be developed that has the potential to allow surgeons to both plan a fixation surgery as well as predict its outcome.  A musculoskeletal model will also be developed to provide a comprehensive analysis of the effect of fixation technique on DRUJ kinematics, kinetics and muscular involvement.  Finally, these models will be incorporated into a clinical setting to assess the effectiveness of rehabilitation strategies.  The research proposed here will make a significant impact not only on the way that distal radius fractures are viewed, but also in the strategies to prevent, treat and rehabilitate them, improving the functional outcome and quality of life of affected patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Knowledge Translation of a Wheelchair Skills Program for Rehabilitation Clinicians: A Feasibility Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CHART AUDITS; FOCUS GROUPS; INTERACTIVE EDUCATIONAL WORKSHOP; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; OUTCOME MEASURES; PARTICIPATION; SURVEYS; WHEELCHAIR; WHEELCHAIR CONFIDENCE; WHEELCHAIR SKILL
Abstract-Résumé: The wheelchair provides mobility options for more than 250,000 Canadians. Less than optimal wheelchair use can be associated with barriers to participation in important activities, mobility dependence, or accidents. The inclusion of standardized wheelchair skills testing and training has been identified as one strategy for improving wheelchair use, yet a gap between best practice and current practice remains. Our aim is to design and implement a knowledge translation intervention specific to a standardized wheelchair skills program, called WheelKnowIt. This study investigates the potential for using WheelKnowIt among experienced clinicians at a rehabilitation centre in Vancouver, BC. The WheelKnowIt includes an interactive educational workshop, clinical champions, educational outreach, and use of a website. We will measure feasibility outcomes related to process, resources and the intervention, as well as establish preliminary estimates of the effectiveness of the intervention. Once we confirm that WheelKnowIt is feasible and effectively improves the usage of standardized wheelchair skills testing and training, broader studies can be conducted including a national randomized controlled trial. WheelKnowIt offers promise for improving the use of standardized outcome measures and interventions for wheelchair skills testing and training in a rehabilitation setting, which may improve wheelchair-related patient outcomes. WheelKnowIt may also serve as a framework for implementing other important rehabilitation outcomes and interventions for other populations, such as spinal cord injury or stroke.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tele-SCOPE - Translation, Evaluation and Learnings Exchanged for Sustainable Childhood Obesity Prevention Through Community Engagement
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTION; CHILDHOOD; COMMUNITY; ENGAGEMENT; EXCHANGE; KNOWLEDGE; OBESITY; PARTICIPATORY; PREVENTION; SUSTAINABLE
Abstract-Résumé: Rates of childhood obesity are increasing all over the world and with this comes increased rates of serious, life-long diseases such as type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, and even cancer. Up until now, treatment strategies for childhood obesity have been mostly ineffective. Therefore, a focus on prevention is necessary and this should start at the level of communities in which children live and play. This project will evaluate a thoughtfully designed system that will support the exchange of knowledge between experts in childhood obesity prevention and the key individuals, leaders, and community members who can inspire, motivate and create long-lasting changes at the community-level that will ultimately support children and their families in leading healthier lifestyles. The results of this project will be important not only to the prevention of childhood obesity and the long-term health of children and youth, but will also be relevant to other health promotion or disease prevention initiatives in Canada, and around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development, testing and feasibility of an interprofessional shared decision-making and goal-setting decision aid for patients with diabetes in clinical care
Keywords-MotsClés: DECISION AID; DIABETES MELLITUS; GUIDELINE ADHERENCE; INTERPROFESSIONAL CARE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTIMORBIDITY; SHARED DECISION-MAKING
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes care is complicated for people with diabetes as well as for health care providers: they have to watch their diet, exercise, take medications, checking blood sugars and blood pressure, get tests and see multiple doctors.  On top of that, many with diabetes have other health problems, such as high blood pressure or arthritis, that make care even more complicated.  Guidelines for improving the care of people with diabetes try to help by summarizing the best practices for care, but because diabetes care is so complicated, it is hard for them to be put into practice.  One solution to this is a tool that can help people with diabetes set health care goals that are important to them, and participate actively in decisions about their own health care, together with health care providers.  This tool would have an information booklet for patients with facts that can help them make a decision, a worksheet to help spell out what their goals are and how they want to get there, and a cheat-sheet for health care providers that gives them tips on how to do this.  The purpose of this project is to find out if a tool like this would be helpful, how we could make it more helpful and usable, and what the best way would be to make sure that people use it.

TitreApplicationTitle: First Nations Emissions Mapping Project: A Knowledge To Action Collaboration
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTAMINANTS; ENVIRONMENT; FIRST NATION; GIS; HEALTH; KNOWLEDGE TO ACTION
Abstract-Résumé: The First Nations Emissions Mapping Project (FN EMP) was developed as a collaborative effort between researchers from CAREX Canada, members of the First Nations Environmental Health Innovation Network (FNEHIN) and representatives of the Assembly of First Nations Environmental Stewardship Unit. The FN EMP is an information base consisting of a broad range of Google Earth files, developed by team members from existing datasets on measured levels of contaminants in outdoor air, water, sediments and soils, as well as reported and estimated emissions of contaminants across Canada. The overall objective of this proposal is to understand how to create meaningful and sustained use of the FN EMP within First Nations organizations, not only in the technical aspects of using the FN EMP, but more importantly, for prioritizing environmental health issues, developing relevant environmental health research questions, and identifying data gaps that require future research or local data collection. We will collaboratively plan and design knowledge to action activities with the guidance of a Knowledge to Action (KTA) advisory committee and in-person workshops with FNEHIN members. Rigorous KTA evaluation will be implemented throughout the project. The FN EMP has the potential to enhance First Nations organizations' participation in provincial and federal environmental impact assessments, and thereby provide more control over local environmental quality. Our KTA activities will identify barriers in the use of spatial data and technologies with the FN EMP, as well as to fulfilling increased capacity goals, and propose solutions which will be beneficial to other KTA researchers.  The process of collaboratively defining goals and metrics and assessing how established KTA activities contribute to reaching these goals provides an important contribution to evaluating the effectiveness of the KTA mechanisms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of occupational radiation exposure on men and women in nuclear industry - from biomarkers to prevention strategies
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMAKERS; EPIGENETICS; KT; OCCUPATIONAL RADIATION EXPOSURE; RADIATION PROTECTION; SEX DIFFERENCES
Abstract-Résumé: Occupational exposure to ionizing radiation (IR) is very common.  The nuclear power industry, health care, and research departments as well as defence sectors all extensively utilize man-made radiation. Currently, the nuclear industry employs approximately 800 000 workers worldwide. Occupational exposure to radiation is of great importance in Canada.  Canadian nuclear science and technology features one of the most significant concentrations of nuclear research, development and technical capability in the world. Nearly 40000 people work in Canada's nuclear industry. Research focused on the health effects of occupational exposure to radiation is of crucial importance to Canadians and worldwide.  Currently radiation protection guidelines are based on males. Historically, this was due to the fact that guidelines were developed soon after inception of the Manhattan Project and were geared towards assumption that the individual receiving a radiation dose is a young male-a Manhattan Project worker. Yet, currently the situation has changed and women constitute a major part of nuclear industry workforce. Are they equally protected? My application is aimed to analyze the effects of occupational radiation on males and females and develop novel sex-specific protection guidelines.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gender, Work and Traumatic Brain Injury: Addressing the Gap in OHS Research, Policy, and Practice
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; RESEARCH-INFORMED THEATRE; SEX AND GENDER ANALYSIS; WOMEN'S HEALTH; WORK RELATED TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY; WORKPLACE ACCOMMODATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Traumatic brain injury is a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. It is a very costly and devastating occupational injury however there is very little information on how to prevent this injury specifically that considers both men and women separately. Also, this research provides us with more information on how to best return people to work after the injury which involves helping the person as well as changing things in the environment. We also examine how problems with sleep can be detected and treated to avoid future injury and improve return to work which has a beneficial effect on quality of life. This proposal provides a plan to improve what we know about brain injury at work considering both men and women by providing funds for trainees and also resources to teach more people about this injury. We also use very effective techniques like research informed drama to increase knowledge about brain injury at work that takes into account differences between men and women. We especially focus on women as in the past, there has not been much attention given to women with respect to traumatic brain injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Working well: understanding how gender influences working conditions and health in long term care settings across Canada and internationally
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE STUDY; DIVISION OF LABOUR; GENDER; LONG TERM CARE; MIXED METHODS RESEARCH; OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY; STAFFING INTENSITY; UNPAID CARE WORK; WORK AND HEALTH; WORKLOAD; WORKPLACE QUALITY INDICATORS
Abstract-Résumé: Long-term care (LTC) in Canada is a tangled web of contradictions. It is a place no one wants to "end up", but it is desperately needed. Women typically perform the care, but their roles as paid workers, unpaid volunteers, students, and family members spill messily together. Women also comprise nearly three-quarters of the residents, though our legislation and public policies ignore its gendered nature. LTC is meant to provide safe and secure care but our research and that of others have found that it is often filled with violence and over-worked, poorly paid, and poorly trained staff.  The best data we have on care for people with Alzheimer's and Dementia has noted the importance of social care, but workers increasingly argue that social care is not possible due to overwork and time constraints.  LTC is supposed to support people no longer able to remain in their own homes, but in Ontario it is challenging to get a publicly funded bed  -- waitlists can top 18 months -- and once in care, great burdens and stress are often placed on people and their families. It is referred to as a home, but there is little that is home-like in terms of the food or the living accommodations. It is a place that is too often filled with care workers who work in careless conditions. Care work in Canada is treated as an assembly line process, though human needs and human dignity for both the worker and the resident can not be manufactured in the same way that a car is assembled.  This program of research, training and knowledge translation aims to contribute to our understandings of the links between the gendered organization of care work and health outcomes for workers. Using surveys, interviews and observations, this research program aims to contribute to the practice environment by offering tools to support worker's health and safety and to the policy environment by contributing gender-sensitive indicators of quality working conditions in LTC

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of an Imaged-Based Tool to Measure Outcomes in Patients with Osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ALIGNMENT; ARTHRITIS/OSTEOARTHRITIS; COHORT STUDY; DISABILITY; IMAGING; JOINT; JOINT MECHANICS; PAIN; TRAUMA; X-RAY COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Fractures of the distal radius account for 1/6th of all fractures treated in the emergency room. Mal-alignment of the wrist following fracture occurs in approximately 71% of patients. This mal-alignment can lead to substantial pain, disability and impairment. The objective of this research proposal is to employ a previously developing imaging technique to visualize joint alignment in a clinical setting. This joint alignment measuring technique was developed in a in vitro environment and has been shown to reduce the effective dose acquired by x-ray CT scanning of the shoulder by up to 90%. The first objective will be to develop low-dose CT images of the wrist. Subsequently a clinical study will be performed to investigate the long-term effect of mal-alignment on joint degradation, pain, physical impairment and disability. Patients will be recruited from two highly equipped and skilled research laboratories in London and Hamilton. These patients will have had a distal radius fracture 8-10 years previously that healed mal-aligned. We will also enroll a group of patients who also had a distal radius fracture but who did not have their wrist heal mal-aligned. Additionally, we will recruit patients who did not suffer from a fracture-related injury. These patients have been previously enrolled in studies ongoing at the Hand and Upper Limb Centre. Therefore, we will have access to their baseline measures of pain, disability and previously acquired CT scans. These patients will be re-tested for these measures and will undergo low-dose CT protocols to measure joint alignment.  We will be able to see the changes in joint alignment and symptoms that occur a decade after fracture and will be able to assess the risk associated with fracture alignment. By gaining a better understanding of the relationship between joint alignment, pain, disability and function, we will define a safe zone of fracture alignment that will be used by physicians in fracture management.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural, Biochemical, and Enzymatic Characterization of the Bacterial Cell Wall Synthesis Enzyme BacA
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMISTRY; ENZYMOLOGY; PROTEIN CRYSTALLOGRAPHY; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Antibiotic resistance has spread in recent decades to as many as 90% of isolates from some species. At the same time there has been a decline in antibiotic discovery; the most recent patent of a novel class of antibiotics was in 1987. Recently, research has focused on modifying successful classes of antibiotics to circumvent resistance mechanisms. However, many of these second generation antibiotics are losing efficacy as bacteria adapt. New classes of antibiotics are urgently needed to address the rise of "superbugs" that are resistant to multiple antibiotics. The process of bacterial cell wall synthesis is unique, and several stages in the process are targeted by successful classes of antibiotics. One potential target in the pathway is recycling of the undecaprenyl pyrophosphate lipid carrier. This process is catalyzed by BacA, an integral membrane lipid phosphatase with no known homologs and an uncharacterized mechanism. This proposal outlines a structural and enzymatic approach for studying the molecular mechanism of BacA. The data obtained from these experiments will be used to identify novel BacA inhibitors in collaboration with the Centre for Drug Research and Development at the University of British Columbia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying Biomarkers for Developmental Delays in Infants Born Prematurely
Keywords-MotsClés: ATYPICAL DEVELOPMENT; COGNITION; DEVELOPMENT; FNIRS; NEURAL DEVELOPMENT; PERCEPTION; PREMATURITY
Abstract-Résumé: Advances in neonatal care have increased the survival of infants born prematurely.  While a significant accomplishment for modern medicine, these infants are at high risk for a number of general and specific cognitive and perceptual delays, estimated at 3 to 6 times higher than their full-term peers (Orchinik et al., 2011) and with learning disabilities at a rate of 25-50% in infants born extremely premature (Litt et al., 2012).  This constitutes a significant public health risk as almost 15% of babies in Canada are born prematurely, a rate that has been rising for over two decades, according to the Public Health Agency of Canada.  The current research project will investigate whether infants born prematurely exhibit deviations in some of the basic neurobiological mechanisms supporting human development and a method to identify infants, at 6 months of age, who will have later developmental delays allow the effective use of early intervention.  Specifically, we will use functional Near Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS) to examine real-time changes in neural activity in the infant brain while they are learning.  Similar to fMRI, fNIRS monitors changes in blood flow in the brain as a proxy for neural activity while effectively sidestepping the methodological hurdles preventing fMRI of infants (e.g., rigid head stabilization. strong magnetic fields). We will compare neural changes in infants born very to extremely prematurely (born after less than 32 and less than 28 weeks, respectively) and infants born at full term (born at 38 weeks to 41 weeks).  Initial recordings will take place when infants are 6 months old (correct gestational age or CGA for preterm infants).  A follow-up experimental assessment (14 months CGA) will identify infants experiencing early delays in perceptual and cognitive development.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying therapeutic targets of the Hox-Meis network that regulate leukemia stem cell fate.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; HOX-MEIS; LEUKEMOGENESIS; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is diagnosed annually in ~1,200 patients in Canada. Treatment for this disease has not changed significantly over the last 30 years and the overall survival of AML patients remains close to 20%. Unfortunately, most AML patients relapse within 3 years of diagnosis and of these only 11% will survive past 5 years. One major reason for relapse is the persistence of a leukemia stem cell (LSC) population following therapy. LSCs are defined by their ability to self-renew and continually repopulate leukemic cells. However, the networks governing self-renewal are unknown. Previously, our group showed that HOXA9 and MEIS1 genes cause leukemia in mice and likely in humans. Deregulation of HOX, MEIS, and PBX genes represents one of the most frequent molecular anomalies in human leukemia (deregulated in approximately 50% of acute leukemias) and are associated with adverse prognosis.  HOX proteins and co-factors (MEIS-PBX) are potent nuclear oncogenes. Over the years, our group has characterized several components involved in HOX-MEIS-PBX leukemia and paved the way to identify, test, and further develop small molecules and therapeutic targets for this disease. In this application, I hypothesize that HOX-MEIS-PBX is an important network that regulates human LSCs. Understanding of this network may allow for LSC targeting and treatment of intermediate-risk AML at its basis, thereby avoiding relapse. Over the course of two separate, yet integrated, aims I propose to characterize the nature (Aim 1) and test the functional importance (Aim 2) of the HOX-MEIS-PBX complex in human LSCs and leukemias. The proposed studies will characterize therapeutic targets both upstream and downstream of HOX-MEIS-PBX. Collectively these results will provide a comprehensive characterization and therapeutic validation of the HOX-MEIS-PBX transforming network and may facilitate targeting and manipulation of LSCs in human acute leukemias.

TitreApplicationTitle: Economic evaluation of a school-based program for the prevention of obesity in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC CONDITIONS; COST-EFFECTIVENESS; ECONOMIC EVALUATION; ECONOMIC MODELING; HEALTH-RELATED QUALITY OF LIFE; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; OBESITY PREVENTION; POPULATION HEALTH; RETURN-ON-INVESTMENT; SCHOOL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Our previous research has identified the Health Promoting Schools Program (HPSP) as very effective in promoting healthy eating and active living and preventing childhood obesity. While better health behaviors and improved health status are important to public health decision makers, cost-effectiveness and return-on-investment are also important. However, economic evaluations of these programs have yielded mixed results and there is no Canadian data available yet.  We propose to conduct an economic evaluation of the HPSP by comparing its program costs with changes in proportions of obesity, health care costs, and quality of life of the Canadian population. We will develop a mathematical model to represent the lifetime progression of school children over five obesity-related health states, including: underweight, normal, overweight, obesity and death. Existing data from Statistics Canada's surveys, the assessments of the HPSP in Nova Scotia and Alberta, and from Medline and Cochrane searches will be used to parameterise the model. The model will project the trends of obesity epidemics in Canada and assess the long-term impacts of the HPSP on future disease burden. The outcome measures include program and health care costs, proportions of obesity and chronic conditions avoided, savings in medical expenditures and absenteeism costs, and quality-adjusted life years gained by the intervention.   Findings of this study will inform resource allocation and justify investments in school-based health promotion. Moreover, effective school-based program in preventing childhood obesity that will also save future health care costs may become a key strategy in curbing the obesity epidemic in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the effects of strategic cognitive enhancement training on executive cognitive functions, neural plasticity, and falls risk in seniors at-risk for falls.
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE TRAINING; DUAL-TASK ABILITY; FALLS RISK; FUNCTIONAL PLASTICITY; IMPAIRED EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONING; MOBILITY; NEUROIMAGING; OLDER ADULTS; VIRTUAL REALITY SIMULATOR
Abstract-Résumé: With approximately 30% of seniors experiencing one or more falls per year, falls are a major health care concern for Canadians. These falls result in injuries, reduced quality of life, and an economic burden on our health care system. Falls are often attributed to physical problems, such as poor balance. Recent research, however, has suggested that impaired cognition also contributes to falls. My research is aimed at examining whether computer game training can improve cognitive functions and reduce falls risk in older adults. In this study, older adults deemed to be at-risk for falls will be assigned to one of two groups: 1) game playing group, or 2) control (no game playing) group. Participants in the game playing group will play Rise of Nations, a commercially available strategy game, for a total of 23.5 hours over an eight week period. After the training period, I will assess changes in cognitive function using standard laboratory tests and examine changes in brain activation using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Additionally, I will compare changes in falls risk after the training period between my two research groups (game players versus controls). My research has important implications for improving multiple components that contribute to falls risk. Given our rapidly aging population, I highlight that developing effective tools for reducing falls risk has the potential to improve quality of life for seniors across Canada and reduce health care costs.

TitreApplicationTitle: A randomized controlled trial examining the effect of aerobic exercise on cognitive decline and brain region volumes in older men and women with mild cognitive impairment: Possible interaction between sex and BDNF polymorphisms.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD DEVELOPMENT; CORTISOL ASSAYS; ENDOCRINOLOGY; EPIGENETICS; HEALTH RESEARCH; MATERNAL HEALTH; MATERNAL STRESS; POPULATION HEALTH; PRENATAL ENVIRONMENT; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Adverse prenatal conditions, such as maternal exposure to stress, can have important consequences for fetal development and increase disease susceptibility across the lifespan. High levels of stress during pregnancy have been shown to alter children's behavioural, emotional, cognitive, immune, and metabolic functioning. Existing evidence suggest that these negative outcomes may be a consequence of changes in the development of the stress axis. Previous studies on prenatal stress, however, begin evaluating maternal stress levels only after pregnancies are clinically recognized, missing the first six weeks of gestation, a 'critical period' for the development of the fetus. Therefore the proposed study will investigate the role maternal stress level has in the programming of the stress axis during that crucial window of vulnerability for the fetus and evaluate its subsequent function during the transition to puberty. To understand the mechanisms involved in the programming of the stress axis we will investigate how relevant genes are activated or de-activated in children and how these patterns of gene expression are associated with maternal stress levels from the first six weeks of gestation. The proposed study will be the first to look at how maternal stress levels during the child's earliest developmental environment, the first six weeks after conception, influence adolescent development. The results from this study will provide novel information critical to understanding how adverse early-life experiences can 'get under the skin' and impact physical and mental health outcomes later in life. Ultimately this research may aid in the development of public policy for prevention and intervention programs for at-risk mothers and children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antibodies Targeting the ErbB2/ErbB3/IGF-1R Complex as Therapeutics for ErbB2 Positive Breast Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY THERAPY FOR BREAST CANCER; ERBB RECEPTORS; IGF-1 RECEPTOR; PHAGE DISPLAY
Abstract-Résumé: The use of the antibody trastuzumab to inhibit human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (erbB2), which is present on specific types of breast cancer, is a paradigm shift in cancer therapy, as it provides a more specific and less toxic approach to treat breast cancer compared to chemotherapy. However, many patients with erbB2 positive breast cancer show no response to trastuzumab or they acquire resistance to trastuzamab treatment with one year. Recently, it has been shown that increased expression of two other surface receptors, human epidermal growth factor receptor 3 (erbB3) and insulin-like growth factor receptor (IGF-1R), is associated with the development of trastuzamab resistance. ErbB3 and IGF-1R form a complex with erbB2, which blocks trastuzamab activity and allows breast cancer cells to survive and proliferate. We propose to develop new antibodies that target erbB3 and IGF- 1R as a promising strategy to treat erbB2-positive trastuzumab sensitive and resistant breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulating the function of SCF ubiquitin ligases through ubiquitin-based binders
Keywords-MotsClés: COMBINATORIAL LIBRARIES; E3 UBIQUITIN LIGASE; F-BOX PROTEIN; HIGH THROUGHPUT SCREENING; PHAGE DISPLAY; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; SCF UBIQUITIN LIGASE; STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS; UBIQUITIN PROTEASOME PATHWAY; UBIQUITIN-BASED INHIBITORS/ACTIVATORS
Abstract-Résumé: The ubiquitin proteasome system is responsible for timely degradation of proteins inside the cell, which is absolutely critical for proper cellular function. Through a series of enzymatic steps, a small protein called ubiquitin is attached to other proteins, marking them for degradation by a large complex of proteins called the proteasome. Recently, it has become apparent that components of the ubiquitin proteasome system are deregulated in many cancers, making them attractive targets for cancer therapy. This has been validated by successful treatment of multiple myeloma with Bortezomib, a drug which prevents the proteasome from functioning normally. The clinical success of this drug, which has a general effect on the proteasome, suggests that a more targeted approach in which the function of specific components of the ubiquitin proteasome system are modulated could result in even better therapeutic action with less side effects. Of particular interest is targeting a group of enzymes called E3 ligases, which mediate the attachment of ubiquitin to the proteins bound for degradation, thus acting as specificity factors in the ubiquitin proteasome system. The main goal of my project is to develop protein-based binders to E3 ligases, with the goal of either preventing or enhancing their function. These protein modulators will provide tools for better understanding E3 ligase biology and perhaps pave way for the development of therapeutic drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pain in Preterm Infants: Long-Term Effects on Neurodevelopment
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; CHILDREN; COGNITIVE PROCESSING; IMAGING; LONG-TERM SEQUELAE; MORPHINE; NEURODEVELOPMENT; PAIN; PREMATURITY; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: It is estimated that nearly 13 million premature infants are born worldwide each year. Due to modern technology the majority of very preterm infants now survive, but the tiniest babies spend weeks to months hospitalized in the neonatal intensive care (NICU) often undergoing essential life-saving invasive procedures that can be painful. In children born very preterm (less than 32 weeks of gestation), rates of cognitive problems remain high despite major advances in neonatal medicine. These infants are biologically very immature and their brains are rapidly developing during this period. Recently it has been shown that greater neonatal procedural pain is associated with reduced brain maturation, and giving morphine does not ameliorate these effects. However, there is no knowledge of the specific brain structures affected, and whether the impact of pain persists into childhood. The proposed project will examine the relationship between neonatal procedural pain, exposure to morphine and brain development in children born very preterm. At present, pain management strategies are advocated in NICU care (e.g. morphine) with no understanding of effects on the developing brain. Methods are needed to evaluate long term effects of both pain exposure and pain management on the brain. Identifying specific areas of the brain that are affected long term and found to be associated with school-age outcomes could become useful markers of these effects on the brain. The proposed study will provide a way to validate if growth in certain brain regions could be used as an indicator of the long-term effects of pain exposure, thereby providing a way to evaluate pain management in the future.

Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; COPD; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; IMMUNE REGULATION; IN VIVO MODELS; INVESTIGATIONAL THERAPEUTICS; T CELL; TRANSLATIONAL MEDICINE; VIRAL INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: COPD patients suffer frequent viral infections due to Human Rhinovirus and Influenza A Virus, which cause substantial morbidity and mortality. In response to cigarette smoke (CS), transcription factor Nrf2 upregulates a broad spectrum of protective defenses, including nearly all cellular antioxidants. Our laboratory has previously shown that lungs of COPD patients have a defective Nrf2 pathway and Nrf2 protects from CS-induced oxidative stress, inflammation and helps fight bacterial infection. The role of Nrf2 during viral infection is not known. Our recent findings suggest we have not only found a novel cause of virus driven COPD deaths, but also a therapeutic solution. My research from past 1 year has uncovered a novel role of Nrf2 in regulating T cell responses which are required to fight viral infections but worsen COPD symptoms. We have found that CS-exposure increased T cell inflammatory responses and caused greater lung damage in Nrf2-/- mice following virus infection and conversely, increasing Nrf2 in T cells blunted the harmful effects in vitro.  We hypothesize that Nrf2 regulates the dangerous effects of T cells without compromising viral clearance and inhibits excessive pulmonary inflammation in CS-exposed mice following viral infection. To prove this we will; 1) Test the hypothesis that Nrf2 inhibits activation of T cells that destroy lung tissue in CS exposed mice following virus infection, 2) Determine whether augmenting Nrf2 by sulforaphane attenuates T cell inflammation in CS-exposed mice following virus infection and 3) Test the hypothesis that activation of Nrf2 suppresses T cell activation through upregulation of self-regulatory molecule SOCS3.  Taken together, this study will identify a novel mechanism of T cell regulation and test the therapeutic potential of sulforaphane, a phytonutrient found in broccoli sprouts and potent Nrf2 activator for the treatment of viral exacerbations of COPD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rapid gene expression and protein profiling for transplantation medicine
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; BIOSENSING; MICROCHIP TECHNOLOGY; TRANSPLANTATION MEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: Lung transplantation (LTx) is a life-saving therapy for patients suffering from end-stage lung disease. While there have been significant advances in procedures for lung transplantation, there are still significant impediments that stand in the way of successful transplantation outcomes. While the number of patients in need of LTx is significantly increasing, the number of donors remains static. The shortage is further aggravated by very low utilization rates of donor lungs (~15%) among multi-organ donors due to the conservative practices of many transplant groups.  Recently, a set of markers were identified by co-PIs Keshavjee, Liu and Cypel that provide a molecular basis for better predicting the quality of donor lungs and thus transplant outcomes. The challenge of using these molecular markers, however, is that they must be assessed rapidly in order for this information to be used. After removal from a donor, lungs must be transplanted within 8 hours, and the clock on the use of the lung may start at times when the services of laboratories equipped to perform molecular analysis are not available. An ideal solution would be an automated testing unit that could perform rapid analysis of marker levels at the site where the donated organs are being assessed and retrieved. A new molecular analysis platform recently developed by Kelley and Sargent will provide a solution enabling marker analysis for organ transplantation. The platform is based on an electronic chip that is highly robust, inexpensive, and straightforward to fabricate. This project will adapt the chip-based detection platform described above for the challenge of transplantation medicine. The automated, highly multiplexed, fast and portable nature of this molecular diagnostic platform makes it an ideal fit for rapid readout of markers predicting lung transplant outcomes. The primary deliverable to be obtained with this support is an integrated protein/RNA detection system for transplantation medicine.

Abstract-Résumé: A novel intravascular imager technology of fatty acids in arteries responsible for heart disease and stroke will be developed. The imager consists of a catheter carrying combined photoacoustic and ultrasonic sources and detectors capable of scanning circumferentially (tomographically) the inside of an artery around a full circle. The catheter is able to move axially along the artery thereby generating cylindrical maps of the internal walls. Using parallel optical-to-ultrasound (photoacoustic) energy conversion and pure ultrasound detection "co-registration", the catheter imager will map the presence of fatty lipids responsible for coronary artery disease at an earlier stage than today's purely ultrasonic and purely optical imaging catheters. This technology can be very valuable for diagnosis and more effective treatment of coronary disease, the leading cause of adult death in developed nations with increasing prevalence worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Computerized Patient Phenotyping to Connect Canadian Clinical Genetics Clinics
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL GENETICS; HEALTH INFORMATICS; PHENOTYPING; RARE DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: Approximately one in 12 Canadians is affected by a rare disorder; many of these conditions are severe, and most are currently untreatable. With the lives of over three million Canadians affected, the impact of rare genetic disorders on the healthcare system and Canadian society as a whole is significant. Currently, databases of systematically collected phenotypic information on humans with rare disorders using a standard terminology do not exist. We have developed PhenoTips, a phenotyping tool for rare diseases utilizing an internationally recognized standard vocabulary, the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO). The software is already public and is used as part of the Finding of Rare Disease Genes (FORGE) project, and has been presented at Rounds at each of our three partner hospitals: SickKids (Toronto), CHEO (Ottawa), and Mt Sinai (Toronto). At all of these presentations, clinicians were uniformly supportive of the general launch of our software for clinical use. As part of the current proposal, we are planning to: (1) Develop a stable version of the phenotyping tool that will be deployed for clinical use at our three partner hospitals; (2) Build novel algorithms and user interfaces within the phenotyping tool to simplify clinical diagnostics; and (3) allow for the interchange of full patient records between the hospitals and transfer of anonymized data of patients consented for research use to a centralized data repository. Our project will simplify clinical workflows at each of the partner sites, and in the future can be deployed at additional hospitals across Canada: all of our software will be made freely available (open source) to encourage wide adoption.

TitreApplicationTitle: Protecting Canadian Health, Security, and Prosperity through the Novel Integration of Global Epidemic Surveillance and Risk Modelling Technologies
Keywords-MotsClés: 1101- HUMAN HEALTH; 2705-SOFTWARE AND DEVELOPMENT; 2960-MATHEMATICAL MODELLING; 802-INFORMATION SYSTEMS AND TECHNOLOGY; EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE; EPIDEMIC AND PANDEMIC THREATS; GLOBAL INFECTIOUS DISEASE SURVEILLANCE; METAPOPULATION EPIDEMIC MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: As the world becomes increasingly interconnected and globalized, infectious diseases emerging in other parts of the world present growing threats to Canadian health, security, and economic prosperity. To strengthen awareness of global infectious disease threats, the Canadian government developed the Global Public Health Intelligence Network (GPHIN) in 2000 - a novel technology to monitor online news about infectious diseases worldwide, around the clock in nine different languages. While this tool has created greater awareness of the many potential global threats that exist every day, it lacks the ability to evaluate those threats and understand their ability to spread into Canada and consequently threaten the nation's health and economic security. We propose (i) to link GPHIN with BioDiaspora - a patented, web-GIS technology developed by our scientific team that is capable of rapidly analyzing massive volumes of worldwide air travel data, and (ii) integrate mathematical modeling of infectious diseases to be able to forecast the global spread of infectious diseases into Canada and identify the most effective and efficient public health countermeasures available. We propose to create an integrated solution that can rapidly generate essential knowledge from anywhere in the world at any moment in time, through a real-time, web-based software system.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Modular Intelligent Power Wheelchair System to Enhance Mobility, Safety and Participation of Users
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE; DECISION MAKING; DISABILITY; MOBILITY; OLDER ADULTS; PLANNING; REHABILITATION; ROBOTICS; WHEELCHAIRS
Abstract-Résumé: Power wheelchairs can help people with mobility problems to be independent. But people with physical, sensory and cognitive disabilities have difficulty using power wheelchairs safely and independently. This project will develop an intelligent power wheelchair system for older adult long term care residents who have multiple disabilities. The technology aims to improve mobility, safety and participation while decreasing dependence on caregivers and health care providers. We will produce a module that can be added to existing power wheelchairs to adapt to user needs for safety and mobility. The module's features will help users to avoid obstacles, get to where they wish to go with guidance if necessary, and make suggestions for activities. The system will include feedback to help users operate and direct the power wheelchair easily. The system, using computer vision and artificial intelligence, will be safety and performance tested. Feedback will be sought from therapists, nursing staff, and caregivers to improve the design and potential for use in care homes. Testing will involve users who are currently excluded from power wheelchair use because of cognitive and other disabilities and will examine user satisfaction and whether features improve safety and skilled driving. The new features can potentially help current power wheelchair users to maintain mobility independence longer, and also expand the mobility options for a growing number of new users. Advances in engineering and computer science will be made in the development of real world obstacle detection and navigation using computer vision and user interfaces to provide assistance to users with multiple disabilities. The new module is aimed to be used with existing power wheelchair, an outcome that has yet to be achieved. This is a joint project with the University of Toronto, Toronto Rehab, University of British Columbia, GF Strong Rehab Centre, and PG Drives Technology (UK).

TitreApplicationTitle: Chitosan-siRNA nanoparticles for gene silencing in Atherosclerosis and Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CANCER; CHITOSAN; GENE SILENCING; GENE THERAPY; NANOTECHNOLOGY; RNAI; SIRNA
Abstract-Résumé: A new class of drugs has been under development for the past decade, based on RNA interference, a mechanism of gene regulation whose discovery was awarded the Nobel prize in 2006. The drugs are short sequences of RNA, the genetic material that drives protein expression in all cells. It is possible to shut down the expression of pathological proteins using this mechanism by introducing RNA molecules into cells. Over the past decade the scientific and pharmaceutical community have recognised that the main limitation of making these drugs work is the lack of effective delivery systems. Our team has been working in this area of RNA delivery for several years and have discovered and published new systems that can deliver RNA molecules to cells using a polymer of glucosamine called chitosan. We previously discovered and developed a product for cartilage repair using this polymer and have now leveraged our ability to produce, modify and characterise these polymers to identify specific entities that are promising for RNA delivery. We have data in animal studies that suggest they may be useful for treating Atherosclerosis. This project aims to produce specific compositions of chitosan and RNA that can treat Atherosclerosis and Cancer based on silencing genes that are proven therapeutic targets. By the end of the project we expect to identify new therapeutic approaches which could be used in people to treat these diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of Magnetic Nanoparticles to Breakthrough the Blood-Brain Barrier
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD-BRAIN BARRIER; BRAIN TUMORS; DRUG DELIVERY; MAGNETIC NANOPARTICLES; NEUROPATHOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Effective treatment of brain related disorders requires an adequate distribution of drugs into the brain.  For many drugs, penetration into the brain is restricted by the brain capillaries that form what is referred to as the blood-brain barrier (BBB). The current research project will develop iron-oxide based nanoparticles as a delivery platform for enhancing the brain penetration of drugs.  Our approach is to utilize the magnetic properties of the nanoparticles to "pull" them through the BBB by applying a magnetic field to the brain.  Optimization of the outer surface properties of the magnetic nanoparticles will be performed to target the nanoparticles to the junctions between the brain capillary endothelial cells which in the presence of a magnetic field will enhance BBB penetration.  Once optimization is achieved, studies will be preformed to determine the bio-compatibility and safety profile of these magnetic nanoparticles at both the cell culture and whole animal (mouse) level. This is important as the potential brain related toxicity of these particular nanoparticles is unknown.  Finally, using a prototype magnetic nanoparticle, we will perform proof-of-principle studies demonstrating the increased delivery of chemotherapeutic agents to target sites in a mouse brain tumor model.  Our overall objective is to determine the optimal surface properties and magnetic field strengths to achieve brain penetration, as well as to characterize the bio-compatibility and safety profile of these magnetic nanoparticles for brain related applications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Universal Smart Guided-Catheter Systems Based on Novel Shape Memory Polymer Brush Actuators for Minimally Invasive Vascular Surgery
Abstract-Résumé: Catheters are widely employed in vascular and cardiovascular disease (CVD) treatment. CVD is the leading cause of death in adult Canadian men and women. In Canada, 70,000 patients die out of 500,000 hospitalized CVD cases per year. Catheters are not only important in these life-saving surgical procedures but are  also inserted into body cavities or vessels for drainage purposes, to administer fluids or allow passage of other instruments for surgery on different parts of the body.  Most catheters are straight. A variety of catheter shapes may be necessary to negotiate an area of the body that would not allow passage of a simple straight catheter in vascular surgery.  The principal innovation of this project is to create a novel catheter technology whereby a catheter's tip can be reversibly deformed into controllable angles using a novel shape memory mechanism in combination with wireless MEMS technology. The control of the catheter tip bending angles or deformation allows the catheter to guide itself through tortuous paths in human blood vessels with minimum physical forces to be applied by the surgeon. Successful realization of this technology will not only improve upon the current state-of-the art but also will lead to a change in clinical practice whereby a single catheter tip can be used to navigate through complex blood vessel geometries over a range of angles. This research will lead to innovative medical devices in vascular surgery, improved surgical procedures, and potentially enhanced surgical outcomes for patients. Drawing expertise from chemists, engineers, and surgeons, this the smart catheter technology developed for vascular surgery in this project will serve as an ideal launching platform for applications in other surgical procedures in future.

Abstract-Résumé: The spread of bacteria from the initial site of infection to other parts of the body via the bloodstream (dissemination) is responsible for most of the mortality caused by bacterial infection. Infectious diseases cost the Canadian economy $3.49B/year. The Canadian biopharmaceutical industry, Industry Canada and CIHR have identified discovery and development of novel classes of antibacterials and molecules for complementing the action of existing antibiotics as a strategic focus for Canadian innovation and development. Disrupting bacterial dissemination may provide an important antibiotic-complementing approach for limiting infectious disease progression. The proposed project will develop rapid, less costly methods for identifying and characterizing bacterial dissemination inhibitors with potential use as novel treatments for bacterial infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Spatial data mining exploring co-location of adverse birth outcomes and environmental variables
Keywords-MotsClés: BIRTH OUTCOMES; DATA MINING; GIS; INDUSTRIAL POLLUTION; MATERNAL/INFANT HEALTH; SOCIO ECONOMIC STATUS
Abstract-Résumé: Adverse birth outcomes (ABO), such as prematurity and low-birth weight, have immediate and long-term health consequences, including serious emotional and economic impacts on society. Current research identified relationships between ABO maternal factors, social factors and certain pollutants. Investigating links between pollutants and ABO has been limited by the challenge of evaluating all those factors in combination. This study will use new methods based on data mining to investigate relationships of industrial emissions and different social factors with ABO, considering wind patterns, urban pollution and maternal factors. We will use data from 1) the National Pollution Release Inventory (>300 chemicals annual emissions); 2) Statistics Canada, CIHR MiCare Program, and the Canadian Perinatal Programs Coalition (birth outcomes, maternal and socioeconomic variables); 3) CAREX (urban air pollution models), and 4) Environment Canada, Ministry of Agriculture (wind data). Maps will be created to present results.  Investigators from different disciplines and institutions will participate (e.g. computing sciences, neonatology, epidemiology, and knowledge translation) as well as interested stakeholders from Health Canada, the Canadian Perinatal Programs Coalition, and the Canadian Partnership for Children's Health & Environment. We anticipate that this study, by identifying complex interactions between all these factors in specific locations, will identify areas of Canada where increased rates of ABO, specific industrial emissions and socioeconomic factors co-exist. The study will also identify areas that may require further investigation, how existing data can be used for the study of pollution/disease and the usefulness of methods developed in this project for addressing complex health problems. Highly qualified personnel will be trained as well. The knowledge gained will contribute to understand the complex problem of ABO and promote Canadian mothers and infants' health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Quality and Patient Safety in Radiation Therapy by Integrating Multi-Disciplinary Criteria into an Artificial Intelligence System
Keywords-MotsClés: 1211 MEDICAL AND HEALTH SCIENCES; 2603 COMPUTER VISION; 2605 PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE; 2804 EXPERT SYSTEMS; 9000 HEALTH SCIENCES; AUTOMATION; MEDICAL PHYSICS; PATIENT SAFETY; QUALITY ASSURANCE; RADIATION ONCOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The delivery of radiation for the treatment of cancer is a complicated process that requires both clinical and technical expertise to ensure radiation treatments are safe and effective. Sub-optimal treatment plans have the potential to result in significant detriment to the patient and several studies have shown radiation therapy (RT) plans, which deviate from established quality assurance (QA) guidelines, result in worse patient outcomes. Therefore, the current RT process requires substantial multi-disciplinary QA resources to reduce the likelihood of errors and to ensure a high standard of patient care.   Technical innovations in RT have improved the quality of treatment plans usually at the cost of increased complexity. Therefore, more information and plan data requires review on the part of the multi-disciplinary RT team. The goal of the current research proposal is to integrate automation into the existing QA process in order to improve the quality of the RT and to develop a system for reducing errors.  In order to achieve these objectives, we are developing sophisticated mathematical algorithms, which represent and store thousands of previous RT plans deemed to be safe and of high quality. For a new radiation treatment plan created, the algorithms examine features of the plan to establish relationships and patterns in the data in order to identify deviations and errors in comparison to the plan knowledge base. These algorithms, once integrated into an automated QA system will simplify the plan review process and provide the RT team essential knowledge to make more informed decisions about patient treatment. This research will also make the RT process more efficient and robust, thereby reducing interruptions in patient treatments and reducing wait times for patients requiring RT. The research will promote widespread dissemination and knowledge translation to other institutions, thus benefiting all patients receiving RT as part of their cancer management.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a research program in HIV-related population health and health services research
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HIV; IMMIGRANTS; POPULATION HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past ten years, there has been an increase in the number of women, straight men and immigrants originally from Africa and the Caribbean living with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in Canada.   However, despite the increased representation of these individuals among the population of persons living with HIV, very little is known about the health of these patients and whether the existing network of health and social support services for persons living with HIV adequately meets their needs. Therefore, the aim of this program of research is to use information obtained from various sources, including large health databases, surveys and focus groups, to learn about the health and patterns of health and social support use of women, straight men and immigrants from African and the Caribbean living with HIV.  The specific projects which make up the program of research include 1) a project looking at various aspects of the health and prenatal care of HIV-infected women and their babies; 2) a project looking at changes in the health of HIV-infected persons originally from Africa and the Caribbean following their arrival in Canada, and the factors that influence these changes and 3) a national survey to identify patterns and barriers in the use of health and support services by heterosexual men with HIV, and the influence of health and support service use on the various aspects of the health of these men.  All of these projects build on the PhD work conducted by the applicant and the collaborations he has forged with other scientists across the country, community members living with HIV and the staff of AIDS service organizations who provide care to these patients.  The results of this program of research will be of relevance and interest to clinicians, policy makers and researchers who are involved in the funding, provision and evaluation of HIV-related services, and will improve the health of Canadians living with HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mobilizing ethnoracial minority and newcomer communities to address HIV/STI stigma and reduce HIV vulnerabilities
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY MOBILIZATION AND CAPACITY BUILDING; ETHNO-RACIAL MINORITY COMMUNITIES; GENDER AND SEXUAL HEALTH; IMMIGRANTS AND REFUGEES; SEXUAL MINORITIES; SOCIAL AND STRUCTURAL DETERMINANTS OF HIV/STI; STIGMA AND SEXUAL HEALTH DISPARITIES
Abstract-Résumé: There is solid evidence to show that social and economic inequities affect the sexual health of Canadians. At the end of 2008, it was estimated that 65,000 people were living with HIV/AIDS in Canada, and 26% of them were not aware of their HIV status. Research also shows that sexually transmitted infections (STI) including HIV/AIDS are not distributed equally across all Canadian populations. Young people who live in neighbourhoods that have high rates of unemployment, low income, lack of access to education, health and social services, and limited community sources tend to have higher rates of STIs. Similarly, newcomer communities bear a disproportionate burden of HIV/AIDS. Research results show racism reinforces HIV stigmas and silence about HIV/AIDS within newcomer. The lack of visible HIV champions also leads to community denial about the true impact of HIV/STI in these vulnerable communities. Mobilizing youth and adults in the affected communities to become HIV champions to reduce stigma and promote open discussion about HIV is critical to effective HIV/STI prevention, treatment and care.   This program of research will engage young people from disadvantaged neighbourhoods, newcomers living with HIV/AIDS, and community faith, media and social justice leaders to study how individual factors (e.g., knowledge, attitude, beliefs) and societal factors (e.g., homophobia, poverty, racism, gendered violence) interact to produce conditions that put marginalized groups at higher risk of HIV/STI. Knowledge and insights gained from this research program will be shared with community members, youth, people living with HIV/AIDS, service providers, students in health sciences, researchers, and policy makers. They will also be used to guide the development of effective HIV prevention programs, promote community collaboration to reduce HIV stigma, and inform policy and practice to improve the health outcomes of PHAs, vulnerable groups, and Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparative Safety and Effectiveness of Antidiabetic Medications
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES; DRUG SAFETY AND EFFECTIVENESS; HEALTH OUTCOMES; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Medications used to treat type 2 diabetes are studied extensively prior to approval by regulatory authorities. However, our understanding of a medication's effectiveness in an everyday clinical setting, the chance of rare adverse effects, and its long-term effects is very limited. In other words for individuals living with type 2 diabetes, a medication's potential to cause unintended side effects - and even any beneficial effects it might have on reducing the complications of diabetes long-term (e.g. cardiovascular disease) - are unknown when the medication is first marketed. Given the increasing numbers of people with type 2 diabetes worldwide, an evaluation of the postmarketing safety and effectiveness of medications for type 2 diabetes is essential for improving the care for these individuals.   My research over the next 5 years will focus on studying the risks and benefits of both the newest antidiabetic medications (the incretins) and older, understudied medications (insulin). I propose to study these medications using a database of detailed healthcare records for individuals with type 2 diabetes.  This database will include information on: prescription medication use, diagnoses, laboratory tests, and hospitalizations and death. Using the information in the database, I will assess the risk and benefits of incretin-based therapies and insulin therapy compared to other commonly used antidiabetic therapies. Moreover, I will systematically assess if there are any specific effects within certain groups of patients such as males and females, those with poor or normal kidney function, and other sociodemographic, clinical, and health system characteristics. Ultimately, my research program will contribute to our understanding of the real world effects of antidiabetic medications, and will inform patients, clinicians, and policymakers of the potential harms and benefits of these medications when used in everyday clinical practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: New Investigator Award: Improving Uncertainty Around Drug Safety, Research Plan for Network Meta-Analysis of RCTs and Observational Studies
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG SAFETY; META-ANALYSIS; NETWORK META-ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal outlines my ambitions for the next 5 years of my research career as part of my application for a New Investigator award in the priority area of drug safety. My planned primary focus is in expanding the application of network meta-analysis to include observational data along with data from randomized trials in analyses for safety. A variety of limitations related to assessing safety from RCTs are known to exist and observational studies may offer a solution to some of these challenges. At the same time, it will be important to assess potential bias within observational studies and account for them quantitatively in analyses.  In the research proposal three objectives are proposed: the first objective of this program will be to develop a framework which will incorporate adjustments for these perceived biases at the individual study level (year 1). As a second objective, I will demonstrate use of this framework while answering a series of drug safety questions outlined below (years 1-3). As a third objective, we plan to report empirical findings related to how the addition of observational data impacted the extent of available evidence for meta-analysis, summary estimates, clinical conclusions, and how bias adjustments impacted results (years 3-4). I believe the proposed work is well suited to the priority topic of the study of drug safety and is well aligned with the objectives of the Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network.

TitreApplicationTitle: The expression and role of soluble IL-7 receptor alpha in HIV-HCV co-infection
Keywords-MotsClés: CD8+ T-CELLS; CYTOKINES; HIV-HCV CO-INFECTION; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNOLOGY; LIVER
Abstract-Résumé: An immune response that effectively clears a viral infection depends on the actions of cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells (CTL). Cellular messengers known as cytokines, particularly interleukin-7 (IL-7), are very important in generating such responses. In progressive HIV and hepatitis-C virus (HCV) infections, CTL function is impaired, and similarly, IL-7 and its receptor CD127, have reduced activity. We have detected increased levels of a soluble form of CD127 (sCD127) in HIV+ individuals, which may function to alter IL-7 activity and contribute to immune impairment. Furthermore, in HIV-HCV co-infected individuals, a co-morbidity affecting approximately 30% of HIV+ individuals, sCD127 may contribute to HIV/AIDS progression. Studies will investigate expression and functions of sCD127 in both HCV mono- and HIV-HCV co-infection. This research could lead to be better understanding of how sCD127 influences anti-viral responses, thereby building the foundation needed for the development of novel immunotherapeutics and vaccine adjuvants to fight HIV and HCV infections.
