TitreApplicationTitle: Applied phylogenetics for HIV prevention
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; HIV PREVENTION; MOLECULAR EVOLUTION; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; PHYLOGENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: HIV evolves extremely rapidly in response to its environment.  As a result, the history of HIV transmission and adaptation leaves a distinct imprint on the genetic composition of each virus population. The overall objective of my research program is to develop computational tools that will enable us to reconstruct the spread and adaptation of HIV from these imprints, with the ultimate goal of directly applying this knowledge to prevent the transmission of HIV among Canadians. HIV genetic variation can be studied at two levels that both hold significant information for HIV prevention. First, we can study the genetic divergence of virus populations as they spread and adapt to different hosts. Second, we can study the accumulation of mutations in a virus population as it evolves within a single individual. A common thread to the study of genetic variation at any level is the use of a tree, called a 'phylogeny', to reconstruct the evolutionary origins of the diversity we see. My research program will use phylogenies to address critical problems in HIV prevention, concerning both the development of anti-HIV vaccines and the global initiative to expand access to HIV treatment known as 'Treatment as Prevention' (TasP). Specific aims of my program include: (1) identifying potential targets of HIV vaccines in virus-encoded proteins; (2) quantifying the impact of TasP on the transmission of HIV, including drug-resistant variants; (3) reconstructing the genetic characteristics of transmitted HIV variants; and (4) directly evaluating the impact of expanding access to HIV testing by reconstructing dates of HIV infection. These projects will directly impact the health of Canadians by evaluating the impact of current HIV prevention initiatives. Furthermore, my research plan includes several knowledge translation goals to ensure the uptake and utilization of these innovations by stakeholders in HIV prevention, including the public release of software and dissemination workshops.

Abstract-Résumé: The worldwide burden of hepatitis C (HCV), especially among those individuals who use illicit injection drugs and those also infected with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), is tremendous. This project proposes to access the long-term impact of increasing HCV testing, treatment coverage and retention into care as means of preventing individuals from dying prematurely and from transmitting both HCV and HIV. This proposed five-year research program has important implications, since we will identify strategies to diminish the gap in the delivery of care to those afflicted by HIV and HCV. This research proposal will employ innovative statistical and mathematical models to answer our research goal. Furthermore, this research program will have different co-investigators and collaborators with strong and diverse backgrounds with an exceptional publication record, and it create great opportunities to trainees to be supported across a variety of disciplines, further enhancing BC's competitive advantage in population-health and in HIV and HCV research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Integrating Indigenous and Western Scientific Approaches in Community-Based Participatory Research to Reduce the Health Inequities of First Nations, Inuit, and Métis Peoples in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH RESEARCH; AND ENVIRONMENT; COMMUNITY; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH; HEALTH; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTHY LANDS; HEALTHY PEOPLE; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOGIES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MIXED RESEARCH METHODS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, no population is in a more disadvantaged health position than Indigenous peoples. Despite decades of biomedical research, their health outcomes have seen little improvement, largely because researchers have focused on pathology and dysfunction, not on understanding the social determinants of health or Indigenous experiences. For example, only recently have we recognized that the health of their land is intimately tied to the health of Indigenous peoples. We also know that industry is degrading the environment and impacting human health to such an extent and at such a rate that there is cause for serious concern. Worse, disproportionate exposures to pollutants are impacting Indigenous peoples, especially given their close proximity to and interdependent relationship on the land around them. We have a reasonable understanding of the historical, cultural, and epidemiological perspectives concerning Indigenous health in Canada. But we do not have an adequate understanding of their health concerns, changes to their health status over time, or the factors that contribute to their health status from their perspectives.   Community-based participatory research is a philosophical and methodological approach that characterizes the traits that CIHR's Institute of Aboriginal Peoples' Health espouses: "to carry out sound and ethical research together in ways that respect community values and allow communities to stand as true partners in the research process". By integrating Indigenous and Western scientific approaches in community-based participatory research - exemplified in the accompanying (funded) operating grant - this research program, unified by a number of interrelated and complementary projects, will offer recommendations for practice, program and policy domains that will ultimately reduce health disparities and work towards health equity by involving Indigenous peoples in Canada in the research enterprise.

TitreApplicationTitle: The MIcroRnas and Congenital Lung Anomalies program: MIRACLA
Keywords-MotsClés: EPITHELIAL CELLS; FIBROBLASTS; LUNG DEVELOPMENT; MICRORNAS; MIR-200B
Abstract-Résumé: Every year up to one hundred children are born in Canada with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Previous research from my group has shown that the abnormal lung development associated with the diaphragmatic defect is responsible for the poor outcome in these babies. Although survival of these babies has improved significantly over the last few decades, the intensive medical treatment, required to achieve this improved survival, results in long term damage to the lungs. At present doctors have a poor understanding of why and how the abnormal lung development occurs in babies with CDH. This knowledge is important if you want to improve or modulate the abnormal lung development.  Recently, microRNAs (small pieces of nucleic acid) have emerged as an important new class of regulators of gene expression during cancer and organ development. Our preliminary results identified one of these microRNAs: miR-200b, to be important for normal lung development. More importantly, miR-200b expression is changed during abnormal lung development due to CDH. My research program aims to improve our understanding of abnormal lung development in babies with CDH. I want to develop the MIRACLA research program that will study microRNA and congenital lung abnormalities. With the results of these novel studies we will potentially be able to design targeted (prenatal) therapies to modulate the natural course of lung development in these babies. This should eventually result in improved outcomes.

Abstract-Résumé: Our team has developed new technology that will allow the rapid detection of blood-borne disease markers, or allow monitoring drug concentrations during treatment. Our affordable, portable prototype apparatus is based on optical detection, using recent innovations to increase sensitivity. Our innovations will allow the detection using small volumes of blood, such that the method is non-invasive. The technology is readily adaptable to detection of a large number of approved biomarkers and can be applied to monitoring the blood concentrations of specific drugs. This project entails the development of detection protocols for blood-borne molecules, related to cancer therapy. The focus will be on the detection of prostate cancer, and on monitoring the course of treatment of childhood amyloid lymphoblastic leukemia. The technology developers will collaboratively adapt the detection assays to the current needs and clinical reality of clinicians from major health centers in Montreal. The assays will be rapidly integrated into clinical environments for validation. Our team is committed to the commercial development of this technology.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nanoconfinement Based Single-Cell Cytogenetic Platform for Pre-/Post-Implantation Genetic Diagnosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CONVEX-LENS IMPOSED CONFINEMENT (CLIC); CYTOGENETICS; NANOFLUIDICS; PRE-IMPLANTATION GENETIC DIAGNOSIS; PRE-IMPLANTATION GENETIC SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: Chromosomal analysis is routinely performed in Canada when there is an elevated risk of chromosomal anomalies (e.g. in the prenatal period due to maternal age, family history of a chromosomal rearrangement). In particular, pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is performed on 8-cell stage embryos as part of in vitro fertilization (IVF) to ensure embryo viability and fetal health: roughly 7000 women undergo IVF each year in Canada, a number that is growing due to increasing maternal age and the legally mandated provision of PGD through public health insurance. PGD must necessarily be performed on single cells. Current methods (ex. fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) can screen only for limited and pre-determined number of genetic defects. Alternatives to FISH, such as array comparative genomic hybridization (array-CGH), require single-cell amplification and cannot detect abnormalities such as triploidy and balanced translocations. There is a need for a single-cell cytogenetic diagnostic tool that is (a) high-throughput and (b) can yield a comprehensive high resolution analysis of single-cells without marker preselection. We propose to develop lab-on-a-chip instrumentation for the direct optical mapping of entire genomes extracted from single-cells with application to prenatal genetic analysis and PGD. The technology approach will be based on using a special instrument that can actively impose confinement in an experiment by deforming a coverslip with a "lens-pusher."  The instrument has the special property that it can shift between low and high confinement states, transforming a microfluidic device suitable for sample preparation steps into a nanofluidic device suitable for molecular analysis via DNA extension in nanofabricated groove structures defined on the coverslip.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-APOPTOTIC PROTEIN BCL-2; ANTISENSE OLIGONUCLEOTIDES; CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKEMIA; DNA CAGES AND NANOTUBES; DRUG RESISTANT TUMORS; ENZYME-MEDIATED REPAIR OF DNA DAMAGE; NUCLEIC ACID DELIVERY; OLIGONUCLEOTIDE ANALOGUES; SIRNA; TARGETED CANCER THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: General drug cytotoxicity and drug resistance are major hurdles in traditional cancer therapies, stemming from the nonspecific delivery of cancer therapeutics to normal and cancerous cells simultaneously. We aim to develop a new method for targeted cancer therapy using non-toxic DNA cages and nanotubes. Length, diameter and composition of these DNA cages can be tuned and modified, to generate delivery molecules that can accommodate a plethora of cargo molecules, including cancer therapeutics. We have shown that DNA cages are able to accumulate in cancer cells, more specifically in drug resistant leukemia cells. We propose to encapsulate a wide range of cancer destroying molecules such as cytotoxic drugs, RNA molecules, and other cancer inhibiting agents. We propose that this novel class of cages made up of DNA bases, will evade the innate immune system, successfully and specifically deliver novel and pre-existing cancer therapeutics to cancer cells without affecting normal cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innovative vascular implants based on electrospinning and bioactive coatings
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS 2006; BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING 1102; BIOMEDICAL MATERIALS 1902; ELECTROSPINNING; GROWTH FACTOR; MEDICAL EQUIPMENT AND APPARATUS 518; PLASMA POLYMERIZATION; STENT-GRAFTS; SURFACE MODIFICATION; VASCULAR IMPLANTS
Abstract-Résumé: Vast numbers of patients world-wide suffer from cardiovascular diseases; this has led to growing use of implants designed to restore normal blood flow in diseased vessels. However, their success is limited: Vascular grafts (tubes made of plastic), sutured to blood vessels to replace diseased arteries, are prone to occlusion and limited to large-diameter vessels, thus excluding arteries of the heart or the lower limbs. Other implants such as stent-grafts are less invasive, because they are inserted by catheter into the diseased blood vessels. However, frequent complications limit their use to patients with high operative risks. These complications are mainly related to the inadequate mechanical and biological properties of the synthetic materials used. The present proposal aims to combine promising innovations developed by two successful multidisciplinary research teams, namely to create a new generation of vascular implants using (i) scaffolds with mechanical properties that better match those of blood vessels; (ii) surface  modification, which enables improved cell response and tissue healing around the implant. Both technologies (even more, their combination) will permit greatly-improved healing and tissue regeneration around these implants, thereby reducing clinical complications and enabling more patients to be treated. Technologies will be tested in vitro and in animals, to confirm their beneficial effects and to enable rapid transfer to industry. This "joint venture" is strongly endorsed and supported by CORONEO, a Montreal-based company that conducts R&D and commercialization of implants and instruments for cardiovascular medicine, as well as by an international leader in the manufacture of endovascular stent-grafts. Therefore, this project will not only address urgent health problems in Canada's ageing population, but will also help develop "made-in-Canada" technology for one of the currently most lucrative medical device markets (16 billion $/yr).

TitreApplicationTitle: Multidimensional separation isolation and characterization of circulating tumour cells
Keywords-MotsClés: AFFINITY-BASED PURIFICATION; ANTIBODY; BREAST CANCER; CELL SIZE; CIRCULATING TUMOR CELL; FILTRATION; HOT EMBOSSING; MICROFABRICATION
Abstract-Résumé: BACKGROUND. If cancer remains localized, it can often be treated, but if it metastasis, it vecome very difficult. Metastasis is thought to occur by so-called circulating tumor cells, or CTCs. These CTCs are emerging as a new element for prognosis of cancer, as well as for measuring the response to therapy, and to diagnose recurrence much earlier. The presence of as little as 3-5 CTCs per 7.5 ml of blood may have prognostic significance, this volume also contains ~ 100,000,000 white blood cells, rendering CTC isolation extremely challenging. In addition, CTCs are heterogeneous, and further it is important to differentiate between dead and live cells with metastatic potential. Although separation systems exist, they typically isolate cells based on a single property, either mechanical or biomolecular, and have been shown to miss many cells.   PROJECT: Here we propose to develop a low cost CTC isolation cartridge that will capture cells from 10 ml of blood in a few minutes based on both mechanical and molecular characteristics. We thus hope to isolate a much greater variety of cells, and make CTCs a much more reliable diagnostic and prognostic tool. We believe that this will also help us understand which cells are responsible for cancer metastasis, which may then lead to targeted therapies to eradicate them. The low cost of our technology should also greatly accelerate the translation to the clinic and its adoption as a standard of care to help treat cancer patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Commissural interneurons in locomotion and spasticity after spinal cord injury
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL TESTING; CENTRAL PATTERN GENERATOR; COMMISSURAL INTERNEURONS; CONTUSION SPINAL CORD INJURY; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; LOCOMOTOR RECOVERY; NEUROANATOMY; OPTOGENETICS; PLASTICITY; SPASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: The spinal cord is the primary neurological link between the brain and the rest of the body. Damage to the spinal cord can cause paralysis to regions below the injury site, followed by secondary symptoms, such as muscle spasticity. Normally, there is limited recovery of motor and sensory function below the site of injury. In most spinal cord injuries, however, there are at least some neurons that are not injured (i.e., spared), which can effectively 'bridge' the injury site. Recent studies have shown that these spared neurons can form new connections below the injury in a process called 'plasticity'. Although they provide important insights, these studies are limited because they do not identify the specific types of neurons responsible for recovery and used spinal cord injury models that are not relevant for human injuries. Knowing the key neuronal players and understanding how they form new connections is a very important step in developing a cure for spinal cord injury. Our project focuses on neural plasticity using transgenic mice and a spinal cord injury model that is relevant to human spinal cord injuries. We will focus specifically on a type of spinal cord neuron that is important for short distance communication in the spinal cord. These neurons are particularly interesting because they have an elevated capacity to form new connections after injury. In a first set of experiments we will examine the roles of these neurons in the normal walking behaviour of mice. In a second set of experiments animals will receive a spinal cord injury, and some animals will be treated to increase the amount of plasticity, whereas others will be treated to block the plasticity. We will then test which group of animals has improved locomotor abilities and reduced spasticity. These experiments are highly relevant to human spinal cord injuries and this project will provide the foundation from which plasticity-based therapies can be developed to treat spinal cord injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Two-Spirited Talking Circle Series
Keywords-MotsClés: TWO-SPIRITED PEOPLES HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Despite findings that both sexual minority and Aboriginal Canadians experience significant health disparities, very little research  has examined the intersection of sexual minority and Aboriginal identity - that is, two-spirited people. We will hold 6 Aboriginal talking circles of 4 hours each: 1 in Thunder Bay, Timmins, and Sudbury and 3 in Toronto, with a total of 72 participants.   These talking circles will: 1) Identify issues impacting the health of two-spirit people in Ontario; 2) Facilitate future research by establishing networks of trust; 3) Provide two-spirited people with cultural resources found to promote health via a sweat lodge ceremony performed by Vern Harper, Resident Elder at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, and through an online audio or video podcast by Mr. Harper; 4) Produce a set of 4 fact sheets on subjects emerging from the talking circles.Participants will be recruited using convenience sampling through Aboriginal and LGBT network and selected based on key demographics (e.g., age, sex).   Talking circles will be facilitated by Dr. Margaret Robinson, led by a semi-structured guide. Discussions will be held in non-colonial space, digitally recorded and transcribed verbatim. Dr. Robinson will analyze and code transcripts, group codes into concept categories, and generate theory related to factors impacting the health of two-spirited people. Participants will be invited to comment on the transcripts and summary of findings.

TitreApplicationTitle: Delineating culturally-appropriate adaptation strategies to the health effects of climate change for a subarctic First Nation community through a community-based participatory research approach
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTATION STRATEGIES; CLIMATE CHANGE ADAPTATION; CLIMATE CHANGE IMPACT; COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; FIRST NATION COMMUNITY; HEALTH EFFECTS; HEALTH INTERVENTION STRATEGIES; RESILIENCE; RURAL HEALTH; SUB-ARCTIC
Abstract-Résumé: Marginalized populations are at greater risk to climate change due to existing socioeconomic, political and health disadvantages. Aboriginal communities in remote locations are vulnerable populations with limited resources and greater health disparities, making them especially susceptible to the impacts of climate change because their subsistence lifestyle is strongly tied to the environment. In a First Nation community located in the western James Bay region, many community members have noticed changes in the timing of seasons, snow type, ice freeze-up/break-up, and weather patterns. These changes have affected animal behaviour, hunting activities and the winter road, which have led to financial strain and well-being issues (e.g. food insecurity). Despite such changes, many First Nation community members have exhibited the ability to adapt. The ability to adapt to climate change is vital. However, as the effects of climate change are continually increasing the difficulty in everyday living, it is unknown whether Aboriginal communities will be able to withstand related stressors in the future. Thus, through a community-based participatory research (CBPR) approach, this research project aims to 1) identify significant determinants of vulnerability to climate change among a First Nation community, 2) develop culturally-appropriate adaptation strategies that would reduce health risks to the effects of climate change, and 3) promote community well-being. A specific area of focus includes examining the health implications from the impacts of climate change on community infrastructure (e.g. housing, winter roads, and water sources), and subsequently, identifying and implementing sustainable interventions strategies. This research would be conducted in partnership with the Fort Albany First Nation community, located in the subarctic region of Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Évaluation des effets d'une pratique réflexive sur l'administration de psychotropes et sur la fréquence et la sévérité des symptômes comportementaux et psychologiques de la démence chez des personnes âgées résidant en centre d'hébergement et de soins de longue durée.
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVIS MIXTE; DEVIS QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL; INTERVENTION EDUCATIVE; INTERVENTIONS NON PHARMACOLOGIQUES; MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER ET MALADIES APPARENTEES; PERSONNEL SOIGNANT (INFIRMIERES; PERSONNES AGEES RESIDANT EN CHSLD; PREPOSES AUX BENEFICIAIRES); RECHERCHE-ACTION; SYMPTOMES COMPORTEMENTAUX ET PSYCHOLOGIQUES DE LA DEMENCE
Abstract-Résumé: Il est estime que 70 a 80 % des personnes agees residant en centre d'hebergement et de soins de longue duree (CHSLD) sont atteintes de la maladie d'Alzheimer ou de maladies apparentees. Jusqu'a 91 % de ces aines presentent des comportements difficiles pour le milieu de vie tels que l'errance, l'agitation ou l'agressivite. Bien qu'il existe des ecrits scientifiques portant sur ces comportements, plusieurs soignants affirment ne pas savoir quelles interventions adopter face a ceux-ci et le recours aux medicaments est souvent la premiere option envisagee. Une intervention educative qui repose sur l'auto-examen, par le soignant, de ses experiences cliniques pourrait permettre l'amelioration des soins dispenses a ces aines et maximiser l'instauration d'interventions non pharmacologiques reposant sur les meilleures pratiques de soins connues. Les buts de cette etude sont: 1) de developper et de mettre a l'essai une intervention educative avec des infirmieres et des preposes aux beneficiaires uvrant en CHSLD aupres d'aines atteints de la maladie d'Alzheimer et presentant des comportements difficiles; 2) d'evaluer les effets de cette intervention sur l'administration de medicaments ainsi que sur la frequence et la severite de ces comportements chez les aines. Cette etude sera realisee au moyen d'un devis mixte. Une approche de recherche-action sera utilisee pour le developpement et la mise a l'essai de l'intervention educative. L'evaluation des effets de l'intervention sera realisee au moyen d'une approche quantitative de type quasi-experimental. Cette etude permettra d'evaluer les effets d'une intervention educative novatrice visant a optimiser l'utilisation d'interventions non pharmacologiques aupres d'une clientele aux prises avec des comportements difficiles, en forte prevalence dans nos CHSLD et pour laquelle les soignants sont quotidiennement mis au defi.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preoperative delays prior to radical cystectomy and its impacts on survival in patients with bladder cancer: a population-based study
Keywords-MotsClés: BLADDER CANCER; PREOPERATIVE DELAYS; RADICAL CYSTECTOMY; RETROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY; SURVIVAL; SURVIVAL ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Bladder cancer is the 2nd most common urological cancer and the 6th most common diagnosed malignancy in Canada. It has the 4th highest cancer incidence in men and the 12th in women. About 80% of bladder tumors are already invasive tumors at initial diagnosis. In addition, half of patients have occult distant metastases at the time of presentation, which is a clear indication of the aggressive nature of the disease. Surgical removal of the bladder remains the recommended treatment for this condition. It has been suggested that delaying surgery is associated with poorer survival, and there is growing concern that waiting time for cancer surgery has been increasing in Canada. However, there is a lack of detailed studies on the magnitude of the problem. Previous data showed that preoperative delays for bladder cancer surgery have been steadily increasing, and a delay of more than 12 weeks is associated with worse long-term survival. Therefore, the objectives of the present research are to: (1) characterize and measure the impact of the different components of delay experienced by bladder cancer patients before surgery; (2) to identify predictors of longer delays and; (3) to determine the impact of the various components of delay on mortality. We will analyze data from patients who underwent surgery for bladder cancer from 2000 to 2009. Data will be obtained from the linkage of two administrative database of the province of Quebec: the RAMQ and the ISQ. These databases provide valuable information on medical services dispensed to patients and demographic data. The results of this study will furnish real evidence-based data on the determinants of preoperative delays and its impact on survival in patients with a diagnostic of bladder cancer. The results of this research will provide indications to physicians and health policy makers to develop interventions addressed to improve survival of patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiovascular disease in patients with breast cancer and lymphoma
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; CANCER; CARDIOMYOPATHY; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE; HEART FAILURE; LYMPHOMA; OUTCOME AND PROCESS ASSESSMENT; QUALITY INDICATORS; TRASTUZUMAB
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of death in cancer patients, and limits their quality of life. It is not well-defined which cancer patients get heart disease after treatment and how it impacts their health. Objectives: 1. To quantify and describe the type of heart disease in breast cancer and lymphoma patients during cancer treatment, and how this affects their treatment and survival in the 5 years after diagnosis.  2. To quantify and describe the type of heart disease in long term survivors of breast cancer and lymphoma, as the well as the time of development of these events 3. To quantify the impact of heart disease development on the lifespan of cancer survivors and their  use of hospital resources 4. To determine which patient characteristics, and which elements of their treatment, can be predictive of who develops heart disease as well as the type of heart disease and its timing 5. Study markers of the quality of care of cancer survivors who develop heart disease and how they compare with other patients with heart disease 6. Particular attention will be paid to the long term effects of trastuzumab, a breast cancer drug  which causes heart disease that is thought to be reversible, although its long term effects are unknown Methods: The Ontario Cancer Registry will be used to identify patients with breast cancer and lymphoma. The Ontario Health Card number will be used to link these patients with the Canadian Institute of Health Information Discharge Abstract Database, Ontario Registered Persons Database, and the Ontario Drug benefit Database. Trastuzumab use will be identified from the New Drug Funding Program database. We will also consider performing targeted chart reviews of patients who are treated with chemotherapy for breast cancer and lymphoma to obtain details of their cancer treatment. This will allow us to identify patient demographics, baseline comorbidities, medications and subsequent hospitalizations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the Premotor and the Parietal Connectivity with Primary Motor Cortex during the Rubber Hand Illusion in Focal Hand Dystonia
Keywords-MotsClés: CORTICAL PLASTICITY; FOCAL HAND DYSTONIA; RUBBER HAND ILLUSION; SENSORIMOTOR INTEGRATION; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Focal hand dystonia (FHD) is a neurological disorder which is characterized by sustained arm muscle contractions and abnormal postures. These muscle movements are involuntary and may interfere with the patient's performance on tasks everyday life. The exact cause and the mechanism of dystonia is not yet fully understood but recent studies have revealed that abnormalities exist not only in the motor cortex, which is a cortical region of the brain involved in the execution of voluntary movement, but also in the sensory cortex, which is another cortical region related to touch, temperature and body position sense. A key mechanism of dystonia lies within the process called sensorimotor integration in which these sensory inputs are processed by the central nervous system and interact with the motor system. The abnormalities in the sensorimotor integration may be indicated by a clinical phenomenon known as a 'sensory trick' which is a temporal suppression of the abnormal muscles contractions induced by just touching the affected or adjacent part of the body.    The aim of this research is to throw some light on the mechanism of the abnormal sensory connection with motor function using a technique known as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). TMS is a non-invasive technique for stimulation of the human brain and can be used to study the interaction between the two brain areas. In this research, the sensorimotor integration process in the healthy controls and the patients with dystonia will be explored by TMS stimulus over the motor cortex and the sensory cortex while the sensory inputs are being processed in the brain. This study will help us to understand the pathophysiology of dystonia and the result will contribute to designing a 'sensory training based treatment' for dystonia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeting the HER2 pathway in breast tumor-initiating cells
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOCRINE NRG1 SIGNALING; BREAST CANCER STEM CELL; CHEMOTHERAPY; HER2/HER3 SIGNALING PATHWAY; RADIATION THEARPY
Abstract-Résumé: Currently only breast cancer patients with HER2-positive tumors are treated with HER2-targeted therapies. However, recent clinical observations suggest that inhibiting HER2 in tumors that express low levels of HER2 may also improve survival. How inhibiting HER2 leads to beneficial effects in HER2-low breast cancer is poorly understood. I hypothesize that the HER2 pathway regulates a subset of tumor cells called cancer stem cells or tumor-initiating cells (TICs). TICs often make up only a small proportion of tumors but are the only cells that are able to divide indefinitely. Current anti-cancer therapies often leave behind a small number of resistant TICs that can cause tumor relapses and successful treatment requires the complete elimination of all TICs in a tumor. I propose that an activator of HER2 called NRG1 is produced by TICs, activates signaling through the pathway, and promotes survival and proliferation of breast TICs. If true, this would explain why anti-HER2 treatments improve survival of some patients with HER2-low tumors. I will evaluate the effect of NRG1 and HER2 inhibition in breast TICs as well as the chemo- and radiosensitizing effects. Importantly, I also plan to apply single cell-based analysis methods to surgical specimens from HER2-low breast cancer patients in order to establish what fraction of these tumors rely on the NRG1/HER2 pathway. This work will directly lead to a clinical assay that will then be used to test a personalized strategy of employing HER2 pathway inhibitors in the subset of HER2-low breast cancer patients whose TICs display pathway activity. This could significantly broaden the applicability of HER2-targeted therapy to a larger group of breast cancer patients in a personalized fashion. Thus, this proposal has a high chance of significantly impacting individual patients with breast cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Profil moléculaire de la double résistance du cancer du sein triple négatif (TN) aux agents anti-tumoraux
Keywords-MotsClés: AGENTS ANTI-TUMORAUX; BIOMARQUEURS; CANCER DU SEIN; GENOMIQUE; PACLITAXEL; PROTEOMIQUE; RESISTANCE EN SERIE
Abstract-Résumé: Les cellules cancereuses continuant a se propager malgre les traitements d'agents anti-tumoraux representent actuellement la problematique la plus importante pour la survie des femmes atteintes du cancer du sein.  En fait, ce phenomene affecte particulierement les femmes atteintes d'une forme tres agressive du cancer du sein, soit le cancer du sein triple negatif (TN). L'approche clinique pour le traitement du cancer du sein TN resistant au Paclitaxel (agent anti-tumoral principalement utilise en clinique) consiste a donner un autre agent anti-tumoral.  Toutefois, dans la plupart des cas, l'efficacite du traitement est temporaire et ces patientes deviennent a nouveau resistantes (resistance en serie) au nouvel agent administre. Il existe peu d'information sur les tumeurs TN resistantes aux agents anti-tumoraux et encore moins sur les tumeurs doublement resistantes. Notre projet vise a etudier en laboratoire des cellules du cancer du sein TN avec lesquelles nous allons identifier les facteurs moleculaires leur permettant de devenir resistantes aux agents anti-tumoraux administres en serie. L'etude proposee s'inscrit dans un projet de grande envergure ayant deja genere des cellules resistantes au Paclitaxel et faisant appel a une biobanque regroupant des echantillons tumoraux et sanguins de patientes atteintes de cancer du sein TN doublement resistantes. Les facteurs de resistance identifies dans notre etude seront par la suite valides dans les lesions tumorales de patientes atteintes du cancer du sein TN provenant de la biobanque. La decouverte de ces facteurs de resistance aidera les oncologues de 2 facons: premierement, en connaissant mieux l'etat de resistance des lesions tumorales, ils pourront privilegier l'utilisation de certains agents anti-tumoraux mieux cibles. Deuxiemement, nos travaux permettront de developper de nouveaux traitements et nous avons espoir qu'ils puissent aider a prevenir ou retarder la mort des femmes atteintes de cancer du sein TN.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetic deregulation of transposable elements contributes to Hodgkin lymphoma microenvironment formation
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA METHYLATION; EPIGENETICS; HISTONE MODIFICATIONS; HODGKIN LYMPHOMA; TRANSCRIPTION REGULATION; TRANSPOSABLE ELEMENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Remnants of transposable elements (TEs) or "mobile DNA" make up almost 50% of the human genome and have played an important role in species evolution. TEs are also responsible for several human diseases and "activation" of TE sequences in cancer is often observed. In order to block such harmful events, the host cell has evolved a series of epigenetic mechanisms to inhibit further movement of TEs.  These epigenetic mechanisms involve the marking or modification of TEs in the genome so they cannot be expressed.  Therefore, global epigenetic abnormalities, which often occur in cancer cells, cause many normally silent TEs to be expressed. We hypothesize that epigenetic alterations of specific TEs may awaken their transcriptional promoters, create host gene transcripts and contribute to the establishment of tumour microenvironments. We have analyzed RNA expression patterns from normal and Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) cell lines in order to find genes differentially expressed due to TE promoters. We have chosen eight genes that are abnormally upregulated in HL compared to normal, and harbor TE derived promoters. Curiously, these genes participate in pathways involved in inflammation, a pathway thought to be responsible for establishment of the HL microenvironment. We will assay for changes in DNA methylation and chromatin modifications, which are epigenetic marks, in the promoters of the eight genes in HL cell lines and normal cells. We will induce epigenetic changes in normal cells to mimic the HL cell lines and hopefully distinguish genes important for HL proliferation and tumour microenvironment. Biological significance of the best gene candidates will be assayed with functional experiments. It is hoped that this work will lend insight into the role of epigenetic abnormalities in HL and how these abnormalities may contribute to the malignant state.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of genomic alterations in C. elegans lacking Fanconi anemia pathway function
Keywords-MotsClés: C. ELEGANS; CANCER GENOMICS; CHROMOSOMAL INSTABILITY; DNA REPAIR; FANCJ; FANCONI ANEMIA PATHWAYS; GENOMIC STRUCTURAL VARIATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Fanconi Anemia (FA) is a devastating disorder associated with increased cancer susceptibility. FA patients will often develop anemia and cancer. FA is caused by mutations in DNA repair system, specifically the interstrand crosslink (ICL) repair. Currently, 15 human genes have been associated with FA. The initiation of the pathway has been well studied, but many of the repair mechanisms after the initiation are not well understood. The model organism Caenorhabditis elegans has been instrumental in understanding the function of FA components. So far, seven FA genes have been identified in C. elegans, including dog-1 as FANCJ. Due to the highly parallel DNA repair system between C. elegans and humans, I want to further develop C. elegans as a model system for studying FA. I will first identify other FA genes in C. elegans using bioinformatics and genomics methods. The Rose lab has hundreds of uncharacterized mutant strains enriched in DNA repair genes. We may find additional FA genes in this library by identifying their molecular identity in a high throughput manner.      The ultimate goal of my research project is to understand the genomic consequences when FA pathway is lost. To accomplish this, I will employ next-generation sequencing technology to sequence and classify the types of mutational changes in mutator strains that have lost FA components. Whole genome sequence will provide a global picture the types of mutation that can accumulate over time. Using the same technology, I will examine the genomic sequences of strains treated with crosslinking agents, such as the common chemotherapy agent mitomycin C, to classify genomic alterations in response to mutagens. Results from my research will give us a better understanding the relationship between mutators and ICL and will help develop therapeutics for FA derived cancers.

NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités : fragilité du chromosome X (PPPOS)
TitreApplicationTitle: Carrier-Mediated Delivery of Therapeutic Proteins into the Brain
Keywords-MotsClés: BLOOD-BRAIN-BARRIER; CARRIER PROTEIN; CRM197; DIPHTHERIA TOXIN; ENDOCYTOSIS; FRAGILE X SYNDROME; INTRACELLULAR DELIVERY MOLECULE; PROTEIN REPLACEMENT THERAPY; RECEPTOR-MEDIATED TRANSCYTOSIS; TOXIN-MEDIATED DELIVERY
Abstract-Résumé: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is the most common single-gene cause of autism and the most common form of inherited mental retardation in boys. The disease is characterized by a range of symptoms from characteristic hand movements to severe mental disability. FXS is currently a disease without a cure or meaningful treatments. FXS stems from the FMR1 gene that is normally expressed in neurons, but is switched off during development due to a mutation, and the result is that the protein FMRP is not produced in FXS patients, resulting in disease. the disease. Although FMRP can be delivered into the bloodstream of FXS patients, there are two major roadblocks that prevent FMRP from doing its job. First, proteins on their own do not cross the blood-brain-barrier and second, even if they did, they do not cross cell membranes to access their targets inside neurons. Our proposal aims to overcome both of these hurdles at once. By fusing FMRP to a non-toxic variant of diphtheria toxin (DT), we can deliver FMRP across the blood-brain-barrier and into neurons. DT is a highly sophisticated protein that binds to its receptor on the cells that make up the blood-brain-barrier and is transported across and into the brain. Once there, it binds to the same receptor on the surface of neurons and is taken up by the cell and deposited into the cytoplasm. We are proposing to take advantage of this delivery vehicle that nature has evolved by fusing FMRP onto a non-toxic DT variant. Experiments have shown that if FMRP is reintroduced into the brains of mice lacking FMRP, it alleviates cognitive impairment and reverses autism-related symptoms. If successful, this will be the first direct treatment for FXS patients, and possibly even a cure.

ProgramNameEN: Fellowship Award - Priority Announcement: Fragile X (SHOPP)
NomDuProgrammeFR: Bourse de recherche - Annonce de priorités : fragilité du chromosome X (PPPOS)
TitreApplicationTitle: Development of synaptic kainate receptors (KARs) in a mouse model of Fragile X Syndrome (FXS)
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBELLUM; DEVELOPMENT; FRAGILE X SYNDROME; IONOTROPIC GLUTAMATE RECEPTORS; KAINATE; METABOTROPIC GLUTAMATE RECEPTORS; PURKINJE CELL
Abstract-Résumé: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is the leading cause of inherited mental impairment. It is known to involve disturbances in the primary excitatory communication system in the brain, the glutamate signaling system. Glutamate communicates by acting at AMPA-type, NMDA-type, kainate-type and metabotropic glutamate receptors. Metabotropic glutamate receptors are promising therapeutic agents for the treatment of FXS. Interestingly, kainate-type receptors are currently the only main type of glutamate receptors that have not been examined in the pathophysiology and therapeutics of FXS. This study proposes to explore the expression and function of kainate-type receptors of Purkinje cells in the mouse cerebellum from birth to adulthood. In particular it will examine how kainate receptors regulate Purkinje cell activity by coupling to other ion channels and question whether this process is disrupted in a mouse model of FXS. Cerebellum Purkinje cells are known to use kainate-type receptors as part of their communication system and these cells are physiologically and physically disturbed in mouse models of FXS. By assigning a potential role for kainate-type receptors in FXS we will identify a novel therapeutic target for the treatment of FXS. To this end, metabotropic glutamate receptor drugs, known to be beneficial in FXS, and kainate-type receptor drugs will be tested alone or in combination to determine if they can correct the known and proposed deficits associated with FXS in cerebellum Purkinje cells.

TitreApplicationTitle: Screening for Novel NS5B-Inhibitors: Toward Selective and Potent Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Therapy.
Keywords-MotsClés: VIROLOGY; VIRTUAL SCREENING
Abstract-Résumé: Over 170 million people are living with persistent hepatitis C (HCV) infection in the world, with about 300,000 infected people in Canada alone. No vaccine or potent, well-tolerated drugs are available despite 23 years of research since the discovery of the virus and there is still no licensed drug that specifically targets the HCV polymerase. Current standard therapy often fails, has very substantial side effects and is very expensive. Our proposal aims at using new computer based methods to develop potent and more tolerable drugs to stop the replication of HCV. Our goal is to inhibit the activity of the viral enzyme that is responsible for HCV replication. The new methods we intend to use have been proven successful for other drug targets recently. Our proposal combines state-of-the-art computer based modeling approaches with cutting-edge experimental validation protocols. Computer-based methods will allow us to screen in silico a large number of small molecules (~1,000,000) based on their ability to bind and stop the activity of this enzyme. We expect to find approximately 100 molecules (hits) by this computer-based method and then these molecules will be subjected to experimental validation. The proposed experimental validation is very specific and is three stages. During the first stage, all small molecules will be tested for their ability to stop HCV replication and for their toxicity to cells. During the second stage, further analysis of toxicity factors related to possible side effects (e.g. myopathy and severe anemia) will be performed. Finally, efficacy of the promising molecules will be tested using a humanized mouse model in which human liver is infected with HCV. Active compounds will then be modified using the initial computational approach, serving as seeds for an optimized collection of small molecules with improved binding abilities to the enzyme. The ultimate goal of our proposal is to develop a rationally designed new class of HCV drugs.

Keywords-MotsClés: & IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; ANIMAL MODELS & THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTION; AUTOIMMUNE HEPATITIS & PATHOGENESIS; CELL CULTURES; CELLULAR IMMUNOLOGY & FLOW CYTOMETRY; CHEMOKINES & RECEPTORS; CYTOKINES; DNA/RNA PURIFICATION & RT-PCR; GASTEROENTEROLOGY & HEPATOLOGY; IMMUNOSTAINING; LIVER BIOPSY; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; PRIMARY BILIARY CIRRHOSIS; PRIMARY SCLEROSING CHOLANGITIS; SEROLOGICAL DIAGNOSTICS BIOMARKERS
Abstract-Résumé: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC), and autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) are three common chronic inflammatory liver diseases (combined prevalence of ~1/1000) that account for a significant number of liver transplantations in North America (PSC is within the top five diseases requiring liver transplantation). The diagnosis of these conditions is suboptimal, invasive and expensive. Furthermore, in the majority of cases, significant liver injury has already occurred by the time of a confirmed diagnosis. In our initial study involving 313 individuals, we have recently identified a novel set of serum markers in patient blood samples that could improve diagnosis substantially. In the current proposal, we will attempt to confirm our serum-based tests using a larger patient cohort derived from national and international patients and investigate the role of these immune markers in the underlying mechanism of disease. Our overall goal is to identify better methods to diagnose such patients and from a better understanding of the mechanism of disease to identify new therapeutic avenues.

TitreApplicationTitle: Longitudinal analysis of immune quiescence and impact of commercial sex work in HIV Exposed Seronegative(HESN) sex workers from Nairobi, Kenya
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES/CHEMOKINES; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HIV; HIV EXPOSED SERONEGATIVE INDIVIDUALS (HESN); IMPACT OF SEX WORK; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; PBMC/ CERVICAL MONONUCLEAR CELLS; REGULATORY T CELL; RESISTANT COMMERCIAL SEX WORKERS; T CELL ACTIVATION MARKERS
Abstract-Résumé: There are 2.6 million new HIV infections every year, more than half of them among women. Finding new strategies to develop HIV-preventive tools, such as vaccine or microbicides, remain our best chance to control the pandemic. Studying individuals who remain seronegative despite multiple exposures to HIV will shed light on what are the natural mechanisms involved in protection against HIV infection. Such individuals have been identified in the Pumwani Sex Worker Cohort from Nairobi, Kenya. Previous studies have provided strong evidence that commercial sex workers who remained uninfected present lower activation of their immune system compared to their counterparts who are susceptible to HIV infection. Our initial findings suggest that having an immune system that is less prone to becoming activated following exposure to stimulants contained in clients semen may protect against HIV acquisition. What factors contribute to that sate and how HIV exposed seronegative sex workers can control immune activation remained to be determined. Preliminary data demonstrated that interruption in sex work affects immune activation level. Women who remained uninfected maintain a state of low immune activation in the female genital tract and, therefore, have fewer targets compared to their counterparts. To identify what are the drivers of that low immune activation protective against HIV acquisition and how sex work influence these factors, a synchronized longitudinal analysis study is currently implemented within the Pumwani Cohort. This study will observe women before, during and following work interruption and measure many immune parameters in their genital tract but also in their blood. We think that HIV resistant women can evolve active regulation mechanisms that control the levels of immune activation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining and promoting health behavior adherence among HIV positive smokers.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHERENCE; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; HIV/AIDS; SMOKING CESSATION
Abstract-Résumé: Rates of smoking in patients living with HIV/AIDS (PHAs) are greater than that of the general Canadian population and they continue to increase. As well, cardiovascular disease (CVD) rates are alarmingly increasing in PHAs. Given the large percentage of PHAs who smoke, this is a critical health care issue and research suggests that smoking is the strongest predictor for new cases of CVD in PHAs. Few effective smoking cessation programs have been developed for PHAs and one of the largest problems faced by smokers is staying quit. Current smoking status is also an important and strong predictor of adherence to highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), a crucial facet of care of PHA. Current smokers' adherence rates to HAART are lower than their non- or ex-smoker counterparts. Taken together, this suggests that smoking cessation and its relationship to adherence to HAART are important health behaviours in PHAs. This study will evaluate the success of a tailored quit smoking intervention for PHA. By comparing the quit smoking intervention and pharmaceutical assistance to quit smoking to pharmaceutical interventions only we will evaluate the importance and success of our psychological intervention. Success will be defined as adherence to health behaviours (a) the quit smoking pharmacotherapy, (b) abstinence from smoking and (c) adherence to HAART regimens. My hypotheses are as follows: 1) PHA receiving pharmacotherapy as well as a smoking cessation counseling program (targeting depression) will have higher rates of smoking abstinence than those receiving smoking cessation pharmacotherapy alone, (2) Adherence to HAART will be highest in those that remain quit vs. current or reduced smokers. This study will inform researchers and clinicians of the importance of smoking cessation in PHA and will provide a better understanding of the challenges (ie., depression) and benefits (increased HAART adherence, decreased risk of CVD) associated with smoking cessation in PHA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Source of and policy responses to HIV/AIDS gender inequality in Sub-Saharan Africa
Keywords-MotsClés: AN EXTENSION OF THE BLINDER-OAXACA EFFECT DECOMPOSITION; DELPHI METHOD; HIV/AIDS GENDER INEQUALITIES; MULTILEVEL ANALYSIS; POLICY RESPONSES TO HIV/AIDS INEQUALITY; SOURCE OF HIV/AIDS INEQUALITY
Abstract-Résumé: Sub-Saharan African women are disproportionately at risk for acquiring and having human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Beyond the biological difference between men and women, it is essential to know the sources of gender disparities in HIV/AIDS infection in order to address the HIV epidemic in each country. In an initial study, we found that gender inequalities in HIV infection were attributable to the unequal distribution of risk factors among men and women in Tanzania and to the differential effect of these factors between groups in Kenya and Lesotho. These different patterns may have important implications for policies to reduce gender inequalities in HIV/AIDS across the three countries. This study will identify and understand sources of HIV infection inequality between men and women in 20 sub-Saharan African countries. With this information, additional work will be done to analyze general social and HIV specific policies' impact on gender disparities in HIV/AIDS infections. This knowledge should help understand how policies may be used to reduce HIV/AIDS gender disparities across sub-Saharan African countries. In Canada, women who come from HIV endemic countries continue to be over-represented and disproportionately affected by HIV/AIDS; they represent more than half (54.2%) of the positive HIV test reports attributed to women. Knowing the causes of gender disparity in HIV infection and the effectiveness of public policies for ameliorating those differences in countries where HIV is endemic could provide important, cost-effective public health benefits for recipient countries such as Canada. Reducing the extent of HIV/AIDS in low-resource, HIV endemic countries, in addition to contributing to global good, could reduce the stress on resources and Canada's health care system due to HIV/AIDS

TitreApplicationTitle: Linking social and basic sciences to understand stress as a social indicator for the lived experiences of Aboriginal women and a biological indicator for the physiological impact of stress on HIV pathogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL WOMEN; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; EMOTIONAL AND SPIRITUAL WELL-BEING; GENDER; HIV; HIV PREVENTION; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOGY; MENTAL; MIXED METHODS RESEARCH; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal women are overrepresented in the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Canada. Among Aboriginal people testing HIV positive during 1998-2008, 48.8% were women compared to 20.7% of women among non-Aboriginal people. Aboriginal women are disproportionately affected by HIV risk factors such as poverty, violence, gender inequity, drug use, housing instability and discrimination. These social determinants of health have an impact on one's well-being. There is a need for addressing the impact of HIV on the mental, spiritual and emotional well-being in Aboriginal Women using culturally-appropriate methods. Research to date has focused on the impact of HIV on physical well-being missing the holistic approach deemed critical in Aboriginal culture. The overall aim of this project is to develop a national stress-reducing therapeutic intervention for Aboriginal Women living with and at risk of HIV infection framed within Aboriginal perspectives with an interdisciplinary research team of Aboriginal Women living with HIV, representatives of Aboriginal AIDS Service Organizations, Aboriginal service providers and researchers and allied researchers. This project will take place in Ontario, Canada, has two phases, and will follow an indigenous methodology. The objectives of phase one are 1) to characterize stress in the lives of Aboriginal women living with and at risk of HIV infection and to discuss 2) stress management approaches and 3) the feasibility of measuring stress levels using questionnaires and proteins in the saliva. During phase two, the objectives are to develop and implement a pilot study of the intervention and the stress measurement study. The findings will inform the development of a national stress-reducing therapeutic intervention for Aboriginal Women living with and at risk of HIV infection framed within Aboriginal perspectives to improve well-being and the acceptability of using biological markers of stress in the saliva and questionnaires to measure stress levels.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cultural determinants of Aboriginal youth health: Translating Indigenous knowledge into quantitative outcomes using the cultural consensus and cultural consonance models
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES HEALTH; ABORIGINAL YOUTH; CULTURAL CONSENSUS; CULTURAL CONSONANCE; FREE LISTING; INDIGENOUS METHODS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTIVARIATE STATISTICS; QUANTITATIVE METHODOLOGIES; SOCIAL AND CULTURAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The health status of Aboriginal peoples remains significantly lower than that of other Canadians. Aboriginal youth are at considerably higher risk in regard to tobacco, alcohol, and drug consumption, risky sexual behaviors, physical inactivity, depression, and suicide. The majority of the research conducted on the health of Aboriginal youth has not included culture as a determining factor of health outcomes. Quantitative research in Aboriginal youth health is also lacking, resulting in reduced possibilities for comparison and generalization of results. These research gaps have an adverse effect on the delivery of health care to Aboriginal youth and ultimately in the overall improvement of their health status. Presently there is great need for Aboriginal youth health research that not only incorporates Indigenous knowledge and recognizes Aboriginal culture as an important determinant of health, but that also employs quantitative methodologies that allow for reliable comparisons between populations, and for extrapolation of results beyond the people surveyed. The proposed research will be part of a Canadian Institute of Health Research-funded research program and will collect data from eleven Aboriginal communities in rural Saskatchewan in order to measure the impact of culture on the health behaviors of Aboriginal youth. It will use sophisticated methods of data collection and analysis that: 1) allow Aboriginal youth to define and explain their culture, in their own terms; and 2) measure the impact that said culture has on their health behavior. This research project will make a significant contribution to the field of Aboriginal youth health, through the use of quantitative methodologies and through the translation of Indigenous knowledge into quantitative health outcomes, which will increase the effectiveness of future knowledge translation efforts, policy formulation initiatives, and health interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Interaction of Microbial Pathogens and the Intestinal Epithelial Lining: Contributions of Inflammatory Cell Death and Barrier Disruption to Inflammatory Bowel Diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL PATHOGEN-CELL INTERACTION; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; CYTOKINE ANALYSIS; EPITHELIAL CELL SHEDDING; FLOW CYTOMETRY; INFLAMMASOMES; PERMEABILITY DYSRUPTION; PYROPTOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Our gut is comprised of a complex society inhabited by bacteria. In this world within a world, there are ten bacteria for every human cell in our body. The relationship we have with bacteria is a symbiotic one; we need the digestive machinery of the bacteria as much as it needs our daily intake of food. In healthy individuals, the intestinal tract separates the bacteria from our body with a layer of cells which are tightly bound to one another. If the cell barrier is damaged, it would cause inflammation (an increase in our body's defense which also damages healthy tissue and organs). Frequent inflammation causes a vicious cycle of damage called Inflammatory Bowel Disease. The disease can cause a loss in weight, diarrhea, and patients are at a higher risk for colon cancer, and surgery.   Our laboratory has discovered that intestinal cells can interact with harmful bacteria, then die and shed from the lining (in other words a selfless suicide to save the others). This cell shedding disturbs the intestinal barrier. We have found that a released bacterial toxin and another protein can disrupt the barrier and cause cell death. We have also used an inhibitor that can promote barrier strength. By identifying bacterial proteins which can cause cell death and methods to inhibit it, we can reduce the inflammation in the intestine and lower patient visits and possibly cases of surgeries.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of autophagy in inflammatory bowel disease-associated colon cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; CANCER; GUT MICROBIOME; INFLAMMATION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; MOUSE MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Canada has amongst the highest rates of inflammatory bowel disease in the world. Inflammatory bowel disease is a condition affecting the intestine that results in damage to the bowel causing debilitating symptoms including pain, diarrhea and bleeding. Individuals with inflammatory bowel disease have an increased risk of developing cancer, which correlates with the length of time they have disease. In fact doctors recommend that people with inflammatory bowel disease should undergo once or twice yearly colonoscopies to screen for cancer. We don't know why people with inflammatory bowel disease get cancer. Recent studies suggest that changes in the microbes in the gut are involved in both inflammatory bowel disease and colon cancer. We think that this could be due to defects in a process called autophagy. Autophagy is a cell recycling system that is also important in getting rid of bacteria in our cells. In addition, studies in animals and humans suggest that autophagy can help to prevent cancer from developing. Our research will test the idea that autophagy causes changes in microbes in the gut and increases the chance of getting colon cancer when you have inflammatory bowel disease. We will cause inflammatory bowel disease in normal mice and in mice that don't have autophagy in their intestine. We will also give them a drug to increase the development of colon cancer. We will determine if the mice without autophagy have different microbes in their gut and if they get more severe cancer earlier. If we determine this pathway is involved then this will open the door for new treatments for colon cancer that specifically affect this pathway.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL BEHAVIOR (SPONTANEOUS PAIN); DEXTRAN SULFATE SODIUM (DSS)-INDUCED COLITIS; DORSAL ROOT GANGLION; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INFLAMMATORY AND NEUROGENIC PAIN; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; PERIPHERAL AND CENTRAL SENSITIZATION; QUANTITATIVE PCR; TRANSIENT RECEPTOR VANILLOID 1; VISCERAL HYPERSENSITIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), including ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, affects more than 200,000 Canadians. This chronic disease of the gastrointestinal tract is associated with severe abdominal pain, which in some cases can persist throughout remission phases of the disease. Beyond its economic impact (estimated to more than one billion annually), IBD significantly decrease the quality of life of both patients and their families. Despite recent advances in our understanding of the mechanisms regulating pain sensation, the efficacy of therapeutic approaches in the treatment of chronic pain symptoms remains variable and clinical improvement modest. The research outlined in the present application focuses on understanding the mechanisms involved in nerve sensitization and pain following colonic inflammation. We hypothesize that, by interfering with these processes, we will be able to reduce chronic pain associated with inflammatory conditions such as IBD. We believe that the results from this study could contribute to the development of novel therapeutics for the treatment of chronic pain in IBD patinets.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of Hydrogen sulfide on Pathogenic Disruptions of Microbiota Biofilms: Therapeutic Potential in Inflammatory Bowel Disease ?
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIA BIOFILMS; DRUG DEVELOPMENT; HYDROGEN SULFIDE; INFLAMMATION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INNATE IMMUNITY; MICE MODELS OF INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; RESOLUTION OF INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: The treatment of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) represents a major medical challenge. Clinical observations implicate bacteria in IBD while antibiotics efficacy is controversial. For survival success, species of intestinal bacteria live in close relationships with other species in a glue-like substance to anchor in tissue. Those communities of bacteria sharing the same physical environment are named biofilms. Within those biofilms shelter, the population of bacteria is likely to enhanced resistance to antibiotics. This is probably why the use of antibiotics to treat IBD patients is inconsistent. The hydrogen sulfide is a gas known for his offensive rotten egg odor. It has useful role in some important functions of the gut. Recent preliminary studies have shown that hydrogen sulfide could modify the formation of a biofilm composed by a single species of human pathogenic bacteria.  We propose that hydrogen sulfide could disrupt biofilms that contribute to IBD, thereby exerting protective effects.  We will focus on human multispecies pathogenic biofilms collected from IBD patients of Foothills Medical Centre of Calgary, Alberta. First, we will evaluate if those biofilms could lead to a gut inflammation in recipient mice. Then, we will expose biofilms to hydrogen sulfide. In those experiments, the microbial composition and structure of biofilms will be performed using advanced techniques of microbial cultures, genetics and microscopy. Eventually, we will evaluate the therapeutic potential of using hydrogen sulfide to treat colitis in mice that received pathogenic biofilms.  This proposal could provide further evidence that hydrogen sulfide can serve as the basis for an effective treatment of IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of endogenous opioids and chronic stress in the expression of pain in IBD
Keywords-MotsClés: DORSAL ROOT GANGLIA; ENDOGENOUS OPIOIDS; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; NOCICEPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Abdominal pain is a major cause of distress in patients suffering from inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Previous research has demonstrated that acute IBD flares are associated with increased abdominal pain, while patients with long-term IBD have a much higher pain threshold, suggesting a balance between factors that signal increased pain vs. dampen pain sensation. In both animal models of IBD as well as from tissues of patients with chronic ulcerative colitis, there is early evidence that endogenous opioids, the body's own class of morphine-like substances, are released from inflammatory cells to dampen pain sensation to spinal cord neurons which supply the gut.  Stress hormones may disrupt the pain-relieving effects of endogenous opioids. The goal of our research is to study the interaction between endogenous opioids and stress on spinal cord neurons which supply the gut and sense pain. We will examine this in both an animal model of IBD and in colonic tissues from patients with IBD flares and chronic disease.   Our research may have a broad impact on the health of patients suffering from IBD as it will give us greater understanding into how abdominal pain is sensed and the role of stress in pain sensation. This may in turn lead to new medications for pain control which will apply not only to patients with IBD, but also to patients suffering with irritable bowel syndrome.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms of Intestinal Inflammation Following Ileal Resection for Crohn's Disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: CROHN'S DISEASE; ILEAL RESECTION; INFLAMMATION; MICROBIOME; POSTOPERATIVE RECURRENCE; TAXONOMIC PROFILE
Abstract-Résumé: Crohn's disease (CD) is a lifelong inflammatory condition affecting the gastrointestinal tract. The cause of which is not fully understood. While it is a relatively uncommon disease the rates of inflammatory bowel disease; an umbrella term for CD and Ulcerative colitis, are on the rise.  It is estimated that more than 200 per 100,000 people in North America and Europe are affected. Canada has the highest reported incidence and prevalence rates for CD. CD is commonly first diagnosed in persons in their teens and early adulthood, affecting them during their most economically and educationally productive years. Up to 80% of persons with CD will undergo some form of intestinal surgery throughout their disease course. Unfortunately the relief from symptoms afforded by surgery is often temporary and the disease recurs in most.  We plan to study the factors which lead to an earlier recurrence of CD after surgery. This will help to better understand the cause of this disease and to help predict which people are more likely to develop a recurrence of their disease at a short interval.  To do this we will invite people undergoing a surgical resection of their small bowel for CD to take part in the study. After gaining their informed consent we will perform colonoscopies, a camera test, to examine the large and small bowel of these subjects at 3-6 months after surgery and then again at 15-18 months. At this time we will take tiny pieces of tissue from the lining of the bowel for analysis, as well as drawing blood samples. The samples taken will be analysed to see if we can identify patterns of bacteria in the bowel, normal people have 10's of 1000's of bacteria in their bowel, which predispose to an early recurrence of CD after surgery.  Ultimately we hope this research will aid us in our understanding of what causes CD and help us customise our treatment of persons who have undergone surgery for their CD, by tailoring treatment to their personal risk of recurrence.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of Nod2 and TLR2 signaling on the modulation of T cell function in colitis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL EXPERIMENTATION; CELL CULTURE-HISTOLOGY; GUT; IMMUNOLOGY; INFECTIOLOGY; INFLAMMATION; MOUSE-PIG; QPCR; T CELLS-EPITHELIAL CELLS; WESTERN BLOT-ELISA
Abstract-Résumé: Controlled interactions between the intestinal immune system and commensal bacteria result in a low level of inflammation. In diseases such as inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), an abnormal immune response towards commensal bacteria contributes to the mucosal inflammation. Indeed, Crohn's disease (CD) is characterized by an altered activation of T cells which produce inflammatory cytokines and contribute to intestinal inflammation and mucosal barrier destruction. Recent data suggests that bacterial products stimulate innate pattern recognition receptors (PPRs) e.g. TLRs and NLRs on T cells and directly regulate T cell function. Given that mutations in the NOD2 gene are linked to susceptibility to CD, innate modulation of T cell phenotype, function and survival may be important for homeostasis and maintenance of an "appropriate" immune responses against commensal bacteria. Defects in this response may lead to increased susceptibility to auto-inflammatory reactions and colitis. We hypothesize that Nod2 and TLR2 signaling cooperate to regulate T cell function in the maintenance of homeostasis. Our preliminary data confirm that TLR2 stimulation modulates T cell phenotype and cytokine secretion and that Nod2 stimulation increases NF-kB activation and MAPK phosphorylation in T cells. Therefore we propose to use normal mice and mice with specific mutations in T cell (conditional knockout) to study Nod2 and TLR2 control of T cell function. Specific Aims will be to define:  1. The signaling pathways modulated by Nod2 and TLR2 stimulation in T cells  2. The interaction of Nod2 and TLR2 stimulation on T cell signaling responses 3. The role of T cell expressed-Nod2 and TLR2 in the induction and the regulation of colitis  This study will identify important interactions between signaling pathways in the control of T cell responses to commensal bacteria and will identify signaling molecules that can serve as targets for development of novel therapies for patients with IBD

TitreApplicationTitle: The Translation of Pre-Clinical to Clinical Research: A Study of Publication Bias.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; CLINICAL TRIALS; ETHICS; POLICY; PRE-CLINICAL RESEARCH; PUBLICATION BIAS; REPORTING BIAS; TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: The goal of health research is to understand the causes and ultimately develop treatments for human disease. The foundation of health research for humans rests with animal research and the reporting of animal research is an essential part of the health research system. Recent research has found the quality of reporting of biomedical animal experiments to be poor, and evidence of publication bias has been found with the growth of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of animal experiments. If animal research is not reported correctly or reported at all, then the scientific and ethical integrity of human health research are jeopardized.  Although criticisms of reporting biases are not new, there is growing evidence that it undermines the ability of animal models to reliably inform us about clinical interventions. For instance, Sena and colleagues examined systematic reviews of animal models for acute ischaemic stroke and found statistical evidence that publication bias caused an exaggerated estimate of effect for treatment of 30%. There are economic costs from publication bias in animal research such as bringing falsely positive treatments to clinical trials, and incorrect reporting or failure to report research findings cannot justify such waste. There are also ethical costs to volunteers in clinical trials and patients awaiting treatments who depend on a health research system that protects them and ensures their welfare is based on sound science, not biased reporting. Similarly, the ethical use of animals in research requires that their use not be wasted due to biases.  This application is to conduct the first direct assessment of publication biases of biomedical animal research.

TitreApplicationTitle: A correlative study of melanoma tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and response to vemurafenib
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; METASTATIC MELANOMA; T-CELL RESPONSES BEFORE AND AFTER VEMURAFINIB TREATMENT; TISSUE BIOPSIES; TUMOR INFILTRATING LYMPHOCYTES
Abstract-Résumé: The incidence of melanoma in North America is rising. In 2011 alone, 75,000 cases will have been newly diagnosed and 14,000 will have died. Metastatic melanoma has a very poor prognosis with less than 5 year survival.  Recently, ipimulimab, a CTLA-4 inhibitor which modulates patients' immune response, and vemurafenib, which targets melanoma cells with the BRAF mutation, have improved survival in metastatic melanoma patients. However, almost all patients will eventually develop resistance to these drugs and better treatment strategies are needed to overcome the limitations of current therapeutic approaches.  T lymphocytes are crucial in mounting anti-tumour immune responses. Therapies which increase T-cell responses such as CTLA-4 inhibitors and adoptive T cell therapy whereby T lymphocytes are isolated from a patient and expanded in ex vivo culture and reinfused into the same patient have produced long lasting tumour control in 20% of patients. Evaluation of tumour tissues has also suggested that increase in number of "tumour infiltrating lymphocytes" (TILs) after treatment with ipimulimab correlated with patients' clinical response. The role of TILs in patients receiving BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib, however, has not been widely studied and it is unknown how critical the immune response is for patients to respond to vemurafenib.  Studying TILs in the tumour microenvironment in vemurafenib treated patients may uncover the underlying immune mechanisms which modulates response and resistance to BRAF inhibition and also shed light on new therapeutic strategies that may be used to optimize current treatment paradigm. The proposed study is novel and unique in seeking to characterize TILs (phenotypic subtypes and function) in paired tumour tissues obtained before and after vemurafenib treatment in sufficient number of patients to gain enough data on TILs to inform future studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Large Scale Isolation of Malignant Melanoma Circulating Tumor Cells for Functional and Molecular Characterization and for Testing Drug Sensitivity
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL MARKERS; CELL SORTING; CIRCULATING TUMOR CELLS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENE MICROARRAY; MELANOMA; THERAPY RESISTANCE
Abstract-Résumé: The major challenge in cancer therapy is to stop its progression to more advanced stages (metastasis) where the disease becomes resistant to most forms of therapeutic interventions. Understanding the mechanisms leading to metastasis is only beginning to emerge and is key to develop specific therapeutic interventions. Another complicating factor in cancer therapy is the diversity of cancer cells within a tumor, also called heterogeneity, that makes it difficult to optimize therapeutic regimen in individual patients, also referred to as personalized medicine. Recent advances have uncovered novel ways to diagnose, follow and potentially treat cancer using a unique therapeutic target known as circulating tumors cells (CTCs). These cells are shed from the primary tumor or its metastatic sites and recapitulate many of the features of tumor heterogeneity. Importantly, CTCs number follow closely the progression or regression of the disease making them ideal candidates for developing personalized therapeutic regimens. However, CTCs circulate in very low number making it difficult to study them using standard blood test procedures. Recently, we have developed a novel approach to isolate CTCs in large numbers from a series of breast cancer patients by a procedure called aphaeresis. Furthermore, we have banked these live cells at ultra-low temperature and we are studying them in detail. We plan to apply the same procedure to melanoma patients where we intend to identify unique CTC markers that can aid us in predicting the course of the disease. Also, we will test the CTCs response to a variety of chemotherapeutic agents in view of developing personalized therapeutic regimen. Finally, the proposed approach could be applied to a variety of cancer types in the near future.
