TitreApplicationTitle: The relationship between muscle mass, density and size to functional measures in pre- and post-menopausal women
Keywords-MotsClés: FALLS RISK; FUNCTIONAL CAPACITY; HIGH RESOLUTION COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; MUSCLE CROSS-SECTIONAL AREA; MUSCLE DENSITY; MUSCULOSKELETAL HEALTH; PERIPHERAL QUANTITATIVE COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMEN; SACROPENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Healthy skeletal muscle plays a key role in activities of daily living and is essential for maintaining posture, balance and bone health. Studies have demonstrated an association between age-related loss of muscle mass and strength (sarcopenia) and adverse clinical outcomes in older populations such as falls, fractures, subsequent mobility limitations and hospitalizations. Sarcopenia is becoming a major public health concern and is costly to the Canadian health care system. Women, in particular, experience an accelerated loss of muscle mass and function around the time of menopause. However, currently there is no established protocol for assessing sarcopenia and its related functional disability, in part due to the lack of a simple standardized measure of muscle loss over time. Muscle imaging has the potential to play an important role in studies of sarcopenia. The proposed study will use two novel muscle imaging techniques to determine the best measures of muscle size and density, and how they relate to functional ability and falls risk in healthy pre- and postmenopausal women, as well as in those with recurrent falls and are at risk for fractures. The knowledge gained from this study will help us to better understand sarcopenia and its predictors. This knowledge is essential for preventative health initiatives both for identifying individuals who are at higher risk of experiencing a fall (but may not have fallen yet) and for assessing the effectiveness of interventions aimed at decreasing falls risk.

Abstract-Résumé: Studies have documented a higher prevalence of disease caused by Haemophilus influenzae in several Aboriginal populations compared to the general population.  Indeed, recent studies at the Northern Ontario School of Medicine have documented this phenomenon in Aboriginal populations in Northern Ontario.  At this time the basis of an increased susceptibility of Aboriginal individuals to this pathogen are unknown.  One possibility is that Aboriginal individuals do not possess adequate natural antibodies to prevent disease.  We propose to survey the immune status of Aboriginal populations in Northern Ontario.  If a lack of natural antibodies is the basis of the increased disease burden then the development of a vaccine could address the issue.

Abstract-Résumé: This is a multi-country, EcoHealth research program with interdisciplinary components including epidemiology, nutrition, qualitative health research, microbiology, toxicology, and ecology. The general objective of this program is to look at the links between oceanic and human health through the lens of food security. Specifically, we examine how fishery decline and the contamination of marine food sources with heavy metals and other pollutants influence human health in small coastal communities. This research will contribute to our understanding of how upscale environmental processes impact population health and what can be done to mitigate the negative impacts of such processes. The postdoctoral fellow, with the support of her mentor-Dr. Eric Dewailly- and his research teams in Nunavik and the Caribbean, will help to develop, lead, and expand the research initiative described in this application. This project is linked to other projects in Nunavik and the Caribbean and will involve both the collecting of new data and the exploiting of pre-existing data sources.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aboriginal Healing from Complex Traumas: Integrating Western and Indigenous Therapies
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; COMPLEX TRAUMAS; HEALING; MENTAL HEALTH; PSYCHOLOGICAL ASSESSMENT; PSYCHOLOGY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH INTERVIEWS; SURVEY; TRADITIONAL INDIGENOUS HEALING; TRAUMA-INFORMED THERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Complex traumas and their mental health sequelae represent contemporary areas of significant concern for Aboriginal peoples, especially with respect to rates of abuse, intimate partner violence, addictions and mental health issues. Mental health outcomes for Aboriginal peoples who have experienced complex traumas, often rooted in historical and intergenerational traumas, have been well outlined in the psychology literature. Many Aboriginal people seeking counselling for issues stemming from complex traumas struggle with a multitude of social, emotional, cognitive and physical health difficulties. Findings from my PhD dissertation with Anishnawbe Health Toronto (an Aboriginal health agency) found that mental health therapies must first be 'Culture-Informed' (culturally competent and contextualized within an understanding of historical factors affecting Aboriginal communities), and they must also be 'Trauma-Informed' (they must address the social, emotional cognitive impairments that have been found to be strongly related to complex traumas). The present research project, also created as a community-based partnership with Anishnawbe Health Toronto, extends from these dissertation findings to explore therapeutic application of these principles of trauma-informed and culture-informed mental health service to therapy. This project will implement and evaluate a culture-based psychotherapy group for addressing trauma in the lives of Aboriginal peoples and will combine Western and Indigenous healing principles. Evaluation of this protocol will inform mainstream health practice, health policy, and the psychological literature on Aboriginal mental health and healing interventions for trauma that are empirically successful at the community level.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Spinal Stenosis Pedometer and Nutrition e-Health Lifestyle Intervention (SSPANLI) Randomized Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION; E-HEALTH; LUMBAR SPINAL STENOSIS; MOBILITY; NUTRITION; OBESITY; PEDOMETER; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; WEIGHT LOSS
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is one of the most important determinants of quality of life and function. People with spinal stenosis may be at increased risk of obesity given walking limitations. Spinal stenosis is a common degenerative condition in people over 45. People with this condition have pain and numbness in the legs during walking, and therefore avoid physical activity. Lack of physical activity is related to weight gain and increased risk of chronic disease. Objective: The objective of this project is test a new e-health (online) pedometer and nutrition intervention aimed at promoting weight loss and increasing physical activity in overweight and obese individuals with spinal stenosis. Methods:  We will recruit 106 people with lumbar spinal stenosis who are overweight or obese. Half of these people will receive the 12-week intervention, and the other half will receive usual care (no intervention). In Weeks 1 and 6, people in the intervention group will meet with a Registered Dietitian and an Exercise Physiologist for personalized sessions. They will receive a pedometer and instructions on how to log in to the e-health site (https://sspanli.mtroyal.ca). They will wear the pedometer daily and log in to the website each week for a nutrition education session, a weekly step goal, and tips. We will look to see whether people in the intervention group show greater change in physical activity, body composition and quality of life compared to the individuals who received usual care. Relevance: The increasing number of people with spinal stenosis represents a huge health care burden in Canada. This intervention could provide a new treatment option that would increase mobility, quality of life, and potentially alleviate the need for expensive treatments like surgery. E-health interventions provide an opportunity for patients to take an active role in their own health, and promote behaviour changes that will result in healthier Canadians less likely to access care in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: First Nations Elders Living with Memory Loss: Family Perspectives on Elder Health Care on Vancouver Island.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; DEMENTIA; FIRST NATIONS HEALTH; FIRST NATIONS STORYTELLING  METHODOLOGY; QUALITATIVE; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The frequency of dementia in North America has grown rapidly in the past couple decades.  While the incidence of cognitive impairment is on the rise in Canada there have been few studies done to increase helath care provider knowledge on the issues that First Nations Elders and their families confront when Elders experience memory loss.  A limited number of epidemiological and exploratory studies have been conducted with Indigenous North American people to garner a greater understanding of the dementia risks, frequency and family care giving in Indigenous populations.  It has been determined that First Nations people face a greater likelihood of   low socio-economic status, diabetes, poverty and obesity.  All of these circumstances increase the risk of developing dementia in later life. Conclusions from some recent studies suggest that there is a need for cultural sensitivity within all professional levels the health care system. Research in the area of Elder brain health and family caring systems is critical in ensuring culturally safe health care practices and resources, for future aging First Nations populations and their caregivers. This proposed study will utilize a qualitative Indigenous storytelling methodology to explore how families in Coast Salish communities on Vancouver Island cope when their family members are diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, as well as the support systems available for families when Elder family members experience dementia.   The findings of this research will inform health care professionals and future health care policies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Where Do I Get Porcupine Quills? An Exploration of Winter Counts as First Nations Ways of Knowing for Youth
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; CULTURE; FIRST NATIONS; HEALTH; ORAL METHODOLOGIES; VISUAL METHODOLOGIES; WAYS OF KNOWING; WINTER COUNT; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: The research will explore the utilization of traditional Dakota "winter counts" as First Nations ways of knowing and sharing their knowledge. It is important to understand what health means to First Nations youth and how these youth come to understand health. Approximately half of the First Nations population in Saskatchewan is under 19 years of age. First Nations youth are at high risk for developing long-term health related problems, being hospitalized, being incarcerated, committing suicide, and becoming infected with HIV. Past health research and health systems efforts have focused on Western knowledge in the effort to reduce the individual's risks and to reduce costs to the health care system. The time has come to reconsider how we engage First Nations youth in learning about their meaning of health and ways of knowing from a First Nations lens. Oral and visual methods such as winter counts may lead to improved health individually and collectively through better health policies, more effective research, and perhaps creative health delivery models. This research will involve be open to mutual capacity building and co-research in the pursuit of meaningful and innovative approaches to understanding and achieving health for First Nations youth.

Abstract-Résumé: Lay Abstract: For decades now social and cultural determinants of health-focused research has pointed to race and ethnicity as key determinants. Yet race and ethnicity require further consideration in the health studies , and for its implications for applied research. This project aims to understand how these determinants of health, in relation to others, shape the sexual health (and vulnerability to HIV) of people who engage in interracial and interethnic intimate relationships in Winnipeg. This research will utilize an anthropological approach through the analysis of sexual health discourses circulating in the city, through spatial mapping of social relationships, and through in-depth interviews with key informants and people engaged in interracial intimate relationships. This study will contribute to the increased body of literature on health disparities by providing important insight into how  complex forms of racial inequality take shape in the interracial relationships   occurring between  two marginalized populations in Winnipeg.

TitreApplicationTitle: Perception of Pain among Aboriginal Individuals: Perspectives of Patients and Care Providers
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; CHRONIC PAIN; COPING AND WELLBEING; PAIN EXPRESSION; PAIN PERCEPTION; QUALITATIVE DATA ANALYSIS; QUANTITATIVE DATA ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: One in five Canadians suffer from chronic pain. Epidemiological surveys in Canada indicate the prevalence of chronic pain is higher among Aboriginal (i.e. First-Nation, Metis, Inuit) populations. This is consistent with the broader scientific literature revealing a large disparity in the health of Non-Aboriginal vs. Aboriginal individuals. Research suggests that the way in which people describe their pain may vary by race and ethnicity and that health care providers may react differently to pain reported by patients of varying racial and ethnic characteristics. However, the extent to which these issues contribute to worse pain and pain treatment among Aboriginal peoples remains relatively unexplored.  The first goal of this research is to understand if there is a systematic difference in how Aboriginal vs. non-Aboriginal individuals describe their pain. The second goal is to assess if formal caregivers perceive pain differently in Aboriginal vs. non-Aboriginal individuals. In the first phase, a small sample of Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal chronic pain suffers will be recruited from community health centers to take part in a brief qualitative interview about their pain experience. In the second phase, formal caregivers, nurses, will be recruited to participate in an online study. Participants will be presented with a random selection of medical case history vignettes, created based on the Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal patients recruited in the first phase, and asked to report on the patient's pain intensity. Differences in treatment suggestions based on patient's ethnicity will be assessed. Related factors such as how empathy impacts caregiver's accuracy in pain assessment will be investigated.  If a systematic difference exists in how Aboriginal vs. non-Aboriginal individuals describe their pain or how formal caregivers assess their pain, care for Aboriginal individuals can be improved by increasing Aboriginal cultural competence during professional training.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reducing the signs and symptoms of Huntingtons disease by manipulating endocannabinoid tone.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANNABINOIDS; CELL CULTURE; HUNTINGTON'S DISEASE; PHARMACOLOGY; SUBSTANCE ABUSE/ADDICTION; TRANSGENIC ANIMAL MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: The endocannabinoid system is a system of receptors and enzymes that interact with cannabinoids, molecules that are naturally produced by the body and related to the active ingredient in marijuana, THC, to cause context-specific effects. In the brain, the type 1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1) is activated by cannabinoids. Activation of CB1 inhibits excessive neuronal activity and assists in the creation of neuron-to-neuron connections. For these reasons, CB1 is considered 'neuro-protective'. In humans, expression of CB1 changes with age. For example, brain CB1 expression is higher during adolescence than during adulthood.   Huntingtons disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the inheritance of one copy of the mutant huntingtin gene. There is no cure for HD and no effective treatment to manage the behavioural, cognitive, and motor symptoms of the disease. During the early phases of HD, CB1 expression decreases in the regions of the brain most affected by HD. Because CB1 is neuro-protective and CB1 expression decreases early in HD, it is thought that decreased CB1 contributes to HD and increasing CB1 levels may reduce the severity of HD symptoms.  Our laboratory has demonstrated that cannabinoids increase CB1 levels in cell models of HD and the viability of these cells is consequently improved. Whether this is possible in an animal or a human is not known. In HD, where CB1 receptor expression is decreased, cannabinoid-based therapies could restore expression, and provide neuro-protective benefits. I hypothesize that 1) increasing the expression of CB1 can reduce the signs and symptoms of HD, and 2)cannabinoid levels influence CB1 expression in the brain.   Because brain CB1 levels are higher during adolescence than adulthood, adolescent and adult cannabinoid exposure may have differential effects on CB1 expression. In HD, where CB1 expression declines, cannabinoid-dependent induction of CB1 expression may restore normal brain function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sowing new seeds: The collaborative development and implementation of food policy interventions by public health and civil society
Keywords-MotsClés: CIVIL SOCIETY; FOOD AND NUTRITION; GOVERNANCE; INTERSECTORAL; POPULATION HEALTH; QUALITATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Rising rate of overweight and obesity pose as a major challenge for public health.  It is well accepted that unhealthy diets are one of the major contributors to the overall burden of disease.  Obesity is a complex problem that requires creative and innovative policies that target the environments where people live, work, and play.  Developing policy interventions for complex problems necessitates action from health and non-health sectors, as well as public health and civil society. This research project investigates how local public health units in Ontario, Canada, are collaborating with civil society organizations to develop and implement novel food policy interventions.  Collaborative policymaking raises important questions regarding processes of governance and decision-making that will be addressed by the following research questions: (1) what are the contextual conditions that enable or constrain the collaborative development of food-related policy; (2) what strategies do civil society actors employ to claim space in public health decision-making, and how are those strategies supported or resisted by public health actors; and (3) how do relevant stakeholders in collaborative policy settings define, measure and evaluate outcomes associated with the policy process.    Qualitative key informant interviews and deliberative dialogues will assist in developing recommendations on processes of policy making for complex problems.

TitreApplicationTitle: AMPK Activation for the Treatment of Mitochondrial Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; MITOCHONDRIA; MITOCHONDRIAL DISEASE; MITOPHAGY
Abstract-Résumé: Our body is made up of millions of cells. Each cell requires energy to function and they must convert the nutrients in our diet to ATP, the form of energy each cell uses. In most cells, specialized compartments called mitochondria perform the majority of this conversion. Mitochondria contain much of the genetic information required to create ATP. So if there is a mutation in this genetic information, the mitochondria cannot produce sufficient ATP. Cells will lack the energy to fully operate and devastating disorders, termed mitochondrial diseases, are the result. This proposed research aims to use a drug, AICAR, to therapeutically treat these disorders. AICAR is unique because, by activating AMP-Activated Protein Kinase (AMPK), it can both activate the creation of new mitochondria and breakdown dysfunctional mitochondria. By activating mitochondrial growth and increasing the ratio of mitochondria that can efficiently make energy, the energy production capacity is restored to levels of healthy cells. Breaking down the dysfunctional mitochondria can prevent the proliferation of poor energy producing mitochondria and improve the overall energy producing capacity of each mitochondrion in the cell. This study will use AICAR to treat skin cells from patients who suffer from these disorders. We will then take functional measurements of the cells to look for improvements and, if found, analyze the origin of these improvements. We hypothesize that this will improve the functional capacity of the cells as indicated by their energy producing potential.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving the Cardiovascular Health of Older Adults: is Cardiac Rehabilitation the Answer?
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING PROCESS; CARDIAC REHABILITATION THERAPY; CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; CARDIOVASULCAR DISEASE; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; OLDER ADULTS; QUALITY OF LIFE; SECONDARY PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: The population of Canadian adults 65 years and older is expected to rapidly increase in the next decade. Given the natural trajectory of the aging process, varying degrees of deterioration in the cardiovascular system are anticipated in this population. Currently, older adults represent 85% of Canadian people with established cardiovascular disease (CVD). CVD is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Canada. A well-accepted secondary prevention modality for CVD is cardiac rehabilitation therapy (CR). CR involves interventions such as exercise programs and dietary modification. Currently, older adults are under-represented in the studies dedicated to cardiovascular health, including those investigating the outcomes of CR. The purpose of this study is to: (1) assess the effectiveness of CR in reducing future cardiovascular events in this age group; (2) investigate the contextual factors of the current CR programs that may hinder the participation of older adults in such programs; (3) investigate the impact of CR on the quality-of-life and on the ability of older adults to maintain their autonomy with the healthcare team. The study will focus on BC residents 65 years and older who have presented with a cardiovascular event to one of two major cardiac centers in BC. Using a quantitative research design, groups of individuals who have completed a CR program will be compared to those who have not completed the program with respect to cardiovascular events and mortality. Furthermore, using a qualitative research design, the study will investigate the experiences of older adults with the current CR programs. This study will obtain evidence demonstrating the extent to which CR is beneficial to the older adult population and ways through which current CR programs could be modified to improve their ability to meet the unique needs of the elderly population. This will decrease the health burden of CVD on older adults, their families, and the healthcare system.

TitreApplicationTitle: The invisible patient in the room: Shifting the focus to include support for the health of family caregivers of cancer patients.
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; DESCRIPTIVE QUALITATIVE DESIGN; EXERCISE; HEALTH PROMOTION; MIXED METHOD; OLDER CANCER CAREGIVERS; PHYSICAL AND PSYCHOLOGICAL HEALTH; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: In our current health care system, family members of cancer patients are expected to provide many supports to patients. Nursing care, emotional support, medication management, personal care, and multiple physician visits are carried out by family members. Unfortunately, this increased demand on family caregivers often leads to increased stress, depression, physical health problems, loss of time at work and lost wages. Family caregivers suffer many of the same physical and emotional problems as the patients themselves. These health and emotional needs are often not the focus when patients are seen by health care providers. The ability of our resource poor system to provide support to the family caregivers is also limited. Although there has been some research looking at the problems faced by family caregivers, there is very little research looking at how best to support the physical and emotional health of caregivers. The goal of this research project is to gain a broader understanding of the needs of older family caregivers to cancer patients. Two separate phases of the research project will be completed. In the first phase, data will be collected about the physical health, emotional health, and physical activity levels of older family caregivers to cancer patients. Family caregivers will then be invited to participate in a physical activity program to test whether or not providing physical activity time will help to ease some of the physical and emotional symptoms they are experiencing. The second phase of the research project will involve asking family caregivers questions about their interactions with the health care team. The goal of this second phase is to understand what role health care providers have in supporting family caregivers. Family caregivers to cancer patients are often invisible partners in the health care team. The overall goal of this research is to make the needs of family caregivers more visible and learn about how best to support them

TitreApplicationTitle: Post-Fall Decision Making among Older Women Living in Continuing Care Retirement Communities: A Mixed Methods Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTINUING CARE RETIREMENT COMMUNITIES; DECISION MAKING; FALLS; GERONTOLOGY; HEALTH; HEALTH COMMUNICATION; INDEPENDENCE; OLDER WOMEN; QUALITATIVE METHODS; QUANTITATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Each year, one in three individuals over the age of 65 will experience a fall. Women experience more falls than men and are three times more likely to be hospitalized for a fall-related injury. The incidence of a fall can change how a woman perceives herself and how she maintains her health and independence. These falls can trigger important decision making among older women, yet little is known about the post-fall decision-making processes. This study proposes to examine post-fall decision making among older women living in continuing care retirement communities to better understand: 1) the types of decisions made by older women after they experience a fall; 2) the content and sources of health information involved in the post-fall decision making; and 3) the influence of individual factors, such as the women's preferences regarding care, on the decision-making process. The findings of this study will contribute to a greater understanding of what happens when an older woman experiences a fall and may help improve future fall prevention programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Motivating Delayed Phase Sleep Syndrome Adolescents to Maintain Early Sleep Onset
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENCE; DELAYED PHASE SLEEP SYNDROME (DPSS); DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOLOGY; HEALTH PSYCHOLOGY; MOTIVATIONAL INTERVEWING; PEDIATRIC SLEEP RESEARCH; SLEEP BEHAVIOUR; SLEEP DISORDERS; TREATMENT ADHERENCE; TREATMENT OF SLEEP DISORDERS
Abstract-Résumé: People with Delayed Phase Sleep Syndrome(DPSS) go to sleep later and wake up later than the rest of the population. This disorder is most prevalent in adolescents. Bright Light Therapy (BLT) is a treatment that advances the circadian rhythm. At first, BLT is effective in making adolescents fall asleep earlier but at follow up times of 3 months adolescents often revert back to later sleeping times. I suggest the reason for that is that they are not motivated to go to sleep earlier. To sustain the impact of BLT, the adolescents need to be motivated to go to bed at an earlier time. Motivational interviewing is a client-centered counseling approach aimed at increasing intrinsic motivation by allowing the client to become aware of the problem and setting their own goals to achieve. This would be suitable for adolescents because they tend to not like following orders from authority and in this approach they would be deciding on their own to go to bed earlier. It is hypothesized that in adolescents with DPSS, those who receive motivational interviewing will maintain earlier bedtimes for a longer period of time than those who do not receive MI after their BLT treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fonctionnement du circuit neuronal de la peur chez des jeunes anxieux, des jeunes à risque de développer un trouble anxieux et des jeunes en bonne santé.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETE; CONDITIONNEMENT; DEVELOPPEMENT; EXTINCTION; FAMILLE; IMAGERIE PAR RESONANCE MAGNETIQUE FONCTIONNELLE; JEUNES; POPULATION A RISQUE
Abstract-Résumé: Les enfants de parents atteints d'un trouble anxieux ont jusqu'a dix fois plus de risque de souffrir d'un trouble anxieux que les enfants de parents qui n'ont pas d'historique similaire. De plus, etre victime d'un trouble anxieux durant l'enfance ou l'adolescence est invalidant par l'augmentation de la sensibilite et de l'anticipation des menaces environnantes, en plus d'etre associe a une augmentation des risques de souffrir de troubles anxieux et de depression a l'age adulte. Ceci refleterait des changements a long terme dans certaines structures du cerveau composant le circuit de la peur. Ces structures seraient liees a l'emergence des troubles anxieux et au risque de les developper, soit les amygdales, au milieu du cerveau, et le cortex prefrontal, a l'avant du cerveau. Tres peu d'etudes ont examine ces liens chez les jeunes. Une meilleure comprehension des changements neuronaux encourus chez les jeunes anxieux ou a risque d'anxiete est essentielle et elle permettra de developper des methodes d'intervention aptes a stopper les troubles anxieux avant que ceux-ci ne deviennent chroniques. L'objectif de cette etude est donc de comprendre le fonctionnement du circuit de la peur en lien avec l'anxiete et le risque d'un trouble anxieux chez les jeunes. Pour atteindre notre objectif, trois groupes de 30 jeunes, ages entre 10-17 ans, seront recrutes : (1) des jeunes qui sont presentement atteints d'un trouble anxieux; (2) des jeunes sans trouble anxieux present ou passe, mais a risque eleve d'anxiete par la presence d'un trouble anxieux, present ou passe, chez les parents; (3) des jeunes en bonne sante mentale de parents en bonne sante mentale. Le fonctionnement du circuit de la peur sera evalue a l'aide de taches sur l'apprentissage et l'extinction d'une reponse de peur grace aux technologies d'imagerie par resonance magnetique fonctionnelle (IRMf). Ces taches sont adaptees pour l'IRMf et sont validees aupres de jeunes en bonne sante, a risque d'anxiete et anxieux.

TitreApplicationTitle: The dissemination of clinical practice guidelines to arthritis health professionals using innovative strategies
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES; EVIDENCE BASED PRACTICE; ONLINE SOCIAL NETWORKING; OSTEOARTHRITIS; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: This pilot study will investigate various strategies using the internet to provide arthritis health professionals with up-to-date evidence on osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis self-management strategies. The evidence which will be provided to arthritis is the The Arthritis Society's People Getting a Grip on Arthritis Program (PGrip). PGrip was developed by the Ottawa Panel who have identified and selected effective strategies which arthritis patients can perform themselves to manage and improve their symptoms. Forty-five arthritis health professionals from the Arthritis Health Professions Association (AHPA)will be randomized to one of three different intervention groups: 1) A Facebook group which will have access to the People Getting a Grip on Arthritis program; 2) A PGrip website group in which participants will be provided with a link to the TAS PGrip website; and 3) A group only receiving electronic arthritis educational pamphlets. Knowledge learnt, actual implementation of the self-management strategies, satisfaction with online learning will be measured at 2 weeks and 3 months after the delivery of each group's respective intervention. These measurements will be conducted using online questionnaires.

TitreApplicationTitle: Determining the Role of Biobehavioral Factors in Early Knee Osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; DISABILITY; HEALTH BEHAVIOUR; KNEE; MUSCULOSKELETAL; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PAIN; PHYSICAL ACITIVITY; PRECLINICAL; QUESTIONNAIRES
Abstract-Résumé: This project will integrate human clinical research and animal laboratory research to understand how health behaviours can result in early detection and management of knee osteoarthritis (OA). Health and disease prevention is promoted by positive behaviours, whereas risk behaviours have the opposite effect. The clinical human studies will: (1) determine the validity of a new screening questionnaire for people with early knee OA prior to full clinical diagnosis, (2) determine if the health behavior questionnaire components are related to several biological indicators of early knee OA. One study group will include persons who have consulted their physical therapist about chronic knee pain symptoms with signs of knee OA that may not be confirmed through diagnosis. The second will include only people with confirmed knee OA. A key aspect of the questionnaire is it's identification of how people alter their activity in response to early symptomatic knee OA symptoms. In the animal research, elements of human activity-modifying behaviour will be measured in a rat model. Activity-modifying behaviour is an adjustment or avoidance of certain physical activity. This approach is important because knee OA develops over many years in humans, whereas with our early knee OA rat model the disease develops over a 12 week period. Measuring activity-modifying behaviour in our rat model will identify how knee OA causes progressive disablement.   We expect that in clinical settings, our questionnaire will become an important tool for recognizing early knee OA. This will improve healthcare delivery where clinicians apply therapies to slow the progression and better manage symptoms, thus improving the personal health of Canadians with early knee OA. In addition, defining activity-modifying behaviour in this early knee OA rat model will aid research on drug therapy to cure progressive disablement in humans with early stage knee OA.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discerning the Utility of Cognitive and Behavioural Measures for the Early Detection of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH ENHANCEMENT; COGNITIVE AGING; DEMENTIA; ERP ANALYSIS; SPEECH PERCEPTION AND RECOGNITION; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Communication difficulties are common in Alzheimer's dementia (AD) and in mild cognitive impairment (MCI; an early mental decline stage prior to dementia). These communication difficulties are due to dementia decline's negative effect on working memory, which is our mind's ability to integrate information and perform tasks. Working memory capacity declines in dementia and with this lack of mental resources comes difficulty in perceiving and comprehending speech. A proposed solution to this difficulty is audiovisual (AV) communication: the presentation of facial communication alongside audio. AV communication has been reliably shown to decrease the degree of mental resources required to perceive and comprehend speech, a phenomena known as the AV enhancement effect. Older adults, due to experiencing hearing decline as part of normal aging, become particularly skilled in using visual information to assist in otherwise challenging communication. The proposed study will utilize the AV enhancement effect with MCI and AD populations to determine how much of an improvement in speech perception and recognition is afforded by AV communication. To measure this, participants will be shown sentences that either have grammatical errors or content errors. These sentences are known to tax working memory significantly due to the effort required to perceive and determine the error. These sentences for MCI and AD populations during normal conditions would be highly challenging, but AV enhancement will ideally overcome this difficulty and facilitate communication. The success of this project will lead to a new understanding of how best to facilitate speech perception and recognition in minds with deteriorating mental resources. This information will be used to inform caregivers and other parties on the most effective means to communicate with dementia patients, overall assisting in alleviating the debilitating consequences of mental decline.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive impairments in anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, and the relationship to day hospital treatment outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: ANOREXIA NERVOSA; BULIMIA NERVOSA; CLINICAL PSYCHOLOGY; COGNITION; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENTS; DAY HOSPITAL TREATMENT; EATING DISORDERS; TREATMENT OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: There is research suggesting that people with anorexia have problems with certain types of thinking. For example, they may have difficulty thinking flexibly, in terms of adapting their thinking to suit the changing needs of tasks. They may also have trouble thinking about the big picture, instead focusing on small details. Some researchers have explored whether people with other eating disorders, such as bulimia, have the same types of thinking difficulties, but currently it is not clear whether this is the case. This study investigates the types of thinking problems that people with different types of eating disorders might have, including how they compare to one another and to people without any eating disorder. It is predicted that people with bulimia and a more general eating disorder will also have difficulties in some types of thinking. This study will also look at whether problems with thinking before entering treatment can tell us how people will respond to hospital treatment, and it is predicted that greater impairments will be related to poorer treatment outcomes. Lastly, this study examines whether problems with thinking are improved after regular hospital treatment, and it is predicted that these thinking styles will change moderately after treatment. This study will ask people with eating disorders to complete a number of tasks looking at thinking style. Their results will be compared to people without eating disorders, and will also be examined in relation to treatment outcomes. This will help researchers to better understand what types of problems in thinking people with eating disorders might have, and how this relates to treatment. Because eating disorders require intensive treatment, and because many patients often do not ever fully recover, better understanding may help us to improve treatments for Canadians with eating disorders, as well as to reduce the health care costs associated with eating disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: VITAH Trial - Vitamin D supplementation and cardiac autonomic tone in hemodialysis: A blinded, randomized-controlled trial
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTONOMIC NERVOUS SYSTEM; CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; HEMODIALYSIS; SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic kidney disease affects 13% of the Canadian population, a portion of the public which has now grown to surpass the number of those suffering from diabetes. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in chronic kidney disease patients in Canada and worldwide, despite treatment of traditional risk factors. In humans, heart rate is controlled by stimulatory and inhibitory input from the cardiac autonomic nervous system. Specialized computer software can quantify the level of activity from these two opposing limbs by assessing the beat-to-beat changes in heart rate, termed "heart rate variability," from a typical heart monitor reading. Abnormal heart rate variability, and thus abnormal autonomic nervous system activity, has been identified as a predictor of both cardiovascular and sudden death.   The prevalence of vitamin D deficiency in those suffering from kidney disease is also extremely high. Many studies have shown that poor vitamin D status (either insufficiency or deficiency), kidney dysfunction, and increased risk of cardiovascular disease are associated with one another. Thus, improving low vitamin D levels with supplementation may lead to an improvement in heart rate variability in this population.   For the first time, this blinded, randomized-controlled trial will investigate the impact of vitamin D supplementation on heart rate variability in a population of high-risk hemodialysis patients. Based on our laboratory's previous findings in humans who are healthy and whom have early stages of kidney dysfunction, we hypothesize that oral vitamin D supplementation to will lead to an improvement in heart rate variability parameters, thus indicating an improvement in cardiovascular risk, specifically during the high-risk period following the two day dialysis-free period. These findings would support the role of vitamin D supplementation in reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease and death within the chronic kidney disease population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multimodal imaging of functional networks involved in selective attention in schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: FUNCTIONAL MRI; MAGNETOENCEPHALOGRAPHY; MULTIVARIATE STATISTICS; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is characterized by deficits in the performance of most mental tasks, and these deficits become more pronounced as the difficulty of these tasks increases. One area in which these deficits are consistently found is in selective attention, which involves directing awareness to particular aspects of the external world that require further processing. Although this is a complex cognitive task, it can be subdivided into two phases: deciding which aspects to process, and the implementation of that processing. The goal of this research project is to elucidate the differences in the implementation of selective attention between schizophrenia patients and healthy volunteers. Specifically, the goal is to capitalize on the excellent spatial and temporal resolution of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG), respectively, to investigate the differences in brain activity involved in the implementation of selective attention. The use of multiple methods of brain imaging will allow a more comprehensive analysis of how these differences in activity lead to performance deficits in schizophrenia, and have the potential to lead to the discovery of new treatments and medications targeted to improving cognitive function in schizophrenia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transgender Individuals' Suicidal Ideation: Disclosure to Medical and Mental Health Care Providers
Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS; MENTAL HEALTH; SUICIDE; SUICIDE PREVENTION; THEORY OF REASONED ACTION; TRANSGENDER; TRANSITION-RELATED CARE
Abstract-Résumé: 41% of transgender (TG) individuals report having attempted suicide (Grant et al., 2010). Although this rate is alarming, there is a dearth of literature regarding TG suicide prevention. Many TG individuals require specialized medical and mental health care (LGBT Health Program, 2009), referred to as transition-related care (TRC). It is recommended that all individuals who experience suicidal ideation (SI) seek help from their health care providers (Health Canada, 2009). However, this approach to suicide prevention may prove ineffective with TG individuals if SI is present while TRC is sought; TG individuals may be reluctant to disclose SI out of fear of being denied TRC. The proposed project will examine TG individuals' decisions to disclose SI using the Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA, Ajzen and Fishbein, 1980). TRA postulates that behaviour is determined by the intent to carry the behaviour out, which is determined by one's attitudes, beliefs, and subjective norms surrounding the behaviour. It is hypothesized that attitudes, beliefs, and social norms in which the disclosure of SI is a barrier to receiving TRC will negatively predict intent to disclose, which in turn will negatively predict actual disclosure of SI to care providers. Focus groups of TG individuals will be held in order to generate an accurate compilation of attitudes, beliefs, and social norms regarding disclosure of SI to care providers. Focus group data will then be used to create realistic items for a TRA-based measure. 200 TG participants will be administered the TRA-based questionnaire, a validated questionnaire to assess intent of disclosing SI to health professionals, and a question to assess disclosure to at least one care provider. Results from the proposed study will clarify reasons why TG individuals do not disclose ideation and will have the potential to inform best practices regarding suicide prevention with TG individuals, thus lowering the suicide attempt rate in this population.

TitreApplicationTitle: An examination of distraction use in exposure therapy for anxiety
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; COGNITION; COGNITIVE-BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; DISTRACTION; EXPOSURE THERAPY; INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES; OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER; TREATMENT OUTCOME; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Anxiety disorders are among the most common mental illnesses. The most effective treatment for anxiety disorders is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT); however, treatment refusal and drop-out rates are high. Exposure, an effective component of CBT, involves gradually exposing oneself to a feared stimuli or situation to habituate to symptoms of anxiety. Although exposure is effective, many clients are unwilling to complete exposures, or refuse treatment due to fear of exposures. Thus, improving the acceptability of exposure may increase treatment acceptance and reduce drop-outs. The current study proposes the use of distraction during exposure to make it more acceptable to clients. There have been mixed findings regarding the impact of distraction use on treatment outcome; thus, it is important to evaluate factors may play a role in whether distraction will aid or interfere with exposure. Specifically, the type of distraction strategy used as well as individual factors may impact the utility of distraction during exposure. The proposed studies will examine different types of distraction as well as their relationship to individual differences in typical distraction use. Study 1 will involve the construction and validation of a questionnaire assessing distraction use, including items assessing perceived necessity of these strategies. Study 2 will involve validating how difficult or taxing a number of potential distraction tasks are, and Study 3 will use these tasks in the context of an exposure session. In this third study, 120 participants with contamination fear complete an exposure session with a feared stimulus (e.g., a dirty toilet), and will be assigned to a no distraction control, mild distraction, moderate distraction, or high distraction condition. They will rate their anxiety throughout the task and at a follow-up visit (when exposed to the same stimulus). This study will also investigate individual differences in outcome.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Population Based Perspective of Children and Youth with Brain Tumours in Ontario, Canada: Who Are They and Where Do They Go?
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOURS; CHILDREN AND YOUTH; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH CARE ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; INTERNATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF DISEASE; SURVEILLANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumours are the leading cause of cancer death in children and youth. Currently, there is little detailed population based information on this group of individuals and even fewer on those that have non-cancerous brain tumours. However, it is important to recognize that non-cancerous brain tumours can still cause serious health problems and negative long term effects that may be improved through rehabilitation. Using health care data from Ontario's publicly funded health care system, this study will identify the number and characteristics of children and youth aged 19 years and younger with cancerous and non-cancerous brain tumours and determine where they are discharged to after emergency department visits and acute care admissions. Patients with cancerous and non-cancerous brain tumours will be compared and geographic variation within Ontario also be examined. Surveillance of brain tumours is important for the planning, evaluating, and transforming health care systems to better address the needs of this population and align resources with needs. The candidate will build upon an already established working relationship with knowledge users throughout the project to ensure the data are utilized in planning of health services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pilot Project for the Promotion of Self-management of Chronic Mobility Limitations Among Vulnerable Seniors at the MUHC: Training the New Generation of Canadian Physiotherapists for this Role
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVITY LIMITATIONS; ELDERLY; HEALTH CARE SERVICES; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PAIN; PARTICIPATION RESTRICTION; QUALITY OF LIFE; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL; SELF-MANAGEMENT PROGRAMS; UPPER AND LOWER BODY IMPAIRMENTS
Abstract-Résumé: The population of Quebec is getting older, therefore chronic conditions are increasing. Chronic conditions are the major causes of pain and mobility problems in seniors. Currently, access to physiotherapy services to ease these conditions is difficult, as the waiting times can be greater than three months. While waiting for these services, many patients may get worse. We need to change the method of providing services and promoting health in seniors, especially for those who have just been in the hospital.  This project will test a new method of promoting function by improving self-management skills. Self-management programs emphasize patients role in managing their illness, by giving them knowledge, skills, and confidence to cope with their problems. We expect that by engaging and instructing elders in the self-management of their mobility limitations, community participation and mobility will be improved. Similarly, visits to emergency or walk-in-clinics, pain and number of falls will be reduced. To test our hypothesis, 60 elders, recently discharged from McGill Teaching Hospitals will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. The first group will be offered an evaluation and treatment plan supervised by a physiotherapist, accompanied by written and visual material to enhance mobility self-management skills, supported by telephone mentoring. The second group will be mailed an exercise guide targeting the key mobility limitations common in the elderly. Outcome measures administered before and after intervention include a self-administered questionnaire package covering health care utilization, self-efficacy, arm and leg function, pain, activity and participation levels as well as quality of life. Basic descriptive statistics will be used to compare both groups at baseline and dependent on the data type, Pearsons correlations and multiple regressions will be performed. The entire study should take 18 to 24 months to complete.

Outcomes will be assessed using depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, self-esteem, and self-harm and suicidality psychological measures.

TitreApplicationTitle: Gaining Insight: Understanding and preventing excessive prenatal weight gain in urban First Nations women.
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; FIRST NATIONS HEALTH; OBESITY; PREGNANCY; PREVENTION; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; WEIGHT-GAIN
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is widespread among First Nations (FN) peoples in Canada; according to Statistics Canada, approximately half of FN women are obese. Excessive weight gain during pregnancy increases the risk of poor maternal and fetal health outcomes that can continue throughout their lifetimes. Research has shown that pregnant Aboriginal women often exceed recommended weight-gain guidelines. Thus, the time period when obesity prevention efforts may be most warranted is during pregnancy.  This research will use the social determinants of health framework to help to understand the factors that influence urban FN weight gain during pregnancy. The social determinants of health are defined by the World Health Organization as the "conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, including the health system." Through community-based research in partnership with the Odawa Native Friendship Centre (ONFC) in Ottawa, Ontario, I seek to understand how obesity prevention programs with pregnant FN women who live in urban centres can be reflective of and sensitive to FN cultural practices. My PhD research will be divided into three distinct stages.  The first stage will use semi-structured interviews, focus groups, and a review of literature to assess the factors that influence urban FN women's weight gain during pregnancy. Using the results from the initial stage of the research, in the second stage I will use focus groups to work with participants to revise current prenatal health promotion resources to better suit participants' unique cultural needs. Finally, in the third stage, I will implement and evaluate an obesity prevention module within the existing pre-natal health program at the ONFC.  This research has the capacity to address health inequalities in Canada through informing and strengthening the development of culturally-safe interventions and policies that can prevent excess weight-gain, adverse maternal and fetal outcomes, and obesity, for FN women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Reproductive Justice as Defined by Urban Aboriginal Women: A Feminist Participatory Action Research Project
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL WOMEN; PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH; REPRODUCTIVE JUSTICE; REPRODUCTIVE RIGHTS
Abstract-Résumé: The colonization and control of Aboriginal women's bodies, enacted through forced sterilization, misuse of long-term reproductive technologies, and child welfare system interventions has not come to an end. Rather, it continues in new forms. In the face of the surveillance, Aboriginal women, particularly Aboriginal women living in poverty, are subjected to there is a call from Indigenous women for reproductive justice. Reproductive justice focuses on the rights of women to choose not only whether or not to have children, but also how to raise them in safe and healthy environments, an understanding consistent with First Nations and Metis peoples holistic views of health. This research uses a collaborative, participatory approach to examine Aboriginal women living in poverty's access (or lack of access) to reproductive justice as well as how this access can be improved. This project seeks to determine: 1) What constrains and fosters Aboriginal women living in poverty's reproductive justice? 2) What changes to social and health services would increase Aboriginal women's access to reproductive justice? 3) What structural and cultural shifts would increase Aboriginal women's access to reproductive justice? In order to examine these questions, this project will collaborate with Aboriginal women living in poverty and service providers who work closely with them as co-researchers. This project will engage ethnographic approaches including qualitative interviews, photography, and field notes. This data will be supplemented by an analysis of the federal and provincial policies relating to reproductive justice. Together, the research team (the Principal Applicant and co-researchers) will determine how to disseminate the study's results and recommendations.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Indian Solution to the Policy Problem: Developing an Indigenous Policy Model to Address First Nations Health and Education Disparities
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES; COMPARATIVE POLICY ANALYSIS; CRITICAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS; EDUCATION; HEALTH; INDIGENOUS RESEARCH METHODOLOGY; POLICY; POLITICS; POST-COLONIALISM; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Prior to contact with settlers, Indigenous peoples had laws and cultural practices that governed their societies and promoted community cohesion. Although it is often overlooked, these laws and practices could also be referred to as policies created by each community's leadership. Post-contact, the locus of control for policy-making amongst Indigenous communities shifted from internal decision-making powers to becoming externalized and located within the power of the Canadian governments through the processes of colonization and assimilation. Under the auspices of assimilation, the ultimate agenda of the government at the time was "the eradication of Indigenous population by eradicating Indigenous differences, and public policy became the weapon of choice" to deal with the "Indian problem" (Episkenew 2009, 26). As a result of this policy history and the policy-making process, both the health gap and education gap (a key social determinant of health) between First Nations and non-First Nations Canadians is widening despite numerous policies designed to improve their health and education levels. These policies are often failing to achieve their desired outcomes due to three key factors: lack of community control/input; racist and oppressive policy structures and institutions; and an ineffective policy-making process that does not take into account traditional Indigenous policy-making procedures or principles. Therefore, it is the formation of policy, and the resulting policy as an instrument itself, that limits their effectiveness in addressing the health and education needs of First Nations people. As a result, the policy-making process needs to be re-examined so that an Indigenous policy framework can be created to help guide the formation of health and education policies that improve First Nations health and education outcomes in Canada through culturally appropriate and lasting methods.

Previous studies have found that levels of parental stress, socioeconomic status, nutrition, and other environmental exposures in early life lead to differences in gene expression, through epigenetic modifications. The proposed research seeks to understand how environmental inputs interact with these epigenetic factors to shape development and lifelong health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Good Health Now, Good Health for the Future: Post-Secondary Education, Physical Activity, and Aboriginal Health.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES; ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE; INTERVENTION; MENTAL HEALTH; PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Education and health go hand in hand; the higher one's education the better one's health. In Canada education is a pivotal issue for Aboriginal people because it is so closely linked with good health. Today, more Aboriginal students are attending post-secondary institutions than ever before. However, attrition rates for Aboriginal students are much higher than for non-Aboriginal students; less than one third of Aboriginal students who start university will acquire a degree. One way to reduce attrition rates is to address barriers that currently face Aboriginal students.  Barriers such as lack of supportive relationships, academic challenges, discrimination, and health issues such as anxiety and depression are commonly faced by Aboriginal students. Physical activity may assist in addressing many these barriers. Physical activity is proven to increase academic performance, and buffers against depression and anxiety. Furthermore, group physical activity can build supportive relationships for young people. Thus, a group physical activity program for Aboriginal students could assist in increasing students' abilities to deal with the many challenges they face at University. Increasing the health of Aboriginal students while attending university ultimately increases their health in the future through the attainment of higher education. The goal of this project is to establish a culturally relevant group physical activity program at the University of Saskatchewan for Aboriginal students and study its effect on physical activity levels, supportive relationships, ability to cope with academic challenges, and mental health.

Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; AGING; CHRONIC DISEASE; COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT; DEMENTIA; EPIDEMIOLOGY; FIRST NATIONS HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The objective of this research project is to identify factors associated with dementia in First Nations communities in Ontario.  To date, no research has been done investigating the impact of dementia on First Nations communities in Canada.  This will be the first Ontario-based project on the prevalence of dementia in First Nations seniors.  Identified risk factors associated with dementia in First Nations populations will be contrasted to the risk factors in the general Ontario population to understand unique health services required (if any).  By having a variety of sampling populations we may identify geographic/environmental risk factors associated with dementia in addition to high risk populations.  The results will be useful for First Nations communities, and also for guiding the clinicians and community organizations who serve them.

TitreApplicationTitle: Differential effects of cognitive remediation therapy and metacognitive training on symptoms, cognition, and functional brain activity in schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE BIASES; COGNITIVE REMEDIATION THERAPY; DELUSIONS; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; METACOGNITIVE TRAINING; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a debilitating disorder that severely impacts the lives of patients and their families. Despite major improvements to the medications used to treat schizophrenia, they are not always effective at improving symptoms, memory and attention, or social functioning. For these reasons, health professionals are actively searching for complementary treatment options that can be used alongside conventional medications. Cognitive training is one of the most common and effective of these alternative treatments, and has been found to improve symptoms, social functioning, as well as memory and attention. However, different types of therapy target different aspects of schizophrenia, and it is important to understand their distinct effects to better tailor treatment to a patient's needs. The goal of this research is to examine whether two cognitive therapies, cognitive remediation therapy (CRT) and metacognitive training (MCT), show distinct benefits to schizophrenia patients. CRT uses training and practice to improve memory and attention whereas MCT focuses on teaching patients to counteract biases in thinking that contribute to symptoms. In this study, groups of 10 schizophrenia patients will take part in either CRT or MCT over an 8-week period, and we will examine changes in social functioning, symptom severity, memory/attention, and brain activity. This research will be the first direct comparison of two popular cognitive therapies for schizophrenia, and could lead to more individualized treatment options for patients by determining which features of schizophrenia are impacted most through CRT vs. MCT. Future research combining CRT and MCT would serve as the first steps in the development of a comprehensive treatment program involving treatment with medications in conjunction with cognitive training.

TitreApplicationTitle: Active Pharmacovigilance and Parkinson's Disease: Identifying Vulnerable Populations at Risk of Developing Cancers or Experiencing Negative Cardiovascular Effects
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS (ADRS); CANCERS; CARDIOVASCULAR EFFECTS; CASE STUDIES; COHORT STUDIES; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PATIENT SAFETY; PHARMACEUTICALS; PHARMACOVIGILANCE; SECONDARY HEALTH DATABASES
Abstract-Résumé: It is well documented that the North American population is aging at a rapid rate and that the incidence of nervous system disorders, specifically Parkinson's disease (PD), will significantly increase in coming years. As such, there is a need to better identify groups of PD patients that are at risk of experiencing severe reactions to their medications.  The objective of my research project is to identify groups of PD patients in North America who are at risk of developing cancers (i.e. prostate cancers and melanomas) or negative cardiovascular outcomes (heart attacks, blood pressure disorders, and cardiac diseases) as a result of taking medications to treat their symptoms. Additionally, I want to identify which medications or classes of medications, if any, are responsible for increasing a PD patient's risk of experiencing these severe reactions.  In order to calculate the risk of severe reactions to medications, I will use quantitative epidemiological methods to analyze de-identified PD patient data from more than 500 North American hospitals. Findings from my study will identify specific medications or classes of medications that increase the risk of cancers and/or development of negative cardiovascular outcomes for certain groups of PD patients. More specifically, I will be able to identify groups of PD patients by age, sex, or place of residence that are at the greatest risk of severe reactions to their medications.  By identifying groups of PD patients at risk of severe reactions to their medications, regulators and health professionals will be able to make informed decisions that will ensure health for all. Additionally, my findings may lead to the implementation of population health interventions targeted at improving specific determinants of health that are associated with poorer health post-diagnosis with PD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel health economic methods to strengthen coverage decision-making of biologic response modifiers for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGIC AGENTS; BIOLOGICAL THERAPY; BIOLOGICS; CLINICAL TRIAL DESIGN; ECONOMIC EVALUATION; INFLAMMATORY DISEASE; META-ANALYSES; METHODOLOGY; MULTIPLE TREATMENT COMPARISON; RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: The current evidence used to inform drug regulatory approvals for biologic response modifiers for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) has focused on efficiency, quantified as incremental cost-effectiveness. However, there are many discrepancies in this evidence base, and there has been substantial debate over the decisions made on this evidence in Canada and elsewhere. No advanced analyses have been undertaken to determine the strength and completeness of the existing evidence base, nor have any robust models been developed to improve the decision-making processes. With many new biologics for RA currently being tested in late stage clinical trials, and the significant costs associated with the use of these drugs, it is pertinent that we further develop the methods and tools used in the evidence synthesis of biologics for RA so that appropriate decisions can be made about their use. I propose to strengthen coverage decision-making in relation to biologics for RA. In order to achieve this goal, I propose the following linked tasks: 1) To develop valid and reliable clinical research evidence; 2) To develop robust economic evaluation and decision models; 3) To review the strength and completeness of existing evidence for informing economic models; and 4) To develop a robust coverage decision making process.

TitreApplicationTitle: The use of insulin glargine and risk of colorectal cancer in patients with type 2 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: BENEFIT-RISK PROFILE; COLORECTAL CANCER; COX PROPORTIONAL HAZARD MODEL; DIABETES MELLITUS; DRUG SAFETY; INSULIN GLARGINE; INSULIN THERAPY; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The high prevalence of colorectal cancer and the increasing incidence of type 2 diabetes in Canada and elsewhere is a public health concern. Diet and obesity, some known risk factors, may influence insulin levels resulting in an increased risk for colorectal cancer. In patients with diabetes, modified human insulin is used as an antidiabetic therapy in order to help patients gain better control of glucose levels. These modified insulin structures such as long-acting insulin may bind more strongly to receptors, which may play an important role in cancer cell growth. Current studies show that there is a link between long-acting insulin therapies and cancer risk in general, but these studies may be flawed in scientific methods and limited in size, and the duration of the therapy is often neglected. Studies on all types of insulin therapy show an increase in risk of colorectal cancer and demonstrate longer use of this therapy elevates the risk even more. This has public health importance because there is an issue of risks and benefits with using long-acting insulin among diabetics and existing research on the effect of long-acting insulin therapies on the risk of colorectal cancer, especially with longer insulin use, is limited. Therefore, the aim of this doctoral research is to evaluate whether a long-acting insulin therapy, glargine, is associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer, and to determine if this risk varies with duration of use.

TitreApplicationTitle: C. elegans p53 family transcription factor has roles in meiotic recombination and DNA interstrand crosslink repair
Keywords-MotsClés: BRCA1; C. ELEGANS; CEP-1; DNA INTERSTRAND CROSSLINKS; DNA REPAIR; FANCONI ANEMIA; GENOMIC INSTABILITY; MEIOTIC RECOMBINATION; P53 FAMILY; P63
Abstract-Résumé: The p53 family of transcription factors (p53,p63,p73) function as tumour suppressors by promoting apoptosis, cell cycle arrest and DNA repair. Recent studies revealed that p63 and p73 promote DNA repair by transcriptionally activating components of the Fanconi anemia (FA) repair network. In addition, dominant negative isoforms of p63 are frequently upregulated in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC), a tumor most FA adult survivors eventually develop. Thus, understanding how p63 promotes DNA repair and genome stability will help elucidate the molecular basis of FA and facilitate development of therapies for HNSCC in FA patients. The presence of multiple paralogues and isoforms with overlapping functions complicate analysis of the p53 family in vertebrates. The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans contains a single p53 family member (CEP-1) and most of the FA repair network proteins. Structurally, CEP-1 is more similar to p63/p73 than p53 and gene profiling studies showed considerable overlap between the targets of CEP-1 and human p63. Recent work in our lab revealed that CEP-1 has a minor role in promoting meiotic recombination and DNA interstrand crosslink (ICL) repair that is similar to several FA genes, but defects in these processes are significantly enhanced when cep-1 is co-ablated with these FA genes. These preliminary results suggest that CEP-1 cooperates in parallel with the FA proteins to promote meiosis and ICL repair. During my PhD studies, I will define the mechanism by which CEP-1 collaborates with the FA network to promote ICL repair using the powerful genetics and in vivo imaging tools available in C. elegans. I will translate my findings in C. elegans to mammalian models to ask whether p63 has conserved interactions with the FA network in promoting ICL repair. My work on CEP-1/p63 will provide new insights into the DNA repair defects of FA and ideally uncover new therapeutic targets for the treatment and prevention of FA-associated phenotypes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of Specific Inhibitors of Alternative Splicing Events Crucial to HIV Replication: A New Anti-HIV/AIDS Strategy
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; DRUG DISCOVERY; ENZYME INHIBITORS; HIV AGENTS; SYNTHETIC CHEMISTRY
Abstract-Résumé: Although access to HAART has changed the prognosis of HIV infection to that of a chronic disease, the long term use of HAART is limited by issues of drug compliance, side effects and drug resistance. To respond to the continued need for new drugs, and in particular, those acting through as yet unexplored mechanisms of action, my PhD thesis research is directed toward the  development small molecule inhibitors of HIV alternative splicing as a new therapy for HIV/AIDS. This project began with the discovery of the tetracyclic indole compound IDC16, the first small molecule known to inhibit the exonic splicing enhancer activity of SRSF1. The splicing factor SRSF1 plays a crucial, but generally redundant role in human RNA splicing. However, in HIV-1 infected cells it specifically regulates alternative splicing events that are vital to the production of critical HIV proteins Tat and Rev. These RNA-binding proteins are key regulators for the expression of HIV-1 viral genes, for the synthesis of full-length genomic RNA and, ultimately, for the production of progeny virions. The advantages of blocking SRSF1 as an anti HIV/AIDS strategy over the use of existing drugs are that: (i) this protein is essential for HIV replication, and (ii) targeting a human protein decreases the chances of mutations and subsequent resistance to drug therapy. Our laboratories effort to design new ring opened mimics of IDC16 has led to identification of several di(hetero)arylamide (DHA) type compounds that block the replication of HIV at concentrations comparable to AZT. Unlike IDC16 these new molecules are not inherently cytotoxic. My PhD thesis research is focused on optimizing the activity/selectivity and in vivo properties of these active molecules. The development of this new class of anti-HIV/AIDS drug with minimal risk of resistance will potentially have considerable impact on the quality of life of HIV/AIDS victims, and will have considerable social/financial impact on Canadian society.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of HIV infection status and carriage of HIV protective/non-protective KIR/HLA genotypes on induction of Natural Killer cell subset responses.
Keywords-MotsClés: CORRELATES OF PROTECTION; CYTOKINE SECRETION; CYTOLYSIS; HOST RESISTANCE TO HIV-1; HUMAN LEUKOCYTE ANTIGEN (HLA); KILLER IMMUNOGLOBULIN-LIKE RECEPTORS (KIRS); MULTI-PARAMETRIC FLOW CYTOMETRY; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; NK CELL EFFECTOR FUNCTION; NK CELL LICENSING
Abstract-Résumé: HIV infection causes AIDS and is one of the top 3 global infectious disease killers. Some people remain uninfected despite multiple exposures to the virus. Of those who become infected, about 5% progress slowly without treatment. Epidemiological studies implicate Natural Killer (NK) cells in HIV resistance and slow time to AIDS in those infected. These protective outcomes are associated with expressing certain NK cell surface receptors called KIRs and their ligands, HLA molecules. KIR and HLA interact with each other to determine how active an NK cell will be when it recognizes virus infected cells. Previous work from Dr. Bernard's group has demonstrated that NK cells from individuals with protective KIR/HLA genotypes had larger numbers of NK cells with stronger and multiple anti-viral functions.  My Ph.D. research will extend this work by identifying which NK cell subset/s respond to HIV infected cells and confer protective outcomes in the context of HIV. I will develop and optimize tools to detect NK cell subsets based on patterns of KIR expression and assess the function of these subsets. I will have access to cells from subjects who are HIV uninfected and HIV positive typical and slow progressors typed for KIR and HLA variants. I will determine which NK cells subsets are activated by HIV infected cells versus by cell stimuli that activate NK cells more broadly (as well as controls). The effect of HIV infection status, KIR/HLA genotype and stimulus on NK function will be measured and compared in terms of frequency of the activated subset/s, intensity of function and number of functions among NK subsets.  Results from this project should deepen our understanding of how NK cells respond to HIV infected cells and how this differs according to KIR/HLA genotypes that are or are not protective. A better understanding of how NK cells function to prevent infection may aid in developing strategies that harness NK cells to prevent HIV infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Strategies to facilitate eradication of the HIV latent reservoir
Keywords-MotsClés: ELIMINATING HIV LATENT RESERVOIR; ENHANCING CTL RESPONSE; HIV LATENCY; HIV NEF; HIV/AIDS; IMMUNE EVASION; IMMUNE EXHAUSTION/TOLERANCE; NEF MHC-I DOWNREGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) has been tremendously successful in controlling HIV replication in infected individuals but it is not a cure. Persons living with HIV need strict adherence to the drug regimen for the rest of their lives to control the virus. If treatment becomes irregular, the once suppressed viral load can resurge rapidly and resume disease progression. Viral outgrowth is due to the presence of long-lived HIV infected cells that escape the killer T cells responsible for eliminating infected cells that are referred to as the latent HIV reservoir. To cure HIV, new therapies need to be designed that can bring these cells out of hiding so that they may be detected and killed by killer T cells. In my research projects I propose two such new strategies. Firstly, studies suggest that latently infected cells express highest amounts of a protein named Tim-3 upon their surface that keeps HIV replication repressed to extremely low levels or none such that the infected cell does not attract a killer T cell towards it. By blocking this Tim-3 protein, I aim to reverse this viral replication brake and thus selectively induce viral outgrowth enough from latently infected cells so that they may be detected and eradicated by killer T cells. Secondly, I wish to suppress the functions of an HIV protein called Nef that is enriched in latently infected cells once they are reactivated. Nef protects these cells from early detection by killer T cells by reducing the expression of another protein called MHC-I that is required for killer T cells to recognize an infected cell. Through collaboration I have acquired novel drugs that help prevent Nef's negative effect on the latently infected cell. By treating these latently infected cells with these new drugs we hope to enhance killer T cells' ability to kill an infected cell. The aim of both of these strategies is to provide a new avenue of HIV therapy that could eventually eradicate HIV and thus cure the patient.
