TitreApplicationTitle: Timing of Initiation of Combined Antiretroviral Therapy in Treatment Naive HIV-Hepatitis C Co-infected Patients: A Collaborative Cohort Study and Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; CD4 LYMPHOCYTE COUNT; COHORT STUDY; COMBINED ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; COST-EFFECTIVENESS ANALYSIS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEPATITIS C INFECTION; HIV INFECTION; LIVER DISEASE; TREATMENT OUTCOMES
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, infection with both HIV and the hepatitis C virus has become an important issue. Since the introduction of HIV treatment, there has been a decrease in mortality from AIDS in HIV-infected people. However, as life expectancies increased, sickness from HCV-associated liver disease has risen and is now one of the leading causes of death in HIV-infected people.  The decision to treat a HIV-infected person with medication is currently based on a patient's level of immunity, which is commonly referred to as their CD4+ cell count. For patients who only are infected with HIV, guidelines suggest that they start treatment once their cell count falls below 350 cells. For people who are co-infected, it is unclear about when the best time to start therapy is. It has been hypothesized that starting treatment earlier may delay liver disease and reduce the risk of developing AIDS. To date, there has been no study that has examined the effect of early therapy in HIV-HCV co-infected patients.  The primary objective of this study is to determine the effect that starting therapy earlier in co-infected patients has on their survival, the occurrence of AIDS, and their liver disease risk, using data from a large Canadian cohort of co-infected individuals. Our secondary objectives will be to investigate health-care utilization and costs associated with the occurrence of toxic side-effects associated with earlier treatment and to determine the cost-effectiveness of starting HIV therapy earlier. In the absence of randomized trials, results from this study will provide information about when is the optimal time to initiate HIV therapy to reduce morbidity and mortality from liver disease and AIDS. We plan to disseminate the results of the study to stakeholders, such as the Canadian Trials Network, the Canadian AIDS Society and the Canadian AIDS Treatment Information Exchange organization.

TitreApplicationTitle: Experience Talks, Resilience Shapes - Revisiting historic trauma: Impact on treatment in Aboriginal males living with HIV/AIDS in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; ACQUIRED IMMUNODEFICIENCY SYNDROME (AIDS); FOCUS GROUP DISCUSSIONS; HISTORIC TRAUMA LEGACY; HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS (HIV); IN-DEPTH INTERVIEWS; PURPOSIVE SAMPLING; QUALITATIVE INTERPRETIVE DESCRIPTION; THEMATIC ANALYSIS; THEORETICAL SAMPLING
Abstract-Résumé: There is an over-representation of HIV and AIDS incidence, prevalence and mortality rates in Aboriginal communities. The eradication of HIV is not yet possible therefore persons undergoing treatment must take highly active anti-retroviral therapy regularly. Yet many do not adhere to treatment. It is a reality that many Aboriginal people still have unresolved trauma secondary to the residential schools legacy, and this explains in part their low adherence to HIV treatment. A critical look at individual experiences can lead to the consideration of the areas of strength and adaptation, and better inform policy and decision-making. The objectives of this study are to: assess the impact of historic trauma on treatment in Aboriginal people living with HIV and AIDS in BC; compare the influence of historic trauma on treatment in BC between youth and adults, across gender, and between survivors and non-survivors of residential schools; examine the role of resilience in those who participate in community development and healing projects or circles to deal with trauma; and offer culturally-sensitive recommendations to better address historic trauma, aimed at improving treatment-seeking behavior and adherence to treatment and reducing deaths due to HIV or AIDS. Aboriginal youth and adults from Vancouver who are currently on highly active anti-retroviral therapy will be interviewed. Recruitment will be through purposive sampling and theoretical sampling. Qualitative interpretive description will be used. A letter of approval for the study has been provided by the Vancouver Native Health Society clinic research committee. Ethics approval will be sought from the Research Ethics Board at the University of Northern BC. Provisions of the Tri-Council Policy Statement on Ethical Conduct for Research Involving Humans will also be followed. In-depth interviews and focus group discussions will be conducted, transcribed and coded. Thematic analysis will be conducted.

TitreApplicationTitle: HIV Epidemic Diversity Among High Risk Populations in Pakistan
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; HIV; INJECTION DRUG USERS; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; NETWORK ANALYSIS; PAKISTAN; SEX WORKERS; TRANSMISSION DYNAMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Pakistan has substantial heterogeneity in HIV prevalence and risk behaviors across different geographic areas and high risk populations. HIV prevalence has reached 50% among injection drug users in some areas and is recently beginning to appear among sex workers - large populations representing significant potential for transmission to the general population. Little is understood about the diversity and trajectory of HIV epidemics in Pakistan. This project will investigate and characterize HIV transmission chains in Pakistan using molecular, behavioural and social network data. By sequencing particular genes isolated from HIV specimens of a sample of infected individuals and grouping them according to sequence similarities, clusters of closely related HIV strains can be identified. Clusters represent specimens that share a common ancestor and therefore are part of the same transmission chain (subepidemic). Clusters may differ a lot in terms of trajectory, population membership and size, behaviours and geographic location and may therefore require unique HIV prevention program configurations in optimal locations targeting that specific transmission chain. Cluster features also reveal the success of interventions, as large clusters suggest that transmission has not been abated. Transmission routes may be further described using network data, which indicates sexual and injection bridging between individuals.  I propose to perform molecular analysis on specimens isolated from dry blood spots from injection drug users in 2011 and 2013 and female, male, and transgender sex workers in 2011 and link these results to accompanying behavioural and geographic data. In 2013 sexual and injection network data among injection drug users will also be collected. This project will provide a uniquely comprehensive understanding of the heterogeneity and population dynamics of HIV subepidemics in Pakistan, which will be critical to strategically design targeted HIV prevention programs.

Abstract-Résumé: The rate of new HIV infections in Canada has increased over the past decade, and unprotected anal sex between men represents the main mode of transmission.  Highly active antiretroviral treatment has increased the life expectancy of HIV-infected people, yet may have contributed to an attitude of HIV complacency. HIV complacency has been broadly defined as the act of minimizing, discounting, or discrediting the threat of HIV and it has been associated with high-risk sexual behaviour. Single-session interventions have been effective at reducing high-risk sexual behaviour, but none have specifically targeted HIV complacency. The current study will pilot-test a single-session intervention to reduce HIV complacency and sexual risk behaviour among 150 sexually active, HIV-negative men who have sex with men (MSM), and will examine HIV complacency in a Canadian sample. The intervention is expected to reduce the frequency of unprotected anal intercourse by introducing discrepancy between an individual's beliefs and sexual health-related behaviour, then by motivating behavioural change. This study will provide descriptive information about HIV complacency in a Canadian context, and is the first study to specifically target HIV complacency in an HIV-prevention intervention. This study will provide initial data on a potentially time- and cost-effective HIV prevention intervention that is easily administered in a community setting by individuals with minimal training.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bone Targeted Therapy for Prostate Cancer in Canada: Practice Patterns and Impact on Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE METASTASES; PROSTATE CANCER
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer, the most common cancer in Canadian men, causes significant morbidity through the development of bone metastases.  These can result in skeletal-related events (SRE) such as fractures, spinal cord compressions, bone pain requiring radiation therapy or surgery to bone.  In addition to the health consequences faced by patients, there is a significant economic burden on the health care system. Recent new treatments include using bisphosphonates and rank-ligand inhibitors to prevent SREs.  Zoledronic acid and denosumab are examples of such agents.  Variable funding of these treatments from one province to the next has resulted in variable access and utilization of these agents.  This study aims to investigate how these agents are used across Canada in men with advanced prostate cancer, how and why these patterns of usage vary, and if these patterns impact on outcomes.  Medical oncologists will be surveyed to determine prescribing patterns and endpoints such as radiation utilization, and incidence of spinal and hip surgeries in men with metastatic prostate cancer will be analyzed.  This information will provide the picture of the current landscape in Canada in regards to how bone metastases are treated in this patient population.  Together these findings will help guide the future use of bone-targeted therapy and will have important implications for how these agents are funded in our public system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predictive and prognostic impacts of quality of life measurements and biomarker discovery in chemotherapy treated advanced pancreatic cancer patients in Northern Alberta
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; DATABASE; PANCREAS CANCER; QUALITY OF LIFE; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Pancreas cancer is a very lethal cancer.  The symptoms, such as a lack of appetite, weight loss, fatigue and abdominal pain, are very vague.  Consequently, approximately 80% of people diagnosed with pancreas cancer have widespread and incurable disease at the time of their diagnosis.  Unfortunately, the treatment options for advanced pancreas cancer are limited.  Medical research has shown that a chemotherapy drug, named gemcitabine, can be used in this setting, but it only increases patient lifespan by an average of six weeks.  However, gemcitabine does improve how patients feel, in terms of their pain, weight, energy and day-to-day functioning.  Because the cure rates for advanced pancreas cancer are so low, it is important to be able to provide these patients with symptom relief and a good quality of life.  Medical research has shown that in some very lethal cancers, such as advanced lung cancer, patients who report a better quality of life before and during treatment experience superior response to chemotherapy and these patients survive longer.  This research project aims to investigate how quality of life is related to response to chemotherapy and survival in patients with advanced pancreas cancer.  We will investigate patients with advanced pancreas cancer treated at the Cross Cancer Institute in Edmonton, Alberta.  In particular, we will collect information on these patients' symptoms, quality of life, treatment, response to therapy and survival.  We will also collect samples of patients' tumours to look at various markers that may help predict patient prognosis and response to therapy.    New and improved treatment options are desperately needed for patients with advanced pancreas cancer.  This study will allow us to investigate the impact of quality of life on response to therapy and survival and may allow us to personalize therapy and improve care for patients with advanced pancreas cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: The influence of air pollution on asthma development and exacerbations : A translational research approach using human clinical exposures and mechanistic in vitro studies.
Keywords-MotsClés: AIR POLLUTION; AIRWAY EPITHELIAL CELLS; ALLERGENS; ASTHMA; DIESEL; IMMUNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a respiratory disease that effects more than 10% of the North America population, including 2.5 million Canadians.  During asthma attacks, exaggerated closing of the airways and lung inflammation makes it hard to breathe, which can lead to death.  To date there is no known cure for the disease.  The exact causes leading to the development of asthma are not perfectly clear, although it is known that air pollution can trigger asthma attacks.  Exactly how air pollution leads to asthma attacks remains a mystery.  One possibility of how air pollution contributes to asthma is that during breathing, air pollution is inhaled into the lungs and irritates the protective barrier of cells that line the lungs.  The protective barrier of cells, called airway epithelial cells, may release molecules in response to air pollution that leads to difficulty in breathing.  We propose to study how air pollution interacts with airway epithelial cells.  We will do this by collecting samples from human subjects with or without asthma that have been exposed to diesel exhaust.  We anticipate that our research will show us how the human body responds to air pollution.  Our studies will provide i) biological data to support public health initiatives aimed at protecting vulnerable populations from air pollution and ii) new targets for the development of drugs for the treatment of asthma.   There are few research groups in the world that perform air pollution studies with human beings.  The combination of air pollution studies in humans and research on airway epithelial cells is even more unique.  Our proposed research studies will therefore have high impact on respiratory research fields by being the first to demonstrate precise and relevant biological consequences of air pollution on asthma.  Our studies will also form a foundation of knowledge for air quality health policy initiatives that are designed to protect the health of all Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental and Occupational Risk Factors for Brain Tumours in the INTEROCC Study
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOURS; CASE-CONTROL STUDY; CELLULAR TELEPHONES; CHEMICALS; EXTREMELY LOW FREQUENCY MAGNETIC FIELDS; GLIOMA; INTERACTIONS; MENINGIOMA; OCCUPATION
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumours are a serious, often highly fatal disease, with few established risk factors, and are an important population health issue in Canada.  Although ionizing radiation has been clearly linked with brain tumours, there are a number of environmental and occupational agents that are suspected.  However, results from previous studies are inconsistent due to small numbers of study subjects and crude methods of exposure assessment. There exists a unique opportunity to further clarify the role of environmental and occupational agents in the etiology of brain tumours using data from a large, multi-national study of brain tumours, INTERPHONE.  INTERPHONE is a 13-country study, including Canada, that was conducted according to a common protocol.  Its primary objective was to examine whether radiofrequency (RF) field exposure from cellular telephones is associated with brain tumours.  A number of INTERPHONE countries, with interest and expertise in occupational hygiene, collected detailed occupational information and participated in the subsequent INTEROCC study.  The objective of INTEROCC is to address outstanding questions concerning environmental and occupational agents, including electromagnetic field (EMF) exposure, particularly extremely low frequency magnetic fields (ELFMF), and chemicals in the disease.  Chemical and ELFMF exposures have been estimated for 3,978 brain tumours (2,054 gliomas and 1,924 meningiomas) and 5,601 controls, providing an extraordinary opportunity to investigate the effect of these agents and their potential interactions for brain tumours, a pressing research gap.  The proposed research seeks to provide new scientific data to help resolve the debate surrounding conflicting previous studies, clarify whether Canadians are at an increased risk of brain tumours due to environmental and occupational agents, and to inform the management of potential occupational and environmental risks to health.

TitreApplicationTitle: PLAY GAME: Post-concussion syndrome Affecting Youth: GABAergic effects of Melatonin
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL OUTCOME; CHILDREN; COGNITIVE TESTING; CONCUSSION; FUNCTIONAL MRI; MELATONIN; MILD TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY; POST-CONCUSSION SYNDROME; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: One in seven children will have had a concussion by age ten, and 11% of those children continue to have symptoms three months later. These symptoms, referred to as post-concussion symptoms (PCS), include headaches, fatigue, sleep disruption, mood and concentration difficulties. They often result in missed school and both physical and psychological consequences to children and their families. The neurological basis of PCS is not clear, although recent evidence suggests dysfunction in GABAergic neurotransmitter systems.   Even though PCS affects thousands of Canadian children every year, there is no evidenced-based medical treatment. Melatonin is produced naturally in our brain and is best known for its actions in maintaining our 24-hour internal clock. Although it is widely available as an over-the-counter sleep aid, there is a growing interest in its pain-relieving, and brain injury protective effects, including its GABAergic effects. Our previous research found that 85% of children with PCS and sleep problems, reported improvement when treated with Melatonin.  The proposed study will compare treatment with oral melatonin to placebo in youth with PCS. We hypothesize that those treated with melatonin will have fewer symptoms. We will examine the relationship between PCS, sleep and response to treatment. We will also use new technologies to examine the GABAergic brain systems and they are affected by melatonin treatment. These methods include functional magnetic resonance imaging and transcranial magnetic stimulation.   Our study has the potential to provide a safe treatment for PCS in children. It will also allow us to discover how neuronal networks and brain connectivity changes during treatment and recovery so that we can provide even better interventions in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Patient Access to Internet Cognitive Behaviour Therapy for Depression and Anxiety: Overcoming Barriers and Fostering Innovation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; DEPRESSION; EFFECTIVENESS RESEARCH; INNOVATION IN MENTAL HEALTH DELIVERY; INTERNET-COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MENTAL HEALTH ASSESSMENT; PATIENT ACCESS; PATIENT EDUCATION
Abstract-Résumé: Depression and anxiety are highly prevalent and disabling conditions that are frequently undertreated. There is strong evidence that Internet Cognitive Behavior Therapy (ICBT) is effective for treating these conditions. ICBT involves patients reviewing strategies for coping with symptoms over the Internet along with patients communicating with a therapist over a secure email system. ICBT is advantageous for those who have difficulties accessing care. Our past research shows that it is feasible to train providers from multiple disciplines in ICBT and for them to deliver ICBT effectively and safely within the community. There are some barriers to delivering ICBT, however, that need to be overcome before this approach can be routinely incorporated into clinical practice. The current research involves a partnership between researchers and decision makers responsible for mental health programming in rural and urban areas of Saskatchewan to improve access to ICBT. Specifically, we aim to: 1) develop and evaluate an online presentation to inform patients about ICBT; 2) develop and evaluate an online diagnostic questionnaire to identify patients who are eligible for ICBT; 3) implement and evaluate a 5-module ICBT program that can be used for depression and or anxiety and can be offered either as a first step in care, as an alternative method of delivering care or as an adjunct to face-to-face care; 4) examine therapist perceptions of ICBT; and 5) explore decision-making related to ongoing use of ICBT in Saskatchewan resulting from this research. We are particularly interested in factors that will facilitate or constrain health regions adopting ICBT in the longer-term. Patient feedback will be sought throughout the project. The research has the potential to significantly influence how ICBT is managed and delivered not only in Saskatchewan, but in other areas of Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autophagy and the maintenance of synaptic function during aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL BIOLOGY; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ENDOCYTOSIS; NEURODEGENERATIVE DISORDERS; NEUROSCIENCE; PROTEOMICS; SUPER-RESOLUTION MICROSCOPY; SYNAPTIC VESICLES
Abstract-Résumé: Neurons in the brain communicate with each other at specialized sites termed synapses via the release of neurotransmitter from synaptic vesicles. These vesicles undergo continual cycles of release and regeneration, the fidelity of which must be maintained for efficient communication. During aging components of these synaptic vesicles start to malfunction, resulting in a reduction in synaptic function and decreased cognitive function. One mechanism cells use to degrade malfunctioning components is a process of self-eating termed autophagy, whereby the cell engulfs and degrades malfunctioning proteins or organelles. Along with a decline in cognitive function during aging there is a reduction in autophagy. Autophagy has been linked to the correct functioning of synaptic vesicle cycling and numerous neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Huntington's disease, therefore drugs that modulate autophagy represent potential therapies for treating neurodegenerative diseases. We will examine how autophagy regulates synaptic vesicle cycling; specifically we aim to determine the molecular mechanisms whereby specific malfunctioning synaptic components are targeted to undergo autophagy, as well as the impact of modulating autophagy on cognitive function in animal models. Understanding the role of autophagy in the mental decline that occurs with aging and during the onset of pathologies will be important for the generation of specific therapies to maintain cognitive function during aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Council on Animal Care (CCAC) Transition Plan 2013-2016
Keywords-MotsClés: DIRECTED GRANT
Abstract-Résumé: The role of the Canadian Council on Animal Care (CCAC) is to provide the Canadian public with an integrated program to enhance the welfare of animals in science. This program challenges if the use of animals in science is absolutely necessary, and if the benefits warrant it, we require that all harm and distress are minimized. We do this by developing science-based and ethical reference standards, and then certifying that these standards are being met. All of this is done by working with a wide range of experts and public representatives.   Although in the past the CCAC program has been funded by federal agencies, they are now restricting their funding to standards development. As a result, the CCAC must find funding for assessment, certification, training and education, from other sources.   This proposal requests funding for a three year transition period to determine and implement an acceptable and sustainable business plan, arrived at through comprehensive stakeholder consultations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implementation and evaluation of a clinical pathway for chronic kidney disease in primary care
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE; CLINICAL PATHWAYS; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; POLICY DECISION-MAKING
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is common, affecting almost 10% of all Canadian adults.However many patients with CKD do not receive optimal care. This may be because they have a number of other health conditions, and their CKD is not recognized, or it may be due to the complexity in the care they require.    New clinical practice guidelines are being published to guide management of patients with CKD. Since the majority of patients with CKD (95%) are managed by primary care physicians, they will be the target for these guidelines. To help facilitate the uptake of the evidence in clinical practice by primary care physicians, the guidelines will be summarized in the form of a clinical pathway.  The purpose of our proposed project is to implement and evaluate this clinical pathway for CKD in primary care.    Specifically we will: 1) assess patient, provider and health system barriers and facilitators to uptake of the clinical pathway for CKD. 2) determine if the clinical pathway improves care for patients with CKD by doing an observational study (pre-post clinical pathway implementation), as well as a randomized trial (randomizing physician practices to electronic reminder and clinical decision support system to facilitate completion of a care plan for CKD).  We will evaluate the impact of the clinical pathway using process of care outcomes (assessment of proteinuria; nephrology referral; completion of CACP), using our chronic disease laboratory (administrative and lab data for all Alberta health regions).   This innovative work builds on extensive background work and has substantial potential to improve the quality and efficiency of care for patients with CKD. TitreApplicationTitle: Association Between Times to Administration of Adjuvant Chemotherapy and Outcomes in Early Breast Cancer: Analysis of Adjuvant Studies Conducted by NCIC Clinical Trials Group
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUVANT TREATMENT; EARLY STAGE BREAST CANCER; META-ANALYSIS; RETROSPECTIVE STUDY; TIME TO TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: In breast cancer, chemotherapy after surgery has an important role.  Studies have shown that adjuvant chemotherapy in certain patients could impact survival by reducing the risk of relapse and death which helped establish the role of adjuvant chemotherapy in high risk breast cancer. Despite decades of research addressing the question of what constitutes the best chemotherapy, there is a striking lack of information regarding when best to give the chemotherapy after surgery.  Other researchers looked at this question in 2006 and suggested that the survival is better when chemotherapy is given up to 12 weeks after surgery compared to wait times longer than 12 weeks. There is an urgent need to examine this question again. We believe that waiting time makes a difference and that we need to further study this question using modern chemotherapy treatments. We are planning two projects. The first project will  involves an analysis of information that was collected in 3 studies that tested different types of chemotherapy in patients with early breast cancer. We will see what impact waiting time has on survival. We will conduct another project that examines  how long it takes patients in Ontario to start chemotherapy after their diagnosis and initial surgery. We will look at the wait times for specific events such as the referral to the cancer centre; being seen by a cancer specialist and receiving the first dose of chemotherapy. We will conduct this project with other cancer centers in Ontario. On the basis of these projects, we hope to provide information regarding what is an appropriate time to wait until start of chemotherapy and how the health care system might be improved to make the wait time as short as possible.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transforming Treatment Services and Housing for People with Mental Illness in Canada: A Systems Approach to Integrated Knowledge Translation
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITIES OF PRACTICE; HOUSING FIRST; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: The purpose of this research project is to create and evaluate partnerships that will strengthen and improve Canada's healthcare system by transforming the way that mental health, health, addiction treatment, and housing services are provided for people who are homeless and diagnosed with mental illness and other co-occurring conditions. More specifically, the mission of the partnership is to disseminate and expand an evidence-based approach to homelessness and mental illness, known as supported housing or Housing First (HF), across Canada. HF is transformative in its emphasis on the principles of consumer choice, the separation of housing and clinical services, recovery, and community integration, all of which serve to shift the status of a person with mental illness from a patient to a citizen. Through the generation and use of applied, policy, and practice relevant research on HF (particularly, evidence from Canada's At Home/Chez Soi project), the creation of national and regional community of practice (CoP) partnerships, and the application of Integrated Knowledge Translation (IKT) strategies, we aim to promote the utilization of HF evidence and the implementation of HF programs with project-specific partners across Canada. The activities and impacts of the CoPs and IKT strategies will be evaluated through a rigorous qualitative, case study approach.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of ROR-alpha in Type-2 Innate Lymphocyte Lineage Selection and Type-2 Inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: ALLERGIC LUNG INFLAMMATION AND ASTHMA; DEVELOPMENT OF THE IMMUNE SYSTEM; DRUG DISCOVERY; FACS/FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENE EXPRESSION ANALYSIS; GENE-REPORTER MOUSE; HAEMATOPOIESIS; IMMUNE REGULATION; SMALL MOLECULE INHIBITORS
Abstract-Résumé: Allergic lung inflammation and asthma are leading causes of morbidity and mortality in children and adults. In Canada alone, over 2.5 million people suffer from asthma. Type-2 Innate Lymphoid (ILC2) cells were recently discovered to be critically important in mediating inflammation in the lung and intestines. Normally ILC2 cells play a role in fighting parasite infections, but in mice and humans they can also be activated by allergens, causing unwanted allergic inflammation in the lung. We have now discovered that the gene Rora is required for ILC2 cell development, because mice that lack Rora do not have ILC2 cells. More importantly, these mice also don't develop allergic lung inflammation, thus proving the inflammatory role of ILC2 cells. My project is designed to discover how the gene Rora is needed for ILC2 cell development, and if we can target Rora in fighting lung inflammation or asthma. The method I intend to use allows me to track cells where Rora is turned on, which include mature and immature ILC2 cells. This is important because the detection of Rora and ILC2 cells is currently very difficult. Furthermore, I will study lung inflammation in mice where Rora has been turned off in only some immune cells, which is important for detailed analysis of ILC2 cells. This is of great importance to scientists in Canada and around the world, as little is known about the function and development of ILC2 cells. Lastly, I will target Rora with compounds designed to inhibit its function. For many years it was believed that other cells were important for lung inflammation and asthma, resulting in drugs designed towards these cells. However, my findings suggest that ILC2 cells play a leading part in lung inflammation. I predict that by targeting Rora we can inhibit the development or function of ILC2 cells, which should have a positive effect on lung inflammation and asthma. These compounds could potentially be developed as future drugs for inflammatory diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of NRXN1 in Autism Spectrum Disorder Using Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
Keywords-MotsClés: GENOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental and highly variable disorder that is poorly understood at the gene level. Several ASD-susceptibility genes were recently identified using new high-throughput DNA sequencing technologies. The study of the expression and causative role of ASD candidate genes in the neuronal circuitry was previously hampered by the fact that neurons from the human brain are not easily accessible. However, this limitation can now be circumvented by reprogramming cells from the skin into stem cells (iPS cells), which can be subsequently converted into brain neurons. These iPS-derived neurons present the advantage of recapitulating the abnormal events observed in ASD such as deficiency in communication between two neurons and propagation of nerve signals. In the present study, iPS cells will be created from ASD subjects in whom the gene NRXN1 was shown to be defective and susceptible to cause the disease. These iPS cells will be used to generate neurons in the laboratory. A normal version of NRXN1 and a few candidate drugs will be delivered into these neurons in order to rescue the deficits observed in neuronal function. This non-invasive concept of "disease-in-a-dish" will help to elucidate networks of factors participating in ASD and will facilitate earlier diagnosis and personalized approaches for the treatment of this affliction.

TitreApplicationTitle: Global characterization of C2H2 transcription factors
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL ONE-HYBRID; BIOINFORMATICS; C2H2 ZINC FINGER; CHIP-SEQ; GENE REGULATION; HIGH-THROUGHPUT SEQUENCING; PROTEIN-BINDING MICROARRAY; SIRNA; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Abstract-Résumé: The human body consists of trillions of cells whose specialized roles are necessary for normal body development and function. The cells themselves are constructed from myriads of molecular building blocks, such as various proteins with different functions in the cell. The blueprint for manufacturing these building blocks is encoded within the genome, a copy of which is embedded within each cell. While the cells of an individual contain the same copy of the genome, and therefore the same blueprint, they differ in various ways, from morphological properties to behaviour and function. It is now clear that the main reason for these differences lies within the amount of each building block that each cell produces. In other words, the genome contains not only instructions for how to build the proteins and other molecules, but also instructions for where, when, and how much of these molecules should be produced. Many diseases are caused by errors in execution of these "regulatory" instructions. For example, over-production of particular proteins in the cell may change its behaviour and drive it into development of cancer. Or, production of particular proteins in the wrong cell or in the wrong developmental stage can result in severe disorders. In this project, we aim to understand the function of the largest group of factors that regulate production of proteins. This group of regulatory molecules, called "C2H2 transcription factors", constitute about half of the factors that regulate the very first steps of production of proteins from genes. We will create models that will tell us where on the genome these factors bind, and how this binding will affect the cell. Deeper understanding of regulatory mechanisms of the cell will eventually enable us to understand the causes of many developmental and genetic diseases. This will bring us a step closer to realizing the goal of modern genetics to identify causes and treatments of diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the Neural Basis of Relapse in Addiction
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; AMYGDALA; BEHAVIOURAL MEASUREMENTS; LEARNING AND MEMORY; TRANSGENIC MICE; VIRAL VECTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Long after an addicted individual has become drug-free, simple events or circumstances that were associated with prior drug use, such as walking through a particular neighbourhood or hearing a particular song, can reawaken powerful memories that can trigger drug craving and provoke a relapse.  These environmental stimuli may render an addict vulnerable to a return to drug use. This type of stimulus-evoked relapse is a major roadblock to treating addicted individuals.  The aim of my study is to understand the neural mechanisms that mediate how stimuli become associated with the rewarding properties of cocaine and to determine if disrupting expression of this memory can help prevent relapse.  To this end, I will use a mouse model of drug-seeking referred to as conditioned place preference.  In this task, an otherwise neutral environment is paired with cocaine administration.  A second neutral environment is paired with saline administration.  Drug-free mice are then given the opportunity to spend time in each of these environments.  Mice that have learned and remember the association between the particular environment and cocaine spend more time in this drug-paired environment.  I will test the hypothesis that the processes that mediate this form of cue-drug learning are similar to those that underlie the formation of fear memory, as these two forms of memories shares many similarities.  I will then go on to determine if I can disrupt this "cue-drug memory" such that mice will no longer seek cocaine even when the stimulus or cue is presented.  I will use the same molecular tools that recently allowed my lab to block the expression of a previously established fear memory.  The results of these studies may not only inform us as to the biology underlying the development and expression of cue-cocaine associations, but, in the future, these findings could serve as a foundation for the development of new pharmacotherapies aimed at treating or even preventing drug relapse.

TitreApplicationTitle: Global analysis of fungal persister cells: understanding environmental signaling and mechanisms of antifungal drug tolerance for the fungal pathogen Candida albicans
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIFUNGAL DRUG TOLERANCE; CELLULAR SIGNALING; CELLULAR STRESS RESPONSE; DRUG RESISTANCE; FUNGAL PATHOGENS; PERSISTER CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Fungal infections have emerged as a global problem amongst an ever-increasing population of immunocompromised individuals, including people with AIDS, or those undergoing cancer chemotherapy or transplants. The fungal pathogen Candida albicans reigns as the leading cause of invasive fungal infections, and the fourth most common cause of all hospital-acquired infections, with mortality rates of invasive infection approaching 50%. The treatment of C. albicans fungal infections is notoriously challenging, and resistance to antifungal drugs is frequently encountered in the clinic. C. albicans forms cellular biofilms, which are surface-associated microbial communities found on medical devices, such as stents and shuts, that may be up to 1000-fold more resistant to drug treatment than other fungal cells. Given the prevalence and importance of drug-tolerant fungal infections, my research aims to explore the mechanisms by which fungal pathogens are able to survive in the presence of antifungal stress. Specifically, this work aims to characterize C. albicans persister cells, which able to tolerate and survive treatment with antifungal drugs. This work will provide the first global assessment of the environmental conditions that trigger fungal persister cell formation, and assess persister cells from either free-floating, or biofilm environments. This work will further provide an in-depth analysis of the mechanisms of antifungal drug tolerance in these persister cells, to further our understanding of how certain cells can survive drug treatment. Last, this work will investigate persister cell formation under host conditions, and establish an animal model in which to study C. albicans persister cell formation and treatment. Together this will provide the first in-depth analysis of fungal persister cells, and enhance our understanding of how fungal pathogens can resist antifungal drug treatment, ultimately informing the treatment of life-threatening invasive fungal infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of antibiotics and environmental exposures on infant gut microbiota and atopic disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBIOTICS; ATOPIC DISEASE; BIODIVERSITY; BREASTFEEDING; CAESAREAN SECTION; DATABASE LINKAGE; ENVIRONMENTAL EXPOSURES; GUT MICROBIOME; INFANT GUT MICROBIOTA; MICROBIOTA COMPOSITION
Abstract-Résumé: Bacteria living in the digestive tract (known as gut microbiota) play a crucial role in immune system development. Disruption of infant gut microbiota has the potential to cause allergic disease later in childhood. We and others have found that antibiotic use, formula feeding and caesarean delivery can significantly alter the infant gut microbiota. These exposures are also important risk factors for allergy and asthma in children. The impact of antibiotic-mediated microbiota disturbance is poorly understood because infants receiving antibiotics are often excluded from studies, and the impact of other environmental factors (e.g. siblings, pets, daycare attendance) has not been widely studied.  My goal is to systematically investigate the impact of antibiotic use and environmental exposures on infant gut microbiota, and subsequent development of allergic disease.  I will employ the Canadian Healthy Infant Longitudinal Development (CHILD) birth cohort study as a research platform. Environmental exposures and type of feeding will be obtained by parent questionnaire, and antibiotic use will be determined from provincial prescription records.  Microbiota profiles will be generated via genetic analysis of fecal samples, and allergic disease will be evaluated by skin prick test for common allergies, diagnosis of allergic eczema, and parent-reported wheeze.  Specialized statistical methods will be used to examine microbiota changes according to exposures, and to test their impact on subsequent development of allergic disease.   The incidence of allergic disease has increased dramatically in recent years, representing a significant global health and economic burden.  New evidence suggests that modifiable environmental exposures may be responsible, through their impact on the gut microbiota.  My proposed research aims to provide evidence for this "microbiota hypothesis", with the potential to impact clinical practice guidelines and prevention strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Attention Bias Modification Training: Efficacy Study of Novel Treatment for Anxiety in Children With and Without Autism Spectrum Disorders
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY & AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDERS; ANXIETY TREATMENT; ATTENTION BIAS MODIFICATION TRAINING; CHILDHOOD ANXIETY
Abstract-Résumé: Attention Bias Modification Treatment (ABMT) is an emerging evidenced-based treatment for anxiety. A number of randomized controlled trials demonstrate that ABMT reduces attentional biases to threat, symptoms of anxiety, and vulnerability to stress in adult populations. Despite these promising findings, only one published study has examined the efficacy of ABMT in treating childhood anxiety, which is the most common mental illness of childhood, and no studies to date have explored the applicability of ABMT for treating anxiety in children with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD), a disorder associated with abnormally high rates of anxiety. This relative dearth of research is surprising when considering that many children do not receive treatment and only half of children who receive existing front-line treatments demonstrate positive treatment gains. To address this gap in the literature, the proposed randomized controlled study will examine the feasibility and efficacy of employing ABMT in treating anxiety in children with and without ASD. 80 children (40 with ASD) and high levels of trait anxiety will be randomly assigned to receive active treatment or placebo treatment. The effect of ABMT on attention bias, anxiety symptomology, and vulnerability to stress will be assessed immediately following treatment and at four-months follow up. This study will contribute critically to the childhood anxiety literature by examining and testing a novel evidenced-based treatment alternative.

TitreApplicationTitle: Connecting youth in custody with mental health services
Keywords-MotsClés: INTERRAI YOUTH JUSTICE CUSTODIAL FACILITIES TOOL; INTERVENTION; JUSTICE SYSTEM; MENTAL HEALTH; SCREENING AND ASSESSMENT; SUBSTANCE USE; TRAINING SERVICE PROVIDERS; TREATMENT NEEDS; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: The teen years are ones of stress and transition. Some youth emerge into adulthood unscathed while others face more challenges, such as difficulties with mental health or substance use, and may find themselves in conflict with the law. While some of the delinquent behaviours may be experimental or transitory, more persistent and serious manifestations may occur. Unless access to age-appropriate services and appropriate care plans are provided, untreated mental illness, often in conjunction with drug problems, may impede the successful transition to adult roles and responsibilities. This lost opportunity can exact a considerable toll on the youth, their families and society.   Young people found in custodial facilites of the justice system display a particularly high level of mental health and substance use problems, and are among the most vulnerable youth sub-group with unmet needs for treatment services. THe extent to which these needs among these high-risk youth are undiagnosed or unmatched with services is largely unknown in Canada, but the prevention of ongoing or future mental health problems, as well as further conflict with the law, requires attention to these difficulties as early as possible.  Knowledge user partners, consisting of decision-makers in the Ontario Ministry of Children and Youth Services, the Forensic Mental Health Section of Ontario's Ministry of Health and Long Term Care, and the Youth Justice and Strategic Initiatives branch of Justice Canada, have identified the pressing mental health and substance use issues of the incarcerated youth justice population. A primary concern is the need for better screening tools to identify youth most in need of further assessment and possible referral to appropriate treatment services. By training relevant staff in a new more senstive instrument, and evaluating its implementation for youth in custody, this study will provide the basis for improved access and care, and better mental health outcomes

TitreApplicationTitle: A generational investigation of traditional food knowledge among First Nation communities in southwestern Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES PREVENTION; DIETARY CHANGE; HEALTH PROMOTION; INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; ORAL HISTORY; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; QUALITATIVE METHODS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; TRADITIONAL FOODS
Abstract-Résumé: Major differences exist in health status between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal groups in Canada. Life expectancies are five to ten years lower than the Canadian averages and diabetes is considered to have reached epidemic proportions. First Nations diabetes prevention programs have primarily focused on behaviour change. To develop effective strategies, more information is needed about local knowledge linked to behaviours impacting health. Nutrition studies in First Nation communities have focused on food intake with less attention towards understanding how traditional knowledge loss may impact food security. Few studies have looked at how food insecurity is related to cultural loss, or the inter-generational impacts of residential schools, particularly in southern Canada. The proposed research project is an extension of collaborative work between the Southwest Ontario Aboriginal Health Access Centre (SOAHAC), and Western University. Building on recommendations, a larger project will develop and evaluate community-based diabetes prevention programs. To inform this work the proposed study will focus on potential mechanisms that have impacted the inter-generational transfer of knowledge related to traditional foods within urban and reserve-based communities. The project will analyse qualitative interviews that took place with First Nations women as part of The SOAHAC Food Choice Study, focusing on traditional food access, availability and preferences. Twenty Elders will be recruited from participating communities. Their life history interviews will explore: historical and environmental changes impacting traditional food availability; social and cultural determinants of food security; geographic and economic issues impacting traditional food access; and traditional knowledge influencing food practices. Results will inform SOAHAC's nutrition programs to better meet the needs of their clients and assist in creating culturally appropriate diabetes prevention programs.

Keywords-MotsClés: APPLIED RESEARCH; ARCHITECTURE; BUILT ENVIRONMENT; COMPLEX CHRONIC DISEASE; DESIGN AND HEALTH; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HEALTHCARE FACILITY DESIGN; INTEGRATED KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; POST OCCUPANCY EVALUATION; QUASI EXPERIMENTAL RESEARCH DESIGN
Abstract-Résumé: A significant amount of money is spent on the construction and redevelopment of healthcare facilities, with expenditures projected to increase substantially as our population ages and requires more complex chronic care. There is a growing interest in how to build and develop health promoting environments. However, there has been little research to understand how building design can influence health outcomes for patients requiring complex care and rehabilitation. As healthcare facilities deteriorate, we have a growing population of patients who will require specialized care and long hospital stays. We need to know more about how to make strategic investments in the built environment to improve health outcomes. The overall goal of this research is to assess the impact of healthcare facility design on health outcomes in complex chronic disease across an existing facility, a new facility, and a comparison facility.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving distress management knowledge and skills for oncology nurses: A Pan-Canadian knowledge translation study
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL CHANGE; CLINICAL GUIDELINE APPLICATION; CONTEXTUAL ANALYSIS; INTERVENTION AND FOLLOW UP; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MEASUREMENTS OF COMPETENCIES; MIXED METHODS; NURSING CONTINUING EDUCATION; PAN CANADIAN RESEARCH; PSYCHOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS
Abstract-Résumé: By the end of 2012, 88,000 Canadian women and 97,600 men will be diagnosed with cancer. A cancer diagnosis and its treatments can lead to considerable emotional distress, including symptoms of depression, anxiety, or fatigue. It is important to attend to these symptoms as they can reduce overall quality of life and lead to greater costs to the health care system if left untreated.  National agencies, such as the Canadian Association of Psychosocial Oncology, have developed clinical guidelines for health care professionals to address cancer related distress. In this study we will provide a comprehensive educational intervention called "The Therapeutic Practices for Distress Management (TDPM) program" to nurses to support their use of clinical guidelines with the aim to improve their distress management skills. The training program includes information on psychosocial care of the adult, assessment and care of cancer related fatigue, and psychosocial assessment and intervention for cancer related distress and will be offered at 6 Canadian centers in NS, QC, ON, MB, and  AB.  This study proposes a two phase approach. In PHASE I, the project team will assess current distress management practice in each setting, identify enablers and barriers to change, and site readiness. Building on that knowledge, the team will roll out PHASE II, to evaluate the TPDM program. The program includes three components:  1) a 16 week online course; 2) a series of reflective practice sessions to improve clinical practice using case studies; and 3) site mentors or champions to support nurses.  The effectiveness of the program will be evaluated using key informant interviews and focus groups as well as nurse questionnaires and patient chart reviews. The study has direct implications for improving cancer care outcomes focusing on the emotional care needs of cancer patients and their families.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interindividual variability in the effect of statin exposure on the tissue transcriptome
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; EXPRESSION QUANTITATIVE TRAIT LOCI (EQTLS); GENE EXPRESSION; GENE REGULATION; PHARMACOGENOMICS; RNA SEQUENCING; STATINS; TISSUE TRANSCRIPTOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Variability in drug response between individuals is an important challenge for clinicians, because it is difficult to predict who will respond well to a medication, and who might have an adverse reaction.  One way that drugs affect the body is by changing the amount or rate at which genes are expressed thereby altering the production of proteins and non-coding RNAs. Genetic diversity can further lead to differences in gene expression between individuals, and the complex interplay between drugs, genetic variation, and gene expression is not well understood.  Statins are a type of medication commonly prescribed to decrease low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, and reduce cardiovascular disease risk. Up to 10% of individuals who take a statin will experience muscle pain or weakness. In very rare cases, a life threatening form of muscle damage may occur. To be effective, statins must enter the liver, where the majority of cholesterol synthesis occurs. There is also evidence to suggest that statins work in other tissues, through inflammation-related pathways, to reduce overall cardiovascular disease risk.  This project seeks to identify the effects of statin use on gene expression in multiple tissues in the body, including liver and muscle, and the role of genetic variation in this expression. By combining information about gene expression with information about an individual's DNA, we aim to identify genetic variants that contribute to variability in statin response.  This project will result in an enhanced understanding of how statin exert their effect over multiple tissues.  This will improve our knowledge of the specificity and biochemical impact of this treatment. In addition, new insight to the role of genetic variation on changes to gene expression following statin exposure will improve our ability to monitor and predict which individuals might suffer from adverse side effects or benefit from their use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Toward Improvement of Augmentative and Alternative Communication Services for Young People with Complex Communication Needs
Keywords-MotsClés: AUGMENTATIVE AND ALTERNATIVE COMMUNICATION; CHILDREN WITH DISABILITIES; HEALTH SERVICES AND POLICY RESEARCH; OUTCOME MEASUREMENT
Abstract-Résumé: More than 12,000 Canadian children need assistive devices because they have difficulty speaking or cannot speak. Despite the availability of specialized communication devices and clinical services, 50% of these children have unmet communication needs. This is worrying because children with unmet needs are unable to participate fully in society. Unfortunately, health services managers and clinicians do not understand why so many children have unmet needs and why as many as 1 in 5 children reject the devices they get. This is because outcome measurement tools that they need to study this and make changes to improve products and services are unavailable.   Our alliance of clinicians and researchers developed a novel questionnaire for parents called the Family Impact of Assistive Technology Scale for Augmentative and Alternative Communication. The purpose of the questionnaire is to detect the effect of communication interventions on the lives of children and their families. Our earlier research involving more than 170 parents and clinical experts showed that the questionnaire is reliable. However, we now need to test whether it can measure change in the lives of children and families when clinical interventions work or do not work well. We need to do this so health professionals can use the questionnaire to learn how to improve their services.   Fifty parents of children with speech problems will take part in the study. Parents will complete the questionnaire twice before and twice after their child gets a new communication device. Clincians believe that children will show no change before the child gets the device, communicate a little better 6 weeks after getting the device, and a lot better 12 weeks after getting the device. Our study will show whether the questionnaire can detect these different amounts of change. The project proposed will launch a new program of clinical research to improve communication services for children with disabilities.

Abstract-Résumé: The purpose of this partnership is to study the healthcare provided to people with developmental disabilities in Ontario. For most things people with developmental disabilities should receive the same care as people without disabilities. People with developmental disabilities, however, also tend to have a greater risk of certain kinds of health problems. In this project, we want to find out if adults with developmental disabilities are receiving all the care they should. We are also interested in seeing whether through empowering people with developmental disabilities and their caregivers, we can improve their care. Right now the information needed to properly study the health and healthcare provided to people with developmental disabilities is held in many different places. The partners on this project are cooperating to put information together in one place, and to work together to study and improve their care.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Cancer Screening Among First Nations and Metis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER SCREENING; COMMUNITY READINESS; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; FIRST NATIONS AND METIS; HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SYSTEM; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: Using a highly collaborative process involving researchers, decision-makers, First Nations and Metis leaders and communities as well as other key knowledge-users, we anticipate that the proposed research will produce highly policy relevant outcomes, that it will have a strong likelihood of being used by decision makers and therefore, that it is highly likely to have an impact on the delivery of cancer screening services to First Nations and Metis in Canada.  Specifically, there are 4 key outcomes for the proposed work: (1) a comprehensive analysis of the policies that govern cancer screening services for First Nations and Metis in Ontario and 2 other Canadian provinces; (2) a pilot analysis in a First Nations or Metis community of its readiness and the system's capacity for cancer screening that will used to develop a strategic plan to improve cancer screening in that community, an approach we anticipate can be replicated in other interested communities across Canada; (3) a rigorous program evaluation of 4 existing initiatives to improve cancer screening in Ontario First Nations or Metis communities, allowing for the identification of promising interventions that can be implemented in other First Nations and Metis communities in Canada; (4) a comprehensive action plan to improve cancer screening that has been developed with the very knowledge-users who are best positioned to effect change, thereby maximizing the potential that this comprehensive action plan will be implemented and will have an impact on cancer screening for FN and Metis in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Contraception Access Research Team - Contraception Cost-effectiveness Modeling (CART-CCM)
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTRACEPTION; COST-EFFECTIVENESS MODELLING; DECISION SUPPORT TOOLS; FAMILY PLANNING; SEXUAL HEALTH; SURVEY
Abstract-Résumé: Family planning is acknowledged to be one of the top ten public health advances of the millennium. Health policy supporting accessible family planning has proven value leading to population-level gains in terms of health equity in developed countries around the world. Canadian health care jurisdictions stand as one of the few among comparable countries that do not provide universal subsidized contraception. Canadian-context  tools to support evidence-informed policies relating to contraception are not currently available. Development requires data on Canadian specific pregnancy determinants, and on the relation of these factors to a broad range of determinants of health. Many of these parameters have not been measured among Canadian populations.   The Contraception Access Research Team (CART) brings together health system leaders, senior academic researchers from a broad range of disciplines, health service delivery professionals and stakeholder groups, to address BC's and Canada's most pressing family planning health service research questions.   CART proposes to undertake development of Canada's first Contraception Cost-effectiveness Model (CCM), using data from BC. The CART-CCM will be used to create decision-making tools capable of supporting evidence-informed policies for optimal contraception strategies in BC and for adaptation to Canadian provinces, territories and federal health jurisdictions.   At the end of this grant, our team of researchers and knowledge users will be positioned to more effectively evaluate policy interventions to improve contraception provision, with the ultimate aim of reducing sexual and reproductive health inequalities experienced by vulnerable subgroups across BC. Through CART partnerships, there is excellent potential for effective scaling up of the CART-CCM tools within the health system to monitor and evaluate investments made in this area not only in BC, but across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adverse Drug Event Reporting in PharmaNet to Improve Patient Safety and Inform Policy
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE DRUG EVENT REPORTING; COMMUNICATION ACROSS HEALTHCARE SECTORS; DRUG SAFETY; ELECTRONIC MEDICAL RECORDS; MEDICATION INFORMATION SYSTEMS; PHARMACOSURVEILLANCE; PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Medications are widely used to treat and prevent debilitating and fatal diseases. Over 73% of Canadians over the age of 65 use at least one prescription medication daily. As a result, adverse drug events (ADEs)-the harmful and unintended consequences of medications-are common, and cause 1.7 million emergency department visits in Canada each year. Many ADEs occur because patients are re-exposed to drugs that have previously caused problems, because information about ADEs is not effectively communicated between healthcare providers (e.g. between physicians and pharmacists) or across healthcare sectors (e.g. between hospitals and community pharmacies).   We have partnered with a broad range of stakeholders to design a new ADE reporting platform in PharmaNet, BC's provincial medication information system, so that front-line clinicians can communicate relevant ADE information between healthcare providers and across healthcare sectors. We will use this platform to collect data about ADEs for research and decision-making.  First, we will determine how a new electronic ADE reporting platform can be integrated into the existing workflow of emergency department healthcare workers. Second, we will determine what information needs to be captured so that the ADE reports are sufficiently detailed to support clinical decisions. Then, we will develop and implement an electronic ADE reporting platform, and will develop computerized alerts that pop up when physicians or pharmacists prescribe or dispense medications that have previously caused problems. Finally, we will evaluate the ADE reports in PharmaNet.  The new ADE reporting platform has a strong potential to make prescribing decisions safer, by warning healthcare providers of medications that have previously caused problems. By creating ADE reports that can be linked to other health data, we will support the data needs of researchers and decision makers to influence health programs and policy decisions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dosage CIN: A comprehensive analysis of gene dosage effects on genome stability
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMOSOME INSTABILITY; GENE AMPLIFICATION; GENE OVER-EXPRESSION; GENOME INSTABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a somatic genetic disease where the genetic changes occur spontaneously in one part of the body. While many of these genetic changes are known, exactly how these changes result in cancer remains to be uncovered. Our work focuses on finding genes that affect the stability of the genome, using the budding yeast as a model organism. Even though it is difficult to perceive what we have in common with yeast, many of the fundamental biological pathways that are essential for life are very well conserved from yeast to man. Yeast is an excellent model system, for ethical and logistical reasons, since we can perform experiments on yeast that are not possible in humans, such as exposing them to chemotherapy drugs and studying the effects of these drugs on every single gene in the yeast. We have used genetic screens to find genes when overproduced decrease the stability of the genome in yeast. Currently, we are extending this work in human cells. The ultimate goal is to find genetic changes that are shared between yeast and human cancers and then utilize these genetic changes to either make cancer more susceptible to the effects of chemotherapy or to identify new chemotherapeutics.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional neuroimaging of non-Invasive brain stimulation in Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN STIMULATION; COGNITION; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RECONANCE IMAGING; MEMORY; SCHIZOPHRENIA; TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Patients with schizophrenia have been shown to have cognitive deficits (such as problems with memory and attention), which have been demonstrated to be strong predictors of patient outcome and quality of life. As a result there has been an increased focus towards treatment methods designed to overcome these cognitive impairments.  A brain stimulation treatment called transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) works by sending a magnetic pulse through the scalp and has shown promise for improving cognitive deficits. TMS is non-invasive and well tolerated with few side effects. Forty patients will be given four weeks of TMS treatment, where we will observe whether cognitive abilities are improved. This study will also use brain imaging (functional magnetic resonance imaging, fMRI) to understand how activity within a patient's brain is changed by TMS. In particular, we are interested in determining if the pattern of brain activity is 'normalized' towards that of healthy controls, or if there is a compensation mechanism in which a different pattern of brain activity is observed. This will help us understand the cognitive deficits in patients and how we should go about treating them.  A second branch of research will use an innovative new research method called TMS-fMRI, in which we can measure changes in brain activity across a wide range of brain areas when we stimulate a specific region. This technique is technically challenging and has only been implemented in a few centers across the world. TMS-fMRI is a powerful method for understanding brain networks involved in specific tasks, such as memory. This method will be used to examine how neural networks in patients differ from those of controls when performing a memory task. This will put us on the forefront of an innovative and exciting new avenue of research into understanding cognitive deficits in schizophrenia, as well as setting Canada up as a world leader in the use of this innovative research technique.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pain communication in couples with chronic pain: Partner interactions and sex differences
Keywords-MotsClés: COUPLES; DISABILITY; HEALTH OUTCOMES; PAIN; PAIN COMMUNICATION; QUALITY OF LIFE; RELATIONSHIP DISTRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Having a partner with health problems, such as chronic pain (CP), can lead to relationship strain. Couples with relationship difficulties report having more physical health and mental health problems than couples in happy relationships.  Although everyone experiences pain, communicating about the pain can be difficult (e.g., due to dysfunctional aspects of the relationship). Being able to communicate pain is vital to good relationships. Poor verbal or non-verbal communication about pain in couples leads to more pain, mental health issues, and more negative emotions in partners. The quality of communication may also be influenced by the sex of the individual with chronic pain. Research in this area is mostly based on observation of couples discussing pain rather than through direct observation during the experience of pain, and sex differences are rarely taken into account. Couples in which one partner reports current CP and couples without CP will be studied. They will complete a safe, experimentally induced pain task where one partner will place his/her hand in ice water and will rate his/her level of pain during the task. The other partner will observe and rate the level of pain he/she believes that his/her partner is experiencing. During the task, both partners' facial expressions will be video-taped for later examination of emotions or pain-related facial expressions, such as grimacing. This research will have important implications for the development of the current understanding of pain communication in couples with CP.  Moreover, the clarification of maladaptive communication patterns in couples with CP will have direct implications for interventions for couples coping with CP. Finally, this study will lead to the development of strategies that could prevent relationship distress, and the associated negative mental health and physical health outcomes, in couples with CP.

TitreApplicationTitle: Managed Alcohol Programs:  Implementation and Effectiveness
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL; HARM REDUCTION; HOMELESSNESS; HOUSING
Abstract-Résumé: Canadians with unstable housing may also experience problems with substance use, which can create barriers to accessing temporary or stable accommodation. Problems may be compounded by use of hazardous non-beverage alcohol such as rubbing alcohol, methanol, mouth wash and hand sanitizers. In Toronto, a Managed Alcohol Program (MAP) was initiated in 1996 following a coronial enquiry into the freezing deaths of three drinkers who had been unable to access to shelter accommodation. Similar programs in four other sites, MAPs involve the provision of accommodation alongside controlled access to alcohol to replace non-beverage alcohol and reduce heavy drinking episodes for individuals for whom abstinence treatment has not been successful. One published study of a Canadian MAP has indicated promising results, notably fewer emergency department presentations, improved access to health care and reduced alcohol consumption. These programs are controversial and not well researched. This application seeks funding for a rigourous evaluation of health and social outcomes for over 200 program participants across five Canadian MAP sites in comparison with similar individuals drawn from nearby non-MAP agencies. Benefits, potential harms and best practices will be investigated by accessing health and police records, conducting brief interviews monthly for up to 2 years and in-depth interviews with clients and program staff.

TitreApplicationTitle: A population-based study on the effect of primary care reforms on health services utilization and quality of care outcomes among vulnerable children in Quebec, Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEALTHCARE REFORM; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PEDIATRICS; PRIMARY CARE; QUALITY OF CARE; QUEBEC; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Children from low income families are often less healthy than children from wealthier backgrounds. Studies have shown how primary care is important to improve health. Primary care includes visits to a doctor for regular health check ups. When a child receives care from a primary care doctor, they may have fewer visits to the emergency room or hospital. The benefit of primary care may be even greater for children in poverty or children with chronic diseases such as asthma. Since 2002, Quebec introduced new ways for family physicians to practice in groups known as family medicine groups (FMGs) or network clinics. These groups allow doctors to share duties. They provide patients with easier access to more complete medical care. Across Canada, similar changes have taken place, referred to as primary care reform. At the moment, we know little about the primary care of children in Quebec: how many have a doctor, who they are seeing, and if it makes any difference who sees them. We do not know if FMGs or network clinics are providing better care to children in poverty or suffering from asthma compared to other types of primary care providers. In our study, we will use provincial databanks containing all visits to doctors and hospitals for children in Quebec. Using a group representing all children and a group of children with asthma, we will look at where they go for primary care. We will see if children seen by certain primary care providers have fewer visits to the emergency room and hospital stays. We will then see if there are differences between low and high income children. Our study is essential to the health of children and the healthcare system. We will see if primary care reform has reduced the large differences in health between poor and rich children. With our team of policy and decision makers, we will advise the government on what kind of care children need and how to plan future resources.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sustaining Recovery: Supporting the Transition from Specialized Services to Community-based Primary Care for At-Risk Youth Who Have Experienced Early Psychosis
Keywords-MotsClés: AT-RISK YOUTH; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; COMMUNITY BASED PRIMARY MENTAL HEALTH CARE; EARLY PSYCHOSIS; EVIDENCE BASED MENTAL HEALTH INTERVENTIONS; MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING; TRANSITIONAL CARE; TRANSITIONS COACHING; YOUTH MENTAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: The onset of a mental illness in young adulthood can have consequences for educational achievement, career opportunities, relationships, and a young person's sense of self. Given these consequences, the importance of early intervention for a first episode psychosis is critical. Early intervention programs are effective. However, the question of how to best support recovery moving from early psychosis programs to discharge to the community is concerning. Research shows that the gains made in early intervention programs are lost once care is transferred to the community. To the best of our knowledge, there are no intervention studies that address ideal follow-up care in primary health care settings following discharge. The challenge is to determine how best to continue with the progress made in early intervention programs. Our research proposes to develop and evaluate an intervention to support the recovery process for youth experiencing psychosis, as they move from specialized services to primary care services. These interventions include two proven approaches: Motivational Interviewing and Cognitive Behaviour Therapy that assist clients to manage their illness and recovery. A Transitions Coach will also work closely with youth and their family, health professionals and peer supports by acting a resource. The youth will also be involved in a Transition Recovery Eight Week Group to help with challenges.  Youth will be divided into two groups. The first group will have 180 participants who will be recruited before the intervention starts. The second group will also have 180 participants who will be recruited after the intervention starts.  The program will be evaluated and the results will be shared with the youth, staff caring for them, health care administrators, and policy makers in order to ensure that recovery continues after discharge from specialized services. The research will be widely shared so individuals and organizations can benefit from the findings.

TitreApplicationTitle: Facilitating Personalized Breast Cancer Therapy via Early Prediction of Patient Responses using Non-invasive Hybrid Imaging Biomarkers
Keywords-MotsClés: EARLY PROGNOSIS; HYBRID IMAGING BIOMARKERS; LOCALLY ADVANCED BREAST CANCER; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; PHOTO-ACOUSTIC IMAGING; QUANTITATIVE ULTRASOUND; SALVAGE THERAPY; SONOELASTOGRAPHY; TEXTURAL ANALYSIS; TREATMENT RESPONSE MONITORING
Abstract-Résumé: This project focuses on developing a new treatment monitoring technique for locally advanced breast cancer. It investigates the coincident use of sonoelastography, quantitative ultrasound and photo-acoustic imaging coupled with textural analysis techniques for the early evaluation of ultimate patient response to such treatment modalities as chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Such early evaluation can be effectively used to improve treatments for patients on an individual basis. Results from this study will permit oncologists to either continue with their initially prescribed treatment regimen or modify the treatment as needed when no response is observed.  The ultimate goal here is to use this method of treatment monitoring to personalize cancer therapies and permit an objective rational change of an ineffective treatment to a more effective one early on during treatment period (within days), as opposed to the time point when it is potentially too late (after several months).  Personalized cancer therapy is expected to offer a considerably better prognosis for cancer patients.  In addition to higher survival rates, it can also help to substantially improve the quality of life for patients during and after their treatment.
