TitreApplicationTitle: "The dangers of lying in bed": How do sedentary behaviours impact the health of hospitalized patients and how can we reduce them?
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; EXERCISE; FRAILTY; HOSPITAL; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SEDENTARY BEHAVIOUR
Abstract-Résumé: Canadian older adults are sedentary for more than 70% of their waking hours. Behaviours such as lying in bed and sitting down to watch TV are now acknowledged as independent health risks even in people who are otherwise active. The risk from prolonged lying/sitting might be even more profound in older adults who become hospitalized. Compared to young people, older adults are more often admitted to hospitals and stay for a longer time. During hospitalization, many spend much of their time lying in bed awake, even when they can walk independently. Hospitalized younger adults experience physiological and cognitive declines, even during short bed rest, and these declines are even greater among older adults. This puts older patients' post-hospital independence at risk. Despite the adverse outcomes associated with bed rest, no comprehensive assessment of sedentary time is done during hospitalization and there is no standard of care for reducing it. It may be possible to improve hospital outcomes in older patients using light physical activities (e.g. standing, walking). These activities could be beneficial even amongst the sickest and most frail, and may help them maintain their independence.   The purpose of this proposed research is to examine whether time spent lying down/sitting affects the health of hospitalized older adults and what physical activity interventions may be helpful in countering these effects. Accelerometers, a state-of-the art device, will be used to monitor the daily sedentary time of older patients during their hospital stay. We expect to determine the minimum sedentary time to reduce the adverse outcomes associated with bed rest during hospitalization. We will also examine the impact of replacing lying down/sitting time with physical activity on health outcomes. For example, we will examine whether substituting 20 minutes/day lying down with 20 minutes/day standing or moving is associated with shorted length of stay during hospitalization

TitreApplicationTitle: Global analysis of the transcriptional circuitry regulating Candida glabrata biofilm formation
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR SIGNALLING; FUNGAL EVOLUTION; GENOMICS; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; MICROBIOLOGY; MOLECULAR GENETICS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Due to its intrinsic resistance to commonly used antifungal drugs, Candida glabrata has rapidly grown in prevalence over recent decades and is now second to Candida albicans as the leading cause of fungal infection in humans. Candida species are commensal yeasts commonly associated with the gut microbiota, however, they can cause life-threatening disease in immunocompromised patients. Treatment of infection is hampered by the ability of certain species including C. glabrata to form biofilms on implanted medical devices including urinary and venous catheters, and artificial joints. Biofilms are extremely resistant to both antifungal drugs and mechanical perturbation and once medical devices are infected, they must often be removed to avoid dissemination of the infection into the blood stream as mortality rates approach 50% for invasive Candida infection. The goal of this research is to elucidate the transcriptional programs, including the regulators and their target genes, which allow C. glabrata to form biofilms through genome-wide approaches. This research will reveal the regulatory networks required for C. glabrata biofilm formation and provide key insights into both novel and conserved mechanisms of biofilm development. This research may directly reveal novel therapeutic targets and comprise new treatment strategies that save human lives through the prevention and treatment of fungal biofilms.

TitreApplicationTitle: Pathophysiological association between epicardial fat accumulation and coronary heart disease-are brown adipocytes the missing link?
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BROWN ADIPOCYTES; CELL CULTURE; CORONARY HEART DISEASE; EPICARDIAL ADIPOSE TISSUE; INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: During obesity, excess fat accumulation can be seen around the heart in a depot named epicardial adipose tissue (EAT), which is thought to contribute to the development of coronary heart disease. However, besides the white fat cells that constitute this depot,  brown adipocytes are also present in this depot. These cells are different from the white fat cells as they can burn fatty acids and also promote an anti-inflammatory environment. In the proposed research, I want to explore if the presence of brown adipocytes can support an anti-atherogenic environment around the heart and hence reduce coronary heart disease. I will address this hypothesis by first establishing animal models that possess EAT and then stimulating this depot to have more brown adipocytes. Next the interaction between EAT (with-and without- brown adipocytes) and the heart cells will be studied using cell culture. Human EAT will be studied to ascertain its nature and regulation. Overall, my studies will help to establish if EAT shares a causal association with the coronary heart disease. Additionally, my work will help to determine if brown adipocytes within EAT can be used as a therapeutic target to manage CVD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving quality of care during transport of sick neonates: A national collaborative partnership for outcome improvement and system enhancement
Keywords-MotsClés: NEWBORN; NEWBORN DISEASES; PATIENT OUTCOMES; PATIENT TRANSFER; PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY; QUALITY INDICATORS
Abstract-Résumé: Since the 1970s, neonatal intensive care in Canada has been mostly regionalized where high risk infants are born and managed in high risk centres for optimal outcomes. However, regionalization has been challenging as unplanned births in a non-high risk centre occur in 30% of at-risk newborns in Canada and inter-facility transfer of such neonates to tertiary neonatal intensive care units (NICU) by expert transport teams is required. Neonatal transport is a resource intense service for sick infants with a major cost to the health care system. Across Canada, 15 inter-facility neonatal transport teams are responsible for the transport of almost 5000 newborns annually. Among the teams, there are wide variations in transport processes and there is no consensus on the standards for performance. The Canadian Neonatal Network (CNN) and its sister network, the Canadian Neonatal Follow Up Network, collect data from NICU admission to 18 months post NICU discharge. While the processes of care during transport prior to NICU admission are major contributors to outcomes, currently no mechanism exists to evaluate these practices. We know that the outcomes of transported neonates are not as good as infants born at high risk centers, and that there is room for improvement. We propose to develop a Canadian Neonatal Transport Network (CNTN) under the umbrella of the CNN, to fill this major gap in the assessment of a full service health care system in the continuum from birth to childhood. The CNTN will pool the expertise available among the transport programs across Canada to share knowledge, generate new knowledge, facilitate collaboration, and disseminate knowledge, to improve outcomes. We will develop key indicators to evaluate the performance of the transport teams and develop national guidelines. These standards will be the catalyst to guide changes to the organization and delivery of neonatal transport systems to improve outcomes in this highly vulnerable group of neonates.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Cardiovascular Health Awareness Program for the South Asian Community in York Region: Assessing volunteer participation and the gender and ethno-specific impacts
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE; PRIMARY CARE; SOUTH ASIAN COMMUNITY
Abstract-Résumé: South Asians are known to have a significant higher prevalence of hypertension than Caucasians. They are also at an elevated risk for premature coronary artery disease and are 3 to 5 times more likely to have diabetes than Caucasians due to an increased prevalence of abdominal obesity, insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome. The Cardiovascular Health Awareness Program (CHAP) is a patient-centred, interdisciplinary, multi-pronged, community-led CVD and stroke prevention and management program targeted at older adults. We propose to use a participatory research approach to adapt CHAP to the needs and realities of a South Asian community in the York region (Ontario), and develop, in partnership with knowledge-users, an integrated knowledge translation plan to disseminate the findings in order to have an impact on programs and policy. The main research question of this project is: What adaptation strategies to the Cardiovascular Health Awareness Program (CHAP) should be put in place in order to successfully prevent and manage chronic disease among the South Asian community? More specifically, how can we address gender and ethno-specific impacts? What are the best strategies to optimize the recruitment, retention and health promotion role of health champions among the South Asian Community?

TitreApplicationTitle: Transforming mental health services: A participatory mixed methods study to promote and evaluate the implementation of recovery-oriented care
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTHROPOLOGY; ETHICS; MENTAL HEALTH; PSYCHIATRY; SOCIAL NETWORK
Abstract-Résumé: Since its creation in 2007, the Mental Health Commission of Canada (MHCC) has worked collaboratively across all provinces to publish a new framework for a Canadian mental health strategy. This federal document has now been mandated as policy for implementation, between 2012-2017. The proposed strategies have been written into provincial health plans, hospital accreditation standards, and the annual objectives of psychiatric departments and community organizations.  The principles for recovery and wellbeing outlined in the framework are based on both values for care and research evidence. The core premise, as exemplified by the MHCC's ongoing process, is to empower persons with mental illness and their families to become participants in designing their own care. These services should be accessible to all, address health promotion as well as illness intervention, while meeting the needs of a diverse Canadian population. However, these recovery principles do not come with a guide for actual implementation in different contexts. This three-year research project (2013-2016) proposes a participatory approach to implementing these principles in a Montreal institute of psychiatry, which serves a highly diverse Canadian, and immigrant population. This project will be conducted in multiple phases: 1) The creation of a partnership amongst health care professionals, researchers, hospital administrators, family organizations and persons with mental illness who are served at this institute, 2) An evaluation of the current attitudes and services towards recovery in mental health, 3) Engagement in participatory approaches to changing attitudes, designing services, and applying the MHCC principles in a manner tailored to the institute's culture and community, 4) Evaluating the outcomes  in relation to the framework guidelines, and finally, (5) Provide applied guidelines for the successful implementation of mental health policy while respecting local complexities and differences.

TitreApplicationTitle: Seasonal Labour Migration and Intra-Household Health Statuses in the Krishnagiri district of Tamil Nadu, India
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-ENGAGED RESEARCH; INTRA-HOUSEHOLD HEALTH STATUS; MIXED METHODS APPROACH; POPULATION HEALTH; SEASONAL LABOUR MIGRATION; SOCIETAL & CULTURAL DIMENSIONS OF HEALTH; SOUTH ASIA
Abstract-Résumé: Seasonal labour migration represents a critical livelihood strategy for millions of rural households throughout India including the state of Tamil Nadu. However, there is limited research that investigates the effects of seasonal labour migration on migrant household health statuses in India. The research question that this project will address is how do patterns of seasonal labour migration impact the health status of different members of migrant households who are small-scale rural farmers in the Krishnagiri district of Tamil Nadu, India. More specifically, this project has three overarching objectives which are to investigate the impact of seasonal labour migration on the overall health status of individual migrants; to examine how seasonal labour migration impacts the overall health statuses of household members who do not seasonally migrate; and to describe the major health problems that constrain agricultural production and community development in this setting. This project will elicit participation from community members in its design and implementation and use several methods including interviews, focus groups, and surveys. Beyond filling several gaps in the academic literature, this project has a strong applied orientation and policy focus. A stronger understanding of the connections among seasonal labour migration, health, and agricultural production is a critical step in the development of improved health policy, food security policy, and inclusive social policy that grasps the complexity of seasonal labour migration in this context and in other areas throughout South Asia.  For these reasons, this study clearly connects to the mandate of CIHR to promote research that addresses the global health concerns of marginalized populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Développer une innovation clinique en oncologie: pour un meilleur continuum de soins et de services pour les patients atteints de cancer.
Keywords-MotsClés: IMPLEMENTATION SCIENCE; INNOVATION CLINIQUE; INTERDISCIPLINARITE; ONCOLOGIE; PLANIFICATION DE CONGE; PORTAIL INTERACTIF WEB2; RECHERCHE COLLABORATIVE; RECHERCHE QUALITATIVE; SCIENCES INFIRMIERES; TRANSFERT DES CONNAISSANCES
Abstract-Résumé: La planification de conge en oncologie constitue un enjeu majeur du continuum de soins pour ameliorer la qualite de soins offerts aux patients. Au Canada, aucune norme ne regit la planification de conge. Pourtant, les ecrits soulignent l'importance de l'education aux patients, de la coordination des services et de l'implantation de suivis reguliers pour assurer une planification de conge optimale. Une meilleure planification de conge peut reduire la duree des sejours a l'hopital et eviter les readmissions. Afin de mieux utiliser les resultats des recherches sur la planification de conge en oncologie, cette etude  vise a developper une innovation clinique interactive, le « Portail d'echange de savoirs » (PES) pour favoriser l'acces rapide aux meilleures pratiques en planification de conge en oncologie. Le but de ce projet est de documenter le processus de developpement du Portail d'echange de savoirs et d'explorer ses effets sur l'implantation de pratiques exemplaires chez les professionnels de la sante et sur l'experience de sante des patients. La recherche se deroulera dans 6 milieux cliniques  et permettra de connaitre les elements facilitants l'integration de nouvelles pratiques et les difficultes rencontrees. Des patients participeront activement a toutes les etapes de la recherche afin d'integrer leurs preoccupations. Cette recherche vise a contribuer au developpement de nouveaux savoirs entre les professionnels, les patients, leurs proches, les chercheurs et les decideurs et a offrir de meilleurs soins et services aux patients. Elle permettra de reduire l'utilisation de services non necessaires et les couts de sante. Les decideurs politiques participants au projet pourront faire evoluer les politiques de sante en s'appuyant sur les resultats obtenus et influencer les decisions prises dans les organisations de soins tout en contribuant aux meilleures prises de decisions par les professionnels de la sante, les patients et leurs proches.

TitreApplicationTitle: L'optimisation de l'utilisation des données de performance pour la gestion et la gouverne des systèmes et organisations de santé
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNICATION; DIFFUSION; PERFORMANCE; SYSTEME; EVALUATION
Abstract-Résumé: Depuis plusieurs annees, l'Institut canadien d'information sur la sante (ICIS) et le Commissaire a la sante et au bien-etre du Quebec (CSBE) produisent des donnees de performance pertinentes a la prise de decision entourant l'organisation et la prestation de service de soins de sante. Malgre l'energie deployee pour fournir ces informations aux differents publics cibles, dont les decideurs, l'utilisation  des systemes d'informations sur la performance  demeure limitee et la situation doit etre corrigee. L'acces a des donnees de performance valides et pertinentes devrait permettre aux decideurs et acteurs d'identifier les forces et les faiblesses de leurs organisations, d'etablir des objectifs d'amelioration de la performance et de prendre des actions en ce sens. Notre projet s'adresse directement a cette problematique de l'utilisation des donnees par differents publics cibles. L'objectif principal est de developper des strategies de communication novatrices qui surmontent les barrieres a l'utilisation afin d'optimiser l'usage des connaissances de performance dans les decisions de gestion et de gouverne des systemes et organisations de sante. Le projet propose permettra d'identifier et d'analyser quelles sont les strategies actuelles de communication utilisees par deux organisations de production de connaissance sur la performance (CSBE et CIHI), quels sont leur niveau de penetration dans les publics-cibles et leur impact aupres de ces publics; d'elaborer et de construire differents outils ou strategies permettant d'optimiser l'utilisation de l'information dans les publics-cibles et d'evaluer les outils et strategies proposees afin d'en mesurer les impacts sur l'utilisation des connaissance sur la performance.

TitreApplicationTitle: AFFORD - Appropriate eFfective eFficient Oncology Reimbursement Decisions
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER DRUG FUNDING; GUIDANCE FOR POLICY; MULTI-CRITERIA DECISIONS; USE OF ECONOMIC ANALYSES
Abstract-Résumé: Two out of five Canadians will experience cancer during their lives. Despite benefits such as a longer and higher quality of life, most patients cannot afford cancer drugs. Canadians rely on government to fund the most appropriate drugs for them. Governments have limited budgets; Provinces choose whether or not to fund new drugs.   Decisions, often based on recommendations of regional committees, have varied across jurisdictions; drugs available in one Province are often unavailable in another. Recently, the pan Canadian Oncology Drug Review (pCODR) was formed to increase consistency by making recommendations relevant to all Canadian regions.  pCODR and Provincial committees rely on multiple criteria: reports of clinical effects, economic costs, ethical principles, patient perspectives, etc. Studies show that committees experience challenges, two of which we address: (i) committee members as knowledge users have different expectations of what economic analyses should offer compared to producers of economic analyses; (ii) there is no explicit, standardized method to balance multiple criteria in the decision process.   pCODR has identified a need for a guidance tool to use in the decision process. We will develop this tool from our analysis of current choices of pCODR committees, their priorities, and their needs. Using mixed methods we will assess: (i) the gap in expectations between producers and users of economic analyses; and (ii) current approaches to weighing multiple criteria. Using a round-table discussion and iterative interviews we will evaluate reactions of committee members to the analysis of their own choices. Using thematic analysis, we will develop the guidance tool and an academic conceptual framework.   The impact will be far-reaching; pCODR recommendations to all jurisdictions will be arrived at in a systematic, standardized, and transparent manner. Patients will better understand why a specific drug was or was not recommended for funding.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modifications neurométaboliques et microstructurales à la suite d'une commotion cérébrale chez les athlètes féminines.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHLETES FEMININES; COMMOTION CEREBRALE; IMAGERIE PAR DIFFUSION DE TENSEURS; IMAGERIE PAR RESONANCE MAGNETIQUE SPECTROSCOPIQUE; METABOLISME CEREBRALE; REHABILITATION; TRAUMATISME AXONAL; TRAUMATOLOGIE SPORTIVE
Abstract-Résumé: De recentes estimations situent entre 1,6 et 3,8 millions le nombre de commotions cerebrales reliees au sport annuellement, aux Etats-Unis seulement. Malgre ces donnees epidemiologiques alarmantes et la presence d'alterations neurophysiologiques chroniques, les impacts a court et a long terme au niveau neurochimique et microstructural sont encore peu connus et pourraient expliquer les effets deleteres des commotions sur le profil neurophysiologique des athletes. A ce sujet, des etudes recentes utilisant l'imagerie par resonance magnetique spectroscopique (IRMs), permettant la detection des modifications neurochimiques, ont demontre des alterations neurometaboliques dans la phase aigue et chronique. De plus, les etudes en traumatologie sportive utilisant l'imagerie par diffusion de tenseurs (IDT) qui fournit des informations sur l'atteinte des faisceaux de matiere blanche, ont egalement mises en evidence des alterations aigues et chroniques dans le profil de diffusion de plusieurs faisceaux de matiere blanche chez des athletes commotionnes. Cependant, aucune etude n'a evalue specifiquement le profil d'alterations post-commotionnel a l'aide de l'IRMs et l'IDT chez des athletes feminines malgre une symptomatologie plus importante et une rehabilitation plus longue chez les femmes. De plus, peu d'etudes portent sur les athletes feminines ayant subi une commotion cerebrale malgre une augmentation du taux de participation des femmes dans les sports. Cette etude a donc pour but d'evaluer les effets d'une commotion reliee au sport par l'utilisation de l'IRMs et de l'IDT chez des athletes feminines. En evaluant ces aspects chez les athletes de sexe feminin, cette etude permettra de mieux comprendre les effets specifiques d'une commotion chez cette population. De facon plus importante, cette etude est une demarche de plus afin d'adapter les interventions et les traitements offerts aux athletes feminines en plus d'assurer un retour au jeu plus securitaire pour ces dernieres.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the process of policy formulation and analysing implications for health promotion: the case of national policy on global health
Keywords-MotsClés: GLOBAL HEALTH; HEALTH IN ALL POLICIES; HEALTH PROMOTION; KEY INFORMANT INTERVIEWS; MULTIPLE CASE STUDY; PUBLIC POLICY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Today, health concerns occupy a prominent place in the realm of global issues and priorities.  Health on a global scale has surpassed the domain of international organisations such as WHO, and penetrated the interests of national policy makers outside the formal health sector. This is demonstrated by recent discussions in the UN General Assembly on the prevention of non-communicable diseases. The effects of globalization have increased the interdependence of countries, therefore adding a global dimension to national policy on health.  Public policies are recognised as instruments with potential to improve population health. The field of health promotion is particularly interested in how equity and a positive concept of health can support the development of national policy on global health.  This research will aim to better understand what role ideas about the promotion of health have in this newly emerging type of policy.  By exploring cases from the United Kingdom and Switzerland, the first two countries to adopt such a policy, the research will examine these policies in terms of their objectives, their resources, the actors involved, and their actions.  It will examine what opportunities exist for the values of health promotion, such as equity, to influence these policies.  To examine this, I will analyse publically available documents and conduct interviews with key actors. This research will contribute to a better understanding of what ideas and values are considered in the face of the challenge to make global health a concern for national public action.  The relevance of this research will be its contribution to reflecting on how national public policy can contribute to global health equity.

TitreApplicationTitle: These women's work: Exploring the meaning of work from the perspective of HIV-positive Black women who live in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: AFRICAN DIASPORA/BLACK RACE; DECOLONIZING METHODOLOGIES; EMPLOYMENT; GENDER; HIV/AIDS; QUALITATIVE METHODOLOGIES; RACE; SOCIAL SCIENCE; WOMEN; WORK
Abstract-Résumé: For people living with HIV, meaningful work engagement has been found to improve mental and physical well-being, and can contribute to self-sufficiency. However, for HIV-positive Black women, meaningful work can be a difficult goal to achieve. Black women are disproportionally impacted by the HIV epidemic. HIV-positive Black women are more likely to be unemployed, underemployed or precariously employed than their HIV-negative or non-racialized counterparts. Furthermore, preliminary evidence suggests that ideas about work contained in Canadian policies are not always well matched to the realities of HIV-positive Black women's lives. Given the links between work and one's well-being and in response to knowledge gaps, this study will explore experiences of paid and unpaid work for HIV-positive Black women. The studies goals are: 1) to explore experiences of work and its health impacts from the perspectives of HIV-positive Black women; and 2) to examine the points of connection and disconnection between women's work narratives, and employment and social policies designed to support them in meaningful work engagement. An integrated KTE plan using multiple forms of dissemination (e.g., scientific papers, policy papers, arts-based approaches, community forums, social media etc.) will ensure that findings are transferred to, exchanged with, and enhanced by knowledge users who can bring them into action. This project examines the intersection of multiple social determinants of health (gender, race, HIV status) in the context of work life, and it will focus on determinants (employment and income) known to impact the health outcomes of racialized women. Additionally, this study addresses a priority population for HIV research, and uses KTE approaches that can foster knowledge into action. Theoretical frameworks developed from this study can inform work-related policies and add to the body of social science literature on decolonized methodologies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the Antiviral Mechanism of Natual Killer cells during HSV-2 Infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL HANDLING; CELL SIGNALLING; ELISAS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS TYPE 2; INTERFERONS; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; NITRIC OXIDE; VIRAL TITERING
Abstract-Résumé: Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) is one of the most prevalent sexually transmitted infections across the globe. As the main cause of genital herpes, it presents a large burden on the health care system. Furthermore, it has been implicated in facilitating the infection, transmission, and disease progression of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), a deadly chronic viral infection with no known cure. Therefore, it is imperative to develop an effective vaccine and treatment strategy against HSV-2. We are investigating a specific immune response responsible for controlling early HSV-2 infection. Natural killer (NK) cells are immune cells that respond rapidly to HSV-2 infection and are a key element in controlling the early stages of infection. The method of activating these NK cells against HSV-2 and how they control infection are not fully known. Type I interferon is an immune component produced by our bodies that initiates an immune response against viral infection. In the case of HSV-2, type I interferon appears to be necessary for the activation, regulation, and function of NK cells against HSV-2 infection. Once the NK cells are activated, there is evidence suggesting that they can then increase the production of nitric oxide (a multi-functional molecule that is produced by the body; NO) at the site of infection. Increased production of NO may prevent the virus from reproducing, which can limit the symptoms and spread of HSV-2. In determining the mechanism of this specific immune response, we can develop therapies based on enhancing this process to control or prevent HSV-2 infection. If we can minimize the symptoms and spread of HSV-2, we will be able to improve the quality of life for those living with genital herpes and lower the HSV-2 related burden on the healthcare system. Furthermore, a treatment for HSV-2 could lower the rate of HIV transmission and improve the outcome for those who are currently infected with HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ethical frameworks to assess health technology: A theoretical and empirical study
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS THEORY; COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT THEORY; HEALTH POLICY ANALYSIS; HEALTH TECHNOLOGY ASSESSMENT; INDUCTIVE ANALYSIS; PARTICIPANT-OBSERVER DESIGN; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH METHODOLOGY; SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: I will explore how ethical frameworks as decision-making tools are utilized by governmental and non-governmental agencies to assess health technologies for public funding. My research will focus on whether these frameworks achieve their designed aim of providing the relevant social values perspective of the communities affected by the technologies, and how social values can be framed and utilized in this policy context to meaningfully reflect community interests. This question of 'what kind of material objects should one make and accept?' preoccupies policy makers because our commitments to technologies shape not only future technology but the contours of society itself. The ideals that shape a society emerge in part from the technologies it employs. Limited qualitative research has been conducted on this topic in Canada and globally, although the need for this perspective is what gave rise to the field of health technology assessment fifty years ago.  My research will address a gap in the foundational theory and implementation of this influential area of health policy by outlining the regulatory/policy and funding context in which HTA is currently practiced, and by comprehensively describing how it is conducted in Canada, focusing on a provincial (Ontario Health Assessment Technology Advisory Committee - OHTAC) and national (Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health - CADTH) program.  I will use the qualitative participant-observer method, together with focused interviews, to describe and interpret stakeholder views on the nature and justifiability of policies and practices in this area, and use inductive analysis to relate these findings to relevant themes in the areas of science and technology ethics, community engagement theory, and policy studies. Finally, I will propose a model for incorporating social values and ethical expertise into decision-making about health technology that can be utilized as efficiently and effectively as other HTA criteria.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Investigation of High Fertility Rates and Local Perspectives of Community-Based Family Planning Programs in northern Ghana
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; CONTRACEPTION; FAMILY PLANNING; INTERNATIONAL HEALTH; MEDICAL ANTHROPOLOGY; MIXED METHODS; REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Family planning programs provide access to contraceptives and education, which allows couples and individuals to limit the number of children they have. These programs provide a wide range of benefits, especially for people in developing areas of the world, where access to contraceptives and reproductive health education has shown to increase reproductive health, decrease poverty and empower women. However, programs in sub-Saharan Africa, where women have on average 5.5 births per lifetime, have been less successful. One of the barriers to gaining a good understanding of family planning programs in sub-Saharan Africa is the reliance on survey-based models of research and the exclusion of participants in program evaluations. This research in Navrongo, Ghana, which has served as a major site for developing family planning programs in sub-Saharan Africa, will use anthropological methods to investigate the social and biological factors that affect contraceptive use and the acceptability of family planning programs from the perspectives of participants. In particular the effectiveness of community-based family planning programs, delivered through community health workers and community-organizations, and promoted as culturally-acceptable and accessible, will be evaluated. Data will be collected using a variety of methods, including open-ended interviews. This research will reveal the multiplicity of factors influencing family planning in Navrongo, filling a substantial gap in our knowledge about family planning in Ghana and West Africa. The views of participants on community-based family planning programs recorded will determine whether these programs offer culturally sensitive, effective and accessible healthcare and will offer recommendations for delivering and evaluating global health programs in developing regions, more generally.

TitreApplicationTitle: The development, implementation and evaluation of a health systems guidance workbook: Supporting the contextualization of the World Health Organization's 'Optimizing the delivery of key interventions to attain Millennium Development Goals 4 and 5' (Optimize4MNH) guidance at the national level
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE STUDY; EVIDENCE-BASED GUIDANCE; HEALTH SYSTEM ASSESSMENT; HEALTH SYSTEMS STRENGTHENING; INTERNATIONAL GUIDANCE CONTEXTUALIZATION; KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE; POLITICAL SYSTEM ASSESSMENT; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SURVEY
Abstract-Résumé: Many low- and middle-income countries around the world have poor health system infrastructures and few resources.  Using research-based international guidance, such as recommendations from the World Health Organization, can help countries improve their health systems and the health of their people in an effective and acceptable way.  However, creating health policy to change health systems is a complex process. And, most guidance documents do not include ways to help countries shape these recommendations to fit their specific needs, especially with regards to their political and health systems.  The World Health Organization is currently working on guidance to improve access to key prevention and treatment measures, through the support and training of health professionals, to help improve the health of mothers and newborns in low- and middle-income countries (the Optimize4MNH guidance).  This study looks at the process of creating and testing the use of a workbook to help decision-makers at the national level adapt these international recommendations to the needs and realities of their respective countries.

TitreApplicationTitle: Feasibility Study and Experimental Evaluation of Microwave Tomographic Imaging for In Vivo Characterization of Tissue as a Diagnostic Technique for Human Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST IMAGING; CANCER; CLINICAL TRIALS; MICROWAVE TOMOGRAPHY; NANOPARTICLES
Abstract-Résumé: Microwave tomography (MWT) is a promising low-cost, portable alternative or complementary biomedical diagnostic technique for conventional soft-tissue imaging modalities. MWT uses microwave scattering measurements in a safe, non-ionizing frequency range of a few hundred megahertz up to a few gigahertz to quantitatively reconstruct the bulk electrical properties, i.e., the permittivity and effective conductivity, of the tissue being imaged with or without the use of a contrast agent. These frequency-dependent properties are not only unique to different tissue types in the human body but also vary with the tissue's physiological state, offering a new quantifiable factor in the diagnosis and investigation of pathological conditions; human breast imaging applications of MWT are well established and a number of promising pilot studies have already been completed.  This proposed study will first explore the use of MWT in relatively unexplored areas of diagnostic medicine, focusing on different anatomical regions of the human body and detectable changes in their bulk electrical properties attributed to physiological distress or abnormality. A corollary to this research will focus on the use of magnetic nanoparticles, a synthetic contrast agent, for contrast-enhanced microwave imaging. MWT will then be experimentally evaluated  through the development of a prototype system designed specifically for breast imaging. Testing of this system will be undertaken using non-biological breast phantoms containing synthetic tissue-mimicking materials with dielectric properties similar to their biological analogues. The experimental component of the feasibility study will culminate in a series of clinical human breast imaging trials involving at least sixteen healthy volunteers using the newly-developed system, without intent to detect any particular breast pathology.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Step Forward for STEPS: An Investigation of the Neural and Behavioural Responses to a Novel Treatment for Functional Outcome in Schizophrenia
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL INTERVENTION; COMMUNICATION; DISABILITY; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC IMAGING; NEURAL CORRELATES; QUALITY OF LIFE; SCHIZOAFFECTIVE DISORDER; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SOCIAL FUNCTIONING
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a serious mental illness characterized by hallucinations, delusions, cognitive deficits, and disorganized behaviour. Disorganized speech has long been recognized as a core feature of the disorder; it does not respond to pharmacological medication and is thought to perpetuate stigma, as it is one of the most salient symptoms of psychosis. Disorganized speech is present across the course of schizophrenia and is a limiter of functioning in domains of social skills, academic achievement, and workplace success. Thus, disordered speech is a challenging barrier on the road to true recovery. However, any type of treatment has been almost completely ignored and we know very little about the malleability of this devastating symptom. I will address this gap in the research by conducting a large-scale multi-site randomized controlled trial to evaluate a treatment that I developed entitled Structured Therapy for the Enhancement of Purposeful Speech (STEPS). STEPS is a novel behavioural treatment designed to increase goal-directed speech and promote gains in interpersonal skills. Treatment incorporates asking participants to engage in conversations and correcting speech errors in real-time as they occur. Replicating and extending the results from our efficacy study, I hypothesize that immediate feedback in this fashion will shape organization of thoughts resulting in a decrease in disordered speech. During STEPS, individuals will practice their newly acquired communication skills in a social setting allowing for generalization to everyday community behaviour. With better communication skills individuals will be able to better advocate for themselves and build social connections thereby increasing quality of life. Through this study we will determine whether disorganized speech can be remediated and further understand how these improvements may be transferred to real-world behaviour to better the lives of the millions of North Americans afflicted by schizophrenia.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the effectiveness of 6-month Isoniazid Preventive Therapy amongst people living with HIV in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
Keywords-MotsClés: HIV-TB CO-INFECTION; ISONIAZID PREVENTIVE THERAPY; MIXED-METHODOLOGY; POPULATION-BASED EFFECTIVENESS TRIAL; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Despite the fact that tuberculosis (TB) is a curable disease, it remains the number one cause of death amongst people with AIDS globally. South Africa has the highest number of people living with HIV (5.6 million) and the highest incidence of TB and HIV-TB worldwide (981 and 591 per 100 000, respectively). Latent TB infection (LTBI) is a dormant stage preceding TB disease. Although treatment for LTBI in the form of Isoniazid Preventive Therapy (IPT) has been commonly used in the developed world, it has not been used in countries with high HIV-TB incidence until now. In 2011, IPT became available community-wide to people living with HIV (PLWH) in the Edendale Hospital catchment of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa (an area of high TB-HIV and MDR-TB prevalence). The present project will follow up all charts of PLWH who completed 6-months of IPT in the catchment area between Dec 1, 2011 and June 30, 2012 to determine changes in TB incidence, TB mortality, and all cause mortality among PLWH compared with previous years. The PhD candidate will also interview a subset of PLWH declining, discontinuing, or completing the IPT regimen to learn more about the experience of patients. The project will build upon a catalyst project which helped to develop community partnerships and identify community perceptions of population-wide IPT. Pre-established advisory teams in a random sample of six Edendale communities will help determine sub-objectives, interview tools, and culturally competent findings and dissemination methods. This study will be the first opportunity globally to evaluate the effectiveness of IPT in a high TB-HIV co-infected environment, as South Africa is the first country to formally adopt the practice of community-wide IPT for PLWH. Findings will directly affect local and international policy guidelines on the use of IPT among PLWH.

TitreApplicationTitle: Orthotic prescription for knee osteoarthritis using a biomechanical personalized-medicine approach
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COMPUTER PROGRAM; FOOTWEAR ORTHOTICS; GAIT ANALYSIS; INVERSE DYNAMICS; KNEE JOINT BIOMECHANICS; ORTHOPEDICS; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PERSONALIZED-MEDICINE; RHEUMATOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Arthritis currently affects approximately 4.5 million Canadians with an economic cost of $33 billion annually. The most common form of arthritis is knee osteoarthritis (OA), which is characterized by degeneration of cartilage and bone tissues within the knee joint, leading to pain, swelling, and often long-term disability. Recent advances in engineering have been able to identify that increased mechanical loading in the knee during movement is related to knee OA development and progression. Therefore, one possible method for preventing and slowing knee OA progression is by reducing these loads. Footwear orthotics can reduce knee joint loading and thus can improve symptoms associated with knee OA; however it is currently not possible to predict the type of orthotic needed to reduce knee joint loading for a given patient. Therefore, the objective of the proposed research is to identify a method for predicting the type of orthotic that a given patient would require to successfully reduce knee joint loading and therefore improve OA symptoms.   I will recruit 180 participants for this study. Eight physical and anatomical variables believed to be associated with knee joint loading will be measured at baseline for each participant, and then, using non-invasive engineering techniques, knee joint loading during walking will be quantified with two different orthotic conditions, and one control condition. Based on these data, I will develop equations that can be used to predict the type of orthotic that will most likely reduce knee joint loading for a given patient based on their physical and anatomical characteristics. This equation will be coded into a computer program that will then be implemented into clinics around Alberta, where long-term clinical outcomes will be monitored. This will be the first-ever personalized approach to knee OA management, and thus has the potential to have an enormous impact on the musculoskeletal health for millions of Canadians each year.

TitreApplicationTitle: Physical Activity and Nutrition in Head/Neck Oncology: Developing a Patient-Oriented, Clinic-Supported Program
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PROGRAMMING; EDUCATION; HEAD AND NECK CANCER; HEALTH PROMOTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; NUTRITION; PATIENT-ORIENTED RESEARCH; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; QUALITY OF LIFE; WELLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: The objective of this research project, to evaluate a Patient-Oriented, Clinic-Supported Physical Activity and Nutrition Program in Head/Neck Oncology, directly aligns with CIHR's vision to advance evidence-based, patient-centered care. The project's goal is to address a current unmet need in head/neck cancer care and respond directly by delivering an intervention combining physical activity, nutritional and educational elements. Research on physical activity and nutrition interventions to positively impact symptom management, treatment-related recovery and quality of life, has largely excluded head/neck cancer populations. This translates into a lack of clinical programming available for these patients. This research is necessary because head/neck cancer patients deal with severe weight loss; with upwards of 70% attributed to lean muscle wasting, leading to extended recovery times, decreased quality of life, impaired physical functioning, and delayed return to work. To date, interventions to address body composition issues have focused solely on diet, despite findings that nutritional therapy alone is insufficient. A combined lifestyle intervention, that also incorporates important educational components, is necessary. Our pilot work suggests large patient demand and clinic support from the health care professionals. Therefore, the purpose of the present study is to investigate the specific benefits of this lifestyle program on patient body composition, physical functioning, blood markers, quality of life, smoking status, depression and return to work. Further, this research will evaluate the effectiveness of this lifestyle intervention at different time points along the cancer care trajectory to identify the most effective clinical intervention point in patient care. This study will promote advancements in cancer survivorship and our work will result in a sustainable, evidence-based program that can be implemented in cancer centers across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluating the effectiveness of neuromuscular training on strength, coordination, and injury prevention in novice runners.
Keywords-MotsClés: BALANCE; COORDINATION; HEALTH; INJURY; LOWER EXTREMITY; MOTOR CONTROL; OVERUSE; RUNNING; STRENGTH; TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: Running is an extremely popular sport with many known health benefits. As the number of runners has increased so has the number of running-related injuries, such as knee pain and shin splints. It has been shown that large rotations at the ankle, knee, and hip joints are predictors of running injury. Some clinicians believe that weak leg muscles are responsible for these large joint rotations. Previous injury prevention training programs have tried to increase leg strength in order to reduce joint movements. However, these training programs have thus far been unsuccessful in preventing running injuries. Poor leg strength and large joint movements have been related to injuries in other sports such as volleyball and soccer where injury prevention training programs have been applied successfully. These particular training programs included the addition of an unstable surface, such as a wobble board, to their exercises. This addition may challenge both the user's leg strength and coordination due to the difficulty of maintaining an upright posture on an unstable surface. While these training protocols have been successful for other sports, they have never been used for recreational running. The goal of this research project will be to determine if this training program is effective in reducing the number of injuries suffered by novice runners. This is particularly attractive as these training programs can be completed at home with equipment that is easily accessible to the public. This will allow for the training program to benefit a larger portion of the population, with minimal economic burden. Reducing the likelihood of injuries has the potential to have a widespread impact due to the popularity of recreational running in Canada. Avoiding injury will allow for Canadians to remain active and enjoy the benefits of participating in running. Additionally, a successful injury prevention program will also reduce the healthcare costs associated with running injuries.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Non-Invasive Evaluation of Elevated Intracranial Pressure in Severe Traumatic Brain Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: INTRACRANIAL HYPERTENSION; INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE; INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE MONITORING; INTRAOCULAR PRESSURE; PREDICTIVE INDEX; PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY; SENSITIVITY; SPECIFICITY; TONOMETRY; TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Over half of hospitalized patients either die or are left severely disabled following severe traumatic brain injury (TBI). Uncontrolled cerebral edema is the leading cause of ongoing brain injury following a severe TBI. Left untreated, cerebral edema represents a life-threatening emergency as the resulting elevated intracranial pressure causes decreased blood flow to the brain, stroke, and eventual death. Alternatively, early diagnosis and invasive monitoring of increased intracranial pressure with subsequent goal directed therapies improves survival. Recognition of uncontrolled cerebral edema immediately following severe TBI is difficult as clinical examination and imaging may be unreliable indicators. Current guidelines for the placement of brain pressure monitors accurately predict elevated pressure in only half of patients. The placement of monitors in patients without elevated intracranial pressure results in potentially avoidable disability and death as hemorrhage or infection occurs in up to a third of patients following the procedure. More importantly, the delayed recognition of elevated pressure results in preventable ongoing brain injury. We propose to establish the use of the measurement of the pressure in the eye as a novel method of non-invasive diagnosis of uncontrolled cerebral edema. Previous studies have demonstrated intracranial pressure is indirectly transmitted to the eye via the intervening venous anatomy. We intend to exploit this relationship to improve upon the current accuracy of the non-invasive diagnosis of uncontrolled cerebral edema. The earlier recognition of uncontrolled cerebral edema and subsequent intervention will prevent progressive cerebral ischemia while sparing those patients with normal intracranial pressure from the undue hazard of invasive monitoring. The successful use of intraocular pressure in the diagnosis of brain swelling will thereby reduce the death and disability due to severe TBI.

TitreApplicationTitle: Detection of severe mental illness among prisoners
Keywords-MotsClés: MENTAL HEALTH; PATHWAYS TO CARE; PRISON; SCREENING; TRAJECTORIES
Abstract-Résumé: Rates of mental illness are high among prison populations. This research will explore existing processes to detect mental illness among prisoners serving sentences of 2 years or longer. First it will measure whether current mental health screening tests can accurately identify offenders with mental illness that require further treatment. Second, it will measure changes in mental health during the first year in prison and events that may cause these changes. Finally, it will look at differences in outcomes for offenders with mental illness depending on if and when they are referred for service. This research will lead to improved identification of mental illness to overcome barriers to accessing treatment at the earliest point possible. It will also seek to clarify how and for whom mental health services can reduce continued involvement with the criminal justice and mental health systems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of mutations in the BMPR2 gene on the phospho-proteome of blood-outgrowth endothelial cells in pulmonary arterial hypertension
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MORPHOGENETIC PROTEIN RECEPTOR 2; CELL SIGNALING PATHWAYS; ENDOTHELIAL DYSFUNCTION; ENDOTHELIAL PROGENITOR CELLS; GENOMICS; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; PROTEOMICS; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION; RIGHT HEART FAILURE; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is disease characterized by abnormally high blood pressure in the vessels of the lungs as well as severe narrowing and scarring in these arteries. It is a chronic, debilitating disease that, if left untreated, can progress to heart failure and eventually death. Unfortunately, there is no medical cure. A major breakthrough in the last decade was the discovery of a loss-of-function single gene mutation identified in up to 80% of cases of hereditary form of PAH (HPAH), and about 25% of patients with sporadic idiopathic PAH (IPAH). The gene responsible is called BMPR2 (bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2), which is crucial to maintaining healthy pulmonary vessels. In particular, the integrity, function and survival of an important cell type known as the endothelial cell (EC) which forms the lining of vessels in the lung is critically dependent on fully functional BMPR2. In fact, the loss of lung ECs has been hypothesized to be the initiating event that triggers PAH. However, the molecular mechanisms of BMPR2 mutations are unclear and there are no specific treatments for this patient population thus far.   Using an approach known as proteomics, we will study the direct effect of the BMPR2 mutation on the entire complement of proteins in ECs derived from peripheral blood of HPAH patients with BMPR2 mutations. Using this powerful technology, we can also detect molecular modifications that reflect changes protein activity and derive a comprehensive profile of cellular processes affected by the BMPR2 gene mutation. With this information, we will validate the function of these targets in patient-derived ECs and in animal models of PAH to better understand the disease. We hope that the knowledge gained from this research will allow us to design personalized interventions aimed at preventing PAH in families with known mutations before the onset of disease, potentially relieving a huge burden on the individual and the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Prenyl Diphosphate Synthase Subunit 1 (PDSS1) in Impaired Cellular Bioenergetics and its Implications in Obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOENERGETICS; GENETICS; HUMANS; MITOCHONDRIA; MOLECULAR/CELLULAR TECHNIQUES; OBESITY; OXPHOS; PDSS1; SKELETAL MUSCLE; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: According to the World Health Organization, obesity has more than doubled globally since 1980, affecting over 1.5 billion adults. In Canada, statistics reveal that in 2008, over 8 million people suffered from obesity, with estimated costs exceeding $4.6 billion. Given that obesity is extremely complex and a major risk factor for other conditions such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, diseases of the joints, and some cancers (including endometrial, breast, and colon), it is clear that it constitutes an important area of research. As such, much effort has been put into elucidating the genetic predictors of obesity in order to contribute to its prevention and treatment. This is the basis from which the proposed project evolves. It was previously established that deficiency of a certain molecule in the "powerplants" of cells, named Coenzyme Q10, increases the risk for obesity. One of the genes that is essential for cellular production of Coenzyme Q10 is called Prenyl Diphosphate Synthase Subunit 1 (PDSS1).  Never before has anyone linked this gene with obesity and we now have preliminary evidence from genetic studies of over 2000 patient records that suggest PDSS1's importance.  Thus, we will investigate the role of PDSS1 in the development of obesity and as a possible target for treatment. Using cultured model cells, we will reduce levels of PDSS1 and evaluate cellular responses. At the clinical level, we will compare PDSS1 levels in obese and lean individuals in order to determine expression patterns. We expect that the PDSS1 gene will be defective in some obese individuals, and our experimental work may demonstrate that we can reverse this defect with CoQ10 supplementation. Ultimately, this translational project will yield an improved understanding of the role of energy expenditure mechanisms in the development of obesity and will also allow the development of novel therapeutic and pharmaceutical strategies to improve weight loss success in clinical programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of oncolytic vaccinia virus using functional genomics
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOTHERAPEUTICS; CANCER THERAPY; DRUG COMBINATION THERAPY; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; HIGH-THROUGHPUT SCREEN; HOST-VIRUS INTERACTION; ONCOLYTIC VIRUS THERAPY; RNAI; TUMOUR GENETICS; TUMOUR MICROENVIRONMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Oncolytic vaccinia virus therapy is a novel cancer therapy that is currently being tested in a multinational phase 2b clinical trial in patients with advanced liver cancer and could be available in the clinic in the next few years. In oncolytic vaccinia virus therapy, cancer patients are administered oncolytic vaccinia virus, which has been shown to selectively destroy tumour cells, yet cause no harm to patients. Previous phase 1 and 2 clinical trials have yielded promising results for a spectrum of cancers, yet we believe that the potential exists to further enhance this therapy so that an even greater number of patients can benefit and/or benefit to an even greater extent. We hypothesize that we can increase the therapeutic efficacy of oncolytic vaccinia virus by improving its ability to spread in tumours, as studies suggest that heightened spread and replication at the tumour site is correlated with enhanced efficacy. We are using robot assisted genetic screens to identify tumour and virus genes across the entire human and vaccinia genomes that modulate its ability to spread. We plan to use the knowledge gleaned from these screens to engineer a more potent oncolytic vaccinia virus, or to custom design drugs to work synergistically with the virus. The outcome of this project has the potential of significantly improving cancer treatment outcomes and the lives of those fighting this devastating disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuro-immune interactions in autism: mechanisms of disease and therapeutic targets
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; IN-VIVO IMAGING; INFECTION AND IMMUNITY; NEURO-IMMUNE INTERACTION; TWO-PHOTON MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: Autism is the most common neurological disorder manifesting in childhood, affecting 1 in 88 children and over 200,000 Canadians. Autism causes problems with communication, social interaction and behavior and carries a heavy burden of healthcare and special educational needs.  We study the origins of autism in early brain development. Though the exact causes of autism are unknown, we know that dysregulation of the immune system in the mother and the fetus is a key feature. The immune system protects us from infections. It exists in a delicate balance between activated and surveillant states. If this balance is perturbed - by maternal infection during pregnancy for example - the immune system can become chronically overactive, damaging the body by fighting infections which aren't there.  Why should this affect brain development? The answer is likely to lie with a group of cells called microglia. These are the immune cells of the brain. When they are activated, they proliferate, chew up brain tissue (looking for infection) and release inflammatory modulators called cytokines. Many of these cytokines can affect the structure and function of the brain. Brain development is thus profoundly sensitive to the state of the immune system.  A number of specific immune factors are dysregulated in autism. To develop therapies, we need to understand when, where and how these factors affect the wiring and function of the brain. To do this, we use cutting-edge imaging techniques to see inside the living, developing brain. We visualize interactions between microglia and other brain cells in conditions of immune activation. We can see how inflammation modulates brain structure and activity. By understanding the mechanisms of neuro-immune interaction, we aim to identify points of leverage for therapeutic intervention. Immune-directed therapy of at-risk pregnant mothers and children with autism is a promising approach to the prevention and treatment of this debilitating condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oxytocin and Depression during the Perinatal Period
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD DEVELOPMENT; MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH; MIND-MINDEDNESS; MOTHER-CHILD INTERACTION; POST-PARTUM DEPRESSION; SOCIAL COGNITION; THEORY OF MIND
Abstract-Résumé: Depression is a common mental health problem during pregnancy and the postpartum period, which adversely affects both the mother and her developing child. However, the processes through which perinatal depression impacts the mother-child relationship and child development remain unclear. Oxytocin is a good candidate as a biological mechanism as it has been related to maternal mood, social cognition, and maternal behavior. The objective of the proposed research is to examine the modulating role of oxytocin as it relates to perinatal depression, maternal theory of mind, maternal interactive behavior, and child's theory of mind development. Specifically, I hypothesize that women with high levels of oxytocin will experience less depression, be more attuned to the mental states of their children, display more sensitive interactive behavior, and in turn their children will demonstrate appropriately developed theory of mind abilities. The current investigation will assess mother-child dyads when the child is 2-3 years old, as a follow-up study of women and their children who participated in a larger longitudinal study. Participants recruited from prenatal clinics (N = 341) were assessed at 12-14 weeks gestation, 32-34 weeks gestation, and 7-9 weeks postpartum. By elucidation the links between oxytocin, social cognition, and maternal behavior, the proposed project will help to develop effective interventions to improve the mother-child relationship in the context of perinatal depression.

TitreApplicationTitle: Group cognitive-behavioural therapy for co-morbid social anxiety in schizophrenia: Efficacy and neuroimaging markers of symptomatic improvement.
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYGDALA; COGNITIVE-BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; EMOTIONAL PROCESSING TASK; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; GROUP THERAPY; LIMBIC ACTIVATION; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SCHIZOPHRENIA; SOCIAL ANXIETY
Abstract-Résumé: Almost 36% of individuals who suffer from schizophrenia experience anxiety in social situations. This causes significant impairment in social functioning in these patients and renders them more susceptible to relapse and suicide attempts. A psychological treatment method known as cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) has been shown to be effective in adult anxiety disorders; however research on its effectiveness in patients with schizophrenia is scant. The present study aims to evaluate the effects of group CBT adapted specifically for social anxiety in schizophrenia. A sample of patients from the Psychosis Program at the Douglas Hospital will be offered the adapted CBT program in groups of 8-10 participants. Symptoms of social anxiety at the end of the program will be compared to symptoms experienced prior to beginning the program using clinical assessment scales. We expect that after partaking in the program, participants will show fewer symptoms associated with social anxiety. To treat patients efficiently, this study will use brain imaging methods in an attempt to predict which individuals are most likely to benefit from the therapy. Studies have shown that the amygdala, a brain structure involved in emotional processing, is over-activated in anxiety disorders. This effect can be reduced with successful treatment. We will use functional magnetic resonance imaging to observe activity in the amygdala while participants perform an emotional processing task. If higher activity in the amygdala prior to group CBT is related to increased symptom improvement after the program, we can predict that individuals with over-activation of the amygdala will benefit most from group CBT. This study is relevant because mental health centres across Canada may offer adapted group CBT therapy to reduce social anxiety and improve functioning in people with schizophrenia. To conserve limited resources, patients most likely to benefit from the therapy can be identified using neuroimaging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurons' electrical activity refines neural circuits by strengthening the connections between neurons with correlated activity while eliminating connections between neurons with uncorrelated activity.
Keywords-MotsClés: CONFOCAL IMAGING; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NEURAL CIRCUITS; NEURAL PLASTICITY; SYNAPTIC ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: During early postnatal life, neural circuits undergo reorganization in which some connections are strengthened while others are eliminated to form efficient circuits. However, we know little about the mechanism underlying this refinement process. Previous studies have shown that altering the strength of electrical signal transmission between neurons disrupts this refinement process, which suggests that electrical signaling has a central role in the development of neural circuits. Given this, here we hypothesize that connections between the neurons with correlated electrical activity are stabilized while connections between the neurons with uncorrelated electrical activity are eliminated. I am using a genetically modified mouse model in which electrical signaling between half of the neurons in the autonomic nervous system has been blocked. To study neural circuit refinement in this model, I am using a multi-disciplinary approach by combining the technique of electrophysiology and confocal imaging. In addition, I am using viral-mediated gene transfer technique at different times after birth, to restore electrical signaling between neurons that were blocked earlier. I predict that, morphological connections between neurons in which electrical signaling has been blocked will be eliminated within a few weeks after the birth, while connections between neurons with normal electrical signaling will be stabilized. On the other hand, restoring electrical signaling during early postnatal life will reorganize neural circuits but there will be no reorganization if the signaling is restored later in life. The results coming from this project will reveal the instructive principles that govern the refinement of neural circuits during development. Further, these experiments will shed light on whether a critical time window exists for the re-organization of neural circuits.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of the tumourigenic ability of glioblastoma stem-like cells
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN CANCER; CANCER STEM CELLS; HIGH THROUGHPUT SEQUENCING; TRANSCRIPTIONAL NETWORKS
Abstract-Résumé: Tumours of glial cell origin (gliomas) are among the most malignant and deadly cancers in the adult human brain and include grade II astrocytoma, grade III anaplastic astrocytoma, and the most common and malignant form, glioblastoma (grade IV). Adult gliomas are quite common with more than 15,000 primary cases diagnosed annually in North America. The majority of these tumours grow rapidly and are widely invasive, resulting in poor patient prognosis. In particular, glioblastoma patients have an average survival time of only 15 months due to the tumour's aggressive and invasive nature that the current advances in neurosurgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy can only temporarily contain. Perhaps the most devastating part of the disease is its recurrent nature; the tumour often recurs within 7 months after surgery. It is hypothesized that the recurrence, and in part occurrence, of glioblastoma is due to a population of cells in the tumour with stem cell-like properties. The main goal of the proposed study is to clarify the molecular events that occur during glioblastoma initiation, progression, and recurrence by focusing on this highly potent cell population which therapy has not yet managed to conquer. In this regard, our laboratory has combined the analysis of surgical glioblastoma specimens with primary tissue culture of glioblastoma-derived cells with stem-like and tumour forming ability. Specifically, we seek to characterize molecular mechanisms important for gene regulation events underlying the self-renewal and tumourigenic potential of glioblastoma stem-like cells. It is anticipated that understanding what has gone awry in these glioblastoma cells at a molecular level will provide important new insights into the pathobiology of this deadly brain cancer. Moreover, we hope that this information will allow us to design new approaches aimed at providing previously unavailable therapeutic options for glioblastoma.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Manipulation of 14-3-3 Proteins to Promote Axonal Regeneration after Injury
Keywords-MotsClés: NEURONAL REGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Traumatic events such as spinal cord injury and stroke have debilitating clinical consequences.  A major cause of persistent disability is that nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord are damaged such that functional communication is disrupted.  In the brain and spinal cord, spontaneous repair of injured nerve cells is blocked by the presence of inhibitory molecules.  Inhibitory molecules play an important role in hard wiring the adult nervous system but unwanted roles in limiting nerve cell regrowth following injury.   A promising strategy to promote the repair of injured nerve cells is to reprogram the cells such that they no longer respond to inhibitory proteins in the brain and spinal cord.  We have identified a family of neuronal proteins called 14-3-3 proteins that are important for neuronal responses to inhibitory proteins and we have shown that blocking the function of these proteins can help nerve cell repair in cultured neurons.   The aim of our studies is to determine the effects of 14-3-3 blockers in promoting nerve cell repair in pre-clinical models of nerve injury. The ultimate goal of our studies is the development of new treatments for brain and spinal cord injury, bringing comfort to the millions of victims of accidents and neurodegenerative diseases worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Translating Research in Elder Care
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; FACILITY-BASED LONG-TERM CARE; INTERVENTION; KNOWLEDGE UTILIZATION; LONGITUDINAL DATA COLLECTION; MDS-RAI; RESIDENT OUTCOMES; SOCIAL NETWORK ANALYSIS; SUSTAINABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: The most rapidly expanding group of Canadians is those >=85 years - the age when complex chronic diseases, in particular dementias, begin to take their greatest toll on ability to live independently. Currently 1 in 5 men >=85 and 1 in 3 women >=85 reside in long-term care (LTC) facilities designed to provide care when family and community no longer can. With our many successes in keeping seniors healthier and in the community longer, residents are admitted later in their decline, with more complex needs and in a much greater state of vulnerability. Within these facilities, the majority of care is provided by unregulated care aides who have low incomes, are most often women with high school education or less, some with little proficiency in either official language. They constitute another at-risk group.  To ensure the best possible quality of life for these two vulnerable populations, the Translating Research in Elder Care (TREC) research program will examine how the work environment in nursing homes affects staff members and residents. Like links in a chain, we believe that favorable work environments lead to enhanced use of research information, provision of better care, and ultimately better outcomes for residents (e.g. fewer pressure sores, less pain, etc).  Improved staff well-being is also a link in the chain. We will be testing the strength of each link to determine where changes can be most effective. We will also test a program aimed at helping staff design and run their own care improvement projects, once again, measuring the associations with the links of the chain. A third component of our work is aimed at understanding how LTC facilities are connected to each other, which ones are the innovators and leaders, and which ones learn from the others. The TREC research will be carried out in nursing homes across the 4 western provinces. The information developed will contribute to better care for Canadian seniors who spend their final years in a nursing home.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using the General Public to Estimate Health-related Quality-of-life in Alzheimer's Disease: Development and Validation of Clinical Vignettes
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; CLINICAL VIGNETTES; CONCURRENT VALIDITY; FOCUS GROUPS; GENERAL PUBLIC SURVEY; HEALTH-RELATED QUALITY-OF-LIFE; MIXED METHODS; TEST-RETEST RELIABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Quality-of-life (QoL) is important in Alzheimer's disease (AD) because no cure exists. Measuring QoL provides a way of assessing the 'humanistic element' of AD treatments. Patients and caregivers currently estimate QoL in AD by answering questionnaires. Question responses are converted into scores ranging from 0 (worst possible QoL or death) to 1 (perfect health). However, patients and caregivers give different QoL scores and very sick AD patients often cannot answer QoL questionnaires.  We will examine whether the general public can provide QoL scores in place of patients and caregivers. To do this, we will develop stories describing what happens to people who have mild, moderate, and severe AD. Patients, caregivers, and physicians will help us develop these stories. Afterward, we will conduct a survey that contains the stories and see if a sample of the general public in Canada gives QoL scores that decrease as disease severity increases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of Platelet Subpopulations based on the Heterogeneity of NOS Signaling: Significance for Hemostasis and Thrombosis
Keywords-MotsClés: AGGREGOMETRY; ENDOTHELIAL NITRIC OXIDE SYNTHASE; FLOW CYTOMETRY; FLUORESCENCE ACTIVATED CELL SORTING; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; NITRIC OXIDE; PLATELET PHARMACOLOGY; PLATELET SUBPOPULATIONS; QUARTZ CRYSTAL MICROBALANCE FLOW ASSAY; STROKE PATIENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Platelets are circulating blood particles normally responsible for stopping bleeding by forming blood clots (platelet aggregates). In conditions such as heart attack and stroke blood clots form inappropriately in sick (atherosclerotic) blood vessels. Recently, we have discovered that two types of platelets exists. One type of platelet generates the signaling molecule nitric oxide and the other type of platelet does not generate this signaling molecule. Nitric oxide is well known to inhibit platelet clot formation. Hence, we propose that platelets that do not generate nitric oxide initiate clot formation, while platelets that do generate nitric oxide limit clot formation. Hence, the purpose of our studies are 1) to investigate the biochemical and structural differences between the two platelet subtypes, 2) to investigate whether the two platelet subtypes play different roles in clot formation, and 3) to study whether patients with cardiovascular disease (specifically those having had a stroke) have altered ratios of one type of platelet to another. By the end of our studies we expect to have established that the two platelet subtypes differ biochemically and structurally, have different roles in clot formation, and that stroke patients have elevated levels of platelets which initiate clot formation. These basic and translational studies of platelet biology have the potential to significantly impact the health of Canadians by better predicting risk and extent of clot formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: From the omics bench to personalized medicine: ethical and scientific challenges
Keywords-MotsClés: DELPHI SURVEY; END-USERS; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; POLICY FRAMEWORK; RESEARCH ETHICS; WEBSITE SURVEY; WHOLE GENOME SEQUENCING TECHNOLOGIES
Abstract-Résumé: Our project aims to explore the socio-ethical challenges of integrating whole genome sequencing approaches into clinical practice. More specifically, we aim to lay an evidence-based empirical foundation that can both anticipate and recognize the socio-ethical and scientific challenges of integrating WGS approaches into clinical practice, both for diseases affecting vulnerable research populations (e.g., bipolar affective disorders, congenital heart disease) as well as in a field holding promise for the general population (e.g., nutrigenomics/metabolic disorders), with a view to develop policy documents to help manage and meet these socio-ethical challenges. In keeping with our recent research work on the ethical and social issues raised by the use of next-generation sequencing technologies to identify genes involved in these three diseases, and anticipating that key genes and biochemical pathways playing an important role in these disorders could lead directly to clinically relevant diagnostic and therapeutic applications for a many individuals affected or at risk for these diseases, coupled to the advent of personalized medicine, and finally to best help researchers and clinicians in ways that anticipate and prevent, rather than react and respond to, socio-ethical conflicts, we therefore aim to analyze the socio-ethical issues and challenges at the juncture between omics research and the clinic.
