TitreApplicationTitle: Health Diplomacy at a Crossroads: Social Justice-Oriented South-South Cooperation in a Time of Global Change
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO ESSENTIAL MEDICINES; COMPREHENSIVE PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; GLOBAL HEALTH; GLOBAL HEALTH DIPLOMACY; HEALTH WORKER MIGRATION; HEALTH WORKFORCE TRAINING; LATIN AMERICA; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOUTH-SOUTH COOPERATION; SOUTHERN AND EAST AFRICA
Abstract-Résumé: In recent years, the global health field has been marked by a new kind of activity - health cooperation between social justice-oriented agencies and governments of the global South. This involves: cross-border public health and medical training; sharing of health care workers; policy support around universal comprehensive primary health care; and addressing the broader social and political factors that affect health. But very little is known about this social justice-oriented South-South health cooperation (SJSSC) and how it differs from other forms of global health diplomacy in terms of political values and how cooperative health activities are carried out.  This project will further understanding of SJSSC and its implications for improving global health by: 1) carrying out a conceptual analysis of the different forms of global health diplomacy and cooperation; 2) providing an in-depth examination of how SJSSC plays out in two key arenas: primary health care and health care workforce issues; and 3) building a dialogue between Africa and Latin America to explore the similarities and differences in the forms of South-South cooperation within and between the two regions.  These issues will be examined through a policy analysis of SJSSC, based on the following case studies: universal, comprehensive primary health care in El Salvador and in Venezuela; health worker deployment to, and regional responses around, health worker migration within and from Southern and East Africa; the rights-based elements of socially progressive South-South policies, and the role of regional health justice networks and cooperation in all of these efforts.  The ultimate goal of this research is to determine whether this new form of South-South health cooperation leads to greater policy autonomy, more sustainable and effective health equity policies, and improved global health diplomacy. This study will help inform Canada's global health activities and policies.

TitreApplicationTitle: End-of-life ethical deliberations: Characterization of interprofessional clinical practices
Keywords-MotsClés: END OF LIFE CARE; ETHICAL DELIBERATION; ETHICS; INTERPROFESSIONAL COLLABORATION; PALLIATIVE CARE; PATIENT AUTONOMY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SHARED MEDICAL DECISION-MAKING
Abstract-Résumé: Healthcare professionals praciticing in end-of-life care settings face numerous ethical challenges, such as disclosure of sensitive information, and decisions about initiating, not initiating, or withdrawing treatment. Terminally ill patients and their families are the most immediately affected by theses challenges. The ethical dillemmas that often result entail decisions and professional conduct that cannot be regulated solely by the deontological norms, the legislation, and the institutional norms and standards. The quality of deliberations hinges primarily on the nature of the interprofessional relationships that exist within the healthcare team. In its most basic form, ethical deliberation is a dialogue consisting of identifying, then acting on, the value the healthcare team deems primordial in a given situation. This deliberative process must help determine the most ethically reeasonable and acceptable course of action, consistent with the values and end-of-life wishes of patients. There is a need to identify and carefully describe the opportunities and limitations of optimal patient-centered interprofessional collaboration in ethical deliberation situations, to characterize those situations likely to compromise or impede this particular form of deliberation and finally, to describe to what extent and how the professional integrate the patients and families' perspectives into the process. The purpose of the study is to examine interprofessional ethical deliberation practices and to identify the factors that facilitate and hinder ethical deliberation processes in end-of-life care settings. The knowledge generated by this study will shed light on interprofessional collaboration practices as regards to ethical deliberations throughout the healthcare network. This information is long-awaited in order to better equip clinicians to relieve the suffering of patients and their families when unresolved ethical dilemmas are the source of their suffering.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ion Channels as Therapeutic Targets in Chronic HIV/AIDS Pain
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL NEUROSCIENCE; CYTOKINE; DORSAL ROOT GANGLION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HCN CHANNELS; K+ CHANNELS; NEUROINFLAMMATION; NEUROPATHIC PAIN; NEUROPATHY; PERIPHERAL NERVE
Abstract-Résumé: AIDS patients frequently suffer from neurological disease as a result of infection by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). One in two patients suffers from chronic pain. Unlike many forms of serious pain which respond to morphine and other drugs, HIV associated "neuropathic" pain fails to respond to currently available drugs. We know that HIV promotes the production of toxic proteins which damage sensory pain nerves whilst causing them to generate pain impulses which constantly enter the spinal cord and brain. To find out how this happens, we will first explore the actions of a toxic viral protein called Vpr. We will use electrical recordings of sensory nerve activity in the presence and absence of the protein to determine which ion channels are affected. Ion channels are protein pores in nerve cell membranes which control their electrical activity and enable them to generate nerve impulses. We will then use drugs such as "K+ channel activators"  to correct the effects of Vpr on sensory neuron activity. Mice which have been genetically engineered to make the viral protein Vpr (in the absence of HIV infection) display pain-related behaviors. We will see if the drugs that correct Vpr induced changes in sensory nerve activity can also stop pain in these animals. If so this will lead to the development of urgently needed treatments for pain in AIDS patients

TitreApplicationTitle: New roads taken to identify and study the biological significance of host-derived molecules incorporated in HIV-1
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS; CD4 T CELLS; HIV-1; MACROPHAGES; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Animal retroviruses are formed by budding through the limiting membranes of producer cells, a process during which the newly formed virions become coated with a lipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane. The low specificity of the process governing glycoprotein incorporation into retroviruses is most likely responsible for the incorporation of a vast array of cell-derived proteins. Previous studies have shown the functional ability of some virus-anchored host cell membrane constituents. Given that virus-associated host proteins can influence several aspects of HIV-1 biology, additional experiments are warranted to shed light on this intriguing phenomenon.  The primary goal of the current research project is to gain novel insights into the role played by some virally acquired host cell membrane molecules in the complex interactions occurring between HIV-1 and its cell targets. A more complete understanding of the contribution of virus-associated host proteins to the HIV-1 life cycle is crucial because it might lead to the development of new drugs, the design of therapeutic agents that can deplete the reservoir of archived viruses in latently infected cells, the use of alternative approaches for the treatment of HIV-1 infection and/or the design of an efficient vaccine strategy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Promoting resilience among first responders: Culturally-sensitive intervention strategies for positive health
Keywords-MotsClés: CULTURAL COMPETENCY; FIRST LINE RESPONDERS; MINDFULNESS; MULTICULTURALISM; POLICE ORGANIZATION & LOCAL COMMUNITY; POLICE POPULATION; POSITIVE PSYCHOLOGY; PREVENTIVE INTERVENTION; PSYCHOLOGICAL AWARENESS; PSYCHOLOGICAL TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: Although countries may differ in the politics of criminal justice, the violence and adversity that police officers face in the line of duty is universal. These traumatic incidents require a variety of urgent responses (e.g., child abuse, gang shootings). Chronic exposure to critical incidents can negatively impact the mental and physical health of the officer. Many first responders do not seek help despite the risks of repeated trauma exposure (e.g., sleep disturbances, irritability, alcohol abuse, anxiety, depression, chronic disease) (Andersen et al., 2010, Brodie & Eppler, 2012, Rajaratnam et al., 2011). Reasons for this include the unique nature of police trauma and the existence of a "police culture" where asking for help from mental health professionals is shunned for fear of stigmatization (e.g., loss of weapon, personal weakness, etc.) (Wester et al., 2010). What is more, this distinct police subculture is dominated by white, masculine, heterosexual ethos (Myers, Forest, & Miller, 2004). This means that officers from minority cultural groups are often marginalized and left to prove they are "real" officers (Cochran & Warren, 2012). To research the heretofore unaddressed complex interactions between police trauma and police culture, I developed a new theoretical framework "police complex spiral trauma" (PCST). This theory proposes a multidimensional spiral form of trauma accumulated through time, tension, and frequency over direct and vicarious exposures to traumatic events (Papazoglou, 2012). In this proposal, I outline a set of studies to show that employing the PCST theory in a series of interventions will a). Improve mental health treatment seeking behavior of trauma exposed police officers, b). Reduce stigmatizing behaviors commonly practiced in police culture both towards minority officers and towards seeking mental health treatment, and c). Promote resilient coping strategies and positive health outcomes among police officers exposed to on-going trauma

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic and cellular origins of relapsed acute myeloid leukemia in remission
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; BIOMARKER; CANCER PROGNOSIS; HYPOXIA; MOUSE XENOGRAFT; PROSTATE CANCER; TUMOUR MICRO-ENVIRONMENT; WHOLE-GENOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Malignancy of the prostate is the most diagnosed cancer type in Canadian males and the third most deadly cancer in this population; however, effective methods for diagnosis, prognosis, and prediction of recurrence are yet undiscovered. A tumour is initiated by a small number of mutations in the DNA, the genetic material of the cell, and progress by creating more mutations which catastrophically transform the genome. In patients, cancer cells are not regulated by normal mechanisms and grow uninhibited, damaging the organ(s). Curing cancer is difficult because each cancer is genetically different and may contain multiple tumours with different behaviours; we term this genetic heterogeneity. We are specifically interested in the oxygen levels of tumours because low level of oxygen, called hypoxia, is responsible for enabling a tumour to resist chemotherapy and radiation therapy. My research objective is to find genes controlling tumour oxygen levels by studying the DNA sequences of tumours with hypoxia and comparing them to those of tumours without hypoxia. The project will utilize cutting-edge DNA sequencing machines and bioinformatics softwares to uncover specific genes responsible for this tumour behaviour. Ultimately, we hope to find genetic biomarkers that can be used in the clinic for improved diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of patients. As a result, the study will benefit patients to receive the most optimized treatments and benefit clinicians to provide the most effective treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Leptin action in a gut-brain axis and involvement in the glucose-lowering effect of duodenal-jejunal bypass surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRUS; DIABETIC ANIMAL MODEL; GASTRIC BYPASS SURGERY; GLUCOSE METABOLISM; GLUCOSE PRODUCTION; GUT-BRAIN-LIVER AXIS; HORMONE ACTION; INTESTINAL SIGNALING; LEPTIN; PANCREATIC GLUCOSE/INSULIN CLAMP
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes and obesity are characterized by a disruption in glucose homeostasis due partly to an elevation in hepatic glucose production. Thus, it is important to understand the mechanism(s) involved. The peptide hormone leptin has been shown to regulate glucose production and food intake by binding to its receptor in the brain, however leptin receptors are also located in the jejunum and it is unknown whether jejunal leptin action has a similar role. Furthermore, gastric duodenal bypass surgery (GBS) lowers blood glucose prior to weight loss in diabetes and obesity, but the possible role of leptin remains unclear. Since leptin is produced in the stomach, in addition to adipose tissue, and leptin receptors are located in the jejunum, and GBS enhances digestive flow from the stomach into the jejunum, increased leptin action in the jejunum may contribute to the glucose-lowering effect of GBS in diabetes. Therefore, our objective is to evaluate whether the jejunum senses leptin to lower glucose production and whether the mechanism(s) involved are enhanced in GBS to lower blood glucose. Leptin will be infused into the jejunum of rodents, and glucose production will be measured using established techniques. To examine the underlying mechanisms, inhibitors of signaling molecules and neuronal transmission to the brain and liver will be infused along with leptin. Leptin will also be infused into the jejunum of diabetic rats to determine its effectiveness in the diseased state. If leptin's effect remains, GBS will be performed in rats with diabetes, followed by jejunal infusion experiments with the same inhibitors that were found to be effective in negating jejunal leptin sensing. These findings will reveal a novel site of leptin's metabolic action and possible new therapeutic strategies, other than GBS which is very invasive, targeting the jejunum to lower glucose levels in diabetes and obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigations of the functional neural circuitry underlying effort-based motivational impairments in schizophrenia: a translational model
Keywords-MotsClés: EFFORT-BASED DECISION MAKING; FUNCTIONAL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING; MOTIVATION; NEURAL CICUITRY; NEUROCOGNITION; PSYCHOSOCIAL FUNCTIONING; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a complex and debilitating disorder that affects approximately one percent of the population and is accompanied by enormous personal, social and economic burden. The symptoms of this illness are typically thought of in discrete domains, including positive (e.g. hallucinations and delusions), cognitive (e.g. attention and planning deficits) and negative symptoms (e.g. lack of motivation, difficulty experiencing pleasure and decreased facial expressions). Although current treatments have helped alleviate the burden of positive symptoms, they have had minimal impact on cognitive and negative symptoms, and goals of recovery of functioning remain elusive. Negative symptoms, particularly amotivation, have been found across a number of clinical studies to be central to functioning. However, there is a paucity of effective measures to tap these symptoms and their underlying neurobiology. In the affective neuroscience literature, decades of research has used the amount of work animals are willing to perform for a given reward as a measure of their motivation. The current research program aims to use an innovative translational paradigm recently developed in humans to measure a key component of motivation: effort expenditure. This novel paradigm will be coupled with functional magnetic resonance imaging to explore the neurobiology of effort-based motivational impairments in schizophrenia, which will ultimately guide the development of novel strategies for treatment of schizophrenia and the promotion of functional recovery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immunological mechanisms of brain injury after experimental subarachnoid hemorrhage
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN INJURY; DELAYED CEREBRAL ISCHEMIA; IMMUNOLOGY; STROKE; SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE; VASOSPASM
Abstract-Résumé: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is a special type of stroke that typically results from a ruptured intracranial aneurysm, a weakening in the wall of a blood vessel. This type of life-threatening bleeding occurs in over 3000 Canadians per year, usually in working-age adults. If one is fortunate enough to survive the initial bleeding episode and the subsequent surgical treatment of the aneurysm, patients may still develop secondary strokes 3 to 14 days after the initial bleeding. These delayed strokes are the most significant cause of morbidity and mortality after SAH and may be potentially preventable. There is only one medication (an anti-hypertensive) that has shown to improve outcomes after SAH. The molecular pathway causing these delayed strokes is still not clear, and this is an active area of research.  Our laboratory hypothesizes that the cause of these delayed strokes is a pro-inflammation molecule called tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFa). Specifically, we hypothesize the breakdown of blood products (hemoglobin) after SAH increases TNFa in the walls of small blood vessels, which results in the delayed strokes. Successful blockage of this pathway with etanercept, may lead to positive results in these experiments, and will provide a new treatment target for clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: A novel use of E2f and Cdk inhibitors to prevent RB1-null tumors in genetically engineered models of retinoblastoma and other cancers
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPY; CELL CYCLE; CHEMOPREVENTION; CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUTS; DRUG DELIVERY; IN VIVO IMAGING; NEUROGENESIS; TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH; TUMORIGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is a multi-step process, consisting of initiation and transformation phase. During initiation, there is continuous and progressive selection for aggressive clones by acquiring mutations.  Apart from mutations in oncogenes and tumor-suppressor, we know surprisingly little regarding the molecular networks that underlie the emergence of cancer-prone cells. This is especially true in adult tumors where initiating mutations have remained largely elusive due to the large milieu of cancer-causing genes present at early stages of the disease. With time, cancer progresses and accrues more mutations, which give the cells an impressive armament to resist chemical and radiation-based therapies. As such, developing effective therapeutics for adult tumors has been challenging and costly. In contrast to adult tumors, paediatric tumors often develop from a single initiating mutation and have predictable outcomes. For instance, newborns that have one inactivating mutation in one RB1 allele (RB1+/-) develop tumors within the first year of life and many of whom die of secondary tumors in the bone, brain, and lung. We can leverage unique cancer properties of retinoblastoma to overcome the challenges of dissecting disease networks, and ultimately, pharmaceutically exploit these networks to prevent heritable cancer. Here, we define molecular properties of cancer-prone cells and use this information to prevent retinoblastoma with only week of targeted therapy (2 months before expected tumor emergence). Surprisingly, the cancer-prone state could be reversed without affecting normal physiological processes. Our current data and future directions suggests that targeting initiation networks may hold great promise towards a cancer-free future in children.

TitreApplicationTitle: Eating-out: A study of the nutritional profile of restaurant foods and interventions to promote healthy-eating
Keywords-MotsClés: CALORIES; FAST-FOOD; FOOD ENVIRONMENT; MENU-LABELLING; NUTRITION; POINT-OF-CONSUMPTION NUTRITION INFORMATION; PUBLIC HEALTH; RESTAURANTS; SODIUM
Abstract-Résumé: Over the past thirty years, obesity and diabetes rates have doubled, while the prevalence of eating outside-the-home has simultaneously increased. Because eating-out is associated with a higher risk for chronic disease, menu-labelling has been proposed as a policy option to address this situation.  To date, many questions about the effect of menu-labelling and other point-of-consumption nutrition interventions remain unknown. Furthermore, the nutritional profile of restaurant foods in Canada has never been analyzed.  This project has three main objectives: first, to analyze the nutritional profile of foods and meals served at Canadian chain fast-food and sit-down restaurants. Secondly, to understand the effect of different methods of menu-labelling on consumer purchase intentions, behaviours and attitudes. And finally, to determine if "focused nutritional messages" at the point-of-consumption (such as "make half your plate fruits and vegetables"), will influence the nutrient intakes of university students.  The nutritional profile of restaurant foods will be analyzed using the "University of Toronto Restaurant Database" which contains nutrition information for over 9000 menu items from the major (n=85) chain restaurants in Canada. The "menu-labelling study" will be conducted using the Canadian Consumer Monitor (n=3081), an online, nationally representative consumer survey panel. And finally, the "focused nutritional messages" intervention will take place over four months in a university dining-hall.  Ultimately, it is hoped that this research will: 1) provide a baseline assessment of Canadian restaurant foods, which can be used to guide reformulation strategies, 2) provide evidence to support menu-labelling policies, and 3) determine if point-of-consumption nutrition information can be used to promote healthy-eating in schools.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Philosophical Analysis of the Current Chronic Disease Model and Implications for the Care of Complex Older Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: CHRONIC DISEASE MODEL; CLINICAL REASONING; DISEASE ONTOLOGY; EPISTEMOLOGY; GERIATRIC CARE; LOGICAL ANALYSIS; MULTI-MORBIDITY; PHILOSOPHY OF MEDICINE; PHILOSOPHY OF SCIENCE; PRIMARY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Canada's provincial health systems face a crisis of aging and chronic disease. The World Health Organization recognizes chronic disease as a serious threat to the health of people globally. As the population ages, more Canadians, especially older individuals, are burdened by multiple chronic diseases. Yet, our current chronic disease model, the way we handle patients with multiple chronic conditions, is insufficient for delivering quality health care. Many have argued that current health care is disease-centered rather than 'whole person'-centered, fractured rather than integrated, and often harmful rather than helpful. We see the evidence for these failings most clearly in the care of complex older patients. These patients may have psychological and social issues that go unaddressed, attend many visits with specialists, and take multiple medications at once, which risks serious side effects and drug interactions, often without direct evidence of therapeutic benefit. This project draws from the theory and methods of the philosophy of medicine to examine the assumptions and reasoning characteristic of our current chronic disease model. It seeks to answer the question: In what ways is our current model inadequate for the care of older patients with multiple chronic conditions and how can we improve upon it? The project will investigate flaws in the ways that our current model explains and manages complex illness through multiple disease diagnosis, along with the ways that it judges the effectiveness of therapies through experimental and theoretical reasoning. It will suggest how these flaws might contribute to the problems identified above. Finally, it will develop more holistic and integrative theories of disease explanation and therapeutic reasoning so that we may provide a higher quality of care to Canadians with chronic disease, including complex older patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: NOD1/2 Mediated Control of Innate and Adaptive T cell function during Chronic Colitis
Keywords-MotsClés: COLITIS; CROHN'S DISEASE; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE; INKT CELLS; INNATE SIGNALING; MUCOSAL IMMUNOLOGY; NOD1/2 RECEPTORS; T CELL TRANSFER MODEL; T CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease is a set of diseases that are defined by chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. Currently, Canada has one of the highest incidences of inflammatory bowel disease worldwide with over 200,000 sufferers and an annual health system cost of over $753 million. Symptoms of inflammatory bowel disease include diarrhea, rectal bleeding, vomiting and low energy levels. Once diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease, sufferers often have a decreased quality of life, with negative impacts on personal lifestyle, intimacy and career choice. While treatments can decrease the severity of the symptoms, there is no known cure, other than surgical removal of the colon. Recent advances in research have shown that people with a mutation to the NOD2 gene have an increased susceptibility to inflammatory bowel disease; however, it is unknown how NOD2 contributes to the disease progression. Alternatively, activation of invariant natural killer T cells (iNKT cells), a fast acting immune system cell, has recently been shown to confer protection against inflammatory bowel disease in mice. In my research I plan to investigate the consequence of NOD2 mutation on iNKT cell activation and the onset of inflammatory bowel disease. This research will provide a clearer understanding of the mechanisms involved in the onset of inflammatory bowel disease and may lead to the discovery of an alternative cure.

TitreApplicationTitle: Spatiotemporal dynamics of the syphilis and HIV syndemic in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: CLUSTER DETECTION; DISEASE SURVEILLANCE; HIV; SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS; SPATIAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; SYPHILIS
Abstract-Résumé: Since the mid-1990s Canadian syphilis rates have increased, with no sustained decrease after nearly twenty years of public health efforts aimed at controlling the epidemic. In British Columbia (BC)-as elsewhere in Canada-most recent syphilis cases are among gay men and other men having sex with men, and as many as half also have human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. With closer examination of these cases, public health investigators may be able to define groups of people who are repeatedly infected or part of disease "clusters". Some researchers in the United States have been able to identify these groups by mapping the geography of cases over time.   In this study I will map cases of syphilis in BC in order to see the distribution of cases across different phases (or "waves") of the syphilis epidemic. I will pay special attention to people who are also HIV-infected and those who have more than one syphilis infection across multiple years. I will find clusters of infection using specialized statistical software and will determine whether those clusters are outbreaks lasting a short period of time or ongoing clusters which may be important to the continuation of the syphilis epidemic. Lastly, I will use Canadian Census data to look at social and economic factors in the neighbourhoods where clusters are occurring.  This research will improve public health in several ways. By finding ongoing clusters of syphilis (and HIV) infection, we may have a better idea of how to geographically target syphilis testing, treatment, and other sexually transmitted infection prevention and control programs. By describing the cases (e.g., age, sexual behaviours, social/economic conditions) at various stages of the epidemic, we may learn how best to tailor interventions. Finally, through comparison of the BC epidemic with those of other jurisdictions, we may find common patterns in the spread of the disease and thus help to better control syphilis around the world.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenomic Profiling of cirDNA in Colorectal Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKER DISCOVERY; COLORECTAL CANCER; DNA METHYLATION; DNA MODIFICATION; EARLY DIAGNOSIS; EPIGENETIC SIGNATURE; EPIGENOMICS; LOW INVASIVENESS; MICROARRAY; PLASMA CIRCULATING DNA
Abstract-Résumé: Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer and the second common cancer-related cause of death in Canada. It is estimated for 2012 that 23,300 Canadians will be diagnosed with colorectal cancer and 9,200 will die of it. Early detection of colorectal cancer increases treatment options and significantly improves a patient's chances of survival. Current detection tests, such as colonoscopy, are not applicable in screening programs because they expensive and are associated to serious complications. Other screening tests, such as fecal occult blood test, are often unreliable due to low accuracy and frequently lead to missed diagnoses.  There is a need for new methods to reliably detect colorectal cancer in its early stages of development.       We believe that such a test may be developed using a blood sample.  During the growth of a tumour, from its earliest stages, some malignant cells die, and the contents of such cells are released into the blood stream. It has been known for some time that cancer cells exhibit numerous genetic and epigenetic changes. Epigenetic changes are chemical modifications to the structure of the genes that are used normally regulate (turn on an off) the gene.  The observation that DNA carrying aberrant epigenetic signatures appears in the blood stream of cancer patients can be used to develop epigenetic markers for early detection of cancer.       We propose to scan epigenetic profiles of DNA floating in blood samples from colorectal cancer patients and controls in order to detect cancer-specific epigenetic differences.  This first genome-wide scan for epigenetic modification in cell-free floating DNA in blood may provide novel, non-invasive markers, with the potential for translation into clinical practice.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of simple-to-complex simulation training on novice skill acquisition and procedural errors in lumbar puncture: a prospective, randomized study
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTCARE DELIVERY; INSTRUCTIONAL DESIGN; LUMBAR PUNCTURE; PATIENT SAFETY; PROSPECTIVE RANDOMIZED STUDY; SIMULATION-BASED TRAINING; SURGICAL EDUCATION
Abstract-Résumé: As a result of work-hour restrictions, budgetary constraints, and technological advances in healthcare, medical trainees are expected to acquire more skills, in less time, and in more complex environments then ever before. Consequently, simulation-based training has become an important tool in medical education. Despite growing evidence supporting its use, little is known about how to design simulation environments to improve skills and reduce procedural errors, especially for complex tasks. The purpose of this research program is to 1) clarify the potential negative effects associated with training in highly complex environments on the acquisition of procedural skills, the frequency of errors, and the mental workload of inexperienced trainees, and 2) to evaluate the usefulness of an innovative instructional design strategy known as simple-to-complex sequencing in reducing these effects. Should this strategy be beneficial, it will inform the best ways to structure simulation-training to optimize skill acquisition and reduce procedural errors, thereby potentially improving patient safety and the efficiency of healthcare delivery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sadhee Sehayth (Our Health): Experiences of Punjabi Ancestry Canadians Living with Cardiovascular Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; CRITICAL ETHNOGRAPHY; FEMINIST THEORY; HEALTHCARE ACCESS AND EQUITY; HEALTHCARE POLICY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; POST/COLONIAL THEORY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH METHODS; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; SOUTH ASIAN ANCESTRY CANADIANS
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) continues to be the leading cause of death among women and men, with one Canadian dying every 7 minutes, and costing the healthcare system in excess of 22 billion dollars per year. For Canada's largest visible minority community, CVD related deaths are decreasing at a significantly slower pace than their European/British ancestry counterparts. South Asian ancestry Canadians experience heart disease at a significantly younger age and have a greater risk of premature death. Researchers have not been able to adequately address the reasons behind the higher prevalence for given the lack of conventional risk factors (i.e. absence of high fat diets, smoking and high rates of obesity). Based on the higher prevalence rate without the presence of conventional risk factors, and newly identified delays in emergency care when heart attack symptoms arise, evaluating how healthcare is accessed can inform if structural barriers are limiting healthcare access. This project aims to understand how one South Asian ancestry community considers, seeks, accesses, values and utilzes cardiovascular disease healthcare; and subsequently what factors shape their CVD healthcare access and uptake. A qualitative approach will be applied to conduct a Critical Ethnography whereby 5-8 cardiac healthcare providers will be interviewed regarding healthcare delivery factors; observational field notes will be collected at cardiac field sites to record how patients are responding to services and interactions with healthcare providers; and finally 30-40 interviews will be conducted with Punjabi ancestry Canadians living with CVD.  Post/colonial, feminist and critical race theory will anchor the qualitative analysis to deliver academic and community based knowledge sharing projects. Policy makers, clinicians, health educators and community members will benefit from a better understanding of how CVD care is sought, accessed and experienced.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of Developmental Pathways Selectively Reactivated in Lung Tumours of Never smokers
Keywords-MotsClés: FETAL DEVELOPMENTAL PATHWAYS; GENOMICS; LUNG CANCER; LUNG DEVELOPMENT; NOVEL THERAPEUTIC TARGETS; TRANSCRIPTOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the number one cause of cancer death worldwide, and the five-year survival rate is less than 17% in Canada. As many as 25% of lung cancer cases arise in never smokers; however, since lung cancer is mostly viewed as a smoker's disease, the risk of never smokers developing lung cancer is often overlooked, leading to delays in diagnosis and poor survival rates. Elucidation of novel molecular mechanisms involved in lung cancer development specifically in never smokers is imperative to advance our understanding of this unique disease and to improve treatment of these patients. Many cellular pathways that are normally only active during the development of an embryo and/or the generation of different organ types in the human body have been found to have roles in cancer biology. These pathways are responsible for controlling developmental processes such as cell proliferation and blood vessel formation, which are key processes that cancer cells need to grow and survive. Activation of these pathways in cancer cells is associated with poor survival outcomes in cancer patients. Because fetal developmental pathways are selectively reactivated in cancer cells, they are ideal targets for the development of novel anti-cancer therapies -- non-cancerous cells in the body in which these pathways are not active would be spared from toxicity, making treatments targeting fetal pathways relatively specific to tumour cells. The goal of my research is to identify fetal lung genes and pathways that are reactivated in lung cancers of never smokers and not expressed in normal adult cells. I will use advanced DNA and RNA sequencing technologies to reveal new genes with critical roles in never smoker lung cancer. The genes I identify may represent novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of never smoker lung cancer, potentially leading to a better prognosis and standard of care for this group of patients in Canada and worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of Genes and Pathways Conferring Cytoprotective Responses and Validation of Potential Targets that will Enhance First-Line Platinum-Based Chemotherapy in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: CISPLATIN; DRUG COMBINATIONS; GENOME-WIDE SCREEN; HIGH CONTENT SCREENING ANALYSIS; NON-SMALL CELL LUNG CANCER; POTENTIATION; REAL-TIME PCR; SMALL INTERFERING RNA; SYNERGY; TARGET VALIDATION
Abstract-Résumé: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer deaths in Canada. In recent years, more non-smokers are being diagnosed with lung cancer, causing a major public concern. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for about 80% of the cases of which two-thirds of the patients have reached the inoperable stage at diagnosis. Standard of care for these patients is a combination of two chemotherapy drugs, with one typically being cisplatin. Even with two agents, the 5-year survival rate is less than 20%, suggesting a great need for new drug combinations to improve treatment outcomes. We propose that certain genes and pathways are activated in cancer cells when they are first exposed to chemotherapy, allowing cancer cells to survive. Inhibiting these genes or gene products should improve the effects of current first-line treatments and, in turn, reduce the chances of cancer recurrence. A recently completed siRNA (small interfering RNA) screen (where each of the 22,000 genes of the human genome was individually knocked out) identified several genes that, when silenced, increased cisplatin activity more than 5-fold. One such gene encodes for 3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) synthase 1 (PAPSS1), an enzyme that makes the biologically usable form of sulfate PAPS from inorganic sulfate. We aim to characterize the role of PAPSS1 and other identified targets in NSCLC and to validate their therapeutic value in multiple NSCLC cell lines as well as in patient-derived NSCLC cells. Therapeutic siRNA will be used in conjunction with high content screening methods to evaluate cisplatin activity under gene silencing conditions. A virtual screen will also help identify existing drug candidates against promising targets to be used as part of a cisplatin chemotherapy cocktail in treating NSCLC. This program will allow us to better understand and ultimately target cytoprotective responses in cancer cells; responses that help cancer cells survive initial exposure to anticancer drugs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studying global proteolysis and N-terminal protein modifications in human cells to determine the mechanisms by which enterohemorrhagic and enteropathogenic Escherichia coli cause human disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL INFECTIONS; BIOCHEMISTRY; CELL CULTURE; CELL CULTURE MODELS; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MICROBIAL PATHOGENESIS; MICROBIOLOGY; PROTEOMICS
Abstract-Résumé: The foodborne pathogens enterohemorrhagic and enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EHEC, EPEC) result in severe diarrheal disease and cause significant morbidity and mortality worldwide. In Canada, EHEC causes an estimated 50 000 infections per year, numerous deaths, and a heavy financial burden. EPEC outbreaks have occurred in Canadian childcare centres. The proposed bio-medical study aims to understand human cellular functions and how they are influenced and disrupted by EHEC and EPEC infection; this understanding is vital to prevent and treat future infections. Studying how the proteins of human cells are altered during infection (the "proteomics" of infection) can further our understanding of how these bacteria affect entire protein networks and how human cells respond to infection.  TAILS (terminal amine isotopic labeling of substrates) is a new proteomics technique that not only identifies and quantifies human proteins but also characterizes how they have been modified (i.e. fragmentation or the addition of chemical groups). The proposed research will use TAILS to study EHEC and EPEC infection of human cells cultured in Petri dishes to see how human protein networks have been altered. I hypothesize that altered human proteins are important during infection and that their study will provide valuable insight into the molecular and system-wide mechanisms by which EHEC and EPEC cause human disease. This research involves a strong collaboration between the TAILS developers and one of the leading Canadian research groups studying bacterial pathogenesis and host-pathogen interactions, forming a uniquely capable group for this project. This study has broad applications to the fields of molecular microbiology and innate immunology, specifically examining how pathogens like EHEC and EPEC cause human disease and how the human cells respond to bacterial infection. This study could also reveal clinical targets against pathogenic E. coli.

TitreApplicationTitle: Who attempts suicide? Predicting attempted suicide among a high-risk population engaging in non-suicidal self-injury.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; CROSS-SECTIONAL; EMOTION; LONGITUDINAL; NON-SUICIDAL SELF-INJURY; RISK ASSESSMENT; SUICIDE; YOUNG ADULTS
Abstract-Résumé: Suicide and attempted suicide are shockingly prevalent. Suicide is the ninth leading cause of death in Canada, and twenty times as many people attempt suicide as die by suicide each year. Non-suicidal self-injury, such as cutting or burning, is also highly prevalent, with an estimated 15% of Canadian adolescents having engaged in these behaviours. Only in the last few years, however, have researchers begun to understand the relationship between non-suicidal and suicidal self-injury. Engaging in non-suicidal self-injury is associated with a much greater likelihood of attempting suicide; this relationship is stronger, in fact, than the relationship between attempted suicide and depression, hopelessness, and previous suicide attempts. Despite this strong relationship, not all self-injurers will make suicide attempts, and little research has investigated what differs between those who do and do not attempt suicide. This proposed research will clarify how aspects of non-suicidal self-injury, such as the frequency of self-injury, the methods used, or the purpose or function of self-injury, are related to suicide attempts among adolescents and young adults. Participants in this research will provide detailed information about their history of non-suicidal self-injury and attempted suicide to determine which aspects of non-suicidal self-injury are most related to suicide risk. Further, some participants will be followed over time to investigate how earlier non-suicidal self-injury is related to later suicide attempts. This research will clarify the relationship between non-suicidal self-injury and suicide, thereby improving not only the ability of researchers to understand the relationship between suicidal and non-suicidal self-injury, but also the ability of clinicians to assess risk of attempted suicide among the already high-risk population of self-injurers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epidemiological insights into increasing postpartum hemorrhage rates in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PRACTICE; GENDER AND HEALTH; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH; PERINATAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; POPULATION AND PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Severe maternal morbidity has received increasing emphasis in the recent international literature for several reasons including the life threatening nature of such conditions and the potential for subsequent disability. Atonic postpartum hemorrhage (bleeding after birth) is one such morbidity. Approximately 14,500 Canadian women experience atonic postpartum hemorrhage each year. In Canada, even though an increase in severe postpartum hemorrhage  was identified in Canada in 2003, no in-depth investigation has been carried out to identify the causes to date. Rates of postpartum hemorrhage in Canada have increased by 34% between 1991 and 2004 (from 29.4 to 39.5 per 1,000 deliveries, respectively). In this application I propose to address this problem through the Canadian Perinatal Network infrastructure using a case-control study. Knowledge gained from this study will be used to facilitate reductions in the frequency of postpartum hemorrhage, prevention of complications and improvements in maternal health.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of thymocyte selection-associated high mobility group box (TOX) in the pathogenesis of cutaneous T cell lymphomas
Keywords-MotsClés: CUTANEOUS T CELL LYMPHOMA; LYMPHOCYTE DEVELOPMENT; MYCOSIS FUNGOIDES; NEOPLASIA; SEZARY SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL) is a rare but fatal disease arising from the T lymphocytes, the most common immune cells of our body. This disease affects more than 3000 Canadians; many of them will die of this disease due to the lack of effective therapies. Normally T lymphocytes have the ability to defend the body against bacterial and viral infections. They stop multiplying at the instruction of the body.  In contrast, the malignant T lymphocytes of CTCL are deficient in infection fighting ability, and they proliferate uncontrollably even when the body tells them to stop.  My research is to understand the fundamental mechanism responsible for the development of the CTCL malignant lymphocytes. Specifically, I study a protein, called TOX that potentially is the key molecular switch present in the malignant T lymphocytes. The results generated will provide vital information on how to turn the malignant T lymphocytes off. Therefore, it will help generate valuable clues for developing effective therapies for this fatal disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: A sticky situation: Defining how bacterial pathogens subvert the intestinal mucus layer.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BACTERIAL VIRULENCE STRATEGIES (MUCINASES); ENTERIC BACTERIAL PATHOGENS; HOST-BACTERIAL INTERACTIONS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; IN VIVO MUCUS QUANTIFICATION; INTESTINAL MICROBIOME; INTESTINAL MUCUS DYNAMICS; PROTEIN PURIFICATION; TISSUE CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: When we eat food or drink water, we are always at risk of consuming dangerous bacteria such Salmonella, Shigella and types of E. coli. These bacteria cause significant illness in millions of North Americans while the same or similar bacteria sicken or kill millions of children each year in the developing world. All these bad bacteria target the cells that line the insides of our intestines, called epithelial cells, either attaching to, or invading these cells. Therefore most research on these dangerous bacteria has focused on understanding how they infect epithelial cells. However, in order for bacteria to reach these epithelial cells, they must pass through a sticky layer of mucus that lies on top of the epithelium. Surprisingly, although essentially every enteric bacterial pathogen must cross this mucus layer to reach the epithelial cells, we know very little about how this is done, and how dangerous bacteria interact with intestinal mucus. My goal is to use mouse models of bacterial infection to study how bacteria cross the mucus layer. I believe that some bacteria are able to swim through the mucus while others cannot swim, and instead chew up the mucus. I also believe that dangerous intestinal bacteria have evolved strategies to use mucus to help them infect their hosts. I therefore plan to test if bacteria, as they cross the mucus layer, actually use mucus as a binding site, to help them invade epithelial cells. I will also test whether some dangerous bacteria release factors that increase their host production of mucus, as a way to improve their chances of spreading to new hosts, and to remove competing resident intestinal bacteria. Taken together, my studies will improve our understanding of how dangerous bacteria infect our intestines, and examine whether targeting the way bacteria interact with the mucus layer may offer novel opportunities to develop new therapeutics, potentially benefitting the health of both children and adults worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phylogenetic clustering: new statistical inference and computational approaches to identify patterns of transmission of HIV and Hepatitis C.
Keywords-MotsClés: BAYESIAN STATISTICAL INFERENCE; CLUSTERING; COMPUTATION AND MARKOV CHAIN MONTE CARLO; EPIDEMIC MODELLING; PHYLOGENETICS; POPULATION HEALTH; TRANSMISSION OF INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: HIV infection represents an ongoing public health concern in the province of Quebec and across Canada.  To better understand patterns of ongoing transmission, viral DNA samples from infected subjects have been cataloged and analyzed to identify closely genetically related ``clusters" of sequences.  A major bottleneck in this process is the vast amount of data now available (several thousands of DNA sequences), which goes beyond the scope of currently existing analytic methods and tools. This project will develop new statistical methods, and computational tools, that will allow researchers to more effectively analyze their data.  In addition to the study of genetic clusters in HIV, the project will also study viral samples from subjects concurrently infected with HIV and Hepatitis C, and examine clustering patterns.

TitreApplicationTitle: Operational Modelling for the Implementation of Treatment as Prevention Programs to Contain the HIV/AIDS Epidemic
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH SYSTEMS; HIGHLY ACTIVE ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; HIV/AIDS; IMPLEMENTATION SCIENCE; MATHEMATICAL MODELLING; NETWORK MODELLING; OPERATIONS RESEARCH; SEEK; SYSTEMS DYNAMICS; TEST; TREAT AND RETAIN PROGRAMS; TREATMENT AS PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) suppresses HIV replication, improving health and extending lives for people living with HIV. Viral suppression also vastly reduces the risk of HIV transmission to uninfected sexual partners. Thus, prioritizing universal, sustained access to HAART also holds significant benefits for the community, through curbing the growth of the HIV epidemic. This strategy - known as Treatment as Prevention - has now become the cornerstone of the global response to the HIV pandemic. Ensuring access to HAART poses great challenges, however. HIV disproportionately affects the most marginalized and only half of those eligible actually access HIV treatment in Canada. Furthermore, treatment delivery is not a single activity but a complex process, which includes HIV testing, referral to care, patient monitoring, activities to ensure treatment adherence and retention in care, as well as coordination with other prevention programs. Treatment delivery also has to be tailored to local epidemiological conditions that often vary by jurisdiction Thus, large-scale expansion of HAART access is an unprecedented operational challenge. The STOP HIV/AIDS initiative in British Columbia is one of the first pilot studies now underway worldwide to evaluate the public health benefits of implementing the Treatment as Prevention strategy. In our proposed project, we will use the methods of operations research and mathematical modelling in conjunction with consultations with public health experts, to develop strategies of effective HIV treatment delivery for optimal public health impact in BC. Efficient treatment delivery can potentially have broad and significant health benefits for Canadians and the Canadian health care system. Therefore, we will seek to generalize our findings to other jurisdictions in Canada. Our team includes HIV, health care operations research, mathematics and health economics experts, as well as key members of the STOP HIV/AIDS team.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autophagy inhibition for the treatment of chemotherapy-refractory triple-negative breast cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; BASAL; BREAST CANCER; CELL SURVIVAL; CHEMOTHERAPY; HUMAN PRIMARY TUMOURS; HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE; TREATMENT RESISTANCE; TRIPLE NEGATIVE; XENOGRAFT MOUSE MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive disease and the most difficult form of breast cancer to treat. For patients with advanced stage disease, the main treatment option is chemotherapy. However, patient response to chemotherapy is variable, and tumors that initially respond often develop chemotherapy resistance. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop new treatment options for TNBC that will help overcome chemotherapy resistance and prevent tumors from coming back. In this study, we propose to generate important evidence supporting a new treatment strategy for TNBC. In combination with chemotherapy, we will treat breast cancer cells with inhibitors that target a cellular process called autophagy. Since autophagy acts to promote both cell survival and chemotherapy resistance, the inhibition of autophagy should result in a more effective treatment response. This prediction is supported by our recent data showing that autophagy inhibition can overcome treatment resistance in a breast cancer cell line model that we developed. In this study, we propose to generate comprehensive evidence, using mouse models and a variety of TNBC samples, to enable the clinical translation of this promising new treatment strategy for TNBC patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Home care case manager work: Understanding workload, caseloads and influencing factors and how these relate to quality of care in various home care contexts
Keywords-MotsClés: CASE MANAGEMENT; CASELOAD; CASELOAD INTENSITY; CASELOAD/WORKLOAD MEASUREMENT; HOME CARE; MIXED METHODS; PHOTOELICITATION; QUALITATIVE; QUALITY OF CARE; WORK
Abstract-Résumé: Home care programs are growing exponentially across Canada both in terms of numbers and acuity of clients. Costs are also on the rise. Home care is a major strategy across Canadian provinces to help manage system pressures and client health care needs. Case management, the process of assessing client needs, care planning, ongoing care coordination and evaluation, is a key strategy; and the one constant, in home care programs across Canada. Unprecedented growth in home care has resulted in higher caseloads of increasing intensity. Measures for the intensity of case manger caseloads and the necessary work associated with their caseloads are not standard. We do not know the impact of caseloads and their intensity on quality of care and resultant outcomes for home care clients and families. The main goal is to understand case manager work, workload, and caseload intensity within different home care contexts (i.e., different populations/geographic regions). Specific objectives are to: 1) identify and examine factors that influence case manager work, workload, and caseload intensity within different home care contexts, 2) explore associations that case managers draw between work-related factors and the quality of care and health outcomes client and families, 3) explore the relationship between case manager caseload/workload factors and client health outcomes, and 4) identify attributes of reasonable, equitable, and manageable caseloads as perceived by case managers, leaders, and case manager teams within different home care contexts. This study will generate new knowledge about case manager work, workload, and caseload intensity. As home care programs continue to grow case manager caseloads must be reasonable and manageable in order to achieve positive client health outcomes, the ultimate goal in any health care delivery program. This work has relevance for rural, suburban and urban areas as it will be carried out in multiple communities with a variety of client types.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of a novel function for small RNAs in alternative splicing
Keywords-MotsClés: ALTERNATIVE SPLICING; ASOS; COMPARATIVE GENOMICS; DOWNREGULATION BY SIRNAS; MACHINE LEARNING; NEXT-GENERATION SEQUENCING; OVARIAN AND BREAST CANCER; PHENOTYPIC ASSAY; RNA PROCESSING; SMALL RNAS; TARGET PREDICTION
Abstract-Résumé: The human genome encodes approximately 22000 protein-coding genes. Depending on the cell type, the actual protein content varies as controlled not only by gene expression regulation but also through the process of alternative splicing, which allows the production of different proteins from a single gene. Although alternative splicing has been extensively investigated, the regulation of many tissue-specific alternative splicing events is poorly understood. Many forms of cancer including ovarian cancer are characterized by alterations in splicing programs highlighting the importance of a comprehensive understanding of this regulation. Small non-coding RNAs represent an abundant and diverse group of molecules, many of which have been recently described as involved in the regulation of essential cellular processes. Preliminary evidence suggests a role for specific types of small RNAs in the regulation of alternative splicing. Some such small RNAs have recently been discovered to be much more abundant in cancer cells including ovarian cancer than in healthy cells.  In light of these recent findings, we propose to characterise specific families of small RNAs and to study their regulatory role in alternative splicing, in normal and ovarian cancer cells, using computational and experimental methods. We will also study the consequences of their deregulation in ovarian cancer, which will be instrumental in devising urgently needed methods for the detection and treatment of this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Evaluation of Blood Product Utilization, Healthcare Resource Consumption and Patient Outcomes in New Oral Anticoagulant-Related Hemorrhage.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE EFFECTS; ANTICOAGULATION; ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; POPULATION COHORT; STROKE PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: Atrial fibrillation is a heart condition that increases the chance of stroke in elderly individuals, and this can be prevented through anticoagulation, or blood-thinning. Too much blood-thinning, however, can lead to bleeding and death. Recently, two new drugs were approved as recommended therapy for blood-thinning in people living with atrial fibrillation based on results of studies that showed their superiority over an older drug, warfarin. However, there have been recent reports of severe bleeding among people taking these new blood-thinners, complicated by the fact that there is no approved antidote to reverse the effect of these drugs in hospital once bleeding begins. The purpose of this study is to find out 1) what are the current types of treatment and their associated medical costs for elderly patients who present to four major hospitals in Ontario with bleeds from new blood-thinners and warfarin; and 2) if the outcomes after treatment are different between these two groups of patients. Health records departments at our participating hospitals and our research unit have unique databases that capture information about diagnosis, treatment, cost and outcomes of hospital encounters. We will also review the charts of individuals who came to hospital with blood-thinner-related bleeds to see which medications they were on when they came in. By looking at costs and outcomes of treating the elderly suffering from new blood-thinner complications using real-world patient data, we hope to provide information about current Canadian practices and provide preliminary information for further research, all aimed at improving the health and well-being of atrial fibrillation patients undergoing blood-thinner treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cognitive Training in the Rural Elderly: A Randomized Trial to Evaluate the Efficacy and Accessibility of a New Approach
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITIVE REHABILITATION; EXPERIMENTAL; MULTIVARIATE ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Much has been made of the fact that Canada's population is aging, and with it, the number of people suffering from thinking problems is climbing. Treatment aimed at addressing the impact of aging is particularly restricted in rural regions of Canada that are in great need of creative solutions to service delivery barriers. The heart of this research is to encourage a wide variety of healthcare professionals to join forces to develop new treatment options that will allow rural Canadians to age gracefully in their thinking abilities. To do so, healthy elderly who consent to participate will be provided with a self-help treatment kit containing specialized thinking activities that are believed to strengthen intellect. Over the course of 4 weeks, participants will be required to engage in the program by themselves 1 hour, 5 days/week. To ensure that the project goes smoothly, participants will be closely monitored and will be provide with one-on-one coaching throughout the treatment period. At the end of the program, participants of the treatment program will be compared to people who were not part of the program in order to see if the program worked in improving thinking ability. What this project highlights is a need for researchers and practitioners to connect in a way that improves the quality and accessibility of care to rural-dwelling Canadians. A program that encourages people to actively participate in overcoming their thinking problems is irrefutably worth pursuing.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effet des mutations responsables de maladies de l'oeil sur la liaison membranaire de la R9AP
Keywords-MotsClés: BRADYOPSIE; LIAISON MEMBRANAIRE; MALADIES DE L'OEIL; MEMBRANES; MUTANTS; PHOTOTRANSDUCTION VISUELLE; PROTEINE; R9AP; RETINE; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: La vision est rendue possible grace a la conversion de la lumiere en un signal electrique par la cascade de phototransduction visuelle dans les cellules photoreceptrices de l'oeil. Cette cascade implique plusieurs proteines dont l'inactivation est primordiale pour que les photorecepteurs retrouvent leur sensibilite aux changements d'intensite lumineuse. Au cours de ce processus, un complexe de proteines inluant la R9AP (RGS9 Anchor Protein) participe a l'inactivation d'une importante proteine de la phototransduction appelee phosphodiesterase (PDE). La structure de la R9AP n'est pas encore connue. On sait toutefois qu'elle est exprimee uniquement dans les photorecepteurs et qu'elle est associee a la membrane de ces cellules par le biais de son segment transmembranaire en helice alpha. La presence de mutations dans le gene de la R9AP empechant sa liaison membranaire et sa fonction d'inactivation se traduit par une adaptation lente des photorecepteurs aux changements de luminosite et a une maladie appelee bradyopsie. Les patients atteints par cette maladie presentent une photophobie, ainsi que des difficultes a adapter leur vision a un eclairage variable et a suivre des objets en mouvement. La bradyopsie est causee par deux mutations de la R9AP qui conduisent a un ralentissement important de l'inactivation de la PDE, ce qui suggere un role majeur de la liaison membranaire de la R9AP dans l'arret de la phototransduction visuelle. Les travaux proposes visent donc a cloner, surexprimer et purifier la R9AP native ainsi que ses differents mutants pour determiner leur liaison membranaire et le role des mutations causant la bradyopsie. De plus, a plus long terme, la determination de la structure de la R9AP et de ses mutants permettra non seulement d'expliquer plus clairement son role dans l'inactivation de la PDE, mais aussi de comprendre comment des mutations de cette proteine peuvent mener a des maladies de l'oeil.

TitreApplicationTitle: Limiting HIV target cells by inducing immune quiescence in the female genital tract
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; CHLOROQUINE; CYTOKINES/CHEMOKINES; HIV EXPOSED SERONEGATIVE; HIV INFECTION; IMMUNE QUIESCENCE
Abstract-Résumé: This proposal's goal is to limit the number of target cells that HIV infects in the female genital tract.  A long-term study of commercial sex workers in Nairobi, Kenya who are intensely exposed to HIV yet remain uninfected has shown us that the immune systems of these women are very unique.  They are exceptional in that they have significantly fewer HIV target cells in their genital tract.  The goal of this study is to try to induce that state of fewer HIV target cells in other women.  To do this we will use a very safe and inexpensive drug, hydroxychloroquine, that limits improper activation of immune cells and prevents them from being targets for HIV infection.  In this proposal, we will assess the role of this drug in a test tube tissue model, in animal studies and in human volunteer studies.  Through this study, we should able to reduce the number of HIV target cells in the female genital tract and in doing so provide a novel level of protection from HIV infection that could be exploited on its own or in combination with other prevention strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Combined late and early HIV-1 protein-specific exosome-targeted T cell-based vaccine capable of stimulating CTL responses in absence of CD4+ T cell help
Keywords-MotsClés: CD4+ T CELL HELP; CD8 CTL; EXOSOME; GAG; GP120; HAART; HIV-1; T CELL VACCINE; TAT
Abstract-Résumé: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) in human immunodeficiency virus type-1 (HIV-1)-infected patients causes millions of individuals died each year. Highly active antiviral therapy (HAART) is currently the only means to halt progression of AIDS. Although HAART  suppressis viral replication and improves prognosis, it is unable to eliminate the proviral latent reservoirs by any vaccine strategies which are dependent on the functional dendritic cells (DC) and CD4+ T cells. However, AIDS patients often have dendritic cell dysfunction and CD4+ T cell dificiency. In this study, we propose to develop a combined late and early HIV-1 protein (Gp120/gag and Tat)-specific exosome (EXO)-targeted T cell-based (Gp120/gag/tat-Texo) vaccine. We will assess the therapeutic efficiency of Gp120/gag/tat-Texo vaccine against Gp120 or Gag-expressing tumor cells in wild-type C57BL/6 abd BALB/c mice and transgenic HLA-A2-expressing A2Kb mice closely mimicking the human situation. This novel Gp120/gag/tat-Texo vaccine capable of stimulating broadened efficient CTL responses and memory may thus be useful in immunotherpay of AIDS patients with DC dysfunction and declined CD4+ T cells, especially those on HAART for cleaning their proviral latent reservoirs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Negative Regulation of Immune Cell Function
Keywords-MotsClés: INOSITOL PHOSPHATASE; INTERLEUKIN-10; MACROPHAGE; PHAGOCYTOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Although macrophage activation is an important step in both innate and acquired immune responses, this inflammatory reaction must be carefully regulated in order to avoid pathological consequences. One cytokine, soluble proteins which cells use to communicate and regulate each other, called interleukin-10 (IL10) is a key regulator of macrophage activation. Studies directed at understanding the mechanism by which IL10 inhibits macrophage activation have focused on examining whether IL10 alters intracellular signalling pathways shown to be essential for the function of macrophage activators. Several studies, for example, have shown that IL10 inhibits the NFkB and the Map kinase pathways involve inLPS activation of macrophages. However, the significance of these observation remain unclear because of the variability of the results and because it has not been possible to link them mechanistically to any IL10 signalling pathway. To approach this problem from a different perspective, my studies will concentrate on characterizing IL10-induced signalling pathways and the role they play in mediating IL10's anti-inflammatory action. An understanding of how IL10 deactivates macrophages may provide new insights into development of anti-inflammatory drugs or therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Derivation of sinoatrial node pacemaker cells from human pluripotent stem cells for the generation of bio-artificial pacemakers.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIO-ARTIFICIAL PACEMAKER; CARDIOMYOCYTE SUBTYPE SPECIFICATION; CARDIOMYOCYTE SURFACE MARKER; CARDIOMYOCYTES; HEART DEVELOPMENT; HUMAN EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; REGENERATIVE THERAPY; SIGNALING PATHWAYS; SINOATRIAL NODE PACEMAKER CELLS; STEM CELL DIFFERENTIATION
Abstract-Résumé: It is now possible to routinely generate cardiomyocytes from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). The heart is composed of two major cardiomyocyte subtypes: the working myocardium consisting of atrial and ventricular myocytes and the pacemaker myocardium consisting of sinoatrial node pacemaker cells and atrioventricular node pacemaker cells. While there is some diversity in the cardiomyocytes that are obtained from hESCs, there are currently no approaches to specifically derive and purify these subtypes of human cardiomyocytes. Sinoatrial node pacemaker cells (SNPCs) represent a myocyte population that is of special interest to cardiac research as these cells are the primary pacemakers of the heart. Patients with a failing sinoatrial node suffer from arrhythmias and bradicardia (too slow heart rhythm). Currently these patients are subjected to implantation of electronic pacemaker devices requiring recurrent surgeries. The ability to replace the sinoatrial node of these patients with pacemaker cells made from stem cells would represent a novel therapy for this type of heart disease. My postdoctoral project aims to specifically derive SNPCs from hESCs. Preliminary findings from my research show that it is possible to isolate hESC-derived SNPC-like cells based on the expression of two different markers. These SNPC-like cells beat faster than control cardiomyocytes and express pacemaker specific genes. The goals of my project are to further characterize these cells to formally demonstrate that they are SNPCs, to identify surface markers that will enable their isolation and to define the signaling pathways that regulate their development. Ultimately, I want to test the hypothesis that SNPCs can pace the working myocardium using an animal model, with the aim to demonstrate that SNPCs can function as bio-artificial pacemaker.

TitreApplicationTitle: Discovering the Mutational Landscape of Hodgkin Lymphoma
Keywords-MotsClés: HODGKIN LYMPHOMA; LYMPHOMAGENESIS; MUTATIONAL LANDSCAPE; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; TARGETED THERAPIES; WHOLE GENOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Primary lymphoid cancer is the fifth most frequent cancer in humans. Among those, Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL) represents the most common type of lymphoid cancer in young people in the Western world. Despite modern treatment strategies, about 20% die following relapse or progressive disease. To construct better treatments for these patients a better understanding of why HL develops is required.    HL is unique amongst all cancers because the malignant cells, so called Hodgkin Reed Sternberg cells (HRS), are greatly outnumbered by normal immune cells surrounding the HRS cells. HRS cells make up only about 1% of the tumor, and this paucity has hampered molecular studies of these cells in the past. In the last 3 years our understanding of cancer biology has rapidly improved based on a technological revolution enabling the analysis of the entire genome of cancer cells. This technology is called "next generation sequencing" and we have already used this technology in our research team uncovering many new genetic characteristics of cancer cells.  In this study, we will perform whole genome sequencing of purified, laser- microdissected HRS cells from HL patients by next generation sequencing. By these experiments we will for the first time uncover the "genetic landscape" of HL and this study will be one of the world's largest and most comprehensive biological studies of HL. The final goal of our research is to discover genetic characteristics that can be used as novel therapeutic targets. Ultimately, our findings will lead to the development of new drugs that will help to cure many young HL patients in the world as well as in Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sexual Well-Being in Couples Living with Fibromyalgia: An Application of the Interpersonal Exchange Model of Sexual Satisfaction
Keywords-MotsClés: COUPLES; FIBROMYALGIA; HEALTH PROMOTION; HEALTH RESEARCH; SEXUAL WELL-BEING; SURVEY STUDY
Abstract-Résumé: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a pain disorder affecting 2 - 4% of the adult population with a ratio of approximately 6-9 women to 1 man suffering from the disorder. There is preliminary evidence that FM has a severe negative impact on women's sexual lives, sexual relationships, and sexual well-being. The proposed research will be comprised of three studies. The first study will determine the nature and extent of compromised sexual well-being in patients with FM compared to individuals who are not living with a pain disorder. Although research has begun to identify the impact of FM on individuals' sexual lives, little is known about their experiences or about why and how FM negatively affects sexual well-being. Therefore, a second goal of this study is to test a model delineating the illness-related mechanisms underlying the relationship between FM and lower sexual well-being. In the second study, the main goal is to test the reciprocal effects of examine the reciprocal effects of individuals with FM and their partner on both partners' sexual well-being by collecting data from both members of the couple. The results of these innovative studies will be used for the third study in which a detailed informational pamphlet will be designed as an intervention to improve sexual well-being for patients with FM and their partner. Thus, the fourth goal of the research proposal is to evaluate the effectiveness of this intervention. The proposed research will offer the first evidence of why FM affects sexual well-being and preliminary evidence of how to promote sexual well-being in individuals with FM.

TitreApplicationTitle: Treating and identifying predictors of treatment success in children with developmental prosopagnosia
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS; DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOLOGY; FACE PERCEPTION; INTERVENTION; NEUROPSYCHOLOGY; PROSOPAGNOSIA; TREATMENT; VISUAL PERCEPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Every day we interact with many people. Our ability to recognize the faces of others relies on a network of brain areas. Impairments to this network produce face recognition deficits. Developmental face blindness (prosopagnosia) is defined by severe face recognition problems resulting from a failure to develop the necessary visual mechanisms for processing faces. These individuals fail to recognize familiar faces, such as friends and family, and sometimes even their own face. Estimates from adults suggest that 2% of the population is affected, meaning that millions of children could suffer from face blindness. It can have a serious impact during childhood, leading to difficulties making friends, participating in social activities, and increased anxiety. Treating children with face blindness is important for promoting their health and wellbeing, but few studies have tested whether interventions improve face processing. The proposed research involves testing a treatment strategy with a group of children who have developmental face blindness. This strategy, which involves training children to pay attention to the spatial relationships between facial features, has been shown to work in an adult case. This research will determine which children respond to treatment, and whether they have certain characteristics that may be predictive of their treatment outcome. We expect that children with less severe and more specific deficits will be more likely to benefit. Identifying useful treatments and determining who is best suited for those treatments will positively impact a large number of children and their families. This research will also provide important information about the development and flexibility of the human visual system. Early intervention for children with developmental disorders is important for improving the quality of life and potential of young Canadians, promoting the likelihood that they will become well-adjusted and productive members of our society.

TitreApplicationTitle: Coordinating targeted delivery of latency-reversing drugs and enhanced antiviral T-cell responses to eradicate HIV infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOPTIVE IMMUNOTHERAPY; BLT HUMANIZED MOUSE; CYTOTOXIC T LYMPHOCYTES; HIV; HIV ERADICATION/CURE; HIV RESERVOIRS; NANOTECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Although current medications can dramatically improve the lives of people living with HIV/AIDS they cannot cure infection. Treatment is an expensive lifelong commitment, and is associated with side-effects which substantially reduce quality of life. There is therefore an urgent need to develop an HIV cure. A major challenge in curing HIV is that the virus hides out in very long-lived cells, where it is invisible to the immune system, but from where it can re-emerge if treatment is ever stopped. We propose to explore a strategy of enhancing T-cells, the natural virus hunters of the immune system, via nanotechnology in a way which both enables them to see this hidden virus, and improves their ability to survive and multiply in the body. This approach is analogous to sonar on a submarine, whereby T-cells will give off a signal as they circulate throughout the body that will expose any hidden virus. We will systematically test these enhanced T-cells in a mouse model of HIV infection with the goal of curing these animals. If we observe success in this model we will develop this strategy towards a cure for HIV/AIDS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Studies on the Development of an Effective Vaccine Against Hepatitis C Virus
Keywords-MotsClés: HEPATITIS C VIRUS (HCV); IMMUNOLOGY; INFECTIOUS DISEASE; LIVER DISEASE; MEDICAL MICROBIOLOGY; PUBLIC HEALTH; VACCINE; VIROLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) remains a major cause of liver disease in Canada and worldwide.  There are 250-350 thousand chronic carriers of HCV in Canada - approximately seven times more than the number of HIV infected people.  An effective vaccine for HCV remains an urgent medical need globally.  Although there has been significant progress in the development of direct acting antiviral agents, these drugs are proving to be very expensive. To address this challenge, my proposed supervisor's research group has recently developed a cell culture system that can increase the production of HCV by 1000 times.  This makes the production of a "killed" viral vaccine for HCV feasible.  My plan is now to produce a new HCV vaccine and test its ability to prevent HCV infection in cell culture as well as in an animal model.  My research has two specific objectives: 1. to produce sufficient amounts of "killed" HCV vaccine to immunize mice, and 2. to compare the various immune responses produced by the new HCV vaccine with another experimental HCV vaccine. I anticipate that my proposed HCV vaccine will result in more complete immune protection than the limited protection afforded by other vaccines.  The proposed studies may provide important leads to the development of a successful vaccine that can protect against many forms of HCV.
