TitreApplicationTitle: Pharmaceutical Innovation, Drug Access, and International Trade Policy in an Era of Global Population Aging
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COMPARATIVE CASE STUDY; COMPULSORY LICENSE; GLOBAL DRUG ACCESS AND TRADE; GLOBAL GOVERNANCE; INDIA; INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY; PHARMACEUTICAL FIRMS; POLITICAL ECONOMY; THAILAND
Abstract-Résumé: The developing world is aging rapidly, creating unprecedented demand for age-associated disease medicines (e.g., cancer, cardiovascular disease)--perhaps the most expensive and often patented category of pharmaceuticals. World Trade Organization member states in the developing world find themselves facing decisions that pit their national trade interests against their public health interests. Multinational pharmaceutical firms find themselves in a conflict paradigm, defending their intellectual property and pricing. The globalized stage is set for a complex drama with multiple actors whose competing and converging interests compel actions with significant impact on other stakeholders. What policy options are the key stakeholders considering vis-a-vis this challenge? How could these change the landscape of drug access and trade, if at all? This study will use Thailand and India's negotiations over patents on and prices of age associated disease medicines (e.g., Clopidogrel/Plavix, Imatinib mesylate/Glivec or Gleevic, Letrozole/Femara) in 2006-2012 with four multinational pharmaceutical firms (i.e., Novartis, Sanofi-Aventis, Roche, and Bayer) to do a comparative analysis of multiple, exploratory case-studies. Detailed, systematic text analysis and 45 interviews with key stakeholders will be conducted. A political economy analysis, drawing from game theory, will be utilized to forecast on outcomes and externalities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Conformity to the Majority: Peer Impact of Medical and Nursing Student's Clinical Skills Performance in a Simulated Training Enviroment
Keywords-MotsClés: DECISION MAKING; GROUP CONFORMITY; HEALTH PROFESSIONALS; INTERPROFESSIONAL TEAM DYNAMICS; MEDICAL STUDENTS; MISCOMMUNICATION; NURSING STUDENTS; PATIENT SAFETY; PEER PRESSURE; SOCIAL BEHAVIOURS
Abstract-Résumé: This study will examine the need for medical and nursing students to gain membership in, and a sense of belonging to, their peer group. Over the last 60 years, researchers around the world have shown that people are likely to conform to the consensus of the group, despite believing that this consensus may be incorrect (Asch, 1951). This is known as group conformity and may be motivated by the need to be seen as a team player. Conformity among healthcare professionals may also occur and explain, in part, the rate of medical error occurrence of 20,000 deaths per year in Canadian hospitals  (Baker et al., 2004). The economic burden of medical errors is estimated at $300 million (Zhan et al., 2006).  The proposed research will shed light on whether nursing students, who may be trained to follow orders given by doctors, are likely to conform to a group of medical students who give incorrect vital sign readings from a simulation mannequin. Specifically, we ask, will nursing students repeat the same incorrect readings for pulse, respiration, and blood pressure they hear from medical students despite taking different readings from a mannequin? If this is the case, it is important that course curriculum include strategies and communication skills to teach students how to assertively manage conflicting or inaccurate information that is likely to occur during multidisciplinary teamwork. These skills will likely reduce conformity behaviors among healthcare professionals to ensure that the best quality of care is provided to Canadian patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Engineering interactions between the macrophage polarization and human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiac tissue to develop an in vitro myocardial infarction model to understand the early disease progression
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIAC STEM CELL ENGINEERING; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES; IMMUNE SYSTEM; INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE; MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of mortality in Canada. Myocardial infarction (MI), also known as a heart attack, occurs when there is a narrowing or a blockage of a blood vessel supplying oxygen and nutrients to the heart. After an MI, the lack of oxygen causes inflammation in the heart muscle that results in scarring. However, the scarred heart tissue is dysfunctional and disrupts normal heart function, eventually leading to heart failure. Very little is known about inflammation occurring in the heart after an MI, and current study tools in the laboratory setting are limited.  In this respect, the discovery of a specific type of stem cell has opened an exciting era of potential for MI research. This type of stem cell, called pluripotent stem cell, is capable of giving rise to different cell types of various human organs. In particular, a set of proteins can cause human cells that are already a specific cell type  to reverse back into cells that are pluripotent, which has a potential to become any cell type. These generated cells are called human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs).    Our lab has shown that cardiac cells can be derived from hiPSCs. In this study, I propose to use hiPSCs to create an engineered heart tissue (EHT). I will combine EHT with cells that produce inflammation and deprive this system of oxygen, to study how the inflammatory system contributes to the early progression of an MI and scarring. Better understanding of these early events in scarring after a heart attack may lead to the development of pharmaceutical interventions to reduce cardiovascular mortality and improve the quality of life of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tumor cell-derived mechanisms underlying lung-specific metastatic behavior of breast cancer cells:  Role of ALDH1A1, CD44 and other stem cell related factors.
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDEHYDE DEHYDROGENASE; BREAST CANCER; CANCER STEM CELL; CD44; LUNG; METASTASIS
Abstract-Résumé: Most breast cancer deaths occur as a result of metastasis, the process whereby tumor cells (or "seeds") leave the breast through the bloodstream and establish themselves in other organs (the "soil"). These metastatic tumors are often difficult to find and have an increased capacity for therapy resistance. However, breast cancer cells do not thrive in all organs, but instead show preference for migrating to and growing in specific organs including lymph node, lung, liver, brain, and bone. In particular, lung metastasis frequently associates with poor outcome. Furthermore, there is strong scientific evidence indicating that (1) not all tumor cells have an equal ability to seed themselves in distant organs and (2) these aggressive tumor cells use specific molecular factors for thriving in distant organs.   We have identified a very specific subgroup of breast cancer cells, known as "cancer stem cells". These cells are responsible for seeding cancer outgrowths in the lung and other organs throughout the body. Our research group has previously demonstrated that these cancer stem cells contribute to metastasis and therapy resistance. Now, we endeavor to identify the molecular factors utilized by these tumor seeds to enter, be planted, and thrive specifically in the lung. Identification and subsequent interference of the action of these factors with new drugs has the potential to improve breast cancer treatment by blocking the lethal seeding activity of breast cancer to the lung.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting molecular phenotypes of SHANK2 mutations using patient-specific neurons from an autistic patient
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; DEVELOPMENT; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELL; NEURON; SYNAPSE
Abstract-Résumé: Autism spectrum disorders affect 1% of all children and is marked by deficits in social interaction. Recent evidence suggests that genes governing mechanisms of neuronal communication, such as SHANK2, are partially responsible for the cause of autism spectrum disorders. I will use human patient-specific neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells to study the mechanisms of SHANK 2 mutations in causing this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Experimental and theoretical investigation of the dynamics of ultrasonically excited micro-bubbles for imaging and therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAT CANCER; HIGH FREQUENCY ULTRASOUND; MICRO-BUBBLES; ULTRASONIC IMAGING; ULTRASOUND ENHANCED DRUG DELIVERY
Abstract-Résumé: Micro-bubbles (MBs) are used to increase the sensitivity of diagnostic ultrasound in detecting cancer. They can also be used as to deliver drugs and genes to tumors. However, how the micro-bubbles respond to ultrasound is poorly understood, especially at higher frequencies of ultrasound. As an example, high frequency clinical ultrasonic imaging (e.g >10 MHz) still cannot produce good ultrasound images with MBs. Understanding the how the MBs respond to ultrasound excitation, especially at higher frequencies, is the key to optimize how MBs are used for imaging but also therapy. I will investigate both theoretically and experimentally the dynamics of MBs at higher frequencies. Previously, I developed efficient experimental and theoretical methods for analyzing the behavior of single MBs. Using these methods we discovered new phenomena in the oscillations of MBs at higher frequencies that were not known before. The new oscillatory behavior of the MBs allows much better approaches to ultrasound imaging and therapy. In this research I will continue my theoretical and experimental investigations on the oscillations of MBs by extending the MB model to MBs confined within elastic walls to replicate the dynamics of MBs within small blood vessels. Our discovery of the new MB dynamics will be used in phantom experiments and in in-vivo models to investigate the improvements expected in clinical settings. We believe that our findings will have significant impact on improving the ultrasound technology used to acquire contrast enhanced images at higher resolution. This may allow early detection of cancer and monitoring of the response of the tumors to treatments. In addition, we expect these findings to improve drug delivery applications of ultrasound. The end goal will be a cost effective, portable, real-time, minimally invasive and nonionizing platform for cancer detection and therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Evidence in Pediatric Intensive Care (EPIC) Research Program
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL EPIDEMIOLOGY; PEDIATRIC CRITICAL CARE; PEDIATRICS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIALS; RESARCH METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: My program of research has two goals, both of which will ultimately improve the care of critically ill children and their families. The first is to improve the ability of clinicians to use currently published randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The second is to improve how future RCTs are designed and conducted.  The program includes four studies, each building on the results of the previous study:  (1)A review of RCTs and systematic reviews to identify and describe previous studies. Compiling this information will make this literature more accessible to clinicians caring for patients and researchers planning studies.  (2)A survey of Canadian physicians and pharmacists who care for critically ill children to help understand how they make decisions for in critically ill children.  This will provide key information on the factors they consider, particularly when there is limited evidence. (3)An observational study of medication use in critically ill children in Canada to understand how medications are used. This study, when combined with the review, will allow us to identify where new research is needed. (4)A study interviewing clinicians caring for critically ill children to understand how they use the results of research studies.  This will help to us design studies that will be more useful to them.    Over 10,000 seriously ill children are admitted to the 18 pediatric intensive care units in Canada. In many cases there are no RCTs to help guide treatment, and those that have been done are often small and of modest quality. Additional problems faced by pediatric clinicians are difficulties finding the studies that have been done and keeping up to date with the latest information. The projects in this research program will identify areas where future research is needed and to ensure that clinicians can keep up to date, we will build a free, regularly updated, database of RCTs done in critically ill children.

TitreApplicationTitle: A New Analytical Paradigm to Predict and Prevent Bladder Toxicity from Pelvic Radiation Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: BLADDER TOXICITY; CLINICAL PRACTICE IMPROVEMENT; DEFORMABLE REGISTRATION; DOSE ACCUMULATION; FUNCTIONAL IMAGING; PELVIC CANCER; PERSONALIZED CANCER TREATMENT; QUALITY OF LIFE; RADIATION THERAPY; UROFLOWMETRY
Abstract-Résumé: Radiotherapy (RT) is a very effective treatment for cancer, and more than 50% of cancer patients will receive RT as part of their treatment. It is not always possible to deliver tumoricidal doses of RT to pelvic cancers without causing side effects because of the proximity of normal organs. Bladder side effects are common after RT for prostate, gynaecologic and rectal cancer and this can have a serious detrimental effect on survivor quality of life.  New techniques that manipulate the spatial distribution of RT dose hold the potential to personalize the design of cancer treatment and provide important opportunities to minimize bladder side effects. But, despite years of investigation, the relationship between bladder dose and the development of side effects remains ill-defined. This is because routine dose calculations do not incorporate the effect of daily bladder filling variations during a 1-2 month RT course and bladder side effects are typically reported using highly subjective symptom scales.  This project will capitalize on recent advances in imaging and RT dose modelling to quantify the actual dose delivered to the bladder. This will involve calculating the dose delivered to the bladder each day from images acquired at the time of daily RT, then summing the daily doses using a special technique (deformable registration) which accounts for changes in bladder shape, size and position. Side effects will be assessed through the novel application of various objective methods to measure bladder function (e.g. uroflowmetry, functional MRI).  The results of this research will enable the generation of highly personalized RT plans that will provide patients with the highest probability of an uncomplicated cure and will facilitate more uniform reporting of side effects in future clinical trials. Overall, this project has the potential to influence clinical RT practice internationally and reduce the toxicity burden on pelvic cancer survivors worldwide.

TitreApplicationTitle: Linking Ventilator-Induced Diaphragm Dysfunction and Weaning Failure to Diaphragm Inactivity During Mechanical Ventilation: A Physiological Clinical Research Program
Keywords-MotsClés: CONTROL OF BREATHING; INTENSIVE CARE; MECHANICAL VENTILATION; OUTCOMES RESEARCH; RESPIRATORY DRIVE; RESPIRATORY MUSCLE WEAKNESS; RESPIRATORY PHYSIOLOGY; WEANING
Abstract-Résumé: The diaphragm is the most important breathing muscle in the human body. When patients experience severe breathing difficulties from acute respiratory failure, artificial ventilation is used to help the patient breathe until they recover. However, artificial ventilation can actually weaken the diaphragm, making it more difficult to breathe on their own (without assistance from the ventilator) once they recover from the acute lung disease.  Previous laboratory research suggests that artificial ventilation may weaken the diaphragm by allowing it to completely rest. Any muscle that is rested will eventually lose muscle mass and strength and this weakness may develop even more rapidly in the diaphragm (within hours), a muscle that ordinarily works around the clock. However, no one has yet studied whether diaphragm over-rest causes diaphragm weakness in real patients receiving artificial ventilation.  We are studying the effects of diaphragm rest in patients on artificial respiration with a variety of acute lung diseases. We are also developing new methods for measuring diaphragm activity and strength that will make it easier for doctors to check whether the patient's diaphragm is working or resting during artificial ventilation.   If our theory (over-rest weakens the diaphragm) proves correct, then doctors will change the method of artificial ventilation to keep the diaphragm working comfortably. This may help patients recover from the ventilator more easily and prevent the complications (pneumonia, death, long-term weakness and disability) associated with a long stay on artificial ventilation. This would also reduce the healthcare costs required to treat acute respiratory failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: The mTOR pathway in HCC using a systems Biology approach
Keywords-MotsClés: EIF4E; HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA; MTOR PATHWAY
Abstract-Résumé: Liver cancer is the 5th most common cancer in the world, and is associated with a poor survival rate because of late cancer diagnosis and few therapeutic options. It is therefore very important to develop more effective diagnostic and therapeutic tools against this cancer. There is a pathway called the mTOR pathway that helps cancers grow by increasing their protein and fat synthesis, and it is upregulated in a large number of liver cancers. The goal of this project is to determine what role a critical protein in the mTOR pathway called eIF4E plays in liver cancer development, and whether this occurs by starving the cancer cells of protein and fat, thereby inducing cell death. We could then possibly target this protein to treat liver cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Endoscopic Ultrasonography in Ontario and Alberta: Healthcare Utilization and Outcomes from 2003 to 2011
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADIAN POPULATION-BASED STUDY; COMPLICATIONS; DEMOGRAPHICS; DIAGNOSIS; ENDOSCOPIC ULTRASOUND; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HOSPITALIZATION; OBSERVATIONAL STUDY; PROCEDURE; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is a relatively new technique that provides high-resolution ultrasound imaging to examine the walls of the digestive tract as well organs near the gastrointestinal tract such as the lungs.  EUS can be used to diagnose and treat diseases of the esophagus, stomach, bile duct, pancreas and colon as well as determine the extent of spread of certain cancers.  The high-resolution imaging offered by EUS allows for safe sampling of lumps and lesions.  EUS with sampling has been shown to be more accurate at determining the extent to lung cancer spread compared to other imaging techniques such as computed tomography scan and positron emission tomography.  On the other hand, it is costly and requires highly trained specialists.    Very little is known about how EUS is currently being used in Canada, how this may have changed over time or potential inequalities in patient access to EUS.  Furthermore, no studies have evaluated health outcomes following EUS in a Canadian setting.  Therefore, the present study aims to confirm the accuracy of EUS procedure codes available through provincial health administrative databases and then describe 1) who receives EUS (including patient demographics and their medical conditions), 2) how EUS is being delivered (patient, procedure and physician characteristics) and 3) important clinical events that occur after EUS is provided in a real world setting.    The overall goals of this study are to raise awareness among physicians and health care managers about how EUS is delivered in Canada as well as important clinical events associated with EUS, and thereby encourage informed decision making regarding patient care and resource allocation for patients who may benefit from EUS.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and validation of novel metabolic biomarkers for osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; METABOLOMICS; OSTEOARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis and results in substantial disability in the elderly. It primarily involves the joints of the knee, hip, spine, hand and foot, and is strongly associated with increasing age. It imposes a great economic burden on society and this societal burden (both in terms of personal suffering and use of health resources) is expected to increase worldwide with the increasing prevalence of obesity and the aging of the community. While there are drugs available on the market that reduce pain and improve function, there are no drugs available that decrease or eliminate the disease, and there is no reliable method of determining the amount of joint destruction in osteoarthritis. There is a pressing need to develop reliable markers - biomarkers, which can indicate the amount of joint destruction. These biomarkers will be of value in early detection of disease, improving earlier treatments for patients with fast progression of the disease. Biomarkers also provide an opportunity of drug development and testing in clinical trials. The emerging field of metabolomics provides the opportunity to identify biomarkers from body fluids or tissues in a single step. We will use this approach to follow-up on our preliminary experiments to identify new biomarkers for osteoarthritis in patients undergoing total joint replacement. This study will provide valuable information about the biomarkers related to osteoarthritis, which can be used to identify patients with fast progression of the disease and provide earlier treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hypothalamic control of energy balance and food reinforcement
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE; FASTING; FOOD INTAKE; HYPOTHALAMUS; OREXIN NEURON; PATCH CLAMP RECORDING; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY; SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
Abstract-Résumé: Overweight and obesity are among the top global health problems as the population of overweight outnumbers the undernourished. In Canada, almost 60% of the population is overweight or obese, causing increased morbidity, expansion of health care costs, diminished quality of life and a reduction in economic productivity. Therefore, there is an urgent need for efficient therapies and prevention strategies to prevent or reduce obesity. Overconsumption of palatable high fat diet often underlies weight gain, which is driven by the brain recognizing food as rewarding. Orexin neurons are known to mediate the motivational aspect of food intake. Therefore, food deprivation or exposure to palatable foods may alter the regulation of these neurons which in turn may promote appetite and excessive food intake. To test this hypothesis, we will use in vitro electrophysiological technique to investigate the mechanisms by which orexin neurons are regulated and how they are affected by palatable diet or fasting. We will also test how modulation of orexin neurons affect food intake. The proposed study will shed some light onto the mechanism by which overfeeding is induced.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding Discharge Instruction for Children and Caregivers in the Transition from Pediatric Emergency Care
Keywords-MotsClés: DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS; EFFECTIVE COMMUNICATION; HEALTH SERVICE DELIVERY; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PEDIATRIC EMERGENCY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Over 87% of children who visit Canadian emergency departments (EDs) are discharged home to their place of residence. Following discharge, many children and their caregivers are unable to list their diagnosis, recount the name and purpose of medications they received, outline the recommended post ED care or know when to return to seek medical advice. The aim of this project is to develop a description of a patient centered approach to discharge instructions in the context of Canadian pediatric emergency care. The description will be developed from data gathered through chart audits, observations parent/clinician interactions in the ED and focus group interviews with parents and clinicians. This work will increase our understanding of discharge communication in Canadian pediatric EDs and lead to national policy recommendations for delivery of discharge instructions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and immunological characterizations of reovirus oncolysis
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-CANCER IMMUNITY; INNNATE IMMUNITY; RAS SIGNALLING; REOVIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: We don't normally think of viruses as beneficial organisms because they are invariably associated with human diseases. In 1998, we demonstrated that a naturally occurring, benign human virus, called reovirus, is a potent cancer killer. This virus is able to infect a variety of cancer cells, eventually killing them. Progeny viruses made in these cells are released and can in turn infect and kill neighboring cancer cells. We have further shown that reovirus is very effective against various human cancers implanted in mice, including brain, breast, pancreas, prostate, ovarian, and colorectal cancers. Reovirus is presently undergoing various phases of clinical trials in Canada, US and the UK.   Current research in my laboratory is focused on the precise mechanisms whereby reovirus specifically infects and kills cancer cells. We aim to understand 1) how reovirus exploits cancer cells' inability to defend against virus invasion, and 2) how reovirus enhances the body's immune system to fight cancer. A thorough understanding of these events should facilitate the use of oncolytic viruses as an anti-cancer therapeutic with the potential to provide long term cancer-free health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of organic anion transporters 1, 2, and 3 in antiviral drug clearance from the eye
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIVIRALS; CILIARY BODY; EPITHELIAL TRANSPORT; EYE; ORGANIC ANION TRANSPORTERS; PHARMACOKINETICS; RABBIT; RETINAL PIGMENTED EPITHELIUM; SLC22A; USSING CHAMBERS
Abstract-Résumé: Viral infections of the eye, such as herpes and cytomegalovirus can cause a variety of complications leading to blindness.  Effective treatment of these infections is challenging since antiviral drugs administered outside of the eye have a difficult time getting in, and once in they are rapidly cleared.  Invasive drug delivery methods, many of which have serious side effects, are being used to bypass this problem.  Despite this we still understand very little about the processes that function to lower antiviral drug concentrations in the eye.  We speculate that the two cell layers (ciliary epithelium and retinal pigmented epithelium) that separate the eye interior from the bloodstream have proteins (drug transporters) that facilitate the clearance of antivirals from the eye, thus reducing their concentration and residence time.  Our focus is on the organic anion transporters 1 (OAT1), 2 (OAT2) and 3 (OAT3), since they are known to transport antivirals and our preliminary data suggest that they are present.  We are measuring the capacity of the two cell layers to preferentially move clinically-relevant antivirals (penciclovir, acyclovir, ganciclovir and cidofovir) in the eye interior-to-blood direction.  We are examining the capacity of the cloned transport proteins to transport antiviral drugs, and we are using molecular and biochemical approaches to identify where the transport proteins reside in the eye.  Drug movement across the two tissues and from the eye in vivo is being measured in the absence versus presence of selective OAT inhibitors to determine their contribution to antiviral clearance.  The goal of this work is to enhance our understanding of how antivirals are cleared from the eye toward developing methods for increasing their concentrations and residence time, such as with OAT inhibitors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Antidepressants as placebo and panacea: Implications for evidence-based practice
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIDEPRESSANTS; DISCOURSE ANALYSIS; EVIDENCE-BASED PRACTICE; OFF-LABEL PRESCRIBING; PLACEBO RESPONSE; QUALITATIVE; SEMI-STRUCTURED INTERVIEWS
Abstract-Résumé: Antidepressants are medications that are widely prescribed to Canadians. Their use, however, is not without controversy. Some of the present controversy centres around claims that they are over-prescribed, in part for diagnoses other than depression. Further controversy evolves from claims that their effects are due to their capacity to engender beliefs on the part of patients that they are receiving an active treatment rather than to their direct influence on brain chemistry. Reports of these claims have received wide-spread coverage in both academic articles and the popular press. I propose to investigate how members of the following groups define and make sense of the evidence for the use and effectiveness of antidepressants and how they negotiate important issues raised by current controversies: (i) family physicians; (ii) patients who have received a prescription for an antidepressant for a diagnosis other than depression; and (iii) pharmacists. Questions that will be explored include how health professionals decide what to disclose to patients about the evidence for the use and effectiveness of antidepressants and how patients with diagnoses other than depression account for their physicians' decisions to prescribe and their own decisions to use antidepressants. This research will contribute to a better understanding of the complex interactions that transpire between patients and health care providers when evidence-based practice is challenged, and will inform evidence-based medicine and the quality of service delivery.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transcriptional control of myelin gene expression and myelination by oligodendrocytes in young adult and aged mice
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; MYELIN; MYELIN OLIGODENDROCYTE GLYCOPROTEIN; OLIGODENDROCYTE; SIRT2; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Oligodendrocytes (OLs) are a cell type in the central nervous system (CNS) that can readily be induced to wrap axons (a long filament that extends from nerve cells) in a smooth fatty protein called myelin. Myelin insulates the axon and is critical for all bodily movements and functions. The myelinating ability of OLs is essential to the proper repair of CNS injury and yet the efficiency of OL remyelination declines with age. This age related impairment of remyelination is relevant to multiple sclerosis (MS), from which patients may suffer for several decades, and to cognitive impairments accompanying several neurological disorders, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia. Little is known about the specific role(s) played by the factors that govern the expression of genes needed for OLs to myelinate axons.  The objective of our research is to determine how myelination is affected by altering the expression of two genes (Hoxd1 and Nkx2.2) and the enzyme Sirtuin 2 (Sirt2). Sirtuins have been shown to increase longevity of yeast, worms, and fruit-flies. We hypothesize these genes and enzyme play important roles in controlling the progression of OLs from immature cells to ones that have assembled a myelin sheath, and that OL myelination/remyelination will be affected during aging in mice as a consequence of impaired Hoxd1 and Nkx2.2 control. Our long-term goal is to determine how Hoxd1, Nkx2.2, and Sirt2 regulate myelination by OLs. Establishing how these factors regulate this process is important for determining how to increase remyelination of damaged CNS axons and reverse the age-related decline in remyelination efficiency. This research is the groundwork for developing therapeutic approaches to repair CNS damage caused by MS or several age-related diseases including AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regenerative neuronal reprogramming: elucidating and enhancing intrinsic neural repair programs
Keywords-MotsClés: NERVE REGENERATION; NEUROTROPHINS; REGENERATION-ASSOCIATED GENE EXPRESSION; SENSORY NEURONS
Abstract-Résumé: Sensory neurons relay information between our body and our spinal cord and brain via peripheral nerves.  When these nerves are injured, they induce an intrinsic repair response we have shown is critically dependent on brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), whose expression is regulated by neuronal activity. But, regeneration of these nerves is still fraught with challenges that result in incomplete  repair and/or pain states. We have identified a therapeutic intervention, brief electrical nerve stimulation at the time of repair, that increases BDNF expression and results in much more robust and accurate repair. Even the axonal electrical discharge at the time of injury, we find is critical to inducing the intrinsic neuronal repair state. But, the underlying early cell and molecular mechanisms linking increased neuronal activity and BDNF to induction of a more robust intrinsic regeneration state are largely unknown and the focus of our research, as they may provide novel therapeutic targets.  The early injury-induced/activity-regulated events that we hypothesize contribute and/or are critical to a robust regenerative state include rapid activity-induced alterations in membrane responsiveness to local neurotrophin cues; increased expression of an activity-regulated cytoskeleton protein we believe is critical to forming the growth cone a component of the growing axon front; and a novel axon-localized transcription factor that we hypothesize serves as an important retrograde injury signal to the sensory neuron to regulate regeneration-associated transcriptional events and help  the neuron cope with injury-associated stressors.  Finally, we will employ nerve stimulation strategies to determine if they can also improve regeneration of peripheral nerves where repair is delayed, a clinically challenging scenario.  We believe that learning how to optimally manipulate the intrinsic repair programs in sensory neurons will vastly improve nerve repair outcomes for Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aboriginal Youth Mentorship Program for increasing Physical Activity in Youth in Northern Aboriginal Communities
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; CHILDHOOD OBESITY; PEER-MENTORING; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; SELF EFFICACY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal youth represent a significant and growing population in Canada and have much to offer in terms of their contributions to their own health and the health and wellness of others. At the same time, Aboriginal youth are at a greater risk for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) and obesity than non-Aboriginal youth. Few school based programs have been developed and tested that are aimed at reducing the risk for T2D Aboriginal youth, especially those living in rural communities. Fewer still involve interventions that are peer-led and reliant upon the strengths, energy and talents of the youth themselves. Building on the successes of a communal, relationship based approach to Aboriginal youth mentoring in an after school physical activity program (AYMP), we are evaluating a peer-led approach for diabetes prevention in Aboriginal schools. With the support of adult community members, high school students (grades 7-12) volunteer as mentors, and develop an after-school physical activity, nutrition and education program that they then deliver to children in grade 4 at a neighbouring school. The high school mentors meet twice a week. The first day, they develop an activity plan which emphasizes vigorously active low organized games and healthy nutrition; together, the mentors decide roles and responsibilities to ensure successful delivery of each activity. The second day, they deliver the program for the children, which incorporates a healthy snack, 45-minutes of physical activity, and educational games and activities. In partnership with our advisory committee and youth mentors we plan to deliver the AYMP intervention in 6 rural communities and 6 urban schools over a period of 3 years. The project incorporates a community-based participatory action research model that is informed by indigenous teachings, values and worldviews (e.g., respect, relevance, responsibility and reciprocity).

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of nuclear protein import in cardiovascular disease states
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARDIOMYOPATHY; HYPERTENSION; MEMBRANE TRANSPORT; NUCLEUS
Abstract-Résumé: All cells must respond and adapt to a changing environment. Each cell must sense what is changing and then make appropriate alterations to maintain function and viability. Most cells in the body contain a nucleus. The nucleus is the storehouse in the cell for its genetic material (DNA). It is essential for cell survival and function that these genes are expressed in coordination with the needs of the cell. Proteins move in and out of the nucleus in a regulated fashion through special channels.  These proteins then initiate and control gene expression. This process appears critical when cells divide and grow. Our proposed study will examine how protein transport through these channels is controlled at a molecular level. The more we understand how this process is regulated, the more we will learn about what factors regulate cell division and growth.  Accelerated cell division and growth are hallmark features of cancer and heart disease. Our data, therefore, will be of great importance in advancing our knowledge regarding the pathogenesis of these two critical diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying demographic, epidemiologic, clinical outcome and health care utilization trends in Canadians with chronic hepatitis C viral infections over the past two decades.
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; FORECAST; HEALTH CARE UTILISATION; HEPATITIS C; LONGITUDINAL; POPULATION-BASED
Abstract-Résumé: Hepatitis C generated intensive scientific, clinical and public interest during the past two decades, since the virus was first described by Choo and colleagues in 1989. It is estimated that 170 million people are infected worldwide, and 3 to 4 million persons are newly infected each year. In Canada, and estimated 275,000 are chronically infected with HCV virus. Thus, chronic hepatitis C (CHC) remains a significant health and economic problem in Canada. Yet population-based data regarding HCV incidence rates, prevalence, and patterns of health care use within North America are limited. A Comprehensive Hepatitis C Research Database (CHCRD) had been developed by the applicant by linking records from multiple administrative and public health sources and all HCV-positive residents of the Canadian province of Manitoba were identified during a twelve year period (1991-2002). To date, important data on the prevalence, natural history and health care utilization have been generated from five clinical and administrative databases. The present proposal represents a continuation of this effort wherein the time trends in the incidence rates and prevalence of newly diagnosed HCV infection during two decades since 1991 (the time when laboratory testing for HCV infections became first available) to 2012 will be documented and the epidemiology of CHC on a population level will be further clarified. Furthermore, the outcome of CHC infection and the rates of progression to end-stage liver disease and HCC will be calculated, health care utilization examined, and the observed data will be the basis for the forecast of future health care use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Psychosocial Predictors of Health and Survival in Late Life
Keywords-MotsClés: APPRAISALS; HEALTH; HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; LONGITUDINAL; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Health is influenced by many psychosocial variables, including the way individuals psychologically appraise life events. For example, appraising events as controllable has salutary effects on health. Because individuals are threatened by precipitous, uncontrollable life challenges as they age, it is critical to understand the implications of perceived control (PC) in late life. Although research generally demonstrates health protective consequences of PC, our paradoxical premise is that appraising health as controllable might have negative consequences when it is part of a toxic appraisal style that fosters an invincible attitude leading to denial of health care needs and disengagement from health. The strengths of our longitudinal study that will assess the role of PC as assessed during interviews with community dwelling older adults include: i) access to a representative sample of very old adults; ii) a long follow up (20 years); iii) the linkage of interview data to other valuable databases (e.g., Manitoba Health Registry); and, iv) an outstanding quality and quantity of the data that provides access to psychological appraisals in a health context and a broad range of outcome variables, including physical activity, emotional well being (depression), physical health (e.g., ,blood oxygen), health care service usage, and longevity. The findings could have diagnostic implications in that they will provide the basis for developing an easy-to-administer screening tool to identify older adults who are at risk of disengaging from health care and who fail to comply with prescribed treatments. To the extent that health is compromised among individuals who deny their health needs, the findings would be relevant to understanding the well being of older Canadians. Because such individuals pose challenges for the informal and formal care systems, our findings would also have implications relevant to caregiver burden and the financial strain on Canada's health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Using regulatory macrophages (Mregs) to promote beta cell regeneration during islet inflammation.
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA CELL; DIABETES; GROWTH FACTORS; INFLAMMATION; ISLET TRANSPLANTATION; REGENERATION; REGULATORY MACROPHAGE
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes is a condition of elevated blood sugar (glucose) where the body does not produce enough insulin to meet the body's demand. Insulin is important because it moves glucose into the body's cells from the blood, storing energy for times when it is required. Prolonged high blood glucose levels are toxic to the body's cells. Diabetes is a devastating disease. Annually it results in approximately 4.6 million deaths globally. Long term complications associated with this condition include heart disease, stroke, blindness, kidney failure, nerve damage and problems with impotence. It is predicted that by 2030, one in ten adults worldwide will be diagnosed with diabetes.   There are two types of diabetes. Type 1 diabetes occurs when our own body attacks and destroys the insulin producing pancreatic beta cells, and type 2 diabetes occurs when the beta cells fail to produce sufficient insulin to overcome insulin resistance and is often associated with obesity.   One potential cure for type 1 diabetes is pancreatic islet transplantation, to replace those beta cells that have been destroyed. Both types of diabetes and islet transplantation are associated with islet inflammation.   The inflamed islets produce proteins called cytokines and other substances that promote inflammation and recruit macrophages (classic immune cells). When macrophages accumulate in and around islets, they can secrete even more cytokines and other pro-inflammatory factors, damaging the tissue further. However, following tissue damage macrophages can also promote tissue healing and regeneration.   This project will use animal models to determine how macrophages can be utilized to dampen islet inflammation and promote beta cell regeneration during diabetes and islet transplantation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering the functional role of proteoglycans in the etiology of osteoarthritis
Keywords-MotsClés: BMP SIGNALLING; CARTILAGE MATRIX; DEVELOPMENTAL GENETICS; IMAGING; OSTEOARTHRITIS; PROTEOGLYCANS; SYNCHROTRON; ZEBRAFISH
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis is a debilitating skeletal disease that affects at least 50% of humans over 60 years of age.  In osteoarthritis, cartilage breaks down at the interacting surfaces of bones (i.e., joints), and its absence causes pain during motion.  Osteoarthritis is caused in part by the loss of proteoglycans (PGs, which are sugar-coated proteins) in cartilage matrix.  PGs are thought to be important for at least two biological roles of cartilage matrix that are relevant to defects in osteoarthritis patients: tissue integrity and growth factor signalling.  Over the course of the New Investigator Salary Award, I will investigate both of these features using a variety of functional genetic and imaging experiments.  Also, collaborations are in place to develop cartilage tissue engineering therapies and relate my findings directly to human osteoarthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Perceptions of cognitive health: An ethnographic inquiry of rural older adults
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COGNITIVE HEALTH; CULTURE; DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; GENDER; GERIATRIC HEALTH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; PERCEPTIONS; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; RURAL HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: "Edna" is a 75 year old woman who lives alone with her husband on a farm. Over the last year, her husband has become increasingly distant and confused. Edna is worried and does not know who to talk to. Last fall, she received a call from the bank informing her that there was no money in their account. Her husband told her that the government had quit sending pension cheques. Three months later and barely surviving on no pension, she discovers the cheques in a bathroom drawer. She is hesitant to discuss her husband's health and when asked, she quietly whispers, "I think he has the Alzheimer's." Despite her reluctance, the news has slowly spread across town, and Edna now finds herself as the local town expert with others coming to her for advice. Edna shared her story with me in an interview on rural aging, and although cognitive health was not the study's focus, undertones of cognitive issues were observed.  Thousands of Canadians suffer from cognitive decline and this number is projected to increase significantly. Exploring the values and perceptions of cognitive health among cultural groups such as rural older adults facilitates the development of culturally acceptable interventions. The limited research and lack of cultural knowledge on rural older adults' cognitive health perceptions and beliefs has an important influence on the policies and interventions designed to support aging in rural communities. However, as a cultural group, rural seniors face important cognitive health challenges which are compounded by barriers to information, lower incomes, less education, lack of adequate housing, insufficient public transportation and limited access to health services. Using qualitative interviews and participant observation, this research will aim to develop an understanding of rural seniors' perceptions of cognitive health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Multifamily Psychoeducation Groups to reduce Expressed Emotion and Caregiver Burden Experienced by Parents of Adolescents who Self-harm
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; CAREGIVER BURDEN; DELIBERATE SELF-HARM; FAMILY FUNCTIONING; GROUP PSYCHOEDUCATION; MENTAL HEALTH; PARENTING; PATIENT ORIENTED CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Deliberate self-harm is increasingly becoming a problem among Canadian adolescents. Parent involvement is an important factor in their self-harming child's prognosis. Unfortunately, these parents feel unsupported by peers and the healthcare system, unprepared to manage their child's behaviour, and overwhelmed by negative emotions. Parents report that communication with their child and their family functioning suffers tremendously. The caregiver burden and distress experienced by these parents can best be explained by the concept of expressed emotion (EE). EE refers to the extent to which burdened family members express critical/hostile and emotionally over-involved attitudes and remarks towards a specific person, and has been shown to be a major predictor of patient relapse in those suffering from mental disorders. Multifamily psychoeducation groups (MFPGs) which address EE have been shown to be effective in reducing caregiver burden as well as EE and its negative effects among parents of youth with various disorders. However, no research has investigated the utility of EE-focused MFPGs for the parents of self-harming adolescents in addressing these caregivers' difficulties. The objective of the proposed study is to develop a MFPG that is effective in providing support and information on self-harm and EE, and thus improve family functioning, communication, and distress. First, a pilot project will be conducted with 10 parents of self-harming adolescents, and their feedback will inform modifications to the MFPGs. Then, 50 parents will be recruited for participation in MFPGs. Participants will complete measures of caregiver burden and distress, family disruption, and EE. Providing education and support to these parents may improve their mental health, family functioning, and prognosis of their child. As self-harming adolescents are a notoriously difficult population in which to intervene, targeting parents may prove to be a more effective health-delivery strategy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring police officers' susceptibility to posttraumatic stress after exposure to fictional and real-world trauma
Keywords-MotsClés: FICTIONAL TRAUMATIC MEDIA; POLICE POPULATIONS; POSTTRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER; RESILIENCE VARIABLES; RISK VARIABLES
Abstract-Résumé: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a serious mental disorder resulting in a constellation of mental, physical, social, and interpersonal symptoms. Police officers are exposed to higher rates of traumatic and work environment stressors relative to civilians, with 13 to 32% of officers reporting PTSD symptoms at any time. Identifying risk (e.g., anxiety sensitivity, intolerance of uncertainty, personality) and resilience (e.g., hope, optimism, perceived social support) variables associated with the development of PTSD in policing populations is clinically and economically advantageous for individual officers, their families, police agencies, and taxpayers. The proposed study will investigate the risk and resilience profile of 60 new Saskatchewan Police College (SkPC) recruits at baseline, following exposure to commercially available horror movie, and following one year of active duty. Each questionnaire battery will be supplemented by a structured clinical interview administered by qualified researcher to assess for psychiatric disorders (e.g., PTSD). Hierarchical linear modelling will be performed after data collection from each re-administration is completed, to assess relationships between the independent variables (i.e., risk and resilience) and the dependent variables (i.e., PTSD symptoms). Key outcomes include conceptualization of the risk and resilience profile which leads police officers to be more susceptible to PTSD following trauma exposure, which has immediate practical implications for assessment, treatment, and potentially even intervention for at risk police officers. Findings from the proposed study would serve as a clear stepping stone for informing future research, policy, and program development for not only municipal police officers but also federal police and military forces.

TitreApplicationTitle: Conformation specific targeting of misfolded superoxide dismutase 1 as an immunotherapeutic strategy for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
Keywords-MotsClés: AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS; CONFORMATION SPECIFIC ANTIBODIES; IMMUNOTHERAPY; PEPTIDE EPITOPE OPTIMIZATION; PROTEIN MISFOLDING; SELF-EPITOPE; SOD1; VACCINE DESIGN
Abstract-Résumé: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), also referred to as "Lou-Gehrig's Disease", is the most common motor neuron disease.  ALS is characterized by a rapidly progressive degeneration of motor neurons, leading to a loss of muscle function, which often results in death within 1-5 years of onset.  There is currently no cure for ALS and symptomatic therapy remains the most beneficial, therefore there is an urgent need for new therapies.  A key cellular enzyme, SOD1, has been implicated in the pathology of ALS.  This enzyme, when functioning normally, is responsible for neutralizing free radicals in the cell.  In ALS, this enzyme misfolds and goes rogue, taking on new functions that are toxic, specifically to motor neurons responsible for controlling voluntary muscle contraction.  The SOD1 form responsible for disease pathology can be distinguished from normal SOD1 by differences in protein structure.  These subtle differences can be recognized by antibodies enabling the neutralization of the toxic effects of this rogue protein without disrupting the properly functioning protein.  Our objective is to design vaccines capable of generating antibodies that can effectively neutralize the toxicity of misfolded SOD1 in the CNS.  We aim to investigate the ability of this treatment strategy to significantly delay the onset of clinical symptoms and/or to increase life expectancy, specifically, by increasing motor neuron survival through the reduction of misfolded SOD1 deposits.  This project encompasses the preliminary research and development stages for a potential treatment of the devastating disease ALS, which currently lacks an effective therapy.  The treatment methodology to be investigated can be applied to other diseases where protein misfolding has been implicated, including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Assessing the analgesic effects of nicotine on pain threshold and tolerance in humans: An exploratory investigation
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALGESIA; ANXIETY; NICOTINE; PAIN; SMOKING; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELING
Abstract-Résumé: Close to 3 million Canadians suffer from pain (Statistics Canada, 2009), and the prevalence of back pain is higher among Canadian smokers (23.3%) than non-smokers (16%; Alkherayf & Agbi, 2009). The youth population is at greatest risk; smokers ages 20 to 29 are 80% more likely to report back pain than nonsmokers in the same age range. Further clarification of the relationship between pain and smoking is necessary to contribute to the improved health of Canadians. Research aimed at elucidating the association between smoking and back pain has revealed a dynamic interrelationship. Smoking has been conceptualized as an indirect causal factor in the development of certain pain conditions (Wei & Hui, 2010), but also as an analgesic, providing temporary relief of pain, thereby reinforcing smoking behaviours (see Shi et al., 2010). Thus, the relationship between pain and smoking might be self-perpetuating. Animal models have consistently demonstrated analgesic effects of nicotine, but results from human studies using experimental pain paradigms have been inconsistent (see Ditre et al., 2011). Differences in pain modality (e.g., heat, cold), pain induction stimuli (e.g., cold pressor, thermal pain, electrical pain), and sex may be responsible for the mixed evidence (Ditre et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2010), but standardization of procedures used to assess such effects is necessary to clarify the mechanisms underlying the observed relationship. The proposed investigation will address methodological short-comings in the smoking and pain perception literature by assessing the effects of nicotine on pain threshold and tolerance across experimental pain modalities and sex while controlling for smoking status. Clarification regarding the analgesic effects of nicotine will provide further insight into mechanisms responsible for the self-perpetuating cycle of smoking and chronic pain, and thereby inform preventative and intervention strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of synaptic plasticity in the lateral hypothalamus: implications for energy homeostasis and obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; ENERGY HOMEOSTASIS; LATERAL HYPOTHALAMUS; OBESITY; OREXIN; PATCH-CLAMP; SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity rates have sharply increased over the past few decades, thereby reducing the quality of life of Canadians. To develop efficient therapies for obesity, we need to understand the regulation of body weight at its source - the brain. The brain coordinates behaviour and physiology to adapt to changing feeding states, such as after a meal or during fasting. However, this balance between food intake and requirement can be overcome by an abundance of rewarding energy-dense food, leading to overeating and obesity. Within the hypothalamus, neurons expressing the neuropeptide orexin are of particular interest for obesity since they are linked to both appetite and reward circuitry and are known to promote consumption of rewarding energy-dense food. Therefore, the goal of my research is to discover how orexin neurons can promote obesity. Recently, research has shown that synaptic plasticity, a process by which appetite circuits change their properties or wiring, is critical for body weight regulation in the brain. Accordingly, my preliminary studies show that a rewarding, energy-dense diet induces plasticity that increases the excitatory drive to orexin neurons. This increased drive would further promote appetite leading these rats to overeat. Therefore, I hypothesize that there are changes to the orexin circuit induced by exposure to a rewarding energy-dense diet, which cause overeating and weight gain.  To test this hypothesis, the electrical activity of orexin neurons will be recorded from rats fed with a normal or rewarding energy-dense diet. I will measure various properties of the circuits within the orexin network to assess how they change between feeding conditions.This study is important as dysfunction in this network could be a beginning or sustaining cause of overeating leading to obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional characterization of the Gct1 gene product in a mouse ovarian tumour model: genetics, biology and translation
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; ENDOCRINOLOGY; GENE SEQUENCING; GENOMICS; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; MOUSE GENETICS; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; OVARIAN CANCER; OVARIAN PHYSIOLOGY; QUANTITATIVE RT-PCR
Abstract-Résumé: Our understanding of cancer susceptibility genes has been greatly enhanced through the study of families that show genetic heritability for specific cancers.  Genes for cancer susceptibility play a particularly important role in the etiology of pediatric cancers, as they appear at a time of life when the impact of environmental factors on cancer risk is very low.  However, the investigational power to identify genetic determinants for cancer susceptibility may be limited if the cancer is rare in the human population.  My research focuses on a particular gene that contributes to spontaneous ovarian granulosa cell (GC) tumour susceptibility in inbred female mice, as a model genetic system for the development of pediatric ovarian tumours that appear with low frequency in infants and young girls.  The genetic region under investigation is located on mouse Chromosome 4, and has been shown to be fundamental for ovarian tumour susceptibility.  In addition, previous research has shown that this region is responsive to the steroid precursor dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), such that treatment with DHEA increases the overall frequency of ovarian tumour appearance.  The mouse model indicates a specific gene target for DHEA exists in the mammalian ovary, and in the correct genetic context, this gene supports ovarian tumour initiation in the cells of the ovarian follicle.  The identification of the tumour susceptibility gene active in the mouse model will provide specific gene candidates for further investigation in human cases of pediatric GC tumours.  Through this research, my ultimate goal is to shed light on the etiological basis of a disease for which such information is severely lacking.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Ethical Inclusion of Adolescents in Canadian Health Research
Keywords-MotsClés: ADOLESCENTS; COMMUNITY HEALTH; POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS; QUALITATIVE METHODS; RESEARCH ETHICS; SOCIAL INCLUSION
Abstract-Résumé: This research will examine and analyze key stakeholder perspectives on the ethical inclusion of adolescents in Canadian health research and provide recommendations for renewed policy direction. Depending on the province, adolescents up to 18 years of age may require parental permission to participate in research. Across research disciplines, there have been calls to allow young people to make decisions for themselves, yet it is unclear how these appeals have been taken up and how to best support the inclusion of adolescents in health research while attending to ethical concerns. The central questions guiding this proposal are: 1) What are the current policies and laws on the inclusion of adolescents in health research in Canada? 2) How do key stakeholders understand and uptake existing legal and ethical guidelines on the inclusion of adolescents in health research? and 3) What changes, if any, do key stakeholders recommend to policy and practice guidelines concerning the inclusion of adolescents in health research? By exploring the perspectives of researchers and decision-makers as well as legal and ethical frameworks, this approach to research shifts the focus away from the traditional research subject and instead researches up, and will integrate a poststructural analysis. There are three core elements: 1) a policy scan of legal and ethical guidelines concerning the participation of adolescents in Canadian health research; 2) a scoping review of recent Canadian health literature involving adolescents and young adults, and 3) thirty-four in-depth interviews with health researchers, policy-makers from across Canada, and decision-makers from research ethics boards. This study will identify gaps in perspectives and practice among key stakeholders and will provide new opportunities to reconsider the risks and benefits of including adolescents in Canadian health research.

Abstract-Résumé: The major objective of this proposal is to evaluate the contribution of a gene known as EZH2 in breast cancer progression. Using a number of well-defined mouse models we will assess whether elevated expression of EZH2 in breast cancer cells confers resistance to many of the drugs currently used to treat breast cancer. The results of these studies will lead to the development of more effective therapeutic strategies to treat breast cancer patients.

Abstract-Résumé: Obesity and diabetes are diseases of increasing importance in Western societies and beyond. The increase in their occurrence in Canada and elsewhere along with clustering of these diseases in families suggests that both environment and genes play a role. In past years the genes have been systematically identified. We propose that systematic mapping of environmental influences on gene function can now also be achieved by using latest high-throughput DNA sequencing technologies with capacity of simultaneous assessment of millions of sites in our genome susceptible for environmental modulation. Using these novel tools we will compare environmental marks in the genome including both fat (adipose) and blood tissues in individuals sharing their genetic make-up (twins) and in French-Canadian population. Our work represents a pioneering effort to understand how to best use new technologies to assess environmental influence important in modulating inherited risks for disease.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; BISULFITE SEQUENCING; EPIGENETICS; FETAL ALCOHOL SPECTRUM DISORDER; KNOCK-OUT MICE; METHYLATION ARRAY; TRANSLATING TO THE COMMUNITY; XENOPUS
Abstract-Résumé: Drinking during pregnancy is known to cause brain damage and physical changes to the developing embryo; however, not every fetus exposed to alcohol will develop into an individual with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD). This would mean that it is a combination of environmental and genetic factors that together, determine the susceptibility and the extent of damage. The gene regulatory changes, especially changes to the methylation patterns of the epigenome during early embryogenesis, have yet to be elucidated. The overarching aim of this project is to discover an "FASD Epi-Code" based on reliable biomarkers that develop in different animal models of FASD. Using the FASD Epi-Code in a personalized medicine approach to patient care, we can improve the diagnosis and care of affected individuals and reduce the secondary disabilities, therefore reducing the direct and indirect costs of care across a person's lifetime. Using the Centre for Epigenome Mapping Technologies and the Epigenome Data Co-ordination Centre, the FASD Epi-Code will be validated in human brain tissue to confirm that the biomarkers discovered in cell culture, rodents, and frogs, is conserved in individuals who were exposed to alcohol in utero. This project is an expansion of an existing international team of researchers and clinicians with a focus on improving the diagnosis, care and prevention of FASD. If successful, the implementation of the FASD Epi-Code could save Canada part of the 6 billion dollars a year spent on FASD and more importantly, greatly improve the care and quality of life in affected individuals.

Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a group of chronic intestinal inflammatory diseases that includes ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Canada has one of the world's highest incidence rates with over 200,000 people suffering from some form of IBD (approximately 0.5% of the population). In addition, there is a strong association between IBD and the development of colon cancer, with IBD patients having a 2 to 3-fold greater lifetime risk of developing colorectal cancer. While 99 genetic associations have been identified for IBD, the risk associated with any individual genetic marker is small suggesting that other factors like environmental effects and "epigenetics" may play an important role. In this research study, we examine how intestinal microorganisms (bacteria) may effect the development of IBD through modulation of the body's immune response to those microorganisms. We think epigenetic mechanism may contribute to this response. Epigenetics is the study of heritable changes in gene expression caused by mechanisms other than changes in the underlying DNA sequence. Epigenetic regulatory proteins are thought to comprise a new generation of drug targets and so this proposal will also use inhibitory compounds to study the biological function of epigenetic regulatory factors and to identify potential new drug targets for treatment of IBD.

Keywords-MotsClés: ASTHMA; ATOPY; ENVIRONMENT; EPIGENETICS; EXPOSURES; GENE-ENVIRONMENT INTERACTIONS; GENETICS; LUNG FUNCTION; RISK ASSESEMENT; SMOKING
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a common chronic disorder that affects both children and adults and causes decreased quality of life for those who suffer from the illness and for their families. Asthma has several associated symptoms including wheezing, coughing and mucus production. These symptoms vary among individuals in their range and severity. Asthma affects as many as 300 million people in the world and is the cause of 1 in every 250 deaths world-wide. The burden of asthma can be calculated in both direct costs (medical care, drugs) and indirect costs mortality, quality of life, time lost from work or school, and reduced productivity). The Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) report ranks Canada as 6th in the world in the prevalence of asthma in 13 and 14 year-old children. Asthma and related phenotypes are complex diseases with multiple genetic susceptibility variants, some of which interact with environmental factors. We need to better understand the causes of asthma 1) to reduce its prevalence; 2) to design better prevention and intervention measures; 3) to develop cost-effective management strategies; and 4) to improve diagnosis and treatment.  There is a genetic predisposition to asthma but increasing evidence shows that environmental insults such as smoking exposure, pollution, viruses, and common allergens are involved in the development of asthma. This study is designed to see how these genetic and environmental factors interact to contribute to asthma. This knowledge could lead to preventative public health policies and/or new therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Epigenetic Modifications Regulating Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Hepatocyte Differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: DIFFERENTITATION; GENE REGULATION; GENOMICS; HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA; HEPATOCYTE; HISTONE MODIFICATION; LIVER; STEM CELLS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: There are over 100 types of liver disease and left untreated, these diseases can develop into liver cirrhosis and potentially into hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Thousands of Canadians die each year from liver cirrhosis causing liver failure. Currently the only treatment for liver failure is a transplant. However, treatment is hindered by a shortage of donor tissue. Thus, viable alternatives to donor liver transplant are required. Many researchers are trying to develop methods to make hepatocytes, the main functional cell of the liver, in the laboratory from cells which are pluripotent, meaning that they can make many different types of cells. Human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) are differentiated into hepatocytes by mimicking the step-wise signals that are used to make hepatocytes in embryos.  Amazingly, HCC exhibits gene expression patterns that are similar to an embryonic hepatocyte suggesting that development of HCC is related to a reversal of differentiation.  In this proposal, we will explore the similarities and differences between HCC and hepatocytes generated from hPSCs. We are particularly interested in factors that regulate DNA packaging and, thus, are able to regulate the expression of genes. We will use genome-wide techniques to map the similarities and differences in these factors between hepatocyte differentiation and HCC development. From this, we will be able to build a picture of how changes in DNA packing can regulate HCC formation, which can lead to better diagnostics and therapeutics. Moreover, our work can contribute to the development of better methods for generating hepatocytes in the laboratory that can be used for transplantation, gene therapy, drug testing and bioartifical livers for bypass machines.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGONISTIC ANTIBODY THERAPY; CD8 T CELLS; CHRONIC VIRAL INFECTION; CO-STIMULATORY MOLECULES; GITR; IMMUNE DYSREGULATION; LCMV; REGULATORY T CELLS; TNFR SUPERFAMILY; TRAFS
Abstract-Résumé: During an acute viral infection, such as influenza virus, cells of the immune system are able to detect the presence of the pathogen, launch a response against it, and finally, eliminate it from the host. However, when the virus persists, such as with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, the immune system is forced to turn down the immune response and "truce" with the pathogen, otherwise chronic activation of the immune system would result in destruction of not only infected cells, but would also cause collateral damage to uninfected cells (termed "immunopathology"). The immune suppressive mechanisms that turn the cells "OFF" to prevent immunopathology are also therefore responsible for increased viral persistence. Although antiretroviral drugs are quite good at limiting HIV infection, they do not completely eliminate virus - and are therefore not a cure. As such, there exists a need for the development of novel therapies to complement drug treatment to eliminate the infection. What we propose is targeting a molecule on these "OFF" state immune cells to turn them back "ON" so that function is restored in hopes of eliminating the virus. Bearing in mind that since the immune system has turned "OFF" these cells to prevent collateral damage, turning it back "ON" is not without risk. However, to date our early studies have shown no negative side effects, but instead have dramatically improved the control of chronic infection in mouse models. We now must: first, gain a complete understanding the mechanism(s) of this therapy to properly evaluate safety and efficacy; and second, aim to translate this knowledge into a therapy for chronic viral infection in human (HIV) settings.

Abstract-Résumé: When cells are exposed to interferon, hundreds of cellular proteins are induced and expressed. Interestingly a handful of these proteins have been shown to stop HIV infection. By learning about these proteins and identifying others, new therapeutics can be created to help combat HIV.  We have found a novel interferon-induced protein called HERC5 that is able to potently stop HIV infection by two different mechanisms of action. First, we have shown that HERC5 interferes with the production of viral proteins and secondly, we have shown that HERC5 is able to trap HIV within the infected cell.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of gender role conflict on the relationship between internalized heterosexism and unprotected anal intercourse among gay men: Testing a moderator effect
Keywords-MotsClés: GAY MEN; GENDER ROLE CONFLICT; HEALTH RISK BEHAVIOR; HIV/AIDS; INTERNALIZED HETEROSEXISM; INTERSECTIONALITY FRAMEWORK; MASCULINITY; MODERATOR EFFECT; STRESS AND COPING; UNPROTECTED ANAL INTERCOURSE
Abstract-Résumé: Internalized heterosexism (IH) occurs when LGBTQ people internalized negative societal attitudes toward their own sexual orientation. In past research, IH and the stress that accompanies it has frequently been used to explain unprotected anal intercourse (UAI) among gay men, a group at increased risk for contracting HIV. A recent review of this research has shown that the link between IH and UAI among gay men is generally small and has decreased with time. Although, these recent findings challenge the usefulness of earlier IH-UAI research, advances in gender and health research may offer a context for the continued utility of IH as a predictor of UAI among gay men. While gender and health research has found evidence for the influence of masculinity on heterosexual men's sexual health practices, similar research on the sexual health practices of gay men has not been investigated.   In the proposed study, we investigate whether adherence to traditional masculinity supports the link between IH and UAI among gay men. The influence of adherence to traditional masculinity may be especially problematic for gay men in terms of risky sexual behavior because of masculine taboos against affectionate behavior between men. Gay men with greater adherence to traditional masculinity may engage in more UIA because taking precautions to safeguard their health and the health of their sexual partner(s) may be seen as feminine given that it may suggest that they are affectionately concerned about the well-being of other men. Thus, the link between IH and UAI will be greater among gay men who adhere to traditional masculinity.   A major application of the proposed study is in HIV intervention among gay men. If the proposed study finds that the link between IH and UIA is greater among gay men with increased adherence to traditional masculinity then, HIV interventions can be designed to focus on the IH and masculine experiences of gay men to reduce UIA.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Cedar Project: Using mobile phone technology to improve HIV treatment and services utilization among young Aboriginal people living with or at risk of HIV.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; ADDICTIONS TREATMENT; CULTURAL SAFETY; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH DISPARITY; HIV TREATMENT; HIV/AIDS; MOBILE HEALTH; PUBLIC HEALTH; SUBSTANCE USE
Abstract-Résumé: Many Canadians with HIV are living longer than ever before, thanks to highly effective medications. However, Aboriginal people with HIV - who make up a disproportionate number of Canadians living with the disease - are more likely to die from HIV-related causes and die without receiving treatment compared to other Canadians living with HIV. This study will test a new approach to helping young Aboriginal people living with HIV who use drugs overcome the barriers to getting and staying on HIV treatment, based on successful trials of a similar approach in Kenya. Researchers in Kenya showed that introducing mobile phone technology into HIV care helped participants overcome issues of poverty, rural living, transience, and stigma to improve HIV treatment adherence and health outcomes.   I will test the feasibility, acceptability and efficacy of using mobile technology to improve uptake and adherence to HIV treatment among young Aboriginal people living with or at high risk of HIV in British Columbia. This study will take place within the Cedar Project, an on-going prospective cohort that monitors HIV and HCV infection among 600 Aboriginal people aged 14-30 who use illicit drugs in Vancouver, Prince George and Chase, BC. A pre-post test design using mixed-methods will evaluate use of mobile phone technology to improve access to HIV treatment among participants by measuring self-reported adherence, CD4 and viral load every six months. Interviews and focus groups will determine the acceptability and cultural safety of the program.   Considering its demonstrated effectiveness, it is critical to determine if mobile technology can foster resiliency, access to treatment, and adherence in a culturally safe setting for young Aboriginal people living with or at risk of HIV. The implications of this research have great significance for developing interventions to improve HIV treatment not only among Aboriginal young people but also among other vulnerable groups in Canada.
