Keywords-MotsClés: BONE MARROW; INCREASING DONATION; INFLAMMATION; ORGAN REPAIR; PEDIATRICS; SOLID ORGANS/CELLS; STEM CELLS; TOLERANCE/IMMUNOMODULATION; TRANSPLANT COMPLICATIONS; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Organ and bone marrow transplants are well-established treatments for patients with incurable medical conditions. However, major gaps and obstacles prevent transplantation from being fully effective. We need to develop new knowledge, policies and health care practices to overcome these barriers. Our transplant research team brings together researchers and stakeholders across Canada from many disciplines to work in an integrated and coordinated manner to increase and improve the promise of transplantation as a 'second chance' at health for Canadians.  Our research program will unify the following projects:  1) Improving organs for transplant through targeted organ protection and repair 2) Increasing organ and cell donation through improved donor identification 3) Examining biologic markers of early problems in transplant function and identifying targets for drug treatments 4) Implementing strategies to avoid rejection of transplants and side-effects of medication 5) Predicting and preventing viral complications of transplantation 6) Targeting age-related and health care system problems experienced by children and teenagers with transplants.  To support these innovative projects, our program will integrate the management of experimental protocols, data, clinical trials, biobanks and registries across all studies. A core team will examine ethical, economic, legal and social issues related to transplantation. Our team's critical priorities include creating and sharing knowledge with a wide range of stakeholders and training new transplant researchers to sustain progress into the future. Overall, we aim to achieve improvements to donation effectiveness, to transplant policies and processes and to individual transplant outcomes. By increasing the effectiveness of donation and transplantation, the proposed research will substantially improve the health of Canadians who are candidates for and recipients of solid organ and bone marrow transplants.

Abstract-Résumé: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma are common obstructive lung diseases that affect more than 20% of people worldwide. For largely unknown reasons, there are more women than men with these lung disease conditions after puberty. These lung conditions produce symptoms such as breathlessness, cough, and sputum (phlegm) production. Excess mucus production may be important in the causes of both COPD and asthma by blocking the airways and thereby increasing airway resistance. Clinical studies showed that lung function fluctuates during the menstrual cycle in female asthmatics, implicating the role of sex hormones in enhancing airways disease. Estrogen may directly cause goblet cells to increase in the airway lining of the lungs. More interesting in our mice model, ovariectomized mice showed greater sensitivity in goblet cell production in the airway with estrogen replacement than intact female mice. After we have elucidated a mechanism by which estrogen controls mucus production, therapeutics targets can be made to control excess mucus being produced in pre-menopausal and post-menopausal patients with COPD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanism and dynamics of mRNA export from the nucleus.
Keywords-MotsClés: DEAD-BOX ATPASE; GENE EXPRESSION PROGRAM; MRNA EXPORT; NUCLEAR PORE COMPLEX; NUCLEUS; SINGLE PARTICLE IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Within almost every cell of our body is a compartment called the nucleus that carries our genetic information in the form of DNA. The nucleus protects and organizes this material, so that it can be used throughout our life to instruct the growth and function of all of our body's cells. The information stored in DNA is shared by copying it in to another material called RNA. RNA carries the gentic information to the rest of the cell, but to perform this task the RNA must first escape the nucleus. This is made possible by large protein assemblies, termed nuclear pore complexes, which act as "gateways" between the nucleus and the rest of the cell. It is known that mutations affecting these gateways and the RNA transport process are associated with multiple human diseases. However, the defects that result from these mutations and subsequently cause these various diseases remain unknown. In this research proposal our work aims to better understand the RNA transport process. Our goal being new knowledge that can provide a foundation for improved understanding, diagnosis, and treatment of human disease caused by defects in RNA transport.

Abstract-Résumé: Inflammatory bowel disease, a term which includes diseases known as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is becoming increasingly common in Canada, particularly among children.  Any child or teenager may develop IBD, including those, whose families have recently moved to Canada from parts of the world where IBD is much less common.  Research has uncovered many important genes that are factors in what makes children and adults susceptible to developing IBD, but there are clearly environmental factors that are equally important and must be identified. Many effective treatments have been developed, but there are still questions as to the best way to use these treatments, and available drug treatment does not work well for all children.  The Canadian Childhood IBD network will bring together medical doctors and scientists working across Canada with the common goals of understanding why IBD affects so many children in Canada and determining the best treatment strategies to heal the bowel inflammation and allow children to grow and enjoy life normally.  To reach these goals, the network will recruit all children at the time they are first discovered to have IBD, and will ask questions about environmental, including dietary, exposures.  We will obtain blood for assessment of genetic risk, and stool and urine for assessment of microorganisms that might be playing a role in the development of IBD. Each child's progress over the years of treatment will be carefully followed in order to critically assess which plans of treatment work best for children with specific types of IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of Novel Prognostic Biomarkers in Stem cell Transplantation and Prostate Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: GERMLINE VARIATIONS; GRAFT-VS-HOST DISEASE; IMMUNOSUPPRESSANTS; POLYMORPHISMS; PROGNOSTIC BIOMARKERS; PROSTATE CANCER; STEM CELL TRANSPLANTATION; STEROID HORMONES
Abstract-Résumé: One of the greatest challenges of the fields of hematology and oncology is to optimize and personalize patient care to overcome the high rate of life-threatening complications and the overall cancer-related mortality. There are also significant limitations in our ability to predict cancer progression or any other adverse events related to treatment approaches. For instance, risk of disease progression and mortality differs greatly between individuals, and the variability in clinical outcome further emphasizes the need to find novel prognostic markers in almost all types of cancer. Consequently, there is a clear unmet hemato-oncological needs to better predict cancer outcomes, and thus far, very few prognostic markers fill this gap in knowledge, particularly in the two areas of the research program; 1) life-threatening complications after stem cell transplantation used to treat cancer patients and 2) prostate cancer (PCa). With this goal in mind, the research program focuses on the discovery of inherited molecular markers to help predict clinical outcome in these specific areas of research. Indeed, a better knowledge of the underlying physiological basis for those critical individual differences is therefore essential in order to minimize risks for adverse events, to prevent toxicity and to personalize treatment. This research program is expected to generate novel prognostic biomarkers with a high translational potential with impending clinical application.

TitreApplicationTitle: Seizure-induced ischemia/hypoxia:  Consequences for brain and behaviour
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL NEUROSCIENCE; EPILEPSY; OXYGEN; RODENT; SEIZURES
Abstract-Résumé: It is well established in people and animals that both seizures and episodes of low tissue oxygen levels result in a number of deleterious effects to the brain that lead to disruptions in cognitive functioning and behaviour.  Given the similarities between these two types of devastating conditions, I reasoned that each seizure may lead to a cascade of events that result in low brain oxygen levels. We implanted a small device that provides accurate and continuous measurements of oxygen levels in a local area of brain tissue in awake freely moving rats and then induced a brief (<1 minute) seizure. We discovered a severe and long-lasting episode of extremely low oxygen that begins minutes after a seizure is terminated and lasts about an hour. We have also measured blood flow and found that the seizure-induced low oxygen episodes are related to reduced blood flow to the brain region involved in the seizure.    My data suggest the following General Hypothesis: Seizures result in very low brain tissue oxygen levels (hypoxia) which is mediated by local blood flow mechanisms (ischemia) that, in turn, results in transient behavioural impairment, a series of injurious outcomes to brain and alterations in learning. Understanding that seizures lead to reduced blood flow and low oxygen levels is critically important, because a key factor by which seizures could result in deleterious effects to the brain is through the resulting low oxygen levels, and not just the immediate seizure itself. Moreover understanding the mechanisms of seizure-induced low oxygen levels is critical for determining and implementing therapies that treat this previously unrecognized source of injury that long outlasts a seizure event.  Our work indicates that in addition to preventing seizures, people with seizure disorders, particularly those who have recurrent spontaneous seizures (epilepsy), may benefit from accessing therapies that prevent the reduced blood flow and resulting low oxygen levels.

Abstract-Résumé: The Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) is a transcription factor that has been widely studied due to its role in the toxic effects of carcinogens. While it usually serves to protect cells from dangerous compounds, in aberrant situations it can instead lead to tumour formation. Due to its role in carcinogenesis, ongoing efforts are being made to develop therapeutic treatments that target the AHR. Recent studies in mouse and rat models have demonstrated that even in the absence of external toxins, the AHR protein significantly affects the transcription of many genes, suggesting that it plays a role in background cellular processes. Understanding the role of the AHR in normal cell physiology is crucial to identifying the mechanisms by which it causes carcinogenesis. Currently, no large-scale comparison of basal AHR effects has been performed. I hypothesize that the AHR exerts common, tissue-specific, and species-specific basal effects and that understanding these effects will shed light on the mechanisms underlying AHR-mediated carcinogenesis. To test this hypothesis, I will perform a large-scale assessment of mRNA abundance in multiple rat and mouse tissues. Gene-wise linear modelling will be used to detect genes whose expression levels are altered by the AHR. The identity of these genes will be used to identify pathways and regulatory networks that are involved in AHR-dependent expression. This study will help clarify the basal role of the AHR, and this understanding will be essential for identifying specific alterations underlying carcinogenesis. My results will provide insight into therapeutic strategies, and an understanding of species- and tissue-specific mechanisms will facilitate better development of targeted AHR therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bridging communication gaps in 'everyday' handoffs beyond discharge transitions
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE CARE; APPRECIATIVE INQUIRY; COMMUNICATION; DEVELOPMENTAL EVALUATION; ETHNOGRAPHY; MIXED-METHODS RESEARCH; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT; TRANSITIONS
Abstract-Résumé: In healthcare-as with all systems-only 10% of the patient journey is 'value added'. In other words, few processes change the patient or the patient information. The degree to which these separate fragments are smoothly linked together is essential to providing quality patient care. Gaps in communication are one of the most commonly cited barriers that prevent interprofessional teams from working along the continuum of care. However, past studies focus narrowly on the discharge process even though it is a small fraction of a patient's total handoffs between providers. Handoffs occur when patients move between departments and also daily in the form of shift changes even when the patient is not physically moved. Although there is little literature on this topic, my experiences and discussions with healthcare providers (HCPs) suggest that communication gaps between staff within the same care setting also greatly impacts seamless care. The goal of my project is to increase health system integration by addressing the oft-overlooked communication gaps between and within hospital departments. One approach is working on quality improvement initiatives - I have connected with one potential supervisor whose students created handoffs storyboards of typical patient journeys. An ideal process was mapped and future work will involve selecting and working on quality improvement initiatives. A second approach is bridging these gaps by leveraging existing data collection tools to guide care plans and create common definitions. In both approaches, quantitative and qualitative methods will measure HCP perspectives and patient outcomes. This project can greatly improve the health delivery system because the learnings apply to every care setting, affect every patient's journey, and has the potential to address underlying reasons for hospital readmissions and ALC days among other pressing issues. The healthcare system should benefit in all areas of safety, quality, delivery, and cost.

Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL CELL CULTURE; HUNTINGTIN PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; HUNTINGTON DISEASE; MICROSCOPY; PALMITOYLATION; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MODIFICATION; PROTEIN PURIFICATION AND ENZYME ASSAYS; THERAPEUTIC TARGETS
Abstract-Résumé: Huntington disease (HD) is a devastating neurodegenerative condition which causes death of the striatal neurons in the brain, leading to cognitive, psychiatric and motor coordination decline during mid-life. The disease is caused by a genetic mutation in the huntingtin (HTT) gene. Palmitoylation- the post-translational addition of a lipid to proteins by a palmitoyl acyltransferase (PAT) enzyme- is believed to play a key role in the disease pathology. Specifically,evidence suggests that the HD-associated PAT HIP14 is dysfunctional in the presence of the HD mutation. Characterizing the interaction between HIP14 and other proteins in the cell will elucidate novel pathways which can be targeted with drugs or biotechnological therapeutics in order to further our knowledge and push towards a cure for this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Innovative Community-Based Approaches to Promote Optimal Aging for Older Adults with Multiple Chronic Conditions and their Caregivers
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS; CAPACITY BUILDING; CLIENT AND FAMILY CENTRED; ECONOMIC EVALUATION; FAMILY CAREGIVERS; INTERPROFESSIONAL TEAM; OLDER ADULTS; PREVENTION & MANAGEMENT OF MULTIPLE CHRONIC CONDITIONS; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE INTERVENTIONS; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Identifying effective interventions to improve quality of life for older adults is a public health priority.  Older adults with multiple chronic conditions (MCC) are most likely to benefit from such interventions. The purpose of this research program is to evaluate innovative community-based primary healthcare interventions to promote optimal aging for older adults living in the community with MCC and to support their family caregivers. The research program is composed of six interrelated studies focused on enhancing our understanding of 1) how older adults with MCC, family caregivers and health professionals manage MCC; 2) the factors, health outcomes and costs associated with MCC; 3) the influence of gender, age, education, income and other factors on the quality of life of family caregivers of older adults with MCC; 4) the effectiveness and costs of a Toolkit and volunteer support for family caregivers of older persons with Alzheimer's disease and MCC; 5) the effectiveness and costs of a client-driven interprofessional intervention to support self-management among older persons with Type 2 Diabetes and MCC; and 6) the effectiveness and costs of a community navigation and rehabilitation intervention for stroke survivors with MCC using home care services. This research will be conducted in Ontario and Alberta by an interdisciplinary team of investigators, health professional scientists and clinicians, advised by patients and families, and supported by senior health system decision-makers. Training opportunities will be included for graduate students and new investigators.  Two knowledge translation events will be held to share study results with key stakeholders and to plan ways to implement successful programs more widely. This research program will result in knowledge that can be used to guide health services policy decisions and the allocation of resources in community-based primary healthcare for older adults with MCC across Canada.

Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS FOR VULNERABLE POPULATION; AVOIDABLE EMERGENCY DEPARTEMENT CONSULTATIONS; INTERNATIONAL COMPARISONS; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE DEVELOPMENT PARTNERSHIP; ORGANISATIONAL INNOVATION; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL DESIGNS; SYSTEMATIC SCOPING AND REVIEWS
Abstract-Résumé: Canada and Australia are two countries trying to improve their systems for delivering primary healthcare (PHC). However many consumers are still unable to access quality care - especially for the sick, the poor, or those who are otherwise disadvantaged. Poor PHC access leads to overloaded emergency departments, avoidable hospitalisations and, in the long run, to increased costs and poor health outcomes. Canada and Australia have introduced a number of programs to improve access to PHC. However many of these programs have been either limited in their scope or restricted to 'pilot studies'. Our team comprises researchers, clinicians and decision makers who have come together to help solve some of these critical problems. We plan to work with consumers and providers in six regions (three in Australia and three in Canada) to identify, refine and then trial 'world's best practice' innovations to assist access, particularly for vulnerable populations. These innovations won't be simply thrust upon communities. We will build upon our team's existing links with community leaders, decision makers and health professionals in each region to develop innovations that enhance the local system, are tailored to local needs and are likely to make a real difference to vulnerable groups. Our evaluation will determine whether these interventions work to improve access to quality care. Our 5 year program will give governments, health services and consumers in both countries a rich understanding of what really matters in access to needed PHC. Decision makers and communities will have a toolkit and a well-tested plan through which to address local access needs. Most importantly, all will have an opportunity to reduce the access gap for vulnerable populations so that better health outcomes can be achieved and healthcare funds can be used to best purpose.

Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; COMMUNITY CARE; HEALTH CARE DELIVERY; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HEALTH POLICY; IMPLEMENTATION; MODELS AND PROGRAMS OF CARE; ORGANIZATIONAL MANAGEMENT; PATIENT CENTERED CARE; PRIMARY CARE
Abstract-Résumé: This research programme addresses the question:  What are the steps to implementing innovative integrated community-based primary health care (CBPHC) models that address the health and social needs of older adults with complex care needs? The program is directed at 4 levels of analysis: policy, organization, provider, and patient and family/caregiver and will be conducted in 3 phases. Phase 1 identifies and describes successful integrated CBPHC models; Phase 2 involves in-depth case studies of exemplar models and creates a framework to explain conditions that lead to successful implementation; Phase 3 evaluates the implementation of innovative CBPHC models. Research methods include reviews of literature, official documents and databases and mixed methods case studies (including surveys, interviews, and analysis of administrative data). Key outcomes will be performance measures at the patient, provider, organization and system levels, and a systematic guide to the design, implementation and scaling-up of innovative models of CBPHC.

TitreApplicationTitle: Canadian Chronic disease Awareness and Management Program (C-CHAMP)
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOMETABOLIC RISK; CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT; COMMUNITY INTERVENTIONS; HYPERTENSION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; MULTIDISCIPLINARY APPROACH; PEER HEALTH EDUCATORS; PRAGMATIC RANDOMIZED TRIALS; PRIMARY HEALTHCARE; PRIMARY PREVENTION
Abstract-Résumé: The most prevalent chronic health conditions are largely the product of interactions among a small set of well-established, modifiable causes, such as smoking, having a sedentary lifestyle, heavy drinking and high salt consumption.  These chronic health conditions, notably obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure, are on the rise nationally and internationally.  In order to combat this epidemic, the Canadian Chronic Disease Awareness and Management Program (C-ChAMP) will address these common problems by implementing a program designed to raise awareness, encourage self-care and transfer the onus of treatment from hospitals into the community.  C-ChAMP will build off of the success of a previous model of treatment, the Cardiovascular Health Awareness Program (CHAP), which has already been shown to significantly decrease hospitalization rates in the communities in which it was established.  The researchers behind CHAP now hope to increase the scope and impact of CHAP by targeting a wider audience with a wider range of chronic diseases.  In order to accomplish this, C-ChAMP will collaborate with community partners, such as local pharmacists, family physicians, and social organizations so that the program can be adjusted to meet local needs.  Information sessions, open to the public at large but targeted at individuals over 40, are held in local pharmacies, where trained volunteers perform tasks that would typically be conducted in the doctor's office.  These include blood pressure monitoring, conducting cardiovascular disease, stroke, diabetes and pre-diabetes risk assessments, and providing information about locally available resources (exercise programs, smoking cessation clubs, etc).  These results are then transmitted to the participant's family physician, pharmacist, and his/herself so that a health profile can be established.  This ensures a continuity of health care monitoring that is currently lacking in our overburdened health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Transforming CBPHC Delivery through Comprehensive Performance Measurement and Reporting
Keywords-MotsClés: INNOVATIONS IN CBPHC; INTERDISCIPLINARY; LINK TO ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; MIXED METHODS; MULTI-JURISDICTIONAL; ORGANIZATIONAL SURVEY; PATIENT SURVEY; PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENT; PROVIDER SURVEY; VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: A strong community-based PHC (CBPHC) system will give Canadians more equitable care with better population outcomes at reduced cost. Canada has invested over $1billion in renewing CBPHC over the last decade. Despite some efforts no one data source can capture or represent innovations in CBPHC performance in Canada. Our goal is to demonstrate the feasibility and usefulness of comparative and comprehensive PHC performance measurement and reporting in regions as a foundation to inform innovation in the delivery and organization of the Canadian PHC system. We will collect survey data (in English and French) from CBPHC organizations, patients, and clinicians in three sociodemographically comparable regions in British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec. We will link their responses to health administrative data and the patients' chart data. We will carry out four conceptually linked research projects. With this program of research, we will help make Canada a leader in evaluating the effectiveness of CBPHC innovations. Our proposal is original in its development and application of methods and measures. We develop a complex vulnerability index and use it to report on healthcare equity. We apply theoretical foundations of complexity theory and an equity lens and use mixed methods to guide conceptualization, data collection and analyses throughout this program of research. Our surveys and innovative data management and collection processes will influence research, quality improvement and policy development across Canada and internationally. Through our case studies we will identify conditions and strategies for scaling-up innovative models of CBPHC. We extend and evaluate a new method to extract data from electronic medical records (EMRs). Our proposal is original in its application of social media to assist with integrated knowledge translation and exchange. We use deliberative dialogue and crowdsourcing.Finally, we are an interprofessional team working together on this research.

TitreApplicationTitle: Correlation of cortical perfusion and neurocognition between Multiple Sclerosis subtypes using a novel quantitative perfusion sequence
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITIVE DYSFUNCTION; MRI PEFUSION; RELAPSING REMITTING MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; SECONDARY PROGRESSIVE MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Disease of the outer layer of the brain or cortex is a previously unrecognized but important cause of both physical and mental disability in Multiple sclerosis (MS). Sparse information exists on the role of the cortex in affecting the ability to think, organize and process information. These skills are critical for social and intellectual functioning and are commonly affected in MS leading to mental disability or cognitive impairment. MRI can directly measure cortical lesions but this is very challenging because the lesions are often very small or difficult to see. This limitation is important because doctors need a reliable and commonly available method to monitor cortical disease so that they can study the effect of cortical lesions on disability. We previously show that a new MRI scan technique (or Bookend perfusion) can measure differences in the cortex between patients with and without cognitive impairment. We think the ability to show differences indirectly reflects differences in cortical disease. We found that cortical abnormality localized to expected brain regions and better predicted cognitive impairment than traditional markers including white matter disease and cortical atrophy. Importantly, we showed strong associations between abnormality and specific cognitive tests associated with information processing speed. The present proposal hopes to expand our study to less affected MS patients (or relapsing remitting MS) to determine whether similar findings are present and allow comparison between MS subtypes. This will test the relationship between disease severity, cognitive impairment and cortical abnormality. We will also assess whether similar spatial differences are seen. The study is important because our new technique is easy to use and may be performed on any MRI scanner allowing routine cortical assessment for all MS patients. The future hope is that the technique can help doctors monitor disease activity and assess the efficacy of new drugs.

Keywords-MotsClés: BTB/KELCH PROTEINS; F-BOX PROTEINS; POXVIRUS; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; UBIQUITIN; UBIQUITIN LIGASE
Abstract-Résumé: The degradation of proteins is necessary for the regulation of many cellular processes. Significantly, alterations in protein degradation have been linked to a number of important human diseases, including cancer. Proteins can be marked for degradation by the addition of a small protein called ubiquitin that is essential for the normal function of healthy cells. Given the importance of protein degradation, many viruses regulate protein degradation to their own advantage. Understanding how viruses regulate protein degradation will provide clues for the future development of therapeutic interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Orexins and Post-traumatic stress disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODEL; ANXIETY; BEHAIVORAL ANALYSIS; MULTICHANNEL ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; NEUROPHARMACOLOGY; OREXIN; POST-TRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER; QPCR; RATS; THALAMUS
Abstract-Résumé: Some people who experience intense fear and horror will develop an anxiety disorder called post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).  The purpose of the proposed experiments is to provide a better understanding of how the brain controls negative emotions like anxiety that can develop after people experience a traumatizing event.  Similar to people, animals exposed to stressful situations will develop anxiety-like behaviors that we can measure in the laboratory.  We have used this rat model of PTSD to discover that a chemical messenger in the brain called orexin is involved in producing the anxiety associated with a stressful event.  In this grant, we propose to further examine the brain mechanisms involved in this stress- and orexin-mediated anxiety.  We also want to provide preclinical evidence that drugs that interfere with the orexin system can reduce anxiety levels in our rat model of PTSD. While this research is entirely animal base, it is realistic to believe that the results from these experiments could lead to the identification of novel drug target for developing drugs that act at some of the underlying neurobiological basis for PTSD.  The development of similar drugs that act on the orexin system to treat insomnia is well underway by several pharmaceutical companies. We hope that our research may generate the interest in testing these drugs for treating anxiety and PTSD.

TitreApplicationTitle: BRUISE CONTROL-2: A randomized controlled trial to investigate whether a strategy of Continued versus Interrupted Dabigatran at the time of device surgery, in patients with moderate to high risk of arterial thrombo-embolic events, leads to a reduction in the incidence of clinically significant hematoma
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICOAGULATION; ATRIAL FIBRILLATON; DABIGATRAN; DEFIBRILLATOR; HEMATOMA; PACEMAKER
Abstract-Résumé: Many patients requiring cardiac arrhythmia device surgery are on chronic blood thinners to prevent stroke. The management of blood thinners around the time of surgery presents a dilemma to physicians. Physicians usually discontinue long acting oral blood thinners (e.g. Coumadin) a few days before the surgery (for the effects of tablet blood thinners to be cleared) and then bridge with injection blood thinners (e.g. Heparin) before and after surgery for a few days while the restarted tablet blood thinner effect is building up to therapeutic levels. There are a number of downsides to bridging anti-coagulation including a substantial risk of significant device pocket hematoma (large collection of blood around the device battery). An alternative strategy of performing device surgery without stopping tablet blood thinners is currently being evaluated in the randomized controlled trial BRUISE CONTROL. Patients undergoing device surgery are randomly assigned to one of two treatment arms. In the conventional arm patents are bridged. In the experimental arm patients continue on tablet blood thinners. Recently, newer shorter acting tablet blood thinners (e.g. dabigatran) have been approved for use for stroke prevention. Given that their onset and offset of action is shorter than Coumadin, bridging anticoagulation with heparin is unlikely required for short periods of discontinuation around the time of device surgery. However, data is limited regarding the incidence of hematoma with peri-operative use of this medication. The important question of whether it safer to stop and restart dabigatran or to operate on continued dabigatran will be assessed in the current randomized controlled trial BRUISE CONTROL-2. Patients will be randomly assigned to either interrupted dabigatran or continued dabigatran at the time of device surgery. The primary outcome will be clinically significant hematoma.

TitreApplicationTitle: ACUTE Study: Acute Congestive Heart Failure Urgent and Transitional Care Evaluation
Keywords-MotsClés: EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT; HEALTH OUTCOMES; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; HEART FAILURE; HOSPITAL DISCHARGE; TRANSITIONAL CARE
Abstract-Résumé: Heart failure is a common condition that occurs when there is excessive fluid in the lungs causing patients to feel shortness of breath, often resulting from prior heart damage. It is one of the leading reasons for hospitalizations, emergency department visits, and cardiovascular death. It is estimated that over 3.3 million Canadians have or will develop heart failure since approximately 1 in 5 adults will be affected. The emergency department is the point of first contact for patients with heart failure, but there are few tools to guide physicians who care for such patients. As a result, some patients who are considered safe to discharge home may die shortly after leaving the emergency department, and conversely, some patients who could be safely discharged home may be admitted to hospital unnecessarily.  We have developed a tool to guide physicians to better assess the risk of the heart failure patients that seek care in the emergency department: the Emergency Heart failure Mortality Risk Grade (EHMRG). In this grant, we will test and optimize the EHMRG and examine how it performs in the real world practices of busy emergency department physicians. We will also examine how using the EHMRG could potentially affect overall admissions or discharges for HF patients in the ED.   We have also found that the type of care received by heart failure patients soon after discharge from the emergency department (e.g., discharge transitional care) has a major impact on whether patients will die, need to revisit the emergency department or require hospital admission. We will conduct a detailed examination of factors that predict whether patients will be more likely to require repeat emergency department visits and hospitalizations. We will determine the impact of different levels of care provided after emergency department discharge, and who might most benefit from such care to reduce the burden of heart failure on the health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Applications of Systematic Review and Meta-Analytic Techniques to Challenge Prevailing Thinking Regarding Effectiveness of Treatments for Reducing Mortality in Critically-Ill Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: CRITICAL ILLNESS; SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYTIC TECHNIQUES
Abstract-Résumé: In clinical medicine, systematic review and meta-analytic techniques systematically search for and combine data from randomized trials and form the basis for evidence-based medicine.  As an active critical care clinician and active researcher, I will use novel applications of systematic review and meta-analytic techniques to re-examine and potentially challenge prevailing thinking regarding the effectiveness of certain treatments to reduce mortality in critically-ill patients.  This proposal focuses on three common clinically-relevant questions in critical care that cannot be readily answered using other means.  First, whether nitric oxide, a very expensive inhaled gas used to improve oxygenation in critically-ill patients requiring mechanical ventilation for lung failure, is actually effective in the sickest patients with life-threateningly low oxygen levels.  Second, whether resource-intensive treatments used to reduce secondary (ventilator-associated) pneumonia which often occurs in patients requiring ventilation also results in improved mortality and length of stay.  And third, whether an optimal duration of follow up in randomized controlled trials (which currently use many different follow up durations) can be identified when mortality effects have stabilized to ensure accurate estimates of the effectiveness of these treatments.  Answering these questions will illustrate how novel applications of meta-analytic techniques can inform more effective decision making by clinicians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Behavioural and Neurobiological Characterization of the Multiple Facets of Motivation in Health and Illness
Keywords-MotsClés: APATHY; DEPRESSION; DTI; FUNCTIONAL MRI; MOTIVATION; REWARD; SCHIZOPHRENIA; STRUCTURAL MRI
Abstract-Résumé: The loss of motivation (i.e., apathy) has emerged as a common symptom in numerous brain disorders, including schizophrenia and depression.  Importantly, apathy in these populations has been consistently linked to poor functioning for affected individuals.  Our understanding of the neurobiology of motivation, and the mechanisms of apathy, to date has come from disparate lines of investigations that have focused primarily on a single illness.  Recent work has highlighted the multiple components of motivation, including reward valuation, effort and willingness to work, reward prediction, action selection, responsiveness to reward attainment, and reward learning.  This multi-faceted structure for the human motivational system suggests that a simultaneous investigation of the multiple components of motivation is needed to develop a comprehensive understanding of the neurobiology of normal human motivation, and its dysfunction across illnesses.  Such an approach can serve to delineate the core components of the motivational network in the brain, as well as providing a foundation for the development of effective treatments for apathy in brain disorders. To address this issue, we are undertaking investigations specifically aimed at uncovering the functional and structural brain circuitry of normal human motivation, as well as the critical pathways in the brain that can cause apathy.  These studies include both behavioural and brain imaging investigations of the multiple components of motivation in healthy adults, and in individuals affected with schizophrenia and depression. This will allow for a comprehensive determination of the specific brain networks that serve specific functions in the human motivational system, and identify key brain regions that need to be targeted by treatments aimed at addressing apathy in mental illnesses. Ultimately, this holds promise for the reduction of the prominent functional impairment characteristically seen in these illnesses.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of periodontal inflammation by the platelet cytoskeleton
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOSKELETON; FILAMIN A; PERIODONTITIS; PLATELETS
Abstract-Résumé: Proper function of the immune system is essential for protection against infectious disease and maintaining human health. During the onset of infection, white blood cells and platelets release signaling molecules known as cytokines, which orchestrate a protective inflammatory response. When cytokine release is de-regulated, excessive inflammation results that causes cell and tissue death and loss of function. This is seen in periodontitis (gum disease), which is characterized by gingival (gum) inflammation and destruction of tooth-supporting connective tissues and bone. The purpose of this grant application is to study the mechanisms and identify the proteins responsible for maintaining the health of periodontal tissues. In addition to regulating blood coagulation (clotting), platelets are emerging as pivotal components of the host inflammatory response. We will study in human and mouse platelets, how infection causes cytokine release. The current project will focus on two major questions. First, we will identify the molecular signals that operate during periodontal infection and learn how these signals affect platelet function. We will also test the hypothesis that a group of proteins known as filamins mediate the release of cytokines from platelets. In this context, an improved understanding of platelet function could have important implications for rational treatment of inflammatory diseases, including periodontitis.

TitreApplicationTitle: rTMS for the Treatment of Working Memory Deficits in Schizophrenia and Effects on Brain Structure
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN STIMULATION; COGNITIVE; MRI; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Schizophrenia is a debilitating disorder that exacts enormous personal, social and economic costs. Currently, 300,000 Canadians suffer from this illness, which is characterized by a constellation of clinical symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, impaired cognition) and life long functional disability. Memory impairments are one of the most difficult to treat problems in SCZ that underlie the poor daily functioning of these patients. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been shown to be an effective and safe in the treatment of schizophrenia. We have recently evaluated rTMS for the treatment of these memory impairments in schizophrenia. Our data shows that by stimulating more frontal regions of the brain there is an improvement in memory. Additionally, we are conducting a type of brain imaging known as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to determine whether the frontal parts of the brain important for this type of memory change with rTMS treatment. This will help us understand better what effects rTMS has on brain structure. Patients with schizophrenia have alterations in frontal parts of their brain that may explain their memory impairments. By conducting MRI before and after the rTMS treatment, we may also find out whether the brain changes in a way that also helps improve memory performance. If our hypotheses are correct, our study will provide promising new treatments for memory impairments in schizophrenia. Having additional treatment options available is vital to improve the quality of life and functioning of our patients that may provide hope for those who would otherwise suffer from persistent illness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving primary healthcare with patients and professionals
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH POLICY; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER; MIXED METHOD RESEARCH; PRIMARY HEALTHCARE; PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT; QUALITY IMPROVEMENT; QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: There is a wide consensus that healthcare improvement requires strong partnerships between patients and professionals. However, little research exists on how patients and the public can effectively be involved in healthcare improvement. In a recent study, we tested an intervention to involve patients together with professionals in setting common priorities for healthcare improvement, which demonstrated that it is feasible to involve patients and the public in strategic healthcare decisions and that it can increase consensus between patients and professionals improvement priorities. The goal of this research program is to test the generalizability of this intervention in different contexts of primary healthcare improvement.   We will first tailor our intervention to three important primary healthcare issues: access, chronic disease management, and end-of-life care. We will then implement our involvement intervention in 8 different sites, each addressing one of these three issues. 200 participants (including 120 patient and public representatives, and 80 professionals) will be recruited. Participants will be informed about the policy issue and available options, consulted about their preferred choices, they will deliberate together to agree on common recommendations, and these recommendations will be communicated to relevant decision-makers. We will explore the relationship of key contextual factors (community, organizations, and policy issue) with the process and outcome of involvement, using research instruments previously tested. This research program will foster the development of robust involvement interventions that are more generalizable to different policy issues, communities and organizations. This research also offers a unique opportunity to engage with patients and the public in key areas of healthcare improvement and policymaking, support health system changes that are better aligned with public needs and expectations.

Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENETICS; DNA SEQUENCING; FLOW CYTOMETRY; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILINE; LEUKEMIA; MURINE MODELS OF CANCER; STEM CELL BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer in humans is often the result of the accumulation of genetic damage over years. Many people seek medical attention with conditions called "pre-cancerous", in the sense that they are known to transform into an aggressive cancer over time. For many of these patients, there is currently no better course of action than observation. The goal of this project is to monitor the evolution of "pre-leukemic" cells in mice over time, as they eventually transform into a disease that makes the mouse sick. I am interested in learning how these cells gradually learn to "escape" the control of their environment in order to become aggressive. This model could be applied to other types of cancer. I hope to have a positive impact on human disease.  By better understanding the transformation of pre-cancerous lesions into aggressive cancer, it might be possible to develop new treatments or monitoring tools for patient affected with these conditions.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic analysis of the nucleotide excision repair pathway in a Drosophila model of tauopathy
Keywords-MotsClés: ALZHEIMER'S DISEASE; DNA DAMAGE; DNA REPAIR; DROSOPHILA; GENETICS; NEURODEGENERATION; NUCLEOTIDE EXCISION REPAIR (NER)
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimer's disease, the most common human neurodegenerative disease, is characterized by the accumulation of several proteins in the brain and the subsequent death of nerve cells. Pathologically, it is classified within a family of diseases called tauopathies. Unfortunately, much remains to be learned about the mechanisms through which the accumulation of  certain proteins in the brain leads to neuronal death.  This project uses a Drosophila model (the fruit fly) to replicate the accumulation of one such protein, tau, in the brain. In the past, this model has proved useful to unravel several important steps in the cascade leading to neurodegeneration in tauopathies and Alzheimer's disease. Here, we will focus on a subset of proteins which play an important protective role against damage to DNA and we will try to determine whether this normal protective response plays a paradoxical role in neurodegeneration. More specifically, we will look for the accumulation of DNA damage in fly brains expressing mutated human tau and test whether the activation of this DNA-repair mechanisms influences cell death in our tauopathy model. If our preliminary results are confirmed, this could open the door to a series of new  therapeutic targets to prevent neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Environmental Contaminants and Adolescent Development
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL HEALTH; ADOLESCENTS DEVELOPMENT AND HEALTH; ENVIRONMENTAL CONTAMINANTS; PRENATAL EXPOSURE; PUBLIC HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: A recent review of evidence from Canadian studies reveals accumulating evidence of learning disabilities and illness attributable to exposure to environmental contaminants (EC). It is, therefore, important to further elucidate the associations of EC with health and development. This requires the design and implementation of longitudinal cohorts of pregnant women and children with exposure assessments at critical windows and sensitive endpoints documented along the continuum of human development. Several effect studies of exposure to EC have been conducted, but follow-ups through adolescence are scarce. The Inuit from Arctic Quebec are among the populations most highly exposed to mercury, polychlorinated biphenyls and chlorinated pesticides due to frequent consumption of fish and marine mammals. We have recruited a pregnancy cohort in Arctic Quebec between 1993-96. Cord blood concentrations of EC were obtained, and the cohort was followed at 1-, 5- and 11-year of age. We are now proposing to follow up this cohort during the adolescent period to document the long-term effects of pre- and postnatal exposure to these contaminants. Outcomes of interests include cognitive, affective and behavioural development, physical growth, and metabolic precursors of obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. The sample will consist of 200 adolescents aged 16 to 19 years. Each child will be evaluated during a 3-hr visit, and current exposure to EC will be assayed from blood samples. The proposed study is of public health importance in light of increasing Hg body burdens in the North due to increasing emissions in developing countries, challenging the health of the Inuit. Although exposure levels in Southern Canada are markedly lower than those found in Arctic Quebec, recent evidence from our studies of the Inuit population indicates adverse effects on development at levels of contaminant exposure commonly found in Southern Canadian populations.

TitreApplicationTitle: Interplay between homologous recombination and anti-recombination activities at broken DNA replication forks and genomic instability
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-RECOMBINATION ACTIVITIES; DNA DOUBLE-STRAND BREAKS; DNA REPAIR; DNA REPLICATION; HOLLIDAY JUNCTION; HOMOLOGOUS RECOMBINATION; RAD51 PARALOGS
Abstract-Résumé: DNA replication is a biological process that occurs in all living organisms and copies their genetic information which is inherited by newly divided cells. Hence, faithful DNA replication is essential to all life. It has been known for many years that compounds that interfere with DNA replication, kill actively proliferating cancer cells. These compounds show severe cytotoxic effects on actively growing cells by inducing DNA damage such as double-strand breaks. In normal cells, DNA repair acts as a defence mechanisms against anticancer drugs, while in cancer cells, this mechanism often causes reduced sensitivity of these cells to the drugs. We aim to understand how DNA repair affects the cell ability to repair double-strand breaks by homologous recombination during DNA replication. This process act by copying DNA sequences from homologous DNA sequences. However, this process is highly regulated by positive (pro-recombination) and negative (anti-recombination) forces. When this balance is compromised,  DNA repair cannot act properly, leading to genomic instability, an hallmark of cancer. Using genetic and cellular tools, we will investigate how/when/why this balance occurs specifically during DNA replication.  In the future, this knowledge will help clinicians to optimize chemotherapy during DNA replication, by selectively inactivating the balance between pro-and anti-recombinases, leading to cancer cell death.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Effects of Exercise on Adipose Tissue Insulin Action
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE; EXERCISE; GLYCOGEN; INSULIN; KNOCKOUT MICE; LIPOLYSIS; LIVER; OBESITY; SIGNALING; SKELETAL MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Owing to its vital role in locomotion and the fact that it accounts for the majority of whole body glucose disposal and fatty acid oxidation the majority of exercise physiology/biochemistry studies investigating the acute effects of exercise on glucose and fat metabolism have examined skeletal muscle. However, there is a growing appreciation for the role of adipose tissue (i.e. fat) in regulating whole body metabolism. Despite this, few if any studies have examined the acute effects of exercise in controlling the function of adipose tissue. In preliminary experiments we have found that a single bout of exercise leads to the development of impaired insulin action in adipose tissue during the recovery from exercise. This is an important adaptation as it allows for a continued release of fatty acids from adipose tissue to be used as a fuel source while sparing blood sugar to be used for the re-synthesis of glycogen in muscle and liver. The purpose of this proposal is to determine the mechanisms mediating the effects of exercise on adipose tissue insulin action. Based on strong preliminary data, we believe that a protein called interleukin 6 (IL-6) is involved in this process. We will explore the involvement of IL-6 in the regulation of adipose tissue function through using special, genetically engineered mice that do not have IL-6. We will determine how rapidly the development of adipose tissue insulin resistance reverses and will also examine how exercise modifies adipose tissue insulin action in obese, insulin resistant mice. These studies will provide novel insight into the mechanisms through which exercise controls the function of adipose tissue during the recovery from exercise. More importantly our studies will provide new information regarding the mechanisms of how adipose tissue becomes dysfunctional during the development of obesity and insulin resistance and how exercise can be used to treat this condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prognostic significance of Fbw7 in human melanoma and its role in cell migration
Keywords-MotsClés: FBW7; HUMAN MELANOMA; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; TISSUE MICROARRAY
Abstract-Résumé: The E3 ubiquitin ligase Fbw7 (F-box and WD repeat domain-containing 7) is broadly considered as a tumor suppressor because of its role in turnover of several well-known onco-proteins. However, the role of Fbw7 in melanomagenesis is not clear. To investigate the expression profile and biological functions of Fbw7 in melanoma, we examined Fbw7 expression level using melanoma tissue microarray and immunohistochemistry. Our data showed that Fbw7 expression is significantly reduced in primary melanoma compared with dysplastic nevi (P = 0.020) and further reduced in metastatic melanoma compared with primary melanoma (P = 0.011). Furthermore, we observed a strong correlation between negative Fbw7 expression and a worse 5-year survival of melanoma patients (P = 0.015). We also found that both Fbw7 protein and mRNA expression was significantly reduced in 9 melanoma cell lines compared with normal melanocytes. Moreover, our in vitro studies showed a remarkable increase of cell migration and stress fibre formation in Fbw7 knockdown cells, and treatment of selective MEK inhibitor abrogated Fbw7 alpha knockdown induced melanoma cell migration. Taken together, our findings indicate that Fbw7 plays an important role in melanoma progression, and Fbw7 inhibits melanoma cell migration through MAPK-ERK signalling pathway and may serve as a prognostic marker.

Abstract-Résumé: La recherche sur les effets de la nutrition sur la sante est en pleine effervescence. Malgre l'avancement des connaissances et la diffusion massive d'informations sur la nutrition, on constate toujours qu'il y a grandement place a l'amelioration en ce qui concerne la qualite de l'alimentation des Canadiens. Pourquoi le fosse est-il si important entre les connaissances et leur mise en application?  Comment pouvons nous retrecir ce fosse? C'est a ces questions principales que nous tenterons de repondre dans le cadre de la programmation de recherche proposee. Plus specifiquement, nous nous interesserons a l'adhesion aux recommandations alimentaires visant la saine alimentation. Pour bien cerner cette question de recherche, nous utiliserons une approche interdisciplinaire qui nous permettra de faire avancer les connaissances de facon integree et ce, sur plusieurs fronts. En effet, puisque nous nous interessons a la qualite de l'alimentation, nous travaillerons au developpement d'outils  optimaux pour mesurer le plus precisement possible l'alimentation des individus. Par la suite, afin d'ameliorer la comprehension du phenomene de l'adhesion a la saine alimentation, nous identifierons les facteurs associes a la qualite de l'alimentation dans le contexte d'une etude d'observation dans la population quebecoise.  Puisque nous souhaitons proposer des solutions pour ameliorer la qualite de l'alimentation, nous testerons des interventions nutritionnelles afin de determiner celles qui sont le plus pertinentes pour favoriser une adhesion a long terme aux changements alimentaires recommandes.  Finalement, pour s'assurer que notre programmation de recherche procure des retombees concretes, un plan de transfert des connaissances  permettra d'informer les utilisateurs potentiels des connaissances globales et specifiques qui decouleront de notre programmation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimizing Mothers' Milk for Preterm Infants
Keywords-MotsClés: BODY COMPOSITION; DONOR MILK; FEEDING TOLERANCE; GASTROINTESTINAL HEALTH; HUMAN MILK; HUMAN MILK FORTIFIERS; INFANT NUTRITION; NEURODEVELOPMENT; PROTEIN; VERY LOW BIRTH WEIGHT INFANTS
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, the leading cause of infant death and disability is preterm birth.  Preventing nutritional deficiencies and provision of mothers' milk are critical in mitigating the consequences of preterm birth in three important areas:  (1) brain and physical development, (2) growth and body composition, and (3) gut health. Health care professionals have responded to the evidence that mothers' milk improves the health of preterm infants and, as result, there has been a dramatic increase in provision of mothers' milk during initial hospitalization.  However, due to maternal illness and other factors related to preterm birth, most mothers are unable to express adequate amounts of breast milk to exclusively feed their infants during hospitalization. Second, mothers' milk alone will not meet the nutritional requirements of very low birth weight (VLBW) infants and so cow milk-based nutrient fortifiers are added to mothers' milk.  We do not know whether adding cow milk-based nutrient fortifiers will affect the protective properties of mothers' milk or what the correct amount of protein is to add to human milk in order to promote optimal development without causing undue risk.  To resolve these challenges, health care professionals from a large consortium of neonatal units have assembled to evaluate the benefits, risks and costs of using pasteurized donor human milk, a human milk-based nutrient fortifier and protein modulars for feeding VLBW infants.  While feeding interventions will occur in hospital, infants will be followed to school age.  In addition to standard clinical assessments, the team will be using sophisticated molecular techniques to study gut colonization (important in protection from life threatening infections) as well as novel neuroimaging and body composition studies to gauge the impact of feeding interventions on brain development and appropriate growth.   This study will be pivotal in setting feeding guidelines for VLBW infants in Canada and globally

Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS AND RELATED DISEASES; BREAST CANCER; COHORT; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HISTOLOGY; MALIGNANCY; RHEUMATIC DISEASE; RHEUMATOLOGY; SYSTEMIC AUTOIMMUNE RHEUMATIC DISEASE; SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer is increasingly common in the developed world. As we focus more on long-term outcomes in arthritis and related disease, there is increasing interest in cancer risk in rheumatic disorders. Individuals with systemic lupus (SLE) have been shown to have distinct cancer risk profiles. Compared to the general population, current data indicate a slight (10-15%) increase in cancer in SLE overall. However, evidence also points to a decreased risk of breast cancer in women with SLE, relative to the general population. The reasons behind a negative association between SLE and breast cancer is unknown. The objective of this project is to provide a brief report of the breast cancer cases from a very large SLE sample population, with respect to age, race, SLE duration cancer stage, receptor status, treatment, and outcomes

TitreApplicationTitle: Physical Activity in Lung Transplant Candidates: defining cut-offs for a frailty index
Keywords-MotsClés: FRAILTY; LUNG TRANSPLANT; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; PHYSICAL THERAPY; REHABILITATION; SARCOPENIA
Abstract-Résumé: Lung transplantation is a life saving surgery for people with severe lung diseases. There is a growing trend for considering older patients and those with more critical illness for lung transplantation. As a result, the assessment of physical frailty is becoming an important issue in lung transplant candidates since it may affect outcomes following the transplant surgery. Frailty is defined in the elderly by unintentional weight loss, muscle weakness, exhaustion, slowness and low physical activity. The goal of our research program is to develop a transplant-specific "frailty index" to assess for frailty in lung transplant candidates. To improve on previous frailty indices used in the elderly, we propose to use an objective measure of physical activity using an activity monitor worn on the hip. The objective of the proposed study it to develop the cut-off values for "low physical activity" in people waiting for lung transplantation, which will be used in a transplant-specific frailty index. This study will be conducted as part of an undergraduate summer studentship through the priority research area in Physical Activity, Mobility & Health.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of telomerase in budding yeast
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMOSOME BIOLOGY; TELOMERASE; TELOMERE MAINTENANCE; TELOMERE REPLICATION
Abstract-Résumé: One could compare our genome to an extraordinarily large library that contains numerous shelves, each with many books. The combined information contained in all the books represents our genetic information and is required to make us what we are. In this paraphrase, the bookshelves could be likened to our chromosomes. Due to a heavy use of the books and also because the whole library, including the shelves, need to be duplicated before each cell division, there is continued wear and tear on the terminal bookends on the shelves. Without continued upkeep and repair, the bookends eventually will become dysfunctional, causing books to fall off the shelves and get lost. The telomerase enzyme that we study basically is the repair enzyme for the bookends of the shelves, thus in real life it is essential to ensure the integrity of our chromosomes. Inside cells, telomerase is composed of a number of components but minimally, two of them are required for the enzyme to work: a protein and an RNA molecule. Inadequate supply of any of those components, causing instability of the chromosomes, is associated with a number of human disease states, foremost cancer, but also dyskeratosis congenita (DKC). In fact, it has been shown that DKC can be caused by mutations in the RNA component of telomerase. Using budding yeast as a model system, here we propose to investigate the biology of the telomerase enzyme. In particular, we wish to determine all the components of the yeast telomerase, learn more about how the RNA is regulated and localized and how the enzyme operates at its most important location, namely the catalytic center. Given the fact that telomerase function and regulation generally is very highly conserved across many species, including humans, we speculate that these studies provide critical clues and input into questions on how this enzyme affects human health.

Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis is a common source of disability, pain, and death in the elderly. Individuals who have a spine fracture are and increased risk of death and future fracture. Exercise is often recommended for individuals with osteoporosis. However, there is very little research about the safety and effectiveness of exercise in high risk individuals such as those with spine fractures. Our team is conducting a large clinical trial of home exercise in women with spine fractures. The proposed undergraduate project will assess the time individuals with spine fractures spend in sedentary activity and in light, moderate and vigorous activity, and will compare self-reported physical activity levels with those measured with accelerometers, to inform the choice of measurement tools in future larger trials. Our ultimate goal is to conduct a large trial examining the effect of exercise on fracture risk in high-risk individuals.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating the role of extracellular pyrophosphate in the induction of ectopic mineralization in a mouse model of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)
Keywords-MotsClés: ARTHRITIS; DIFFUSE IDIOPATHIC SKELETAL HYPEROSTOSIS; INTERVERTEBRAL DISC; MINERALIZATION; PYROPHOSPHATE
Abstract-Résumé: The Arthritis Society lists DISH (diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis) as the second most common form of arthritis after osteoarthritis. Unlike many types of arthritis, DISH occurs more often among men than women (25% of men versus 15% of women over age 50). The condition has an overall prevalence estimated at 6-12% of North Americans, and given our aging population, is expected to increase significantly within the coming decade.  Although the symptoms of DISH have been described in the literature for over 100 years, it was only recognized as a distinct disorder in 1997. Consequently, it is underdiagnosed and often misdiagnosed. Symptoms include thoracic spine pain and stiffness and, in advanced cases, dysphagia and compression of the spinal cord and nerve roots. Importantly, the etiology of DISH is unknown. Moreover, apart from surgical removal of hyperostoses in severe cases, there are no specific treatments for this common disorder.  To better understand the causes underlying this condition, our group has recently reported a transgenic mouse model that mimics DISH in humans.  The current proposal will continue these studies, developing a cell culture model to begin to understand the signals present in the microenvironment of affected cell types that triggers the development of this disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Insulin receptor signaling in joint fibrosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULAR CONTRACTION; FIBROSIS; IGF RECEPTOR SIGNALING; IGF-II SIGNALING; INSULIN RECEPTOR HYBRIDS; TYPE-2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: We have recently identified insulin-like growth factor-II (IGF-II) levels as abnormally high in Dupuytren's Disease (DD) and Frozen Shoulder Syndrome (FSS).  DD and FSS are  diseases of the hand and shoulder respectively that are approximately 10 times more common in patients with diabetes than in the general population.  Why patients with diabetes are more prone to these conditions is not understood.  Serum IGF-II levels are increased in patients with type-2 diabetes and we have shown that IGF-II significantly enhances cellular contractility.  IGF-II signals through  a form of the insulin receptor that can form hybrids with IGF receptors, and these hybrids can cause insulin resistance, a characteristic of type-2 diabetes.   This project will determine if IGF-II signaling through insulin  receptor hybrids promotes DD and FSS development.

TitreApplicationTitle: International Orthopaedic Multicentre Fracture Study
Keywords-MotsClés: FRACTURE; GLOBAL HEALTH; ORTHOPAEDICS; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: This study will address the demographics and injury characteristics  that lead to negative outcomes after orthopaedic injuries in low and middle income countries. This will be done as a prospective cohort study. The study will continue the work of McMaster University on the global burden of fractures done previously. About 16,500 patients presenting to emergency departments with orthopaedic injuries will be examined. Some specific outcomes to be examined are the demographics and injury characteristics associated with 30-day mortality,  unplanned re-operation, and injury-related infections in adult (age 18+) patients presenting to emergency departments with fractures and/or dislocations of the pelvis, spine, and/or extremities in low and middle income countries.

TitreApplicationTitle: Predictors of reoperations and other complications in patients with complex open fractures of the extremities: A sub-study of the FLOW trial
Keywords-MotsClés: FRACTURE; GLOBAL HEALTH; ORTHOPAEDICS; TRAUMA
Abstract-Résumé: Open fractures are often complicated by infections, wound healing problems and failure of fracture healing - many of which necessitate a reoperation. The most effective antibiotic regimen in preventing postoperative deep infections remains controversial, and the current state of practice varies widely, particularly with respect to antibiotic duration. Further, the question of which characteristics are most predictive of risk of a negative outcome following open extremity fracture repair remains unresolved.  The primary aim of this study is to evaluate the effect of different implementation methods and duration of administered antibiotics, as well as other potential predictors for reoperations and complications in surgically - treated complex open fractures of the extremities. This will be a predictors sub-analysis of the mentor's Fluid Lavage of Open Wounds (FLOW) trial of over 2000 patients evaluating the effect of alternative irrigating solutions and pressures on reoperations in patients with open fractures. Analyses will include a multivariable logistic regression using reoperations as the dependent variable. This study will potentially inform clinical guidelines. The devastation these injuries create for patients as well as the challenges to our practice as orthopedic surgeons will be tremendously impacted by these findings, allowing for the successful management of complex open fractures in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Is CCN1 necessary for skin fibrosis?
Keywords-MotsClés: CCN1; CCN2; FIBROSIS; SCARS; SCLERODERMA; SKIN
Abstract-Résumé: Currently there is no treatment available to patients who suffer from skin fibrosis such as scleroderma. A gene called CCN2 has been shown to play an important role in skin fibrosis and is a possible target for treatment intervention. Another gene closely related to CCN2 called CCN1 has been shown to work similarly in cell based studies, suggesting they function similarly in the body as well. Data shows that both CCN1 and CCN2 are present in skin fibrosis and may be working together, or one may be a more optimal target then the other. My aim is to study these two genes in mouse models to get a better understanding of their roles in fibrosis. If we understand the functional importance of CCN2 and CCN1 we can then determine which target is best for treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of the differential roles of MyoD and myogenin in establishing the muscle gene expression program
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE EXPRESISON; MUSCLE DEVELOPMENT; PROGRAMMING STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Stem cells have the potential to treat numerous diseases that currently have no cure, especially degenerative diseases such as muscular dystrophy. Stems cells have given us this exciting possibility due to their capacity to, not only self-renew but also differentiate into every type of cell in the body; thus providing the material that can be used to regenerate diseased tissue. The long-term goal of the research group is to use stem cells as a treatment for muscular dystrophy, but we must first be able to create protocols to direct the differentiation of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells to skeletal muscle. In order to do this, we must increase our knowledge of the specific gene expression and molecular mechanisms that direct muscle development, or myogenesis. The purpose of this proposal is to determine the role of muscle regulatory factors (MRFs) to differentially activate gene expression. Also to possibly identify coactivators that differentially interact with MRFs to allow muscle specific gene expression and muscle development. The coactivators will be determined with the pull-down methods using MRF bound promoter extracts and will be identified using quantitative mass spectrometry. The specific role of the identified coactivators will be determined using RNA interference to knockdown their activity and the expression of genes of interest will be examined using qualitative Real-time PCR. This research will help to define the roles of MRFs, as well as identify new proteins that were not known to be involved in myogenesis. The completion of this research will bring us one step closer to finding a treatment for muscular dystrophy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Prevention and control of chronic and respiratory viral diseases using PapMV nanoparticles.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADJUVANT; IMMUNOMODULATOR; INFLUENZA; INNATE IMMUNITY; LCMV CLONE 13; PAPMV NANOPARTICLES; PREVENTION VIRAL INFECTION; ROD LIKE STRUCTURE; TLR7 AGONIST; TREATMENT VIRAL INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: We have recently developed a novel adjuvant that is a rod-shape nanoparticle made of the coat protein of a plant virus assemble around a RNA. We showed that the nanoparticles are able to expand and increase significantly the immune response to the seasonal flu vaccine antigens. In addition we also showed that the adjuvant induce a strong innate immune response that lead to protection to viral respiratory diseases (like flu) or viral chronic disease (like LCMV). Based on those exciting results, we wish to investigate the mechanism of recognition of the nanoparticles by the immune system. In brief, we will (1) study the importance of aggregation of PapMV nanoparticles in the immune response, (2) identify the immune receptor(s) of PapMV nanoparticles, (3) investigate the involvement of platelets in the immune response response induced by PapMV nanoparticles,  (4) identify the modulation of the transcriptome in immune cells induced with PapMV nanoparticles  Finally, we will attempt to treat established infections with influenza or LCMV using PapMV nanoparticles alone or in combination with other drugs to evaluate the potential of this technology in the treatment of viral diseases. Because PapMV nanoparticles are very well tolerated in mammals, we are confident that the technology has a strong potential to be used for several applications, including the preventions and treatment of various viral infections.

TitreApplicationTitle: Contribution of intracellular sodium to paralytic attack in HyperKPP muscle
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTION POTENTIAL; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; HYPERKALEMIC PERIODIC PARALYSIS; INTRACELLULAR SODIUM; MEMBRANE POTENTIAL; MUSCLE CONTRACTION; SODIUM CHANNEL
Abstract-Résumé: Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis (HyperKPP) is a disease primarily characterized by myotonic discharges between and during periods of paralysis that mainly affect limb muscles. The paralysis completely incapacitates patients because they are unable to move, often confined to bed for a period of time varying from a few hours to days. So far, none of the available treatments are fully effective and some loss effectiveness with time.  The disease is caused by a mutation of sodium channel that disrupt the excitability of the cell membrane in skeletal muscle. The disruption first starts with an over excitability (myotonic discharge) of the membrane followed by a complete loss of excitability (paralysis). So far, we have always worked on the assumption that only changes in membrane potential are responsible for the paralysis. However, it is known that the intracellular concentration of sodium increases drastically during paralysis to levels that can actually contribute and accentuate the loss of membrane excitability. However, at the present time the contribution of the intracellular Na+ to a loss of membrane excitability is unknown. The objective of this study is to determine how much each of the disturbances in membrane potential and of increases in [Na+]i contribute to the paralysis. The experiments are designed to measure membrane excitability at different membrane potentials while intracellular sodium concentration is constant and vice versa at different intracellular Na+ concentrations while the membrane potential is maintained at a given values. The results from these experiments will then provide valuable information as to whether new treatment for HyperKPP will require solely a correction in membrane potential or simultaneously a correction in intracellular sodium concentration.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of mechanical stress in regulating integrin binding to latent transforming growth factor TGF-beta1
Keywords-MotsClés: FIBROSIS; MECHANICAL STRESS; MYOFIBROBLAST; TGF BETA; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: After injury, our body rapidly repairs the damage, often leaving behind a stiff scar. Scarring is a clinical burden because affected organs are losing vital functions. A scarred heart cannot pump properly, scarred lung tissue impairs proper gas exchange, and scarred skin becomes inflexible which impedes the function of muscles, limbs and digits. This condition, called fibrosis, is fatal in skin systemic sclerosis and in lung, heart, liver, and kidney fibrosis. Fibrosis always accompanies cancer and promotes metastasis of the transformed epithelium. It is estimated that 60-70% of all disease-related deaths are ultimately caused by fibrosis-related organ failure. To date, no therapy is effective to treat fibrosis. Fibroblasts promote tissue repair and fibrosis by secreting massive amounts of fibrous collagen. As fibroblasts crawl they pull on the initially soft fibre matrix and make it stiffer. At one point, the matrix is too stiff to be reorganized but still too weak to stabilize the organ. Then, fibroblasts turn into contractile myofibroblasts that stiffen the tissue even more and thereby stimulate other fibroblasts to become contractile - a vicious cycle is established. In this project, we investigate how organ stiffness directly influences the availability of a growth factor that is stored in the tissue and that worsens the situation once pulled out by the fibroblasts.
