TitreApplicationTitle: Determine the functional role of Xin within skeletal muscle in vivo
Keywords-MotsClés: GENE EXPRESSION; MUSCLE FUNCTION; MUSCLE REGENERATION; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY; SATELLITE CELLS; STEM CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Muscular dystrophy is a disease state defined by muscle wasting, which can be caused by mutations in proteins integral to maintaining the shape and function of muscle. The role of many of these proteins are poorly understood, one of which is Xin. The Dr. Hawke lab has demonstrated that Xin is expressed in two locations within adult skeletal muscle. In uninjured muscle, it is localized to the myotendinous junction (between muscle and tendon) where it is believed to support areas experiencing high mechanical stress. In injured muscle, Xin is highly expressed within muscle stem cells, suggesting it contributes significantly to muscle repair. The studies described herein serve to further define the function of Xin in skeletal muscle and to provide insight into the potential symptoms expected in patients with Xin mutations.   These experiments involve a comparison of the functional capacities of skeletal muscles from normal mice and mice lacking Xin protein. After conducting in situ muscle stimulation, these experiments will determine if the absence of Xin leads to impairments in force production and fatigability in skeletal muscle. Complementing these tests, the structure of muscle tissue will be analyzed using Evans Blue Dye and other markers of muscle damage to assess whether the absence of Xin leads to increased susceptibility to damage in unstimulated and contracting (stimulated) muscle fibers.  Overall, with a greater understanding of Xin, we believe we can help explain the heterogeneity of muscular dystrophy and possibly identify a novel form of muscular dystrophy. This will help healthcare professionals to definitively diagnose and identify appropriate therapeutic strategies to improve quality of life and assist patients in coping with Xin-related muscular diseases.  Secondly, understanding the function of Xin will introduce new insight and understanding of the muscle stem cell population, which will help improve their therapeutic potential.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hip Fracture Evaluation with Alternatives of Total Hip Arthroplasty versus Hemi-Arthroplasty
Keywords-MotsClés: DISABILITY; HEMI-ARTHROPLASTY; HIP FRACTURES; MULTI-CENTRED; ORTHOPAEDIC TRAUMA MANAGEMENT; RANDOMIZED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Hip fractures are associated with a 30% mortality rate at 1 year and profound temporary, and sometimes permanent, impairment of independence and quality of life. Hip fractures account for more hospital days than any other musculoskeletal injury and represent more than two thirds of all hospital days due to fractures. Length of hospital stays in Canada is estimated at 465,000 patient-days annually with a projected increase to 1.8 million days annually by 2040. The disability adjusted life-years lost as a result of hip fractures ranks in the top 10 of all cause disability globally. The lack of definitive evidence regarding the optimal approach for surgical management has fueled debates at international orthopaedic surgical meetings. Despite the fact that most surgeons prefer hemi-arthroplasty, available evidence suggests that, if there is a difference in patient-important outcomes, it likely favours total hip arthroplasty. The discordance between surgeon preference and trends, in evidence to date, reinforces the need for a large definitive trial.

TitreApplicationTitle: Tissue origin determines the susceptibility of fibroblasts to mechanically induced fibrogenesis
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CONTRACTION; FIBROSIS; MYOFIBROBLAST; ONCOLOGY; TISSUE REPAIR; WOUND HEALING
Abstract-Résumé: Fibrosis is a major cause for organ failure with no effective therapy available. Fibrosis is characterized by the accumulation of a collagen-rich and stiff extracellular matrix. The stiffness of fibrotic tissues activates resident non-contractile fibroblastic cells into highly contractile myofibroblasts. Enhanced myofibroblast contraction is detrimental by producing the tissue contractures that impair organ function.Based on previous observations in the Hinz lab, we hypothesize that fibroblasts are heterogeneous in their ability to differentiate into fibrogenic myofibroblasts upon mechanical stimulation. The aim of this study is to evaluate whether the mechanical environment of their origin tissue influences the potential of fibroblasts to differentiate into myofibroblasts. The research priority areas directly relevant to this proposal are 'Tissue Injury, Repair and Replacement' and 'Chronic Disease'. The project aims in understanding the role of contractile myofibroblasts in physiological tissue repair and in causing pathological and chronic tissue fibrosis. Fibrosis is a major burden for the Canadian Health Care System. It is estimated that 60-70% of all disease-related deaths are ultimately caused by fibrosis-related organ failure. To date, no therapy is effective to treat fibrosis. Long term benefits of the proposed research will be improved health of Canadians who are impacted by fibrosis, and recipients of implants and regenerative cell therapy. The understanding of cell regulation gained from this research is crucial for the rational design of more efficient therapies for fibrocontractive diseases. In particular, anti-fibrosis therapies may need to be tuned to different fibroblast populations in different organs.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of FHL2 in matrix stiffness-mediated mesenchymal stem cell osteogenic differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMATERIALS; BIOMECHANICS; BONE; STEM CELLS; TISSUE ENGINEERING
Abstract-Résumé: Musculoskeletal diseases are among the most significant economic and health burdens in Canada. A promising approach to repair or replace diseased or damaged tissue is to use adult mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) delivered to the repair site with a biomaterial. However, for MSC-based therapies to realize their full potential, biomaterials that predictably guide MSC function to restore tissue function are needed. Interestingly, a biomaterial's mechanical stiffness has profound impact on the ability of the MSCs to mature to functional cells, like those that make bone. If we can understand and harness this phenomenon, we should be able to design better biomaterials for the regeneration of bone and other tissues.  Based on preliminary work in our lab, we hypothesize that a molecule called FHL2 is required for a biomaterial's stiffness to direct bone formation by MSCs. In this summer research project, an undergraduate researcher will test this hypothesis. Using genetics and drugs, she will manipulate FHL2 levels in human and mouse MSCs grown in the lab and then test whether they can become bone cells on biomaterials with different mechanical stiffnesses. We expect that FHL2 will be required for MSCs to become bone cells on different biomaterials. These studies will provide significant new insights into the molecular mechanisms that link biomaterial design to MSC-based tissue regeneration. Longer term, this work is expected to lead to novel strategies to regenerate bone by modulating FHL2 activity using drugs or customized biomaterials.  More immediately, this project will introduce a promising young scientist to research in regenerative medicine and musculoskeletal health and train her in an interdisciplinary research environment with a track record of success in training new scientists. By equipping and encouraging her to pursue this field, our goal is that she will contribute to advances in health technology in the future to improve the health of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Utilization of Novel Image Processing Algorithms to Generate Accurate Computational Models of the Craniofacial Skeleton
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTATIONAL MODELING; SURGERY; TISSUE/BONE INJURY
Abstract-Résumé: Mechanical behaviour of the Craniofacial Skeleton (CFS) under physiological loads is poorly understood. The complex structure of the CFS defies reduction to analogous or simpler components, and demands a complete characterization of its biomechanics to gain insight into its key structural components. High rates of morbidity and revision surgery in the CFS (up to 50%) due to an inability to accurately optimize bone healing and long-term stability are issues due to lack of knowledge of CFS biomechanics. The objective of this research is to characterize the mechanical behaviour of thin bone structures in the CFS under physiological loads based on morphologically accurate computational finite element (FE) models. This project involves the use of micro-level image analysis, development and analysis of experimentally validated FE models along with mechanical design, materials science and biomechanical testing. Additionally, a newly developed and validated automated deconvolution filter based algorithm will be used to locally correct intensity and geometry data from clinical CT scans; allowing for accurate segmentation and modeling of thin bone regions and articulations (sutures). The performance of the specimen specific FE models (n=6) is measured through a strain-based comparison to mechanical testing data under temporalis and masseter muscle loading. If the characterization of the mechanical patterns in CFS are successful, automated segmentation techniques optimized for thin bone structures can be implemented to rapidly generate FE models. These models will allow for accurate representations of strain patterns in the CFS. Ultimately, they can serve as a biomechanical framework for rational design of new treatments and practices for CFS injuries and pathologies. In addition, this project maybe significant to other orthopaedic applications with respect to understanding biomechanical behaviour such as preventing musculoskeletal injury and improving repair and regeneration.

TitreApplicationTitle: Benefits and Harms of Taking Opioids for Chronic Non-cancer Pain
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BENEFIT-HARM ANALYSIS; CAREGIVER PERSPECTIVE; CHRONIC PAIN; MIXED METHODS; MUSCULOSKELETAL DISEASE; OPIOIDS; PATIENT PERSPECTIVE
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain, defined as pain that persists for at least three to six months, has become an enormous societal burden that affects many people and can endure for many years. It is very important to manage chronic pain properly because this condition can impair an individual's ability to work, their quality of life and their ability to function. Musculoskeletal conditions are very prominent causes of chronic pain. Opioids are effective treatments for acute moderate to severe pain, but have limited evidence of benefit for chronic pain. In addition, there are risks of harmful side effects such as constipation, vomiting, over-sedation and confusion. At a wider level, many patients are concerned about taking a medication that is commonly associated with addiction, crime and overdose. Since chronic pain is very common and all pain medications have limitations, opioid use has expanded dramatically in Canada over the past decade. Data from Ontario shows that opioid-related deaths have increased dramatically as well, making the need for research on the benefits and harms of opioids a priority. In the proposed study, we will interview patients with chronic non-cancer pain and their caregivers, to gain an in-depth understanding of their experiences related to the patient's use of opioid medications - benefits, harms, nature of the painful condition, coping strategies, difficulties with usage, adherence, concerns regarding effect on family and friends, and overall weighing of positive and negative effects. We expect that caregivers may have a somewhat different perspective than patients on the overall weight of opioid benefit and harm. Although we expect some variation of opinion among the sample, it is likely that key themes will readily emerge.  There has been surprisingly little research on the total patient experience with opioids and virtually none involving caregivers or situated in Canada. This study will add useful information for clinicians and for future studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Induction of hyperglycemia by infection with the Lyme arthritis pathogen in susceptible hosts
Keywords-MotsClés: BACTERIAL INFECTION; DIABETES; DIET INDUCED OBESITY; LYME ARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Lyme disease is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi (Bb). The most common complication of Lyme disease is arthritis. Rates of Lyme disease are increasing rapidly throughout the industrialized world, in parallel with rising rates of obesity and diabetes. We found recently that obesity and diabetes enhance Bb infection, and that Bb infection results in elevated blood sugar. Diabetes and poorly controlled blood sugar are associated with some forms of arthritis. In this project we will investigate whether increases in blood sugar induced by Bb infection increase the severity of Lyme arthritis, and whether control of blood sugar by insulin treatment can limit Lyme arthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Correction du gène de la dystrophine avec des protéines ZFNs et TALENs.
Keywords-MotsClés: DYSTROPHIE MUSCULAIRE DE DUCHENE; DYSTROPHINE; FLUORESCENCE; GENIE GENETIQUE; MICRODELETION; NON HOMOLOGOUS END JOINING (NHEJ); TAL EFFECTOR NUCLEASE (TALEN); THERAPIE GENIQUE; ZINC FINGER NUCLEASE (ZFN)
Abstract-Résumé: La dystrophie musculaire de Duchenne est une maladie hereditaire touchant environs  1 garcon sur 4000. Elle conduit a un affaiblissement des muscles au cours du grandissement de l'enfant atteint. Cette maladie est causee par une mutation genetique dans le chromosome X qui ne permet pas la production d'une proteine musculaire, soit la dystrophine. Ceci contribue a affaiblir les cellules musculaires conduisant l'enfant a avoir des difficultes a marcher. La maladie evolue par un esoin obligatoire d'un fauteuil roulant. Ensuite, la maladie finit par affaiblir tous les muscles, incluant les muscles cardiaques et respiratoires. Au cours du stage, il sera question de developper des proteines tres specifiques pouvant ouvrir l'ADN pour qu'il puisse etre repare par des micro-deletions dans le gene mute, afin de corriger ce gene et ainsi permettre que la dystrophine soit produite. Les proteines etudiees seront les nucleases a doit de zinc (ZFN) et les Trascription Activator-Like Effector Nuclease (TALEN). Suite aux micro-deletions, le gene sera reassemble par des methodes de correction cellulaires, soit par recombinaison non-homologue des extremites. Le developpement des proteines TALEN se fera pour differents segments codants du gene qui causent la maladie. Une autre approche qui sera etudie pour ce traitement est d'utiliser une paire de TALEN avec un plasmide donneur d'ADN afin de reparer le gene par recombinaison homologue. Au cours du stage, il sera aussi question de produire les proteines TALEN  chez les bacteries. Les TALEN produites seront ensuite utilisees afin de verifier que ces proteines peuvent corriger le cadre de lecture du gene qui cause la dystrophie. La correction du gene produira une proteine pouvant avoir des fonctions partielles, tel est le cas de la dystrophie musculaire de Becker, soit une variante de la maladie beaucoup moins grave et moins evolutive, ce qui ameliorera grandement la vie des personnes atteints de la Dystrophie musculaire de Duchenne.

TitreApplicationTitle: Post-transcriptional gene regulation during Drosophila development
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; GENE REGULATION; GENETICS; GERM CELLS; RNA LOCALIZATION; RNA STABILITY; RNA-BINDING PROTEIN; TRANSLATIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: Genes can be regulated at many different levels. Best understood are the machineries that make a messenger RNA (mRNA) copy from the DNA and then translate the information encoded in the mRNA into protein. It is well known that cells are instructed to take on different fates (skin, nerves, muscle, etc.) during development in large part through different genes being turned 'on' or 'off' in their ability to make mRNA. Recently it has become clear that a great deal of control is exerted, not in the making of the mRNA, but also after the mRNA is made. For example, an mRNA may be made in two cell types (say nerve and muscle) but only be allowed to be translated into protein one of these (say, nerves). Likewise the mRNA may be produced in both cell types but its stability may be regulated such that it is chewed up and eliminated in one cell type but not the other. Furthermore, where an mRNA is placed within a cell is very important and highly controlled and can ensure that the protein is made in the right part of the cell (say in the axon of a nerve rather than in its dendrites). Defects in these sorts of processes - called post-transcriptional processes - can lead to developmental defects and disease. The machinery of post-transcriptional processes is evolutionarily highly conserved so that fruit flies and humans have very similar machinery. We use the fruit fly - which is amenable to highly sophisticated molecular, cellular and genetic methods - to understand the post-transcriptional machinery and its role in development and disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Composition, ontogeny and function of specific GPCR signalling complexes.
Keywords-MotsClés: BRET/FRET; G PROTEIN-COUPLED RECEPTORS; HEART DISEASE; IMAGING; SIGNALLING COMPLEX ASSEMBLY; SIGNALLING SPECIFICITY
Abstract-Résumé: Most of the drugs currently used to treat heart failure and related diseases (including beta-blockers) are directed against the largest family of cell surface receptors (which transduce signals outside of the cell into activity inside the cell), the so-called G protein-coupled receptors or GPCRs. These drugs target ligand-binding sites, i.e. the site where endogenous compounds interact with the receptor. Drugs thus act as either agonists, mimicking the effects of the natural ligand or as antagonists, which block the effects of the natural ligand. The problem is that all of these drugs produce significant side effects. This, in part is due to the fact that targetting the ligand binding site may not be specific or selective enough to elicit or block only the desired effect. This is likely due to the nature of the receptor and how it's downstream signalling pathways are organized. These receptors do not as previously believed interact with their signalling partners in a random fashion as a result of agonist stimulation. Recent data has shown that 1) each single receptor can be coupled to multiple signalling pathways in the same cell ; 2) receptors are physically and stably associated with their signalling pathways even before agonist stimulation and 3) these complexes form during biosynthesis, i.e. before the receptor gets to it's final destination in the cell membrane. How then, can we make drugs that are more specific and have less side effects? This project is aimed at characterizing individual receptor signalling complexes, their organization and specificity and how they are assembled. Once we know 1) what is in any given signalling complex and 2) how it is assembled and localized in the cell we can in principle, we can thus reduce the number of side effects seen with current therapeutic approaches to diseases such as heart failure.

Keywords-MotsClés: MEDICATION ADHERENCE; OSTEOPOROSIS; PILOT EXPERIMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoporosis is a growing public health concern in our aging population. Although effective medications are available for reducing the risk of broken bones, many patients are not taking them as directed or they stop taking their osteoporosis medication. The Arthritis Program (TAP) at Southlake Regional Health Centre is an award-winning model of care that provides assessment, treatment and education to patients with rheumatic diseases. It has been providing a comprehensive education program for those living with osteoporosis since 2006. This program aims to increase patients' knowledge and confidence in managing the disease. Patients receive consultation and follow-up care in a clinic with a rheumatologist, a pharmacist, and a kinesiologist. TAP patients are also invited to attend a one-day education workshop which covers topics such as medications, Calcium and Vitamin D, nutrition, falls prevention, and exercise. The proposed study will measure compliance with osteoporosis medication in those patients who attend the Program. A comparison will be made to similar patient groups who did not attend the program.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of maternal high fat feeding on the development and integration of metabolic and reward-related brain circuits in the offspring
Keywords-MotsClés: DOPAMINE; GHRELIN; HIGH FAT INTAKE; INDEPENDENT FEEDING; INTRACELLULAR SIGNALLING; LATERAL HYPOTHALAMUS; LEPTIN; NEONATAL DEVELOPMENT; VENTRAL TEGMENTAL AREA
Abstract-Résumé: Exposure of the mother to calorie dense food in the peri-conceptional period, pregnancy and/or early postpartum periods leads to obesity in the offspring by programming the brain circuits controlling energy balance and the rewarding value of food.  However, the precise mechanisms of this metabolic programming are still unclear. We have previously documented that the long term effects of maternal high fat feeding during the end of gestation and lactation on the adult rat offspring are quite similar to the hypofunction in dopamine neurotransmission observed in human pre-obese and obese individuals. In this proposal, we will take advantage of the rodent model to examine whether dopamine function is altered early by maternal diet (i.e. during the neonatal period) and whether high fat exposure accelerates the onset of independent feeding in pups. We will also explore the role of two metabolic hormones, leptin- (that is increased in high fat fed pups) and ghrelin on the establishment of the neuronal circuitry linking both the metabolic and reward aspects of feeding in pups. These studies should help us understand how programmed developmental neurotransmission is altered by maternal diet and where are the potential targets for early intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Treadmill training and SOX9 ablation: a combination therapy to improve locomotor recovery of spinal cord-injured mice
Keywords-MotsClés: CHONDROITIN SULFATE PROTEOGLYCANS; INCOMPLETE SPINAL CORD INJURY; LOCOMOTOR RECOVERY; NEURAL PLASTICITY; SOX9 ABLATION; TISSUE REPAIR; TREADMILL TRAINING
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a catastrophic event that is a major health care issue, causing lifelong disability. In the USA and Canada, more than 12,000 spinal cord injuries occur annually, and ~275,000 people live with permanent, serious disabilities due to SCI (Cdn. Paraplegic Assoc.). Since SCI usually occurs in young males it represents a lifelong burden to the patient and a socioeconomic challenge to our society.  Currently, there are no effective treatments for SCI however recent work suggests that weight-supported treadmill training may offer some hope of improving outcomes when combined with other therapies.  In this study we propose to test the therapeutic effectiveness of combining weight-supported treadmill training with a strategy for reducing scar protein expression in the injured spinal cord.  Scar proteins, and in particular chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, have been demonstrated to limit regeneration in the injured spinal cord.  We have recently demonstrated that we can reduce scar protein expression after SCI by blocking the expression of a protein called SOX9 that normally up-regulates these inhibitory proteins.   Importantly, blocking SOX9 expression after SCI not only reduces scar protein expression but also leads to improved locomotor outcomes.  The present study will evaluate whether combining SOX9 inhibition with treadmill training increases locomotor recovery in spinal cord-injured mice over and above what is achieved through either treatment alone. Improving recovery and regeneration after SCI will relieve pressure on our healthcare system and produce priceless improvements to the quality of life of SCI patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Ultrasound-guided facet joint injection training using Perk Tutor
Keywords-MotsClés: FACET JOINT INJECTION; MEDICAL EDUCATION; SIMULATION TRAINING; ULTRASOUND-GUIDANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Facet syndrome is a condition that may cause 15-45% of chronic lower back pain. It is commonly diagnosed and treated using facet joint injections, a procedure that involves injecting anesthetic into the facet joints (the joints linking adjacent vertebrae together). Because facet joint injections require accurate needle placement, computed tomography (CT) and fluoroscopy imaging are often used to guide the needle insertion; however, more recently ultrasound (US) has also been shown to be a promising modality for guidance. US is a particularly attractive alternative to CT and fluoroscopy because it is affordable, time efficient and obviates radiation risks. US-guided injections, however, require physicians to interpret 2-D US images while simultaneously manipulating an US probe and needle; this is a particularly difficult task with a long learning curve. It follows that in order to establish US as the standard guidance modality for facet joint injections, and reap its benefits, improved training methodologies that will allow trainees to quickly master the requisite skills are needed. To address this need, we have developed the Perk Tutor, an augmented reality training system for US-guided needle insertions. Results from a recent pilot study suggest that Perk Tutor training leads improved improved trainee performance. The project aims to strengthen the results of this pilot study through an expanded study that will comprehensively establish the effectiveness of Perk Tutor training.

TitreApplicationTitle: Production de pansements biologiques humains en milieux définis pour la guérison de plaies cutanées
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOCYTES; BIOCHIMIE; BIOLOGIE CUTANEE; CELLULES SOUCHES; DIFFERENCIATION CELLULAIRE; GUERISON DE PLAIES; GENIE TISSULAIRE; INTERACTIONS CELLULAIRES; KERATINOCYTES; REEPITHELIALISATION
Abstract-Résumé: Les plaies chroniques et les ulceres cutanes affectent de nombreuses personnes a travers le monde, en particulier les personnes atteintes du diabete. Ce type de blessures chroniques requiert des ressources importantes du systeme de sante et cree de fortes douleurs chez les gens qui en souffrent. Dans cette optique, le soin des plaies est un enjeux important. L'utilisation des cellules souches pour stimuler la guerison des plaies est etudiee par plusieurs equipes de recherches. Les cellules souches extraites du tissu adipeux (du gras) sont particulierement attrayantes : leur abondance, leur accessibilite et leurs modes de prelevement peu invasif en font un choix de premier ordre. Par ailleurs, ces cellules souches ont la capacite de se differencier en adipocytes matures. Les adipocytes sont les cellules contenues dans les tissus graisseux. Toutefois, ces adipocytes ne font pas que stocker les graisses: ils secretent de nombreuses molecules qui ont des roles dans la croissance cellulaire, le metabolisme, l'inflammation et la revascularisation. Les effets de ces molecules sur les cellules de la peau et la guerison des plaies sont encore peu connus. Toutefois, un modele innovateur et unique permettant d'etudier en detail ces interactions a ete developpe par notre equipe. Cette methode originale consiste a creer en laboratoire des tissus reconstruits pouvant agir comme des «pansements biologiques». Nous pensons que les pansements biologiques, contenant des adipocytes ou des cellules souches du gras, auront une influence benefique sur la guerison des plaies et sur la qualite de la peau regeneree.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of cartilage homeostasis by the nuclear receptor RXR.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANABOLIC/CATABOLIC CARTILAGE MARKERS; ARTICULAR CARTILAGE EXPLANT CULTURE; BONE; CHONDROCYTE; ELISA; EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX; NUCLEAR RECEPTOR RXR; OSTEOARTHRITIS; RT-PCR
Abstract-Résumé: The degeneration of articular cartilage in joints is a hallmark of osteoarthritis, which has a large impact on mobility and overall health of affected individuals, especially the elderly.  The activity of chondrocytes (cells of cartilage) directly influence cartilage degeneration, thus making these cells a promising target for potential treatments of osteoarthritis.  This study proposes that a group of proteins called RXRs may offer protection of articular cartilage when activated, based on what is known about the role of these proteins in skeletal development.  Based on our preliminary data, RXR's are thought to regulate the expression of genes that are directly responsible for the production and degradation of cartilage.  We will be examining the expression of genes responsible for cartilage degeneration when RXRs are active and inactive to determine whether the activation of RXRs confer any protective properties to articular cartilage by repressing the expression of these genes.  We will also examine the expression of genes that produce or regenerate cartilage under similar conditions of RXR activation and inactivation.  In this experiment, articular cartilage will be cultured and treated with molecules which can activate or repress RXR activity.  We will then assess the effect these conditions have on the activity of genes involved in the maintenance of cartilage homeostasis. The aim of this project is to provide an improved understanding of the role of RXRs in cartilage physiology which could lead to improved management of osteoarthritis through specific drug targeting in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of Sox7 during myogenesis in mouse embryonic stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: MYOGENESIS
Abstract-Résumé: Treatments for patients with neuromuscular diseases, such as muscular dystrophy, have not been as easy to achieve as would be expected. Gene therapy approaches, while still promising, have had several setbacks. A method to repair and reverse muscle wasting would greatly enhance the outcome for these patients. Developing novel therapeutic methods will require enhancing our basic understanding of how skeletal muscle is made and repairs itself.  The current proposal addresses the way that muscle is formed in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells.  ES cells are cells that are derived from an early embryo.  These cells can divide to create more stem cells, termed proliferation, but can also differentiate into almost any other cell type.  The major difficulty with using ES cells for cell therapy is that only a small population of ES cells can differentiate into skeletal muscle.  Understanding how ES cells differentiate into skeletal muscle will provide insight into novel cell therapeutic approaches.  We have shown that the protein Sox7 can increase the production of the Pax3 protein.  This is important because Pax3 is found in muscle progenitor cells.  These are stem cells that are able to proliferate and also to differentiate efficiently into skeletal muscle. We hypothesize that Sox7 can regulate the formation of muscle progenitor cells, since Sox7 could increase the amount of Pax3 in P19 cells.  We will determine if the overexpression of Sox7 is able to increase the formation of skeletal muscle in mouse ES cells.  We predict that Sox7 will be able to regulate the muscle progenitor gene, Pax3, during skeletal muscle development in ES cells and lead to enriched populations of ES-derived skeletal muscle.  These studies will shed light on novel future approaches for cell therapy and will also provide an embryonic muscle population for future molecular and biochemical analysis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Optimisation des peaux humaines reconstruites par génie tissulaire : réduction du temps nécessaire à la production.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELLULES SOUCHES; CULTURE CUTANEE; DIFFERENCIATION ET PROLIFERATION DES CELLULES CUTANEES; GENIE TISSULAIRE; PEAU; PLAIES ET BRULES
Abstract-Résumé: La technique de production de peau du LOEX est tres prometteuse pour le traitement des grands brules. La methode presentement utilisee permet de conserver les cellules souches dans la peau a long-terme contrairement a d'autres methodes de production, ce qui permet une regeneration de l'epiderme a long terme. Cependant, le temps de production (45 jours) est un facteur qui pourrait etre ameliore. Une nouvelle methode de production utilisant des cellules sans materiel genetique d'un donneur pourrait permettre de diminuer le temps necessaires a la production de peaux en laboratoire. Ces cellules peuvent etre conserves a long terme et utilise au besoin. Mon premier objectif est de comparer 3 methodes de production de peau afin d'evaluer le temps necessaire a leur production et leur capacite a conserver les cellules souches. La suite du projet viserait a confirmer la fonctionnalite des peaux apres la greffe chez l'animal et a determiner les mecanismes responsables de la preservation/perte des cellules souches. CONTRIBUTION A L'AVANCEMENT DES CONNAISSANCES  Ces experimentations fourniront de nouvelles connaissances fondamentales sur la preservation des cellules epitheliales de la peau humaine ainsi que les facteurs qui en sont responsables. Ce projet vise une meilleure comprehension de l'impact des methodes de production du derme, (utilisation d'un support de cellules sans materiel genetique que l'on reensemence avec des cellules du patient) ainsi que le moment ou les cellules de l'epiderme sont ensemencees sur la qualite et la fonctionnalite des substituts cutanes. Nous anticipons que l'usage de cellules sans materiel genetique d'un donneur ne stimulera pas le rejet des greffes. A terme, ces resultats pourraient ameliorer le traitement des patients souffrant de brulures graves et etendues en permettant de fermer leurs plaies avec des substituts de peau de qualite produits plus rapidement en laboratoire.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular role of MLIP in myoblast differentiation and regeneration.
Keywords-MotsClés: LAMINOPATHY; MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Genetic disorders caused by mutations in the Lamin A/C gene (LMNA) are defined as laminopathies and affect muscle, heart, gastrointestinal and nervous systems, endocrine glands, skin, eyes and other organs. Muscular dystrophy is one of the most common muscle related laminopathies that arise from specific mutations in LMNA that result in progressive muscle weakness. Very little is known about the process from which mutations in the LMNA gene result in muscular dystrophy. We have recently identified a novel protein, MLIP, that interacts directly with A - type lamins. This provides us with a unique opportunity to investigate and understand a group of new genes and networks that may work together and are involved in muscular dystrophy. By directly manipulating the behaviour of MLIP in muscle and evaluating MLIPs effects on the muscle with a wide variety of molecular and biochemical experimental methods, we will define the role of the MLIP in muscle, in health and disease. We will map the activation and inactivation of MLIP through normal and abnormal muscle development. By recognizing the difference between the normal and abnormal muscle form and function within the context of the type of MLIP manipulation applied we will delineate the role of MLIP in muscle. The successful execution of this research will substantially expand out scientific understanding of muscular dystrophy and lead to the development of more effective therapeutic treatment of muscular dystrophy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Unasked questions: The perspectives of hip fracture patients on clinical assessments
Keywords-MotsClés: CARE TRANSITIONS; ELECTRONIC HEALTH INFORMATION SYSTEMS; HEALTH CARE PROVIDERS; INTERRAI; PATIENTS AND FAMILIES; REHABILITATION THERAPY; SENIORS; STANDARDIZED ASSESSMENT TOOLS
Abstract-Résumé: Elderly hip fracture patients often experience multiple care transitions following discharge from hospital. Inadequate information sharing among patients, families and health care providers can result in compromised patient safety and poor care quality. The CIHR-funded InfoRehab Transitions project seeks to improve the quality of care during transitions for older adults who have musculoskeletal disorders, through enhanced use and sharing of health information.   As part of the InfoRehab Transitions project, a series of interviews were conducted with hip fracture patients, informal caregivers, and health care providers to learn about their experiences with transitional care. These interviews will be analyzed to determine what information patients prioritize as most important for their health care providers, whether they believe this information is taken into account by clinicians in their decision-making, and whether these priority areas are included in currently mandated standardized assessment tools. The results of the analysis will be presented in a focus group interview with health care providers, older persons, and their family members to assess their potential for wider applicability. The project is intended to generate prompts or guides that can be used by health care providers to address information gaps identified by patients and informal caregivers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Fidélité et validité des mesures d'imagerie quantitative par ultrasonographie du tendon d'Achille : Une étude préliminaire auprès de personnes atteintes d'une tendinopathie et de personnes en bonne santé
Keywords-MotsClés: FIABILITE; IMAGERIE PAR ULTRASONOGRAPHIE; MESURE; PHYSIOTHERAPIE; READAPTATION; TENDINOPATHIE; TENDON D'ACHILLE; VALIDITE
Abstract-Résumé: L'integrite du tendon d'Achille est frequemment atteinte puisque ce tendon figure parmi les plus longs et les plus forts du corps humain, tout en etant l'un des moins bien vascularise. A ce jour, les physiotherapeutes ne disposent d'aucune mesure objective pour directement caracteriser l'integrite du tendon d'Achille in vivo. L'imagerie quantitative par ultrasonographie (IQUS), une approche emergente en physiotherapie, pourrait corriger cette lacune. Aucune etude n'a etabli les qualites psychometriques de mesures du tendon d'Achille obtenues par IQUS et aucun protocole de mesure standardise  n'est disponible en pratique clinique. Les principaux objectifs du projet visent a 1) mesurer la fiabilite des mesures de resultats obtenus par l'IQUS du tendon d'Achille et 2) determiner le meilleur protocole d'evaluation pour mesurer le tendon d'Achille par IQUS. Vingt  individus ayant une tendinopathie unilaterale ou bilaterale du tendon d'Achille et vingt individus sans atteinte au tendon d'Achille participeront a deux seances d'enregistrement d'images des tendons d'Achille  par ultrasonographie, separees de 30 minutes. Lors de chacune de ces seances, trois images longitudinales et trois images transversales seront enregistrees par un physiotherapeute et un physiatre suivant un protocole standardise. Les images enregistrees seront fragmentees en micropixels avant d'etre traitees a l'aide d'un programme d'analyse des images specialement developpe pour ce projet. Ce programme quantifiera, entre autres, l'epaisseur et l'echogenecite, d'une region d'interet du tendon. Pour chaque mesure de resultat, une etude de generalisabilite quantifiera leur fiabilite et precision, alors qu'une etude de decision confirmera le meilleur protocole a utiliser en pratique clinique. Ultimement, l'IQUS du tendon d'Achille permettra aux physiotherapeutes d'evaluer l'efficacite des interventions therapeutiques offertes aux individus atteints d'une tendinopathie.

Abstract-Résumé: It is essential that people with diabetes visit a physician as the physician has a key-role in monitoring diabetes progression and delivering recommended care components such as HbA1C testing, foot checking and urine checking. They are also able to advise the patient when changes to lifestyle or medication are necessitated. The aim of this research was to ascertain whcih factors are associated with self-reported use of diabetes healthcare in 1,175 people with type 2 diabetes who took part in the Diabetes Health Study in Quebec. We also wanted to ascertain the impact of major depression on reported utilization of and access to diabetes healthcare and received care components. We found that those people who reported not using diabetes healthcare were more likely to have a household income less than $15,000, be controlling diabetes through diet/exercise, have a normal body-mass index, not have received recommended care components and have major depression. People with major depression were more likely to report problems getting advice and being less likely to have feet checked by their doctor.

TitreApplicationTitle: Homelessness, mental illness and justice issues: what is the evidence?
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO HEALTH SERVICES; CRIMINAL JUSTICE INVOLVEMENT; HOMELESSNESS; SEVERE MENTAL ILLNESS; SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW; TRAUMA; VICTIMIZATION
Abstract-Résumé: The aim of this literature review is to have a better understanding of how many homeless persons who have a mental illness commit crimes, are involved with the justice system, or are the victims of crimes. Another goal of the study is to identified the factors associated with these issues. The findings indicate high levels of criminal justice involvement, crime commission and victimization. Between 62.9% to 90% of homeless persons with a mental illness have ever been arrested, between 48% to 67% of them have ever been incarcerated and between 73.7% and 87% have ever been the victims of crime. Results also indicate that young men with a longer duration of homelessness who also have substance abuse difficulties and who report high psychiatric and medical needs are more likely to be involved with justice. Women with a history of child abuse and depression are more likely to be the victims of crimes. We discuss the implications of these findings, particularly for the development of trauma-oriented services for homeless individuals with a mental illness throughout Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aberrant expresion of autophagy markers during Osteoarthritis.
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY MARKERS; OSTEOARTHRITIS
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is commonly described by joint pain and reduced joint movement associated cartilage destructionand changes in bone formation. It is a disease that tends to get worse over time as the cartilage continues to wear away. OA is a leading cause of disability in Canada and with increasing life expectancy; OA is a major clinical and economic concern. The pathological mechanisms by which OA can be halted is still unknown. Therefore, it is utmost important to identify new targets which will help us understand the exact pathology of this disease and will further help us in stopping OA. In this context, our animal and human cell based studies suggest that a biological factor called autophagy may be an attractive target for the treatment of OA. However, we are still uncertain as to what is the exact role of autophagy in OA. Therefore, this study for the first time will investigate the specific role of autophagy in OA using mice, dog and human cells to investigate the expression pattern of autophagy markers. Te data we get from mice, dog compared to cartilage samples collected from normal human and OA patients and specifically answer the following questions: (1) What is the exact role of autophagy markers in cartilage and bone destruction associated with OA. (2) What is the exact role of autophagy on inflammation associated with OA. (3) How does autophagy control the production of harmful biological factors involved in OA. (4) What is the exact signalling mechanism by which autophagy works in OA. To answer these questions I will use a combination of techniques such as quantitative PCR and immunohistochemistry methods. I anticipate that this study will show that autophagy is the key target likely to control inflammation and damage to bone and cartilage observed in OA. Therefore, this project has the potential to generate new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of OA and related disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of 1,25hydroxyvitaminD3 on the viability of peripheral blood eosinophils from allergic and/or asthmatic donors.
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: Allergic diseases remain an important economic strain on health care systems. In fact, the issue is predominant in northern areas since asthma and allergy cases are more numerous in countries which tend to lack sunlight. Since natural light is needed for the human body to produce vitamin D, some researchers have begun to speculate that there is a link between asthma, allergies and vitamin D deficiency. Furthermore, it may be related to the effect of vitamin D deritives on the human body's natural defenses such as white blood cells. The research project at hand tends to focus on a specific white blood cell which is often involved in allergic diseases: the eosinophil. This white blood cell type is known to be a 'hot tempered' toxic body which releases deadly compounds in response to various triggers. This study will investigate the direct effect of metabolized vitamin D on the viability of eosinophils. Blood will be taken from allergic and/or asthmatic donors in order to isolate eosinophils. These cells will be incubated with diverse survival factors either seperately or in combination with vitamin D. The eosinophils' viability will be measured at diverse time points. This study will allow for a better understanding of the beneficial role attributed to vitamin D in allergic asthma. It could also clarify the reasons behind lung tissue damage in asthma. The intent is to reveal a mode of action which can be utilized in a therapy against allergic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adaptation to the Health Effects of Climate Change among Indigenous Peoples in the Global South (IP-ADAPT)
Keywords-MotsClés: CLIMATE CHANGE; ECOHEALTH; GLOBAL HEALTH; INDIGENOUS TRADITIONAL KNOWLEDGE; INTERVENTION RESEARCH; PERU; UGANDA; VULNERABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: The Adaptation to the Health Effects of Climate Change among Indigenous Peoples in the Global South (IP-ADAPT) project is a multidisciplinary, international collaborative research project that will develop and apply a framework for adaptation assessment, evaluating pilot interventions for adaptation to the health effects of climate change among Indigenous populations in the global south, and providing an evidence base for targeted intervention programs and adaptation policy. Recent international commitments under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) have created funding opportunities to implement adaptation programs in low and middle income countries. Allocation of these funds requires evidence that interventions are feasible and successful. Despite the magnitude of the adaptation challenge, there is a lack of evidence-based research to support access to funding. There is widespread recognition of particularly high vulnerability among Indigenous peoples, yet these populations have been largely neglected in literature and discourse on climate change. Working with Indigenous community partners in Amazonian Peru and southwestern Uganda, the IP-ADAPT project is the first research initiative to explicitly evaluate adaptation interventions to promote climate change adaptation in the context of Indigenous health. The research team consists of international leaders in climate change adaptation, Indigenous health research, and health policy, and the project is guided by an integrated knowledge translation model. The research will contribute to the development of a sparse but critically needed evidentiary base to support policy formulation and funding allocation for adaptation among Indigenous peoples.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding the mechanisms of stem cell lineage development and tumour suppression using freshwater planarians
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; LINEAGE DEVELOPMENT; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; NUCLEAR PORE COMPLEX; PLANARIANS; RNAI; RNASEQ; STEM CELL BIOLOGY; TUMOUR SUPPRESSOR GENES
Abstract-Résumé: Humans owe their longevity and their ability to fix tissues throughout their lives to the activity of a specific cell type called "adult stem cell".  Adult stem cells exist throughout the life of an organism and when they divide, they renew themselves and also produce a daughter cell in order to replace cells that are lost due to aging or injury.  For example, human blood stem cells will replace the millions of blood cells we turnover every day.  In addition, humans have stem cells in most of our tissues, especially tissues which turnover rapidly such as the skin, blood, lungs, and intestines.  Interestingly, those tissues are also the most common sites of tumour formation, which suggests a connection between adult stem cells and the development of cancer.  In addition, cancers often have their own stem cells, called cancer stem cells, which behave very similarly to normal adult stem cells, but simply in a less-regulated fashion.  Therefore, it stands to reason that if we can learn more about the biology that drives normal stem cells, we will understand how this biology goes awry during cancer development.  Here we will use a non-traditional model system, the freshwater planarian, to investigate the role of cancer-causing genes in normal adult stem cell biology as well as discover new mechanisms that regulate stem cells.  Planarians possess a large population of adult stem cells that can be easily manipulated and studied in the adult.  We propose to use the advantages of planarians to discover new stem cell regulators in the hopes that any new molecule found may be a potential target for future therapies in human cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Building a systems biology view of Salmonella-host interactions
Keywords-MotsClés: INTERACTOME; KINASE; PHOSPHORYLATION; PROTEOMICS; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY; VIRULENCE FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Salmonella bacteria reside in the intestinal tracts of livestock or wild animals and can be transmitted to humans via contaminated food or water to cause typhoid fever and diarrhoea, which pose major health problems throughout the world. White blood cells can normally destroy invading microorganisms by engulfing them and then delivering destructive enzymes that kill the bacteria. This part of our innate immune system is one of the primary lines of defence against invading pathogens but Salmonella species have evolved mechanisms to avoid this destruction; the bacteria is able to get into other cell types on its own, such as the cells lining our intestines, where it can halt the delivery of the destructive enzymes, allowing the bacteria to live and multiply within the cell. Ultimately the bacteria can either cause food poisoning-like symptoms from inside these cells or it can escape the confines of the cell and spread throughout the body to cause typhoid fever. The work proposed here focuses on trying to understand, from a broad view, how Salmonella is able to so efficiently control its host cells. Previous work from many other laboratories has made significant progress in understanding some aspects of this process but we aim to apply some cutting edge technology that we have had a role in developing in order to take a step backwards and ask 'What is going on in the cell as a whole?' As our group has led some of the technology development and also has significant background in the biological aspects of this problem, we have a unique ability to contribute to the overall picture of how this important pathogen affects us. The anticipated benefit of this work will be a much better understanding of how pathogens such as Salmonella are able to bypass our immune system. Such knowledge will allow us to make a more rational approach to drug design and therapies since we will be able to target specific processes unique to Salmonella.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification of Genetic Factors for Familial Lymphoid Cancers
Keywords-MotsClés: EXOME SEQUENCING; FAMILIAL CANCER; HODGKIN LYMPHOMA; LYMPHOID CANCER; LYMPHOID LEUKEMIA; LYMPHOMA; MULTIPLE MYELOMA; NEXT GENERATION SEQUENCING; NON-HODGKIN LYMPHOMA
Abstract-Résumé: We will use next-generation sequencing methods to reveal genetic variants responsible for lymphoid cancers in families. Lymphoid cancers include Hodgkin lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocytic leukemias, multiple myeloma and some other rarer cancers.      Over the last 6 years we have identified 101 lymphoid cancer families interested in participating in research, and have collected DNA samples from members of these families. These families were identified, in part, by means of a database maintained in the Lymphoma Tumour Group of the BC Cancer Agency by Dr. Joseph Connors for 30 years. We will study both large and small families. We will look for genetic variants that are shared between different affected individuals within each family, and that are not carried by certain clearly unaffected family members. In addition, we will look for commonalities between specific genes and types of genes, between families.      This will result in the identification of genes and genetic variants that contribute to lymphoid cancers in families, better risk prediction for family members, and biological insights that may help in treatment or prevention of such cancers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Structural and Functional Analysis of Pneumococcal Carbohydrate-Processing Pathways.
Keywords-MotsClés: CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS; ENZYME INHIBITION; ENZYME MECHANISM; GLYCOBIOLOGY; GLYCOSIDE HYDROLASE; INHIBITOR; PROTEIN BIOCHEMISTRY; SMALL ANGLE X-RAY SCATTERING; STRUCTURAL BIOLOGY; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding the structure and function of proteins has served to illuminate their critical functions in diverse organisms. Here we focus on a family of related enzymes from the Streptococcus pneumonia (the pneumococcus), which is a bacterium that often lives in the nose and throats of humans. This microorganism is an accomplished disease-causing germ that can cause mild ailments, such as earaches, to lethal illnesses like pneumonia, blood poisoning, and infections of the brain and central nervous system. Current vaccines and medicines (antibiotics) for treating pneumococcus infections are not always effective since this germ is constantly adapting to avoid both of these medical interventions. The importance of S. pneumoniae as a major disease-causing germ dictates intense research efforts be directed to understand how it causes infections with the aim of using this knowledge to guide eventual new treatment strategies.  The human body has large amounts of carbohydrates with complex structures, termed glycans, displayed on the surface of cells and coating the surfaces of tissues (e.g. mucous). Remarkably, the pneumococcus relies on its ability to attack these glycans to colonize humans and ultimately cause disease.   Our research is aimed at determining how this happens, at the molecular level. What glycans does the germ attack? What pneumococcal factors do this? What do these pneumococcal factors look like? What are the consequences of destroying certain host sugars? What effect do molecules that block these factors have on pneumococcal attack of host glycans. The results of this research will yield important research tools for the community but also such molecules are proving useful provide fundamewntal knowledge that could be used by other to develop new treatments to combat S. pneumoniae infections.

Abstract-Résumé: Most of the drugs most commonly taken for pain and inflammation, including for arthritis, frequently cause significant damage and bleeding in the intestine. This is a very serious effect of these drugs, that often goes undetected, and for which there are no effective treatments.   Drugs taken to protect the stomach from these drugs actually worsen the damage and bleeding caused in the intestine.  Our research project will identify the main mechanisms through which this damage and bleeding is produced, and we will develop a method for preventing this life-threatening side effect of very commonly used medications.

TitreApplicationTitle: Autonomous and unobtrusive monitoring of the physiology and physical activity of seniors within the smart home environment.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING-IN-PLACE; AUTONOMOUS MONITORING; CARDIAC REHABILITATION; HEART FAILURE MANAGEMENT; PHYSIOLOGICAL MEASUREMENTS; SEDENTARY BEHAVIOUR DETECTION; SMART HOME DESIGN; ZERO-EFFORT TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The senior population in Canada is growing at an unparalleled rate and many seniors will need to self-manage their health conditions. Many seniors do not know how or when to monitor their chronic diseases. Those who do are often given standard devices, such as arm cuffs or chest straps, which can be difficult to operate effectively and reliably. This research project will design a system that can monitor seniors in their homes with no effort required on their part. The system will also provide ongoing feedback about their vital signs and physical activity to caregivers and healthcare providers. This project is composed of three specific objectives. The first is to hold focus groups with seniors, their caregivers and healthcare providers to learn about their monitoring needs and preferences. Our lab currently measures vital signs such as heart rate, breathing rate, blood pressure, body weight, body temperature, and sedentary behaviour through sensors embedded into common household items such as chairs, beds, ceilings and flooring. The second objective of the project is to tailor our zero-effort measurement technologies into a system that will respond to the needs identified in the focus groups. The third objective is to measure the accuracy of the new system through pilot tests in a lab setting with 40 senior heart failure (HF) patients enrolled in cardiac rehabilitation. The measurements from the new system will be compared to standard home care devices such as heart rate straps and blood pressure cuffs. This research project expects to improve the health monitoring of seniors by providing them and their caregivers with automatic and reliable information without interfering with their daily activities. The smart system is expected to reduce the burden of chronic monitoring on seniors and their loved ones, reduce hospitalization rates and improve quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of a mutant human coagulation protein as a novel antidote for new direct factor Xa anticoagulant drugs, and as a tool for investigating the activity and regulation of intrinsic and extrinsic tenase, key enzyme complexes in blood coagulation.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTICOAGULATION; ANTITHROMBIN; COAGULATION; ENZYME KINETICS; FACTOR XA; FONDAPARINUX; HEMOPHILIA; HEPARIN; ICS TRAVEL AWARDS; THROMBIN
Abstract-Résumé: Heart attacks and strokes, the number one cause of death and disability in Canada, are often caused by defective blood clotting in the human body. This research project aims to translate discoveries made on the scientific bench to the bedside by figuring out the way blood clots are controlled in the body in order to develop a way to counteract the clotting system. In the past several years, numerous new anti-clotting drugs have entered the market worldwide for the treatment of strokes that target the blood clotting system. Unfortunately, given the biological nature of these new agents, readily accessible and effective antidotes and unavailable. This creates a major barrier to the widespread use of these easy to administer lifesaving drugs because for some patients, these drugs can cause life-threatening bleeding. These at-risk patients would need an antidote to quickly reverse their anticoagulation. Our laboratory has engineered a new molecule for which we have pilot data on a novel way to use this molecule to measure the action of the critical parts of the blood clotting system called tenase and prothrombinase. Because this part of the system is also the target for these new drugs, a clearer understanding of how they work aid in the development of an effective antidote for the new anti-clotting agents. Because our molecule also directly targets the tenase and prothrombinase systems, this new molecule or versions of it also has the potential to become a new anti-clotting therapy for the treatment of heart attacks and stroke.

Keywords-MotsClés: APICAL COMPLEX; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; ERYTHROCYTE; MALARIA; MOLECULAR AND CELL BIOLOGY; PHOSPHOINOSITIDES; PROTEIN INTERACTIONS; PROTEIN TRAFFICKING; SUBCELLULAR
Abstract-Résumé: Malaria is one of the world's most common infectious diseases, with approximately 274 million cases each year and 1 million deaths, and thus represents one of the most devastating global public health problems. The lack of an effective vaccine, the emergence of resistance to first-line drugs like chloroquine and antifolates and recent reports of clinical cases of reduced susceptibility to artemisinine in Cambodia, combined with the small number of suitable new drugs against the malaria parasite demonstrate the urgent need for the development and implementation of novel intervention strategies in the form of drugs, vector control measures and an effective vaccine. Indeed, it is expected that if the trend in malaria prevalence stays on its current upwards course, the death rate could double in the next twenty years. Invasion of a red blood cell by Plasmodium falciparum parasites is an essential step in the malaria lifecycle and host response to parasite antigens are an important component of human malarial immunity. Consequently, the molecular players involved in erythrocyte invasion are key targets for both therapeutic and vaccine-based strategies to block parasite development. Several of these invasion proteins are stored in the apical complex of the parasite, a structure containing secretory organelles called dense granules, micronemes and rhoptries, and are released at different times during invasion. Because of its essential role, interfering with the generation of the apical complex represents a very attractive target for the design of a new kind of antimalarial. Our studies will focus on trying to understand how the parasite directs proteins to the different structures of the apical complex. Understanding this complex process will likely provide a wealth of new targets for the development of strategies to block apical complex generation and preventing malaria pathogenesis.

This work might reveal new strategies to target cancer but in the shorter term, this work will result an understanding of how the RNF8 and RNF168 proteins participate in maintaining the integrity of our genome.

TitreApplicationTitle: The impact of drug-induced dyskinesia and its management on the daily life activities of patients with Parkinson's disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL SCALES; DYSKINESIA; EVALUATION; LEVODOPA; MAGNETIC TRACKER; MOVEMENT PATTERNS; PARKINSON; PERSONALIZED MEDICINE; QUALITY OF LIFE; QUANTIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: THE PROBLEM. Side effects such as involuntary movements called drug-induced dyskinesia (DID) in Parkinson's disease still represent a huge obstacle for maintaining social interaction, independence and quality of life. No studies has tried to determine when DID becomes problematic for patients, and how reduction of DID through drug regimen modification will affect the daily activities of patients. HYPOTHESES. We believe that for patients with DID, (a) success of a particular task is dependent on the amplitude of the intended voluntary movement (signal), the amplitude of DID and the magnitude of other underlying symptoms (noise); and (b) improvement in how many daily activities one can perform is dependent on how drug regimen modification aiming to reduce DID will alter the signal-to-noise ratio. AIMS. (1) determine the which activities available to patients having DID; (2) assess the impact of a change of medication aiming at reducing DID on the activities of patients; (3) survey clinicians about their original goal when changing drug regimen, and verify whether the goals were reached; (4) test the ability of patients to evaluate the impact of DID on daily life activities. THE METHOD. Whole-body DID of patients will be recorded with a 15-sensor magnetic tracker system as they perform daily life motor tasks. Amplitude of DID will be measured in every limb at rest and during voluntary movement, and will be correlated with motor performance to determine the detrimental signal-to-noise ratio for each task. CLINICAL OUTCOME OF THIS RESEARCH. The proposed research will help us build a model of interaction between motor symptomatology and activities available to patients having DID. It will help determine how drug regimen modification to avoid DID affects activities of patients. The end goal is to develop better methods of evaluating treatment efficacy that focus on optimizing participation during daily life activities.

TitreApplicationTitle: The regulatory mechanism of spermatogonial stem cell proliferation and differentiation
Keywords-MotsClés: BASIC RESEARCH; CANCER SURVIVORS; CELL CULTURE; FATE DECISION CONTROL; GENETIC MODIFICATION; MALE FERTILITY PRESERVATION & RESTORATION; MALE REPRODUCTION; MOUSE; STEM CELLS; TRANSPLANTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Our research aims at elucidating the mechanism that regulates the survival, proliferation, and differentiation of sperm-producing stem cells, using the mouse as a model species. Spermatogenesis is the process to generate the male gamete, sperm, and continues for a lifetime after puberty. Sperm-producing stem cells are the foundation of this process. Our ability to understand the biology of these stem cells is crucial for preserving male fertility, producing healthy sperm, and maintaining the health of our children. For example, although the survival rate of cancer patients has significantly increased, anti-cancer treatments often cause infertility. This is particularly a serious problem for childhood cancer patients, because freeze-storing sperm is not an option for them to have their own children, due to their developmental immaturity. Therefore, encouraging the survival and function of stem cells during and after anti-cancer treatments will provide these patients with a great hope to establish their family in the post-cancer life. Our research will significantly contribute to realizing such a therapeutic strategy and to improving the quality of life of cancer survivors.

TitreApplicationTitle: Signal cross talk in lung injury and repair
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY; AIRWAY INJURY; ANIMAL PHYSIOLOGY; CELL MIGRATION; REPAIR AND REGENERATION; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TRANSGENIC MICE
Abstract-Résumé: If one cannot breath, nothing else matters. Through breath, many infectious or noxious substances that are inhaled can cause damage to the airways and the lung. If this injury cannot be properly repaired, it will lead to chronic lung disease. Therefore, knowledge regarding the repair and regeneration of the airway and the lung after injury is very important. However, the mechanisms of repair are not well known.  My lab has discovered a new gene/protein, called XB130. In cell culture, this protein has been shown to protect cells from death, and promote cell proliferation and migration. In animal studies, mice lacking this gene are more susceptible to airway and lung injury. We speculate that this protein, and related molecules, can reduce lung injury in living species by protecting cells from death, and promote epithelial repair through cell proliferation and migration. We will further study these important mechanisms using animal models and state-of-the-art cellular and molecular technologies.   New knowledge from these studies will help us to develop strategies to prevent or reduce lung injury, promote repair and avoid chronic lung diseases.

Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHIMIE; GENETIQUE; ONCOLOGIE; TRANSCRIPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Bourse de voyage de l'ACI. La nucleophosmine (NPM) est une proteine du noyau de la cellule, impliquee dans la division cellulaire. En effet, elle est situee dans une partie du noyau de la cellule appele nucleole et permet la separation des chromosomes lors de la mitose.  Depuis quelques annees, son role dans le developpement de la leucemie est fortement etudie. Ainsi, il a ete montre que dans plus d'un tiers des leucemies myeloides aigues (LMA), la proteine NPM est mutee. Cette proportion est augmentee a 60% dans le cas des leucemies dont le caryotype (nombre et nature des chromosomes) est normal. C'est pourquoi, il nous semble de plus en plus important de comprendre l'ensemble des roles de NPM, et les changements d'action engendres par les mutations de cette proteine. Dans cette etude, nous nous interessons essentiellement a deux mutations de NPM qui conduisent a la formation dans la cellule de deux proteines appelees NPM-MLF1 (mutant contenant une partie de la proteine MLF1 pour myeloide leukemia factor 1) et le mutant NPMc+ (qui conduit a une nouvelle localisation de NPM, hors du noyau, dans le cytoplasme de la cellule).  Nous cherchons a caracteriser les differentes voies de signalisation de la cellule, dans lesquelles NPM joue un role. Pour cela, nous voulons isoler et identifier les complexes de proteines dans lesquels on retrouve la nucleophosmine. Nous souhaitons egalement voir si NPM peut avoir une action dans la regulation de la stabilite du genome (ensemble des genes).  Dans un second temps, nous souhaitons observer l'evolution des complexes precedemment definis, en presence des formes mutees de NPM. Puis, nous essayerons de lier les changements observes au niveau moleculaire aux phenomenes connus en oncogenese.  Cette approche nous permettra a la fois de comprendre le role de NPM dans la cellule mais egalement son implication dans le developpement des LMA et nous permettra eventuellement de definir de nouvelles strategies de traitement.

TitreApplicationTitle: mTOR Regulation of CTL Responses

Abstract-Résumé: T cells that can recognize and destroy malignant cells are present in cancer patients, yet they fail to eradicate cancer. Constant efforts are made to understand how anticancer T cells operate and how their responses can be boosted. Rapamycin is an immunosuppressive drug that targets an important enzyme called mTOR inside mammalian cells, thereby altering numerous cellular functions. Rapamycin is routinely used in the clinic to weaken immune responses in transplanted organ recipients, but also paradoxically exhibits anticancer properties. In fact, rapamycin is approved for treatment of several types of cancer including advanced kidney cancer. Our preliminary results obtained in a mouse model indicate that rapamycin can surprisingly improve both the vigor and the quality of anticancer T cells. The proposed investigation will utilize mouse models to reveal how exactly rapamycin strengthens antitumor immunity. We will also explore whether the therapeutic benefit of rapamycin in kidney cancer patients can be linked to its positive effect(s) on T cells. These studies will advance our understanding of T cell responses in cancer and are likely to uncover new immune enhancing mechanisms of action for a family of drugs represented by rapamycin. This may in turn result in development of novel vaccination strategies for human cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neural control of posture and movement
Keywords-MotsClés: BASAL GANGLIA; LOCOMOTION; MOTOR CONTROL; POSTURE
Abstract-Résumé: Trying to pick up an object that is just out of reach an inherently dangerous activity as it potentially leads to an unstable body position ... and a fall. The same is true of most reaching movements to objects that are outside the support base provided by the feet. To prevent this unfortunate outcome, the central nervous system (CNS) has devised a strategy whereby adjustments of posture obligatorily anticipate the potential destabilisation produced by the movement and provide a stable platform upon which the movement can be superimposed. These postural adjustments are made unconsciously as part of the intention to move and prior experimental evidence, in part from patients with Parkinson's disease, suggests that the basal ganglia may be particularly involved in assuring the planning and coordination of the posture and the movement. One of the major aims of the current experimental program is to determine, by using an animal model, the involvement of the basal ganglia in assuring the coordination of posture and movement.

Abstract-Résumé: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are used for the treatment of pain and inflammation caused by arthritis and such other rheumatic diseases. Arthritis is not only a disease of the elderly, but children can also be affected by the disease. According to WHO there are 1.2 billion arthritis patients around the world, 51 million  in US and 4.2 million in Canada. About 30-50% of  the arthritis patients are chronic user of NSAIDs, but their use is restricted due to their side effects of the various bodily systems  including cardiovascular (CV)  system through unknown mechanisms. Recently, we have reported that a major blood pressure controlling mechanism in the body called renin angioten system (RAS) and its metabolic product peptides (cardiotoxic-ANGII; cardioprotective-ANG1-7) are disrupted in the rat heart under inflammatory condition. Studies have shown that most of cardiovascular disease have an inflammatory component involved in their pathogenesis.  Simultaneously,  the use of NSAIDs  for treatment of such inflammatory condition have also been reported to adversely influence the cardiac function. Thus, we aimed to assess if inflammation and NSAIDs can influence the RAS by altering the activity of ists enzymes (ACE and ACE2)and their active metabolic products (Ang-II, Ang1-7). We studied this in rat heart in a model of rheumatoid arthritis , using Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). We concluded that both inflammation and NSAIDs influnece the RAS by altering its component enzymes (ACE, ACE2). This results in a results in a significant increase in their metabolic product peptides namely; cardiotoxic(Ang-II)and cardioprotective(Ang-1-7). But for those NSAIDs that are know for their cardiotoxic potential the proportional(i.e. rofecoxib) the increase in cardiotoxic peptide (Ang-II) is more compared to the increase in cardioprotective peptide (Ang01-7). That might explains the increased risk of cardiotoxicity associated with the use of some NSAIDs.

Abstract-Résumé: Mitochondria are the organelles responsible for energy (ATP) production in most cell types.  As we age, there is evidence that mitochondrial function is impaired and that the concentration of mitochondria in muscle cells is reduced.  This can result in poor energy production, fatigue and decreased quality of life. However, the reasons for the reduced mitochondrial concentration and function are not well known.  In addition, evidence exists that exercise prevents this decrease, but the underlying mechanisms are not established.  These questions will be addressed in the current research proposal. TitreApplicationTitle: The structural basis for plasmid segregation by bacterial actins
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIN; BACTERIAL CYTOSKELETON; CRYO-EM; PLASMID MAINTENANCE; X-RAY CRYSTALLOGRAPHY
Abstract-Résumé: Historically, bacteria have been viewed as simple organisms with little internal organization, often described as mere 'bags of enzymes'. More recently we have come to appreciate the often elaborate schemes bacteria adopt to organize their internal spaces, including filamentous cytoskeletons that move and position objects within the cell. Like more complex organisms, bacteria use cytoskeletal filaments to move DNA and ensure that both daughter cells get a copy when the cell divides. This process of DNA segregation is important not only for the bacterial genome, but also for plasmids - small pieces of DNA that can be spread among bacteria and often encode bacterial toxins and virulence factors. Without active segregation by the cytoskeleton many plasmids are lost from bacterial populations. Understanding how the machinery of plasmid segregation works at the detailed molecular level will provide opportunities to effectively disrupt the process in combating pathogenic bacteria.    Here, we focus on segregation systems driven by bacterial actins, distant relatives of the cytoskeletal filament actin that plays roles in cell movement, cell division, intracellular organization, cell-cell interactions, and muscle contraction in higher organisms. Great progress has been made in recent years in characterizing bacterial actins both in vitro and in cells, revealing a surprising diversity of filament forms and dynamic behaviours. One of the central challenges now is to understand the detailed structures of the molecular machines that drive plasmid segregation. To achieve this, we propose work that integrates multiple structural approaches, allowing us to visualize in three dimensions single molecules, large molecular machines, and entire cells. This work will provide a framework for understanding both the diversity and the common features of plasmid segregation in these systems, as well as insight into more basic features of actin function.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relational ethics of the parental experience of congenital anomaly in the NICU
Keywords-MotsClés: CONGENITAL ANOMALIES; LIVED EXPERIENCE; NEONATOLOGY; PEDAGOGY; PHENOMENOLOGY; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; RELATIONAL ETHICS; TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Some babies' births are complicated by prematurity or other medical problems prompting admission to a newborn intensive care unit. A  number of these children are born with congenital anomalies. Certain anomalies may be identified during pregnancy, and others are not recognized until after birth. While anomalies may not outwardly appear visible, some occur along with striking changes in the physical appearance of a child. To parents, this appearance may be unexpected and distressing. Parents may experience a divisive bodily encounter with a child who appears so "other" than them, different from their body, yet also so clearly from them, a child of their body. Limited research has addressed this ethical experience from the perspective of the parent in spite of the fact that this relational encounter may shape subsequent parent-child interactions and moral decision-making.  The aim of the proposed study is to develop a rich understanding of the parental experience of the birth of a child with a visible congenital anomaly who requires hospital care in a newborn intensive care unit. This study will use a qualitative methodology to empirically explore a variety of such parental experiences. The final research texts and knowledge translation media, which present the study findings, will facilitate knowledge translation by developing understandings in lay and professional readers. As such, this study will effect the healthcare provider to become more understanding of the experiences of parents who are faced with the birth of a child with a visible congenital anomaly. Ultimately, this knowledge is fundamental to the reflective ethical practice of the various health discipline practitioners responsible for the infant patient and family.
