TitreApplicationTitle: Cadherin Adhesion Complexes in Cocaine Addiction
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; BETA-CATENIN; CADHERIN-BASED ADHESION; COCAINE; CONDITIONED PLACE PREFERENCE; DOPAMINERGIC NEURONS; ELECTRON MICROSCOPY; SYNAPSE PLASTICITY; TRANSGENIC MICE; VENTRAL TEGMENTAL NUCLEUS
Abstract-Résumé: Researchers believe that drugs of abuse act on the part of the brain which functions to regulate our experience of pleasure and reward. According to researchers, drug addiction is a type of memory disorder - but instead of memory loss, drugs of abuse "hijack" the reward circuit in the brain and promote the learning of drug-related behaviours with such efficiency that these behaviours become compulsive.  Similar to learning in other regions of the brain, this learning is mediated by changes at the level of the "synapse".  Synapses are specialized junctions where nerve cells communicate with one another. This type of learning occurs in all mammals, so why is it that some people are more prone to addiction than others? Although the exact mechanisms are unknown, experts widely agree that some people are genetically vulnerable to developing addiction disorders. Cadherin adhesion molecules are great candidate proteins that may regulate the predisposition to drug addiction.  Indeed, cadherins are 1) expressed in the reward circuitry of the brain, 2) important regulators of learning and memory, and 3) mutated in people with addiction disorders. We will examine the involvement of the cadherins in mediating drug-induced changes in synapses as well as in addiction behaviours.

TitreApplicationTitle: Duration of the antiviral response: phospho-dependent regulation mechanisms
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL SIGNALING; CYTOKINES; INNATE IMMUNITY; INTERFERON; NUCLEIC ACID SENSOR; POST-TRANSLATIONAL MIDIFICATIONS; PROTEIN PHOSPHATASE; RESOLUTION; VIRUS INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: The body's first line of defense against a virus infection is to trigger an adapted immune response in order to limit replication and spread of the virus. However, there is a fine line between enough response to limit the virus-associated disease and too much response that can cause secondary illnesses in the individual (host). Indeed, an uncontrolled response in term of intensity or duration is harmful to the host, possibly leading to disease such as chronic inflammation and a response whereby the body begins to attack its own cells, known as autoimmune disease. Consequently to prevent this, the strength and duration of the immune response need to be tightly regulated to achieve the best balance between efficiently fighting the infection and the generation of adverse side effects for the host's survival. Although much improvement has been achieved in our understanding of how the response is initiated, far much less is known about how this response is sustained or resolved. Our research endeavor is aimed at characterizing the intracellular mechanisms allowing the host's cells to positively or negatively regulate the duration of the immune response to a safe level. We believe that our research will help design new drugs agents, which ultimately could reduce the cost of virus-induced secondary diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: The descending control of locomotion by dopamine in the adult mouse
Keywords-MotsClés: CATECHOLAMINES; CENTRAL PATTERN GENERATORS; DOPAMINE; MONOAMINES; MOVEMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last decade impressive advances have been made in our understanding of spinal cord injury (SCI) and identification of possible therapies. One of the success stories in treatment of spinal cord injury has been the adoption of active locomotor-based rehabilitation. Perhaps the most publicized case was that of Christopher Reeve, who showed a recovery of sensorimotor function following an extensive aquatherapy and assisted cycling exercise regimen. While the underlying mechanisms of Reeve's recovery and that of others using treadmill based therapies may never be fully known, a consensus has emerged that part of the recovery is due to activity-driven reorganization of spinal circuits. These spinal circuits are essential for producing many motor behaviors including walking. Despite the success of these programs, patients do plateau in their recovery over time, and indeed activity-dependent rehabilitation does not work for some patients. Rehabilitation appears to work because it provides an excitatory stimulus to spinal cord circuits, allowing networks to be expressed, and remodeled. Our work and that of others has established that spinal circuits can be awakened by application of exogenous drugs or by electrical stimulation of nerves. Another approach is direct activation of descending pathways projecting to the brain. Our work explores this issue by activating dopamine pathways to the spinal cord. We show that centres within the brain that contain dopamine are particularly effective in activating locomotor activity. This raises the possibility that stimulation of these dopamine centres could facilitate locomotion in patients with movement disorders.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effect of a six week exercise training program on proteolytic enzyme activity, ROS generation and autophagy in the white gastrocnemius and left ventricle of normotensive and hypertensive rats
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS; AUTOPHAGY; CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE; HYPERTENSION; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; SKELETAL MUSCLE
Abstract-Résumé: Hypertension is a cardiovascular disease associated with increased cell death and proteolytic enzyme activity in both skeletal and cardiac muscle. Autophagy is a degradative system that plays an essential role in muscle health and has been shown to influence cell death processes. Although acute exercise can alter markers of autophagy, little is known about the effects of exercise training on autophagy in healthy or diseased states. The purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of exercise training on markers of autophagy, proteolytic activity, and ROS levels in white gastrocnemius (WG) and left ventricle (LV) of Wistar Kyoto (WKY) and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR. Male WKY and SHR were assigned to a sedentary condition or exercise consisting of treadmill running for 6 wks.In the WG muscle of SHR, significantly greater LC3I protein and a lower LC3II/I ratio was observed compared to WKY rats. Exercise training did not alter the WG LC3II/I protein ratio, a common marker of autophagosome production; however,exercise training significantly upregulated factors contributing to the regulation of autophagy such as Beclin,LC3,and p62 mRNA and reduced ATG7 and Beclin protein levels. Following exercise training, the proteolytic enzyme activity of caspase-3 and cathepsin was lower and a trend towards lower ROS production was observed in the WG. In the LV, SHR had a significantly lower LC3II/I protein ratio and a greater accumulation of p62 protein compared to WKY rats suggesting increased autophagy. Training increased both Beclin and p62 mRNA levels in the LV; however, no change in the LC3II/I protein ratio was observed. Exercise training lowered LV caspase-3 and calpain activity, as well as tended to reduce cathepsin activity and ROS production. Together, these results suggest that autophagy is altered in the SHR muscle and heart, and exercise training can alter upstream regulators of autophagy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Do EMRs in Primary care Improve Care and outcomes? (EPIC)
Keywords-MotsClés: ELECTRONIC MEDICAL RECORD (EMR); PRIMARY CARE RESEARCH; QUALITY OF CARE INDICATORS; QUALITY OF CARE MEASURES
Abstract-Résumé: Canada has historically been behind other industrialized countries in terms of implementing electronic medical records (EMRs) but in recent years significant resources have been put towards the uptake of EMRs particularly in primary care. Yet, whether EMRs improve patient health and healthcare delivery has not been clearly established. We propose a program of research to examine the question, "Do EMRs in primary care improve quality of patient care?" This program of research will develop methods to accurately measure quality both within the EMR and in administrative data, determine the if the EMR, physician or patient factors lead to better quality of care and test if quality of care can be improved with EMR tools. This program of research will utilize the unique resource of the Electronic Medical Record Administrative data Linked Database (EMRALD) at the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES). EMRs contains detailed clinical information but are not necessarily readily accessible for analysis whereas as administrative data (hospitalization information, physician billing and drug benefit data) is much broader in scope and covers the entire population of a province or even the country. The environment of full primary care EMR data linked to administrative data is not available anywhere else in Canada. This program of research will expand the capacity for doing health services and health informatics research in the primary care setting by bring together the methods and experience developed with EMRALD in Ontario with the theoretical frameworks (EMR adoption, circle of care) and technologic skills and tools developed by the eHealth Observatory in BC. An additional goal of this program of research is to provide an excellent training ground for students in the disciplines of health informatics and primary care research, both of which are rapidly developing fields of research in Canada.

Abstract-Résumé: Hydatidiform mole (HM) is a human pregnancy with no embryo. The paradoxical nature of this condition has fascinated and puzzled scientists in all civilizations since the time of Hippocrates. In western countries, HM occurs once in every 600 pregnancies, but at higher incidences in developing and underdeveloped countries. Among women with one HM, 1-6% will develop a second mole and 10-25% will have a second reproductive wastage, mostly as a spontaneous abortion. Molar pregnancies are the most common trophoblastic tumours, usually benign, but may degenerate into malignant choriocarcinomas and lead to the death of the patients. My group initiated genetic research on familial recurrent HM, identified and characterized the functions of the first known gene, NLRP7, for this condition. Patients with this condition are now offered DNA testing and counselled for future pregnancies. The aim of this proposal is to complete the validation of two identified genes during the last funding period and elucidate their functions in order to provide help for more patients with this condition

Keywords-MotsClés: GENE EXPRESSION; INSULIN-RESISTANCE; INTESTINAL LIPOPROTEIN METABOLISM; NUTRITION; PROTEOMIC
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes and pre-diabetes are metabolic disorders affecting more than 15% of the world's population and their prevalences are on the increase due mainly to more sedentary lifestyles associated with rising obesity rates and aging of the population. Because diabetes and pre-diabetes are so closely associated with major health problems such as high blood pressure, high blood cholesterol and cardiovascular disease (CVD), they have a huge impact on the health care costs of our society. Major efforts should therefore be undertaken to tackle from a societal perspective this critical problem. Although elevated blood cholesterol levels observed in diabetes and pre-diabetes have largely been attributed to overproduction by the liver, recent studies from our group have indicated that the small intestine also contributes significantly to elevated blood cholesterol levels. Nutritional guidelines currently focus on substitution of saturated fatty acids (SFA) by polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) and this is largely based on the evidence that consumption of PUFA in place of SFA reduces CVD risk. Recent data suggest that PUFA may exert beneficial effects on CVD risk by reducing intestinal cholesterol production but no studies have examined this issue in patients with diabetes or pre-diabetes. This study will allow us to investigate whether substitution of SFA by PUFA could reduce intestinal cholesterol production in patients with pre-diabetes. We will also examine the impact of PUFA on the expression of the major genes and proteins involved in the regulation of intestinal cholesterol metabolism. Identification of therapeutic strategies using non-pharmacologic agents such as PUFA is likely to lead to significant advances in our attempts to reduce CVD risk in this vulnerable population.

Keywords-MotsClés: DENDRITIC CELLS/PHAGOCYTES; EPIGENETICS; INNATE LYMPHOCYTES; MICROBIOME; MOUSE MODELS OF DISEASE; MUCOSAL IMMUNE RESPONSES; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; PATTERN RECOGNITION RECEPTORS; PHAGOCYTE CONTROL OF ILCS; TYROSINE KINASE
Abstract-Résumé: Development of inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs) is the result of multiple factors, including inappropriate immune responses to normal gut bacteria, and disruption of the intestinal epithelium (the barrier between gut and surrounding tissues) leading to bacterial escape. Distinct populations of immune cells govern the nature/magnitude of protective immunity in the gut. Recent studies suggest that previously unrecognized populations of cells called innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) might be important in dampening the immune responses leading to IBD. However, researchers currently have a rudimentary understanding of the physiological roles of ILCs in intestinal health/disease. Understanding how ILCs contribute to inflammation in the gut promises to uncover new and exciting approaches toward controlling IBD.        We recently discovered that a protein present in immune cells, called Lyn, is key in indirectly activating ILCs (through dendritic cells (DCs), inducing them to secrete a protective factor IL-22.  We also discovered that Lyn increases barrier function during gut inflammation.  Using sophisticated mouse models, we showed that loss of Lyn led to an increase in the development of colitis (a form of intestinal inflammation) while enhancing Lyn-dependent signals in the immune system was protective against colitis.       Here we propose to use Lyn loss-and gain-of function approaches together with mouse intestinal inflammatory disease models to determine the biochemical mechanisms underlying the control of DCs and/or ILCs by Lyn, elucidate the roles played by the different subsets of ILCs, and understand how Lyn controls barrier integrity, thereby better understanding how Lyn regulates IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improving Glucocorticoid Therapy in Leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH; FATTY ACID OXIDATION; GLUCOCORTICOIDS; GLYCOLYSIS; LEUKEMIA; MOUSE MODELS; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; PPAR; PROTEOMICS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia or CLL is the most common type of leukemia in Canada. This blood cancer cannot be cured with chemotherapy. Glucocorticoids, or steroids, are another form of treatment that can help patients whose tumor cells develop resistance to chemotherapy. Unfortunately CLL cells can develop ways to resist steroids as well. Dr. Spaner's group has found that steroids act by turning off the ability of a tumor cell to produce the energy it needs to grow from sugar and protein. If the tumor cells use fat to generate their energy, or if they turn up their ability to burn sugar or protein, then they become resistant to steroids. If they are prevented from burning fat, or their ability to burn sugar or protein is decreased, then they can again be killed by steroids.       In this grant, Dr. Spaner will try to determine the most effective ways to improve the results of steroid therapy. He will compare a number of chemicals that are able to block energy generation by leukemia cells in a test tube and in mice in order to determine one that can be used to develop a treatment for patients. If these studies are successful, they may result in better treatments for CLL that may also work for other cancers.

Abstract-Résumé: Bone is a hard tissue that protects internal organs, helps locomotion and serves as a reservoir for essential mineral ions required for proper body function. Bone is a living tissue that undergoes a constant process of growth and resorption, called remodeling. In health individuals, this process is tightly balanced. However, any disruption in this equilibrium results in serious health concerns. A relative increase in bone resportion causes the disease osteoporosis, while an increase in bone formation causes the disease osteopetrosis.  The long term goal of this proposal is to understand the mechanism that regulates the equilibrium between bone resorption and bone formation.  Recent studies have pointed out that bone activity is probably regulated by the subconscious part of the brain, however, it is still not well understood the mechanisms behind this regulation. In the current proposal we plan to investigate how a series of signals generated from the brain, that are well known to regulate food digestion, sleep and heart rate, might as well be responsible for controlling the strength of our bones. By understanding this process we will be able to develop a new family of therapies for osteoporosis, and new drugs to accelerate the healing of bone fractures. In fact our preliminary experiments have already discovered two drugs are able to make our bones stronger and heal faster by stimulating these novel signaling pathways.

Abstract-Résumé: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a chronic progressive systemic inflammatory condition, leads to considerable pain and joint destruction, diminished function and disability. RA is associated with excess morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular complications. Evidence suggests that common pro-inflammatory cytokines, which are produced in the body in response to the disease, are involved in the development and progression of RA as well as other inflammatory diseases such as atherosclerosis. In the body, renin-angiotensin system (RAS) regulates blood pressure and fluid balance and contributes to the inflammatory response in the vascular wall. The activation of RAS by inflammation plays an important role in the physiology and pathophysiology of cardiovascular system. An important therapeutic approach in dealing with cardiovascular complications of RA, therefore, is to mitigate the process of activation of RAS. We have focused on a therapeutic intervention that may prevent cardiovascular events by inhibiting the activation of RAS caused by experimental arthritis. Glucosamine is a naturally occurring aminosugar that in our preliminary studies appears to exert anti-inflammatory effects in the heart through the RAS. We showed that inflammation activates RAS in rat heart and increases its cardiotoxic metabolites and disrupts the physiological balance of the RAS system. Administration of glucosamine, however, restored the normal balance and proved to be cardioprotective by decreasing cardiotoxic and increasing cardioprotective metabolites of RAS.

TitreApplicationTitle: T follicular helper cell differentiation and function in immunity and infection
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIBODY; CHEMOKINES; CYTOKINES; HUMORAL IMMUNITY TO INFECTION; INTEGRINS; PARASITIC INFECTION; T HELPER CELL DIFFERENTIATION; VIRAL INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Infections ranging from viruses to parasites elicit vigorous antibody responses critical for host protection. In fact, vaccine efficacy is defined by the generation of robust pathogen-specific antibodies. These effective humoral immune responses depend on white blood cells called helper T cells to directly interact with and instruct other immune cells called B cells to produce antibodies that neutralize pathogens. However, important questions remain as to how these immune cells orchestrate these responses effectively. This research proposal applies animal models of infection combined with cell biology and genetic manipulation to advance our understanding of how leukocytes work together to fight disease and generate protection from infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Investigating a motor skill intervention for preschool age children with autism spectrum disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER; CHILDREN; DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITY; EARLY INTERVENTION; FUNDAMENTAL MOVEMENT SKILLS; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; MOTOR DEVELOPMENT; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: The physical inactivity of children is a public health crisis that has been linked to a number of chronic diseases including obesity. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a common development disability that is characterized by delays in communication, social reciprocity, and repetitive behaviours; it is often associated with intellectual disability. Children with ASD have significant delays in their fine and gross motor skills which may inhibit them from engaging in active play; thus, increasing their risk of inactivity. Although little is known about the variables that contribute to physical activity (PA) in children, particularly in children with disabilities, potential factors include sport involvement, lack of transportation and finances. Many of these factors known to influence PA are not modifiable. Proficiency in fundamental movement skills (FMS) is arguably one of the most important predictors of PA in children because it is modifiable - FMS can be improved through intervention, finances are not likely to change. FMS are the basic movement skills that are essential to the future acquisition of the more complex skills required in games and recreational physical activities. Research has clearly demonstrated that FMS competency is positively related to PA yet, children with ASD experience significant delays in their FMS; thus, early intervention is of utmost importance. The purpose of this study is to examine the effects of a FMS intervention on PA levels and social behaviour in preschool-aged children with ASD. Participants will engage in a 12-hour intervention over the course of 6 or 12 weeks depending on group assignment. Participants' FMS, PA, and social behaviour will be measured multiple times throughout the study: pre- and post-intervention and at a follow-up point. The findings of this study will fill an important gap in the literature and contribute to future wide-scale interventions targeting FMS competency and physical inactivity in children with ASD.

TitreApplicationTitle: S-sulfhydration regulation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: Nitric oxide (NO) is a main regulatory determinant of vascular homeostasis. Endothelial NO synthase (eNOS), the main NO-producing enzyme in the vascular walls, can be regulated by posttranslational modifications, such as phosphorylation and S-nitrosylation. In the present study, we found that H2S stimulates NO production via S-sulfhydration modification of eNOS. Treatment with dithiothreitol abolished H2S-mediated eNOS S-sulfhydration and NO production in endothelial cells. GSNO (NO-donor) reduced the S-sulfhydration effect of H2S on eNOS, while GSNO alone had little effect on eNOS S-sulfhydration. Treatment with NaHS and GSNO has divergent effect on S-sulfhydration and S-nitrosylation of eNOS. Furthermore, incubation of endothelial cell lysates with NO donor decreased eNOS dimer stability but increased the monomer formation. Inhibition of H2S production by DL-propargylglycine decreased the dimer formation of eNOS in endothelial cells. The ratio of eNOS monomer to functional dimer in aortic tissue was significantly higher in wild type mice than in CSE-knockout which has a targeted deletion of the CSE gene, the major H2S- producing enzyme in vascular tissues. In addition, incubation of endothelial cell lysates with NO and H2S together restored the stability of the eNOS dimer. Mutation of eNOS protein at cysteine 443 eliminated eNOS S-sulfhydration and S-nitrosylation as well as dimer formation. In summary, H2S induces eNOS S-sulfhydration and causes eNOS dimer stabilization in endothelial cells. H2S may be a valuable therapeutic agent for endothelial dysfunction and increases the functional eNOS stability in vascular tissues.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functions of Hedgehog-GLI-dependent signaling in stromal cells during normal and malformed mammalian kidney development.
Keywords-MotsClés: DEVELOPMENTAL GENETICS; HEDGEHOG SIGNALING; NEPHROGENESIS; RENAL DEVELOPMENT; RENAL MALFORMATION; URETEROPELVIC JUNCTION
Abstract-Résumé: The kidney consists of hundreds of thousands of functional units termed nephrons. Nephrons empty urine into a central space, the pelvis, which is connected to the ureter via the ureteropelvic junction. Formation of these structures is complete by the end of human pregnancy. Kidney function after birth is dependent on a critical number of nephrons and a patent ureteropelvic junction. Kidney malformation, the major cause of childhood renal failure, frequently involves abnormal nephron formation, low nephron number and obstruction of the ureteropelvic junction. Despite the contribution of kidney formation to health and disease, the causes of kidney malformation are poorly defined and no specific treatments exist. The goal of our research is to define molecule mechanisms that control formation of the normal and malformed kidney. We have discovered that a protein family, termed Hedgehogs, control a poorly characterized population of kidney cells, the stromal cells, and that stromal cells control nephron number and the integrity of the ureteropelvic junction. In this proposal we will test our hypothesis that Hedgehog-dependent stromal cell differentiation controls nephron number and formation of the ureteropelvic junction. We propose three Aims.  First, we will identify the molecules within stromal cells that respond to Hedgehogs and which medicate stromal cell function. Second, we will determine how Hedgehog-mediated signals influence the choice that cells make to become nephrons versus stromal cells during kidney development. Third, we will characterize a novel population of cells, resembling stromal cells, that can block the ureteropelvic junction and determine the contribution of these cells to human ureteropelvic junction obstruction. Together, our studies will elucidate the functions of an under-evaluated cell population in the fetal kidney and will provide a basis for the development of treatments aimed at treating kidney malformation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Perception - language relationships in autism
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE; COMPLEXITY; FMRI; PERCEPTION
Abstract-Résumé: Whereas most persons within the autistic spectrum present a major speech delay and/or impairment, other individuals, known as Asperger syndrome, exhibit early language development while presenting similar social and repetitive symptoms. Better understanding this puzzling pattern of language performance in autism spectrum is particularly important, because communication deficits are the major predictor of adaptive outcome in autism. New results from our laboratory suggest an explanation of this puzzle through a common brain plasticity mechanism, which are the way our brain compensated for an injury or a deficit. In autistic people with language impairment, speech would be mainly processed through an enhanced functioning of perception. This would result in language impairment and superior visuospatial and auditory performance. In contrast, in those with Asperger's syndrome most information would be processed through an overextension of language-related processes, resulting in language, but not visuo-spatial or auditory performance peaks. We will therefore test the hypothesis that the two presentations within the autistic spectrum, autism and Asperger, are the result of a common mechanism of brain plasticity, applied to two different domains. This will be done by comparing the perceptual and language performance of autistic children with and without language impairment, and compare them with language impaired non autistic children and typical children without autism. We will also use visual and auditory tasks and fMRI in adults autistic participants with and without an history of language impairment. This will allow detecting how the brain regions typically devoted to perception and language are differently overextended in these two groups. Beyond the development of future educational techniques of language based on language of perceptual strengths, this project, if successful, will represent a major step in our understanding of brain mechanisms associated to autism.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of ALDH1A3 in breast cancer progression and cancer stem cell biology
Keywords-MotsClés: ALDEHYDE DEHYDROGENASE 1A3; BREAST CANCER; CANCER STEM CELLS; RETINOIC ACID SIGNALLING; THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: We need to understand why cancer spreads and comes back years later after treatment. This will help treat cancer patients more effectively. Tumors are made up of different cancer cells. Of all the tumor cells, cancer stem cells (CSCs) have the greatest ability to form new tumors and are also very hard to kill. By understanding the biology of CSCs, we will gain new insight into how cancer develops and be able to make new anti-cancer drugs that kill CSCs better, decreasing the chance that the patient's cancer will return years later.  Previously, we found that breast CSCs make an enzyme called aldehyde dehydrogenase 1A3 (ALDH1A3). Breast cancer patients with higher levels of ALDH1A3 in their tumors have more aggressive cancer and are less likely to survive in the long term. We have new data showing that ALDH1A3 also drives breast cancer tumor growth and promotes the spread of the cancer by producing retinoic acid (RA). Based on these observations, we propose the following research aims to determine the role of the ALDH1A3/RA pathway in breast cancer progression and CSC biology and if we can treat cancer with drugs that stop ALDH1A3 function. In Aim 1, we will to determine how the ALDH1A3/RA pathway drives breast cancer growth and spread by identifying the other key upstream and downstream factors in the ALDH1A3/RA pathway.  In Aim 2, we will determine how the ALDH1A3/RA pathway regulates CSC growth and affects their ability make new tumors. Finally, in Aim 3, we will test if drugs that block ALDH1A3 function in cancer cells stop breast tumor growth and kill CSCs.  This proposal will use laboratory assays, animal models and breast cancer patient tumor samples to understand why breast CSCs have the greatest ability to make new tumors and spread the cancer, and how the ALDH1A3/RA pathway contributes to this process. This will make a major impact in both understanding cancer biology and in devising new strategies for more effective treatments for cancer patients

TitreApplicationTitle: Biology and pathobiology of alpha-synuclein
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN; LEWY BODIES; NEURODEGENERATION; NEURONS; PARKINSON DISEASE; PRION; PROTEIN AGGREGATION; PROTEIN DEGRADATION; PROTEIN SECRETION; PROTEIN UPTAKE
Abstract-Résumé: Alpha-Synuclein (alpha-syn) is a major protein in neurons that is implicated in Parkinson disease (PD). We have identified high molecular weight protein complexes that contain alpha-syn in rodents and human brains and have identified some components of these complexes. Because these complexes represent an important link to the pathological alpha-syn aggregates that build up in PD brains, it is essential that we investigate the intermediary biochemical changes that cause them to become impaired and dysfunctional. Recent studies also implicate the transfer of misfolded alpha-syn from one neuron to another as a major culprit in the spread of PD pathology such as Lewy bodies. It is possible that oxidative stress and dysfunctional protein breakdown pathways alter the balance of alpha-syn binding partners causing premature disassembly or accumulation of aberrant and toxic complexes, which can then be transferred to adjacent neurons and propagate the neurotoxicity. Therefore we will develop a novel system to measure the neuron-to-neuron movement of alpha-syn and also test whether aggregated alpha-syn can be used to seed pathology in otherwise healthy tissue.

TitreApplicationTitle: Self-esteem and physical health in older adults: A longitudinal analysis
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING RESEARCH; CORTISOL; DEPRESSION; DEVELOPMENTAL RESEARCH; HEALTH OUTCOMES; INFLAMMATORY MARKERS; PHYSICAL FUNCTIONING; PHYSICAL HEALTH; SELF-ESTEEM; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Levels and variability in self-esteem are important personality factors influencing both psychological and physical health. Research has shown that self-esteem can be associated with psychological benefits such as reduced negative emotions and stress. Negative emotions and stress represent risk factors for disturbances in individuals' biological systems and physical health. In fact, if people experience stress, self-esteem has been shown to buffer associated effects on increases in cortisol secretion. It may prevent exposure to negative impacts of a person's immune functioning. This biological dysregulation is likely to increase older adults' vulnerability to developing a variety of age-related diseases. Self-esteem could protect physical health among people who experience stressful life events. Furthermore, research suggests that older adulthood is associated with a linear decline in self-esteem. This possibility will be investigated through analysis of data from a longitudinal study of older adults who have been followed over a period of 8 years (Montreal Aging and Health Study). It is hypothesized that declines in self-esteem will predict biological dysregulation of immune systems and increased physical health problems. The results from this research project are likely to discover mechanisms of successful aging that could be targeted in clinical interventions. It may thus contribute to improving quality of life among the elderly population and reduce associated costs for public health services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the impact of responsibility beliefs on reassurance seeking in OCD
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; COGNITION; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL TREATMENT; EMOTION; MENTAL HEALTH; MOTIVATION; OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE DISORDER; REASSURANCE SEEKING; RESPONSIBILITY BELIEFS; SOCIAL IMPACT
Abstract-Résumé: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a mental health problem which can have deleterious consequences for interpersonal and mental well-being. Excessive reassurance seeking (ERS) is thought of as seeking confirmation from others that an action has been performed or that a negative outcome will not occur, despite having received this information previously. Researchers have suggested that the function of ERS in OCD is to gain certainty that one is safe from potential harm, or to allay feelings of anxiety by reducing the perceived threat or by increasing the coping resources an individual believes s/he has, usually involving seeking the support of others to reduce feelings of personal responsibility. This study thus seeks to examine the influence of inflated responsibility beliefs on ERS behaviour in OCD. 120 participants will be randomly assigned to receive either low or high feedback ambiguity, and to participate in the study either with a trusted individual or with a confederate. Participants will be told that they are helping to validate a new biohazard scanner, and will be asked to place their hand in a container of liquid in which a fictitious contaminant has been placed. Participants will be given the opportunity to wash their hands in the laboratory kitchen, and will then be asked to place their hand in a scanner. Participants in the high ambiguity condition will receive feedback that there is a 50% chance that the contaminant remains, while those in the low ambiguity condition will be told that there is only a 2% chance. Participants will have the opportunity to discuss the situation for 3 minutes either with their trusted person, or with the confederate. The results of this study will clarify how ERS changes when participants are in the company of significant others vs. relative strangers in clear and ambiguous situations, which may have implications for generating effective targets for the treatment of responsibility and ERS during interventions for OCD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dopamine regulation of clock gene expression in the dorsal striatum; Relevance to Parkinson's disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS; CLOCK GENE EXPRESION; DOPAMINE; DORSAL STRIATUM; DOUBLE IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; GLUTAMATE; NEUROTOXIC CORTICAL LESIONS; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; PER2; SLEEP-WAKE DISTURBANCES
Abstract-Résumé: Circadian rhythms are biological processes which influence behaviour, physiology and health and which help an organism adapt to its environment.  These rhythms are disrupted in many clinical conditions, including depression, drug abuse and Parkinson's disease, and in natural processes such as aging.  To better understand the underlying causes of circadian dysregulation in these populations, it is important to first understand the fundamental mechanisms which help to regulate them. Despite the complex array of conditions which can lead to disruption in circadian rhythms, a potential common mechanism that is being investigated is dopamine regulation of the circadian clock genes PER1 and PER2.  It has been found that by reducing dopamine in the dorsal striatum, a similar reduction of PER1 and PER2 expression also occurs.  Initial information is suggesting a role of a specific type of dopamine receptor, the D2 type receptor, for being responsible for this relationship.  For my MSc project, I propose to define more specifically the type of cells involved in clock gene function in the dorsal striatum and how dopamine interacts with signals coming from the cortex in order to regulate these clock genes.  I plan to do double immunohistochemistry to identify the cell type expressing PER2 and compare the differences in PER2 expression when dopamine and/or cortical inputs are removed.  I hope that my findings will lead to new insight on sleep-wake disturbances in diseases such as Parkinson's.

TitreApplicationTitle: Differences in Immune Reactivity to Respiratory Challenges in Asthmatic Patients with and without Panic Disorder
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; ASTHMA; BEHAVIORAL MEDICINE; HEALTH PSYCHOLOGY; IMMUNE SYSTEM; PANIC DISORDER; RESPIRATORY SYSTEM; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Asthma is a chronic airway disease characterized by the walls of the airway narrowing and having inflammation (the process which normally repairs damaged cells in the body but can be dangerous when it goes wrong, as in asthma). This condition affects over 8% of Canadians over the age of 12, with more than half of those people having difficulty controlling their asthma symptoms, despite many using asthma medication. The reasons for this lack of control remain poorly understood. Patients with asthma tend to have more mental health problems (e.g., psychiatric disorders) than the general population and these kinds of problems have been shown to worsen asthma symptoms. For example, panic disorder (PD) is up to six times more common in asthmatics than in the general population. This high rate is thought to be in part due to the fact that asthma and panic attacks have similar characteristic symptoms: anxiety, difficulty breathing, and chest tightness. While this similarity may cause patients and their doctors to misinterpret the nature of an attack (be it asthma or panic), it is also possible that panic attacks may trigger asthma attacks. It is possible that that a sudden stressful event, such as a panic attack, may cause an increase in inflammation, thus worsening the person's asthma. Identifying the links between panic and asthma attacks may lead to better and quicker treatment, and may help doctors distinguish asthma-related and PD-related attacks more effectively, which is particularly important in the Emergency Department. This work may also lead to the development of tools for patients, ultimately helping them to better understand their symptoms as asthma-related or not, which would in turn help them to make better medical decisions (e.g., choosing to go to the Emergency Department or not) and lead to reductions in unnecessary medical use.

TitreApplicationTitle: Sleep, Autonomic Dysfunction, and Childhood Obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: CARDIOVASCULAR; DAILY ROUTINE; HEART RATE VARIABILITY; OBESITY/OVERWEIGHT; PEDIATRICS; SLEEP
Abstract-Résumé: Childhood obesity is a major public concern that is associated with a number of health issues, including cardiovascular and metabolic dysfunctions. Shorter sleep duration has been linked to the development of obesity in cross-sectional and prospective studies, as well as through meta-analytic research, yet the underlying mechanisms between the two have yet to be identified. One possible mechanism is through heart rate variability (HRV), an indicator of autonomic nervous system functioning measured through non-invasive ECG recordings. The aim of the present study is to compare the links between obesity, sleep, and HRV in two large samples of Quebec children aged 10-12. The first is a population-based sample of children in Quebec, and the second is a cohort of youth at risk for developing obesity identified as having one biological parent who is obese. Each group completed detailed questionnaires asking about their sleep, and had anthropometric and physiological data measured by trained research assistants. Data analysis will be conducted to determine if there is a link between obesity and HRV across both groups, if this link is influenced by short total sleep time or disrupted circadian regularity, and whether the relation is stronger in the cohort at risk for obesity. The results will provide information to help scientists better understand the relation between sleep and obesity in youth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Es-x in lipid metabolism

Abstract-Résumé: Obesity is strongly associated with excessive fat storage in multiple tissues including the liver, where this fat deposition leads to abnormal liver functions and risk for cardiovascular disease and diabetes. Increased liver fat deposition stimulates the export of particles that carry bad cholesterol (LDL). We have shown that a protein called Es-x plays an important role in regulating the cholesterol export from the intestine and from the liver into blood. We have developed mice that are deficient in this protein and have shown that these animals have more harmful blood lipid levels and are less protected from fat accumulation in the liver and adipose tissue and have impaired insulin action. Therefore, increasing the function of this protein would seem beneficial in treatment of obesity-related metabolic complications. In the proposed research we plan to investigate the mechanisms by which Es-x regulates fat absorption, and fat deposition, and research novel animal models in effort to gain more information about this protein. This new information will be important not only in understanding of the protective role of this protein in fat metabolism but also in the development of therapeutics for the treatment obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Rescue of diabetic sensory neurodegeneration through insulin signaling
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETIC POLYNEUROPATHY; EXPERIMENTAL DIABETES; INSULIN; NEURODEGENERATION; SENSORY NEURONS
Abstract-Résumé: Diabetes mellitus is rising in prevalence worldwide. The development of polyneuropathy, or damage to nerves, is a challenging complication of diabetes, noted in up to 50% of persons with diabetes mellitus. This condition, currently irreversible, results in loss of sensation, pain and increases the risk of lower limb amputation in patients. Our lab works on experimental models of diabetic polyneuropathy in mice and rats to understand how this condition develops and how it might be reversed. In this grant, we build on exciting findings that insulin, acting directly on neurons can encourage them to regrow and repair themselves from diabetic damage. This effect of insulin does not depend on blood glucose levels and in part involves a novel form of direct delivery to insulin receptors within the nervous system: intranasal insulin administration. We propose to enhance insulin's benefits by adding insulin sensitizing agents, by combining insulin with newly discovered insulin-related peptides, by removing barriers to insulin actions on neurons (reversing insulin 'resistance') and by discovering how diabetes and insulin alter gene function in nerve cells. Our goal is to identify how these approaches might lead to effective treatment of polyneuropathy in humans.

TitreApplicationTitle: Influenza and acute lung injury: priming, platelets and permeability
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LUNG INJURY; BACTERIAL SUPERINFECTION; INFLUENZA; LUNG ENDOTHELIUM; LUNG EPITHELIUM; MICROVASCULAR LEAK; PLATELET ADHESION; PRIMING; STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS; VASCULAR STABILITY
Abstract-Résumé: Seasonal infections with the influenza virus cause more than just a few days off work. In some patients, a secondary bacterial pneumonia can occur, triggering leaking of the blood vessels in the lung and resulting in respiratory failure. In other patients, such as the elderly or in those with a poor immune system, the virus itself can cause an overwhelming pneumonia, leading to respiratory failure even in the absence of any bacterium. In both settings, patients develop leaky blood vessels in their lungs, leading to filling of the lungs with fluid and preventing gas exchange. How influenza affects the lungs' blood vessels to make them leak is not known. In this application, we propose that infection with influenza, even at a low dose, alters or primes the lung blood vessels, making them much leakier when they are subsequently exposed to bacteria. We also suggest that high titers of the virus, such as may occur in the setting of a deficient immune system, can cause blood clots to form in the lung. These blood clots then cause the lung's blood vessels to leak. Other infected cells in the lung release chemical signals called cytokines that further stimulate blood vessels to leak.  Finally, we hypothesize that preventing the lung's blood vessels from leaking will improve survival from severe influenza. This research has the potential to identify new drug targets for the treatment of severe influenza, which is one of the most common infectious causes of death in Canada.

Keywords-MotsClés: ASSESSMENT; ATTITUDES; CONCUSSION; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; EVENT RELATED POTENTIALS -P300; EVIDENCE-BASED BEST PRACTICE; MILD TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY; PREVENTION; QUESTIONNAIRE; RETURN-TO-PLAY
Abstract-Résumé: Concussion is the third leading cause of traumatic injury in Canada, and is a growing public health concern given its potential for serious long-term consequences. Unfortunately, there is no consensus regarding how to determine safe return-to-play time frames for athletes after brain injury. Although most overt symptoms diminish within 7-10 days, recent electrophysiological (EEG) research finds evidence that brain activity may remain dysfunctional for a longer period of time. This abnormality in brain function may represent a window of vulnerability where a secondary injury can result in even more serious brain dysfunction. This research will examine evidence-based practices for determining safe return-to-play time frames by integrating EEG and standardized neuropsychology measures for child, adolescent and adult athletes. In addition, an examination of attitudes and beliefs surrounding the causes, symptoms and seriousness of concussion, and the use of objective measures of concussion in determining return-to-play readiness will be conducted.  This research will impact health delivery systems by implicating evidence-based best practice following sports-related concussion, and by highlighting attitudes held by those most closely associated with the effects of this form of mild traumatic brain injury in order to determine likelihood of adopting new return-to-play protocol.

TitreApplicationTitle: Use Of Narratives To Uncover The Dynamics Of Male Sexual Risk And Agency
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARD
Abstract-Résumé: Connell's (1995) concept of hegemonic masculinities has been invaluable for prevention efforts that seek to promote a shift in hegemonic male norms that drive the HIV epidemic. However, most work on masculinities is non-narrative and positivist, which fails to appreciate how individual men both conform to and resist hegemonic norms in multiple and sometimes conflicting ways. This limits our comprehension of how to promote the transformation of men's identities, which is necessary for effective and sustainable HIV prevention efforts. A narrative approach, for privileging the diversity in men's lived experiences, could address such concerns. 50 sexual history interviews with men and 25 interviews with women were conducted with participants purposively sampled from a wide range of cultural and racial backgrounds, age categories, and in urban and rural sites across five provinces in South Africa. The data was analyzed using a narrative approach, which pays attention to both content and process including how men perform to constructions of masculinity in sometimes unconscious ways. The narratives reveal the fluid and divergent nature of male sexuality, and provide a platform for understanding under what conditions men resist gender norms that can be damaging to their sexual and reproductive health (SRH). Such nuanced and contextualized understandings of men's SRH are critical for gender transformative HIV prevention efforts and point to the value of a narrative approach in more deeply understanding male sexual risk and agency and the meanings and experiences that underlie it.

TitreApplicationTitle: Potential roles of Semaphorin 3A in atherosclerosis
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; INFLAMMATION; MACROPHAGES; SEMAPHORIN
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiovascular diseases are by far the most prevalent cause of death in developed countries. These diseases, including heart attacks and strokes, often result from atherosclerosis, a fatty deposit of cholesterol, blood cells and fibers in the wall of arteries. Macrophages are the most abundant cells in atherosclerotic plaques. They are attracted by the inflammation caused by the fatty deposits in the wall. Normally, macrophages should enter the plaques, clean up the fatty deposit, and migrate out. However, for reasons that are not well understood, macrophages in plaques lose their ability to move around, so they accumulate locally, become loaded with lipids, and die. In this proposal, we will investigate how semaphorin 3a, a secreted protein that can be detected in the blood, may be protective in the context of atherosclerosis. We found that treatment with semaphorin reduced disease progression in a mouse model of atherosclerosis. Using cell experiments, we also discovered that semaphorin increases macrophage migration and enhances the clearance of dead cells by macrophages. We propose to investigate the molecular mechanisms that underlie these effects of semaphorin. This is the first study to demonstrate an effect of semaphorin in macrophages. Our work will provide insight into the potential of semaphorin as a therapeutic option for patients with atherosclerosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Targeted Proteomics Analysis of the Adaptor Protein Grb2 Signaling Network Dynamics in Breast Cancer.

Abstract-Résumé: Communication between cells that make up tissues in our body is essential. It is required not only to ensure that all parts of our body will develop properly from conception, but also that they will function accurately during our lifetime. Failure for cells to send, to receive or to correctly understand signals to/from their environment or other cells may lead to problems for the whole organism, such as cancer. The cellular actors responsible for such tasks are called proteins. Most, if not all proteins do not act individually but rather function as pairs, small groups (complexes) or larger groups (networks). We are particularly interested with a group of proteins, called adaptors, whose function is to bridge different proteins with one another in order to help a cell integrating signals from outside. Our work seeks to identify which proteins will associate with adaptors to form complexes and networks in normal cells, how different they are in cancer cells, and how they change during cancer progression and metastasis. We will investigate what are the rules that govern this process, as we know that it is not random. To achieve these goals, we will use a combination of protein separation and quantification tools, as well as cellular imaging, in a breast cancer model. We assert that our work will provide unique insights into protein networks that are essential for cellular communication and life, and how they can be utilized as predictive tools or targeted for therapeutic purposes in breast cancer treatment.

Specifically we have shown that mice which spontaneously develop diabetes have fewer DN T cells than mice which never develop disease. Abstract-Résumé: Eight-five percent of Canadian adults do not meet the recommended amount of weekly physical activity at an intensity to achieve health benefits. Individuals also do not have the supports they require in primary health care to adopt more physical activity into their daily lives. Primary health care workers often say that they do not have enough time to talk with their patients about adopting a more physically active lifestyle and also report that they do not know enough about physical activity counseling. Therefore, we have designed a 4 month physical activity counseling program within primary health care to provide individuals with the supports they need to be more physically active by adding an exercise specialist (i.e. kinesiologist) into primary care. Based on our findings so far, individuals are accumulating almost +10 minutes of physical activity at an intensity to achieve health benefits in bouts of 10 minutes or longer after completing the program. Even larger physical activity improvements (i.e. +100 minutes per week) were observed when physical activity was assessed in 30 second bouts or longer. This improvement suggests that our program was helping individuals re-schedule their lives in which they were able to be physically active for about 1 hour and 40 minutes a week more than they were before receiving our physical activity program.  This type if physical activity counseling program is one potential strategy to help support individuals to become more physically active.

Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY/PATCH-CLAMP; ENDOCYTOSIS; FRET; IMAGING; ION CHANNEL; NEONATE CARDIOMYOCYTES; RAB PROTEINS; TARGETING; WESTERN BLOTS
Abstract-Résumé: In the human body, electricity controls life. Electrical signals are generated by the combined work of many different proteins, called ion channels. Each of these ion channels plays a unique role in the heart normal function. Since contractions are controlled by the influx of calcium cations (positively charged molecules), the calcium channel is very important in the heart function. The L-type calcium channel opens and closes in response to changes in electrical activity in cardiac muscle. It is very important that calcium ions enter the cell for the cardiac muscle to contract but the amount of calcium ions has to be exquisitely determined. Too many calcium ions or too few calcium ions will cause important disturbances, called arrhythmias, in the heart electrical activity. We made it our lifelong goal to understand the molecular mechanisms that link the heart electrical activity and the activity (opening and closing) of the calcium channel. Tremendous progress has been made over the last 20 years. We are now able to modify the molecular structure of proteins such as the L-type calcium channels using standard molecular biology techniques and to test the function of the modified proteins using classical electrophysiological methods (whereby we measure the currents generated by the ion channels). We are also able to track the movement of these proteins within cells by tagging the channel proteins with fluorescent labels. By comparing the changes in the electrical pattern and the change in the level of fluorescence between the normal and the modified protein, we are able to identify portions of the protein that are important for its function. We hope that the knowledge we will gain by understanding these fundamental mechanisms will provide additional therapeutic avenues to treat heart failure and lethal arrhythmias.

Keywords-MotsClés: MOUSE MODELS; MYOGENESIS; NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION; RHO-KINASE INHIBITORS; SPINAL MUSCULAR ATROPHY; SYNAPTOSOMES; THERAPEUTICS
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is the number one genetic killer of young children. It is a group of inherited and often fatal diseases that destroys the nerves controlling voluntary muscle movement, with the result that activities like crawling, walking, head and neck control, and even swallowing are affected. At present there is no cure for this devastating disorder. Fortunately, there has been great success at the development of appropriate mouse models for the severe and intermediate forms of the disease. These mice are helping us to get a better understanding of the pathological steps in the progression of the disease, and serve as pre-clinical models for the development and testing of novel therapeutics. Indeed, our work has shown that both motor neurons and skeletal muscle have intrinsic defects, and that both cell types need to be targeted for effective therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Characterization of Platelet Subpopulations based on the Heterogeneity of NOS Signaling: Significance for Hemostasis and Thrombosis
Keywords-MotsClés: AGGREGOMETRY; ENDOTHELIAL NITRIC OXIDE SYNTHASE; FLOW CYTOMETRY; FLUORESCENCE ACTIVATED CELL SORTING; FLUORESCENCE MICROSCOPY; NITRIC OXIDE; PLATELET PHARMACOLOGY; PLATELET SUBPOPULATIONS; QUARTZ CRYSTAL MICROBALANCE FLOW ASSAY; STROKE PATIENTS
Abstract-Résumé: Platelets are circulating blood particles normally responsible for stopping bleeding by forming blood clots (platelet aggregates). In conditions such as heart attack and stroke blood clots form inappropriately in sick (atherosclerotic) blood vessels. Recently, we have discovered that two types of platelets exists. One type of platelet generates the signaling molecule nitric oxide and the other type of platelet does not generate this signaling molecule. Nitric oxide is well known to inhibit platelet clot formation. Hence, we propose that platelets that do not generate nitric oxide initiate clot formation, while platelets that do generate nitric oxide limit clot formation. Hence, the purpose of our studies are 1) to investigate the biochemical and structural differences between the two platelet subtypes, 2) to investigate whether the two platelet subtypes play different roles in clot formation, and 3) to study whether patients with cardiovascular disease (specifically those having had a stroke) have altered ratios of one type of platelet to another. By the end of our studies we expect to have established that the two platelet subtypes differ biochemically and structurally, have different roles in clot formation, and that stroke patients have elevated levels of platelets which initiate clot formation. These basic and translational studies of platelet biology have the potential to significantly impact the health of Canadians by better predicting risk and extent of clot formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Frontal-Plane Knee Joint Loading Magnitude Is Not Related To Pain Severity in Runners with Patellofemoral Pain
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMECHANICS; BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING; INVERSE DYNAMICS; JOINT LOADING; KNEE; ORTHOPAEDICS; OVERUSE INJURY; PAIN; RUNNING; SPORT MEDICINE
Abstract-Résumé: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is the most common running injury, characterized by pain beneath and around the knee-cap during movement. Runners with PFPS experience larger mechanical loads in the knee joint during the stance phase of running compared to uninjured runners. It has been proposed that these greater loads induce greater stress within the joint, thereby increasing pain. If this is the case, one might suspect knee load magnitude and pain severity to be related.   In this study, 35 runners with diagnosed PFPS reported pain during running on a scale from 0-100. Then, each runner completed 5 trials running along a runway in a biomechanics laboratory where 3-dimentional leg movements were measured using an 8-camera system, and the forces exerted on the ground during running were measured using a force platform. Combining the movement and force data, knee joint loads were calculated. Statistical analysis revealed that knee joint loading magnitude was not related to pain severity. Based on this result, it is believed that rather than increasing stress at a given location within the knee, which would lead to greater pain, greater knee loads shift the knee-cap to a new location, inducing new mechanical stress and pain, which is then perceived differently for different patients. This theory is currently being investigated using animal models.

TitreApplicationTitle: Specific inhibition of Notch2 as a novel therapy for invasive bladder cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: Background: Notch signaling guides decisions regarding cell fate, establishment of cell lineages, stem cell maintenance and differentiation during early development. Notch is active in many adult malignancies where it has been shown to regulate tumor cell proliferation and progression to aggressive disease. We report outcomes of Notch2 knockdown or treatment in our bladder cancer cell models. Methods: UMUC3, UMUC13 and UMUC16 cells were transduced with Notch2 or non-targeting shRNA and were stably propogated. A Notch2-inactivating monoclonal antibody, NRR2Mab, was kindly provided by Genentech. Cells were grown under adherent (AH) or anchorage-independent conditions (AI) and the effects of Notch2 silencing or NRR2Mab inactivation were quantitatively assessed for changes in proliferation, migration and invasive activities using in vitro assays and, for expression of Notch2 or other common stem cell-related genes using quantitative RT-PCR, Western blotting and immunohistochemistry. In vivo effects were evaluated in an orthotopic bladder cancer xenograft model. Results: Cells transduced with the Notch2 shRNA or treated with NRR2Mab demonstrated markedly decreased Notch2 expression. Stable silencing of Notch2 or treatment with NRR2Mab in UMUC3 and 13 diminished cell proliferation under AI but not AH conditions. Likewise, when grown in AI conditions, UMUC3 and 13 were found to be enriched for expression of stem cell genes but Notch2 silencing or NRR2Mab diminished the expression of these genes. Coincidentally, Notch silencing and NRR2Mab treatment significantly inhibited cell migration and invasion of these cells. In vivo, stable Notch2 knockdown cells significantly inhibited xenograft growth for all 3 cell lines. NRR2Mab treatment of host mice also inhibited UMUC13 xenograft growth and metastasis. Conclusions: Our results provide preclinical evidence that Notch2 may be a useful target to block aggressive behaviors and to prevent growth and progression of bladder cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Respiratory-gated radiotherapy in filter-free photon mode for the treatment of liver carcinomas
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS
Abstract-Résumé: Cancer of the liver can often not be removed with surgery, and so other methods of treatment like radiation therapy must be considered. In stereotactic radiotherapy, very large doses are delivered to a tumor making it very important to ensure the location of a lesion in the liver is known accurately. A patient's breathing moves organs in the surrounding chest area, the liver being one. This creates a difficulty in precisely knowing the exact location of a liver cancer at any instant of a patient's breath.   Gating in radiotherapy refers to the act of delivering radiation to a cancer only in one part of a patient's breath such as at the point of maximum inhale or exhale. In this way a precise dose is hypothetically delivered to the tumor, while the surrounding healthy tissue is spared. It is not yet well established whether gating allows for delivery of an accurate prescribed dose to a tumor, and if it alters the survival of cells following radiotherapy. Because gating provides dose to a tumor only in certain part of a patient's respiratory cycle, the overall treatment time increases up to 7 times in duration. 'Filter free' accelerators are able to deliver a dose ~4 times faster than their predecessors, making their use favorable. This research explores how dose accumulation differs when radiation delivery is gated as opposed to being delivered in one instance. Further, the change in cell survival following the two methods of radiotherapy is measured. For this purpose, the respiratory patterns of 10 patients are obtained and simulated on an acrylic phantom - a model of the human body used to test the response of patients to different radiation treatments. An insert made to accommodate cell vials or radiation dosimeters is attached to the phantom body, and moves to mimic the breathing of the selected patient.  Positive outcomes of the study could imply that respiratory-gated radiotherapy is the next step in improving liver cancer patient quality of life and survival.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring the role of D4 receptors in controlling reward expectancy in a rat model of slot machine play.
Keywords-MotsClés: ADDICTION; DOPAMINE; GAMBLING; RAT; REWARD
Abstract-Résumé: As opportunities to gamble continue to grow in our society, pathological gambling (PG) is increasingly recognised as a significant public health concern. However, effective treatments remain elusive. Among those who seek treatment for PG, compulsive engagement in slot machine play is the most commonly reported gambling activity. Psychologists have suggested that one reason why slot machines can be so "addictive" is due to the prevalence of near-miss events i.e. when 2 out of 3 stimuli match on the payline. Although people find these experiences frustrating, the occurrence of near-misses can galvanise further game play, and these stimuli also activate similar brain areas as true wins. Helping subjects to reclassify near-misses as losses, rather than wins, can decrease the desire to play a slot machine. The development of pharmacological treatments which reduce the power of near-misses to drive slot machine play could therefore represent a significant advance in treating this form of PG. To study the neurobiology underlying the near-miss effect, we developed a rat model of slot machine play, and have found that dopamine D4 receptor antagonists selectively decrease the degree to which rats respond to losses as if they were wins. Dopamine is a brain chemical that plays a critical role in signalling how motivated we are to earn rewards, and the addictive nature of drugs like cocaine has been attributed to their ability to increase dopamine levels. D4 antagonists could therefore represent a very promising treatment for compulsive slots play. We want to follow-up on these findings and determine where in the brain these D4 antagonists are acting to produce such beneficial effects in our rat model. We also want to analyse the effects of chronic administration of D4 antagonists, to observe whether the improvement in performance is consistent over time, and also whether these drugs can reduce reinstatement of play after a period of abstinence i.e. reduce a marker of relapse.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immediate vs. Delayed Stenting after Primary Percutaneous Reperfusion in ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION; ANTICOAGULATION; CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE; INTERVENTIONAL CARDIOLOGY; PRIMARY PCI; RANDOMIZED TRIAL; STENT
Abstract-Résumé: Stenting during STEMI has become a standard of care in industrialized countries. A primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) typically consists of restoring flow in the occluded coronary artery, after which the culprit lesion is immediately sealed with a stent to prevent a reocclusion of the artery. However, a growing body of evidence suggests that delaying stent implantation may be superior to traditional immediate stenting. During a STEMI, stents are implanted in a thrombotic environment which paradoxically impairs myocardial reperfusion because of distal embolization. The potential drawbacks of immediate stenting should be considered in the context of improved anti-platelet agents and safer systemic anticoagulation which have virtually eliminated the risk of an acute coronary reocclusion. Ideally, stents should be withheld until adjunctive anticoagulation has been administered long enough to reduce the thrombus burden.   The primary objective of the PRIMACY trial is to assess whether delayed stenting is superior to immediate stenting at improving cardiovascular outcomes in patients with ST elevation myocardial infarction. We hypothesize that delayed stenting will reduce the combined occurrence of cardiac death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, and target vessel revascularization at 9 months. Patients with STEMI successfully reperfused will be randomized to either immediate stenting or to delayed stenting where anticoagulation will be administered for 24 hours before stenting is allowed. The PRIMACY trial will be ran using Bayesian assumptions; an independent board of experts will determine the prior probability of efficacy and will supervise the evolution of the Bayesian monitoring. This trial is critically important because delayed stenting carries the potential to improve survival and quality of life in the large and vulnerable population of Canadian with STEMI who are in the greatest need of more effective therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relationship-Focused Intervention for Maternal Substance Abuse Improves Maternal Outcomes and Reduces Child Behavioral Problems
Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARD
Abstract-Résumé: Interventions for maternal substance abuse are becoming increasingly integrated in nature (including prenatal, parenting, or child-related services). However, intervention is often limited to basic information regarding parenting and child behavior management. Children are rarely included in service and the mother-child relationship is seldom seen as a critical target of treatment. Breaking the Cycle (BTC) is a children's (aged 0 to 6) mental health agency in downtown Toronto that aims to improve child outcomes through intervention for maternal substance abuse that aims at fostering the mother-child relationship. The goal of this study was to compare the relative efficacy of this novel approach to standard, integrated treatment. Participants were 65 mothers from BTC and 25 comparison mothers. Three maternal outcome domains were assessed including: addiction severity (ASI; DTCQ), relationship capacity (PSS; AAS), and mental health (CES-D; BAI). Both groups showed significant improvement on measures of addiction severity, but only BTC mothers made significant gains on measures of relationship capacity and mental health (ds = small to moderate). One-year follow-up data were available for 45 children of BTC mothers. Improvements in maternal relationship capacity and mental health significantly predicted improvements in total parenting stress on the Parent Stress Index, total child behavioral difficulties on the Child Behavior Checklist, and working memory on the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (all ps < .05). These findings suggest that relationship-focused intervention supports mothers with substance abuse issues to make broad changes across multiple domains of functioning, including changes in their mental health and relationship capacity. Findings also indicate that improvements in maternal functioning are associated with better child behavioral outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Étude des différences entre les femmes dans le traitement au propranolol chez une population souffrant d'un état de stress post-traumatique.
Keywords-MotsClés: MEMOIRE; PROPRANOLOL; RECONSOLIDATION; REACTIVATION; SANTE MENTALE; STRESS; TRAITEMENT; TRAUMA; ETAT DE STRESS POST-TRAUMATIQUE
Abstract-Résumé: L'etat de stress post-traumatique (ESPT) affecte actuellement un million d'individus au Canada seulement. De plus, les hommes et les femmes ne reagissent pas de la meme maniere a un evenement traumatique. En effet, une fois expose a un trauma, les femmes sont deux fois plus a risque que les hommes de developper un ESPT. Etant donne la souffrance liee a ce trouble, il importe de fournir une aide appropriee aux personnes ayant un ESPT. Malheureusement, les traitements psychotherapeutiques et pharmacologiques developpes pour l'ESPT montrent une efficacite plus ou moins satisfaisante. Afin d'offrir des soins plus adaptes aux patients, de recentes decouvertes proposent le blocage de la reconsolidation comme traitement prometteur. La reconsolidation presume que lorsqu'on se rappelle d'un souvenir, il devient instable et il est possible a ce moment la de le modifier avant qu'il se restabilise a nouveau dans le cerveau. D'autre part, de recentes recherches montrent qu'il serait possible de diminuer la memoire negative en bloquant le processus de reconsolidation a l'aide de differentes substances. Ce blocage peut se faire durant la periode d'instabilite mentionnee precedemment. Une des substances utilisees est le propranolol. La personne raconte son trauma sous l'influence du medicament, ce qui diminue les emotions negatives associees a ce souvenir traumatique. D'ailleurs, il semblerait que ce traitement est plus efficace chez les femmes que chez les hommes. Cependant, le(s) mecanismes expliquant cette difference demeurent inexpliques a ce jour. Par consequent, il est important de determiner pourquoi cette nouvelle intervention par le propranolol est plus efficace chez les femmes. Les resultats nous permettront de mieux personnaliser les traitements pour les gens, plus particulierement chez les femmes, qui souffrent d'un ESPT.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Aboriginal Youth Mentorship Program (AYMP): A peer-led healthy living after-school program for achieving healthy weights in First Nations children living in a northern remote setting.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL YOUTH; DIABETES; OBESITY; PEER-MENTORING; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal youth represent a significant and growing population in Canada and have much to offer in terms of their contributions to their own health and the health and wellness of others. At the same time, they are at greater risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity than non-Aboriginal youth. Few school based programs have been developed and tested that are aimed at reducing the risk for Aboriginal youth, especially those living in rural communities. Fewer still involve interventions that are peer-led and reliant upon the strengths, energy, and talents of the youth themselves. Building on the successes of a communal, relationship based approach to Aboriginal youth mentoring in an after school physical activity program (AYMP), we are evaluating a peer-led approach for diabetes prevention in Aboriginal schools. With the support of adult community members, high school volunteer as mentors, and develop an after-school physical activity, nutrition and education program that they then deliver to children in grade 4 at a neighbouring school. The high school mentors meet twice a week. The first day, they develop an activity plan which emphasizes vigorously active low organized games and healthy nutrition; together, the mentors decide roles and responsibilities to ensure successful delivery of each activity. The second day, they deliver the program for the children.The project incorporates a community-based participatory action research model that is informed by indigenous teachings, values and worldviews.

Keywords-MotsClés: BARRIERS TO ACCESS TO HEALTH CARE; DIFFERENCE-IN-DIFFERENCES REGRESSION ANALYSIS; HEALTH SERVICES ACCESSBILITY; ICS TRAVEL AWARDS; POTENTIAL ACCESS TO HEALTH CARE; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE REFORM; TEAM-CENTERED MODELS OF CARE
Abstract-Résumé: A decade after their implementation, we investigate the impact of Quebec's Groupes de medicine de famille (GMFs) on access to primary care and perceived remaining barriers. We emphasize potential access - i.e. several measures that capture whether an individual reports having timely access to needed care. We use data from seven waves of the Canadian Community Health Survey to capture reported access to primary care and barriers to access. GMF participation is voluntary and they emerged at different rates in different health regions across Quebec. We constructed a GMF 'participation' measure using the share of primary care physicians participating in GMFs in each health region and year. Our primary measure of potential access is having a regular doctor. We verified that regions with ultimately high vs. low rates of GMF participation were not systematically different in the pre-policy period in terms socioeconomic characteristics or health care access, making comparisons of these regions appropriate. Preliminary results suggest that rates of having a regular doctor have increased over time in all Quebec health regions. However, this measure of access varies across regions and some, including Montreal, always report lower rates of access. Individual characteristics that predict access to primary care are age, sex, education, income, immigrant status, language spoken, number of chronic diseases and self-reported health. Controlling for time trends, fixed differences between regions, and individual characteristics, reported access does not change significantly as GMF participation increases. Improved access to primary health care was one of the primary objectives of Quebec's primary care reform a decade ago. Our findings suggest that increased GMF participation has not improved several important measures of access, and that additional measures may be necessary to increase potential access to primary care.
