Keywords-MotsClés: ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; HEALTH ECONOMICS; PAYMENT MODELS; PRIMARY CARE; RELATIVE DISTRIBUTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Ontario has supplemented fee-for-service with several payment schemes for primary care physicians (PCPs), many based on age-sex adjusted capitation payments. Recent studies have demonstrated that changes in payment have coincided with increasing provincial expenditures. One possible explanation for increases in primary care costs is that the new payment schemes are overpaying for the majority of patients that use a small quantity of services. The objective of this paper is to compare cost distributions for different payment schemes in Ontario to determine how patient costs differ; and to determine whether these differences are due to increases in costs across all patients, or differences in make-up of patient populations enrolled to different payment schemes. Data was obtained from the Institute for Clinical Evaluation Sciences (ICES) in Ontario, which stores all administrative health data for the province. The time frame for this study covered a cross-section of two fiscal years (2010/11 to 2011/12). We analyzed relative distributions of patient costs across primary care practice types (i.e., different payment schemes) controlling for patient case-mix, location and practice characteristics. We also computed statistical tests to test whether there are significant differences in the distributions. Analysis is underway, but preliminary results suggest that there are uniform increases in primary care costs for patients assigned to capitation-remunerated PCPs, and that capitation-remunerated PCPs also have fewer high-cost patients on their rosters than FFS-remunerated PCPs.  It is possible that age and sex adjusted capitation payments do not adequately predict patient complexity and cost, incentivizing PCPs with healthier (and less costly) patient rosters to self-select into the capitation-based payment schemes. Further studies are underway using panel methods to determine the causal relationship between payment change and the characteristics of physician rosters.

TitreApplicationTitle: Disrupting Surgical Practice: The Rise of Minimally Invasive Surgery, 1980-2000
Keywords-MotsClés: HISTORY OF SURGERY; HISTORY OF TECHNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: The proposed project examines how keyhole surgery was adopted by surgeons in Europe and North America to replace open operations during the 1980s and 1990s, and how this new method transformed the nature of surgical practice.  What began as a diagnostic technique in the fields of gynecology, urology and internal medicine in the mid-twentieth century had revolutionized general practice by the beginning of the twenty-first.  Because keyhole methods required a completely different set of skills than traditional 'open' surgery, their introduction into new areas was at first controversial, and took considerable perseverance from both within and beyond the medical profession. We propose to investigate why and how surgeons at first ignored and then learned to use the new techniques, and how they cultivated and spread new skills through personal experience with their peers and colleagues. We will look at the role of technical devices and their manufacturers in shaping the spread of keyhole procedures, and the ways surgeons convinced themselves and the public that the benefits outweighed the risks.  Finally, we will analyze the role of patient demand in accelerating the rise of keyhole surgery. The project focuses on an unexplored revolution in the history of modern surgery, the effects of which are still unraveling.  Its results will therefore provide a better basis for future policy decisions about supporting and guiding technical innovations in surgery and other areas of health care.

Abstract-Résumé: Children born with heart problems are much more likely to have other health problems, such as being overweight, having diabetes, or being anxious or sad. Physical activity is important for all children, but it could also help children with heart problems to be healthier. Active children are less likely to be overweight, have diabetes or be anxious or sad. Our study was designed to find out why children with heart problems do not have healthy lifestyles. We have asked children with heart problems and their parents to tell us what it is like, what makes it difficult and what would help. We also talked to doctors, nurses, recreation leaders, and mental health professionals to find out what they know and what changes they think would help. From talking to all of these groups, we learned that: a) children think health is more than just about their heart, b) that trying to be healthy often feels like a struggle that they have to fight on their own, and c) children, families and professionals think that having more information would make it easier to be healthy. The results of this project are changing what doctors and nurses do when children with heart problems come to see them.

Abstract-Résumé: I will study a molecule that is a potential new treatment for colon cancer. Colon cancer is the 3rd leading cause of cancer death in Canada, with 24 patients dying of colorectal cancer in Canada each day. Current strategies to treat advanced colorectal cancer include chemotherapies, but many of the molecules used have severe side-effects for patients and are expensive to the Canadian health care system. The molecule we propose to study (cladoniamide) has been shown to kill colon cancer cells in the laboratory, and this molecule may be a good drug to treat advanced colon cancer patients. The drug may also be useful against other types of cancers.   The molecule is isolated from a bacterial species that lives in the wild. We propose a program to make this bacterially-derived molecule in the laboratory. High-level production of the molecule in the laboratory will help lower the cost of the molecule. Further, we will use advanced techniques to make related molecules with small modifications that may have improved properties, i.e. better drugs. Finally, we will study the mechanisms that the bacteria uses to make this molecule. Proteins called enzymes are likely to be involved in making this drug. We want to understand how these enzymes work and use this information to make additional anti-cancer molecules for testing.

Abstract-Résumé: Child neglect is among the top reasons for jurisdictions to take custody of children. The SafeCare program was developed in the U.S. to specifically address neglect in families involved in the child welfare system. SafeCare is an evidence-based in-home parent-training program that is being implemented in U.S. states, in the U.K., and in Belarus. Within Ontario child welfare agencies, however, there currently exist no such evidence-based neglect-specific interventions. The objective of the current proposal is to deliver the SafeCare program in several Ontario agencies (that are representative of diversity in terms of culture and geographic location) and to evaluate important implementation issues such as acceptability and feasibility using multiple informants and mixed methods (interviews, questionnaires). We will also gather information prior to and following completion of the SafeCare program to evaluate the effects on participating families. The current project not only has the potential to impact the health of individual children and families but it also has population health implications. Specifically, child neglect is expensive from a community point of view (medical care, out-of-home placement, poor educational outcomes), and once established, it tends to remain persistent. By evaluating the acceptability, feasibility, and effects of the SafeCare program, our project has significant applied relevance because it may lead to the adoption of this program by Ontario child welfare agencies, which then has the potential to help families and to safeguard against the establishment of child neglect as a chronic societal condition.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of blood platelets in the regulation of inflammation

Abstract-Résumé: PURPOSE: Proper function of blood cells is essential for protection against infectious disease and maintaining human health. During the onset of infection or following injury, white blood cells and platelets release signaling molecules known as cytokines, which orchestrate a protective inflammatory response. When cytokine release is de-regulated, excessive inflammation results that causes cell and tissue death and loss of function. In addition to regulating blood coagulation (clotting), platelets are emerging as pivotal components of the host inflammatory response. Notably, platelets are an important source of transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGF-B1), a cytokine that regulates wound healing, inflammation and cell-mediated immunity. The mechanisms underlying cytokine secretion from platelets are undefined but likely involve the structural framework of the cell (cytoskeleton). The Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASp) controls the actin cytoskeleton in white blood cells but has other function(s) in platelets. We hypothesized that WASp may control the release of TGF-B1 from platelets.  RESULTS: Upon activation, WASp-deficient platelets released more TGF-B1 than normal (wild-type) platelets. Similarly, blocking WASp function with a chemical inhibitor augmented TGF-B1 release in human platelets. Chemical disruption of the actin cytoskeleton also increased TGF-B1 release, but this was independent of WASp function.  CONCLUSION: WASp function restricts TGF-B1 secretion from platelets independently of the actin cytoskeleton.  IMPACT: Identifying the biochemical mechanisms of cytokine secretion will improve our understanding of platelets and their role in the host inflammatory response.

Abstract-Résumé: Smooth muscle plays an important role in the regulation of vascular tone as well as a myriad of other biological functions. Central to this proposal, tone management is a key contribution of the vascular smooth muscle (VSM) tissue, which when functioning normally, contributes to general health and wellness but when dysfunctional is associated with morbidity and mortality. For example, an increase in VSM contractility is known to contribute to the severe arterial narrowing observed in cerebral and coronary vasospasm, in chronic hypertension and in the decreased dilatory responses of arteries in obesity, diabetes and aging. The fine control of VSM tone is essential for maintenance of normal cardiovascular function. The biochemical systems that govern VSM are complex, yet zipper-interacting protein kinase (ZIPK) has emerged as one of the most important factors that regulate this mechanism. Indeed, research suggests that ZIPK can promote VSM contractility in health and disease. More recent studies suggest that there is a strong correlation between ZIPK and cancer development and progresion. Taken togther, I will investigate the role of ZIPK in cardiovascular diseases and cancer . During the timeline of this proposal, I propose to address a number of knowledge limitations and develop important tools to better interrogate the physiological function(s) of ZIPK. These investigations will reveal the potential for development of inhibitors of ZIPK for attenuation of its cellular activity. Accordingly, the validation of specific inhibitors (or activators) of ZIPK would be particularly advantageous, not only in promoting our basic understanding of this signalling module but also for clinical application for treatment of contractile disorders. Furthermore, knowledge gained by my investigations will enable exploration of additional functions of this critically important kinase in cancer disease.

Abstract-Résumé: When older adults with multiple illnesses get discharged from a hospital stay, they have high chances of being readmitted to the hospital or visiting the Emergency Department in the months following their discharge. Many of these older adults are forced to return to hospital so soon because of medication errors, lack of ability to manage their conditions at home, and communication lapses between hospital staff and community caregivers. In the United States and New Zealand, Nurse Practitioner-led care transition programs have helped older adults transition home and stay out of hospital longer. These programs feature a pre-discharge visit while the patient is in hospital and post-discharge home visits, all by the same Nurse Practitioner. During these visits, the Nurse Practitioner checks patients' medications and guides them through a personalized care plan.   This study is the first to look at whether a Nurse Practitioner-led care transition program can help older adults in Canada transition home more smoothly, thereby avoiding Emergency Department visits and readmissions. In addition to testing whether this type of hospital-to-home program reduces hospital readmissions, this study also identifies why certain components of the program did or did not meet their goals. This information on the processes that led to program successes and failures can be used to guide future hospital-to-home programs in Canada and abroad.

Abstract-Résumé: Blood vessels formation or angiogenesis is  complex process that requires coordination of different cell types and involves various cellular processes such as activation, proliferation, migration, and differentiation. The PI 3-kinase catalytic isoform p110 beta is important in signaling molecule that has multiple activities inside the cell. We demonstrate that the inhibition of p110b activity in endothelial cells has an adverse effect on new blood vessels formation in vitro. The loss of p110 beta reduced sprouting of tip cells, which are the cells that lead the sprouts that eventually develop into new blood vessel.  The loss of p110 beta reduced capillary-like structures in vivo using matrigel plugs injected under the mouse skin. The deletion of p110 beta in mouse rendered the mouse more susceptible to kidney injury in a kidney injury animal model as the injured kidney small blood vessels failed to get repaired. This research project advances our knowledge of an important physiological process, which can help devise new strategies in the treatment of cardiovascular diseases and the regeneration of small blood vessels

Keywords-MotsClés: ICS TRAVEL AWARDS; YI FORUM 2013 CIHR_ICRH
Abstract-Résumé: Cardiac remodeling is the process by which cardiac structure and/or function change in response to pathophysiological derangements such as disease states, chronic arrhythmic conditions or altered hormone balance. Cardiac remodeling promotes mechanical dysfunction of the heart and arrhythmia generation. The traditional view of the signal transduction pathways leading to the gene-expression changes that cause remodeling has been that molecules interact with cell membrane receptors and modulate the production and/or breakdown of intracellular second messengers, which diffuse into the nucleus and modify gene-transcription. Recent work has suggested that ligands may also act via receptors on intracellular organelles, and not just exclusively via surface-membrane receptors: so-called "intracrine signaling". There is evidence that AT1R (Angiotensin Type 1 receptor) and AT2R (Angiotensin Type 1 receptor) localized to the nuclear envelope may play significant roles in cardiac remodeling. Nuclear receptors with the ability to regulate cardiac gene-expression have been demonstrated for Ang-II, endothelin, beta-adrenergic agonists and opioid ligands. How do peptide ligands get into the cell to act on intracellular receptors? Intracrine ligands may be synthesized de novo intracellularly (e.g. FB growth factor, opioids, Ang-II), may be transported actively (noradrenaline) or via passive diffusion (leukotrienes) from the extracellular space, or may move into the cell within internalized endosomes. The nucleus contains all the key components of G-protein receptor-coupled signaling pathways, which if activated would be strategically located to regulate gene-transcription pathways. Relevant consequences could be the development of compounds selected for their ability to concentrate (or not) intracellularly, as well as novel drug-delivery approaches to the development of agents that act principally within the cell.

Abstract-Résumé: The kidneys play an important role in keeping our bones healthy. When an individual's kidney function begins to decline they often develop bone problems. The best treatment for an individual with severe declines in kidney function is kidney transplantation. Past research has suggested that kidney transplant recipients have an increased risk of fracture compared to the general population. However, information on the burden of fracture and risk factors for fracture have not been efficiently sumarized. We conducted a systematic review to sumarize this information. We found that the burden of fracture varied widely in the literature and the risk factors for fracture were not consistent across studies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploring cholinergic mechanisms to understand behavioral deficits in dementia.
Keywords-MotsClés: ACETYLCHOLINE; ATTENTION; BEHAVIOR; BEHAVIORAL FLEXIBILITY; BRAIN CIRCUITS; CELLULAR MECHANISMS; DEMENTIA; DEPRESSION; MOUSE MODELS; PHARMACOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Aging is the major risk-factor for a number of diseases that lead to dementia. In Canada, due to a significant aging of its population, it has been estimated that by the year 2031 there will be approximately 4 million Canadians with dementia. Behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia include memory loss, reasoning loss, delusions, hallucinations, agitation, anxiety, irritability, depression, apathy, disinhibition, and sleep or appetite impairment. Thus, besides being debilitating for the patients and a huge health care cost, the disease also brings an enormous load on caregivers. Therefore, novel approaches are urgently needed to find more effective therapeutic interventions to decrease the burden of dementia. To communicate with each other, brain cells (or neurons) use a combination of chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. The neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh) seems to be an  important player in dementia as dysfunction of particular groups of ACh-releasing neurons is present in a number of neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Dementia with Lewy bodies. Here we propose to use a number of different genetically modified mouse models, each of them showing impairment in the release of ACh from different groups of ACh neurons in the brain, to define how changes in ACh release influence the regulation of brain communication circuits and behavioral manifestations related to dementia. These mice, which provide a model for chemical changes in dementia, will also be used to investigate mechanisms for novel drugs that can be used to  alleviate behavioral problems in dementia. These studies will pinpoint specific molecular and behavioral abnormalities relating ACh deficits to dementia and will define novel pharmacological mechanisms tailored to improve specific ACh-mediated symptoms.

NomDuComitéFR: Investigation clinique-A : Reproduction, santé de la mère, de l'enfant et de l'adolescent
TitreApplicationTitle: Treating the cardiovascular dysfunction of newborns with asphyxia
Keywords-MotsClés: ASPHYXIA; HEMODYNAMICS; MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASE; NEONATES; TRANSLATION
Abstract-Résumé: When newborns lacking oxygen (asphyxia) are resuscitated, they may develop poor heart function and multiple organ failure during recovery. This contributes to significant mortality, short-term and long-term morbidity. The current treatment consists mainly of supportive therapies. We recently observed an improved recovery of the heart with the administration of an antibiotics, doxycycline, using an established model of newborn resuscitation. The "protective" effect of doxycycline could be related to the regulation of activity of a cardiac-specific enzyme and excessive oxygen stress. We propose to perform sophisticated experiments to detail the protective effects of doxycycline in an intact animal model of asphyxia and resuscitation (specifically in the heart and brain), the administration protocol, mechanism of action as well as the correlation between functional recovery, oxygen stress and histological and biochemical markers of injury. The findings would lay the foundation for future clinical studies in the treatment of asphyxia-injured newborns which is the cause of a million deaths worldwide every year.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of vascular endothelial cell  bioenergetics by H2S in health and under oxidative stress
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; BIOENERGETICS; CARDIOVASCULAR; ENDOTHELIUM; HYDROGEN SULFIDE; HYPERTENSION; ION CHANNELS; MITOCHONDRIA; OXIDATIVE STRESS; REDOX SIGNALING
Abstract-Résumé: Recent work has demonstrated that the rotten-egg gas, hydrogen sulfide (also known as "sewer gas" or "swamp gas") is produced by our cells and tissues, and regulates the metabolism and function of various cells including endothelial cells that form a thin layer of the inner wall of our blood vessels. Endothelial cells play a critical role in controlling blood flow and the integrity of blood vessels. The current project, based on multiple lines of new discoveries, will investigate the role of hydrogen sulfide in the alterations in endothelial  metabolism and blood flow under healthy conditions, and in two models of blood vessel diseases; high blood pressure and atherosclerosis. We will study how the enzymes that produce hydrogen sulfide are moving inside the cell controlling the cellular production and utilization of energy and the way the cell can survive or die during cardiovascular diseases. With this project, Dr. Katalin Modis (a young Ph.D. pharmacist who has received specialized training in hydrogen sulfide biology at the University of Texas) will have the opportunity to join Lakehead University, Canada, to learn and to conduct cutting-edge studies with Dr. Rui Wang, a pioneer and leader of hydrogen sulfide biological research. The results of our studies will directly lead to the formulation of rational therapeutic concepts and are fundamentally relevant for multiple vascular diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Moving from Custodial Housing to Autonomous Living: The Lived Experience of Residents and Their Recovery from Serious Mental Illness
Keywords-MotsClés: CUSTODIAL HOUSING; HOUSING; INNOVATIVE PARTNERSHIPS; MENTAL HEALTH; MENTAL HEALTH RECOVERY; NARRATIVES; QUALITATIVE METHODS; SERIOUS MENTAL ILLNESS
Abstract-Résumé: This study will explore the experiences of people recovering from serious mental illness who move into autonomous housing. Mental health recovery is a unique process of personal change aimed at living a more satisfying, hopeful, productive life, even within the limitations caused by mental illness. Recovery-oriented services go beyond traditional clinical care to help people achieve better quality of life, employment, friendships, and better living conditions. New innovative housing has been created throughout Canada through intersectoral partnerships involving community organizations, local health & social service centres, and psychiatric hospitals. This study will explore 1) how residents experience recovery in these autonomous housing units; and 2) how the different stakeholders view the recovery orientation of their services and their impact on residents' recovery. Having a decent, affordable home is a basic human right and a priority for people with serious mental illness. Inter-sectorial partnerships are viewed as an effective way to deal with the complex challenges of providing housing in the community for this population. Yet recovery is not about finding an ideal housing type, but understanding how housing meets people's personal goals, priorities and life circumstances. We know very little about what difference new housing will make in people's lives. We will collect narratives or stories from residents living in four housing projects, Montreal, Toronto St John's and Sherbrooke. We will also interview 4 other stakeholder groups(family members, mental health service providers; housing staff;  and regional planning board members). Other data sources include observation & document analysis. Findings will be compared and contrasted within/across the four housing projects. We hope that this research will provide a better understanding of how new housing influences the recovery of residents.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the nuclear receptor corepressor-1 in blocking inflammatory gene expression
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CULTURE; GENE EXPRESSION ASSAYS; GENE SILENCING; GENE TRANSCRIPTION; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASES; MOUSE CONDITIONAL KNOCKOUT
Abstract-Résumé: Both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease represent the major inflammatory diseases (IBD) that affect more than 200,000 youngsters and adults over the country per year. It is thus imperative to better understand genes as well as modifying factors that confer susceptibility for the initiation and progression of these significant illnesses. The main objective of this grant proposal is to elucidate the overall mechanisms that restrict gene expression of pro-inflammatory molecules.  The progress of our research has led to the identification of a nuclear co-repressor (NCoR1) as being crucial to restrict expression of inflammatory mediators at the gene level.  This research project proposes to sequentially delete this protein in different cellular counterparts of the gut tissue (epithelial, myofibroblastic and immune cells) and measure the biological and functional consequences of such deletions on the severity of experimental colitis.   Sequencing of the whole transcriptome in absence of this gene repressor will allow us to identify novel direct genetic targets for this repressor of functional relevance for these diseases.  Finally, the exact annotation of the repressor complex composition upon inflammatory stress should allow the identification of key molecules required for the gene repressive action of this repressor. These molecular approaches will offer a better understanding of the mechanisms that restrain intestinal inflammatory response.  These findings might then lead to the exploration of novel therapeutic strategies to limit exaggerated and relapsing inflammation during IBD.

TitreApplicationTitle: An International Study to Develop a Patient-Reported Outcome Instrument for Cleft-Lip and/or Palate Patients: The CLEFT-Q
Keywords-MotsClés: CLEFT LIP; CLEFT PALATE; GLOBAL HEALTH; PATIENT SATISFACTION; PSYCHOMETRICS; QUALITATIVE; QUALITY OF LIFE; QUESTIONNAIRES; RELIABILITY; VALIDITY
Abstract-Résumé: Cleft lip and/or palate (CLP) is the most common congenital craniofacial anomaly. The management of this condition is complex, beginning in infancy and often extending into adulthood. Patients undergo at least one operation, and depending on the severity of the cleft, may have more than six operations before the age of 18 years. While the goal of treatment is to improve patient's physical, psychological, and social well-being, the measurement of outcomes has typically ignored the patients' perspective to focus on objective and more readily analyzed outcomes. Our international team of experts from Canada, USA and United Kingdom has come together to develop and validate a new patient-reported outcome (PRO) instrument called the CLEFT-Q. A PRO instrument for patients with CLP needs to measure the domains of health of importance to patients (e.g., appearance, speech, psychosocial interaction) and to do this in a way that captures differences in aspects of quality of life as patients matures, as well as differences between countries. Progress to date by our team includes a literature review of health concepts in patients with CLP, interviews with 136 patients with CLP from 6 countries and the development of a conceptual framework with 4 main domains (Appearance, Physical Health, Psychological Health and Social Health). The framework was used to guide the development of 13 new CLEFT-Q scales. All scale items now need to be tested for cultural and cognitive understanding. We then plan to conduct a large scale field-test and use modern psychometric methods to choose the best possible items for inclusion in the final CLEFT-Q scales. Finally, the CLEFT-Q will be included in a psychometric evaluation study to examine validity, reliability and responsiveness. Once developed, the CLEFT-Q will be used to support patient advocacy, clinical audit for quality improvement, and local, national and international research efforts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Examining the practice of informal caregiving in medical tourism: Qualitatively exploring caregiver-companions' roles and responsibilities
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREGIVING; MEDICAL TOURISM; QUALITATIVE METHODS
Abstract-Résumé: Medical tourism (MT) occurs when individuals travel across international borders with the intention of accessing non-emergency medical care, which they pay for privately. Canadian medical tourists often do not travel abroad on their own; typically, friends and/or family accompany them and take on various supporting and caregiving roles. My research will qualitatively examine if and how Canadian caregiver-companions' roles and responsibilities change as they engage in medical tourism.  Participating in informal caregiving impacts both medical tourists' and caregivers' health and wellbeing. As such, my research can be used to identify ways to assist with maintaining the health of both parties. In addition, my research will contribute to knowledge about medical tourism and can help inform Canadian health policy responses to this phenomenon.

TitreApplicationTitle: Biopsychosocial Predictors of the Effectiveness of If-then Plans and Mental Practice in Pre-Diabetic Patients
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL VARIABLES; DIABETES PREVENTION; HABIT FORMATION; IF-THEN PLANS; ILLNESS ANXIETY; IMPULSIVITY; LIFESTYLE MODIFICATION PROGRAM; MENTAL PRACTICE; SELF-EFFICACY; SOCIAL SUPPORT
Abstract-Résumé: Pre-diabetes is an increasingly widespread health care epidemic that is currently affecting the lives of over five million Canadians. The costs and health consequences associated with pre-diabetes are tremendous. As a result, several lifestyle modification programs, which aim to bring about significant changes in one's eating and physical activity behaviours have been developed in order to prevent the progression of pre-diabetes into type 2 diabetes. However, these programs are complex and costly, and the health-related changes that participants make are not sufficiently maintained for a long period of time. Currently, a randomized controlled trial is investigating whether evidence-based lifestyle modification programs, specifically the Group Lifestyle Balance Program, can be rendered more feasible and effective by integrating two habit formation tools (if-then plans and mental practice) early on and throughout the program. The present research proposes that biomedical, psychological and social variables predict and mediate the efficacy of these two habit formation tools. I expect that (1) higher levels of illness anxiety and impulsivity will decrease the effectiveness of if-then plans and mental practice, especially when co-occurring with biomedical risk factors and low levels of social support and (2) self-efficacy for physical activity at the beginning of the intervention will mediate the increase in physical activity levels and habit strength from the beginning to the end of the intervention. Ultimately, this research can be used to significantly improve short and long-term treatment outcomes for individuals with pre-diabetes in a feasible and effective manner.

TitreApplicationTitle: FBW7-dependent regulation of cMYC and MXD1 function by the vitamin D receptor
Keywords-MotsClés: CHIPSEQ; CMYC; FBW7; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; MXD1; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Growing epidemiological evidence suggests that maintaining vitamin D sufficiency reduces the risk of developing certain types of cancers, particularly cancers of the digestive tract. We have been interested in how the active form of vitamin D can control cancer cell proliferation, and have found that it inhibits both the production and function of cMYC in cancer cells through inhibiting the rate of production of new cMYC protein and through reducing the stability of existing cMYC protein. We also found that vitamin D stimulates the production and function of an antagonist of cMYC called MAD1/MXD1. Our goals are to understand in full the molecular mechanisms by which vitamin D controls cMYC and MXD1 function. These studies are important because they will provide a molecular basis for the potential cancer chemopreventive activities of vitamin D.

TitreApplicationTitle: Microscopic underpinnings of brain oxygen delivery with aging.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ATHEROSCLEROSIS; FMRI; MICRO-VASCULATURE; OXYGEN DELIVERY; TWO-PHOTON MICROSCOPY
Abstract-Résumé: In this project we will investigate the microscopic mechanisms associated with oxygen delivery to the brain and their changes with age and disease. Using new technological advances based on two-photon microscopy and optical coherence tomography, imaging of the microscopic distribution of oxygen will be performed and related to changes in blood flow within the micro-vasculature. As a last step, the impact of our results for clinical imaging and disease prevention will be investigated.

TitreApplicationTitle: Implication of atherosclerotic pathways and metabolic risk factors in the structural deterioration of bioprosthetic heart valves-II
Keywords-MotsClés: INFLAMMATION; LIPID; STRUCTURAL DETERIORATION; VALVE BIOPROSTHESES
Abstract-Résumé: Bioprosthesis (BP) are animal's derived tissues used by surgeons to replace diseased heart valves. These substitutes have many advantages for patients, including among them, the fact that these valves obviate the need for anti-coagulation treatment. However, their longevity after implantation is plagued by a phenomenon called structural valve deterioration (SVD). While it was thought for years that SVD was a passive process, for which no active treatment could prevent its development, our laboratory has recently identified that active mechanism (thus potentially modifiable) were involved in the deterioration of valve function. We have found that patients with obesity, diabetes, and renal failure have an increased risk to develop SVD. In addition, the ongoing research of our laboratory has also shown that a mechanism akin to atherosclerosis (a common disease of blood vessels in westernized societies) is participating to the development of SVD. Thus, the objective of our work is to understand the mechanisms that participate to SVD. These new and exciting discoveries open a new field of investigations with the hope to reduce or abolish in a near future the development of SVD increasing, therefore, the quality of life for patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: A prospective study of the impact of fear-avoidance variables and anxiety sensitivity on genital pain and sexual impairment after childbirth.
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY SENSITIVITY; FEAR-AVOIDANCE MODEL OF PAIN; GENITAL PAIN; POSTPARTUM PAIN; PROSPECTIVE STUDY; WOMEN'S HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic pain problems involving the female reproductive system are major health concerns and entail a great personal cost to affected women and their families since they are poorly understood and often ignored. One such condition is genital pain that develops after childbirth. The majority of women resume regular intercourse by three months postpartum, and about half experience it as painful. Under treated genital pain is a risk factor for developing chronic pain. According to the fear-avoidance model of pain, a woman may interpret pain as threatening leading to a fear of pain, anxiety, and excessive attention to the pain. Consequently, the woman avoids the painful activity, further strengthening the interpretation of the pain as threatening. Extensions of this model suggest that a higher fear of anxiety-related body sensations (anxiety sensitivity) may lead to excessive fear-avoidance. This model has been partially supported in a retrospective study of women with chronic genital pain. However, women from this study were previously diagnosed with genital pain and the study did not include anxiety sensitivity so the influence of fear-avoidance on the development of the pain could not be examined. The aim of the proposed study is to examine whether greater fear-avoidance and anxiety sensitivity in pregnancy predict the onset and severity of genital pain and decreased sexual functioning postpartum. First time mothers will complete measures of fear-avoidance and anxiety sensitivity during pregnancy, and measures of genital pain intensity and sexual functioning three months after childbirth. Results may identify women at greater risk for this condition and inform the development of interventions, which may lower genital pain intensity, improve sexual functioning, and reduce the risk of developing chronic pain. Findings could thus improve the health and quality of life of many women, since postpartum genital pain is a highly prevalent but neglected women's health problem.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dysregulation of neuronal mitochondrial function in diabetic sensory neuropathy.
Keywords-MotsClés: AMPK; ANIMAL MODELS; CONFOCAL IMAGING; DIABETES; METABOLISM; MITOCHONDRIA; NERVE REGENERATION; NEUROPATHY; TRANSGENIC MICE; VIRAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: Background. Diabetic neuropathy is a major complication of diabetes with no effective therapy. The incidence of peripheral nerve damage in diabetic patients can be 50% or higher and leads to incapacitating pain, sensory loss, foot ulceration (up to 2 million North Americans have this complaint) and lower extremity amputation often follows (accounts for 90,000 cases each year in North America). A primary feature of the disease is loss of nerve endings leading to denervation of the skin and subsequent sensory loss. Our recent work shows that mitochondria, the ells energy generator, are abnormal in sensory neurons, the cells that innervate the peripheral tissues, in diabetic rodents. Preliminary work. We show for the first time that an intracellular signaling pathway comprising AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), that senses the energy demands of cells and regulates mitochondrial function accordingly, is dysfunctional in animals models of type 1 and 2 diabetes. Hypothesis. We propose that in neurons under diabetic conditions the excess glucose causes AMPK to be deactivated and results in diminishment of mitochondrial activity. An innovative translational component of our work is the identification of cytokine treatment or blockade of the muscarinic acetylcholine type 1 receptor (M1R) as novel mechanisms to activate the AMPK pathway and mitochondrial function in neurons. Objectives. This proposal will determine if the AMPK signaling pathway is indeed a central regulator of mitochondrial function in neurons in diabetes. We wish to: (i)characterize the regulatory pathways that control this critical signaling axis, (ii)investigate global changes in gene expression, (iii)identify novel means of modulating pathway activity, for example using antimuscarinic drugs, in order to initiate new therapeutic opportunities for diabetic sensory neuropathy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Expression and Function of PPARgamma in Articular Joint Tissues
Keywords-MotsClés: CARTILAGE; CHROMATIN; CYTOKINES; EPIGENETICS; L-PGDS; METALLOPROTEINASES; OSTEOARTHRITIS; POLYMORPHISMS; PPARGAMMA; PROSTAGLANDINS
Abstract-Résumé: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most prevalent form of arthritis and the leading cause of disability in Canada and the rest of the world. The impact of this disease is expected to increase dramatically as a result of increased life expectancy and population aging. OA is characterized by chronic pain, cartilage degradation and loss of function. These processes are due to increased production of several inflammatory and catabolic mediators. So far, there is no efficient treatment for OA. We have demonstrated for the first time that PPARgamma activators inhibited several inflammatory and catabolic responses in vitro and were protective in animal models of the disease. We have also demonstrated that the L-PGDS products have anti-arthritic effects in vitro. In this project we will utilize different approaches to characterize the pattern of PPARg expression during OA and to define the role of L-PGDS in animal models of the disease. With regard to PPARg expression, we will analyse the role of DNA methylation in the regulation of this gene expression. With regard to L-PGDS, we will investigate the course of OA in L-PGDS deficient mice These studies will improve our understanding of the pathogenesis of OA and will be very helpful in developing more efficient therapeutic strategies for the treatment of OA and possibly other arthritic diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clonal evolution of medulloblastoma BTICs (brain tumor initiating cells) in response to therapy: Discovering the refractory BTIC population through genes regulating stem cell self-renewal
Keywords-MotsClés: BRAIN TUMOR INITIATING CELL (BTIC); BRAIN TUMORS; CD133 REPORTER AND LINEAGE TRACING; CLONAL TRACKING THROUGH THERAPY; FLOW CYTOMETRY AND CELL SORTING; GENE EXPRESSION PROFILING; HUMAN-MOUSE XENOGRAFTS; PEDIATRIC MEDULLOBLASTOMA; STEM CELL BIOLOGY; TREATMENT-REFRACTORY BTIC
Abstract-Résumé: Brain tumors represent the leading cause of childhood cancer mortality, due to their highly aggressive and often incurable nature. For medulloblastoma, the most frequent malignant pediatric brain tumor, a stem cell origin has long been implicated. The current project examines the molecular factors governing stem cell regulation that may be disrupted to result in medulloblastoma formation and tumor recurrence despite best current therapy. Self-renewal, a unique property of stem cells, is defined as the ability of the parental stem cell to generate another daughter stem cell, along with a second cell. We will examine how genes that regulate self-renewal of normal neural stem cells may be disrupted to give rise to abnormal brain cancer stem cells, known as brain tumor initiating cells (BTICs). BTIC populations are known to be resistant to both radiotherapy and chemotherapy, and higher fractions of BTICs escaping therapy may explain why some patients relapse despite current best therapy. We will study the function of these BTIC self-renewal genes and their molecular pathways in regulating stem cell populations in human medulloblastoma, using stem cell biology experimental approaches and animal models. Using an animal model that adapts current radiation and chemotherapy for medulloblastoma patients to mice, we can profile BTIC self-renewal throughout therapy to discover how BTICs evolve and change to evade therapy and cause tumor relapse. Currently, a specific subset of medulloblastoma patients still suffers from poor outcomes and relapse leading to death. Discovery of stem cell self-renewal pathways activated in these subtypes could provide much-needed BTIC-specific therapeutic targets, leading to an improved risk-benefit profile for current survivors, and an overall improved survivorship for all medulloblastoma patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modeling the reproducibility of blood assays for TB infection
Keywords-MotsClés: DIAGNOSIS; INTERFERON-GAMMA RELEASE ASSAYS; MODELING; REPEAT TESTING; TUBERCULOSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Tuberculosis (TB) infects a third of the world's population, and nearly 9 million cases occur every year. Health care workers (HCWs) are at higher risk of TB and therefore are repeatedly tested (for example, every year) with a skin test to identify latent TB infection (not yet an active disease). Over the past few years, blood-based tests called interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) have been increasingly used instead of the skin test. While IGRAs are more accurate than skin tests, evidence is showing that in some cases, if you test someone more than once (as is the case with HCWs) their IGRA result could be different each time: some tests change from negative to positive (conversion) and some from positive to negative (reversion). Because of this variation of IGRA test results, hospitals face a challenge: how to interpret a HCW's IGRA test results if these differ every year? In this context, it's important to understand how likely these variations are to occur and how to interpret them clinically (for example, what is the risk of disease in a patient who is positive one year and negative in the next year without intervention). To do this, we will construct a mathematical model with 100,000 hypothetical individuals that will be representative of North American HCWs. Within this model, we will assess the different factors that can affect the variability of the test. The data for the model will come from a systematic review of all available literature on IGRA testing reproducibility and from experiments of one of our collaborators. This model should allow us to understand how many conversions are true new TB infections, and how many are random (not new cases of TB), and to define new guidelines on how to interpret results from IGRAs in serial testing. We hope that the results from this project can inform policies on TB diagnosis in HCWs in North America.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms regulating mRNA localization and translational control
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL CYCLE REGULATION; CELL DIFFERENTIATION; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; FLUORESCENT IN SITU HYBRIDIZATION; MRNA TRANSPORT AND LOCALIZATION; RNA-BINDING PROTEINS; TRANSLATIONAL CONTROL; YEAST
Abstract-Résumé: Some proteins are needed all over the cell, but others need to be expressed only at a specific site within the cell. Cells can achieve local synthesis of proteins by transporting and localizing mRNA to a specific site. This process plays an important role in the development of multicellular organisms, in cell motility and in neuronal growth.  Defects in the localization pathway or local translation of specific mRNAs are linked to increased cancer cell motility and neurological diseases, such as Fragile X syndrome and motor neurons disorders, so understanding this process is medically relevant.  Our research aims at identifying the mechanism of action of various factors involved in the assembly and regulation of the mRNA localization and translational control machineries. It is important for the synthesis of proteins to be inhibited until the mRNA reaches its final destination so that proteins are made only where the cell needs them. We are using the budding yeast as a model system for studying these mechanisms, as several mRNAs are known to be sorted and locally translated at the bud tip of yeast cells. Furthermore, key factors involved in this process in yeast have homologs in human. This is an organism of choice for the characterization of molecular processes because of the multiple genetic, cellular and molecular biology tools available. In this proposal, we will investigate the coupling between the mRNA localization and translational control machineries during their recruitment on nascent localized transcripts.  Moreover, we will study the role of post-translational modifications in the regulation of the localization process during the cell cycle and in the local activation of protein synthesis, when mRNAs reach their destination.  This grant will support our continuing effort to characterize the localization and translational control machineries, and explore their role in the spatio-temporal regulation of mRNA translation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Novel Adhesion Molecules Regulating CNS Inflammation
Keywords-MotsClés: ADHESION MOLECULES; ANTIGEN PRESENTING CELLS; BLOOD BRAIN BARRIER; ENDOTHELIUM; IMMUNOPHARMACOLOGY; LYMPHOCYTES; MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS; NEURO-INFLAMMATION
Abstract-Résumé: Immune cells, called leukocytes travel from the blood to local sites of inflammation where they initiate and maintain tissue-specific immune responses. Normally, the brain is not easily accessible to cells of the immune system due to the presence of the endothelial blood-brain barrier (BBB). However, in the disease Multiple Sclerosis (MS), an autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system (CNS), a large number of inflammatory immune cells known as pro-inflammatory lymphocytes readily cross the BBB to infiltrate the brain and to trigger the formation of lesions. The movement of such aggressive lymphocytes, from the blood to the CNS, is orchestrated by many factors, including cell adhesion molecules (CAMs). CAMs enable immune cells to adhere and cross over the BBB to infiltrate the CNS. We have identified MCAM (for Melanoma Cell Adhesion Molecule) as a novel CAM expressed by endothelial cells of the BBB, and found it to play a central role in the migration of aggressive immune cells into the CNS. The current research application focuses on this newly discovered molecule used by immune cells to enter the CNS and to promote the development of MS lesions, and more specifically on the role of MCAM on the trans-migration of very aggressive and CNS-attacking CD8 lymphocytes. Using a combination of human in vitro and in situ experiments, combined with mouse in vivo models of MS, we propose to elucidate the role of MCAM in CD8 lymphocyte migration and to identify novel biological therapeutics (Antibodies that can be used in human) to neutralize MCAM and to reduce the formation of inflammatory plaques in MS. This project expands our research program which aims at identifying attractive target for the development of novel therapies for the treatment of MS and other inflammatory diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Adaptive Cortical Plasticity Following Deafness
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY CORTEX; CORTICAL CONNECTIONS; CORTICAL DEVELOPMENT; CORTICAL PLASTICITY; DEAFNESS; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL RECORDING; FMRI; HEARING; REVERSIBLE DEACTIVATION; VISUAL CORTEX
Abstract-Résumé: Hearing loss is the third most common chronic disability, affecting one in ten Canadians. Moreover, hearing loss is the most common birth defect in Canada, yet little is known about what occurs to the brain as a consequence of deafness. In this proposal we will be studying what happens inside the brain following the onset of deafness shortly after birth or in adulthood. Specifically, we will be studying the regions of the brain that normally process sounds in hearing individuals. To do this we will examine deafness in an animal model. This approach will permit us to examine the activity of individual neurons, to examine changes in brain circuitry and activity, and to examine how changes in the brain affect perception and behavior. If the part of the brain that normally processes hearing is not receiving sound, then what is it doing? Is it processing visual information? Is it processing information concerning touch? If it is processing sight, then it may very well help explain the increased visual abilities of deaf humans. Changes in the brain such as this are known as "plastic" changes, or simply "plasticity". These changes are also called "adaptive" because they help the subject enhance their ability to use their remaining senses. Therefore, the goal of this study is to examine the natural adaptive plasticity of the brain. Knowing how the brain responds to changes in its inputs in this way will help us develop appropriate therapeutic strategies to help increase brain plasticity and help patients to overcome conditions such as deafness and blindness.

TitreApplicationTitle: Criminal charges of HIV non-disclosure: impacts on the lives of people living with HIV and AIDS
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HEALTH AND CRIMINAL LAW; HIV NON-DISCLOSURE AND CRIMINAL LAW; HIV-RELATED STIGMA AND DISCRIMINATION; IN-DEPTH SEMI-STRUCTURED INTERVIEWS; INTERSECTIONAL ANALYSIS OF HIV; QUALITATIVE HEALTH RESEARCH; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, HIV positive people are increasingly charged criminally for not telling their HIV status to sexual partners. This is known as the criminalization of HIV non-disclosure. There is no evidence that this helps prevent the spread of HIV. In fact, people with HIV have been imprisoned even when they have used condoms or when there has been no HIV transmission. This punitive climate is driving people away from proven HIV prevention and support services. HIV is not what it once was. Treatments for HIV have dramatically improved quality of life and have made HIV very hard to transmit. But still today, HIV is a highly stigmatized disease. Telling people your HIV-positive status can result in discrimination and violence. Experts state that the complexities underlying HIV disclosure and prevention are not suited to a criminal law context. The recent Supreme Court of Canada decision reinforced a legal approach on this issue and has opened the door for further charges. Up until 2010 there have been 122 cases, with charges ranging from sexual assault to attempted murder. This project will ask the question: How has the experience of being charged in relation to HIV non-disclosure impacted peoples lives, and what are the implications for human rights and the HIV response? This Community Based Research project will interview up to 20 people who have been charged in relation to not disclosing their HIV status. Interview participants will include men and women from across Canada. This project will be conducted in partnership with Concordia University, Ontario Working Group on Criminal Law and HIV Exposure, Prisoners AIDS Support Action Network, and the HIV and AIDS Legal Clinic Ontario. There has been no study of the experiences of people in Canada who faced these charges firsthand. This research will offer new insight to help understand the personal, social and human rights implications of this practice to help inform responses and alternatives.

TitreApplicationTitle: An evaluation of governmental policy relating to HIV/AIDS funding and service delivery within First Nations communities in Ontario, Canada.
Keywords-MotsClés: FIRST NATIONS; FUNDING; HEALTH POLICY; HIV/AIDS; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOGIES
Abstract-Résumé: This research will examine how policy (namely the Indian Act, Canada Health Act, Indian Transfer payments, and Constitution Acts 1867 to 1982) impacts funding distribution and the accessibility of HIV/AIDS programs for status First Nations (FN) people within reserves of Ontario. Grounded in Indigenous and Critical Race Theory, this research will utilize a variety of academic and Indigenous research approaches to examine how the aforementioned policies affect funding and resources for HIV/AIDS within FNs. This study will explore the policies and funding arrangements for HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment. Particular attention will be given to the origin of funding/services, how they are utilized, and the specific role each level of government (Federal/Provincial) plays in the delivery of HIV/AIDS services. Furthermore, this research project will seek participants in four FN communities who have received HIV/AIDS services. Participants will complete surveys and take part in Sharing Circles to discuss their ability to access needed services, their experiences with the services, and changes they would suggest.   Overall, this research will expose the availability and sufficiency of funding and services within communities while analyzing the policies that have created systemic barriers. The objective is to examine how federal policy impacts the funding and service delivery of HIV/AIDS services (and how those services are perceived by clients and practitioners) and therefore, what processes/actions can be taken by the federal/provincial governments and FN communities to reevaluate current practices of funding and service delivery to improve any inefficiencies' which may be found. This is done in order to offer better services to people and communities that are affected by the HIV/AIDS epidemic and to find ways policy can help in stopping the spread of HIV/AIDS within these communities.

TitreApplicationTitle: Arts-based HIV/AIDS Education for Aboriginal Youth in Labrador: A community-based participatory action research project
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; ARTS-BASED; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HIV PREVENTION; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOGIES; LABRADOR; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: In Canada, Aboriginal people continue to be overrepresented in the HIV/AIDS epidemic with rates of infection three times higher than the general population. In Labrador, the need for an HIV/AIDS prevention program was identified by Labrador HIV/AIDS Surveillance Study.  Arts-based approaches (such as music, storytelling and photography) have been recognized as innovative and promising strategies for HIV/AIDS education with Aboriginal youth. However, there is a lack of research exploring how these interventions work, as well as how they are implemented and experienced by both the participants and implementers. Working in collaboration with the Labrador Friendship Centre HIV Project, we will develop, implement and evaluate an arts-based program for the youth they serve to evaluate the effectiveness and experience of participating in an arts-based program. A community-based participatory action research design incorporating Indigenous methodologies will be implemented.  This HIV/AIDS education program will be guided by a Steering Committee, comprised of stakeholders including community leaders, elders and youth targeted by this program. Tools to assess the effectiveness and value of the program will be created in consultation with the Steering Committee. Interviews will be conducted with key informants. The findings of this research project will have a direct and immediate impact on HIV/AIDS education in Labrador and will inform future arts-based HIV/AIDS education initiatives.

TitreApplicationTitle: Kw'amkw'um S'uli Tst; Strengthening our Spirit. Culture as Intervention among the Cowichan Tribes
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; COMMUNITY BASED RESEARCH; COMMUNITY CAPACITY BUILDING; CULTURE AS INTERVENTION; ELDERS; INTERGENERATIONAL TRAUMA; INTERVENTION PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS; TRADITIONAL CULTURAL KNOWLEDGE
Abstract-Résumé: Kw'makw'um S'uli works with Elders to learn the content and applicability of Traditional Cultural Knowledge (TCK).   Our objectives are two pronged. Our team will develop Elders' capacity through education on the social and clinical aspects of HIV/AIDS, including the need for early testing and adherence to treatment; Secondly, once Elders are familiar with the issues, they will share advice about feelings of loss, fear, stigma and addiction.   The last decade has seen a dramatic increase in research finding the benefit and need for the inclusion of TCK into Aboriginal intervention programs. But, What is TCK, and does it have the capacity to discuss contemporary issues of sex, intravenous drugs and HIV/AIDS?   Our research has found that Elders' advice is rich with suggested applications of TCK for intervention programming. It is also rich with specific coping mechanisms for stigma, fear and despair; optimistic perspectives on an individual's responsibility to the self and community, prayers and personal stories of overcoming addiction and trauma. Very often, the advice comes in the Hul'q'umi'num', Coast Salish language. These quotes will be translated to English, and included in a booklet with accompanying CD. These will be a useful tools for future intervention program development, such as would bring youth together with Elders. The audio and textual materials can be used to expand the capacity of a further pool of Elders. As critical as these materials will be to future intervention programmers, much will also be learned from the process of KT from Western clinical paradigms into traditional ones.  Subsequent translation of traditional advice into relevant information for the research community will be published in journals for this purpose.

TitreApplicationTitle: Inquiring into HIV prevention and care for pregnant and early parenting women experiencing homelessness.
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; AIDS; HIV; HOMELESS; INTERVENTION; QUALITATIVE; STREET INVOLVED; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: The purpose of the proposed research is to inquire into a community-based program for vulnerable street involved and homeless pregnant and early parenting women at risk for Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)infection. People who are homeless are at increased risk for HIV and HIV infection rates are significantly higher amongst this population. According to the Federal Initiative to Address HIV/AIDS in Canada, poverty, lack of affordable housing, homelessness, racism and stigma, all contribute to disease progression and a person's ability to manage and live with the disease. A community based research approach will provide the conceptual framework for this study, as this ensures that research priorities meet the interests of the community; community members are active participants in the process, and the research contributes to social change. In collaboration with Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal agencies we will inquire narratively into the life experiences of street involved and pregnant and early parenting women in precarious housing situations who are HIV positive or at risk for HIV, as well as the experiences of care providers as they provide care for this population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Refining the Research Response: An Aboriginal HIV & AIDS Research Strategy for Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; AIDS; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HEALTH RESEARCH; HIV; INDIGENOUS METHODOLOY; RESEARCH
Abstract-Résumé: Rates of HIV continue to increase within the Aboriginal population in Canada, particularly within the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. In response to this alarming trend, diverse stakeholders are seeking new evidence to inform strategic responses to prevent new infections, eliminate stigma and discrimination and reduce AIDS-related deaths. The Canadian Aboriginal AIDS Network (CAAN) is strategically positioned as a national leader in Aboriginal Community-based Research and has identified this project as a priority. The aim of this operating grant is to contribute to the creation, dissemination and use of a strategic research agenda in response to HIV & AIDS in the Aboriginal community for Canada.   Our research will be implemented in three phases and consistent with conducting research with Aboriginal peoples, the First Nation ethical principles of OCAP will be adhered to. CBR emphasizes capacity building, thus a research coordinator and peer research associates will work together taking responsibility for the research activities guided by our highly skilled team. Phase 1 activities include preparing a literature review, to be presented as the launch of strategic consultations. Phase 2 will consist of planning, organizing and holding 14 focus groups across the country. The outcome of each focus group will be compiled into a report for review and approval from the participants and then made immediately available online as part of our integrated KTE plan. Phase 3 activities include in-depth analysis of the focus group data to be conducted by the research team members. The data analysis findings and literature review will then be compiled into a final document and presented at the Wise Practices V, Aboriginal HIV & AIDS CBR Gathering in 2015. Each phase of this research project will build upon the previous one with careful attention to the KTE process to ensure that engagement and uptake of the research contributes to new knowledge.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Resonance Project - Emerging Biomedical Discourses and Decisions within Gay Men's Knowledge Networks
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMEDICAL KNOWLEDGE; COMMUNICATION TOOLS; CULTURAL RESONANCE; GAY MEN; HIV PREVENTION; KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION AND EXCHANGE
Abstract-Résumé: This project was conceived by CATIE, the Canadian AIDS Society, the Interagency Coalition on AIDS and Development, and the Canadian Public Health Association. Recognizing the steadily growing and evolving biomedical knowledge of HIV, the Resonance Project has the objectives to critically examine: - if/how gay men are taking up biomedical knowledge of HIV - if/how biomedical knowledge of HIV has resonance for their everyday lives  - the discourses men use to make sense of risk, and inform their sexual decision-making and practices, and - the roles and responsibilities of institutions and service providers in shaping these discourses.    The research questions are: 1. In what ways do gay and bisexual men living in Canada - individually and as communities - make sense of, incorporate into their understanding, and modify their behaviours based on, biomedical knowledge of HIV? 2. How are community-based organizations and service providers succeeding and struggling in integrating new biomedical knowledge of HIV within their existing (and evolving) social, structural and behavioural prevention efforts?   3. What key elements - main messages, precautions and caveats - must be incorporated into communication about biomedical knowledge of HIV to be sensitive to the lived realities of gay and bisexual men and their communities?   This research project will be conducted through 5 phases, moving through an iterative process from understanding to knowledge translation and exchange.  The outcomes of this research project will help HIV prevention stakeholders to identify how they should be integrating recent and emerging biomedical knowledge of HIV into current prevention programs and policies in Canada in ways that are best supported by, and supportive of, people at risk of HIV.

TitreApplicationTitle: Positive Living, Positive Homes: Navigating HIV and Housing Policies and Programs in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: AIDS SERVICE ORGANIZATIONS; CASE STUDY METHODOLOGY; HIV/AIDS; HOUSING POLICY; QUALITATIVE; SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
Abstract-Résumé: Positive Living, Positive Homes (PLPH) will be the first study in BC to focus specifically on housing and HIV. This study will use a qualitative case study approach to examine how local and provincial policies and programs interact with and impact PHAs' abilities to manage their health and wellbeing and to highlight policies and programs that can be used as models across jurisdictions in BC. PLPH will document the successes and challenges of various housing-related programs, services and policies from three case study communities - Vancouver, Kamloops and Prince George - each of which face significantly different housing needs and pressures, and have distinct housing and HIV service structures. To achieve this, we will interview 125 people living with HIV at two time points and a total of 60 service providers, service users, and decision makers from the three communities. These qualitative findings will complement the descriptive, quantitative data on the housing circumstances and needs of over 300 PHAs in BC available through the Food Security and HIV Study as well as the policy analysis data from Phase I of PLPH. The result will be actionable evidence about PHA's housing experiences and program, service and policy best practices with HIV-related housing service providers and community based organizations. This community-based research project is the culmination of a four-year community-driven process to respond to an identified need for HIV housing. PLPH has already been an important catalytic agent for CBR in BC through the collaborative process of PHASE I, and the PHASE II will provide the tools for aligning housing policy in BC with coordinated responses to HIV/AIDS in order to achieve outcomes that will enhance the health and wellbeing of PHAs throughout the province.

TitreApplicationTitle: Au-delà du VIH: être femme plurielle. Recherche évaluative participative pour le bien-être sexuel des femmes vivant avec le VIH du Québec
Keywords-MotsClés: APPLICATION DES CONNAISSANCES; EFFETS; FEMMES VIVANT AVEC LE VIH (FVVIH); INTERVENTION CIBLEE; RECHERCHE EVALUATIVE-PARTICIPATIVE; SANTE SEXUELLE
Abstract-Résumé: Rares sont les interventions axees sur la sante sexuelle et affective des femmes vivant avec le VIH (FVVIH). Les thematiques telles que l'intimite, l'affirmation de ses besoins sexuels, le sentiment d'etre desirable, la feminite, les relations amoureuses ou encore les dysfonctions sexuelles, sont peu explorees. Voulant repondre a cette preoccupation, une equipe de chercheurs de Montreal, en partenariat avec des organismes communautaires quebecois de lutte contre le VIH/sida et des FVVIH souhaite developper, valider et evaluer un programme d'empowerment visant le bien-etre sexuel des FVVIH du Quebec. La presente etude, d'une duree de trois ans (2013-2016, est un projet de recherche participative de nature evaluative. L'objectif general est de mobiliser les utilisatrices des connaissances (FVVIH et intervenantes des organismes communautaires) dans le but d'adapter, d'implanter et d'evaluer l'intervention a l'echelle provinciale (Quebec). Pour ce faire, une formation sera developpee et offerte aux utilisatrices des connaissances. Par la suite, l'intervention sera implantee per ces dernieres dans plusieurs milieux a Montreal et en regions, et evaluee aupres des FVVIH. De plus, des activites de valorisation des experiences et de partage des connaissances seront realisees. Les elements qui constituent l'evaluation, comme les methodes et les instruments de collecte de donnees, ainsi que les strategies de partage des connaissances seront choisis, developpes et precises par, avec et pour les utilisatrices des connaissances. Etant donne la rarete des programmes d'intervention visant l'amelioration de la sante sexuelle et affective des FVVIH, si l'intervention developpee est efficace et implantee de facon persistante, d'autre FVVIH quebecoises et, a plus long terme, d'autre FVVIH canadiennes et d'ailleurs pourront profiter des benefices d'une telle intervention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cross-Canada best practice recommendations for harm reduction programs - research evidence syntheses and dissemination
Keywords-MotsClés: BEST PRACTICE RECOMMENDATIONS; COMMUNITY-BASED RESEARCH; HARM REDUCTION; HIV PREVENTION; INJECTION DRUG USERS
Abstract-Résumé: Drug use practices that can lead to transmission of HIV and blood-borne infections are pressing issues affecting communities throughout Canada. Existing best practice recommendations for needle and syringe programs are out of date. To stay current with the best available scientific evidence and ensure that people have access to high-quality services that help prevent HIV transmission, best practices must undergo review and update. Our goal is to create an updated set of user-friendly recommendations that will benefit harm reduction programs across the country. Our community-based team has members from across Canada representing people who use drugs, service providers, researchers, and policy makers. We use a consensus process to make all project decisions. We are applying to complete Phases 3 and 4 of our project. Phase 1, during which we designed the project, was funded by a CIHR MPD grant. In Phase 2, funded by the AIDS Bureau, we reviewed scientific evidence to create best practice recommendations related to distribution of needles, distribution of other injecting equipment, distribution of safer crack use equipment, disposal of used drug equipment, and safer drug use education.  Phase 3 involves reviewing scientific evidence and creating best practice recommendations related to: program delivery models; safer sex education; overdose prevention; other services; primary care; relationships with other agencies; involvement of people who use drugs in program delivery; program monitoring; and staffing.  In Phase 4, the best practice recommendations will be reviewed by external experts. Using the reviews, we will finalise the recommendations and then make the recommendations available through online seminars and workshops, "chat with the expert" events, and electronic copies. By using a broad dissemination strategy, we will reach a wide audience who will use the document, including people who use drugs and service providers, at harm reduction programs across Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: The cellular life and function of pannexins
Keywords-MotsClés: CHANNELS; CONNEXINS; GENETICALLY-MODIFIED MICE; PANNEXINS; SKELETON; SKIN
Abstract-Résumé: Most cells in the human body need to consistently talk to each other and exchange information.  Cell to cell communication can be mediated by connexin channels called gap junctions that directly allow the exchange of signals.  In other cases, information encoded in small molecules are released through specialized channels only to be recaptured by receptors or channels that reside on the surface of neighboring cells. In the present study we are focusing on a new class of channel forming proteins called pannexins that allow small molecules carrying important signals to enter and leave the cell.  Already these unique channels have been demonstrated to be important in sending find me signals to clear dead or dying cells. In disease, pannexin channels have been linked to ischemic and epileptic damage in the brain.  In addition, our evidence suggests that these channels are very important in skeletal development and skin differentiation. In the present study we will determine what regulates the function of the channels allowing them to release or uptake important signalling molecules. Using newly generated genetically-modified mice that lack one or two members of the pannexin family we will assess the skin and skeleton for abnormalities. Finally, since preliminary data suggests pannexin channels may be important in skeletal diseases, we will determine if the loss of one or more pannexins will lead to the acceleration or reversion of osteoarthritis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and functional properties of mucosal pathogenic dendritic cells in chronic inflammatory bowel diseases
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGY OF DENDRITIC CELLS; HUMAN IMMUNOLGY; INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASES; NEW TARGET FOR IBD
Abstract-Résumé: Crohn's disease (CD) and Ulcerative colitis (UC) are common chronic inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) of modern society. IBD patients experience symptoms such as abdominal pain, cramping, weight loss, fever, fatigue, nausea/vomiting and diarrhea. The incidence of IBD is rising, especially in Canada, where its prevalence is said to be among the highest in the world. Inflammation and tissue injury characteristic of CD can be found anywhere along the digestive tract while that of UC is restricted to the colon. The disease pathogenesis is thought to result from an inappropriate, exaggerated immune response in genetically-prone individuals. The currently available therapies for IBD, more particularly CD are often associated with serious side effects and highlight the need for continued research in this field. Dendritic cells (DCs) are a specialized cell type implicated in the initiation and perpetuation of immune responses. Therefore, when dysregulated, DCs may misinterpret a harmless encounter as being harmful and initiate an unnecessary immune response, leading to chronic intestinal inflammation. We identified the human counterpart of the mouse DCs (CD172a+ DCs) that promote intestinal inflammation in an experimental model of CD. We further showed that CD172a+ DCs accumulate in lymphoid and inflamed gut tissues of CD patients where they represent the major source of pro-inflammatory cytokines. In this proposal, we plan to investigate the cellular origin, the molecular signature and the detailed functional properties of CD172a+ DCs. We also plan to search for these pathogenic cells in tissues of UC patients with the aim of identifying properties (for instance biomarkers) that may help in the differential diagnosis between UC and CD. As such, detailed analysis of molecular and functional characteristics of these cells may contribute to our knowledge of disease pathogenesis and/or translate into the development of new diagnosis and therapeutic targets.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Effects of Acute Exercise on Cognitive Processes in Children with ADHD
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE EXERCISE; ATTENTION; ATTENTION-DEFICIT HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER; CHILDREN; CLINICAL; DIVIDED ATTENTION; EXERCISE; MENTAL HEALTH; SUSTAINED ATTENTION; WORKING MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: Exercise is effective in reducing behavioural symptoms of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). This study will examine whether acute exercise is also beneficial to the cognitive processes that are often impaired in children with ADHD (e.g., impaired sustained attention, divided attention, and working memory). Cognitive processes will be assessed for 36 children with ADHD, who will be randomly assigned to exercise (e.g., 20 minutes of moderate intensity exercise) or control (e.g., 20 minute exercise video) groups.   It is expected that a single session of exercise will improve the cognitive processes of children with ADHD. The implications of the present study are that it will assess executive functioning processes that have yet to be examined, the findings will offer health practitioners a multimodal perspective on ADHD, and will inform education and health communities on ideal learning conditions for children with ADHD. Further, the results of the present study will provide clinicians with potential recommendations for managing cognitive symptoms in a classroom setting.
