TitreApplicationTitle: Chloride homeostasis in neural development and disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CHLORIDE TRANSPORT; EPIGENETICS; GENE EXPRESSION; INTERNEURONS; MICROARRAY; NEURAL DEVELOPMENT; NEUROPATHY; NOTCH; STEM CELL; ZEBRAFISH EMBRYO
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding how the nervous system develops normally, as well as abnormally in hereditary diseases, requires an understanding of the genes that are critical for brain development.  Furthermore, repairing the diseased or damaged nervous system will ultimately require manipulating the expression of these genes.  The zebrafish has emerged as a leading model for studies of vertebrate (and by extension human) developmental genetics because of the ease in manipulating and studying their embryos.  Our group has defined key elements of the circuitry in the embryonic zebrafish spinal cord that are conserved across species.  It is hypothesized that the cellular concentration of chloride ions is important for regulating the generation of neurons and development of connections between them in neural circuits.  To directly test the role of chloride signaling, we propose to manipulate gene expression in the zebrafish embryo in order to alter the chloride ion concentration during development of the spinal cord circuitry.  We will then examine the consequences of these manipulations by studying neural development and a model for peripheral neuropathy.  Based on the mechanisms discovered in zebrafish embryos, we will test gene activities in stem cells from the adult mouse brain to determine the potential of regulating the production of new adult neurons.

TitreApplicationTitle: Plasma non-esterified fatty acids and the progression of insulin resistance and pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction: a novel targeted omics approach.
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA CELL DYSFUNCTION; DIABETES MELLITUS; INSULIN RESISTANCE; NON-ESTEREFIED FATTY ACIDS; TYPE 2
Abstract-Résumé: Elevations in total blood free fatty acids can be used to predict the risk of developing insulin resistance, which increases the risk of type 2 (adult-onset) diabetes mellitus. In the blood, fatty acids are found in specific compartments, commonly called pools. Furthermore, about 25 fatty acids commonly make up the total free fatty acid pool. It is well known that the 25 individual fatty acids are chemically and biologically very different. In this study we will separate out four individual blood fatty acid pools and, using sophisticated equipment, measure the 16 fatty acids that make up the free fatty acid pool. We hypothesize that specific fatty acids will predict the risk of developing insulin resistance more than others. To test this hypothesis we will examine baseline blood fatty acids from 712 subjects at risk for type 2 DM who have been followed for over 3 years. If specific fatty acids predict insulin resistance, we could develop improved screening methods and have new mechanistic insight as to how elevated fatty acids lead to adult-onset diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Linguistic Analysis of Communication Between Therapist and Patient During the Course of Therapist-Assisted Internet Cognitive Behaviour Therapy for Generalized Anxiety
Keywords-MotsClés: GENERALIZED ANXIETY DISORDER; HEALTH PSYCHOLOGY; INTERNET COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; LINGUISTIC ANALYSIS
Abstract-Résumé: Therapist-assisted Internet Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (ICBT) is an empirically supported method of treating mental health disorders including generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).  In addition to the standard cognitive and behavioural elements found within face-to-face Cognitive Behaviour Therapy, therapist-assisted ICBT includes elements of expressive writing, through email communication with a therapist.  Expressive writing has been associated with numerous positive outcomes; furthermore, certain linguistic dimensions in expressive writing have been associated with psychological and physical health benefits.  No research to date has analyzed linguistic dimensions in patient communication over the course of a therapist-assisted ICBT program.  The purpose of the current study is to understand how patients with GAD are communicating with their online therapists, and if their communication style has an impact on their psychotherapeutic outcome.  Participants are patients (n = 100) with GAD that completed a 12-module therapist-assisted ICBT program at the Online Therapy Unit for Service, Education, and Research at the University of Regina. A set of outcome variables, including anxiety symptoms, worry symptoms, adjustment, and quality of life was assessed pre-treatment, mid-treatment, and post-treatment.  Text communication from patients to their therapists over the course of therapy will be analyzed by a text analysis program that categorizes text, word-by word, into different linguistic categories (e.g., positive or negative emotion, insight words; reported as percentage of total words).  If communication style does impact treatment outcomes, findings could impact the way therapist-assisted ICBT is delivered in the future.  For example, clients may be provided with guidance on how to write more effectively, in hopes optimizing beneficial outcomes from the program.

TitreApplicationTitle: Theoretical Studies of Ion Translocation in Membrane Proteins
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPUTER SIMULATIONS; CYTOCHROME C OXIDASE; FREE ENERGY CALCULATIONS; ION CHANNELS; ION TRANSLOCATION; IONIC SELECTIVITY; MOLECULAR MECHANISM; SINGLE-CHANNEL CONDUCTANCE; SODIUM CHANNEL; VOLTAGE-GATED PROTON CHANNEL
Abstract-Résumé: The movement of ions such as protons, sodium, and potassium, across biological membranes fulfills a myriad of physiological functions involved in vital processes such as heartbeat, muscle contraction, egg fertilization, and respiration.   We know that the movement of these ions is controlled by tiny, specialized molecular machines called proteins, which are embedded in biological membranes and which work either as pumps or as mills that use the flow of ions productively.  However, we don't understand how these machines work.  Because ions are extremely small (a million times smaller than the width of a hair) and move extremely fast (a million go through each protein every second), it is very hard to follow their movement using experimental techniques.  In order to figure out how membrane proteins work, we use large computers to mimic or simulate the movement of ions across membranes.   The insight gained from this work will help understand important processes of relevance to human health and disease.  We will study three molecular machines required for breathing, for fighting infections, for fertility, and for the propagation of electrical impulses in the heart, in muscles, and in nerve cells.  Ultimately, this work will also help us figure out the role that these machines play in breast cancer, brain damage, hemiplegic migraine, extreme pain, and periodic paralysis, and may contribute to developing cures to these devastating diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clinical and molecular heterogeneity of Paget's disease of Bone
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTOPHAGY; BONE REMODELING; BONE RESORPTION; CLINICAL PHENOTYPE; FUNCTIONAL ANALYSIS; MEASLES VIRUS NUCLEOCAPSID PROTEIN; OPTINEURIN GENE; OSTEOCLASTIC PHENOTYPE; PAGET'S DISEASE OF BONE; SQSTM1/P392L MUTATION
Abstract-Résumé: Paget's disease of bone (PDB) is a common bone disorder, affecting approximately three percent of people over 55 years of age. This disease may lead to severe disabilities, including most frequently bone pain, fractures and bone deformity. A genetic component of this disease is already known and a mutation in a gene linked to PDB has been described in some French-Canadian families. However this genetic variation does not fully explain the development of the disease, in particular when some common virus envelopes are absent, and in more than half of families with PDB, the causal genes are still unknown.  In this study, we aim at 1) studying how three other genes may be involved in the development of this disease, 2) determining the factors that give rise to early clinical symptoms and cellular changes in healthy relatives carrier of the already known mutation, and 3) explaining how about one third of patients may develop PDB even in the absence of common virus envelopes cited above.  This research project will lead to a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms of this and other similar bone diseases which are increasingly prevalent in our aging Canadian population, such as osteoporosis and bone metastases.  Enhancing our knowledge of the factors associated with the early stages of development of these common bone diseases will facilitate the discovery of new innovative treatments to better control bone cells activity. Preventing and appropriately treating bone diseases would have a major impact on public health by decreasing the direct and indirect costs associated with chronic bone diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: microRNA Regulation of PGC-1alpha: Role in Atherosclerosis and Obesity
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; DIABETES; FATTY ACID METABOLISM; INFLAMMATION; MICRORNA; MITOCHONDRIA; OBESITY
Abstract-Résumé: Heart disease affects over one million Canadians, and costs the Canadian healthcare system over 20 billion dollars annually. Atherosclerosis, a leading cause of heart disease, is a buildup of cholesterol, immnune cells and calcium in the arteries that feed your heart muscle with blood. Diabetes is also an important risk factor for heart disease, and can develop in a similar way to atherosclerosis. The goal of our research is to investigate new mechanisms that contribute to atherosclerosis and diabetes and to design new therapies to treat these diseases. We propose to study how a small RNA molecule, called microRNA-33, affects the risk factors for heart disease. Specifically, we want to know if miR-33 turns on/off a gene called PGC-1alpha, which is an important factor involved in how our bodies use energy. PGC-1alpha can increase "good" fat (brown fat), reduce diabetes, and improve heart disease. We believe that miR-33 controls PGC-1alpha, so therapies to inhibit miR-33 would increase PGC-1alpha and would improve diabetes and atherosclerosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Identifying policy interventions to reduce household food insecurity in Canada
Keywords-MotsClés: DOCOSAHEXAENOIC ACID; INFLAMMATION RESOLUTION; MOUSE MODEL; RESOLVINS
Abstract-Résumé: Uncontrolled and excessive inflammation is linked to several chronic diseases including vascular and neurological disease. Recent evidence suggests resolution of inflammation is not a passive clearance of pro-inflammatory mediators, as was once thought, but is an active process with its own anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving mediators.   Specialized Pro-resolving Mediators (SPM) including Resolvins and Protectins are a genus of bioactive mediators, produced naturally in our bodies from omega-3 fatty acids like docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) that we get in our diet. These compounds were discovered in the proposed training laboratory and potently resolve inflammation, with certain SPM 10,000 times more potent than commonly prescribed non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Structures, receptors, and target cellular pathways have been identified for several SPM in many disease models; however, the metabolism of DHA in bacterial infection and the effects of increased precursor DHA has yet to be investigated. The proposed study will test the impact of DHA and bioactive DHA metabolites in an animal model of bacterial infection, which has implications for human infection. I hypothesize that increasing DHA levels in the blood will reduce inflammation and promote resolution of bacterial infection, and that it does so though the production of novel SPM. Important for translation to the clinic, these studies will determine how long a dose of DHA can be given before infection while still promoting healthy resolution, and investigate the mechanism through which this might be happening.   This research will help to map the new terrain of inflammation resolution with the goal to better appreciate the role of nutrition in the innate immune response and infection. It will also help identify new pathways and tools from a pre-clinical model to consider for future human studies and the evaluation of novel therapies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Women who are breastfeeding: Increasing self-efficacy to improve outcomes (WISE) Trial
Keywords-MotsClés: BREASTFEEDING; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL; SELF-EFFICACY
Abstract-Résumé: Leading health authorities all recommend exclusive breastfeeding to 6 months postpartum. Unfortunately, only 27% of Canadian mothers achieve this recommendation, a rate significantly lower than many industrialized countries. A Cochrane systematic review clearly indicates that professional support alone is insufficient to improve breastfeeding outcomes to 6 months postpartum. However, a promising intervention is the combination of professional and lay support. While most interventions have targeted women based on non-modifiable demographic risk variables, breastfeeding self-efficacy has been shown internationally to be predictive of breastfeeding exclusivity and duration and is a potentially modifiable risk factor. The purpose of this trial is to evaluate the effect of a breastfeeding self-efficacy enhancing intervention provided by combined nurse and peer mentor support on breastfeeding exclusivity among primiparous mothers. Women will be randomly allocated to either a control group (standard postpartum care) or intervention group (standard postpartum care plus a breastfeeding self-efficacy enhancing intervention) group. A research assistant blinded to group allocation will telephone all mothers at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months postpartum to collect outcome data. The results from this trial will make substantive contributions in five areas: (1) advance the body of knowledge concerning the effectiveness of a breastfeeding self-efficacy enhancing intervention on improving breastfeeding outcomes; (2) examine the utility of providing professional and lay support in the provision of breastfeeding care; (3) provide an economic evaluation of a breastfeeding support intervention;  (4) examine maternal and infant health service utilization in relation to infant feeding method; and (5) present valuable information regarding breastfeeding behaviours across the first year postpartum in a diverse Canadian sample.

TitreApplicationTitle: Impact of Maternal and Paternal Postpartum Depression: Assessing Concurrent Depression in The Family (IMPACT) Study
Keywords-MotsClés: ANXIETY; INFANT DEVELOPMENT; LONGITUDINAL STUDY; MARITAL RELATIONSHIP; MATERNAL DEPRESSION; PARENTING; PARENTING STRESS; PATERNAL DEPRESSION; POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Depression has become a major public health priority. Over 8 million parents in North America will experience depression each year, putting at least 16 million children at risk for adverse outcomes. Based on evidentiary studies, major depression can interfere with parenting quality and increase the risk of children developing mental, behavioural, and social problems - and evidence is accumulating that these negative effects begin in the early infant environment. Research that focuses on both parents to examine the onset, course, and consequences of postpartum depression (PPD) is urgently needed. The proposed study will incorporate a longitudinal design where 4288 new mothers and fathers will be followed for the first 24 months postpartum. Our proposed research is novel because it will advance our understanding of the mediating and moderating effects of single (maternal or paternal) parental PPD versus dual (maternal and paternal) parental PPD on infant development. Families will be categorized into four PPD risk models (no parental PPD, maternal-only PPD, paternal-only PPD, dual parental PPD). We will also provide information about the prevalence, course, and relationship between maternal and paternal PPD. Rates of dual depressed parents will be described and we will increase our knowledge about the clinical presentation of PPD among fathers. The results from this study will produce urgently needed knowledge that will assist in the development of targeted interventions for parents based on whether the family has one or two parents with PPD and whether the depressed parent is the mother or the father. Experts have identified parental depression as a major childhood adversity and that effective interventions to address this condition are one of the most preventive strategies to reduce negative developmental outcomes among children. Our study will inform the development of effective parental PPD interventions with the aim of preventing negative child outcomes.

TitreApplicationTitle: Extra-telomeric functions of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) isoforms
Keywords-MotsClés: EMBRYONIC STEM CELLS; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS (IPSC); MORPHOLINO; NAIVE PLURIPOTENCY; PLURIPOTENCY; PRIMED PLURIPOTENCY; SELF RENEWAL; SPLICE VARIANTS; TELOMERASE; TERT
Abstract-Résumé: Currently, over 14% of Canada's population is over age 65 and by 2026, one in five Canadians will be over age 65. With this senior population increase there will be an affiliated rise in age-related diseases and injuries along with their associated economic impact on our health care system. Along with promoting healthy living and improving health policies and systems affecting life and health, we need to focus on advancing our knowledge with respect to tissue repair and regeneration to help prevent/treat various diseases and injuries that disable a growing number of aging Canadians.  Stem cells exist in most mammalian organs and tissues and are essential for normal tissue function and repair. The aging process coincides with a reduction in the regenerative ability of various tissues and a decline in stem cell function. It is now generally accepted that stem cell functionality limits organ homeostasis and repair, but emerging work suggests they also fuel tumour growth.  We have discovered novel and existing forms of the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) enzyme that are more highly expressed in conditions that maintain stem cell function. These roles of telomerase appear to be not associated with it's known activity in synthesizing the ends of chromosomes (telomeres). We hypothesize that telomerase isoforms promote stem cell function by extra-telomeric means.      This research project will clarify the non-telomeric roles of TERT isoforms in maintaining stem cell function. We aim to discover novel TERT targets that maintain/induce stem cell behavior. Our findings will open up opportunities for drug discovery and strategies to identify compounds that can be used to manipulate stem cells for therapeutic purposes to enhance tissue regeneration and repair and to treat age-related diseases such as cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: HIV antiretrovirals and their impact on sex steroids during pregnancy;  a potential mechanism for the increased adverse pregnancy outcomes in women with HIV.
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOMARKERS; DRUG SAFETY; HIV ANTIRETROVIRALS; HUMAN PREGNANCY; LOW BIRTH WEIGHT; MOUSE MODEL; PLACENTA; SEX STEROIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Combination antiretroviral therapy is now recommended by the WHO for all HIV+ women that are pregnant. However, very little information is available on how these drugs can impact on pregnancy outcome. HIV-positive women are at a higher risk for pre-term delivery and low birth weight babies, and several studies have found an association between these adverse outcomes and being on combination antiretroviral therapy. Sex steroids are extremely important for a healthy pregnancy, and changes in these factors could contribute to the smaller babies and the pre-mature births seen in HIV+ women. Changes in the levels of sex steroids have been observed in HIV+ patients treated with combination antiretroviral therapy, however, no one has tested this in the context of pregnancy. We are proposing to investigate the impact of currently recommended antiretroviral drug regimens, and regimens that are increasingly being used during pregnancy, on the levels of sex steroids and on pregnancy outcome. Our hypothesis is that some combination antiretroviral regimens will alter the levels of sex steroids during pregnancy, and this will affect how the fetus develops and the initiation of labour. We will use in vitro studies using placental cells, a mouse pregnancy model, and also two cohorts of HIV+ pregnant women (a Canadian and a Zambian cohort) to test if different HIV antiretroviral regimens affect the levels of sex steroids, and if alteration in sex steroid levels are related to adverse birth outcomes. This research will increase our understanding of the impact of HIV therapy on pregnancy outcome, and will help inform treatment recommendations for women with HIV that are pregnant, or are contemplating pregnancy.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Longitudinal Assessment of Cognitive Risk for Insomnia
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL/APPLIED RESEARCH; COGNITION; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOUR THERAPY; COGNITIVE VULNERABILITY; FATIGUE; INSOMNIA; LONGITUDINAL; MECHANISMS; PREVENTION; RISK FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Insomnia affects about 10% of Canadians; it is chronic and debilitating in part because it is recurrent, and carries significant risk for developing other costly conditions such as cardiovascular and mental disorders. Understanding the cognitive vulnerability factors for other psychological conditions has led to significant treatment improvements; thus, advancing understanding of cognitive risk factors for insomnia will likely pay the same healthcare and well-being dividends. Compared with good sleepers, people with insomnia have unhelpful thinking about sleep. For example, they believe they must exert effort to sleep and to cope with sleep loss. Unfortunately such thoughts underlie compensatory behaviours that interfere with the body's natural compensatory system for sleep loss and perpetuate insomnia. In this project, we will investigate whether cognitive factors predict risk for future insomnia. In Study 1, people who have never experienced insomnia, and people with past but not current insomnia will complete an innovative cognitive reactivity test (CRT) to measure a latent tendency towards unhelpful thinking when experiencing fatigue. In Study 2 we will follow participants for one year, during which they will complete measures and track their sleep. We will test whether specific thinking styles predict the development or recurrence of insomnia across the year. Also, we will test the value of the CRT for uncovering a latent cognitive vulnerability to insomnia in those with asymptomatic sleep. In Study 3, we will assess the extent to which cognitive-behavioural insomnia treatment (CBT-I) modifies cognitive risk for insomnia. These studies will help us predict cognitive risk for insomnia occurrence and recurrence and to what extent CBT-I reduces cognitive vulnerability. The findings will be used to inform prevention and refinements to existing insomnia interventions.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES MULTIDISCIPLINAIRES; RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the nuclear pore complex in genome organization and gene silencing
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL BIOLOGY; CELL CYCLE; CHROMATIN; EPIGENETICS; FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS; MASS SPECTROMETRY; NUCLEAR PORE COMPLEX; NUCLEAR STRUCTURE; NUCLEAR TANSPORT; NUCLEOPORINS
Abstract-Résumé: Understanding the molecular basis for many acute and chronic diseases is a daunting challenge facing the biomedical community today. It is clear that comprehending processes that control cell growth and differentiation is central to this goal, and we strive to understand how gene expression controls these processes. Many factors contribute to controlling gene expression including the environment in which genes are stored. In every eukaryotic cell, including humans, genes are housed within a spherical, membrane-enclosed compartment, termed the nucleus. The nucleus segregates the genes from the rest of the cell and controls access of molecules to the genome, and thus what genes are turned on or off. Structures termed nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) sit on the surface of the nucleus and act as sentinels, allowing only certain molecules to enter or leave the nucleus. Recent evidence from our laboratory and others suggests that this is not the only way that NPCs influence genes. We have shown that NPCs can also grab on to genes and, like puppeteers, they can alter their structure and, in this way, control whether a specific set of genes are turned on or off. Using state-of-the-art techniques, we are investigating how the NPC, in particular how one component termed Nup170p, accomplishes this feat by defining how Nup170p physically interacts with specific genes to define their structure and control their functions. As the NPCs are highly conserved in eukaryotes as diverse as humans and yeast, these studies can be conducted in a yeast model system where powerful genetic and biochemical approaches can be used to explore NPC function. It is clear that defects in NPC proteins, including those related to Nup170p, lead to diseases including heart abnormalities and cancer. Understanding their functions in nuclear organization will provide us with a critical understanding of the underlying causes of these diseases and provide an avenue for eventual rational intervention.

ClasseRechercheFR: CANCER DU SEIN; MUSCLES ET OS
TitreApplicationTitle: DNA demethylation blockers; novel preventive and therapeutic approach to breast cancer development, progression and metastasis
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER; DNA METHYLATION; TRANSGENIC MICE; TUMOR METASTASIS
Abstract-Résumé: Metastasis of cancer cells to other organs is responsible for a large fraction of the morbidity and mortality from breast cancer. There are no effective therapies that could block breast cancer metastasis. A large number of genes play a role in breast cancer metastasis; we therefore reasoned that inhibiting metastasis would be possible only if the principal process that coordinates the activation of a significant fraction of these genes is reversed or inhibited. Our genes are regulated by a set of chemical marks on DNA called DNA methylation. DNA methylation silences genes. Our labs have discovered in previous studies that the process that turns on metastatic genes in cancer involves the removal of DNA methylation. Interestingly, we identified a protein that is responsible for this loss of DNA methylation, MBD2. We also discovered that if we used specific drugs that blocked the process of removal of DNA methylation, cancer metastasis was inhibited as well. Interestingly, the process of metastasis could be blocked with (S-adenosylmethionine) SAMe a natural compound. This compound interferes with DNA demethylation and MBD2 activity. These studies were mostly done in tissue culture. However, to know whether SAM could serve as a therapy in human breast cancer it has to be tested first in living animals. In this study we are going to use different mouse models of breast cancer metastasis as well as human metastasizing breast cancer cells explanted in mice to test the hypothesis that depletion of MBD2, or treatment with SAMe reverse and prevent breast cancer metastasis. The study will look as well at the mechanism of action of these agents. Since SAMe is an approved nontoxic nutritional supplement this study could be translated into new therapeutics and preventatives of breast cancer metastasis.

TitreApplicationTitle: In situ characterization of MeCP2-containing chromatin domains
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALYTICAL ULTRACENTRIFUGE; CHROMATIN; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; FLUORESCENCE RECOVERY AFTER PHOTOBLEACHING; HISTONES; MASS SPECTROMETRY; MECP2; RETT SYNDROME
Abstract-Résumé: Rett syndrome is a slow progressing neurodevelopmental disease,that affects approximately 1 in 10,000 infant females. 85% of the clinical cases have been traced to mutations of MeCP2, a vital regulatory protein that cannot function properly when mutated, leading to severe language and learning disabilities.  MeCP2 binds specifically to methylated DNA sequences and these complex interactions are modulated by the state of chromatin.  Chromatin consists of a DNA wrapped around proteins known as histones, and is prevalent in the cells of higher organisms (i.e., plants and animals including humans).  The functions and interactions of MeCP2 with chromatin are not well understood. Recently, our lab has provided well-supported evidence that MeCP2 is abundant in the brain, prefers binding to specific chromatin sequences, and is highly enriched in certain chromatin regions.  In this proposed study, we plan to further investigate the MeCP2-chromatin interactions by characterizing MeCP2 containing chromatin structures and determining specific MeCP2 interaction sites with histones.  Results of this study will assist us to better understand the functions of MeCP2 in the context of chromatin, to develop strategies and interventions to possibly reverse the impairments associated with Rett syndrome.

NomDuComitéFR: Santé publique, santé communautaire et santé des populations
TitreApplicationTitle: Is mental health changing over time?
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL; CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDIES; DISTRESS; EPIDEMIOLOGICAL STUDIES; HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; MENTAL DISORDERS; PHARMACOEPIDEMIOLOGY; PREVALENCE; PSYCHOTROPIC MEDICATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Is mental health in Canada getting better or worse? The goal of this project is to provide an answer this question. Diminished stigmatization of mental illness (which may encourage more people to seek help sooner), new therapies and safer and more effective medications may be leading to improved mental health. On the other hand health-system ineffectiveness and changing social and economic conditions may be causing a deterioration.   Statistics Canada has recently completed a 2012 national mental health survey - the "Canadian Community Health Survey, Mental Health." The firm release date for the survey data set is September 19, 2013. Data  from a nearly identical 2002 survey are also available. The objectives of this project will be accomplished by comparative analyses of the 2002 and 2012 survey results supplemented by data from a variety of other national surveys, some of which date back to the mid-1990s.   If we find improvements in mental health status this will provide  encouragement to continue with current policies. The results will help to identify areas of greater or lesser progress, providing information useful for improvement of health care systems. On the other hand, a finding of no change or deteriorating mental health would trigger a major "rethink" in the mental health field.

TitreApplicationTitle: Effects of maternal high fat feeding on skeletal muscle development and body composition in first generation rat offspring
Keywords-MotsClés: ADIPOSE TISSUE; BODY COMPOSITION; DEVELOPMENT; DUAL ENERGY X-RAY ABSORPTIOMETRY; HIGH FAT FEEDING; MICRO-COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; MUSCLE; NUTRITION; NUTRITIONAL PROGRAMMING; RATS
Abstract-Résumé: Research has demonstrated that children of obese parents are likely to become obese themselves. Obesity is strongly related with chronic diseases such as high blood pressure and type II diabetes, accounting for over four billion dollars a year in health care related costs alone. This creates a huge strain on Canada's health care system. The leading cause of obesity is believed to be due to a habitual diet high in fat and sugar. However, new evidence suggests that what a mother eats before and during pregnancy can affect the growth and development of her child. This may lead to smaller muscle size and altered muscle activity, which may affect body movement. High fat diets are also shown to increase body fat surrounding the internal organs, which is related to the development of disease. Whether expecting mothers (who have higher than normal amounts of body fat) can negatively affect muscle growth, and predict body fat levels of their baby, remains unclear. As such, the purpose of this study is to measure the effects of early life high fat feeding in female rats (before and during pregnancy), on muscle and fat development in their pups. To carry out this study, there will be two groups of rats: one fed a high fat diet, and another fed a 'healthy' balanced diet. The pups born to these rats will be measured for muscle size and body fat at twenty one days (childhood) and three months (young adulthood) of age. This study is highly relevant to Canadians as the trend of obesity is increasing. Conclusions may shed light on the origins of obesity aside from food intake alone, setting the stage for identifying lifestyle strategies for expecting mothers to follow, promoting healthy skeletal muscle and fat development of their baby. Overall, research on the causes of obesity may show promise in helping to reduce the prevalence of obesity and health care related costs, ultimately improving the quality of life and life expectancy for many Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Dietary Intakes and Periodontal Outcomes After Sanative Therapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM; DIETARY SUPPLEMENTS; FATTY ACIDS; INFLAMMATION; NUTRITION; PERIODONTAL DISEASE; SANATIVE THERAPY; TOOTH LOSS; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Oral health, specifically the retention of teeth, is inextricably and positively linked with nutritional status of an individual. Researchers have shown that specific nutrients such as vitamin D, calcium, and omega-3 fatty acids are associated with better oral health. When patients are treated for periodontal disease (infection of the gums and loss of jaw bone resulting in lost teeth), the first line of treatment is sanative therapy. Sanative therapy is a deep cleaning procedure that removes the agents that cause inflammation below the gum line. If successful, sanative therapy reduces the need for further invasive and costly treatment, and it allows patients to keep their natural teeth. If sanative therapy fails, however, teeth will be lost along with bone from the jaw. Evidence shows that individuals with fewer teeth have poorer nutritional status, which has a significant impact on overall health. Because we know that nutrition plays a crucial role in oral health (for example, some nutrients can promote the formation of stronger teeth and some nutrients can reduce inflammation) it is likely that nutrition can modulate a patient's response to sanative therapy. This research will determine what dietary patterns, specific nutrients, or nutritional supplements improve a patient's response to sanative therapy. Throughout the study, we will be measuring improvements in periodontal health (such as reduced inflammation and tooth loss) after they receive sanative therapy, and comparing that to the patients diet and use of dietary supplements. Knowing these relationships may help us develop dietary strategies to ensure a successful and full recovery from sanative therapy, and allow a patient to retain their natural teeth.

TitreApplicationTitle: Validation of two novel pancreatic cancer biomarkers: CUZD1 and LAMC2
Keywords-MotsClés: EARLY DIAGNOSIS; IMMUNOASSAYS; PANCREATIC CANCER; TUMOR MARKERS; VALIDATION STUDIES
Abstract-Résumé: With a five-year survival rate less than 5%, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most aggressive of all solid malignancies. Most patients are diagnosed once the disease has progressed into an advanced stage, making the only curative approach of resection surgery impossible. The delayed or missed diagnosis of PDAC can be attributed to the absence of specific symptoms in the early stages of cancer development and to the lack of efficient non-invasive diagnostic tests in clinical practice. As such, a major unmet clinical need is for serum biomarkers with sufficient sensitivity and specificity to help diagnose PDAC early. The classical pancreatic cancer serum biomarker, CA19-9, suffers from poor diagnostic sensitivity and specificity and is mainly used in the clinic to monitor therapeutic response. Even with this application, approximately 10% of the general population does not produce CA 19-9 (Lewis negative phenotype). These individuals with PDAC cannot be therapeutically monitored by assessing CA 19-9 serum levels. Thus another immediate need is to identify novel markers that are useful for monitoring CA 19-9 negative patients. The objective of our grant application is to perform extended clinical validation studies on two novel pancreatic cancer serum biomarkers (CUB and zona pellucida-like domains 1 (CUZD1) and laminin gamma C2 (LAMC2)) discovered in our laboratory. The diagnostic potential of these two markers, either alone or in combination with CA 19-9, will be carefully examined through a retrospective and a prospective study. The therapeutic monitoring potential of these markers will also be examined. The clinical implications: early detection of PDAC will reduce the burden of this disease through administration of effective treatment and identifying markers for monitoring therapeutic response in those patients that are CA 19-9 negative will aid in predicting whether therapy was successful earlier than imaging and clinical signs.

ClasseRechercheFR: ANOMALIES CONGENITALES; SANTE DES POPULATIONS - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Identification and characterization of genes predisposing to neural tube defects in humans
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOCHEMICAL ASSAYS; BIOINFORMATICS; CANDIDATE GENE SEQUENCING; CANONICAL WNT PATHWAY; GENETIC INTERACTION STUDIES; MOUSE MUTANT; NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS; PLANAR CELL POLARITY; WHOLE EXOME SEQUENCING; ZEBRAFISH MODEL
Abstract-Résumé: Neural tube defects (NTDs) represent a group of very common malformations in humans that are present at birth (1-2 infants per 1000 births). They are caused by a partial or complete failure of the spinal column to close during early development of the embryo. The most common forms of NTDs are anencephaly and spina bifida. They arise from a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Rare novel mutations in genes that form part of a signaling pathway called the planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling pathway have been associated with NTDs in humans. In the proposed project, we will study the effect of these mutations on protein function using cell-based and zebrafish models and we will determine how these mutations genetically interact together to modulate the incidence of the NTD phenotype in the same patient. To identify novel genes predisposing to NTDs, we will also re-sequence the whole protein coding regions in families affected  with NTDs. Our study will help better understand the underlying pathological mechanisms and is crucial for studying and characterizing the gene-environment interactions. These studies will help design novel preventive strategies and better counseling for couples at risk.

TitreApplicationTitle: Relationship between healthcare service utilization, costs and highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) uptake among HIV-positive persons in British Columbia
Keywords-MotsClés: EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTHCARE COST; HEALTHCARE SERVICE UTILIZATION; HIGHLY ACTIVE ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY; HIV/AIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Although not a cure, present-day HIV medicines commonly referred to as highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) has been established globally as an effective therapy for reducing HIV/AIDS-related morbidity and mortality. An emerging body of research suggests that expanding access to HAART may be a powerful strategy for reducing new HIV infections. Despite this evidence, British Columbia (BC), which has one of the highest HIV prevalence rates in Canada, has less than a fifty percent rate of HAART uptake. HAART's use among HIV-positive individuals clinically indicated for treatment remains suboptimal in BC where access to HAART is free via its universal health care system. It is unclear how HAART uptake affects healthcare service utilization and cost in BC. This proposal includes a set of inter-related objectives that seeks to understand the relationship between healthcare service utilization, costs and HAART uptake in BC. It aims to explore how clinical and socio-demographic characteristics of a BC cohort of HIV-positive individuals and their uptake of HAART impact healthcare service utilization and cost over time. It is hypothesized that HIV-positive individuals receiving HAART will have lower healthcare service needs compared to those not receiving HAART and thus will present an overall lower economic burden to society. This research will benefit the Canadian public by helping them understand how the proportion of HIV-positive people receiving treatment has changed (increased, decreased, or remain constant) over time. This knowledge is necessary to understand the impact of HIV on healthcare service utilization and associated costs. For policy makers, this understanding will be useful in informing resource-allocation decisions regarding how best to target underserved HIV-positive individuals, potentially reduce new HIV infections, improve overall HIV health outcomes and ultimately reduce healthcare cost in the long-term.

TitreApplicationTitle: Linkage between innate and adaptive immunity in chlamydial infection
Keywords-MotsClés: HOST DEFENSE; IMMUNE RESPONSES; INFECTIOUS DISEASES; MEDICAL MICROBIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Chlamydiae are globally important human bacterial pathogens that cause infectious diseases with serious sequelae. C. pneumoniae (Cpn) is the only chlamydial species causing acquired community pneumonia and possibly atherosclerosis and Alzheimer's disease There is no vaccine for this infection. The lack of a clear understanding of the mechanisms of protective/ pathological reactions has been a major obstacle for the rational development of a vaccine. We recently demonstrated that that Cpn induces significant response of natural killer T cells (NKT) which had a promoting impact on the function of dendritic cells (DC) and T cells which are important for host defense against the infection. We also found that a Cpn lipid antigen can activate NKT. Our objective for the proposed study is to examine mechanism by which NKT promotes the function of DC and T cell responses and protection including bacterial clearance and reduction of pathology. In addition, we will test if the lipid antigen can be used as an adjuvant to enhance the function of current vaccine candidates. We will use mouse model of lung infection with Cpn to examine the interaction of NKT and DCs and the outcome effect on T cell function and protection. Different types of mice including those with deficiency in particular cells and molecules will be tested. We will examine the immune responses, disease process and the outcome of infection in the special and normal control mice. We will also examine the changes related to how the cells look like and how the cell function especially from the aspects related to host dense against chlamydial infections and diseases. The study may lead to identification of new mechanisms and molecules related to chlamydial immunity and pathogenesis. Such knowledge will be very useful for the rational design of an effective and safe chlamydial vaccine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of SirT1 in the regulation of pancreatic beta-cell mass and function
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; APOPTOSIS; DIABETES; GENE EXPRESSION; INSULIN SECRETION; METABOLISM; PANCREATIC BETA-CELLS; PROLIFERATION; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Insulin is produced in the pancreas by specialized cells, named beta-cells. Type 1 diabetes results from selective destruction of beta-cells. Type 2 diabetes is characterized by both insulin resistance and a progressive deterioration of beta-cells. Therefore, diabetes treatment should aim at preserving and expanding surviving beta-cells.  In this project, we are going to study the role of a particular protein called SirT1 in the regulation of beta-cell survival and expansion. We will also try to understand how the activity of this protein is regulated. The ultimate goal of our research proposal is to characterize SirT1 as a target for diabetes treatment.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cardiac and vasculoendothelial assessment following a pre-eclamptic pregnancy.
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL MARKERS; HEART DISEASE; PREGNANCY AND PRE-ECLAMPSIA; SCREENING AND PREVENTION; WOMEN
Abstract-Résumé: The Canadian Heart Health Strategy and Action Plan and the Heart & Stroke Foundation Annual Report on Canadians' Health state that women's heart health is a key national priority that needs to be addressed to reduce care inequities for women. Given the costs of treating heart disease and screening for it, new and innovative ways to identify women who should undergo screening are critical to achieve this goal. A significant number of heart attacks occur in in women in the absence of major heart disease risk factors (e.g. age, high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, cholesterol or lipid problems) and many women with these risk factors do not experience heart attacks which highlights the need for assessment of new markers of heart disease risk and at different times during a woman's lifetime. Pregnancy and the period after delivery are often one of the first times that women access the health care system on a regular basis and are seen by a trained health-care provider. Therefore, for the majority of Canadian women of reproductive age, pregnancy is a window of opportunity to improve their longterm health which has not previously been considered. The 2011 Update for the American Heart Association's Evidence-Based Guidelines for the Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease in Women now identifies pre-eclampsia as relevant in the determination of a woman's cardiovascular risk; "Future research should evaluate the potential for exposures, events, or interaction with the medical system during periods of potential vulnerability across a woman's lifespan such as menarche, pregnancy, and menopause to identify women at risk and to determine the effectiveness of diagnostic and preventive interventions during these critical times". The Maternal Health Clinic which we set up to follow women with pre-eclampsia is internationally unique and affords us a real opportunity to not only carry out screening but to establish new and innovative ways to screen and treat these women.

TitreApplicationTitle: Phase I/II clinical trial of myoblast transplantation to Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy patients.
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL THERAPY; CELL TRANSPLANTATION; CLINICAL TRIAL; DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
Abstract-Résumé: The present submission for a Phase I/II of the clinical trial is to permit us to investigate whether the transplantation of normal myoblasts throughout one muscle (the extensor carpi radialis longus) of the patients will permit to increase the strength of that muscle. During this Phase I/II, the patients will be transplanted with myoblasts grown from the muscle biopsy of the donor and kept frozen in liquid nitrogen. Thirty million myoblasts will be injected per cm3 in a progressively higher surface of the radialis (i.e., 3, 7 and 10 cm2). The contralateral muscle will be injected with saline to serve as a negative control. The strength of both muscles will be measured at 3 months to verify whether the myoblast transplantation increase the strength of the muscle. If there is no significant strength increase the protocol will be terminated immediately for that patient. If there is a significant strength increase, the patient will be maintained under immunosuppression until 6 months and his strength will be re-evaluated.

ClasseRechercheFR: THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL; TUMEURS
TitreApplicationTitle: Investigation of Dendritic Cell De-differentiation in Cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: DENDRITIC CELLS; TUMOR IMMUNOLOGY; TUMOR IMMUNOTHERAPY; TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT; TUMOR VACCINE
Abstract-Résumé: The failure of the body's immune system to kill cancer cells is a major factor in cancer development and progression. This problem of tumor tolerance also contributes to the poor success of cancer vaccines and cancer immunotherapy. Dr. Cattral's research team is studying a specialized population of white blood cells, called dendritic cells (DC). They have made the exciting and important discovery that a specialized population of cells that arise from tumor DC is responsible for tumor tolerance.  Blocking the development of these cells was found to increase the success of immunotherapy.  The proposed studies will refine our understanding of how these cells develop, and lead to new ways to treat cancer in patients.

TitreApplicationTitle: Immune plasticity of natural killer cell function in cancer and surgery
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER; CANCER METASTATSIS; IMMUNE MODULATION; IMMUNE PLASTICITY; INNATE IMMUNITY; NATURAL KILLER CELLS; ONCOLYTIC VIRUS; PERIOPERATIVE IMMUNE THERAPY; SURGICAL STRESS; TRANSLATIONAL IMMUNOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Surgery is one of the most important steps in curative cancer treatment. Most patients with solid tumors, like breast, colon or lung cancer, have an operation to remove the tumor, but for a number of patients the cancer will come back, often spreading to distant organs (metastasis). My work in Drs. Auer/Bell's lab and others has shown that surgery itself can increase the spread of cancer to distant sites. Many patients get toxic treatments, like chemotherapy, many weeks after surgery to try and prevent this. Our research is focused on trying to understand how cells of the immune system, specifically natural killer (NK) cells are involved in the spread of tumor cells after surgery so that more effective and less toxic treatments can be given to patients around the time of their operation. In this proposal, I will find out how NK cells are profoundly suppressed after surgery and more importantly, I will reverse this effect by using novel virotherapy that targets tumor cells and spares normal healthy cells.  Cancer treatments that are specifically aimed at preventing recurrence of cancer following surgery will improve survival in all cancer patients undergoing surgery to remove their tumor.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; TRAUMATISME,REGENERATION
TitreApplicationTitle: Topical susceptibility to TGF-beta: a new concept and key mechanism in myofibroblast generation
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOSKELETON; EPITHELIAL-MESENCHYMAL TRANSTION; MRTF; MYOFIBROBLAST; PRIMARY CILIUM; PROMOTER STUDIES; TGFBETA SIGNALING; TIME-LAPSE CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Organ fibrosis is a chronic scarring process due to cycles of tissue injury and failed repair.  It is estimated that 45% of all deaths in the western world can be attributed to some form of chronic fibrotic disease, which can develop as a consequence of chronic inflammation, diabetes, hypertension, drug abuse and environmental toxins.  It is the major and death-inducing mechanism in many chronic lung and kidney diseases and liver cirrhosis.  Stunningly, the overall life expectancy of people with progressive fibrosis is worse than that of the cancer patients. Currently there is no cure to halt or reverse the process. A main culprit of the disease is a matrix producing muscle-like cell type the so called myofibroblast. These cells can develop from epithelial cells that, in a disease-inducing environment, undergo epithelial-myofibroblast transition.  In order to lessen fibrotic processes, we have to understand how myofibrobalst are generated. Our previous work has shown that growth factors and injury to the cell contacts act in synergy to provoke the transformation of epithelial cells to myofibroblasts. Recently we have found novel molecular and cellular mechanisms that involve changes in the cell skeleton and the cell's sensory antenna, the primary cilium. However currently we do not understand how these act together to induce the deleterious process. This proposal aims to clarify how the cell skeleton, the primary cilium and fibrosis-inducing growth factors bring about major changes in cell fate. We will use an array of cell and molecular biology techniques, including changes in gene expression and life cell imaging analysis on cellular models and cells from patients with fibrosis.  The gained knowledge will help us understand the fundamental mechanisms underlying this devastating disease entity define targets for therapeutic interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The genetic analysis of multiple traits of time-dependent effects in longitudinal studies
Keywords-MotsClés: DISCRETE LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS; JOINT ANALYSIS OF TIME-TO EVENT AND LONGITUDINAL TRAITS; LONGITUDINAL MULTIVARIATE TRAITS
Abstract-Résumé: Many complex diseases are of a dynamic nature and understanding them often require of expensive and time consuming designs that collect phenotype data as well as other relevant repeated measurements on a group of individuals. Modelling data from these cohort studies requires to consider at least two kinds of dependence: i) individuals may have common ancestry and/or shared environment; and ii) the correlated nature of repeated measures. Ignoring the dependence structure or replacing it with a simplified 'working correlation' for computational purposes could greatly preclude the advantages conferred by the cohort design and even the validity of the inference.  In spite of this, most studies of longitudinal traits use over-simplified models that fail not only to capture the dynamics of the disease but also may yield misleading results regarding the nature and extent of genetic effects. Furthermore, in longitudinal studies there are events that happen (like death, drop-out or other milestone stage) that cannot be ignored in the analysis because these events affect data collection and the longitudinal outcomes are likely to affect the time on which these events happen. Thus, the genetic analysis of data from cohorts requires of the development of methods for models able to deal with these issues. Although no in a human genetics context, joint modelling of continuous longitudinal outcomes and time-to-event has received considerable attention in the last decade. However, methods considering discrete longitudinal outcomes, quite common in medical studies, are almost absent in the statistical literature. The objectives of this proposal are to develop methods for genetic models of longitudinal and event history data that use the true dependence structure of the data under study and are computationally sound. Particular attention will be given to models for discrete longitudinal traits. These methods will be of immediate utility in the analysis of on-going medical research.

ClasseRechercheFR: TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX; MALADIE D'ALZHEIMER
TitreApplicationTitle: Involvement of AMPA receptor endocytosis in Alzheimers disease:  Examining memory and structural plasticity deficits in mouse models
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIORAL NEUROSCIENCE; BEHAVIOUR; FEAR CONDITIONING; HIPPOCAMPUS; MEMORY; MOUSE; RECALL; RECONSOLIDATION; SHORT TERM MEMORY; WATER MAZE
Abstract-Résumé: Alzheimers disease (AD) was first described in 1906. Despite intense research in the intervening 100 years, there is no cure for AD and available treatments are far from ideal.  Progressive memory loss is the defining feature of AD.  The early stages of AD are characterized by inability to acquire new memories, often observed as difficulty in recalling recent events.  The ability to remember older events is then disrupted.  Symptoms gradually worsen over time and many aspects brain function become affected.   Although the precise cause(s) of AD remains elusive, b-amyloid (Ab), a small protein derived from amyloid precursor protein (APP), is widely implicated.  Mutations in APP cause familial AD (FAD) and increase Ab levels.  While high Ab may eventually trigger cell death, memory deficits are observed in AD patients before evidence of cell death, suggesting that high levels of Ab itself may interferes with the ability to acquire memories in the early stages of this disease.  Indeed, recent findings in cells suggest that increased Ab decreases the surface expression proteins that are key players in memory formation.  However, whether a similar process underlies the memory deficits in whole organisms such as mouse models of AD is unknown.  Here we will test this prediction using mice genetically-designed to mimic AD.  Importantly, these mice show memory deficits, similar to people with early-stage AD.  Our exciting preliminary results suggest that interfering with the decrease in the surface expression of this key protein, indeed rescues the memory deficits in these mice designed to model AD.  We will verify and extend this finding and explore possible ways to translate this finding into the clinic.   Currently, there are few clinical therapeutic options for AD.  Our results will not only increase our understanding of the neurobiological bases of AD, but may advance future treatments for AD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Critical role of the transcription factor FoxO3a in host survival during a chronic infection
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DEATH; CELL SIGNALING; HOST-PATHOGEN INTERACTIONS; INFLAMMATION; T CELL MEMORY
Abstract-Résumé: To circumvent the rapid proliferation of intracellular bacteria, the immune system must operate rapidly.  Cells of the innate and acquired immune system are endowed with different roles in order to control the pathogen comprehensively during early- and late-stages.  However, some evasive pathogens, such as Salmonella Typhimurium (ST), which induces a typhoid-like disease in mice and gasteroenteritis in humans, are highly virulent and cause a chronic and sometimes fatal infection. Outbreaks of such food- and water-borne pathogens are on the rise, and they are often the reason for co-morbidity in other chronic inflammatory diseases.  Vaccines available are not highly efficacious.  In this proposal we will unravel the role of a critical molecule called FoxO3a.  This molecule is normally present in the nucleus of cells where it modulates the expression of genes that play role in cell survival, cell proliferation and inflammation.   Our preliminary data indicates that FoxO3a plays a critical role in promoting survival of hosts during a chronic infection with Salmonella Typhimurium, as hosts die rapidly in the absence of FoxO3a.  We will use various cell biological, immunological and biochemical techniques to unravel the mechanisms that allow FoxO3a to promote survival of hosts during a chronic infection.   These studies will lead to the identification of strategies that can be exploited for development of therapeutics against chronic inflammatory diseases.

ClasseRechercheFR: PROMOTION DE LA SANTE; RECHERCHES SUR LES SERVICES DE SANTE - GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Effectiveness of a consumer-targeted pharmacist-led educational intervention to reduce inappropriate prescriptions
Keywords-MotsClés: EDUCATIONAL INTERVENTION; INAPPROPRIATE PRESCRIBING; PATIENTS; PHARMACISTS; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: As Canadians age, the probability of suffering from different medical conditions and having to take many medications increases. As the number of medications increases, so too does the risk of side effects. Some medications pose greater risks than others. For example, some medications can cause a person to fall, have trouble with their memory, or lead to hospital emergency room visits for low blood sugar. When medications are prescribed for which safer alternatives exist, it is called "inappropriate prescribing". National specialist consensus panels regularly publish lists of inappropriate drugs that pose an elevated risk of adverse effects, yet unfortunately inappropriate prescribing persists. As many as 1 in 4 Canadian seniors on public drug programs consume one or more inappropriate medications. Our project proposes a novel intervention whereby pharmacists provide educational materials to both seniors and their primary care providers on the risks of taking inappropriate prescriptions. Recommendations to change inappropriate prescriptions to safer alternatives are provided. Forty-six community pharmacies in Quebec will help us recruit 400 of clients to this project. We hope to show that empowered patients can play a role in helping health professionals reduce inappropriate prescriptions and increase medication safety in the elderly.

TitreApplicationTitle: The effect of dietary calcium intake as compared to calcium supplementation on vascular and bone health in postmenopausal women
Keywords-MotsClés: BONE HEALTH; CALCIUM SUPPLEMENTS; CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH; DIETARY CALCIUM; MENOPAUSE; MICRONUTRIENTS; RANDOMIZED CONTROL TRIAL; VITAMIN D
Abstract-Résumé: Calcium and vitamin D are essential nutrients for optimal bone health throughout life. Research has shown that postmenopausal women who take appropriate amounts of these nutrients have better bone strength and fewer fractures than those who don't. However, researchers have recently questioned the safety of calcium and vitamin D obtained through supplements as they might increase the risk of cardiovascular events such as heart attacks and strokes. Because there are methodological concerns with these studies and because the exact cause behind these negative effects is not yet determined, many questions remain. Could calcium supplements be good for your bones but bad for your heart? Many individuals count on supplements to ensure an adequate intake of calcium and vitamin D to protect their bones against osteoporosis and fractures. It may be possible that calcium obtained from the diet have a better effect on vascular health than that obtained from supplements. Because this has never been studied prospectively, we propose to estimate the effect of dietary intake of calcium as compared to supplemental calcium on markers of vascular and bone health in postmenopausal women. We hope to enroll postmenopausal women who will be assigned to one of three interventions: to receive 1200 mg of calcium though milk and dairy foods or to receive a calcium supplement once daily or to be in a control group without specific intervention. At baseline and after 12 months, we will measure the health of the vascular system through assessment of the arteries with an ultrasound technique, monitoring of blood pressure and various blood tests. We think this study is well designed to provide information on whether calcium supplements have a different effect on vascular health than calcium obtained from the diet and shed light on the mechanisms that underlie these effects.

TitreApplicationTitle: Closed-loop regulation of glucose levels in patients with type 1 diabetes
Keywords-MotsClés: CLOSED-LOOP SYSTEM; GLUCAGON; HYPOGLYCEMIA; INSULIN; TYPE 1 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: In healthy individuals, blood sugar levels are tightly controlled by 2 hormones: insulin and glucagon. Secretion of insulin, a vital hormone to reduce blood sugar, is lost in type 1 diabetes (T1D). Thus, T1D patients are currently treated by intensive insulin therapy. Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is frequent in T1D individuals. Hypoglycemia causes physical and psychological morbidity and sometimes leads to death. In case of hypoglycemia, patients might need glucagon, a key hormone to raise blood glucose. Poor glycemic control in T1D leads to long-term complications such as heart disease, blindness, kidney failure and amputation.   We have developed a wearable artificial pancreas (WAP) that regulates sugar levels for adults with T1D. Two configurations of the WAP have been developed, one that infuses insulin and another that infuses insulin and glucagon. The systems are composed of 3 components: continuous glucose sensor (to read blood sugar changes), insulin infusion pumps (to provide insulin with or without glucagon) and an intelligent dosing method that links the sensor with the pump (to suggest dose changes to the pump based on the information provided). In a controlled environment, we have shown that the WAP improved glucose time in target by 17% while reducing hypoglycemic risk by 8-fold over 15 hours.  In order to show the effectiveness of the 2 systems, we aim to compare it in 20 adults with T1D for a 60-hour in a far less controlled environment. The study will be conducted under close to free-living conditions. The participants will have the freedom in their day schedule, food intake and physical exercise. This study is an essential step leading to out-patient studies to be conducted under completely free-living conditions.    The WAP has a great potential to improve patients quality of life, improve health outcomes, promote physical activities and alleviate the burden of diabetes management from the patients and their health care providers.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular characterization of VHL-HIF axis
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA METHYLATION; E3; HIF; HYPOXIA; KIDNEY CANCER; VHL
Abstract-Résumé: Oxygen homeostasis or balance is a vital organizing principle for human development and physiology. A universal response to compromised oxygen availability involves a protein called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), which accumulates during low oxygen levels or hypoxia to trigger the expression of numerous genes including those that promote new blood vessel formation (angiogenesis), anaerobic metabolism, and the production of oxygen-carrying red blood cells. These cellular responses facilitate adaptation and survival in low oxygen environment and help to restore normal oxygen balance. The significance of HIF in cancer is underscored by the finding that HIF is inordinately overexpressed in virtually all human tumours, and the extent of HIF expression correlates with disease aggressiveness, resistance to radiation and chemotherapy, and poor prognosis. Tumour cells express increasing levels of HIF because regions within a growing tumour mass inevitably and progressively become more hypoxic as the diffusional capacity of oxygen from the nearest blood vessel is surpassed. In addition, cancer-causing mutations on critical tumour suppressor genes have been shown to increase the expression of HIF. The objective of this research proposal is to elucidate the molecular mechanisms governing the activity of HIF with the supposition that lessons learned would provide significant insight into the multifaceted adaptive response to hypoxia and advance our fundamental understanding of cancer biology.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genetic Basis of Murine Fibrotic Lung Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: BLEOMYCIN; CONGENIC; FIBROSIS; GENETICS; IDIOPATHIC PULMONARY FIBROSIS; IMMUNE RESPONSE; LUNG; MOUSE MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: The lung disease of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis could be more effectively treated if the altered genes which contribute to its development were known.  Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a genetically complex disease which can result from known (environmental, therapeutic) exposures and involves a pathology of excessive scar formation in the lung which can result in impaired lung function and, ultimately, respiratory failure. This devastating disease has an estimated annual incidence of 1 case per 10000 members of general population and an associated mortality of 50-70% at 5 years post diagnosis. Genetic differences among people likely contribute to who develops this response and who does not. In the proposed research we will study animal models which present the same lung disease as patients suffer, to identify specific inflammatory responses and genes which predispose to the development of these effects. Such genes are more easily detected in animal models (than in the clinic) as breeding permits the needed number of animals to be created.  The proposed investigations will use the latest advances and approaches of genomics research, related to the Human Genome project, to uncover specific lung response genes for later testing in a patient population. It is anticipated that the mouse studies will provide evidence for variation within specific genes leading to fibrosis, and that these genes could then be investigated in the clinic. The elucidation of genetic differences leading to fibrosis will also provide potential targets for therapeutic intervention.  New targets are needed, as there are presently no approved drugs for pulmonary fibrosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Eph and Insulin Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Signaling in C. elegans Neurodevelopment
Keywords-MotsClés: AXON GUIDANCE; C. ELEGANS; CANCER; CELL MIGRATION; EPH RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASE; GENETICS; INSULIN SIGNALING; MORPHOGENESIS; PTEN; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION
Abstract-Résumé: One of the greatest challenges of medical research is to understand how the brain functions. Many diseases are caused by malfunctions of the nervous system, for example neurodegeneration can cause diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, epilepsy and stroke. In addition, brain tumors that start to metastasize (move) can lead to a quick death if left untreated.  If we are to develop cures for such diseases it is crucial that we understand how the nervous system functions at the molecular level. Dr. Chin-Sang's research is devoted to understanding cell movements and in particular cells of the nervous system. Dr. Chin-Sang's lab has obtained some exciting data on certain receptors found in the nervous system. These receptors guide cells called neurons to their proper location to make proper connections. One can imagine just like a computer that is not wired correctly, brain cells that are not connected properly will cause the brain to function abnormally.  Dr. Chin-Sang uses a tiny worm called C. elegans as a model organism to study the nervous system. Why worms? Many of the genes that control this tiny worm's nervous system are also found in humans and function in an identical manner. Therefore, the knowledge gained from Dr. Chin-Sang's research will certainly help us understand the molecular mechanisms during abnormal nervous system function in humans. Neurological diseases are devastating for the patient and very expensive to care for. Dr. Chin-Sang's research in neuroscience and cell biology will provide the necessary information to help in the design of drugs and identify drug targets for therapeutic intervention of neurological diseases and cancer. The Chin-Sang lab will provide a valuable resource for students who want to pursue graduate work in molecular genetics. Currently, Dr. Chin-Sang's research on C. elegans presents one of the few genetic models for understanding how these receptor genes function in a living animal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Boundaries and Borderlands: Negotiating Care Work in Long-term Residential Settings
Keywords-MotsClés: CARE WORK; CRITICAL ETHNOGRAPHY; INFORMAL CAREGIVERS; INTERSECTIONALITY; LONG-TERM RESIDENTIAL CARE; POWER RELATIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Family members make significant contributions to Canada's healthcare system through their role as unpaid caregivers for older people living at home. This has been the focus of many research studies, however very little research has examined the role of families in long-term residential care (LTRC). Recent policy papers have pointed to the need to address this gap in order to develop effective, equitable and ethical policies and practices necessary to foster supportive and collaborative relations among those engaged in care work in this setting - that is residents, family members and staff. The purpose of this research study is to develop a better understanding of how care is negotiated in LTRC, including the influence of social relations such as gender, class, racialization and age on this process. This study will be conducted in three long-term residential care facilities in British Columbia. We will conduct in-depth interviews with family members, residents, and staff members, gathering detailed information about their experiences of negotiating care work. We will spend time with family members when they are at the facility, observing the negotiation of care work during informal and formal interactions (e.g. 'hands-on' personal care, helping with facility routines such as meal times, and participating in Family Councils). We will also review documents (e.g. provincial licensing guidelines, facility-level policies) that shape care work in LTRC. We expect that this study will provide a current, contextualized portrayal of how care work is negotiated in the complex healthcare environment of LTRC. Findings will be used to inform health policies and practice-ready strategies (e.g. communication, conflict resolution workshops) that foster supportive and collaborative relations among those engaged in care work. Knowledge translation and exchange activities will involve a blog on a study-specific website, community forums, in addition to academic dissemination.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cultural Safety of Physical Activity Programming for Aboriginal Elders
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL; CULTURAL SAFETY; CULTURE; ELDERS; LEISURE; OLDER ADULTS; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; RECREATION
Abstract-Résumé: The 2006 Canadian Census states that the Canadian Aboriginal population aged 65 and over has increased 43.0% since 2001 (Statistics Canada, 2010). Despite this dramatic increase in older Aboriginal peoples, there is a dearth of research concerning this cohort (Wilson, Rosenberg, & Abonyi, 2011), especially in regard to their physical activity. Physical inactivity is a major risk factor for many chronic diseases that are prevalent in Aboriginal populations (Waldram, Herring, & Young, 2006). Physical activity interventions can be highly effective for improving the overall health of adults over the age of 65 (Taylor et al., 2004). It is thus especially important to have physical activity programs that are culturally safe. I will use a case study methodology for my community-based research, which will expand on the current body of literature pertaining to older Aboriginal peoples' participation in physical activity. I will examine the "Elders in Motion" program in Yellowknife and Fort Resolution, run by the Northwest Territories Recreation and Parks Association (NWTRPA). Through focus groups and semi-structured interviews, I will determine how the organizers of the program view older adults' participation in physical activity and if Elders in Motion is a culturally safe program.

TitreApplicationTitle: Exploiting the immunogenic properties of tumor antigens to potentiate oncolytic virus vaccines
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNE RESPONSE; ANIMAL STUDIES; CANCER THERAPEUTICS; ELISAS; FLOW CYTOMETRY; IMMUNOCHEMISTRY; INFECTED CELL VACCINE; ONCOLYTIC VIRUSES; TUMOR ASSOCIATED ANTIGENS
Abstract-Résumé: Over the last decade oncolytic viruses (OV) have been shown to be very effective anti-cancer agents - they are able to target tumor cells while leaving normal cells intact. Oncolytic viruses are able to control tumor growth and disease progression in many ways including by mounting an immune response to directly target the cancer. One of the ways that we are able to amplify this immune response is by altering the genetic make-up of the virus to make it better able to stimulate the immune system. There are certain alterations to the genetic make up of the virus that makes it more immunogenic and more able to control tumor growth and we are trying identify the changes which are most immune stimulatory. Once we have identified these changes we can create an even more potent and effective oncolytic virus platform than the one that we already have. In a therapeutic setting, these changes would make the therapy more tumor specific and have fewer side effect for patients. Oncolytic viruses have already shown tremendous success as a cancer therapeutic and being able to improve them even more will put us that much closer to being able to create a therapy that is effective for everyone.

TitreApplicationTitle: Development of optimized adenovirus-based vectors for evaluation in a mouse model of Spinal Muscular Atrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: ADENOVIRUS; DISSECTION; GENE THERAPY; IN VITRO AND IN VIVO INFECTIONS; IP AND IV INJECTIONS; MOUSE MODEL; SOLID AND LIQUID OVERLAYS; SPINAL MUSCULAR ATROPHY; TITERS; VIRAL PURIFICATION
Abstract-Résumé: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) is a genetic disorder affecting 1 in 6000 live births. In its most severe form, children with SMA are never able to sit and succumb to the disease within the first 2 years of life.  The disease is caused by mutations in the gene encoding a protein called survival motor neuron (SMN).  This protein is essential for proper function and health of motor neurons and, in the absence of SMN, motor neurons die leading to muscle weakness and atrophy.  Currently there is no known cure.  In our studies, we are using attenuated viruses to deliver a good copy of the SMN gene to a mouse model of SMA in order to achieve disease correction.  In the first part of our research, we will screen a panel of viruses that infect cells through different routes to identify the virus that targets infection to motor neurons.  In the second part of the research, we will use the virus identified above to deliver the SMN gene to a mouse model of SMA.  These mice will be monitored at varying times after gene delivery for overall health and muscle strength.  We believe that this therapy will improve motor neuron and muscle function in the animals, and will dramatically extend their lifespan (untreated animals typically only survive one month).  These studies will provide important preliminary preclinical data that may help in developing a new therapeutic approach for treatment of SMA.
