TitreApplicationTitle: Balancing benefits and harms from cervical cancer screening: additional analysis of the CoHIPP trial
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER SCREENING; CASE CONTROL STUDY; CERVICAL CANCER; COLPOSCOPY; HARM FROM SCREENING; HPV TESTING; HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUSES; SQUAMOUS INTRA-EPITHELIAL LESION; TREATMENT FAILURE
Abstract-Résumé: We will use information and samples collected for an ongoing project to identify ways of reducing unnecessary interventions in women found to have precancer by cervical cancer screening. Our first goal is to better understand why some women found to have precancer on cervical biopsy, have no precancer on the cervical treatment specimen.  Cervical precancer treatment can weaken the cervix and lead to complications in future pregnancies, such as preterm birth.  This is why we want to identify factors we could act on to reduce the number of women who are treatment unnecessarily. We will investigate the role of  pathology diagnosis on the biopsy, and investigate factors linked to spontaneous regression of the lesion between biopsy and treatment.  We will also look at the viral characteristics of the human papillomaviruses (the cause of cervical precancers) found in the cervical specimens. In another analysis, we will investigate if some patients and/or disease characteristics would help further define women truly at risk of recurrence of precancer after treatment.  We firmly believe that, in combination, those analyses will help balance benefits and harms from cervical cancer screening, by enabling more targeted intervention strategies.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of nuclear protein import in cardiovascular disease states
Keywords-MotsClés: ATHEROSCLEROSIS; CARDIOMYOPATHY; DIABETES; HYPERTENSION; MEMBRANE TRANSPORT; NUCLEUS
Abstract-Résumé: All cells must respond and adapt to a changing environment. Each cell must sense what is changing and then make appropriate alterations to maintain function and viability. Most cells in the body contain a nucleus. The nucleus is the storehouse in the cell for its genetic material (DNA).  It is essential for cell survival and function that these genes are expressed in coordination with the needs of the cell. Proteins move in and out of the nucleus in a regulated fashion through special channels. These proteins then initiate and control gene expression. This process appears critical when cells divide and grow. Our proposed study will examine how protein transport through these channels is controlled at a molecular level. The more we understand how this process is regulated, the more we will learn about what factors regulate cell division and growth. Accelerated cell division and growth are hallmark features of cancer and heart disease. Our data, therefore, will be of great importance in advancing our knowledge regarding the pathogenesis of these two critical diseases.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Prospective Study to Evaluate the Impact of Behavioural and Psychosocial Factors on Gestational Weight Gain and Postpartum Weight Retention
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL; POSTPARTUM; PREGNANCY; PROSPECTIVE DESIGN; PSYCHOSOCIAL; WEIGHT
Abstract-Résumé: Each year among the 380 000 women who deliver an infant in Canada, 50% will exceed the recommended weight gain guidelines during pregnancy. Excessive weight gain during pregnancy has been associated with negative health outcomes for both mother and infant. Interventions to promote healthy weight gain during pregnancy have reported mixed results. Eating behaviour and weight gain is recognized as complex, influenced by sociodemographic, biomedical, behavioural and psychosocial factors. In comparison to other dimensions, psychosocial factors have been largely neglected in relation to weight gain during pregnancy. While pregnancy is considered a joyful occasion, it is also a major life event with the potential for increased stress, anxiety and depressed mood. Little is known about how a woman's mental state during pregnancy is related to eating behaviour, weight gain and weight retention postpartum. The present study is timely, in that is proposes to examine the role of these modifiable variables to weight gain during this critical period. The findings will inform clinical practice guidelines and guide the design of more effective interventions to prevent excess weight gain during pregnancy, and ultimately improve outcomes for both mothers and their infants.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Deep Phenotyping Approach to Assess the Effect of Uric Acid Lowering in Patients with Uncomplicated Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
Keywords-MotsClés: DIABETES MELLITUS; ENDOTHELIAL FUNCTION; HYPERGLYCEMIC CLAMP; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; RENAL HEMODYNAMIC FUNCTION; RENAL HYPERFILTRATION; RENIN ANGIOTENSIN SYSTEM; TRANSLATIONAL PHYSIOLOGY; URIC ACID; URINE BIOMARKERS
Abstract-Résumé: Brief background of issue: High blood sugars stimulate renin angiotensin system (RAS) hormones in patients with diabetes mellitus (DM). RAS activation leads to high kidney pressure, inflammation and scarring in the kidney, and stiff arteries. These changes cause kidney failure, heart attacks, strokes and blindness. Despite the use of conventional medications to block the RAS, patients still develop kidney and blood vessel injury. Recent studies have shown that a substance called "uric acid" may also contribute to diabetic kidney and blood vessel damage. Furthermore, medications that block uric acid such as "febuxostat" can also block the RAS. Whether lowering uric acid protects against kidney and blood vessel injury in young type 1 DM patients is, however, unknown. Objective: The objective of this study is to examine the impact of febuxostat on kidney and blood vessel function and molecules that cause kidney damage in patients with early type 1 DM. Brief description of the research project: After admission to the hospital, insulin and sugar will be given intravenously to achieve normal blood sugars. Five hours later, we will test the urine for harmful inflammatory proteins. Blood vessel function will be assessed by ultrasound. We will then measure kidney function using gold-standard "inulin tests" to test the level of kidney RAS activation. The next day, kidney and blood vessel function will be measured when blood sugar levels are high. Patients will then be treated with the uric acid blocker febuxostat for 8 weeks and the same tests will be performed. Relevance to diabetes: This physiology study has important implications for patients with early type 1 DM. Information from our study could be used to design larger clinical trials which will determine whether or not uric acid lowering reduces the chance of developing blood vessel diseases, including kidney failure, heart attacks, strokes and limb amputations.

ClasseRechercheFR: RETARD MENTAL; TROUBLES MENTAUX ET COMPORTEMENTAUX
TitreApplicationTitle: The role of network activity in the developing cerebellum
Keywords-MotsClés: CEREBELLUM; DEVELOPMENT; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; IMAGING; NETWORK ACTIVITY; PURKINJE CELL; TRANSGENIC MICE; TRAVELING WAVES
Abstract-Résumé: Years before you can play a Mozart Sonata on the piano, your brain has already developed into a structure that has the capacity to acquire new motor skills for the rest of your life. Playing the piano, and other motor skills, involves the cerebellum, or "little brain" at the base of the brain. Diseases of the cerebellum, like ataxia, lead to devastating motor impairments. My research focuses on how the cerebellum develops. We hope that by the understanding we gain of cerebellar development may help us to uncover what goes wrong in cerebellar disorders and even eventually how to treat or prevent them.  Early in the developing brain, patterns of activity that resemble waves have been observed across many different brain structures. These early waves have been best studied in the visual parts of the brain, where they have been shown to be important for visual brain regions to develop properly.  My recent work has identified early waves of activity in the developing cerebellum, which are similar to waves seen in other brain regions. We are now undertaking a deeper study of these waves, to learn more about when and where they are found, and what mechanisms turn them on and off in the developing cerebellum. Finally, we will block these early waves to directly test what their function is in development.  Results from this research will give us insight into how early waves function in non-visual brain regions, which will tell us if wave function is conserved across the developing nervous system, and thus will have impact for other brain regions as well. Furthermore, we expect that this work will give us insights into the problems underlying cerebellar diseases, and may ultimately lead to new strategies for their treatment or prevention.

TitreApplicationTitle: Opening Doors to Participation of Youth with Physical Disabilities in Community Activities: An Intervention Study
Keywords-MotsClés: COACHING; ENVIRONMENTAL BARRIERS; INTERRUPTED TIME SERIES; INTERVENTION; PARTICIPATION; PHYSICAL DISABILITIES; YOUTH
Abstract-Résumé: Active participation of adolescents with physical disabilities in extracurricular activities is vital to their health, well-being and overall quality of life. Examples of such activities include playing team sports, joining a youth group, or going on an outing such as to the movies with friends. Taking part in leisure activities is an excellent opportunity for adolescents with disabilities to make friends, build social networks and develop social skills; qualities that help them prepare for adulthood. Unfortunately, youth with physical disabilities are at risk of experiencing lower levels of participation in community activities, which in turn can lead to isolation and decreased quality of life. The current problem is that health professionals have very little evidence about how to promote adolescents' involvement in community activities. The purpose of this study, therefore, is to test if an environment-based intervention can improve youth participation.  This intervention focuses on removing environmental barriers (e.g., lack of accessibility to community programs, lack of information made available for parents) and coaching parents to identify and implement strategies that can enhance their child's participation. Thirty youth with physical disabilities, aged 12-16 years will be invited to participate in a 12-week intervention. A clinician will work individually with each youth to remove environmental barriers that prevent or restrict them from engaging in specific desired activities. Performance in each activity will be monitored multiple times throughout the entire study. A follow-up will take place to see if change in performance remains in place post-intervention. Findings from this study can indicate not only if the intervention works, but also for whom and under what conditions it is most effective.  Such knowledge can guide clinical practice and assist therapists in making informed decisions when working with similar populations.

ClasseRechercheFR: MUSCLES ET OS; AFFECTIONS DENTAIRES (ET BIOLOGIE BUCCO-DENTAIRE)
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Characterization of Bone Sialoprotein
Keywords-MotsClés: ANIMAL MODELS; BIOMINERALIZATION; BONE; BONE REPAIR; COLLAGEN BINDING; COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY; CRYSTAL CHARACTERIZATION; HYDROXYAPATITE; PERIODONTAL TISSUES
Abstract-Résumé: The organic matrices of mineralized tissues consist principally of type I collagen and a variety of non-collagenous proteins. These proteins are postulated to have critical roles in tissue  development and the mineralization process. Studies conducted in our laboratories and elsewhere have shown that one of these proteins, bone sialoprotein, is a multifunctional protein that can interact with the mineral, cells and collagen. Bone sialoprotein can initiate mineral formation, promote osteoblast differentiation and has been shown to promote bone repair. We have shown in a mouse model that in the absence of bone sialoprotein there are major defects in the periodontal tissues and in the enthesis, which represents tendon/ligament insertion sites into bone. We will determine the mechanism by which bone sialoprotein mediates biomineralization using both physical-chemical protocols and the mouse that lacks bone sialoprotein.  Furthermore we will determine the critical functional domains of bone sialoprotein that mediates biomineralization in vivo.  By understanding the mechanism we will be able to develop novel therapeutic agents for the promotion of mineralized tissue repair.

TitreApplicationTitle: An Analysis of Integrated Care Systems and Policies for Older Adult Populations: Lessons from Canada and Abroad
Keywords-MotsClés: COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS; HEALTH CARE SYSTEMS; HEALTH POLICIES; HEALTH SERVICES; INTEGRATED CARE SYSTEMS; OLDER ADULTS
Abstract-Résumé: Canada's population is aging and as a result the health care needs of our population are changing. Currently14.8% of Canadians are seniors and by the year 2036 it is estimated that approximately 24.5% of the population will be seniors. Seniors require more health services than younger members of the population, and are more likely to require long-term care, complex care, and care for chronic conditions. While the Canadian health care system is very good at providing emergency care, improvements can be made in the way the system delivers non-emergency care. Fragmentation within the health care system makes it very difficult for patients requiring long-term, complex, or chronic disease care to navigate the health care system and receive the care they need. Integrated care systems have been proposed as a way to make the Canadian health care system more efficient and to meet the needs of our aging population. Integrated care systems seek to connect the different parts of the health care system in order to create more efficient systems of care and better experiences of care for patients. The purpose of my research is to examine the integrated care systems in place in Canada, and other countries, in order to learn how integrated care systems for seniors can best be implemented in Canada.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES A VIRUS; THERAPIE DU CANCER EN GENERAL
TitreApplicationTitle: Reovirus-induced immune modulation during oncotherapy
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTI-CANCER IMMUNITY; REOVIRUS
Abstract-Résumé: We don't normally think of viruses as beneficial organisms because they are invariably associated with human diseases. In 1998, we demonstrated that reovirus, a benign, naturally occurring human virus that does not cause any serious illness, is a potent cancer killer. This virus has the unique ability to preferentially kill cancer cells while leaving healthy, normal cells unaffected. Thus far, reovirus has been shown to kill cancers of almost every origin, including breast, pancreas, prostate, ovarian, brain, and colorectal. Reovirus is currently undergoing various cancer trials in Canada, the US, Belgium and the UK.   Recently our laboratory discovered that reovirus-based anti-cancer therapy bears a "beneficial" side effect to it. We observed that, apart from its direct cancer killing activity, reovirus additionally educates the body's immune system to attack cancer.  Importantly, this virus-induced anti-cancer immunity is capable of not only killing existing cancer cells, but also targeting any relapsing cancer cells in the future. Thus, reovirus-based therapy can simultaneously target cancers with two distinct mechanisms: 1) virus-mediated direct killing of cancer cells, and 2) virus-induced anti-tumor immunity.  It is now acknowledged that anti-tumor immune activities are the indispensible components of reovirus therapy.   For the last decade, we have comprehensively studied how reovirus directly kills cancer cells. We now focus on understanding the virus-induced immunological events in the context of cancers. For this purpose, we will first dissect the interaction between reovirus and the cancer-associated immune entities that dictate anti-cancer immunity. We will then use this knowledge to design strategies that can further enhance the efficacy of reovirus therapy. It is our hope that the knowledge generated through this project will result in better cancer outcomes, and further promote long-term cancer-free health even after discontinuation of therapy.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of cytochrome P450 enzymes in pathogenesis of cardiac hypertrophy
Keywords-MotsClés: ARACHIDONIC ACID; CARDIAC HYPERTROPHY; CARDIOVASCULAR PHARMACOLOGY; CYTOCHROME P450; DRUG METABOLISM; GENE EXPRESSION
Abstract-Résumé: Enlargement of the heart is one of the most common causes of heart failure in Canada. Once cardiac failure develops, the condition is irreversible and is associated with a very high death rate. Fifty percent of patients whose heart failure has progressed to include shortness of breath without physical activity do not survive beyond one year. As the heart becomes enlarged, it also disrupts the production of small lipid molecules that control the heart function, causing further damage and increasing the risk of sudden cardiac death. The heart enlargement reduces the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules called epoxyeicosatrienoic acids and increases the production of cardiotoxic molecules called hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid. While most patients can be treated with drug therapy, these treatments have side effects and are not effective in all patients. The objectives of our work are to control and prevent enlargement of the heart to improve treatment options for patients and reduce mortality. By increasing the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules (epoxyeicosatrienoic acids) and inhibiting the production of cardiotoxic molecules (hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid) in the heart, we can prevent the progressive deterioration of heart function and the development of heart failure. Our research will identify the molecules that are responsible for the enlargement of the heart and heart failure. In addition, we will test new chemicals that are known to increase the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules and inhibit the production of cardiotoxic molecules in the heart. This will prevent the progressive deterioration of heart function and the development of heart failure. This research will help to diminish health care costs, as well as to design strategies that improve treatment of heart failure.

TitreApplicationTitle: SirT1 mediates adaptation to chronic stress and resistance to chronic disease.
Keywords-MotsClés: HIGH CALORIE DIETS; HOMOLOGOUS RECOMBINATION; HYPOXIA; METABOLIC SYNDROME; MOUSE MUTATIONS; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION; SIRTUIN
Abstract-Résumé: Many of the common diseases in humans arise primarily in the elderly or in individuals who are at risk due to a physiological compromise such as obesity, elevated blood pressure, etc.  Our thesis is that some of the important diseases arise as a consequence of reduced ability of the patients to physiologically adapt to chronic stresses.  We believe that SirT1 is a key component of the adaptation machinery and that by elevating the abundance of SirT1 we will be able to delay the onset and perhaps reverse the development of some of the diseases caused by such chronic stresses as obesity.  Our approach is to use genetically modified strains of mice that we have create to first establish the validity of our idea (that increased SirT1 is of therapeutic benefit) and then to identify pharmacological agents that can increase SirT1 in normal mice and can thus affect therapeutic benefit more universally.

TitreApplicationTitle: Leveraging a literacy initiative to extend the reach of immunization in underserved populations in India: a synergy for child development
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILD HEALTH; HEALTH EQUITY; HEALTH LITERACY; IMMUNIZATION; INDIA; POPULATION HEALTH INTERVENTION RESEARCH; UNDERSERVED POPULATIONS; VACCINES
Abstract-Résumé: Globally and in India, vaccination rates are lower for children whose families and communities are less educated and whose socioeconomic position is worse. This project proposes to leverage a highly successful child literacy initiative to increase the reach of immunization and other essential child health services in India. The project team will develop novel methods for effective grassroots health education in low-literacy communities and pioneer approaches to improve community engagement in health and health services.

TitreApplicationTitle: Postprandial energy metabolism of brown fat in humans
Keywords-MotsClés: BROWN ADIPOSE TISSUE; DIABETES MELLITUS; INSULIN RESISTANCE; LIPID METABOLISM; POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; POSTPRANDIAL LIPOPROTEIN METABOLISM; POSTPRANDIAL THERMOGENESIS; STABLE ISOTOPES
Abstract-Résumé: Recent studies using positron emission tomography (PET), a diagnostic tool that allows quantification of tissue glucose uptake, have demonstrated the presence of brown adipose tissue (BAT) in humans. Metabolism of this tissue is activated by cold exposure and appears to be less active in obese and diabetic individuals. We demonstrated the contribution of BAT to energy expenditure and glucose and fatty acid utilization in healthy humans and found that it is less activated in subjects with diabetes. Using sophisticated PET and tracer techniques that allows quantification of tissue energy utilization and glucose and dietary fatty acid uptake, we will determine how much energy and fat BAT dissipates after a meal prior to and after increasing BAT activity using a validated 4-week cold acclimation protocol in otherwise healthy men with and without pre-diabetes (glucose intolerance). Energy expenditure, shivering, hormonal and metabolic responses to cold will be simultaneously determined. The proposed study will determine the true potential of activating BAT to dissipate energy and dietary fat after meal intake as a strategy to prevent and treat obesity and type 2 diabetes.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Role of Deubiquitination Enzymes in Mitochondrial Quality Control
Keywords-MotsClés: MITOCHONDRIA; NEURONAL CELL DEATH; PARKINSON'S DISEASE; QUALITY CONTROL
Abstract-Résumé: Beyond being the powerhouse of the cell, mitochondria are critical machines that can determine the overall health of the cell, and when they malfunction, can contribute to the death of the cell.  Mitochondrial dysfunction has been linked to many human diseases including Parkinson's disease.  This proposal will uncover new aspects of mitochondrial biology and function and lead the way to future therapeutics for Parkinson's disease.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comprehensive Health Assessments for Adults with Intellectual Disability (ID) in Manitoba: A Feasibility Study
Keywords-MotsClés: CAREGIVERS; COMMUNITY-BASED PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; COMPREHENSIVE HEALTH ASSESSMENT; COMPREHENSIVE HEALTH ASSESSMENT PROGRAM (CHAP); FOCUS GROUP; GENERAL PRACTITIONERS; HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA SETS; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; SEMI-STRUCTURED INTERVIEWS
Abstract-Résumé: Intellectual disabilities (IDs) affect approximately 300,000 Canadians and about 5,000 Manitobans, about 1,000 of whom are at least 45 years of age. Prior research shows that persons with ID have poorer health and more difficulty accessing proper health care than the general population. Thus, they will more likely have unmet health-care needs, which may result in preventable mortality and illnesses. Several factors may explain why persons with ID might not receive sufficient health care, for example, because of their communication difficulties or because their physicians and other health care providers may lack knowledge of their specific needs. The Comprehensive Health Assessment Program (CHAP), an assessment tool used by physicians and caregivers, can minimize the barriers to proper health care facing those with ID. Research from other countries has demonstrated the effectiveness of using the CHAP. In this grant application, we are proposing to send a copy of the CHAP to physicians and other individuals providing care to persons with ID to ask whether they would be willing to use this assessment tool for their clients. We will then meet with the study participants in groups to discuss any difficulties that they reported in using the tool and to brainstorm solutions. Using the CHAP can improve the overall health and well-being of persons with ID by facilitating their access to health care and in particular, preventive care, such as immunization, oral health care, regular checks on brain, heart, hearing, and vision, and care for a number of health risks that commonly affect persons with ID.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of epithelial polarity
Keywords-MotsClés: BLINDNESS; CANCER; CELL POLARITY; CRUMBS; DROSOPHILA; EPITHELIAL POLARITY; GENETIC ANALYSIS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY; TRANSGENEIC ANIMALS; YURT
Abstract-Résumé: The human retina contains cells called photoreceptors that are specialized to receive light and thus allow us to see. Photoreceptor cells have a complex architecture that emerges during development and that is essential for the normal function and survival of these cells. Mutations in several genes are known that seem to compromise photoreceptor cell structure and lead to the degeneration of the retina and blindness. The crumbs gene that we study is one of those genes. Humans that carry a mutant crumbs gene become blind during early childhood. Photoreceptors belong to a large group of cells known as epithelial cells, which include cells in our skin, gut, liver, and lungs to mention a few examples. All epithelial cells share a polarized cell structure that is critical for their shape and function as in the case of photoreceptors. Crumbs is needed to shape many different epithelial cells in addition to photoreceptors. On a fundamental level, we try to understand the mechanisms that shape epithelial cells by studying crumbs and several other genes that interact with crumbs. Our work is also highly relevant for the understanding of cancer. In most organs, cancer cells originate from epithelial cells in these organs. In fact, more than 80% of all cancers derive from epithelial cells. Thus, understanding epithelial tissue organization and developing strategies for maintaining epithelial tissue integrity is critical for addressing the cancer problem.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nursing Practice in Rural and Remote Canada II
Keywords-MotsClés: CANADIAN; HEALTH HUMAN RESOURCES; PRIMARY HEALTH CARE; QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS; QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS; REMOTE NURSING; RURAL NURSING; SURVEY
Abstract-Résumé: People who live in rural and remote parts of Canada (including the North) tend to have more health challenges than people living in urban areas. Rural and remote communities also have chronic shortages of health care workers, including nurses. The Nature of Nursing Practice in Rural and Remote Canada study (2001-04) was the first nation-wide study to look at these issues. In order to keep improving health services and support nurses in rural and remote communities, planners and policy makers need up-to-date information. Nursing Practice in Rural and Remote Canada II will provide that information. This research will survey over 9,000 licensed practical nurses (LPNs), registered nurses (RNs), registered psychiatric nurses (RPNs), and nurse practitioners (NPs) in rural and remote communities in every province and territory of Canada. The survey will ask questions about the nurses, their practice and what contributes to their recruitment and retention. The study will take place over three years, from 2013 to 2016. It will be done in partnership with planners and policy makers, who will make sure that the findings can be used to improve nursing services and access to care in rural and remote Canada.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of Prenatal Excess Vitamins in the Programming of Energy Balance Regulatory Pathways in Wistar Rat Dams and Offspring
Keywords-MotsClés: ENERGY HOMEOSTASIS; EPIGENETICS; FOOD INTAKE; HYPOTHALAMUS; METABOLIC DISORDERS; METABOLISM AND NUTRITION; OBESITY; RATS; REWARD SYSTEM; VITAMINS
Abstract-Résumé: Limited understanding of the complex contributors of obesity and related disorders has imposed a significant socioeconomic burden in Canada. Popularity and use of multivitamin supplements along with liberal food fortification policy contribute to risk of excessive intakes during pregnancy with largely unknown long term health effects in offspring. During the past 8 years our research group has provided novel evidence that high multivitamin consumption during pregnancy, in excess or inadequate amounts, programs the fetus for obesity and metabolic disorders in later life. As well, it has long lasting effects on food intake and characteristics of metabolic syndrome in the mothers. Our hypothesis is that the obese phenotype is a result of altered fetal and postnatal programming interactions of central and peripheral energy homeostasis pathways in response to excessive vitamin intake. Our work has potential to lead to a new understanding of the role of vitamins in the development of regulatory systems for food intake and metabolism. This research will identify the vitamins responsible and the molecular mechanisms underlying high vitamin diet-induced metabolic dysfunctions. The results will encourage research in humans to determine if excess of vitamins during pregnancy and early life contribute to a higher risk of obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Melatonin MT1 receptor as a target for antidepressant drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIDEPRESSANTS; DRUG DISCOVERY; IN VIVO ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MELATONIN; MELATONIN RECEPTORS; MOLECULAR BIOLOGY
Abstract-Résumé: Major depression, a condition affecting 3.2-6% of Canadians and with elevated health care costs, is characterized by depressed mood, anhedonia, weight loss or gain, insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue, despair, and/or cognitive impairments. The discovery and validation of new targets for the treatment of depression is of extreme importance, since the available treatments are clinically effective in only one third of the patients and importantly, they can also cause serious side effects. A new promising target for depression seems to be the melatonergic system. In mammals, melatonin acts through MT1 and MT2 receptors and the impact of these receptors on mood disorders, together and separately, is still unknown. The present proposal will combine behavioral, in vivo electrophysiological, molecular biology approaches to investigate the role of MT 1 receptors in the pathogenesis of depression and clarify the mechanism of action. For the first time, a novel cutting-edge selective MT1 agonist (called UCM871), recently synthetized in collaboration with a group of Italian chemists will be tested. The present research will thus validate a novel target for antidepressant drugs, representing an alternative to current therapies.

ClasseRechercheFR: MALADIES DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF; CANCER DE L'APPAREIL DIGESTIF
TitreApplicationTitle: Signaling Networks in Pancreatic Disease
Keywords-MotsClés: ACTIVATING TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR 3; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION; GENE MICROARRAY; GENETICALLY MODIFIED MICE; MIST1; PANCREATIC ADENOCARCINOMA; PANCREATITIS; POLYCOMB REPRESSOR COMPLEX 2; TRANSCRIPTION; UNFOLDED PROTEIN RESPONSE
Abstract-Résumé: The pancreas consists of two compartments; one which regulates blood sugar levels and the other that is involved in food digestion. This organ is also the target of a number of devastating diseases including pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer. There is an established link between pancreatitis and cancer of the pancreas with pancreatitis patients 20 times more likely to be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in their life time. My laboratory is interested in how normal pancreatic function and gene expression is altered to increase the susceptibility and severity to pancreatitis, and how these events then increase susceptibility to pancreatic cancer. We propose that the unfolded protein response, a signaling pathways that allows cells to deal with stress, also leads to changes in the mature pancreas that promote disease and conversion of mature pancreatic cells to immature cells that can undergo acinar to duct cell metaplasia, an early event in pancreatic cancer. We propose to use unique genetically modified mouse lines to manipulate the expression of ATF3, a mediator of the unfolded protein response, and PRC2, which is involved in gene silencing, and determine their roles in affecting the severity of pancreatitis and increasing the susceptibility to pancreatic cancer. From this work, we intend to determine the cellular mechanisms that are hijacked during disease, and identify potential cellular pathways that be targeted therapeutically.

TitreApplicationTitle: Deciphering the characteristics and functions of a novel growth hormone-releasing hormone receptor in the kidney
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL PROLIFERATION; CELL SIGNALING; CELL SURVIVAL; IN VIVO STUDIES; KIDNEY; RAT MODELS; RECEPTOR CHARACTERIZATION; RENAL CELL CULTURE
Abstract-Résumé: The growth hormone-releasing hormone receptor (GHRH-R) belongs to a family of proteins termed receptors, carrying external signals into the cells. They activate messengers systems leading to biological actions.   In the pituitary hormonal gland, localized at the base of the brain, activation of this very important protein target by a specific brain factor (growth hormone-releasing hormone or GHRH), leads to the production of growth hormone (GH). Its secretion into the blood allows important actions in the various part of the body, such as cell growth. It also increases lean body mass and decrease fat.  My research team has made an important discovery: the kidney contains a novel GHRH-R functional protein. Our recent results, using rat, mouse, pig and human kidneys, indicate that the structure of the kidney GHRH-R protein is different from that in the pituitary, suggesting specific roles in the kidney. Our results suggest that this receptor could protect the renal cells against oxidative stress and help injured cells to recover and take back their normal functions. In our rat model, this has been observed in specific portions of the inner kidney involved in urine concentration.  The general objective of the present project is therefore to use various biological approaches to determine the features of this novel GHRH-R in the kidney. We will also determine how it sends information into the cells and what type of information it sends into the cells. We will study its role in healthy rat tissues as well as in experimental models of high oxidative cellular stress.  Our results will allow determining the potential of the renal GHRH-R as a new target to consider in the maintenance of kidney functions, particularly in medical conditions of increased renal oxidative stress, such as diabetes, oxygen deprivation or ischemia, antibiotic toxicity, infections, inflammation and aging.

TitreApplicationTitle: Universal Childhood Varicella Vaccination Program: Will It Protect or Harm the Immigrant Population?
Keywords-MotsClés: COST-EFFECTIVENESS; EPIDEMIOLOGY; HEALTH DISPARITIES; HEALTH POLICY; IMMIGRANTS; VARICELLA; VARICELLA VACCINATION PROGRAMS
Abstract-Résumé: Varicella (Chickenpox) was a common infection in young children until a universal childhood vaccination program was implemented across Canada in 2005.  Rates of varicella and related complications have decreased dramatically since the introduction of the vaccination program.  To prevent outbreaks of varicella all persons who are not immune should be vaccinated.  Adult immigrants from tropical countries are more likely to be susceptible (non-immune) to varicella because varicella occurs at an older age in tropical countries and immigrants are not given varicella vaccine before arriving in Canada.    A fifth of Canadians are foreign born and the majority of new immigrants come from tropical countries therefore there is a large proportion adult immigrants who are probably non-immune to varicella.  This is important because adults are more likely to develop severe varicella and to be hospitalized or to die from varicella than children.  A safe and effective vaccine (~85%) has been available in Canada since 1999 but there are no programs in Canada to routinely give varicella vaccine to the new immigrants.   This is because there are no good studies to prove that immigrants are more likely to get varicella, to become more sick from varicella or how this may have changed since the introduction of a varicella vaccination program in children.   We propose to do a study where we will measure and compare the number of cases of varicella and associated hospitalizations and complications due to varicella in the immigrant compared to the Quebec born population before and after introduction of the childhood vaccination program.  We will use this data to do an economic analysis to determine what is the best vaccination strategy for this population.  The results from this study will provide policy makers with the information they need to develop targeted varicella vaccination programs for the immigrant population to ensure that they stay healthy and are not involved in outbreaks.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular-physiological characterization of Dbx1, putative XII inspiratory premotoneurons
Keywords-MotsClés: CALCIUM IMAGING; DBX1; HYPOGLOSSAL PREMOTONEURON; LASER ABLATION; MOUSE; MUSCLE ATONIA; OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA; RESPIRATORY DISEASE; SLEEP; WHOLE-CELL RECORDING
Abstract-Résumé: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a serious health issue, affecting more than 4% of individuals. It is characterized by repeated episodes (hundreds) of airway blockage and apnea (periods when breathing stops) during the night. OSA patients suffer from excessive daytime sleepiness, are at great risk for accidents and at high risk for cardiovascular disease. A major factor in OSA is that during sleep, especially dreaming sleep, muscles of the airway undergo almost complete relaxation because regions of the brain that normally keep these muscles active shut-down. When you try to breathe in, the negative pressure in the airway pulls the airway muscles, especially the tongue, backwards which blocks the airway. A major focus of research in OSA has been on the motoneurons that control the tongue muscle and how their activity changes with sleep-wake cycling. The ultimate objective of this work is to find ways to increase tongue muscle activity in sleep to prevent OSA.      The activity of the tongue muscle, however, is not just determined by the activity tongue motoneurons but by a whole circuit that transmits activity from regions in the brain the generate breathing, through an intermediate group of neurons called premotoneurons that ultimately communicate with the motoneurons. As with motoneurons, reduced activity of these premotoneurons during sleep could be an important contributor to OSA. However, virtually nothing is known about these premotoneurons because they are widely dispersed amongst many other neurons and extremely difficult to find. We have recently identified a molecular marker for these neurons that has been used to engineer mice in which these neurons light up under a fluorescent light. Therefore, the objective of this study is to use these engineered mice to learn as much as possible about these neurons so that we can develop strategies to manipulate them in naturally sleeping animals and understand how they contribute to airway control in sleep.

TitreApplicationTitle: Randomized controlled trial of a community-based exercise program for preventing functional decline among individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY; COPD; EXERCISE; FUNCTION; REHABILITATION
Abstract-Résumé: Research shows that participation in a formal rehabilitation program leads to improvements in physical function and quality of life. However following discharge from such programs, individuals often experience a decline in function, often to pre-rehabilitation levels. This decline is likely a result of non-adherence to home exercise programs. Community-based exercise programs represent a cost-effective way to address this issue, using existing resources to improve the health of individuals living with lung disease. This project will evaluate the effects of a one-year, community-based exercise program on physical function and quality of life. Participants will be asked to attend the program at least twice a week, at a location that is most convenient for them. Physical function and quality of life for individuals enrolled in the program will be compared to those who received standard care. If the program proves to be superior to standard care, it represents a cost-effective way to improve the health of individuals with chronic lung disease, with no additional strain on the healthcare system.

OrgNm: Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre/Institut de recherche du Centre universitaire de santé McGill
TitreApplicationTitle: Therapeutic implications of macrophage apoptosis in TB
Keywords-MotsClés: ADAPTIVE IMMUNITY; ANIMAL MODEL; CELL DEATH PROGRAM; EICOSANOIDS; INNATE IMMUNITY; MACROPHAGES BIOLOGY; MITOCHONDRIA; MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS; NANOPARTICLES; PULMONARY INFECTION
Abstract-Résumé: Ever since German scientist Robert Koch first discovered the infectious agent of tuberculosis (TB), (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mtb) in 1882, TB has defied efforts by scientists to prevent or cure the disease. The presence of Mtb DNA in the lung tissues of ancient Egyptian mummy (dated 1550-1080 BC) suggests a long-standing historical evolutionary relationship between M.tb and humans. Despite the world-wide application of BCG vaccination and other anti-Mtb interventions, Mtb remains one of the most deadly human pathogens killing annually two million people. Eight to ten million new cases of active tuberculosis occur each year due in large part to asymptomatic people chronically infected with Mtb. The ability of Mtb to persist in individuals with apparently normal immune systems implies that Mtb has developed strategies to avoid, evade, and even subvert innate and adaptive immunity. The major objective of this proposal is to develop a novel vaccine employing a pharmacological approach or recombinant BCG as tools to enhance immunity and ultimately protection against pulmonary Mtb infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Modulation of the androgenic message in adipose tissue
Keywords-MotsClés: 5ALPHA-REDUCTASES; ADIPOCYTE; ANDROGENS; DIHYDROTESTOSTERONE; OBESITY; TESTOSTERONE
Abstract-Résumé: Excess accumulation of fat inside the abdomen, termed visceral obesity, is generally predominant in men. The presence of those large visceral fat stores has been closely linked to metabolic abnormalities which lead to diabetes and heart disease. Would it be possible to reduce fat storage in adipose tissue located inside the abdominal cavity and favor accumulation of fat tissues located under the skin, or subcutaneous fat? If so, this could delay the onset of diseases in men with abdominal obesity. This has in fact been done before with agents called thiazolidinediones, which have been widely used before their withdrawal due to adverse side effects. A new mode of action for anti-diabetes drugs is to block the synthesis cortisol, a steroid hormone favoring visceral fat storage, directly in adipose tissue. Our main postulate is that this can also be done with another type of steroid hormone, that is, the male sex hormone testosterone. While the testes are a main source of testosterone in men, we have evidence that adipose tissues can also generate a portion of their own testosterone from other hormones secreted by the adrenals (termed adrenal androgen precursors). We wish to prove that blocking testosterone synthesis or inactivation in some fat compartments will change the availability of the hormone in each fat compartment and will direct excess dietary lipids away from the visceral fat stores. To reach this goal, we will use cultures of adipose cells or explants obtained from various fat compartments of lean, overweight and obese men. We have access to pharmacological inhibitors that can block the reactions leading to testosterone synthesis. These inhibitors have never been tested in the context of obesity. We postulate that studying androgen production in fat will contribute to identify new targets for the remodeling of adipose tissue distribution in men.

TitreApplicationTitle: Bioethics on the Ground: Criminalization and the Changing Landscape of HIV/AIDS Advocacy
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS; CRIMINALIZATION; HIV/AIDS; INTERSECTIONALITY; NON-DISCLOSURE; RISK
Abstract-Résumé: The criminalization of HIV/AIDS non-disclosure has emerged as one of the more complex legal questions to face Canada's Supreme Court (SCC) in recent years. From its landmark Cuerrier decision in 1998 through to the jointly heard D.C. and Mabior cases in 2012, the SCC has tried to grapple with medico-ethical-legal questions regarding the duty to disclose one's HIV positive sero-status to a sexual partner.  While it has sustained significant legal, scholarly and activist attention, there has been considerably less interest in how ethical issues are transforming the field of HIV/AIDS advocacy. In this project, we explore how the ethically uncertain and emotionally charged nature of the issue of HIV/AIDS non-disclosure is transforming the ethical field of HIV/AIDS. What obligations do HIV-positive people have to their sexual partners? What constitutes a significant risk for HIV infection? Courts have struggled to answer these questions in a clear, consistent, and direct manner, with some cases finding that condom use reduced the risk of transmission to an insignificant level while others found that it did not. AIDS service organizations advocate that the risk of transmission varies with the gender of the parties and with sexual position and activity, which complicates the court's desire to craft a uniform legal duty to disclose.

TitreApplicationTitle: Does anxiety sensitivity moderate the relation between post traumatic stress severity and alcohol abuse?
Keywords-MotsClés: ALCOHOL; ANXIETY; ANXIETY SENSITIVITY; COGNITION; COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY; MODERATOR; PREVENTION; SUBSTANCE; TRAUMA; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Most people will experience a traumatic event at some point in their lives. For many, the memory and distress of the event will fade with time, but for others the experience can leave them with lasting feelings of panic, anxiety, sleep difficulties, and a host of other unpleasant symptoms. This cluster of symptoms is referred to as Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), and impacts approximately 7% of the population, it can be lifelong in the absence of treatment. A significant proportion of those with PTSD will go on to develop alcohol dependence (AD), which can severely exacerbate symptoms, and decrease the likelihood of a full recovery. In the past, this lethal combination has lead to extremely poor quality of life, loss of job, isolation, and even suicide. It is important to understand risk factors to the development of AD following a traumatic event in order to apply early intervention and increase the odds of recovery. Anxiety sensitivity (AS), which is defined as ones fear of experiencing anxiety symptoms, may be a key player in the development of PTSD and subsequent AD. The goal of the proposed study is to examine the role anxiety sensitivity (AS) has in the development of AD following trauma exposure. Understanding factors that lead to the development of alcohol problems following trauma will allow therapists to alter their treatment to prevent a downward spiral that could result in lifelong impairment. This line of research can arm us with the ability to apply early intervention, and can also provide greater insight into risk factors that may lead to understanding the causes of PTSD and AD on a more fundamental level.

TitreApplicationTitle: iPSC-based in vitro modeling of prostate cancer
Keywords-MotsClés: 3D TISSUE CULTURE; CANCER RESEARCH; CANCER STEM CELLS; CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY; INDUCED PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; MESENCHYMAL-EPITHELIAL TRANSITION; REAL-TIME RT-PCR; TISSUE ENGINEERING; TUMOUR MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: The transformation of a cancer cell into a metastatic body is the main cause of death in patients with cancer. Cancer stem cells have the ability to give rise to all cell types found in a particular cancer sample, and therefore these cells are tumorigenic. Cancer stem cells are proposed to persist in tumours as a distinct subpopulation and cause relapse and metastasis by giving rise to secondary tumours. It is suggested that by selectively targeting cancer stem cells it would be possible to treat patients with aggressive tumors and prevent metastasis. Our research project proposes a model of tumour formation that will allow us to study cancer stem cell tumour development in three dimensional (3D) tissue culture. It can further be used for high throughput small molecule screening for drugs that suppress tumour formation. Recently researchers have called for better cancer models where tumour formation can be studied in 3D culture within a tissue context. Our approach can lead to a new field of cancer tissue engineering, which will allow the study of cancer stem cells mediated tumour formation in culture. Engineered tissues provide physiologically relevant, yet controllable models for the fundamental research, for example, to study stem cells in native-like 3D context of the development or a disease, or to perform drug screening with engineered human tissues.  Development of specific therapies targeted at cancer stem cells has a great potential for improvement of survival and quality of life of cancer metastatic patients. Our research will contribute significantly to the understanding of the mechanism and regulation of cancer stem cell tumour development and provide a valuable 3D model of tumour formation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Genotypic and functional evolution of HIV-1 Vif over the course of HIV/AIDS epidemic
Keywords-MotsClés: APOBEC3G; HIV-1; IMMUNE ESCAPE; MOLECULAR EPIDEMIOLOGY; VIF
Abstract-Résumé: HIV-1 infects 34 million people worldwide. Although current HIV treatments can suppress viral loads in the in the blood to undetectable levels, the need for a vaccine is still present. A major challenge to vaccine design is the virus' capacity to adapt to the human immune system through the selection of mutations, a process called "immune escape". Analysis at the population level has revealed that the specific mutational pathways of immune escape are highly reproducible based on the specific genetic profiles expressed by the host.  The extent to which HIV has adapted to immune selection pressure over the course of the pandemic remains incompletely understood. Furthermore, the extent to which immune-driven evolution has influenced HIV protein function and viral pathogenesis remains unknown. Ongoing research in the Brumme laboratory aims to identify the impact of immune selection pressure on HIV protein function. I will specifically look at the HIV-1 Vif (viral infectivity factor) protein responsible for antagonizing the human antiviral immune protein APOBEC3G. Characterizing and comparing HIV-1 Vif sequences collected from patients dating back to 1979, I will use current laboratory techniques to understand the extent to which HIV-1 Vif sequences have evolved in response to immune selection pressures imposed by human hosts over the course of the epidemic in North America. In addition, I will use a published assay to assess the ability of historic and modern patient derived Vif sequences to enhance virion infectivity by modulating the host APOBEC3G protein.  This study will advance our understanding of the extent and pathogenic implications of host-driven adaptation of HIV accessory proteins over the course of the epidemic, yielding results of relevance to HIV vaccine design.

TitreApplicationTitle: Parallel control of the micro-vasculature by neurons and astrocytes
Keywords-MotsClés: ASTROCYTES; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MICRO-VASCULATURE; NEOCORTEX; NEURO-VASCULAR COUPLING; NEURONS; NEUROSCIENCE; OPTOGENETICS; TWO-PHOTON IMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: The control of brain blood flow is absolutely critical for maintaining brain function.  Brain blood flow control requires intimate communication from brain cells to nearby small blood vessels.  This communication results in diameter changes to the vessels, to speed up or slow down nutrient delivery from the blood to ensure appropriate supply.  Deficiencies in this fundamental process can have devastating consequences to brain health, which include stroke, vascular dementia and migraine.  Surprisingly, how brain cells coordinate blood vessel diameter changes is not fully understood.  Currently it is believed that neurons and brain support cells called astrocytes are important players in blood flow control.  However, the current model of blood flow control posits that neurons and astrocytes act in series (neuron to astrocyte to blood vessel) to make adjustments in blood vessel diameter.  Here we propose a new conceptual framework for blood flow control by detailing a new way in which neurons and astrocytes act in parallel with one another, each regulating a different aspect of blood vessel diameter control.  The results from our proposed experiments will provide novel insights into the fundamental mechanisms of blood flow control in the brain.  The knowledge gained will be an important step towards developing therapeutics for conditions impacted by abnormal brain blood flow.

TitreApplicationTitle: Aboriginal Youth Mentor Program
Keywords-MotsClés: COMMUNITY-BASED PARTICIPATORY ACTION; MENTORSHIP; OBESITY; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY; TYPE 2 DIABETES
Abstract-Résumé: Aboriginal youth represent a significant and growing population in Canada and have much to offer in terms of their contributions to their own health and the health and wellness of others. At the same time, they are at a greater risk for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) and obesity than non-Aboriginal youth. Few school based programs have been developed and tested that are aimed at reducing the risk for T2D Aboriginal youth, especially those living in rural communities. Fewer still involve interventions that are peer-led and reliant upon the strengths, energy and talents of the youth themselves. Building on the successes of a communal, relationship based approach to Aboriginal youth mentoring in an after school physical activity program (AYMP), we are evaluating a peer-led approach for diabetes prevention. First Nations high school students volunteer as mentors, and develop an after-school program that they then deliver to children in grade 4. The mentors meet twice a week. The first day, they develop an activity plan and decide roles and responsibilities to ensure successful delivery of each activity. The second day, they deliver the program to the grade 4s, which incorporates a healthy snack, 45-minutes of physical activity, and educational games/activities. Our primary goal is to determine the health benefits of AYMP; guided by our youth mentors and community advisors, we will also develop a number of research questions that will help us to better understand the social, emotional, physical and spiritual outcomes of the peer-led mentor program. To answer these questions, we will train community members in both qualitative and quantitative methods. The quantitative outcomes of this study include physical activity, waist circumference, obesity rates, and self-esteem. Qualitative methods may include photovoice and focus group interviews. All of these will be used to assess the social determinants of health and contextual features of the program.

TitreApplicationTitle: Preclinical models of natural killer cell-based immunotherapy to cure refractory childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CHILDHOOD LEUKEMIA; CORD BLOOD TRANSPLANTATION; CYTOKINE INDUCED KILLER CELLS; DENDRITIC CELLS; IMMUNOTHERAPY; MOUSE MODEL OF CORD BLOOD TRANSPLANTATION; MOUSE MODEL OF HUMAN LEUKEMIA XENOGRAFT; NATURAL KILLER CELLS
Abstract-Résumé: Forty to fifty percent of children whose leukemia reappears following treatment die of their disease, underscoring an urgent need to improve current therapies. The only hope of a cure for these children is intensive highly toxic chemotherapy followed by the replacement of their immune system, also called hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.  The reappearance of leukemia is due to the persistence of leukemic cells, despite intensive chemotherapy. These cancer cells are recognized and eliminated by the recovering immune system provided by the hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. This recognition, called graft-versus-leukemia effect, can be enhanced by stimulating immune cells that recover following the transplantation. The first immune cells that are present in the blood of transplanted children are highly effective as killers of tumour cells. We, therefore, aim to stimulate these cells following hematopoietic transplantation in order to eradicate the residual cancer cells that are responsible for the relapse. We propose to use mouse models to test new therapeutic approaches following hematopoietic transplantation. We will also evaluate the safety of these therapies, as well as the possible interaction with immune suppressive drugs that are commonly administrated to transplanted patients. Collectively, our results will establish the best possible approaches to prevent leukemia relapse for testing in future clinical trials.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neuropeptides and peptidomimetics as pharmacological tools and potential drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: ANALGESICS FOR NEUROPATHIC PAIN; BIFUNCTIONAL OPIOID/ANTIOXIDANT ANALGESICS; CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS OF PEPTIDES AND PEPTIDOMIMETICS; OPIOID ANALGESICS; PEPTIDE HORMONES AND NEUROTRANSMITTERS; PEPTIDE-BASED DRUG DEVELOPMENT
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic, severe pain is a significant health problem. One third of North-Americans suffer from some form of chronic pain, and in over 30% it is resistant to analgesic therapy. The economic impact of pain is enormous, at approximately $ 100 billion annually. While non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and opiate narcotics are effective for acute pain relief, adequate therapies for the treatment of chronic pain, including neuropoathic pain, complex regional pain syndrome, chemotherapy-induced pain, post-operative pain and inflammatory pain, are lacking. Medications currently used in the in the management of neuropathic pain states, such as tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants (e.g. gabapentin), serotonin/noradrenalin reuptake inhibitors and opioid analgesics, are ineffective and produce side effects. There is convincing evidence that mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) at the spinal level are involved in the generation and maintenance of neuropathic and inflammatory pain. Administration of various antioxidants (free radical quenchers) was somewhat effective in animal models of neuropathic pain, but very high doses were required because these agents were not targeted to mitochondria.  A mitochondria-targeted mu opioid analgesic with antioxidant properties discovered in our laboratory, [Dmt1]DALDA, was found to be superior to morphine in animal models of neuropathic pain and complex regional pain syndrome, likely due to a synergistic effect between mu opioid- and antioxidant activity. We now propose to synthesize [Dmt1]DALDA analogues with further improved antioxidant capacity and to test them in vitro for opioid and antioxidant activity, and in vivo as pharmacological tools and drug candidates in animal models of the neuropathic pain states described above.  The compounds to be developed are expected to be highly effective for neuropathic pain relief and to have low propensity to induce analgesic tolerance.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cerebral erythropoietin as a novel mechanism to explain sex-specific respiratory depression in neonates
Keywords-MotsClés: APNEA; BRAINSTEM; ERYTHROPOIETIN; HYPOXIA; MASCULINIZATION; NEONATES; RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION; SEX DIMORPHISM; SIDS; TESTOSTERONE
Abstract-Résumé: The morbidity and the mortality related to respiratory disordered in newborn and during infancy are more observed in males than females. The underlying mechanisms of such sex-specific differences are still un-determined. Interestingly, we found that erythropoietin (Epo) prevents respiratory depression in newborn mice, and that this effect is more important in male than female mice. Originally, Epo was discovered as a hormone able to increase the production of red blood cells (such occurring in anemia or doping). Now we know that Epo is also synthesized in neuronal tissue (cerebral Epo) and exert in brain crucial protective function upon conditions of poor oxygen availability (hypoxia). Brainstem is the region located in the posterior part of the brain that holds the major centers associated with control of respiration. In newborn mammals the respiratory control system in the brainstem is in full process of maturation and development, thus hypoxia-induced respiratory depression is more important than in adult animals. Hence, developing strategies allowing the respiratory control system to maintain adequate and efficient breathing responses to hypoxia would be a significant breakout in the development of new clinical interventions and biomedical sciences. Based on our exciting findings, we propose to that testosterone (the hormone that promotes the "masculinization" of the male brain around birth) interacts with Epo in the regulation of respiration in newborn mice. We will define: the sex specific expression of Epo and its receptors in the brainstem; the sex-dependent respiratory depression in absence (inactivation) of cerebral Epo; and whether the testosterone suppression (castration) or metabolization abolishes the impact of Epo on respiratory depression. These measurements will be performed in conditions of both normal and limited oxygen availability, thus mimicking conditions of respiratory diseases. The potential health and social benefits are very significant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Étude longitudinale de la relation entre les pratiques sportives risquées et l'occurrence de blessures chez des adeptes de sports alpins de glisse
Keywords-MotsClés: BLESSURE; IMPULSIVITE; PERSONNALITE; PRISE DE RISQUE; PREVENTION DES BLESSURES; SENSATIONS FORTES; SKI ALPIN; SPORT; SURF DES NEIGES
Abstract-Résumé: Les sports consideres comme extremes ou a risque sont de plus en plus populaires de nos jours, particulierement chez les adolescents et les jeunes adultes. La pratique de ces sports est a l'origine de nombreuses blessures. Les blessures d'origine recreative et sportive representent deja une preoccupation importante sur le plan de la sante publique. A chaque annee, les couts socioeconomiques imputables aux blessures d'origine recreative et sportive se chiffrent a pres de 272 millions de dollars pour la seule province du Quebec. Le ski alpin et le surf des neiges font partie des sports occasionnant les taux de blessures graves les plus eleves. En 2009-2010,ils se situaient respectivement au 3e rang et au 4e rang des sports ayant les plus haut taux de blessures graves, avec 42,7 % des blessures recensees chez les skieurs et 37,1 % chez les surfeurs des neiges etant considerees comme severes. Le nombre de blessures est en hausse depuis 2010. A ce jour, plusieurs etudes ont porte sur les types de blessures associees aux sport de glisse de meme que l'efficacite du casque comme equipement de protection. Par contre, peu d'etudes ont porte sur la relation entre la prise de risques et l'occurrence de blessures et sur les divers facteurs psychosociaux venant l'influencer. Les blessures d'origine sportive peuvent compromettre le developpement des jeunes en leur laissant des sequelles physiques ou intellectuelles permanentes, ce pourquoi il importe de mener des recherches afin de mieux comprendre les mecanismes relies a la prise de risques et aux blessures, en vue de developper des outils de prevention des blessures et de la prise de risque aupres des adeptes de sports de glisse.

TitreApplicationTitle: DNA Copy Number Variation in Li-Fraumeni Syndrome
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER GENETICS; CANCER GENOMICS; GENETIC MODIFIERS; LI-FRAUMENI SYNDROME; P53; TUMOR SURVEILLANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Li-Fraumeni syndrome, LFS, is a familial disorder characterized by the development of multiple cancers, in children and young adults. These individuals carry a mutation in a gene, called TP53. TP53 normally behaves to protect cells from becoming cancerous. It does so by being able to recognize when the DNA in a cell is unstable, and then directing the cell to stop dividing or to kill itself. But people with LFS carry an abnormal copy of the TP53 gene in every cell of their body, so every cell is at risk of becoming a cancer cell. We do not know what other genetic changes are required that determine what age or what type of cancer will develop in any particular LFS individual. However, using novel experimental techniques we have shown that there may be other abnormalities in the DNA of a person that modify the effect of the mutant TP53 gene. It appears that, in addition to the abnormal TP53 gene, these people also inherit or acquire dramatic sub-microscopic structural alterations in their DNA in every cell in their body, and in cells that become cancerous, these changes become even more pronounced. In addition, these patients carry variants (polymorphisms) in other genes or in TP53 itself that appear to modify the risk of getting cancer. In this study, we will examine the DNA from blood of LFS patients - both those with TP53 mutations and those with normal TP53. In the first set, we will be looking for variants in genes other than TP53 that play a role in determining the types and age of onset of cancer; in the second set, we will look for mutations in genes that may cause the cancers in these patients and families. This information would be enormously helpful in predicting who develops cancer, when and what cancers occur, as well lead to a better understanding of the underlying genetic basis of cancer. With this information, we will also be able to develop better surveillance methods to detect cancers early with the hope to improve survival.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of TGF-beta in spinal cord damage and repair
Keywords-MotsClés: AXONAL REGENERATION; CONFOCAL AND 2-PHOTON MICROSCOPY; CYTOKINE; GLIA SCAR; IMMUNE RESPONSE; MACROPHAGE; NEURODEGENERATION; SPINAL CORD INJURY; TRANSGENIC AND CHIMERIC MICE; WALLERIAN DEGENERATION
Abstract-Résumé: Over four million of individuals are afflicted by different types of spinal cord injury (SCI). One of the consequences of SCI is the loss of neural tissue at the site of injury and the damage to neuronal projections that traverse the length of the spinal cord. Damage to these descending and ascending neuronal projections -termed axons- can result in loss of motor, sensory, and autonomic functions. Because the natural capacity of the mammalian central nervous system (CNS) to regenerate is extremely limited, unlike the peripheral nervous system (PNS), axonal damages sustained after SCI often lead to permanent functional deficits for which no cure is currently available. Among the many factors that prevent CNS neurons from regenerating their axons are molecules associated with degenerating myelin. Although these molecules are present in both the CNS and PNS, myelin-associated axon growth inhibitors are eliminated very rapidly by macrophages after peripheral nerve injury. In addition to remove myelin debris, macrophages release molecules that allow non-neuronal resident cells to switch into a growth-support mode. The direct result of this being the expression of trophic and guidance molecules for regenerating axons. In the human CNS, the macrophage response is deficient and can take up months to years to fully develop. The main goal of this research proposal is to identify the cellular and molecular mechanisms employed by macrophages to create a growth permissive environment for regenerating axons and utilized this knowledge to promote axonal regeneration in the injured CNS. Instructing immune cells to remove myelin and its inhibitors of axonal regeneration and provide adequate trophic support will have implications for regeneration following brain and spinal cord injury.

TitreApplicationTitle: Psychosocial Predictors of Health and Survival in Late Life
Keywords-MotsClés: APPRAISALS; HEALTH; HEALTH CARE UTILIZATION; LONGITUDINAL; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: Health is influenced by many social and psychological variables, such as the way individuals psychologically appraise life events. For example, appraising events as controllable has positive effects on health. Because individuals are threatened by uncontrollable life challenges as they age, it is critical to understand the implications of perceived control (PC) in late life. Although research generally demonstrates health protective consequences of PC, our paradoxical premise is that appraising health as controllable might have negative consequences when it is part of a toxic appraisal style that results in denial of health care needs and disengagement from health. The strengths of our longitudinal study of community dwelling older adults include: i) access to a representative sample of very old adults; ii) a long follow up (20 years); iii) the linkage of interview data to  valuable databases (e.g., Manitoba Health Registry); and iv) an outstanding quality and quantity of data on psychological appraisals in a health context, and outcomes that include physical activity, emotional well being (depression), physical health (e.g., blood oxygen), health care service usage (e.g., physician visits, hospitalizations), and mortality. To the extent that a maladaptive appraisal style corresponds to disengagement from health care and compromised health, the findings would be relevant to understanding the well being of older Canadians. Our findings would also have implications relevant to caregiver burden that results when individuals neglect their health and pose challenges for the informal and formal care systems. This would have further implications for the mounting political pressures and the financial challenges facing the Canadian health care system. The development of an intervention to foster an adaptive appraisal style would have the potential to offset health care costs, relieve caregiver burden, and ultimately, to improve the well being and longevity of Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Developing a Built Environment Assessment Tool for Aboriginal Communities
Keywords-MotsClés: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES' HEALTH; BUILT ENVIRONMENT; ENVIRONMENTAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH; PARTICIPATORY RESEARCH; PHYSICAL ACTIVITY
Abstract-Résumé: The disenfranchising effects of colonial practices have deprived Aboriginal youth from participating fully in physical activity (PA), preventing them from achieving a balanced state of health. Although research has demonstrated a link between the built environment and PA, understanding this relationship from an Aboriginal perspective is important when considering health disparities between Aboriginal peoples and the general population. My Master's project is an ancillary study to an ongoing CIHR-funded project (2012-2015) that is evaluating Active Circle programming and its effect on positive youth development. As part of the Active Circle project, photovoice will be used to understand how youth from 10 urban and rural communities perceive the quality of PA opportunities in their community. Photovoice is a participatory research method that engages participants to take pictures of their community in a way that allows them to share personally meaningful dialogue about community issues. For my project, I will use the Rural Active Living Assessment (RALA), an established built environment assessment tool, to assess the physical environment in rural Aboriginal communities (about 4-5 communities) participating in the Active Circle study. The RALA assesses physical environment features that affect PA in rural communities. I will conduct a quantitative analysis of RALA outcomes and use the photovoice results to determine what elements are missing for understanding the built environment and its effect on PA from an Aboriginal perspective. The revised tool will then be validated within the Active Circle project. The results of my study will increase our understanding of the relationship between the built environment and PA. This will help reduce health disparities, such as higher rates of type II diabetes, among Aboriginal peoples. My project will also provide practitioners with a tool to assess the built environment of Aboriginal communities in a culturally meaningful way.

TitreApplicationTitle: Mechanisms in compulsive drug use
Keywords-MotsClés: BEHAVIOURAL TRAINING; CELLULAR NEUROSCIENCE; ELECTROPHYSIOLOGY; MECHANISM OF DRUG ADDICTION; NEUROPEPTIDES
Abstract-Résumé: Substance abuse, which carries an enormous social and economical toll, continues to propagate at an alarming rate in Canada. Research has been relatively successful in understanding how drugs of abuse act on the brain to produce exaggerated reinforcement. The next challenge for researchers in the field of drug addiction is to identify the cellular and molecular neuroadaptations that characterize voluntary drug intake and the brain's transformation in addiction. Specifically, our research focuses on understanding the cellular changes, which underlie human addict's transition between habitual to compulsive drug use. Our laboratory has identified a specific mechanism which shows promising evidence towards its role in compulsive behaviour. Therefore, my project will consist of investigating neural modulators that may have an effect on this mechanism. Ultimately, we will try to investigate whether blocking these neural modulators could be used for potential treatment to counter the compulsive behaviour seen in addicts.

TitreApplicationTitle: Understanding mechanisms of elevated blood clotting during acute psychological stress in those with and without heart disease
Keywords-MotsClés: CLOTTING; HAEMOCONCENTRATION; HEART DISEASE; SEX AND GENDER; STRESS
Abstract-Résumé: Acute stress, for example an argument with a spouse, may increase the chance of getting heart disease or even having a heart attack, though we don't know exactly how this happens. During this kind of stress blood may be more prone to clotting. That is, the blood goes from being a liquid to being a sticky solid. Clotting is what happens to blood to stop the bleeding when we have a cut, but should not happen otherwise. It is possible that this 'stress-induced clotting' could be due to the blood temporarily losing some of its liquid part (called heamoconcentration), that the 'fight or flight' (called the autonomic nervous system) response to stress may change the parts of the blood responsible for the clotting, or that other parts of the blood or the blood vessel change to make it more likely that the blood will clot. The aims of this project are: 1) Explore why blood clotting increases during stress; 2) Compare the stress-induced clotting responses between those with and without heart disease; and 3) Compare this response between men and women. To do this, we will recruit men and women with heart disease and age- and sex-matched healthy individuals from the Montreal area. Measures of blood and general functioning of the heart will be taken during rest and two standardized laboratory mental stress tasks (a math task and a picture viewing task). We will look at how the blood, the factors in the blood, and the blood vessel change in response to these tasks. We expect that this study will help us understand how stress might lead to heart disease and how this might differ between men and women. Once we understand this process better we will be able to develop interventions which may help reduce how stress affects the heart and lower peoples chances of having a heart attack.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining molecular pathways underlying craniofacial birth defects
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL DIFFERENTIATION; CRANIOFACIAL BIRTH DEFECTS; MOUSE GENTICS; NEURAL CREST
Abstract-Résumé: Malformations in head structures, such as the bones and palate, are estimated to account for approximately 50% of all human birth defects and have been associated with a wide variety of syndromes including the Pierre Robin and DiGeorge syndromes. The prevalence of craniofacial malformations is likely related to the intricate relationship that exists between the various components of the head and the complex molecular pathways that regulate their development.In this proposal, we investigate the involvement of a specific receptor at the surface of neural crest cell, called Neogenin, to regulate the differentiation of these cells into cells that form bones of the face. Understanding how this receptor regulates this process will provide important information on how dysregulation of its function during development can lead to craniofacial defects at birth.
