TitreApplicationTitle: Deconvoluting the role of diet and obesity in prostate cancer susceptibility through epigenomics
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOINFORMATICS; CHROMATIN IMMUNOPRECIPITATION-SEQUENCING; DIET; DNASE I HYPERSENSITIVE SITES; EPIGENOMICS; HUMAN TISSUES; MOUSE MODELS; OBESITY; PROSTATE CANCER; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Prostate cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in North American men and the second leading cause of cancer-related death. Still, androgen deprivation therapy has remained the sole treatment for advance disease since its description in 1941, although it ultimately leads to an incurable castration-resistant disease. Therefore, the field urgently needs an innovative approach to prevent and treat prostate cancer before it reaches a more advanced stage.  Diet and obesity are among the risk factors associated with prostate cancer. Strikingly, the disparity in prostate cancer incidence between the Eastern and the Western part of the World clearly advocate for the crucial role of environmental factors in the etiology of the disease. Prostate cancer is characterized by complex genomic alterations that are highly heterogeneous and greatly varies from a patient to another and even within the same tumor. Such disparities could be partly explained by an underlying genomic instability. In fact, prostate cancer has been described as an epigenome catastrophe, suggesting that epigenetic changes (i.e. modifications to the DNA) are pivotal events in prostate cancer initiation. Diet can induce various epigenetic modifications that result as global alterations in DNA packaging. Such stable and heritable changes regulate the access of the transcriptional machinery to their target genes and completely alter cellular behavior.  Our working hypothesis is that specific diets and chronic obesity induce profound epigenetic modifications leading to increased genomic instability, which contributes to prostate cancer development. Tackling this hypothesis using various animal models, human tissues and cutting edge genome-wide technologies represent a novel and promising approach in prostate cancer research. We trust that understanding those epigenetic modifications will allow us to point to non-pharmacological means as well as targeted therapy to prevent or treat prostate cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Population-based assessment of sleep deprivation in staff physicians and its impact on patient care and outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: ADVERSE EVENTS; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; OUTCOMES; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SLEEP-DEPRIVATION; SURGERY
Abstract-Résumé: Sleep deprivation is a significant problem among medical trainees and can adversely impact patient care.  To date however, we have no knowledge of whether this applies to staff physicians who perform the great bulk of patient care.  We have very little data on how frequently patients are treated by sleep-deprived staff physicians, and more importantly, whether their patients' outcomes suffer as a result.  In this study, we will first explore the physician workforce that is involved in treating patients emergently in the overnight hours as well as the next day - that is, after a period of overnight sleep loss.  Second, we will study whether patient outcomes are impacted if their physician is sleep deprived.  Finally, we will use surveys and interviews to assess the factors influencing physician sleep deprivation and patient care, and to assess the perspectives of patients and physicians. To conduct this study, we will utilize unique high-quality data sources that allow us to characterize all physician-patient encounters that take place in the province, and study their outcomes.  The findings from this study are relevant to all Ontarians and fully generalizable to other jurisdictions in Canada.  If we find that patients do worse when they receive care by sleep-deprived physicians, we can develop strategies that can have a major impact on improving patient safety and quality of care.  These strategies will need to take into account physician workforce issues as well as the perspectives of physicians and patients.  Since we are studying these issues as well, we will be able to tailor strategies that are beneficial to patients while being acceptable and feasible to implement broadly.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Genetic Epidemiology of Autism; Family and Molecular Studies
Keywords-MotsClés: AUTISM; GENETICS; WHOLE GENOME SEQUENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Although there has been remarkable progress in understanding the genetic architecture of autism spectrum disorders (ASDs)in recent years many unanswered questions. We do not know if all the variants have been discovered and with the advent of newer technologies there remains the possibility that a number of genetic variants known as Single Nucleotide Variants (or SNVs) may be uncovered as well. Moreover, most of the variants described to date appear to arise spontaneously (de novo)in subjects affected with ASD and so do not explain the fact that ASD runs in families. Finally, correlations between genetic variants and the clinical expression of ASD have been difficult to replicate consistently; information that is essential for genetic counselling.  The objective of this renewal is to test hypotheses about correlations between specific genetic variants and clinical expression in families with an ASD child. We will first exploit our existing sample by going back to families with a subject with ASD who also have at least two other siblings. We will also recruit new families with the same family structure. Each affected subject will undergo Whole Genome Sequencing and rare SNVs that are "potentially causal" or ASD will be identified. Families with these variants will be then clinically characterized using a comprehensive battery of measures that include ASD traits, ASD associated features, and medical co-morbidities. Other family members will also undergo WGS to see if they carry the same genetic variant as the affected child.  The relevance of this research program is to begin to fill in the "evidence-gaps" in understanding the influence of genetic variants on the clinical expression in ASD. This information is crucial in helping families understand the meaning of a particular genetic variant on their ASD child's life course and the risk posed to their other children who may have inherited the same variant.

TitreApplicationTitle: Culture Stress and the Preimplantation Embryo: Implications for Single Embryo Transfer
Keywords-MotsClés: APOPTOSIS AND CELL DEATH; ASSISTED REPRODUCTIVE TECHNOLOGIES; BLASTOCYST; CELL SIGNALLING; EMBRYO CULTURE; PREIMPLANTATION DEVELOPMENT; REACTIVE OXYGEN SPECIES; REPRODUCTION; SINGLE EMBRYO TRANSFER
Abstract-Résumé: Fertility clinics are moving rapidly to single embryo transfer (SET) to reduce the numbers of "multiple" ie twin, triplet or greater pregnancies. "Multiple" pregnancies are high risk and are accompanied by high rates of premature delivery and low birth weight with all of their accompanying medical and social concerns and costs. It is important single embryo transfer becomes standard practice. This will only be safely accomplished by understanding how the early embryo can adapt to laboratory environments. Thus to increase the safety of fertility treatments and to ensure the health of offspring produced by the application of fertility treatments it is essential that research defines the impact of exposure to laboratory environments on early development. Through their combined expertise Dr(s) Watson and Betts propose to investigate the mechanisms underlying one of the most pressing concerns that the fertility field has which is why laboratory environments have such a profound immediate and often long term impact on embryo health, pregnancy and postpartum development. We will investigate the roles of two cell signalling pathways called p66Shc and AMPK (PRKAA1/2). We hypothesize that these pathways regulate the development of early embryos and also responses to culture stress. Thus our studies will determine if these pathways are important for allowing embryos to survive laboratory environments and this knowledge will allow us to apply single embryo transfer in a much safer and more efficient way. The proposed experiments will be applied to mouse, cow and human preimplantation embryos. Our long-term goal is to translate our findings from the mouse to the human to enable the effective application of fertility treatments.

TitreApplicationTitle: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Housing First for Homeless People with Mental Illness: Long-term Outcomes
Keywords-MotsClés: ASSERTIVE COMMUNITY TREATMENT; ETHNO-RACIAL; HOMELESSNESS; HOUSING FIRST; INTENSIVE CASE MANAGEMENT; MENTAL ILLNESS; RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL
Abstract-Résumé: Homeless people with mental illness suffer from very poor health and many unmet health care needs. The Housing First model is an intervention that addresses the needs of this population by providing immediate access to subsidized housing in conjunction with supports. Although several studies of the effectiveness of Housing First have been conducted, several knowledge gaps remain. In particular, the long-term effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of this highly resource-intensive intervention is not known. In 2009, the Mental Health Commission of Canada initiated the At Home study, the world's largest randomized controlled trial of a Housing First intervention for people who are homeless and have mental illness. In Toronto, Ontario, the study enrolled 400 men and 175 women who were randomized to a Housing First intervention or treatment-as-usual and assessed regularly for 2 years following randomization.  This study will extend the At Home study beyond this point to determine the long-term outcomes (up to 6 years) of the Housing First model for homeless people with mental illness. Knowledge about the long-term effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of this intervention will inform efforts to improve the health of this population and reduce adverse impacts on the health care, social service, and justice systems.

TitreApplicationTitle: Stress-induced dopamine release in subjects at clinical high risk for psychosis: a [11C]-FLB457 PET study
Keywords-MotsClés: POSITRON EMISSION TOMOGRAPHY; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: People with schizophrenia experience symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions. It is a devastating illness for those affected, estimated at more than 240,000 Canadians, and their families (Goeree et al 2004). A natural chemical present in the brain called dopamine carries signals between nerve cells and plays an important role in schizophrenia.  People who have the disease, or those at very high risk of developing it, become worse when they are in stressful situations. Repeated exposure to stressors may change the amount of dopamine released in the brain and could explain why the disease develops in vulnerable individuals, and why those who have the illness relapse.  It is possible to detect brain levels of dopamine in humans by using a radioactive dye and a positron emission tomography (PET) camera. In this study, PET will be used to measure brain levels of dopamine in the cerebral cortex during a stressful task in healthy volunteers, individuals at very high risk of developing schizophrenia, and patients. Information on changes in dopamine release in the brain, hormonal changes and psychological characteristics will be collected, and the interactions between them explored. This is anticipated to provide the knowledge needed to detect the disease at an earlier stage and for identification of socio-psychological risk factors that will help target mental health interventions.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of transcription factors Nur77 and retinoid X receptor (RXR) in the effect of antipsychotic drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: ANTIPSYCHOTIC DRUGS; DOPAMINE D2 RECEPTORS; DRUG-INDUCED BIOMARKER; DYSKINESIA; GENE EXPRESSION; NEUROPHARMACOLOGY; NUCLEAR RECEPTORS; RETINOIDS; SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE POLYMORPHISM; TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: Dopamine is an important neurotransmitter. It modulates various activity including, locomotion, motivated behaviors and neuroendocrine processes. Antipsychotic drugs are used to alleviate schizophrenia symptoms and share the common property to interact with dopamine receptors. But, their cellular and molecular mechanisms of action remain poorly understood. In recent years, we have identified an important role for transcription factors of the nuclear receptor family Nur77 and retinoid X receptor (RXR) in the action of dopaminergique drugs. In the present proposal we would like 1) to demonstrate the formation of the transcriptional complex Nur77/RXR following antipsychotic drug administration; 2) to identify gene targets of Nur77/RXR transcriptional activity in antipsychotic drug-induced gene expression; and 3) to evaluate the putative functional effect of a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the human Nur77 messenger RNA. Data generate from these experiments should improve our understanding on the role of Nur77 and RXR in antipsychotic drug effects. Since Nur77 and RXR are associated with maintenance of homeostatic dopamine activity and potential beneficial effects against antipsychotic drug-induced side effects, targeting Nur77/RXR transcriptional activity might represent a new way to ameliorate dopamine related disorder treatments. Characterization of the Nur77 SNP may help to predict individuals with higher risk to develop dopamine drug side effects leading to a better and more individualize therapeutic approach.

TitreApplicationTitle: The role of TRPM7 channel in neurite outgrowth during development and regeneration following injury.
Keywords-MotsClés: IMMUNOBLOT; IMMUNOCYTOCHEMISTRY; LASER CONFOCAL MICROSCOPY; NEURONAL DEVELOPMENT; NEURONAL OUTGROWTH; NEURONAL REGENERATION; PRIMARY CELL CULTURE; VIRUS-MEDIATED GENE SILENCING
Abstract-Résumé: Central nervous system is comprised of the networks of highly specialized cells, neurons, that interact through extending their axons and dendrites, or collectively, neurites. Neurons are highly susceptible to abnormalities, disease and injury during development and adulthood; thus, understanding the development and loss of their function is highly important. Evidence suggests that Transient Receptor Potential Melastatin 7 (TRPM7), a channel that allows calcium and magnisium ions to enter the cells, plays a role in a variety of physiological and pathophysiological conditions. TRPM7 has been shown to be critical to neuron survival and play a role in neuronal growth. It is hypothesized that decreasing the expression of TRPM7 channel in neonatal mouse neurons will promote neuronal outgrowth and synapse formation. This hypothesis will be tested by comparing the changes of morphological features associated with growth and synapse formation in cells with normal and low numbers of TRPM7 channels. As well, similar methods will be applied to neurons with injured neurites to test the potential involvement of TRPM7 channel in regeneration of neurons following injury. The results of this study can assist in the development of new therapies for neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental diseases and nervous system injury in the future.

TitreApplicationTitle: Clarifying ethical and evidence-based values of beneficiary input for humanitarian healthcare missions
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOETHICS; CROSS-CULTURAL HEALTH TRANSACTIONS; GLOBAL HEALTH ETHICS; HEALTHCARE ETHICS; HUMANITARIANISM; QUALITATIVE ASSESSMENTS OF HEALTHCARE
Abstract-Résumé: Medical humanitarian missions set up clinics and operating theatres for the poorest throughout the world with the intention of alleviating their suffering in the absence of adequate or affordable local health services and medicines. The question is, do the choices made by medical volunteers, often in clinically and culturally unfamiliar contexts, coincide with the expectations and priorities of beneficiaries? What role can and should suggestions from beneficiary communities play in shaping what medical missionaries do or aim to do? Combining analysis of existing policies and empirical research, and working in collaboration with Canada's leading humanitarian healthcare ethics research team, this evidence-based study seeks to improve the effective and ethical delivery of healthcare services in humanitarian settings. Ensuring there is resonance between medical aid and beneficiary values and needs is central to safeguarding and improving the ethical performance of medical humanitarian projects. As federal funding for international aid interventions comes under increasing pressure due to global financial pressures, yet global disasters and demand for aid increase, it is crucial to make best use of available funds. The better understanding of beneficiary experiences of medical missions this study yields will inform the training and preparation of healthcare professionals for medical missions in unfamiliar cultural and clinical contexts, while providing guidelines on how beneficiary input can be integrated into humanitarian healthcare planning and delivery to ensure limited resources are strategically situated to do the most good.

TitreApplicationTitle: Restoring binaural hearing to children who are deaf
Keywords-MotsClés: AUDITORY DEVELOPMENT AND PLASTICITY; BILATERAL AND BINAURAL HEARING; CHILDREN; COCHLEAR IMPLANTS; DEAFNESS; HEARING AIDS
Abstract-Résumé: Cochlear implants are devices which help children who are deaf to hear. Until recently, they were only placed into one ear which left the other ear without hearing. We found that the hearing nerves on the implanted side begin to work better as children use their CI while those on the other side do not. This mismatch between the two ears helps to explain why children with one cochlear implant find it hard to tell where sounds are coming from and often cannot understand conversations in a noisy place. We tried giving a group of young cochlear implant users a second implant in their other ear; they heard slightly better but did not get the full advantage of listening with both ears.  In this study, we want to improve hearing for children with hearing loss by encouraging better development from both ears.  We are asking whether this can be done by either giving children hearing in both ears at the same time or by turning off the first cochlear implant for regular periods to help the hearing nerves on the second implanted side catch up to the first.  To answer these questions, we will monitor hearing in children who use 2 cochlear implants or a cochlear implant in one ear and a hearing aid in the other.  We will measure how the hearing nerves and brain respond to information from both ears and whether children can use this information to hear better.  We might find that: 1) abnormal auditory development can be avoided by giving hearing to both ears at the same time, 2) the hearing nerves and brain can use information coming from two implants or from an implant on one side and a hearing aid in the other, and 3) hearing nerves on the side implanted second can be strengthened if allowed to work alone. If any one of these proves correct, we will have discovered that children who are deaf can develop important hearing advantages from listening with two ears and will have shown which strategies can best accomplish this goal.

TitreApplicationTitle: Cancer Cachexia: Phenotype Definition, Markers for Genetic Predisposition and Prognosis
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER CACHEXIA; GENOTYPE; PALLIATIVE CARE
Abstract-Résumé: The majority of patients who are affected by advances cancer (in Canada about 75,000 people per year), are affected by malnutrition and wasting.  The losses of body weight, muscles and fat tissue are asociated with poor immunity, and poor tolerance to cancer therapy, and the associated weakness and fatigue place a large burden on patients and families.  The malnutrition and wasting syndrome do not affect all cancer patients equally and while some will be less affected and have minimal weight losses, others are very susceptible and may lose so much weight as to appear as "skin and bones".  This variation suggests that indeed some people may be genetically more likely to lose weight, just as some individuals have a family tendancy for other conditions such as obesity, diabetes or cancer.  Our research focuses on identifying the genetic characteristics of cancer patients who are highly susceptible (or resistant) to wasting.

TitreApplicationTitle: Employment needs and experiences of workers with arthritis and diabetes: Keeping the Boom(ers) in the labour market.
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; ARTHRITIS; BABY BOOMERS; CHRONIC EPISODIC HEALTH CONDITIONS; DIABETES; EMPLOYMENT; OLDER WORKERS; PSYCHOLSOCIAL FACTORS
Abstract-Résumé: The large size of the Canadian baby boomer generation (born 1946 to 1964) has created concerns for older workers. A loss of skills in the labour market as older workers retire has meant the need for strategies to keep individuals working and delay retirement. Yet, not everyone enjoys good health when working. Individuals are more likely to report chronic diseases and activity limitations with age. To date, we don't have information about how characteristics of many chronic health conditions that arise with age may create unique challenges for workers, including conditions like arthritis and diabetes that do not have a continuous impact but result in episodes of disability, unpredictable symptoms, and stress related to working and disclosing health problems to colleagues. This proposal focuses on women and men 50-67 yrs of age who work with arthritis and/or diabetes compared to workers with no disabling health conditions. The research aims to: 1) Describe the extent to which remaining employed is a priority among baby boomers as they age; 2) Examine the experiences and perceived impact of working with an episodic health condition, as well as factors that act as barriers or facilitate working; and 3) Examine characteristics of episodic health conditions (e.g., symptom unpredictability, invisibility) and their association with work outcomes (e.g., job disruptions, absenteeism). A telephone-administered or on-line questionnaire will be given to a sample of individuals with arthritis (n = 500), diabetes (n = 500), and no chronic health conditions causing disability (n = 500). Questionnaires will ask for information on demographic (e.g., age, gender), health, work context, worker attitudes, and social factors. With increased life expectancies and the disappearance of mandatory retirement, Canadians are expected to age while working. This study forms an important step in understanding the interplay of health and work and will provide information to help sustain employment.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Capacity of Formal Community Based Mentoring Relationships to Improve the Health of Canadian Children
Keywords-MotsClés: ADULT VOLUNTEERS; CHILDREN'S DEVELOPMENTAL OUTCOMES; CHILDREN'S HEALTH AND WELL-BEING; DEVELOPMENTAL TRAJECTORIES; FORMAL COMMUNITY MENTORING PROGRAMS; GROWTH CURVE MODELLING; NATIONAL MENTORING SURVEY; STRUCTURAL EQUATION MODELLING; SURVIVAL ANALYSIS; YOUTH MENTORING RELATIONSHIPS
Abstract-Résumé: This study will examine the capacity of Big Brothers Big Sisters (BBBS) community mentoring relationships involving children and adult volunteers to improve the health and well-being of Canadian children. Information will come from an existing national survey of BBBS mentoring relationships. Specific aims will focus on the potential of mentoring relationships to improve children's developmental outcomes in the areas of physical health and mental well-being, social relationships, academic performance, and risky behaviors. Other aims will seek to better understand how mentoring works to foster positive change in children's lives, for whom and under what conditions positive change is most likely to occur, the key aspects of mentoring relationships (e.g., perceived quality, similarity of interests, longevity, frequency of contact, type of activities) that are critical for attaining positive developmental outcomes, and mentoring agency practices (e.g., mentor training, caseworker support) and other environmental factors (e.g., parent support) that improve the quality and functioning of mentoring relationships. The results are ultimately expected to lead to better health for children by making recommendations that would further improve the content and delivery of mentoring services and programs.

TitreApplicationTitle: Access to Specialist Healthcare Services in Ontario
Keywords-MotsClés: ACCESS TO HEALTHCARE; SPECIALIST HEALTHCARE
Abstract-Résumé: Access to healthcare services is a vital determinant of a population health, extending to the treatment, diagnosis, and prevention of disease and ill-health. While the majority of research on healthcare access has focused on primary care, we know relatively less about access to specialist care (e.g., cardiologist, allergists, oncologists). More specifically, a major gap in knowledge exists related to the ways in which patients experience accessing specialty care in terms of barriers to access, and impacts of wait times. Recognizing that barriers may relate to patient, provider, and community level factors, this research will analyze data related to specialist access with this lens. This research will contribute by exploring inequities in access to specialist care that may arise because of individual and/or community-level factors. By identifying vulnerable groups, this research will be vital for informing policies aimed at improving healthcare delivery for all Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Nesfatin-1 Regulation of Glucose and Energy Homesotasis
Keywords-MotsClés: BETA CELLS; BLOOD GLUCOSE; BODY WEIGHT; FOOD INTAKE; GASTROINTESTINAL TRACT; GLUCONEOGENESIS; INSULIN; LIVER; METABOLISM; PANCREATIC ISLETS
Abstract-Résumé: Obesity and diabetes are debilitating diseases reaching pandemic proportions in several parts of the world. According to Statistics Canada reports, ~25% of Canadians are obese. Approximately 1 billion of the global population is obese. About 5% of Canadians have diabetes. Several hormones are involved in regulating blood glucose levels and body weight. Defects in the production, secretion and/or action of these hormones could contribute to certain types of obesity and/or diabetes. There is a great deal of interest in using naturally occurring hormones for the treatment of diabetes and obesity. Nesfatin-1 is a recently discovered natural hormone found in humans and other animals. Our research determined that the insulin producing cells in the pancreas are an abundant source of nesfatin-1. Nesfatin-1 also stimulates insulin secretion from the pancreas. We, as well others identified that nesfatin-1 inhibits the quantity of food eaten, and promote weight loss. Together, these research results highlight the important roles played by nesfatin-1 in regulating body weight and blood glucose levels. How does nesfatin-1 elicit the above-mentioned functions? Currently, this question is poorly understood. I predict that nesfatin-1 has specific effects on target organs/tissues in regulating blood glucose levels, food intake and body weight. We will elucidate how nesfatin-1 affects the stomach, pancreas and liver, three organs critical in the regulation of feeding and metabolism. In a second approach, we will determine what will happen to the body weight and blood glucose if nesfatin-1 is not produced in the body. This will be achieved using a mouse model with a dysfunctional gene encoding nesfatin-1. Together, the studies proposed here will significantly improve our understanding on nesfatin-1, an important protein. The outcome of this research will also help us further explore nesfatin-1 as a potential target molecule for innovative therapies for diabetes and obesity.

TitreApplicationTitle: Hepatic Bile Acid and Organic Anion Transporting Polypeptide (OATP) drug uptake transporters as determinants of drug disposition
Keywords-MotsClés: CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY; DRUG DISPOSITION; DRUG TRANSPORTERS; LIVER TRANSPORTERS; PHARMACOGENETICS
Abstract-Résumé: Liver is widely known as an organ capable of breaking down (metabolism) foreign chemicals and drugs that we ingest, and then secrete such breakdown products into bile for subsequent elimination out of the body. Specifically, we now know that the cells that make up organs such as the liver possess proteins called transporters on their cell membrane that allow drugs, foreign chemicals, hormones, and nutrients to enter or leave the cell. For many drugs that circulate in our body, a subset of drug transporters known as Organic Anion Transporting Polypeptide (OATP) found in liver cells facilitate the movement of drugs from blood into liver. In 2001 my laboratory was the first to identify genetic variation in a liver-specific OATP known as OATP1B1 which in recent years have been shown to be the most clinically relevant predictor of muscle injury associated with the use of cholesterol lowering drugs called statins. More recently, with the support of CIHR funds, we were able to study the effects of OATP1B1 genetic variations in a large cohort of patients that resulted in a clinically useful algorithm for predicting at risk patients. Unexpectedly, identified another hepatic transporter, the liver-specific bile acid uptake transporter known as Sodium Taurocholate Co-transporting Polypeptide (NTCP), is not only key to how the liver clears bile acids from circulation, but also capable of drug transport. Importantly, preliminary data from our group would indicate there is a key region in NTCP essential to how it recognizes drugs such as statins. Therefore we plan to study transporter activity, function, and regulation of liver-specific OATP and NTCP transporters using novel model systems, as well as by conducting proof-of-principle human studies. It is expected that our findings will provide important new insights to how drugs are cleared by the liver and thereby further enable the emerging field of personalized medicine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Do Primary Care Reforms Influence Physician Performance and Patient Outcomes? Econometric Analyses of Ontario's Primary Healthcare Delivery Models
Keywords-MotsClés: HEALTH ADMINISTRATIVE DATA ANALYSIS; HEALTH ECONOMETRICS METHODOLOGY; HEALTH ECONOMICS; HEALTH POLICY ANALYSIS; PANEL DATA ECONOMETRICS; PRIMARY CARE DELIVERY MODELS
Abstract-Résumé: During the past decade, strategies have been introduced across Canadian provinces to address issues of around the clock access to primary care, the adequacy of preventive care and the cost effective management of chronic diseases. In Ontario, two types of primary care reform models (enhanced fee-for-service model (fee-for-service plus incentives) like in Family Health Groups (FHGs) and blended capitation (fixed rate per patient plus incentives) such as in Family Health Organizations (FHOs)) as well as extensive multidisciplinary team-based practice approaches, like Family Health Teams (FHTs), are now driving change in what was traditionally a predominantly fee-for-service based province - approaches that are quickly becoming role models for other jurisdictions in Canada and abroad. However, only limited evidence exists to date on the impact of these reforms on the supply of healthcare services, the attendant costs and health system outcomes. We propose to undertake a comprehensive study of the impact of primary care reform over several dimensions of outcomes such as healthcare services supplied by physicians, costs per patient, after-hours access, referrals to specialists, emergency department visits, avoidable hospitalizations and self-reported patient outcomes in Ontario's dominant primary care delivery models. This project will use rich longitudinal population-based health administrative data from Ontario, recent Canadian Community Health Survey and health econometrics methodology. Our study will provide empirical evidence concerning the relative strengths and weaknesses of alternative primary care delivery models relative to the traditional fee-for-service model, and provide guidance for evidence-based health policy decision making in Ontario and beyond.

TitreApplicationTitle: Comparative Study of the Human and Monkey Cortex
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOARCHITECTURE; HUMAN BRAIN; MACAQUE MONKEY BRAIN
Abstract-Résumé: The association cortex of the human brain, which is involved in the highest aspects of cognition, comprises several areas that exhibit differences in their cellular structure (i.e. cytoarchitecture). In recent years, developments in functional neuroimaging with positron emission tomography (PET) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have made it possible to demonstrate distinct changes in neuronal activity within the human brain in relation to specific aspects of cognitive processing. A proper interpretation of these activation foci requires their integration with what is known about the anatomy and physiology of the primate cortex, i.e. information that has been gathered almost exclusively in experimental work in the monkey. Unfortunately, for many regions of the cortex, the architecture in the monkey and the human brains were not studied in parallel and with the same criteria. There are therefore several inconsistencies in the organizational schemes of the monkey and the human cortex that prevent the effective utilization of basic knowledge about anatomy and physiology to interpret findings from functional neuroimaging studies in human subjects. The present grant proposes a research program to resolve some of the above problems. The research plan involves a comparative examination of human and macaque monkey brains stained for cytoarchitecture in order to define areas in the regions of interest according to the same criteria in these two primate species and then examine whether the areas defined relate to particular sulci of the human brain. The studies should provide a solid basis on which to interpret human functional activation studies.

ClasseRechercheFR: RECHERCHES SE RAPPORTANT A PLUSIEURS MALADIES; LEUCEMIES
TitreApplicationTitle: Dissecting a novel gene regulatory function for histone H2B ubiquitylation
Keywords-MotsClés: CHROMATIN; HISTONE H2B UBIQUITYLATION; HISTONES; P-TEFB; RNA-SEQ; TRANSCRIPTION ELONGATION
Abstract-Résumé: The human genome (and indeed, the genome of every animal) is comprised of long strands of DNA (known as chromosomes) that need to be tightly packaged within cells.    An important consequence of this packaging is that it limits access of cellular gene expression machinery to the genetic information, and thus cells have evolved elaborate mechanisms to regulate DNA packaging. In cells, DNA strands are compacted by wrapping around groups of dedicated packaging proteins called histones.  By introducing modifications onto the histones, cells can modulate how DNA is packaged to allow access to certain DNA sequences such as genes.  Intriguingly, these modifications can also serve as signals that help to localize cellular machinery involved in gene expression to specific regions of the chromosome.     I study one such modification called ubiquitylation.  Histone ubiquitylation has been detected in a wide variety of organisms, including humans, and altered levels of this modification are associated with certain types of cancer.  However, its function in modulating DNA packaging and gene expression is still poorly understood.  Using a model organism that is easy to manipulate genetically (the fission yeast Schizossacharomyces pombe), I have found that cells unable to ubiquitylate their histones suffer from gene expression defects, morphological abnormalities and slow growth.  I have also linked ubiquitylation to the function of other known regulators of gene expression using genetic and biochemical approaches.  My current experiments involve using high-resolution RNA sequencing technology to identify which genes are affected by ubiquitylation and which stage of gene expression is compromised.     I hope to characterize in detail how the ubiquitylation of histones contributes to the proper regulation of genes.  Ultimately, such information may provide insight into how gene regulation may be perturbed in disease states such as cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Troubles du sommeil, changements neuro-anatomiques et perception de douleur un an après un traumatisme craniocérébral (TCC) modéré/sévère.
Keywords-MotsClés: DENSITE DE MATIERE GRISE; DOULEUR CHRONIQUE; IMAGERIE PAR RESONANCE MAGNETIQUE; INTEGRATION CORTICALE; PERCEPTION DE DOULEUR; POLYSOMNOGRAPHIE; POTENTIELS EVOQUES NOCICEPTIFS; SOMMEIL; TRAUMATISME CRANIOCEREBRAL; ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAMME
Abstract-Résumé: Selon des resultats probants, la qualite du sommeil des patients TCC dans les mois suivant leur traumatisme pourrait amener des changements dans des regions du cerveau associees a la perception de la douleur et les predisposer au developpement du syndrome de douleur chronique. Cette etude vise donc a comprendre l'association entre les troubles du sommeil, les changements neuro-anatomiques et la sensibilite a la douleur un an apres un TCC modere/severe. Pour y parvenir, une methode de collecte de donnees novatrice alliant des techniques d'imagerie medicale ainsi que d'autres techniques de stimulation sensorielle sera utilisee. Plus precisement, un an apres l'occurrence d'un TCC modere ou severe, les participants passeront  une polysomnographie nocturne afin d'identifier les caracteristiques specifiques du sommeil chez les TCC comme la duree du sommeil moyenne et le nombre d'interruptions pendant la nuit. Le matin suivant, ils seront exposes a une sequence de stimuli douloureux (chocs de faible intensite projetes sur le dos de la main et connu sous le nom de potentiels evoques) afin de documenter des variables relatives a leur sensibilite a la douleur. Par la suite, une imagerie par resonance magnetique cerebrale sera employee pour examiner la presence de changements structuraux au niveau des regions associees a la perception de douleur. A ce jour, les troubles du sommeil et la douleur chronique sont frequemment rapportes par les patients survivant a un TCC modere/severe. En plus d'affecter la qualite de vie, ces symptomes peuvent compromettre le retablissement et le retour a la productivite a court et a long terme. Cette etude permettrait de mieux comprendre le role specifique du sommeil dans la chronicisation de la douleur chez les patients TCC - une etape primordiale pour le developpement d'interventions ciblees permettant d'attenuer les troubles du sommeil et de prevenir le developpement de douleur chronique chez cette clientele.

TitreApplicationTitle: Molecular and cellular characterization of early human hematopoietic lineage determination
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; GENOMICS; HEMATOPOIESIS; MIRNA; ONTOGENY; SELF-RENEWAL
Abstract-Résumé: Blood stem cells are unique because they are unspecialized and able to make any mature blood cell type, when they divide, they have the potential to generate another stem cell, a process called self-renewal, or other types of cells that lack stem cell function and begin a process of specialization, a process called differentiation. We know very little about how self-renewal occurs; knowledge that is important in understanding many human blood diseases. Our lab's long-term goal is to gain a deep understanding of how human blood stem cells self-renew and differentiate. In our previous work, we created a map of the cell types in human blood and identified the purest human blood stem cells: hematopoietic stem cells (HSC). We propose to use this map to isolate and investigate how blood cells and human HSCs are regulated in different stages in life, in early life (fetal liver), at birth (cord blood), and in adults (bone marrow). This is important because, although the process and the genes that control it are not well understood, it has been shown that the ability to renew in stem cells decreases in aging. By watching how the gene programs in HSC change as they lose self-renewal function, we will be able to uncover the gene programs that govern this process. We will determine first how HSC cells change across a lifespan by measuring the potential of HSCs to generate other cell types at different ages. Then we will look at the all the genes expressed in HSC taken from each stage of life to narrow the list down to those that change at the same time as HSC self-renewal changes. With this short list, we will perform a deep analysis on them via sophisticated approaches to understand the function of these elements. This proposal will harness our unique abilities to investigate the human blood system and achieve unprecedented insight into the self-renewal and aging processes of human HSCs that may allow us to manipulate these elements in the future for regenerative medicine.

TitreApplicationTitle: Role of the FRMD5 protein in Purkinje cell biology.
Keywords-MotsClés: ATAXIA; CYTOSKELETON; FRMD5 FUNCTION; NEURONAL SURVIVAL; PURKINJE CELLS; SEIZURES
Abstract-Résumé: Using chemicals to mutate their DNA, mice were derived that displayed seizures, tremor and an abnormal gait. On inspection, we discovered that these defects were associated with a single base pair change in the DNA that encodes a protein known as FRMD5. Very little is known about FRMD5, but it is thought to play an important role in function of the cell cytoskeleton; i.e., the scaffolding that supports cell shape and numerous internal signaling functions. Our analysis of the FRMD5 mutant mice suggests that the change in FRMD5 leads to the partial loss of special cells in the cerebellum, a major motor control area of the brain. This investigation is designed to expose the precise cellular mechanisms that are disrupted by this abnormal protein. These studies will identify critical pathways used by neurons for normal function and survival, providing deeper insight into the characteristics that serve to protect some neurons from death while making others susceptible. Our studies will also elucidate new mechanisms whereby cerebellar neurons develop functional connections and will delineate the extent to which FRMD5 mutation may also cause human cerebellar disease. This knowledge will deepen our understanding of the factors that can lead to cerebellar dysfunction and other debilitating neurological conditions that are particularly common in the aging population.

TitreApplicationTitle: Functional and genomic characterization of clonal heterogeneity in human leukemia
Keywords-MotsClés: ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA; ACUTE MYELOID LEUKEMIA; CLONAL HETEROGENEITY; CNV; DIAGNOSIS VS. RELAPSE; LIMITED DILUTION ASSAY; TARGETED SEQUENCING; TARGETED THERAPEUTICS; XENOGRAFTS
Abstract-Résumé: Our goal is to study how gene mutations that cause cancer increase in number over time making the cancer more aggressive and resistant to therapy. Similar to investigating a family tree, we can use advanced genetic tests to trace the individual trees, where one mutation after another is added onto those accumulated before, making the leukemia more aggressive and resistant to therapy. We will study two kinds leukemia and find out how many trees exist when the tumor is first diagnosed and then again when the tumor comes back when treatment fails. By studying these matched pairs we will find out which trees are failing therapy and causing the disease to come back. With information we can develop new drugs that target the worst trees and we will also develop a test for personalized therapy to make sure the worst tree is killed.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of FGF receptor 1 by Nedd4
Keywords-MotsClés: ENDOCYTOSIS; SIGNAL TRANSDUCTION; TYROSINE KINASE; UBIQUITIN
Abstract-Résumé: Cell growth, proliferation and differentiation are critical events in normal cell and body functions, and when dis-regulated can cause serious diseases, such as developmental defects and cancer. Breakdown of specific proteins is an integral part of these normal processes. We have been working on a family of proteins, called the Nedd4 family, that are responsible for breakdown of other proteins to which they bind. Recently, we discovered that Nedd4 leads to degradation of a very important protein, FGF receptor 1 (FGFR1), which control cellular differentiation, animal development and cancer. When unable to bind Nedd4, FGFR1 stays active for prolonged times, leading to severe developmental defects in animal models, to defects in differentiation of human stem cells and to cancer. However, the mechanism by which this occurs is not known. As well, we found recently that Nedd4 is also involved in regulating tumor growth in the body by controlling other proteins aside from FGFR1. Here we propose to investigate HOW Nedd4 is involved in regulating normal animal development and in cancer

TitreApplicationTitle: Perceptions of innovative orally administered treatment for long-term opioid dependent participants in the SALOME clinical trial
Keywords-MotsClés: DATA TRIANGULATION; HEALTH SERVICES RESEARCH; OPIOID DEPENDENCE; OPIOID SUBSTITUTION TREATMENT; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH METHODS; TREATMENT PERCEPTIONS
Abstract-Résumé: Opioid dependence (i.e., heroin dependence) is a chronic illness that poses great harm to the individual, their family and the wider community. Substitution with oral methadone is the gold standard treatment for opioid dependence, but is not effective for 15 to 25% of chronic opioid dependent individuals. SALOME (Study to Assess Longer-Term Opioid Medication Effectiveness; CIHR-funded) is a randomized, double blind clinical trial testing the effectiveness of hydromorphone (a licensed pain medication; [HDM]) and diacetylmorphine (active ingredient in heroin; [DAM]) as alternative treatments for this population.  In Stage I of SALOME, participants are treated with injectable HDM or DAM and in Stage II, half of the participants switch to an oral formulation of HDM or DAM treatment.  Despite its effectiveness, treatment with an injectable medication poses some challenges for the health care system (e.g., clinic logistics) and society (e.g., stigma). Thus, the oral treatments in SALOME, if proven effective, have the potential to significantly expand available treatment options for a population that has not benefited from available treatments in Canada.   SALOME does not collect data about the delivery of the oral treatment; information that is critical to consider in the planning of future health delivery systems. Therefore, the proposed study is dedicated to analyzing participant's perceptions of oral treatment in SALOME and determining the association between participant's treatment satisfaction with street opioid use at 12 months. Using a mixed qualitative (in-depth interviews) and quantitative (i.e., urinalysis reports, client satisfaction questionnaire) methods approach, data will be triangulated to enrich the theoretical framework being developed.  The proposed study will identify the perceptions and outcomes of an innovative treatment alternative for a population that remains outside of the Canadian health care system.

TitreApplicationTitle: Enhanced syphilis screening among HIV-positive men who have sex with men: Evaluation of a clinic-based intervention
Keywords-MotsClés: DIAGNOSIS; HEALTH SERVICES; HIV/AIDS; INTERVENTIONS; MEN WHO HAVE SEX WITH MEN; POPULATION HEALTH; SCREENING; SYPHILIS
Abstract-Résumé: Syphilis is on the rise among HIV-positive men who have sex with men (MSM), with rates now more than 300 times higher than among the general male population. Untreated syphilis is of great concern. It may progress to serious outcomes such as neurosyphilis, in which symptoms such as meningitis or dementia may develop. Moreover, untreated and infectious syphilis can be spread to partners; as well, it can increase the likelihood of further spread of HIV. On the other hand, syphilis testing and treatment of new infections, if detected early, is simple and inexpensive. We aim to enhance syphilis testing among HIV-positive MSM, so that more men will undergo testing, they will test more often, and more cases will be treated early. The intervention will combine syphilis tests with the standard HIV blood tests that are routinely done every 3-6 months for persons in care at 4 hospital-based HIV clinics in Toronto and Ottawa. First, we will describe the proportion tested, how frequently men were tested, and how many new cases were diagnosed during the period prior to the intervention. Next, we will observe rates of testing and new syphilis diagnoses following implementation of the intervention to determine how well it worked. We will draw our observations using data from lab results of syphilis tests, patients' medical charts, and also information obtained from male patients of these clinics who are volunteer participants of an ongoing research study which includes annual interviews. Our results will inform future decisions on whether the intervention should be continued in the participating clinics and also whether it should be introduced to clinics elsewhere. Most importantly, if the intervention proves to ensure more rapid and timely treatment of syphilis, this will prevent serious syphilis-related disease, and, ultimately, may help to control its spread among MSM.

TitreApplicationTitle: Estimating female sex workers' early HIV risk and the implications for HIV epidemic control: A multi-country observational and mathematical modeling study
Keywords-MotsClés: BIOLOGICAL AND BEHAVIOURAL SURVEY; FEMALE SEX WORKERS; HIV/AIDS; INDIA; KENYA; MODELLING; PREVENTION; TARGETED INTERVENTIONS; UKRAINE
Abstract-Résumé: Female sex workers (FSWs) experience a much higher risk of HIV than the general population, and programs targeted to FSWs are a critical component of HIV prevention globally. However, preventive interventions for FSWs only reach women after they identify as sex workers. Evidence suggests that young women may also exchange sex for money, drugs, or gifts (undeclared transactional sex) prior to identifying as a sex worker. The goal of this research project is to (i) estimate HIV risk, and characterize the behaviours (such as undeclared transactional sex) that influence HIV risk, during the transition period from first sex until self-declared entry into sex work; (ii) estimate HIV risk during the first two years of "formal" sex work, if before access to local HIV prevention services (access gap); and (iii) explore the importance of this early HIV risk for epidemic control. We will use innovative geographic mapping tools and perform a cross-sectional biological and behavioural survey of young women residing in established sex work "hot spots" in south India, Kenya, and Ukraine. Mathematical modelling will use these data to replicate diverse HIV epidemics in each of the three study sites, to understand how HIV infection acquired before "formal" entry into sex work or during the access gap could potentially limit the ability of existing programs to protect FSWs and the general population from HIV, and to estimate the added benefit of feasibly expanding existing programs to prevent these early HIV infections. The findings will contribute significantly to our understanding of HIV risk in young, high-risk women and self-identified FSWs, and will inform the strategic design and expansion of HIV prevention programs in regions where "formal" sex work and undeclared transactional sex fuel and sustain HIV epidemics.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Effect of an Inter-Disciplinary Program, Including Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, on Psychosocial Function, Pain Perception, Disability, and Quality of LIfe in Breast Cancer Survivors with Chronic Neuropathic Pain.
Keywords-MotsClés: BREAST CANCER SURVIVORS; CHRONIC NEUROPATHIC PAIN; DISABILITY; INTERDISCIPLINARY TREATMENT; MINDFULNESS-BASED STRESS REDUCTION; QUALITY OF LIFE
Abstract-Résumé: Chronic neuropathic pain is a common problem for breast cancer survivors. Even with the best medical treatments, some survivors continue to experience disabling pain. It is well-established that an interdisciplinary approach is key to the treatment of chronic pain, but little research has been performed on the effectiveness of this approach for cancer survivors with chronic neuropathic pain. We will evaluate the effectiveness of such a program combining medical treatment and mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) to reduce disability and improve quality of life among breast cancer survivors with chronic neuropathic pain. The benefits of mindfulness training on neuropathic pain among cancer survivors will be assessed in 108 women survivors of breast cancer with neuropathic pain who will be randomly assigned to either medical treatment only or medical treatment with an 8-week MBSR program.  We will compare the proportion of participants who experience a substantial reduction in pain-related disability in each group. We will also investigate whether participating in MBSR results in reduced stress hormones and changes in immune system activity as has been found in previous studies with other groups.

TitreApplicationTitle: Electrical and metobolic analysis of human epileptogenic lesions
Keywords-MotsClés: EPILEPSY; NEUROIMAGING
Abstract-Résumé: Some forms of epilepsy are caused by localized brain lesions such as tumors, vascular malformations, cysts and brain developmental abnormalities resulting from intra-uterine injury or genetic factors. Patients suffering from an epilepsy that is refractory to medical treatment can be helped by surgical treatment if the region generating seizures can be identified, localized and safely removed. The presence of such an epileptogenic region is assessed with brain imaging methods such as MRI and by recording the electrical activity of the brain (EEG). In many patients, however, no lesion can be seen on MRI or the relationship between the lesion and the epilepsy is uncertain. The EEG shows epileptic activity in most patients but it does not provide accurate localization. The combination of functional MRI and EEG is showing great promise to significantly improve our ability to find the epileptogenic region in a non-invasive way and to understand better the relationship between the lesion and the epileptic disorder. We propose to establish the clinical parameters for which the method can be used practically and to develop exciting new MRI technology that will render this approach simpler and even more powerful. We also propose studies that will help us understand better the relationship between this method and the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying epileptic discharges in the brain.

TitreApplicationTitle: Efficacy of regular aerobic exercise as an adjuvant or stand alone treatment for PTSD: A randomized controlled trail
Keywords-MotsClés: AEROBIC; ANXIETY; DEPRESSION; EXERCISE; POSTTRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER; RCT; TREATMENT
Abstract-Résumé: People who exercise are less likely to suffer from significant anxiety, depressed mood, and other mental health issues when compared to inactive individuals; yet, despite this and recommendations from health authorities that adults participate in 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity every week to obtain health benefits, less than 1 in 6 Canadian adults report doing so. There is preliminary evidence that regular aerobic exercise may be an effective intervention for anxiety disorders, now the most common and costly group of mental disorders, for which accessible evidence-based treatment alternatives are needed. Of the anxiety disorders, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is particularly common and devastating, being associated with development of other significant mental health issues, diminished physical health, and suicidality; as such, it is now considered a public health concern. The purpose of this research program is to systematically evaluate the impact of regular aerobic exercise, both alone and when combined with a known effective psychotherapy-based treatment, on symptom severity and general physical health of people diagnosed with PTSD. Knowledge obtained from this research will help us understand of the potential value of aerobic exercise in the treatment of PTSD and, if shown effective on its own, will pave the way for an evidence-based treatment that is accessible to most Canadians.

TitreApplicationTitle: Neurophysiology of 3-D Gaze and Head Control
Keywords-MotsClés: EYE MOVEMENTS; FRONTAL CORTEX; GAZE MOVEMENTS; HEAD MOVEMENTS; MONKEYS; NEUROPHYSIOLOGY; PARIETAL CORTEX; SUPERIOR COLLICULUS; UNIT RECORDING; VISION
Abstract-Résumé: Diseases and disorders of the nervous system make up the largest class of medical problems in the world. One way to address this huge problem is study basic brain mechanisms so that we can then try to understand how they are affected by multiple diseases. For example, sensory-motor transformations underlay most aspects of daily living, work, and leisure, and are affected by nearly all diseases, disorders, and injuries to the brain. Most of what we know about such basic brain processes comes from animal studies. Despite advances in human brain science, it is still very limited in what it can test, for example it cannot differentiate between different neurons in an area of the brain, and it often forces unnatural behaviors, like fixing the head in place or making subjects lie down. For this reason neural recordings in monkeys are still needed, because they are very close to the human in brain and behavior. However, monkey studies have often times been limited by the need to test very simple behaviors in rather unnatural conditions, and by two-dimensional approximations to the real three-dimensional (3-D) motion. Here, we propose to use a monkey model to examine some of the most fundamental questions of sensorimotor control with the use of a new method for analyzing neural activity recorded during naturally variable 3-D behaviors (especially with the head free to move naturally). This will enable us to describe how visual signals are processed, stored and converted into neural commands for eye and head movements. We will also study how the brain encodes future sequences of coordinated movement, and we will test, for the first time, if a specific part of parietal cortex is involved in sensorimotor integration for head control. Importantly, this new work will allow us to obtain very precise quantitative measurements from more natural behaviors that should therefore apply more closely to real-world situations than most previous neural recordings of this type.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: Functional Brain Networks Underlying Non-pharmaceutical Interventions for Psychosis
Keywords-MotsClés: COGNITION; DELUSIONS; FMRI; FUNCTIONAL NEUROIMAGING; HALLUCINATIONS; PSYCHOSOCIAL TREATMENT; SCHIZOPHRENIA
Abstract-Résumé: The moderate effect sizes associated with pharmaceutical intervention in psychosis have opened the door for development of a range of novel non-pharmaceutical treatment methods that can supplement the impact of medication. The objective of this study is to demonstrate that although neurocognition-focused (cognitive remediation therapy; CRT) and thought-focused (metacognitive training; MCT) group therapy methods both improve social/everyday functioning in psychosis, they produce distinct patterns of efficacy, differentially affecting symptoms, and producing distinct changes in cognitive and functional neuroimaging measures. All participants will be inpatients with a primary diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder from the BC Psychosis program. Participants will be randomly assigned CRT or MCT, with the treatment as usual (TAU) comparison captured within subjects as a baseline condition. All measures will be collected at three timepoints, baseline, pre-intervention, and post intervention (TAU followed by CRT/MCT). Groups will consist of approximately 10 participants. We hypothesize that (1) CRT and MCT will produce greater change in social/everyday functioning than TAU, (2) MCT will have more impact on positive symptoms than CRT, (3) CRT (but not MCT) will improve basic attention and memory measures and their biological underpinnings, whereas MCT (but not CRT) will reduce targeted cognitive biases on reasoning tasks and their biological underpinnings. Evidence that different psychosocial treatments lead to different brain responses in people with psychosis is an important development in the field because neural responses to psychosocial interventions are relatively unknown. This knowledge could pave the way for more precise biological targets for both pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions, and adds to the literature on the effectiveness of non-pharmaceutical interventions in psychosis.

TitreApplicationTitle: Regulation of pluripotency and differentiation in human stem cells
Keywords-MotsClés: CELL LINEAGE SPECIFICATION; CELLULAR HIERARCHIES; DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY; GENE FUNCTION; HUMAN PLURIPOTENT STEM CELLS; STEM CELL DIFFERENTIATION
Abstract-Résumé: The differentiation potential captured within cultures of human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) have driven expectations that these cells will provide a model for insights into human development and a resource for the production of tissues compatible with therapeutic transplantations. Human PSCs have until recently only been accessible by harvesting them from the early embryo, but a recent exciting discovery has revealed that hPSCs can be generated by "reprogramming" cells in the adult body. Harnessing the potential of hPSCs requires understanding how pluripotency is gained during reprogramming, maintained and then lost during the process differentiation into adult tissues. Although some of the major players that control pluripotency have been identified, our understanding of pluripotency in hPSCs is largely based on studies of mouse PSCs, which show a number of differences with their human counterparts. Our laboratory has made human cell lines that report the expression of the pluripotency associated gene REX1 and revealed two previously unappreciated populations in seemingly uniform PSCs. These two populations appear to represent steppingstones in the process of differentiation into tissues that could have therapeutic potential in the clinic. We are proposing to studying how entry and exit through the stages that these populations represent can be manipulated to provide greater control of cellular fate. We anticipate that advances arising from our work will have direct relevance to human health via the generation of cells and tissues amenable to drug screening and transplantation.

TitreApplicationTitle: Iron homeostasis and the pathogenesis of malarial anemia
Keywords-MotsClés: CYTOKINES; ERYTHROPOIESIS; INFLAMMATORY RESPONSES; IRON METABOLISM; IRON TRANSPORTER PROTEINS; MACROPHAGE; MALARIAL ANEMIA
Abstract-Résumé: Malaria remains a major global human health threat. The high prevalence of malaria infections in endemic areas in the developing world is due to several factors, including the lack of an effective vaccine, resistance of the parasite to anti-malarial drugs, and insecticide resistance among mosquito vectors. Plasmodium falciparum is the most virulent and deadly human parasite especially in sub-Saharan Africa, where it is responsible for high morbidity and mortality. In this region, children under the age of 5 and pregnant women have the highest risk for severe malarial anemia (SMA) and cerebral malaria, which are severe complications of P. falciparum infection. The goal of our studies is to provide a better understanding of the etiology of SMA. Observations in P. falciparum infected humans and experimental malaria models in monkeys and mice indicate that suppressed erythropoiesis or red blood cell (RBC) production plays a major role in SMA. Iron is an essential element of life in vertebrates and their microbial invaders. Importantly, iron is critical for erythropoiesis to replace RBC lost or destroyed during episodes of anemia. We propose that iron homeostasis may be disrupted or abnormal during malaria and contribute to suppressed erythropoiesis underlying malarial anemia. The proposed studies will utilize multidisciplinary approaches including hematology, immunology, cell biology, and molecular biology. The proposed experiments will be conducted using a well-characterized mouse malaria model and in serum samples obtained from Kenyan children with malaria. Our studies will lead to a comprehensive understanding of iron homeostasis during malaria and will identify potential molecules and mechanisms that will be useful for the development of urgently needed novel therapy to treat SMA, a severe and often fatal complication of P. falciparum infection.

TitreApplicationTitle: Oncogene-mediated signal transduction in ErbB2 transgenic models of mammary tumour progression
Keywords-MotsClés: DRUG RESISTANCE; ERBB2; EZH2; MAMMARY TUMORIGENESIS; SRC; TRANSGENIC
Abstract-Résumé: Breast cancer development involves the activation of genes that promote tumour development (oncogenes) and the inactivation of genes that prevent it (tumour suppressor genes) through genetic changes such as gene mutations and chromosome rearrangements. Based on this, rationally designed therapies to inhibit proteins activated in breast cancer have entered clinical use. Two important examples are Herceptin and Lapatinib, which target the ErbB2 oncogene amplified in 20-30% of breast cancers. While these drugs are a major breakthrough, their use is plagued by lack of response in many patients and the inevitable emergence of drug resistance in most others. In this project we will use powerful new in vivo and in vitro models of breast cancer to study the function of c-Src a protein that regulates human breast cancers growth. We will identify genes that are epigenetically modified by c-Src and determine whether this is involved in breast cancer initiation and progression. We will also investigate the significance of a c-Src in other cell types that support breast cancer. Finally, we will test the hypothesis that c-Src is involved in the development of Herceptin and Lapatinib resistance, building on our initial observations that c-Src is significantly increased in breast cancer cells that have acquired resistance to targeted therapy. Our studies will clarify the role of c-Src in contributing to breast cancer and establish whether it can serve as a novel therapeutic target to improve treatments and outcomes for ErbB2-positive patients.

CommitteeNameEN: Biological and Clinical Aspects of Aging
NomDuComitéFR: Aspects biologiques et cliniques du vieillissement
TitreApplicationTitle: Lighting up the aging brain
Keywords-MotsClés: AGING; BRAIN IMAGING; COGNITION; LIGHT; VIGILANCE
Abstract-Résumé: Much of the research on aging has focused on how to age cognitively well, or at least better. Several proposed and validated approaches have addressed physical activity, nutritional aspects, or cognitive training. The long-term goal of this research program is to use light as a simple, non-invasive intervention to enhance vigilance and cognition in the elderly. Light exposure can rapidly improve alertness and increase performance on several cognitive tasks in young subjects, even under sleep loss. We hypothesize that systematic light exposure is an efficient therapeutic strategy to enhance alertness, performance and cognition in older individuals. Some studies suggest that aging may decrease the beneficial effects of light. This in turn may prevent optimized cognitive performance in the elderly. The overall aim of this research program is to understand the effects of light on cognition in aging. First, we will use brain imaging to assess whether the effect of light on cerebral activity during a cognitive task is reduced in healthy elderly compared to young individuals.  We will also evaluate whether age-related changes in the eyes (i.e. lens yellowing) may affect the impact of light on cognition. Hence, we will assess whether light sensitivity is enhanced in cataract patients for whom yellowed lens is replaced with a clear lens, rendering the lens of an elderly patient more transparent than that of a teenager. Finally, we will assess whether systematic light exposure may enhance alertness and cognition in healthy elderly individuals under sleep deprivation, despite lower light sensitivity. This research will provide important cues on how to use light to improve cognition and alertness in aging populations. After completing the proposed program, we will perform similar investigations in clinical populations presenting alertness and cognitive deficits, such as patients with Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease.

NomDuComitéFR: Sciences du comportement - B: Études cliniques du comportement
TitreApplicationTitle: Using neuroimaging to assess cognitive function after serious brain injury
Keywords-MotsClés: COMA; CONSCIOUSNESS; EEG; FMRI; MINIMALLY CONSCIOUS STATE; NEUROIMAGING; SERIOUS BRAIN INJURY; VEGETATIVE STATE
Abstract-Résumé: The vegetative state (VS) is one of the least understood and most challenging conditions in modern medicine. The term describes a condition in which patients who emerge from coma appear to be awake, but show no signs of awareness. The minimally conscious state (MCS) is a related condition in which patients show inconsistent signs of awareness. In both cases, it is extremely difficult to assess residual brain function using standard clinical methods, leading to an alarmingly high rate of misdiagnosis (43%). In a series of recent studies, we have demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalograpy (EEG) can identify residual cognitive function, and even awareness, in some patients who are assumed to be VS or MCS, but still have abilities that cannot be detected using standard clinical methods. This new proposal builds on these studies in a number of important ways. First, we will apply our new methods to a large group of Canadian VS and MCS patients in order to establish how frequently aspects of cognitive function (including awareness and the ability to communicate using EEG or fMRI) are preserved and whether these covert signs can inform diagnosis and prognosis. We will also use state-of-the-art structural neuroimaging to determine why some of these patients remain conscious, yet behaviourally entirely non-responsive. Finally, for the first time, we will use our methods in the intensive care unit setting, to assess residual cognitive function in patients who are still comatose. This research will have a profound and direct impact on the assessment, diagnosis and clinical care of patients with severe brain injury and will have significant implications for the delivery of health care resources across Canada. The results will inform medical ethics and legal discussions (in terms of withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies) and drive future efforts to develop interventions to facilitate recovery and quality of life.

TitreApplicationTitle: The Peritoneal Dialysis Outcomes and Practice Patterns Study  (P-DOPPS)
Keywords-MotsClés: COLLABORATION; HOSPITALIZATION; PERITONEAL DIALYSIS; PERITONEAL DIALYSIS TREATMENT TIME; PRATICE PATTERNS; PROSPECTIVE OBSERVATIONAL COHORT STUDY; QUALITY OF LIFE; SURVIVAL
Abstract-Résumé: For the 36000 Canadians living with end stage kidney disease, hospital based hemodialysis (HD) is the most common therapy. Less than 20 percent of patients are treated with home based peritoneal dialysis (PD). PD requires a catheter which is inserted in the patient's peritoneum in the abdomen to allow for the removal of fluid and wastes. Compared to HD, PD is associated with similar survival, superior patient satisfaction, and is administered at home by a patient or caregiver at a lower cost. Increasing the use of PD represents an attractive strategy to improve patient outcomes and minimize healthcare costs of dialysis therapy. Yet, over 30 percent of Canadian patients on PD will ultimately require a transfer to HD after 3 years.  The transfer to HD may be related to ongoing infection of the PD fluid, complications of the PD catheter, inability of peritoneal membrane to remove the necessary fluid and toxins needed, and difficulty for patients to manage their treatments at home. Across facilities in Canada and between countries, the rates of these treatment related complications vary significantly. This finding may be the result of differences in patient characteristics across facilities. However, it also may relate to the different ways in which PD patients are cared for. The present study will be the Canadian arm of The Peritoneal Dialysis Outcomes and Practice Patterns Study (PDOPPS) that will be performed in Canada, Japan, UK and USA. PDOPPS will be one of the largest studies following patients on PD. PDOPPS will collect information on the differences in facility practices, and will follow patients over a 3 year period. The study will provide an opportunity to identify different practices in how patients on PD are cared for within 20 representative facilities within Canada comparing these to those facilities in participating countries. This will allow us to identify practices that minimize the need to transfer to HD and improve outcomes for patients on PD.

TitreApplicationTitle: Defining the causes of heterogeneous riboucleotide reductase gene transcription in response to DNA damage and anti-cancer drugs
Keywords-MotsClés: DNA DAMAGE CHECKPOINT; DRUG RESPONSES; QUANTITATIVE BIOLOGY; SYSTEMS BIOLOGY OF MODEL ORGANISMS; TRANSCRIPTIONAL REGULATION
Abstract-Résumé: The outcome of drug therapy can vary significantly from one individual to the next. Studies of model systems, such as breast and lung cancer cell lines, have shown that variability in drug responses can originate at the level of individual cells, even under stringently controlled laboratory conditions. Understanding the causes of this variability is important because it can reduce effectiveness of drug treatment, and facilitate the development of drug resistance.  The proposed research will identify causes of high cell-to-cell variability in drug-induced transcription of genes encoding the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) among genetically identical budding yeast cells. This organism is used extensively in health-related biomedical research because it shares many important genes and pathways with humans, including those involved in DNA replication and repair. Moreover, increased expression of the RNR enzyme is required for DNA damage repair in all organisms, and the enzyme is the direct target of drugs used in established and experimental cancer therapies.   Our preliminary investigations demonstrate that variability in single-cell responses to DNA damage and certain anti-cancer drugs involves the suppression of RNR gene transcription in some cells, but not in others. Moreover, our studies implicate multiple conserved genes and pathways involved in cell cycle control and the stress response. Correspondingly, we anticipate that the proposed research will provide new important insights into the mechanisms that cells use to integrate information about DNA damage, cell growth and stress, and enable new research to improve the efficacy of disease therapies, including those that target the RNR enzyme.

TitreApplicationTitle: Polymer-based Bioengineering Approaches for Systemic Iron Removal
Keywords-MotsClés: BIODEGRADABLE POLYMERS; BIOMATERIALS; CONTROLLED POLYMERIZATION; IRON CHELATION; IRON OVERLOAD; LONG CIRCULATING CHELATORS; POLYGLYCEROL; POLYMER BASED IRON CHELATORS; THALASSEMIAS
Abstract-Résumé: Iron overload disease is primarily caused by the repeated transfusion of red blood cells as implicated in the case of thalassemia, sickle cell anaemia and myelodysplastic syndromes or by the enhanced uptake of dietary iron. These conditions affect millions of people worldwide. Since humans do not have an iron excretion mechanism, excess iron will get deposited in the human body.  Free iron is highly toxic to critical organs and tissues. Organ injury is the most important reason for the premature death among iron overloaded patients. To date, the only treatment option available is the life-long iron chelation therapy by administering small iron specific organic molecules which aid in excreting iron either through the kidney or feces. Toxicity, adverse side effects, poor patient compliance and high cost, limit the current treatment with small molecular weight organic molecules. In this project, we propose macromolecular engineering of low molecular weight chelators in the development of novel biodegradable polymer constructs which are non-toxic, long circulating and can remove iron specifically from vasculature or from organs that are mostly affected by iron burden. We anticipate that this novel approach will increase vascular residence time of iron chelators and increase the efficiency of chelation. Macromolecular chelators will provide high patient compliance and improved quality of life to patients by decreasing the adverse side effects.. This would benefit numerous patients worldwide, especially sickle cell and thalassemic patients, suffering from iron overload diseases undergoing iron chelation therapy. The availability of biodegradable non-toxic polymeric chelators will also provide novel methods to treat infection, neurodegenerative diseases and cancer.

TitreApplicationTitle: Improved treatment of cervical cancer through heat-activated delivery of chemo-radiosensitizing agents in combination with radiotherapy
Keywords-MotsClés: CANCER THERAPY; CERVICAL CANCER; CHEMOTHERAPY; CISPLATIN; HYPERTHERMIA; IMAGING; LIPOSOMES; NANOTECHNOLOGY; RADIOSENSITIZATION; RADIOTHERAPY
Abstract-Résumé: Although much progress has been made in the past decade in the treatment of cervical cancer, disease control is still a challenge in 10-20% of patients and a further 10-20% develop pelvic recurrence after an initial complete response. A study at the Princess Margaret Hospital in Toronto found that disease recurrence is less frequent if patients are treated with radiation therapy and the drug cisplatin instead of radiation alone. This proposal aims to build on this finding by encapsulating cisplatin into a liposome delivery system that will increase the amount of drug reaching the primary tumor site. This strategy will increase the local concentration of drug within the pelvic region, while continuing to control metastatic spread without an increase in toxicity. The liposome delivery system proposed here is thermosensitive, and only releases cisplatin when heat is applied. We propose to use high intensity focused ultrasound to apply heat at tumor sites, with the guidance of magnetic resonance imaging. We hypothesize that the combination of radiation therapy with increased delivery of cisplatin to tumor sites using a thermosensitive liposome will improve the treatment of cervical cancer. We propose to assess this using models of human cervical cancer in mice.
